name: 2-methylacyl-CoA racemase deficiency
formal: Autosomal recessive peroxisomal disorder of branched-chain fatty acid and bile acid metabolism (AMACR) causing adult sensorimotor neuropathy, retinopathy, seizures, encephalopathy and pristanic acid accumulation.
simple: A rare inherited metabolic disease in which the body cannot process certain fats, causing nerve damage, vision problems and sometimes seizures or confusion.
th: โรคเพอรอกซิโซมแบบยีนด้อยที่หายากมาก ทำให้ pristanic acid คั่ง ผู้ใหญ่มีปลายประสาทเสื่อม จอประสาทตาเสื่อม ชัก และภาวะสมองผิดปกติเป็นพัก ๆ
tempoNote: Adult form: slowly progressive neuropathy and retinopathy with superimposed episodes of encephalopathy or stroke-like events; infantile form presents with cholestasis
feat: Adult-onset sensorimotor neuropathy and pigmentary retinopathy
Episodes of encephalopathy, seizures or stroke-like events, sometimes triggered by illness
Cognitive decline, tremor, ataxia or migraine-like headaches in some
Infants may instead present with cholestatic liver disease and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency
inv: Plasma pristanic acid markedly raised; phytanic acid normal or mildly raised (differs from Refsum disease)
Abnormal C27 bile acid intermediates in plasma or urine
AMACR gene sequencing
MRI may show white matter, thalamic or cortical lesions during acute episodes

case.story: Several years of numb feet and poor night vision; admitted after a generalised seizure and two days of confusion following a febrile illness.
case.exam: Distal sensory loss, absent ankle jerks, pigmentary changes in both retinas, mild cerebellar ataxia.
case.tests: Pristanic acid raised many-fold, phytanic acid near normal; MRI shows bilateral thalamic T2 changes; AMACR biallelic variants.
case.q: Which metabolic pathway is affected, and what dietary measure is advised?
case.a: Peroxisomal branched-chain fatty acid oxidation (AMACR deficiency); restrict dietary phytanic and pristanic acid (dairy, ruminant fat, some fish).

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — peroxisomal disorders

det.patho: AMACR converts branched-chain fatty acyl-CoA esters (from pristanic acid and bile acid precursors) into the stereoisomer that peroxisomal beta-oxidation can use. Loss of function causes pristanic acid and C27 bile acid intermediates to accumulate. How these lead to neuropathy, retinopathy and episodic brain dysfunction is not fully understood. Fewer than a few dozen patients have been reported.
det.clinical: Adults present with peripheral neuropathy, retinitis pigmentosa, cognitive impairment, epilepsy and relapsing encephalopathy, sometimes with stroke-like episodes. Some have only subtle signs until an acute episode. Infants may show neonatal cholestasis and coagulopathy from vitamin K deficiency. The natural history is incompletely described because the disease is so rare.
det.diagnosis: Measure plasma pristanic and phytanic acid in adults with unexplained neuropathy plus retinopathy, epilepsy or episodic encephalopathy. A high pristanic to phytanic ratio is the clue. Bile acid analysis supports it, and AMACR genetic testing confirms. Broader peroxisomal and mitochondrial panels help exclude other causes.
det.treatment: Dietary restriction of phytanic and pristanic acid lowers levels and may reduce episodes, although evidence is limited to case reports. Bile acid therapy (cholic acid) has been used in infantile cases. Seizures and acute encephalopathy need standard supportive management, and fat-soluble vitamins should be supplemented in infants. Genetic counselling is recommended.
det.prognosis: Not well defined; reported adults have variable progression with risk from acute encephalopathic episodes.
pearls: Neuropathy plus retinopathy with high pristanic but near-normal phytanic acid points to AMACR deficiency.
Standard very long chain fatty acid testing alone misses it; request pristanic and phytanic acid.
Acute stroke-like or encephalopathic episodes may be triggered by intercurrent illness.
det.thd: AMACR deficiency เป็นโรคเพอรอกซิโซมที่หายากมาก ทำให้ pristanic acid และกรดน้ำดีตัวกลางคั่ง ผู้ใหญ่มีปลายประสาทเสื่อม จอประสาทตาเสื่อม ชัก และสมองผิดปกติเป็นพัก ๆ บางครั้งคล้ายโรคหลอดเลือดสมอง ตรวจพบ pristanic acid สูงแต่ phytanic acid ปกติหรือสูงเล็กน้อย ยืนยันด้วยยีน AMACR รักษาด้วยการจำกัดอาหารที่มี phytanic และ pristanic acid

ddx.pt: Neuropathy, retinitis pigmentosa, anosmia and ichthyosis with very high phytanic acid
Spastic paraparesis with neuropathy and adrenal failure; very long chain fatty acids raised
Umbrella group; specific metabolite profile and gene testing define the disorder

name: 3-methylglutaconic aciduria
formal: Heterogeneous group of inherited disorders with raised urinary 3-methylglutaconic acid, linked to mitochondrial dysfunction; neurological forms feature optic atrophy, dystonia, spasticity and developmental delay.
simple: A group of rare inherited conditions where a chemical builds up in the urine because of faulty energy production in cells, often causing movement problems and developmental delay.
th: กลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่ปัสสาวะมี 3-methylglutaconic acid สูง สัมพันธ์กับความผิดปกติของไมโทคอนเดรีย อาการทางประสาทได้แก่ ประสาทตาฝ่อ dystonia เกร็ง และพัฒนาการช้า
tempoNote: Onset in infancy or childhood; slowly progressive or static
feat: Raised urinary 3-methylglutaconic acid as the shared biochemical marker
Costeff syndrome (OPA3): early optic atrophy with later ataxia, chorea or spasticity
MEGDEL (SERAC1): deafness, encephalopathy, Leigh-like basal ganglia lesions
Barth syndrome (TAZ): cardiomyopathy, neutropenia, myopathy in boys
Others (TMEM70, DNAJC19, CLPB, AUH) with cardiomyopathy, cataract or neutropenia
inv: Urine organic acids (3-MGA and 3-methylglutaric acid), repeated if borderline
Lactate, echocardiogram, blood count for neutropenia, audiology, ophthalmology
Gene panel or exome; MRI for basal ganglia and cerebellar changes

case.story: Poor vision since age 3, now jerky dance-like movements and stiff legs.
case.exam: Bilateral optic disc pallor, choreiform movements, brisk reflexes, mild ataxia.
case.tests: Urine 3-methylglutaconic acid raised; OPA3 biallelic variants.
case.q: Which syndrome is this?
case.a: Costeff syndrome (3-MGA type III): infantile optic atrophy followed by extrapyramidal and pyramidal signs.

det.patho: Primary 3-MGA type I is a true leucine catabolism defect (AUH). The remaining forms are disorders of mitochondrial membrane function, phospholipid remodelling or ATP synthase assembly, where 3-MGA is a secondary marker of mitochondrial stress rather than the cause of symptoms. Consequently the clinical picture depends on the gene involved.
det.clinical: Type I may cause leukoencephalopathy in adults or be mild. Barth syndrome presents in infant boys with dilated cardiomyopathy and neutropenia. Costeff syndrome begins with optic atrophy then movement disorders. MEGDEL causes infantile deafness, dystonia and encephalopathy; CLPB deficiency adds cataracts and neutropenia; TMEM70 causes neonatal cardiomyopathy and hyperammonaemia.
det.diagnosis: Urine organic acid analysis detects the marker, but levels fluctuate and are not specific. Genetic testing identifies the subtype. Investigate the heart, blood count, hearing and eyes in every case.
det.treatment: Mostly supportive: cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia management, G-CSF for neutropenia, treatment of dystonia and spasticity, visual and hearing aids. Leucine restriction is considered only for AUH deficiency. Elamipretide has been studied in Barth syndrome.
det.prognosis: Ranges from near normal (some type I) to death in infancy (TMEM70, severe MEGDEL); Costeff syndrome is slowly progressive.
pearls: 3-MGA is a marker of mitochondrial dysfunction in most subtypes, not the cause.
Optic atrophy in early childhood followed by chorea: Costeff syndrome.
Boy with cardiomyopathy and neutropenia: Barth syndrome.
det.thd: 3-methylglutaconic aciduria เป็นกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมหลายชนิดที่ปัสสาวะมีกรด 3-methylglutaconic สูง ส่วนใหญ่เป็นตัวบ่งชี้ว่าไมโทคอนเดรียทำงานผิดปกติ อาการขึ้นกับยีน เช่น Costeff syndrome มีประสาทตาฝ่อแล้วตามด้วย chorea และขาเกร็ง Barth syndrome มีกล้ามเนื้อหัวใจผิดปกติและนิวโทรฟิลต่ำ วินิจฉัยด้วยตรวจปัสสาวะและยีน รักษาตามอาการ

ddx.pt: X-linked TAZ disorder in boys with cardiomyopathy and neutropenia, a 3-MGA cause
OPA1-related optic atrophy with deafness, neuropathy or ophthalmoplegia; urine 3-MGA usually normal
Symmetric brainstem and basal ganglia lesions from many mitochondrial genes, regression with lactate rise

aN: 3 mga | 3 mga uria | mgca | costeff syndrome type iii | megdel syndrome

name: 4-hydroxybutyric acidaemia
formal: Autosomal recessive succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency causing GABA and gamma-hydroxybutyrate accumulation; presents with developmental delay, hypotonia, ataxia, seizures and behavioural problems.
simple: A rare inherited disorder where brain chemicals are not broken down properly, leading to delayed development, poor muscle tone, unsteadiness and seizures.
th: ภาวะขาดเอนไซม์ SSADH ถ่ายทอดแบบยีนด้อย ทำให้ GABA และ gamma-hydroxybutyrate คั่ง เด็กพัฒนาการช้า กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง เดินเซ ชัก และมีพฤติกรรมก้าวร้าวหรือวิตกกังวล
tempoNote: Slowly progressive or static from infancy and early childhood; seizures and behavioural problems emerge during childhood
feat: Developmental delay with marked speech and language impairment and intellectual disability
Hypotonia in infancy with later ataxia
Seizures in over half of patients, including generalised tonic-clonic, absence and myoclonic types
Behavioural problems: hyperactivity, anxiety, obsessive features, aggression and self-injury
Hyperkinetic movement disorder with choreoathetosis, dystonia or myoclonus in the more severe early-onset forms
inv: Urine organic acids showing raised 4-hydroxybutyric acid; the peak can be hidden under the large urea peak, so request specific attention
ALDH5A1 gene sequencing to confirm
MRI with symmetric T2 hyperintensity in the globus pallidus and brainstem, and EEG with background slowing and spikes

case.story: He sat late, speaks only a few words and has started falling often. Two months ago he had a generalised seizure; he is hyperactive and bites his hand when frustrated. A neighbouring clinic labelled him as cerebral palsy.
case.exam: Axial hypotonia, wide-based gait, mild dysarthria, no spasticity, normal growth.
case.tests: Urine organic acids show a marked 4-hydroxybutyric acid peak; MRI shows bilateral T2 hyperintensity in the globus pallidus; ALDH5A1 homozygous variant.
case.q: Why did the first urine screen miss it in a previous laboratory, and which anti-seizure drug should be avoided?
case.a: The 4-hydroxybutyric acid peak co-elutes with urea unless the lab looks for it; valproate should be avoided because it can inhibit the residual enzyme.

read.where: Chapter 31: EPILEPSY IN THE SETTING OF INHERITED METABOLIC AND MITOCHONDRIAL DISORDERS

det.patho: Succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency (SSADH) is an autosomal recessive disorder of GABA degradation caused by ALDH5A1 variants. The block causes build-up of gamma-hydroxybutyrate and GABA and their metabolites, which disturb the balance of excitation and inhibition and produce brain dysfunction, seizures and behavioural disturbance.
det.clinical: Presentation is usually non-specific, and many children are labelled cerebral palsy or intellectual disability. Slow development, hypotonia, speech delay and ataxia are typical, with seizures in more than half. Behavioural symptoms such as hyperactivity, anxiety and self-injury become prominent later, and in some patients a movement disorder with dystonia, chorea or myoclonus appears. Sleep disturbance and psychiatric symptoms can continue into adulthood. Course is variable, and a small proportion deteriorate in early life.
det.diagnosis: Suspicion arises from the combination of delay, ataxia, seizures and behavioural problems, supported by basal ganglia signal change on MRI. Urine organic acid analysis shows raised 4-hydroxybutyric acid, but the peak can be overlooked because it overlaps the urea peak, so the laboratory must be alerted. Glycine may be mildly elevated. Enzyme assay or ALDH5A1 sequencing confirms the diagnosis. EEG may show slowing and spike discharges.
det.treatment: Management is symptomatic: seizure control with usual drugs while avoiding valproate, behavioural and psychiatric care, physiotherapy and speech therapy. Vigabatrin has helped some patients but made others worse, so it is used only with specialist guidance. Genetic counselling is advised for families, and gene or enzyme therapies remain investigational.
det.prognosis: Survival into adulthood is common; outcomes are limited by intellectual disability, epilepsy and psychiatric symptoms.
pearls: Ask the laboratory to look for 4-hydroxybutyric acid specifically, since it can hide beneath the urea peak.
Valproate is contraindicated because it may block residual SSADH activity.
Consider it in children labelled as cerebral palsy who have ataxia, seizures and aggression without perinatal injury.
det.thd: ภาวะ 4-hydroxybutyric acidaemia หรือ SSADH deficiency เกิดจากยีน ALDH5A1 บกพร่อง ทำให้ GABA และ gamma-hydroxybutyrate คั่ง เด็กพัฒนาการช้า พูดช้า เดินเซ ชัก และมีพฤติกรรมวิตกหรือก้าวร้าว มักถูกวินิจฉัยเป็นสมองพิการก่อน ตรวจ urine organic acids ต้องแจ้งห้องปฏิบัติการให้มองหา 4-hydroxybutyric acid ยืนยันด้วยยีน หลีกเลี่ยง valproate และรักษาตามอาการ

Static perinatal injury with spasticity; no progression and normal metabolic screen
Low CSF glucose, paroxysmal movement disorder and seizures responding to ketogenic diet

name: 5-MTHF deficiency
formal: Disorder of cerebral folate transport or metabolism (e.g. FOLR1 or MTHFR defects) with low CSF 5-methyltetrahydrofolate, causing irritability, ataxia, seizures, developmental regression; folinic acid responsive.
simple: A shortage of an active form of folate in the brain that can cause developmental problems, unsteadiness and seizures, and may improve with folinic acid treatment.
th: ภาวะขาดโฟเลตในสมอง (5-MTHF ในน้ำไขสันหลังต่ำ) จากความผิดปกติของการขนส่งหรือเมตาบอลิซึมโฟเลต ทำให้เด็กหงุดหงิด เดินเซ ชัก และพัฒนาการถดถอย ตอบสนองต่อ folinic acid
tempoNote: Typically begins after a few months of normal infancy (FOLR1 often age 2–3), with progressive regression if untreated
feat: Irritability, sleep disturbance and slowed head growth after early normal development
Psychomotor regression, ataxia, dyskinesia and spasticity
Refractory epilepsy, often myoclonic
Autistic features or visual and hearing loss in some forms
inv: CSF 5-methyltetrahydrofolate low, with normal or high serum folate
MRI: hypomyelination and cerebellar atrophy in FOLR1 deficiency
Folate receptor alpha autoantibodies; FOLR1 and MTHFR genes; check for mitochondrial causes (for example Kearns-Sayre)

case.story: Developed normally until 2 years, then became irritable, lost words and began falling; myoclonic jerks started two months ago.
case.exam: Truncal ataxia, brisk reflexes, frequent myoclonic jerks, poor eye contact.
case.tests: Serum folate normal; CSF 5-MTHF very low; MRI shows delayed myelination; FOLR1 biallelic variants.
case.q: What treatment should be started, and which form of folate is wrong?
case.a: High-dose oral or intravenous folinic acid (calcium folinate); avoid folic acid, which may compete for transport and worsen CNS folate.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Neurotransmitter Disorders

det.patho: 5-MTHF enters the brain via folate receptor alpha at the choroid plexus. Biallelic FOLR1 variants, blocking autoantibodies against the receptor, severe MTHFR deficiency, mitochondrial disease and some drugs reduce CNS folate. Low brain folate impairs methylation, neurotransmitter synthesis and myelination.
det.clinical: Genetic FOLR1 deficiency causes regression, ataxia, epilepsy and hypomyelination from early childhood. Autoantibody-mediated forms have been linked to infantile-onset autistic regression, though this association remains debated. Severe MTHFR deficiency causes homocystinuria with encephalopathy, seizures and thrombosis.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires measuring CSF 5-MTHF, as blood folate is usually normal. Then search for the cause: FOLR1 and MTHFR sequencing, folate receptor antibodies, plasma homocysteine and mitochondrial studies. Interpret CSF values against age-specific ranges and process samples correctly, since 5-MTHF is unstable.
det.treatment: Folinic acid (calcium folinate or the active 5-MTHF form) bypasses the receptor; doses are much higher than nutritional doses and adjusted to CSF levels. Early treatment in FOLR1 deficiency can control seizures and allow developmental progress; intravenous or intrathecal routes have been used in refractory cases. Betaine and other measures are needed for MTHFR deficiency. Avoid folic acid and drugs that interfere with folate where possible.
det.prognosis: Early diagnosis and folinic acid treatment can greatly improve outcome; delayed treatment leaves permanent deficits.
pearls: Normal blood folate does not exclude brain folate deficiency; measure CSF 5-MTHF.
Treat with folinic acid, not folic acid.
Consider it in any child with unexplained regression plus ataxia and myoclonic epilepsy.
det.thd: ภาวะขาด 5-MTHF ในสมองเกิดจากการขนส่งโฟเลตเข้าสมองผิดปกติ เช่น ยีน FOLR1 หรือภูมิคุ้มกันต่อตัวรับโฟเลต เด็กพัฒนาการปกติช่วงแรกแล้วถดถอย หงุดหงิด เดินเซ และชัก ระดับโฟเลตในเลือดปกติแต่ในน้ำไขสันหลังต่ำ รักษาด้วย folinic acid ขนาดสูงซึ่งได้ผลดีหากเริ่มเร็ว และไม่ควรใช้ folic acid

name: Abducens (VIth) nerve palsy
formal: Lesion of the sixth cranial nerve causing impaired ipsilateral abduction and horizontal diplopia; causes include raised intracranial pressure (false localising), microvascular ischaemia, trauma and pontine lesions.
simple: Weakness of the nerve that moves the eye outward, so the eye cannot turn sideways properly and the person sees double.
th: อัมพาตเส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 6 ตากลอกออกด้านนอกไม่ได้ เห็นภาพซ้อนแนวนอนชัดเมื่อมองไกลและมองไปข้างที่เป็น อาจเป็น false localising sign จากความดันในกะโหลกสูง
tempoNote: Microvascular palsy appears over hours to days; subacute palsy with headache suggests raised pressure; slowly progressive palsy suggests skull-base tumour
feat: Horizontal double vision worse at distance and on looking towards the affected side
Esotropia with limited abduction; head may be turned toward the weak side
Isolated in microvascular, raised ICP and skull-base lesions; with ipsilateral facial palsy or gaze palsy if in the pons
Headache, papilloedema and pulsatile tinnitus suggest raised intracranial pressure (bilateral VI palsy possible)
With ipsilateral V1 and Horner's: cavernous sinus; with ear pain and facial pain after otitis: petrous apex (Gradenigo)
inv: Fundoscopy for papilloedema; MRI brain with contrast (with MRV if raised ICP suspected)
Lumbar puncture with opening pressure when imaging is normal and papilloedema present
Glucose, HbA1c, BP; ESR/CRP in older patients
AChR antibodies or ice/rest test if variable; thyroid tests if restrictive pattern

case.who: 29-year-old woman, BMI 36, call-centre worker from Chonburi
case.story: Three months of daily headache worse lying down, whooshing sounds in both ears; for one week she sees two images side by side when watching TV.
case.exam: Left abduction deficit with esotropia worse at distance; bilateral papilloedema; otherwise normal.
case.tests: MRI/MRV: empty sella and transverse sinus narrowing, no mass; LP opening pressure 38 cmH2O with normal CSF.
case.q: Why is the sixth nerve affected and what is the diagnosis?
case.a: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension; the long intracranial course of VI makes it vulnerable to raised pressure — a false localising sign.

det.patho: The abducens nerve arises in the pons, climbs the clivus, bends over the petrous apex under the petroclinoid (Gruber's) ligament, crosses the cavernous sinus beside the internal carotid artery and passes into the orbit via the superior orbital fissure. This long intracranial course makes it susceptible to stretching from raised or reduced intracranial pressure and to skull-base disease. Causes include microvascular ischaemia, raised ICP, trauma, tumour (clival chordoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, meningioma), Wernicke's encephalopathy, infection and post-lumbar puncture low pressure.
det.clinical: Patients report horizontal diplopia worse at distance and towards the side of the lesion. Lesions of the abducens nucleus cause a horizontal gaze palsy rather than an isolated abduction deficit, often with facial weakness because the facial fibres loop around it. Children may develop a benign, post-viral sixth nerve palsy. In Thailand, nasopharyngeal carcinoma is an important cause of progressive sixth palsy with ear fullness or neck nodes.
det.diagnosis: Look at the fundi first, then image with MRI including skull base and cavernous sinus. An isolated painless palsy in an older vascular patient may be observed for three months, but nasopharynx examination and imaging are mandatory for progression, other cranial nerve signs or young age. Distinguish restrictive causes (thyroid eye disease, medial wall fracture) with forced duction, and Duane syndrome by the congenital history and globe retraction on adduction.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying cause (e.g. weight loss and acetazolamide or CSF diversion for IIH, radiotherapy for NPC, thiamine for Wernicke). Relieve diplopia with occlusion or Fresnel prisms. Botulinum toxin to the medial rectus may prevent contracture; strabismus surgery is considered after 6–12 months of stable deviation.
det.prognosis: Microvascular and benign childhood palsies usually recover in weeks to three months; tumour-related palsies depend on the lesion.
pearls: Sixth nerve palsy can be a false localising sign of raised (or low) ICP — always check the fundi.
Gaze palsy rather than abduction weakness points to the VI nucleus, not the nerve.
In a Thai adult with progressive VI palsy, scope the nasopharynx.
det.thd: อัมพาตเส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 6 ทำให้ตากลอกออกด้านนอกไม่ได้ เห็นภาพซ้อนแนวนอนชัดขึ้นเมื่อมองไกลหรือมองไปด้านที่เป็น เส้นประสาทนี้ยาวจึงถูกกระทบง่ายเมื่อความดันในกะโหลกสูง เช่น IIH จึงต้องตรวจจอประสาทตาทุกราย สาเหตุอื่นได้แก่หลอดเลือดเล็กขาดเลือด เนื้องอกฐานกะโหลก โดยเฉพาะมะเร็งหลังโพรงจมูกในคนไทย ทำ MRI และรักษาตามสาเหตุ ส่วนภาพซ้อนแก้ด้วยปิดตาหรือปริซึม

qx.stem: A 38-year-old woman from Nakhon Pathom with no vascular risk factors has two weeks of horizontal diplopia worse on looking right, with a limited abduction of the right eye. Visual acuity, pupils, other eye movements, fundi and the rest of the neurological examination are normal.
qx.q: What is the best next step?
opts: Observe for three months because microvascular palsy is likely
Start oral steroids empirically
Brain MRI with contrast (with venography or other targeted imaging as indicated)
Reassure and give an eye patch only
No investigation, because isolated palsies are always benign
qx.why: In patients younger than about 50, or without vascular risk factors, an isolated sixth nerve palsy has a meaningful chance of an intracranial neoplasm, demyelination, infection, raised intracranial pressure or brainstem lesion, so prompt neuroimaging is advised. Observation without imaging is traditionally reserved for older patients with vascular risk factors, although many experts now image them too given occasional non-ischaemic findings. Empirical steroids and reassurance risk delaying a treatable cause.

name: Abetalipoproteinemia (Bassen-Kornzweig disease)
formal: Autosomal recessive MTTP defect abolishing apoB-lipoprotein assembly, causing fat malabsorption, acanthocytosis, retinitis pigmentosa, and spinocerebellar ataxia with large-fibre neuropathy from vitamin E deficiency.
simple: A rare inherited problem absorbing fats and vitamin E, leading to unsteady walking, weak nerves, and vision loss if untreated.
more: Very low cholesterol and absent apoB; acanthocytes on smear. High-dose vitamin E with fat-soluble vitamin supplements and a low-fat diet slow or prevent neurological decline when started early. Abetalipoproteinaemia from MTTP mutation with fat malabsorption, acanthocytosis, retinitis pigmentosa and progressive spinocerebellar degeneration due to vitamin E deficiency. Diagnosis by low or absent cholesterol, triglycerides and vitamin A/E/K with no apoB-containing lipoproteins; blood smear shows acanthocytes. Treat with a low-fat diet and high-dose vitamin E and A supplementation.
th: โรคยีนด้อยที่สร้าง lipoprotein ชนิด apoB ไม่ได้ — ท้องเสียไขมันตั้งแต่ทารก cholesterol ต่ำมาก acanthocyte และขาด vitamin E จนเกิด ataxia กับจอตาเสื่อม
tempoNote: Gut symptoms from infancy; neurological and retinal signs appear in childhood or adolescence if vitamin E is not replaced
feat: Fatty, foul stools, vomiting and poor weight gain from early infancy
Later sensory ataxia, areflexia with impaired vibration and proprioception
Night blindness and pigmentary retinopathy
Acanthocytes on the blood film; possible bleeding tendency from vitamin K deficiency
Myopathy or ophthalmoplegia in long-standing untreated cases
inv: Very low total cholesterol and near-absent triglycerides; apoB and LDL undetectable
Blood smear: acanthocytes; low vitamins E, A, D and K (prolonged INR)
Parents have normal lipid levels (contrast familial hypobetalipoproteinaemia)
MTTP genetic testing; ophthalmology and NCS baseline

case.story: Greasy diarrhoea since infancy and small for age; now stumbles in the dark and her legs feel 'asleep'.
case.exam: Thin, short; wide-based gait worse with eyes closed, absent ankle jerks, reduced vibration to the knees; fundi show peripheral pigment clumps.
case.tests: Cholesterol 0.9 mmol/L, triglycerides 0.1 mmol/L, apoB undetectable; acanthocytes; vitamin E unmeasurably low; parents' lipids normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the key long-term treatment?
case.a: Abetalipoproteinaemia (MTTP); low-fat diet with very high-dose vitamin E plus vitamins A, K and D, and monitored essential fatty acids.

read.where: Review: Autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxias for which treatment is available; Table 3
8 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System

det.patho: Loss of microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTTP) prevents assembly of apoB-containing lipoproteins in gut and liver, so chylomicrons, VLDL and LDL are absent. Fat and fat-soluble vitamin absorption fail; the neurological and retinal disease results mainly from severe vitamin E deficiency, with vitamin A deficiency adding to retinopathy. Red cell membranes become spiky (acanthocytes) because of abnormal lipid composition.
det.clinical: Infants present with steatorrhoea and failure to thrive. Without replacement, the first decade brings loss of reflexes and proprioception, then a spinocerebellar syndrome, neuropathy and retinitis pigmentosa leading to visual loss. Coagulopathy, liver steatosis and occasionally myopathy or cardiomyopathy occur.
det.diagnosis: Strikingly low cholesterol and triglycerides with absent apoB, acanthocytes and very low vitamin E make the diagnosis; MTTP sequencing confirms it. Normal parental lipids separate it from homozygous familial hypobetalipoproteinaemia (APOB). Track vitamin levels, INR, liver ultrasound and retinal function.
det.treatment: A low-long-chain-fat diet controls diarrhoea, with essential fatty acid supplements. High-dose vitamin E (on the order of 100–300 IU/kg/day) is the key neuroprotective measure, together with vitamin A, K and D replacement adjusted to levels. Early, sustained therapy prevents or limits neurological and retinal disease; late treatment stabilises but rarely reverses deficits.
det.prognosis: Good if treatment begins in infancy or early childhood; untreated, disabling ataxia and blindness develop by early adulthood.
pearls: Ataxia + retinitis pigmentosa + acanthocytes + near-zero cholesterol: abetalipoproteinaemia.
Serum vitamin E is low partly because carrier lipoproteins are absent; adipose or red-cell levels are better guides on treatment.
Treatable — begin vitamin E on suspicion, without waiting for confirmation.
det.thd: Abetalipoproteinemia เกิดจากยีน MTTP ร่างกายสร้าง lipoprotein ที่มี apoB ไม่ได้ ทารกจึงถ่ายเป็นไขมันและโตช้า ต่อมาขาด vitamin E อย่างรุนแรงทำให้เดินเซ reflex หาย และจอตาเสื่อม เลือดพบ acanthocyte cholesterol และ triglyceride ต่ำมาก รักษาด้วยอาหารไขมันต่ำร่วมกับ vitamin E ขนาดสูงมากและวิตามิน A, K, D

ddx.pt: Normal lipids and no malabsorption or acanthocytes
Normal lipids and vitamin E; cardiomyopathy; FXN repeat expansion
Also retinopathy and neuropathy, but phytanic acid high and lipids normal

name: Abversive seizures
formal: Focal seizures with forced, sustained turning of the eyes and head away from the epileptic focus (contraversive), often arising from frontal eye field or adjacent frontal regions.
simple: Seizures in which the eyes and head are forced to turn to one side without the person controlling it.
th: ชักเฉพาะส่วนที่ตาและศีรษะหันออกด้านข้างอย่างรุนแรงและค้างไว้ ทิศทางการหันตาเริ่มแรกบอกว่าจุดกำเนิดชักอยู่ฝั่งตรงข้าม มักมาจาก frontal eye field หรือ frontal lobe (เรียกอีกชื่อว่า adversive)
tempoNote: Seconds to minutes; often precedes a generalised tonic-clonic seizure
feat: Forced, sustained turning of the eyes and often the head to one side at seizure onset
Direction of the early forced deviation points to the contralateral hemisphere in most cases
Frequently followed by arm posturing (fencing), clonic jerking or secondary generalisation
Awareness may be retained at onset, especially when the focus is frontal
Late, weak or transient deviation after generalisation is not reliable for lateralising
inv: Video-EEG monitoring with careful note of the first forced movement
MRI brain with epilepsy protocol (focal cortical dysplasia, tumour, stroke, cavernoma)
FDG-PET, ictal SPECT or MEG in refractory cases for surgical evaluation

case.story: Several times a month he suddenly notices his eyes and head dragged to the left, his left arm stiffens, and then he has a convulsion. After the first seizure he was weak briefly on the right.
case.exam: Between events normal. A witnessed episode on video shows forced leftward head and eye deviation with left arm extension and then secondary generalisation.
case.tests: Video-EEG shows right frontal onset; MRI shows a small cortical dysplasia in the right frontal lobe.
case.q: What does the head and eye deviation tell you?
case.a: An adversive seizure from the right frontal region. Early forced deviation to the left indicates the contralateral hemisphere, so a right frontal focus; treat with an anti-seizure drug and refer for surgical assessment if drug-resistant.

read.where: Chapter 8 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System — versive seizures

det.patho: Cortical networks of the frontal eye field and its connections to the pontine horizontal gaze centre drive contraversive eye movements. An epileptic discharge in this region produces forced conjugate deviation to the opposite side, while destructive lesions initially drive the eyes toward the lesion. Parietal and occipital foci can also cause deviation, occasionally ipsilateral.
det.clinical: Seizures begin with an abrupt turn of the eyes and head, then the body may rotate, followed by tonic posturing of the contralateral arm and often a convulsion. The patient may be aware, sensing the eyes pulled sideways. The initial forced deviation lateralises to the opposite hemisphere; weak or late head turning is non-specific and may even be ipsilateral. A post-ictal deficit can follow.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis relies on history from witnesses and video-EEG with the first movement analysed. MRI finds structural causes, and functional imaging is used when surgery is considered. Mimics include psychogenic non-epileptic events, dystonic or oculogyric crises from drugs, and acute stroke with gaze preference. Always distinguish seizure from a gaze palsy due to a lesion.
det.treatment: Treat as a focal epilepsy with an appropriate anti-seizure medication such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine or levetiracetam. Surgical resection is considered when seizures persist after two adequate drug trials and a focal lesion is found. Counsel on driving, safety and adherence.
det.prognosis: Depends on the underlying lesion; many patients achieve control with drugs, and well-localised lesional epilepsy has good surgical results.
pearls: Early forced deviation lateralises to the contralateral hemisphere.
Late or weak head turning does not lateralise reliably.
Destructive frontal lesions pull the eyes toward the lesion; irritative ones push away.
det.thd: Abversive (adversive) seizure คือชักที่ตาและหัวหันไปด้านข้างอย่างรุนแรง มักมาจาก frontal eye field ทิศทางที่ตาเริ่มหันบอกว่าจุดกำเนิดชักอยู่สมองซีกตรงข้าม ต้องตรวจ video-EEG และ MRI สมองหาสาเหตุ การรักษาใช้ยากันชักแบบ focal และพิจารณาผ่าตัดถ้าควบคุมไม่ได้ ต้องแยกจากอัมพาตการมองด้านข้างที่เกิดจากรอยโรคถาวร

name: Acanthocytes/acanthocytosis
formal: Presence of spiny, irregularly contracted red cells on blood film, characteristic of neuroacanthocytosis syndromes (chorea-acanthocytosis, McLeod) and abetalipoproteinaemia, with chorea, orofacial dyskinesia and myopathy.
simple: Red blood cells with spiky edges, seen in some rare inherited diseases that cause abnormal movements, muscle disease and nerve problems.
th: เม็ดเลือดแดงรูปหนามไม่สม่ำเสมอบนสเมียร์เลือด เป็นผลตรวจไม่ใช่โรค พบในกลุ่ม neuroacanthocytosis (chorea-acanthocytosis, McLeod) และ abetalipoproteinaemia ซึ่งมี chorea ขยับปาก ลิ้น และกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง
tempoNote: Laboratory finding; associated neurological syndromes progress over years
feat: A blood film finding: red cells with several irregular thorny projections
Chorea-acanthocytosis (VPS13A): orolingual dystonia with tongue protrusion when eating, lip and tongue biting, tics, seizures
McLeod syndrome (XK, X-linked): chorea, cardiomyopathy, raised CK and weak Kell antigens
Abetalipoproteinaemia: fat malabsorption, retinopathy, ataxia from vitamin E deficiency
Also seen in severe liver disease (spur cell anaemia) and some HDL2 and PKAN cases
inv: Fresh wet blood film diluted with saline (repeat several times; sensitivity is limited)
CK, liver enzymes, lipid profile and vitamin E; Kell antigen typing
MRI caudate atrophy; genes VPS13A, XK, MTTP, JPH3

case.story: Two years of involuntary movements, bites his tongue and lips, and food is pushed out of his mouth by his tongue; one seizure last year.
case.exam: Generalised chorea, feeding dystonia with tongue protrusion, absent ankle jerks.
case.tests: CK 1,500; wet blood film shows 15% acanthocytes; HTT gene normal; VPS13A biallelic variants.
case.q: What does the blood film add here?
case.a: It points to neuroacanthocytosis, specifically chorea-acanthocytosis, once Huntington disease has been excluded.

det.patho: Acanthocytes result from altered red cell membrane lipids or membrane protein interactions, so the cell surface buckles into spicules. In neuroacanthocytosis the same gene defects that alter red cell membranes (VPS13A, XK) disturb basal ganglia neurons, especially the caudate. In abetalipoproteinaemia, lack of lipoproteins changes membrane lipid composition.
det.clinical: The finding itself causes little haemolysis. Its importance is as a clue in a patient with chorea, tics, orofacial dystonia, seizures, psychiatric change, neuropathy or myopathy, especially with high CK and liver enzymes. A normal film does not exclude neuroacanthocytosis because the proportion of acanthocytes varies.
det.diagnosis: Request a fresh, saline-diluted wet preparation rather than a routine dried smear, and repeat if negative. Combine with CK, lipids, vitamin E, Kell antigens and genetic tests for the candidate syndromes.
det.treatment: Depends on the underlying disorder: vitamin E and fat-soluble vitamins with a low-fat diet for abetalipoproteinaemia; symptomatic treatment (tetrabenazine, antiseizure drugs, mouth guards, DBS in selected cases) for chorea-acanthocytosis and McLeod; cardiac surveillance in McLeod.
det.prognosis: Neuroacanthocytosis syndromes progress over 15–30 years; abetalipoproteinaemia outcome depends on early vitamin E therapy.
pearls: Chorea + tongue-protrusion feeding dystonia + high CK: ask for a wet blood film for acanthocytes.
Routine smears miss acanthocytes; a fresh diluted preparation is better.
McLeod patients need Kell-negative compatible blood if transfused.
det.thd: Acanthocytes คือเม็ดเลือดแดงรูปมีหนามบนสเมียร์เลือด เป็นผลตรวจไม่ใช่โรค มีความสำคัญเพราะช่วยชี้ไปที่กลุ่ม neuroacanthocytosis เช่น chorea-acanthocytosis ที่มี chorea ลิ้นดันอาหารออกขณะกิน กัดลิ้นและริมฝีปาก CK สูง และ McLeod syndrome รวมถึง abetalipoproteinaemia ควรขอตรวจเลือดสดเจือจางด้วยน้ำเกลือและตรวจซ้ำ การรักษาขึ้นกับโรคต้นเหตุ

ddx.pt: Autosomal dominant chorea and dementia with CAG expansion; normal CK and blood film
X-linked, older onset, cardiomyopathy and weak Kell antigens
Childhood malabsorption, very low cholesterol and vitamin E, ataxia and retinopathy

aN: acanthocytosis | acanthocytes | spur cells | neuroacanthocytosis

name: Acetazolamide benign paroxysmal tonic upgaze and ataxia of childhood
formal: Childhood-onset episodic tonic upward gaze deviation with ataxia, linked to CACNA1A variants, tending to resolve with age and sometimes improving with acetazolamide or levodopa.
simple: A childhood condition with repeated episodes where the eyes drift upward and balance is poor; it usually settles with age.
ab: Paroxysmal tonic upgaze of childhood with ataxia (acetazolamide-responsive)
th: กลุ่มย่อยของ paroxysmal tonic upgaze ในเด็กที่มีตาเหลือกขึ้นเป็นพัก ๆ ร่วมกับเดินเซ มักเกี่ยวกับยีน CACNA1A และตอบสนองต่อ acetazolamide
tempoNote: Starts in the first year; episodes cluster, then fade over several years
feat: Not a separate disease: a descriptive variant of paroxysmal tonic upgaze that responds to acetazolamide
Sustained upward eye deviation with downbeating saccades on attempted downgaze
Ataxia during or between episodes; worse with fatigue or illness
Consciousness preserved; normal horizontal eye movements
May be followed by episodic ataxia type 2 or mild developmental issues
inv: MRI brain usually normal
Video-EEG during an episode to exclude seizures
CACNA1A testing, especially with family history of episodic ataxia or hemiplegic migraine

case.story: Episodes of eyes rolling up for hours with chin tucked down, worse when tired; she stumbles while cruising during these days. Mother has episodic ataxia.
case.exam: Between episodes mild truncal unsteadiness; during an episode sustained upgaze with downbeat nystagmus on looking down.
case.tests: MRI and video-EEG normal; heterozygous CACNA1A variant.
case.q: What treatment trial is reasonable and what is the outlook?
case.a: Acetazolamide (as in EA2); episodes usually fade within a few years, though some children have later ataxia or learning difficulty.

det.patho: CACNA1A encodes the P/Q-type calcium channel, crucial in cerebellar Purkinje cells and brainstem gaze circuits. Loss-of-function variants are thought to disturb the vertical gaze integrator and cerebellar output intermittently. Acetazolamide may stabilise neuronal excitability by altering pH, as in EA2.
det.clinical: Infants develop bouts of tonic upward gaze lasting hours, sometimes with neck flexion compensation and ataxia, often worse with fatigue and infections. Horizontal eye movements are normal and the child remains alert. Episodes usually resolve in early childhood. A subset later shows episodic ataxia, hemiplegic migraine or developmental delay.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical after excluding seizures and structural lesions of the midbrain with EEG and MRI. CACNA1A testing is reasonable, particularly with family history. Response to acetazolamide supports the label but is not required.
det.treatment: Many children need no treatment. Acetazolamide can reduce attacks in some; levodopa has also been reported to help in some series. Developmental follow-up is advised.
det.prognosis: Usually benign with resolution; a minority has persisting motor or cognitive issues.
pearls: Tonic upgaze in an alert infant: exclude seizure and midbrain lesion, then think CACNA1A.
Downbeating nystagmus on attempted downgaze is characteristic.
Ask about family episodic ataxia or hemiplegic migraine.
det.thd: ภาวะนี้คือ paroxysmal tonic upgaze ในเด็กเล็กที่มีตาเหลือกขึ้นค้างเป็นชั่วโมงร่วมกับเดินเซ เด็กรู้ตัวดี มักเกี่ยวกับยีน CACNA1A และบางรายตอบสนองต่อ acetazolamide ต้องตรวจ EEG และ MRI เพื่อตัดชักและรอยโรคที่ midbrain ส่วนใหญ่หายเองภายในไม่กี่ปี บางรายมีเดินเซหรือพัฒนาการช้าภายหลัง

ddx.pt: The parent entity; this label highlights response to acetazolamide
Later-onset attacks of ataxia, EA2 also from CACNA1A
Episodes of head tilt rather than upgaze, also CACNA1A-linked

aN: acetazolamide responsive paroxysmal tonic upgaze | paroxysmal tonic upgaze of childhood with ataxia acetazolamide responsive | cacna1a related tonic upgaze | ptu with ataxia

name: Achoreic Huntington’s disease (Huntington sine chorea)
formal: Huntington disease presenting without chorea, with cognitive-psychiatric decline, bradykinesia, rigidity or dystonia, but with a pathological CAG repeat expansion in HTT; seen with juvenile or late-stage disease.
simple: Huntington disease that appears without the typical jerky dance-like movements, showing instead as stiffness, slowness, or changes in thinking and mood.
more: Genetically confirmed Huntington disease presenting with cognitive, psychiatric or hypokinetic-rigid features but without chorea, as in the juvenile Westphal variant or late disease.
th: โรคฮันติงตันที่ไม่มีอาการ chorea แต่มีสมองเสื่อม อาการทางจิต เคลื่อนไหวช้า แข็งเกร็ง หรือ dystonia ยืนยันด้วย CAG repeat ในยีน HTT พบในชนิดเด็ก/วัยรุ่นหรือระยะท้าย
tempoNote: Insidious, progressive over 10–20 years
feat: Cognitive slowing, apathy, executive dysfunction and psychiatric disorder without chorea
Bradykinesia, rigidity, dystonia and gait impairment (parkinsonian picture)
Juvenile onset (Westphal variant) often with seizures and very large CAG expansions
Slow saccades and impersistence may still be present
Family history may be missing because of paternal anticipation or non-paternity
inv: HTT CAG repeat testing with pre- and post-test counselling
MRI caudate atrophy; neuropsychology
Exclude Wilson disease, DRPLA, SCA17 and other HD phenocopies when HTT is normal

case.story: School grades collapsed over two years, became stiff and slow; first seizure this year. His father, who left the family, was said to have 'restless movements'.
case.exam: Rigidity, bradykinesia, dystonic posturing, slow saccades, no chorea.
case.tests: HTT CAG 72 repeats; MRI caudate atrophy.
case.q: Why does this patient lack chorea despite Huntington disease?
case.a: Juvenile HD with large paternally inherited expansion typically presents as an akinetic-rigid (Westphal) form.

read.where: 12 The Many Faces of Parkinsonism: A Review of the Parkinson Look-alike Syndromes

det.patho: The CAG expansion in HTT produces mutant huntingtin with a long polyglutamine tract that injures striatal medium spiny neurons and cortex. Chorea reflects early loss of indirect pathway neurons; when direct pathway neurons are lost early or in later disease, a hypokinetic-rigid picture predominates. Very long repeats, usually inherited from the father, give juvenile onset.
det.clinical: Juvenile HD presents before 20 with behavioural and learning problems, rigidity, dystonia and seizures. Adult patients may have prominent psychiatric or cognitive change for years before or without chorea, and late-stage disease becomes rigid and akinetic as chorea fades. Dysphagia, weight loss and falls follow.
det.diagnosis: Genetic testing for HTT CAG repeat length confirms (40 or more fully penetrant). Absence of chorea should not stop testing when family history, cognitive and psychiatric features suggest HD. Counselling is essential.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy is approved; huntingtin-lowering therapies are in trials, and AMT-130 gene therapy reported encouraging early data in 2025. Levodopa or dopamine agonists may help rigidity modestly; antiseizure medication for juvenile epilepsy; psychiatric care, speech, swallow and physiotherapy. Avoid VMAT2 inhibitors when chorea is absent because they worsen parkinsonism.
det.prognosis: Progressive, with death 10–20 years after onset; juvenile cases often progress faster.
pearls: No chorea does not exclude HD, especially in juvenile cases.
Juvenile HD: rigidity + seizures + paternal transmission + large CAG repeat.
Tetrabenazine helps chorea but worsens a hypokinetic-rigid presentation.
det.thd: Huntington sine chorea คือโรคฮันติงตันที่ไม่มีการเคลื่อนไหวแบบ chorea แต่มีสมองเสื่อม อาการทางจิต แข็งเกร็ง เคลื่อนไหวช้า และ dystonia พบมากในชนิดเด็กและวัยรุ่นที่ได้รับยีนจากพ่อซึ่งมี CAG ยาวมาก และพบในระยะท้ายของโรค ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน HTT ยังไม่มียาที่ชะลอโรคได้ รักษาตามอาการ

name: Acid-base disorders
formal: Disturbances of systemic pH balance (metabolic or respiratory acidosis or alkalosis) that can cause encephalopathy, seizures, tetany, hyperventilation and altered consciousness depending on severity and rate of change.
simple: Imbalances of acid and alkali levels in the blood that can cause confusion, seizures, muscle cramps and drowsiness.
th: ความผิดปกติของสมดุลกรด-ด่างในร่างกาย ซึ่งเป็นโรคทางระบบอื่นที่ทำให้เกิดอาการทางสมองได้ เช่น สับสน ชัก tetany และหายใจเร็ว ขึ้นกับความรุนแรงและความเร็ว
tempoNote: Neurological effects depend on how quickly pH changes; rapid shifts cause more symptoms than slowly developing ones
feat: Systemic (not primarily neurological) disorders that frequently present with brain symptoms
Respiratory or metabolic alkalosis: perioral and digital tingling, carpopedal spasm, light-headedness, sometimes seizures
Acute respiratory acidosis (CO2 retention): headache, drowsiness, asterixis, papilloedema, coma
Severe metabolic acidosis: lethargy, deep rapid breathing (Kussmaul), confusion
inv: Arterial or venous blood gas with electrolytes, anion gap and osmolar gap
Lactate, ketones, creatinine, toxicology (salicylate, methanol, ethylene glycol)
Ionised calcium and magnesium in tetany

case.story: During an exam developed breathlessness, tingling around the mouth and both hands, and her fingers cramped into a claw shape.
case.exam: Rapid breathing, carpopedal spasm, positive Trousseau sign, otherwise normal neurology.
case.tests: Blood gas: pH 7.55, PCO2 24 mmHg, total calcium normal.
case.q: What causes the tetany, and how is it managed?
case.a: Acute respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation lowers ionised calcium; reassure, slow breathing and treat anxiety, after excluding organic causes.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Acid-Base Disorders
Chapter 14: Neurologic Manifestations Of Acid–Base Derangements, Electrolyte Disorders, And Endocrine Crises

det.patho: pH changes alter neuronal excitability and cerebral blood flow. Alkalosis increases protein binding of calcium, lowering ionised calcium and raising nerve excitability, and causes cerebral vasoconstriction. Hypercapnia dilates cerebral vessels, raising intracranial pressure and depressing consciousness. CSF pH lags behind blood pH, so rapid correction can transiently worsen neurological function.
det.clinical: This is not a neurological disease but a systemic disturbance with common neurological presentations. Hyperventilation-related tetany is frequent in emergency departments. CO2 narcosis occurs in COPD, neuromuscular respiratory failure and over-oxygenation. Toxic causes of high anion gap acidosis (methanol, ethylene glycol) also cause specific brain and optic nerve injury.
det.diagnosis: Measure blood gas and electrolytes, determine primary disorder and compensation, and calculate anion gap. Look for the underlying cause such as sepsis, diabetic ketoacidosis, kidney failure, toxins, lung disease or neuromuscular weakness. In a patient with neuromuscular disease, rising CO2 signals impending respiratory failure.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: insulin and fluids for DKA, ventilation for hypercapnia, dialysis or antidotes for toxins, controlled breathing for hyperventilation. Correct pH changes gradually. Watch for hypocalcaemia, hypokalaemia and hypophosphataemia, which add neurological effects.
det.prognosis: Neurological symptoms usually reverse once the acid-base problem is corrected, unless hypoxic or toxic injury has occurred.
pearls: Bilateral perioral and hand tingling with carpopedal spasm during anxiety: respiratory alkalosis.
Rising PCO2 in GBS or myasthenia indicates late respiratory failure; do not wait for it to intubate.
High anion gap acidosis with visual loss: think methanol.
det.thd: ความผิดปกติของกรด-ด่างเป็นโรคทางระบบ ไม่ใช่โรคทางประสาทโดยตรง แต่ทำให้เกิดอาการทางสมองได้บ่อย เช่น ภาวะด่างจากหายใจเร็วทำให้ชารอบปากและมือจีบเกร็ง ส่วน CO2 คั่งทำให้ปวดหัว ซึม และหมดสติ วินิจฉัยด้วย blood gas และเกลือแร่ แล้วรักษาตามสาเหตุอย่างค่อยเป็นค่อยไป

name: Acoustic trauma
formal: Cochlear injury from loud noise or blast producing sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and sometimes hyperacusis, due to hair cell damage particularly at 3 to 6 kHz.
simple: Hearing damage caused by very loud noise, leading to hearing loss and ringing in the ears.
th: การบาดเจ็บของหูชั้นในจากเสียงดังหรือแรงระเบิด ทำให้หูตึงแบบประสาทรับเสียง เสียงดังในหู และไวต่อเสียง โดยมักเสียที่ความถี่ 3–6 kHz
tempoNote: Acute after a single blast, or gradual after years of occupational noise
feat: Muffled hearing, tinnitus and ear fullness after gunfire, explosion or loud music
Chronic occupational form is bilateral and gradual
Audiogram notch at 4 kHz with recovery at 8 kHz
Hyperacusis; blast injury may also rupture the eardrum or cause vertigo
inv: Pure-tone audiometry, speech audiometry and tympanometry
Otoscopy for drum perforation after blast
MRI internal auditory canals if asymmetric loss or vestibular symptoms

case.story: After a rifle range session without ear protection, his right ear has rung for three days and voices sound dull.
case.exam: Intact eardrums; Rinne positive bilaterally, Weber lateralises to the left.
case.tests: Audiogram: right sensorineural loss maximal at 4 kHz.
case.q: What is the management?
case.a: Acute acoustic trauma; early oral or intratympanic corticosteroids are often given, plus strict noise avoidance and hearing protection.

read.where: Chapter 23 Neuro-Otology: Dizziness, Balance and Hearing — Sensorineural Hearing Loss

det.patho: Excess sound energy damages outer hair cells, their stereocilia and supporting structures in the cochlea, with the 3–6 kHz region most vulnerable owing to ear canal resonance. Synapses between inner hair cells and auditory nerve fibres can be lost even when thresholds recover ('hidden hearing loss'). Blasts add mechanical injury to the drum, ossicles and inner ear membranes.
det.clinical: A temporary threshold shift may resolve within days; repeated exposure leads to permanent loss. Patients complain of tinnitus and difficulty hearing speech in noise. It is an ear disorder, not a central neurological disease, but presents to neurologists as tinnitus or hearing loss.
det.diagnosis: Based on history of exposure and the typical audiometric notch. Asymmetric loss without clear exposure, or neurological signs, warrants MRI to exclude a retrocochlear lesion. Document baseline for occupational compensation.
det.treatment: Acute trauma is often treated like sudden sensorineural hearing loss with corticosteroids, although evidence is limited. Avoid further noise. Hearing aids and tinnitus management (sound therapy, CBT) for permanent loss. Prevention through hearing conservation programmes is central.
det.prognosis: Temporary shifts often recover; permanent loss does not reverse and worsens with continued exposure.
pearls: Audiometric notch at 4 kHz with recovery at 8 kHz = noise injury.
Asymmetric sensorineural loss without exposure: image the internal auditory canals.
Prevention (ear protection) is the only reliable treatment.
det.thd: Acoustic trauma คือการบาดเจ็บของเซลล์ขนในหูชั้นในจากเสียงดังมาก เช่น เสียงปืน ระเบิด หรือเสียงดังจากการทำงานนาน ๆ ทำให้หูอื้อ เสียงดังในหู และได้ยินลดลงโดยเฉพาะที่ 4 kHz ตรวจด้วย audiogram ระยะเฉียบพลันอาจให้ steroid ส่วนการสูญเสียถาวรใช้เครื่องช่วยฟัง สิ่งสำคัญที่สุดคือการป้องกันด้วยอุปกรณ์ป้องกันเสียง

name: Acquired ataxia syndromes
formal: Ataxias of non-hereditary origin including alcohol, vitamin deficiency, immune-mediated, paraneoplastic, toxic, vascular and infectious causes; subacute progressive cerebellar syndrome needs urgent aetiological work-up.
simple: Unsteadiness and poor coordination that develops from causes such as alcohol, vitamin lack, immune reactions, cancer or infection rather than being inherited.
th: กลุ่ม ataxia ที่ไม่ได้เกิดจากพันธุกรรม เช่น แอลกอฮอล์ ขาดวิตามิน ภูมิคุ้มกัน paraneoplastic ยาหรือสารพิษ หลอดเลือด และการติดเชื้อ หากเป็นแบบกึ่งเฉียบพลันต้องหาสาเหตุเร่งด่วน
tempoNote: Tempo is the key clue: acute (stroke, toxin), subacute (immune, paraneoplastic, deficiency), chronic (alcohol, drugs)
feat: Gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria and nystagmus without a clear family history
Alcohol: midline (vermis) gait ataxia with relatively spared arms
Subacute pancerebellar syndrome over weeks suggests paraneoplastic or autoimmune cause
Drugs (phenytoin, lithium, metronidazole, chemotherapy) and vitamin E/B1 deficiency are reversible
Associated clues: neuropathy, opsoclonus, myoclonus, coeliac symptoms, thyroid disease
inv: MRI brain (stroke, demyelination, tumour, atrophy pattern)
Vitamin B1, B12, E, thyroid, coeliac serology, drug levels, alcohol history
Onconeural and cell-surface antibodies (Yo, Hu, CV2, Ri, Tr/DNER, mGluR1, GAD65, VGCC); CT chest-abdomen-pelvis or PET
CSF for inflammation; test for MSA and late-onset genetic ataxias (RFC1, FGF14) if workup negative

case.story: Over six weeks became unable to walk without support, speech slurred, sees objects jumping.
case.exam: Severe gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, downbeat nystagmus; breast lump on examination.
case.tests: MRI normal; serum anti-Yo positive; CSF mild pleocytosis; breast biopsy carcinoma.
case.q: Why does the tempo matter here?
case.a: A rapidly progressive pancerebellar syndrome over weeks suggests paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration; early tumour treatment and immunotherapy give the best chance of stabilisation.

read.where: Chapter 24 Cerebellar Ataxias and Related Conditions — Acquired Ataxia Syndromes
Chapter 73: Cerebellar Disorders and Ataxias: Acquired Disorders

det.patho: The cerebellum is sensitive to toxins (alcohol, drugs), nutritional deficiency (thiamine, vitamin E), immune attack against Purkinje cells, ischaemia, demyelination and infection. Damage may be focal (stroke, tumour), regional (vermis in alcohol) or diffuse (paraneoplastic).
det.clinical: Acute ataxia suggests stroke, haemorrhage, toxicity, Wernicke encephalopathy or post-infectious cerebellitis. Subacute ataxia over weeks to months points to paraneoplastic, autoimmune (GAD, gluten), prion, or deficiency causes. Chronic acquired ataxia is commonly alcohol-related or due to long-term drugs. Superficial siderosis gives ataxia with deafness.
det.diagnosis: Start with MRI and a careful drug, alcohol and diet history. Blood tests for vitamins, thyroid and coeliac disease are inexpensive and treatable. Antibody panels and cancer screening are needed for subacute presentations. When all is negative in late-onset sporadic ataxia, consider MSA and genetic causes such as RFC1 (CANVAS) and FGF14 (SCA27B).
det.treatment: Treat the cause: stop offending drugs, thiamine for Wernicke, vitamin E replacement, gluten-free diet, tumour removal and immunotherapy for paraneoplastic and autoimmune forms. Rehabilitation with balance training benefits all. Riluzole and 4-aminopyridine have some evidence for symptomatic benefit in certain ataxias.
det.prognosis: Reversible causes may recover substantially; paraneoplastic and prion causes generally do not.
pearls: Tempo first: acute, subacute or chronic narrows the cause.
Always check thiamine, vitamin E, drugs and coeliac antibodies; they are treatable.
Subacute pancerebellar syndrome in an adult: search for cancer and send onconeural antibodies.
det.thd: Acquired ataxia คือ ataxia ที่ไม่ได้มาจากพันธุกรรม สาเหตุมีหลายอย่าง เช่น แอลกอฮอล์ ยา เช่น phenytoin ขาดวิตามิน B1 หรือ E โรคภูมิคุ้มกัน paraneoplastic หลอดเลือดสมอง และการติดเชื้อ การดูความเร็วของอาการช่วยมาก หากแย่ลงภายในสัปดาห์ต้องหามะเร็งและตรวจแอนติบอดี ตรวจ MRI และเลือดหาสาเหตุที่รักษาได้ แล้วรักษาตามต้นเหตุร่วมกับกายภาพบำบัด

name: Acquired cardiac disease
formal: Cardiac conditions arising after birth (valvular disease, arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, endocarditis) that are major sources of cardioembolic stroke and cerebral hypoperfusion.
simple: Heart problems developed during life, such as valve disease or irregular rhythm, that can send clots to the brain and cause stroke.
th: โรคหัวใจที่เกิดภายหลัง เช่น ลิ้นหัวใจ หัวใจเต้นผิดจังหวะ กล้ามเนื้อหัวใจ และเยื่อบุหัวใจอักเสบ ซึ่งเป็นแหล่งของลิ่มเลือดอุดตันในสมองและสมองขาดเลือด
tempoNote: Underlying heart disease is chronic; neurological events such as embolic stroke are abrupt
feat: Not a single neurological disease: an umbrella for heart conditions that cause brain injury
Atrial fibrillation, rheumatic mitral disease, recent myocardial infarction, cardiomyopathy and endocarditis are main embolic sources
Embolic strokes: abrupt maximal deficit, cortical signs, multiple territories
Low cardiac output causes syncope, watershed infarcts or cognitive impairment
Rheumatic heart disease remains a relevant stroke cause in younger Thai patients
inv: ECG and prolonged rhythm monitoring (Holter, loop recorder)
Transthoracic echocardiography; transoesophageal echo for valves, left atrial appendage or endocarditis
Blood cultures if fever or new murmur; troponin and BNP as indicated

case.story: Known rheumatic heart disease, irregular follow-up. Sudden right weakness and inability to speak while sewing.
case.exam: Irregularly irregular pulse, mid-diastolic murmur, global aphasia, right hemiplegia; NIHSS 18.
case.tests: CT: no haemorrhage; CTA left M1 occlusion; echo: severe mitral stenosis with large left atrium; ECG atrial fibrillation.
case.q: What is the stroke mechanism and the secondary prevention of choice?
case.a: Cardioembolism from rheumatic mitral stenosis with AF; after thrombectomy, long-term warfarin (DOACs are not preferred in moderate–severe rheumatic mitral stenosis).

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Neurological Complications of Acquired Cardiac Disease
Chapter 5 Neurologic Manifestations of Acquired Cardiac Disease and Arrhythmias
27 Fits, faints, funny turns, and falls in the differential diagnosis of the dizzy patient
Chapter 6: What caused this transient or persisting ischemic event?

det.patho: Stasis in a fibrillating or dilated atrium, akinetic ventricular segments after infarction, damaged or prosthetic valves and infected vegetations all produce emboli that lodge in brain arteries. Heart failure and arrhythmia also reduce cerebral perfusion, contributing to border-zone infarcts and cognitive decline. Endocarditis adds septic emboli, abscess and mycotic aneurysm.
det.clinical: Cardioembolic strokes tend to be large, sudden and cortical, sometimes with early haemorrhagic transformation. Recurrent events in different territories suggest a central embolic source. Syncope with focal signs, unexplained encephalopathy or headache with fever may point to endocarditis. Many patients have known heart disease, but AF is often paroxysmal and undiscovered.
det.diagnosis: Every ischaemic stroke needs an ECG and rhythm monitoring; extended monitoring increases AF detection after cryptogenic stroke. Echocardiography identifies thrombus, valve disease, low ejection fraction and vegetations. Modified Duke criteria guide endocarditis diagnosis. Classify the stroke mechanism (e.g. TOAST) to guide prevention.
det.treatment: Acute stroke management follows usual pathways; thrombolysis is contraindicated in endocarditis, but thrombectomy can be considered. Secondary prevention: DOACs for non-valvular AF, warfarin for mechanical valves and moderate–severe rheumatic mitral stenosis, heart failure optimisation and surgery when indicated. Anticoagulation timing after stroke depends on infarct size.
det.prognosis: Cardioembolic strokes carry higher early mortality and recurrence than other subtypes unless the source is treated.
pearls: Stroke in a young Thai adult: listen for a mitral murmur.
Embolic infarcts in several territories point to the heart or aortic arch.
Do not thrombolyse suspected endocarditis.
det.thd: Acquired cardiac disease คือโรคหัวใจที่เกิดภายหลัง เช่น AF โรคลิ้นหัวใจรูมาติก กล้ามเนื้อหัวใจตายหรือหัวใจล้มเหลว และเยื่อบุหัวใจอักเสบติดเชื้อ ซึ่งเป็นแหล่งของลิ่มเลือดที่หลุดไปอุดหลอดเลือดสมอง ผู้ป่วยมักมีอาการอ่อนแรงเฉียบพลันรุนแรง ควรตรวจ ECG ติดตามจังหวะหัวใจ และทำ echocardiography การป้องกันซ้ำใช้ยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือดตามชนิดโรคหัวใจ

name: Acquired metabolic disorders
formal: Non-genetic metabolic derangements (hypoglycaemia, uraemia, hepatic failure, electrolyte disturbance, thyroid disease, vitamin deficiency) producing encephalopathy, neuropathy, myopathy or movement disorders.
simple: Body chemistry problems such as low sugar, kidney or liver failure or vitamin shortage that can affect the brain, nerves or muscles.
th: ความผิดปกติทางเมตาบอลิกที่ไม่ใช่พันธุกรรม เช่น น้ำตาลต่ำ ไตวาย ตับวาย เกลือแร่ผิดปกติ ไทรอยด์ และขาดวิตามิน ทำให้เกิดภาวะสมองผิดปกติ ปลายประสาท กล้ามเนื้อ หรือการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติ
tempoNote: Usually acute or subacute, following the systemic derangement
feat: Fluctuating confusion, inattention and drowsiness without focal signs (delirium)
Asterixis, multifocal myoclonus and tremor in uraemia, liver failure and hypercapnia
Seizures with hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia or hypomagnesaemia
Movement disorders: hemichorea with non-ketotic hyperglycaemia, parkinsonism in acquired hepatocerebral degeneration
Neuropathy and myopathy in chronic kidney disease, hypothyroidism or deficiency states
inv: Glucose, sodium, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, urea, creatinine, liver function, ammonia, blood gas
TSH, cortisol, B1, B12, folate
EEG (triphasic waves, slowing, non-convulsive status); MRI (osmotic demyelination, pallidal T1 signal, PRES)

case.who: 70-year-old woman from Suphan Buri with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes
case.story: Two days of involuntary flinging movements of the left arm and leg; no headache.
case.exam: Left hemichorea-hemiballism, alert, no weakness.
case.tests: Glucose 32 mmol/L without ketones; CT shows right putaminal hyperdensity; MRI T1 putaminal hyperintensity.
case.q: What is the diagnosis?
case.a: Non-ketotic hyperglycaemic hemichorea; correct the glucose, and movements usually settle over days to weeks.

read.where: Chapter 28 Disorders of Consciousness and Intensive Care Neurology — Metabolic Encephalopathy
Chapter 61 Disorders of Consciousness in Systemic Diseases
Chapter 4: The Phenomenology of Movement Disorders

det.patho: The brain, nerves and muscles depend on stable glucose, oxygen, osmolality, electrolytes and clearance of toxins. Failure of any organ that maintains this balance disturbs neurotransmission and cell volume, giving diffuse dysfunction. Rapid correction can itself injure the brain, as in osmotic demyelination after fast sodium correction.
det.clinical: Encephalopathy is the commonest manifestation; focal signs may occur with hypoglycaemia (transient hemiparesis) or hyperglycaemia (hemichorea). Chronic states cause neuropathy (uraemic, hypothyroid), myopathy (thyroid, steroid excess, hypokalaemia) and cerebellar or extrapyramidal syndromes. Several disturbances often coexist in ill patients. This is an umbrella term rather than one disease.
det.diagnosis: Screen all patients with altered consciousness for glucose and electrolytes immediately, then broader organ function. EEG helps exclude non-convulsive status. MRI patterns can be suggestive. Look for a precipitant and medicine effects.
det.treatment: Correct the derangement at an appropriate speed (sodium no faster than 8–10 mmol/L per 24 h in chronic hyponatraemia); give thiamine before glucose in at-risk patients; dialysis for uraemia; lactulose and rifaximin for hepatic encephalopathy; hormone replacement for endocrine causes. Treat seizures and avoid sedatives that mask recovery.
det.prognosis: Usually reversible if corrected promptly; prolonged hypoglycaemia or osmotic demyelination can cause permanent injury.
pearls: Check glucose in every confused or seizing patient before anything else.
Hemichorea in an elderly diabetic: non-ketotic hyperglycaemia with putaminal T1 hyperintensity.
Asterixis suggests metabolic rather than structural encephalopathy.
det.thd: Acquired metabolic disorders หมายถึงความผิดปกติทางเมตาบอลิกที่เกิดภายหลัง เช่น น้ำตาลต่ำหรือสูง โซเดียมผิดปกติ ไตวาย ตับวาย ไทรอยด์ และขาดวิตามิน ทำให้สับสน ชัก มือสั่นแบบ asterixis หรือการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติ ตรวจเลือดหาสาเหตุทันที และแก้ไขด้วยความเร็วที่เหมาะสม เช่น ไม่เพิ่มโซเดียมเร็วเกินไป ส่วนใหญ่อาการกลับคืนได้หากรักษาเร็ว

name: Acquired muscle diseases
formal: Non-hereditary myopathies such as inflammatory, toxic, endocrine, metabolic and critical illness muscle disease, presenting with proximal weakness, myalgia and raised creatine kinase.
simple: Muscle diseases that develop during life from inflammation, drugs, hormone problems or illness, causing weakness and sometimes pain.
th: กลุ่มโรคกล้ามเนื้อที่ไม่ได้เกิดจากพันธุกรรม เช่น การอักเสบ ยา ต่อมไร้ท่อ เมตาบอลิก และกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงในผู้ป่วยวิกฤต
tempoNote: Days in necrotising and critical-illness myopathy, weeks to months in dermatomyositis and polymyositis, years in inclusion body myositis and endocrine myopathy
feat: Symmetric proximal limb weakness: trouble rising from a chair, climbing stairs, combing hair; sensation and reflexes are preserved until late
Myalgia and raised CK in inflammatory, necrotising and toxic forms; normal CK in steroid, thyroid and many endocrine myopathies
Skin signs (heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, shawl sign) mark dermatomyositis; finger flexor and quadriceps weakness mark inclusion body myositis
Drug and toxin clues: statins, glucocorticoids, colchicine, alcohol, zidovudine, immune checkpoint inhibitors
Eye muscle forms exist: thyroid orbitopathy, ocular myositis, mitochondrial CPEO, and ocular myasthenia is the main look-alike
inv: CK, aldolase, TSH, electrolytes (K, Ca, phosphate), vitamin D, ESR/CRP and a medication review
EMG showing myopathic units, with fibrillations in irritable (inflammatory or necrotising) myopathy
Myositis antibodies (anti-HMGCR, SRP, Jo-1, Mi-2, TIF1-gamma, NXP2, cN-1A) and muscle MRI to target biopsy
Muscle biopsy for diagnosis and subtype; cancer screening in dermatomyositis and necrotising myopathy

case.story: For two months stairs and getting up from the toilet had become a struggle. She had muscle aches but no eye or swallowing symptoms. Statin had been taken for four years; weakness persisted for weeks after stopping it.
case.exam: Proximal weakness of hips and shoulders MRC 4, neck flexor mild weakness, normal reflexes and sensation, no rash.
case.tests: CK 7,800 U/L; EMG myopathic with fibrillations; anti-HMGCR antibody positive; biopsy shows necrotic fibres with minimal inflammation.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what treatment is needed?
case.a: Statin-associated immune-mediated necrotising myopathy. Stop the statin and start immunosuppression: corticosteroid with methotrexate or IVIG, and screen for cancer.

read.where: Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Acquired Muscle Diseases

det.patho: Acquired myopathies arise from immune attack (dermatomyositis through complement-mediated microangiopathy and interferon signalling, polymyositis and inclusion body myositis through cytotoxic T cells, necrotising myopathy through anti-SRP or anti-HMGCR antibodies), from toxins and drugs that injure fibres, and from systemic illness such as thyroid or cortisol excess, electrolyte disorders and critical illness. The effect is fibre necrosis, atrophy or dysfunction without a primary genetic defect.
det.clinical: Most present with progressive proximal weakness over weeks to months, but the pace and companions differ. Dermatomyositis shows skin changes, interstitial lung disease and associated cancer; necrotising myopathy has very high CK and may follow statins; inclusion body myositis begins after age 50 with asymmetric finger flexor and quadriceps weakness and dysphagia; critical illness myopathy appears in the ICU after sepsis, steroids and neuromuscular blockers. Ocular involvement ranges from the proptosis and restricted gaze of thyroid orbitopathy to isolated painful ocular myositis.
det.diagnosis: Combine pattern of weakness, CK, EMG, antibodies, MRI and muscle biopsy to assign a subtype. Normal CK does not exclude steroid or endocrine myopathy, and the EMG distinguishes myopathy from neuropathic and junction disorders. Exclude metabolic causes (hypothyroidism, hypokalaemia, hypophosphataemia, hypercalcaemia, vitamin D deficiency), toxins, infection (HIV, parasitic myositis) and mimics such as muscular dystrophy and Pompe disease.
det.treatment: Remove culprits (statin, alcohol, steroid) and correct endocrine or electrolyte problems. Inflammatory myopathies are treated with corticosteroid plus a steroid-sparing agent (methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate), with IVIG for severe, dysphagic or refractory disease, and rituximab in selected cases; inclusion body myositis rarely responds. Add exercise, dysphagia care, bone protection and cancer screening, and monitor lungs and heart.
det.prognosis: Toxic, endocrine and necrotising forms improve when the cause is treated; dermatomyositis and polymyositis need long therapy; inclusion body myositis progresses slowly to disability.
pearls: Myopathy with a normal CK still occurs: think steroid, hypothyroid, hypokalaemic or inclusion body causes.
Weakness persisting after stopping a statin should prompt anti-HMGCR testing.
In new dermatomyositis, search for an underlying cancer.
det.thd: โรคกล้ามเนื้อที่เกิดภายหลัง ได้แก่ myositis จากภูมิคุ้มกัน (dermatomyositis, polymyositis, IBM, necrotising myopathy) ยาและสารพิษ (statin, steroid, สุรา) ต่อมไร้ท่อ (ไทรอยด์ คอร์ติซอล) และ ICU myopathy ผู้ป่วยมักอ่อนแรงบริเวณต้นแขนต้นขาและลุกจากเก้าอี้ลำบาก CK อาจสูงมากหรือปกติก็ได้ ตรวจ EMG แอนติบอดี MRI และชิ้นเนื้อ เพื่อจำแนกชนิด การรักษาคือเลิกสารก่อโรค แก้ภาวะผิดปกติของฮอร์โมนและอิเล็กโทรไลต์ และให้ยากดภูมิคุ้มกันในกลุ่ม myositis

ddx.pt: Fatigable weakness with ptosis and diplopia and normal CK
Proximal leg weakness with areflexia, dry mouth and facilitation after exercise
Neurogenic EMG, fasciculations and a very slow course; SMN1 deletion

aN: acquired myopathies | non hereditary myopathies | secondary myopathies | acquired myopathy

name: Acquired peripheral nerve diseases
formal: Neuropathies from non-genetic causes including diabetes, immune-mediated, toxic, nutritional, infectious, paraproteinaemic and vasculitic mechanisms, causing sensory loss, weakness and pain.
simple: Nerve damage in the arms and legs from causes such as diabetes, immune attack, toxins, infection or poor nutrition.
th: โรคเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายที่ไม่ใช่พันธุกรรม เช่น เบาหวาน ภูมิคุ้มกัน ยาและสารพิษ ขาดสารอาหาร ติดเชื้อ paraprotein และหลอดเลือดอักเสบ ทำให้ชา อ่อนแรง และปวด
tempoNote: Hours to 4 weeks in GBS and vasculitis, weeks to months in toxic, nutritional and some immune neuropathies, years in diabetic and paraproteinaemic forms
feat: Length-dependent glove-and-stocking sensory loss with burning pain (diabetes, alcohol, drugs, B12 deficiency)
Rapid ascending weakness with areflexia (GBS), or relapsing and progressive weakness with proximal involvement (CIDP)
Painful asymmetric mononeuritis multiplex from vasculitis, diabetes, leprosy or HIV
Sensory ataxia from dorsal root ganglion damage (Sjögren, paraneoplastic, B6 toxicity, cisplatin)
Autonomic features such as postural hypotension, gastroparesis and sweating change, especially in amyloid and diabetic neuropathy
inv: Nerve conduction and EMG to define axonal versus demyelinating, symmetric versus multifocal, and large versus small fibre
First-line blood tests: HbA1c or glucose, B12 with methylmalonic acid, serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and light chains, renal, liver and thyroid function
Targeted tests: HIV, hepatitis B/C, ANCA, ENA, anti-MAG, nodal/paranodal antibodies, paraneoplastic panel, leprosy smear, CSF
Nerve ultrasound, skin biopsy for small fibre neuropathy, and nerve biopsy in selected vasculitic or infiltrative cases

case.who: 63-year-old man from Udon Thani with 10-year type 2 diabetes
case.story: Over a year he developed numb feet and burning at night, and recently his hands tingle too. He also loses balance in the dark. He drinks alcohol moderately and takes metformin.
case.exam: Reduced pinprick and vibration to the knees, absent ankle reflexes, positive Romberg sign, normal strength apart from mild toe weakness.
case.tests: HbA1c 9.1%; B12 low-normal with raised methylmalonic acid; SPEP shows an IgG kappa band; NCS shows length-dependent axonal sensorimotor neuropathy.
case.q: Is it all diabetic neuropathy? What else should be considered?
case.a: Diabetes is probable but not sufficient: B12 deficiency (metformin, alcohol) and a monoclonal gammopathy are additional contributors that need treatment or haematology work-up.

read.where: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves — Acquired Neuropathies

det.patho: Acquired neuropathies arise through metabolic injury (diabetes, uraemia), immune attack on myelin or axon (GBS, CIDP, vasculitis, paraproteinaemia), toxins and drugs (alcohol, chemotherapy, nitrofurantoin, pyridoxine excess), nutritional deficiency (B12, thiamine, copper), infection (leprosy, HIV, hepatitis, Lyme) and neoplastic mechanisms. The nerve responds with distal axonal degeneration, segmental demyelination or ganglionopathy, patterns that EDX can distinguish and that point to causes.
det.clinical: Pattern recognition is the core skill: tempo (acute, subacute, chronic), symmetry, length dependence, motor versus sensory predominance and pain. Distal symmetric polyneuropathy is the commonest form and most often diabetic, alcoholic or drug-related. Acute severe weakness suggests GBS, relapsing proximal and distal weakness suggests CIDP, and painful stepwise multifocal deficits suggest vasculitis. Prominent sensory ataxia raises sensory ganglionopathy, and autonomic failure suggests amyloid or diabetes.
det.diagnosis: Approach by history, examination and nerve conduction studies, then laboratory evaluation guided by pattern. Guidelines support first-line testing of glucose or HbA1c, B12 with metabolites and serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation because yield is highest. Further tests (CSF, antibodies, imaging, skin or nerve biopsy, genetics) are tailored. Always consider hereditary mimics, especially when the course is long, there is foot deformity or family history, and note that more than one cause may coexist.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: glycaemic control and risk-factor management in diabetes, vitamin replacement, stopping offending drugs or alcohol, antibiotics for leprosy or infection, and immunotherapy for immune-mediated forms (IVIG 2 g/kg, plasma exchange or steroids for GBS and CIDP; cyclophosphamide with steroids for vasculitis). Treat neuropathic pain with gabapentinoids, SNRIs or tricyclics, and use foot care, balance training and ankle-foot orthoses to prevent complications.
det.prognosis: Highly cause-dependent: immune neuropathies often respond to treatment, metabolic and toxic forms stabilise when the cause is removed, while established axonal loss recovers slowly or incompletely.
pearls: Order HbA1c, B12 with methylmalonic acid and SPEP with immunofixation in nearly every chronic polyneuropathy.
Rapid course, proximal weakness or asymmetry in a neuropathy should prompt a search for an immune or vasculitic cause.
Diabetes does not exclude another contributing cause, so look further.
det.thd: โรคเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายที่เกิดภายหลังมีหลายสาเหตุ เช่น เบาหวาน ภูมิคุ้มกัน (GBS, CIDP) หลอดเลือดอักเสบ ยาและสารพิษ ขาดวิตามิน B12 ติดเชื้อ เช่น โรคเรื้อน และ paraprotein การวินิจฉัยเริ่มจากแยกรูปแบบ ได้แก่ ความเร็วของโรค ความสมมาตร ชนิดของใยประสาท และอาการเด่น ตามด้วย NCS/EMG และตรวจเลือดเบื้องต้น คือ HbA1c, B12 กับ MMA และ SPEP พร้อม immunofixation จากนั้นตรวจเพิ่มตามความสงสัย การรักษาคือแก้สาเหตุ ให้ยากดภูมิคุ้มกันในโรคภูมิคุ้มกัน และจัดการอาการปวดจากเส้นประสาท
