name: Acquired prion diseases
formal: Transmissible spongiform encephalopathies acquired by exposure, including kuru, iatrogenic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and variant CJD from bovine spongiform encephalopathy, with rapid dementia and myoclonus.
simple: Fatal brain diseases caused by abnormal proteins passed on through contaminated tissue, medical procedures or food, causing rapid memory loss and jerking.
th: โรคพรีออนที่ได้รับจากภายนอกมี 3 กลุ่ม ได้แก่ kuru จากพิธีกรรมกินศพ iatrogenic CJD จากฮอร์โมน เนื้อเยื่อหรือเครื่องมือผ่าตัดปนเปื้อน และ variant CJD จากเนื้อวัวที่ติดโรควัวบ้า พบน้อยกว่า 1% ของโรคพรีออนทั้งหมด ฟักตัวนานหลายปีถึงหลายสิบปี
tempoNote: Silent incubation of years to decades (kuru mean 12 years, up to 50; vCJD ~17; iatrogenic 1.5–30+), then ataxia or dementia and death within about a year
feat: Fewer than 1% of human prion disease; three forms: kuru (ritual endocannibalism), iatrogenic CJD (grafts, hormones, instruments) and variant CJD (BSE beef; rarely transfusion)
Not contagious by ordinary contact, since a large dose of prions is needed; the risk is inoculation, transfusion or eating infected tissue
Kuru and growth-hormone cases start with cerebellar ataxia; dura-graft cases with ataxia, visual symptoms and dementia; vCJD with psychiatric and painful sensory symptoms
Species barrier protects humans against scrapie and probably chronic wasting disease, but classic BSE crossed it and caused vCJD
Prions resist heat, formalin and ordinary disinfectants, so hospital transmission is the main modern risk
inv: Exposure history first: grafts, pituitary hormone, neurosurgery, corneal transplant, transfusion, residence in BSE countries
MRI DWI/ADC and FLAIR (pulvinar sign in vCJD), CSF RT-QuIC and total tau; EEG periodic complexes are rare in vCJD
PRNP sequencing and codon 129 genotype; tonsil biopsy only for suspected vCJD without the pulvinar sign

case.who: 49-year-old man from Chonburi who had neurosurgery for a brain tumour in Europe in the 1980s
case.story: Four months of unsteady walking and slurred speech, now forgetfulness and startle jerks.
case.exam: Gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, myoclonus, impaired recall; no family history.
case.tests: MRI caudate and cortical restricted diffusion; CSF RT-QuIC positive; PRNP wild type.
case.q: Which acquired form is suspected, and what protects staff and later patients?
case.a: Iatrogenic CJD from a contaminated dural graft or instrument; notify authorities, use single-use or incinerated instruments, and avoid reprocessing neurosurgical sets.

read.where: Chapter 95 Prion Diseases — Acquired Prion Disease: Kuru, Variant CJD, Iatrogenic Prion Disease
CJD board tutorial — spectrum table (variant CJD, iatrogenic and kuru rows)
Chapter 11 Cognitive Impairment and Dementia — Acquired Prion Diseases

det.patho: Exogenous prions seed conversion of host PrPC after entering through the brain, peripheral tissue or the gut. Prions need a large infectious dose, resist ordinary disinfection and bind tightly to metal surfaces. Variant CJD spreads through lymphoid tissue before reaching the CNS, so tonsil biopsy is positive, whereas kuru and iatrogenic cases usually lack lymphoreticular involvement. Species barriers stop most animal prions, such as scrapie, from infecting humans, yet the BSE epidemic showed that a barrier can be crossed after passage through cattle.
det.clinical: Kuru among the Fore of Papua New Guinea was spread by mortuary rites, struck women and children most, and is essentially extinct, with rare cases after incubation as long as 50 years. Iatrogenic CJD has caused about 400 cases from growth hormone, dura grafts, corneas and instruments. Variant CJD (232 cases worldwide, none confirmed since 2019) mainly came from BSE-contaminated beef in the UK and France, with transfusion transmission in a few recipients. Animal prion diseases such as chronic wasting disease have not so far caused human cases.
det.diagnosis: Record a detailed exposure history, then apply sCJD criteria with RT-QuIC and MRI, and vCJD criteria when the young age, psychiatric onset and pulvinar sign are present. Lymphoreticular PrPSc is found in vCJD only, so tonsil biopsy is not appropriate in the other acquired forms. Confirmation is by neuropathology with Western blot typing. PRNP sequencing excludes a genetic cause.
det.treatment: Supportive and palliative; no approved drug. Prevention is the main intervention: single-use instruments, incineration of exposed equipment, and where reprocessing is unavoidable, extended steam sterilisation at 132 °C for at least 30 minutes with caustic denaturants. Surveillance centres trace people exposed to the same batch or instrument set, and public-health agencies restrict blood and tissue donation for people at risk.
det.prognosis: All forms are fatal, usually within months to a year after symptoms appear.
pearls: Acquired means exposure, not contagion; casual contact and sexual contact do not transmit prions.
Ataxia-first CJD in a younger patient raises iatrogenic or kuru-type disease.
Absence of PrPSc in tonsils does not exclude iatrogenic CJD.
det.thd: โรคพรีออนที่ได้รับจากภายนอกมี kuru, iatrogenic CJD และ variant CJD โดยไม่ติดต่อจากการสัมผัสทั่วไป ต้องมีการรับ prion ปริมาณมากผ่านการกินเนื้อเยื่อ ปลูกถ่ายอวัยวะ ใช้เครื่องมือผ่าตัดปนเปื้อน หรือรับเลือด ผู้ป่วยมักเริ่มด้วยเดินเซหรือพฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน ตามด้วยสมองเสื่อมเร็ว การวินิจฉัยต้องซักประวัติการสัมผัสร่วมกับ MRI และ RT-QuIC และไม่มียารักษา การป้องกันคือจัดการเครื่องมือผ่าตัดอย่างเข้มงวด

ddx.pt: Same clinical picture without any exposure; by far the commonest prion disease
PRNP mutation, often with family history; GSS, fatal familial insomnia or genetic CJD
Treatable rapidly progressive dementia with antibodies; RT-QuIC negative

aN: acquired cjd | transmissible spongiform encephalopathies acquired | iatrogenic cjd | kuru | vcjd

name: Acquired retrocochlear hearing disorders
formal: Hearing loss from lesions of the auditory nerve or central auditory pathways, such as vestibular schwannoma, demyelination or stroke, with poor speech discrimination and abnormal brainstem responses.
simple: Hearing loss caused by a problem in the hearing nerve or brain rather than the ear itself, often making speech hard to follow.
more: Central auditory disorders from lesions beyond the cochlea (auditory nerve, brainstem, cortex) causing impaired speech discrimination and processing out of proportion to pure-tone loss.
ab: Auditory nerve and brainstem hearing loss
th: การสูญเสียการได้ยินจากรอยโรคที่เส้นประสาทการได้ยินหรือทางเดินประสาทการได้ยินส่วนกลาง เช่น vestibular schwannoma, MS หรือ stroke
tempoNote: Acute with stroke or demyelination; slowly progressive with tumours
feat: Usually asymmetric or unilateral sensorineural loss with tinnitus
Speech understanding worse than the pure-tone audiogram predicts
May be accompanied by imbalance, facial numbness or facial weakness (cerebellopontine angle lesions)
Causes: vestibular schwannoma, meningioma, MS, brainstem stroke (AICA), infection, superficial siderosis
Bilateral cortical lesions can give cortical deafness with intact pure tones in some cases
inv: Pure-tone audiometry with speech discrimination; stapedial reflex testing
Auditory brainstem responses show prolonged interpeak latencies or absent waves
Gadolinium MRI of internal auditory canals and brainstem is the definitive test

case.story: Two years of right-sided hearing loss and ringing; recently trouble understanding phone calls in her right ear and unsteady walking.
case.exam: Weber lateralises left, Rinne positive both sides; reduced right corneal reflex; mild right limb ataxia.
case.tests: Audiogram: right high-frequency loss with speech discrimination 40%; MRI: 2.8-cm enhancing right CPA mass entering the internal acoustic canal.
case.q: What is the lesion and why is speech discrimination so poor?
case.a: Right vestibular schwannoma; neural (retrocochlear) loss degrades the timing of auditory signals, so words are less clear than tone thresholds suggest.

read.where: Chapter 23 Neuro-Otology: Dizziness, Balance and Hearing — Aetiology of Hearing Loss
Chapter 23 Neuro-Otology: Dizziness, Balance and Hearing — Sensorineural Hearing Loss
Chapter 23 Otoneurologic Manifestations of Otologic and Systemic Disease

det.patho: Damage to the cochlear nerve, cochlear nuclei or central auditory pathways disrupts neural synchrony and transmission even when hair cells are healthy. Tumours compress the nerve and its blood supply; demyelination slows conduction; infarction of AICA territory can damage both inner ear and brainstem. Central lesions above the cochlear nuclei rarely cause deafness unless bilateral because of crossed pathways.
det.clinical: Unilateral progressive hearing loss with tinnitus is the classic tumour presentation; sudden loss occurs in a minority. Associated cranial nerve V and VII signs or cerebellar features suggest a CPA mass. Sudden hearing loss with vertigo and brainstem signs should be treated as stroke. Patients with central disorders may complain of difficulty following speech in noise.
det.diagnosis: Asymmetric sensorineural loss (commonly defined as a 15 dB difference at two adjacent frequencies) or unilateral tinnitus warrants MRI. ABR is less sensitive than MRI for small tumours and is now mostly used when MRI is not possible. Distinguish cochlear from neural loss using otoacoustic emissions (preserved in neural lesions) and speech testing.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: observation, stereotactic radiosurgery or microsurgery for schwannomas; immunotherapy for demyelination; stroke pathways for AICA infarction. Hearing aids, CROS devices or cochlear/auditory brainstem implants aid rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause; tumour treatment often does not restore lost hearing, while demyelinating loss may recover.
pearls: Unilateral sensorineural loss or tinnitus: MRI, not just reassurance.
Poor word recognition out of proportion to thresholds suggests a neural lesion.
Sudden hearing loss plus vertigo and ataxia may be AICA stroke.
det.thd: Acquired retrocochlear hearing disorders คือการได้ยินลดลงจากรอยโรคที่เส้นประสาทการได้ยินหรือก้านสมอง เช่น vestibular schwannoma, MS หรือ stroke ผู้ป่วยมักมีหูอื้อข้างเดียวและฟังคำพูดไม่ชัดมากกว่าระดับการได้ยินที่วัดได้ อาจมีเดินเซหรือชาใบหน้าร่วม การตรวจสำคัญคือ audiogram และ MRI ของ internal auditory canal การรักษาตามสาเหตุร่วมกับเครื่องช่วยฟัง

name: Acquired symptomatic parkinsonian syndromes
formal: Parkinsonism due to an identifiable cause such as drugs, vascular disease, toxins, infection, trauma or structural lesions, as opposed to idiopathic Parkinson disease.
simple: Parkinson-like symptoms such as slowness, stiffness and tremor that are caused by a drug, stroke, toxin or other identifiable problem.
th: parkinsonism ที่มีสาเหตุชัดเจน เช่น ยา หลอดเลือดสมอง สารพิษ การติดเชื้อ การบาดเจ็บ หรือก้อนในสมอง ต่างจากโรคพาร์กินสันชนิดไม่ทราบสาเหตุ
tempoNote: Weeks to months after a drug or toxin; stepwise with vascular disease
feat: Drug-induced: symmetric bradykinesia and rigidity after dopamine blockers (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, flunarizine)
Vascular: lower-body parkinsonism with shuffling gait, upright posture and arms relatively spared
Toxic: manganese (welders), carbon monoxide, MPTP, methanol with pallidal or putaminal lesions
Post-infectious (Japanese encephalitis), normal pressure hydrocephalus, tumours, repeated head trauma
Poor or absent levodopa response in most
inv: Full drug history including calcium channel blockers and antiemetics
MRI brain: white matter disease, basal ganglia lesions, ventriculomegaly, mass
Dopamine transporter SPECT: normal in drug-induced parkinsonism, abnormal in PD
Selected: blood manganese, carboxyhaemoglobin history, Wilson screen in young patients

case.story: Taking flunarizine for dizziness for one year; now slow, stiff and shuffling, with a mild symmetric tremor.
case.exam: Symmetric bradykinesia and rigidity, mild postural tremor, no rest tremor asymmetry.
case.tests: MRI unremarkable; DAT-SPECT normal.
case.q: What is the next step?
case.a: Drug-induced parkinsonism; stop flunarizine and reassess, as recovery may take weeks to months.

read.where: 8 Overview of Parkinsonism and Approach to Differential Diagnosis
4 - Parkinsonism: Clinical features and differential diagnosis

det.patho: Any process that blocks striatal dopamine receptors, depletes dopamine or damages the nigrostriatal pathway or basal ganglia output can cause parkinsonism. Drugs act at receptors without neuronal loss; vascular disease interrupts frontal-subcortical connections; toxins selectively injure the globus pallidus or substantia nigra.
det.clinical: Drug-induced parkinsonism is the commonest secondary form and often unrecognised in older adults; flunarizine and cinnarizine are frequent culprits in Thailand. Vascular parkinsonism follows small vessel disease with gait apraxia, frontal signs and urinary urgency. Toxic causes have exposure histories. Unmasking of subclinical PD by drugs is common, so persistent symptoms after withdrawal suggest underlying degeneration.
det.diagnosis: Clinical history is key; MRI and DAT-SPECT help when uncertain. A normal DAT scan in suspected drug-induced parkinsonism predicts recovery after withdrawal. Consider NPH when gait dominance, dementia and urinary symptoms coexist.
det.treatment: Remove the cause where possible (stop offending drugs; switch to quetiapine or clozapine if an antipsychotic is essential). Levodopa trial is worthwhile in vascular and other forms, though responses are modest. Shunting for NPH, chelation for manganese in selected cases. Physiotherapy and falls prevention.
det.prognosis: Drug-induced forms usually resolve within months; vascular and toxic forms tend to persist or progress.
pearls: Ask about flunarizine, metoclopramide, antipsychotics and valproate in every new parkinsonism.
Normal DAT-SPECT supports drug-induced rather than degenerative parkinsonism.
Lower-body parkinsonism with white matter disease suggests vascular parkinsonism.
det.thd: Acquired symptomatic parkinsonism คือภาวะเคลื่อนไหวช้า แข็งเกร็ง ที่มีสาเหตุชัดเจน พบบ่อยที่สุดจากยา เช่น flunarizine, metoclopramide และยารักษาโรคจิต รองลงมาคือโรคหลอดเลือดสมองขนาดเล็ก สารพิษ เช่น แมงกานีส คาร์บอนมอนอกไซด์ และ NPH ซักประวัติยา ตรวจ MRI และ DAT-SPECT ในรายที่สงสัย รักษาโดยเอาสาเหตุออก ยา levodopa ได้ผลน้อยกว่าในโรคพาร์กินสัน

name: Action dystonia
formal: Dystonia that appears or worsens during voluntary movement, as in task-specific dystonias such as writer's cramp, and is typically absent at rest.
simple: Abnormal muscle twisting or posturing that happens only when moving or doing a specific action, and not when resting.
th: dystonia ที่เกิดหรือแย่ลงเมื่อเคลื่อนไหวโดยตั้งใจ เช่น writer’s cramp หรือ musician’s dystonia และมักไม่มีขณะพัก เป็นลักษณะของอาการ ไม่ใช่โรคเฉพาะ
tempoNote: Gradual onset; may spread from task-specific to general action dystonia
feat: Abnormal postures or twisting appear only during a specific action or voluntary movement
Task-specific forms: writing, playing an instrument, typing, golf putting (yips), speaking
Mirror dystonia: dystonia in the affected hand when the other hand performs the task
Sensory trick (geste antagoniste) may lessen symptoms
Often the earliest stage of primary dystonia; rest dystonia suggests secondary cause or progression
inv: Clinical diagnosis by observing the task
MRI brain if atypical (rest dystonia, hemidystonia, other neurological signs)
Wilson screen (caeruloplasmin, slit lamp) under age 50; genetic testing in early-onset or generalised cases

case.story: For a year her right hand cramps and her wrist flexes and twists after writing a few lines; typing is fine.
case.exam: Normal at rest; writing provokes wrist flexion, finger curling and slowed script; mirror dystonia present.
case.tests: MRI normal; caeruloplasmin normal.
case.q: What is the treatment of choice?
case.a: Writer's cramp (task-specific action dystonia); botulinum toxin injections guided by EMG are first line, with occupational therapy and writing aids.

read.where: 1 - Clinical overview and phenomenology of movement disorders
2 Approach to History Taking and Examination of the Movement Disorder Patient

det.patho: Action dystonia reflects abnormal sensorimotor integration, reduced surround inhibition and maladaptive plasticity in basal ganglia-cerebellar-cortical circuits. Repetitive highly practised tasks are a risk factor for task-specific forms. In genetic dystonias, action dystonia of a limb is often the first manifestation.
det.clinical: Primary (isolated) dystonias usually begin as action dystonia and may later appear at rest, a sign of progression. Adult-onset focal forms tend to stay focal; childhood-onset leg action dystonia often generalises (e.g. DYT-TOR1A). New dystonia at rest in an adult, hemidystonia, or rapid progression should prompt search for a structural or secondary cause.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical; watch the patient do the triggering task. Distinguish compensatory postures from primary dystonic movements. Investigate atypical cases with MRI, Wilson screen and genetic tests.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin targeted to overactive muscles is the main treatment for focal action dystonia. Oral drugs (trihexyphenidyl, clonazepam, baclofen) help some, particularly younger patients. Retraining therapy, ergonomic aids and switching hands are useful. Pallidal (GPi) DBS is reserved for disabling generalised or segmental dystonia.
det.prognosis: Focal adult forms are usually stable but persistent; spread to adjacent regions occurs in a minority.
pearls: Dystonia that is present only with action is usually primary; rest dystonia raises suspicion of secondary causes.
Mirror dystonia helps identify the muscles to inject.
Young-onset leg action dystonia: test for TOR1A and consider dopa-responsive dystonia with a levodopa trial.
det.thd: Action dystonia คือ dystonia ที่เกิดเฉพาะเมื่อทำกิจกรรมหรือเคลื่อนไหว เช่น เขียนหนังสือแล้วมือเกร็งบิด เล่นดนตรีแล้วนิ้วงอ ขณะพักปกติ มักเป็นจุดเริ่มต้นของ dystonia ปฐมภูมิ วินิจฉัยจากการดูผู้ป่วยทำกิจกรรมนั้น หากมีอาการขณะพักหรือเป็นครึ่งซีกต้องหาสาเหตุทุติยภูมิ การรักษาหลักคือฉีด botulinum toxin ร่วมกับการฝึกและอุปกรณ์ช่วย

name: Action myoclonus
formal: Brief shock-like jerks triggered or aggravated by voluntary movement, typical of cortical myoclonus, posthypoxic Lance-Adams syndrome and progressive myoclonic epilepsies.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks that are set off by trying to move, making it hard to perform everyday tasks.
th: การกระตุกสั้น ๆ เหมือนไฟช็อตที่เกิดหรือแย่ลงเมื่อเคลื่อนไหวโดยตั้งใจ พบใน cortical myoclonus, Lance-Adams syndrome และ progressive myoclonic epilepsy
tempoNote: A clinical sign whose time course depends on the cause: may follow acute hypoxia, or progress over years in progressive myoclonic epilepsies
feat: A sign, not a single disease: jerks appear when the patient moves or tries to hold a posture
Brief, irregular jerks that disrupt reaching, writing, drinking and speech; often absent at rest
Negative myoclonus (sudden lapses of tone) causes falls when standing (bouncy gait)
Stimulus sensitivity to touch, noise or light suggests cortical origin
inv: EEG and EMG with back-averaging: cortical spike preceding jerks, short EMG bursts
Somatosensory evoked potentials: giant cortical responses
Search for cause: renal and hepatic function, drugs, hypoxic history, MRI, genetic tests for progressive myoclonic epilepsy

case.story: Survived a cardiac arrest three months ago with good cognitive recovery; now jerks violently whenever he lifts a cup or tries to walk.
case.exam: Multifocal jerks on reaching and posture, falls from leg jerks and lapses on standing; still at rest.
case.tests: EEG shows spikes time-locked to jerks; MRI normal.
case.q: What is the syndrome, and which medicines help?
case.a: Lance–Adams syndrome (post-hypoxic action myoclonus); levetiracetam, valproate, clonazepam and piracetam are used, often in combination.

read.where: Chapter 18 - Myoclonus: Phenomenology, etiology, physiology, and treatment

det.patho: Action myoclonus is usually cortical: hyperexcitable sensorimotor cortex fires brief bursts when voluntary motor commands are generated. Loss of inhibitory interneurons, as after hypoxia or in neurodegenerative and metabolic disease, increases cortical excitability. Cortical-subcortical loops involving the cerebellum may also contribute.
det.clinical: The jerks are often worse with precise or effortful movements, causing major disability despite normal strength. Causes include post-hypoxic myoclonus, progressive myoclonic epilepsies (Unverricht–Lundborg, Lafora, MERRF, sialidosis, AMRF), metabolic disorders (renal, hepatic), drugs (opioids, gabapentinoids, lithium), and neurodegenerative diseases such as CJD, corticobasal syndrome and Alzheimer disease.
det.diagnosis: Distinguish myoclonus from tremor, tics and chorea clinically. Electrophysiology helps confirm cortical origin. Then identify the cause through history (hypoxia, medications), metabolic tests, imaging and, in young patients with epilepsy, genetic testing.
det.treatment: Remove offending drugs and correct metabolic causes. Effective medicines for cortical myoclonus include levetiracetam, valproate, clonazepam and piracetam, often combined; perampanel and brivaracetam are options. Phenytoin, carbamazepine and other sodium channel blockers can worsen myoclonus in progressive myoclonic epilepsies. Physiotherapy and walking aids reduce falls.
det.prognosis: Variable by cause; post-hypoxic myoclonus may improve over months to years.
pearls: Jerks on movement with a still patient at rest suggest action myoclonus.
Negative myoclonus in the legs causes falls and is often under-recognised.
Avoid sodium channel blockers in progressive myoclonic epilepsies.
det.thd: Action myoclonus คืออาการกระตุกสั้น ๆ เหมือนไฟช็อตเมื่อเคลื่อนไหวหรือพยายามคงท่า มักมาจากเปลือกสมองที่ไวเกิน สาเหตุสำคัญคือภาวะสมองขาดออกซิเจน (Lance-Adams), progressive myoclonic epilepsy, ไตหรือตับวาย และยา ตรวจ EEG/EMG ช่วยยืนยัน รักษาด้วย levetiracetam, valproate, clonazepam หรือ piracetam และหลีกเลี่ยงยากลุ่ม sodium channel blocker

name: Action myoclonus renal failure syndrome
formal: Progressive myoclonic epilepsy with action myoclonus, tremor, ataxia and later renal failure with proteinuria, caused by SCARB2 mutations affecting lysosomal function.
simple: A rare inherited disease causing movement-triggered jerking, tremor and unsteadiness along with kidney failure.
th: progressive myoclonic epilepsy แบบยีนด้อยจาก SCARB2 มี action myoclonus สั่น เดินเซ และต่อมาไตวายจากโปรตีนรั่ว แม้บางรายไม่มีไตวาย
tempoNote: Onset usually in late adolescence or early adulthood (15–25 years), with progressive myoclonus over years; renal disease may precede, accompany or follow neurological features
feat: Disabling action myoclonus and tremor, with generalised tonic-clonic seizures
Progressive cerebellar ataxia and dysarthria
Cognition usually preserved, distinguishing it from many other progressive myoclonic epilepsies
Proteinuria progressing to renal failure (collapsing focal segmental glomerulosclerosis), absent in some
Demyelinating peripheral neuropathy or hearing loss in some patients
inv: Urinalysis for proteinuria and renal function; renal biopsy if indicated
EEG: generalised epileptiform discharges with photosensitivity; SEPs may be giant
SCARB2 gene sequencing; MRI often normal

case.who: 21-year-old male university student from Surat Thani
case.story: For two years has had jerks when writing or eating and has fallen several times; had a generalised seizure six months ago. Grades remain good.
case.exam: Action myoclonus in arms and legs, intention tremor, mild ataxia, normal cognition.
case.tests: Urine protein 3 g/day, creatinine mildly raised; EEG with generalised spike-wave; SCARB2 biallelic variants.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and does kidney transplantation treat the neurological disease?
case.a: Action myoclonus–renal failure syndrome; transplant treats kidney failure but does not stop neurological progression.

read.where: Chapter 18 - Myoclonus: Phenomenology, etiology, physiology, and treatment

det.patho: SCARB2 encodes LIMP-2, a lysosomal membrane protein that transports beta-glucocerebrosidase into lysosomes. Loss leads to lysosomal dysfunction in neurons and kidney podocytes. SCARB2 variants are also linked to Parkinson disease risk, reflecting shared glucocerebrosidase biology.
det.clinical: Most patients present between 15 and 25 with tremor and action myoclonus, followed by seizures and ataxia. Kidney disease (proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome) may appear before or after the neurological onset, or not at all. Cognition is usually spared, while motor disability becomes severe. Some patients have hearing loss or demyelinating neuropathy.
det.diagnosis: Consider it in any progressive myoclonic epilepsy, especially with proteinuria. Check urinalysis and kidney function, and test SCARB2; gene panels for progressive myoclonic epilepsy include it. Kidney biopsy shows collapsing glomerulosclerosis, and inclusions may be seen.
det.treatment: Myoclonus and seizures are treated as in other progressive myoclonic epilepsies: valproate, levetiracetam, clonazepam, piracetam, perampanel or zonisamide, while avoiding phenytoin and carbamazepine. Dose adjustments for kidney function are needed. Dialysis and transplantation manage renal failure but do not change neurological progression. Rehabilitation and fall prevention are important.
det.prognosis: Progressive neurological disability; life expectancy shortened, especially with renal failure.
pearls: Progressive myoclonic epilepsy plus proteinuria: think SCARB2.
Cognitive preservation helps distinguish it from Lafora disease and neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses.
Adjust renally cleared antiseizure drugs such as levetiracetam.
det.thd: AMRF เป็น progressive myoclonic epilepsy จากยีน SCARB2 ซึ่งทำให้ไลโซโซมผิดปกติ ผู้ป่วยวัยรุ่นหรือผู้ใหญ่ตอนต้นมีกระตุกเมื่อเคลื่อนไหว สั่น เดินเซ และชัก แต่ความคิดยังดี ร่วมกับมีโปรตีนรั่วในปัสสาวะจนไตวาย ยืนยันด้วยยีน SCARB2 รักษาด้วยยากันชักที่เหมาะกับ myoclonus และปรับขนาดตามการทำงานของไต การปลูกถ่ายไตไม่หยุดโรคทางสมอง

name: Action myotonia
formal: A non-dystrophic myotonia phenotype where muscle stiffness is provoked by voluntary action, usually from chloride or sodium channel dysfunction, without a prominent warm-up effect or weakness.
simple: Muscles stiffen and are slow to relax when you try to use them, for example when gripping something firmly.
more: EMG shows myotonic discharges; genetic testing of CLCN1 or SCN4A helps. Mexiletine is the usual first-line drug; the course is generally benign.
th: กล้ามเนื้อคลายตัวช้าหลังหดตัวโดยตั้งใจ เช่น กำมือแล้วแบช้า เกิดจากความผิดปกติของ chloride หรือ sodium channel ในกลุ่ม non-dystrophic myotonia หรือใน myotonic dystrophy
tempoNote: Lifelong stiffness from childhood, varying with rest, cold and activity
feat: Stiffness on starting movement after rest; slow release of grip
Warm-up phenomenon in chloride channel myotonia (improves with repetition)
Paradoxical myotonia worsening with repetition and cold in paramyotonia (sodium channel)
Muscle hypertrophy in myotonia congenita; transient weakness in recessive Becker type
Percussion myotonia on tapping thenar eminence or tongue
inv: EMG: myotonic discharges with waxing-waning frequency and amplitude
Short and long exercise tests and cooling studies to separate channel types
Genetic testing: CLCN1, SCN4A; DMPK and CNBP if weakness or systemic features
CK, ECG (essential if myotonic dystrophy possible)

case.story: Since childhood, legs feel stiff when he first stands up and he cannot release a handshake quickly; it eases after a few movements.
case.exam: Well-developed muscles, grip myotonia improving with repetition, percussion myotonia, normal strength.
case.tests: EMG myotonic discharges; CLCN1 heterozygous variant; ECG normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and first-line drug?
case.a: Thomsen myotonia congenita; mexiletine if symptoms limit daily life (check ECG first).

read.where: 36: Myotonic Muscle Disorders and Periodic Paralysis Syndromes

det.patho: Myotonia results from muscle membrane hyperexcitability. Reduced chloride conductance (CLCN1) or impaired sodium channel inactivation (SCN4A) causes repetitive firing after voluntary activation, delaying relaxation. In myotonic dystrophy, abnormal splicing of the chloride channel produces the same effect.
det.clinical: Action myotonia is a sign shared by several disorders. Myotonia congenita (Thomsen dominant, Becker recessive) is the commonest non-dystrophic myotonia. Sodium channel myotonias may be painful or fluctuate with potassium intake. Myotonic dystrophy has myotonia plus multisystem disease, and missing this distinction risks overlooking cardiac danger.
det.diagnosis: Clinical demonstration (grip, eyelid, percussion) and EMG confirm myotonia. Exercise and cooling tests classify the channel type, and genetic testing confirms. Always assess for features of myotonic dystrophy.
det.treatment: Mexiletine is first line for disabling non-dystrophic myotonia, with ECG screening; lamotrigine is an alternative. Avoid depolarising muscle relaxants and be cautious with anaesthesia. Regular gentle warm-up helps chloride channel myotonia.
det.prognosis: Non-dystrophic myotonias are usually benign and do not shorten life.
pearls: Warm-up = chloride channel; worsening with repetition or cold = sodium channel.
Rule out myotonic dystrophy before labelling myotonia as benign.
Suxamethonium can trigger severe masseter spasm in myotonic patients.
det.thd: Action myotonia คือกล้ามเนื้อคลายตัวช้าหลังหดตัว เช่น กำมือแล้วแบช้า พบใน myotonia congenita จากยีน CLCN1 ซึ่งดีขึ้นเมื่อขยับซ้ำ และในโรคของ sodium channel ซึ่งแย่ลงเมื่อเย็นหรือขยับซ้ำ รวมถึง myotonic dystrophy วินิจฉัยด้วย EMG และตรวจยีน ยาหลักคือ mexiletine หลังตรวจ ECG และต้องระวังยาดมสลบบางชนิด

name: Action tremor
formal: Tremor occurring during voluntary muscle activation, including postural, kinetic and intention subtypes, as in essential tremor, cerebellar disease or enhanced physiological tremor.
simple: A shaking that appears when the person holds a position or moves, rather than when the limb is resting.
th: อาการสั่นที่เกิดขณะกล้ามเนื้อทำงาน รวมถึงสั่นขณะยกค้างท่า สั่นขณะเคลื่อนไหว และสั่นเมื่อใกล้เป้าหมาย พบใน essential tremor โรคสมองน้อย และ physiological tremor ที่เพิ่มขึ้น
tempoNote: Usually chronic; acute onset suggests drugs, metabolic cause or a structural lesion
feat: Postural tremor when holding the arms outstretched
Kinetic tremor during writing, pouring or finger-nose testing
Intention tremor that increases near the target (cerebellar outflow)
Task-specific tremor (primary writing tremor) as a separate form
Absent or minimal at rest, distinguishing it from parkinsonian rest tremor
inv: Thyroid function, glucose, drug and caffeine review
Under 50: caeruloplasmin and slit lamp for Wilson disease
MRI if intention tremor, asymmetric or with other neurological signs; accelerometry in selected cases

case.story: Hand shaking for 10 years when drinking soup; better after a small amount of alcohol; his mother had the same.
case.exam: Bilateral postural and kinetic tremor, mild head tremor, no bradykinesia or rigidity.
case.tests: TSH normal; no tremorogenic drugs.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and first-line treatment?
case.a: Essential tremor; propranolol or primidone, with focused ultrasound or DBS for refractory disabling tremor.

det.patho: Action tremors arise from oscillations in the cerebello-thalamo-cortical network. Essential tremor involves cerebellar dysfunction, while intention tremor results from lesions of the cerebellum or its outflow (dentate nucleus, superior cerebellar peduncle). Enhanced physiological tremor reflects increased peripheral drive from adrenergic stimulation.
det.clinical: Essential tremor is the commonest cause, often familial and alcohol responsive. Enhanced physiological tremor occurs with anxiety, thyrotoxicosis, caffeine, beta-agonists, valproate, lithium and withdrawal states. Cerebellar intention tremor accompanies ataxia from MS, stroke or degeneration. Holmes tremor combines rest, postural and intention components after midbrain lesions.
det.diagnosis: Classify by activation condition, distribution and associated signs (2018 consensus). Exclude drug and metabolic causes. MRI is needed when signs suggest a structural lesion. DAT-SPECT helps when parkinsonism is uncertain.
det.treatment: Remove triggers; propranolol or primidone for essential tremor, with topiramate or gabapentin as alternatives. Botulinum toxin for head or voice tremor. MR-guided focused ultrasound thalamotomy or DBS for disabling drug-refractory tremor. Cerebellar intention tremor responds poorly to drugs; weighted utensils help.
det.prognosis: Essential tremor slowly worsens over years but does not shorten life; others depend on the cause.
pearls: Action tremor = postural + kinetic + intention; rest tremor is a separate category.
Always check thyroid function and drugs in new action tremor.
Intention tremor points to the cerebellum or its outflow.
det.thd: Action tremor คืออาการสั่นขณะใช้กล้ามเนื้อ ได้แก่ สั่นตอนยกแขนค้าง สั่นตอนเคลื่อนไหว และสั่นมากขึ้นเมื่อเข้าใกล้เป้าหมาย สาเหตุพบบ่อยคือ essential tremor ส่วน physiological tremor เพิ่มจากกาแฟ ไทรอยด์เป็นพิษ หรือยา และ intention tremor จากรอยโรคในสมองน้อย ตรวจไทรอยด์และทบทวนยา รักษา essential tremor ด้วย propranolol หรือ primidone

Variable frequency, entrainment and distractibility

name: Acute akathisia
formal: Subjective inner restlessness with an urge to move and objective pacing or shifting, appearing hours to days after starting a dopamine blocker such as an antipsychotic or antiemetic.
simple: A distressing feeling that you cannot sit still, usually brought on by a medicine, making a person pace or fidget.
more: Diagnosis is clinical. Reduce or change the drug, and treat with propranolol, benzodiazepines, mirtazapine or anticholinergics; it usually resolves when the cause is removed.
th: Acute akathisia คือภาวะกระวนกระวายภายในและต้องขยับตัวตลอดเวลาที่เกิดภายในไม่กี่ชั่วโมงถึงไม่กี่วันหลังเริ่มหรือเพิ่มยาต้านโดพามีน เช่น haloperidol, aripiprazole, metoclopramide ในห้องฉุกเฉินมักถูกเข้าใจผิดว่าเป็นอาการวิตกกังวล การรักษาคือลดหรือหยุดยาที่เป็นสาเหตุ ให้ propranolol หรือ benzodiazepine และห้ามเพิ่มยาต้านโรคจิตเพิ่มเติม
tempoNote: Begins within hours to days of a new dopamine-blocking drug or a dose rise and usually settles within days to weeks once the drug is reduced
feat: Inner restlessness and an urge to move appearing soon after a dopamine blocker, often within the first days of treatment or after an injection
Objective pacing, rocking, marching in place and crossing the legs; patients cannot sit through a meal or a consultation
A frequent consequence of antiemetics given in emergency or surgical care, such as metoclopramide or prochlorperazine, and of oral or depot antipsychotics
Can lead to refusal of medicines, aggression, falls and suicidal thoughts, so early recognition is a safety issue
Treatment is dose reduction, change of drug and propranolol or a benzodiazepine; additional antipsychotic makes the problem worse
inv: Clinical recognition with a drug timeline; Barnes Akathisia Rating Scale
Exclude agitation from delirium, withdrawal, mania, anxiety and hyperthyroidism with a brief history and examination
Look for coexisting acute dystonia or parkinsonism, and for NMS if fever or rigidity develops

case.who: 34-year-old woman from Ayutthaya in the emergency room
case.story: She was given intravenous metoclopramide for vomiting; within an hour she is pacing the corridor, wringing her hands and begging to leave.
case.exam: Cannot remain seated, shifts weight constantly, describes a terrible inner restlessness; tone normal, no fever.
case.tests: Observations stable; glucose and electrolytes normal.
case.q: How would you treat and what advice would you give?
case.a: Acute akathisia from metoclopramide. Stop the drug, reassure her, give a small dose of propranolol or a short-acting benzodiazepine, and record metoclopramide as a drug to avoid.

det.patho: Acute akathisia is linked to dopamine receptor blockade, with serotonergic and noradrenergic modulation. Rapid titration, high-potency drugs, parenteral doses and previous episodes raise risk. Newer partial agonists such as aripiprazole can cause it too, particularly early in treatment.
det.clinical: The patient is aware, can describe the sensation and is distressed by it, which separates the disorder from agitation with disorganised thinking. Common signs are marching on the spot, sitting and standing repeatedly and crossing the legs. In emergency and surgical wards the culprit is frequently an antiemetic. If missed, the patient may be sedated, restrained or given more of the offending drug, which prolongs the problem.
det.diagnosis: Diagnose from the sequence of drug exposure and the combination of subjective urge and motor restlessness. Document the Barnes score. Rule out delirium, withdrawal states, mania, anxiety and thyroid disease, and consider NMS if fever, rigidity and autonomic change develop. Remember that akathisia may accompany acute dystonia or parkinsonism.
det.treatment: Withdraw or reduce the drug, or switch to one with a lower risk. First-line symptomatic therapy is propranolol 10–20 mg two or three times daily or a benzodiazepine, and low-dose mirtazapine is an alternative. Anticholinergics are less effective when akathisia stands alone. Do not give more of the same drug class. Review medicines before discharge and warn the patient about future exposure.
det.prognosis: Most patients improve within days to weeks of drug reduction. A minority progress to persistent or tardive akathisia.
pearls: Antiemetics are a common hidden cause in the emergency room.
The subjective urge is as important as the movement.
More dopamine blocker equals more akathisia.
det.thd: Acute akathisia คือภาวะที่ผู้ป่วยกระวนกระวายภายในและต้องขยับตัวหลังได้ยาต้านโดพามีน เช่น metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, haloperidol หรือ aripiprazole มักเกิดภายในไม่กี่ชั่วโมงถึงไม่กี่วัน ผู้ป่วยรู้ตัวดีแต่นั่งนิ่งไม่ได้ ต้องแยกจากความวิตกกังวลและ delirium รักษาโดยหยุดหรือลดยา ให้ propranolol หรือ benzodiazepine และหลีกเลี่ยงยาต้านโดพามีนซ้ำ

name: Acute cerebellar ataxia of childhood
formal: Self-limited post-infectious cerebellar syndrome in young children with abrupt gait ataxia, with or without nystagmus or tremor, usually recovering over weeks to months.
simple: A sudden unsteadiness in young children, usually after a viral illness, that normally gets better by itself over weeks.
th: เดินเซเฉียบพลันในเด็กเล็กหลังติดเชื้อไวรัส เช่น อีสุกอีใส ส่วนใหญ่หายเองภายในสัปดาห์ถึงเดือน เป็นการวินิจฉัยหลังแยกโรคอันตรายแล้ว
tempoNote: Abrupt onset over hours, peaks within days, recovers over weeks
feat: Child aged 2–5 years with sudden unsteady gait or refusal to walk
Onset days to weeks following vaccination or a viral infection, classically varicella
Truncal ataxia more than limb ataxia; nystagmus and dysarthria possible
Alert, no fever at onset, no headache, normal mental state
Gradual full recovery in most within weeks

case.exam: Alert, broad-based staggering gait, mild nystagmus, normal tone and reflexes, healing varicella crusts.
case.tests: Toxicology negative; MRI brain normal.
case.q: What course is expected?
case.a: Post-infectious acute cerebellar ataxia; supportive care, with most children recovering fully over weeks.

det.patho: The cerebellum is targeted by a post-infectious immune response or, less often, direct viral invasion. Varicella, EBV, enteroviruses, influenza and mycoplasma are common triggers. Antibodies to cerebellar antigens have been found in some children, supporting an autoimmune mechanism.
det.clinical: It is the commonest cause of acute ataxia in young children. Onset is abrupt with gait instability that can be severe; arms are less affected. Behaviour is normal apart from irritability. Recovery begins within days and is usually complete within weeks to a few months. Persistent or recurrent symptoms suggest another diagnosis. Acute cerebellitis with swelling is a more severe variant.
det.diagnosis: A diagnosis of exclusion. Toxins (anticonvulsants, benzodiazepines, alcohol, antihistamines) are the most important alternative. Imaging is needed if there is headache, vomiting, altered consciousness, focal signs, or no improvement. Look for opsoclonus, which changes the diagnosis to OMS and requires tumour screening.
det.treatment: Supportive care and safety measures; most need no specific treatment. Steroids or IVIG are sometimes used in severe or prolonged cases or acute cerebellitis, but evidence is limited. Physiotherapy if recovery is slow.
det.prognosis: Excellent in most; a minority have persistent mild coordination or behavioural problems.
pearls: Toddler + sudden ataxia + recent varicella + normal consciousness: acute cerebellar ataxia.
Always exclude drug ingestion first.
Look carefully at the eyes; opsoclonus means OMS and a neuroblastoma search.

name: Acute cervical cord disorders
formal: Acute myelopathies of the cervical spinal cord from trauma, compression, infarction, inflammation or infection producing quadriparesis, sensory level and sphincter dysfunction.
simple: Sudden damage to the spinal cord in the neck causing weakness or paralysis of the arms and legs, numbness and bladder problems.
th: กลุ่มโรคไขสันหลังส่วนคอที่เกิดเฉียบพลัน จากการบาดเจ็บ การกดทับ การขาดเลือด การอักเสบ หรือการติดเชื้อ ทำให้แขนขาอ่อนแรง มีระดับชาและปัสสาวะผิดปกติ
tempoNote: Minutes (trauma, infarction) to days (inflammation, abscess)
feat: Weakness of all four limbs or arms more than legs, with a sensory level at or below the neck
Bladder retention and bowel dysfunction; possible respiratory compromise if C3–C5 involved
Early flaccidity and areflexia in spinal shock, later spasticity and hyperreflexia
Neck pain suggests trauma, disc, abscess or dissection; fever suggests infection
Autonomic instability: hypotension, bradycardia with high lesions
inv: Urgent MRI whole spine with contrast

Vital capacity monitoring

case.exam: Arms MRC 2, legs MRC 4, burning hands, preserved sacral sensation; urinary retention.
case.tests: CT: no fracture, multilevel spondylosis; MRI: C4–C5 cord T2 signal with canal stenosis.

det.patho: Acute cervical cord injury arises from mechanical trauma, rapid compression (disc, haematoma, abscess, metastasis), ischaemia (anterior spinal artery, vertebral dissection), inflammation (MS, NMOSD, MOGAD, myelitis) or infection. Secondary injury from oedema, ischaemia and inflammation extends damage over hours. High lesions affect phrenic outflow and sympathetic control.
det.clinical: Patterns include complete transection, central cord (arms worse, often in elderly with spondylosis), anterior cord, Brown-Séquard and posterior cord syndromes. Spinal shock can mask upper motor neuron signs. Respiratory failure and autonomic dysreflexia are key complications.
det.diagnosis: Any acute quadriparesis with a sensory level or sphincter involvement needs emergency MRI. Compressive lesions need surgery; non-compressive cases require CSF and antibody testing. Exclude GBS and bilateral brain lesions clinically.
det.treatment: Stabilise the spine and airway; maintain mean arterial pressure (commonly 85–90 mmHg) for several days after trauma. Urgent decompression for compressive causes; high-dose steroids and plasma exchange for inflammatory myelitis; antibiotics and drainage for abscess. Early rehabilitation, bladder and pressure care.
det.prognosis: Depends on completeness and cause; incomplete injuries and inflammatory causes recover better than complete traumatic lesions.
pearls: Arms weaker than legs after a fall in an elderly person: central cord syndrome.
Check vital capacity in any high cervical lesion.
Do not wait for neurological deterioration before imaging.
det.thd: Acute cervical cord disorders คือโรคไขสันหลังส่วนคอที่เกิดเฉียบพลันจากหลายสาเหตุ เช่น อุบัติเหตุ หมอนรองกระดูกกดทับ ฝี ไขสันหลังขาดเลือด หรือการอักเสบ ผู้ป่วยมีแขนขาอ่อนแรง ระดับชา ปัสสาวะไม่ออก และอาจหายใจลำบาก ต้องทำ MRI ด่วน การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ เช่น ผ่าตัดลดการกดทับ ให้ steroid หรือยาปฏิชีวนะ

name: Acute chorea
formal: Abrupt onset of irregular, flowing involuntary movements due to causes such as Sydenham chorea, stroke affecting basal ganglia, drugs, metabolic disease, lupus or hyperthyroidism.
simple: Sudden onset of irregular dance-like jerky movements that the person cannot control.
th: การเคลื่อนไหวกระตุกไม่สม่ำเสมอไหลต่อเนื่องที่เกิดขึ้นทันที จากสาเหตุเช่น stroke ที่ basal ganglia น้ำตาลสูง ยา SLE หรือ Sydenham chorea
tempoNote: Develops over hours to weeks rather than years
feat: Brief, random, flowing movements that flit between body parts; motor impersistence
Unilateral (hemichorea) suggests a contralateral structural or hyperglycaemic striatal lesion
Generalised chorea suggests metabolic, drug, autoimmune or infectious causes
In Thailand, non-ketotic hyperglycaemic hemichorea in older diabetic women is a frequent cause
Children: Sydenham chorea after streptococcal infection

CT/MRI brain: striatal T1 hyperintensity in hyperglycaemia, infarct or haemorrhage
ANA, antiphospholipid antibodies, ASO/anti-DNase B; pregnancy test; drug review
Autoimmune encephalitis antibodies if subacute with cognitive change

case.who: 72-year-old female rice farmer from Roi Et
case.story: Poorly controlled diabetes; three days of continuous flinging movements of the left arm and leg.
case.exam: Left hemichorea-hemiballism, no weakness, orientated.
case.tests: Glucose 520 mg/dL, no ketones, HbA1c 14%; CT: right putaminal hyperdensity without mass effect; MRI T1 hyperintensity.
case.q: What is the cause and treatment?
case.a: Non-ketotic hyperglycaemic hemichorea; correct glucose, and use haloperidol or tetrabenazine if movements persist.

read.where: Chapter 28 Disorders of Consciousness and Intensive Care Neurology — Movement Disorder Emergencies

det.patho: Chorea reflects reduced output of the indirect basal ganglia pathway, often from striatal or subthalamic dysfunction, causing disinhibition of thalamocortical motor drive. Acute causes include vascular lesions, hyperglycaemic striatal changes, drugs that increase dopaminergic tone (levodopa, stimulants, oral contraceptives), hyperthyroidism, autoimmune antibodies and infections.
det.clinical: Onset over hours to weeks distinguishes acute from hereditary chorea. Hemichorea points to a contralateral lesion; generalised forms suggest systemic causes. Associated features (fever, carditis, rash, cognitive change, pregnancy, psychiatric symptoms) direct testing.
det.diagnosis: Start with glucose, electrolytes, thyroid function and a drug history, then image the brain. Consider lupus, antiphospholipid syndrome, polycythaemia, HIV and autoimmune encephalitis (e.g. anti-CASPR2, anti-IgLON5) according to context. In children, look for streptococcal evidence and carditis.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: correct glucose or thyroid state, stop offending drugs, anticoagulate antiphospholipid syndrome. Symptomatic options include tetrabenazine or other VMAT2 inhibitors, or low-dose antipsychotics. Sydenham chorea may need antibiotic prophylaxis and sometimes steroids or IVIG.
det.prognosis: Often improves over weeks to months once the cause is treated; vascular hemichorea typically regresses.
pearls: Hemichorea plus very high glucose: think striatal hyperglycaemia before stroke.
Check pregnancy and contraceptive use in young women with chorea.
Sydenham chorea warrants an echocardiogram.
det.thd: Acute chorea คือการเคลื่อนไหวแบบกระตุกไหลไม่เป็นจังหวะที่เกิดขึ้นเร็ว ถ้าเป็นข้างเดียวมักเกิดจากรอยโรคที่ basal ganglia ฝั่งตรงข้าม เช่น stroke หรือภาวะน้ำตาลสูงที่พบบ่อยในผู้สูงอายุไทย ถ้าเป็นทั้งตัวให้นึกถึงยา ไทรอยด์ SLE หรือ Sydenham chorea การตรวจเริ่มจากน้ำตาล เกลือแร่ ไทรอยด์ และภาพสมอง การรักษาคือแก้สาเหตุร่วมกับยา VMAT2 inhibitor หรือ antipsychotic

name: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM)
formal: Monophasic immune-mediated inflammatory demyelination of brain and spinal cord, often post-infectious in children, with encephalopathy, multifocal deficits and widespread MRI white matter lesions.
simple: An immune reaction, usually after an infection, causing brain and spinal cord swelling with confusion, weakness and vision or balance problems.
th: สมองและไขสันหลังอักเสบแบบกระจายเฉียบพลัน มักตามหลังการติดเชื้อในเด็ก มีซึมหรือสับสนร่วมกับอาการทางประสาทหลายตำแหน่ง
tempoNote: Polyfocal deficits and encephalopathy evolve over days, peaking within about 3 months; usually monophasic
feat: Encephalopathy (drowsiness, irritability or altered behaviour) not explained by fever
Multifocal deficits: weakness, ataxia, cranial nerve palsies, optic neuritis, myelitis
Commonly 1–3 weeks after a viral illness or, rarely, vaccination
Mostly children under 10; fever, headache, vomiting and meningism may occur
Seizures in a minority; can deteriorate rapidly to need ventilation
inv: MRI: large, bilateral, poorly marginated T2/FLAIR lesions in white matter, deep grey matter (thalami, basal ganglia), brainstem and cord, mostly of similar age
CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis and raised protein; oligoclonal bands usually absent
MOG IgG and AQP4 IgG in serum; infectious screen (PCR, cultures) to exclude encephalitis
Repeat MRI at 3 months and later to confirm monophasic course

case.story: Ten days after a febrile rash illness she becomes sleepy and irritable, then cannot walk steadily and her speech is slurred.
case.exam: GCS 12, bilateral extensor plantars, truncal ataxia, left sixth nerve palsy, mild neck stiffness.
case.tests: MRI: multiple fluffy FLAIR lesions in both hemispheres, both thalami and the pons. CSF: 40 lymphocytes, protein 80 mg/dL, OCB negative, viral PCR negative. MOG IgG positive.
case.q: What diagnosis best fits, and what does the MOG result add?
case.a: ADEM; MOG positivity places it within the MOGAD spectrum and identifies a risk of further demyelinating events, so follow-up imaging and clinical review are needed.

det.patho: ADEM is an immune-mediated, typically monophasic inflammatory demyelination of the CNS, thought to follow molecular mimicry or bystander activation after infection. Perivenous demyelination with lymphocyte and macrophage cuffs is the pathological hallmark, distinguishing it from confluent MS plaques. A large share of paediatric cases carry MOG antibodies.
det.clinical: Onset usually follows a prodrome of fever, malaise and headache, then encephalopathy with multifocal neurological signs develops over days. Brainstem involvement can compromise breathing, and concurrent myelitis causes paraparesis and bladder retention. Adults can be affected, often with more severe illness. A new event after 3 months suggests multiphasic ADEM, MOGAD, NMOSD or MS.
det.diagnosis: Paediatric consensus criteria require a first polyfocal CNS event of presumed inflammatory cause, encephalopathy, compatible MRI and no new features after 3 months. Infective encephalitis must be excluded before steroids where possible, but acyclovir can be started in parallel. Check MOG and AQP4 antibodies, and consider mitochondrial, metabolic, vasculitic and neoplastic mimics such as CNS lymphoma or HLH.
det.treatment: First line is IV methylprednisolone for 3–5 days followed by an oral taper over several weeks. IVIG or plasma exchange is used for steroid-refractory or severe disease. Supportive care includes airway protection, seizure control and treatment of raised intracranial pressure; decompressive surgery is rarely needed in fulminant forms.
det.prognosis: Most children recover fully or nearly so, though subtle cognitive or behavioural sequelae occur; adults and haemorrhagic variants fare worse.
pearls: Encephalopathy is required for ADEM; multifocal lesions without it suggest MS or MOGAD.
Deep grey matter involvement favours ADEM over MS.
Check MOG IgG in every case because it predicts relapse risk.
det.thd: ADEM เป็นการอักเสบและทำลายปลอกประสาทแบบกระจายในสมองและไขสันหลัง มักเกิดหลังติดเชื้อไวรัสในเด็ก ผู้ป่วยซึม สับสน ร่วมกับอาการทางระบบประสาทหลายตำแหน่ง MRI พบรอยโรคใหญ่ขอบไม่ชัดทั้งเนื้อขาวและ thalamus ต้องแยกการติดเชื้อสมองและตรวจ MOG IgG รักษาด้วย IV methylprednisolone ตามด้วยการลด steroid ช้า ๆ ถ้าไม่ดีขึ้นให้ IVIG หรือ PLEX ส่วนใหญ่หายดี

qx.stem: A 7-year-old boy from Chachoengsao has a cough and fever, and twelve days later becomes drowsy and irritable with ataxia and weakness of all four limbs. MRI shows large, fluffy, poorly marginated T2 lesions in both cerebral hemispheres, both thalami and the middle cerebellar peduncles, and a long cervical cord lesion. CSF has 40 lymphocytes/µL; viral PCR panel and cultures are negative. He improves on IV methylprednisolone.
qx.q: Which test result most influences his long-term relapse risk and follow-up plan?
opts: CSF oligoclonal bands
Serum anti-nuclear antibody titre
EEG showing diffuse slowing
Repeat MRI at 1 week
Serum MOG-IgG by cell-based assay
qx.why: Monophasic ADEM after an infection is common in children, and around half of paediatric ADEM is MOG-IgG positive. MOG-IgG positivity, especially if it stays positive at follow-up, predicts relapsing MOGAD (e.g. ADEM followed by optic neuritis) and guides whether long-term immunotherapy and monitoring are needed. Bands are usually absent in ADEM and would raise MS concern, but they matter less than MOG serostatus here; EEG and early repeat MRI do not predict relapse.

name: Acute dystonia
formal: Sudden sustained muscle spasms of face, neck or trunk (oculogyric crisis, torticollis) shortly after starting dopamine-blocking drugs, responding to anticholinergics.
simple: Sudden painful muscle spasms of the face, neck or eyes that can happen soon after taking certain medicines such as anti-sickness or antipsychotic drugs.
more: Treat with IV or IM benztropine or diphenhydramine, usually relieving symptoms within minutes. More common in young men on high-potency antipsychotics or metoclopramide; consider laryngeal dystonia as an emergency, and switch or reduce the offending drug.
th: Acute dystonia (acute dystonic reaction) คือท่าบิดเกร็งของคอ ขากรรไกร ลิ้น หรือตา (oculogyric crisis) เกิดภายในไม่กี่ชั่วโมงถึงไม่กี่วันหลังได้ยาต้านโดพามีน เช่น haloperidol, metoclopramide หรือ prochlorperazine ผู้ป่วยรู้ตัวและเจ็บ อาจมี laryngeal dystonia ทำให้หายใจลำบาก รักษาเร็วด้วย anticholinergic หรือ diphenhydramine ทางหลอดเลือดดำหรือกล้ามเนื้อ อาการมักหายภายในไม่กี่นาที
tempoNote: Occurs within a couple of days of starting or raising a dopamine blocker; episodes last minutes to hours and respond within minutes to an anticholinergic
feat: Sudden twisting of the neck (torticollis, retrocollis), jaw (trismus or opening), tongue, trunk (opisthotonus) or eyes after a dopamine-blocking drug
Oculogyric crisis: the eyes are held upward, often with neck extension, fear, anguish and intrusive thoughts; the patient stays alert
Highest risk in young men and children, with high-potency antipsychotics, antiemetics and accidental ingestions; incidence in chronic neuroleptic treatment up to about 10% for oculogyric crises
Laryngeal or pharyngeal dystonia causes stridor, dysphagia and respiratory distress, which is the dangerous form
Other causes include withdrawal of dopamine agonists, levodopa in some parkinsonian patients, tetrabenazine, lithium, carbamazepine, gabapentin and brain lesions
inv: Drug history including antiemetics, antihistamine-type vertigo drugs and herbal products
Airway assessment and pulse oximetry if the voice changes or stridor appears; endoscopy for suspected laryngeal dystonia
Calcium, magnesium and glucose if the story is atypical; EEG or imaging only if consciousness is altered

case.who: 22-year-old man from Chon Buri taking haloperidol after an injection in the emergency room
case.story: Six hours later his eyes roll up, his neck arches back, his jaw is clamped and his tongue feels thick; he is frightened and in pain.
case.exam: Alert, bilateral upward gaze deviation, retrocollis and trismus; oxygen saturation 98%; no fever, tone otherwise normal.
case.tests: Capillary glucose and electrolytes normal.
case.q: What is the immediate treatment and what should follow?
case.a: Acute dystonic reaction with oculogyric crisis. Give diphenhydramine 25–50 mg or an anticholinergic such as benztropine or biperiden intravenously or intramuscularly; relief within minutes confirms the diagnosis. Continue an oral anticholinergic for 3 to 5 days and review the antipsychotic.

det.patho: Acute dystonia follows blockade of striatal dopamine D2 receptors, with a relative excess of cholinergic activity and altered nigral output, producing sustained contractions. Risk rises with potent blockers, rapid titration, parenteral administration and previous episodes. Oculogyric crises were first described in encephalitis lethargica and may also occur in postencephalitic parkinsonism and in some patients with Wilson's disease or dopa-responsive dystonia.
det.clinical: Dystonic reactions are frightening and painful, and the patient is awake and able to complain. The eyes may lock upward and sideways, and Sacks recorded associated terror, rage, thought compulsions and autonomic overactivity. Tongue protrusion, trismus and neck twisting are common. Respiratory dystonia, with grunting or stridor, is uncommon but dangerous. Accidental ingestion in children causes oculogyric crisis in a large proportion.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis rests on the time relation to the drug and the typical postures, and it is confirmed by prompt relief after an anticholinergic. Review all drugs, including antiemetics bought without prescription. Consider tetanus, seizures, hypocalcaemia, meningitis, functional dystonia and NMS when the story is atypical, and examine the airway whenever the voice changes.
det.treatment: Administer an anticholinergic or antihistamine intravenously or intramuscularly: diphenhydramine 25–50 mg, benztropine 1–2 mg or biperiden are standard; relief comes within minutes. Benzodiazepines are alternatives if anticholinergics are contraindicated. Ensure airway safety in laryngeal dystonia and call for expert airway help. After relief, give an oral anticholinergic for 3 to 5 days, reduce or change the antipsychotic, and counsel the patient. Oral clonazepam can help patients with recurrent oculogyric crises.
det.prognosis: Prompt treatment ends the episode; recurrences occur if the drug and dose are unchanged. Rare tardive dystonia may follow long exposure.
pearls: An awake patient with sudden twisting after a new drug: give an anticholinergic.
Always ask about metoclopramide and other antiemetics.
Stridor and drooling suggest laryngeal dystonia; check the airway.
det.thd: Acute dystonia เกิดภายในไม่กี่ชั่วโมงถึงไม่กี่วันหลังได้ยาต้านโดพามีน เช่น haloperidol, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine ผู้ป่วยรู้สึกตัวแต่ตาเหลือกขึ้นบน (oculogyric crisis) คอบิด ขากรรไกรแน่น ลิ้นแข็ง และเจ็บมาก บางรายมี laryngeal dystonia หายใจลำบาก ให้ diphenhydramine 25–50 มก. หรือ benztropine/biperiden ทางหลอดเลือดดำหรือกล้ามเนื้อ อาการมักดีขึ้นใน 1–5 นาที จากนั้นให้ anticholinergic ทางปาก 3–5 วัน และทบทวนยา

qx.stem: A 19-year-old woman is seen in the emergency room with vomiting and given intravenous metoclopramide. Forty minutes later her eyes roll upward and cannot be brought back to the primary position, her neck is arched backwards and she cries that her tongue feels thick. She is awake and frightened, temperature is 36.8 °C, tone elsewhere is normal and oxygen saturation is 99%.
qx.q: What is the best next step?
opts: Intravenous haloperidol to relax the spasm
Urgent CT head and lumbar puncture before any treatment
Intravenous diphenhydramine or an anticholinergic such as benztropine
Observation only, because the reaction is harmless
Oral clonazepam and discharge in two hours without further medication
qx.why: Oculogyric crisis with retrocollis soon after a dopamine blocker in an awake patient is an acute dystonic reaction. A parenteral anticholinergic or diphenhydramine usually terminates it within minutes, followed by a few days of oral cover and avoidance of the offending antiemetic. Haloperidol would worsen it, imaging is not needed without atypical features, and the reaction is painful and can involve the larynx, so it should be treated rather than watched.

name: Acute flaccid paralysis
formal: Syndrome of rapid-onset limb weakness with hypotonia and areflexia, caused by poliovirus, enteroviruses, Guillain-Barre syndrome, myelitis or other anterior horn cell, nerve or muscle disease.
simple: Sudden floppy weakness of one or more limbs, often in children, with a range of possible causes including viral infections.
th: กลุ่มอาการแขนขาอ่อนแรงแบบปวกเปียกเฉียบพลัน reflex ลดลง เกิดจากโรคของ anterior horn เส้นประสาท รอยต่อประสาทกล้ามเนื้อ หรือกล้ามเนื้อ เป็นตัวชี้วัดการเฝ้าระวังโปลิโอในเด็ก
tempoNote: Maximum weakness within hours to 4 days in poliovirus and acute flaccid myelitis, up to 4 weeks in GBS
feat: Rapidly progressive limb weakness with low tone and reduced or absent reflexes, reaching peak in under 4 weeks
Asymmetric weakness after a febrile illness, with preserved sensation, suggests anterior horn cell disease: poliovirus, enterovirus D68 or A71, West Nile and other flaviviruses
Symmetric ascending weakness with distal paraesthesia or back pain and areflexia suggests Guillain–Barré syndrome
Other causes: transverse myelitis (early spinal shock), botulism, periodic paralysis, tick paralysis, myasthenic crisis, toxins, critical illness neuromuscular weakness
Respiratory, bulbar and autonomic failure are the immediate dangers; any child under 15 with AFP must be notified for polio surveillance
inv: Two stool specimens 24–48 hours apart within 14 days of onset (WHO polio surveillance); nasopharyngeal swab for enteroviruses
MRI spine (longitudinal grey-matter T2 lesions in acute flaccid myelitis), CSF cells, protein, and viral PCR
NCS/EMG after 3–7 days: demyelinating or axonal neuropathy, anterior horn pattern, junction decrement, or myopathy
Potassium, CK, glucose, and serial forced vital capacity with bulbar and autonomic monitoring

case.story: He had fever and diarrhoea for two days. On day 4 he began to refuse to walk, complained of leg pain and the left leg became limp. There were no sensory complaints. Immunisation record is incomplete.
case.exam: Febrile, alert, left leg flaccid with absent reflexes, right leg mildly weak, intact sensation, no bladder involvement, normal breathing.
case.tests: CSF 40 cells/mm3 (lymphocytes), protein mildly raised; MRI spine shows grey matter lesion at the lumbar cord; stool poliovirus screen sent in two samples.
case.q: What is the syndrome, what must be done within 24 hours, and what is the differential?
case.a: Acute flaccid paralysis with anterior horn pattern. Notify the surveillance system, collect two stool samples, monitor breathing and bulbar function, and consider polio, enterovirus acute flaccid myelitis, and GBS.

read.where: Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — Viral Infections of the Nervous System

det.patho: Acute flaccid paralysis is a syndromic label for lower motor neuron-type weakness of rapid onset. Poliovirus and other neurotropic enteroviruses destroy anterior horn cells; Guillain–Barré syndrome is immune attack on nerve roots and peripheral nerves; transverse myelitis causes initial spinal shock; botulism blocks release of acetylcholine; periodic paralysis and myositis affect the muscle membrane; and toxins affect various levels. Precise localisation guides the cause.
det.clinical: Start by asking about fever, preceding infection, pain, vaccination and exposure, then check symmetry, sensory loss, reflexes, bladder, cranial nerves and breathing. A febrile prodrome followed by painful, asymmetric flaccid weakness without sensory loss indicates poliovirus or enterovirus myelitis. Symmetric ascending weakness with areflexia and sensory symptoms indicates GBS. Descending bulbar weakness with dilated pupils suggests botulism. Normal sensation with recurrent weakness and low potassium indicates periodic paralysis.
det.diagnosis: Use CSF (pleocytosis versus albuminocytologic dissociation), MRI spine and brain, NCS/EMG, and laboratory tests (potassium, CK, glucose) to localise the lesion. In children under 15 with AFP, stool collection within 14 days is mandatory for poliovirus detection and typing. Enterovirus D68 or A71 PCR from respiratory secretions, CSF and stool, and a toxin or botulism screen are added by context. West Nile and Japanese encephalitis virus are also recognised causes in endemic areas.
det.treatment: Immediately secure airway, breathing and swallowing: monitor FVC, admit to intensive care if falling, and watch autonomic stability. Specific therapy follows the cause: immunoglobulin (total 2 g/kg, split across several days) or plasma exchange for GBS, antitoxin for botulism, potassium for hypokalaemic paralysis, and supportive care with rehabilitation for polio and acute flaccid myelitis. No specific antiviral has proven effective for enterovirus myelitis. Maintain high routine polio immunisation coverage.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause: most GBS patients recover, whereas polio and acute flaccid myelitis often leave permanent asymmetric weakness; periodic paralysis resolves fully.
pearls: Asymmetric flaccid paralysis with fever and normal sensation is anterior horn disease until proven otherwise.
Collect two stool samples within 14 days for every AFP case in a child.
Monitor forced vital capacity and bulbar function, because breathing fails before limbs worsen.
det.thd: Acute flaccid paralysis คือกลุ่มอาการอ่อนแรงปวกเปียกเฉียบพลัน reflex ลดลง สาเหตุเกิดได้ตั้งแต่เซลล์ anterior horn (โปลิโอ enterovirus) เส้นประสาท (GBS) รอยต่อประสาทกล้ามเนื้อ (botulism) จนถึงกล้ามเนื้อ (periodic paralysis) ถ้าไข้นำมาแล้วอ่อนแรงไม่สมมาตรโดยไม่มีอาการชา ให้นึกถึงโรคของ anterior horn ต้องแจ้งระบบเฝ้าระวังโปลิโอ เก็บอุจจาระ 2 ครั้งห่างกัน 24–48 ชั่วโมงภายใน 14 วัน ตรวจ CSF MRI และ NCS/EMG เฝ้าระวังการหายใจและการกลืน การรักษาตามสาเหตุ เช่น IVIG หรือ plasma exchange ใน GBS

name: Acute haemorrhagic leukoencephalitis (AHL)
formal: Hyperacute fulminant, usually post-infectious, haemorrhagic demyelinating encephalitis (Hurst disease) with fever, rapid coma and cerebral oedema; considered a severe variant of ADEM.
simple: A rare, very severe brain inflammation with bleeding and swelling that comes on quickly, usually after an infection.
more: Acute haemorrhagic leukoencephalitis, a fulminant post-infectious demyelinating disease with perivascular haemorrhage and necrosis, causing rapid fever, coma and seizures; a hyperacute ADEM variant.
th: สมองอักเสบชนิดทำลายปลอกประสาทแบบมีเลือดออกที่รุนแรงและเร็วมาก มักตามหลังการติดเชื้อ ถือเป็น ADEM ชนิดรุนแรงที่สุด
tempoNote: Hyperacute: from first symptoms to coma within hours to a few days
feat: Fever, headache and rapidly falling consciousness days after a viral or respiratory infection
Seizures, focal deficits and signs of raised intracranial pressure
Large white matter lesions with oedema, petechial haemorrhage and mass effect on MRI
CSF may show neutrophils, raised protein and red cells
Mortality has historically been very high, though aggressive treatment has improved outcomes
inv: MRI with susceptibility-weighted imaging to show microhaemorrhages
CSF analysis and PCR to exclude HSV and other infections
AQP4 and MOG antibodies; consider brain biopsy if the diagnosis is uncertain

case.who: 24-year-old male nursing student from Chon Buri
case.story: One week after influenza-like illness developed headache, confusion and left-sided weakness, becoming unrousable within 36 hours.
case.exam: GCS 7, left hemiplegia, bilateral extensor plantars, papilloedema.
case.tests: MRI: large confluent right hemispheric white matter lesions with oedema, SWI petechial haemorrhages, midline shift; CSF: 180 cells (70% neutrophils), protein 1.4 g/L, PCR negative.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what treatment should start at once?
case.a: Acute haemorrhagic leukoencephalitis; high-dose methylprednisolone with plasma exchange and/or IVIG, ICP control and possible decompressive craniectomy.

read.where: Chapter 19 Multiple Sclerosis and Demyelinating Diseases — Acute Haemorrhagic Leukoencephalitis

det.patho: AHL is regarded as the hyperacute end of the ADEM spectrum. An immune response triggered by infection causes fibrinoid necrosis of small vessels, perivascular haemorrhage, neutrophil infiltration and demyelination. Severe cerebral oedema follows. Anti-MOG antibodies have been detected in a minority of cases.
det.clinical: After a prodromal infection, patients develop fever, encephalopathy, seizures and focal signs that progress rapidly to coma. Lesions can be one-sided or both-sided and may involve brainstem and cerebellum. Death results mainly from herniation.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows large tumefactive white matter lesions with haemorrhagic foci and mass effect; SWI is sensitive for petechiae. CSF often shows neutrophilic pleocytosis with red cells and high protein. Exclude infective encephalitis, abscess, vasculitis and tumour; biopsy can confirm in uncertain cases.
det.treatment: Begin high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone early, often combined with plasma exchange, IVIG or cyclophosphamide. Aggressive ICP management with osmotherapy and decompressive craniectomy has been associated with survival. Cover empirically with aciclovir and antibiotics until infection is excluded.
det.prognosis: Historically most cases were fatal; with early combined immunotherapy and surgery, survival with variable deficits is now reported in a substantial proportion.
pearls: Post-infectious encephalopathy with haemorrhagic white matter lesions: think AHL and treat immediately.
CSF neutrophils do not exclude an immune cause here.
Decompressive craniectomy can be life-saving.
det.thd: Acute haemorrhagic leukoencephalitis หรือ Hurst disease เป็นสมองอักเสบทำลายปลอกประสาทชนิดมีเลือดออกที่รุนแรงที่สุดในกลุ่ม ADEM มักเกิดหลังติดเชื้อไวรัส ผู้ป่วยมีไข้ สับสน ชัก อ่อนแรง และโคม่าในเวลาไม่กี่วัน MRI พบรอยโรคเนื้อขาวขนาดใหญ่ บวมและมีจุดเลือดออก การรักษาต้องให้ steroid ขนาดสูง plasma exchange หรือ IVIG ทันที และควบคุมความดันในกะโหลกศีรษะ

name: Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP)
formal: Most common form of Guillain-Barre syndrome: immune-mediated demyelination causing ascending areflexic weakness with albuminocytological dissociation and slowed nerve conduction.
simple: The common type of Guillain-Barre syndrome in which the immune system attacks nerve coverings, causing weakness that spreads upward from the legs.
more: Nerve conduction shows prolonged distal latencies, conduction block and absent F waves or H reflexes; CSF protein rises after the first week. IVIG or plasma exchange speeds recovery; ventilatory and autonomic monitoring are essential.
th: Guillain–Barré ชนิดที่พบบ่อยที่สุด ภูมิคุ้มกันทำลายไมอีลินของเส้นประสาท ทำให้อ่อนแรงขึ้นจากขาและรีเฟล็กซ์หายภายในไม่กี่วัน
tempoNote: Weakness progresses over days, peaking within 4 weeks (usually 2), then plateau and recovery
feat: Often follows a respiratory or diarrhoeal infection 1–4 weeks earlier
Symmetric ascending weakness with reduced or absent reflexes; distal tingling and back pain
Facial and bulbar weakness, respiratory failure in about a quarter
Autonomic instability: arrhythmia, labile blood pressure, ileus, urinary retention
Monophasic, nadir within 4 weeks
inv: NCS: prolonged distal latencies, slowed conduction, conduction block, absent F-waves (may be normal in first days)
CSF: raised protein with normal or near-normal cell count (< 50/µL), often normal in week one
Serial FVC, single-breath count and NIF; ECG monitoring
Exclude mimics: electrolytes (K, Mg, phosphate), CK, HIV, spinal MRI if sensory level or bladder signs early

case.story: Two weeks after a bout of diarrhoea his feet tingled, then over five days he could not climb stairs and now struggles to lift his arms. Lower back pain is prominent.
case.exam: Symmetric proximal and distal weakness (MRC 3/5 legs, 4/5 arms), bilateral facial weakness, areflexia, mild distal sensory loss; HR fluctuates 50–130.
case.tests: CSF protein 1.2 g/L, cells 2/µL; NCS shows prolonged distal latencies and conduction block; FVC 1.9 L falling.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the two key immediate decisions?
case.a: AIDP (Guillain–Barré syndrome); start IVIG (2 g/kg total, split over 5 days) or plasma exchange, and admit to ICU-level monitoring because FVC is falling with autonomic instability.

det.patho: An antecedent infection (Campylobacter, CMV, EBV, influenza, Zika, SARS-CoV-2, Mycoplasma) or occasionally vaccination triggers an immune response that cross-reacts with Schwann cell or myelin antigens. Macrophages strip myelin under complement and T-cell influence, especially at roots and distal nerve terminals where the blood–nerve barrier is weak. Secondary axonal damage determines slow or incomplete recovery. AIDP predominates in Europe and North America, while axonal forms are proportionally more common in Asia.
det.clinical: Paraesthesia and back or limb pain often precede symmetric weakness that ascends over days. Reflexes become reduced or absent, though a minority with normal reflexes exist. Facial diplegia, bulbar weakness and respiratory failure occur in a substantial proportion; dysautonomia can cause fatal arrhythmias. Variants include Miller Fisher, pharyngeal–cervical–brachial and paraparetic forms. Red flags for another diagnosis are marked asymmetry, a sensory level, early severe bladder dysfunction, CSF cells over 50/µL and fever at onset.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by CSF albuminocytological dissociation and electrodiagnostic demyelination; both may be normal in the first week, so repeat studies help. Brighton criteria are used for classification and the 2023 EAN/PNS guideline describes a practical approach. EGRIS predicts need for ventilation and mEGOS predicts outcome. Screen for mimics including hypokalaemia, botulism, tick paralysis, myasthenic crisis, porphyria and spinal cord lesions.
det.treatment: Patients unable to walk unaided within 2–4 weeks of onset should receive IVIG (2 g/kg total, divided across 5 days) or plasma exchange (about five exchanges); neither combining the two nor repeating IVIG is recommended. Corticosteroids are ineffective. Monitor FVC and autonomic function; intubate early if FVC falls below about 20 mL/kg or bulbar weakness threatens the airway. DVT prophylaxis, neuropathic pain treatment, bowel and bladder care and early rehabilitation are essential. Complement inhibitors are under study.
det.prognosis: About 80% walk independently by 6 months; mortality is 3–7%, and older age, preceding diarrhoea and severe weakness predict poorer recovery.
pearls: Normal CSF protein and NCS in week one do not exclude GBS — repeat later.
Monitor FVC, not oxygen saturation; desaturation is a late sign.
Worsening after 8 weeks or ≥3 relapses after initial improvement: reconsider as acute-onset CIDP.
det.thd: AIDP เป็น Guillain–Barré syndrome ชนิดทำลายไมอีลินที่พบบ่อย มักเกิดหลังติดเชื้อทางเดินหายใจหรือท้องเสีย 1–4 สัปดาห์ ผู้ป่วยอ่อนแรงขึ้นจากขาทั้งสองข้าง รีเฟล็กซ์หาย อาจหายใจล้มเหลวและระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติแปรปรวน ตรวจ CSF พบโปรตีนสูงแต่เซลล์ปกติ และ NCS พบลักษณะ demyelination รักษาด้วย IVIG หรือ plasma exchange และต้องเฝ้าระวัง FVC ใกล้ชิด

name: Acute inflammatory myopathy
formal: Acute onset immune-mediated or infectious muscle inflammation (e.g. polymyositis, viral or bacterial myositis) producing myalgia, proximal weakness and elevated creatine kinase.
simple: Sudden inflammation of muscles causing pain and weakness, usually in the shoulders and hips.
th: กลุ่มภาวะกล้ามเนื้ออักเสบเฉียบพลันจากการติดเชื้อหรือภูมิคุ้มกัน ทำให้ปวดกล้ามเนื้อ อ่อนแรง โดยเฉพาะน่อง/ต้นขา และ CK สูง อาจมี rhabdomyolysis และไตวายได้
tempoNote: Hours to days after a viral prodrome (post-influenza or enteroviral); immune forms over days to weeks
feat: Sudden severe muscle pain, tenderness and symmetric weakness, often worst in the calves in children
Preceding fever, cough or sore throat for several days, commonly influenza or other respiratory viruses
Tendon reflexes are preserved, differentiating from acute neuropathy
Dark urine from myoglobinuria in severe cases, with risk of acute kidney injury
Skin rash or sustained proximal weakness points to dermatomyositis, polymyositis or necrotising forms
inv: Creatine kinase (often marked rise), renal function, potassium and urine myoglobin
Viral studies (influenza PCR, enterovirus) and muscle MRI showing oedema
Myositis antibody panel and muscle biopsy if subacute, relapsing or persistent
Nerve conduction studies and EMG to separate neuropathy and neuromuscular junction disorders

case.story: After four days of fever and cough, he refused to walk because of severe calf pain and weak legs. Urine looked tea-coloured.
case.exam: Afebrile now, tender calf muscles, difficulty standing, power 3 out of 5 in thighs, reflexes preserved, sensation normal.
case.tests: CK greatly elevated, creatinine slightly high, influenza B PCR positive; nerve conduction normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what is the main risk?
case.a: Acute infectious (influenza-associated) myositis with rhabdomyolysis. Give IV fluids to protect the kidneys, analgesia and rest; weakness usually resolves in days to weeks.

read.where: Chapter 28 Disorders of Consciousness and Intensive Care Neurology — Neuromuscular Disease

det.patho: Muscle injury results from direct viral invasion, cytokine-mediated damage or, in autoimmune forms, T-cell and antibody-driven inflammation. In children influenza B and enteroviruses are the usual culprits. Severe cases involve massive myofibre necrosis with myoglobin release.
det.clinical: A prodromal respiratory illness is followed by abrupt severe muscle pain and weakness with calf tenderness and toe walking. Reflexes are preserved and sensation is normal. Immune forms such as polymyositis and dermatomyositis develop over weeks and show proximal weakness, often with rash in dermatomyositis. Necrotising myopathy after statin use or malignancy also presents subacutely.
det.diagnosis: A markedly raised CK with normal nerve conduction supports myositis. Test renal function and electrolytes, search for viral cause, and use MRI to show oedema. Immune myopathy needs a myositis antibody panel and biopsy to classify. Exclude Guillain–Barré syndrome, periodic paralysis, metabolic myopathy, botulism and drug- or toxin-induced rhabdomyolysis.
det.treatment: Treatment of infectious myositis is supportive: hydration, analgesia, monitoring of renal function and potassium, and antivirals such as oseltamivir for influenza. Immune-mediated forms need corticosteroids with steroid-sparing agents, IVIG in selected cases, and management of the associated malignancy or drug cause. Check for respiratory and swallowing muscle involvement.
det.prognosis: Infectious myositis recovers fully within days to weeks; outcome in immune forms depends on subtype and response to treatment.
pearls: Painful calves plus preserved reflexes and high CK after flu means myositis, not GBS.
Check renal function and potassium in every case with dark urine.
Persisting or relapsing weakness needs antibodies and biopsy.
det.thd: ภาวะกล้ามเนื้ออักเสบเฉียบพลันมักเกิดหลังติดเชื้อไวรัส เช่น ไข้หวัดใหญ่ ทำให้ปวดและอ่อนแรงที่น่องและขา ปัสสาวะสีเข้ม รีเฟล็กซ์ยังปกติ CK สูงมาก ต้องระวังไตวายจาก rhabdomyolysis การรักษาคือให้สารน้ำ ยาแก้ปวดและรักษาโรคไวรัส ส่วนชนิดภูมิคุ้มกันต้องใช้สเตียรอยด์และยากดภูมิคุ้มกัน
