name: Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP)
formal: Autosomal dominant hepatic porphyria from porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency causing attacks of abdominal pain, autonomic instability, psychosis, seizures and motor neuropathy, triggered by drugs, fasting or hormones.
simple: An inherited disorder causing attacks of severe belly pain, confusion, seizures and nerve weakness that can be triggered by certain drugs or fasting.
th: โรคพอร์ไฟเรียเฉียบพลัน — ปวดท้องรุนแรง อาการทางจิต ระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติผิดปกติ แล้วแขนขาอ่อนแรงแบบแอกซอน
tempoNote: Attacks over days, often triggered by drugs, fasting, alcohol or the menstrual cycle
feat: Severe abdominal pain without peritonism, vomiting, constipation
Tachycardia, hypertension, hyponatraemia (SIADH), seizures, confusion or psychosis
Rapid motor axonal neuropathy, often proximal and arm-predominant; may need ventilation
Dark or reddish urine that darkens further on standing in light
inv: Urine porphobilinogen (PBG) and ALA markedly raised during the attack
Sodium, magnesium; NCS: motor axonal pattern
HMBS gene testing and family screening

case.story: After starting a new anticonvulsant and dieting, 4 days of colicky abdominal pain, then agitation and arm weakness.
case.exam: Pulse 130, BP 170/100, proximal arm weakness MRC 3/5, reduced reflexes, soft abdomen.
case.tests: Sodium 122 mmol/L; urine PBG markedly raised; urine turned port-wine colour on the window sill.
case.q: What are the first treatment steps?
case.a: Stop porphyrinogenic drugs, give IV glucose and haem arginate (hemin), treat pain and seizures with porphyria-safe drugs, monitor breathing.

qx.stem: A 26-year-old woman from Nonthaburi is admitted for the third time with severe abdominal pain, vomiting, tachycardia and hyponatraemia (Na 124 mmol/L) a few days before menstruation. She becomes confused and then develops proximal arm weakness and areflexia. Abdominal CT is normal. A spot urine porphobilinogen is markedly raised.
qx.q: Which treatment is most appropriate for this acute attack?
opts: High-dose IV glucose alone and oral contraceptive pill to suppress cycles
Carbamazepine for neuropathic pain and IVIG for the weakness
Plasma exchange for presumed Guillain–Barré syndrome
IV haem arginate (hemin) daily for about 4 days, stop porphyrinogenic drugs, and plan givosiran prophylaxis for recurrent attacks
Laparoscopy to exclude an acute surgical abdomen
qx.why: Neurovisceral attacks with raised urinary PBG and motor axonal neuropathy indicate an acute hepatic porphyria. Intravenous haem is the definitive treatment, glucose is only supportive, and unsafe drugs (e.g. carbamazepine, many hormonal preparations) must be stopped. Givosiran, an siRNA against ALAS1, markedly reduces attacks in patients with recurrent episodes. IVIG and plasma exchange do not treat porphyric neuropathy.

Wrist drop, anaemia with basophilic stippling, high blood lead

aN: aip | acute intermittent porphyria | acute porphyria | porphyric neuropathy | hepatic porphyria

det.patho: AIP is an autosomal dominant deficiency of hydroxymethylbilane synthase (HMBS, also called PBG deaminase) in haem synthesis, with low penetrance. Triggers that induce hepatic ALAS1 — cytochrome P450-inducing drugs, fasting, alcohol, progesterone, infection and stress — cause accumulation of ALA and PBG. ALA is thought to be directly neurotoxic, causing the visceral, autonomic, central and peripheral nerve manifestations. Attacks are most common in women of reproductive age.
det.clinical: Attacks begin with severe, poorly localised abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and constipation, with tachycardia and hypertension. Anxiety, insomnia, confusion, hallucinations, seizures and hyponatraemia from SIADH may follow; PRES can occur. A motor-predominant axonal neuropathy may develop over days, often proximal and arm-first, sometimes with cranial nerve and respiratory involvement. Recurrent attacks can lead to chronic pain, hypertension, kidney disease and an increased risk of liver cancer.
det.diagnosis: A spot urine PBG (with creatinine) that is markedly elevated during symptoms establishes an acute porphyria attack and should be sent urgently, not deferred. ALA is also raised. Plasma fluorescence, faecal porphyrins and enzyme or HMBS gene testing distinguish AIP from other acute porphyrias and allow family screening. NCS shows a motor axonal pattern. Check sodium, magnesium and liver function.
det.treatment: Stop all unsafe drugs, treat pain with opioids, control nausea, and correct electrolytes. Give intravenous haem (hemin or haem arginate, usually a 4-day course at 3–4 mg/kg per day) as early as possible; glucose loading is only a holding measure for mild attacks. Treat seizures with porphyria-safe drugs and monitor vital capacity. For frequent recurrent attacks, givosiran (an siRNA silencing hepatic ALAS1) reduces attack rates; liver transplantation is a last resort.
det.prognosis: Most attacks resolve with early haem therapy, but established neuropathy recovers slowly over months and may be incomplete.
pearls: Abdominal pain + hyponatraemia + psychiatric change + new weakness: send a urine PBG.
Many antiepileptic drugs trigger attacks; check a porphyria drug database before prescribing.
AIP has no skin photosensitivity, unlike variegate porphyria and hereditary coproporphyria.
det.thd: AIP เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมจากการขาดเอนไซม์ HMBS ในการสร้างฮีม เมื่อมีตัวกระตุ้น เช่น ยาบางชนิด การอดอาหาร แอลกอฮอล์ หรือฮอร์โมน จะเกิดการสะสมของ ALA และ PBG ซึ่งเป็นพิษต่อระบบประสาท ผู้ป่วยมีอาการปวดท้องรุนแรง ใจสั่น ความดันสูง สับสน ชัก โซเดียมต่ำ และแขนขาอ่อนแรงแบบแอกซอน การวินิจฉัยคือพบ PBG ในปัสสาวะสูงมากขณะมีอาการ การรักษาคือหยุดยาที่กระตุ้น ให้ hemin ทางหลอดเลือดดำโดยเร็ว และใช้ givosiran ป้องกันในรายที่เป็นซ้ำบ่อย

name: Acute ischaemic stroke
formal: Sudden focal neurological deficit due to arterial occlusion and cerebral infarction, treated with thrombolysis or thrombectomy within defined time windows.
simple: A stroke caused by a blocked blood vessel in the brain, leading to sudden weakness, speech or vision problems.
th: สมองขาดเลือดเฉียบพลัน — หลอดเลือดสมองอุดตันทำให้เนื้อสมองบางส่วนตาย อาการเกิดทันทีและตรงกับบริเวณที่หลอดเลือดนั้นเลี้ยง
tempoNote: Maximal deficit within minutes; time last known well drives treatment
feat: Sudden focal deficit that fits one arterial territory
Negative symptoms (loss of power, sensation, speech or vision) rather than spreading positive phenomena
Cortical signs (aphasia, neglect, gaze deviation) point to a large-vessel anterior circulation occlusion
Crossed signs, vertigo with ataxia, or diplopia suggest the posterior circulation
inv: Non-contrast CT immediately to exclude haemorrhage; CT angiography for large-vessel occlusion
Capillary glucose before any reperfusion decision
MRI DWI confirms infarction when CT is unrevealing
ECG/Holter, echocardiography, carotid imaging and lipid/HbA1c for mechanism

case.who: 68-year-old man with hypertension and atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated)
case.story: Found by his wife at breakfast unable to speak; he was normal when he went to the toilet 50 minutes earlier.
case.exam: Global aphasia, left gaze preference, right face-and-arm weakness worse than leg, right hemianopia.
case.tests: CT brain: no blood, hyperdense left MCA; CTA: left M1 occlusion; glucose 6.1 mmol/L.
case.q: Which vessel is occluded and what two reperfusion options should be considered now?
case.a: Left middle cerebral artery (M1). Within the window he is a candidate for IV thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy; AF is the likely embolic source.

qx.stem: A 68-year-old farmer from Buriram wakes with a left hemiparesis; he was last seen well 11 hours earlier. NIHSS is 11. Non-contrast CT shows no haemorrhage, CTA shows a right M1 occlusion, and CT perfusion shows a small core of 18 mL with a penumbral volume of 90 mL (mismatch ratio over 4).
qx.q: Which statement best applies to his reperfusion options?
opts: He should be excluded from all reperfusion treatment because onset exceeds 6 hours
Intravenous alteplase is mandatory before any thrombectomy decision
Reperfusion is contraindicated until an MRI is completed
A repeat CT in 24 hours should be done before deciding
He is eligible for thrombectomy because perfusion imaging shows salvageable tissue in an extended window
qx.why: Trials such as DAWN and DEFUSE-3 showed that large-vessel occlusion with a small core and large mismatch benefits from thrombectomy up to 24 hours, so a fixed 6-hour cut-off is obsolete. Lytic therapy may be added if the patient meets criteria, but it is not mandatory. Waiting for MRI or 24-hour imaging simply loses penumbra.

qx.stem: A 59-year-old man arrives 90 minutes after sudden aphasia and right arm weakness. Non-contrast CT shows loss of grey-white differentiation of the left insula and lentiform nucleus, with ASPECTS 6. The CTA confirms a left M1 occlusion.
qx.q: How should the CT finding be interpreted?
opts: Established infarct that rules out any treatment
A venous infarct needing anticoagulation
Artefact from beam hardening requiring repeat CT
Haemorrhagic transformation requiring blood pressure lowering
Early ischaemic change reflecting reduced attenuation from cytotoxic oedema; ASPECTS 6 does not preclude thrombectomy
qx.why: Within hours, water uptake in ischaemic tissue lowers CT attenuation, producing insular ribbon loss and a blurred lentiform nucleus. ASPECTS of 5 or higher (and larger cores in selected trials such as SELECT2 and ANGEL-ASPECT) still showed benefit from thrombectomy when LVO is present. The pattern is arterial, not venous, and not haemorrhage.

qx.stem: A 45-year-old woman has transient vertigo and right facial numbness lasting 20 minutes. At 3 hours the exam is normal. Non-contrast CT is normal. MRI diffusion-weighted imaging shows a small area of high signal with low ADC in the left lateral medulla.
qx.q: What does the DWI/ADC combination indicate?
opts: T2 shine-through from an old lesion
Vasogenic oedema from a demyelinating plaque
Acute cytotoxic oedema consistent with infarction, so the transient episode is a minor stroke rather than TIA by tissue definition
Gadolinium enhancement from blood-brain barrier breakdown
Normal variant from susceptibility artefact
qx.why: Restricted diffusion (bright DWI with low ADC) marks cytotoxic oedema, which appears within minutes and persists for about 1–2 weeks. T2 shine-through has normal or high ADC, and demyelinating or vasogenic lesions have high ADC. A symptom-resolved event with a DWI lesion is an infarct by the tissue-based definition and needs stroke work-up and dual antiplatelet therapy as appropriate.

qx.stem: A 72-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation has sudden left lower limb weakness and abulia, with relative sparing of the arm and face. MRI shows a diffusion-restricting wedge along the inner hemispheric surface, involving frontal and parietal cortex on the right.
qx.q: Which artery is occluded?
opts: Right middle cerebral artery superior division
Right posterior cerebral artery
Right lenticulostriate branches
Right anterior cerebral artery
Right anterior choroidal artery
qx.why: ACA infarction affects the medial frontoparietal cortex, causing contralateral leg-predominant weakness and abulia. MCA infarcts spare the medial surface and cause arm and face predominance. PCA infarcts involve the occipital and medial temporal regions, and lenticulostriate or anterior choroidal infarcts are deep, small-volume lesions.

qx.stem: A 64-year-old rice farmer from Suphan Buri was last seen well at 22:00 and woke at 06:00 with right arm and face weakness and word-finding difficulty (NIHSS 7). Glucose and platelets are normal, BP 172/94 mmHg. Non-contrast CT is unremarkable and CTA shows no large-vessel occlusion. A rapid MRI shows a diffusion-bright lesion in the left insula and corona radiata with no matching signal change on FLAIR.
qx.q: Which is the most appropriate acute treatment decision?
opts: No thrombolysis, because the onset time is unknown and more than 4.5 hours have passed since last known well
Start aspirin plus clopidogrel and admit for observation only
Proceed to catheter angiography for thrombectomy
Give IV thrombolysis, because the DWI–FLAIR mismatch suggests the infarct is probably under 4.5 hours old
Repeat the MRI in 24 hours before any treatment
qx.why: A DWI lesion that is not yet visible on FLAIR implies a likely age within about 4.5 hours, and imaging-selected thrombolysis in wake-up stroke improved outcomes (WAKE-UP). Unknown onset alone is therefore not a contraindication when this tissue clock is available. There is no occlusion to retrieve, and DAPT or waiting would forgo an effective reperfusion therapy.

qx.stem: A 69-year-old man has a left M1 occlusion successfully opened by thrombectomy (final eTICI 2c) 4 hours after onset. In the recovery area his BP is 168/88 mmHg and the junior doctor proposes an infusion to bring the systolic pressure below 120 mmHg to protect against reperfusion haemorrhage.
qx.q: Which statement best reflects current evidence on blood pressure after successful thrombectomy?
opts: Systolic below 120 mmHg improves functional outcome and should be targeted
Aggressive lowering below 140 mmHg has been associated with worse functional outcome; keep systolic below about 180 mmHg and avoid steep drops
Blood pressure should not be treated at any level for 72 hours
Target a mean arterial pressure above 130 mmHg to drive collateral flow
Induced hypertension is the standard of care after complete reperfusion
qx.why: After ischaemia, cerebral autoregulation is impaired, so perfusion of recovering tissue follows systemic pressure passively. Randomised trials of intensive targets after thrombectomy (for example ENCHANTED2/MT, OPTIMAL-BP, BP-TARGET) found no benefit and some harm for functional outcome compared with a conventional limit of about 180/105 mmHg. Leaving severe hypertension untreated or deliberately inducing it is not supported either.

qx.stem: A 59-year-old man weighing 80 kg arrives 2 hours after onset of aphasia and right hemiparesis (NIHSS 12). CT shows no haemorrhage and CTA shows a left M2 occlusion. Transfer to the thrombectomy centre will take 90 minutes. The hospital has switched its thrombolytic to tenecteplase.
qx.q: Which regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Tenecteplase 0.4 mg/kg bolus followed by a 60-minute infusion
Tenecteplase 0.1 mg/kg bolus repeated every 30 minutes
Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg as a single IV bolus (20 mg), then transfer for thrombectomy
No thrombolytic, because thrombectomy is planned
Alteplase 0.6 mg/kg because tenecteplase is contraindicated before transfer
qx.why: Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg (maximum 25 mg) as a single bolus is at least as effective and safe as alteplase within 4.5 hours, and its bolus administration simplifies drip-and-ship transfer; it may also improve early reperfusion before thrombectomy (EXTEND-IA TNK). The 0.4 mg/kg dose gave no added benefit with more bleeding. Eligible patients should still receive thrombolysis on the way to thrombectomy.

qx.stem: A 66-year-old woman is independent at baseline and arrives 5 hours after onset of left hemiplegia, gaze deviation and neglect (NIHSS 20). CT shows ASPECTS 4 and CTA shows a right terminal ICA occlusion. CT perfusion estimates an ischaemic core of about 90 mL. Her family asks whether anything can still be done.
qx.q: What is the most appropriate recommendation?
opts: Offer endovascular thrombectomy, because recent large-core trials showed better functional outcome despite more haemorrhage
Comfort care only, because a core above 70 mL excludes reperfusion therapy
IV thrombolysis alone, then reassess at 24 hours
Thrombectomy only if repeat CT in 6 hours shows no further infarct growth
Decompressive craniectomy now, before any reperfusion attempt
qx.why: Several randomised trials of large-core anterior-circulation occlusions (SELECT2, ANGEL-ASPECT, RESCUE-Japan LIMIT, TENSION, TESLA, LASTE) found that thrombectomy shifted functional outcomes favourably even with ASPECTS 3–5 or cores over 50–70 mL, despite more symptomatic haemorrhage. She is beyond the thrombolysis window, waiting wastes salvageable tissue, and craniectomy is reserved for malignant oedema.

ddx.pt: Clinically indistinguishable — only imaging separates them; headache, vomiting and falling GCS favour bleeding
Follows a witnessed seizure and fades over hours; no matching DWI lesion
Positive symptoms that march over 5–60 min, then headache; recurrent stereotyped history
Low capillary glucose; deficit reverses with dextrose
Positive Hoover sign and inconsistency; deficit not in a vascular territory

aN: ais | ischemic stroke | cerebral infarction | brain attack | cva

det.patho: Sudden arterial occlusion starves a region of brain; a densely ischaemic core dies within minutes while a surrounding penumbra stays salvageable for hours if flow returns, and how fast the core grows depends largely on collateral supply. The usual TOAST-style mechanisms are cardioembolism (AF above all), large-artery atherosclerosis (extracranial carotid in Western series, intracranial stenosis much more often in Asian patients), small vessel (lacunar) occlusion, other determined causes such as dissection or vasculitis, and cryptogenic or embolic stroke of undetermined source. After occlusion, energy failure, excitotoxicity and cytotoxic oedema evolve over hours, while blood–brain barrier breakdown later drives vasogenic swelling and haemorrhagic transformation. Worldwide, stroke is still among the top causes of death and adult disability, with a rising burden in Asia, Thailand included.
det.clinical: Deficits appear abruptly and map onto one arterial territory: MCA strokes give contralateral face-arm weakness, aphasia (dominant) or neglect (non-dominant) and gaze deviation toward the lesion, while ACA strokes favour the leg and PCA strokes give a homonymous hemianopia. Lacunar syndromes (pure motor, pure sensory, ataxic hemiparesis, dysarthria–clumsy hand, sensorimotor) lack cortical signs and may fluctuate over the first day as a capsular warning syndrome. Posterior circulation strokes are easily missed when they present as vertigo, imbalance, diplopia or dysarthria; basilar occlusion may announce itself with stuttering symptoms before coma or locked-in state. Early worsening comes from clot propagation, failing collaterals, malignant oedema (large MCA infarcts peak at days 2–4) or haemorrhagic transformation. Examiners like the NIHSS, territory localisation, the time-last-known-well logic and recognition of a large-vessel occlusion at the bedside (forced gaze, aphasia or neglect plus dense hemiplegia).
det.diagnosis: The first goal is to exclude haemorrhage and mimics within minutes: non-contrast CT plus capillary glucose, then CT angiography from arch to vertex to find a large-vessel occlusion, without waiting for creatinine. ASPECTS on CT estimates early ischaemic change in the MCA territory, and CT perfusion (core–penumbra mismatch) or MRI (DWI–FLAIR mismatch) selects patients who wake up with symptoms, have unknown onset or arrive beyond the standard windows. DWI is the most sensitive test but can miss very small brainstem infarcts in the first hours, so a negative scan does not overrule a convincing posterior circulation syndrome. Mimics include seizure with Todd paresis, hypoglycaemia, migraine aura, functional weakness, tumour, subdural haematoma and sepsis unmasking an old deficit. Once stable, define the mechanism with prolonged rhythm monitoring (including implantable loop recorders for cryptogenic stroke), echocardiography, vessel imaging, lipids, HbA1c and, in the young, tests for dissection, PFO, thrombophilia and vasculitis.
det.treatment: IV thrombolysis is given within 4.5 hours of last known well, using tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg as a single bolus (maximum 25 mg) or alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (maximum 90 mg, 10% as bolus); beyond 4.5 hours or for wake-up stroke it remains an option up to 9 hours when perfusion or DWI–FLAIR imaging shows salvageable tissue, but it adds little for minor non-disabling deficits, where dual antiplatelet therapy is preferred. Mechanical thrombectomy is standard for ICA or proximal MCA occlusion up to 24 hours with imaging selection, recent trials extend benefit to large established cores (ASPECTS roughly 3–5), and basilar occlusion with moderate–severe deficit also benefits up to about 24 hours; routine thrombectomy for medium or distal vessel occlusions has not shown benefit. Keep BP at or below 185/110 before and 180/105 for 24 hours after reperfusion, and avoid driving systolic pressure well below 140 after successful thrombectomy, since intensive targets worsened outcome. Admit to a stroke unit, screen swallowing, treat fever and hyperglycaemia, prevent aspiration, DVT (intermittent pneumatic compression) and falls, and start early rehabilitation; decompressive hemicraniectomy within 48 hours saves lives in malignant MCA infarction. Secondary prevention follows mechanism: 21 days of aspirin plus clopidogrel after minor stroke or high-risk TIA, a DOAC for AF started early (within about 2 days for minor and 6–7 days for severe strokes per recent trials), high-intensity statin with LDL target below 70 mg/dL, BP control and carotid revascularisation when indicated.
det.prognosis: Outcome depends on infarct size, age, collateral status and speed of reperfusion; roughly a third of survivors remain dependent. Recurrence risk is highest in the first weeks, especially with large-artery disease.
pearls: Time is brain: always record the time last seen well, not the time found.
Check glucose before calling a stroke — hypoglycaemia is the classic reversible mimic.
A dizzy patient with a normal CT can still have a cerebellar stroke; look for gait ataxia and use HINTS.
A large core is no longer an automatic exclusion for thrombectomy, and basilar occlusion is treated up to about 24 hours.

name: Acute lymphocytic leukaemia (ALL)
formal: Malignancy of lymphoid precursor cells that can involve the CNS with leukaemic meningitis, cranial neuropathies and treatment-related neurotoxicity such as leukoencephalopathy and neuropathy.
simple: A fast-growing blood cancer that can spread to the brain coverings or cause nerve problems, including from its treatment.
th: มะเร็งเม็ดเลือดขาวชนิด lymphoblast ซึ่งลุกลามระบบประสาทได้ เช่น เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบจากเซลล์มะเร็ง เส้นประสาทสมองพิการ และพิษจากการรักษา เช่น leukoencephalopathy จาก methotrexate และปลายประสาทเสื่อมจาก vincristine

Methotrexate toxicity: stroke-like episodes with diffusion restriction, or chronic leukoencephalopathy
Vincristine neuropathy: distal paraesthesia, foot drop, constipation, jaw pain, ptosis

case.who: 7-year-old boy from Nan in consolidation therapy for ALL
case.story: Eight days after intrathecal methotrexate he suddenly had right arm weakness and slurred speech, then recovered over 24 hours.
case.exam: Mild residual right pronator drift.
case.tests: MRI: left centrum semiovale diffusion restriction without vascular territory; CSF clear of blasts.
case.q: What is the likely cause and can methotrexate continue?
case.a: Subacute methotrexate neurotoxicity; it usually resolves, and many children safely resume methotrexate (sometimes with dextromethorphan) after discussion with oncology.

Chapter 7: Neurological complications of lymphoid malignancies

det.patho: ALL is the commonest childhood cancer. Blasts can seed the leptomeninges, a sanctuary site, which is why CNS-directed therapy (intrathecal and high-dose systemic methotrexate, cytarabine) is part of every protocol. Treatment toxicities arise from folate pathway disruption, microtubule inhibition by vincristine and asparaginase-induced coagulopathy.
det.clinical: CNS involvement at diagnosis is uncommon but more likely in T-cell disease and high counts. Neurological complications during therapy include methotrexate stroke-like syndromes, posterior reversible encephalopathy, sinus thrombosis, seizures, vincristine neuropathy and infections. Long-term survivors may have neurocognitive deficits, particularly after cranial irradiation, which is now used rarely.
det.diagnosis: CSF assessment with cytospin and flow cytometry stages CNS disease. MRI separates leukaemic infiltration, toxicity, thrombosis and infection. Consider timing relative to drug doses.
det.treatment: CNS disease receives intensified intrathecal and systemic therapy; immunotherapy (blinatumomab, CAR-T cells) may cause its own neurotoxicity (ICANS), managed with steroids. Vincristine neuropathy is handled by dose modification and avoiding azole antifungals that raise its levels. CVT is treated with anticoagulation.
det.prognosis: Childhood ALL cure rates exceed 85–90% in high-resource settings; neurological toxicities are usually reversible but late cognitive effects can persist.
pearls: New cranial nerve palsy in a child with ALL: check CSF for relapse.
Transient stroke-like deficit 1–2 weeks after methotrexate: think methotrexate neurotoxicity.
Azoles markedly worsen vincristine neuropathy.

name: Acute motor and sensory axonal neuropathies (AMSAN)
formal: Severe axonal form of Guillain-Barre syndrome with motor and sensory involvement, rapid progression, marked axonal degeneration and poor, slow recovery.
simple: A severe form of Guillain-Barre syndrome that damages the nerve fibres themselves, causing weakness and numbness with slow recovery.
more: Nerve conduction shows low motor and sensory amplitudes with relatively preserved velocities; sural response often lost. Treat with IVIG or plasma exchange as in other GBS forms; mechanical ventilation is frequently needed and long-term disability is common.
ab: Acute motor and sensory axonal neuropathies

Cranial nerve and autonomic involvement common

case.who: 29-year-old male construction worker from Pathum Thani
case.story: Diarrhoea 10 days ago; now within 3 days unable to walk, tingling hands and feet and difficulty breathing.
case.exam: Flaccid tetraparesis MRC 1–2, areflexia, glove-and-stocking sensory loss, bilateral facial weakness, FVC 15 mL/kg.
case.tests: CSF protein 1.2 g/L, cells 2; NCS absent sensory potentials and very low CMAPs without slowing; anti-GM1 IgG positive.
case.q: Which GBS variant is this and what treatment is given?
case.a: AMSAN; IVIG (total 2 g/kg, divided across 5 days) or plasma exchange with ICU support.

read.where: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves — Variants of Guillain–Barré Syndrome

det.patho: Molecular mimicry between bacterial lipo-oligosaccharides and gangliosides at nodes of Ranvier triggers antibody and complement attack on motor and sensory axons. Severe cases progress to Wallerian-like degeneration. AMSAN is considered the severe end of the AMAN spectrum, with sensory fibres also affected.
det.clinical: Weakness evolves quickly to severe tetraparesis, often with respiratory failure, cranial nerve palsies and autonomic instability. Sensory symptoms and pain are prominent. Recovery is slow and incomplete because axons must regrow. Wasting can be marked.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis uses GBS criteria plus neurophysiology showing axonal changes in motor and sensory nerves. Early studies can mislead because reversible conduction failure looks axonal; repeat studies help. CSF protein rises after the first week. Exclude porphyria, toxins, critical illness neuropathy and spinal cord disease.
det.treatment: IVIG (total 2 g/kg split across 2–5 days) or plasma exchange; there is no proven benefit of combining them or of steroids. Intensive care for ventilation, autonomic monitoring, DVT prophylaxis and pain control is essential. Early rehabilitation prevents contractures. Complement inhibitors are under trial.
det.prognosis: Many have prolonged disability; a significant minority remain unable to walk at 1 year.
pearls: Axonal GBS with sensory loss after diarrhoea: AMSAN.
Repeat nerve conduction to separate true axonal loss from reversible conduction failure.
Severe early nadir predicts ventilation and slow recovery.

det.patho: Most cases follow Campylobacter jejuni enteritis: lipo-oligosaccharide on the bacterium mimics GM1 and GD1a gangliosides of motor axons. Cross-reacting IgG binds the nodal axolemma, activates complement and disrupts sodium channels. Mild injury causes reversible nodal conduction failure; heavier injury leads to Wallerian-like axonal degeneration. AMAN is proportionally more frequent in East and South Asia and Latin America, and in younger patients.
det.clinical: Weakness ascends over days without sensory symptoms, often with deep tendon reflexes that are preserved or briefly brisk. Cranial nerves are less often affected than in AIDP, but respiratory failure still occurs. Recovery follows one of two tracks: rapid improvement within weeks (reversible conduction failure) or slow recovery over many months (axonal degeneration, sometimes with permanent distal weakness). Pain and dysautonomia are generally milder than in AIDP.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the GBS clinical criteria plus electrophysiology showing reduced CMAPs, normal sensory responses and no persistent demyelinating features. Early studies may mimic demyelination; repeat at 3–6 weeks to classify correctly. CSF protein may be normal in the first week. IgG anti-GM1/GD1a supports the diagnosis and Campylobacter can be sought in stool or serology. Exclude poliomyelitis and other acute flaccid myelitis, hypokalaemia, botulism and porphyria.
det.treatment: Management is the same as GBS: IVIG (total 2 g/kg, split across 5 days) or plasma exchange, ideally within the first two weeks. Corticosteroids are not effective. Monitor vital capacity, swallowing and autonomic function and anticipate ventilation. Thromboprophylaxis, pain control and early rehabilitation are part of standard care.
det.prognosis: Most patients walk again; those with reversible conduction failure recover quickly, while extensive axonal loss predicts slow and incomplete recovery. The modified Erasmus GBS outcome score helps estimate prognosis.
pearls: Preserved or brisk reflexes do not exclude GBS — this is classic for AMAN.
One early NCS can mislabel AMAN as demyelinating; serial studies are needed.
Normal sensory potentials in an acute flaccid paralysis point to AMAN, poliomyelitis-like illness or NMJ disease.
det.thd: AMAN เป็น GBS ชนิดที่ทำลายแอกซอนของเส้นประสาทสั่งการ มักเกิดหลังท้องเสียจาก Campylobacter ซึ่งทำให้ร่างกายสร้างแอนติบอดีต่อ GM1/GD1a ผู้ป่วยอ่อนแรงขึ้นจากขาไปแขนภายในไม่กี่วัน แต่ไม่มีอาการชา และรีเฟล็กซ์อาจยังปกติ การตรวจไฟฟ้าพบ CMAP ต่ำโดย sensory ปกติ ควรตรวจซ้ำเพื่อแยกจาก AIDP การรักษาเหมือน GBS คือ IVIG หรือ plasma exchange และเฝ้าระวังการหายใจ

name: Acute necrotising encephalopathy
formal: Rapidly progressive post-infectious encephalopathy with symmetric multifocal brain lesions involving thalami, brainstem and cerebellum, associated with RANBP2 mutations in familial recurrent cases.
simple: A rare severe brain illness in children after a viral infection, causing fever, seizures and coma with damage in deep brain areas.
th: สมองอักเสบรุนแรงเฉียบพลันหลังติดเชื้อไวรัส (เช่น ไข้หวัดใหญ่) มีรอยโรคสมมาตรที่ thalamus ทั้งสองข้าง ชักและโคม่าภายในวัน
tempoNote: Coma and seizures within 1–3 days of a febrile viral illness; familial RANBP2 cases may recur with later infections
feat: Fever and a viral prodrome (influenza, HHV-6, SARS-CoV-2) followed within days by seizures and falling consciousness
Symmetric multifocal lesions, always involving both thalami, often with brainstem, cerebellum and periventricular white matter
Mostly young children, especially East Asian; adults occasionally
Liver enzymes may rise without hyperammonaemia; CSF protein high with few or no cells
Recurrent or familial episodes suggest RANBP2 variant (ANE1)
inv: MRI: bilateral thalamic swelling with central haemorrhage or diffusion restriction (concentric 'tricolour' pattern)
CSF: raised protein, no pleocytosis; viral PCR from respiratory samples
Blood: transaminases, cytokines (IL-6) where available; exclude metabolic and toxic causes
RANBP2 testing in recurrent or familial cases

case.story: Two days into an influenza A illness she has a long generalised seizure and does not wake up afterwards.
case.exam: GCS 6, brisk reflexes, intermittent decerebrate posturing; no neck stiffness.
case.tests: CSF: 2 cells, protein 1.4 g/L; MRI: symmetric swollen thalami with central haemorrhage and pontine tegmentum lesions; AST 410 U/L.
case.q: What is the syndrome and which early treatments are commonly considered?
case.a: Acute necrotising encephalopathy; ICU care with early high-dose steroids, sometimes IVIG or IL-6 blockade, plus oseltamivir, though evidence is limited.

read.where: Chapter 28 Disorders of Consciousness and Intensive Care Neurology — Conditions of Particular Concern on Neurological Critical Care
Chapter 13: Neurologic Complications Of Cardiac Arrest

det.patho: A cytokine storm triggered by a viral infection disrupts the blood–brain barrier, producing vasogenic oedema, petechial haemorrhage and necrosis in a striking symmetric distribution centred on the thalami. There is no direct viral invasion of the brain in most cases. Heterozygous missense variants in RANBP2 cause an incompletely penetrant familial form (ANE1) with recurrences after later infections.
det.clinical: Children develop seizures, encephalopathy and coma soon after the fever begins, typically inside 72 hours. Shock and multiorgan failure may coexist. Survivors frequently have motor, cognitive and behavioural sequelae. Adult cases are recognised, notably after influenza and COVID-19.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the clinical setting plus characteristic MRI: symmetric multifocal lesions with obligatory bilateral thalamic involvement. CSF typically shows high protein without cells. Mizuguchi criteria require exclusion of other similar diseases such as fulminant infections, Reye syndrome, mitochondrial and toxic encephalopathies. A severity score using shock, brainstem lesions, age and CSF protein helps predict outcome.
det.treatment: No therapy is proven in trials. Supportive ICU care with seizure and pressure control is fundamental. Early high-dose methylprednisolone (ideally within the first day) is associated with better outcomes in observational series; IVIG, plasma exchange, therapeutic hypothermia and tocilizumab have been used. Treat the triggering virus when possible, and vaccinate against influenza, especially in RANBP2 families.
det.prognosis: Mortality is roughly a quarter to a third, and many survivors have lasting deficits; brainstem involvement predicts worse outcome.
pearls: Symmetric thalamic lesions days after flu in a toddler: ANE until proven otherwise.
CSF protein high with no cells — the inflammation is systemic and vascular, not meningitic.
Ask about previous episodes and family history; RANBP2 carriers need flu vaccination and early care.
det.thd: Acute necrotising encephalopathy เป็นสมองอักเสบรุนแรงในเด็กเล็กหลังติดเชื้อไวรัส เช่น ไข้หวัดใหญ่ เกิดจากพายุ cytokine มิใช่เชื้อเข้าสมองโดยตรง เด็กชักและซึมลงจนโคม่าภายในไม่กี่วัน MRI เห็นรอยโรคสมมาตรที่ thalamus ทั้งสองข้าง CSF โปรตีนสูงแต่เซลล์ไม่ขึ้น รักษาประคับประคองใน ICU และให้ steroid ขนาดสูงโดยเร็ว

name: Acute necrotising myopathy
formal: Rapid muscle fibre necrosis with markedly elevated creatine kinase, caused by statins, immune-mediated disease, cancer, infection or toxins, presenting with severe proximal weakness.
simple: Sudden breakdown of muscle fibres causing marked weakness and pain, with a very high muscle enzyme level in blood.
more: Rapid-onset myopathy with myofibre necrosis and marked CK elevation, seen with rhabdomyolysis, toxins, drugs, infection, or paraneoplastic and autoimmune causes, often with myoglobinuria. Check CK, renal function, potassium, and drug or toxin history; biopsy shows necrosis with little inflammation. Treat the cause, give fluids, and protect the kidneys; recovery is often good.
th: กล้ามเนื้อตายอย่างรวดเร็ว CK สูงมาก สาเหตุจาก statin ภูมิคุ้มกัน มะเร็ง การติดเชื้อ หรือสารพิษ ทำให้อ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขารุนแรง และอาจมีปัสสาวะสีโคล่า
tempoNote: Days (toxic, rhabdomyolysis) to weeks (immune-mediated)
feat: Rapid symmetric proximal weakness with muscle pain
Very high CK (often over 10,000 IU/L), myoglobinuria and risk of acute kidney injury
Causes: statins (anti-HMGCR), anti-SRP, cancer, viral infections, alcohol, snake envenomation, drugs
Dysphagia, neck and respiratory weakness in severe cases
Biopsy shows necrotic fibres with little inflammation
inv: CK, renal function, potassium, calcium, urine myoglobin
Myositis antibodies: anti-HMGCR, anti-SRP; drug and toxin history
MRI muscle (oedema), EMG (irritable myopathy), muscle biopsy; cancer screening

case.who: 63-year-old man from Ratchaburi on atorvastatin for 2 years
case.story: Six weeks of difficulty climbing stairs and rising from chairs, now struggling to lift his arms; statin stopped a month ago without improvement.
case.exam: Proximal weakness grade 3/5 in hips and shoulders, neck flexor weakness.
case.tests: CK 14,000; anti-HMGCR positive; MRI thigh oedema; biopsy necrotic fibres with scant inflammation.
case.q: Why did stopping the statin not help, and what treatment is needed?
case.a: Anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotising myopathy continues after the trigger is removed; IVIG with steroids and a steroid-sparing agent.

read.where: Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Inflammatory Myopathies
Chapter 1 Breathing and the Nervous System

det.patho: Muscle fibres undergo necrosis from direct toxic injury (statins at high dose, alcohol, envenomation, drugs), autoimmune attack (complement deposition on fibres in anti-HMGCR and anti-SRP disease), infection or paraneoplastic mechanisms. Unlike polymyositis, inflammatory cell infiltration is sparse, and regeneration accompanies necrosis.
det.clinical: Presentation is subacute or acute proximal weakness, often severe, with myalgia and very high CK. Toxic forms follow exposure and improve after removal, whereas immune forms progress despite stopping the trigger. Respiratory, bulbar and cardiac muscle may be involved. Myoglobinuric renal failure is a key acute risk.
det.diagnosis: Measure CK and renal function urgently. Obtain myositis-specific antibodies, MRI to guide biopsy and EMG. Muscle biopsy distinguishes necrotising from inflammatory myopathy. Screen for cancer, especially in seronegative and anti-HMGCR cases.
det.treatment: Treat the cause and protect the kidneys with IV fluids and monitoring of potassium. Stop statins and other offending drugs. Immune-mediated forms require IVIG plus corticosteroids, often with methotrexate, azathioprine or rituximab (especially anti-SRP). Rehabilitation after the acute phase.
det.prognosis: Toxic forms often recover well; immune-mediated forms may need long-term therapy and some patients retain weakness.
pearls: Very high CK + weakness after a statin that persists after stopping it: test anti-HMGCR.
Necrosis without inflammation on biopsy points to IMNM or toxic myopathy rather than polymyositis.
Watch potassium and kidney function in severe rhabdomyolysis.
det.thd: Acute necrotising myopathy คือกล้ามเนื้อตายอย่างรวดเร็ว CK สูงมาก ผู้ป่วยอ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขา ปวดกล้ามเนื้อ และอาจปัสสาวะสีเข้มจนไตวาย สาเหตุมีทั้งสารพิษ ยา เช่น statin การติดเชื้อ และภูมิคุ้มกัน เช่น anti-HMGCR หรือ anti-SRP ตรวจ CK การทำงานของไต แอนติบอดี และตัดชิ้นเนื้อ รักษาด้วยการให้สารน้ำ หยุดยาที่เป็นสาเหตุ และให้ยากดภูมิคุ้มกันในกลุ่ม immune-mediated

name: Acute necrotising myopathy of intensive care
formal: Critical illness myopathy variant with acute rhabdomyolysis and muscle fibre necrosis, associated with sepsis, high-dose steroids and neuromuscular blockers, causing flaccid quadriparesis and ventilator weaning difficulty.
simple: Severe muscle damage in very ill patients in intensive care that causes generalised weakness and makes it hard to come off the ventilator.
th: กล้ามเนื้อตายเฉียบพลันในผู้ป่วย ICU ที่ได้ steroid ขนาดสูงหรือยาหย่อนกล้ามเนื้อ ร่วมกับ sepsis ทำให้อ่อนแรงทั้งตัวและ CK สูงมาก
tempoNote: Develops over days during critical illness, often noticed when sedation is lifted or weaning fails
feat: Flaccid generalised weakness in a ventilated patient, limbs and often diaphragm
Risk factors: sepsis, multiorgan failure, high-dose IV corticosteroids, non-depolarising blockers
CK markedly raised, sometimes with myoglobinuria and acute kidney injury
Sensation and eye movements largely preserved; reflexes reduced or absent
The most severe end of the critical illness myopathy spectrum
inv: Serum CK, urine myoglobin, renal function and potassium
Nerve conduction: low CMAP with normal sensory responses; direct muscle stimulation shows inexcitable muscle
EMG: short small units and fibrillations where activation is possible
Muscle biopsy (if needed): widespread fibre necrosis with little inflammation

case.who: 52-year-old man in the medical ICU at a provincial hospital in Khon Kaen
case.story: Admitted with severe asthma and pneumonia; received high-dose methylprednisolone and a vecuronium infusion for 5 days. After sedation stopped he could barely move his limbs and failed weaning.
case.exam: Symmetric flaccid weakness of all limbs, neck flexors weak, reflexes depressed, facial and eye movements intact, withdraws to pain normally.
case.tests: CK 18,000 U/L, dark urine positive for blood without red cells, creatinine rising; NCS show low CMAPs with normal sensory potentials.
case.q: What is the cause of his weakness and what is the immediate priority?
case.a: Acute necrotising myopathy of intensive care; protect the kidneys with fluids, stop the blocking agent and taper steroids where possible.

read.where: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves — Critical Illness Neuromyopathy
Chapter 28 Disorders of Consciousness and Intensive Care Neurology — Neuromuscular Disease

det.patho: In critical illness, inflammatory cytokines, corticosteroids and pharmacological denervation from neuromuscular blockers combine to cause loss of myosin and frank fibre necrosis. Muscle membrane excitability falls because of sodium channel dysfunction, so fibres do not respond even to direct stimulation. The necrotising form shows widespread destruction of fibres and high CK, unlike the thick-filament form where CK may be near normal.
det.clinical: Weakness becomes obvious once sedation is reduced, with flaccid limbs, neck weakness and an inability to come off the ventilator. Facial weakness can occur but eye movements are usually spared. Pigmented urine and kidney injury may accompany the necrosis. It often coexists with critical illness polyneuropathy, and the two can be hard to separate at the bedside.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the context, a high CK and electrophysiology showing small motor responses with preserved sensory potentials. Direct muscle stimulation, where available, helps distinguish myopathy from neuropathy. Biopsy is reserved for unclear cases and shows scattered or extensive necrosis with minimal inflammation. Exclude pre-existing neuromuscular disease, spinal cord lesions and electrolyte disorders such as hypophosphataemia.
det.treatment: There is no specific drug therapy. Management is supportive: treat sepsis, avoid or minimise neuromuscular blockers and high-dose steroids, maintain renal perfusion and correct electrolytes. Tight glucose control and early mobilisation reduce the risk of ICU-acquired weakness. Prolonged rehabilitation is often needed after ICU discharge.
det.prognosis: Many patients recover over weeks to months, but severe necrotising cases carry higher mortality and can leave residual weakness.
pearls: Normal sensory potentials plus low CMAPs in an ICU patient point to myopathy rather than neuropathy.
Steroids together with neuromuscular blockers in status asthmaticus are the classic trigger.
Check CK early in any patient who cannot be weaned and moves poorly after sedation stops.
det.thd: เป็นภาวะกล้ามเนื้อตายเฉียบพลันที่เกิดในผู้ป่วยวิกฤต โดยเฉพาะเมื่อมี sepsis และได้ steroid ขนาดสูงร่วมกับยาหย่อนกล้ามเนื้อ ผู้ป่วยจะอ่อนแรงทั้งตัวและหย่าเครื่องช่วยหายใจไม่ได้ ตรวจพบ CK สูงมาก NCS มี CMAP ต่ำแต่ sensory ปกติ การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง ป้องกันไตวาย หยุดยาที่เป็นสาเหตุ และฟื้นฟูสมรรถภาพ

name: Acute otitis media
formal: Infection of the middle ear that may cause neurological complications such as mastoiditis, lateral sinus thrombosis, meningitis, brain abscess and facial palsy.
simple: A middle ear infection that can sometimes spread to cause facial weakness, meningitis or brain abscess.
th: การติดเชื้อหูชั้นกลาง ซึ่งอาจลุกลามทำให้เกิดภาวะแทรกซ้อนทางระบบประสาท เช่น mastoiditis, lateral sinus thrombosis, เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ ฝีในสมอง และอัมพาตใบหน้า
tempoNote: Ear infection over days; intracranial complications may follow within days to weeks
feat: Primarily an ENT disease: ear pain, fever, bulging tympanic membrane, otorrhoea
Facial nerve palsy from inflammation in a dehiscent facial canal
Spread causes mastoiditis, meningitis, epidural or temporal/cerebellar abscess
Lateral (sigmoid) sinus thrombosis gives headache, papilloedema (otitic hydrocephalus)
Petrous apicitis gives Gradenigo syndrome: ear discharge, VI palsy, retro-orbital pain
inv: Otoscopy; culture of discharge
Contrast CT temporal bone and brain, or MRI with MR venography if complications are suspected
Lumbar puncture only after imaging excludes mass effect

case.story: Two weeks of left ear discharge treated at a clinic; now severe headache, vomiting and double vision.
case.exam: Purulent left otorrhoea, mastoid tenderness, bilateral papilloedema, left VI nerve palsy.
case.tests: MRV: thrombosis of the left sigmoid and transverse sinuses; CT: opacified mastoid air cells.
case.q: What complication has occurred?
case.a: Otogenic lateral sinus thrombosis with raised intracranial pressure; needs antibiotics, mastoid surgery and usually anticoagulation.

read.where: Chapter 23 Neuro-Otology: Dizziness, Balance and Hearing

det.patho: Bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae infect the middle ear, usually after eustachian tube dysfunction. Infection may spread through bone, along veins or through dehiscences to the meninges, venous sinuses, facial canal and brain. Chronic suppurative disease with cholesteatoma carries higher intracranial risk.
det.clinical: Children are most affected. Warning signs of complication include persistent fever despite antibiotics, severe headache, vomiting, drowsiness, neck stiffness, seizures, facial weakness, vertigo or diplopia. Otitic hydrocephalus is raised ICP from venous sinus thrombosis.
det.diagnosis: Uncomplicated AOM is diagnosed clinically. Suspected complications need contrast imaging of temporal bone and brain, including venography. CSF analysis is essential for meningitis once safe.
det.treatment: Antibiotics (amoxicillin first line for uncomplicated AOM). Complications require intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, mastoidectomy or drainage, abscess drainage, and anticoagulation is often used for sinus thrombosis. Facial palsy from AOM usually recovers with antibiotics and myringotomy.
det.prognosis: Uncomplicated AOM resolves; intracranial complications still carry meaningful morbidity and mortality, especially abscess.
pearls: Ear discharge plus headache and papilloedema: image the venous sinuses.
Gradenigo triad points to petrous apex infection.
Always examine the ear in a child with facial palsy.
det.thd: Acute otitis media คือหูชั้นกลางอักเสบติดเชื้อ ซึ่งเป็นโรคทางหู คอ จมูก แต่อาจลุกลามเข้าสู่กะโหลกศีรษะทำให้เกิด mastoiditis เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ ฝีในสมอง หลอดเลือดดำ sigmoid sinus อุดตัน และอัมพาตใบหน้า อาการเตือนคือปวดศีรษะมาก อาเจียน ซึม ตามัวหรือเห็นภาพซ้อน ต้องทำ CT หรือ MRI พร้อม venography และรักษาด้วยยาปฏิชีวนะทางหลอดเลือดร่วมกับการผ่าตัด

name: Acute parkinsonism
formal: Subacute-onset rigid-akinetic syndrome from drugs, toxins, encephalitis, basal ganglia stroke or metabolic causes, differing from slowly evolving idiopathic Parkinson disease.
simple: Parkinson-like stiffness and slowness that starts suddenly, often caused by a medicine, toxin, infection or stroke.
th: Acute parkinsonism คือภาวะเคลื่อนไหวช้าและกล้ามเนื้อแข็งที่เกิดภายในไม่กี่วันถึงสัปดาห์ ต่างจาก Parkinson’s disease ที่ค่อยเป็นค่อยไป สาเหตุสำคัญได้แก่ยา (โดยเฉพาะยาต้านโดพามีนและยากันคลื่นไส้) สารพิษ การติดเชื้อสมองอักเสบ โรคหลอดเลือดสมอง hydrocephalus และ catatonia ต้องแยก NMS และ catatonia ให้ได้เพราะรักษาต่างกัน
tempoNote: Evolves over hours to a few weeks; secondary forms usually appear faster than idiopathic Parkinson's disease
feat: Bradykinesia and rigidity, often symmetrical, with tremor present in only some patients, appearing over days to weeks
Commonest causes are drugs: dopamine blockers (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine), flunarizine and cinnarizine, valproate and lithium
Toxic and metabolic causes: carbon monoxide, manganese, methanol, cyanide, disulfiram, osmotic demyelination, anoxia, alcohol withdrawal
Infection and inflammation: viral encephalitis (Japanese encephalitis), encephalitis lethargica, post-measles, HIV with opportunistic infection, lupus
Fever, confusion or high CK point to NMS, serotonin syndrome or encephalitis; sudden akinesia with open eyes and no tremor may be catatonia
inv: Detailed drug history (including antiemetics, vertigo and herbal products) and toxicology
MRI brain: basal ganglia or midbrain lesions, hydrocephalus, pontine and extrapontine myelinolysis, stroke or tumour
CK, electrolytes with sodium trend, glucose, liver and thyroid tests, HIV, and CSF with viral studies if encephalitis is possible
Lorazepam challenge and EEG when catatonia is a possibility; a trial of levodopa as both treatment and diagnostic test

case.who: 38-year-old farmer from Sukhothai, ten days after a febrile illness with headache and drowsiness in the rainy season
case.story: As the fever settled he became slow and expressionless, spoke in a whisper and could no longer rise from a chair; his wife says he was well a fortnight ago.
case.exam: Mask-like face, bilateral rigidity with cogwheeling, mild rest tremor of the right hand, slow but appropriate answers; no fever now.
case.tests: MRI shows T2 hyperintensity in the substantia nigra and thalami; CSF has a few lymphocytes with a positive Japanese encephalitis IgM.
case.q: What is the likely cause and what treatment is reasonable?
case.a: Parkinsonism after Japanese encephalitis. Give supportive care and a slowly titrated trial of levodopa; unlike idiopathic disease, many patients improve over weeks to months, but dyskinesias can appear at low doses.

read.where: Chapter 28 Disorders of Consciousness and Intensive Care Neurology — Movement Disorder Emergencies

det.patho: Acute parkinsonism arises when dopaminergic transmission in the nigrostriatal system, or the striatal and pallidal circuits downstream, is disrupted over a short time. Mechanisms include receptor blockade by drugs, mitochondrial or oxidative toxicity (carbon monoxide, MPTP, manganese), infarction or demyelination, and inflammation. In the encephalitis lethargica epidemic, tangle-type pathology destroyed the midbrain, producing the delayed postencephalitic parkinsonism. The varied causes share the same motor picture.
det.clinical: The history is often unreliable, because families notice the slowing only after a fall or an episode of incontinence, so ask carefully when it began. Parkinsonism may be the main complaint or only a minor part of a serious illness such as encephalitis or NMS. Features that argue against idiopathic disease are rapid onset, symmetry, absence of rest tremor, early drowsiness or fever, and lack of response to levodopa. Psychogenic parkinsonism should be considered in young patients, and catatonia whenever there is sudden akinesia and mutism without a structural cause.
det.diagnosis: Start with the drug and toxin history, then MRI and a metabolic and infection screen guided by the context. The lorazepam challenge with an EEG helps to identify catatonia. Reversible structural causes such as hydrocephalus (including shunt blockage) must be sought. Dopamine transporter imaging can show whether the nigrostriatal terminals are intact, distinguishing drug-induced from degenerative disease.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: stop the offending drug, remove the toxin, treat infection, or correct sodium slowly. Where the cause is unclear a levodopa trial is sensible and may be diagnostic; the book recommended a dopamine agonist in NMS, and amantadine (about 200–400 mg a day if renal function is normal) as an alternative. Patients with postencephalitic disease are very sensitive to dopaminergic drugs, so start low and increase slowly. Catatonia needs lorazepam or ECT, not antiparkinson drugs, and NMS needs intensive care.
det.prognosis: Outcome depends on cause: drug-induced, post-infectious and toxic forms often improve over weeks to months, whereas anoxic, ischaemic or postencephalitic damage may persist.
pearls: Ask for drug exposure first, including antiemetics and vertigo pills.
Open eyes, silence and no tremor in a stiff patient suggest catatonia, not Parkinson's disease.
Postencephalitic patients need slow levodopa titration.

name: Acute reversible hyperglycaemic neuropathy
formal: Transient painful or sensory neuropathy occurring with severe hyperglycaemia and resolving once glucose is normalised, distinct from chronic diabetic polyneuropathy.
simple: Nerve pain or numbness that appears with very high blood sugar and goes away once the sugar is brought under control.
th: อาการชาหรือปวดปลายประสาทชั่วคราวที่เกิดขณะน้ำตาลในเลือดสูงมาก และหายไปเมื่อควบคุมน้ำตาลได้ ต่างจากปลายประสาทเสื่อมจากเบาหวานเรื้อรัง
tempoNote: Appears with severe hyperglycaemia; improves within weeks of glucose control
feat: Distal sensory symptoms (tingling, burning) in newly diagnosed or decompensated diabetes
Associated with marked hyperglycaemia and weight loss
Mild slowing of nerve conduction that corrects with euglycaemia
Rapid improvement after glucose normalises, unlike chronic diabetic neuropathy
Must be distinguished from treatment-induced neuropathy (insulin neuritis), which starts after rapid glucose lowering
inv: Glucose and HbA1c; ketones and osmolality in decompensation
Nerve conduction studies (baseline and follow-up)
B12, renal and thyroid function to exclude other causes

case.who: 45-year-old man from Kamphaeng Phet with newly diagnosed diabetes
case.story: Polyuria, weight loss and tingling feet for a month; glucose 25 mmol/L, HbA1c 13%.
case.exam: Mild distal reduction of vibration sense, ankle reflexes present.
case.tests: NCS mild slowing of sensory and motor conduction; B12 and TSH normal.
case.q: What is expected after treatment?
case.a: Acute reversible hyperglycaemic neuropathy; symptoms should settle as glucose is corrected gradually; new severe pain after rapid correction would suggest insulin neuritis instead.

read.where: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves — Endocrine Disorders

det.patho: High glucose causes reversible metabolic and osmotic changes in nerves: polyol pathway activation, altered sodium-potassium ATPase function and axonal swelling. These slow conduction without causing structural loss, so correction restores function. The entity is described mainly in older literature and is less commonly diagnosed today.
det.clinical: Patients with uncontrolled diabetes (often new diagnosis) report distal sensory symptoms that improve in parallel with glucose control. Weakness is unusual. It may coexist with early chronic diabetic neuropathy, making attribution difficult.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is supported by temporal link with hyperglycaemia and improvement after control. Nerve conduction slowing that normalises on follow-up is confirmatory. Exclude other neuropathy causes.
det.treatment: Gradual glucose control is the treatment; avoid very rapid HbA1c reduction to limit the risk of treatment-induced neuropathy. Short-term neuropathic pain medication if needed.
det.prognosis: Good; symptoms usually resolve over weeks to a few months.
pearls: Symptoms that start with hyperglycaemia and improve with control: reversible hyperglycaemic neuropathy.
Symptoms that start after rapid control: insulin neuritis.
Lower HbA1c gradually (roughly no more than 2% over 3 months) when possible.
det.thd: Acute reversible hyperglycaemic neuropathy คืออาการชาหรือปวดปลายประสาทที่เกิดขณะน้ำตาลในเลือดสูงมาก เช่น เบาหวานที่เพิ่งวินิจฉัย และหายไปเมื่อควบคุมน้ำตาลได้ เพราะเส้นประสาทยังไม่เสียหายถาวร ตรวจ nerve conduction อาจพบการนำกระแสช้าเล็กน้อยที่กลับมาปกติ ต้องแยกจาก insulin neuritis ที่เกิดหลังลดน้ำตาลเร็วเกินไป รักษาด้วยการควบคุมน้ำตาลอย่างค่อยเป็นค่อยไป

name: Acute small fiber sensory neuropathy
formal: Abrupt-onset neuropathy of thinly myelinated and unmyelinated fibres presenting with burning pain and autonomic symptoms with preserved strength and reflexes and normal nerve conduction studies.
simple: A sudden nerve problem causing burning pain and odd skin sensations, usually without weakness.
more: Skin biopsy shows reduced intra-epidermal nerve fibre density; look for diabetes, post-infectious, and drug causes. Treat pain symptomatically; some cases improve spontaneously or with immunotherapy.
th: เส้นประสาทเส้นเล็กเสียหายแบบเฉียบพลัน ปวดแสบร้อนและมีอาการระบบอัตโนมัติ แต่กำลังกล้ามเนื้อ reflex และผลตรวจ NCS ปกติ
tempoNote: Burning pain develops over days to a few weeks; many improve over months
feat: Rapid burning, prickling or electric pain, often patchy or starting in hands, face or trunk rather than feet
Allodynia; reduced pinprick and temperature sense with normal vibration and joint position
Autonomic features: sweating change, flushing, orthostatic dizziness, gut upset
Strength and tendon reflexes preserved; nerve conduction normal
Triggers include infection or vaccination, new glucose disturbance, rapid glycaemic control and drugs
inv: Skin punch biopsy for intra-epidermal nerve fibre density (distal leg plus proximal thigh)
Glucose tolerance/HbA1c, B12, thyroid, HIV, hepatitis C, ANA, Ro/La, SPEP
Autonomic tests (QSART, tilt) and quantitative sensory testing where available
NCS to confirm large fibres are spared

case.who: 41-year-old man, rubber plantation owner in Rayong
case.story: Three weeks after a gastrointestinal infection, burning pain spreads over his face, hands and chest; he cannot bear his shirt touching his skin and feels faint on standing.
case.exam: Patchy loss of pin and cold sensation, preserved vibration, full strength, normal reflexes; postural BP drop 25 mmHg.
case.tests: NCS normal; skin biopsy shows reduced fibre density at thigh more than ankle; HbA1c 5.4%.
case.q: Why might this be a ganglionopathy-like, possibly immune small fibre disorder?
case.a: Non-length-dependent (proximal) loss and acute post-infectious onset suggest an immune small fibre neuropathy; screen for Sjögren and consider a trial of immunotherapy if severe.

det.patho: Thinly myelinated A-delta and unmyelinated C fibres carry pain, temperature and autonomic signals. An acute insult — post-infectious autoimmunity, metabolic stress such as rapid lowering of glucose ('treatment-induced neuropathy'), or toxic drugs — causes their terminals or dorsal root ganglion cell bodies to degenerate. When the attack targets ganglia, loss is patchy and non-length-dependent.
det.clinical: Pain is the main complaint and can be severe and disproportionate to signs. Distribution may be length-dependent or patchy involving the face, scalp and trunk. Autonomic involvement varies from mild sweating change to disabling orthostatic intolerance. Examination is often near normal apart from reduced small-fibre modalities, which can lead to the condition being dismissed as functional.
det.diagnosis: Normal nerve conduction does not exclude neuropathy; small fibre disease needs skin biopsy, autonomic testing or quantitative sensory testing. Proximal-predominant loss on biopsy suggests a ganglionopathy. Screen for diabetes and prediabetes, Sjögren syndrome, HIV, hepatitis C, coeliac disease, paraproteins and drug exposure. Consider Fabry disease and hereditary sodium channel disorders when onset is early or family history is positive.
det.treatment: Treat the cause where found and avoid overly fast glucose correction. Neuropathic pain responds partially to gabapentinoids, duloxetine or tricyclic agents, with topical lidocaine or capsaicin for focal pain. Autonomic symptoms are managed with fluids, salt, compression and drugs such as midodrine. IVIG or steroids are sometimes used for severe immune-mediated cases, but controlled evidence is limited.
det.prognosis: Many acute cases improve over months, especially post-infectious and treatment-induced forms; some leave chronic pain.
pearls: Normal NCS plus burning pain: think small fibres and order a skin biopsy, not just reassurance.
Rapid HbA1c reduction can itself trigger acute painful neuropathy with autonomic failure.
Face or trunk involvement points to a ganglionopathy and a search for Sjögren or paraneoplastic cause.
det.thd: Acute small fiber sensory neuropathy คือการเสียหายของเส้นใยประสาทขนาดเล็กอย่างรวดเร็ว ผู้ป่วยปวดแสบร้อน สัมผัสเบา ๆ ก็เจ็บ และอาจมีอาการระบบอัตโนมัติ เช่น หน้ามืดเวลาลุก แต่แรงกล้ามเนื้อ reflex และ NCS ปกติ ยืนยันด้วย skin biopsy หาเหตุ เช่น น้ำตาล Sjögren ยา และการติดเชื้อ รักษาสาเหตุร่วมกับยาลดปวดประสาท

name: Acute stroke
formal: Abrupt focal neurological deficit from cerebral infarction or haemorrhage, requiring urgent imaging and reperfusion or haemorrhage management.
simple: Sudden loss of brain function, such as weakness or speech trouble, caused by a blocked or bleeding blood vessel in the brain.
th: ความผิดปกติทางระบบประสาทเฉพาะที่ที่เกิดทันทีจากสมองขาดเลือดหรือเลือดออกในสมอง ต้องทำภาพสมองด่วนเพื่อพิจารณาเปิดหลอดเลือดหรือจัดการเลือดออก
tempoNote: Sudden onset over seconds to minutes; treatment windows measured in hours
feat: Sudden face droop, arm or leg weakness, speech disturbance, visual loss or imbalance (BE FAST)
About 80% ischaemic, the remainder intracerebral or subarachnoid haemorrhage
Severity graded by NIHSS; large vessel occlusion suggested by gaze deviation, aphasia or neglect
Mimics: hypoglycaemia, seizure with Todd paresis, migraine aura, functional disorders
Time of last known well defines eligibility for reperfusion
inv: Immediate capillary glucose
Non-contrast CT ± CT angiography/perfusion, or MRI with diffusion
ECG, full blood count, coagulation, renal function

case.story: Found by his wife at 07:00 unable to speak with right-sided weakness; last seen well at 06:15.
case.exam: BP 182/100, global aphasia, left gaze preference, right hemiplegia; NIHSS 20; glucose 132 mg/dL.
case.tests: CT: no haemorrhage, ASPECTS 9; CTA: left M1 occlusion.
case.q: What acute treatments are indicated?
case.a: IV thrombolysis (alteplase or tenecteplase) within 4.5 hours plus mechanical thrombectomy for the large vessel occlusion.

read.where: Chapter 8 Stroke and Cerebrovascular Diseases — Treatment of Acute Ischaemic Stroke
Chapter 11: What are this patient’s problems? A problem‐based approach to the general management of stroke
Section 6 Systemic Disorders That Also Involve the Cerebrovascular System

det.patho: Ischaemic stroke results from thrombotic or embolic occlusion (large artery atherosclerosis, cardioembolism, small vessel disease, other causes). Haemorrhagic stroke results from vessel rupture, most often from hypertensive arteriopathy or amyloid angiopathy, or from aneurysm rupture. A salvageable penumbra surrounds the infarct core for a variable time, which is the target of reperfusion.
det.clinical: Presentation depends on territory: anterior circulation gives hemiparesis, aphasia or neglect; posterior circulation gives vertigo, diplopia, ataxia, crossed signs or visual field loss. Headache, vomiting and depressed consciousness favour haemorrhage but are not reliable. Early complications include oedema, haemorrhagic transformation, aspiration, seizures and infections.
det.diagnosis: Rapid assessment with a stroke scale, glucose check and brain imaging is essential. CT excludes haemorrhage; CTA identifies large vessel occlusion; perfusion imaging or MRI mismatch selects late-window patients. Wake-up strokes may qualify for thrombolysis based on DWI–FLAIR mismatch.
det.treatment: Eligible ischaemic stroke receives IV thrombolysis within 4.5 hours and thrombectomy for proximal occlusions in selected patients as late as a day after onset. Haemorrhage requires blood pressure lowering, reversal of anticoagulants and neurosurgical review. All patients benefit from stroke unit care, swallow screening, early mobilisation and secondary prevention.
det.prognosis: Outcome depends on severity, age and speed of treatment; reperfusion therapies substantially increase the proportion of independent survivors.
pearls: Check glucose before calling it a stroke.
Time is brain: every minute of delay loses neurons.
Gaze deviation with cortical signs suggests a large vessel occlusion — call the thrombectomy team.
det.thd: Acute stroke คือภาวะที่มีอาการทางระบบประสาทเฉพาะที่เกิดทันที จากหลอดเลือดสมองตีบอุดตันหรือแตก อาการเช่นปากเบี้ยว แขนขาอ่อนแรง พูดไม่ชัด ต้องตรวจน้ำตาลและทำ CT ทันที ถ้าเป็นชนิดขาดเลือดและมาทันเวลาจะได้รับยาละลายลิ่มเลือดและ/หรือการลากลิ่มเลือด ถ้าเป็นเลือดออกต้องควบคุมความดันและแก้ฤทธิ์ยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือด

qx.stem: A 71-year-old woman on twice-daily premixed insulin is brought by EMS 50 minutes after her daughter found her confused, sweaty and unable to move the left arm. NIHSS is 9. She has not eaten since the previous evening. The stroke team is assembling and the CT scanner is ready.
qx.q: Before any decision about thrombolysis, which step is most important?
opts: Check capillary glucose and, if low, correct it with IV dextrose and re-examine
Give tenecteplase immediately because every minute of delay costs neurons
Obtain a CT perfusion study to estimate the ischaemic core
Wait for the full coagulation profile before imaging
Give a loading dose of aspirin through a nasogastric tube
qx.why: Hypoglycaemia is a classic stroke mimic that can produce focal weakness, and glucose is the only laboratory result required before thrombolysis in most patients. If the deficit resolves with dextrose, thrombolysis is avoided; if it persists after correction, the stroke pathway continues. Waiting for coagulation results is unnecessary unless anticoagulant use or a bleeding disorder is suspected, and aspirin should not be given before haemorrhage is excluded.

name: Acute vestibular syndrome
formal: Acute onset of vertigo, nausea, nystagmus and gait imbalance lasting days, caused by vestibular neuritis or posterior circulation stroke; HINTS examination helps distinguish them.
simple: Sudden spinning dizziness with nausea and unsteadiness lasting days, caused by an inner ear nerve problem or sometimes a stroke.
th: กลุ่มอาการเวียนศีรษะบ้านหมุนต่อเนื่องเฉียบพลัน คลื่นไส้ ตากระตุก และเดินเซ นานหลายวัน สาเหตุหลักคือ vestibular neuritis หรือ stroke ของ posterior circulation

feat: Continuous vertigo, nausea, vomiting, head-motion intolerance and unsteadiness
Spontaneous nystagmus; peripheral type is unidirectional and suppressed by fixation
HINTS: positive head impulse, unidirectional nystagmus and no skew favour a peripheral cause
Central red flags: normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, skew, severe truncal ataxia, new hearing loss
About 1 in 4 to 1 in 5 cases in emergency settings is a stroke

Video head impulse testing where available

case.who: 55-year-old male fisherman from Rayong with hypertension
case.story: Woke with severe spinning dizziness and vomiting; cannot stand unaided.
case.exam: Left-beating nystagmus on left gaze turning right-beating on right gaze, normal head impulse both sides, right skew deviation, unable to sit unsupported.
case.tests: CT normal; MRI at 24 hours: small right cerebellar infarct.
case.q: Which examination findings pointed to a central cause?
case.a: Normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, skew deviation and severe truncal ataxia — posterior circulation stroke.

read.where: Chapter 23 Neuro-Otology: Dizziness, Balance and Hearing — Acute (Central) Vestibular Syndrome

det.patho: Sudden imbalance between left and right vestibular inputs produces vertigo and nystagmus. Peripheral causes involve the vestibular nerve or labyrinth (neuritis, labyrinthitis); central causes involve the vestibular nuclei or cerebellum (stroke, demyelination). AICA strokes can affect both labyrinth and brainstem, creating mixed signs.
det.clinical: Patients have continuous vertigo with nausea and imbalance lasting days. Peripheral cases usually can stand and walk with support, whereas central cases often cannot sit unaided. Headache, neck pain, diplopia, dysarthria or numbness suggest stroke or dissection, but many central cases have no obvious focal signs.
det.diagnosis: The HINTS examination performed by trained clinicians is more sensitive for stroke than early MRI. CT is poor for posterior fossa infarcts. Vascular risk factors raise suspicion but do not decide the diagnosis.
det.treatment: Short-term vestibular suppressants and antiemetics, early mobilisation and vestibular rehabilitation for neuritis; a brief steroid course is sometimes used. Stroke pathways (thrombolysis if eligible, antiplatelets, monitoring for cerebellar oedema) for central causes.
det.prognosis: Vestibular neuritis compensates over weeks; cerebellar stroke can swell and compress the brainstem in the first days.
pearls: A normal head impulse in a patient with continuous vertigo is a danger sign.
Direction-changing gaze-evoked nystagmus is central.
Negative early MRI does not exclude a small posterior fossa infarct.

read.where: Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — Viral Infections of the Nervous System
Part I: Introduction: An Insight into Central Nervous System (CNS) Infections
Chapter 42 Nervous System Complications of Systemic Viral Infections
Chapter 111: DNA and RNA Viral Infections of the Nervous System

det.patho: Viruses reach the nervous system through blood, by crossing the barrier in infected leucocytes, or by travelling inside peripheral nerves (herpes viruses, rabies, enteroviruses). Damage comes from direct cell infection, the host inflammatory response, or later molecular mimicry that drives autoimmune syndromes. Systemic illness can also cause encephalopathy without CNS infection through fever, hypoxia, metabolic upset or cytokines.
det.clinical: This entry is a broad heading for teaching. Patterns to recognise are aseptic meningitis, encephalitis with seizures and confusion, brainstem encephalitis, acute flaccid paralysis, transverse myelitis, and delayed immune conditions such as GBS, ADEM or acute cerebellar ataxia. In Thailand, dengue, Japanese encephalitis, enterovirus, influenza and rabies are important; travel and animal exposure matter.
det.diagnosis: Lumbar puncture (after imaging when indicated) is central, with PCR panels and paired serology. Timing helps: neurological illness during fever implies invasion, whereas onset after recovery suggests post-infectious immunity. MRI pattern (temporal, thalamic, brainstem, anterior horn) narrows the list. Always consider bacterial, fungal and autoimmune mimics.
det.treatment: Start aciclovir empirically for suspected encephalitis until HSV is excluded. Specific antivirals exist for some agents (ganciclovir for CMV, oseltamivir for influenza), but most care is supportive with seizure control, airway protection and management of raised pressure. Post-infectious immune syndromes receive immunotherapy such as IVIG or steroids. Vaccination (JE, measles, polio, influenza, rabies post-exposure) remains the best prevention.
det.prognosis: Ranges from full recovery in viral meningitis to death or severe disability in some encephalitides.
pearls: Separate 'during the fever' (infection) from 'after the fever' (immune) — treatments differ.
Aciclovir first, questions later, for any febrile encephalopathy.
Hand-foot-mouth illness plus myoclonus in a child is a warning sign for EV-A71 brainstem disease.
det.thd: หัวข้อนี้เป็นกลุ่มการติดเชื้อไวรัสเฉียบพลันที่อาจกระทบระบบประสาท ทั้งเชื้อเข้าสู่ระบบประสาทโดยตรงช่วงที่มีไข้ เช่น เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ สมองอักเสบ ไขสันหลังอักเสบ และภาวะภูมิคุ้มกันหลังหายไข้ เช่น GBS หรือ ADEM ตรวจน้ำไขสันหลังและ PCR ให้ aciclovir ทันทีเมื่อสงสัยสมองอักเสบ ส่วนใหญ่รักษาประคับประคอง และป้องกันด้วยวัคซีน

name: Acute viral myositis
formal: Self-limited inflammatory muscle injury after viral infection, commonly influenza B, with severe myalgia, tender calves, raised CK, and occasionally rhabdomyolysis.

Tender calves; strength and reflexes otherwise normal
Recent influenza B (less often A or other viruses) with fever and cough
CK commonly raised to a few thousand; myoglobinuria uncommon but possible
Recurrences or very high CK should prompt a search for a metabolic myopathy
inv: CK, renal function and urine dipstick for blood (myoglobin)
Influenza rapid test or PCR
Repeat CK after recovery; biopsy rarely needed

case.story: Four days after a flu-like fever he wakes up unable to walk normally, insisting on tiptoes because his calves hurt.
case.exam: Bilaterally tender calves, pain on ankle dorsiflexion, full power when coaxed, normal reflexes.
case.tests: CK 4,200 U/L, creatinine normal, urine dipstick negative; influenza B antigen positive.
case.q: What management is needed?
case.a: Benign acute childhood myositis: reassurance, fluids, simple analgesia and a follow-up CK; admit only if urine darkens or kidney function changes.

det.patho: The mechanism is thought to be direct viral invasion of muscle fibres or immune injury during the acute infection, causing focal necrosis especially in the gastrocnemius and soleus. Influenza B is the classic agent, followed by influenza A and other respiratory viruses. Biopsy, rarely needed, shows necrotic fibres with modest inflammation.
det.clinical: The child typically has had fever and respiratory symptoms for a few days, then suddenly develops calf pain and an abnormal gait, either toe-walking or a wide stiff gait. Weakness is apparent rather than real, limited by pain. Adults can have more diffuse myalgia and a higher risk of rhabdomyolysis. Symptoms settle in about three to seven days.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical in the right setting with raised CK and a positive influenza test. Confirm reflexes are present and there are no sensory signs, which excludes GBS. Check urine and creatinine for rhabdomyolysis. Persistent weakness, recurrent episodes or extreme CK warrant evaluation for an underlying metabolic or dystrophic myopathy.
det.treatment: Treatment is supportive: hydration, rest and paracetamol or ibuprofen if kidney function is normal. Oseltamivir may be given per influenza guidance but does not clearly shorten myositis. Admit for IV fluids if there is pigmenturia, rising creatinine or inability to drink. Influenza vaccination reduces risk.
det.prognosis: Excellent; full recovery is the rule and recurrence is rare.
pearls: Toe-walking child after flu with tender calves and normal reflexes: benign acute childhood myositis.
Check reflexes — absent reflexes change the diagnosis to GBS.
Recurrent episodes mean a metabolic myopathy screen.
det.thd: Acute viral myositis พบบ่อยในเด็กหลังเป็นไข้หวัดใหญ่ B เด็กปวดน่องมากจนเดินเขย่งหรือไม่ยอมเดิน กดน่องเจ็บ reflex ปกติ CK สูงเป็นพัน รักษาด้วยน้ำ ยาแก้ปวด และติดตามปัสสาวะกับการทำงานของไต ส่วนใหญ่หายภายในหนึ่งสัปดาห์ ถ้าเป็นซ้ำควรตรวจหาโรคกล้ามเนื้อจากเมแทบอลิก

name: ADA2 deficiency
formal: Autosomal recessive autoinflammatory vasculopathy (DADA2) from CECR1 mutations causing recurrent fever, livedo, early-onset ischaemic and haemorrhagic strokes and polyarteritis nodosa-like disease.
simple: A rare inherited condition causing fevers, skin rash and strokes at a young age due to inflamed blood vessels.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมด้อยที่ขาดเอนไซม์ ADA2 ทำให้หลอดเลือดอักเสบ มีไข้เป็นพัก ๆ ผื่น livedo และ stroke ตั้งแต่อายุน้อยทั้งขาดเลือดและเลือดออก
tempoNote: Starts in childhood; recurrent strokes and fevers over years
feat: Recurrent lacunar strokes in deep grey matter or brainstem in children or young adults
Intermittent fevers, livedo racemosa, skin nodules or ulcers
Polyarteritis nodosa-like disease: hypertension, abdominal or renal aneurysms, neuropathy
Cytopenias, hypogammaglobulinaemia, hepatosplenomegaly in some
Wide phenotypic range, from severe vasculitis to haematological presentations
inv: Plasma ADA2 enzyme activity (low or absent)
ADA2 (CECR1) gene sequencing
MRI brain with SWI; angiography if PAN-like features
Inflammatory markers and immunoglobulins

case.story: Recurrent fevers since age 3 with a lace-like rash on the legs; now two episodes of sudden facial droop and slurred speech within six months.
case.exam: Livedo racemosa on thighs, mild right facial weakness, dysarthria.
case.tests: MRI: small infarcts in left thalamus and pons; ESR 70 mm/h; ADA2 activity markedly reduced; biallelic ADA2 variants.
case.q: What treatment best prevents further strokes?
case.a: TNF inhibitor therapy (e.g. etanercept or adalimumab); antiplatelets alone are not adequate and may raise haemorrhage risk.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Deficiency of Adenosine Deaminase 2

det.patho: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in ADA2 reduce extracellular adenosine deaminase 2 activity. This skews macrophages towards a pro-inflammatory phenotype and damages endothelium, producing a small- and medium-vessel vasculopathy. Strokes typically affect lenticulostriate and brainstem perforators.
det.clinical: Most present in childhood with fevers, livedo and lacunar strokes, sometimes with haemorrhage. Other features include PAN-like organ involvement, peripheral neuropathy, immunodeficiency, cytopenia or pure red cell aplasia. Adults may present with stroke or vasculitis only.
det.diagnosis: Consider DADA2 in any child or young adult with recurrent lacunar strokes, especially with systemic inflammation or livedo. Low serum ADA2 activity with biallelic pathogenic variants confirms it. Exclude other vasculitides and genetic small vessel diseases.
det.treatment: TNF inhibitors are highly effective in preventing strokes and controlling inflammation. Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is used for severe haematological or immunodeficient forms. Avoid anticoagulation and use antiplatelets cautiously given haemorrhage risk.
det.prognosis: With TNF blockade, new strokes become rare; untreated disease causes recurrent strokes and organ damage.
pearls: Childhood lacunar stroke plus fever and livedo: test ADA2.
TNF inhibitors, not steroids alone, prevent DADA2 strokes.
Some patients present only with cytopenias — the phenotype is broad.
det.thd: ADA2 deficiency หรือ DADA2 เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมด้อยจากการกลายพันธุ์ของยีน ADA2 ทำให้หลอดเลือดขนาดเล็กและกลางอักเสบ เด็กมักมีไข้เป็นพัก ๆ ผื่นลายร่างแห และ stroke ชนิด lacunar ที่ก้านสมองหรือ basal ganglia ซ้ำ ๆ การวินิจฉัยด้วยการวัดเอนไซม์ ADA2 และตรวจยีน การรักษาที่ได้ผลคือยา TNF inhibitor
