name: Addison’s disease
formal: Primary adrenal insufficiency, usually autoimmune, causing fatigue, hypotension, hyponatraemia and hyperpigmentation; may cause neurological symptoms such as weakness, confusion and myopathy.
simple: A condition where the adrenal glands do not make enough hormones, causing tiredness, low blood pressure and weakness.
th: ต่อมหมวกไตชั้นนอกทำงานบกพร่อง (ส่วนใหญ่จากภูมิคุ้มกัน) ทำให้ขาด cortisol และ aldosterone เกิดอ่อนเพลีย ความดันต่ำ ผิวคล้ำ และอาจมีอาการทางประสาทเช่นอ่อนแรง ตะคริว สับสน
tempoNote: Months of fatigue and weight loss; may crash into adrenal crisis within hours during infection or surgery
feat: Fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, nausea, salt craving and light-headedness on standing
Hyperpigmentation of palmar creases, scars, gums and pressure areas from raised ACTH
Hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia, sometimes hypoglycaemia
Neuromuscular and cognitive echoes: diffuse weakness, cramps, myalgia, apathy, confusion or delirium
In boys and men with negative adrenal antibodies, consider adrenoleukodystrophy
inv: Early-morning cortisol with ACTH; cosyntropin (ACTH) stimulation test if equivocal
Plasma renin and aldosterone; 21-hydroxylase antibodies
Electrolytes, glucose, calcium, thyroid function; very-long-chain fatty acids in antibody-negative males
Adrenal imaging (CT) when TB, fungal infection, metastasis or haemorrhage is suspected

case.who: 38-year-old woman, a factory worker from Samut Prakan
case.story: Eight months of tiredness, poor appetite, 8 kg weight loss and cramps in the legs, with dizziness when standing and craving for salty snacks; referred as 'myopathy' after a normal CK.
case.exam: Supine BP 90/55, 70/45 on standing; darkened palmar creases and buccal mucosa; mild generalised weakness without wasting; reflexes normal.
case.tests: Na 127, K 5.6 mmol/L, glucose 3.6 mmol/L; 8 am cortisol low with markedly raised ACTH; 21-hydroxylase antibodies positive; CK normal.
case.q: Why is the weakness not a primary muscle disorder, and what should be started?
case.a: Autoimmune primary adrenal insufficiency causes weakness through cortisol and aldosterone deficiency and electrolyte disturbance; give hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone and teach stress dosing and crisis warning signs.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Adrenal Disorders
Chapter 15: Neurologic Complications Of Acute Renal Disease

det.patho: In most cases the adrenal cortex is destroyed by an autoimmune process marked by antibodies against 21-hydroxylase; tuberculosis, fungal disease, HIV-related infection, metastasis, haemorrhage and adrenoleukodystrophy are other causes. Loss of cortisol impairs blood pressure support, glucose production and stress responses, while loss of aldosterone causes salt wasting and potassium retention. The pituitary raises ACTH in compensation, and this stimulates melanocytes to darken the skin.
det.clinical: Addison disease sits at the border of neurology because patients are often first seen for weakness, cramps, mood change or cognitive complaints. Fatigue is nearly universal, but proximal weakness is functional rather than a true myopathy and CK is typically normal. Muscle and joint pain, rare flexion contractures, and psychiatric symptoms such as apathy or depression occur. Adrenal crisis presents with vomiting, abdominal pain, hypotension, hypoglycaemia and altered consciousness, and can be triggered by infection or surgery.
det.diagnosis: A low morning cortisol with high ACTH is highly suggestive, and equivocal values call for a stimulation test; raised renin with low aldosterone indicates mineralocorticoid deficiency. Positive 21-hydroxylase antibodies point to an autoimmune cause. If negative, look for infection, infiltration or haemorrhage on adrenal imaging, and measure VLCFA in men to find adrenoleukodystrophy. Never withhold treatment while awaiting results in suspected crisis.
det.treatment: Replacement is lifelong, using hydrocortisone in divided doses plus fludrocortisone, titrated to symptoms, blood pressure, electrolytes and renin. Patients must raise glucocorticoid doses during fever or other illness, carry a steroid card and learn injectable hydrocortisone use. In crisis, give hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenously at once with isotonic saline and glucose, and search for the trigger. Correct hyponatraemia carefully, since overly rapid rise can cause osmotic demyelination.
det.prognosis: With dependable replacement and education about sick-day rules, life expectancy is close to normal. Unrecognised crisis is the main preventable cause of death.
pearls: Hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and fatigue: check cortisol before calling the weakness neuromuscular or psychiatric.
Male Addison disease with negative antibodies requires a VLCFA test for adrenoleukodystrophy.
Rapid sodium correction after steroid start can cause osmotic demyelination.
det.thd: Addison’s disease คือภาวะต่อมหมวกไตชั้นนอกเสียหน้าที่ ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจากภูมิคุ้มกันทำลาย ทำให้ขาด cortisol และ aldosterone ผู้ป่วยอ่อนเพลีย น้ำหนักลด ความดันต่ำเวลายืน อยากกินเค็ม ผิวคล้ำ และอาจมีอ่อนแรง ตะคริว สับสน ซึ่งอาจถูกเข้าใจผิดว่าเป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้อหรือจิตเวช เลือดมักพบ Na ต่ำ K สูง วินิจฉัยด้วย cortisol ตอนเช้า ACTH และ ACTH stimulation test รักษาด้วย hydrocortisone และ fludrocortisone ตลอดชีวิต และเพิ่มขนาดยาเมื่อเจ็บป่วย ในผู้ชายที่ไม่พบ antibody ควรตรวจ VLCFA เพื่อหา adrenoleukodystrophy

name: Adenosine deaminase (ADA2) deficiency
formal: Autosomal recessive vasculopathy from CECR1 mutation causing deficient adenosine deaminase 2, with fevers, livedoid rash, recurrent lacunar strokes and immunodeficiency features.
simple: A rare inherited enzyme deficiency that inflames blood vessels, causing fevers, rashes and strokes in young people.
th: ภาวะพร่องเอนไซม์ adenosine deaminase 2 ซึ่งเป็นโรค autoinflammatory ทางพันธุกรรม ทำให้เกิด lacunar stroke ซ้ำ ไข้ ผื่น livedo และภูมิคุ้มกันบกพร่องในบางราย
tempoNote: Episodes of fever and stroke recurring from childhood or young adulthood
feat: Young-onset recurrent small deep infarcts, sometimes intracranial haemorrhage
Systemic inflammation: fevers, raised CRP, livedoid rash
Medium-vessel vasculitis features resembling PAN
Immune and blood abnormalities: low IgM or IgG, neutropenia, red cell aplasia
Peripheral neuropathy and ocular involvement occasionally
inv: Serum ADA2 enzymatic activity
Genetic confirmation of biallelic ADA2 variants
Brain MRI and vascular imaging; skin biopsy may show vasculitis

case.who: 19-year-old male vocational student from Surat Thani
case.story: Childhood diagnosis of 'PAN' treated with steroids on and off; now sudden double vision and left-sided numbness.
case.exam: Right INO, left hemisensory loss, livedo racemosa on legs, BP 160/100.
case.tests: MRI: acute right pontine lacune and old thalamic infarct; low IgM; ADA2 activity absent.
case.q: Why does the earlier diagnosis need revisiting?
case.a: Childhood PAN with lacunar strokes may be DADA2, which responds to TNF inhibitors rather than steroids alone.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Deficiency of Adenosine Deaminase 2

det.patho: ADA2 is secreted mainly by monocytes and macrophages and influences their differentiation; its deficiency shifts cells toward inflammatory M1 types and impairs vascular integrity. The disease bridges autoinflammation, vasculitis and immunodeficiency.
det.clinical: Neurological involvement appears in a large proportion, typically lacunar strokes in deep nuclei and brainstem. Cranial neuropathies and peripheral neuropathy are reported. Systemic features vary from minimal to severe PAN-like disease.
det.diagnosis: Measure ADA2 activity early in children with stroke and inflammation; confirm with sequencing. Note that many reported variants are rare, so enzyme testing helps interpret uncertain variants.
det.treatment: Long-term TNF inhibitor therapy prevents vascular events; dose and choice are guided by specialist teams. HSCT is considered for marrow failure or immunodeficiency. Manage hypertension and avoid unnecessary anticoagulants.
det.prognosis: Good stroke control on TNF blockade; morbidity mainly from accumulated strokes before diagnosis.
pearls: Reconsider childhood-onset PAN as DADA2.
Lacunar stroke in a child is never 'just small vessel disease'.
Screen siblings — inheritance is autosomal recessive.
det.thd: Adenosine deaminase 2 deficiency เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมแบบด้อยที่ทำให้มีการอักเสบของหลอดเลือดและภูมิคุ้มกันผิดปกติ ผู้ป่วยมี stroke ขนาดเล็กซ้ำ ๆ ตั้งแต่อายุน้อย ไข้ ผื่น livedo และบางรายมีภูมิคุ้มกันต่ำหรือเม็ดเลือดต่ำ วินิจฉัยด้วยการวัดเอนไซม์และตรวจยีน การรักษาหลักคือยาต้าน TNF ซึ่งป้องกัน stroke ได้ดี

name: Adhesive arachnoiditis
formal: Chronic inflammation of the arachnoid membrane following surgery, infection, haemorrhage or contrast, leading to scarring and tethering of nerve roots with chronic pain and neurological deficits.
simple: Scarring of the spinal cord coverings that makes nerve roots stick together and causes long-lasting pain, numbness and weakness.
th: การอักเสบเรื้อรังของเยื่อ arachnoid จนเกิดพังผืดดึงรั้งรากประสาท หลังผ่าตัด ติดเชื้อ เลือดออก หรือฉีดสารเข้าช่องไขสันหลัง ทำให้ปวดเรื้อรังและมีความผิดปกติทางระบบประสาท
tempoNote: Develops months to years after the triggering insult and usually persists
feat: Constant burning back and leg pain, often in several root distributions
Patchy sensory loss, weakness, reduced reflexes; sphincter disturbance in severe cases
History of multiple spinal operations, oil-based myelography, epidural or intrathecal injections, meningitis (including TB) or subarachnoid haemorrhage
Can extend to cord tethering, syringomyelia or arachnoid cysts
inv: MRI lumbar spine: clumped roots adherent centrally or to the thecal sac ('empty sac'), sometimes a soft-tissue mass
EMG: chronic multilevel radiculopathy
CSF only if active infection or inflammation is suspected

case.who: 56-year-old female rubber plantation owner from Songkhla
case.story: Three lumbar operations over ten years; persistent burning in both legs and new difficulty passing urine.
case.exam: Patchy loss of sensation L4–S1 both legs, absent ankle jerks, mild ankle weakness, no upper motor neuron signs.
case.tests: MRI: nerve roots clumped and stuck to the dural sac wall from L3 to S1; no recurrent disc.
case.q: What explains her symptoms and what are realistic treatment goals?
case.a: Adhesive arachnoiditis; the aim is pain control and function with neuropathic agents and rehabilitation — further surgery rarely helps.

read.where: Section III Other Inflammatory CNS Disorders and Neuroimmunologic Mimics

det.patho: Injury to the arachnoid causes an inflammatory exudate with fibrin deposition that matures into collagenous scar. Roots become bound together or to the dura, impairing their blood supply and CSF flow. Historical oil-based contrast and intrathecal steroids were notorious causes; today surgery, haemorrhage and infection predominate.
det.clinical: Pain is typically constant, burning and worse with activity, often with paraesthesia, cramps and fasciculation. Neurological deficits are multiradicular and asymmetric. Bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction occur in advanced cases. Thoracic involvement can cause myelopathy or syringomyelia.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows three patterns: central clumping of roots, peripheral adhesion (empty sac), or an intrathecal soft-tissue mass obliterating the sac. Correlation with history is essential because postoperative change can mimic it. Exclude recurrent disc, tumour and infection.
det.treatment: Management is multidisciplinary: neuropathic pain agents (gabapentinoids, SNRIs, tricyclics), physiotherapy, psychological support and sometimes spinal cord stimulation. Surgical adhesiolysis has disappointing long-term results except for selected syrinx or cyst decompression. Avoid further intrathecal procedures where possible.
det.prognosis: Usually chronic and stable; a minority progress slowly with worsening deficits.
pearls: Multiple back operations plus diffuse burning leg pain: look for clumped roots on MRI.
Further surgery seldom helps and may worsen adhesions.
TB meningitis can leave spinal arachnoiditis in Thai patients.
det.thd: Adhesive arachnoiditis คือการอักเสบเรื้อรังของเยื่อ arachnoid จนเกิดพังผืดยึดรากประสาท มักตามหลังผ่าตัดหลังหลายครั้ง การติดเชื้อ เช่น วัณโรคเยื่อหุ้มสมอง หรือการฉีดสารเข้าช่องไขสันหลัง ผู้ป่วยปวดแสบร้อนหลังและขาเรื้อรัง ชาหลายราก อาจปัสสาวะลำบาก MRI พบรากประสาทจับกลุ่มหรือแนบผนัง การรักษาเน้นควบคุมอาการปวดและฟื้นฟู

name: Adrenal insufficiency
formal: Inadequate cortisol production causing fatigue, hypotension, hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia; may present with confusion, myopathy or encephalopathy, and occurs in adrenoleukodystrophy.
simple: The adrenal glands do not produce enough hormones, leading to weakness, tiredness, low blood pressure and sometimes confusion.
more: Confirm with morning cortisol, ACTH and a short synacthen stimulation test; primary disease shows high ACTH and autoantibodies to 21-hydroxylase. Treat with hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone; adrenal crisis needs urgent IV hydrocortisone and saline.
th: ภาวะสร้าง cortisol ไม่พอ จากต่อมหมวกไตเอง (primary) หรือจากต่อมใต้สมอง/การหยุดสเตียรอยด์ (secondary) ทำให้อ่อนเพลีย ความดันต่ำ น้ำตาลต่ำ และสับสนได้

feat: Systemic endocrine disorder: fatigue, anorexia, nausea, postural hypotension
Hyponatraemia in all forms; hyperkalaemia and pigmentation only in primary disease
Hypoglycaemia, especially in children and secondary forms
Neurological presentations: encephalopathy, seizures from low sodium or glucose, diffuse weakness
Most common secondary cause in practice: stopping long-term glucocorticoids

Electrolytes, glucose; renin and aldosterone for primary disease
Pituitary MRI and other pituitary hormones when ACTH is low
21-hydroxylase antibodies; VLCFA in males without autoimmunity

case.story: Took a herbal powder (later found to contain dexamethasone) for knee pain for two years, stopped it a month ago; now drowsy and vomiting after a chest infection.
case.exam: Confused, BP 82/50, no pigmentation, cushingoid face, no focal neurological signs.
case.tests: Na 124 mmol/L, glucose 2.9 mmol/L; random cortisol 40 nmol/L with low ACTH.
case.q: What is the likely mechanism and the first step in management?
case.a: Secondary (HPA-axis suppression) adrenal insufficiency from hidden steroid use; give IV hydrocortisone and fluids at once, then taper slowly.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — endocrine disorders
Chapter 21 The Skin and Neurologic Disease

det.patho: Cortisol deficiency arises from adrenal destruction (primary: autoimmune, infection, haemorrhage, metastasis, ALD), from lack of pituitary ACTH (secondary: tumour, apoplexy, hypophysitis, surgery, radiotherapy) or from suppression of the axis by exogenous steroids, opioids or immune checkpoint inhibitors. Aldosterone is lost only in primary forms because renin, not ACTH, drives it. In Thailand, unregulated steroid-containing traditional remedies are a frequent cause of axis suppression.
det.clinical: Not a primary neurological disease, but it presents to neurologists as fatigue, weakness, myalgia, confusion, low mood or seizures. Weakness is usually global and non-fatigable without consistent CK rise. Crisis produces shock, vomiting, abdominal pain, fever and altered consciousness, sometimes misattributed to sepsis or encephalitis. Hyponatraemia may be severe in secondary disease because cortisol deficiency increases ADH release.
det.diagnosis: Measure morning cortisol and ACTH together; very low cortisol confirms the diagnosis, and intermediate values need a 250 µg ACTH stimulation test (interpret with assay-specific cut-offs). High ACTH means primary, low or normal ACTH means secondary or tertiary. Primary disease then needs antibodies, adrenal imaging and VLCFA in males; secondary needs pituitary MRI and other pituitary axes. Patients on steroids or oral oestrogen give misleading cortisol values.
det.treatment: Treat suspected crisis first: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV then 200 mg/day by infusion or divided doses, with saline and glucose. Maintenance is oral hydrocortisone in two or three doses, adding fludrocortisone only in primary disease. Teach sick-day dose increases, provide an emergency injection kit and medical alert card. In steroid-induced cases taper slowly while retesting the axis.
det.prognosis: Good with adequate replacement; recurrent crises and over-replacement both shorten survival and impair quality of life.
pearls: Secondary disease spares aldosterone, so potassium is normal and the skin is not dark.
Ask about clinic powders and herbal pills in every Thai patient with unexplained low cortisol.
In a hypotensive, hyponatraemic, drowsy patient, give hydrocortisone first and test later.

name: Adrenal-induced myopathy
formal: Proximal muscle weakness resulting from excess or deficient adrenal corticosteroids, including Cushing syndrome and chronic steroid therapy, with normal creatine kinase.
simple: Muscle weakness, mainly of the thighs and shoulders, caused by too much or too little steroid hormone.

tempoNote: Develops over weeks to months of hormone excess; acute form rarely after high-dose IV steroids
feat: Painless proximal weakness, worst in hip flexors and thighs, difficulty rising from a chair
Cushingoid features: central obesity, moon face, striae, thin skin
CK normal or low; reflexes and sensation preserved
Adrenal insufficiency can instead cause fatigue, cramps and weakness with hyperkalaemia

case.who: 38-year-old woman from Chiang Rai seen in medical clinic
case.story: Took a local herbal powder for knee pain for a year; noticed weight gain, easy bruising and trouble climbing stairs for 3 months.
case.exam: Round face, abdominal striae, thin skin, hip flexor and shoulder abductor weakness grade 4, reflexes normal, no sensory loss.
case.tests: CK 45 U/L; morning cortisol suppressed and ACTH low, consistent with exogenous steroid; EMG near normal.
case.q: What explains the weakness and what should be done?
case.a: Exogenous glucocorticoid myopathy from adulterated herbal medicine; stop the source with supervised steroid weaning and cover for adrenal insufficiency, then exercise rehabilitation.

read.where: Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Endocrine Myopathies

det.patho: Glucocorticoid excess promotes muscle protein breakdown, inhibits protein synthesis and impairs insulin signalling, mainly affecting fast-twitch type 2 fibres. Fluorinated steroids such as dexamethasone and triamcinolone are more myopathic. Adrenal insufficiency causes weakness via electrolyte disturbance, reduced muscle blood flow and impaired carbohydrate metabolism.
det.clinical: The chronic form is common in people on long-term oral steroids and in endogenous Cushing syndrome, giving symmetric proximal leg-predominant weakness without pain. An acute form can follow very high IV doses, overlapping with critical illness myopathy. In Thailand, steroid-adulterated herbal remedies are a recurrent hidden cause. Addison disease presents with fatigue, cramps and sometimes flexion contractures rather than marked weakness.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical, supported by a normal CK and evidence of hormone imbalance. Endocrine testing confirms Cushing syndrome or adrenal insufficiency; with exogenous steroids, endogenous cortisol is suppressed. EMG and biopsy mainly exclude alternatives. In a patient with inflammatory myositis on steroids, worsening weakness with falling CK suggests steroid myopathy rather than relapse.
det.treatment: Reduce the steroid dose to the lowest effective level or switch to a non-fluorinated agent, and use steroid-sparing drugs where possible. Treat endogenous Cushing syndrome surgically or medically. Resistance and aerobic exercise help, and adequate protein intake is important. In adrenal insufficiency, hormone replacement usually resolves symptoms.
det.prognosis: Recovery occurs over weeks to months once the hormone balance is restored, though older patients may recover incompletely.
pearls: Normal CK with proximal weakness in a steroid-treated patient favours steroid myopathy.
Ask about herbal or traditional medicines in any unexplained cushingoid patient.
Never stop long-term steroids abruptly; taper and watch for adrenal crisis.
det.thd: Cortisol ที่มากเกินไปจาก Cushing syndrome หรือการกินยา steroid นาน ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อสลายและต้นขาอ่อนแรงโดยไม่ปวด ค่า CK มักปกติ ส่วนภาวะต่อมหมวกไตทำงานน้อยทำให้อ่อนเพลียและเป็นตะคริว วินิจฉัยจากประวัติและตรวจฮอร์โมน รักษาโดยลดหรือหยุด steroid อย่างค่อยเป็นค่อยไปและออกกำลังกาย

name: Adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD)
formal: X-linked peroxisomal disorder from ABCD1 mutation with very long chain fatty acid accumulation, causing childhood cerebral demyelination, adrenal insufficiency or adult adrenomyeloneuropathy.
simple: An inherited disease in which fatty substances build up and damage the brain's white matter, spinal cord and adrenal glands.
more: Screen with plasma very long chain fatty acids (raised C26:0); MRI shows posterior-predominant symmetric white matter change with rim enhancement. Early cerebral disease is treated by stem cell transplant; steroid replacement for adrenal failure. X-linked ABCD1 peroxisomal disorder with very long chain fatty acid accumulation, cerebral demyelination, adrenal insufficiency or adrenomyeloneuropathy.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมถ่ายทอดทางโครโมโซม X จากยีน ABCD1 กรดไขมันสายยาวมากสะสม ทำให้เนื้อขาวสมองถูกทำลาย ต่อมหมวกไตล้มเหลว หรือไขสันหลังเสื่อม
tempoNote: Cerebral form in boys (4–10 y) progresses over months; AMN in adults progresses slowly over years
feat: Boys: school decline, attention and behaviour problems, visual and hearing loss, then rapid spastic quadriparesis
Adult men: adrenomyeloneuropathy — slowly progressive spastic paraparesis, sensory ataxia, bladder and erectile dysfunction
Primary adrenal insufficiency (bronzed skin, fatigue, hypotension), may precede neurological signs
Female carriers often develop a milder myelopathy after age 40
Same mutation can cause different phenotypes within one family
inv: Plasma very long chain fatty acids (raised C26:0 and C26:0/C22:0 ratio); C26:0-lysophosphatidylcholine for screening
MRI: symmetric parieto-occipital white matter lesions with enhancing leading edge; Loes score
Morning cortisol and ACTH (adrenal function)
ABCD1 genetic testing (essential in women, whose VLCFA can be normal)

case.story: Teachers report his grades have dropped and he bumps into things; over three months he has become clumsy and irritable. He tans easily.
case.exam: Hyperpigmented gums and skin creases, impaired visual fields, brisk reflexes with bilateral Babinski signs.
case.tests: MRI symmetric posterior white matter T2 lesions with contrast-enhancing rim; C26:0 raised; ACTH high, cortisol low.
case.q: Which disorder fits, and what treatment is time-critical?
case.a: Cerebral X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy; urgent referral for haematopoietic stem cell transplant (or gene therapy) while disease is early, plus steroid replacement.

read.where: Adult-Onset Inherited Leukodystrophies — X-Linked Adrenoleukodystrophy, p. 994

det.patho: Loss of the ABCD1 peroxisomal transporter prevents very long chain fatty acids from entering peroxisomes for beta-oxidation, so they accumulate in myelin, adrenal cortex and testis. The cerebral form involves an inflammatory demyelinating process that breaks the blood–brain barrier (enhancing edge), while AMN is a non-inflammatory distal axonopathy of long spinal tracts. There is no genotype–phenotype correlation, so family members with the same variant can differ greatly.
det.clinical: Childhood cerebral ALD typically begins between 4 and 10 years with inattention and school decline, then visual, auditory and motor loss leading to a vegetative state within a few years if untreated. Adolescent and adult cerebral forms also occur, including conversion from AMN. AMN presents in the twenties or thirties with slowly worsening stiff legs, sensory ataxia and sphincter problems. Adrenal insufficiency affects most males and may be the only finding. Heterozygous women commonly develop late-onset myelopathy.
det.diagnosis: Raised plasma VLCFA confirms the diagnosis in males; women require ABCD1 testing. MRI with contrast and Loes scoring identifies cerebral disease; boys diagnosed by family or newborn screening need MRI surveillance every 6–12 months to catch early lesions. Check adrenal function at diagnosis and periodically. Newborn screening for ALD is now implemented in many countries.
det.treatment: Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation halts cerebral disease if done early (low Loes score, minimal symptoms); autologous lentiviral gene therapy (elivaldogene autotemcel) is an alternative in some regions. Adrenal insufficiency needs lifelong steroid replacement and stress dosing. AMN is managed with spasticity treatment, bladder care and rehabilitation; leriglitazone and other agents have been studied in trials. Lorenzo's oil does not alter established disease.
det.prognosis: Untreated childhood cerebral ALD is fatal within several years; AMN progresses slowly over decades.
pearls: Any boy with Addison disease needs VLCFA testing — and any boy with leukodystrophy needs adrenal testing.
Posterior symmetric white matter lesions with an enhancing rim are typical of cerebral ALD.
Female carriers can be symptomatic and may have normal VLCFA; use gene testing.
det.thd: Adrenoleukodystrophy เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมทางโครโมโซม X จากยีน ABCD1 ทำให้กรดไขมันสายยาวมาก (VLCFA) สะสม เด็กชายมีการเรียนถดถอย การมองเห็นและการเดินแย่ลงอย่างรวดเร็ว ผู้ใหญ่มีขาเกร็งค่อย ๆ เป็น (AMN) และหลายคนต่อมหมวกไตล้มเหลว ตรวจพบ VLCFA สูงและ MRI มีรอยโรคเนื้อขาวด้านหลังขอบ enhance การปลูกถ่ายไขกระดูกระยะแรกช่วยหยุดโรคได้ และต้องให้ steroid ทดแทน

name: Adrenomyeloneuropathy (AMN)
formal: X-linked ABCD1-related adult phenotype of adrenoleukodystrophy with very-long-chain fatty acid accumulation causing spastic paraparesis, mild axonal neuropathy, and adrenal insufficiency.
simple: An inherited disorder, mainly in men, causing slowly worsening leg stiffness and weakness, along with adrenal gland problems.
more: Elevated plasma very-long-chain fatty acids and ABCD1 mutation confirm it. Replace adrenal hormones; Lorenzo's oil is of limited benefit; progression is slow over decades. Adult-onset X-linked ABCD1 disorder (adrenomyeloneuropathy) with progressive spastic paraparesis, sensory and sphincter disturbance and adrenal insufficiency, due to distal axonopathy of long tracts.
th: รูปแบบผู้ใหญ่ของ X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy จากยีน ABCD1 ทำให้ขาเกร็งอ่อนแรงช้า ๆ ชาปลายเท้า ปัสสาวะผิดปกติ และต่อมหมวกไตทำงานไม่พอ

feat: Slowly progressive spastic paraparesis with brisk knee jerks and extensor plantars
Impaired vibration and joint position in the feet; ankle jerks may be lost from coexisting axonal neuropathy
Urgency, incontinence and erectile dysfunction appear early relative to the weakness

case.story: Three years of stiff, tiring legs and urinary urgency; he was treated for Addison disease at 25 after collapsing with low sodium.
case.exam: Spastic gait, hyperreflexia with Babinski signs, reduced vibration to the knees, absent ankle jerks, tanned palmar creases.
case.tests: MRI spine shows diffuse thoracic cord atrophy without compression; C26:0 markedly raised.
case.q: What single-gene disorder unifies the adrenal and spinal findings, and which relatives need testing?

det.patho: Pathogenic variants in ABCD1 impair the peroxisomal transporter that imports very-long-chain acyl-CoA for beta-oxidation, so these fats build up in myelin, adrenal cortex and Leydig cells. In AMN the dominant lesion is a dying-back degeneration of the longest spinal tracts (corticospinal and dorsal columns) with a milder axonal neuropathy. The same genotype can give childhood cerebral ALD, AMN or isolated Addison disease even within one family, so other modifiers must operate.
det.clinical: Men usually notice leg stiffness and imbalance in early adulthood, followed by bladder and sexual symptoms; the course is slowly progressive over decades. Adrenal insufficiency is present in most men and may be the first clue, sometimes years earlier. Carrier women commonly develop a milder myelopathy with prominent sensory ataxia after middle age, often misdiagnosed as MS or spondylosis. A minority of men convert to cerebral ALD with behavioural change and rapid decline, which is the main threat to life.
det.diagnosis: Measure plasma VLCFA in any man with unexplained progressive myelopathy, particularly with adrenal failure; in women VLCFA may be normal, so genetic testing is needed. Confirm with ABCD1 sequencing and check adrenal function. Brain MRI identifies cerebral involvement, scored with the Loes scale. Nerve conduction often shows an axonal sensorimotor neuropathy.
det.treatment: Lifelong glucocorticoid replacement for adrenal insufficiency, with stress dosing during illness. Spasticity, bladder and pain are treated symptomatically, with physiotherapy and mobility aids. Lorenzo's oil has not shown convincing benefit for AMN; leriglitazone and other agents are under study. Men need periodic brain MRI so that cerebral conversion is caught early, when haematopoietic stem cell transplantation or gene therapy may be considered.
det.prognosis: Pure AMN progresses slowly, many needing a walking aid within 10–20 years; cerebral conversion carries a poor outlook.
pearls: Spastic paraparesis plus Addison disease in a man: send VLCFA.
Women carriers are not merely carriers; many develop symptoms later in life.
Do routine brain MRI surveillance because cerebral ALD can still appear in adults.
det.thd: AMN เป็นโรคทางพันธุกรรมแบบ X-linked จากยีน ABCD1 ทำให้กรดไขมันสายยาวมากสะสม ผู้ชายวัยหนุ่มมีขาเกร็งอ่อนแรง ชาปลายเท้า ปัสสาวะกะปริบกะปรอย และมักมีต่อมหมวกไตบกพร่อง ตรวจ VLCFA ในเลือดและยีน ABCD1 เพื่อยืนยัน การรักษาเน้นให้ฮอร์โมนทดแทน ลดเกร็ง และตรวจ MRI สมองเป็นระยะเพื่อจับการลุกลามเข้าสมอง

simple: A rare inherited disorder where abnormal sugar deposits build up in nerves, causing stiff weak legs, numbness and bladder problems.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมสะสม polyglucosan ในผู้ใหญ่จากยีน GBE1 ทำให้ขาเกร็งอ่อนแรง ปัสสาวะผิดปกติก่อน ชาปลายเท้า และความจำลดลง

case.story: Has had urinary urgency for five years, then over three years his legs became stiff and he now uses a cane; his feet feel numb.
case.exam: Spastic legs with brisk knee jerks, absent ankle jerks, extensor plantars, distal leg wasting, reduced vibration to the knees.
case.tests: MRI: diffuse white matter change and atrophy of medulla and thoracic cord; NCS axonal neuropathy; reduced GBE activity and biallelic GBE1 variants.
case.q: Which combination of findings should prompt this diagnosis?
case.a: Adult polyglucosan body disease — early neurogenic bladder plus spastic paraparesis with neuropathy and leukoencephalopathy with cord atrophy.

det.patho: Reduced activity of glycogen branching enzyme leads to poorly branched glycogen (polyglucosan) that is insoluble and accumulates as bodies in axons, astrocytes and other tissues. Long central and peripheral axons are most vulnerable, explaining the combination of myelopathy and neuropathy. It is the adult end of the GBE1 spectrum that includes fatal infantile glycogen storage disease type IV.
det.clinical: Most patients present in their 40s to 60s. Bladder dysfunction commonly precedes leg stiffness by years, then a gait disorder mixing upper and lower motor neuron features, plus distal sensory loss, develops. Cognitive slowing, mild dysarthria and autonomic failure may appear later. It is often misdiagnosed as progressive MS, spondylotic myelopathy or ALS.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in late-onset progressive paraparesis with early bladder involvement and neuropathy. MRI showing leukoencephalopathy with medullary and cord atrophy is characteristic. Confirm with GBE enzyme activity and GBE1 sequencing, including the common p.Y329S variant and deep intronic variants. Biopsy is now rarely needed.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy is established; triheptanoin and other approaches have been explored in small studies. Management is supportive: antispasticity drugs, bladder management (clean intermittent catheterisation, antimuscarinics with caution), physiotherapy, walking aids and treatment of orthostatic hypotension. Genetic counselling is appropriate.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive over 10–20 years, with many patients eventually needing a wheelchair.
pearls: Neurogenic bladder years before spastic paraparesis is a strong clue.
Upper and lower motor neuron signs plus sensory neuropathy in a middle-aged adult: consider APBD alongside AMN.
MRI combining white matter change and medulla/cord atrophy points the way.
det.thd: Adult polyglucosan body disease เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมแบบยีนด้อยจากยีน GBE1 ทำให้ไกลโคเจนผิดรูป (polyglucosan) สะสมในแกนประสาท ผู้ป่วยวัยกลางคนมักเริ่มด้วยปัสสาวะผิดปกติก่อน แล้วขาเกร็งอ่อนแรง ชาปลายเท้า และอาจความจำลดลง MRI พบรอยโรคเนื้อขาวร่วมกับไขสันหลังและก้านสมองฝ่อ วินิจฉัยด้วยการวัดเอนไซม์และตรวจยีน การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง

simple: A set of inherited diseases damaging the brain's white matter in adults, causing memory loss, mood changes, stiffness and walking problems.
more: Genetic white matter disorders presenting in adulthood, including ALSP, adrenomyeloneuropathy, Alexander disease and CADASIL-like disorders, with spastic gait, ataxia and cognitive decline.
ab: Inherited white matter disease of adults
th: กลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมของเนื้อขาวสมองที่เริ่มอาการในวัยผู้ใหญ่ เช่น X-ALD, CSF1R-related leukoencephalopathy, Alexander disease และ MLD ทำให้ความจำ พฤติกรรม และการเคลื่อนไหวเสื่อมลง

Clues: family history, adrenal failure (ALD), palatal tremor and bulbar signs (Alexander), early dementia with calcifications (CSF1R)
Symmetric confluent white matter change on MRI unlike patchy vascular or MS lesions
Peripheral neuropathy in metachromatic leukodystrophy and Krabbe disease

case.who: 42-year-old male bank manager from Chiang Rai
case.story: Two years of personality change, poor planning and later stiff legs; his mother died of 'early dementia' in her fifties.
case.exam: Frontal release signs, apathy, mild spastic paraparesis, brisk reflexes.
case.tests: MRI: confluent bifrontal white matter T2 signal with thinned corpus callosum and small diffusion-restricting foci; CT: punctate frontal white matter calcifications; CSF1R pathogenic variant.
case.q: Which leukodystrophy is this?
case.a: CSF1R-related disease (ALSP), an adult-onset leukoencephalopathy featuring axonal spheroids and pigmented glia.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Adult-Onset Inherited Leukodystrophies

det.patho: Each disorder disrupts a different part of white matter biology: peroxisomal fatty acid handling (X-ALD), lysosomal sulfatide breakdown (MLD), astrocyte intermediate filaments (Alexander, GFAP), microglial signalling (CSF1R), mitochondrial or translation machinery (AARS2, eIF2B). Adult-onset forms usually reflect milder residual function. Inheritance may be X-linked, dominant or recessive.
det.clinical: Presentation is often psychiatric or cognitive in mid-adulthood with later motor decline. X-ALD in men may begin as adrenomyeloneuropathy with spastic paraparesis; women carriers can develop a later myelopathy. Alexander disease favours brainstem features with palatal tremor; MLD can show neuropathy and psychosis. Many are misdiagnosed as MS, vascular dementia or psychiatric illness.
det.diagnosis: Start with MRI pattern analysis and targeted biochemical tests, then a broad genetic panel or exome. Exclude acquired causes such as vascular disease, MS, toxic leukoencephalopathy, HIV, PML and B12 deficiency. Family testing aids variant interpretation.
det.treatment: Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can halt early cerebral ALD and some MLD and CSF1R cases if done before major disability. Adrenal replacement is mandatory in ALD with insufficiency. Otherwise care is supportive: spasticity, seizures, psychiatric symptoms, nutrition and genetic counselling.
det.prognosis: Generally progressive over years to a decade or more; outcome depends on subtype and timing of any transplant.
pearls: Symmetric confluent white matter disease in a young adult is not 'small vessel disease' — think genetic.
Check adrenal function in a man with spastic paraparesis and white matter change.
CT calcifications help flag CSF1R disease.
det.thd: Adult-onset inherited leukodystrophies คือกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมของเนื้อขาวสมองที่เริ่มในวัยผู้ใหญ่ เช่น X-ALD, CSF1R, Alexander และ MLD ผู้ป่วยมักเริ่มด้วยพฤติกรรมเปลี่ยนหรือความจำเสื่อม ตามด้วยขาเกร็งและเดินเซ MRI พบเนื้อขาวผิดปกติสมมาตรเป็นแผ่น การวินิจฉัยใช้รูปแบบ MRI ผลตรวจทางชีวเคมี และการตรวจยีน การปลูกถ่ายไขกระดูกช่วยได้บางชนิดถ้าทำเร็ว นอกนั้นเป็นการรักษาประคับประคอง

name: Adult-onset Niemann–Pick disease type C
formal: Lysosomal cholesterol transport disorder from NPC1 or NPC2 mutation presenting in adulthood with psychiatric symptoms, cognitive decline, ataxia, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and dystonia.
simple: An inherited disease affecting how cells handle cholesterol, causing psychiatric symptoms, memory trouble, clumsiness and difficulty moving the eyes up and down.
th: โรคสะสมคอเลสเตอรอลในไลโซโซมจากยีน NPC1/NPC2 ที่เริ่มในผู้ใหญ่ มีอาการจิตเวช สมองเสื่อม เดินเซ กลอกตาแนวดิ่งไม่ได้ และ dystonia
tempoNote: Insidious onset in late teens to 40s, with psychiatric or cognitive change often preceding motor signs by years
feat: Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, often first as slowed downward saccades
Progressive cerebellar ataxia and dysarthria
Psychosis, depression or executive cognitive decline, sometimes labelled schizophrenia first
Dystonia, cataplexy triggered by laughter (gelastic cataplexy) and dysphagia
History of neonatal jaundice or mild splenomegaly in some patients
inv: Plasma oxysterols, lysosphingomyelin-509 or bile acid markers as screening tests
NPC1 and NPC2 genetic testing; filipin staining of fibroblasts if variants are uncertain
Abdominal ultrasound for spleen size; MRI may show cerebellar or frontal atrophy

case.story: Treated for psychosis for two years, then colleagues noticed clumsy walking and slurred speech; she sometimes drops to the floor when laughing.
case.exam: Slow vertical saccades with limited downgaze that improves with doll's-eye manoeuvre, limb ataxia, mild arm dystonia.
case.tests: Spleen 14 cm on ultrasound; plasma oxysterols elevated.
case.q: Which treatable lysosomal disorder fits, and what drug is used?
case.a: Niemann–Pick type C; miglustat (and in some countries arimoclomol) may slow neurological progression.

det.patho: NPC1 (about 95%) or NPC2 loss impairs export of unesterified cholesterol and glycosphingolipids from late endosomes and lysosomes. Lipids accumulate in neurons, especially Purkinje cells and brainstem nuclei, with neurofibrillary tangles resembling those of Alzheimer disease. Visceral storage in spleen and liver is variable and tends to be mild in adult forms.
det.clinical: Adult presentations cluster into psychiatric, cognitive and movement patterns that overlap over time. Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy is the most specific sign and should be looked for in any young patient with psychosis plus neurological signs. Gelastic cataplexy, dysphagia, seizures and dystonia emerge as the disease advances. Splenomegaly may be absent or detected only on imaging.
det.diagnosis: Screening biomarkers (oxysterols, lyso-SM-509, bile acid metabolites) are sensitive and quick; confirm with NPC1/NPC2 sequencing. Filipin staining of cultured fibroblasts is a functional backup when variants are of uncertain significance. Suspicion indices combining visceral, neurological and psychiatric items help decide whom to test. Exclude Wilson disease, which is more common and also treatable.
det.treatment: Miglustat, a substrate-reduction drug, is approved in many countries and may stabilise swallowing and ambulation; arimoclomol and levacetylleucine were approved in the US in 2024 as additions. Symptomatic care covers psychosis (with caution about dopamine blockers worsening movement), seizures, cataplexy, dysphagia and dystonia. Speech and swallow therapy, nutrition and genetic counselling are core.
det.prognosis: Adult-onset disease progresses over one to several decades; death most often follows aspiration from failing swallow.
pearls: Psychosis plus vertical gaze palsy in a young adult: check NPC biomarkers.
Laughter-triggered falls are gelastic cataplexy, a strong clue.
Downward saccade slowing is often the earliest eye sign.
det.thd: Niemann–Pick type C ชนิดเริ่มในผู้ใหญ่ เกิดจากยีน NPC1/NPC2 ทำให้คอเลสเตอรอลค้างในไลโซโซมของเซลล์ประสาท ผู้ป่วยอาจมาด้วยอาการจิตเวชหรือความจำเสื่อมก่อน แล้วตามด้วยเดินเซ พูดไม่ชัด มองลงล่างไม่ได้ และล้มเมื่อหัวเราะ ตรวจ oxysterol หรือ lyso-SM-509 แล้วยืนยันด้วยยีน รักษาด้วย miglustat ร่วมกับการรักษาตามอาการ

name: Advanced sleep–wake phase disorder
formal: Circadian rhythm disorder with sleep onset and waking much earlier than desired, due to an advanced circadian phase; some familial cases involve PER2 mutations.
simple: A body-clock problem in which a person gets sleepy very early in the evening and wakes up far too early in the morning.
th: นาฬิกาชีวภาพเร็วกว่าปกติ ทำให้ง่วงมากตั้งแต่หัวค่ำและตื่นเช้ามืดเกินต้องการ พบในผู้สูงอายุ และบางครอบครัวเกิดจากยีน PER2 หรือ CK1delta
tempoNote: Usually middle or older age, persisting for at least 3 months; familial forms can start in youth
feat: Irresistible sleepiness from about 7–8 pm and spontaneous waking around 2–5 am
Sleep is normal in length if allowed to follow the early schedule
Complaint is often early-morning waking, mistaken for insomnia or depression
Less common than the delayed type; more common in older adults
Familial advanced sleep phase with autosomal dominant inheritance (PER2, CSNK1D)
inv: Sleep diary and actigraphy for at least 7 days
Morningness–eveningness questionnaire shows strong morning type
DLMO is early, if available
Screen for depression, which also causes early waking

case.story: She falls asleep in front of the television at 7:30 pm and wakes wide awake at 3:30 am; she cannot stay up for family dinners. Her mother had the same pattern.
case.exam: Normal; no depressive symptoms on screening.
case.tests: Actigraphy: stable sleep from 8 pm to 4 am, about 7.5 h per night.
case.q: Which light timing helps?
case.a: Advanced sleep–wake phase disorder; evening bright light (about 7–9 pm) delays the clock, with avoidance of early-morning light.

read.where: Chapter 29 Disorders of Sleep — Advanced Sleep–Wake Phase Disorder

det.patho: The circadian clock runs early, often with a shorter intrinsic period. Familial forms are caused by mutations affecting clock protein phosphorylation such as PER2 and casein kinase 1 delta. Ageing also advances circadian phase and reduces the strength of the circadian signal.
det.clinical: Patients become very sleepy in the early evening and wake in the early morning unable to return to sleep. If they force themselves to stay up, they still wake early and become sleep deprived. The disorder is often missed or labelled as insomnia or depression in older adults.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires a stable advance of the main sleep period with distress or impairment, shown by at least 7 days of diary or actigraphy. Sleep is of normal length and quality on the preferred schedule. Depression and early waking from other sleep disorders such as OSA must be excluded.
det.treatment: Evening bright light delays the clock and is the main treatment, combined with avoiding early-morning light, for example with sunglasses on early walks. Keep a regular schedule and plan evening activities. Low-dose morning melatonin is theoretically sensible but has little evidence and may cause daytime drowsiness. Hypnotics do not fix the timing problem.
det.prognosis: Tends to be lifelong, especially in familial cases, but symptoms are manageable with light.
pearls: Light in the evening delays the clock; light in the early morning advances it further.
Early waking with normal mood and early sleepiness suggests circadian advance, not depression.
det.thd: Advanced sleep–wake phase disorder คือนาฬิกาชีวภาพเร็ว ง่วงตั้งแต่หัวค่ำและตื่นตีสามตีสี่ แต่ถ้านอนตามเวลาที่ร่างกายต้องการจะได้ชั่วโมงนอนปกติ พบในผู้สูงอายุและบางครอบครัวมียีน PER2 หรือ CK1delta วินิจฉัยด้วย sleep diary หรือ actigraphy และต้องแยกจากโรคซึมเศร้า การรักษาหลักคือรับแสงสว่างช่วงหัวค่ำและหลีกเลี่ยงแสงเช้ามืด

name: Agnosia
formal: Inability to recognise objects, faces or sounds despite intact primary sensation and intellect, due to lesions in modality-specific association cortex such as occipitotemporal regions.
simple: Being unable to recognise things such as objects, faces or sounds even though the eyes or ears work normally.
th: การไม่สามารถจดจำวัตถุ ใบหน้า หรือเสียง แม้การรับรู้ขั้นต้นและสติปัญญาปกติ จากรอยโรคที่ association cortex เฉพาะประสาทสัมผัส
tempoNote: Acute after stroke; gradual in neurodegenerative disease
feat: A clinical sign or syndrome rather than a disease
Visual agnosia: cannot recognise objects by sight but can by touch
Prosopagnosia: face blindness, usually bilateral or right fusiform lesions
Auditory agnosia: cannot recognise sounds despite normal hearing
Causes: posterior cerebral artery stroke, posterior cortical atrophy, encephalitis, trauma
inv: Bedside: naming objects by sight vs touch, face recognition, copying
Neuropsychological testing
MRI brain; amyloid/tau biomarkers when degenerative

case.story: Gradually cannot find objects on the table and failed to recognise his grandson at the door, though memory is relatively preserved.
case.exam: Cannot name a key by sight but names it immediately by touch; visual acuity normal; simultanagnosia.
case.tests: MRI: bilateral occipitoparietal atrophy; CSF profile consistent with Alzheimer pathology.
case.q: What syndrome is this?
case.a: Visual agnosia and simultanagnosia from posterior cortical atrophy, usually an atypical presentation of Alzheimer disease.

Chapter 11 Cognitive Impairment and Dementia — Perception

det.patho: Agnosia reflects damage to association cortex that links primary sensory input with stored knowledge. Apperceptive forms arise from impaired perceptual integration; associative forms from disconnection between percept and meaning. The ventral visual stream (occipitotemporal) handles object and face recognition.
det.clinical: Patients can see, hear or feel but cannot recognise. Visual agnosia causes difficulty identifying objects; prosopagnosia affects faces; auditory agnosia affects environmental sounds or words; astereognosis affects touch. Patients often compensate with other senses.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires showing intact primary sensation, attention and language, then impaired recognition in one modality. Neuropsychological tests and imaging identify the lesion.
det.treatment: Treat the cause (stroke, dementia). Rehabilitation teaches compensatory strategies such as using voice, clothing or context to recognise people.
det.prognosis: Partial recovery after stroke; progressive in degenerative disease.
pearls: Recognises by touch but not by sight = visual agnosia.
Prosopagnosia usually involves the right fusiform gyrus.
Posterior cortical atrophy often presents as visual agnosia with relative memory sparing.
det.thd: Agnosia คือการจดจำสิ่งต่าง ๆ ไม่ได้ทั้งที่การมองเห็น การได้ยิน หรือการสัมผัสปกติ เป็นอาการทางคลินิก ไม่ใช่โรค เช่น visual agnosia, prosopagnosia (จำหน้าไม่ได้) และ auditory agnosia เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ association cortex เช่น stroke ของ PCA หรือ posterior cortical atrophy วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจข้างเตียง การทดสอบทางประสาทจิตวิทยา และ MRI

name: Aicardi–Goutières syndrome (AGS)
formal: Genetic interferon-driven encephalopathy (AGS) with basal ganglia calcification, white matter changes, CSF lymphocytosis and progressive microcephaly, often resembling congenital infection.
simple: A rare inherited illness in which the immune system is overactive in the brain, causing small head size, seizures and developmental delay.
more: Inherited type I interferonopathy (TREX1, RNASEH2A-C, SAMHD1 and others) with early-onset encephalopathy, intracranial calcification, leukodystrophy, raised CSF interferon and chilblain-like skin lesions.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมที่ interferon ชนิดที่ 1 ถูกกระตุ้นต่อเนื่อง ทารกมีสมองอักเสบเรื้อรัง หินปูนในสมอง เนื้อขาวผิดปกติ ศีรษะเล็ก และผื่นคล้ายถูกความเย็นกัด ดูคล้ายติดเชื้อแต่กำเนิดแต่ตรวจเชื้อไม่พบ
tempoNote: Typical onset in the first year with a subacute encephalopathic phase over weeks to months, then a largely fixed but severe deficit; late-onset genotypes evolve slowly
feat: Irritability, poor feeding, jitteriness and sterile low-grade fevers in a previously normal infant
Loss of milestones with acquired microcephaly, spasticity, dystonia and axial hypotonia
Chilblain-like purple lesions on toes, fingers and ears, worse in cool weather
Basal ganglia and subcortical calcification with leukoencephalopathy and progressive atrophy
Some genotypes (ADAR, IFIH1, RNASEH2B) give later-onset spastic paraparesis, bilateral striatal necrosis or near-normal cognition
inv: CT for calcification (basal ganglia, thalami, dentate, periventricular); MRI for white-matter signal change and atrophy
CSF: mild lymphocytosis early, raised interferon-alpha and neopterin, infection studies negative
Blood interferon-stimulated gene expression score, often persistently high
Gene panel or exome: TREX1, RNASEH2A/B/C, SAMHD1, ADAR, IFIH1, LSM11, RNU7-1

case.story: Normal at birth. From about 3 months she became fretful, stopped social smiling and had repeated fevers with no focus. Her toes turn purple and sore in the cool season. A sibling died in infancy of an unexplained brain disease.
case.exam: Head circumference crossing down the centiles, poor head control, increased limb tone with dystonic posturing, chilblain-like toe lesions.
case.tests: CT: symmetric basal ganglia calcification. CSF: 12 lymphocytes/mm3, negative bacterial culture, viral PCR and TORCH studies. Blood interferon signature strongly raised.
case.q: Why should this infant not simply be labelled congenital infection?
case.a: Repeated negative infection tests, chilblains, a family history and a high interferon signature point to Aicardi–Goutières syndrome, a genetic interferonopathy; the gene panel confirms it.

read.where: Aicardi-Goutières syndrome: differential diagnosis and aetiopathogenesis (Funct Neurol 2003)

det.patho: AGS is the prototype type I interferonopathy. Variants in nucleic-acid handling genes (TREX1 DNA exonuclease; RNASEH2A, B and C; SAMHD1; ADAR1 RNA editing; the RNA sensor IFIH1; and more recently the histone-processing genes LSM11 and RNU7-1) allow self DNA or RNA to accumulate and trigger innate antiviral sensors. Chronic interferon-alpha signalling injures small brain and skin vessels, microglia and oligodendroglia, producing calcification and white-matter disease. Inheritance is mostly autosomal recessive, though dominant or de novo variants occur in TREX1, ADAR and IFIH1.
det.clinical: The classic early form resembles a congenital infection: a normal or slightly small head at birth, then irritability, feeding trouble, sterile fevers and regression within months. Examination shows acquired microcephaly, spasticity with dystonia and poor visual contact, and about half have seizures. Chilblains, glaucoma, hypothyroidism, cytopenias and lupus-like autoantibodies may accompany. After the active phase, neurological status often plateaus, though many remain profoundly disabled. Later-onset and mild phenotypes are well recognised, including isolated spastic paraparesis, striatal necrosis after a febrile illness, and cases with normal intellect.
det.diagnosis: Suspect AGS when infantile encephalopathy with calcification and leukoencephalopathy has a negative infection work-up. CT shows calcification best, MRI shows white-matter change and atrophy, and early CSF may show lymphocytosis with raised interferon-alpha or neopterin. A raised blood interferon-stimulated gene score supports the diagnosis and is positive in most genotypes, although a normal score does not fully exclude it. Confirm with a gene panel or exome and offer counselling. Exclude congenital infection, Cockayne syndrome, mitochondrial disease, hypoparathyroidism and lupus.
det.treatment: Management is supportive: feeding and nutrition, seizure control, treatment of spasticity and dystonia, and surveillance for glaucoma, thyroid disease and cytopenias. JAK inhibitors, notably baricitinib and ruxolitinib, lower interferon signalling and have improved skin disease, interferon scores and in some children neurological function in open-label studies. Benefit appears greatest when started early, before established injury. Treatment is given in specialist centres with monitoring for infection and blood counts, and the evidence is still limited.
det.prognosis: Early-onset disease usually carries severe disability and reduced survival, whereas later-onset or ADAR- and IFIH1-related forms vary widely and can allow long survival with partial function.
pearls: Pseudo-TORCH picture with negative infection studies: order an interferon signature and genes.
Chilblains in an encephalopathic infant, or a sibling with the same illness, are strong bedside clues.
Calcification, white-matter disease and CSF lymphocytes form the classic triad, but late-onset forms may lack calcification.
det.thd: AGS เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมที่ร่างกายจัดการกรดนิวคลีอิกของตัวเองไม่ได้ จึงสร้าง interferon ชนิดที่ 1 มากเกินไปต่อเนื่อง ทารกจะงอแง ไข้โดยไม่พบเชื้อ พัฒนาการถดถอย ศีรษะเล็ก และมีผื่นคล้ายถูกความเย็นกัดที่นิ้วมือเท้า ภาพสมองพบหินปูนและเนื้อขาวผิดปกติคล้ายติดเชื้อแต่กำเนิดแต่ตรวจเชื้อไม่พบ ยืนยันด้วย interferon signature และตรวจยีน เช่น TREX1 RNASEH2 SAMHD1 ADAR IFIH1 การรักษาหลักคือประคับประคอง และยากลุ่ม JAK inhibitor เช่น baricitinib เป็นทางเลือกใหม่ที่ยังอยู่ระหว่างการศึกษา

name: Akathisia
formal: Subjective inner restlessness with compulsion to move, with pacing and shifting of the legs, typically a side effect of dopamine-blocking drugs such as antipsychotics.
simple: An uncomfortable inner restlessness that makes a person feel they must keep moving, often caused by certain medicines.
th: Akathisia คือความรู้สึกกระวนกระวายภายในร่วมกับแรงผลักให้ขยับตัวตลอดเวลา พบบ่อยหลังได้ยาต้านโดพามีน เช่น antipsychotic, metoclopramide และ prochlorperazine ผู้ป่วยนั่งนิ่งไม่ได้ ขยับขา โยกตัว หรือเดินวน อาจถูกวินิจฉัยผิดว่าเป็นโรควิตกกังวลหรืออาการทางจิตกำเริบ และเสี่ยงต่อการฆ่าตัวตาย ต้องลดขนาดยาหรือเปลี่ยนยาและให้ propranolol หรือ benzodiazepine
tempoNote: Acute akathisia starts hours to days after a new drug or dose rise; tardive forms follow months of exposure and can outlast the drug
feat: A distressing inner restlessness with an urge to move that is relieved only briefly by moving, plus rocking, pacing, crossing and uncrossing the legs
Worse when asked to sit or stand still; the trunk and legs are affected much more than the arms
Dopamine blockers (antipsychotics including aripiprazole, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine) are the commonest cause, and SSRIs, antidepressants and calcium channel blockers can cause it too
Often misread as anxiety, agitation or relapse of psychosis, so doses are wrongly raised and the patient stops treatment
Linked to suicidal thoughts and violence; a tic patient given pimozide may be thought to have worse tics when this is actually akathisia
inv: Clinical diagnosis; timeline of drug starts, increases and withdrawals
Barnes Akathisia Rating Scale for severity and monitoring
Iron studies and ferritin when restless legs syndrome or iron deficiency might be present
Screen for risk of self-harm and for coexistent parkinsonism or dystonia

case.who: 28-year-old man from Rayong admitted with first-episode psychosis
case.story: After haloperidol was increased he paces the ward, cannot sit through meals and says he wants to 'crawl out of his skin'. The nurses think his psychosis is worse.
case.exam: Constant weight-shifting between the legs on standing and rocking when seated; no rigidity or tremor; he says the urge is intolerable.
case.tests: Barnes global score 4; ferritin normal; no other cause on review.
case.q: What is the right response?
case.a: Acute akathisia. Do not raise the antipsychotic; reduce the dose or switch to a lower-risk agent, and add propranolol 10–20 mg, two to three doses daily, or a short course of a benzodiazepine; mirtazapine at low dose is another option.

17 - The tardive syndromes: Phenomenology, concepts on pathophysiology and treatment, and other neuroleptic-­induced syndromes

det.patho: Akathisia is associated with blockade of dopamine D2 receptors in mesocortical and mesolimbic pathways, with contributions from serotonergic, noradrenergic, GABAergic and opioid systems. The effect of 5-HT2A antagonists and beta-blockers supports multiple mechanisms. Dose, speed of titration, high-potency agents and iron deficiency raise risk.
det.clinical: Patients describe a compelling need to move, particularly in the legs, and objective signs include pacing, shifting weight, rocking and repeatedly crossing the legs. The inner feeling distinguishes akathisia from the involuntary but not compelled movements of dyskinesia. It appears early after a new or increased dose and is the most common acute movement disorder seen on antipsychotics. The consequences include poor adherence, agitation, aggression, falls and, in some patients, suicidal thoughts, which have been reported in patients with and without psychiatric illness.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, built on the subjective urge and objective restlessness, in the context of a dopamine-blocking drug. Rating scales, especially the Barnes scale, document severity. Check for other causes of restlessness: anxiety, agitated depression, mania, withdrawal, stimulant use, hyperthyroidism and restless legs syndrome. The key diagnostic act is to look at the timing against the drug dose rather than at the behaviour alone.
det.treatment: Lower the dose of the offending drug or switch to an agent with less risk when possible. Propranolol (for example 10–20 mg, two to three doses daily) and benzodiazepines such as clonazepam give prompt relief, and low-dose mirtazapine, 5-HT2A antagonists and vitamin B6 have supporting data. Anticholinergics help when akathisia is accompanied by parkinsonism but are less reliable alone. Persistent forms may need VMAT2 inhibitors or a change to clozapine. Stopping the drug is the surest cure when it is practical.
det.prognosis: Acute akathisia usually resolves within days to weeks of reducing the drug. Tardive and persistent forms can last for years and are difficult to treat.
pearls: More restless on more antipsychotic? Think akathisia, not worse psychosis.
Ask 'do you feel you must keep moving?'; the subjective answer makes the diagnosis.
Propranolol or a benzodiazepine gives quick relief.
det.thd: Akathisia คือความรู้สึกกระวนกระวายภายในที่ทำให้ต้องขยับตัวตลอดเวลา เกิดหลังเริ่มหรือเพิ่มยา antipsychotic, metoclopramide หรือ prochlorperazine ผู้ป่วยโยกตัว ขยับขา และเดินวน ซึ่งมักถูกเข้าใจผิดว่าเป็นอาการทางจิตที่แย่ลง ทำให้เพิ่มยาและยิ่งแย่ รักษาโดยลดขนาดยาหรือเปลี่ยนยา ให้ propranolol, benzodiazepine หรือ mirtazapine ขนาดต่ำ และสังเกตความเสี่ยงฆ่าตัวตาย

name: Akinesia
formal: Poverty and slowness of spontaneous and voluntary movement with difficulty initiating motion, a cardinal feature of parkinsonism due to basal ganglia dysfunction.
simple: A reduced ability to start movements, so the person moves very little, as seen in Parkinson disease.
th: ภาวะเคลื่อนไหวน้อยและเริ่มเคลื่อนไหวได้ยาก เป็นอาการหลักของ parkinsonism จากความผิดปกติของ basal ganglia
tempoNote: Usually insidious in degenerative parkinsonism; acute in drug-induced, vascular or toxic causes
feat: Reduced spontaneous movement: less blinking, facial expression and arm swing
Difficulty starting movements and turning in bed; may freeze at doorways
Often paired with bradykinesia (slowness and amplitude decrement on repetition)
Soft voice, small handwriting and slowed daily activities
A clinical sign, not a disease; causes include PD, atypical parkinsonism and drugs
inv: Clinical assessment with repetitive finger tapping, hand opening and foot tapping
Medication review for dopamine blockers
MRI brain and DaT-SPECT when the cause is uncertain

case.story: His wife says he sits for hours without moving, rarely blinks, and takes an hour to dress; he denies feeling weak.
case.exam: Hypomimia, reduced blink, slow small finger taps that fade, no arm swing on the right, cogwheel rigidity right wrist.
case.tests: MRI brain unremarkable.
case.q: Is this weakness? What is the sign and its likely cause?
case.a: No, power is normal; this is akinesia with bradykinesia, most likely from Parkinson disease.

read.where: 1 - Clinical overview and phenomenology of movement disorders

det.patho: Akinesia reflects reduced dopaminergic drive through the basal ganglia motor loop, increasing inhibitory output from the output nuclei (GPi and SNr) onto the thalamus and brainstem. The cortex receives less facilitation, so self-generated movements are poorly initiated and scaled.
det.clinical: This entry describes a clinical sign rather than a disease. Patients show fewer spontaneous movements and a delay in starting voluntary ones, often accompanied by bradykinesia and hypokinesia. It is a core feature of Parkinson disease, multiple system atrophy, PSP, drug-induced and vascular parkinsonism, and is also seen in frontal lobe and catatonic states. Examiners expect it to be distinguished from weakness, apraxia and depression.
det.diagnosis: Look for decrement in speed and amplitude with repeated movements, reduced facial expression and blink rate, and difficulty initiating gait. Identify the cause from tempo, symmetry, drug history and associated signs; DaT-SPECT separates presynaptic dopaminergic loss from drug-induced parkinsonism.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying cause: levodopa or dopamine agonists for Parkinson disease, withdrawal of offending drugs, and physiotherapy using external cues. Atypical parkinsonism responds poorly to dopaminergic therapy.
det.prognosis: Depends entirely on the cause; drug-induced akinesia usually reverses over weeks to months.
pearls: Akinesia is poverty of movement; bradykinesia is slowness with decrement.
Normal strength distinguishes akinesia from weakness.
Visual or auditory cues can transiently unlock movement.
det.thd: Akinesia คือการเคลื่อนไหวเองได้น้อยและเริ่มต้นเคลื่อนไหวยาก ไม่ใช่กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง เกิดจากโดปามีนในวงจร basal ganglia ลดลง พบใน Parkinson disease, parkinsonism จากยา และโรคกลุ่ม atypical parkinsonism ตรวจด้วยการเคาะนิ้วซ้ำ ๆ ดูความช้าและความกว้างที่ลดลง การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ เช่น levodopa หรือหยุดยาที่เป็นต้นเหตุ

aN: bradykinesia | hypokinesia | poverty of movement | akinesia sign

name: Akinesia paradoxica
formal: Sudden transient ability of severely akinetic parkinsonian patients to move normally in response to emotional or external stimuli, such as fire or visual cues.
simple: A surprising short burst of normal movement in a person with severe Parkinson disease when stimulated, for example by an emergency.
th: ปรากฏการณ์ที่ผู้ป่วย parkinsonism ที่ขยับตัวแทบไม่ได้ กลับเคลื่อนไหวได้ดีชั่วคราวเมื่อเจอสิ่งกระตุ้นทางอารมณ์หรือสัญญาณภายนอก
tempoNote: Seconds to minutes during a sudden emotional or sensory trigger
feat: Abrupt, brief normal movement in a severely akinetic patient
Triggered by danger (fire, earthquake), strong emotion or external cues
Lines on the floor, rhythmic sounds or a thrown ball can release frozen gait
Reflects a phenomenon, not a separate disease
Often misread as malingering or functional disorder
inv: Clinical observation; video recording of freezing and cue response
No specific test; investigate the underlying parkinsonism

case.who: 72-year-old woman with advanced Parkinson disease in Khon Kaen
case.story: She needs help to walk and freezes at doors, yet when a gas stove caught fire she ran out of the kitchen unaided.
case.exam: Severe bradykinesia with freezing on turning; stepping improves when she walks over tape lines on the floor.
case.tests: Not required.
case.q: Is her sudden running evidence of a functional disorder?
case.a: No; it is kinesia paradoxa, an emergency-driven release of movement that can be harnessed with cueing strategies.

det.patho: The mechanism is incompletely understood. Leading ideas are that strong arousal recruits noradrenergic and limbic pathways and alternative motor routes (cerebellar-thalamocortical and brainstem) that bypass the defective basal ganglia loop, and that external cues replace the impaired internal timing of movement.
det.clinical: This is a phenomenon rather than a disease. It is best known in Parkinson disease, especially with freezing of gait, but occurs in other parkinsonian syndromes. The release is short-lived and cannot be reproduced on demand, which can confuse families and clinicians.
det.diagnosis: Recognise it from the history and the response to cues; it supports, rather than argues against, an organic basal ganglia disorder. Distinguish from motor fluctuations linked to levodopa timing.
det.treatment: No specific treatment. Physiotherapists exploit the principle with visual (floor lines, laser canes) and auditory (metronome, music) cueing to reduce freezing. Optimise dopaminergic therapy for the underlying disorder.
det.prognosis: Benign as a phenomenon; outlook depends on the underlying parkinsonism.
pearls: Running from a fire does not mean the parkinsonism is fake.
Cueing therapy for freezing is built on this phenomenon.
It shows the motor programme is intact but poorly triggered.
det.thd: Akinesia paradoxica หรือ kinesia paradoxa คือการที่ผู้ป่วยพาร์กินสันที่ขยับตัวลำบากมาก กลับลุกเดินหรือวิ่งได้ทันทีเมื่อเจอเหตุฉุกเฉินหรือสัญญาณภายนอก เช่น เส้นบนพื้นหรือเสียงจังหวะ เป็นปรากฏการณ์ ไม่ใช่โรคแยก และไม่ใช่การแกล้งทำ นักกายภาพนำหลักนี้มาใช้ฝึกเดินแก้ freezing ด้วย visual หรือ auditory cue

The usual setting; motor fluctuations with levodopa produce different timing

aN: kinesia paradoxa | paradoxical kinesia | kinesia paradoxica

name: Akinetic mutism
formal: State of wakefulness with absent speech and voluntary movement but preserved eye tracking, caused by lesions of the medial frontal, diencephalic or reticular systems.
simple: A state in which a person is awake but does not speak or move, though the eyes may follow things.
th: ภาวะตื่นแต่ไม่พูดและแทบไม่เคลื่อนไหวเอง ทั้งที่ตามองตามได้ เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ frontal ส่วนกลาง ไดเอนเซฟาลอน หรือระบบ reticular
tempoNote: Usually acute after stroke, haemorrhage or hydrocephalus; subacute in prion disease or tumours
feat: Eyes open and track, sleep-wake cycles present, yet almost no speech or spontaneous movement
Can obey simple commands with strong prompting, showing preserved awareness
Motor pathways intact; no paralysis to explain the immobility
Causes: bilateral anterior cerebral artery infarcts, ACoA aneurysm rupture, hydrocephalus, paramedian thalamic or mesencephalic lesions, CJD
Lies at the extreme end of the abulia spectrum
inv: MRI brain with DWI to locate medial frontal, cingulate or diencephalic lesions
CT angiography if subarachnoid haemorrhage or vasospasm suspected
EEG to exclude non-convulsive status; CSF and RT-QuIC if prion disease possible

case.who: 55-year-old man in a neurosurgical ward in Bangkok
case.story: Ten days after clipping of an anterior communicating artery aneurysm, he lies awake with eyes open but does not speak or eat unless repeatedly urged.
case.exam: Follows the examiner with his eyes, squeezes hand after several prompts, no limb paralysis, bilateral grasp reflexes, urinary incontinence.
case.tests: MRI shows bilateral medial frontal and anterior cingulate infarcts from vasospasm.
case.q: How does this state differ from locked-in syndrome?
case.a: This is akinetic mutism: motor pathways work but drive is lost; in locked-in syndrome drive is intact but the motor output is paralysed except vertical eye movement.

read.where: 23 The Localization of Lesions Causing Coma
Chapter 4: Which arterial territory is involved?

det.patho: The syndrome results from interruption of the circuits that convert motivation into action: anterior cingulate and supplementary motor areas, their connections through the ventral striatum and medial thalamus, and ascending dopaminergic and reticular inputs. Bilateral lesions are usually required, though large unilateral lesions occasionally suffice.
det.clinical: Patients appear awake and may follow with their eyes, but rarely speak or move unless stimulated, and responses are delayed and brief. Incontinence and frontal release signs are common. The state can improve partially into abulia as swelling or vasospasm settles. It must be distinguished from coma, unresponsive wakefulness, locked-in syndrome and catatonia.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by imaging that shows medial frontal, cingulate, thalamic or midbrain damage, or hydrocephalus. EEG excludes non-convulsive seizures, and metabolic and drug causes should be screened.
det.treatment: Treat the cause (shunt hydrocephalus, manage vasospasm, remove tumour). Dopaminergic agents such as bromocriptine, levodopa or amantadine, and stimulants like methylphenidate, are used with variable benefit. Nursing care, swallow safety and prevention of complications are essential.
det.prognosis: Variable; reversible causes such as hydrocephalus may recover well, whereas extensive infarcts often leave lasting abulia.
pearls: Eyes track, motor system works, but nothing is initiated.
Think bilateral ACA territory after ACoA aneurysm rupture.
A shunt-responsive cause (hydrocephalus) must never be missed.
det.thd: Akinetic mutism คือผู้ป่วยตื่น ลืมตา มองตามได้ แต่แทบไม่พูดและไม่เคลื่อนไหวเองแม้กำลังกล้ามเนื้อปกติ เกิดจากรอยโรคสองข้างของ frontal ด้านใน cingulate หรือ thalamus เช่น หลังหลอดเลือด ACoA แตกหรือภาวะน้ำในโพรงสมองคั่ง ตรวจ MRI หาตำแหน่งรอยโรค รักษาตามสาเหตุและอาจลองยากลุ่มโดปามีน แยกจาก locked-in syndrome ซึ่งผู้ป่วยอยากตอบแต่ขยับไม่ได้

name: Akinetic–abulic syndrome
formal: Frontal lobe syndrome with apathy, reduced spontaneous activity and speech and loss of initiative, due to damage to medial frontal, cingulate or frontal-subcortical circuits.
simple: A condition of marked lack of drive, in which a person barely moves, speaks or shows interest after frontal brain damage.
th: กลุ่มอาการ frontal ที่ผู้ป่วยเฉยเมย ไม่ริเริ่มทำอะไร พูดและเคลื่อนไหวน้อย จากรอยโรค frontal ส่วนกลาง cingulate หรือวงจร frontal-subcortical
tempoNote: Acute after stroke or haemorrhage; chronic in degenerative or vascular cognitive disorders
feat: Apathy and loss of initiative with reduced spontaneous speech and action
Long delays before answering; replies are short but often correct
Can perform tasks when prompted but stops when prompting stops
Often accompanied by incontinence, grasp reflex and gait apraxia
Lesions: medial frontal, anterior cingulate, caudate, globus pallidus, medial thalamus
inv: MRI brain to locate lesions in frontal-subcortical circuits
Screen for depression, hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency and sedating drugs
Cognitive testing focused on executive function

case.story: After a stroke last month her family says she sits all day, no longer cooks or chats, but is not sad; she eats only when food is placed in her hand.
case.exam: Answers after long pauses with one-word replies, bilateral grasp reflex, no hemiparesis, normal mood on questioning.
case.tests: MRI: bilateral caudate head and anterior limb internal capsule lacunes.
case.q: Is this depression?
case.a: More likely abulia from frontal-subcortical circuit damage; she lacks drive rather than low mood.

read.where: 20 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Cerebral Hemispheres

det.patho: Initiative depends on a loop linking anterior cingulate and medial prefrontal areas, via the ventral striatum, globus pallidus and medial thalamus, modulated by dopamine. Damage anywhere along this circuit, especially bilaterally, reduces the conversion of goals into action.
det.clinical: Abulia ranges from mild apathy to near akinetic mutism. Patients are passive, slow to respond and show little concern, yet do not report sadness. Common causes include ACA strokes, caudate or pallidal lesions (e.g. carbon monoxide), thalamic infarcts, hydrocephalus, traumatic brain injury and frontotemporal or vascular dementia.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical, distinguishing lack of drive from depression, aphasia, parkinsonism and sedation. Apathy scales help quantify severity. MRI identifies the circuit lesion.
det.treatment: Treat reversible causes and review sedating medication. Dopaminergic drugs (bromocriptine, amantadine, levodopa) or methylphenidate may help some patients. Structured routines, caregiver education and prompting-based rehabilitation are practical cornerstones.
det.prognosis: Acute vascular causes often improve partly over months; degenerative causes worsen.
pearls: Abulia is loss of drive; depression is low mood with negative thoughts.
Patients respond correctly but only after long delays.
Look for bilateral caudate or medial frontal lesions.
det.thd: Akinetic-abulic syndrome คือผู้ป่วยขาดแรงจูงใจ ไม่ริเริ่มทำอะไรเอง พูดน้อย ตอบช้าแต่มักตอบถูก เกิดจากรอยโรคในวงจร frontal-subcortical เช่น cingulate, caudate หรือ thalamus ต่างจากซึมเศร้าตรงที่ไม่ได้รู้สึกเศร้า วินิจฉัยจากอาการและ MRI รักษาตามสาเหตุ อาจใช้ยากลุ่มโดปามีนหรือ methylphenidate และฝึกตามกิจวัตรโดยมีผู้ดูแลกระตุ้น

name: Akinetic–rigid syndromes
formal: Disorders such as Parkinson disease, MSA, PSP and CBD that combine slowness of movement with rigidity, due to basal ganglia or nigrostriatal dysfunction.
simple: Conditions in which slow movement is combined with muscle stiffness, as in Parkinson disease and related disorders.
th: กลุ่มโรคที่มีการเคลื่อนไหวช้าร่วมกับกล้ามเนื้อแข็งเกร็ง เช่น Parkinson, MSA, PSP และ CBD จากความผิดปกติของ basal ganglia
tempoNote: Mostly insidious degenerative course; subacute in drug-induced, toxic or vascular forms
feat: Bradykinesia with rigidity, with or without rest tremor and postural instability
Umbrella category: Parkinson disease, MSA, PSP, CBD, DLB, drug-induced and vascular parkinsonism
Red flags for atypical forms: early falls, early autonomic failure, gaze palsy, apraxia, poor levodopa response
Young-onset forms raise Wilson disease, juvenile Huntington disease and genetic parkinsonism
inv: Detailed drug history; MRI brain for atrophy patterns and vascular lesions
DaT-SPECT to confirm presynaptic dopaminergic deficit
Levodopa trial; caeruloplasmin and slit-lamp exam if under 50

case.story: Two years of slowness and stiffness; he fell backwards several times in the first year, and levodopa did little.
case.exam: Symmetric axial rigidity, slowed vertical saccades, square-wave jerks, positive applause sign.
case.tests: MRI shows midbrain atrophy with relative pons preservation.
case.q: Which akinetic-rigid syndrome is this?
case.a: Progressive supranuclear palsy, Richardson syndrome.

read.where: 1 - Clinical overview and phenomenology of movement disorders
8 Overview of Parkinsonism and Approach to Differential Diagnosis

det.patho: These syndromes share loss of nigrostriatal dopaminergic input or of striatal and pallidal neurons that receive it. In PD and DLB alpha-synuclein accumulates in neurons; in MSA it accumulates in oligodendroglia; PSP and CBD belong to the 4-repeat tau group. Drugs blocking D2 receptors and vascular lesions of the basal ganglia produce similar physiology.
det.clinical: This is a syndromic heading rather than a single disease. The task is to classify: PD typically starts asymmetrically with tremor and responds well to levodopa, while atypical forms progress faster and add early falls, autonomic failure, eye movement disorders or cortical signs. Drug-induced parkinsonism tends to be symmetric and reverses after drug withdrawal.
det.diagnosis: Apply clinical criteria for each disorder (MDS criteria for PD, PSP and MSA). MRI patterns (midbrain atrophy in PSP, putaminal and pontine changes in MSA) and DaT-SPECT add support. Skin biopsy or CSF seed amplification for alpha-synuclein is increasingly used to support synucleinopathy.
det.treatment: Levodopa is tried in all patients; response is strong in PD and partial or brief in atypical forms. Rehabilitation, speech and swallow therapy, management of autonomic symptoms and falls prevention are central. Remove offending drugs where possible.
det.prognosis: Ranges from decades in PD to roughly 6–10 years in MSA and PSP.
pearls: Early falls, early autonomic failure and poor levodopa response suggest atypical parkinsonism.
Always ask about metoclopramide, flunarizine and antipsychotics.
Check caeruloplasmin in parkinsonism under 50.
det.thd: Akinetic-rigid syndromes คือกลุ่มอาการพาร์กินสันที่มีเคลื่อนไหวช้าและกล้ามเนื้อแข็ง ได้แก่ Parkinson disease, MSA, PSP, CBD และ parkinsonism จากยาหรือหลอดเลือด หน้าที่ของแพทย์คือแยกชนิดจากลักษณะเริ่มต้น การตอบสนองต่อ levodopa และอาการเตือน เช่น ล้มเร็ว ระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติล้มเหลว หรือกลอกตาผิดปกติ ใช้ MRI และ DaT-SPECT ช่วย การรักษาคือ levodopa ร่วมกับกายภาพบำบัด
