name: Alcohol-induced cramps
formal: Painful muscle cramps related to alcohol intake or withdrawal, due to electrolyte disturbance, myopathy or neuropathy.
simple: Painful muscle cramps linked to heavy drinking or stopping alcohol.
th: ตะคริวกล้ามเนื้อที่สัมพันธ์กับการดื่มสุราหรือถอนสุรา จากเกลือแร่ผิดปกติ โรคกล้ามเนื้อ หรือเส้นประสาทเสื่อมจากสุรา
tempoNote: Recurrent painful episodes, often nocturnal, on a background of chronic heavy drinking
feat: Painful calf, foot or thigh cramps, frequently at night (a symptom, not a separate disease)
Reported by a large proportion of people with alcohol use disorder
Associated hypomagnesaemia, hypokalaemia, hypocalcaemia or liver cirrhosis
Coexisting alcoholic neuropathy (burning feet) or myopathy
Worse during withdrawal
inv: Electrolytes including magnesium, potassium, calcium and phosphate
Liver function, CK, thiamine status
Nerve conduction if neuropathic symptoms

case.who: 50-year-old male fisherman from Chanthaburi drinking rice whisky daily
case.story: Wakes most nights with agonising calf cramps; feet burn when walking.
case.exam: Reduced ankle jerks, stocking pinprick loss, tender calves, palmar erythema.
case.tests: Mg 0.5 mmol/L, K 3.1 mmol/L; GGT raised; NCS length-dependent axonal neuropathy.
case.q: What is driving his cramps and how should they be treated?
case.a: Alcohol-related cramps from hypomagnesaemia and neuropathy; correct electrolytes, give thiamine and support abstinence.

det.patho: Cramps arise from spontaneous high-frequency discharges in motor nerve terminals. Alcohol promotes them through electrolyte losses (magnesium, potassium, calcium), axonal neuropathy, direct muscle toxicity and liver disease. Withdrawal-related hyperexcitability adds to the risk.
det.clinical: Cramps are sudden, painful, palpable contractions relieved by stretching. They cluster at night or after exertion and often accompany neuropathic burning and weakness. This entry describes a symptom pattern in alcohol misuse rather than a distinct neurological disease. Cirrhosis independently causes frequent cramps.
det.diagnosis: History of heavy alcohol use, typical cramps and supportive findings are enough. Check electrolytes, liver function and CK. Nerve conduction confirms neuropathy. Exclude other causes such as diuretics, hypothyroidism and statin use.
det.treatment: Correct magnesium and potassium, give thiamine and B-complex vitamins, and support alcohol reduction. Stretching before bed helps. In cirrhosis, short-term options include taurine or baclofen; quinine is avoided because of safety concerns. Manage neuropathic pain if present.
det.prognosis: Cramps lessen with abstinence and electrolyte correction; neuropathy recovers slowly.
pearls: Check magnesium in any drinker with cramps.
Cramps in cirrhosis improve when ascites and electrolytes are managed.
Give thiamine before glucose in malnourished drinkers.
det.thd: ตะคริวจากสุราเป็นอาการ ไม่ใช่โรคเฉพาะ เกิดจากแมกนีเซียมและโพแทสเซียมต่ำ เส้นประสาทเสื่อมจากสุรา โรคกล้ามเนื้อ และโรคตับ มักเป็นตอนกลางคืนที่น่องหรือเท้า ตรวจเกลือแร่ การทำงานของตับ และ NCS การรักษาคือแก้เกลือแร่ ให้ thiamine ยืดกล้ามเนื้อ และช่วยให้ลดหรือเลิกสุรา

ddx.pt: Painful length-dependent neuropathy that often underlies the cramps
Proximal weakness or acute rhabdomyolysis with raised CK
Cramps with widespread fasciculations, not tied to alcohol

aN: alcohol related muscle cramps | alcoholic cramps | withdrawal cramps

name: Alcoholic myopathy
formal: Muscle disease from chronic heavy alcohol use, either acute necrotising with rhabdomyolysis or chronic proximal atrophy with type II fibre loss, partly reflecting nutritional deficiency.
simple: Muscle damage and weakness caused by heavy long-term drinking.
more: CK may be high in the acute form; biopsy shows type II fibre atrophy. Stopping alcohol and improving nutrition usually brings recovery over months.
th: โรคกล้ามเนื้อจากการดื่มสุราหนักเรื้อรัง มีทั้งแบบเฉียบพลัน (กล้ามเนื้อสลาย) และแบบเรื้อรัง (ต้นขาลีบอ่อนแรง)
tempoNote: Acute necrotising episodes after binges; chronic proximal atrophy develops over months to years
feat: Chronic form: painless proximal wasting and weakness, mostly hips and thighs
Acute form: painful swollen muscles after a binge, dark urine, very high CK
Often coexists with alcoholic neuropathy, cerebellar degeneration and liver disease
Hypokalaemia and hypophosphataemia aggravate the acute form
Improves with abstinence and nutrition
inv: CK, potassium, phosphate, magnesium, renal and liver function
Urine myoglobin in acute presentations
NCS/EMG to identify coexisting neuropathy; biopsy shows type 2 atrophy in chronic cases

case.story: Daily heavy rice-whisky drinker; over a year noticed thin thighs and difficulty getting up from squatting. Feet tingle at night.
case.exam: Proximal leg wasting and weakness grade 4, reduced ankle reflexes, glove-stocking pinprick loss, mild gait ataxia, palmar erythema.
case.tests: CK 260 U/L, GGT high, potassium 3.1 mmol/L; NCS show mild axonal sensorimotor neuropathy.
case.q: What explains his proximal weakness alongside the neuropathy?
case.a: Chronic alcoholic myopathy with coexisting alcoholic neuropathy; advise abstinence, thiamine, nutrition and electrolyte correction.

read.where: Chapter 34 Neurologic Complications of Recreational Drugs
Myopathies of Systemic Disease and Toxic Myopathies

det.patho: Ethanol and acetaldehyde impair muscle protein synthesis, particularly in fast-twitch type 2 fibres, and disturb mitochondrial function and calcium handling. Malnutrition, electrolyte losses and immobility during intoxication add to fibre injury. The acute form reflects frank necrosis, sometimes triggered by prolonged pressure during stupor.
det.clinical: Chronic alcoholic myopathy is common but frequently overlooked, giving gradual proximal wasting in heavy drinkers. Acute necrotising myopathy presents with painful, tender, swollen muscles and myoglobinuria after a binge and can cause kidney failure. Cardiomyopathy may accompany skeletal muscle disease. Coexisting neuropathy, Wernicke encephalopathy and cerebellar degeneration should be looked for.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical, based on drinking history, the pattern of weakness and exclusion of other causes. CK is normal or mildly raised in chronic disease and very high in acute disease. Electrolytes must be checked because hypokalaemia or hypophosphataemia can mimic or worsen it. Biopsy is rarely needed.
det.treatment: Abstinence is the cornerstone, combined with nutritional repletion, thiamine before glucose, and correction of potassium, phosphate and magnesium. Acute rhabdomyolysis requires IV fluids and monitoring of renal function and potassium. Physiotherapy aids recovery. Alcohol use disorder services should be involved.
det.prognosis: Muscle strength improves over months with abstinence; continued drinking leads to progressive wasting.
pearls: In a heavy drinker with proximal weakness, check potassium and phosphate before calling it alcoholic myopathy.
Acute alcoholic rhabdomyolysis can follow a long period lying unconscious; look for compartment syndrome.
Give thiamine first in any malnourished drinker.
det.thd: การดื่มสุราหนักเป็นเวลานานทำให้กล้ามเนื้อต้นขาลีบและอ่อนแรงอย่างช้า ๆ ส่วนการดื่มหนักครั้งเดียวอาจทำให้กล้ามเนื้อสลายเฉียบพลัน ปวดบวม ปัสสาวะสีเข้มและไตวาย ควรตรวจ CK และเกลือแร่ทุกครั้ง การรักษาหลักคือหยุดดื่ม ให้ thiamine โภชนาการ และแก้ไขโพแทสเซียมหรือฟอสเฟต

name: Alcoholic neuropathy
formal: Length-dependent axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy from chronic alcohol exposure and thiamine and other B-vitamin deficiency, with painful distal paraesthesia and sometimes autonomic features.
simple: Nerve damage in the feet and hands from long-term heavy drinking, causing burning pain, numbness, and weakness.
more: Nerve conduction studies show axonal loss; rule out other causes. Abstinence, thiamine and B-vitamin replacement, and neuropathic pain drugs help; recovery is slow and partial.
th: ปลายประสาทเสื่อมจากสุราเรื้อรังร่วมกับขาดสารอาหาร — ชา แสบร้อนเท้า เดินเซ
tempoNote: Gradual over months to years of heavy drinking; a faster subacute form occurs with thiamine deficiency
feat: Painful burning feet with distal sensory loss, starting in the toes
Later distal weakness and wasting; ankle jerks lost early
Sensory ataxia when large fibres are involved
Autonomic features: sweating changes, impotence, postural dizziness
Associated signs: cerebellar gait, Wernicke features, liver disease, myopathy
inv: NCS: length-dependent axonal sensorimotor neuropathy
Thiamine, B12, folate, B6, LFT, GGT, MCV, glucose
Exclude other causes when atypical: HbA1c, TSH, serum protein electrophoresis

case.who: 52-year-old male rice farmer from Roi Et
case.story: Drinks local rice spirit daily for 20 years and eats little. Feet burn at night and he stumbles in the dark.
case.exam: Thin, tender calves, stocking loss of pinprick and vibration to mid-shin, absent ankle jerks, Romberg positive, mild ankle dorsiflexion weakness.
case.tests: NCS: absent sural responses and low peroneal CMAP; MCV 104 fL, GGT high, thiamine low.
case.q: Besides abstinence, what simple treatment is essential?
case.a: Thiamine (and multivitamin) replacement with a balanced diet; start thiamine before any glucose load to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy.

read.where: 16. THE TOXIC NEURONOPATHY: PRINCIPLES OF GENERAL AND PERIPHERAL NEUROTOXICOLOGY; PHARMACEUTICAL AGENTS

det.patho: Damage reflects both direct ethanol and acetaldehyde toxicity to axons and nutritional deficiency, especially thiamine. Pure alcohol toxicity tends to cause a slow, painful small-fibre-predominant neuropathy, while thiamine lack produces a quicker, more motor large-fibre form. Lifetime alcohol dose correlates with severity.
det.clinical: Usually affects people with many years of heavy drinking. Pain and burning are frequent and may be the main complaint. Weakness and wasting appear later, and sensory ataxia combined with cerebellar degeneration makes falls common. Look for coexisting Wernicke–Korsakoff, myopathy, compressive palsies (radial 'Saturday night' palsy) and liver disease.
det.diagnosis: A length-dependent axonal neuropathy in a heavy drinker with no other cause supports it. Check nutritional markers and screen for diabetes, B12 deficiency, thyroid disease and paraproteins. Rapid or asymmetric progression should prompt a broader work-up, including vasculitis or GBS.
det.treatment: Abstinence and nutrition are the core: thiamine, B-complex and a balanced diet, plus support for alcohol use disorder. Painful symptoms may respond to duloxetine, amitriptyline or gabapentinoids. Foot care, balance training and fall prevention help.
det.prognosis: Slow partial recovery over months to years after abstinence; established severe axonal loss may not fully reverse.
pearls: Always give thiamine before glucose in malnourished drinkers.
Burning feet plus ataxia: check both neuropathy and cerebellar vermis signs.
Recurrent radial or peroneal pressure palsies occur after intoxicated sleep.
det.thd: Alcoholic neuropathy เกิดจากพิษของแอลกอฮอล์ร่วมกับขาดวิตามินโดยเฉพาะ thiamine ผู้ป่วยชาและแสบร้อนเท้า เดินเซ และต่อมาอ่อนแรงปลายเท้า NCS พบ axonal neuropathy แบบเริ่มจากปลาย การรักษาคือหยุดสุรา ให้ thiamine และวิตามินบีรวม ร่วมกับยาลดปวดประสาท อาการดีขึ้นช้า ๆ หลังหยุดดื่ม

name: Alexander disease
formal: Leukodystrophy from GFAP gain-of-function mutations with Rosenthal fibres, causing infantile macrocephaly and seizures or adult bulbar signs, ataxia and spasticity with periventricular or brainstem MRI changes.
simple: A rare inherited disease damaging the brain's white matter, causing a large head, seizures and developmental problems in babies or swallowing and walking trouble in adults.
th: โรค leukodystrophy จากยีน GFAP ที่ผิดปกติแบบเด่น เด็กเล็กมีศีรษะโตและชัก ส่วนผู้ใหญ่มีอาการก้านสมองส่วนล่าง เช่น กลืนลำบาก พูดไม่ชัด เดินเซ เกร็ง
tempoNote: Infantile form progresses over a few years; adult form evolves slowly over years to a decade or more
feat: Infants: enlarging head, developmental delay or regression, seizures and spasticity
Adults: bulbar symptoms (dysphagia, dysphonia), palatal tremor/myoclonus, ataxia and spastic weakness
Autonomic problems such as constipation, urinary dysfunction and sleep apnoea
Frontal-predominant white matter change in children; medulla and upper cord atrophy ('tadpole') in adults
Usually a new (de novo) dominant GFAP variant, so family history is often absent
inv: MRI brain and cervical cord: frontal white matter, periventricular rim, basal ganglia or medullary signal change/atrophy, sometimes enhancement
GFAP gene sequencing confirms the diagnosis
Other leukodystrophy screens (VLCFA, arylsulfatase A) when GFAP is negative

case.story: Over three years her voice became nasal, she coughs when drinking and her legs feel stiff; she also snores heavily now.
case.exam: Palatal tremor, tongue fasciculation absent, brisk reflexes with bilateral Babinski, mild gait ataxia.
case.tests: MRI shows marked atrophy of the medulla and upper cervical cord with signal change; GFAP sequencing finds a pathogenic missense variant.
case.q: Which imaging pattern points to this diagnosis in adults?
case.a: Medullary and cervical cord atrophy ('tadpole' sign) in adult-onset Alexander disease.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Alexander Disease
8 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System

det.patho: Dominant gain-of-function variants in GFAP, the main intermediate filament of astrocytes, cause the protein to aggregate into Rosenthal fibres. Astrocytes become dysfunctional, which disturbs myelin maintenance and neuronal support. It is a primary astrocytopathy rather than a disorder of myelin itself. Most cases arise de novo; adult forms may be inherited.
det.clinical: Type I (early onset) presents in infancy or early childhood with macrocephaly, seizures, feeding problems and developmental failure. Type II (later onset, juvenile to adult) is dominated by bulbar and brainstem signs, palatal myoclonus, spastic paraparesis, ataxia and autonomic dysfunction, with relatively preserved cognition. Some adults are found incidentally on MRI. Severity correlates partly with the specific variant.
det.diagnosis: MRI is highly suggestive: in children, frontal-predominant white matter loss with a periventricular rim and contrast enhancement; in adults, atrophy and signal change in the medulla and upper cord. Confirmation is by GFAP sequencing; brain biopsy is no longer needed. Exclude other leukodystrophies and inflammatory disease where imaging is atypical.
det.treatment: No approved disease-modifying therapy exists; an antisense oligonucleotide lowering GFAP (zilganersen) has been in clinical trials. Care is supportive: antiseizure medication, swallow assessment and gastrostomy, management of spasticity, bladder and bowel care, and treatment of sleep apnoea. Genetic counselling is advised.
det.prognosis: Infantile forms often cause death within the first decade; adult forms progress slowly over many years.
pearls: Big head + frontal white matter disease in an infant: think Alexander or Canavan disease.
Adult palatal tremor + bulbar palsy + medullary atrophy suggests adult Alexander disease.
Rosenthal fibres are the pathological hallmark, but genetics now replaces biopsy.
det.thd: Alexander disease เป็น leukodystrophy จากยีน GFAP ทำให้ astrocyte ผิดปกติและมี Rosenthal fibres ในเด็กเล็กมีศีรษะโต ชัก พัฒนาการช้า ส่วนผู้ใหญ่มีอาการกลืนลำบาก พูดเสียงขึ้นจมูก palatal tremor เดินเซและขาเกร็ง MRI ในผู้ใหญ่เห็นก้านสมองส่วน medulla และไขสันหลังส่วนคอฝ่อ ยืนยันด้วยตรวจยีน GFAP การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง

qx.stem: A 36-year-old woman from Trang has progressive dysphagia, dysarthria, palatal myoclonus, spastic gait and ataxia. MRI shows atrophy of the medulla extending into the upper cervical cord with scattered T2 hyperintense brainstem lesions and only modest white matter change.
qx.q: Which gene analysis is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
opts: PLP1
GFAP
ASPA
GALC
NOTCH3
qx.why: Bulbar dysfunction, palatal myoclonus and spastic ataxia with medullary and cervical cord atrophy suggest adult-onset Alexander disease, which results from dominant GFAP variants and no longer needs brain biopsy for confirmation. PLP1 causes Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease, ASPA causes Canavan disease, GALC causes Krabbe disease and NOTCH3 causes CADASIL.

name: Allgrove syndrome
formal: Autosomal recessive triple A syndrome from AAAS mutations with achalasia, adrenal insufficiency, alacrima and progressive neuropathy, ataxia and autonomic features.
simple: A rare inherited disease causing swallowing difficulty, dry eyes, adrenal gland weakness and nerve problems.
th: โรคพันธุกรรม autosomal recessive จากยีน AAAS มี achalasia ต่อมหมวกไตทำงานไม่พอ น้ำตาไม่ไหล ร่วมกับเส้นประสาทเสื่อมและระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติผิดปกติ
tempoNote: Alacrima from infancy; adrenal crisis or achalasia in childhood; neurological features progress in adolescence and adulthood
feat: Alacrima (no tears) from birth, often the earliest sign
Achalasia with dysphagia and vomiting; ACTH-resistant adrenal insufficiency (hypoglycaemia, pigmentation)
Progressive motor or sensorimotor neuropathy, distal amyotrophy, bulbar signs and spasticity mimicking MND
Autonomic dysfunction: postural hypotension, abnormal pupils, sweating changes
Ataxia, cognitive impairment, optic atrophy and hyperkeratosis in some
inv: Schirmer test; barium swallow or manometry for achalasia
Morning cortisol and ACTH, ACTH stimulation test
Nerve conduction and EMG; autonomic testing
AAAS gene sequencing

case.story: Had a hypoglycaemic seizure at age 4, was told he never cries tears, had dilatation for swallowing difficulty, and now has weak, thin hands.
case.exam: Dry eyes, nasal speech, distal hand wasting with brisk reflexes, postural BP drop of 30 mmHg, darkened skin creases.
case.tests: Schirmer test minimal; low cortisol with very high ACTH; EMG chronic denervation; biallelic AAAS variants.
case.q: What unifying syndrome is present and which treatable feature is life-threatening?
case.a: Allgrove (triple A) syndrome; adrenal insufficiency requires glucocorticoid replacement.

read.where: Chapter 15 Disorders of the Motor Cells: The Motor Neuron Diseases — Other Forms

det.patho: Biallelic AAAS variants disrupt ALADIN, a nuclear pore complex protein. Defective nuclear import, especially of DNA repair and antioxidant proteins, leaves adrenal, autonomic and neuronal cells vulnerable to oxidative stress. Expression and severity vary even within families.
det.clinical: Childhood features are alacrima, achalasia and adrenal insufficiency, which may present with hypoglycaemia or crisis. Neurological involvement develops later and can include distal motor neuropathy, bulbar weakness, UMN signs, ataxia and autonomic failure, sometimes resembling ALS. Not all patients have all three 'A's.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it when two of the cardinal features occur, or in young patients with MND-like disease plus alacrima or achalasia. Endocrine testing, Schirmer test and oesophageal studies support it. Nerve conduction and EMG show axonal neuropathy and denervation. Genetic testing for AAAS confirms.
det.treatment: Glucocorticoid replacement with stress dosing prevents adrenal crises; mineralocorticoid is sometimes needed. Achalasia is treated with dilatation, myotomy or POEM. Artificial tears protect the cornea. Neurological care is supportive with physiotherapy and orthoses, and antioxidant strategies remain experimental.
det.prognosis: With adrenal replacement survival is good; neurological disability progresses slowly.
pearls: Ask about tears in a young patient with an MND-like picture.
Recurrent childhood hypoglycaemia plus achalasia: think triple A.
Steroid replacement is the life-saving step.
det.thd: Allgrove หรือ triple A syndrome เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมจากยีน AAAS มีสามอาการหลักคือ achalasia ต่อมหมวกไตทำงานไม่พอ และไม่มีน้ำตา ร่วมกับปัญหาระบบประสาท เช่น เส้นประสาทเสื่อม กล้ามเนื้อลีบคล้าย ALS และระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติผิดปกติ วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจฮอร์โมน Schirmer test และตรวจยีน การให้สเตียรอยด์ทดแทนช่วยชีวิต ส่วนอาการทางประสาทดูแลแบบประคับประคอง

name: Alpers–Huttenlocher syndrome
formal: Mitochondrial POLG-related disease with intractable seizures, psychomotor regression and liver failure, typically in early childhood; valproate may precipitate fatal hepatotoxicity.
simple: A severe inherited energy-production disorder in children causing hard-to-control seizures, loss of skills and liver failure.
ab: Progressive neuronal degeneration of childhood with liver disease
th: โรคไมโตคอนเดรียจากยีน POLG ในเด็กเล็ก มีชักรุนแรงรักษายาก พัฒนาการถดถอย และตับวาย ห้ามใช้ valproate
tempoNote: Usually begins between infancy and age 5 (rarely adolescence) with stepwise decline over months
feat: Drug-resistant focal seizures, often occipital, that can become continuous focal motor status
Developmental regression, hypotonia, ataxia and cortical visual loss
Liver dysfunction that may appear late or be triggered by valproate
Episodes of decline often follow an intercurrent infection
Recessive POLG variants in most cases
inv: EEG: high-amplitude slow activity with polyspikes, often occipital predominance
MRI: cortical signal change (occipital), later atrophy; MR spectroscopy may show lactate
Liver function tests serially; POLG gene sequencing
CSF protein and lactate may be raised

case.story: Previously normal, she developed jerking of the right hand that would not stop for days after a febrile illness; she has since lost words.
case.exam: Continuous focal clonic jerks of the right arm, reduced visual attention, hypotonia.
case.tests: EEG shows left occipital rhythmic high-amplitude delta with polyspikes; ALT mildly raised; POLG compound heterozygous variants.
case.q: Which antiseizure drug must be avoided and why?
case.a: Valproate — it can provoke fulminant, often fatal liver failure in POLG disease.

read.where: Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Metabolic Muscle Disease

det.patho: Biallelic POLG variants impair mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma, leading to depletion of mitochondrial DNA in brain and liver. Energy failure affects highly active cortical neurons, especially in occipital cortex, and hepatocytes. Metabolic stress from infection or certain drugs unmasks the deficit.
det.clinical: Children develop normally then present with refractory focal seizures, often with episodes of epilepsia partialis continua, followed by regression, ataxia, cortical blindness and hypotonia. Liver involvement ranges from mild enzyme rise to fulminant failure. Juvenile and adolescent forms are recognised. Migraine-like headaches with visual aura may precede seizures in older children.
det.diagnosis: Suspect in any child with new refractory focal or occipital seizures and regression, especially with abnormal liver tests. EEG and MRI support the diagnosis; POLG sequencing confirms it. Liver biopsy is avoided where possible because of bleeding risk. Test POLG before starting valproate in unexplained childhood epilepsy with regression.
det.treatment: There is no cure. Seizure control uses non-hepatotoxic agents (for example levetiracetam, lacosamide, benzodiazepines) and status epilepticus protocols; valproate is contraindicated. Supportive care includes nutrition, avoidance of prolonged fasting and liver monitoring. Liver transplant is generally not offered because neurological decline continues. Genetic counselling is important.
det.prognosis: Poor; most children die within a few years of onset from status epilepticus or liver failure.
pearls: Child with intractable occipital or focal motor status plus liver dysfunction: test POLG.
Never start valproate before POLG disease is considered in this setting.
Liver disease may be absent at onset, so a normal LFT does not exclude it.
det.thd: Alpers–Huttenlocher syndrome เป็นโรคไมโตคอนเดรียจากยีน POLG พบในเด็กเล็ก เริ่มด้วยชักเฉพาะที่ซึ่งรักษายากมาก บางครั้งชักต่อเนื่อง ตามด้วยพัฒนาการถดถอย ตาบอดจากสมองส่วนท้ายทอยและตับวาย EEG มักผิดปกติที่ occipital ยืนยันด้วยตรวจยีน POLG ห้ามให้ valproate เพราะทำให้ตับวายรุนแรง

name: ALS-like syndrome
formal: Motor neuron syndrome mimicking amyotrophic lateral sclerosis from other causes such as lead, hexosaminidase deficiency, paraneoplastic disease, lymphoma and hyperthyroidism, with mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs.
simple: A condition that resembles motor neuron disease but has another identifiable, sometimes treatable cause.
more: Search for reversible causes with metals, serology, thyroid and imaging. Treatment of the underlying cause may stabilise symptoms.
th: กลุ่มอาการคล้าย ALS ที่มีทั้ง UMN และ LMN แต่เกิดจากสาเหตุอื่น เช่น cervical myelopathy, MMN, ไทรอยด์เป็นพิษ, ตะกั่ว หรือ hexosaminidase deficiency ซึ่งบางสาเหตุรักษาได้
tempoNote: Weeks to years depending on cause
feat: Mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs mimicking ALS
Treatable mimics: cervical spondylotic myelopathy, multifocal motor neuropathy, hyperthyroidism, B12 and copper deficiency
Rarer causes: lead, adult hexosaminidase A deficiency, lymphoma or paraneoplastic disease, Kennedy disease
Sensory signs, sphincter involvement or conduction block argue against true ALS
inv: MRI cervical and brain; EMG/NCS with conduction block search
Thyroid, B12, copper, calcium, serum protein electrophoresis and free light chains
Heavy metals if exposure; anti-GM1 antibodies; genetic tests (androgen receptor CAG, HEXA) when suggested

case.story: Eight months of hand wasting and leg stiffness; recently abdominal colic and constipation.
case.exam: Wasting of hand muscles with fasciculations, brisk reflexes, wrist extensor weakness, gingival blue line.
case.tests: Blood lead 78 µg/dL; anaemia with basophilic stippling; no conduction block.
case.q: Why must this not be labelled ALS without further work-up?
case.a: Lead toxicity can cause a motor neuronopathy mimic; chelation and removing exposure may halt progression.

det.patho: ALS-like syndromes arise when a separate process damages both corticospinal tracts and lower motor neurons or their axons, or when two disorders coexist (for example cervical myelopathy plus radiculopathy). Toxic, metabolic, immune, structural and genetic mechanisms are all represented.
det.clinical: Up to about one in ten patients initially thought to have ALS turn out to have something else. Features that should prompt doubt include prominent sensory symptoms, sphincter failure early, very slow progression, conduction block, purely lower motor neuron or purely upper motor neuron involvement, and systemic features such as weight loss with tremor (thyrotoxicosis) or gynaecomastia (Kennedy disease).
det.diagnosis: A structured mimic screen includes neuraxis MRI, careful NCS/EMG, metabolic and haematological blood tests, paraprotein studies, and targeted genetic or toxic tests. Gold Coast criteria for ALS require exclusion of alternative causes, so a negative screen is part of the ALS diagnosis.
det.treatment: Treat the identified cause: decompression surgery for myelopathy, IVIG for MMN, antithyroid therapy, vitamin or copper replacement, chelation and exposure removal for lead, oncological treatment for lymphoma. Some causes stabilise rather than reverse.
det.prognosis: Generally better than ALS when a reversible cause is found early; genetic mimics progress slowly.
pearls: Always image the cervical spine before diagnosing ALS.
Conduction block points to MMN, a treatable mimic.
Gynaecomastia and perioral fasciculations suggest Kennedy disease.
det.thd: ALS-like syndrome คือภาวะที่มีอาการเหมือน ALS ทั้งกล้ามเนื้อลีบ เต้นพลิ้ว และ reflex ไว แต่เกิดจากสาเหตุอื่น เช่น กระดูกคอกดไขสันหลัง MMN ไทรอยด์เป็นพิษ ขาดวิตามินบี 12 หรือทองแดง พิษตะกั่ว หรือโรคพันธุกรรม ต้องตรวจ MRI คอ EMG และเลือดก่อนสรุปว่าเป็น ALS เพราะหลายสาเหตุรักษาได้

name: Altered mental status
formal: Acute change in awareness, attention or cognition, ranging from confusion to coma, with causes including metabolic, infective, toxic, structural and epileptic factors.
simple: A sudden change in how alert or clear-thinking a person is, such as confusion or unusual sleepiness.
th: การเปลี่ยนแปลงของระดับความรู้สึกตัว สมาธิ หรือความคิดแบบเฉียบพลัน ตั้งแต่สับสนจนถึงโคม่า เป็นอาการนำ ไม่ใช่โรค ต้องหาสาเหตุ
tempoNote: Minutes to days; speed of onset helps separate vascular, toxic, metabolic and infective causes
feat: Presenting problem rather than a disease: ranges from inattention and confusion to stupor and coma
Fluctuating attention suggests delirium; fixed focal signs suggest a structural lesion
Fever, neck stiffness or rash point to CNS infection
Asterixis, myoclonus or tremor favour metabolic or toxic causes
Subtle twitching or fluctuating unresponsiveness may hide non-convulsive status
inv: Bedside glucose immediately; electrolytes, sodium, calcium, renal and liver function, blood gas, toxicology
CT brain for focal signs, trauma or anticoagulation; MRI if CT unrevealing
Lumbar puncture when infection or inflammation suspected (after imaging if indicated)
EEG for unexplained or fluctuating consciousness to exclude NCSE

case.who: 72-year-old man from a Bangkok nursing home
case.story: Became drowsy and muddled over two days; staff note poor intake and a new urine smell.
case.exam: GCS 13, inattentive, picking at sheets, no focal deficit, no neck stiffness, asterixis absent.
case.tests: Glucose 6 mmol/L, sodium 158 mmol/L, creatinine raised, urine positive for leucocytes and nitrite; CT brain shows only atrophy.
case.q: What is the likely mechanism of his altered mental status?
case.a: Delirium from hypernatraemic dehydration and urinary sepsis; treat the causes and use non-drug delirium measures.

det.patho: Consciousness depends on the ascending reticular activating system in the upper brainstem and thalamus and on widespread cortical function. Diffuse insults (metabolic, toxic, septic, hypoxic) impair both hemispheres, while focal lesions cause AMS only if they involve the brainstem or thalamus, or produce mass effect. Epileptic activity can disrupt awareness without visible convulsions.
det.clinical: This is not a neurological disease but a symptom category. Presentations range from subtle inattention and disorientation to agitation, somnolence, stupor and coma. Key bedside questions are the speed of onset, fluctuation, focal signs, meningism, pupils and eye movements, and abnormal movements. Older adults with dementia, infection or new drugs are at highest risk.
det.diagnosis: Start with airway, breathing, circulation and capillary glucose. A structured search covers metabolic disturbances, infection, drugs and toxins, structural brain disease, seizures and endocrine causes. Neuroimaging is needed for focal signs, head injury, anticoagulation or no clear systemic cause. EEG should be considered early when the cause is unclear, and LP when infection or autoimmune encephalitis is possible.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: correct glucose and electrolytes gradually, give thiamine before glucose in at-risk patients, start empirical antimicrobials for suspected meningitis or encephalitis, reverse toxins and stop offending drugs. Supportive measures include airway protection, orientation strategies, sleep hygiene and family presence. Antipsychotics are reserved for dangerous agitation.
det.prognosis: Depends entirely on the cause; delirium in older adults predicts longer stay, later cognitive decline and higher mortality.
pearls: Check glucose first and give thiamine early in anyone malnourished or drinking alcohol.
A fluctuating confused patient with no clear cause deserves an EEG for NCSE.
Focal signs change the work-up: image the brain before blaming metabolism.
det.thd: Altered mental status คือภาวะที่ระดับความรู้สึกตัวหรือความคิดเปลี่ยนไปเฉียบพลัน เป็นอาการนำ ไม่ใช่โรคเฉพาะ สาเหตุมีทั้งเมตาบอลิก ติดเชื้อ ยาและสารพิษ รอยโรคในสมอง และชักแบบไม่เกร็งกระตุก ควรเจาะน้ำตาลทันที ตรวจเกลือแร่ การทำงานของไตและตับ ถ่ายภาพสมองถ้ามีอาการเฉพาะที่ และทำ EEG ถ้ายังหาสาเหตุไม่ได้ การรักษาคือแก้ที่ต้นเหตุ

name: Alternating hemiplegia of childhood
formal: Rare neurodevelopmental disorder, usually ATP1A3-related, with recurrent episodes of hemiplegia alternating sides from infancy, plus dystonia, nystagmus, seizures and cognitive impairment.
simple: A rare childhood condition with repeated episodes of weakness affecting one side of the body, sometimes switching sides.
th: โรคหายากในเด็กจากยีน ATP1A3 มีอาการอ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกเป็นพัก ๆ สลับข้าง เริ่มก่อนอายุ 18 เดือน หายเมื่อหลับ ร่วมกับ dystonia ตากระตุกและชัก
tempoNote: Attacks last minutes to days and begin before 18 months; developmental impairment accumulates over years
feat: Recurrent attacks of hemiplegia affecting either side, sometimes both, starting in infancy
Attacks stop during sleep and may return a few minutes after waking
Paroxysmal nystagmus (often monocular), dystonic spells and autonomic changes
Triggers: emotion, bathing in water, temperature change, light, fatigue
Developmental delay, ataxia, chorea; epilepsy in about half
inv: ATP1A3 sequencing (positive in most); ATP1A2 or SLC2A1 if negative
Video-EEG of attacks: hemiplegic spells lack ictal discharges, though true seizures also occur
MRI usually normal at onset; exclude stroke and structural lesions

case.story: Since 4 months he has had odd eye wobbling, then spells where the left side goes floppy for hours; last week it was the right side. A bath seemed to trigger one.
case.exam: Between attacks mild hypotonia and delayed motor milestones; during a filmed attack, flaccid right hemiparesis with preserved alertness.
case.tests: MRI brain normal; EEG during attack shows no seizure; ATP1A3 de novo variant (D801N).
case.q: Which feature of the attacks is most characteristic?
case.a: Hemiplegia that switches sides and disappears on sleeping — alternating hemiplegia of childhood.

det.patho: Most cases result from de novo heterozygous variants in ATP1A3, which encodes the alpha-3 subunit of the neuronal Na+/K+-ATPase. Impaired pump function destabilises neuronal membrane potentials, especially in basal ganglia, cerebellum and cortex, giving paroxysmal dysfunction. The same gene underlies rapid-onset dystonia-parkinsonism and CAPOS syndrome.
det.clinical: Onset is before 18 months, often with abnormal eye movements or dystonic spells before the first hemiplegia. Episodes of one-sided or bilateral weakness last minutes to days and resolve with sleep. Persistent problems include developmental and intellectual disability, ataxia, chorea, dystonia and behavioural difficulties. Epilepsy and sudden death risk are increased.
det.diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis uses consensus features: onset under 18 months, repeated hemiplegic attacks alternating in laterality, other paroxysms (dystonia, nystagmus, autonomic signs), bilateral episodes, relief with sleep, and developmental impairment. Video recordings by parents are invaluable. Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis in most; EEG and MRI exclude mimics.
det.treatment: Treatment is supportive. Flunarizine is commonly used to lessen attack frequency or severity, with variable benefit. Teaching families to induce sleep early in an attack and avoid known triggers helps. Benzodiazepines may abort spells; seizures need antiseizure drugs. Multidisciplinary developmental support is essential.
det.prognosis: Lifelong with variable cognitive and motor disability; some risk of sudden unexpected death.
pearls: Infant with side-switching hemiplegia that clears with sleep: think ATP1A3.
Paroxysmal nystagmus in early infancy often precedes the first hemiplegic attack.
Ask parents to video attacks and to try to induce sleep — it shortens the spell.
det.thd: Alternating hemiplegia of childhood เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมหายาก ส่วนใหญ่จากยีน ATP1A3 เริ่มก่อนอายุ 18 เดือน มีอาการแขนขาอ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกเป็นพัก ๆ สลับซ้ายขวา หายเมื่อเด็กหลับ ร่วมกับตากระตุก dystonia ชัก และพัฒนาการช้า การวินิจฉัยอาศัยอาการและตรวจยีน การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง เช่น flunarizine และช่วยให้เด็กหลับเมื่อเริ่มมีอาการ

name: Aluminium neurotoxicity
formal: Neurotoxicity from aluminium exposure, historically dialysis encephalopathy with speech disturbance, myoclonus, seizures and dementia, and associated with microcytic anaemia and bone disease.
simple: Brain damage caused by too much aluminium exposure, historically in kidney dialysis patients, leading to speech problems, jerks and confusion.
th: พิษอะลูมิเนียมต่อสมองในผู้ป่วยไตวายที่ได้รับอะลูมิเนียมสะสม เช่นจากน้ำฟอกไตหรือยาจับฟอสเฟต ทำให้พูดติดขัด กระตุก ชัก และสมองเสื่อม ร่วมกับโลหิตจางและโรคกระดูก
tempoNote: Months of accumulation in kidney failure; speech disturbance can fluctuate, often worse after dialysis
feat: Halting, stuttering speech or speech arrest as the earliest sign
Multifocal myoclonus, asterixis and seizures
Progressive cognitive decline, apraxia, personality change or psychosis
Microcytic anaemia unresponsive to iron and bone pain from osteomalacia
Sources: contaminated dialysate, aluminium phosphate binders, long-term parenteral nutrition, some infusions in renal failure
inv: Serum aluminium (use aluminium-free tubes); desferrioxamine challenge for body burden
EEG: frontal bursts of high-voltage slow waves with spikes
Dialysis water and dialysate audit
Bone biopsy with aluminium stain when osteomalacia is in question

case.who: 55-year-old woman on thrice-weekly haemodialysis at a community dialysis centre in Udon Thani
case.story: Over two months she has trouble starting sentences, the speech stammers during dialysis, and her husband notes jerking of her arms and forgetfulness. Two other patients at the centre have similar complaints.
case.exam: Hesitant, dysarthric speech, multifocal myoclonus, asterixis, mild disorientation, normal strength.
case.tests: Serum aluminium markedly elevated, Hb 8 g/dL with MCV 72 and normal ferritin; EEG shows bilateral frontal slow bursts with spikes.
case.q: What must be investigated at the unit and how is the patient treated?
case.a: Dialysis water treatment and any aluminium-containing binders; remove the source, switch to non-aluminium binders and give chelation with desferrioxamine under specialist supervision.

read.where: Neurologic Dysfunction and Kidney Disease; Neurologic Disorders Associated with Bone and Joint Disease (osteomalacia)
Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Neurological Consequences of Renal Disease and its Treatment

det.patho: When renal excretion fails, aluminium from dialysate, binders or intravenous solutions accumulates, binds to transferrin and enters brain, bone and bone marrow. In the cortex it disturbs enzyme activity, neurotransmission and iron handling, and in bone it blocks mineralisation, while in marrow it blocks haem synthesis. Children and patients on prolonged parenteral nutrition are also at risk. Environmental aluminium has not been proven to cause Alzheimer disease.
det.clinical: Dialysis encephalopathy typically begins with speech arrest or stammering that is first noticeable during or after dialysis and then becomes continuous. Myoclonus, seizures, dyspraxia, psychosis and dementia follow. Combined features of microcytic anaemia and proximal bone pain or fractures indicate systemic overload. Today the syndrome is rare because of water purification standards and non-aluminium binders, but clusters still occur when treatment plants fail.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in a dialysis or advanced CKD patient who has speech change, myoclonus and cognitive decline. Raised serum aluminium confirms exposure and a desferrioxamine challenge or bone biopsy assesses tissue load. The EEG pattern supports encephalopathy, and MRI mainly serves to exclude other causes. Rule out uraemia, dialysis disequilibrium, drug toxicity, stroke and prion disease.
det.treatment: Eliminate the source: repair reverse-osmosis and water treatment, test dialysate, and replace aluminium binders with calcium or non-calcium alternatives. Desferrioxamine chelation with dialysis, preferably on high-flux membranes, lowers the burden but must be given cautiously because it can worsen neurotoxicity transiently and predispose to mucormycosis. Treat seizures and myoclonus with agents such as benzodiazepines or valproate.
det.prognosis: Advanced untreated encephalopathy was progressive and fatal; early detection and removal of the source can stabilise or improve patients.
pearls: Stuttering speech and myoclonus in a dialysis patient prompt a check of serum aluminium and the water plant.
Iron-resistant microcytic anaemia and bone pain suggest aluminium overload.
Clusters of cases in one unit point to a contaminated water supply.
det.thd: พิษอะลูมิเนียมต่อสมองพบในผู้ป่วยไตวายเรื้อรังหรือฟอกไต เมื่ออะลูมิเนียมจากน้ำฟอกไต ยาจับฟอสเฟต หรือสารน้ำสะสมในร่างกาย อาการเริ่มจากพูดติดขัดหรือพูดตะกุกตะกัก ตามด้วยกล้ามเนื้อกระตุก ชัก สมองเสื่อม ร่วมกับโลหิตจางชนิด microcytic และกระดูกเปราะ ตรวจ serum aluminium และ EEG ตรวจสอบระบบน้ำของหน่วยไต การรักษาคือกำจัดแหล่งที่มา เปลี่ยนยาจับฟอสเฟต และให้ desferrioxamine โดยแพทย์เฉพาะทาง

name: Alzheimer’s disease (AD)
formal: Most common neurodegenerative dementia with progressive amnestic cognitive decline, amyloid plaques and tau tangles, and early hippocampal and medial temporal atrophy.
simple: A brain disease that slowly destroys memory and thinking skills, and is the most common cause of dementia.
more: Diagnosis by clinical criteria plus CSF amyloid-beta 42 reduced with raised tau/phosphotau, or amyloid PET and FDG-PET temporoparietal hypometabolism. APOE e4 raises risk; autosomal dominant APP, PSEN1 and PSEN2 mutations cause early onset.
th: สมองเสื่อมที่พบบ่อยที่สุด — จำเรื่องใหม่ไม่ได้ ถามซ้ำ ค่อย ๆ แย่ลงหลายปี

Later language, visuospatial and executive decline
Neurological examination otherwise normal early
Atypical variants: posterior cortical atrophy, logopenic aphasia
inv: Cognitive testing; reversible causes (B12, thyroid, syphilis, depression)
MRI: medial temporal/hippocampal atrophy
CSF or plasma amyloid/tau, amyloid PET when disease-modifying therapy considered

case.story: Over two years she repeats questions, forgets recent conversations and recently got lost driving home.
case.exam: Delayed recall 0/5 not helped by cues, mild word-finding difficulty, normal motor examination.

qx.stem: A 61-year-old secondary-school headmistress from Chiang Mai feels her memory is not as sharp as it was, but she still runs the school budget without errors and her husband notices no change. MoCA is 29/30 and a full neuropsychological battery is normal for age and education. A private wellness clinic ordered a plasma p-tau217 test, which came back clearly elevated, and she now asks to begin lecanemab.
qx.q: Which response best reflects current practice?
opts: Start lecanemab now, because treatment works best before symptoms begin
Order amyloid PET first and start donanemab if it is positive
Explain that anti-amyloid antibodies are not indicated in cognitively unimpaired people; counsel her, manage risk factors and arrange follow-up or a prevention trial
Tell her the result proves she will develop dementia within five years
Start donepezil 5 mg daily as a preventive measure
qx.why: The 2024 revised Alzheimer's Association criteria define AD biologically, so an abnormal core biomarker in an unimpaired person indicates preclinical disease, but the same document advises against testing or treating asymptomatic people outside research. Lecanemab and donanemab are licensed only for MCI or mild dementia with confirmed amyloid, and many amyloid-positive people never become impaired in their lifetime. Cholinesterase inhibitors have no preventive role.

qx.stem: A 70-year-old retired pharmacist in Khon Kaen has had 18 months of repeating questions and misplacing his phone; he still drives and manages his money with a little help. MoCA is 22/30 with poor delayed recall that does not improve with cues. He and his daughter want to know whether he can receive an anti-amyloid antibody.
qx.q: Which work-up is required before lecanemab or donanemab can be considered?
opts: CT brain and serum B12 only, because the clinical picture is typical
EEG and CSF 14-3-3 protein
FDG-PET alone, since temporoparietal hypometabolism confirms amyloid
A trial of donepezil for six months first, then reassess
Confirmation of amyloid pathology (PET, CSF or a validated plasma p-tau217 assay), a recent MRI including SWI, and APOE genotyping with counselling
qx.why: Appropriate-use recommendations require biomarker proof of amyloid, a baseline MRI to exclude more than four microbleeds, superficial siderosis, prior macro-haemorrhage or extensive vascular disease, and APOE testing because ε4 homozygotes carry the greatest ARIA risk. FDG-PET shows neurodegeneration but not amyloid. A prior cholinesterase inhibitor trial is not a prerequisite, and 14-3-3 belongs to the prion work-up.

qx.stem: A 73-year-old retired nurse from Nakhon Pathom has 18 months of progressive amnestic cognitive decline with a MoCA of 20/30. Her memory clinic has no access to PET, and CSF is declined. A validated plasma p-tau217 assay with two cut-offs gives a clearly positive result.
qx.q: Which statement reflects current use of plasma biomarkers?
opts: A single plasma result is too unreliable to use in any patient
In a symptomatic patient, a high-accuracy plasma p-tau217 result above the upper cut-off can support amyloid pathology without PET or CSF, whereas the intermediate zone needs confirmatory testing
Plasma p-tau217 should be used to screen all cognitively normal adults
A positive plasma result proves the dementia is due to Alzheimer disease alone
Plasma p-tau217 replaces clinical assessment and MRI
qx.why: Recent frameworks accept high-performance plasma p-tau217 assays for supporting biological confirmation in people with cognitive symptoms, using two cut-offs so that intermediate results trigger CSF or PET. They are not recommended for screening unimpaired people, and a positive test does not exclude co-pathologies such as vascular disease, Lewy bodies or TDP-43, so clinical assessment and MRI remain essential.

det.patho: Extracellular amyloid-beta plaques and intraneuronal tau tangles accumulate over decades, spreading from the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus to association neocortex, with synaptic loss correlating best with cognition. APOE e4 is the major genetic risk factor; rare early-onset autosomal dominant forms result from APP, PSEN1 or PSEN2 mutations. Age is the strongest risk factor, and vascular risk factors, hearing loss, inactivity and low education add to risk.
det.clinical: The typical amnestic form begins with trouble learning and keeping new information: repeated questions, misplaced items and forgotten appointments, while remote memories are relatively intact. Word-finding problems, getting lost, and difficulty managing money or medication follow; insight is often poor. Behavioural symptoms such as apathy, depression, agitation and delusions increase in moderate stages. Atypical presentations include posterior cortical atrophy (visuospatial and reading difficulty), logopenic aphasia (slow speech with poor repetition of sentences) and a frontal variant. Early prominent parkinsonism, hallucinations or gait failure suggest another cause.
det.diagnosis: Assess cognition objectively (MoCA or MMSE, then neuropsychology if needed), obtain a collateral history, and screen for reversible contributors: B12, thyroid, syphilis, HIV where relevant, depression, sleep apnoea and anticholinergic drugs. MRI typically shows hippocampal and medial temporal atrophy, and helps exclude vascular disease, tumour or NPH. Biological confirmation uses CSF (low Aβ42 or Aβ42/40 ratio, raised p-tau), amyloid PET, or increasingly blood p-tau217, and is required before anti-amyloid therapy. Biomarkers indicate pathology, not necessarily the cause of symptoms in an older person with mixed disease.
det.treatment: Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) give modest symptomatic benefit in mild to moderate disease; memantine is added or used in moderate to severe stages. Anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab) slow decline modestly in early, biomarker-confirmed disease but require MRI monitoring for ARIA, and APOE e4 homozygotes carry the highest risk. Non-drug care — exercise, cognitive and social engagement, hearing correction, caregiver support, safety and driving review, and advance care planning — matters as much as medication. Avoid antipsychotics where possible and minimise anticholinergic burden.
det.prognosis: Average survival after diagnosis is roughly 8–10 years, with wide variation; late stages bring dependence, dysphagia and infection.
pearls: A spouse who answers for the patient (head-turning sign) is a common clue to cognitive impairment with poor insight.
Normal neurological examination early is expected — focal signs should make you look for another cause.
Biomarker positivity is not dementia: interpret it alongside the clinical picture.

Blood p-tau217 is meant for people who already have cognitive complaints and are being assessed in a memory service — ideally early, at the mild stage — not for screening healthy people; a clearly positive or negative result can spare PET or lumbar puncture, while an intermediate result needs CSF or PET.

The 2025 Lancet series stresses that a molecular diagnosis (amyloid plus tau evidence) is now the entry ticket for anti-amyloid therapy, so access to biomarkers, MRI safety monitoring and specialist pathways must expand together.

name: Alzheimer’s disease and Parkinson’s disease
formal: Two most common neurodegenerative diseases, often overlapping clinically and pathologically, with cognitive decline in Alzheimer disease and dopaminergic motor disorder in Parkinson disease.
simple: Two common brain diseases of ageing: one mainly affects memory and thinking, the other mainly affects movement.
th: การทับซ้อนของสองโรคเสื่อมที่พบบ่อยที่สุด คือ Alzheimer (ความจำเสื่อม) และ Parkinson (การเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติ) ซึ่งมักมีพยาธิสภาพร่วมกันในผู้สูงอายุ
tempoNote: Both are insidious and progressive over years; overlap becomes more likely with age
feat: Comparison or overlap heading rather than a single disease
AD: early episodic memory loss from hippocampal involvement; PD: asymmetric bradykinesia, rigidity, rest tremor
Many PD patients with dementia have co-existing amyloid plaques and tau tangles
Many AD brains contain Lewy pathology, giving parkinsonism, hallucinations or fluctuation
Mixed pathology speeds decline and blurs clinical boundaries
inv: Cognitive testing (MoCA) and motor examination
Amyloid and tau biomarkers (CSF or plasma p-tau217, amyloid PET)
DaT-SPECT or alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay to detect Lewy co-pathology

case.story: Five years of Parkinson disease with good levodopa response; over the last year he forgets recent conversations and repeats questions.
case.exam: Moderate parkinsonism; MoCA 18 with poor delayed recall not helped by cues.
case.tests: Plasma p-tau217 raised; MRI shows bilateral hippocampal atrophy.
case.q: What explains his amnestic decline beyond the expected PD dementia profile?
case.a: Co-existing Alzheimer pathology; mixed AD and Lewy disease is common and influences prognosis and trial eligibility.

det.patho: AD is defined by amyloid-beta plaques and tau neurofibrillary tangles; PD by alpha-synuclein Lewy pathology with loss of nigral dopaminergic neurons. Autopsy series show that co-pathology is usual, not exceptional, in older adults, and that amyloid and tau in PD predict faster cognitive decline. Shared risk factors include age, and APOE e4 increases risk of dementia in both.
det.clinical: This entry is an overlap or comparison label, not a distinct disease. Clinically, pure AD tends to start with episodic memory loss, whereas PD dementia shows attention, executive and visuospatial deficits with relatively preserved storage. Mixed patients may show both patterns, and parkinsonism in AD is often symmetric and axial.
det.diagnosis: Biological diagnosis is increasingly possible: amyloid and tau biomarkers identify AD pathology, and alpha-synuclein seed amplification assays or DaT-SPECT identify Lewy disease. Clinical criteria for DLB and PDD help classify the dominant syndrome.
det.treatment: Cholinesterase inhibitors help both AD and PD dementia; rivastigmine is licensed for PDD. Levodopa treats motor features. Anti-amyloid antibodies are approved for early AD, but co-existing Lewy pathology and cerebrovascular disease affect suitability, and safety in PD has not been established. Avoid typical antipsychotics.
det.prognosis: Mixed pathology is associated with faster progression and shorter survival than either alone.
pearls: In older brains, mixed pathology is common; clinical labels are approximations.
Rivastigmine is used for PD dementia; avoid haloperidol in Lewy disease.
Biomarkers can reveal AD co-pathology in PD patients.
det.thd: หัวข้อนี้กล่าวถึงความสัมพันธ์ระหว่าง Alzheimer และ Parkinson ซึ่งเป็นโรคเสื่อมที่พบบ่อยที่สุด ในผู้สูงอายุมักพบพยาธิสภาพทั้ง amyloid, tau และ alpha-synuclein ร่วมกัน ทำให้มีทั้งความจำเสื่อมและอาการพาร์กินสัน การตรวจ biomarker ช่วยแยก การรักษาใช้ cholinesterase inhibitor และ levodopa ตามอาการ ผู้ป่วยที่มีพยาธิสภาพผสมมักแย่ลงเร็วกว่า

name: Amantadine akathisia
formal: Restlessness and urge to move as a rare adverse effect of amantadine, resolving after dose reduction or withdrawal.
simple: Inner restlessness that can occur as a side effect of the medicine amantadine.
th: อาการกระวนกระวายและอยากขยับตัวที่เป็นผลข้างเคียงพบน้อยของ amantadine หายได้เมื่อลดหรือหยุดยา
tempoNote: Appears within days to weeks of starting or increasing amantadine; resolves within days of dose reduction
feat: Inner restlessness and urge to move, pacing, inability to sit still
Rare adverse effect of amantadine, used for Parkinson disease, dyskinesia, influenza or fatigue in MS
More likely with high doses, renal impairment and older age because the drug is renally cleared
Often accompanied by other amantadine toxicity: insomnia, hallucinations, confusion, livedo reticularis, ankle oedema
Resolves after dose reduction or withdrawal
inv: Medication history and timing; renal function (creatinine, eGFR)
Barnes Akathisia Rating Scale
Exclude RLS (ferritin), anxiety and other drug causes

case.who: 74-year-old man with Parkinson disease from Nakhon Si Thammarat
case.story: Amantadine 300 mg/day was added for dyskinesia; two weeks later he paces at night, cannot sit through meals and feels driven to move.
case.exam: Restless shifting and pacing, livedo reticularis on the legs, mild confusion.
case.tests: Creatinine 2.0 mg/dL (eGFR 32); ferritin normal.
case.q: What is the cause and the management?
case.a: Amantadine-induced akathisia from accumulation in renal impairment; reduce the dose or stop amantadine and adjust dosing to kidney function.

det.patho: Amantadine is an NMDA receptor antagonist that also enhances dopamine release and has anticholinergic effects. Why it occasionally causes akathisia is not clear; proposed mechanisms include altered dopaminergic and glutamatergic balance in mesocortical and striatal pathways. Because it is excreted unchanged by the kidneys, impaired renal function raises plasma levels and toxicity.
det.clinical: Patients develop subjective restlessness and an urge to move, often with pacing, fidgeting and insomnia, after starting or increasing amantadine. Signs of broader toxicity, such as hallucinations, confusion and myoclonus, suggest high levels. In Parkinson disease, akathisia can also occur as an off-period symptom, so timing relative to doses helps.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical and depends on a temporal link to amantadine and improvement after dose reduction. Check renal function and review other drugs that cause akathisia, such as antipsychotics, SSRIs and metoclopramide. Distinguish from RLS, off-period restlessness, anxiety and agitated delirium.
det.treatment: Reduce or stop amantadine, adjusting the dose to renal function; symptoms generally settle within days. Avoid abrupt withdrawal in patients taking it for Parkinson disease because rebound parkinsonism or withdrawal delirium can occur. Propranolol or a short course of a benzodiazepine can help if symptoms are distressing during withdrawal.
det.prognosis: Fully reversible after dose adjustment or discontinuation.
pearls: Check eGFR in any older patient with new amantadine side effects.
Taper amantadine rather than stopping suddenly in Parkinson disease.
Livedo reticularis and ankle oedema are clues that the patient is taking amantadine.
det.thd: Amantadine akathisia คืออาการกระวนกระวาย อยากขยับตัว นั่งไม่ติดที่ ซึ่งเป็นผลข้างเคียงที่พบน้อยของยา amantadine ที่ใช้รักษา Parkinson หรือ dyskinesia มักเกิดเมื่อใช้ขนาดสูงหรือไตทำงานบกพร่องเพราะยาขับออกทางไต อาจมีสับสน ประสาทหลอน และผื่น livedo ร่วมด้วย การรักษาคือลดขนาดยาตามการทำงานของไตหรือค่อยๆ หยุดยา อาการมักหายในไม่กี่วัน

name: Amino acid and organic acid metabolism disorders
formal: Inherited aminoacidopathies and organic acidurias (e.g. phenylketonuria, maple syrup urine disease, methylmalonic aciduria) causing encephalopathy, seizures, developmental delay and metabolic crises.
simple: A group of inherited conditions in which the body cannot break down certain protein parts, causing brain problems, seizures and developmental delay.
ab: Inborn errors of amino acid metabolism
th: กลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมของการเผาผลาญกรดอะมิโนและกรดอินทรีย์ เช่น PKU, MSUD, MMA ทำให้ภาวะสมองผิดปกติ ชัก พัฒนาการช้า และวิกฤตเมตาบอลิกเมื่อเจ็บป่วย
tempoNote: Neonatal crises after feeding starts, intermittent decompensation with illness or fasting, or slowly progressive developmental impairment
feat: Neonate well at birth then poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy and coma after a few days
Recurrent decompensations with infection or fasting: ketoacidosis, hyperammonaemia, hypoglycaemia
Developmental delay, seizures, movement disorder (e.g. basal ganglia stroke in MMA or glutaric aciduria)
Odd odours (maple syrup in MSUD, musty in PKU) and specific dietary intolerance to protein
Some forms detected by newborn screening before symptoms
inv: Blood gas, ammonia, glucose, lactate, ketones and anion gap during a crisis
Plasma amino acids, urine organic acids, acylcarnitine profile

case.who: 5-day-old boy born at a provincial hospital
case.story: Fed well for two days, then became sleepy, vomited and stopped feeding; now has abnormal stiffening episodes.
case.exam: Lethargic neonate, alternating hypotonia and hypertonia with bicycling movements, sweet burnt-sugar odour of urine.
case.tests: Ketones strongly positive; plasma leucine, isoleucine and valine high with alloisoleucine present.
case.q: Which disorder fits and what are the urgent steps?
case.a: Maple syrup urine disease; stop protein, give high-calorie glucose and lipid, and remove leucine by haemofiltration if severe.

Section II: Epidemiology, Etiology, and Diagnosis

det.patho: Defects in enzymes or transporters of amino acid breakdown cause upstream accumulation of toxic metabolites (for example phenylalanine, branched-chain ketoacids, propionyl or methylmalonyl compounds) and secondary disturbances such as acidosis and hyperammonaemia. These injure neurons, myelin and the basal ganglia. Most are autosomal recessive.
det.clinical: This entry is a group heading rather than one disease. Presentations include acute neonatal encephalopathy, intermittent crises in infancy or later triggered by illness, chronic developmental and behavioural problems, and late-onset psychiatric or movement disorders. Specific patterns include basal ganglia strokes in MMA and glutaric aciduria type 1, and intellectual disability in untreated PKU.
det.diagnosis: During illness collect blood gas, ammonia, glucose, lactate and ketones before treatment changes them, plus plasma amino acids, urine organic acids and acylcarnitines. Newborn screening by tandem mass spectrometry identifies many disorders early. Confirm by enzyme assay or gene panel. Always consider these disorders in a neonate with unexplained encephalopathy or sepsis-like illness.
det.treatment: Acute management stops protein intake briefly, provides high-calorie glucose and lipids to reverse catabolism, corrects acidosis, and uses ammonia scavengers or dialysis when needed. Long-term care uses tailored low-protein diets with medical formulas and specific cofactors (e.g. vitamin B12 in responsive MMA, carnitine, biotin, sapropterin in some PKU). Liver transplantation is an option for selected disorders. Emergency letters for intercurrent illness are standard.
det.prognosis: Variable; early detection and strict treatment give near-normal outcomes in PKU, while severe organic acidaemias carry risks of recurrent crises and disability.
pearls: A neonate who was well then deteriorates after feeding: send ammonia, gas and metabolic screen with the sepsis work-up.
Metabolic acidosis with high anion gap + hyperammonaemia suggests an organic acidaemia.
Keep emergency plans: illness or fasting can trigger crises.
det.thd: กลุ่มโรคความผิดปกติของการเผาผลาญกรดอะมิโนและกรดอินทรีย์เป็นโรคพันธุกรรม ทำให้สารพิษคั่งในร่างกาย ทารกมักปกติแรกเกิดแล้วซึม ไม่ดูดนม อาเจียน ชัก หลังเริ่มกินนม หรือมีวิกฤตเมื่อเจ็บป่วย ตรวจ blood gas แอมโมเนีย กรดอะมิโนในพลาสมา กรดอินทรีย์ในปัสสาวะ และ acylcarnitine รักษาด้วยหยุดโปรตีนชั่วคราว ให้พลังงานสูง และอาหารเฉพาะโรคระยะยาว

name: Amiodarone neuropathy
formal: Dose- and duration-related toxic neuropathy with demyelinating and axonal features, tremor, and ataxia, from the antiarrhythmic amiodarone.
simple: Nerve damage causing numbness, tingling, and weakness in people taking the heart rhythm drug amiodarone.
more: Nerve conduction studies show mixed demyelination and axonal loss; reducing or stopping the drug leads to slow improvement.
th: เส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเสื่อมจากยา amiodarone ขึ้นกับขนาดและระยะเวลา มีทั้ง demyelinating และ axonal อาจมีมือสั่นและเดินเซร่วมด้วย
tempoNote: Months to years after starting, usually with higher daily doses; slow recovery after stopping
feat: Distal symmetric sensorimotor neuropathy, sometimes with proximal weakness
Postural tremor and ataxia are common accompaniments
Conduction slowing may mimic CIDP; axonal loss also present
Other toxicity clues: thyroid dysfunction, blue-grey skin, corneal deposits, pulmonary fibrosis, optic neuropathy
inv: NCS/EMG: mixed demyelinating and axonal features
Thyroid function, liver tests
Nerve biopsy (rarely needed) shows lysosomal lamellar inclusions

case.who: 70-year-old man with atrial fibrillation from Phrae
case.story: On amiodarone 400 mg daily for two years; numb feet, shaky hands and unsteady walking for six months.
case.exam: Stocking sensory loss, absent ankle jerks, mild distal weakness, postural tremor, blue-grey facial skin.
case.tests: NCS shows slowed conduction velocities with reduced amplitudes; TSH low.
case.q: What is the likely cause and what should be done?
case.a: Amiodarone neuropathy; discuss an alternative rhythm drug with cardiology and expect slow improvement over months.

det.patho: Amiodarone is a cationic amphiphilic drug that accumulates in lysosomes, forming lamellar inclusions in Schwann cells, endothelial cells and other tissues. This produces both segmental demyelination and axonal degeneration. Its long half-life means tissue levels fall very slowly after stopping.
det.clinical: Neuropathy develops after months of therapy, especially above 400 mg daily, with distal numbness, weakness and sometimes proximal involvement. Tremor and gait ataxia are frequent, and optic neuropathy can cause visual loss. Other systemic toxicities provide useful clues.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the temporal link with amiodarone, a compatible NCS pattern and exclusion of other causes such as diabetes, B12 deficiency, CIDP and paraproteinaemia. Nerve biopsy is reserved for unclear cases.
det.treatment: Reduce or stop amiodarone in consultation with cardiology, using an alternative antiarrhythmic or rate control where possible. Manage neuropathic pain symptomatically and treat thyroid dysfunction. Recovery is gradual because of the drug's long elimination.
det.prognosis: Most improve partially over months after withdrawal; severe axonal loss may leave residual deficit.
pearls: Amiodarone can cause neuropathy, tremor, ataxia and optic neuropathy.
Demyelinating NCS pattern may mislead toward CIDP.
Improvement is slow because the drug persists for months.
det.thd: Amiodarone neuropathy เกิดจากยารักษาหัวใจเต้นผิดจังหวะ amiodarone ที่สะสมในเซลล์ ทำให้ปลอกประสาทและแกนประสาทเสื่อม ผู้ป่วยมีชาปลายมือปลายเท้า อ่อนแรง มือสั่น และเดินเซ อาจมีไทรอยด์ผิดปกติหรือผิวสีเทาอมฟ้าร่วม ตรวจ NCS พบทั้ง demyelinating และ axonal การรักษาคือปรึกษาแพทย์โรคหัวใจเพื่อลดหรือเปลี่ยนยา อาการดีขึ้นช้า

name: Amnesia
formal: Impaired ability to form new memories or recall past ones, due to lesions of the hippocampus, thalamus or basal forebrain, or to transient global amnesia, trauma or Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.
simple: Loss of memory, either for recent events or for things from the past.
th: ความผิดปกติในการสร้างความจำใหม่หรือเรียกความจำเดิม เกิดจากรอยโรคของ hippocampus thalamus หรือ basal forebrain หรือจากภาวะอื่น เช่น TGA การบาดเจ็บ หรือ Wernicke-Korsakoff
tempoNote: Can be transient (TGA, seizures), acute and persistent (stroke, encephalitis, hypoxia), or gradually progressive (Alzheimer disease)
feat: Inability to learn new information despite normal attention (anterograde amnesia)
Loss of memories formed before the onset, often with a temporal gradient (retrograde amnesia)
Other cognitive domains relatively spared in pure amnesia
Confabulation in Korsakoff syndrome or basal forebrain lesions
This is a symptom/syndrome; the cause determines treatment
inv: Bedside memory tests (delayed recall) and neuropsychological testing
MRI brain with DWI: hippocampal, thalamic or fornix lesions, medial temporal atrophy
Thiamine, glucose, B12, thyroid; EEG for transient epileptic amnesia
CSF for encephalitis (HSV PCR, autoimmune antibodies)

case.story: After shovelling sand in the heat he repeatedly asked his wife what day it was for six hours, then returned to normal.
case.exam: During the episode he was alert, knew his name, and had no focal signs.
case.tests: MRI two days later shows tiny DWI dot in the left hippocampus; EEG normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis?
case.a: Transient global amnesia — a benign episode of anterograde amnesia.

read.where: Chapter 11 Cognitive Impairment and Dementia — Transient Global Amnesia
18 The Anatomic Localization of Lesions in the Thalamus

det.patho: Memory formation relies on the Papez circuit: hippocampus, fornix, mammillary bodies, anterior thalamus and cingulate cortex. Damage to any part — bilateral hippocampi, anterior/medial thalamus, mammillary bodies or basal forebrain — can cause amnesia. Causes include stroke, herpes or autoimmune encephalitis, hypoxia, trauma, thiamine deficiency, tumours, epilepsy and neurodegenerative disease.
det.clinical: Amnesia is a sign rather than a disease. Anterograde amnesia shows as repeating questions and inability to recall recent events; retrograde amnesia affects older memories, often recent ones first. Transient global amnesia lasts hours; transient epileptic amnesia recurs briefly and often on waking. Progressive amnesia is typical of Alzheimer disease.
det.diagnosis: Establish onset and duration, other cognitive deficits, and risk factors. MRI with diffusion imaging identifies strokes, encephalitis or atrophy; EEG detects epileptic causes; blood tests and CSF evaluate metabolic, infectious and autoimmune causes. Neuropsychological testing defines the profile.
det.treatment: Treatment targets the cause: thiamine for Wernicke-Korsakoff, antivirals for HSV encephalitis, immunotherapy for autoimmune encephalitis, antiseizure drugs for epileptic amnesia, and secondary prevention for stroke. Rehabilitation strategies, memory aids and caregiver support help persistent deficits.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause: TGA resolves completely; amnesia from structural damage often persists; neurodegenerative amnesia progresses.
pearls: Give thiamine before glucose in any confused or amnestic malnourished patient.
Loss of personal identity suggests functional/dissociative amnesia, not organic.
Brief recurrent amnesia on waking: think transient epileptic amnesia.
det.thd: Amnesia คือความจำเสื่อม เป็นอาการไม่ใช่โรค อาจเป็นการจำสิ่งใหม่ไม่ได้หรือลืมความจำเก่า เกิดจากรอยโรคในวงจรความจำ เช่น hippocampus, thalamus หรือ mammillary bodies สาเหตุมีทั้งชั่วคราว เช่น TGA และชัก หรือถาวร เช่น สมองขาดเลือด สมองอักเสบ ขาดวิตามินบี 1 ตรวจ MRI, EEG และเลือดเพื่อหาสาเหตุ แล้วรักษาตามสาเหตุ

name: Amniotic fluid embolism
formal: Obstetric emergency with sudden hypoxia, shock, coagulopathy and seizures or coma, which may produce hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury in the mother.
simple: A rare, life-threatening childbirth complication where amniotic fluid enters the mother's blood, causing collapse and sometimes brain injury.
th: ภาวะฉุกเฉินทางสูติกรรมที่มีน้ำคร่ำเข้าสู่กระแสเลือดมารดา ทำให้ขาดออกซิเจน ช็อก เลือดออกผิดปกติ ชักหรือหมดสติ และอาจเกิดสมองขาดออกซิเจน
tempoNote: Sudden collapse during labour, delivery or shortly after
feat: Primarily an obstetric and critical care emergency, not a primary neurological disease
Sudden breathlessness, hypoxia, hypotension and cardiac arrest around delivery
Seizures or abrupt confusion may be the first sign
Disseminated intravascular coagulation with massive haemorrhage
Survivors may have hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury or haemorrhagic stroke
inv: Clinical diagnosis of exclusion; no confirmatory test
Coagulation profile, fibrinogen, blood gases, echocardiography (right heart failure)
CT/MRI brain for seizures or persistent coma; EEG

case.story: During an induced labour she became breathless, had a generalised seizure and then cardiac arrest; return of circulation after 15 minutes.
case.exam: Comatose post-resuscitation, oozing from cannula sites.
case.tests: Fibrinogen 0.6 g/L, platelets 45,000; echo shows dilated right ventricle; MRI day 4 shows bilateral cortical and basal ganglia diffusion restriction.
case.q: What caused her brain injury?
case.a: Amniotic fluid embolism with cardiac arrest causing hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy.

det.patho: Fetal material entering the maternal circulation is thought to trigger an abnormal immune and coagulation response, rather than simple mechanical obstruction. Acute pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular failure, followed by left ventricular dysfunction and consumptive coagulopathy, produce collapse. Brain injury follows global hypoxia, hypotension or intracranial haemorrhage from coagulopathy.
det.clinical: Onset is abrupt during labour, caesarean section or within about half an hour after delivery. Seizures, agitation or sudden loss of consciousness can precede cardiovascular collapse. Survivors often have multi-organ failure; neurological sequelae include coma, cortical blindness, cognitive impairment and seizures.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, requiring sudden cardiorespiratory collapse plus coagulopathy near delivery after excluding pulmonary embolism, anaphylaxis, sepsis, haemorrhage and eclampsia. Neuroimaging defines the extent of brain injury and excludes haemorrhage.
det.treatment: Immediate resuscitation, rapid delivery if undelivered, ventilatory and inotropic support, aggressive correction of coagulopathy with blood products. Neuroprotective care follows post-arrest principles: temperature control, seizure treatment and avoidance of hypotension and hypoxia.
det.prognosis: Maternal mortality remains substantial and many survivors have neurological deficits.
pearls: Peripartum seizure with collapse and bleeding: think AFE, not only eclampsia.
Neurological outcome is driven mostly by duration of hypoxia.
Check fibrinogen early.
det.thd: Amniotic fluid embolism เป็นภาวะฉุกเฉินทางสูติกรรมที่น้ำคร่ำเข้าสู่กระแสเลือดมารดา ทำให้หายใจลำบาก ความดันตก หัวใจหยุดเต้น และเลือดไม่แข็งตัว ทางระบบประสาทอาจเริ่มด้วยการชักหรือหมดสติ และผู้รอดชีวิตมักมีสมองขาดออกซิเจน การวินิจฉัยเป็นทางคลินิก การรักษาคือกู้ชีพ ทำคลอด แก้ภาวะเลือดออก และดูแลสมองหลังหัวใจหยุดเต้น

name: Amyloid myopathy
formal: Myopathy from amyloid deposition in muscle, usually AL type, causing progressive proximal weakness, macroglossia, and pseudohypertrophy with a raised or normal CK.
simple: Weakness of muscles caused by an abnormal protein called amyloid building up inside them.
more: Biopsy with Congo red staining shows amyloid; screen for plasma cell disorder with serum and urine immunofixation. Treat the underlying clone with chemotherapy; prognosis depends on cardiac involvement.
th: กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงจากการสะสม amyloid (ส่วนใหญ่ชนิด AL) ในกล้ามเนื้อ มีลิ้นโตและกล้ามเนื้อแข็งโตเทียม
tempoNote: Progressive over months
feat: Progressive proximal weakness in an older adult
Macroglossia, firm enlarged muscles (pseudohypertrophy), jaw claudication or dysphagia
Systemic clues: nephrotic proteinuria, heart failure, periorbital purpura, carpal tunnel
Coexisting sensory-autonomic neuropathy common
Usually AL from a plasma cell dyscrasia; rarely hereditary forms
inv: Serum and urine immunofixation and serum free light chains
Muscle biopsy with Congo red (apple-green birefringence) and amyloid typing (mass spectrometry)
Echocardiogram/cardiac MRI, NT-proBNP, troponin; bone marrow biopsy
CK normal or mildly raised; EMG myopathic

case.who: 64-year-old woman referred to a Bangkok university hospital
case.story: Six months of difficulty standing from a chair, hoarse voice and a swollen tongue that she bites while eating; legs swell.
case.exam: Enlarged tongue with dental indentations, firm bulky shoulders, proximal weakness grade 4, bilateral carpal tunnel signs, periorbital bruising.
case.tests: CK 380 U/L; lambda free light chains high; urine protein 4 g/day; muscle biopsy with Congo-red-positive vessel deposits.
case.q: What is the unifying diagnosis?
case.a: AL amyloidosis with amyloid myopathy; refer urgently to haematology for plasma-cell-directed therapy and cardiac staging.

read.where: Myopathies of Systemic Disease and Toxic Myopathies

det.patho: Misfolded immunoglobulin light chains deposit in vessel walls and around muscle fibres, causing ischaemia and mechanical disruption. Rarely transthyretin, gelsolin or other hereditary amyloid proteins are responsible. Deposits in tongue and limb muscles produce firmness and enlargement despite weakness.
det.clinical: Patients are usually middle-aged or elderly with progressive proximal weakness, sometimes the first sign of systemic AL amyloidosis. Macroglossia, dysphagia, hoarseness, jaw claudication and muscle pseudohypertrophy are characteristic clues. Cardiac and renal involvement determine outcome. Neuropathy, carpal tunnel syndrome and orthostatic hypotension often coexist.
det.diagnosis: Muscle biopsy with Congo red or thioflavin staining shows amyloid, especially around vessels; sampling may need several sites. The amyloid type must be confirmed, ideally by mass spectrometry, as it changes treatment. Monoclonal protein screening is essential, and cardiac imaging stages the disease. Fat pad aspirate is less sensitive for muscle involvement.
det.treatment: AL amyloidosis is treated by haematology with plasma-cell-directed regimens, commonly daratumumab-based combinations, and selected patients receive autologous stem cell transplantation. Transthyretin forms are treated with stabilisers or silencers. Supportive care covers swallowing, nutrition, heart failure and physiotherapy.
det.prognosis: Prognosis depends mainly on cardiac involvement; muscle weakness may stabilise once the haematological response is achieved.
pearls: Macroglossia plus proximal weakness should prompt free light chain testing.
Large firm muscles do not always mean a dystrophy; amyloid can mimic pseudohypertrophy.
Always type the amyloid before treatment.
det.thd: Amyloid myopathy เกิดจากการสะสมโปรตีน amyloid ซึ่งส่วนใหญ่เป็น light chain จาก plasma cell ในกล้ามเนื้อ ทำให้ต้นแขนขาอ่อนแรง ลิ้นโต และกล้ามเนื้อแข็งโต วินิจฉัยโดยตัดชิ้นเนื้อย้อม Congo red และตรวจ free light chain รักษาโดยส่งต่อโลหิตวิทยาเพื่อให้ยารักษา plasma cell พยากรณ์โรคขึ้นกับการมีหัวใจผิดปกติ

Higher CK, inflammatory infiltrates rather than amyloid; responds to immunotherapy
Also linked to paraprotein but biopsy shows rods, not amyloid

name: Amyloid neuropathy
formal: Neuropathy from extracellular amyloid deposition in nerves, as in hereditary transthyretin or AL amyloidosis, with painful small fibre loss, autonomic failure and carpal tunnel syndrome.
simple: Nerve damage caused by abnormal protein deposits, leading to pain, numbness, weakness and problems with blood pressure and digestion.
more: Length-dependent axonal sensorimotor and autonomic neuropathy caused by amyloid deposited in nerves, from hereditary transthyretin, AL, or rarer types, often with early pain and temperature loss. Diagnosed by tissue biopsy with typing and genetic or monoclonal testing. Treatments include TTR silencers and stabilisers, chemotherapy for AL, and liver transplantation in selected patients.
th: เส้นประสาทเสื่อมจากการสะสมของ amyloid เช่น transthyretin ทางพันธุกรรมหรือ AL มีปวดแสบปลายเท้า ระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติล้มเหลว และ carpal tunnel syndrome
tempoNote: Progressive over months (AL) to years (ATTR), often with prior bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome
feat: Length-dependent painful small-fibre neuropathy with early pain and temperature loss
Autonomic failure: orthostatic hypotension, diarrhoea or constipation, erectile dysfunction
Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, sometimes years earlier
Systemic clues: cardiomyopathy, weight loss, nephrotic syndrome, macroglossia (AL), vitreous opacities (ATTR)
Rapid progression and weight loss favour AL or late-onset ATTR
inv: Serum and urine immunofixation with free light chains
TTR gene sequencing; echocardiography and cardiac MRI or bone scintigraphy
Tissue biopsy (fat pad, nerve, or other) with Congo red and mass spectrometry typing
NCS and autonomic testing

case.story: One year of burning feet, dizziness on standing and weight loss of 8 kg; had bilateral carpal tunnel surgery three years ago.
case.exam: Loss of pinprick to mid-shin with relatively preserved vibration, postural BP drop 35/15 mmHg.
case.tests: Echo shows thick ventricular walls; TTR sequencing shows a pathogenic variant; fat-pad biopsy is Congo-red positive.
case.q: Which treatment classes can slow this disease?
case.a: Hereditary ATTR amyloidosis; TTR stabilisers (tafamidis) or gene silencers (patisiran, vutrisiran, inotersen, eplontersen).
