det.patho: Misfolded proteins deposit as amyloid fibrils in endoneurium, around vessels and in dorsal root and autonomic ganglia. In hereditary ATTR, destabilising variants in TTR (e.g. V30M or many others) lead to fibrils; wild-type ATTR affects older men and mostly heart and carpal tunnel. In AL amyloidosis, a clonal plasma cell disorder produces amyloidogenic light chains.
det.clinical: The usual pattern is a painful, length-dependent neuropathy affecting small fibres first, followed by large-fibre loss and weakness, combined with autonomic failure. Cardiac involvement determines survival. Late-onset ATTR in non-endemic regions may be misdiagnosed as CIDP or idiopathic neuropathy.
det.diagnosis: Evaluate for a monoclonal protein first because AL needs urgent haematological treatment. Confirm amyloid in tissue and type it by mass spectrometry; sequence TTR. Fat-pad biopsy has limited sensitivity, so a negative result does not exclude disease. Cardiac imaging stages heart involvement.
det.treatment: Hereditary ATTR: TTR stabilisers (tafamidis, diflunisal) or silencers (siRNA patisiran and vutrisiran; antisense inotersen and eplontersen); liver transplantation is now rarely used. AL: chemotherapy such as daratumumab-based regimens with or without autologous stem cell transplant. Supportive care for neuropathic pain and orthostatic hypotension is essential.
det.prognosis: Untreated ATTR polyneuropathy leads to severe disability within about 10 years; AL with cardiac involvement can be rapidly fatal without treatment. Modern therapies substantially slow progression.
pearls: Painful neuropathy + autonomic failure + carpal tunnel: think amyloid.
Always check for a monoclonal protein; AL is a haematological emergency.
A negative fat-pad biopsy does not rule out amyloid.
det.thd: Amyloid neuropathy เกิดจากโปรตีน amyloid ไปสะสมในเส้นประสาท จากยีน TTR ที่ผิดปกติหรือจากเซลล์พลาสมาสร้าง light chain (AL) ผู้ป่วยมีปวดแสบปลายเท้า หน้ามืดเวลาลุกยืน ท้องเสียสลับท้องผูก และมักเคยมี carpal tunnel สองข้าง ตรวจหาโปรตีนผิดปกติในเลือด ยีน TTR และชิ้นเนื้อย้อม Congo red ปัจจุบันมียา TTR stabiliser และ gene silencer และเคมีบำบัดสำหรับ AL

name: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)
formal: Progressive neurodegeneration of upper and lower motor neurons causing weakness, wasting, fasciculations and bulbar involvement, leading to respiratory failure; some cases are familial and associated with frontotemporal dementia.
simple: A progressive disease destroying the nerve cells controlling muscles, causing weakness, muscle wasting, and eventually difficulty speaking, swallowing and breathing.
more: Alternative name for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, a progressive degenerative disorder of upper and lower motor neurons causing weakness, wasting and bulbar failure. Diagnosed clinically with EMG; riluzole and edaravone modestly prolong survival, tofersen for SOD1; median survival 3-5 years, usually from respiratory failure.
th: เซลล์ประสาทสั่งการเสื่อมทั้งในสมองและไขสันหลัง — กล้ามเนื้อลีบ เต้นพลิ้ว ร่วมกับรีเฟล็กซ์ไว ไม่มีอาการชา
tempoNote: Relentless progression over months
feat: UMN and LMN signs coexisting within one body region
Asymmetric painless weakness and wasting with fasciculations
Bulbar onset: dysarthria, dysphagia, tongue fasciculation, emotional lability
Sensation, eye movements and sphincters usually spared; may overlap with FTD
inv: EMG: active denervation with chronic reinnervation in ≥2–3 regions; normal sensory studies
MRI cervical spine/brain to exclude structural mimics
B12, thyroid, calcium, paraprotein; genetic testing when familial

case.story: Eight months of a weak right hand and cramps; now his left hand and speech are affected.
case.exam: Wasted first dorsal interosseous and thenar muscles, widespread fasciculations, brisk reflexes with Hoffmann sign, normal sensation.
case.tests: EMG: fibrillations and large polyphasic units in cervical, thoracic and lumbar segments; MRI spine unremarkable.
case.q: Which combination at the bedside is the key clue?
case.a: Wasting and fasciculations (LMN) with preserved or brisk reflexes (UMN) in the same limb, and no sensory loss.

qx.stem: A 61-year-old teacher from Nakhon Si Thammarat has had 8 months of right hand weakness, cramps and fasciculations. Examination shows wasting of the right first dorsal interosseous, brisk reflexes in the legs and a positive Hoffmann sign, with preserved sensation. Needle EMG shows active denervation with chronic reinnervation in the cervical and lumbosacral regions and in the genioglossus.
qx.q: What is the principal role of electromyography in this evaluation?
opts: To prove upper motor neuron involvement
To replace MRI of the cervical spine
To demonstrate widespread lower motor neuron involvement across regions and to exclude mimics such as multifocal motor neuropathy
To measure antibody levels
To diagnose isolated cervical spondylotic myelopathy
qx.why: EMG confirms active and chronic denervation across several body regions, and the Gold Coast criteria accept fasciculation potentials as evidence of active denervation. Nerve conduction studies help exclude mimics like multifocal motor neuropathy. Upper motor neuron signs are clinical, antibodies are blood tests, and cervical imaging is still needed to exclude compressive disease.

qx.stem: A 62-year-old man from Nakhon Sawan has four months of right hand weakness. The thenar CMAP amplitude is normal, yet a motor unit number estimate (MUNE) is clearly reduced compared with the opposite side and controls.
qx.q: Why can the CMAP remain normal in early ALS?
opts: The CMAP measures sensory fibres, which are spared
Conduction block in the motor nerve raises the amplitude
Surviving motor neurons sprout and reinnervate orphaned muscle fibres, so CMAP stays normal while the number of motor units falls
Fibrillation potentials add to the CMAP amplitude
The MUNE is an artefact of the stimulator position
qx.why: In motor neuron disease, collateral sprouting enlarges the surviving motor units, so the maximum CMAP and strength are maintained for a time even though many motor neurons have died. Motor unit number estimation counts the loss directly and may fall rapidly in the first months of disease. Thus a normal CMAP does not exclude significant motor neuron loss, and large, polyphasic units on needle EMG confirm reinnervation.

det.patho: Progressive loss of cortical upper motor neurons and of lower motor neurons located in the bulbar nuclei and anterior horn. Most cases show TDP-43 protein aggregates; around 10% are familial, and the commonest genes are C9orf72 repeat expansion, SOD1, TARDBP and FUS, which are also found in some apparently sporadic cases. Mechanisms include impaired protein handling, RNA processing defects, glutamate excitotoxicity and glial toxicity. ALS overlaps clinically and genetically with frontotemporal dementia.
det.clinical: Onset is usually focal and asymmetric — limb onset (hand wasting, foot drop) in about two-thirds, bulbar onset (dysarthria, dysphagia) in about a quarter — then spreads to contiguous regions. Mixed UMN and LMN signs coexist: wasting and fasciculations with brisk reflexes, spasticity and pseudobulbar affect. Eye movements, sensation and sphincters are typically spared. Cognitive or behavioural change occurs in up to half, with frank FTD in some. Respiratory muscle weakness causes orthopnoea, morning headache and disturbed sleep. Variants include progressive muscular atrophy, primary lateral sclerosis and flail-arm syndrome.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by EMG, using the Gold Coast criteria: progressive motor impairment with UMN and LMN dysfunction in one region or LMN dysfunction in two regions, after excluding other causes. EMG shows active denervation and chronic reinnervation, with fasciculation potentials, and normal sensory nerve studies. MRI of brain and spine excludes compressive myelopathy and other structural mimics. Bloods and targeted tests exclude MMN, Kennedy disease, IBM, paraproteinaemia and hyperparathyroidism; offer genetic testing, now relevant for SOD1-targeted therapy.
det.treatment: Riluzole modestly prolongs survival; edaravone is available in some countries, and tofersen is an antisense therapy for SOD1-ALS. Multidisciplinary clinic care improves survival and quality of life. Non-invasive ventilation for respiratory insufficiency extends survival, and gastrostomy should be placed before vital capacity falls too far. Manage sialorrhoea, cramps, spasticity, pseudobulbar affect and communication needs, and discuss advance care planning early.
det.prognosis: Median survival is about 2–4 years from symptom onset, mainly ending in respiratory failure; around one in ten live beyond 10 years.
pearls: Upper and lower motor neuron signs coexisting in one limb with normal sensation = ALS until proven otherwise.
Always exclude cervical myelopathy and MMN — both are treatable mimics.
Split hand: thenar and first dorsal interosseous wasted more than hypothenar.
det.thd: ALS คือโรคเซลล์ประสาทสั่งการเสื่อมทั้ง upper และ lower motor neuron เริ่มจากอ่อนแรงและลีบเฉพาะที่ข้างเดียว แล้วลามไปบริเวณอื่น พบกล้ามเนื้อลีบ เต้นพลิ้ว ร่วมกับรีเฟล็กซ์ไวในแขนขาเดียวกัน แต่ไม่มีอาการชา การกลอกตาและหูรูดปกติ บางรายมีความจำและพฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน (FTD) วินิจฉัยด้วยอาการร่วมกับ EMG และต้องตัดโรคที่รักษาได้ เช่น cervical myelopathy และ MMN รักษาด้วย riluzole การดูแลแบบสหสาขา เครื่องช่วยหายใจแบบ NIV และใส่สายให้อาหารทางหน้าท้องเมื่อกลืนลำบาก

name: Anaemia
formal: Reduced haemoglobin with neurological consequences including fatigue, headache, tinnitus, stroke risk and, in B12 or iron deficiency, neuropathy and cognitive effects.
simple: A low level of red blood cells or haemoglobin, causing tiredness, headache and breathlessness.
th: ภาวะฮีโมโกลบินต่ำ ซึ่งส่งผลทางระบบประสาท เช่น อ่อนเพลีย ปวดศีรษะ เสียงในหู เพิ่มความเสี่ยง stroke และถ้าขาด B12 หรือธาตุเหล็กอาจมีปลายประสาทอักเสบและความจำบกพร่อง
tempoNote: Usually develops over weeks to months; acute blood loss causes rapid symptoms
feat: A haematological condition with neurological consequences rather than a neurological disease
Fatigue, poor concentration, headache, dizziness, pulsatile tinnitus, syncope
B12 deficiency: subacute combined degeneration, neuropathy, cognitive change — can occur with little or no anaemia
Iron deficiency: restless legs, breath-holding spells in children, association with venous sinus thrombosis and stroke
Sickle cell disease and thalassaemia cause stroke, moyamoya-like vasculopathy and extramedullary haematopoiesis
inv: FBC with MCV, reticulocytes, blood film
Ferritin, B12, folate, methylmalonic acid/homocysteine
Haemoglobin typing in Thailand (thalassaemia, HbE)

case.who: 35-year-old female seamstress from Phayao with heavy menstrual bleeding
case.story: Months of fatigue and pulsatile whooshing in both ears; new severe headache and blurred vision over a week.
case.exam: Pale conjunctivae, bilateral papilloedema, no focal deficits.
case.tests: Hb 6.2 g/dL, MCV 62 fL, ferritin 3 ng/mL; MRV: superior sagittal and right transverse sinus thrombosis.
case.q: How is her anaemia linked to the neurological problem?
case.a: Severe iron deficiency anaemia is a recognised risk factor for cerebral venous thrombosis; treat with anticoagulation and iron replacement.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Anaemia
Chapter 11: Neurological complications of red blood cell disorders

det.patho: Reduced oxygen-carrying capacity provokes compensatory cerebral vasodilation; severe anaemia lowers the ischaemic threshold. Iron is a cofactor for dopamine synthesis and myelination, explaining links to restless legs and developmental delay. B12 and folate deficiency impair methylation needed for myelin. Haemoglobinopathies damage vessel walls and increase viscosity.
det.clinical: Nonspecific symptoms dominate mild anaemia. Severe anaemia can cause syncope, worsening of existing ischaemia (TIA-like symptoms), retinal haemorrhages and high-output heart failure. Specific deficiencies produce characteristic syndromes such as myelopathy or neuropathy.
det.diagnosis: Characterise the anaemia (micro-, normo- or macrocytic), then look for cause. Measure B12 in any unexplained myelopathy, neuropathy or cognitive decline regardless of haemoglobin. In Thailand, screen for thalassaemia traits before attributing microcytosis to iron deficiency.
det.treatment: Treat the cause and replace deficient nutrients: iron orally or intravenously, B12 intramuscularly when neurological deficits exist. Transfusion is reserved for severe or symptomatic anaemia. Stroke prevention in sickle cell disease uses transfusion programmes and hydroxyurea.
det.prognosis: Symptoms of anaemia resolve with correction; neurological damage from prolonged B12 deficiency may be partly permanent.
pearls: Normal haemoglobin does not exclude B12-related neurological disease.
Profound iron deficiency raises the odds of venous sinus thrombosis and arterial stroke.
Check ferritin in restless legs.
det.thd: Anaemia หรือภาวะซีดเป็นโรคทางโลหิตวิทยาแต่มีผลต่อระบบประสาท เช่น อ่อนเพลีย ปวดศีรษะ เวียนศีรษะ เสียงในหู ภาวะขาดเหล็กสัมพันธ์กับ restless legs และหลอดเลือดดำสมองอุดตัน ส่วนการขาด B12 ทำให้ไขสันหลังและเส้นประสาทเสื่อมได้แม้ไม่ซีด การตรวจคือ CBC, ferritin, B12 และ Hb typing การรักษาคือแก้สาเหตุและเสริมสารที่ขาด

name: Anaesthetic-induced myoclonus
formal: Involuntary myoclonic jerks occurring on induction or emergence from anaesthesia due to certain agents such as etomidate, propofol or opioids.
simple: Brief muscle jerks that can happen when certain anaesthetic drugs are given.
th: การกระตุกแบบ myoclonus ระหว่างนำสลบหรือฟื้นจากยาสลบ จากยาเช่น etomidate, propofol หรือ opioid
tempoNote: Seconds to minutes at induction or emergence; rarely persists for hours to days
feat: Brief, shock-like jerks of limbs or trunk during induction or emergence
Most frequent with etomidate; also propofol, methohexital, high-dose opioids and sevoflurane
Can resemble a seizure, prompting unnecessary anticonvulsant treatment
Usually self-limited and benign
inv: Clinical; EEG if jerks persist or a seizure is suspected
Check electrolytes, glucose and renal function when prolonged

case.who: 35-year-old woman undergoing elective surgery in Songkhla
case.story: After an etomidate bolus for induction she has jerks of both arms for about 20 seconds; no prior seizures.
case.exam: Jerks stop spontaneously; vital signs stable.
case.tests: No investigation needed; recovery uneventful.
case.q: Is this a seizure requiring long-term treatment?
case.a: No; it is anaesthetic-induced myoclonus, typically benign and self-limiting.

det.patho: Etomidate and other agents can transiently suppress cortical inhibitory circuits before subcortical structures, releasing brainstem or spinal myoclonic generators. Some agents (e.g. opioids, propofol) may also act on glycine or GABA systems in ways that disinhibit motor neurons.
det.clinical: Jerks are typically multifocal or generalised, short-lived and seen at induction or emergence. Rarely, prolonged myoclonus or opisthotonus after propofol has been reported. Patients have no lasting sequelae.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical in context. EEG is reserved for persistent or atypical events to rule out seizures, especially in patients with epilepsy.
det.treatment: Usually none is needed. Pretreatment with small doses of opioids, benzodiazepines or lidocaine reduces etomidate-related myoclonus. Prolonged events can be treated with benzodiazepines.
det.prognosis: Excellent; self-limiting.
pearls: Etomidate is the classic cause at induction.
Avoid labelling as epilepsy without EEG support.
Benzodiazepine or opioid premedication reduces it.
det.thd: Anaesthetic-induced myoclonus คือการกระตุกของแขนขาช่วงสั้น ๆ ขณะนำสลบหรือฟื้นจากยาสลบ พบบ่อยกับ etomidate และ propofol เกิดจากยากดวงจรยับยั้งในสมองชั่วคราว มักหายเองไม่มีผลระยะยาว ไม่ต้องให้ยากันชัก ยกเว้นเป็นนานหรือสงสัยชักจริงจึงตรวจ EEG

simple: A fast-growing cancer of brain support cells that needs surgery, radiation and chemotherapy.
th: เนื้องอก astrocyte ชนิดแทรกซึมเกรด 3 มี mitosis เพิ่ม ตามระบบ WHO 2021 เรียก astrocytoma IDH-mutant grade 3 ผู้ป่วยมักอายุน้อยกว่า glioblastoma และรักษาด้วยฉายรังสีตามด้วย temozolomide

feat: Mean age in the 40s, a decade or two earlier than glioblastoma; may follow a long history of a low-grade glioma

case.who: 44-year-old man, a rubber-plantation manager from Surat Thani
case.story: Eight weeks of worsening morning headache and trouble finding words, then a focal seizure of the right face.
case.exam: Mild expressive aphasia and subtle right pronator drift; papilloedema absent.
case.tests: MRI shows a left frontal mass with patchy enhancement and no necrosis. Resection: astrocytoma, IDH1-mutant, ATRX-lost, brisk mitoses, CDKN2A/B retained, CNS WHO grade 3.
case.q: What adjuvant treatment is used after surgery for this tumour?
case.a: Focal radiotherapy (about 59.4 Gy) followed by adjuvant temozolomide, which improved survival in the CATNON trial; concurrent temozolomide added little. Residual vorasidenib is not indicated for grade 3.

det.patho: Anaplastic astrocytoma shows increased cellularity, nuclear atypia and brisk mitotic activity but lacks the necrosis and microvascular proliferation required for grade 4 by histology. Most cases are IDH-mutant with ATRX and TP53 changes, and arise from or alongside lower-grade lesions. Under WHO CNS5 the name is replaced by astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, grade 3, and tumours with homozygous CDKN2A/B deletion are graded 4. IDH-wildtype lesions of this appearance are tested for TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification and 7+/10-, which define glioblastoma.
det.clinical: Presentation is subacute: headache, seizures, progressive focal deficit or cognitive change over weeks to months. Imaging often shows greater mass effect and oedema than in grade 2 disease. Median survival is better than glioblastoma but the tumour recurs and may transform to grade 4; patients with preserved performance status can live several years.
det.diagnosis: Pathologic confirmation with molecular typing is required. Conventional MRI cannot separate grade 3 from grade 4 reliably; perfusion and spectroscopy help choose a biopsy target. IDH, ATRX, 1p/19q and CDKN2A/B are mandatory for classification, and MGMT promoter status guides alkylator expectations. The older concept of mixed oligoastrocytoma has been abolished by molecular testing.
det.treatment: Maximal safe resection is followed by radiotherapy (about 59.4 Gy in 33 fractions) and adjuvant temozolomide for 12 cycles in IDH-mutant tumours, based on the CATNON trial; PCV is an alternative where available. IDH-wildtype grade 3 histology with glioblastoma molecular features is treated like glioblastoma. Dexamethasone for symptomatic oedema, and antiseizure drugs for epilepsy, are supportive. In earlier decades nitrosourea-based regimens were the standard chemotherapy and temozolomide was introduced at recurrence; today temozolomide is used earlier.
det.prognosis: IDH-mutant grade 3 astrocytoma has a median survival of roughly 5-8 years; IDH-wildtype lesions fare much worse, and recurrence is the norm.
pearls: Grade 3 IDH-mutant astrocytoma: radiotherapy then adjuvant temozolomide; concurrent temozolomide is not required.
Homozygous CDKN2A/B deletion makes an IDH-mutant astrocytoma grade 4 regardless of histology.
Mixed oligoastrocytoma is no longer a diagnosis; molecular testing places the tumour as astrocytoma or oligodendroglioma.

name: Andersen–Tawil syndrome
formal: Autosomal dominant KCNJ2 channelopathy with periodic paralysis, ventricular arrhythmia with prolonged QU interval and dysmorphic features such as low-set ears and small mandible.
simple: An inherited condition causing episodes of muscle weakness, heart rhythm problems and distinctive facial and skeletal features.
more: Autosomal dominant KCNJ2 channelopathy of Kir2.1 presenting with periodic paralysis, ventricular arrhythmia with long QT or U waves, and dysmorphic features such as low-set ears and small jaw. Genetic testing of KCNJ2 and ECG monitoring are key. Potassium-level management, acetazolamide or dichlorphenamide, and antiarrhythmic therapy or ICD are used as needed.

36: Myotonic Muscle Disorders and Periodic Paralysis Syndromes

det.patho: Most cases result from dominant-negative mutations in KCNJ2, encoding the inward-rectifier potassium channel Kir2.1 expressed in skeletal muscle, heart and bone. Reduced inward-rectifier current destabilises the resting potential in muscle, prolongs terminal repolarisation in the heart, and disturbs skeletal development. The condition follows dominant transmission with variable expression; de novo cases are frequent.
det.clinical: The full triad is present in only a portion of patients, so diagnosis is often delayed. Attacks of weakness resemble other periodic paralyses but can occur with any potassium level. Cardiac features range from asymptomatic ectopy to syncope; sudden death is uncommon but reported. Dysmorphic features are subtle and require deliberate inspection of face, hands and feet. A fixed proximal weakness may develop later.
det.diagnosis: Suspect ATS in any periodic paralysis with ventricular arrhythmia or characteristic ECG changes (enlarged U waves, long QU, ventricular ectopy). ECG and Holter are essential, together with potassium in attacks and a long exercise test. Genetic testing for KCNJ2 confirms most cases; first-degree relatives should be screened with ECG.
det.treatment: Neuromuscular attacks are reduced with carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide or dichlorphenamide) and careful potassium management, keeping in mind cardiac effects. Cardiology manages arrhythmia, often with beta-blockers or flecainide; ICD is considered for syncope or sustained VT. Avoid drugs that prolong repolarisation and severe hypokalaemia.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is usually close to normal with treatment; disability comes from attacks and later fixed weakness.
pearls: Always do an ECG in periodic paralysis — U waves and bidirectional VT unmask ATS.
Look at the hands and jaw: clinodactyly and micrognathia are easy to miss.
Potassium may be low, normal or high in attacks.

Pupil-involving third nerve palsy suggests a posterior communicating aneurysm; a sentinel headache may precede rupture

Severity graded by Hunt–Hess or WFNS; modified Fisher grade predicts vasospasm

case.who: 54-year-old man, truck driver from Ubon Ratchathani, heavy smoker with untreated hypertension; his sister had SAH at 50
case.story: While lifting a load he felt an explosive headache, vomited and lost consciousness for a minute.
case.exam: GCS 14, neck stiffness, blood pressure 185/105 mm Hg, no focal deficit.
case.tests: CT: thick blood in the basal cisterns and interhemispheric fissure; CTA: 5-mm irregular anterior communicating artery aneurysm.
case.q: The aneurysm is small; why does that not reassure, and what are the priorities?
case.a: Small aneurysms are far more numerous than large ones, so most ruptures come from lesions under 10 mm, and size alone does not exclude rupture. Secure the aneurysm early (coiling when anatomically suitable, otherwise clipping), give oral nimodipine, treat blood pressure carefully before securing, and monitor for hydrocephalus and delayed ischaemia.

det.patho: Saccular aneurysms at branch points of the circle of Willis rupture when wall stress overcomes a wall weakened by inflammation and remodelling. Blood in the subarachnoid space abruptly raises intracranial pressure and causes global ischaemia; breakdown products later provoke arterial narrowing and microvascular dysfunction. Smoking, hypertension, heavy alcohol use, female sex, family history and polycystic kidney disease increase risk, and a first-degree family history is linked to rupture at smaller sizes and younger ages. Aneurysm size, location and shape inform the risk of rupture but small aneurysms still account for many events.
det.clinical: Up to half of patients report a sentinel headache in the preceding weeks. Initial severity ranges from isolated headache to coma. Rebleeding is most likely in the first hours, delayed cerebral ischaemia peaks between days 3 and 14, and hydrocephalus can occur early or late. In a patient with a known aneurysm, a new thunderclap headache is never routine and demands immediate imaging. Cognitive and mood problems are common among survivors.
det.diagnosis: CT within six hours of onset is nearly always positive; its sensitivity falls with time, so lumbar puncture is needed for later negative scans. CTA identifies most aneurysms, with DSA as the reference. Exclude non-aneurysmal causes such as dissection, RCVS, perimesencephalic haemorrhage, AVM and trauma.
det.treatment: Secure the ruptured aneurysm as soon as feasible, ideally within 24 hours; endovascular coiling is preferred when anatomy permits, based on trials showing better disability-free survival than clipping in suitable lesions. Oral nimodipine for 21 days improves outcome; control severe hypertension before securing, avoid hypovolaemia, and treat acute hydrocephalus with an external ventricular drain. Prolonged antifibrinolytic therapy does not improve outcome, and the endothelin antagonist clazosentan reduced vasospasm without clear clinical benefit. Delayed ischaemia is managed with euvolaemia, blood pressure support and, if refractory, endovascular rescue.
det.prognosis: Roughly a third die, and many survivors have cognitive or mood problems even after good physical recovery.
pearls: Thunderclap headache needs CT and, if late or negative, lumbar puncture or CTA.
Pupil-involving third nerve palsy with headache is an aneurysm until proven otherwise.
Nimodipine is given orally; intravenous boluses can drop blood pressure.
det.thd: Aneurysmal SAH คือเลือดออกใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมองจากหลอดเลือดโป่งพองแตก ผู้ป่วยปวดศีรษะรุนแรงทันที อาเจียน คอแข็ง และอาจหมดสติ ปัจจัยเสี่ยงคือสูบบุหรี่ ความดันโลหิตสูง ดื่มจัด และประวัติครอบครัว ต้องทำ CT ถ้าผลลบแต่มาช้าให้เจาะหลังหรือทำ CTA การรักษาคือปิดหลอดเลือดโป่งพองโดยเร็วด้วย coiling หรือ clipping ให้ nimodipine และเฝ้าระวัง hydrocephalus กับ vasospasm หลังรักษาต้องติดตามภาพหลอดเลือดและควบคุมความดัน

qx.stem: A 50-year-old woman has a thunderclap headache. Non-contrast CT performed 2 hours after onset shows diffuse subarachnoid blood filling the basal cisterns plus the Sylvian fissure with a focal thick clot in the interhemispheric fissure. CTA is performed.
qx.q: What is the next step if CTA shows a 6 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm?
opts: Repeat CT in two weeks
Wait for vasospasm to resolve before any intervention
Start high-dose steroids
Secure the aneurysm early by endovascular coiling or clipping after multidisciplinary review, with nimodipine
Lumbar puncture to confirm xanthochromia
qx.why: A positive CT within 6 hours and a culprit aneurysm on CTA means urgent securing, ideally within 24 hours, to prevent rebleeding, plus nimodipine to reduce delayed ischaemia. Lumbar puncture is not needed when CT is positive. Steroids and delay increase risk, and vasospasm management follows rather than delays securing the aneurysm.

Repeat CT in 48 hours

Cranial CT angiography (with digital subtraction angiography if needed) to find the aneurysm

Sodium is 136 mmol/L, CT shows no new bleed or hydrocephalus, and transcranial Doppler velocities in the anterior cerebral arteries have risen sharply. Start prophylactic phenytoin and observe
Give IV dexamethasone for cerebral oedema

Prophylactic hypervolaemia and fluid restriction are both harmful, and steroids or routine phenytoin have no role.

Chapter 8 Stroke and Cerebrovascular Diseases — Subarachnoid Haemorrhage
Chapter 16: Specific interventions to prevent intracranial hemorrhage
Section 3 Hereditary and Genetic Conditions and Malformations

det.patho: Saccular aneurysms develop at bifurcations from loss of the internal elastic lamina, endothelial dysfunction, haemodynamic stress and inflammation. Smoking and hypertension add to the risk, and genetic predisposition is seen in polycystic kidney disease, Ehlers–Danlos syndrome and familial clusters. Fusiform and dissecting aneurysms follow arterial wall injury or atherosclerosis, and infectious aneurysms arise from septic emboli. Up to one in five patients have more than one aneurysm.
det.clinical: Unruptured aneurysms are mostly silent. Compression symptoms depend on site: posterior communicating and basilar aneurysms cause third nerve palsy, ophthalmic or ACoA aneurysms affect vision, and cavernous carotid lesions cause ophthalmoplegia and facial pain. Thrombus within the sac may embolise and cause TIA or stroke. A thunderclap headache is a ruptured aneurysm until excluded, and new headaches in a patient with a known aneurysm should be taken seriously.
det.diagnosis: CTA and MRA detect most aneurysms, with DSA for the smallest lesions and for planning. Risk tools such as PHASES, ELAPSS and UIATS summarise rupture, growth and treatment considerations but leave out factors such as smoking and family history. Size under 7 mm in the anterior circulation carries a low annual risk, while 7 mm or more, posterior circulation location, irregular shape and growth carry more. A multidisciplinary team and shared decision making are expected.
det.treatment: Small low-risk aneurysms are observed with blood pressure control, smoking cessation and repeat imaging. Endovascular treatment (coiling, stent-assisted coiling, flow diversion, intrasaccular devices) has a lower procedural risk but more recurrence than clipping, which is more durable but more invasive. Symptomatic, enlarging or higher-risk aneurysms deserve prompt treatment. Antiplatelet drugs needed for another indication are generally continued, and stents or flow diverters require a planned course of dual antiplatelet therapy.
det.prognosis: Annual rupture risk of small unruptured aneurysms is low but rises with size, posterior location and growth; outcome after rupture is often poor.
pearls: Painful pupil-involving third nerve palsy: urgent angiography.
Stopping smoking and controlling blood pressure are essential whether or not repair is chosen.
Mycotic aneurysm: think endocarditis.
det.thd: Aneurysm ในสมองคือหลอดเลือดแดงโป่งพอง มักเป็นแบบ saccular ที่จุดแยกของ circle of Willis ส่วนใหญ่ไม่มีอาการและพบโดยบังเอิญ บางรายกดเส้นประสาทสมองที่ 3 ทำให้ตาตกและม่านตาขยาย หรือแตกเป็น SAH ตรวจด้วย CTA หรือ MRA ส่วนการรักษาพิจารณาจากขนาด ตำแหน่ง รูปร่าง และปัจจัยเสี่ยงโดยใช้ PHASES ร่วมกับการตัดสินใจร่วมกับผู้ป่วย ผู้ป่วยทุกรายควรเลิกบุหรี่และคุมความดันโลหิต

qx.stem: A 61-year-old man from Samut Songkhram with treated hypertension and a 30 pack-year history has an incidental 3-mm saccular aneurysm of the right middle cerebral artery on MR angiography for dizziness. He has no family history of subarachnoid haemorrhage and no neurological deficit.
qx.q: Which management is most appropriate?
opts: Immediate surgical clipping
Flow diverter placement within a week
Smoking cessation, blood pressure control, and surveillance imaging with MRA or CTA, reserving intervention for growth or higher-risk features
Lifelong anticoagulation
No follow-up at all, as aneurysms of this size never rupture
qx.why: Small unruptured aneurysms under 7 mm in the anterior circulation have a low annual rupture risk, and the main steps are modifiable risk factor control (smoking cessation, blood pressure) and periodic imaging surveillance, with treatment for growth, symptoms, irregular shape or higher-risk location. Procedures carry risk that outweighs benefit here, and anticoagulation is not indicated.

qx.stem: A neurovascular multidisciplinary meeting reviews five patients, each with an incidental unruptured intracranial aneurysm.
qx.q: Which patient should be prioritised for endovascular or surgical repair?
opts: A man aged 70 with a 2-mm paraclinoid aneurysm and no risk factors
A 52-year-old smoker with hypertension, a family history of subarachnoid haemorrhage and an 8-mm irregular anterior communicating artery aneurysm with a daughter sac
A 78-year-old woman whose 3-mm calcified cavernous carotid aneurysm
A 66-year-old man with a 4-mm stable MCA aneurysm unchanged over 3 years
A woman aged 59 with a 2-mm infundibulum of the posterior communicating artery origin
qx.why: Risk of rupture increases with size of 7 mm or more, anterior communicating or posterior circulation location, irregular morphology or daughter sacs, growth, hypertension, smoking and a family history of aneurysmal SAH. qx.stem: A 60-year-old woman has three days of right periorbital pain, then complete ptosis with the eye down and out and a 6-mm poorly reactive pupil. CT shows no subarachnoid blood.
qx.q: Which is the most important next step?

Start high-dose corticosteroids for presumed giant cell arteritis only
Urgent CT or MR angiography, with prompt neurovascular referral if an aneurysm is found
Reassure and arrange outpatient review in six weeks
Order an edrophonium test
qx.why: A painful third nerve palsy involving the pupil suggests a posterior communicating aneurysm that is symptomatic and may be expanding, so urgent vascular imaging is required. Microvascular palsy typically spares the pupil, and waiting risks rupture. Steroids may follow if arteritis is later proven, and an edrophonium test does not apply because the pupil is involved.

name: Angelman syndrome
formal: Neurodevelopmental disorder with severe intellectual disability, absent speech, ataxia, tremulous movements, epilepsy and a happy demeanour, due to loss of maternal UBE3A function on chromosome 15q11-13.
simple: A genetic condition causing developmental delay, no speech, unsteady walking, seizures and frequent smiling or laughter.
more: Confirmed by methylation testing and other chromosome 15 studies. Management includes antiseizure drugs, sleep and behavioural therapy; life expectancy is near normal.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมจากการสูญเสียหน้าที่ยีน UBE3A จากแม่บนโครโมโซม 15 ทำให้พัฒนาการช้ามาก ไม่พูด เดินเซ ชัก และหัวเราะยิ้มบ่อย
tempoNote: Delay evident from 6–12 months; seizures typically begin before age 3; non-progressive course
feat: Severe developmental delay with minimal or absent speech but better receptive language
Ataxic, jerky gait with raised flexed arms and tremulous limb movements
Frequent laughter, excitable happy demeanour, hand flapping, fascination with water
Epilepsy in most, often with myoclonic and atypical absence seizures
Microcephaly, sleep disturbance; hypopigmentation with deletion type

case.story: Not yet walking alone or saying words; she laughs easily, sleeps poorly and had her first seizure with fever.
case.exam: Microcephaly, fair skin compared with parents, wide-based jerky stepping with arms up, frequent smiling, hand flapping.
case.tests: EEG shows high-amplitude 2–3 Hz rhythmic delta with spikes; methylation test shows only paternal pattern; microarray finds 15q11-q13 deletion.
case.q: Which parent's chromosome 15 is missing the active gene?
case.a: Maternal — Angelman syndrome results from loss of maternally expressed UBE3A.

read.where: Section II: Epidemiology, Etiology, and Diagnosis

det.patho: UBE3A, a ubiquitin ligase gene, is imprinted in neurons so only the maternal copy is active. Loss of the maternal copy by deletion (about 70%), paternal uniparental disomy, imprinting centre defect or UBE3A mutation leaves neurons without the protein, disturbing synaptic function. The paternal deletion of the same region causes Prader–Willi syndrome instead.
det.clinical: Infants may have feeding problems and hypotonia, and slowed development becomes clear around 6–12 months. Speech is minimal, though children understand more and use gestures or devices. Gait is ataxic and tremulous; behaviour is cheerful and excitable with short attention. Epilepsy, sleep disturbance, scoliosis and obesity in some subtypes are common. Deletion cases tend to be the most severe.
det.diagnosis: Clinical consensus criteria guide suspicion. Methylation analysis of 15q11-q13 detects about 80% of cases; further testing (microarray, UPD studies, UBE3A sequencing) defines the mechanism, which matters for recurrence risk counselling. The EEG pattern is a useful early clue.
det.treatment: Management is supportive: antiseizure drugs (valproate, levetiracetam, clobazam; avoid carbamazepine which can worsen myoclonic and absence seizures), sleep measures including melatonin, augmentative communication, physiotherapy and behavioural support. Antisense oligonucleotides aimed at reactivating the silent paternal UBE3A copy are in clinical trials.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is near normal; adults need lifelong support.
pearls: Maternal loss = Angelman; paternal loss of the same region = Prader–Willi.
Absent speech with relatively strong understanding and frequent laughter is the key behavioural picture.
Recurrence risk depends on mechanism: low for deletion, up to 50% for UBE3A mutation or imprinting defects.
det.thd: Angelman syndrome เกิดจากยีน UBE3A บนโครโมโซม 15 ที่ได้จากแม่ไม่ทำงาน เด็กมีพัฒนาการช้ามาก แทบไม่พูดแต่เข้าใจได้มากกว่า เดินเซกระตุก ยกแขน ชัก หัวเราะง่ายและนอนหลับยาก EEG มีลักษณะเฉพาะ ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจ methylation ของ 15q11-q13 รักษาแบบประคับประคอง ใช้ยากันชัก ฝึกสื่อสาร และดูแลการนอน

name: Ankylosing spondylitis
formal: Chronic inflammatory spondyloarthropathy with sacroiliitis and spinal fusion, associated with HLA-B27 and neurological complications such as cauda equina syndrome and spinal fracture myelopathy.
simple: A long-term inflammatory disease that stiffens the spine and can occasionally damage the spinal cord or nerves.
th: โรคข้อกระดูกสันหลังอักเสบเรื้อรังที่มี sacroiliitis และกระดูกสันหลังเชื่อมติด สัมพันธ์กับ HLA-B27 มีภาวะแทรกซ้อนทางระบบประสาท เช่น กระดูกคอหัก cauda equina และ atlantoaxial subluxation
tempoNote: Chronic inflammatory back disease starting in young adults; neurological complications may be acute (fracture) or slowly progressive (cauda equina)
feat: Rheumatological disease, not primarily neurological; neurologists see its spinal complications
Inflammatory back pain with morning stiffness in young adults, improving with exercise
Rigid, fused 'bamboo' spine fractures easily after minor trauma, often cervical, with high cord injury risk
Cauda equina syndrome from dural ectasia and arachnoid diverticula in long-standing disease
Atlantoaxial subluxation, uveitis, aortitis and heart block
inv: HLA-B27, CRP, ESR
MRI sacroiliac joints and spine; CT for suspected fracture even after minor falls
MRI lumbar spine for dural ectasia in cauda equina features
Nerve conduction/EMG for radiculopathy

case.who: 58-year-old man from Udon Thani with 30 years of ankylosing spondylitis
case.story: Slipped in the bathroom and hit his forehead; next day severe neck pain and tingling in both hands.
case.exam: Fixed kyphotic neck, weakness of hand grip, brisk reflexes in legs.
case.tests: Plain X-ray unclear; CT shows an unstable fracture through C6–7 with epidural haematoma on MRI.
case.q: Why is minor trauma dangerous in AS?
case.a: The fused, osteoporotic spine behaves like a long brittle bone, so minor trauma causes unstable fractures and cord injury; CT/MRI and urgent stabilisation are needed.

read.where: Chapter 14 Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders — Rheumatological Disorders Affecting the Spine and Spinal Cord
Chapter 22 Neurologic Disorders Associated with Bone and Joint Disease
Section 6 Systemic Disorders That Also Involve the Cerebrovascular System
Chapter 16: Anatomy and Degenerative Diseases of the Spine

det.patho: AS is an HLA-B27-associated spondyloarthritis in which enthesitis and the IL-23/IL-17 axis drive inflammation of the sacroiliac joints and spine, followed by new bone formation and ankylosis. The fused spine loses flexibility and becomes osteoporotic, so it fractures easily. Chronic arachnoiditis and dural ectasia can erode the posterior lumbar elements and compress cauda equina roots.
det.clinical: Inflammatory back pain begins before age 45, with morning stiffness and improvement with exercise. Neurological complications include cervical fractures after minimal trauma, epidural haematoma, atlantoaxial subluxation, spinal stenosis and the slowly progressive cauda equina syndrome with sensory loss, sphincter dysfunction and leg weakness. Extra-articular features include anterior uveitis, aortic regurgitation and inflammatory bowel disease.
det.diagnosis: ASAS criteria combine imaging sacroiliitis or HLA-B27 with clinical features. For neurological complications, CT detects fractures that may be invisible on plain films, and MRI shows cord injury, haematoma and dural ectasia with diverticula. Any patient with AS and new neck pain after a fall should have CT of the whole spine.
det.treatment: Disease control uses NSAIDs, physiotherapy and biologics (TNF or IL-17 inhibitors) or JAK inhibitors. Fractures require careful immobilisation in the patient's existing posture and usually surgical fixation. Cauda equina syndrome from dural ectasia is managed surgically in selected cases, with variable benefit. Fall prevention and bone health measures are important.
det.prognosis: Most patients have good function with modern therapy; spinal fractures carry high rates of neurological deficit and mortality.
pearls: Minor fall + AS + neck pain = CT the spine; plain films miss fractures.
Never force the neck into a 'neutral' position — immobilise in the patient's usual posture.
Slowly progressive cauda equina in long-standing AS suggests dural ectasia.
det.thd: Ankylosing spondylitis เป็นโรคข้อกระดูกสันหลังอักเสบเรื้อรังที่สัมพันธ์กับ HLA-B27 ทำให้ปวดหลังแบบอักเสบในคนหนุ่ม และกระดูกสันหลังเชื่อมติดกันจนแข็ง เป็นโรคทางรูมาติสซั่ม แต่มีภาวะแทรกซ้อนทางระบบประสาท เช่น กระดูกคอหักง่ายจากอุบัติเหตุเล็กน้อย cauda equina syndrome และ atlantoaxial subluxation หากล้มแล้วปวดคอต้องทำ CT ทันที การรักษาใช้ NSAIDs, biologics และกายภาพบำบัด

name: Anoctamin-5-related muscular dystrophy (LGLD
formal: Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (LGMD R12) from ANO5 mutations with asymmetric proximal or distal weakness, calf atrophy, myalgia and markedly raised creatine kinase.
simple: An inherited muscle disease causing weakness of the hips, shoulders or calves and very high muscle enzyme levels.
th: กล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมชนิด limb-girdle จากยีน ANO5 พบในผู้ใหญ่ อ่อนแรงไม่สมมาตร น่องลีบ ปวดกล้ามเนื้อ และ CK สูงมาก
tempoNote: Adult onset, slowly progressive over decades; some only have raised CK or myalgia for years
feat: Onset in adulthood, more severe in men
Asymmetric weakness of quadriceps or hamstrings, or calf (Miyoshi-like) presentation
Calf atrophy (sometimes early hypertrophy), exercise myalgia
CK often 10–50 times normal, even in asymptomatic carriers of two variants
Cardiac and respiratory involvement uncommon
inv: CK; EMG myopathic
Muscle MRI: asymmetric involvement of medial gastrocnemius, adductors and hamstrings
Gene panel: biallelic ANO5 variants (a common founder variant in Europeans; other variants in Asians)
Biopsy: dystrophic changes, sometimes amyloid deposits, normal dysferlin

case.who: 41-year-old male motorcycle taxi driver from Bangkok
case.story: Calf aching after long walks for several years; recently struggles to climb stairs, worse on the right leg.
case.exam: Asymmetric thigh wasting right more than left, right calf thin, unable to stand on tiptoes on the right, arms normal, reflexes reduced at the knees.
case.tests: CK 4,500 U/L; MRI shows fatty replacement of right medial gastrocnemius and adductors; panel finds two ANO5 variants.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and which test excluded the main alternative?
case.a: ANO5-related muscular dystrophy (LGMD R12); normal dysferlin expression and the gene result excluded dysferlinopathy.

read.where: Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Muscular Dystrophies

det.patho: ANO5 encodes anoctamin-5, a membrane protein thought to function as a scramblase involved in sarcolemmal repair. Loss of function impairs resealing after exercise-induced membrane damage, giving a dystrophic process. Inheritance is autosomal recessive; in parts of northern Europe it is among the commonest adult LGMDs.
det.clinical: Presentation varies from isolated high CK or exercise myalgia to proximal or distal weakness beginning in the 20s to 50s. Asymmetry is a useful clue. Men tend to be more severely affected than women. Progression is slow, and most remain ambulant for decades.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in adults with very high CK and asymmetric posterior thigh or calf involvement on MRI. Genetic panel testing is the main confirmatory step. Biopsy shows non-specific dystrophic changes and normal dysferlin, which helps separate it from dysferlinopathy. Many cases were previously misdiagnosed as polymyositis.
det.treatment: No disease-specific therapy exists. Management involves graded exercise avoiding excessive eccentric loading, physiotherapy, orthoses and periodic cardiac review. Steroids are not effective and should be avoided. Genetic counselling is appropriate.
det.prognosis: Usually slowly progressive with preserved ambulation into later life; life expectancy is generally normal.
pearls: Asymmetric calf or thigh weakness with very high CK in an adult should suggest ANO5.
Steroid-unresponsive 'polymyositis' with high CK deserves an LGMD gene panel.
Amyloid deposits can be seen on biopsy in some ANO5 cases.
det.thd: โรคกล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมทางพันธุกรรมแบบ autosomal recessive จากยีน ANO5 ซึ่งช่วยซ่อมผนังเซลล์กล้ามเนื้อ เริ่มอาการในวัยผู้ใหญ่ อ่อนแรงต้นขาหรือน่องแบบไม่สมมาตร ปวดหลังออกแรง และ CK สูงมาก วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI กล้ามเนื้อและตรวจยีน ยังไม่มียาจำเพาะ ใช้กายภาพบำบัดและติดตามอาการ

name: Anterior canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (a-BPPV)
formal: Rare form of BPPV in which displaced otoconia affect the anterior semicircular canal, causing brief positional vertigo with downbeating torsional nystagmus, treated with repositioning manoeuvres.
simple: A rare type of brief spinning dizziness triggered by head position, caused by tiny crystals in a part of the inner ear.
ab: Anterior canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
th: BPPV ชนิดพบน้อยที่ตะกอนหินปูนอยู่ในหลอดกึ่งวงกลมด้านหน้า ทำให้เวียนศีรษะสั้น ๆ ตามท่าและพบ downbeating nystagmus
tempoNote: Brief attacks (< 1 min) with head movements, recurring over days to weeks
feat: Brief positional vertigo, e.g. lying down or bending forward
Downbeating nystagmus, often with a small torsional component, in Dix–Hallpike or straight head-hanging
Accounts for a small minority of BPPV; may follow posterior canal repositioning
Short latency and fatigable, unlike most central positional nystagmus
inv: Dix–Hallpike both sides and deep head-hanging under Frenzel/video goggles
MRI brain if nystagmus is persistent, non-fatigable, or with other neurological signs (central positional downbeat)

case.story: Two days after Epley treatment for right posterior canal BPPV, she has new brief spins when lying back and when bending to wash her hair.
case.exam: Straight head-hanging provokes downbeating nystagmus with slight torsion lasting 15 seconds and fatiguing; no other signs.
case.tests: No imaging needed after typical response; resolved with a deep head-hanging manoeuvre.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what must be considered if nystagmus does not fatigue?
case.a: Anterior canal BPPV; persistent downbeat positional nystagmus suggests a central (cerebellar) cause needing MRI.

read.where: Chapter 23 Neuro-Otology: Dizziness, Balance and Hearing — Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo

det.patho: Otoconia displaced from the utricle enter the anterior semicircular canal and move with gravity during head positioning, producing ampullofugal endolymph flow and excitation of the canal. The anterior canal's upward orientation makes it rarely affected, and debris tends to clear spontaneously.
det.clinical: Patients describe brief spinning when lying down, looking up or bending forward. Positional testing produces downbeating nystagmus, with the torsional component often subtle. Anterior canal BPPV may follow treatment of the posterior canal form. It is usually self-limiting.
det.diagnosis: The key is distinguishing it from central positional downbeat nystagmus, which is commoner than anterior canal BPPV in many series. Features favouring peripheral origin are brief latency, crescendo-decrescendo course, fatigability and the absence of other neurological signs. When in doubt or if the response to treatment is poor, MRI is required.
det.treatment: Deep head-hanging manoeuvres (such as the Yacovino manoeuvre) are effective and do not require identifying the side. Many cases resolve spontaneously. Vestibular suppressants are not recommended beyond short-term symptom relief.
det.prognosis: Good; recurrences can occur as with other BPPV.
pearls: Positional downbeat nystagmus: think central first, anterior canal BPPV second.
Yacovino manoeuvre treats a-BPPV without needing to know the side.
No fatigue or atypical features → MRI posterior fossa.
det.thd: Anterior canal BPPV เป็น BPPV ชนิดพบน้อยที่ตะกอนหินปูนเข้าไปในหลอดกึ่งวงกลมด้านหน้า ทำให้เวียนหัวสั้น ๆ เมื่อนอนหงายหรือก้ม ตรวจพบ downbeating nystagmus ที่มี latency สั้นและล้าได้ ต้องแยกจาก central positional nystagmus จากโรคสมองน้อย รักษาด้วยท่า deep head-hanging เช่น Yacovino และถ้าไม่ตอบสนองควรทำ MRI

name: Anterior cingulate syndrome
formal: Frontal syndrome from anterior cingulate damage causing apathy, akinetic mutism, reduced motivation and impaired error monitoring, as in stroke from anterior cerebral artery occlusion.
simple: Loss of drive, speech and emotion after damage to a front part of the brain.
th: กลุ่มอาการจากรอยโรคที่ anterior cingulate cortex ทำให้เฉยเมย ขาดแรงจูงใจ พูดและเคลื่อนไหวน้อย จนถึง akinetic mutism เช่นในโรคหลอดเลือด anterior cerebral artery อุดตัน
tempoNote: Acute after stroke, haemorrhage or surgery; insidious with tumours or degeneration
feat: Apathy, abulia and reduced spontaneous speech and movement
Akinetic mutism when lesions are bilateral: eyes follow but patient barely moves or speaks
Poor error monitoring, perseveration and reduced emotional response
Often with leg weakness, urinary incontinence and grasp reflex in ACA territory stroke
Causes: ACA infarction, ACoA aneurysm rupture or surgery, butterfly glioma, frontotemporal dementia, hydrocephalus
inv: MRI brain with diffusion; MRA or CTA of anterior cerebral arteries
Cognitive screening emphasising initiation and executive tasks
EEG if fluctuating responsiveness raises suspicion of non-convulsive seizures

case.story: After surgical clipping of an anterior communicating aneurysm he lies still, answers only after long delays and is incontinent.
case.exam: Eyes open and track, speaks single words when pushed, bilateral grasp reflexes, legs weaker than arms.
case.tests: MRI: bilateral medial frontal and anterior cingulate infarcts.
case.q: What syndrome is present and what may help?
case.a: Bilateral anterior cingulate (medial frontal) syndrome with akinetic mutism; dopaminergic agents such as bromocriptine or amantadine with rehabilitation may improve initiation.

det.patho: The anterior cingulate cortex integrates motivation, attention and action selection through connections with prefrontal cortex, ventral striatum and thalamus. Damage, particularly bilaterally, disconnects drive from motor output. Lesions of connected structures (medial thalamus, ventral striatum) produce similar syndromes.
det.clinical: Mild cases show apathy and slowed responses; severe bilateral lesions cause akinetic mutism where patients are awake but initiate almost nothing. Responses may emerge with strong stimulation. Associated ACA signs include contralateral leg weakness and incontinence.
det.diagnosis: Clinical recognition plus imaging localises the lesion. Distinguish from depression, catatonia, locked-in syndrome, disorders of consciousness and non-convulsive status.
det.treatment: Treat the cause (stroke prevention, tumour management, CSF diversion). Dopamine agonists, amantadine or methylphenidate have small-study support for apathy and akinetic mutism. Structured rehabilitation with external cueing helps.
det.prognosis: Unilateral lesions often improve substantially; bilateral lesions may leave lasting apathy.
pearls: Awake but not initiating, yet tracking you with the eyes: think akinetic mutism.
ACoA aneurysm rupture or clipping can damage both medial frontal lobes.
Do not mislabel apathy as depression without examining frontal signs.
det.thd: Anterior cingulate syndrome เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ anterior cingulate cortex ทำให้ผู้ป่วยเฉยเมย ขาดแรงจูงใจ พูดและเคลื่อนไหวน้อย ถ้าเป็นทั้งสองข้างอาจเป็น akinetic mutism คือตื่นและมองตามแต่แทบไม่พูดหรือขยับ สาเหตุเช่น ACA infarction หลอดเลือดโป่งพอง ACoA เนื้องอก หรือ FTD การรักษาคือแก้สาเหตุ ให้ยา dopaminergic และฟื้นฟู

name: Anterior cord syndrome
formal: Spinal cord infarction or injury in the anterior spinal artery territory with loss of motor function and pain and temperature sensation below the lesion, with preserved dorsal column function.
simple: Spinal cord damage causing paralysis and loss of pain and temperature sensing below the injury, while touch and position sense stay normal.
th: กลุ่มอาการจากไขสันหลังส่วนหน้าขาดเลือดหรือบาดเจ็บ ทำให้ขาอ่อนแรงทันทีและเสียการรับรู้เจ็บและอุณหภูมิใต้รอยโรค แต่ยังรับรู้สั่นสะเทือนและตำแหน่งข้อได้
tempoNote: Pain followed within minutes to hours by weakness, reaching nadir within about 12 hours
feat: Abrupt paraparesis or tetraparesis, flaccid at first and spastic later, with a sensory level
Pinprick and thermal sensation are lost below the lesion, with vibration and joint position spared because the dorsal columns are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries
Sudden radicular or band-like back or neck pain at onset in many infarcts
Bladder retention, bowel dysfunction and sometimes autonomic instability
Causes: aortic surgery or dissection, severe hypotension, atherosclerosis, fibrocartilaginous embolism, vertebral artery disease, and flexion injuries or disc herniation in trauma
inv: MRI of the whole spine with diffusion imaging: T2 hyperintensity of anterior grey matter (owl’s-eye or pencil-like), diffusion restriction; repeat in 24–72 hours if first scan is normal
Exclude compression, myelitis and haematoma; CT angiography or MRA of aorta and cervical vessels
Blood pressure history, cardiac assessment, inflammatory and thrombophilia screen in selected cases

case.who: 66-year-old man from Chiang Rai who has hypertension and diabetes
case.story: While being treated in hospital after a ruptured aortic aneurysm repair he woke with sudden back pain, then within an hour could not move either leg. Blood pressure fell to 70/40 during the operation.
case.exam: Flaccid paraplegia, absent pinprick and cold sensation below T8, vibration and joint position intact in both feet, urinary retention, absent reflexes initially.
case.tests: MRI shows anterior grey matter T2 hyperintensity from T7 to T10 with diffusion restriction; no cord compression; CT angiogram shows the repaired graft is patent.
case.q: Why is vibration preserved, and what is the key management?
case.a: The dorsal columns are fed by the paired posterior spinal arteries, unlike the anterior cord territory. Management is raising spinal perfusion pressure (maintain blood pressure, consider CSF drainage), supportive care and rehabilitation; steroids are unproven.

read.where: Chapter 49: Ischemic Stroke: Uncommon and Special Situations — Spinal Cord Infarction
Chapter 14 Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders — Clinical Assessment of Spinal Disorders
Chapter 30: The Neurologist And Icu Ethical Dilemmas

det.patho: The anterior spinal artery perfuses the ventral part of the cord (about two-thirds of its cross-section), including the corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts, while the posterior spinal arteries feed the dorsal columns. The thoracolumbar segment is a watershed zone and is the most vulnerable to low perfusion. Infarction results from hypoperfusion, embolism or thrombosis; in trauma, the anterior cord is injured by flexion forces, disc fragments or vertebral bone.
det.clinical: Back pain is followed by weakness within minutes or hours, accompanied by loss of pain and temperature sensation and retention of urine. Flaccid weakness and areflexia at first become spastic with hyperreflexia over days to weeks, and lower motor neuron signs appear at the segment of infarction. Dorsal column function remains. Posterior spinal artery or sulcal artery syndromes are much rarer, and diagnosis requires attention to recent aortic surgery, dissection, hypotension and embolic sources.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical and relies on MRI, which shows a sagittal pencil-like or axial owl’s-eye pattern of T2 signal with early diffusion restriction, and on exclusion of mimics. A normal early MRI does not exclude infarction. Imaging of the aorta, vertebral arteries and heart identifies the source. Proposed criteria require acute non-traumatic myelopathy, no compression, and supportive or specific imaging.
det.treatment: No therapy is proven for the acute infarct. Keep mean arterial pressure up, correct the cause, and in aortic surgery or dissection cases consider CSF drainage to lower intrathecal pressure; corticosteroids have been tried with mixed results. Secondary prevention targets the source, such as antiplatelet therapy or anticoagulation for embolic cause and control of vascular risk factors. Rehabilitation, bladder and bowel programmes, pressure sore prevention and pain management determine recovery.
det.prognosis: Variable: about a fifth to a quarter do not improve, around a fifth make a good recovery, and the rest remain moderately to severely disabled. Chronic neuropathic pain is common.
pearls: Preserved vibration and joint position with loss of pain and temperature points to the anterior cord.
Think aorta first: dissection and aneurysm surgery are classic causes.
Repeat MRI with diffusion if the first scan is clear but the story is typical.
det.thd: Anterior cord syndrome เกิดจากไขสันหลังส่วนหน้าขาดเลือดจาก anterior spinal artery หรือจากการบาดเจ็บ ผู้ป่วยปวดหลังเฉียบพลันแล้วขาอ่อนแรงภายในไม่กี่ชั่วโมง เสียความรู้สึกเจ็บและอุณหภูมิใต้ระดับรอยโรค ปัสสาวะไม่ออก แต่ vibration และ joint position ยังดีเพราะ dorsal column ได้เลือดจากหลอดเลือดอีกชุด MRI เห็นสัญญาณผิดปกติรูปตาเค้าและ DWI จำกัดการแพร่ การรักษาคือรักษาความดันเลือด แก้สาเหตุ และฟื้นฟู

name: Anterior horn cell disease
formal: Disorders of spinal motor neuron cell bodies such as ALS, spinal muscular atrophy and poliomyelitis, causing lower motor neuron weakness, wasting and fasciculations without sensory loss.
simple: Diseases that damage the nerve cells in the spinal cord that control muscles, causing weakness and muscle wasting.
th: กลุ่มโรคที่เซลล์ประสาทสั่งการใน anterior horn ของไขสันหลังเสื่อมหรือติดเชื้อ ทำให้อ่อนแรง กล้ามเนื้อลีบ fasciculation โดยไม่มีอาการชา

feat: Pure motor weakness with wasting, fasciculations and cramps
Asymmetric or segmental onset is common; sensation entirely spared

case.who: 58-year-old male rice farmer from Suphan Buri
case.story: Over eight months his right hand became clumsy and thin, and he now notices twitching in both arms and cramps at night.
case.exam: Wasted first dorsal interosseous and thenar muscles, widespread fasciculations, brisk biceps and knee jerks, no sensory loss.
case.tests: EMG: denervation in cervical, thoracic paraspinal and lumbar segments; sensory NCS normal; MRI cervical spine unremarkable.
case.q: Why is this classified as anterior horn disease and which specific diagnosis is most likely?
case.a: Pure motor LMN signs with normal sensation localise to the anterior horn; combined UMN signs across regions point to ALS.

det.patho: Spinal motor neuron somata sit in the ventral horn grey matter, with equivalents in the brainstem motor nuclei. They can be lost through degeneration (ALS, SMA from SMN1 deletion, Kennedy disease from androgen receptor repeat expansion), viral infection (poliovirus, enterovirus A71, West Nile, JE) or rarely toxic and paraneoplastic processes. Loss of motor units leads to denervation, wasting and compensatory reinnervation.
det.clinical: The core picture is weakness and atrophy without sensory involvement. Fasciculations and cramps are frequent. Acute infective forms produce asymmetric flaccid paralysis with fever and meningism, while degenerative forms creep over months to years. Look for upper motor neuron signs (ALS), gynaecomastia and sensory neuronopathy (Kennedy), or childhood onset with proximal symmetric weakness (SMA).
det.diagnosis: EMG is the key test, showing widespread denervation with normal sensory nerve action potentials. Exclude conduction block (MMN), compressive myelopathy or radiculopathy, and myopathy. Gold Coast criteria are now often used for ALS. Genetic tests confirm SMA and Kennedy disease, while CSF and PCR help in acute flaccid myelitis.
det.treatment: Treatment depends on cause. SMA has disease-modifying options (nusinersen, risdiplam, onasemnogene). ALS care includes riluzole, tofersen for SOD1 cases, non-invasive ventilation and gastrostomy within a multidisciplinary clinic. Acute viral forms need supportive and respiratory care; polio is prevented by vaccination.
det.prognosis: Varies from stable residual weakness after polio to median survival of 3–5 years in ALS.
pearls: Wasting + fasciculation + no sensory loss = anterior horn until proven otherwise.
Normal sensory nerve potentials on NCS support localisation to the cell body or root rather than the nerve.
Always exclude treatable mimics: MMN, cervical myelopathy, thyrotoxicosis.
det.thd: Anterior horn cell disease คือโรคของเซลล์ประสาทสั่งการในไขสันหลัง ทำให้อ่อนแรง ลีบ กล้ามเนื้อกระตุก (fasciculation) โดยไม่ชา สาเหตุมีทั้งการเสื่อม เช่น ALS, SMA, Kennedy และการติดเชื้อ เช่น โปลิโอ ตรวจ EMG พบ denervation หลายบริเวณ ต้องแยกโรคที่รักษาได้ เช่น MMN และไขสันหลังถูกกด การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ

name: Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (AION)
formal: Optic nerve head infarction, non-arteritic from small vessel disease or arteritic in giant cell arteritis, causing sudden painless monocular vision loss with disc swelling.
simple: Sudden painless loss of vision in one eye from poor blood supply to the front of the optic nerve.
th: ขั้วประสาทตาขาดเลือด ชนิด non-arteritic จากโรคหลอดเลือดเล็ก หรือ arteritic จาก giant cell arteritis ทำให้ตามัวข้างเดียวทันทีโดยไม่ปวด และขั้วประสาทตาบวม
tempoNote: Sudden, often noticed on waking; may worsen over days to two weeks
feat: Painless sudden monocular visual loss, often inferior altitudinal field defect
Relative afferent pupillary defect and swollen disc, sometimes with splinter haemorrhages
NAION: age 50+, vascular risk factors, small crowded fellow disc ('disc at risk'), sleep apnoea
Arteritic AION: older, jaw claudication, headache, scalp tenderness, polymyalgia, chalky-white swollen disc
Fellow eye later affected in about 15% with NAION but much more frequently and quickly in untreated GCA
inv: ESR, CRP and platelets urgently in anyone over 50
Temporal artery ultrasound (halo sign) or biopsy if GCA suspected
Visual fields, OCT; fluorescein angiography shows choroidal delay in arteritic cases

case.exam: Right VA counting fingers, right RAPD, pale swollen right disc; tender non-pulsatile temporal arteries.
case.tests: ESR 98 mm/h, CRP 64 mg/L, platelets 520,000; temporal artery ultrasound shows halo sign.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what must happen today?

det.patho: The anterior optic nerve head is perfused by short posterior ciliary arteries. In NAION, nocturnal hypotension, a crowded small disc and small vessel disease create a compartment-like ischaemia. In arteritic AION, granulomatous inflammation occludes the ciliary arteries. Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists have been linked to NAION in observational studies.
det.clinical: NAION presents with painless visual loss, typically altitudinal, in middle-aged or older patients with vascular risk. Arteritic AION is usually more severe and accompanied by GCA symptoms; transient visual obscurations or diplopia may precede it. Disc swelling resolves into sectoral or diffuse pallor over 6–8 weeks.
det.diagnosis: Fundoscopy shows disc oedema at onset. Urgent ESR, CRP and platelets screen for GCA; temporal artery ultrasound or biopsy confirms. Atypical features (pain on eye movement, young age, bilateral simultaneous loss) prompt MRI to exclude optic neuritis or compressive or infiltrative lesions.
det.treatment: Arteritic AION: immediate high-dose glucocorticoids, followed by tocilizumab as steroid-sparing therapy. NAION: no proven treatment; manage vascular risk factors, sleep apnoea and nocturnal hypotension, and review drugs implicated in the condition.
det.prognosis: NAION visual loss usually stabilises with modest recovery in some; arteritic loss rarely recovers and threatens the fellow eye without prompt steroids.
pearls: Any patient over 50 with AION needs ESR/CRP the same day.
A chalky-white swollen disc suggests arteritic AION.
Look at the fellow disc: small crowded discs predispose to NAION.
det.thd: AION คือขั้วประสาทตาขาดเลือด ทำให้ตามัวข้างเดียวทันทีโดยไม่ปวด ขั้วประสาทตาบวม มีสองชนิดคือ non-arteritic จากโรคหลอดเลือดเล็กและขั้วประสาทตาแออัด กับ arteritic จาก giant cell arteritis ในผู้สูงอายุ ซึ่งมีปวดศีรษะ ปวดกรามเวลาเคี้ยว และ ESR/CRP สูง ชนิด arteritic ต้องให้ steroid ขนาดสูงทันทีเพื่อป้องกันตาอีกข้าง ส่วน NAION ยังไม่มีการรักษาที่พิสูจน์ได้ ให้ควบคุมปัจจัยเสี่ยง

name: Antibody-mediated neurological diseases
formal: Neurological diseases caused by antibodies against neuronal surface or synaptic antigens (e.g. NMDA receptor, LGI1, AQP4), producing encephalitis, seizures, psychiatric features or neuromuscular disease.
simple: Brain and nerve illnesses in which the body's antibodies wrongly attack the nervous system.
th: กลุ่มโรคที่แอนติบอดีโจมตีโปรตีนบนผิวเซลล์ประสาทหรือรอยต่อประสาท เช่น NMDA receptor, LGI1, AQP4, AChR ทำให้สมองอักเสบ ชัก อาการทางจิต หรือโรคประสาท-กล้ามเนื้อ ตอบสนองต่อการกดภูมิคุ้มกัน
tempoNote: Most evolve over days to weeks (under 3 months for autoimmune encephalitis); some relapse
feat: Group heading covering encephalitis, NMOSD, myasthenia, LEMS, stiff-person spectrum and others
Subacute memory loss, psychiatric change or new seizures (faciobrachial dystonic seizures in LGI1)
Antibodies to surface antigens are usually pathogenic and treatment-responsive
Some are paraneoplastic (e.g. ovarian teratoma with NMDAR)
Relapses can occur, especially with delayed treatment
inv: Paired serum and CSF neuronal antibody panels (cell-based assays)
MRI (limbic T2 change, optic nerve or long cord lesions) and EEG
CSF: pleocytosis, oligoclonal bands; tumour screening by CT/MRI/ultrasound or PET

case.story: Over two weeks became anxious, then psychotic with insomnia; now she has seizures, lip-smacking movements and fluctuating blood pressure.
case.exam: Mute, orofacial dyskinesia, catatonic posturing, tachycardia.
case.tests: CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis; NMDA receptor antibodies positive in CSF; pelvic MRI shows an ovarian teratoma.
case.q: What are the first-line treatments?
case.a: Tumour removal plus first-line immunotherapy (IV methylprednisolone, IVIG and/or plasma exchange); rituximab if no improvement.

det.patho: Antibodies directed against extracellular parts of receptors, ion channels or associated proteins alter their function by internalisation, blocking or complement activation, causing potentially reversible dysfunction. By contrast, antibodies to intracellular antigens mainly flag a cytotoxic T-cell response with neuronal loss. Triggers include tumours, preceding infections (HSV encephalitis) and immune checkpoint inhibitors.
det.clinical: This is an umbrella term. Central syndromes include NMDAR encephalitis (psychiatric onset, dyskinesia, autonomic instability), LGI1 encephalitis (faciobrachial dystonic seizures, hyponatraemia, older men), CASPR2, GABA-B, AMPA and GAD65 syndromes, and AQP4/MOG demyelinating disease. Peripheral examples are myasthenia gravis, LEMS and autoimmune nodopathies.
det.diagnosis: Use published clinical criteria for possible autoimmune encephalitis to start treatment before antibody results. Test serum and CSF with cell-based assays; some antibodies (NMDAR) are more sensitive in CSF, others (LGI1, AQP4) in serum. Interpret low-titre serum-only results cautiously. Screen for tumours appropriate to the antibody.
det.treatment: First-line immunotherapy is high-dose corticosteroids, IVIG and/or plasma exchange, started early. Rituximab or cyclophosphamide is used for inadequate response, and maintenance agents prevent relapse in some disorders. Specific monoclonal therapies (complement or FcRn inhibitors, IL-6 receptor blockade) are approved for MG and NMOSD. Remove any associated tumour.
det.prognosis: Most surface-antibody encephalitides improve substantially with early therapy, though recovery may take months and residual cognitive deficits are common.
pearls: Surface antibodies usually mean treatable disease; intracellular antibodies mean likely cancer and poorer response.
Do not wait for antibody results when the syndrome fits — start immunotherapy.
Faciobrachial dystonic seizures plus hyponatraemia point to LGI1.
det.thd: โรคประสาทที่เกิดจากแอนติบอดีเป็นกลุ่มโรคที่ภูมิคุ้มกันสร้างแอนติบอดีโจมตีโปรตีนบนผิวเซลล์ประสาท เช่น NMDA receptor, LGI1, AQP4 และ AChR ทำให้เกิดสมองอักเสบ อาการทางจิต ชัก ปลอกประสาทอักเสบ หรือกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง ตรวจแอนติบอดีในเลือดและน้ำไขสันหลัง ร่วมกับ MRI, EEG และหาเนื้องอก รักษาด้วยสเตียรอยด์ IVIG หรือเปลี่ยนถ่ายพลาสมาโดยเร็ว ส่วนใหญ่ฟื้นตัวดีถ้ารักษาเร็ว

name: Anticholinergic syndrome
formal: Toxidrome from muscarinic receptor blockade with confusion, delirium, dry skin and mouth, mydriasis, tachycardia, urinary retention and hyperthermia.
simple: A reaction to certain drugs causing confusion, dry mouth, wide pupils, fast heartbeat and difficulty passing urine.
th: พิษจากการปิดกั้น muscarinic receptor ทำให้เพ้อสับสน ผิวแห้งแดง ปากแห้ง รูม่านตาขยาย หัวใจเร็ว ปัสสาวะคั่ง และไข้ ยาที่พบบ่อยคือยาแก้แพ้ ยาต้านซึมเศร้า และพืชลำโพง
tempoNote: Hours after ingestion or after general anaesthesia; usually resolves over 24–48 hours once the agent is cleared
feat: Delirium with agitation, disorientation, vivid visual hallucinations and picking or grasping movements
Peripheral blockade: dry flushed skin without sweating, dry mouth, dilated poorly reactive pupils, tachycardia, low-grade fever
Urinary retention and reduced bowel sounds; muscle tone and reflexes are normal
Central form after anaesthesia or ICU sedation: seizures, stupor or coma and respiratory depression without peripheral signs
Causes: antihistamines, tricyclics, antipsychotics, trihexyphenidyl, scopolamine, atropine eye drops, Datura (ลำโพง) and other Solanaceae plants
inv: Clinical diagnosis; 12-lead ECG for sinus tachycardia and for QRS or QT prolongation (tricyclics)
Temperature, bladder scan, glucose, electrolytes, creatine kinase; toxicology screen and paracetamol level in overdose
Consider EEG if seizures or persistent stupor, and brain imaging if signs are lateralised

case.who: 74-year-old woman with Parkinson disease on trihexyphenidyl, Songkhla
case.story: Her family bought a cough and cold mixture containing an antihistamine on top of her usual tablets. That night she became agitated, said there were insects on the bed sheet and could not pass urine.
case.exam: Temperature 38.1 C, heart rate 124, dry flushed skin, pupils 7 mm and sluggish, dry mucosa, bladder palpable, bowel sounds diminished, no rigidity or clonus, delirium with picking at the air.
case.tests: ECG sinus tachycardia with normal QRS; glucose, electrolytes and creatine kinase normal; bladder scan 600 mL.
case.q: How would you separate this from serotonin syndrome, and what is the treatment?
case.a: Dry skin, normal tone and absent clonus favour anticholinergic toxicity (sweating, clonus and hyperreflexia indicate serotonin toxicity). Stop all anticholinergics, give supportive care with catheterisation, cooling and a benzodiazepine for agitation, and use physostigmine only for severe cases without conduction block.

det.patho: Muscarinic antagonists block acetylcholine at central and peripheral receptors. In the brain this disrupts attention, memory and arousal, producing delirium, hallucinations and sometimes seizures, while parasympathetic blockade in the periphery causes dry mucosa, mydriasis, tachycardia, urinary retention and anhidrotic hyperthermia. The central anticholinergic syndrome of anaesthesia is clinically similar to atropine poisoning and can follow opioids, ketamine, etomidate, propofol, nitrous oxide, volatile agents and H2-blockers such as cimetidine, with unpredictable individual susceptibility.
det.clinical: Patients are agitated, disoriented and have fluctuating hallucinations, often reaching for objects that are not there. Skin is hot, dry and flushed, pupils are wide, the heart is fast and the bladder distended. Seizures, stupor, coma and apnoea can occur in severe poisoning, and tricyclic drugs add arrhythmia risk. Older people with dementia or Parkinson disease are especially vulnerable, since cumulative anticholinergic load from several drugs is enough. In Thailand, accidental or recreational Datura (ลำโพง) ingestion causes similar presentations.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by exclusion of mimics: sepsis and meningitis, thyroid storm, alcohol withdrawal, sympathomimetic toxicity, serotonin syndrome and NMS. Dry skin and normal bowel tone distinguish it from sympathomimetic and serotonergic states. ECG is essential in any tricyclic exposure. Physostigmine response was once used as a diagnostic challenge but is now reserved for therapy in selected patients.
det.treatment: Stop the drug and give supportive care: IV fluids, cooling, bladder catheterisation, a quiet environment, and benzodiazepines for agitation or seizures. Avoid antipsychotics and other anticholinergic drugs, which add to the burden. Physostigmine, given slowly in small increments, is the specific antidote for severe delirium, uncontrolled agitation or seizures, but it is contraindicated with QRS widening or heart block, as in tricyclic overdose, and requires monitoring for bradycardia and cholinergic effects. Activated charcoal helps early after oral ingestion in a protected airway.
det.prognosis: Usually full recovery within one to two days; serious outcomes follow arrhythmia, hyperthermia, aspiration or seizures in massive overdose.
pearls: Dry and flushed skin with delirium and normal tone is the anticholinergic fingerprint; wet skin with clonus is serotonin.
Postoperative confusion with seizures or coma can be central anticholinergic syndrome, treatable with physostigmine.
Review the whole medication list in older patients: many common drugs have hidden anticholinergic effects.
det.thd: Anticholinergic syndrome เกิดจากสารที่ปิดกั้นตัวรับ muscarinic เช่น ยาแก้แพ้ ยาต้านซึมเศร้ากลุ่ม tricyclic trihexyphenidyl atropine และพืชลำโพง ผู้ป่วยสับสน เพ้อ เห็นภาพหลอน ผิวแห้งแดง ปากแห้ง รูม่านตาขยาย หัวใจเต้นเร็ว ปัสสาวะไม่ออก และมีไข้ ต่างจาก serotonin syndrome ที่เหงื่อออกและกล้ามเนื้อกระตุก การรักษาคือหยุดยา ดูแลประคับประคอง ให้ benzodiazepine เมื่อกระสับกระส่าย และใช้ physostigmine เฉพาะรายรุนแรงที่ ECG ไม่มี QRS กว้าง

case.story: Started on trihexyphenidyl for dystonia; within a week feels unable to sit still and paces at night.

det.patho: The mechanism is uncertain; altered cholinergic-dopaminergic balance in striatal and limbic circuits may produce restlessness, or the restlessness may be part of central anticholinergic toxicity.
det.clinical: Patients report inner restlessness and show movements such as pacing or crossing and uncrossing legs. Coexisting confusion or anticholinergic signs suggest toxicity. Older adults are more vulnerable.
det.diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis based on temporal relation to the drug and exclusion of other causes, especially dopamine blockers and RLS.
det.treatment: Reduce or stop the anticholinergic; symptoms usually settle. Benzodiazepines or propranolol may help temporarily.
det.prognosis: Usually resolves after withdrawal.
pearls: Always check for concurrent dopamine-blocking drugs.
Restlessness plus confusion suggests anticholinergic toxicity.
Evidence for this entity is limited.

name: Antimicrotubular myopathies
formal: Drug-induced vacuolar myopathy from colchicine or vincristine impairing microtubule function, producing proximal weakness with a modestly raised CK, often alongside neuropathy and renal impairment.
simple: Muscle weakness caused by drugs such as colchicine that interfere with the internal scaffolding of muscle cells.
more: EMG shows myopathic and neuropathic features; biopsy shows autophagic vacuoles. It usually resolves within weeks after stopping the drug.
th: โรคกล้ามเนื้อจากยาที่รบกวนไมโครทูบูล เช่น colchicine และ vincristine ทำให้ต้นแขนขาอ่อนแรงและ CK สูงเล็กน้อย มักร่วมกับเส้นประสาทเสื่อม

feat: Proximal weakness developing on long-term colchicine, especially with renal impairment

Drug interactions raising colchicine levels: clarithromycin, cyclosporin, statins, azoles

case.who: 70-year-old man from Nan with gout and chronic kidney disease (eGFR 32)
case.story: Taking colchicine 1.2 mg daily for a year; recently added simvastatin; now cannot rise from a chair.
case.exam: Proximal weakness MRC 4-/5, absent ankle jerks, mild distal sensory loss.
case.tests: CK 1,800 U/L; EMG myopathic with fibrillations and complex repetitive discharges; biopsy shows rimmed-like autophagic vacuoles.
case.q: What is the cause and the treatment?
case.a: Colchicine neuromyopathy, aggravated by kidney disease and statin; stop colchicine and statin, expect recovery in weeks.

det.patho: Colchicine and vinca alkaloids bind tubulin and impair microtubule polymerisation, disrupting autophagosome trafficking and lysosomal fusion. Undigested material accumulates as autophagic vacuoles in muscle, and axonal transport in long nerves fails. Toxicity rises when clearance is impaired by renal or hepatic disease or interacting drugs.
det.clinical: Patients develop subacute proximal weakness and sometimes myalgia, with mild distal sensory loss from neuropathy. It mimics polymyositis or IBM. Severe overdose causes multiorgan failure with rhabdomyolysis. Vincristine mainly produces painful sensorimotor and autonomic neuropathy.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in anyone on colchicine with weakness and raised CK. EMG shows irritable myopathy proximally and axonal changes distally. Biopsy, when done, shows vacuoles without inflammation. Improvement after stopping the drug is the best confirmation.
det.treatment: Stop or reduce colchicine and address interacting drugs and renal function. Supportive physiotherapy aids recovery. Dose colchicine according to renal function in future. For vincristine, dose modification is negotiated with the oncology team.
det.prognosis: Myopathy recovers within weeks to months; neuropathy improves more slowly.
pearls: Colchicine plus CKD plus a CYP3A4 inhibitor or statin: watch for myopathy.
Vacuolar myopathy without inflammation — look at the drug chart.
Neuromyopathy: proximal myopathy plus distal neuropathy.
det.thd: Antimicrotubular myopathy คือโรคกล้ามเนื้อจากยา colchicine หรือ vincristine ที่รบกวนไมโครทูบูล พบมากในผู้ป่วยโรคไตที่ได้ colchicine นานหรือใช้ร่วมกับยาที่เพิ่มระดับยา เช่น clarithromycin หรือ statin อาการคือต้นแขนขาอ่อนแรง CK สูง และมีเส้นประสาทปลายเสื่อม ชิ้นเนื้อพบ autophagic vacuole การรักษาคือหยุดยา แล้วอาการมักดีขึ้นในไม่กี่สัปดาห์

simple: An immune disorder that makes blood clot too easily, leading to strokes, clots in veins and pregnancy losses.
