det.patho: Autoantibodies directed against phospholipid-binding proteins, mainly beta-2-glycoprotein I and prothrombin, activate endothelial cells, platelets, monocytes and complement, producing a prothrombotic state in arteries, veins and microvessels. Valve thickening and vegetations add an embolic route. It may be primary or accompany SLE and other autoimmune diseases; transient positivity also follows infections and some drugs.
det.clinical: Stroke and TIA are the commonest arterial events, typically in young adults and often recurrent. Other presentations include cerebral venous thrombosis, multi-infarct cognitive decline, migraine-like headache, seizures and chorea. Pregnancy morbidity and thrombocytopenia are clues. Catastrophic APS is a rare storm of microvascular thrombosis in three or more organs within a week, carrying high mortality.
det.diagnosis: Requires a clinical event plus persistent laboratory positivity (lupus anticoagulant, medium-high titre anticardiolipin or anti-β2GPI) on two occasions at least 12 weeks apart; the 2023 ACR/EULAR criteria weight the features. Lupus anticoagulant testing is unreliable during heparin, DOAC or warfarin therapy and in the acute phase. Low titres and isolated IgM are of uncertain significance. Screen for SLE and look for valve lesions on echocardiography.
det.treatment: Acute stroke follows standard pathways; thrombolysis is not contraindicated by the antibodies alone, but a prolonged aPTT must be interpreted carefully. For definite APS with arterial events, long-term warfarin at INR 2–3 is usual, with some experts adding aspirin or aiming higher in recurrent cases. DOACs are not recommended for arterial or triple-positive APS. Low-antibody profiles without a full syndrome may be managed with aspirin alone. Catastrophic APS needs anticoagulation, glucocorticoids and plasma exchange or IVIG.
det.prognosis: Recurrence is common without adequate anticoagulation; triple positivity and arterial events predict a worse course.
pearls: Prolonged aPTT that fails to correct with mixing in a young stroke patient = check for lupus anticoagulant.
One positive test is not APS: repeat after 12 weeks.
Arterial APS: warfarin, not rivaroxaban or apixaban.

det.patho: Bilateral damage to the primary visual cortex causes cortical blindness. The denial is attributed to disconnection between visual areas and language or monitoring networks, so the brain fails to register the absence of input, combined with frontal or memory dysfunction that enables confabulation. It is a form of anosognosia.
det.clinical: Patients act as if they can see, describe objects that are not there and attribute collisions to darkness or clumsiness. Pupils are reactive and the fundi normal. Additional features include amnesia, agitated delirium and other signs of top-of-basilar ischaemia such as vertical gaze palsy. The denial may resolve over days to weeks.
det.diagnosis: Clinical recognition depends on noting the mismatch between severe visual failure and the patient's claims. MRI identifies bilateral occipital lesions and their cause; vascular imaging assesses the basilar and posterior cerebral arteries. Functional visual loss must be distinguished; in Anton syndrome patients deny loss, whereas functional patients complain of it.
det.treatment: Treat the cause promptly: reperfusion therapy for acute basilar or bilateral PCA occlusion when eligible, secondary stroke prevention, blood pressure control and withdrawal of offending drugs in PRES. Safety measures against falls and supported rehabilitation are needed.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause; PRES often recovers fully, while infarction may leave permanent cortical visual loss.
pearls: Blind with reactive pupils and normal fundi = cortical blindness.
Denial plus confabulation = Anton syndrome.
Bilateral occipital infarcts: image the basilar artery.

det.patho: Atherosclerotic plaques in the ascending aorta and arch shed debris and thrombus into brachiocephalic vessels. Aneurysms and dissections compromise branch arteries including intercostal and lumbar feeders of the spinal cord. Inflammatory aortitis narrows arch branches.
det.clinical: Patients present with embolic strokes, TIAs or retinal emboli; procedural strokes occur during cardiac catheterisation or surgery. Spinal cord ischaemia produces anterior cord syndrome. Large arch aneurysms compress the left recurrent laryngeal nerve or sympathetic chain.

det.treatment: Arch atheroma: antiplatelet therapy, statins and blood pressure control; the role of anticoagulation is uncertain. det.prognosis: Complex arch plaque carries a high recurrence risk; outcomes after spinal cord infarction vary.

det.patho: An intimal tear lets blood split the media and create a false lumen that propagates and occludes branches. Carotid involvement or hypotension causes stroke; occlusion of intercostal or lumbar arteries causes spinal cord ischaemia; peripheral nerve ischaemia occurs when limb arteries are compromised.
det.clinical: Neurological symptoms occur in a meaningful minority of type A dissections and can dominate the presentation. Painless presentations are more common in older patients and those with altered consciousness. Syncope may reflect tamponade or carotid involvement.
det.diagnosis: CT angiography of chest, abdomen and pelvis confirms. In acute stroke, a CTA that includes the arch may reveal a flap. Raised D-dimer is sensitive but non-specific. Echocardiography supports the diagnosis in unstable patients.
det.treatment: Type A dissection requires emergency surgery; type B is often managed with blood pressure and heart rate control, with endovascular repair for complications. Thrombolysis and anticoagulants are contraindicated. Spinal protection measures are used during repair.
det.prognosis: Untreated type A dissection has high early mortality; neurological deficits at presentation predict worse outcome.
pearls: Stroke plus chest pain, hypotension or arm BP difference: suspect dissection before thrombolysis.
Right-sided hemisphere stroke reflects common involvement of the brachiocephalic trunk.

det.patho: Language depends on a left-hemisphere network in most people, including the inferior frontal gyrus, superior temporal gyrus, arcuate fasciculus, angular gyrus and subcortical structures. Damage from stroke, tumours, trauma, infection or neurodegeneration disrupts specific components. Subcortical and thalamic aphasias are also recognised.
det.clinical: Classic syndromes include Broca (non-fluent, preserved comprehension), Wernicke (fluent, poor comprehension), conduction (poor repetition), global (all components impaired), transcortical (preserved repetition) and anomic. Patients may be frustrated or unaware of errors. Aphasia must be distinguished from dysarthria (motor speech disorder) and from confusion.
det.diagnosis: Bedside testing of fluency, comprehension, repetition and naming classifies the aphasia and suggests lesion location. Acute onset is a stroke until proven otherwise and needs immediate imaging. Progressive aphasia requires MRI, PET and sometimes biomarkers to identify neurodegenerative causes.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: thrombolysis or thrombectomy for acute stroke, surgery for tumours. Speech and language therapy improves outcomes and should be intensive; communication aids and family training are valuable. Depression is common and should be treated.
det.prognosis: Recovery after stroke is often substantial in the first months; progressive aphasias worsen over time.
pearls: Sudden nonsense speech is stroke, not psychosis, until proven otherwise.
Test repetition — it helps distinguish conduction and transcortical aphasias.
Aphasia is a language disorder, not a motor speech problem.
det.thd: Aphasia คือความผิดปกติทางภาษาที่เกิดภายหลัง มักเกิดจากรอยโรคในสมองซีกซ้าย แบ่งเป็นชนิด Broca พูดไม่คล่องแต่เข้าใจ ชนิด Wernicke พูดคล่องแต่ไม่มีความหมายและไม่เข้าใจ และชนิดอื่น ๆ หากเกิดเฉียบพลันให้คิดถึงหลอดเลือดสมองและตรวจภาพสมองทันที หากค่อย ๆ เป็นอาจเป็น primary progressive aphasia รักษาตามสาเหตุร่วมกับการฝึกพูด

formal: Rare disorder of absent or reduced ceruloplasmin (aceruloplasminaemia) causing brain iron accumulation with diabetes, retinal degeneration, ataxia, dystonia and cognitive decline.
simple: A rare inherited disease where iron builds up in the brain and organs, causing movement problems, memory loss and diabetes.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมหายากที่ไม่มี caeruloplasmin ทำให้เหล็กสะสมในสมอง ร่วมกับเบาหวาน จอประสาทตาเสื่อม เดินเซ dystonia และสมองเสื่อม
tempoNote: Anaemia and diabetes from the 20s–30s; neurological features usually from the 40s–50s
feat: Triad: diabetes mellitus, retinal degeneration, neurological disease in mid-adulthood
Ataxia, dysarthria, chorea, dystonia, parkinsonism and cognitive decline
Mild microcytic anaemia with low serum iron but high ferritin
MRI: marked iron-related hypointensity of basal ganglia, thalamus, dentate and cortex
inv: Serum caeruloplasmin absent or very low; low copper, low iron, high ferritin
MRI with T2*/SWI for iron deposition
CP gene sequencing; fundoscopy and glucose tests

case.story: Diabetic since 35 and treated for mild anaemia that never responded to iron; now unsteady with twitching facial movements and forgetfulness.
case.exam: Gait ataxia, facial chorea, blepharospasm, peripheral retinal degeneration.
case.tests: Caeruloplasmin undetectable; ferritin 1,200 ng/mL with low serum iron; MRI shows diffuse basal ganglia and dentate hypointensity.
case.q: Why is iron supplementation harmful here?
case.a: Aceruloplasminaemia causes tissue iron overload despite low serum iron; iron chelation, not supplementation, is indicated.

det.patho: Caeruloplasmin is a ferroxidase that oxidises ferrous iron so it can be exported from cells and loaded onto transferrin. Biallelic CP variants abolish this function, so iron accumulates in astrocytes, neurons, pancreas, liver and retina, causing oxidative damage. It belongs to the neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA) group.
det.clinical: Most cases are reported from Japan, though worldwide distribution exists. Diabetes and anaemia precede neurological features by years. Neurological signs include cerebellar ataxia, involuntary movements, parkinsonism, psychiatric change and dementia.
det.diagnosis: Absent caeruloplasmin with low copper, low iron and high ferritin, plus MRI iron deposition, strongly suggests the diagnosis; confirm with CP sequencing. Heterozygotes may have half-normal caeruloplasmin and are usually asymptomatic.
det.treatment: Iron chelation (deferasirox, deferiprone, desferrioxamine) can reduce iron load and may stabilise symptoms if started early; anaemia limits chelation. Fresh-frozen plasma has been used to supply caeruloplasmin. Diabetes and neurological symptoms are treated conventionally.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; early chelation may delay neurological decline, but evidence is limited.
pearls: Low serum iron + high ferritin + anaemia unresponsive to iron: think aceruloplasminaemia.
Diabetes plus retinal degeneration plus movement disorder is the triad.
Both Wilson disease and aceruloplasminaemia have low caeruloplasmin; urinary copper separates them.
det.thd: Aceruloplasminaemia เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมหายากที่ไม่มี caeruloplasmin ทำให้เหล็กออกจากเซลล์ไม่ได้และสะสมในสมอง ตับอ่อน และจอตา ผู้ป่วยมีเบาหวานและโลหิตจางตั้งแต่อายุน้อย ต่อมาเดินเซ มีการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติและสมองเสื่อม ตรวจพบ caeruloplasmin ต่ำมาก ferritin สูงแต่เหล็กในเลือดต่ำ MRI พบเหล็กสะสม รักษาด้วยยาขับเหล็ก ห้ามให้ธาตุเหล็กเสริม

name: Apolipoprotein A1-related amyloidosis
formal: Rare autosomal dominant hereditary amyloidosis from APOA1 variants causing visceral deposition of amyloid and sometimes a sensory or autonomic neuropathy, with laryngeal or skin involvement in some families.
simple: An inherited disease in which an abnormal cholesterol-carrying protein forms deposits in organs, occasionally including nerves.
more: Diagnosed by biopsy with mass-spectrometry typing and APOA1 sequencing. Management is supportive; liver or kidney transplantation is considered in advanced organ failure.
th: amyloidosis ทางพันธุกรรมจากยีน APOA1 สะสมที่ตับ ไต หัวใจ และบางรายทำให้เส้นประสาทรับความรู้สึกและระบบอัตโนมัติเสื่อม
tempoNote: Adult onset with slowly progressive organ dysfunction over years
feat: Autosomal dominant; mostly visceral disease (kidney, liver, heart, larynx, testes, skin)
Painful length-dependent sensory or sensorimotor neuropathy in some variants (e.g. Iowa G26R)
Autonomic features: postural hypotension, GI dysmotility
Renal failure and hepatomegaly common
Low HDL cholesterol may be a clue
inv: Tissue biopsy (fat pad, nerve, kidney) with Congo red and mass spectrometry typing
APOA1 gene sequencing
NCS, autonomic tests, renal and liver function, echocardiography

case.story: Burning feet for 3 years, dizziness on standing and worsening kidney function; her father had kidney failure.
case.exam: Distal pinprick loss to the ankles, absent ankle jerks, postural BP fall of 25 mmHg, hepatomegaly.
case.tests: Proteinuria; NCS axonal sensory neuropathy; fat pad Congo red positive, typed as ApoA-I by mass spectrometry; APOA1 variant.
case.q: Why is typing the amyloid essential?
case.a: Hereditary ApoA-I amyloidosis is managed differently from AL or TTR amyloid, avoiding chemotherapy and TTR-specific drugs.

read.where: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves — Apolipoprotein A-1 Related Familial Amyloid Polyneuropathy

det.patho: Missense or deletion variants in APOA1 destabilise apolipoprotein A-I, which misfolds and deposits as amyloid fibrils. Deposits favour kidney, liver, heart, larynx and gonads, while some variants also involve peripheral and autonomic nerves. Penetrance and organ pattern depend on the specific variant.
det.clinical: Most patients present with renal disease or hepatomegaly; a smaller group, classically the Iowa kindred, have neuropathy resembling TTR amyloidosis. Neuropathic pain, autonomic failure and cardiomyopathy can coexist. It is very rare in Thailand and largely unknown in local series.
det.diagnosis: Demonstrate amyloid in tissue and type it by mass spectrometry or immunoelectron microscopy, then confirm with APOA1 sequencing. Exclude monoclonal proteins to rule out AL amyloid. Assess kidney, liver, heart and nerves at baseline. Family screening follows a positive result.
det.treatment: No specific drug therapy is approved; care is supportive with pain management, autonomic measures and organ support. Kidney and liver transplantation have been used successfully in selected patients. Experimental approaches target fibril stabilisation and removal.
det.prognosis: Often slowly progressive over decades; renal failure is a common major complication.
pearls: Always type amyloid; therapy depends on the precursor protein.
Low HDL with renal amyloid hints at ApoA-I disease.
Neuropathic presentations closely resemble TTR amyloidosis.
det.thd: ApoA-I amyloidosis เป็น amyloidosis ทางพันธุกรรมจากยีน APOA1 ส่วนใหญ่สะสมที่ไตและตับ บางสายพันธุ์ทำให้เส้นประสาทรับความรู้สึกและระบบอัตโนมัติเสื่อมคล้าย TTR amyloidosis วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจชิ้นเนื้อย้อม Congo red และระบุชนิดด้วย mass spectrometry ร่วมกับตรวจยีน ยังไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ ใช้การดูแลประคับประคองและปลูกถ่ายอวัยวะในบางราย

name: Apperceptive visual agnosia
formal: Failure to perceive object form despite preserved elementary vision, due to bilateral occipitotemporal damage, often from carbon monoxide poisoning or hypoxia; patients cannot copy or match shapes.
simple: Inability to recognise objects because the brain cannot put what the eyes see together, even though vision is otherwise normal.
th: ภาวะที่ไม่สามารถรับรู้รูปร่างของวัตถุ แม้การมองเห็นพื้นฐานยังดี เกิดจากรอยโรค occipitotemporal ทั้งสองข้าง เช่น พิษคาร์บอนมอนอกไซด์
tempoNote: Usually follows an acute brain insult; may also appear in neurodegenerative disease (posterior cortical atrophy)
feat: Cannot copy, match or describe the shape of objects despite adequate acuity, colour and brightness detection
Recognises objects by touch, sound or context
Often preserved visually guided reaching (dissociation between perception and action)
Classic causes: carbon monoxide poisoning, hypoxia, bilateral posterior strokes, posterior cortical atrophy
inv: Bedside: ask to copy a simple figure and match shapes; contrast with associative agnosia (can copy, cannot name)
Neuropsychological testing (e.g. VOSP battery)
MRI brain; FDG-PET or amyloid tests if neurodegenerative

case.story: Found unconscious in a closed room with a charcoal grill; after recovery he cannot recognise his own motorcycle or cups at home.
case.exam: Acuity 6/9, colour vision intact, but cannot copy a square or match shapes; names a key at once when it is placed in his hand.
case.tests: MRI shows bilateral lateral occipital and globus pallidus lesions.
case.q: What is the deficit and how does it differ from associative agnosia?
case.a: Apperceptive visual agnosia — he cannot form a percept (cannot copy); in associative agnosia the copy is good but meaning is lost.

read.where: Chapter 66: Visual Impairment after Cortical Injury

det.patho: Lesions of lateral occipital and adjacent occipitotemporal cortex interrupt grouping of edges and contours into coherent shapes, while primary visual cortex may be partly spared. Carbon monoxide and hypoxia produce diffuse laminar damage there; bilateral involvement is usually required.
det.clinical: Patients may say they see things as blurred fragments. They cannot copy drawings or discriminate simple forms, yet they can identify objects by touch or sound and may navigate surprisingly well. Some patients can still guide hand posture to objects through the dorsal stream. Associated deficits include alexia, prosopagnosia and visual field loss.
det.diagnosis: The defining test is failure to copy or match shapes with adequate elementary vision. Neuropsychological batteries quantify perception. Imaging shows the lesion; in progressive cases posterior cortical atrophy (usually Alzheimer pathology) is the main consideration.
det.treatment: No specific drug therapy. Rehabilitation emphasises compensatory strategies using touch, verbal descriptions, environmental labelling and occupational therapy. Treat the cause and support carers.
det.prognosis: Partial recovery possible after acute insults; progressive in degenerative causes.
pearls: Cannot copy = apperceptive; can copy but not name = associative.
Carbon monoxide poisoning is the textbook cause.
Progressive visual-perceptual problems in a 60-year-old: think posterior cortical atrophy.
det.thd: Apperceptive visual agnosia คือภาวะที่ตายังมองเห็นแสงและสีได้ แต่ไม่สามารถรวมเส้นขอบเป็นรูปร่างของวัตถุ จึงวาดตามและจับคู่รูปทรงไม่ได้ แต่จำวัตถุได้เมื่อจับหรือได้ยินเสียง เกิดจากรอยโรค occipitotemporal ทั้งสองข้าง เช่น พิษคาร์บอนมอนอกไซด์ หรือ posterior cortical atrophy การรักษาเน้นฟื้นฟูโดยใช้ประสาทสัมผัสอื่นช่วย

name: Apraxia
formal: Impaired execution of learned purposeful movements not explained by weakness, sensory loss or incoordination, often from left parietal or frontal lesions; includes ideomotor and ideational types.
simple: Difficulty carrying out skilled, purposeful movements on request, even though the muscles are strong and the person understands the task.
th: ความบกพร่องในการทำการเคลื่อนไหวที่เรียนรู้มาแล้ว ทั้งที่ไม่มีอ่อนแรง ชา หรือเสียการประสานงาน มักจากรอยโรคที่ parietal หรือ frontal ซีกซ้าย
tempoNote: Acute after stroke; progressive in corticobasal syndrome or dementia
feat: A sign or syndrome, not a disease
Ideomotor: errors pantomiming tool use (uses hand as the tool)
Ideational: cannot sequence multistep tasks
Limb-kinetic: clumsy fine movements
Other types: buccofacial, gait, dressing and constructional apraxia
inv: Bedside: gesture on command, imitation, tool use, sequence tasks
MRI brain
Neuropsychological assessment

case.story: After a left MCA stroke, nurses note he cannot use a toothbrush properly though his right hand strength is good.
case.exam: Mild non-fluent aphasia; when asked to show how to comb hair, uses his fingers as the comb; imitation also impaired.
case.tests: MRI: left inferior parietal and frontal infarct.
case.q: What deficit is this and which hemisphere is usually responsible?
case.a: Ideomotor apraxia, usually from left (dominant) parietal or frontal lesions.

det.patho: Learned skilled movements depend on a left hemisphere network linking parietal representations of actions to premotor and motor areas. Damage to the network or its connections produces apraxia.
det.clinical: Patients struggle with tool use, gestures and multistep tasks, despite normal strength and coordination. Deficits often coexist with aphasia. Apraxia predicts dependence in daily activities.
det.diagnosis: Test gestures to command, imitation and actual tool use, after confirming comprehension. MRI identifies the lesion.
det.treatment: Occupational therapy with strategy training and errorless learning improves daily function. Treat the underlying disease.
det.prognosis: Partial improvement after stroke; progressive in degenerative disease.
pearls: Using a body part as the tool is typical of ideomotor apraxia.
Test imitation to separate apraxia from comprehension problems.
Progressive asymmetric apraxia suggests corticobasal syndrome.
det.thd: Apraxia คือความบกพร่องในการทำการเคลื่อนไหวที่เรียนรู้มาแล้ว เช่น ใช้แปรงสีฟันหรือทำท่าทางตามสั่งไม่ได้ ทั้งที่ไม่มีอ่อนแรงหรือชา มักเกิดจากรอยโรคที่ parietal หรือ frontal ซีกซ้าย เช่น stroke หรือ corticobasal syndrome เป็นอาการไม่ใช่โรค การรักษาคือดูแลโรคต้นเหตุและกิจกรรมบำบัด

name: Arachnoiditis
formal: Inflammation of the arachnoid mater causing nerve root adhesions and chronic back pain, leg pain, sensory change and sphincter disturbance, following surgery, infection, haemorrhage or intrathecal agents.
simple: Inflammation of one of the membranes around the spinal cord and nerves, causing long-standing pain, numbness and weakness.
th: Arachnoiditis คือการอักเสบและพังผืดของเยื่อหุ้มไขสันหลัง (arachnoid ร่วมกับ pia และ dura) ทำให้รากประสาทเกาะกลุ่มกัน ปวดหลังและขาแบบแสบร้อน ชา อ่อนแรงหลายราก และกลั้นปัสสาวะผิดปกติ สาเหตุได้แก่ การติดเชื้อ (วัณโรค) เลือดออก การผ่าตัดหลายครั้ง สารทึบรังสีหรือยาฉีดเข้าช่องไขสันหลัง MRI พบรากประสาทเกาะกลุ่มหรือถุง thecal ว่างเปล่า การรักษาเน้นรักษาสาเหตุและควบคุมอาการปวด
tempoNote: An inflammatory phase after the insult is followed by chronic adhesive scarring lasting years
feat: Chronic burning back and leg pain, often multiradicular and bilateral, with sensory loss, weakness, reflex loss and bladder, bowel or sexual dysfunction

Causes: meningitis (bacterial, tuberculous, syphilitic, fungal), spinal surgery especially repeated operations, subarachnoid or epidural blood, myelographic contrast (oil-based agents), intrathecal drugs or steroids, trauma, neoplasm and idiopathic cases
It accounts for roughly 6–16% of persistent symptoms after lumbar surgery in some series, but imaging evidence of arachnoiditis may be present without symptoms
Thoracic or extensive disease can cause myelopathy, syringomyelia, cysts or hydrocephalus
Peridural scar is common after surgery but usually asymptomatic and should not be confused with arachnoiditis
inv: MRI with gadolinium: nerve roots clumped centrally, roots stuck to the sac wall producing an empty thecal sac appearance, or a sac filled with soft tissue; active inflammation may enhance, chronic scarring less
CSF in the active phase: protein often raised, cells, glucose, culture, TB PCR, cytology to exclude infection or malignancy
EMG to define the roots involved; myelography is mostly historical and shows blocks or 'candle-guttering' defects

case.story: He completed treatment for tuberculous meningitis a year ago and now has progressive leg weakness, numbness and urinary hesitancy, with burning pain in both legs.
case.exam: Asymmetrical leg weakness with absent reflexes, sensory loss L2–S2, reduced anal tone.
case.tests: MRI shows thickened enhancing lumbar meninges with clumped roots and loculated CSF; CSF protein 2.1 g/L, few lymphocytes, TB PCR negative.
case.q: What is the likely cause and what treatment is available?
case.a: Adhesive arachnoiditis after tuberculous meningitis. Confirm there is no active infection, continue pain management with neuropathic agents and rehabilitation, consider corticosteroids in the active phase, and reserve surgery for a syrinx, cyst or focal compression because decompression of scarred roots gives poor results.

det.patho: Inflammation of the meninges, injury or irritation leads to a fibrinous exudate that organises into collagen and scars, tethering the nerve roots to each other and to the dura and obstructing CSF flow. The term is a misnomer since the process involves pia, arachnoid and dura. The root ischaemia and fibrosis explain pain and deficit. Putative triggers include meningitis, blood, trauma, spinal surgery, neoplasm, spinal anaesthesia agents, detergent contaminants, oil-based contrast agents and intrathecal injection of drugs.
det.clinical: Lumbar and sacral roots are most often affected, causing chronic burning pain, paraesthesia and mixed multiradicular deficits, with bladder and bowel disturbance in advanced cases. Thoracic arachnoiditis can compress the cord or cause syringomyelia and arachnoid cysts. The infective forms evolve with fever and CSF inflammation, while those following a procedure present weeks to years later. Some patients with imaging changes have no complaint.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the history and MRI. Three patterns are recognised: central clumping of roots into one or two cords, roots adherent to the periphery of the sac (empty sac), and a sac filled with inflammatory tissue with no visible CSF. Gadolinium enhancement suggests active disease. CSF analysis excludes infection and malignancy in the active phase, and tumour spread (leptomeningeal) may mimic central adhesions. Distinguish residual disc, scar and arachnoiditis in the failed-back patient, because only the first responds to repeat surgery.
det.treatment: Treat any infection or underlying cause. In early inflammatory arachnoiditis, especially tuberculous, corticosteroids may reduce inflammation. For chronic disease, treat as neuropathic pain with gabapentinoids, serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors or tricyclics, physiotherapy, psychological support and sometimes neuromodulation (spinal cord stimulation). Surgery is limited to decompression of a syrinx, cyst or focal compression, because lysis of adhesions has poor and short-lived benefit. Avoid repeat intrathecal and epidural injections and use water-soluble non-ionic contrast only when necessary.
det.prognosis: Usually chronic and fluctuating; infective forms do better when the infection is treated early.
pearls: Root clumping or an empty thecal sac on MRI is the radiological hallmark.
Arachnoiditis may appear months after tuberculous or bacterial meningitis.
Surgery for adhesions generally fails; reserve it for a syrinx or focal compression.
det.thd: Arachnoiditis คือการอักเสบและเกิดพังผืดของเยื่อหุ้มไขสันหลัง ทำให้รากประสาทที่หางม้าเกาะกลุ่มกัน มีอาการปวดแสบร้อนหลังและขา ชา อ่อนแรงหลายรากและปัสสาวะผิดปกติ สาเหตุที่พบได้แก่ การติดเชื้อเยื่อหุ้มสมอง (เช่น วัณโรค) เลือดออก การผ่าตัดกระดูกสันหลังหลายครั้ง สารทึบรังสีหรือยาที่ฉีดเข้าช่องไขสันหลัง MRI พบรากประสาทเกาะกลุ่มหรือ thecal sac ว่างเปล่า ตรวจน้ำไขสันหลังเพื่อแยกการติดเชื้อและมะเร็ง รักษาสาเหตุ ควบคุมอาการปวดแบบ neuropathic และกายภาพบำบัด ผ่าตัดเฉพาะกรณี syrinx ซีสต์ หรือกดทับเฉพาะที่

name: Arachnoiditis fibrosis
formal: Chronic stage of arachnoiditis with fibrotic scarring of the meninges and nerve roots, producing clumped roots on MRI, chronic radicular pain and cauda equina deficits.
simple: Scarring of the membranes around the spinal nerves that causes ongoing pain and nerve problems.
th: ระยะเรื้อรังของเยื่อ arachnoid อักเสบที่กลายเป็นพังผืด ทำให้รากประสาทเกาะกลุ่ม ปวดร้าวเรื้อรัง และอาการ cauda equina
tempoNote: Develops months to years after spinal surgery, infection, haemorrhage or intrathecal injection; then persistent
feat: Chronic burning back and leg pain, often bilateral and not following one root
Sensory loss, weakness, reflex loss and bladder dysfunction in cauda equina pattern
History of multiple spinal surgeries, myelography with oil contrast, intrathecal drugs, meningitis or SAH
MRI: clumped roots, empty thecal sac sign, or roots adherent peripherally
inv: MRI lumbar spine with T2 axial images; CT myelography if MRI equivocal
EMG for multiple root involvement
CSF only if infection or inflammation is suspected

case.story: Three lumbar operations over ten years; for two years has constant burning in both legs and needs to strain to pass urine.
case.exam: Patchy sensory loss in L4–S2 distribution on both sides, absent ankle jerks, weak toe flexors.
case.tests: MRI shows nerve roots stuck to the dural wall giving an empty sac appearance from L3 to S1.
case.q: Why is further decompressive surgery unlikely to help?
case.a: This is adhesive arachnoiditis; repeated surgery tends to worsen scarring, so pain management and rehabilitation are preferred.

det.patho: Injury to the arachnoid by blood, infection, surgery or chemical irritants triggers inflammation with fibrin exudate, followed by collagen deposition. Nerve roots adhere to each other and to the dura, impairing their blood supply and CSF flow; occasionally the scar calcifies or forms cysts and syrinx.
det.clinical: The dominant complaint is persistent neuropathic pain in the back and legs, often worse with activity. Neurological deficits can involve several roots and the sphincters. Progression is usually slow, but cord tethering, syrinx formation or ossification can cause new myelopathy.
det.diagnosis: MRI features include central clumping, peripheral adhesion (empty sac) or a soft-tissue mass replacing the subarachnoid space. Correlation with history is essential because postoperative change alone can look similar.
det.treatment: Management is mainly symptomatic: neuropathic pain drugs, physiotherapy and multidisciplinary pain care. Spinal cord stimulation helps some. Surgery is generally avoided except for specific complications such as syrinx or focal cyst; steroids are of uncertain benefit.
det.prognosis: Chronic and often disabling; most patients stabilise rather than recover.
pearls: Clumped roots or an empty thecal sac on MRI suggest arachnoiditis.
Repeated spinal surgery is a key risk factor.
More surgery usually worsens rather than improves it.
det.thd: Arachnoiditis fibrosis คือเยื่อหุ้มไขสันหลังชั้น arachnoid อักเสบเรื้อรังจนเป็นพังผืด รากประสาทติดกันหรือติดกับผนังถุงหุ้ม มักเกิดหลังผ่าตัดหลังหลายครั้ง ติดเชื้อ เลือดออก หรือฉีดยาเข้าช่องไขสันหลัง ผู้ป่วยปวดแสบร้าวลงขาเรื้อรัง ชา อ่อนแรง และปัสสาวะลำบาก MRI พบรากประสาทเกาะกลุ่ม การรักษาเน้นยาลดปวดชนิด neuropathic และกายภาพ หลีกเลี่ยงการผ่าตัดซ้ำ

files.chapter: Chapter 22 Neurologic Disorders Associated with Bone and Joint Disease

ddx.pt: Acute compression from a disc or tumour needing urgent surgery
Mechanical stenosis with neurogenic claudication; roots not clumped
Cape-like dissociated sensory loss from a cord cavity; may itself complicate arachnoiditis

aN: adhesive arachnoiditis | chronic arachnoiditis | fibrotic arachnoiditis | arachnoiditis ossificans calcified form

name: Arginase deficiency
formal: Urea cycle disorder from ARG1 mutation presenting with progressive spastic diplegia, developmental delay and seizures, with hyperargininaemia and sometimes hyperammonaemia.
simple: A rare inherited metabolic condition causing leg stiffness, delayed development and seizures because a waste-removing enzyme is missing.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมด้อยของวงจรยูเรียจากยีน ARG1 ทำให้พัฒนาการช้าแล้วถดถอย ขากลายเป็นเกร็ง spastic ค่อยเป็นค่อยไป และชัก โดย arginine ในเลือดสูง
tempoNote: Normal or slow early course, then progressive spasticity and regression from about 1 to 4 years; metabolic crises are infrequent
feat: Progressive spastic paraplegia or quadriplegia that begins in early childhood, often with toe walking
Developmental slowing, then loss of skills and intellectual disability
Seizures, recurrent vomiting, irritability and ataxia; aversion to protein foods
The rarest of the urea cycle disorders, autosomal recessive
Easily labelled cerebral palsy or hereditary spastic paraplegia if blood amino acids are not checked
inv: Plasma amino acids: raised arginine, often several times normal
Blood ammonia (often raised but can be near normal) and urine orotic acid
Red cell arginase activity or ARG1 sequencing; expanded newborn screening where available
MRI brain for atrophy and exclusion of structural causes

case.story: He walked at 13 months but for a year has walked on tiptoe, trips often and has had two seizures. His mother says he refuses meat and eggs and vomits after big meals.
case.exam: Spastic legs with brisk reflexes and bilateral extensor plantars, mild cognitive delay; arms near normal.
case.tests: Plasma arginine several times the upper limit; ammonia mildly raised; MRI shows mild cerebral atrophy.
case.q: Why is cerebral palsy the wrong label, and what test finds the answer?
case.a: The spasticity is progressive with regression, which is not cerebral palsy; plasma amino acids reveal high arginine, pointing to treatable arginase deficiency.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Arginase Deficiency

det.patho: Biallelic ARG1 variants remove the cytosolic arginase that splits arginine into ornithine and urea, the last step of the urea cycle. Arginine and related guanidino compounds build up and are thought to injure corticospinal and cortical neurons. Because other pathways dispose of some nitrogen, ammonia rises less than in proximal cycle defects.
det.clinical: Infancy is usually unremarkable. Between one and four years the child slows, then loses skills and develops stiffness in the legs, sometimes progressing to the arms. Seizures, vomiting and growth failure may appear, and some children suffer ammonia crises during infections. The chief clinical lesson is that this is a metabolic cause of progressive paraplegia in a child.
det.diagnosis: Measure plasma amino acids in any child with progressive spastic paraplegia, especially if cognition is falling. A markedly raised arginine is the key result, and about nine in ten children also show raised ammonia. Confirm with ARG1 sequencing or the absent red cell enzyme activity, and note that newborn screening detects many cases early.
det.treatment: Dietary protein restriction with essential amino acid supplements lowers arginine and can slow or partly reverse the disease. Ammonia scavengers such as sodium benzoate or phenylbutyrate are added for hyperammonaemia. Pegzilarginase, an enzyme that degrades arginine, has been approved in some regions for older children and adults and lowers plasma arginine in trials. Physiotherapy, orthoses, botulinum toxin and baclofen manage spasticity, and an emergency plan covers intercurrent illness.
det.prognosis: Early treatment can stabilise or improve function; untreated disease leads to fixed spasticity and severe intellectual disability.
pearls: Progressive, not static, spastic diplegia means look for a cause: send plasma amino acids.
Ammonia may be only modestly raised, so do not be reassured by a normal value.
A treatable mimic of cerebral palsy and hereditary spastic paraplegia.
det.thd: Arginase deficiency เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมแบบถ่ายทอดยีนด้อยของวงจรยูเรียจากยีน ARG1 ทำให้ arginine สะสม เด็กมักปกติช่วงทารก แล้วพัฒนาการถดถอย ขาเกร็งมากขึ้นเรื่อย ๆ ชัก อาจอาเจียนซ้ำ จึงถูกวินิจฉัยผิดเป็นสมองพิการหรือ HSP ได้ง่าย วินิจฉัยโดยตรวจ plasma amino acid พบ arginine สูง รักษาด้วยจำกัดโปรตีน เสริมกรดอะมิโนจำเป็น ยาขับแอมโมเนีย และ pegzilarginase ในบางประเทศ

ddx.pt: Plasma amino acids and ammonia normal; a specific SPG gene on the panel
Fixed injury from the perinatal period, no regression and no metabolic abnormality
Proximal enzyme defects cause hyperammonaemic coma rather than progressive spastic paraparesis

aN: argininemia | hyperargininemia | arg1 deficiency | arginase 1 deficiency

name: Arginosuccinic aciduria
formal: Urea cycle disorder from argininosuccinate lyase deficiency causing hyperammonaemia, seizures, developmental delay and brittle hair, with citrulline and argininosuccinate elevation.
simple: An inherited condition where ammonia builds up in the blood, causing seizures, developmental problems and brittle hair.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมของวงจรยูเรียจากการขาดเอนไซม์ argininosuccinate lyase ทำให้แอมโมเนียสูง ชัก พัฒนาการช้า ผมเปราะ และตับโต
tempoNote: Severe neonatal hyperammonaemia in the first days, or later intermittent crises and chronic developmental problems
feat: Neonatal form: lethargy, poor feeding, vomiting, hyperventilation and coma after a few days
Late form: episodic hyperammonaemia with illness, behavioural problems, developmental delay
Brittle, knotted hair (trichorrhexis nodosa)
Hepatomegaly, liver fibrosis and systemic hypertension
Cognitive impairment may occur even without major hyperammonaemic episodes
inv: Plasma ammonia; blood gas often respiratory alkalosis
Plasma amino acids: raised citrulline and argininosuccinic acid (also in urine)
ASL gene testing; newborn screening detects many cases

case.who: 3-day-old girl at a regional neonatal unit
case.story: Healthy term delivery with normal Apgar scores; by day 3 she became floppy, fed poorly and breathed fast.
case.exam: Drowsy, hypotonic, tachypnoeic without lung findings; liver palpable 2 cm.
case.tests: Ammonia 450 µmol/L, respiratory alkalosis; plasma citrulline moderately raised with large argininosuccinic acid peak.
case.q: What is the emergency approach?
case.a: Stop protein, give IV glucose, arginine and ammonia scavengers, and start haemodialysis if ammonia stays very high.

read.where: Chapter 17: Preventing recurrent stroke and other serious vascular events
Section 9 Vasospastic Conditions and Other Miscellaneous Vasculopathies

det.patho: Biallelic ASL variants block cleavage of argininosuccinate into arginine and fumarate, causing ammonia accumulation and arginine deficiency. ASL is also needed for nitric oxide production, which helps explain hypertension, liver disease and cognitive effects independent of ammonia. It is the second most common urea cycle disorder.
det.clinical: Severe forms present in the newborn period with hyperammonaemic encephalopathy. Later-onset forms present with recurrent vomiting, lethargy or behavioural change during illness, plus developmental delay, seizures, ataxia, trichorrhexis nodosa, hepatomegaly with fibrosis and hypertension. Some are found only by newborn screening.
det.diagnosis: Measure ammonia in any sick neonate or child with unexplained encephalopathy. Argininosuccinic acid in plasma or urine is diagnostic; citrulline is moderately raised. Confirm with ASL gene testing. Monitor liver function, blood pressure and development.
det.treatment: Acute crises need cessation of protein, IV glucose, IV arginine, ammonia scavengers (sodium benzoate, phenylbutyrate) and haemodialysis for severe hyperammonaemia. Long-term care uses a protein-restricted diet with arginine supplements and emergency plans for illness. Liver transplantation corrects ammonia handling in selected patients but not all neurological features.
det.prognosis: Neonatal forms carry risk of death or disability; later forms often have learning difficulties despite good metabolic control.
pearls: Hyperammonaemia + respiratory alkalosis in a neonate: think urea cycle disorder.
Brittle knotted hair is a distinctive clue to ASL deficiency.
Arginine supplementation is central because arginine becomes an essential amino acid.
det.thd: Argininosuccinic aciduria เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมของวงจรยูเรียจากการขาดเอนไซม์ ASL ทำให้แอมโมเนียสูง ทารกอาจซึม ไม่ดูดนม หายใจเร็วและโคม่าในไม่กี่วันแรก หรือมีอาการเป็นพัก ๆ เมื่อเจ็บป่วยในเด็กโต ร่วมกับพัฒนาการช้า ผมเปราะ ตับโต ตรวจพบ argininosuccinic acid ในเลือดและปัสสาวะ รักษาด้วยหยุดโปรตีน ให้ arginine ยาจับแอมโมเนีย และฟอกเลือดเมื่อรุนแรง

files.chapter: Chapter 17: Preventing recurrent stroke and other serious vascular events
Section 9 Vasospastic Conditions and Other Miscellaneous Vasculopathies

ddx.pt: Other enzyme defects (OTC, citrullinaemia) lack argininosuccinic acid and the hair change
High anion gap metabolic acidosis and ketosis accompany hyperammonaemia
Acquired liver failure with coagulopathy and jaundice

aN: argininosuccinic aciduria | asa | asl deficiency | argininosuccinate lyase deficiency

name: Argyll Robertson syndrome
formal: Pupils that accommodate but do not react to light, with small irregular pupils, classically due to neurosyphilis involving the midbrain pretectal area.
simple: Small pupils that tighten when focusing on near objects but not in response to light, classically caused by late syphilis.
th: รูม่านตาเล็ก รูปร่างไม่กลม ไม่หดเมื่อส่องไฟแต่หดเมื่อมองใกล้ ทั้งสองข้าง คลาสสิกจาก neurosyphilis
tempoNote: Develops insidiously years after untreated syphilis infection
feat: Small (often <3 mm), irregular, usually bilateral but may be asymmetric pupils
Poor or absent light reaction with brisk constriction to near (light-near dissociation)
Pupils dilate poorly with mydriatics; vision itself is normal
May accompany tabes dorsalis or general paresis
inv: Serum treponemal and non-treponemal tests (TPHA/TPPA, VDRL/RPR) and HIV
CSF: cells, protein, CSF-VDRL
MRI brain to exclude dorsal midbrain lesions if serology negative

case.story: His relatives note he has become forgetful and walks unsteadily in the dark; he mentions lightning pains in his legs.
case.exam: Both pupils 2 mm and irregular, no reaction to bright light, brisk constriction on near effort; positive Romberg, absent ankle jerks.
case.tests: Serum TPHA positive, RPR 1:16; CSF 18 lymphocytes, CSF-VDRL reactive.
case.q: What do the pupils and other findings indicate, and what is the treatment?
case.a: Argyll Robertson pupils with tabes dorsalis — neurosyphilis; treat with IV aqueous penicillin G for 10–14 days and test for HIV.

read.where: Chapter 22 Neuro-Ophthalmology — Central (Midbrain) Lesions of the Light Reflex

det.patho: The lesion is classically placed in the rostral dorsal midbrain near the Edinger–Westphal nucleus, interrupting fibres from the pretectal light reflex pathway while sparing the more ventral near-response input. Iris involvement may contribute to the small irregular shape. Neurosyphilis is the classic cause; diabetes, sarcoidosis, MS and other midbrain lesions can produce similar pupils.
det.clinical: The sign appears as an incidental finding or in the context of tabes dorsalis (lightning pains, sensory ataxia, areflexia) or general paresis. Visual acuity is preserved, so poor light response is not due to blindness. Pupils are small, unlike the mid-dilated pupils of dorsal midbrain syndrome and the large tonic pupil of Adie.
det.diagnosis: Confirm light-near dissociation by testing light in dim conditions and near with an accommodative target. Any patient with this sign needs syphilis and HIV serology, and lumbar puncture if positive. If serology is negative, look for diabetes and midbrain pathology with MRI.
det.treatment: Neurosyphilis is treated with IV aqueous penicillin G for 10–14 days (ceftriaxone is an alternative in allergy, or desensitisation). Repeat CSF and serology to confirm response. The pupil abnormality itself usually persists even after cure.
det.prognosis: Pupil changes are permanent; the course of neurosyphilis depends on how early treatment is given.
pearls: Light-near dissociation with SMALL pupils: Argyll Robertson; with LARGE pupil: Adie or dorsal midbrain.
Mnemonic: 'accommodates but does not react' (ARP).
Check HIV in every patient with neurosyphilis.
det.thd: Argyll Robertson pupil คือรูม่านตาเล็ก ไม่กลม ไม่หดเมื่อส่องไฟแต่หดเมื่อมองใกล้ เกิดจากรอยโรคบริเวณ dorsal midbrain พบคลาสสิกใน neurosyphilis โดยเฉพาะร่วมกับ tabes dorsalis ต้องตรวจ syphilis serology, HIV และน้ำไขสันหลัง รักษาด้วย penicillin G ทางหลอดเลือด แต่รูม่านตามักไม่กลับเป็นปกติ

ddx.pt: Large unilateral tonic pupil with slow near reaction and redilation; reduced reflexes
The underlying disease; look for tabes, general paresis or meningovascular stroke
Dorsal midbrain lesions give light-near dissociation with mid-dilated pupils and upgaze palsy

aN: argyll robertson pupil | arp | light near dissociation syphilitic | prostitute pupil

name: Argyrophilic grain disease (AGD)
formal: Late-onset tauopathy with 4-repeat tau argyrophilic grains in limbic regions, producing slowly progressive amnestic cognitive impairment and behavioural change.
simple: A slowly progressive brain disease of older people, causing gradual memory loss and personality change.
more: Usually diagnosed only at autopsy, often coexisting with Alzheimer or other tauopathies; there are no specific biomarkers. Management is symptomatic only.
th: tauopathy ชนิด 4-repeat ในผู้สูงอายุ มี argyrophilic grain ในระบบ limbic ทำให้ความจำเสื่อมช้า ๆ และพฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน มักวินิจฉัยได้จากการชันสูตรศพ
tempoNote: Very slow amnestic decline in people over 75
feat: Late-life amnestic cognitive impairment, slower than typical Alzheimer disease
Irritability, agitation, emotional instability or psychosis may be prominent
Asymmetric anterior medial temporal atrophy on MRI in some cases
Frequently coexists with AD, PSP, CBD or LATE pathology
No validated in-vivo biomarker; diagnosis is usually post mortem
inv: MRI brain; amyloid and tau biomarkers to exclude or identify AD co-pathology
Neuropsychological testing

case.story: Four years of gradually worsening forgetfulness with new irritability and suspiciousness toward her daughter.
case.exam: MoCA 21 with impaired recall; no parkinsonism.
case.tests: MRI shows asymmetric left anterior hippocampal and amygdala atrophy; CSF amyloid normal.
case.q: Which non-Alzheimer pathology might explain amnestic decline with normal amyloid?
case.a: Argyrophilic grain disease or LATE; both are limbic-predominant and confirmable only post mortem.

read.where: 9 - Atypical parkinsonism, parkinsonism-­plus syndromes and secondary parkinsonian disorders

det.patho: AGD is defined by small spindle-shaped tau-positive grains in dendrites of limbic neurons, beginning in the ambient gyrus and spreading to entorhinal cortex, hippocampus and amygdala. The tau is 4-repeat, linking it to PSP and CBD. Prevalence rises steeply with age and the grains are often found in very old brains with few symptoms.
det.clinical: Clinically AGD resembles slow amnestic mild cognitive impairment or late-onset dementia, often with behavioural and mood change. Because it so often coexists with other pathologies, its independent contribution to symptoms is debated.
det.diagnosis: There is currently no specific in-vivo test; diagnosis is neuropathological. Amyloid-negative amnestic decline with asymmetric anterior temporal atrophy raises the possibility, alongside LATE and primary age-related tauopathy. 4R-tau PET tracers are in development.
det.treatment: Management is symptomatic: cognitive support, treatment of mood and behaviour, and caregiver education. Cholinesterase inhibitors are of uncertain benefit when AD pathology is absent.
det.prognosis: Generally slow progression compared with Alzheimer disease.
pearls: AGD is a common 4R tauopathy of the very old.
Think of it in amyloid-negative amnestic decline after 80.
Often a co-pathology rather than a sole cause.
det.thd: Argyrophilic grain disease เป็นโรคสมองเสื่อมจากโปรตีน tau ชนิด 4R ในผู้สูงอายุมาก มีการสะสมของ grain ในฮิปโปแคมปัสและอะมิกดาลา ทำให้ความจำเสื่อมช้า ๆ และอารมณ์หงุดหงิด มักพบร่วมกับ Alzheimer หรือโรคอื่น ยังไม่มีการตรวจยืนยันขณะมีชีวิต วินิจฉัยได้จากการชันสูตร การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคองตามอาการ

files.chapter: 9 - Atypical parkinsonism, parkinsonism-­plus syndromes and secondary parkinsonian disorders
Chapter 77: Mild Cognitive Impairment and Alzheimer Disease

ddx.pt: Positive amyloid and tau biomarkers
Severe hippocampal neuron loss, often with TDP-43 (LATE)
Younger onset, prominent behavioural or language change

aN: agd | argyrophilic grain disease | braak disease | grain disease | 4r tauopathy with grains

name: Arm tremor
formal: Rhythmic involuntary oscillation of the upper limb that may be rest, postural or kinetic, with causes including Parkinson disease, essential tremor, cerebellar lesions and drugs.
simple: Shaking of the arm that may occur at rest, while holding a position, or during movement.
th: การสั่นเป็นจังหวะของแขน อาจเป็นขณะพัก ขณะยกค้าง หรือขณะเคลื่อนไหว สาเหตุเช่น Parkinson, essential tremor, รอยโรคสมองน้อย และยา
tempoNote: Usually chronic; acute onset suggests drugs, metabolic causes or a structural lesion
feat: A sign classified by activation: rest, postural or kinetic/intention
Rest tremor: Parkinson disease; postural/kinetic: essential tremor, enhanced physiological tremor
Intention tremor with dysmetria: cerebellar disease; rest plus postural plus intention: Holmes tremor
Drugs: valproate, lithium, salbutamol, amiodarone, SSRIs; metabolic: thyrotoxicosis, hypoglycaemia
Functional tremor shows variable frequency, distractibility and entrainment
inv: Thyroid function, glucose, drug review; caeruloplasmin under 50
Spiral drawing and handwriting samples
MRI for asymmetric or intention tremor; DaT-SPECT when PD vs ET uncertain

case.story: Hand shaking when holding a cup for three years; father had the same; improves after a beer.
case.exam: Bilateral 7 Hz postural and kinetic tremor, mild head tremor, no rigidity or bradykinesia.
case.tests: TSH normal.
case.q: Which diagnosis fits best, and what is the first-line drug?
case.a: Essential tremor; propranolol or primidone.

det.patho: Tremor arises from oscillation in central loops (cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuit, basal ganglia-thalamic loop) or from mechanical-reflex resonance of the limb. Different diseases engage different oscillators, which explains the distinct activation conditions and frequencies.
det.clinical: This entry describes a sign, not a disease. Classification follows the MDS 2018 two-axis scheme: clinical features (activation, distribution, frequency, associated signs) and aetiology. Combined tremor syndromes, such as dystonic tremor or Holmes tremor, are important to recognise because treatment differs.
det.diagnosis: Observe at rest, with arms outstretched and during finger-nose testing; look for associated parkinsonism, dystonia, ataxia or neuropathy. Simple blood tests and a drug review identify reversible causes. Accelerometry and EMG help in uncertain cases, especially for functional tremor.
det.treatment: Treat the cause. Essential tremor: propranolol, primidone, topiramate; refractory cases: deep brain stimulation or focused ultrasound thalamotomy. Parkinsonian tremor: levodopa, anticholinergics in younger patients, DBS. Cerebellar tremor responds poorly to drugs.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause; essential tremor progresses slowly, drug-induced tremor resolves on withdrawal.
pearls: Ask whether tremor occurs at rest, posture or action.
Asymmetric rest tremor with slowness means PD until proven otherwise.
Always review drugs and thyroid function.
det.thd: Arm tremor คือการสั่นเป็นจังหวะของแขน เป็นอาการแสดงไม่ใช่โรค แบ่งเป็นสั่นขณะพัก (มักเป็น Parkinson) สั่นขณะยกค้างหรือเคลื่อนไหว (เช่น essential tremor) และสั่นเมื่อใกล้เป้าหมาย (สมองน้อย) ควรตรวจไทรอยด์ ทบทวนยา และดูอาการร่วม การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ เช่น propranolol สำหรับ essential tremor หรือ levodopa สำหรับ Parkinson

ddx.pt: Bilateral action tremor, family history, alcohol response
Asymmetric rest tremor with bradykinesia
Fine fast tremor from drugs, anxiety, thyroid excess

aN: upper limb tremor | hand tremor | action tremor of the arm | rest tremor of the arm

name: Arrhythmic myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus with irregular, non-repetitive jerks, typical of cortical or subcortical myoclonus, unlike rhythmic myoclonus seen with focal brainstem or spinal lesions.
simple: Muscle jerks that happen at random, with no regular pattern.
th: myoclonus ที่กระตุกไม่สม่ำเสมอ ไม่เป็นจังหวะ พบใน cortical หรือ subcortical myoclonus ต่างจาก rhythmic myoclonus จากรอยโรคก้านสมองหรือไขสันหลัง
tempoNote: Depends on cause: acute in toxic-metabolic states, chronic in degenerative and genetic disorders
feat: Descriptive sign: irregular, non-repetitive shock-like jerks
Typical of cortical myoclonus (stimulus-sensitive, action-induced) and many subcortical forms
Causes: metabolic (uraemia, liver failure), hypoxia, drugs, CJD, progressive myoclonus epilepsies
Contrasts with rhythmic myoclonus from segmental brainstem or spinal lesions (e.g. palatal tremor)
inv: Renal and liver function, electrolytes, drug levels
EEG with back-averaging, somatosensory evoked potentials (giant SEPs in cortical myoclonus)
MRI brain; prion work-up if rapidly progressive

case.who: 68-year-old man on haemodialysis in Pathum Thani
case.story: Missed two dialysis sessions; family notices irregular jerks of his hands and that he drops cups.
case.exam: Multifocal irregular jerks, asterixis, mild confusion.
case.tests: Urea and creatinine markedly raised; EEG shows diffuse slowing.
case.q: What type of myoclonus is this and how is it treated?
case.a: Arrhythmic multifocal metabolic myoclonus; correct the uraemia with dialysis.

det.patho: Arrhythmic jerks reflect irregular firing of hyperexcitable cortical or subcortical neurons, often due to loss of inhibitory interneurons or metabolic disruption. Cortical generators conduct rapidly down the corticospinal tract, giving brief, focal or multifocal jerks.
det.clinical: This is a descriptive term rather than a disease. Arrhythmic myoclonus is often multifocal, stimulus-sensitive and worse with action. It occurs in toxic-metabolic encephalopathy, post-hypoxic states, neurodegenerative disorders and epilepsy syndromes. Rhythmicity helps localise: rhythmic jerks suggest segmental generators.
det.diagnosis: Describe distribution, rhythmicity and triggers, then search for causes with metabolic tests, drug review, EEG, SEPs and MRI. Neurophysiology confirms cortical origin and short burst duration.
det.treatment: Treat the cause where possible. For cortical myoclonus, levetiracetam, valproate, clonazepam and piracetam are used; avoid phenytoin and carbamazepine in some myoclonic epilepsies, which can worsen jerks.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause; metabolic myoclonus resolves with correction.
pearls: Rhythmicity separates segmental from cortical-subcortical myoclonus.
Asterixis is negative myoclonus and often accompanies metabolic arrhythmic jerks.
Levetiracetam is a good first choice for cortical myoclonus.
det.thd: Arrhythmic myoclonus คือการกระตุกที่ไม่เป็นจังหวะ พบบ่อยในชนิด cortical หรือ subcortical เช่น จากไตวาย ตับวาย ขาดออกซิเจน ยา หรือโรคเสื่อม ต่างจาก rhythmic myoclonus ที่มักเกิดจากรอยโรคก้านสมองหรือไขสันหลัง ตรวจเลือดหาสาเหตุ EEG และ SEP การรักษาคือแก้สาเหตุและใช้ยาเช่น levetiracetam หรือ clonazepam

name: Arsenic neurotoxicity
formal: Toxic exposure causing gastrointestinal illness, Mees lines, painful sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy resembling Guillain-Barre, and encephalopathy, diagnosed by urine arsenic levels.
simple: Nerve and brain damage from arsenic poisoning, causing painful numbness, weakness, confusion and white lines on the nails.
th: พิษสารหนูทำให้ท้องเสียอาเจียน เส้นประสาทปลายเสื่อมแบบปวดแสบคล้าย GBS ผิวหนังเปลี่ยนสี และเล็บมี Mees lines
tempoNote: Neuropathy 1–3 weeks after acute ingestion; insidious with chronic contaminated groundwater
feat: Acute: vomiting, diarrhoea, hypotension, QT prolongation, then encephalopathy
Painful ascending sensorimotor axonal neuropathy 1–3 weeks later, can mimic GBS
Mees lines (transverse white nail bands) appear weeks later
Chronic: hyperpigmentation, palmar-plantar hyperkeratosis, skin cancers
Thailand: historic groundwater contamination around tin-mining areas (Ron Phibun, Nakhon Si Thammarat)
inv: 24-hour urine arsenic (avoid seafood for 48 hours before testing) with speciation
Hair and nail arsenic for chronic exposure
NCS: axonal sensorimotor neuropathy; early studies can look demyelinating
ECG, renal and liver function, blood count

case.story: Two weeks after a severe bout of vomiting and diarrhoea she developed burning feet and could not climb stairs.
case.exam: Distal weakness, glove-and-stocking sensory loss, absent ankle jerks, white transverse bands on nails, hyperkeratotic palms.
case.tests: 24-hour urine inorganic arsenic markedly raised; NCS sensorimotor axonal neuropathy.
case.q: What toxin is responsible and what is the treatment?
case.a: Arsenic poisoning; remove exposure and give chelation (e.g. dimercaprol acutely, then DMSA).

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System

det.patho: Inorganic arsenic binds sulfhydryl groups and interferes with pyruvate dehydrogenase and oxidative phosphorylation, damaging highly metabolic tissues. Long sensory and motor axons degenerate in a dying-back pattern. Chronic exposure comes from contaminated groundwater, industrial sources and some traditional remedies; acute poisoning is usually intentional or accidental ingestion.
det.clinical: Acute poisoning starts with gastrointestinal illness, cardiovascular instability and possibly encephalopathy, followed by painful neuropathy. Early neurophysiology can mimic demyelinating GBS. Chronic poisoning causes skin pigmentation, keratoses, peripheral neuropathy and cancers. Mees lines appear about a month after exposure.
det.diagnosis: Urine arsenic is the key test, separating inorganic from seafood-derived organic arsenic. Hair and nails document chronic exposure. NCS shows axonal sensorimotor neuropathy. Investigate the source for public-health reasons.
det.treatment: Remove the source. Acute symptomatic poisoning needs supportive care and chelation, commonly dimercaprol initially, followed by oral succimer (DMSA) or DMPS when tolerated. Monitor QT, renal function and fluid balance. Neuropathy management includes pain control and rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: Recovery of neuropathy is slow and often incomplete, particularly after severe acute poisoning.
pearls: GI illness then painful neuropathy two weeks later: test urine arsenic.
Mees lines are a delayed clue — look at the nails.
Seafood raises total urinary arsenic; ask the lab for speciation.
det.thd: พิษสารหนูทำให้มีอาการทางเดินอาหารรุนแรงก่อน แล้ว 1–3 สัปดาห์ต่อมามีเส้นประสาทปลายเสื่อมแบบปวดแสบลุกลามคล้าย GBS พิษเรื้อรังทำให้ผิวคล้ำ ฝ่ามือฝ่าเท้าหนา และเล็บมี Mees lines ในไทยเคยพบที่อำเภอร่อนพิบูลย์ วินิจฉัยด้วยระดับสารหนูในปัสสาวะ 24 ชั่วโมง การรักษาคือหยุดการสัมผัสและให้ยาขับโลหะ เช่น dimercaprol หรือ DMSA

name: Arteriolosclerosis
formal: Hyaline thickening and narrowing of small arterioles from chronic hypertension and ageing, underlying lacunar infarcts, white matter disease and vascular cognitive impairment.
simple: Hardening and narrowing of the smallest blood vessels, often from high blood pressure, which can cause small strokes and memory problems.
th: การหนาตัวแบบ hyaline และตีบแคบของหลอดเลือดแดงเล็กจากความดันสูงเรื้อรังและอายุ เป็นพื้นฐานของ lacunar infarct โรคเนื้อขาว และ vascular cognitive impairment
tempoNote: Accumulates silently over decades; punctuated by acute lacunes or haemorrhages
feat: A pathological process rather than a single disease
Clinical expressions: lacunar strokes, white matter hyperintensities, microbleeds, deep intracerebral haemorrhage
Slowed thinking, executive dysfunction, gait disturbance and urinary urgency
Strongest risk factors: hypertension, age, diabetes, smoking
inv: MRI: white matter hyperintensities, lacunes, perivascular spaces, deep microbleeds
Blood pressure monitoring including ambulatory recordings
Glucose, lipids; consider genetic small vessel disease if young or familial

case.who: 71-year-old male retired policeman from Nakhon Ratchasima with long-standing hypertension
case.story: Two years of slowing, forgetfulness for appointments and short shuffling steps.
case.exam: Slow processing, reduced verbal fluency, wide-based short-stepped gait, brisk reflexes.
case.tests: MRI: extensive confluent periventricular and deep white matter hyperintensities, multiple lacunes in basal ganglia and pons, deep microbleeds.
case.q: What underlying vascular pathology is most likely?
case.a: Hypertensive arteriolosclerosis causing small vessel disease and vascular cognitive impairment.

read.where: Chapter 8 Stroke and Cerebrovascular Diseases — Lacunar Syndromes and Subcortical Ischaemic Stroke

Chapter 4: Which arterial territory is involved?

det.patho: Chronic hypertension damages small penetrating arteries: smooth muscle cells are replaced by hyaline material, walls thicken and lumens narrow. Lipohyalinosis and microatheroma lead to occlusion (lacunes) or rupture (deep haemorrhage), while chronic hypoperfusion and blood–brain barrier leakage damage white matter.
det.clinical: Many changes are silent. Clinical manifestations include classic lacunar syndromes, stepwise or insidious cognitive decline, gait apraxia, mood change and urinary dysfunction. Deep haemorrhages occur in basal ganglia, thalamus, pons and cerebellum.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is built on characteristic MRI markers in someone with hypertension or other vascular risks. STRIVE criteria standardise imaging terms. Consider monogenic causes (CADASIL, CARASIL, COL4A1) in young or familial cases and amyloid angiopathy when microbleeds are lobar.
det.treatment: Blood pressure control is the most effective measure for slowing progression. Manage diabetes, lipids and smoking; antiplatelets for symptomatic lacunar stroke. Physical activity and cognitive rehabilitation help function.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; heavy white matter burden predicts stroke, dementia, falls and death.
pearls: Deep microbleeds point to hypertensive arteriolosclerosis; lobar ones to amyloid.
Blood pressure control is disease-modifying therapy for small vessel disease.
Gait slowing and urgency often accompany cognitive change.
det.thd: Arteriolosclerosis คือหลอดเลือดแดงเล็กในสมองหนาตัวและตีบจากความดันโลหิตสูงเรื้อรังและอายุ เป็นพื้นฐานของโรคหลอดเลือดสมองขนาดเล็ก ได้แก่ lacunar infarct เนื้อขาวผิดปกติ microbleeds และเลือดออกในสมองส่วนลึก ทำให้ความคิดช้า ความจำและการเดินแย่ลง การวินิจฉัยใช้ MRI การรักษาที่สำคัญที่สุดคือควบคุมความดันและปัจจัยเสี่ยงอื่น

name: Arteriovenous malformation (AVM)
formal: Congenital tangle of dilated arteries and veins with direct shunting causing haemorrhage, seizures, headache or focal deficits.
simple: An abnormal tangle of blood vessels in the brain that can bleed or cause seizures.
th: กลุ่มหลอดเลือดผิดปกติแต่กำเนิดในสมองที่หลอดเลือดแดงต่อกับหลอดเลือดดำโดยตรงผ่าน nidus ไม่มี capillary คั่นกลาง มาด้วยเลือดออกในสมองในคนอายุน้อย ชัก หรือปวดศีรษะ
tempoNote: Present from birth; becomes evident with a sudden haemorrhage (often age 20–40), seizures or chronic headache
feat: Intracerebral (lobar), intraventricular or subarachnoid haemorrhage in a young person
Focal or focal-to-bilateral seizures
Chronic migraine-like headache, sometimes always on the same side
Progressive focal deficit from steal or venous congestion (uncommon)
Cranial bruit; association with hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT)
inv: CT/CTA: haematoma with calcification or enlarged vessels; MRI shows flow voids and the nidus
Catheter angiography (gold standard): feeders, nidus, venous drainage, associated aneurysms
Spetzler–Martin grading: size, eloquent location, deep venous drainage
Screen for HHT if multiple AVMs or family history of epistaxis/telangiectasia

case.story: Collapsed with sudden severe headache and vomiting during football; became drowsy, with right-sided weakness and word-finding difficulty.
case.exam: GCS 13, right hemiparesis 3/5, expressive aphasia; BP 136/82.
case.tests: CT: 30 mL left frontal lobar haematoma with serpiginous calcified vessels; CTA and angiography: 3-cm nidus fed by MCA branches with superficial cortical venous drainage.
case.q: What is the Spetzler–Martin grade and the management plan?
case.a: Size 3–6 cm (2) + eloquent cortex (1) + superficial drainage (0) = grade III; stabilise, then multidisciplinary decision on microsurgery ± embolisation or radiosurgery to prevent rebleeding.

det.patho: A brain AVM is a tangle of dysplastic vessels (nidus) through which arterial blood shunts directly into veins without a capillary bed. High flow and pressure cause venous dilatation, flow-related aneurysms on feeders and fragile walls prone to rupture. Most are sporadic, with somatic KRAS/BRAF mutations found in endothelial cells; multiple AVMs suggest HHT (ENG, ACVRL1). Prevalence is about 15–20 per 100,000, and AVMs cause a disproportionate share of haemorrhagic strokes in young adults.
det.clinical: About half present with haemorrhage, typically lobar or intraventricular, often less devastating than hypertensive bleeds. Seizures are the second commonest presentation; headache, progressive deficits and incidental discovery make up the rest. Risk factors for (re)bleeding include prior rupture, deep location, exclusively deep venous drainage, associated aneurysms and venous outflow stenosis.
det.diagnosis: CT/CTA in acute haemorrhage, MRI/MRA for unruptured lesions, and digital subtraction angiography to define architecture before treatment. Spetzler–Martin grade (I–V) predicts surgical risk; supplementary scores add age, prior haemorrhage and compactness. If an early angiogram is negative because of haematoma compression, repeat imaging after resorption.
det.treatment: Ruptured AVMs are generally treated to eliminate the nidus, as rebleeding risk is high in the first year. Options: microsurgical resection (low grade, accessible), stereotactic radiosurgery (small, deep or eloquent nidus; obliteration takes 2–3 years), and embolisation mainly as an adjunct or for feeder aneurysms. For unruptured AVMs, the ARUBA trial found medical management alone gave fewer strokes or deaths over several years than intervention, so many are observed with seizure and headache control, though selected low-grade lesions in young patients may still be treated. Anti-seizure medication for seizures; acute haemorrhage care as for ICH.
det.prognosis: Unruptured AVMs bleed at roughly 1–3% per year, rising to perhaps 5–15% in the first year after a rupture; mortality per haemorrhage is lower than for hypertensive ICH.
pearls: Lobar haemorrhage in a young normotensive adult: image for an AVM.
Spetzler–Martin = size + eloquence + deep venous drainage.
Unruptured AVMs: intervention is not automatically better (ARUBA).
det.thd: AVM คือกลุ่มหลอดเลือดผิดปกติแต่กำเนิดที่หลอดเลือดแดงต่อตรงกับหลอดเลือดดำผ่าน nidus มักมาด้วยเลือดออกในสมองในคนอายุน้อย ชัก หรือปวดศีรษะ วินิจฉัยด้วย CTA/MRI และ angiography จัดระดับด้วย Spetzler–Martin (ขนาด, ตำแหน่ง eloquent, การระบายเลือดดำลึก) รายที่แตกแล้วควรรักษาด้วยผ่าตัด radiosurgery หรือ embolisation ส่วนรายที่ยังไม่แตกพิจารณาเป็นราย ๆ ไป เพราะการรักษาไม่ได้ดีกว่าการติดตามเสมอ

qx.stem: A 27-year-old man presents with a first generalised seizure. MRI shows a compact cluster of tubular signal voids in the left parietal lobe with no mass effect and no surrounding oedema. Early arterial-phase enhancement is seen in an enlarged draining cortical vein, and the intervening brain shows gliosis.
qx.q: Which finding on conventional angiography would best confirm the diagnosis?
opts: A venous-phase blush only
Delayed capillary stain with a single feeding artery of normal calibre
A smooth segmental stenosis of the middle cerebral artery
A cluster of beaded small vessels with a puff-of-smoke appearance
A nidus with early filling of the draining vein through arteriovenous shunting
qx.why: An AVM is defined by a nidus linking feeding arteries directly to draining veins without a capillary bed, so the draining vein opacifies early in the arterial phase. Flow voids without mass effect reflect high-flow channels, and gliosis from steal or prior bleeds. Puff-of-smoke collaterals describe moyamoya, not an AVM.

name: Arteritis
formal: Inflammation of arterial walls, such as giant cell, Takayasu or primary CNS vasculitis, producing stroke, visual loss, headache and systemic symptoms.
simple: Inflammation of blood vessel walls that can reduce blood supply and cause strokes, headaches or vision loss.
th: การอักเสบของผนังหลอดเลือดแดง เช่น giant cell arteritis, Takayasu หรือ primary CNS vasculitis ทำให้เกิด stroke ตามัว ปวดศีรษะ และอาการทั่วร่างกาย
tempoNote: Weeks to months of systemic symptoms, punctuated by acute ischaemic events
feat: Umbrella term covering many arteritides
Giant cell arteritis: over 50, new headache, jaw claudication, visual loss, high ESR/CRP
Takayasu: young women, absent pulses, arm claudication, bruits, stroke
Primary CNS vasculitis: subacute headache, cognitive change and multifocal infarcts
Infection-related arteritis: TB, syphilis, varicella zoster, fungal
inv: ESR, CRP, full blood count; ANCA and autoimmune screen
Vascular imaging: ultrasound, CTA/MRA, vessel wall MRI, PET in large-vessel disease
Temporal artery or brain/leptomeningeal biopsy as appropriate; CSF in CNS vasculitis

case.story: Months of fatigue, low fever and left arm pain on writing; now transient left visual loss and right-sided weakness.
case.exam: Weak left radial pulse, BP 150/90 right arm and 100/70 left arm, carotid bruit, right hemiparesis.
case.tests: ESR 78 mm/h; CTA: long smooth stenosis of left subclavian and left common carotid arteries.
case.q: What type of arteritis is this?
case.a: Takayasu arteritis; treat with glucocorticoids plus a steroid-sparing agent (methotrexate or tocilizumab/TNF inhibitor).

det.patho: Immune-mediated inflammation of the arterial wall leads to thickening, stenosis, occlusion or aneurysm. Granulomatous inflammation characterises giant cell and Takayasu arteritis; infectious arteritis arises from direct invasion or immune response. The pattern of vessel size (large, medium, small) guides classification.
det.clinical: Symptoms combine systemic inflammation (fever, weight loss, fatigue) with ischaemia of the territories supplied. GCA causes visual loss and posterior circulation stroke; Takayasu causes arm claudication, pulse deficits and stroke; CNS vasculitis causes headache, encephalopathy and multifocal infarcts.
det.diagnosis: Inflammatory markers, vascular imaging and tissue diagnosis are combined. Normal ESR/CRP make GCA unlikely but do not exclude CNS vasculitis. Exclude infection and mimics such as RCVS, atherosclerosis and moyamoya before immunosuppression.
det.treatment: High-dose glucocorticoids are first line; steroid-sparing agents include tocilizumab (GCA, Takayasu), methotrexate, cyclophosphamide or rituximab depending on type. Treat infections with specific antimicrobials. Antiplatelets are often added for ischaemic complications.
det.prognosis: Usually controllable; relapses are common and steroid toxicity is a major long-term issue.
pearls: Absent radial pulse in a young woman with stroke: Takayasu.
Over 50 with headache and visual symptoms: check ESR/CRP that day.
Rule out infection before strong immunosuppression.
det.thd: Arteritis คือการอักเสบของผนังหลอดเลือดแดง ได้แก่ giant cell arteritis ในผู้สูงอายุ Takayasu ในหญิงสาว และ primary CNS vasculitis รวมทั้งจากการติดเชื้อ ผู้ป่วยมีไข้ อ่อนเพลีย ปวดศีรษะ ตามัว หรือ stroke การตรวจคือ ESR/CRP ภาพหลอดเลือด และชิ้นเนื้อ การรักษาหลักคือ steroid ขนาดสูงร่วมกับยากดภูมิที่ช่วยลด steroid

name: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) deficiency
formal: Scurvy from vitamin C deficiency with perifollicular haemorrhage, gum bleeding and bone pain; it may cause intracranial or muscle bleeding and, in children, pseudoparalysis.
simple: Lack of vitamin C causing bleeding gums, bruising, joint pain and weakness.
th: ภาวะขาดวิตามินซี (scurvy) ทำให้เลือดออกง่าย เหงือกบวม ปวดกระดูกและข้อจนเด็กไม่ยอมเดิน ซึ่งอาจถูกวินิจฉัยผิดเป็นโรคทางระบบประสาท
tempoNote: Develops over one to three months of very low intake
feat: Perifollicular haemorrhage, corkscrew hairs, swollen bleeding gums and poor wound healing
Painful legs with refusal to bear weight in children (pseudoparalysis) from subperiosteal bleeding
Tiredness, irritability and low mood early in the course
Rarely muscle haematoma, subdural bleeding or compressive neuropathy
At risk: selective eaters including children with autism, heavy drinkers, elderly people living alone, dialysis and malabsorption
inv: Plasma ascorbate, taken before supplementation is started
Clotting profile and platelet count, usually normal, to exclude coagulopathy
Long-bone radiographs or MRI showing subperiosteal haemorrhage and marrow oedema

case.story: For a year he has eaten only white rice and fried chicken nuggets. In the past two weeks he has stopped standing and cries when his legs are touched. He has no fever.
case.exam: Lies with hips and knees flexed, tender swollen knees, purple swollen gums, perifollicular petechiae on the legs; reflexes and sensation are normal.
case.tests: Plasma vitamin C very low; platelets and clotting normal; MRI femurs show patchy marrow oedema with subperiosteal blood.
case.q: Why will he not walk, and is this a neurological weakness?
case.a: No. It is scurvy with painful subperiosteal haemorrhage causing pseudoparalysis. Treat with vitamin C replacement and dietary correction; improvement is rapid.

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid)
8 Vitamin E deficiency and its neurological effects

det.patho: Humans cannot synthesise ascorbate, which is a cofactor for the hydroxylases that stabilise collagen and for dopamine beta-hydroxylase in catecholamine synthesis. Without it, collagen is fragile, capillaries leak and bone matrix forms poorly. Intake below about 10 mg a day for weeks leads to clinical scurvy, while the body pool is depleted over one to three months.
det.clinical: Fatigue and aching limbs come first, followed by bruising, gum disease, tooth loosening and corkscrew hairs. In children, pain around the metaphyses and a frog-leg posture lead to refusal to stand and are often mistaken for leukaemia, osteomyelitis or neuromuscular disease. Adults can develop anaemia, joint effusions and oedema. Neurological effects are uncommon and mostly consequences of bleeding or depression and apathy. Ask about diet in anyone with unexplained bleeding and bone pain.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical, supported by low plasma ascorbate and radiographic signs such as a dense metaphyseal line and Wimberger ring in children. Normal coagulation tests help exclude haematological disease. A rapid response to replacement is itself confirmatory. Evaluate for the underlying cause of poor intake, including eating disorders, sensory food aversion and alcohol use.
det.treatment: Give oral vitamin C, typically 100–300 mg per day in adults and a weight-based paediatric dose, for one to three months. Symptoms such as pain and irritability improve within days and gum and skin findings within weeks. Add nutritional counselling and treat associated deficiencies. Hospitalise patients with intracranial bleeding or severe haemorrhage and treat them as a bleeding emergency.
det.prognosis: Recovery is complete with replacement and a corrected diet. Delay in recognition leads to repeated needless investigations rather than permanent damage.
pearls: A child who will not walk, has swollen gums and a normal blood count and clotting: think scurvy.
A very restricted diet in autism is the commonest modern setting.
Check vitamin C level before treatment, as it normalises within hours of supplementation.
det.thd: ภาวะขาดวิตามินซีหรือโรค scurvy เกิดจากกินอาหารที่ขาดผักผลไม้นานเป็นเดือน ทำให้คอลลาเจนอ่อนแอและเลือดออกง่าย อาการคือเหงือกบวมเลือดออก จุดเลือดออกรอบรูขุมขน ขนม้วนงอ และในเด็กจะปวดขาจนไม่ยอมเดิน ซึ่งไม่ใช่อัมพาตจริง ผลเลือดการแข็งตัวปกติ ระดับวิตามินซีในพลาสมาต่ำ การรักษาคือให้วิตามินซีและแก้ไขอาหาร อาการดีขึ้นเร็วภายในไม่กี่วัน

name: Aseptic meningitis
formal: Meningeal inflammation with lymphocytic pleocytosis and negative bacterial cultures, most often viral, but also from drugs, autoimmune disease or malignancy.
simple: Inflammation of the brain's coverings causing headache, fever and neck stiffness, but with no bacteria found, most often caused by a virus.
th: กลุ่มอาการเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบที่ย้อมและเพาะเชื้อแบคทีเรียไม่พบ ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจากไวรัส (enterovirus, HSV-2, VZV, HIV) แต่ต้องคิดถึงยา (NSAIDs, TMP-SMX, IVIG, lamotrigine) โรคภูมิต้านตนเอง มะเร็ง และการติดเชื้อที่รักษาได้ เช่น วัณโรค cryptococcus ซิฟิลิส และแบคทีเรียที่ได้ยามาก่อน
tempoNote: Viral and drug causes evolve over hours to days and settle within 1-2 weeks; TB, fungal, syphilitic or malignant causes progress over weeks
feat: Fever, headache, photophobia and neck stiffness with preserved consciousness and no focal signs
Viruses dominate: enteroviruses, HSV-2 (including recurrent Mollaret meningitis), VZV even without rash, HIV seroconversion, mumps, LCMV and arboviruses
Drug-induced meningitis within hours to days of NSAIDs, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, IVIG, lamotrigine, carbamazepine, isoniazid or intrathecal agents
Non-infectious causes: SLE, Sjogren, Behcet, sarcoidosis, Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada, leptomeningeal cancer, ruptured epidermoid cyst
Must exclude partially treated bacterial meningitis, a parameningeal focus, TB, cryptococcus, syphilis, leptospirosis and Lyme disease
inv: CSF: usually lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal or mildly raised protein, normal glucose; early viral and drug-induced cases can be neutrophil predominant
CSF PCR (enterovirus, HSV-1/2, VZV; multiplex panel where available), cryptococcal antigen, Gram stain and culture; TB tests and repeat tap if glucose is low or illness prolonged
HIV test, syphilis serology, blood cultures; consider Leptospira, scrub typhus and arbovirus serology in Thailand
MRI with contrast for parameningeal infection, leptomeningeal disease or a dermoid if the course is atypical

case.who: 26-year-old female nursing student from Khon Kaen with lupus
case.story: Six hours after taking ibuprofen 400 mg for period pain she develops severe headache, fever and neck pain; the same happened after ibuprofen a year ago.
case.exam: Temperature 38.4 C, neck stiffness, alert, no rash or focal signs.
case.tests: CSF 650 cells (70% neutrophils), protein 1.1 g/L, glucose normal; Gram stain negative; culture and multiplex PCR negative at 48 hours; she improves within two days without antibiotics after the first doses.
case.q: What is the likely cause and how can recurrence be prevented?
case.a: Drug-induced aseptic meningitis from ibuprofen (lupus is a risk factor); stop empirical antibiotics once cultures are negative, label the allergy and avoid ibuprofen and related NSAIDs.
