det.patho: The term describes meningeal inflammation with a CSF pleocytosis but no organism on routine Gram stain and bacterial culture. Viruses reach the meninges through the bloodstream (enteroviruses, arboviruses) or along nerves (HSV-2 from sacral ganglia). Drug-induced meningitis is thought to be a hypersensitivity or direct irritant reaction, more frequent in people with autoimmune disease. Malignant, granulomatous and autoimmune causes inflame the meninges more slowly and can lower CSF glucose.
det.clinical: Acute viral cases resemble a severe headache with fever and meningism but a clear sensorium; the illness settles in days. Drug-induced meningitis begins within hours to days of exposure and resolves within days of stopping, recurring with rechallenge. Recurrent episodes suggest HSV-2, drug exposure, an epidermoid cyst or autoimmune disease. Confusion, seizures or focal signs mean encephalitis or another diagnosis and change the work-up.
det.diagnosis: Lumbar puncture defines the syndrome; CT first only when there are focal signs, papilloedema, seizure, immunosuppression or reduced consciousness. A normal glucose with lymphocytes and a positive enterovirus or HSV PCR settles most cases, but a negative multiplex panel does not exclude HSV, TB or fungi, so targeted tests remain necessary. Neutrophils early on do not mean bacterial infection when glucose is normal and Gram stain negative, and a repeat tap after 12-24 hours often shows a shift to lymphocytes in viral cases. Low glucose points to TB, fungi, malignancy, sarcoid or partially treated bacteria, and needs further testing rather than a viral label.
det.treatment: Give empirical bacterial meningitis therapy if there is any doubt, and stop it when cultures are negative at 48 hours and the picture fits a viral or drug cause. Aciclovir is given if encephalitis is suspected; in immunocompetent adults with HSV-2 meningitis antivirals have not been shown to shorten the illness, and suppressive valaciclovir did not prevent recurrences in a trial, although many clinicians still treat severe cases. Remove the culprit drug and document it, and treat underlying autoimmune or infectious causes specifically. Analgesia, antiemetics and hydration are the mainstay.
det.prognosis: Viral and drug-induced aseptic meningitis recover fully, although headache and fatigue may linger for weeks; the prognosis of other causes depends on the underlying disease.
pearls: Ibuprofen, TMP-SMX and IVIG are the classic drug triggers, and lupus increases the risk.
Aseptic does not mean benign: always think of TB, cryptococcus, syphilis, partially treated bacteria and cancer when glucose is low or the course is long.
HSV-2 is the main cause of recurrent benign lymphocytic (Mollaret) meningitis.
det.thd: Aseptic meningitis คือเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบที่ย้อมและเพาะเชื้อแบคทีเรียไม่พบ ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจากไวรัส เช่น enterovirus และ HSV-2 แต่ยาก็เป็นสาเหตุได้ เช่น ibuprofen, TMP-SMX และ IVIG ซึ่งอาจทำให้น้ำไขสันหลังมีนิวโทรฟิลเด่นในช่วงแรก ต้องแยกโรคที่รักษาได้ เช่น วัณโรค cryptococcus ซิฟิลิส และแบคทีเรียที่ได้ยามาก่อน โดยเฉพาะเมื่อน้ำตาลในน้ำไขสันหลังต่ำหรือป่วยนาน รักษาตามสาเหตุ หยุดยาปฏิชีวนะเมื่อเพาะเชื้อไม่ขึ้นที่ 48 ชั่วโมง และหยุดยาที่เป็นต้นเหตุ

qx.stem: A 34-year-old woman with systemic lupus has fever, severe headache and neck stiffness 8 hours after taking ibuprofen for toothache. She had a similar episode last year. CSF shows 900 cells with 75% neutrophils, protein 1.0 g/L, glucose within normal limits; the Gram stain is negative. Empirical ceftriaxone is started.
qx.q: If CSF culture and PCR are negative at 48 hours and she is improving, what is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Partially treated pneumococcal meningitis
Lupus cerebritis
Tuberculous meningitis
Drug-induced aseptic meningitis
Mollaret meningitis due to HSV-2
qx.why: NSAIDs, especially ibuprofen, are classic triggers of drug-induced aseptic meningitis, lupus increases the risk and recurrence on rechallenge is typical. The CSF is often neutrophilic with normal glucose, which can mimic bacterial infection. Antibiotics can be stopped once cultures are negative, and the drug should be avoided in future.

name: Asperger’s syndrome
formal: Former diagnostic label for a form of autism spectrum disorder with social communication difficulty and restricted interests but preserved language and cognition.
simple: A previous name for a form of autism in which a person has difficulty with social interaction and has narrow interests, but normal language ability.
ab: autism spectrum disorder without intellectual or language impairment
th: ชื่อเดิมของภาวะออทิสติกสเปกตรัมที่มีปัญหาการสื่อสารทางสังคมและความสนใจจำกัด แต่ภาษาและสติปัญญาปกติ ปัจจุบันรวมเป็น ASD ใน DSM-5
tempoNote: Neurodevelopmental from early childhood; often recognised at school age or even in adulthood
feat: Neurodevelopmental condition, not a degenerative neurological disease; term retired in DSM-5 and ICD-11
Difficulty with reciprocal social interaction and reading non-verbal cues
Intense restricted interests and preference for routine
Normal early language milestones and average or higher intelligence
Motor clumsiness, sensory sensitivities, anxiety and ADHD are common co-occurrences
inv: Developmental and psychiatric assessment using DSM-5 criteria (e.g. ADOS-2, ADI-R)
Hearing and vision screen; genetic testing if dysmorphic or intellectual disability present
EEG only if seizures are suspected

case.story: Top of his class in mathematics but has no friends, talks at length about train timetables and becomes upset when routines change.
case.exam: Formal pedantic speech, limited eye contact, normal neurological examination.
case.tests: ADOS-2 consistent with autism spectrum disorder; IQ above average.
case.q: What is the current diagnostic label?
case.a: Autism spectrum disorder without intellectual or language impairment (formerly Asperger syndrome).

det.patho: Autism spectrum disorder is highly heritable, with contributions from many common variants and some rare de novo variants affecting synaptic and chromatin genes. Differences in brain connectivity and social-cognitive networks are described, but no single lesion exists. Vaccines do not cause autism.
det.clinical: This is a neurodevelopmental, not a neurological degenerative, condition and the name has been absorbed into ASD. Children typically present with social difficulties at school, rigid routines and specialised interests; adults may present with anxiety, depression or workplace difficulties. Neurologists meet it in the context of comorbid epilepsy, tics, sleep problems or motor coordination disorder.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical by trained teams using developmental history and standardised observation. Rule out hearing loss, language disorder, ADHD, anxiety and genetic syndromes where suggested.
det.treatment: Support is behavioural and educational: social skills training, cognitive behavioural therapy for anxiety, and school accommodations. Medication targets comorbidities (e.g. ADHD, anxiety, sleep), not core features.
det.prognosis: Lifelong but often compatible with independent living and employment with appropriate support.
pearls: Asperger syndrome is now classified as ASD in DSM-5 and ICD-11.
Normal early language distinguishes it from classic autism.
Screen for anxiety, ADHD and sleep problems.
det.thd: Asperger syndrome เป็นชื่อเดิมของภาวะออทิสติกสเปกตรัมที่มีสติปัญญาและพัฒนาการภาษาปกติ แต่มีปัญหาการเข้าสังคม อ่านสีหน้าท่าทางไม่ค่อยออก และสนใจเรื่องเฉพาะอย่างมาก เป็นภาวะทางพัฒนาการ ไม่ใช่โรคสมองเสื่อม วินิจฉัยโดยทีมพัฒนาการเด็กหรือจิตแพทย์ การดูแลเน้นฝึกทักษะสังคม ปรับการเรียน และรักษาภาวะร่วม เช่น วิตกกังวลหรือสมาธิสั้น

name: MOG antibody-associated disease (MOGAD)
formal: Antibody-mediated demyelinating disease with anti-MOG antibodies causing optic neuritis, myelitis, ADEM-like illness or brainstem syndromes, distinct from MS and neuromyelitis optica.
simple: An immune disease in which antibodies attack a protein on nerve coverings, causing optic nerve inflammation, spinal cord inflammation or brain inflammation.
th: โรคจากแอนติบอดีต่อ MOG — ประสาทตาอักเสบสองข้างหรือบวมมาก ไขสันหลังอักเสบยาว ADEM ในเด็ก และ cortical encephalitis มักตอบสนองดีต่อ steroid
tempoNote: Attacks peak over days; monophasic in many, especially children, with relapses in a minority of adults
feat: Optic neuritis, often bilateral and with marked disc swelling and painful eye movement
Longitudinal or conus-involving myelitis with bladder, bowel and erectile dysfunction
ADEM-like encephalopathy, especially in children
Unilateral cortical encephalitis with seizures (FLAMES)
Brainstem or cerebellar syndromes; marked recovery between attacks is typical
inv: MOG IgG by live cell-based assay; serum preferred, low titres need clinical correlation
MRI orbits: long anterior optic nerve lesion with perineural enhancement; spinal cord: H-sign of grey matter, conus lesions
MRI brain: fluffy, poorly demarcated lesions; few Dawson-finger or juxtacortical MS-type lesions
CSF: pleocytosis possible; oligoclonal bands usually absent; AQP4 IgG negative

case.story: Pain behind both eyes on moving them, then over three days vision falls to counting fingers in each eye.
case.exam: Visual acuity CF bilaterally, bilateral swollen optic discs with haemorrhages, sluggish pupils, no other deficits.
case.tests: MRI orbits: enhancement of the anterior half of both optic nerves with perineural sheath enhancement. AQP4 IgG negative, MOG IgG positive (1:1000). CSF no oligoclonal bands.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and how should steroids be tapered?
case.a: MOGAD optic neuritis; give IV methylprednisolone then a slow oral taper over weeks to months, because rapid withdrawal is a common trigger of early relapse.

det.patho: MOG is a minor component on the outermost surface of CNS myelin and oligodendrocytes. Antibodies to it, usually IgG1, together with T-cell and complement-mediated inflammation produce demyelination with relative axonal preservation, unlike the astrocytopathy of AQP4-NMOSD. It is now regarded as a separate disease from MS and NMOSD.
det.clinical: Children commonly present with ADEM or encephalitis, adults with optic neuritis or myelitis. Optic neuritis is frequently bilateral with severe swelling; myelitis tends to involve the conus and grey matter and may cause lasting sphincter problems even after motor recovery. Cortical encephalitis with seizures and headache, and brainstem syndromes, are characteristic additional phenotypes. Around a third to half of adults relapse, most often optic neuritis.
det.diagnosis: International criteria (2023) require a core demyelinating event plus MOG IgG on a cell-based assay, with supporting MRI or clinical features when titres are low or only CSF is positive. Serum should ideally be taken before treatment, since titres fall after steroids or plasma exchange. Always check AQP4 IgG and assess for MS. MOG positivity in a phenotype typical of MS should be interpreted with caution.
det.treatment: Treat attacks with IV methylprednisolone, adding plasma exchange or IVIG for severe or poor responses, followed by a slow steroid taper. Maintenance therapy is reserved for relapsing disease: options include maintenance IVIG, azathioprine, mycophenolate, rituximab or tocilizumab, with IVIG showing the strongest observational data. Several MS disease-modifying drugs are ineffective or harmful here.
det.prognosis: Recovery after each attack is often good, especially vision, but residual bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction from myelitis is common; persistent seropositivity predicts relapse risk.
pearls: Bilateral swollen discs with long anterior optic nerve enhancement: test MOG before giving steroids.
Conus involvement and the spinal-cord H-sign point towards MOGAD.
Do not taper steroids too fast; early relapse is often withdrawal-related.
det.thd: MOGAD เกิดจากแอนติบอดีต่อ MOG บนผิวปลอกประสาท ทำให้เกิดประสาทตาอักเสบซึ่งมักเป็นสองข้างและขั้วประสาทตาบวม ไขสันหลังอักเสบโดยเฉพาะ conus ADEM ในเด็ก และ cortical encephalitis ที่มีชัก วินิจฉัยด้วย MOG IgG แบบ cell-based assay และต้องแยกจาก NMOSD และ MS รักษาช่วงกำเริบด้วย IV methylprednisolone แล้วลด steroid อย่างช้า ถ้ากำเริบซ้ำให้ IVIG ระยะยาวหรือยากดภูมิ

qx.stem: A 15-year-old boy from Surat Thani develops painful loss of vision in both eyes over three days. Both optic discs are markedly swollen. Orbital MRI shows enhancement along more than half the length of each optic nerve with enhancement of the surrounding sheath. Serum MOG-IgG on fixed cell-based assay is positive at 1:40 (laboratory low-positive range); AQP4-IgG is negative and brain MRI is normal.
qx.q: How should this result be interpreted using the 2023 international MOGAD criteria?
opts: MOGAD cannot be diagnosed because the titre must always be at least 1:100
A brain lesion is required before MOGAD can be diagnosed
He fulfils MOGAD criteria: low-positive MOG-IgG is acceptable with negative AQP4-IgG and supportive features
MOG-IgG must be confirmed in CSF before it counts
A second attack is needed to fulfil the criteria
qx.why: The 2023 criteria need a core demyelinating event plus MOG-IgG by cell-based assay. A clear positive titre stands alone, whereas a low-positive or untitred result also requires AQP4-IgG negativity and at least one supportive feature; for optic neuritis these include bilateral simultaneous involvement, long-segment (>50%) nerve involvement, perineural enhancement and disc oedema, all present here. CSF testing, brain lesions and relapse are not required.

name: Astrocytoma
formal: Glial tumour arising from astrocytes, ranging from pilocytic (grade 1) to diffuse and anaplastic forms and glioblastoma, presenting with seizures, headache or focal deficits.
simple: A brain tumour that grows from star-shaped support cells in the brain, ranging from slow-growing to aggressive.
th: เนื้องอกสมองชนิด glioma ที่เกิดจากเซลล์ astrocyte ตั้งแต่ pilocytic astrocytoma ที่ผ่าตัดหายได้ในเด็ก ไปจนถึง IDH-mutant astrocytoma และ glioblastoma ในผู้ใหญ่ การจัดกลุ่มตาม WHO 2021 ใช้ผล molecular (IDH, ATRX, CDKN2A/B, H3) ร่วมกับพยาธิวิทยา
tempoNote: Low-grade tumours behave over years (a first seizure may precede imaging change by a long time); grade 3-4 tumours progress within weeks or a few months, producing worsening deficit or raised pressure
feat: Adults: a first focal or generalised seizure is the commonest opening in low-grade tumours, usually with a normal examination; roughly half of patients have no deficit at diagnosis
Higher grades add headache, personality or memory change, aphasia or hemiparesis according to the lobe involved, and papilloedema when the mass or oedema raises pressure
Children: pilocytic astrocytoma of cerebellum, optic pathway or hypothalamus with ataxia, hydrocephalus, visual loss or diencephalic signs; the optic pathway form is linked to NF1

WHO CNS5 splits astrocytic tumours into circumscribed (pilocytic, BRAF-driven), adult diffuse (IDH-mutant astrocytoma, grade 2-4) and IDH-wildtype glioblastoma; molecular results can override the microscopic grade
Frontal lobe is the favourite site in adults, then temporal and parietal; deep and brainstem sites are more common in children
inv: Contrast MRI: non-enhancing T2/FLAIR mass in low grade, rim enhancement with necrosis and oedema in glioblastoma; enhancement can appear in grade 2 so imaging alone does not assign grade
Tissue diagnosis with molecular panel: IDH1/2, ATRX, TP53, 1p/19q, CDKN2A/B, TERT promoter, MGMT promoter methylation, and H3 K27 or BRAF V600E when the site and age suggest them
MR spectroscopy, perfusion and functional MRI/tractography to support grading and plan a resection that spares eloquent cortex and tracts
EEG only if seizures are difficult to classify; a post-operative MRI within 72 hours to measure the residual tumour

case.who: 38-year-old woman, primary-school teacher from Khon Kaen
case.story: A 2-minute episode of right-hand jerking progressing to a convulsion while marking exam papers; she recovers fully and feels well. No headache or weight loss.
case.exam: Normal examination including fundi, language and power. No neurocutaneous stigmata.
case.tests: MRI shows a non-enhancing left frontal cortical-subcortical FLAIR-bright mass with no restricted diffusion. At awake craniotomy a near-total resection is achieved; pathology: diffuse astrocytoma, IDH1 R132H-mutant, ATRX lost, CNS WHO grade 2.
case.q: Which two molecular findings define this tumour type under WHO 2021, and what drug can postpone radiotherapy if residual tumour remains?
case.a: IDH mutation with ATRX/TP53 changes and intact 1p/19q define astrocytoma, IDH-mutant. Vorasidenib, an oral IDH1/2 inhibitor, delays progression in residual grade 2 disease and may defer radiotherapy and chemotherapy.

read.where: Chapter 1 Pathology and Classification of Tumors of the Nervous System

det.patho: Astrocytic tumours are glial neoplasms with astrocytic differentiation. In adults the dominant biology is an IDH1/2 mutation producing the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate, usually with ATRX loss and TP53 mutation; glioblastoma without IDH mutation has a different origin and a far worse course. Pilocytic astrocytoma instead carries MAPK-pathway alterations, classically KIAA1549::BRAF fusion. WHO CNS5 grades IDH-mutant astrocytoma 2 to 4 and calls a tumour grade 4 when CDKN2A/B is homozygously deleted even without necrosis.
det.clinical: Seizures lead the story in slow tumours; the interval from first seizure to diagnosis can be long. In a modern series about half of patients with low-grade tumour have a normal examination. Mass effect, headache and focal deficit become common with grade 3-4 disease, and frontal or temporal lesions add personality, memory and language change. Low-grade diffuse tumours often progress to a higher grade after several years; the book from which this entry draws reports a wide range of transformation rates and times. Children with posterior fossa or optic pathway tumours present with hydrocephalus, ataxia or visual loss instead of seizures.
det.diagnosis: MRI with contrast defines the lesion, but histology plus molecular testing assigns type and grade, and a biopsy may under-grade a heterogeneous tumour, so sampling across the lesion matters. Standard panel: IDH1 R132H immunostain with sequencing if negative, ATRX, p53, 1p/19q, CDKN2A/B, TERT promoter, MGMT methylation and, in midline or young patients, H3 K27M and BRAF V600E. Spectroscopy for 2-hydroxyglutarate can suggest IDH mutation non-invasively. Differential diagnosis includes lymphoma, demyelination, infarct, encephalitis and metastasis.
det.treatment: Maximal safe resection guided by awake mapping and navigation is the first step; extent of resection and low residual volume are linked to longer control. For IDH-mutant grade 2 tumours with residual disease and no urgent need for radiotherapy, vorasidenib (INDIGO trial; approved in the USA in 2024) prolongs progression-free survival. Higher-risk or grade 3 disease receives radiotherapy followed by temozolomide (CATNON) or PCV; glioblastoma follows the Stupp pathway. Pilocytic astrocytoma is often cured by resection alone, and BRAF/MEK inhibitors serve unresectable BRAF-altered tumours. Control seizures with non-enzyme-inducing drugs such as levetiracetam or lamotrigine, and use dexamethasone only for symptomatic oedema.
det.prognosis: Pilocytic tumours have a ten-year survival above 90% after resection; IDH-mutant astrocytomas live many years (median roughly 10 years for grade 2, shorter for grade 3-4) while IDH-wildtype glioblastoma is measured in about 15-20 months.
pearls: First adult seizure plus a non-enhancing cortical mass: think diffuse glioma and send tissue for molecular typing, not only histology.
IDH status and CDKN2A/B deletion now outweigh the microscopic grade for prognosis.
Cerebellar cyst with a mural nodule in a child is pilocytic astrocytoma until proved otherwise, and complete excision cures it.
det.thd: Astrocytoma เป็นเนื้องอกสมองกลุ่ม glioma ที่เกิดจาก astrocyte อาการในผู้ใหญ่มักเริ่มจากชักครั้งแรก ส่วนชนิดรุนแรงทำให้ปวดศีรษะ อ่อนแรง หรือสับสนค่อยเป็นค่อยไป การวินิจฉัยต้องใช้ MRI และตรวจชิ้นเนื้อร่วมกับ molecular เช่น IDH, ATRX, 1p/19q, CDKN2A/B ซึ่งกำหนดทั้งชนิดและเกรดตาม WHO 2021 การรักษาเริ่มจากผ่าตัดให้มากที่สุดเท่าที่ปลอดภัย แล้วพิจารณาฉายรังสี เคมีบำบัด หรือยา vorasidenib สำหรับ IDH-mutant เกรด 2 ที่ยังมีเนื้องอกเหลือ

name: Asymptomatic alcoholic myopathy
formal: Subclinical muscle involvement in chronic drinkers, detected by raised CK, EMG, or biopsy showing type II fibre atrophy without overt weakness.
simple: Muscle changes from heavy drinking that show up on tests but cause no noticeable weakness.
more: Often an incidental finding; abstinence and adequate nutrition may reverse it, preventing progression to symptomatic myopathy.
th: ภาวะกล้ามเนื้อผิดปกติจากสุราที่ยังไม่มีอาการ ตรวจพบ CK สูง EMG หรือชิ้นเนื้อพบ type II fibre atrophy โดยยังไม่อ่อนแรง
tempoNote: Develops silently with years of heavy drinking; may progress to symptomatic chronic myopathy
feat: No weakness, but raised CK or myopathic changes found incidentally
Biopsy shows type II fibre atrophy without major necrosis
Linked to cumulative alcohol intake; often coexists with neuropathy or liver disease
Can be reversible with abstinence and good nutrition
inv: CK, liver function, electrolytes (K, Mg, phosphate), thyroid tests
EMG if symptoms appear; biopsy rarely needed

case.story: Drinks a bottle of rice whisky daily for 20 years; attends clinic for a liver check and has no muscle complaints.
case.exam: Normal strength; mild loss of ankle jerks.
case.tests: CK 420 U/L, GGT high; TSH normal.
case.q: How should the raised CK be interpreted?
case.a: Likely subclinical alcoholic myopathy; advise abstinence, correct nutrition and recheck, rather than biopsy.

det.patho: Ethanol and acetaldehyde impair muscle protein synthesis, particularly in fast-twitch type II fibres, and cause mitochondrial and oxidative injury. Malnutrition, low potassium, magnesium and phosphate add to the damage.
det.clinical: Patients are asymptomatic; the finding is a laboratory or neurophysiological abnormality. A proportion will later develop proximal weakness and wasting typical of chronic alcoholic myopathy. Alcoholic neuropathy often coexists.
det.diagnosis: Interpret raised CK in heavy drinkers after excluding thyroid disease, drug effects (statins), recent exertion or trauma, and inflammatory myopathy if CK is very high. Muscle biopsy is not usually required.
det.treatment: Abstinence, balanced nutrition, thiamine and correction of electrolytes. Recheck CK after a period of abstinence.
det.prognosis: Usually reversible over months with abstinence.
pearls: Raised CK in a drinker is not always benign; exclude other causes.
Type II fibre atrophy is non-specific; also seen with steroids and disuse.
Abstinence is the treatment.
det.thd: Asymptomatic alcoholic myopathy คือกล้ามเนื้อผิดปกติจากการดื่มสุราเรื้อรังโดยยังไม่มีอาการอ่อนแรง ตรวจพบ CK สูงหรือชิ้นเนื้อมี type II fibre atrophy ต้องแยกจากสาเหตุอื่น เช่น ไทรอยด์ต่ำหรือยา statin การรักษาคือหยุดสุรา กินอาหารให้ครบ แก้เกลือแร่ และมักกลับเป็นปกติได้

ddx.pt: Symptomatic chronic proximal weakness or acute rhabdomyolysis
Raised CK after statin start; may coexist
Raised CK with slow relaxing reflexes and high TSH

name: Asymptomatic carotid stenosis
formal: Carotid narrowing found without prior stroke or TIA, carrying a modest annual stroke risk, managed with medical therapy and in selected cases endarterectomy or stenting.
simple: A narrowing of the neck artery to the brain found without having caused symptoms, which raises stroke risk.
th: ICA ตีบที่ตรวจพบโดยบังเอิญหรือจากการคัดกรอง โดยไม่มีอาการทางตาหรือสมองข้างเดียวกันใน 6 เดือน ความเสี่ยง stroke ต่ำ (< 1–2% ต่อปี) ภายใต้ยาที่ดี การผ่าตัดหรือใส่ stent พิจารณาเฉพาะราย
tempoNote: Clinically silent; found on screening, by a bruit or before cardiac surgery, and followed over years
feat: No ipsilateral TIA, amaurosis or stroke in the last 6 months (check carefully — vague symptoms are often missed)
Often discovered by a neck bruit, routine ultrasound or pre-operative screening
Commonly coexists with coronary and peripheral artery disease
Annual stroke risk with modern medical therapy is low, roughly 0.5–1%
inv: Carotid duplex with velocity criteria; repeat to watch for progression
CTA/MRA if intervention is being considered
Markers of higher risk: silent ipsilateral infarcts, rapid progression, intraplaque haemorrhage, microemboli on TCD
Global cardiovascular risk assessment (lipids, HbA1c, BP, renal function)

case.who: 71-year-old woman from Chon Buri awaiting coronary artery bypass surgery
case.story: Pre-operative duplex shows a left ICA stenosis; she denies any visual loss, weakness, numbness or speech trouble, now or ever.
case.exam: Left carotid bruit; neurological examination normal.
case.tests: Duplex peak systolic velocity 290 cm/s (≈ 75% stenosis); MRI brain: no infarcts; LDL 132 mg/dL.
case.q: What is the cornerstone of management?
case.a: Intensive medical therapy (antiplatelet, high-intensity statin, BP and diabetes control, stop smoking); revascularisation is reserved for selected higher-risk plaques in centres with very low complication rates.

read.where: Chapter 17 Preventing recurrent stroke and other serious vascular events

det.patho: The plaque biology is identical to symptomatic disease, but without evidence of recent embolisation. Most asymptomatic plaques remain stable; risk rises with greater degree, progression, lipid-rich necrotic cores, intraplaque haemorrhage and ulceration. Prevalence of ≥ 50% stenosis is around 2–5% in people over 65 and higher in those with coronary disease.
det.clinical: By definition there are no relevant symptoms, so a careful history is the key step: brief monocular dimming or transient hand weakness reclassifies the patient as symptomatic. Patients usually die of cardiac rather than cerebrovascular causes, so the stenosis is mainly a marker of systemic atherosclerosis. A bruit is a poor guide to severity.
det.diagnosis: Duplex grades the stenosis; screening the general population is not recommended. Imaging the brain may reveal silent ipsilateral infarcts, which increase future risk. Identify patients who may benefit from intervention by risk markers (progression on serial scans, intraplaque haemorrhage on MRI, microembolic signals, reduced cerebrovascular reserve) and estimate life expectancy, which should exceed about 5 years for intervention to make sense.
det.treatment: Best medical therapy is mandatory for everyone: antiplatelet, high-intensity statin (with ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitor as needed), BP and glucose control, exercise and smoking cessation. Older trials showed a small absolute benefit of endarterectomy for 60–99% stenosis, but medical therapy has improved since; recent randomised data comparing intensive medical care with and without revascularisation are mixed, with some benefit of stenting suggested in selected severe stenoses. Intervention is therefore individualised for severe stenosis with high-risk features, in centres whose procedural stroke/death rate is under 3%. Carotid screening before CABG does not routinely justify prophylactic surgery.
det.prognosis: Ipsilateral stroke risk is generally under 1% per year on modern therapy; cardiovascular events and death are considerably more frequent.
pearls: Ask about symptoms carefully — a missed amaurosis fugax changes the patient to symptomatic.
Treat the patient's whole vascular risk; the heart is the usual killer.
Intervene only when expected survival is long, risk markers are present and the centre's complication rate is very low.
det.thd: Asymptomatic carotid stenosis คือ ICA ตีบที่ไม่มีอาการทางสมองหรือตาข้างเดียวกันใน 6 เดือน มักพบจากการคัดกรองหรือได้ยิน bruit ความเสี่ยง stroke ต่ำมากภายใต้การรักษาด้วยยาเต็มที่ (antiplatelet, statin, คุมความดัน เบาหวาน เลิกบุหรี่) การผ่าตัดหรือ stent พิจารณาเฉพาะรายที่ตีบมากร่วมกับลักษณะเสี่ยงสูงและคาดว่ามีชีวิตยืนยาว และต้องซักประวัติให้แน่ใจว่าไม่เคยมีอาการ

name: Ataxia
formal: Incoordination of movement and gait from cerebellar or sensory pathway dysfunction, with dysmetria, intention tremor, dysarthria and wide-based gait; causes are genetic, toxic, autoimmune, vascular or nutritional.
simple: Poor balance and clumsy, uncoordinated movements, such as staggering walking and slurred speech.
more: MRI, vitamin and thyroid tests, antibodies and genetic panels identify causes. Treat reversible causes; otherwise physiotherapy, speech therapy and supportive care.
th: การเคลื่อนไหวไม่ประสานกัน เดินเซ จากความผิดปกติของสมองน้อยหรือทางรับความรู้สึก มี dysmetria, intention tremor, พูดไม่ชัด และเดินขากว้าง
tempoNote: Tempo is the main clue: acute (stroke, toxins), subacute (immune, nutritional, paraneoplastic), chronic (genetic, degenerative), episodic (episodic ataxias)
feat: A sign/syndrome, not a single disease
Cerebellar: dysmetria, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, scanning speech, nystagmus, wide-based gait
Sensory: positive Romberg, loss of joint position sense, worse in the dark
Vestibular: vertigo, gait veering to one side, nystagmus without limb ataxia
Causes: alcohol, drugs (phenytoin), stroke, MS, B1/B12/E deficiency, hypothyroidism, autoimmune, genetic
inv: MRI brain (cerebellum, posterior fossa); MRI spine if sensory ataxia
B12, vitamin E, thyroid, anti-TTG, anti-GAD, paraneoplastic panel, drug levels
NCS for sensory neuronopathy; genetic panel (SCA, FA, RFC1) when chronic

case.story: Three months of increasingly unsteady gait and slurred speech; heavy smoker, weight loss 6 kg.
case.exam: Bilateral limb and gait ataxia, gaze-evoked nystagmus, dysarthria; normal sensation.
case.tests: MRI normal; anti-Yo negative, anti-Hu negative, anti-Tr (DNER) positive; CT chest shows mediastinal lymphadenopathy.
case.q: What tempo-based category is this, and what must be searched for?
case.a: Subacute cerebellar ataxia; paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, search for lymphoma or lung cancer.

read.where: Chapter 24 Cerebellar Ataxias and Related Conditions — Approach to the Patient with Ataxia

det.patho: Coordination needs the cerebellum to compare intended and actual movement using proprioceptive and vestibular input. Lesions of the cerebellum or its connections cause errors in timing and scaling; loss of proprioceptive input (dorsal root ganglia, large-fibre nerves, dorsal columns) causes sensory ataxia; vestibular lesions disturb balance.
det.clinical: This entry is a syndrome heading. Midline (vermis) lesions mainly affect stance and gait, whereas hemisphere lesions affect ipsilateral limb coordination. Associated signs (neuropathy, pyramidal signs, eye movement disorders, cognitive change) narrow the cause. In Thailand, alcohol, drugs, stroke, SCA3 and MS/NMOSD are common considerations.
det.diagnosis: Classify by type (cerebellar, sensory, vestibular), tempo and family history. Acute ataxia needs urgent imaging to exclude stroke or haemorrhage. Subacute ataxia prompts autoimmune, paraneoplastic, nutritional and prion work-up. Chronic ataxia warrants genetic testing after acquired causes are excluded.
det.treatment: Treat reversible causes (stop alcohol or phenytoin, replace vitamins, treat coeliac disease, immunotherapy for autoimmune ataxia). Physiotherapy focusing on balance and coordination helps across causes. Omaveloxolone is approved for Friedreich ataxia; acetazolamide or 4-aminopyridine for some episodic ataxias.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause; acquired and treatable forms may improve, degenerative forms progress.
pearls: Romberg positive points to sensory, not cerebellar, ataxia.
Tempo is the first branch point in the ataxia work-up.
Always exclude acute posterior circulation stroke.
det.thd: Ataxia คือการเคลื่อนไหวไม่ประสานกัน เดินเซ เป็นกลุ่มอาการ ไม่ใช่โรคเดียว เกิดจากสมองน้อย ทางรับความรู้สึกตำแหน่ง หรือระบบทรงตัว แยกชนิดจากการตรวจร่างกาย เช่น Romberg และแยกสาเหตุจากระยะเวลาที่เกิด เช่น เฉียบพลันคิดถึงหลอดเลือดสมอง กึ่งเฉียบพลันคิดถึงภูมิคุ้มกันหรือมะเร็ง เรื้อรังคิดถึงพันธุกรรม การรักษาคือแก้สาเหตุที่รักษาได้และทำกายภาพบำบัด

name: Ataxia with oculomotor apraxia (AOA1, AOA2)
formal: Autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxias (AOA1, AOA2, etc.) with oculomotor apraxia, peripheral neuropathy and hypoalbuminaemia or raised alpha-fetoprotein, caused by DNA repair gene defects such as APTX and SETX.
simple: Inherited conditions causing unsteadiness together with difficulty starting eye movements and nerve damage, usually starting in childhood.
th: ataxia ยีนด้อยกลุ่มซ่อมแซม DNA ที่มีกลอกตาเริ่มยาก ร่วมกับเส้นประสาทเสื่อมรุนแรง — AOA1 (APTX) albumin ต่ำ, AOA2 (SETX) AFP สูง
tempoNote: AOA1 usually starts in early-to-mid childhood; AOA2 in the teens; both progress over years to wheelchair use
feat: Progressive gait and limb ataxia with cerebellar dysarthria
Difficulty launching saccades, compensated by head turns or blinks (more consistent in AOA1 than AOA2)
Marked axonal sensorimotor neuropathy: areflexia, distal wasting, foot deformity
Chorea or dystonia, especially early in AOA1; head tremor in some
No telangiectasia, immunodeficiency or high cancer risk
inv: AOA1: low albumin and high LDL/total cholesterol that become clearer with disease duration
AOA2: AFP moderately raised (useful screening marker); CK sometimes up
NCS: axonal sensorimotor neuropathy; MRI: cerebellar atrophy
Gene testing: APTX (AOA1), SETX (AOA2), ideally within a recessive-ataxia panel

case.story: Since age 13 she trips more and her handwriting has become shaky; her parents are cousins.
case.exam: Gait and limb ataxia, absent reflexes, distal leg wasting with pes cavus, reduced vibration at the toes; saccades are slightly hypometric but she starts them normally.
case.tests: AFP 32 ng/mL (age norm < 10); albumin normal; NCS axonal sensorimotor neuropathy; MRI cerebellar atrophy.
case.q: Which subtype fits best, and which gene would you test first?
case.a: AOA2 — teenage onset, neuropathy, cerebellar atrophy and a modest AFP rise; test SETX.

read.where: Review: Ataxias with oculocephalic dissociation; Biomarkers; Table 3
Chapter 24 Cerebellar Ataxias and Related Conditions — Inherited Ataxia Syndromes

det.patho: Both are recessive disorders of nucleic-acid processing. Aprataxin (APTX) repairs abortive DNA ligation intermediates at single-strand breaks; senataxin (SETX) is a helicase that resolves RNA–DNA hybrids during transcription. Cerebellar and peripheral sensory neurons seem especially vulnerable. AOA1 is frequent in Japan and Portugal, while AOA2 is among the commoner recessive ataxias after Friedreich's in Europe.
det.clinical: AOA1 typically begins before 10 with ataxia, choreic movements and later a severe neuropathy that can dominate the picture; cognitive slowing may occur. AOA2 starts in adolescence with ataxia and neuropathy, and oculomotor apraxia is present in only around half, so its absence should not deter testing. Both lack the immune and cancer features of A-T. Wheelchair dependence usually arrives within one to three decades.
det.diagnosis: Think of these after Friedreich's ataxia is excluded in a young patient with cerebellar atrophy and axonal neuropathy. AFP points towards AOA2 (or A-T), and low albumin with high cholesterol towards AOA1. Confirm with gene testing; a multigene ataxia panel or exome is efficient. Note that dominant SETX variants cause a juvenile ALS (ALS4), a different disease.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy exists. Rehabilitation, foot orthoses, speech therapy and management of dyskinesia are the mainstays. Coenzyme Q10 has been tried because some AOA1 patients have low muscle levels, but evidence is weak. Genetic counselling is important for siblings.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; life expectancy is often reduced but many survive into middle age.
pearls: Ataxia + neuropathy + cerebellar atrophy + high AFP in a teenager: AOA2.
AOA1 biomarker pair: low albumin and high cholesterol.
A diagnosis of AOA2 can be made without oculomotor apraxia.
det.thd: AOA เป็น ataxia ยีนด้อยที่มีปัญหาเริ่มกลอกตา ร่วมกับเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเสื่อมชนิด axonal และสมองน้อยฝ่อ AOA1 จากยีน APTX เริ่มในวัยเด็ก มี chorea และ albumin ต่ำ cholesterol สูง ส่วน AOA2 จากยีน SETX เริ่มวัยรุ่นและมี AFP สูงปานกลาง ต่างจาก AT ตรงที่ไม่มีภูมิคุ้มกันบกพร่องหรือมะเร็ง รักษาแบบประคับประคองและให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

name: Ataxia autosomal dominant hereditary
formal: Group of dominantly inherited progressive cerebellar ataxias (spinocerebellar ataxias), often from CAG repeat expansions, with gait ataxia, dysarthria and variable extrapyramidal or pyramidal features.
simple: Inherited conditions passed down in families that cause gradually worsening balance, clumsiness and slurred speech.
more: Genetic testing identifies subtypes such as SCA1, 2, 3 and 6, with anticipation seen in repeat disorders. No disease-modifying therapy exists; physiotherapy and symptomatic care are used.
th: กลุ่มโรคสมองน้อยเสื่อมที่ถ่ายทอดแบบยีนเด่น (spinocerebellar ataxias) มักเกิดจาก CAG repeat ขยาย มีเดินเซ พูดไม่ชัด และอาการ extrapyramidal หรือ pyramidal ร่วม
tempoNote: Onset usually 20–50 years; earlier and more severe in later generations for repeat disorders (anticipation)
feat: Progressive gait and limb ataxia with dysarthria and nystagmus
Family history in successive generations; anticipation in CAG repeat types
SCA3 (Machado-Joseph) most common in Thailand and worldwide; also SCA1, 2, 6, 7
Extra features: slow saccades (SCA2), retinal degeneration (SCA7), pure late cerebellar (SCA6), dystonia and parkinsonism (SCA3)
inv: MRI: cerebellar and/or brainstem atrophy
Repeat expansion testing for SCA1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 17 and DRPLA; panel or genome sequencing for non-repeat SCAs
Exclude acquired causes (alcohol, vitamin E, thyroid, autoimmune)

case.story: Five years of unsteadiness and slurred speech; his mother and uncle used wheelchairs from their 50s.
case.exam: Gait ataxia, gaze-evoked nystagmus, bulging-eye appearance, mild leg spasticity, faciolingual fasciculations.
case.tests: MRI shows pontocerebellar atrophy; ATXN3 CAG expansion confirmed.
case.q: Which SCA is this and what is its inheritance risk to his children?
case.a: SCA3 (Machado-Joseph disease); each child has a 50% risk.

read.where: Chapter 74: Cerebellar Disorders and Ataxias: Inherited Disorders

det.patho: Most common SCAs (1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 17, DRPLA) are caused by expanded CAG repeats encoding polyglutamine tracts that cause toxic protein aggregation and neuronal loss in cerebellum and brainstem. Other SCAs result from non-coding repeat expansions (e.g. SCA27B, FGF14 GAA) or conventional variants in channel and signalling genes.
det.clinical: Gait ataxia is usually first, followed by limb ataxia, dysarthria and dysphagia. Additional features vary by subtype and help direct testing. Longer repeats give earlier onset and more severe phenotypes, especially with paternal transmission in some types.
det.diagnosis: A dominant family history plus progressive ataxia warrants repeat expansion testing, then wider genetic panels. Absent family history does not exclude SCA because of incomplete penetrance, early parental death or non-paternity. Genetic counselling must precede presymptomatic testing.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy is approved; antisense oligonucleotides are in trials. Intensive physiotherapy, speech and swallow therapy, and treatment of spasticity, dystonia or restless legs improve function. Riluzole and troriluzole have mixed evidence.
det.prognosis: Progressive over 10–30 years; dysphagia and aspiration are major late risks.
pearls: SCA3 is the most frequent dominant ataxia in Thailand.
Slow saccades suggest SCA2; visual loss suggests SCA7.
Counsel families before predictive testing.
det.thd: Spinocerebellar ataxia กลุ่มนี้ถ่ายทอดแบบยีนเด่น ลูกมีโอกาสเป็น 50% ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจาก CAG repeat ขยาย ทำให้สมองน้อยและก้านสมองเสื่อม ผู้ป่วยเดินเซ พูดไม่ชัด กลืนลำบาก และอาจมีอาการพาร์กินสันหรือขาเกร็ง ในไทยพบ SCA3 มากที่สุด ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน ยังไม่มียารักษาให้หาย การรักษาคือกายภาพบำบัดและดูแลตามอาการ

name: Ataxia telangiectasia (AT)
formal: Autosomal recessive ATM disorder presenting in early childhood with progressive ataxia, oculomotor apraxia, telangiectasia, immunodeficiency, sensitivity to radiation and lymphoid malignancy risk.
simple: An inherited disease causing progressive clumsiness in children, visible tiny blood vessels, frequent infections and high cancer risk.
more: Raised serum alpha-fetoprotein is a key marker; MRI shows cerebellar atrophy. Cells are radiosensitive, so avoid unnecessary radiation; there is no cure, with care being supportive and many patients reaching adolescence or early adulthood. Alternative name for ataxia-telangiectasia, an autosomal recessive ATM disorder with cerebellar ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasia, immunodeficiency and malignancy risk. Autosomal recessive DNA repair disorder from ATM mutation with progressive cerebellar ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasia, immunodeficiency, raised alpha-fetoprotein and cancer predisposition.
th: ataxia แบบถ่ายทอดยีนด้อยที่เริ่มตั้งแต่เด็กเล็ก มีเส้นเลือดฝอยขยายที่ตาขาว กลอกตาเริ่มยาก ภูมิคุ้มกันบกพร่อง และเสี่ยงมะเร็งเม็ดเลือดสูง AFP สูง
tempoNote: Wobbly gait from the time the child starts walking (1–4 years), steady worsening; most need a wheelchair by about 10
feat: Toddler-onset truncal and gait ataxia that keeps worsening rather than improving with age
Head thrusts to shift gaze because saccades are hard to start (oculomotor apraxia); slurred speech and drooling
Dilated vessels on the bulbar conjunctiva and ears, usually appearing after ataxia (age 3–6)
Chorea, dystonia or myoclonus in later childhood; reflexes fade as an axonal neuropathy develops
Repeated sinus and chest infections, growth failure, early greying; lymphoma or leukaemia risk
inv: Serum alpha-fetoprotein: raised above the age norm in almost all patients after about 2 years old
Immunoglobulins (low IgA, IgG2, IgE) and lymphocyte subsets; karyotype may show 7;14 rearrangements
MRI: cerebellar atrophy becomes obvious with age; avoid unnecessary CT and X-rays (radiosensitivity)
ATM gene sequencing; ATM protein absent or reduced on immunoblot

case.story: Walked late and has always swayed; teachers notice he falls more each term. He has had pneumonia twice and constant runny ears.
case.exam: Broad-based gait, intention tremor, turns head before eyes when asked to look sideways, red thread-like vessels on both sclerae, depressed ankle jerks.
case.tests: AFP 180 ng/mL; IgA undetectable; MRI shows mild vermian atrophy.
case.q: Which gene is responsible, and what change in imaging practice follows?
case.a: ATM — ataxia telangiectasia; limit ionising radiation (prefer MRI and ultrasound) because cells are radiosensitive and cancer risk is high.

read.where: Review: Clinically common syndromes — Ataxia telangiectasia; Table 3

det.patho: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in ATM, a kinase that senses DNA double-strand breaks and triggers repair and cell-cycle arrest, cause genomic instability. Cerebellar Purkinje cells degenerate early, lymphocytes fail to rearrange antigen-receptor genes properly, and all cells are hypersensitive to ionising radiation. It is the second most common recessive ataxia in most populations; carriers have a modestly raised breast cancer risk.
det.clinical: The classic form begins in the second year with truncal sway, then oculomotor apraxia, dysarthria and dyskinesias; telangiectasia appear only later, so their absence early does not exclude it. Intellect is usually preserved at first but learning slows. Sinopulmonary infection, bronchiectasis and interstitial lung disease are leading causes of morbidity; lymphoid malignancy affects roughly a quarter. Milder 'variant' A-T with residual ATM activity presents in adolescence or adulthood with dystonia, tremor or neuropathy and less immune and cancer burden.
det.diagnosis: A progressive childhood ataxia with raised AFP is A-T until proved otherwise. Confirm with ATM sequencing (with deletion analysis) or absent ATM protein; radiosensitivity assays are supportive. Check immunoglobulins and vaccine responses, and screen lung function. Cerebellar atrophy is often absent in the first years, so a normal early MRI does not exclude it.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying therapy approved; dexamethasone delivered within autologous red cells has been studied in trials. Care is multidisciplinary: physio and speech therapy, nutrition and gastrostomy when swallowing fails, prophylactic antibiotics or immunoglobulin replacement for antibody deficiency, and vigilant cancer surveillance using non-ionising imaging. Oncologists must reduce radiotherapy and some chemotherapy doses. Offer genetic counselling and breast screening advice to carrier relatives.
det.prognosis: Most patients now survive into their 20s or 30s; death usually follows malignancy or chronic lung disease.
pearls: Ataxic toddler + head thrusts + high AFP: think A-T even before telangiectasia appear.
Avoid needless X-rays and CT; radiation tolerance is very low.
Normal AFP with an A-T picture suggests ATLD (MRE11) or another DNA-repair ataxia.
det.thd: Ataxia telangiectasia เกิดจากยีน ATM ซึ่งซ่อมแซม DNA ผิดปกติ เด็กเริ่มเดินเซตั้งแต่ขวบปีที่สองและแย่ลงเรื่อย ๆ กลอกตาเริ่มยากต้องหันศีรษะนำ มีเส้นเลือดฝอยขยายที่ตาขาวตามมา ติดเชื้อทางเดินหายใจบ่อยและเสี่ยงมะเร็งต่อมน้ำเหลือง ตรวจพบ AFP สูงและ IgA ต่ำ ยืนยันด้วยยีน ATM รักษาแบบประคับประคอง ป้องกันติดเชื้อ และหลีกเลี่ยงรังสีที่ไม่จำเป็น

ddx.pt: Starts later, no telangiectasia or immune defect; AOA2 has milder AFP rise, AOA1 has low albumin
MRE11 defect with similar neurology but normal AFP and no telangiectasia
Non-progressive deficit from early brain injury; AFP normal and no new signs over time

name: Ataxia-ocular motor apraxic syndrome
formal: Cerebellar ataxia with impaired voluntary horizontal gaze initiation due to saccade failure, seen in ataxia with oculomotor apraxia types 1 and 2 and ataxia-telangiectasia.
simple: Unsteadiness together with difficulty moving the eyes quickly to look at things, seen in some inherited ataxias.
ab: Cerebellar ataxia with saccade initiation failure
th: ภาวะเดินเซจากสมองน้อยร่วมกับไม่สามารถเริ่มกลอกตาไปด้านข้างตามใจได้ (oculomotor apraxia) พบใน AOA1, AOA2 และ ataxia telangiectasia
tempoNote: Childhood or adolescent onset; slowly progressive
feat: Progressive cerebellar ataxia from childhood or adolescence
Difficulty initiating horizontal saccades; head thrusts or blinks used to shift gaze
Sensorimotor axonal neuropathy; chorea or dystonia in some
Laboratory markers: low albumin and high cholesterol (AOA1), high AFP (AOA2, AT)
Autosomal recessive (APTX, SETX, ATM and others)
inv: AFP, albumin, cholesterol, immunoglobulins
MRI: cerebellar atrophy
Nerve conduction: axonal sensorimotor neuropathy
Recessive ataxia gene panel

case.story: Unsteady since age 12, now needs support on stairs. To look at someone beside her she turns her whole head first.
case.exam: Gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, absent ankle jerks, distal sensory loss, delayed initiation of horizontal saccades overcome by head thrusts.
case.tests: AFP 45 ng/mL, MRI cerebellar atrophy, axonal neuropathy, biallelic SETX variants.
case.q: Which form of ataxia with oculomotor apraxia fits?
case.a: AOA2 (SETX), with raised AFP and later-childhood onset.

det.patho: The causative genes encode DNA single-strand break repair and transcription-related proteins (aprataxin in AOA1, senataxin in AOA2, ATM in ataxia telangiectasia). Neurons, particularly Purkinje cells and long peripheral axons, are vulnerable to accumulated DNA damage, leading to cerebellar degeneration and neuropathy.
det.clinical: Ataxia starts in childhood (AOA1, AT) or adolescence (AOA2) and is followed by neuropathy. Oculomotor apraxia means voluntary saccades are delayed or hypometric, so patients thrust or turn the head; it may be absent in some AOA2 patients. Chorea, dystonia and cognitive impairment occur. AT adds telangiectasias, infections and malignancy.
det.diagnosis: Biochemical clues guide testing: hypoalbuminaemia and hypercholesterolaemia point to AOA1; raised AFP to AOA2 or AT. Imaging shows cerebellar atrophy, and nerve studies confirm axonal neuropathy. Multigene panels or exome sequencing provide the diagnosis.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy exists. Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, orthoses, speech and swallowing support and management of chorea are used. In AT, infection prophylaxis and cancer surveillance, avoiding unnecessary ionising radiation, are essential. Coenzyme Q10 is given in AOA1 cases with documented deficiency.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; many become wheelchair users in early adulthood.
pearls: Head thrusts to shift gaze in an ataxic teenager: think AOA.
AFP is the cheapest screening test for AOA2 and AT.
Low albumin and high cholesterol suggest AOA1.
det.thd: Ataxia–oculomotor apraxia syndrome คือการเดินเซจากสมองน้อยร่วมกับไม่สามารถเริ่มกลอกตาไปด้านข้างตามใจ ผู้ป่วยต้องหันศีรษะนำ พบใน AOA1, AOA2 และ ataxia telangiectasia ซึ่งเป็นโรคยีนด้อยเกี่ยวกับการซ่อม DNA ตรวจ AFP, albumin และ cholesterol ช่วยแยกชนิด ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง

name: Ataxia-telangiectasia-like disorder (ATLD)
formal: Ataxia-telangiectasia-like disorder from MRE11 mutations, causing slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, dysarthria and oculomotor apraxia without telangiectasia or immunodeficiency.
simple: A rare inherited disorder similar to ataxia-telangiectasia causing slowly worsening unsteadiness and slurred speech.
th: ataxia แบบถ่ายทอดยีนด้อยจากยีน MRE11 อาการคล้าย ataxia telangiectasia แต่เริ่มช้ากว่า ไม่มีเส้นเลือดฝอยขยายที่ตา ภูมิคุ้มกันปกติ และ AFP ปกติ
tempoNote: Childhood onset, slower progression than classic A-T
feat: Progressive cerebellar ataxia from early childhood, slower than A-T
Oculomotor apraxia and dysarthria; dystonia or chorea in some
No telangiectasia and usually no immunodeficiency or high cancer risk (though tumours reported)
Cells are radiosensitive, as in A-T
inv: Normal serum AFP and immunoglobulins
MRI cerebellar atrophy
MRE11 gene sequencing; cellular radiosensitivity assay supportive

case.who: 9-year-old girl from Ubon Ratchathani, parents first cousins
case.story: Unsteady walking noticed from age 4, worsening slowly; speech slurred; no frequent infections.
case.exam: Gait and limb ataxia, head thrusts on lateral gaze, no conjunctival telangiectasia.
case.tests: AFP and immunoglobulins normal; MRI cerebellar atrophy; biallelic MRE11 variants.
case.q: Which disorder is mimicked and what distinguishes this one?
case.a: Ataxia telangiectasia; ATLD lacks telangiectasia, raised AFP and immune deficiency, and is due to MRE11 rather than ATM.

det.patho: MRE11 forms part of the MRN complex (MRE11–RAD50–NBN) that detects DNA double-strand breaks and activates ATM. Hypomorphic biallelic variants impair this signalling, giving cellular radiosensitivity and Purkinje cell loss. It is very rare, with families reported mainly from the UK, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Japan.
det.clinical: Children develop ataxia, dysarthria and oculomotor apraxia resembling A-T but milder and slower, often walking independently into adolescence. Telangiectasia and frequent infections are absent. Microcephaly and developmental delay are seen in some families, and lung adenocarcinoma has been reported in a few, so cancer risk is not fully known.
det.diagnosis: Consider it when a child has an A-T-like ataxia with normal AFP. Genetic testing with an ataxia or DNA-repair gene panel or exome confirms MRE11 variants. Radiosensitivity assays support it but are not widely available.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy exists. Rehabilitation, speech therapy and management of dystonia are supportive. Minimise ionising radiation because cells are radiosensitive. Offer genetic counselling to the family.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; life expectancy is thought to be longer than in classic A-T, but data are limited.
pearls: A-T phenotype with normal AFP and no telangiectasia: think ATLD.
MRE11, RAD50 and NBN are partners; defects give overlapping DNA-repair syndromes.
Radiosensitivity still applies; avoid unnecessary CT.
det.thd: ATLD เกิดจากยีน MRE11 ซึ่งทำงานร่วมกับ ATM ในการซ่อม DNA เด็กมีเดินเซ พูดไม่ชัด และกลอกตาเริ่มยากคล้าย ataxia telangiectasia แต่ช้ากว่า ไม่มีเส้นเลือดฝอยขยายที่ตา ภูมิคุ้มกันและ AFP ปกติ ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน ไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ ควรหลีกเลี่ยงรังสีที่ไม่จำเป็น

ddx.pt: Raised AFP, telangiectasia, immunodeficiency and lymphoma risk; ATM gene
Similar eye signs; AOA1 has low albumin, AOA2 mildly high AFP and later onset
Areflexia, posterior column loss, cardiomyopathy and diabetes; GAA expansion in FXN

name: Atherosclerosis
formal: Chronic arterial disease with intimal lipid-laden plaques causing stenosis and thromboembolism, leading to ischaemic stroke, TIA and vascular dementia.
simple: Fatty build-up that hardens and narrows arteries, which can cause strokes and heart attacks.
th: โรคหลอดเลือดแดงเรื้อรังที่มีคราบไขมันในผนังชั้นใน ทำให้หลอดเลือดตีบและเกิดลิ่มเลือด นำไปสู่ stroke, TIA และ vascular dementia
tempoNote: Develops over decades; presents with acute ischaemic events
feat: Systemic arterial process affecting carotid bifurcation, vertebral origin, intracranial arteries and aortic arch
Causes TIA, ischaemic stroke, amaurosis fugax and vascular cognitive impairment
Intracranial atherosclerosis is especially common in Asian populations
Risk factors: hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidaemia, smoking, obesity, age
Often coexists with coronary and peripheral arterial disease
inv: Carotid duplex ultrasound; CTA or MRA of neck and intracranial arteries
Lipid profile, HbA1c, blood pressure assessment
Vessel wall MRI to distinguish plaque from vasculitis when uncertain

case.who: 66-year-old male retired engineer from Bangkok with diabetes and smoking history
case.story: Two brief episodes of right-hand clumsiness and difficulty finding words over a week.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination; left carotid bruit.
case.tests: Carotid duplex: 80% left internal carotid stenosis; MRI: small acute left frontal cortical infarct.
case.q: What is the best next step?
case.a: Symptomatic severe carotid stenosis — carotid endarterectomy (or stenting) within two weeks, plus antiplatelets, statin and risk factor control.

det.patho: Lipoproteins enter the arterial intima, are oxidised and engulfed by macrophages, forming foam cells and a lipid core beneath a fibrous cap. Inflammation thins the cap; rupture exposes thrombogenic material, causing thrombosis and artery-to-artery embolism. Slowly growing plaques cause haemodynamic stenosis, while branch-occlusive disease blocks penetrating arteries.
det.clinical: Neurological consequences range from silent stenosis to TIA and stroke. Carotid disease causes ipsilateral retinal or hemispheric events; intracranial disease causes territorial, border-zone or perforator infarcts. Chronic hypoperfusion and multiple infarcts contribute to cognitive decline.
det.diagnosis: Imaging of extracranial and intracranial arteries quantifies stenosis and plaque features. In stroke, classify mechanism (TOAST, ASCOD). Look for coronary and peripheral disease.
det.treatment: Lifestyle change and risk factor control; antiplatelet therapy and high-intensity statin (LDL target below 70 mg/dL, often lower). Short-term dual antiplatelet therapy after minor stroke or TIA. Carotid revascularisation for symptomatic 50–99% stenosis; intensive medical management for intracranial stenosis.
det.prognosis: Risk of recurrent stroke is highest in the first weeks after a symptomatic event and falls with aggressive management.
pearls: Symptomatic carotid stenosis: revascularise early, ideally within two weeks.
Intracranial atherosclerosis is common in Thai stroke patients.
Atherosclerosis is systemic — treat the patient, not just the plaque.
det.thd: Atherosclerosis คือการสะสมของไขมันในผนังหลอดเลือดแดงทำให้ตีบและเกิดลิ่มเลือด เป็นสาเหตุสำคัญของ TIA, stroke และ vascular dementia ในคนไทยพบหลอดเลือดในกะโหลกตีบบ่อย การตรวจคือ carotid duplex, CTA หรือ MRA การรักษาคือยาต้านเกล็ดเลือด statin ควบคุมความดัน เบาหวาน และหยุดบุหรี่ ผู้ที่มี carotid ตีบมากและมีอาการควรผ่าตัดหรือใส่ stent

name: Atherothrombotic stroke
formal: Ischaemic stroke due to rupture or stenosis of an atherosclerotic plaque in large extracranial or intracranial arteries with thrombosis or artery-to-artery embolism.
simple: A stroke caused by a blood clot forming on a fatty plaque in one of the major arteries to the brain.
th: stroke ขาดเลือดจากคราบไขมันในหลอดเลือดแดงใหญ่ภายนอกหรือภายในกะโหลกแตกหรือตีบ ทำให้เกิดลิ่มเลือดหรือลิ่มเลือดหลุดไปอุดหลอดเลือดปลายทาง
tempoNote: Sudden or stuttering onset; often preceded by TIAs
feat: Preceding TIAs in the same territory are common
Stuttering or fluctuating course, especially with intracranial stenosis
Cortical or border-zone infarcts in carotid disease; perforator infarcts in intracranial plaque
Carotid bruit, amaurosis fugax and other atherosclerotic disease
TOAST requires ≥50% stenosis of a relevant artery and exclusion of other causes
inv: CTA or MRA of head and neck; carotid duplex
MRI DWI pattern: border-zone or multiple small infarcts in one territory
Cardiac evaluation to exclude a competing embolic source

case.who: 62-year-old female noodle vendor from Phetchabun with diabetes
case.story: Weakness of the left arm that fluctuated over 24 hours, worse when sitting up.
case.exam: Left hemiparesis arm more than leg, mild dysarthria; NIHSS 6.
case.tests: MRI: string of small infarcts in right internal border zone; MRA: 85% right MCA M1 stenosis.
case.q: What mechanism explains the fluctuation, and what medical regimen is preferred?
case.a: Haemodynamic and embolic effects of symptomatic intracranial stenosis; short-term dual antiplatelets, high-intensity statin and blood pressure management without over-lowering in the acute phase.

det.patho: Unstable plaques rupture and trigger thrombosis, which can occlude the artery locally or shed emboli downstream. Severe stenosis also reduces perfusion distal to the lesion, especially in border zones. Branch atheromatous disease occludes perforator origins.
det.clinical: Presentations include sudden deficits after preceding TIAs, stepwise worsening, and positional or blood-pressure-dependent symptoms. Intracranial disease is common in Asians and causes a high early recurrence rate.
det.diagnosis: Requires imaging demonstration of significant stenosis or occlusion in the relevant artery, with a compatible infarct pattern and absence of cardiac embolic source. Vessel wall MRI and transcranial Doppler can add information.
det.treatment: Acute: thrombolysis and thrombectomy as for any stroke. Secondary prevention: short-term dual antiplatelet therapy, statin, blood pressure and diabetes control, smoking cessation. Carotid endarterectomy or stenting for symptomatic extracranial stenosis; intracranial stenting is reserved for refractory selected cases.
det.prognosis: Recurrence risk is highest early; aggressive medical therapy has lowered it substantially.
pearls: Repeated TIAs in one territory point to large artery disease.
Avoid aggressive blood pressure lowering acutely with critical stenosis.
Intracranial stenosis: medical therapy first.
det.thd: Atherothrombotic stroke คือ stroke ขาดเลือดจากคราบไขมันในหลอดเลือดแดงใหญ่แตกหรือตีบ ทำให้เกิดลิ่มเลือดอุดตันหรือหลุดไปอุดปลายทาง มักมี TIA นำมาก่อนและอาการขึ้นลง การตรวจคือ CTA หรือ MRA ของหลอดเลือดคอและสมอง การรักษาระยะเฉียบพลันเหมือน stroke ทั่วไป การป้องกันซ้ำใช้ยาต้านเกล็ดเลือดสองตัวช่วงสั้น statin และผ่าตัดหลอดเลือด carotid เมื่อมีข้อบ่งชี้

qx.stem: A 61-year-old shopkeeper presents 48 hours after a sudden weak, clumsy right hand that has partly improved (NIHSS 3). He was not given thrombolysis. MRI shows two small left frontal infarcts, and CTA shows 70% stenosis of the left middle cerebral artery. He has no history of bleeding.
qx.q: Which antithrombotic plan is best supported by trial data?
opts: Aspirin alone indefinitely
Warfarin aiming for an INR between 2 and 3
Aspirin plus clopidogrel for 12 months
Full-dose rivaroxaban for 3 months
Aspirin plus clopidogrel for about 21 days, then a single antiplatelet, with intensive risk-factor control
qx.why: Short-course dual antiplatelet therapy reduces early recurrence after minor stroke or high-risk TIA (CHANCE, POINT), and INSPIRES extended the benefit to patients of presumed atherosclerotic cause treated within 72 hours. Long-term DAPT increases bleeding without added benefit, and warfarin was no better than aspirin for intracranial stenosis (WASID). Intensive statin, BP and lifestyle measures, as in SAMMPRIS, are central to management.

qx.stem: A 64-year-old man is discharged after a left MCA infarct attributed to a 50% left carotid plaque. He takes atorvastatin 40 mg and his LDL cholesterol at 6 weeks is 2.6 mmol/L (100 mg/dL). He tolerates the statin without muscle symptoms. He asks what LDL level he should aim for.
qx.q: Which lipid strategy is best supported by trial evidence?
opts: Keep the current dose, because any statin is sufficient
Stop the statin once the plaque is stable on imaging
Add fish oil capsules instead of changing therapy
Target LDL below 1.8 mmol/L (70 mg/dL), intensifying the statin and adding ezetimibe or a PCSK9 inhibitor if needed
Switch to fibrate monotherapy
qx.why: After atherosclerotic ischaemic stroke, a target LDL below 1.8 mmol/L reduced major cardiovascular events compared with a looser target (Treat Stroke to Target), building on SPARCL. High-intensity statins are first line, with ezetimibe and then PCSK9 inhibitors added when the target is not reached. Fish oil and fibrates do not replace LDL lowering, and stopping the statin increases risk.

name: Athetosis
formal: Slow, writhing involuntary movements of distal limbs, often combined with chorea, resulting from basal ganglia damage as in dyskinetic cerebral palsy.
simple: Slow, twisting, writhing movements of the fingers, hands and feet that the person cannot control.
th: การเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติแบบบิดช้า ๆ คล้ายงูเลื้อย มักที่มือและนิ้ว พบร่วมกับ chorea จากความเสียหายของ basal ganglia เช่น สมองพิการชนิด dyskinetic
tempoNote: Usually present from infancy (perinatal injury); acquired forms follow stroke or drugs
feat: A movement sign: slow, continuous, sinuous writhing of fingers, hands, face or feet
Often merges with chorea (choreoathetosis) or dystonia
Main cause: dyskinetic cerebral palsy from kernicterus or hypoxic-ischaemic injury
Pseudoathetosis from proprioceptive loss appears with eyes closed and must be distinguished
inv: MRI brain (globus pallidus, putamen, thalamus)
Neonatal history; metabolic and genetic tests if no clear perinatal cause
Sensory examination to exclude pseudoathetosis

case.story: Born at home with severe neonatal jaundice; walked late and has constant twisting of hands and face, worse when he tries to write.
case.exam: Slow writhing of fingers and wrists, facial grimacing, dysarthria, upward gaze limitation, sensorineural hearing loss.
case.tests: MRI shows bilateral globus pallidus T2 hyperintensity.
case.q: What caused his athetosis?
case.a: Kernicterus (bilirubin encephalopathy) damaging the globus pallidus, with associated hearing loss and gaze palsy.

det.patho: Athetosis reflects dysfunction of the basal ganglia indirect and direct pathways, especially pallidal and putaminal damage, leading to unstable motor output. Bilirubin preferentially injures the globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus and auditory nuclei; hypoxia injures putamen and thalamus.
det.clinical: This is a sign, not a disease. Movements are slow, continuous and distal, often worsened by voluntary action and emotion and absent during sleep. Combination with chorea or dystonia is common. Pseudoathetosis due to severe proprioceptive loss resembles it but appears when vision is removed.
det.diagnosis: Clinical recognition plus search for the cause: perinatal history, MRI and, if needed, metabolic and genetic testing (e.g. GLUT1, ADCY5, glutaric aciduria).
det.treatment: Treatment is often disappointing. Options include anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl), tetrabenazine, baclofen and botulinum toxin for focal problems; pallidal DBS helps some dyskinetic cerebral palsy patients. Physiotherapy and communication aids are central.
det.prognosis: Persistent in cerebral palsy; acquired forms may improve.
pearls: Athetosis plus hearing loss plus upgaze palsy suggests kernicterus.
Close the eyes: pseudoathetosis worsens, true athetosis does not depend on vision.
Choreoathetosis is often a better description than either term alone.
det.thd: Athetosis คือการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติแบบบิดช้า ๆ ต่อเนื่องที่นิ้ว มือ หรือใบหน้า เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ basal ganglia สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยคือสมองพิการจากตัวเหลืองรุนแรงในทารก (kernicterus) หรือขาดออกซิเจน ต้องแยกจาก pseudoathetosis ที่เกิดจากสูญเสียการรับรู้ตำแหน่ง การรักษาใช้ยา trihexyphenidyl, baclofen หรือ botulinum toxin และกายภาพบำบัด

ddx.pt: Faster, flowing, random jerks rather than slow writhing
Sustained twisting postures rather than continuous movement
The commonest underlying disease of childhood athetosis

name: Athetotic cerebral palsy
formal: Dyskinetic cerebral palsy with writhing involuntary movements and fluctuating tone, commonly following perinatal basal ganglia injury such as kernicterus or hypoxia.
simple: A type of cerebral palsy caused by early brain injury, with slow twisting uncontrolled movements and changing muscle tone.
th: สมองพิการชนิด dyskinetic มีการเคลื่อนไหวบิดช้าและความตึงตัวขึ้นลง จากการบาดเจ็บของ basal ganglia และ thalamus ช่วงปริกำเนิด เช่น ขาดออกซิเจนรุนแรงเฉียบพลันหรือ kernicterus
tempoNote: Non-progressive injury; involuntary movements usually emerge after the early hypotonic months, in the first one to three years
feat: Early hypotonia and gross motor delay, then writhing choreoathetosis, dystonia and fluctuating tone
Movements worsen with effort and emotion and disappear in sleep
Speech, swallowing and drooling are heavily affected; understanding is often better than output suggests
Typical causes in a term infant: brief profound hypoxia-ischaemia or severe neonatal jaundice (kernicterus)
High energy needs from constant movement can cause undernutrition
inv: MRI: deep grey matter injury (posterior putamen, ventrolateral thalamus) or pallidal signal change in kernicterus
Hearing assessment, since auditory neuropathy accompanies bilirubin injury
Metabolic and genetic work-up if MRI is normal, course is progressive or tone fluctuates through the day
Swallow study and nutritional review

case.story: Born at term after cord prolapse with poor Apgar scores; she was floppy as a baby and now twists her trunk and arms whenever she reaches. She is thin despite eating well.
case.exam: Fluctuating tone, dystonic arm posturing, oromotor dyskinesia with drooling and clear comprehension.
case.tests: MRI shows bilateral posterior putamen and ventrolateral thalamus lesions.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and which treatable mimic should be excluded with a drug trial?
case.a: Dyskinetic (athetotic) cerebral palsy after acute hypoxic-ischaemic injury; a levodopa trial excludes dopa-responsive dystonia.

det.patho: A term infant's metabolically busy deep grey matter, especially putamen and thalamus, is selectively damaged by short severe hypoxia-ischaemia, while high unconjugated bilirubin injures the globus pallidus and brainstem nuclei. The resulting loss of basal ganglia-thalamocortical regulation causes unwanted movement and unstable tone. The lesion is fixed, so the picture changes only with growth.
det.clinical: Dyskinetic forms make up roughly 10 to 20 percent of cerebral palsy. Parents notice delay and floppiness, and the writhing movements follow. Severe cases add spastic quadriparesis, seizures and intellectual disability, whereas milder ones keep normal intelligence but struggle to speak, write and feed. Careful nutrition planning matters because movement burns many calories, and some children need tube feeding.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, using birth history and a dyskinesia rating tool, with MRI showing the deep grey matter lesion. A normal scan, a family history, regression or marked diurnal change should prompt targeted tests for DRD, GLUT1 deficiency, ADCY5 disease and other genetic dyskinesias. Hearing and vision must be tested.
det.treatment: Start early physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy with augmentative communication and well-fitted seating. A trial of levodopa can reduce abnormal movement and improve gait and also excludes DRD. Trihexyphenidyl, baclofen (oral or intrathecal), gabapentin and clonidine help selected children, and botulinum toxin treats focal dystonia. Pallidal deep brain stimulation gives modest benefit in carefully chosen cases.
det.prognosis: The lesion does not progress; many reach adulthood, with independence set by motor severity, communication and access to therapy.
pearls: Give a levodopa trial before accepting the label.
Check hearing and nutrition in every child.
Regression or marked day-to-day variation means the diagnosis needs rethinking.
det.thd: Athetotic cerebral palsy หรือสมองพิการชนิด dyskinetic เกิดจาก basal ganglia และ thalamus บาดเจ็บช่วงคลอด เช่น ขาดออกซิเจนรุนแรงเฉียบพลันหรือตัวเหลืองรุนแรง kernicterus ทารกอ่อนปวกเปียกก่อน แล้วมีการเคลื่อนไหวบิดไม่ตั้งใจและ dystonia พูดกลืนลำบาก แต่ความเข้าใจอาจดี วินิจฉัยจากประวัติและ MRI ควรลอง levodopa เพื่อแยก DRD ตรวจการได้ยิน ดูแลโภชนาการ รักษาแบบสหวิชาชีพ ยาที่ใช้ ได้แก่ trihexyphenidyl, baclofen และ botulinum toxin

Macrocephaly and striatal injury after a febrile illness; urine organic acids diagnostic
Umbrella term; the spastic type is far more common than the dyskinetic type

name: Athetotic hemiplegia, hereditary
formal: Congenital or hereditary hemiplegia with unilateral slow writhing movements from contralateral basal ganglia or thalamic damage.
simple: Weakness of one side of the body combined with slow writhing movements, caused by damage to deep brain structures.
th: อัมพาตครึ่งซีกที่มีการเคลื่อนไหวบิดช้าในข้างเดียวกัน จากรอยโรค basal ganglia หรือ thalamus ฝั่งตรงข้าม ซึ่งอาจเป็นมาแต่กำเนิดหรือในบางรายพบในครอบครัว
tempoNote: Present from early childhood or emerging months after an early-life hemispheric injury
feat: Hemiparesis with slow writhing movements of the same limbs
Contralateral basal ganglia or thalamic lesion; delayed onset after the injury is typical
Hereditary forms are poorly characterised historical descriptions
Consider alternating hemiplegia and genetic dystonias when family members are affected
inv: MRI brain to identify contralateral lesion
Genetic testing (e.g. ATP1A3, ADCY5) if familial or episodic

case.story: Mild left-sided weakness since infancy after a neonatal stroke; in recent years her left hand makes slow twisting movements.
case.exam: Left hemiparesis with hemiathetosis and dystonic posture of the hand.
case.tests: MRI: old right putaminal and thalamic infarct.
case.q: Why can movement disorders appear years after the original lesion?
case.a: Delayed post-lesional movement disorders arise as the developing brain reorganises; this is acquired hemiathetosis rather than a hereditary disease.

read.where: 1 - Clinical overview and phenomenology of movement disorders
Section 3 Hereditary and Genetic Conditions and Malformations

det.patho: Unilateral lesions of the striatum, pallidum or thalamus disturb the motor output to the opposite limbs. Delayed movement disorders reflect maladaptive plasticity and sprouting. Clearly hereditary unilateral athetosis is rare, and the label comes from older literature; modern genetic diagnoses usually replace it.
det.clinical: Weakness and abnormal movements coexist on one side. Onset of athetosis is often delayed months to years after an early injury. Familial or paroxysmal cases warrant consideration of channelopathies and genetic dyskinesias.
det.diagnosis: MRI usually identifies a structural contralateral lesion. Where none is found, or several relatives are affected, genetic testing is appropriate. Historical terms should be translated into current etiological diagnoses.
det.treatment: Physiotherapy and occupational therapy, botulinum toxin, trihexyphenidyl or tetrabenazine, and in selected cases DBS.
det.prognosis: Usually stable once established.
pearls: Hemiathetosis often appears long after the causative lesion.
Look for a contralateral putaminal or thalamic lesion.
Familial cases should prompt modern genetic testing.
det.thd: Athetotic hemiplegia คือแขนขาซีกหนึ่งอ่อนแรงร่วมกับการเคลื่อนไหวบิดช้า ๆ ในข้างเดียวกัน เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ basal ganglia หรือ thalamus ฝั่งตรงข้าม มักเกิดหลังสมองบาดเจ็บตั้งแต่เด็กและอาการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติปรากฏทีหลังหลายเดือนหรือหลายปี ชนิดที่ถ่ายทอดในครอบครัวพบน้อยมากและควรตรวจยีนสมัยใหม่ การรักษาใช้กายภาพ botulinum toxin และยาตามอาการ

name: Atonic seizure
formal: Brief generalised seizure with sudden loss of muscle tone causing head drops or falls, typical in Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, with EEG showing generalised slow spike-wave or electrodecrement.
simple: A seizure in which the muscles suddenly go limp, so the person drops their head or falls to the ground.
th: อาการชักแบบทั่วไปที่กล้ามเนื้อหมดแรงทันที ทำให้คอตกหรือล้มลง พบบ่อยใน Lennox–Gastaut syndrome
tempoNote: Sudden events lasting about a second or less, often many times a day
feat: Sudden loss of postural tone: head nod, jaw drop, knee buckling or a full fall
Very brief (usually under 2 seconds) with rapid recovery
Injuries to face and head are common
Often coexists with tonic, atypical absence and myoclonic seizures in DEEs
May be preceded by a myoclonic jerk (myoclonic-atonic seizure in Doose syndrome)
inv: Video-EEG with surface EMG: generalised spike/polyspike-wave or electrodecrement with EMG silence
MRI to identify a structural cause in DEE
Genetic testing in developmental and epileptic encephalopathies

case.story: Several times a day he suddenly drops to the floor, gets up immediately and has scars on his chin; he also has staring spells and stiffening in sleep.
case.exam: Moderate intellectual disability, healed facial lacerations, wearing a helmet.
case.tests: EEG: slow spike-wave at about 2 Hz interictally, generalised paroxysmal fast activity in sleep; a captured drop shows polyspike-wave with EMG silence.
case.q: Which epilepsy syndrome is most likely?
case.a: Lennox–Gastaut syndrome with atonic seizures; consider valproate, clobazam, rufinamide, cannabidiol and corpus callosotomy for injurious drops.

read.where: Chapter 10 Epilepsy and Related Disorders — Generalised Seizures
10 Electro-Clinical Syndromes by Age of Onset—Childhood, Adolescence, and Adult

det.patho: A generalised discharge transiently inhibits the motor systems that maintain posture, producing a brief silent period in muscle activity. It reflects widespread cortical-subcortical network involvement typical of epileptic encephalopathies. Distinguishing atonic from tonic or myoclonic drops often requires polygraphy.
det.clinical: Atonic seizures are a seizure type, not an epilepsy syndrome. They occur in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, Doose syndrome, other DEEs and occasionally in structural epilepsy. Events can be as minor as a head nod or as dramatic as a sudden fall causing injury. Many 'drop attacks' in epilepsy are actually tonic, which matters for treatment choice.
det.diagnosis: Video-EEG with EMG is the gold standard: the EEG shows generalised spike-wave, polyspike-wave or electrodecrement, and EMG shows silence. History from witnesses and home video help. Evaluate for an underlying syndrome and cause with MRI and genetic testing.
det.treatment: Broad-spectrum antiseizure medicines are preferred: valproate, clobazam, lamotrigine, rufinamide, topiramate, cannabidiol and fenfluramine in LGS. Ketogenic diet and vagus nerve stimulation help some. Corpus callosotomy reduces injurious drop attacks when drugs fail. Protective helmets reduce injury. Avoid carbamazepine, which may worsen generalised seizures.
det.prognosis: Often drug-resistant when part of an epileptic encephalopathy; Doose syndrome may remit.
pearls: EMG silence on polygraphy separates atonic from tonic or myoclonic drops.
Callosotomy is most effective specifically for drop attacks.
Emotion-triggered drops with clear consciousness suggest cataplexy, not epilepsy.
det.thd: Atonic seizure คืออาการชักแบบทั่วไปที่กล้ามเนื้อหมดแรงทันทีชั่ววินาที ทำให้คอตก ขาทรุด หรือล้มลงจนบาดเจ็บ มักพบใน Lennox–Gastaut syndrome และ Doose syndrome ยืนยันด้วย video-EEG ร่วมกับ EMG ที่เห็นกล้ามเนื้อเงียบ รักษาด้วยยากันชักกลุ่มกว้าง เช่น valproate, clobazam, rufinamide อาหาร ketogenic หรือผ่าตัด corpus callosotomy และสวมหมวกกันน็อกป้องกันบาดเจ็บ
