name: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)
formal: Neurodevelopmental disorder with persistent inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity, linked to dopaminergic and noradrenergic dysfunction in frontostriatal circuits.
simple: A condition beginning in childhood that makes it hard to focus, sit still and control impulses.
th: โรคสมาธิสั้น เป็นโรคพัฒนาการทางระบบประสาทที่มีอาการขาดสมาธิ ซน และหุนหันพลันแล่นต่อเนื่องตั้งแต่วัยเด็ก
tempoNote: Symptoms begin before age 12 and often persist into adulthood in modified form
feat: Persistent inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity in at least two settings (home, school, work)
Presentations: predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive or combined
Frequent comorbidity: tic disorders, learning disorders, autism, anxiety, sleep problems, epilepsy
Highly heritable; associated with prematurity and prenatal alcohol or tobacco exposure
Stimulant medication plus behavioural support is effective
inv: Clinical diagnosis using DSM-5-TR criteria with teacher and parent rating scales
Hearing, vision and sleep assessment; consider absence epilepsy if staring spells
Cardiovascular history and BP before stimulants
Developmental and learning assessment

case.who: 8-year-old boy from Udon Thani brought by his mother
case.story: Teachers report he cannot stay seated, interrupts, loses his books and does not finish work; the same happens at home with homework.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination; fidgety and distractible in clinic; occasional eye blinking tic.
case.tests: Parent and teacher rating scales strongly positive; hearing and vision normal; no staring spells.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the first-line medication?
case.a: ADHD, combined presentation, with a mild tic; methylphenidate together with parent training and school support.

det.patho: ADHD has strong genetic loading, with heritability around 70–80% and many common variants of small effect. Imaging studies show delayed cortical maturation and altered fronto-striatal and fronto-cerebellar networks. Catecholamine signalling, especially dopamine and noradrenaline, is implicated, which explains the benefit of stimulants and atomoxetine. Environmental contributors include preterm birth and prenatal toxin exposure.
det.clinical: Symptoms must start in childhood, persist for at least six months and cause impairment in more than one setting. Hyperactivity often lessens with age, while inattention and restlessness persist in many adults. Comorbid tics, epilepsy, autism, learning disability and sleep disorders are common in neurology clinics. Absence seizures, hearing loss and obstructive sleep apnoea can mimic inattention.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, using DSM-5-TR or ICD-11 criteria and standardised rating scales from at least two informants. There is no diagnostic blood test, EEG or scan. Neurological examination looks for soft signs, dysmorphism or features of a genetic syndrome. EEG is ordered only if there are staring spells or other seizure features.
det.treatment: Management combines parent training, classroom adjustments and medication for school-age children. Methylphenidate is the first-line drug in Thailand; atomoxetine, guanfacine and lisdexamfetamine are alternatives. Monitor growth, appetite, sleep, heart rate and blood pressure. Stimulants do not worsen tics in most children, and they are generally safe in well-controlled epilepsy.
det.prognosis: Many children continue to have symptoms in adulthood; treatment reduces academic failure, injuries and substance use.
pearls: Check for absence epilepsy and sleep apnoea before labelling inattention as ADHD.
Mild tics are not a contraindication to stimulants.
Symptoms must be present in more than one setting.
det.thd: ADHD หรือโรคสมาธิสั้นเป็นโรคพัฒนาการทางระบบประสาทที่มีอาการขาดสมาธิ ซนอยู่ไม่นิ่ง และหุนหันพลันแล่น เริ่มก่อนอายุ 12 ปีและเห็นในหลายสถานที่ มีพันธุกรรมเกี่ยวข้องมาก และมักพบร่วมกับโรค tic ความบกพร่องในการเรียนรู้ หรือ autism การวินิจฉัยใช้เกณฑ์ทางคลินิกและแบบประเมินจากผู้ปกครองและครู การรักษาคือยา methylphenidate ร่วมกับการปรับพฤติกรรมและการช่วยเหลือในโรงเรียน

name: Atypical absence seizure
formal: Generalised seizure with slower onset and offset of impaired awareness, often with tone changes, and slow 1.5 to 2.5 Hz spike-wave EEG, typical in Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and developmental epileptic encephalopathy.
simple: A type of seizure with staring and reduced awareness that starts and stops more slowly, usually in children with other developmental problems.
th: อาการชักแบบเหม่อลอยที่เริ่มและหยุดค่อย ๆ นานกว่าแบบ typical มักมีการเปลี่ยนแปลงความตึงกล้ามเนื้อ EEG เป็น slow spike-wave 1.5–2.5 Hz พบใน Lennox–Gastaut
tempoNote: Episodes last several seconds to minutes and can cluster into atypical absence status
feat: Impaired awareness with gradual onset and offset, often incomplete loss of responsiveness
Head nodding, loss of tone, eyelid myoclonus or automatisms commonly accompany
Not reliably provoked by hyperventilation
Occurs in children with developmental delay, DEEs and Lennox–Gastaut syndrome
May evolve into prolonged non-convulsive status with stupor
inv: EEG: generalised slow spike-wave at 1.5–2.5 Hz, often asymmetric, on an abnormal slow background
Video-EEG to separate from behavioural staring and typical absence
MRI and genetic testing to find the cause of the underlying encephalopathy

case.story: Known to have learning delay; teachers notice she drifts off for 10–20 seconds, slowly slumping forward, then gradually resumes activity.
case.exam: Mild intellectual disability; during an event she looks dazed with slight head drop and lip movements.
case.tests: EEG shows 2 Hz generalised slow spike-wave during the event on a slowed background.
case.q: How does this differ from a typical absence seizure?
case.a: Atypical absences start and stop gradually, have more tone change, and show slower (<2.5 Hz) spike-wave on an abnormal background; ethosuximide alone is often insufficient.

read.where: Chapter 10 Epilepsy and Related Disorders — Generalised Seizures

det.patho: Atypical absences arise from abnormal thalamocortical oscillations superimposed on diffuse cortical dysfunction, giving slower and more irregular spike-wave discharges than typical absence. They are a marker of a broader epileptic encephalopathy rather than an isolated genetic generalised epilepsy.
det.clinical: This is a seizure type. Awareness may be only partially reduced, and onset and end are subtle, so events are often missed or attributed to the child's baseline. Changes in tone and mild myoclonic or automatic movements are common. Seen in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, CSWS spectrum, Dravet and other DEEs.
det.diagnosis: EEG confirms the slow (under 2.5 Hz) generalised spike-wave and abnormal background; video-EEG correlates behaviour with discharges. Identify the underlying syndrome and aetiology with MRI and genetic testing. Exclude NCSE when a child becomes persistently less responsive.
det.treatment: Valproate, lamotrigine, ethosuximide (often in combination), clobazam and rufinamide are used; carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin and vigabatrin can worsen them. Ketogenic diet is an option for resistant cases. Treat atypical absence status with benzodiazepines.
det.prognosis: Usually persistent and drug-resistant, tracking the underlying encephalopathy.
pearls: Gradual onset, slow spike-wave and abnormal background = atypical; abrupt and 3 Hz with normal background = typical.
Sodium-channel blockers may aggravate these seizures.
A child with DEE who becomes slowly more 'switched off' may be in atypical absence status.
det.thd: Atypical absence seizure เป็นการชักแบบเหม่อลอยที่เริ่มและหยุดแบบค่อยเป็นค่อยไป นานกว่า typical absence และมักมีคอตกหรือกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนตัวร่วม EEG แสดง slow spike-wave ช้ากว่า 2.5 Hz บนพื้นหลังผิดปกติ พบในเด็กที่มีพัฒนาการช้า เช่น Lennox–Gastaut syndrome รักษาด้วย valproate, lamotrigine, clobazam และควรหลีกเลี่ยงยา carbamazepine ที่อาจทำให้แย่ลง

name: Atypical Parkinsonian disorders
formal: Neurodegenerative parkinsonian syndromes such as MSA, PSP, corticobasal syndrome and dementia with Lewy bodies, with poor levodopa response, early falls, autonomic failure or cognitive features.
simple: Parkinson-like diseases that progress faster and respond poorly to usual Parkinson drugs.
more: Diagnosed by clinical red flags and MRI patterns such as hot cross bun or hummingbird signs. Treatment is symptomatic with limited drug benefit, and prognosis is worse than Parkinson disease. Parkinsonian syndromes such as multiple system atrophy, progressive supranuclear palsy and corticobasal degeneration with early falls, poor levodopa response and additional neurological signs. Atypical parkinsonian disorders such as MSA, PSP and corticobasal degeneration, with poor levodopa response, early falls, autonomic failure or gaze palsy.
th: กลุ่มโรคพาร์กินสันเสื่อมที่ไม่ใช่ Parkinson ทั่วไป ได้แก่ MSA, PSP, CBS และ DLB ตอบสนองต่อ levodopa ไม่ดี ล้มเร็ว ระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติล้มเหลว หรือมีปัญหาความคิด
tempoNote: Faster progression than PD; many need a wheelchair within 5 years
feat: Poor or short-lived levodopa response
Early falls (PSP), early autonomic failure and cerebellar signs (MSA), apraxia and alien limb (CBS), fluctuations and hallucinations (DLB)
Symmetric onset and absence of classic rest tremor are common
Early dysarthria, dysphagia and stridor (MSA)
MRI markers: hummingbird/morning glory (PSP), hot cross bun and putaminal rim (MSA)
inv: MRI brain with attention to midbrain, pons, putamen and cortex
Autonomic testing (tilt, bladder scan)
DaT-SPECT is abnormal in all, so does not separate them from PD; cardiac MIBG and alpha-synuclein assays may help

case.story: Two years of slowness, fainting on standing, urinary incontinence and loud snoring with nocturnal stridor; levodopa helped a little.
case.exam: Symmetric parkinsonism, mild gait ataxia, orthostatic BP drop 40/20 mmHg, cold blue hands.
case.tests: MRI: hot cross bun sign in pons and posterior putaminal hypointensity.
case.q: Which atypical parkinsonism is this?
case.a: Multiple system atrophy, parkinsonian type.

read.where: Chapter 9 Movement Disorders — Atypical Forms of Parkinsonism

Chapter 8: Rating Scales in Movement Disorders

det.patho: MSA and DLB are synucleinopathies (glial versus neuronal inclusions); PSP and CBD belong to the 4-repeat tau group. Neurodegeneration extends beyond the nigrostriatal system to the striatum, brainstem, cerebellum and cortex, explaining poor response to dopamine replacement.
det.clinical: Red flags that suggest an atypical disorder include rapid progression, early falls, early severe dysarthria or dysphagia, early autonomic failure, cerebellar signs, gaze palsy, apraxia and early dementia or hallucinations. Prodromal REM sleep behaviour disorder is common in synucleinopathies but uncommon in tauopathies.
det.diagnosis: Use MDS clinical criteria for PSP and MSA, the 2017 criteria for DLB, and the Armstrong criteria for CBD. MRI planimetry, autonomic testing, cardiac MIBG (normal in MSA, reduced in PD and DLB) and skin or CSF alpha-synuclein assays support classification; final confirmation is pathological.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy. A full levodopa trial (up to about 1,000 mg/day) should be given. Treat orthostatic hypotension (fludrocortisone, midodrine, droxidopa), bladder dysfunction, sleep disorders and hallucinations (low-dose quetiapine or pimavanserin; avoid typical antipsychotics in DLB). Early speech, swallow and physiotherapy and palliative planning are important.
det.prognosis: Median survival is roughly 6–10 years from onset for MSA and PSP; DLB and CBS have variable but shorter courses than PD.
pearls: Wheelchair within 5 years or falls in the first year should make you doubt PD.
DaT-SPECT cannot separate PD from atypical parkinsonism.
Nocturnal stridor in parkinsonism suggests MSA and needs airway assessment.
det.thd: Atypical parkinsonian disorders คือกลุ่มโรคพาร์กินสันเสื่อมชนิดพิเศษ ได้แก่ MSA, PSP, CBS และ DLB โรคลุกลามเร็วกว่าพาร์กินสันทั่วไป ตอบสนองต่อ levodopa ไม่ดี มีอาการเตือน เช่น ล้มเร็ว ความดันตกเวลาลุก กลอกตาลำบาก หรือประสาทหลอน MRI ช่วยแยกชนิด เช่น hot cross bun ใน MSA และ hummingbird ใน PSP การรักษาเป็นการรักษาตามอาการและการดูแลแบบประคับประคอง

name: Atypical parkinsonism on Guadeloupe
formal: Cluster of parkinsonism with dementia and PSP-like features in Guadeloupe, associated with consumption of annonaceous fruits and herbal teas containing acetogenins, a probable environmental tauopathy.
simple: A form of parkinsonism seen in Guadeloupe with memory loss, linked to eating certain tropical fruits and teas.
th: กลุ่มผู้ป่วยพาร์กินสันชนิดผิดปกติร่วมกับสมองเสื่อมและอาการคล้าย PSP บนเกาะ Guadeloupe สัมพันธ์กับการกินผลไม้และชาสมุนไพรตระกูล Annonaceae ที่มี acetogenin
tempoNote: Insidious onset around age 60–70, progressing over years
feat: Geographic cluster of levodopa-unresponsive parkinsonism in the French Caribbean
PSP-like features: vertical gaze palsy, early falls; frontal dementia, myoclonus, hallucinations in some
Epidemiological link to soursop and related fruits and teas containing annonacin, a mitochondrial complex I inhibitor
Pathology shows a tauopathy; causality from the plant toxin is probable but not proven
inv: MRI brain; dietary history of Annonaceae consumption
Exclude classical PSP, PD and other causes

case.who: 68-year-old man originally from Guadeloupe, now visiting relatives in Bangkok
case.story: Three years of falls, slowness and memory loss; he drank soursop leaf tea daily for decades.
case.exam: Symmetric akinetic-rigid syndrome, slowed vertical saccades, frontal release signs; no levodopa response.
case.tests: MRI shows midbrain atrophy.
case.q: Which environmental exposure is suspected?
case.a: Annonacin from Annonaceae plants (soursop, sweetsop), linked to Guadeloupean atypical parkinsonism.

det.patho: Acetogenins such as annonacin, abundant in soursop (Annona muricata) and related species, inhibit mitochondrial complex I and induce tau redistribution and neuronal death in experimental systems. Autopsy cases show tau pathology resembling PSP or a distinct tauopathy. Genetic susceptibility may contribute.
det.clinical: Guadeloupe has an unusually high frequency of atypical parkinsonism, two-thirds of which resembles PSP or a PSP-dementia complex. Patients show symmetric parkinsonism, early postural instability, gaze palsy and frontal cognitive decline.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on clinical features, geographic origin and dietary exposure, after excluding other causes. There is no specific biomarker.
det.treatment: Symptomatic management as for PSP; avoid further consumption of Annonaceae products, though reversal is not expected. Levodopa trial is reasonable.
det.prognosis: Progressive like PSP; data are limited.
pearls: A model of environmental tauopathy linked to a dietary mitochondrial toxin.
Soursop products are also sold as herbal remedies elsewhere, including Asia.
Ask about long-term herbal tea use in atypical parkinsonism.
det.thd: Atypical parkinsonism บนเกาะ Guadeloupe เป็นกลุ่มผู้ป่วยพาร์กินสันชนิดผิดปกติคล้าย PSP ที่พบมากผิดปกติ สัมพันธ์กับการกินทุเรียนเทศและชาสมุนไพรจากพืชตระกูล Annonaceae ซึ่งมีสาร annonacin ที่ยับยั้ง mitochondrial complex I พยาธิสภาพเป็น tauopathy ผู้ป่วยไม่ตอบสนองต่อ levodopa การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคองและควรหยุดบริโภคพืชกลุ่มนี้

name: Auditory agnosia
formal: Failure to recognise environmental sounds or speech despite intact hearing, from bilateral temporal lesions, including pure word deafness and cortical deafness.
simple: Inability to make sense of sounds or speech even though hearing is normal, from damage to hearing areas in the brain.
th: ภาวะที่หูได้ยินปกติแต่แปลความหมายเสียงพูดหรือเสียงในสิ่งแวดล้อมไม่ได้ จากรอยโรค temporal lobe ทั้งสองข้าง
tempoNote: Often after sequential bilateral temporal strokes; gradual in degenerative or developmental forms
feat: Pure tone thresholds near normal yet speech or meaningful sounds are not understood
Pure word deafness: cannot understand or repeat speech but reads, writes and speaks fluently
Non-verbal form: cannot identify a doorbell, dog bark or phone ring; amusia for music
Patients often say speech sounds like a foreign language or noise
Classically after a second temporal stroke on the other side, or a deep left lesion cutting both inputs
inv: Pure tone and speech audiometry, otoacoustic emissions and auditory brainstem responses
MRI for bilateral superior temporal (Heschl gyrus) or subcortical temporal lesions
Neuropsychological testing of speech discrimination, sound identification and reading

case.who: 66-year-old market vendor from Nakhon Ratchasima with prior left temporal stroke
case.story: After a second stroke he suddenly could not understand his family, though he heard them talking.
case.exam: Speaks fluently, reads and follows written commands, cannot repeat spoken words, startles to a hand clap.
case.tests: Audiogram near normal; MRI shows new right superior temporal infarct with an old left one.
case.q: Why can he read but not understand speech?
case.a: Pure word deafness (auditory agnosia) from bilateral auditory cortex damage; the language system is intact but cut off from auditory input.

read.where: Chapter 23 Neuro-Otology: Dizziness, Balance and Hearing
Chapter 23 Neuro-Otology: Dizziness, Balance and Hearing — Auditory Processing Disorders
20 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Cerebral Hemispheres

det.patho: Sound meaning depends on primary auditory cortex in Heschl gyrus and its connections with superior temporal association areas. Bilateral cortical damage, or a deep left lesion disconnecting both auditory radiations from Wernicke area, abolishes recognition while the cochlea and brainstem work. Causes include strokes, herpes encephalitis, trauma, Landau-Kleffner syndrome in children and degenerative disease.
det.clinical: Presentations range from complete cortical deafness, through generalised auditory agnosia, to selective forms affecting speech, environmental sounds or music. Patients may seem deaf, but brainstem reflexes such as startle remain. Reading and writing separate pure word deafness from aphasia. Psychiatric or functional labels are a common early misdiagnosis.
det.diagnosis: Document near-normal peripheral hearing with audiometry, otoacoustic emissions and brainstem evoked responses. Then test speech discrimination, sound identification and music perception in quiet. MRI shows the lesions; cortical evoked potentials may be abnormal. Compare reading versus spoken comprehension to separate it from aphasia.
det.treatment: Treat the cause and use written communication, lip reading and gesture. Speech and language therapy can train phoneme discrimination. Hearing aids do not help since thresholds are normal. Recovery after stroke is variable.
det.prognosis: Some improvement over months is common, but bilateral lesions often leave lasting difficulty.
pearls: Hears the clap, cannot understand the word: auditory agnosia.
Written commands obeyed but spoken ones not: pure word deafness, not Wernicke aphasia.
A second temporal stroke on the opposite side is the classic trigger.
det.thd: Auditory agnosia คือการได้ยินเสียงแต่แปลความหมายไม่ได้ เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ auditory cortex ทั้งสองข้างหรือรอยโรคลึกด้านซ้ายที่ตัดทางเข้าเสียง ชนิด pure word deafness ผู้ป่วยอ่านเขียนและพูดได้ปกติแต่ฟังคำพูดไม่เข้าใจ ตรวจการได้ยินพื้นฐานมักปกติ ใช้ MRI หารอยโรค การรักษาเน้นสาเหตุและสื่อสารด้วยการเขียนหรือท่าทาง

name: Auditory neuropathy
formal: Hearing disorder with preserved outer hair cell function (present otoacoustic emissions) but absent or abnormal auditory brainstem responses, causing poor speech understanding out of proportion to audiogram.
simple: A hearing problem in which the ear detects sound but the nerve sends it poorly to the brain, so speech is hard to understand.
th: ความผิดปกติของการได้ยินที่เซลล์ขนชั้นนอกยังทำงาน (OAE ปกติ) แต่ ABR ผิดปกติหรือไม่มี ทำให้ฟังคำพูดไม่เข้าใจมากกว่าที่ audiogram บ่งบอก
tempoNote: Often congenital or neonatal (hyperbilirubinaemia, prematurity); some genetic forms present later
feat: Poor speech understanding, especially in noise, out of proportion to pure-tone thresholds
Present otoacoustic emissions or cochlear microphonic with absent or abnormal ABR
Risk factors: neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia, prematurity, hypoxia; genetic (OTOF, OPA1, PMP22)
Associated with peripheral neuropathies (CMT, Friedreich ataxia) in older patients
Hearing aids often give limited benefit
inv: OAE, ABR with both polarities, audiometry
MRI of internal auditory canals for nerve deficiency
Genetic testing (OTOF, OPA1) and neurological assessment for neuropathy

case.story: Severe neonatal jaundice needing exchange transfusion; passed newborn OAE screening but speech is delayed and she does not respond in noisy rooms.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination.
case.tests: OAE present; ABR absent with preserved cochlear microphonic; MRI shows normal nerves.
case.q: Why did she pass the newborn screen?
case.a: OAE tests outer hair cell function, which is normal in auditory neuropathy; ABR is needed in high-risk infants.

read.where: Chapter 23 Neuro-Otology: Dizziness, Balance and Hearing — Definitions of Hearing Loss
Chapter 23 Otoneurologic Manifestations of Otologic and Systemic Disease

det.patho: Sound is transduced normally by outer hair cells, but transmission from inner hair cells through the synapse or auditory nerve is impaired or desynchronised. Lesions may be presynaptic (otoferlin defects), synaptic, or neural (demyelination, axonal loss, nerve hypoplasia).
det.clinical: Children show delayed speech despite apparently mild hearing loss; thresholds may fluctuate. Older patients complain of hearing but not understanding. Some forms, like OTOF-related, are temperature-sensitive.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires present OAE or cochlear microphonic with absent or grossly abnormal ABR. Newborn screening with OAE alone misses it, so high-risk infants need ABR. MRI excludes cochlear nerve deficiency.
det.treatment: Management includes trial of hearing aids, FM systems, sign language and cochlear implantation, which works best for presynaptic forms such as OTOF. Gene therapy for OTOF deafness has shown early success in trials (2024).
det.prognosis: Variable; some infants with hyperbilirubinaemia improve, others need cochlear implantation.
pearls: OAE present, ABR absent: auditory neuropathy.
Screen high-risk neonates with ABR, not OAE alone.
OTOF-related cases respond well to cochlear implants.
det.thd: Auditory neuropathy คือการได้ยินผิดปกติที่หูชั้นในส่วน outer hair cell ยังทำงานปกติ (OAE ผ่าน) แต่สัญญาณประสาทการได้ยินผิดปกติ (ABR ไม่มี) ผู้ป่วยได้ยินเสียงแต่ฟังคำพูดไม่เข้าใจ โดยเฉพาะที่มีเสียงดัง พบในทารกที่ตัวเหลืองรุนแรงหรือคลอดก่อนกำหนด และจากยีน เช่น OTOF ทารกเสี่ยงสูงต้องตรวจ ABR การรักษาอาจใช้เครื่องช่วยฟังหรือประสาทหูเทียม

name: Auditory processing disorder (APD)
formal: Impaired central processing of auditory information despite normal peripheral hearing, causing difficulty with speech in noise, localisation and temporal processing.
simple: Trouble understanding what is heard, especially in noisy places, even though hearing tests are normal.
th: ความผิดปกติในการประมวลผลเสียงที่สมอง ทั้งที่หูปกติ ทำให้ฟังพูดในที่เสียงดังไม่รู้เรื่อง แยกทิศทางหรือจังหวะเสียงได้ไม่ดี
tempoNote: Developmental forms present in school age; acquired forms follow brain injury, stroke or ageing
feat: Difficulty following speech in noisy rooms despite a normal audiogram
Poor sound localisation, slow processing and frequent requests for repetition
Children: classroom difficulty, overlaps with ADHD, language and learning disorders
Adults: after head injury, stroke, MS, or with ageing and cognitive decline
inv: Full audiological assessment to exclude peripheral and retrocochlear hearing loss
Central auditory test battery: speech in noise, dichotic listening, gap detection, temporal patterns
MRI brain when acquired, asymmetric or accompanied by other neurological signs

case.story: Teachers say he does not listen in class and misunderstands instructions, but at home one-to-one he is fine.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination and otoscopy.
case.tests: Normal audiogram and tympanometry; poor scores on speech-in-noise and dichotic tests; nonverbal IQ average.
case.q: What condition fits and what classroom measure helps?
case.a: Developmental auditory processing disorder; preferential seating and a remote-microphone (FM) system to improve signal-to-noise.

read.where: Chapter 23 Neuro-Otology: Dizziness, Balance and Hearing — Auditory Processing Disorders
Chapter 23 Otoneurologic Manifestations of Otologic and Systemic Disease

det.patho: APD reflects inefficient neural handling of auditory signals in the brainstem, thalamus and auditory cortex, especially timing, binaural integration and separating speech from background. In children it is thought to relate to delayed maturation and often coexists with language and attention disorders; repeated otitis media may contribute. Acquired forms follow traumatic brain injury, stroke, demyelination, neurotoxic exposure and ageing.
det.clinical: The hallmark is struggling to hear speech in noise or reverberant rooms while hearing seems fine in quiet. Children appear inattentive or slow and may have reading and spelling problems. Adults report difficulty in restaurants and meetings and may have tinnitus or hyperacusis. Because symptoms overlap with ADHD, language disorder and cognitive decline, multidisciplinary assessment is important.
det.diagnosis: First exclude peripheral hearing loss with pure tone audiometry, tympanometry and otoacoustic emissions, and retrocochlear disease with brainstem responses or MRI where indicated. A battery of central auditory tests then shows deficits in at least two domains relative to age norms. Testing is unreliable in young children and with significant cognitive or attention problems. The diagnosis remains debated, so findings should guide support rather than serve as a label alone.
det.treatment: Environmental changes come first: reduce noise, use preferential seating, written instructions and remote-microphone systems. Auditory training programmes and language therapy can help some patients. Manage coexisting ADHD, learning or mood disorders. In acquired cases, treat the underlying neurological condition.
det.prognosis: Developmental cases often improve with maturation and support; acquired cases vary with the cause.
pearls: Normal audiogram does not mean normal listening.
Speech-in-noise difficulty is the key complaint.
Always exclude peripheral and retrocochlear loss before labelling APD.
det.thd: APD คือการที่หูได้ยินปกติแต่สมองประมวลผลเสียงได้ไม่ดี โดยเฉพาะฟังพูดในที่เสียงดัง พบในเด็กวัยเรียนและผู้ใหญ่หลังบาดเจ็บสมองหรือสูงอายุ ต้องตรวจการได้ยินพื้นฐานให้ปกติก่อนแล้วจึงใช้ชุดทดสอบ central auditory การดูแลเน้นปรับสิ่งแวดล้อม ใช้ระบบไมโครโฟน FM และฝึกการฟัง ควรประเมินภาวะร่วม เช่น ADHD

name: Autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy (AAG)
formal: Autoimmune disorder with antibodies against ganglionic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors causing subacute pan-autonomic failure with orthostatic hypotension, anhidrosis, dry mouth and gut dysmotility.
simple: An immune attack on the nerve junctions of the autonomic system, causing dizziness on standing, dry mouth, constipation and abnormal sweating.
more: Antibody-mediated autonomic failure, often with ganglionic acetylcholine receptor antibodies, causing orthostatic hypotension, anhidrosis, dry eyes and mouth, gut dysmotility, and urinary retention. Check anti-ganglionic AChR antibodies and autonomic tests; screen for cancer. Plasma exchange, IVIG, and immunosuppression help; many patients improve partially.
th: ระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติล้มเหลวทั่วไปจากแอนติบอดีต่อ ganglionic (α3) AChR — ความดันตกเมื่อยืน ตาแห้งปากแห้ง ลำไส้ไม่เคลื่อน รักษาได้
tempoNote: Often subacute over days to weeks, sometimes after infection; a slowly progressive form mimics pure autonomic failure
feat: Severe orthostatic hypotension with fainting on standing
Dry eyes and mouth, reduced sweating
Gut dysmotility: early satiety, vomiting, constipation or ileus
Urinary retention and erectile failure
Poorly reacting, dilated pupils; motor and sensory function largely preserved
inv: Ganglionic (α3) AChR antibody — higher titres are more specific
Autonomic testing: tilt with BP/HR, Valsalva, QSART or thermoregulatory sweat test, heart-rate variability
Low supine and standing noradrenaline; NCS to show sparing of large fibres
Cancer screening (CT chest/abdomen) because of paraneoplastic associations

case.story: Two weeks after a febrile illness she cannot stand without blacking out; she vomits after meals, passes little urine and her mouth is parched.
case.exam: BP 132/84 lying, 74/50 standing with HR unchanged at 84; pupils 6 mm sluggish to light; dry skin; normal strength, sensation and reflexes.
case.tests: α3-AChR antibody strongly positive; tilt test shows neurogenic OH; sweat test widespread anhidrosis; CT chest–abdomen unremarkable.
case.q: What treatment can be offered beyond symptomatic care?
case.a: Immunotherapy — IVIG, plasma exchange or steroids, with rituximab or mycophenolate for maintenance — alongside OH management (fluids, midodrine, droxidopa if available).

read.where: Companion to Peripheral Neuropathy: chapters (see text)

det.patho: Antibodies against the α3 subunit of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor in autonomic ganglia block fast synaptic transmission in both sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia and enteric neurons. Titres correlate with severity, and passive transfer reproduces the disorder in animals. Some cases are paraneoplastic (small-cell lung cancer, thymoma, others).
det.clinical: Two patterns exist: an acute-subacute onset with widespread failure, often after a viral prodrome, and a slow form closely resembling pure autonomic failure. Cholinergic failure (sicca, pupils, gut, bladder) is usually more prominent than in degenerative autonomic failure. Somatic nerves are largely spared, though mild sensory symptoms or cognitive complaints can occur.
det.diagnosis: Combine objective evidence of generalised autonomic failure with a positive ganglionic AChR antibody; low titres are seen in other disorders and must be interpreted cautiously. Seronegative cases exist and may still respond to immunotherapy. Rule out diabetes, amyloidosis (including TTR), Sjögren syndrome, porphyria, botulism and paraneoplastic anti-Hu disease.
det.treatment: Treat OH with fluids, salt, compression, midodrine, fludrocortisone or droxidopa, and manage gut motility and bladder. Immunotherapy is reasonable once diagnosed: IVIG 2 g/kg, plasma exchange or steroids, then maintenance with mycophenolate, azathioprine or rituximab. Search for and treat any tumour.
det.prognosis: About a third recover well spontaneously or with treatment; many have partial improvement, and the chronic form often needs long-term immunotherapy.
pearls: Prominent dry eyes/mouth, fixed pupils and gut failure in subacute autonomic collapse: test α3-AChR antibody.
Unlike MSA, the brain examination stays normal.
Pyridostigmine can help some patients by boosting ganglionic transmission.
det.thd: AAG เป็นโรคภูมิคุ้มกันที่สร้างแอนติบอดีต่อ α3 AChR ที่ปมประสาทอัตโนมัติ ทำให้ความดันตกเมื่อยืน ตาแห้ง ปากแห้ง เหงื่อไม่ออก ลำไส้ไม่เคลื่อน ปัสสาวะคั่ง และรูม่านตาขยาย โดยกล้ามเนื้อและความรู้สึกยังปกติ วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจระบบอัตโนมัติร่วมกับแอนติบอดี และควรค้นหามะเร็ง รักษาด้วย IVIG, PLEX, steroid หรือ rituximab ร่วมกับรักษาอาการความดันตก

qx.stem: A 44-year-old schoolteacher from Chiang Rai develops, over five weeks after a febrile illness, fainting on standing, early satiety with vomiting, severe constipation, dry eyes and mouth and inability to sweat. Lying blood pressure is 128/80 mmHg and falls to 72/48 mmHg after 2 minutes standing without a rise in heart rate. The pupils are dilated with a sluggish light response. Strength, reflexes and sensation are normal.
qx.q: Which antibody test best supports the diagnosis?
opts: Anti-MAG IgM
Anti-GQ1b IgG
Anti-VGCC (P/Q-type) antibody
Ganglionic (α3-subunit) nicotinic acetylcholine receptor antibody
Muscle acetylcholine receptor binding antibody
qx.why: Subacute pandysautonomia (adrenergic, cholinergic and enteric failure with tonic pupils) and no somatic deficit suggests autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy; ganglionic α3-AChR antibodies are found in about half, and higher titres correlate with severity. A paraneoplastic search (ANNA-1, CT chest) is still needed. Treatment includes IVIG, plasma exchange or rituximab plus symptomatic midodrine or droxidopa. Muscle AChR antibodies cause myasthenia, not dysautonomia.

name: Autoimmune chorea
formal: Chorea arising from immune-mediated mechanisms, including Sydenham chorea, lupus, antiphospholipid syndrome and paraneoplastic or anti-CV2 and anti-LGI1 syndromes.
simple: Jerky, dance-like movements caused by the immune system attacking the brain.
th: chorea ที่เกิดจากภูมิคุ้มกัน เช่น Sydenham, SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome และ paraneoplastic (anti-CV2, anti-LGI1)
tempoNote: Develops over days to weeks; Sydenham follows streptococcal infection by 1–6 months
feat: Subacute generalised or hemichorea with behavioural change
Children: Sydenham chorea with emotional lability, OCD symptoms, carditis
Young women: SLE or antiphospholipid syndrome; may appear in pregnancy or with oral contraceptives
Older adults: paraneoplastic (CRMP5/CV2 with small cell lung cancer) or LGI1 with faciobrachial seizures
Responds to immunotherapy; distinguish from genetic and metabolic choreas
inv: ASO, anti-DNase B, echocardiography (Sydenham)
ANA, anti-dsDNA, antiphospholipid antibodies
Neuronal antibody panels (CRMP5, LGI1, NMDAR, CASPR2) and cancer screening
MRI brain; glucose and thyroid tests to exclude metabolic causes

case.story: Two weeks of involuntary jerky movements of the left arm and face after starting the combined oral contraceptive pill; one prior miscarriage.
case.exam: Left hemichorea, livedo reticularis.
case.tests: Lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin positive; MRI normal; glucose normal.
case.q: What is the likely cause and management?
case.a: Antiphospholipid syndrome-related chorea; stop the oestrogen pill, consider anticoagulation and symptomatic tetrabenazine or haloperidol.

read.where: Chapter 21 - Abnormal Movements in Neurological Autoimmune Disorders

det.patho: Antibodies or immune complexes target basal ganglia neurons or their vasculature. Sydenham chorea involves cross-reactive antibodies after group A streptococcal infection; antiphospholipid antibodies may act on striatal neurons directly as well as through thrombosis; paraneoplastic antibodies cause striatal inflammation.
det.clinical: Onset is usually subacute, often with psychiatric features. The context strongly suggests the cause: age, sex, pregnancy, systemic signs or weight loss. Asymmetric chorea is common in Sydenham and antiphospholipid cases.
det.diagnosis: Search systematically for streptococcal, lupus, antiphospholipid and neuronal antibodies while excluding hyperglycaemia, hyperthyroidism, drugs and genetic disorders. MRI may show striatal T2 changes in paraneoplastic and autoimmune encephalitis.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: penicillin prophylaxis for Sydenham, anticoagulation when antiphospholipid thrombosis is present, cancer treatment and immunotherapy for paraneoplastic forms. Symptomatic options include tetrabenazine, valproate or antipsychotics. Steroids, IVIG or plasma exchange are used in severe or refractory cases.
det.prognosis: Sydenham usually resolves in months, though recurrence occurs; paraneoplastic forms depend on tumour control.
pearls: New chorea on oral contraceptives: test for antiphospholipid antibodies.
Older patient with subacute chorea and weight loss: CRMP5 and lung imaging.
Sydenham may present months after the sore throat; ASO may already be normal.
det.thd: Autoimmune chorea คือ chorea ที่เกิดจากภูมิคุ้มกัน ได้แก่ Sydenham ในเด็กหลังติดเชื้อ streptococcus, SLE และ antiphospholipid syndrome ในหญิงวัยเจริญพันธุ์ และ paraneoplastic ในผู้สูงอายุ มักเกิดภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์และมีอาการทางจิตร่วม ตรวจ ASO, ANA, antiphospholipid และ antibody ต่อเซลล์ประสาท การรักษาคือแก้สาเหตุ ใช้ยาลดการเคลื่อนไหว และยากดภูมิในรายรุนแรง

name: Autoimmune disease
formal: Condition in which the immune system attacks self-tissues; neurological examples include multiple sclerosis, myasthenia gravis, Guillain-Barre syndrome and autoimmune encephalitis.
simple: A disease in which the body's immune system wrongly attacks its own tissues, including parts of the brain and nerves.
th: กลุ่มโรคที่ระบบภูมิคุ้มกันทำร้ายเนื้อเยื่อของตัวเอง ทางระบบประสาทเช่น MS, myasthenia gravis, GBS และ autoimmune encephalitis

feat: Umbrella category rather than a single disease
Can target CNS (MS, NMOSD, autoimmune encephalitis), PNS (GBS, CIDP), NMJ (myasthenia) or muscle (myositis)

case.story: Has known Hashimoto thyroiditis; now presents with fluctuating double vision and drooping eyelids worse in the evening.
case.exam: Fatigable ptosis, variable diplopia, neck flexion 4/5; pupils normal.
case.tests: AChR antibodies positive; CT chest normal thymus; TSH controlled.

det.patho: Autoimmune disease arises when tolerance to self-antigens fails, through genetic susceptibility (HLA and immune-regulatory genes), environmental triggers such as infection (molecular mimicry), tumours (paraneoplastic) or drugs including immune checkpoint inhibitors. Effector mechanisms include pathogenic antibodies (myasthenia, NMOSD, NMDAR encephalitis), cytotoxic T cells (paraneoplastic intracellular-antigen syndromes) and complement. This entry is a general category, not a specific diagnosis.
det.clinical: Neurological autoimmunity may affect any level of the neuraxis and may be organ-specific or part of a systemic disease. Clues include subacute onset, relapsing course, inflammatory CSF, coexisting autoimmune diseases, recent infection or cancer, and response to steroids or other immunotherapy. Clinical features are those of the specific disease involved.
det.diagnosis: The approach is to localise the problem, then test for the relevant antibodies and inflammatory markers and exclude infection and malignancy. Antibody results must match the clinical syndrome; low-titre or non-specific antibodies (e.g. ANA, anti-TPO) are common in healthy people. Tumour screening is needed where paraneoplastic disease is possible.
det.treatment: Treatment depends on the disease but generally follows acute immunotherapy (corticosteroids, IVIG, plasma exchange) and maintenance immunosuppression or targeted biologics (rituximab, complement and FcRn inhibitors, anti-IL-6R). Infection prophylaxis, bone protection on steroids and vaccination planning are part of care. Remove triggers such as tumours or offending drugs.
det.prognosis: Highly variable — many neurological autoimmune diseases are treatable, and early therapy improves outcome.
pearls: Autoimmune diseases cluster in individuals and families.
An antibody result is only meaningful when it fits the clinical picture.
Immune checkpoint inhibitors are an important new trigger of neurological autoimmunity.
det.thd: Autoimmune disease เป็นชื่อกลุ่มโรคที่ภูมิคุ้มกันโจมตีเนื้อเยื่อของตัวเอง ไม่ใช่โรคเดี่ยว ทางระบบประสาทมีได้ทุกระดับ เช่น สมอง (MS, autoimmune encephalitis) เส้นประสาท (GBS, CIDP) รอยต่อประสาทกล้ามเนื้อ (myasthenia gravis) และกล้ามเนื้อ (myositis) การวินิจฉัยใช้ antibody ที่สอดคล้องกับอาการ ร่วมกับ MRI และ CSF ส่วนใหญ่รักษาได้ด้วย steroid, IVIG, plasma exchange หรือยากดภูมิ

det.patho: Loss of tolerance leads to antibodies against neural surface or intracellular antigens, cytotoxic T-cell attack, or immune-complex and vascular inflammation. Triggers include infection, cancer (paraneoplastic), immune checkpoint inhibitors and genetic susceptibility. Surface-antibody diseases often respond well to immunotherapy, whereas intracellular-antigen (T-cell) diseases respond less well.
det.clinical: Presentations reflect the target: optic neuritis, myelitis, encephalitis, seizures, movement disorders, neuropathy, neuromuscular junction failure or myositis. Subacute evolution over days to weeks and coexisting autoimmunity are helpful clues.
det.diagnosis: Combine clinical syndrome, MRI, CSF and specific antibody testing (preferably cell-based assays). Exclude infection and malignancy. Formal criteria exist for MS, NMOSD, MOGAD and autoimmune encephalitis.
det.treatment: Acute: high-dose steroids, IVIG or plasma exchange. Maintenance: disease-specific agents (B-cell depletion, complement inhibitors, FcRn blockers, conventional immunosuppressants). Treat associated tumours.
det.prognosis: Highly variable; early recognition and treatment improve outcomes in most antibody-mediated diseases.
pearls: Subacute neurological illness with inflammatory CSF: think autoimmune as well as infection.
Use cell-based antibody assays where available.
Some MS drugs worsen NMOSD — get the diagnosis right first.
det.thd: Autoimmune disorders ทางระบบประสาทคือโรคที่ภูมิคุ้มกันของร่างกายทำร้ายระบบประสาท เช่น MS, NMOSD, autoimmune encephalitis, GBS และ myasthenia gravis อาการมักเกิดแบบกึ่งเฉียบพลันหรือกำเริบเป็นพัก ๆ การวินิจฉัยใช้ MRI น้ำไขสันหลัง และแอนติบอดีจำเพาะ การรักษาคือ steroid, IVIG, plasma exchange และยากดภูมิระยะยาวตามชนิดโรค

name: Autoimmune encephalitis

simple: Brain inflammation caused by the immune system, leading to memory loss, seizures, confusion and behaviour changes.

case.story: Over 6 weeks he has had brief episodes, dozens a day, where his left face grimaces and left arm stiffens for a second; then he started repeating questions and getting lost on familiar routes.
case.exam: Disoriented to date, recalls 0/3 words at 5 minutes; observed brief left faciobrachial dystonic jerks.
case.tests: Sodium 126 mmol/L; MRI bilateral mesial temporal FLAIR hyperintensity; CSF 3 cells, protein normal; serum LGI1 antibody positive.
case.q: Which antibody syndrome is this and why should treatment start promptly?
case.a: LGI1 encephalitis (faciobrachial dystonic seizures, hyponatraemia, limbic involvement); early immunotherapy (IV methylprednisolone ± IVIG) controls seizures better than antiseizure drugs and helps prevent permanent amnesia.

det.patho: Two broad mechanisms exist. Antibodies against neuronal surface or synaptic proteins (NMDAR, LGI1, CASPR2, AMPAR, GABA-A/B receptors and others) directly and often reversibly alter receptor function, so these forms respond well to immunotherapy. Antibodies against intracellular antigens (Hu, Ma2, CV2, GAD) are markers of cytotoxic T-cell attack, frequently paraneoplastic and less reversible. Triggers include tumours, prior HSV encephalitis (which can induce NMDAR encephalitis weeks later) and immune checkpoint inhibitors.
det.clinical: NMDAR encephalitis typically affects young women and children with psychiatric symptoms, then seizures, dyskinesia, mutism, autonomic instability and hypoventilation. LGI1 encephalitis mostly affects older men with faciobrachial dystonic seizures, amnesia and hyponatraemia. CASPR2 causes Morvan syndrome or limbic encephalitis with neuromyotonia and pain; GABA-B and AMPAR present with seizures or limbic encephalitis, often with lung cancer or thymoma. Antibody-negative cases are common and still treatable.
det.diagnosis: The 2016 Graus criteria allow treatment before antibody results. Possible autoimmune encephalitis requires: (1) subacute onset (under 3 months) of working-memory deficits, psychiatric features or altered mental status; (2) at least one of new focal CNS findings, unexplained seizures, CSF pleocytosis (over 5 cells/mm³) or MRI features suggesting encephalitis; and (3) reasonable exclusion of alternative causes. Further tiers define definite limbic encephalitis, probable or definite NMDAR encephalitis and probable antibody-negative autoimmune encephalitis. Test serum and CSF with cell-based assays, interpret low-titre serum-only results cautiously, and actively exclude infection, toxic-metabolic causes, prion disease, primary psychiatric illness and CNS lymphoma or vasculitis.
det.treatment: Start first-line immunotherapy once infection is reasonably excluded: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days, IVIG (total 2 g/kg given across 2–5 days), or plasma exchange, often combined. Remove any tumour (e.g. ovarian teratoma) promptly. If there is no clear improvement in about 2 weeks, escalate to rituximab or cyclophosphamide; tocilizumab or bortezomib are options in refractory cases. Treat seizures, autonomic instability and psychiatric symptoms supportively (antipsychotics can worsen dyskinesia and NMS-like reactions in NMDAR). Maintenance immunotherapy may be needed in relapsing forms.
det.prognosis: Most patients with surface-antibody encephalitis improve substantially, though recovery takes months and memory or behavioural sequelae persist in some; intracellular-antibody paraneoplastic forms respond poorly.
pearls: Use the Graus criteria — do not wait for antibody results to start treatment.
Faciobrachial dystonic seizures + low sodium = LGI1; early steroids prevent progression to amnesia.
A young woman with psychosis, seizures and dyskinesia needs NMDAR testing in CSF and a pelvic scan for teratoma.
Relapse with new symptoms weeks after HSV encephalitis may be NMDAR encephalitis rather than viral recurrence.
det.thd: Autoimmune encephalitis คือสมองอักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกันต่อโปรตีนของเซลล์ประสาท เช่น NMDAR, LGI1, CASPR2 อาการความจำเสื่อม สับสน พฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน และชักภายในไม่เกิน 3 เดือน เกณฑ์ Graus 2016 ใช้วินิจฉัย possible AE ได้เมื่อมีอาการข้างต้นร่วมกับ focal sign ชัก CSF เซลล์เพิ่ม หรือ MRI เข้ากับสมองอักเสบ และตัดสาเหตุอื่นแล้ว จึงเริ่มรักษาได้ก่อนผลแอนติบอดี รักษาด้วย methylprednisolone, IVIG หรือ plasma exchange ถ้าไม่ดีขึ้นให้ rituximab หรือ cyclophosphamide และต้องหาเนื้องอกร่วม เช่น teratoma ในรังไข่

name: Autoimmune inner ear disease
formal: Progressive bilateral sensorineural hearing loss with vestibular symptoms from immune-mediated cochlear damage, responsive to corticosteroids and associated with systemic autoimmune disease.
simple: Hearing loss, sometimes with dizziness, caused by the immune system attacking the inner ear, which may improve with steroid treatment.
th: หูชั้นในอักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกัน ทำให้การได้ยินเสื่อมแบบประสาทหูทั้งสองข้างภายในสัปดาห์ถึงเดือน มักมีเวียนศีรษะร่วม และตอบสนองต่อสเตียรอยด์

feat: Bilateral, often asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss progressing over weeks to months
Fluctuating hearing, tinnitus and aural fullness; may look like bilateral Ménière disease
Imbalance or vertigo; bilateral vestibular loss gives oscillopsia when walking

case.story: Over six weeks she cannot hear students in class, right ear first then left, with ringing and unsteadiness in the dark. She has had recurrent painful red eyes.
case.exam: Rinne positive both sides with lateralisation-free Weber; positive head impulse test bilaterally; no cranial neuropathy or ataxia.
case.tests: Audiogram: 50–60 dB bilateral sensorineural loss, worse than one month before; MRI normal; treponemal test negative.
case.q: What systemic syndrome should be considered given the eye history?
case.a: Cogan syndrome (interstitial keratitis plus audiovestibular loss) as a cause of immune-mediated inner ear disease; give prompt high-dose steroids and involve ophthalmology and rheumatology.

read.where: Chapter 23 Neuro-Otology: Dizziness, Balance and Hearing — Sensorineural Hearing Loss

det.patho: Immune attack on the cochlea and labyrinth, involving antibodies, T cells and cytokines such as IL-1, damages hair cells and stria vascularis. No single inner-ear antigen has been convincingly proven; anti-HSP70 and anti-cochlin antibodies proved neither sensitive nor specific. It may be primary (organ-restricted) or secondary to systemic autoimmune disease. It is rare, accounting for under 1% of hearing loss.
det.clinical: Typical patients are middle-aged women with hearing that drops in steps over weeks, affecting both ears within months. Episodes of vertigo, persistent imbalance and oscillopsia reflect vestibular damage. Untreated, hearing can fall to profound levels. Ask about eye inflammation, rash, arthritis, sinus disease and renal symptoms to identify a systemic cause.
det.diagnosis: There is no definitive test; the diagnosis rests on rapidly progressive bilateral sensorineural loss, exclusion of other causes, and a measurable improvement with corticosteroids. MRI with contrast removes vestibular schwannoma, inflammation and demyelination from the list; syphilis, Lyme disease, ototoxic drugs and Ménière disease must also be considered. Screening for systemic autoimmunity and eye examination are routine.
det.treatment: High-dose oral prednisolone (around 1 mg/kg/day for 4 weeks, then taper if responsive) is the first step; intratympanic steroid can supplement it. Steroid-dependent patients need sparing agents such as methotrexate, though trial evidence is weak; biologics including anakinra and rituximab have been tried in refractory cases. Cochlear implantation works well when hearing is lost. Vestibular rehabilitation helps imbalance.
det.prognosis: Most respond at first, but many relapse when steroids are reduced; a proportion progress to bilateral deafness.
pearls: Bilateral sensorineural loss developing over weeks is not age-related: test for syphilis and autoimmunity.
Steroid response is part of the diagnosis, so document audiometry before and after.
Red eyes plus deafness and vertigo: think Cogan syndrome.
det.thd: Autoimmune inner ear disease คือหูชั้นในอักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกัน การได้ยินแบบประสาทหูลดลงทั้งสองข้างภายในหลายสัปดาห์ถึงเดือน อาจมีเสียงในหู เวียนศีรษะ และเสียการทรงตัว บางรายมีโรคภูมิคุ้มกันทั้งตัว เช่น vasculitis หรือ Cogan syndrome ไม่มีการตรวจเลือดเฉพาะ วินิจฉัยจากการดำเนินโรค การตัดสาเหตุอื่นด้วย MRI และ serology และการตอบสนองต่อสเตียรอยด์ รักษาด้วย prednisolone ขนาดสูง ถ้าหูหนวกถาวรพิจารณา cochlear implant

det.patho: The node of Ranvier and its flanking paranodes are held together by a protein complex: neurofascin-155 on the glial side binds contactin-1 and Caspr1 on the axon, while neurofascin-186 sits in the nodal gap. Antibodies against these proteins — most often of the IgG4 subclass — loosen the axo-glial junction and disperse sodium channels, so conduction fails without the macrophage-driven myelin stripping seen in classic CIDP. Because IgG4 barely activates complement, the disease is driven by functional blockade rather than inflammation. Since the 2021 EAN/PNS guideline these patients are classed as a separate entity, no longer as a CIDP subtype.
det.clinical: Many patients are first labelled GBS or CIDP; the clue is a course that keeps advancing past 8 weeks or a striking lack of response to IVIG. Each antibody carries a typical profile: NF155 in young adults with tremor, ataxia and huge roots; CNTN1 in older adults with rapid axonal loss and membranous nephropathy; Caspr1 with severe neuropathic pain; pan-neurofascin with a catastrophic GBS-like illness. Weakness is usually distal and motor-predominant and the nadir is deep. Cranial, respiratory and autonomic involvement mark the most aggressive cases.
det.diagnosis: Request a nodal–paranodal antibody panel by cell-based assay whenever a CIDP-like or GBS-like patient has atypical features: tremor, sensory ataxia, poor IVIG response, nephrotic syndrome or very high CSF protein. Report the IgG subclass, as IgG4 predicts IVIG resistance. Nerve conduction may look demyelinating (very long distal latencies) or show reversible conduction failure that recovers without dispersion. CSF protein is often above 1–2 g/L and MRI or ultrasound may show enlarged roots and plexuses. Check urine protein and immunofixation because renal and haematological associations change management.
det.treatment: Rituximab is the most effective long-term option for IgG4-mediated disease and often produces sustained remission after one or two cycles. Plasma exchange and high-dose corticosteroids are used for rapid control while rituximab takes effect. IVIG may help early or in IgG1/IgG3-predominant cases but rarely suffices alone. Associated membranous nephropathy or lymphoproliferative disease should be managed together with nephrology or haematology. Antibody titres can be followed as a rough marker of response.
det.prognosis: With timely rituximab most patients improve substantially, though axonal damage accumulated during a delayed diagnosis may leave residual weakness. Untreated or IVIG-only cases often progress to severe disability.
pearls: IVIG failure in 'CIDP' should prompt antibody testing before simply escalating IVIG.
IgG4 does not fix complement — this is why IVIG works poorly and B-cell depletion works well.
Conduction block that reverses without temporal dispersion points to a nodal, not myelin, problem.
det.thd: Nodopathy เกิดจากแอนติบอดี (ส่วนใหญ่เป็น IgG4) ที่จับโปรตีนบริเวณ node และ paranode ของเส้นใยประสาท ทำให้กระแสประสาทถูกขัดขวางโดยไม่มีการอักเสบทำลายปลอกประสาทแบบ CIDP ทั่วไป ผู้ป่วยมักถูกวินิจฉัยเป็น GBS หรือ CIDP ก่อน แต่ไม่ตอบสนองต่อ IVIG และอาการรุนแรงกว่า ควรส่งตรวจแอนติบอดี NF155, CNTN1, Caspr1 และ pan-NF พร้อม IgG subclass เมื่อมีลักษณะผิดปกติ เช่น มือสั่น เดินเซ โปรตีนใน CSF สูงมาก หรือมีโปรตีนรั่วในปัสสาวะ การรักษาหลักคือ rituximab ร่วมกับ plasma exchange หรือสเตียรอยด์ในช่วงแรก

name: Autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes
formal: Multi-gland autoimmune endocrine failure: type 1 (AIRE) with candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism and Addison disease; type 2 with Addison, thyroid disease and diabetes; may overlap with myasthenia.
simple: Conditions in which the immune system attacks several hormone glands at once, sometimes also affecting nerves and muscles.
more: Diagnosed with organ-specific autoantibodies and hormone testing, plus AIRE testing in type 1. Treat with hormone replacement and monitor for new glands being affected.
th: กลุ่มโรคที่ภูมิคุ้มกันทำลายต่อมไร้ท่อหลายต่อมพร้อมกันหรือทยอยกัน เช่น ต่อมหมวกไต ไทรอยด์ พาราไทรอยด์ และตับอ่อน บางรายมี myasthenia ร่วม
tempoNote: Gland failures accumulate over years; APS-1 starts in childhood, APS-2 in young to middle adulthood
feat: APS-1: chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism and Addison disease starting in childhood
APS-2: Addison disease with autoimmune thyroid disease and/or type 1 diabetes, mostly in adults
Neurological links: hypocalcaemic tetany or seizures, hypoglycaemia, myopathy, and occasional myasthenia gravis
Other associations: vitiligo, alopecia, pernicious anaemia (B12 neuropathy), coeliac disease, hypogonadism
New gland failures can appear years after the first
inv: Organ-specific antibodies: 21-hydroxylase, TPO, GAD65, intrinsic factor, tissue transglutaminase
Hormone panels: cortisol/ACTH, TSH/FT4, calcium/PTH, glucose/HbA1c, B12
AIRE gene testing and anti-interferon-omega antibodies for suspected APS-1

case.story: Thrush in the mouth since early childhood; had a generalised seizure and hand cramps last year; now tired with darkening skin.
case.exam: Oral candidiasis, dystrophic nails, positive Chvostek sign, hyperpigmented gums.
case.tests: Calcium 1.6 mmol/L with low PTH; morning cortisol low with high ACTH; anti-interferon-omega antibody positive.
case.q: Which syndrome and gene, and why did she seize?
case.a: APS-1 (APECED) from biallelic AIRE variants; the seizure was hypocalcaemic from hypoparathyroidism.

det.patho: APS-1 is autosomal recessive (rarely dominant-negative) loss of AIRE, which normally displays tissue antigens in the thymus to delete self-reactive T cells; neutralising antibodies to IL-17 and IL-22 explain the candidiasis. APS-2 is polygenic with HLA-DR3/DR4 links and is far more common. Additional categories (APS-3/4) describe thyroid or other combinations without Addison disease. Thymoma can produce an APS-1-like picture through secondary AIRE loss.
det.clinical: These are endocrine-immunological syndromes; neurology is involved through metabolic consequences rather than direct nerve attack. Hypocalcaemia causes tetany, seizures and basal ganglia calcification; adrenal failure and diabetes give hypoglycaemia and encephalopathy; B12 deficiency gives myeloneuropathy; hypothyroidism adds myopathy and carpal tunnel syndrome. Myasthenia gravis and stiff-person syndrome (via GAD antibodies) occasionally cluster with these disorders.
det.diagnosis: Diagnose when two or more autoimmune endocrine failures occur, or one plus candidiasis in APS-1. Confirm each gland with hormone tests and specific antibodies, and screen asymptomatic organs periodically. AIRE sequencing and interferon-omega antibodies (highly sensitive for APS-1) settle the type. First-degree relatives should be screened.
det.treatment: Replace each deficient hormone; always correct cortisol before or together with thyroxine, as thyroxine can precipitate adrenal crisis. Hypoparathyroidism needs calcium and active vitamin D with careful urine calcium monitoring. Candidiasis needs antifungals and surveillance for oral cancer. Monitor yearly for new endocrine and non-endocrine components.
det.prognosis: Good with replacement and surveillance; APS-1 carries extra risk from crises, infection, hepatitis and oral squamous carcinoma.
pearls: Seizure plus candidiasis in a child: check calcium and think APS-1.
Give hydrocortisone before thyroxine when both glands fail.
Interferon-omega antibodies are a near-universal marker of APS-1.
det.thd: Autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes คือกลุ่มโรคที่ภูมิคุ้มกันทำลายต่อมไร้ท่อหลายต่อม ชนิดที่ 1 เกิดจากยีน AIRE มีเชื้อราในปากเรื้อรัง พาราไทรอยด์ทำงานต่ำ และ Addison ตั้งแต่เด็ก ชนิดที่ 2 พบในผู้ใหญ่ มี Addison ร่วมกับโรคไทรอยด์หรือเบาหวานชนิดที่ 1 อาการทางระบบประสาทเกิดจากแคลเซียมต่ำ น้ำตาลต่ำ หรือ B12 ต่ำ และอาจพบ myasthenia ร่วม รักษาด้วยการทดแทนฮอร์โมน โดยให้ hydrocortisone ก่อน thyroxine

name: Autoinflammatory disease
formal: Disorders of innate immune dysregulation with recurrent systemic inflammation, such as cryopyrin-associated syndromes, some causing aseptic meningitis, hearing loss and papilloedema.
simple: Conditions with repeated unprovoked inflammation, such as fevers and rashes, which can affect the brain coverings.
th: กลุ่มโรคที่ระบบภูมิคุ้มกันโดยกำเนิดทำงานผิดปกติ ทำให้อักเสบทั่วร่างกายเป็นพัก ๆ เช่น CAPS บางชนิดทำให้เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบแบบ aseptic หูเสื่อม และ papilloedema
tempoNote: Recurrent fever episodes from childhood, with chronic organ damage over years
feat: Recurrent fevers, rash, serositis and arthritis without autoantibodies or infection
Examples: CAPS (NLRP3), familial Mediterranean fever, TRAPS, HIDS, DADA2, VEXAS
Neurological: chronic aseptic meningitis, sensorineural hearing loss, papilloedema (NOMID/CINCA)
DADA2 causes early-onset lacunar strokes; Behcet-like overlap
AA amyloidosis is a long-term complication
inv: CRP, SAA during and between attacks
Genetic panels for autoinflammatory genes; ADA2 enzyme activity
CSF analysis, audiometry and fundoscopy in neurological involvement

case.story: Since infancy has urticarial rash, fevers and joint pains; now has chronic headache and is losing hearing.
case.exam: Urticaria-like rash, bilateral papilloedema, knee overgrowth.
case.tests: CRP persistently high; CSF lymphocytes 40, protein mildly raised; NLRP3 variant identified.
case.q: Which treatment targets the mechanism?
case.a: Neonatal-onset multisystem inflammatory disease (severe CAPS); IL-1 blockade with anakinra or canakinumab.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Autoinflammatory Syndromes

det.patho: Autoinflammatory diseases result from dysregulation of innate immune pathways, especially the inflammasome and interleukin-1 signalling, TNF receptor handling, interferon or NF-kB pathways. Unlike autoimmunity, autoantibodies and autoreactive T cells are not central.
det.clinical: This entry is a group heading. Neurological involvement includes aseptic meningitis, raised intracranial pressure, sensorineural hearing loss, strokes (DADA2), and vasculitic neuropathy. Adult-onset VEXAS syndrome in older men can involve relapsing chondritis and vasculitis.
det.diagnosis: Recognise recurrent inflammation without infection or autoantibodies, then confirm genetically. CSF, MRI, audiometry and eye examination define neurological involvement.
det.treatment: Targeted therapy: IL-1 inhibitors (anakinra, canakinumab, rilonacept) for CAPS; colchicine for FMF; TNF inhibitors for DADA2 (which reduce strokes); JAK inhibitors for interferonopathies. Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is used in selected cases.
det.prognosis: Good with targeted therapy if started before irreversible deafness, brain damage or amyloidosis.
pearls: Recurrent aseptic meningitis with fever and rash may be CAPS.
Early lacunar strokes in a child: test ADA2 activity.
IL-1 blockade can prevent deafness in CAPS.
det.thd: Autoinflammatory disease คือกลุ่มโรคที่ภูมิคุ้มกันโดยกำเนิดทำงานผิดปกติ ทำให้ไข้และอักเสบซ้ำ ๆ โดยไม่มีเชื้อหรือ autoantibody เช่น CAPS, FMF และ DADA2 ผลต่อระบบประสาทได้แก่ เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบเรื้อรัง หูเสื่อม ความดันในกะโหลกสูง และหลอดเลือดสมองตีบในเด็ก ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน การรักษาใช้ยาเฉพาะ เช่น IL-1 blocker, colchicine หรือ TNF inhibitor

name: Autonomic disorders
formal: Conditions of impaired sympathetic, parasympathetic or enteric function, such as orthostatic hypotension, MSA, pure autonomic failure and autonomic neuropathy.
simple: Problems with the body's automatic functions such as blood pressure, heart rate, sweating and bladder control.
th: กลุ่มภาวะที่ระบบประสาท sympathetic, parasympathetic หรือ enteric ทำงานผิดปกติ เช่น ความดันตกเวลาลุกยืน MSA, pure autonomic failure และ autonomic neuropathy
tempoNote: Acute (GBS, botulism), subacute (autoimmune ganglionopathy), chronic (diabetes, synucleinopathies), episodic (reflex syncope, PoTS)
feat: Umbrella heading for central and peripheral autonomic disorders
Orthostatic hypotension, syncope, postural tachycardia
Bladder, bowel, sexual and sweating dysfunction; dry eyes and mouth; pupil abnormalities
Central: MSA, PD, DLB; peripheral: diabetic, amyloid, autoimmune, hereditary neuropathies
inv: Orthostatic BP and heart rate; tilt-table testing
Autonomic reflex screen (deep breathing, Valsalva, QSART)
Glucose, HbA1c, B12, paraprotein, ganglionic AChR antibodies

case.story: Faints after standing up from meals, urinary retention and dry eyes developing over six weeks after a flu-like illness.
case.exam: Orthostatic BP drop 50/20 mmHg without heart rate rise, sluggish pupils.
case.tests: Ganglionic AChR antibody strongly positive.
case.q: Which treatable autonomic disorder is this?
case.a: Autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy; treat with immunotherapy (IVIG, plasma exchange, steroids).

read.where: Chapter 32 Autonomic Aspects of Neurology — Classification of Autonomic Dysfunction

det.patho: The autonomic nervous system includes central networks (insula, hypothalamus, brainstem), preganglionic neurons in brainstem and spinal cord, autonomic ganglia and postganglionic fibres, plus the enteric system. Disorders may affect any level: neurodegeneration, autoimmunity, metabolic injury or genetic defects.
det.clinical: This is a group heading. Orthostatic hypotension is the most disabling feature, with supine hypertension often coexisting in central disorders. Gut, bladder, sexual and sudomotor symptoms vary. Distinguishing central from peripheral autonomic failure guides prognosis.
det.diagnosis: Bedside orthostatic vital signs, standard autonomic tests, plasma noradrenaline (low supine in peripheral failure), skin biopsy and antibody tests help locate the lesion. Search for underlying diabetes, amyloidosis, paraprotein and neurodegeneration.
det.treatment: Non-drug measures (fluids, salt, compression garments, head-up tilt at night) come first. Drugs include midodrine, fludrocortisone, droxidopa and pyridostigmine. Treat the underlying cause and individual symptoms.
det.prognosis: Depends on the cause; synucleinopathies progress, autoimmune forms may improve with treatment.
pearls: Orthostatic hypotension without compensatory tachycardia suggests neurogenic cause.
Subacute pandysautonomia: test ganglionic AChR antibodies.
Treat supine hypertension when treating orthostatic hypotension.
det.thd: Autonomic disorders คือกลุ่มโรคที่ระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติทำงานผิดปกติ ทั้งส่วนกลาง เช่น MSA และพาร์กินสัน และส่วนปลาย เช่น เบาหวาน amyloid หรือภูมิคุ้มกัน อาการได้แก่ หน้ามืดเวลาลุก ปัสสาวะลำบาก ท้องผูก เหงื่อผิดปกติ และสมรรถภาพทางเพศเสื่อม ตรวจวัดความดันท่านอนและยืน tilt test และหาสาเหตุ การรักษาเริ่มจากเพิ่มน้ำและเกลือ ถุงน่องรัด แล้วใช้ยาเช่น midodrine หรือ fludrocortisone

name: Autonomic failure
formal: Failure of autonomic regulation, causing orthostatic hypotension, anhidrosis, impaired heart rate control and gut and bladder dysfunction, in conditions such as MSA, Parkinson disease and diabetes.
simple: Loss of the body's automatic controls, causing dizziness on standing, abnormal sweating and bladder and bowel problems.
th: ระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติล้มเหลว ทำให้ความดันตกเวลาลุกยืน ไม่มีเหงื่อ หัวใจปรับอัตราเต้นไม่ได้ และลำไส้กระเพาะปัสสาวะผิดปกติ พบใน MSA, Parkinson และเบาหวาน
tempoNote: Usually chronic progressive; subacute in autoimmune or paraneoplastic forms
feat: Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension: sustained fall of at least 20/10 mmHg within 3 minutes with little heart-rate rise
Coat-hanger neck pain, dizziness after meals or heat, syncope
Anhidrosis, constipation, urinary retention or urgency, erectile dysfunction
Supine hypertension frequently coexists
Pure autonomic failure may later convert to PD, DLB or MSA
inv: Orthostatic BP and HR; tilt test; 24-hour ambulatory BP
Autonomic reflex screen and plasma noradrenaline
Search for cause: MRI, DaT-SPECT, glucose, paraprotein, amyloid, antibodies

case.story: Three years of fainting when standing up after breakfast, constipation and acting out dreams at night; no tremor or stiffness.
case.exam: BP 150/90 lying, 90/60 standing at 3 minutes with HR change of 4 bpm; no parkinsonism.
case.tests: Supine noradrenaline low; cardiac MIBG uptake reduced.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and long-term concern?
case.a: Pure autonomic failure; many patients later phenoconvert to Parkinson disease, DLB or MSA.

read.where: Chapter 32 Autonomic Aspects of Neurology — Clinical Features in Patients with Autonomic Failure

det.patho: Autonomic failure arises from loss of central autonomic neurons (MSA), postganglionic sympathetic neurons (PD, DLB, pure autonomic failure), or peripheral fibres (neuropathies). Impaired noradrenaline release on standing leads to blood pooling and hypotension.
det.clinical: Patients describe light-headedness, blurred vision, neck and shoulder ache, or cognitive slowing on standing, worse in the morning, after meals and in heat. Supine hypertension is common, especially at night. REM sleep behaviour disorder suggests synucleinopathy.
det.diagnosis: Confirm neurogenic orthostatic hypotension by sustained BP drop with a heart rate rise of less than about 0.5 bpm per mmHg fall. Classify central versus peripheral using noradrenaline levels, MIBG and skin biopsy for alpha-synuclein.
det.treatment: Remove offending drugs, increase salt and fluids, use compression garments, sleep with head up and drink water before standing. Midodrine, droxidopa, fludrocortisone and pyridostigmine are options; avoid lying flat at night if supine hypertension. Treat bladder and bowel symptoms.
det.prognosis: Variable: pure autonomic failure may remain isolated for years; MSA progresses quickly.
pearls: A heart rate that barely rises with a big BP fall is neurogenic.
Pure autonomic failure is a prodrome of synucleinopathy in many.
Bolus water drinking can raise BP for about an hour.
det.thd: Autonomic failure คือระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติล้มเหลว ผู้ป่วยหน้ามืดหรือเป็นลมเวลาลุกยืน โดยเฉพาะหลังอาหารหรืออากาศร้อน โดยที่หัวใจไม่เต้นเร็วขึ้นชดเชย ร่วมกับท้องผูก ปัสสาวะผิดปกติ และไม่มีเหงื่อ พบใน MSA, Parkinson, DLB, pure autonomic failure และเบาหวาน การรักษาคือดื่มน้ำ เพิ่มเกลือ ถุงน่องรัด นอนหัวสูง และยา midodrine หรือ fludrocortisone

name: Autonomic neuropathy
formal: Damage to autonomic nerves causing orthostatic hypotension, anhidrosis, bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction, caused by diabetes, amyloid, autoimmunity or toxins.
simple: Nerve damage affecting automatic functions like blood pressure, digestion and sweating.
more: Autonomic reflex testing; treat cause and symptoms such as with fludrocortisone and midodrine. Damage to autonomic nerve fibres from diabetes, amyloidosis, autoimmune disease or toxins, producing orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis, sweating abnormalities and bladder dysfunction.
th: เส้นประสาทอัตโนมัติเสียหาย ทำให้ความดันตกเวลาลุก ไม่มีเหงื่อ ปัสสาวะ ลำไส้ และสมรรถภาพทางเพศผิดปกติ จากเบาหวาน amyloid ภูมิคุ้มกัน หรือสารพิษ
tempoNote: Chronic in diabetes and amyloid; subacute in autoimmune or paraneoplastic; acute in GBS or botulism
feat: Orthostatic hypotension, resting tachycardia, exercise intolerance
Gastroparesis, diarrhoea or constipation, bladder retention, erectile dysfunction
Distal anhidrosis with compensatory sweating elsewhere
Often accompanied by painful small-fibre sensory neuropathy
Causes: diabetes, amyloidosis, autoimmune ganglionopathy, Sjogren, paraneoplastic, HIV, toxins (vincristine), hereditary (HSAN)
inv: Autonomic reflex screen, QSART or sudomotor tests, tilt test
Skin biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fibre density
HbA1c, paraprotein, TTR, ganglionic AChR antibodies, anti-Hu, anti-Ro/La, HIV

case.who: 49-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes for 25 years from Nakhon Ratchasima
case.story: Vomiting undigested food after meals, dizziness on standing and nocturnal diarrhoea.
case.exam: Resting HR 105, orthostatic drop 30/10 mmHg, stocking sensory loss, retinopathy.
case.tests: Gastric emptying delayed; heart rate variability to deep breathing absent.
case.q: What unifies her symptoms?
case.a: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy affecting cardiovascular and gut function.

det.patho: Thin myelinated and unmyelinated fibres carrying autonomic signals are damaged by metabolic injury, amyloid deposition, immune attack on ganglia or toxins. Vagal fibres, being long, are often affected early, causing resting tachycardia.
det.clinical: Patients have varied symptoms depending on organs affected. Cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy increases cardiac and perioperative risk. Gastroparesis complicates glucose control. Hypoglycaemia unawareness can coexist.
det.diagnosis: Standardised autonomic testing quantifies severity. Cause-directed work-up is essential, especially for treatable causes (autoimmune, amyloid, paraneoplastic).
det.treatment: Treat the cause (glycaemic control, immunotherapy, TTR therapies, tumour treatment). Symptomatic care includes midodrine and fludrocortisone for orthostatic hypotension, prokinetics and dietary changes for gastroparesis, bladder catheterisation, and PDE5 inhibitors for erectile dysfunction.
det.prognosis: Cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy in diabetes is associated with higher mortality.
pearls: Fixed resting tachycardia in diabetes suggests cardiac vagal neuropathy.
Subacute onset demands search for autoimmune or paraneoplastic cause.
Small-fibre sensory symptoms often accompany it.
det.thd: Autonomic neuropathy คือเส้นประสาทอัตโนมัติส่วนปลายเสียหาย ทำให้หน้ามืดเวลาลุก หัวใจเต้นเร็วตลอด อาหารค้างในกระเพาะ ท้องเสียกลางคืน ปัสสาวะไม่ออก และเหงื่อผิดปกติ สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยคือเบาหวาน รองลงมาคือ amyloid ภูมิคุ้มกัน มะเร็ง และยาเคมีบำบัด ตรวจ autonomic test และหาสาเหตุ การรักษาคือแก้สาเหตุร่วมกับการรักษาอาการแต่ละระบบ

name: Autosomal dominant Emery—Dreifuss muscular dystrophy (EDMD)/
formal: LMNA or EMD-associated muscular dystrophy with early elbow, Achilles, and spine contractures, humeroperoneal weakness, and cardiac conduction disease and arrhythmias risking sudden death.
simple: A genetic muscle disease causing early joint tightening, weakness in the upper arms and lower legs, and heart rhythm problems.
more: Genetic testing of LMNA confirms it; cardiac monitoring and early pacemaker or defibrillator are crucial. Physiotherapy and contracture release help; heart disease drives prognosis.
th: กล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมจากยีน LMNA (หรือ EMD ในชนิด X-linked) มีข้อติดที่ข้อศอก เอ็นร้อยหวาย และกระดูกสันหลังตั้งแต่เนิ่น อ่อนแรงแบบ humeroperoneal และโรคการนำไฟฟ้าหัวใจเสี่ยงเสียชีวิตเฉียบพลัน

feat: Early contractures of elbows, Achilles tendons and posterior neck (rigid spine) before major weakness
Humeroperoneal weakness: biceps, triceps, tibialis anterior and peronei
Cardiac conduction block, atrial arrhythmias, dilated cardiomyopathy and sudden death
Autosomal dominant LMNA forms; X-linked EMD form (emerin) is the classic type
inv: ECG, Holter, echocardiography and cardiac MRI
CK normal or mildly raised
LMNA (and EMD, FHL1) genetic testing

case.story: Could never straighten his elbows fully, walks on toes since childhood; his mother had a pacemaker at 35 and died suddenly.
case.exam: Elbow flexion contractures, tight Achilles tendons, limited neck flexion, weak biceps and ankle dorsiflexors.
case.tests: ECG shows first-degree AV block; CK 450 U/L; LMNA pathogenic variant.
case.q: What is the most urgent management step?
case.a: Cardiac assessment for ICD (not just pacemaker), as LMNA carriers are at high risk of sudden arrhythmic death.

read.where: Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Muscular Dystrophies

det.patho: Lamin A/C and emerin are nuclear envelope proteins; defects weaken the nucleus under mechanical stress and disturb gene regulation in muscle and heart. LMNA variants also cause other laminopathies (lipodystrophy, progeria, LGMD1B, isolated cardiomyopathy).
det.clinical: The triad is early contractures, humeroperoneal weakness and cardiac disease. Cardiac involvement can be the presenting or only feature in some family members. Atrial standstill, AV block and ventricular arrhythmias occur.
det.diagnosis: Clinical pattern, cardiac findings and family history guide genetic testing. Muscle MRI shows characteristic patterns. Cardiac evaluation is needed even in asymptomatic carriers.
det.treatment: Annual cardiac monitoring. ICD rather than pacemaker is often recommended in LMNA carriers with risk factors because of ventricular arrhythmias; anticoagulation for atrial arrhythmias. Physiotherapy, stretching and selective tendon surgery for contractures; heart transplant for end-stage cardiomyopathy.
det.prognosis: Cardiac disease drives survival; with modern cardiac care many live into later adulthood.
pearls: Contractures before weakness plus heart block: think EDMD.
LMNA carriers often need an ICD, not just a pacemaker.
Screen relatives with ECG even if they have no muscle symptoms.
det.thd: Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy ชนิดยีนเด่นเกิดจากยีน LMNA ผู้ป่วยมีข้อศอก ข้อเท้า และคอติดตั้งแต่เด็กก่อนจะอ่อนแรง กล้ามเนื้อต้นแขนและหน้าแข้งอ่อนแรง และที่สำคัญคือโรคหัวใจ ทั้งการนำไฟฟ้าผิดปกติและหัวใจเต้นผิดจังหวะที่อาจเสียชีวิตเฉียบพลัน ต้องตรวจหัวใจเป็นประจำและมักต้องใส่ ICD ญาติควรได้รับการตรวจ ECG และยีน

ddx.pt: Collagen VI disorder with contractures but no cardiac involvement
X-linked emerin form in boys with similar phenotype
Facial and scapular weakness without early contractures or conduction block

name: Autosomal dominant frontal lobe epilepsy (ADNFLE)
formal: Familial focal epilepsy with clustered brief nocturnal hypermotor seizures from sleep, often caused by mutations of nicotinic receptor subunit genes (CHRNA4, CHRNB2) or KCNT1.
simple: An inherited form of epilepsy with brief, violent-looking seizures from sleep, caused by a gene change affecting brain signalling.
more: Ictal EEG and interictal MRI are often normal, so video-EEG or polysomnography is needed to distinguish from parasomnias and functional events. Carbamazepine is first-line; pharmacoresistance in around a third, and the disorder is often misdiagnosed.
th: โรคลมชักเฉพาะที่ถ่ายทอดทางพันธุกรรมแบบเด่น มีอาการชักแบบเคลื่อนไหวรุนแรงสั้น ๆ เป็นชุดขณะหลับ จากยีน CHRNA4, CHRNB2 หรือ KCNT1 ปัจจุบันเรียก ADSHE
tempoNote: Begins in childhood or adolescence; brief seizures cluster during NREM sleep, often nightly
feat: Clusters of brief (under 2 minutes) seizures arising from sleep, often stage 2 NREM
Hypermotor movements: thrashing, pedalling, dystonic posturing, vocalisation
Abrupt onset and offset; patient often aware and remembers events
Family history of similar 'nightmares' or sleepwalking in multiple generations
Frequently misdiagnosed as parasomnia or psychogenic events
inv: Video-polysomnography or video-EEG to capture events
Scalp EEG often normal even during attacks; MRI usually normal
Genetic testing: CHRNA4, CHRNB2, CHRNA2, KCNT1, DEPDC5

case.story: Wakes several times a night with sudden thrashing and shouting lasting 30 seconds; he remembers some of them. His father had similar 'night attacks' as a teenager.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination.
case.tests: Video-polysomnography captures stereotyped hypermotor events from NREM stage 2 with little EEG change; MRI normal; CHRNA4 variant found.
case.q: Which features separate this from NREM parasomnia?
case.a: Highly stereotyped, brief, clustered events through the night, often with awareness, versus longer variable confused arousals in the first third of sleep; carbamazepine is effective.

det.patho: Variants in genes for neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunits (CHRNA4, CHRNB2, CHRNA2) increase receptor sensitivity and alter thalamocortical arousal circuits. KCNT1 variants cause more severe forms with intellectual disability; DEPDC5 and other mTOR pathway genes also contribute. Penetrance is about 70%.
det.clinical: Onset is usually in childhood or teenage years. Seizures emerge from NREM sleep in clusters, with sudden arousal, hyperkinetic or tonic-dystonic movements, and sometimes fear or vocalisation. Daytime seizures are rare. Intellectual function is usually normal except in KCNT1 cases; psychiatric comorbidity can occur. The syndrome is now called sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy (SHE) because not all seizures arise from the frontal lobe.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on history from bed partners, home video and video-polysomnography. Interictal and even ictal scalp EEG may be normal or obscured by artefact, so a normal EEG does not exclude it. Stereotypy, brevity and clustering help separate it from parasomnias. Genetic testing supports familial cases.
det.treatment: Carbamazepine at low-to-moderate doses is first-line, with oxcarbazepine or topiramate as alternatives; nicotine patches have helped some CHRNA4 cases. About a third are drug-resistant; epilepsy surgery is considered for those with a lesional focus. Counselling about inheritance is important.
det.prognosis: Lifelong but often improves in middle age; seizures rarely cause harm beyond disturbed sleep.
pearls: Brief, stereotyped, clustered events every night from NREM sleep: think SHE/ADNFLE.
Normal EEG does not exclude it — capture the events on video.
Carbamazepine usually works well.
det.thd: ADNFLE หรือปัจจุบันเรียก sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy เป็นโรคลมชักทางพันธุกรรมแบบเด่น เกิดจากยีนตัวรับ nicotinic acetylcholine อาการคือชักสั้น ๆ ขณะหลับ มีการดิ้น เตะ ตะโกน เกิดเป็นชุดหลายครั้งต่อคืน มักถูกวินิจฉัยผิดว่าเป็นละเมอหรือฝันร้าย EEG อาจปกติ ต้องอัดวิดีโอหรือทำ video-polysomnography รักษาด้วย carbamazepine ได้ผลดีในส่วนใหญ่

ddx.pt: NREM arousal disorders are longer, less stereotyped, occur early in the night and rarely cluster
Arise from wakefulness on EEG, prolonged, fluctuating with eye closure
Dream enactment in later night REM sleep, older adults, REM without atonia on PSG
