name: Autosomal dominant leukodystrophy
formal: Inherited CNS white matter disorders with dominant transmission, including adult-onset LMNB1 duplication leukodystrophy with autonomic dysfunction, pyramidal signs and cerebellar ataxia.
simple: An inherited disease passed from one parent that gradually damages the brain's white matter, causing stiffness, imbalance and autonomic problems.
th: โรคเนื้อสมองขาวเสื่อมทางพันธุกรรมแบบเด่นในผู้ใหญ่ จากยีน LMNB1 มีระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติล้มเหลวก่อน แล้วตามด้วยอาการ pyramidal และ ataxia
tempoNote: Onset in 40s–50s, slowly progressive over 10–20 years
feat: Autosomal dominant; onset typically in the fifth or sixth decade
Early autonomic failure: bladder and bowel dysfunction, erectile dysfunction, orthostatic hypotension
Later spastic paraparesis, cerebellar ataxia and cognitive slowing
MRI: symmetric frontoparietal and cerebellar white matter change, often sparing periventricular rims
Mimics primary progressive multiple sclerosis or multiple system atrophy
inv: Brain and spinal MRI
Genetic testing for LMNB1 duplication or upstream deletion
Autonomic function tests; exclude other adult leukodystrophies (VLCFA, arylsulfatase A)

case.who: 52-year-old man from Phitsanulok whose mother had a similar walking problem
case.story: Three years of urinary urgency and dizziness on standing, then stiff legs and unsteady gait over the past year.
case.exam: Postural blood pressure drop of 35 mmHg without heart-rate rise, spastic legs with brisk reflexes, bilateral extensor plantars, heel-shin ataxia.
case.tests: MRI shows confluent symmetric cerebral and middle cerebellar peduncle white matter signal; CSF without oligoclonal bands; LMNB1 duplication detected.
case.q: Why was this not primary progressive MS?
case.a: Prominent early autonomic failure, symmetric white matter change, a dominant family history and no oligoclonal bands point to LMNB1 autosomal dominant leukodystrophy.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Adult-Onset Inherited Leukodystrophies

det.patho: Duplication of LMNB1, or deletions upstream that boost its expression, increases lamin B1 in the nuclear envelope. Oligodendrocytes appear especially sensitive, leading to myelin loss with relative axonal preservation. The reason for early autonomic involvement is not fully understood.
det.clinical: Autonomic symptoms, particularly bladder and bowel disturbance and orthostatic hypotension, often precede motor signs by years. Pyramidal weakness of the legs, upper limb involvement and cerebellar ataxia follow, with mild cognitive change late. The course spans one to two decades. Family history may be missed if relatives were labelled as MS.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows symmetric white matter abnormality in frontal and parietal lobes, corticospinal tracts and cerebellar peduncles, often extending into the cord. Genetic testing by copy-number analysis confirms LMNB1 duplication or upstream deletion; standard sequencing may miss it. Exclude X-ALD, metachromatic leukodystrophy, CADASIL and MS.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy is available. Management targets orthostatic hypotension, bladder and bowel symptoms, spasticity and mobility. Physiotherapy and assistive devices maintain function. Genetic counselling is important for relatives.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive, leading to severe disability and death typically 10–20 years after onset.
pearls: Adult leukodystrophy starting with autonomic failure suggests LMNB1.
Request copy-number testing, as sequencing panels can miss duplications.
Relatives labelled with 'progressive MS' may be a clue to dominant inheritance.
det.thd: เป็นโรคเนื้อสมองขาวเสื่อมทางพันธุกรรมแบบเด่นในผู้ใหญ่ เกิดจาก lamin B1 มากเกินไปจาก duplication ของ LMNB1 อาการเริ่มด้วยระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติผิดปกติ เช่น ปัสสาวะผิดปกติและความดันตกเมื่อลุกยืน ต่อมาขาเกร็งและเดินเซ MRI พบ white matter ผิดปกติแบบสมมาตร ยังไม่มียาเฉพาะ รักษาตามอาการ

qx.stem: A 48-year-old woman from Nan has orthostatic dizziness, constipation and urinary urgency for five years, followed by leg stiffness and mild ataxia. Her mother had similar symptoms in her fifties. MRI shows symmetric white matter change extending into the middle cerebellar peduncles, with corticospinal tract involvement.
qx.q: What is the likely genetic mechanism?
opts: Duplication of LMNB1
Expansion of CGG repeats in FMR1
Biallelic DARS2 variants
Mitochondrial DNA point mutation
ABCD1 deletion
qx.why: Early autonomic failure followed by pyramidal and cerebellar signs, dominant inheritance and extensive white matter disease with middle cerebellar peduncle involvement characterise adult-onset autosomal dominant leukodystrophy, usually due to duplication of the LMNB1 gene (overexpression of lamin B1). FMR1 premutation gives FXTAS, DARS2 gives LBSL, and ABCD1 gives X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.

ddx.pt: Autonomic failure with parkinsonism or ataxia but no diffuse white matter disease
Asymmetric periventricular lesions and oligoclonal bands; no family history
X-linked, raised VLCFA, adrenal insufficiency; spinal cord predominant

name: Autosomal dominant optic atrophy
formal: Inherited optic neuropathy, usually OPA1-related, causing bilateral slowly progressive central visual loss with temporal disc pallor and colour vision defects from childhood.
simple: An inherited eye nerve disease that slowly reduces central vision in both eyes, usually starting in childhood.
more: Autosomal dominant optic atrophy from OPA1 mutation, with childhood onset of slowly progressive bilateral central visual loss and temporal disc pallor, with blue-yellow colour defect.
th: โรคประสาทตาเสื่อมทางพันธุกรรม มักจากยีน OPA1 ทำให้มองเห็นตรงกลางลดลงช้า ๆ ทั้งสองตาตั้งแต่เด็ก ขั้วประสาทตาซีดด้าน temporal และตาบอดสีน้ำเงิน-เหลือง
tempoNote: Insidious visual decline beginning in the first decade, slowly progressive
feat: Bilateral symmetric gradual central or centrocaecal visual loss
Temporal or diffuse optic disc pallor
Blue-yellow (tritan) colour vision defect
OPA1-plus: sensorineural deafness, ataxia, myopathy, ophthalmoplegia, neuropathy
Variable expressivity within families
inv: Visual fields, colour vision testing, OCT showing temporal RNFL thinning
OPA1 (and OPA3) genetic testing
Audiology and neurological examination for OPA1-plus

case.story: Struggles to read the board; her father and grandmother also have poor vision since childhood.
case.exam: Visual acuity 6/24 both eyes, bilateral temporal disc pallor, central scotomas, tritan defect.
case.tests: OCT shows temporal RNFL thinning; OPA1 variant confirmed.
case.q: What distinguishes this from LHON?
case.a: ADOA is insidious, symmetric and dominant from childhood; LHON is acute, sequential, maternally inherited and more often in young men.

read.where: Chapter 22 Neuro-Ophthalmology — Autosomal Dominant Optic Atrophy

det.patho: OPA1 encodes a mitochondrial inner membrane protein needed for fusion and cristae maintenance. Haploinsufficiency or dominant-negative variants impair energy production, and retinal ganglion cells, especially the papillomacular bundle, degenerate.
det.clinical: Vision declines insidiously from childhood, often unnoticed until school screening. Severity ranges from near normal to legal blindness. About 20% have OPA1-plus features, particularly with missense variants.
det.diagnosis: Clinical pattern with family history plus OCT and genetic confirmation. Exclude compressive, toxic, nutritional and other hereditary optic neuropathies.
det.treatment: No approved disease-modifying treatment; idebenone has been tried with uncertain benefit and gene therapies are in development. Low-vision aids, educational support and genetic counselling. Avoid tobacco, excess alcohol and mitochondrial toxins.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; most retain useful navigational vision.
pearls: Childhood bilateral optic atrophy with dominant family history: OPA1.
Tritan colour defect is characteristic.
Look for deafness and neuromuscular signs (OPA1-plus).
det.thd: Autosomal dominant optic atrophy หรือ Kjer เกิดจากยีน OPA1 ที่ทำให้ไมโทคอนเดรียทำงานผิดปกติ เซลล์ประสาทจอตาเสื่อม เด็กจะมองเห็นตรงกลางลดลงช้า ๆ ทั้งสองตา ขั้วประสาทตาซีดด้าน temporal และตาบอดสีน้ำเงิน-เหลือง มักมีคนในครอบครัวเป็นด้วย บางรายมีหูหนวกหรือเดินเซร่วม ยังไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ ใช้อุปกรณ์ช่วยการมองเห็นและให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

ddx.pt: Acute painless sequential loss in young men; maternal inheritance
Similar centrocaecal scotomas; nutritional deficiency or toxin exposure
Cupping with arcuate field loss; raised or normal pressure

aN: kjer optic neuropathy | adoa | opa1 optic atrophy | dominant optic atrophy

name: Autosomal recessive cardiomyopathy and ophthalmoplegia (ARCO)
formal: Mitochondrial disorder due to recessive variants in mitochondrial genes such as MT-ND or related nuclear genes, producing dilated cardiomyopathy with progressive external ophthalmoplegia.
simple: A rare inherited condition causing weak heart muscle together with drooping eyelids and trouble moving the eyes.
more: Diagnosed through muscle biopsy with ragged-red or COX-negative fibres and gene panels. Treatment is supportive with heart failure therapy; transplantation may be considered.
th: โรคไมโทคอนเดรียทางพันธุกรรมแบบด้อยที่มีกล้ามเนื้อหัวใจผิดปกติร่วมกับกลอกตาไม่ได้ (ophthalmoplegia) และกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง
tempoNote: Childhood or early adult onset with slow progression; cardiac failure may dominate
feat: Progressive external ophthalmoplegia and ptosis
Dilated cardiomyopathy, sometimes the first or the life-limiting feature
Proximal myopathy and exercise intolerance
Recessive inheritance; reported mainly with nuclear-encoded mitochondrial gene defects
Very rare; clinical spectrum incompletely defined
inv: Echocardiogram, ECG, cardiac MRI
CK, lactate; muscle biopsy for COX-negative or ragged-red fibres
Muscle mtDNA analysis for multiple deletions; nuclear gene panel or exome

case.who: 19-year-old man from Ubon Ratchathani; parents are first cousins
case.story: Droopy eyelids since age 12, now double vision rarely; recent breathlessness on climbing to the second floor.
case.exam: Bilateral ptosis, restricted eye movements in all directions, mild neck and proximal weakness, displaced apex beat.
case.tests: Echo LVEF 30% with dilated LV; lactate mildly high; biopsy shows COX-negative fibres and multiple mtDNA deletions.
case.q: Why must cardiac assessment be part of the work-up for ptosis here?
case.a: This is a recessive mitochondrial cardiomyopathy-ophthalmoplegia picture (ARCO); heart failure drives prognosis and needs early heart failure therapy.

det.patho: ARCO describes a recessively inherited mitochondrial disorder in which defective nuclear genes affecting mtDNA maintenance or oxidative phosphorylation produce secondary mtDNA deletions in muscle and heart. Extraocular and cardiac muscle are particularly vulnerable because of their high energy demands. The precise genes and frequency are not well established, and the label appears in only a few reports.
det.clinical: Patients develop ptosis and progressive external ophthalmoplegia, usually without diplopia, together with dilated cardiomyopathy. Limb myopathy and exercise intolerance are common. Cardiac failure or arrhythmia may be the presenting problem. Because evidence is limited, the full range of features remains uncertain.
det.diagnosis: Combine cardiac imaging with a mitochondrial work-up: lactate, muscle biopsy for COX-negative and ragged-red fibres, and long-range PCR for multiple mtDNA deletions. Exome or mitochondrial nuclear gene panels identify the causative gene. Exclude myasthenia, oculopharyngeal dystrophy and Kearns–Sayre syndrome.
det.treatment: There is no curative therapy. Cardiac care follows heart failure guidelines and may include devices or transplant evaluation. Ptosis surgery is considered when vision is obstructed. Exercise, avoidance of mitochondrial toxins such as valproate, and genetic counselling are recommended.
det.prognosis: Determined largely by severity of the cardiomyopathy; data are limited.
pearls: Ophthalmoplegia with cardiomyopathy should trigger a mitochondrial evaluation and cardiac surveillance.
Multiple mtDNA deletions suggest a nuclear maintenance gene defect, not a sporadic single deletion.
Little is known about this rare label; treat it as part of the mitochondrial PEO-plus spectrum.
det.thd: ARCO เป็นโรคไมโทคอนเดรียหายากที่ถ่ายทอดแบบด้อย ทำให้หนังตาตกและกลอกตาไม่ได้ร่วมกับกล้ามเนื้อหัวใจโตอ่อนแรง ตัดชิ้นเนื้อกล้ามเนื้อมักพบ COX-negative fibre และ mtDNA หลายตำแหน่งขาดหาย ไม่มีการรักษาจำเพาะ แต่ต้องดูแลหัวใจอย่างใกล้ชิดเพราะเป็นตัวกำหนดพยากรณ์โรค

ddx.pt: Sporadic single deletion, onset before 20, retinopathy and conduction block rather than dilated cardiomyopathy
Ophthalmoplegia and ptosis without significant cardiomyopathy
X-linked hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with myopathy and intellectual disability, no ophthalmoplegia

name: Autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxias
formal: Heterogeneous group including Friedreich ataxia, ataxia-telangiectasia, AOA and others, typically of childhood onset with neuropathy, extracerebellar signs and early-onset progressive ataxia.
simple: A group of inherited diseases needing a faulty gene from both parents, causing unsteadiness and poor coordination, usually from childhood.
th: กลุ่มโรคเดินเซทางพันธุกรรมแบบด้อย เช่น Friedreich ataxia, ataxia-telangiectasia, AOA มักเริ่มในเด็กหรือวัยรุ่น ร่วมกับเส้นประสาทเสื่อมและอาการนอกสมองน้อย
tempoNote: Usually onset before 25 years with slow progression; late-onset forms (e.g. some Friedreich, CANVAS) exist
feat: Progressive gait and limb ataxia with dysarthria, often beginning in childhood
Sensory neuronopathy or axonal neuropathy, areflexia, pes cavus, scoliosis
Extra features point to subtype: cardiomyopathy and diabetes (Friedreich), telangiectasia and infections (AT), oculomotor apraxia (AOA), spasticity (ARSACS)
Consanguinity or affected siblings with healthy parents
Treatable forms: AVED, cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis, coenzyme Q10 deficiency, Refsum
inv: MRI brain and spine (cerebellar or spinal atrophy)
NCS and EMG; ECG and echocardiogram
Bloods: vitamin E, alpha-fetoprotein, albumin, cholesterol, cholestanol, phytanic acid, lactate
Genetic testing: FXN repeat, then NGS ataxia panel or exome, RFC1 for late onset

case.who: 14-year-old girl from Phetchabun with consanguineous parents
case.story: Clumsy since age 9, now falls often and her writing has deteriorated; recent palpitations.
case.exam: Gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, absent reflexes, impaired vibration and joint position sense, extensor plantars, pes cavus, scoliosis.
case.tests: ECG shows T-wave inversion; echo left ventricular hypertrophy; FXN GAA repeat expansion on both alleles.
case.q: Which recessive ataxia is this and what non-neurological screening is needed?
case.a: Friedreich ataxia; regular cardiac surveillance and diabetes screening; omaveloxolone is approved from age 16.

read.where: Chapter 24 Cerebellar Ataxias and Related Conditions — Inherited Ataxia Syndromes
Chapter 73: Cerebellar Disorders and Ataxias: Acquired Disorders

det.patho: These disorders result from biallelic variants affecting mitochondrial function (frataxin), DNA repair (ATM, APTX, SETX), lipid metabolism, protein folding and other pathways. Cerebellar Purkinje cells, dorsal root ganglia and spinal tracts are especially vulnerable. Friedreich ataxia is the commonest worldwide but is less frequent in East Asian populations, where AOA and other forms may be relatively more common.
det.clinical: Most present before age 25 with progressive gait ataxia, often with neuropathy and areflexia. Non-neurological features (cardiomyopathy, diabetes, telangiectasia, immunodeficiency, cataract, tendon xanthomas) are diagnostic clues. Some forms have Babinski signs despite areflexia. Disability progresses over years to wheelchair dependence in many.
det.diagnosis: Use age of onset, MRI pattern, neuropathy type and biomarkers to narrow the list, then targeted or broad genetic testing. Always screen for treatable causes early: vitamin E, cholestanol, phytanic acid, CoQ10 and others. Alpha-fetoprotein is raised in ataxia-telangiectasia and AOA2. Family history may be negative in recessive disorders.
det.treatment: Treatable forms respond to vitamin E, chenodeoxycholic acid, dietary phytanate restriction or CoQ10. Omaveloxolone is approved for Friedreich ataxia. For others, physiotherapy, speech therapy, orthopaedic and cardiac care are central. Genetic counselling is essential for siblings and future pregnancies.
det.prognosis: Variable; Friedreich ataxia often shortens life through cardiomyopathy, while others progress slowly.
pearls: Areflexia with extensor plantars in a teenager: Friedreich until proven otherwise.
Check vitamin E in every unexplained recessive ataxia.
Raised AFP points to ataxia-telangiectasia or AOA2.
det.thd: กลุ่ม autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxia เป็นโรคเดินเซทางพันธุกรรมแบบด้อย มักเริ่มในเด็กหรือวัยรุ่น ตัวอย่างคือ Friedreich ataxia ataxia-telangiectasia และ AOA มักมีเส้นประสาทเสื่อมและอาการนอกระบบประสาทที่ช่วยแยกชนิด วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI NCS ตรวจเลือด และตรวจยีน ต้องคัดกรองชนิดที่รักษาได้ เช่น AVED เสมอ

name: Autosomal recessive mitochondrial ataxic syndrome
formal: POLG-related disorder with sensory ataxia, neuropathy, dysarthria, epilepsy and ophthalmoplegia (also called MIRAS), caused by recessive POLG variants affecting mitochondrial DNA replication.
simple: An inherited mitochondrial disease causing poor balance, nerve damage, seizures and eye muscle weakness.

det.patho: Biallelic POLG variants weaken the mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma, causing mtDNA depletion and accumulating deletions. Dorsal root ganglion neurons, cerebellar pathways, thalamus, olives and occipital cortex are especially vulnerable. Energy failure during infection or seizures may provoke acute neuronal necrosis that appears as stroke-like lesions on MRI.
det.clinical: MIRAS and SANDO belong to the POLG ataxia-neuropathy spectrum: sensory ataxia, cerebellar signs, ptosis and ophthalmoparesis arise in adolescence or adulthood. Epilepsy, often occipital and prone to status or epilepsia partialis continua, may be the first dramatic event and shapes the outcome. Headache resembling migraine, depression, myoclonus and liver dysfunction may follow, and symptoms can worsen sharply with illness or fasting.
det.diagnosis: Suspect POLG disease in any young adult with sensory or mixed ataxia, ophthalmoplegia or occipital seizures, particularly when no dominant family history exists. Nerve studies show a sensory neuronopathy, and MRI often reveals thalamic and cerebellar abnormalities. POLG sequencing confirms the diagnosis, and muscle biopsy is supportive but no longer essential. Check liver function and avoid valproate before any treatment decision is made.
det.treatment: Management is supportive: use non-valproate antiseizure drugs, treat status epilepticus early and aggressively, and arrange physiotherapy, balance aids and ptosis care when needed. Avoid prolonged fasting and other mitochondrial toxins. No disease-modifying therapy is established, and genetic counselling should be offered to the family.
det.prognosis: Variable. Progression is slow in some, but status epilepticus and liver failure account for much of the disability and many deaths.
pearls: Sensory ataxia plus ophthalmoplegia plus occipital seizures: test POLG.
Never give valproate until POLG disease is excluded in an unexplained ataxia-epilepsy picture.
Absent sensory potentials with ataxia point to a ganglionopathy, not only cerebellar disease.
det.thd: โรคนี้เกิดจากความผิดปกติของยีน POLG แบบ autosomal recessive ทำให้ mtDNA สร้างได้ไม่ดี พบในวัยรุ่นถึงผู้ใหญ่ตอนต้น อาการคือเดินเซจากการรับความรู้สึกเสียและสมองน้อยผิดปกติ ร่วมกับหนังตาตก กลอกตาไม่ได้ พูดไม่ชัด และอาจชักแบบ occipital จนเกิด status epilepticus การตรวจพบ sensory potential หายไปและ MRI พบรอยโรคที่ thalamus หรือสมองน้อย ยืนยันด้วยตรวจยีน POLG การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคองและต้องห้ามใช้ valproate เพราะเสี่ยงตับวายรุนแรง

det.patho: ARSACS results from biallelic SACS variants encoding sacsin, a very large protein that interacts with chaperones and regulates mitochondrial and neurofilament organisation. First described in a founder population in the Charlevoix and Saguenay regions of Quebec, it is now found worldwide and is one of the more frequent recessive ataxias outside Friedreich's. Purkinje cell loss, corticospinal degeneration and peripheral demyelination combine to produce the phenotype. Sacsin is abundant in Purkinje cells and motor neurons, and its loss leaves intermediate filaments bundled abnormally and mitochondria poorly divided. The Quebec founder alleles account for nearly all French-Canadian patients, whereas patients elsewhere mostly carry private truncating or missense variants, which partly explains why the eye and nerve findings vary between populations.
det.clinical: Children are noted to be unsteady when they start to walk (usually between 1 and 5 years), then develop progressive leg spasticity, ataxia, dysarthria, nystagmus and distal amyotrophy. The mix of pyramidal signs (brisk knees, Babinski) with lost ankle reflexes is typical, and pes cavus, hammer toes, distal wasting and reduced vibration sense accumulate as the neuropathy advances. Urinary urgency, mitral valve prolapse and thinning of the cervical cord are additional reported features; cognition is usually normal, though some have mild learning difficulties. Hypermyelinated retinal fibres are common in Quebec but often absent in patients from Asia and elsewhere, and many such children are first labelled as spastic diplegic cerebral palsy. Later-onset forms may resemble spastic paraplegia or a pure neuropathy.
det.diagnosis: Look for the triad of early cerebellar ataxia, lower-limb spasticity and sensorimotor neuropathy, with retinal nerve fibre thickening as a bonus finding. Nerve conduction typically shows prolonged distal motor latencies and slowed motor velocities with absent or tiny sensory potentials; ARSACS and Refsum disease are the recessive ataxias in which a demyelinating component is prominent, unlike the axonal sensory neuropathy of Friedreich ataxia. MRI shows atrophy of the upper vermis with the lower vermis relatively spared, linear T2/FLAIR dark bands across the pons, thick middle cerebellar peduncles and later cervical cord thinning, while the cerebral white matter stays normal; OCT is a cheap bedside supplement. Screening tests that rule out mimics — AFP, albumin, cholesterol, vitamin E, echocardiography and frataxin repeat testing — are normal. Confirm with SACS testing, including copy-number analysis since deletions occur.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying therapy; management is supportive: physiotherapy, stretching, antispasticity drugs or botulinum toxin for focal spasticity, ankle–foot orthoses, and orthopaedic care for foot deformity. Muscle coenzyme Q10 may be secondarily reduced in ARSACS, but high-dose CoQ10 given to affected patients has not improved ataxia scores, so it should not be promised as treatment. Bladder symptoms, falls and fractures, and later swallowing need attention. Speech and swallowing assessment and genetic counselling of siblings and parents should be offered.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive over decades; most patients need a wheelchair somewhere between their 30s and 50s, and typical survival reaches the sixth or seventh decade.
pearls: Spastic + ataxic + absent ankle jerks + thick retinal fibres: ARSACS.
Pontine 'stripes' on T2 MRI are a strong clue.
OCT is an inexpensive screening test before genetic confirmation.
A normal fundus does not exclude ARSACS outside Quebec; low muscle CoQ10 here is secondary and does not predict a response to supplements.

det.patho: Most cases are due to heterozygous mutations in VCP, encoding valosin-containing protein involved in protein degradation and autophagy. det.clinical: Myopathy is present in most patients, Paget disease in about half, and frontotemporal dementia in around a third. Motor neuron disease and parkinsonism can occur. Presentation varies widely even within families.
det.diagnosis: Suspect in a patient with myopathy plus Paget disease or FTD, or a family with mixed phenotypes. Muscle biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles; genetic testing confirms. Bone and cognitive screening are needed.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy exists; trials of VCP modulators are ongoing. Treat Paget disease with bisphosphonates, and manage cognitive and motor symptoms supportively. Respiratory and cardiac monitoring are advisable; genetic counselling for families.

det.patho: After transection or focal destruction, the distal axon undergoes an active program of self-destruction driven by SARM1 activation and NAD+ depletion, followed by myelin breakdown and macrophage clearance. In dying-back neuropathies, metabolic or toxic stress affects the longest axons first, causing distal-to-proximal degeneration. Schwann cells then form bands that guide regeneration.
det.clinical: Consequences depend on which fibres are lost: weakness and wasting from motor axons, numbness and pain from sensory axons, and autonomic disturbance from small fibres. Focal lesions produce territory-specific deficits; generalised processes cause length-dependent polyneuropathy. This entry describes a process and is not a standalone diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: Electrophysiology shows reduced amplitudes and denervation with near-normal velocities, but only after degeneration has occurred (about a week for NCS, two to three weeks for EMG). Biopsy confirms axonal loss and can show vasculitis or amyloid. Blood neurofilament light is an emerging biomarker of active axonal injury.
det.treatment: Treat the cause, such as decompression, nerve repair, immunotherapy or removal of a toxin. Rehabilitation, splinting and pain management bridge the regeneration period. SARM1 inhibitors are being studied as axon-protective drugs.
det.prognosis: Regeneration is slow and incomplete over long distances; proximal lesions recover poorly.
pearls: Early NCS after nerve injury can be falsely reassuring.
Axons regrow about 1 mm a day — estimate recovery time from lesion distance.
Low amplitude, normal velocity equals axonal.
det.thd: Axonal degeneration คือกระบวนการสลายของแกนประสาท แบบ Wallerian หลังบาดเจ็บเฉพาะที่ หรือแบบ dying-back จากปลายประสาทเข้ามาในโรคพิษหรือเมแทบอลิก เป็นพยาธิสภาพ ไม่ใช่โรคเฉพาะ NCS จะพบ amplitude ลดลงเมื่อผ่านไปประมาณหนึ่งสัปดาห์ และ EMG พบ fibrillation หลัง 2–3 สัปดาห์ การรักษาคือแก้สาเหตุและฟื้นฟูระหว่างรอแกนประสาทงอกใหม่

det.patho: In axonopathies the axon itself fails, typically because metabolic, toxic or genetic stress overwhelms axonal transport and energy supply in the longest fibres. The longest fibres to the feet fail first, explaining the stocking distribution. Schwann cells and myelin are secondarily affected.
det.clinical: Sensory symptoms begin in the toes and climb; by the time they reach the knees, the fingertips begin to be involved. Pain, imbalance and later distal weakness follow. Autonomic features accompany small-fibre involvement. Severity correlates with cause and duration.
det.diagnosis: Nerve conduction confirms axonal pattern and length dependence. A focused screen (glucose, B12, thyroid, renal, protein electrophoresis) identifies most treatable causes. Atypical features — rapid onset, asymmetry, proximal involvement, motor predominance — prompt further tests including CSF, nerve biopsy or genetics. A substantial fraction remain idiopathic.
det.treatment: Address the cause: glycaemic control, alcohol cessation, vitamin replacement, drug modification. Neuropathic pain responds to duloxetine, pregabalin, gabapentin or amitriptyline. Foot care, footwear and balance training prevent ulcers and falls.
det.prognosis: Usually slowly progressive or stable if the cause is controlled; recovery is limited once axons are lost.
pearls: Distal-first symmetrical sensory loss is the classic axonopathy.
Check B12 in diabetics on metformin.
Asymmetry or arm-first symptoms are red flags for a different process.

det.patho: Zidovudine, a thymidine analogue, inhibits mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma, leading to mtDNA depletion, impaired oxidative phosphorylation and lipid accumulation in muscle fibres. The same mechanism explains lactic acidosis, neuropathy and fat redistribution from other nucleoside analogues. Risk rises with dose and duration of therapy.
det.clinical: Symptoms include muscle pain, proximal weakness and easy fatigue developing after many months of treatment. Weakness is usually mild to moderate and symmetric, with muscle bulk preserved or reduced. Features of systemic mitochondrial toxicity may appear. HIV itself can cause polymyositis-like illness, so the two may coexist.
det.diagnosis: Check CK, lactate, and a medication timeline. EMG shows myopathic changes and biopsy demonstrates ragged-red fibres and COX-deficient fibres, in contrast to dense inflammatory infiltrates in HIV polymyositis. A trial of withdrawal both confirms and treats. Exclude statins, hypothyroidism, rhabdomyolysis and other infections.
det.treatment: Replace zidovudine with a regimen free of thymidine analogues, such as one based on tenofovir, lamivudine or an integrase inhibitor. Symptoms normally improve within weeks. Analgesia and graded exercise help, and steroids are reserved for coexisting inflammatory myopathy. Monitor lactate and liver function.
det.prognosis: Good; most patients recover strength after withdrawal.
pearls: Ragged-red fibres in an HIV patient on nucleoside analogues should prompt drug review.
Improvement after withdrawal supports the diagnosis.
Zidovudine is now rarely used, so the diagnosis is often historical.
det.thd: AZT myopathy เป็นกล้ามเนื้อเป็นพิษจากยา zidovudine ที่ยับยั้ง mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma ในผู้ติดเชื้อ HIV ที่ใช้ยานาน มีปวดกล้ามเนื้อ อ่อนแรงต้นขา CK สูงเล็กน้อย ตรวจชิ้นเนื้อพบ ragged-red fibres ต้องแยกจาก HIV myopathy จากการอักเสบ การรักษาคือหยุดหรือเปลี่ยนยา ส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นใน 2–6 สัปดาห์

name: Bacterial meningitis
formal: Acute purulent infection of the meninges with fever, headache, neck stiffness and altered consciousness, commonly caused by pneumococcus, meningococcus or Haemophilus, requiring urgent antibiotics.
simple: A serious bacterial infection of the membranes around the brain causing fever, severe headache, stiff neck and drowsiness, needing emergency treatment.

Cranial nerve palsies, seizures, hearing loss

qx.q: According to the WHO guidelines, which patient should have cranial imaging before lumbar puncture?
opts: A 2-year-old with fever, neck stiffness and a single brief seizure who is now alert
A 52-year-old man with fever, headache and a Glasgow Coma Score of 9
A 30-year-old with fever, neck stiffness, GCS 15 and no focal signs
A 10-year-old with petechiae, GCS 15 and neck stiffness
A 25-year-old with fever, photophobia, GCS 14 and no focal deficit
qx.why: WHO advises against routine imaging in suspected meningitis. Where CT is readily available it should precede lumbar puncture if the Glasgow Coma Score is below 10, there are focal neurological signs, cranial nerve palsies, swollen optic discs, a new seizure in an adult or severe immunosuppression. A first isolated seizure in a child without other risk features does not need imaging, and treatment must never be delayed for imaging.

det.patho: Most adult infections start with colonisation of the nasopharynx; encapsulated strains then enter the blood, resist complement and slip across the choroid plexus or brain capillaries into CSF, a space with little antibody or complement defence. Bacterial lysis releases wall components that drive a cytokine- and complement-led inflammatory storm, and it is this host reaction that produces brain swelling, failed autoregulation, arteritis, cortical vein and sinus thrombosis and hydrocephalus. Pneumococcus and meningococcus account for most adult cases; Listeria monocytogenes becomes important beyond about 50, in pregnancy, alcohol misuse and impaired T-cell immunity, while staphylococci and Gram-negative rods dominate after neurosurgery or shunting. Across South-East Asia, including Thailand, Streptococcus suis caught from raw pork dishes or handling pigs is a major adult cause and very often leaves permanent deafness.
det.clinical: Illness usually builds over hours to a day or two, but older or immunosuppressed people can drift in over several days with confusion as the main sign. The full fever–stiff neck–altered mentation triad is present in fewer than half, yet almost everyone has at least two of fever, headache, meningism and reduced consciousness; Kernig and Brudzinski signs are seldom positive, so their absence reassures little. A petechial or purpuric rash points to meningococcus but is also seen with pneumococcus and S. suis. Seizures, cranial nerve palsies (especially VIII), arterial or venous infarcts, hydrocephalus, subdural effusion or empyema, ventriculitis and cord infarction can arise at any stage, even after antibiotics finish, so any fresh deterioration needs repeat imaging. Always ask about ear or sinus infection, CSF leak or skull fracture, splenectomy, alcohol, HIV and pork exposure.
det.diagnosis: Draw blood cultures and give antibiotics within the first hour; neither scanning nor LP should hold treatment up. CT before LP is needed only for a GCS below about 12 or falling, focal signs, papilloedema, recent seizures or severe immunosuppression, and LP is deferred in shock, coagulopathy, a fast-spreading rash or skin sepsis at the puncture site. The classic CSF is turbid under high pressure, with hundreds to tens of thousands of mainly neutrophils, CSF:blood glucose below about 0.4 and protein usually above 1 g/L; a CSF lactate near 4 mmol/L or higher, if sampled before antibiotics, strongly favours bacteria over viruses. Gram stain, culture (still needed for susceptibility) and species-specific or multiplex PCR on CSF and EDTA blood identify the organism, and PCR often stays positive for days after antibiotics have sterilised cultures. Partial treatment and Listeria can make the CSF look lymphocytic; offer an HIV test to everyone.
det.treatment: Adult empirical cover is ceftriaxone 2 g IV 12-hourly (or cefotaxime), with vancomycin added where penicillin-resistant pneumococci are a concern, high-dose IV amoxicillin or ampicillin for Listeria in older, pregnant or immunocompromised patients, and acyclovir until HSV encephalitis is excluded; after neurosurgery use vancomycin with an anti-pseudomonal agent such as meropenem or ceftazidime. Dexamethasone 10 mg IV 6-hourly is begun with or just before the first antibiotic and continued for 4 days when pneumococcus is proven or likely, but stopped if another organism is identified. Once the isolate is known, narrow therapy: roughly 5–7 days for meningococcus, 10–14 days for pneumococcus and about 21 days for Listeria. Manage sepsis, seizures, raised pressure, hyponatraemia and fluids in a monitored bed, with ventricular drainage for symptomatic hydrocephalus. Report to public health, give close contacts of meningococcal cases prophylaxis (single-dose ciprofloxacin or rifampicin) and book a hearing test before discharge.
det.prognosis: Adult case fatality is still about 15–20% overall, highest with pneumococcus, older age, coma, seizures and delayed antibiotics; up to half of survivors carry deafness, cognitive slowing or focal deficits.
pearls: Antibiotics first; scan and LP afterwards whenever they would cause delay.
Deafness after meningitis in someone who eats raw pork dishes (e.g. larb or koi): suspect Streptococcus suis.
Fever with a non-blanching rash is meningococcal sepsis until proved otherwise.
A lymphocytic CSF does not rule out bacteria — think Listeria or prior antibiotics.
det.thd: เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบจากแบคทีเรียเป็นภาวะฉุกเฉินที่ต้องให้ยาภายในชั่วโมงแรก เชื้อหลักในผู้ใหญ่คือ pneumococcus และ meningococcus ผู้สูงอายุ หญิงตั้งครรภ์ และผู้ภูมิคุ้มกันต่ำต้องครอบคลุม Listeria ส่วนในไทยต้องนึกถึง Streptococcus suis จากการกินหมูดิบ ซึ่งมักทำให้หูหนวกถาวร อาการคือไข้ ปวดศีรษะ คอแข็ง ซึมสับสน แต่ไม่ครบทุกข้อเสมอ ให้เจาะเลือดเพาะเชื้อแล้วให้ ceftriaxone (± vancomycin, ampicillin, acyclovir) ร่วมกับ dexamethasone ทันที ทำ CT ก่อนเจาะหลังเฉพาะรายที่มีข้อบ่งชี้ น้ำไขสันหลังมี neutrophil สูง น้ำตาลต่ำ โปรตีนสูง ส่ง Gram stain เพาะเชื้อ และ PCR หลังหายควรตรวจการได้ยินและแจ้งควบคุมโรค

name: Bacterial spinal infection
formal: Infections of vertebrae, discs or epidural space (vertebral osteomyelitis, discitis, epidural abscess) causing back pain, fever and risk of cord compression.
simple: A bacterial infection in the spine that causes back pain and fever and can press on the spinal cord.
th: การติดเชื้อแบคทีเรียของกระดูกสันหลัง ได้แก่ vertebral osteomyelitis, discitis และ spinal epidural abscess ผู้ป่วยปวดหลังตำแหน่งชัด กดเจ็บ มีไข้หรือไม่ก็ได้ และมีปัจจัยเสี่ยง เช่น เบาหวาน ฉีดยาเข้าเส้น ไตวายเรื้อรัง ต้องส่ง MRI ทั้งแนวกระดูกสันหลังเร็ว เพาะเชื้อจากเลือดหรือชิ้นเนื้อก่อนให้ยาปฏิชีวนะ แล้วให้ยานานอย่างน้อย 6 สัปดาห์ ผ่าตัดเมื่อมีอ่อนแรง ไม่เสถียร หรือรักษาไม่ได้ผล
tempoNote: Axial pain for days to weeks, then radicular pain, weakness and paralysis can follow within days to hours
feat: Localised, worsening spinal pain with percussion tenderness, often worse at night; fever, sweats or rigors are frequent, yet a sizeable minority lack them and the white count may be normal
Risk factors: diabetes, injection drug use, chronic renal failure or dialysis, alcohol, immunosuppression, recent spinal surgery or injection, bacteraemia, endocarditis, a skin boil in only about 15%
Epidural abscess is most often thoracic (about half), then lumbar and cervical, and usually lies posterior to the cord; the classic sequence is spinal pain, radicular pain, weakness, then paralysis
Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest organism; in Thailand consider Burkholderia pseudomallei (melioidosis) in diabetics and TB (Pott disease), and Brucella and fungi in selected settings
Discitis and osteomyelitis often coexist, so finding one means looking for the other; children under 3 may refuse to walk or sit
inv: Urgent contrast MRI of the whole spine (skip lesions and multilevel abscess occur); CT guides biopsy and shows bone destruction
ESR and CRP (sensitive but non-specific), blood cultures before antibiotics, echocardiography if bacteraemia or a new murmur
Image-guided or open biopsy for culture, histology and TB or fungal studies when blood cultures are negative, preferably before antibiotics in a stable patient

case.who: 62-year-old diabetic rice farmer from Ubon Ratchathani
case.story: Three weeks of worsening lower thoracic back pain after a leg abscess; yesterday his legs became heavy and today he cannot pass urine.
case.exam: Temperature 38.4 degrees, midline tenderness at T10, legs 3/5, sensory level T11, retained urine, extensor plantars.
case.tests: CRP 190 mg/L, white count 17,000; MRI shows T9–T10 discitis with a dorsal epidural abscess compressing the cord; blood cultures later grow Burkholderia pseudomallei.
case.q: What is the management?
case.a: Spinal epidural abscess with myelopathy from spondylodiscitis. Emergency surgical decompression and drainage with cultures, then prolonged targeted antimicrobial therapy (intensive ceftazidime or meropenem followed by oral eradication therapy for melioidosis), glucose control and rehabilitation.

read.where: Chapter 21 Skull, Spine, and Post-Surgical Infections — Spinal epidural abscess; Vertebral osteomyelitis; Discitis
Chapter 14 Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders
Chapter 22 Neurologic Disorders Associated with Bone and Joint Disease

det.patho: Bacteria seed the vertebral endplate by the arterial or venous (Batson plexus) route from skin, urinary tract, endocarditis or intravascular devices, then spread to the disc and adjacent vertebrae; direct inoculation follows surgery, injections or epidural catheters. Pus tracking into the epidural space compresses the cord or cauda equina, and septic thrombophlebitis or arterial compromise can infarct the cord. Infection of the disc is typically early because the adult disc is avascular but the endplate is well perfused; in children the disc itself is perfused, which explains juvenile discitis.
det.clinical: Pain in the spine with local tenderness is the commonest feature. Radicular pain follows, then limb weakness and sphincter disturbance, with the interval between each stage shortening: a few days from back pain to root pain, then a few days to weakness and as little as a day from weakness to paralysis. Fever, sweats, rigors and encephalopathy may be present, and postoperative infection may show few signs except local pain. Meningism can occur. Delay in diagnosis is common because back pain is common.
det.diagnosis: Consider spinal infection in any patient with fever or a predisposing condition plus spinal pain or tenderness, and obtain MRI with gadolinium of the entire spine. Findings are endplate erosion, disc hyperintensity on T2 and enhancement; tumours usually spare the disc, infections involve it. Obtain blood cultures, and if negative, a CT-guided or open biopsy before antibiotics when the neurological status permits. Inflammatory markers help monitor response, and imaging often lags behind the clinical improvement.
det.treatment: Neurologically intact patients with discitis or osteomyelitis can be treated with organism-directed antibiotics for at least 6 weeks; trials support 6 weeks overall and an early switch from IV to oral agents with good bone penetration in selected patients, while epidural abscess, hardware infection or resistant organisms often need longer courses. Surgery (decompression, drainage, debridement and stabilisation, which does not preclude instrumentation) is indicated for neurological deficit, spinal instability, failure of medical treatment, or large epidural abscess; many centres operate early for abscess with any deficit. Immobilise in a brace if unstable, control diabetes, remove infected devices and monitor CRP. Melioidosis and TB need different regimens.
det.prognosis: Neurological recovery relates to the deficit and its duration before decompression; paralysis for more than a day or two rarely recovers fully.
pearls: Back pain plus fever or a risk factor plus spinal tenderness: MRI the whole spine promptly.
Infection crosses the disc space; tumour usually does not.
Absence of fever or a normal white count does not exclude epidural abscess.
det.thd: การติดเชื้อแบคทีเรียของกระดูกสันหลัง (vertebral osteomyelitis, discitis, epidural abscess) ผู้ป่วยปวดหลังเฉพาะที่ กดเจ็บ อาจมีไข้ มักมีเบาหวาน ไตวาย ใช้ยาเสพติดฉีด หรือเพิ่งผ่าตัด เมื่อลุกลามอาจมีขาอ่อนแรงและปัสสาวะไม่ออกภายในไม่กี่วัน MRI ฉีดสีทั้งแนวกระดูกสันหลังเป็นการตรวจที่ดีที่สุด เพาะเชื้อจากเลือดหรือชิ้นเนื้อก่อนให้ยา รักษาด้วยยาปฏิชีวนะอย่างน้อย 6 สัปดาห์ ผ่าตัดเมื่อมีอ่อนแรง กระดูกสันหลังไม่มั่นคง หรือรักษาด้วยยาไม่ได้ผล ในไทยควรนึกถึง melioidosis และวัณโรค

name: Balance disorders
formal: Disturbances of equilibrium from vestibular, cerebellar, proprioceptive or visual dysfunction, causing unsteadiness, dizziness and falls.
simple: Problems staying steady on the feet, causing dizziness, unsteadiness and falls.
th: กลุ่มภาวะที่การทรงตัวผิดปกติจากระบบการทรงตัวในหูชั้นใน สมองน้อย ประสาทรับความรู้สึกตำแหน่ง หรือการมองเห็น ทำให้เดินไม่มั่นคงและล้ม

feat: Umbrella symptom category, not a single disease
Sources: vestibular (peripheral or central), cerebellar, proprioceptive (neuropathy, dorsal columns), visual, extrapyramidal, frontal gait, functional
Older adults often have multisensory deficits plus fear of falling
Romberg test separates sensory from cerebellar ataxia
Red flags: acute onset with headache, focal signs, inability to stand
inv: Bedside: Romberg, tandem gait, head impulse, nystagmus, positional tests, proprioception, orthostatic BP
Targeted tests: vestibular function (vHIT, calorics), MRI, nerve conduction, B12
Medication review (sedatives, antihypertensives, antiseizure drugs)

case.story: A year of unsteady walking, worse in the dark and on uneven ground; two falls. Takes gentamicin courses for recurrent UTI, metformin for diabetes.
case.exam: Romberg positive, reduced vibration at the ankles, bilateral abnormal head impulse tests, oscillopsia when walking.
case.tests: Video head impulse test shows bilateral reduced gain; B12 low-normal; nerve conduction shows mild axonal neuropathy.
case.q: What are the contributors to this man's imbalance?
case.a: Multisensory imbalance: bilateral vestibulopathy (likely aminoglycoside) plus diabetic and possibly B12-related neuropathy.

read.where: Chapter 23 Neuro-Otology: Dizziness, Balance and Hearing — The Clinical Presentation of Balance Disorders
19 - Gait disorders: Pathophysiology and clinical syndromes

det.patho: Upright balance requires integration of vestibular, visual and proprioceptive input in the brainstem and cerebellum, with output through vestibulospinal and motor pathways. Failure of any input, or of central integration, produces instability; the nervous system can compensate for a single deficit but often not for several, which is why older adults are vulnerable.
det.clinical: History should establish whether the problem is vertigo, light-headedness, unsteadiness or fear of falling, and whether it is acute, episodic or chronic. Oscillopsia suggests bilateral vestibular loss; worsening in the dark suggests sensory or vestibular deficit; associated parkinsonian, cerebellar or cognitive features suggest central causes. Falls and their consequences are the main risk.
det.diagnosis: A structured bedside examination usually localises the problem. Vestibular laboratory testing, posture studies, MRI and neurophysiology are selected according to the suspected component. Medication review is essential, as polypharmacy is a common reversible factor.
det.treatment: Treat specific causes (repositioning for BPPV, stopping vestibulotoxic drugs, B12 replacement), and use vestibular rehabilitation and balance training, which have good evidence. Address vision, footwear, home hazards and orthostatic hypotension. Walking aids are prescribed where needed.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause; many improve with rehabilitation even when the underlying deficit persists.
pearls: Ask 'worse in the dark?' — points to vestibular or proprioceptive loss.
Bilateral vestibulopathy is easily missed; test head impulses both sides.
Several mild deficits add up to serious imbalance in older people.
det.thd: Balance disorders เป็นกลุ่มอาการทรงตัวผิดปกติจากหลายระบบ ได้แก่ หูชั้นใน สมองน้อย ประสาทรับตำแหน่ง และการมองเห็น ผู้สูงอายุมักมีความผิดปกติหลายอย่างร่วมกัน การตรวจข้างเตียง เช่น Romberg, head impulse และ positional test ช่วยแยกสาเหตุ การรักษาตามต้นเหตุร่วมกับ vestibular rehabilitation และป้องกันการล้ม

name: Balint syndrome
formal: Triad of simultanagnosia, optic ataxia and oculomotor apraxia from bilateral parieto-occipital lesions, seen in posterior cortical atrophy and watershed infarcts.
simple: Damage to both sides of the back of the brain causing difficulty seeing more than one thing at a time, reaching for objects and directing gaze.
th: กลุ่มอาการสามอย่าง คือ simultanagnosia, optic ataxia และ oculomotor apraxia จากรอยโรค parieto-occipital ทั้งสองข้าง พบใน posterior cortical atrophy และ watershed infarct
tempoNote: Abrupt after watershed stroke or hypoxia; gradual in posterior cortical atrophy
feat: Simultanagnosia: sees individual items but cannot grasp the whole scene
Optic ataxia: misreaching for objects under visual guidance despite normal strength
Ocular (oculomotor) apraxia: difficulty voluntarily shifting gaze to a new target
Patients may appear blind yet have normal acuity in the small area they attend to
Causes: posterior border-zone infarcts after hypotension, PCA strokes, PCA variant of Alzheimer disease, CJD, PML
inv: Bedside: cookie-theft picture, reaching tests, overlapping figures
MRI brain: bilateral parieto-occipital lesions or atrophy
FDG-PET or amyloid/tau biomarkers when degenerative

case.who: 61-year-old male lottery seller from Khon Kaen
case.story: Two years of bumping into things, difficulty reading and finding objects on a cluttered table; memory relatively spared.
case.exam: Visual acuity 6/9; describes single items in a picture but not the scene; misreaches for a pen; struggles to look at a target on command.
case.tests: MRI: bilateral parieto-occipital atrophy; CSF amyloid low, p-tau raised.
case.q: What syndrome is this and what is the underlying disease?
case.a: Balint syndrome due to posterior cortical atrophy (visual variant of Alzheimer disease).

read.where: 8 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System

det.patho: Damage to the dorsal visual stream in both parieto-occipital regions disrupts spatial attention, visuomotor coordination and gaze control. Ventral stream function (object recognition) is relatively preserved, which explains recognising single objects but not their spatial arrangement.
det.clinical: Patients describe difficulty seeing more than one thing at once, losing their place while reading, and reaching inaccurately. They often consult ophthalmologists first. Partial forms are common; associated features include Gerstmann elements, visual field defects and dressing apraxia.
det.diagnosis: Recognise the triad at the bedside; acuity and fields may be near normal. MRI identifies infarcts, atrophy or other lesions. In degenerative cases, Alzheimer biomarkers clarify the cause; consider CJD if rapid.
det.treatment: Treat the cause. Occupational therapy, verbal strategies, reduction of visual clutter and low-vision aids help. Cholinesterase inhibitors are used when Alzheimer pathology underlies PCA.
det.prognosis: Stroke-related cases may improve; degenerative cases progress.
pearls: Normal acuity plus inability to see the whole scene: test for simultanagnosia.
Patients often present first to eye clinics.
Bilateral watershed infarcts after hypotension can cause acute Balint syndrome.
det.thd: Balint syndrome ประกอบด้วย simultanagnosia (มองเห็นทีละอย่างแต่ไม่เห็นภาพรวม), optic ataxia (เอื้อมจับของไม่แม่น) และ oculomotor apraxia (กลอกตาไปยังเป้าหมายได้ยาก) เกิดจากรอยโรค parieto-occipital ทั้งสองข้าง เช่น watershed infarct หรือ posterior cortical atrophy ผู้ป่วยมักไปพบจักษุแพทย์ก่อนเพราะคิดว่าตามัว การวินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจข้างเตียงและ MRI การรักษาตามสาเหตุและฝึกการใช้ชีวิตประจำวัน

qx.stem: A 59-year-old Thai badminton coach has two years of trouble judging where the shuttle is; she reaches beside objects she is looking straight at and, when shown a picture of a market, describes only one stall at a time. Visual acuity and fields are normal and memory for recent events is fairly preserved. MRI shows bilateral parieto-occipital atrophy with sparing of the hippocampi.
qx.q: Where is the dominant damage and what process most often underlies this presentation?
opts: Bilateral inferior temporal lobes; semantic-variant FTLD
Primary visual cortex; occipital lobe infarcts
Left frontal operculum; tau pathology
Bilateral dorsal parieto-occipital (dorsal-stream) cortex; Alzheimer's disease pathology
Optic chiasm; pituitary macroadenoma
qx.why: Simultanagnosia, optic ataxia and impaired gaze direction form Balint syndrome, which localises to the bilateral dorsal visual stream in the parieto-occipital cortex. In a slowly progressive picture with relative memory sparing this is posterior cortical atrophy, most often due to Alzheimer pathology, so amyloid and tau biomarkers are usually positive. Normal fields exclude chiasmal or calcarine disease, and inferior temporal damage produces object or face recognition loss instead.

Cortical blindness with denial of blindness
Rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus; Heidenhain variant visual onset

name: Ballism
formal: Violent, large-amplitude flinging movements of proximal limbs, usually unilateral (hemiballismus) from lesions of the contralateral subthalamic nucleus or its connections.
simple: Wild, flinging, uncontrolled movements of the arm or leg, often after damage to a deep brain area.
th: Ballism คือการเหวี่ยงแขนขาอย่างรุนแรงจากโคนแขนขา มักเป็นครึ่งซีก (hemiballismus) เกิดเฉียบพลันจากรอยโรคของ basal ganglia ซึ่งพบบ่อยที่สุดคือหลอดเลือดสมองตีบเล็ก ๆ และภาวะน้ำตาลในเลือดสูงแบบ non-ketotic และมักดีขึ้นเองในหลายสัปดาห์ถึงหนึ่งปี
tempoNote: Starts abruptly over hours to days, usually after a small basal ganglia stroke or severe hyperglycaemia; most cases fade over weeks to a year
feat: Violent, wide, flinging or rotatory movements of the proximal arm and leg, often on one side only, present throughout waking and gone in sleep
Worse with action and stress and only briefly suppressible; the patient may strike the bed rail or wall and bruise or lacerate the limb
Stroke (usually a small lacunar infarct) and non-ketotic hyperglycaemia are the two commonest causes; the lesion lies in the subthalamic nucleus in only a minority
Other causes: tumour, abscess or granuloma in the basal ganglia, demyelination, lupus or antiphospholipid disease, drugs added to an old lesion
Exhaustion, dehydration, limb injury and rhabdomyolysis are the dangers; smaller-amplitude hemichorea often replaces ballism as the illness settles
inv: Capillary and venous glucose, HbA1c and urine ketones at once, because correcting glucose may end the movements
MRI brain with diffusion imaging; T1 hyperintensity of the putamen points to the hyperglycaemic form, and CT may show a dense putamen
Stroke work-up (vessel imaging, cardiac rhythm, lipids) and HIV serology with toxoplasma testing when risk factors exist
Creatine kinase and renal function when movements are continuous or the urine is dark

case.who: 66-year-old retired teacher from Nakhon Si Thammarat with hypertension
case.story: The right arm and leg began to fling about while he was eating breakfast. By the next day he had bruised his hand on the table edge and could not rest.
case.exam: Large proximal flinging movements of the right limbs, stopping in sleep; power full; blood pressure 178/98 mmHg; glucose normal.
case.tests: MRI shows a small acute infarct in the left subthalamic region; CK normal; vessel imaging shows small-vessel disease only.
case.q: What treatment is needed for the movements, and what must not be forgotten?
case.a: Pad the limb and give a dopamine antagonist or a dopamine depleter, for example haloperidol or risperidone at low dose or a VMAT2 inhibitor, for about 3 months before a trial of withdrawal; start antiplatelet and blood-pressure control because the stroke itself carries a risk of recurrence.

det.patho: Classical teaching tied hemiballism to the subthalamic nucleus, since monkeys develop it when more than a fifth of that nucleus is destroyed. Modern imaging shows that most human lesions lie elsewhere, such as the putamen, caudate, pallidum or thalamus, so the movements reflect disturbed basal ganglia output rather than a single nucleus. The pattern of pauses in firing of pallidal neurons, rather than the average rate, seems to produce the ballistic bursts. In hyperglycaemic cases the picture is of striatal injury with reactive astrocytes, though the exact mechanism remains uncertain.
det.clinical: Ballism is dramatic and usually brings the patient to the emergency room within a day or two. The flinging movements involve the shoulder or hip more than the hand, may have a rotatory component and can be so violent that the limb is injured. Patients are alert, strength is normal and the movements vanish in sleep. Bilateral forms (biballism) or leg-predominant forms (paraballism) are rare and imply bilateral lesions. As recovery begins, amplitude falls and the picture becomes hemichorea, and later some patients develop dystonia in the same limbs.
det.diagnosis: Treat ballism as a syndrome that needs a cause. Check glucose first, then image the brain with MRI, looking for infarction, haemorrhage, mass lesions, demyelination and the striatal T1 hyperintensity of hyperglycaemia. In an HIV-positive or immunosuppressed patient think of toxoplasma, cryptococcal and tuberculous lesions. In younger patients test for lupus and antiphospholipid antibodies and review drug exposure, since levodopa, anticonvulsants and oral contraceptives can unmask the movements on a previously damaged striatum.
det.treatment: First treat the cause: glucose correction, secondary stroke prevention and treatment of infection or mass lesions. Mild cases need only padding of the limb, hydration and watchfulness, because they settle on their own. When treatment is needed, dopamine blockers such as haloperidol or risperidone and dopamine depleters such as tetrabenazine are the best-studied options, with response in roughly nine of ten patients; valbenazine and deutetrabenazine belong to the same class but are not established for this use. Pain, exhaustion and rhabdomyolysis in the worst cases may call for sedation in an intensive care unit. Keep drug treatment for about 3 months, then taper. For disabling ballism lasting beyond 3 months, lesioning of the pallidum or thalamus, pallidal stimulation and focused ultrasound have all been reported; the book favoured lesioning, but today stimulation and focused ultrasound are also used.
det.prognosis: The old view that hemiballism was a grave disease is wrong: most patients recover within months, particularly the hyperglycaemic type, which can clear in days. One caution is that a patient who had a stroke may have a high later vascular risk, so secondary prevention matters.
pearls: Always check the glucose first in acute hemiballism.
Most causative lesions are not in the subthalamic nucleus.
Dopamine blockers treat it, and levodopa can make it worse.
det.thd: Ballism คืออาการเหวี่ยงแขนขาแรง ๆ มักเป็นข้างเดียว เกิดจากรอยโรคใน basal ganglia ที่พบบ่อยคือหลอดเลือดตีบเล็ก ๆ และน้ำตาลในเลือดสูงแบบ non-ketotic ผู้ป่วยรู้ตัวดี กำลังกล้ามเนื้อปกติ และอาการหายไปเมื่อหลับ ต้องตรวจน้ำตาลและทำ MRI ทันที แก้สาเหตุ ป้องกันแขนขากระแทก ให้น้ำให้เพียงพอ และใช้ยา haloperidol หรือ risperidone หรือ tetrabenazine เมื่ออาการรุนแรง ส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นเองภายในไม่กี่เดือน ถ้าไม่ดีอาจพิจารณาผ่าตัด pallidotomy หรือ DBS

name: Ballism–chorea
formal: Spectrum of hyperkinetic movements from basal ganglia dysfunction, with ballism as proximal large-amplitude flinging and chorea as distal flowing jerks, often coexisting after subthalamic or striatal lesions.
simple: Uncontrolled flinging and dance-like movements that come from damage to deep brain structures.
th: กลุ่มการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติแบบ hyperkinetic จาก basal ganglia ที่ ballism (เหวี่ยงกว้างจากต้นแขนขา) และ chorea (กระตุกเลื่อนไหลปลายแขนขา) มักพบร่วมกันหลังรอยโรคที่ subthalamic หรือ striatum
tempoNote: Abrupt onset, typically improving from ballism toward chorea over days to weeks
feat: Continuum from large proximal flinging (ballism) to smaller distal flowing movements (chorea)
Causes: lacunar stroke, non-ketotic hyperglycaemia, hyperthyroidism, autoimmune, drugs
Same patient may shift from ballism to chorea as recovery occurs
Usually unilateral with contralateral lesion
inv: Glucose, thyroid function, electrolytes
MRI brain with DWI and T1 sequences
Autoimmune and antiphospholipid tests in young patients

case.story: Sudden onset of flinging right arm movements three weeks ago; now the movements are smaller and involve fingers and face.
case.exam: Right-sided chorea with occasional proximal flinging; mild right sensory loss.
case.tests: MRI shows small left subthalamic infarct on DWI.
case.q: Why has the movement pattern changed?
case.a: Ballism and chorea are a spectrum; as the lesion recovers, high-amplitude ballism commonly softens into chorea.

det.patho: Both phenomena result from reduced output of the internal globus pallidus to the thalamus, whether via subthalamic damage or striatal dysfunction. The amplitude difference reflects the degree and site of disinhibition.
det.clinical: This entry describes a phenomenological spectrum rather than a single disease. Patients often have mixed movements, and clinicians may label them differently depending on timing. Underlying causes guide management.
det.diagnosis: Same work-up as for ballism and chorea: glucose, thyroid, imaging, drug history and immune tests, with genetic testing for chronic or familial cases.
det.treatment: Treat the cause; symptomatic options include VMAT2 inhibitors (tetrabenazine), dopamine antagonists, and anticonvulsants. Most acute vascular cases improve spontaneously.
det.prognosis: Usually favourable for vascular and metabolic causes.
pearls: Ballism and chorea differ mainly in amplitude and proximal involvement.
Expect ballism to evolve into chorea during recovery.
Hyperglycaemia is a reversible cause to check first.
det.thd: Ballism-chorea คือกลุ่มการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติที่ต่อเนื่องกัน ballism เป็นการเหวี่ยงแรงจากต้นแขนขา ส่วน chorea เป็นการกระตุกเล็กกว่าที่ปลายแขนขา มักเกิดร่วมกันจากรอยโรคที่ subthalamic nucleus หรือ striatum เช่น หลอดเลือดสมองหรือน้ำตาลสูง เมื่ออาการดีขึ้น ballism มักกลายเป็น chorea การรักษาคือแก้สาเหตุและใช้ยาลดการเคลื่อนไหวตามความจำเป็น

Children, post-streptococcal, often bilateral

name: Barth syndrome
formal: X-linked mitochondrial disease from TAZ mutation with cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy, neutropenia and 3-methylglutaconic aciduria.
simple: An inherited condition in boys causing heart and muscle weakness and low white blood cell counts.
th: โรคไมโทคอนเดรียที่ถ่ายทอดทางโครโมโซม X จากยีน TAZ ในเด็กชาย มีกล้ามเนื้อหัวใจผิดปกติ กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง เม็ดเลือดขาว neutrophil ต่ำ และตัวเตี้ย
tempoNote: Presents in infancy or early childhood; cardiac risk highest in early years
feat: Boys with dilated or non-compaction cardiomyopathy, often in infancy
Proximal myopathy, fatigue and delayed motor milestones
Intermittent or persistent neutropenia with recurrent infections and mouth ulcers
Growth delay with catch-up in adolescence; characteristic facial features
Raised urinary 3-methylglutaconic acid
inv: Echocardiogram and Holter for arrhythmia
Full blood count repeated to detect neutropenia
Urine organic acids; monolysocardiolipin to cardiolipin ratio (specific)
TAFAZZIN gene sequencing

case.who: 2-year-old boy at a regional children's hospital in Songkhla
case.story: Admitted with pneumonia and mouth ulcers; poor weight gain and late walking. A maternal uncle died in infancy of 'heart failure'.
case.exam: Below 3rd centile weight, generalised hypotonia, proximal weakness, gallop rhythm and hepatomegaly.
case.tests: Absolute neutrophil count 300/µL; echo shows dilated LV with non-compaction; urine 3-methylglutaconic acid raised.
case.q: Which unifying X-linked diagnosis fits?
case.a: Barth syndrome; confirm with cardiolipin ratio and TAFAZZIN sequencing, start heart failure treatment and G-CSF support.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Disorders of Phospholipid Synthesis

det.patho: TAFAZZIN (TAZ) encodes an acyltransferase that remodels cardiolipin, a phospholipid essential for inner mitochondrial membrane structure. Deficiency reduces mature cardiolipin and raises monolysocardiolipin, impairing respiratory chain function in heart, skeletal muscle and neutrophils. It is X-linked recessive, so affected individuals are almost always male.
det.clinical: Cardiomyopathy usually appears in the first year and may cause heart failure or ventricular arrhythmia. Skeletal myopathy, exercise intolerance and hypotonia are common. Neutropenia predisposes to bacterial infections and can be cyclical. Growth is delayed, and some have mild learning difficulty.
det.diagnosis: An elevated monolysocardiolipin/cardiolipin ratio in blood spots or cells is highly specific. Urine 3-methylglutaconic acid is supportive but not universal. TAFAZZIN sequencing confirms and enables carrier testing of female relatives.
det.treatment: Management is multidisciplinary: standard heart failure therapy, arrhythmia monitoring, sometimes transplantation; G-CSF and prophylactic antibiotics for neutropenia; nutrition and physiotherapy. Elamipretide has been studied and gained conditional US approval in 2025; access is limited. Avoid prolonged fasting.
det.prognosis: Early infant mortality is high from cardiac failure or sepsis, but survival into adulthood is increasingly common with specialist care.
pearls: Cardiomyopathy plus neutropenia in a boy suggests Barth syndrome.
Repeat blood counts; neutropenia can be intermittent.
3-methylglutaconic aciduria is a clue but not specific.
det.thd: Barth syndrome เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมที่ถ่ายทอดทาง X จากยีน TAZ ทำให้ cardiolipin ในไมโทคอนเดรียผิดปกติ เด็กชายมีหัวใจโต อ่อนแรง เม็ดเลือดขาวต่ำติดเชื้อง่าย และโตช้า ตรวจพบ 3-methylglutaconic acid ในปัสสาวะ และยืนยันด้วยตรวจยีน การรักษาเป็นการดูแลหัวใจ ให้ G-CSF และโภชนาการ

name: Basal cell naevus syndrome
formal: Gorlin syndrome, an autosomal dominant PTCH1 disorder with multiple basal cell carcinomas, jaw keratocysts, medulloblastoma risk, falx calcification and skeletal anomalies.
simple: An inherited condition causing many skin cancers, jaw cysts and an increased chance of a childhood brain tumour.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมเด่นจากยีน PTCH1 หรือ SUFU มี basal cell carcinoma หลายก้อน ซีสต์กรามชนิด keratocyst หลุมที่ฝ่ามือฝ่าเท้า ซี่โครงแฉก หินปูนที่ falx และเสี่ยง medulloblastoma ในเด็กเล็ก
tempoNote: Features accrue from infancy to adulthood; medulloblastoma risk is concentrated in the first years of life
feat: Multiple basal cell carcinomas from teens or twenties, extensive on sun-exposed skin
Odontogenic keratocysts of the jaw with swelling or loose teeth
Palmar and plantar pits, bifid or splayed ribs, macrocephaly, frontal bossing
Early lamellar calcification of the falx cerebri
Desmoplastic/nodular SHH-medulloblastoma in infancy, especially with SUFU variants
inv: PTCH1 and SUFU testing
MRI brain; avoid ionising radiation where possible, since irradiation provokes basal cell carcinomas
Panoramic dental imaging and dermatological surveillance; MRI brain screening in young children with SUFU variants

case.story: Dozens of small skin lesions on his back and face, a jaw swelling, and a headache work-up showed calcified falx.
case.exam: Frontal bossing, macrocephaly, multiple pearly papules, palmar pits.
case.tests: Biopsy of a lesion confirms basal cell carcinoma; panoramic film shows multiple jaw cysts; PTCH1 pathogenic variant.
case.q: What neurological surveillance and what imaging cautions apply?
case.a: Gorlin syndrome: brain MRI for medulloblastoma surveillance in young carriers where indicated, and avoid radiotherapy and CT when alternatives exist.

det.patho: Gorlin syndrome is autosomal dominant and caused by loss of function in PTCH1, or less often SUFU, genes that restrain the sonic hedgehog pathway. Unchecked pathway activity drives basal cell carcinoma, keratocysts and SHH-subgroup medulloblastoma. Ionising radiation markedly raises tumour burden in treated areas.
det.clinical: The usual mode of discovery is multiple early basal cell carcinomas or jaw cysts, though some are found after medulloblastoma in infancy. Skeletal and craniofacial signs such as bifid ribs, macrocephaly and frontal bossing, palmar pits, falx calcification and ovarian fibromas support the diagnosis. Meningioma, cardiac fibroma and cleft palate also occur.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis uses major and minor clinical criteria and is confirmed by detecting PTCH1 or SUFU variants. A first medulloblastoma with desmoplastic histology in an infant should trigger germline testing. Panoramic radiographs show keratocysts and MRI documents brain tumours.
det.treatment: Multidisciplinary lifelong care: sun protection, early treatment of basal cell carcinoma with surgery, topical agents or photodynamic therapy, and hedgehog inhibitors such as vismodegib for advanced disease. Medulloblastoma is treated with surgery and chemotherapy, with radiotherapy avoided in the youngest children when possible. Jaw cysts are enucleated and family members offered testing.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is near normal for most with careful skin surveillance; outcome depends on medulloblastoma, which is relatively favourable in the desmoplastic type.
pearls: Young patient with many basal cell carcinomas needs a genetic work-up.
Radiotherapy can create dense tumour fields.
Infant desmoplastic medulloblastoma suggests SUFU Gorlin syndrome.
det.thd: Basal cell naevus (Gorlin) syndrome เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมเด่นจากยีน PTCH1 หรือ SUFU มี basal cell carcinoma หลายก้อนตั้งแต่อายุน้อย ซีสต์กราม หลุมที่ฝ่ามือฝ่าเท้า ซี่โครงแฉก หินปูนที่ falx และเสี่ยง medulloblastoma ในเด็กเล็ก ควรหลีกเลี่ยงการฉายแสง ตรวจ MRI ติดตาม และใช้การรักษาผิวหนังตามระยะ รวมทั้งให้คำปรึกษาครอบครัว

name: Basal ganglia calcification
formal: Mineral deposits in basal ganglia seen on imaging, either incidental or in Fahr disease (SLC20A2, PDGFRB, XPR1), hypoparathyroidism and infections, causing parkinsonism, dystonia, cognitive decline and psychiatric features.
simple: Calcium deposits in deep parts of the brain that may cause movement problems, memory decline or mood changes.
more: Symmetric calcium deposits in basal ganglia, dentate and cortex (primary familial brain calcification or secondary to hypoparathyroidism); presents with parkinsonism, dystonia, cognitive and psychiatric change.
th: หินปูนสะสมในปมประสาทฐานบนภาพ CT อาจพบโดยบังเอิญ หรือเกิดจากพันธุกรรม (PFBC) และภาวะพาราไทรอยด์ต่ำ ทำให้มี parkinsonism, dystonia และอาการทางจิตประสาท
tempoNote: Slowly progressive over years; many imaging findings are incidental and stay silent
feat: Symmetric calcification of globus pallidus, often also dentate nuclei, thalamus and subcortical white matter
Small pallidal specks are common incidental CT findings in older adults
Symptomatic cases: parkinsonism, dystonia, chorea, ataxia, seizures
Cognitive slowing, depression, psychosis or apathy may precede the motor picture
Hypoparathyroidism gives a reversible-cause clue: tetany, cramps, low calcium
inv: CT is the most sensitive test for calcium; MRI susceptibility sequences help
Serum calcium, phosphate, PTH, magnesium, vitamin D and renal function
Gene panel in familial or young cases: SLC20A2, PDGFRB, PDGFB, XPR1 (dominant), MYORG, JAM2 (recessive)

case.story: Two years of slowness and low mood; recently stiff hands and occasional finger cramps. She had a thyroidectomy 15 years ago.
case.exam: Mild bradykinesia and rigidity both sides, positive Chvostek sign, normal eye movements.
case.tests: Calcium 1.6 mmol/L, PTH undetectable; CT dense symmetric calcification of pallida and dentate nuclei.
case.q: What is the cause of the calcification and what should be corrected first?
case.a: Post-surgical hypoparathyroidism; replace calcium and active vitamin D carefully, which may ease symptoms though calcium deposits persist.

read.where: 9 - Atypical parkinsonism, parkinsonism-­plus syndromes and secondary parkinsonian disorders

det.patho: Calcium phosphate is laid down in and around small vessels of the deep grey nuclei. Secondary forms come from disturbed calcium-phosphate balance (hypoparathyroidism, pseudohypoparathyroidism), congenital infections (CMV, toxoplasma), HIV, radiation or mitochondrial disease. Primary familial brain calcification arises from variants in genes that handle phosphate transport (SLC20A2, XPR1) or keep the neurovascular unit intact (PDGFB, PDGFRB, MYORG, JAM2). Mild pallidal calcification increases with age and usually means nothing.
det.clinical: Most people with small deposits have no symptoms. Symptomatic patients present usually between 30 and 60 years with a mix of parkinsonism, dystonia, chorea, gait ataxia, dysarthria, headache, seizures and neuropsychiatric change; the burden of calcium correlates only loosely with disability. Children with congenital infection or Aicardi–Goutières syndrome show calcification with developmental problems. Always ask about neck surgery, tetany and family history.
det.diagnosis: CT confirms and maps the calcium; MRI shows variable T1/T2 change and is less sensitive. Check calcium, phosphate, PTH, magnesium and vitamin D to find treatable secondary causes; consider infection serology in young patients and mitochondrial testing when there are other system clues. Genetic testing is appropriate when calcification is extensive, early or familial and biochemistry is normal.
det.treatment: Correct hypocalcaemia and hypoparathyroidism with calcium and calcitriol, avoiding hypercalciuria; symptoms may improve though calcium rarely clears. For primary forms treatment is symptomatic: levodopa (variable response), drugs for dystonia, antiseizure medicines and psychiatric care. Neuroleptics should be used cautiously because parkinsonism may worsen. Offer genetic counselling for familial forms.
det.prognosis: Incidental calcification is benign; symptomatic primary forms progress slowly over years, while secondary hypoparathyroid forms stabilise once calcium is controlled.
pearls: Bilateral pallidal plus dentate calcium on CT: check calcium and PTH before calling it Fahr.
A prior thyroidectomy is the commonest clue to secondary hypoparathyroidism.
Calcium load on imaging predicts symptoms poorly; treat the patient, not the scan.
det.thd: หินปูนในปมประสาทฐานเห็นชัดใน CT ส่วนน้อยมีอาการ เช่น parkinsonism, dystonia และอาการทางจิต ต้องตรวจแคลเซียม ฟอสเฟต และ PTH เสมอ เพราะภาวะพาราไทรอยด์ต่ำ (โดยเฉพาะหลังผ่าตัดไทรอยด์) รักษาได้ ถ้าเคมีเลือดปกติและเป็นในครอบครัวให้นึกถึง PFBC ซึ่งรักษาตามอาการ

Examination shows mild symmetric parkinsonism, positive Chvostek sign and dry skin. Non-contrast CT shows dense symmetric calcification of the globus pallidus, caudate and dentate nuclei.
qx.q: Which investigation should be done first?

Copper and ceruloplasmin
CSF analysis for oligoclonal bands
Serum calcium, phosphate, magnesium and parathyroid hormone

qx.why: Symmetric basal ganglia and dentate calcification has a treatable metabolic cause that must be excluded first; post-surgical hypoparathyroidism with hypocalcaemia (seizures, Chvostek sign, cramps) is the leading candidate here. Correcting calcium and vitamin D can improve seizures and tetany. Genetic testing for primary familial brain calcification is appropriate only after normal calcium–phosphate–PTH studies.

name: Batten disease
formal: Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, a group of inherited lysosomal storage disorders with progressive visual failure, seizures, dementia and motor deterioration, most often juvenile onset from CLN3 mutations.
simple: An inherited childhood disease causing gradual vision loss, seizures, loss of skills and movement difficulty.
th: กลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมสะสมไขมันในไลโซโซม (NCL) ทำให้ตามัวลงเรื่อย ๆ ชัก สมองเสื่อม และการเคลื่อนไหวแย่ลง ส่วนใหญ่เป็นแบบเด็กโตจากยีน CLN3
tempoNote: CLN3: visual loss at 4–7 years, then seizures and decline over the next decade; CLN2 starts at 2–4 years with seizures
feat: Progressive visual loss from retinopathy (CLN3) as the first sign in school-age children
Seizures (generalised and myoclonic), often the first sign in CLN2
Cognitive decline, behavioural change and later dementia
Parkinsonism, ataxia, speech decline and eventual loss of mobility
Autosomal recessive inheritance

Blood film: vacuolated lymphocytes in CLN3; enzyme assay TPP1 (CLN2), PPT1 (CLN1)

case.story: Teachers noticed he could not see the board; glasses did not help. Over two years his school performance dropped and he had his first convulsion.

det.patho: The NCLs are recessively inherited lysosomal disorders caused by variants in at least 13 CLN genes, leading to accumulation of autofluorescent lipopigment in neurons and retina. Neuronal death in cortex, cerebellum and retina underlies symptoms. 'Batten disease' strictly referred to CLN3 juvenile NCL but is now used for the whole group.
det.clinical: Forms are grouped by age at onset: infantile (CLN1), late infantile (CLN2 and variants), juvenile (CLN3) and adult (Kufs). Juvenile CLN3 typically begins with rapid visual decline in early school years, followed by cognitive slowing, seizures, psychiatric symptoms and parkinsonism in adolescence. CLN2 begins at 2–4 years with seizures and language regression, then motor decline and blindness.
det.diagnosis: Consider in a child with unexplained visual failure, seizures and regression. Ophthalmology with ERG, blood film for vacuolated lymphocytes, enzyme assays for TPP1 and PPT1, and gene panels confirm the type. Skin or rectal biopsy electron microscopy is largely replaced by genetics. EEG in CLN2 often shows a photoparoxysmal response at low flash frequencies.
det.treatment: Cerliponase alfa, an intraventricular enzyme replacement, slows motor and language decline in CLN2 disease. Other forms rely on supportive care: antiseizure drugs, visual aids, mobility and nutrition support, management of behavioural and sleep issues, and palliative care. Genetic counselling is essential.
det.prognosis: Progressive; juvenile CLN3 usually causes death in the third decade, earlier in infantile forms.
pearls: School-age child with rapid unexplained visual loss and then seizures: think CLN3.
Toddler with new seizures and language regression: test TPP1 (CLN2), as early ERT helps.
Vacuolated lymphocytes on blood film are a cheap clue to CLN3.

name: Becker muscular dystrophy
formal: X-linked dystrophinopathy with partially functional dystrophin causing later-onset, slower progressive proximal limb weakness, calf hypertrophy and raised creatine kinase.
simple: An inherited muscle disease in males that causes slowly progressing weakness, milder than Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
more: Diagnosed by DMD gene deletion or duplication testing, with muscle biopsy showing reduced, truncated dystrophin on Western blot; reading frame is preserved. Cardiomyopathy surveillance is crucial; steroids are used less consistently than in Duchenne.

case.story: Cramps in the calves after football since his teens; recently breathless on exertion.
case.exam: Mild hip weakness, calf hypertrophy.
case.tests: CK 3,200 U/L; echo: dilated left ventricle, EF 35%; in-frame DMD deletion.
