det.patho: Becker dystrophy results from dystrophin gene mutations, usually in-frame deletions, that permit production of a shortened, partly functional dystrophin. The amount and quality of residual protein broadly determine severity. Cardiac muscle may be disproportionately affected because it receives less protection from the residual protein and has a high workload.
det.clinical: Onset ranges from childhood to adulthood with exercise-induced myalgia, cramps or myoglobinuria, then proximal leg weakness and calf hypertrophy. Patients remain ambulant past 16 and often into adulthood, with a wide range of severity. Dilated cardiomyopathy may be the presenting or dominant problem, sometimes in men with little weakness. Some present only with an incidentally raised CK.
det.diagnosis: CK is raised (moderately to markedly). Genetic testing shows a DMD deletion or duplication that usually preserves the reading frame; muscle biopsy, if done, shows reduced or patchy dystrophin. Exclude LGMD (especially FKRP-related), which can look identical. Echocardiography or cardiac MRI and ECG are needed at diagnosis and periodically.
det.treatment: There is no approved disease-modifying drug; corticosteroids are not routinely used. Management centres on cardiac surveillance and early heart-failure therapy (ACE inhibitors or ARBs, beta blockers, mineralocorticoid antagonists), with heart transplantation for end-stage disease. Physiotherapy, avoidance of extreme eccentric exercise and anaesthetic precautions apply. Female carriers should be offered cardiac screening.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is reduced mainly by cardiomyopathy, often in middle age; with good cardiac care many live into their 50s or beyond.
pearls: In Becker, the heart can be severely affected even when walking is good.
Exercise-induced cramps and myoglobinuria in a man can be the only early sign.
det.thd: Becker muscular dystrophy เกิดจากการกลายพันธุ์ของยีน dystrophin แบบที่ยังสร้างโปรตีนได้บางส่วน อาการจึงช้ากว่าและเบากว่า Duchenne ผู้ป่วยยังเดินได้หลังอายุ 16 ปี อาจมีปวดหรือเป็นตะคริวหลังออกกำลังกาย น่องโต และ CK สูง ปัญหาสำคัญคือกล้ามเนื้อหัวใจโตผิดปกติ ซึ่งอาจรุนแรงแม้แขนขาจะยังแข็งแรง จึงต้องตรวจหัวใจเป็นระยะ และให้ยารักษาหัวใจล้มเหลวตั้งแต่ระยะแรก รวมถึงตรวจหัวใจในพาหะผู้หญิงด้วย

name: Becker’s disease
formal: Recessive form of myotonia congenita from CLCN1 mutations causing muscle stiffness that eases with exercise, with transient weakness and mild hypertrophy.
simple: An inherited condition in which muscles are stiff after rest but loosen with repeated movement.

tempoNote: Onset in childhood (often 4–12 years), lifelong, may worsen slightly until early adulthood
feat: Stiffness on starting movement that eases with repetition (warm-up)
Transient weakness at the start of activity, especially in recessive form

case.story: Stiff legs at the start of school sports races and falls when first standing up; after a few minutes he runs normally.
case.exam: Muscular calves and thighs, delayed release of grip improving after several repetitions, percussion myotonia of thenar eminence, strength normal after warm-up.

case.q: Which channel is affected and what is a first-line drug if symptoms are disabling?

det.patho: Loss-of-function variants in CLCN1 reduce chloride conductance of the muscle membrane. Without the stabilising chloride current, potassium accumulating in the T-tubules after activity depolarises fibres and triggers repetitive after-discharges, perceived as stiffness. Recessive variants cause greater loss of function than most dominant ones, explaining the more severe Becker phenotype.
det.clinical: Children develop generalised stiffness, often legs first, worst after rest and relieved by continued activity. Transient weakness lasting seconds is a typical feature of the recessive form and may cause falls. Hypertrophy gives a muscular look. Cold has less effect than in sodium channel myotonias.
det.diagnosis: EMG shows widespread myotonic discharges with no dystrophic features. The short exercise test with cooling helps separate chloride from sodium channel disorders. Genetic testing of CLCN1 confirms, and parental testing clarifies inheritance.
det.treatment: Many need no drug. Mexiletine is the best-supported treatment; check ECG beforehand. Alternatives include lamotrigine, carbamazepine or acetazolamide. Warn anaesthetists that depolarising agents and cold may trigger severe myotonia.
det.prognosis: Non-progressive in adulthood; life expectancy normal.
pearls: Warm-up phenomenon points to chloride channel myotonia.
Transient weakness at movement onset is more typical of the recessive form.
Becker's disease (myotonia) and Becker muscular dystrophy are unrelated.
det.thd: Becker's disease คือ myotonia congenita แบบด้อยจากยีน CLCN1 ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อคลายตัวช้า แข็งเมื่อเริ่มขยับและดีขึ้นเมื่อขยับซ้ำ บางครั้งอ่อนแรงชั่วคราว กล้ามเนื้อมักโต วินิจฉัยด้วย EMG และตรวจยีน ยาที่ใช้ได้คือ mexiletine ไม่ใช่โรคเดียวกับ Becker muscular dystrophy

formal: Abnormalities of conduct, mood or personality that may result from neurological disease such as frontal lobe damage, dementia or epilepsy.
simple: Problems with behaviour or emotions that can be caused by brain disease.

det.patho: Behaviour depends on frontal-subcortical circuits (orbitofrontal, anterior cingulate, dorsolateral prefrontal), limbic structures and their connections. Damage from degeneration, trauma, stroke, tumour, inflammation, epilepsy or drugs can release, blunt or distort behaviour. Psychiatric disorders and neurodevelopmental conditions overlap with these pathways.
det.clinical: This is a descriptive category rather than one disease. Common pictures include apathy-abulia, disinhibition, emotional lability, aggression, compulsive behaviour and psychosis. In dementia these are called BPSD and are a major source of carer burden. A new, sustained personality change in an adult with no psychiatric history should prompt a neurological search.
det.diagnosis: Obtain a collateral history describing the onset, course and specific behaviours. Bedside frontal tests, cognitive screening and neurological examination look for accompanying signs. MRI, EEG and blood screening identify structural, epileptic, metabolic or infective causes; neuropsychology and psychiatry assessment help define the pattern.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying cause where possible. Non-drug approaches come first: carer education, routine, environmental changes and addressing pain, infection or sleep loss. Medications are symptom-targeted (SSRIs for disinhibition or compulsion in FTD, cautious antipsychotic use for dangerous agitation or psychosis with attention to stroke and mortality risk in dementia).
det.prognosis: Depends on the cause, from reversible (drug or metabolic) to progressive (neurodegenerative).
pearls: New personality change after age 40 is neurological until proven otherwise.
Ask about medicines: levetiracetam, steroids and dopamine agonists commonly alter behaviour.
Use behavioural strategies before antipsychotics in dementia.
det.thd: Behavioral disorders หมายถึงความผิดปกติของพฤติกรรม อารมณ์ หรือบุคลิกภาพ ซึ่งอาจเกิดจากโรคสมอง เช่น สมองส่วนหน้าเสียหาย สมองเสื่อม โรคลมชัก หรือผลข้างเคียงยา เป็นกลุ่มอาการ ไม่ใช่โรคเฉพาะ ผู้ใหญ่ที่บุคลิกเปลี่ยนใหม่ควรตรวจหาสาเหตุทางสมองด้วยประวัติจากญาติ ตรวจความจำ MRI และเลือด การรักษาคือแก้ที่สาเหตุ ใช้วิธีไม่ใช้ยาก่อน แล้วจึงใช้ยาตามอาการ

det.patho: bvFTD reflects frontotemporal lobar degeneration, most often with TDP-43 or tau inclusions and less often FUS. A family history is present in as many as one patient in three; the main genes are C9orf72 (hexanucleotide expansion, also causing ALS), MAPT and GRN. It is a leading cause of dementia below 65.
det.clinical: Personality and social conduct change first: disinhibition, tactlessness, loss of sympathy, apathy, compulsive or ritualised routines and a change in eating, with sweet cravings and overeating. Insight is typically absent, so the history must come from family. Memory and visuospatial function are relatively intact early, which can mislead clinicians toward a psychiatric diagnosis. Some patients develop motor neuron disease or parkinsonism; C9orf72 carriers may present with psychosis. Overlap with semantic dementia and progressive non-fluent aphasia is common later.
det.diagnosis: International (Rascovsky) criteria require three of six features — disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, perseverative behaviour, hyperorality and a dysexecutive profile — for possible bvFTD, with imaging support for probable disease. MRI shows frontal and/or anterior temporal atrophy, often asymmetric; FDG-PET can reveal hypometabolism when MRI is still normal. Exclude primary psychiatric illness (late-onset bipolar disorder, depression), frontal tumours, AD with a frontal presentation and the bvFTD phenocopy syndrome, which does not progress. Examine for fasciculations and consider EMG and genetic testing.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying treatment. SSRIs or trazodone may reduce disinhibition, compulsions and eating changes; cholinesterase inhibitors are not helpful and may worsen behaviour. Antipsychotics are used sparingly for severe agitation. Key work is carer education, legal and financial protection, safety (driving, finances, impulsive spending) and planning support.
det.prognosis: Survival is about 6–11 years from onset and shorter when ALS coexists.
pearls: A middle-aged person with new socially inappropriate behaviour and no insight needs a neurological work-up, not only psychiatric care.
Always look for tongue and limb fasciculations — FTD and ALS lie on one spectrum.
Early MRI can be normal; FDG-PET or repeat imaging helps.

det.patho: Behçet's is a variable-vessel vasculitis with prominent neutrophil and Th1/Th17 activity, linked to HLA-B51 and clustered along the old Silk Road from the Mediterranean to Japan and Korea. In parenchymal neuro-Behçet, perivenular inflammation affects small venules of the brainstem and diencephalon; in the non-parenchymal type, venous sinus thrombosis results from vessel wall inflammation. Neurological involvement occurs in roughly 5–10% of patients, is more frequent in men, and arterial events are rare.
det.clinical: Parenchymal disease (about three quarters) presents subacutely with headache, fever and a brainstem or diencephalic syndrome, sometimes with hemiparesis, behavioural change or seizures; attacks may relapse or become progressive. Cerebral venous thrombosis tends to be the milder form and can be the first manifestation of Behçet's. Ask about recurrent mouth ulcers, genital scars, eye redness and skin lesions in any young adult with a brainstem lesion. Neurotoxicity with ciclosporin and isolated headache are common confounders.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on neurological syndrome plus established Behçet's (International Study Group or ICBD criteria) after excluding infection, MS, lymphoma and other vasculitides. MRI typically shows a large, poorly marginated lesion at the midbrain–diencephalic junction or pons, spreading upward, with oedema that is larger than its enhancement. CSF shows inflammatory cells, often neutrophil-rich early, with high protein and usually no oligoclonal bands. In Thailand, Behçet's is uncommon, so tuberculosis, melioidosis and lymphoma need firm exclusion.
det.treatment: Acute parenchymal attacks are treated with high-dose IV methylprednisolone followed by a tapering oral course over months. Maintenance therapy uses azathioprine; severe or relapsing disease merits an anti-TNF agent such as infliximab early. Avoid ciclosporin in neuro-Behçet as it can trigger or worsen CNS disease. Venous thrombosis is treated with corticosteroids; anticoagulation is commonly used but only after excluding pulmonary artery aneurysms, which can bleed.
det.prognosis: Venous thrombosis usually recovers well; parenchymal disease carries risk of relapse and disability, worse with progressive course, brainstem atrophy or high CSF cell counts.
pearls: Young man + recurrent oral ulcers + subacute brainstem lesion spreading to the thalamus: think neuro-Behçet.
MS has oligoclonal bands; neuro-Behçet usually does not.
Do not use ciclosporin for neuro-Behçet.
det.thd: Behçet เป็นโรคหลอดเลือดอักเสบที่สัมพันธ์กับ HLA-B51 มีแผลในปากเป็นซ้ำ แผลที่อวัยวะเพศ และม่านตาอักเสบ เมื่อเป็นที่ระบบประสาทแบ่งเป็นชนิดเนื้อสมองซึ่งมักเป็นรอยโรคใหญ่ที่ก้านสมองลามขึ้น thalamus และชนิดหลอดเลือดดำสมองอุดตัน CSF มีเซลล์อักเสบแต่ไม่มี oligoclonal band รักษาช่วงกำเริบด้วย methylprednisolone ตามด้วย azathioprine หรือ infliximab และหลีกเลี่ยง ciclosporin ในไทยพบไม่บ่อย จึงต้องแยกวัณโรคและมะเร็งต่อมน้ำเหลืองก่อน

name: Belly dancer’s dyskinesia
formal: Rhythmic involuntary movements of the abdominal wall, associated with spinal or peripheral nerve lesions, abdominal surgery or radiculopathy, or idiopathic.
simple: Continuous wave-like twitching movements of the belly muscles that the person cannot control.
th: การเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติของกล้ามเนื้อหน้าท้องเป็นจังหวะคล้ายระบำหน้าท้อง เกิดหลังผ่าตัดช่องท้อง รอยโรคไขสันหลังหรือรากประสาท ยา หรือไม่ทราบสาเหตุ
tempoNote: Usually persists for months to years once established
feat: Slow writhing or rhythmic contractions of the abdominal wall that make the umbilicus move sideways
Often continuous, may be uncomfortable or painful, lessens in sleep
Triggers: abdominal surgery or trauma, thoracic root or cord lesions, dopamine blockers
May coexist with diaphragmatic flutter, tardive dyskinesia or functional movement disorder
inv: Surface EMG of abdominal and paraspinal muscles to show pattern and segmental spread
MRI of thoracic spine when a segmental (spinal) generator is suspected
Medication review; consider fluoroscopy if diaphragm involvement is suspected

case.story: Three months after a laparotomy she notices her belly 'moving by itself' all day, worse when she is tense.
case.exam: Continuous undulating contractions of the rectus and oblique muscles, umbilicus shifting side to side; neurological exam otherwise normal.
case.tests: Surface EMG shows rhythmic bursts at about 1 Hz confined to lower thoracic segments; thoracic MRI normal.
case.q: Name the phenomenon and a first treatment option.
case.a: Belly dancer's dyskinesia after abdominal surgery; EMG-guided botulinum toxin into the active abdominal muscles is a reasonable first option.

read.where: 1 - Clinical overview and phenomenology of movement disorders

det.patho: The term describes a phenotype rather than one disease. Generators may be segmental spinal circuits after root or cord injury, peripheral nerve irritation after surgery, basal ganglia dysfunction as in tardive syndromes, or functional mechanisms; many cases remain idiopathic. Evidence comes mainly from case reports and small series.
det.clinical: Patients describe continuous rolling or jerking of the belly wall, sometimes with pain or breathing discomfort. The pattern can be slow and writhing or more rhythmic, and the umbilicus is often seen to move. Look for associated orofacial dyskinesia (tardive), segmental sensory signs (root/cord), or features suggesting a functional disorder such as distractibility and entrainment.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by multichannel surface EMG to characterise burst duration and rhythmicity and to test for propriospinal spread. Thoracic spine MRI and a review of dopamine-blocking drugs are standard. Electrophysiology with back-averaging or Bereitschaftspotential can help when a functional cause is considered.
det.treatment: Remove or reduce provoking drugs if possible. Botulinum toxin injections to the most active abdominal muscles help many patients; tetrabenazine, clonazepam, levetiracetam or other anticonvulsants are tried with variable success. Functional cases are managed with explanation and specialised physiotherapy or psychotherapy.
det.prognosis: Course is variable; some cases fade spontaneously while others persist for years with partial treatment response.
pearls: Watch the umbilicus: lateral wandering is the visual hallmark.
Always ask about abdominal surgery and dopamine blockers.
Surface EMG separates segmental spinal patterns from functional ones.
det.thd: belly dancer's dyskinesia คือกล้ามเนื้อหน้าท้องหดตัวเองเป็นคลื่นจนสะดือขยับไปมา เป็นลักษณะทางคลินิกที่เกิดได้จากหลายสาเหตุ เช่น หลังผ่าตัดช่องท้อง รอยโรครากประสาทหรือไขสันหลัง ยาต้านโดปามีน หรือเป็น functional ควรตรวจ surface EMG และ MRI ไขสันหลังส่วนอก รักษาด้วยการหยุดยาที่เป็นสาเหตุ และ botulinum toxin ได้ผลในหลายราย

name: Bell’s palsy
formal: Acute idiopathic unilateral lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy, often with ear pain or taste change, thought to be post-viral, with usual recovery over weeks.
simple: Sudden weakness of one side of the face, often improving over weeks, thought to follow a viral nerve inflammation.
th: เส้นประสาทใบหน้าอ่อนแรงเฉียบพลันข้างเดียว — หน้าเบี้ยวทั้งซีกรวมหน้าผาก หลับตาไม่สนิท
tempoNote: Peaks within 72 hours
feat: Unilateral facial weakness involving the forehead (LMN pattern)
Postauricular pain, hyperacusis, altered taste
Incomplete eye closure with Bell phenomenon
Most recover; early prednisolone improves outcome
inv: Clinical diagnosis; check for vesicles (Ramsay Hunt), bilateral involvement, other cranial nerves
Glucose, BP; imaging if atypical or no recovery by 3–4 months

case.story: Woke up with drooling from the left side of her mouth and unable to close the left eye; ached behind the ear yesterday.
case.exam: Complete left facial weakness including forehead, eyeball rolls up on attempted closure, no ear vesicles, other cranial nerves normal.
case.tests: Glucose normal.
case.q: Why does forehead involvement localise the lesion to the nerve rather than the cortex?
case.a: The upper face receives bilateral cortical input; a cortical (UMN) lesion spares the forehead, whereas a nerve (LMN) lesion paralyses it.

ddx.pt: Vesicles in the ear or palate, vertigo/hearing loss; VZV
Forehead spared, arm weakness or dysarthria
Bilateral facial weakness with limb areflexia
Travel/tick exposure, often bilateral

aN: bell palsy | idiopathic facial palsy | facial nerve palsy | lmn facial palsy | cn vii palsy

det.patho: Idiopathic acute lower motor neuron facial palsy, thought to result mainly from reactivation of herpes simplex virus in the geniculate ganglion, causing inflammation and swelling of the facial nerve within the narrow labyrinthine segment of the facial canal. Risk is higher in pregnancy (third trimester), diabetes and obesity. Annual incidence is roughly 20–30 per 100,000.
det.clinical: Unilateral weakness of upper and lower face develops over hours to 72 hours, often preceded by pain behind the ear. Patients cannot raise the eyebrow, close the eye fully or smile symmetrically, and the eye rolls upward on attempted closure (Bell phenomenon). Taste loss on the anterior tongue, hyperacusis and reduced tearing localise the lesion along the nerve. Red flags include gradual progression beyond 3 weeks, other cranial neuropathies, bilateral palsy, ear vesicles, a parotid mass, recurrent same-side palsy or no recovery by 3–4 months.
det.diagnosis: Bell palsy is a diagnosis of exclusion based on history and examination. Look carefully in the ear and mouth for vesicles (Ramsay Hunt), examine other cranial nerves and the parotid, and check glucose and BP. Laboratory tests and imaging are not routinely needed; MRI with contrast is indicated for atypical features. Electroneurography after the first week helps predict recovery in complete palsy. Bilateral palsy suggests GBS, Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, HIV or leukaemia.
det.treatment: Start oral corticosteroids within 72 hours, e.g. prednisolone 50 mg daily for 10 days or 60 mg daily for 5 days followed by a taper; this increases complete recovery. Adding an antiviral offers at most a small benefit and may be considered in severe palsy. Eye protection is vital: lubricating drops by day, ointment and taping at night, and urgent ophthalmology review if the eye becomes red or painful. Persistent severe weakness or synkinesis may benefit from physiotherapy, botulinum toxin and reanimation surgery.
det.prognosis: About 70% recover fully without treatment and over 80% with steroids; complete palsy, older age and absent early recovery predict incomplete recovery and synkinesis.
pearls: Forehead involved = LMN (nerve) lesion; forehead spared = UMN (central) lesion.
Always look in the ear for vesicles — Ramsay Hunt has a worse prognosis.
Protect the cornea; exposure keratopathy is the main early complication.
det.thd: Bell's palsy คือเส้นประสาทใบหน้า (CN VII) อ่อนแรงเฉียบพลันข้างเดียวโดยไม่ทราบสาเหตุ เชื่อว่าเกิดจากเชื้อ herpes simplex ทำให้เส้นประสาทบวมในช่องกระดูก อาการคือหน้าเบี้ยวทั้งซีกรวมหน้าผาก หลับตาไม่สนิท อาจปวดหลังหู รับรสผิดปกติ และได้ยินเสียงดังผิดปกติ วินิจฉัยโดยแยกสาเหตุอื่นออก เช่น ดูตุ่มน้ำในหู (Ramsay Hunt) และตรวจเส้นประสาทสมองเส้นอื่น รักษาด้วย prednisolone ภายใน 72 ชั่วโมงและปกป้องกระจกตา ส่วนใหญ่หายดี

name: Benedikt’s syndrome
formal: Midbrain tegmental lesion causing ipsilateral third nerve palsy with contralateral tremor, ataxia or involuntary movements from red nucleus involvement.
simple: A brainstem stroke syndrome with a drooping eye on one side and tremor or jerky movement of the opposite arm and leg.
th: กลุ่มอาการสมองส่วนกลางด้าน tegmentum จากรอยโรคใกล้ red nucleus ทำให้เส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 3 อัมพาตข้างเดียวกัน ร่วมกับสั่น เดินเซ หรือเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติด้านตรงข้าม
tempoNote: Usually abrupt from a paramedian midbrain infarct; slower with tumour, tuberculoma or demyelination
feat: Ipsilateral oculomotor palsy: ptosis, eye down and out, often a dilated pupil
Contralateral tremor (rest, postural and intention, Holmes-type), ataxia or choreoathetosis
Contralateral hemiparesis if the adjacent cerebral peduncle is involved, which merges it with Weber syndrome
Possible vertical gaze limitation or contralateral sensory loss
Crossed pattern: cranial nerve sign on one side, limb signs on the other
inv: MRI brain with DWI and thin cuts through the midbrain
Vascular imaging of the posterior circulation (CTA/MRA)
Stroke work-up: ECG/Holter, lipids, glucose; consider tumour, tuberculoma or demyelination if not vascular

case.story: He woke with a drooping right eyelid and double vision; by evening his left hand shook whenever he reached for a cup.
case.exam: Right ptosis, right eye abducted and depressed with a sluggish pupil; coarse left arm intention and postural tremor with mild dysmetria; power nearly normal.
case.tests: MRI: small DWI-bright lesion in the right paramedian midbrain tegmentum involving the red nucleus.
case.q: Which midbrain syndrome is this, and which structures are damaged?
case.a: Benedikt syndrome: oculomotor fascicles plus the red nucleus and cerebellothalamic fibres in the right tegmentum.

det.patho: The lesion lies in the paramedian midbrain tegmentum, supplied by interpeduncular perforators of the basilar tip and posterior cerebral artery. It involves the third nerve fascicles together with the red nucleus and the crossed dentatorubrothalamic pathway, hence the tremor and ataxia on the opposite side. Infarction is the common cause; haemorrhage, tumour, tuberculoma, abscess and demyelination are rarer.
det.clinical: The ipsilateral third nerve palsy is combined with contralateral tremor, which may be rest, postural or intention in type, together with ataxia or chorea. When the cerebral peduncle is also involved, contralateral hemiparesis appears, and the picture overlaps with Weber syndrome. Tremor may emerge days to weeks after the stroke (delayed Holmes tremor). Neuro-ophthalmology texts list it among the alternating syndromes with oculomotor paresis.
det.diagnosis: Localise first by the crossed signs: a third nerve palsy with opposite limb tremor means midbrain tegmentum. MRI with DWI confirms infarction and vascular imaging looks at the basilar tip and posterior cerebral arteries. Search for other causes in younger patients or when onset is gradual, including tumour, tuberculoma and demyelination.
det.treatment: Manage as an acute posterior circulation stroke, with reperfusion therapy where indicated, antithrombotic therapy, blood pressure and risk-factor control. Tremor is hard to treat and may respond to levodopa, propranolol, clonazepam, primidone or, in refractory cases, thalamic deep brain stimulation. Ptosis and diplopia are managed with patching or prisms, and surgery is considered after the deficit has stabilised.
det.prognosis: Oculomotor recovery is often partial; tremor can persist and be disabling.
pearls: Crossed signs equal brainstem: ipsilateral cranial nerve, contralateral limbs.
Third nerve palsy with contralateral tremor or chorea localises to the red nucleus region.
Holmes tremor may appear weeks to months after a midbrain stroke.
det.thd: Benedikt’s syndrome เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ tegmentum ของสมองส่วนกลางใกล้ red nucleus ทำให้ตาข้างเดียวกันกลอกไม่ได้จาก CN III ตกหนังตา ตาเหลือบลงนอก และมีอาการสั่น เดินเซ หรือ chorea ของแขนขาด้านตรงข้าม มักเกิดจากหลอดเลือดสมองตีบแขนงของ basilar หรือ PCA วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI รักษาตามแนวทางโรคหลอดเลือดสมองเฉียบพลัน ส่วนอาการสั่นอาจใช้ levodopa, propranolol หรือ clonazepam

qx.q: Which additional structure is involved compared with Weber syndrome?
opts: Medial lemniscus
Spinal trigeminal tract

Weber syndrome involves the peduncle with prominent hemiparesis but little tremor. Posterior commissure damage gives Parinaud features.

Fatigable ptosis and diplopia with pupil sparing and no limb tremor
Bilateral ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia after infection; anti-GQ1b positive

name: Benign hereditary chorea (BHC)
formal: Autosomal dominant NKX2-1 disorder with early-onset non-progressive chorea, mild gait delay and sometimes thyroid and lung abnormalities.
simple: An inherited childhood condition with mild non-worsening jerky movements, sometimes with thyroid or lung problems.
th: chorea ที่ถ่ายทอดทางพันธุกรรมแบบเด่นจากยีน NKX2-1 เริ่มตั้งแต่เด็กเล็ก ไม่ค่อยลุกลาม อาจมีปัญหาไทรอยด์และปอดร่วม
tempoNote: Begins in infancy or early childhood; static or improves by adulthood
feat: Generalised chorea from infancy or early childhood, often with hypotonia and delayed walking
Non-progressive or improving course; cognition usually normal or mildly affected
Congenital hypothyroidism and neonatal respiratory distress or later interstitial lung disease (brain-lung-thyroid triad)
Family history with dominant inheritance, though de novo variants are common
inv: Thyroid function and lung assessment (chest imaging, lung function)
MRI usually normal; exclude other causes of childhood chorea
NKX2-1 sequencing and deletion testing; ADCY5 and others in a chorea panel if negative

case.story: Walked at 22 months and has always had fidgety, dancing movements of arms and face; she was treated for congenital hypothyroidism. Her father had similar movements that faded in his twenties.
case.exam: Continuous generalised chorea, mild hypotonia, normal reflexes and eye movements.
case.tests: MRI normal; TSH controlled on thyroxine; NKX2-1 heterozygous variant.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what other organ needs monitoring?
case.a: NKX2-1-related benign hereditary chorea; monitor the lungs (risk of interstitial disease and recurrent infection).

read.where: Chapter 9 Movement Disorders — Benign Hereditary Chorea

det.patho: Most cases are caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants or deletions of NKX2-1, a transcription factor needed for development of the ventral forebrain (including striatal interneurons), thyroid and lung. Haploinsufficiency explains the variable combination of chorea, thyroid and lung disease. Some families with a similar phenotype carry variants in other genes such as ADCY5 or PDE10A.
det.clinical: Chorea usually appears in the first years, sometimes preceded by hypotonia and delayed motor milestones. It typically stays stable or lessens in adolescence and adulthood, though some adults keep mild chorea, myoclonus or dystonia. Thyroid disease ranges from congenital hypothyroidism to subtle dysfunction; lung disease ranges from neonatal respiratory distress to chronic interstitial disease and increased lung cancer risk in adults. Learning difficulties and ADHD can occur.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in childhood-onset non-progressive chorea, particularly with thyroid or lung problems. MRI is usually normal. Genetic testing of NKX2-1 (including deletion analysis) confirms; a broader movement panel is used when negative.
det.treatment: Tetrabenazine or levodopa improve chorea in some children; many need no drug. Thyroid hormone replacement, respiratory follow-up and avoidance of smoking are important. Educational support and genetic counselling for the family are part of care.
det.prognosis: Neurological outlook is generally good; lung disease drives most serious morbidity.
pearls: Childhood chorea + hypothyroidism + lung disease = think NKX2-1.
'Benign' refers to the neurology; the lungs may not be benign.
Unlike Huntington disease, the chorea does not progress.
det.thd: Benign hereditary chorea เกิดจากยีน NKX2-1 ถ่ายทอดแบบเด่น เด็กเริ่มมีการเคลื่อนไหวกระตุกแบบ chorea ตั้งแต่ขวบปีแรก ๆ มักไม่ลุกลามและดีขึ้นเมื่อโต อาจมีไทรอยด์ทำงานต่ำแต่กำเนิดและโรคปอดร่วม ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน รักษาตามอาการด้วย tetrabenazine หรือ levodopa และติดตามไทรอยด์กับปอด

qx.stem: An 8-year-old girl from Nakhon Sawan has had mild, non-progressive chorea and gait clumsiness since age 2, with normal cognition. Her father had similar movements in childhood, and she has had several respiratory infections. Brain MRI is normal.
qx.q: Which additional assessment is most relevant?
opts: CAG repeat in the HTT gene for Huntington disease
Thyroid function and pulmonary evaluation, with NKX2-1 testing
Serum ceruloplasmin only

qx.why: Early-onset, non-progressive chorea with a dominant family history and normal MRI suggests benign hereditary chorea due to NKX2-1 variants, where the 'brain-lung-thyroid' syndrome can include hypothyroidism and recurrent lung disease. Huntington disease has progressive course and adult onset, Sydenham chorea follows streptococcal infection, and NMDA receptor encephalitis has other features.

name: Benign hereditary myoclonus
formal: Familial myoclonus with early onset, non-progressive course, often alcohol-responsive, with normal cognition and EEG.
simple: An inherited condition of mild muscle jerks that begins in childhood and does not get worse.
th: myoclonus ที่ถ่ายทอดในครอบครัว เริ่มในวัยเด็ก ไม่ลุกลาม มักดีขึ้นเมื่อดื่มแอลกอฮอล์ สติปัญญาและ EEG ปกติ ส่วนใหญ่เป็นกลุ่ม myoclonus-dystonia (SGCE)
tempoNote: Onset in childhood or adolescence; stable or slowly fluctuating over life
feat: Brief lightning-like jerks of neck, trunk and arms, worse with action and posture
Often mild dystonia (cervical dystonia or writer's cramp)
Marked improvement after alcohol
Psychiatric features common: anxiety, OCD, depression, alcohol misuse
Normal cognition and EEG; no seizures or ataxia
inv: EEG normal; neurophysiology shows subcortical (non-cortical) myoclonus
MRI brain normal
SGCE testing (paternally inherited due to imprinting); panel if negative (e.g. KCTD17)

case.story: Jerky arms since age 8 make him spill drinks; he discovered that two beers make his hands steady. His father had the same jerks.
case.exam: Multifocal jerks of neck and arms on posture and action, mild right torticollis, otherwise normal.
case.tests: EEG normal, no giant SEPs; MRI normal; SGCE pathogenic variant.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and why might the mother be unaffected carrier in other families?
case.a: Myoclonus-dystonia (SGCE); maternal imprinting means the gene is expressed mainly from the paternal copy, so inheritance via the mother is usually silent.

read.where: 11 - Dystonia: Phenomenology, classification, etiology, pathology, biochemistry, and genetics

det.patho: Most familial non-progressive myoclonus with alcohol response is now classed as myoclonus-dystonia, mainly due to SGCE variants (epsilon-sarcoglycan). SGCE is maternally imprinted, so disease usually appears when the variant is inherited from the father. Dysfunction of cerebellar-thalamic and basal ganglia circuits is thought to produce the subcortical myoclonus.
det.clinical: Jerks start in the first two decades and mainly involve the upper body; they are brief, often with action and posture, and may disable writing or drinking. About half have mild dystonia. Psychiatric comorbidity is frequent and may need more attention than the movements. The disorder does not cause dementia, seizures or progressive ataxia, which separates it from progressive myoclonic epilepsies.
det.diagnosis: Clinical features plus family history suggest it; a normal EEG and absence of cortical myoclonus markers support it. Confirm with SGCE testing, remembering the imprinting pattern. Exclude Wilson disease and drug causes in sporadic young patients.
det.treatment: Clonazepam, levetiracetam, zonisamide or sodium valproate may help jerks; anticholinergics or botulinum toxin help dystonia. Globus pallidus internus deep brain stimulation is effective for disabling cases. Counsel against self-treatment with alcohol and treat psychiatric symptoms actively.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is normal; symptoms tend to plateau in adulthood.
pearls: Alcohol-responsive jerks in a teenager with a normal EEG: test SGCE.
Paternal transmission pattern is the clue to imprinting.
Screen for alcohol misuse, anxiety and OCD.
det.thd: Benign hereditary myoclonus ปัจจุบันส่วนใหญ่จัดเป็น myoclonus-dystonia จากยีน SGCE ผู้ป่วยมีอาการกระตุกสั้น ๆ ที่คอและแขนตั้งแต่วัยเด็ก อาจมี dystonia เล็กน้อย ดีขึ้นชัดเมื่อดื่มเหล้า EEG และสติปัญญาปกติ ยีนนี้แสดงออกจากฝั่งพ่อ รักษาด้วย clonazepam หรือ DBS ที่ GPi และต้องดูแลปัญหาจิตเวชและการดื่มสุราด้วย

name: Benign myoclonus of infancy
formal: Self-limited infantile condition with brief spasms of head and arms during feeding, mimicking infantile spasms but with normal EEG and development.
simple: Harmless brief jerks in a baby, especially during feeding, which stop by themselves.
th: ภาวะกระตุกเป็นชุดของศีรษะ ลำตัว และแขนในทารก ซึ่งดูเหมือน infantile spasms แต่ EEG ระหว่างที่กระตุกปกติ พัฒนาการปกติ และหายเองภายในไม่กี่เดือน (ปัจจุบันบางตำราเรียกว่า benign spasms of infancy)
tempoNote: Clusters of brief jerks, often around feeds, building over weeks to months and then fading spontaneously; usually gone by 2 years
feat: Begins during infancy as clusters of quick head nods, trunk flexion or arm jerks
Events often occur at mealtimes and look identical to epileptic spasms to the eye
Child is alert between clusters and neurologically and developmentally normal
Intensity builds over weeks to months, then clusters abate and stop, with no events after about 2 years
Ictal EEG during a typical spasm shows no epileptiform discharge and no hypsarrhythmia
inv: Video-EEG capturing a typical event: normal background and normal ictal tracing is the key test
Home video from caregivers to document the movements and their timing
Neuroimaging and metabolic work-up only if development stalls or exam is abnormal

case.who: 6-month-old boy brought to the paediatric neurology clinic in Songkhla by his mother
case.story: For three weeks, during bottle feeding, he has clusters of quick head drops with both arms jerking forward, 5–10 jerks each, several times a day. He smiles, tracks and rolls over normally; no regression and no fever.
case.exam: Alert and interactive, head circumference on the 50th centile, normal tone, no skin lesions, normal fundus and fixation.
case.tests: Video-EEG with three captured clusters: normal sleep and wake background with no hypsarrhythmia, and no electrographic change during the jerks.
case.q: Which diagnosis is being tested for, and why is the ictal EEG so decisive?
case.a: Benign myoclonus (spasms) of infancy. The movements mimic infantile spasms, so only a normal EEG during an event allows reassurance; hypsarrhythmia would instead mandate urgent ACTH, prednisolone or vigabatrin. Counsel the parents and review development at intervals.

det.patho: The cause is unknown and no structural, genetic or metabolic lesion has been found; it is presumed to be a transient, age-limited quirk of maturing motor circuits. It is rare and appears to be non-epileptic, so cortical discharges are not demonstrated. Nomenclature is unsettled, since the term benign myoclonus of infancy has been partly replaced by benign spasms of infancy.
det.clinical: Onset is in infancy, with clusters of brief flexor jerks of the head, trunk and arms that are often seen during feeding. Frequency and intensity build over several weeks to months before fading, and they have typically stopped by around 3 months after peak and certainly before age 2. Between events the infant looks well, feeds, tracks and develops normally. Because the semiology cannot be told apart from infantile spasms by looking, parents are often alarmed and clinicians must treat the first presentation as possible West syndrome until proven otherwise.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on capturing events during video-EEG and showing a normal ictal and interictal recording. Without that, the label should not be applied. Normal development, examination and, where done, imaging support it. Mimics to exclude include infantile spasms, benign sleep myoclonus, gastro-oesophageal reflux with posturing, shuddering attacks and early myoclonic epilepsies; any abnormal tracing, stalling of milestones or eye-contact loss should reopen the question.
det.treatment: No anti-seizure drugs are needed; the management is education, reassurance and a clear plan for follow-up. Parents should be told which features (loss of skills, new seizure types, hypsarrhythmia on repeat EEG) should prompt early review. Avoid starting steroids or vigabatrin before the EEG result is known unless the picture is strongly typical of West syndrome.
det.prognosis: Excellent: spontaneous resolution with normal neurodevelopment is the rule, and the diagnosis is made retrospectively when the course holds up.
pearls: Looks like infantile spasms, behaves like nothing: only a normal EEG during the event separates them.
Never label it benign on history alone; a missed West syndrome costs developmental outcome.
Jerks restricted to sleep point to benign sleep myoclonus rather than this condition.
det.thd: โรคนี้ทำให้ทารกมีอาการหัวพับหรือแขนกระตุกเป็นชุด ๆ มักเกิดช่วงกินนม ดูคล้าย infantile spasms แต่ไม่ใช่โรคลมชัก สมองและพัฒนาการปกติ การวินิจฉัยต้องทำ video-EEG ขณะมีอาการ ซึ่งต้องปกติ จึงจะแยกจาก West syndrome ได้ ไม่ต้องให้ยากันชัก เน้นให้ความรู้พ่อแม่และติดตามพัฒนาการ ส่วนใหญ่หายเองก่อนอายุ 2 ปี

name: Benign paraproteinaemic neuropathy
formal: Peripheral neuropathy associated with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (often IgM anti-MAG) producing distal demyelinating sensory-predominant neuropathy with tremor and ataxia.
simple: Nerve damage associated with an abnormal blood protein that is not cancer, causing numbness, imbalance and tremor in the legs and hands.
th: เส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเสื่อมที่สัมพันธ์กับ monoclonal gammopathy ชนิดที่ยังไม่ใช่มะเร็ง (MGUS) โดยเฉพาะ IgM anti-MAG ให้อาการชาปลายเท้า เดินเซ และมือสั่น
tempoNote: Slowly progressive over years, usually in people over 60
feat: Distal, symmetric, sensory-predominant neuropathy in older adults, men more than women
Sensory ataxia with positive Romberg sign; postural/action hand tremor common in IgM cases
Mild distal weakness only; reflexes reduced or absent
IgG/IgA MGUS neuropathies are more heterogeneous and the link may be coincidental
inv: Serum protein electrophoresis plus immunofixation and free light chains
NCS: demyelinating with very prolonged distal motor latencies in anti-MAG
Anti-MAG antibody titre; haematology review (bone marrow, imaging) to exclude Waldenström, myeloma, AL amyloid, POEMS

case.story: Three years of numb feet and unsteadiness in the dark; recently his handwriting has become shaky.
case.exam: Reduced vibration and joint position at toes and ankles, Romberg positive, absent ankle jerks, mild toe extension weakness, fine postural tremor of the hands.
case.tests: IgM-kappa paraprotein 4 g/L; NCS distal-predominant demyelination with long distal latencies; high anti-MAG titre.
case.q: What is the likely neuropathy and which drug has the best evidence?
case.a: Anti-MAG IgM paraproteinaemic neuropathy; rituximab is the usual choice for progressive disabling cases.

read.where: 15. Paraproteinemic Neuropathy: Distinguishing the Ominous From the Ordinary
Chapter 52: Distal Acquired Demyelinating Symmetric (DADS) Neuropathy
Part I: Peripheral Nerve, Neuromuscular Junction and Motor Neuron Disorders

det.patho: A clonal plasma-cell or B-cell population produces a monoclonal immunoglobulin. In about half of IgM cases the antibody binds myelin-associated glycoprotein, deposits on myelin and widens myelin lamellae, causing a distal demyelinating neuropathy. With IgG or IgA MGUS the relationship is less certain and many patients actually have CIDP or an unrelated neuropathy.
det.clinical: Typical patients are older men with slowly ascending numbness, sensory ataxia and falls, with a hand tremor in many IgM cases. Weakness is mild and distal. Rapid progression, pain, weight loss, autonomic failure or organomegaly should prompt a search for amyloidosis, POEMS, lymphoma or myeloma rather than 'benign' disease.
det.diagnosis: Screen all unexplained neuropathies with electrophoresis and immunofixation, because small bands are missed on electrophoresis alone. Nerve conduction defines demyelinating versus axonal patterns. Measure anti-MAG in IgM cases and refer to haematology to stage the clone; MGUS requires the absence of end-organ damage from a malignancy. VEGF and skeletal survey are needed if POEMS is possible.
det.treatment: Mild, slowly progressive disease can be observed. Rituximab is the main option for disabling anti-MAG neuropathy, though benefit is modest; IVIG gives short-lived help in some. IgG/IgA MGUS with a CIDP-like picture is treated like CIDP (IVIG, steroids, plasma exchange). Any underlying haematological malignancy is treated on its own merits, and the clone is monitored over time for transformation.
det.prognosis: Disability usually accumulates slowly over many years; a minority progress to lymphoproliferative disease.
pearls: Always use immunofixation; electrophoresis alone misses small paraproteins.
IgM + distal demyelination + tremor + sensory ataxia = anti-MAG pattern.
Lambda light chain with a motor-predominant demyelinating neuropathy: check VEGF for POEMS.

name: Benign paroxysmal infantile torticollis
formal: Recurrent episodes of head tilt in infants, lasting hours to days, with pallor, irritability or vomiting, and linked to CACNA1A variants and later migraine or vertigo.
simple: Repeated episodes where a baby's head tilts to one side, with fussiness or vomiting, that settle with age.
th: อาการคอเอียงเป็นพัก ๆ ในทารก นานหลายชั่วโมงถึงหลายวัน อาจมีซีด อาเจียน หรืองอแง หายเองได้ สัมพันธ์กับ CACNA1A และไมเกรนในภายหลัง
tempoNote: Starts in the first year of life, recurs every few weeks, and usually stops by age 3–5
feat: Recurrent attacks of head tilt to one side (side may alternate), lasting hours to days
Pallor, irritability, vomiting, malaise or ataxia during attacks
Normal neurological examination and development between attacks
Family history of migraine is common
Often evolves into benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood and later migraine
inv: Clinical diagnosis per ICHD-3 episodic syndromes associated with migraine
MRI of posterior fossa and cervical spine if atypical, persistent or with abnormal signs

case.story: Every three to four weeks her head tilts to the right or left for about two days with pallor and vomiting; between episodes she is happy and developing normally.
case.exam: Between attacks normal tone, eye movements and milestones.
case.tests: MRI brain and cervical spine normal.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and expected outcome?
case.a: Benign paroxysmal infantile torticollis; it usually resolves by preschool age, though migraine may develop later.

det.patho: It is regarded as an early-life migraine equivalent, probably involving transient dysfunction of vestibular or cerebellar circuits. Some families carry CACNA1A or PRRT2 variants, linking it to channelopathies such as familial hemiplegic migraine and episodic ataxia. In most children no genetic cause is identified.
det.clinical: Episodes begin in the first months and recur, often monthly, lasting minutes to days. The infant tilts the head and may rotate it; attempts to straighten may be resisted. Pallor, vomiting, irritability and unsteadiness in older infants are common. Development is normal, although mild motor delay is reported in some.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 criteria require recurrent attacks in a young child with at least one associated feature (pallor, irritability, malaise, vomiting, ataxia) and a normal examination between attacks. Exclude posterior fossa tumours, gastro-oesophageal reflux, atlanto-axial problems, dystonia and seizures, particularly when attacks are atypical.
det.treatment: No treatment is usually needed; reassurance and documentation of attacks are key. Preventive drugs are rarely justified. Follow up for the emergence of benign paroxysmal vertigo or migraine.
det.prognosis: Resolves spontaneously in early childhood; many children later develop migraine.
pearls: Intermittent head tilt with completely normal interictal exam = think migraine equivalent.
Persistent tilt or abnormal signs require posterior fossa imaging.
Family history of migraine or episodic ataxia supports the diagnosis.

formal: Brief positional vertigo from displaced otoconia in the semicircular canals, causing characteristic torsional nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike testing, treated with the Epley manoeuvre.
simple: Short bouts of spinning dizziness when moving the head, caused by tiny crystals in the inner ear.

feat: Brief rotatory vertigo turning in bed, looking up or bending down
Posterior canal most common

case.exam: Right Dix–Hallpike: after 3 s latency, upbeating torsional nystagmus toward the right ear lasting 20 s.

det.patho: Otoconia (calcium carbonate crystals) break loose from the utricular macula and drift into a semicircular canal, most often the posterior canal because it is the lowest part of the labyrinth when lying down. When the head moves in the plane of that canal the free particles sink under gravity and drag endolymph, deflecting the cupula and producing brief vertigo with canal-specific nystagmus (canalithiasis); less often the debris sticks to the cupula itself (cupulolithiasis), giving longer-lasting nystagmus. The posterior canal accounts for roughly 80–90% of cases, the horizontal canal for most of the rest, and the anterior canal is rarely affected. BPPV is the commonest cause of vertigo, with a lifetime prevalence of about 2–3%, a peak between 50 and 70 years and a female excess. Secondary BPPV follows head injury, vestibular neuritis, Ménière disease or prolonged bed rest, and low vitamin D and osteoporosis are associated.
det.clinical: Patients describe short bursts of spinning lasting under a minute, triggered by rolling over in bed, lying down, sitting up, looking up to a shelf or bending forward, often worst on first rising in the morning. Nausea and a lingering sense of unsteadiness may persist between spells, but there is no hearing loss, headache or neurological deficit. Horizontal canal BPPV causes violent vertigo on turning the head to either side while lying supine. Older patients may report only imbalance or falls rather than spinning, so BPPV is under-diagnosed in the elderly. Spells cluster over days to weeks and often relapse months or years later.
det.diagnosis: The Dix–Hallpike manoeuvre for posterior canal BPPV provokes, once a brief delay of seconds has passed, upbeating-torsional nystagmus whose fast phase twists the top of each eye toward the undermost ear, building and fading within a minute, reversing direction on sitting up and lessening with repetition. The supine roll test detects horizontal canal BPPV: geotropic nystagmus (beating toward the ground, from free particles) is stronger when the affected ear is down, whereas apogeotropic nystagmus (from cupular or anterior-arm debris) is stronger when the healthy ear is down. In typical cases neither imaging nor vestibular laboratory testing is needed. Atypical findings — no latency, nystagmus that does not fade, pure downbeat or direction not matching any canal, failure of repeated manoeuvres, or other neurological signs — require MRI to exclude central positional nystagmus from a cerebellar or fourth-ventricle lesion.
det.treatment: Canalith repositioning is curative in most patients: the Epley or Semont manoeuvre for posterior canal BPPV, each clearing about 80% after one or two sessions, and the Lempert (barbecue) roll or Gufoni manoeuvre for horizontal canal BPPV; apogeotropic forms may first need conversion to geotropic. Post-manoeuvre restrictions on posture are not required. Vestibular suppressants have no role beyond brief nausea control, and Brandt–Daroff exercises are less effective than repositioning. Patients with recurrences can be taught self-treatment, older patients should have a falls assessment, and vitamin D supplementation reduces recurrence in those who are deficient. Very rare intractable cases are considered for posterior canal occlusion surgery.
det.prognosis: Most cases resolve with one to three manoeuvres, but about a third to a half recur within a few years, sometimes in a different canal.
pearls: Vertigo lasting seconds on lying down or turning in bed = BPPV until proved otherwise.
Nystagmus without latency, without fatigue or in a non-canal direction is a central warning sign.
Repositioning beats medication — betahistine and antihistamines do not cure BPPV.
Look for BPPV after head injury or vestibular neuritis — it is a common secondary cause of positional vertigo.

name: Benign paroxysmal tonic upgaze and ataxia of childhood
formal: Childhood paroxysmal disorder with intermittent tonic upgaze deviation and ataxia, often CACNA1A related, typically self-limiting with normal development.
simple: A childhood condition where the eyes drift upward in episodes with unsteadiness, usually going away with age.
th: ภาวะในเด็กเล็กที่ตาเหลือกขึ้นค้างเป็นพัก ๆ ร่วมกับเดินเซ เด็กรู้ตัวดี มักหายเองเมื่อโตขึ้น บางรายเกี่ยวกับยีน CACNA1A
tempoNote: Begins in infancy, episodes last hours to days, usually resolve within 1–4 years
feat: Episodes of sustained conjugate upward gaze with chin-down head posture
Downbeating nystagmus when the child attempts to look down; horizontal movements normal
Ataxia during episodes; normal consciousness
Triggered or worsened by fatigue and infection; relieved by sleep
Most develop normally; some show mild language or motor delay
inv: MRI brain to exclude midbrain or pineal lesions
EEG/video-EEG to exclude seizures
Consider CACNA1A testing; metabolic tests if atypical

case.story: Episodes of eyes staring upward for several hours, with his chin tucked, mostly when tired or feverish; he sways when sitting during episodes.
case.exam: Between episodes normal; video shows sustained upgaze with downbeat nystagmus on attempted downgaze, alert and smiling.
case.tests: MRI normal; video-EEG during an episode shows no epileptiform activity.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what is the typical outcome?
case.a: Benign paroxysmal tonic upgaze of childhood; episodes usually stop within a few years, with follow-up for development.

det.patho: The mechanism is uncertain. Proposed explanations include transient dysfunction of the vertical gaze centres in the rostral midbrain or immaturity of cerebellar–brainstem control. Some cases have CACNA1A variants and a family history of episodic ataxia or hemiplegic migraine, suggesting a channelopathy.
det.clinical: It typically begins in infancy. Episodes of upward eye deviation last hours and recur over days, with the child flexing the neck to see forward. Ataxia commonly accompanies episodes. Consciousness is normal and episodes disappear during sleep. The condition usually remits by early childhood.
det.diagnosis: It is a diagnosis of exclusion: seizures, oculogyric crises from drugs, midbrain lesions and metabolic disorders must be ruled out with EEG, MRI and history. Normal horizontal eye movements and preserved alertness are reassuring.
det.treatment: Reassurance is often enough. Levodopa and acetazolamide have been reported to help in some children. Developmental surveillance is advised because a minority show delays.
det.prognosis: Usually benign; a subset has later ataxia, learning difficulties or migraine.
pearls: Alert infant with episodic upgaze and normal horizontal movements: think PTU.
Always exclude drug-induced oculogyric crisis and midbrain lesions.
Ask for family history of episodic ataxia or hemiplegic migraine.

case.story: Parents film rhythmic jerks of both arms and legs lasting several minutes, only while he sleeps; they stop when he is picked up and he feeds well.
case.exam: Normal tone, alert, normal fontanelle and reflexes.
case.tests: Video-EEG during a cluster shows normal sleep background without seizures.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what is the management?

det.patho: Thought to reflect immaturity of brainstem and spinal inhibitory control during sleep. It is not epileptic and not associated with structural brain disease. Its cause is otherwise unknown; some cases follow maternal drug use.
det.clinical: Onset is in the first month, with clusters of jerks during quiet (non-REM) sleep involving arms, legs or both. Episodes can be frequent and long, alarming parents and sometimes leading to wrong treatment. The infant wakes normally and is neurologically normal.
det.diagnosis: History and home video are often sufficient; waking the baby stopping the jerks is the key test. Video-EEG is used in doubtful cases and shows no ictal change. Metabolic checks are reserved for babies who look unwell.
det.treatment: Reassure the parents. No drug is required; benzodiazepines may increase jerks. Follow development routinely.
det.prognosis: Excellent; resolves within months with normal development.
pearls: Jerks only in sleep that stop on waking = benign neonatal sleep myoclonus.
Avoid starting antiseizure drugs on the basis of a typical video.
An unwell baby or jerks in wakefulness needs full seizure work-up.

name: Benign tremulous Parkinson’s disease
formal: Parkinson disease with prominent tremor, slow progression, mild bradykinesia and relatively preserved cognition and gait.
simple: A form of Parkinson disease with mainly tremor that progresses slowly and causes few other problems.

Mild bradykinesia and rigidity that progress slowly

case.story: Eight years of shaking hands that embarrasses her at the market, yet she still cooks, gardens and drives.
case.exam: Bilateral rest tremor and re-emergent postural tremor, mild right bradykinesia, normal gait and pull test.
case.tests: DaT-SPECT shows asymmetric reduced putaminal uptake.
case.q: How is this different from typical Parkinson disease prognosis?

det.patho: It is considered a slowly progressive phenotype of Lewy body Parkinson disease rather than a separate disorder. Dopaminergic deficit is present on imaging, but the rate of spread appears slower; why tremor-dominant patients fare better is not fully understood.
det.clinical: Patients have conspicuous tremor for years with only mild slowness and stiffness and minimal axial involvement. Disability comes mostly from tremor itself. Some show a family history of tremor, raising debate about overlap with essential tremor. Long follow-up is required to label the course 'benign'.
det.diagnosis: Apply MDS clinical criteria; DaT-SPECT supports a degenerative dopaminergic cause when the picture overlaps with essential or dystonic tremor. Exclude drug-induced parkinsonism and Wilson disease in younger patients.
det.treatment: Levodopa or dopamine agonists treat bradykinesia; tremor may need higher doses, anticholinergics in younger patients, clozapine, or propranolol for postural components. Refractory tremor responds well to deep brain stimulation or focused ultrasound thalamotomy. Exercise and physiotherapy are encouraged as in any PD.
det.prognosis: Better than average for PD; many remain independent for over a decade.
pearls: Tremor that looks dramatic does not mean a bad prognosis in PD.
Levodopa-resistant tremor is common; consider DBS or focused ultrasound.
Normal DaT-SPECT should make you reconsider the diagnosis.
det.thd: Benign tremulous Parkinson's disease คือ Parkinson ชนิดที่อาการสั่นเด่นแต่ช้าและแข็งเพียงเล็กน้อย การเดินและความจำดีอยู่ได้นาน ลุกลามช้ากว่าแบบทั่วไป DaT-SPECT ผิดปกติซึ่งช่วยแยกจาก essential tremor อาการสั่นอาจตอบสนองต่อ levodopa ไม่ดี รายที่สั่นมากพิจารณา DBS หรือ focused ultrasound

name: Bent spine/dropped head syndrome

simple: A condition where back or neck muscles are too weak to hold the trunk or head upright, so the spine bends forward.
more: Investigate with EMG, MRI, CK, and biopsy to find the cause. Treat the underlying disease, and use bracing and physiotherapy; response varies by cause.

case.exam: Neck extensors 3/5, flexors 4/5, fatigable ptosis after sustained upgaze, no fasciculations.
case.tests: AChR antibody positive; repetitive stimulation decrement in trapezius; CK normal.
case.q: What is the cause of the head drop here?

det.patho: The posture results from weakness or dystonic imbalance of axial extensor muscles. Causes include isolated axial (focal) myopathy of the elderly, inflammatory myositis, inclusion body myositis, myasthenia, motor neuron disease, late-onset Pompe disease, FSHD, mitochondrial and nemaline myopathies, hypothyroidism, and parkinsonian disorders where dystonia and rigidity contribute.
det.clinical: Ask about speed of onset, fatigability, bulbar or respiratory symptoms and other limb weakness. Camptocormia in Parkinson disease and MSA is common and partly dystonic; head drop is particularly associated with MG, ALS and isolated neck extensor myopathy. Respiratory involvement is crucial to identify in ALS, Pompe and MG.
det.diagnosis: Screen bloods (CK, thyroid, antibodies), EMG including paraspinals, and muscle MRI to choose a biopsy site and show oedema versus fat. Spinal imaging excludes structural deformity. Dried blood spot for acid alpha-glucosidase helps detect Pompe disease.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying disease: immunotherapy for MG or myositis, enzyme replacement for Pompe, optimisation of dopaminergic therapy in PD (camptocormia often responds poorly). Collars, braces and walking aids improve function; physiotherapy strengthens extensors. Botulinum toxin and DBS have selected roles in dystonic parkinsonian forms.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause: good in treated MG, poor in ALS, often static in isolated axial myopathy.
pearls: Head drop: think MG and ALS first, then myopathy.
Always check respiratory function in head drop.
Muscle MRI of paraspinals guides biopsy and distinguishes active from end-stage myopathy.

name: Bethlem myopathy
formal: Collagen VI-related autosomal dominant myopathy with slowly progressive proximal weakness, distal joint hyperlaxity and finger contractures.
simple: An inherited muscle disease causing slowly progressive weakness with stiff finger and elbow joints.
more: Diagnosed by COL6A1, COL6A2 or COL6A3 mutations or collagen VI immunostaining of muscle or skin fibroblasts; CK is normal or mildly raised. MRI shows a rim of fatty change in muscle; management is supportive with contracture care and respiratory monitoring.

case.tests: CK 420 U/L; thigh MRI shows peripheral fatty rim in vastus lateralis; dominant COL6A1 variant.

det.patho: Collagen VI is an extracellular matrix protein that anchors muscle fibres to the surrounding basement membrane and supports tendon and skin integrity. Dominant-negative or haploinsufficient variants in COL6A1–3 disturb microfibril assembly, causing gradual fibre loss and connective tissue changes. Fibroblasts, not muscle cells, produce collagen VI.
det.clinical: Weakness can start in infancy with hypotonia or later in adult life. Joint contractures, particularly of finger flexors, elbows and Achilles tendons, coexist with laxity of distal joints. Skin findings such as keratosis pilaris and abnormal scars are helpful clues. Many patients walk into older age, though some need aids after middle age.
det.diagnosis: Clinical pattern plus typical muscle MRI appearances strongly suggest the diagnosis. Genetic testing of the three COL6 genes confirms it; some deep intronic variants require RNA studies. Collagen VI staining on cultured fibroblasts is reduced or abnormal.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy exists. Stretching, splinting and physiotherapy reduce contractures. Monitor respiratory function, including nocturnal hypoventilation. Surgery for contractures is occasionally helpful.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; about half of patients over 50 need walking aids, and lifespan is generally normal.
pearls: Contractures with distal hyperlaxity is the collagen VI combination.
Rectus femoris 'central shadow' on MRI is characteristic.
Bethlem and Ullrich are ends of the same collagen VI spectrum.

name: Biballism
formal: Bilateral ballism with large proximal flinging movements on both sides, usually due to bilateral subthalamic nucleus lesions or metabolic causes.
simple: Wild, uncontrolled flinging movements of limbs on both sides of the body.

feat: Large-amplitude, flinging proximal movements of limbs on both sides

case.exam: Bilateral violent proximal flinging movements, more on the left, conscious and oriented.

det.patho: Ballism reflects reduced output from the subthalamic nucleus or striatal circuits, leading to disinhibition of thalamocortical motor drive. Bilateral involvement needs a bilateral or diffuse process: hyperglycaemia, multiple infarcts, drugs (levodopa, anticonvulsants), autoimmune encephalitis, or metabolic disorders. Ballism and chorea are thought to be points on one continuum.
det.clinical: The movements are proximal, violent and continuous during wakefulness, settling in sleep. Patients may be injured, exhausted or dehydrated. As the condition improves the amplitude falls and chorea emerges. Underlying causes are often more urgent than the movements themselves.
det.diagnosis: Check glucose immediately, then MRI with diffusion and T1 sequences. Review medications and toxins. In unexplained cases, test for autoimmune and paraneoplastic antibodies and consider CSF analysis.
det.treatment: Correct the cause (glucose, stop the drug, immunotherapy). Symptomatic options include tetrabenazine or deutetrabenazine, and antipsychotics such as haloperidol or risperidone in severe cases. Protect the patient with padding and maintain fluids and nutrition; check CK.
det.prognosis: Metabolic and vascular cases usually improve over weeks to months; some persist.
pearls: Bilateral ballism in an elderly diabetic: check glucose before any scan.
Ballism and chorea are the same spectrum with different amplitude.
Monitor CK and hydration in severe ballism.

formal: Autoimmune brainstem encephalitis with anti-GQ1b antibodies causing ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and impaired consciousness, belonging to the Miller Fisher-Guillain-Barre spectrum.
simple: An immune illness after infection causing drowsiness, unsteady walking and weakness of eye movements.

feat: Bilateral external ophthalmoplegia and ataxia, like Miller Fisher syndrome
Drowsiness or coma, which marks central (brainstem reticular) involvement
Reflexes may be brisk with extensor plantars, or lost if overlapping with GBS

case.story: Ten days after diarrhoea he developed double vision and could not walk straight; over three days he became sleepy and confused.
case.exam: GCS 12, almost complete external ophthalmoplegia, truncal ataxia, brisk reflexes with bilateral extensor plantars.
case.tests: MRI brain normal; CSF protein 0.9 g/L, 3 cells; serum anti-GQ1b IgG strongly positive.

det.patho: Molecular mimicry between infectious lipo-oligosaccharides and the ganglioside GQ1b, which is concentrated in ocular motor nerve paranodes and also present in the brainstem reticular formation, leads to antibody-mediated dysfunction. BBE sits with Miller Fisher syndrome and GBS on a continuous anti-GQ1b spectrum. It is rare, with a slight male predominance and a peak in young adults.
det.clinical: Onset is acute, usually following infection, with diplopia and unsteadiness, then disturbed consciousness. Signs include ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, hyperreflexia or areflexia, facial weakness and bulbar palsy; about half develop limb weakness overlapping with GBS, and some need ventilation. Autonomic instability may occur. Most reach nadir within a few weeks.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical: progressive, fairly symmetric ophthalmoplegia and ataxia with impaired consciousness or hyperreflexia, after excluding stroke, Wernicke encephalopathy, infection, botulism and other encephalitides. Anti-GQ1b IgG supports but is not mandatory. MRI is normal in most; brainstem lesions do not exclude the diagnosis. CSF and EEG are nonspecific.
det.treatment: Supportive care with airway protection and monitoring is central. IVIG or plasma exchange is widely used, extrapolating from GBS evidence; steroids are sometimes added without strong data. Give thiamine empirically until Wernicke encephalopathy is excluded. Rehabilitation follows the acute phase.
det.prognosis: Generally favourable, with most recovering well within six months; a minority have residual deficits or die from complications.
pearls: Ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + drowsiness: BBE; same without drowsiness: Miller Fisher.
Brisk reflexes do not exclude an anti-GQ1b disorder.
Always give thiamine while working up ophthalmoplegia with confusion.

det.patho: Bilateral optic neuritis can be the first event in aquaporin-4 antibody astrocytopathy (NMOSD), in MOG antibody-associated disease (MOGAD), or occasionally in MS, post-infectious and systemic autoimmune settings. In AQP4 disease, complement-activating IgG1 binds the astrocyte water channel, causing astrocyte death, demyelination and axonal loss, with predilection for optic nerve, spinal cord and area postrema. MOG antibodies target the oligodendrocyte surface and tend to produce swollen, steroid-responsive optic neuritis.
det.clinical: Visual loss progresses over days in one or both eyes with pain on eye movement and dyschromatopsia, and visual field defects are usually central. AQP4-NMOSD often brings devastating, incompletely reversible loss, may involve the chiasm, and can be accompanied by longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, intractable vomiting and hiccups from the area postrema. MOGAD frequently presents with bilateral swollen discs, is more steroid-responsive and may relapse when steroids are tapered. Typical MS rarely begins with simultaneous bilateral optic neuritis.
det.diagnosis: Use clinical evaluation, MRI of orbits, brain and spine, and cell-based serology for AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG, ideally before steroid or plasma exchange. A flowchart approach to relapsing or bilateral optic neuritis places brain MRI and AQP4 testing first, then CSF oligoclonal bands, spinal imaging and alternative diagnoses if seronegative. Exclude infection (syphilis, TB, HIV), sarcoidosis, lupus, compressive and infiltrative lesions, nutritional or toxic neuropathy and LHON.
det.treatment: Treat suspected attacks without waiting for antibody results: intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily over three to five days, then plasma exchange or immunoadsorption within days when response is poor or the attack is severe. For AQP4-NMOSD, start long-term prevention at once with rituximab, inebilizumab, satralizumab or a complement inhibitor (eculizumab, ravulizumab), or azathioprine or mycophenolate where access is limited. MOGAD after repeated relapses may need long-term immunotherapy; interferon-beta and some MS drugs can worsen NMOSD and should be avoided.
det.prognosis: AQP4-NMOSD carries significant risk of permanent visual and motor disability without prevention; MOGAD often recovers well but may relapse.
pearls: Bilateral or very severe optic neuritis means test AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG before treatment.
Start intravenous steroid early; do not wait for the antibody result.
Avoid interferon-beta in AQP4-NMOSD.
det.thd: Optic neuritis ทั้งสองข้างพบน้อยใน MS ทั่วไป ควรนึกถึง NMOSD (AQP4-IgG) และ MOGAD เป็นอันดับแรก ผู้ป่วยตามัวเร็ว เจ็บเวลากลอกตา มองสีผิดปกติ และ MRI อาจเห็นการอักเสบยาวตามเส้นประสาทตาหรือถึง chiasm ควรเจาะเลือดตรวจแอนติบอดีก่อนให้ยา และตรวจหาสาเหตุอื่น เช่น ซิฟิลิส วัณโรค ขาดวิตามิน B12 หรือ LHON การรักษาเฉียบพลันคือ methylprednisolone ทางหลอดเลือด และทำ plasma exchange ถ้าไม่ตอบสนอง ใน NMOSD ต้องให้ยาป้องกันการกลับเป็นซ้ำระยะยาว และหลีกเลี่ยง interferon-beta

name: Bilateral vestibular failure (BVF)
formal: Loss of vestibular function on both sides, causing oscillopsia, unsteadiness worse in the dark and a positive head impulse test, from ototoxins, meningitis or idiopathic causes.
simple: Loss of balance function in both inner ears, causing unsteadiness and a bouncing view of the world when walking.
th: การทำงานของระบบการทรงตัวในหูชั้นในเสียทั้งสองข้าง ทำให้เดินเซโดยเฉพาะในที่มืด และภาพสั่นไหวเวลาเดินหรือขยับศีรษะ
tempoNote: Gradual or stepwise over months to years; occasionally sudden after aminoglycosides or meningitis
feat: Unsteadiness worse in the dark, on uneven ground or with eyes closed; little or no vertigo
Oscillopsia: the visual world jumps when walking or turning the head
Bilaterally abnormal head impulse test with catch-up saccades
Causes: gentamicin ototoxicity, meningitis, bilateral Ménière, CANVAS, autoimmune; about half idiopathic
inv: Video head impulse test (reduced gain both sides); caloric testing; rotational chair
Audiogram
MRI brain and internal auditory canals; nerve conduction if CANVAS suspected
Review drug history; RFC1 repeat testing when neuropathy or cerebellar signs coexist

case.story: After two weeks of IV gentamicin for pyelonephritis, she finds the world bounces when she walks and she falls at night walking to the toilet.
case.exam: Bilateral catch-up saccades on head impulse, Romberg positive, dynamic visual acuity drops 4 lines; no nystagmus or cerebellar signs.
case.tests: vHIT gain 0.3 bilaterally; audiogram mild high-frequency loss.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the main treatment?
case.a: Aminoglycoside-induced bilateral vestibular failure; vestibular rehabilitation, fall prevention and avoidance of further ototoxins.

read.where: Chapter 23 Neuro-Otology: Dizziness, Balance and Hearing — Bilateral Peripheral Vestibulopathy

det.patho: Loss of vestibular hair cells or vestibular nerve function on both sides removes the vestibulo-ocular reflex and part of the input to postural control. Aminoglycosides (especially gentamicin) destroy hair cells, sometimes after short courses; other causes include bacterial meningitis, bilateral sequential neuritis, Ménière disease, autoimmune inner ear disease, superficial siderosis and RFC1-related CANVAS.
det.clinical: Patients complain of imbalance and oscillopsia rather than spinning vertigo. Symptoms are minimal when sitting still with the head steady, and worse in the dark when vision cannot compensate and on soft surfaces when proprioception is reduced. Coexisting neuropathy or cerebellar disease amplifies disability and raises suspicion of CANVAS.
det.diagnosis: The Bárány Society criteria require chronic unsteadiness plus objective bilateral reduction of vestibular function (vHIT gain, caloric responses or rotational chair). The bedside head impulse test and dynamic visual acuity are useful screens. Investigate for drugs, prior meningitis, neuropathy, cerebellar signs and hearing loss; MRI excludes structural causes.
det.treatment: There is no restorative treatment. Vestibular rehabilitation emphasising substitution with vision and proprioception, home safety, a stick, and night lighting reduce falls. Stop ototoxic drugs and avoid sedatives. Vestibular implants remain experimental.
det.prognosis: Function rarely returns, but many adapt; falls and reduced quality of life are major risks.
pearls: Imbalance in the dark + oscillopsia with no vertigo: test head impulses on both sides.
Ototoxicity spares hearing more than balance with gentamicin — a normal audiogram does not exclude it.
BVF + neuropathy + cerebellar signs: test for RFC1 (CANVAS).
det.thd: Bilateral vestibular failure คือการเสียการทำงานของระบบทรงตัวในหูชั้นในทั้งสองข้าง ผู้ป่วยไม่ค่อยเวียนหัวหมุน แต่เดินเซโดยเฉพาะในที่มืดและเห็นภาพสั่นเวลาเดิน สาเหตุสำคัญคือยา gentamicin เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ และ CANVAS ตรวจด้วย head impulse test หรือ vHIT รักษาด้วยการฝึกการทรงตัว (vestibular rehabilitation) และป้องกันการล้ม

name: Bilateral vestibular schwannoma
formal: Hallmark of neurofibromatosis type 2 with bilateral eighth nerve tumours causing progressive hearing loss, tinnitus and imbalance, often with meningiomas and spinal ependymomas.
simple: Tumours on both hearing and balance nerves, typical of an inherited condition called neurofibromatosis type 2.
th: เนื้องอก schwannoma ของเส้นประสาทเวสติบูลาร์ทั้งสองข้าง เป็นลักษณะสำคัญของ NF2 ทำให้หูตึงลงช้า ๆ มีเสียงรบกวนในหูและทรงตัวไม่ดี
tempoNote: Hearing and balance decline over years, usually starting in the teens to thirties
feat: Slowly worsening hearing loss in both ears with tinnitus and unsteadiness in a young adult
Companion tumours: meningiomas, spinal ependymomas, schwannomas on other nerves and under the skin
Early-life lens opacity (posterior subcapsular cataract); café-au-lait patches are few
Big tumours squeeze the brainstem, facial and trigeminal nerves and can block CSF flow
Family history of brain or spinal tumours, though many cases are new mosaic changes
inv: Contrast MRI of the brain with thin slices through the internal auditory canals, plus MRI of the whole spine
Pure-tone and speech audiometry to monitor function
NF2 testing on blood and, if needed, tumour tissue (mosaicism is frequent)
Eye and skin examination; offer surveillance to at-risk relatives

case.story: She has trouble hearing lecturers, first with the left ear and then the right, and now feels wobbly when descending stairs. Her father died young of 'brain tumours'.
case.exam: Sensorineural hearing loss on both sides, mild left facial weakness, a couple of raised skin plaques and a cloudy posterior lens.
case.tests: MRI shows enhancing masses filling both internal auditory canals (left 2.5 cm), a falx meningioma and a cervical intramedullary lesion.
case.q: Which single condition links these findings, and which drug may slow tumour growth?
case.a: NF2-related schwannomatosis; bevacizumab can stabilise growing vestibular tumours and protect hearing, with surgery or radiosurgery chosen by a specialist team.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Neurocutaneous Syndromes
23 Genetics of episodic and progressive vestibulocerebellar syndromes

det.patho: Inactivation of both copies of the NF2 gene on chromosome 22 removes merlin, a growth-suppressing membrane-cytoskeleton protein, so Schwann cells multiply. A person inherits one faulty copy (autosomal dominant) or carries a post-conception mosaic change, and a second hit arises in each tumour. By the third decade nearly everyone with the gene has tumours on both vestibular nerves. An international group in 2022 retitled the condition NF2-related schwannomatosis.
det.clinical: Hearing loss, tinnitus and poor balance appear in adolescence or early adulthood; some children first show facial palsy, cataract, skin lumps or spinal cord signs. Additional meningiomas and spinal tumours add disability. Truncating variants tend to give earlier, more aggressive disease than missense or mosaic ones, so course differs between families. Board-style questions often present a young patient with bilateral deafness and ask for the underlying syndrome.
det.diagnosis: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas on MRI are enough to meet diagnostic criteria. Gadolinium MRI of brain and spine defines the tumour load, and gene sequencing of blood, then tumour tissue if blood is negative, identifies the variant. Close relatives should be offered genetic testing and scheduled MRI from childhood. Audiometry sets a baseline for follow-up.
det.treatment: Care belongs in a multidisciplinary centre and aims to keep hearing and function as long as possible. Choices include watchful waiting with serial MRI and audiometry, microsurgery, radiosurgery (used with caution because of malignant-change concerns in NF2) and bevacizumab for enlarging tumours that threaten hearing. Cochlear or auditory brainstem implants help after hearing is lost. Targeted drugs are still in trials.
det.prognosis: Survival is shortened mainly by intracranial tumour burden, but expert multidisciplinary follow-up has improved outcomes.
pearls: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas equal NF2-related schwannomatosis.
Bilateral hearing loss in a young adult: image the internal auditory canals.
Cataract in youth and few café-au-lait spots separate NF2 from NF1.
det.thd: Bilateral vestibular schwannoma คือเนื้องอกของเส้นประสาทหู-ทรงตัวทั้งสองข้าง เป็นเกณฑ์วินิจฉัยโรค NF2 (NF2-related schwannomatosis) จากความผิดปกติของยีน NF2 ที่สร้างโปรตีน merlin ผู้ป่วยวัยหนุ่มสาวจะหูตึงช้า ๆ มีเสียงในหู และเดินเซ อาจมี meningioma หรือ ependymoma ร่วมด้วย ตรวจด้วย MRI สมองและไขสันหลังร่วมกับตรวจยีน รักษาโดยทีมเฉพาะทางด้วยการเฝ้าติดตาม ผ่าตัด รังสี หรือ bevacizumab
