name: Binswanger’s disease
formal: Subcortical arteriosclerotic leukoencephalopathy with hypertensive small vessel disease, white matter lesions and lacunes causing slowly progressive dementia, gait disturbance and pseudobulbar signs.
simple: A form of dementia caused by long-term damage to small brain vessels, with slow thinking, trouble walking and mood changes.
more: MRI shows periventricular and deep white matter T2 hyperintensities sparing U-fibres, with lacunes and microbleeds; CADASIL and amyloid angiopathy should be considered. Control blood pressure and vascular risk factors; no specific therapy exists.
th: ภาวะสมองเสื่อมจากโรคหลอดเลือดเล็กในเนื้อขาว มักสัมพันธ์กับความดันสูงเรื้อรัง ทำให้คิดช้า เฉยเมย เดินก้าวสั้น ปัสสาวะราด และ pseudobulbar affect ปัจจุบันจัดเป็น subcortical ischaemic vascular dementia
tempoNote: Gradual decline over years, often with step-like worsening after small strokes
feat: Extensive small vessel disease of deep white matter in a long-term hypertensive patient
Slowing, apathy and executive dysfunction, with memory affected less than in Alzheimer disease
Short-stepped, broad-based or magnetic gait with falls
Urinary urgency or incontinence, dysarthria and pseudobulbar affect
Prior lacunar strokes or transient deficits in many, with brisk reflexes and corticobulbar signs
inv: MRI: confluent periventricular and deep white matter hyperintensities, lacunes and microbleeds
Cognitive testing stressing attention, speed and executive tasks
Vascular risk work-up: BP monitoring, glucose, lipids, ECG; consider NOTCH3 testing in younger or familial cases

case.who: 73-year-old man, retired rice farmer from Roi Et, hypertensive for 25 years with poor adherence
case.story: Two years of becoming quiet and indifferent, taking longer to finish tasks, needing help with money, and recently urgent bladder with small-step walking and two falls.
case.exam: Slow responses, poor letter fluency, emotional lability, brisk jaw jerk, small shuffling steps with wide base, normal eye movements.
case.tests: MRI: widespread confluent periventricular and deep white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensity, multiple lacunes in basal ganglia, a few microbleeds; hippocampi relatively preserved; ventricles proportionate to sulcal enlargement.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and the most effective intervention?
case.a: Subcortical ischaemic vascular dementia of the Binswanger type; lasting control of blood pressure and other vascular risks, plus gait and bladder rehabilitation.

read.where: Chapter 11 Cognitive Impairment and Dementia — Vascular cognitive impairment
Chapter 11 Cognitive Impairment and Dementia — Vascular Dementia and Vascular Cognitive Impairment
9 - Atypical parkinsonism, parkinsonism-­plus syndromes and secondary parkinsonian disorders
Section 6 Systemic Disorders That Also Involve the Cerebrovascular System

det.patho: Chronic hypertension and ageing cause arteriolosclerosis and lipohyalinosis of the long penetrating vessels that supply the deep white matter. Resulting hypoperfusion, leaky blood-brain barrier and repeated small infarcts produce patchy loss of myelin and axons while the subcortical arcuate fibres are largely spared. Interruption of frontal-subcortical circuits explains the dysexecutive state, gait failure and urinary symptoms.
det.clinical: The picture develops slowly, often with interspersed stepwise declines from fresh lacunes. Early on there is slowed thinking, trouble planning, apathy and mood change, while recall improves with cueing. Walking becomes slow with short steps and falls, and urgency incontinence and pseudobulbar affect appear. The label is somewhat controversial and many authors regard it as the severe end of cerebral small vessel disease, but it remains a useful description of this clinical syndrome.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is made at the bedside and supported by MRI, which should show widespread deep white matter change and lacunes in someone with vascular risk factors and a frontal-subcortical cognitive profile. Imaging severity does not map precisely to cognition, so correlate with function. Exclude NPH, inherited arteriopathies such as CADASIL, amyloid angiopathy and inflammatory or infectious white matter disease, and correct contributors like B12 deficiency. Concomitant Alzheimer pathology is frequent and may need biomarkers to clarify.
det.treatment: No treatment reverses established lesions, so management centres on prevention of progression. Aim for sustained blood pressure control, treat diabetes and lipids, stop smoking, and use antiplatelet therapy when lacunar infarcts have occurred. Cholinesterase inhibitors give small benefit in some patients. Add physiotherapy for gait and falls, bladder management, treatment for depression, and support for caregivers.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive over years with growing dependence, and the risk of further stroke is raised. Good vascular risk control slows decline.
pearls: Gait disorder plus urgency plus slowing: think small vessel disease as well as NPH.
Cued recall is relatively helpful, unlike the encoding failure of Alzheimer disease.
Modern terminology often says subcortical ischaemic vascular dementia instead of Binswanger.
det.thd: Binswanger’s disease คือภาวะสมองเสื่อมจากโรคหลอดเลือดเล็กในเนื้อขาวสมอง สัมพันธ์กับความดันสูงเรื้อรัง ผู้ป่วยคิดช้า เฉยเมย วางแผนไม่ได้ เดินก้าวสั้น ล้มบ่อย ปัสสาวะราด และหัวเราะหรือร้องไห้ง่ายผิดปกติ MRI พบเนื้อขาวผิดปกติเป็นบริเวณกว้างและ lacunes หลายแห่ง ต้องแยกจาก NPH, CADASIL และ Alzheimer การรักษาหลักคือควบคุมความดัน น้ำตาล ไขมัน เลิกบุหรี่ ให้ยาต้านเกล็ดเลือดเมื่อมี lacunar stroke ร่วมกับกายภาพบำบัด

name: Biotin-responsive basal ganglia disease (BBGD)
formal: Autosomal recessive thiamine transporter-2 disorder (SLC19A3) with recurrent encephalopathy, confusion, dysarthria, dystonia and seizures with bilateral caudate and putamen necrosis on MRI.
simple: An inherited childhood brain disease with episodes of confusion, stiffness and seizures that improves with vitamins.
more: Treatment with high-dose biotin and thiamine given early can reverse episodes and prevent disability, and should be lifelong; delays in treatment risk permanent dystonia.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมแบบด้อยจากยีน SLC19A3 (ตัวขนส่ง thiamine) มีภาวะสมองผิดปกติเป็นพัก ๆ dystonia ชัก และ caudate/putamen เสียหาย รักษาได้ด้วย biotin และ thiamine ขนาดสูง
tempoNote: Subacute encephalopathic episodes, often after fever or minor illness, from infancy to adulthood; recovery with treatment, relapse if stopped
feat: Episodes of confusion, irritability, vomiting, dysarthria and dysphagia after an illness
Dystonia, rigidity, external ophthalmoplegia and seizures during crises
Infantile form resembles Leigh syndrome with lactic acidosis
Bilateral caudate and putamen lesions, sometimes thalami and cortex
Treatable: rapid response to biotin plus thiamine
inv: MRI: bilateral symmetric caudate and putamen T2 hyperintensity, swelling or necrosis
SLC19A3 gene testing
Blood/CSF lactate may be raised in infantile cases; exclude other Leigh causes

case.story: After a febrile illness he became confused, could not swallow and developed twisting of his limbs over 3 days.
case.exam: Encephalopathic, generalised dystonia, dysarthria, partial external ophthalmoplegia.
case.tests: MRI shows bilateral swollen caudate and putamen; biallelic SLC19A3 variants confirmed later.
case.q: What empirical treatment should start immediately?
case.a: High-dose biotin and thiamine — the episode may reverse and treatment must continue lifelong.

det.patho: Biallelic SLC19A3 variants impair thiamine transporter-2, reducing thiamine entry into brain cells. Thiamine-dependent enzymes (pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase) fail, causing energy failure in basal ganglia. Biotin appears to increase transporter expression, explaining its partial benefit. Many cases are reported from the Middle East but it occurs worldwide.
det.clinical: Classic childhood BBGD presents at 3–10 years with subacute encephalopathy, dystonia, dysarthria, seizures and ophthalmoplegia, often triggered by fever or stress. An early infantile Leigh-like form has severe lactic acidosis and high mortality, and adult-onset Wernicke-like presentations are recognised. Untreated episodes leave permanent dystonia and cognitive deficit.
det.diagnosis: Suspect in any child with acute encephalopathy and bilateral basal ganglia lesions, especially with dystonia. Start empirical biotin and thiamine before results. SLC19A3 testing confirms; low free thiamine in CSF supports. Exclude other metabolic, mitochondrial, toxic and post-infectious causes.
det.treatment: High-dose biotin with high-dose thiamine, started early and continued lifelong, is standard; thiamine appears to be the key element. Supportive care includes treatment of seizures and dystonia, nutrition and rehabilitation. Stopping treatment risks relapse.
det.prognosis: Good with early continuous treatment; delayed treatment leads to residual dystonia, intellectual disability or death.
pearls: Acute encephalopathy + bilateral striatal lesions: give biotin and thiamine empirically.
It is one of the few treatable Leigh-like disorders.
Lifelong treatment is needed even after full recovery.
det.thd: Biotin-responsive basal ganglia disease เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมแบบด้อยจากยีน SLC19A3 ซึ่งขนส่ง thiamine เข้าสมอง เด็กมักมีอาการซึม สับสน กลืนลำบาก พูดไม่ชัด dystonia และชักหลังเป็นไข้ MRI พบ caudate และ putamen บวมทั้งสองข้าง รักษาโดยให้ biotin และ thiamine ขนาดสูงทันทีโดยไม่ต้องรอผลยีน และต้องให้ตลอดชีวิต ถ้ารักษาเร็วจะฟื้นตัวดี

name: Biotin-responsive encephalopathy
formal: Subacute encephalopathy with confusion, seizures, dysarthria and dystonia from SLC19A3 mutation with bilateral basal ganglia necrosis, responsive to biotin and thiamine.
simple: An inherited illness causing episodes of confusion, seizures and abnormal movements that improves with vitamin treatment.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมยีนด้อย SLC19A3 ที่ขนส่ง thiamine เข้าสมองไม่ได้ เกิดสมองอักเสบเฉียบพลันพร้อมแกนสมองส่วน basal ganglia ตาย ตอบสนองดีต่อ thiamine และ biotin ขนาดสูง
tempoNote: Attacks over days, often after a fever or minor illness; can recur, and untreated each episode leaves more damage
feat: Episodes of confusion, drowsiness or coma, often after a febrile illness
Dystonia, rigidity, dysarthria and swallowing difficulty during or after episodes
Seizures and ophthalmoplegia or ataxia in some; infantile form can mimic Leigh syndrome
Dramatic improvement within days when high-dose thiamine and biotin are started early
inv: MRI: bilateral swelling then necrosis of caudate and putamen, often with cortical, thalamic or brainstem change
Serum/CSF lactate may be raised in the infantile form; routine metabolic screen often normal
SLC19A3 sequencing confirms; do not wait for the result before giving vitamins

case.who: 4-year-old boy from Nakhon Ratchasima, parents are second cousins
case.story: Three days after a viral fever he became sleepy, slurred his words and then could not swallow or walk. He had a milder similar spell a year ago.
case.exam: Drowsy, generalised dystonic posturing, dysarthria, brisk reflexes; no meningism.
case.tests: MRI shows symmetric swollen T2-bright caudate heads and putamina; CSF cells normal.
case.q: What should you give immediately, and which gene would you test?
case.a: High-dose thiamine plus biotin without delay; test SLC19A3 for biotin-thiamine-responsive basal ganglia disease.

det.patho: Biallelic variants in SLC19A3 impair thiamine transporter 2, so thiamine uptake into brain cells falls, especially when metabolic demand rises during illness. Thiamine-dependent enzymes such as pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase fail, producing energy failure in the highly active striatum. Why biotin helps is not fully explained; it may increase transporter expression, and thiamine appears to be the more important of the two. Many reported families come from the Middle East, but cases occur worldwide.
det.clinical: The classic childhood form presents with subacute encephalopathy, dystonia, dysarthria, dysphagia and sometimes seizures or external ophthalmoplegia, often after fever or vaccination. An early-infantile form looks like Leigh syndrome with lactic acidosis and has a worse outcome. Adult cases can resemble Wernicke encephalopathy. Without treatment, patients may die or be left with severe dystonia and cognitive impairment.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in any child with acute encephalopathy and symmetric bilateral striatal T2 lesions, especially with a recurrent pattern or consanguinity. MRI typically shows caudate and putamen swelling that later becomes atrophic or cystic, sometimes with cortical and subcortical involvement. Confirm with SLC19A3 genetic testing; low free thiamine in CSF supports it. Exclude mitochondrial disease, organic acidurias, Wilson disease and infectious or post-infectious encephalitis.
det.treatment: Start high-dose oral or IV thiamine with biotin immediately on suspicion, then continue lifelong; doses are weight-based and set by a metabolic specialist. Treat seizures and dystonia symptomatically, and support swallowing and nutrition during crises. Increase vigilance and keep vitamins uninterrupted during illness. Offer genetic counselling and test siblings, who can be treated before symptoms.
det.prognosis: Early and sustained vitamin therapy usually brings marked recovery and prevents further crises; delayed treatment leaves fixed dystonia and disability.
pearls: Symmetric striatal necrosis in a child: give thiamine and biotin first, investigate second.
Infantile SLC19A3 disease can masquerade as mitochondrial Leigh syndrome.
Stopping the vitamins can trigger a relapse; adherence is life-long.
det.thd: โรคนี้เกิดจากยีน SLC19A3 ทำให้ thiamine เข้าเซลล์สมองไม่พอ เมื่อเด็กไม่สบายหรือมีไข้จะเกิดอาการซึม พูดไม่ชัด กลืนลำบาก และเกร็งบิด MRI เห็น caudate และ putamen บวมทั้งสองข้าง ควรให้ thiamine และ biotin ขนาดสูงทันทีที่สงสัยและให้ต่อเนื่องตลอดชีวิต ถ้ารักษาเร็วมักฟื้นตัวได้ดี

ddx.pt: Mitochondrial; brainstem and basal ganglia lesions with high lactate and no clear vitamin response
Acquired thiamine deficiency; mamillary body and periaqueductal lesions rather than striatal necrosis
Post-viral with symmetric thalamic necrosis and multi-organ involvement; not vitamin responsive

name: Bismuth toxicity
formal: Toxic accumulation from excessive bismuth compounds causing encephalopathy, myoclonus, tremor and renal impairment.
simple: Harmful effects of too much bismuth medicine, including confusion, tremor and muscle jerks.
more: Reversible encephalopathy from chronic bismuth subsalicylate exposure with confusion, myoclonus, ataxia, tremor and speech disturbance.
th: พิษจากการได้รับสารบิสมัทมากเกินหรือนาน ทำให้สับสน กระตุก myoclonus เดินเซ สั่น และไตบกพร่อง ส่วนใหญ่หายได้เมื่อหยุดสาร
tempoNote: Builds over weeks of excess intake; reverses over weeks once exposure stops
feat: Confusion, apathy, hallucinations or delirium
Multifocal myoclonus, tremor, ataxia and dysarthria
Seizures in severe cases
Renal impairment and grey-black discolouration of gums or stool
inv: Blood and urine bismuth levels
Renal function; CT may show hyperdense cortex/basal ganglia in some cases
EEG diffuse slowing; exclude other metabolic, infectious and prion causes

case.story: Taking large amounts of an over-the-counter bismuth stomach remedy daily for months; family notes confusion and jerking over three weeks.
case.exam: Disoriented, multifocal myoclonus, broad-based gait, dark-coloured tongue.
case.tests: Blood bismuth markedly raised; creatinine elevated; EEG diffuse slowing; MRI unremarkable.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the key step in treatment?
case.a: Bismuth encephalopathy; stop the bismuth and support renal clearance — chelation (e.g. DMSA or dimercaprol) is considered in severe cases.

det.patho: Bismuth salts used for dyspepsia, H. pylori eradication or wound care are poorly absorbed, but large chronic doses, renal impairment or specific formulations allow accumulation in brain tissue. The exact neurotoxic mechanism is unclear. Outbreaks were described historically with insoluble salts; modern cases are sporadic.
det.clinical: A prodrome of apathy, poor concentration and insomnia is followed by confusion, myoclonus, tremor, gait ataxia and dysarthria; seizures and coma can occur. Renal failure may coexist and worsen accumulation. The picture can mimic prion disease, which is the critical misdiagnosis to avoid.
det.diagnosis: Ask specifically about stomach remedies and supplements. Measure blood or urine bismuth; interpret alongside renal function. EEG shows non-specific slowing; MRI helps exclude CJD and structural disease.
det.treatment: Stop all bismuth sources. Supportive care, hydration and treatment of seizures are central; myoclonus may need benzodiazepines or levetiracetam. Chelation with dimercaprol or DMSA and haemodialysis in renal failure have been used in severe cases, though evidence is limited.
det.prognosis: Most patients recover over weeks to months after exposure ends; deaths are rare.
pearls: Myoclonic encephalopathy: always take a full over-the-counter medicine history.
Bismuth toxicity can mimic CJD — a reversible cause not to miss.
Kidney failure greatly increases the risk.
det.thd: พิษบิสมัทเกิดจากการกินยาเคลือบกระเพาะที่มีบิสมัทปริมาณมากหรือนาน โดยเฉพาะเมื่อไตเสื่อม ผู้ป่วยมีอาการสับสน กระตุก สั่น เดินเซ อาจชัก คล้ายโรค CJD ต้องซักประวัติยาที่ซื้อเองและตรวจระดับบิสมัทในเลือด รักษาโดยหยุดสารและประคับประคอง รายรุนแรงพิจารณา chelation หรือฟอกไต ส่วนใหญ่ฟื้นตัวได้

ddx.pt: Rapid dementia with myoclonus but no toxin, with DWI cortical ribboning and positive RT-QuIC
Uraemic, hepatic or electrolyte encephalopathy with asterixis and multifocal myoclonus
Other reversible toxic encephalopathy; check lithium level

aN: bismuth encephalopathy | bismuth poisoning | bismuth subsalicylate toxicity | bismuth neurotoxicity

name: Blepharospasm
formal: Focal dystonia of orbicularis oculi causing involuntary forceful eyelid closure, often idiopathic in middle-aged women and treated with botulinum toxin.
simple: Uncontrolled, forceful blinking and eyelid closing that can make the person functionally blind.
th: Blepharospasm คือ focal dystonia ของกล้ามเนื้อรอบตา (orbicularis oculi) ทำให้กะพริบถี่และหลับตาแน่นโดยไม่ตั้งใจ จนอาจตาบอดเชิงหน้าที่ พบมากในหญิงวัยกลางคน แสงจ้าและความเครียดทำให้แย่ลง การรักษาหลักคือฉีด botulinum toxin ซ้ำทุก 3–4 เดือน
tempoNote: Insidious onset in the fifties or sixties, worsening over months to a few years, then usually plateauing; spread to the lower face occurs in a minority
feat: Increased blinking that progresses to bilateral forceful eyelid closure lasting seconds to minutes, with the brow pulled down; the episodes are worse in bright light, driving, reading, stress and fatigue
Sensory tricks (touching the eyelid, temple or nose, wearing dark glasses, humming, chewing gum) can stop an attack briefly, and spasms are minimal in sleep and while talking or concentrating
Eye irritation, dryness, photophobia or blepharitis often precede or accompany the spasm and are treated alongside it
Apraxia of eyelid opening, an inability to start eyelid opening without orbicularis contraction, may coexist or mimic it; reciprocal inhibition of levator palpebrae contributes in some patients
May extend to oromandibular muscles (Meige syndrome); secondary forms follow dopamine blockers, parkinsonian and other degenerative diseases, or brainstem lesions
inv: Clinical diagnosis; ophthalmology review for dry eye, blepharitis, uveitis and corneal disease that can trigger reflex blepharospasm
Medication review (dopamine blockers, levodopa, dopamine agonists); examination for parkinsonism, PSP-type features or myasthenia
MRI brain if onset is early, unilateral or accompanied by other neurological signs; EMG of orbicularis oculi and levator rarely needed

case.story: For 18 months her eyes shut tightly when she walks out into sunlight or reads; twice she narrowly avoided an accident on her motorbike. She can open her eyes by touching her eyebrow and the spasm is gone while she sleeps.
case.exam: Frequent blinking and runs of forceful bilateral eye closure lasting about 10 seconds; no ptosis at rest; eye movements, pupils and visual acuity normal; no lower face or jaw spasm.
case.tests: Ophthalmology: mild dry eye; no drug exposure; MRI not required.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the treatment of choice?
case.a: Benign essential blepharospasm; botulinum toxin injected into the orbicularis oculi (starting low and avoiding the midline of the upper lid to limit ptosis), repeated every 3–4 months, with lubricants and tinted lenses.

det.patho: Blepharospasm is a focal dystonia in which abnormal basal ganglia and brainstem circuits, together with disturbed sensorimotor integration, produce excessive blink drive and loss of inhibition of the orbicularis oculi. The blink reflex has an enhanced excitability, and reciprocal inhibition between the orbicularis oculi and the levator palpebrae is faulty, which explains the lid-opening apraxia seen in some patients. Ocular surface disease and photophobia contribute to the vicious circle through the trigeminal afferent pathway.
det.clinical: Most patients are in their fifties or sixties and women outnumber men about two to one. The disorder begins as increased blinking, then spreads to sustained forced closure, and the main disability is functional blindness during spasms with falls, driving risk and loss of employment. Spasms are suppressed by sensory tricks, speaking and in sleep, and aggravated by bright light, stress and fatigue. About one in five patients spreads to other cranial muscles, and Meige syndrome combines eyelid and oromandibular involvement. A careful look for secondary causes, including dopamine blockers and parkinsonian or other degenerative diseases, is part of the assessment.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical. Ophthalmic assessment is needed because dry eye, blepharitis and photophobia are frequent and treatable contributors, and because apraxia of lid opening or a ptosis from myasthenia can be mistaken for blepharospasm. Brain imaging is reserved for young onset, unilateral spasm or additional neurological signs, since structural lesions of the brainstem or thalamus can produce a secondary form. The Jankovic rating scale or the Blepharospasm Disability Index records severity.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin type A (onabotulinumtoxinA, incobotulinumtoxinA or abobotulinumtoxinA) injected into the pretarsal orbicularis oculi is the standard therapy and gives relief for 3–4 months in most patients; injections avoiding the central upper lid lower the risk of ptosis, and tolerance is uncommon with modern preparations. Treat eye surface disease with lubricants and consider tinted (FL-41) lenses for light sensitivity. Oral drugs such as clonazepam or trihexyphenidyl help little; when toxin fails, upper eyelid myectomy gives lasting relief and pallidal (GPi) deep brain stimulation is an option in very severe cases. Lid-opening apraxia may need pretarsal injection or lid crutches.
det.prognosis: The condition is lifelong but not life-shortening; with regular toxin treatment most patients return to work and driving.
pearls: Touching the eyebrow or humming that stops the spasm is a sensory trick, a hallmark of dystonia.
Inject pretarsal and away from the midline of the upper lid to avoid ptosis.
A dry-eye work-up is part of the treatment, not an optional extra.
det.thd: Blepharospasm คือภาวะ dystonia ของกล้ามเนื้อรอบตา ทำให้กะพริบตาถี่และหลับตาแน่นจนมองไม่เห็นชั่วคราว พบบ่อยในหญิงวัยกลางคน แสงจ้า การขับรถ และความเครียดทำให้แย่ลง ส่วนการแตะขมับหรือคิ้วอาจช่วยให้ลืมตาได้ (sensory trick) ควรตรวจตาเพื่อหาตาแห้งหรือการอักเสบ และทบทวนยาที่ใช้ การรักษามาตรฐานคือฉีด botulinum toxin ทุก 3–4 เดือน ถ้าไม่ได้ผลอาจผ่าตัดตัดกล้ามเนื้อหรือใช้ DBS

name: Bobble-head doll syndrome
formal: Rhythmic anteroposterior head nodding at 2 to 3 Hz, suppressed by voluntary effort or sleep, associated with third ventricle cysts, hydrocephalus and cerebellar lesions.
simple: A rare condition in children with slow, constant head nodding, sometimes linked to a fluid-filled cyst in the brain.
th: ศีรษะผงกไปหน้าหลังเป็นจังหวะ 2–3 ครั้งต่อวินาทีในเด็ก หยุดเมื่อตั้งใจหรือหลับ สัมพันธ์กับถุงน้ำในโพรงสมองที่สามและภาวะน้ำในโพรงสมองคั่ง
tempoNote: Develops gradually in infancy or early childhood as the cyst enlarges
feat: Rhythmic anteroposterior (yes-yes) head bobbing at about 2–3 Hz
Disappears with voluntary effort, concentration and sleep
Caused by suprasellar arachnoid cysts, third ventricle cysts or aqueductal stenosis with hydrocephalus
Associated macrocephaly, developmental delay, visual loss, endocrine dysfunction
Resolves or improves after CSF diversion or cyst fenestration
inv: MRI brain with attention to the third ventricle and suprasellar region
Ophthalmology for visual acuity and optic atrophy
Endocrine screening (growth, puberty, thyroid)

case.story: Parents notice that for months his head nods forward and back rhythmically when he sits; it stops when he concentrates on a toy or sleeps.
case.exam: Head circumference above 97th centile, rhythmic head nodding, mild truncal ataxia, pale optic discs.
case.tests: MRI shows a large suprasellar arachnoid cyst compressing the third ventricle with hydrocephalus.
case.q: What is this movement and how is it treated?
case.a: Bobble-head doll syndrome; endoscopic cyst fenestration (ventriculocystocisternostomy) usually abolishes the movement.

det.patho: The exact mechanism is uncertain. The leading idea is that a cyst or dilated third ventricle compresses the dorsomedial thalamus and its connections, disrupting motor control circuits and generating a rhythmic movement. Some propose a learned compensatory movement that intermittently relieves CSF obstruction. The movement is not a seizure.
det.clinical: Children typically aged 2–6 years develop rhythmic yes-yes head bobbing, sometimes extending to the trunk, at roughly 2–3 per second. It ceases during sleep and can be stopped voluntarily. Associated features include macrocephaly, developmental delay, ataxia, visual impairment and endocrine disturbances such as precocious puberty or obesity.
det.diagnosis: The characteristic movement should prompt urgent MRI of the brain. Typical findings are a suprasellar arachnoid cyst, third ventricle cyst or aqueductal stenosis. EEG is not needed unless seizures are suspected. Visual and endocrine assessment identify associated complications.
det.treatment: Surgical decompression of the cyst or relief of hydrocephalus is the treatment, with endoscopic fenestration preferred over shunting. The movement often stops promptly after surgery. Visual and endocrine follow-up continues afterward.
det.prognosis: The movement usually resolves after surgery; developmental outcome depends on the duration of hydrocephalus.
pearls: Rhythmic yes-yes head nodding in a toddler warrants MRI of the third ventricle region.
It stops with concentration and sleep, which helps separate it from seizures.
Endoscopic cyst fenestration usually cures the movement.
det.thd: Bobble-head doll syndrome คือการผงกศีรษะไปหน้าหลังเป็นจังหวะประมาณ 2–3 ครั้งต่อวินาทีในเด็กเล็ก หยุดเมื่อเด็กตั้งใจทำอะไรหรือหลับ สัมพันธ์กับถุงน้ำ arachnoid เหนือ sella หรือในโพรงสมองที่สามและภาวะน้ำในโพรงสมองคั่ง เด็กอาจหัวโต พัฒนาการช้า และสายตาเสีย ต้องทำ MRI และรักษาด้วยการผ่าตัดเจาะถุงน้ำซึ่งมักทำให้อาการหาย

Older patients, often with essential tremor or dystonia; persists in concentration
Underlying mechanism in many cases; headache, vomiting and macrocephaly

name: Bodily distress disorder
formal: Mental health condition with persistent distressing bodily symptoms and excessive attention to them, in the ICD-11 classification, often presenting to neurology as functional disorders.
simple: A condition where a person has ongoing physical symptoms that cause great worry, without a clear physical cause.
th: ภาวะทางจิตเวชใน ICD-11 ที่มีอาการทางกายต่อเนื่องและรบกวน ร่วมกับให้ความสนใจอาการมากเกินไป ไม่ใช่โรคทางระบบประสาท
tempoNote: Symptoms persist for months, often years
feat: Psychiatric diagnosis (ICD-11), not a neurological disease
Persistent distressing bodily symptoms such as pain, fatigue, dizziness or palpitations
Excessive attention, worry and repeated consultations about symptoms
May coexist with medical or neurological disease
Common presentation in neurology clinics alongside functional neurological disorder
inv: Appropriate, limited investigations guided by clinical findings
Screen for depression and anxiety

case.story: Several years of headaches, widespread pain, fatigue and dizziness; multiple normal investigations; she worries about a serious illness.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination.
case.tests: Normal MRI and blood tests.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and approach?
case.a: Bodily distress disorder; explain the condition positively, avoid unnecessary tests, and provide CBT and treatment of comorbid anxiety or depression.

det.patho: Current models describe altered processing of bodily signals in which attention, expectation and emotion amplify ordinary or disease-related sensations. Predisposing factors include adverse life experiences, anxiety and illness beliefs. Symptoms are maintained by repeated checking, reassurance seeking and avoidance, which keep attention focused on the body.
det.clinical: Patients present with multiple or single persistent symptoms causing distress. They often seek repeated reassurance and investigations. Severity ranges from mild to severe disability.
det.diagnosis: The ICD-11 diagnosis requires persistent, distressing bodily symptoms with excessive attention to them, causing impairment; it does not depend on an absent medical explanation. Severity is graded mild, moderate or severe. Investigate what the history and examination justify, then stop. Screen for depression, anxiety and coexisting medical disease.
det.treatment: Validate symptoms, give a clear explanation, set goals, and coordinate care. CBT and physical rehabilitation are effective; antidepressants may help with pain and mood. Limit repetitive investigations.
det.prognosis: Variable; earlier recognition and treatment improve outcomes.
pearls: Diagnosis is positive, not just exclusion.
Medical illness can coexist; reassess new symptoms.
Avoid repeated unnecessary tests.
det.thd: Bodily distress disorder เป็นการวินิจฉัยทางจิตเวชใน ICD-11 ผู้ป่วยมีอาการทางกายเรื้อรังและกังวลมาก เช่น ปวด อ่อนเพลีย เวียนศีรษะ แม้ตรวจหลายครั้งไม่พบโรค ไม่ใช่โรคทางระบบประสาทโดยตรง การรักษาคืออธิบายอย่างเข้าใจ หลีกเลี่ยงการตรวจซ้ำ ทำ CBT และรักษาภาวะซึมเศร้าหรือวิตกกังวลร่วม

Neurological symptoms with positive clinical signs of functional origin

name: Border-zone infarction
formal: Ischaemic stroke in watershed territory between major arteries, usually from hypoperfusion or microembolism, causing proximal limb weakness (man-in-a-barrel) or visual deficits.
simple: A stroke in areas at the edge between two blood vessel regions, often caused by a drop in blood pressure.
more: Watershed infarcts at the junction of major arterial territories (cortical or internal), caused by haemodynamic compromise or microemboli, often with carotid stenosis.
th: สมองขาดเลือดบริเวณรอยต่อระหว่างเขตหลอดเลือดใหญ่ (cortical) หรือระหว่างแขนงลึกกับแขนงผิว (internal) มักเกิดเมื่อความดันเลือดตกร่วมกับหลอดเลือดแดงใหญ่ตีบ หรือจาก microemboli
tempoNote: Sudden, often on standing, after cardiac surgery, arrhythmia, dehydration or over-treatment of BP; may stutter with repeated hypotensive episodes
feat: Cortical (external) border zones: ACA–MCA gives proximal arm and shoulder weakness ('man-in-a-barrel' when bilateral); MCA–PCA gives visual and parieto-occipital deficits
Internal border zone: chain of small infarcts in centrum semiovale/corona radiata, often with fluctuating hemiparesis
Transcortical motor or sensory aphasia from anterior or posterior border-zone infarcts in the dominant hemisphere
Precipitant: hypotension, cardiac arrest, bypass surgery, haemodialysis, aggressive antihypertensives
Usually severe ipsilateral ICA stenosis/occlusion when unilateral
inv: MRI DWI: wedge-shaped cortical strips or a rosary-like row of deep lesions between territories
CTA/MRA/duplex for ipsilateral carotid or MCA stenosis/occlusion
CT or MR perfusion: prolonged transit time in the affected hemisphere
Cardiac evaluation for arrhythmia, low output, and BP records around onset

case.who: 74-year-old man from Lampang with known left ICA occlusion
case.story: Started on three new BP tablets last week; this morning he stood up quickly, felt faint, then noticed his right shoulder and hip were weak and his words came out slowly.
case.exam: BP 98/60 lying. Right proximal arm weakness more than hand, mild right leg weakness, sparse speech with preserved repetition.
case.tests: MRI DWI: string of small lesions in the left corona radiata and a cortical strip between ACA and MCA territories; CTA confirms left ICA occlusion.
case.q: What is the mechanism and the immediate management?
case.a: Haemodynamic border-zone infarction distal to an occluded ICA; stop excess antihypertensives, hydrate, keep the patient flat and allow higher BP.

det.patho: Distal fields between two arterial supplies sit at the end of each tree and receive the lowest perfusion pressure, so when systemic pressure falls or a proximal artery is severely narrowed or occluded with poor collaterals, these zones fail first. Cortical (external) border zones lie between the ACA, MCA and PCA surface territories; internal (deep) border zones lie in the corona radiata and centrum semiovale between lenticulostriate and medullary penetrators, which are themselves end arteries. Small emboli wash out poorly from low-flow regions, so reduced perfusion and microembolism (from carotid plaque, the heart or a valve) often act together — Caplan's 'impaired washout' concept — and cortical border-zone lesions are more often embolic while internal ones are more strongly tied to haemodynamic failure and early recurrence. Systemic disorders can produce the same pattern: cardiac arrest or bypass surgery, severe anaemia or sickle cell disease, hyperviscosity (polycythaemia, myeloproliferative disease), hypereosinophilic syndrome with microvascular thrombosis, and infective endocarditis with showers of tiny emboli.
det.clinical: Bilateral anterior (ACA–MCA) border-zone infarcts after cardiac arrest or bypass cause proximal arm and shoulder weakness with relatively spared face, hands and legs ('man-in-a-barrel'), sometimes with transcortical motor aphasia when dominant. Posterior (MCA–PCA) border-zone lesions cause visuospatial and visual disturbances such as Balint features, cortical blindness or transcortical sensory aphasia. Internal border-zone infarcts present with hemiparesis that fluctuates or progresses in steps over hours to days and are a warning of exhausted haemodynamic reserve. A unilateral pattern points to ipsilateral ICA or MCA stenosis or occlusion and may be heralded by orthostatic TIAs or limb-shaking TIAs; symptoms that appear on standing, after a meal, during dialysis or with a new antihypertensive and settle lying flat are a strong clue.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the DWI pattern plus a plausible haemodynamic trigger or vascular lesion: wedge-shaped cortical strips between territories, or a chain ('rosary') of lesions in the centrum semiovale parallel to the lateral ventricle. Map the territories carefully because individual anatomy and collateral supply shift the borders. Image the carotid and intracranial arteries with CTA, MRA or duplex, and use CT or MR perfusion (or cerebrovascular reactivity testing) to demonstrate delayed transit and impaired reserve. Check the blood pressure record and drug chart, fluid balance, haemoglobin and haematocrit, cardiac rhythm and output, and recent anaesthesia or procedures; scattered bilateral border-zone lesions without a large-artery cause should prompt echocardiography and a search for blood disorders such as hypereosinophilia or polycythaemia. Distinguish from global hypoxic-ischaemic injury, which also involves cortex, basal ganglia and hippocampi.
det.treatment: Restore perfusion first: correct hypotension and hypovolaemia, stop or reduce antihypertensives in the acute phase, keep the head flat early if tolerated, treat arrhythmia, anaemia or low cardiac output, and mobilise cautiously while watching for orthostatic worsening. Standard reperfusion treatment (thrombolysis or thrombectomy) applies when there is a qualifying occlusion. For the underlying lesion, offer endarterectomy or stenting for symptomatic carotid stenosis; for symptomatic intracranial stenosis, use intensive medical therapy (short-term dual antiplatelets, high-intensity statin, risk-factor control), since stenting has not beaten medicine and EC–IC bypass has not shown benefit for carotid occlusion in trials. Blood pressure should be lowered gradually over weeks: for symptomatic intracranial stenosis guidelines favour a systolic target below 140 rather than 130 mmHg, because patients with low distal flow did worse when pressure was pushed lower. Treat systemic causes such as hyperviscosity or hypereosinophilia specifically.
det.prognosis: Outcome depends on infarct size and the haemodynamic substrate; internal border-zone infarcts beyond a severe stenosis or occlusion carry a high early risk of progression and recurrence, whereas cortical border-zone infarcts after a single correctable hypotensive episode often have a good outlook.
pearls: Proximal arm and shoulder weakness with hand sparing = ACA–MCA border zone ('man-in-a-barrel' if bilateral).
A rosary of deep white matter infarcts points to haemodynamic failure beyond a carotid or MCA lesion — treat it as an unstable patient.
Check the drug chart and the lying–standing BP: new antihypertensives and dehydration are frequent, reversible triggers.
Bilateral scattered watershed infarcts with no large-artery disease: think microemboli (endocarditis, NBTE) or blood disorders (hyperviscosity, hypereosinophilia).
det.thd: Border-zone (watershed) infarction คือสมองขาดเลือดบริเวณรอยต่อระหว่างเขตหลอดเลือด ซึ่งเป็นปลายทางที่ความดันเลือดต่ำที่สุด เกิดเมื่อความดันเลือดตก (หลังหัวใจหยุดเต้น ผ่าตัดหัวใจ ขาดน้ำ ยาลดความดันมากเกิน) ร่วมกับหลอดเลือดแดงใหญ่ตีบหรืออุดตัน และมักมี emboli เล็ก ๆ ที่ถูกชะล้างออกได้ไม่ดีในเขตเลือดไหลช้าร่วมด้วย แบบ cortical ทำให้อ่อนแรงต้นแขนและไหล่หรือมีปัญหาการมองเห็น ส่วนแบบ internal เป็นแถวลูกประคำใน corona radiata มักอ่อนแรงขึ้น ๆ ลง ๆ และเสี่ยงกำเริบซ้ำสูง วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI DWI ร่วมกับ CTA/MRA และ perfusion imaging พร้อมทบทวนความดันและยา รักษาโดยแก้ความดันต่ำ งดยาลดความดันช่วงแรก แก้ไขภาวะซีดหรือหัวใจเต้นผิดจังหวะ และรักษาหลอดเลือดที่ตีบ (ผ่าตัด carotid หรือยาเต็มที่สำหรับหลอดเลือดในกะโหลก) โดยลดความดันระยะยาวอย่างค่อยเป็นค่อยไป เป้าหมาย systolic ต่ำกว่า 140 mmHg ในรายที่หลอดเลือดในกะโหลกตีบ

qx.stem: A 63-year-old man collapses during coronary artery bypass surgery with a mean arterial pressure of 40 mmHg for several minutes. On awakening he has proximal arm and leg weakness bilaterally and cortical visual disturbance. MRI shows bilateral diffusion-restricting lesions in the parieto-occipital regions and a linear chain of lesions in the deep white matter.
qx.q: Which description best fits this pattern?
opts: Lacunar infarcts from lipohyalinosis
Cerebral venous infarcts from sagittal sinus thrombosis
Embolic infarcts from the aorta in a random distribution
Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome
Bilateral watershed infarcts from systemic hypoperfusion
qx.why: Border-zone (watershed) infarcts lie between major arterial territories, either cortical (ACA–MCA, MCA–PCA) or internal as a chain of deep white matter lesions, and are classically from low perfusion pressure in severe stenosis or cardiac surgery hypotension. 'Man in the barrel' proximal weakness follows ACA–MCA border-zone damage. Emboli are scattered, and lacunes are single small deep lesions.

name: Borderline leprosy
formal: Unstable leprosy classification (BT, BB, BL) with variable nerve involvement, multiple asymmetric skin patches and risk of type 1 reactions with nerve palsy.
simple: An in-between form of leprosy with skin patches and nerve damage that can flare up into painful weakness.
th: โรคเรื้อนกลุ่มกึ่งกลางที่ภูมิคุ้มกันไม่คงที่ มีวงผื่นชาหลายวงไม่สมมาตรและเส้นประสาทโต เสี่ยงเกิด reversal reaction ทำให้เส้นประสาทเสียหายเฉียบพลัน
tempoNote: Indolent skin and nerve disease over months to years, punctuated by acute type 1 reactions
feat: Several to many asymmetric hypopigmented or reddish patches with reduced sensation
Thickened peripheral nerves (ulnar, common peroneal, great auricular, posterior tibial)
Mononeuritis multiplex: claw hand, foot drop, facial weakness, lagophthalmos
Type 1 (reversal) reaction: inflamed patches and painful nerves with rapid loss of function
Can shift toward tuberculoid or lepromatous pole depending on immunity
inv: Slit-skin smear (bacterial index); skin biopsy with Fite stain
Nerve conduction to document mononeuropathies; nerve ultrasound for thickening
Voluntary muscle and monofilament testing to track nerve function
PCR for M. leprae where available

case.story: He has had several numb pale patches on his back and arm for a year; over the past week the patches turned red and swollen and his right hand became weak and painful at the elbow.
case.exam: Seven asymmetric erythematous anaesthetic plaques, tender thickened right ulnar nerve, weak interossei with ulnar claw.
case.tests: Slit-skin smear BI 1+; biopsy shows borderline tuberculoid granulomas with oedema.
case.q: What is happening and how should the neuritis be treated?
case.a: Borderline leprosy in type 1 (reversal) reaction with acute ulnar neuritis; start oral prednisolone (e.g. 40 mg/day tapered over months) plus WHO multidrug therapy and protect the hand.

read.where: Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — Borderline Leprosy

det.patho: Mycobacterium leprae invades Schwann cells and skin macrophages. In borderline disease, cell-mediated immunity is intermediate and unstable, so the number of bacilli and the extent of granulomatous inflammation sit between the tuberculoid and lepromatous poles (Ridley–Jopling BT, BB, BL). Sudden increases in cell-mediated immunity cause type 1 reactions, in which inflammatory swelling within nerve sheaths produces compression and rapid nerve damage.
det.clinical: Skin lesions are more numerous than tuberculoid disease but less symmetric than lepromatous disease, with variable loss of sensation, sweat and hair. Disability stems mostly from nerve injury, which can progress silently. Type 1 reactions often occur in the first year after starting treatment, during pregnancy or after delivery, and require urgent recognition. BL patients can also develop erythema nodosum leprosum.
det.diagnosis: WHO cardinal signs are anaesthetic skin patches, thickened nerves with sensory or motor loss, and acid-fast bacilli on smear or biopsy. Ridley–Jopling classification uses histology and bacterial index; for treatment WHO groups patients as paucibacillary or multibacillary. Regular sensory and motor nerve function testing detects early neuritis.
det.treatment: WHO multidrug therapy (rifampicin, clofazimine and dapsone) is now recommended for all patients — 6 months for paucibacillary and 12 months for multibacillary. Type 1 reactions with neuritis are treated with corticosteroids, typically several months of tapering prednisolone. Self-care for anaesthetic hands, feet and eyes, splinting and reconstructive surgery prevent deformity. Contacts may receive single-dose rifampicin prophylaxis.
det.prognosis: Bacterial cure is reliable; disability depends on early detection and prompt treatment of reactions.
pearls: Leprosy is still seen in Thailand: anaesthetic patch + thick nerve = check for leprosy.
Reversal reaction is a neurological emergency for the nerve — start steroids promptly.
Borderline disease is 'unstable' and can down- or upgrade toward either pole.
det.thd: Borderline leprosy คือโรคเรื้อนกลุ่มกลางที่ภูมิคุ้มกันไม่คงที่ มีวงผื่นชาหลายวงไม่สมมาตรและเส้นประสาทโต เช่น ulnar หรือ peroneal ทำให้มือหงิกหรือเท้าตก อาจเกิด reversal reaction ผื่นอักเสบและเส้นประสาทปวดบวมเสียหายเร็ว รักษาด้วยยาหลายขนานตาม WHO และให้ prednisolone เมื่อมี reaction ร่วมกับดูแลมือเท้าตาที่ชา

name: Borderline personality disorder
formal: Psychiatric condition with unstable mood, relationships and self-image and impulsivity, commonly encountered in functional and neuropsychiatric presentations.
simple: A mental health condition with intense swings in emotions, unstable relationships and impulsive behaviour.
th: ความผิดปกติทางบุคลิกภาพที่มีอารมณ์ ความสัมพันธ์ และภาพลักษณ์ตนเองไม่มั่นคง หุนหันพลันแล่น เป็นภาวะทางจิตเวช ไม่ใช่โรคทางระบบประสาท
tempoNote: Long-standing pattern from adolescence or early adulthood
feat: Psychiatric condition, not a neurological disease
Unstable emotions, relationships and self-image; impulsivity
Chronic feelings of emptiness, fear of abandonment
Higher rates of functional neurological symptoms and functional seizures
Associated with childhood adversity
inv: Psychiatric assessment
Neurological investigations only when indicated by symptoms

case.story: Repeated hospital visits with attacks of shaking and unresponsiveness after interpersonal conflicts; long history of unstable relationships.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination.
case.tests: Video-EEG captures a typical event without EEG change.
case.q: What conditions underlie these events?
case.a: Functional seizures in a person with borderline personality disorder; psychological therapy (e.g. DBT) and coordinated care.

read.where: Chapter 30 Neuropsychiatry — Personality Disorder and Personality Change
Chapter 48: Sleep in other psychiatric disorders

det.patho: The condition arises from an interaction of inherited temperament, such as emotional sensitivity and impulsivity, with environmental factors including childhood trauma or neglect. Neuroimaging studies suggest altered frontolimbic regulation of emotion, but there is no diagnostic biomarker. It is a psychiatric diagnosis, not a neurological disease.
det.clinical: Core features are rapidly shifting mood, impulsive behaviour, unstable relationships and identity, fear of abandonment and recurrent self-harm. In neurology services, patients may present with functional symptoms, functional seizures or frequent emergency attendances. Comorbid depression, substance use and eating disorders are common. Suicide risk is significant and should always be assessed.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is made by a psychiatrist using DSM-5 or ICD-11 criteria (ICD-11 codes it as a borderline pattern specifier of personality disorder). Neurological tests are used only to answer specific clinical questions, for example video-EEG for suspected functional seizures. Care is needed not to attribute new neurological signs automatically to the personality disorder.
det.treatment: Psychotherapy (dialectical behaviour therapy, mentalisation-based therapy) is first line. Medication for comorbid conditions. Coordinated care between neurology and psychiatry helps.
det.prognosis: Symptoms often improve over time with treatment.
pearls: Not a neurological disease but common in functional neurology.
Stigma-free, consistent care is important.
Psychotherapy is the mainstay.
det.thd: Borderline personality disorder เป็นความผิดปกติทางบุคลิกภาพที่อารมณ์ ความสัมพันธ์ และภาพลักษณ์ตนเองไม่มั่นคง หุนหันพลันแล่น ไม่ใช่โรคทางระบบประสาท แต่พบร่วมกับอาการทางระบบประสาทแบบ functional และ functional seizures รักษาด้วยจิตบำบัดเช่น DBT และดูแลร่วมกับจิตแพทย์

name: Bovine spongiform encephalopathy
formal: Prion disease of cattle caused by misfolded prion protein, transmissible to humans as variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease through contaminated beef.
simple: A fatal brain disease of cattle, commonly called mad cow disease, which can cause a similar disease in humans.
th: โรคพรีออนของวัว (โรควัวบ้า) เกิดจากโปรตีนพรีออนที่พับผิดรูป ติดต่อสู่คนผ่านเนื้อหรือผลิตภัณฑ์วัวปนเปื้อน ทำให้เกิด variant CJD ในคนอายุน้อย
tempoNote: In humans, vCJD follows an incubation period of about 10–15 years, then progressive illness of roughly 1–2 years
feat: Fatal prion disease of cattle spread by feed containing infected meat-and-bone meal
In humans it causes variant CJD with an average onset age in the late twenties
Early psychiatric symptoms and painful limb sensory symptoms, followed by ataxia, myoclonus and dementia
Illness lasts around 14 months on average after symptom onset
Atypical BSE strains also occur sporadically in old cattle without contaminated feed
inv: MRI with pulvinar sign (bilateral posterior thalamic hyperintensity) in most cases of vCJD
EEG nonspecific and CSF 14-3-3 often negative; RT-QuIC on CSF or nasal brushings and tonsil or brain tissue for PrP
PRNP codon 129 genotype, typically methionine homozygous in vCJD

case.who: 29-year-old graphic designer from Bangkok who studied in the United Kingdom as a teenager
case.story: Nine months of depression and anxiety, then burning pain in the feet and hands and difficulty walking. In recent months, forgetfulness and jerks of the arms.
case.exam: Gait ataxia, painful dysaesthesia of the legs, myoclonus, impaired memory and executive function.
case.tests: MRI shows bilateral pulvinar hyperintensity on FLAIR; CSF RT-QuIC positive; PRNP codon 129 methionine homozygous.
case.q: Which exposure explains this young patient's disease, and what characteristic MRI sign supports it?
case.a: Dietary exposure to BSE-contaminated beef in the United Kingdom in the 1990s causing variant CJD, with the pulvinar sign on MRI.

read.where: Chapter 116: Prion Disorders: Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease and Related Disorders

Part II: Viral Pathogens: Pathogenesis, Pathology, Diagnosis and Treatment

det.patho: BSE is a transmissible spongiform encephalopathy in which the normal cellular prion protein (PrPC, encoded by PRNP) is converted into a protease-resistant, beta-sheet-rich form (PrPSc) that propagates and accumulates in the brain. Cattle were infected through meat-and-bone meal feed. Humans exposed to the classic BSE strain develop variant CJD, and the methionine homozygous genotype at codon 129 is found in all confirmed cases so far.
det.clinical: The UK epidemic peaked in the early 1990s, and the first human cases appeared in 1996. In vCJD, young adults develop psychiatric symptoms and limb dysaesthesia, followed by ataxia, chorea or myoclonus and progressive dementia. Illness averages about 14 months, longer than in sporadic CJD. Reported cases fell sharply after feed bans and removal of high-risk cattle tissues, but cases of atypical BSE continue to be detected in surveillance.
det.diagnosis: Suspect vCJD in young patients with psychiatric onset, painful sensory symptoms and later neurological decline. MRI showing the pulvinar sign is strongly supportive; periodic sharp wave EEG is usually absent and CSF 14-3-3 is less often positive than in sporadic CJD. RT-QuIC testing and tonsil biopsy for PrP help in life, while definite diagnosis rests on neuropathology with florid plaques. Exposure history to the UK or other affected countries matters.
det.treatment: There is no curative treatment, and care is supportive: symptom control for myoclonus and anxiety, nutrition, palliative care and infection control for instruments. Public health control rests on bans of ruminant protein in feed, removal of specified risk materials and surveillance of cattle and human cases. Blood donor deferral policies exist in several countries.
det.prognosis: Invariably fatal, usually within about 14 months of symptom onset.
pearls: Young age, psychiatric onset and painful dysaesthesia point to vCJD rather than sporadic CJD.
The pulvinar sign on MRI is seen in about 9 of 10 patients with vCJD.
BSE is the cattle disease; vCJD is the human disease.
det.thd: BSE หรือโรควัวบ้าเป็นโรคพรีออนของวัว ติดต่อผ่านอาหารสัตว์ที่ปนเปื้อน และทำให้คนที่บริโภคเนื้อปนเปื้อนเป็น variant CJD ซึ่งพบในคนอายุน้อย เริ่มด้วยอาการทางจิตและปวดแสบปลายมือเท้า ตามด้วยเดินเซ กระตุก และสมองเสื่อม MRI พบ pulvinar sign ตรวจ RT-QuIC และพันธุกรรมช่วยวินิจฉัย ไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ จึงเน้นการป้องกันด้วยการควบคุมอาหารสัตว์และเฝ้าระวัง

name: Boxers’ encephalopathy
formal: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (dementia pugilistica) from repeated head blows, with cognitive decline, parkinsonism, dysarthria, ataxia and tau deposition.
simple: Long-term brain damage in boxers after repeated head blows, causing memory loss, slurred speech and slowness.
th: สมองเสื่อมจากการถูกกระแทกศีรษะซ้ำ ๆ เช่น นักมวย มีความจำเสื่อม พฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน parkinsonism พูดไม่ชัด เดินเซ พยาธิสภาพเป็น tau
tempoNote: Symptoms appear years after exposure and progress slowly
feat: History of many years of repetitive head impacts (boxing, Muay Thai, contact sports, military)
Cognitive impairment: memory, executive function, slowed processing
Behavioural and mood change: irritability, impulsivity, depression
Parkinsonism, dysarthria, gait ataxia in the classic boxer picture
inv: MRI: atrophy, cavum septum pellucidum, microbleeds; excludes subdural haematoma
Neuropsychological testing
Exclude treatable causes (B12, thyroid, depression); diagnosis of CTE pathology is post-mortem

case.who: 52-year-old retired Muay Thai fighter from Buriram
case.story: Over 300 bouts in his youth; for five years he has become forgetful, short-tempered and slower in movement.
case.exam: MoCA 19/30, mild bilateral bradykinesia, dysarthria, wide-based gait.
case.tests: MRI generalised atrophy with a large cavum septum pellucidum; no subdural collection.
case.q: What clinical syndrome is suspected and how is CTE confirmed?
case.a: Traumatic encephalopathy syndrome (clinical correlate of CTE); confirmation of CTE requires neuropathology showing perivascular p-tau at sulcal depths.

det.patho: Repeated concussive and subconcussive impacts lead to hyperphosphorylated tau aggregating in neurons and astrocytes around small vessels at the depths of cortical sulci, later spreading widely. TDP-43, amyloid and Lewy pathology often coexist. The relation between exposure dose, genetics and disease risk is not fully defined.
det.clinical: Early features include mood and behavioural change; later cognitive decline and motor signs dominate. The 2021 consensus criteria define 'traumatic encephalopathy syndrome' as the clinical diagnosis, with core features of cognitive impairment and/or neurobehavioural dysregulation plus a progressive course after substantial exposure. Parkinsonism, dysarthria and ataxia were typical of heavily exposed boxers.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis in life is clinical and probabilistic; exclude other dementias and treatable causes. MRI may show atrophy and cavum septum pellucidum; tau PET and fluid biomarkers are research tools. Definite CTE is a neuropathological diagnosis.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying treatment exists. Manage depression, behavioural symptoms and parkinsonism symptomatically (levodopa has limited benefit). Prevention through rule changes, medical supervision and limiting exposure is the key public health approach.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive over years to decades; severity relates partly to exposure.
pearls: Ask every dementia patient about contact sports and boxing, including Muay Thai.
Cavum septum pellucidum is a common imaging clue but not diagnostic.
CTE is confirmed only at autopsy; TES is the living diagnosis.
det.thd: Boxers' encephalopathy หรือ CTE เกิดจากศีรษะถูกกระแทกซ้ำ ๆ เป็นเวลานาน เช่น นักมวยไทยหรือนักกีฬาปะทะ หลายปีต่อมามีความจำเสื่อม อารมณ์ฉุนเฉียว parkinsonism และพูดไม่ชัด ยืนยันได้เฉพาะการตรวจสมองหลังเสียชีวิต (tau รอบหลอดเลือดที่ร่องสมอง) ไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ ดูแลตามอาการและเน้นการป้องกัน

name: Brachial neuritis
formal: Immune-mediated inflammation of the brachial plexus (neuralgic amyotrophy) with sudden severe shoulder pain, then patchy weakness and wasting of upper limb muscles.
simple: Sudden shoulder pain followed by weakness of the arm because of inflammation of the nerves in the shoulder region.
more: Idiopathic inflammatory brachial plexopathy (Parsonage-Turner syndrome) with abrupt severe shoulder pain followed by patchy upper limb weakness and wasting, often after infection or vaccination.
th: เส้นประสาทแขนอักเสบเฉียบพลัน — ปวดไหล่รุนแรงเป็นวันแล้วตามด้วยอ่อนแรงลีบเป็นหย่อม ๆ สะบักยก
tempoNote: Severe pain for days to weeks, then patchy weakness; recovery over months to years
feat: Sudden severe shoulder/arm pain, often at night, sometimes after infection, surgery, vaccination or childbirth
As pain settles: patchy weakness and wasting — serratus anterior (winging), anterior interosseous, suprascapular, axillary
Mild sensory loss; can be bilateral or recurrent (hereditary form: SEPT9)
inv: EMG after 2–3 weeks: multifocal denervation outside a single root or nerve
MRI neurography/ultrasound: nerve hourglass constrictions

case.story: Woke with excruciating right shoulder pain a week after a viral illness; 10 days later the pain eased but he could not lift his arm or pinch.
case.exam: Medial scapular winging, weak shoulder abduction, weak flexion of the thumb tip and index fingertip (cannot make an 'OK' sign), minimal sensory loss.
case.tests: EMG: denervation in serratus anterior, deltoid and flexor pollicis longus; cervical MRI normal.
case.q: Why can't the patient make an 'OK' sign?
case.a: Anterior interosseous nerve involvement — a classic branch affected in neuralgic amyotrophy.

ddx.pt: Neck pain, dermatomal pattern, imaging correlate
Painless, progressive, UMN signs
Painless, slowly progressive, conduction block

aN: acute brachial neuritis | neuralgic amyotrophy | parsonage turner syndrome | brachial plexitis

det.patho: Neuralgic amyotrophy is thought to be an immune-mediated inflammation of brachial plexus nerves and branches, triggered by infection, surgery, vaccination, childbirth or strenuous exercise in a genetically or mechanically susceptible person. Pathology shows perivascular inflammation, and imaging can reveal focal hourglass-like constrictions of nerve fascicles. A hereditary form linked to SEPT9 causes recurrent attacks. Incidence is higher than once thought, roughly 1 in 1,000 per year in some estimates.
det.clinical: The illness begins with sudden severe shoulder or arm pain, often at night, unrelieved by usual analgesia and lasting days to weeks. As pain subsides, patchy weakness and wasting appear, commonly affecting the long thoracic nerve (scapular winging), suprascapular, axillary and anterior interosseous nerves, sometimes the phrenic nerve with orthopnoea. Sensory loss is modest and patchy. Bilateral involvement occurs in a minority. A second phase of persistent fatigue and residual pain is common.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by EMG showing denervation in a patchy distribution that does not fit a single root or nerve, best performed after 2–3 weeks. MRI of the cervical spine excludes radiculopathy; MRI neurography or high-resolution ultrasound may show nerve swelling or constrictions. Check diaphragm movement if breathless lying flat. Exclude rotator cuff disease, cervical radiculopathy, ALS, MMN and Pancoast tumour.
det.treatment: Adequate pain relief is the immediate priority, often requiring a combination of NSAID and a long-acting opioid. A short course of oral corticosteroids in the first weeks may shorten pain and speed recovery, although evidence is limited. Rehabilitation focuses on scapular stability and compensatory movement patterns; surgery (neurolysis or nerve transfer) is considered for constrictions without recovery.
det.prognosis: Most patients improve over 1–3 years, but many have residual weakness, pain or fatigue. Recurrence is common in hereditary forms.
pearls: Severe pain then weakness as pain fades — the sequence is the clue.
Isolated anterior interosseous or long thoracic palsy without trauma: think neuralgic amyotrophy.
Ask about orthopnoea: phrenic nerve involvement is under-recognised.
det.thd: Brachial neuritis (neuralgic amyotrophy) เป็นการอักเสบของเส้นประสาทแขนเชื่อว่าเกิดจากภูมิคุ้มกัน มักตามหลังติดเชื้อ ผ่าตัด วัคซีน หรือคลอดบุตร เริ่มด้วยปวดไหล่รุนแรงฉับพลันหลายวัน แล้วเมื่อปวดลดลงจะมีอ่อนแรงและลีบเป็นหย่อม ๆ เช่น สะบักยก ทำสัญลักษณ์ OK ไม่ได้ วินิจฉัยทางคลินิกร่วมกับ EMG และ MRI เพื่อแยกโรครากประสาท รักษาด้วยยาแก้ปวดเต็มที่ steroid ระยะสั้นช่วงแรก และกายภาพบำบัด ฟื้นตัวช้าเป็นปี

name: Brachial plexopathy
formal: Lesion of the brachial plexus from trauma, neuralgic amyotrophy, tumour, radiation, or other causes, with pattern of weakness and sensory loss matching trunk, cord, or branch involvement.
simple: Damage to the network of nerves in the shoulder that supply the arm, causing weakness, pain, and numbness.
more: MRI and EMG define the site and cause. Treatment depends on the cause: surgery for trauma, steroids for inflammatory forms, and rehabilitation. Disorders of the brachial plexus from trauma, tumour infiltration, radiation, inflammation or thoracic outlet compression, causing arm weakness, sensory loss and pain. Diagnose with EMG, nerve conduction and MRI plexus imaging; radiation plexopathy shows myokymia whereas tumour infiltration is painful. Treat the cause, with analgesia, physiotherapy and surgical repair for traumatic avulsions in the early months.
th: รอยโรคของ brachial plexus จากอุบัติเหตุ อักเสบ เนื้องอก หรือรังสี ทำให้แขนอ่อนแรงและชาตามรูปแบบของ trunk/cord ที่เสียหาย
tempoNote: Acute after trauma or neuralgic amyotrophy; subacute–chronic with tumour or radiation
feat: Weakness and sensory loss not fitting a single root or nerve
Upper trunk lesions affect shoulder abduction and elbow flexion; lower trunk affects hand muscles and medial forearm
Severe pain with tumour infiltration (often lower trunk) or neuralgic amyotrophy
Painless progression with myokymia suggests radiation plexopathy
Horner syndrome suggests lower trunk/T1 root involvement near the spine
inv: EMG/NCS: low sensory nerve action potentials (post-ganglionic) and denervation pattern localise the lesion
MRI brachial plexus with contrast (or MR neurography); CT myelography for root avulsion
PET-CT in suspected malignant infiltration; chest imaging for apical tumours

case.story: Thrown off his motorcycle and landed on his shoulder; now cannot lift his arm or bend his elbow.
case.exam: Weak deltoid, biceps, infraspinatus and brachioradialis, absent biceps reflex, numb lateral arm; hand function intact.
case.tests: EMG at 3 weeks: denervation in C5–C6 muscles, absent lateral antebrachial cutaneous SNAP; MRI shows upper trunk swelling without avulsion.
case.q: Where is the lesion and when should surgery be considered?
case.a: Upper trunk (Erb pattern) post-ganglionic injury; if no recovery by about 3–6 months, refer for nerve repair or transfer.

read.where: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves — Plexopathies

det.patho: The plexus may be stretched, compressed, avulsed, infiltrated or inflamed. Traction injuries from motorcycle accidents are the leading cause in young adults; birth injury affects infants. Other causes include neuralgic amyotrophy, tumour (Pancoast, breast, lymphoma), radiation fibrosis, thoracic outlet syndrome, surgical positioning and diabetes.
det.clinical: Localise by pattern: upper trunk (C5–6) shoulder and elbow flexion; middle trunk mimics C7; lower trunk (C8–T1) intrinsic hand muscles and medial forearm; cords produce mixed nerve patterns. Pain intensity and Horner sign help separate tumour infiltration from radiation injury. Root avulsion means intradural damage and a poorer outlook.
det.diagnosis: Electrodiagnosis is central: sensory potentials are reduced in plexus lesions but preserved in root avulsions. Timing matters—denervation appears after 2–3 weeks. MRI or MR neurography shows mass, swelling or avulsion pseudomeningocele; PET-CT helps distinguish tumour from radiation.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: early surgical exploration for open injuries, nerve grafting or transfers for traumatic lesions without recovery in 3–6 months, oncological therapy for tumour, and steroids in early neuralgic amyotrophy. Physiotherapy keeps joints mobile; neuropathic pain needs gabapentinoids, antidepressants or interventional approaches.
det.prognosis: Highly variable—good for neurapraxia and mild traction, poor for avulsion and radiation plexopathy.
pearls: Normal SNAPs with weakness = pre-ganglionic (root) lesion.
Painful lower trunk plexopathy with Horner = think apical lung tumour.
Myokymia on EMG favours radiation over tumour.
det.thd: Brachial plexopathy คือรอยโรคของ brachial plexus ทำให้แขนอ่อนแรงและชาไม่ตรงกับรากประสาทเส้นเดียว สาเหตุพบบ่อยในไทยคืออุบัติเหตุจักรยานยนต์ ตรวจ EMG/NCS ช่วยบอกตำแหน่งและแยกจากรากประสาทขาด MRI ช่วยหาสาเหตุ รักษาตามสาเหตุ ถ้าบาดเจ็บแล้วไม่ฟื้นใน 3–6 เดือนควรส่งผ่าตัดต่อเส้นประสาท

ddx.pt: Neck pain and dermatomal symptoms with normal SNAPs (pre-ganglionic)
Acute severe shoulder pain followed by patchy weakness and wasting
Lower trunk compression by a cervical band: thenar wasting and medial forearm numbness

name: Brain abscess
formal: Focal suppurative collection in brain parenchyma from contiguous infection, haematogenous spread or trauma, presenting with headache, fever, seizures and focal deficits, with ring-enhancing lesion on imaging.
simple: A pocket of pus in the brain due to infection, causing headache, fever, seizures and weakness.
more: Focal pyogenic infection of brain parenchyma from contiguous spread or bacteraemia, producing headache, fever, focal deficits; ring-enhancing lesion on MRI.
th: ฝีหนองในเนื้อสมองจากการติดเชื้อลามจากหู ไซนัส ฟัน หรือผ่านกระแสเลือด ปวดศีรษะ ไข้ อาการเฉพาะที่ CT/MRI เป็นก้อนขอบวงแหวน ตรงกลาง DWI restriction
tempoNote: Usually develops over 1–3 weeks from cerebritis to a walled-off capsule; sudden worsening suggests rupture into the ventricles or herniation
feat: Progressive headache (most common symptom), often without fever or neck stiffness
Focal deficit or seizures depending on site; cerebellar abscess from ear infection gives ataxia and hydrocephalus
Look for a source: chronic otitis media, sinusitis, dental infection, endocarditis, lung infection, cyanotic heart disease, trauma or surgery
Immunocompromised hosts: Nocardia, toxoplasma, fungi, TB; in Thailand consider melioidosis in diabetics
inv: MRI with contrast and DWI: ring-enhancing lesion with a smooth thin rim and restricted diffusion in the core
Blood cultures, echocardiography, ENT/dental imaging, chest imaging for source
Aspirate for Gram stain, aerobic/anaerobic, fungal and mycobacterial culture (and 16S PCR)
Avoid LP when there is mass effect; low yield and risk of herniation

case.who: 52-year-old diabetic rice farmer from Ubon Ratchathani
case.story: Two weeks of worsening headache and fever, then right arm weakness and one focal seizure; he had a leg abscess last month.
case.exam: Temperature 38.4 °C, right pronator drift, mild expressive aphasia, no neck stiffness.
case.tests: MRI two adjacent left frontal ring-enhancing lesions with DWI restriction and oedema; blood culture grows Burkholderia pseudomallei.
case.q: Which organism and what treatment plan?
case.a: Melioidosis brain abscess; IV ceftazidime or meropenem for several weeks, neurosurgical drainage of large lesions, then prolonged oral eradication therapy (co-trimoxazole).

read.where: Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System (Cerebral abscess)

Part III: Fungal Pathogens: Pathogenesis, Pathology, Diagnosis and Treatment

det.patho: Infection seeds the brain from a contiguous focus (middle ear, mastoid, sinus, teeth), via the blood (endocarditis, lung abscess, right-to-left shunts) or directly after trauma or surgery. Streptococci of the anginosus group and anaerobes dominate contiguous and dental cases, Staphylococcus aureus follows trauma or surgery, and Gram-negatives arise from ear sources. Over about 2 weeks an area of cerebritis forms a collagen capsule, thinner on the ventricular side, which is why rupture tends to occur into the ventricle.
det.clinical: Headache is the commonest complaint; the full triad of fever, headache and focal deficit is present in only a minority. Seizures, vomiting, papilloedema and declining consciousness reflect mass effect. Location reflects source: frontal lobe from sinuses, temporal lobe or cerebellum from the ear, and multiple lesions from blood-borne spread. Sudden deterioration with meningism suggests intraventricular rupture, which carries high mortality.
det.diagnosis: MRI with DWI is the key test: pus restricts diffusion, which separates abscess from necrotic tumour in most cases. Blood cultures, echocardiography and a careful ENT and dental search identify the source. Stereotactic aspiration provides both diagnosis and drainage; send material for full microbiology, including Nocardia, fungi, TB and molecular testing. In Thailand, Burkholderia pseudomallei, Klebsiella and TB are important causes to culture for.
det.treatment: Combine drainage and antibiotics. Aspirate or excise lesions larger than about 2.5 cm, those causing mass effect or near the ventricle, and any uncertain diagnosis. Empirical therapy commonly uses a third-generation cephalosporin plus metronidazole, adding vancomycin after trauma or neurosurgery; use ceftazidime or meropenem when melioidosis is possible. Continue IV therapy for about 6–8 weeks guided by imaging; treat the source, use antiseizure drugs for seizures, and give steroids only for dangerous oedema.
det.prognosis: Mortality has fallen to around 10% with MRI and early drainage; poor consciousness at presentation and ventricular rupture predict death, and survivors often have epilepsy.
pearls: Restricted diffusion in the centre of a ring lesion favours abscess over tumour.
Absence of fever does not exclude an abscess.
Think melioidosis in a diabetic farmer from northeast Thailand.
det.thd: Brain abscess คือฝีหนองในเนื้อสมอง เกิดจากเชื้อลามจากหู ไซนัส ฟัน หรือมาทางกระแสเลือด อาการเด่นคือปวดศีรษะที่แย่ลง อาจมีไข้ ชัก และอาการเฉพาะที่ MRI พบก้อนขอบวงแหวนที่ตรงกลางมี diffusion restriction ช่วยแยกจากเนื้องอก รักษาด้วยการเจาะดูดหนองหรือผ่าตัดร่วมกับยาปฏิชีวนะทางหลอดเลือด 6–8 สัปดาห์ ในไทยต้องนึกถึง melioidosis ในผู้ป่วยเบาหวานจากภาคอีสาน

name: Brain tumour
formal: Intracranial neoplasm, primary or metastatic, presenting with progressive headache, seizures, focal deficits or raised intracranial pressure.
simple: An abnormal growth of cells in or around the brain that may cause headache, seizures or weakness.
more: Primary or metastatic neoplasms of the brain causing headache, seizures, focal deficits and raised intracranial pressure; gliomas and metastases are most frequent.
th: เนื้องอกในสมองทั้งชนิดปฐมภูมิและมะเร็งแพร่กระจาย ทำให้ปวดศีรษะที่ค่อย ๆ เป็นมากขึ้น ชัก อ่อนแรงเฉพาะที่ หรือความดันในกะโหลกสูง
tempoNote: Usually weeks to months of progression; a seizure or bleed into the tumour can make the first presentation abrupt
feat: Progressive focal deficit (weakness, aphasia, field cut) over weeks to months
New-onset seizures in an adult, focal or focal to bilateral
Headache worse on waking or bending, with vomiting or papilloedema when pressure rises
Personality change, apathy or memory decline with frontal or callosal tumours
Metastases often multiple and at the grey-white junction; known cancer in many
inv: MRI brain with gadolinium (CT if MRI unavailable); perfusion and spectroscopy can help grading
Search for a primary: CT chest-abdomen-pelvis, breast exam, skin check
Tissue diagnosis with integrated histology and molecular markers (IDH, 1p/19q, MGMT, H3 K27M)
Avoid steroids before biopsy if primary CNS lymphoma is possible

case.story: Six weeks of morning headaches and his wife says he leaves sentences unfinished. Yesterday his right hand jerked for a minute.
case.exam: Mild right pronator drift, word-finding difficulty, early papilloedema.
case.tests: MRI: two ring-enhancing lesions at the left frontal and right parietal grey-white junction with surrounding oedema; chest CT shows a right hilar mass.
case.q: Which diagnosis fits best, and what are the first two management steps?
case.a: Brain metastases from lung cancer; start dexamethasone for oedema and an antiseizure drug, then obtain tissue (often from the lung) and plan surgery or radiosurgery.

det.patho: In adults, metastases (lung, breast, melanoma, kidney, colorectal) outnumber primary brain tumours. The commonest primary tumours are meningioma, glioblastoma and other diffuse gliomas, and primary CNS lymphoma; in children, pilocytic astrocytoma, medulloblastoma and diffuse midline glioma lead. The 2021 WHO CNS classification defines many tumours by molecular features, for example IDH mutation and 1p/19q codeletion. Symptoms come from local invasion, mass effect and vasogenic oedema, and from blocked CSF pathways.
det.clinical: Presentation depends on site and growth rate: slow tumours often present with seizures, fast ones with weeks of escalating deficit and raised pressure. Isolated headache is an uncommon sole presentation, but headache with vomiting, papilloedema, new neurological signs or a change in pattern deserves imaging. Posterior fossa tumours give ataxia and hydrocephalus; pituitary lesions give endocrine change and bitemporal field loss. Red flags for herniation are falling consciousness, a dilated pupil and Cushing response.
det.diagnosis: Contrast MRI is the key test; CT may show only oedema or calcification. Look for a primary cancer if lesions are multiple or the patient is older or a smoker. Final diagnosis requires tissue with molecular profiling, except for typical meningiomas that may be observed. Mimics include abscess, tumefactive demyelination, subacute infarct, tuberculoma, cysticercosis and vasculitis.
det.treatment: Dexamethasone reduces oedema-related symptoms but should be held until biopsy if lymphoma is possible. Give antiseizure drugs to patients who have had seizures; prophylaxis in seizure-free patients is not routinely advised. Definitive care is maximal safe resection followed by tailored radiotherapy and chemotherapy (for example temozolomide with radiation for glioblastoma; IDH inhibitor vorasidenib is an option for selected IDH-mutant low-grade glioma). Metastases are managed with surgery, stereotactic radiosurgery or systemic therapy that crosses the barrier. Address venous thromboembolism, steroid side effects, rehabilitation and palliative needs.
det.prognosis: Ranges from cure for many meningiomas to a median survival of well under two years for glioblastoma; molecular markers strongly guide outlook.
pearls: First seizure in an adult with focal signs: get contrast MRI.
Hold steroids before biopsy when lymphoma is on the list.
Multiple lesions at the grey-white junction suggest metastases; search for the primary.
det.thd: เนื้องอกสมองในผู้ใหญ่ที่พบบ่อยที่สุดคือมะเร็งที่แพร่กระจายมาจากปอด เต้านม หรือผิวหนัง ส่วนชนิดปฐมภูมิที่พบบ่อยคือ meningioma และ glioma อาการได้แก่ปวดศีรษะที่เป็นมากขึ้น ชัก และอ่อนแรงหรือพูดผิดปกติที่ค่อย ๆ แย่ลง วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI ที่ฉีดสารทึบรังสีและยืนยันด้วยชิ้นเนื้อพร้อมตรวจ molecular marker รักษาด้วย dexamethasone ลดสมองบวม การผ่าตัด รังสีรักษา และยาเคมีตามชนิดของเนื้องอก

name: Brainstem encephalitis
formal: Inflammation of the brainstem from infection (Listeria, enterovirus 71, herpes), autoimmune or paraneoplastic causes, with cranial neuropathies, ataxia and altered consciousness.
simple: Inflammation of the brainstem causing double vision, trouble swallowing, unsteadiness and drowsiness.
th: สมองส่วนก้านสมองอักเสบจากเชื้อ (Listeria, enterovirus 71, herpes) หรือภูมิคุ้มกัน/paraneoplastic ทำให้เส้นประสาทสมองผิดปกติ เดินเซ และระดับความรู้สึกตัวลดลง
tempoNote: Develops over hours to days in infections; days to weeks in autoimmune forms
feat: Multiple cranial neuropathies: diplopia, facial weakness, dysphagia
Ataxia, nystagmus, long tract signs
Fever and headache in infective cases; altered consciousness
Myoclonic jerks, tremor and autonomic instability in EV71 infection of young children
Respiratory failure from medullary involvement
inv: MRI with contrast (T2/FLAIR brainstem lesions, abscesses)
CSF cell count, protein, glucose, culture, PCR (HSV, EV, Listeria) — blood cultures for Listeria
Anti-GQ1b, paraneoplastic and autoimmune panels; screen for underlying cancer and Behçet when relevant

case.who: 65-year-old woman on steroids for rheumatoid arthritis, from Nan
case.story: Four days of fever and headache, then double vision, facial droop and choking on fluids.
case.exam: Febrile, right CN VI and VII palsies, dysphagia, left limb ataxia, GCS 13.
case.tests: MRI: patchy T2 lesions in pons and medulla with ring enhancement; blood culture grows Gram-positive rods.
case.q: Which organism and which antibiotics?
case.a: Listeria rhombencephalitis; high-dose IV ampicillin (often with gentamicin), since cephalosporins do not cover Listeria.

read.where: Chapter 28 Disorders of Consciousness and Intensive Care Neurology — Brainstem Encephalitis
Chapter 109: Paraneoplastic and Other Autoimmune Neurologic Disorders

det.patho: The brainstem can be invaded by organisms with tropism for it (Listeria monocytogenes via cranial nerves, enterovirus 71, HSV, flaviviruses) or targeted by immune processes (anti-GQ1b, paraneoplastic anti-Ri/Ma2/KLHL11, Behçet, MS, NMOSD, CLIPPERS). Damage to nuclei and tracts in a compact region causes rapid, combined deficits.
det.clinical: Infective cases often begin with a febrile prodrome before cranial nerve and cerebellar signs and progress to reduced consciousness and respiratory failure. EV71 affects young children during hand-foot-mouth outbreaks with myoclonus, tremor, ataxia and cardiopulmonary collapse. Autoimmune cases are subacute and less febrile.
det.diagnosis: MRI with contrast and CSF analysis are first-line; CSF may be only mildly abnormal in Listeria, so blood cultures are crucial. Test PCR for viruses, antibody panels when infection is excluded, and screen for malignancy in paraneoplastic suspicion.
det.treatment: Start empirical ampicillin plus aciclovir alongside standard meningitis cover while awaiting results. Treat EV71 supportively with intensive care; IVIG is used in some centres. Autoimmune forms receive steroids, IVIG or plasma exchange, and tumour treatment if paraneoplastic. Protect the airway early when bulbar function fails.
det.prognosis: Listeria rhombencephalitis has high mortality and frequent sequelae; outcome is better with early treatment.
pearls: Fever + cranial neuropathies + ataxia: add ampicillin for Listeria.
Hand-foot-mouth outbreak + toddler with myoclonic jerks = EV71 brainstem involvement.
Brainstem encephalitis can cause sudden respiratory arrest; monitor closely.
det.thd: Brainstem encephalitis คือก้านสมองอักเสบ สาเหตุติดเชื้อสำคัญคือ Listeria ในผู้สูงอายุหรือภูมิต่ำ และ enterovirus 71 ในเด็กเล็กช่วงระบาดมือเท้าปาก ส่วนสาเหตุภูมิคุ้มกัน ได้แก่ anti-GQ1b และ paraneoplastic อาการคือเส้นประสาทสมองหลายเส้นผิดปกติ เดินเซ ซึม อาจหยุดหายใจ ต้องทำ MRI เจาะน้ำไขสันหลัง เพาะเชื้อเลือด และให้ ampicillin กับ aciclovir ทันที
