name: Brainstem encephalitis in adults
formal: Brainstem inflammation in adults from Listeria, viruses, Behcet disease, anti-GQ1b antibodies or paraneoplastic causes, with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and long tract signs.
simple: Inflammation of the lower brain in adults, often from infection or immune disease, causing double vision, unsteadiness and weakness.
th: ก้านสมองอักเสบในผู้ใหญ่ สาเหตุหลักคือ Listeria ไวรัส Behçet anti-GQ1b และ paraneoplastic อาการกลอกตาผิดปกติ เดินเซ และ long tract signs
tempoNote: Infections over days; immune and paraneoplastic forms over days to weeks
feat: Ophthalmoplegia, facial and bulbar weakness
Ataxia and nystagmus; pyramidal signs
Drowsiness or coma as the reticular system is involved
Clues: oral ulcers (Behçet), recent diarrhoea or infection (GQ1b), weight loss or smoking (paraneoplastic)

case.who: 41-year-old man from Phrae with recurrent mouth ulcers
case.story: Ten days of headache, slurred speech and unsteadiness; previous painful genital sores.
case.exam: Bilateral INO, dysarthria, right hemiparesis with brisk reflexes; oral aphthae.
case.tests: MRI: T2 lesion extending from the midbrain into the pons with patchy enhancement; CSF neutrophilic pleocytosis; HLA-B51 positive.
case.q: What is the likely cause and treatment?
case.a: Parenchymal neuro-Behçet; high-dose steroids plus an immunosuppressant (azathioprine or anti-TNF such as infliximab).

det.patho: Adult brainstem encephalitis arises from direct infection (Listeria, HSV, VZV, tuberculosis, flaviviruses), from autoimmune attack (anti-GQ1b antibodies, Behçet vasculitis, CLIPPERS, demyelinating disease) or from paraneoplastic immunity directed against neuronal antigens. Each mechanism produces focal inflammation in a region packed with cranial nuclei and long tracts.
det.clinical: Presentation combines eye-movement disorders, bulbar weakness, ataxia and corticospinal signs with variable consciousness. Fever and rapid course favour infection; preceding diarrhoea or respiratory infection with areflexic weakness suggests the GQ1b spectrum; oral and genital ulcers suggest Behçet; an older smoker with opsoclonus or jaw dystonia points to paraneoplastic disease.
det.diagnosis: MRI, CSF analysis and blood cultures are first steps. Add anti-GQ1b, onconeural and autoimmune panels; a pathergy test or HLA-B51 helps in Behçet. Search for occult cancer in paraneoplastic suspicion and repeat screening if negative.
det.treatment: Empirical ampicillin and aciclovir until infection is excluded. Bickerstaff encephalitis responds to IVIG or plasma exchange; Behçet needs steroids plus immunosuppressants or anti-TNF drugs; paraneoplastic disease requires tumour therapy plus immunotherapy. CLIPPERS is steroid-responsive but often steroid-dependent.
det.prognosis: Varies by cause—good for Bickerstaff, variable for Behçet, poor for many paraneoplastic forms.
pearls: Treat as Listeria until proved otherwise in an unwell adult with fever and brainstem signs.
Ask about oral and genital ulcers in every brainstem lesion of a young adult.
Hyperreflexia with ophthalmoplegia and drowsiness suggests Bickerstaff, not Miller Fisher.
det.thd: ก้านสมองอักเสบในผู้ใหญ่ เกิดได้จากเชื้อ Listeria และไวรัส จากภูมิคุ้มกัน เช่น anti-GQ1b (Bickerstaff) และ Behçet หรือจาก paraneoplastic อาการคือกลอกตาผิดปกติ กลืนลำบาก เดินเซ และอ่อนแรงครึ่งซีก ตรวจ MRI น้ำไขสันหลัง และแอนติบอดี ให้ยาฆ่าเชื้อครอบคลุม Listeria ก่อน แล้วรักษาตามสาเหตุ

name: Brainstem meningoencephalitis
formal: Infectious inflammation of the brainstem and meninges, typically Listeria or viral, causing fever, cranial nerve palsies, ataxia and drowsiness.
simple: Infection of the lower brain and its coverings, causing fever, double vision, unsteady walking and drowsiness.
th: การติดเชื้อที่ก้านสมองร่วมกับเยื่อหุ้มสมอง เช่น Listeria หรือไวรัส ทำให้ไข้ เส้นประสาทสมองอ่อนแรงหลายเส้น เดินเซ และซึม

feat: Biphasic course: flu-like prodrome then asymmetric cranial nerve palsies

Listeria in older, pregnant, diabetic or immunosuppressed patients — but also healthy adults
Other causes: HSV, enterovirus A71, TB, Japanese encephalitis, Behçet, autoimmune

det.patho: Listeria reaches the brainstem either through the blood or, as suggested by animal studies, by travelling along cranial nerves from the oropharynx, forming microabscesses in the pons and medulla. Viruses such as HSV and enterovirus A71 can invade the same region. Inflammation of nuclei and long tracts in a compact area gives multiple cranial nerve and long-tract signs.
det.clinical: Expect fever, headache, nausea and then evolving asymmetric cranial neuropathies (VI, VII, IX, X), cerebellar signs, hemiparesis and somnolence. Meningeal signs may be mild. Respiratory failure from medullary involvement is an important cause of death. Children with hand-foot-mouth disease may develop EV-A71 rhombencephalitis with myoclonus and autonomic instability.
det.diagnosis: Brainstem lesions are often invisible on CT, so MRI is the imaging of choice. CSF findings vary and may be only modestly abnormal; Listeria may not be seen on Gram stain, so blood cultures are crucial. Use PCR panels for HSV and enterovirus and consider TB, Behçet, lymphoma and paraneoplastic causes.
det.treatment: Empirical meningitis therapy in at-risk adults should include ampicillin to cover Listeria. Confirmed listeriosis needs high-dose IV ampicillin or penicillin, often with gentamicin initially, for several weeks (longer if abscesses); co-trimoxazole is an alternative in penicillin allergy. Add aciclovir until HSV is excluded. Supportive care includes airway protection and nasogastric feeding.
det.prognosis: Listeria rhombencephalitis has substantial mortality and residual deficits are common even with treatment.
pearls: Fever + multiple cranial nerve palsies + ataxia: think Listeria and give ampicillin.
Cephalosporins do not cover Listeria.
Blood cultures are often more useful than CSF Gram stain.
det.thd: Brainstem meningoencephalitis คือการติดเชื้อที่ก้านสมองและเยื่อหุ้มสมอง สาเหตุสำคัญคือ Listeria ซึ่งพบในผู้สูงอายุ หญิงตั้งครรภ์ หรือภูมิต่ำ ผู้ป่วยมีไข้ปวดหัวนำมาก่อนแล้วตามด้วยเส้นประสาทสมองหลายเส้นอ่อนแรง เดินเซ และซึม ตรวจ MRI และเพาะเชื้อจากเลือด รักษาด้วย ampicillin ขนาดสูงเพราะ cephalosporin ไม่ครอบคลุม Listeria

name: Brainstem myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus generated in the brainstem, including startle syndromes (hyperekplexia) and reticular reflex myoclonus, with generalised jerks propagating up and down the neuraxis.
simple: Sudden whole-body or facial jerks arising from the lower part of the brain, often provoked by sound or touch.
th: myoclonus ที่เกิดจากก้านสมอง เช่น startle syndrome (hyperekplexia) และ reticular reflex myoclonus ทำให้กระตุกทั้งตัวกระจายขึ้นลงตามแกนประสาท
tempoNote: Stimulus-triggered jerks; course depends on cause (lifelong in hereditary hyperekplexia, variable after hypoxia)
feat: Generalised axial jerks with shoulder elevation, head flexion and arm flexion
Often triggered by sound, touch or tapping the nose/face
Exaggerated startle with falls but preserved consciousness
Causes: hereditary hyperekplexia, post-hypoxic injury, brainstem lesions, autoimmune (glycine receptor antibodies)

case.exam: Repeated glabellar taps produce non-habituating whole-body jerks; otherwise normal.
case.tests: EMG: startle response beginning in sternocleidomastoid and spreading; GLRA1 pathogenic variant.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the drug of choice?

det.patho: Abnormal hyperexcitability of the brainstem reticular formation leads to jerks that start in muscles supplied by the lower brainstem and propagate rostrally and caudally. In hyperekplexia, defects in inhibitory glycinergic transmission (GLRA1, GLRB, SLC6A5) reduce inhibition of startle circuits. Acquired forms follow hypoxia, brainstem stroke, inflammation or glycine receptor antibody disease (PERM).
det.clinical: Jerks are generalised and stimulus-sensitive, often with falls. Neonates with hyperekplexia are stiff and may have apnoea that improves with flexion of head and legs (Vigevano manoeuvre). Post-hypoxic patients show reticular reflex myoclonus in addition to cortical myoclonus.
det.diagnosis: Multichannel EMG demonstrates the brainstem pattern (earliest in SCM, then cranial and limb muscles). MRI and antibody testing identify acquired causes; genetic testing confirms hereditary forms.
det.treatment: Clonazepam is first-line for hyperekplexia; levetiracetam, valproate and piracetam help some reticular myoclonus. Immunotherapy treats glycine receptor antibody disease. Teach neonatal caregivers the flexion manoeuvre for apnoea.
det.prognosis: Hereditary hyperekplexia improves with age; acquired forms depend on the cause.
pearls: Non-habituating nose-tap jerks are a bedside sign of hyperekplexia.
SCM fires first in brainstem myoclonus on EMG.
Stiff neonate with apnoea and startles: think glycinergic defect.
det.thd: Brainstem myoclonus คือการกระตุกทั้งตัวที่เกิดจากก้านสมอง มักถูกกระตุ้นด้วยเสียงหรือการสัมผัส เช่น hyperekplexia ทางพันธุกรรม (ยีน GLRA1) และ reticular myoclonus หลังสมองขาดออกซิเจน ตรวจ EMG พบกล้ามเนื้อ SCM กระตุกก่อนแล้วกระจายขึ้นลง รักษาด้วย clonazepam ส่วนชนิด autoimmune ให้ยากดภูมิ

name: Brainstem reticular myoclonus
formal: Generalised myoclonus originating in the brainstem reticular formation, with jerks spreading caudally and rostrally, often provoked by action or stimuli after hypoxic injury.
simple: Sudden body jerks that start in the brainstem and spread, sometimes after oxygen deprivation to the brain.
more: Cortical-subcortical myoclonus arising from the brainstem reticular formation, producing generalised jerks with startle-like characteristics, often after hypoxic brain injury or in hyperekplexia. Brainstem-generated generalized jerks, with muscle activation ascending from the caudal medulla and rostral spread; triggered by action or stimuli, as in hypoxic brain injury.
th: myoclonus ทั่วตัวที่เกิดจาก reticular formation ของก้านสมอง กระจายขึ้นลง ถูกกระตุ้นด้วยการเคลื่อนไหวหรือสิ่งเร้า พบหลังสมองขาดออกซิเจน
tempoNote: Appears early after hypoxic or toxic brainstem injury; may persist or fade
feat: Generalised, synchronous axial and proximal jerks
Triggered by movement, touch or sound; may occur spontaneously
Common after cardiac arrest, also with uraemia and some toxins
Often accompanies cortical myoclonus in Lance–Adams syndrome
inv: Multichannel EMG: activity starts in muscles of the lower brainstem (e.g. SCM) and spreads
EEG often shows no time-locked cortical discharge
MRI brainstem; metabolic and drug screen

case.exam: Awake, follows commands, generalised flexion jerks on tapping or passive movement.
case.tests: EMG: jerks start in SCM and spread to face and limbs; EEG no time-locked spikes.
case.q: What type of myoclonus and which drugs may help?
case.a: Post-hypoxic reticular reflex myoclonus; levetiracetam, clonazepam or valproate.

det.patho: Damage or toxicity in the medullary reticular formation releases reflex circuits, so stimuli trigger generalised jerks. Hypoxic-ischaemic injury is the classic cause; uraemia, some drugs and brainstem lesions also produce it. Unlike startle, the response does not involve a normal startle pattern and is not habituating.
det.clinical: Patients show generalised jerks often affecting proximal limbs and trunk more than distal ones, provoked by movement or touch. Post-hypoxic patients may also have cortical myoclonus and action myoclonus. In acute post-arrest coma, distinguish reticular myoclonus from status myoclonus with poor prognosis.
det.diagnosis: Polygraphic EMG timing establishes the brainstem origin; EEG back-averaging lacks a cortical correlate. Imaging and metabolic tests identify the cause.
det.treatment: Treat the cause where possible (correct uraemia, stop drugs). Levetiracetam, clonazepam and valproate are commonly used; piracetam may help. Avoid excessive sedation in recovering patients.
det.prognosis: Depends on the underlying injury; myoclonus may improve over months.
pearls: Proximal, generalised and stimulus-sensitive jerks after hypoxia suggest a reticular source.
EMG order of activation separates brainstem from cortical myoclonus.
Do not equate all post-arrest myoclonus with poor prognosis; assess with EEG and clinical context.
det.thd: Brainstem reticular myoclonus เกิดจาก reticular formation ในก้านสมองไวผิดปกติ มักพบหลังสมองขาดออกซิเจน เช่น หลังหัวใจหยุดเต้น หรือภาวะยูรีเมีย ผู้ป่วยกระตุกทั้งตัวเมื่อถูกสัมผัสหรือเคลื่อนไหว ตรวจ EMG พบเริ่มที่กล้ามเนื้อจากก้านสมองส่วนล่าง รักษาสาเหตุร่วมกับ levetiracetam หรือ clonazepam

feat: Effortful, halting, short-phrase speech with omitted function words (agrammatism)
Impaired repetition and naming; comprehension of simple speech relatively preserved
Patient aware and frustrated; writing similarly affected

Vascular imaging and stroke work-up

det.patho: Damage to the left inferior frontal gyrus (pars opercularis and triangularis) and surrounding frontal operculum, insula and subcortical white matter disrupts speech planning and grammar. Lesions confined to Broca's area alone often give transient deficits; persistent Broca aphasia usually needs larger lesions.
det.clinical: Speech is slow, effortful and short, with content words preserved but grammar lost. Repetition and naming are poor; comprehension is good for simple material but struggles with complex syntax. Right hemiparesis (face and arm) and apraxia of speech often coexist. Patients are aware and may become depressed.
det.diagnosis: Bedside: assess fluency, comprehension, repetition, naming, reading and writing. Imaging confirms the lesion; stroke is the commonest cause, but tumours, abscesses and degenerative disease (PNFA) are alternatives when onset is gradual.
det.treatment: Treat the cause—acute stroke with thrombolysis or thrombectomy if eligible. Speech and language therapy is the mainstay; intensive therapy improves outcomes. Support communication with gestures, writing and communication aids, and screen for depression.
det.prognosis: Improvement occurs over months, particularly in the first 3–6 months; many patients regain functional communication.
pearls: Non-fluent + good comprehension + poor repetition = Broca.
Sudden aphasia is a stroke until proven otherwise; call the stroke team.
Gradual non-fluent aphasia suggests PNFA, not Broca stroke.
det.thd: Broca's aphasia คือภาวะพูดไม่คล่อง พูดช้า ติดขัด ไม่มีคำเชื่อม พูดตามไม่ได้ แต่ฟังเข้าใจค่อนข้างดี เกิดจากรอยโรคสมองส่วนหน้าซีกซ้ายด้านล่าง ส่วนใหญ่จาก stroke ในเขต MCA มักมีแขนขวาอ่อนแรงร่วม ต้องรีบตรวจและรักษาแบบ stroke เร่งด่วน แล้วฝึกพูดกับนักแก้ไขการพูด

name: Brody disease
formal: Autosomal recessive exercise-induced muscle stiffness from ATP2A1 mutation affecting SERCA1 calcium pump, causing painless delayed relaxation with electrically silent cramp.
simple: An inherited problem where muscles become stiff and slow to relax after exercise, especially in the cold.
more: Diagnosed by ATP2A1 testing and reduced SERCA1 activity; EMG is silent during stiffness. Dantrolene may help; it is generally non-progressive.
th: โรคกล้ามเนื้อทางพันธุกรรมแบบด้อยจากยีน ATP2A1 (SERCA1) ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อคลายตัวช้าเมื่อออกแรง แต่ EMG ไม่พบ myotonia
tempoNote: Lifelong exercise-induced stiffness starting in childhood, provoked by each bout of exertion
feat: Painless or mildly painful stiffness after repeated or vigorous exercise
Delayed relaxation worsens with continued exercise and cold
Electrically silent: no myotonic discharges on EMG
Arms, legs and eyelids affected; strength usually normal
Autosomal recessive ATP2A1 variants; a dominant Brody syndrome also exists

case.story: His hands lock after repeatedly gripping a badminton racket and his legs stiffen running uphill, easing after a few minutes of rest.
case.exam: Normal bulk and strength; after 20 rapid fist closures, hand opening is markedly slow, no percussion myotonia.
case.tests: EMG at rest normal and during the stiffness shows no myotonic discharges; CK 210 U/L; two ATP2A1 variants identified.
case.q: Why does an electrically silent stiffness point away from myotonia congenita?
case.a: Slow relaxation here comes from slow calcium re-uptake by SERCA1 (Brody disease), not from membrane hyperexcitability.

read.where: 8. Cramps, Muscle Stiffness, and Exercise Intolerance
8 - Cramps, Muscle Stiffness, and Exercise Intolerance

det.patho: SERCA1, encoded by ATP2A1, pumps calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum of fast-twitch fibres after contraction. Reduced activity slows relaxation, especially during repeated contractions when cytosolic calcium accumulates. Because the membrane is normal, there is no electrical after-discharge.
det.clinical: Symptoms begin in childhood with stiffness and cramp-like slowing after exertion, eased by rest. Cold aggravates symptoms. Muscle strength and bulk are usually normal, though some have mild hypertrophy or rhabdomyolysis episodes. The disorder is rare and underdiagnosed.
det.diagnosis: Key clue is clinical delayed relaxation without myotonic potentials on EMG. ATP2A1 genetic testing confirms the recessive form; a dominant 'Brody syndrome' without identified ATP2A1 variants is described. Exclude metabolic myopathies with forearm exercise testing where needed.
det.treatment: Avoid triggering exercise patterns and cold. Calcium channel blockers such as verapamil or dantrolene have helped some patients, but evidence is anecdotal. Anaesthetists should be informed, though malignant hyperthermia risk is not clearly increased.
det.prognosis: Non-progressive and compatible with normal life expectancy.
pearls: Exercise-induced stiffness with a silent EMG suggests Brody disease.
Unlike myotonia congenita, symptoms worsen rather than improve with continued activity.
Think of it in 'atypical myotonia' with no CLCN1 or SCN4A variant.
det.thd: Brody disease เกิดจากความผิดปกติของ SERCA1 ที่สูบแคลเซียมกลับเข้า sarcoplasmic reticulum ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อคลายตัวช้าหลังออกแรงซ้ำ ๆ และในอากาศเย็น ต่างจาก myotonia ตรงที่ EMG ไม่พบ myotonic discharge วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีน ATP2A1 การรักษาคือหลีกเลี่ยงสิ่งกระตุ้น บางรายใช้ยา dantrolene หรือ verapamil

Same-side dorsal column loss (position and vibration)

det.patho: Hemisection of the cord interrupts the descending corticospinal tract and ascending dorsal columns, which cross only in the medulla, and the spinothalamic tract, whose fibres have already crossed near their entry level. This gives ipsilateral motor and proprioceptive loss with contralateral pain and temperature loss. Damage to entering roots and the dorsal horn adds a band of ipsilateral sensory loss at the lesion level.
det.clinical: Pure hemisection is rare outside penetrating trauma; most patients show partial patterns. Multiple sclerosis, NMOSD, disc herniation, meningioma, schwannoma, radiation myelopathy and idiopathic spinal cord herniation are common causes. Sphincter function is often relatively preserved. Pain at the lesion level may precede other signs in compressive causes.
det.diagnosis: Clinical localisation from the crossed sensory pattern should guide targeted MRI. Imaging characterises the lesion: eccentric short T2 lesions favour MS, longitudinally extensive lesions suggest NMOSD, and extramedullary masses require surgery. In thoracic cases with ventral cord displacement, consider cord herniation.
det.treatment: Treatment is directed at the cause: surgical stabilisation and decompression for trauma or tumour, corticosteroids and disease-modifying therapy for demyelination, and dural repair for herniation. Rehabilitation addresses gait and protection of the anaesthetic limb from burns and injury.
det.prognosis: Generally the best prognosis among incomplete cord syndromes, with most patients regaining independent walking.
pearls: Weak leg on one side, numb to pain on the other side: hemicord.
The pain level is a little lower than the actual lesion.
Warn patients to protect the analgesic limb from hot water and injury.
det.thd: Brown–Séquard syndrome เกิดจากรอยโรคครึ่งซีกของไขสันหลัง ทำให้ด้านเดียวกับรอยโรคอ่อนแรงและเสียความรู้สึกตำแหน่งข้อและการสั่น ส่วนด้านตรงข้ามเสียความรู้สึกเจ็บและร้อนเย็น เพราะใยประสาท spinothalamic ข้ามฝั่งตั้งแต่ระดับที่เข้าไขสันหลัง สาเหตุมีทั้งอุบัติเหตุ ปลอกประสาทอักเสบ หมอนรองกระดูก และเนื้องอก ตรวจด้วย MRI และรักษาตามสาเหตุ โดยรวมพยากรณ์โรคค่อนข้างดี

formal: Riboflavin transporter deficiency neuronopathy from SLC52A2 or SLC52A3 mutations with progressive bulbar palsy, sensorineural deafness, respiratory compromise and motor weakness; responsive to riboflavin.
simple: An inherited condition with hearing loss, weakness of face and throat muscles and breathing difficulty, which can improve with vitamin B2.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมขนส่งไรโบฟลาวิน — หูหนวก กลืนพูดลำบาก แขนลีบในเด็ก/วัยรุ่น รักษาได้ด้วยวิตามินบี 2 ขนาดสูง
feat: Childhood or adolescent onset of sensorineural deafness
Progressive bulbar palsy, facial weakness, tongue wasting; respiratory failure
Arm and neck weakness; some have sensory ataxia and optic atrophy
inv: SLC52A2 / SLC52A3 genetic testing; acylcarnitine profile may be abnormal
EMG: neurogenic change; audiometry

case.story: Gradual hearing loss from age 8, now nasal speech and difficulty swallowing; neck feels weak.
case.exam: Bilateral sensorineural deafness, facial weakness, wasted fasciculating tongue, weak neck flexors and shoulders.
case.tests: EMG: active denervation in bulbar and cervical muscles; SLC52A3 variants.
case.q: Why must treatment start before genetic confirmation?
case.a: High-dose riboflavin is safe and can halt or reverse the disease; delays allow irreversible respiratory and bulbar failure.

ddx.pt: Adult, no deafness, UMN signs
Adult male, gynaecomastia, AR expansion
Fatigable bulbar weakness without wasting or deafness

aN: bvvl | riboflavin transporter deficiency | rtd | slc52a3 | slc52a2 | fazio londe

det.patho: BVVL is an autosomal recessive riboflavin transporter deficiency caused by mutations in SLC52A3 (RFVT3) or SLC52A2 (RFVT2). Reduced riboflavin uptake impairs flavin-dependent mitochondrial enzymes, including fatty acid oxidation and the respiratory chain. Cochlear neurons, cranial nerve motor nuclei, anterior horn cells, sensory neurons and optic nerves are especially vulnerable. Fazio–Londe disease, its counterpart without deafness, belongs to the same spectrum.
det.clinical: Progressive sensorineural hearing loss usually comes first in childhood or adolescence, followed by bulbar palsy with dysarthria, dysphagia, facial weakness and tongue fasciculations. Neck and shoulder weakness, often with a 'dropped head', and respiratory failure from diaphragmatic weakness may follow. SLC52A2 cases more often have sensory ataxia, optic atrophy, nystagmus and prominent upper limb weakness. Infantile forms can be rapidly fatal.
det.diagnosis: Genetic testing for SLC52A2 and SLC52A3 confirms the diagnosis. Plasma acylcarnitine and urine organic acid profiles may show a MADD-like pattern, though they can be normal. EMG shows neurogenic changes in bulbar and limb muscles, NCS may show a sensory neuronopathy, and audiometry documents hearing loss. Consider in any young patient with deafness and motor neuron disease features.
det.treatment: Start high-dose oral riboflavin immediately when the diagnosis is suspected, without waiting for genetic results; it is inexpensive and safe. Supportive care includes respiratory support, gastrostomy, hearing aids or cochlear implants, and physiotherapy. Families should be offered genetic counselling.
det.prognosis: Early riboflavin can stabilise or improve motor, bulbar and respiratory function; hearing loss responds less consistently. Untreated disease often leads to respiratory failure.
pearls: Childhood deafness + bulbar palsy + neck weakness = give riboflavin now.
This is one of the few treatable causes of motor neuron disease in the young.
det.thd: Brown–Vialetto–Van Laere syndrome เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมแบบยีนด้อยจากความผิดปกติของตัวขนส่งไรโบฟลาวิน (วิตามินบี 2) ทำให้เซลล์ประสาทหลายกลุ่มเสื่อม อาการเริ่มด้วยหูหนวกในเด็กหรือวัยรุ่น ตามด้วยพูดและกลืนลำบาก ลิ้นลีบ คอและไหล่อ่อนแรง และอาจหายใจไม่ได้ การวินิจฉัยใช้การตรวจยีน SLC52A2/SLC52A3 ส่วนการรักษาคือให้ riboflavin ขนาดสูงทางปากทันทีที่สงสัย โดยไม่ต้องรอผลยีน เพราะช่วยหยุดหรือฟื้นอาการได้

name: Bucco-linguo-masticatory (BLM)
formal: Repetitive involuntary chewing, tongue and lip movements, most often tardive dyskinesia after dopamine-blocking drugs or edentulous orofacial dyskinesia in older people.
simple: Repeated uncontrolled chewing, lip smacking and tongue movements, often from long-term use of certain medicines.
th: การเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติซ้ำ ๆ ของปาก ลิ้น และขากรรไกร เช่น เคี้ยว ดุนลิ้น เม้มปาก มักเป็น tardive dyskinesia จากยาต้านโดปามีน หรือในผู้สูงอายุที่ไม่มีฟัน
tempoNote: Develops over months of drug exposure; may persist long after the drug is stopped
feat: Repetitive chewing, lip smacking, pouting and tongue protrusion or rolling
Suppressible briefly, decreases during speech or when eating, disappears in sleep
Usually follows months of antipsychotic or metoclopramide use
Elderly edentulous people may show similar movements without drug exposure
inv: Detailed drug history including antiemetics (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine)
AIMS scale to grade severity and follow response
Dental assessment; MRI/blood tests only if atypical (e.g. Huntington, Wilson, chorea-acanthocytosis)

case.story: Took metoclopramide daily for two years for 'gastritis'; now her family says she chews constantly even when not eating.
case.exam: Continuous chewing, lip pursing and tongue darting; mild finger chorea; good dentures.
case.tests: Glucose, thyroid and calcium normal; MRI unremarkable.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and the first management steps?
case.a: Tardive dyskinesia (BLM pattern) from metoclopramide; stop the drug and consider a VMAT2 inhibitor such as tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine or valbenazine.

det.patho: Long-term dopamine D2 receptor blockade is thought to cause receptor supersensitivity and maladaptive plasticity in the striatum, producing hyperkinetic orofacial movements. Risk rises with age, female sex, diabetes, duration of exposure and first-generation antipsychotics. In the elderly without teeth, loss of oral sensory input may drive similar movements.
det.clinical: BLM movements are stereotyped and rhythmic, with chewing, tongue protrusion and lip puckering. They can interfere with eating, speech and denture fit, and may cause tongue ulcers. Trunk, limb or respiratory dyskinesia may coexist. Stopping the drug can briefly worsen movements (withdrawal emergence).
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, based on exposure to a dopamine-blocking drug for at least a few months and the typical movement pattern. Exclude other causes of chorea or orofacial movements when exposure is absent or other neurological signs are present.
det.treatment: Remove or reduce the offending drug where psychiatrically safe, or switch to clozapine or quetiapine. VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine, tetrabenazine) are first-line pharmacological therapy; clonazepam and ginkgo biloba have weak evidence. Botulinum toxin helps focal oromandibular components. Avoid anticholinergics, which can worsen TD.
det.prognosis: Often persistent, though improvement occurs in a proportion after the drug is withdrawn, especially in younger patients.
pearls: Ask about metoclopramide; it is a common hidden cause in the elderly.
Anticholinergics help acute dystonia but not tardive dyskinesia.
Check dentures before diagnosing drug-induced BLM in an older person.
det.thd: Bucco-linguo-masticatory คือการเคี้ยว ดุนลิ้น และเม้มปากซ้ำ ๆ โดยไม่ตั้งใจ ส่วนใหญ่เป็น tardive dyskinesia จากยาต้านโรคจิตหรือ metoclopramide ที่ใช้นาน ผู้สูงอายุที่ไม่มีฟันอาจมีอาการคล้ายกันได้ รักษาโดยหยุดหรือเปลี่ยนยา และใช้ยา VMAT2 inhibitor เช่น tetrabenazine หลีกเลี่ยงยา anticholinergic

ddx.pt: Elderly without well-fitting dentures; no drug history; often improves with dental care
Blepharospasm with jaw-opening or jaw-closing dystonia, more sustained and patterned
Generalised chorea, motor impersistence and cognitive decline, with family history

aN: blm | bucco linguo masticatory | blm syndrome | orofacial dyskinesia | oro bucco lingual dyskinesia | tardive orofacial dyskinesia | blm dyskinesia

name: Bulbar palsy
formal: Lower motor neuron weakness of cranial nerves IX to XII muscles causing dysarthria, dysphagia, tongue wasting and fasciculation, seen in ALS, brainstem lesions and myasthenia.
simple: Weakness of the muscles of the tongue, throat and mouth, causing slurred speech and trouble swallowing.
th: กลุ่มอาการอ่อนแรงแบบ lower motor neuron ของกล้ามเนื้อที่เลี้ยงด้วยเส้นประสาทสมองคู่ 9–12 ทำให้พูดเสียงขึ้นจมูก กลืนลำบาก ลิ้นลีบและเต้นระริก gag reflex ลดลง ต่างจาก pseudobulbar และ opercular syndrome ที่ reflex ยังอยู่หรือไวขึ้น
tempoNote: Acute in medullary stroke, Guillain–Barré syndrome or botulism; subacute to chronic in motor neuron disease, myasthenia and compressive lesions
feat: A syndrome, not a single disease: lower motor neuron weakness of palate, pharynx, larynx and tongue
Nasal speech, nasal regurgitation, weak cough and aspiration risk
Wasted, fasciculating tongue; reduced or absent gag and jaw jerk, and voluntary and reflex movements fail together
Contrast with pseudobulbar and opercular syndromes, where the tongue is stiff or normal, the jaw jerk and gag are preserved, and automatic movements such as yawning or laughing remain
Causes: ALS or progressive bulbar palsy, Kennedy disease, medullary stroke, syringobulbia, GBS and its pharyngeal-cervical-brachial variant, botulism, skull-base tumours, myasthenia
inv: MRI brain stem and skull base, with CT or MR angiography if a vascular cause is suspected
EMG for widespread denervation (motor neuron disease) and repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fibre studies; AChR, MuSK and LRP4 antibodies
CSF and nerve conduction studies if GBS variants are suspected; toxin tests if botulism is plausible
Swallow assessment (videofluoroscopy or FEES); androgen receptor CAG repeat testing in men with gynaecomastia

case.story: Over six months her speech became nasal and slurred, fluids come out through her nose, and she has lost 6 kg.
case.exam: Wasted tongue with fasciculations, poor palatal movement, absent gag, normal jaw jerk, brisk limb reflexes and fasciculations in the shoulders; she cannot yawn widely or cough effectively.
case.tests: MRI brain stem normal; EMG shows active and chronic denervation in tongue, cervical and lumbar segments; AChR antibodies negative.
case.q: What does lost reflex movement together with brisk limb reflexes tell you?
case.a: Lower motor neuron bulbar failure combined with pyramidal signs in the limbs indicates bulbar-onset amyotrophic lateral sclerosis; plan early gastrostomy discussion, riluzole, noninvasive ventilation assessment, speech therapy and communication aids.

det.patho: Bulbar palsy results from damage to the lower cranial motor nuclei in the medulla (nucleus ambiguus, hypoglossal nucleus), their axons, the neuromuscular junction or the muscles themselves. The common substrate is loss of lower motor neuron drive to oropharyngeal and laryngeal muscles, so both voluntary and reflex actions of those muscles fail. This contrasts with supranuclear lesions, where the final common pathway stays intact and reflexes persist or are exaggerated. Causes range from degeneration to vascular, inflammatory, toxic, infiltrative and compressive lesions.
det.clinical: Speech becomes nasal and indistinct, swallowing is difficult with coughing on liquids, and the cough is weak. The tongue is wasted with fasciculation and the gag reflex reduced or absent. Aspiration pneumonia and weight loss are key risks. Accompanying signs such as limb fasciculation, sensory loss, ophthalmoplegia or fatigability point towards the cause.
det.diagnosis: Distinguish LMN bulbar palsy from UMN pseudobulbar palsy at the bedside by examining tongue bulk and fasciculation, gag, jaw jerk and whether reflex movements survive. MRI of the brain stem and skull base excludes structural disease, and EMG, repetitive stimulation and antibody tests separate motor neuron disease, myasthenia and myopathy. A rapid course with areflexia suggests GBS variants or botulism. Do not label a patient with isolated, abrupt voluntary loss and preserved reflexes as bulbar palsy until opercular syndromes are considered.
det.treatment: Treat the cause where possible, such as immunotherapy for myasthenia or GBS and surgery for compressive lesions. In bulbar-onset ALS, riluzole is standard, edaravone is available in some systems, and tofersen is used in SOD1-related disease. Supportive care includes speech and swallow therapy, diet modification, early discussion of gastrostomy, saliva management, communication aids and respiratory monitoring with noninvasive ventilation when indicated.
det.prognosis: Variable with cause: progressive in motor neuron disease, often reversible in myasthenia and GBS.
pearls: Wasted, fasciculating tongue with absent gag points to LMN bulbar palsy.
If voluntary movement is lost but yawning, smiling and gag remain, think supranuclear or opercular syndrome, not bulbar palsy.
Bulbar signs with brisk limb reflexes: bulbar-onset ALS until proven otherwise.
det.thd: Bulbar palsy คือการอ่อนแรงแบบ LMN ของกล้ามเนื้อที่เลี้ยงด้วยเส้นประสาทสมองคู่ 9–12 ทำให้พูดเสียงขึ้นจมูก กลืนลำบาก ลิ้นลีบและเต้นระริก gag reflex ลดลงหรือหายไป ทั้งการเคลื่อนไหวตามสั่งและแบบอัตโนมัติเสียไปด้วยกัน ต่างจาก pseudobulbar และ opercular syndrome ที่ reflex ยังอยู่ ต้องแยกสาเหตุ เช่น ALS, myasthenia, GBS และรอยโรคก้านสมอง รักษาตามสาเหตุและดูแลการกลืน การหายใจ และการสื่อสาร

Fatigable bulbar weakness without wasting or fasciculation, often with ptosis; antibodies and decrement on repetitive stimulation
Men with perioral fasciculation, gynaecomastia and sensory neuropathy; androgen receptor CAG expansion

aN: lower motor neuron bulbar palsy | lmn bulbar weakness | bulbar syndrome | progressive bulbar weakness

name: Burning mouth syndrome
formal: Chronic idiopathic intraoral burning pain with normal mucosa, usually in peri/postmenopausal women; thought to reflect small-fibre or central pain mechanisms; exclude secondary causes first.
simple: A long-lasting burning feeling in the mouth or tongue even though the mouth looks normal.
th: อาการปวดแสบร้อนในช่องปากเรื้อรังโดยเยื่อบุปกติ มักพบในหญิงวัยหมดประจำเดือน เชื่อว่าเกี่ยวกับ small fibre หรือกลไกปวดส่วนกลาง
tempoNote: Persists for months to years; at least 2 hours daily for over 3 months by ICHD-3 criteria
feat: Burning of tongue tip and sides, lips or palate
Often worsens through the day; eating may relieve it
Dry mouth sensation and altered taste
Normal oral examination
Associated with anxiety, depression and sleep disturbance
inv: Exclude secondary causes: candida, diabetes, B12, iron, folate, zinc, thyroid, xerostomia, drugs (ACE inhibitors), denture problems
Oral examination and sometimes swabs
Taste tests or biopsy only in research or selected cases

case.story: Eight months of burning tongue starting mid-morning and worsening by evening; eating eases it.
case.exam: Normal oral mucosa and tongue; no candidiasis.
case.tests: Normal blood count, B12, iron, glucose and thyroid.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and first-line therapy?
case.a: Primary burning mouth syndrome; topical clonazepam (dissolve and spit) and cognitive behavioural therapy.

read.where: Chapter 31 Pain in Neurological Disorders — Conditions of Uncertain Aetiology that may Present to Neurology
Chapter 31 Pain in Neurological Disorders — Burning Mouth Syndrome

det.patho: Evidence points to small fibre neuropathy of oral mucosa, changes in trigeminal processing and reduced central dopaminergic inhibition. Hormonal changes after menopause may contribute.
det.clinical: Continuous burning pain with normal oral examination, often with dysgeusia and dry mouth. Pain tends to worsen during the day. Psychological comorbidity is common.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out local and systemic causes.
det.treatment: Topical clonazepam, alpha-lipoic acid, capsaicin rinses, CBT; systemic clonazepam, gabapentinoids or tricyclics for refractory cases. Reassurance is important.
det.prognosis: Chronic; spontaneous remission occurs in a minority.
pearls: Normal mouth plus chronic burning = burning mouth syndrome after excluding causes.
Topical clonazepam is effective.
Check for dentures, candida and nutritional deficiency first.
det.thd: Burning mouth syndrome คืออาการปวดแสบร้อนในปากเรื้อรังโดยตรวจช่องปากปกติ มักพบในหญิงวัยหมดประจำเดือน อาการมักแย่ลงตอนบ่ายและเย็น เชื่อว่าเกิดจาก small fibre neuropathy และกลไกปวดส่วนกลาง ต้องแยกสาเหตุอื่น เช่น เชื้อรา ขาดวิตามิน เบาหวาน และยา รักษาด้วย clonazepam ชนิดอมแล้วบ้วนทิ้งและ CBT

ddx.pt: Brief electric paroxysms rather than continuous burning
True xerostomia with dry eyes and positive antibodies
Glossitis with red, smooth tongue

aN: bms | glossodynia | stomatodynia | oral dysesthesia

name: C5 radiculopathy
formal: Compression of the C5 nerve root, usually at C4-5, causing neck and shoulder pain with weakness of deltoid and biceps, reduced biceps reflex, and lateral shoulder sensory loss.
simple: A pinched nerve in the neck causing pain and weakness lifting the arm to the side.
more: MRI and EMG confirm it. Most improve with conservative care; surgery is used for severe or persistent deficits.
th: รากประสาท C5 ถูกกด มักที่ระดับ C4-5 ทำให้ปวดคอและไหล่ ไหล่และต้นแขนอ่อนแรง และ biceps reflex ลดลง
tempoNote: Pain often abrupt; weakness may follow; post-operative C5 palsy appears days after decompression
feat: Neck pain radiating to the shoulder and lateral upper arm
Weakness of deltoid, supraspinatus/infraspinatus and biceps
Reduced biceps and brachioradialis reflexes
Numbness over the lateral upper arm (regimental badge area)
Pain worsened by neck extension and rotation to the affected side (Spurling)
inv: MRI cervical spine (foraminal stenosis, disc at C4-5)
EMG: denervation in deltoid, spinati, biceps and C5 paraspinals; normal sensory potentials
Shoulder imaging if pain is mainly with arm movement

case.story: Two weeks of right neck and shoulder pain, now cannot lift his arm to comb his hair.
case.exam: Deltoid and supraspinatus 3/5, biceps 4/5, reduced biceps jerk, numb lateral upper arm, Spurling positive.
case.tests: MRI shows right C4-5 foraminal stenosis from uncovertebral osteophyte; EMG confirms C5 root denervation.
case.q: How can you tell this from a rotator cuff tear?
case.a: Reflex loss, sensory change and EMG denervation in several C5 muscles indicate radiculopathy; cuff tears cause painful weakness without neurological signs.

read.where: Chapter 14 Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders — Cervical Spine

det.patho: The C5 root exits above the C5 vertebra at the C4-5 level and is compressed by foraminal stenosis, uncovertebral osteophytes or disc herniation. A short root and tethering may explain its vulnerability after decompressive surgery (post-operative C5 palsy). Inflammation contributes to pain.
det.clinical: Patients have neck and shoulder pain and weakness of shoulder abduction and elbow flexion. Sensory change over the lateral arm is often subtle. Biceps reflex reduction is a key sign. Shoulder disease is the main mimic because both cause pain on arm movement.
det.diagnosis: Clinical localisation plus MRI showing concordant compression. EMG helps if MRI findings are multilevel or uncertain. Because the lesion sits before the dorsal root ganglion, sensory nerve action potentials remain normal. Consider neuralgic amyotrophy when weakness follows severe pain without compression.
det.treatment: Most improve with analgesia, short-term NSAIDs, physiotherapy and activity modification. Selective nerve root injections can ease pain. Surgery (foraminotomy, ACDF or disc replacement) is considered for persistent pain or progressive or significant weakness. Post-operative C5 palsy usually recovers over months.
det.prognosis: Good in most cases; severe weakness may recover incompletely.
pearls: Biceps reflex reduced plus deltoid weakness: C5.
SNAPs are preserved in radiculopathy.
Shoulder pain without reflex or sensory change suggests local shoulder pathology.
det.thd: C5 radiculopathy คือรากประสาท C5 ถูกกดที่ระดับ C4-5 ทำให้ปวดคอร้าวไหล่ ยกแขนลำบากจากกล้ามเนื้อ deltoid และ spinati อ่อนแรง biceps reflex ลดลง และชาต้นแขนด้านนอก วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจร่างกาย MRI และ EMG ต้องแยกโรคข้อไหล่และ neuralgic amyotrophy ส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นด้วยการรักษาแบบอนุรักษ์ ผ่าตัดเมื่ออ่อนแรงมากหรือปวดไม่หาย

ddx.pt: Severe pain then patchy weakness (often long thoracic, suprascapular), not dermatomal
Weakness spans several roots; sensory potentials reduced
Painless, spreading weakness with fasciculations and UMN signs

aN: c5 root lesion | c4 5 radiculopathy | c5 nerve root compression | c5 palsy

name: C6 radiculopathy
formal: Compression of the C6 root, commonly from C5-6 disc or spondylosis, causing weakness of biceps, brachioradialis, and wrist extensors, reduced biceps reflex, and thumb and index paraesthesia.
simple: A pinched nerve in the neck causing pain down the arm into the thumb, with weak elbow bending and wrist lifting.
more: Diagnosed by exam, MRI, and EMG. Usually settles with physiotherapy and analgesia; surgery for refractory pain or progressive weakness.
th: รากประสาท C6 ถูกกด มักจากหมอนรองกระดูกหรือกระดูกงอกที่ C5-6 ทำให้ปวดร้าวถึงนิ้วโป้ง biceps และ wrist extensor อ่อนแรง
tempoNote: Acute disc herniation presents over days; spondylosis produces a slower course
feat: Neck pain radiating along the lateral arm and forearm into the thumb and index finger
Weakness of elbow flexion (biceps, brachioradialis) and wrist extension (extensor carpi radialis), with pronator teres and sometimes spinati involved
Reduced biceps and brachioradialis reflexes
Paraesthesia or numbness of thumb and index finger
Spurling manoeuvre, shoulder abduction relief sign and neck extension reproduce or relieve radicular pain
inv: MRI cervical spine (disc, foraminal narrowing, cord status)

NCS/EMG: sensory potentials (thumb, lateral antebrachial cutaneous) are normal because the lesion lies proximal to the dorsal root ganglion; needle EMG of C6 muscles and paraspinals shows denervation after 2–3 weeks
Plain films with flexion-extension if instability is suspected

case.story: Two weeks of neck pain shooting down to the thumb, worse with looking up; her right elbow feels weak lifting patients' charts and the thumb is numb.
case.exam: Reduced right biceps and brachioradialis reflexes, mild weakness of elbow flexion and wrist extension, reduced pinprick on thumb and index finger, positive Spurling test.
case.tests: MRI shows a right paracentral C5-6 disc protrusion compressing the C6 root; NCS shows normal median and radial sensory responses.
case.q: Which nerve-conduction finding separates this from carpal tunnel syndrome?
case.a: Normal thumb SNAP (preganglionic lesion) plus weakness of proximal C6 muscles; in carpal tunnel the median sensory response is abnormal.

det.patho: The C6 root leaves the spine at the C5-6 level, where disc herniation and uncovertebral or facet osteophytes narrow the foramen. Nerve root compression and local inflammation cause pain, sensory change and sometimes axonal loss. C6 is, with C7, the commonest cervical root affected, since the mobile mid-cervical segments take the most strain.
det.clinical: Patients report unilateral neck and arm pain in the C6 dermatome, often worse with extension and rotation toward the symptomatic side. Examination finds weak biceps, brachioradialis and wrist extensors, reduced biceps and brachioradialis reflexes and sensory loss over the thumb and index finger. An inverted supinator reflex suggests concurrent cord compression. Weakness is usually mild, and most cases improve.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis rests on history and focused examination, confirmed by MRI that matches the clinical level. NCS/EMG is used when the picture is unclear or to distinguish from carpal tunnel syndrome, brachial plexopathy or neuralgic amyotrophy; normal sensory potentials with denervation in C6 muscles and paraspinals supports radiculopathy. C6 and C7 are the levels most difficult to separate electrodiagnostically, so sample several muscles. EMG may be normal in the first two weeks, so repeat if suspicion remains.
det.treatment: Most patients improve with conservative care: relative rest, NSAIDs, neuropathic pain agents, physiotherapy, short courses of oral steroid or image-guided epidural injection in selected patients. Surgery (anterior discectomy and fusion or arthroplasty, or foraminotomy) is considered for progressive or severe weakness, myelopathy, or pain that fails around 6–12 weeks of treatment. Look for red flags such as infection, tumour and myelopathy.
det.prognosis: Favourable; most improve within months without surgery.
pearls: Thumb and index numbness plus reduced biceps reflex: C6.
Inverted supinator reflex hints at C5-6 cord compression.
Carpal tunnel and C6 radiculopathy can coexist (double crush).
det.thd: C6 radiculopathy คือรากประสาท C6 ถูกกดทับ มักจากหมอนรองกระดูก C5-6 หรือกระดูกงอก ทำให้ปวดคอร้าวลงแขนด้านนอกถึงนิ้วโป้งและนิ้วชี้ กล้ามเนื้อ biceps และข้อมือเหยียดอ่อนแรง รีเฟล็กซ์ biceps และ brachioradialis ลดลง ตรวจ MRI คอ และตรวจ NCS/EMG เพื่อแยกจาก carpal tunnel โดยรากประสาทที่ถูกกดมักมี sensory potential ปกติ ส่วนใหญ่หายได้ด้วยการรักษาแบบไม่ผ่าตัด ถ้าอ่อนแรงมากหรือมีไขสันหลังถูกกดจึงพิจารณาผ่าตัด

ddx.pt: Night-time hand paraesthesia, thenar weakness only, abnormal median SNAP, no neck pain or biceps reflex change
Middle-finger numbness, triceps weakness and reduced triceps reflex rather than biceps
Severe shoulder pain followed by patchy weakness of upper trunk muscles with a plexus pattern

aN: c6 root lesion | c5 6 radiculopathy | c6 nerve root compression

name: C7 radiculopathy
formal: Most common cervical radiculopathy from C6-7 disease, with triceps, wrist flexor, and finger extensor weakness, reduced triceps reflex, and middle finger paraesthesia.
simple: A pinched nerve in the neck causing pain and weakness when straightening the arm, with tingling in the middle finger.
more: MRI and EMG confirm it. Conservative treatment helps most; surgery if severe weakness or myelopathy occurs.
th: รากประสาทคอที่พบถูกกดบ่อยที่สุด จากระดับ C6-7 ทำให้ triceps กล้ามเนื้องอข้อมือและเหยียดนิ้วอ่อนแรง triceps reflex ลด และชานิ้วกลาง
tempoNote: Pain onset abrupt or over days; most settle within 3 months
feat: Neck and scapular pain radiating down the back of the arm to the middle finger
Weakness of triceps, wrist flexors and finger extensors
Reduced triceps reflex
Numbness of the middle finger
Shoulder abduction relief sign may ease pain
inv: MRI cervical spine (C6-7 disc or foraminal stenosis)
EMG to distinguish from radial neuropathy and plexopathy

case.who: 39-year-old male tuk-tuk driver from Chiang Mai
case.story: Pain from the neck down the back of the left arm to the middle finger for 3 weeks; weak when pushing himself up from bed.
case.exam: Left triceps 4-/5, finger extensors 4/5, absent left triceps jerk, numb middle finger, pain eased by resting the hand on his head.
case.tests: MRI shows left C6-7 foraminal disc herniation.
case.q: Which root is affected and how does it differ from radial nerve palsy?
case.a: C7; radial palsy spares wrist flexors and the triceps reflex is usually preserved unless the lesion is very proximal.

read.where: Chapter 14 Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders — Cervical Spine

det.patho: The C7 root exits at C6-7 and is the commonest cervical root affected by disc herniation and spondylosis. Compression and inflammation cause pain; prolonged compression leads to axonal loss in C7-supplied muscles. Sensory potentials stay normal because the ganglion lies distal to the lesion.
det.clinical: Pain spreads from the neck and medial scapula down the posterior arm and forearm to the middle finger. Weakness of elbow extension, wrist flexion and finger extension is typical. The triceps reflex is reduced or lost. Sleep disturbance from pain is common.
det.diagnosis: Clinical pattern with MRI confirmation. EMG localises when MRI is multilevel or neuropathy is suspected. Remember anatomical variation can blur root territories. Red flags warrant urgent imaging.
det.treatment: Conservative care with analgesics, NSAIDs, physiotherapy and education first; most settle by 6–12 weeks. Image-guided steroid injection for persistent pain. Surgery for progressive or disabling weakness or intractable pain.
det.prognosis: Favourable in most patients; recurrence is possible.
pearls: C7 is the most frequently affected cervical root.
Triceps reflex loss with middle finger numbness localises well.
Wrist flexor weakness separates C7 from radial nerve lesions.
det.thd: C7 radiculopathy เป็นรากประสาทคอที่ถูกกดบ่อยที่สุด จากระดับ C6-7 ทำให้ปวดคอร้าวลงหลังแขนถึงนิ้วกลาง triceps กล้ามเนื้องอข้อมือและเหยียดนิ้วอ่อนแรง triceps reflex ลดลง วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจร่างกายและ MRI EMG ช่วยแยก radial nerve palsy ส่วนใหญ่หายด้วยการรักษาแบบอนุรักษ์ภายใน 3 เดือน

ddx.pt: Wrist drop with sparing of wrist flexors; sensory loss on dorsum of hand
Biceps weakness and thumb sensory changes
Intrinsic hand weakness and medial forearm or little finger numbness

aN: c7 root lesion | c6 7 radiculopathy | c7 nerve root compression

name: C8/T1 radiculopathy
formal: Lower cervical root compression causing weakness and wasting of finger flexors and hand intrinsics with medial forearm and hand sensory loss, requiring differentiation from ulnar neuropathy and thoracic outlet.
simple: A pinched nerve low in the neck causing a weak, numb hand and small hand muscle wasting along the little finger side.
more: EMG shows involvement outside ulnar-innervated muscles; MRI looks for disc, tumour, or Pancoast lesion. Treatment depends on the cause.
th: รากประสาท C8/T1 ถูกกดทับ ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อมือและนิ้วอ่อนแรง ชาด้านในของแขนและมือ
tempoNote: Disc-related cases come on over days; tumour or spondylotic causes creep up over months
feat: Neck or shoulder-blade pain radiating down the inner arm to the little and ring fingers
Weak finger flexion, finger spreading and thumb abduction; grip clumsy
Numbness of the medial forearm and medial hand, unlike ulnar lesions which spare the forearm
Triceps and finger-flexor jerks may be reduced; Horner syndrome points to T1 or apical lung disease
Uncommon compared with C6 and C7 lesions, so look hard for a non-disc cause
inv: MRI cervical spine with views through C7–T1 foramina
Chest X-ray or CT of the lung apex when T1 signs, Horner or smoking history are present
EMG: denervation in median- and ulnar-supplied hand muscles plus paraspinals; sensory nerve action potentials preserved

case.who: 58-year-old male rubber-tapper from Rayong, smoker for 40 years
case.story: Three months of aching in the left scapula and inner arm, then trouble buttoning shirts and gripping a knife.
case.exam: Wasting of first dorsal interosseous and thenar muscles, weak finger flexors, numb medial forearm, small left pupil with mild ptosis.
case.tests: EMG shows chronic denervation in C8/T1 muscles with normal ulnar sensory responses; CT chest shows a left apical mass.
case.q: Why should a disc not be assumed here, and what is the lesion?
case.a: Horner plus progressive lower-root signs in a smoker suggests an apical lung tumour invading C8/T1 roots and the lower trunk.

det.patho: The C8 root leaves between C7 and T1 vertebrae and the T1 root below T1, and the two merge into the plexus lower trunk. Disc herniation at C7–T1 is unusual because that segment moves little, so spondylotic foraminal narrowing, tumours of the lung apex, schwannomas and metastases make up a larger share. T1 also carries sympathetic fibres for the eye, explaining Horner syndrome.
det.clinical: Patients describe pain along the inner arm with weakness that mainly affects the hand, so they report dropping things or poor dexterity rather than shoulder weakness. Sensory change covers the medial forearm and ulnar side of the hand. Wasting of intrinsic hand muscles may be the most visible sign. Progressive pain at night, weight loss or Horner syndrome are red flags for malignant infiltration.
det.diagnosis: Clinical localisation distinguishes root from ulnar nerve or plexus: forearm sensory loss and involvement of median-innervated thenar muscles argue against an ulnar lesion. EMG shows denervation across multiple nerves sharing C8/T1 with preserved sensory potentials, since the damage sits before the sensory ganglion. MRI of the cervical spine, and chest imaging of the apex when indicated, identify the structural cause.
det.treatment: Disc or spondylotic lesions usually settle with analgesia, short activity modification and physiotherapy; neuropathic agents help radicular pain. Decompression is offered for progressive weakness or intractable pain. Tumour-related cases need oncological management including radiotherapy and pain control. Hand therapy preserves function while waiting for recovery.
det.prognosis: Compressive degenerative cases usually improve over weeks to months; recovery of intrinsic hand wasting is slow and may be incomplete.
pearls: Medial forearm numbness separates C8/T1 or lower trunk from an ulnar nerve lesion.
Horner syndrome with lower-root weakness is an apical lung tumour until proven otherwise.
Normal sensory nerve action potentials in a numb hand suggest a pre-ganglionic (root) lesion.
det.thd: รากประสาท C8/T1 ควบคุมกล้ามเนื้อมือและรับความรู้สึกด้านในของแขน เมื่อถูกกดจะมีปวดร้าวลงแขนด้านใน มืออ่อนแรงและลีบ ต่างจาก ulnar neuropathy ตรงที่ชาถึงแขนท่อนล่างด้านในและกล้ามเนื้อ thenar อ่อนแรงด้วย ถ้ามี Horner syndrome ต้องนึกถึงเนื้องอกปอดส่วนยอด ตรวจด้วย MRI คอ EMG และภาพถ่ายทรวงอก รักษาตามสาเหตุ

qx.stem: A 52-year-old man from Phitsanulok has weakness of thumb abduction and finger abduction with numbness along the medial forearm and little finger that began after neck extension during a fall. The median and ulnar CMAPs are low, but both ulnar and median SNAPs and the medial antebrachial cutaneous response are normal on testing.
qx.q: What does the pattern of low CMAPs with normal SNAPs indicate about lesion location?
opts: A lesion of the dorsal root ganglia
A distal axonal polyneuropathy
A lesion in the mid-forearm affecting only motor fibres
A lesion lying central to the dorsal root ganglion, for example in a root
A brachial plexus lesion of the lower trunk distal to the ganglion
qx.why: The sensory cell body lies in the dorsal root ganglion outside the spinal canal, so a lesion proximal to it (a root or cord lesion) damages the motor axon and spares the sensory nerve, leaving SNAPs normal despite sensory symptoms. A plexus or postganglionic lesion causes wallerian degeneration of the sensory axons and reduces SNAPs. Polyneuropathy would affect SNAPs as well.

ddx.pt: Spares the medial forearm and thenar muscles; abnormal ulnar sensory potential
Lower-trunk plexus lesion with abnormal medial antebrachial cutaneous sensory response

name: Caffeine-related headache
formal: Headache triggered by caffeine intake or by withdrawal after regular use, typically diffuse and pressing or migrainous, resolving after stable intake or abstinence.
simple: A headache caused by too much caffeine or by suddenly stopping usual caffeine.
th: ปวดศีรษะที่สัมพันธ์กับคาเฟอีน ทั้งจากดื่มมากเกินและที่พบบ่อยกว่าคือจากการหยุดดื่มกะทันหันหลังดื่มเป็นประจำ หายได้ภายในไม่กี่วัน
tempoNote: Withdrawal headache appears within a day of the final intake and settles within about a week of abstinence
feat: Usually withdrawal: regular intake (often over 200 mg/day for 2 weeks or more) then abrupt stop
Diffuse, pressing or throbbing pain, with tiredness, poor concentration and low mood
Typical scenarios: weekends, fasting before surgery, Ramadan, hospital admission
Relieved within an hour by 100 mg caffeine; resolves within 7 days of abstinence
Heavy intake also contributes to medication overuse headache and poor sleep
inv: Detailed intake diary: coffee, tea, energy drinks, combination analgesics containing caffeine
No tests needed if the pattern is typical and examination normal
Look for red flags that would point to a secondary headache

case.story: Drinks four strong iced coffees on workdays; every Saturday morning she wakes with a heavy, throbbing headache and feels sluggish.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination and blood pressure.
case.tests: None required.
case.q: What is the likely explanation and plan?
case.a: Caffeine withdrawal headache; keep intake consistent and taper total caffeine gradually by about 25% per week.

det.patho: Caffeine is an adenosine receptor antagonist; chronic use upregulates adenosine receptors. When intake stops, unopposed adenosine causes cerebral vasodilatation and altered nociceptive signalling, producing headache and fatigue. High intake can also aggravate migraine and disturb sleep.
det.clinical: Withdrawal headache appears 12–24 hours after the last dose, peaks at 1–2 days and lasts up to a week. It may be accompanied by drowsiness, irritability and flu-like feelings. Postoperative or fasting headache is often caffeine withdrawal. Overuse of caffeine-containing analgesics contributes to chronic daily headache.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 recognises caffeine-withdrawal headache when regular use is followed by interruption and the pain resolves after resuming or stopping completely. Diagnosis is clinical, provided the examination is normal and there are no red flags.
det.treatment: Acute relief comes from a small dose of caffeine or simple analgesics. Long-term, either keep a stable modest intake or taper gradually. Before elective surgery or prolonged fasting, a planned taper or a morning caffeine dose can prevent headache.
det.prognosis: Benign and self-limiting.
pearls: Weekend or post-operative headache — ask about coffee.
Combination analgesics with caffeine drive both overuse and withdrawal.
Taper caffeine slowly to avoid rebound.
det.thd: Caffeine-related headache มักเป็นปวดศีรษะจากการขาดคาเฟอีนหลังดื่มกาแฟหรือชาเป็นประจำแล้วหยุดกะทันหัน เช่น วันหยุดหรือก่อนผ่าตัด เกิดจาก adenosine receptor ที่เพิ่มขึ้นจากการได้คาเฟอีนนาน ปวดตื้อทั้งศีรษะร่วมกับง่วงและเพลีย หายภายในหนึ่งสัปดาห์ การป้องกันคือดื่มสม่ำเสมอหรือค่อย ๆ ลดปริมาณ

ddx.pt: Daily headache from frequent analgesic or triptan use, often including caffeine combinations
Featureless pressing headache without a clear caffeine timing pattern
Older adult woken at a fixed time every night, not tied to weekend abstinence

aN: caffeine withdrawal headache | caffeine induced headache | weekend headache | coffee withdrawal headache

name: Caisson disease
formal: Decompression sickness from nitrogen bubbles after rapid pressure drop; spinal cord (thoracolumbar) and inner ear are commonly involved, with pain, weakness and vertigo.
simple: Illness in divers or compressed-air workers when gas bubbles form in the body after surfacing too fast, which can affect nerves and the spinal cord.
th: โรคจากการลดความดันเร็วเกินไป เช่น นักดำน้ำ ทำให้ฟองไนโตรเจนอุดตันและทำลายไขสันหลัง หูชั้นใน และสมอง
tempoNote: Symptoms begin within minutes to a few hours of surfacing; spinal forms can worsen over hours
feat: Recent scuba dive, caisson or tunnel work, or flying soon after diving
Joint pain ('bends'), skin marbling, fatigue
Spinal cord DCS: back or girdle pain, then leg weakness, sensory level and urinary retention (thoracic cord typical)
Inner-ear DCS: vertigo, vomiting, hearing loss and tinnitus, linked to right-to-left shunt
Cerebral involvement or arterial gas embolism: confusion, hemiparesis, seizures soon after surfacing
inv: Clinical diagnosis; do not delay recompression for imaging
MRI spine and brain after stabilisation (often normal early)
Later: bubble-contrast echocardiography for patent foramen ovale in inner-ear or cerebral cases

case.who: 34-year-old dive instructor working in Koh Tao
case.story: After a deep third dive with a rapid ascent he developed band-like abdominal pain and leg tingling within 30 minutes, then could not pass urine.
case.exam: Paraparesis MRC 3/5, sensory level at T10, brisk knee jerks, palpable bladder.
case.tests: Initial MRI thoracic spine unremarkable; oxygen saturation normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the definitive treatment?
case.a: Spinal cord decompression sickness; give 100% oxygen and transfer urgently for hyperbaric recompression.

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Decompression Sickness
Chapter 128: Toxins and Environmental Neurologic Injury

det.patho: Inert gas dissolved in tissues under pressure comes out of solution as bubbles if pressure drops too quickly. Bubbles block venous drainage of the spinal cord, injure tissue directly and trigger inflammation and coagulation; arterial bubbles crossing a patent foramen ovale can embolise to brain or inner ear. Deep, repetitive or prolonged dives, rapid ascent, dehydration and flying afterwards increase risk.
det.clinical: Mild forms produce joint pain, itching and fatigue. Neurological DCS most often affects the thoracic cord with girdle pain, paraesthesia, weakness and sphincter disturbance. Inner-ear DCS causes vertigo and hearing loss and must be separated from inner-ear barotrauma, which needs different care. Cerebral arterial gas embolism appears within minutes of surfacing with stroke-like deficits or loss of consciousness.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical and based on symptoms after a pressure reduction. Imaging can be normal and must not delay transfer for recompression. After treatment, MRI documents cord or brain injury, and divers with inner-ear or cerebral events should be screened for right-to-left shunts. Dive computer data help estimate the exposure.
det.treatment: Give 100% oxygen, lie the patient flat, rehydrate and arrange urgent hyperbaric oxygen therapy using a standard treatment table, repeated if deficits persist. Avoid air transport at altitude where possible. Rehabilitation follows for residual deficits. Return to diving needs specialist assessment and sometimes PFO closure.
det.prognosis: Most recover fully with early recompression; delayed treatment and severe spinal involvement leave lasting deficits.
pearls: Back pain and leg tingling after a dive is cord DCS until proven otherwise.
Oxygen and recompression first; imaging later.
Inner-ear DCS strongly associates with a patent foramen ovale.
det.thd: Caisson disease หรือ decompression sickness เกิดจากการลดความดันเร็วเกินไปจนก๊าซไนโตรเจนกลายเป็นฟอง พบในนักดำน้ำ ทำลายไขสันหลังส่วนอกบ่อยที่สุด ทำให้ปวดหลังรอบเอว ขาอ่อนแรง และปัสสาวะไม่ออก บางรายมีเวียนศีรษะและหูดับจากหูชั้นใน การวินิจฉัยอาศัยประวัติดำน้ำ การรักษาคือให้ออกซิเจน 100% และส่งทำ hyperbaric oxygen โดยเร็ว

name: Calcium channelopathies
formal: Disorders of voltage-gated calcium channels such as CACNA1S hypokalaemic periodic paralysis, CACNA1A episodic ataxia type 2 and migraine, and malignant hyperthermia susceptibility.
simple: Inherited conditions where faulty calcium channels cause episodes of muscle weakness, unsteadiness, or other attacks.
more: Genetic testing identifies the variant. Acetazolamide helps periodic paralysis and episodic ataxia; avoid triggers and triggering anaesthetics when relevant.
th: กลุ่มโรคที่เกิดจากช่องแคลเซียมผิดปกติ เช่น hypokalaemic periodic paralysis (CACNA1S) episodic ataxia type 2 และ hemiplegic migraine (CACNA1A) และ malignant hyperthermia
tempoNote: Most present as attacks lasting minutes to days; some develop fixed deficits over years
feat: CACNA1S: hypokalaemic periodic paralysis, malignant hyperthermia susceptibility
CACNA1A: episodic ataxia type 2, familial hemiplegic migraine type 1, SCA6
Attacks triggered by exertion, stress, carbohydrate load or anaesthesia
Interictal signs may include nystagmus, slowly progressive ataxia or proximal myopathy
Autoimmune counterpart: antibodies to P/Q-type channels cause Lambert–Eaton syndrome
inv: Potassium during attacks; CK; ECG
MRI brain for cerebellar atrophy in CACNA1A disease
Genetic testing (CACNA1A, CACNA1S, RYR1 panels)

case.story: Since adolescence has attacks of vertigo and staggering lasting hours after stress or exercise; his mother has similar attacks.
case.exam: Between attacks: downbeat nystagmus on lateral gaze, otherwise normal.
case.tests: MRI mild vermian atrophy; CACNA1A truncating variant.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and a drug that reduces attacks?
case.a: Episodic ataxia type 2; acetazolamide (or 4-aminopyridine) reduces attack frequency.

det.patho: Voltage-gated calcium channels control excitation-contraction coupling in muscle (CaV1.1, CACNA1S) and neurotransmitter release in neurons (CaV2.1, CACNA1A). Loss-of-function variants in CACNA1A cause EA2; gain-of-function variants cause hemiplegic migraine; small polyglutamine expansions cause SCA6. CACNA1S variants cause hypokalaemic periodic paralysis or malignant hyperthermia susceptibility.
det.clinical: The common theme is paroxysmal dysfunction: attacks of ataxia, migraine with hemiparesis, or flaccid weakness. Attacks may be triggered by stress, exertion or diet. Over time, fixed features such as ataxia or proximal myopathy may appear. Malignant hyperthermia presents only on exposure to volatile anaesthetics or succinylcholine.
det.diagnosis: Clinical pattern, family history and ictal tests (potassium, CK) guide targeted gene testing. EMG long exercise test is useful for periodic paralysis. MRI may show cerebellar atrophy in CACNA1A disorders.
det.treatment: Acetazolamide or dichlorphenamide reduce periodic paralysis and EA2 attacks; 4-aminopyridine helps EA2. Hemiplegic migraine uses standard preventives such as verapamil, flunarizine or lamotrigine and avoids triptans in some guidelines. Patients susceptible to malignant hyperthermia must avoid triggering anaesthetics and wear an alert card.
det.prognosis: Generally compatible with normal life span; quality of life depends on attack frequency and fixed deficits.
pearls: One gene (CACNA1A) — three phenotypes: EA2, FHM1, SCA6.
Acetazolamide works in both EA2 and many periodic paralyses.
Flag malignant hyperthermia risk before any surgery.
det.thd: Calcium channelopathies คือโรคที่ช่องแคลเซียมผิดปกติทางพันธุกรรม ยีน CACNA1A ทำให้เกิด episodic ataxia type 2, hemiplegic migraine และ SCA6 ส่วน CACNA1S ทำให้เกิด hypokalaemic periodic paralysis และเสี่ยง malignant hyperthermia อาการมาเป็นพัก ๆ ตรวจยีนยืนยัน รักษาด้วย acetazolamide และหลีกเลี่ยงยาดมสลบที่กระตุ้น

ddx.pt: Prototype CACNA1A channelopathy with hours-long ataxia attacks and interictal nystagmus
Flaccid weakness attacks with low potassium; CACNA1S or SCN4A
Myotonia and hyperkalaemic paralysis from SCN4A; epilepsy syndromes from SCN1A

aN: cacna1a disorders | cacna1s disorders | voltage gated calcium channel disorders | calcium channel diseases

name: Calcium deficiency
formal: Hypocalcaemia causing neuromuscular irritability: perioral paraesthesia, tetany, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, seizures and prolonged QT.
simple: Low blood calcium, causing tingling around the mouth, muscle spasms and sometimes seizures.
th: แคลเซียมในเลือดต่ำ ทำให้ประสาทและกล้ามเนื้อไวเกิน มีชารอบปากและปลายมือ มือจีบเกร็ง ชัก และ QT ยาว
tempoNote: Acute drops (e.g. after thyroid surgery) cause tetany within hours; long-standing hypoparathyroidism gives slow basal ganglia calcification
feat: Tingling around the mouth and in fingers and toes
Carpopedal spasm, muscle cramps; laryngospasm in severe cases
Positive Chvostek and Trousseau signs
Seizures, confusion; chronic cases may develop parkinsonism or cataracts
inv: Albumin-corrected or ionised calcium, magnesium, phosphate, creatinine
PTH and 25-hydroxy vitamin D to identify the cause
ECG for prolonged QT; CT brain in chronic cases for basal ganglia calcification

case.who: 42-year-old woman in a provincial hospital in Lampang
case.story: A day after total thyroidectomy she reports pins and needles around her lips and her hands cramp into a claw.
case.exam: Facial twitch on tapping in front of the ear; carpal spasm when a BP cuff is inflated above systolic for 3 minutes.
case.tests: Corrected calcium 1.6 mmol/L, magnesium low-normal, PTH low; QTc 500 ms.
case.q: What is the cause and the immediate treatment?
case.a: Post-surgical hypoparathyroidism; give IV calcium gluconate slowly with cardiac monitoring, correct magnesium, then oral calcium and calcitriol.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — endocrine disorders

det.patho: Low extracellular ionised calcium lowers the depolarisation threshold of nerve membranes, so axons fire spontaneously; peripheral nerves are most sensitive, causing paraesthesia and tetany. Common causes are hypoparathyroidism after neck surgery, vitamin D deficiency, hypomagnesaemia (which blocks PTH release and action), chronic kidney disease, pancreatitis, massive transfusion and drugs such as bisphosphonates or denosumab. Alkalosis, as in hyperventilation, lowers ionised calcium without changing total calcium. Long-standing hypoparathyroidism leads to calcification of basal ganglia and dentate nuclei.
det.clinical: This is a metabolic disorder rather than a primary neurological disease, but its first features are often neurological. Acute hypocalcaemia gives perioral and acral paraesthesia, cramps, carpopedal spasm and, when severe, laryngospasm, seizures and arrhythmia. Chronic deficiency may be surprisingly quiet but can cause cognitive change, parkinsonism or chorea from basal ganglia calcification, raised intracranial pressure and cataracts. Neonates present with jitteriness and seizures.
det.diagnosis: Measure ionised calcium or correct total calcium for albumin, and always check magnesium. PTH distinguishes hypoparathyroidism (low or inappropriately normal) from secondary causes where PTH is high. Vitamin D, phosphate and renal function complete the picture. Chvostek sign is present in some normal people, while Trousseau sign is more specific.
det.treatment: Symptomatic or severe hypocalcaemia needs slow IV calcium gluconate with ECG monitoring, followed by an infusion if needed. Replace magnesium first or simultaneously, since calcium will not correct otherwise. Chronic hypoparathyroidism is managed with oral calcium and active vitamin D (calcitriol or alfacalcidol), aiming for low-normal calcium to protect the kidneys; recombinant PTH analogues are options for difficult cases. Seizures from hypocalcaemia respond poorly to antiseizure drugs until calcium is corrected.
det.prognosis: Acute symptoms resolve quickly with correction; basal ganglia calcification and cataracts from chronic deficiency are irreversible.
pearls: Always check magnesium in refractory hypocalcaemia.
Seizure with prolonged QT after neck surgery: think calcium.
Bilateral basal ganglia calcification: check calcium, phosphate and PTH.
det.thd: แคลเซียมต่ำทำให้เส้นประสาทไวเกินไป จึงชารอบปากและปลายนิ้ว มือเกร็งจีบ และอาจชักหรือหัวใจเต้นผิดจังหวะ สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยคือหลังผ่าตัดไทรอยด์ ขาดวิตามินดี และแมกนีเซียมต่ำ ตรวจ calcium, magnesium, PTH และ ECG รักษาเฉียบพลันด้วย calcium gluconate ทางหลอดเลือดอย่างช้า ๆ และแก้แมกนีเซียมควบคู่ไป

name: Calpainopathy (LGMD R1/2A)
formal: Autosomal recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophy from CAPN3 mutations with proximal pelvic and shoulder girdle weakness, scapular winging, and contractures.
simple: An inherited muscle disease that slowly weakens muscles around the hips and shoulders.
th: กล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมชนิด limb-girdle ที่พบบ่อยจากยีน CAPN3 อ่อนแรงสะโพกและไหล่ สะบักยก และข้อเท้าติด
tempoNote: Onset usually 8–15 years; loss of walking often 10–30 years after onset
feat: Symmetric pelvic and shoulder girdle weakness, posterior thigh and hip adductors early
Scapular winging; calf atrophy rather than hypertrophy
Early Achilles tendon contractures, toe walking
CK high (often 5–20 times normal) early, falls later
Heart and intellect usually spared
inv: CK; EMG myopathic
Muscle MRI: early involvement of adductors, semimembranosus and medial gastrocnemius
CAPN3 sequencing; biopsy western blot for calpain-3 (normal protein does not exclude)
Spirometry intermittently

case.story: Slower at running than classmates since age 10; now has trouble climbing bus steps and walks on her toes.
case.exam: Waddling gait, scapular winging, hip adductor and gluteal weakness, thin calves, tight Achilles tendons, normal face.
case.tests: CK 3,200 U/L; MRI thighs shows posterior compartment fatty change; biallelic CAPN3 variants.
case.q: Which girdle finding helps separate this from a dystrophinopathy?
case.a: Calpainopathy (LGMD R1): calf atrophy and scapular winging rather than calf hypertrophy, with no cardiac involvement.

read.where: Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Muscular Dystrophies

det.patho: CAPN3 encodes calpain-3, a muscle-specific protease involved in sarcomere remodelling and calcium handling. Loss of function leads to defective repair and fibre degeneration. Most cases are autosomal recessive; specific in-frame deletions cause a milder dominant form (LGMD D4).
det.clinical: Presentation is in late childhood or adolescence with difficulty running and climbing. Weakness is symmetric, involving hip adductors, extensors and posterior thigh more than quadriceps, with scapular winging. Contractures of the heel cords and spine stiffness may occur. Cardiac and respiratory function are usually preserved until late.
det.diagnosis: Very high CK with a typical MRI pattern suggests the diagnosis. Genetic testing confirms; calpain-3 western blot can support variants of uncertain significance, but about 20% of patients have normal protein amount. Early biopsies may show eosinophilic infiltrates, mimicking myositis.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy is approved; gene therapy research is ongoing. Physiotherapy, stretching and orthoses address contractures. Monitor respiratory function and scoliosis. Avoid steroids, which are ineffective.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; many lose ambulation in adulthood; lifespan usually near normal.
pearls: Thin calves plus girdle weakness and high CK suggests calpainopathy.
Eosinophilic myositis in a young person may be early calpainopathy.
Normal calpain-3 on western blot does not exclude CAPN3 disease.
det.thd: Calpainopathy เป็น LGMD ที่พบบ่อยจากยีน CAPN3 มักถ่ายทอดแบบด้อย เริ่มในวัยเด็กโตหรือวัยรุ่น อ่อนแรงสะโพกและไหล่ สะบักยก น่องลีบ และข้อเท้าติด CK สูง หัวใจมักปกติ วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI และตรวจยีน ยังไม่มียาเฉพาะ รักษาด้วยกายภาพบำบัด

name: Camptocormia (bent spine syndrome)
formal: Marked involuntary forward flexion of the trunk when standing or walking that disappears when lying; seen in parkinsonism, axial myopathy and idiopathic paraspinal myopathy.
simple: A stooped, bent-forward posture of the back that appears when standing or walking and eases when lying down.
more: Marked forward flexion of the trunk when standing, which disappears when lying down, seen in Parkinson disease, axial myopathy, dystonia and ageing.
th: ลำตัวงอไปข้างหน้ามากเมื่อยืนหรือเดิน แต่หายเมื่อนอนราบ พบใน parkinsonism โรคกล้ามเนื้อหลัง และ dystonia
tempoNote: Usually evolves over months; rapid onset suggests inflammatory myopathy
feat: Thoracolumbar forward flexion of 45 degrees or more when upright, worse with walking
Fully corrects when lying supine or leaning against a wall (no fixed kyphosis)
Back pain and fatigue; walking with hands on thighs or a walker
Associated parkinsonism, myopathy or dystonia depending on cause
inv: Spine X-ray to exclude fixed structural deformity
Paraspinal muscle MRI and EMG; CK
Myopathy or MG work-up as appropriate

case.who: 69-year-old man from Lopburi with Parkinson disease for 9 years
case.story: Over six months he bends further forward when walking, with back pain; he straightens completely in bed.
case.exam: Bradykinesia and rigidity; 60-degree trunk flexion when standing, corrected supine; no fixed kyphosis.
case.tests: Spine X-ray mild spondylosis; paraspinal MRI shows mild oedema; CK normal.
case.q: What is the posture called and what treatment options exist?
case.a: Camptocormia in Parkinson disease; adjust dopaminergic therapy, physiotherapy and bracing, with botulinum toxin or DBS in selected cases.

det.patho: Camptocormia results from imbalance between trunk flexors and extensors. In parkinsonism it is attributed to axial dystonia, rigidity and secondary paraspinal myopathy. Primary paraspinal myopathies, inflammatory myositis, FSHD and late-onset Pompe disease are myopathic causes; osteoporotic fractures and degenerative spine disease contribute in older people.
det.clinical: The patient walks bent forward and corrects when supine. In Parkinson disease, onset is usually years into the illness. Pain and walking limitation reduce quality of life. Examine for parkinsonian signs, proximal or axial weakness and spinal deformity.
det.diagnosis: Measure the angle of flexion and confirm passive correctability. Obtain spinal imaging, CK, EMG and paraspinal MRI to separate myopathic, dystonic and structural causes.
det.treatment: Management is often disappointing. Optimise dopaminergic therapy, offer physiotherapy, back-extension exercises and braces or walkers. Botulinum toxin into iliopsoas or rectus abdominis and DBS help some patients. Treat myopathy when found.
det.prognosis: Tends to be persistent; partial improvement is common with therapy.
pearls: Correctable when supine distinguishes camptocormia from fixed kyphosis.
Paraspinal MRI is key to separating myopathy from dystonia.
Levodopa rarely fixes camptocormia completely.
det.thd: Camptocormia คือลำตัวงอไปข้างหน้ามากเวลายืนหรือเดินแต่ตรงได้เมื่อนอน พบบ่อยใน Parkinson ระยะหลังและโรคกล้ามเนื้อหลัง ตรวจ X-ray กระดูกสันหลัง EMG และ MRI กล้ามเนื้อหลังเพื่อหาสาเหตุ รักษาด้วยการปรับยา กายภาพบำบัด อุปกรณ์พยุง และบางรายใช้ botulinum toxin หรือ DBS
