name: CAP disease
formal: Rare congenital myopathy defined by peripheral caps of disorganised sarcomeres under the sarcolemma, caused by TPM2, TPM3, or ACTA1 mutations, with hypotonia, weakness, and respiratory problems.
simple: A rare inherited muscle disease present from early life, causing floppiness and weakness.
more: Biopsy shows subsarcolemmal caps lacking myofibrillar ATPase. Care is supportive, focusing on breathing, swallowing, and scoliosis; severity varies.
th: congenital myopathy หายากที่ชิ้นเนื้อพบ cap บริเวณใต้ผนังเซลล์ จากยีน TPM2 TPM3 หรือ ACTA1 ทำให้ตัวอ่อนปวกเปียกและอ่อนแรงใบหน้า
tempoNote: Congenital or early childhood onset; static or slowly progressive
feat: Neonatal hypotonia, facial weakness and high-arched palate
Proximal and neck weakness; scoliosis and respiratory weakness
Caps: peripheral crescents of disorganised myofibrils on biopsy
Overlaps with nemaline myopathy (same thin-filament genes)
Very rare; natural history known from small series
inv: CK normal or slightly raised
Muscle biopsy: subsarcolemmal caps on Gomori trichrome and NADH; electron microscopy
Gene panel: TPM2, TPM3, ACTA1
Spirometry and sleep study

case.story: Floppy as a baby, sat late, walks with a wide-based waddle and cannot keep up with peers; frequent chest infections.
case.exam: Long thin face, high palate, neck flexor weakness, mild proximal weakness, early scoliosis, reflexes reduced.
case.tests: CK 90 U/L; biopsy shows peripheral cap-like zones lacking ATPase activity; TPM2 de novo variant.
case.q: What respiratory test should be arranged even though he is walking?
case.a: CAP disease (congenital myopathy) – overnight oximetry/sleep study, as nocturnal hypoventilation may be silent.

det.patho: Variants in thin-filament genes, mostly TPM2 and TPM3, disturb myofibrillar organisation at the fibre periphery, producing cap structures composed of disorganised thin filaments and Z-disc material. The relationship with nemaline rods suggests a shared pathway. Most cases are dominant, often de novo.
det.clinical: Infants show hypotonia, feeding difficulty and facial weakness. Motor milestones are delayed, and weakness is mostly proximal and axial. Respiratory insufficiency and scoliosis can develop. Information is limited to case series, so long-term course is uncertain.
det.diagnosis: Biopsy is diagnostic when caps are seen, though their proportion varies and may increase with age. Genetic testing confirms the gene and inheritance. Exclude other congenital myopathies and myasthenic syndromes.
det.treatment: Supportive care only: respiratory surveillance and non-invasive ventilation, physiotherapy, scoliosis care, nutrition and genetic counselling. Anaesthetic precautions for respiratory weakness apply.
det.prognosis: Varies from mild, slowly progressive disease to severe respiratory involvement; data are sparse.
pearls: Caps and rods can occur in the same TPM2/TPM3 patient.
Respiratory weakness may outstrip limb weakness in congenital myopathies.
Normal CK is typical; do not let it reassure you.
det.thd: CAP disease เป็น congenital myopathy ที่หายาก ชิ้นเนื้อกล้ามเนื้อพบโครงสร้าง cap ใต้ผนังเซลล์ เกิดจากยีน TPM2 TPM3 หรือ ACTA1 เด็กมีตัวอ่อนปวกเปียก หน้าอ่อนแรง และอาจมีปัญหาการหายใจและหลังคด ไม่มีการรักษาจำเพาะ ต้องติดตามการหายใจและทำกายภาพบำบัด

name: Carbamate poisoning
formal: Reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibition causing cholinergic crisis with miosis, salivation, bronchorrhoea, fasciculations and weakness; treated with atropine.
simple: Poisoning from certain insecticides that overstimulates nerves, causing small pupils, drooling, muscle twitching and weakness.
th: พิษจากสารกำจัดแมลงกลุ่ม carbamate ยับยั้ง acetylcholinesterase แบบผันกลับได้ ทำให้เกิดภาวะ cholinergic crisis คล้าย organophosphate แต่สั้นกว่า
tempoNote: Symptoms within minutes to a few hours of exposure; usually settle within 24–48 hours because enzyme binding is reversible
feat: Muscarinic excess: pinpoint pupils, drooling, sweating, wet chest with bronchorrhoea, vomiting, diarrhoea, bradycardia
Nicotinic effects: fasciculations, cramps, then weakness that can involve breathing muscles
Central effects (agitation, drowsiness, seizures) are milder than with organophosphates because most carbamates cross the blood–brain barrier poorly
Garlic-free, often a solvent or chemical smell; history of farm work or deliberate ingestion
Course is shorter and intermediate syndrome is uncommon compared with organophosphates
inv: Clinical diagnosis; do not delay atropine for laboratory results
Red-cell or plasma cholinesterase may be low but can recover in the tube, so a normal value does not exclude carbamates
Arterial blood gas, chest X-ray, ECG (bradycardia, QT prolongation) and serial bedside spirometry or neck-flexion strength

case.who: 34-year-old male rice farmer from Suphan Buri
case.story: Brought in an hour after drinking an insecticide labelled carbofuran after a family argument. Vomiting, sweating and short of breath.
case.exam: Pupils 1 mm, profuse salivation, crackles both lungs, HR 48/min, fasciculations over the calves and chest wall, GCS 14.
case.tests: SpO2 86% on air; plasma cholinesterase markedly reduced; chest X-ray shows bilateral perihilar shadowing.
case.q: What is the priority treatment and how does the expected course differ from an organophosphate?
case.a: Escalating atropine until the chest is dry with heart rate above 80, airway support and decontamination; recovery is usually within a day or two and late weakness is uncommon.

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Organophosphates and Carbamates

det.patho: Carbamates carbamylate the serine site of acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine builds up at muscarinic, nicotinic and central synapses. Unlike organophosphates the bond hydrolyses spontaneously within hours and the enzyme does not age. Most agricultural carbamates are quaternary or poorly lipophilic, which limits brain penetration, although some (e.g. aldicarb) can still cause seizures and coma.
det.clinical: The picture is a cholinergic toxidrome: secretions, bronchospasm, miosis, bradycardia and gut hyperactivity, combined with nicotinic muscle fasciculation and weakness. Respiratory failure from bronchorrhoea plus muscle weakness is the main cause of death. Severe poisoning can still be lethal despite the reversibility, especially with highly toxic agents such as carbofuran or methomyl. Children may show more CNS depression and fewer muscarinic signs.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on exposure history, container label and the toxidrome. Cholinesterase activity supports the diagnosis but carbamylated enzyme can reactivate in the sample, giving falsely reassuring results. Mimics include organophosphate poisoning, opioid overdose (miosis without secretions) and nicotine poisoning. Monitor vital capacity, neck flexion and oxygenation every few hours in the first day.
det.treatment: Secure the airway and decontaminate skin and clothing. Give atropine in doubling boluses until the chest is clear, heart rate is adequate and systolic pressure is maintained, then continue by infusion. Benzodiazepines treat seizures and agitation. Oximes are generally not needed because the enzyme recovers spontaneously; many toxicologists still use them when the agent is unknown or mixed with an organophosphate.
det.prognosis: Most patients who reach hospital and receive timely atropine and ventilatory support recover fully within 1–2 days; deaths follow early respiratory failure or aspiration.
pearls: Treat the toxidrome, not the label: if unsure whether it is a carbamate or organophosphate, manage as organophosphate.
A normal cholinesterase level does not rule out carbamate exposure.
Endpoint of atropine is dry lungs, not pupil size.
det.thd: Carbamate เป็นยาฆ่าแมลงที่ยับยั้ง acetylcholinesterase แบบผันกลับได้ ทำให้มี acetylcholine คั่ง ผู้ป่วยมีรูม่านตาเล็ก น้ำลายและเสมหะมาก หลอดลมตีบ หัวใจเต้นช้า กล้ามเนื้อกระตุกและอ่อนแรง การวินิจฉัยอาศัยประวัติสัมผัสและอาการ โดยระดับ cholinesterase อาจดูปกติได้ การรักษาสำคัญคือดูแลทางเดินหายใจ ล้างสารพิษ และให้ atropine จนปอดแห้ง โรคมักหายภายใน 1–2 วัน

name: Carbamyl phosphate synthetase deficiency
formal: Urea cycle disorder causing hyperammonaemia with vomiting, lethargy, seizures and encephalopathy, mainly in neonates; low citrulline and absent orotic acid.
simple: An inherited problem in clearing ammonia from the blood, causing sleepiness, vomiting and seizures.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมยีนด้อยของวงจรยูเรีย ทำให้แอมโมเนียในเลือดสูงมาก ทารกแรกเกิดซึม อาเจียน ชัก และโคม่า
tempoNote: Classic form appears within days of birth after protein feeding; partial deficiency gives later episodic crises triggered by illness or protein load
feat: Newborn well at first, then poor feeding, vomiting and lethargy within days
Rapid progression to seizures, hypothermia, apnoea and coma
Late-onset forms: episodic confusion, ataxia or psychiatric change after protein or catabolic stress
Respiratory alkalosis early in a hyperammonaemic crisis
inv: Plasma ammonia urgently on free-flowing sample (often several hundred µmol/L in crisis)
Plasma amino acids: high glutamine, low citrulline and arginine; urine orotic acid low or normal
CPS1 gene sequencing confirms; distinguishes from NAGS deficiency

case.who: 3-day-old term boy at a regional hospital in Khon Kaen
case.story: Fed well on day 1 but on day 3 is sleepy, vomiting and breathing fast.
case.exam: Lethargic, hypotonic, intermittent cycling movements; no focal signs.
case.tests: Ammonia 680 µmol/L, blood gas respiratory alkalosis, normal glucose; plasma citrulline very low, urine orotic acid not raised.
case.q: Which urea cycle defects fit, and what is the emergency plan?
case.a: CPS1 or NAGS deficiency; stop protein, give high-calorie IV glucose, ammonia scavengers and arginine, and start haemodialysis given the level; N-carbamylglutamate trial helps separate NAGS deficiency.

det.patho: CPS1 catalyses the first committed mitochondrial step of the urea cycle, joining ammonia and bicarbonate to form carbamyl phosphate; it requires N-acetylglutamate as an activator. Biallelic CPS1 variants block nitrogen disposal, so ammonia and glutamine accumulate, causing astrocyte swelling and cerebral oedema. Because the block is before ornithine transcarbamylase, carbamyl phosphate does not spill into pyrimidine synthesis and orotic acid stays low, unlike OTC deficiency. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
det.clinical: The severe neonatal form presents after a short symptom-free interval with feeding refusal, vomiting, tachypnoea, lethargy, seizures and coma, and can be fatal within days. Partial forms present at any age with recurrent encephalopathy, headache, behavioural change or ataxia, often triggered by infection, fasting, surgery, pregnancy or high-protein meals. Survivors of severe crises often have intellectual disability and cerebral palsy-like deficits. Some children self-select a low-protein diet.
det.diagnosis: Measure ammonia in any newborn or adult with unexplained encephalopathy, collecting on ice and analysing fast. Plasma amino acids (low citrulline, high glutamine) with low or normal urine orotic acid point to CPS1 or NAGS deficiency; molecular testing separates them. Exclude organic acidurias with blood gas, ketones and urine organic acids. Many countries now include urea cycle markers on newborn screening, though proximal defects are hard to detect by citrulline alone.
det.treatment: Emergency care: stop protein, give generous glucose and lipid calories to halt catabolism, start IV ammonia scavengers (sodium benzoate and sodium phenylacetate) with arginine, and use haemodialysis for very high or rising ammonia. Long term, patients need a protein-restricted diet with essential amino acids, oral scavengers (sodium or glycerol phenylbutyrate) and citrulline or arginine supplements, plus an emergency sick-day plan. N-carbamylglutamate is curative for NAGS deficiency and helps some CPS1 variants. Liver transplantation is considered for severe early-onset disease.
det.prognosis: Neonatal-onset disease carries high mortality and disability; outcome depends mainly on the peak and duration of hyperammonaemia.
pearls: Sick neonate with respiratory alkalosis: check ammonia, not just sepsis screen.
Low citrulline with normal orotic acid points to CPS1 or NAGS deficiency; high orotic acid points to OTC deficiency.
Ammonia above about 250–500 µmol/L in a newborn usually needs dialysis.
det.thd: CPS1 deficiency เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมยีนด้อยของวงจรยูเรีย ร่างกายกำจัดแอมโมเนียไม่ได้ ทารกแรกเกิดจะปกติช่วงแรกแล้วซึม อาเจียน หายใจเร็ว ชัก และโคม่า ตรวจพบแอมโมเนียสูงมาก citrulline ต่ำ และ orotic acid ไม่สูง รักษาฉุกเฉินด้วยการงดโปรตีน ให้พลังงาน ให้ยาจับแอมโมเนีย arginine และฟอกเลือด ระยะยาวต้องคุมอาหารโปรตีนและอาจพิจารณาปลูกถ่ายตับ

name: Carbohydrate metabolism disorders
formal: Inherited disorders of sugar metabolism such as galactosaemia and glycogen storage diseases, with hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly, myopathy or encephalopathy.
simple: A group of inherited conditions in which the body cannot properly handle sugars, which can harm muscles, liver and brain.
more: Detect with newborn screening, urine reducing substances, red cell GALT activity, plasma lactate and muscle biopsy enzymology. Treatment depends on the defect, with galactose exclusion in galactosaemia and diet or enzyme therapy in glycogenoses.

feat: Umbrella group: glycogen storage diseases, galactosaemia, hereditary fructose intolerance, GLUT1 deficiency and others
Liver forms: fasting hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly, growth failure
Muscle forms: exercise intolerance, cramps, myoglobinuria or progressive weakness
Neurological: seizures from hypoglycaemia, cataract and cognitive impairment in galactosaemia, epilepsy in GLUT1 deficiency
Most autosomal recessive

CK; forearm exercise test for muscle glycogenoses

case.who: 10-day-old girl in a neonatal unit in Udon Thani
case.story: Vomiting and poor feeding after starting formula, becoming jaundiced and drowsy.
case.exam: Lethargic, hepatomegaly, bilateral cataracts on red reflex testing, bulging fontanelle absent.
case.tests: Glucose low, liver enzymes high, urine reducing substances positive; E. coli in blood culture; GALT activity absent.
case.q: Which carbohydrate disorder is this and what is the immediate dietary change?

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Disorders of Carbohydrate Metabolism

det.patho: These disorders result from defects in enzymes or transporters that handle glucose, galactose, fructose or glycogen. Consequences include energy failure in muscle or brain, accumulation of toxic metabolites such as galactitol, and inability to release glucose from the liver. The organ affected depends on where the enzyme is expressed.
det.clinical: This is a group heading rather than a single disease. Hepatic forms present in infancy with hypoglycaemia and hepatomegaly, while muscle forms present with exercise intolerance or weakness from childhood to adult life. Galactosaemia presents in newborns with feeding problems, liver failure, cataract and E. coli sepsis. GLUT1 deficiency causes early epilepsy, movement disorders and microcephaly.
det.diagnosis: Clinical pattern guides biochemical tests: glucose, lactate and ketones during episodes, CK and exercise testing for muscle disease, and newborn screening for galactosaemia. Enzyme assays and genetic panels confirm the specific defect. Low CSF glucose with normal blood glucose suggests GLUT1 deficiency.
det.treatment: Treatment is specific to the disorder: lactose exclusion for galactosaemia, frequent feeds and cornstarch for hepatic glycogenoses, enzyme replacement for Pompe disease, ketogenic diet for GLUT1 deficiency and avoidance of fructose in hereditary fructose intolerance. Metabolic dietitian input is essential.
det.prognosis: Variable; early treatment improves outcomes, though galactosaemia may leave learning and ovarian problems despite diet.
pearls: Cataract plus liver dysfunction and sepsis in a newborn suggests galactosaemia.
Low CSF glucose with normal blood glucose: think GLUT1 deficiency.
Muscle glycogenoses cause cramps and myoglobinuria with brief intense exercise.
det.thd: เป็นกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมของการใช้น้ำตาลในร่างกาย เช่น galactosaemia, glycogen storage disease และ GLUT1 deficiency อาการขึ้นกับอวัยวะ ได้แก่ น้ำตาลต่ำและตับโตในทารก ตะคริวและปัสสาวะสีเข้มหลังออกกำลัง หรือชักในเด็ก การวินิจฉัยใช้ผลเลือดขณะมีอาการ ตรวจเอนไซม์และยีน การรักษาขึ้นกับโรค เช่น งดนม lactose หรือให้อาหารบ่อย

Fat oxidation defect: rhabdomyolysis with fasting or prolonged exercise, no cramps during brief effort
Raised lactate with multisystem involvement and normal carbohydrate enzymes

name: Carbon disulphide poisoning
formal: Industrial solvent toxicity causing polyneuropathy, parkinsonism, psychosis and encephalopathy, with basal ganglia and optic nerve involvement.
simple: Poisoning by an industrial chemical that can damage nerves and brain, causing weakness, tremor and mood changes.
th: พิษจากตัวทำละลายอุตสาหกรรม carbon disulphide (เช่นโรงงานเรยอน) ทำให้ปลายประสาทเสื่อม parkinsonism อาการทางจิต และสมองเสื่อม
tempoNote: Chronic occupational exposure over months to years; very high exposure can cause acute psychosis
feat: Distal sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy
Parkinsonism and other extrapyramidal signs
Mood change, irritability, psychosis and cognitive impairment
Retinopathy, optic neuropathy, hearing loss; accelerated atherosclerosis and small vessel strokes
inv: Occupational history; workplace air monitoring
Urinary TTCA (2-thiothiazolidine-4-carboxylic acid) as exposure marker
NCS/EMG; MRI brain (white matter and basal ganglia lesions); eye examination

case.story: Fifteen years in a viscose rayon plant; two years of numb feet, slowness and irritability.
case.exam: Distal sensory loss, absent ankle jerks, mild bradykinesia and rigidity.
case.tests: NCS axonal neuropathy; MRI multiple white matter hyperintensities; elevated urinary TTCA.
case.q: What occupational toxin is likely, and what is the key management?
case.a: Carbon disulphide; remove from exposure and treat symptomatically.

det.patho: Carbon disulphide reacts with amino groups of proteins, causing cross-linking of neurofilaments and axonal swelling, similar to hexacarbon neuropathy. It also damages vascular endothelium, accelerating atherosclerosis, and affects basal ganglia and cortex. Exposure is mainly occupational in viscose rayon and some chemical industries.
det.clinical: Chronic exposure produces neuropathy, extrapyramidal syndromes, neuropsychiatric symptoms and cognitive decline, along with retinal, auditory and cardiovascular effects. Acute high exposure can cause delirium, mania or psychosis and coma.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on documented exposure plus compatible findings. Urinary TTCA reflects recent exposure. NCS, MRI and eye examination document organ damage; exclude other causes of neuropathy and parkinsonism.
det.treatment: Stop exposure immediately and notify occupational health authorities. Treatment is supportive: neuropathic pain management, rehabilitation, and trial of levodopa for parkinsonism (response is often limited). Workplace controls are the main preventive measure.
det.prognosis: Neuropathy may partly improve after exposure ends; CNS damage often persists.
pearls: Always take an occupational history in neuropathy plus parkinsonism.
Rayon industry is the classic setting.
Vascular damage and early strokes are part of chronic CS2 toxicity.
det.thd: พิษ carbon disulphide พบในคนงานโรงงานเรยอนและเคมี สัมผัสเรื้อรังทำให้เส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเสื่อม parkinsonism อารมณ์แปรปรวน สมองเสื่อม และหลอดเลือดแข็งเร็ว วินิจฉัยจากประวัติการทำงานและตรวจ TTCA ในปัสสาวะ รักษาโดยหยุดสัมผัสและดูแลตามอาการ

name: Carbon monoxide poisoning
formal: Hypoxic poisoning from carboxyhaemoglobin with headache, confusion and coma; delayed leukoencephalopathy and bilateral globus pallidus lesions may follow.
simple: Poisoning from breathing carbon monoxide gas, which causes headache, confusion and unconsciousness and can injure the brain.
more: Toxic brain injury from carbon monoxide exposure causing tissue hypoxia, with acute encephalopathy and possible delayed cognitive and parkinsonian sequelae.
th: ภาวะพิษจากคาร์บอนมอนอกไซด์ทำให้เนื้อเยื่อขาดออกซิเจน อาจเกิดอาการสมองเสื่อมหรือพาร์กินสันตามมาภายหลังได้
tempoNote: Hours of exposure; delayed syndrome after a lucid interval of days to about six weeks
feat: Headache, dizziness, nausea and confusion, often in several people at the same place
Coma, seizures, cardiac ischaemia and lactic acidosis in severe exposure
Pulse oximetry reads falsely normal
Delayed neurological sequelae: cognitive decline, apathy, parkinsonism, incontinence
Bilateral globus pallidus lesions and diffuse white-matter change on MRI
inv: Carboxyhaemoglobin by co-oximetry on arterial or venous blood
ECG, troponin and lactate to assess cardiac injury and acidosis
MRI brain with DWI and FLAIR, seen in the pallidum and periventricular white matter
Consider cyanide in smoke inhalation

case.story: She was found drowsy in a closed room with a charcoal stove, and her child was also unwell. After three weeks of recovery she became slow, apathetic and incontinent.
case.exam: Slow responses, poor attention, bradykinesia and frontal release signs.
case.tests: Initial COHb 30%; MRI now shows bilateral pallidal lesions with confluent white-matter hyperintensity.
case.q: What is this late presentation called, and how was the first-day treatment given?
case.a: Delayed neurological sequelae of carbon monoxide poisoning. Initial care is 100% oxygen, and hyperbaric oxygen is considered for coma, neurological deficit, pregnancy or high COHb.

read.where: Chapter 24: Neurologic Complications Of Drug Overdose, Poisoning, And Terrorism
Chapter 13: Neurologic Complications Of Cardiac Arrest
Chapter 28 Disorders of Consciousness and Intensive Care Neurology — Carbon Monoxide Poisoning

det.patho: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin with about 200-fold the affinity of oxygen, shifts the dissociation curve to the left and impairs mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase, so tissues become hypoxic despite normal PaO2. Brain areas with high metabolic demand and watershed supply, especially the globus pallidus and hippocampus, are most vulnerable. Delayed injury involves lipid peroxidation and immune-mediated demyelination.
det.clinical: Acute symptoms are non-specific and easily blamed on influenza, so clustering of cases at home, in winter braziers, charcoal stoves, generators or car exhaust is the clue. Severe cases show coma, seizures, myocardial injury and rhabdomyolysis. Cherry-red skin is uncommon. In some survivors, a delayed syndrome of memory loss, mood change, parkinsonism and mutism develops after a symptom-free interval of several days to weeks.
det.diagnosis: Measure COHb by co-oximetry; values from smokers can be elevated and the level falls fast on oxygen, so a normal level late does not exclude exposure. Obtain ECG and troponin, and cranial MRI for neurological findings. Pulse oximetry cannot be relied on. Consider coexisting cyanide and intoxication in fires.
det.treatment: Remove the patient from exposure and give 100% oxygen by tight-fitting mask or ventilator until the level is normal and symptoms resolve, which shortens the half-life from hours to about an hour. Hyperbaric oxygen is considered for loss of consciousness, neurological deficit, ischaemic cardiac changes, pregnancy or very high COHb, but evidence for preventing sequelae is mixed. Treat seizures, acidosis and cardiac complications and plan follow-up cognitive assessment.
det.prognosis: Many recover, but up to a third of significant exposures develop cognitive or neuropsychiatric sequelae, usually improving over months. Severe pallidal injury predicts poor recovery.
pearls: A normal SpO2 and a cluster of headache cases: think CO.
Symmetric pallidal lesions on MRI are the classic imaging sign.
Warn survivors about delayed symptoms and arrange follow-up.
det.thd: พิษจากคาร์บอนมอนอกไซด์เกิดเมื่อก๊าซ CO จับฮีโมโกลบินแน่นกว่าออกซิเจนมาก ทำให้เนื้อเยื่อขาดออกซิเจน ผู้ป่วยปวดศีรษะ เวียนศีรษะ สับสน อาจชักหรือหมดสติ และ pulse oximeter อ่านค่าปกติจึงหลอกได้ ต้องวัด COHb รักษาด้วยออกซิเจน 100% และพิจารณา hyperbaric oxygen ในรายรุนแรง ผู้รอดชีวิตบางรายมีอาการสมองเสื่อมหรือพาร์กินสันตามหลังได้หลายวันถึงสัปดาห์ MRI พบรอยโรคสมมาตรที่ globus pallidus

name: Carbon tetrachloride poisoning
formal: Solvent poisoning causing hepatorenal toxicity plus headache, confusion, coma and sometimes peripheral neuropathy or optic neuritis.
simple: Poisoning by a cleaning solvent that damages the liver and kidneys and can cause confusion and nerve damage.
th: พิษจากตัวทำละลาย carbon tetrachloride ทำลายตับและไตเป็นหลัก ร่วมกับปวดศีรษะ สับสน หมดสติ และบางครั้งปลายประสาทอักเสบหรือเส้นประสาทตาอักเสบ
tempoNote: Neurological symptoms within hours; liver and kidney failure over 1–4 days
feat: Acute CNS depression: headache, dizziness, confusion, coma
Centrilobular hepatic necrosis and acute kidney injury follow days later
Alcohol use increases toxicity
Optic neuropathy or peripheral neuropathy reported with chronic exposure
inv: Liver and renal function, coagulation
Occupational or ingestion history; blood levels are rarely available
Eye examination and NCS if visual or sensory symptoms

case.story: Cleaned a tank without ventilation; became confused and vomited. Two days later he is jaundiced and producing little urine.
case.exam: Drowsy, jaundiced, tender liver.
case.tests: ALT 4,000 U/L, INR 3, creatinine rising; CT brain normal.
case.q: What toxin is suspected and which treatment is sometimes used early?
case.a: Carbon tetrachloride; N-acetylcysteine is often given early, with supportive care for liver and kidney failure.

det.patho: Carbon tetrachloride is metabolised by hepatic CYP2E1 to the trichloromethyl radical, which causes lipid peroxidation and necrosis in the liver and kidneys. It is also a CNS depressant. Alcohol induces CYP2E1 and increases toxicity. It has largely been withdrawn from consumer use.
det.clinical: Acute exposure causes narcosis, headache and vomiting; hepatorenal failure develops over days. Chronic low-level exposure is associated with nonspecific neurological symptoms and, rarely, optic or peripheral neuropathy. The neurological picture is overshadowed by liver and kidney involvement.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, based on exposure plus the pattern of liver and kidney injury. Exclude viral hepatitis and paracetamol toxicity.
det.treatment: Remove from exposure, decontaminate and provide supportive care. N-acetylcysteine is used empirically. Severe cases may require dialysis or liver transplant.
det.prognosis: Depends on the severity of liver and kidney damage; survivors usually recover neurologically.
pearls: Solvent exposure + liver failure: think carbon tetrachloride.
Alcohol users are at greater risk.
The neurological features are usually secondary to liver failure.
det.thd: พิษ carbon tetrachloride เกิดจากสูดหรือกินตัวทำละลายนี้ ทำให้ซึม สับสน ปวดหัวในไม่กี่ชั่วโมง และตามด้วยตับวายและไตวายใน 1–4 วัน ผู้ดื่มสุราเสี่ยงสูงกว่า รักษาประคับประคอง ให้ N-acetylcysteine และฟอกไตหรือปลูกถ่ายตับในรายรุนแรง

name: Cardioencephalomyopathy
formal: Multisystem mitochondrial disorder with heart, brain and muscle involvement, such as cytochrome oxidase deficiency from SCO2 variants, with infantile hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and lactic acidosis.
simple: A severe inherited energy disease affecting the heart, brain and muscles in infants.
more: Genetic testing and enzyme studies make the diagnosis. No cure and treatment is supportive; prognosis is poor.
th: โรคไมโทคอนเดรียที่กระทบหัวใจ สมอง และกล้ามเนื้อพร้อมกัน เช่นการขาด cytochrome c oxidase จากยีน SCO2 ทำให้ทารกมีกล้ามเนื้อหัวใจหนาและอ่อนแรง
tempoNote: Infantile onset with rapid progression in classic SCO2 disease
feat: Infantile hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Hypotonia, muscle weakness and respiratory insufficiency
Encephalopathy with developmental delay, sometimes Leigh-like lesions
Lactic acidosis
inv: Plasma and CSF lactate; echocardiography
Muscle biopsy: COX-deficient fibres; respiratory chain enzyme assays
Genetic testing (SCO2 and nuclear mitochondrial gene panels)

case.story: Poor feeding, breathlessness and floppiness since 2 months of age.
case.exam: Hypotonia, weak cry, enlarged liver, gallop rhythm.
case.tests: Echo: severe hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; lactate 6 mmol/L; biopsy COX-deficient fibres; biallelic SCO2 variants.
case.q: What is the diagnosis?
case.a: SCO2-related fatal infantile cardioencephalomyopathy with cytochrome c oxidase deficiency.

det.patho: SCO2 encodes a copper chaperone needed to assemble cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV). Biallelic variants reduce complex IV activity in heart, muscle and brain, impairing oxidative phosphorylation. Other nuclear genes affecting complex IV assembly cause similar multisystem disease.
det.clinical: Infants present in the first months with cardiomyopathy, hypotonia, feeding difficulty and respiratory failure; some have spinal muscular atrophy-like anterior horn involvement. Course is usually rapid. Milder or later-onset variants exist but are less well characterised.
det.diagnosis: Lactic acidosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in an infant with hypotonia should prompt metabolic and genetic work-up. Muscle biopsy histochemistry and enzyme assays show complex IV deficiency; genetic testing confirms. Exclude Pompe disease with enzyme testing.
det.treatment: No curative therapy; supportive care including cardiac management, respiratory support and nutrition. Copper supplementation has been tried with limited evidence. Genetic counselling is important.
det.prognosis: Classic infantile form is usually fatal in infancy.
pearls: Infant with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy + hypotonia: check GAA (Pompe) and lactate.
SCO2 disease can mimic SMA type 1.
Recessive inheritance; offer counselling to parents.
det.thd: Cardioencephalomyopathy คือโรคไมโทคอนเดรียที่กระทบหัวใจ สมอง และกล้ามเนื้อพร้อมกัน ตัวอย่างคือยีน SCO2 ทำให้ขาด cytochrome c oxidase ทารกมีกล้ามเนื้อหัวใจหนา อ่อนปวกเปียก และกรดแลคติกสูง ยืนยันด้วยตัดชิ้นกล้ามเนื้อและตรวจยีน ไม่มีการรักษาเฉพาะ ดูแลประคับประคองและให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

Brainstem and basal ganglia lesions with lactic acidosis; cardiomyopathy less constant

name: Cardiomyopathy
formal: Primary disease of heart muscle, dilated, hypertrophic or restrictive, which is often present in neuromuscular disorders such as muscular dystrophies, Friedreich ataxia and mitochondrial disease.
simple: A disease of the heart muscle that weakens the heart, often seen alongside inherited muscle and nerve diseases.
more: Echocardiography, cardiac MRI and ECG monitor it. Treat with ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers and devices; screening is routine in dystrophies. Primary heart muscle diseases that can cause cardioembolic stroke, syncope and arrhythmia; also associated with neuromuscular diseases such as dystrophies and Friedreich ataxia.
th: โรคของกล้ามเนื้อหัวใจชนิดขยาย หนาตัว หรือแข็งตัว ซึ่งพบร่วมกับโรคประสาทและกล้ามเนื้อหลายโรค และเป็นแหล่งลิ่มเลือดอุดตันในสมอง
tempoNote: Progresses over years; may present abruptly with embolic stroke, arrhythmia or sudden death
feat: A cardiac disease relevant to neurology in two ways: as a stroke source and as part of neuromuscular disorders
Dilated cardiomyopathy in Duchenne/Becker dystrophy (including female carriers), laminopathies, desmin and some limb-girdle dystrophies
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in Friedreich ataxia, Danon disease, Pompe and mitochondrial disease
Conduction disease and arrhythmia dominate in myotonic dystrophy and Emery–Dreifuss dystrophy
Low ejection fraction and ventricular thrombus cause cardioembolic stroke
inv: ECG and Holter; echocardiography; cardiac MRI for early fibrosis
BNP/NT-proBNP and troponin
Genetic testing guided by the neuromuscular phenotype

case.who: 17-year-old male student from Udon Thani with Duchenne muscular dystrophy
case.story: Wheelchair user since age 11; mother notes he is more breathless and tired, but he cannot exercise to reveal symptoms.
case.exam: Resting tachycardia, mild ankle oedema, displaced apex beat.
case.tests: Echo: LVEF 32% with dilated left ventricle; cardiac MRI: lateral wall late gadolinium enhancement.
case.q: Why was cardiac surveillance needed before symptoms appeared?
case.a: Dystrophinopathy cardiomyopathy is often silent in non-ambulant patients; early ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers slow progression.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Cardiomyopathies
Chapter 5 Neurologic Manifestations of Acquired Cardiac Disease and Arrhythmias

det.patho: Many genes causing skeletal myopathy are also expressed in heart muscle, so loss of dystrophin, lamin A/C, desmin or mitochondrial function damages cardiomyocytes. Fibrosis leads to dilatation, hypertrophy or conduction disease. Poor contraction and arrhythmia favour intracardiac thrombus formation.
det.clinical: Cardiac symptoms are often masked by limited mobility. Palpitations, syncope or sudden death reflect arrhythmia. Embolic strokes may be the first sign of cardiomyopathy in otherwise undiagnosed patients.
det.diagnosis: Routine screening with ECG and echo (or cardiac MRI) is recommended in at-risk neuromuscular disorders, often yearly from diagnosis or adolescence. Holter monitoring is important in myotonic dystrophy and laminopathies. In stroke, echo looks for low ejection fraction and thrombus.
det.treatment: Heart failure medications (ACE inhibitors or ARBs, beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid antagonists, SGLT2 inhibitors), pacemakers or ICDs for conduction disease, and anticoagulation for thrombus or AF. Cardiac transplantation is occasionally considered in selected neuromuscular patients.
det.prognosis: Cardiomyopathy is a major killer in Duchenne dystrophy and Friedreich ataxia; early treatment improves survival.
pearls: Female dystrophinopathy carriers can develop cardiomyopathy — screen them.
In myotonic dystrophy, sudden death relates to conduction disease; check ECG intervals.
Echocardiography belongs in every young stroke workup.
det.thd: Cardiomyopathy คือโรคกล้ามเนื้อหัวใจ ซึ่งเกี่ยวข้องกับระบบประสาทสองทาง คือเป็นแหล่งลิ่มเลือดอุดตันในสมอง และพบร่วมกับโรคกล้ามเนื้อเช่น Duchenne, Friedreich ataxia และ myotonic dystrophy ผู้ป่วยมักไม่มีอาการชัดเพราะเคลื่อนไหวน้อย จึงต้องตรวจคัดกรองด้วย ECG และ echocardiography เป็นระยะ การรักษาใช้ยารักษาหัวใจล้มเหลว เครื่องกระตุ้นหัวใจ และยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือดเมื่อมีข้อบ่งชี้

name: Cardiovascular autonomic failure
formal: Failure of autonomic cardiovascular regulation causing orthostatic hypotension and abnormal heart rate control; seen in MSA, pure autonomic failure and neuropathies.
simple: Failure of the nerves that control blood pressure and heart rate, causing dizziness or fainting on standing.
th: ระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติคุมความดันและชีพจรล้มเหลว ทำให้ความดันตกเมื่อลุกยืน หน้ามืด เป็นลม พบใน MSA pure autonomic failure และโรคปลายประสาท เช่น เบาหวาน amyloid
tempoNote: Usually develops over months to years; acute in autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy
feat: Orthostatic hypotension: drop ≥20 mmHg systolic or ≥10 diastolic within 3 minutes of standing
Lack of compensatory heart rate rise (neurogenic pattern)
Supine hypertension, postprandial hypotension
Light-headedness, coat-hanger neck pain, falls, syncope
Other autonomic features: urinary and erectile dysfunction, constipation, anhidrosis
inv: Lying and standing BP and heart rate; head-up tilt test
Autonomic function tests (Valsalva, deep breathing heart rate variability)
Cause work-up: glucose, B12, amyloid testing, AAG antibodies; MRI brain if MSA suspected

case.story: Two years of dizziness on standing and urinary urgency; recently clumsy speech and unsteady gait.
case.exam: BP 150/90 supine, 90/60 standing with heart rate unchanged; cerebellar ataxia and mild rigidity.
case.tests: Tilt test confirms neurogenic orthostatic hypotension; MRI pontine 'hot cross bun' sign.
case.q: What is the cause of the autonomic failure?
case.a: Multiple system atrophy (cerebellar type) with cardiovascular autonomic failure.

read.where: Chapter 32 Autonomic Aspects of Neurology — Manifestations of Orthostatic Hypotension
11 Non-motor Symptom Management in Parkinson’s Disease

det.patho: Failure of sympathetic vasoconstriction on standing results from lesions of central autonomic pathways (MSA), postganglionic neurons (Parkinson disease, pure autonomic failure, diabetic and amyloid neuropathy) or autonomic ganglia (autoimmune ganglionopathy). The baroreflex cannot raise vascular tone or heart rate, so blood pressure falls on standing.
det.clinical: Symptoms include dizziness, blurred vision, fatigue and neck pain on standing, worse after meals, heat or exertion. Supine hypertension is common and complicates treatment. Ask about bladder, bowel, sexual and sweating problems, and look for parkinsonism, ataxia or neuropathy.
det.diagnosis: Bedside orthostatic measurement plus heart rate response is the first test; a heart rate rise of less than about 15 bpm in the face of a significant drop suggests neurogenic cause. Tilt testing and autonomic function tests confirm. Investigate underlying cause with blood tests, NCS, MRI and specific tests for amyloid or antibodies.
det.treatment: Non-drug measures first: review drugs, increase fluid and salt, compression garments, head-up tilt of the bed, small meals, and counter-manoeuvres. Drug options include midodrine, fludrocortisone, droxidopa and pyridostigmine. Monitor and manage supine hypertension. Treat the underlying cause (e.g. immunotherapy for AAG, tafamidis or gene silencers for TTR amyloid).
det.prognosis: Depends on cause — poor in MSA, better in treatable neuropathies.
pearls: Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension: low BP on standing with little heart rate change.
Always check supine BP before increasing pressor drugs.
Early autonomic failure with parkinsonism suggests MSA rather than PD.
det.thd: Cardiovascular autonomic failure คือระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติไม่สามารถปรับความดันเมื่อลุกยืน ทำให้ความดันตกแต่ชีพจรไม่เพิ่ม หน้ามืดหรือหมดสติ สาเหตุ ได้แก่ MSA, Parkinson, pure autonomic failure, เบาหวาน และ amyloid ตรวจวัดความดันท่านอนท่ายืนและ tilt test รักษาด้วยการเพิ่มน้ำและเกลือ ถุงน่องรัด ยา midodrine หรือ fludrocortisone และระวังความดันสูงขณะนอน

name: Carnitine palmitoyl transferase II (CPT-II) deficiency
formal: Autosomal recessive disorder of long-chain fatty acid oxidation causing exercise-, fasting- or illness-induced myalgia and rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria.
simple: An inherited problem burning fat for energy that causes muscle pain and breakdown after exercise or fasting.
more: Autosomal recessive disorder of mitochondrial long-chain fatty acid oxidation causing recurrent exertional rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria triggered by prolonged exercise, fasting, or fever. Acylcarnitine profile and CPT2 testing; avoid fasting, use carbohydrate before exercise and a low-fat diet; medium-chain triglycerides may help.
th: สาเหตุพันธุกรรมที่พบบ่อยที่สุดของกล้ามเนื้อสลายซ้ำในผู้ใหญ่ — เกิดหลังออกกำลังนาน อดอาหาร หรือมีไข้
tempoNote: Attacks follow prolonged exertion, fasting, infection or cold; normal between episodes
feat: Recurrent myalgia and myoglobinuria after long-duration exercise rather than brief bursts
Provoked by fasting, fever, cold, general anaesthesia or certain drugs (valproate, ibuprofen in high doses)
Normal strength and usually normal CK between attacks
No second-wind phenomenon (unlike McArdle)
inv: CK and renal function during attacks
Plasma acylcarnitine profile (raised long-chain C16, C18:1) — may be normal between episodes
CPT2 gene sequencing (S113L common); enzyme assay in muscle or fibroblasts if needed

case.story: Third episode of dark urine: first after a marathon, second during dengue fever, now after skipping meals during a long hike.
case.exam: Tender calves and thighs, mild weakness; neurologically normal between episodes per old records.
case.tests: CK 62,000 U/L; acylcarnitines show raised C16 and C18:1; homozygous CPT2 S113L.
case.q: What practical advice prevents further attacks?
case.a: Avoid prolonged fasting and exhausting exercise, eat carbohydrates before and during exertion, treat fever early, and alert anaesthetists; some benefit from triheptanoin or a high-carbohydrate, lower-fat diet.

det.patho: CPT2 on the inner mitochondrial membrane converts long-chain acylcarnitines back into acyl-CoA for beta-oxidation. Partial deficiency, as in the adult myopathic form, limits fatty-acid fuel when muscle depends on it—during prolonged exercise, fasting or fever—so energy failure and fibre breakdown follow. Inheritance is autosomal recessive; the S113L variant is common in European populations, while other variants are found in Asia. Severe neonatal and infantile forms are multisystemic.
det.clinical: The adult form produces episodes of muscle pain, stiffness, weakness and myoglobinuria, typically starting in adolescence or early adulthood. Exercise tolerance for short bursts is normal; endurance activity is the problem. Some attacks occur with no clear trigger or with viral illness. Acute kidney injury is the main danger, and respiratory muscle involvement is occasionally reported.
det.diagnosis: Suspect CPT2 deficiency in recurrent rhabdomyolysis linked to prolonged activity, fasting or fever, with normal CK between attacks. Acylcarnitine profiling, ideally during or soon after an attack or after fasting, shows increased long-chain species. Genetic testing confirms; enzyme assay is used if only one variant is found. Muscle biopsy is often normal and may not show lipid storage.
det.treatment: Acute attacks are treated as rhabdomyolysis with IV fluids plus intravenous glucose to suppress fat oxidation. Prevention focuses on regular carbohydrate intake, avoiding prolonged fasting and exhausting exertion, early treatment of fever, and an emergency letter for hospitals. Triheptanoin or medium-chain triglycerides may help some patients; avoid valproate and prolonged fasting before surgery.
det.prognosis: The adult form has good long-term prognosis if renal failure is avoided; attacks often become less frequent with lifestyle adaptation.
pearls: Long exertion, fasting, fever = CPT2; short intense effort with second wind = McArdle.
Normal CK and biopsy between attacks do not exclude the diagnosis.
Give IV glucose during attacks and perioperatively to prevent fat-dependent energy crises.
det.thd: CPT II deficiency เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมแบบด้อยที่ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อใช้กรดไขมันเป็นพลังงานไม่ได้ จึงเกิดกล้ามเนื้อสลายซ้ำเมื่อออกกำลังเป็นเวลานาน อดอาหาร มีไข้ หรือหนาว ระหว่างอาการกำลังและ CK ปกติ วินิจฉัยด้วย acylcarnitine profile และตรวจยีน CPT2 การรักษาคือให้สารน้ำและกลูโคสขณะเกิดอาการ และป้องกันด้วยการกินคาร์โบไฮเดรตสม่ำเสมอ ไม่อดอาหาร และรักษาไข้เร็ว

qx.stem: A 17-year-old schoolboy from Nakhon Si Thammarat has recurrent muscle pain and dark urine after prolonged exercise, fasting during Ramadan and a flu-like illness. There is no second-wind phenomenon and a high-carbohydrate meal improves his tolerance. His forearm exercise test gives a normal lactate rise, and acylcarnitine analysis shows raised long-chain species.
qx.q: Which advice is the most appropriate?
opts: Fast regularly to induce ketosis
Avoid prolonged fasting and heavy exercise, eat frequent carbohydrate-rich meals and consider medium-chain triglyceride or triheptanoin supplementation
Start long-term corticosteroids
Begin high-dose coenzyme Q10 as the main treatment
Restrict carbohydrate and take a fat-rich diet
qx.why: Exertional rhabdomyolysis triggered by fasting, prolonged effort or infection with a normal lactate response and abnormal long-chain acylcarnitines indicates CPT II deficiency, a long-chain fatty acid oxidation defect. Management centres on avoiding fasting and prolonged exercise, high-carbohydrate intake, and medium-chain substrates; a fat-rich diet is harmful. McArdle disease differs by second wind and blunted lactate.

name: Carnitine transporter deficiency
formal: Autosomal recessive SLC22A5 defect causing primary systemic carnitine deficiency with hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy, and myopathy, due to impaired fatty acid transport.
simple: An inherited inability to move carnitine into cells, which weakens muscles and the heart and can cause low blood sugar.
more: Plasma carnitine is very low; confirm with gene testing. Lifelong oral L-carnitine is very effective at preventing complications.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมยีนด้อย SLC22A5 ทำให้ขาดคาร์นิทีนทั่วร่างกาย เกิดน้ำตาลต่ำโดยไม่มีคีโตน กล้ามเนื้อหัวใจผิดปกติ และกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง รักษาได้ดีด้วย L-carnitine
tempoNote: Metabolic crises in infancy with fasting or illness; cardiomyopathy and myopathy later
feat: Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and encephalopathy in infants during fasting or infection
Dilated or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in childhood
Proximal myopathy, hypotonia, raised CK
Liver dysfunction and hyperammonaemia during crises
Adults may be asymptomatic or present with arrhythmia
inv: Very low plasma free and total carnitine
High urinary carnitine loss (reduced renal reabsorption)
SLC22A5 genetic testing; echocardiography and ECG

case.story: Became floppy and unrousable after two days of vomiting; previously tired easily.
case.exam: Lethargic, hepatomegaly, hypotonia.
case.tests: Glucose 1.8 mmol/L with no ketones, ammonia raised; plasma free carnitine very low; echo dilated cardiomyopathy.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and treatment?
case.a: Primary carnitine deficiency (SLC22A5); lifelong oral L-carnitine with avoidance of fasting.

det.patho: SLC22A5 encodes OCTN2, the high-affinity carnitine transporter in kidney, heart and muscle. Loss of function causes renal carnitine wasting and low tissue carnitine, so long-chain fats cannot be shuttled across the inner mitochondrial membrane for burning. Energy failure occurs when fat is the main fuel—during fasting and illness, and continuously in the heart.
det.clinical: Infants present with hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and Reye-like encephalopathy; older children with cardiomyopathy and myopathy. Sudden cardiac death is a risk. Newborn screening detects many cases, including affected mothers identified through their infants.
det.diagnosis: Plasma carnitine is markedly low; urine carnitine excretion is inappropriately high. Confirm with SLC22A5 sequencing or reduced carnitine uptake in fibroblasts.
det.treatment: Oral L-carnitine supplementation corrects cardiomyopathy and myopathy in most patients. Avoid prolonged fasting, and give IV glucose during illness. Monitor carnitine levels, heart function and ECG.
det.prognosis: Excellent with early treatment; untreated disease can cause sudden death.
pearls: Treatable cause of cardiomyopathy: always check carnitine in childhood cardiomyopathy.
Low carnitine in a newborn screen may reveal an affected mother.
Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia points to fatty acid oxidation defects.
det.thd: Carnitine transporter deficiency เกิดจากยีน SLC22A5 ทำให้ไตขับคาร์นิทีนออกมากและร่างกายขาดคาร์นิทีน เด็กเล็กมีน้ำตาลต่ำแบบไม่มีคีโตนและซึมเมื่ออดอาหาร เด็กโตมีกล้ามเนื้อหัวใจผิดปกติและอ่อนแรง ตรวจระดับคาร์นิทีนต่ำและยืนยันด้วยยีน รักษาด้วย L-carnitine ตลอดชีวิตซึ่งได้ผลดีมาก

name: Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS)
formal: Median nerve entrapment at the wrist causing thumb-to-ring finger paraesthesia, nocturnal symptoms, thenar weakness; confirmed by slowed distal median conduction.
simple: Pressure on a nerve in the wrist that causes numbness, tingling and weakness in the thumb and first fingers.
more: Electrodiagnostic study shows prolonged median sensory and motor latencies with preserved ulnar responses across the wrist; ultrasound shows an enlarged median nerve. Treat with wrist splinting, steroid injection or surgical carpal tunnel release.
th: เส้นประสาท median ถูกกดที่ข้อมือ — ชานิ้วโป้งถึงนิ้วนางครึ่งนิ้ว ปวดชาตอนกลางคืน สะบัดมือแล้วดีขึ้น
feat: Nocturnal paraesthesia in the thumb to radial ring finger; relief by shaking the hand
Sensation over the thenar eminence spared (palmar cutaneous branch leaves before the tunnel)
Late thenar (APB) wasting
Associations: pregnancy, hypothyroidism, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, amyloidosis
inv: NCS: prolonged median distal latency, slowed sensory conduction across the wrist
Ultrasound: enlarged median nerve cross-sectional area

case.story: Wakes at night with numb right fingers and shakes her hand to relieve it.
case.exam: Reduced sensation on the thumb, index and middle fingers, normal palm sensation, Phalen positive, mild APB weakness.
case.tests: Median sensory latency prolonged; ulnar normal.
case.q: Why is palm sensation spared?
case.a: The palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the carpal tunnel.

qx.stem: A 44-year-old noodle-shop cook in Bangkok reports nocturnal numbness of the thumb, index and middle fingers that wakes her from sleep and eases when she shakes her hand. Examination shows reduced sensation over the median digits and a positive Tinel sign at the wrist. She asks which electrodiagnostic result would be most sensitive for early disease.
qx.q: Which comparison study is most useful when routine median conduction studies are borderline?
opts: Median-versus-ulnar or radial sensory latency comparison over the same distance to the ring finger and thumb
Median nerve F-wave latency
Needle EMG of the biceps brachii
H-reflex of the soleus
Repetitive stimulation of the abductor pollicis brevis
qx.why: Comparing the median sensory latency with an ulnar or radial latency on the same limb over an identical distance cancels out systemic factors such as temperature and polyneuropathy, so it detects focal slowing earlier than absolute values. F-waves are poor at detecting distal focal lesions. Biceps EMG and the soleus H-reflex test other segments, and repetitive stimulation is a junction test.

qx.stem: A 45-year-old seamstress from Chiang Rai has nocturnal hand tingling relieved by shaking. Standard median sensory and motor conduction values are at the upper limit of normal.
qx.q: Which approach raises the sensitivity of electrodiagnostic testing?
opts: Check the F-wave persistence in the median nerve alone
Perform needle EMG of the paraspinal muscles only
Record the H-reflex from the thenar muscles
Compare median with ulnar (or radial) sensory latency in the same hand over equal distances, for example the ring finger
Record a blink reflex
qx.why: Mild carpal tunnel syndrome can hide behind a normal absolute median latency, so within-hand comparisons with an adjacent unaffected nerve (median versus ulnar or radial, or palm-to-wrist segments) detect early slowing, because they correct for temperature, age and height. Distal motor latency is less sensitive than sensory testing. F-waves, H-reflexes and blink reflexes assess other pathways.

det.patho: Compression of the median nerve beneath the transverse carpal ligament raises local pressure, impairs epineurial blood flow and leads to focal demyelination, then axonal loss if prolonged. Contributing factors include female sex, obesity, pregnancy, diabetes, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly, wrist fractures, dialysis and transthyretin amyloidosis (bilateral CTS often predates amyloid cardiomyopathy). It is the most common entrapment neuropathy.
det.clinical: Numbness, tingling and pain affect the thumb, index, middle and radial half of the ring finger, typically waking the patient at night and relieved by shaking the hand (flick sign). Symptoms may be felt more diffusely or radiate to the forearm. Repetitive grip or wrist flexion aggravates them. Advanced cases show thenar wasting and weakness of thumb abduction. The palm over the thenar eminence is spared because its cutaneous branch bypasses the tunnel.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by provocative tests (Phalen, Tinel, carpal compression) that have moderate accuracy. Nerve conduction studies confirm focal slowing of median sensory and motor fibres across the wrist and grade severity; comparison techniques (median vs ulnar or radial) increase sensitivity. Ultrasound shows an enlarged median nerve cross-sectional area at the tunnel inlet. Consider C6–C7 radiculopathy, proximal median neuropathy, polyneuropathy and thoracic outlet syndrome, which can coexist (double crush).
det.treatment: Mild to moderate cases respond to neutral-position night splinting, activity modification and treatment of underlying conditions; local corticosteroid injection gives short- to medium-term relief. Surgical carpal tunnel release (open or endoscopic) is indicated for persistent symptoms, constant numbness, thenar weakness or wasting, or severe electrodiagnostic changes. Pregnancy-related CTS usually settles after delivery.
det.prognosis: Most improve with conservative care or surgery; advanced axonal loss may leave persistent numbness or weakness.
pearls: Spared palm sensation separates CTS from a more proximal median lesion.
Bilateral CTS in an older man: consider transthyretin amyloidosis.
Neck pain, reflex changes or forearm sensory loss suggest radiculopathy instead.
det.thd: CTS คือเส้นประสาท median ถูกกดที่อุโมงค์ข้อมือ พบบ่อยที่สุดในบรรดาโรคเส้นประสาทถูกกดทับ ปัจจัยเสี่ยงคือเพศหญิง อ้วน ตั้งครรภ์ เบาหวาน ไทรอยด์ต่ำ และ amyloidosis อาการคือชาและปวดนิ้วโป้งถึงครึ่งนิ้วนาง ตื่นกลางดึกแล้วสะบัดมือจึงดีขึ้น ระยะท้ายมีกล้ามเนื้อโคนนิ้วโป้งลีบ ฝ่ามือส่วน thenar ไม่ชาเพราะแขนงประสาทแยกก่อนเข้าอุโมงค์ วินิจฉัยจากอาการร่วมกับ NCS หรืออัลตราซาวด์ รักษาด้วยเฝือกอ่อนตอนกลางคืน ฉีดสเตียรอยด์ และผ่าตัดเมื่ออาการรุนแรงหรือกล้ามเนื้อลีบ

name: Castleman disease
formal: Lymphoproliferative disorder with angiofollicular lymph node hyperplasia, linked to POEMS syndrome with sensorimotor demyelinating neuropathy, high VEGF, and plasma cell dyscrasia.
simple: A rare disease causing enlarged lymph nodes, which can be linked with nerve damage in some patients.
more: Lymph node biopsy diagnoses it. Treatment includes surgery for localised disease and rituximab, siltuximab, or chemotherapy for multicentric disease.
th: โรคต่อมน้ำเหลืองโตชนิดไม่ใช่มะเร็ง ชนิดหลายตำแหน่งสัมพันธ์กับ POEMS syndrome ที่มีเส้นประสาทอักเสบแบบ demyelinating
tempoNote: Unicentric disease is often indolent; multicentric disease has subacute systemic flares
feat: Not a primary neurological disease: lymphoproliferative disorder with unicentric and multicentric forms
Multicentric form: fever, night sweats, weight loss, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, oedema and anaemia
Neurological link is mainly through POEMS syndrome: sensorimotor demyelinating neuropathy with lambda paraprotein and high VEGF
HHV-8 drives one multicentric subtype, especially with HIV
TAFRO subtype: thrombocytopenia, anasarca, fever, reticulin fibrosis, organomegaly
inv: Excision biopsy of an enlarged lymph node for histology
HHV-8 PCR, HIV serology, CRP, IL-6, albumin, blood count
Serum and urine immunofixation and plasma VEGF if neuropathy is present (POEMS screen)
NCS: uniform demyelination with axonal loss, more in lower limbs, in POEMS-associated cases

case.story: Over a year he has developed numb, weak feet and then hands, with darkening skin, swollen legs and enlarged neck nodes.
case.exam: Distal symmetric weakness and sensory loss with areflexia, hepatosplenomegaly, skin hyperpigmentation, white nails, pitting oedema.
case.tests: Lymph node biopsy: Castleman disease, plasma cell variant; small IgA lambda paraprotein; VEGF markedly raised; NCS demyelinating.
case.q: Which syndrome links his nodes and his neuropathy, and why does it matter?
case.a: POEMS syndrome associated with Castleman disease; it is often misdiagnosed as CIDP and responds to treating the plasma cell disorder, not to IVIG.

det.patho: Castleman disease is a group of lymph node disorders with characteristic histology driven by excess cytokines, particularly IL-6. Unicentric disease involves one node region; multicentric disease is subdivided into HHV-8-associated, POEMS-associated and idiopathic (iMCD, including TAFRO). In POEMS, a monoclonal plasma cell population produces VEGF, which increases vascular permeability and contributes to nerve damage.
det.clinical: Unicentric disease is often found incidentally as a mass. Multicentric disease causes systemic inflammation with fever, lymphadenopathy, organomegaly, effusions and cytopenias. Neuropathy occurs mainly in the POEMS context: a progressive, symmetric, sensorimotor polyradiculoneuropathy, painful in many, often mistaken for CIDP. Castleman-variant POEMS may have a less prominent neuropathy.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires excision lymph node biopsy with compatible histology, plus exclusion of infections, autoimmune disease and lymphoma that can mimic it. Test HHV-8 and HIV. In any patient with Castleman disease and neuropathy, screen for a lambda light-chain paraprotein and measure VEGF, skeletal survey for sclerotic lesions, and look for endocrine dysfunction.
det.treatment: Unicentric disease is usually cured by surgical excision. Idiopathic multicentric disease is treated first-line with the anti-IL-6 antibody siltuximab (or tocilizumab), with rituximab, steroids or chemotherapy for refractory cases. HHV-8 disease uses rituximab with or without antivirals and antiretroviral therapy. POEMS-associated neuropathy responds to treatment of the plasma cell clone (radiotherapy for isolated lesions, lenalidomide-based therapy or autologous stem cell transplant).
det.prognosis: Unicentric disease has an excellent outcome; multicentric disease is variable, and neuropathy improves slowly over months to years after successful therapy.
pearls: Demyelinating neuropathy plus lymphadenopathy and organomegaly: screen for POEMS and Castleman disease.
A 'CIDP' that fails IVIG with a lambda paraprotein — measure VEGF.
Siltuximab targets IL-6, the key cytokine in idiopathic multicentric disease.
det.thd: Castleman disease เป็นโรคต่อมน้ำเหลืองโตที่ไม่ใช่มะเร็ง เกิดจาก cytokine โดยเฉพาะ IL-6 มากเกิน ชนิดเดียวตำแหน่งรักษาด้วยการผ่าตัด ชนิดหลายตำแหน่งมีไข้ ต่อมน้ำเหลืองและตับม้ามโต ทางระบบประสาทสัมพันธ์กับ POEMS syndrome ซึ่งมีเส้นประสาทอักเสบแบบ demyelinating คล้าย CIDP แต่มี lambda paraprotein และ VEGF สูง การรักษาต้องรักษาโรคต้นเหตุ เช่น siltuximab หรือรักษา plasma cell clone

name: Cat scratch disease
formal: Bartonella henselae infection after cat scratch or bite, with regional lymphadenopathy; neurological complications include encephalopathy, neuroretinitis and myelitis.
simple: An infection from a cat scratch causing swollen glands, and rarely brain or eye problems.
th: การติดเชื้อ Bartonella henselae จากการสัมผัสแมวหรือลูกแมว ทำให้ต่อมน้ำเหลืองโตใกล้แผล ภาวะแทรกซ้อนทางประสาทที่สำคัญคือ encephalopathy ที่มักชัก (รวมถึง status epilepticus) ในเด็ก และ neuroretinitis ที่มี macular star ส่วนใหญ่หายดี
tempoNote: Papule within a week of contact, nodes after 1-7 weeks, encephalopathy days to about 2 months after the nodes
feat: Contact with cats, especially kittens or cats with fleas; a scratch or bite is not always remembered
Papule or pustule at the inoculation site followed by tender regional lymphadenopathy, sometimes suppurating
Encephalopathy in a small percentage of cases: headache, agitation or combative behaviour, then seizures in about half, sometimes status epilepticus
Neuroretinitis: painless, usually unilateral visual loss with disc swelling and a macular star of exudates
Rarer: facial and other cranial neuropathies, transverse myelitis, radiculitis, vertebral osteomyelitis; in advanced HIV, bacillary angiomatosis of the brain
inv: Bartonella henselae IgG/IgM serology (a high IgG titre supports recent infection) and PCR of node aspirate, tissue or blood
CSF is often normal or shows mild lymphocytosis and raised protein; low glucose is rare
MRI brain is usually normal; EEG shows diffuse slowing or focal discharges
Dilated fundoscopy and OCT for disc oedema and macular exudates; repeat a week later as the star may appear late

case.who: 9-year-old girl from Nakhon Pathom whose family adopted two stray kittens
case.story: A tender lump in her left armpit for three weeks, then sudden confusion, aggression and a 40-minute generalised seizure needing two doses of midazolam.
case.exam: Drowsy but rousable after the seizure, healed scratch on the left forearm, tender 3 cm axillary node, no focal signs, normal fundi.
case.tests: CSF 6 cells, protein 0.5 g/L, glucose normal; HSV PCR negative; MRI normal; EEG diffuse slowing; Bartonella henselae IgG 1:1024 and node PCR positive.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what outcome should the parents expect?
case.a: Cat scratch encephalopathy; control seizures, give supportive care and a Bartonella-active antibiotic (for example azithromycin or rifampicin, doxycycline if older), and expect full recovery within days to weeks in most children.

det.patho: Bartonella henselae is a fastidious Gram-negative bacillus carried by cats and spread among them by fleas; humans are infected through a scratch, bite or flea faeces in the skin. Typical disease is a granulomatous, sometimes suppurative, lymphadenitis. Whether encephalopathy is due to direct invasion, vasculitis or an immune response is uncertain, since the organism is rarely found in the brain. In profound immunosuppression the organism causes vascular proliferative lesions (bacillary angiomatosis), which can involve the brain.
det.clinical: About one in ten patients has atypical disease, including Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome, neuroretinitis, encephalopathy, hepatosplenic granulomas and prolonged fever. Encephalopathy affects children and young adults, begins abruptly with headache and altered behaviour, and seizures are frequent; fever may be absent. Neuroretinitis causes a sudden drop of vision with an afferent pupil defect, disc swelling and a macular star that may only develop after one to two weeks. Recovery is usually complete, but persistent cognitive problems, ataxia or seizures occasionally occur.
det.diagnosis: The key is to ask about cat contact, not only about scratches. Serology is the usual test and PCR of a node or aspirate adds specificity. CSF and MRI are mostly used to exclude other causes such as HSV, enterovirus or autoimmune encephalitis. In neuroretinitis, serology for syphilis, Lyme and Toxoplasma and a check of blood pressure are part of the work-up.
det.treatment: Uncomplicated lymphadenitis is often self-limited, and azithromycin for 5 days hastens node resolution. For neurological or ocular disease many experts give doxycycline with rifampicin for 4-6 weeks (azithromycin or rifampicin-based combinations in young children), although no trial proves benefit. Seizures and status epilepticus are managed in the usual way, and short-term antiseizure medicine is usually sufficient. Corticosteroids are sometimes added for neuroretinitis with severe swelling, but evidence is limited.
det.prognosis: Encephalopathy and neuroretinitis usually resolve over weeks to months with a good final outcome; a few patients keep mild optic neuropathy or neurological sequelae.
pearls: Ask about kittens: a child with new-onset status epilepticus and regional lymphadenopathy may have cat scratch encephalopathy.
Disc swelling with a macular star (which may appear late) is neuroretinitis, not optic neuritis, and does not predict multiple sclerosis.
Normal MRI and nearly normal CSF are typical; serology makes the diagnosis.

Visual evoked potentials
Bartonella henselae serology
Oligoclonal bands in CSF
Temporal artery biopsy

name: Cataplexy
formal: Sudden bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion with preserved consciousness, characteristic of narcolepsy type 1 due to hypocretin deficiency.
simple: Sudden muscle weakness or collapse triggered by strong emotions such as laughter, while staying awake.
th: กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงฉับพลันสองข้างเมื่อมีอารมณ์ เช่น หัวเราะ โดยยังรู้สึกตัวดี เป็นลักษณะเฉพาะของ narcolepsy type 1 จากการขาด hypocretin (orexin)
tempoNote: Attacks last seconds to about 2 minutes, triggered by emotion; usually begins within a few years of the onset of sleepiness
feat: Brief bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by laughter, joking, surprise or anger
Consciousness and memory preserved; partial attacks cause jaw sagging, head drop, facial twitching or knee buckling
Tendon reflexes are transiently lost during an attack
Occurs with daytime sleepiness, hypnagogic hallucinations, sleep paralysis and broken night sleep
Children may show facial grimacing and tongue protrusion near onset (cataplectic facies)
inv: Overnight PSG then MSLT: average latency to sleep of 8 min or under plus at least two SOREMPs (a SOREMP on the night PSG counts)
CSF hypocretin-1 110 pg/mL or below confirms narcolepsy type 1
HLA-DQB1*06:02 is supportive but not diagnostic
MRI brain if atypical features suggest secondary narcolepsy (hypothalamic lesion, Niemann–Pick C, anti-Ma2)

case.who: 19-year-old female university student from Chiang Mai
case.story: When friends make her laugh, her knees buckle and her head drops for a few seconds while she stays aware; she has fallen asleep in lectures for two years and sees vivid figures as she drifts off.
case.exam: Normal between attacks; during a filmed attack her knee reflexes are absent.
case.tests: MSLT mean latency 3 minutes with four SOREMPs; HLA-DQB1*06:02 positive.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and which drugs treat both sleepiness and cataplexy?
case.a: Narcolepsy type 1 with cataplexy; oxybate (including low-sodium oxybate) or pitolisant treats both, while venlafaxine or an SSRI can be added for cataplexy.

read.where: Chapter 51 Neurologic Aspects of Sleep Medicine

det.patho: Cataplexy results from loss of hypothalamic hypocretin (orexin) neurons, most likely by an autoimmune T-cell process in people carrying HLA-DQB1*06:02. Without orexin, the brainstem circuits that produce REM atonia are released by emotional input from the amygdala and medial prefrontal cortex. It is therefore an intrusion of REM-sleep paralysis into wakefulness.
det.clinical: Positive emotions, especially laughter, are the classic trigger. Attacks are bilateral, brief and evolve over seconds, and consciousness is clear throughout. Partial attacks affecting face, neck or knees are more common than full collapse. Sudden stopping of antidepressants can provoke status cataplecticus with repeated attacks for hours.
det.diagnosis: A clear history of emotion-triggered bilateral weakness with preserved awareness is nearly diagnostic. Confirm narcolepsy type 1 with MSLT showing short sleep latency and SOREMPs, or with low CSF hypocretin-1. Filming an attack and checking reflexes helps when the history is uncertain. Exclude seizures, syncope and functional attacks, and look for secondary causes when onset is atypical.
det.treatment: Oxybates are highly effective for cataplexy and sleepiness; options now include twice-nightly sodium oxybate, low-sodium mixed oxybate salts and once-nightly extended-release sodium oxybate. Pitolisant, an H3 inverse agonist, reduces cataplexy and sleepiness and is not a controlled drug. Venlafaxine, SSRIs or clomipramine suppress cataplexy through REM suppression but must not be stopped abruptly. Orexin-2 receptor agonists are in late-phase trials for narcolepsy type 1.
det.prognosis: Cataplexy is lifelong but often lessens with age and responds well to treatment.
pearls: Cataplexy is the only symptom specific to narcolepsy type 1; sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations are common in healthy people.
Reflexes disappear during an attack, which helps separate it from functional collapse.
Abrupt withdrawal of antidepressants can trigger status cataplecticus.
det.thd: Cataplexy คืออาการกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงทันทีสองข้างเมื่อหัวเราะหรือมีอารมณ์ โดยยังรู้สึกตัว เกิดจากการสูญเสียเซลล์ hypocretin ใน hypothalamus ทำให้ภาวะ atonia ของ REM แทรกเข้ามาตอนตื่น เป็นลักษณะเฉพาะของ narcolepsy type 1 ยืนยันด้วย MSLT หรือ CSF hypocretin ต่ำ ยาที่ได้ผลคือ oxybate (รวมสูตรโซเดียมต่ำ) pitolisant และยากลุ่ม venlafaxine/SSRI

qx.stem: A 22-year-old male motorcycle courier from Pathum Thani has fallen asleep at red lights for 3 years. When colleagues tease him, his jaw drops and his knees give way for a few seconds while he hears everything around him. He was started on venlafaxine by a psychiatrist last year and stopped it abruptly 2 days ago; since then he has had dozens of attacks a day.
qx.q: What best explains the new increase in attacks?
opts: Emergence of atonic seizures from sleep deprivation
Rebound cataplexy after abrupt withdrawal of a REM-suppressing antidepressant
Development of functional collapses after psychiatric treatment
Progression to idiopathic hypersomnia
Serotonin syndrome from venlafaxine
qx.why: Antidepressants suppress cataplexy, and stopping them suddenly can cause a severe rebound called status cataplecticus. The emotional trigger, preserved awareness and brief bilateral loss of tone are typical of cataplexy in narcolepsy type 1. Atonic seizures impair awareness and are not emotion-triggered, and idiopathic hypersomnia has no cataplexy.

qx.stem: A 31-year-old man with narcolepsy type 1 has controlled his cataplexy with venlafaxine for two years. After running out of tablets while travelling, he stops them suddenly. Two days later he has near-continuous episodes of facial and knee weakness that leave him unable to stand, with preserved awareness and no loss of consciousness. EEG during an episode shows wakefulness and the examination is otherwise normal.
qx.q: What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Intravenous levetiracetam for non-convulsive status epilepticus
High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone
Plasma exchange for autoimmune myasthenic crisis
Restart venlafaxine and review the long-term anticataplectic plan
Treat with intravenous thiamine and glucose
qx.why: Abrupt withdrawal of antidepressants that suppress REM sleep can precipitate rebound cataplexy and status cataplecticus. The treatment is to restart the drug and then review long-term options such as oxybate or pitolisant. Preserved awareness with a wake EEG excludes non-convulsive seizures, and the context makes immune therapy or Wernicke encephalopathy unlikely.

name: Catatonia
formal: Psychomotor syndrome with stupor, mutism, posturing, negativism, waxy flexibility or excitement; occurs in psychiatric and medical disorders and responds to benzodiazepines or ECT.
simple: A state in which a person becomes unusually still and unresponsive, or sometimes agitated, and may hold odd postures.
th: Catatonia คือกลุ่มอาการของการเคลื่อนไหวและพฤติกรรมที่ผิดปกติ ได้แก่ นิ่งเฉย ไม่พูด ค้างท่า ต่อต้าน หรือกระวนกระวายมากผิดปกติ พบทั้งในโรคอารมณ์สองขั้ว โรคจิต และโรคทางกาย เช่น autoimmune encephalitis ตอบสนองดีต่อ lorazepam และ ECT และต้องระวังชนิดที่มีไข้สูง (malignant catatonia)
tempoNote: Appears over days to a few weeks; may continue for months untreated, and the malignant form can become life-threatening within a day or two
feat: Stupor with mutism and little response to the surroundings, or the opposite pole of purposeless excitement; some patients alternate between both
Negativism and posture signs: refusal to cooperate, resisting passive movement, holding odd postures, waxy flexibility, mitgehen, echolalia and echopraxia
Refusal to eat or drink leads to dehydration, immobility to thrombosis and pressure sores; the eyes are often open, which separates it from coma
Causes include bipolar and depressive illness, schizophrenia, autoimmune encephalitis (anti-NMDA receptor), drugs, metabolic and structural brain disease
Malignant catatonia adds fever, unstable blood pressure, tachycardia and sweating, and is hard to separate from neuroleptic malignant syndrome
inv: Bedside rating (Bush-Francis scale) and a lorazepam challenge of 1–2 mg intravenously with re-examination after 5–10 minutes
CK, renal function, electrolytes, iron, thyroid, infection screen and drug toxicology; EEG, MRI brain and CSF with autoimmune antibodies at first presentation
Leg veins and D-dimer or imaging when the patient has been immobile, because pulmonary embolism is a common cause of death

case.who: 23-year-old woman, a call-centre worker from Chiang Mai, with bipolar disorder
case.story: After several days of elevated mood and no sleep she became silent, stopped eating and drinking, and stayed rigidly in bed with her eyes open. She had been given haloperidol injections in the emergency room two days earlier.
case.exam: Mute, staring, resists any movement, holds a raised arm in position and repeats the examiner's gesture. Temperature 37.9 °C, pulse 112.
case.tests: CK 3,200 U/L; CT head, EEG and CSF are normal; lorazepam 2 mg intravenously produces speech and eating within minutes, with relapse after a few hours.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what treatment must be avoided or considered if lorazepam fails?
case.a: Catatonia in bipolar illness, with early malignant features. Stop the antipsychotic, continue scheduled lorazepam, give fluids and thromboprophylaxis, and refer for ECT if there is no clear response within a day or two or if fever and instability worsen.

read.where: 2. Acute Parkinsonism — catatonia as a psychiatric cause of acute akinesia
1 - Clinical overview and phenomenology of movement disorders

det.patho: Catatonia is a syndrome of disordered frontal-subcortical circuits that regulate movement, emotion and behaviour. Reduced GABA-A and dopamine activity and altered glutamate signalling are all implicated, which fits the response to lorazepam and the harm from dopamine blockers. It occurs in mood disorders more often than in schizophrenia, and also with encephalitis, metabolic disease and drug toxicity. Pre-existing low dopamine tone and stress may add to the vulnerability.
det.clinical: The core features are reduced responsiveness, mutism, negativism and abnormal posture. Many clinicians think of waxy flexibility as the defining sign, but it is not needed, and a patient who simply will not move or talk with open eyes and intact brainstem reflexes should raise the question. Excited forms look like extreme agitation with purposeless movement. Malignant catatonia is the form with fever and autonomic instability; it was described in the nineteenth century, carried a very high mortality before modern care, and now has a much lower one when treated early.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical and relies on a structured examination for several of the typical signs, most often with the Bush-Francis scale or DSM-5 criteria. A positive response to a lorazepam challenge supports it but a negative response does not exclude it. Always search for a medical cause: autoimmune encephalitis, epileptic status, delirium, infection, metabolic and structural disease, and drug causes including antipsychotics, valproate, lithium and withdrawal states. Check CK, iron and white count, since they are raised in the malignant form.
det.treatment: Lorazepam is first-line, usually 1–2 mg every 6–8 hours with upward titration if tolerated. ECT should be given without delay when the response is partial, when catatonia is malignant, or when the patient is not eating or drinking; in the malignant form the book urged ECT within one to two days of non-response. Antipsychotics should be withheld in the acute phase because they can worsen catatonia and trigger NMS. Treat the underlying illness, including immunotherapy for autoimmune encephalitis, and give fluids, nutrition and prophylaxis against venous thrombosis. NMDA antagonists such as amantadine or memantine are used as adjuncts in resistant cases.
det.prognosis: Most patients respond well to lorazepam or ECT, but relapse is common while the underlying illness persists. Malignant catatonia is potentially lethal, with a recent mortality of around one in ten in published cases when recognised early.
pearls: Open eyes, mutism and no movement in a patient who resists examination: think catatonia before coma.
Do not use antipsychotics in the acute phase; ECT is life-saving in the malignant form.
Always look for autoimmune encephalitis or epileptic status as the cause.
det.thd: Catatonia คือกลุ่มอาการที่ผู้ป่วยนิ่งเฉย ไม่พูด ลืมตาแต่ไม่ตอบสนอง ค้างท่า ต่อต้านการเคลื่อนไหว หรือกระสับกระส่ายแบบไร้จุดหมาย พบได้ในโรคอารมณ์ โรคจิต และโรคทางกาย เช่น anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis ตรวจทดสอบด้วย lorazepam ทางหลอดเลือดดำ ซึ่งมักตอบสนองภายในไม่กี่นาที ต้องหลีกเลี่ยงยาต้านโรคจิตในช่วงเฉียบพลันเพราะอาจกระตุ้น NMS หากมีไข้สูงและระบบอัตโนมัติรวน (malignant catatonia) หรือ lorazepam ไม่ได้ผลใน 1–2 วัน ควรรักษาด้วย ECT ทันที

qx.stem: A 30-year-old woman with bipolar disorder from Chiang Mai stops eating and speaking over four days. She holds rigid postures, resists passive movement and echoes the nurse's words. Temperature is 39.1 °C, heart rate 128/min, BP fluctuating, CK 3,500 U/L. She has received no antipsychotic for six months. MRI brain and CSF are normal; EEG shows diffuse slowing without seizures.
qx.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
opts: Haloperidol IM to control agitation
Dantrolene alone without benzodiazepine
Olanzapine orally once she can swallow
Observation until the fever settles
IV lorazepam, with early electroconvulsive therapy if there is no rapid response
qx.why: Catatonic signs with fever and autonomic instability define malignant catatonia, a medical emergency. Benzodiazepines (IV lorazepam, escalated as needed) are first-line, and ECT is life-saving when the response is inadequate. Antipsychotics can worsen it or provoke a neuroleptic malignant-like state, and autoimmune encephalitis (e.g. anti-NMDAR) should be considered in new-onset cases.

qx.stem: A 26-year-old man from Ubon Ratchathani with bipolar disorder lies in bed with open eyes, will not speak or eat, resists passive movement and holds his arm in the air when it is lifted. Temperature is 37.6 °C. CT head and EEG are normal. He received a haloperidol injection yesterday. Two milligrams of intravenous lorazepam is given; ten minutes later he answers questions and drinks water.
qx.q: What does this response indicate and what should be done?
opts: The response proves a psychogenic disorder; the antipsychotic should be increased
The response indicates catatonia; give scheduled lorazepam, avoid antipsychotics, and plan ECT if improvement is incomplete or malignant features appear
The response excludes any organic cause, so no further investigations are needed
The response is diagnostic of non-convulsive status epilepticus
The response suggests NMS, so dantrolene is the first-line treatment
qx.why: Mutism, negativism and posturing in an awake patient with a prompt response to lorazepam point to catatonia. Treatment is scheduled benzodiazepine with withdrawal of antipsychotics, which can precipitate NMS, and ECT when response is partial or malignant features such as fever and autonomic instability develop. A positive challenge does not exclude medical causes such as autoimmune encephalitis, so a cause search remains necessary, and it does not point to NCSE, in which the EEG is abnormal.
