name: Catheter-related infections
formal: Device-associated bloodstream or local infections, including intrathecal or ventricular catheter infection causing meningitis or ventriculitis.
simple: Infections that start from a tube placed in the body, which can sometimes spread to the brain coverings.
th: การติดเชื้อที่เกิดจากสายหรืออุปกรณ์ในระบบประสาท เช่น ท่อระบายน้ำไขสันหลังจากโพรงสมอง (EVD) ท่อ shunt หรือ Ommaya reservoir ทำให้เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบหรือโพรงสมองอักเสบ
tempoNote: Most internalised shunt infections appear within weeks to months of surgery; externalised drains usually within days to a couple of weeks
feat: Fever, headache, irritability or drowsiness in a patient with a shunt, drain or reservoir
Signs of shunt malfunction (vomiting, bulging fontanelle, lethargy) may be the only clue
Redness or discharge along the tract; abdominal pain or peritonitis when the distal end is infected
Commonest organisms are skin flora: coagulase-negative staphylococci and Staphylococcus aureus
Early-onset infection after placement and repeated revisions are strong risk factors
inv: CSF from the device or lumbar puncture for cell count, Gram stain and culture, held for at least 10 days to detect slow growers such as Cutibacterium
Blood cultures and inflammatory markers, with abdominal imaging if the distal catheter is suspected
Neuroimaging (CT or MRI) for hydrocephalus, ventriculitis or abscess

case.story: Three weeks after revision of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt for hydrocephalus he has fever, vomiting and unusual sleepiness.
case.exam: Temperature 38.8 C, drowsy, bulging anterior fontanelle is closed, mild neck stiffness, redness along the scalp part of the shunt tract.
case.tests: Shunt tap CSF has 450 cells with 80% neutrophils, low glucose; culture grows coagulase-negative Staphylococcus; CT shows ventricular enlargement.
case.q: What should be done to the hardware and how should empirical antibiotics be chosen?
case.a: Remove the infected shunt and place an external ventricular drain, then give IV antibiotics; vancomycin is the standard empirical choice for skin flora, adjusted to culture.

read.where: Chapter 113: Bacterial Infections of the Nervous System
Part I: Introduction: An Insight into Central Nervous System (CNS) Infections

det.patho: Neurosurgical hardware provides a surface for biofilm formation, usually seeded from the patient's own skin flora at the time of placement. Internalised shunts such as ventriculoperitoneal or ventriculoatrial systems, and externalised devices such as external ventricular drains and Ommaya reservoirs, all carry a risk. Infection rates are estimated at roughly 5–15% of shunts placed.
det.clinical: Internalised shunt infections mostly emerge in the first weeks or months after surgery, and repeated revisions or prior infection increase risk. The presentation can be mild: fever, headache and lethargy, with symptoms of shunt malfunction. Proximal infection usually involves coagulase-negative staphylococci or S. aureus, whereas distal infection, particularly after bowel perforation, brings gram-negative enteric organisms and peritonitis. Externalised drains risk ventriculitis, with change in CSF cell count and sudden fever.
det.diagnosis: No CSF biomarker beyond culture reliably predicts shunt infection, so samples should be obtained from the device or ventricle before antibiotics whenever safe. A high proportion of neutrophils in CSF is supportive. Laboratories should keep CSF cultures going for ten days or more so that slow-growing organisms are not missed. Blood cultures, imaging for hydrocephalus or abscess, and abdominal assessment for distal infection are added.
det.treatment: Standard treatment is removal of the infected hardware, temporary external ventricular drainage and systemic antibiotics tailored to the organism, with later reimplantation once CSF is sterile. Vancomycin is the usual empirical drug for skin flora, and a fourth-generation cephalosporin is added when nosocomial gram-negative organisms are possible. When an enteric source is suspected, broad-spectrum cover including anaerobes is chosen. Intraventricular antibiotics are reserved for cases in which the device cannot be removed.
det.prognosis: Usually good with prompt device removal and appropriate antibiotics, although infection can cause hydrocephalus complications and neurodevelopmental harm in children.
pearls: In a patient with a shunt, fever plus drowsiness is infection until proved otherwise.
Culture CSF for at least 10 days to catch Cutibacterium acnes.
Antibiotics alone rarely cure device infection; remove the hardware.
det.thd: การติดเชื้อจากสายหรืออุปกรณ์ในระบบประสาท เช่น EVD, VP shunt และ Ommaya reservoir เกิดจากเชื้อประจำผิวหนัง เช่น coagulase-negative Staphylococcus และ S. aureus พบบ่อยในช่วงสัปดาห์ถึงเดือนแรกหลังผ่าตัด ผู้ป่วยมีไข้ ปวดศีรษะ ซึม หรืออาการคล้าย shunt ทำงานผิดปกติ ต้องเพาะเชื้อน้ำไขสันหลังอย่างน้อย 10 วัน การรักษาคือเอาอุปกรณ์ออก ใส่ EVD ชั่วคราว และให้ยาปฏิชีวนะ เช่น vancomycin ตามผลเพาะเชื้อ

name: Cauda equina syndrome
formal: Compression of lumbosacral nerve roots causing saddle anaesthesia, sphincter dysfunction and lower limb weakness with areflexia; a surgical emergency.
simple: Pressure on the nerves at the bottom of the spine causing numbness in the groin and loss of bladder or bowel control.
th: รากประสาทกลุ่มหางม้า (cauda equina) ถูกกดทับ มักจากหมอนรองกระดูกเคลื่อนขนาดใหญ่ ชาบริเวณก้นและฝีเย็บ ปัสสาวะผิดปกติ ปวดร้าวลงขาสองข้าง ต้อง MRI และผ่าตัดด่วน
tempoNote: Usually acute over hours to days with a large disc; slower over weeks with tumour or stenosis
feat: Low back pain with sciatica, often bilateral or alternating
Reduced perineal and saddle sensation, altered sensation when wiping or passing urine
Bladder dysfunction: hesitancy, poor stream, painless retention with overflow
Bowel and sexual dysfunction; reduced anal tone
Lower motor neuron leg weakness with absent ankle jerks; no sensory level or Babinski
inv: Emergency MRI lumbosacral spine (same day)
Post-void residual by bladder scan (large residual supports retention)
Perianal sensation and anal tone examination documented; CT myelography if MRI contraindicated

case.story: Long-standing back pain; after lifting cement bags yesterday he developed pain down both legs and since this morning feels numb 'like sitting on nothing' and has not passed urine.
case.exam: Reduced sensation over buttocks and perineum, weak plantar flexion bilaterally, absent ankle jerks, reduced anal tone; bladder scan 900 mL.
case.tests: MRI: massive central L4–L5 disc extrusion filling the canal.
case.q: Which stage is this and what is the management?
case.a: Cauda equina syndrome with urinary retention (CES-R); catheterise and arrange emergency surgical decompression.

read.where: Chapter 14 Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders (Degenerative disease of the spine: lumbar spine)
Chapter 13 Other Neurologic Disorders Associated with Gastrointestinal Disease

det.patho: Below L1–L2 the spinal canal contains the lumbosacral roots, which control the legs, perineal sensation, bladder, bowel and sexual function. Compression, most commonly from a large central disc at L4–L5 or L5–S1, impairs these roots together. Other causes include tumours, epidural abscess or haematoma, fractures, severe stenosis and iatrogenic injury.
det.clinical: Warning symptoms are bilateral sciatica, altered saddle sensation and new urinary difficulty; painless retention with overflow is a late sign. It is graded as suspected, incomplete (CES-I: altered urinary sensation or difficulty but control retained) and with retention (CES-R). Pain may paradoxically lessen as roots stop conducting. Conus medullaris lesions give earlier sphincter loss, less pain and possible upper motor neuron signs.
det.diagnosis: Clinical findings alone are unreliable; many patients referred with red flags have normal MRI, but the stakes justify a low threshold. Emergency MRI is mandatory when CES is suspected. Document perineal sensation, anal tone and post-void residual. Consider a functional overlay only after imaging excludes compression.
det.treatment: Urgent surgical decompression (usually discectomy or laminectomy) as soon as possible, ideally in the incomplete stage before retention develops, is the standard. Catheterise if in retention. Arrange follow-up for bladder, bowel and sexual function, psychological support and pain management. Treat other causes appropriately (antibiotics for abscess, radiotherapy or surgery for tumour).
det.prognosis: Patients operated at the incomplete stage usually regain sphincter control; those with established retention often have lasting bladder, bowel or sexual dysfunction.
pearls: Ask every back pain patient about saddle numbness and bladder change.
Operate before retention: CES-I has a much better outcome than CES-R.
Do not be reassured if leg pain improves; it can mean worsening compression.
det.thd: Cauda equina syndrome เกิดจากรากประสาทกลุ่มหางม้าในช่องกระดูกสันหลังส่วนเอวถูกกด ส่วนใหญ่จากหมอนรองกระดูกเคลื่อนตรงกลางขนาดใหญ่ อาการคือปวดร้าวลงขาสองข้าง ชาบริเวณก้นและฝีเย็บ ปัสสาวะลำบากหรือคั่ง และกลั้นอุจจาระไม่ได้ ต้องตรวจความรู้สึกรอบทวารและ tone ของหูรูด ทำ MRI ฉุกเฉิน และผ่าตัดลดการกดทับโดยเร็ว ผลจะดีกว่าถ้าผ่าตัดก่อนเกิดปัสสาวะคั่ง

name: Causalgia and dystonia
formal: Complex regional pain syndrome type 2 after nerve injury with burning pain, autonomic change, and sometimes fixed dystonic posture of the limb.
simple: Severe burning pain after nerve injury, sometimes with painful twisted muscle postures.
th: complex regional pain syndrome type 2 หลังบาดเจ็บเส้นประสาท มีปวดแสบร้อน ระบบอัตโนมัติผิดปกติ และบางครั้งแขนขาเกร็งค้างแบบ fixed dystonia
tempoNote: Begins days to weeks after injury and often persists for months to years
feat: Burning pain, allodynia and hyperalgesia beyond the territory of the injured nerve
Swelling, colour and temperature change, sweating abnormalities
Fixed flexed posture of fingers, wrist or ankle that resists passive correction
Trophic changes in skin, hair and nails
inv: Clinical diagnosis using Budapest criteria
NCS/EMG to document nerve injury
Bone scan or X-ray for osteopenia in selected cases

case.story: After a wrist fracture with median nerve injury, she develops burning pain and her fingers curl tightly closed.
case.exam: Swollen, sweaty, mottled hand, allodynia, fixed finger flexion that cannot be opened passively.
case.tests: NCS median neuropathy at wrist; X-ray patchy osteopenia.
case.q: What is the syndrome and what rehabilitation principle is key?
case.a: CRPS type II with fixed dystonia; graded physiotherapy and pain management with multidisciplinary rehabilitation.

det.patho: CRPS type II follows a definable nerve injury. Mechanisms include peripheral and central sensitisation, inflammation, autonomic dysfunction and cortical reorganisation. The fixed dystonia associated with CRPS often has features overlapping with functional dystonia, and it does not behave like primary dystonia.
det.clinical: Pain and autonomic change dominate early; the limb then becomes fixed in flexion. Spread to other limbs and coexisting functional features are reported. Disability can be marked.
det.diagnosis: Use the Budapest criteria for CRPS and document nerve injury. Assess for functional features. Exclude infection, vascular disease and other causes of fixed posture.
det.treatment: Multidisciplinary rehabilitation with physiotherapy, occupational therapy and psychological therapy is central. Neuropathic pain drugs, short courses of steroids early, bisphosphonates and sympathetic blocks are options. Botulinum toxin is sometimes used but response is variable; surgery should be avoided.
det.prognosis: Many improve over time, but a subset have persistent pain and disability.
pearls: Fixed dystonia after minor injury often has functional overlap.
Rehabilitation, not immobilisation, is the key.
Budapest criteria standardise CRPS diagnosis.

name: Cavernous malformation
formal: Cluster of dilated thin-walled vascular channels without intervening brain, causing seizures, haemorrhage or focal deficits; may be familial (CCM1-3).
simple: A cluster of abnormal blood vessels in the brain that can cause seizures or bleeding.
th: กลุ่มหลอดเลือดฝอยขยายผนังบางแบบมีลักษณะคล้ายลูกหม่อน ไม่มีเนื้อสมองคั่น เลือดไหลช้า มักมีเลือดซึมซ้ำ ๆ ทำให้ชักหรืออาการทางระบบประสาทเป็นพัก ๆ เห็นชัดใน MRI (popcorn + วงแหวน haemosiderin) แต่ไม่เห็นใน angiography
tempoNote: Often silent for years; symptomatic bleeds give acute or subacute deficits that improve over weeks, and may cluster
feat: Seizures from supratentorial cortical lesions (most common presentation)
Acute focal deficits from small haemorrhages, especially in brainstem lesions (diplopia, facial numbness, ataxia)
Headache; many lesions found incidentally on MRI
Familial form: multiple lesions, autosomal dominant inheritance
Often adjacent developmental venous anomaly in sporadic cases; may follow cranial radiotherapy
inv: MRI with SWI/GRE: mixed-signal 'popcorn' core with dark haemosiderin rim; SWI reveals additional small lesions
Catheter angiography is usually normal (low-flow lesion)
Genetic testing (KRIT1, CCM2, PDCD10) when multiple lesions or family history
EEG in patients with seizures

case.story: Two days of double vision and numbness of the left face, after a mild headache. A year ago she had similar but briefer symptoms that resolved.
case.exam: Right internuclear ophthalmoplegia, reduced left facial sensation, mild gait ataxia.
case.tests: MRI: 12-mm pontine lesion with mixed signal core, dark rim and fresh blood products; SWI shows three further tiny dark dots in both hemispheres; CTA normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what genetic implication do the extra lesions carry?
case.a: Brainstem cavernous malformation with a recent bleed; multiple lesions suggest familial CCM — test KRIT1/CCM2/PDCD10 and screen relatives with MRI.

Section 3 Hereditary and Genetic Conditions and Malformations

det.patho: Cavernous malformations are clusters of dilated, thin-walled sinusoidal channels lined by a single endothelial layer without intervening brain. Loss of function in the CCM protein complex (KRIT1/CCM1, CCM2, CCM3/PDCD10) disrupts endothelial junctions through MEKK3–KLF2/4 signalling; familial forms carry a germline mutation plus a second somatic hit, while sporadic lesions often carry somatic PIK3CA and MAP3K3 variants. Repeated low-pressure bleeding produces the haemosiderin rim and lesion growth. They occur in about 0.2–0.5% of people.
det.clinical: Supratentorial lesions present mainly with seizures; brainstem and spinal cord lesions with acute deficits after haemorrhage. Bleeds are small and rarely fatal, but brainstem bleeding causes cumulative disability. Haemorrhage tends to cluster in time, so a recent bleed raises short-term rebleed risk. Familial disease (common in Hispanic families of Mexican descent through a KRIT1 founder) gives multiple lesions, and CCM3 causes the most aggressive phenotype.
det.diagnosis: MRI is diagnostic: a reticulated popcorn lesion with mixed signal and a complete haemosiderin rim on T2, blooming on GRE/SWI. Angiography is normal unless an associated developmental venous anomaly is shown. The Zabramski classification describes MRI types. Multiple lesions prompt genetic testing and family screening; post-radiation cavernomas should be considered in patients treated for childhood tumours.
det.treatment: Asymptomatic lesions are observed. Seizures are treated with anti-seizure medicines; surgical resection, including the haemosiderin ring, is considered for drug-resistant epilepsy and offers good seizure control. Surgery is offered for accessible lesions after symptomatic haemorrhage, especially repeated brainstem bleeds reaching a pial surface. Radiosurgery is controversial. Propranolol and statins are under investigation; antithrombotic drugs are not contraindicated when needed for other reasons. Avoid unnecessary cranial irradiation in familial forms.
det.prognosis: Annual haemorrhage risk is under 1% for incidental lesions but can reach 5–30% for brainstem lesions in the first years after a bleed, falling thereafter.
pearls: Popcorn lesion with a black rim on MRI and a normal angiogram = cavernous malformation.
SWI is the best sequence for counting lesions in familial disease.
Brainstem cavernomas cause step-by-step deficits from repeated small bleeds.
det.thd: Cavernous malformation (cavernoma) คือกลุ่มหลอดเลือดขยายผนังบาง เลือดไหลช้า มักมีเลือดซึมซ้ำ ๆ ทำให้ชัก หรือเกิดอาการทางระบบประสาทเฉียบพลันโดยเฉพาะในก้านสมอง MRI เห็นเป็นรูปคล้ายข้าวโพดคั่วมีวงแหวนดำของ haemosiderin แต่ angiography ปกติ ถ้ามีหลายตำแหน่งให้นึกถึงชนิดถ่ายทอดทางพันธุกรรม (KRIT1, CCM2, PDCD10) รักษาโดยเฝ้าติดตาม ให้ยากันชัก และผ่าตัดในรายที่เลือดออกซ้ำหรือชักดื้อยา

qx.stem: A 35-year-old woman has had two focal seizures. CT is unremarkable apart from a tiny density. MRI shows a rounded lesion with a mixed-signal core resembling popcorn, surrounded by a complete low-signal rim; on susceptibility-weighted imaging the lesion blooms strongly and two further small foci are seen. A tiny venous anomaly lies adjacent. There is no oedema and no flow void.
qx.q: Which statement is most accurate?
opts: Catheter angiography will show a large arteriovenous shunt
These lesions represent low-flow vascular channels that are often angiographically occult, and multiple lesions may be familial
The hemosiderin rim indicates malignancy
Embolisation is the preferred treatment
The adjacent venous anomaly is the cause of the bleeding
qx.why: Cavernous malformations are low-flow, thin-walled sinusoids with repeated microhaemorrhage, producing a popcorn core, hemosiderin rim and blooming on SWI, yet angiography is usually normal. Multiple lesions suggest a familial form (CCM1-3). Management of seizure-associated lesions is by antiseizure medication, with surgery or radiosurgery for refractory or eloquent-sparing cases.

qx.stem: A 27-year-old man has his first focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizure. His father had brain surgery for a 'blood-filled lesion' and his sister has headaches. CT shows a small calcified right frontal lesion. MRI shows a mixed-signal 'popcorn' lesion with a dark haemosiderin rim and, on susceptibility-weighted imaging, more than 20 additional tiny dark foci. Catheter angiography is normal.
qx.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Multiple cerebral amyloid angiopathy microbleeds
Arteriovenous malformation with nidus calcification
Familial cerebral cavernous malformations, for example from a KRIT1 (CCM1) variant
Haemorrhagic metastases from melanoma
Developmental venous anomaly only
qx.why: Cavernous malformations are angiographically occult low-flow lesions with a popcorn core and haemosiderin rim; many lesions on SWI with an affected relative indicate the familial form caused by KRIT1, CCM2 or PDCD10 variants. CAA microbleeds occur in older adults in a lobar pattern, AVMs show a nidus and early venous drainage on angiography, and metastases usually enhance with surrounding oedema.

name: Cavernous sinus syndrome
formal: Lesion of the cavernous sinus involving cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI, with ophthalmoplegia and facial sensory loss; causes include tumour, thrombosis, aneurysm and Tolosa-Hunt.
simple: Damage near the base of the brain that affects eye movement and facial feeling nerves.
th: รอยโรคที่ cavernous sinus ทำให้เส้นประสาทสมองที่ 3, 4, 5 (V1, V2) และ 6 เสีย มีอัมพาตกล้ามเนื้อตาและชาใบหน้า สาเหตุเช่นเนื้องอก ลิ่มเลือด หลอดเลือดโป่งพอง และ Tolosa–Hunt
tempoNote: Acute with thrombosis, fistula or apoplexy; gradual with tumours
feat: Combination of III, IV and VI palsies with forehead/cheek numbness
Horner syndrome from sympathetic involvement, sometimes with VI palsy (Parkinson sign)
Pain suggests inflammation, infection or aneurysm; proptosis and chemosis suggest fistula or thrombosis
Causes: meningioma, pituitary adenoma, metastasis, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, carotid-cavernous fistula, septic thrombosis, Tolosa–Hunt, fungal infection
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is an important cause in Southeast Asia
inv: MRI with contrast and fat-suppressed coronal views of the cavernous sinus
CTA or catheter angiography for aneurysm or fistula
FBC, glucose, ESR/CRP, blood cultures; nasopharyngoscopy and EBV serology
Biopsy when imaging is indeterminate before labelling Tolosa–Hunt

case.story: Two months of right-sided facial numbness, double vision and nasal stuffiness with occasional blood-stained discharge.
case.exam: Right III (pupil-involving), IV and VI palsies, reduced sensation V1–V2, right neck lymph node.
case.tests: MRI: nasopharyngeal mass invading skull base and right cavernous sinus; biopsy: undifferentiated carcinoma, EBV positive.
case.q: Where is the lesion and what is the cause?
case.a: Right cavernous sinus syndrome from invasive nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

read.where: Chapter 13 Cranial Nerve Disorders — Multiple Cranial Neuropathies

det.patho: The cavernous sinus contains the internal carotid artery and sympathetic plexus, with III, IV, V1 and V2 in its lateral wall and VI free within the sinus. Any space-occupying, inflammatory, thrombotic or vascular lesion here affects several nerves together. Septic thrombosis follows facial, sinus or dental infection.
det.clinical: Diplopia, ptosis and facial numbness are core; pupil may be dilated, small (Horner) or mid-position if both are affected. Carotid-cavernous fistulas cause pulsatile proptosis, chemosis and bruit. Septic thrombosis brings fever, periorbital swelling and bilateral spread. Diabetic patients with sinus disease may have mucormycosis.
det.diagnosis: High-resolution contrast MRI is essential; angiography assesses aneurysm or fistula. Systemic work-up includes infection, inflammation and cancer screening. Tolosa–Hunt remains a diagnosis of exclusion; steroid response alone does not exclude lymphoma.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: antibiotics and possibly anticoagulation for septic thrombosis, antifungals and debridement for mucormycosis, endovascular closure for fistula, oncology treatment for tumours, steroids for Tolosa–Hunt.
det.prognosis: Depends on the cause; septic and fungal disease carry significant mortality, while inflammatory causes usually recover.
pearls: III, IV, VI plus V1/V2 numbness localises to the cavernous sinus.
Diabetic with ketoacidosis and facial numbness: think mucormycosis.
Always examine the nasopharynx in Southeast Asian patients.
det.thd: Cavernous sinus syndrome คือรอยโรคที่ cavernous sinus ทำให้เส้นประสาทสมองที่ 3, 4, 6 และ V1–V2 เสียพร้อมกัน ผู้ป่วยหนังตาตก เห็นภาพซ้อน และชาหน้าผากหรือแก้ม สาเหตุมีหลายอย่าง เช่น มะเร็งหลังโพรงจมูก meningioma, pituitary adenoma, ลิ่มเลือดติดเชื้อ, carotid-cavernous fistula และ Tolosa–Hunt การตรวจสำคัญคือ MRI พร้อมสารทึบรังสี และรักษาตามสาเหตุ

qx.stem: A 57-year-old man from Ubon Ratchathani has had a week of dull pain behind the right eye followed by horizontal diplopia. Examination shows an abduction deficit of the right eye, a right ptosis with a pupil 2 mm smaller than the left that dilates slowly in the dark, and normal visual acuity, colour vision and optic discs. Sensation over the right forehead is reduced and the corneal reflex is slightly diminished.
qx.q: Which localisation best explains the combination of an abducens palsy with an oculosympathetic palsy?
opts: Right orbital apex, where the optic nerve is compressed with the extraocular nerves
Right midbrain tegmentum, involving the oculomotor nucleus and descending sympathetic fibres
Right cavernous sinus, where the sympathetic fibres briefly travel with the abducens nerve beside the internal carotid artery
Right pontine tegmentum, involving the abducens nucleus and the facial colliculus
Right superior orbital fissure, where all three ocular motor nerves lie close together
qx.why: Within the cavernous sinus the post-ganglionic sympathetic fibres leave the carotid plexus and run briefly alongside the sixth nerve before reaching the ophthalmic division, so a lesion here can produce a sixth nerve palsy together with a mild Horner syndrome and V1 sensory loss. Preserved vision and a normal fundus argue against the orbital apex. A pontine lesion would affect the facial nerve and long tracts, and a midbrain lesion would cause oculomotor, not abducens, deficits.

name: CD8+ encephalitis
formal: Rare T-cell mediated encephalitis in HIV with CD8 lymphocytic infiltration and viral escape, causing subacute cognitive decline and seizures.
simple: A brain inflammation in people with HIV caused by overactive immune cells.
th: สมองอักเสบจาก CD8 T cell ที่พบในผู้ติดเชื้อ HIV มักสัมพันธ์กับไวรัสในน้ำไขสันหลังหลุดการควบคุม ทำให้สับสนเฉียบพลันถึงกึ่งเฉียบพลันและชัก ตอบสนองต่อ steroid
tempoNote: Develops over days to weeks, often after stopping or changing ART or with CSF viral escape
feat: Person with HIV, usually on ART with good blood viral suppression
Subacute confusion, headache and cognitive decline
Seizures, sometimes status epilepticus, and reduced consciousness
Can follow ART interruption or appear with drug-resistant virus in CSF
inv: MRI: diffuse bilateral white matter T2 hyperintensity, often with patchy perivascular enhancement
CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein; HIV RNA higher than plasma (CSF escape)
CSF HIV genotype for resistance; exclude opportunistic infection (JC, CMV, toxoplasma, cryptococcus)
Brain biopsy shows perivascular and parenchymal CD8+ T-cell infiltrates

case.who: 38-year-old man from Bangkok, HIV on ART for 8 years
case.story: Two weeks of headache and increasing confusion; he admits stopping his pills for a few months last year then restarting.
case.exam: Disoriented, slow responses, no focal weakness; one generalised seizure in the ward.
case.tests: Plasma HIV RNA undetectable; CSF 40 lymphocytes, HIV RNA 12,000 copies/mL; MRI diffuse white matter T2 change with perivascular enhancement; JC virus PCR negative.
case.q: What process is suspected and what are the treatment steps?
case.a: CD8+ encephalitis with CSF viral escape; start high-dose corticosteroids and change ART according to the CSF resistance genotype.

det.patho: Cytotoxic CD8+ T cells infiltrate the brain parenchyma and perivascular spaces in large numbers, with few CD4 cells, causing inflammatory white matter injury. The trigger is thought to be ongoing HIV replication in the CNS, as in CSF viral escape, ART interruption, or immune reconstitution, but the exact antigen is not established. It is recognised as a severe form of CNS escape or a variant of neuro-IRIS. It is rare, and most knowledge comes from case series.
det.clinical: Patients with HIV, often with controlled plasma virus, develop subacute encephalopathy with headache, confusion, seizures and sometimes coma. Focal signs are less prominent than in PML. Some cases follow ART interruption, others arise with resistant virus in the CSF. Without treatment it can be fatal within weeks.
det.diagnosis: Consider it in a person with HIV who has subacute encephalopathy, diffuse enhancing white matter change and CSF HIV RNA exceeding plasma. Exclude opportunistic infections and lymphoma with CSF PCR, cryptococcal antigen, cultures and imaging. Brain biopsy showing a dense CD8+ lymphocytic infiltrate confirms the diagnosis but is not always needed when the picture is typical. Send CSF for HIV genotyping.
det.treatment: High-dose corticosteroids (IV methylprednisolone, then a tapering oral course) form the mainstay and often produce rapid improvement. Optimise ART, guided by CSF resistance testing, and favour drugs with good CNS penetration as a practical consideration. Treat seizures and raised intracranial pressure as needed. Monitor for relapse during steroid taper.
det.prognosis: Many patients improve substantially with steroids and ART adjustment; delayed treatment can lead to death or lasting cognitive impairment.
pearls: Suppressed plasma HIV does not exclude active HIV in the CSF.
Diffuse enhancing white matter change in HIV after ART interruption: think CD8+ encephalitis.
Unlike most HIV brain disease, steroids are the key treatment here.
det.thd: CD8+ encephalitis เป็นสมองอักเสบที่พบน้อยในผู้ติดเชื้อ HIV เกิดจาก CD8 T cell เข้าไปในสมองจำนวนมาก มักสัมพันธ์กับไวรัสในน้ำไขสันหลังสูงกว่าในเลือดหรือหลังหยุดยาต้านไวรัส ผู้ป่วยสับสน ปวดศีรษะ และชัก MRI มีรอยโรคเนื้อสมองสีขาวกระจายพร้อมการ enhance รักษาด้วย steroid ขนาดสูงและปรับยาต้านไวรัสตามผลดื้อยาในน้ำไขสันหลัง

qx.stem: A 44-year-old man from Chiang Mai with HIV on suppressive ART develops headache, confusion and seizures over 10 days. MRI shows extensive contrast-enhancing perivascular white matter lesions. CSF HIV RNA is low, and brain biopsy shows dense perivascular CD8+ lymphocytic infiltrates.
qx.q: Which treatment is most appropriate alongside continuing ART?
opts: High-dose corticosteroids
Intrathecal amphotericin B
Intravenous ganciclovir alone
Ivermectin
Pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine
qx.why: CD8+ encephalitis is an immune-mediated encephalopathy in people with controlled HIV, with perivascular CD8+ infiltrates, and most patients respond to corticosteroids. It overlaps with CSF escape, so CSF viral load and resistance testing should be performed and ART optimised if discordance is found. The other treatments target fungal, CMV, parasitic or toxoplasma infection.

name: Central cord syndrome
formal: Cervical cord injury with disproportionate weakness of the arms compared with legs, variable sensory loss and bladder dysfunction; typical after hyperextension in spondylosis.
simple: A neck spinal cord injury that weakens the arms more than the legs.
th: กลุ่มอาการไขสันหลังส่วนคอบาดเจ็บที่ทำให้แขนโดยเฉพาะมืออ่อนแรงมากกว่าขา มักเกิดในผู้สูงอายุที่ล้มคออแอ่นร่วมกับโรคกระดูกคอเสื่อม
tempoNote: Immediate after hyperextension injury; improves over weeks to months
feat: Arm and especially hand weakness out of proportion to leg weakness
Variable sensory loss below the injury and burning dysaesthesia of the hands
Bladder retention or incomplete emptying
Typical after a forward fall with neck hyperextension on a spondylotic canal, often with no fracture
Recovery usually proceeds legs first, then bladder, then proximal arms, with fine hand function last
inv: CT cervical spine to detect fracture, instability and canal diameter
MRI cervical spine for cord oedema, haemorrhage, disc and ligament injury
Serial standardised motor and sensory scoring (ISNCSCI) to track recovery
Bladder scan and early assessment of swallowing and respiratory function

case.story: He slipped on a wet bathroom floor and struck his forehead on the tiles. Afterwards he could not hold a cup but could stand with help.
case.exam: Forehead abrasion; grip 1/5, shoulder abduction 3/5, leg power 4/5; patchy reduced pinprick below C5 with burning hands; urinary retention.
case.tests: CT shows no fracture; MRI shows multilevel spondylotic narrowing with T2 hyperintensity of the cord at C4–C5.
case.q: Which cord syndrome is this and what should be done in the first days?
case.a: Central cord syndrome. Immobilise the neck, maintain mean arterial pressure, monitor cardiorespiratory function, and discuss early versus delayed decompression with spinal surgeons.

det.patho: Hyperextension drives the ligamentum flavum and osteophytes into an already narrowed cervical canal, bruising the central grey matter and medial corticospinal fibres that serve the arms. Laminated tract organisation, with cervical fibres more medial, explains the arm predominance. It is the commonest incomplete cord injury and mostly affects older people after low-energy trauma.
det.clinical: Patients have weak hands and arms, may walk with a spastic or stiff gait and often complain of burning hands. Bladder dysfunction varies, and sensation is patchy. It must be assessed together with the neck, head injury and associated chest or airway problems. Neurological recovery is usually considerable in the first weeks, but hand dexterity and spasticity remain a problem. Exam questions often ask for the relationship between fibre lamination and the pattern of weakness.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical, combined with CT to look for bone injury and MRI to show the cord injury, canal stenosis and ligament disruption. Rule out vascular causes such as anterior spinal artery infarct and cord compression by haematoma. Use ISNCSCI grading to document baseline and follow recovery, repeating it regularly.
det.treatment: Initial care includes spinal immobilisation, avoiding hypotension and maintaining blood pressure targets (commonly mean arterial pressure above 85 mmHg for several days) in specialised units, airway surveillance and prevention of complications such as pressure sores, thrombosis and urinary infection. Steroids are not recommended. Surgery is advised for instability, progressive deficit or persisting compression, and timing is individualised with early decompression increasingly favoured. Rehabilitation, spasticity management and bladder training are central.
det.prognosis: The prognosis is better than for other incomplete cord syndromes, with most patients regaining walking and bladder control, although hand function is often incomplete. Younger age and higher initial strength predict better recovery.
pearls: Arms worse than legs after a neck hyperextension fall: central cord until proven otherwise.
Recovery runs legs, bladder, proximal arm, then hand.
A normal CT does not exclude a significant cord injury; get an MRI.
det.thd: Central cord syndrome เกิดจากการบาดเจ็บไขสันหลังส่วนคอ มักในผู้สูงอายุที่หกล้มหน้าคะมำและคอแอ่นขณะมีกระดูกคอเสื่อม ผู้ป่วยจะแขนและมืออ่อนแรงมากกว่าขา มีอาการชาแสบร้อนที่มือและปัสสาวะไม่ออก การตรวจ MRI พบไขสันหลังบวมหรือมีสัญญาณผิดปกติ แม้ CT จะไม่พบกระดูกหัก การรักษาคือตรึงคอ ควบคุมความดันโลหิตไม่ให้ต่ำ ผ่าตัดเมื่อไม่มั่นคงหรือกดทับต่อเนื่อง และทำกายภาพบำบัด ส่วนใหญ่ฟื้นการเดินได้แต่การใช้มือมักฟื้นไม่สมบูรณ์

name: Central core disease (CCD)
formal: Congenital myopathy from RYR1 mutations with central cores lacking oxidative enzyme activity, hypotonia and malignant hyperthermia susceptibility.
simple: An inherited muscle disease with weak, floppy muscles from birth and risk of a dangerous reaction to some anaesthetics.
more: Congenital myopathy from RYR1 mutations with hypotonia, proximal weakness, and well-defined cores lacking oxidative activity on biopsy, and association with malignant hyperthermia. Confirm with RYR1 sequencing and biopsy; avoid volatile anaesthetics and succinylcholine. Treatment is supportive; usually non-progressive.
th: โรคกล้ามเนื้อแต่กำเนิดจากยีน RYR1 ชิ้นเนื้อพบ central core ที่ไม่มีเอนไซม์ออกซิเดชัน กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงไม่มาก และเสี่ยง malignant hyperthermia
tempoNote: Onset in infancy or childhood; static or very slowly progressive
feat: Mild hypotonia and delayed motor milestones; proximal and axial weakness
Facial weakness mild; extraocular muscles usually spared
Scoliosis, hip dislocation, foot deformities
Malignant hyperthermia susceptibility; exertional rhabdomyolysis in some
inv: CK usually normal or mildly raised
Muscle MRI: selective involvement (e.g. vasti, sartorius, adductors) with sparing of rectus femoris and gracilis
Muscle biopsy: cores lacking oxidative enzyme staining; RYR1 testing

case.story: Late walking and difficulty climbing stairs; her uncle had a severe reaction during anaesthesia.
case.exam: Mild proximal weakness, scoliosis, normal eye movements.
case.tests: CK normal; biopsy central cores in type 1 fibres; RYR1 dominant variant.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and which precaution is crucial?
case.a: RYR1-related central core disease; avoid volatile anaesthetics and succinylcholine (malignant hyperthermia risk).

read.where: Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Congenital Myopathies

det.patho: Most CCD is caused by dominant RYR1 variants affecting the skeletal muscle ryanodine receptor, the calcium release channel of the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Leaky or dysfunctional channels cause disordered excitation-contraction coupling and mitochondrial depletion in the core of fibres. RYR1 variants also underlie malignant hyperthermia susceptibility.
det.clinical: Most children have mild, non-progressive proximal weakness with skeletal features. Severe neonatal forms exist, especially with recessive variants. Some adults present with exertional myalgia, rhabdomyolysis or anaesthetic reactions only.
det.diagnosis: Muscle MRI pattern and biopsy guide testing; RYR1 sequencing confirms. Family screening is important due to malignant hyperthermia risk.
det.treatment: Supportive care: physiotherapy, orthopaedic management of scoliosis and hips, and respiratory monitoring. Salbutamol has shown some benefit in small studies. Mark the patient and family as malignant hyperthermia susceptible; use trigger-free anaesthesia.
det.prognosis: Usually good with normal life expectancy in typical dominant cases.
pearls: Congenital myopathy + anaesthetic reaction in family = RYR1.
CK is often normal in congenital myopathies.
Muscle MRI pattern can point directly to RYR1.
det.thd: Central core disease เกิดจากยีน RYR1 ทำให้กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงแต่กำเนิดแบบไม่รุนแรง เดินช้า กระดูกสันหลังคด ชิ้นเนื้อพบ central core ที่ไม่ติดสีเอนไซม์ สำคัญที่สุดคือเสี่ยง malignant hyperthermia ต้องหลีกเลี่ยงยาดมสลบชนิดระเหยและ succinylcholine และตรวจคัดกรองญาติ

ddx.pt: Multiple small cores, often recessive RYR1 or SEPN1 with respiratory involvement
Rods on Gomori trichrome, facial and bulbar weakness
Fasciculations of tongue, areflexia and neurogenic EMG

aN: ccd | central core disease | central core myopathy | ryr1 related myopathy | ryr1 core myopathy

name: Central neurocytomas
formal: Rare intraventricular neuroglial tumours near the foramen of Monro in young adults, causing hydrocephalus; low-grade with good prognosis after resection.
simple: A slow-growing brain tumour in the fluid spaces of the brain that can block fluid flow.
th: เนื้องอก neuroglial ชนิดหายากในโพรงสมองใกล้ foramen of Monro ในผู้ใหญ่ตอนต้น ทำให้ hydrocephalus มักพยากรณ์ดีหลังผ่าตัด
tempoNote: Slow growth over years; decompensation of hydrocephalus can be rapid
feat: Young adults (20s–40s) with headache, vomiting and papilloedema from obstructive hydrocephalus
Lateral ventricle mass attached to the septum pellucidum near the foramen of Monro
Calcification and cysts give a 'bubbly' appearance on MRI
WHO grade 2; atypical forms have higher Ki-67
Sudden deterioration possible with ventricular obstruction or haemorrhage
inv: MRI with contrast: intraventricular heterogeneous mass with cysts
CT for calcification
Histology: uniform round cells, synaptophysin positive

case.story: Two months of morning headaches and vomiting, recently blurred vision.
case.exam: Bilateral papilloedema, no focal deficit.
case.tests: MRI: lobulated, cystic lateral ventricle mass attached to the septum causing hydrocephalus; biopsy shows synaptophysin-positive neurocytic cells.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the main treatment?
case.a: Central neurocytoma; maximal safe resection, with radiotherapy or radiosurgery for residual or atypical tumours.

det.patho: Central neurocytoma is a low-grade glioneuronal tumour of uniform neuronal-lineage cells, arising from the septum pellucidum or ventricular walls. It grows slowly and obstructs CSF pathways. Atypical neurocytoma with high proliferation has a greater risk of recurrence.
det.clinical: Symptoms reflect raised intracranial pressure from hydrocephalus: headache, vomiting, visual blurring and papilloedema. Focal deficits are rare. Tumour haemorrhage or acute obstruction can cause rapid deterioration.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows a heterogeneous intraventricular mass with cysts and calcification. Histology with synaptophysin and NeuN positivity confirms it and distinguishes it from oligodendroglioma and ependymoma. Methylation profiling can resolve uncertain cases.
det.treatment: Gross total resection is the treatment of choice and often curative. Residual or atypical tumours receive radiotherapy or stereotactic radiosurgery. Hydrocephalus may need a shunt if not relieved by surgery.
det.prognosis: Excellent after complete resection; atypical and incompletely resected tumours may recur.
pearls: Bubbly mass attached to the septum pellucidum in a young adult: think neurocytoma.
Synaptophysin positive, unlike ependymoma.
Hydrocephalus is the main presenting problem.
det.thd: Central neurocytoma เป็นเนื้องอกในโพรงสมองด้านข้างใกล้ foramen of Monro ในผู้ใหญ่ตอนต้น โตช้าและอุดทางเดินน้ำไขสันหลังจนเกิด hydrocephalus ทำให้ปวดศีรษะ อาเจียน และ papilloedema MRI พบก้อนที่มี cyst และหินปูน ติดกับ septum pellucidum การรักษาหลักคือผ่าตัดออกให้มากที่สุด และฉายรังสีเสริมถ้าเหลือ พยากรณ์โรคดี

ddx.pt: Often fourth ventricle in children; GFAP positive, perivascular pseudorosettes
Children; enhancing frond-like mass in the atrium or fourth ventricle
Intraventricular meningioma in the trigone of older adults

aN: central neurocytoma | intraventricular neurocytoma | cn

name: Central post-stroke pain (CPSP)
formal: Neuropathic pain from thalamic or other central somatosensory lesions after stroke, often burning or allodynic and delayed by weeks to months.
simple: Long-lasting burning or painful sensations that develop after a stroke damages pain pathways in the brain.
th: ปวดชนิด neuropathic จากรอยโรคทางเดินรับความรู้สึกส่วนกลางหลัง stroke โดยเฉพาะ thalamus มักปวดแสบร้อนหรือเจ็บเมื่อถูกสัมผัส และเริ่มช้าหลัง stroke เป็นสัปดาห์ถึงเดือน
tempoNote: Begins weeks to months after the stroke and often persists
feat: Burning, aching, freezing or lancinating pain in the body region affected by the stroke
Allodynia (touch or cold provokes pain) and hyperalgesia
Abnormal pain and temperature sensation in the painful area is required
Classic after ventral posterolateral thalamic infarct; also lateral medullary, capsular and cortical strokes
Pain worsened by cold, emotion and movement; disturbs sleep and mood
inv: Clinical diagnosis with careful sensory mapping
MRI to confirm a lesion in the somatosensory pathway
Exclude shoulder pain, spasticity, CRPS and musculoskeletal causes

case.story: Three months after a left thalamic stroke with right-sided numbness, she develops burning pain in the right arm and leg, worse when the fan blows on her.
case.exam: Reduced pinprick and cold sense on the right, with cold allodynia; strength nearly normal.
case.tests: MRI: chronic left ventrolateral thalamic lacune.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the first-line drug options?
case.a: Central post-stroke pain; amitriptyline or a gabapentinoid (pregabalin/gabapentin), with lamotrigine as an alternative.

read.where: Chapter 31 Pain in Neurological Disorders — Brain
Chapter 58: Central pain in the face and head JÖRGEN

det.patho: Damage to the spinothalamic–thalamocortical pathway leads to loss of normal inhibitory control and hyperexcitability of deafferented thalamic and cortical neurons. Central sensitisation and imbalance between lemniscal and spinothalamic inputs are proposed. Not all patients with such lesions develop pain.
det.clinical: Onset is often delayed; pain is constant or paroxysmal and typically within the area of sensory loss. It frequently coexists with depression, anxiety and poor sleep. Prevalence is a few percent of all strokes but higher after thalamic and lateral medullary infarction.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires pain in a body territory corresponding to a central lesion, with sensory abnormalities in that area, and exclusion of nociceptive or peripheral neuropathic causes. Grading systems for neuropathic pain help.
det.treatment: Amitriptyline and gabapentinoids are commonly used first; lamotrigine, duloxetine and combinations follow. Refractory cases may be considered for repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation of motor cortex or deep brain/motor cortex stimulation. Address mood, sleep and function.
det.prognosis: Often chronic with partial response to drugs; meaningful reduction rather than complete relief is realistic.
pearls: New burning pain on the stroke side weeks later: CPSP, not a new stroke.
Check for altered temperature sense — it is almost always present.
Lateral medullary infarcts can cause facial and contralateral body pain.
det.thd: Central post-stroke pain คืออาการปวดชนิด neuropathic หลัง stroke ที่ทำลายทางเดินรับความรู้สึก โดยเฉพาะ thalamus ผู้ป่วยปวดแสบร้อนหรือเย็นเจ็บในบริเวณที่ชา เริ่มหลัง stroke หลายสัปดาห์ถึงเดือน และเจ็บเมื่อถูกสัมผัสหรือความเย็น การวินิจฉัยเป็นทางคลินิกร่วมกับ MRI การรักษาใช้ amitriptyline, pregabalin หรือ gabapentin, lamotrigine และการกระตุ้นสมองในรายที่ดื้อยา

ddx.pt: Swelling, colour and sweating change, often in a hemiplegic hand
Broader thalamic deficits; pain is one component

name: Centronuclear myopathy
formal: Congenital myopathy with centrally placed nuclei in fibres; X-linked myotubular (MTM1) and autosomal forms (DNM2, BIN1) cause hypotonia and weakness.
simple: An inherited muscle disease with weakness and low muscle tone starting early in life.
more: Muscle biopsy shows central nuclei with radial sarcoplasmic strands; CK is usually normal, and genetics identifies MTM1 in males with severe neonatal disease. Prognosis ranges from early ventilator dependence to milder adult forms, and care is supportive.
th: โรคกล้ามเนื้อแต่กำเนิดที่นิวเคลียสอยู่กลางเส้นใย ชนิด X-linked (MTM1) รุนแรงในทารกชาย ชนิด autosomal (DNM2, BIN1, RYR1) อ่อนกว่า
tempoNote: X-linked form severe from birth; autosomal forms from childhood or adulthood, slowly progressive
feat: Severe neonatal hypotonia and respiratory failure in X-linked myotubular myopathy
Ptosis and ophthalmoparesis common, facial weakness
Distal and proximal weakness in DNM2-related adult form
Long thin face, high-arched palate; liver haemorrhage risk in XLMTM
inv: Muscle biopsy: centrally placed nuclei, radial sarcoplasmic strands (DNM2)
Genetic testing (MTM1, DNM2, BIN1, RYR1, TTN)
Respiratory function and liver assessment

case.story: Born floppy, needed ventilation from birth; reduced fetal movements and polyhydramnios in pregnancy.
case.exam: Profound hypotonia, weak facial muscles, ptosis, absent reflexes.
case.tests: CK normal; biopsy small fibres with central nuclei; MTM1 pathogenic variant.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and inheritance?
case.a: X-linked myotubular myopathy (MTM1); the mother may be a carrier.

read.where: Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Congenital Myopathies

det.patho: Genes involved in membrane trafficking and T-tubule formation (MTM1 myotubularin, DNM2 dynamin 2, BIN1 amphiphysin 2) are affected, leading to disorganised triads and impaired excitation-contraction coupling. Nuclei remain in the centre of fibres, as in fetal muscle.
det.clinical: XLMTM affects boys with severe hypotonia and ventilator dependence; carrier females may have mild weakness. Autosomal dominant DNM2 disease starts in childhood or adulthood with slowly progressive weakness, ptosis and ophthalmoparesis. Recessive BIN1 and RYR1 forms vary.
det.diagnosis: Biopsy shows central nuclei; genetic testing confirms the subtype. Exclude myotonic dystrophy with maternal examination and testing.
det.treatment: Supportive: ventilation, feeding support, physiotherapy and orthopaedic care. Gene therapy trials for XLMTM were halted after liver toxicity; research continues. Pyridostigmine helps some patients with fatigable features.
det.prognosis: XLMTM has high early mortality; DNM2 forms have near-normal life expectancy.
pearls: Floppy male neonate with ptosis and ophthalmoparesis: consider XLMTM.
Examine the mother for myotonia before biopsy.
Watch for liver haemorrhage in XLMTM survivors.
det.thd: Centronuclear myopathy คือโรคกล้ามเนื้อแต่กำเนิดที่นิวเคลียสอยู่กลางเส้นใย ชนิด X-linked (MTM1) ทารกชายอ่อนปวกเปียกรุนแรงและต้องใช้เครื่องช่วยหายใจ ชนิด DNM2 อาการเบากว่าเริ่มในวัยเด็กหรือผู้ใหญ่ มีหนังตาตกและกลอกตาจำกัด ยืนยันด้วยชิ้นเนื้อและยีน รักษาประคับประคอง

ddx.pt: Floppy neonate with maternal myotonia and CTG expansion
Tongue fasciculations, alert face without ptosis
Rods on biopsy rather than central nuclei

aN: cnm | myotubular myopathy | xlmtm | mtm1 myopathy | dnm2 myopathy

name: Cerebellar ataxia
formal: Syndrome of incoordination with gait ataxia, dysmetria and dysarthria from cerebellar dysfunction; causes include genetic, toxic, immune, paraneoplastic and degenerative.
simple: Poor balance and clumsy movement due to cerebellum problems.
th: กลุ่มอาการเสียการประสานงานจากสมองน้อย เดินเซ แขนขาวัดระยะผิด พูดไม่ชัด สาเหตุได้ทั้งพันธุกรรม พิษ ภูมิคุ้มกัน มะเร็ง และความเสื่อม
tempoNote: Tempo is the key to cause: acute (stroke, toxin), subacute (immune, paraneoplastic), chronic (genetic, degenerative)
feat: Wide-based unsteady gait and difficulty with tandem walking
Dysmetria, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia
Scanning dysarthria
Nystagmus and saccadic abnormalities
inv: MRI brain (atrophy pattern, stroke, demyelination, tumour)
Blood tests: B12, vitamin E, thyroid, coeliac and anti-GAD antibodies, alcohol history
Paraneoplastic antibodies for subacute cases; genetic panel for chronic familial cases

case.story: Over eight weeks she has become unable to walk without help and her speech is slurred; she has lost weight.
case.exam: Severe gait and limb ataxia, scanning dysarthria, downbeat nystagmus.
case.tests: MRI normal; anti-Yo positive; CT shows ovarian mass.
case.q: What is the cause of the ataxia?
case.a: Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration (anti-Yo) associated with ovarian cancer.

read.where: Chapter 24 Cerebellar Ataxias and Related Conditions — Approach to the Patient with Ataxia

det.patho: The cerebellum coordinates movement by comparing intended with actual motion. Damage to the vermis causes truncal and gait ataxia; hemisphere lesions cause ipsilateral limb ataxia. Causes include vascular, toxic (alcohol, drugs), immune, paraneoplastic, infectious, genetic and degenerative processes.
det.clinical: Classify by tempo and distribution. Acute cerebellar syndromes need urgent imaging for stroke or haemorrhage. Subacute pancerebellar ataxia suggests immune or paraneoplastic causes. Chronic ataxia with family history suggests genetic disease; sporadic adult-onset progressive ataxia raises MSA, alcohol and idiopathic late-onset ataxia.
det.diagnosis: MRI is first-line. Laboratory screening addresses treatable causes (vitamin deficiencies, hypothyroidism, gluten ataxia, anti-GAD). Antibody panels and cancer screening for subacute cases. Genetic testing including repeat expansions (SCAs, FA, RFC1/CANVAS) for chronic progressive ataxia.
det.treatment: Treat the cause where possible: thiamine, vitamin E, gluten-free diet, immunotherapy, tumour removal. Omaveloxolone is approved for Friedreich ataxia in adults and adolescents. Physiotherapy improves balance and function. Acetazolamide or 4-aminopyridine for episodic ataxias.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause.
pearls: Acute vertigo with inability to walk: exclude cerebellar stroke.
Always check thiamine, B12, vitamin E and thyroid in new ataxia.
Subacute pancerebellar syndrome in an adult: search for cancer.
det.thd: Cerebellar ataxia คือกลุ่มอาการจากสมองน้อยผิดปกติ เดินเซ ขากว้าง แขนขากะระยะผิด สั่นเวลาเคลื่อนไหว และพูดไม่ชัด ช่วงเวลาที่เกิดอาการช่วยบอกสาเหตุ เช่น เฉียบพลันจาก stroke กึ่งเฉียบพลันจากภูมิคุ้มกันหรือมะเร็ง เรื้อรังจากพันธุกรรม ตรวจ MRI และเลือดหาสาเหตุที่รักษาได้ เช่น ขาดวิตามิน ไทรอยด์ต่ำ และ gluten

Slowly progressive, dominant family history

name: Cerebellar atrophy and variants
formal: Progressive cerebellar degeneration with ataxia, dysarthria and nystagmus; may be hereditary, alcoholic, paraneoplastic or idiopathic.
simple: Shrinking of the balance centre of the brain, causing unsteady walking and slurred speech.
th: สมองน้อยฝ่อเสื่อมแบบลุกลาม มีเดินเซ พูดไม่ชัด ตากระตุก อาจเกิดจากพันธุกรรม สุรา paraneoplastic หรือไม่ทราบสาเหตุ
tempoNote: Usually progressive over years; subacute in paraneoplastic or immune forms
feat: Progressive gait ataxia, dysarthria, limb incoordination
Nystagmus and broken pursuit
Vermis-predominant atrophy in alcohol-related degeneration (legs and gait more than arms)
Additional features suggest MSA, SCA, FXTAS or mitochondrial disease
inv: MRI pattern: vermian, hemispheric, pontocerebellar atrophy
Alcohol history, nutritional screen, thyroid, anti-GAD, gliadin antibodies
Genetic testing (SCA, FXTAS, RFC1); paraneoplastic antibodies if subacute

case.story: Heavy rice whisky drinker for 30 years; progressive unsteadiness of gait for two years, arms nearly normal.
case.exam: Wide-based gait, heel-shin ataxia, mild dysarthria, minimal arm ataxia.
case.tests: MRI anterior superior vermian atrophy; low thiamine.
case.q: What is the likely cause?
case.a: Alcohol-related cerebellar degeneration (anterior vermis), possibly with nutritional contribution.

read.where: Chapter 33 Alcohol and the Nervous System
9 - Atypical parkinsonism, parkinsonism-­plus syndromes and secondary parkinsonian disorders

det.patho: Cerebellar Purkinje cells and their connections degenerate from genetic defects, toxins (alcohol, phenytoin, chemotherapy), vitamin deficiencies, immune attack or unknown causes. The pattern of atrophy (vermis vs hemispheres, involvement of pons) gives diagnostic clues.
det.clinical: Gait ataxia comes first; limb ataxia, dysarthria and eye movement disorders follow. Additional non-cerebellar features are crucial: autonomic failure (MSA), neuropathy (FA, CANVAS), tremor and cognitive change (FXTAS).
det.diagnosis: Imaging confirms atrophy. Systematic screening for acquired causes precedes genetic testing. Repeat expansion testing is needed because panels may miss them.
det.treatment: Treat reversible causes (stop alcohol, thiamine, vitamin E, gluten-free diet, discontinue toxic drugs). Rehabilitation is the mainstay; specific drugs exist for a few subtypes.
det.prognosis: Variable; alcohol-related degeneration may stabilise with abstinence.
pearls: Leg-predominant ataxia with vermian atrophy: think alcohol.
Add autonomic history to every ataxia assessment.
Atrophy pattern on MRI narrows the differential.
det.thd: Cerebellar atrophy คือสมองน้อยฝ่อแบบลุกลาม ทำให้เดินเซ พูดไม่ชัด ตากระตุก สาเหตุ ได้แก่ สุรา (ฝ่อที่ vermis ส่วนหน้า ขาเซมากกว่าแขน) พันธุกรรม MSA และ paraneoplastic ตรวจ MRI ดูรูปแบบการฝ่อและหาสาเหตุที่รักษาได้ รักษาโดยกำจัดสาเหตุและฝึกการทรงตัว

name: Cerebellar disease
formal: General term for processes affecting the cerebellum causing ataxia, nystagmus, hypotonia, and intention tremor; ipsilateral signs for hemisphere lesions.

det.patho: This umbrella term covers any process affecting the cerebellum: stroke, haemorrhage, tumour, demyelination, infection, toxins and degenerations. Unilateral hemisphere lesions cause ipsilateral signs because cerebellar output and input pathways cross twice before reaching the limbs. Midline (vermis and flocculonodular) damage affects posture, gait and eye movements more than the limbs. It is a localisation label, not a single disease.
det.clinical: Signs include ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, hypotonia, nystagmus and dysarthria. Acute cerebellar stroke can present as isolated vertigo and vomiting, so the inability to stand or walk is an important clue. Swelling from infarct or haemorrhage in the posterior fossa can cause hydrocephalus and brainstem compression within hours to days, a neurosurgical emergency. Chronic lesions are often well compensated, especially in children.
det.diagnosis: MRI with diffusion imaging is the investigation of choice; CT is used first when haemorrhage or mass effect is suspected, though it misses small posterior fossa infarcts. At the bedside, the HINTS examination (head impulse, nystagmus pattern, skew) helps separate central from peripheral acute vertigo. Further tests follow the suspected cause.
det.treatment: Management depends on cause. Large cerebellar haemorrhages (often above about 3 cm) or swollen infarcts with deterioration or hydrocephalus need urgent neurosurgical decompression and sometimes ventricular drainage. Ischaemic stroke follows standard reperfusion and secondary prevention pathways. Balance and gait rehabilitation helps all chronic deficits.
det.prognosis: Variable; young patients often compensate well.
pearls: Cerebellar hemisphere lesions cause ipsilateral signs.
Large cerebellar strokes can deteriorate rapidly; monitor consciousness.
HINTS exam helps identify central vertigo.
det.thd: Cerebellar disease เป็นคำกว้างสำหรับภาวะที่สมองน้อยผิดปกติ มีเดินเซ กะระยะผิด สั่นเวลาเคลื่อนไหว และตากระตุก รอยโรคที่ซีกสมองน้อยทำให้เกิดอาการด้านเดียวกัน ต้องตรวจ MRI หาสาเหตุ หากเป็นเลือดออกหรือก้อนขนาดใหญ่อาจต้องผ่าตัดด่วน

det.patho: Cerebellar disorders include any process disrupting the cerebellum or its connections in the brainstem and thalamus. Major categories are vascular, demyelinating, neoplastic, infectious, immune, toxic-nutritional, genetic and degenerative. Purkinje cells are especially vulnerable to toxins, antibodies and many inherited defects.
det.clinical: Ataxia, dysarthria and abnormal eye movements are core; the cerebellum also contributes to cognition and emotion. History of onset, family history, drug and alcohol use, and extra-cerebellar features guide classification.
det.diagnosis: MRI is the first test and often points to the category. Laboratory screening looks for treatable causes such as thiamine, B12 or vitamin E deficiency, hypothyroidism and gluten sensitivity. Subacute cases need antibody testing and cancer screening; chronic progressive cases need genetic testing including repeat expansions.
det.treatment: Treat the specific cause, for example immunotherapy for MS or immune ataxias, vitamin replacement for deficiencies, and withdrawal of toxic drugs or alcohol. Physiotherapy focused on balance and coordination, occupational therapy and speech therapy benefit nearly all patients. Walking aids and fall prevention are important in progressive disease.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause.
pearls: Group ataxias by tempo: acute, subacute, chronic.
Extra-cerebellar signs provide the diagnosis.
Remember the cerebellum's role in cognition.
det.thd: Cerebellar disorders คือกลุ่มโรคที่ทำให้สมองน้อยทำงานผิดปกติ มีอาการเดินเซเป็นหลัก สาเหตุมีหลายกลุ่ม ได้แก่ หลอดเลือด MS เนื้องอก ติดเชื้อ ภูมิคุ้มกัน พิษ พันธุกรรม และความเสื่อม การแยกตามความเร็วของอาการช่วยวางแผนการตรวจ

det.patho: Hypertensive arteriolopathy of the superior cerebellar and posterior inferior cerebellar artery branches typically causes bleeding near the dentate nucleus. The tight posterior fossa means modest haematomas can compress the brainstem and fourth ventricle.
det.clinical: Patients present with headache, vomiting, vertigo and gait failure. Consciousness may be preserved initially and then decline abruptly. Signs of brainstem compression include ipsilateral gaze palsy, facial weakness, small reactive pupils and abnormal breathing.
det.diagnosis: CT makes the diagnosis. Measure haematoma diameter, check fourth ventricle effacement and ventricular size. Look for secondary causes in younger or normotensive patients.
det.treatment: Lower blood pressure (target systolic around 140 mmHg), reverse anticoagulation and monitor in a neurocritical care unit. Surgical evacuation is recommended for haematomas over about 3 cm or with brainstem compression or hydrocephalus. External ventricular drainage alone may worsen upward herniation if used without decompression.
det.prognosis: Good recovery is possible after timely surgery; delayed treatment of compression is often fatal.
pearls: Cannot stand plus headache and vomiting: CT before calling it vertigo.
Gaze palsy towards the lesion signals brainstem compression.
Surgery is lifesaving for large cerebellar bleeds.

det.patho: Lesions of the cerebellar nuclei or outflow pathways (superior cerebellar peduncle, red nucleus region, ventrolateral thalamus) disrupt feed-forward correction of movement. Delayed or inaccurate correction produces oscillation that grows as precision demand rises.
det.clinical: Tremor appears during goal-directed movements and is maximal near the target. Associated cerebellar signs are almost always present. Axial titubation involves the head and trunk. Severe tremor can be highly disabling for feeding and writing.
det.diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis based on tremor characteristics and accompanying cerebellar signs. MRI identifies the lesion; review medications and alcohol. Electrophysiology can distinguish from functional or essential tremor.
det.treatment: Medications (propranolol, primidone, topiramate, isoniazid, clonazepam) have limited effect. Occupational therapy, wrist weights and assistive devices help. Severe tremor in selected patients may be eased by deep brain stimulation targeting the thalamic Vim nucleus, or by focused ultrasound in selected patients.
det.prognosis: Post-relapse or post-stroke tremor may improve partially; degenerative causes progress.
pearls: Tremor that worsens on approach to the target = intention (cerebellar) tremor.
Rest component plus intention tremor suggests Holmes tremor.
Check lithium and phenytoin levels.
det.thd: Cerebellar tremor คืออาการสั่นความถี่ต่ำที่สั่นมากขึ้นเมื่อมือเข้าใกล้เป้าหมาย เกิดจากรอยโรคที่สมองน้อยหรือทางเดินออกของสมองน้อย มักพบใน MS, stroke, เนื้องอก, สุรา หรือยาบางชนิด มักมีอาการเดินเซหรือชี้เป้าพลาดร่วม การวินิจฉัยใช้การตรวจร่างกายและ MRI ยามักได้ผลน้อย การฟื้นฟู อุปกรณ์ช่วย และ DBS อาจช่วยในรายรุนแรง

det.patho: The cerebellopontine angle is a CSF-filled space between cerebellum, pons and petrous bone, crossed by cranial nerves V, VII and VIII. Slow-growing masses stretch these nerves and later compress cerebellum and brainstem, eventually blocking the fourth ventricle. Vestibular schwannomas account for most lesions, followed by meningiomas and epidermoid cysts.
det.clinical: Hearing loss and tinnitus usually come first, imbalance next, and trigeminal symptoms and loss of corneal reflex follow. The facial nerve is surprisingly resistant to slow compression, so early facial palsy suggests a non-schwannoma lesion such as meningioma, cholesteatoma or malignancy. Large lesions add ataxia, raised pressure and dysphagia. Sudden worsening may reflect haemorrhage or cyst expansion.
det.diagnosis: Any unexplained asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss deserves MRI of the internal auditory canals. Enhancement pattern, canal widening, dural tail and diffusion restriction help separate schwannoma, meningioma and epidermoid. Audiology defines baseline hearing for surgical decisions. Bilateral lesions should prompt NF2-related schwannomatosis assessment.
det.treatment: Options include observation with serial MRI for small lesions, stereotactic radiosurgery for small to medium tumours and microsurgery for large or compressive ones. Facial nerve monitoring is standard during surgery. Hydrocephalus may need shunting or resolve after resection. Hearing rehabilitation includes CROS aids or cochlear implant in selected cases.
det.prognosis: Benign lesions have excellent survival; outcome is mainly about hearing and facial nerve preservation.
pearls: Absent corneal reflex is an early sign of a CPA mass.
Early facial weakness argues against vestibular schwannoma.
Asymmetric hearing loss of unknown cause needs MRI.

det.patho: The cerebellopontine angle is a CSF space containing cranial nerves V, VII and VIII and the anterior inferior cerebellar artery. Tumours arising from these nerves, the dura, or embryonic remnants compress the nerves first and then the pons and cerebellum. Hearing loss reflects cochlear nerve or vascular compromise.
det.clinical: Progressive unilateral hearing loss is the classic presentation, though sudden deafness can also occur. Vertigo is uncommon because vestibular loss is gradual and compensated. Tumours over about 3 cm cause facial numbness, cerebellar signs and hydrocephalus. Epidermoids can cause hemifacial spasm or trigeminal neuralgia.
det.diagnosis: Any asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss or unilateral tinnitus warrants MRI of the internal auditory canals. Imaging features distinguish common lesions: schwannomas extend into the canal, meningiomas have a dural tail, epidermoids are diffusion-restricting and non-enhancing, and lipomas are T1 bright. Audiometry documents baseline hearing.
det.treatment: Small schwannomas may be observed with serial MRI. Growing or medium tumours are treated with stereotactic radiosurgery or microsurgery, chosen by size, age, hearing and patient preference. Large tumours causing brainstem compression need surgery. Facial nerve preservation and hearing outcomes are key surgical goals.
det.prognosis: Most are benign with excellent survival; morbidity relates to hearing loss and facial nerve injury.
pearls: Unilateral sensorineural hearing loss = MRI internal auditory canals.
Corneal reflex loss is an early sign of trigeminal involvement by CPA mass.
Epidermoid: bright on DWI; arachnoid cyst: dark.

det.patho: Beta-amyloid (mainly Aβ40) deposits in the walls of small cortical and leptomeningeal arteries replace smooth muscle and make them brittle, causing lobar haemorrhages, cortical microbleeds, convexity SAH and cortical superficial siderosis, while impaired perivascular drainage produces white matter injury and enlarged centrum semiovale perivascular spaces. Prevalence rises steeply with age, and APOE e4 (amyloid deposition) and e2 (vessel rupture) genotypes modify risk. Hereditary forms (e.g. Dutch type, APP mutations) start earlier, and iatrogenic CAA appears decades after childhood neurosurgery or cadaveric dura or pituitary hormone exposure, implying seeded transmission. An inflammatory variant (CAA-ri) reflects an immune reaction against vascular amyloid, closely resembling ARIA from anti-amyloid antibody drugs.
det.clinical: Presentations include spontaneous lobar haemorrhage in older adults, transient focal neurological episodes (spreading paraesthesia, weakness or visual symptoms lasting minutes, from convexity SAH or siderosis), progressive cognitive decline with slowed processing, and incidental microbleeds on MRI. Cerebellar superficial haemorrhages can occur, whereas deep basal ganglia or brainstem bleeds point elsewhere. CAA-related inflammation causes subacute headache, confusion, seizures and focal signs with asymmetric confluent white matter oedema. Recurrent bleeds are common, cumulative disability follows, and amyloid spells that herald convexity bleeding predict a high short-term risk of ICH.
det.diagnosis: The Boston criteria v2.0 apply to people aged 50 or older presenting with spontaneous ICH, transient focal episodes or cognitive impairment. Probable CAA requires at least two strictly lobar haemorrhagic lesions in any combination (ICH, microbleeds, foci of cortical superficial siderosis or convexity SAH), or one such lesion plus one white matter feature (severe centrum semiovale perivascular spaces or a multispot subcortical white matter hyperintensity pattern), with no deep haemorrhagic lesion; possible CAA needs only one of these. Cerebellar lesions are not counted as deep. On CT alone, the Edinburgh criteria use finger-like projections and subarachnoid extension of a lobar haematoma. Pathology remains definitive; exclude vascular malformation, tumour, venous thrombosis, coagulopathy and trauma, and support CAA-ri with CSF anti-amyloid antibodies or biopsy.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying therapy; management focuses on preventing bleeding: strict BP control (the single most effective measure) and minimising antithrombotic exposure. After ICH, restarting an antiplatelet for a firm indication is reasonable, but long-term anticoagulation carries a high rebleeding risk in CAA, especially with siderosis or convexity SAH, so left atrial appendage occlusion is preferred for AF where feasible. Statins are not contraindicated when indicated. Transient focal episodes should not be treated as TIA with antithrombotics; some clinicians use antiseizure drugs or simply observe. CAA-ri responds to corticosteroids, sometimes with steroid-sparing immunosuppressants, and patients with CAA markers face higher ARIA risk on lecanemab or donanemab, which is why SWI is checked before treatment.
det.prognosis: Recurrent lobar haemorrhage occurs at several percent per year, highest with disseminated cortical siderosis; cognitive impairment and dementia are frequent.
pearls: Lobar bleed + microbleeds + siderosis in the elderly = probable CAA.
Amyloid spells mimic TIA or migraine aura; antithrombotics may cause harm.
Check SWI before starting anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies for Alzheimer disease.
Lobar bleeding before age 55 with remote childhood neurosurgery should raise iatrogenic CAA.

det.patho: Mutations in NOTCH3, almost all altering the number of cysteine residues in the extracellular EGF-like repeats, cause accumulation of the NOTCH3 ectodomain and granular osmiophilic deposits around degenerating vascular smooth muscle cells. Small penetrating arteries become thickened and fibrotic with narrowed lumens, leading to chronic hypoperfusion of white matter and lacunar infarcts. It is the most common monogenic cause of stroke; variants in EGFr 1–6 cause more severe disease than those in EGFr 7–34. An Asian variant spectrum (e.g. R544C in Taiwan) often gives later onset without the temporal pole sign.
det.clinical: Course typically runs: migraine with aura in young adulthood, then recurrent subcortical ischaemic events, mood disturbance (depression, bipolar features) and apathy, and finally subcortical dementia with gait failure and pseudobulbar palsy. Strokes are lacunar, not territorial. Intracerebral haemorrhage is uncommon but more frequent in Asian series. Phenotype varies greatly even within one family.
det.diagnosis: Suspect in young lacunar stroke, extensive WMH out of proportion to age and risk factors, or a family history. Anterior temporal pole involvement is highly suggestive in European patients but less consistent in East Asians. Genetic testing for cysteine-altering NOTCH3 variants is the reference standard; skin biopsy with electron microscopy showing GOM is highly specific. Differentials include other monogenic SVDs (HTRA1, COL4A1/2, Fabry), MS and leukodystrophies.
det.treatment: No disease-specific therapy. Manage vascular risk aggressively, stop smoking, and use antiplatelet after ischaemic events (avoid routine anticoagulation). Migraine: standard preventives are fine; triptans and ergots are generally avoided because of vasoconstriction concerns. IV thrombolysis has been given without clear excess harm but evidence is limited. Treat depression, provide rehabilitation, and offer genetic counselling with careful pre-symptomatic testing protocols.
det.prognosis: Most patients become dependent by their 60s; median age at death is around 65–70, earlier in men and in carriers of EGFr 1–6 variants.
pearls: Migraine with aura + young lacunar strokes + family history = CADASIL until NOTCH3 tested.
WMH in anterior temporal poles and external capsules is a classic MRI clue.
Patients are often normotensive — extensive WMH without risk factors should prompt testing.
det.thd: CADASIL เป็นโรคหลอดเลือดเล็กในสมองถ่ายทอดทางพันธุกรรมแบบยีนเด่นจากยีน NOTCH3 เริ่มด้วย migraine with aura ในวัยหนุ่มสาว ตามด้วย lacunar stroke ซ้ำ ๆ ในวัยกลางคน อารมณ์ซึมเศร้า เฉยเมย และสมองเสื่อม MRI มี white matter hyperintensities ที่ anterior temporal pole และ external capsule ยืนยันด้วยตรวจยีน NOTCH3 หรือ skin biopsy ยังไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ เน้นคุมปัจจัยเสี่ยง งดบุหรี่ และให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

det.patho: Folate enters the brain mainly through folate receptor alpha on the choroid plexus. Biallelic FOLR1 variants abolish this transport, and blocking or binding autoantibodies against the receptor impair it, so CSF 5-methyltetrahydrofolate falls despite normal blood folate. Secondary cerebral folate deficiency occurs in mitochondrial disorders (especially Kearns-Sayre), some inborn errors and with certain drugs. Low brain folate disturbs methylation, myelination and neurotransmitter synthesis.
det.clinical: Classic infantile onset follows a normal first few months with irritability, slow head growth, developmental regression, ataxia, dyskinesia, spasticity and seizures. FOLR1 cases often show severe myelination failure and refractory epilepsy beginning in early childhood. Antibody-associated cases overlap with autism spectrum features, and the strength of that link remains debated. Visual and hearing loss may develop later.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis rests on low CSF 5-MTHF with normal systemic folate, so a lumbar puncture with properly handled CSF (protected from light, frozen) is essential. Test for FOLR1 variants and serum receptor autoantibodies, and look for underlying mitochondrial or metabolic disease. MRI may show hypomyelination or cerebellar atrophy. Exclude nutritional folate deficiency and drug causes.
det.treatment: Folinic acid (calcium folinate or levofolinate) bypasses the receptor and raises CSF folate; doses are higher than nutritional replacement and adjusted by response and repeat CSF levels. Avoid high-dose folic acid. In antibody-positive children, a milk-free diet has been tried to reduce antibody titres, but evidence is limited. Treat seizures and provide developmental therapy.
det.prognosis: Early treatment, particularly in FOLR1 disease, can improve seizures and development; late treatment leaves fixed deficits.
pearls: Normal blood folate does not exclude brain folate deficiency; CSF 5-MTHF is the test.
Treat with folinic acid, not folic acid.
Look for Kearns-Sayre or other mitochondrial disease as a secondary cause.

det.patho: Infarction follows arterial occlusion from thrombosis or embolism, or hypoperfusion; haemorrhage follows rupture of small arteries weakened by hypertension or amyloid, or of aneurysms and malformations. Both cause focal neuronal loss; haemorrhage adds mass effect.
det.clinical: Both present abruptly with focal signs matching the territory involved. Haemorrhage more often causes headache, vomiting, raised blood pressure and reduced consciousness, but small bleeds look exactly like infarcts.
det.diagnosis: CT distinguishes bleeding from infarction immediately; MRI is more sensitive for small or posterior infarcts and microbleeds. Further work-up seeks the mechanism.
det.treatment: Infarction: reperfusion when eligible, then antithrombotic secondary prevention. Haemorrhage: blood pressure control, anticoagulant reversal and neurosurgical review. Both: stroke unit care, dysphagia screening and rehabilitation.

det.patho: Cerebral palsy describes a group of permanent motor disorders due to non-progressive injury to the developing brain. Major causes include prematurity (periventricular leukomalacia, intraventricular haemorrhage), perinatal arterial stroke, hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, infection, kernicterus and brain malformations; a genetic cause is found in a growing minority. Prevalence is about 2 per 1,000 live births.
det.clinical: Spastic forms are commonest; dyskinetic CP (dystonia, choreoathetosis) follows basal ganglia injury, often from term hypoxia or kernicterus, and ataxic CP is least common. Motor severity is graded with the Gross Motor Function Classification System. Musculoskeletal complications progress with growth even though the brain lesion is static, and adults face early ageing, pain and falling mobility.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the history, examination and MRI; high-risk infants can be identified early with the General Movements Assessment and the Hammersmith Infant Neurological Examination. A normal MRI, family history, regression, or atypical signs (pure ataxia, fluctuating dystonia) should prompt genetic and metabolic testing because several treatable mimics exist (DRD, arginase deficiency, GLUT1 deficiency).
det.treatment: Management is multidisciplinary: physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy, orthoses, and assistive devices. Spasticity is managed with oral agents (baclofen, tizanidine), focal botulinum toxin, intrathecal baclofen or selective dorsal rhizotomy; dystonia may respond to trihexyphenidyl or deep brain stimulation. Orthopaedic surgery corrects contractures and hip displacement. Seizures, nutrition, drooling, communication and education need attention.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is near normal for mildly affected people but reduced in severe quadriplegia with feeding and respiratory problems.
pearls: Regression or progression means it is not CP — look for a metabolic, genetic or structural cause.
Preterm with stiff legs and scissoring: spastic diplegia from periventricular leukomalacia.
Trial levodopa in any 'dystonic CP' without a clear cause.

name: Cerebral trauma and dystonia
formal: Post-traumatic dystonia after brain injury, often delayed by months to years, typically hemidystonia contralateral to basal ganglia or thalamic damage.
simple: Painful twisting muscle postures that develop after a head injury.
th: dystonia หลังสมองบาดเจ็บ มักเกิดช้าเป็นเดือนหรือปี มักเป็นครึ่งซีกด้านตรงข้ามกับรอยโรคที่ basal ganglia หรือ thalamus

Delayed onset, often months to years after injury
May coexist with tremor, chorea or myoclonus
Often occurs after severe injury, frequently in young people

case.story: Severe head injury in a motorcycle crash at 18; recovered well, but over the past year his left arm twists when writing.
case.exam: Left arm and leg dystonic posturing, mild left hemiparesis.
case.tests: MRI old right putaminal and thalamic lesions.
case.q: What is the diagnosis?

det.patho: Damage to the basal ganglia or thalamus disrupts the circuits that select and inhibit movements. The delay between injury and dystonia suggests that maladaptive plasticity, axonal sprouting or ongoing inflammation contribute rather than the lesion alone. Putaminal lesions are the commonest substrate, followed by thalamic ones. Peripheral injury can also be followed by dystonia, but that is a separate and more contested entity.
det.clinical: Dystonia affects the side opposite the lesion, with the arm generally worse than the leg, and may progress for months before stabilising. Tremor, myoclonus or chorea can coexist, and hemiparesis from the original injury is common. Without treatment, painful postures and fixed contractures develop. Younger patients appear more susceptible.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on a clear history of significant head injury and an MRI lesion in the contralateral basal ganglia or thalamus. Exclude Wilson disease, drug-induced dystonia and genetic dystonias, particularly when imaging is normal. A long gap between injury and onset does not argue against the link.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin is useful for focal or segmental components. Oral options include trihexyphenidyl, baclofen and clonazepam, with modest benefit. Pallidal or thalamic deep brain stimulation may help refractory cases, though responses are smaller than in isolated genetic dystonia. Physiotherapy and splinting help prevent contractures.
det.prognosis: Often persistent; partial response to treatment.
pearls: Dystonia can appear years after brain injury.
Putaminal lesions are the classic substrate.
Secondary dystonia responds less well to DBS than primary.
det.thd: Dystonia หลังสมองบาดเจ็บมักเกิดช้าเป็นเดือนหรือปี มักเป็นครึ่งซีกตรงข้ามกับรอยโรคที่ putamen หรือ thalamus วินิจฉัยจากประวัติและ MRI รักษาด้วย botulinum toxin ยารับประทาน และ DBS ในรายที่ดื้อยา
