name: Cerebral vasculitis
formal: Inflammation of CNS vessels, primary or secondary to systemic disease or infection, causing stroke-like events, headache and encephalopathy.
simple: Inflammation of brain blood vessels, which can cause strokes and confusion.
th: การอักเสบของหลอดเลือดในสมอง — ชนิดปฐมภูมิ (PACNS) มาแบบค่อยเป็นค่อยไป ปวดหัว ความคิดถดถอย stroke หลายจุด CSF อักเสบ ต้องพิสูจน์และรักษาด้วย steroid ร่วมกับ cyclophosphamide/rituximab
tempoNote: Usually builds up over weeks to months with stepwise events; acute presentations occur but are less typical
feat: Persistent, non-thunderclap headache with gradually worsening cognition or behaviour
Recurrent strokes in several territories, often of different ages on MRI
Seizures and encephalopathy; spinal cord involvement occasionally
Systemic features (rash, arthritis, renal or lung disease, high ESR) suggest secondary vasculitis rather than primary
inv: MRI: multiple infarcts in different stages, microbleeds, leptomeningeal or parenchymal enhancement; a normal MRI makes PACNS very unlikely
CSF: mild lymphocytic pleocytosis and raised protein in most; also screen for infection (VZV, TB, syphilis, fungi)
Vessel imaging (CTA/MRA, catheter angiography, vessel-wall MRI) — beading is neither sensitive for small vessels nor specific
Brain and leptomeningeal biopsy from an enhancing, non-eloquent area is the reference standard

case.story: Three months of dull daily headache, forgetfulness and slowing at work; two episodes of transient left arm numbness, then new word-finding difficulty.
case.exam: Mild expressive aphasia, right pronator drift, MoCA 21/30; no rash or joint signs.
case.tests: MRI: small infarcts in both hemispheres of different ages with patchy leptomeningeal enhancement; CSF 18 lymphocytes, protein 95 mg/dL, cultures and VZV PCR negative; ESR normal.
case.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis and why are steroids alone not enough?
case.a: Brain-leptomeningeal biopsy to show transmural vessel inflammation (PACNS) and exclude lymphoma or infection; induction usually combines glucocorticoids with cyclophosphamide or rituximab.

det.patho: Inflammation of the vessel wall narrows or occludes arteries and causes ischaemia, sometimes haemorrhage. In PACNS the process is confined to the brain and spinal cord vessels and is granulomatous, lymphocytic or necrotising on histology; one subset is linked to amyloid deposition. Secondary CNS vasculitis complicates infections (VZV, TB, syphilis, fungi, HIV), systemic vasculitides, connective tissue diseases, drugs and lymphoma.
det.clinical: Primary angiitis has a median age around 50 and slightly more men. The common pattern is headache plus cognitive decline with or without multifocal strokes; seizures, cranial neuropathies and myelopathy occur less often. Large-to-medium vessel disease presents more like strokes, while small vessel disease looks like a progressive encephalopathy with enhancing lesions. Fever, weight loss and raised inflammatory markers should prompt a search for systemic or infectious causes.
det.diagnosis: There is no single blood marker. Combine MRI evidence of multifocal ischaemia or enhancement, inflammatory CSF and vessel imaging, then aim for biopsy because angiographic beading is non-specific and small-vessel disease can have normal angiograms. Rule out RCVS (normal CSF, reversibility), infection, lymphoma, atherosclerosis, moyamoya, CAA-ri and demyelination. Vessel-wall MRI showing concentric enhancement supports but does not prove inflammation.
det.treatment: Induction typically uses high-dose glucocorticoids (often an intravenous methylprednisolone pulse then oral prednisolone) together with cyclophosphamide or rituximab for more severe or biopsy-proven disease. Maintenance with azathioprine, mycophenolate or methotrexate for 1–2 years or more follows. Secondary vasculitis is managed by treating the cause (e.g. aciclovir for VZV, antituberculous therapy). Use antithrombotics cautiously and monitor with serial MRI.
det.prognosis: With treatment many patients stabilise or improve; relapse occurs in about a quarter and mortality is higher with large-vessel involvement, infarcts at presentation or delayed diagnosis.
pearls: Normal CSF and normal MRI argue strongly against PACNS.
An abnormal angiogram is not proof of vasculitis — think RCVS, atheroma and infection.
Always exclude VZV and TB before immunosuppression.
det.thd: Cerebral vasculitis คือการอักเสบของผนังหลอดเลือดสมอง ชนิดปฐมภูมิ (PACNS) เกิดเฉพาะในระบบประสาทส่วนกลาง ผู้ป่วยปวดศีรษะเรื้อรัง ความจำหรือพฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน และมี stroke หลายตำแหน่งต่างเวลา CSF มักมีเซลล์และโปรตีนสูง การวินิจฉัยแน่นอนต้องตัดชิ้นเนื้อสมอง และต้องแยกจาก RCVS การติดเชื้อ และ lymphoma รักษาด้วย steroid ร่วมกับ cyclophosphamide หรือ rituximab

name: Cerebral vasospasm
formal: Reversible narrowing of intracranial arteries, classically 4-14 days after subarachnoid haemorrhage, causing delayed cerebral ischaemia.
simple: Narrowing of brain arteries, often after bleeding around the brain, which can cause a stroke.
more: Narrowing of cerebral arteries, usually after subarachnoid haemorrhage, causing delayed cerebral ischaemia.
th: Vasospasm คือภาวะหลอดเลือดสมองตีบแคบชั่วคราวหลังเลือดออกใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมองแตกจากหลอดเลือดโป่งพอง มักเกิดวันที่ 4–14 ทำให้เกิดสมองขาดเลือดล่าช้า (DCI) ผู้ป่วยซึมลง หรือมีอาการอ่อนแรงใหม่ ต้องแยกสาเหตุอื่นก่อน เช่น เลือดออกซ้ำ น้ำคั่งโพรงสมอง โซเดียมต่ำ ชัก
tempoNote: Almost never before day 3 after aneurysmal SAH, peaks between days 7 and 10, and has usually settled by about day 14 to 21; angiographic narrowing takes a few weeks to resolve
feat: A new headache, drowsiness, confusion or focal deficit that evolves gradually in the second week after aneurysmal SAH; the picture can fluctuate and is a diagnosis of exclusion

Anterior cerebral artery territory spasm gives abulia, slowed speech, grasp or suck reflexes and urinary incontinence (bilateral frontal infarcts after anterior communicating aneurysm rupture); MCA spasm gives hemiparesis, aphasia or neglect
Angiographic narrowing appears in roughly half of SAH patients but only about a third become symptomatic; delayed cerebral ischaemia (DCI) is the broader clinical term used in research and guidelines
Risk rises with thick cisternal clot or intraventricular blood (modified Fisher 3–4), poor clinical grade, smoking and younger age; early aneurysm treatment does not prevent it
Mimics that must be excluded: rebleeding, hydrocephalus, seizure, hyponatraemia (including cerebral salt wasting), sepsis, hypoxia and cerebral oedema
inv: Daily neurological examination and transcranial Doppler: mean MCA velocity above about 120 cm/s suggests spasm and above 200 cm/s severe spasm; a Lindegaard ratio (MCA:ICA) above 3 separates spasm from hyperaemia, and a rise of more than 50 cm/s in a day is a warning
CT angiography with CT perfusion (or MRI with perfusion) when a deficit appears; digital subtraction angiography remains the reference and allows treatment in the same sitting
Urgent non-contrast CT for rebleeding or hydrocephalus, sodium and osmolality, glucose, infection screen and EEG (continuous EEG can show delayed ischaemia early in comatose patients)

case.who: 46-year-old woman, a market trader from Nakhon Ratchasima
case.story: On day 8 after coiling of a ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm (Hunt-Hess 3, thick basal cistern clot) she becomes slow to speak and sleepy, and her nurse notes she has stopped asking for the bedpan.
case.exam: GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6), abulia with whispered speech, grasp reflex on both sides, mild left leg weakness, no neck rigidity beyond baseline.
case.tests: CT shows no new blood and stable small ventricles; sodium 134 mmol/L, glucose normal; TCD mean ACA and MCA velocities have risen from 70 to above 180 cm/s with a Lindegaard ratio of 5; CT perfusion shows prolonged transit time in both anterior cerebral territories.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what is the stepwise plan?
case.a: Delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm after SAH. Confirm nimodipine is being given, keep euvolaemia and correct sodium, raise blood pressure with vasopressor under monitoring, and if she does not improve or worsens go to angiography for intra-arterial vasodilator or balloon angioplasty.

det.patho: Breakdown products of subarachnoid blood, especially oxyhaemoglobin, reduce nitric oxide, raise endothelin-1 and trigger smooth-muscle contraction, inflammation and structural wall change in the arteries bathed in clot. The spasm mainly affects the proximal ACA and MCA segments. Delayed cerebral ischaemia is however multifactorial: early brain injury, microvascular constriction and microthrombi, cortical spreading depolarisations and impaired autoregulation all contribute, which is why relieving large-artery narrowing does not always prevent infarction.
det.clinical: Symptoms rarely begin before day 3, peak around the second week and resolve by about the third. The onset is usually gradual, with a new or increasing headache, lethargy, disorientation and sometimes meningism, followed by focal signs that follow the arterial territory. The anterior cerebral syndrome (abulia, grasp reflex, slowness, incontinence) is especially common after anterior communicating aneurysm rupture. Radiographic spasm without symptoms and symptoms without visible spasm both occur, so the term delayed cerebral ischaemia is preferred. In unconscious patients the diagnosis depends on monitoring because the examination cannot be followed.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical and by exclusion: a delayed deficit compatible with an arterial territory in the right time window after exclusion of rebleeding, hydrocephalus, seizure, metabolic upset, hypoxia and infection. Transcranial Doppler is a bedside trend tool whose velocities are specific but only moderately sensitive in the middle cerebral artery and unreliable in the anterior cerebral artery. CT angiography is specific but may overstate the degree of narrowing; CT or MR perfusion shows the tissue at risk, and catheter angiography confirms and allows treatment. Baseline Doppler studies taken before the spasm period make later values more useful.
det.treatment: Oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days (or 30 mg every 2 hours if blood pressure falls) is the one drug proven to improve outcome, probably by neuroprotection rather than by dilating arteries. Maintain euvolaemia, normal sodium and normothermia; routine prophylactic hypervolaemia and haemodilution are no longer used. For symptomatic delayed ischaemia the usual first step is to raise blood pressure with a vasopressor once the aneurysm is secured, although randomised evidence for induced hypertension is limited. If this fails or complications arise, intra-arterial vasodilators (such as nicardipine, verapamil or milrinone) or balloon angioplasty of accessible vessels are used. Magnesium and statins did not help in trials, and clazosentan lowers angiographic spasm but did not clearly improve clinical outcome in the large phase 3 trial.
det.prognosis: Delayed ischaemia is a major cause of poor outcome and death after SAH, but prompt treatment can reverse deficits, and early recognition matters more than any single therapy.
pearls: A new deficit in the second week after SAH is vasospasm until the mimics are excluded: always check CT, sodium and ventilation first.
Nimodipine improves outcome without reversing the narrowing; give it on schedule to everyone with aneurysmal SAH.
Hyponatraemia after SAH is often salt wasting with hypovolaemia; fluid restriction can worsen ischaemia.

qx.stem: A 52-year-old market vendor from Nakhon Pathom had a Fisher grade 3 subarachnoid haemorrhage from an anterior communicating artery aneurysm that was coiled on day 1. She is on oral nimodipine and is euvolaemic. On day 7 she becomes newly drowsy and develops weakness of the right leg. CT shows no rebleed or hydrocephalus, sodium is normal, and transcranial Doppler shows a sharp rise in velocities in both anterior cerebral arteries.
qx.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Give prophylactic triple-H therapy with hypervolaemia and haemodilution
Stop nimodipine and start intravenous labetalol
Induce hypertension with a vasopressor and arrange angiography for possible intra-arterial vasodilator or angioplasty
Start intravenous heparin for presumed cardioembolism
Perform an urgent lumbar drain and await clinical change
qx.why: New focal deficit in the day 4-14 window, with rebleed, hydrocephalus and hyponatraemia excluded, suggests delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm. Current practice is to keep euvolaemia, raise blood pressure with a vasopressor and escalate to endovascular rescue if the deficit persists. Hypervolaemia and haemodilution are no longer recommended, lowering pressure worsens perfusion, and anticoagulation does not treat vasospasm.

det.patho: Cerebrovascular diseases arise from arterial occlusion (atherosclerosis, embolism, small vessel disease), vessel rupture, venous occlusion and structural malformations. Shared mechanisms include endothelial dysfunction, hypertension-driven vessel injury and thrombosis.
det.clinical: Presentations range from silent infarcts and white matter changes to TIA, stroke, haemorrhage, headache, seizures and progressive cognitive decline.
det.diagnosis: Imaging defines the type; aetiological work-up classifies mechanism. Risk factor screening applies to all.
det.treatment: Acute treatments depend on subtype; secondary prevention centres on blood pressure, lipids, antithrombotics, diabetes management and lifestyle. Public education on stroke recognition shortens time to treatment.
det.prognosis: Highly variable; aggressive risk factor control substantially lowers recurrence.
pearls: Of all the risk factors that can be modified, hypertension matters most.
Silent infarcts count — treat risk factors.
Every TIA is an opportunity to prevent a stroke.

det.patho: Age-related disc degeneration, osteophytes, ligamentum flavum thickening and ligament ossification narrow the canal and foramina. Repeated neck flexion and extension add dynamic injury and local ischaemia to the cord. Posterior longitudinal ligament ossification (OPLL) is particularly common in East Asians, including Thai patients.
det.clinical: Radiculopathy causes dermatomal pain and weakness; myelopathy causes hand clumsiness, gait imbalance and later bladder dysfunction. Symptoms can worsen suddenly after minor trauma (central cord syndrome).
det.diagnosis: MRI confirms compression and any cord signal change; it must be matched to clinical findings because degenerative changes are very common in asymptomatic older adults. CT shows OPLL and bony detail for surgical planning. EMG and NCS help separate radiculopathy from entrapment neuropathy and ALS, and B12 testing excludes a metabolic mimic.
det.treatment: Most radiculopathies settle with analgesia, short-term activity modification and physiotherapy; selective root injections help some, and surgery is offered for persistent pain or progressive weakness. Current guidance recommends decompression for moderate or severe degenerative myelopathy, while mild cases can be offered surgery or careful structured follow-up. Avoid neck manipulation in myelopathy.
det.prognosis: Radiculopathy usually improves; myelopathy tends to progress without surgery.
pearls: Clumsy hands + hyperreflexia in older adult: think cervical myelopathy.
Imaging degeneration is common; correlate clinically.
OPLL is frequent in Asians.
det.thd: Cervical degenerative disease คือกระดูกคอเสื่อม อาจกดรากประสาททำให้ปวดร้าวลงแขน หรือกดไขสันหลังทำให้มือเงอะงะ เดินเซ reflex ไว ตรวจ MRI ยืนยัน รักษา radiculopathy ด้วยการรักษาแบบอนุรักษ์ และผ่าตัดเมื่อเป็น myelopathy ระดับปานกลางขึ้นไป

ddx.pt: No sensory loss, bulbar involvement, widespread fasciculations
B12 deficiency with posterior column loss and neuropathy
Gait disorder with urinary incontinence and cognitive change, no cord signs

aN: cervical spondylosis | degenerative cervical spine disease | degenerative cervical myelopathy | dcm

name: Cervical disk disease
formal: Herniation or degeneration of cervical discs compressing roots or cord, producing arm pain, sensory loss, weakness and sometimes myelopathy.
simple: A slipped or worn disc in the neck pressing on nerves, causing arm pain and weakness.
th: ก้อนหมอนรองกระดูกคอ (cervical disc herniation) กดรากประสาทที่ออกจากรูในระดับเดียวกัน เช่น หมอนรอง C6–7 กดราก C7 ทำให้ปวดคอร้าวลงแขน ชาตามผิวหนัง และกล้ามเนื้อบางมัดอ่อนแรง ตรวจ Spurling, shoulder abduction relief และใช้ MRI ยืนยัน ส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นด้วยการรักษาแบบอนุรักษ์ ผ่าตัด ACDF เมื่ออ่อนแรงมากขึ้น ปวดรุนแรงที่ไม่ดีขึ้น หรือมี myelopathy
tempoNote: Soft disc herniation: pain often present on waking, evolves over days; spondylosis: months to years of radiculopathy or myelopathy
feat: The cervical root exits above the pedicle of the vertebra of the same number, so a herniated cervical disc usually compresses the root of that level (C6–7 disc compresses C7); about two-thirds of herniations are at C6–7 and a fifth at C5–6

C5: shoulder abduction weakness and lateral shoulder numbness; C6: biceps and wrist extension weakness, thumb and index numbness; C7: triceps weakness and middle finger numbness with reduced triceps jerk; C8: hand intrinsic weakness and ring and little finger numbness
Neck pain worse on extension, painful limitation of motion, relief by placing the hand on the head (shoulder abduction relief sign); Spurling manoeuvre provokes arm pain
C6 radiculopathy on the left may mimic angina; C8–T1 involvement may give a partial Horner sign
Large central herniation or traumatic extrusion can cause cord syndromes (central cord, Brown-Séquard) or myelopathy with Lhermitte sign, clumsy hands and spastic gait
inv: MRI cervical spine is the first-line investigation and also images the cord; CT or CT myelography when MRI is contraindicated or bone detail (OPLL, osteophyte) is needed
Electrodiagnosis (needle EMG with paraspinals) to confirm radiculopathy, exclude carpal tunnel syndrome, ulnar neuropathy, plexopathy or motor neuron disease
Red flags for fever, weight loss, cancer, trauma or rapid deficit prompt urgent imaging with contrast

case.story: She woke with neck pain and a burning ache down the back of the left arm into the middle finger that is worse when she looks up; her left hand feels weak when she squeezes a pair of scissors.
case.exam: Left triceps 4/5 and wrist flexion 4+/5, reduced triceps reflex, numb middle finger, Spurling test reproduces the pain, relieved by lifting the arm onto the head; gait and reflexes in the legs normal.
case.tests: MRI shows a left posterolateral C6–7 disc extrusion compressing the C7 root, cord not compressed; EMG shows denervation in the triceps and flexor carpi radialis.
case.q: Which root and what is the plan?
case.a: C7 radiculopathy from a C6–7 disc herniation. Offer conservative care (NSAIDs, neuropathic agent, physiotherapy, a trial of epidural steroid if needed) for 6–12 weeks; surgery (ACDF or foraminotomy) if pain is intractable or weakness progresses.

read.where: Chapter 67 Cervical Disc Herniation — Cervical nerve root syndromes; Physical examination; Radiologic evaluation
Chapter 22 Neurologic Disorders Associated with Bone and Joint Disease

det.patho: Cervical discs dehydrate and fissure with age, and the nucleus may herniate posterolaterally into the foramen or centrally into the canal. Unlike the lumbar spine, the exiting root passes immediately over the disc space at the same level, so a lateral herniation compresses the root of the numbered level. Chemical irritation from disc material adds to mechanical compression. Chronic uncovertebral and facet hypertrophy produce spondylotic foraminal stenosis, and central disc, osteophyte or OPLL reduces the canal for the cord.
det.clinical: Radicular pain, often present on waking without obvious trauma, radiates from the neck to the shoulder blade, arm and hand with dermatomal paraesthesia and sometimes myotomal weakness. C6 and C7 account for most cases. Symptoms worsen with neck extension and rotation to the affected side, while holding the arm overhead relieves them. Atrophy and fasciculations may appear in chronic cases. Lhermitte sign, spastic legs or sphincter symptoms signal cord involvement and change management.
det.diagnosis: Localise the root clinically (deltoid, biceps and brachioradialis, triceps and finger flexor reflexes, sensory map), then confirm with MRI at the corresponding level because asymptomatic disc bulges are very common in adults. Spurling, axial traction and shoulder abduction signs are specific but not sensitive. EMG is valuable when localisation is uncertain and for excluding peripheral entrapment and plexopathy. Look for upper motor neuron signs such as Hoffmann reflex, clonus and extensor plantars.
det.treatment: Most patients improve over weeks to months without surgery: analgesia, NSAIDs, a short course of oral steroid in selected cases, neuropathic agents, physiotherapy and activity modification; a soft collar is only for brief comfort. Epidural steroid injection may give temporary relief and carries rare serious neurovascular risks with transforaminal technique. Surgery is for progressive weakness, intractable pain after an adequate trial, or myelopathy: anterior cervical discectomy with fusion or disc arthroplasty, or posterior foraminotomy for a lateral soft disc. Myelopathy from central compression usually warrants decompression because it progresses.
det.prognosis: Radiculopathy has a favourable natural history with most patients improving in 3–6 months; motor recovery after surgery is good if compression is relieved before prolonged atrophy.
pearls: In the neck the disc compresses the root of the same number (C6–7 disc, C7 root); in the lumbar spine it is the root below.
Spurling positive, shoulder abduction relief positive: think root compression, not shoulder disease.
Hand clumsiness, gait imbalance or brisk reflexes turn a radiculopathy into a myelopathy question.
det.thd: ก้อนหมอนรองกระดูกคอส่วนใหญ่เกิดที่ C6–7 และ C5–6 และกดรากประสาทที่ออกจากรูระดับเดียวกัน (หมอนรอง C6–7 กดราก C7) ผู้ป่วยปวดคอร้าวลงแขน ชาเป็นแนว dermatome มีกล้ามเนื้อบางมัดอ่อนแรงและรีเฟล็กซ์ลดลง ตรวจ Spurling และ shoulder abduction relief ยืนยันด้วย MRI และ EMG เมื่อไม่แน่ใจ ส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นเองหรือด้วยยาและกายภาพบำบัด ผ่าตัดเมื่ออ่อนแรงมากขึ้น ปวดรุนแรงที่ไม่ดีขึ้น หรือมีอาการของไขสันหลังถูกกด

ddx.pt: Long-tract signs, gait disturbance and hyperreflexia from cord compression rather than a single root pattern

aN: cervical disc disease | cervical disc herniation | cervical disc prolapse | cervical degenerative disc disease | cervical spondylosis

name: Cervical meningioma
formal: Benign dural tumour in the cervical canal, more often in women, causing slowly progressive cord compression with weakness, sensory loss and gait trouble.
simple: A slow-growing non-cancerous tumour pressing on the neck spinal cord.
th: เนื้องอกของเยื่อดูราที่กระดูกต้นคอ พบในหญิงมากกว่าชาย กดไขสันหลังช้า ๆ ทำให้อ่อนแรง ชา และเดินลำบาก
tempoNote: Symptoms develop slowly over months to years before diagnosis
feat: Middle-aged or older woman with slowly progressive myelopathy
Neck or radicular arm pain, clumsy numb hands, spastic gait
Foramen magnum lesions give unusual patterns: rotating weakness, lower cranial nerve signs, 'numb clumsy hands'
Brisk reflexes, Hoffmann sign and Babinski below the level; possible Brown-Séquard pattern
inv: MRI cervical spine with gadolinium: intradural extramedullary dural-based enhancing mass
CT to look for calcification
Neurophysiology rarely needed; exclude degenerative cervical myelopathy

case.story: For 18 months her hands have felt numb and clumsy, she drops her keys, and walking has become stiff; she was treated for carpal tunnel without benefit.
case.exam: Bilateral hand numbness, brisk reflexes in all limbs, positive Hoffmann and Babinski signs, spastic gait.
case.tests: MRI: homogeneously enhancing 2 cm dural-based mass anterolateral at C2 with cord displacement.
case.q: What is the likely lesion and the treatment?
case.a: Cervical meningioma; surgical resection usually gives good functional recovery.

det.patho: Meningiomas arise from arachnoid cap cells. Spinal meningiomas occur mostly at thoracic levels, but cervical and foramen magnum lesions are clinically important. They are usually WHO grade 1, slow-growing, and compress the cord from outside, often laterally or anteriorly. Hormonal factors and prior radiation are associated.
det.clinical: Symptoms can be present for a long time before diagnosis, and atypical patterns such as hand numbness may be misattributed to peripheral nerve problems. Foramen magnum meningiomas can cause occipital pain, weakness that progresses around the limbs, and lower cranial nerve signs. Sphincter disturbance is usually late.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows an intradural extramedullary mass with broad dural attachment, dural tail and avid homogeneous enhancement; the cord is displaced and compressed. Calcification may be seen on CT. Differentiation from schwannoma relies on shape (meningioma less often dumbbell) and enhancement.
det.treatment: Surgical removal is the standard and is often complete with good outcome. Small asymptomatic tumours may be monitored. Radiotherapy is reserved for residual, recurrent or higher-grade tumours.
det.prognosis: Good; most patients improve after surgery, though severe pre-operative deficits may not fully resolve.
pearls: Numb clumsy hands with brisk reflexes: image the cervical cord, not just the carpal tunnel.
Foramen magnum lesions can mimic MS or motor neuron disease.
Intradural extramedullary + dural tail + middle-aged woman = meningioma.
det.thd: Cervical meningioma คือเนื้องอกชนิดไม่ร้ายของเยื่อหุ้มที่ไขสันหลังส่วนคอ พบในผู้หญิงวัยกลางคนขึ้นไป โตช้าและกดไขสันหลัง ทำให้มือชาและงุ่มง่าม เดินเกร็ง reflex ไว อาจถูกวินิจฉัยผิดเป็น carpal tunnel ตรวจ MRI พบก้อนติดเยื่อดูราและเพิ่มสารทึบรังสีชัด รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัดซึ่งผลมักดี

aN: cervical spinal meningioma | spinal meningioma | foramen magnum meningioma | intradural extramedullary meningioma

name: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy (CSM)
formal: Compression of the cervical spinal cord by age-related degeneration of the spine — disc bulges, osteophytes, ligamentum flavum buckling and ossified posterior longitudinal ligament — causing a slowly progressive spastic gait, clumsy numb hands, hyperreflexia and later bladder disturbance.
simple: Wear-and-tear changes in the neck bones narrow the spinal canal and squeeze the spinal cord, making the hands clumsy and walking stiff and unsteady.
ab: ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament
th: ไขสันหลังส่วนคอถูกกดจากกระดูกคอเสื่อม (หมอนรอง กระดูกงอก เอ็นหนาหรือ OPLL) มือชาและงุ่มง่าม เดินเกร็งไม่มั่นคง reflex ไว Hoffmann บวก ผ่าตัดเมื่ออาการปานกลางหรือแย่ลง
tempoNote: Gradual or step-wise decline over months to years; acute worsening after minor neck trauma (central cord injury) is possible
feat: Numb, clumsy hands: difficulty with buttons, handwriting and chopsticks; 'myelopathy hand' with finger escape sign
Spastic, unsteady gait with poor tandem walking and falls
Hyperreflexia, Hoffmann sign, inverted supinator reflex, extensor plantars; Lhermitte phenomenon
Neck pain and radicular arm pain or wasting at the compressed level
Late urinary urgency and frequency
inv: MRI cervical spine: canal narrowing with cord compression; T2 intramedullary signal change
CT cervical spine to define ossification (OPLL is common in East Asians) for surgical planning
Exclude mimics: B12/copper, HIV/HTLV-1 and syphilis serology, and EMG if anterior horn disease suspected
Severity scoring with the modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association (mJOA) scale

case.story: Over 18 months his hands have become numb and clumsy, he cannot thread needles or do up buttons, and he now holds walls when walking.
case.exam: Broad, stiff gait, brisk reflexes in all limbs, positive Hoffmann signs, inverted supinator jerks, extensor plantars, intrinsic hand wasting, normal cranial nerves.
case.tests: MRI: multilevel C3–C6 spondylosis with cord flattening and T2 hyperintensity at C4–C5; CT shows continuous OPLL C3–C6; B12 normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the recommended management?
case.a: Degenerative cervical (spondylotic) myelopathy with OPLL, moderate severity; refer for surgical decompression (often posterior laminoplasty or laminectomy and fusion for multilevel OPLL).

read.where: Chapter 14 Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders (Degenerative disease of the spine: cervical spine)
Chapter 14 Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders — Degenerative Disease of the Spine
Section VI: Epilepsy Surgery and Neurostimulation

det.patho: With age, discs lose height and bulge, uncovertebral and facet joints form osteophytes, and the ligamentum flavum thickens and folds; ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament is particularly common in East and Southeast Asians. A developmentally narrow canal adds risk. Static compression combined with repeated movement-related stretch reduces cord blood flow, causing ischaemia, demyelination and eventually neuronal loss, especially in the lateral corticospinal tracts and central grey matter.
det.clinical: Among adults past middle age, no other cause of cord dysfunction is seen as often. Typical features are numb clumsy hands, gait imbalance and spasticity, with upper motor neuron signs in the legs and mixed signs at the arm level. Course is usually slow with plateaus but may be stepwise, and a fall can provoke acute central cord syndrome. Many patients are labelled as 'old age' or carpal tunnel syndrome.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis needs both clinical myelopathy and MRI evidence of cord compression; radiological compression alone is common and not an indication for surgery. T2 high signal (and especially T1 low signal) within the cord indicates more advanced injury. CT helps identify OPLL. Rule out B12, copper, HIV, HTLV-1 and syphilis myelopathy, MS and motor neuron disease, particularly when sensory features are absent or wasting is widespread.
det.treatment: Surgical decompression is recommended for moderate and severe myelopathy (mJOA 14 or below) and for mild disease that is progressing; anterior (discectomy or corpectomy with fusion) or posterior (laminoplasty, laminectomy with fusion) approaches are chosen according to levels, alignment and OPLL. Mild stable disease can be monitored closely with supervised rehabilitation, avoiding neck manipulation. Patients should be warned about the risk of injury in falls and minor trauma.
det.prognosis: Surgery usually halts progression and improves function in many; longer symptom duration and severe preoperative deficits predict less recovery.
pearls: Clumsy numb hands in an older adult are cervical myelopathy until proved otherwise — not just carpal tunnel.
Inverted supinator reflex localises around C5–C6.
OPLL is common in Thai and other East Asian patients; ask for CT.
det.thd: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy เกิดจากกระดูกคอเสื่อม หมอนรองกระดูกโป่ง กระดูกงอก เอ็นหนา หรือ OPLL ที่พบบ่อยในคนเอเชีย กดไขสันหลังส่วนคอ ผู้ป่วยมือชางุ่มง่าม ติดกระดุมหรือใช้ตะเกียบลำบาก เดินเกร็งเซ ตรวจพบ reflex ไว Hoffmann บวก และ Babinski บวก วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI ร่วมกับอาการทางคลินิก และต้องแยกขาด B12 HIV HTLV-1 และ ALS ผ่าตัดลดการกดทับเมื่ออาการปานกลางขึ้นไปหรือแย่ลง

aN: csm | degenerative cervical myelopathy | dcm | cervical myelopathy | spondylotic myelopathy | cervical canal stenosis | opll | ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament | myelopathy hand

name: Cervical myelopathy with quadriplegia
formal: Severe cervical cord compression or injury with tetraparesis or tetraplegia, spasticity, sensory level and sphincter loss.
simple: Serious neck spinal cord damage causing weakness or paralysis of all four limbs.
th: ไขสันหลังส่วนคอถูกกดหรือบาดเจ็บรุนแรงจนแขนขาทั้งสี่อ่อนแรงหรือเป็นอัมพาต มีระดับความรู้สึกและเสียการควบคุมหูรูด
tempoNote: Acute with trauma, haemorrhage, infarction or abscess; subacute with tumour or myelitis; chronic with spondylosis
feat: Weakness of all four limbs with upper motor neuron signs below the lesion and lower motor neuron signs at the level
Sensory level in the neck or upper chest; bladder and bowel dysfunction
Lesions at C3–C5 threaten the diaphragm (phrenic nerve) and breathing
Autonomic dysfunction: neurogenic shock, bradycardia, later autonomic dysreflexia
Causes: trauma, spondylosis, disc, epidural abscess or metastasis, transverse myelitis, haemorrhage
inv: Emergency MRI of the cervical spine (whole spine if metastasis or abscess suspected)
CT in trauma; blood cultures and inflammatory markers if infection
Vital capacity monitoring for respiratory failure
CSF and antibody studies if inflammatory myelitis

case.story: Fever and severe neck pain for five days; today he cannot move his arms or legs and has not passed urine.
case.exam: Febrile, neck tenderness, flaccid tetraplegia, sensory level at C5, urinary retention, shallow breathing.
case.tests: MRI shows a C4–C6 ventral epidural collection compressing the cord; blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus; vital capacity 1.1 L.
case.q: What is the emergency and the treatment?
case.a: Cervical spinal epidural abscess with myelopathy and tetraplegia; urgent surgical decompression, IV antibiotics and ICU airway monitoring.

read.where: Chapter 28 Disorders of Consciousness and Intensive Care Neurology — Acute Cervical Cord Disorders

det.patho: Compression, contusion, ischaemia or inflammation of the cervical cord interrupts descending motor and ascending sensory tracts to all four limbs and damages anterior horn cells at the level. Above C5, the phrenic nucleus is at risk, and disruption of descending sympathetic pathways causes neurogenic shock and later autonomic dysreflexia. Secondary injury from swelling and ischaemia evolves over hours to days.
det.clinical: Patients present with weakness or paralysis of all limbs, sensory loss below a cervical level and sphincter failure. Initially there may be spinal shock with flaccidity and areflexia, followed by spasticity. Respiratory compromise, hypotension, bradycardia and poikilothermia are dangerous early complications. The tempo and associated features (fever, trauma, cancer, neck pain) suggest the cause.
det.diagnosis: Urgent MRI is essential and should not be delayed for other tests. CT defines fractures. Laboratory tests target infection and malignancy, and CSF examination is done when imaging shows no compression. The ASIA impairment scale grades severity and helps prognosis.
det.treatment: Compressive causes need urgent decompression and stabilisation; abscesses require surgery plus prolonged IV antibiotics, and metastases need steroids with radiotherapy or surgery. Inflammatory myelitis is treated with high-dose steroids and plasma exchange. Supportive care includes airway protection, ventilation if vital capacity falls, blood pressure support, bladder catheterisation, thromboprophylaxis, pressure care and rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause, completeness and speed of treatment; complete lesions beyond 72 hours rarely recover meaningful function.
pearls: Tetraparesis with a sensory level is a cord emergency — MRI now.
Measure vital capacity; lesions at C3–5 can stop breathing.
Fever plus neck pain plus weakness: epidural abscess until proved otherwise.
det.thd: Cervical myelopathy with quadriplegia คือไขสันหลังส่วนคอถูกกดหรือบาดเจ็บรุนแรงจนแขนขาทั้งสี่อ่อนแรง มีระดับความรู้สึกที่คอและเสียการควบคุมปัสสาวะ ถ้ารอยโรคสูงกว่า C5 อาจทำให้หายใจล้มเหลว สาเหตุมีทั้งอุบัติเหตุ ฝีในช่องไขสันหลัง เนื้องอก กระดูกคอเสื่อม และไขสันหลังอักเสบ ต้องทำ MRI ด่วน ผ่าตัดลดการกดทับตามสาเหตุ และดูแลการหายใจและความดันโลหิต

name: Cervical radiculopathies
formal: Disorders of cervical nerve roots, usually from disc herniation or spondylosis, giving neck and arm pain with dermatomal sensory loss and myotomal weakness, most often C6 and C7.
simple: Pinched nerves in the neck causing pain, numbness, and weakness in the arm and hand.
more: MRI and EMG confirm it. Most cases improve in weeks to months with conservative care; surgery for progressive or severe deficits.
th: รากประสาทส่วนคอถูกกดทับจากหมอนรองกระดูกหรือกระดูกงอก ทำให้ปวดคอร้าวลงแขน ชาและอ่อนแรงตามรากประสาท
tempoNote: Soft disc herniation gives abrupt pain; spondylotic foraminal narrowing evolves gradually
feat: Neck pain with shooting arm pain in a dermatomal band, often worse on looking up or turning toward the painful side
Relief by resting the hand on top of the head (shoulder abduction relief sign)
Myotomal weakness and a reduced matching reflex: C5 biceps, C6 brachioradialis, C7 triceps
C7 is the commonest level, followed by C6
Upper motor neuron signs in the legs indicate coexisting myelopathy
inv: MRI cervical spine (first-line when imaging is needed)
EMG and nerve conduction when imaging and symptoms disagree or to exclude entrapment
Plain films add little except for instability or trauma

case.story: Woke with severe right neck pain shooting down the back of the arm to the middle finger after a long weekend of phone use.
case.exam: Spurling manoeuvre reproduces pain, weak elbow and wrist extension, reduced triceps jerk, numb middle finger; legs normal.
case.tests: MRI shows right C6–C7 posterolateral disc protrusion compressing the C7 root.
case.q: Which root is involved and what is the usual first step?
case.a: Right C7 radiculopathy; conservative care with analgesia, neuropathic agents and physiotherapy, as most recover within weeks.

read.where: Chapter 14 Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders — Degenerative Disease of the Spine

det.patho: Roots are compressed in the intervertebral foramen by disc material or by osteophytes from uncovertebral and facet joints. Mechanical pressure plus local inflammatory mediators from the disc cause radicular pain, and conduction block or axon loss produces weakness and reflex change. In younger adults soft disc is typical, while older adults usually have spondylotic narrowing.
det.clinical: Pain usually dominates, radiating in the affected dermatome, with paraesthesia in the hand for C6–C8 lesions. Weakness follows the myotome but overlap between roots blurs the picture. Neck extension and rotation toward the side provoke symptoms. Red flags include fever, cancer history, progressive weakness, bilateral symptoms or myelopathic signs.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by MRI when symptoms persist beyond several weeks, deficits progress or red flags exist. Imaging abnormalities are common in asymptomatic people, so correlation with level is essential. EMG helps separate root from plexus or entrapment and estimates axon loss; sensory potentials stay normal in root disease.
det.treatment: Most patients improve without surgery using analgesics, short-term activity adjustment, physiotherapy and neuropathic agents; brief oral steroids or image-guided epidural injection are options for severe pain. Surgery (anterior discectomy and fusion, disc arthroplasty or posterior foraminotomy) is reserved for progressive or disabling weakness, myelopathy or pain unresponsive after several weeks. Prolonged collar use is discouraged.
det.prognosis: The majority recover substantially within 6–12 weeks; a minority have recurrent or persistent symptoms.
pearls: Hand-on-head relief favours radiculopathy over shoulder disease, which is worsened by abduction.
Always check the legs: radiculopathy with myelopathy changes urgency.
Imaging disc bulges are common in healthy adults; treat the patient, not the scan.

det.patho: This umbrella term includes degenerative, inflammatory (rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis), infectious (tuberculosis, pyogenic, melioidosis), neoplastic and traumatic disease of the neck. Each can compress nerve roots or the cord, or destabilise the spine. Rheumatoid disease erodes the atlantoaxial joint, while ankylosing spondylitis makes the spine rigid and prone to fracture after minor trauma.
det.clinical: Presentations range from neck pain alone to radiculopathy and myelopathy. Red flags such as fever, weight loss, night pain, cancer history, immunosuppression or trauma should change the work-up. Tuberculous spondylitis and melioidosis are important infections in Thailand. Rapidly evolving weakness needs same-day imaging.
det.diagnosis: MRI with contrast is the key test for cord, roots, discs and epidural collections. CT shows bony destruction and fractures, and flexion-extension films assess instability where safe. Blood cultures, inflammatory markers and image-guided biopsy identify infection or tumour.
det.treatment: Treatment follows the cause: urgent decompression for cord compression with deficit, prolonged targeted antibiotics for infection, radiotherapy or surgery for tumour, and fixation for instability. Degenerative disease is managed as described for cervical spondylosis. Rehabilitation is needed after any significant cord injury.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause and pre-treatment deficit.
pearls: Fever + neck pain + weakness: epidural abscess.
Consider TB and melioidosis in Thai patients.
Rheumatoid patients need cervical spine assessment before intubation.

feat: Exposure: birth or long residence in rural Latin America, a mother from an endemic area, transfusion or organ transplant; very rare in Thailand but seen in migrants
Acute phase: chagoma at the bite site or unilateral painless eyelid swelling (Romaña sign); meningoencephalitis mainly in young children

Acute or reactivated disease: blood smear or buffy coat, quantitative PCR; trypomastigotes may be seen in centrifuged CSF

Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — American Trypanosomiasis (Chagas Disease)

det.patho: Trypanosoma cruzi is passed in the faeces of triatomine bugs, by transfusion, organ transplantation, the oral route or from mother to child. Parasites persist for life in heart and smooth muscle, where chronic inflammation and fibrosis cause cardiomyopathy and destroy autonomic ganglia. The brain is involved in three ways: meningoencephalitis in acute infection, embolism from a diseased heart, and reactivation in immunosuppression, when parasites multiply in glia and form necrotic, mass-like lesions. Reactivated brain lesions are not seen in immunocompetent people.
det.clinical: Most infected adults are in the indeterminate phase and well; about a third develop cardiac or digestive disease over decades. Ischaemic stroke may be the first manifestation of Chagas heart disease and can occur even with mild ventricular dysfunction. In people with HIV, reactivation causes headache, fever, focal deficits and seizures with ring-enhancing lesions, and can be fatal if untreated. Transplant recipients from infected donors, or infected recipients on immunosuppression, need monitoring for acute disease.
det.diagnosis: Chronic infection is diagnosed by two concordant serological tests; parasitological tests are insensitive at this stage. Acute and reactivated infection is shown by parasites in blood or CSF and by rising quantitative PCR. Cardiac evaluation with ECG, echocardiography and rhythm monitoring is needed in every seropositive patient with stroke. In an HIV patient with brain lesions from an endemic area, Chagas should be tested alongside toxoplasmosis and lymphoma.
det.treatment: Antiparasitic treatment is benznidazole (about 5-7 mg/kg/day for 60 days) or nifurtimox (about 8-10 mg/kg/day for 60-90 days); it is clearly indicated in acute, congenital and reactivated disease and in children and women of child-bearing age, and individualised in adults with established cardiomyopathy. Side effects include rash, neutropenia and peripheral neuropathy with benznidazole, and gastrointestinal upset and weight loss with nifurtimox. Stroke prevention relies on anticoagulation for thrombus, aneurysm with embolism or atrial fibrillation, plus heart-failure therapy and devices as needed. Reactivation in HIV is treated with benznidazole and ART.
det.prognosis: Prognosis depends mostly on the cardiomyopathy; reactivated CNS disease has high mortality without prompt antiparasitic therapy.
pearls: Young stroke plus right bundle branch block with left anterior fascicular block in a Latin American migrant: test for T. cruzi.
Chagas reactivation is a mimic of toxoplasmosis in advanced HIV; look at the birthplace.
Screen the children and other family members of an infected woman, because vertical transmission is a major route outside endemic areas.

name: Channelopathies
formal: Disorders of ion channel genes causing episodic phenotypes such as periodic paralysis, myotonia, epilepsy, ataxia, migraine and pain.
simple: Diseases caused by faulty electrical channels in cells, producing attacks of weakness, seizures or pain.
th: กลุ่มโรคที่เกิดจากยีนหรือภูมิต้านทานต่อช่องไอออน ทำให้มีอาการเป็นพัก ๆ เช่น อัมพาตเป็นช่วง กล้ามเนื้อคลายตัวช้า ชัก เดินเซเป็นพัก และไมเกรน
tempoNote: Typically attacks with normal function between them, though some develop fixed weakness or ataxia over years
feat: Stereotyped attacks with recovery between episodes
Triggers such as rest after exercise, carbohydrate meals, cold, stress or fever
Family history often dominant; same gene can give different phenotypes
Examples: periodic paralysis, myotonia, Dravet syndrome, episodic ataxia, hemiplegic migraine, erythromelalgia
inv: Targeted tests during attacks: potassium, EEG, video of events
EMG for myotonia and long exercise test for periodic paralysis
Gene panel (e.g. SCN4A, CACNA1S, CLCN1, SCN1A, KCNA1, CACNA1A, SCN9A); antibodies for acquired forms

case.story: Since age 15 he wakes 2–3 times a year unable to lift his arms and legs after a large rice and sweet dessert dinner; it lasts a few hours. His father had similar spells.
case.exam: Normal between attacks; during one attack proximal flaccid weakness with reduced reflexes, normal sensation.
case.tests: Potassium 2.4 mmol/L during attack; thyroid function normal.
case.q: What broad category of disease is this, and what must be excluded in a young Asian man?
case.a: A skeletal muscle channelopathy, likely familial hypokalaemic periodic paralysis (CACNA1S or SCN4A); exclude thyrotoxic periodic paralysis.

det.patho: Ion channels control the resting and action potentials of nerve and muscle; variants that alter gating or trafficking make membranes either hyperexcitable (myotonia, seizures, pain) or inexcitable (paralysis). Autoantibodies against channels or associated proteins cause acquired channelopathies such as Lambert-Eaton syndrome or Isaacs syndrome. A single gene can cause several phenotypes (for example CACNA1A in episodic ataxia, hemiplegic migraine and SCA6), and one phenotype can arise from several genes. The tendency to episodic symptoms reflects a membrane that works normally until a trigger shifts it past a threshold.
det.clinical: This is an umbrella term, not a single disease. Muscle channelopathies give periodic paralysis and myotonia; brain channelopathies give genetic epilepsies, episodic ataxia and familial hemiplegic migraine; peripheral nerve channelopathies cause pain syndromes or insensitivity to pain. Many patients develop fixed problems later, such as permanent myopathy in periodic paralysis or interictal ataxia. Symptoms often begin in childhood or adolescence.
det.diagnosis: Capture the attack: serum potassium during paralysis, EEG or video for spells, and careful trigger history. Neurophysiology (EMG myotonia, long exercise test, short exercise tests with cooling) helps localise muscle disorders. Genetic panels confirm most familial cases. Always exclude acquired mimics, such as thyrotoxicosis, drugs, renal potassium loss and autoimmune encephalitis.
det.treatment: Management is phenotype-specific: carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and potassium for periodic paralysis, mexiletine for myotonia, acetazolamide or 4-aminopyridine for episodic ataxia type 2, and antiseizure drugs chosen by gene (for example avoiding sodium channel blockers in SCN1A Dravet syndrome). Trigger avoidance is central. Anaesthetists must be told because of malignant hyperthermia or anaesthetic risk in some muscle channelopathies. Precision therapies are emerging for several genes.
det.prognosis: Most are compatible with normal lifespan; outcome depends on the specific disorder, with severe early epileptic encephalopathies the main exception.
pearls: Episodic symptoms with normal examination between attacks suggest a channelopathy.
Genotype can change drug choice: sodium channel blockers can worsen SCN1A epilepsy.
Hypokalaemic paralysis in an Asian man: check thyroid function first.
det.thd: Channelopathy คือกลุ่มโรคที่ช่องไอออนของเซลล์ประสาทหรือกล้ามเนื้อทำงานผิดปกติจากพันธุกรรมหรือภูมิต้านทาน อาการมักเป็นพัก ๆ เช่น อ่อนแรงเป็นช่วง กล้ามเนื้อคลายตัวช้า ชัก เดินเซ หรือไมเกรนชนิดอ่อนแรงครึ่งซีก ระหว่างอาการตรวจร่างกายมักปกติ วินิจฉัยจากการตรวจขณะมีอาการ EMG และการตรวจยีน การรักษาขึ้นกับชนิดของโรคและการหลีกเลี่ยงสิ่งกระตุ้น

Most common inherited neuropathy with distal wasting, pes cavus, foot drop and sensory loss; many genes including PMP22 and MFN2. det.patho: A genetically diverse group of inherited motor and sensory neuropathies with over 100 causative genes. CMT1A, from duplication of PMP22 on chromosome 17p, is by far the most common; other frequent causes are GJB1 (X-linked CMTX1), MPZ and MFN2 (the commonest axonal CMT2A). Demyelinating forms (CMT1) have uniformly slow conduction, axonal forms (CMT2) have preserved velocities with low amplitudes, and intermediate forms sit between. Length-dependent axonal loss underlies the clinical deficit in all types.
det.clinical: Symptoms usually begin in the first two decades with tripping, ankle sprains and difficulty running. Examination shows distal wasting and weakness of the legs (inverted champagne bottle appearance), foot drop with steppage gait, pes cavus and hammer toes, depressed reflexes and distal sensory loss, with hands affected later. Sensory symptoms are typically mild relative to signs. Severity varies widely, even within families. Additional features in some subtypes include hearing loss, optic atrophy, vocal cord paresis and scoliosis.
det.diagnosis: Nerve conduction studies classify the type: in CMT1 the upper-limb motor conduction velocity is below 38 m/s and slowing is uniform without conduction block. Family history and pedigree guide inheritance pattern. Test for PMP22 duplication first in demyelinating cases; then use multigene panels or exome sequencing. Distinguish from CIDP (patchy slowing, conduction block, proximal weakness, raised CSF protein), HNPP and acquired axonal neuropathies.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy is available, although trials are ongoing. Management involves physiotherapy and stretching to prevent contractures, ankle-foot orthoses, orthopaedic foot surgery for severe deformity, occupational therapy for hand function and pain control. Avoid neurotoxic drugs, especially vincristine, which can cause severe weakness in CMT. Offer genetic counselling.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive with normal life expectancy; most remain ambulant, though many need orthoses.
pearls: Uniform slowing points to inherited demyelination; patchy slowing with block suggests acquired disease.
Pes cavus in a family with clumsy feet = check PMP22 duplication.
Vincristine is dangerous in CMT.
Track disability with a standard scale such as the CMT Neuropathy Score, and screen for hearing loss, vocal cord weakness, scoliosis and (in children) hip dysplasia.
Subtype names are shifting toward labels that state inheritance, nerve-conduction pattern and gene together (e.g. AD-CMTde-PMP22), rather than numbered types alone.

det.patho: CMT1 is the dominant demyelinating group of hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy. About 70% of cases are CMT1A, a 1.4 Mb duplication containing PMP22 that causes overproduction of a compact myelin protein; MPZ (CMT1B) and other genes account for the rest. Schwann cells repeatedly lose and rebuild myelin, producing onion bulbs and, over time, secondary axonal loss that drives the weakness. CMT overall affects roughly 1 in 2,500 people.
det.clinical: Children are often described as clumsy, slow runners or prone to ankle sprains; foot deformity and toe walking may be the earliest sign. Weakness and wasting climb slowly from feet to lower legs and later to hands, while sensory symptoms are surprisingly mild. Postural hand tremor occurs in some (historically called Roussy–Lévy). Rapid deterioration, marked asymmetry, pain or cranial nerve involvement should prompt a search for a second, acquired cause such as superimposed CIDP or neurotoxic drugs.
det.diagnosis: Nerve conduction is the key step: diffuse, symmetrical slowing below 38 m/s in arm motor nerves defines the demyelinating form, and it is present from early childhood. Test PMP22 copy number first, then use a multigene neuropathy panel if negative. Family examination and NCS of a parent can clarify inheritance. Avoid labelling as CIDP based on slow velocities alone, and remember that vincristine can cause severe weakness in undiagnosed CMT1A.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy is approved; PMP22-lowering approaches (antisense, gene silencing) are in trials and ascorbic acid was not effective. Management relies on physiotherapy, stretching, ankle-foot orthoses, appropriate footwear and orthopaedic procedures for severe cavus or contractures. Weight control and safe exercise help maintain function. Review medicines for neurotoxicity, especially vincristine, and offer genetic counselling.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is normal; most remain ambulant throughout life, though some need orthoses or aids in later years.
pearls: Uniform slowing equals inherited; patchy slowing with block suggests acquired demyelination.
Check PMP22 duplication before any gene panel in a demyelinating CMT picture.
Ask about CMT before giving vincristine; it can precipitate severe weakness.

qx.stem: A 15-year-old girl from Kanchanaburi has high arches, hammer toes, distal leg wasting, steppage gait and absent ankle reflexes since early teens. Her mother has a similar foot shape. Median motor conduction velocity is 21 m/s in both arms and CMAP amplitudes are only mildly reduced.
qx.q: Which finding suggests this subtype of the inherited neuropathy?
opts: Median velocity above 45 m/s with markedly reduced amplitudes
Asymmetric conduction block with normal velocities
Normal conduction studies
Sensory responses present with absent motor responses
Uniform, symmetric velocity slowing below 38 m/s in the upper limbs
qx.why: Upper-limb median motor velocities under 38 m/s with uniform slowing identify a demyelinating CMT (type 1, most commonly PMP22 duplication), whereas axonal CMT2 has velocities above 38 m/s with low amplitudes. Conduction block suggests acquired demyelination and normal studies exclude a neuropathy.

qx.stem: A 25-year-old man from Surin has pes cavus, high-stepping gait and a similarly affected father. Motor conduction velocities are 18 to 24 m/s in every nerve tested, equal in all nerves, with reduced CMAP amplitudes and no conduction block.
qx.q: Which electrophysiological pattern does this represent?
opts: Uniform, symmetric slowing without conduction block, typical of hereditary demyelinating neuropathy such as PMP22 duplication
Multifocal slowing with conduction block, as in acquired inflammatory demyelinating neuropathy
Normal velocities with low amplitudes, as in axonal CMT2
Absent sensory potentials with normal motor studies, as in a ganglionopathy
A decrement at 3 Hz repetitive stimulation
qx.why: Hereditary demyelinating neuropathies such as CMT1A cause uniformly slow conduction in all nerves, often below 38 m/s, because every internode is affected, and conduction block and dispersion are absent. Acquired demyelination (CIDP) is patchy and asymmetric with block. Axonal neuropathies keep velocity near normal with low amplitudes. A family history and uniform slowing point to a hereditary cause and PMP22 testing.

name: Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease type 2 (CMT2)
formal: Axonal hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy with near-normal conduction velocities, reduced amplitudes; MFN2 is common, with later onset than CMT1.
simple: An inherited nerve disease where the nerve fibres themselves degenerate, causing foot weakness and numbness.
more: Axonal CMT with near-normal conduction velocities but reduced amplitudes, caused by MFN2, GDAP1 and others, with distal weakness and sensory loss. Genetic panels identify the mutation; treatment is supportive; onset and severity vary, MFN2 forms can be severe.

Pes cavus is less prominent than in CMT1; nerves are not thickened

Some subtypes add optic atrophy, vocal cord palsy, hearing loss or pyramidal signs (e.g. MFN2)
Dominant inheritance mostly; recessive and de novo forms exist

case.story: Several years of tripping and burning feet; her father walked with a slapping gait and her son is clumsy.
case.exam: Bilateral foot drop, distal calf wasting, absent ankle reflexes, reduced pinprick to mid-shin, normal-calibre nerves.
case.tests: Peroneal CMAP low, median motor velocity 51 m/s; HbA1c, B12 and immunofixation normal; MFN2 pathogenic variant.
case.q: What distinguishes this from CMT1 electrically?
case.a: Velocities are near normal with small amplitudes, an axonal pattern (CMT2).

det.patho: CMT2 results from primary failure of the axon rather than its myelin. MFN2, a mitochondrial fusion protein, explains about a fifth of cases; others involve neurofilaments (NEFL), heat-shock proteins, axonal transport and tRNA synthetases. The longest axons suffer first, giving a length-dependent pattern. Unlike CMT1 there is no single dominant mutation, so molecular diagnosis is less frequent.
det.clinical: The picture resembles CMT1 but onset is often later and sensory loss and pain may be more prominent. MFN2 disease can be severe in childhood with early wheelchair use, sometimes with optic atrophy (formerly HMSN VI). Some subtypes are motor-predominant and overlap with distal hereditary motor neuropathy. A slowly progressive axonal neuropathy with a family history and foot deformity is the usual clue.
det.diagnosis: NCS shows low amplitudes with preserved or only mildly reduced velocity (arm motor above about 45 m/s). Because acquired axonal neuropathies are common, screen for diabetes, B12 deficiency, alcohol, thyroid disease, paraproteinaemia and drugs before attributing it to genetics. A next-generation sequencing panel or exome is the usual genetic test; variants of uncertain significance are frequent and need segregation studies.
det.treatment: Care is supportive: physiotherapy, orthoses, foot care, pain management with standard neuropathic agents and orthopaedic surgery when needed. Avoid neurotoxic drugs where possible. Gene-specific therapies are still experimental. Genetic counselling is important given variable penetrance.
det.prognosis: Usually slowly progressive with normal lifespan; early-onset MFN2 forms can be disabling.
pearls: Arm motor velocity above 45 m/s with small amplitudes = axonal CMT pattern.
Always exclude common acquired axonal causes before a genetic label.
Optic atrophy plus axonal neuropathy suggests MFN2.
det.thd: CMT2 เป็น CMT ชนิด axonal ที่ตัวแกนประสาทเสื่อมเอง ความเร็วการนำกระแสเกือบปกติแต่ amplitude ต่ำ ยีนที่พบบ่อยคือ MFN2 อาการคล้าย CMT1 คือขาส่วนปลายอ่อนแรงลีบ แต่มักเริ่มช้ากว่าและมีชาหรือปวดมากกว่า ต้องแยกสาเหตุ axonal neuropathy ที่ได้มาภายหลัง เช่น เบาหวาน ขาด B12 ก่อนส่งตรวจยีน การรักษาเป็นกายภาพและอุปกรณ์ช่วยเดิน

det.patho: When input to the visual cortex is reduced, cortical neurons become hyperexcitable through homeostatic plasticity, producing spontaneous activity perceived as images. The content reflects which association areas fire, so faces, figures or patterns appear. The syndrome can occur with eye disease or lesions anywhere along the visual pathway.
det.clinical: Hallucinations are typically well-formed, vivid and soundless, lasting seconds to hours, more common in dim light and when inactive. They may be simple (patterns, grids) or complex. Insight is kept. Many patients have never told anyone. It may appear within a hemianopic field after occipital stroke.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical in a person with substantial visual loss, preserved insight and no other psychiatric or neurological explanation. Screening for cognitive impairment and parkinsonism helps exclude Lewy body disease. Medication review (dopaminergic, anticholinergic) is sensible.
det.treatment: Explanation and reassurance are often enough. Optimising vision, improving lighting, reducing isolation and simple manoeuvres (blinking, looking away, turning on a light) help. Medication such as low-dose antipsychotics or antiseizure drugs is rarely needed and has limited evidence.
det.prognosis: Benign; hallucinations often lessen over a year or more as the brain adapts.
pearls: Ask every patient with severe visual loss about hallucinations — they rarely volunteer them.
Insight preserved and cognition normal: CBS rather than dementia or psychosis.
Can appear in a hemianopic field after occipital stroke.
det.thd: Charles Bonnet syndrome คือภาพหลอนที่เห็นชัดเจนในผู้ที่สายตาเสียมาก เช่น จอตาเสื่อม หรือต้อหิน ผู้ป่วยรู้ตัวว่าไม่จริงและไม่มีอาการทางจิตอื่น เกิดจากสมองส่วนการมองเห็นทำงานเองเมื่อขาดสัญญาณเข้า การรักษาหลักคืออธิบายให้เข้าใจ ปรับแสงสว่าง และหาสาเหตุอื่น เช่น Lewy body dementia ถ้ามีอาการไม่เข้ากัน

name: Cherry-red spot-myoclonus syndrome (sialidosis type I)
formal: Sialidosis type I from NEU1 deficiency with macular cherry-red spot, action myoclonus, ataxia and seizures in adolescence or adulthood.
simple: An inherited metabolic disease causing jerky movements, seizures and a red spot in the eye.
th: โรคกลุ่มลิโซโซมจากเอนไซม์ neuraminidase ต่ำ พบในวัยรุ่น มีกล้ามเนื้อกระตุกเวลาเคลื่อนไหว ชัก เดินเซ และจุด cherry-red ที่จอตาโดยสติปัญญายังดี
tempoNote: Starts in the teens and worsens slowly over years
feat: Action- and stimulus-triggered myoclonus that gradually disables hand use and walking
Generalised tonic-clonic seizures with cerebellar ataxia
Cherry-red macular spot with slow visual loss; cataract in some
Intellect largely spared; no coarse face or enlarged organs in type I
Autosomal recessive NEU1 disease with progression to wheelchair dependence

case.story: For two years his hands jerk when he reaches, so he spills drinks and drops his phone. Last month he had a first generalised convulsion, yet his school marks remain high.
case.exam: Action myoclonus in all limbs, ataxic gait and red-centred macular spots in both eyes.
case.tests: Urine sialyloligosaccharides elevated; leucocyte neuraminidase activity very low.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and which antiseizure drug class should be avoided?
case.a: Sialidosis type I (NEU1); sodium channel blockers such as phenytoin and carbamazepine can aggravate myoclonus, so favour valproate, levetiracetam or clonazepam.

det.patho: Biallelic NEU1 variants lower lysosomal alpha-neuraminidase, so sialylated oligosaccharides and glycoproteins build up in neurons and retinal cells. Some residual enzyme activity accounts for the milder type I; near-absent activity causes the dysmorphic type II with organomegaly. The disorder is one of the progressive myoclonic epilepsies. It is rare but has been reported across Asia.
det.clinical: Onset is commonly in the second decade with action myoclonus, often first mistaken for clumsiness or tremor. Generalised seizures, ataxia and falling vision follow. The cherry-red spot is a helpful clue yet may be subtle or vanish later. Because cognition is typically preserved until late, the picture contrasts with many other storage disorders.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in any adolescent with action myoclonus and macular change. Screen urine for sialyloligosaccharides, confirm with low neuraminidase activity and sequence NEU1. EEG shows a fast low-voltage background and somatosensory evoked potentials are giant, in keeping with cortical myoclonus. Distinguish from other progressive myoclonic epilepsies by fundoscopy and enzyme testing.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying treatment exists. Myoclonus is eased with valproate, levetiracetam, clonazepam, piracetam or perampanel, often combined. Avoid phenytoin, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, gabapentin and pregabalin. Offer physiotherapy, falls prevention, low-vision support and genetic counselling.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; many become wheelchair-bound within one to two decades, though intellect and lifespan are often relatively preserved.
pearls: Cherry-red spot plus myoclonus with intact intellect points to sialidosis I.
Sodium channel blockers can worsen myoclonus.
Cherry-red spot in infancy suggests Tay–Sachs or Sandhoff instead.
det.thd: Sialidosis type I เกิดจากยีน NEU1 กลายพันธุ์ทำให้เอนไซม์ neuraminidase ในไลโซโซมต่ำ ผู้ป่วยวัยรุ่นมีกล้ามเนื้อกระตุกเวลาใช้งาน ชัก เดินเซ และตามัวลง พบจุด cherry-red ที่จอตาแต่สติปัญญามักปกติ ตรวจปัสสาวะหา sialyloligosaccharides และวัดเอนไซม์เพื่อยืนยัน รักษาตามอาการด้วย valproate, levetiracetam หรือ clonazepam และหลีกเลี่ยงยา phenytoin กับ carbamazepine

det.patho: A small, underdeveloped posterior fossa crowds the hindbrain, pushing the tonsils down through the foramen magnum, which blocks normal CSF pulsation between cranium and spinal canal, producing pressure dissociation during Valsalva and, in some, a syrinx. Rarely it is familial or linked to connective tissue and craniovertebral junction anomalies.
det.clinical: Tussive occipital headache is the hallmark symptom. Others present with syringomyelia (dissociated sensory loss, wasting, painful dysaesthesia), brainstem or cerebellar signs, or central sleep apnoea. Neck pain and diffuse symptoms like fatigue or dizziness are common but nonspecific and unreliable for deciding surgery. Incidental Chiari I is found on about 1% of MRIs.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows tonsils at least 5 mm below the basion–opisthion line, often peg-like, with reduced CSF at the foramen magnum. Image the whole spine for syrinx. Correlate symptoms carefully; exclude intracranial hypotension and raised pressure as causes of acquired descent, because their treatment differs.
det.treatment: Asymptomatic patients without syrinx are observed. Typical Valsalva headache, syrinx or brainstem signs justify posterior fossa decompression, with or without duraplasty; most syrinxes shrink afterwards. Avoid lumbar puncture in symptomatic crowded posterior fossa. Shunting is reserved for persistent syrinx or hydrocephalus.
det.prognosis: Cough headache usually improves after surgery; established sensory loss and wasting improve less.
pearls: Cough headache + downbeat nystagmus → image the craniocervical junction.
Not every low-lying tonsil is Chiari — think SIH if headache is orthostatic.
Always image the whole spine to look for syrinx.
det.thd: Chiari I malformation คือทอนซิลของสมองน้อยยื่นลงต่ำกว่า foramen magnum ตั้งแต่ 5 มม. ขึ้นไป เพราะแอ่งสมองส่วนหลังเล็ก ทำให้น้ำไขสันหลังไหลไม่สะดวก อาการเด่นคือปวดท้ายทอยเวลาไอหรือเบ่ง อาจมี syringomyelia ทำให้ชาแบบเสื้อคลุมและกล้ามมือลีบ หรือมีอาการก้านสมอง วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI สมองและไขสันหลังทั้งหมด ถ้ามีอาการชัดหรือมี syrinx รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัด decompression

det.patho: Chiari type I is a heterogeneous group with one common feature, impaired CSF flow at the foramen magnum. Many are congenital with a small posterior fossa (underdeveloped occipital bone, low tentorium), others are acquired from a mass in the posterior fossa, hydrocephalus, craniosynostosis, lumboperitoneal shunting or repeated lumbar puncture. In type II a neural tube defect with myelomeningocele is accompanied by a small posterior fossa, downward displacement of the vermis, medulla and fourth ventricle, and a kinked medulla. The altered CSF dynamics drive syrinx formation and cough-related headache.
det.clinical: Type I is typically diagnosed at around 40 years (range from teenage to old age), with a slight female predominance. Pain, mostly headache in the suboccipital area, is the leading complaint, provoked by Valsalva and neck extension. Weakness, sensory change, Lhermitte symptoms, downbeat nystagmus and spasticity depend on the combination of brainstem compression, syrinx and hydrocephalus. The natural history is poorly documented: patients may be stable for years with occasional deterioration. Type II presents in infancy with hydrocephalus, respiratory distress and swallowing difficulty.
det.diagnosis: MRI of the brain and cervical (preferably whole) spine is the investigation of choice, and the clinical picture must decide the significance because tonsillar ectopia is often incidental; the degree of crowding and obliteration of CSF at the foramen magnum is more informative than the number of millimetres. Cine MRI of CSF flow is optional and rarely changes management. Exclude causes of secondary descent, especially intracranial hypotension and a posterior fossa mass, before operating. Consider a neurophysiology and sleep study when apnoea or dysphagia is suspected.
det.treatment: Asymptomatic patients without syrinx are observed. Symptomatic patients with typical headache, progressive deficit or a syrinx are offered posterior fossa decompression, usually with C1 laminectomy and duraplasty, sometimes with tonsil reduction; the exact technique is debated. Syrinx shrinks in most patients, and patients do best when operated within two years of symptoms; pain and cerebellar signs respond better than weakness and atrophy. Perioperative respiratory depression, sometimes at night, CSF leak and pseudomeningocele are the main risks, so close monitoring is needed. Hydrocephalus is treated by shunting or third ventriculostomy, and type II needs closure of the myelomeningocele and long-term surveillance.
det.prognosis: Decompression relieves headache and stabilises or improves the syrinx in most patients; established sensory loss and wasting may persist.
pearls: Cough headache lasting seconds in a young adult: image the craniocervical junction.
Downbeat nystagmus points to the foramen magnum region.
Tonsillar descent alone is not a diagnosis; exclude intracranial hypotension before decompressing.
det.thd: Chiari malformation ชนิดที่ 1 คือภาวะที่ทอนซิลสมองน้อยหย่อนลงต่ำกว่า foramen magnum ทำให้น้ำไขสันหลังไหลผ่านไม่สะดวก ผู้ป่วยมักปวดท้ายทอยเมื่อไอหรือเบ่ง ตากระตุกลง เดินเซ หรือมี syrinx ที่ทำให้สูญเสียการรับรู้ความเจ็บปวดและอุณหภูมิ ชนิดที่ 2 พบร่วมกับ myelomeningocele และ hydrocephalus ในทารก วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI สมองและไขสันหลัง ต้องแยก intracranial hypotension ออกก่อนรักษา การผ่าตัดขยายท้ายทอยทำเมื่อมีอาการชัดหรือ syrinx และผลดีกว่าถ้าผ่าตัดภายใน 2 ปีหลังเริ่มมีอาการ

qx.stem: A 27-year-old office worker in Bangkok has occipital headaches that last seconds to minutes and are brought on by coughing, laughing and straining. Neurological examination is normal. MRI shows the cerebellar tonsils pointed and lying 8 mm below the foramen magnum, crowding of the cisterna magna, and no syrinx. The brain is otherwise normal and there is no hydrocephalus.
qx.q: Which is the most appropriate management for her symptomatic hindbrain herniation?
opts: Ventriculoperitoneal shunt as first-line treatment
Lumbar drain to reduce pressure before surgery
Observation only, since symptoms never relate to tonsillar descent
Posterior fossa decompression with suboccipital craniectomy, C1 laminectomy and usually duraplasty
Transoral odontoidectomy
qx.why: Valsalva-provoked short occipital headache with tonsillar descent over 5 mm is the typical symptomatic Chiari I picture, and posterior fossa decompression is the operation of choice when symptoms are clear. Lumbar drainage or lumbar puncture can worsen herniation. Shunting is reserved for coexisting hydrocephalus, and transoral surgery is for ventral compression such as basilar invagination.
