ddx.pt: A syrinx from trauma, tumour or arachnoiditis rather than a hindbrain cause; tonsils normal
Orthostatic headache with tonsillar sag and pachymeningeal enhancement; decompression would be harmful
Broader developmental group (Dandy-Walker spectrum, rhombencephalosynapsis) rather than isolated tonsillar descent

aN: chiari malformation | arnold chiari malformation | hindbrain herniation | cm1 | cm2

name: Chiasmal disease
formal: Lesions at the optic chiasm, e.g. pituitary tumours or craniopharyngioma, causing bitemporal hemianopia and reduced acuity.
simple: Damage near where the eye nerves cross, causing loss of side vision in both eyes.
th: รอยโรคที่ optic chiasm เช่น pituitary tumour หรือ craniopharyngioma ทำให้ลานสายตาด้านขมับหายทั้งสองข้างและสายตามัว
tempoNote: Usually insidious over months; sudden with pituitary apoplexy or aneurysm expansion
feat: Bitemporal field loss, often upper quadrants first with pituitary tumours compressing from below
Gradual blurring of vision; patients may bump into objects on both sides
Optic atrophy, sometimes 'bow-tie' pallor, with relative afferent pupil defect if asymmetric
Endocrine features (amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, acromegaly, hypopituitarism) with pituitary lesions
Junctional scotoma: central loss in one eye plus upper temporal defect in the other
inv: Formal perimetry (Humphrey 24-2 or Goldmann) respecting the vertical meridian
MRI pituitary/sellar region with gadolinium; CT for calcification in craniopharyngioma
Pituitary hormone panel (prolactin, IGF-1, cortisol, TSH/FT4, LH/FSH); OCT for nerve fibre layer

case.story: Has had two minor side-swipe accidents this year and complains of reduced libido and headache.
case.exam: Acuity 6/9 both eyes, bitemporal hemianopia on confrontation, mild temporal disc pallor.
case.tests: MRI: 3 cm sellar mass lifting the chiasm; prolactin 60 ng/mL, low testosterone.
case.q: Where is the lesion and what is the likely cause?
case.a: Optic chiasm compressed by a non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma (modest prolactin rise from stalk effect).

det.patho: At the chiasm the nasal retinal fibres from each eye cross, so pressure on its centre damages both temporal fields. Causes include pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma, meningioma of the tuberculum or diaphragma sellae, aneurysm, glioma, inflammation (sarcoid, demyelination), trauma and radiation necrosis. The direction of compression affects which quadrant fails first.
det.clinical: Loss is often unnoticed until advanced because each eye covers the other's nasal field; difficulty with driving or depth perception may be the first complaint. Hemifield slide can cause double vision without nerve palsy. Pituitary apoplexy produces sudden headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia and adrenal crisis and is an emergency. Children with craniopharyngioma may present with growth failure and raised pressure.
det.diagnosis: Confrontation testing should compare red targets across the vertical meridian, but formal perimetry is required. MRI with contrast through the sella is the definitive study; check pituitary hormones in all sellar lesions. OCT thickness of retinal nerve fibres and ganglion cells helps predict visual recovery after decompression.
det.treatment: Treatment targets the cause: prolactinomas usually respond to cabergoline, while other compressive adenomas are removed via transsphenoidal surgery. Craniopharyngioma and meningioma need neurosurgery with or without radiotherapy. Apoplexy requires urgent hydrocortisone and often decompression. Replace hormones as needed and follow fields after treatment.
det.prognosis: Vision often improves after decompression, especially when nerve fibre layer thickness is preserved; long-standing atrophy predicts limited recovery.
pearls: Bitemporal field loss = chiasm until proved otherwise; always image the sella.
Junctional scotoma localises to where one optic nerve joins the chiasm.
Sudden headache plus visual loss plus ophthalmoplegia: think pituitary apoplexy and give steroids.
det.thd: Chiasmal disease คือรอยโรคที่ optic chiasm ซึ่งเป็นจุดที่ใยประสาทจากจอตาด้านจมูกไขว้กัน จึงทำให้เกิด bitemporal hemianopia สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยคือเนื้องอกต่อมใต้สมองและ craniopharyngioma ผู้ป่วยมักไม่รู้ตัวจนลานสายตาเสียมาก ตรวจด้วย perimetry, MRI sella และฮอร์โมนต่อมใต้สมอง รักษาตามสาเหตุ เช่น ผ่าตัด หรือยา cabergoline สำหรับ prolactinoma

ddx.pt: Most common chiasmal cause in adults; endocrine profile and sellar mass on MRI
Children and older adults; calcified cystic suprasellar mass, diabetes insipidus
Painful monocular loss with central scotoma; does not respect the vertical meridian

aN: chiasmal syndrome | optic chiasm lesion | chiasmopathy | bitemporal hemianopia syndrome

name: Childhood bulbar SMA
formal: Fazio-Londe disease, a juvenile motor neuron disorder related to riboflavin transporter mutations, causing progressive bulbar palsy with facial weakness, dysphagia, and respiratory failure.
simple: A rare childhood condition in which nerves to the face, tongue, and throat degenerate, causing trouble swallowing and speaking.
more: SLC52A3 testing is useful; high-dose riboflavin can stabilise or improve the course, so early treatment matters. Respiratory support may be needed.
th: โรคเซลล์ประสาทสั่งการในเด็กที่กระทบก้านสมองเด่น ทำให้กลืนลำบาก พูดไม่ชัด หน้าอ่อนแรง สัมพันธ์กับยีนขนส่ง riboflavin ซึ่งรักษาได้ด้วย riboflavin ขนาดสูง
tempoNote: Months to a few years of progressive bulbar signs, often punctuated by sudden worsening with infection; deafness may open the illness
feat: Progressive dysarthria, dysphagia, facial weakness and tongue wasting with fasciculation from lower cranial nerve motor nuclei (IX, X, XII, VII)
Respiratory compromise with stridor from vocal cord palsy or diaphragm weakness; infections may trigger rapid decline
Sensorineural hearing loss, often the first symptom, defines the Brown–Vialetto–Van Laere end of the spectrum; the juvenile bulbar palsy end is hearing-sparing
Later arm more than leg weakness with absent reflexes, sensory ataxia, optic atrophy and nystagmus; intellect is usually preserved
Autosomal recessive; biallelic SLC52A2 or SLC52A3 variants cause a riboflavin transporter deficiency and are the treatable cause
inv: Genetic panel for SLC52A2, SLC52A3 and SLC52A1; start riboflavin on suspicion without waiting for results
Nerve conduction and EMG: sensory more than motor axonal neuropathy with chronic denervation; evoked potentials and audiometry
MRI brainstem to exclude glioma; acylcarnitine profile and plasma flavin levels as supportive tests
Swallow study, vital capacity, and sleep or nocturnal oximetry for respiratory planning

case.story: Her mother noticed she was missing words in class, then over a year her speech became nasal, she choked on liquids and her voice turned hoarse. Two weeks ago a cold left her breathless at night. Her hearing had been slightly worse since age 5.
case.exam: Facial diplegia, tongue atrophy with fasciculations, weak palate, mild stridor; arm weakness with absent reflexes; reduced vibration at ankles; normal cognition.
case.tests: Audiometry shows bilateral high-frequency sensorineural loss; NCS show reduced sensory amplitudes; MRI brain stem is normal; panel finds biallelic SLC52A2 variants.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what should be started at once?
case.a: Riboflavin transporter deficiency (Brown–Vialetto–Van Laere spectrum). Start high-dose oral riboflavin and give nutritional and ventilatory support; early treatment can stabilise or improve function.

read.where: 17. Lower Brainstem and Cranial Nerve Dysfunction
Chapter 15 Disorders of the Motor Cells: The Motor Neuron Diseases — Rare Forms of Spinal Muscular Atrophy and Differential Diagnosis

det.patho: Riboflavin (vitamin B2) is the precursor of FAD and FMN, which carry electrons in mitochondrial respiratory and fatty-acid oxidation pathways. Defective cellular uptake through the transporters encoded by SLC52A2 and SLC52A3 deprives motor neurons, sensory neurons, and the auditory and optic pathways of flavin cofactors and leads to axonal degeneration. Inheritance is autosomal recessive and carrier parents are healthy.
det.clinical: The age at onset runs from infancy to adolescence. Hearing loss often opens the illness, followed within a year or two by cranial neuropathy: weak face, palate and tongue, a weak voice and swallowing trouble. Peripheral axonal neuropathy causes arm-predominant weakness, areflexia and sensory ataxia, and respiratory weakness can appear suddenly. Vision loss from optic atrophy and nystagmus occurs in some. Untreated disease can progress to ventilator dependence within months to years.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in any child with progressive bulbar palsy, neuropathy and hearing loss, particularly when myasthenia serology is negative. MRI is needed to exclude a pontine glioma. EMG shows chronic denervation and NCS show a sensory predominant axonal neuropathy; abnormal flavin or acylcarnitine results support the diagnosis but may be normal. Molecular confirmation identifies biallelic pathogenic variants in SLC52A2 or SLC52A3.
det.treatment: Begin oral riboflavin at once on clinical suspicion, in the range of 10–50 mg/kg/day divided in doses, and keep it going lifelong; some centres add riboflavin derivatives or CoQ10 but evidence is limited. Response is best when treatment is early, with stabilisation of strength, hearing and breathing. Provide gastrostomy and aspiration prevention, noninvasive ventilation when forced vital capacity falls, cochlear implant assessment for severe hearing loss, and physiotherapy.
det.prognosis: Depends strongly on how soon riboflavin is started; many treated children stabilise or improve, while those treated late may have lasting weakness or ventilator needs.
pearls: Treatable cause of motor neuron-like disease in a child: never wait for genetic results before starting riboflavin.
Progressive bulbar palsy plus deafness in childhood means think Brown–Vialetto–Van Laere first.
Tongue fasciculation with preserved intellect and absent reflexes points to lower motor neuron disease, not myasthenia.
det.thd: โรคนี้เกิดจากการขนส่ง riboflavin เข้าเซลล์บกพร่อง (SLC52A2 หรือ SLC52A3) ทำให้เซลล์ประสาทสั่งการของก้านสมองและเส้นประสาทเสื่อม เด็กจะกลืนลำบาก พูดไม่ชัด ลิ้นลีบและสั่นพลิ้ว หน้าอ่อนแรง บางรายหูตึงนำมาก่อน และอาจมีแขนอ่อนแรง ชาและเดินเซ ควรตรวจ MRI ก้านสมองเพื่อแยกเนื้องอก ตรวจ NCS/EMG และส่งตรวจยีน แต่ให้ riboflavin ขนาดสูงทันทีเมื่อสงสัย เพราะการรักษาเร็วทำให้อาการคงที่หรือดีขึ้นได้ ต้องดูแลการกลืนและการหายใจร่วมด้วย

Fatigable bulbar weakness with no atrophy, fasciculation or sensory ataxia; antibodies and decrement on repetitive stimulation

name: Children and young adults alternating hemiplegia of childhood
formal: Rare ATP1A3-related disorder with episodes of hemiplegia or dystonia, onset before 18 months, eye movement abnormalities and developmental delay.
simple: A rare childhood condition with repeated attacks of weakness on one side of the body.
th: โรคหายากจากยีน ATP1A3 มีอาการอัมพาตครึ่งซีกสลับข้างเป็นพัก ๆ ร่วมกับ dystonia ตาผิดปกติ เริ่มก่อนอายุ 18 เดือน และพัฒนาการช้า
tempoNote: Attacks last minutes to days, beginning in infancy; a chronic developmental and motor deficit accumulates
feat: Recurrent episodes of hemiplegia affecting either side, or both, beginning before 18 months
Attacks stop during sleep and resume on waking
Paroxysmal nystagmus, often monocular, and dystonic attacks in early infancy
Triggers: bathing in water, heat, emotion, light, fatigue
Persistent developmental delay, ataxia, chorea and epilepsy in about half
inv: ATP1A3 sequencing (positive in most); ATP1A2 or SLC2A1 in some atypical cases
EEG during attacks to separate seizures (EEG usually lacks ictal activity in hemiplegic spells)
MRI brain (usually normal) and metabolic screen including CSF glucose for GLUT1 deficiency

case.story: Since 4 months she has had episodes of jerky eye movements of one eye followed by limpness of one side lasting hours; the side changes and spells vanish when she falls asleep.
case.exam: Between attacks: hypotonia, mild ataxia, delayed sitting; during an attack, flaccid right hemiparesis with alertness preserved.
case.tests: MRI normal; ictal EEG shows no seizure discharge; ATP1A3 heterozygous de novo variant.
case.q: Which feature most helps separate this from epilepsy with Todd paralysis?
case.a: Weakness switches sides, starts with eye movements or dystonia, lacks EEG seizure activity and disappears in sleep — AHC.

det.patho: Most patients carry de novo heterozygous variants in ATP1A3, the alpha-3 subunit of the neuronal sodium-potassium pump. Impaired pump function leaves neurons vulnerable to depolarisation under stress, causing transient motor failure. The same gene underlies rapid-onset dystonia-parkinsonism and CAPOS syndrome, forming a spectrum.
det.clinical: Paroxysmal eye movements and dystonic spells usually precede hemiplegia in the first months of life. Attacks vary from minutes to days and may be bilateral; consciousness is preserved. Over time a fixed deficit emerges with intellectual disability, ataxia, choreoathetosis and dysarthria; epilepsy and status epilepticus are frequent and may be life threatening. Some patients survive into adulthood with ongoing attacks (the reason for the 'young adults' label).
det.diagnosis: Clinical criteria (Aicardi) combine onset before 18 months, alternating hemiplegia, other paroxysms, relief with sleep and developmental issues; ATP1A3 testing confirms. EEG and video help separate seizures from non-epileptic attacks. Exclude GLUT1 deficiency, mitochondrial disease and hemiplegic migraine.
det.treatment: Teach families to induce sleep early in attacks, which aborts them; avoid known triggers. Flunarizine is the most used preventive, with variable benefit; acute benzodiazepines or chloral hydrate help induce sleep. Seizures are treated with standard anti-seizure medicines, and rescue plans are essential. Multidisciplinary developmental support is needed; gene-based therapies are under study.
det.prognosis: Chronic disability is common; sudden death and status epilepticus are recognised risks.
pearls: Hemiplegia that switches sides and vanishes in sleep: think ATP1A3 AHC.
Monocular nystagmus attacks in a young infant are an early clue.
Sleep is the most effective acute treatment.
det.thd: Alternating hemiplegia of childhood เกิดจากการกลายพันธุ์ของยีน ATP1A3 ที่ควบคุมปั๊มโซเดียม-โพแทสเซียมในเซลล์ประสาท เด็กเริ่มมีอาการก่อน 18 เดือน อัมพาตครึ่งซีกสลับข้างเป็นพัก ๆ ร่วมกับตากระตุกและ dystonia อาการหายเมื่อหลับ ระยะยาวมีพัฒนาการช้าและโรคลมชัก วินิจฉัยด้วยเกณฑ์ทางคลินิกและตรวจยีน รักษาด้วยการพาเด็กให้นอนหลับ หลีกเลี่ยงตัวกระตุ้น และใช้ flunarizine ป้องกัน

ddx.pt: Follows a visible seizure, same side each time, resolves within hours
Low CSF glucose; paroxysmal events improve with ketogenic diet
Later onset, headache, family history; hemiplegic forms involve CACNA1A/ATP1A2

name: Chin tremor
formal: Rhythmic 4-7 Hz tremor of the chin, hereditary autosomal dominant or sporadic, appearing in childhood and worsening with stress.
simple: Shaking of the chin, often running in families, that gets worse with stress.
th: อาการคางสั่นเป็นจังหวะ มักถ่ายทอดทางกรรมพันธุ์แบบยีนเด่น เริ่มในวัยเด็ก และเป็นมากขึ้นเมื่อเครียดหรือตื่นเต้น
tempoNote: Bouts lasting seconds to hours, provoked by emotion; lifelong tendency that often eases with age
feat: Rapid rhythmic up-and-down movement of the chin (mentalis muscle), present from infancy or childhood
Provoked by stress, concentration or emotion; absent in sleep but may occur with sleep transitions
Usually otherwise neurologically normal
Autosomal dominant family history in hereditary geniospasm
Rare association with nocturnal tongue biting
inv: Clinical diagnosis; surface EMG shows bursts in mentalis
Neurological examination to exclude other tremor; MRI only if atypical or progressive

case.story: When nervous before school exams his chin quivers for several minutes; his father and grandfather had the same since childhood.
case.exam: Brief chin tremor at about 6 Hz provoked by a stressful task; no tremor elsewhere and normal neurology.
case.tests: Surface EMG confirms rhythmic mentalis bursts; no further tests needed.
case.q: Is this a seizure and does it need treatment?
case.a: No — hereditary geniospasm is benign; reassurance is usually enough, botulinum toxin to mentalis if troublesome.

read.where: Chapter 71: Hyperkinetic Movement Disorders: Tremor and Myoclonus

det.patho: Hereditary geniospasm is a dominantly inherited, highly penetrant disorder; a locus on chromosome 9q13–q21 was reported in one family but the gene is not established. The mentalis muscles contract rhythmically, probably from a brainstem generator. Chin tremor can also be a component of essential tremor, Parkinson disease or drug effects.
det.clinical: Episodes begin in infancy or early childhood, are triggered by emotion and may be noticed during crying or laughing. Severity often declines with age. A neurological examination is otherwise normal. Secondary chin tremor in older adults suggests parkinsonism or drug-induced tremor, so age of onset is crucial.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by family history and normal examination; EMG can document the pattern. Imaging and EEG are only needed when features are atypical, such as progression, other neurological signs or impaired awareness.
det.treatment: Most families need only explanation. Botulinum toxin injection into mentalis is effective when episodes are distressing. Oral drugs are rarely used.
det.prognosis: Benign; tends to improve with age.
pearls: Childhood-onset emotional chin quiver with similar relatives = hereditary geniospasm.
New chin tremor in an older adult: look for Parkinson disease or drugs.
Mentalis botulinum toxin works well if treatment is needed.
det.thd: Chin tremor หรือ hereditary geniospasm เป็นอาการคางสั่นเป็นจังหวะจากกล้ามเนื้อ mentalis มักถ่ายทอดทางกรรมพันธุ์แบบยีนเด่น เริ่มตั้งแต่เด็ก เกิดเมื่อเครียดหรือมีอารมณ์ ตรวจร่างกายส่วนอื่นปกติ วินิจฉัยจากอาการ ไม่อันตราย ส่วนใหญ่ให้คำอธิบายพอ ถ้ารบกวนมากใช้ botulinum toxin ฉีดได้ ถ้าเริ่มในผู้สูงอายุให้นึกถึงพาร์กินสันหรือยา

Variable frequency, distractible and entrainable

name: Chloride channelopathies
formal: Disorders of CLCN1 channel function causing myotonia congenita, either dominant Thomsen or recessive Becker form, with muscle stiffness that eases with repeated use.
simple: Inherited conditions where faulty chloride channels leave muscles stiff, easing after repeated movement.
more: EMG shows myotonic discharges; confirmed by CLCN1 testing. Mexiletine is first-line; prognosis is good.
th: กลุ่มโรค myotonia congenita จากช่องคลอไรด์ CLCN1 ทั้งแบบเด่น (Thomsen) และแบบด้อย (Becker) กล้ามเนื้อแข็งและดีขึ้นเมื่อขยับซ้ำ
tempoNote: Childhood onset; lifelong, non-progressive in adulthood
feat: Stiffness after rest that improves with repeated movement (warm-up)
Grip and percussion myotonia; muscle hypertrophy
Dominant Thomsen form milder; recessive Becker form more severe with transient weakness
Normal strength and no systemic features
Symptoms may worsen in pregnancy or hypothyroidism
inv: EMG: myotonic discharges
Short exercise test: transient CMAP fall that recovers (especially recessive)
CLCN1 sequencing

case.who: 30-year-old male soldier from Lopburi; father has similar stiffness
case.story: Stiff legs when he starts marching after sitting, improving after a few steps; hands slow to open after a firm handshake.
case.exam: Hypertrophic thighs, grip myotonia that eases after 4–5 repetitions, percussion myotonia, normal strength.
case.tests: EMG shows myotonic runs in all muscles; a heterozygous CLCN1 variant shared with father.
case.q: What is the inheritance pattern and the clinical form?
case.a: Autosomal dominant chloride channel myotonia (Thomsen disease).

read.where: Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Skeletal Muscle Channelopathies
36: Myotonic Muscle Disorders and Periodic Paralysis Syndromes

det.patho: The ClC-1 chloride channel provides most resting membrane conductance in skeletal muscle. Reduced chloride current leaves the membrane prone to depolarise from potassium accumulating in T-tubules, so a single voluntary activation sets off repetitive action potentials. Dominant variants usually have a dominant-negative effect on the dimeric channel; recessive ones cause loss of function.
det.clinical: The two classic forms are Thomsen (dominant) and Becker (recessive). Both cause generalised stiffness with warm-up and muscle enlargement. The recessive form typically begins later in childhood, is more severe, and includes brief weakness at the start of exertion. There is no involvement of heart, eyes or endocrine glands.
det.diagnosis: EMG detects myotonic discharges. Exercise and cooling protocols help separate chloride from sodium channel myotonias. Genetic testing confirms; some families show variable penetrance, blurring the dominant and recessive distinction.
det.treatment: Mexiletine is first-line for disabling symptoms, after an ECG. Alternatives include lamotrigine, carbamazepine, phenytoin and acetazolamide. Warm-up strategies help. Inform anaesthetists to avoid suxamethonium.
det.prognosis: Not progressive; normal life expectancy.
pearls: Warm-up improvement points to chloride channel disease; worsening with repetition points to sodium channel.
Transient weakness at the start of activity favours recessive Becker form.
Mexiletine is first-line.

name: Chloroquine neuropathy
formal: Toxic neuromyopathy from chloroquine or hydroxychloroquine causing sensorimotor neuropathy with vacuolar myopathy, with curvilinear bodies on biopsy.
simple: Nerve and muscle problems caused by the malaria and arthritis drug chloroquine.
more: Stopping the drug generally leads to recovery; biopsy shows autophagic vacuoles.
th: ภาวะพิษจากยา chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อต้นแขนขาอ่อนแรงและเส้นประสาทเสื่อม ชิ้นเนื้อพบ curvilinear bodies
tempoNote: Develops after months to years of continuous treatment, usually with higher cumulative dose
feat: Gradual proximal leg weakness in a patient on long-term antimalarial therapy (lupus, rheumatoid arthritis)
Mild distal sensory loss and depressed reflexes from accompanying neuropathy
Cardiomyopathy or conduction block may coexist
Retinopathy may be present; renal impairment increases risk
CK normal or mildly raised
inv: EMG: myopathic units with fibrillations; mild axonal neuropathy
Muscle biopsy: autophagic vacuoles and curvilinear bodies on electron microscopy
ECG, echocardiogram or cardiac MRI to screen for cardiotoxicity

case.who: 52-year-old woman from Khon Kaen with SLE on hydroxychloroquine for 9 years and chronic kidney disease
case.story: Six months of trouble rising from a squat and climbing onto the songthaew; feet feel slightly numb.
case.exam: Symmetric hip and shoulder weakness, absent ankle jerks, mild distal vibration loss.
case.tests: CK 420 U/L; EMG shows irritable myopathy plus mild axonal neuropathy; biopsy shows rimmed autophagic vacuoles with curvilinear bodies.
case.q: What is the likely cause and what is the main step?
case.a: Hydroxychloroquine neuromyopathy; stop the drug and assess the heart.

det.patho: Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine are lysosomotropic, raising lysosomal pH and impairing autophagic degradation. Undigested membranes accumulate as autophagic vacuoles and curvilinear bodies in muscle, nerve Schwann cells and cardiac muscle. Risk rises with dose, duration and reduced renal clearance.
det.clinical: The presentation is a slowly evolving proximal myopathy, sometimes with a mild length-dependent neuropathy. Cardiac involvement (cardiomyopathy, conduction disease) can be the most dangerous feature. Because these patients have autoimmune disease, weakness is often wrongly attributed to inflammatory myositis or steroids.
det.diagnosis: Consider it in anyone on long-term antimalarials with new weakness. EMG often shows myopathic potentials with spontaneous activity, mimicking myositis. Muscle biopsy with electron microscopy is decisive, showing curvilinear bodies. Cardiac evaluation is part of the work-up.
det.treatment: Withdraw the drug and liaise with the rheumatologist for alternative disease control. Supportive physiotherapy is used during recovery. Steroids are not helpful and may worsen weakness. Monitor cardiac status.
det.prognosis: Muscle strength usually improves over months after withdrawal; neuropathy and cardiac damage may recover less completely.
pearls: Irritable myopathy on EMG in a lupus patient is not always myositis; check the drug list.
Curvilinear bodies on electron microscopy are the hallmark.
Renal impairment raises the risk of antimalarial toxicity.
det.thd: Chloroquine และ hydroxychloroquine ทำให้ lysosome ทำงานผิดปกติ เกิด vacuole ในกล้ามเนื้อ เส้นประสาท และหัวใจ ผู้ป่วยที่กินยานานมีกล้ามเนื้อต้นแขนขาอ่อนแรงช้าๆ อาจชาปลายเท้า EMG อาจคล้าย myositis การตัดชิ้นเนื้อพบ curvilinear bodies เป็นหลักฐานสำคัญ รักษาโดยหยุดยาและตรวจหัวใจ

name: Cholesteatomas
formal: Epidermoid lesions of keratinising squamous epithelium in middle ear or petrous apex that erode bone and cause hearing loss, facial palsy and vertigo.
simple: A skin-cell growth in the ear or skull base that slowly destroys bone and affects hearing and the face nerve.
th: ก้อนเยื่อบุผิว squamous ที่สะสมเคราตินในหูชั้นกลางหรือ petrous apex กัดกร่อนกระดูก ทำให้หูหนวก เวียนศีรษะ และอัมพาตใบหน้า
tempoNote: Slow growth over years with intermittent infected discharge; complications can arise acutely
feat: Chronic foul-smelling ear discharge and conductive hearing loss (primary ENT disease)
Retraction pocket or white keratin mass seen on otoscopy, often attic (pars flaccida)
Labyrinthine fistula: vertigo with pressure on the tragus or loud sound
Facial nerve palsy from erosion of the fallopian canal
Intracranial spread: meningitis, temporal lobe or cerebellar abscess, sigmoid sinus thrombosis
inv: Otomicroscopy and audiometry
High-resolution CT temporal bone for bone erosion
MRI with non-echo-planar diffusion to detect or confirm residual cholesteatoma

case.story: Years of smelly left ear discharge, now dizzy when he presses on the ear and his face droops on the left.
case.exam: Attic retraction with keratin debris in left ear, left conductive hearing loss, positive fistula test, left lower motor neuron facial palsy.
case.tests: CT temporal bone: erosion of ossicles, lateral semicircular canal and tympanic facial canal.
case.q: What is the lesion and why is the face weak?
case.a: Middle ear cholesteatoma eroding the facial canal and labyrinth; needs urgent mastoid surgery.

det.patho: Cholesteatoma is not a true tumour but a sac of keratinising squamous epithelium growing into the middle ear and mastoid. Acquired forms arise from tympanic membrane retraction or perforation; congenital forms come from embryonic epithelial rests behind an intact drum or at the petrous apex. Enzymes and chronic inflammation erode ossicles, labyrinth, facial canal and tegmen.
det.clinical: This is primarily an otological disease that matters to neurologists through its complications. Patients have chronic discharge and conductive hearing loss. Erosion into the labyrinth gives vertigo and sensorineural loss; facial palsy, meningitis, brain abscess and venous sinus thrombosis can follow. Petrous apex lesions may present with VI, V or VII nerve palsies without obvious ear disease.
det.diagnosis: Otomicroscopy usually shows the mass or retraction pocket. CT delineates bone destruction, while diffusion-weighted MRI is highly specific because keratin restricts diffusion. Intracranial complications need contrast MRI or CT and lumbar puncture only after imaging excludes a mass. Neurologists should examine the ear in any facial palsy with otorrhoea.
det.treatment: Surgery is the treatment: canal wall up or down mastoidectomy with complete removal, followed by surveillance for recurrence with diffusion MRI. Topical and systemic antibiotics settle infection preoperatively. Complications such as abscess or sinus thrombosis need neurosurgical and medical care. Hearing reconstruction may be staged.
det.prognosis: Good with complete excision, but recurrence is common and lifelong follow-up is advised.
pearls: Facial palsy plus smelly otorrhoea is not Bell's palsy.
Keratin restricts diffusion, making DWI MRI the key imaging test.
A positive fistula sign suggests labyrinthine erosion.
det.thd: Cholesteatoma คือถุงเยื่อบุผิวที่สะสมเคราตินในหูชั้นกลางหรือ petrous apex เป็นโรคทางหูเป็นหลัก แต่กัดกร่อนกระดูกจนทำให้เวียนศีรษะ อัมพาตใบหน้า และติดเชื้อเข้าสมองได้ ผู้ป่วยมักมีหูน้ำหนวกกลิ่นเหม็นเรื้อรัง ตรวจด้วย CT temporal bone และ MRI DWI การรักษาคือผ่าตัดเอาออกให้หมดและติดตามการกลับเป็นซ้ำ

name: Choline acetyltransferase deficiency
formal: Congenital myasthenic syndrome from CHAT mutations causing presynaptic failure of ACh synthesis, with hypotonia and episodic apnoea precipitated by fever or excitement.
simple: An inherited disorder in which nerve endings cannot make enough chemical messenger, causing weakness and sudden breathing pauses.
more: Decrement on repetitive stimulation, especially after exertion; CHAT sequencing. Pyridostigmine is helpful; families need apnoea monitoring.
th: congenital myasthenic syndrome ชนิดก่อนไซแนปส์จากยีน CHAT สร้าง acetylcholine ไม่พอเมื่อใช้งานต่อเนื่อง ทารกอ่อนแรงและมีหยุดหายใจเป็นพัก ๆ ขณะป่วยมีไข้
tempoNote: Neonatal or infantile onset; sudden apnoeic crises on a background of mild or even absent weakness
feat: Newborn hypotonia, weak cry, poor suck and ptosis, sometimes needing ventilation
Recurrent apnoea and bulbar weakness set off by fever, vomiting, infection or excitement
Strength may look nearly normal between crises, so the diagnosis is easily missed
Risk of hypoxic brain injury or sudden infant death; arthrogryposis in some
Autosomal recessive; antibody-negative and unresponsive to immunosuppression or thymectomy
inv: Repetitive nerve stimulation: 2–3 Hz decrement, which may appear only after prolonged 10 Hz stimulation or exercise
Anti-AChR and anti-MuSK antibodies negative
CHAT sequencing or a congenital myasthenic syndrome gene panel
Edrophonium or pyridostigmine trial under monitoring in infants

case.who: 3-month-old boy followed after a NICU stay in Bangkok
case.story: Born floppy and ventilated for two days, he later turned blue twice during febrile colds. He recovered fully each time.
case.exam: Mild bilateral ptosis and weak suck; limb strength near normal between episodes.
case.tests: Resting RNS normal; after five minutes of 10 Hz stimulation there is marked decrement; biallelic CHAT variants.
case.q: Why can a normal resting RNS miss this disease, and what long-term drug prevents apnoea?
case.a: The defect in acetylcholine resynthesis only shows after sustained firing depletes the stores; regular pyridostigmine (with a home apnoea plan) protects during illness.

det.patho: Choline acetyltransferase makes acetylcholine from choline and acetyl-CoA in the motor nerve terminal. Biallelic CHAT variants reduce transmitter resynthesis, so quanta released at rest suffice but the store runs down during sustained or fast firing. This explains the episodic failure of neuromuscular transmission with illness, fever and exertion.
det.clinical: Many infants have respiratory insufficiency or feeding trouble at birth and need brief ventilation, then improve over weeks. Ptosis and generalised weakness fluctuate, extraocular movements are often spared and episodes of life-threatening apnoea recur through infancy and sometimes later childhood. Crises are provoked by infection, vomiting and excitement. Other children are well between episodes, which makes families doubt the diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: Suspect the condition in an antibody-negative infant with apnoeic spells and fluctuating weakness. Low-frequency RNS shows decrement in weak muscles, and a negative result at rest does not exclude the disease if stimulation is not prolonged. Antibodies against AChR and MuSK are absent, and immunotherapy brings no gain. Gene panel or exome sequencing confirms CHAT disease.
det.treatment: Long-term pyridostigmine or neostigmine prevents sudden apnoea during illness, and some children also benefit from 3,4-diaminopyridine. Parents need training in resuscitation, a home oximeter or apnoea monitor and an emergency letter for hospitals. Avoid drugs that impair transmission, such as aminoglycosides and magnesium. Thymectomy and immunosuppression do not help.
det.prognosis: Crises become fewer with age and outcome is good if hypoxic injury is avoided.
pearls: Apnoea with infection in a floppy antibody-negative infant: think CHAT-related congenital myasthenic syndrome.
Resting RNS can be normal; prolong stimulation.
Aminoglycosides can precipitate a crisis.
det.thd: Choline acetyltransferase deficiency เป็น congenital myasthenic syndrome ชนิดถ่ายทอดยีนด้อยจากยีน CHAT ทำให้สร้าง acetylcholine ที่ปลายประสาทไม่พอเมื่อใช้งานต่อเนื่อง ทารกแรกเกิดอ่อนปวกเปียก หนังตาตก ดูดนมอ่อน และหยุดหายใจเป็นพัก ๆ เมื่อมีไข้หรืออาเจียน ตรวจ RNS ต้องกระตุ้นนานพอจึงเห็น decrement แอนติบอดีเป็นลบ ยืนยันด้วยยีน รักษาด้วย pyridostigmine ต่อเนื่อง ไม่ใช้ thymectomy หรือภูมิคุ้มกันบำบัด และหลีกเลี่ยงยากลุ่ม aminoglycoside

qx.stem: A 4-month-old girl from Khon Kaen is brought to the emergency department cyanotic and limp after two days of vomiting and fever. She recovers after bag-mask ventilation. She had a similar episode at 6 weeks. Between episodes she has only mild ptosis, a normal eye movement range and fairly normal strength. Repetitive stimulation at 3 Hz is normal at rest, but a decrement appears after a prolonged 10 Hz train.
qx.q: Which long-term approach is most appropriate for the likely diagnosis?
opts: Daily prednisolone to prevent relapses of autoimmune myasthenia
Daily pyridostigmine with a home plan for illness, including apnoea monitoring and rescue ventilation or neostigmine during infections
Fluoxetine to shorten the open time of the receptor channel
Salbutamol alone, with pyridostigmine avoided
Observation only, as the episodes will stop spontaneously by one year
qx.why: Episodic apnoea triggered by infection or vomiting, with mild interictal weakness, ptosis without ophthalmoplegia and a decrement only after prolonged stimulation, suggests ChAT deficiency, a presynaptic CMS in which transmitter resynthesis cannot keep up with demand. Cholinesterase inhibitors prevent most crises, while cerebral hypoxia from unrecognised apnoea is the main danger. Fluoxetine is for slow channel syndrome and immunosuppression has no role.

name: Chondrosarcomas
formal: Malignant cartilaginous tumours of the skull base or spine causing cranial neuropathies or cord compression; slow-growing but locally invasive.
simple: Cancers of cartilage at the skull base or spine that can press on nerves.
th: มะเร็งกระดูกอ่อนที่ฐานกะโหลกหรือกระดูกสันหลัง โตช้าแต่ลุกลามเฉพาะที่ กดเส้นประสาทสมองหรือไขสันหลัง
tempoNote: Slow growth over years; symptoms accrue gradually
feat: Skull base tumours arise off-midline at the petroclival synchondrosis
Abducens palsy and diplopia are the most frequent presenting cranial nerve deficit
Headache, facial numbness or hearing loss depending on extension
Spinal tumours cause local pain and cord or root compression
Often low grade with local recurrence rather than distant spread
inv: MRI: lobulated very T2-bright lesion with ring-and-arc enhancement
CT: chondroid matrix calcification and bone destruction
Biopsy or resection specimen; IDH1/2 mutations support chondrosarcoma over chordoma

case.story: Eight months of horizontal double vision when looking left and a dull ache behind the left ear.
case.exam: Left abducens palsy, reduced left facial sensation in V2, other cranial nerves normal.
case.tests: MRI shows a lobulated T2-hyperintense left petroclival mass; CT shows arc-like calcification; pathology is brachyury-negative.
case.q: Why is this not a chordoma?
case.a: Off-midline petroclival site, chondroid calcification and brachyury negativity favour chondrosarcoma.

read.where: 8 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System

det.patho: Chondrosarcomas are malignant cartilage-producing tumours. At the skull base they arise from residual cartilage in synchondroses, most often petroclival. Many conventional cases carry IDH1 or IDH2 mutations, and they are associated with Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome.
det.clinical: Symptoms reflect slow compression of nearby cranial nerves: diplopia from the abducens nerve, facial sensory change, hearing loss or lower cranial nerve palsies. Spinal tumours present with pain and myelopathy or radiculopathy. Because growth is slow, deficits may be tolerated for long periods before diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: MRI and CT together characterise the lesion. Pathology confirms the diagnosis and grade; immunohistochemistry distinguishes chondrosarcoma (brachyury negative) from chordoma (brachyury positive). Staging is mainly local, with chest imaging for higher-grade tumours.
det.treatment: Maximal safe resection, usually through endoscopic or skull base approaches, is followed by high-dose radiotherapy, often proton or carbon ion therapy for residual tumour. Chemotherapy has a limited role except in mesenchymal or dedifferentiated forms. Long-term MRI surveillance is needed.
det.prognosis: Low-grade skull base tumours have good long-term control after surgery plus particle therapy; higher grades fare worse.
pearls: Midline clivus suggests chordoma; off-midline petroclival suggests chondrosarcoma.
Brachyury staining separates the two on pathology.
Isolated sixth nerve palsy with a slowly growing skull base mass is a classic presentation.
det.thd: Chondrosarcoma เป็นมะเร็งกระดูกอ่อน ที่ฐานกะโหลกมักอยู่ข้างแนวกลางบริเวณ petroclival โตช้าและกดเส้นประสาทสมอง โดยเฉพาะเส้นที่ 6 ทำให้เห็นภาพซ้อน MRI พบก้อนสว่างมากใน T2 CT พบหินปูนแบบกระดูกอ่อน ชิ้นเนื้อ brachyury ลบช่วยแยกจาก chordoma รักษาด้วยผ่าตัดร่วมกับรังสีรักษาขนาดสูง

name: Chordoma
formal: Rare locally aggressive tumour from notochordal remnants at clivus or sacrum, causing diplopia, headache and cranial nerve palsies.
simple: A rare slow-growing tumour at the skull base or tailbone that can press on nerves.
th: เนื้องอกหายากที่เกิดจากเศษ notochord ที่ clivus หรือ sacrum โตช้าแต่ทำลายกระดูกและกลับเป็นซ้ำบ่อย ทำให้เห็นภาพซ้อน ปวดศีรษะ และเส้นประสาทสมองอัมพาต การรักษาคือผ่าตัดให้มากที่สุดร่วมกับ proton beam
tempoNote: Months to years of headache and diplopia; time to diagnosis often exceeds a year
feat: Midline clival tumour (about a quarter to a third of chordomas), sacral tumour (about half) and mobile spine; peak age 30-50 years, rare in children
Diplopia from sixth nerve palsy is the first symptom in many; headache, hypoglossal, facial and lower cranial nerve deficits follow
Compression of the brainstem or cerebellum causes long-tract signs; retropharyngeal or nasal extension causes dysphagia, nasal obstruction or epistaxis

MRI: T2-hyperintense, lobulated enhancing mass with septations; involvement of vertebrobasilar and carotid vessels; MRA when vascular encasement is possible

case.who: 46-year-old man, a market vendor from Phetchabun
case.story: Eight months of progressive horizontal diplopia, deep headache and a nasal voice; he lost 3 kg.
case.exam: Left abducens palsy, mild left hypoglossal weakness and a retropharyngeal bulge on nasal endoscopy.
case.tests: CT shows an expansile lytic midline clival mass with fragments; MRI shows a T2-bright lobulated enhancing tumour compressing the pons. Endoscopic endonasal biopsy: brachyury-positive chordoma.
case.q: What are the key principles of treatment and one precaution for the surgical route?

det.patho: Chordoma arises from notochordal remnants along the neuraxis, most often at the spheno-occipital synchondrosis and the sacrococcygeal region. Histology shows lobules of physaliphorous (bubbly vacuolated) cells in a mucoid matrix, expressing cytokeratin, EMA and brachyury, the notochordal transcription factor that defines the tumour. Poorly differentiated chordoma with SMARCB1 (INI1) loss occurs in children. The book also discusses chondroid chordoma as a subtype; the current WHO classification no longer uses it. Local recurrence is driven by invasion into bone.
det.clinical: Skull base lesions are slow, with years of headache and abducens palsy preceding diagnosis. Cranial neuropathies are found in 40-90 percent at presentation. Large lesions compress the brainstem or extend into the cavernous sinus, sphenoid sinus and craniocervical junction. Sacral lesions present late with pain and sphincter loss. Seeding of the surgical tract and distant metastasis to lung, bone or liver are late events.
det.diagnosis: Imaging combines CT (bone destruction, calcified fragments) and MRI (extent, brainstem and vascular relationship). The diagnosis needs tissue, ideally via a nasal route, with brachyury staining. A midline origin and destruction without hyperostosis differentiate chordoma from meningioma, while chondrosarcoma is more lateral and brachyury-negative. Staging for metastases and discussion at a skull base multidisciplinary meeting are standard.
det.treatment: Radical resection through endoscopic endonasal or open skull base routes followed by high-dose radiation is the best chance of control. Doses of 70-80 Gy are needed, so proton or carbon-ion therapy is preferred to spare brainstem; photon IMRT and radiosurgery are alternatives. Cerebrospinal fluid leak occurs in 8-30 percent after surgery. Tumour seeding along the operative route can be limited by changing instruments and gloves before fat grafting. Systemic options for recurrence are limited; imatinib, EGFR inhibitors and brachyury-targeted vaccines are investigational.
det.prognosis: Median survival is about 6-10 years with modern treatment; recurrence rates 12-60 percent are reported depending on prior surgery and resection extent.
pearls: Midline clival bone destruction plus sixth nerve palsy in a middle-aged adult: chordoma until proved otherwise.
Brachyury is the confirmatory immunostain.
Proton or carbon beam therapy allows 70+ Gy to the tumour with brainstem sparing.
det.thd: Chordoma เป็นเนื้องอกหายากที่เกิดจากเศษ notochord ที่ clivus หรือ sacrum โตช้าแต่ทำลายกระดูก ผู้ป่วยมาด้วยภาพซ้อน ปวดศีรษะ และเส้นประสาทสมองอัมพาตหลายเส้น ภาพ CT เห็น clivus ถูกทำลายโดยไม่มีกระดูกหนาตัว ชิ้นเนื้อย้อมติด brachyury การรักษาคือผ่าตัดให้มากที่สุดร่วมกับฉายรังสีขนาดสูง โดยเฉพาะ proton beam เพราะเนื้องอกกลับเป็นซ้ำได้บ่อย

name: Chorea
formal: Hyperkinetic movement disorder with irregular, brief, flowing involuntary movements; causes include Huntington disease, drugs, Sydenham and metabolic disorders.
simple: Irregular, jerky dance-like movements that flow from one body part to another.
more: Work up by history for drugs, then check thyroid, glucose, calcium, ESR, antibodies (ASO titre, antiphospholipid), pregnancy test and MRI; genetic HTT testing if familial. Treat with dopamine-depleting agents (tetrabenazine) or antipsychotics for severe cases.
th: การเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติแบบกระตุกสั้น ๆ ไม่เป็นจังหวะ ไหลจากส่วนหนึ่งไปอีกส่วนหนึ่ง สาเหตุมีทั้ง Huntington ยา Sydenham และโรคเมตาบอลิก
tempoNote: Acute with stroke or hyperglycaemia, subacute with autoimmune/infectious causes, chronic in genetic disease
feat: Irregular, unpredictable, brief movements that flit across face, trunk and limbs
Motor impersistence: cannot keep tongue out or maintain grip ('milkmaid grip')
Patients may blend movements into purposeful-looking actions (parakinesia)
Can be generalised, hemichorea (contralateral basal ganglia lesion) or focal
Often accompanied by hypotonia; ballism is its large-amplitude extreme
inv: Drug review (levodopa, antipsychotics, antiepileptics, oral contraceptives) and pregnancy test
Glucose/HbA1c, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid, liver and renal function, full blood count with smear for acanthocytes
ASO/anti-DNase B, ANA, antiphospholipid antibodies; autoimmune encephalitis panel if subacute
MRI brain; genetic testing (HTT first) when familial or progressive

case.who: 72-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes from Nakhon Ratchasima
case.story: Over two days developed flinging, writhing movements of her left arm and leg; no headache.
case.exam: Continuous left hemichorea-hemiballism, alert, no weakness.
case.tests: Glucose 520 mg/dL without ketones; CT shows right putaminal hyperdensity, MRI T1 hyperintense putamen.
case.q: What is the likely cause and treatment?
case.a: Non-ketotic hyperglycaemic hemichorea; correct glucose, add a short course of dopamine blocker or tetrabenazine if severe.

det.patho: Chorea reflects reduced output of the indirect basal ganglia pathway, mainly from striatal or subthalamic dysfunction, leading to disinhibition of thalamocortical motor drive. Causes fall into genetic (Huntington, HDL2, neuroacanthocytosis, benign hereditary chorea, C9orf72), structural (stroke, tumour), metabolic (hyperglycaemia, hyperthyroidism, hyponatraemia correction), drug-induced, autoimmune (Sydenham, SLE, antiphospholipid, anti-NMDA, paraneoplastic) and infectious (HIV, toxoplasma).
det.clinical: Mild chorea can look like fidgeting; ask the patient to sit quietly or hold arms out. Age, tempo and distribution guide the search: hemichorea suggests a focal lesion or hyperglycaemia; childhood onset raises Sydenham, benign hereditary chorea or metabolic disease; pregnancy suggests chorea gravidarum. Cognitive and behavioural change with a family history points to Huntington disease.
det.diagnosis: Start with drug history, glucose and basic chemistry, then autoimmune and infectious tests guided by age. MRI identifies strokes, putaminal T1 hyperintensity in hyperglycaemia and caudate atrophy in Huntington. Genetic testing for HTT should follow counselling. A blood smear for acanthocytes and CK help detect neuroacanthocytosis.
det.treatment: Correct the cause wherever possible: stop the drug, fix glucose, treat autoimmune disease. Symptomatic options include VMAT2 inhibitors (tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine, valbenazine), antipsychotics or, in some cases, amantadine, valproate or benzodiazepines. Watch for depression with tetrabenazine and for parkinsonism with antipsychotics. Treat only if the movements are disabling.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause: metabolic, drug and Sydenham chorea often resolve; genetic chorea progresses.
pearls: Hemichorea in an elderly diabetic: check glucose and look for T1-bright putamen.
Motor impersistence (darting tongue, milkmaid grip) helps identify subtle chorea.
Always check a pregnancy test and drug list in young women with new chorea.
det.thd: Chorea คือการเคลื่อนไหวกระตุกสั้น ๆ ไม่เป็นจังหวะ ไหลไปตามส่วนต่าง ๆ ของร่างกาย เกิดจากความผิดปกติของ basal ganglia สาเหตุมีหลายกลุ่ม ได้แก่ พันธุกรรม (Huntington) ยา น้ำตาลในเลือดสูง โรคภูมิคุ้มกัน (Sydenham, SLE) และรอยโรคหลอดเลือด การตรวจเริ่มจากประวัติยา น้ำตาล เกลือแร่ แอนติบอดี และ MRI รักษาที่สาเหตุ และใช้ VMAT2 inhibitor หรือยาต้าน dopamine เมื่ออาการรบกวนมาก

name: Chorea and dystonia
formal: Combination of choreiform movements and dystonic postures seen in Huntington disease, neuroacanthocytosis, drug-induced and paediatric disorders.
simple: A mix of dance-like jerks and twisting postures caused by basal ganglia disorders.
th: กลุ่มอาการที่มีทั้ง chorea และท่าทาง dystonia พร้อมกัน พบใน Huntington, neuroacanthocytosis, ยา และโรคในเด็ก
tempoNote: Most causes are chronic genetic or degenerative; drug-induced and autoimmune forms evolve over weeks
feat: Brief flowing involuntary movements alongside sustained twisting postures
Orofacial and feeding dystonia (tongue protrusion) suggests chorea-acanthocytosis
Juvenile Huntington and many metabolic disorders mix the two patterns
Dyskinetic cerebral palsy and kernicterus produce lifelong choreoathetosis with dystonia
Levodopa-induced dyskinesia in Parkinson disease often combines both
inv: MRI brain (caudate atrophy, iron or metal deposition, basal ganglia lesions)
Blood smear for acanthocytes, CK, copper and caeruloplasmin, lactate, amino and organic acids in children
Genetic panels (HTT, VPS13A, ADCY5, NKX2-1, GNAO1, PANK2 and others)

case.story: Two years of involuntary face movements, tongue pushing food out of his mouth, and recent seizures; he bites his lips.
case.exam: Generalised chorea, feeding dystonia with tongue protrusion, lip mutilation, absent ankle reflexes.
case.tests: CK 1,500 U/L; acanthocytes on fresh smear; MRI caudate atrophy; HTT normal.
case.q: Which disorder fits best?
case.a: Chorea-acanthocytosis (VPS13A), a form of neuroacanthocytosis.

read.where: Chapter 58 Movement Disorders Associated With General Medical Diseases

det.patho: Chorea and dystonia often coexist because both arise from abnormal basal ganglia output; striatal degeneration, metabolic toxins and dopaminergic excess can disturb several pathways at once. Typical causes include Huntington disease, chorea-acanthocytosis, McLeod syndrome, Wilson disease, PKAN, ADCY5 and GNAO1 disorders, dyskinetic cerebral palsy, glutaric aciduria and drugs (levodopa, dopamine blockers).
det.clinical: Describe which pattern predominates since it guides the work-up. Childhood onset with fluctuating, sleep-related or paroxysmal exacerbations suggests ADCY5 or GNAO1. Adult onset with psychiatric change, seizures and neuropathy points to neuroacanthocytosis. Parkinson patients on levodopa show peak-dose choreodystonia.
det.diagnosis: Combine history (drugs, perinatal events, family history) with MRI and targeted laboratory tests. Copper studies are mandatory in anyone under about 50. Next-generation sequencing panels are now first-line when acquired causes are excluded.
det.treatment: Treat the cause (e.g. chelation for Wilson, adjust levodopa). Symptomatic therapy is tailored: VMAT2 inhibitors for chorea, anticholinergics or botulinum toxin for focal dystonia, and deep brain stimulation for selected genetic dystonia-chorea syndromes. Mouth guards and nutrition support help feeding dystonia.
det.prognosis: Varies by cause; degenerative forms progress over years while drug-induced forms usually improve once adjusted.
pearls: Feeding dystonia with tongue pushing food out: chorea-acanthocytosis.
Check copper studies in every young patient with mixed hyperkinesia.
Peak-dose levodopa dyskinesia commonly blends chorea and dystonia.
det.thd: Chorea and dystonia คือกลุ่มอาการที่มีทั้งการกระตุกไหลแบบ chorea และท่าบิดเกร็งแบบ dystonia ในคนเดียวกัน สาเหตุสำคัญได้แก่ Huntington, neuroacanthocytosis, Wilson, ยา levodopa และโรคพันธุกรรมในเด็ก ควรตรวจ MRI, copper studies, blood smear หา acanthocyte, CK และตรวจยีน การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ ร่วมกับยาตามอาการเช่น VMAT2 inhibitor หรือ botulinum toxin

name: Chorea gravidarum
formal: Chorea first occurring or relapsing in pregnancy, often linked to prior rheumatic fever, antiphospholipid syndrome or lupus; usually resolves after delivery.
simple: Dance-like involuntary movements during pregnancy that usually settle after birth.
more: Chorea arising during pregnancy, often in women with prior rheumatic chorea, lupus or antiphospholipid antibodies; usually resolves after delivery.
th: chorea ที่เริ่มหรือกลับมาในระหว่างตั้งครรภ์ สาเหตุเดิมคือ rheumatic fever แต่ปัจจุบันพบจาก antiphospholipid syndrome และ SLE มากที่สุด มักหายเองภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์ถึงเดือน
tempoNote: Appears over days to weeks, usually in months 2–5 of pregnancy (sometimes after delivery) and settles within weeks to months
feat: Generalised chorea or hemichorea with motor impersistence beginning in pregnancy, typically the second to fifth month
Past Sydenham chorea, rheumatic fever or lupus in many; can recur in later pregnancies or with oral contraceptives
Today antiphospholipid antibodies (with or without SLE) are the commonest identified cause
Mood change, anxiety or psychosis may accompany severe cases, and cognition may dip
Most resolve spontaneously, often after delivery
inv: Antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-beta2-glycoprotein I), ANA and anti-dsDNA
ASO or anti-DNase B and echocardiography for rheumatic heart disease
TSH, glucose, calcium and magnesium; Wilson screen if a young woman has other signs
MRI brain without gadolinium if atypical (basal ganglia infarct or lesion)

case.story: For two weeks she drops cups and her arms writhe. At 11 she had a 'dancing illness' with joint pain after a sore throat.
case.exam: Mild generalised chorea, motor impersistence of the tongue, and a soft apical systolic murmur.
case.tests: Antiphospholipid antibodies and ANA negative, TSH normal; echocardiography shows rheumatic mitral valve changes.
case.q: What is the likely mechanism, and what are the management priorities?
case.a: Recrudescent Sydenham (rheumatic) chorea triggered by pregnancy; reassure, look for APS and lupus, give penicillin prophylaxis, and treat symptoms only if disabling.

Chapter 20 Sex Hormone, Pituitary, Parathyroid, and Adrenal Disorders and the Nervous System

det.patho: Chorea reflects dysfunction of the striatum and its connections. In pregnancy, raised oestrogen is thought to sensitise dopamine receptors, and autoimmune triggers (post-streptococcal antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies, lupus) add to the risk. A past episode of Sydenham chorea predisposes to recurrence.
det.clinical: Chorea typically begins between months two and five of gestation, with a few cases after delivery. Movements are irregular, flowing and worsen with stress; hemichorea suggests a structural lesion such as infarct. Mild cases are disabling mainly by clumsiness, and severe ones threaten nutrition and can be accompanied by psychiatric symptoms. In many women it settles within weeks to months, but antiphospholipid syndrome carries risk of thrombosis and miscarriage.
det.diagnosis: Evaluate every pregnant woman with new chorea for rheumatic fever, antiphospholipid syndrome and lupus, and check thyroid and metabolic causes. Imaging is not usually needed except for focal signs or atypical course, and gadolinium should be avoided. Rule out Wilson disease, drugs (neuroleptics, antiemetics), and Huntington disease from family history.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: penicillin prophylaxis for rheumatic chorea, anticoagulation with low-molecular-weight heparin and aspirin for antiphospholipid syndrome, and steroids or hydroxychloroquine for lupus as guided by obstetric and rheumatology teams. Mild chorea needs only rest and reassurance. For disabling movements, haloperidol or low-dose risperidone is used cautiously; valproate is avoided in pregnancy, and the decision is shared with obstetrics.
det.prognosis: Usually self-limited with good recovery, though recurrence in later pregnancy is possible and the underlying disease needs long-term follow-up.
pearls: New chorea in pregnancy equals antiphospholipid antibodies until proven otherwise.
Avoid valproate and gadolinium; plan with obstetrics.
Past Sydenham chorea predicts recurrence in pregnancy or on oral contraceptives.

name: Chorea insaneins
formal: Historical term for severe chorea associated with psychiatric disturbance and mania, now largely obsolete.
simple: An old term for severe jerky movements combined with serious mental disturbance.
th: ศัพท์ประวัติศาสตร์ หมายถึง chorea รุนแรงร่วมกับอาการทางจิต สับสน หรือ mania ปัจจุบันแทบไม่ใช้แล้ว
tempoNote: Historically described as rapidly escalating over days in severe Sydenham or pregnancy chorea
feat: Historical label (correct spelling 'chorea insaniens') — not a separate disease today
Violent generalised chorea with delirium, agitation, hallucinations or mania
Classically seen in severe Sydenham chorea or chorea gravidarum before antibiotics
Exhaustion, injury, fever and dehydration contributed to high historical mortality
inv: Investigate as for acute chorea with encephalopathy: infection, autoimmune encephalitis, SLE, metabolic and drug causes
MRI brain, EEG and CSF if confused; NMDA receptor and other neuronal antibodies

case.who: 17-year-old girl brought to a provincial hospital in Sakon Nakhon
case.story: Ten days of worsening jerking movements, then insomnia, shouting and seeing people in the room; sore throat a month earlier.
case.exam: Severe generalised chorea, agitated and disoriented, tachycardic, no neck stiffness.
case.tests: ASO raised; CSF mild lymphocytosis; NMDA receptor antibodies positive in CSF.
case.q: Why is the old label 'chorea insaniens' unhelpful here?
case.a: It describes a picture, not a cause; this patient has anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, which needs immunotherapy and tumour screening.

det.patho: In nineteenth- and early twentieth-century texts this label described chorea so severe that patients became maniacal or delirious. Many such cases were probably rheumatic or pregnancy-related chorea complicated by fever and exhaustion, and some would now be recognised as autoimmune encephalitis, lupus or infection. No distinct pathology is defined.
det.clinical: The term survives mainly in historical classifications of chorea alongside chorea major, minor, mollis and gravidarum. A modern patient with combined chorea and psychosis needs urgent evaluation for treatable causes rather than a descriptive label.
det.diagnosis: Approach as acute encephalopathy with a movement disorder: MRI, EEG, CSF with autoimmune panels, infection screening, lupus serology, thyroid and metabolic studies, drug and toxin history.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying cause (immunotherapy for autoimmune encephalitis or Sydenham, management of lupus, antibiotics for infection) plus sedation, hydration and protection from injury. Symptomatic agents include benzodiazepines and dopamine blockers with careful monitoring.
det.prognosis: Historically fatal in some cases; with modern diagnosis outcome reflects the treatable cause.
pearls: Historical descriptive term; translate it into a modern cause-based diagnosis.
Chorea plus psychosis in a young woman: test for anti-NMDA receptor antibodies.
Spelling in old texts varies (insaniens/insaneins).
det.thd: Chorea insaniens เป็นศัพท์เก่าใช้เรียก chorea รุนแรงที่มีอาการทางจิตร่วม เช่น เพ้อ คลั่ง หรือประสาทหลอน มักพบใน Sydenham chorea รุนแรงหรือ chorea ระหว่างตั้งครรภ์สมัยก่อนมียาปฏิชีวนะ ปัจจุบันไม่ถือเป็นโรคเฉพาะ ผู้ป่วยที่มีอาการแบบนี้ต้องหาสาเหตุที่รักษาได้ เช่น anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, SLE หรือการติดเชื้อ แล้วรักษาตามสาเหตุ

Psychosis, dyskinesia, seizures, autonomic instability; CSF antibodies

name: Chorea major
formal: Historical term for severe, violent chorea such as chorea gravidarum or severe Sydenham chorea.
simple: An old name for very severe, violent dance-like movements.
th: ศัพท์ประวัติศาสตร์ เดิมหมายถึงการเต้นรำผิดปกติเป็นกลุ่มในยุคกลาง (dancing mania) ต่อมาใช้กับ chorea รุนแรง ปัจจุบันไม่ใช้แล้ว
tempoNote: Historical outbreaks lasted days to weeks; modern use not defined
feat: Historical term contrasting with 'chorea minor' (Sydenham chorea)
Originally described medieval European epidemics of frenzied dancing (dancing mania)
Those outbreaks are now generally viewed as mass psychogenic illness
Some later authors used it loosely for any violent chorea, including chorea gravidarum
Not a diagnosis in modern classifications
inv: Not a current diagnosis; investigate any patient with severe chorea as for chorea of unknown cause
Video assessment for functional features if movements are bizarre or variable

case.who: Medical student preparing a history-of-neurology talk in Bangkok
case.story: Finds 'chorea major' and 'chorea minor' in an old textbook and asks which is Sydenham chorea.
case.exam: Not applicable — terminology question.
case.tests: Not applicable.
case.q: What did each term mean?
case.a: Chorea minor = Sydenham chorea; chorea major = historical dancing epidemics (largely psychogenic) or loosely any severe chorea.

det.patho: The term derives from Paracelsus-era descriptions of dancing plagues along the Rhine in the fourteenth to sixteenth centuries, attributed then to St Vitus or St John. Historians and neurologists now interpret these mostly as mass psychogenic or socially driven phenomena, possibly amplified by hardship; ergotism has been proposed but is unproven. Thomas Sydenham's later description of childhood chorea became 'chorea minor'.
det.clinical: No defined clinical entity corresponds to chorea major today. When students encounter the label, it signals historical writing. Patients with violent, bizarre, variable movements need assessment for both organic hyperkinesia and functional movement disorder.
det.diagnosis: Not applicable as a diagnosis. Use modern categories: cause-based chorea, ballism, or functional movement disorder supported by positive clinical signs.
det.treatment: Treat whichever modern diagnosis applies, e.g. physiotherapy-led rehabilitation for functional movement disorder or cause-directed therapy for organic chorea.
det.prognosis: Not applicable.
pearls: Chorea minor = Sydenham; chorea major = historical dancing mania.
St Vitus dance became a popular name for Sydenham chorea.
Avoid historical terms in clinical notes.
det.thd: Chorea major เป็นศัพท์ประวัติศาสตร์ เดิมใช้เรียกโรคระบาดการเต้นรำผิดปกติเป็นกลุ่มในยุโรปยุคกลาง (dancing mania) ซึ่งปัจจุบันเชื่อว่าส่วนใหญ่เป็นปรากฏการณ์ทางจิตสังคม ตรงข้ามกับ chorea minor ซึ่งหมายถึง Sydenham chorea ปัจจุบันไม่ใช้เป็นการวินิจฉัย ถ้าพบผู้ป่วย chorea รุนแรงให้หาสาเหตุตามแนวทางปัจจุบัน

name: Chorea paralytica
formal: Historical term for chorea with such profound hypotonia that it mimics paralysis, in severe Sydenham chorea.
simple: An old term for chorea so severe that the muscles go floppy as if paralysed.
th: ศัพท์เก่าสำหรับ Sydenham chorea ที่กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนปวกเปียกมากจนดูเหมือนอัมพาต
tempoNote: Develops over days to weeks after streptococcal infection, like other Sydenham chorea
feat: Severe hypotonia and apparent weakness with only sparse chorea
Child may be unable to walk, sit or speak clearly, mimicking acute flaccid paralysis
Reflexes are preserved or pendular; sensation normal
Recent streptococcal infection, carditis or arthritis support the diagnosis
inv: ASO and anti-DNase B, throat culture, ESR/CRP, echocardiography
Nerve conduction and MRI spine if true paralysis cannot be excluded

case.story: Over a week she became floppy, could not hold a spoon and stopped walking; a sore throat six weeks ago.
case.exam: Marked hypotonia, small irregular twitches of the fingers and face, pendular knee jerks, normal sensation.
case.tests: Anti-DNase B high; echo mild mitral regurgitation; NCS normal.
case.q: Why is this not Guillain–Barré syndrome?
case.a: Reflexes are present, NCS is normal and subtle chorea is visible — paralytic (limp) Sydenham chorea.

det.patho: A subtype of Sydenham chorea: antibodies induced by group A streptococcus cross-react with basal ganglia neurons, and in this form hypotonia dominates over hyperkinesia. The name reflects an era when profound limpness was mistaken for paralysis.
det.clinical: Children appear paralysed but strength on careful testing is limited by impersistence and hypotonia rather than true weakness. Subtle chorea, emotional lability and rheumatic carditis provide clues. Recovery follows the usual Sydenham timeline of weeks to months.
det.diagnosis: Diagnose as Sydenham chorea with streptococcal serology and echo. Exclude acute flaccid paralysis, myelitis and Guillain–Barré with NCS and spinal imaging if uncertain.
det.treatment: Penicillin to eradicate streptococcus followed by long-term secondary prophylaxis, as for rheumatic fever. Symptomatic drugs (valproate, carbamazepine, antipsychotics) are less useful when chorea is minimal; supportive physiotherapy is key. Corticosteroids or IVIG are used in severe cases in some centres.
det.prognosis: Generally good, with recovery over months; relapse risk persists as for other Sydenham chorea.
pearls: Floppy child with preserved reflexes after strep throat: consider limp Sydenham chorea.
Look carefully for small choreic jerks and motor impersistence.
Secondary penicillin prophylaxis applies as for any rheumatic chorea.
det.thd: Chorea paralytica หรือ chorea mollis เป็นศัพท์เก่าของ Sydenham chorea ชนิดที่กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนปวกเปียกมากจนดูเหมือนอัมพาต แต่ reflex ยังอยู่และ NCS ปกติ มักพบในเด็กหลังเจ็บคอจาก streptococcus ควรตรวจ ASO/anti-DNase B และ echocardiography รักษาด้วย penicillin และป้องกันระยะยาวแบบไข้รูมาติก ร่วมกับกายภาพบำบัด

Areflexia, sensory symptoms and abnormal nerve conduction
Inconsistent weakness with positive signs such as Hoover sign

name: Chorea-acanthocytosis (ChAc)
formal: Autosomal recessive neuroacanthocytosis from VPS13A mutations, with progressive chorea, orofacial dyskinesia, self-biting, seizures, myopathy, neuropathy and cognitive change, plus acanthocytes and raised CK.
simple: A rare inherited disease with uncontrolled movements, biting of the tongue and lips, and mood and memory changes.
more: Blood film may show acanthocytes; MRI shows caudate atrophy and genetics confirm. There is no cure and treatment is symptomatic; deep brain stimulation has helped some. Autosomal recessive VPS13A disease with chorea, orofacial dyskinesia, tongue and lip biting, acanthocytes, seizures, myopathy and raised creatine kinase. Autosomal recessive VPS13A disease with chorea, orofacial dyskinesia, lip biting, acanthocytes and myopathy. Neuroacanthocytosis from VPS13A variants with chorea, orofacial dyskinesia with tongue and lip biting, seizures, neuropathy, myopathy, raised CK and acanthocytes, with caudate atrophy. Diagnosis by blood film, CK, MRI and VPS13A testing; chorein loss can be shown on Western blot. Treatment is symptomatic with no cure, and progression takes years. Eponym for neuroacanthocytosis (chorea-acanthocytosis), with progressive orofacial dyskinesia, tongue biting, chorea, seizures, neuropathy and acanthocytosis on blood film. VPS13A mutations underlie it and CK is raised. Treatment is symptomatic with antiseizure drugs and movement therapies; no cure.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมยีนด้อย VPS13A ในผู้ใหญ่ตอนต้น มี chorea บริเวณปากและลิ้น กัดลิ้นกัดปาก ลิ้นดันอาหารออก ชัก กล้ามเนื้อและเส้นประสาทเสื่อม CK สูง และพบ acanthocyte
tempoNote: Begins in the 20s–30s and progresses over 15–30 years
feat: Generalised chorea with prominent orofacial dyskinesia
Lip and tongue biting; feeding dystonia with the tongue pushing food out
Vocal and motor tics, psychiatric change, executive dysfunction
Seizures (often temporal), areflexia from axonal neuropathy, mild myopathy
inv: Fresh wet blood film for acanthocytes (repeat; may be absent early)
CK raised, often with mildly raised liver enzymes
MRI caudate atrophy; chorein (VPS13A protein) absent on western blot; VPS13A testing
Kell antigen expression normal (distinguishes McLeod syndrome)

case.story: Two years of restlessness, odd tongue movements and repeated biting of her lips; food falls out when she tries to eat. Recently had two seizures.
case.exam: Generalised chorea, tongue protrusion dystonia, scarred lower lip, absent ankle reflexes; parents are first cousins, no family history of chorea.
case.tests: CK 1,400 U/L; blood film shows acanthocytes; HTT CAG repeats normal; MRI caudate atrophy.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and confirmatory test?
case.a: Chorea-acanthocytosis; confirm with VPS13A sequencing or absent chorein on red-cell western blot.

read.where: 12 The Many Faces of Parkinsonism: A Review of the Parkinson Look-alike Syndromes

det.patho: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in VPS13A abolish chorein, a lipid-transfer protein at membrane contact sites, disturbing lipid flow between organelles. The striatum (especially caudate) degenerates, and red cells become spiky acanthocytes from abnormal membranes. Muscle and peripheral nerve are also affected. The disease is rare and reported worldwide, including in Japan and other Asian countries.
det.clinical: Onset is typically in early adulthood with chorea, orofacial dyskinesias, self-mutilating lip and tongue biting, and characteristic feeding dystonia. Tics, vocalisations, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, depression and frontal-type cognitive decline are common, and some present with psychiatric disease or epilepsy first. Later, parkinsonism can replace chorea. Axonal neuropathy causes areflexia and myopathy raises CK, sometimes with mild weakness.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in a young adult with chorea plus lip biting, seizures, areflexia or high CK, with no dominant family history. Acanthocytes support it but have limited sensitivity, so a fresh, carefully prepared film should be repeated. Chorein western blot and VPS13A sequencing confirm. Exclude Huntington disease, McLeod syndrome (Kell antigens), Wilson disease and autoimmune chorea.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying treatment exists. Chorea may respond to VMAT2 inhibitors or antipsychotics; feeding dystonia and biting may be helped by botulinum toxin and mouth guards. Seizures are treated with standard antiseizure drugs, and psychiatric symptoms need active management. GPi deep brain stimulation has helped selected patients. Dietitian, speech therapy and genetic counselling are important.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive over decades with cumulative disability; sudden death related to seizures has been reported.
pearls: Chorea + lip biting + high CK: think chorea-acanthocytosis.
Normal blood film does not exclude it; acanthocytes can be missed.
Kell antigens are normal in ChAc and weak in McLeod syndrome.
det.thd: Chorea-acanthocytosis เกิดจากยีน VPS13A แบบยีนด้อย ผู้ป่วยวัยผู้ใหญ่ตอนต้นมีการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติแบบ chorea โดยเฉพาะที่ปากและลิ้น กัดริมฝีปาก ลิ้นดันอาหารออกเวลากิน ชัก และมีอาการทางจิตเวช ตรวจพบ CK สูง acanthocyte ในเลือด และ caudate ฝ่อ ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน รักษาตามอาการด้วยยาลด chorea, botulinum toxin ยากันชัก และบางรายใช้ DBS

Acanthocytes support it but may be missed on routine smears, so genetic testing or reduced chorein on red cell Western blot confirms. McLeod syndrome (XK, Kell antigens) is the main mimic; biopsy is never needed.

name: Choroid plexus tumours
formal: Neoplasms of choroid plexus epithelium, papilloma to carcinoma, mainly in children, causing hydrocephalus from CSF overproduction or obstruction.
simple: Tumours in the fluid-making tissue of the brain, mostly in young children, that can cause head swelling.
th: เนื้องอกจากเยื่อบุ choroid plexus ตั้งแต่ papilloma (grade I) ถึง carcinoma (grade III) พบมากในทารกและเด็กเล็ก ทำให้ความดันในกะโหลกสูงจากน้ำไขสันหลังคั่ง
tempoNote: Weeks to months of enlarging head, vomiting and drowsiness in infants; headache and visual blurring over a similar period in older patients
feat: Intraventricular tumour in the lateral ventricle (usually children), the fourth ventricle (all ages, the usual site in adults) or, rarely, the third ventricle
Raised intracranial pressure: enlarging head and tense fontanelle in infants, vomiting, reduced alertness, headache and visual impairment in older children
Hydrocephalus arises from true overproduction of CSF, from blockage of its pathway or from tumour bleeding; this is the clinical hallmark
Papilloma is far more frequent than carcinoma; about 80% of carcinomas occur in children
Carcinoma (WHO grade III) is associated with germline TP53 variants, so Li–Fraumeni syndrome should be considered
inv: MRI with contrast: lobulated, cauliflower-like, brightly enhancing intraventricular mass; carcinoma may show necrosis, bleeding, brain oedema and seeding
Imaging of the whole spine and CSF cytology when carcinoma or dissemination is suspected
Histology (papilloma, atypical papilloma, carcinoma) and germline TP53 testing for carcinoma

case.story: Her mother noticed that her head had grown quickly over six weeks. She vomits after feeds, smiles less and no longer tracks toys well.
case.exam: Head circumference well above the 97th centile, tense anterior fontanelle, sunsetting eyes on downgaze, mild truncal hypotonia. Fundi hard to see.
case.tests: MRI shows a lobulated, strongly enhancing mass in the right lateral ventricle atrium with marked enlargement of the ventricles. Spine imaging is clean.
case.q: Why is the ventricle large, and what is the preferred treatment?
case.a: The tumour secretes CSF and can also obstruct outflow. Gross total surgical resection, after steroid and CSF diversion planning, is usually curative for papilloma; a shunt is needed only if hydrocephalus persists.

read.where: Chapter 104: Nonglial Central Nervous System Tumors — Choroid Plexus Tumors
8 - Cramps, Muscle Stiffness, and Exercise Intolerance

det.patho: These tumours arise from the epithelium that makes CSF. Choroid plexus papilloma (WHO grade I) is a papillary neoplasm of uniform cuboidal cells on fibrovascular cores, atypical papilloma (grade II) shows more mitoses, and carcinoma (grade III) has sheet-like growth, necrosis and invasion. Together they are only a fraction of 1% of intracranial tumours at all ages, but in infants they reach 10–20%. Germline TP53 alterations underlie a share of carcinomas.
det.clinical: Presentation follows the effect on CSF dynamics. Infants show enlarging head size, bulging fontanelle, vomiting, irritability and loss of developmental skills; older children and adults report headache, nausea and blurred vision, and may have gait ataxia when the fourth ventricle is involved. Hydrocephalus can occur even when the tumour is small because of CSF overproduction. Carcinoma behaves aggressively with local invasion and spread along CSF pathways.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows a lobulated, intensely enhancing intraventricular mass, often with flow voids and sometimes calcification. Features that favour carcinoma include irregular margins, adjacent oedema, haemorrhage or necrosis and drop metastases, which makes whole neuraxis imaging mandatory. Tissue confirms the grade. Test the germline TP53 gene in carcinoma and offer family counselling.
det.treatment: Complete surgical removal is the treatment of choice and cures most papillomas, with five-year survival near 100% after gross total resection. Pre-operative embolisation or early vessel control limits bleeding, which is an important risk in small infants. Hydrocephalus resolves in many cases after resection; a shunt or third ventriculostomy is kept for persistent cases. Carcinoma needs maximal resection with adjuvant chemotherapy; radiotherapy is avoided where possible in the very young and in TP53 carriers because of second-cancer risk.
det.prognosis: Papilloma carries an excellent outlook after full resection. Carcinoma has a guarded prognosis that depends on resection extent, age and TP53 status.
pearls: Lateral ventricle in a child, fourth ventricle in an adult: the site tracks age.
Hydrocephalus can be produced by the tumour itself because it secretes CSF, not only by obstruction.
Always ask about family cancer history in choroid plexus carcinoma and test TP53.
det.thd: เนื้องอก choroid plexus เกิดจากเซลล์ที่สร้างน้ำไขสันหลัง จึงทำให้เกิดน้ำคั่งในโพรงสมองได้ทั้งจากการผลิตมากและการอุดตัน พบมากในทารกและเด็กเล็กที่ lateral ventricle ส่วนผู้ใหญ่พบที่ ventricle ที่ 4 MRI เห็นก้อนเป็นพูคล้ายดอกกะหล่ำที่ติดสีเข้มชัด การรักษาหลักคือผ่าตัดเอาออกให้หมด ซึ่งมักหายขาดใน papilloma ส่วน carcinoma ต้องใช้เคมีบำบัดร่วมและควรตรวจยีน TP53

name: Chronic acquired hepatocerebral degeneration
formal: Hepatic encephalopathy complication from portosystemic shunting with parkinsonism, ataxia, cognitive decline and manganese deposition in basal ganglia.
simple: Long-term brain damage in severe liver disease causing slowness, tremor and thinking problems.
th: ภาวะสมองเสื่อมจากโรคตับเรื้อรังหรือ portosystemic shunt ทำให้เกิด parkinsonism, ataxia, ความคิดถดถอย และมีแมงกานีสสะสมที่ basal ganglia
tempoNote: Develops over months to years in established cirrhosis or shunting, often after repeated encephalopathy
feat: Symmetrical akinetic-rigid parkinsonism with early gait and postural problems, little rest tremor
Dysarthria, ataxia, action tremor, chorea or myoclonus
Slowed thinking, inattention and apathy (subcortical cognitive pattern)
Persists between episodes of overt hepatic encephalopathy
Rarely accompanied by hepatic myelopathy (spastic paraparesis)
inv: MRI: bilateral symmetric T1 hyperintensity in globus pallidus (manganese)
Liver function, ammonia, imaging for portosystemic shunts
Exclude Wilson disease (caeruloplasmin, urine copper, slit-lamp) in younger patients

case.who: 58-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis from Chachoengsao
case.story: Over a year has become slow, shuffling and soft-spoken despite abstaining from alcohol; prior admissions for confusion.
case.exam: Symmetric bradykinesia and rigidity, postural tremor, mild asterixis, wide-based gait.
case.tests: MRI shows bright pallidum on T1; ammonia mildly raised; caeruloplasmin normal.
case.q: What does the T1 pallidal signal reflect?
case.a: Manganese deposition from impaired hepatobiliary clearance — acquired hepatocerebral degeneration.

det.patho: Portosystemic shunting lets neurotoxins bypass the liver. Manganese, normally excreted in bile, accumulates in the globus pallidus and disrupts dopaminergic function; ammonia-driven astrocyte injury (Alzheimer type II astrocytes) and neuronal loss in cortex and basal ganglia contribute. It affects a small proportion of cirrhotic patients, more often with large shunts.
det.clinical: Unlike episodic hepatic encephalopathy, the neurological deficits are persistent and slowly progressive. The parkinsonism is usually symmetric and poorly levodopa-responsive. Cognitive slowing and gait instability raise fall risk.
det.diagnosis: Diagnose in a patient with chronic liver disease or shunt, compatible neurological signs and T1 pallidal hyperintensity, after excluding Wilson disease, drug-induced parkinsonism and other neurodegenerative disorders.
det.treatment: Optimise treatment of hepatic encephalopathy (lactulose, rifaximin), nutrition and shunt closure where appropriate. Liver transplantation can improve or reverse signs, though not in all patients. Levodopa helps only a minority; trial it. Physiotherapy and fall prevention are important.
det.prognosis: Often progressive without transplant; partial reversibility after transplantation is reported.
pearls: T1-bright globus pallidus in cirrhosis = manganese.
Persistent parkinsonism between encephalopathy episodes suggests AHD.
Rule out Wilson disease in younger patients with liver and movement disorders.
det.thd: Chronic acquired hepatocerebral degeneration เป็นภาวะที่ผู้ป่วยโรคตับเรื้อรังหรือมี portosystemic shunt เกิดอาการทางระบบประสาทถาวร เช่น parkinsonism แบบสองข้างเท่ากัน เดินเซ พูดไม่ชัด และความคิดช้า เกิดจากแมงกานีสและแอมโมเนียสะสม MRI พบ T1 สว่างที่ globus pallidus ต้องแยกจาก Wilson disease รักษาด้วยการควบคุม hepatic encephalopathy และการปลูกถ่ายตับอาจช่วยได้

name: Cerebellar ataxia, neuropathy and vestibular areflexia syndrome (CANVAS)
formal: CANVAS: late-onset cerebellar ataxia, sensory neuropathy and bilateral vestibular areflexia, due to biallelic RFC1 expansions.
simple: A slowly progressive condition of poor balance, numb feet and inner ear failure.

Diagnose by RFC1 biallelic AAGGG repeat expansion on repeat-primed PCR or Southern blot, with cerebellar vermis atrophy on MRI and absent sensory potentials on NCS. Late-onset, autosomal recessive; no disease-modifying therapy, so give rehabilitation.
ab: Chronic ataxic neuropathy and vestibular areflexia
Cerebellar ataxia with neuropathy and bilateral vestibular areflexia
