feat: Unsteadiness worsening in the dark from combined sensory, vestibular and cerebellar failure
Distal numbness with absent sensory responses but usually preserved reflexes early
Bilaterally abnormal head impulse test and impaired visually enhanced VOR
Long-standing dry cough often predates neurological symptoms by years
Autonomic symptoms and oscillopsia are common; dysarthria develops later
inv: Nerve conduction: absent or reduced sensory potentials with normal motor studies (ganglionopathy pattern)
Bilateral vestibular loss shown by video head impulse or calorics
MRI: cerebellar vermis atrophy, often anterior and dorsal
Genetic testing for biallelic RFC1 intronic pentanucleotide expansions

case.story: Dry cough for 15 years, then 4 years of imbalance that is worse on uneven ground at night; recently says the world jumps when walking.
case.exam: Broad-based gait, Romberg positive, bilateral catch-up saccades on head impulse, mild limb ataxia, reduced vibration at toes.
case.tests: Sural and radial sensory responses absent with normal motor conduction; MRI shows vermian atrophy.
case.q: Which genetic test is most likely to be positive?
case.a: Biallelic RFC1 AAGGG repeat expansion (CANVAS).

det.patho: Most cases result from biallelic expansion of an intronic pentanucleotide repeat (classically AAGGG) in RFC1, which encodes a DNA replication factor subunit. Neuronal loss involves dorsal root ganglia, vestibular and other cranial ganglia, and cerebellar Purkinje cells. The mechanism appears to be loss of function rather than toxic RNA, though details remain under study.
det.clinical: Presentation is usually after age 50 with slowly progressive imbalance. A sensory neuronopathy is almost universal and may be the only feature for years, so many patients first carry a label of idiopathic sensory neuropathy. Vestibular areflexia causes oscillopsia with head movement. Chronic cough, dysautonomia and later dysarthria and dysphagia complete the picture; the full triad is present in only a portion of carriers.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in late-onset ataxia with a non-length-dependent sensory neuronopathy, particularly with chronic cough. Bedside head impulse testing with video confirmation shows bilateral vestibular hypofunction. Standard ataxia panels and exome sequencing miss the expansion, so a dedicated repeat-primed PCR and Southern blot or long-read test is needed. Exclude acquired ganglionopathies such as Sjögren, paraneoplastic and toxic causes.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy exists. Management uses vestibular and balance physiotherapy, walking aids, fall prevention and speech-swallow assessment. Neuropathic pain and cough may need symptomatic medication. Genetic counselling is relevant because siblings can be affected though the disorder is recessive.
det.prognosis: Slow decline over a decade or more; many need a walking aid after about ten years and dysphagia is a late risk.
pearls: A chronic unexplained cough plus a sensory neuronopathy should prompt RFC1 testing.
Exome sequencing does not detect RFC1 expansions; order the specific test.
Vestibular loss is easily missed when cerebellar signs blunt the head impulse test; use video testing.
det.thd: CANVAS เกิดจากการขยายของ repeat ใน RFC1 แบบ recessive ทำให้เสียทั้ง dorsal root ganglion ระบบ vestibular และสมองน้อย ผู้ป่วยสูงอายุเดินเซ เวลามืดจะแย่ลง ภาพสั่นเวลาขยับศีรษะ และมักไอแห้งเรื้อรังมานาน การตรวจ NCS พบ sensory potential หาย head impulse ผิดปกติสองข้าง ต้องส่งตรวจ RFC1 โดยเฉพาะเพราะ exome ตรวจไม่เจอ การรักษาเป็นการฟื้นฟูและป้องกันการล้ม

name: Chronic daily headache
formal: Headache occurring 15 or more days per month for over 3 months, including chronic migraine, tension-type and medication overuse headache.
simple: A headache that occurs on most days for months.

feat: A descriptive umbrella, not a single diagnosis

case.story: Long history of monthly migraine; over two years headaches became almost daily, and she takes paracetamol-caffeine tablets on 20 days a month.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination and fundi; BMI 31.
case.tests: None needed initially.

det.patho: Most chronic daily headache represents progression of episodic migraine or tension-type headache through central sensitisation of trigeminovascular pathways. Risk factors for transformation include high baseline frequency, medication overuse, obesity, sleep disorders, depression and stressful life events. Population prevalence is around 3–5%.
det.clinical: Patients describe near-daily headaches of varying severity, often with superimposed migraine attacks. Comorbid mood disorders, insomnia and neck pain are common and reduce quality of life. Separating long-duration (over 4 hours) from short-duration daily headaches helps direct diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: Classify according to ICHD-3 subtype using diaries and history. Count medication days to detect overuse. Examine for papilloedema and focal signs; image or test when red flags such as new onset over 50, positional features, systemic symptoms or abnormal examination are present.
det.treatment: Educate, address overuse (simple advice or structured withdrawal), and treat comorbidities. Preventive options for chronic migraine include topiramate, amitriptyline, propranolol, onabotulinumtoxinA and CGRP monoclonal antibodies or gepants. Behavioural therapy, sleep hygiene, exercise and weight loss add benefit.
det.prognosis: Many improve with treatment of overuse and prevention, but relapse is common.
pearls: Always count analgesic days — overuse is often hidden in combination tablets.
Chronic daily headache is a starting label; refine to the ICHD subtype.
Check fundi in every chronic daily headache.

case.who: 34-year-old woman, factory worker in Samut Prakan
case.story: Seizures since age 12 with a rising feeling then staring and lip smacking, 4–6 times a month despite carbamazepine and levetiracetam taken correctly.
case.exam: Normal neurological exam; mild verbal memory problems on testing.
case.tests: MRI shows left hippocampal sclerosis; video-EEG captures three seizures from the left temporal region.

read.where: Section VI: Epilepsy Surgery and Neurostimulation

det.patho: Persistent seizures reflect an established epileptogenic network, commonly hippocampal sclerosis, focal cortical dysplasia, tumour, vascular malformation or post-injury scarring, or a severe genetic epilepsy. Proposed mechanisms of drug resistance include altered drug targets, increased efflux transporters and network reorganisation. Around one third of people with epilepsy do not achieve control with medication. Recurrent seizures and drugs both contribute to cognitive and mood burden.
det.clinical: Patients have recurrent seizures over years, often focal impaired awareness seizures, with periods of clustering. Comorbidities such as memory complaints, depression, anxiety, sleep disturbance, osteoporosis and drug side effects frequently matter as much as seizures. Mortality is raised from SUDEP, injury, drowning and suicide. Pseudoresistance from wrong diagnosis, wrong drug, inadequate dose or poor adherence is common and must be excluded.
det.diagnosis: The ILAE definition of drug-resistant epilepsy is failure of two tolerated, appropriately chosen and used antiseizure medication schedules to achieve sustained seizure freedom. Confirm the diagnosis and syndrome with video-EEG, review drug choice and adherence, and image with a high-resolution epilepsy protocol MRI. Consider functional seizures, syncope, sleep disorders and autoimmune or metabolic causes. Early referral to a comprehensive epilepsy centre is advised.
det.treatment: Resective surgery is the most effective option for suitable focal epilepsies; laser ablation, vagus nerve stimulation, responsive neurostimulation and thalamic deep brain stimulation are alternatives. Newer drugs (for example cenobamate) and ketogenic dietary therapy may help when surgery is unsuitable. Address mood, bone health, contraception and pregnancy planning, driving and employment, and provide SUDEP counselling and seizure first-aid education. Rescue medication such as buccal or intranasal midazolam reduces prolonged clusters.
det.prognosis: Each additional failed drug lowers the chance of medical control; surgery yields seizure freedom in a majority of well-selected temporal lobe cases.
pearls: Two failed appropriate drugs = drug-resistant; refer early, not after ten years.
Check the diagnosis and adherence before labelling epilepsy refractory.
Hippocampal sclerosis with concordant EEG has the best surgical outcome.
det.thd: Chronic หรือ drug-resistant epilepsy คือโรคลมชักที่ยังชักอยู่แม้ใช้ยากันชักที่เหมาะสมมาแล้วอย่างน้อยสองตัว ควรตรวจยืนยันด้วย video-EEG และ MRI แบบ epilepsy protocol และทบทวนการกินยา ผู้ป่วยกลุ่มนี้มีปัญหาความจำ ซึมเศร้า และเสี่ยง SUDEP ทางเลือกการรักษาที่ได้ผลมากคือการผ่าตัดถ้าจุดกำเนิดชัด หรือใช้ VNS, DBS, ยาใหม่ และอาหาร ketogenic

name: Chronic idiopathic sensory polyneuropathy
formal: Slowly progressive, length-dependent sensory axonal polyneuropathy in older adults with no identifiable cause after thorough work-up.
simple: Slowly worsening numbness and tingling in the feet and hands in older people, with no known cause found.
more: Diagnosis requires excluding diabetes, B12 deficiency, toxins, paraproteins, and other causes. Treat symptoms and prevent falls; prognosis is benign.
th: เส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเสื่อมชนิดรับความรู้สึก ค่อยๆ เป็นในผู้สูงอายุ โดยหาสาเหตุไม่พบหลังตรวจครบ
tempoNote: Very slowly progressive over years, usually after age 50
feat: Numbness, tingling or burning starting in the toes and creeping up symmetrically
Ankle jerks lost; mild distal vibration and pinprick loss
Minimal or no weakness; at most toe extensor weakness
Balance mildly affected in older patients
A diagnosis of exclusion; up to a quarter of polyneuropathies remain unexplained
inv: Glucose tolerance test or HbA1c, B12 with methylmalonic acid, TSH, renal and liver function
Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and free light chains
Nerve conduction: length-dependent axonal sensory or sensorimotor pattern
Skin biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fibre density if conduction studies are normal

case.story: Four years of burning soles and a feeling of walking on cotton; worse at night.
case.exam: Absent ankle reflexes, reduced pinprick to mid-shin, vibration reduced at the toes, normal strength.
case.tests: Glucose tolerance, B12, TSH, immunofixation and HIV all normal; NCS shows reduced sural amplitudes only.
case.q: What label fits and what should the follow-up focus on?
case.a: Chronic idiopathic sensory polyneuropathy; symptom control, foot care and periodic review for new features suggesting a treatable cause.

read.where: Companion to Peripheral Neuropathy: chapters (see text)

det.patho: By definition no cause is found. Proposed contributors include metabolic syndrome, prediabetes, obesity, hypertriglyceridaemia and ageing of distal axons. Some cases later prove to be genetic (for example RFC1) or paraproteinaemic, which is why the label should be revisited.
det.clinical: The typical patient is over 50 with slowly ascending distal sensory symptoms and minimal disability. Pain is present in many. Progression is gradual and severe weakness or rapid change should prompt reconsideration. Falls may occur in elderly patients with additional vestibular or visual problems.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires a typical length-dependent pattern and a thorough negative screen: glucose tolerance, B12 status, thyroid, renal and hepatic function, paraprotein studies, HIV and hepatitis serology where relevant, alcohol and drug history, and family history. Non-length-dependent, asymmetric or motor-predominant features suggest an alternative diagnosis. Small fibre testing helps when nerve conduction is normal.
det.treatment: Treat neuropathic pain with gabapentinoids, duloxetine or tricyclics, adjusted for age and comorbidity. Address modifiable metabolic factors such as weight, lipids and glucose. Teach daily foot inspection and fall prevention. Review periodically for evolution.
det.prognosis: Usually mild and slowly progressive; few patients become severely disabled.
pearls: A 2-hour glucose tolerance test catches cases a fasting glucose misses.
Rapid progression, asymmetry or weakness means the idiopathic label is probably wrong.
Re-test for paraprotein and consider RFC1 if the picture changes.
det.thd: เป็นเส้นประสาทเสื่อมแบบรับความรู้สึกที่ปลายเท้าในผู้สูงอายุ ค่อยๆ ลามขึ้นช้าๆ และหาสาเหตุไม่พบหลังตรวจเบาหวาน B12 ไทรอยด์ paraprotein และอื่นๆ ครบแล้ว อาการมักชา แสบร้อน แต่ไม่อ่อนแรง รักษาตามอาการด้วยยาลดปวดประสาท ดูแลเท้าและป้องกันการล้ม ควรทบทวนใหม่ถ้าอาการเปลี่ยน

name: Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy
formal: Immune-mediated neuropathy with progressive or relapsing proximal and distal weakness and sensory loss for 8 weeks or more; demyelination on nerve conduction; responds to IVIG, steroids or plasma exchange.
simple: A long-term immune attack on nerves causing weakness and numbness that responds to immune treatments.
more: Diagnose with nerve conduction showing demyelination (conduction block, prolonged distal latencies) and raised CSF protein; nerve MRI or ultrasound shows enlargement. Maintenance IVIG or subcutaneous immunoglobulin is common; rituximab in refractory cases. Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy with progressive or relapsing symmetric weakness and sensory loss over more than 8 weeks; responds to steroids, IVIG or plasma exchange. Supportive criteria include raised CSF protein, nerve conduction showing demyelination and, if unclear, nerve ultrasound or biopsy. Maintenance IVIG or subcutaneous immunoglobulin is often needed; steroid dependence and relapses are common.

feat: Symmetric proximal AND distal weakness — proximal involvement separates it from length-dependent neuropathy

Relapsing or steadily progressive course
Responds to IVIG, steroids or plasma exchange
inv: NCS: demyelinating features (slowing, conduction block, prolonged F-waves) in multiple nerves
CSF raised protein; MRI roots/plexus enlargement
Screen for paraprotein (POEMS, anti-MAG), diabetes, HIV; nodo-paranodal antibodies if poor response

case.story: Five months of slowly worsening difficulty rising from chairs and buttoning shirts, with numb feet; fell twice in the dark.
case.exam: Hip flexors and finger extensors 4/5, absent reflexes everywhere, reduced vibration and positive Romberg.
case.tests: NCS: conduction velocity 50% of normal with temporal dispersion; CSF protein 1.0 g/L.
case.q: Why does weakness of hip flexors argue against diabetic neuropathy?
case.a: Length-dependent axonal neuropathies affect distal muscles first; proximal weakness implies root/demyelinating involvement such as CIDP.

qx.stem: A 63-year-old man from Ratchaburi with type 2 diabetes for 15 years has three years of numbness and burning in the feet up to the mid-shin, with normal strength. Ankle jerks are absent. Nerve conduction shows reduced sural amplitudes and mildly reduced motor velocities in the peroneal nerve only, with no conduction block. CSF protein is 0.72 g/L. Another hospital diagnosed CIDP and offered long-term IVIG.
qx.q: Which statement best applies the 2021 EAN/PNS CIDP guideline to this patient?
opts: He has typical CIDP because CSF protein is raised
He has distal CIDP and should start IVIG maintenance
He does not meet CIDP criteria; motor demyelinating features in at least two nerves are required and raised CSF protein is only supportive
Nerve ultrasound alone is enough to confirm CIDP here
An IVIG trial is the best way to confirm the diagnosis
qx.why: The 2021 EAN/PNS guideline requires a compatible clinical picture plus motor conduction abnormalities meeting demyelinating criteria in at least two nerves; CSF protein, imaging and treatment response are supportive only. A length-dependent, purely sensory diabetic neuropathy with slight slowing in one nerve and mildly raised CSF protein (common in diabetes) is a frequent cause of CIDP over-diagnosis. Subjective improvement after IVIG is unreliable for confirming the diagnosis.

src.where: Case 42 Painless, Symmetric, Ascending Weakness and Sensory Loss

qx.stem: A 58-year-old retired bus conductor from Lampang has had 7 months of progressive leg and arm weakness with numbness and absent reflexes throughout. Nerve conduction studies show distal latencies prolonged to 150% of the upper limit, conduction velocities of 28 m/s in the median and peroneal nerves, and a drop of 60% in CMAP amplitude between wrist and elbow of the ulnar nerve with a duration increase of 40% across the segment.
qx.q: Which electrodiagnostic finding best supports an acquired rather than a hereditary demyelinating neuropathy?
opts: Uniform slowing of conduction velocities in every nerve tested
Prolonged distal latencies in the median nerve alone
Non-uniform slowing with conduction block and temporal dispersion in motor nerves
Absent sensory responses in the lower limbs only
Reduced CMAP amplitudes with normal velocities
qx.why: Acquired demyelination (CIDP) is patchy, so velocities differ between nerves and between segments, and motor studies show conduction block or abnormal temporal dispersion. Hereditary neuropathies such as CMT1 produce uniform, length-dependent slowing without block. Axonal neuropathies lower amplitudes with near-normal velocities, and isolated median latency delay indicates entrapment.

qx.stem: A 36-year-old woman from Pathum Thani, two months post-partum, has progressive leg-predominant weakness, numbness and back pain with absent reflexes. CSF protein is 400 mg/dL with 6 cells and MRI shows diffuse nerve root enhancement. Nerve conduction studies show absent H-reflexes and mildly prolonged F-latencies but no focal slowing or conduction block. She improves with prednisolone and periodic IVIG.
qx.q: What best explains the lack of demyelination on routine studies?
opts: CIDP can be excluded, since demyelination on nerve conduction is mandatory
The illness must be axonal Guillain-Barré syndrome
Predominantly proximal root involvement, which routine conduction studies cannot sample, so root MRI or somatosensory evoked potentials can help
Postpartum polyradiculopathy is always diabetic
A steroid response excludes an inflammatory cause
qx.why: Electrodiagnostic criteria rely on motor conduction and can miss CIDP when the disease is mild, secondarily axonal, sensory-predominant or confined to proximal segments such as the nerve roots. Absent H-reflexes, prolonged F-waves, markedly raised CSF protein and root enhancement on MRI are supportive, and somatosensory evoked potentials may reveal proximal conduction delay. A treatment response to steroids or IVIG supports rather than excludes an immune cause.

src.where: Case series - Case 1: A young female with quadriparesis

qx.stem: A 70-year-old woman from Phrae with multifocal CIDP did not respond to prednisone, then improved on IVIG 2 g/kg then 1 g/kg at three-week intervals. She now notices diplopia and weakness returning about 2.5 weeks after each infusion.
qx.q: What would you do next?
opts: Stop all immunotherapy
Add monthly plasma exchange alone and halve the IVIG dose
Switch to weekly subcutaneous immunoglobulin to give steadier immunoglobulin levels
Change to prednisone alone at low dose
Lower the IVIG dose to 0.2 g/kg every 3 weeks
qx.why: Wearing-off before the next IVIG dose suggests treatment-related fluctuation rather than failure. Subcutaneous or facilitated subcutaneous immunoglobulin prevents relapse in CIDP and provides more stable IgG levels; shortening the interval or raising the dose are alternatives. Corticosteroids, IVIG, SCIG, efgartigimod and plasma exchange are effective therapies, and most patients, roughly 80% to 90%, respond to at least one.

aN: polyradiculoneuropathy cidp | cidp | polyradiculoneuropathy | chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy | chronic gbs

det.patho: An immune-mediated demyelinating disorder of nerves and roots involving both cellular and humoral mechanisms; inflammation at the roots and plexuses explains proximal weakness and the high CSF protein. A subgroup has IgG4 antibodies against nodal or paranodal proteins (neurofascin-155, contactin-1, Caspr1, neurofascin-186), now classified separately as autoimmune nodopathies because they behave differently. Prevalence rises with age and men are affected more often.
det.clinical: Typical CIDP produces symmetric proximal and distal weakness with sensory loss and generalised hypo- or areflexia, progressing over more than 8 weeks with a progressive or relapsing course. Variants include distal (DADS), multifocal (Lewis–Sumner), focal, motor and sensory forms. Tremor, sensory ataxia and cranial nerve involvement can occur. Around one in six starts acutely, mimicking GBS. Pain, prominent autonomic failure or weight loss suggests POEMS, amyloidosis or another mimic.
det.diagnosis: The 2021 EAN/PNS guideline relies on clinical criteria plus electrodiagnostic evidence of demyelination (prolonged distal latency, slowed conduction velocity, conduction block, temporal dispersion, prolonged or absent F waves) affecting two or more nerves. Supportive features are raised CSF protein, nerve root or plexus enlargement on MRI or ultrasound, objective response to treatment and nerve biopsy. Screen for paraprotein (IgM with anti-MAG, POEMS with VEGF), diabetes, HIV, hepatitis and hereditary neuropathy. Over-diagnosis based on mild slowing is a frequent pitfall.
det.treatment: First-line options are IVIG (2 g/kg loading, then maintenance about 1 g/kg every 3 weeks titrated to response), corticosteroids (daily prednisolone or pulsed dexamethasone/methylprednisolone) and plasma exchange. Subcutaneous immunoglobulin and efgartigimod are maintenance options. Pure motor CIDP may worsen with steroids, so IVIG is preferred. Refractory cases may need rituximab (especially nodopathies) or other immunosuppressants. Use objective measures (grip strength, INCAT, I-RODS) to guide dose tapering.
det.prognosis: Most patients respond to treatment and many reach remission, but a substantial fraction need long-term therapy and some accumulate axonal damage.
pearls: Proximal plus distal weakness with global areflexia = think CIDP, not length-dependent neuropathy.
Poor IVIG response with tremor or sensory ataxia: test nodal/paranodal antibodies.
IgM paraprotein with distal sensory ataxia: check anti-MAG.
det.thd: CIDP คือเส้นประสาทและรากประสาทอักเสบแบบทำลาย myelin เรื้อรังจากภูมิคุ้มกัน อาการค่อย ๆ เป็นนานเกิน 8 สัปดาห์ อ่อนแรงทั้งต้นแขนต้นขาและปลายมือปลายเท้า ชา และรีเฟล็กซ์หายทั่วไป วินิจฉัยตามเกณฑ์ EAN/PNS 2021 ด้วยการตรวจ NCS ที่พบลักษณะ demyelination ร่วมกับโปรตีนในน้ำไขสันหลังสูงหรือรากประสาทโตใน MRI และต้องหา paraprotein หรือโรคอื่นที่เลียนแบบ รักษาด้วย IVIG สเตียรอยด์ หรือ plasma exchange และกลุ่มที่มีแอนติบอดี nodal/paranodal ตอบสนองดีต่อ rituximab

name: Chronic inflammatory neuropathies
formal: Immune-mediated neuropathies lasting beyond 8 weeks including CIDP, MMN, anti-MAG and nodopathies, with demyelinating or axonal changes.
simple: Long-lasting nerve problems caused by the immune system attacking nerves.
th: กลุ่มโรคเส้นประสาทอักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกันที่เป็นนานเกิน 8 สัปดาห์ เช่น CIDP, MMN, anti-MAG neuropathy และ nodopathy
tempoNote: Progressive or relapsing course lasting more than 8 weeks
feat: Umbrella group: typical CIDP, CIDP variants (distal, multifocal, focal, motor, sensory), MMN, anti-MAG neuropathy, autoimmune nodopathies
Proximal and distal weakness with areflexia in typical CIDP; asymmetric arm weakness without sensory loss in MMN
Sensory ataxia and tremor in anti-MAG and nodopathies
Course over more than 8 weeks, progressive or relapsing
Most are treatable, so diagnosis and correct subtype matter
inv: NCS: demyelinating features (slowing, prolonged latencies, conduction block, temporal dispersion)
CSF protein, serum and urine immunofixation, anti-MAG, anti-GM1, nodal/paranodal antibodies (NF155, CNTN1, Caspr1, NF186/140)
Nerve root/plexus MRI or nerve ultrasound showing enlargement
Screen for diabetes, HIV, hepatitis, POEMS (VEGF) as indicated

case.story: Over five months he has had trouble standing from a squat and buttoning shirts, with tingling in hands and feet.
case.exam: Symmetric proximal and distal weakness (MRC 4/5), global areflexia, reduced vibration to the knees, mild sensory ataxia.
case.tests: NCS: slowing to 60% of normal with conduction blocks in several nerves; CSF protein 1.1 g/L; immunofixation negative; nodal antibodies negative.
case.q: Which chronic inflammatory neuropathy is most likely and what is first-line treatment?
case.a: Typical CIDP; IVIG, corticosteroids or plasma exchange are all first-line options.

read.where: Chapter 46 Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP), pp. 721–742

det.patho: These disorders result from immune attack on myelin, Schwann cells or the node of Ranvier. In CIDP, macrophage-mediated demyelination with T-cell involvement is typical, while autoimmune nodopathies are driven mostly by IgG4 antibodies that disrupt paranodal junctions without inflammation. MMN involves IgM anti-GM1 antibodies and complement at motor nerve nodes, and anti-MAG neuropathy reflects IgM paraprotein binding to myelin-associated glycoprotein.
det.clinical: Typical CIDP produces symmetric proximal and distal weakness with sensory loss and areflexia over more than two months. Variants include distal CIDP (formerly DADS), multifocal and focal CIDP, and pure motor or sensory forms. MMN causes asymmetric, mostly arm, motor weakness with preserved sensation. Nodopathies cause subacute severe weakness, tremor, ataxia and poor IVIG response. Anti-MAG neuropathy presents in older men with distal sensory ataxia and tremor.
det.diagnosis: The 2021 EAN/PNS criteria define CIDP by clinical features plus electrodiagnostic demyelination, with supportive CSF, imaging, biopsy and treatment response. Test for paraproteins, MAG and nodal antibodies because these change management and are now classed separately from CIDP. Over-diagnosis of CIDP is common, especially from borderline conduction findings in diabetic neuropathy; be strict with criteria.
det.treatment: Typical CIDP responds to IVIG, corticosteroids or plasma exchange; subcutaneous immunoglobulin and FcRn blockers such as efgartigimod are maintenance options. MMN responds to IVIG but may worsen with steroids. Nodopathies and anti-MAG neuropathy respond best to rituximab. Treatment response should be measured objectively (grip strength, disability scales) and doses periodically tapered to find the lowest effective dose.
det.prognosis: Most patients with CIDP improve with treatment and many achieve remission; residual deficits depend on axonal loss.
pearls: Steroids help CIDP but can worsen MMN.
Poor IVIG response, tremor and very high CSF protein: test for nodal/paranodal antibodies.
Distal sensory-predominant demyelination with IgM paraprotein: check anti-MAG.
det.thd: Chronic inflammatory neuropathies คือกลุ่มโรคเส้นประสาทอักเสบเรื้อรังจากภูมิคุ้มกันที่เป็นนานกว่า 8 สัปดาห์ ได้แก่ CIDP และชนิดย่อย, MMN, anti-MAG neuropathy และ autoimmune nodopathy อาการคืออ่อนแรงทั้งต้นและปลาย รีเฟล็กซ์หาย ชา หรืออ่อนแรงไม่สมมาตรใน MMN NCS พบลักษณะ demyelination ควรตรวจ paraprotein และ antibody ต่อ node เพราะเปลี่ยนการรักษา CIDP รักษาด้วย IVIG, steroid หรือ plasma exchange ส่วน nodopathy และ anti-MAG ตอบสนองดีต่อ rituximab

name: Chronic liver disease
formal: Hepatic disease with neuromuscular consequences including hepatic encephalopathy, myopathy and sarcopenia, axonal polyneuropathy, and movement disorders such as asterixis.
simple: Long-term liver damage that can affect the brain, nerves, and muscles.
more: Management centres on treating liver disease, using lactulose or rifaximin for encephalopathy, and nutrition; transplantation may reverse neurological features.
th: โรคตับเรื้อรังที่ส่งผลต่อระบบประสาท เช่น hepatic encephalopathy, กล้ามเนื้อลีบ, เส้นประสาทอักเสบ และ asterixis

feat: Not a primary neurological disease: neurological complications of hepatic failure
Hepatic encephalopathy ranging from minimal (subtle attention deficits) to coma, with asterixis
Sarcopenia and muscle cramps; axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy
Acquired hepatocerebral degeneration and hepatic myelopathy in long-standing shunting
Associated causes bring their own neurology: alcohol, Wilson disease, hepatitis C, haemochromatosis

case.who: 55-year-old man with hepatitis B cirrhosis from Chonburi
case.story: Family notes day-night reversal and confusion over 3 days after constipation and a minor GI bleed.
case.exam: Drowsy but rousable, asterixis, no focal signs, ascites.
case.tests: Ammonia raised, sodium 128, glucose normal; CT brain unremarkable.
case.q: What precipitated the encephalopathy and how is it treated?
case.a: GI bleeding and constipation increased gut ammonia load; treat precipitants plus lactulose with rifaximin for prevention.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Hepatic Encephalopathy

det.patho: Failure of hepatic detoxification and portosystemic shunting expose the brain to ammonia, manganese, inflammatory mediators and false neurotransmitters, causing astrocyte swelling and altered neurotransmission. Malnutrition and inflammation drive muscle wasting; metabolic and toxic factors cause polyneuropathy.
det.clinical: Hepatic encephalopathy is graded from minimal (detectable only on testing) to coma (West Haven grades). Precipitants include infection, bleeding, constipation, electrolyte disturbance, sedatives and dehydration. Chronic complications include hepatocerebral degeneration, hepatic myelopathy, neuropathy and sarcopenia. Coexisting alcohol-related syndromes (Wernicke, cerebellar degeneration) are common.
det.diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy is a diagnosis of exclusion in a patient with liver disease: exclude hypoglycaemia, sepsis, intracranial haemorrhage, drugs and Wernicke. Ammonia levels support but do not grade severity. Imaging is required with focal signs or head injury.
det.treatment: Address precipitants, give lactulose titrated to two to three soft stools daily, and add rifaximin for recurrence. Avoid benzodiazepines and correct sodium slowly. Provide nutrition with adequate protein and late-evening snacks, and thiamine in alcohol use. Liver transplantation can reverse many neurological complications.
det.prognosis: Overt encephalopathy marks advanced disease and predicts reduced survival without transplantation.
pearls: Always look for a precipitant of hepatic encephalopathy.
Give thiamine before glucose in alcohol-related liver disease.
Protein restriction is outdated; malnutrition worsens outcome.
det.thd: โรคตับเรื้อรังไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาทโดยตรง แต่ทำให้เกิดภาวะแทรกซ้อนทางประสาทหลายอย่าง ที่สำคัญคือ hepatic encephalopathy ซึ่งผู้ป่วยสับสน ง่วงซึม และมี asterixis มักมีตัวกระตุ้นเช่นเลือดออกในทางเดินอาหาร ติดเชื้อ หรือท้องผูก รักษาด้วยการแก้ตัวกระตุ้น lactulose และ rifaximin นอกจากนี้อาจมีเส้นประสาทอักเสบ กล้ามเนื้อลีบ และ parkinsonism จากแมงกานีสสะสม

formal: B-cell malignancy that may cause neurological complications such as meningeal infiltration, paraneoplastic syndromes, and opportunistic infections.

Chapter 7: Neurological complications of lymphoid malignancies

det.patho: CLL is a clonal expansion of mature CD5+ B cells. Immune dysfunction (hypogammaglobulinaemia, T-cell defects) and therapies such as purine analogues, anti-CD20 antibodies and BTK inhibitors predispose to opportunistic CNS infection. Direct CNS infiltration is uncommon clinically, though often found at autopsy; Richter transformation carries higher CNS risk.
det.clinical: Neurological symptoms in CLL most often come from infection or treatment rather than leukaemic infiltration. Shingles and post-herpetic neuralgia are common; PML, cryptococcal meningitis and listeria must be considered. Leptomeningeal disease presents with headache, cranial nerve palsies or radicular pain. Ibrutinib increases bleeding risk, including subdural haematoma.
det.diagnosis: Image with contrast MRI and analyse CSF for cells, flow cytometry, cytology and pathogens; a few CLL cells in CSF may be incidental, so interpret with clinical findings. Biopsy may be needed for transformation.
det.treatment: Treat infection specifically; reduce immunosuppression for PML. CNS CLL or Richter transformation needs haematology-directed systemic or intrathecal therapy and sometimes radiotherapy. Immunoglobulin replacement and antiviral prophylaxis lower infection risk.
det.prognosis: CLL itself is often indolent; CNS infection or transformation markedly worsen prognosis.
pearls: Neurological problems in CLL are more often infection or drug-related than infiltration.
Non-enhancing white matter lesion in CLL: test CSF for JC virus.
Watch for subdural bleeding on BTK inhibitors.

case.exam: Mild neck stiffness, right sixth nerve palsy, slow responses, no papilloedema.
case.tests: CSF 180 cells (80% lymphocytes), protein 2.1 g/L, glucose 1.5 mmol/L (serum 6.0); MRI basal meningeal enhancement with early hydrocephalus; HIV negative, CrAg negative, Xpert Ultra negative.

Part I: Introduction: An Insight into Central Nervous System (CNS) Infections

det.patho: Chronic meningitis is a syndrome in which organisms or immune or tumour cells persist in the subarachnoid space and provoke ongoing inflammation. Thick basal exudate entraps cranial nerves, blocks CSF flow and inflames penetrating arteries. Worldwide and in Thailand, tuberculosis and Cryptococcus dominate; other fungi (Coccidioides, Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Sporothrix, Talaromyces and some moulds) are rarer but important when exposure fits. Non-infectious causes form a sizeable minority, and a fraction remain unexplained.
det.clinical: Patients present with weeks of headache, malaise and behaviour change, sometimes with only mild meningism. Cranial nerve palsies, hearing loss, visual loss, seizures, hydrocephalus and stroke are complications. Fungal causes cluster by host and place: high-pressure Cryptococcus in HIV; Coccidioides in people who have been in desert regions; Talaromyces with skin lesions in advanced HIV in the north of Thailand. Systemic clues help narrow the cause, and relapsing courses point to Behcet, Mollaret meningitis, drugs or chemical causes.
det.diagnosis: Generous CSF volumes, repeated taps and a plan that includes fungal culture raise the yield. Fungal work-up now extends beyond CrAg: Histoplasma antigen (urine, serum, CSF), Coccidioides and Blastomyces antigen or antibody, and CSF beta-D-glucan and galactomannan, whose negative values make non-cryptococcal, non-mucoral, non-blastomyces infection unlikely. Imaging looks for basal enhancement, hydrocephalus and infarcts, and biopsy of enhancing meninges is considered when the syndrome persists undiagnosed.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: anti-TB drugs with dexamethasone, amphotericin-based induction for cryptococcus with aggressive pressure control (see Cryptococcus neoformans (pathogen)), high-dose fluconazole for coccidioidal disease (see Coccidioides species (pathogen)), liposomal amphotericin B then itraconazole for histoplasma, blastomyces and sporothrix, penicillin for neurosyphilis, immunotherapy for sarcoidosis, and appropriate therapy for malignancy. Empirical anti-TB treatment is reasonable in endemic settings when the CSF profile fits. Avoid steroid-only treatment before infection and lymphoma are excluded. Shunt or drain hydrocephalus as needed.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause and stage; delayed TB treatment, hydrocephalus and infarction predict death or disability, and fungal causes need long courses with relapse risk.
pearls: Four weeks of abnormal CSF defines it; in Thailand think TB and Cryptococcus first, then ask about travel for Coccidioides and Histoplasma.
Repeat large-volume taps raise diagnostic yield, and CSF fungal markers can rescue a negative serum screen.

Steroids before diagnosis can hide lymphoma and worsen fungal infection; organism pages include Cryptococcus neoformans (pathogen), Coccidioides species (pathogen) and Histoplasma capsulatum (pathogen).

name: Chronic ocular ischaemic syndromes
formal: Visual loss from chronic hypoperfusion due to carotid stenosis or occlusion, with venous stasis retinopathy, neovascular glaucoma and ocular pain.
simple: Eye damage from poor blood flow, usually from a narrowed neck artery.

feat: Older patient with vascular risk factors; usually one eye (about 80%); males outnumber females about 2 to 1

Chapter 22 Neuro-Ophthalmology — Chronic Ocular Ischaemic Syndromes

det.patho: Ocular ischaemic syndrome results from sustained hypoperfusion of the eye, usually from severe atherosclerotic stenosis or occlusion of the ipsilateral internal or common carotid artery, with reduced ophthalmic artery pressure. The retina and anterior segment both suffer: the retina releases angiogenic factors that drive new vessel growth on the iris and disc, while the ciliary body underperfuses, producing inflammation and low aqueous production. Collateral flow through the external carotid may be inadequate.
det.clinical: Vision is lost slowly, often with persistent after-images and a long recovery after bright light. A dull ache around the eye or brow is common and may be eased by lying down. Examination shows rubeosis iridis, mid-dilated pupil, venous dilatation without tortuosity, mid-peripheral haemorrhages and retinal arterial pulsation. It signals diffuse atherosclerotic disease: five-year mortality is about 40%, mostly from cardiac disease.
det.diagnosis: Recognition requires suspicion, since the findings may be subtle or mistaken for diabetic retinopathy or central retinal vein occlusion. Confirm with carotid imaging and fluorescein angiography, which shows delayed filling of the choroid and prolonged transit. Intraocular pressure can be misleadingly low. In an older patient, also rule out giant cell arteritis and the other causes of anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy.
det.treatment: Ocular treatment treats the consequences: topical steroid and mydriatic for inflammation, management of neovascular glaucoma, panretinal photocoagulation or intravitreal anti-VEGF for proliferative disease, and anti-VEGF or steroid for macular oedema. Carotid endarterectomy or stenting reduces stroke risk and can stabilise vision when done before ischaemia is advanced, but may raise pressure transiently and cannot be done with total occlusion. Intensive antiplatelet, statin, blood pressure and glucose control, and smoking cessation, are essential, with cardiology review.
det.prognosis: Visual outcome is often poor, though better presenting acuity predicts better outcome. Systemic prognosis is dominated by coronary and cerebrovascular disease.
pearls: Pain, rubeosis and low intraocular pressure with dilated veins and blot haemorrhages should make you listen to the carotid.
Slow recovery of vision after bright light is a clue to chronic retinal ischaemia.
OIS is a stroke and heart attack warning: refer for vascular work-up, not only for retinal laser.

15 Vestibular symptoms, balance, and their disorders: How will we classify them?

det.patho: After a unilateral peripheral vestibular injury, central compensation normally restores balance over weeks. Compensation can fail because of ongoing fluctuating disease, poor movement, sedative drugs, visual or proprioceptive impairment, age or anxiety. Bilateral loss removes the vestibulo-ocular reflex altogether, so the eyes cannot stabilise images during head movement.
det.clinical: Patients describe constant unsteadiness rather than attacks of spinning, with oscillopsia when walking if loss is bilateral. Darkness and soft ground make things worse because vision and proprioception must substitute. Falls, reduced activity and psychological distress are common. Look for the cause: previous neuritis, Ménière disease, ototoxic drugs, CANVAS, autoimmune inner-ear disease or meningitis.
det.diagnosis: Bedside head impulse, dynamic visual acuity and Romberg tests are informative. Video head impulse and caloric tests quantify loss; audiometry looks for cochlear involvement. Central causes must be excluded, especially when the head impulse is normal. PPPD may coexist and changes management.
det.treatment: Customised vestibular rehabilitation with gaze stabilisation, balance and habituation exercises is the cornerstone. Withdraw vestibular suppressants and sedatives that block compensation. Treat associated anxiety with CBT or SSRIs, particularly with PPPD features. Fall prevention and walking aids help bilateral loss; vestibular implants remain experimental.
det.prognosis: Unilateral loss usually improves with rehabilitation; bilateral loss tends to leave permanent oscillopsia and fall risk.
pearls: Long-term betahistine or vestibular suppressants hinder compensation.
Oscillopsia on walking with a positive bilateral head impulse means bilateral vestibulopathy.
Ask about gentamicin exposure in every bilateral loss.

name: Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO)
formal: Mitochondrial disorder with progressive ptosis and bilateral ophthalmoparesis with minimal diplopia, from mtDNA deletions or POLG mutations; part of Kearns-Sayre spectrum.

more: Muscle biopsy shows ragged-red fibres and COX-negative fibres with large-scale deletions; check ECG for conduction block and screen for endocrinopathy. Mostly sporadic; no cure, so use ptosis crutches or surgery, and monitor cardiac status. Slowly progressive bilateral ptosis and ophthalmoparesis, mostly mitochondrial DNA deletions or POLG, sometimes with myopathy; part of Kearns-Sayre syndrome. Muscle biopsy shows ragged red fibres and COX-negative fibres, and long-range PCR detects single large deletions in muscle DNA; CK is normal or mildly raised. Treatment is supportive, with ptosis surgery or crutches and cardiac monitoring for conduction block. Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia with ptosis and slowly worsening eye movement paralysis, usually mitochondrial DNA deletion or POLG-related disease; part of Kearns-Sayre syndrome.

case.who: 48-year-old woman, office clerk in Nakhon Pathom
case.story: Eyelids have drooped for 10 years; colleagues say she looks sleepy. She never sees double.
case.exam: Bilateral ptosis covering upper pupil, eyes move only a few millimetres in every direction, weak orbicularis oculi, normal pupils; no worsening with sustained upgaze.
case.tests: AChR antibody negative; RNS normal; deltoid biopsy shows ragged-red and COX-negative fibres; long-range PCR finds a single mtDNA deletion.
case.q: Why does she not complain of diplopia despite marked ophthalmoplegia?
case.a: The paresis is symmetric and very slowly progressive, so the eyes stay roughly aligned and the brain adapts; this contrasts with fluctuating, asymmetric ocular myasthenia.

read.where: 8 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System

det.patho: CPEO results from defective mitochondrial respiration in extraocular muscle, which has very high energy demand and many mitochondria. Sporadic cases usually carry a single large mtDNA deletion arising early in development; familial cases (dominant or recessive) usually come from nuclear genes that maintain mtDNA, such as POLG, TWNK or RRM2B, which lead to multiple deletions.
det.clinical: Ptosis comes first, followed over years by symmetric limitation of gaze; Bell's phenomenon may be lost. Patients rarely notice diplopia but may have trouble reading in downgaze. In 'PEO-plus' there is also limb myopathy, dysphagia, sensory ataxic neuropathy, parkinsonism, hearing loss or premature ovarian failure, especially with POLG. Examiners look for absence of fatigability and preserved pupils.
det.diagnosis: Myasthenia must be excluded first with antibodies, repetitive stimulation or single-fibre EMG and, if needed, an ice-pack test. Muscle biopsy showing ragged-red and COX-negative fibres plus mtDNA analysis of muscle confirms the diagnosis; blood is often uninformative for single deletions. Check ECG because conduction block can occur even without full Kearns–Sayre features.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying drug. Ptosis can be helped by lid crutches or conservative frontalis-sling surgery, avoiding overcorrection because corneal exposure is a risk with weak eye closure. Prisms help rare diplopia. Monitor swallowing, heart conduction and, in POLG cases, avoid valproate. Exercise training is safe and helpful.
det.prognosis: Usually a slowly progressive disorder with normal lifespan in isolated CPEO; outlook depends on extra-ocular involvement, especially cardiac.
pearls: Severe ophthalmoplegia without diplopia points to a myopathic, symmetric cause rather than MG.
Single deletion: sporadic, low recurrence risk; multiple deletions: think nuclear gene and family risk.
Lift ptosis cautiously: weak orbicularis plus lost Bell's phenomenon invites exposure keratitis.

simple: A nerve disease that keeps coming back with weakness and numbness.
th: โรคเส้นประสาทชนิด axonal ที่มีอาการอ่อนแรงและชากำเริบเป็นพัก ๆ เป็นรูปแบบหนึ่งของ polyneuropathy เรื้อรัง เช่น จาก vasculitis หรือการอักเสบ
tempoNote: Repeated attacks over months to years with incomplete recovery between them
feat: Descriptive label rather than one disease: episodes of weakness and sensory loss with axonal NCS
May be asymmetric and painful (vasculitis) or symmetric (inflammatory, toxic, porphyric)
Incomplete recovery leaves step-wise accumulating deficit
Consider acute intermittent porphyria, recurrent toxin exposure, vasculitis, nodopathy
inv: Serial NCS/EMG to confirm axonal pattern and pattern of spread
ESR, CRP, ANCA, cryoglobulins, hepatitis B/C, HIV, porphobilinogen during attacks, heavy metals
Nodal/paranodal antibodies (NF155, CNTN1, NF186) and nerve biopsy if vasculitis suspected

case.story: Third episode in two years of burning feet and left foot drop over weeks; each time partial recovery.
case.exam: Left peroneal and right ulnar weakness, patchy sensory loss, purpuric rash on shins.
case.tests: Axonal multifocal NCS; cryoglobulins and hepatitis C positive; sural biopsy shows vasculitis.
case.q: What underlies her relapsing axonal neuropathy?
case.a: Hepatitis C-related cryoglobulinaemic vasculitic neuropathy.

det.patho: Relapsing axonal injury can result from repeated ischaemic nerve infarction (vasculitis), immune attack on axolemma or nodes (nodopathy, axonal CIDP variants), metabolic crises (porphyria) or recurring toxin exposure. The term was used historically when no specific cause was identified.
det.clinical: Each relapse produces new deficits over days to weeks with partial recovery. Pattern matters: multifocal and painful suggests vasculitis; symmetric with proximal weakness suggests immune nodopathy; with abdominal pain and hyponatraemia suggests porphyria. Overlap with relapsing GBS is described.
det.diagnosis: Characterise the pattern with electrodiagnosis and search for systemic disease. Nerve (plus muscle) biopsy is the standard for non-systemic vasculitic neuropathy. Test nodal antibodies because nodopathies can appear axonal early. Urine porphobilinogen must be measured during an attack.
det.treatment: Treat the identified cause: corticosteroids with cyclophosphamide or rituximab for vasculitis; IVIG or rituximab for immune nodopathies; haem arginate and avoidance of triggers in porphyria. Supportive care includes pain management and rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause and cumulative axonal loss; recovery is slower than in demyelinating disease.
pearls: Relapsing axonal neuropathy is a pattern, not a final diagnosis.
Painful multifocal relapses: think vasculitis and biopsy.
Test porphobilinogen during an attack, not weeks later.
det.thd: Chronic relapsing axonal neuropathy เป็นคำบรรยายลักษณะโรคเส้นประสาทชนิด axonal ที่กำเริบเป็นพัก ๆ และฟื้นไม่หมด ไม่ใช่โรคเดียว สาเหตุที่ต้องหา ได้แก่ vasculitis, nodopathy จากภูมิคุ้มกัน, porphyria และสารพิษ ตรวจ NCS ซ้ำ เลือดหาสาเหตุ แอนติบอดี และตัดชิ้นเนื้อเส้นประสาทเมื่อสงสัย vasculitis รักษาตามสาเหตุ

ddx.pt: Painful asymmetric stepwise mononeuropathies with systemic vasculitis markers
Demyelinating NCS features, raised CSF protein, IVIG response
Abdominal pain, psychiatric change, raised urinary porphobilinogen during attacks

aN: relapsing axonal polyneuropathy | axonal cidp historical | recurrent axonal neuropathy | relapsing axonal gbs

name: Chronic relapsing inflammatory optic neuropathy (CRION)
formal: Steroid-dependent recurrent optic neuritis with pain and visual loss, often MOG or GFAP antibody related, lacking systemic disease.
simple: Repeated painful eye nerve inflammation that needs long steroid treatment.
th: เส้นประสาทตาอักเสบที่กำเริบซ้ำ ปวดตาและตามัว ตอบสนองต่อสเตียรอยด์แต่กำเริบเมื่อลดยา ปัจจุบันพบว่าส่วนมากเป็น MOGAD
tempoNote: Recurrent attacks of subacute visual loss, typically flaring as steroids are tapered
feat: Painful optic neuritis attacks that recur, uni- or bilateral
Marked steroid responsiveness with relapse on withdrawal (steroid dependence)
No brain or spinal lesions and no systemic disease at diagnosis
Severe acuity loss with disc swelling common in MOG-positive cases
inv: MOG-IgG and AQP4-IgG (cell-based assays); many CRION cases are MOG-positive
MRI orbits (long-segment, perineural enhancement) and brain/spine
Exclude sarcoidosis, syphilis, lupus (ACE, chest CT, serology)

case.story: Fourth episode in 18 months of painful vision loss; each time improves on prednisolone but worsens when the dose drops below 10 mg.
case.exam: Acuity 6/36 right, RAPD right, swollen right disc.
case.tests: MRI: long-segment right optic nerve enhancement with perineural sheath involvement; MOG-IgG positive, AQP4 negative.
case.q: What is the modern diagnosis and long-term plan?
case.a: MOG antibody-associated disease presenting as CRION; needs maintenance immunotherapy (e.g. IVIG, azathioprine, mycophenolate) rather than repeated steroid courses.

read.where: Chapter 22 Neuro-Ophthalmology — Optic Neuritis: Chronic Relapsing Inflammatory Optic Neuropathy

det.patho: CRION was described in 2003 as a recurrent inflammatory optic neuropathy outside MS and NMO. Since antibody testing became available, a large proportion of cases turn out to be MOG antibody-associated disease, with a minority AQP4-positive or seronegative. It is thus increasingly a phenotype rather than a separate disease.
det.clinical: Attacks are painful with significant vision loss, often with optic disc swelling. Steroid withdrawal triggers relapses. Cumulative attacks cause optic atrophy and permanent visual loss if untreated.
det.diagnosis: Test MOG-IgG and AQP4-IgG with cell-based assays, ideally before or early in treatment. MRI typically shows anterior, long-segment optic nerve involvement with perineural enhancement. Exclude infection, sarcoid and other systemic inflammatory disease.
det.treatment: Acute attacks: high-dose IV methylprednisolone, with plasma exchange for poor response. Long term: slow steroid taper and a steroid-sparing agent — IVIG maintenance, azathioprine, mycophenolate or rituximab (less consistent in MOGAD); AQP4-positive patients follow NMOSD regimens.
det.prognosis: Good recovery from each attack is typical in MOG-positive cases, but repeated attacks can cause permanent damage.
pearls: Steroid-dependent recurrent optic neuritis: test MOG-IgG.
CRION is now largely viewed within MOGAD.
Avoid abrupt steroid withdrawal; plan a steroid-sparing agent.
det.thd: CRION คือเส้นประสาทตาอักเสบที่กำเริบซ้ำ ปวดตาและตามัวมาก ตอบสนองดีต่อสเตียรอยด์แต่กลับเป็นใหม่เมื่อลดยา ปัจจุบันพบว่าผู้ป่วยส่วนใหญ่มี MOG antibody จึงถือเป็นส่วนหนึ่งของ MOGAD ควรตรวจ MOG-IgG และ AQP4-IgG และ MRI เส้นประสาทตา รักษาระยะเฉียบพลันด้วย methylprednisolone และระยะยาวด้วยยากดภูมิที่ช่วยลดสเตียรอยด์ เช่น IVIG หรือ azathioprine

qx.stem: A 33-year-old female accountant in Chon Buri has had four episodes of painful visual loss in alternating eyes over two years. Each responded well to high-dose steroids, but every relapse occurred within weeks of tapering prednisolone below about 10 mg daily. Brain and spinal MRI show no lesions outside the optic nerves, and CSF bands are absent.
qx.q: Which serum antibody is most likely to be positive?
opts: MOG-IgG
AQP4-IgG
CRMP5-IgG
ANCA (PR3 or MPO)
Anti-recoverin antibody
qx.why: Relapsing, steroid-dependent optic neuritis with relapses on taper is the CRION phenotype, and a large proportion of such patients are MOG-IgG positive on cell-based assay, which reclassifies them as MOGAD. AQP4-IgG must also be tested because it changes treatment, but it is less frequent in this pattern. CRMP5 causes painless paraneoplastic optic neuropathy, recoverin a retinopathy, and ANCA vasculitis rarely presents as isolated recurrent optic neuritis.

ddx.pt: Most CRION is MOG-positive; same disease reframed
AQP4-positive, severe attacks, longitudinal myelitis, area postrema
Systemic granulomatous features, chest imaging and biopsy evidence

name: Chronic vestibular disorders
formal: Persistent inner ear or central vestibular disorders, such as Meniere disease, vestibular migraine and persistent postural-perceptual dizziness, with chronic vertigo and imbalance.
simple: Long-lasting balance system conditions causing dizziness.
th: กลุ่มโรคที่ทำให้เวียนหรือเสียการทรงตัวเรื้อรังจากหูชั้นในหรือระบบทรงตัวส่วนกลาง เช่น Ménière, vestibular migraine และ PPPD
tempoNote: Persistent or recurrent symptoms lasting more than three months
feat: Umbrella term grouping recurrent or persistent vestibular problems
Episodic: Ménière disease, vestibular migraine, recurrent BPPV
Persistent: PPPD, bilateral vestibulopathy, uncompensated unilateral loss, cerebellar degeneration
Imbalance worse in the dark (bilateral loss) or in busy visual environments (PPPD)
Anxiety and fall fear frequently amplify disability
inv: Bedside: head impulse, nystagmus, positional tests, Romberg, gait
Audiometry, video head impulse test, caloric testing, VEMPs
MRI with internal auditory meatus views for asymmetric hearing loss or central signs

case.story: Six months after a bout of acute vertigo she feels rocking and unsteady every day, worse in supermarkets and when scrolling her phone.
case.exam: Normal head impulse, no nystagmus, normal gait with cautious steps.
case.tests: vHIT and calorics show good compensation; MRI normal.
case.q: What diagnosis explains her ongoing symptoms?
case.a: Persistent postural-perceptual dizziness triggered by previous vestibular neuritis; treat with vestibular rehabilitation, CBT and an SSRI.

read.where: Chapter 23 Neuro-Otology: Dizziness, Balance and Hearing — Chronic Vestibular Disorders

det.patho: Causes include peripheral disorders (endolymphatic hydrops in Ménière, bilateral hair cell loss from aminoglycosides or ageing), central disorders (vestibular migraine, cerebellar degeneration) and functional maladaptation (PPPD) where postural control remains in a high-alert, visually dependent mode after an initial insult. Several can coexist in one patient.
det.clinical: Episodic disorders produce discrete attacks: Ménière with hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness for hours; vestibular migraine with variable duration and migraine features. Persistent disorders give daily non-spinning dizziness or imbalance. Oscillopsia suggests bilateral loss; visual and motion provocation suggests PPPD.
det.diagnosis: Use Bárány Society criteria for Ménière disease, vestibular migraine, PPPD and bilateral vestibulopathy. Vestibular function tests quantify deficits. MRI is required for asymmetric hearing loss, central signs or atypical features.
det.treatment: Treatment is cause-specific: vestibular rehabilitation for almost all, SSRIs and CBT for PPPD, migraine prevention for vestibular migraine, salt reduction, betahistine (limited evidence), intratympanic steroid or gentamicin for refractory Ménière. Avoid long-term vestibular suppressants, which slow compensation.
det.prognosis: Most improve with rehabilitation and targeted treatment, though symptoms often fluctuate.
pearls: Chronic dizziness is rarely one disease — look for overlapping causes.
Stop chronic vestibular sedatives; they block compensation.
Visual-motion provocation suggests PPPD.
det.thd: Chronic vestibular disorders เป็นคำรวมของโรคที่ทำให้เวียนศีรษะหรือเสียการทรงตัวเรื้อรังเกิน 3 เดือน เช่น Ménière, vestibular migraine, PPPD และการเสียการทำงานของหูชั้นในสองข้าง ต้องตรวจร่างกายระบบทรงตัว ตรวจการได้ยินและทดสอบ vestibular รักษาตามสาเหตุ โดยการฝึกกายภาพการทรงตัวมีประโยชน์เกือบทุกโรค และควรเลี่ยงยากดการทรงตัวระยะยาว

name: Circadian rhythm disorders
formal: Disorders of timing of the sleep-wake cycle such as delayed phase, advanced phase, non-24-hour and shift work disorder.
simple: Problems where the body clock is out of step with normal day and night, causing trouble sleeping.
th: กลุ่มความผิดปกติของเวลานอนตื่นจากนาฬิกาชีวภาพไม่ตรงกับเวลาที่ต้องการ เช่น นอนช้า นอนเร็ว non-24 และ shift work disorder
tempoNote: Persistent or recurrent misalignment over months; jet lag and shift work forms are situational
feat: Sleep is normal in quality but occurs at the wrong time relative to social demands
Types: delayed phase, advanced phase, irregular sleep–wake rhythm, non-24-hour, shift work, jet lag
Irregular rhythm common in dementia and institutionalised patients; non-24 in totally blind people
Presents as insomnia, daytime sleepiness or both
Treated with timed light, timed melatonin and schedule changes
inv: Sleep diary and actigraphy for 1–2 weeks
Chronotype questionnaires
Dim-light melatonin onset where available
Polysomnography when a coexisting sleep disorder is suspected

case.who: 45-year-old nurse in a Bangkok hospital working rotating night shifts
case.story: Cannot sleep more than 3–4 hours after night shifts and feels very sleepy driving home; symptoms ease on holidays.
case.exam: Normal; BMI 23; no snoring reported.
case.tests: Actigraphy shows fragmented daytime sleep after nights and normal sleep on off days.
case.q: Which circadian disorder fits and what helps?
case.a: Shift work disorder; bright light during the shift, dark glasses on the way home, a dark quiet bedroom and planned naps, with melatonin before daytime sleep.

read.where: Chapter 29 Disorders of Sleep — Circadian Rhythm Disorders
Chapter 51 Neurologic Aspects of Sleep Medicine
Chapter 134: Circadian Disorders, Insomnia, and Parasomnias

det.patho: The suprachiasmatic nucleus generates a roughly 24-hour rhythm that is entrained mainly by light via the retinohypothalamic tract and secondarily by melatonin, activity and meals. Disorders arise from intrinsic changes in clock timing or entrainment (delayed, advanced, non-24) or from external schedules conflicting with the clock (shift work, jet lag). Neurodegeneration and blindness weaken entrainment.
det.clinical: Patients complain of insomnia at the intended bedtime, excessive sleepiness at intended waking times, or both. When allowed to sleep on their own schedule, sleep is usually normal. Irregular sleep–wake rhythm, with fragmented sleep spread across 24 hours, is common in dementia, autism and after brain injury. Non-24 disorder produces cycles of good and bad sleep that drift over weeks.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on history and objective documentation with sleep diaries and actigraphy. Melatonin phase markers support diagnosis in specialist centres. Rule out insomnia due to psychiatric illness, sleep apnoea and medication effects. Polysomnography is not needed for diagnosis.
det.treatment: Treatment uses appropriately timed light exposure and melatonin to shift the clock, with structured sleep schedules and attention to light hygiene. Tasimelteon is approved for non-24 in blind people in some countries. Irregular rhythm in dementia improves with daytime light, activity and reduced night-time disruption. Hypnotics are generally avoided.
det.prognosis: Many improve with chronotherapy, though relapse is common if schedules lapse.
pearls: Ask when the patient sleeps on holidays — normal sleep at their own time points to a circadian problem.
Timing matters: light and melatonin shift the clock in opposite directions depending on when given.
Totally blind patients with cyclic insomnia may have non-24.
det.thd: Circadian rhythm disorders เป็นกลุ่มความผิดปกติที่นาฬิกาชีวภาพไม่ตรงกับเวลาที่ต้องการนอนหรือตื่น เช่น นอนดึกตื่นสาย นอนเร็วตื่นเช้ามืด non-24 ในคนตาบอด และ shift work disorder ผู้ป่วยนอนไม่หลับหรือง่วงกลางวัน แต่ถ้านอนตามเวลาของตัวเองก็หลับดี การวินิจฉัยใช้บันทึกการนอนและ actigraphy การรักษาคือการรับแสงและใช้ melatonin ในเวลาที่เหมาะสมร่วมกับจัดตารางการนอน

name: Clival chordoma
formal: Chordoma at the clivus with headache, diplopia from sixth nerve palsy and brainstem compression; locally recurrent.
simple: A slow-growing tumour at the base of the skull that can cause double vision.
th: เนื้องอก chordoma ที่ clivus ฐานกะโหลก ทำให้ปวดศีรษะ เห็นภาพซ้อนจากเส้นประสาทสมองที่ 6 และกดก้านสมอง
tempoNote: Slow growth over years with insidious symptoms
feat: Midline clival mass in adults, typically 30s to 60s
Headache and horizontal diplopia from abducens nerve compression
Lower cranial nerve palsies, nasal obstruction or brainstem compression in larger tumours
Locally aggressive with frequent recurrence
Rarely metastasises but can seed along the surgical tract
inv: MRI: midline T2-bright lobulated mass destroying the clivus, heterogeneous enhancement
CT: lytic bone destruction with sequestered fragments
Pathology: physaliferous cells, brachyury-positive

case.story: One year of occipital headache and recent double vision on distant gaze.
case.exam: Bilateral abducens weakness worse on the right; otherwise normal.
case.tests: MRI shows a midline lobulated T2-hyperintense mass eroding the clivus and indenting the pons; biopsy is brachyury-positive.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the preferred treatment approach?
case.a: Clival chordoma; maximal safe resection followed by high-dose particle radiotherapy.

det.patho: Chordomas arise from remnants of the embryonic notochord at the skull base, sacrum or mobile spine. Brachyury (TBXT), a notochordal transcription factor, is expressed in virtually all cases and duplication of TBXT confers familial risk. Growth is slow but invasive through bone.
det.clinical: Headache and diplopia from abducens involvement are the commonest early symptoms. Extension can involve other cranial nerves, the pituitary region, nasopharynx or brainstem. Recurrence after treatment is common and often defines the long-term course.
det.diagnosis: MRI and CT define the midline destructive lesion. Biopsy or resection specimen shows physaliferous cells; brachyury immunostaining confirms the diagnosis and separates it from chondrosarcoma. Poorly differentiated subtypes (SMARCB1 loss) occur in children and young adults.
det.treatment: Treatment combines maximal safe resection, often endoscopic endonasal, with high-dose proton or carbon ion radiotherapy. Recurrence is managed with re-resection or re-irradiation; systemic therapies are investigational. Multidisciplinary skull base teams achieve the best outcomes.
det.prognosis: Long-term local control is achievable but recurrence is common; extent of resection is the strongest predictor.
pearls: Bilateral sixth nerve palsy plus headache: image the clivus.
Brachyury is the diagnostic immunostain.
Particle therapy is preferred because the required dose is high near the brainstem.
det.thd: Chordoma เกิดจากเศษ notochord ที่ค้างอยู่ บริเวณ clivus กลางฐานกะโหลก โตช้าแต่ทำลายกระดูก ผู้ป่วยปวดศีรษะและเห็นภาพซ้อนจากเส้นประสาทสมองเส้นที่ 6 MRI พบก้อนสว่างใน T2 กลางแนว ชิ้นเนื้อ brachyury บวก รักษาด้วยผ่าตัดให้มากที่สุดอย่างปลอดภัยร่วมกับรังสีอนุภาค มักกลับเป็นซ้ำ

name: Clivus/skull base syndromes
formal: Lesions at the clivus and skull base, such as chordoma, chondrosarcoma and metastases, causing multiple cranial neuropathies and headache.
simple: Problems at the base of the skull that press on several nerves.
ab: Multiple cranial neuropathies from skull base lesion
th: กลุ่มอาการจากรอยโรคที่ clivus และฐานกะโหลก ทำให้เส้นประสาทสมองหลายเส้นเสียร่วมกับปวดศีรษะ
tempoNote: Metastases and infection progress over weeks; benign tumours over months to years
feat: Combination of cranial nerve palsies on one or both sides, often VI first
Deep headache, sometimes occipital or retro-orbital
Lower cranial nerves (IX–XII) in jugular foramen or occipital condyle syndromes
Causes: nasopharyngeal carcinoma, metastases, chordoma, chondrosarcoma, meningioma, skull base osteomyelitis
Pattern of nerves involved localises the lesion along the skull base
inv: MRI with contrast and fat-suppressed sequences of the skull base
CT skull base for bone erosion
Nasoendoscopy, EBV DNA and biopsy when nasopharyngeal carcinoma is possible

case.who: 55-year-old man from Udon Thani with diabetes
case.story: Two months of severe right ear pain and headache, then hoarseness and choking on fluids.
case.exam: Right abducens palsy, reduced palatal elevation, weak right sternomastoid and tongue deviating to the right.
case.tests: MRI shows enhancing soft tissue around the right clivus and jugular foramen; nasoendoscopy and biopsy confirm nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
case.q: How do you approach multiple unilateral cranial neuropathies?
case.a: Image the whole skull base and look for malignancy (especially NPC in Thailand) or skull base osteomyelitis in diabetics.

read.where: Skull base syndromes: anatomy, step approach, foramen syndromes

det.patho: The skull base hosts cranial nerve exit foramina in close proximity, so a single infiltrative or compressive lesion damages several nerves. Neoplasms (nasopharyngeal carcinoma, metastases, chordoma, chondrosarcoma, meningioma, lymphoma), infection (malignant otitis externa, fungal) and inflammatory disease are the main causes.
det.clinical: Named patterns help localisation: cavernous sinus (III, IV, V1–2, VI), petrous apex (V, VI), jugular foramen (IX–XI), occipital condyle (XII with occipital pain) and a combined clival picture affecting VI and lower nerves. Pain is often prominent and precedes deficits. Progressive accumulation of palsies over weeks is a malignancy red flag.
det.diagnosis: Contrast MRI of the skull base with fat suppression is the main test, combined with CT to judge bone erosion. In Thai patients nasopharyngeal examination with biopsy is important. Inflammatory markers and cultures matter in diabetics with ear pain. Biopsy is usually required for definitive diagnosis.
det.treatment: Treatment depends on cause: chemoradiation for nasopharyngeal carcinoma, surgery plus particle therapy for chordoma and chondrosarcoma, prolonged antibiotics or antifungals for skull base osteomyelitis. Supportive care includes swallowing assessment and eye protection.
det.prognosis: Varies with cause; malignant infiltration carries a poor outlook if untreated.
pearls: Multiple cranial neuropathies on one side are a skull base lesion until imaging says otherwise.
In Thailand always think of nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
A diabetic with ear pain and lower cranial palsies may have skull base osteomyelitis.
det.thd: ฐานกะโหลกเป็นที่ผ่านของเส้นประสาทสมองหลายเส้น รอยโรคเดียวจึงทำให้หลายเส้นเสียพร้อมกัน สาเหตุสำคัญคือ nasopharyngeal carcinoma มะเร็งแพร่กระจาย chordoma และการติดเชื้อฐานกะโหลกในผู้ป่วยเบาหวาน ต้องตรวจ MRI ฐานกะโหลกร่วมกับ CT และส่องตรวจโพรงหลังจมูก รักษาตามสาเหตุ

ddx.pt: Commonest malignant cause in Southeast Asia; check nasopharynx and neck
Petrous apex infection with VI palsy, retro-orbital pain and ear discharge
Painful ophthalmoplegia confined to the cavernous sinus; steroid responsive

aN: skull base syndromes | clivus syndrome | petroclival syndrome | multiple cranial neuropathies from skull base lesion

name: Clonazepam akathisia
formal: Akathisia-like restlessness related to clonazepam, usually from withdrawal or paradoxical reaction, with inner restlessness and inability to sit still.
simple: A feeling of inner restlessness related to taking or stopping clonazepam.
th: อาการกระสับกระส่ายนั่งไม่ติดที่สัมพันธ์กับ clonazepam ส่วนใหญ่เกิดตอนหยุดหรือลดยา หรือเป็นปฏิกิริยาตรงข้าม (paradoxical)
tempoNote: Appears days after abrupt reduction or stopping, or within hours of a dose in a paradoxical reaction
feat: Inner restlessness and a felt need to move, pacing or shifting weight while standing
Usually linked to a fall in clonazepam dose rather than to the drug itself
Accompanied by withdrawal features: anxiety, insomnia, tremor, sweating, perceptual sensitivity
Paradoxical agitation can occur in children, older adults or those with brain injury
Clonazepam is more often a treatment for akathisia than a cause
inv: Careful medication timeline: dose changes, missed doses, other drugs started (antipsychotics, SSRIs)
Barnes Akathisia Rating Scale to document severity
Exclude restless legs (iron studies), hyperthyroidism and stimulant use when the picture is unclear

case.story: Took clonazepam 2 mg nightly for two years for panic disorder; stopped it herself a week ago. Now cannot sit through meetings, paces at night and feels 'electric inside'.
case.exam: Restless shifting while seated, fine postural tremor, sweaty palms, no rigidity, no chorea; reflexes brisk symmetrical.
case.tests: TSH normal, ferritin 85 ng/mL; urine drug screen negative for stimulants.
case.q: What explains her restlessness and how should it be managed?
case.a: Benzodiazepine withdrawal with akathisia-like restlessness; restart clonazepam at a tolerated dose and taper slowly over weeks to months.

det.patho: Benzodiazepines enhance GABA-A inhibition; long use downregulates receptor function, so abrupt withdrawal produces a hyperexcitable state with anxiety, motor restlessness and sometimes seizures. Paradoxical reactions reflect disinhibition, perhaps from reduced frontal control. True dopamine-blockade akathisia is not a recognised effect of clonazepam, and the drug is used to treat akathisia.
det.clinical: Patients describe inner tension and difficulty staying still, which can be hard to separate from anxiety rebound. The timing after a dose drop is the strongest clue. Other withdrawal symptoms such as insomnia, tremor, depersonalisation, hyperacusis and, in heavy users, seizures may coexist. Paradoxical reactions present as agitation, talkativeness or aggression soon after a dose.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, based on the medication history and observed restlessness. Check for co-prescribed dopamine antagonists or antidepressants, which are more common causes of akathisia. Consider restless legs, thyrotoxicosis, stimulant misuse and primary anxiety. Rating scales help track response.
det.treatment: For withdrawal, reinstate a benzodiazepine and taper gradually, often by 5–10% of the dose every few weeks, sometimes switching to a longer-acting agent. For paradoxical reactions, stop the drug; flumazenil is rarely needed. If an antipsychotic is also involved, treat that akathisia separately with dose reduction, propranolol or mirtazapine.
det.prognosis: Symptoms usually resolve with slow tapering; protracted withdrawal symptoms can persist for months in a minority.
pearls: Restlessness after stopping a benzodiazepine is withdrawal until proven otherwise.
Clonazepam is a therapy for akathisia; look for another culprit drug.
Never stop long-term benzodiazepines abruptly because of seizure risk.
det.thd: อาการกระสับกระส่ายนั่งไม่ติดที่สัมพันธ์กับ clonazepam มักไม่ใช่ akathisia จากการปิดกั้น dopamine แต่เกิดจากการถอนยา benzodiazepine หรือปฏิกิริยาตรงข้าม ผู้ป่วยรู้สึกกระวนกระวายภายใน ร่วมกับนอนไม่หลับ ใจสั่น มือสั่น การวินิจฉัยใช้ประวัติการปรับยา และแยกโรค restless legs ไทรอยด์เป็นพิษ และยาอื่น การรักษาคือกลับมาให้ยาแล้วค่อย ๆ ลดขนาดอย่างช้า ๆ

formal: Brief, repeated rhythmic jerking seizures, focal or generalised, with loss of awareness when generalised.
simple: Seizures in which the limbs jerk rhythmically.

feat: Sustained rhythmic jerking at a regular rate, unlike the single jerks of myoclonus
Focal form may march from hand to arm to face (Jacksonian)
Awareness preserved in focal clonic seizures, lost when generalised
Postictal weakness of the affected limb (Todd paresis)
Common seizure type in neonates
inv: EEG: rhythmic spike or polyspike discharges time-locked to the jerks
MRI to find a structural lesion in focal clonic seizures

case.who: 67-year-old man from Ayutthaya, 6 months after a left MCA infarct
case.story: His right hand began jerking rhythmically, spreading to the forearm and right face over 30 seconds; he could talk throughout. Afterwards his right hand was weak for an hour.
case.exam: Old mild right hemiparesis; no new deficit after recovery.
case.tests: EEG shows left fronto-central sharp waves; MRI old cortical infarct only.
case.q: How would you classify this seizure, and what is the cause?
case.a: Focal aware clonic (motor) seizure with Jacksonian march, from post-stroke epilepsy; start an antiseizure drug.

det.patho: Clonic jerks arise when a cortical epileptic discharge repeatedly excites corticospinal neurons, interrupted by brief inhibitory pauses. Focal clonic seizures usually come from the primary motor cortex, and spread along the motor strip produces the Jacksonian march. In neonates, immature networks make focal and multifocal clonic seizures the commonest motor seizure type. Generalised clonic seizures without a tonic phase are uncommon outside infancy.
det.clinical: Focal clonic seizures cause rhythmic jerking of one face, arm or leg, usually with retained awareness, and may spread or become bilateral tonic-clonic. Postictal Todd paresis can last minutes to hours and may mimic stroke. In newborns clonic seizures are often caused by stroke, hypoxic-ischaemic injury, infection or metabolic disturbance. Persistent focal clonic activity raises concern for epilepsia partialis continua.
det.diagnosis: Video description or recording plus EEG showing rhythmic discharges in step with the jerks establishes the seizure type. Focal clonic seizures need MRI to look for a lesion; in neonates continuous EEG is preferred because many seizures are subtle. Check glucose and electrolytes, especially sodium, calcium and magnesium. Distinguish from tremor, myoclonus, rigors and functional events.
det.treatment: Treat the cause and use antiseizure drugs as for focal or generalised epilepsy; most focal options (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, carbamazepine, lacosamide) work. Prolonged seizures follow the status epilepticus pathway with benzodiazepines first. Neonatal seizures are treated with phenobarbital first line in most guidelines, with levetiracetam as an alternative. Address metabolic triggers before escalating drugs.
det.prognosis: Depends on the underlying cause; focal clonic seizures from a stable lesion usually respond to medication.
pearls: Clonic = rhythmic repeated jerks; myoclonic = brief single or irregular jerks.
Todd paresis after a clonic seizure can mimic stroke.
Neonatal clonic seizures need a search for stroke, HIE, infection and electrolyte problems.
det.thd: Clonic seizure คืออาการชักที่แขนขาหรือใบหน้ากระตุกเป็นจังหวะต่อเนื่อง ถ้าเป็นเฉพาะที่ผู้ป่วยมักรู้สึกตัวและอาจลามจากมือไปแขนและหน้า หลังชักอาจอ่อนแรงชั่วคราว (Todd paresis) ตรวจด้วย EEG และ MRI หาสาเหตุ และตรวจเกลือแร่ในเลือด รักษาด้วยยากันชักและแก้สาเหตุ ในทารกแรกเกิดมักใช้ phenobarbital

name: Clonidine akathisia
formal: Akathisia-like restlessness related to clonidine, often on withdrawal, with sympathetic overactivity.
simple: Restlessness and inability to stay still related to clonidine.
th: อาการกระสับกระส่ายคล้าย akathisia ที่สัมพันธ์กับ clonidine โดยเฉพาะเมื่อหยุดยากะทันหัน ร่วมกับระบบซิมพาเทติกทำงานมาก
tempoNote: Usually within 1–3 days of stopping or missing clonidine
feat: Inner restlessness, pacing and inability to sit still
Most often a feature of abrupt clonidine withdrawal with rebound hypertension, tachycardia, sweating and anxiety
True akathisia caused by clonidine itself is poorly documented; clonidine is more often used to treat akathisia or tics
Higher risk with high doses, combination with beta-blockers or after long-term use
inv: Medication history and timing of last dose; blood pressure and heart rate
Exclude other causes of restlessness: dopamine blockers, hyperthyroidism, drug or alcohol withdrawal, RLS

case.story: Ran out of clonidine 0.3 mg twice daily two days ago; now agitated, cannot sit, has headache and palpitations.
case.exam: BP 210/120, pulse 118, sweating, constantly shifting legs and pacing, no rigidity.
case.tests: ECG sinus tachycardia; TSH normal; no antipsychotic exposure.
case.q: What explains his restlessness and how is it managed?
case.a: Clonidine withdrawal hyperadrenergic state; restart clonidine and taper slowly, avoid beta-blocker monotherapy.

det.patho: Clonidine stimulates central alpha-2 receptors, reducing noradrenergic outflow from the locus coeruleus. Sudden withdrawal causes rebound sympathetic overactivity that produces anxiety, tremor and motor restlessness resembling akathisia. Direct akathisia from clonidine is described only in scattered reports, and evidence is weak; in practice clonidine has been used as a treatment for akathisia.
det.clinical: Restlessness appears within a day or two of a missed dose and is accompanied by hypertension, tachycardia, headache and sweating. In children treated for tics or ADHD, withdrawal can produce irritability and hyperactivity. Hypertensive crisis is the main danger.
det.diagnosis: Clinical, based on timing and autonomic signs. Exclude other drug-induced akathisia, thyrotoxicosis, substance withdrawal and anxiety disorders.
det.treatment: Reinstate clonidine then taper over 1–2 weeks. Manage severe hypertension with combined alpha and beta blockade or other agents; avoid beta-blocker alone, which can worsen hypertension through unopposed alpha activity. Educate patients on not stopping abruptly.
det.prognosis: Resolves quickly once clonidine is restarted or tapered properly.
pearls: Clonidine-related restlessness is mostly a withdrawal phenomenon.
Never stop high-dose clonidine abruptly — taper.
Clonidine is more often a treatment for akathisia than a cause.
det.thd: Clonidine akathisia คืออาการกระสับกระส่ายนั่งไม่ติดที่สัมพันธ์กับยา clonidine ส่วนใหญ่เกิดเมื่อหยุดยากะทันหัน ทำให้ระบบซิมพาเทติกทำงานเกิน ความดันสูง ใจสั่น เหงื่อออก หลักฐานว่าตัวยาเองทำให้เกิด akathisia มีน้อย รักษาโดยกลับไปให้ยาแล้วค่อย ๆ ลดขนาด และควบคุมความดันโดยไม่ใช้ beta-blocker เดี่ยว ๆ

feat: Excruciating strictly unilateral orbital/temporal pain
Ipsilateral lacrimation, conjunctival injection, rhinorrhoea, ptosis/miosis
