det.patho: Cluster headache is the most frequent trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia. Pain comes from activation of the trigeminovascular system with release of neuropeptides such as CGRP and PACAP, and the same circuit triggers a cranial parasympathetic reflex (tearing, nasal discharge), while sympathetic fibres around the carotid are disturbed, producing a partial Horner syndrome. The clock-like timing of attacks and seasonal bouts point to the hypothalamus as a pacemaker, supported by functional imaging and by the effect of hypothalamic stimulation. Prevalence is about 1 per 1,000; men outnumber women (roughly three to one in recent series), onset is typically between the 20s and 40s, and most patients are current or former heavy smokers. Genetic studies have identified several susceptibility loci.
det.clinical: Pain is strictly one-sided around the eye or temple, peaks within minutes at an excruciating level and lasts 15–180 minutes untreated, recurring anywhere from every second day to eight times a day, often at fixed hours and typically an hour or two after falling asleep. Restlessness is characteristic — patients pace, rock or strike their head — the opposite of the stillness of migraine. Ipsilateral tearing, red eye, nasal blockage or discharge, lid swelling, sweating, ptosis and miosis accompany the pain, and ptosis or miosis can persist between attacks. In episodic cluster (the large majority) bouts of weeks to a few months alternate with remissions of at least three months; in chronic cluster remission is absent or shorter. Alcohol, nitroglycerin and volatile smells provoke attacks within a bout but not during remission, and the severity carries a real risk of suicidal thoughts.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical with ICHD-3 criteria: at least five severe attacks of one-sided pain around the orbit, above the orbit or at the temple, each 15–180 minutes long, with ipsilateral autonomic signs and/or restlessness. MRI brain with pituitary views is recommended at first presentation, because pituitary adenomas, parasellar meningiomas, aneurysms and arterial dissection can mimic it; atypical features such as continuous background pain, other neurological signs or no response to oxygen and triptans raise the yield. Separate it from paroxysmal hemicrania (shorter, more frequent attacks with absolute indomethacin response), SUNCT/SUNA (seconds-long stabs with cutaneous triggers), hemicrania continua (continuous pain), migraine and trigeminal neuralgia. A new painful Horner syndrome needs carotid imaging to exclude dissection. Diagnostic delay of years is still common, often after dental or sinus procedures.
det.treatment: Acute attacks respond best to 100% oxygen at 12–15 L/min through a non-rebreather mask for 15–20 minutes, subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg, or intranasal zolmitriptan; oral triptans act too slowly. At the start of a bout, a short transitional course of oral prednisolone or an ipsilateral greater occipital nerve block with steroid suppresses attacks while prevention is built up. Verapamil is the first-line preventive, increased gradually in divided doses (commonly 240–480 mg/day, sometimes higher) with an ECG before each increment because of heart block; lithium and topiramate are alternatives, and galcanezumab is approved for episodic cluster. Non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation helps some patients, and refractory chronic cluster may be referred for occipital nerve or sphenopalatine ganglion stimulation. Advise stopping smoking and avoiding alcohol during bouts, and screen for depression.
det.prognosis: The disorder may persist for decades, though bouts often become less frequent with age; some episodic cases convert to chronic and vice versa, and chronic cluster is harder to control.
pearls: Restless pacing during attacks separates cluster from migraine at a glance.
Order an ECG before each verapamil dose increase.
Oral triptans are too slow for cluster attacks — use injected or nasal routes.
Cluster-like attacks beginning after 50, or with neck pain and a new Horner, need imaging for a secondary cause.

formal: Autosomal recessive demyelinating CMT with early onset and severe disability, caused by mutations in genes such as GDAP1, MTMR2, SH3TC2, and PRX.
simple: A group of inherited nerve diseases passed on by both parents, with early-onset weakness and foot deformities.
more: Genetic testing identifies the subtype; scoliosis is common; supportive care and surgery for deformities; progression is often significant.

tempoNote: Infantile or early childhood onset with more rapid progression than dominant CMT1
feat: Early-onset distal then proximal weakness, delayed walking, frequent loss of ambulation
Marked scoliosis and foot deformities
Gene-specific extras: vocal cord palsy (GDAP1), cranial nerve involvement, deafness (SH3TC2), sensory ataxia (PRX)

Very slow conduction velocities, often below 20 m/s

case.who: 8-year-old girl from Pattani, parents first cousins
case.story: Walked at 2 years, falls frequently and now has a curving spine; an older brother uses a wheelchair.
case.exam: Distal and proximal leg weakness, pes cavus, thoracic scoliosis, areflexia, mild hand wasting.
case.tests: Median motor velocity 14 m/s; homozygous SH3TC2 variant.

case.a: Autosomal recessive CMT4C; monitor and treat scoliosis early.

det.patho: CMT4 subtypes involve Schwann cell genes controlling myelin maintenance, membrane trafficking and phosphoinositide signalling (MTMR2, SBF2, FIG4), endosomal function (SH3TC2), mitochondrial dynamics (GDAP1) and the periaxin complex (PRX). Biallelic loss leads to dysmyelination, focal myelin outfoldings or onion bulbs. More common in populations with consanguinity.
det.clinical: Begins in infancy or the toddler years, with delayed milestones and faster progression than CMT1; many lose ambulation by the second or third decade. Scoliosis, respiratory involvement and cranial neuropathies are more frequent. Some subtypes (CMT4D/NDRG1, Lom) are geographically clustered.
det.diagnosis: Very slow, uniform conduction in a child of consanguineous parents strongly suggests CMT4. Genetic panels identify the subtype; nerve biopsy patterns (e.g. myelin outfoldings in CMT4B) can guide testing when genetics is inconclusive.
det.treatment: Supportive: orthoses, physiotherapy, early scoliosis surveillance and surgery, respiratory monitoring, hearing and vocal cord assessment. No disease-modifying treatment is approved. Genetic counselling for the family.
det.prognosis: More disabling than dominant CMT; some forms shorten life through respiratory compromise.
pearls: Severe early demyelinating CMT with consanguinity: think CMT4.
Screen spine and respiratory function regularly.
Vocal cord palsy with neuropathy suggests GDAP1.

6 Neurological effects of Vitamin B12 deficiency
Chapter 125: Neurologic Complications of Nutritional Disorders
11. NEUROPATHIES ASSOCIATED WITH VITAMIN AND ESSENTIAL MINERAL DEFICIENCIES AND MALABSORPTION

det.patho: Cobalamin is a cofactor for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; deficiency disrupts DNA synthesis and myelin maintenance. Causes include pernicious anaemia (autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor), gastrectomy or bariatric surgery, ileal disease, strict vegan diet, metformin and long-term acid suppression, and nitrous oxide exposure. Demyelination with vacuolation affects dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts.
det.clinical: Symptoms start with symmetrical distal paraesthesia, then sensory ataxia, spasticity and cognitive or psychiatric changes. Neurological disease may occur with normal haemoglobin and MCV. Untreated, it progresses to paraplegia and dementia. Recreational nitrous oxide use can produce rapid myelopathy in young people.
det.diagnosis: Low B12 confirms deficiency, but values in the low-normal range need MMA and homocysteine. Look for the cause (intrinsic factor antibodies, dietary and drug history). MRI of the spine supports SCD; changes may be absent early. Folate supplementation without B12 can worsen neurology.
det.treatment: Give intramuscular hydroxocobalamin or cyanocobalamin (e.g. 1 mg) frequently at first, such as alternate days for 1–2 weeks, then maintenance every 1–3 months lifelong in pernicious anaemia; high-dose oral B12 is an option for dietary deficiency. Stop nitrous oxide. Monitor potassium and platelets in severe anaemia when therapy starts.
det.prognosis: Improvement occurs over months; recovery is best with short symptom duration and is often incomplete if treatment is delayed.
pearls: Neurological B12 deficiency can occur without anaemia.
Extensor plantars with absent ankle jerks: think B12, Friedreich, or copper.
Ask young patients with myelopathy about nitrous oxide ('whippets').

det.patho: Cobblestone malformation arises when the pial basement membrane and glia limitans break down, letting migrating neurons spill past the cortical plate into the leptomeningeal space. Most cases trace to faulty sugar-chain decoration of alpha-dystroglycan, which normally anchors radial glial end-feet to the extracellular matrix. Variants in laminin, collagen IV or adhesion-GPCR genes can disrupt the same barrier. Inheritance is mostly autosomal recessive.
det.clinical: Babies are hypotonic and developmentally delayed from the start, and many develop seizures and hydrocephalus in the first months. Eye and muscle involvement set the severity: Walker-Warburg lies at the worst end, with MEB disease and Fukuyama-type CMD somewhat gentler. Cognitive and motor gains are limited, and swallowing and breathing problems accumulate. Families often present after an affected sibling or an abnormal antenatal scan.
det.diagnosis: MRI is the key test, showing a thick, irregular cortex with an unclear grey-white junction, white-matter signal change, a kinked or hypoplastic brainstem and cerebellar cysts. Markedly raised CK and reduced glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan on muscle immunostaining support the dystroglycan pathway. Molecular testing by multigene panel or exome now establishes the specific gene. Differentiate smooth classic lissencephaly, polymicrogyria and congenital infection such as CMV.
det.treatment: No cure exists, so care is multidisciplinary: antiseizure medication, CSF diversion for progressive hydrocephalus, gastrostomy and airway care, physiotherapy and visual aids. Discuss goals of care early in the severe forms. Genetic counselling, carrier testing and prenatal or pre-implantation diagnosis are offered for later pregnancies.
det.prognosis: Walker-Warburg usually leads to death in infancy or early childhood; milder phenotypes survive longer with severe disability.
pearls: Bumpy cortex plus very high CK in a floppy infant points to a dystroglycanopathy.
Cobblestone is an over-migration disorder; classic lissencephaly is an under-migration one.
Look at the eyes and the brainstem shape on MRI when the cortex looks abnormal in a hypotonic baby.
det.thd: Cobblestone malformation คือความผิดปกติของเปลือกสมองที่เซลล์ประสาทเคลื่อนที่เลยขอบเขตออกไปนอกเยื่อฐานของสมอง ทำให้ผิวสมองเป็นปุ่มขรุขระ มักเกิดจากความผิดปกติของ alpha-dystroglycan ทารกจะตัวอ่อนปวกเปียก พัฒนาการช้า ชัก ศีรษะโตจากน้ำคั่งในสมอง และมีความผิดปกติของตา วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI สมอง ค่า CK สูงมาก และตรวจพันธุกรรม การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคองและให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุศาสตร์แก่ครอบครัว

formal: Cocaine-related stroke from vasospasm, vasculitis, thrombosis or hypertension with intracranial haemorrhage or infarction.
simple: Blood vessel damage and strokes caused by cocaine use.

tempoNote: Usually within hours of use; recurrent with continued use
feat: Stroke in a young adult within hours of cocaine use (crack smoking or nasal use)
Haemorrhage (ICH, SAH from previously unknown aneurysm or AVM) or infarction
Severe hypertension, tachycardia, chest pain, agitation

case.exam: BP 220/130, HR 128, agitated, left hemiparesis.
case.tests: CT: right frontal lobar haemorrhage; CTA: no aneurysm or AVM; urine positive for cocaine metabolites.

det.patho: Cocaine blocks reuptake of noradrenaline, dopamine and serotonin, causing abrupt hypertension and vasoconstriction, while also activating platelets and promoting thrombosis. Chronic use accelerates atherosclerosis. True vasculitis is uncommon; adulterants such as levamisole provoke immune-mediated vascular injury.
det.clinical: Haemorrhagic strokes are frequent and often lobar; underlying aneurysms or AVMs are unmasked. Ischaemic strokes may be large-vessel or small-vessel. Seizures, myocardial infarction and arrhythmia often coexist.
det.diagnosis: Ask directly about drug use; check urine toxicology early. Vascular imaging looks for structural lesions and vasoconstriction. Distinguish RCVS from vasculitis: in cocaine use, narrowing usually reverses within weeks.
det.treatment: Standard stroke care with attention to cocaine toxicity: benzodiazepines for agitation and hypertension; calcium-channel blockers or other vasodilators. Thrombolysis is not absolutely contraindicated but bleeding risk and mimics need care. Addiction services are central to secondary prevention.
det.prognosis: Recurrence risk is high with continued use; abstinence markedly lowers it.
pearls: Ask every young stroke patient about stimulant use.
Cocaine bleeds may unmask aneurysms — always do vascular imaging.
Avoid unopposed beta-blockade in acute cocaine toxicity.
det.thd: Cocaine vasculopathy คือ stroke ที่สัมพันธ์กับการใช้โคเคน เกิดจากความดันพุ่งสูง หลอดเลือดหดตัว ลิ่มเลือด และบางรายมีหลอดเลือดอักเสบจากสารปน เช่น levamisole ผู้ป่วยมักเป็นคนหนุ่มสาวที่มีเลือดออกในสมองหรือสมองขาดเลือดภายในไม่กี่ชั่วโมงหลังเสพ ต้องตรวจสารเสพติดในปัสสาวะและภาพหลอดเลือด การรักษาคือดูแลแบบ stroke ให้ benzodiazepine เลี่ยง beta-blocker และส่งต่อบำบัดยาเสพติด

name: Cockayne’s syndrome
formal: Autosomal recessive DNA repair disorder with growth failure, photosensitivity, microcephaly, deafness, retinopathy, neuropathy and leukodystrophy.
simple: An inherited condition with slow growth, sun sensitivity, hearing loss and brain and nerve problems.
more: Caused by ERCC6 (CSB) or ERCC8 (CSA) mutations; MRI shows basal ganglia calcification and white matter hypomyelination. Skin cells show impaired transcription-coupled repair; treatment is supportive, with early childhood death in severe types.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมด้อยที่การซ่อม DNA บกพร่อง ทำให้เด็กโตช้า ศีรษะเล็ก ไวต่อแสง หูหนวก จอตาเสื่อม และสารขาวสมองเสื่อม
tempoNote: Growth and development normal at birth in type I, then falter during the first two years; relentless neurological decline over years
feat: Postnatal growth failure with cachectic dwarfism, sunken eyes and a beaked nose; head circumference also falls below the fifth percentile
Psychomotor delay then regression, with ataxia, spasticity, tremor and dystonia
Photosensitive skin without the high skin cancer risk of xeroderma pigmentosum
Sensorineural hearing loss, pigmentary retinopathy and cataracts; demyelinating neuropathy in many
Types I (classic), II (severe, early onset), III (mild, later) and COFS (cerebro-oculo-facio-skeletal, prenatal); autosomal recessive ERCC6 or ERCC8
inv: MRI: hypomyelination or leukodystrophy, cerebellar and cerebral atrophy; CT: basal ganglia and cortical calcification
Nerve conduction studies: slowed demyelinating velocities; audiometry and electroretinography

case.story: She was born at term at a normal weight but stopped gaining weight in the second year. She is now very thin, has not progressed to sentences, and her skin burns after short sun exposure. Hearing was reduced at the school screening.
case.exam: Height and weight well below 3rd percentile, microcephaly, sunken eyes, ataxic broad-based gait, tremor, spasticity in the legs, absent ankle jerks.
case.tests: MRI shows hypomyelination and cerebellar atrophy; CT shows basal ganglia calcification; NCV slow; ERCC8 biallelic mutation.
case.q: Which two long-term precautions are specific to this disease?
case.a: Strict sun protection and sunglasses for photosensitivity, and avoidance of metronidazole (reports of fatal liver injury) with careful liver monitoring.

det.patho: Cockayne syndrome belongs to the transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair disorders. CSA (ERCC8) and CSB (ERCC6) proteins remove RNA polymerase stalled at DNA lesions, so unrepaired damage accumulates in highly active, non-dividing cells such as neurons and oligodendrocytes. The consequences are premature ageing, myelin loss, neuronal death and calcification, with additional mitochondrial dysfunction contributing.
det.clinical: In type I, birth growth is normal and decline begins in the first two years, producing a thin, short child with small head, deep-set eyes and a prematurely aged face. Hearing and vision deteriorate, with pigmentary retinopathy and cataracts; neurological disease adds ataxia, spasticity, tremor and demyelinating polyneuropathy, with cognitive disability. Types II and COFS are earlier and more severe, and type III is milder with later onset. Hypertension, renal and hepatic problems, dental caries and diabetes may occur.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis rests on the clinical constellation and genetic confirmation of biallelic ERCC6 or ERCC8 variants. Imaging showing hypomyelination, atrophy and basal ganglia calcification is characteristic, and nerve conduction studies show demyelination. Differentiate from other leukodystrophies, mitochondrial disease, xeroderma pigmentosum with neurological features (XP/CS), Bardet-Biedl syndrome and other causes of cachexia and retinal degeneration.
det.treatment: Treatment is symptomatic and multidisciplinary: sun protection and sunglasses, nutrition and feeding support, hearing aids and cataract surgery, spasticity and contracture management, physiotherapy and educational support. Watch for liver, renal and blood pressure complications. Avoid metronidazole because of liver failure reports, and monitor for sensory aids and dental care. Genetic counselling is essential.
det.prognosis: Type I causes severe disability with death usually before the end of the second decade; type II is earlier and type III later.
pearls: Photosensitivity without skin cancer separates Cockayne syndrome from xeroderma pigmentosum.
Normal birth growth, then failure by age two: think type I.
Avoid metronidazole; liver failure is reported.
det.thd: Cockayne syndrome เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมด้อยที่การซ่อม DNA ที่เกิดจากการถอดรหัสบกพร่อง (ERCC6 หรือ ERCC8) เด็กเกิดมาปกติ แต่ภายใน 2 ปีแรกจะโตช้า ผอมมาก ศีรษะเล็ก ตาลึก ไวต่อแสงแดดแต่ไม่เสี่ยงมะเร็งผิวหนังสูง มีหูตึง จอตาเสื่อม ต้อกระจก เดินเซ เกร็ง และเส้นประสาท demyelinating MRI พบ hypomyelination และ CT พบหินปูนที่ basal ganglia วินิจฉัยยืนยันด้วยยีน การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง ใช้ครีมกันแดด แว่นกันแดด และเลี่ยง metronidazole

det.patho: Coeliac disease is a gastrointestinal autoimmune disorder, not a primary neurological disease. In HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 carriers, gluten peptides modified by tissue transglutaminase activate T cells that damage small intestinal villi. Neurological complications are thought to arise from cross-reacting antibodies (for example against transglutaminase 6 in gluten ataxia), from malabsorption of vitamins and copper, or both. It is common in Europeans but appears much less common in Thailand, though awareness is increasing.
det.clinical: Neurological features include progressive cerebellar ataxia, sensory-predominant neuropathy, epilepsy with bilateral parieto-occipital calcifications, refractory myoclonic ataxia, headache and inflammatory myopathy. Many patients with neurological presentations have few gut symptoms. Whether some entities such as gluten ataxia without enteropathy are truly distinct remains debated. Associated deficiencies of B12, copper and vitamin E can cause myelopathy or neuropathy in their own right.
det.diagnosis: Test tTG-IgA with total IgA (or IgG-based tests in IgA deficiency) while the patient still eats gluten. Confirm with duodenal biopsy in adults; negative HLA-DQ2/DQ8 makes the disease very unlikely. Anti-TG6 antibodies support gluten ataxia but are not widely available. Look for other ataxia causes before attributing it to coeliac disease, since antibodies can be incidental.
det.treatment: A strict lifelong gluten-free diet with expert dietitian support is the main treatment; neurological stabilisation can take a year or more and established cerebellar loss may not recover. Correct any vitamin or copper deficiency. Refractory neurological disease sometimes receives immunotherapy, but evidence is limited. Monitor adherence with serology and screen for refractory coeliac disease or lymphoma when symptoms progress despite diet.
det.prognosis: Early dietary treatment often stabilises or improves ataxia and neuropathy; delayed treatment leaves permanent deficits.
pearls: Test for coeliac antibodies before the patient goes gluten-free.
Neurological coeliac disease often has no gut symptoms.
Check copper, B12 and vitamin E in any coeliac patient with myelopathy or neuropathy.

det.patho: An autoimmune process targeting antigens shared by corneal and inner ear tissues is suspected, possibly triggered by infection. Vasculitis of variable vessel size occurs in some, particularly aortitis. Inner ear damage involves inflammation of the labyrinth and cochlea.
det.clinical: Eye and audiovestibular symptoms typically occur within two years of each other. Hearing loss can become profound quickly. Vestibular failure leaves oscillopsia and imbalance. Systemic vasculitis, especially aortic involvement, determines long-term risk.
det.diagnosis: Clinical, based on typical ocular inflammation with audiovestibular dysfunction after excluding infection (syphilis, Lyme, TB, viral keratitis) and other autoimmune disease. No specific antibody test exists.
det.treatment: High-dose glucocorticoids early for inner ear disease, with methotrexate, azathioprine, TNF inhibitors or other agents for steroid sparing. Topical steroids for keratitis. Cochlear implantation for profound deafness. Monitor aorta and heart valves.
det.prognosis: Hearing outcome is often poor despite treatment; vasculitis can cause significant morbidity.
pearls: Red eye plus vertigo and deafness in a young adult: Cogan syndrome.
Exclude congenital or acquired syphilis first.
Check the aortic valve and aorta.
det.thd: Cogan syndrome เป็นโรคภูมิคุ้มกันผิดปกติที่พบน้อย มักในผู้ใหญ่ตอนต้น มีกระจกตาอักเสบตาแดงปวด ร่วมกับเวียนศีรษะบ้านหมุน เสียงในหู และหูหนวกทั้งสองข้างอย่างรวดเร็ว บางรายมีหลอดเลือดแดงใหญ่อักเสบ ต้องแยกโรคซิฟิลิสก่อน การรักษาคือ steroid ขนาดสูงโดยเร็วร่วมกับยากดภูมิ และพิจารณา cochlear implant ในรายที่หูหนวก

name: Cognitive disorders
formal: Conditions with impaired memory, attention, language, executive or visuospatial function, including mild cognitive impairment, delirium and dementias.
simple: Conditions that affect thinking, memory and reasoning.
th: กลุ่มภาวะที่ความจำ สมาธิ ภาษา การบริหารจัดการ หรือการรับรู้มิติสัมพันธ์บกพร่อง รวมถึง mild cognitive impairment, delirium และ dementia
tempoNote: Acute (delirium) or chronic progressive (dementia); mild cognitive impairment is an intermediate stage
feat: Memory, attention, language, executive or visuospatial impairment
Delirium: acute, fluctuating inattention and confusion
Mild cognitive impairment: measurable decline without loss of independence
Dementia: decline impairing daily function
Behavioural and psychological symptoms common
inv: Cognitive screening (MoCA, MMSE) and functional assessment
Bloods: B12, thyroid, glucose, electrolytes, syphilis, HIV
MRI brain; amyloid/tau biomarkers or PET when needed

case.story: Two years of gradually forgetting recent conversations; still manages her shop independently.
case.exam: MoCA 23/30 with delayed recall deficit; neurological exam otherwise normal.
case.tests: B12, thyroid normal; MRI mild hippocampal atrophy.
case.q: What is the diagnosis?
case.a: Amnestic mild cognitive impairment, possibly prodromal Alzheimer disease.

read.where: 4 - Parkinsonism: Clinical features and differential diagnosis

det.patho: Cognitive disorders arise from neurodegenerative (Alzheimer, Lewy body, frontotemporal), vascular, metabolic, infectious, toxic, inflammatory or psychiatric causes. Delirium reflects acute global brain dysfunction from systemic illness. Mixed pathologies are common in older adults.
det.clinical: Presentations range from subjective decline to severe dementia. Delirium develops over hours to days with fluctuating attention. Dementia types differ: memory-first in Alzheimer disease, behavioural or language changes in FTD, visual hallucinations and parkinsonism in DLB, stepwise decline in vascular dementia.
det.diagnosis: History from an informant, cognitive screening and functional assessment establish severity. Blood tests identify reversible contributors. MRI assesses atrophy and vascular lesions; CSF or PET biomarkers characterise neurodegenerative causes, especially when anti-amyloid therapy is considered.
det.treatment: Treat reversible causes and delirium triggers. Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine for Alzheimer and Lewy body dementia; anti-amyloid antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab) for selected early Alzheimer disease. Manage vascular risk factors, hearing loss and depression; caregiver support and planning are essential.
det.prognosis: Delirium is often reversible but associated with long-term decline; dementias are usually progressive.
pearls: Always rule out delirium before diagnosing dementia.
Check for treatable causes: B12, thyroid, depression, NPH.
Informant history is key.
det.thd: Cognitive disorders คือกลุ่มภาวะที่ความสามารถทางสมองบกพร่อง ได้แก่ delirium ที่เกิดเฉียบพลัน mild cognitive impairment และ dementia ที่ทำให้ใช้ชีวิตประจำวันลำบาก สาเหตุมีทั้งโรคเสื่อม หลอดเลือด และภาวะที่รักษาได้ ตรวจด้วยแบบทดสอบความจำ เลือด และภาพสมอง รักษาตามสาเหตุและให้ยาในรายที่เหมาะสม ร่วมกับการดูแลผู้ดูแล

name: Collagen vascular diseases
formal: Autoimmune diseases like SLE and vasculitis with neurological features such as stroke, myelitis, neuropathy and seizures.
simple: Immune diseases such as lupus that inflame blood vessels and can affect the nerves and brain.
th: กลุ่มโรคภูมิคุ้มกันทั่วร่างกาย เช่น SLE และหลอดเลือดอักเสบ ที่มีอาการทางระบบประสาท เช่น stroke, ไขสันหลังอักเสบ, ปลายประสาทอักเสบ และชัก
tempoNote: Relapsing–remitting systemic disease with acute or subacute neurological events
feat: Historical umbrella for SLE, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren syndrome, dermatomyositis and vasculitides
CNS: stroke (often antiphospholipid-related), seizures, psychosis, cognitive impairment, myelitis, aseptic meningitis
PNS: mononeuritis multiplex, sensory neuronopathy (Sjögren), trigeminal neuropathy (scleroderma), myositis
Rheumatoid arthritis: atlantoaxial subluxation with cervical myelopathy
Treatment-related complications: infections, PML, PRES, steroid myopathy
inv: ANA, anti-dsDNA, ENA panel, complement, ANCA, rheumatoid factor/anti-CCP
Antiphospholipid antibodies; MRI brain/spine; CSF
Nerve conduction and EMG; tissue biopsy where needed

case.who: 24-year-old female garment worker from Samut Sakhon
case.story: Known SLE with lupus nephritis; now a week of numbness rising to the chest and urinary retention.
case.exam: Sensory level T8, paraparesis, brisk reflexes.
case.tests: MRI: longitudinally extensive T2 lesion T4–T11; AQP4-IgG negative; anti-dsDNA high, C3 low; antiphospholipid antibodies positive.
case.q: What is the neurological complication and the treatment?
case.a: Lupus myelitis; high-dose IV methylprednisolone with cyclophosphamide or rituximab, plus consideration of anticoagulation for antiphospholipid antibodies.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Neurological Involvement in Systemic Vasculitides and Related Disorders
Chapter 4: Vascular Diseases of the Brain

det.patho: Mechanisms include autoantibody-mediated neuronal injury, immune complex vasculitis, antiphospholipid-associated thrombosis, accelerated atherosclerosis and complications of renal failure or hypertension. The term 'collagen vascular disease' is dated; 'systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases' is preferred.
det.clinical: Neurological features may occur during systemic flares or as the first presentation. SLE gives the broadest range; vasculitides cause mononeuritis multiplex and stroke; Sjögren causes ganglionopathy and NMOSD-like disease; scleroderma causes trigeminal neuropathy and myopathy.
det.diagnosis: Assess systemic activity and serology, then use imaging, CSF and neurophysiology to define the neurological syndrome. Exclude infection, drug toxicity and metabolic causes, which are common in immunosuppressed patients.
det.treatment: Inflammatory complications: glucocorticoids plus cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate or rituximab. Thrombotic complications: anticoagulation. Symptomatic treatment of seizures, pain and mood. Close rheumatology collaboration.
det.prognosis: Depends on disease and organ involvement; neurological involvement worsens overall prognosis in SLE.
pearls: Stroke in lupus: check antiphospholipid antibodies.
Rheumatoid neck: beware atlantoaxial subluxation before intubation.
Always exclude infection in immunosuppressed patients with new neurological signs.
det.thd: Collagen vascular diseases คือกลุ่มโรคภูมิคุ้มกันทั่วร่างกาย เช่น SLE, Sjögren, scleroderma, rheumatoid arthritis และหลอดเลือดอักเสบ ทำให้เกิด stroke ชัก ไขสันหลังอักเสบ ปลายประสาทอักเสบ และกล้ามเนื้ออักเสบ การตรวจคือ autoantibody, antiphospholipid, MRI และน้ำไขสันหลัง ต้องแยกการติดเชื้อจากยากดภูมิด้วย การรักษาคือ steroid และยากดภูมิ หรือยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือดตามกลไก

name: Colour vision disorders
formal: Congenital (X-linked red-green) or acquired (optic nerve, occipital lesions, drugs) impairment of colour perception; central achromatopsia arises from ventral occipital lesions.
simple: Difficulty telling colours apart, either from birth or after eye or brain damage.
th: ความผิดปกติของการรับรู้สี มีทั้งแบบแต่กำเนิด (ตาบอดสีแดง-เขียวถ่ายทอดทางโครโมโซม X) และแบบเกิดภายหลังจากโรคเส้นประสาทตา ยา หรือรอยโรคที่สมองส่วนท้ายทอยด้านล่าง
tempoNote: Congenital types are lifelong and stable; acquired types follow the underlying retinal, optic nerve or cortical disease
feat: Congenital red-green deficiency affects about 8% of men and under 1% of women, is symmetric, stable and usually first found on screening
Acquired loss is often asymmetric and described as colours looking dull, faded or darker, with other visual symptoms
Red desaturation in one eye is a sensitive bedside sign of optic neuropathy; optic nerve disease tends to hit red-green axis, macular and outer retinal disease the blue-yellow axis
Cerebral achromatopsia: loss of colour in a hemifield or the whole field from lesions of the lingual and fusiform gyri, often with prosopagnosia or an upper quadrant defect
Congenital achromatopsia (rod monochromacy) comes with poor acuity, photophobia and nystagmus; drugs such as ethambutol and hydroxychloroquine impair colour discrimination
inv: Ishihara plates (screen for red-green defects); Hardy–Rand–Rittler or Farnsworth D-15 and 100-hue to define type and severity
Acuity, pupils for RAPD, visual field, dilated fundus examination and OCT to look for optic neuropathy or maculopathy
MRI brain or orbits if acquired and unexplained; ERG and genetic testing for congenital cone dysfunction
Medication and toxin review; B12 and nutritional assessment when bilateral and progressive

case.story: He saw a flash and, over two days, noticed red traffic lights looked brownish in his left eye only. He has no pain. He has been on a tuberculosis regimen with ethambutol for 4 months.
case.exam: Acuity 20/40 left, 20/20 right; Ishihara 1/17 plates left, 17/17 right; central scotoma on perimetry; swollen discs not seen; mild RAPD on the left.
case.tests: OCT shows thinned retinal nerve fibre layer later; MRI orbits normal; renal function is normal.
case.q: What does the colour finding suggest and what should be done?
case.a: Acquired dyschromatopsia from an optic neuropathy, here likely ethambutol toxicity. Stop the drug in consultation with the TB team and monitor recovery.

read.where: Chapter 66: Visual Impairment after Cortical Injury
Chapter 36: Hereditary Diseases of the Retina

det.patho: Colour vision depends on three cone types (long, middle and short wavelength) and opponent processing along the retinogeniculate pathway to the ventral occipitotemporal cortex. Congenital red-green defects are X-linked mutations of the OPN1LW or OPN1MW genes, blue-yellow defects are autosomal, and complete achromatopsia results from CNGA3 or CNGB3 variants. Acquired loss reflects damage to cones, the optic nerve (particularly the papillomacular bundle) or the lingual and fusiform cortex.
det.clinical: Congenital dichromacy or anomalous trichromacy is lifelong, symmetric and rarely recognised except by screening, though it can affect occupations such as transport or electrical work. Acquired dyschromatopsia is typically noticed by patients as desaturation, and a difference in red colour between the two eyes points to a unilateral optic neuropathy. Cortical lesions produce hemiachromatopsia, where one half of the visual field loses colour, or complete cerebral achromatopsia that follows bilateral ventral occipitotemporal damage.
det.diagnosis: Screen with pseudo-isochromatic plates, then classify with arrangement tests (Farnsworth D-15, 100-hue) or anomaloscopy. Cross-check acuity, field, pupils and fundus to separate retinal, optic nerve and cortical causes. A reduced Ishihara score with relatively good acuity is a clue to optic neuropathy. Genetic and electrophysiological testing helps with congenital cone disorders.
det.treatment: No treatment reverses congenital colour vision deficiency; counselling, occupational advice and tinted filters or digital aids can help. Acquired loss is managed by treating the cause: stopping toxic drugs, steroids for optic neuritis when appropriate, vitamin replacement, and rehabilitation for cortical lesions. Monitor colour vision during use of ethambutol, hydroxychloroquine and similar drugs.
det.prognosis: Congenital forms are stable; acquired forms improve in proportion to recovery of the underlying lesion, and cortical achromatopsia often persists.
pearls: Red desaturation in one eye is a quick bedside test for optic neuropathy.
A normal Ishihara score does not exclude blue-yellow loss.
Hemifield colour loss localises to the contralateral lingual or fusiform region.
det.thd: ความผิดปกติของการมองเห็นสีมีทั้งแบบแต่กำเนิด (ตาบอดสีแดง-เขียวพบราว 8% ในผู้ชาย ถ่ายทอดทางโครโมโซม X) และแบบเกิดภายหลังจากโรคจอตา เส้นประสาทตา ยา เช่น ethambutol หรือรอยโรคสมองส่วนท้ายทอยด้านล่าง การตรวจใช้ Ishihara และ Farnsworth D-15 ร่วมกับตรวจ visual acuity, RAPD, visual field และ OCT ถ้ามองสีแดงจางลงข้างเดียวให้สงสัยโรคเส้นประสาทตา แบบแต่กำเนิดไม่มีวิธีรักษา ส่วนแบบเกิดภายหลังต้องรักษาที่สาเหตุ

name: Coma
formal: State of unarousable unresponsiveness with eyes closed from bilateral hemispheric or brainstem reticular activating dysfunction; many causes.
simple: A deep unconsciousness in which a person cannot be woken.
th: ภาวะไม่ตอบสนองและปลุกไม่ตื่น ตาปิด เกิดจากความผิดปกติของสมองใหญ่ทั้งสองซีกหรือ reticular activating system ในก้านสมอง มีหลายสาเหตุ
tempoNote: Usually acute; outcome depends on cause
feat: Eyes closed, no response to voice or pain beyond reflex movements
Structural causes: haemorrhage, large infarct, trauma, herniation
Metabolic/toxic: hypoglycaemia, drugs, sepsis, hepatic or uraemic encephalopathy, hypothermia
Other: seizures (non-convulsive status), meningitis, encephalitis
Clinical state, not a disease
inv: Immediate glucose; ABC; GCS and pupils
CT brain; blood gases, electrolytes, renal and liver function, toxicology
EEG for non-convulsive status; lumbar puncture when indicated

case.who: 52-year-old man found unresponsive at home in Udon Thani
case.story: Known hypertension; complained of headache in the morning.
case.exam: GCS 5, right pupil fixed and dilated, left hemiparesis, Cheyne-Stokes breathing.
case.tests: CT: large right putaminal haemorrhage with midline shift and uncal herniation.
case.q: What does the right fixed pupil indicate?
case.a: Right uncal herniation compressing CN III; requires urgent airway protection, osmotherapy and neurosurgical evaluation.

read.where: Chapter 28 Disorders of Consciousness and Intensive Care Neurology — Coma

det.patho: Consciousness depends on the ascending reticular activating system in the upper brainstem and thalamus projecting to both hemispheres. Coma results from bilateral hemispheric dysfunction, brainstem tegmental lesions or diffuse metabolic suppression.
det.clinical: Assess GCS, pupils, eye movements (oculocephalic, caloric), motor response and breathing pattern. Asymmetric signs suggest structural lesions; preserved pupils with absent eye movements suggest metabolic or drug causes.
det.diagnosis: Rapid glucose check, CT, metabolic and toxicology screens, EEG and CSF identify the cause. MRI defines brainstem lesions and hypoxic injury.
det.treatment: Secure airway, breathing and circulation; give thiamine and glucose; treat raised ICP, seizures, infection and specific poisonings; consult neurosurgery for mass lesions.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause; metabolic and drug-induced coma often reversible, anoxic coma with absent pupillary reflexes after 72 hours has poor outcome.
pearls: Check glucose in every comatose patient.
Reactive pupils with absent eye movements suggest a toxic or metabolic cause.
Consider non-convulsive status when coma is unexplained.
det.thd: Coma คือภาวะไม่รู้สึกตัว ปลุกไม่ตื่น ตาปิด เกิดจากสมองใหญ่สองซีกหรือ reticular activating system ในก้านสมองทำงานผิดปกติ สาเหตุได้แก่ เลือดออกในสมอง stroke ขนาดใหญ่ อุบัติเหตุ น้ำตาลต่ำ ยา และการติดเชื้อ ต้องดูแล ABC ตรวจน้ำตาล ทำ CT และตรวจเลือดทันที แล้วรักษาตามสาเหตุ

name: Compartment syndromes
formal: Raised pressure within a closed fascial compartment compromising perfusion, causing severe pain, tense swelling, and nerve and muscle ischaemia.
simple: Pressure builds in a muscle space, cutting off blood supply and risking nerve and muscle damage.
more: Diagnosed clinically with pressure measurement; urgent fasciotomy is required to avoid permanent damage.
th: ความดันในช่องกล้ามเนื้อที่ล้อมด้วยพังผืดสูงขึ้นจนเลือดไปเลี้ยงไม่พอ ทำให้ปวดรุนแรง บวมตึง และเส้นประสาทกับกล้ามเนื้อขาดเลือด
tempoNote: Acute over hours after injury; chronic exertional form recurs with exercise
feat: Primarily a surgical/orthopaedic emergency with neuromuscular consequences
Pain out of proportion to injury, worse with passive stretch of the compartment muscles
Tense swelling; paraesthesia then weakness of nerves passing through (e.g. deep peroneal in anterior leg)
Pulses often remain present until late
Causes: fractures, crush injury, reperfusion, tight casts, prolonged immobilisation (drug overdose), snakebite, rhabdomyolysis
inv: Clinical diagnosis; compartment pressure measurement (delta pressure under 30 mmHg supports it)
CK, renal function, potassium, urine myoglobin
Later: EMG/NCS for residual nerve injury

case.who: 22-year-old male construction worker from Nakhon Sawan
case.story: Tibial fracture fixed yesterday; now severe leg pain despite morphine and numbness between his first and second toes.
case.exam: Tense anterior leg, severe pain on passive toe flexion, weak ankle dorsiflexion, sensory loss first web space, dorsalis pedis palpable.
case.tests: Anterior compartment pressure 48 mmHg with diastolic BP 70 (delta 22); CK 18,000 U/L.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the necessary treatment?
case.a: Acute anterior compartment syndrome with deep peroneal nerve ischaemia; emergency fasciotomy.

det.patho: Rising pressure inside a non-expansile fascial compartment exceeds capillary perfusion pressure, causing muscle and nerve ischaemia. Nerves are affected within hours and muscle necrosis follows. Reperfusion after vascular repair can trigger it.
det.clinical: Pain is the earliest and most important symptom, typically severe and resistant to analgesia. Sensory symptoms in the territory of compartment nerves follow, then weakness. Late sequelae include contracture (Volkmann) and permanent nerve deficits. Chronic exertional forms cause recurrent pain and paraesthesia during exercise that resolves with rest.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical in alert patients; pressure measurement helps when examination is unreliable (sedation, coma). Do not wait for pulselessness.
det.treatment: Remove casts or dressings and perform urgent fasciotomy of all involved compartments. Manage rhabdomyolysis with fluids. Chronic exertional compartment syndrome may require activity modification or elective fasciotomy.
det.prognosis: Fasciotomy within about six hours usually preserves function; delays lead to permanent nerve and muscle damage.
pearls: Pain on passive stretch is an early warning; pulses are a late sign.
Foot drop after a leg fracture: check the anterior compartment.
Consider compartment syndrome in unconscious patients found after prolonged immobility.
det.thd: Compartment syndrome คือภาวะความดันในช่องกล้ามเนื้อที่มีพังผืดหุ้มสูงจนเลือดไปเลี้ยงไม่พอ มักเกิดหลังกระดูกหัก ถูกกดทับนาน หรือใส่เฝือกแน่น ผู้ป่วยปวดมากเกินสัดส่วน ปวดมากเมื่อยืดกล้ามเนื้อ บวมตึง และมีชาหรืออ่อนแรงจากเส้นประสาทขาดเลือด ชีพจรมักยังคลำได้ การรักษาคือผ่าเปิดพังผืดโดยด่วน

name: Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS)
formal: Chronic limb pain with allodynia, oedema, vasomotor and sudomotor change, trophic change and motor dysfunction after injury, type 1 without and type 2 with nerve lesion.
simple: Long-lasting severe limb pain with swelling and skin changes, usually after an injury.
more: Chronic limb pain disproportionate to an inciting injury, with allodynia, oedema, vasomotor and sudomotor change, and motor features such as dystonia; type I has no nerve lesion, type II follows nerve injury. Diagnosed clinically by the Budapest criteria. Early physiotherapy, neuropathic pain drugs, bisphosphonates, steroids and sympathetic blocks are used; many improve within a year but some are left with chronic disability.
th: CRPS คือกลุ่มอาการปวดเรื้อรังที่แขนหรือขา ปวดมากเกินกว่าการบาดเจ็บเดิม มี allodynia บวม สีผิวและอุณหภูมิเปลี่ยน เหงื่อผิดปกติ และผิวหนังกล้ามเนื้อเปลี่ยนแปลง หลังกระดูกหักหรือผ่าตัด Type 1 ไม่มีรอยโรคเส้นประสาท Type 2 มี ใช้เกณฑ์ Budapest วินิจฉัย การรักษาหลักคือกายภาพบำบัดและการฟื้นฟู ร่วมกับยาบรรเทาปวด
tempoNote: Starts within days to weeks of an injury, surgery or immobilisation; many improve within a year, a minority persist
feat: Pain, usually burning and disproportionate to the injury, spreading beyond a single nerve territory and worsened by touch (allodynia), movement or dependency
Vasomotor change (limb warm and red or cold and blue), sweating change, oedema, and later trophic changes in skin, hair, nails and joints
Motor features: weakness, tremor, dystonic posturing and reduced range of motion; stiff joints can be partly due to immobility
Type 1 follows fractures, sprains or surgery without a defined nerve lesion; type 2 (formerly causalgia) follows a recognisable nerve injury, most often the median, ulnar or sciatic nerve
Clinical picture is heterogeneous, and mimics (vascular, inflammatory, infectious, entrapment, disuse and functional disorders) must be excluded
inv: Clinical diagnosis using the Budapest criteria: continuing disproportionate pain, symptoms in at least three of four categories, signs in at least two, and no better explanation

Nerve conduction studies and EMG to identify a nerve lesion (type 2) or entrapment; X-ray for patchy osteopenia, and three-phase bone scan or MRI only in doubtful cases, noting that they are not diagnostic
Tests to exclude alternatives: infection, deep vein thrombosis, arterial disease, inflammatory arthritis, compartment syndrome, malignancy

case.who: 55-year-old woman, a vegetable seller from Chiang Mai
case.story: Six weeks after a cast was removed for a wrist fracture her hand is constantly burning and swollen and she cannot bear a bracelet or the sleeve touching it.
case.exam: Swollen, shiny, red and sweaty hand, 1.5 degrees warmer than the other side, allodynia, stiff fingers and tremor on movement.
case.tests: X-ray: healed fracture with patchy osteopenia; NCS normal; no infection or thrombosis.
case.q: What criteria support the diagnosis and what is the treatment?
case.a: Budapest-criteria CRPS type 1 after fracture. Treat with early graded physiotherapy and occupational therapy, desensitisation, mirror therapy, analgesics (and a short oral steroid course in an early inflammatory phase or bisphosphonate in selected cases), with attention to mood and sleep.

read.where: Chapter 28 Pain — Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS)
Chapter 31 Pain in Neurological Disorders — Complex Regional Pain Syndrome

det.patho: The mechanisms are multiple and not fully understood: inflammation with neuropeptide release, peripheral and central sensitisation, altered sympathetic-nociceptive coupling, changes in cortical representation of the limb, and sometimes small-fibre loss; autoantibodies have been implicated in some patients. Older ideas that sympathetic overactivity is the central mechanism are no longer held for all cases. The syndrome is best thought of as a phenomenology with several contributing causes, and many of the autonomic and trophic features may follow disuse.
det.clinical: CRPS begins soon after an injury, surgery or immobilisation, with pain usually in the hand or foot, and the vascular pattern can be warm and pink or cold and mottled. Sensory, vasomotor, sudomotor and trophic features evolve, and motor disturbance includes weakness, tremor and fixed dystonia. Median, ulnar and sciatic nerve injuries are classic triggers of type 2. Risk factors include fractures, particularly distal radius, casting, female sex and older age. Spread to another limb is uncommon.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical. The Budapest criteria have good sensitivity and specificity and require signs on examination as well as symptoms. Older diagnostic aids such as thermography, three-phase bone scan, radiographic osteoporosis and response to sympathetic block have not held up and should not be relied on to establish or rule out CRPS. Investigations aim to exclude other causes and to identify a nerve lesion (type 2) or entrapment that needs separate treatment.
det.treatment: Rehabilitation is the foundation: graded desensitisation, physiotherapy, occupational therapy, mirror therapy and graded motor imagery, with early mobilisation and avoidance of prolonged immobilisation. Pain control uses simple analgesics, NSAIDs, gabapentinoids or tricyclics, topical agents and, for early inflammatory CRPS, a short oral corticosteroid course; bisphosphonates and sometimes calcitonin or ketamine are used in specialist centres. Sympathetic blocks give only temporary relief in controlled trials, and neurostimulation (spinal cord or dorsal root ganglion) is considered in refractory cases. Psychological support is important; long-term opioids are discouraged. Prevention after distal radius fracture includes vitamin C 500 mg daily for 50 days, supported by some trials.
det.prognosis: Many patients improve substantially within a year with early treatment; a minority have persistent pain and disability.
pearls: Budapest criteria need observable signs, not symptoms alone.
Bone scan, thermography and sympathetic block are not reliable diagnostic tests.
Keep the limb moving: immobilisation worsens the syndrome.
det.thd: CRPS คืออาการปวดเรื้อรังที่แขนหรือขาซึ่งปวดมากกว่าการบาดเจ็บเดิม ร่วมกับ allodynia บวม สีและอุณหภูมิผิวหนังเปลี่ยน เหงื่อออกผิดปกติ และผิวหนังกล้ามเนื้อเปลี่ยนแปลง มักเกิดหลังกระดูกหัก ใส่เฝือก หรือผ่าตัด Type 1 ไม่พบรอยโรคของเส้นประสาท Type 2 พบรอยโรคเส้นประสาทชัดเจน วินิจฉัยตามเกณฑ์ Budapest ซึ่งต้องมีทั้งอาการและอาการแสดง ไม่มีการตรวจเฉพาะเจาะจง การรักษาเน้นกายภาพบำบัด กิจกรรมบำบัด mirror therapy และยาบรรเทาปวด หลีกเลี่ยงการตรึงอวัยวะนาน

qx.stem: A 46-year-old seamstress from Ayutthaya had a distal radius fracture treated in a cast. Eight weeks later her whole left hand is burning and very sensitive to light touch, swollen and shiny, warmer and redder than the right, with sweating and stiff fingers. Nerve conduction studies show no nerve injury.
qx.q: Which is the best description and first-line approach?

Cellulitis; intravenous antibiotics

qx.why: Disproportionate pain with sensory, vasomotor, sudomotor and trophic changes after a fracture, without a defined nerve lesion, meets the Budapest criteria for CRPS type I. Type II requires a definable nerve injury. Early graded movement-based rehabilitation is the core treatment, with drugs and sympathetic blocks or spinal cord stimulation for refractory cases.

Chapter 43: Hereditary Neuropathy with Pressure Palsy (HNPP)

det.patho: Pressure causes ischaemia and mechanical deformation of myelin, giving focal demyelination and conduction block; more severe or prolonged compression causes axonal degeneration. Nerves are vulnerable where they run superficially or through fibro-osseous tunnels.
det.clinical: Symptoms follow the anatomy of the affected nerve. Acute palsies are often painless and noticed on waking. Chronic entrapments produce paraesthesia, pain and later wasting. A systematic search for predisposition (diabetes, hypothyroidism, pregnancy, HNPP) is warranted when lesions are multiple or recurrent.
det.diagnosis: Clinical localisation is confirmed by nerve conduction studies showing focal slowing or block. EMG quantifies denervation, which matters for prognosis. Ultrasound or MRI can detect space-occupying lesions such as ganglia or tumours.
det.treatment: Remove the pressure, protect the limb and use splints (wrist or ankle-foot orthosis) while recovering. Entrapments may need steroid injection or surgical release when conservative care fails or axon loss is present. Physiotherapy maintains range of movement.
det.prognosis: Conduction block lesions recover in weeks to months; axonal lesions recover slowly and incompletely.
pearls: Distinguish block from axon loss: block recovers quickly.
Several pressure palsies in one patient warrants HNPP testing.
Radial palsy at the spiral groove spares triceps.
det.thd: เส้นประสาทถูกกดจากภายนอกหรือในช่องแคบทางกายวิภาค ทำให้ชาและอ่อนแรงเฉพาะเส้น เช่น median ที่ข้อมือ ulnar ที่ข้อศอก peroneal ที่เข่า radial ที่ต้นแขน ยืนยันด้วย NCS ที่พบ conduction block หรือ focal slowing รักษาโดยเลี่ยงการกด ใส่เฝือกพยุง และผ่าตัดคลายเมื่อจำเป็น ถ้าเป็นหลายเส้นให้นึกถึงเบาหวานหรือ HNPP

name: Compressive neuropathy and radiculopathy
formal: Combined focal nerve root compression and entrapment neuropathy causing pain, sensory loss and weakness; double crush phenomenon may exist.
simple: Nerves pinched at the spine or along the limb causing pain, numbness and weakness.
th: รากประสาทและเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายถูกกดทับพร้อมกัน เช่น C6/C7 radiculopathy ร่วมกับ carpal tunnel syndrome

feat: Neck pain with radicular symptoms plus nocturnal hand paraesthesia
Symptoms out of proportion to either lesion alone
Common pairs: cervical root with median at wrist, lumbar root with fibular nerve

case.who: 61-year-old female seamstress from Lampang with type 2 diabetes
case.story: Hand numbness wakes her at night, and for two years she has neck pain radiating to the thumb; carpal tunnel release last year helped only partly.
case.exam: Weak biceps and wrist extensors, reduced brachioradialis jerk, positive Phalen test, numb thumb and index finger.
case.tests: NCS: prolonged median distal latency; EMG: chronic denervation in C6 muscles; MRI: C5–C6 foraminal stenosis.
case.q: Why was the operation only partly helpful?
case.a: Coexisting C6 radiculopathy (double crush); both lesions need treatment.

det.patho: The double crush hypothesis proposes that proximal compression impairs axonal transport, making the distal nerve more vulnerable to a second compression. Evidence for a true mechanistic interaction is mixed, but co-occurrence of root and entrapment lesions is common in older adults and diabetics.
det.clinical: Patients show features of both lesions, and treatment of one gives incomplete relief. Careful mapping of sensory loss, reflexes and muscle involvement helps reveal both. Systemic neuropathy can be a third contributing factor.
det.diagnosis: Electrodiagnosis is key: distal median slowing indicates carpal tunnel, while denervation in muscles sharing a root across different nerves with normal sensory responses indicates radiculopathy. MRI corroborates the root lesion. Avoid attributing everything to one finding.
det.treatment: Treat each component on its merits: splinting or release for entrapment, conservative care or decompression for the root lesion. Optimise glycaemic control in diabetics. Set realistic expectations when both lesions coexist.
det.prognosis: Outcome depends on axon loss at each site; recovery is better when both are addressed.
pearls: Incomplete response to carpal tunnel release should prompt a search for a cervical root lesion.
Paraspinal EMG abnormalities support a root component.
The term describes coexistence; the mechanistic theory remains debated.
det.thd: ผู้ป่วยบางรายมีรากประสาทถูกกดร่วมกับเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายถูกกด เช่น รากประสาท C6 ร่วมกับ carpal tunnel เรียก double crush ทำให้อาการมากและรักษาจุดเดียวไม่หาย ต้องใช้ NCS/EMG ร่วม MRI เพื่อแยกแต่ละส่วน แล้วรักษาทั้งสองตำแหน่ง ผู้ป่วยเบาหวานพบได้บ่อย

name: Compressive optic neuropathy
formal: Optic nerve compression from tumour, aneurysm, thyroid eye disease or hyperostosis causing progressive painless visual loss with colour desaturation and disc pallor.
simple: Pressure on the eye nerve, causing slow vision loss.

tempoNote: Insidious loss over weeks to months; occasionally faster with pituitary apoplexy, aneurysm or orbital haemorrhage
feat: Painless, gradually progressive visual loss, often with colour desaturation out of proportion to acuity
Relative afferent pupillary defect and field loss that follows the compressed segment (central, altitudinal or temporal)
Disc may be normal early, then swollen or pale with optociliary shunt vessels in optic sheath meningioma
Eye movement-evoked visual dimming, proptosis, diplopia or headache point to an orbital or parasellar mass

case.who: 52-year-old woman, rubber plantation owner from Trang
case.story: Right eye has grown dim over eight months; colours look washed out and the eye sometimes blurs when she looks to the side. Headache is mild; no eye pain.
case.exam: Right visual acuity 20/60, left 20/20; right RAPD, red desaturation, mild proptosis and a pale disc with optociliary shunt vessels.
case.tests: MRI orbit shows a tubular, enhancing thickening of the right optic nerve sheath with a tram-track sign; automated perimetry shows a constricted field with central scotoma.
case.q: What is the most likely lesion and how should it be managed?
case.a: Optic nerve sheath meningioma causing compressive optic neuropathy. Proceed with a multidisciplinary plan: fractionated stereotactic radiotherapy is usually favoured over surgery for preserving vision, with regular perimetry and imaging follow-up.

det.patho: Any mass or bone lesion in the orbit, optic canal or intracranial prechiasmatic space can compress the nerve. Sheath meningioma and optic glioma arise from the nerve, whereas sphenoid wing meningioma, pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma and aneurysms act from outside. In thyroid eye disease the swollen muscles squeeze the nerve at the orbital apex. Compression causes slow axoplasmic block and then ischaemia and axon loss.
det.clinical: Typical patients report monocular dimming, colour fading or a creeping scotoma without pain. A relative afferent pupillary defect appears early and visual acuity may lag behind field and colour changes. The disc looks normal at first because the lesion is retrobulbar, later it becomes pale; optociliary shunt veins, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia or hormonal symptoms hint at the cause. Rapid worsening suggests apoplexy, haemorrhage or aneurysm expansion. Bilateral or chiasmal pattern fields change the localisation.
det.diagnosis: Start with careful measurement of acuity, colour, pupils, fields and OCT, since these quantify damage and give a baseline. MRI with contrast and orbit protocols is the key test; CT shows hyperostosis and calcification. Mimics include optic neuritis, ischaemic optic neuropathy, hereditary and toxic-nutritional neuropathy and glaucoma, so lack of pain, progression beyond four weeks, and failure to recover are red flags for compression.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying lesion: surgery or radiotherapy for tumours, endocrine therapy or decompression for pituitary lesions, aneurysm clipping or coiling, and corticosteroids, teprotumumab or orbital decompression for sight-threatening thyroid eye disease. Timing matters because axonal loss can become irreversible, so earlier decompression gives better outcome. Optic nerve sheath meningioma is generally irradiated rather than resected.
det.prognosis: Visual recovery depends on duration and severity of compression; stabilisation is common, and good recovery is likely when treatment is early and the disc is not yet atrophic.
pearls: Painless, progressive, colour-first visual loss with RAPD means compression until imaging says otherwise.
Normal disc does not exclude it; the lesion is retrobulbar.
Optociliary shunt vessels, proptosis and hyperostosis suggest sheath meningioma.
det.thd: ภาวะที่เส้นประสาทตาถูกก้อนหรือกระดูกกดทับ เช่น meningioma, ก้อนที่ต่อมใต้สมอง, aneurysm หรือ thyroid eye disease ทำให้ตามัวช้า ๆ ไม่ปวด เห็นสีผิดปกติ และมี RAPD การตรวจสำคัญคือ visual field, OCT และ MRI วงโคจรพร้อมสารเปรียบต่าง การรักษาคือแก้ที่สาเหตุ เช่น ฉายรังสี ผ่าตัด หรือรักษาไทรอยด์ ยิ่งรักษาเร็วโอกาสฟื้นยิ่งดี

name: Compulsive behavioral disorders
formal: Impulse control and compulsive behaviours such as gambling, hypersexuality, binge eating and punding, most often triggered by dopamine agonists in Parkinson disease or restless legs syndrome.
simple: Out-of-control urges such as gambling, shopping or repetitive tasks, often caused by Parkinson medicines.
more: Treat by reducing or stopping the dopamine agonist, with counselling and sometimes naltrexone or amantadine; withdrawing the drug too fast can cause an agonist withdrawal syndrome.

case.a: Dopamine agonist-induced impulse control disorder; taper the agonist gradually while compensating with levodopa and counsel the family.

Chapter 30 Sexual Dysfunction in Patients with Neurologic Disorders

det.patho: Dopamine agonists, particularly those favouring D3 receptors, overstimulate the ventral striatum and mesolimbic reward circuitry, which are relatively preserved in Parkinson disease. This biases decision making towards immediate reward and reduces sensitivity to loss. Genetic and personality factors influence susceptibility.
det.clinical: Impulse control disorders affect roughly one in six Parkinson patients on agonists, and also occur in restless legs and pituitary patients treated with dopaminergic drugs. Behaviours escalate quietly and may cause severe social and financial harm. Punding and dopamine dysregulation syndrome often coexist.
det.diagnosis: Ask directly and involve a carer, using validated screens such as QUIP-RS. Link onset to dose changes. Assess for depression, anxiety and cognitive impairment, and consider other causes if there is no dopaminergic exposure.
det.treatment: Gradually reduce or stop the dopamine agonist, replacing motor benefit with levodopa as needed; watch for dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome (anxiety, dysphoria, pain). Cognitive behavioural therapy and financial safeguards help. Amantadine or naltrexone have mixed evidence. Deep brain stimulation can allow dopaminergic reduction but outcomes for ICDs vary.
det.prognosis: Most improve after agonist reduction, though some persist and withdrawal symptoms may limit tapering.
pearls: Warn every patient and family before starting a dopamine agonist.
Screen for impulse control disorders at each follow-up.
Taper agonists slowly to avoid withdrawal syndrome.
det.thd: Compulsive behavioral disorders หรือ impulse control disorders เป็นพฤติกรรมหุนหันหรือย้ำทำ เช่น การพนัน ซื้อของ กินมาก หรือเรื่องเพศ พบบ่อยในผู้ป่วยพาร์กินสันที่ใช้ยา dopamine agonist เพราะยากระตุ้นวงจรรางวัลของสมองมากเกินไป ผู้ป่วยมักปิดบัง จึงต้องถามญาติและคัดกรองทุกครั้ง รักษาโดยลดยา agonist ช้า ๆ ทดแทนด้วย levodopa และให้คำปรึกษาครอบครัว

name: Conduct disorder
formal: Persistent pattern of violating rules or others' rights in childhood and adolescence, with aggression, deceit and truancy; psychiatric diagnosis often comorbid with ADHD.

case.who: 13-year-old boy from Samut Prakan referred from a juvenile court clinic
case.story: Over two years: fights at school, stole a motorcycle, skips class and has hurt a neighbour's dog; previously diagnosed with ADHD but stopped medication.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination; little remorse when describing events.
case.tests: School reports confirm truancy and aggression; ADHD scales still elevated; no developmental regression.
case.q: What psychiatric diagnosis fits and what is the main treatment?
case.a: Conduct disorder with comorbid ADHD; family-based behavioural interventions and treatment of ADHD, coordinated with child psychiatry.

det.patho: Conduct disorder arises from combined genetic vulnerability and environmental adversity, including harsh or inconsistent parenting, abuse, peer influences and poverty. Studies of youths with callous-unemotional traits show reduced amygdala responsiveness to distress cues. Prenatal exposures and head injury may contribute in some. It is a psychiatric diagnosis included here for differential diagnosis.
det.clinical: Behaviour falls into aggression, property destruction, deceitfulness or theft, and serious rule-breaking such as running away and truancy. Onset before age 10 predicts persistence and adult antisocial behaviour. ADHD and learning disability are common companions. Neurologists should consider frontal lobe epilepsy, head injury and rare neurogenetic syndromes only when there are atypical features.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis uses DSM-5-TR criteria based on history from family, school and sometimes legal sources. Coexisting disorders must be assessed because they change management. Brain imaging and EEG are not routine and are reserved for neurological red flags such as seizures, regression or focal deficits.
det.treatment: Parent management training, multisystemic therapy and school-based programmes have the best evidence. Treat comorbid ADHD with stimulants, which also reduce aggression. Antipsychotics such as risperidone are used short-term for severe aggression with careful monitoring. Child protection issues must be addressed.
det.prognosis: Many adolescents improve, but childhood-onset cases have higher risk of adult antisocial behaviour, substance misuse and incarceration.
pearls: Treating coexisting ADHD often reduces aggression.
Look for abuse and learning disability in every child with conduct problems.
Neurological testing is guided by red flags, not by behaviour alone.

formal: Early-onset non-progressive or slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia due to cerebellar malformation or genetic causes, with hypotonia and delayed motor milestones.

th: ภาวะเดินเซจากสมองน้อยที่เริ่มตั้งแต่แรกเกิดหรือวัยทารก มักไม่ลุกลามหรือลุกลามช้า เกิดจากความผิดปกติของโครงสร้างสมองน้อยหรือพันธุกรรม มีกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนปวกเปียกและพัฒนาการช้า
tempoNote: Present from infancy; often stable or slowly improving with development, sometimes slowly progressive
feat: Neonatal or infant hypotonia, then delayed sitting and walking
Truncal and gait ataxia, intention tremor and dysarthria once the child develops
Abnormal eye movements (nystagmus, oculomotor apraxia) common
Often accompanied by intellectual disability
Causes include malformations (Joubert, Dandy–Walker, cerebellar hypoplasia), genes (CACNA1A, ITPR1) and perinatal injury

case.story: Floppy at birth, sat at 12 months and still cannot walk alone; parents noticed jerky eye movements and episodic fast breathing in infancy.
case.exam: Hypotonia, truncal titubation, oculomotor apraxia, mild developmental delay.
case.tests: MRI shows molar tooth sign; renal ultrasound normal; ciliopathy panel identifies CC2D2A variants.
case.q: Which disorder and which organs need surveillance?
case.a: Joubert syndrome; monitor kidneys, liver and retina.

1 - Clinical overview and phenomenology of movement disorders

det.patho: Congenital ataxias reflect abnormal cerebellar development or early injury. Malformative causes include ciliopathies (Joubert), Dandy–Walker spectrum, pontocerebellar hypoplasias and rhombencephalosynapsis. Non-malformative genetic forms involve ion channels (CACNA1A, ITPR1) and synaptic proteins; congenital disorders of glycosylation and mitochondrial disease can also present this way.
det.clinical: Hypotonia dominates early, and ataxia becomes visible as the child attempts posture and walking. Many children improve functionally with maturation even when the underlying condition is fixed. Progression, regression, seizures or systemic involvement suggest metabolic or degenerative disease.
det.diagnosis: MRI is the first step and classifies most malformations. Next-generation sequencing has a substantial yield in non-malformative forms. Check eyes, kidneys and liver for syndromic associations and screen for treatable metabolic disorders.
det.treatment: No cure for most; early physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy, and educational support are central. Treat associated problems (seizures, scoliosis, renal disease). Acetazolamide helps some channel-related episodic forms. Genetic counselling guides recurrence risk.
det.prognosis: Variable; many walk with aid and stabilise, while syndromic or metabolic forms carry more disability.
pearls: Floppy infant who later becomes ataxic: image the cerebellum.
Non-progression is reassuring; regression is a red flag for metabolic disease.
Molar tooth sign = Joubert and its ciliopathy relatives.
det.thd: Congenital ataxia คือภาวะเดินเซจากสมองน้อยที่มีมาตั้งแต่แรกเกิดหรือวัยทารก เด็กมักตัวอ่อนปวกเปียกก่อนแล้วจึงเห็นอาการเซเมื่อเริ่มนั่งเดิน สาเหตุได้แก่ความผิดปกติของโครงสร้างสมองน้อย (เช่น Joubert) ความผิดปกติทางพันธุกรรม หรือการบาดเจ็บช่วงคลอด ตรวจ MRI และตรวจยีน ส่วนใหญ่ไม่ลุกลาม รักษาด้วยกายภาพบำบัดและการฟื้นฟูพัฒนาการ

name: Congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy (CHN)
formal: Early-onset neuropathy with severely slowed conduction, hypotonia and arthrogryposis, from myelin gene mutations (EGR2, PMP22, MPZ).
simple: A rare inherited nerve disease in newborns with floppy muscles and poor movement.
th: เส้นประสาทส่วนปลายสร้าง myelin ไม่ได้ตั้งแต่กำเนิด ทำให้ทารกตัวอ่อนปวกเปียก ข้อติด และหายใจลำบาก

Arthrogryposis and areflexia
Respiratory insufficiency in severe cases

case.who: Newborn girl at a provincial hospital in Nakhon Ratchasima
case.story: Born with stiff, flexed knees and ankles, weak suck and needed oxygen for poor breathing effort.
case.exam: Profound hypotonia, areflexia, contractures of knees and feet, alert face.

case.a: Peripheral nerve myelin; congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy.

read.where: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves — Autosomal Dominant Charcot–Marie–Tooth Disease Type 1

det.patho: Pathogenic variants in myelin structure or Schwann cell transcription genes (MPZ, PMP22, EGR2, PRX, SOX10, MTMR2 and others) prevent formation of normal myelin during development. Biopsy shows axons with absent or very thin myelin, sometimes with basal lamina onion bulbs.
det.clinical: Infants present at birth with hypotonia, weakness, contractures and feeding or respiratory problems. Some improve modestly with maturation, while others have progressive weakness. SOX10 cases may include Waardenburg-Hirschsprung features.
det.diagnosis: Extremely slow conduction velocities point to a severe demyelinating neuropathy. Genetic testing via neuropathy panel or exome confirms the gene. Exclude other causes of floppy infant with normal conduction.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy. Supportive care includes respiratory support, nutrition, orthopaedic management of contractures, physiotherapy and genetic counselling.
det.prognosis: Variable; severe forms may be fatal in infancy, milder forms survive with significant disability.
pearls: A floppy infant with conduction velocities in single digits has CHN or Dejerine–Sottas spectrum disease.
SOX10 variants link neuropathy with pigmentary and gut innervation defects.
Many are de novo dominant, so parents may be unaffected.
det.thd: CHN เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมที่เส้นประสาทส่วนปลายสร้าง myelin ไม่ได้ตั้งแต่กำเนิด ทารกตัวอ่อนปวกเปียก ข้อติด ดูดนมและหายใจไม่ดี reflex หาย NCS ช้ามากหรือวัดไม่ได้ ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน เช่น MPZ PMP22 EGR2 การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง

name: Congenital inherited ataxic disorders
formal: Group of genetic cerebellar ataxias present from birth including Joubert syndrome, Gillespie syndrome and cerebellar hypoplasias.
simple: Inherited conditions in which poor coordination is present from infancy.
th: กลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่มีอาการเดินเซจากสมองน้อยตั้งแต่กำเนิด เช่น Joubert syndrome, Gillespie syndrome และ cerebellar hypoplasia

Joubert syndrome: molar tooth sign, breathing irregularities, oculomotor apraxia, renal and retinal disease
Gillespie syndrome: partial aniridia, ataxia and intellectual disability (ITPR1)
Pontocerebellar hypoplasias: severe, often with microcephaly and seizures

Exome or genome sequencing; targeted panels for ciliopathies

case.exam: Fixed dilated-looking pupils with partial absent iris, gait ataxia, mild learning delay.
case.tests: MRI: cerebellar vermis hypoplasia; de novo ITPR1 variant.
case.q: Which syndrome is this?

det.patho: These disorders result from defects in genes governing cerebellar neuron generation, migration and primary cilia function, or in neuronal calcium signalling. Inheritance may be recessive (Joubert, VLDLR, most pontocerebellar hypoplasias), dominant de novo (ITPR1, CACNA1A), or X-linked (OPHN1, CASK).
det.clinical: Presentation is with hypotonia and delayed motor milestones; extra-neurological features guide diagnosis (kidney cysts, liver fibrosis, retinal dystrophy in Joubert; aniridia in Gillespie). Cognitive outcome ranges from normal to severe impairment.
det.diagnosis: Combine MRI pattern and systemic findings, then confirm with sequencing. Reanalysis of exome data over time increases yield. Provide syndromic surveillance once a diagnosis is reached.
det.treatment: Supportive rehabilitation, education support and management of organ-specific complications (dialysis or transplant for renal disease in Joubert, low-vision support). Genetic counselling for recurrence risk.
det.prognosis: Highly variable by gene; Joubert and Gillespie are typically non-progressive, while pontocerebellar hypoplasias often shorten life.
pearls: Look at the eyes: aniridia suggests Gillespie, retinal dystrophy suggests Joubert.
MRI pattern recognition narrows the genetic search.
Joubert needs lifelong renal and hepatic surveillance.
det.thd: Congenital inherited ataxic disorders เป็นกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่เด็กมีอาการเดินเซจากสมองน้อยตั้งแต่กำเนิด เช่น Joubert syndrome ที่มี molar tooth sign และโรคไต Gillespie syndrome ที่มีม่านตาหายบางส่วน และ pontocerebellar hypoplasia ที่รุนแรง ตรวจ MRI ร่วมกับการตรวจยีน และตรวจตา ไต ตับ รักษาแบบฟื้นฟู ติดตามภาวะแทรกซ้อนเฉพาะโรค และให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

formal: Inherited muscle diseases onset at birth or infancy with hypotonia and weakness; subtypes include merosin deficiency and dystroglycanopathies, sometimes with brain involvement.
simple: Inherited muscle diseases causing floppy, weak muscles from birth.
th: กลุ่มโรคกล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมที่มีอาการตั้งแต่แรกเกิดหรือขวบปีแรก ตัวอ่อนปวกเปียก ข้อติด และบางชนิดมีสมองหรือตาผิดปกติ

feat: Neonatal hypotonia, weakness, delayed milestones and contractures
Main groups: LAMA2 (merosin), dystroglycanopathies, collagen VI, SELENON, LMNA
Brain involvement: white matter changes (LAMA2), cobblestone cortex (severe dystroglycanopathy)
Respiratory failure, scoliosis and feeding problems common

case.story: Weak at birth, never sat unsupported, needs frequent suction for secretions; cognition appears appropriate.
case.exam: Generalised weakness and hypotonia, contractures at hips and ankles, normal social smile, no eye abnormalities.
case.tests: CK 1,800 U/L; MRI shows diffuse white matter T2 hyperintensity with normal cortex; biopsy shows absent laminin-alpha2.
case.q: Which subtype is this and what does the white matter change mean for cognition?
case.a: LAMA2-related (merosin-deficient) CMD; the white matter change is typical and usually not associated with intellectual disability.

7: Molecular Diagnostic Procedures and Genetics in Neuromuscular Disorders

det.patho: CMDs arise from defects in proteins linking the muscle cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix (laminin-alpha2, collagen VI, glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan), the nuclear envelope (lamin A/C) or the endoplasmic reticulum (selenoprotein N). Many of these proteins are also expressed in brain and eye, explaining CNS involvement. Most are autosomal recessive; collagen VI and LMNA forms can be dominant de novo.
det.clinical: Children present as floppy infants or with delayed motor milestones and early contractures. LAMA2 CMD shows profound weakness with white matter change but often normal intelligence. Dystroglycanopathies range from Walker-Warburg to limb-girdle forms. Collagen VI forms feature distal laxity, while SELENON causes rigid spine and early respiratory failure.
det.diagnosis: Combine CK, MRI brain, eye examination and muscle biopsy immunohistochemistry to target genetic testing. Muscle MRI patterns may suggest a gene. Exome sequencing is now often the first test. Exclude SMA and congenital myasthenic syndromes.
det.treatment: No approved disease-modifying drug exists; management follows international consensus: respiratory monitoring and non-invasive ventilation, scoliosis surveillance, contracture management, nutrition and cardiac review where relevant. Seizures are treated as usual.
det.prognosis: Highly variable by subtype, from early death to adult survival with stable weakness.
pearls: White matter change with normal cognition suggests LAMA2 CMD.
Respiratory failure may occur while walking in SELENON and collagen VI forms.
Check the eyes and brain in any floppy infant with high CK.
det.thd: CMD คือกลุ่มโรคกล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมที่เริ่มตั้งแต่แรกเกิด เด็กตัวอ่อน อ่อนแรง ข้อติด บางชนิดมีความผิดปกติของสมองหรือตา เช่น merosin-deficient CMD และ dystroglycanopathy วินิจฉัยด้วย CK, MRI สมอง ชิ้นเนื้อกล้ามเนื้อ และตรวจยีน การดูแลเน้นการหายใจ หลังคด ข้อติด และโภชนาการ

name: Congenital myasthenic syndrome (CMS)
formal: Inherited neuromuscular junction disorders with fatigable weakness since early life, ptosis and feeding problems; mutations in CHRNE, RAPSN, DOK7 and others.
simple: Inherited conditions where nerves cannot signal properly to muscles, causing tiring weakness.

Family history or consanguinity; antibodies negative
Clues to subtype: limb-girdle pattern without eye involvement (DOK7, GFPT1), episodic apnoea (CHAT), repetitive CMAP (slow-channel, COLQ)

AChR and MuSK antibodies negative
Genetic panel (CHRNE, RAPSN, DOK7, COLQ, GFPT1 …)

case.exam: Limb-girdle fatigable weakness, mild ptosis, normal eye movements.
case.tests: RNS decrement 30%; AChR/MuSK negative; DOK7 compound heterozygous variants.
case.q: Which drug is usually helpful in DOK7 CMS?
case.a: Salbutamol (or ephedrine); acetylcholinesterase inhibitors often worsen DOK7 and COLQ forms — hence the genetic diagnosis matters.

qx.stem: An 8-month-old boy from Nakhon Sawan has had drooping eyelids since birth, a weak cry and poor feeding, with two admissions for respiratory infections needing oxygen. He has a high-arched palate, ptosis that is worse in the evening, and mild limb hypotonia. His mother has no weakness, AChR and MuSK antibodies are negative, and low-rate repetitive stimulation shows a decremental CMAP response.
qx.q: What is the best next step before choosing long-term treatment?
opts: Plan thymectomy as for juvenile myasthenia gravis
Give a course of intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg
Start azathioprine for seronegative myasthenia
Send a gene panel for congenital myasthenic syndromes, because drug choice depends on the molecular subtype
Begin rituximab because anti-MuSK antibodies may be missed
qx.why: Early onset, seronegative status, skeletal features such as a high-arched palate and a decrement suggest a genetic neuromuscular junction disorder, which is autoimmune-negative and does not respond to immunotherapy or thymectomy. Because some subtypes improve with pyridostigmine and amifampridine while others (slow channel, DOK7, COLQ) are worsened by them and need fluoxetine, quinidine, salbutamol or ephedrine, genetic subtyping guides safe therapy.
