det.patho: CMS are inherited defects of neuromuscular transmission caused by mutations in presynaptic, synaptic basal lamina, postsynaptic or glycosylation genes. The most frequent are AChR subunit mutations (especially CHRNE) causing receptor deficiency, followed by RAPSN, DOK7, COLQ and GFPT1. Kinetic defects either prolong channel opening (slow-channel, usually dominant) or shorten it (fast-channel). Most forms are autosomal recessive.
det.clinical: Fatigable weakness of ocular, bulbar, axial or limb muscles begins at birth or in childhood, though some forms present in adolescence or adulthood. Neonates may have hypotonia, poor feeding, arthrogryposis or episodic apnoea (CHAT, RAPSN). DOK7 and GFPT1 forms often show limb-girdle weakness with little eye involvement. Slow-channel and COLQ forms may show selective neck, wrist and finger extensor weakness and pupils that react slowly.
det.diagnosis: RNS decrement and increased jitter on single-fibre EMG establish a transmission defect; a repetitive CMAP after a single stimulus suggests slow-channel syndrome or COLQ deficiency. AChR, MuSK and LRP4 antibodies should be negative. Next-generation sequencing panels or exome sequencing identify the gene. Consider CMS in any 'seronegative MG' with early onset, family history or poor response to immunotherapy.
det.treatment: Therapy is genotype-specific. AChR deficiency and fast-channel forms respond to pyridostigmine, often with 3,4-diaminopyridine. Slow-channel syndrome is treated with open-channel blockers such as fluoxetine or quinidine, and cholinesterase inhibitors should be avoided. DOK7 and COLQ forms respond to beta-2 agonists (salbutamol, ephedrine) and may worsen with pyridostigmine. Immunotherapy has no role.
det.prognosis: Many forms are static or slowly progressive and compatible with normal life expectancy if crises are managed; some have life-threatening apnoeic episodes in childhood.
pearls: Antibody-negative 'MG' that worsens with pyridostigmine suggests DOK7, COLQ or slow-channel CMS.
A repetitive CMAP after one stimulus is a key electrophysiological clue.
det.thd: CMS เป็นกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่ทำให้การส่งสัญญาณที่รอยต่อประสาทกล้ามเนื้อผิดปกติ มีอาการอ่อนแรงแบบล้าง่ายตั้งแต่เด็ก เช่น หนังตาตก กลืนลำบาก หรืออ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขา โดยไม่มีแอนติบอดี AChR หรือ MuSK การวินิจฉัยใช้ RNS, single-fibre EMG และตรวจยีน การรักษาขึ้นกับชนิดของยีน บางชนิดตอบสนองต่อ pyridostigmine แต่ชนิด DOK7, COLQ และ slow-channel อาจแย่ลงจากยานี้ และควรใช้ salbutamol หรือ fluoxetine แทน

name: Congenital myopathies
formal: Inherited muscle diseases with hypotonia and weakness from birth, with distinct structural features: nemaline, core and centronuclear myopathies.
simple: A group of inherited muscle diseases causing weak, floppy muscles from early life.
more: Diagnosis uses CK, EMG, muscle MRI pattern and biopsy with enzyme histochemistry, but a next-generation sequencing panel is now first line. Management is mainly supportive with respiratory, orthopaedic and cardiac follow-up, and prognosis depends on the gene.

Facial weakness, high-arched palate, long face; ptosis/ophthalmoparesis in centronuclear forms
RYR1 core myopathy: malignant hyperthermia susceptibility
inv: CK normal or mildly raised; EMG myopathic
Muscle biopsy: rods (nemaline), cores (central core), central nuclei (centronuclear)
Gene panel (RYR1, ACTA1, NEB, MTM1, DNM2 …)

case.story: Floppy at birth, walked at 2 years, always last in sports; no worsening.
case.exam: Mild proximal and neck flexor weakness, long thin face, high palate, normal reflexes.
case.tests: CK 180 U/L; biopsy: central cores; RYR1 variant.
case.q: Why should the anaesthetist be told?
case.a: RYR1-related core myopathy carries a risk of malignant hyperthermia with volatile anaesthetics and suxamethonium.

aN: congenital myopathy | nemaline myopathy | central core disease | centronuclear myopathy | myotubular myopathy | ryr1

det.patho: Congenital myopathies are genetic disorders of muscle structure and excitation–contraction coupling, defined historically by biopsy features: cores (RYR1, SELENON), rods (NEB, ACTA1 and others), central nuclei (MTM1, DNM2, BIN1, RYR1) and fibre-type disproportion. RYR1 is the most common gene overall. One gene can cause several pathological pictures, and one picture can come from several genes, so genetic diagnosis now takes priority.
det.clinical: Most present at birth or in infancy with hypotonia, weakness, feeding problems and delayed motor milestones, followed by a static or slowly progressive course. Facial weakness, a long narrow face, high-arched palate, scoliosis and joint contractures are common. Respiratory weakness may be disproportionate to limb weakness, especially in nemaline, SELENON and centronuclear forms. X-linked myotubular myopathy causes severe neonatal weakness in boys, often with ventilator dependence; ptosis and ophthalmoparesis suggest centronuclear myopathy or some RYR1 forms.
det.diagnosis: CK is normal or mildly raised and EMG shows myopathic or non-specific changes. Muscle MRI patterns can point to particular genes. Biopsy with histochemistry and electron microscopy remains useful, but next-generation sequencing panels or exome sequencing usually establish the diagnosis. Exclude SMA, congenital myasthenic syndromes, congenital myotonic dystrophy and Pompe disease.
det.treatment: There is no approved disease-modifying therapy. Management focuses on respiratory monitoring with nocturnal ventilation when needed, nutrition, scoliosis care, physiotherapy and orthopaedic support. Patients with RYR1 variants should avoid triggering anaesthetic agents. Some CMS-like transmission defects in centronuclear myopathy may respond to pyridostigmine.
det.prognosis: Ranges from near-normal life with mild weakness to early death from respiratory failure in severe neonatal forms.
pearls: Check FVC lying down — diaphragm weakness can be hidden.
RYR1 myopathy: alert the anaesthetist about malignant hyperthermia.
A floppy infant with normal CK and a myopathic face suggests congenital myopathy.
det.thd: Congenital myopathies เป็นกลุ่มโรคกล้ามเนื้อทางพันธุกรรมที่เป็นตั้งแต่เกิด ทารกตัวอ่อน กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง ดูดนมลำบาก พัฒนาการช้า แต่โรคมักไม่ค่อยลุกลาม เดิมแบ่งชนิดตามลักษณะชิ้นเนื้อ เช่น core, rod และ central nuclei ยีนที่พบบ่อยที่สุดคือ RYR1 การวินิจฉัยปัจจุบันใช้การตรวจยีนเป็นหลัก การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง โดยเฉพาะการเฝ้าระวังการหายใจ และผู้ป่วยที่มี RYR1 ต้องแจ้งวิสัญญีแพทย์เพราะเสี่ยงต่อ malignant hyperthermia

name: Congenital myotonic dystrophy
formal: Severe neonatal form of DM1 with large maternal CTG expansions causing hypotonia, respiratory failure, facial weakness, and intellectual disability.
simple: A serious form of myotonic dystrophy present at birth, causing floppiness and breathing problems.
more: Genetic testing in baby and mother; ventilatory support and feeding care; survivors improve in motor strength but have cognitive impairment.
th: DM1 รูปแบบรุนแรงในทารกแรกเกิด เกิดจาก CTG repeat ยาวมากที่ถ่ายทอดจากแม่ มีตัวอ่อนปวกเปียก หายใจล้มเหลว ใบหน้าอ่อนแรง และสติปัญญาบกพร่อง
tempoNote: Present at birth, with gradual motor improvement in survivors and later development of adult DM1 features
feat: Polyhydramnios and reduced fetal movement in pregnancy
Severe neonatal hypotonia, facial diplegia with tented upper lip, poor suck and swallow
Respiratory failure needing ventilation; talipes and other contractures
Clinical myotonia absent in infancy; appears later in childhood
Mother usually affected, sometimes mildly and unaware
inv: DMPK CTG repeat sizing in the infant (typically above 1,000 repeats)
Examine the mother for grip myotonia, ptosis, facial weakness; test her DMPK
Echocardiography, ECG, feeding and swallowing assessment

case.who: Newborn boy delivered at a regional hospital in Nakhon Sawan
case.story: Pregnancy complicated by polyhydramnios; at birth he is floppy, cannot suck and needs intubation.
case.exam: Facial diplegia with open tented mouth, bilateral talipes, generalised hypotonia; mother cannot release her handshake quickly.
case.tests: Infant DMPK expansion about 1,500 CTG repeats; mother has 300 repeats.
case.q: Why did the infant inherit a more severe form than his mother?
case.a: Maternal transmission favours large CTG expansion (anticipation), causing congenital DM1.

read.where: 11. The Diagnostic Approach to the Hypotonic and Weak Infant

det.patho: DM1 results from CTG repeat expansion within DMPK; the expanded RNA sequesters splicing regulators (MBNL1), producing widespread mis-splicing. Very large expansions, almost always passed through the mother, disturb muscle and brain development in utero. Muscle shows immaturity rather than classic adult changes.
det.clinical: Neonatal mortality is substantial in infants needing prolonged ventilation. Survivors gain motor skills over the first decade but have intellectual disability, speech problems, behavioural issues and later develop typical myotonia, cardiac conduction disease and cataracts. Gastrointestinal dysmotility is common.
det.diagnosis: Suspect in any floppy newborn with facial diplegia and talipes; examine the mother. DMPK repeat analysis confirms. EMG in infants may not show myotonia. Prenatal testing is available for affected mothers.
det.treatment: Supportive neonatal care with ventilation and feeding support; physiotherapy, orthotics and casting for talipes; speech and educational support. Lifelong cardiac surveillance with ECG and Holter, anaesthesia precautions, and family genetic counselling. Disease-modifying RNA-targeted therapies are in trials.
det.prognosis: Infants surviving beyond the neonatal period usually improve motorly; cognitive impairment and adult DM1 complications persist.
pearls: Floppy baby with tented upper lip: shake the mother's hand.
Myotonia is not seen clinically or on EMG in newborns.
Anticipation is strongest through maternal transmission.
det.thd: Congenital myotonic dystrophy เป็น DM1 รูปแบบรุนแรงที่สุด เกิดจาก CTG repeat ยาวมากในยีน DMPK ซึ่งส่วนใหญ่ถ่ายทอดจากแม่ ทารกตัวอ่อนปวกเปียก หน้าอ่อนแรงปากรูปตัวเอ็มคว่ำ ดูดนมไม่ได้ หายใจล้มเหลว และเท้าปุก ระหว่างตั้งครรภ์มักมีน้ำคร่ำมาก ควรตรวจแม่ด้วยเพราะอาจมีอาการน้อยจนไม่รู้ตัว ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน รักษาแบบประคับประคอง เด็กที่รอดมักดีขึ้นด้านกำลังแต่มีสติปัญญาบกพร่อง

qx.stem: A term male newborn in Khon Kaen is born with polyhydramnios noted late in pregnancy, severe hypotonia, bilateral talipes, a tented upper lip and feeding failure. He requires ventilation. Examination of the mother reveals a myopathic face, ptosis and grip myotonia that she can barely release.
qx.q: What is the mechanism and recurrence implication?
opts: Autosomal recessive SMN1 deletion
Paternal imprinting disorder at 15q11-q13
Neonatal transfer of anti-AChR antibodies
Duchenne carrier state
Maternal CTG repeat expansion in DMPK is transmitted with further expansion, so the mother (and siblings) require counselling
qx.why: Congenital myotonic dystrophy almost always arises from a mother with DM1, because large CTG expansions occur with maternal transmission, causing anticipation. The mother may not know she is affected and needs examination and genetic counselling. The other options do not explain the maternal myotonia or the clinical pattern.

name: Connective tissue diseases
formal: Heterogeneous group including Ehlers-Danlos, Marfan and SLE; neurological complications include dissection, stroke, aneurysm and myelopathy.
simple: Diseases of the supporting tissue of the body that can sometimes affect blood vessels, nerves and the spine.
th: กลุ่มโรคเนื้อเยื่อเกี่ยวพันหลากหลาย เช่น Ehlers–Danlos, Marfan และ SLE ซึ่งมีภาวะแทรกซ้อนทางระบบประสาท เช่น หลอดเลือดฉีกขาด stroke หลอดเลือดโป่งพอง และโรคไขสันหลัง
tempoNote: Lifelong conditions with acute vascular or spinal events
feat: Mixed category: heritable disorders (Marfan, vascular EDS, Loeys–Dietz, pseudoxanthoma elasticum) and autoimmune ones (SLE, scleroderma)
Cervical artery dissection and intracranial aneurysms, especially in vascular EDS and Loeys–Dietz
Carotid-cavernous fistula and spontaneous arterial rupture in vascular EDS
Dural ectasia, spontaneous CSF leak and intracranial hypotension in Marfan
Craniocervical instability and Chiari-like problems reported in hypermobile EDS (evidence debated)
inv: Clinical features: joint hypermobility, skin, lens dislocation, family history
Genetic testing (FBN1, COL3A1, TGFBR1/2, SMAD3)
Vascular imaging of head, neck and aorta; spine MRI for dural ectasia or CSF leak

case.who: 33-year-old male graphic designer from Bangkok, tall with long fingers
case.story: Orthostatic headache for two weeks, better lying down; previous lens dislocation.
case.exam: Marfanoid habitus, arm span exceeding height; neurological examination normal.
case.tests: MRI brain: pachymeningeal enhancement and brain sagging; spine MRI: lumbosacral dural ectasia with extradural fluid; FBN1 variant.
case.q: What is the cause of his headache?
case.a: Spontaneous intracranial hypotension from a CSF leak associated with Marfan dural ectasia.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Neurological Involvement in Systemic Vasculitides and Related Disorders
Chapter 50 Connective Tissue Diseases, Vasculitis, and the Nervous System
Section 3 Hereditary and Genetic Conditions and Malformations
3. EVALUATION AND MANAGEMENT OF THE PATIENT WITH PERIPHERAL NEUROPATHY

det.patho: Heritable connective tissue disorders weaken vessel walls and dura through defective collagen, fibrillin or TGF-beta signalling, predisposing to dissection, aneurysm, fistula and CSF leaks. Autoimmune connective tissue diseases cause injury through inflammation and thrombosis.
det.clinical: Young-onset dissection, aneurysm or spontaneous intracranial hypotension should prompt examination for skin hyperextensibility, joint hypermobility, marfanoid habitus, lens dislocation and family history. Systemic features (aortic dilatation, bowel or uterine rupture) carry high risk.
det.diagnosis: Clinical criteria (Ghent for Marfan, 2017 EDS criteria) supported by genetic testing. Vascular imaging assesses the head, neck and aorta.
det.treatment: Blood pressure and heart rate control, aortic surveillance and timely surgery. Conservative or endovascular management of dissections and aneurysms, mindful of fragile vessels in vascular EDS where catheter procedures carry high risk. Epidural blood patch for CSF leak.
det.prognosis: Vascular EDS and Loeys–Dietz carry reduced life expectancy; Marfan survival has improved greatly with aortic care.
pearls: Young dissection or carotid-cavernous fistula: look for connective tissue clues.
Vascular EDS patients tolerate invasive angiography poorly.
Spontaneous intracranial hypotension may be the first sign of Marfan dural ectasia.
det.thd: Connective tissue diseases ในบริบทนี้รวมโรคพันธุกรรมของเนื้อเยื่อเกี่ยวพัน เช่น Marfan, Ehlers–Danlos, Loeys–Dietz และโรคภูมิคุ้มกัน เช่น SLE ภาวะแทรกซ้อนทางระบบประสาทได้แก่ หลอดเลือดคอฉีกขาด หลอดเลือดโป่งพอง carotid-cavernous fistula และน้ำไขสันหลังรั่ว ควรสังเกตลักษณะร่างกายและประวัติครอบครัว ตรวจยีน และตรวจหลอดเลือด การรักษาคือควบคุมความดันและเฝ้าระวังหลอดเลือด

name: Constructional apraxia
formal: Inability to copy or assemble spatial figures, a disorder of visuospatial organisation, usually from right parietal lesions.
simple: Trouble drawing or building shapes, caused by damage to a part of the brain involved with space.
th: การไม่สามารถวาดหรือประกอบรูปทรงตามแบบได้ เป็นความผิดปกติด้าน visuospatial มักเกิดจากรอยโรค parietal ด้านขวา
tempoNote: Acute after stroke, gradual in dementia
feat: Cannot copy a cube, intersecting pentagons or clock
Right parietal lesions: disorganised drawings with neglect of left side
Left parietal lesions: simplified drawings with preserved overall layout
Common in Alzheimer disease, DLB, hepatic encephalopathy
Sign, not a disease
inv: Bedside copying tasks (MoCA cube, clock drawing)
Neuropsychology; MRI
Metabolic tests (ammonia) if encephalopathy suspected

case.story: Gets lost driving and cannot assemble a simple bookshelf.
case.exam: Cannot copy a cube or intersecting pentagons; mild memory deficit; fluctuating attention and visual hallucinations.
case.tests: MRI: mild atrophy; DAT scan reduced uptake.
case.q: Which neurodegenerative disease is suggested?
case.a: Dementia with Lewy bodies, where visuospatial and constructional deficits are early and prominent.

read.where: Chapter 11 Cognitive Impairment and Dementia — Cognitive Functions and their Clinical Syndromes
Chapter 11 Cognitive Impairment and Dementia — Voluntary Action
20 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Cerebral Hemispheres

det.patho: Copying and assembling figures requires visual perception, spatial analysis and motor planning integrated in parietal-frontal networks. Right parietal damage impairs spatial organisation; left damage impairs planning.
det.clinical: Patients struggle with drawings, puzzles, dressing and navigation. It is often part of broader visuospatial dysfunction.
det.diagnosis: Simple copying tasks reveal the deficit; pattern of errors hints at lesion side. Imaging and cognitive testing find the cause.
det.treatment: Treat the cause; occupational therapy and environmental adaptation help.
det.prognosis: Depends on the cause.
pearls: Failed pentagon copying is an early clue to DLB.
Left-sided omissions suggest right parietal lesion.
Constructional apraxia is a classic sign of hepatic encephalopathy.
det.thd: Constructional apraxia คือการวาดหรือประกอบรูปทรงตามแบบไม่ได้ เช่น ลอกรูปลูกบาศก์หรือห้าเหลี่ยมซ้อนกันไม่ได้ เป็นความผิดปกติด้าน visuospatial มักจากรอยโรค parietal ขวา พบใน DLB, Alzheimer และ hepatic encephalopathy เป็นอาการ ไม่ใช่โรค รักษาตามสาเหตุ

name: Copper deficiency
formal: Acquired deficiency from malabsorption or zinc excess causing myeloneuropathy resembling B12 deficiency, with anaemia and neutropenia.
simple: Too little copper in the body, causing numbness, balance problems and low blood counts.
more: Diagnosed by low serum copper and caeruloplasmin, with MRI spinal cord dorsal column signal change as in B12 deficiency; marrow shows vacuolated precursors. Replace copper and remove zinc excess; haematology recovers but neurological improvement is partial.
th: ภาวะขาดทองแดงจากการดูดซึมผิดปกติหรือได้รับสังกะสีมาก ทำให้เกิดโรคไขสันหลังและเส้นประสาทคล้ายขาด B12 ร่วมกับโลหิตจาง
tempoNote: Develops over months after the precipitating cause
feat: Spastic-ataxic gait with posterior column sensory loss
Distal sensory neuropathy
Anaemia and neutropenia; sometimes myelodysplastic-looking marrow
Risk factors: bariatric or gastric surgery, malabsorption, excess zinc (supplements or denture cream)
Can coexist with B12 deficiency
inv: Serum copper and caeruloplasmin low; serum zinc often high
MRI spine: T2 signal in dorsal columns of cervical/thoracic cord
FBC: anaemia, neutropenia
B12 and methylmalonic acid to exclude combined deficiency

case.who: 47-year-old woman from Pathum Thani with gastric bypass 8 years ago
case.story: Progressive unsteady gait and tingling feet over 6 months despite B12 injections.
case.exam: Spastic legs, brisk knee jerks, absent ankle jerks, extensor plantars, Romberg positive, loss of joint position at toes.
case.tests: Copper 25 µg/dL (low), caeruloplasmin low, neutropenia; MRI shows dorsal column hyperintensity.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and treatment?
case.a: Copper deficiency myeloneuropathy; oral or intravenous copper replacement and stop any zinc source.

read.where: Chapter 14 Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders — Diagnosis of Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders

Chapter 15 Neurologic Manifestations of Nutritional Disorders

11 Neurological consequences of copper and zinc deficiency

det.patho: Copper is a cofactor for enzymes such as cytochrome c oxidase and dopamine beta-hydroxylase and is needed for myelin maintenance. It is absorbed in the stomach and proximal small bowel, so upper GI surgery impairs it. Excess zinc induces enterocyte metallothionein, which traps copper and prevents absorption.
det.clinical: The neurological picture is a myeloneuropathy closely resembling subacute combined degeneration, with gait ataxia, spasticity and sensory loss. Optic neuropathy can occur. Haematological abnormalities (anaemia, neutropenia) often accompany. Symptoms progress if the cause is not identified.
det.diagnosis: Low serum copper and caeruloplasmin, with low urinary copper, confirm deficiency. Look for a cause: surgery history, zinc intake and malabsorption. MRI may show dorsal column signal change. Distinguish from Wilson disease, in which caeruloplasmin is also low but copper is excess in tissues.
det.treatment: Remove zinc sources and replace copper orally, or intravenously when severe or absorption is poor. Monitor copper and blood counts. Haematological abnormalities correct quickly; neurological recovery is slower.
det.prognosis: Haematological recovery is usual; neurological deficits often stabilise but may only partly recover.
pearls: B12-replete myelopathy after bariatric surgery: check copper.
Excess zinc from denture cream or supplements is a classic cause.
Neurological recovery is incomplete, so early recognition matters.
det.thd: ทองแดงจำเป็นต่อการทำงานของ myelin การขาดเกิดหลังผ่าตัดกระเพาะ ลำไส้ดูดซึมผิดปกติ หรือได้รับสังกะสีมากเกิน ทำให้เดินเซ ขาเกร็ง ชาปลายเท้า คล้ายขาดวิตามิน B12 พร้อมโลหิตจางและเม็ดเลือดขาวต่ำ ตรวจ copper และ caeruloplasmin ต่ำ MRI พบ dorsal column ผิดปกติ รักษาด้วยการให้ทองแดงทดแทนและหยุดสังกะสี

qx.stem: A 59-year-old woman from Udon Thani has nine months of a worsening wide-based, stiff gait, numb feet and falls in the dark. For two years she has taken several high-dose zinc tablets daily, bought online 'for immunity'. She has brisk knee jerks, absent ankle jerks, extensor plantars and impaired joint position sense. Blood count shows anaemia and neutropenia. Vitamin B12 and methylmalonic acid are normal; MRI shows T2 signal in the cervical dorsal columns.
qx.q: Which set of laboratory results is most likely?
opts: High copper, high ceruloplasmin and low zinc
Normal copper with a low folate
Low copper, low ceruloplasmin and raised serum zinc
Raised 24-hour urine copper with Kayser–Fleischer rings
Low vitamin E with normal copper
qx.why: Copper-deficiency myeloneuropathy mimics subacute combined degeneration and often comes with cytopenias. Excess zinc induces enterocyte metallothionein, which traps copper and blocks its absorption; other causes are bariatric surgery and malabsorption. Treatment is to stop zinc and replace copper. Haematological changes recover well but neurological deficits often improve only partly, so early recognition matters.

name: Copper dystonia
formal: Dystonia in Wilson disease from copper accumulation in basal ganglia, with Kayser-Fleischer rings and hepatic disease.
simple: Twisting muscle postures caused by copper build-up in the brain.
th: dystonia ใน Wilson disease จากทองแดงสะสมใน basal ganglia มักพบร่วมกับ Kayser-Fleischer ring และโรคตับ
tempoNote: Develops over months in adolescents and young adults; can worsen early after starting chelation
feat: Generalised or segmental dystonia, often with risus sardonicus (fixed grin) and drooling
Dysarthria and dysphagia; wing-beating tremor and parkinsonism may coexist
Psychiatric symptoms (mood change, impulsivity) common
Kayser–Fleischer rings present in nearly all neurological Wilson cases
Hepatic disease may be overt or subclinical
inv: Serum caeruloplasmin (low), 24-hour urinary copper (high), slit-lamp exam
MRI: T2 hyperintensity in putamen, thalamus and brainstem ('face of the giant panda' in midbrain)
ATP7B genetic testing; liver function and liver copper if needed

case.who: 19-year-old male university student in Chiang Mai
case.story: A year of slurred speech, worsening handwriting and a strange fixed smile; his grades have dropped and he is irritable.
case.exam: Oromandibular and limb dystonia, risus sardonicus, golden-brown corneal rings.
case.tests: Caeruloplasmin 5 mg/dL, urinary copper 350 µg/24 h, MRI putaminal T2 signal.
case.q: What treatment caution applies when starting chelation?
case.a: Neurological worsening can occur early, particularly with penicillamine; start low, consider trientine or zinc, and monitor closely.

det.patho: Biallelic ATP7B variants impair biliary copper excretion and incorporation into caeruloplasmin. Copper accumulates first in the liver and then in the brain, injuring the putamen, thalamus, midbrain and pons. Neurological presentation usually follows hepatic copper overload in the second or third decade.
det.clinical: Dystonia is one of the main neurological phenotypes alongside tremor, parkinsonism and ataxia. Bulbar dystonia causes dysarthria, drooling and swallowing problems; facial dystonia produces a fixed smile. Psychiatric change may precede motor symptoms.
det.diagnosis: Test any patient under 50 with unexplained dystonia for Wilson disease. Low caeruloplasmin, raised urinary copper and KF rings support it; Leipzig scoring combines findings. MRI and ATP7B genotyping add confirmation and allow family screening.
det.treatment: Lifelong copper removal with chelators (penicillamine or trientine) or zinc to block absorption; trientine or zinc may carry less risk of paradoxical neurological deterioration. Dystonia is treated symptomatically with anticholinergics, botulinum toxin and physiotherapy. Severe liver failure may need transplantation. Screen siblings.
det.prognosis: Often improves substantially with adherence over months to years; long-standing dystonia may leave residual deficit.
pearls: Test copper studies in every young person with dystonia.
Neurological Wilson disease almost always has KF rings.
Early neurological worsening after chelation is a known risk.
det.thd: Copper dystonia คือ dystonia ที่เกิดใน Wilson disease ซึ่งเป็นโรคพันธุกรรมจากยีน ATP7B ทำให้ทองแดงสะสมในตับและสมองส่วน basal ganglia ผู้ป่วยวัยรุ่นหรือผู้ใหญ่ตอนต้นมีท่าทางบิดเกร็ง พูดไม่ชัด น้ำลายไหล ยิ้มค้าง และมี Kayser-Fleischer ring ตรวจ caeruloplasmin ต่ำ ทองแดงในปัสสาวะสูง รักษาด้วยยาขับทองแดงหรือ zinc ตลอดชีวิต ระวังอาการแย่ลงช่วงเริ่มยา

ddx.pt: Pallidal 'tiger eye' MRI pattern, retinal degeneration, normal copper studies
Rigid-dystonic picture with family history and HTT expansion
Older cirrhotic patient, T1 pallidal brightness, normal caeruloplasmin

aN: wilsonian dystonia | wilson disease dystonia | dystonic wilson disease | hepatolenticular dystonia

name: Copper metabolism disorders
formal: Disorders including Wilson disease, Menkes disease and acquired copper deficiency, causing neurological, hepatic and haematological disease.
simple: Conditions where the body has too much or too little copper.
th: กลุ่มโรคที่การเผาผลาญทองแดงผิดปกติ ได้แก่ Wilson disease, Menkes disease และภาวะขาดทองแดงที่เกิดภายหลัง ทำให้เกิดโรคทางระบบประสาท ตับ และเลือด
tempoNote: Menkes presents in infancy; Wilson in youth; acquired deficiency evolves over months
feat: Copper excess: Wilson disease (ATP7B) with hepatic, movement and psychiatric disease
Copper deficiency, inherited: Menkes disease (ATP7A) with kinky hair, seizures, regression in infant boys; occipital horn syndrome is milder
Acquired copper deficiency: myeloneuropathy resembling B12 deficiency, with anaemia and neutropenia
Rare others: aceruloplasminaemia (iron accumulation), MEDNIK syndrome, ATP7A motor neuropathy
inv: Serum copper and caeruloplasmin, 24-hour urinary copper, serum zinc
MRI brain and spine; slit lamp for KF rings
Genetic testing (ATP7B, ATP7A); full blood count

case.who: 52-year-old woman 8 years after gastric bypass, from Bangkok
case.story: Gradually unsteady gait and numb feet over a year despite regular B12 injections.
case.exam: Sensory ataxia, spastic legs, absent ankle jerks.
case.tests: Serum copper and caeruloplasmin very low, B12 normal, neutropenia; MRI dorsal column T2 signal.
case.q: Which nutrient deficiency explains her myelopathy?
case.a: Acquired copper deficiency after bariatric surgery; replace copper and check zinc intake.

det.patho: Copper is essential for cytochrome c oxidase, dopamine beta-hydroxylase, lysyl oxidase and other enzymes, yet toxic in excess. ATP7A transports copper across the gut and into the brain; its failure causes systemic deficiency (Menkes). ATP7B exports copper into bile and caeruloplasmin; its failure causes overload (Wilson). Excess zinc intake or upper gut surgery reduces copper absorption.
det.clinical: Wilson disease presents with liver disease, tremor, dystonia, parkinsonism and psychiatric change in youth. Menkes disease causes hypotonia, intractable seizures, sparse kinky hair and connective tissue problems in infant boys. Acquired deficiency mimics B12 deficiency with sensory ataxia, spasticity and cytopenias.
det.diagnosis: Measure copper, caeruloplasmin and urinary copper; interpret caeruloplasmin carefully since it is an acute-phase reactant and low in malnutrition. Genetic testing confirms inherited forms. Spine MRI and NCS characterise acquired myeloneuropathy.
det.treatment: Wilson: chelation or zinc lifelong. Menkes: early subcutaneous copper histidinate may help if started in the newborn period, especially with residual ATP7A function. Acquired deficiency: oral or IV copper replacement and stop excess zinc (including zinc-containing denture creams).
det.prognosis: Wilson outcomes are good with adherence; Menkes is usually fatal in early childhood; acquired deficiency improves haematologically but neurologically only partially.
pearls: Myelopathy with normal B12 after gastric surgery: check copper and zinc.
Menkes: infant boy, kinky hair, seizures, low copper.
Caeruloplasmin can be falsely normal in inflammation.
det.thd: Copper metabolism disorders เป็นกลุ่มโรคที่ร่างกายจัดการทองแดงผิดปกติ ได้แก่ Wilson disease ซึ่งทองแดงเกิน ทำให้โรคตับ การเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติ และอาการทางจิต Menkes disease ซึ่งขาดทองแดงตั้งแต่ทารก มีผมหยิกเปราะและชัก และภาวะขาดทองแดงภายหลัง เช่น หลังผ่าตัดกระเพาะหรือได้ zinc มาก ทำให้ไขสันหลังเสื่อมคล้ายขาด B12 ตรวจระดับทองแดงและ caeruloplasmin รักษาตามชนิด

name: Cortical agnosia
formal: Failure to recognise objects despite intact primary sensation from cortical lesion, such as visual, tactile or auditory agnosia.
simple: Not being able to recognise things like objects or sounds despite seeing or hearing them normally, due to brain damage.
th: ภาวะที่ไม่สามารถจดจำวัตถุผ่านประสาทสัมผัสหนึ่ง เช่น การมองเห็น การสัมผัส หรือการได้ยิน แม้ประสาทรับความรู้สึกพื้นฐานปกติ เกิดจากรอยโรคที่เปลือกสมอง

feat: Umbrella term for modality-specific recognition failure: visual, tactile (astereognosis), auditory
Primary sensation intact enough to explain normal recognition
Recognition succeeds through another sense
Subtypes: apperceptive vs associative; prosopagnosia, pure word deafness, finger agnosia
Causes: stroke, hypoxia, encephalitis, tumour, neurodegeneration (PCA, semantic dementia)
inv: Bedside testing of each modality with control of primary sensation
Neuropsychological assessment
MRI brain; FDG-PET or amyloid/tau markers if progressive

case.story: After a right parietal stroke she cannot identify coins or keys in her left pocket without looking, though she feels them clearly.
case.exam: Normal touch, pain and position sense in the left hand; cannot identify objects by touch on the left but does so immediately on the right or by sight.
case.tests: MRI shows right inferior parietal infarct.
case.q: What is this deficit?
case.a: Tactile agnosia (astereognosis) from parietal cortical damage — a form of cortical agnosia.

read.where: Chapter 22 Neuro-Ophthalmology — Disorders of Higher Visual Function

det.patho: Recognition depends on cortical association areas that link sensory representations with stored knowledge. Damage to modality-specific association cortex (occipitotemporal for vision, parietal for touch, superior temporal for sound) leaves basic sensation but disrupts the formation or use of percepts. Lesions are usually bilateral for visual and auditory agnosia and contralateral for tactile.
det.clinical: Patients may appear confused or careless but can name the same objects when another sense is used. Apperceptive forms disturb perception itself; associative forms preserve perception but lose meaning. Prosopagnosia, colour agnosia and pure word deafness are specific types. Anosognosia may coexist.
det.diagnosis: The examiner must first show adequate primary sensation, attention and language, since aphasia or neglect can mimic agnosia. Structured tests of copying, matching and naming in different modalities define the type. Imaging locates the lesion and helps separate acute from degenerative causes.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying cause and provide rehabilitation focusing on compensatory strategies, cueing via intact senses and environmental adaptation. Educating families avoids misinterpretation as confusion or malingering.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause; partial recovery after stroke, progression in neurodegeneration.
pearls: Recognises by another sense = agnosia, not naming failure.
Check primary sensation first; otherwise it is not agnosia.
Progressive visual agnosia in middle age suggests posterior cortical atrophy.
det.thd: Cortical agnosia เป็นคำรวมของภาวะที่จำวัตถุผ่านประสาทสัมผัสหนึ่งไม่ได้ แม้ประสาทรับความรู้สึกพื้นฐานปกติ เช่น จำด้วยตาไม่ได้ จำด้วยการสัมผัสไม่ได้ หรือจำเสียงไม่ได้ แต่จำได้เมื่อใช้ประสาทสัมผัสอื่น เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ association cortex เช่น stroke หรือโรคสมองเสื่อม การตรวจต้องยืนยันว่าการรับความรู้สึกพื้นฐานปกติก่อน

name: Cortical dementia
formal: Dementia with predominant cortical features such as aphasia, apraxia, agnosia and amnesia, as in Alzheimer disease and frontotemporal dementia.
simple: Memory loss and language and thinking problems from damage to the brain's outer layer.
th: dementia ที่เด่นด้านเปลือกสมอง เช่น ความจำใหม่เสียเร็ว aphasia apraxia agnosia และ visuospatial ผิดปกติ ตัวอย่างคืออัลไซเมอร์และ FTD ต่างจาก subcortical dementia ที่คิดช้า เฉยเมย
tempoNote: Insidious onset with steady worsening over several years
feat: Early learning failure: new information is lost quickly and does not improve with cueing
Aphasia, apraxia, agnosia and acalculia from association cortex dysfunction
Visuospatial and constructional difficulty, getting lost in familiar places
Motor speed, gait and mood are relatively spared early on
Contrasts with subcortical dementia: slowing, apathy, retrieval deficit and motor signs
inv: Neuropsychological testing profiling memory, language, praxis and visuospatial skills
MRI looking for hippocampal, temporal, parietal or frontal atrophy pattern
Biomarkers when available: amyloid PET, CSF or plasma p-tau and amyloid; FDG-PET for atypical cases
Screen for reversible contributors: B12, thyroid, depression, medications

case.who: 71-year-old retired schoolteacher from Nakhon Si Thammarat
case.story: Three years of repeating questions, misplacing items and getting lost on the way home; recently she cannot find the right words for common objects.
case.exam: Fluent speech with naming errors, 0/3 recall after delay, unable to copy intersecting pentagons or draw a clock; gait, tone and eye movements normal.
case.tests: MoCA 14/30; MRI shows medial temporal and parietal atrophy; CSF amyloid low with raised p-tau.
case.q: Which cortical dementia fits, and how does she differ from subcortical dementia?
case.a: Alzheimer disease; she shows poor learning, language and visuospatial deficits with preserved motor function, whereas subcortical dementia mostly shows slowing, apathy and improved performance with cues.

det.patho: Cortical dementias arise from neurodegeneration of association cortices. In Alzheimer disease, amyloid plaques and tau tangles begin in the medial temporal lobes and spread to parietal and frontal regions. Frontotemporal lobar degeneration involves tau, TDP-43 or FUS pathology in frontal and anterior temporal lobes. The cortical versus subcortical division is a clinical shorthand with considerable overlap, not a strict pathological boundary.
det.clinical: Patients show prominent amnesia with rapid forgetting, along with aphasia, apraxia, agnosia and visuospatial failure, often with reduced insight. Alzheimer disease classically starts with memory loss, though variants begin with visual (posterior cortical atrophy) or language (logopenic aphasia) problems. FTD begins with behavioural change or language disorder, while memory is relatively intact early. Motor signs usually appear late, which distinguishes this pattern from subcortical syndromes.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis combines the clinical syndrome with neuropsychological profile, MRI atrophy pattern and, increasingly, biomarkers such as amyloid PET or CSF and plasma p-tau. Distinguishing cortical from subcortical features guides the differential: recognition memory is poor in cortical disease but better than recall in subcortical disease. Always exclude reversible factors, including depression, B12 deficiency, thyroid disease, medications and sleep apnoea. Check for mixed pathology in older adults.
det.treatment: Treatment depends on the cause. In Alzheimer disease, cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine give modest symptomatic benefit, and anti-amyloid antibodies such as lecanemab may be considered in selected early cases with ARIA monitoring and APOE genotyping. FTD has no approved disease-modifying drug, so behavioural symptoms are managed with non-drug measures and carefully chosen medication. All patients need risk factor control, safety assessment, driving and legal planning, and caregiver support.
det.prognosis: Gradually progressive over years, ending in dependence; the rate varies by cause and age at onset.
pearls: Aphasia, apraxia and agnosia suggest cortical involvement.
Cueing helps recognition in subcortical dementia but not in Alzheimer encoding failure.
Terms are a bedside heuristic; biomarkers define the actual pathology.
det.thd: Cortical dementia คือกลุ่มอาการสมองเสื่อมที่เกิดจากเปลือกสมองเสียหาย มีความจำใหม่เสียเร็วและไม่ดีขึ้นแม้ได้ตัวช่วย ร่วมกับ aphasia, apraxia, agnosia และมองพื้นที่ไม่ถูก ตัวอย่างคืออัลไซเมอร์ และ FTD ต่างจาก subcortical dementia ที่คิดช้า เฉยเมย และมีอาการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติเร็ว วินิจฉัยโดยทดสอบ neuropsychology, MRI และ biomarker เช่น amyloid PET หรือ p-tau รักษาตามสาเหตุ เช่น cholinesterase inhibitor ในอัลไซเมอร์ พร้อมดูแลผู้ป่วยและผู้ดูแล

name: Cortical disease
formal: Disorders involving cerebral cortex, with focal deficits, seizures or cognitive dysfunction such as aphasia, agnosia and neglect.
simple: Problems in the outer layer of the brain that affect thinking, language, senses or cause seizures.

Cortical sensory loss: impaired graphaesthesia, stereognosis and two-point discrimination

Weakness or field defects that are partial and patterned (e.g. face-arm more than leg)
Cortical dementias with early amnesia, aphasia or visuospatial loss

case.story: Woke unable to find words and her right hand felt clumsy; she can walk normally.
case.exam: Non-fluent aphasia, right face and hand weakness, leg strength normal, cannot identify a coin in the right hand by touch.
case.tests: MRI DWI: restricted diffusion in the left frontal operculum and precentral cortex.
case.q: Is this cortical or subcortical, and which signs tell you?
case.a: Cortical (left MCA superior division branch); aphasia and astereognosis with face-hand weakness are cortical signs that a pure subcortical lacune would not give.

det.patho: This is a localisation concept rather than a single disease. The cerebral cortex holds specialised regions for language, praxis, spatial attention, recognition and primary motor and sensory functions, so damage produces characteristic higher-function deficits. Causes include infarcts and haemorrhages in cortical branches, tumours, encephalitis, trauma, cortical dysplasia and neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer disease, frontotemporal degeneration and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Cortical grey matter is also the generator of most epileptic seizures.
det.clinical: Clues to cortical localisation include aphasia (dominant hemisphere), neglect and anosognosia (usually non-dominant), apraxia, agnosia, Gerstmann or Balint syndromes, cortical sensory loss and homonymous field defects. Motor deficits are usually partial and patchy rather than dense face-arm-leg hemiplegia. Seizures point strongly to cortical involvement. Subcortical disease, by contrast, gives slowed processing, dense pure motor or sensory deficits, and gait and mood disturbance without these higher-function signs.
det.diagnosis: Bedside testing of language, praxis, attention, visuospatial function and cortical sensation identifies the syndrome and side. MRI then defines the lesion and its likely cause; EEG supports seizures or encephalopathy. In slowly progressive syndromes, neuropsychology, amyloid or tau biomarkers and FDG-PET help separate the neurodegenerative causes.
det.treatment: Treatment is directed at the cause: reperfusion and secondary prevention in stroke, surgery or oncological therapy for tumour, antimicrobials or immunotherapy for encephalitis, and disease-specific therapy for dementia. Speech and occupational therapy target aphasia, neglect and apraxia. Antiseizure drugs are used when seizures occur.
det.prognosis: Highly variable; recovery after acute cortical stroke is often substantial within the first months.
pearls: Aphasia, neglect, astereognosis and seizures localise to cortex.
Dense equal face-arm-leg weakness without cortical signs suggests a subcortical lesion.
Cortical ribboning on DWI in rapid dementia suggests CJD.
det.thd: Cortical disease เป็นคำบอกตำแหน่งรอยโรคที่เปลือกสมอง ไม่ใช่โรคเดียว อาการที่บ่งว่าเป็นเปลือกสมองได้แก่ พูดผิดปกติ (aphasia) ละเลยซีกหนึ่ง (neglect) จำสิ่งของไม่ได้ ทำท่าทางไม่ได้ (apraxia) สูญเสียความรู้สึกระดับสูง และชัก สาเหตุมีทั้งหลอดเลือดสมอง เนื้องอก สมองอักเสบ และโรคสมองเสื่อม ตรวจด้วย MRI และ EEG แล้วรักษาตามสาเหตุ

name: Cortical myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus from sensorimotor cortex hyperexcitability, focal, action- or stimulus-sensitive, with giant SEPs; in post-hypoxic, metabolic and progressive myoclonic epilepsies.
simple: Quick shock-like jerks of muscles caused by overactive brain surface cells.

feat: Very brief (under about 50 ms) shock-like jerks, mostly distal (fingers, hand, face), spontaneous or provoked by action, touch, sound or light
Focal, multifocal or generalised; spread to adjacent muscles and into epilepsia partialis continua or generalised seizures can occur
Action myoclonus after hypoxic brain injury (Lance–Adams syndrome) makes reaching and standing difficult; negative myoclonus (asterixis-like lapses) often coexists

Causes: post-hypoxic injury, metabolic encephalopathy (uraemia, liver failure), drugs and toxins, stroke, tumour or Rasmussen encephalitis in focal forms; neurodegenerative disease; and progressive myoclonic epilepsies
In epilepsy patients, myoclonus may be part of a syndrome such as juvenile myoclonic epilepsy or Unverricht–Lundborg disease
inv: EEG with jerk-locked back-averaging shows a cortical spike or sharp wave preceding the jerk by about 20 ms for hand muscles
Somatosensory evoked potentials may show giant cortical potentials and an enhanced long-loop C reflex on EMG

case.who: 52-year-old man from Phuket, three weeks after a drowning and cardiac arrest
case.story: He is now awake and speaking, but every attempt to reach for a cup produces violent jerks of the arm, and he cannot stand without his legs jerking.
case.exam: Action- and stimulus-sensitive multifocal myoclonus, worse with intention and little at rest; mild ataxia; cognition relatively preserved.
case.tests: EEG with back-averaging shows a cortical spike before each jerk; SEPs are giant.
case.q: What is the syndrome and what are the drugs of first choice?
case.a: Lance–Adams syndrome (chronic post-hypoxic cortical action myoclonus); levetiracetam, valproate, clonazepam or piracetam, often in combination.

18 - Myoclonus: Phenomenology, etiology, physiology, and treatment

det.patho: Cortical myoclonus results from hyperexcitable sensorimotor cortex that produces a brief synchronised discharge, which travels quickly through the corticospinal tract to muscles. The cortical hyperexcitability is shown by giant SEPs and enhanced transcortical reflexes; the cerebellum and thalamus contribute through loss of inhibitory control. In post-hypoxic cases, selective loss of cerebellar and cortical inhibitory neurons is proposed.
det.clinical: Jerks may arise at rest but action and sensory stimuli usually provoke them, and the stimulus-sensitive forms impair writing, reaching and walking. Focal cortical myoclonus due to a lesion can coexist with epilepsia partialis continua. Multifocal and generalised cortical myoclonus occur in metabolic encephalopathies, neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer disease, corticobasal syndrome and Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease, and in progressive myoclonic epilepsies. Negative myoclonus is a short lapse of muscle activity that accompanies positive jerks.
det.diagnosis: Start with a thorough bedside description and exclude reversible causes: electrolytes, uraemia, liver failure, hypoxia, infection and drugs (for example opioids, antibiotics such as cefepime, gabapentinoids, lithium and bismuth). The EEG-EMG tests show cortical spikes preceding jerks, giant SEPs and a C reflex; long-latency reflexes support a cortical origin. MRI looks for structural lesions, and gene or antibody testing is used in progressive and encephalitic presentations. Distinguish from subcortical and functional jerks by the duration and polymyography pattern.
det.treatment: Treat the cause, withdraw offending drugs and correct metabolic disturbances. Symptomatic therapy relies on levetiracetam (up to about 3,000 mg/day), valproate, piracetam and clonazepam, often in combination; brivaracetam, perampanel and zonisamide are alternatives, particularly in progressive myoclonic epilepsies, while phenytoin and carbamazepine may worsen some syndromes. Avoid lamotrigine in some myoclonic epilepsies. Rehabilitation and adaptive devices help action myoclonus.
det.prognosis: Depends on the cause: metabolic and drug-related jerks resolve with correction, while Lance–Adams syndrome is chronic but often improves over years, and degenerative forms progress.
pearls: Action- and stimulus-sensitive jerks of the hands after cardiac arrest point to Lance–Adams syndrome.
Back-averaged EEG showing a spike before the jerk proves a cortical origin.
Levetiracetam, valproate and piracetam are the backbone of therapy; carbamazepine can make myoclonus worse.
det.thd: Cortical myoclonus คือการกระตุกสั้น ๆ ที่เกิดจากการปล่อยไฟฟ้าผิดปกติของ sensorimotor cortex มักที่มือและนิ้ว ไวต่อการเคลื่อนไหวและสิ่งกระตุ้น พบหลังขาดออกซิเจน (Lance–Adams syndrome), metabolic encephalopathy, ยาบางชนิด และ progressive myoclonic epilepsy การตรวจ EEG back-averaging และ giant SEP ช่วยยืนยันตำแหน่ง รักษาโดยแก้สาเหตุและใช้ levetiracetam, valproate, piracetam หรือ clonazepam

qx.stem: A 40-year-old woman from Songkhla has brief, irregular, action-induced jerks of the right hand after a left frontal stroke, worse when she reaches for objects. Back-averaging of EEG against rectified EMG shows a cortical spike preceding the jerk by about 20 ms, and somatosensory evoked potentials show giant cortical potentials.
qx.q: Which drug is commonly used?

Levetiracetam, piracetam or valproate
Haloperidol

qx.why: A time-locked cortical correlate and giant SEPs confirm cortical myoclonus, which responds to levetiracetam, piracetam, valproate and clonazepam. Carbamazepine, phenytoin and sometimes lamotrigine can aggravate some myoclonic epilepsies and progressive myoclonic syndromes, and neither haloperidol nor baclofen treats cortical hyperexcitability.

qx.stem: A 55-year-old man survived a cardiac arrest from ventricular fibrillation three months ago. He is now alert but has disabling jerks of his arms and legs whenever he reaches for objects or tries to stand, while he is still at rest. Somatosensory evoked potentials show giant cortical responses, and back-averaging reveals a cortical spike before each jerk.
qx.q: Which medication combination is most appropriate?
opts: Levetiracetam with clonazepam or valproate
Haloperidol with benztropine
Carbidopa-levodopa
Phenytoin and carbamazepine
Tetrabenazine
qx.why: Chronic post-hypoxic action myoclonus (Lance-Adams syndrome) is cortical in origin, as shown by giant SEPs and a preceding cortical spike. Levetiracetam, valproate, clonazepam and piracetam are the effective agents, often combined. Sodium-channel drugs such as phenytoin and carbamazepine can worsen myoclonus, and dopaminergic or antidopaminergic agents do not help.

det.patho: Cortical tremor is a rhythmic form of cortical myoclonus: hyperexcitable sensorimotor cortex fires repeated brief discharges that look like tremor. It is the hallmark of familial adult myoclonic epilepsy (FAME), caused by intronic TTTCA/TTTTA pentanucleotide repeat expansions in genes such as SAMD12 (common in Japan and reported in Thailand and China), STARD7, MARCHF6, YEATS2 and others. Cerebellar involvement is also proposed, since Purkinje cell pathology has been described. Acquired cortical tremor occasionally follows other cortical disease.
det.clinical: Patients have fine, jerky hand tremor on posture and action from early adulthood, sometimes with voice or leg involvement, and generalised tonic-clonic seizures that are typically infrequent and well controlled. Photosensitivity and sleep deprivation aggravate symptoms. Many are misdiagnosed with essential tremor for years. Mild cognitive or cerebellar features may appear with age.
det.diagnosis: Suspect cortical tremor when a tremor looks jerky, is drug-resistant to beta-blockers, or coexists with seizures or a dominant family history. EMG shows short irregular bursts, and neurophysiology reveals giant SEPs, enhanced C-reflexes and a back-averaged cortical potential. EEG may be normal or show generalised discharges and photosensitivity. Repeat-expansion testing requires long-read or repeat-primed methods, as standard panels miss it.
det.treatment: Antiseizure drugs with anti-myoclonic effect, such as valproate, levetiracetam, clonazepam, perampanel or primidone, reduce jerks and prevent seizures. Avoid drugs that may worsen myoclonus (carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine in some). Advise about sleep and photic triggers. Provide genetic counselling for this dominant condition.
det.prognosis: Generally benign with slow progression; seizures are usually easily controlled, though tremor may worsen in later life.
pearls: Jerky 'essential tremor' plus a seizure history: think cortical tremor and FAME.
Giant SEPs separate cortical tremor from essential tremor.
FAME is caused by intronic repeat expansions that routine exome sequencing misses.

det.patho: In this neurophysiological category the jerk arises from abnormal interaction between cortex and thalamus, so the discharge is widespread and bilaterally synchronous rather than coming from a focal cortical site. It is best exemplified by myoclonic seizures in genetic generalised epilepsies such as juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, and is linked to the same thalamocortical circuits that generate spike-wave discharges. It may also contribute to myoclonus in some progressive myoclonic epilepsies and post-hypoxic states. The exact boundaries of this category are not uniformly defined.
det.clinical: Patients have brief bilateral jerks, mostly of the arms and shoulders, often in the morning and triggered by sleep deprivation, alcohol, stress or photic stimulation. Consciousness is preserved during isolated jerks. Generalised tonic-clonic seizures and absences commonly accompany them. In progressive conditions there are additional cognitive, cerebellar or visual signs.
det.diagnosis: EEG with sleep deprivation and photic stimulation typically shows generalised polyspike-wave discharges, time-locked to jerks on simultaneous EMG. MRI is normal in genetic generalised epilepsy; abnormal imaging, progressive deficits or a slow background suggest a progressive myoclonic epilepsy or other symptomatic cause. History of morning jerks is often missed unless specifically asked.
det.treatment: Broad-spectrum antiseizure drugs are used: valproate is the most effective but should be avoided in women of childbearing potential where possible; levetiracetam, lamotrigine (may worsen myoclonus in some) and topiramate are alternatives. Avoid carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin and gabapentin, which can aggravate myoclonic seizures. Regular sleep and avoiding alcohol excess are essential.
det.prognosis: Usually well controlled in genetic generalised epilepsy, though lifelong treatment is often needed.

det.patho: Corticobasal degeneration is a four-repeat tauopathy with ballooned neurons and astrocytic plaques in frontoparietal cortex, basal ganglia and substantia nigra. The term corticobasal syndrome describes the bedside picture, which matches CBD pathology in only about half of cases; the rest prove to be PSP, Alzheimer disease, FTLD-TDP or others. It is sporadic, rare and usually begins after 60.
det.clinical: Classically one limb becomes stiff, slow and useless, with dystonic posturing, myoclonus and apraxia that make the hand clumsier than weakness would explain. Alien-limb behaviour, cortical sensory deficits and mirror movements may appear. Other presentations include a frontal behavioural-spatial syndrome, non-fluent aphasia (often with apraxia of speech) and a PSP-like picture. Over time the other side becomes involved, followed by dysphagia, falls and dementia.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, using consensus criteria that separate possible and probable CBD by the combination of asymmetric motor and cortical signs. MRI and FDG-PET show asymmetric frontoparietal involvement; DAT imaging is abnormal and does not distinguish it from PD. Amyloid or tau biomarkers identify an Alzheimer cause, which matters for counselling and trials. Exclude stroke, tumour, CJD (rapid course, DWI cortical ribbon) and functional disorders.
det.treatment: No therapy modifies the disease. Levodopa trials (up to about 1 g/day) are reasonable but benefit is usually small. Botulinum toxin eases painful fixed dystonia, and levetiracetam or clonazepam may reduce myoclonus. Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and swallow care, and planning for advanced care are the core.
det.prognosis: Median survival from first symptoms is roughly six to eight years, with death usually from aspiration or immobility.
pearls: A useless, stiff, jerky hand with apraxia and poor levodopa response: think corticobasal syndrome.
CBS is a clinical label; CBD is a pathological one — they do not always coincide.
Check for Alzheimer biomarkers; a substantial minority of CBS is due to AD.

det.patho: CBS is a clinical syndrome. Corticobasal degeneration (a 4-repeat tauopathy with ballooned neurons and astrocytic plaques) explains roughly half; other causes include PSP, Alzheimer disease, FTLD-TDP (notably GRN mutations) and occasionally prion disease. Atrophy affects perirolandic and parietal cortex and basal ganglia asymmetrically.
det.clinical: Typically a limb becomes stiff, clumsy and apraxic, followed by dystonia, myoclonus and cortical sensory loss. Alien limb behaviour may include levitation or intermanual conflict. Speech apraxia, nonfluent aphasia, executive dysfunction and gait failure follow; some patients present primarily with cognitive or language problems.
det.diagnosis: Armstrong 2013 criteria define probable and possible CBS based on asymmetric motor and cortical signs. Biomarkers help identify underlying pathology: amyloid/tau PET or CSF for Alzheimer, and genetic testing (GRN, MAPT) if familial. DWI MRI and RT-QuIC exclude CJD when progression is fast.
det.treatment: Treatment is symptomatic: trial of levodopa (usually limited effect), levetiracetam or clonazepam for myoclonus, botulinum toxin for painful dystonia, physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy. Plan for swallowing, falls and advance care. Tau-targeted therapies remain experimental.
det.prognosis: Progressive with median survival around 6–8 years from onset.
pearls: Asymmetric rigidity plus apraxia plus cortical sensory loss = CBS.
CBS describes the clinic; CBD names the pathology.
Test Alzheimer biomarkers — a quarter may have AD pathology.

det.patho: Valsalva transiently raises intrathoracic and intracranial venous pressure. In primary cough headache this may activate pain-sensitive structures in a person with relatively crowded posterior fossa or venous sensitivity. In secondary forms, obstruction at the foramen magnum creates pressure dissociation that pulls the hindbrain downward.
det.clinical: Primary cough headache is uncommon, typically affects men over 40, and produces brief, explosive bilateral pain. Secondary cough headache tends to start younger, last longer and coexist with dizziness, ataxia or sensory symptoms. Thunderclap-like severity alone does not distinguish them.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 requires headache brought on only by coughing, straining or Valsalva, with sudden onset and duration up to two hours. Neuroimaging is mandatory because a substantial proportion are secondary. Exclude SIH, RCVS and aneurysm when features are atypical.
det.treatment: Indomethacin is the usual preventive for primary cough headache; acetazolamide, topiramate or propranolol are alternatives. Treat underlying chronic cough. Secondary forms are managed by their cause, for example decompression for symptomatic Chiari I.
det.prognosis: Primary cough headache often remits within months to a few years.
pearls: Every cough headache deserves an MRI looking at the foramen magnum.
Indomethacin response does not prove a primary cause.

det.patho: Task-specific dystonia reflects maladaptive plasticity: reduced cortical inhibition and blurring of sensory representations of the fingers after prolonged repetitive practice, in a predisposed individual. Basal ganglia–cerebellar networks controlling skilled movement are implicated.
det.clinical: Onset is gradual, often noticed as loss of control or speed. The dystonia is restricted to the task initially, and sensory tricks may help. It can spread to related tasks or the other hand over years. Embouchure dystonia affects brass and woodwind players.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical by observing the triggering task. Rule out entrapment neuropathy, orthopaedic problems and early parkinsonism; consider Wilson disease in patients under 50 with any atypical feature.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin injected into the overactive muscles under EMG or ultrasound guidance is first line. Sensorimotor retraining, ergonomic adaptations (thicker pens, instrument changes) and occupational therapy help. Trihexyphenidyl is used occasionally. Selected severe cases have been treated with thalamotomy or DBS in specialised centres.
det.prognosis: Usually persistent but often stable; careers can be maintained with treatment and adaptation.
pearls: Normal at rest, abnormal only with the task = task-specific dystonia.
Examine during the actual task — bring the pen or instrument.
Botulinum toxin works best with precise muscle targeting.
det.thd: Craft cramp หรือ task-specific dystonia คือ dystonia เฉพาะที่ซึ่งเกิดเมื่อทำงานเฉพาะอย่าง เช่น เขียนหนังสือ เล่นดนตรี หรือพิมพ์ดีด นิ้วหรือข้อมือบิดเกร็งเองขณะทำงานนั้น แต่ทำงานอื่นได้ปกติ เกิดจากวงจรสมองควบคุมการเคลื่อนไหวปรับตัวผิดปกติหลังฝึกซ้ำนาน ๆ วินิจฉัยจากการดูขณะทำงาน รักษาด้วย botulinum toxin การฝึกใหม่ และปรับอุปกรณ์

name: Cramp-fasciculation syndrome
formal: Benign peripheral nerve hyperexcitability disorder with muscle cramps, fasciculations, and myokymia, sometimes associated with CASPR2 or LGI1 antibodies.
simple: A condition of frequent muscle cramps and twitching with no weakness.
more: EMG shows fasciculations; check CASPR2 antibodies; carbamazepine or sodium channel blockers help.
th: ภาวะเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายไวเกิน ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อเป็นตะคริวบ่อย เต้นกระตุก และปวดหลังออกกำลัง แต่ไม่มีอ่อนแรงหรือลีบ มักเป็นโรคไม่ร้ายแรง

feat: Frequent painful cramps, especially calves and feet, triggered by exercise
Widespread fasciculations, muscle aching, stiffness and exercise intolerance
No weakness, wasting or upper motor neuron signs; reflexes normal

case.story: Eight months of night cramps and twitching in both calves and thighs; he read about ALS online and is anxious.
case.exam: Visible fasciculations in both calves, full strength, no wasting, normal reflexes, no Babinski.
case.tests: CK 260 U/L; EMG shows fasciculations with no fibrillations or chronic neurogenic change; CASPR2 negative.
case.q: Why is this not motor neuron disease, and what can help?

det.patho: Spontaneous ectopic firing arises in distal motor axons and terminals, producing fasciculations and cramps. Some cases are autoimmune, with antibodies to CASPR2 or LGI1 reducing potassium channel function at juxtaparanodes; most are idiopathic. Associations include thymoma, other autoimmune disease and anxiety. Familial forms exist but are rare.
det.clinical: Patients are usually young to middle-aged adults with cramps, twitching, muscle pain and fatigue that worsen after exercise. Strength and muscle bulk stay normal throughout, which is the key distinction from motor neuron disease. Symptoms fluctuate and may persist for years. Health anxiety about ALS is common and part of the burden.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis combines the clinical picture with EMG showing fasciculations and no denervation; repetitive nerve stimulation may show after-discharges. Exclude metabolic causes (hypothyroidism, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia), drugs and early ALS. Neuromyotonic discharges point instead toward Isaacs syndrome. Antibody testing identifies an autoimmune subgroup that warrants a tumour search.
det.treatment: Explanation and reassurance form the foundation. For bothersome symptoms, sodium-channel–blocking drugs such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine or mexiletine reduce cramps; gabapentin or pregabalin help some. Stretching and hydration are reasonable adjuncts. Immunotherapy is reserved for antibody-positive patients with severe disease.
det.prognosis: Benign; most patients stabilise or improve, and progression to ALS is not expected.
pearls: Fasciculations with normal strength and a clean EMG are almost never ALS.
Check CASPR2 antibodies in severe or treatment-resistant cases.
Sodium-channel blockers are the main symptomatic treatment.
det.thd: Cramp-fasciculation syndrome คือภาวะปลายประสาทไวเกิน มีตะคริวบ่อยและกล้ามเนื้อเต้นกระตุกทั่วตัว แต่ไม่มีอ่อนแรงหรือลีบ ต่างจาก ALS ตรวจ EMG พบ fasciculation โดยไม่มี denervation บางรายมี CASPR2 antibody ต้องตัดสาเหตุจากเกลือแร่และไทรอยด์ รักษาด้วยการอธิบายให้สบายใจ และยากลุ่ม sodium-channel blocker เช่น carbamazepine เมื่ออาการรบกวน โรคไม่ลุกลาม

8. Cramps, Muscle Stiffness, and Exercise Intolerance

det.patho: Cramps arise from hyperexcitable distal motor nerve terminals firing at high frequency, producing involuntary sustained contraction of a shortened muscle. Factors that increase nerve excitability (electrolyte shifts, denervation, fatigue) promote them. True cramps are electrically active, unlike metabolic contractures.
det.clinical: Most cramps are benign, nocturnal, and affect calves or feet. They are common in older adults, pregnancy and during dialysis. Clinically important associations include motor neuron disease, neuropathy, radiculopathy, cirrhosis, hypothyroidism and drugs. Persistent soreness afterwards is common.
det.diagnosis: History is usually sufficient. A focused exam for weakness, wasting, fasciculations and reflex change determines whether further testing is needed. Blood tests target reversible causes. EMG is reserved for abnormal signs.
det.treatment: Regular calf stretching and correction of precipitating factors are first steps. Quinine is no longer recommended for routine use because of serious haematological and cardiac risks. Options with limited evidence include magnesium (mainly in pregnancy), mexiletine, gabapentinoids and vitamin B complex; treat underlying disease.
det.prognosis: Benign cramps are troublesome but harmless; prognosis depends on any underlying disorder.
pearls: Cramps with fasciculations and wasting need EMG for motor neuron disease.
Contractures in McArdle disease are electrically silent, unlike cramps.
Check the medication list: diuretics and statins are common culprits.
det.thd: ตะคริวคือการหดเกร็งของกล้ามเนื้อเองที่เจ็บปวด มักเป็นที่น่องตอนกลางคืน เกิดจากปลายประสาทสั่งการทำงานไวเกิน พบบ่อยในผู้สูงอายุ คนตั้งครรภ์ ผู้ฟอกไต และผู้ใช้ยาขับปัสสาวะ ตรวจเกลือแร่และทบทวนยา ถ้ามีกล้ามเนื้อลีบหรือเต้นกระตุกต้องส่ง EMG รักษาโดยยืดกล้ามเนื้อและแก้สาเหตุ

name: Cranial dystonias
formal: Focal dystonias affecting face, jaw, tongue, eyelids or neck, including blepharospasm, oromandibular dystonia and Meige syndrome.
simple: Involuntary muscle spasms of the face, mouth, jaw or eyelids.
th: Cranial dystonias คือ focal dystonia ของใบหน้า ปาก ขากรรไกร ลิ้น และกล่องเสียง ได้แก่ blepharospasm, oromandibular dystonia, Meige syndrome และ spasmodic dysphonia มักเริ่มช่วงอายุ 50–60 ปี มีตัวช่วยเฉพาะ (sensory trick) และรักษาหลักด้วย botulinum toxin เป็นรายกล้ามเนื้อ
tempoNote: Gradual onset in middle or later life; spread to neighbouring cranial regions during the first few years, then a stable course with fluctuation tied to stress and fatigue
feat: Blepharospasm: frequent blinking progressing to forced eye closure, with functional blindness in severe cases
Oromandibular dystonia: jaw opening, closing or deviation, lip pursing, tongue protrusion or curling, which interfere with eating, speech and swallowing, and may cause tooth damage or jaw pain
Meige syndrome combines blepharospasm and oromandibular dystonia; laryngeal dystonia (spasmodic dysphonia) and cervical dystonia are related craniocervical forms
Sensory tricks (touching the face, chewing gum, a toothpick or cigarette in the mouth) briefly relieve spasms, and speech or concentration may reduce them
Tardive forms follow dopamine blockers and tend to be more disabling; some cases follow dental or facial procedures or trauma
inv: Clinical diagnosis; medication and dental history, with questions about onset after dental work or trauma
Exclude tardive syndromes, Wilson disease (copper studies under about 50 years), neuroacanthocytosis and neurodegenerative parkinsonism when there are other signs
MRI brain when onset is young, asymmetric or accompanied by additional neurological signs; EMG guidance at toxin injection for deep jaw muscles

case.who: 63-year-old woman, retired seamstress from Nakhon Pathom
case.story: Two years of heavy blinking, then her jaw began to clench and open while she eats and her tongue pushes against her teeth. Chewing gum or touching her chin stops the movements for a while. She has never taken antipsychotic drugs.
case.exam: Bilateral forceful eyelid closure, intermittent jaw opening with tongue protrusion, normal strength, no rigidity or tremor; speech slightly distorted during jaw spasms.
case.tests: Copper and ceruloplasmin normal; MRI shows only mild small-vessel change.
case.q: Name the syndrome and the first-line approach.
case.a: Meige syndrome (blepharospasm with oromandibular dystonia); botulinum toxin to orbicularis oculi and to the affected jaw muscles, with a dental review.

read.where: 12 Dystonia: Phenomenology, classification, etiology, pathology, biochemistry, and genetics

Chapter 34: Functional (Psychogenic) Movement Disorders: Phenomenology, Diagnosis and Treatment

det.patho: Cranial dystonias are adult-onset focal dystonias with disordered basal ganglia and brainstem sensorimotor integration, reduced inhibition at cortical and brainstem levels, and altered blink and jaw reflex excitability. Most are idiopathic; a minority carry mutations in dystonia genes, and others are secondary to drugs, brainstem or basal ganglia lesions, or degenerative disease.
det.clinical: Blepharospasm is the commonest and may stay isolated or spread to the lower face and jaw. Oromandibular dystonia is classified as jaw-closing, jaw-opening, jaw-deviating or lingual, and some patients combine them. Activities that use the mouth, like eating or speaking, may trigger or suppress the spasm, and sensory tricks are classically present. Patients are often misdiagnosed as having temporomandibular joint disease, a psychiatric disorder or a stroke before the diagnosis is made. Task-specific forms occur in wind instrument players, singers and speakers.
det.diagnosis: Recognition is clinical. The abnormal movements are patterned, action-induced and have a geste antagoniste. The key work is to find secondary causes: drug exposure, neuroleptic-induced tardive syndromes, Wilson disease and neuroacanthocytosis in young patients, and parkinsonian disorders when bradykinesia or gait change is present. MRI is not needed in classic typical adult-onset cases. Electromyography can map the involved muscles before botulinum toxin treatment.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin is first-line: pretarsal orbicularis oculi for blepharospasm, masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid for jaw closing, and lateral pterygoid or submental muscles for jaw opening, with doses adjusted to avoid dysphagia. Oral agents (trihexyphenidyl, baclofen, clonazepam, tetrabenazine or deutetrabenazine) help some patients but cause sedation or cognitive effects. Dental splints and bite guards protect teeth; for severe, drug-resistant disease, globus pallidus internus deep brain stimulation can be very effective, especially in Meige syndrome. Speech and swallowing therapy are useful additions.
det.prognosis: The course is chronic and lifelong with periods of variable severity; botulinum toxin or stimulation usually gives long-term control and patients keep function.
pearls: Jaw or tongue spasms in an older woman who has never taken a neuroleptic still count as dystonia, not temporomandibular joint disease.
Always ask for tardive causes in cranial dystonia.
Injecting jaw-opening muscles with toxin needs care because of swallowing difficulty.
det.thd: Cranial dystonias คือ dystonia ที่ใบหน้า ปาก ขากรรไกร ลิ้น และกล่องเสียง เช่น blepharospasm, oromandibular dystonia และ Meige syndrome มักเริ่มช่วงวัยกลางคนและมีการแตะหน้าหรือเคี้ยวหมากฝรั่งแล้วดีขึ้นชั่วคราว ควรซักประวัติยาปิดกั้น dopamine และตรวจหา Wilson disease ในคนอายุน้อย การรักษาหลักคือฉีด botulinum toxin เฉพาะกล้ามเนื้อ และใช้ DBS ที่ GPi ในรายรุนแรงที่ดื้อต่อการรักษา

formal: Disease of one or more cranial nerves with sensory, motor or autonomic dysfunction; causes include compression, infection, ischaemia and inflammation.
simple: Damage to one of the nerves running from the brain to the face, eyes, ears or throat.
th: ความผิดปกติของเส้นประสาทสมองหนึ่งเส้นหรือหลายเส้น ทำให้การรับความรู้สึก การเคลื่อนไหว หรือหน้าที่อัตโนมัติเสีย สาเหตุเช่นการกดทับ ติดเชื้อ ขาดเลือด และการอักเสบ

Microvascular palsies in diabetics: painful, pupil-sparing III, isolated VI or IV, improving over 3 months

det.patho: Cranial nerves can be damaged in the brainstem, subarachnoid space, skull base foramina, cavernous sinus, orbit or face. Mechanisms include compression, ischaemia of the vasa nervorum, demyelination, inflammation, infection and infiltration by tumour.
det.clinical: Clinical features depend on the nerve affected. Pain, multiplicity, progression, systemic symptoms or other neurological signs raise concern for a serious cause. Pattern recognition (e.g. cavernous sinus, jugular foramen, cerebellopontine angle) localises the lesion.
det.diagnosis: Localise the lesion clinically, then image the entire nerve path with contrast MRI. Laboratory and CSF tests follow the clinical context. Biopsy of skull base lesions or meninges may be necessary.
det.treatment: Treat the cause. Microvascular palsies are managed with risk factor control and observation; Bell palsy with early steroids; infections with antimicrobials; tumours with oncological therapy. Symptomatic care includes eye protection, prisms or patching for diplopia, and swallowing support.
det.prognosis: Microvascular and idiopathic palsies usually recover; outcomes in infiltrative or compressive disease depend on the cause.
pearls: Painful pupil-involving III palsy needs urgent vascular imaging.
More than one cranial nerve = not microvascular; investigate fully.
In Thailand, numb chin or progressive cranial palsies: examine the nasopharynx.
det.thd: Cranial neuropathy คือความผิดปกติของเส้นประสาทสมองเส้นเดียวหรือหลายเส้น สาเหตุมีทั้งการขาดเลือด เช่น ในผู้ป่วยเบาหวาน การกดทับจากเนื้องอก การติดเชื้อ เช่น วัณโรค cryptococcus และงูสวัด และการอักเสบ ถ้าเป็นหลายเส้นหรือเป็นมากขึ้นต้องตรวจละเอียด การตรวจหลักคือ MRI พร้อมสารทึบรังสีตลอดแนวเส้นประสาท และน้ำไขสันหลัง การรักษาตามสาเหตุ

name: Craniopharyngioma
formal: Suprasellar epithelial tumour from Rathke pouch remnants causing bitemporal hemianopia, endocrine deficits and hydrocephalus.
simple: A non-cancerous tumour near the pituitary gland that can affect vision and hormones.
th: เนื้องอกไม่ร้ายแต่ผ่าตัดยากบริเวณ sellar และ suprasellar มีถุงน้ำและหินปูน ทำให้ตามัว ฮอร์โมนต่ำ เบาจืด และน้ำหนักขึ้นจากการทำลาย hypothalamus มี 2 ชนิด คือ adamantinomatous (CTNNB1) ในเด็ก และ papillary (BRAF V600E) ในผู้ใหญ่ ซึ่งตอบสนองต่อยา BRAF/MEK inhibitor

feat: Bimodal age: children 5-14 years and adults 50-75 years
Visual loss with asymmetric bitemporal or irregular field defects and optic atrophy in the majority; papilloedema in about a third of children
Pituitary and hypothalamic dysfunction: growth hormone and gonadotropin deficiency first, diabetes insipidus in about a fifth, obesity and sleep or temperature disturbance

case.story: Six months of headaches, slowing growth, and difficulty seeing the blackboard; he has been drinking more water.
case.exam: Height below the 3rd percentile, bitemporal field loss, optic disc pallor, mild papilloedema.
case.tests: MRI shows a 4 cm suprasellar cystic and solid mass with calcification and hydrocephalus; pituitary tests show low IGF-1, low free T4 and low cortisol, with polyuria. Resection: adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma, beta-catenin mutated.
case.q: What factors determine surgical strategy and what is the new option for the papillary type?
case.a: Hypothalamic involvement guides how radical to be (limited resection plus proton radiotherapy often preferred to preserve the hypothalamus and quality of life). Papillary tumours with BRAF V600E respond to BRAF plus MEK inhibitors (dabrafenib plus trametinib or vemurafenib plus cobimetinib).

read.where: Chapter 9 Adult Tumors of Pediatric Origin
Chapter 11: Sella and Central Skull Base

det.patho: Craniopharyngiomas are benign epithelial tumours (CNS WHO grade 1) of the sellar region, from remnants of Rathke pouch. CNS5 separates adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma, which predominates in children, with CTNNB1 mutation, cysts of motor-oil fluid, calcification and wet keratin, from papillary craniopharyngioma of adults with BRAF V600E mutation and no calcification. Both adhere to the hypothalamus and optic apparatus and incite gliosis, making complete removal risky.
det.clinical: The book highlights the three clusters: visual disturbance (early field loss and optic atrophy), endocrine insufficiency (growth failure, delayed puberty, hypogonadism, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, diabetes insipidus) and neurological effects (headache, hydrocephalus, memory problems, appetite and sleep disturbance). Children often present late with unrecognised deficits. Hypothalamic damage before or after surgery causes hyperphagia, obesity, and behavioural problems, often more disabling than the tumour itself.
det.diagnosis: MRI with contrast and thin-slice CT for calcification usually suggest the diagnosis; sellar pathology (pituitary adenoma, Rathke cleft cyst, germinoma, optic pathway glioma, hypothalamic hamartoma) is the differential. Ophthalmological and endocrine evaluation precede surgery. Molecular testing for BRAF V600E and CTNNB1 supports histology and identifies candidates for targeted therapy. Preoperative steroids should be given before surgery to avoid adrenal crisis.
det.treatment: Management is multimodal. Options include gross total resection when the hypothalamus is spared, or limited resection with proton or photon radiotherapy for tumours that involve the hypothalamus, because radiation after subtotal removal gives similar control with less endocrine and hypothalamic injury. Cysts can be drained or treated with Ommaya reservoir and intracystic interferon or bleomycin. For BRAF V600E papillary tumours BRAF plus MEK inhibitors can shrink the tumour dramatically, sometimes avoiding surgery. Lifelong endocrine replacement and visual and hypothalamic obesity management are required; GLP-1 agonists and setmelanotide are being tested for hypothalamic obesity.
det.prognosis: Overall survival is high (about 85-95 percent at ten years) but recurrence is frequent and morbidity from visual, endocrine and hypothalamic sequelae is substantial.
pearls: Child with growth failure, bitemporal hemianopia and calcified suprasellar cyst: craniopharyngioma.
BRAF V600E in papillary craniopharyngioma allows neoadjuvant targeted therapy.
Give stress-dose hydrocortisone before surgery and watch sodium and urine output for diabetes insipidus afterward.
det.thd: Craniopharyngioma เป็นเนื้องอกไม่ร้ายบริเวณ sella และ suprasellar มักมีถุงน้ำและหินปูน ทำให้ตามัว ปวดศีรษะ ฮอร์โมนต่ำ เด็กเตี้ยลง เบาจืด และน้ำหนักเพิ่มจากการทำลาย hypothalamus ชนิด adamantinomatous พบในเด็ก ส่วนชนิด papillary พบในผู้ใหญ่และมี BRAF V600E ซึ่งตอบสนองต่อ dabrafenib ร่วมกับ trametinib การรักษาคือผ่าตัดและ/หรือฉายรังสี พร้อมฮอร์โมนทดแทนตลอดชีวิต

qx.stem: A 46-year-old man from Chanthaburi has loss of the outer halves of both visual fields and fatigue. MRI shows a mostly solid suprasellar mass within the third ventricle without calcification. Morning cortisol and free T4 are low. Partial resection is performed, and pathology shows a papillary craniopharyngioma with a BRAF V600E mutation; the residual tumour grows within six months.
qx.q: Which systemic therapy is most likely to shrink the residual tumour?
opts: Temozolomide
Dabrafenib combined with trametinib
Imatinib
Cabergoline
Intracystic bleomycin
qx.why: Papillary craniopharyngiomas of adults carry BRAF V600E in almost all cases, and combined BRAF and MEK inhibition with dabrafenib and trametinib has produced high response rates in a phase 2 trial. Adamantinomatous tumours of children instead have CTNNB1 mutations and are often cystic, where intracystic therapy was used. Cabergoline treats prolactinoma and the other drugs have no proven role.

qx.stem: A 7-year-old boy from Ubon Ratchathani has slow growth, bitemporal visual field loss and headache. CT shows a suprasellar mass containing coarse calcification and cystic components. MRI shows a multiloculated cystic lesion with a thick enhancing wall, T1-hyperintense cyst contents and extension toward the third ventricle; the sella itself is normal in size.
qx.q: Which diagnosis best explains the findings?
opts: Pituitary macroadenoma with apoplexy
Adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma
Rathke cleft cyst with no calcification
Optic pathway glioma in NF1
Suprasellar germinoma
qx.why: A calcified, cystic suprasellar mass with T1-bright proteinaceous fluid in a child is characteristic of adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma (CTNNB1-mutated in WHO CNS5). A macroadenoma enlarges the sella and arises from below, and a Rathke cleft cyst rarely calcifies or enhances thickly. Hypopituitarism and diabetes insipidus should be assessed before and after surgery.
