name: Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD)
formal: Prion disease with rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, ataxia and akinetic mutism; MRI cortical ribboning, periodic EEG complexes and positive RT-QuIC.
simple: A rare, rapidly worsening brain disease from abnormal prion proteins, causing dementia and jerking.
more: Diagnostic EEG, DWI MRI and CSF 14-3-3 or total tau support; RT-QuIC on CSF has high sensitivity and specificity. Sporadic form predominates, with PRNP mutation in genetic types and variant CJD linked to bovine spongiform encephalopathy. Old term for combined degeneration of cortex, striatum and spinal cord, referring to Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
th: โรคพรีออน — สมองเสื่อมเร็วมากภายในเดือน กระตุก (myoclonus) เดินเซ
tempoNote: Rapidly progressive over weeks to months
feat: Rapidly progressive dementia
Startle-sensitive myoclonus
Ataxia, visual disturbance, pyramidal/extrapyramidal signs, akinetic mutism
inv: MRI DWI: cortical ribboning and/or caudate–putamen restriction
CSF RT-QuIC (high specificity), 14-3-3
EEG periodic sharp-wave complexes

case.story: Within 3 months went from working to needing help dressing; jerks when startled.
case.exam: Disoriented, startle myoclonus, gait ataxia.
case.tests: MRI DWI: cortical ribboning and bilateral caudate restriction; RT-QuIC positive.
case.q: What must be excluded before accepting this diagnosis?
case.a: Treatable rapidly progressive dementias — autoimmune encephalitis, Hashimoto encephalopathy, CNS vasculitis, lymphoma, metabolic causes.

qx.stem: A 64-year-old woman from Songkhla has had six weeks of rapidly progressive confusion, visual distortion and gait unsteadiness, with startle myoclonus. CT is normal. MRI diffusion shows cortical ribboning in the temporal and parietal lobes with bilateral caudate and putamen restriction, with little T2 change and no enhancement.
qx.q: Which investigation adds most to the diagnosis?
opts: CSF RT-QuIC for prion seeding activity
Serum anti-NMDA receptor antibody only
Lumbar puncture with India ink stain
Carotid ultrasound
Fundus fluorescein angiography
qx.why: Cortical ribboning and basal ganglia diffusion restriction are the classic MRI pattern of sporadic CJD, and CSF RT-QuIC has high sensitivity and near-perfect specificity. Autoimmune encephalitis and non-convulsive seizures are valid mimics, but RT-QuIC and EEG complete the work-up. Carotid and fundus studies would not explain the picture.

qx.stem: A 66-year-old woman from Lopburi develops rapid memory loss and unsteady gait over six weeks, followed by startle myoclonus and akinetic mutism. EEG shows generalised periodic sharp wave complexes, and MRI diffusion imaging shows cortical ribboning with bright signal over the caudate and putamen. CSF cell count is normal.
qx.q: Which CSF test has the highest specificity for the diagnosis?
opts: CSF protein above 100 mg/dL
Oligoclonal bands
CSF lactate
RT-QuIC seeding assay for abnormal prion protein
CSF glucose ratio
qx.why: A rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus, periodic EEG complexes and diffusion restriction in cortex and striatum is typical of sporadic CJD. RT-QuIC of CSF detects seeding-active prion protein with high sensitivity and specificity close to 100 percent, outperforming 14-3-3 and total tau. Protein, oligoclonal bands, lactate and glucose are non-specific.

ddx.pt: Antibody-mediated, CSF inflammation, responds to immunotherapy
Years not months
Slower, fluctuations, hallucinations

det.patho: Prion disease results from conversion of normal cellular prion protein (PrPC) into a misfolded, protease-resistant form (PrPSc) that templates further misfolding, causing spongiform change, neuronal loss and gliosis. Sporadic CJD (about 85%) arises spontaneously, with codon 129 polymorphism of PRNP shaping the phenotype; genetic forms (PRNP mutations) and acquired forms (iatrogenic, variant CJD from BSE) make up the rest. Incidence is roughly 1–2 per million per year.
det.clinical: Sporadic CJD usually starts in the 60s with rapidly progressive cognitive decline, often with behavioural change, visual disturbance (Heidenhain variant) or ataxia (Brownell–Oppenheimer variant) as early features. Myoclonus, frequently startle-provoked, appears in most patients, together with pyramidal and extrapyramidal signs. Within months the patient becomes mute and immobile (akinetic mutism). Variant CJD affects younger people, begins with psychiatric symptoms and painful sensory symptoms, and has a longer course.
det.diagnosis: Updated international criteria combine the clinical syndrome with supportive tests. MRI DWI/FLAIR showing cortical ribboning and/or caudate and putamen hyperintensity is highly sensitive. CSF RT-QuIC is the most specific test; 14-3-3 and total tau are sensitive but non-specific. EEG may show periodic sharp-wave complexes, mostly in later stages. Definite diagnosis requires neuropathology. Always look for treatable mimics: autoimmune encephalitis, Hashimoto encephalopathy, CNS lymphoma, vasculitis, metabolic and toxic encephalopathies, and non-convulsive status.
det.treatment: There is no effective treatment; care is supportive and palliative, with clonazepam or levetiracetam for myoclonus and attention to nutrition, comfort and family support. Notify public health authorities as required, and follow infection-control guidance for neurosurgical and ophthalmic instruments. Routine nursing contact poses no transmission risk. Genetic counselling is offered for familial forms.
det.prognosis: Median survival in sporadic CJD is about 4–6 months, with most patients dying within a year.
pearls: Rapid dementia over weeks to months plus myoclonus: get DWI MRI and CSF RT-QuIC.
Cortical ribboning is best seen on DWI and can be missed on routine T2.
Exclude autoimmune encephalitis before labelling a patient with CJD.
det.thd: CJD เป็นโรคพรีออนที่โปรตีน prion พับผิดรูปแล้วชักนำโปรตีนปกติให้ผิดตาม ทำให้สมองเป็นรูพรุนแบบฟองน้ำ ผู้ป่วยสมองเสื่อมเร็วมากภายในสัปดาห์ถึงเดือน มีกระตุกเมื่อตกใจ เดินเซ ตามัว จนพูดและขยับไม่ได้ การตรวจที่ช่วยมาก ได้แก่ MRI DWI เห็น cortical ribboning และ basal ganglia และ CSF RT-QuIC ซึ่งจำเพาะสูง ก่อนวินิจฉัยต้องตัดสาเหตุที่รักษาได้ เช่น autoimmune encephalitis ยังไม่มียารักษา เน้นดูแลแบบประคับประคองและแจ้งหน่วยงานสาธารณสุข

name: Crigler–Najjar syndrome
formal: Inherited disorder of bilirubin conjugation (UGT1A1) causing severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; type I may lead to kernicterus.
simple: An inherited liver enzyme problem that causes high bilirubin and can damage the baby's brain if untreated.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมที่ตับจับคู่ bilirubin ไม่ได้จากยีน UGT1A1 ทำให้ bilirubin ชนิด unconjugated สูงมาก ชนิดที่ 1 เสี่ยง kernicterus ทำลายสมอง
tempoNote: Jaundice from the first days of life; brain injury can occur in infancy or later during illness
feat: Severe persistent unconjugated jaundice from birth without haemolysis
Type I: absent enzyme, bilirubin often above 340 µmol/L (20 mg/dL), no response to phenobarbital
Type II (Arias): partial enzyme, lower bilirubin, falls with phenobarbital
Kernicterus: dystonia, choreoathetosis, upgaze palsy, hearing loss, dental enamel defects
Late encephalopathy can be triggered by fever, fasting or bilirubin-displacing drugs
inv: Total and direct bilirubin, liver enzymes (normal), haemolysis screen (negative)
Phenobarbital trial to separate type I from type II
UGT1A1 gene testing; MRI showing globus pallidus signal change in kernicterus
Brainstem auditory evoked responses for auditory neuropathy

case.story: Deeply jaundiced since birth despite phototherapy; parents are cousins. Development is delayed and she arches her back.
case.exam: Intense jaundice, dystonic posturing, limited upgaze, no hepatosplenomegaly.
case.tests: Unconjugated bilirubin 420 µmol/L, normal liver enzymes, no haemolysis; no fall after phenobarbital.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the definitive treatment?
case.a: Crigler–Najjar type I with early bilirubin encephalopathy; long daily phototherapy as a bridge to liver transplantation.

det.patho: Recessive variants in UGT1A1 abolish (type I) or reduce (type II) hepatic glucuronidation of bilirubin. Unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble and, when free bilirubin is high, crosses the blood–brain barrier and injures neurons of the globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, hippocampus, cranial nerve and auditory nuclei. Gilbert syndrome lies at the mild end of the same gene.
det.clinical: Type I presents with relentless neonatal jaundice; without aggressive phototherapy kernicterus develops, leaving dyskinetic cerebral palsy, gaze palsy and sensorineural or auditory neuropathy hearing loss. Phototherapy becomes less effective with age as skin thickens. Type II is milder and often compatible with a near-normal life, though encephalopathy can still occur during illness. This entry is primarily a hepatic disorder with neurological consequences.
det.diagnosis: Persistent unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with normal liver function and no haemolysis suggests it. Response to phenobarbital (bilirubin falls by more than about 25–30%) indicates type II. Genetic testing confirms. MRI may show pallidal T2 hyperintensity in kernicterus.
det.treatment: Type I needs 10–12 hours of daily phototherapy, plus exchange transfusion or plasmapheresis during crises; liver transplantation is curative and should be planned before brain injury. Type II responds to phenobarbital. Avoid drugs that displace bilirubin from albumin (for example ceftriaxone, sulfonamides). Hepatocyte and AAV gene therapies are in clinical trials.
det.prognosis: Without transplantation type I usually leads to kernicterus by young adulthood; type II has a good outlook.
pearls: Unconjugated jaundice with normal liver enzymes and no haemolysis — think UGT1A1.
Kernicterus triad: dystonia/athetosis, upgaze palsy, auditory neuropathy.
Phenobarbital response separates type II from type I.
det.thd: Crigler–Najjar syndrome เกิดจากยีน UGT1A1 ทำให้ตับจับคู่ bilirubin ไม่ได้ bilirubin ชนิด unconjugated จึงสูงมากตั้งแต่แรกเกิด ชนิดที่ 1 รุนแรงและเสี่ยง kernicterus ซึ่งทำให้เกิด dystonia กลอกตาขึ้นไม่ได้ และหูตึง ชนิดที่ 2 ตอบสนองต่อ phenobarbital การรักษาชนิดที่ 1 คือส่องไฟวันละหลายชั่วโมงจนได้ปลูกถ่ายตับ

Later-onset movement disorder with liver disease and Kayser–Fleischer rings
Inherited encephalopathy driven by ammonia, not bilirubin

name: Critical illness myopathy (CIM)
formal: Acute myopathy with flaccid weakness in ICU patients, associated with steroids, neuromuscular blockers and sepsis; with thick filament loss.
simple: Muscle weakness that develops in very sick patients in intensive care.
more: Acute flaccid weakness with selective myosin loss in ICU patients, linked to steroids, neuromuscular blockers, and sepsis, with low-amplitude CMAPs, normal sensory studies, and mildly raised CK. Direct muscle stimulation and biopsy showing thick-filament loss confirm it. Treatment is supportive with early mobilisation; most survivors recover over weeks to months.
th: กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงที่เกิดระหว่างป่วยหนักใน ICU — สูญเสีย myosin โดยเฉพาะหลังได้ steroid และยาหย่อนกล้ามเนื้อ
tempoNote: Develops during the first 1–2 weeks of critical illness; often noticed at ventilator weaning
feat: Flaccid, often proximal-predominant quadriparesis with failure to wean from the ventilator
Facial weakness possible; eye movements usually spared
Reflexes reduced; sensation preserved (if testable)
Risk factors: sepsis, multiorgan failure, high-dose corticosteroids, neuromuscular blockers, hyperglycaemia
inv: CK normal or modestly raised
NCS: low CMAP amplitudes with long CMAP duration, normal sensory potentials; direct muscle stimulation shows reduced excitability
Muscle biopsy (if needed): selective loss of thick myosin filaments, scattered necrosis

case.story: Ventilated 10 days for status asthmaticus with IV methylprednisolone and a cisatracurium infusion; now awake but cannot lift arms or breathe unaided.
case.exam: Flaccid quadriparesis, worse proximally, mild bilateral facial weakness, reduced reflexes; withdraws to pain normally and reports touch.
case.tests: CK 900 U/L; NCS: low broad CMAPs, normal sural SNAPs; needle EMG: short, small units with early recruitment.
case.q: What distinguishes CIM from CIP electrophysiologically?
case.a: CIM preserves sensory potentials, shows broad low CMAPs and myopathic units, and muscle is inexcitable on direct stimulation; CIP reduces both sensory and motor amplitudes with neurogenic EMG.

det.patho: Sepsis-related inflammation, immobility and high-dose glucocorticoids trigger rapid proteolysis that preferentially removes myosin heavy chains, together with sodium-channel dysfunction that makes the muscle membrane electrically inexcitable. Neuromuscular blocking agents add to the risk, probably through functional denervation. CIM frequently coexists with critical illness polyneuropathy.
det.clinical: Weakness is usually discovered when sedation is lightened or weaning fails. It is generalised and flaccid, often proximal more than distal, and may involve facial and neck muscles while sparing the eyes. Sensory examination, when possible, is intact. Prolonged ventilation, longer ICU and hospital stay, and post-ICU functional impairment are typical consequences.
det.diagnosis: ICU-acquired weakness is defined clinically (for example MRC sum score below 48 in a cooperative patient) after excluding other causes. Electrophysiology distinguishes myopathy from neuropathy: preserved SNAPs, low-amplitude prolonged CMAPs, and myopathic or inexcitable muscle on needle and direct stimulation favour CIM. CK can be normal. Biopsy showing myosin loss confirms but is rarely necessary.
det.treatment: There is no specific treatment. Prevention and mitigation include treating sepsis, avoiding hyperglycaemia, minimising steroid doses and paralytic agents, daily sedation interruption and early mobilisation. Rehabilitation, nutritional support and staged ventilator weaning are central.
det.prognosis: Recovery is often good over weeks to months, generally faster and more complete than in CIP, though some patients have lasting weakness and fatigue.
pearls: Normal sural SNAP with tiny motor responses in an ICU patient favours myopathy over neuropathy.
Steroids plus neuromuscular blockade in asthma is the textbook setting.
Eye movements are spared — ptosis and ophthalmoplegia suggest another diagnosis such as MG or botulism.
det.thd: CIM คือกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงที่เกิดในผู้ป่วยวิกฤต โดยเฉพาะผู้ที่ติดเชื้อรุนแรง ได้ steroid ขนาดสูงหรือยาหย่อนกล้ามเนื้อ เกิดจากการสูญเสีย myosin และเยื่อหุ้มกล้ามเนื้อไม่ตอบสนองต่อไฟฟ้า ผู้ป่วยแขนขาอ่อนแรงแบบปวกเปียกและถอดเครื่องช่วยหายใจไม่ได้ แต่ความรู้สึกปกติ NCS พบ SNAP ปกติ CMAP เล็กและกว้าง การรักษาคือคุมปัจจัยเสี่ยงและฟื้นฟู ส่วนใหญ่หายดีภายในหลายสัปดาห์ถึงเดือน

qx.stem: A 56-year-old man in an ICU in Bangkok recovering from septic shock, ventilated for 3 weeks with high-dose steroids and neuromuscular blockers, cannot be weaned. He has flaccid quadriparesis with preserved sensation, and CK is mildly raised. Motor CMAPs are low and prolonged, with sensory nerve action potentials normal.
qx.q: Which additional test best separates CIM from critical illness polyneuropathy?
opts: F-wave latency
Sural nerve biopsy
Direct muscle stimulation showing reduced muscle excitability, with myopathic motor units on EMG
Median-ulnar comparison study
Brain MRI
qx.why: Normal SNAPs with low CMAPs favour myopathy, and direct muscle stimulation reveals inexcitable muscle membrane in CIM, whereas in polyneuropathy the nerve is abnormal and the muscle responds normally. EMG shows short-duration, small motor units in CIM. Biopsy is invasive and unnecessary, and F-waves and imaging add little.

name: Critical illness polyneuropathy (CIP)
formal: Axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy in ICU patients with sepsis or multi-organ failure, causing flaccid limb weakness and ventilator weaning difficulty.
simple: Widespread nerve damage in very ill patients, causing weakness and slow recovery.
more: Nerve conduction shows reduced compound muscle and sensory amplitudes with spontaneous denervation on EMG; CK is normal and the facial muscles are spared. Treat sepsis and optimise glycaemic control; recovery takes weeks to months and can be incomplete. Axonal sensorimotor neuropathy in ICU patients with sepsis, causing limb weakness and difficulty weaning from ventilation.
th: เส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเสื่อมแบบ axonal ระหว่างป่วยหนัก/ติดเชื้อในกระแสเลือด — อ่อนแรงส่วนปลายและถอดเครื่องช่วยหายใจยาก

feat: Symmetric distal-predominant flaccid weakness and wasting with reduced or absent reflexes
Distal loss of pain, temperature and vibration sense
Difficulty weaning due to phrenic nerve and diaphragm involvement
Facial muscles relatively spared; often combined with CIM
inv: NCS: reduced motor and sensory amplitudes with normal conduction velocity (axonal)

CSF normal protein (helps exclude GBS) when the diagnosis is uncertain

case.story: Three weeks in ICU with leptospirosis, septic shock and renal failure; now alert but legs are floppy and she fails spontaneous breathing trials.
case.exam: Distal > proximal weakness, foot drop, absent ankle jerks, stocking sensory loss, grimaces normally.
case.tests: NCS: low CMAPs and absent sural SNAPs with preserved velocities; needle EMG: fibrillations in leg and diaphragm.
case.q: Why is GBS unlikely, and what is the prognosis?
case.a: Weakness began during critical illness, NCS show pure axonal loss without demyelination and CSF protein is normal. Recovery is slow over months and may be incomplete.

det.patho: Systemic inflammation in sepsis impairs nerve microcirculation, increases vascular permeability and causes bioenergetic failure of axons; sodium-channel inactivation produces early functional block before structural degeneration. The result is a length-dependent sensorimotor axonal neuropathy. Hyperglycaemia and multiorgan failure increase risk, and severity tracks with the duration of sepsis.
det.clinical: Most cases present as failure to wean or limp limbs once sedation is reduced. Weakness is distal-predominant with reduced reflexes and distal sensory loss, though examination is limited by encephalopathy. Phrenic neuropathy prolongs ventilation. CIP and CIM overlap in many patients and together form ICU-acquired weakness, a major cause of long-term disability after intensive care.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis combines a compatible setting with NCS showing reduced CMAP and SNAP amplitudes and normal velocities, and EMG showing denervation. Phrenic NCS and diaphragm EMG help explain ventilator dependence. Preserved SNAPs, inexcitable muscle on direct stimulation or a pure motor pattern suggest CIM instead. Exclude GBS, myasthenia, botulism, high cervical cord lesions and drug effects.
det.treatment: There is no proven specific therapy. Intensive insulin therapy reduces incidence but must be balanced against hypoglycaemia; current practice targets moderate glucose control. Treat sepsis aggressively, minimise sedation, mobilise early and provide physiotherapy, splints and long-term rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: Recovery takes months; many patients regain walking, but residual distal weakness, sensory loss and fatigue are common, more so than with CIM.
pearls: Absent sural SNAP plus low CMAP with normal velocities in a septic patient = CIP pattern.
Check phrenic nerve function in unexplained weaning failure.
CIP and CIM often coexist; electrophysiology defines the mix.
det.thd: CIP คือเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเสื่อมชนิด axonal ที่เกิดระหว่างติดเชื้อรุนแรงหรืออวัยวะล้มเหลวหลายระบบ ผู้ป่วยอ่อนแรงส่วนปลาย reflex หาย ชาแบบถุงเท้า และถอดเครื่องช่วยหายใจยากเพราะเส้นประสาท phrenic เสีย NCS พบ amplitude ลดลงทั้ง motor และ sensory แต่ความเร็วปกติ ไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ เน้นรักษาการติดเชื้อ คุมน้ำตาล เคลื่อนไหวเร็ว และฟื้นฟูยาวนานหลายเดือน

qx.stem: A 58-year-old man from Nonthaburi has been ventilated for 24 days after septic shock from perforated diverticulitis. Sedation is off, he is alert, but he cannot be weaned and has flaccid limb weakness with reduced reflexes and little response to pain in the feet. Facial movements are normal. Electrodiagnosis reveals small motor and sensory potentials with normal conduction velocities, and CSF protein is normal.
qx.q: Which finding best distinguishes this condition from Guillain-Barre syndrome?
opts: Facial sparing
Areflexia
Axonal sensorimotor pattern with reduced SNAP amplitudes, preserved velocities and normal CSF protein in a patient with prolonged sepsis
Respiratory failure
Limb weakness that is symmetric
qx.why: Critical illness polyneuropathy is a primary axonal sensorimotor neuropathy that follows sepsis and multiorgan failure, with reduced SNAP and CMAP amplitudes, mostly normal velocities and non-elevated CSF protein. GBS typically shows demyelinating features, raised CSF protein after the first week and facial or bulbar involvement. Symmetry, areflexia and respiratory failure occur in both, so they do not discriminate.

name: CRMP-5 neuronal antibody-associated limbic encephalitis
formal: Paraneoplastic limbic or multifocal encephalitis with anti-CV2/CRMP5 antibodies, associated with small cell lung cancer and thymoma, often with neuropathy and chorea.
simple: Brain inflammation triggered by the immune system reacting to a hidden cancer, causing memory and mood changes.
th: สมองอักเสบแบบ paraneoplastic ที่สัมพันธ์กับ anti-CV2/CRMP5 พบร่วมกับมะเร็งปอดชนิดเซลล์เล็กและ thymoma มักมีเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายอักเสบและ chorea ร่วม
tempoNote: Evolves over weeks to a few months, often before the tumour is known
feat: Memory loss, confusion, seizures and psychiatric change (limbic encephalitis)
Chorea or other movement disorders, sometimes the presenting feature
Optic neuropathy with disc swelling and retinitis; cerebellar ataxia; myelopathy
Sensorimotor or sensory neuropathy, often coexisting with anti-Hu
Strongly associated with smoking-related small cell lung cancer and thymoma
inv: Serum and CSF CRMP5 (CV2) antibodies with a full paraneoplastic panel
MRI brain (mesial temporal or striatal T2 change), EEG, CSF (pleocytosis, oligoclonal bands)
CT chest and FDG-PET to find the tumour; repeat screening if negative

case.story: Two months of forgetfulness, irritability and new writhing movements of his arms; also numb feet and blurred vision.
case.exam: Disoriented to date, generalised chorea, bilateral disc swelling, absent ankle reflexes.
case.tests: MRI bilateral mesial temporal and caudate T2 signal; CRMP5-IgG positive; PET-CT shows mediastinal node, biopsy small cell carcinoma.
case.q: What is the priority treatment?
case.a: Treat the small cell lung cancer, combined with immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG or plasma exchange).

det.patho: CRMP5 is an intracellular neuronal protein involved in axon guidance. Antibodies are markers of a cytotoxic T-cell response triggered by tumour expression (mainly small cell lung carcinoma, also thymoma). Because the target is intracellular, damage is largely T-cell mediated and less reversible than with surface-antibody encephalitis.
det.clinical: The syndrome is often multifocal: encephalopathy, chorea, optic neuritis with retinitis, cerebellar ataxia, myelopathy and neuropathy can occur in various combinations. Symptoms precede the cancer diagnosis in most patients. Coexisting anti-Hu or other antibodies are common.
det.diagnosis: 2021 paraneoplastic criteria rate CRMP5 as a high-risk antibody. Confirm with cell-based or tissue-based assays plus line blot, and search intensively for cancer with CT and PET; if the first search is negative, rescreen at 4–6-month intervals for two years.
det.treatment: Tumour treatment is the most important intervention. First-line immunotherapy includes high-dose corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange; cyclophosphamide or rituximab may be considered. Symptomatic treatment covers seizures, chorea and neuropathic pain. Immune checkpoint inhibitors can trigger or worsen the syndrome.
det.prognosis: Neurological recovery is usually partial; survival depends mainly on the cancer.
pearls: Chorea plus optic neuropathy plus neuropathy in a smoker: test CRMP5.
Intracellular antibody = T-cell disease, limited immunotherapy response.
Find and treat the tumour; repeat screening if first search is negative.
det.thd: CRMP5 encephalitis เป็นสมองอักเสบแบบ paraneoplastic ที่สัมพันธ์กับมะเร็งปอดชนิดเซลล์เล็กและ thymoma อาการได้แก่ความจำเสื่อม สับสน ชัก ร่วมกับ chorea เส้นประสาทตาอักเสบ เดินเซ และปลายประสาทอักเสบ ตรวจแอนติบอดี CRMP5 ในเลือดและน้ำไขสันหลัง และค้นหามะเร็งด้วย CT/PET การรักษาสำคัญคือรักษามะเร็งร่วมกับยากดภูมิ อาการทางประสาทมักฟื้นได้บางส่วน

name: Crohn’s disease
formal: Inflammatory bowel disease with neurological complications including peripheral neuropathy, cerebral venous thrombosis, myelopathy and treatment-related effects.
simple: A bowel inflammatory disease that can also affect nerves and brain blood vessels.
more: Check for ulcerative thrombotic complications, B12 and folate deficiency, vitamin deficiency and anti-TNF-related demyelination; neuropathy and CNS involvement should be sought on imaging. Treat the bowel disease, anticoagulate venous thrombosis.
th: โรคลำไส้อักเสบเรื้อรังที่มีภาวะแทรกซ้อนทางระบบประสาท เช่น ปลายประสาทอักเสบ หลอดเลือดดำสมองอุดตัน โรคไขสันหลัง และผลข้างเคียงจากยา
tempoNote: Relapsing gut disease; neurological complications can be acute (thrombosis) or gradual (deficiency)
feat: A gastrointestinal disease with secondary neurological complications
B12 deficiency after terminal ileal disease or resection: myelopathy, neuropathy, cognitive change
Hypercoagulability in active disease: cerebral venous thrombosis and arterial stroke
Peripheral neuropathy (axonal, demyelinating, small-fibre) and associated myasthenia or myositis
Drug effects: anti-TNF demyelination, metronidazole neuropathy, natalizumab PML, steroid myopathy, calcineurin inhibitor PRES
inv: B12, folate, copper, vitamin E, vitamin D
MRI brain/spine; MRV for venous thrombosis
Nerve conduction studies; drug history review

case.story: Crohn's disease with ileal resection five years ago, not on B12 injections; now numb feet and unsteady walking in the dark.
case.exam: Reduced vibration and joint position in feet, positive Romberg, brisk knee reflexes but absent ankle jerks, extensor plantars.
case.tests: B12 95 pg/mL, methylmalonic acid high; MRI: dorsal column T2 signal C3–T2.
case.q: What has happened and how should it be treated?
case.a: Subacute combined degeneration from B12 malabsorption after ileal resection; intramuscular hydroxocobalamin with lifelong maintenance.

det.patho: Neurological complications arise from malabsorption (B12, copper, vitamin E), a prothrombotic state during inflammation, immune cross-reactivity, and adverse effects of therapies. Anti-TNF agents can unmask or trigger CNS and peripheral demyelination.
det.clinical: Presentations include sensory neuropathy, myelopathy, ataxia, stroke, venous thrombosis, seizures and headache. Neurological events may coincide with disease flares or occur during remission due to deficiency or drugs.
det.diagnosis: Correlate timing with disease activity, surgery and medications. Screen for nutritional deficiencies, imaging for vascular events, and nerve conduction for neuropathy. New demyelination on anti-TNF therapy warrants stopping the drug and evaluating for MS.
det.treatment: Correct deficiencies, anticoagulate venous thrombosis, stop offending drugs and control intestinal inflammation. Demyelination from anti-TNF often improves after withdrawal, sometimes needing steroids. Natalizumab requires JC virus monitoring.
det.prognosis: Most complications improve with targeted treatment; delayed B12 replacement can leave permanent deficits.
pearls: Ileal resection = lifelong B12 replacement.
Active IBD raises the risk of cerebral venous thrombosis.
New demyelinating symptoms on anti-TNF therapy: stop the drug.

name: Cruciate paralysis
formal: Weakness of both arms with relative sparing of legs, caused by a lesion at the cervicomedullary junction affecting decussating pyramidal fibres.
simple: A weakness mostly in the arms, due to damage at the junction of brain and spinal cord.
th: อ่อนแรงแขนสองข้างโดยขาค่อนข้างปกติ จากรอยโรคที่ cervicomedullary junction บริเวณ pyramidal decussation
tempoNote: Usually acute after trauma; sometimes progressive with tumours
feat: Bilateral arm weakness with little or no leg weakness
Due to anatomy: arm fibres decussate more rostrally and medially than leg fibres
Causes: odontoid fracture, atlantoaxial injury, foramen magnum tumours, syrinx
Can be mistaken for central cord syndrome
Variable sensory loss and cranial nerve signs
inv: CT and MRI of the craniocervical junction
Flexion-extension imaging after trauma when safe
Neurosurgical assessment

case.story: After a crash, cannot lift either arm but can walk a few steps.
case.exam: Profound bilateral arm weakness, mild leg weakness, neck tenderness.
case.tests: CT: type II odontoid fracture; MRI: cervicomedullary contusion.
case.q: Why are the arms weaker than the legs?
case.a: Cruciate paralysis: arm fibres decussate at a slightly different level from leg fibres at the pyramidal decussation.

det.patho: At the pyramidal decussation, corticospinal fibres for the arms cross slightly rostrally and medially compared with leg fibres. A small lesion at the decussation can therefore affect arm fibres selectively. The anatomical explanation is debated, but the clinical pattern is accepted.
det.clinical: Bilateral or asymmetric arm weakness with relative leg sparing after craniocervical trauma or with foramen magnum lesions. Sensory involvement varies. Lower cranial nerve or respiratory problems may coexist.
det.diagnosis: MRI and CT of craniocervical junction identify fracture, contusion or tumour.
det.treatment: Immobilise and stabilise the spine, treat associated injuries, decompress when needed; rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: Often good recovery in traumatic cases.
pearls: Arm weakness more than leg after neck trauma: think central cord or cruciate paralysis.
Odontoid fractures are a classic cause.
Image the craniocervical junction.
det.thd: Cruciate paralysis คือแขนสองข้างอ่อนแรงมากโดยขาค่อนข้างปกติ เกิดจากรอยโรคเล็ก ๆ ที่ cervicomedullary junction บริเวณ pyramidal decussation เช่น กระดูก odontoid หัก หรือเนื้องอกที่ foramen magnum ต้องแยกจาก central cord syndrome ทำ CT และ MRI รอยต่อกะโหลกกับกระดูกคอ และรักษาตามสาเหตุ

name: Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome
formal: Autoinflammatory NLRP3 disease including CINCA/NOMID with chronic aseptic meningitis, hearing loss, papilloedema and rashes.
simple: An inherited inflammatory condition causing fever, rash, joint pain and brain-lining inflammation.
th: โรค autoinflammatory จากยีน NLRP3 รวมถึง CINCA/NOMID มีเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบแบบปลอดเชื้อเรื้อรัง หูตึง papilloedema และผื่นลมพิษ
tempoNote: Begins in infancy or childhood; recurrent flares on top of chronic inflammation in severe forms
feat: Spectrum: familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome (mild), Muckle–Wells (intermediate), NOMID/CINCA (severe)
Urticaria-like rash from early life, fevers, conjunctivitis, joint pain
Chronic aseptic meningitis, raised intracranial pressure, papilloedema, headache
Progressive sensorineural hearing loss
NOMID: intellectual disability, ventriculomegaly, bony overgrowth of the knees

CSF: neutrophilic pleocytosis with raised opening pressure, sterile cultures

case.story: Daily hive-like rash since infancy, recurrent fevers, headaches and difficulty hearing in class.
case.exam: Urticarial rash, bilateral papilloedema, sensorineural hearing loss, enlarged knees.
case.tests: CRP 80 mg/L; CSF neutrophils 50/µL, sterile; NLRP3 gain-of-function variant.
case.q: What treatment can prevent progressive deafness and brain damage?
case.a: IL-1 blockade (anakinra or canakinumab), started early.

det.patho: Gain-of-function NLRP3 variants make the cryopyrin inflammasome overactive, leading to excess caspase-1 activity and IL-1β release. Inflammation affects skin, joints, eyes, cochlea and meninges. Inheritance is autosomal dominant, often de novo, and severe NOMID may arise from somatic mosaicism.
det.clinical: Symptoms start in the newborn period or infancy. Mild forms flare with cold exposure; Muckle–Wells brings hearing loss and AA amyloidosis risk; NOMID shows chronic meningitis, raised pressure, optic atrophy, cognitive impairment and arthropathy. Untreated CNS inflammation causes lasting deficits.
det.diagnosis: Diagnose by clinical criteria (raised inflammatory markers plus features like urticaria, cold triggers, hearing loss, eye inflammation, skeletal changes) supported by NLRP3 testing. CSF and MRI (leptomeningeal enhancement, cochlear enhancement) document CNS involvement. Exclude infection.
det.treatment: IL-1 inhibitors (anakinra, canakinumab, rilonacept) are highly effective and should be titrated to normalise inflammation and CSF findings. Monitor hearing, vision, growth and renal function (amyloid). Hearing aids or cochlear implants support hearing loss.
det.prognosis: With early IL-1 blockade, many complications can be prevented; untreated NOMID causes severe disability and amyloidosis.
pearls: Lifelong urticaria plus aseptic meningitis plus deafness: think CAPS.
IL-1 blockade transforms outcome — start early.
Negative germline testing does not exclude somatic mosaicism.
det.thd: Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome หรือ CAPS เป็นโรคอักเสบจากพันธุกรรมยีน NLRP3 ทำให้ร่างกายหลั่ง IL-1 มากเกินไป เด็กมีผื่นคล้ายลมพิษตั้งแต่เล็ก ไข้เป็นพัก ๆ ปวดข้อ ในรายรุนแรงมีเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบแบบปลอดเชื้อเรื้อรัง ความดันในสมองสูง หูตึง และสติปัญญาบกพร่อง ตรวจ CRP สูง น้ำไขสันหลังมีเม็ดเลือดขาว และตรวจยีน รักษาด้วยยาต้าน IL-1 ตั้งแต่เนิ่น ๆ

det.patho: Cryptococcus yeast is inhaled from soil and bird droppings, lies dormant, and disseminates to the meninges when cellular immunity fails. Its capsule dampens the immune response, and yeast with capsular polysaccharide blocks CSF outflow at the arachnoid granulations, producing very high pressure. Southeast Asia, including Thailand, carries a heavy burden linked to late-presenting HIV. See Cryptococcus neoformans (pathogen) and Cryptococcus gattii (pathogen) for the two species.
det.clinical: A subacute illness of headache, fever and vomiting over weeks, with minimal meningism. Pressure effects dominate harm: visual loss, cranial neuropathies and falling consciousness. In HIV, disease often surfaces soon after diagnosis, and IRIS can follow ART. Without HIV, patients are older, the course is indolent and the diagnosis is often missed for weeks.
det.diagnosis: Lateral-flow CrAg on CSF is highly sensitive and specific and has replaced India ink; serum CrAg is positive in most HIV-related cases and is used for screening when CD4 is low. Culture confirms and allows susceptibility testing and is the better test for relapse, since CrAg can stay positive for months after cure. CSF may be almost bland in deeply immunosuppressed patients, so a normal cell count does not exclude it.
det.treatment: The current preference is a single high dose of liposomal amphotericin B with flucytosine and fluconazole, with conventional amphotericin-based regimens where the liposomal product is unavailable. Consolidation with high-dose fluconazole is followed by lower-dose maintenance for 6-12 months. Aggressive pressure control with repeat lumbar punctures is as important as the antifungal. Steroids are not given, and ART is delayed 4-6 weeks to reduce IRIS-related deaths. Monitor potassium, magnesium and renal function on amphotericin.
det.prognosis: A substantial minority still die, especially with coma, high fungal burden or uncontrolled pressure; survivors can be left with visual loss or hydrocephalus.
pearls: Headache plus a sixth nerve palsy in advanced HIV: check CrAg and opening pressure.
Normal CSF cells do not exclude cryptococcal meningitis in profound immunosuppression.
CrAg is not a test of cure; use clinical course and culture. See Cryptococcus neoformans (pathogen).
det.thd: Cryptococcal meningitis เป็นเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบจากเชื้อราที่พบบ่อยในผู้ติดเชื้อ HIV ระยะท้ายในไทย อาการคือปวดศีรษะเรื้อรัง อาเจียน เห็นภาพซ้อนจากความดันในกะโหลกสูง ต้องวัด opening pressure ทุกครั้ง ตรวจ CrAg ใน CSF หรือเลือด ซึ่งไวและจำเพาะสูง รักษาด้วย amphotericin B ชนิด liposomal ร่วมกับ flucytosine และ fluconazole แล้วต่อด้วย fluconazole ระยะยาว เจาะหลังระบายความดันซ้ำ ไม่ใช้ steroid และเริ่ม ART หลังรักษาเชื้อราประมาณ 4-6 สัปดาห์

qx.stem: A 37-year-old construction worker from Surat Thani, newly found to be HIV positive with CD4 count 38 cells/µL, has three weeks of headache and blurred vision. opts: Fluconazole 400 mg daily alone and start antiretroviral therapy this week
Acetazolamide and dexamethasone to lower intracranial pressure, with amphotericin for two weeks
Single high-dose liposomal amphotericin B with 14 days of flucytosine and fluconazole, serial therapeutic lumbar punctures, and ART delayed for about 4–6 weeks
Ventriculoperitoneal shunt today before antifungal therapy
Start ART immediately and add antifungal treatment only if symptoms persist
qx.why: WHO (2022) recommends induction with one dose of liposomal amphotericin B 10 mg/kg plus flucytosine and fluconazole for 14 days (AMBITION regimen), followed by consolidation fluconazole. Raised pressure is treated with repeated therapeutic lumbar punctures, not steroids or acetazolamide, which worsened outcomes in trials. ART is deferred 4–6 weeks because early start increased mortality from immune reconstitution.

det.patho: Inhaled Cryptococcus yeasts spread through blood to the brain, where the polysaccharide capsule damps immune recognition. Yeast and capsular material clog the arachnoid granulations, so CSF cannot drain and pressure climbs far above what meningitis alone would cause. Defects in cellular immunity (advanced HIV, transplant drugs, steroids, anti-GM-CSF antibodies) allow the organism to persist and multiply. Both C. neoformans and C. gattii can invade brain tissue, which is why meningoencephalitis is the more accurate label.
det.clinical: The picture is a slow-burning headache over weeks with a surprisingly bland examination until pressure rises. Visual blurring, diplopia, hearing loss and drowsiness mean high pressure rather than inflammation. In people without HIV, inflammation is stronger, the course longer and diagnosis later. After ART starts, a paradoxical IRIS can bring new headache, fever and worse pressure.
det.diagnosis: CrAg by lateral flow on CSF or serum is quick, cheap and the main test; India ink is obsolete. The 2026 review reminds readers that culture is slow but still valuable for relapse, and that beta-D-glucan is usually negative in this infection. Always record opening pressure, and image with MRI when mass lesions or hydrocephalus are suspected. Screening serum CrAg in HIV with a low CD4 count finds disease before symptoms.
det.treatment: Induction is liposomal amphotericin B with flucytosine, and a single high dose of the liposomal drug has been shown to be as good as a two-week course; follow with high-dose fluconazole consolidation and then low-dose maintenance for 6-12 months. Longer induction (4-6 weeks) is chosen for high fungal burden, cryptococcoma or slow response. Treat pressure by draining CSF daily if needed until pressure is 25 cm CSF or lower and symptoms resolve. Reduce immunosuppression where safe, avoid steroids, and delay ART for 4-6 weeks if it was not already running.
det.prognosis: Mortality remains substantial, higher in low-resource settings; reduced consciousness, high fungal burden and uncontrolled pressure carry the worst outlook, and relapse is a risk if maintenance therapy is stopped early.
pearls: Headache plus sixth nerve palsy or papilloedema in a person with HIV: opening pressure and CrAg the same day.
Repeat lumbar punctures are treatment, not just diagnosis; acetazolamide and steroids do not help.

Do not follow CrAg titres to judge cure; judge by symptoms, CSF culture and time on therapy. Organism details: Cryptococcus neoformans (pathogen); healthy-host variant: Cryptococcus gattii (pathogen).
det.thd: Cryptococcal meningoencephalitis เกิดจากเชื้อรา Cryptococcus ที่ติดทางการหายใจแล้วเข้าสู่เยื่อหุ้มสมองและเนื้อสมอง พบบ่อยในผู้ป่วย HIV ที่ CD4 ต่ำ ผู้ป่วยปวดศีรษะนานเป็นสัปดาห์ อาเจียน ตามัวหรือเห็นภาพซ้อนจากความดันในกะโหลกสูง ต้องวัด opening pressure และตรวจ CrAg ใน CSF หรือเลือด การรักษาคือ liposomal amphotericin B ร่วมกับ flucytosine และ fluconazole เจาะหลังระบายน้ำไขสันหลังซ้ำเมื่อความดันสูง ไม่ใช้ steroid และเริ่ม ART หลังรักษาเชื้อราไปแล้วประมาณ 4-6 สัปดาห์

name: Cryptogenic myoclonic epilepsy
formal: Myoclonic epilepsy without an identifiable cause, with seizures featuring brief myoclonic jerks.
simple: Epilepsy with sudden muscle jerks for which no cause is found.
ab: Cryptogenic generalised epilepsy with myoclonic seizures

tempoNote: Recurrent myoclonic seizures over years; course depends on the eventual syndrome
feat: Recurrent brief myoclonic jerks, sometimes with falls or other seizure types
No identified structural, metabolic, infectious or genetic cause after work-up
Historical label; many such patients are now reclassified as specific genetic syndromes
Development may be normal or impaired depending on the case
inv: Video-EEG to confirm myoclonic seizures and define the syndrome
MRI brain with epilepsy protocol

case.story: Previously well, he started having sudden jerks and drop attacks several times a day over the past 3 months.
case.exam: Normal neurological exam; slightly behind in speech.
case.tests: EEG shows generalised 2–3 Hz spike-wave with myoclonic and atonic seizures; MRI normal; initial metabolic screen normal.
case.q: Why is 'cryptogenic' no longer used, and which syndrome should be considered?
case.a: The 2017 ILAE scheme uses 'unknown' cause; this picture fits Doose syndrome (myoclonic-atonic epilepsy), and genetic testing (e.g. SLC6A1, SCN1A, GLUT1) is reasonable.

read.where: Chapter 17: Myoclonic Epilepsy in Infancy and Epilepsy With Myoclonic Atonic Seizures

det.patho: Cryptogenic was used in older ILAE classifications for epilepsies presumed to have a cause that could not be found, as opposed to idiopathic (genetic, otherwise normal) and symptomatic (known lesion). Myoclonic epilepsies placed here included some childhood epileptic encephalopathies. With MRI and genetic testing, many are now explained by variants in genes such as SLC2A1, SCN1A, SLC6A1 or CHD2. The term therefore describes the limits of investigation rather than a disease mechanism.
det.clinical: Patients have myoclonic seizures, sometimes with atonic, absence or tonic-clonic seizures, without a demonstrated cause. Prognosis varies widely from self-limited to an epileptic encephalopathy with developmental slowing. Any progressive cognitive or neurological decline should prompt reconsideration of a progressive myoclonic epilepsy or metabolic disorder.
det.diagnosis: Use the current ILAE framework: classify seizure types, epilepsy type and syndrome, then aetiology (structural, genetic, infectious, metabolic, immune or unknown). Video-EEG, high-quality MRI and genetic testing are central; CSF glucose may detect GLUT1 deficiency. Repeat evaluation over time as new tests become available.
det.treatment: Choose broad-spectrum drugs suited to myoclonic seizures, such as valproate, levetiracetam, clobazam or topiramate; ketogenic diet is effective in myoclonic-atonic epilepsy. Avoid carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin and vigabatrin, which can worsen myoclonic seizures. Treat any later-identified cause specifically, for example ketogenic diet in GLUT1 deficiency.
det.prognosis: Variable; depends on the final syndrome and whether development is affected.
pearls: Cryptogenic is obsolete; say 'unknown aetiology' and keep searching.
Myoclonic seizures are aggravated by sodium channel blockers.
Progressive decline means this is not a simple cryptogenic epilepsy.
det.thd: Cryptogenic myoclonic epilepsy เป็นคำเก่าใช้เรียกโรคลมชักที่มีอาการกระตุกเป็นหลักและหาสาเหตุไม่พบ ปัจจุบัน ILAE ใช้คำว่า unknown etiology และผู้ป่วยหลายรายพบสาเหตุทางพันธุกรรมเมื่อตรวจยีน ควรตรวจ video-EEG, MRI และยีนเพื่อระบุกลุ่มอาการ รักษาด้วยยากันชักแบบกว้าง เช่น valproate หรือ levetiracetam และหลีกเลี่ยงยากลุ่ม sodium channel blocker

name: Cuban epidemic neuropathy
formal: Epidemic optic and peripheral neuropathy and myeloneuropathy during 1990s in Cuba, linked to nutritional deficiency including B vitamins.
simple: A nutritional illness in Cuba that caused vision loss and numb, weak limbs.
ab: Cuban epidemic optic and peripheral neuropathy
th: การระบาดของโรคเส้นประสาทตาและเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายในคิวบาช่วงทศวรรษ 1990 สัมพันธ์กับการขาดสารอาหารโดยเฉพาะวิตามินบี
tempoNote: Cases developed over weeks during 1991–1993; most improved with vitamin supplementation
feat: Historical epidemic affecting about 50,000 people during severe food shortages in Cuba
Optic form: bilateral painless visual loss, centrocaecal scotomas, impaired colour vision, temporal disc pallor
Peripheral form: painful sensory neuropathy with burning feet, sometimes hearing loss and dorsolateral myelopathy
Risk linked to smoking (cyanide), alcohol, low dietary thiamine, B12, folate and sulfur amino acids
Epidemic declined after mass vitamin supplementation
inv: Today: equivalent cases need B1, B12, folate, copper levels and toxin history
Visual fields, colour testing, OCT; NCS for neuropathy
Exclude LHON (mtDNA testing) when optic neuropathy is bilateral and sequential

case.who: Neurology resident reviewing a journal club case in Bangkok
case.story: A 1993 report describes a Cuban farm worker who smoked cigars, lost weight and developed painless blurred vision and burning feet.
case.exam: Bilateral centrocaecal scotomas, reduced colour vision, stocking pinprick loss.
case.tests: Low thiamine and folate; recovery after vitamin B complex.
case.q: Which modern Thai patients may develop a similar picture?
case.a: Malnourished people with heavy alcohol or tobacco use, or after bariatric surgery — nutritional optic neuropathy and neuropathy.

read.where: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves — Toxic, Nutritional and Metabolic Peripheral Neuropathies

det.patho: The epidemic followed economic collapse in the early 1990s with sharp falls in dietary B vitamins, protein and fat. Tobacco-derived cyanide, alcohol and high physical work may have increased demand and toxicity, damaging the papillomacular bundle and long sensory axons. Mitochondrial dysfunction is the proposed common pathway; no infectious agent was confirmed.
det.clinical: Two overlapping forms were described: optic neuropathy with central visual loss and peripheral sensory neuropathy with dysaesthesia, sometimes with hearing loss, myelopathy and autonomic symptoms. Middle-aged men and smokers were mostly affected.
det.diagnosis: Historically diagnosed epidemiologically and clinically. Equivalent modern cases are evaluated as nutritional optic and peripheral neuropathy, measuring vitamins, copper and toxins, and excluding hereditary and compressive causes.
det.treatment: Nationwide B-vitamin and folate supplementation ended the epidemic. Individual cases are treated with thiamine, B12, folate and multivitamins, improved diet and stopping tobacco and alcohol.
det.prognosis: Most recovered substantially with supplementation; some had permanent optic atrophy or neuropathy.
pearls: Nutritional optic neuropathy gives bilateral centrocaecal scotomas with colour loss.
Smoking and alcohol add to nutritional risk.
Public health supplementation reversed the epidemic.
det.thd: Cuban epidemic neuropathy คือการระบาดของโรคเส้นประสาทตาและเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายในคิวบาช่วงปี 1991–1993 ขณะเกิดภาวะขาดแคลนอาหาร ผู้ป่วยมีตามัวทั้งสองข้างแบบ centrocaecal scotoma การมองสีเสีย และปลายเท้าชาแสบร้อน ปัจจัยเสี่ยงคือขาดวิตามินบี สูบบุหรี่ และดื่มสุรา การระบาดหายไปหลังให้วิตามินทั้งประเทศ บทเรียนนี้ใช้กับผู้ป่วยขาดสารอาหารในปัจจุบัน

name: Cushing syndrome
formal: Endogenous or exogenous glucocorticoid excess causing proximal myopathy, psychiatric symptoms, hypertension and stroke risk.
simple: A condition of too much cortisol hormone, which can cause muscle weakness and mood changes.
more: Confirm with 24-hour urinary free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol and dexamethasone suppression test; CK is normal in steroid myopathy and EMG is often normal. Treat the underlying cause and reduce steroids.
th: ภาวะ glucocorticoid เกินจากในร่างกายหรือจากยา ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อต้นแขนขาอ่อนแรง อาการทางจิต ความดันสูง และเพิ่มความเสี่ยง stroke
tempoNote: Develops over months; iatrogenic forms track steroid dose
feat: An endocrine disorder with neurological and psychiatric effects
Proximal leg weakness (difficulty rising from a chair) with normal CK — steroid myopathy
Depression, anxiety, insomnia, psychosis and cognitive impairment
Central obesity, moon face, purple striae, bruising, hypertension, diabetes, osteoporosis
Pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease) may cause headache; vertebral fractures can compress roots or cord
inv: 24-hour urinary free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol, overnight dexamethasone suppression
ACTH level to separate pituitary/ectopic from adrenal causes; pituitary MRI
CK (normal) and EMG (often normal or mildly myopathic) for weakness

case.who: 52-year-old female herbal medicine user from Ubon Ratchathani
case.story: Taking an unlabelled 'arthritis herbal remedy' for a year; now struggles to stand up from the floor and climb stairs.
case.exam: Moon face, buffalo hump, thin skin with bruising, proximal hip flexor weakness MRC 4-, reflexes normal.
case.tests: CK 60 U/L; morning cortisol suppressed and ACTH low; remedy analysed and found to contain dexamethasone.
case.q: What causes the weakness and what is the management?
case.a: Iatrogenic Cushing syndrome with steroid myopathy from adulterated herbal medicine; slow supervised steroid taper with adrenal insufficiency precautions and physiotherapy.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Adrenal Disorders

det.patho: Excess glucocorticoids induce muscle protein breakdown and atrophy of type 2 fibres, alter mood-regulating limbic circuits and promote hypertension, diabetes and dyslipidaemia, raising vascular risk. Causes are exogenous steroids (commonest, including adulterated herbal products in Thailand), pituitary ACTH adenoma, ectopic ACTH and adrenal tumours.
det.clinical: Weakness affects hip girdle first, with wasting but preserved reflexes and sensation. Neuropsychiatric symptoms are frequent and may persist after cure. Vascular complications include stroke and venous thromboembolism. Pituitary macroadenomas may cause visual field defects.
det.diagnosis: Exclude exogenous steroid use carefully, including herbal remedies and injections. Biochemical confirmation needs two abnormal screening tests; ACTH and imaging localise the source. In myopathy, normal CK and a non-irritable EMG favour steroid myopathy.
det.treatment: Withdraw exogenous steroids gradually to avoid adrenal crisis; treat endogenous causes surgically (transsphenoidal surgery or adrenalectomy) or medically (steroidogenesis inhibitors). Exercise and physiotherapy aid recovery of myopathy. Treat hypertension and diabetes.
det.prognosis: Muscle strength usually recovers over weeks to months after cortisol normalises; cognitive and mood symptoms may improve more slowly.
pearls: Proximal weakness with normal CK in someone on steroids: steroid myopathy.
Ask about herbal or 'yaa chud' remedies — often steroid-adulterated in Thailand.
Never stop chronic steroids abruptly.
det.thd: Cushing syndrome คือภาวะมี glucocorticoid เกิน ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจากยา steroid รวมถึงยาสมุนไพรหรือยาชุดที่ผสม steroid ผู้ป่วยหน้ากลม พุงย้อย ผิวบาง ความดันและน้ำตาลสูง กล้ามเนื้อต้นขาอ่อนแรงลุกจากเก้าอี้ลำบาก โดย CK ปกติ และอาจมีซึมเศร้าหรือโรคจิต การวินิจฉัยใช้การตรวจ cortisol และ ACTH การรักษาคือค่อย ๆ ลด steroid หรือผ่าตัดเนื้องอกต้นเหตุ ร่วมกับกายภาพบำบัด

name: Cutaneous neurofibromas
formal: Benign peripheral nerve sheath tumours in the skin, characteristic of neurofibromatosis type 1 and appearing from adolescence.
simple: Soft skin bumps made of nerve tissue, typical of neurofibromatosis.
th: ก้อนเนื้องอกชนิดไม่ร้ายของเปลือกหุ้มเส้นประสาทในชั้นผิวหนัง พบมากหลายก้อนใน NF1 เริ่มตั้งแต่วัยรุ่น นิ่ม และกดแล้วยุบเข้าได้ ไม่กลายเป็นมะเร็งเหมือน plexiform neurofibroma
tempoNote: Appear from adolescence and pregnancy and gradually increase in number and size through adulthood
feat: Soft, skin-coloured or violaceous papules and nodules that may invaginate with finger pressure (buttonhole sign)
Usually multiple in NF1, numbering from a few to hundreds; solitary cases are usually sporadic
Typically painless, with itching or tenderness in some, and little functional impairment
Increase in number around puberty and during pregnancy
Distinct from plexiform neurofibromas, which are deeper, congenital and prone to malignant change
inv: Clinical diagnosis against NF1 criteria (café-au-lait macules, freckling, Lisch nodules, plexiform neurofibroma, optic glioma, bone dysplasia, family history)
Skin biopsy when atypical: spindle cells with wavy nuclei, shredded-carrot collagen and S-100 positivity
NF1 gene testing for confirmation or in children with café-au-lait macules only; MRI only for symptomatic or deep lesions

case.story: Since age 15 she has noticed soft skin bumps on her trunk and arms that have increased in number. Her mother had similar lumps and many brown patches.
case.exam: Over 30 soft cutaneous nodules, more than six café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, two Lisch nodules on slit-lamp examination.
case.tests: Biopsy of one nodule shows a benign neurofibroma; NF1 gene testing identifies a pathogenic variant.
case.q: What does the buttonhole sign suggest, and which neurofibroma type needs surveillance for malignant change?
case.a: The soft nodule invaginates under the finger, typical of a cutaneous neurofibroma; plexiform neurofibromas need surveillance for MPNST.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Neurocutaneous Syndromes

det.patho: Neurofibromas are benign peripheral nerve sheath tumours composed of Schwann cells, fibroblasts, perineurial-like cells and mast cells in a collagenous matrix. In NF1 they arise after both copies of the chromosome 17 NF1 gene are inactivated; this gene produces neurofibromin, a negative regulator of Ras signalling. Cutaneous neurofibromas are confined to the dermis and the surface of nerves in skin.
det.clinical: Cutaneous neurofibromas begin to appear in late childhood or adolescence, and their number rises with age and often in pregnancy. They are soft, rubbery and may be flesh coloured or bluish, sometimes with a buttonhole sign. Most are painless, but some itch or cause cosmetic and psychosocial distress. They are not premalignant, unlike plexiform neurofibromas that can transform into malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumours.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical, relying on the NF1 diagnostic criteria, with careful search for café-au-lait macules, freckling and Lisch nodules. Histology shows low-cellularity spindle cells with wavy nuclei and a loose or myxoid background that stains for S-100. Genetic testing is helpful in young children and atypical presentations. Pain, rapid growth or neurological deficit in an associated deep lesion should prompt MRI and referral.
det.treatment: No treatment is needed for most lesions. Surgical excision, electrodesiccation or laser ablation can remove troublesome or disfiguring lesions, and recurrence at new sites is expected because new tumours continue to form. Selumetinib, a MEK inhibitor, is used for symptomatic inoperable plexiform neurofibromas in children rather than for cutaneous lesions. Care is best coordinated in a multidisciplinary neurofibromatosis clinic, including psychological support.
det.prognosis: Benign and cosmetically progressive; lifelong follow-up for NF1 complications is determined by other features.
pearls: Cutaneous neurofibromas rarely, if ever, turn malignant; a growing painful deep nodule needs evaluation.
The buttonhole sign helps distinguish them from lipomas and dermatofibromas.
A solitary neurofibroma is usually sporadic and is not by itself NF1.
det.thd: Cutaneous neurofibroma คือเนื้องอกไม่ร้ายของเปลือกหุ้มเส้นประสาทในผิวหนัง พบเป็นตุ่มนิ่มหลายก้อนใน NF1 เริ่มช่วงวัยรุ่นและเพิ่มขึ้นตามอายุหรือขณะตั้งครรภ์ เกิดจากยีน NF1 บนโครโมโซม 17 ที่สร้าง neurofibromin บกพร่อง วินิจฉัยจากเกณฑ์ทางคลินิก เช่น café-au-lait macules และ Lisch nodules อาจตัดชิ้นเนื้อยืนยัน ไม่ต้องรักษาถ้าไม่รบกวน หากต้องการนำออกใช้ผ่าตัดหรือเลเซอร์ ต่างจาก plexiform neurofibroma ที่อาจกลายเป็นมะเร็ง

name: Cyanide poisoning
formal: Cytochrome oxidase inhibition causing histotoxic hypoxia with headache, seizures, coma and lactic acidosis; delayed parkinsonism possible.
simple: Poisoning by cyanide that stops cells using oxygen, causing collapse, seizures and coma.
more: Mitochondrial toxicity from cyanide exposure with histotoxic hypoxia and basal ganglia injury, including konzo from cassava.
th: ไซยาไนด์ขัดขวางการใช้ออกซิเจนของเซลล์ ทำให้ปวดศีรษะ ชัก โคม่า และ lactate สูงมาก ผู้รอดชีวิตอาจมี parkinsonism หรือ dystonia ตามมา
tempoNote: Inhalation or large ingestion acts within minutes; chronic cassava exposure acts over months
feat: Headache, anxiety, breathlessness and confusion, quickly followed by seizures and coma
Profound lactic acidosis with deceptively normal oxygen saturation and pink skin without cyanosis
Circulatory collapse; smoke victims often have carbon monoxide poisoning as well
Dilated pupils and violent tonic-clonic seizures after heavy inhalation
Survivors may develop delayed parkinsonism or dystonia; chronic cassava exposure causes konzo

case.who: 33-year-old worker at a gold-processing plant in Phichit
case.story: He collapsed after a tank leak; colleagues say he first complained of headache and breathlessness.
case.exam: GCS 7, seizure on arrival, low blood pressure; pulse oximetry 98% on oxygen.
case.tests: Lactate 14 mmol/L, pH 7.05; venous blood looks bright red.
case.q: Which toxin is likely, and what is the antidote?

det.patho: Cyanide binds cytochrome c oxidase, stopping mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, so tissues cannot use oxygen that is delivered normally. Anaerobic metabolism then produces lactic acidosis, and brain and heart fail first. Sources include smoke from burning plastics, gold extraction and electroplating, sodium nitroprusside, cyanogenic plants such as cassava and deliberate poisoning. The basal ganglia are especially vulnerable, which explains late movement disorders.
det.clinical: Acute exposure produces headache, dizziness, tachypnoea and confusion, then seizures, coma, hypotension and cardiac arrest. Patients die with pink skin because cyanosis is absent, and heavy inhalation can kill at the scene. Weeks later survivors may show parkinsonism or dystonia. Chronic exposure to poorly processed cassava with low protein intake underlies konzo, an abrupt permanent spastic paraparesis, and tropical ataxic neuropathy.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical: exposure history, sudden collapse and marked lactic acidosis despite normal saturation. In smoke inhalation a lactate above roughly 8 to 10 mmol/L suggests cyanide. Measure carboxyhaemoglobin and look for co-ingestions; blood cyanide confirms later. MRI in survivors shows basal ganglia and sometimes cortical injury.
det.treatment: Remove from exposure, give 100% oxygen and support circulation. Give hydroxocobalamin promptly (adult 5 g IV, repeatable), which binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin, and add sodium thiosulfate to promote conversion to thiocyanate. Avoid nitrites when carbon monoxide poisoning is possible because they produce methaemoglobin. Control seizures with benzodiazepines and treat later parkinsonism symptomatically, bearing in mind levodopa response is often limited.
det.prognosis: Rapid antidote improves survival; prolonged coma predicts death or lasting movement and cognitive deficits.
pearls: Coma with severe lactic acidosis and normal SpO2: think cyanide.
Smoke victim with high lactate: give hydroxocobalamin.
Bilateral pallidal-putaminal injury with delayed parkinsonism can follow cyanide or carbon monoxide.
det.thd: ไซยาไนด์ยับยั้งเอนไซม์ cytochrome oxidase ทำให้เซลล์ใช้ออกซิเจนไม่ได้ ผู้ป่วยปวดศีรษะ หอบ สับสน ชัก และหมดสติเร็ว ผิวสีชมพู ตรวจพบ lactate สูงมากแต่ค่าออกซิเจนปลายนิ้วปกติ พบในโรงงานสกัดทอง ควันไฟ และมันสำปะหลังที่ไม่ผ่านการเตรียมอย่างเหมาะสม รักษาด้วยออกซิเจนและ hydroxocobalamin ร่วมกับ sodium thiosulfate ผู้รอดชีวิตอาจมี parkinsonism ตามมา

Follows documented cardiac arrest or hypoxia rather than toxin exposure

name: Cycad toxicity
formal: Neurotoxicity from cycad seed consumption (BMAA), linked to Guam ALS-parkinsonism-dementia complex.
simple: Brain harm from eating cycad seeds that has been linked to a disease similar to motor neuron disease and dementia.
th: พิษต่อระบบประสาทจากการกินเมล็ดปรง (สาร BMAA และ cycasin) ถูกเสนอว่าเกี่ยวข้องกับโรค ALS-parkinsonism-dementia complex บนเกาะกวม
tempoNote: Acute poisoning causes vomiting and liver injury within hours; the proposed chronic neurodegeneration appears years to decades later
feat: Cycad seeds contain cycasin (hepatotoxic, carcinogenic) and BMAA (excitotoxic amino acid)
Acute ingestion: vomiting, diarrhoea, liver dysfunction, sometimes seizures; reported in animals and occasionally in people
Chronic exposure hypothesis: Guam ALS-parkinsonism-dementia complex among the Chamorro people
The causal link remains debated; the Guam disease declined as diets westernised
inv: Exposure history (traditional flour, flying fox consumption, herbal products)
Liver function, glucose; EEG if seizures
For chronic neurodegeneration, standard ALS, parkinsonism and dementia work-up

case.story: Ate boiled seeds of an ornamental cycad (ปรง) believing them edible; six hours later repeated vomiting and abdominal pain.
case.exam: Dehydrated, mildly drowsy, no focal deficit.
case.tests: ALT 420 U/L, glucose normal.
case.q: Is long-term neurodegeneration expected from one exposure?
case.a: No — acute toxicity is mainly gastrointestinal and hepatic; the neurodegeneration hypothesis concerns chronic dietary exposure and is unproven.

det.patho: Cycas seeds contain cycasin, which is converted to methylazoxymethanol, a DNA-alkylating hepatotoxin, and beta-N-methylamino-L-alanine (BMAA), which can act on glutamate receptors and be misincorporated into proteins. BMAA was proposed to biomagnify through flying foxes that eat cycad seeds. Experimental models show neurotoxicity at high doses, but human causation for chronic disease is unproven.
det.clinical: Acute poisoning presents with gastrointestinal upset and hepatotoxicity; in livestock a chronic ataxic syndrome is recognised. The Guam ALS-PDC featured ALS, parkinsonism with dementia, and overlapping forms, with tau-predominant pathology. Its incidence has fallen dramatically since the mid-twentieth century.
det.diagnosis: Acute toxicity is diagnosed by exposure history and liver tests. No validated biomarker for BMAA exposure exists in clinical practice. Patients with neurodegenerative disease are diagnosed by standard criteria.
det.treatment: Supportive care for acute ingestion: fluids, antiemetics, liver monitoring, seizure management; activated charcoal early may be considered. No specific antidote exists. Neurodegenerative syndromes receive standard symptomatic treatment.
det.prognosis: Acute poisoning usually resolves with supportive care; chronic neurological risk remains uncertain.
pearls: Cycad hypothesis links BMAA to Guam ALS-PDC but remains controversial.
Acute cycad seed ingestion is primarily a liver and gut poisoning.
Guam ALS-PDC declined with dietary change, supporting an environmental factor.
det.thd: Cycad toxicity คือพิษจากการกินเมล็ดปรง ซึ่งมีสาร cycasin ที่เป็นพิษต่อตับ และ BMAA ที่อาจเป็นพิษต่อเซลล์ประสาท พิษเฉียบพลันทำให้อาเจียน ท้องเสีย และตับอักเสบ ส่วนสมมติฐานว่าการกินปรงเรื้อรังทำให้เกิดโรค ALS-parkinsonism-dementia บนเกาะกวมยังไม่ได้รับการพิสูจน์ชัดเจน การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง ไม่มียาต้านพิษเฉพาะ

ddx.pt: The endemic disease the cycad hypothesis attempts to explain
Sporadic ALS without dietary exposure; genetic forms in about 10%
Tauopathy with vertical gaze palsy; Guam PDC also shows tau pathology

aN: cycad poisoning | bmaa neurotoxicity | cycasin toxicity | cycad hypothesis of guam als pdc

name: Cyclothymic disorder
formal: Chronic mood instability with numerous hypomanic and depressive episodes insufficient for bipolar disorder.
simple: Ongoing mood swings between mild highs and lows.
th: ภาวะอารมณ์แปรปรวนเรื้อรังทางจิตเวช ขึ้นลงระหว่างช่วงคึกเล็กน้อยกับช่วงซึมบ่อยครั้งนานอย่างน้อย 2 ปี แต่ไม่ถึงเกณฑ์ bipolar disorder
tempoNote: Fluctuating mood for at least 2 years (1 year in adolescents), never symptom-free for more than 2 months
feat: Repeated short spells of raised energy and confidence alternating with low, flat periods
Neither phase is severe or long enough to count as hypomania-plus-depression episodes of bipolar disorder
Usually begins in adolescence or early adulthood; relationships and work feel unstable
Roughly one in three people later develop bipolar I or II disorder
Psychiatric, not neurological — but organic mood swings must be excluded
inv: Mood charting over months and collateral history from family
Thyroid function, drug and alcohol screen, review of steroids and stimulants
Neuroimaging only if late onset, focal signs, cognitive change or seizures

case.story: For three years she swings between weeks of little sleep, many plans and chatty overconfidence, and weeks of tiredness and low motivation. She has never been hospitalised or psychotic.
case.exam: Neurological examination normal; mildly elevated but organised speech at interview.
case.tests: TSH normal, urine drug screen negative.
case.q: What diagnosis fits, and what future risk should be discussed?
case.a: Cyclothymic disorder; she carries a substantial risk of evolving into bipolar disorder, so follow-up and caution with antidepressant monotherapy are advised.

det.patho: Cyclothymia is a mood disorder on the bipolar spectrum with strong familial clustering; first-degree relatives often have bipolar disorder. The mechanism is not well defined but is thought to share genetic and circadian vulnerabilities with bipolar illness. Lifetime prevalence is around 0.4–1%.
det.clinical: Patients describe a restless, changeable temperament: bursts of productivity, reduced sleep need and irritability, then dips of fatigue and pessimism lasting days. Symptoms persist for most of at least two years and cause distress or impairment. Substance misuse, anxiety and ADHD are frequent companions. A neurologist meets it mainly when the question is whether mood instability reflects a brain lesion, epilepsy or a drug effect.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical by DSM-5-TR or ICD-11 criteria and requires that full hypomanic, manic and major depressive episodes have never occurred. Exclude thyroid disease, stimulant or steroid use and, when onset is late or atypical, frontal lobe disease, multiple sclerosis or seizures. A mood diary is the most useful tool.
det.treatment: Management belongs to psychiatry: psychoeducation, regular sleep routines, cognitive behavioural or interpersonal therapy, and avoidance of alcohol and stimulants. Mood stabilisers such as lithium, lamotrigine or valproate may be used when impairment is significant. Antidepressants alone can provoke mood elevation and are used cautiously.
det.prognosis: Course is chronic and fluctuating; a sizeable minority progress to bipolar I or II disorder.
pearls: New mood swings after 50 deserve a neurological look before a psychiatric label.
Avoid antidepressant monotherapy in anyone on the bipolar spectrum.
Valproate, a common neurologic drug, also stabilises mood — but avoid it in women who could become pregnant.
det.thd: Cyclothymic disorder เป็นโรคทางจิตเวชในกลุ่ม bipolar spectrum ผู้ป่วยมีอารมณ์ขึ้นลงบ่อยนานอย่างน้อย 2 ปี แต่ความรุนแรงไม่ถึงเกณฑ์ mania หรือ major depression การวินิจฉัยอาศัยประวัติและบันทึกอารมณ์ และควรตรวจแยกสาเหตุทางกาย เช่น ไทรอยด์ ยา หรือรอยโรคสมองถ้าเริ่มเป็นตอนอายุมาก การรักษาโดยจิตแพทย์ ใช้จิตบำบัดและยาปรับอารมณ์เมื่อจำเป็น

ddx.pt: Bipolar disorder has full manic or major depressive episodes rather than milder ongoing swings
Hyper- or hypothyroidism can mimic mood cycling; TSH settles the question
New disinhibition and apathy after 50 with progressive decline and frontal atrophy

name: Cystic fibrosis
formal: CFTR genetic disease with chronic lung and pancreatic disease; neurological aspects include vitamin E deficiency, stroke and ataxia.
simple: An inherited disease causing sticky mucus in lungs and gut, which can sometimes affect nerves.
ab: Cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator disorder
th: โรคพันธุกรรมจากยีน CFTR มีโรคปอดและตับอ่อนเรื้อรัง ทางระบบประสาทพบการขาดวิตามินอี stroke และเดินเซ
tempoNote: Lifelong; neurological complications emerge over years of malabsorption
feat: A multisystem genetic disease (lung and pancreas) — neurological features are secondary
Vitamin E deficiency: ataxia, loss of proprioception, areflexia, ophthalmoplegia, retinopathy
Other deficiencies: vitamin A (raised intracranial pressure in infants), vitamin K (intracranial bleeding), B12
Hypoxia and hypercapnia causing headache and encephalopathy in advanced lung disease
Very rare in Thai populations; more common in people of European ancestry
inv: Vitamin E (adjusted for lipids), A, D, K and coagulation profile
Nerve conduction studies (sensory neuropathy), spine MRI if myelopathy
Blood gases in respiratory failure

case.who: 19-year-old female exchange student from Europe studying in Chiang Mai
case.story: Cystic fibrosis with poor adherence to pancreatic enzymes; increasing clumsiness and unsteady walking over a year.
case.exam: Gait ataxia, absent reflexes, loss of joint position sense in feet, mild ophthalmoplegia.
case.tests: Vitamin E undetectable; NCS: sensory axonal neuropathy; MRI brain normal.
case.q: What is causing her ataxia?
case.a: Vitamin E deficiency from CF-related fat malabsorption; high-dose vitamin E and optimised enzyme replacement.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Cystic Fibrosis
Chapter 15 Neurologic Manifestations of Nutritional Disorders

det.patho: CFTR dysfunction thickens secretions, damaging lungs, pancreas and liver. Fat malabsorption leads to deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins; vitamin E deficiency causes oxidative damage to dorsal root ganglia, posterior columns and spinocerebellar tracts. Chronic lung disease adds hypoxia and hypercapnia.
det.clinical: Neurological complications are uncommon when enzymes and vitamins are taken consistently. Deficiency produces a Friedreich-like syndrome with ataxia and areflexia. Infants may develop bulging fontanelle from vitamin A imbalance or bleeding from vitamin K deficiency. Advanced lung disease causes morning headaches and confusion.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis of CF itself relies on sweat chloride and CFTR testing. In neurological presentations, measure fat-soluble vitamins and perform nerve conduction studies; MRI may show posterior column changes.
det.treatment: Supplement vitamins (high-dose vitamin E), optimise pancreatic enzymes and nutrition, and treat respiratory failure. CFTR modulators (e.g. elexacaftor–tezacaftor–ivacaftor) have transformed lung outcomes and improve nutrition.
det.prognosis: Deficiency-related deficits stabilise or partly improve with replacement; survival in CF has greatly improved with modulators.
pearls: Ataxia in CF: check vitamin E first.
Fat malabsorption from any cause can mimic Friedreich ataxia.
Morning headache in advanced CF suggests hypercapnia.
det.thd: Cystic fibrosis เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมจากยีน CFTR พบน้อยมากในคนไทย ทำให้ปอดและตับอ่อนเสียเรื้อรัง ทางระบบประสาทเกิดจากการดูดซึมไขมันไม่ดี ทำให้ขาดวิตามินอี มีเดินเซ ไม่มีรีเฟล็กซ์ รับรู้ตำแหน่งข้อเสีย คล้าย Friedreich ataxia และอาจขาดวิตามิน A, K การรักษาคือเสริมวิตามิน ให้เอนไซม์ตับอ่อน และยา CFTR modulator

name: Cytokine-driven neurological disease
formal: Neurological disease from excessive cytokine activity, such as in CRES, neuroinflammation and autoinflammatory conditions.
simple: Brain and nerve problems caused by too much immune signalling.
th: กลุ่มภาวะทางระบบประสาทที่เกิดจาก cytokine ถูกปล่อยออกมามากเกิน เช่น หลังการรักษาด้วย CAR-T, HLH และโรค autoinflammatory
tempoNote: Usually develops over hours to days after a trigger such as CAR-T infusion, infection or a systemic inflammatory flare
feat: Umbrella concept, not a single disease: neurological dysfunction driven by IL-1, IL-6, interferon-gamma and related mediators
Encephalopathy with word-finding trouble, tremor, handwriting change, seizures and, at worst, cerebral oedema
Usually accompanied by fever and systemic inflammation (cytokine release syndrome, HLH, autoinflammatory flare)
Settings: CAR-T and bispecific antibody therapy, HLH, monogenic autoinflammatory syndromes, severe sepsis
Often reversible when the inflammatory drive is switched off quickly
inv: Ferritin, CRP, fibrinogen, triglycerides, blood count, liver tests; IL-6 where available
EEG for subclinical seizures or diffuse slowing; MRI to exclude other causes and look for oedema
CSF to exclude infection; may show raised protein or pleocytosis
Structured scoring such as the ICE score in immune-effector-cell patients

case.who: 52-year-old man at a Bangkok university hospital, day 5 after CAR-T for relapsed lymphoma
case.story: Had fever and hypotension on day 2 that settled with tocilizumab; now cannot name objects and his writing has deteriorated.
case.exam: Drowsy but rousable, expressive dysphasia, postural tremor, no focal weakness, no neck stiffness.
case.tests: Ferritin very high, CRP raised; EEG shows generalised slowing without seizures; MRI brain normal.
case.q: What process links his symptoms, and what is the mainstay of treatment?
case.a: Cytokine-driven neurotoxicity (ICANS); corticosteroids with seizure prophylaxis and close monitoring, as tocilizumab alone does not treat the CNS component.

det.patho: Activated immune cells release large amounts of IL-1, IL-6, TNF and interferon-gamma. These mediators activate endothelium, loosen the blood–brain barrier and switch on microglia and astrocytes, so neuronal function falters even without direct immune attack on neurons. Raised CSF cytokines, endothelial activation markers and pericyte injury have been shown in CAR-T neurotoxicity, which serves as the model for the whole group.
det.clinical: This is a mechanistic umbrella rather than a single clinical diagnosis. Patterns include encephalopathy after immune-effector-cell therapy, the CNS phase of HLH, aseptic meningitis or sensorineural deafness in cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes, and septic encephalopathy. Language disturbance and dysgraphia are early signals after CAR-T; seizures, motor weakness and diffuse cerebral oedema mark severe disease. Fever and systemic inflammation usually precede or accompany the neurological picture.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on context: a known trigger, systemic inflammatory markers and exclusion of infection, drugs, metabolic causes and tumour progression. Ferritin, CRP and blood counts help identify HLH or cytokine release syndrome. EEG detects non-convulsive seizures, and MRI is chiefly used to exclude other pathology or show oedema. In autoinflammatory disease, genetic testing for inflammasome-related genes confirms the cause.
det.treatment: Treatment targets the driving cytokine pathway and supports the brain. After CAR-T, corticosteroids are the core therapy for neurotoxicity, with anakinra used for refractory cases; tocilizumab treats systemic cytokine release but does not cross well into the CNS. HLH is managed with steroids, etoposide-based regimens or emapalumab and treatment of the trigger. IL-1 blockade (anakinra, canakinumab) controls cryopyrin-associated disease. Levetiracetam is commonly used for seizure prevention or treatment.
det.prognosis: Most immune-effector-cell neurotoxicity resolves within days to weeks; fulminant cerebral oedema is rare but can be fatal. Outcome in HLH depends on trigger control and speed of treatment.
pearls: After CAR-T, a change in handwriting or naming is often the earliest sign of neurotoxicity.
Tocilizumab calms fever and hypotension but is not the main treatment for the brain component.
Very high ferritin in a febrile encephalopathic patient should prompt a search for HLH.
det.thd: Cytokine-driven neurological disease เป็นแนวคิดรวมของภาวะที่ cytokine เช่น IL-1, IL-6 และ interferon-gamma ถูกหลั่งมากจนทำให้ blood–brain barrier รั่วและสมองทำงานผิดปกติ ตัวอย่างสำคัญคือ ICANS หลังให้ CAR-T, HLH และโรค autoinflammatory ผู้ป่วยมักมีไข้ร่วมกับสับสน พูดไม่ออก มือสั่น หรือชัก การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ เช่น steroid สำหรับ ICANS, การรักษา HLH และยาต้าน IL-1 สำหรับโรค autoinflammatory
