name: D-glyceric acidaemia
formal: Autosomal recessive organic aciduria from GLYCTK deficiency or related defect, with hypotonia, seizures and developmental delay.
simple: A rare inherited metabolic condition causing developmental delay and seizures.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมยีนด้อยที่หายากมากจากเอนไซม์ glycerate kinase บกพร่อง มีกรด D-glyceric ในปัสสาวะสูง อาการหลากหลายตั้งแต่ไม่มีอาการจนถึงกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนปวกเปียก ชัก และพัฒนาการช้า
tempoNote: Severe cases present in the newborn period or infancy; others are found incidentally
feat: Neonatal or infantile hypotonia and poor feeding in severe cases
Seizures, sometimes early and refractory
Developmental delay, microcephaly
Some affected relatives have few or no symptoms; causality debated
inv: Urine organic acids: raised glyceric acid; chiral analysis to confirm D- rather than L-form
GLYCTK sequencing
Plasma glycine (some early cases had high glycine); MRI and EEG for severity

case.who: 2-month-old girl from Pattani, parents are cousins
case.story: Floppy since birth with poor sucking; now has daily brief stiffening spells.
case.exam: Axial hypotonia, poor visual fixation, small head circumference.
case.tests: Urine organic acids show high glyceric acid, confirmed as the D-isomer; GLYCTK biallelic variant found; MRI shows delayed myelination.
case.q: How certain is it that this metabolite explains her disease, and what treatment is available?
case.a: D-glyceric aciduria is linked to such cases, but asymptomatic people with the same defect exist, so other causes must still be sought; treatment is supportive with antiseizure drugs.

read.where: Chapter 36: Seizures Due to Inborn Errors of Metabolism

det.patho: GLYCTK encodes glycerate kinase, which phosphorylates D-glycerate arising from serine and fructose metabolism. Biallelic variants cause D-glycerate to accumulate and spill into urine. Why this would injure the brain is unclear; early cases were associated with features of non-ketotic hyperglycinaemia, and the toxicity of D-glycerate itself has not been established. It is extremely rare, with only a few dozen reported patients.
det.clinical: Reported phenotypes range from severe neonatal encephalopathy with hypotonia, seizures, microcephaly and early death to mild speech delay, and some siblings with identical biochemistry have been healthy. Because of this spread, ascertainment bias is likely, and the disorder may be partly benign. Clinicians should not stop looking for another explanation in a severely affected child.
det.diagnosis: Urine organic acid analysis shows increased glyceric acid; chiral separation is needed to distinguish D-glyceric aciduria from L-glyceric aciduria (primary hyperoxaluria type 2). GLYCTK testing confirms. Exome sequencing is advisable to look for a second cause. Assess with EEG, MRI and developmental evaluation.
det.treatment: There is no proven specific therapy. A handful of patients have trialled fructose restriction with unclear benefit. Management is supportive: seizure control, feeding support, physiotherapy and developmental therapy. Offer genetic counselling.
det.prognosis: Highly variable; with so few reported patients, the outlook is poorly defined.
pearls: Ask the lab to separate D- and L-glyceric acid; the L-form means hyperoxaluria type 2.
Asymptomatic affected siblings suggest the metabolite may not explain everything.
Do exome sequencing to look for a second diagnosis in severe cases.
det.thd: D-glyceric acidaemia เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมยีนด้อยที่หายากมากจากยีน GLYCTK ตรวจพบกรด D-glyceric สูงในปัสสาวะ ผู้ป่วยบางรายมีกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนปวกเปียก ชัก และพัฒนาการช้า แต่บางรายไม่มีอาการเลย จึงยังไม่แน่ชัดว่าสารนี้ทำให้เกิดโรคจริงหรือไม่ วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจกรดอินทรีย์ในปัสสาวะแยกชนิด D/L และตรวจยีน ยังไม่มีการรักษาเฉพาะ ให้การรักษาประคับประคอง

name: DADS neuropathy
formal: Distal acquired demyelinating symmetric neuropathy, a sensory-predominant chronic demyelinating neuropathy often with IgM anti-MAG antibodies, causing distal numbness and ataxia.
simple: A chronic nerve disease with damage to the nerve insulation of the feet and hands, causing numbness and unsteadiness.
more: Search for anti-MAG IgM; rituximab for anti-MAG cases; IVIG for others.
th: เส้นประสาทอักเสบเรื้อรังแบบ demyelinating ที่เด่นปลายมือปลายเท้าและด้านความรู้สึก มักพบ IgM paraprotein และ anti-MAG ในผู้ชายสูงอายุ
tempoNote: Slow progression over months to years
feat: Distal symmetric numbness and imbalance, mainly in the legs, with sensory ataxia
Mild distal weakness only; proximal strength spared
Postural or action tremor of the hands in many anti-MAG cases
Typically older men; IgM monoclonal gammopathy in about two-thirds
Now termed distal CIDP when no paraprotein; anti-MAG cases are classified separately
inv: NCS: markedly prolonged distal motor latencies (high terminal latency index) with relatively less proximal slowing
Serum immunofixation for IgM paraprotein; anti-MAG antibody titre
Haematology work-up for Waldenström macroglobulinaemia or lymphoma when IgM is present

case.story: Over two years his feet have gone numb and he sways in the dark; his hands shake when he holds a cup.
case.exam: Reduced vibration and joint position to the ankles, positive Romberg, absent ankle jerks, mild toe extensor weakness, postural tremor.
case.tests: NCS: very prolonged distal motor latencies; IgM kappa paraprotein 6 g/L; anti-MAG strongly positive.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and which therapy has the best evidence?
case.a: Anti-MAG neuropathy with a DADS phenotype; rituximab is the main option when disability progresses, and IVIG or steroids are usually ineffective.

read.where: Chapter 46 Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP), pp. 721–742

det.patho: In about two-thirds of cases an IgM monoclonal antibody binds myelin-associated glycoprotein in non-compact myelin, causing widened myelin lamellae and preferential distal demyelination. Cases without anti-MAG behave more like distal CIDP and are thought to share CIDP's immune mechanisms. Underlying IgM MGUS is most common, but Waldenström macroglobulinaemia or other B-cell disorders must be sought.
det.clinical: Patients, usually men over 60, report gradually spreading numbness and imbalance more than weakness. Gait ataxia, falls in the dark and an action tremor are typical. Progression is slow and many remain ambulant for years. DADS without paraprotein can occur at younger ages and may respond to standard CIDP therapies.
det.diagnosis: NCS shows disproportionately prolonged distal motor latencies, a low terminal latency index and slowed conduction. Serum immunofixation should always be done, followed by anti-MAG ELISA if IgM is present. Haematology input is needed for bone marrow examination when IgM is high or there are systemic features. Under the 2021 EAN/PNS classification, anti-MAG neuropathy is separated from CIDP and paraprotein-negative cases are labelled distal CIDP.
det.treatment: Mild, stable anti-MAG neuropathy may simply be observed. Rituximab is the most used treatment for progressive disability, with benefit in a subset; ibrutinib or other B-cell therapies are used when Waldenström disease coexists. IVIG gives short-lived benefit at best and steroids are usually ineffective in anti-MAG cases, whereas distal CIDP without paraprotein may respond to IVIG or steroids. Balance training and tremor management help function.
det.prognosis: Usually slowly progressive with moderate disability after many years; a minority become significantly disabled.
pearls: Distal sensory ataxia + tremor + prolonged distal latencies in an older man: check IgM and anti-MAG.
Anti-MAG neuropathy usually does not respond to IVIG or steroids; rituximab is the option.
Always look for Waldenström macroglobulinaemia when IgM paraprotein is found.
det.thd: DADS neuropathy คือเส้นประสาทอักเสบเรื้อรังแบบ demyelinating ที่เด่นปลายและด้านความรู้สึก ผู้ป่วยมักเป็นชายสูงอายุ ชาปลายเท้า เดินเซในที่มืด และมือสั่น ประมาณสองในสามมี IgM paraprotein และ anti-MAG NCS พบ distal motor latency ยาวมาก กรณี anti-MAG ไม่ตอบสนองต่อ IVIG หรือ steroid มักใช้ rituximab และต้องตรวจหา Waldenström ด้วย

name: Danon disease
formal: X-linked LAMP2 deficiency with vacuolar cardiomyopathy and skeletal myopathy, usually with intellectual disability, retinopathy, and Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern.
simple: An inherited disease causing thickened weak heart muscle, muscle weakness, and sometimes learning difficulties.
more: Biopsy shows autophagic vacuoles lacking LAMP2; confirm genetically. Heart transplant is often required; gene therapy is under study.
ab: Lysosomal glycogen storage disease with normal acid maltase
th: โรคพันธุกรรมถ่ายทอดทางโครโมโซม X จากการขาด LAMP2 ทำให้เกิดกล้ามเนื้อหัวใจหนาและกล้ามเนื้อลายอ่อนแรง มักมีสติปัญญาบกพร่อง จอตาผิดปกติ และ WPW
tempoNote: Males present in childhood or adolescence; females later in adulthood, mostly with cardiac disease
feat: Severe hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, often with Wolff–Parkinson–White pre-excitation and arrhythmia
Mild proximal skeletal myopathy with raised CK
Intellectual disability or learning problems in many males
Pigmentary retinopathy and visual impairment
Female carriers develop cardiomyopathy later, sometimes dilated
inv: ECG (pre-excitation, very high voltages), echocardiography and cardiac MRI
CK (moderately raised), liver enzymes; ophthalmology review
Muscle biopsy: autophagic vacuoles with sarcolemmal features, absent LAMP2; LAMP2 gene testing

case.story: Faints during school sports; teachers note he struggles academically and tires on stairs.
case.exam: Mild hip-girdle weakness, loud systolic murmur, pigmentary changes on fundoscopy.
case.tests: ECG short PR with delta waves and huge QRS voltages; echo septal thickness 30 mm; CK 900 U/L; LAMP2 deletion.
case.q: What is the main determinant of survival?
case.a: The cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia; early cardiology care, ICD and transplant evaluation are critical.

det.patho: LAMP2 is a lysosomal membrane protein essential for autophagosome–lysosome fusion. Its deficiency causes autophagic vacuoles with glycogen accumulation in cardiac and skeletal muscle, while acid maltase activity is normal. It is X-linked dominant, so heterozygous women are also affected but later and more mildly.
det.clinical: Affected males typically present in adolescence with cardiomyopathy, which can rapidly progress to heart failure or sudden death by the second or third decade. Skeletal myopathy is usually mild. Cognitive and retinal involvement is common. Women develop cardiac disease in middle age.
det.diagnosis: Suspect in young males with massive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and pre-excitation, especially with raised CK or learning problems. Genetic testing confirms; biopsy shows LAMP2 absence. Screen female relatives with ECG and echo.
det.treatment: Management is cardiological: ICD for sudden death prevention, careful arrhythmia management (accessory pathway ablation), heart failure treatment and early referral for heart transplantation. Neuromuscular and educational support are supportive. AAV gene therapy is in clinical trials.
det.prognosis: Without transplantation, many males die before 30 from heart failure or arrhythmia.
pearls: Massive cardiac hypertrophy + WPW + raised CK in a boy: Danon disease.
Acid maltase is normal, unlike Pompe disease.
Heterozygous females can develop cardiomyopathy — screen them.
det.thd: Danon disease เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมถ่ายทอดทางโครโมโซม X จากการขาดโปรตีน LAMP2 ทำให้เกิดการสะสมในกล้ามเนื้อหัวใจและกล้ามเนื้อลาย ผู้ชายมีอาการตั้งแต่วัยรุ่น ได้แก่ กล้ามเนื้อหัวใจหนามาก มี WPW เสี่ยงหัวใจเต้นผิดจังหวะ กล้ามเนื้อต้นแขนขาอ่อนแรงเล็กน้อย CK สูง สติปัญญาบกพร่อง และจอตาผิดปกติ ผู้หญิงมีอาการช้ากว่า รักษาหลักที่หัวใจ เช่น ICD และปลูกถ่ายหัวใจ

name: Davidenkow disease
formal: Scapuloperoneal syndrome with weakness of shoulder girdle and peroneal muscles, due to neurogenic or myopathic causes such as SPSMA or TRPV4.
simple: A rare condition in which weakness affects the shoulder and front leg muscles.
more: EMG and gene testing; supportive therapy with orthoses. Neurogenic scapuloperoneal syndrome with shoulder girdle and peroneal weakness from SMA or nerve disease (Davidenkow syndrome). Dominant; EMG shows neurogenic changes; supportive.
th: กลุ่มอาการอ่อนแรงบริเวณไหล่-สะบักและกล้ามเนื้อ peroneal ของขา จากสาเหตุทางเส้นประสาทหรือ anterior horn เช่น TRPV4 หรือ CMT
tempoNote: Slowly progressive from childhood to mid-adult life
feat: Weakness of scapular stabilisers and ankle dorsiflexors (foot drop)
Scapular winging and steppage gait
Neurogenic origin: distal sensory loss may accompany in Davidenkow's original description
Causes include TRPV4 (scapuloperoneal SMA), PMP22-related neuropathy and others
Myopathic scapuloperoneal syndromes (FHL1, MYH7, desmin) must be separated
inv: NCS/EMG to separate neuropathy, neuronopathy and myopathy
CK (normal or slightly raised in neurogenic forms)
Gene panel: TRPV4, PMP22, FHL1, MYH7, DES and others

case.story: Foot slapping when walking for 5 years and difficulty lifting his arms to put things on a shelf.
case.exam: Bilateral scapular winging, deltoid sparing, weak tibialis anterior, high-stepping gait, absent ankle reflexes, mild distal vibration loss.
case.tests: NCS show length-dependent demyelinating changes; CK normal; PMP22 duplication found.
case.q: What syndrome pattern does this show and why is EMG/NCS the key first step?
case.a: Scapuloperoneal (Davidenkow) syndrome of neurogenic origin; electrophysiology separates neurogenic from myopathic scapuloperoneal disorders.

det.patho: Davidenkow described a scapuloperoneal pattern of weakness with distal sensory loss, attributed to a hereditary neuropathy. Today it is regarded as a clinical pattern with several causes, including TRPV4-related spinal muscular atrophy and some demyelinating neuropathies. The selective involvement of scapular and peroneal muscles is not fully explained.
det.clinical: Patients develop foot drop and scapular winging, often slowly over years. Sensory loss and reduced reflexes suggest a neuropathic cause, while their absence suggests SMA. Vocal cord weakness may accompany TRPV4 disease. Course is usually slow.
det.diagnosis: Electrophysiology is central: neurogenic changes with normal sensory studies suggest SMA, and abnormal sensory responses suggest neuropathy. Genetic panels for neuropathy and SMA genes identify many causes. Biopsy is rarely needed.
det.treatment: No disease-specific treatment is available. Ankle-foot orthoses, physiotherapy, scapular bracing and occupational therapy improve function. Monitor for respiratory or laryngeal involvement in TRPV4 disease.
det.prognosis: Usually slowly progressive with preserved independence for many years.
pearls: Scapuloperoneal weakness can be neurogenic or myopathic; EMG decides.
Laryngeal or vocal cord weakness suggests TRPV4.
Davidenkow is a pattern, not a single gene.
det.thd: Davidenkow disease คือกลุ่มอาการอ่อนแรงบริเวณสะบักและกล้ามเนื้อหน้าแข้ง ทำให้สะบักยกและเท้าตก เกิดจากสาเหตุทางเส้นประสาทหรือเซลล์ประสาทสั่งการ เช่น TRPV4 หรือ CMT ต้องตรวจ EMG/NCS เพื่อแยกจากโรคกล้ามเนื้อแบบ scapuloperoneal และตรวจยีน การรักษาเน้นอุปกรณ์ช่วยและกายภาพบำบัด

Facial weakness, asymmetry and D4Z4 contraction

name: Degenerative spinal disease
formal: Age-related disc and facet degeneration with canal stenosis causing back pain, radiculopathy, neurogenic claudication or myelopathy.
simple: Wear and tear of the spine that can press on the spinal cord or nerves.
th: Degenerative spine disease คือการเสื่อมของหมอนรองกระดูก ข้อต่อ facet เอ็น ligamentum flavum และกระดูกงอก ทำให้ช่องไขสันหลังและรูรากประสาทแคบ ผลคือปวดคอหรือหลัง รากประสาทอักเสบ neurogenic claudication (ปวดขาเมื่อเดิน นั่งแล้วดีขึ้น) หรือ myelopathy ส่วนใหญ่รักษาแบบไม่ผ่าตัด ผ่าตัดเมื่ออ่อนแรงมากขึ้น ปวดรุนแรงที่ไม่ดีขึ้น myelopathy หรือ cauda equina
tempoNote: Gradual over years with intermittent flares; acute change usually means a disc extrusion or cauda equina
feat: The process involves disc dehydration and collapse, annular tears, facet hypertrophy, osteophytes, thickened ligamentum flavum and sometimes spondylolisthesis; the term degenerative spine disease is preferred to disc disease alone

Lumbar stenosis (most at L4–5, then L3–4) causes back and leg pain on standing and walking that eases with sitting or bending forward (neurogenic claudication), unlike vascular claudication which settles on stopping in any posture
Central canal, lateral recess (the commonest cause of a single root syndrome, often L5 at L4–5) and foraminal stenosis give different patterns of pain, numbness and weakness
Cervical spondylosis causes neck stiffness, radiculopathy or myelopathy with clumsy hands, gait imbalance and brisk reflexes; symptomatic thoracic stenosis is rare and usually a calcified disc
Imaging change is almost universal with age and often asymptomatic; congenital short pedicles or achondroplasia predispose to early symptoms
inv: MRI of the symptomatic region for canal, recess and foraminal narrowing, disc extrusions and cord signal; CT for bone anatomy or when MRI is contraindicated
Standing flexion-extension radiographs for instability or spondylolisthesis; whole-spine films for alignment before fusion
EMG and nerve conduction studies when the root level is uncertain or peripheral neuropathy or entrapment is in doubt; ankle-brachial index when vascular claudication is possible

case.story: For two years he has had aching in both buttocks and thighs after walking 150 metres in the paddy, relieved within a minute by squatting or leaning on his hoe. He can cycle for an hour without trouble.
case.exam: Normal pulses, normal strength and sensation at rest, absent ankle jerks, symptoms reproduced after 3 minutes of walking and extension.
case.tests: MRI shows multilevel lumbar stenosis, worst at L4–5, with facet hypertrophy and thickened ligamentum flavum; ankle-brachial index normal.
case.q: How do you separate this from vascular claudication and what are the options?
case.a: Neurogenic claudication from lumbar canal stenosis: relief by flexion and the ability to cycle point to a neural cause, and pulses are normal. Start with exercise, weight and analgesia advice; if disabling despite conservative care, offer decompressive laminectomy, with fusion only for instability or spondylolisthesis.

det.patho: With age the disc loses proteoglycan and water, develops tears and loses height, which transfers load to the facet joints and ligamentum flavum and promotes osteophytes, hypertrophy and instability. Acquired narrowing is often superimposed on a congenitally shallow canal. Neurological involvement occurs at three sites: the central canal, the lateral recess where the root enters its foramen, and the foramen itself. Stable stenosis consists of facet and ligament hypertrophy with disc collapse; unstable forms add degenerative spondylolisthesis or scoliosis.
det.clinical: Symptoms range from mechanical neck or back pain through radiculopathy to claudication and myelopathy. Lumbar stenosis causes gradual back and leg pain with walking and standing that eases on sitting or lying and with forward flexion, often with a normal examination at rest. Cervical myelopathy is insidious and progressive and may present with leg or hand symptoms. A large extruded disc can suddenly cause cauda equina syndrome. Thai farmers and labourers who lift heavy loads form a large part of the patient population.
det.diagnosis: Clinical history and examination come first because imaging degeneration is nearly universal in older adults. MRI maps the compression and is concordant when the root level and symptoms match; flexion-extension films show dynamic instability. EMG helps separate root from nerve or plexus disease. Red flags (fever, weight loss, cancer, trauma, progressive deficit, sphincter loss) call for urgent imaging. Vascular claudication, hip disease and peripheral neuropathy should be considered.
det.treatment: Most patients are managed non-surgically with activity, physiotherapy and exercise, weight control, short courses of analgesics or NSAIDs, neuropathic agents for radicular pain and sometimes epidural steroid injection for short-term relief. Decompressive laminectomy or laminotomy is offered for disabling neurogenic claudication, progressive deficit, myelopathy or cauda equina syndrome. Fusion adds benefit mainly for instability or spondylolisthesis; in lumbar stenosis without slip, trials show decompression alone is as good as adding fusion, and interspinous spacers have largely been abandoned. Cauda equina syndrome requires urgent decompression.
det.prognosis: Back pain tends to fluctuate; claudication is often stable for years; cervical myelopathy tends to progress without decompression.
pearls: Relief by sitting or bending forward and the ability to ride a bicycle favour neurogenic over vascular claudication.
Always ask about hand clumsiness: cervical myelopathy can produce leg symptoms that tempt a lumbar-only work-up.
Match symptoms to imaging; a degenerate MRI alone is not a diagnosis.
det.thd: Degenerative spine disease คือการเสื่อมของหมอนรองกระดูก ข้อต่อ facet เอ็นหนา และกระดูกงอก ทำให้ช่องไขสันหลังและรูรากประสาทแคบ ผู้ป่วยมีปวดคอหรือหลัง รากประสาทอักเสบ หรือ neurogenic claudication คือปวดหรือชาขาเมื่อยืนเดิน และดีขึ้นเมื่อนั่งหรือก้มตัว ต่างจากหลอดเลือดขาตีบซึ่งดีขึ้นเมื่อหยุดเดินแม้ยืนอยู่ MRI ต้องดูร่วมกับอาการเพราะพบความเสื่อมได้ในคนส่วนใหญ่ รักษาด้วยกายภาพบำบัดและยาก่อน ผ่าตัดเมื่ออาการรุนแรง อ่อนแรงมากขึ้น myelopathy หรือ cauda equina

name: Degenerative vascular disease
formal: Atherosclerotic or small vessel degeneration causing cerebral ischaemia, white matter disease and vascular cognitive impairment.
simple: Age-related damage to blood vessels that supply the brain.
ab: Cerebral small vessel and large artery degeneration
th: กลุ่มโรคหลอดเลือดสมองเสื่อมจากอายุและปัจจัยเสี่ยง (atherosclerosis, arteriolosclerosis) ทำให้เกิดสมองขาดเลือด white matter disease และสมองเสื่อมจากหลอดเลือด
tempoNote: Silent accumulation over years, punctuated by acute strokes or stepwise decline
feat: Umbrella label for wear-and-tear arterial disease: large-artery atheroma plus small-vessel arteriolosclerosis
Presents as TIA, ischaemic stroke, lacunes, or slowly accumulating white matter change
Cognitive picture is slowed processing and executive dysfunction more than amnesia
Gait slowing, urinary urgency and mood change often accompany the cognitive decline
Driven by hypertension, diabetes, smoking, dyslipidaemia and age
inv: MRI with FLAIR, DWI and SWI: white matter hyperintensities, lacunes, microbleeds, old infarcts
Carotid duplex or CTA/MRA for large-artery stenosis
Vascular risk work-up: BP profile, HbA1c, lipids, ECG
Cognitive screen (MoCA) with attention to executive items

case.who: 74-year-old retired teacher from Ratchaburi with 20 years of poorly controlled hypertension
case.story: Family notes two years of slower thinking, shuffling gait and new urinary urgency, with one brief episode of right-hand clumsiness last year.
case.exam: Slowed responses, poor verbal fluency, brisk reflexes on the right, short-stepped gait with preserved arm swing.
case.tests: MRI: confluent periventricular white matter change, several old lacunes in basal ganglia; carotids show 40% plaque only.
case.q: What process links these findings and what is the main treatment target?
case.a: Degenerative small-vessel disease causing vascular cognitive impairment; strict BP control and overall risk-factor management.

read.where: Chapter 11 Cognitive Impairment and Dementia — Vascular Dementia and Vascular Cognitive Impairment

det.patho: Two overlapping processes are lumped here. Large and medium arteries develop atheromatous plaque that narrows lumens or throws emboli, while penetrating arterioles undergo lipohyalinosis and wall thickening that reduces perfusion of deep white matter and basal ganglia. Chronic hypoperfusion, blood-brain barrier leak and impaired autoregulation produce white matter rarefaction, lacunes and microbleeds.
det.clinical: Patients may have discrete strokes, but many accumulate damage silently and present with slowed thinking, apathy, gait change and bladder urgency. Stepwise worsening suggests repeated infarcts, while a smooth decline points toward diffuse small-vessel change. Depression and emotional lability are common. This is a descriptive term rather than a single disease, and mixed pathology with Alzheimer change is frequent in older patients.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on matching the clinical picture to imaging: white matter hyperintensities, lacunes, enlarged perivascular spaces and microbleeds on MRI, together with vascular risk factors. Vessel imaging looks for treatable carotid or intracranial stenosis. Genetic small-vessel disease should be considered when onset is young or risk factors are absent. Neuropsychology helps separate executive-predominant vascular profiles from amnestic neurodegeneration.
det.treatment: Management is prevention: target blood pressure control, statins, diabetes care, smoking cessation and exercise. Antiplatelet therapy is used after ischaemic events but is not routinely given for white matter change alone. Symptomatic carotid stenosis may need revascularisation. Cholinesterase inhibitors give modest benefit in some patients with vascular cognitive impairment; rehabilitation addresses gait and falls.
det.prognosis: Progression is variable and slows with good risk-factor control; high white matter burden predicts stroke, dementia and disability.
pearls: Executive slowing plus gait change plus urgency in a hypertensive patient: think small-vessel disease before Alzheimer disease.
After 75, mixed vascular and neurodegenerative pathology is usual rather than exceptional.
SWI microbleed pattern (deep versus lobar) hints at hypertensive arteriopathy versus amyloid angiopathy.
det.thd: โรคหลอดเลือดสมองเสื่อมเกิดจากหลอดเลือดแดงใหญ่มีคราบไขมันและหลอดเลือดเล็กผนังหนาตัวตามอายุและปัจจัยเสี่ยง ทำให้สมองขาดเลือดทั้งแบบเฉียบพลันและแบบเรื้อรัง ผู้ป่วยมักคิดช้า เดินซอยเท้า และปัสสาวะกลั้นไม่อยู่ MRI พบ white matter hyperintensity และ lacune การรักษาเน้นคุมความดันโลหิต เบาหวาน ไขมัน และเลิกบุหรี่

name: Degos’ disease
formal: Malignant atrophic papulosis, a thrombo-occlusive vasculopathy with porcelain-white skin papules, bowel infarction and cerebral infarcts and haemorrhage.
simple: A rare blood vessel disease with white skin spots that can cause strokes and bowel problems.
th: โรคหลอดเลือดอุดตันที่พบน้อยมาก มีตุ่มผิวหนังสีขาวขุ่นตรงกลางขอบแดง ร่วมกับลำไส้ขาดเลือดและสมองขาดเลือดหรือเลือดออก
tempoNote: Skin lesions may be present for months or years before sudden systemic involvement
feat: Small papules with a porcelain-white depressed centre and a red telangiectatic rim, mainly on trunk and limbs
Systemic form attacks bowel (perforation, peritonitis) and the nervous system
Neurological involvement: ischaemic strokes, haemorrhages, cranial neuropathies, myelopathy, polyradiculopathy
Benign cutaneous-only form exists and may stay limited to skin
Some cases overlap with lupus, dermatomyositis or other connective tissue disease
inv: Skin biopsy: wedge-shaped dermal infarct with occluded small vessels and mucin, little inflammation
MRI brain and spine for infarcts, haemorrhage or meningeal enhancement
CSF: may show raised protein; exclude infection and vasculitis
Autoimmune screen to look for an associated connective tissue disease

case.who: 32-year-old man from Udon Thani with a two-year history of odd skin spots
case.story: Presents with sudden left-sided weakness; a month earlier he had abdominal pain treated as gastritis.
case.exam: Dozens of small atrophic papules with white centres on chest and thighs; left hemiparesis.
case.tests: MRI shows right-sided cortical infarcts and a small lobar haemorrhage; skin biopsy shows a dermal wedge infarct with thrombosed venules.
case.q: Which rare vasculopathy unifies skin, bowel and brain findings?
case.a: Malignant atrophic papulosis (Degos disease), systemic form.

read.where: Chapter 8 Stroke and Cerebrovascular Diseases — Degos’ Disease
Section 6 Systemic Disorders That Also Involve the Cerebrovascular System

det.patho: Degos disease is a thrombo-occlusive endotheliopathy of small arteries and veins. Complement activation, notably C5b-9 deposition, and interferon-alpha signatures have been described, suggesting an immune-mediated endothelial injury, but the cause remains unknown. Vessels become blocked with little true vasculitis, producing infarcts in skin, gut and nervous system.
det.clinical: Most patients first notice the characteristic papules. A subset develops systemic disease, often within a few years, with bowel perforation the main killer. Neurological involvement includes multifocal ischaemic strokes, intracranial haemorrhage, cranial nerve palsies, myelopathy and radiculopathy, sometimes with headache from meningeal involvement.
det.diagnosis: The skin lesions are almost pathognomonic, and a deep skin biopsy confirms the dermal infarct pattern. Brain and spine MRI document the extent of CNS disease. Screening for lupus, antiphospholipid antibodies and other connective tissue disorders is essential because Degos-like lesions occur in them. Endoscopy and abdominal imaging assess gut involvement.
det.treatment: No therapy is proven. Antiplatelet agents such as aspirin and dipyridamole are commonly used for skin-limited disease. For systemic disease, the complement inhibitor eculizumab and subcutaneous treprostinil have produced responses in case series. Immunosuppression with steroids is generally unhelpful unless an associated connective tissue disease is present.
det.prognosis: Skin-limited disease may be benign; systemic Degos disease historically carried high mortality within a few years, mainly from bowel perforation and CNS events.
pearls: White-centred atrophic papules plus stroke or acute abdomen: think Degos.
Biopsy shows occlusion rather than inflammatory vasculitis, so steroids usually fail.
Eculizumab is the main rescue option reported for systemic disease.
det.thd: Degos disease เป็นโรคที่หลอดเลือดขนาดเล็กอุดตันจากความผิดปกติของ endothelium โดยไม่ทราบสาเหตุชัดเจน ลักษณะเด่นคือตุ่มผิวหนังกลางขาวขุ่นขอบแดง บางรายมีลำไส้ทะลุและสมองขาดเลือดหรือเลือดออก วินิจฉัยด้วยการตัดชิ้นเนื้อผิวหนัง การรักษายังไม่มีมาตรฐาน ใช้ยาต้านเกล็ดเลือด และใน systemic form อาจใช้ eculizumab หรือ treprostinil

name: Dejerine–Roussy syndrome
formal: Thalamic pain syndrome after thalamic stroke with contralateral sensory loss, hemiataxia, burning pain and allodynia, later with choreoathetoid movements.
simple: One-sided burning pain and numbness that follow a stroke in the thalamus.
ab: Central post-stroke pain of thalamic origin
th: กลุ่มอาการหลังสมองส่วน thalamus ขาดเลือด มีชาครึ่งซีก ร่วมกับปวดแสบร้อนและไวต่อการสัมผัสผิดปกติด้านตรงข้าม
tempoNote: Pain typically emerges weeks to months after the thalamic stroke, then persists
feat: Contralateral hemisensory loss after a lateral (ventral posterior) thalamic lesion
Delayed burning, aching or lancinating pain in the numb territory
Allodynia and hyperpathia: light touch or cold provokes exaggerated pain
May have mild hemiparesis, hemiataxia and later choreoathetoid or dystonic posturing of the hand
Pain worsened by emotion, temperature change and movement
inv: MRI brain: infarct or haemorrhage in the ventral posterolateral thalamus (thalamogeniculate territory)
Quantitative sensory testing documents impaired thermal sensation in the painful area
Exclude peripheral causes (radiculopathy, shoulder pathology) of limb pain

case.who: 63-year-old diabetic woman from Phitsanulok, three months after a small left thalamic infarct
case.story: Her right-sided numbness had improved, but she now reports constant burning in the right arm and face, unbearable when bedsheets touch the skin.
case.exam: Reduced pinprick and temperature sense on the right; stroking the right forearm provokes intense pain; mild right hand clumsiness.
case.tests: MRI shows an old lacunar infarct in the left ventral posterolateral thalamus.
case.q: What syndrome is this and which drug classes are first-line?
case.a: Dejerine–Roussy (thalamic central post-stroke pain); amitriptyline or gabapentinoids such as pregabalin.

read.where: 22 Vascular Syndromes of the Forebrain, Brainstem, and Cerebellum

det.patho: Damage to the ventral posterior thalamic nuclei and spinothalamic projections disrupts normal sensory processing. Loss of thermosensory input is thought to release thalamocortical circuits from inhibition, producing spontaneous neuronal bursting and central sensitisation. Not all thalamic lesions cause pain; involvement of spinothalamic relay regions is the key risk factor.
det.clinical: The full syndrome combines hemisensory loss, mild transient hemiparesis, hemiataxia, astereognosis and later severe pain. Pain usually appears after a delay of weeks to months as sensation partly recovers. Patients describe burning, freezing or crushing pain, with allodynia to touch or cold. Involuntary movements of the hand, such as pseudoathetosis, may follow loss of proprioception.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical: neuropathic pain confined to a body region corresponding to a thalamic lesion, with sensory abnormalities in the same area. MRI confirms the lesion. Alternative causes of pain in the hemiplegic limb, especially shoulder subluxation, spasticity and CRPS, must be excluded.
det.treatment: First-line options are amitriptyline and gabapentinoids, with lamotrigine as an alternative; duloxetine is sometimes used. Responses are often partial. Refractory cases may be considered for repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation of motor cortex or, in specialist centres, motor cortex or deep brain stimulation. Psychological support and sleep management help coping.
det.prognosis: Pain tends to be chronic and resistant; partial relief is a realistic goal for most.
pearls: Delay between stroke and pain onset is typical, so patients rarely link the two.
Thermal sensory loss in the painful zone strongly supports central pain.
Opioids work poorly in central post-stroke pain.
det.thd: Dejerine–Roussy syndrome คืออาการปวดจากสมองส่วนกลางหลัง thalamus ขาดเลือดหรือเลือดออก ผู้ป่วยมีอาการชาครึ่งซีกก่อน แล้วอีกหลายสัปดาห์ถึงหลายเดือนเกิดอาการปวดแสบร้อนและสัมผัสเบาๆ ก็เจ็บ วินิจฉัยจากอาการร่วมกับ MRI ที่พบรอยโรคใน thalamus การรักษาใช้ amitriptyline หรือ pregabalin/gabapentin และผลตอบสนองมักไม่เต็มที่

ddx.pt: Broader category; lesions anywhere along the spinothalamic pathway, not only the thalamus
Swelling, colour and sweating changes in a limb, often after trauma
Cape-like dissociated sensory loss with amyotrophy; cord cavity on MRI

aN: thalamic pain syndrome | thalamic syndrome | central post stroke pain of thalamic origin | dejerine roussy syndrome

name: Dejerine–Sottas disease (DSD)
formal: Hereditary demyelinating neuropathy (CMT3) with severe early-onset weakness, hypertrophic nerves, marked conduction slowing and high CSF protein.
simple: An inherited nerve disease starting in childhood with severe weakness and thickened nerves.
more: Dejerine-Sottas disease, severe early-onset demyelinating neuropathy with very slow conduction velocities, hypotonia, delayed motor milestones, and often de novo PMP22, MPZ, or EGR2 mutations. Nerve biopsy shows hypomyelination and onion bulbs; genetic testing confirms. Treatment is supportive with rehabilitation; disability is significant.
th: โรคเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายกรรมพันธุ์ชนิดปลอกไมอีลินเสื่อมรุนแรง เริ่มตั้งแต่ทารก เส้นประสาทโต การนำกระแสช้ามาก และโปรตีนในน้ำไขสันหลังสูง
tempoNote: Starts in infancy or the toddler years with delayed motor milestones and slow progression
feat: Infantile hypotonia, delayed walking and sensory ataxia
Distal and later proximal weakness, areflexia
Palpably enlarged peripheral nerves
Pes cavus, scoliosis; sometimes pupillary abnormalities and nystagmus
Motor conduction velocities extremely slow, often below 10 m/s
inv: NCS: profound uniform slowing; sensory responses absent
CSF protein often raised (root hypertrophy)
Gene testing: PMP22, MPZ, EGR2, PRX (dominant de novo or recessive)

case.story: Did not walk until 26 months, falls frequently and his gait is unsteady; parents are healthy.
case.exam: Hypotonia, distal weakness, areflexia, thickened ulnar nerves, sensory ataxia.
case.tests: Median motor velocity 6 m/s; CSF protein 90 mg/dL; de novo MPZ variant.
case.q: Why might this be mistaken for CIDP?
case.a: Raised CSF protein and slowed conduction, but uniform extreme slowing from infancy points to a hereditary neuropathy.

read.where: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves — Autosomal Dominant Charcot–Marie–Tooth Disease Type 1

det.patho: DSD is the severe end of demyelinating CMT, caused by dominant de novo point mutations (PMP22, MPZ, EGR2) or recessive variants (PRX, MTMR2). Myelin is thin or absent, with prominent onion bulbs and enlarged nerves; spinal roots may hypertrophy and compress the cord in rare cases.
det.clinical: Children present with delayed motor development and weakness, then progress to significant disability. Sensory ataxia, foot deformities and scoliosis are common. Some need wheelchairs by adolescence. Cranial nerve involvement and hearing loss can occur.
det.diagnosis: Very slow, uniform conduction (often under 10 m/s) in a child with early-onset neuropathy suggests DSD. Genetic testing defines the subtype; CSF protein elevation reflects root involvement and should not prompt treatment for CIDP without evidence.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy. Physiotherapy, orthoses, mobility aids, scoliosis management and respiratory monitoring. Avoid neurotoxic drugs. Genetic counselling given de novo dominant or recessive mechanisms.
det.prognosis: More severe than typical CMT; many remain ambulant with aids into adulthood but some lose walking early.
pearls: Infant with nerve conduction under 10 m/s: think DSD.
Raised CSF protein does not equal CIDP in a child with hereditary neuropathy.
DSD is now regarded as severe CMT1 or CMT4 rather than a separate entity.
det.thd: Dejerine–Sottas disease หรือ CMT3 เป็นโรคเส้นประสาทกรรมพันธุ์ชนิดปลอกไมอีลินเสื่อมที่รุนแรง เริ่มตั้งแต่ทารก เด็กเดินช้า ล้มบ่อย อ่อนแรง reflex หาย และคลำเส้นประสาทได้โต ตรวจ NCS พบการนำกระแสช้ามาก มักต่ำกว่า 10 m/s และโปรตีนในน้ำไขสันหลังสูง เกิดจากยีน PMP22, MPZ, EGR2 หรือ PRX รักษาแบบประคับประคองด้วยกายภาพและอุปกรณ์ช่วยเดิน

ddx.pt: Neonatal onset with near-absent myelin; even more severe
Recessive early-onset demyelinating CMT; overlap with DSD
Normal sensory responses and conduction; SMN1 deletion

name: Delayed post-hypoxic encephalopathy
formal: Neurological deterioration days to weeks after apparent recovery from hypoxic injury such as carbon monoxide, with leukoencephalopathy and cognitive change.
simple: Brain problems appearing weeks after recovery from oxygen shortage such as carbon monoxide poisoning.
th: ภาวะสมองเสื่อมที่เกิดขึ้นหลังฟื้นจากภาวะขาดออกซิเจน (เช่น พิษคาร์บอนมอนอกไซด์) ไปแล้วหลายวันถึงหลายสัปดาห์ จากการทำลายเนื้อสมองสีขาว
tempoNote: Biphasic: initial recovery, then a lucid interval of about 1–6 weeks before cognitive and motor decline over days to weeks
feat: Apparent full recovery after a hypoxic event (often carbon monoxide or opioid overdose), then new decline weeks later
Apathy, confusion, memory loss and frontal behaviour change that can progress to akinetic mutism
Parkinsonism with rigidity, shuffling gait, incontinence and sometimes pyramidal signs
Diffuse symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensity of cerebral white matter, sparing U-fibres
Many patients improve partly over months to a year
inv: MRI brain with DWI: confluent periventricular and centrum semiovale white-matter change, often restricted diffusion early; globus pallidus lesions after CO
Exclude mimics: metabolic panel, B12, thyroid, toxicology, EEG for non-convulsive seizures
Arylsulfatase A activity (low pseudodeficiency levels have been linked to susceptibility)
MR spectroscopy may show reduced NAA and raised choline or lactate

case.story: Found unconscious in a closed room with a charcoal stove; recovered fully after 2 days of oxygen. Three weeks later his wife notices he sits silently, forgets meals and wets himself.
case.exam: Abulic, slow to answer, bilateral rigidity and bradykinesia, brisk reflexes with extensor plantars.
case.tests: MRI shows symmetric confluent white-matter FLAIR hyperintensity with restricted diffusion and small pallidal lesions.
case.q: What explains the second decline after initial recovery?
case.a: Delayed post-hypoxic leukoencephalopathy after carbon monoxide exposure; supportive care and rehabilitation, with gradual partial recovery common.

det.patho: After a hypoxic insult that is often not severe enough to cause lasting coma, oligodendrocytes and myelin undergo delayed injury, giving a demyelinating leukoencephalopathy. Proposed mechanisms include impaired myelin turnover, oxidative and inflammatory injury, and with carbon monoxide additional lipid peroxidation. Partial arylsulfatase A deficiency may increase susceptibility in some patients. The exact frequency is uncertain; after CO poisoning, delayed neuropsychiatric sequelae are reported in a substantial minority.
det.clinical: The defining pattern is recovery followed by relapse after a lucid gap of days to weeks. Patients develop apathy, disorientation, memory and executive failure, mutism, incontinence and parkinsonism; some show chorea, spasticity or psychosis. Severity ranges from subtle cognitive change to akinetic mutism. Families often describe a person who was back at work and then 'switched off'.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the biphasic history and MRI showing diffuse symmetric white-matter signal change, sometimes with restricted diffusion early in the relapse. The globus pallidus is commonly affected after carbon monoxide. Work-up should exclude metabolic encephalopathy, seizures, infection, drug toxicity and leukodystrophy. No single blood test confirms it.
det.treatment: There is no proven disease-modifying therapy; care is supportive, with nutrition, prevention of aspiration and pressure injury, and active rehabilitation. Hyperbaric oxygen during acute CO poisoning may lower the risk of delayed sequelae, although trial evidence is mixed and its role after onset is unproven. Dopaminergic drugs or amantadine are sometimes tried for parkinsonism and abulia with variable benefit. Counsel families that improvement may take many months.
det.prognosis: Many patients recover substantially over 3–12 months, but a proportion keep permanent cognitive or motor deficits, and some die of complications.
pearls: Ask about charcoal stoves, generators and overdoses in any unexplained subacute white-matter dementia.
The lucid interval after hypoxia is the clue; the acute injury and the relapse are separate events.
Pallidal lesions plus diffuse white matter change after a lucid gap strongly suggest delayed CO injury.
det.thd: ภาวะนี้เกิดหลังผู้ป่วยขาดออกซิเจน เช่น สูดควันถ่านในห้องปิดหรือใช้ยาเกินขนาด แล้วฟื้นตัวดีในช่วงแรก แต่ราว 1–6 สัปดาห์ต่อมากลับซึม เฉยเมย ความจำเสีย กลั้นปัสสาวะไม่ได้ และแข็งเกร็งคล้ายพาร์กินสัน MRI พบเนื้อสมองสีขาวผิดปกติกระจายทั้งสองข้าง การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคองและฟื้นฟู หลายรายดีขึ้นช้า ๆ ภายในหลายเดือน

ddx.pt: Acute toxic phase itself; delayed form appears after an interval of improvement
Other toxins (heroin vapour, chemotherapy) produce similar white matter injury without a preceding hypoxic event
Rapid dementia with myoclonus and cortical ribboning on DWI rather than confluent white-matter change

aN: dphl | delayed post hypoxic leukencephalopathy | grinker myelinopathy | delayed neuropsychiatric sequele | dns after co poisoning

name: Delayed sleep–wake phase disorder
formal: Circadian disorder with persistent late sleep and wake times, causing difficulty falling asleep and waking for conventional hours.
simple: Being unable to fall asleep until very late and waking late, because the body clock runs behind.
th: นาฬิกาชีวภาพล่าช้า ทำให้หลับได้หลังตีสองถึงตีสามและตื่นเช้าไม่ไหว แต่ถ้าได้นอนตามเวลาที่ร่างกายต้องการจะหลับได้ปกติ พบบ่อยในวัยรุ่น
tempoNote: Usually starts in adolescence and persists for at least 3 months; worsens with school or work schedules
feat: Habitual sleep onset 2 hours or more later than desired, often after 2–3 am, with great difficulty waking in the morning
Sleep length and quality are normal when allowed to sleep on the preferred schedule (weekends, holidays)
Morning sleepiness, late arrival, absenteeism and poor school grades; evening alertness
Most common in teenagers and young adults; associated with depression, ADHD and heavy evening screen use
Some families carry CRY1 variants that lengthen the circadian period
inv: Sleep diary and actigraphy for at least 7 days, ideally 14, including free days
Morningness–eveningness questionnaire
Dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO) if available, which is delayed
Polysomnography is reserved for suspected coexisting sleep disorders

case.story: He cannot fall asleep before 3 am, misses morning classes and sleeps until noon at weekends, feeling fine afterwards; he games online until late.
case.exam: Normal; mood screening mildly low.
case.tests: Actigraphy over 2 weeks: stable sleep from 3:15 am to 11 am on free days with normal sleep length.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the timed treatment?
case.a: Delayed sleep–wake phase disorder; low-dose melatonin about 3–5 hours before current sleep onset, bright light on waking, evening light avoidance and gradual advancing of the schedule.

read.where: Chapter 29 Disorders of Sleep — Delayed Sleep–Wake Phase Disorder
Chapter 21: Shift work sleep disorder and jet lag
Chapter 51 Neurologic Aspects of Sleep Medicine

det.patho: The internal circadian clock sits late relative to clock time, so melatonin rises and the sleep window opens hours after conventional bedtime. Contributing factors include a longer intrinsic period, greater sensitivity to evening light, reduced morning light exposure and slower build-up of sleep pressure. Gene variants such as in CRY1 explain some familial cases, and adolescent biology adds a normal delay.
det.clinical: The typical patient is a teenager or young adult who lies awake until the early hours and then cannot get up. When free to choose, sleep is consolidated and of normal length, which separates it from insomnia. Morning absenteeism, academic decline and conflict at home are common, and depression often coexists. Behavioural choices such as late gaming worsen but do not fully explain it.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on a chronic delay of the sleep period with difficulty sleeping and waking at required times, confirmed by at least 7 days of diary or actigraphy, including free days. DLMO testing, where available, shows the delayed phase. Exclude insufficient sleep, depression, substance use and non-24-hour rhythm disorder by looking for a stable rather than drifting pattern.
det.treatment: Treatment shifts the clock earlier using timed melatonin taken several hours before the current sleep onset and bright light soon after waking. Avoid bright light and screens in the evening, keep a fixed wake time every day including weekends, and advance bedtime gradually. Chronotherapy by progressive delay is rarely used now. School start-time or work adjustments can help, and comorbid mood disorder should be treated.
det.prognosis: Often improves after adolescence but relapses easily if the routine slips.
pearls: Good sleep on holidays on a late schedule is the key clue that the problem is timing, not insomnia.
Melatonin advances the clock when given in the evening well before sleep; light advances it when given in the morning.
A fixed wake time, every day, matters more than an early bedtime.
det.thd: Delayed sleep–wake phase disorder คือนาฬิกาชีวภาพล่าช้า ทำให้หลับหลังตีสองตีสามและตื่นสาย แต่ถ้าได้นอนตามเวลาที่ร่างกายต้องการจะหลับปกติ พบบ่อยในวัยรุ่น วินิจฉัยด้วย sleep diary หรือ actigraphy อย่างน้อย 7 วัน การรักษาคือให้ melatonin ขนาดต่ำหลายชั่วโมงก่อนเวลาหลับ รับแสงสว่างตอนเช้า ลดแสงหน้าจอตอนค่ำ และตื่นเวลาเดิมทุกวัน

qx.stem: An 18-year-old male first-year university student from Bangkok cannot fall asleep before 3 am and misses 8 am lectures. On holidays he sleeps from 3 am to 11 am and feels well. Two weeks of actigraphy confirm a stable late sleep period of normal length.
qx.q: Which combination is most likely to shift his sleep earlier?
opts: Bright light at 10 pm and melatonin on waking
Low-dose melatonin in the early evening and bright light soon after waking
Zolpidem nightly at 11 pm
Modafinil in the evening
Bright light at 3 am and melatonin at midday
qx.why: Melatonin given in the early evening, several hours before current sleep onset, and bright light after waking both advance the circadian clock. Evening light delays the clock further. Hypnotics do not correct timing, and modafinil in the evening would worsen sleep onset.

qx.stem: A 17-year-old boy from Bangkok cannot fall asleep before 3 a.m. and wakes at noon when allowed, with normal sleep quality and duration on holidays. On school days he sleeps 4 hours, is late for classes and falls asleep in lessons. Actigraphy shows a consistently delayed pattern. Mood and physical examination are normal.
qx.q: Which treatment is best?
opts: Zolpidem at 10 p.m.
Modafinil in the morning only
Alprazolam at bedtime
Low-dose melatonin several hours before the target bedtime, with morning light and evening light restriction
Staying awake all night to reset the clock
qx.why: Delayed sleep–wake phase disorder is a circadian timing problem. Timed low-dose melatonin taken some hours before the desired bedtime, bright light soon after the target waking time, and dim light in the evening advance the clock gradually. Hypnotics treat sleep but not the delay, and wake-promoting drugs mask the consequences.

ddx.pt: Cannot sleep even when bedtime matches the body clock; sleep is poor on holidays too
Sleep time drifts later every day instead of staying stably late
Chronic short sleep by choice or schedule rather than a shifted body clock

aN: dswpd | delayed sleep phase syndrome | dsps | delayed sleep phase disorder | night owl syndrome

name: Delayed-onset dystonia
formal: Dystonia appearing months or years after perinatal or acquired brain injury, such as hypoxic-ischaemic injury or kernicterus.
simple: Twisting muscle postures that develop long after a brain injury.
th: dystonia ที่เกิดหลังสมองบาดเจ็บนานหลายเดือนถึงหลายปี เช่น หลังขาดออกซิเจนแรกเกิด kernicterus หรือ stroke
tempoNote: Appears after a latent period of months to decades following a static brain injury, then may progress for years
feat: History of a remote, apparently static brain insult (perinatal asphyxia, kernicterus, stroke, head injury, encephalitis)
Dystonia begins after a delay, sometimes in adolescence after a childhood injury
Often focal or hemidystonia contralateral to a putaminal or thalamic lesion
Can progress over years before stabilising
Other signs of the old injury (spasticity, choreoathetosis, cognitive deficits) may coexist
inv: MRI: putamen, globus pallidus or thalamic lesion matching the side of dystonia
Exclude a new progressive cause (Wilson disease, NBIA, genetic dystonia) if history is unclear
Review perinatal records and earlier imaging if available

case.who: 19-year-old man from Chiang Rai who had severe birth asphyxia but walked and attended school normally
case.story: Over two years his right hand has twisted when writing and now his right foot inverts while walking.
case.exam: Right arm and leg dystonia with action-induced posturing; mild right-sided brisk reflexes; no Kayser-Fleischer rings.
case.tests: MRI shows an old left putaminal scar; serum caeruloplasmin normal.
case.q: Why did dystonia appear so long after the birth injury?
case.a: Delayed-onset dystonia from maturing and maladaptive reorganisation of basal ganglia circuits after early putaminal damage.

det.patho: Lesions of the putamen, pallidum or thalamus may not produce symptoms immediately. Ongoing brain maturation, aberrant sprouting and maladaptive plasticity in surviving basal ganglia-thalamocortical circuits are thought to generate dystonia later. The mechanism of the latent period is not fully understood.
det.clinical: The latency ranges from months after adult strokes to years or even decades after perinatal injury. Dystonia is often focal or segmental at first and can spread to hemidystonia. Progression for several years followed by a plateau is typical. Patients with perinatal injury may already have spasticity or mild choreoathetosis.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis needs a convincing earlier insult, a compatible structural lesion and exclusion of new progressive causes. Copper studies, slit-lamp examination and, where appropriate, genetic or iron-sensitive MRI are used when the history is uncertain. Functional dystonia is a further differential.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin is the mainstay for focal symptoms. Oral agents such as trihexyphenidyl, baclofen or clonazepam help some patients. Pallidal (GPi) deep brain stimulation is less effective than in isolated genetic dystonia but can benefit selected patients with intact pallidal tissue. Physiotherapy and orthoses support function.
det.prognosis: Dystonia often stabilises after several years; complete remission is uncommon.
pearls: A long gap between injury and dystonia does not exclude a causal link.
Always check copper studies in young-onset dystonia, even with an old injury on record.
Pallidal DBS works less well when the pallidum itself is damaged.
det.thd: Delayed-onset dystonia คือ dystonia ที่เกิดหลังสมองบาดเจ็บนานเป็นเดือนหรือเป็นปี เช่น ขาดออกซิเจนแรกเกิด หรือ stroke เชื่อว่าเกิดจากการปรับตัวผิดปกติของวงจร basal ganglia ระหว่างที่สมองเจริญเติบโต MRI มักพบรอยโรคเก่าที่ putamen หรือ thalamus ต้องตัดโรคที่ลุกลามได้ เช่น Wilson disease ออกก่อน รักษาด้วย botulinum toxin ยารับประทาน และบางรายพิจารณา DBS

ddx.pt: Progressive dystonia with liver disease, KF rings and low caeruloplasmin
No prior brain injury; normal MRI; starts in a limb and generalises
Abnormal movements present from early childhood rather than after a latent period

aN: delayed onset secondary dystonia | post injury dystonia | late onset acquired dystonia | delayed progressive dystonia

name: Delirium
formal: Acute fluctuating disturbance of attention and cognition from medical illness, drug or withdrawal; may be hyperactive, hypoactive or mixed.
simple: A sudden state of confusion and reduced awareness that fluctuates, often during illness.
ab: ภาวะสับสนเฉียบพลัน
th: ภาวะสับสนเฉียบพลันที่ความใส่ใจและระดับการรู้สติแปรปรวนตลอดวัน เกิดจากโรคทางกาย ยา หรือการถอนยา พบบ่อยในผู้สูงอายุที่นอนโรงพยาบาล ชนิดซึมเงียบมักถูกมองข้าม
tempoNote: Develops over hours to days and fluctuates through the day, often worse at night; may last days to weeks and leave lasting cognitive decline
feat: Acute onset and fluctuating course with impaired attention (cannot do months backwards or serial sevens)
Disorganised thinking, disorientation, perceptual disturbances (often visual hallucinations) and sleep–wake reversal
Hypoactive (quiet, drowsy), hyperactive (agitated) or mixed forms; hypoactive is commonest and most missed
Predisposed by age, dementia, frailty, sensory loss, polypharmacy; precipitated by infection, drugs, metabolic upset, surgery, pain, retention, withdrawal
Associated with longer stay, falls, institutionalisation and death
inv: Screen with 4AT or CAM (CAM-ICU in ventilated patients)
Search for causes: observations, glucose, sodium, calcium, renal and liver function, blood count, infection screen, ECG, oxygenation, medication review
Brain imaging if focal signs, head injury, anticoagulation or no cause found; EEG for suspected non-convulsive status; LP if meningitis or encephalitis possible

case.who: 81-year-old woman from Ratchaburi with mild dementia
case.story: Two days after hip fracture surgery she became sleepy by day, pulled at her cannula at night and accused nurses of stealing. She had been given diphenhydramine to sleep and tramadol for pain.
case.exam: Drowsy, cannot recite months backwards, picks at the bedsheet; no focal signs; bladder palpable.
case.tests: Sodium 128 mmol/L; urinalysis positive nitrite; bladder scan 800 mL.
case.q: What is going on and how should it be managed?
case.a: Post-operative delirium with several precipitants (anticholinergic drug, opioid, urinary retention, infection, hyponatraemia); stop diphenhydramine, adjust analgesia, catheterise, treat infection and sodium, and use non-drug measures — reserve low-dose antipsychotic only for dangerous distress.

read.where: Chapter 28 Disorders of Consciousness and Intensive Care Neurology
Chapter 54 Preoperative and Postoperative Care of Patients With Neurologic Disorders
Chapter 4: Coma And Other States Of Altered Awareness In The Intensive Care Unit

det.patho: Delirium reflects widespread failure of brain network function, with cholinergic deficiency, dopamine excess, inflammatory cytokines crossing a leaky blood–brain barrier, and impaired cerebral metabolism. A vulnerable brain (older, demented) needs only a small insult, while a healthy brain needs a large one. Delirium itself may injure neurons and accelerate later dementia.
det.clinical: The cardinal feature is inattention arising over hours to days, with fluctuation, altered arousal and disorganised thinking. Patients may be agitated, hallucinating and pulling lines, or quietly drowsy and withdrawn — hypoactive cases are easily mistaken for depression or fatigue. It affects up to a third of older medical inpatients and more after hip fracture and in intensive care. Symptoms can persist for weeks and long-term cognitive decline is common.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, using DSM-5 features or validated tools such as the 4AT and CAM. Collateral history from family establishes the baseline. Look for multiple contributing causes rather than one: drugs (anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, opioids, steroids), infection, hypoxia, electrolyte and glucose disturbance, organ failure, retention, constipation, pain, withdrawal (alcohol, benzodiazepines), and intracranial events. Neurological causes include encephalitis, non-convulsive status and subdural haematoma.
det.treatment: Treat each cause and remove deliriogenic drugs. Non-drug care is central: reorientation, glasses and hearing aids, family presence, sleep protection, early mobilisation, hydration, nutrition and avoiding restraints and catheters. Antipsychotics do not shorten delirium; reserve low-dose haloperidol or an atypical for severe distress or danger, short-term, and avoid haloperidol in Parkinson's disease or Lewy body dementia. Benzodiazepines are for alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal only. Multicomponent prevention programmes cut incidence by about a third.
det.prognosis: Associated with higher mortality, longer hospital stay, loss of independence and later dementia; many patients recover fully when the cause is reversed quickly.
pearls: Test attention — months of the year backwards is a quick bedside check.
Hypoactive delirium is the commonest and the most often missed.
Look for urinary retention, constipation and anticholinergic drugs in every confused older patient.
det.thd: Delirium คือภาวะสับสนเฉียบพลันที่ความใส่ใจลดลงและอาการขึ้นลงตลอดวัน เกิดภายในชั่วโมงถึงวัน พบบ่อยในผู้สูงอายุ ผู้ป่วยสมองเสื่อม หลังผ่าตัด หรือใน ICU สาเหตุมักมีหลายอย่างร่วมกัน เช่น ติดเชื้อ ยา (anticholinergic, benzodiazepine, opioid) เกลือแร่ผิดปกติ ปัสสาวะคั่ง ท้องผูก หรือถอนสุรา คัดกรองด้วย 4AT หรือ CAM รักษาที่สาเหตุร่วมกับการดูแลแบบไม่ใช้ยา ยาต้านโรคจิตใช้เฉพาะเมื่อกระวนกระวายจนเป็นอันตรายเท่านั้น

name: Dementia
formal: Acquired decline in multiple cognitive domains interfering with independence, from Alzheimer, vascular, Lewy body, frontotemporal or other causes.
simple: A decline in memory and thinking that gets in the way of everyday life.
th: กลุ่มอาการที่ความสามารถทางสติปัญญาหลายด้านเสื่อมลงจนกระทบการใช้ชีวิตประจำวัน เกิดได้จากหลายสาเหตุ เช่น Alzheimer, หลอดเลือดสมอง, Lewy body
tempoNote: Usually insidious over months to years; decline over weeks suggests rapidly progressive dementia and a different work-up
feat: Acquired decline from a previous level in memory, language, executive, visuospatial or social cognition
Loss of independence in complex daily activities (finances, medication, travel)
Not explained by delirium or a primary psychiatric disorder
Pattern hints at cause: amnestic (Alzheimer), stepwise with focal signs (vascular), fluctuation and hallucinations (Lewy), behaviour first (frontotemporal)
Behavioural and psychological symptoms (apathy, agitation, psychosis, sleep disruption) drive carer burden
inv: Cognitive screen (MoCA, MMSE, Thai versions) and informant history
Reversible-cause bloods: B12, thyroid function, glucose, electrolytes, calcium, liver and renal function, syphilis and HIV when risk
MRI brain (or CT) for atrophy pattern, vascular burden, hydrocephalus or mass
Selected cases: CSF or plasma amyloid/tau biomarkers, FDG-PET, DaT scan, EEG

case.story: Over two years she repeats questions, misses bill payments and got lost driving to a familiar market. Her daughter now manages her pills.
case.exam: MoCA 17/30 with poor delayed recall and clock drawing; no focal deficits, no parkinsonism.
case.tests: B12 and TSH normal; MRI shows bilateral hippocampal atrophy with mild white-matter change.
case.q: Does she meet criteria for dementia, and what is the most likely cause?
case.a: Yes — multidomain decline with lost independence; amnestic pattern with hippocampal atrophy favours Alzheimer disease.

det.patho: Dementia is a syndrome rather than one disease. Alzheimer disease is the commonest cause, followed by vascular disease, Lewy body disease and frontotemporal lobar degeneration; mixed pathology is the rule in very old people. Prevalence roughly doubles every five years after 65. Modifiable risks include hypertension, diabetes, hearing loss, smoking, inactivity, low education, depression, social isolation, air pollution and untreated vision loss.
det.clinical: Onset is usually gradual, with family members noticing repetition, misplaced objects, word-finding trouble or poor judgement before the patient does. Mild cognitive impairment describes measurable decline that has not yet removed independence. Red flags for a different process include young onset, rapid progression over weeks to months, early gait or focal signs, seizures, and systemic illness. Behavioural symptoms, falls, weight loss and swallowing problems emerge in later stages.
det.diagnosis: Confirm decline with a reliable informant and objective testing, then exclude delirium, depression, medication effects (anticholinergics, sedatives) and treatable causes. Structural imaging is recommended for nearly all patients. Biomarkers (CSF Abeta42/40 and p-tau, amyloid PET, or validated plasma p-tau217) help define Alzheimer pathology and are required before anti-amyloid antibody therapy. Rapid or atypical cases warrant EEG, CSF studies, autoimmune and prion testing.
det.treatment: Treat the cause where possible and control vascular risk. Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) help Alzheimer, Lewy body and Parkinson disease dementia modestly; memantine is used in moderate to severe stages. Anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab) are approved in some countries for early Alzheimer disease with confirmed amyloid, with MRI monitoring for ARIA. Non-drug care — carer education, structured routine, hearing aids, exercise, safety and advance care planning — is central; avoid antipsychotics where possible.
det.prognosis: Course depends on cause; typical survival after diagnosis of Alzheimer disease is about 4–10 years, shorter with older age and frailty.
pearls: Always ask an informant; patients with dementia commonly underestimate their deficits.
Exclude delirium first — acute confusion on top of dementia is common and treatable.
Rapid decline over weeks is not ordinary dementia: think prion, autoimmune, infectious or neoplastic causes.
det.thd: Dementia คือกลุ่มอาการที่สมองเสื่อมหลายด้าน เช่น ความจำ ภาษา การวางแผน จนผู้ป่วยทำกิจวัตรเองไม่ได้ สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยคือ Alzheimer และโรคหลอดเลือดสมอง การวินิจฉัยต้องซักประวัติจากญาติ ตรวจคัดกรองความคิดความจำ เจาะเลือดหาสาเหตุที่รักษาได้ และทำภาพถ่ายสมอง การรักษาประกอบด้วยยากลุ่ม cholinesterase inhibitor, memantine ควบคุมปัจจัยเสี่ยง และการดูแลโดยผู้ดูแลอย่างเหมาะสม

name: Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB)
formal: Alpha-synucleinopathy with fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, REM sleep behaviour disorder and neuroleptic sensitivity; dementia precedes parkinsonism by one year or less.
simple: A dementia with fluctuating thinking, vivid hallucinations and stiff slow movements.
more: Amyloid and tau biomarkers are usually negative; DAT-SPECT shows reduced striatal uptake and polysomnography confirms RBD. Cholinesterase inhibitors help cognition and hallucinations; avoid typical antipsychotics. Alpha-synuclein disease with fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and REM sleep behaviour disorder; dementia precedes or occurs within a year of motor signs. DaT scan, polysomnography and cognitive testing help; avoid neuroleptic drugs. Cholinesterase inhibitors help cognition and hallucinations, and survival averages about 8 years. Dementia with Lewy bodies, with fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and REM sleep behaviour disorder, from alpha-synuclein pathology. Alpha-synucleinopathy with widespread cortical and subcortical Lewy bodies, causing dementia, parkinsonism and psychosis; synonym for dementia with Lewy bodies. Pathologically widespread Lewy bodies on alpha-synuclein staining, often with Alzheimer-type changes; DAT-SPECT is abnormal. Management follows DLB with cholinesterase inhibitors; avoid dopamine antagonists, since neuroleptic sensitivity is severe. Dementia with Lewy bodies, with fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and REM sleep behaviour disorder due to alpha-synuclein pathology.
ab: Senile dementia of Lewy body type (SDLT)
Senile dementia of Lewy body type
merged: Senile dementia of Lewy body type (SDLT)
th: สมองเสื่อมจากโปรตีน Lewy — ความตื่นตัวขึ้นลง เห็นภาพหลอนชัดเจน มีอาการพาร์กินสัน แพ้ยาต้านโรคจิต
feat: Fluctuating attention and alertness
Well-formed visual hallucinations (people, animals)
REM sleep behaviour disorder
Parkinsonism; severe sensitivity to antipsychotics
inv: DAT SPECT reduced uptake; MIBG cardiac scintigraphy reduced
Polysomnography for REM sleep without atonia

case.story: Some days he is sharp, other days confused; he sees small children sitting in the living room. Gets worse rigid after haloperidol given in hospital.
case.exam: Poor attention and visuospatial copying, mild symmetric bradykinesia.
case.tests: DAT SPECT: reduced striatal uptake.
case.q: Why was haloperidol dangerous?
case.a: Neuroleptic sensitivity in DLB can cause severe rigidity, confusion and even death.

qx.stem: A 76-year-old retired rice merchant in Ayutthaya has a year of good and bad days, sees small children sitting on his sofa, and kicks in his sleep. He has mild symmetric bradykinesia. After a single dose of haloperidol for night-time agitation at another hospital he became rigid, febrile and drowsy for several days. His family asks how to manage the hallucinations now.
qx.q: What is the most appropriate first-line approach?
opts: Restart haloperidol at a lower dose
Add risperidone 2 mg at night
Increase levodopa to treat the visual hallucinations
Prescribe diazepam at bedtime
A cholinesterase inhibitor such as rivastigmine or donepezil, with environmental measures; reserve low-dose quetiapine or clozapine for persistent distressing psychosis
qx.why: Fluctuations, well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder and parkinsonism fulfil the core features of DLB, and the reaction to haloperidol is severe neuroleptic sensitivity. Cholinesterase inhibitors improve hallucinations and attention and are first line. Typical and most atypical antipsychotics should be avoided; if needed, low-dose quetiapine or clozapine (with blood monitoring) is used. Raising dopaminergic drugs and benzodiazepines tend to worsen confusion.

qx.stem: A 74-year-old man from Chiang Rai has had 10 months of fluctuating attention, staring spells and well-formed visions of children in the garden. Mild bradykinesia and rigidity appeared three months after the cognitive change. His wife says he has punched in his sleep for years. He was admitted with agitation and the ward doctor wants to give haloperidol.
qx.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
opts: Haloperidol is safe at low doses and is preferred for agitation in this setting
Avoid haloperidol because of severe neuroleptic sensitivity; use a cholinesterase inhibitor and, if needed, low-dose quetiapine or clozapine
Start high-dose levodopa to treat the hallucinations
The diagnosis must be Parkinson's disease dementia, so standard antipsychotics are acceptable
Order an EEG and treat with valproate
qx.why: Dementia appearing before or within a year of parkinsonism, fluctuations, visual hallucinations and REM sleep behaviour disorder meet the core features of DLB. Patients are prone to severe and sometimes fatal reactions to D2-blocking antipsychotics, so haloperidol should be avoided. Cholinesterase inhibitors help cognition and hallucinations; pimavanserin, quetiapine or clozapine are used cautiously for psychosis. The one-year rule separates DLB from PDD by convention only.

aN: dlb | dementia with lewy bodies | dementia with lewy body | lewy body dementia | diffuse lewy body disease dlbd | dlbd | diffuse lewy body disease | senile dementia of lewy body type sdlt | sdlt | senile dementia of lewy body type | lbd

det.patho: Alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies are widespread in limbic and neocortical regions as well as the brainstem, often with coexisting Alzheimer pathology. Profound cholinergic deficit from basal forebrain loss contributes to fluctuations and hallucinations and explains the good response to cholinesterase inhibitors. Among older adults it ranks just behind Alzheimer disease as a cause of neurodegenerative dementia.
det.clinical: Cognitive decline affects attention, executive function and visuospatial skills earlier than memory. Core features are fluctuating cognition and alertness (staring spells, daytime drowsiness), recurrent detailed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder and parkinsonism. Supportive features include severe antipsychotic sensitivity, falls, syncope, autonomic dysfunction, hypersomnia, anosmia, delusions and depression. By convention, if dementia appears before or within a year of parkinsonism the label is DLB; if parkinsonism precedes dementia by more than a year it is PD dementia. Episodes of delirium-like confusion are common and may be the first presentation.
det.diagnosis: The 2017 consortium criteria classify probable DLB as dementia with two or more core features, or one core feature plus an indicative biomarker. Indicative biomarkers are reduced striatal DAT uptake on SPECT/PET, low cardiac MIBG uptake, and polysomnographic REM sleep without atonia. MRI shows relative preservation of the medial temporal lobes compared with AD; FDG-PET may show occipital hypometabolism with a cingulate island sign. CSF alpha-synuclein seed amplification is a promising test. Delirium, AD and vascular dementia are the main mimics.
det.treatment: Cholinesterase inhibitors (rivastigmine, donepezil) often help cognition, fluctuations and hallucinations. Levodopa can be tried cautiously for disabling parkinsonism but may worsen psychosis. For distressing psychosis use the lowest dose of quetiapine or clozapine; avoid haloperidol and other potent D2 blockers. Melatonin or clonazepam help RBD; manage orthostasis, constipation and falls. Educate carers and hospital staff about neuroleptic sensitivity.
det.prognosis: Decline is often faster than in AD, with survival of around 5–8 years from diagnosis.
pearls: Hallucinations of small people or animals in the room, often without distress, are typical.
Haloperidol in an agitated patient with DLB can trigger catastrophic rigidity — flag the notes.
Visuospatial failure (poor pentagon copy) with relatively better recall points to DLB over AD.
det.thd: DLB เป็นสมองเสื่อมจากโปรตีน alpha-synuclein กระจายในเปลือกสมอง อาการหลักคือ ความตื่นตัวและความคิดขึ้นลงเป็นวัน เห็นภาพหลอนชัดเจน ละเมอตามความฝัน และมีอาการพาร์กินสัน ผู้ป่วยไวต่อยาต้านโรคจิตมากจนอาจเกร็งรุนแรงหรือเสียชีวิต วินิจฉัยด้วยเกณฑ์ 2017 ร่วมกับ DAT scan, MIBG หรือ polysomnography รักษาด้วย rivastigmine หรือ donepezil ถ้าจำเป็นใช้ quetiapine ขนาดต่ำ หลีกเลี่ยง haloperidol

name: Dental disease
formal: Dental conditions such as infection or abscess that may cause trigeminal pain or neurological complications including brain abscess.
simple: Tooth or gum problems that can cause facial pain or spread infection to the brain.
th: โรคฟันและเหงือก เช่น ฟันผุหรือฝีรากฟัน ไม่ใช่โรคทางประสาทโดยตรง แต่ทำให้ปวดใบหน้าคล้ายเส้นประสาท trigeminal และอาจลามเป็นฝีในสมองได้
tempoNote: Toothache is acute or recurrent; intracranial spread evolves over days to weeks
feat: Not a primary neurological disease: important as a mimic of facial pain and as an infection source
Pain provoked by hot, cold, sweet food or biting; tender tooth on tapping
Can imitate trigeminal neuralgia, sinusitis or temporomandibular disorder
Odontogenic spread: facial cellulitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis, brain abscess (often frontal)
Numb chin (mental nerve) after dental work, or as a sign of jaw metastasis
inv: Dental examination and panoramic X-ray or cone-beam CT
MRI brain with contrast if fever, headache or focal signs follow dental infection
Blood cultures for suspected bacteraemia or endocarditis

case.story: Referred for 'trigeminal neuralgia' with a month of throbbing left jaw pain lasting hours, worse when drinking iced water.
case.exam: Normal facial sensation and corneal reflex; percussion of the lower left molar reproduces pain.
case.tests: Dental X-ray: periapical abscess of the lower left first molar.
case.q: Why is this unlikely to be trigeminal neuralgia?
case.a: Neuralgia gives seconds-long electric shocks triggered by light touch, not hours of throbbing pain; dental pathology explains it and needs dental treatment.

det.patho: Caries and periodontal disease let oral bacteria invade the pulp and periapical tissue, causing inflammation inside a rigid space and intense pain carried by trigeminal branches. Infection can spread through fascial planes, veins communicating with the cavernous sinus, or the bloodstream to the brain and heart valves. Streptococci (including the S. anginosus group) and anaerobes predominate.
det.clinical: This is a dental condition rather than a neurological one, included because it often reaches neurology clinics. Pulpitis gives poorly localised pain that may radiate to the ear or temple, while periapical abscess pain is well localised and worse on biting. Neurological complications include brain abscess, cavernous sinus thrombosis and, rarely, spinal or meningeal infection.
det.diagnosis: Dental assessment and imaging confirm the source. In patients with brain abscess of unknown origin, a dental check is part of the work-up. Persisting facial pain after dental treatment should prompt re-evaluation for neuralgia, persistent idiopathic facial pain or tumours along the trigeminal nerve.
det.treatment: Treatment is dental: drainage, root canal therapy or extraction, with antibiotics if there is spreading infection. Brain abscess needs neurosurgical drainage and prolonged antibiotics covering streptococci and anaerobes. Avoid repeated extractions for pain that is actually neuralgic.
det.prognosis: Excellent with dental care; brain abscess outcomes depend on speed of diagnosis.
pearls: Ask what triggers facial pain: thermal and biting triggers point to teeth.
Unexplained brain abscess — look in the mouth.
Many patients with trigeminal neuralgia lose healthy teeth before the right diagnosis.
det.thd: Dental disease เป็นโรคฟันไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาทโดยตรง แต่ทำให้ปวดใบหน้าคล้าย trigeminal neuralgia ได้ อาการปวดฟันมักตุบ ๆ นานเป็นชั่วโมงและกระตุ้นด้วยของร้อนเย็นหรือการกัด การติดเชื้อที่ฟันอาจลามเป็นฝีในสมองหรือหลอดเลือดดำ cavernous sinus อุดตัน รักษาโดยทันตแพทย์และยาปฏิชีวนะ ผู้ป่วยฝีในสมองไม่ทราบสาเหตุควรตรวจฟันเสมอ
