name: Dentatorubral pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA)
formal: Autosomal dominant CAG-repeat disease (ATN1) with ataxia, chorea, myoclonus, epilepsy and dementia; anticipation, juvenile and adult forms.
simple: An inherited brain disease causing clumsiness, jerking movements, seizures and dementia.
more: Diagnosis by genetic testing for ATN1 CAG expansion; MRI shows cerebellar and brainstem atrophy with white matter changes. Epilepsy is more frequent in juvenile onset, and chorea in adults; therapy is symptomatic and prevalence is higher in Japan. Autosomal dominant CAG-repeat disease with ataxia, chorea, myoclonus, epilepsy and dementia, more common in Japan. Misspelled form of DRPLA, CAG-repeat ATN1 disease with ataxia, chorea, myoclonus, epilepsy and dementia.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมยีนเด่นจาก CAG repeat ในยีน ATN1 อาการได้แก่เดินเซ chorea กล้ามเนื้อกระตุก ชัก และสมองเสื่อม เด็กมักเป็นแบบ PME ผู้ใหญ่มักคล้าย Huntington พบมากในญี่ปุ่น
tempoNote: Onset from childhood to late adulthood; younger onset with larger repeats and more severe course
feat: Juvenile onset (< 20 years): progressive myoclonic epilepsy with cognitive decline
Adult onset (> 40 years): ataxia, choreoathetosis, dementia, psychiatric change
Mixed picture in early adult onset
Autosomal dominant with marked anticipation, stronger with paternal transmission
inv: ATN1 CAG repeat analysis (expanded alleles roughly 48 or more)
MRI: cerebellar and brainstem (especially pontine tegmentum) atrophy; diffuse white matter T2 change in older adults
EEG in juvenile cases: generalised discharges, photosensitivity

case.who: 12-year-old boy whose father, now 45, has unsteady gait and chorea
case.story: From age 9 he has had falling grades, frequent jerks and several generalised seizures; drugs help only partly.
case.exam: Action myoclonus, gait ataxia, mild dysarthria, cognitive decline.
case.tests: MRI cerebellar and brainstem atrophy; father's HTT test was normal; ATN1 CAG repeat expanded in both, larger in the boy.
case.q: What explains the different pictures in father and son?
case.a: DRPLA with paternal anticipation: a larger repeat in the son produces a juvenile progressive myoclonic epilepsy, while the father's smaller repeat gives adult-onset ataxia and chorea.

read.where: 14 - Chorea, Ballism, and Athetosis — Other Huntington disease–like disorders

det.patho: An expanded CAG repeat in ATN1 (atrophin-1) produces a polyglutamine protein that accumulates in neuronal nuclei. Degeneration targets the dentate nucleus and its red nucleus output plus the globus pallidus and subthalamic (Luys) nucleus, giving the name. Longer repeats mean earlier onset, and expansion is especially unstable through the father. Prevalence is highest in Japan; it is rare elsewhere, including Southeast Asia.
det.clinical: Children and adolescents usually present with myoclonus, epilepsy and intellectual decline, resembling a progressive myoclonic epilepsy. Adults over about 40 present with ataxia, choreoathetosis, dementia and psychiatric symptoms, closely mimicking Huntington disease. Between these, patients show mixed features. Disease progresses over years to severe disability.
det.diagnosis: Consider DRPLA in a dominant family with ataxia plus chorea or dementia, or in a child with progressive myoclonic epilepsy and an affected parent. Genetic testing of ATN1 CAG repeat length confirms. MRI shows cerebellar and brainstem atrophy, with white matter hyperintensities in long-standing adult disease. Exclude Huntington disease and SCA17, which can look similar.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying treatment. Seizures and myoclonus are treated with valproate, levetiracetam, clonazepam or perampanel, avoiding drugs that worsen myoclonus. Chorea and psychiatric symptoms can be treated as in Huntington disease. Multidisciplinary rehabilitation and genetic counselling, including predictive testing guidelines, are essential.
det.prognosis: Progressive; juvenile forms have the worst course, and survival is often 10–20 years from onset in severe cases.
pearls: Ataxia + chorea + dementia with normal HTT: test ATN1 (DRPLA) and SCA17.
Juvenile DRPLA presents as a progressive myoclonic epilepsy.
Anticipation is strongest through paternal transmission.
det.thd: DRPLA เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมยีนเด่นจาก CAG repeat ในยีน ATN1 พบมากในญี่ปุ่น ถ้าเริ่มในวัยเด็กจะมีกล้ามเนื้อกระตุก ชัก และสติปัญญาถดถอยคล้าย PME ถ้าเริ่มในผู้ใหญ่จะเดินเซ มี chorea และสมองเสื่อมคล้าย Huntington ยิ่งส่งต่อทางพ่อ repeat ยิ่งยาวและอาการเริ่มเร็วขึ้น วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีน รักษาตามอาการด้วยยากันชักและยาคุมการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติ

ddx.pt: Similar adult chorea and dementia but less ataxia; HTT CAG expansion
Recessive PME with preserved cognition and no dominant family history
Dominant ataxias; SCA17 can also give chorea and dementia

name: Dermatomyositis
formal: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy with proximal weakness, heliotrope rash and Gottron papules; perifascicular atrophy on biopsy; associated with malignancy and anti-MDA5, Mi-2 or TIF1 antibodies.
simple: An immune disease causing muscle weakness and a typical skin rash.
more: Check CK and myositis-specific antibodies, and screen for malignancy with age-appropriate imaging; MRI shows muscle oedema and EMG shows irritability. First-line is corticosteroids with methotrexate, azathioprine or IVIG; skin disease needs sun protection.
th: กล้ามเนื้อและผิวหนังอักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกัน — ต้นแขนต้นขาอ่อนแรง ผื่นม่วงรอบตา ผื่นที่ข้อนิ้ว ต้องหามะเร็งแฝง
feat: Symmetric proximal weakness over weeks
Heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, shawl sign, nailfold changes
Interstitial lung disease (anti-MDA5) and malignancy association (anti-TIF1γ)
inv: CK, myositis-specific antibodies
EMG myopathic with fibrillations; MRI STIR oedema
Biopsy: perifascicular atrophy
Cancer screening; HRCT chest

case.story: Six weeks of difficulty combing her hair and climbing stairs, with a purplish rash on the eyelids.
case.exam: Neck flexors and proximal limbs 4−/5, heliotrope rash, scaly papules over the knuckles.
case.tests: CK 5,800 U/L; anti-TIF1γ positive.
case.q: What must be searched for next?
case.a: An underlying malignancy (anti-TIF1γ carries a high cancer association).

qx.stem: A 58-year-old man from Chon Buri has two months of difficulty rising from a chair and lifting his arms, with a violaceous rash on the eyelids, scaly papules over the knuckles and a V-shaped neck rash. CK is 2,900 U/L. The myositis panel shows anti-TIF1-γ antibody; chest CT shows no interstitial lung disease.
qx.q: Which further investigation is most important now?
opts: Repeat CK weekly without other tests
Comprehensive cancer screening, e.g. CT chest–abdomen–pelvis or PET-CT plus age-appropriate tests including nasopharyngeal examination
Genetic testing for limb-girdle muscular dystrophy
Acetylcholine receptor antibodies and repetitive nerve stimulation
Serial high-resolution CT of the chest every month
qx.why: Anti-TIF1-γ (and anti-NXP2) dermatomyositis in adults carries a high risk of associated malignancy, so thorough cancer screening is required at diagnosis and repeated over the next few years; in Thailand nasopharyngeal carcinoma should be considered. Interstitial lung disease is more strongly linked to anti-MDA5 and antisynthetase antibodies. Dystrophy and myasthenia do not fit the rash and antibody profile.

aN: dm | dermatomyositis | idiopathic inflammatory myopathy

det.patho: An immune-mediated myopathy driven largely by type I interferon, with complement-mediated injury to small vessels causing capillary loss and perifascicular fibre damage. Myositis-specific antibodies define clinical subsets: anti-Mi-2 (classic skin and muscle, good response), anti-TIF1γ and anti-NXP2 (cancer association in adults), anti-MDA5 (minimal myositis, rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease, notable in East Asia) and anti-SAE. Adult disease carries an increased risk of malignancy, especially within three years of diagnosis.
det.clinical: Symmetric proximal weakness evolves over weeks to months, often with myalgia, dysphagia and neck flexor weakness. Skin signs may precede weakness: heliotrope rash, Gottron papules over the knuckles, V-sign and shawl sign, nailfold capillary changes and mechanic's hands. Some patients have skin disease without weakness (amyopathic). Interstitial lung disease, arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, calcinosis (especially in juvenile disease) and cardiac involvement occur. Ovarian, lung, gastric, nasopharyngeal and haematological cancers are typical associations.
det.diagnosis: The EULAR/ACR 2017 classification criteria combine age, weakness pattern, skin features, CK, anti-Jo-1 and biopsy findings. CK is often raised but may be normal. EMG shows an irritable myopathy and MRI STIR shows muscle and fascial oedema guiding biopsy. Biopsy features perifascicular atrophy, MxA expression and capillary loss. Screen all adults for cancer (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, gynaecological and age-appropriate tests, PET in high-risk subsets) and for lung involvement with HRCT and lung function.
det.treatment: First-line treatment is corticosteroids (e.g. prednisolone around 1 mg/kg/day, with IV pulses in severe cases) combined early with methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate to limit steroid exposure. IVIG is effective for refractory disease and dysphagia, and rituximab, calcineurin inhibitors and JAK inhibitors are further options. Anti-MDA5 ILD needs aggressive combined immunosuppression. Treat associated cancer, protect skin from sun, use hydroxychloroquine for skin disease, and give rehabilitation plus bone and infection prophylaxis.
det.prognosis: Most patients improve with treatment, though relapses are common; survival is reduced mainly by malignancy and rapidly progressive lung disease.
pearls: Rash plus proximal weakness in an adult = search for cancer.
Anti-MDA5: little weakness, ulcerating skin lesions, rapidly progressive lung disease.
Perifascicular atrophy on biopsy is the classic pathological clue.
det.thd: Dermatomyositis เป็นโรคภูมิคุ้มกันที่ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อและผิวหนังอักเสบ เกี่ยวข้องกับ interferon และการทำลายหลอดเลือดเล็กในกล้ามเนื้อ อาการคืออ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขาสองข้างเท่ากันภายในหลายสัปดาห์ ผื่นม่วงรอบตา (heliotrope) ผื่นที่ข้อนิ้ว (Gottron) และอาจมีปอดอักเสบ ในผู้ใหญ่ต้องค้นหามะเร็งแฝงโดยเฉพาะเมื่อพบ anti-TIF1γ วินิจฉัยด้วย CK, myositis antibodies, MRI และตัดชิ้นเนื้อพบ perifascicular atrophy รักษาด้วยสเตียรอยด์ร่วมกับยากดภูมิ เช่น methotrexate และให้ IVIG ในรายที่ดื้อยา

name: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs)
formal: Severe early-onset epilepsies in which epileptic activity and the underlying cause contribute to developmental slowing, e.g. West, Dravet and Lennox-Gastaut syndromes.
simple: Severe childhood epilepsies in which frequent seizures also hold back development.
th: กลุ่มโรคลมชักรุนแรงที่เริ่มในวัยทารกหรือเด็กเล็ก ทั้งตัวโรคต้นเหตุและการชักที่ถี่ทำให้พัฒนาการช้าหรือถดถอย
tempoNote: Seizures usually begin in the first months or years of life; development stalls or regresses over months
feat: Begins in the first months or early years of life with frequent, often multiple seizure types (spasms, tonic, myoclonic, atypical absence)
Developmental delay present before seizures, worsening with them, or regression after seizure onset
Markedly abnormal EEG: hypsarrhythmia, burst-suppression, slow spike-wave or multifocal discharges
Seizures are commonly resistant to two or more appropriate antiseizure medicines
Includes West, Dravet, Lennox–Gastaut and many single-gene encephalopathies (SCN1A, STXBP1, CDKL5, KCNQ2, SCN2A)
inv: Prolonged video-EEG including sleep to define the electroclinical syndrome
MRI brain (epilepsy protocol) for malformations, injury or tuberous sclerosis
Genetic testing early: epilepsy gene panel or exome/genome, plus chromosomal microarray
Targeted metabolic screen for treatable causes (glucose, lactate, amino and organic acids, CSF glucose, pyridoxine/PLP trial)

case.story: Had prolonged one-sided seizures with each fever since 5 months; now also brief jerks, and she has stopped babbling and reaching.
case.exam: Hypotonic, poor visual tracking, no focal deficit; head size normal.
case.tests: EEG shows generalised and multifocal discharges; MRI normal; gene panel reveals a de novo SCN1A truncating variant.
case.q: What syndrome is this, and which drug class should be avoided?
case.a: Dravet syndrome, a DEE; avoid sodium-channel blockers such as carbamazepine and lamotrigine, which can worsen seizures.

read.where: Chapter 26: Infantile Epileptic Encephalopathies and De Novo Mutations

det.patho: The term recognises two overlapping drivers of impairment: the underlying cause (often a single-gene variant affecting ion channels, synaptic proteins or chromatin regulators) and the abnormal epileptic activity itself. Many cases arise from de novo variants, so family history is usually negative. Structural, metabolic and acquired causes such as hypoxic injury or infection can produce the same picture. The 2022 ILAE classification groups these by age of onset and named syndrome.
det.clinical: Presentation depends on age and cause: infantile epileptic spasms syndrome (West), Dravet with fever-sensitive prolonged seizures, Lennox–Gastaut with tonic seizures in sleep and drop attacks, and early-infantile DEE with tonic seizures in the first weeks. Comorbidities are common, including autism features, movement disorders, sleep disturbance, feeding difficulty and scoliosis. Some children have a fixed developmental impairment even when seizures are controlled. Sudden unexpected death in epilepsy risk is higher than in other childhood epilepsies.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on age at onset, seizure types, EEG pattern and developmental course. Early genetic testing has a diagnostic yield of roughly a third to a half and can change management. Look first for treatable causes: pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy, GLUT1 deficiency, biotinidase deficiency and inborn errors. MRI may reveal cortical malformations or tuberous sclerosis suitable for surgery or mTOR inhibitors.
det.treatment: Treatment is syndrome- and gene-guided where possible: ACTH or prednisolone and vigabatrin for infantile spasms, stiripentol, fenfluramine, valproate, clobazam or cannabidiol for Dravet, and rufinamide, clobazam, fenfluramine or cannabidiol for Lennox–Gastaut. Ketogenic diet is first-line for GLUT1 deficiency and useful in many others. Epilepsy surgery, vagus nerve stimulation or corpus callosotomy are options for selected children. Multidisciplinary rehabilitation, rescue plans for prolonged seizures and family support are essential.
det.prognosis: Most children have lasting intellectual disability and many continue to have seizures into adulthood; earlier control can improve developmental outcome in some syndromes.
pearls: Infant with spasms or fever-provoked prolonged seizures and stalling development: think DEE and order EEG plus genetics early.
Sodium-channel blockers worsen SCN1A Dravet but may help SCN2A or SCN8A gain-of-function disease.
Always exclude treatable metabolic causes such as pyridoxine dependency and GLUT1 deficiency.
det.thd: DEE คือกลุ่มโรคลมชักรุนแรงในเด็กเล็ก ซึ่งทั้งสาเหตุ (มักเป็นยีนผิดปกติแบบเกิดใหม่) และการชักที่ถี่ทำให้พัฒนาการช้าหรือถดถอย ตัวอย่างคือ West, Dravet และ Lennox–Gastaut syndrome EEG ผิดปกติชัดเจนและการชักมักดื้อยา ควรตรวจ EEG, MRI และพันธุกรรมตั้งแต่เนิ่น ๆ รวมถึงหาสาเหตุที่รักษาได้ การรักษาเลือกตามกลุ่มอาการ เช่น ACTH/vigabatrin สำหรับ spasms และอาหาร ketogenic

name: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy
formal: Small-fibre autonomic neuropathy in diabetes causing orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction, bladder dysfunction, resting tachycardia, and hypoglycaemia unawareness.
simple: Damage to the nerves that run automatic body functions in people with diabetes, causing dizziness, stomach and bladder problems.
more: Autonomic reflex testing and tilt table assess it. Tight glucose control, fludrocortisone or midodrine, prokinetics, and symptomatic care are used.
th: โรคเส้นประสาทอัตโนมัติในผู้ป่วยเบาหวาน ทำให้ความดันตกเมื่อลุกยืน กระเพาะบีบตัวช้า หย่อนสมรรถภาพทางเพศ กระเพาะปัสสาวะผิดปกติ หัวใจเต้นเร็วขณะพัก และไม่รู้สึกตัวเมื่อน้ำตาลต่ำ
tempoNote: Develops over years of diabetes, usually alongside distal sensory neuropathy
feat: Resting tachycardia and loss of heart-rate variability; exercise intolerance
Orthostatic hypotension with dizziness on standing
Gastroparesis (early satiety, vomiting, erratic glucose), diarrhoea or constipation
Erectile dysfunction, neurogenic bladder, abnormal sweating (gustatory sweating)
Hypoglycaemia unawareness and silent myocardial ischaemia
inv: Cardiovascular reflex tests: heart-rate variation with deep breathing, the Valsalva ratio and the standing response; orthostatic BP
Gastric emptying scintigraphy or breath test for gastroparesis
Post-void residual and urodynamics; sudomotor testing

case.who: 52-year-old man with 15 years of type 1 diabetes from Songkhla
case.story: Dizzy when standing, bloated after meals, frequent unpredictable low blood sugars without warning symptoms.
case.exam: BP 140/80 lying, 100/60 standing without heart-rate rise; resting pulse 104; stocking sensory loss.
case.tests: Loss of heart-rate variation on deep breathing; delayed gastric emptying on scintigraphy.
case.q: Why are his hypoglycaemic episodes dangerous?
case.a: Autonomic neuropathy blunts adrenergic warning symptoms (hypoglycaemia unawareness).

read.where: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves — Endocrine Disorders

det.patho: Chronic hyperglycaemia damages small myelinated and unmyelinated autonomic fibres via metabolic, oxidative and microvascular injury. The long vagus nerve is affected early, causing parasympathetic loss and resting tachycardia, followed by sympathetic failure. Prevalence rises with duration and poor glycaemic control.
det.clinical: Cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy predicts mortality and silent ischaemia. Gastrointestinal, genitourinary and sudomotor symptoms vary between patients. Orthostatic hypotension can be aggravated by antihypertensives and diuretics. Hypoglycaemia unawareness complicates intensive glucose management.
det.diagnosis: Formal reflex testing (deep breathing, Valsalva, standing) is the most reliable assessment of CAN; at least two abnormal tests confirm it. Use orthostatic BP measurements routinely and scintigraphy for suspected gastroparesis after excluding obstruction. Exclude other causes of autonomic neuropathy.
det.treatment: Optimise glucose control and cardiovascular risk factors. Orthostatic hypotension: review drugs, fluids and salt, compression garments, then midodrine, fludrocortisone or droxidopa. Gastroparesis: small low-fat meals, metoclopramide for limited periods or domperidone (with QT caution), and adjust insulin timing. Erectile dysfunction responds to PDE5 inhibitors; manage bladder with timed voiding or catheterisation.
det.prognosis: Cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy is associated with higher mortality; symptoms can be managed but rarely reverse.
pearls: Resting tachycardia with fixed heart rate in diabetes suggests CAN.
Orthostatic BP without compensatory tachycardia = neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.
Erratic glucose with vomiting: think gastroparesis.
det.thd: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy เป็นภาวะที่เส้นประสาทอัตโนมัติเสียจากเบาหวานเรื้อรัง ทำให้หัวใจเต้นเร็วขณะพัก ความดันตกเมื่อลุกยืน กระเพาะบีบตัวช้า ท้องอืดอาเจียน หย่อนสมรรถภาพทางเพศ ปัสสาวะผิดปกติ และไม่รู้สึกตัวเมื่อน้ำตาลต่ำ ตรวจด้วยการวัดความดันท่านอน-ยืน และการทดสอบ heart rate variability รักษาโดยคุมน้ำตาลและรักษาตามอาการ เช่น midodrine หรือ fludrocortisone

name: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
formal: Metabolic complication of insulin deficiency with hyperglycaemia and acidosis; may cause cerebral oedema, particularly in children, and altered consciousness.
simple: A dangerous complication of diabetes with very high blood sugar and acid build-up, causing drowsiness and sometimes brain swelling.
th: ภาวะแทรกซ้อนเฉียบพลันจากการขาดอินซูลิน มีน้ำตาลสูงและเลือดเป็นกรด อาจทำให้สมองบวมโดยเฉพาะในเด็ก และระดับความรู้สึกตัวลดลง
tempoNote: Develops over hours to a day or two; cerebral oedema typically 4–12 hours after treatment starts
feat: A systemic metabolic emergency rather than a primary neurological disease
Polyuria, thirst, vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul breathing and dehydration
Altered consciousness proportional to serum osmolality and acidosis
Cerebral oedema in children: headache, falling GCS, bradycardia, hypertension, inappropriate slowing of heart rate
Other neurological complications: stroke, venous thrombosis, rhino-orbital mucormycosis
inv: Glucose, blood ketones (beta-hydroxybutyrate), venous blood gas, anion gap, electrolytes, osmolality
Hourly neurological observations in children
CT or MRI only after stabilisation if focal signs persist; do not delay treatment of suspected cerebral oedema for imaging

case.who: 10-year-old girl from Phrae with new type 1 diabetes
case.story: Admitted with DKA (pH 6.95); 6 hours into treatment she complains of severe headache and becomes drowsy.
case.exam: GCS falls from 15 to 11, pulse drops from 120 to 70, BP rises.
case.tests: Glucose falling appropriately; sodium not rising as expected.
case.q: What is happening and what is the immediate treatment?
case.a: DKA-related cerebral oedema; give mannitol or hypertonic saline immediately, raise the head and call the PICU team.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Diabetes Mellitus

det.patho: Insulin deficiency with counter-regulatory hormone excess causes hyperglycaemia, lipolysis and ketone production, producing metabolic acidosis and osmotic diuresis. Cerebral oedema in children involves vasogenic and cytotoxic mechanisms linked to cerebral hypoperfusion and reperfusion, not simply rapid fluid shifts. Risk factors include new-onset diabetes, young age, severe acidosis, high urea and low pCO2.
det.clinical: Most patients have reduced alertness only when severely hyperosmolar or acidotic. Cerebral oedema occurs in roughly 0.5–1% of paediatric DKA episodes, with high morbidity and mortality. Warning signs include headache, irritability, vomiting after improvement, falling GCS and Cushing response.
det.diagnosis: DKA is defined by hyperglycaemia (or known diabetes), ketonaemia and acidosis. Cerebral oedema is a clinical diagnosis using bedside criteria; imaging can follow treatment. Consider stroke, CVT, infection and hypoglycaemia in neurological deterioration.
det.treatment: Treat with fluid resuscitation, fixed-rate intravenous insulin, potassium replacement and identification of the precipitant, following local paediatric or adult protocols. Recent trial data suggest fluid rate within standard ranges does not change cerebral oedema risk. For suspected cerebral oedema give mannitol (0.5–1 g/kg) or 3% saline, elevate the head and arrange intensive care; avoid excessive hyperventilation.
det.prognosis: DKA mortality is low with protocolised care; paediatric cerebral oedema carries significant risk of death or lasting brain injury.
pearls: Headache and falling heart rate during paediatric DKA treatment = cerebral oedema until proved otherwise.
Treat cerebral oedema before imaging.
Look for mucormycosis in diabetics with facial pain, black eschar or ophthalmoplegia.

name: Diabetic mononeuropathies
formal: Focal nerve lesions in diabetes, including cranial nerve III and VI palsies, and median, ulnar, and peroneal neuropathies, mediated by ischaemia and entrapment.
simple: Damage to a single nerve in people with diabetes, such as a sudden eye-movement palsy.
more: Control glucose, treat entrapment; cranial palsies usually recover in 2 to 3 months.
th: เส้นประสาทเส้นเดียวเสียในผู้ป่วยเบาหวาน เช่น เส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 3 หรือ 6 และ median, ulnar, peroneal จากการขาดเลือดหรือถูกกดทับ
tempoNote: Ischaemic forms start over hours to days; entrapment forms evolve slowly
feat: Painful pupil-sparing third nerve palsy with ptosis and diplopia is the classic cranial form
Sixth and seventh nerve palsies also occur; fourth less often
Limb nerves at entrapment sites (median at wrist, ulnar at elbow, peroneal at fibular head) are vulnerable
Truncal (thoracic) radiculopathy can mimic abdominal or cardiac pain
Ischaemic cranial palsies usually recover within about 3 months
inv: Check pupils carefully; pupil involvement in third nerve palsy needs urgent CTA or MRA to exclude aneurysm
MRI brain for atypical, progressive or multiple cranial palsies
Nerve conduction studies for limb mononeuropathies; background polyneuropathy often present
HbA1c, BP and lipids; ESR/CRP if over 50 to consider giant cell arteritis

case.who: 58-year-old man from Nakhon Pathom with type 2 diabetes for 12 years
case.story: Woke with aching above the left eye, then drooping of the left lid and double vision the next day.
case.exam: Left ptosis, eye down and out, impaired adduction, elevation and depression; pupils equal and reactive.
case.tests: HbA1c 9.4%; CTA shows no aneurysm; MRI brain unremarkable.
case.q: What is the likely mechanism and expected course?
case.a: Microvascular ischaemic diabetic third nerve palsy sparing the peripheral pupillary fibres; recovery expected over weeks to three months.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Diabetes Mellitus

det.patho: Two mechanisms predominate. Acute cranial and some limb mononeuropathies result from occlusion of vasa nervorum, producing a central nerve infarct that tends to spare the superficial pupillomotor fibres of the third nerve. Diabetic nerves are also more susceptible to compression at entrapment sites because of metabolic and microvascular changes.
det.clinical: The third nerve palsy often starts with pain around the eye and evolves over a day or two, with the pupil spared in most cases. Sixth nerve palsy causes horizontal diplopia worse at distance. Limb mononeuropathies mirror those in non-diabetics but are more frequent. Thoracic radiculopathy causes band-like pain and abdominal wall bulging.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is partly one of exclusion. Any pupil-involving or incomplete but progressive third nerve palsy needs vascular imaging for aneurysm. Older patients need ESR and CRP to exclude giant cell arteritis. Multiple or progressive cranial neuropathies warrant MRI and CSF to look for infiltration, infection or inflammation. Nerve conduction studies localise limb lesions.
det.treatment: Ischaemic palsies are managed supportively with eye patching or prisms and vascular risk control; improvement starts within weeks. Entrapment neuropathies are treated as usual with splinting, injection or surgical release. Pain may need neuropathic agents. Better glycaemic control helps long-term nerve health.
det.prognosis: Ischaemic cranial palsies usually recover well within 2–3 months; failure to improve should prompt re-investigation.
pearls: Pupil sparing is reassuring but not absolute; image if in doubt.
Pain does not distinguish ischaemic from aneurysmal third nerve palsy.
Truncal diabetic radiculopathy is often mistaken for an abdominal emergency.
det.thd: Diabetic mononeuropathy คือเส้นประสาทเส้นเดียวเสียในผู้ป่วยเบาหวาน ที่พบบ่อยคือเส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 3 ขาดเลือดทำให้หนังตาตกและเห็นภาพซ้อนแต่รูม่านตาปกติ และเส้นประสาทแขนขาถูกกดทับ ถ้ารูม่านตาขยายต้องตรวจหาหลอดเลือดโป่งพองทันที ส่วนใหญ่อาการดีขึ้นเองใน 2–3 เดือน ร่วมกับคุมเบาหวานและปัจจัยเสี่ยง

name: Diabetic neuropathic cachexia
formal: Acute painful diabetic neuropathy with severe weight loss, burning pain, allodynia, and depression, often after starting insulin or glycaemic improvement.
simple: A rare form of painful diabetic nerve damage with marked weight loss, often after blood sugar is brought under control.
more: Pain control with neuropathic agents and good nutrition; it generally improves spontaneously within about a year.
th: ปลายประสาทอักเสบจากเบาหวานชนิดปวดแสบรุนแรงเฉียบพลัน ร่วมกับน้ำหนักลดมากและซึมเศร้า มักดีขึ้นเองภายในราวหนึ่งปี
tempoNote: Pain and weight loss build over weeks to a few months; recovery over 6–18 months with weight regain
feat: Mostly men with type 2 (sometimes type 1) diabetes, often with only modestly abnormal glucose
Severe burning and contact allodynia in the legs, sometimes trunk; sleep is ruined
Marked unintentional weight loss (often more than 10–20% of body weight), anorexia and depressed mood
Little objective weakness; sensory signs may be mild compared with the pain
Overlaps with treatment-induced neuropathy that follows rapid improvement of HbA1c
inv: Exclude cancer, thyroid disease, coeliac disease and other causes of weight loss before accepting the label
Nerve conduction may be near normal; small-fibre tests (skin biopsy, QST) show the main deficit
HbA1c trend: a rapid recent fall supports a treatment-induced component

case.who: 58-year-old man from Khon Kaen with type 2 diabetes
case.story: Over three months he lost 14 kg and developed burning feet so tender that the bed sheet hurts; he barely eats or sleeps and feels hopeless.
case.exam: Thin, withdrawn; allodynia from the knees down, reduced pinprick distally, ankle jerks reduced, power normal.
case.tests: CT chest–abdomen and endoscopy normal; TSH normal; NCS shows mild sural amplitude reduction only.
case.q: What is the likely syndrome and what course should you explain to him?
case.a: Diabetic neuropathic cachexia; with pain control, nutrition and mood support most patients regain weight and improve over about a year.

det.patho: The cause is uncertain. Proposed mechanisms include acute injury to small unmyelinated fibres, microvascular changes in nerve when glucose falls quickly, and a catabolic state that feeds the weight loss. It is uncommon and probably under-recognised. Many reported patients fit what is now called treatment-induced neuropathy of diabetes.
det.clinical: Patients describe constant burning, lancinating jabs and skin hypersensitivity, usually symmetric in the feet and legs and occasionally on the trunk. Weight loss and anorexia are striking and depression is almost universal, so the picture can be mistaken for malignancy or a primary psychiatric illness. Motor findings are minor. Autonomic symptoms such as postural dizziness or erectile dysfunction may accompany it.
det.diagnosis: It is a clinical diagnosis made after careful exclusion of occult cancer, hyperthyroidism, malabsorption, alcohol and other neuropathies. Small-fibre measures are more informative than standard conduction studies. A history of recent intensive glucose lowering is a helpful clue.
det.treatment: Treat pain with first-line neuropathic agents (duloxetine, pregabalin or gabapentin, or a tricyclic) and combine them when needed. Keep glucose controlled without further abrupt swings, support nutrition with dietitian input, and treat depression actively. Avoid long-term opioids where possible.
det.prognosis: Usually good: pain eases and weight returns over roughly 6–18 months, although some residual sensory symptoms may remain.
pearls: Painful feet plus dramatic weight loss in a diabetic: exclude cancer, then think neuropathic cachexia.
Ask whether HbA1c fell sharply in the preceding months.
Reassurance about the expected recovery is part of treatment.
det.thd: Diabetic neuropathic cachexia เป็นภาวะปลายประสาทเสื่อมจากเบาหวานที่ปวดแสบรุนแรงที่ขาร่วมกับน้ำหนักลดมาก เบื่ออาหาร และซึมเศร้า มักเกิดหลังคุมน้ำตาลลงเร็ว ต้องตัดมะเร็งและสาเหตุอื่นของน้ำหนักลดก่อน รักษาด้วยยาแก้ปวดประสาท ดูแลโภชนาการและอารมณ์ ส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นเองในราวหนึ่งปี

ddx.pt: Asymmetric proximal thigh pain followed by clear weakness and wasting, not a purely sensory picture
Similar painful small-fibre onset but without the profound weight loss; look for other triggers
Weakness and areflexia dominate with demyelinating conduction changes and high CSF protein

name: Diabetic neuropathy
formal: Most common form is length-dependent sensory polyneuropathy with painful feet, numbness and loss of ankle reflexes, from chronic hyperglycaemia and small-vessel disease.
simple: Nerve damage from diabetes, usually causing numb, tingling or painful feet.
more: Neuropathies due to diabetes: distal symmetric polyneuropathy, autonomic neuropathy, radiculoplexopathy, mononeuropathies and cranial neuropathies.
th: กลุ่มโรคเส้นประสาทจากเบาหวาน ที่พบมากที่สุดคือชาปลายเท้าแบบถุงเท้า ร่วมกับชนิดอื่น เช่น autonomic, mononeuropathy และ radiculoplexopathy
tempoNote: Distal symmetric form creeps up over years; focal and radiculoplexus forms are subacute
feat: Distal symmetric sensory-predominant polyneuropathy in a stocking-glove pattern is the commonest form
Burning or electric pain, numbness, loss of ankle jerks and reduced vibration at the toes
Autonomic involvement: postural hypotension, gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction, sweating changes
Focal forms: carpal tunnel, third nerve palsy sparing the pupil, truncal radiculopathy, painful lumbosacral plexopathy
Insensate feet lead to ulcers, Charcot joints and amputation
inv: Annual screening: 10 g monofilament, 128 Hz tuning fork, pinprick, ankle reflexes
Check B12 (especially on metformin), TSH, renal function and serum protein electrophoresis in atypical cases
Nerve conduction studies when the picture is asymmetric, motor-predominant or rapidly progressive

case.who: 63-year-old woman from Nakhon Ratchasima, diabetic for 15 years
case.story: Tingling feet for several years, now burning at night; she did not feel a blister from new shoes.
case.exam: Reduced pinprick and vibration to mid-shin, absent ankle jerks, monofilament not felt at 4 of 10 sites, healing ulcer on the right forefoot.
case.tests: HbA1c 9.1%; B12 low-normal on long-term metformin; NCS shows length-dependent axonal sensorimotor neuropathy.
case.q: Which other treatable cause should be checked, and what is the most important preventive step?
case.a: B12 deficiency from metformin; regular foot inspection, proper footwear and podiatry to prevent ulcers and amputation.

det.patho: Chronic hyperglycaemia damages axons through polyol and advanced glycation pathways, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction and microvascular ischaemia of nerve. Dyslipidaemia, obesity and hypertension add independent risk. Longest fibres fail first, giving the length-dependent pattern. About half of people with long-standing diabetes develop some form.
det.clinical: Distal symmetric polyneuropathy may be painless and found only on screening, or painful with burning and allodynia. Small-fibre symptoms often precede large-fibre signs. Autonomic neuropathy carries cardiovascular risk and causes gastroparesis and bladder problems. Asymmetric forms include mononeuropathies, thoracic radiculopathy and diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy with weight loss and thigh weakness.
det.diagnosis: Typical symptoms and signs in a person with diabetes are enough for distal symmetric disease, after excluding other common causes (B12, thyroid, alcohol, paraprotein, renal failure, drugs). Conduction studies are needed if the pattern is atypical. Small-fibre disease may need skin biopsy for epidermal nerve fibre density. Cardiovascular reflex tests assess autonomic involvement.
det.treatment: Optimise glucose, blood pressure and lipids, and encourage weight loss and exercise; tight control mainly prevents progression in type 1 diabetes. For pain use duloxetine, pregabalin, gabapentin or amitriptyline, with topical capsaicin or lidocaine as additions; avoid routine opioids. Foot care education and podiatry are essential. Treat autonomic features specifically (e.g. prokinetics, orthostatic measures).
det.prognosis: Sensory loss is largely irreversible; good metabolic control slows progression and foot care prevents most amputations.
pearls: Check B12 in any diabetic on metformin with neuropathy.
Prominent motor weakness or rapid progression is not typical; look for CIDP or another cause.
Pupil-sparing third nerve palsy in diabetes is usually microvascular, but image if any feature is atypical.
det.thd: Diabetic neuropathy คือโรคเส้นประสาทจากเบาหวาน ที่พบบ่อยที่สุดคือชาและปวดแสบที่ปลายเท้าแบบถุงเท้า reflex ข้อเท้าหาย อาจมีระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติผิดปกติหรือเส้นประสาทเส้นเดียวเสีย ตรวจคัดกรองด้วย monofilament และส้อมเสียงทุกปี และตรวจ B12 ในผู้ที่กิน metformin รักษาด้วยการคุมน้ำตาล ยาแก้ปวดประสาท และดูแลเท้าเพื่อป้องกันแผลและการตัดขา

name: Diabetic polyradiculopathy
formal: Diabetic lumbosacral or thoracic radiculoplexus syndrome with asymmetric severe pain, weight loss, and proximal leg weakness, thought to be microvasculitic and immune-mediated.
simple: Sudden severe pain and weakness in the thigh or trunk in people with diabetes, usually on one side.
more: MRI excludes compressive lesions; nerve biopsy may show microvasculitis. Treatment is pain control and rehabilitation, sometimes with immunotherapy; recovery is slow.
th: ภาวะรากประสาทและ plexus ส่วนเอวอักเสบในผู้ป่วยเบาหวาน ปวดต้นขารุนแรงข้างเดียว น้ำหนักลด แล้วกล้ามเนื้อต้นขาอ่อนแรงลีบ
tempoNote: Pain-dominated onset over days to weeks, weakness progresses for weeks to months, then slow recovery
feat: Severe asymmetric thigh, hip or buttock pain, often nocturnal, at onset
Followed by proximal leg weakness and wasting (quadriceps, hip flexors) with lost knee jerk
Marked weight loss, frequently after improved glucose control
Often spreads to the other leg within weeks to months
Typically older men with relatively mild type 2 diabetes
inv: EMG/NCS: multifocal axonal changes in roots, plexus and nerves, paraspinal denervation
MRI lumbosacral spine and plexus to exclude compression or infiltration
CSF protein may be raised; cell count normal
Exclude malignancy if weight loss is prominent; nerve biopsy (rarely) shows microvasculitis

case.who: 66-year-old man from Suphan Buri with type 2 diabetes, recently started on insulin
case.story: Six weeks of intense right thigh pain keeping him awake, 8 kg weight loss, and now buckling of the right knee on stairs.
case.exam: Wasted right quadriceps, weak hip flexion and knee extension, absent right knee jerk, patchy sensory loss over anterior thigh.
case.tests: MRI lumbar spine shows only mild spondylosis; EMG shows denervation in L2–L4 myotomes including paraspinals; CSF protein 0.8 g/L.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and how should the patient be counselled?
case.a: Diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy; pain control and rehabilitation, with slow and often incomplete recovery over months.

det.patho: The condition is thought to arise from an immune-mediated microvasculitis affecting lumbosacral roots, plexus and peripheral nerves, causing ischaemic axonal injury. It occurs in diabetes but a non-diabetic counterpart exists, so diabetes is a risk factor rather than the direct cause. Rapid improvement in glucose control and weight loss often precede onset.
det.clinical: Onset is with severe deep pain in hip, buttock or thigh, then weakness of proximal and later distal leg muscles. The process is asymmetric but frequently becomes bilateral. Weight loss can be striking, raising concern for cancer. Thoracic and cervical counterparts exist. Autonomic involvement is possible.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the clinical pattern plus EMG showing multisegmental axonal involvement including paraspinal muscles. Imaging excludes structural lesions and plexus infiltration; MRI sometimes shows plexus or nerve swelling. CSF protein is often elevated. Nerve biopsy is reserved for uncertain cases.
det.treatment: Pain control with neuropathic agents and sometimes short-term opioids is the immediate need. Physiotherapy and walking aids support mobility. Immunotherapy with corticosteroids or IVIG has been tried; evidence from trials is limited, and benefit for weakness is unproven, though steroids may ease pain. Steroids worsen glycaemia and require close monitoring.
det.prognosis: Most patients improve gradually over months to a few years, but residual weakness and pain are common.
pearls: Severe thigh pain plus weight loss plus quadriceps wasting in an older diabetic: think diabetic amyotrophy.
Paraspinal denervation shows root-level involvement beyond the plexus.
Recurrence is uncommon; contralateral spread is not.
det.thd: Diabetic polyradiculopathy หรือ diabetic amyotrophy เกิดจากหลอดเลือดเล็กของรากประสาทและ plexus อักเสบ ผู้ป่วยมักเป็นชายสูงอายุที่เป็นเบาหวาน เริ่มด้วยปวดต้นขารุนแรง น้ำหนักลด แล้วต้นขาอ่อนแรงและลีบ EMG พบการบาดเจ็บหลายระดับรากประสาท รักษาด้วยยาแก้ปวด neuropathic กายภาพบำบัด และค่อยๆ ฟื้นตัวในหลายเดือน

name: Diabetic radiculoplexus neuropathy
formal: Painful asymmetric lumbosacral or cervical radiculoplexus syndrome in diabetes, with proximal weakness and weight loss, linked to microvasculitis.
simple: A painful nerve disease in diabetes affecting the thigh or hip, with wasting and weight loss.
more: Pain control, glycaemic control, and sometimes immunotherapy such as IVIG or steroids; recovery over months to years.
th: เส้นประสาทเอว-ก้นอักเสบในผู้ป่วยเบาหวาน — ปวดต้นขารุนแรง น้ำหนักลด แล้วต้นขาลีบอ่อนแรง
tempoNote: Pain and weakness evolve over weeks to months; slow partial recovery
feat: Often type 2 diabetes with good control and recent weight loss
Severe thigh/hip pain, then asymmetric proximal leg weakness and wasting (quadriceps, hip flexors)
Absent knee jerk; often spreads to the other side; caused by microvasculitis
inv: EMG: denervation in multiple roots and plexus territories including paraspinals
MRI lumbar spine and plexus to exclude compression or tumour; CSF protein may be raised

case.story: Lost 8 kg over 2 months with burning pain in the right thigh keeping him awake; now his knee buckles.
case.exam: Wasted right quadriceps and weak hip flexion and adduction, absent right knee jerk, patchy anterior thigh numbness.
case.tests: EMG: denervation in L2–L4 muscles and paraspinals; MRI: no compression; HbA1c 7.0%.
case.q: What is the usual natural history?
case.a: Gradual improvement over months to years, often incomplete; pain control and rehabilitation are central (immunotherapy is debated).

ddx.pt: Back pain, single root, disc on MRI
Symmetric, demyelinating NCS, no weight loss
Systemic vasculitis markers, upper limb mononeuropathies

det.patho: Diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy is caused by an immune-mediated microvasculitis of small epineurial and perineurial vessels, leading to ischaemic axonal injury across roots, plexus and peripheral nerves. It typically occurs in older people with type 2 diabetes, often with relatively mild or recently improved glycaemic control, so it is not simply a consequence of hyperglycaemia. Similar non-diabetic and cervical/thoracic forms exist.
det.clinical: Onset is usually with intense unilateral thigh, hip or buttock pain, followed within days to weeks by weakness of proximal leg muscles (quadriceps, iliopsoas, adductors) and sometimes distal muscles. Substantial unintentional weight loss is very common. The opposite leg is often involved weeks to months later. The knee jerk is lost on the affected side, and patients may need walking aids or a wheelchair at the nadir. Thoracic radiculopathy can coexist, causing abdominal pain or bulging.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the clinical picture plus EMG showing active denervation in multiple lumbosacral root and nerve territories, including paraspinals. MRI of the lumbar spine and plexus excludes compressive or neoplastic lesions and may show plexus enhancement. CSF protein is often raised. Consider malignancy, lymphoma infiltration, retroperitoneal haematoma, CIDP and vasculitis in the differential.
det.treatment: Management is largely supportive: aggressive neuropathic pain control, physiotherapy, falls prevention and maintaining diabetes control. Immunotherapy (IV methylprednisolone or IVIG) has been used, particularly for severe pain, but randomised evidence shows benefit mainly for pain and sensory symptoms rather than motor recovery, so use is individualised. Steroids worsen glycaemic control and require close monitoring.
det.prognosis: The illness is monophasic in most; pain improves first and strength recovers gradually over months to years, often incompletely. Recurrence is uncommon.
pearls: Painful thigh wasting with weight loss in a diabetic: DLRPN — exclude cancer and compression.
Often follows a period of improved or tight glucose control.
Contralateral spread is common; warn the patient.
det.thd: Diabetic radiculoplexus neuropathy (diabetic amyotrophy) เกิดจากหลอดเลือดเล็กที่เลี้ยงรากประสาทและ plexus อักเสบ มักในผู้สูงอายุเบาหวานชนิดที่ 2 ซึ่งคุมน้ำตาลได้ไม่แย่ เริ่มด้วยปวดต้นขาหรือสะโพกรุนแรงข้างเดียว น้ำหนักลด แล้วต้นขาลีบอ่อนแรง knee jerk หาย และมักลามไปอีกข้าง วินิจฉัยด้วย EMG และ MRI เพื่อแยกการกดทับหรือมะเร็ง รักษาหลักคือคุมปวด กายภาพ ส่วน steroid/IVIG พิจารณาเป็นราย ๆ และค่อย ๆ ฟื้นตัวเป็นเดือนถึงปี

name: Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome
formal: Cerebral oedema from rapid osmotic shifts during haemodialysis, causing headache, nausea, confusion and seizures.
simple: Headache, confusion or seizures during or after dialysis because of fast changes in body fluids.
th: สมองบวมจากการเปลี่ยนแปลงออสโมลาริตีเร็วเกินไประหว่างหรือหลังฟอกเลือด ทำให้ปวดศีรษะ คลื่นไส้ สับสน และชัก
tempoNote: Develops during or within hours after a haemodialysis session, typically the first few sessions
feat: Headache, nausea, vomiting, restlessness and blurred vision during or soon after dialysis
Severe forms: confusion, seizures, reduced consciousness, rarely coma or herniation
Risk highest with the first dialysis sessions, very high pre-dialysis urea, children and the elderly
Pre-existing brain disease (stroke, trauma, tumour) and acidosis raise susceptibility
Symptoms usually settle within hours to a day once dialysis is slowed or stopped
inv: Clinical diagnosis of exclusion: check glucose, sodium, calcium and blood gases
CT brain to exclude subdural or intracerebral haemorrhage (common in anticoagulated dialysis patients); may show oedema
EEG if consciousness is impaired to look for non-convulsive seizures

case.who: 58-year-old man from Nakhon Sawan with newly diagnosed end-stage kidney disease
case.story: During his first 4-hour haemodialysis for urea 310 mg/dL he develops headache and vomiting, then a generalised seizure in the third hour.
case.exam: Drowsy but rousable, no focal deficit, blood pressure 160/90 mmHg.
case.tests: Glucose and sodium normal; CT brain shows no bleed and mild diffuse swelling.
case.q: What happened, and how should future sessions be planned?
case.a: Dialysis disequilibrium; use short, low-flow, low-efficiency sessions on consecutive days (with higher dialysate sodium or mannitol as needed) to lower urea gradually.

det.patho: Rapid removal of urea lowers plasma osmolality faster than urea and other osmolytes leave the brain, so water moves into brain cells. Shifts in brain pH and organic osmolytes probably contribute. The result is cerebral oedema and raised intracranial pressure. It has become uncommon because modern starting regimens are gentler.
det.clinical: Mild forms with headache, nausea, muscle cramps and restlessness are frequent and easily missed; severe forms bring confusion, seizures or coma. It usually occurs in the first sessions or after missed sessions when urea is very high. Patients with pre-existing cerebral lesions or hyponatraemia are vulnerable. It can also follow rapid continuous therapies in critically ill patients.
det.diagnosis: The timing in relation to dialysis is the key clue; there is no specific test. Exclude hypoglycaemia, electrolyte disorders, hypertensive encephalopathy, intracranial haemorrhage, drug toxicity and stroke. CT or MRI may show diffuse oedema but can be normal in mild cases.
det.treatment: Prevention is central: slow initial dialysis with lower blood flow, smaller dialysers and short sessions aiming for limited urea reduction, sometimes using continuous modalities in unstable patients. If symptoms occur, slow or stop the session; hypertonic saline or mannitol can be given for significant oedema. Treat seizures with benzodiazepines and standard antiseizure drugs, and protect the airway if consciousness falls.
det.prognosis: Usually reversible within a day; deaths are rare and linked to severe oedema or delayed recognition.
pearls: First dialysis plus very high urea plus neurological symptoms during the run = think disequilibrium.
Always CT to exclude haemorrhage before attributing coma to disequilibrium in anticoagulated patients.
Gentle, frequent early sessions prevent it.
det.thd: Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome เกิดจากการฟอกเลือดลดยูเรียในเลือดเร็วเกินไป น้ำจึงเคลื่อนเข้าเซลล์สมองจนสมองบวม มักเกิดในการฟอกครั้งแรก ๆ ผู้ป่วยปวดศีรษะ อาเจียน สับสน หรือชักระหว่างหรือหลังฟอก วินิจฉัยจากช่วงเวลาร่วมกับตัดสาเหตุอื่น เช่น เลือดออกในสมองและเกลือแร่ผิดปกติ ป้องกันโดยฟอกช้า ๆ ระยะสั้นในช่วงแรก และรักษาด้วยการหยุดฟอก ให้ hypertonic saline หรือ mannitol เมื่อจำเป็น

name: Dialysis encephalopathy
formal: Progressive encephalopathy in long-term dialysis from aluminium toxicity, with speech arrest, myoclonus, seizures and dementia.
simple: A brain disorder in long-term dialysis patients, once from aluminium, with speech problems and seizures.
th: สมองเสื่อมแบบก้าวหน้าในผู้ป่วยฟอกเลือดระยะยาว จากพิษอะลูมิเนียมในน้ำยาหรือยาจับฟอสเฟต มีพูดติดขัด กระตุก ชัก และความจำเสื่อม ปัจจุบันพบน้อยมาก

Multifocal myoclonus, facial grimacing and focal or generalised seizures

case.who: 58-year-old man on haemodialysis for 12 years, Chiang Mai
case.story: For four months he has hesitated and stammered during dialysis and then speech became halting all day. Jerks of the face and hands began, followed by a generalised seizure. He takes phosphate binders containing aluminium.
case.exam: Drowsy, nonfluent speech with stuttering, multifocal myoclonus of face and arms, proximal weakness and bone tenderness.
case.tests: Serum aluminium markedly elevated; EEG shows bursts of frontal high-voltage delta; MRI brain shows mild atrophy only.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what are the key steps?
case.a: Dialysis encephalopathy (dialysis dementia) due to aluminium intoxication. Remove the source (aluminium-containing binders, check dialysate and water), switch to non-aluminium binders, consider chelation with desferrioxamine, and consider transplantation or intensified dialysis.

det.patho: Aluminium enters the body from contaminated dialysate, inadequately treated water or aluminium-based phosphate binders, and cannot be cleared by the failing kidney. It accumulates in cortex and bone and disrupts neuronal metabolism. The syndrome was recognised in the 1970s and fell sharply once water treatment and non-aluminium binders became standard.
det.clinical: It starts with stammering or hesitancy of speech that is worst around dialysis sessions, evolves to persistent dysarthria or speech arrest, and is followed by myoclonus, seizures, personality change and dementia. Bone disease and microcytic anaemia often co-exist. In children the syndrome may begin with delayed motor skills and ataxia, then progress to myoclonus and seizures. Without correction, death from bulbar failure occurs over months.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by high serum aluminium and a characteristic frontal delta EEG. Exclusion of other causes is required: dialysis disequilibrium, uraemic encephalopathy, hypertensive encephalopathy and PRES, subdural haematoma, opportunistic infection, drug toxicity and electrolyte disorders. A desferrioxamine challenge can help confirm a body burden of aluminium.
det.treatment: Eliminate aluminium exposure first by testing and treating dialysate water and replacing aluminium-containing binders. Desferrioxamine chelation can mobilise aluminium and may improve the course, but it carries risks, so use under specialist guidance with high-flux dialysis. Benzodiazepines may help seizures and myoclonus. Renal transplantation can stop progression.
det.prognosis: Poor if recognised late; early detection and removal of exposure can produce stabilisation or partial reversal.
pearls: Speech stammering around dialysis is the classic first sign.
Now rare: its presence signals a failure in water treatment or binder choice.
Do not confuse with disequilibrium syndrome, which is fluid shift and brief.
det.thd: โรคสมองจากการฟอกเลือดเกิดจากอะลูมิเนียมสะสมในผู้ป่วยไตวายที่ฟอกเลือดมานาน เริ่มจากพูดติดขัดเวลาฟอกเลือด แล้วมีกระตุก ชัก และสมองเสื่อม ตรวจพบระดับอะลูมิเนียมในเลือดสูง และ EEG มีคลื่นช้าเด่นที่ด้านหน้า การรักษาคือหยุดแหล่งอะลูมิเนียม ปรับน้ำและยาจับฟอสเฟต ใช้ desferrioxamine ในบางราย และพิจารณาปลูกถ่ายไต

name: Diaphragmatic myoclonus/flutter
formal: Rhythmic involuntary diaphragm contractions, with 'belly dancer' movements, seen with phrenic nerve irritation or brainstem lesions.
simple: Repeated jerks or flutters of the breathing muscle.
more: Rhythmic or irregular involuntary contractions of the diaphragm, causing hiccup-like belly jerks, often from phrenic nerve irritation or drugs.
th: การหดตัวของกระบังลมเป็นจังหวะโดยไม่ตั้งใจ ทำให้หน้าท้องกระตุกคล้ายสะอึก อาจเกิดจากการระคายเส้นประสาท phrenic รอยโรคก้านสมอง ยา หรือเป็น functional
tempoNote: Bouts lasting minutes to hours, may recur for months or years
feat: Rhythmic epigastric pulsation or 'belly dancing' movement, often 1–8 per second, faster than hiccups
Breathlessness, chest or epigastric discomfort, grunting sounds; no glottic closure click as in hiccup
Movements may stop with sleep or breath-holding in some, persist in others
Causes: phrenic irritation (thoracic surgery, infection), brainstem or cervical cord lesions, drugs, or functional
inv: Fluoroscopy or ultrasound of the diaphragm; surface EMG of diaphragm and abdominal wall muscles
MRI brainstem and cervical cord; chest imaging along the phrenic course
Polygraphy with variability and entrainment testing when a functional cause is suspected

case.story: Since a viral chest infection two months ago she has had rhythmic jumping of her upper abdomen with breathlessness, worse when tired.
case.exam: Regular epigastric pulsation about 4 per second independent of pulse; no other neurological signs.
case.tests: Fluoroscopy confirms rapid diaphragmatic contractions; MRI brain and cervical cord normal; chest CT normal.
case.q: What is the condition and what treatment options exist?
case.a: Diaphragmatic flutter; options include treating the trigger, trial of carbamazepine, clonazepam or other drugs, and phrenic nerve block or crush in refractory cases.

read.where: 1 - Clinical overview and phenomenology of movement disorders
Chapter 1 Breathing and the Nervous System

det.patho: Rhythmic bursts reach the diaphragm via the phrenic nerve from a generator in the brainstem respiratory network, the cervical cord or an irritated phrenic nerve. In some patients no structural cause is found and the features suggest a functional disorder. It is rare and descriptions are mainly case reports.
det.clinical: Patients notice visible epigastric jerking, a sense of fluttering and sometimes dyspnoea or palpitations. Rates are typically higher than hiccup and there is no sudden glottic closure. Symptoms can mimic cardiac or gastrointestinal disease. Functional cases tend to show distractibility and variable frequency.
det.diagnosis: Confirmation comes from seeing diaphragm movement on fluoroscopy or ultrasound and recording rhythmic bursts on diaphragm EMG. Imaging of brainstem, cord and the phrenic pathway searches for a lesion. Drug lists should be reviewed. Electrophysiology with entrainment or distraction tests can support a functional diagnosis.
det.treatment: Treat any underlying cause and stop offending drugs. Medication trials (e.g. carbamazepine, clonazepam, valproate, haloperidol or baclofen) give variable results based on small series. Phrenic nerve block, crush or section has been used in disabling, refractory cases. Functional cases benefit from explanation and physiotherapy-based approaches.
det.prognosis: Variable; some resolve spontaneously, others persist for years.
pearls: Faster than hiccups and without the glottic click: think diaphragmatic flutter.
Image both brainstem and the phrenic route.
Check for distractibility; a sizeable proportion are functional.
det.thd: Diaphragmatic myoclonus หรือ flutter คือกระบังลมหดตัวเป็นจังหวะโดยไม่ตั้งใจ เห็นหน้าท้องส่วนบนกระตุกเร็วกว่าการสะอึก อาจหอบหรือแน่นอก สาเหตุมีทั้งการระคายเส้นประสาท phrenic รอยโรคก้านสมองหรือไขสันหลัง ยา และแบบ functional ยืนยันด้วย fluoroscopy หรือ EMG กระบังลม รักษาตามสาเหตุ ลองยาหลายชนิด และพิจารณา phrenic nerve block ในรายดื้อยา

ddx.pt: Writhing abdominal wall movements, often drug-related or after abdominal surgery, not diaphragm-only rhythmic jerks
Axial flexion jerks spreading up and down the trunk, typically when lying down at sleep onset
Cause diaphragm weakness and orthopnoea rather than involuntary contractions

aN: diaphragmatic myoclonus | diaphragmatic flutter | leeuwenhek disease | respiratory myoclonus

name: Diazepam akathisia
formal: Akathisia-like restlessness related to diazepam, usually on withdrawal, with inability to sit still.
simple: A feeling of restlessness related to using or stopping diazepam.
th: อาการนั่งไม่ติดที่สัมพันธ์กับ diazepam ส่วนใหญ่เกิดเมื่อถอนยาหลังใช้นาน เป็นอาการของการถอนยามากกว่าผลข้างเคียงโดยตรง
tempoNote: Because diazepam has a long half-life, withdrawal restlessness may start 3–10 days after the last dose
feat: Inner restlessness, pacing and inability to sit, emerging days after stopping or cutting diazepam
Delayed onset compared with short-acting benzodiazepines because of active metabolites
Accompanied by anxiety, insomnia, tremor and autonomic arousal
Paradoxical agitation can follow intravenous or high doses, especially in elderly patients
inv: Drug history including alcohol and other sedatives
Basic bloods, TSH, glucose and urine drug screen
EEG only if seizures or fluctuating confusion suggest withdrawal delirium

case.who: 58-year-old male motorbike-taxi driver from Chiang Mai
case.story: Used diazepam 10 mg three times daily for back spasm for a year; ran out ten days ago. Feels he must keep walking and cannot sleep.
case.exam: Paces the room, mild tremor, BP 152/94, HR 104; no rigidity or dyskinesia; orientated.
case.tests: Electrolytes normal; urine screen positive only for benzodiazepines (residual).
case.q: Why did symptoms begin over a week after the last dose?
case.a: Diazepam and its metabolite desmethyldiazepam clear slowly, so withdrawal appears late; manage with a supervised taper.

det.patho: Chronic diazepam exposure causes GABA-A receptor adaptation; when levels fall, unopposed excitatory activity produces motor restlessness and anxiety. The long half-life of diazepam and desmethyldiazepam delays and softens withdrawal but can prolong it. There is little evidence that diazepam causes dopamine-mediated akathisia.
det.clinical: Restlessness appears gradually after discontinuation, often with insomnia, irritability, muscle tension and sensory hypersensitivity. In heavy long-term users, confusion, hallucinations and seizures may follow. Paradoxical excitation can occur acutely in older adults, those with learning disability and children.
det.diagnosis: Establish the timeline and total dose. Distinguish from akathisia due to concurrent antipsychotics, metoclopramide or SSRIs, from alcohol withdrawal, and from primary anxiety or agitated depression. Consider hyperthyroidism and stimulant intoxication.
det.treatment: Reinstate diazepam at a dose that controls symptoms and taper slowly with patient agreement. Address the original indication with non-drug options. Avoid adding antipsychotics, which can introduce true akathisia. Admission is warranted if seizures or delirium develop.
det.prognosis: Good with gradual taper; protracted symptoms are possible but usually fade over months.
pearls: Late-onset restlessness after stopping a long half-life benzodiazepine is still withdrawal.
Diazepam is often the preferred agent for tapering from other benzodiazepines.
Check for alcohol use: combined withdrawal is more dangerous.
det.thd: Diazepam akathisia ส่วนใหญ่คืออาการถอนยา benzodiazepine เนื่องจาก diazepam ออกฤทธิ์ยาว อาการจึงอาจเริ่มหลังหยุดยาเป็นสัปดาห์ ผู้ป่วยกระสับกระส่าย เดินไปมา นอนไม่หลับ ใจสั่น ต้องแยกจาก akathisia จากยาต้าน dopamine และการถอนสุรา การรักษาคือกลับมาให้ยาแล้วลดลงอย่างช้า ๆ

ddx.pt: Usually from dopamine blockers or SSRIs started recently
Leg-focused evening urge with sensory discomfort
Starts soon after a new or higher dose of a dopamine blocker

aN: diazepam withdrawal restlessness | benzodiazepine withdrawal akathisia | diazepam related restlessness

name: Diffuse astrocytoma
formal: WHO grade 2 infiltrating glioma, often IDH mutated, in young adults presenting with seizures; slow growth with eventual malignant transformation.
simple: A slow-growing but spreading brain tumour, often first noticed through seizures.
th: เนื้องอก astrocyte ชนิดแทรกซึมเกรดต่ำ (เดิม WHO grade II) ในปัจจุบันส่วนใหญ่คือ astrocytoma ที่มี IDH mutation มักเริ่มด้วยอาการชักในวัยหนุ่มสาว โตช้าแต่มักกลายเป็นเกรดสูงขึ้นในหลายปี
tempoNote: Grows over years; seizures can precede visible mass effect; progression to grade 3 or 4 typically occurs after several years
feat: Most patients are aged roughly 20-50, with a second smaller peak in childhood; males slightly outnumber females
Seizure is the presenting problem in about half to two-thirds, and many patients have a normal examination
Frontal lobe most often, then temporal and parietal; tumours may also infiltrate insula, thalamus or brainstem

Under WHO CNS5, a diffuse astrocytoma in an adult is now labelled an IDH-mutant astrocytoma (grade 2 in the CNS WHO scheme); the same-looking IDH-wildtype lesion needs further molecular work-up and is often glioblastoma-like
Headache and cognitive change appear late, when mass effect or transformation occurs
inv: MRI: ill-defined T2/FLAIR-bright mass, often cortical, with T1 hypointensity and little or no enhancement; no restricted diffusion; calcification more typical of oligodendroglioma
Biopsy or resection with IDH1/2, ATRX, TP53, 1p/19q and CDKN2A/B; sample the whole lesion because focal anaplasia is easy to miss
MR spectroscopy and perfusion map the most aggressive area to target for biopsy
Serial MRI at 3-6 month intervals after treatment to catch enhancement, which signals transformation

case.who: 29-year-old man, motorbike taxi driver from Chiang Mai
case.story: Two brief episodes of strange smell followed by lip-smacking and confusion over 6 months; the second was witnessed by a passenger.
case.exam: Neurologically normal.
case.tests: MRI shows a non-enhancing right temporal FLAIR-hyperintense lesion extending into the insula. Resection of most of the lesion: IDH1-mutant, ATRX-lost, 1p/19q intact astrocytoma, grade 2, MIB-1 index 2%.
case.q: He is seizure-free after surgery with a small residual. What are the options besides immediate radiotherapy?
case.a: Surveillance MRI is acceptable, and vorasidenib is now an approved option for residual or recurrent IDH-mutant grade 2 tumour that does not yet need radiotherapy or chemotherapy.

det.patho: Diffuse astrocytoma is an infiltrating tumour of astrocytic cells that blends into brain tissue along white-matter tracts and often presents as a microcystic, moderately cellular lesion. In adults it is nearly always IDH-mutant with ATRX loss and TP53 mutation; IDH-wildtype lesions with this histology are re-assigned by WHO 2021 to pathways that behave like glioblastoma when TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification or chromosome 7 gain with 10 loss are found. The older gemistocytic and fibrillary labels are no longer separate entities.
det.clinical: Seizures account for the majority of presentations. Because growth is slow, large lesions can sit in silent areas with mild or no deficit. Focal signs depend on site: frontal tumours give apathy or disinhibition, dominant temporal lesions give word-finding trouble, insular lesions give autonomic or sensory seizures. Transformation to a higher grade is common over time, and a new enhancing nodule or rapid clinical change should prompt re-imaging and possibly re-resection.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows an infiltrative non-enhancing mass. Because imaging overlaps with oligodendroglioma, dysplasia, low-grade epilepsy-associated tumours and demyelination, tissue is required. The pathologist reports IDH1 R132H immunostain, ATRX loss, p53 overexpression, 1p/19q status and CDKN2A/B; absence of codeletion with ATRX loss supports astrocytoma. A Ki-67 index above about 5% raises suspicion of a higher-grade focus. Radiology and pathology are best reviewed together, especially when specimen is small.
det.treatment: Treatment is individualised by age, resection extent and residual tumour. Maximal safe resection with awake mapping is preferred. After a complete resection in a young patient, observation is reasonable; with residual disease, vorasidenib can delay further therapy, while high-risk patients (older, large residual, symptomatic) receive radiotherapy (54 Gy) followed by PCV or temozolomide. Older lower-risk strategies of early radiation without survival benefit have been replaced by this tailored plan. Antiseizure treatment should avoid enzyme inducers that interact with chemotherapy.
det.prognosis: Median survival for IDH-mutant grade 2 astrocytoma is around 10 years or more; age under 40, gross resection, normal examination and absence of enhancement are favourable.
pearls: Young adult, temporal or frontal seizure, non-enhancing infiltrative lesion: IDH-mutant astrocytoma is the usual answer, and tissue still decides.
A new focus of enhancement in a known grade 2 tumour means transformation until shown otherwise.
Residual grade 2 IDH-mutant disease is the main indication for vorasidenib.
det.thd: Diffuse astrocytoma เป็นเนื้องอก astrocyte เกรด 2 ที่แทรกซึมในเนื้อสมอง พบบ่อยในวัยหนุ่มสาวและมักเริ่มด้วยอาการชัก ตาม WHO 2021 ส่วนใหญ่เป็น astrocytoma ที่มี IDH mutation และ ATRX loss การวินิจฉัยต้องตัดชิ้นเนื้อตรวจ molecular การรักษาคือผ่าตัดให้มากที่สุด ถ้าเหลือเนื้องอกและยังไม่จำเป็นต้องฉายรังสีทันที อาจใช้ vorasidenib หรือติดตามด้วย MRI ผู้ที่มีความเสี่ยงสูงให้ฉายรังสีร่วมกับ PCV หรือ temozolomide

ddx.pt: Cortically based, calcified, 1p/19q-codeleted and ATRX-retained, with a better response to chemoradiation
Bubbly cortical lesion without infiltration and without mass effect, static for years
Enhancing, necrotic, rapidly progressive; IDH-wildtype with TERT promoter, EGFR amplification or +7/-10

name: Diffuse fasciitis with eosinophilia/Shulman syndrome
formal: Eosinophilic fasciitis with rapid skin and fascial induration, peripheral eosinophilia, groove sign, and responsiveness to corticosteroids.
simple: A rare disease where tissue under the skin thickens, tightening the limbs.
more: Deep biopsy and MRI; prednisolone with methotrexate for steroid sparing. Eosinophilic fasciitis (Shulman syndrome) with sudden skin thickening and induration of limbs sparing hands, peripheral eosinophilia, and inflammation of fascia on MRI or biopsy. Full-thickness biopsy including fascia is diagnostic; corticosteroids work well, with methotrexate as an adjunct.
th: โรคพังผืดอักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกันที่ผิวหนังแขนขาตึงแข็งเร็ว มี eosinophil สูง เป็นโรคทางรูมาโตโลยีที่อาจเลียนแบบโรคกล้ามเนื้อ ตอบสนองต่อสเตียรอยด์
tempoNote: Skin and limb tightening develops over weeks, sometimes after strenuous exertion
feat: Symmetric painful swelling then woody induration of forearms and legs, sparing hands, feet and face
Groove sign along superficial veins and peau d'orange skin; joint contractures follow
Peripheral eosinophilia and raised ESR or IgG, with usually normal CK
Raynaud phenomenon and sclerodactyly are absent, unlike systemic sclerosis
Associations: haematological disorders such as aplastic anaemia or lymphoma
inv: MRI of limbs: fascial thickening and enhancement
Full-thickness en bloc biopsy from skin to muscle showing inflamed thickened fascia
Full blood count with eosinophils, CK, blood film and screening for blood dyscrasia

case.story: Six weeks after a period of heavy lifting his forearms and calves became swollen, then hard and tight; he can no longer fully straighten his elbows.
case.exam: Woody induration of both forearms and lower legs, linear depressions along veins on arm elevation, hands and face normal, power normal.
case.tests: Eosinophils 2,800/µL; CK normal; MRI shows thickened enhancing fascia; full-thickness biopsy confirms fasciitis.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the first-line treatment?
case.a: Eosinophilic fasciitis; high-dose corticosteroids, often with methotrexate as a steroid-sparing agent.

det.patho: An immune-mediated inflammation of the deep fascia with lymphocyte, plasma cell and eosinophil infiltrates leads to fibrosis and thickening. The trigger is unknown; strenuous exercise, trauma, drugs and infections have been reported before onset. It is a rheumatological disorder, not primarily neurological, but it reaches neurology clinics as stiffness, contracture or suspected myopathy.
det.clinical: Onset is with symmetric limb swelling and pain that becomes indurated, giving a cobblestone or orange-peel texture. The groove sign appears when the limb is raised. Contractures and secondary carpal tunnel syndrome can occur. Systemic sclerosis features (Raynaud, nailfold changes, visceral involvement) are typically absent.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the clinical pattern supported by MRI and a deep full-thickness biopsy. Eosinophilia is common early but may be absent, especially after steroids. Screen for haematological disease. Distinguish from scleroderma, morphoea, eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome and inflammatory myopathy.
det.treatment: Systemic corticosteroids are first line, frequently combined early with methotrexate. Other options for refractory disease include mycophenolate, IVIG, JAK inhibitors or other immunosuppressants based on small series. Physiotherapy to prevent contracture is important.
det.prognosis: Many patients improve substantially within months to a few years; late treatment and extensive involvement predict residual contracture.
pearls: Indurated limbs sparing hands with eosinophilia: think eosinophilic fasciitis, not scleroderma.
Biopsy must include fascia; skin punch alone misses it.
Look for an associated blood disorder.
det.thd: Eosinophilic fasciitis หรือ Shulman syndrome เป็นโรคพังผืดอักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกัน แขนขาบวมแล้วแข็งตึงเหมือนไม้ ไม่เป็นที่มือและหน้า มี eosinophil สูง มี groove sign ตามแนวหลอดเลือดดำ วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI และตัดชิ้นเนื้อลึกถึงพังผืด รักษาด้วยสเตียรอยด์ร่วมกับ methotrexate และกายภาพบำบัดป้องกันข้อติด

name: Diffuse inflammatory lymphocytosis syndrome (DILS)
formal: HIV-related CD8 lymphocytosis with salivary gland swelling, sicca and extraglandular disease including peripheral neuropathy, meningitis and cranial neuropathies.
simple: A condition in HIV with dry mouth, swollen glands and sometimes nerve damage.
th: กลุ่มอาการในผู้ติดเชื้อ HIV ที่มี CD8 lymphocyte สูงและแทรกซึมอวัยวะ ต่อมน้ำลายโต ปากตาแห้ง และอาจมีเส้นประสาทอักเสบหรือเส้นประสาทสมองผิดปกติ
tempoNote: Gland swelling and sicca over months; neuropathy evolves over weeks to months
feat: HIV (often untreated) with persistent CD8 lymphocytosis (>1000/µL)
Bilateral painless parotid swelling with dry eyes and mouth; anti-Ro/La negative
Painful, often asymmetric or multifocal axonal neuropathy; facial palsy
Lymphocytic interstitial pneumonitis, nephritis, hepatitis or aseptic meningitis
inv: CD4/CD8 counts, HIV viral load
Salivary gland biopsy or imaging (cystic parotids); Ro/La antibodies negative
Nerve conduction; nerve biopsy shows CD8 perivascular infiltrates with HIV p24
CSF if meningitis or cranial neuropathy

case.who: 38-year-old woman from Chiang Rai who stopped ART two years ago
case.story: Swollen cheeks for months, gritty eyes, and now painful numb patches on her right forearm and left foot with a left foot drop.
case.exam: Bilateral parotid enlargement, dry mucosa, right ulnar and left peroneal deficits.
case.tests: CD8 1,850/µL, CD4 210/µL; Ro/La negative; NCS: multifocal axonal neuropathy; sural biopsy with CD8 angiocentric infiltrate.
case.q: What is the syndrome and treatment?
case.a: DILS with multiple mononeuropathy; restart effective ART, adding a short steroid course for severe neuropathy.

read.where: Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — HIV-Associated Peripheral Neuropathy

det.patho: DILS represents a strong CD8 T-cell response to HIV infection, with CD8 cells infiltrating salivary glands, lungs, kidneys and nerves. Certain HLA types are associated. In nerves, angiocentric CD8 infiltrates with HIV-infected macrophages produce multifocal axonal damage. It has become uncommon with widespread ART.
det.clinical: Patients show salivary gland swelling and sicca resembling Sjögren syndrome but lacking typical autoantibodies. Neurological involvement includes painful multifocal or symmetric axonal neuropathy, facial nerve palsy and aseptic meningitis. Systemic involvement includes lymphocytic interstitial pneumonitis and hepatitis; lymphoma risk is increased.
det.diagnosis: Requirements include HIV infection, persistent CD8 lymphocytosis and evidence of CD8 tissue infiltration without other explanation. Biopsy of salivary gland or nerve supports diagnosis. Exclude CMV mononeuritis, lymphoma and Sjögren syndrome.
det.treatment: Effective ART is first-line and often leads to improvement. Corticosteroids are used for severe neuropathy or organ involvement. Neuropathic pain agents help symptoms.
det.prognosis: Generally favourable with ART; neuropathy usually improves.
pearls: Sicca + parotid swelling + negative Ro/La in HIV = DILS.
Rising CD8 count is the clue; it is not simply HIV neuropathy.
ART is the treatment.
det.thd: DILS เป็นภาวะในผู้ติดเชื้อ HIV ที่ CD8 lymphocyte สูงและแทรกซึมอวัยวะต่าง ๆ ทำให้ต่อมน้ำลายโต ปากตาแห้งคล้าย Sjögren แต่ไม่มี anti-Ro/La ระบบประสาทอาจมีเส้นประสาทอักเสบหลายเส้น ปวดชา หรือ facial palsy รักษาด้วยการให้ยาต้านไวรัส ART และอาจใช้ steroid ในรายรุนแรง

ddx.pt: Sicca with anti-Ro/La positivity, CD4 lymphocytic infiltrates, no HIV
Multifocal neuropathy in HIV from CMV or vasculitis, usually with low CD4
