name: Diffuse neurofibrillary tangles with calcification (DNTC)
formal: Rare tauopathy with neurofibrillary tangles and basal ganglia calcification without amyloid plaques, causing dementia and parkinsonism, mainly in Japan.
simple: A rare dementia with tangles and calcium deposits in the brain.
more: Rare tauopathy with neurofibrillary tangles and calcification without amyloid plaques, causing dementia and parkinsonism. Diffuse Lewy body disease variant described by Kosaka, with widespread cortical Lewy bodies, dementia and parkinsonism; an earlier term for dementia with Lewy bodies.
ab: Non-Alzheimer presenile dementia with Fahr-type calcification
th: โรคสมองเสื่อมชนิด tauopathy ที่หายาก พบมากในญี่ปุ่น มีปมเส้นใยประสาททั่วเปลือกสมองโดยแทบไม่มี senile plaque ร่วมกับหินปูนที่ globus pallidus และ dentate nucleus
tempoNote: Usually presenile onset (40s–60s); slow decline over many years, reported 3 to over 20 years
feat: Slowly progressive cortical dementia with naming difficulty (anomia), perseveration and apathy; some patients are restless instead
Temporal or frontotemporal signs outweigh parieto-occipital signs; parietal features (apraxia, agnosia) in a subset
Parkinsonism, often emerging during follow-up; late rigidity, contractures and mutism
Visual hallucinations, disorientation to time and sleep disturbance can mimic Lewy body disease
Normal serum calcium, phosphate and PTH despite bilateral pallidal and dentate calcification
inv: CT: bilateral pallidal (and often dentate) calcification with temporal or frontotemporal atrophy; MRI shows atrophy plus nonspecific white-matter change
Calcium, phosphate, PTH, alkaline phosphatase, thyroid, liver and renal tests to exclude secondary calcification
SPECT/FDG-PET: temporal or frontotemporal hypoperfusion/hypometabolism, with basal ganglia uptake unchanged
Definite diagnosis is neuropathological: many tangles, few or no plaques, no Pick bodies

case.story: Three years of worsening trouble finding names for everyday objects, loss of interest in hobbies and repeating the same questions. Last year he began seeing children in the house at night and sleeping poorly. Cholinesterase inhibitor made him more agitated. No toxin exposure; no relatives with dementia.
case.exam: MoCA 16/30 with marked naming errors and perseveration, disoriented to date, mild bilateral rigidity and slowed gait, positive glabellar tap, no focal weakness.
case.tests: CT head: symmetric dense calcification of both globi pallidi and dentate nuclei. MRI: temporal predominant atrophy with mild periventricular T2 change. Calcium, phosphate, PTH, thyroid and renal function normal. FDG-PET: temporal hypometabolism, striatum preserved.
case.q: Why is this not simply Fahr disease or Lewy body dementia, and what is the main limit of making this diagnosis in life?
case.a: Dementia led the illness and temporal atrophy was prominent, whereas primary brain calcification usually begins with movement or psychiatric features and secondary causes were excluded; hallucinations and parkinsonism overlap with DLB but the CT pattern favours DNTC. Calcification and neuronal loss appear to be separate processes, so imaging only supports a probable diagnosis; confirmation needs pathology.

read.where: Diffuse neurofibrillary tangles with calcification (DNTC): Kosaka-Shibayama disease in America

det.patho: The hallmark is abundant neurofibrillary tangles throughout the cortex, especially temporal (hippocampus included) with few or absent senile plaques, plus Fahr-type mineral deposits in the pallidum and dentate nucleus. Small argyrophilic ‘plaque-like structures’ are relatively specific, alpha-synuclein is frequently abundant, and arteriosclerotic vessel change occurs without hypertension. Imaging suggests that calcification and neuronal degeneration develop independently. Almost all cases come from Japan, with a female predominance in the original series; a possible role for lead has been suggested but is unproven.
det.clinical: Onset is usually presenile with progressive cortical dementia in which anomic or sensory aphasia, palilalia and apathy are common. Temporo-frontal signs outweigh parieto-occipital ones, although a parietal-predominant variant with apraxia and agnosia is described. Parkinsonism is the commonest neurological sign and tends to appear later; hallucinations, time disorientation and sleep disturbance may lead to a Lewy-body label. Cholinesterase inhibitors may worsen confusion in some patients. Late disease brings rigidity, contractures, falls and an averbal, bedbound state; duration ranges from a few years to over two decades.
det.diagnosis: Proposed clinical criteria require presenile, slowly progressive cortical dementia, temporo-frontal focal signs, frontotemporal atrophy on CT or MRI, bilateral pallidal and dentate calcification, frontotemporal hypoperfusion on SPECT or PET, and normal serum calcium and phosphate. The key step is excluding secondary calcification (hypoparathyroidism, pseudohypoparathyroidism, mitochondrial, infectious or toxic causes) and primary familial brain calcification genes. MRI white-matter hyperintensity correlates with cognition better than calcium load, so do not over-read the CT. Even when criteria are met the diagnosis stays probable, and the entity must be separated from AD, Pick disease, DLB and the parkinsonian-plus disorders.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy exists. Care is symptomatic: non-drug behavioural strategies first, cautious dosing of any cholinesterase inhibitor with prompt stop if confusion worsens, minimal use of antipsychotics, and a trial of levodopa for disabling parkinsonism. Address falls, swallowing, nutrition, sleep and contracture prevention with physiotherapy, and give carers education and advance-care planning.
det.prognosis: Relentless decline; survival after diagnosis varies widely, from under a decade to more than 20 years in reported series.
pearls: Dementia plus pallidal and dentate calcification: always check calcium, phosphate and PTH before calling it neurodegeneration.
Tangles without plaques, no Pick bodies, and plaque-like structures separate DNTC from AD and Pick disease at autopsy.
Calcification burden does not track cognition; white-matter change and temporal atrophy matter more.
det.thd: DNTC หรือ Kosaka–Shibayama disease เป็นโรคสมองเสื่อมก่อนวัยชราที่หายาก พบมากในญี่ปุ่น พยาธิสภาพคือมี neurofibrillary tangle กระจายทั่วเปลือกสมองโดยมี plaque น้อยมาก ร่วมกับหินปูนที่ globus pallidus และ dentate nucleus ผู้ป่วยมักเริ่มด้วยความจำและการเรียกชื่อสิ่งของแย่ลง เฉยเมย หรือกระสับกระส่าย ตามด้วย parkinsonism และภาพหลอน ต้องตัดภาวะต่อมพาราไทรอยด์ต่ำและ Fahr’s disease ออกก่อน CT พบหินปูนสองข้าง MRI พบฝ่อที่ temporal lobe การวินิจฉัยแน่นอนต้องอาศัยพยาธิวิทยา การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคองตามอาการ

ddx.pt: Calcification-led disorder with early movement or psychiatric signs and a family history or gene variant; dementia is rarely the sole presentation
Fluctuation, REM sleep behaviour disorder and abnormal dopamine transporter imaging; no pallidal calcification
Overlapping behavioural and language decline, but without dense symmetric basal ganglia and dentate calcification

name: Diffuse non-necrotising cachectic myopathy
formal: Muscle wasting in cachexia from cancer or chronic disease with atrophic non-necrotic fibres, without inflammation.
simple: Muscle wasting and weakness in people who are severely underweight from long-term illness.
th: กล้ามเนื้อลีบอ่อนแรงจากภาวะ cachexia ในมะเร็งหรือโรคเรื้อรัง ชิ้นเนื้อพบใยกล้ามเนื้อฝ่อโดยไม่มีการตายหรือการอักเสบ
tempoNote: Wasting progresses in parallel with the underlying illness over weeks to months
feat: Generalised muscle wasting with proximal weakness and fatigue in cancer, heart failure, COPD, CKD or AIDS
CK normal or low; reflexes preserved until late
Weight loss involving both fat and muscle, not explained by reduced intake alone
Often coexists with steroid exposure and disuse
inv: CK, inflammatory markers, albumin, thyroid function
EMG: normal or mildly myopathic, no spontaneous activity
Muscle biopsy (rarely needed): type 2 fibre atrophy without necrosis or inflammation

case.who: 67-year-old man from Udon Thani with metastatic lung cancer
case.story: Over two months he lost 9 kg and now struggles to rise from a chair; appetite is poor.
case.exam: Temporal and limb wasting, proximal weakness MRC 4/5, reflexes present, sensation normal.
case.tests: CK 30 U/L; CRP raised; EMG without fibrillations; no anti-VGCC or myositis antibodies.
case.q: Which paraneoplastic disorders must be excluded before attributing weakness to cachexia?
case.a: Lambert–Eaton syndrome and paraneoplastic myositis (dermatomyositis); cachectic myopathy is a diagnosis of exclusion.

read.where: Chapter 63 Care at the End of Life

det.patho: Inflammatory cytokines (such as TNF, IL-6), tumour-derived factors and altered anabolic signalling increase muscle protein breakdown through ubiquitin-proteasome and autophagy pathways while synthesis falls. Fast-twitch type 2 fibres shrink most. Fibres atrophy without necrosis or inflammation.
det.clinical: This is a systemic, not a primary neuromuscular, disorder. Patients show global wasting, proximal weakness and reduced endurance. It worsens quality of life, tolerance of chemotherapy and survival. Contributing steroid myopathy, disuse, malnutrition and electrolyte disturbance are common.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, based on weight loss, reduced muscle mass and the underlying disease, after excluding myositis, Lambert–Eaton syndrome, neuropathy, thyroid disease and drug myopathy. CK is usually normal. Biopsy is reserved for doubtful cases.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying disease where possible. Provide nutritional support with adequate protein and calories, encourage resistance exercise as tolerated and minimise steroid exposure. Pharmacological options such as progestogens, short-term corticosteroids for appetite, or anamorelin (approved in some countries) have limited effect on function.
det.prognosis: Tracks the underlying illness; cachexia is an adverse prognostic marker in cancer.
pearls: Normal CK and bland EMG in a wasted cancer patient fit cachexia, but always test for LEMS.
Steroid myopathy and cachexia often coexist.
Type 2 fibre atrophy is nonspecific (also in disuse and steroids).
det.thd: Cachectic myopathy คือกล้ามเนื้อลีบอ่อนแรงจากภาวะผอมหนังหุ้มกระดูกในมะเร็งหรือโรคเรื้อรัง เกิดจากไซโตไคน์อักเสบที่เร่งการสลายโปรตีนกล้ามเนื้อ CK ปกติ ชิ้นเนื้อพบใยกล้ามเนื้อ type 2 ฝ่อโดยไม่มีการตายหรืออักเสบ ต้องตัด LEMS กล้ามเนื้ออักเสบ และยาสเตียรอยด์ก่อน รักษาด้วยการรักษาโรคต้นเหตุ โภชนาการ และการออกกำลังกาย

name: Diphasic dyskinesias
formal: Levodopa-induced dyskinesias occurring at onset and end of dose, with improvement during peak dose, mainly involving the legs.
simple: Involuntary movements in Parkinson disease that appear when levodopa starts and wears off.
th: dyskinesia จาก levodopa ที่เกิดตอนยาเริ่มออกฤทธิ์และตอนยาหมด แต่ดีขึ้นช่วงระดับยาสูงสุด มักเป็นที่ขา
tempoNote: Appears 15–30 minutes after a dose and again as the dose wears off, each episode lasting minutes to an hour
feat: Mostly young-onset Parkinson disease patients on levodopa
Repetitive, stereotyped, often violent kicking or ballistic leg movements, sometimes mixed with dystonia
Occurs at transition into 'on' and again on the way 'off'; peak-dose period is relatively calm
Often unilateral or worse on the more affected side
inv: Timed motor diary or home video linked to dose times
Observed levodopa challenge to map onset, peak and decline phases

case.who: 44-year-old man from Bangkok with Parkinson disease for 9 years
case.story: About 20 minutes after each levodopa dose his legs kick wildly for a while, settle when he is fully 'on', then the kicking returns before he goes 'off'.
case.exam: During video review: alternating leg flinging at dose onset, smooth movement at peak, leg dystonia then kicking as dose fades.
case.tests: Timed diary confirms biphasic pattern; MRI unremarkable.
case.q: How does management differ from peak-dose dyskinesia?
case.a: Reducing levodopa often worsens it; instead give larger or more frequent doses to avoid low-level transitions, add a dopamine agonist or continuous therapy, and consider DBS.

det.patho: Diphasic dyskinesia appears when striatal dopamine rises through or falls through an intermediate concentration in a sensitised, denervated striatum. Fluctuating pulsatile stimulation and young age at onset increase risk. The exact circuit mechanism is not fully understood.
det.clinical: It is less common than peak-dose dyskinesia and more disabling, with forceful, rhythmic or ballistic leg movements and dystonic posturing that can cause falls. Symptoms cluster at the beginning and end of each dose cycle. Patients often misreport timing, so careful observation matters.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is made by timing movements against dosing with diaries, videos or an observed levodopa test. Distinguish from peak-dose chorea and off-period dystonia because treatments differ.
det.treatment: Strategies aim to shorten or abolish the transition zones: larger, more frequent levodopa doses, dopamine agonists, or continuous delivery such as levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel, subcutaneous foslevodopa or apomorphine infusion. Amantadine may help some. Subthalamic or pallidal DBS is effective in suitable patients.
det.prognosis: Often persists with disease progression; continuous dopaminergic delivery or DBS gives the most durable control.
pearls: Dyskinesia that improves at peak dose is diphasic, not peak-dose.
Cutting levodopa usually makes diphasic dyskinesia worse.
Young-onset PD patients are most at risk.
det.thd: Diphasic dyskinesia คือการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติจาก levodopa ที่เกิดช่วงยาเริ่มออกฤทธิ์และช่วงยาหมด แต่สงบช่วงระดับยาสูงสุด มักเป็นการเตะขาแรง ๆ ในผู้ป่วยพาร์กินสันอายุน้อย วินิจฉัยด้วยการบันทึกเวลาเทียบกับมื้อยา ต่างจาก peak-dose ตรงที่การลดยามักทำให้แย่ลง รักษาด้วยการปรับยาให้ระดับสม่ำเสมอ ยาแบบให้ต่อเนื่อง หรือ DBS

name: Diphasic dystonia
formal: Levodopa-induced dystonia occurring when drug levels rise and fall, mostly in legs.
simple: Painful muscle twisting in Parkinson disease when levodopa starts to work or wear off.
th: dystonia จาก levodopa ที่เกิดช่วงระดับยาขึ้นและลง มักเป็นที่ขาและเท้า ดีขึ้นช่วงยาออกฤทธิ์เต็มที่
tempoNote: Brief dystonic spells at dose onset and wearing-off
feat: Sustained foot inversion, toe curling or leg twisting during rising and falling levodopa levels
Often mixed with diphasic kicking dyskinesia
Painful cramps can accompany the posture
Usually young-onset Parkinson disease on long-term levodopa
inv: Timed diary and video against dose times
Supervised levodopa challenge

case.who: 49-year-old woman from Songkhla with Parkinson disease for 10 years
case.story: Her right foot twists inward painfully shortly after each pill takes effect and again as it wears off; at the best part of the dose it is fine.
case.exam: Observed right foot inversion with toe flexion 20 minutes after levodopa, resolving at peak, recurring 3 hours later.
case.tests: Diary confirms biphasic timing.
case.q: Which other levodopa-related dystonia must be distinguished, and how?
case.a: Off-period (early-morning) dystonia, which occurs at low levels and resolves once the dose works; timing against doses separates them.

det.patho: Like diphasic dyskinesia, it reflects abnormal striatal responses as dopamine concentration passes through a sub-therapeutic range in a denervated, sensitised striatum. Mechanistic detail remains uncertain.
det.clinical: Patients have painful lower-limb postures at onset and offset of each dose, sometimes alternating with kicks. It can impair walking and cause falls. Upper limb or axial involvement is less common.
det.diagnosis: Careful timing with diaries, videos or an observed challenge is needed to separate diphasic, off-period and peak-dose dystonia, because management diverges.
det.treatment: Aim for steadier dopaminergic levels: shorter dosing intervals, adequate dose size, extended-release preparations, dopamine agonists or continuous infusion therapies. Focal botulinum toxin can help a troublesome fixed foot posture. DBS is an option for refractory motor fluctuations.
det.prognosis: Usually persists but can be controlled with smoothing of dopaminergic delivery or DBS.
pearls: Ask exactly when the posture occurs relative to the last dose.
Peak-dose, off-period and diphasic dystonia need different adjustments.
Botulinum toxin is a useful adjunct for focal foot dystonia.
det.thd: Diphasic dystonia คือ dystonia จาก levodopa ที่เกิดตอนระดับยาขึ้นและลง มักเป็นเท้าบิดเกร็งและเจ็บ แต่หายช่วงยาออกฤทธิ์เต็มที่ ต้องแยกจาก off-period dystonia และ peak-dose dystonia ด้วยการจับเวลาเทียบมื้อยา รักษาด้วยการทำให้ระดับยาสม่ำเสมอ ยาให้ต่อเนื่อง botulinum toxin หรือ DBS

ddx.pt: Same timing but repetitive kicking rather than sustained posture
Dystonia during low levodopa, classically first thing in the morning
Peak-dose dystonia occurs when benefit is maximal

name: Diphtheritic neuropathy
formal: Demyelinating neuropathy following diphtheria toxin, starting with palatal and accommodation paralysis, then generalised sensorimotor neuropathy.
simple: Nerve damage that follows infection with diphtheria bacteria, with throat and eye muscle weakness first.
more: Antitoxin and antibiotics for infection; prevention by vaccination; most patients recover fully.
th: เส้นประสาทเสื่อมจากพิษเชื้อคอตีบ — เริ่มที่เพดานอ่อนและคอ แล้วลามเป็น demyelinating neuropathy ทั่วตัวหลายสัปดาห์ต่อมา
tempoNote: Biphasic: bulbar/palatal palsy in weeks 1–4, then generalised neuropathy at weeks 5–8
feat: Recent membranous pharyngitis (grey adherent membrane) or skin diphtheria, often in unvaccinated people
Early palatal weakness: nasal speech and fluid regurgitating through the nose
Blurred near vision from accommodation paralysis with relatively preserved pupillary light reaction
Weeks later: ascending or generalised weakness, sensory loss and areflexia; may need ventilation
Myocarditis with arrhythmia, often in the same time window
inv: Throat swab culture and toxin PCR for Corynebacterium diphtheriae
NCS: demyelinating features with prolonged latencies and slowed conduction
CSF: raised protein, normal cells
ECG and troponin for myocarditis

case.who: 11-year-old boy from a remote northern village, incompletely vaccinated
case.story: Severe sore throat with a grey membrane three weeks ago; now his voice is nasal and water comes out of his nose when drinking. Two weeks later his legs become weak.
case.exam: Palatal palsy, impaired near focusing, symmetric limb weakness, global areflexia, distal sensory loss.
case.tests: Throat culture grew toxigenic C. diphtheriae; NCS shows marked slowing; CSF protein 1.2 g/L, cells 2; ECG first-degree AV block.
case.q: What does the time course tell you compared with GBS?
case.a: The biphasic course — bulbar palsy weeks after a throat infection followed later by limb neuropathy — reflects toxin action; GBS usually evolves to nadir within 4 weeks of a non-specific infection without the palatal-accommodation start.

det.patho: Diphtheria toxin, produced by toxigenic C. diphtheriae, is absorbed from the local infection and enters Schwann cells, where it blocks protein synthesis. This causes a non-inflammatory demyelination, first in nerves near the infection (palate, pharynx) and later in the peripheral nerves generally, with the dorsal root ganglia and roots also affected. Severity relates to the size of the membrane and delay in antitoxin.
det.clinical: Neurological complications occur in a sizeable minority of severe cases. Palatal paralysis appears in the first weeks, followed by cranial neuropathies including accommodation failure, then a generalised sensorimotor demyelinating neuropathy at about 5–8 weeks. Respiratory muscle weakness and cardiac involvement can be fatal. Cases still occur in under-vaccinated communities, including outbreaks in parts of Southeast Asia.
det.diagnosis: Key is the history of membranous pharyngitis or skin ulcer, the biphasic course and isolation of a toxin-producing strain. NCS shows demyelination that may lag behind the clinical course; CSF protein is raised. Distinguish from GBS, botulism and poliomyelitis.
det.treatment: Give diphtheria antitoxin as early as possible during the acute infection, plus antibiotics (penicillin or erythromycin) and isolation. Once neuropathy begins antitoxin has limited effect, so care is supportive: airway protection, ventilation, cardiac monitoring and rehabilitation. IVIG is not of proven benefit. Vaccinate after recovery and trace contacts.
det.prognosis: Survivors usually recover fully over weeks to months as remyelination occurs.
pearls: Nasal voice and nasal regurgitation weeks after a sore throat in an unvaccinated child: think diphtheria.
Accommodation paralysis with preserved light reflex is characteristic.
Watch the heart — myocarditis kills more often than neuropathy.
det.thd: Diphtheritic neuropathy เกิดจากพิษของเชื้อคอตีบที่ทำลาย Schwann cell อาการเป็นสองช่วง ช่วงแรกเพดานอ่อนอ่อนแรง เสียงขึ้นจมูก สำลักน้ำออกจมูก และมองใกล้ไม่ชัด ต่อมา 5–8 สัปดาห์มีแขนขาอ่อนแรงแบบ demyelinating neuropathy คล้าย GBS และอาจมีกล้ามเนื้อหัวใจอักเสบ การรักษาคือให้ antitoxin และยาปฏิชีวนะแต่เนิ่น ๆ ร่วมกับดูแลการหายใจและหัวใจ

Fatigable weakness with normal sensation and reflexes

name: Disequilibrium syndrome
formal: Imbalance and unsteadiness from vestibular, cerebellar or osmotic shifts, including dialysis disequilibrium; subjective unsteadiness without true vertigo.
simple: A feeling of being unsteady and off balance.
th: คำเรียกกลุ่มอาการทรงตัวไม่มั่นคงโดยไม่มีอาการบ้านหมุน มีหลายสาเหตุ เช่น ระบบ vestibular สมองน้อย ประสาทรับรู้ข้อต่อ หรือการเปลี่ยนแปลงออสโมลาร์จากการฟอกเลือด
tempoNote: Acute in dialysis disequilibrium; chronic and progressive in multisensory or cerebellar causes
feat: Unsteadiness when standing or walking, without the illusion of spinning
Worse in the dark or on uneven ground when vision or proprioception is reduced
In older people often multifactorial: neuropathy, bilateral vestibular loss, small vessel disease, poor vision
The term also refers to the osmotic dialysis disequilibrium syndrome and to a rare congenital ataxia (VLDLR-related)
inv: Romberg, tandem gait, head impulse test, vibration and proprioception testing
MRI brain for cerebellar or white matter disease; nerve conduction studies
Video head impulse or caloric testing for bilateral vestibulopathy

case.story: Two years of feeling unsteady on her feet, especially at night walking to the toilet; no spinning, no hearing loss.
case.exam: Romberg positive, reduced vibration at toes, bilateral abnormal head impulse catch-up saccades, mild cataracts.
case.tests: NCS mild axonal neuropathy; vHIT bilaterally reduced gain; MRI moderate small vessel change.
case.q: Why is treatment of a single cause unlikely to fix her balance, and what helps most?
case.a: Imbalance is multisensory; vestibular rehabilitation, balance training, lighting, walking aids and cataract surgery reduce falls.

det.patho: Balance depends on vestibular, visual and proprioceptive input integrated by cerebellum and basal ganglia-frontal circuits. Loss or mismatch of any input produces disequilibrium. In dialysis disequilibrium, rapid urea removal creates an osmotic gradient and brain swelling. The congenital 'disequilibrium syndrome' (VLDLR) involves cerebellar hypoplasia with intellectual disability.
det.clinical: Patients report unsteadiness, fear of falling and reduced confidence rather than vertigo. Examination looks for sensory ataxia, vestibular hypofunction, cerebellar signs, parkinsonism and frontal gait disorder. Medications (sedatives, antihypertensives) commonly contribute. It is a symptom complex, not one disease.
det.diagnosis: Identify each contributor with targeted bedside tests, vestibular function testing, nerve studies and brain imaging. Orthostatic blood pressure and medication review are essential. In dialysis patients, link of symptoms to treatment sessions makes the diagnosis.
det.treatment: Treat reversible contributors, reduce sedating drugs, correct vision and use vestibular and balance rehabilitation. Provide walking aids and home safety measures. Dialysis disequilibrium is prevented by slower, shorter initial dialysis and managed with osmotic agents when severe.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause; multifactorial imbalance improves partly with rehabilitation, and dialysis disequilibrium is usually reversible.
pearls: Disequilibrium is unsteadiness without spinning; look for several small contributors.
Bilateral vestibulopathy is often missed; do the head impulse test.
Worse in the dark points to sensory (proprioceptive or vestibular) loss.
det.thd: Disequilibrium syndrome คือการทรงตัวไม่มั่นคงโดยไม่มีอาการบ้านหมุน มักเกิดจากหลายปัจจัยร่วมกัน เช่น vestibular เสื่อมสองข้าง ปลายประสาทเสื่อม สมองน้อย หรือ small vessel disease และยังใช้เรียกภาวะ dialysis disequilibrium จากการฟอกเลือด ตรวจหาแต่ละสาเหตุด้วยการตรวจร่างกายและ vestibular test รักษาด้วยการแก้สาเหตุ ลดยากดประสาท และฝึกการทรงตัว

name: Disorders of glycosylation
formal: Congenital disorders of glycosylation: inherited defects of glycan synthesis causing hypotonia, ataxia, cerebellar hypoplasia, seizures, coagulopathy and liver disease; PMM2-CDG is commonest.
simple: Inherited problems in attaching sugar chains to proteins, causing developmental delay, poor balance and seizures.
th: กลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่ร่างกายสร้างสายน้ำตาลบนโปรตีนผิดปกติ ทำให้กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนปวกเปียก เดินเซ สมองน้อยเล็ก ชัก และมีปัญหาตับและการแข็งตัวของเลือด
tempoNote: Usually evident in infancy; neurological deficits are largely static or slowly progressive, with episodic stroke-like events in some
feat: Infantile hypotonia, failure to thrive, developmental delay and strabismus
Cerebellar ataxia with cerebellar hypoplasia/atrophy on MRI (PMM2-CDG)
Abnormal fat distribution (fat pads), inverted nipples in some; later peripheral neuropathy and retinitis pigmentosa
Seizures and stroke-like episodes, often triggered by fever
Multisystem: liver dysfunction, coagulopathy (low factor XI, antithrombin, protein C), endocrine and cardiac problems
inv: Serum transferrin isoform analysis (isoelectric focusing or mass spectrometry) — screens N-glycosylation defects
MRI: cerebellar hypoplasia or atrophy
Coagulation factors, liver enzymes, thyroid and cardiac echo
Gene panel or exome sequencing (over 160 CDG genes); normal transferrin does not exclude O-glycosylation or some CDG types

case.story: Floppy since birth, poor weight gain and not yet sitting alone; had a fever-related episode of left-sided weakness that recovered over a week.
case.exam: Hypotonia, esotropia, truncal ataxia, unusual fat pads over the buttocks, inverted nipples.
case.tests: MRI cerebellar hypoplasia; low antithrombin and factor XI; abnormal transferrin isoform pattern (type 1).
case.q: Which diagnosis fits best, and which gene is most often involved?
case.a: Congenital disorder of glycosylation, most commonly PMM2-CDG (phosphomannomutase 2 deficiency).

read.where: Chapter 36: Seizures Due to Inborn Errors of Metabolism
Progressive Encephalopathies With Onset Before Age 2

det.patho: Glycosylation adds sugar chains to proteins and lipids; defects in the enzymes or transporters of this pathway cause CDG. PMM2-CDG, an autosomal recessive defect in mannose activation, is the most frequent. Because glycosylation affects most secreted and membrane proteins, many organs are involved, including clotting factors, hormones and neuronal proteins.
det.clinical: The classic PMM2-CDG infant has hypotonia, strabismus, ataxia, feeding difficulties and fat pads, sometimes with severe early multiorgan failure. Survivors have intellectual disability, non-progressive cerebellar ataxia, neuropathy, retinal degeneration and skeletal deformity. Stroke-like episodes and thrombosis or bleeding occur due to coagulation factor abnormalities. Other CDG types present with epilepsy, myopathy or isolated liver disease.
det.diagnosis: Transferrin glycoform analysis is the standard screening test for N-glycosylation disorders, though false positives occur with alcohol use, liver disease or transferrin variants and results may normalise with age. Confirmation is by enzyme assay and genetic testing. Exome sequencing is increasingly first-line given the number of genes.
det.treatment: Most CDG types have no curative treatment; care is supportive with nutrition, physiotherapy, seizure management and monitoring of coagulation before surgery. Oral mannose treats MPI-CDG, and galactose helps PGM1-CDG; acetazolamide and epalrestat are being studied in PMM2-CDG. Genetic counselling is important.
det.prognosis: Infantile mortality is significant in severe PMM2-CDG; those surviving infancy usually live into adulthood with stable disability.
pearls: Infant with cerebellar hypoplasia, strabismus and fat pads: send transferrin isoforms.
Low antithrombin and factor XI explain stroke-like and thrombotic events.
MPI-CDG is treatable with oral mannose — never miss it.
det.thd: Congenital disorders of glycosylation เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมที่การเติมสายน้ำตาลบนโปรตีนบกพร่อง ชนิดพบบ่อยคือ PMM2-CDG ทารกมีกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนปวกเปียก ตาเหล่ เดินเซ สมองน้อยเล็ก ไขมันสะสมผิดที่ ชัก และปัญหาตับกับการแข็งตัวของเลือด ตรวจคัดกรองด้วย transferrin isoform และยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน ส่วนใหญ่รักษาแบบประคับประคอง แต่บางชนิดรักษาได้ เช่น MPI-CDG ด้วย mannose

name: Dissociative amnesia
formal: Reversible inability to recall autobiographical information, usually after stress or trauma, in the absence of structural brain disease.
simple: Sudden memory loss for personal information after stress, with no brain injury.
th: การสูญเสียความจำเรื่องราวของตนเองหลังความเครียดหรือบาดแผลทางใจ โดยความจำใหม่ยังดี อาจเดินทางไปที่อื่นโดยจำไม่ได้ (fugue) ต้องแยกจาก TGA ชัก และโรคสมองก่อน
tempoNote: Sudden onset after a stressor, lasting hours to months, often recovering spontaneously or with therapy; recurrences occur
feat: Inability to recall important personal information, usually traumatic or stressful, out of proportion to ordinary forgetting
Retrograde loss is much greater than new learning difficulty, and personal identity may be lost while general knowledge and skills remain
Fugue subtype: purposeful travel or wandering with loss of identity, now a specifier in DSM-5-TR
Often coexists with PTSD, depression, other dissociative symptoms and functional seizures
Normal neurological examination and imaging
inv: Detailed history with a collateral account, including stressors, alcohol and drug use, head injury and seizures
MRI brain with diffusion and EEG when onset is atypical, to exclude stroke, encephalitis, transient epileptic amnesia and other organic causes
Neuropsychological testing looking at the pattern of loss and performance validity

case.who: 38-year-old male bus driver from Nakhon Ratchasima
case.story: Police find him in a Bangkok bus terminal unable to give his name or address; his family later report a serious business failure and threats from creditors a week before he disappeared.
case.exam: Alert and oriented to place and time, learns the doctors' names and today's news normally, but cannot state who he is or recall his family; neurological examination is normal.
case.tests: MRI brain with diffusion and EEG are normal; blood alcohol and toxicology are negative; memories return over 10 days with supportive therapy.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and why is an organic amnesia unlikely?
case.a: Dissociative amnesia with fugue; loss of personal identity with intact new learning is the reverse of organic amnesia, in which recent memory is lost first and identity is preserved.

read.where: 10.4 Amnestic Disorders and Mild Cognitive Impairment

det.patho: Dissociative amnesia is believed to reflect a retrieval block for autobiographical memory under extreme stress, rather than a failure of storage. Functional imaging in single cases shows increased prefrontal activity with reduced activity in hippocampal and right temporofrontal regions during attempted recall. Repeated, early or interpersonal trauma and current overwhelming stress are the main risk factors.
det.clinical: The usual form is localised amnesia for a stressful period; selective, generalised and systematised forms are rarer. Generalised loss of identity is unusual and often occurs with fugue, when the person travels and may assume a vague identity. Ability to learn new information is usually intact, which distinguishes the condition from organic amnesia. Depression, suicidal ideation and self-harm are common, so safety must be checked.
det.diagnosis: DSM-5-TR requires loss of autobiographical memory inconsistent with ordinary forgetting, causing distress or impairment, and not explained by substances, neurological disease, PTSD alone or other disorders. Organic causes to exclude include TGA, transient epileptic amnesia, head injury, stroke, encephalitis, hypoglycaemia and alcohol blackouts. Performance validity testing helps when malingering or factitious disorder is suspected, for example in legal settings.
det.treatment: Provide a safe setting and supportive therapy, avoid confrontation and allow memories to return gradually. Psychotherapy targeting the trauma and current stressors is the main treatment, with care for comorbid depression and PTSD. Drug-facilitated interviews have historical interest but are no longer routine practice. Follow-up should look for recurrence and other dissociative symptoms.
det.prognosis: Memory often returns within days to weeks, but some patients have persistent gaps or recurrent episodes.
pearls: Organic amnesia spares identity; losing one's own name with intact new learning points to dissociative amnesia.
Fugue is no longer a separate disorder but a subtype of dissociative amnesia.
Always ask about safety and suicidal thoughts; these patients often face overwhelming stress.
det.thd: Dissociative amnesia คือการลืมเรื่องราวสำคัญของตนเองหลังความเครียดรุนแรง บางรายลืมแม้แต่ชื่อตัวเองและเดินทางไปที่อื่น (fugue) แต่ยังเรียนรู้เรื่องใหม่ได้ปกติ ซึ่งตรงข้ามกับความจำเสื่อมจากโรคสมองที่มักจำเรื่องใหม่ไม่ได้แต่จำตัวเองได้ ต้องตรวจแยก TGA ชัก stroke และสมองอักเสบก่อน การรักษาคือจิตบำบัดแบบประคับประคอง ส่วนใหญ่ความจำกลับมาในไม่กี่วันถึงไม่กี่สัปดาห์

qx.stem: A 27-year-old female university student from Chiang Mai is escorted to the emergency room by railway staff. She cannot give her name, home or family, but she reads the timetable, follows conversation and remembers the doctors' names an hour later. She has a bruise-free scalp, normal neurological examination, normal MRI with diffusion and normal EEG. Her family later says she was assaulted 2 weeks earlier.
qx.q: Which feature most strongly distinguishes her condition from organic amnesia?
opts: Loss of personal identity with intact ability to learn new information
Normal MRI brain
History of recent trauma
Young age
Normal EEG
qx.why: Organic amnesias impair new learning first and spare personal identity, whereas loss of identity with preserved new learning is typical of dissociative amnesia, here with the fugue subtype. Normal imaging and EEG are supportive but do not rule out organic causes alone. A history of trauma and young age raise suspicion but are not distinguishing features.

ddx.pt: Dense anterograde amnesia with repeated questions, identity always preserved, resolving within 24 hours
Severe anterograde amnesia with confabulation after thiamine deficiency, often with residual ataxia or eye signs
Brief stereotyped episodes with automatisms; transient epileptic amnesia recurs on waking in older adults

aN: psychogenic amnesia | functional amnesia | dissociative fugue | functional retrograde amnesia

name: Dissociative disorders
formal: Disorders with disruption of consciousness, memory, identity or perception, including depersonalisation, dissociative amnesia and identity disorder.
simple: Conditions where a person feels detached from their memory, identity or surroundings.
th: กลุ่มโรคที่การรับรู้ตนเอง ความจำ ตัวตน หรือสิ่งแวดล้อมแยกขาดจากกัน ได้แก่ dissociative amnesia, depersonalisation-derealisation disorder และ dissociative identity disorder สัมพันธ์กับบาดแผลทางใจและพบร่วมกับ functional seizures
tempoNote: Episodes may last minutes (depersonalisation, dissociative attacks) to months (amnesia); identity and depersonalisation disorders are often chronic with fluctuations under stress
feat: Depersonalisation (feeling detached from one's body or thoughts) or derealisation (surroundings seem unreal or dreamlike) with intact reality testing
Dissociative amnesia for personal information, now including fugue as a subtype rather than a separate disorder
Dissociative identity disorder: two or more distinct personality states, with recurrent gaps in recall for everyday events
Strong links with childhood trauma, PTSD (including a dissociative subtype), depression and functional neurological symptoms
Transient depersonalisation is common with panic, sleep loss, cannabis, ketamine and hallucinogens
inv: Clinical assessment; the Dissociative Experiences Scale screens, and structured interviews confirm
Video-EEG and MRI when attacks resemble focal seizures or when onset is late, sudden or accompanied by neurological signs
Urine toxicology and medication review for drug-induced depersonalisation

case.story: For a year she has felt as if she is watching herself from outside, and the hospital ward sometimes looks flat like a film set; each episode lasts hours and is worse after night shifts.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination; she knows the feelings are not real and worries she is going mad.
case.tests: EEG including sleep-deprived recording is normal; MRI brain is normal; urine toxicology negative; Dissociative Experiences Scale is high.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what treatment is recommended?
case.a: Depersonalisation-derealisation disorder; explain the condition, address sleep, anxiety and any trauma, and use CBT-based therapy, treating comorbid depression or anxiety with an SSRI.

read.where: 8 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System

det.patho: Dissociation is thought to be a defensive alteration of integration between memory, identity, emotion and perception, often learned during overwhelming early trauma. Imaging studies suggest increased prefrontal inhibition of limbic and insular activity in depersonalisation, and altered connectivity between self-referential networks in identity disorder. Drug-induced states with ketamine, cannabis and hallucinogens show that glutamate and cannabinoid systems can produce similar experiences.
det.clinical: Depersonalisation-derealisation disorder causes persistent or recurrent episodes of unreality with insight preserved, often starting in adolescence. Dissociative amnesia causes inability to recall autobiographical information beyond ordinary forgetting, sometimes with purposeful travel. Dissociative identity disorder presents with identity shifts, time loss, voices, self-harm and multiple somatic and functional neurological symptoms. Patients may first reach neurologists with blackouts, memory gaps or functional seizures.
det.diagnosis: DSM-5-TR groups dissociative identity disorder, dissociative amnesia (with or without fugue), depersonalisation-derealisation disorder and other specified forms, while ICD-11 places dissociative neurological symptom disorder in the same chapter. Screening with the Dissociative Experiences Scale and structured interviews increases detection. Exclude temporal lobe seizures, migraine aura, substance use, head injury and delirium, especially with brief stereotyped or late-onset episodes.
det.treatment: Treatment is psychological and phase-based: establish safety and stabilisation, then work on trauma memories, then integration. Grounding techniques and CBT help depersonalisation, and comorbid depression, anxiety and PTSD are treated with SSRIs and trauma-focused therapy. No drug is licensed for dissociation itself; lamotrigine and opioid antagonists have weak evidence. Avoid repeated invasive tests once neurological causes have been excluded.
det.prognosis: Course varies; depersonalisation and identity disorders are often chronic, but many patients improve with sustained specialist therapy.
pearls: Insight is preserved in depersonalisation: the patient knows the feeling of unreality is not true.
Brief stereotyped unreality with déjà vu or rising epigastric sensation is a temporal lobe aura until proven otherwise.
Dissociative fugue is now a subtype of dissociative amnesia.
det.thd: Dissociative disorders เป็นกลุ่มโรคที่การรับรู้ตนเอง ความจำ หรือสิ่งแวดล้อมแยกขาดจากกัน เช่น รู้สึกเหมือนดูตัวเองจากภายนอก โลกดูไม่จริง ลืมเรื่องราวของตัวเอง หรือมีหลายบุคลิก มักสัมพันธ์กับบาดแผลทางใจในวัยเด็กและ PTSD ต้องแยกจากชักแบบ focal ของ temporal lobe ไมเกรน และการใช้สาร การรักษาหลักคือจิตบำบัดแบบเป็นขั้นตอน ร่วมกับรักษาโรคซึมเศร้าและวิตกกังวลที่พบร่วม

name: Distal acquired demyelinating sensory neuropathy
formal: Slowly progressive sensory neuropathy with distal numbness, ataxia and demyelinating changes, with anti-MAG IgM in many.
simple: A nerve condition causing numbness in the hands and feet and unsteady walking.
th: เส้นประสาทอักเสบแบบ demyelinating ที่ค่อย ๆ เป็นด้านความรู้สึกส่วนปลาย ชาและเดินเซ หลายรายมี anti-MAG IgM (ชื่อเดียวกับ DADS)
tempoNote: Insidious, slowly progressive over years
feat: Same clinical entity as DADS neuropathy (alternative name)
Distal symmetric sensory loss, gait ataxia and minimal distal weakness
Hand tremor common when anti-MAG antibodies are present
Older men with IgM paraprotein form the largest group
Proximal muscles and cranial nerves spared
inv: NCS: prolonged distal motor latencies out of proportion to proximal slowing
Serum and urine immunofixation; anti-MAG titre if IgM paraprotein
Bone marrow and imaging if haematological malignancy suspected

case.story: Slowly progressive numbness from the toes to mid-shin over three years; he now needs a light on at night to walk to the bathroom.
case.exam: Stocking sensory loss affecting proprioception, positive Romberg, absent ankle reflexes, normal proximal strength.
case.tests: NCS: demyelinating pattern with very long distal latencies; immunofixation negative; anti-MAG negative.
case.q: How is this case classified under current criteria and what treatment can be tried?
case.a: Distal CIDP (paraprotein-negative DADS); a trial of IVIG or corticosteroids is reasonable, unlike anti-MAG cases.

read.where: Chapter 52: Distal Acquired Demyelinating Symmetric (DADS) Neuropathy

det.patho: The term describes a phenotype rather than a single mechanism. Most cases carry an IgM paraprotein with anti-MAG reactivity, producing distal myelin injury; the remainder are thought to be a distal form of CIDP. The distal emphasis reflects antibody access and the vulnerability of terminal nerve segments.
det.clinical: Patients develop slowly progressive distal numbness and unsteadiness, often with paraesthesia and an action tremor, while strength is largely preserved. Men and people older than 50 are affected more often. Disability comes chiefly from ataxia and falls.
det.diagnosis: Confirm demyelination on NCS with prominent distal latency prolongation, and always screen for monoclonal protein. Anti-MAG positivity places the patient in the anti-MAG neuropathy category; negative cases meet criteria for distal CIDP under the 2021 EAN/PNS guideline. Exclude hereditary demyelinating neuropathy, diabetes-related changes and POEMS.
det.treatment: Treatment depends on the subgroup: rituximab for disabling anti-MAG neuropathy and IVIG, steroids or plasma exchange for paraprotein-negative distal CIDP. Physiotherapy and fall prevention are important in all. Haematological disease, if present, is treated in its own right.
det.prognosis: Slow progression is typical; paraprotein-negative cases have a better treatment response.
pearls: DADS is a pattern; the paraprotein and anti-MAG results decide the treatment.
Terminal latency index helps flag distal-predominant demyelination.
Paraprotein-negative DADS is now called distal CIDP.
det.thd: Distal acquired demyelinating sensory neuropathy เป็นชื่อเรียกอีกแบบของ DADS คือเส้นประสาทอักเสบแบบ demyelinating ที่เด่นด้านความรู้สึกส่วนปลาย ผู้ป่วยชาและเดินเซ อ่อนแรงเพียงเล็กน้อย หลายรายมี IgM paraprotein และ anti-MAG ซึ่งมักรักษาด้วย rituximab ส่วนรายที่ไม่มี paraprotein จัดเป็น distal CIDP และอาจตอบสนองต่อ IVIG หรือ steroid

name: Distal hereditary motor neuropathies (distal HMN)
formal: Inherited length-dependent motor axonal neuropathies with distal weakness and wasting without sensory loss, from HSPB1, GARS, BSCL2 and others.
simple: Inherited nerve diseases that weaken and thin the muscles in the hands and feet without numbness.
more: Distal hereditary motor neuropathy, with progressive distal weakness and wasting without sensory loss, from mutations in HSPB1, GARS, BSCL2, and others. EMG shows motor axonal loss; gene panels; supportive care. Inherited length-dependent motor axonopathies without clinically significant sensory loss, resembling Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease, with distal weakness and wasting. Length-dependent motor axonopathy without sensory loss, due to variants such as HSPB1, HSPB8, GARS or BSCL2, causing distal limb wasting and weakness. Nerve conduction shows motor axonal loss with normal sensory responses. Genetic panel testing confirms it; management is supportive with orthoses and rehabilitation.

feat: Slowly progressive distal weakness and wasting, legs first; pes cavus
Clinically and electrically normal sensation
Subtype clues: hand-predominant (GARS, BSCL2), vocal cord palsy, pyramidal signs
inv: NCS: low motor amplitudes with normal sensory responses
Gene panel (HSPB1, HSPB8, GARS1, BSCL2, DYNC1H1 …)

case.story: Trips over steps since her teens; her father 'walked on high arches'.
case.exam: Bilateral foot drop, pes cavus, absent ankle jerks, normal sensation to all modalities.
case.tests: Low peroneal CMAPs, normal sural SNAPs; HSPB1 variant.
case.q: What single finding separates this from CMT2?
case.a: Preserved sensory nerve action potentials (pure motor neuropathy).

nN: distal hereditary motor neuropathies distal hmn
aN: distal hmn | distal hereditary motor neuropathies | distal sma | hereditary motor neuropathies hmns | hmns | hereditary motor neuropathies | hereditary motor neuropathy | dhmn | distal spinal muscular atrophy | dsma | hmn

det.patho: Distal HMNs are a genetically heterogeneous group of length-dependent degenerations of lower motor neurons and their axons, sparing sensory fibres. Genes involve protein folding (HSPB1, HSPB8), tRNA synthetases (GARS1), axonal transport (DYNC1H1, BICD2, DCTN1), RNA processing (SETX, IGHMBP2) and ion channels (TRPV4). Many genes overlap with CMT2, so the distinction from axonal CMT is a spectrum. Biallelic SORD variants have recently been recognised as a relatively common recessive cause.
det.clinical: Most patients develop slowly progressive distal leg weakness and wasting in childhood to early adulthood, with foot drop, pes cavus and reduced ankle reflexes. Specific features suggest genes: hand-first weakness (GARS1, BSCL2), pyramidal signs (BSCL2, SETX), vocal cord paresis (DCTN1, TRPV4), and infantile diaphragmatic paralysis (IGHMBP2, also called SMARD1). Sensory symptoms are absent or minimal.
det.diagnosis: Nerve conduction shows reduced motor amplitudes with normal sensory responses, and EMG shows chronic distal denervation. Next-generation sequencing panels for motor neuropathy and CMT genes are the main test; serum sorbitol helps when SORD neuropathy is suspected. Exclude MMN (conduction block), distal SMA variants, distal myopathies and acquired motor neuronopathies.
det.treatment: Most forms lack any disease-modifying drug; therapies targeting sorbitol accumulation in SORD neuropathy are in trials. Management involves ankle-foot orthoses, physiotherapy, orthopaedic foot surgery and hand therapy. Patients with SMARD1 need early respiratory support. Genetic counselling is recommended.
det.prognosis: Usually slowly progressive with preserved walking for decades, except for severe infantile forms such as SMARD1.
pearls: CMT picture with normal sensory potentials = distal HMN.
Hand weakness plus leg spasticity suggests BSCL2 (Silver syndrome).
det.thd: Distal HMN เป็นกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่ทำให้เซลล์ประสาทสั่งการและแอกซอนส่วนปลายเสื่อม โดยไม่มีผลต่อระบบรับความรู้สึก มีหลายยีน เช่น HSPB1, GARS1 และ SORD ผู้ป่วยมีขาอ่อนแรงปลายเท้า เท้าตก และอุ้งเท้าสูงคล้าย CMT แต่การรับความรู้สึกและ SNAP ปกติ บางชนิดเริ่มที่มือ มีสายเสียงอัมพาต หรือมีกล้ามเนื้อเกร็ง การวินิจฉัยใช้ NCS และตรวจยีนแบบ panel ส่วนการรักษาเน้นกายอุปกรณ์และกายภาพบำบัด

name: Distal limb dystonia
formal: Focal dystonia affecting the foot or hand, such as striatal toe, equinovarus foot or writer's cramp, arising from primary, drug-related, Parkinson-related or structural causes.
simple: Involuntary twisting or cramping of the hand or foot that interferes with writing or walking.
more: Examine for a secondary cause. Botulinum toxin is first-line, with anticholinergics, levodopa trial and sometimes deep brain stimulation for severe cases.
th: dystonia เฉพาะที่มือหรือเท้า เช่น writer's cramp หรือเท้าบิดเข้าใน อาจเป็นแบบปฐมภูมิ จากยา จากพาร์กินสัน หรือจากรอยโรคในสมอง
tempoNote: Usually gradual onset over months; task-specific forms appear only with the action
feat: Task-specific hand dystonia (writing, playing instruments) in otherwise healthy adults
Foot inversion or toe extension (striatal toe) when walking
Adult-onset foot dystonia is a red flag for Parkinson disease or other secondary causes
Sensory tricks and mirror dystonia may be present
inv: Neurological examination for parkinsonism, pyramidal signs, cortical sensory loss
MRI brain if onset is acute, progressive, unilateral with other signs, or in childhood
Levodopa trial in childhood- or young adult-onset limb dystonia; copper studies under age 50

case.story: Over a year his right foot started turning inward when he walks, but he can walk backwards normally.
case.exam: Right foot inversion on walking forward, mild right hand bradykinesia on finger tapping, reduced arm swing.
case.tests: DaT-SPECT shows reduced left putaminal uptake.
case.q: What does adult-onset foot dystonia suggest here?
case.a: An early sign of Parkinson disease; levodopa often improves it.

read.where: 11 - Dystonia: Phenomenology, classification, etiology, pathology, biochemistry, and genetics

det.patho: Abnormal sensorimotor integration, loss of surround inhibition and maladaptive plasticity in basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical and cerebellar circuits produce co-contraction and overflow. Secondary forms arise from striatal lesions, dopamine deficiency, drugs or neurodegeneration.
det.clinical: Hand dystonia is commonly task-specific in adults and may stay focal. Foot dystonia in children often heralds generalised genetic dystonia, whereas in adults it often accompanies Parkinson disease or follows a structural lesion. Look for tremor, mirror movements and sensory tricks.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical. Associated signs, age and tempo guide investigation: imaging for structural lesions, dopamine transporter imaging for parkinsonism, levodopa trial for DRD and copper studies for Wilson disease in younger patients.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin injection guided by EMG or ultrasound is first line for focal limb dystonia. Oral anticholinergics, levodopa (in DRD or PD) and occupational therapy or retraining help selected patients. DBS is reserved for severe, refractory cases.
det.prognosis: Task-specific hand dystonia is usually stable; secondary forms follow the underlying disease.
pearls: Adult-onset isolated foot dystonia: look carefully for parkinsonism.
Childhood limb dystonia deserves a levodopa trial.
Walking backwards normally despite forward foot dystonia is typical of dystonia, not a functional clue alone.
det.thd: Distal limb dystonia คือ dystonia เฉพาะที่มือหรือเท้า เช่น writer's cramp หรือเท้าบิดเข้าในตอนเดิน ในผู้ใหญ่ที่เท้าบิดอาจเป็นอาการแรกของพาร์กินสัน ในเด็กควรลอง levodopa เพื่อหา DRD ตรวจหาสาเหตุทุติยภูมิตามอายุและอาการร่วม รักษาหลักด้วย botulinum toxin ร่วมกับยาและกายภาพ DBS ในรายรุนแรง

name: Distal myopathies
formal: Inherited or acquired myopathies with weakness starting in hands or feet, such as Welander, Miyoshi (dysferlin), GNE and titinopathy.
simple: Muscle diseases that weaken the hands, feet and lower legs first.
more: Diagnosis via CK (mild to markedly raised), muscle MRI patterns, biopsy with rimmed vacuoles or dystrophic change, and gene panels. Mostly slowly progressive with no specific cure; GNE myopathy spares the quadriceps, and dysferlin can be checked by immunoblot. Group of inherited or acquired myopathies with predominantly distal weakness, such as dysferlinopathy, GNE myopathy, Welander, Miyoshi, and ZASP types. CK, MRI, biopsy, and genetic panels determine type; supportive treatment; progression is usually slow.
th: กล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมแบบเริ่มที่ปลายแขนปลายขา — แยกชนิดตามกล้ามเนื้อที่เป็นก่อน (หน้าแข้ง vs น่อง)
feat: Weakness starts distally with preserved reflexes and sensation
Anterior leg (foot drop) — GNE (quadriceps spared), Laing; posterior calf (cannot tiptoe) — dysferlin/Miyoshi; hands — Welander
Proximal spread later
inv: CK: very high in dysferlin, mild in GNE
EMG myopathic (excludes neuropathy); muscle MRI pattern
Biopsy: rimmed vacuoles in GNE; gene panel

case.story: Slapping feet for 5 years, now weak hips but strong thighs.
case.exam: Bilateral foot drop, weak hamstrings, strikingly preserved quadriceps, normal sensation and knee jerks.
case.tests: CK 600 U/L; biopsy: rimmed vacuoles; biallelic GNE variants.
case.q: Which muscle sparing is characteristic here?
case.a: Quadriceps sparing in GNE myopathy, despite marked anterior leg and hamstring weakness.

ddx.pt: Sensory loss, absent reflexes, neuropathic NCS
Older, finger flexors and quadriceps affected
Myotonia, ptosis, cataract

aN: distal myopathy | miyoshi myopathy | gne myopathy | nonaka myopathy | welander myopathy | udd myopathy

det.patho: Distal myopathies are genetic muscle diseases that begin in hand, foreleg or calf muscles. Causes include dysferlin (Miyoshi), GNE (sialic acid synthesis; Nonaka/GNE myopathy), titin (Udd tibial), MYH7 (Laing), TIA1 (Welander), ANO5, and myofibrillar myopathy genes such as desmin, myotilin and ZASP. Inheritance can be recessive or dominant depending on the gene. Several show rimmed vacuoles or protein aggregates on biopsy.
det.clinical: The first muscles involved help identify the type. Anterior leg weakness with foot drop occurs in GNE (quadriceps spared), Laing (early adulthood, toe extensors and neck flexors) and Udd (late onset, mild); posterior calf weakness with inability to stand on tiptoe occurs in dysferlin and ANO5 disease; finger and wrist extensor weakness occurs in Welander. Cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia are important in myofibrillar myopathies and some MYH7 cases. Reflexes and sensation are preserved early.
det.diagnosis: CK is very high in dysferlinopathy and normal to modestly raised in most others. EMG confirms a myopathic process and excludes neuropathy. Muscle MRI patterns are highly informative, and biopsy may show rimmed vacuoles (GNE, Welander), inflammation (dysferlin) or myofibrillar aggregates. Genetic panels confirm the subtype. Exclude CMT, distal HMN, inclusion body myositis and myotonic dystrophy.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying treatment is approved; sialic acid replacement for GNE myopathy has been studied without clear benefit. Management includes ankle-foot orthoses, hand splints, physiotherapy and, where relevant, cardiac surveillance with pacemaker or ICD. Steroids are not helpful.
det.prognosis: Most forms progress slowly and life expectancy is near normal, except when cardiac or respiratory involvement is significant.
pearls: Foot drop with preserved reflexes and normal sensation suggests a distal myopathy rather than neuropathy.
Quadriceps sparing is the signature of GNE myopathy.
Myofibrillar myopathies need cardiac screening.
det.thd: Distal myopathies เป็นกลุ่มโรคกล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมทางพันธุกรรมที่เริ่มอ่อนแรงจากปลายแขนหรือปลายขา แยกชนิดได้จากกล้ามเนื้อที่เป็นก่อน เช่น หน้าแข้งอ่อนแรงจนเท้าตกใน GNE myopathy ซึ่ง quadriceps ยังแข็งแรง หรือน่องอ่อนแรงจนเขย่งไม่ได้ใน Miyoshi (dysferlin) ซึ่ง CK สูงมาก รีเฟล็กซ์และการรับความรู้สึกยังปกติในระยะแรก ช่วยแยกจากโรคเส้นประสาท การวินิจฉัยใช้ EMG, MRI กล้ามเนื้อ ชิ้นเนื้อ และตรวจยีน การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง และบางชนิดต้องเฝ้าระวังหัวใจ

name: Distal sensory peripheral neuropathy (DSPN)
formal: Common form of diabetic and other length-dependent neuropathy with distal numbness, tingling and burning pain in the feet and loss of ankle reflexes.
simple: Nerve damage causing numbness, tingling or pain in the feet and hands, often caused by diabetes.
more: Nerve conduction shows reduced sural amplitudes with preserved large-fibre velocities; skin biopsy nerve fibre density or QSART assess small-fibre involvement. Treat glycaemia, give foot care, and use duloxetine, pregabalin or amitriptyline for pain.
th: ปลายประสาทเสื่อมแบบรับความรู้สึกเป็นหลักตามความยาวของเส้นประสาท ชา ปวดแสบปลายเท้า reflex ข้อเท้าหาย พบบ่อยในเบาหวาน HIV และยาบางชนิด
tempoNote: Gradual ascent of symptoms from toes upward over years
feat: Symmetric numbness, tingling or burning starting in toes and spreading upward; hands involved when legs affected to the knees
Reduced vibration, pinprick and temperature distally; ankle reflexes reduced or lost
Weakness, if any, is late and mild (toe extensors)
Common causes: diabetes, prediabetes, alcohol, B12 deficiency, HIV and its older antiretrovirals, chemotherapy
inv: Fasting glucose or HbA1c (and OGTT if borderline), B12, TSH, renal function, SPEP with immunofixation
NCS: reduced sural sensory amplitudes; normal studies suggest small-fibre disease
Skin biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fibre density when NCS is normal

case.who: 47-year-old man from Bangkok living with HIV
case.story: Burning soles and pins and needles for a year, worse at night; earlier he took stavudine for several years.
case.exam: Reduced pinprick to ankles, vibration absent at big toes, absent ankle jerks, normal strength.
case.tests: HbA1c 5.6%; B12 normal; sural amplitudes reduced on NCS.
case.q: What is the likely cause and the main treatment?
case.a: HIV-associated and drug-related DSPN (prior stavudine); symptomatic neuropathic pain therapy and foot care.

read.where: Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — HIV-Associated Peripheral Neuropathy
Companion to Peripheral Neuropathy: chapters (see text)

det.patho: Axonal degeneration starts at the distal ends of the longest nerve fibres, so symptoms begin in the feet. Metabolic, toxic and inflammatory insults impair axonal transport and mitochondrial energy supply. Small fibres often fail first, producing pain before measurable large-fibre loss.
det.clinical: Symptoms include positive phenomena (burning, prickling) and negative ones (numbness, imbalance). When sensory level reaches the knees, fingertips begin to be affected. Imbalance, falls and foot ulcers follow in advanced cases. Rapid progression, asymmetry or marked weakness suggest another diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: Typical history and examination with a focused screening panel identifies most causes; about a quarter remain idiopathic (often associated with metabolic syndrome). NCS confirm axonal sensory neuropathy; skin biopsy detects small-fibre loss. Genetic testing is considered with a family history or pes cavus.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: glucose and weight control, alcohol cessation, B12 replacement, review neurotoxic drugs. Neuropathic pain responds to duloxetine, pregabalin, gabapentin or tricyclics, with topical capsaicin or lidocaine as additions. Foot care, footwear and balance training prevent complications.
det.prognosis: Usually slowly progressive or stable; recovery is limited once axons are lost, but progression slows if the cause is controlled.
pearls: Check B12, glucose tolerance and paraprotein in every new DSPN.
Normal NCS do not exclude small-fibre neuropathy.
Prominent weakness is not typical of DSPN.
det.thd: DSPN คือปลายประสาทเสื่อมตามความยาวเส้นประสาท เริ่มชาและปวดแสบที่ปลายเท้าแล้วลามขึ้น reflex ข้อเท้าหาย สาเหตุบ่อยคือเบาหวาน แอลกอฮอล์ ขาด B12 HIV และยา ตรวจคัดกรองน้ำตาล B12 ไทรอยด์ และ paraprotein ถ้า NCS ปกติอาจต้องตัดชิ้นเนื้อผิวหนัง รักษาตามสาเหตุ ใช้ยาแก้ปวดประสาท และดูแลเท้า

name: Distal symmetric sensory neuropathy (DSSN)
formal: Length-dependent sensory axonal neuropathy with burning feet and numbness, often from diabetes and chemotherapy.
simple: Nerve damage causing numb and burning feet.
th: เส้นประสาทรับความรู้สึกเสื่อมแบบสมมาตรเริ่มที่ปลายเท้า ชาแสบร้อน พบบ่อยในเบาหวาน HIV และยาเคมีบำบัด
tempoNote: Usually chronic; drug-induced forms may evolve over weeks
feat: Burning, tingling or numb feet starting at the toes
Symmetric glove-and-stocking spread over time
Reduced ankle jerks and distal pinprick and vibration loss
Common causes: diabetes, HIV, neurotoxic chemotherapy (taxanes, platinum, vinca), alcohol
Pain often dominates; weakness minimal
inv: HbA1c or glucose tolerance, B12, TSH, renal function, HIV serology
Nerve conduction: reduced sural amplitudes
Skin biopsy when only small fibres are involved

case.who: 39-year-old man from Chonburi with HIV on antiretrovirals for 10 years
case.story: Two years of burning soles making walking on the beach painful.
case.exam: Absent ankle jerks, reduced pinprick to ankles, allodynia over soles, normal strength.
case.tests: Viral load undetectable; sural responses reduced; glucose and B12 normal.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis?
case.a: HIV-associated distal symmetric sensory neuropathy, possibly with past dideoxynucleoside drug contribution.

read.where: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves — Endocrine Disorders
23. Neuropathies Associated With HIV Infection and Antiretroviral Therapy
Companion to Peripheral Neuropathy: chapters (see text)

det.patho: Distal axons are the most metabolically vulnerable part of the neuron, so diverse insults (hyperglycaemia, viral proteins, mitochondrial toxicity, chemotherapy) cause dying-back degeneration starting at the longest fibres. In HIV, macrophage activation and older antiretrovirals contributed.
det.clinical: Patients report painful or numb feet and later hands. Symptoms are symmetric and slowly ascending. Chemotherapy-induced forms appear during treatment and can worsen for weeks after stopping (coasting), particularly with platinum agents.
det.diagnosis: Clinical pattern plus nerve conduction usually suffice, with targeted blood tests for causes. Small fibre neuropathy needs skin biopsy or quantitative sensory testing because conduction may be normal. Asymmetry or motor predominance should prompt reconsideration.
det.treatment: Treat the cause (glycaemic control, adjust chemotherapy, avoid neurotoxic drugs). Duloxetine has the best evidence for chemotherapy-related pain; gabapentinoids, tricyclics and topical capsaicin or lidocaine are options for other causes. Foot care is essential.
det.prognosis: Usually chronic and slowly progressive; drug-induced forms may partially improve.
pearls: Platinum neuropathy may keep worsening for weeks after the last dose.
Normal conduction studies do not exclude small fibre disease.
Duloxetine has the strongest evidence for painful chemotherapy neuropathy.
det.thd: DSSN คือเส้นประสาทรับความรู้สึกเสื่อมจากปลายเท้าแบบสมมาตร เกิดจากเบาหวาน HIV ยาเคมีบำบัด และสุรา ผู้ป่วยมีอาการชาแสบร้อนเท้า reflex ข้อเท้าลด ตรวจ NCS ร่วมกับเลือดหาสาเหตุ ถ้า NCS ปกติอาจต้องตัดชิ้นเนื้อผิวหนัง รักษาที่สาเหตุและใช้ยาลดปวดประสาท ร่วมกับดูแลเท้า

name: Dok-7 myasthenia
formal: Congenital myasthenic syndrome from DOK7 mutation causing limb-girdle weakness, ptosis, and fatigue, with endplate maldevelopment, and worsening with pyridostigmine.
simple: An inherited neuromuscular junction disorder with weakness of the hips and shoulders, presenting in childhood.
more: Salbutamol or ephedrine is effective; pyridostigmine can worsen symptoms.
th: congenital myasthenic syndrome จากยีน DOK7 ทำให้อ่อนแรงแบบ limb-girdle หนังตาตก และอ่อนล้า แย่ลงเมื่อได้ pyridostigmine แต่ตอบสนองต่อ salbutamol
tempoNote: Onset early childhood after initially normal walking; fluctuating course with episodic worsening
feat: Limb-girdle weakness with waddling gait, often after normal early walking
Ptosis common, eye movements usually spared
Fatigability and episodic worsening for days to weeks
Stridor and respiratory crises in infancy possible
Worsens with acetylcholinesterase inhibitors; improves with beta-2 agonists
inv: Repetitive nerve stimulation: decrement (often in proximal muscles)
Single-fibre EMG: increased jitter
AChR and MuSK antibodies negative
Genetic testing: biallelic DOK7 variants

case.story: Walked normally until age 3, then developed a waddling gait and droopy eyelids; weakness fluctuates and worsened after pyridostigmine was started for 'seronegative MG'.
case.exam: Bilateral ptosis without ophthalmoparesis, proximal weakness worse after repeated squats, waddling gait.
case.tests: RNS shows 20% decrement in trapezius; AChR and MuSK antibodies negative; two DOK7 variants.
case.q: What treatment change should be made?
case.a: DOK7 congenital myasthenic syndrome: stop pyridostigmine and start oral salbutamol (or ephedrine).

read.where: Chapter 17 Disorders of the Neuromuscular Junction — Congenital Myasthenic Syndromes

det.patho: DOK7 is an adaptor protein that activates MuSK, which organises AChR clustering at the endplate. Loss of function causes small, simplified endplates with fewer synaptic folds. Neuromuscular transmission fails intermittently, especially in proximal muscles. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
det.clinical: Many children walk normally then develop proximal weakness and a waddling gait in early childhood. Ptosis and facial weakness occur, but ophthalmoparesis is uncommon. Weakness fluctuates over days to weeks and may worsen with illness or pregnancy. Neonatal stridor from vocal cord weakness and respiratory crises can occur.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in seronegative myasthenia, limb-girdle weakness with fatigability, or a child whose weakness worsens on pyridostigmine. RNS shows decrement, and single-fibre EMG increased jitter. Biopsy may suggest myopathy, misleading toward LGMD. Genetic testing confirms.
det.treatment: Beta-2 adrenergic agonists such as salbutamol or ephedrine are the mainstay and improve strength gradually over months. Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors usually worsen the condition and should be avoided. Respiratory support during crises and physiotherapy are important.
det.prognosis: With beta-2 agonists many patients improve substantially and remain ambulant.
pearls: A child who worsens on pyridostigmine: think DOK7 or slow-channel CMS.
Limb-girdle pattern with ptosis but full eye movements is characteristic.
Salbutamol takes weeks to months to show full benefit.
det.thd: Dok-7 myasthenia เป็น congenital myasthenic syndrome แบบด้อย ทำให้ endplate ของรอยต่อประสาท-กล้ามเนื้อเล็กและทำงานไม่ดี เด็กมักเดินได้ปกติก่อนแล้วจึงอ่อนแรงต้นขาและไหล่ หนังตาตก อาการขึ้นลง ตรวจ RNS พบ decrement แต่ antibody เป็นลบ ห้ามใช้ pyridostigmine เพราะทำให้แย่ลง ควรใช้ salbutamol หรือ ephedrine

qx.stem: A 4-year-old boy from Buriram walked at 22 months, has difficulty climbing stairs and a waddling gait, and has had ptosis without limitation of eye movements. He has intermittent stridor. His weakness worsened after pyridostigmine was started and after amifampridine was added. Antibodies are negative and repetitive stimulation shows a decrement.
qx.q: What is the best change in therapy?
opts: Increase pyridostigmine to the maximum dose
Add fluoxetine for suspected slow channel syndrome
Stop the cholinesterase inhibitor and amifampridine, and start salbutamol or ephedrine
Treat with intravenous immunoglobulin for seronegative myasthenia
Start ocular patching and surgery for ptosis alone
qx.why: A limb-girdle pattern with ptosis but preserved eye movements, stridor and deterioration on pyridostigmine suggests DOK7-related CMS, in which endplates are small and simplified. The beta-2 agonists salbutamol and ephedrine are the usual effective drugs through an uncertain mechanism, and cholinesterase inhibitors and amifampridine often worsen the disease. Fluoxetine and immunotherapy are unrelated to this mechanism.

ddx.pt: Antibody positive, later onset, responds to pyridostigmine
No fatigability or decrement; high CK
Also worsens with pyridostigmine but MuSK antibodies present and bulbar-predominant

aN: dok7 congenital myasthenic syndrome | dok7 cms | limb girdle congenital myasthenia | cms with dok7 mutation

name: Dominant intermediate CMT disease
formal: Group of CMT subtypes with intermediate conduction velocities of 25-45 m/s and dominant inheritance, e.g. DNM2, YARS, MPZ.
simple: An inherited nerve disease with mid-range nerve damage causing weakness and wasting in the feet and hands.
more: Nerve conduction velocity intermediate between demyelinating and axonal types, and nerve biopsy shows both features; genetics confirms the subtype. Management is supportive with foot care and orthoses; avoid neurotoxic drugs.
th: CMT ชนิดถ่ายทอดแบบยีนเด่นที่ความเร็วการนำกระแสประสาทอยู่ระหว่างชนิด demyelinating และ axonal (ราว 25–45 m/s) เช่น DNM2, YARS1, MPZ
tempoNote: Onset childhood to adulthood, very slow progression
feat: Distal weakness and wasting of legs then hands, foot drop, pes cavus and hammer toes
Distal sensory loss and reduced or absent ankle reflexes
Median motor conduction velocity typically 25–45 m/s with dominant family history
Some subtypes have extra features (e.g. DNM2 with neutropenia or cataracts)
inv: NCS: intermediate velocities, often variable between nerves and family members
Gene panel including DNM2, YARS1, MPZ, GJB1 (exclude CMTX1, which also gives intermediate values)

case.story: Trips over her toes since her teens; her father and brother have high-arched feet and thin calves.
case.exam: Pes cavus, bilateral foot drop, distal calf wasting, absent ankle jerks, reduced vibration at toes.
case.tests: Median motor CV 36 m/s; ulnar 38 m/s; heterozygous DNM2 variant.
case.q: Why is it important to look at male-to-male transmission when interpreting intermediate velocities?
case.a: CMTX1 also gives intermediate velocities but cannot pass father to son; male-to-male transmission points to an autosomal dominant intermediate form.

read.where: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves

det.patho: Variants in genes for dynamin 2 (membrane trafficking), tyrosyl-tRNA synthetase and myelin protein zero among others disturb both axon and Schwann cell function, giving conduction slowing that is neither clearly demyelinating nor axonal. Genotype-phenotype data for some rarer genes are limited.
det.clinical: The picture resembles classic CMT with length-dependent motor and sensory deficits and foot deformity. Severity ranges widely even within a family. Some DNM2 families show neutropenia, cataracts or overlap with centronuclear myopathy.
det.diagnosis: An autosomal dominant neuropathy with median motor velocities in the 25–45 m/s range prompts gene panel testing. Exclude CMTX1 by family pattern and GJB1 testing. Conduction values may differ across nerves and relatives.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy. Management includes physiotherapy, ankle-foot orthoses, orthopaedic surgery for deformity and avoidance of neurotoxic drugs such as vincristine. Genetic counselling for families.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; most remain ambulant throughout life.
pearls: Intermediate velocities: think CMTX1 first, then dominant intermediate genes.
Check family tree for male-to-male transmission.
Avoid vincristine in all CMT types.
det.thd: Dominant intermediate CMT เป็น CMT ถ่ายทอดแบบยีนเด่นที่มีความเร็วการนำกระแสประสาทระดับกลาง 25–45 m/s เกิดจากยีนเช่น DNM2, YARS1, MPZ อาการเหมือน CMT ทั่วไปคือเท้าตก อุ้งเท้าสูง กล้ามเนื้อปลายขาลีบ ต้องแยกจาก CMTX1 ด้วยประวัติครอบครัวและยีน GJB1 รักษาแบบประคับประคองด้วยกายภาพ อุปกรณ์พยุงข้อเท้า และหลีกเลี่ยงยาที่เป็นพิษต่อเส้นประสาท

name: Dopa-responsive dystonia (DRD)
formal: Dystonia due to GCH1 or TH deficiency with childhood onset, diurnal fluctuation and dramatic response to low-dose levodopa.
simple: A childhood movement disorder with twisting postures that worsens through the day and responds well to a small dose of levodopa.
more: Normal DAT-SPECT and no neurodegeneration; CSF biopterin and neopterin are low in GCH1 and a phenylalanine loading test is abnormal. Autosomal dominant with reduced penetrance. Dopa-responsive dystonia from GCH1 deficiency with childhood leg dystonia, diurnal fluctuation and dramatic response to low-dose levodopa. Childhood-onset dystonia, often with diurnal fluctuation and sometimes parkinsonism, due to dopamine synthesis defects such as GCH1, TH or SPR variants, dramatically responsive to low-dose levodopa. Diagnosed by CSF pterins and genetic tests, or a levodopa trial. Long-term low-dose levodopa works lifelong without causing dyskinesia.
ab: hereditary progressive dystonia with diurnal fluctuation
th: dystonia ในเด็กที่เริ่มจากขาและแย่ลงตอนเย็น ตอบสนองดีมากต่อ levodopa ขนาดต่ำ ส่วนใหญ่จากยีน GCH1
tempoNote: Childhood onset (often 5–8 years), slowly progressive, with marked worsening as the day goes on
feat: Foot or leg dystonia in a child causing toe-walking or an odd gait, often first noticed by teachers
Clear diurnal fluctuation: near-normal in the morning, worse in the evening or after exercise
Brisk reflexes and apparent extensor plantar responses that mimic spastic diplegia
Adult-onset cases may show mild parkinsonism or arm tremor
Dramatic and lasting response to small doses of levodopa without motor fluctuations
inv: Therapeutic levodopa trial — the key bedside test
Genetic testing: GCH1 (dominant, reduced penetrance); TH and SPR in recessive forms
CSF neurotransmitters: low HVA, low biopterin and neopterin in GCH1 deficiency; phenylalanine loading test where available
DAT-SPECT normal, which helps separate it from juvenile parkinsonism

case.story: Since age 7 she tiptoes and her right foot turns in, mainly after school; she runs well in the morning. Diagnosed as cerebral palsy at a district hospital, but birth and milestones were normal.
case.exam: Right foot inverted and plantar-flexed while walking, mild left-arm posturing at dusk, reflexes brisk, cognition normal.
case.tests: MRI brain normal. On carbidopa/levodopa at low dose, gait normal within two weeks. GCH1 heterozygous pathogenic variant.
case.q: Which feature of the history should have prompted a levodopa trial before labelling cerebral palsy?
case.a: Normal early development with later-onset gait problems and clear diurnal worsening — classic dopa-responsive dystonia.

det.patho: Most cases are autosomal dominant GCH1 mutations reducing GTP cyclohydrolase 1, the first step in tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) synthesis. Low BH4 limits tyrosine hydroxylase, so striatal dopamine falls although nigral neurons survive. Penetrance is incomplete and higher in girls; recessive TH or SPR deficiency gives a more severe infantile phenotype.
det.clinical: Typical onset is around the first decade with leg dystonia that later spreads; symptoms fluctuate through the day and improve after sleep. Some develop parkinsonism in adulthood, and adult-onset relatives may present with tremor or mild parkinsonism alone. Recessive forms can show infantile hypotonia, oculogyric crises, developmental delay and autonomic features.
det.diagnosis: Every child or young adult with unexplained dystonia, or a spastic-diplegia picture without a clear cause, deserves a levodopa trial. Genetic testing confirms most cases, but a negative GCH1 result does not exclude DRD because some mutations are deletions or intronic. CSF pterins and amines and the phenylalanine loading test help when genetics are unhelpful. A normal DAT scan separates DRD from early-onset Parkinson disease.
det.treatment: Levodopa with a decarboxylase inhibitor, often only 50–300 mg/day of levodopa, yields near-complete and sustained benefit; start low and titrate. Long-term dyskinesia and wearing-off are uncommon. Severe recessive forms may need higher doses, 5-HTP or other neurotransmitter replacement.
det.prognosis: Excellent with treatment; most patients lead a normal life on stable low doses for decades.
pearls: Any childhood-onset dystonia: give a levodopa trial before investigations become exhausted.
Diurnal worsening is the historical clue.
DRD can masquerade as spastic diplegic cerebral palsy.
det.thd: DRD หรือ Segawa disease เกิดจากยีน GCH1 ทำให้สร้าง BH4 และ dopamine ได้น้อย เด็กมี dystonia ที่ขา เดินเขย่ง อาการแย่ช่วงเย็นและดีขึ้นหลังนอนหลับ มักถูกวินิจฉัยผิดเป็น cerebral palsy วินิจฉัยด้วยการลองให้ levodopa ขนาดต่ำซึ่งได้ผลดีมากและยั่งยืน ร่วมกับตรวจยีน

qx.stem: A 9-year-old girl from Nakhon Sawan has had 18 months of toe-walking and inward turning of the left foot. Her mother notes she runs well in the morning but drags the leg and falls after school. Examination in the afternoon shows left foot dystonia, mild bradykinesia of the left hand and brisk reflexes with flexor plantars. MRI brain and spine are normal. Her paternal aunt was labelled with 'cerebral palsy' but walked better on a Parkinson tablet.
qx.q: What should be done next?
opts: Arrange tendon-lengthening surgery for presumed spastic diplegia
Start a trial of low-dose levodopa/carbidopa and review the response over weeks
Request DaT-SPECT and defer treatment until it is reported
Start trihexyphenidyl and refer for bilateral GPi deep brain stimulation
Inject botulinum toxin into the tibialis posterior only
qx.why: Childhood-onset leg dystonia with diurnal worsening, mild parkinsonism and a dominant family history suggests GCH1-related dopa-responsive dystonia. A levodopa trial is both diagnostic and therapeutic: small doses usually give a dramatic and lasting response without the motor fluctuations of PD. DaT-SPECT is normal in DRD (useful against juvenile PD) but should not delay treatment, and surgery or DBS would be wrong before a levodopa trial.
