name: Dopamine dysregulation syndrome
formal: Compulsive overuse of dopaminergic medication in Parkinson disease, causing hypomania, impulse control disorders, and dyskinesia.
simple: Compulsive over-use of Parkinson medicine, causing mood and behaviour changes.
more: Recognise by escalating levodopa dose despite motor control, with craving; treat by reducing levodopa and dopamine agonists, adding quetiapine or clozapine, and psychiatric support. Risk factors are young onset and prior substance use.
th: ภาวะที่ผู้ป่วยพาร์กินสันใช้ยาโดปามีนเกินขนาดอย่างบังคับใจตนเองไม่ได้ ร่วมกับอารมณ์คึกคัก พฤติกรรมหุนหันพลันแล่น และ dyskinesia
tempoNote: Develops insidiously over months to years of treatment
feat: Taking extra levodopa or rescue doses beyond motor need, despite severe dyskinesia
Hypomania, irritability, grandiosity, insomnia when 'on'; dysphoria and anxiety when 'off'
Often accompanied by impulse control disorders and punding
Risk: young-onset PD, male sex, novelty seeking, prior substance use or depression
inv: Collateral history from family; medication counting and pharmacy records
Screening tools such as QUIP-RS for impulse control behaviours

case.who: 51-year-old man from Bangkok with young-onset Parkinson disease
case.story: His wife finds hidden levodopa bottles; he takes doses every hour, sleeps little and has spent savings on online purchases.
case.exam: Severe generalised choreic dyskinesia, pressured speech, irritable when questioned.
case.tests: Calculated levodopa intake more than twice the prescription.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the main management principle?
case.a: Dopamine dysregulation syndrome; supervised gradual reduction of dopaminergic drugs with psychiatric support and controlled dispensing.

read.where: 11 Non-motor Symptom Management in Parkinson’s Disease

det.patho: Pulsatile stimulation of a sensitised mesolimbic reward system by short-acting dopaminergic drugs leads to addiction-like wanting. Ventral striatal sensitisation is shown in imaging studies. Personality traits and young age increase vulnerability.
det.clinical: Patients self-medicate to avoid off-period dysphoria and to chase euphoria. Behavioural features include hypomania, aggression, hypersexuality, gambling or compulsive shopping, and punding. Family relationships and finances suffer. Patients frequently minimise the problem.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis relies on history from carers showing use above prescribed doses together with behavioural change. Screen all PD patients on dopaminergic therapy for impulse control symptoms at each visit.
det.treatment: Reduce dopaminergic drugs gradually under supervision, with family-controlled dispensing. Withdrawal may trigger dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome or severe off states. Treat psychosis or mania with quetiapine or clozapine; psychological therapy helps. Continuous delivery therapies or subthalamic DBS can help some, but DBS outcomes for DDS are mixed.
det.prognosis: Difficult to treat and often relapsing; outcomes improve with early recognition.
pearls: Ask the spouse, not only the patient, how many tablets are taken.
Young men with young-onset PD are at highest risk.
Severe dyskinesia that the patient tolerates gladly is a clue.
det.thd: Dopamine dysregulation syndrome คือภาวะที่ผู้ป่วยพาร์กินสันกินยาโดปามีนเกินกว่าที่สั่งอย่างควบคุมไม่ได้ คล้ายการติดยา มีอารมณ์คึกคัก หงุดหงิด พฤติกรรมหุนหันพลันแล่น และ dyskinesia รุนแรง พบมากในผู้ชายที่เป็นพาร์กินสันอายุน้อย ต้องสอบถามจากญาติ รักษาด้วยการค่อย ๆ ลดยาภายใต้การควบคุมของครอบครัว ร่วมกับจิตแพทย์และยา antipsychotic ที่เหมาะสม

qx.stem: A 49-year-old man with young-onset PD is brought in by his wife because he takes extra levodopa tablets every two hours, buys more from online sellers and becomes irritable if she hides them. He stays up all night rearranging the garage and has severe dyskinesia most of the day, yet insists he is 'off' and needs more. His prescribed dose was 600 mg/day.
qx.q: Which is the best management approach?
opts: Increase his prescribed levodopa to match his perceived needs
Add a high-dose dopamine agonist to smooth the response
Supervised dose control with family involvement, gradual reduction to the lowest effective dose, and psychiatric support
Abruptly stop all dopaminergic medication
Start haloperidol for the compulsive behaviour
qx.why: Compulsive overuse of dopaminergic drugs beyond motor need, with craving, punding and dyskinesia, is dopamine dysregulation syndrome, most common in young-onset men with novelty-seeking traits. Management is controlled dispensing, a slow taper to the lowest effective dose and psychiatric input; abrupt withdrawal risks severe off states, apathy or a withdrawal-hyperpyrexia syndrome. Agonists raise the risk of impulse control disorders, and typical antipsychotics worsen parkinsonism.

name: Dopamine β-hydroxylase (DβH) deficiency
formal: Congenital autonomic disorder causing noradrenaline deficiency with severe orthostatic hypotension, ptosis and low plasma noradrenaline.
simple: A rare inherited condition where the body cannot make noradrenaline, causing dizziness on standing and droopy eyelids.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมยีนด้อยที่ร่างกายสร้าง noradrenaline ไม่ได้ ทำให้ความดันตกเมื่อลุกยืนรุนแรง หนังตาตก และระดับ noradrenaline ในเลือดแทบตรวจไม่พบ
tempoNote: Present from birth; orthostatic intolerance usually recognised in childhood or early adulthood
feat: Severe orthostatic hypotension with syncope, while sweating (cholinergic) is preserved
Bilateral ptosis, nasal stuffiness, hyperextensible joints
Neonatal hypoglycaemia, hypothermia and hypotension in some
Retrograde ejaculation in males; exercise intolerance
inv: Plasma noradrenaline and adrenaline undetectable with markedly raised dopamine
Tilt-table testing showing orthostatic hypotension without compensatory tachycardia
DBH gene sequencing

case.story: Since childhood she faints when standing for long; now she cannot stand in class without blacking out.
case.exam: Bilateral mild ptosis, BP 110/70 lying and 60/40 after 2 minutes standing with heart rate barely rising, joints hypermobile.
case.tests: Plasma noradrenaline undetectable; dopamine strikingly high; biallelic DBH variants.
case.q: Which drug replaces the missing neurotransmitter?
case.a: Droxidopa (L-DOPS), a prodrug that DOPA decarboxylase turns straight into noradrenaline, so DβH is not needed.

read.where: Case 35: Lifelong refractory syncope, hypoglycemia, and small digits

det.patho: DβH converts dopamine to noradrenaline in sympathetic nerve terminals and the adrenal medulla. Biallelic DBH loss means sympathetic nerves release dopamine instead, so vasoconstriction fails on standing. Cholinergic sympathetic sweating is spared. Very few cases are known worldwide.
det.clinical: Patients have lifelong orthostatic intolerance that may be labelled vasovagal. Ptosis and nasal congestion reflect absent sympathetic tone. Perinatal complications occur in some. Cognition is normal.
det.diagnosis: The biochemical signature is absent plasma noradrenaline and adrenaline with high dopamine and high dopamine-to-noradrenaline ratio. Autonomic testing shows sympathetic noradrenergic failure with preserved sudomotor and parasympathetic function. Genetic testing confirms.
det.treatment: Droxidopa restores noradrenaline and transforms symptoms in most patients. Supportive measures include fluids, salt, compression garments and avoiding triggers. Treatment is lifelong.
det.prognosis: Excellent on droxidopa, with normal life expectancy expected when treated.
pearls: Orthostatic hypotension plus ptosis in a young patient: measure plasma catecholamines.
High dopamine with absent noradrenaline is diagnostic.
Droxidopa is a targeted, highly effective therapy.
det.thd: DβH deficiency เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมยีนด้อยที่ไม่สามารถเปลี่ยน dopamine เป็น noradrenaline ทำให้ความดันตกเมื่อยืนรุนแรงตั้งแต่เด็ก มีหนังตาตกและคัดจมูก แต่เหงื่อออกปกติ ตรวจเลือดพบ noradrenaline แทบไม่มีแต่ dopamine สูงมาก ยืนยันด้วยยีน DBH รักษาได้ผลดีมากด้วย droxidopa

name: Dorsal cord syndrome
formal: Posterior column spinal lesion with loss of proprioception and vibration, sensory ataxia and Romberg sign, with preserved motor function.
simple: Damage to the back part of the spinal cord that causes poor position sense and unsteady walking.
th: รอยโรคที่ dorsal column ของไขสันหลัง ทำให้เสีย proprioception และ vibration เดินเซแบบ sensory ataxia Romberg บวก แต่กำลังกล้ามเนื้อยังดี
tempoNote: Usually evolves over weeks to months (B12, copper, tabes); acute when caused by trauma or posterior spinal artery infarct
feat: Loss of joint position and vibration sense below the lesion with strength largely preserved
Sensory ataxia: wide-based stamping gait, worse in the dark, positive Romberg sign
Pseudoathetosis of outstretched fingers and Lhermitte phenomenon in cervical lesions
Pain and temperature sensation relatively spared
Causes: B12 or copper deficiency, nitrous oxide, tabes dorsalis, HIV/HTLV, compression from behind, posterior spinal artery infarct
inv: MRI spine: T2 signal confined to the posterior columns (inverted V sign in subacute combined degeneration)
B12, methylmalonic acid, homocysteine, copper, zinc; ask about nitrous oxide
Syphilis serology, HIV and HTLV-1 testing
Nerve conduction studies to separate sensory neuronopathy or neuropathy

case.who: 24-year-old man from a Bangkok party scene seen in a neurology clinic
case.story: Six weeks of tingling feet and hands and stumbling at night; uses whipped-cream chargers several times a week.
case.exam: Normal strength, absent vibration to the iliac crests, impaired toe position sense, positive Romberg, brisk knee jerks.
case.tests: B12 low-normal, methylmalonic acid high; MRI shows posterior column T2 hyperintensity from C2 to C6.
case.q: Which tract is affected and what is the likely cause?
case.a: Dorsal columns — functional B12 deficiency from nitrous oxide abuse (subacute combined degeneration); stop exposure and give parenteral B12.

read.where: Chapter 14 Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders — Diagnosis of Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders
Chapter 14 Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders — Clinical Assessment of Spinal Disorders

det.patho: The dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus) carry large-fibre proprioceptive and vibratory input to the medulla. Their long, heavily myelinated axons are vulnerable to deficiency of B12 or copper, to toxins such as nitrous oxide, to syphilis affecting the dorsal roots and columns, and to compression from posterior lesions. The posterior spinal arteries supply this region, so infarction there is a rare vascular cause.
det.clinical: Patients describe numbness, tightness or a feeling of walking on cotton wool, with unsteadiness that worsens in the dark or when washing the face. Examination finds impaired vibration and position sense with a positive Romberg test, while power and pain sensation are relatively preserved. Cervical lesions can produce useless clumsy hands with pseudoathetosis. When corticospinal tracts are also involved, spastic weakness and extensor plantars appear, as in combined degeneration.
det.diagnosis: Localisation is clinical: a sensory ataxia with spared strength and a spinal sensory pattern. MRI may show T2 hyperintensity restricted to the dorsal columns; a normal scan does not exclude metabolic causes. Blood tests should cover B12 with metabolites, copper and zinc, syphilis, HIV and HTLV-1. Nerve conduction studies distinguish a pure cord process from dorsal root ganglionopathy or large-fibre neuropathy, which can look identical at the bedside.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: intramuscular B12 replacement with cessation of nitrous oxide, copper replacement with withdrawal of excess zinc, or intravenous penicillin for neurosyphilis. Compressive lesions need surgical decompression. Gait rehabilitation with visual compensation strategies and walking aids reduces falls.
det.prognosis: Recovery is better when metabolic causes are corrected early; long-standing deficits often improve only partly.
pearls: Romberg tests proprioception, not cerebellar function.
Ask every young patient with sensory ataxia about nitrous oxide use.
Normal serum B12 does not exclude functional deficiency — check methylmalonic acid or homocysteine.
det.thd: Dorsal cord syndrome เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ dorsal column ซึ่งนำความรู้สึกตำแหน่งข้อและการสั่นสะเทือน ผู้ป่วยจะเดินเซ โดยเฉพาะในที่มืด Romberg บวก แต่กำลังกล้ามเนื้อยังปกติ สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยคือขาด B12 หรือทองแดง การสูดไนตรัสออกไซด์ และซิฟิลิส ตรวจ MRI ไขสันหลังและเลือดหาสาเหตุ แล้วรักษาตามสาเหตุ

name: Dorsal root ganglionopathies
formal: Sensory neuronopathies with asymmetric non-length-dependent sensory loss, ataxia, and areflexia from paraneoplastic, Sjogren, toxic, or idiopathic causes.
simple: Damage to sensory nerve cell bodies, causing numbness and severe loss of position sense and balance.
more: Look for anti-Hu, Sjogren markers, and cisplatin or pyridoxine toxicity; treat the cause and immunotherapy where indicated. Selective dorsal root ganglion neuron disease causing nonlength-dependent asymmetric sensory loss and sensory ataxia; associated with Sjogren, cisplatin and paraneoplastic anti-Hu. Selective destruction of dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons causing sensory ataxia, pseudoathetosis and areflexia, with paraneoplastic, autoimmune or toxic causes.
th: ปมประสาทรับความรู้สึกเสีย — ชาและเสียการรับรู้ตำแหน่งแบบไม่สมมาตร ทั้งแขนขา มือขยับเองไม่รู้ตัว (pseudoathetosis)
feat: Asymmetric, non-length-dependent sensory loss — arms or face may be affected early
Severe proprioceptive loss: sensory ataxia, pseudoathetosis of outstretched fingers, Romberg
Areflexia with preserved strength
Causes: paraneoplastic (anti-Hu, small-cell lung cancer), Sjögren, cisplatin, B6 excess, idiopathic
inv: NCS: widespread reduced or absent SNAPs (including arms) with normal motor studies
Anti-Hu/CV2, anti-Ro/La, Schirmer test; CT/PET for cancer; B6 level; drug history
MRI spine: dorsal column T2 signal

case.story: Over 8 weeks her left hand became clumsy and numb, then both legs; she cannot find her keys in her bag without looking.
case.exam: Pseudoathetoid movements of the left hand with eyes closed, loss of joint position in all limbs, areflexia, normal power.
case.tests: Absent SNAPs in all four limbs, normal motor conduction; anti-Hu positive; CT: hilar mass.
case.q: Why is the asymmetric arm onset a clue?
case.a: Length-dependent neuropathies start in the feet; a ganglion (cell body) disorder can start anywhere, including the arms.

aN: sensory ganglionopathy | sensory neuronopathy | ganglionopathy | sjogren neuronopathy | paraneoplastic sensory neuronopathy

det.patho: Sensory neuronopathy results from damage to the cell bodies of primary sensory neurons in the dorsal root ganglia, which lack a tight blood–nerve barrier and are exposed to circulating toxins and immune attack. Because the whole neuron degenerates, both the peripheral and central (dorsal column) processes are lost, independent of axon length. Main causes are paraneoplastic immunity (anti-Hu with small-cell lung cancer), Sjögren syndrome, platinum chemotherapy, pyridoxine toxicity, genetic causes such as RFC1 (CANVAS) and idiopathic cases.
det.clinical: Onset can be acute, subacute or chronic. Sensory loss is asymmetric and non-length-dependent, may begin in the hands, face or trunk, and is dominated by proprioceptive loss: clumsy hands, writhing pseudoathetoid fingers, an unsteady gait and Romberg positivity. Reflexes are diffusely lost while strength is preserved. Small-fibre forms cause pain and autonomic symptoms. Paraneoplastic cases may have associated encephalomyelitis, cerebellar or autonomic features, and the neuropathy can precede tumour discovery.
det.diagnosis: NCS show reduced or absent SNAPs in a non-length-dependent distribution (upper limb SNAPs as abnormal as lower) with normal motor studies. Validated diagnostic criteria weight asymmetric onset, upper limb involvement and SNAP pattern. Work-up includes onconeural antibodies (Hu, CV2/CRMP5), CT chest and PET when negative, anti-Ro/La with Schirmer test and salivary gland biopsy, vitamin B6, drug and toxin history, HIV, and RFC1 testing in chronic ataxia with cough or vestibular failure. MRI may show T2 hyperintensity in the dorsal columns.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying cause: tumour therapy for paraneoplastic disease (with immunotherapy, though response is usually modest), stopping pyridoxine or neurotoxic chemotherapy, and immunotherapy (IVIG, steroids, rituximab) in Sjögren-associated or idiopathic inflammatory cases. Early treatment is crucial because ganglion cells do not regenerate. Rehabilitation for ataxia and neuropathic pain management are supportive.
det.prognosis: Paraneoplastic forms usually leave severe disability; toxic forms may stabilise after removal of the cause. Established loss of ganglion neurons is generally permanent.
pearls: Absent arm SNAPs with normal motor studies and asymmetric onset = ganglionopathy.
Search for small-cell lung cancer in smokers, even if the CT is initially clear.
Pseudoathetosis of the outstretched hand with eyes closed is a bedside clue.
det.thd: Dorsal root ganglionopathy เกิดจากเซลล์ประสาทรับความรู้สึกในปมประสาทหลังถูกทำลาย จึงไม่ขึ้นกับความยาวของเส้นประสาท อาการชาไม่สมมาตรเริ่มที่แขนหรือหน้าได้ เสียการรับรู้ตำแหน่งข้อ มือขยับเองไม่รู้ตัว เดินเซ รีเฟล็กซ์หายแต่กำลังปกติ NCS พบ SNAP หายทั้งแขนขาโดย motor ปกติ สาเหตุสำคัญคือ paraneoplastic (anti-Hu กับมะเร็งปอด small-cell), Sjögren, cisplatin, วิตามิน B6 เกิน ต้องหาสาเหตุและรักษาเร็วเพราะเซลล์ที่ตายแล้วไม่ฟื้น

name: Dorsolateral prefrontal syndrome
formal: Frontal lobe syndrome from dorsolateral prefrontal damage with executive dysfunction, poor planning, perseveration and impaired working memory.
simple: Problems with planning, organising and flexible thinking from damage to the front of the brain.
th: กลุ่มอาการจากรอยโรคสมองส่วนหน้าด้านข้าง ทำให้วางแผน แก้ปัญหา ยืดหยุ่นความคิด และความจำใช้งานบกพร่อง พูดหรือทำซ้ำ ๆ
tempoNote: Acute after stroke, trauma or surgery; gradual in tumours and neurodegeneration
feat: Poor planning, organisation and problem solving; cannot follow multi-step tasks
Perseveration and difficulty shifting set (Luria sequence, alternating patterns)
Reduced verbal fluency, especially letter fluency
Impaired working memory and attention with relatively preserved recognition memory
Apathy and slowness more than disinhibition (contrast orbitofrontal lesions)
inv: Bedside: Frontal Assessment Battery, letter fluency, Luria hand sequence, trail making B
MRI brain to define lesion (infarct, tumour, contusion, atrophy)
Formal neuropsychology (Wisconsin card sort, Stroop) for rehabilitation planning

case.story: After a left frontal haemorrhage he can do simple sums but cannot organise the monthly accounts; he repeats the same step over and over.
case.exam: Letter fluency 4 words/min, cannot complete fist-edge-palm sequence, perseverates on alternating loops; no weakness.
case.tests: MRI shows chronic haemosiderin-lined cavity in left dorsolateral frontal cortex.
case.q: Which frontal syndrome is this, and how does it differ from orbitofrontal damage?
case.a: Dorsolateral prefrontal (dysexecutive) syndrome; orbitofrontal lesions mainly cause disinhibition and social misconduct with relatively spared executive tests.

det.patho: The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, together with its loop via the caudate, globus pallidus and dorsomedial thalamus support working memory, planning, set-shifting and goal-directed behaviour. Damage anywhere along this loop — cortex, white matter, caudate or thalamus — can produce the syndrome. Common causes include stroke, traumatic brain injury, tumours, hydrocephalus and frontotemporal or vascular neurodegeneration.
det.clinical: Patients may look normal in conversation but fail at real-world tasks requiring organisation. They perseverate, are stimulus-bound and struggle with abstraction and novel problems. Apathy and slowed thinking are common, and insight is often reduced. It is one of the three classic prefrontal syndromes alongside orbitofrontal (disinhibited) and medial frontal (apathetic) types, though overlap is usual.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical and neuropsychological. Bedside tests include letter fluency, motor sequencing, go/no-go and the Frontal Assessment Battery; MMSE is insensitive. Imaging identifies the cause and may show lesions in subcortical parts of the circuit rather than the cortex itself.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying cause. Cognitive rehabilitation using goal management training, external aids, checklists and structured routines is the main intervention. Drug evidence is limited; stimulants or dopaminergic agents are occasionally used for apathy and attention after brain injury.
det.prognosis: Static lesions may improve partially with rehabilitation; degenerative causes progress.
pearls: MMSE can be normal — test fluency and sequencing.
Subcortical lesions (caudate, thalamus) can mimic frontal cortical damage.
Dorsolateral = executive; orbitofrontal = disinhibition; medial = apathy.
det.thd: Dorsolateral prefrontal syndrome เกิดจากรอยโรคสมองส่วนหน้าด้านข้างหรือวงจรที่เชื่อมกับ caudate และ thalamus ผู้ป่วยวางแผนและแก้ปัญหาไม่ได้ ทำซ้ำ ๆ เปลี่ยนความคิดยาก และความจำใช้งานบกพร่อง แม้คุยดูปกติ ตรวจด้วย letter fluency, Luria sequence และ FAB การรักษาคือแก้สาเหตุและฟื้นฟูความคิดด้วยเทคนิคช่วยจัดระบบ

name: Double athetosis
formal: Bilateral athetosis, slow writhing movements of limbs on both sides in cerebral palsy from perinatal basal ganglia injury.
simple: Slow twisting, writhing movements on both sides of the body, usually from early brain injury.
th: การเคลื่อนไหวบิดช้า ๆ ของแขนขาทั้งสองข้างในเด็ก cerebral palsy จากการบาดเจ็บของ basal ganglia ช่วงปริกำเนิด เช่น ขาดออกซิเจนหรือ bilirubin สูง
tempoNote: Movements emerge in the first 1–3 years after initial hypotonia and then remain static
feat: Slow, writhing, continuous movements of hands, face and feet on both sides, worse with action and emotion
Early hypotonia and delayed milestones, then dyskinesia appears
Dysarthria and feeding difficulty; intellect often relatively preserved
Perinatal history of severe hypoxic-ischaemic injury or kernicterus
inv: MRI: bilateral putamen and thalamus injury (hypoxia) or globus pallidus T2 signal (kernicterus)
Hearing test (auditory neuropathy with kernicterus)
Metabolic and genetic tests if no clear perinatal cause or if progressive

case.story: Born after a difficult delivery needing resuscitation; floppy as an infant and later developed constant twisting arm and face movements.
case.exam: Bilateral writhing distal movements, grimacing, dysarthria, good understanding.
case.tests: MRI shows bilateral posterior putamen and ventrolateral thalamic signal change.
case.q: Why is a levodopa trial and genetic review still reasonable in some children like this?
case.a: Dopa-responsive dystonia and other genetic dyskinesias can mimic cerebral palsy, especially when no clear perinatal injury or typical MRI lesions exist.

det.patho: Selective vulnerability of the deep grey matter to acute profound hypoxia-ischaemia at term, or to unconjugated bilirubin toxicity (kernicterus), damages putamen, thalamus or globus pallidus. Disrupted basal ganglia output produces involuntary writhing. The injury itself is static.
det.clinical: Children are hypotonic in infancy and dyskinesia emerges as motor development proceeds. Choreoathetosis and dystonia mix, worsening with effort and emotion. Speech, swallowing and hand use are affected; cognition varies. Kernicterus adds hearing loss and upgaze limitation.
det.diagnosis: A consistent perinatal history and characteristic MRI support the diagnosis. Progressive course, normal birth history or normal MRI should prompt metabolic and genetic evaluation, including a levodopa trial.
det.treatment: Multidisciplinary rehabilitation, communication aids and seating. Medications such as trihexyphenidyl, baclofen or gabapentin may help; botulinum toxin for focal problems. Pallidal DBS gives modest benefit in selected dyskinetic cerebral palsy.
det.prognosis: Non-progressive brain injury, but musculoskeletal complications and cervical myelopathy can develop in adults.
pearls: Athetosis in CP appears after initial hypotonia.
Normal MRI in 'athetoid CP' warrants genetic testing and a levodopa trial.
Adults with athetoid CP can develop cervical myelopathy from constant neck movement.
det.thd: Double athetosis คือการเคลื่อนไหวบิดช้า ๆ ทั้งสองข้างในเด็กสมองพิการชนิด dyskinetic จากการบาดเจ็บของ basal ganglia และ thalamus ช่วงคลอด เช่น ขาดออกซิเจนรุนแรงหรือ bilirubin สูง เด็กตัวอ่อนปวกเปียกก่อนแล้วจึงมีอาการบิด MRI ช่วยยืนยัน ถ้าไม่มีประวัติชัดเจนควรลอง levodopa และตรวจพันธุกรรม รักษาด้วยการฟื้นฟูและยาบรรเทาอาการ

Progressive dystonia with eye-of-the-tiger sign, not static

name: Down syndrome
formal: Trisomy 21 with intellectual disability, hypotonia, and neurological associations including early Alzheimer disease, epilepsy and atlantoaxial instability.
simple: A genetic condition from an extra chromosome 21, with learning difficulty, low muscle tone and distinctive features.
more: Trisomy 21 with intellectual disability, hypotonia, early Alzheimer pathology, epilepsy and atlantoaxial instability.
th: ความผิดปกติของโครโมโซมคู่ที่ 21 เกินมา ทำให้มีภาวะบกพร่องทางสติปัญญา กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง และเสี่ยงอัลไซเมอร์เร็ว ลมชัก และข้อกระดูกคอส่วนบนไม่มั่นคง
tempoNote: Present from birth; Alzheimer-type decline typically begins in the late 40s–50s
feat: Intellectual disability, neonatal hypotonia and characteristic facial features
Very high lifetime risk of early-onset Alzheimer disease (APP gene triplication), often starting with behaviour change
Epilepsy peaks in infancy (infantile spasms) and again in later adulthood with dementia (late-onset myoclonic epilepsy)
Atlantoaxial instability can cause cervical myelopathy: neck pain, gait change, hyperreflexia, new incontinence
Increased risk of moyamoya stroke, hypothyroidism, obstructive sleep apnoea, hearing and visual impairment
inv: Karyotype (standard trisomy, translocation or mosaicism) — usually done at birth
Baseline adult cognitive and functional assessment by the late 30s for later comparison
MRI cervical spine if myelopathic symptoms; thyroid function, B12, sleep study and hearing tests in cognitive decline

case.who: 49-year-old man with Down syndrome from a care home in Nonthaburi
case.story: Over a year he has become withdrawn and irritable, lost his self-care routine, and recently had morning jerks and one generalised seizure.
case.exam: Disoriented compared with his baseline, myoclonic jerks on waking, no long-tract signs.
case.tests: TSH normal; MRI shows generalised and medial temporal atrophy; EEG background slowing with generalised discharges.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis, and which reversible problems must be checked first?
case.a: Alzheimer disease in Down syndrome with late-onset myoclonic epilepsy; first exclude hypothyroidism, depression, sensory loss, sleep apnoea and drug effects.

read.where: Chapter 14 Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders — Craniocervical Junction Anomalies

det.patho: An extra copy of chromosome 21 (usually from maternal meiotic non-disjunction) increases dosage of genes including APP. Excess amyloid precursor protein leads to amyloid plaques in almost all adults by age 40 and Alzheimer dementia in most by their 60s. Developmental brain changes include reduced neuron number and hypoplasia of the cerebellum and hippocampus. Ligamentous laxity underlies atlantoaxial instability.
det.clinical: Children have hypotonia, developmental delay, congenital heart disease and higher rates of infantile spasms. Adults face premature ageing problems: dementia often presents with personality change, apathy or loss of skills rather than memory complaints. New seizures in a middle-aged adult with DS frequently herald or accompany dementia. Symptomatic atlantoaxial subluxation, moyamoya and cervical spondylotic myelopathy are important neurological complications.
det.diagnosis: DS itself is confirmed by karyotype. Dementia is diagnosed by decline from the person's own baseline, so serial structured assessments are recommended. Amyloid and tau biomarkers in plasma, CSF and PET are abnormal early and used in research and trials. Systematically exclude hypothyroidism, depression, hearing or visual loss, sleep apnoea and medication effects.
det.treatment: Support development with early intervention, education and therapy. Treat infantile spasms promptly with ACTH/steroids or vigabatrin. Cholinesterase inhibitors are used in DS dementia with modest evidence; anti-amyloid antibodies carry high ARIA risk because of amyloid angiopathy and are not routinely recommended. Levetiracetam is often used for late-onset myoclonic epilepsy. Annual thyroid testing, sleep and sensory checks are standard.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy now exceeds 60 years; most older adults with DS die from complications of Alzheimer disease.
pearls: New seizures in a middle-aged person with DS: think Alzheimer disease.
Change in gait, neck pain or incontinence: image the craniocervical junction.
Dementia in DS presents with behaviour change and lost skills; compare to the person's own baseline.
det.thd: Down syndrome เกิดจากโครโมโซมคู่ที่ 21 เกิน ทำให้มีภาวะบกพร่องทางสติปัญญาและกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนตั้งแต่เกิด ยีน APP ที่เพิ่มขึ้นทำให้เกิดอัลไซเมอร์ตั้งแต่อายุราว 40–50 ปี มักเริ่มด้วยพฤติกรรมเปลี่ยนและชักกระตุก ภาวะแทรกซ้อนอื่น ได้แก่ ข้อกระดูกคอบนไม่มั่นคงกดไขสันหลัง moyamoya และไทรอยด์ต่ำ ควรประเมินสมรรถภาพเทียบกับพื้นฐานของผู้ป่วยเองและตรวจหาสาเหตุที่แก้ไขได้ก่อน

name: Dravet syndrome
formal: SCN1A-related developmental epileptic encephalopathy beginning with febrile prolonged hemiclonic seizures at about six months, then multiple seizure types, ataxia and cognitive decline.
simple: A severe childhood epilepsy that starts in infancy with fever-triggered seizures and affects development.
th: ทารกปกติดีแต่มีชักนานร่วมกับไข้หรืออากาศร้อนตั้งแต่ขวบปีแรก ต่อมาชักหลายแบบและพัฒนาการช้า — SCN1A ห้ามใช้ sodium channel blocker
tempoNote: First seizure usually 4–8 months; frequent prolonged seizures in early childhood, developmental slowing from the second year
feat: Prolonged febrile or afebrile hemiclonic or generalised clonic seizures in the first year in a previously normal infant
Triggers: fever, warm baths, hot weather, exertion, vaccination-associated fever
From the second year: myoclonic jerks, atypical absences, focal seizures and repeated status epilepticus
Developmental plateau, behavioural problems, ataxia and later crouch gait
High risk of SUDEP
inv: SCN1A sequencing and deletion/duplication testing (positive in most), or epilepsy gene panel
EEG often normal at first, later generalised and multifocal discharges with photosensitivity in some
MRI usually normal; mainly used to exclude other causes

case.story: Three seizures since 5 months: a 40-minute left-sided clonic seizure with a mild fever after vaccination, then right-sided after a warm bath, then generalised during a cold. Development so far normal.
case.exam: Alert, normal tone and milestones.
case.tests: EEG normal between seizures; MRI normal. Gene panel: de novo truncating SCN1A variant.
case.q: Which common antiseizure drugs should be avoided, and what does the vaccine association mean for the family?
case.a: Avoid sodium-channel blockers (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine) as they worsen seizures. The vaccine fever only unmasked an existing genetic disorder; it did not cause it, and vaccination should continue with fever prophylaxis.

read.where: Chapter 26 Infantile Epileptic Encephalopathies and De Novo Mutations
Chapter 18 Generalized Epilepsy Febrile Seizure Plus (GEFs+)

det.patho: About 80–90% carry a heterozygous loss-of-function SCN1A variant, usually de novo, reducing Nav1.1 sodium channel function mainly in inhibitory interneurons. Loss of inhibition makes the network hyperexcitable, which explains why further sodium channel blockade worsens seizures. Incidence is roughly 1 in 15,000–20,000; a few cases involve PCDH19 or other genes.
det.clinical: The first year features long hemiclonic seizures that switch side, triggered by fever or heat in an infant who is otherwise normal. Between ages 1 and 5 multiple seizure types emerge and development slows, with attention, language and motor problems; ataxia and a crouch gait appear later. Status epilepticus is frequent, and SUDEP risk is among the highest of all epilepsies. Milder SCN1A variants cause GEFS+ in families, a separate, less severe spectrum.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it with two or more prolonged or hemiclonic seizures before 1 year, especially with fever or heat, in a developmentally normal infant with normal MRI. Early EEG is often normal, so a normal early tracing does not rule the diagnosis out. Genetic testing confirms it and should be done early so that harmful drugs are avoided.
det.treatment: Valproate and clobazam are common first choices, with stiripentol, fenfluramine and cannabidiol as approved add-ons; topiramate and ketogenic diet also help. Avoid carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin and lamotrigine. Each family needs a written rescue plan with buccal or intranasal midazolam, temperature control, avoidance of overheating, and SUDEP counselling. Antisense therapies targeting SCN1A expression are in clinical trials.
det.prognosis: Most have lasting intellectual disability and persistent seizures into adulthood; mortality is raised, chiefly from SUDEP and status.
pearls: Prolonged, side-switching febrile hemiclonic seizures in a normal infant: test SCN1A.
Sodium-channel blockers make Dravet worse.
Vaccines do not cause Dravet; they may unmask it via fever.
det.thd: Dravet syndrome เกิดจากยีน SCN1A ผิดปกติ (มักเกิดใหม่ ไม่ได้ถ่ายทอด) ทำให้เซลล์ประสาทยับยั้งทำงานลดลง ทารกที่ปกติดีจะชักนานร่วมกับไข้หรือความร้อนตั้งแต่ขวบปีแรก มักชักครึ่งซีกสลับข้าง ต่อมามีชักหลายแบบและพัฒนาการช้า ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน รักษาด้วย valproate, clobazam, stiripentol, fenfluramine หรือ cannabidiol ห้ามใช้ยากลุ่ม sodium channel blocker เช่น carbamazepine ครอบครัวควรมียาฉุกเฉิน midazolam ติดบ้านและรับคำแนะนำเรื่อง SUDEP

By 18 months she has myoclonic jerks, atypical absences and slowing development. Early EEGs were normal; genetic testing reveals a de novo truncating SCN1A variant.

opts: Valproate
Stiripentol
Fenfluramine
Lamotrigine

qx.why: Prolonged febrile hemiclonic seizures alternating sides in infancy, then myoclonus and developmental slowing with an SCN1A loss-of-function variant, indicate Dravet syndrome. Sodium-channel blockers such as lamotrigine, carbamazepine and phenytoin typically worsen seizures. Valproate, clobazam, stiripentol, fenfluramine and cannabidiol are recommended.

name: Dropped head syndrome
formal: Severe neck extensor weakness with chin-on-chest posture, from myopathy, ALS, myasthenia, parkinsonism or isolated neck extensor myopathy.
simple: The head falls forward because the neck muscles are too weak to hold it up.
th: กล้ามเนื้อเหยียดคออ่อนแรงมากจนคางชิดอก มีหลายสาเหตุ เช่น ALS กล้ามเนื้ออักเสบ myasthenia พาร์กินสัน หรือ isolated neck extensor myopathy
tempoNote: Weeks to months; acute only in some myasthenic or inflammatory cases
feat: Chin falls toward chest when upright, correctable passively unless contracture has formed
Neck pain, difficulty looking ahead, dysphagia from posture
Fatigability, ptosis and diplopia suggest myasthenia; fasciculations and wasting suggest ALS
Antecollis with rigidity suggests MSA or Parkinson disease (dystonic mechanism, not weakness)
inv: CK, AChR and MuSK antibodies, thyroid function
EMG of paraspinal, limb and bulbar muscles; repetitive nerve stimulation
MRI of cervical spine and paraspinal muscles; muscle biopsy if myopathy suspected

case.story: Over three months his head keeps dropping forward; he props his chin with his hand to eat.
case.exam: Neck extension 2/5, flexion 4/5, tongue fasciculations, wasting of first dorsal interossei, brisk reflexes.
case.tests: CK mildly raised; EMG shows active denervation in cervical, thoracic paraspinal and tongue muscles.
case.q: What diagnosis explains the dropped head?
case.a: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with prominent neck extensor weakness.

det.patho: Weakness of cervical paraspinal extensors from muscle, junction or motor neuron disease cannot hold the head against gravity. In parkinsonian syndromes, flexor dystonia or rigidity pulls the head forward. Isolated neck extensor myopathy is an inflammatory or degenerative focal myopathy of older adults.
det.clinical: The key clinical task is to decide between weak extensors and overactive flexors. Associated features point to cause: bulbar and limb signs, fatigability, rash, parkinsonism or isolated findings. Late fixed deformity, neck pain and swallowing problems add disability.
det.diagnosis: Investigation targets the commonest causes: ALS, myasthenia, inflammatory myopathy, isolated neck extensor myopathy, hypothyroidism and parkinsonism. EMG and MRI of paraspinal muscles are particularly useful; biopsy helps in suspected myopathy.
det.treatment: Treat the cause (e.g. immunotherapy for myasthenia or myositis). Supportive care includes neck collars, physiotherapy and swallowing assessment. Botulinum toxin to neck flexors may help selected dystonic antecollis. Surgical fixation is rarely appropriate.
det.prognosis: Depends on aetiology; myasthenic and inflammatory causes can improve, ALS progresses.
pearls: Passive correction test: easily lifted head suggests weakness, resistance suggests dystonia.
Always test for myasthenia; it is treatable.
Neck extensor weakness greater than flexor weakness is classic for ALS and myasthenia.
det.thd: Dropped head syndrome คือกล้ามเนื้อเหยียดคออ่อนแรงจนคางตกชิดอก สาเหตุหลักคือ ALS, myasthenia gravis, กล้ามเนื้ออักเสบ, isolated neck extensor myopathy และ antecollis ในพาร์กินสันหรือ MSA ตรวจ CK แอนติบอดี EMG และ MRI กล้ามเนื้อคอ รักษาตามสาเหตุร่วมกับเฝือกคอและกายภาพ

name: Drug-induced akathisia
formal: Akathisia from drugs like neuroleptics, with subjective inner restlessness and inability to stay still; treat by lowering dose, propranolol or anticholinergics.
simple: Inner restlessness and need to keep moving caused by a medicine.
th: ภาวะกระวนกระวายภายในใจและอยู่นิ่งไม่ได้ที่เกิดจากยา โดยเฉพาะยาต้านโรคจิตและยาแก้อาเจียน
tempoNote: Usually within days to weeks of starting or increasing the drug
feat: Subjective inner restlessness and urge to move, often described as anxiety
Rocking from foot to foot, crossing and uncrossing legs, pacing, unable to sit through an interview
Triggered by antipsychotics (including aripiprazole), metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, SSRIs
Can lead to non-adherence, agitation and increased suicidality
inv: Clinical; Barnes Akathisia Rating Scale for severity
Medication history including recent dose changes and antiemetics

case.who: 26-year-old woman from Ayutthaya started on aripiprazole
case.story: A week after the dose was raised she cannot stop pacing and says she feels like jumping out of her skin.
case.exam: Shifting weight constantly while standing, repeatedly crosses legs when seated; no rigidity or tremor.
case.tests: None needed; Barnes scale moderate.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and first-line management?
case.a: Drug-induced acute akathisia; lower the dose or switch drug, and add propranolol (or mirtazapine or a benzodiazepine).

read.where: 17 - The tardive syndromes: Phenomenology, concepts on pathophysiology and treatment, and other neuroleptic-­induced syndromes

det.patho: Blockade of dopamine D2 receptors in mesocortical and striatal pathways is the main mechanism, with serotonergic and noradrenergic contributions explaining responses to propranolol and mirtazapine. High-potency drugs and rapid titration increase risk.
det.clinical: It is common and frequently mistaken for worsening psychosis or anxiety, which can lead to dose increases that make it worse. Patients feel distressed and may be aggressive or suicidal. Objective movements are mainly lower limb.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, relying on the subjective restlessness plus characteristic movements in a temporal relation to the drug. Rating scales help monitoring. Exclude anxiety, agitation, RLS and drug withdrawal.
det.treatment: Reduce dose, slow titration or switch to a lower-risk agent. Propranolol is first-line, low-dose mirtazapine is an alternative, and benzodiazepines can help short term; anticholinergics are less effective unless parkinsonism coexists. Intravenous antiemetic-induced akathisia is reduced by slow infusion.
det.prognosis: Acute akathisia usually resolves within days to weeks after the drug is reduced or stopped.
pearls: Ask 'Do you feel restless inside?' in anyone on antipsychotics.
Increasing the antipsychotic for 'agitation' can worsen akathisia.
Propranolol is first-line.
det.thd: Drug-induced akathisia คือความรู้สึกกระวนกระวายภายในและอยู่นิ่งไม่ได้จากยา โดยเฉพาะยาต้านโรคจิตและยาแก้อาเจียน ผู้ป่วยเดินไปมา โยกตัว สลับไขว้ขา มักถูกเข้าใจผิดว่าเป็นอาการทางจิตกำเริบ รักษาด้วยการลดหรือเปลี่ยนยา และให้ propranolol หรือ mirtazapine

name: Drug-induced choreas
formal: Chorea caused by medicines such as levodopa, neuroleptics, stimulants, antiepileptics and oral contraceptives; resolves after stopping.
simple: Dance-like involuntary movements caused by a medicine.
th: อาการ chorea ที่เกิดจากยา เช่น levodopa ยาต้านโรคจิต ยากระตุ้น ยากันชัก และยาคุมกำเนิด มักดีขึ้นเมื่อหยุดหรือลดยา

feat: Irregular, flowing, non-rhythmic movements that flit unpredictably between body regions
Clear temporal link to starting, increasing or withdrawing a drug
Common culprits: levodopa and dopamine agonists, antipsychotics (tardive or withdrawal), stimulants (amphetamine, cocaine), phenytoin and other antiseizure drugs, oestrogens, lithium
Often orofacial and limb movements; may coexist with dystonia or tics
Improves after the drug is stopped, except tardive forms which may persist
inv: Careful medication and substance history (including over-the-counter and herbal products)
Drug levels where relevant (phenytoin, lithium); glucose, sodium, calcium, thyroid and liver tests
MRI brain if focal, asymmetric or not resolving; pregnancy test and lupus/antiphospholipid screen in young women on oestrogens

case.who: 34-year-old woman from Lampang on phenytoin for epilepsy
case.story: Over 2 weeks she has developed restless twisting movements of the face and hands; she has also felt unsteady and sleepy.
case.exam: Generalised chorea, horizontal nystagmus and gait ataxia.
case.tests: Serum phenytoin 32 mg/L (toxic); MRI normal.
case.q: What is the cause of her chorea, and what should be done?
case.a: Phenytoin toxicity causing chorea; reduce or switch the drug — movements resolve as levels fall.

det.patho: Most drug-induced chorea reflects relative excess dopaminergic activity in the striatum, from direct stimulation (levodopa, agonists, stimulants) or receptor supersensitivity after blockade (tardive and withdrawal-emergent forms). Antiseizure drugs, lithium and oestrogens act through less clear mechanisms, often unmasking an underlying basal ganglia vulnerability. Previous Sydenham chorea, lupus or structural lesions increase susceptibility.
det.clinical: Levodopa-induced peak-dose chorea is the commonest form in clinical practice and appears in advanced Parkinson disease. Stimulant chorea can be acute and severe ('crack dancing'). Oral contraceptives and pregnancy may provoke chorea in women with previous rheumatic chorea or antiphospholipid antibodies. Withdrawal-emergent dyskinesia occurs in children after abrupt stopping of antipsychotics.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, based on drug timing and resolution after withdrawal. Exclude metabolic causes (hyperglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperthyroidism), autoimmune chorea and genetic disease when the course is atypical. Imaging is needed if chorea is unilateral or persists.
det.treatment: Stop or reduce the offending drug where possible; in Parkinson disease, adjust levodopa dosing or add amantadine. If treatment is needed, VMAT2 inhibitors (tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine, valbenazine) are used, especially for tardive forms. Avoid starting new dopamine blockers when possible because they may worsen tardive syndromes over time.
det.prognosis: Most non-tardive drug-induced chorea resolves within days to weeks of stopping the drug.
pearls: Always review the drug list in new chorea, including phenytoin levels and oral contraceptives.
Chorea in a woman on oestrogens: test for antiphospholipid antibodies and lupus.
Peak-dose levodopa dyskinesia is the commonest drug-induced chorea seen in clinic.
det.thd: Drug-induced chorea คืออาการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติแบบไหลไม่เป็นจังหวะที่เกิดจากยา เช่น levodopa ยาต้านโรคจิต ยากระตุ้น phenytoin ลิเทียม และยาคุมกำเนิด เกิดจากโดพามีนใน striatum ทำงานมากเกินหรือ receptor ไวเกิน วินิจฉัยจากความสัมพันธ์กับการเริ่มยาและหายเมื่อหยุดยา ควรตรวจระดับยาและสาเหตุเมตาบอลิก รักษาโดยหยุดหรือลดยา และใช้ VMAT2 inhibitor ในกรณีจำเป็น

ddx.pt: Insidious progression, family history, cognitive and psychiatric change; CAG expansion in HTT
Child or adolescent after streptococcal infection with carditis or behavioural change
Repetitive stereotyped orobuccolingual movements after long-term dopamine blockade; may worsen on stopping

aN: drug induced chorea | medication induced chorea | iatrogenic chorea | levodopa induced chorea | tardive chorea

name: Drug-induced dystonias
formal: Dystonia from drugs, especially dopamine blockers and antiemetics, as acute reactions or tardive dystonia.
simple: Twisting muscle spasms caused by medicines, especially nausea or psychiatric drugs.
more: Withdraw the offending drug; acute dystonic reactions respond within minutes to anticholinergics such as benztropine. Tardive dystonia may persist and needs switching to clozapine or quetiapine, VMAT2 inhibitors, botulinum toxin or sometimes DBS.
th: Drug-induced dystonia แบ่งเป็นแบบเฉียบพลัน (acute dystonic reaction) ที่เกิดเร็วและตอบสนองต่อ anticholinergic และแบบ tardive ที่เกิดหลังรับยาต้านโดพามีนมานาน อาจกินเวลานานหลายปี ภาวะฉุกเฉินที่พบ ได้แก่ laryngeal dystonia หายใจลำบาก กลืนลำบาก ล้ม กระดูกหัก และ rhabdomyolysis การรักษาคือหยุดหรือเปลี่ยนยา anticholinergic, VMAT2 inhibitor, botulinum toxin และ DBS ในรายรุนแรง
tempoNote: Acute reactions appear within days of exposure and last minutes to hours; tardive dystonia emerges after months to years and may persist for years after the drug is stopped
feat: Acute type: torticollis, trismus, tongue protrusion, oculogyric crisis and opisthotonus soon after a dopamine blocker, especially in young males
Tardive type: persistent cranial, cervical or truncal dystonia (retrocollis, jaw or lingual dystonia, trunk arching) after prolonged exposure, often with other tardive movements

Culprits include antipsychotics, antiemetics (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, domperidone less often), calcium channel blockers (flunarizine, cinnarizine), and some antidepressants and anticonvulsants
Emergency complications: respiratory irregularity or stridor from laryngeal dystonia, dysphagia and aspiration, falls and fractures, inability to eat from jaw dystonia, myoglobinuria
Respiratory dysrhythmia was found in about 7% of patients with tardive syndromes in one series, often unnoticed
inv: Careful drug history including antiemetics and OTC preparations, with timing of dose changes
Airway assessment, oximetry and laryngoscopy if stridor, voice change or breathing irregularity occurs
Swallowing evaluation (videofluoroscopy or FEES) when there is choking or weight loss
Calcium, magnesium, copper studies and brain MRI if features are atypical, onset is young or the course does not fit exposure

case.who: 54-year-old woman with schizophrenia on long-term depot antipsychotic from Nakhon Ratchasima
case.story: For 2 years her neck has pulled backward and her jaw clamps shut during meals; this week she cannot eat solids and has noisy, irregular breathing at night.
case.exam: Retrocollis, jaw-closing and lingual dystonia, mild orobuccal dyskinesia; saturation 94% asleep; weight down 4 kg.
case.tests: Laryngoscopy shows irregular vocal fold movements without a mass; swallow study shows poor bolus transport; copper and MRI normal.
case.q: How does this differ from an acute dystonic reaction, and what are the management options?
case.a: It is tardive dystonia, a persistent syndrome that does not respond reliably to anticholinergics. Where possible reduce the dopamine blocker or move to a safer agent such as clozapine, add VMAT2 inhibitors or botulinum toxin to affected muscles, support nutrition, and consider pallidal DBS if disabling.

read.where: 7. Movement Disorder Emergencies of the Upper Aerodigestive Tract — drug-induced tardive dystonia
17 - The tardive syndromes: Phenomenology, concepts on pathophysiology and treatment, and other neuroleptic-­induced syndromes

det.patho: Acute reactions probably arise from abrupt dopamine receptor blockade with relative cholinergic overactivity. Tardive dystonia is attributed to receptor supersensitivity and maladaptive plasticity in the basal ganglia after chronic blockade, though the mechanism is not settled. Genetic and age factors modify risk, and neuroleptic exposure is not required for all patients with these syndromes.
det.clinical: Acute dystonia is painful and frightening and settles quickly with treatment. Tardive dystonia tends to affect young men more than tardive dyskinesia does, and it often involves the neck and trunk, with retrocollis and arching of the back. Severe jaw or tongue dystonia prevents chewing, and laryngeal involvement can cause stridor or sudden respiratory distress. Other effects are falls, fractures, intractable vomiting from air swallowing, myoglobinuria and suicide risk when the disease is chronic.
det.diagnosis: Link the movement disorder to drug exposure by history, document all dopamine blockers, and examine the larynx and swallowing when there are respiratory or feeding symptoms. Exclude other secondary dystonias such as Wilson's disease, structural lesions, tetanus and hypocalcaemia. Tardive forms can persist after the drug is withdrawn, so a history of exposure alone is enough to explain them only if the timeline fits.
det.treatment: Acute episodes respond to parenteral anticholinergics or diphenhydramine within minutes, followed by a few days of oral cover. Tardive dystonia is harder: reduce or stop the offending drug when psychiatric stability allows, or change to clozapine or another low-risk agent. VMAT2 inhibitors (tetrabenazine, valbenazine, deutetrabenazine) are widely used for tardive syndromes, with evidence strongest for dyskinesia, and anticholinergics, baclofen, benzodiazepines and botulinum toxin help selected patients. Pallidal DBS is a late option. Airway emergencies need intubation or surgical airway while the dystonia is treated.
det.prognosis: Acute reactions are self-limited once treated. Tardive dystonia is often long-lasting and sometimes disabling, though a fraction remit after drug withdrawal.
pearls: Acute dystonia answers to anticholinergics; tardive dystonia often does not.
Think of the larynx when a patient on neuroleptics has unexplained stridor or hypoxia.
Antiemetics are a frequent hidden cause.
det.thd: Drug-induced dystonia มี 2 แบบ แบบเฉียบพลันเกิดภายในไม่กี่วันหลังรับยาต้านโดพามีน ตอบสนองดีต่อ anticholinergic ส่วนแบบ tardive เกิดหลังได้ยานานเป็นเดือนถึงปี มักเป็นที่คอ ขากรรไกร ลิ้น และลำตัว อาจทำให้หายใจผิดปกติ กลืนลำบาก ล้ม กินอาหารไม่ได้ ถ้ารุนแรงต้องดูแลทางเดินหายใจ ลดหรือเปลี่ยนยา ให้ VMAT2 inhibitor, botulinum toxin และ DBS ในรายที่ไม่ตอบสนอง

Sudden onset fixed posture, inconsistency, often after minor injury

aN: acute dystonic reaction | tardive dystonia | neuroleptic induced dystonia | medication induced dystonia

name: Drug-induced movement disorders (DMID)
formal: Movement disorders caused by dopamine receptor blockers and other drugs, including acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
simple: Movement problems such as stiffness, tremor, restlessness and twitching caused by medicines, especially antipsychotics.
more: Diagnosis relies on temporal link with the drug. Reduce or switch the agent; treat with anticholinergics, VMAT2 inhibitors for tardive dyskinesia or clozapine alternative.
th: กลุ่มความผิดปกติของการเคลื่อนไหวที่เกิดจากยา เช่น acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia และ NMS ส่วนใหญ่จากยาต้าน dopamine
tempoNote: Acute (dystonia, NMS), weeks (akathisia, parkinsonism) or months to years (tardive syndromes)
feat: Timing after drug start helps: hours–days (dystonia), days–weeks (akathisia, parkinsonism), months+ (tardive)
Major culprits: antipsychotics, metoclopramide, flunarizine/cinnarizine, valproate, lithium, SSRIs
Drug-induced parkinsonism is often symmetric, with early postural tremor and possible orofacial tremor
NMS: fever, rigidity, altered mental state, autonomic instability, high CK
inv: Detailed medication history including over-the-counter and antiemetics
DaT-SPECT to separate drug-induced from unmasked Parkinson disease when uncertain
CK, renal function and temperature monitoring if NMS suspected

case.story: Taking flunarizine for dizziness for a year; now walks slowly with small steps and both hands tremble.
case.exam: Symmetric bradykinesia and rigidity, postural and rest tremor, subtle perioral tremor.
case.tests: None at first; after stopping flunarizine symptoms improve gradually over 4 months.
case.q: Why is this commonly missed in Thailand?
case.a: Flunarizine and cinnarizine are widely prescribed for dizziness and are calcium channel blockers with D2-blocking effect; they often are not seen as 'antipsychotics'.

read.where: Chapter 37: Botulinum Toxin Use in Movement Disorders and Spasticity

det.patho: Most result from D2 receptor blockade or dopamine depletion in the striatum. Other mechanisms include serotonergic excess, GABA or calcium channel effects and mitochondrial toxicity (valproate). Tardive syndromes reflect long-term receptor supersensitivity and maladaptive plasticity.
det.clinical: The phenotype spans hypokinetic (parkinsonism) and hyperkinetic (dystonia, chorea, akathisia, tics, tremor, myoclonus) disorders. Elderly patients and women are prone to parkinsonism; young men to acute dystonia. Tardive dyskinesia classically involves the mouth, tongue and face.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis depends on temporal association with exposure and improvement after withdrawal, which may take months. DaT imaging is normal in pure drug-induced parkinsonism. Always consider whether an underlying disorder was unmasked.
det.treatment: Withdraw or reduce the offending drug when possible, or switch to lower-risk agents (quetiapine, clozapine). Acute dystonia responds to anticholinergics; akathisia to propranolol; tardive dyskinesia to VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine, tetrabenazine). NMS requires stopping the drug, ICU care, and consideration of dantrolene or bromocriptine.
det.prognosis: Most acute syndromes resolve; drug-induced parkinsonism may take months, and tardive syndromes can be permanent.
pearls: Ask specifically about flunarizine, cinnarizine and metoclopramide.
Persistent parkinsonism after drug withdrawal suggests unmasked Parkinson disease.
Anticholinergics can worsen tardive dyskinesia.
det.thd: DMID คือความผิดปกติของการเคลื่อนไหวจากยา ส่วนใหญ่จากยาต้าน dopamine รวมถึง flunarizine และ metoclopramide ที่ใช้บ่อยในไทย มีทั้ง acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia และ NMS ระยะเวลาหลังเริ่มยาช่วยบอกชนิด วินิจฉัยจากประวัติยาและการดีขึ้นหลังหยุดยา รักษาด้วยการหยุดหรือเปลี่ยนยาและยาเฉพาะแต่ละชนิด

name: Drug-induced myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus from drugs including opioids, antidepressants, lithium, antibiotics and levodopa, usually reversible after stopping.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks caused by a medicine.
th: การกระตุกเร็วของกล้ามเนื้อที่เกิดจากยา เช่น opioid ยาต้านซึมเศร้า lithium ยาปฏิชีวนะ และ gabapentinoid มักหายเมื่อหยุดยา
tempoNote: Appears within days of starting, raising the dose, or drug accumulation in renal failure
feat: Multifocal irregular jerks at rest or with action, often with confusion
Common culprits: opioids (especially morphine in renal failure), gabapentin/pregabalin, cefepime, lithium, SSRIs, tramadol
Serotonin toxicity: inducible clonus and hyperreflexia, worse in legs
Renal or hepatic failure increases drug levels and risk
inv: Renal and liver function, electrolytes, glucose; drug levels such as lithium
EEG to exclude non-convulsive status (e.g. cefepime neurotoxicity)

case.who: 68-year-old man from Nonthaburi with CKD stage 4
case.story: Started on pregabalin for shingles pain; within four days he became drowsy with jerking arms and dropping objects.
case.exam: Multifocal action myoclonus, asterixis, mild confusion, no focal signs.
case.tests: eGFR 18; electrolytes normal; EEG diffuse slowing without seizures.
case.q: What caused the myoclonus and what is the fix?
case.a: Pregabalin accumulation in renal failure; stop or reduce the drug and the jerks resolve.

det.patho: Drugs cause myoclonus by increasing cortical excitability, enhancing serotonergic transmission, blocking GABA receptors (beta-lactams) or through toxic metabolites (morphine-3-glucuronide). Organ failure reduces clearance.
det.clinical: Myoclonus is often multifocal and accompanied by encephalopathy. It may be mild and unnoticed or severe enough to impair function. Serotonin toxicity and cefepime neurotoxicity are important severe causes.
det.diagnosis: Link onset to drug exposure, check organ function and levels, and exclude metabolic, hypoxic or infectious causes. EEG helps when consciousness is impaired.
det.treatment: Stop or reduce the drug; adjust dosing for renal function. Opioid rotation helps opioid-induced myoclonus. Clonazepam or levetiracetam can be used short term if jerks are disabling. Dialysis may be needed for lithium or cefepime toxicity.
det.prognosis: Usually fully reversible after drug withdrawal.
pearls: New myoclonus in a renal patient: review gabapentinoids, opioids and antibiotics first.
Cefepime neurotoxicity can cause non-convulsive status.
Inducible clonus plus serotonergic drugs: think serotonin syndrome.
det.thd: Drug-induced myoclonus คือการกระตุกของกล้ามเนื้อจากยา เช่น opioid, gabapentin, pregabalin, cefepime, lithium และยาต้านซึมเศร้า โดยเฉพาะในผู้ป่วยไตวายที่ยาสะสม มักมีสับสนร่วม ตรวจการทำงานของไต ระดับยา และ EEG รักษาด้วยการหยุดหรือปรับยา ส่วนใหญ่หายได้

name: Drug-induced parkinsonism (DIP)
formal: Parkinsonism from dopamine receptor blockers such as antipsychotics and metoclopramide, typically symmetric with bradykinesia and rigidity; usually resolves after stopping.
simple: Parkinson-like stiffness and slowness caused by certain medicines.
th: พาร์กินสันที่เกิดจากยา เช่น ยาต้านโรคจิต metoclopramide flunarizine มักเป็นสองข้าง หายได้หลังหยุดยาแต่ใช้เวลาเป็นเดือน
tempoNote: Develops over weeks to a few months after starting or increasing the drug; resolves over weeks to months (sometimes up to a year) after stopping
feat: Bradykinesia and rigidity, often fairly symmetric, on a dopamine-blocking or dopamine-depleting drug
Postural/action tremor more than rest tremor; perioral 'rabbit' tremor is a clue
May coexist with akathisia or orofacial dyskinesia
Few non-motor prodromal features (normal smell, no REM sleep behaviour disorder)
inv: Medication review: antipsychotics, metoclopramide, flunarizine/cinnarizine, valproate, reserpine, tetrabenazine, lithium, amiodarone
DAT-SPECT normal in pure DIP; abnormal if underlying PD has been unmasked
Smell test can support unmasked PD if impaired

case.story: Taking flunarizine for 'vertigo' for 9 months from a private clinic; over 3 months he walks slowly and his voice softened.
case.exam: Symmetric bradykinesia and rigidity, mild postural tremor of both hands, reduced arm swing bilaterally, no gaze palsy.
case.tests: Routine blood tests normal; DAT-SPECT not available.
case.q: What should be done first, and when would you investigate for Parkinson disease?
case.a: Drug-induced parkinsonism from flunarizine: stop it and review over 3–6 months; if signs persist or progress beyond that, suspect unmasked PD and consider DAT imaging or a levodopa trial.

read.where: Chapter 9 Atypical parkinsonism, parkinsonism-plus syndromes and secondary parkinsonian disorders

det.patho: Drugs that block striatal D2 receptors (typical and some atypical antipsychotics, antiemetics such as metoclopramide, the calcium-channel blockers flunarizine and cinnarizine) or deplete presynaptic dopamine (tetrabenazine, reserpine) reduce dopaminergic signalling. Risk rises with age, female sex, higher dose and pre-existing subclinical nigrostriatal loss. It is the commonest cause of secondary parkinsonism.
det.clinical: Symptoms often appear within three months of starting the drug and can be indistinguishable from PD, including asymmetry in some cases. Gait slowing and falls are common in older people and may be blamed on age. Some patients have a latent degenerative process; their signs improve on withdrawal then return later as PD.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is made by temporal association and resolution after withdrawal, which may take many months. A normal DAT scan supports pure DIP; an abnormal scan suggests unmasked degeneration. Remember that many patients do not report over-the-counter or clinic-dispensed drugs such as flunarizine or prochlorperazine.
det.treatment: Stop or reduce the causative drug where possible, or switch to an antipsychotic with lower D2 affinity (quetiapine or clozapine). Anticholinergics or amantadine can help while waiting, though anticholinergics are poorly tolerated in the elderly. Levodopa is reserved for disabling or persistent cases. Educate patients and prescribers to avoid re-exposure.
det.prognosis: Most recover within months of drug withdrawal; persistent or progressive signs after 6–12 months suggest underlying PD.
pearls: Ask specifically about flunarizine, cinnarizine and metoclopramide — common in Thai practice.
Recovery can lag drug withdrawal by months; do not label PD too early.
Normal DAT-SPECT favours pure drug-induced parkinsonism.
det.thd: Drug-induced parkinsonism เกิดจากยาที่ปิดกั้นหรือทำให้โดปามีนลดลง เช่น ยาต้านโรคจิต metoclopramide flunarizine ผู้ป่วยมีอาการเคลื่อนไหวช้า แข็งเกร็ง มือสั่น มักเป็นสองข้าง เกิดหลังเริ่มยาไม่กี่เดือน วินิจฉัยจากประวัติยา การรักษาคือหยุดหรือเปลี่ยนยา อาการอาจใช้เวลาหลายเดือนกว่าจะหาย ถ้ายังไม่หายควรคิดถึง Parkinson disease ที่ซ่อนอยู่

qx.stem: A 76-year-old woman from Ratchaburi has become slow, stooped and quiet over four months, with a symmetric postural and rest tremor. A village clinic gave her flunarizine for dizziness eight months ago, and she also takes domperidone and omeprazole. There is no family history, smell is normal, and MRI is unremarkable.
qx.q: What should be done next?
opts: Start levodopa and continue all current drugs
Stop flunarizine and review over several months; consider DaT-SPECT if parkinsonism persists
Diagnose PD and refer for DBS evaluation
Start a VMAT2 inhibitor
Add trihexyphenidyl as first-line therapy in this age group
qx.why: Subacute symmetric parkinsonism after starting a calcium-channel blocker with D2-blocking activity, common in Thai primary care, is typical of drug-induced parkinsonism. The culprit should be withdrawn; recovery may take months, and persistent signs suggest underlying PD unmasked by the drug, for which DaT-SPECT is helpful (normal in pure DIP). VMAT2 inhibitors would worsen parkinsonism, and anticholinergics are poorly tolerated in older people.

ddx.pt: Asymmetric onset, rest tremor, hyposmia, RBD; DAT-SPECT abnormal; no causative drug
Lower-body predominant, shuffling gait, pyramidal signs, white-matter disease on MRI
Action tremor without bradykinesia or rigidity, long history and family history

aN: dip | drug induced parkinsonism | neuroleptic induced parkinsonism | secondary parkinsonism drug | pseudoparkinsonism

name: Drug-induced restlessness
formal: Akathisia-like inner restlessness due to a medication such as antipsychotics or SSRIs.
simple: A feeling of restlessness caused by a medicine.
th: ความรู้สึกกระสับกระส่ายอยู่นิ่งไม่ได้คล้าย akathisia ที่เกิดจากยา เช่น ยาต้านโรคจิต SSRIs และยาแก้อาเจียน
tempoNote: Begins within days to weeks of starting or increasing a drug
feat: Subjective inner tension with an urge to keep moving
Pacing, fidgeting, shifting weight while standing
Culprits: antipsychotics, metoclopramide, SSRIs and SNRIs, calcium channel blocking antivertigo drugs
Often misread as anxiety or psychotic agitation
inv: Clinical; medication timeline and dose changes
Ferritin and iron studies if leg-predominant and evening-related (to consider RLS)

case.story: Started fluoxetine for depression; after ten days she feels unable to sit still and cannot sleep.
case.exam: Fidgeting constantly, crossing and uncrossing legs, otherwise normal.
case.tests: Ferritin normal.
case.q: What is the likely cause and management?
case.a: SSRI-induced akathisia-like restlessness; lower dose or switch, consider propranolol, and monitor mood and suicidality.

det.patho: Most cases reflect dopamine D2 blockade or serotonergic inhibition of dopaminergic neurons, reducing striatal and mesocortical dopamine signalling. Individual susceptibility varies and rapid dose escalation increases risk.
det.clinical: This is essentially akathisia from medication. Patients describe distress rather than a specific movement, and objective restlessness may be subtle. It can worsen psychiatric symptoms and adherence, and may raise suicidal risk with antidepressants.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical: temporal link to a drug, typical subjective restlessness and improvement after reduction. Distinguish from anxiety, mania, RLS, withdrawal states and hyperthyroidism.
det.treatment: Reduce or stop the drug, or switch. Propranolol is first line; mirtazapine (low dose) or a short course of benzodiazepine are alternatives. Review all medications for combined effects.
det.prognosis: Generally resolves within days to weeks after adjusting the drug.
pearls: SSRIs, not only antipsychotics, can cause akathisia.
Do not treat drug-induced restlessness by escalating the culprit.
Ask about suicidal thoughts in restless patients on antidepressants.

det.patho: Tic generation involves cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loops in which excess dopaminergic drive lowers the threshold for released movements. Stimulants and levodopa raise synaptic dopamine, whereas long dopamine-receptor blockade can cause receptor hypersensitivity and so tardive tics. How anticonvulsants such as lamotrigine provoke tics is unclear; some patients may carry a latent predisposition that the drug unmasks.
det.clinical: Motor and vocal tics are sudden, brief and stereotyped, and they look the same as in primary tic disorders. The tell is timing: onset follows a new agent or a dose change, often in an adult with no tic history. Tardive tourettism is seen after prolonged exposure to dopamine blockers and may come with other tardive phenomena. Many children with ADHD and tics tolerate stimulants without worsening, so a tic disorder alone is not an absolute bar to treatment.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on a careful chronology and exclusion of other causes rather than a test. Ask about prescription, over-the-counter and recreational substances, and about childhood tics, which are often forgotten. Adult-onset tics with additional signs such as chorea, cognitive decline or oral self-injury call for evaluation for Huntington disease and neuroacanthocytosis. Resolution after dechallenge, followed for several weeks to months, confirms the link; persistence suggests a primary disorder that was unmasked or a tardive process.
det.treatment: Stop or lower the offending drug when the underlying indication allows, or switch to an alternative with a lower tic liability. If tics are bothersome and persist, comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics is first choice, with alpha-2 agonists such as clonidine or guanfacine as pharmacological options. Tardive tics may respond to VMAT2 inhibitors, and the need for any continuing antipsychotic should be reviewed. Explain that this is a drug reaction and not a psychiatric disorder.
det.prognosis: Most stimulant- or anticonvulsant-related tics settle within weeks to months of withdrawal. Tardive forms can persist for years, and some patients turn out to have a primary tic disorder.
pearls: New tics in an adult: list every drug before labelling it Tourette.
Stimulants usually do not worsen tics in children with ADHD, so avoid reflex discontinuation.
Tardive tics follow dopamine blockers and may coexist with akathisia or orofacial dyskinesia.

det.patho: Most drugs enhance physiological tremor by increasing beta-adrenergic or peripheral muscle spindle sensitivity; others affect cerebellar function (lithium toxicity) or dopamine signalling (parkinsonism). Dose and individual susceptibility matter.
det.clinical: Tremor typically begins soon after starting or increasing a drug and is symmetric. Asymmetry, rest tremor or other neurological signs should prompt consideration of an unmasked or separate disorder. Severity often tracks dose.
det.diagnosis: Criteria include exclusion of other medical causes, temporal relation to the drug and dose-response. Check drug levels and thyroid status. Persistence after withdrawal suggests an underlying tremor disorder.
det.treatment: Lower the dose, use extended-release forms or switch drugs. If the drug must continue, propranolol or primidone can reduce tremor. Avoid caffeine and treat coexisting thyroid disease.
det.prognosis: Usually resolves or improves after dose reduction or withdrawal.
pearls: Valproate and lithium are the commonest culprits in neurology and psychiatry.
New coarse tremor with ataxia on lithium: check for toxicity.
Tremor that persists after withdrawal suggests essential tremor or PD unmasked.

19: A Quick Glance at the Therapeutic Approaches for Neuromuscular Disorders
Chapter 17: Dystrophinopathies: Duchenne and Becker Muscular Dystrophies

det.patho: Dystrophin connects the internal actin cytoskeleton to the dystroglycan complex in the sarcolemma. Out-of-frame deletions abolish the protein, causing DMD, while in-frame deletions allow a shortened partly functional protein and BMD (the reading-frame rule, with exceptions). Without dystrophin, the membrane tears with contraction, causing calcium influx, necrosis and replacement by fat and fibrosis. The gene is on Xp21, and about one third of cases are new mutations.
det.clinical: DMD presents in early childhood with delayed walking, frequent falls and a Gowers sign; without treatment walking is lost around age 10–12, followed by scoliosis, respiratory failure and cardiomyopathy. BMD presents later and more variably, from cramps with high CK to limb-girdle weakness in adulthood, and cardiomyopathy can outpace limb weakness. Female carriers may have mild weakness or cardiomyopathy. Cognitive and behavioural issues (ADHD, autism, learning problems) occur in some boys with DMD.
det.diagnosis: A very high CK in a weak boy is the key clue; raised transaminases are muscle-derived. MLPA detects deletions or duplications in most, and sequencing finds point mutations in the rest. Biopsy is reserved for unclear genetic findings. All patients need baseline cardiac and respiratory assessment, and mothers should be offered carrier testing.
det.treatment: Glucocorticoids are standard from about age 4–5 to prolong walking and preserve lung function, with attention to bone health, growth and weight. Exon-skipping antisense drugs and microdystrophin gene therapy are approved in some countries for specific genotypes, and givinostat is approved in some regions; access in Thailand is limited. Early ACE inhibitors or ARBs, mineralocorticoid antagonists for cardiomyopathy, non-invasive ventilation, cough assistance, scoliosis surgery and multidisciplinary care extend survival. Avoid suxamethonium and volatile anaesthetics in DMD because of rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalaemia risk.
det.prognosis: With modern care, many men with DMD live into their 30s or beyond; BMD life expectancy is often into middle age, largely determined by heart disease.
pearls: Unexplained raised ALT/AST in a boy: check CK.
Reading-frame rule predicts DMD versus BMD in most cases.
Screen the heart in carriers and in BMD even with mild limb weakness.

det.patho: DMD is X-linked and caused by mutations (mostly deletions) in the dystrophin gene that disrupt the reading frame and abolish dystrophin expression. Without dystrophin the sarcolemma is fragile during contraction, leading to repeated fibre necrosis, inflammation, failed regeneration and replacement by fat and fibrous tissue. It affects about 1 in 3,500–5,000 male births, and about a third of cases arise from new mutations.
det.clinical: Boys show delayed walking and speech, frequent falls, toe walking, Gowers manoeuvre and calf pseudohypertrophy between 2 and 5 years. Without treatment, walking is lost around age 10–12, followed by scoliosis, respiratory failure and dilated cardiomyopathy. Learning difficulties, ADHD and autism spectrum features are more common. Female carriers can have cardiomyopathy or mild weakness.
det.diagnosis: A very high CK (often 50–100 times normal) is the first clue. Genetic testing with MLPA for deletions and duplications, followed by sequencing if negative, confirms the diagnosis and identifies eligibility for mutation-specific therapies. Muscle biopsy is now only needed if genetics is inconclusive. Baseline cardiac, respiratory and bone health assessments are required.
det.treatment: Daily corticosteroids (prednisone or deflazacort; vamorolone as an alternative with fewer growth and bone effects) are standard from early childhood and prolong walking. Exon-skipping antisense drugs are approved in some countries for eligible deletions, and givinostat is approved in some regions. An AAV micro-dystrophin gene therapy is licensed in some countries with restrictions after serious liver-related safety events. Multidisciplinary care includes cardioprotection with ACE inhibitors, non-invasive ventilation, scoliosis surgery, bone health and stress-dose steroid awareness.
det.prognosis: With modern multidisciplinary care, survival commonly extends into the 30s and beyond; cardiac and respiratory failure are the main causes of death.
pearls: A very high ALT/AST in a young boy may come from muscle — check CK before investigating the liver.
Avoid suxamethonium and volatile anaesthetics because of rhabdomyolysis/hyperkalaemia risk.
Reading frame, not deletion size, predicts Duchenne versus Becker.

det.patho: DNETs are WHO grade 1 glioneuronal tumours arising in cortex, thought to have developmental origins and often associated with adjacent focal cortical dysplasia. Most carry FGFR1 alterations. They are a leading tumour cause of chronic focal epilepsy in children and young adults.
det.clinical: The typical patient has years of focal seizures, often with an aura, and normal neurology. Seizures may be frequent and refractory to medication. Rarely, DNETs change in size or appearance on follow-up, and atypical cases need review to exclude other low-grade tumours.
det.diagnosis: MRI is highly suggestive: a well-demarcated cortical lesion with cystic appearance, high T2 signal, a bright FLAIR rim and little enhancement. Video-EEG and sometimes functional imaging confirm that the lesion drives seizures. Diagnosis is confirmed histologically.
det.treatment: Early surgical resection is recommended for drug-resistant seizures, with complete removal of the lesion and associated dysplastic cortex giving the best results. Chemotherapy and radiotherapy are not needed. Antiseizure drugs may be withdrawn gradually after a seizure-free period post-surgery.
det.prognosis: Excellent: 80–90% become seizure-free after complete resection, and recurrence is rare.
pearls: Bubbly cortical temporal lesion + years of drug-resistant seizures in a young person: DNET.
Early surgery improves both seizure and developmental outcomes.
No oedema or mass effect despite a sizeable lesion.
