name: Dysexecutive syndrome
formal: Frontal-subcortical cognitive syndrome with impaired planning, set shifting, inhibition and working memory, causing poor judgement and behavioural change; seen after frontal lesions, trauma or in neurodegeneration.
simple: Difficulty planning, organising, solving problems and controlling behaviour because of frontal lobe problems.
more: Assessed with the frontal assessment battery and trail making. Treat the cause and use cognitive rehabilitation; response to drugs is limited.
th: ภาวะที่การวางแผน การยับยั้ง การเปลี่ยนความคิด และความจำใช้งานบกพร่อง ทำให้ตัดสินใจและควบคุมพฤติกรรมไม่ดี พบหลังรอยโรคสมองส่วนหน้าหรือในโรคสมองเสื่อม
tempoNote: Acute after stroke or head injury; insidious in neurodegenerative and small vessel disease
feat: Trouble planning, organising, multitasking and adapting to change
Impulsivity or poor inhibition alongside apathy
Perseveration and concrete thinking
Reduced insight; family reports more problems than the patient
Seen after frontal injury and in small vessel disease, Parkinson disease, Huntington disease, bvFTD and PSP
inv: Frontal Assessment Battery, trail making A/B, letter fluency, clock drawing
MRI brain for frontal lesions, white-matter disease, atrophy or hydrocephalus
Neuropsychological assessment including ecological tests of daily function

case.story: Over three years he has become slow, indecisive and unable to manage the rice farm accounts, though he remembers recent events.
case.exam: Slowed thinking, poor letter fluency, fails trail making B; short-stepped gait; brisk reflexes.
case.tests: MRI shows confluent periventricular white-matter hyperintensities and lacunes.
case.q: What cognitive pattern is this and what is the likely cause?
case.a: Dysexecutive syndrome from subcortical small vessel disease (vascular cognitive impairment); control vascular risk and use rehabilitation strategies.

read.where: Chapter 11 Cognitive Impairment and Dementia — Executive Function

det.patho: Executive functions depend on frontal-subcortical loops linking prefrontal cortex with striatum, pallidum and thalamus, plus long white-matter tracts. Disruption anywhere in these networks — focal lesions or diffuse white-matter injury — yields the syndrome. That is why small vessel disease, basal ganglia degenerations and traumatic axonal injury produce executive deficits as readily as frontal cortical lesions.
det.clinical: Patients struggle with novel or complex tasks, show poor judgement and planning, and may be either apathetic or impulsive. Memory complaints often reflect poor retrieval and organisation rather than true storage failure, so cueing helps. Insight is frequently limited, which affects driving, finances and adherence. It is the dominant cognitive profile of vascular cognitive impairment and of subcortical dementias.
det.diagnosis: It is a descriptive syndrome; identify it with executive tests and then search for the cause. MMSE is insensitive, while MoCA and FAB detect executive impairment better. MRI clarifies vascular, traumatic, neoplastic or degenerative causes.
det.treatment: Address the cause and vascular risk factors. Rehabilitation uses goal management training, external aids, routines and environmental structuring. Drug benefit is limited; cholinesterase inhibitors may help in Parkinson disease dementia or Lewy body disease, and treating depression or sleep apnoea can improve executive performance.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause; static lesions may plateau or improve, degenerative causes progress.
pearls: Executive impairment often matters more for independence than memory loss.
Retrieval memory problems improve with cues; hippocampal amnesia does not.
Use FAB or trail making — MMSE misses it.
det.thd: Dysexecutive syndrome คือภาวะที่ความสามารถวางแผน ตัดสินใจ ยับยั้งตนเอง และปรับเปลี่ยนความคิดบกพร่อง เกิดได้ทั้งจากรอยโรคสมองส่วนหน้าและวงจรใต้เปลือกสมอง เช่น โรคหลอดเลือดสมองขนาดเล็ก พาร์กินสัน หรือการบาดเจ็บศีรษะ ตรวจด้วย FAB, trail making และ fluency การรักษาคือแก้สาเหตุ ควบคุมความเสี่ยงหลอดเลือด และฟื้นฟูด้วยการจัดระบบชีวิตประจำวัน

ddx.pt: Common cause of dysexecutive decline with stepwise or slowly progressive course and MRI vascular burden
Early disinhibition, loss of empathy and dietary change with frontal-temporal atrophy
Gait disturbance and urinary urgency with ventriculomegaly

name: Dysferlinopathy (LGMD R2/2B)
formal: Autosomal recessive limb-girdle or distal (Miyoshi) myopathy from dysferlin mutations, with young-adult onset, very high CK, calf atrophy and inflammatory-looking biopsies.
simple: An inherited muscle disease starting in young adults that weakens the hip, shoulder or calf muscles slowly over time.
th: กล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมแบบด้อยจากยีน dysferlin เริ่มในวัยหนุ่มสาว อ่อนแรงน่องหรือต้นขา CK สูงมาก บางครั้งวินิจฉัยผิดเป็น polymyositis
tempoNote: Onset late teens to early 30s after normal or even athletic childhood; slowly progressive
feat: Young adult onset, often in previously sporty people
Distal Miyoshi pattern (calf, cannot tiptoe) or proximal limb-girdle pattern
CK extremely high (10–100 times normal)
Calf atrophy; biopsy may show inflammatory cells, mimicking myositis
Cardiac and respiratory involvement uncommon
inv: CK; EMG myopathic
Muscle MRI: posterior calf and thigh involvement
Dysferlin absent on biopsy or reduced in blood monocytes
DYSF genetic testing

case.story: Over 2 years, cannot rise onto his toes and has lost speed; was treated with prednisolone for 'polymyositis' without benefit.
case.exam: Thin calves, cannot walk on toes, mild hip extensor weakness, normal arms, ankle reflexes absent.
case.tests: CK 12,000 U/L; MRI shows fatty change of gastrocnemius and soleus; biopsy absent dysferlin; DYSF biallelic variants.
case.q: Why did steroids fail?
case.a: This is dysferlinopathy (Miyoshi pattern), a genetic dystrophy; inflammatory cells on biopsy are secondary and steroids are ineffective.

read.where: Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Muscular Dystrophies

det.patho: Dysferlin is a calcium-sensitive protein that helps patch the sarcolemma after injury by fusing repair vesicles. Without it, small membrane tears accumulate, leading to necrosis and inflammation. The disorder is autosomal recessive, with founder variants in some populations.
det.clinical: Symptoms typically begin between 15 and 30 years in previously strong individuals. Two main patterns exist: distal calf weakness (Miyoshi) and proximal girdle weakness, which may coexist or evolve into each other. Progression is slow, with many losing walking after 10–30 years. Hearts and breathing are usually spared.
det.diagnosis: Extremely high CK with a calf-predominant MRI pattern strongly suggests the diagnosis. Absent dysferlin on immunohistochemistry or western blot supports it; blood monocyte assays are a less invasive option. Genetic testing confirms. Inflammatory infiltrates on biopsy frequently lead to a mistaken diagnosis of myositis.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying therapy. Steroids are ineffective and may worsen strength. Physiotherapy, avoidance of extreme eccentric exercise, ankle-foot orthoses and assistive devices maintain function. Gene therapy research is ongoing.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; life expectancy normal or near normal.
pearls: Young athlete with very high CK and calf weakness: think dysferlin.
Steroid-resistant 'polymyositis' in a young adult deserves a dystrophy work-up.
Monocyte dysferlin testing can avoid muscle biopsy.
det.thd: Dysferlinopathy เป็นกล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมแบบด้อยจากยีน DYSF ทำให้การซ่อมแซมผนังเซลล์กล้ามเนื้อบกพร่อง มักเริ่มในวัยหนุ่มสาวที่เคยแข็งแรง อ่อนแรงที่น่อง (Miyoshi) หรือต้นขา CK สูงมาก และมักวินิจฉัยผิดเป็น polymyositis ยืนยันด้วยการย้อม dysferlin และตรวจยีน steroid ไม่ได้ผล การรักษาเป็นกายภาพบำบัดและอุปกรณ์ช่วย

ddx.pt: Usually older onset, proximal arms involved, responds to immunotherapy
Similar calf pattern but often asymmetric and normal dysferlin
Calf hypertrophy rather than atrophy, cardiomyopathy, abnormal dystrophin

name: Dyskinesia
formal: Involuntary, excessive, purposeless movements, including chorea, athetosis and stereotypies, seen as levodopa-induced or tardive syndromes and reflecting basal ganglia dysfunction.
simple: Unwanted, uncontrolled twisting or jerking movements, often caused by long-term medicines for Parkinson disease or psychiatric illness.
more: Treatment depends on cause; levodopa-induced dyskinesia is managed by amantadine, dose fractionation or DBS, while tardive dyskinesia is managed with VMAT2 inhibitors. Examine for peak-dose pattern versus biphasic pattern in Parkinson disease.
th: คำรวมเรียกการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติที่เกินและไร้จุดหมาย เช่น chorea athetosis stereotypy มักพบจาก levodopa หรือ tardive dyskinesia
tempoNote: Depends on cause: fluctuating with doses in PD, persistent in tardive dyskinesia, paroxysmal in channelopathies
feat: Involuntary, non-rhythmic, flowing or writhing movements of face, trunk or limbs
Levodopa-related forms: peak-dose chorea, diphasic leg movements, off dystonia
Tardive dyskinesia: orofacial-lingual chewing and tongue movements after dopamine blockers
Paroxysmal dyskinesias occur in brief attacks with normal intervals
inv: Video recording and medication timing
MRI, metabolic and genetic tests if no drug cause is clear

case.who: 60-year-old woman from Saraburi with Parkinson disease for 8 years
case.story: Her body sways and her head bobs about an hour after each levodopa dose, when she otherwise moves best.
case.exam: Choreic movements of trunk and neck at peak dose, rigid and slow before the next dose.
case.tests: Diary links movements to peak levodopa effect.
case.q: What type of dyskinesia is this and how is it managed?
case.a: Peak-dose levodopa-induced dyskinesia; smaller, more frequent doses, amantadine, and DBS if disabling.

read.where: Chapter 9 Movement Disorders — Medical Treatment of Parkinson’s Disease
6 - Medical treatment of the motor features of Parkinson disease

det.patho: Dyskinesias reflect reduced activity in the indirect pathway output and abnormal firing patterns in the basal ganglia, leading to disinhibited thalamocortical drive. Causes include dopaminergic drugs, dopamine receptor supersensitivity, structural, metabolic, autoimmune and genetic disease.
det.clinical: Dyskinesia is a descriptive umbrella rather than a disease. The task is to classify the movement (chorea, athetosis, dystonia, stereotypy, ballism) and its timing, then search for the cause. Patients may be unaware of their movements, especially in tardive dyskinesia.
det.diagnosis: Classify phenomenology with video, record timing relative to drugs and look for associated signs. Investigations follow the pattern: drug history, MRI, glucose, thyroid, autoimmune and genetic testing where appropriate.
det.treatment: Treatment depends on cause. Levodopa-induced dyskinesia: dose adjustment, amantadine, continuous delivery therapies or DBS. Tardive dyskinesia: VMAT2 inhibitors and review of antipsychotic. Paroxysmal dyskinesias may respond to carbamazepine (PKD).
det.prognosis: Varies by cause; drug-related forms often improve with treatment changes but tardive dyskinesia can persist.
pearls: Name the movement precisely before choosing a treatment.
Dyskinesia may bother carers more than the patient.
Anticholinergics can worsen tardive and choreic dyskinesia.
det.thd: Dyskinesia เป็นคำรวมสำหรับการเคลื่อนไหวเกินที่ไม่ตั้งใจ เช่น chorea athetosis และ stereotypy พบบ่อยจาก levodopa ในผู้ป่วยพาร์กินสัน และ tardive dyskinesia จากยาต้าน dopamine ต้องระบุชนิดของการเคลื่อนไหวและเวลาเกิดเทียบกับยา แล้วรักษาตามสาเหตุ เช่น ปรับยา amantadine, VMAT2 inhibitor หรือ DBS

name: Dysmyelinating diseases
formal: Inherited disorders of myelin formation or maintenance, such as metachromatic leukodystrophy, adrenoleukodystrophy and Pelizaeus-Merzbacher, producing progressive motor and cognitive decline with white matter change.
simple: Genetic diseases in which the protective coating of nerve fibres forms badly or breaks down, causing progressive weakness and developmental loss.
more: MRI shows symmetrical white matter signal change; enzyme assays and gene tests identify the type. Stem cell transplant or gene therapy helps some; most care is supportive.
th: กลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่สร้างหรือรักษาไมอีลินผิดปกติ เช่น MLD, ALD, Pelizaeus–Merzbacher ทำให้การเคลื่อนไหวและสติปัญญาถดถอยร่วมกับเนื้อขาวผิดปกติ
tempoNote: Infantile to adult onset; usually progressive, hypomyelinating forms may be slowly progressive or static
feat: Developmental regression or failure to achieve milestones, spasticity and ataxia
Cognitive and behavioural decline, sometimes psychiatric presentation in adults
Peripheral neuropathy in MLD and Krabbe; adrenal failure in ALD; nystagmus in PMD
Symmetric white matter change on MRI
inv: MRI pattern recognition (frontal vs posterior predominance, hypomyelination, U-fibres)
Arylsulfatase A, galactocerebrosidase, very long chain fatty acids, urine sulfatides
Gene panels or exome sequencing

case.story: Walked at 15 months, but over the past six months falls frequently, now cannot walk unaided and speech has regressed.
case.exam: Spastic legs with absent ankle jerks, ataxia, irritability.
case.tests: MRI symmetric periventricular white matter T2 signal with tigroid pattern; NCS slowed; arylsulfatase A low.
case.q: Which disorder fits and why does the combination of upper and lower motor signs matter?
case.a: Late-infantile metachromatic leukodystrophy; central and peripheral myelin are both affected, a clue to MLD or Krabbe.

det.patho: Dysmyelination means myelin is never formed normally or is unstable because of genetic defects in myelin proteins, lipid metabolism or peroxisomal function. This differs from demyelination, where normal myelin is destroyed by an acquired process such as inflammation.
det.clinical: Presentation varies by disorder and age: infants show regression and spasticity, children decline in motor and school performance, and adults may present with psychiatric or cognitive change and gait disorder. Peripheral nerve and endocrine features help.
det.diagnosis: MRI pattern recognition guides targeted biochemical tests, then genetic confirmation. Many conditions are now diagnosed by exome or genome sequencing. Newborn screening exists for some (e.g. X-ALD, Krabbe in some regions).
det.treatment: Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation helps selected presymptomatic or early patients with ALD, MLD and Krabbe. Gene therapies are approved for early MLD (atidarsagene autotemcel) and cerebral ALD (elivaldogene autotemcel) in some countries. Otherwise care is supportive: spasticity management, seizure control, nutrition and family support.
det.prognosis: Generally progressive with reduced life expectancy; outcomes are better when treated before symptoms.
pearls: Dysmyelination is inherited and defective; demyelination is acquired destruction.
Central plus peripheral demyelination: think MLD or Krabbe.
Early diagnosis matters because transplant and gene therapy work best before symptoms.
det.thd: Dysmyelinating diseases คือกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่สร้างไมอีลินไม่ปกติหรือไม่คงทน เช่น MLD, ALD และ Pelizaeus–Merzbacher ต่างจาก demyelination ที่ไมอีลินปกติถูกทำลายภายหลัง ผู้ป่วยมีพัฒนาการถดถอย เกร็ง เดินเซ และ MRI มีเนื้อขาวผิดปกติแบบสมมาตร ตรวจเอนไซม์และยีนเพื่อยืนยัน บางโรครักษาได้ด้วยการปลูกถ่ายไขกระดูกหรือยีนบำบัดหากวินิจฉัยเร็ว

name: Dystonia
formal: Movement disorder of sustained or intermittent muscle contractions causing twisting, repetitive movements or abnormal postures, arising from basal ganglia and cerebello-thalamic network dysfunction.
simple: A condition where muscles tighten on their own and twist the body into abnormal, sometimes painful, positions.
more: Classified as isolated, combined or acquired with focal, segmental or generalised distribution; MRI is normal in isolated forms. Treat with anticholinergics, botulinum toxin for focal forms, and DBS of globus pallidus internus for generalised dystonia.
th: Dystonia คือกลุ่มอาการที่กล้ามเนื้อหดเกร็งต่อเนื่องหรือเป็นพัก ๆ ทำให้เกิดท่าบิดผิดปกติและการเคลื่อนไหวซ้ำ ๆ ส่วนใหญ่เป็นโรคเรื้อรัง แต่มีภาวะฉุกเฉินสำคัญ ได้แก่ dystonic storm หรือ status dystonicus, acute dystonic reaction จากยา, laryngeal dystonia ที่ทำให้หายใจลำบาก และโรคที่ต้องแยกจาก pseudodystonia เช่น tetanus และ atlantoaxial subluxation
tempoNote: Usually a chronic disorder of months to years; emergencies appear over hours to days as acute drug reactions, dystonic storm or airway dystonia
feat: Patterned, twisting or sustained postures and movements, triggered or worsened by voluntary action and eased by sensory tricks (geste antagoniste)
Classified along two axes: clinical features (onset age, distribution, course, associated signs) and cause; focal forms (cervical dystonia, blepharospasm, writer's cramp) are commonest in adults

Emergency forms: status dystonicus (escalating generalised spasms with fever and rhabdomyolysis), acute dystonic reactions to dopamine blockers, laryngeal or pharyngeal dystonia with stridor or aspiration
Severe oromandibular dystonia can stop eating, and powerful jaw-closing spasms have fractured the facial skeleton
Some treatable causes must not be missed: dopa-responsive dystonia, Wilson's disease, drug-induced dystonia, and mimics such as tetanus
inv: Clinical diagnosis with attention to age, tempo, distribution and associated signs; MRI brain in young-onset, generalised, hemi-dystonic or rapidly progressive cases
Trial of levodopa for childhood-onset dystonia; copper, caeruloplasmin and slit-lamp examination for patients under 50
Gene panel or exome for early-onset and combined dystonia; medication review
Emergency tests when systemic involvement: CK, renal function, blood gases, infection screen and airway assessment

case.who: 24-year-old man from Bangkok with generalised dystonia since childhood
case.story: After his dystonia drugs were stopped during hospitalisation for a fever, he developed relentless opisthotonic spasms with pain, difficulty swallowing and dark urine.
case.exam: Temperature 39 °C, pulse 140, continuous generalised dystonic spasms, sweating, mild dehydration.
case.tests: CK 25,000 U/L, creatinine slightly raised; chest X-ray shows aspiration changes.
case.q: What emergency has occurred, and what is the plan?
case.a: Dystonic storm. Admit to intensive care, correct fluids and treat infection, give midazolam or other sedation, restart and escalate the dystonia drugs, and consider pallidal DBS or intrathecal baclofen if the storm persists.

read.where: Review — diagnosis and pathogenesis of dystonia (2024 consensus definition and classification)
11 - Dystonia: Phenomenology, classification, etiology, pathology, biochemistry, and genetics

det.patho: Dystonia reflects abnormal motor network function involving the basal ganglia, cerebellum, thalamus and cortex, with loss of surround inhibition and maladaptive plasticity. Isolated, combined and complex dystonias can be genetic, acquired or idiopathic, and the 2024 consensus emphasised network-based and aetiological classification. Emergencies arise when a trigger such as infection, drug withdrawal or device failure destabilises a pre-existing severe dystonia.
det.clinical: Most patients have a chronic disorder with variable severity, but certain features are red flags: sudden worsening, fever, continuous spasms, difficulty breathing or swallowing, and dark urine. Laryngeal dystonia causes stridor, breathy voice breaks or sudden airway obstruction, and pharyngeal dystonia causes dysphagia. Oromandibular dystonia can lead to weight loss and tongue injury. Pseudodystonia from tetanus, atlantoaxial subluxation, infection or tumour of the neck must be recognised because the treatment differs.
det.diagnosis: Dystonia is a clinical diagnosis. Search for treatable causes: levodopa trial in children and young adults, copper studies for Wilson's disease, drug review and imaging. In acute presentations assess airway, hydration and rhabdomyolysis before extensive investigation. Remember to image the neck in a child with acute torticollis and not to assume dystonia.
det.treatment: Chronic treatment is botulinum toxin for focal forms and oral drugs (anticholinergics, baclofen, benzodiazepines, tetrabenazine) and DBS for generalised and refractory dystonia. Emergencies require intensive care with sedation, fluids and cooling, avoidance of suxamethonium, dystonia-specific drugs, and early consideration of intrathecal baclofen or pallidal DBS. Acute dystonic reactions respond to parenteral anticholinergics. Airway dystonia needs rapid expert airway management and botulinum toxin to the responsible laryngeal muscles.
det.prognosis: Chronic dystonia is persistent but often manageable. Emergencies carry risk of death or lasting deficit but usually settle with intensive treatment.
pearls: Trial levodopa in every child or young adult with unexplained dystonia.
Dystonia plus fever and dark urine is an emergency.
Acute torticollis in a child needs imaging, not just a muscle relaxant.
det.thd: Dystonia คือกลุ่มอาการที่กล้ามเนื้อหดเกร็งเป็นท่าบิด ส่วนใหญ่เรื้อรัง แต่มีภาวะฉุกเฉินที่ต้องรู้ ได้แก่ dystonic storm ที่ผู้ป่วยมีไข้ ปวด กล้ามเนื้อสลาย acute dystonic reaction จากยา และ laryngeal dystonia ที่ทำให้หายใจลำบาก ต้องแยก pseudodystonia เช่น tetanus และ atlantoaxial subluxation ออก ทดลองให้ levodopa ในเด็กและผู้ป่วยอายุน้อย และตรวจ Wilson’s disease การรักษา ได้แก่ botulinum toxin ยา anticholinergic baclofen tetrabenazine และ DBS ส่วนภาวะฉุกเฉินต้องดูแลในไอซียู

name: Dystonia and retinitis pigmentosa
formal: Combination of dystonia with pigmentary retinal degeneration, seen in neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation phenotypes such as PKAN (HARP) and some mitochondrial disorders.
simple: A rare inherited combination of twisting muscle spasms and slowly worsening vision from damage to the retina.
th: กลุ่มอาการ dystonia ร่วมกับจอประสาทตาเสื่อมแบบ pigmentary พบในกลุ่ม NBIA เช่น PKAN (รวม HARP) และโรคไมโทคอนเดรียบางชนิด
tempoNote: Childhood or adolescent onset, progressive
feat: Progressive dystonia, often oromandibular and limb, with dysarthria
Night blindness and visual field constriction from pigmentary retinopathy
Possible acanthocytosis and hypoprebetalipoproteinaemia (HARP, now within PKAN)
Mitochondrial causes may add neuropathy, ataxia or deafness
inv: MRI with iron-sensitive sequences (eye-of-the-tiger in PKAN)
Electroretinography and fundoscopy
Blood film for acanthocytes, lipoproteins, lactate; PANK2 and mitochondrial genetic testing

case.story: Clumsy gait for two years, now foot twisting and difficulty speaking; trouble seeing in dim light.
case.exam: Generalised dystonia with oromandibular involvement, bone-spicule pigment in both retinae.
case.tests: MRI of the globus pallidus shows the 'eye of the tiger' appearance; PANK2 biallelic variants.
case.q: Which gene is responsible and what does the retinal finding add?
case.a: PANK2 (PKAN); retinopathy is common in classic PKAN and supports the diagnosis.

det.patho: Pantothenate kinase 2 deficiency impairs coenzyme A synthesis, leading to iron accumulation in globus pallidus and degeneration of retina. Mitochondrial disorders cause energy failure in both basal ganglia and retina. Not all mechanisms are fully understood.
det.clinical: Children present with gait problems and dystonia, often with prominent oromandibular involvement and dysarthria. Retinopathy causes night blindness and peripheral field loss. Cognitive decline and psychiatric features can accompany. Atypical later-onset PKAN has more speech and psychiatric symptoms and less retinopathy.
det.diagnosis: Combine MRI (eye-of-the-tiger), ophthalmology (ERG, fundus), blood film and lipid studies, then genetic testing. Lactate and mitochondrial DNA testing are needed if a mitochondrial cause is suspected.
det.treatment: No cure. Symptomatic care includes anticholinergics, baclofen, botulinum toxin, pallidal DBS for severe dystonia, low-vision aids and nutritional support. Iron chelation (deferiprone) has not shown clear clinical benefit in trials.
det.prognosis: Progressive; classic PKAN often leads to loss of ambulation within 10–15 years of onset.
pearls: Child with dystonia plus night blindness: think PKAN.
HARP syndrome is now classified within the PKAN spectrum.
Check a blood film for acanthocytes.

det.patho: Dopaminergic deficiency (presynaptic in PD, synthetic in DRD), striatal degeneration (Lubag, Wilson) or neuronal pump failure (ATP1A3) can each produce both dystonia and parkinsonism. Most causes are genetic or metabolic.
det.clinical: Presentation depends on cause: DRD has diurnal fluctuation; PRKN PD starts with foot dystonia; ATP1A3 has abrupt onset with bulbar features after a trigger; Lubag begins with focal dystonia and evolves to parkinsonism. Wilson disease adds psychiatric and hepatic signs.
det.diagnosis: Age, tempo, family history and ethnicity guide testing. Copper studies, MRI, DaT-SPECT, a levodopa trial and genetic panels are key.
det.treatment: Levodopa for DRD and PRKN; chelation or zinc for Wilson disease; avoidance of exposure for manganese. Symptomatic treatment includes botulinum toxin and anticholinergics. DBS benefits selected genetic forms such as Lubag and some PD cases.
det.prognosis: Highly variable: DRD has normal life with treatment; others progress.
pearls: Young-onset dystonia-parkinsonism: exclude Wilson disease and try levodopa.
Normal DaT-SPECT with dramatic levodopa response points to DRD.

det.patho: These disorders affect dopamine synthesis (GCH1, TH), neuronal membrane proteins (SGCE) or the sodium-potassium pump (ATP1A3) without structural degeneration. The circuit dysfunction is functional rather than neurodegenerative.
det.clinical: The term grouped DRD, myoclonus-dystonia and rapid-onset dystonia-parkinsonism. Each has distinctive features: diurnal fluctuation and levodopa response in DRD; alcohol responsiveness and psychiatric features in myoclonus-dystonia; abrupt onset with bulbar signs in ATP1A3.
det.diagnosis: Characterise associated movements and response to levodopa, then confirm genetically. MRI is normal and helps exclude heredodegenerative disease.
det.treatment: DRD responds to low-dose levodopa for life. Myoclonus-dystonia may respond to clonazepam, zonisamide or pallidal DBS. ATP1A3 has no specific therapy; supportive and symptomatic treatment.
det.prognosis: DRD has excellent prognosis; myoclonus-dystonia is lifelong but compatible with normal life span; ATP1A3 deficits often persist.

name: Dystonic storms
formal: Life-threatening episodes of severe generalised dystonia (status dystonicus) with fever, rhabdomyolysis and respiratory compromise, often triggered by infection or drug changes in people with dystonia.
simple: A dangerous flare of severe, constant muscle spasms that can cause exhaustion, muscle breakdown and breathing problems.
th: Dystonic storm คือภาวะ dystonia ทั่วร่างกายที่รุนแรงต่อเนื่องจนคุกคามชีวิต มีไข้ ปวดมาก กล้ามเนื้อสลาย และหายใจลำบาก มักเกิดในผู้ที่มี dystonia ชนิดทั่วร่างกายเดิมอยู่แล้วหลังการติดเชื้อหรือการหยุดและเปลี่ยนยา ต้องรักษาในห้องไอซียู ด้วยการให้น้ำ ยากล่อมประสาท และยารักษา dystonia โดยเฉพาะ และอาจต้องผ่าตัด DBS
tempoNote: Escalates over hours to days from a baseline of poorly controlled generalised dystonia, often after a trigger
feat: Severe, continuous generalised dystonic spasms with opisthotonus and pain, quite different from the patient's usual baseline
Fever, sweating, tachycardia and dehydration; bulbar involvement can cause anarthria, aphagia and airway compromise
Rhabdomyolysis with raised CK, myoglobinuria and acute kidney injury, plus metabolic acidosis and cardiac strain
Occurs in primary (including DYT1) and secondary dystonia, cerebral palsy, Wilson's disease, PKAN and neuroacanthocytosis, and in people on dopamine blockers
Triggers: infection, fever, surgery, abrupt stopping of tetrabenazine, anticholinergics or intrathecal baclofen, penicillamine in Wilson's disease; many have none
inv: CK, creatinine, electrolytes, urine myoglobin, blood gas and lactate, repeated frequently
Infection work-up, including lumbar puncture when there is fever, headache or altered mind, especially in patients with an intrathecal baclofen pump
Medication history (dopamine blockers, recent withdrawals) and device check of any baclofen pump or DBS system
Investigation of the underlying dystonia if unknown: MRI, copper studies, genetic testing

case.who: 17-year-old girl from Samut Prakan with generalised dystonia from a childhood brain injury
case.story: After a feverish illness her usual twisting became continuous over three days with severe pain, and she could no longer swallow or speak; her trihexyphenidyl had been stopped on admission.
case.exam: Temperature 39.2 °C, pulse 150, opisthotonic posture, sweating, dark urine; alert but exhausted.
case.tests: CK 38,000 U/L, creatinine rising, chest X-ray with right lower lobe consolidation.
case.q: What are the priorities in the first day?

11 - Dystonia: Phenomenology, classification, etiology, pathology, biochemistry, and genetics

det.patho: Disinhibition of basal ganglia output in a brain already prone to dystonia leads to relentless simultaneous contraction of opposing muscle groups. The muscular work generates heat and causes breakdown of muscle, with fever, myoglobinuria and kidney injury, and exhausts the respiratory muscles. A trigger such as infection, pain or drug change probably lowers the threshold. Dystonic storm and status dystonicus describe the same emergency.
det.clinical: Patients with severe baseline dystonia, usually generalised, become suddenly far worse over hours to days. They experience unremitting spasms with intense pain, cannot sleep, and may lose the ability to swallow and speak. Complications include dehydration, tongue biting, gastrointestinal bleeding, aspiration, cardiac strain and acute renal failure. Early recognition matters because the condition is fluctuating and sometimes fatal.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, in a person with known dystonia whose spasms escalate to a continuous, systemically damaging state. Look for a trigger, including infection and device malfunction, and exclude NMS, malignant hyperthermia, serotonin syndrome, intrathecal baclofen withdrawal, meningitis and seizures. Serial CK, kidney function and blood gases guide intensity of care.
det.treatment: Care is divided into supportive treatment, temporising sedation and dystonia-specific therapy. Supportive care covers the airway, fluids with attention to the kidneys, cooling, analgesia, nutrition and treating infection. Midazolam infusion is a reasonable first temporising drug, and propofol with a non-depolarising muscle relaxant is used when spasms threaten life; suxamethonium should be avoided. Dystonia-specific drugs include high-dose anticholinergics, baclofen, tetrabenazine and benzodiazepines; the old Marsden regimen of tetrabenazine, pimozide and an anticholinergic is rarely used now. When drugs fail, intrathecal baclofen or pallidal DBS (or lesioning) can end the storm, even though surgery in the acute phase carries risk.
det.prognosis: Outcome ranges from full recovery to new permanent disability, and some patients die despite good care. Relapse is possible, so the baseline regimen should be reviewed.
pearls: Measure CK early and repeat it; rhabdomyolysis is the killer.
A baclofen pump or DBS system must be checked in every storm.
Do not treat the picture as NMS and stop the dystonia drugs.
det.thd: Dystonic storm คือภาวะ dystonia รุนแรงทั่วร่างกายที่ทรุดลงอย่างรวดเร็วในผู้ป่วย dystonia เดิม มักตามหลังการติดเชื้อ ไข้ หรือการหยุดยา ผู้ป่วยปวดมาก กลืนและพูดไม่ได้ มีไข้ กล้ามเนื้อสลาย (CK สูง) และไตวายได้ ต้องรักษาในไอซียูด้วยการให้น้ำ ลดไข้ แก้ปวด รักษาการติดเชื้อ ยากล่อมประสาท เช่น midazolam ร่วมกับยา dystonia เช่น anticholinergic, baclofen, tetrabenazine และหากไม่ตอบสนองพิจารณา intrathecal baclofen หรือ pallidal DBS

name: Dystonic tremor

simple: A shaking that occurs in a part of the body affected by dystonia and usually changes with position or touch.

det.patho: Dystonic tremor reflects abnormal oscillation in the same network that causes dystonia, involving basal ganglia and cerebellum. The tremor's irregularity reflects co-contraction and abnormal sensorimotor integration.
det.clinical: It is common in cervical dystonia and writer's cramp. Head tremor is often 'no-no' and directional. Arm tremor may be asymmetric and worse with specific postures. Some patients previously labelled SWEDDs have dystonic tremor.
det.diagnosis: Look for dystonic posture, null point and sensory trick. DaT-SPECT is normal. Distinguish from essential tremor (symmetric, regular), PD (rest tremor, abnormal DaT) and functional tremor.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin targeting dystonic muscles is most effective for head and focal arm tremor. Propranolol, primidone, clonazepam and anticholinergics have variable benefit. Thalamic (Vim) or pallidal DBS helps selected severe cases.
det.prognosis: Chronic but usually stable; good control often achieved with botulinum toxin.
pearls: Find the null point: tremor vanishes there.
Asymmetric 'essential tremor' with posturing may be dystonic tremor.
Normal DaT-SPECT separates it from PD.

7: Molecular Diagnostic Procedures and Genetics in Neuromuscular Disorders

det.patho: Via the dystrophin-associated glycoprotein complex, dystrophin anchors the muscle cytoskeleton to the surrounding matrix. Out-of-frame mutations remove dystrophin (Duchenne); in-frame mutations leave a shortened partially functional protein (Becker). Membrane fragility causes repeated necrosis and replacement with fat and fibrous tissue.
det.clinical: Duchenne presents in early childhood with delayed walking or frequent falls and progressive weakness, loss of ambulation in adolescence, then cardiac and respiratory failure. Becker begins later with variable severity. X-linked dilated cardiomyopathy can occur without skeletal weakness. Carriers need cardiac screening.
det.diagnosis: High CK in a boy with proximal weakness is the trigger. MLPA identifies deletions or duplications in most; sequencing finds point mutations. The reading-frame rule predicts severity. Biopsy is reserved for unresolved cases.
det.treatment: Glucocorticoids slow progression; vamorolone and givinostat are newer approved options in some countries. Exon-skipping antisense drugs (e.g. for exon 51, 53, 45) and micro-dystrophin gene therapy (delandistrogene moxeparvovec) are approved in some countries for selected patients. Standard care includes ACE inhibitors and mineralocorticoid antagonists for the heart, non-invasive ventilation, scoliosis management, bone health and rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: With modern multidisciplinary care Duchenne survival often extends into the 30s or beyond; Becker life expectancy is longer, often limited by cardiomyopathy.
pearls: Unexplained high ALT/AST in a boy may be muscle, not liver: check CK.
Out-of-frame = Duchenne, in-frame = Becker (mostly).
Screen female carriers for cardiomyopathy.
det.thd: Dystrophinopathies คือกลุ่มโรคจากยีน dystrophin บนโครโมโซม X ได้แก่ Duchenne ที่อาการรุนแรงในเด็กชายเล็ก Becker ที่อาการช้ากว่า และหัวใจผิดปกติอย่างเดียว ผู้ป่วยมี Gowers sign น่องโต CK สูงมาก ยืนยันด้วย MLPA และ sequencing รักษาด้วยสเตียรอยด์ ยา exon skipping หรือยีนบำบัดในบางราย และดูแลหัวใจ ปอด และกระดูกสันหลัง

det.patho: Loss of periodontal sensory input and disturbed occlusion may alter brainstem and basal ganglia sensorimotor control of the jaw. Ageing-related changes in dopaminergic function may contribute. The mechanism remains uncertain.
det.clinical: Movements are repetitive and orofacial, usually mild, and may bother family more than the patient. It must be distinguished from tardive dyskinesia, which may coexist if patients took antiemetics or antipsychotics.
det.diagnosis: Clinical: orofacial dyskinesia in an edentulous elderly person without causative drug exposure, often improving with dentures. Consider other causes (Huntington disease, dystonia, drug effects).
det.treatment: Dental rehabilitation with proper dentures or implants is the main intervention. Avoid dopamine blockers. Medication is rarely needed.
det.prognosis: Benign; may improve with dental treatment.
pearls: Always ask about teeth and dentures in elderly orofacial dyskinesia.

Improvement with dentures in place supports the diagnosis.

name: Ehlers–Danlos syndrome
formal: Heritable connective tissue disorders with joint hypermobility, skin hyperextensibility and tissue fragility; neurological complications include vascular dissection, aneurysm, neuropathic pain and Chiari symptoms.
simple: An inherited weakness of the body's connective tissue causing very flexible joints and fragile skin and blood vessels.
th: กลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมของเนื้อเยื่อเกี่ยวพัน ข้อหลวม ผิวยืดได้มาก เนื้อเยื่อเปราะ ทางระบบประสาทพบหลอดเลือดฉีก โป่งพอง และ carotid-cavernous fistula
tempoNote: Lifelong connective tissue disorder; neurovascular events are sudden
feat: Joint hypermobility, easy bruising, fragile or stretchy skin, poor wound healing
Vascular type (COL3A1): arterial dissection or rupture, aneurysms, spontaneous carotid-cavernous fistula
Bowel or uterine rupture in vascular EDS; thin translucent skin with visible veins
Hypermobile type is associated with chronic pain, fatigue and orthostatic intolerance
Spontaneous intracranial hypotension from dural fragility in some patients
inv: Genetic testing for the suspected subtype (e.g. COL3A1, COL5A1); hypermobile EDS has no known gene
CTA or MRA of head and neck for dissection or aneurysm
Avoid conventional catheter angiography in vascular EDS when possible because of arterial fragility
Echocardiography and aortic imaging in vascular forms

case.who: 28-year-old woman from Chon Buri with lifelong easy bruising and a sister who died of a bowel rupture
case.story: Sudden right-sided neck pain followed by left arm weakness and blurred vision in the right eye.
case.exam: Thin translucent skin with visible chest veins, right Horner syndrome, mild left hemiparesis.
case.tests: CTA shows right internal carotid dissection; genetic testing identifies a COL3A1 variant.
case.q: Which EDS subtype is this and what procedural caution applies?
case.a: Vascular EDS; invasive arterial procedures carry high rupture risk and should be avoided unless essential.

det.patho: EDS comprises 13 subtypes in the 2017 classification, caused by variants in collagen genes or collagen-processing enzymes. Vascular EDS results from COL3A1 variants that weaken arterial walls and hollow organs. Classical EDS involves COL5A1/COL5A2. Hypermobile EDS, the commonest, has no identified gene and is diagnosed on clinical criteria.
det.clinical: Neurologically, vascular EDS presents with cervical or intracranial dissection, aneurysm rupture causing subarachnoid haemorrhage, and spontaneous direct carotid-cavernous fistula with pulsatile proptosis and chemosis. Hypermobile EDS brings chronic widespread pain, headaches, dysautonomia and sometimes craniocervical instability claims that are controversial. CSF leaks causing orthostatic headache occur more often in EDS.
det.diagnosis: Clinical features guide which genes to test. Family history of sudden death, organ rupture or arterial events should prompt testing for vascular EDS. Non-invasive vascular imaging is preferred. Hypermobile EDS is a clinical diagnosis using the 2017 criteria.
det.treatment: There is no cure. Vascular EDS is managed with surveillance imaging, blood pressure control and avoidance of contact sports and invasive procedures; celiprolol has been used to reduce arterial events. Dissections are managed with antithrombotic therapy as in other patients. Hypermobile EDS care focuses on physiotherapy, pain management and treating orthostatic intolerance.
det.prognosis: Vascular EDS shortens life expectancy because of arterial and organ rupture; other types usually have normal lifespan with variable disability.
pearls: Young dissection plus thin skin or family history of organ rupture: test for vascular EDS.
Spontaneous carotid-cavernous fistula in a young adult should raise suspicion of vascular EDS.
Hypermobile EDS is common; vascular EDS is rare but dangerous.
det.thd: Ehlers–Danlos syndrome เป็นกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมของ collagen ทำให้ข้อหลวม ผิวยืด และเนื้อเยื่อเปราะ ชนิด vascular จากยีน COL3A1 อันตรายที่สุด เพราะหลอดเลือดฉีกขาด โป่งพอง หรือเกิด carotid-cavernous fistula ได้เอง การวินิจฉัยใช้อาการร่วมกับการตรวจยีน ควรตรวจหลอดเลือดด้วยวิธีที่ไม่รุกล้ำ และหลีกเลี่ยงหัตถการที่ไม่จำเป็น

name: Electrical status epilepticus in sleep
formal: Epileptic encephalopathy with near-continuous spike-wave discharges during non-REM sleep and regression in cognition and behaviour, as in Landau–Kleffner and CSWS syndromes.
simple: A childhood epilepsy disorder where abnormal brain electrical activity during sleep leads to loss of language, learning or behaviour skills.
ab: epileptic encephalopathy with spike-wave activation in sleep
developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with spike-wave activation in sleep
th: เด็กที่เคยปกติพัฒนาการถดถอยด้านภาษา/สติปัญญา/พฤติกรรม ร่วมกับ spike-wave เกือบต่อเนื่องตอนหลับ — LKS คือกลุ่มที่สูญเสียการเข้าใจภาษาพูด
tempoNote: Regression over weeks to months, usually between ages 3 and 9; EEG activation tends to burn out by adolescence
feat: New loss of language, learning, attention or behaviour in a child who had been developing normally or had a stable prior problem
Landau–Kleffner type: verbal auditory agnosia — the child seems deaf to speech though hearing is normal, then expressive language deteriorates
Seizures are often infrequent and may be nocturnal focal or atypical absences; some children have none
Negative myoclonus, falls or unsteadiness can appear
May evolve from Rolandic epilepsy or follow early structural injury such as thalamic lesions
inv: Overnight or sleep EEG: marked activation of spike-wave in non-REM sleep, often occupying a large proportion of slow sleep
Formal audiology (normal pure-tone hearing in LKS) and neuropsychological/language assessment
MRI for structural causes (thalamic injury, polymicrogyria); genetic testing (e.g. GRIN2A) where appropriate

case.story: Spoke in full sentences until six months ago; now ignores his name, does not follow spoken instructions and says only a few words, but turns to the sound of a motorbike. Two brief night-time seizures.
case.exam: Normal motor examination; responds to gesture and pictures but not speech.
case.tests: Audiogram normal. Awake EEG: occasional left temporal spikes. Overnight EEG: near-continuous bilateral spike-wave dominating non-REM sleep. MRI normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and which classes of treatment are commonly used?
case.a: Landau–Kleffner syndrome within the EE-SWAS spectrum; corticosteroids, high-dose nocturnal benzodiazepines, sulthiame, valproate or ethosuximide, aiming to suppress sleep activation, with speech and language therapy.

det.patho: Sustained spike-wave activity during non-REM sleep is thought to interfere with sleep-dependent synaptic downscaling and consolidation, producing regression in the networks the discharges involve: temporal language cortex in LKS, frontal or global networks in the wider syndrome. Causes include early thalamic or other structural injury, genetic variants such as GRIN2A, and evolution from self-limited focal epilepsies; many cases are of unknown cause.
det.clinical: Under ILAE 2022 terms, a previously typical child is classed as epileptic encephalopathy with spike-wave activation in sleep (EE-SWAS), while a child with pre-existing impairment is called DEE-SWAS; Landau–Kleffner syndrome is the variant led by acquired verbal auditory agnosia. Regression may involve language, cognition, attention, behaviour or motor skills. Seizures vary and may be rare, so the problem may present as a 'behaviour' or 'hearing' issue. Duration of the sleep activation relates to how much function is lost.
det.diagnosis: Any child with unexplained regression, especially of language, needs a sleep EEG; a short awake EEG can be almost normal. Confirm normal hearing and document cognitive and language baselines to track response. Exclude autism-related regression, metabolic and neurodegenerative disease, and autoimmune encephalitis when the history fits.
det.treatment: Treatment aims to suppress sleep activation quickly. Options include corticosteroids (oral prednisolone or pulsed methylprednisolone), high-dose nocturnal diazepam or clobazam, sulthiame, valproate, ethosuximide and levetiracetam; IVIG and ketogenic diet are used in resistant cases, and surgery is considered for a focal structural cause. Carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine and phenytoin may aggravate the pattern. Intensive speech-language therapy, educational support and sign language where needed are essential.
det.prognosis: EEG activation and seizures usually remit by adolescence, but cognitive and language deficits may persist, particularly with long untreated activation or structural cause.
pearls: A child who suddenly seems 'deaf' to words with a normal audiogram: get a sleep EEG.
Seizures can be few — the regression is the main problem.
Sodium-channel drugs can aggravate sleep spike-wave activation.
det.thd: EE-SWAS (เดิมเรียก ESES/CSWS) คือภาวะที่ EEG มี spike-wave เกือบต่อเนื่องตอนหลับ ทำให้เด็กที่เคยพัฒนาการปกติถดถอยด้านภาษา การเรียนรู้หรือพฤติกรรม Landau–Kleffner syndrome เป็นชนิดย่อยที่เด็กเหมือนหูหนวกต่อคำพูดแต่การได้ยินปกติ อาการชักอาจมีน้อย ต้องตรวจ EEG ขณะหลับจึงจะเห็น รักษาด้วย steroid, benzodiazepine ขนาดสูงก่อนนอน, sulthiame, valproate หรือ ethosuximide ร่วมกับฝึกพูด และควรเลี่ยง carbamazepine

qx.stem: A 7-year-old boy with known centrotemporal spikes had rare nocturnal seizures until 6 months ago. Now his teacher reports he has trouble understanding speech, is hyperactive, and his handwriting is worse. Overnight EEG shows near-continuous bilateral spike-and-wave occupying over 85% of non-REM sleep, while waking EEG shows only occasional spikes.
qx.q: What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Reassure that SeLECTS is benign and no action is needed
Add carbamazepine to suppress centrotemporal spikes
Treat the sleep EEG pattern, e.g. with steroids or high-dose benzodiazepine, and monitor cognition
Arrange speech therapy only
Repeat EEG in 2 years
qx.why: Cognitive and behavioural regression with spike-wave activation in sleep (developmental/epileptic encephalopathy with spike-wave activation in sleep) can evolve from SeLECTS. Prompt treatment of the EEG pattern with corticosteroids, high-dose diazepam/clobazam, sulthiame or valproate aims to protect cognition. Carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine may aggravate this pattern.

name: Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy
formal: Muscular dystrophy with early joint contractures, humeroperoneal weakness and cardiac conduction disease, due to EMD, LMNA or related nuclear envelope gene variants.
simple: An inherited muscle disease with stiff joints, weakness in upper arms and lower legs, and heart rhythm problems.
more: X-linked (EMD) or autosomal dominant (LMNA) forms; CK mildly raised. Cardiac monitoring with pacemaker or defibrillator is life-saving; sudden cardiac death is the main prognostic concern. Nuclear envelope disorders (EMD, LMNA and others) with early joint contractures of elbows, Achilles and spine, humeroperoneal weakness and cardiac conduction defects with arrhythmia risk.
th: กล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมเอเมอรี-ไดรฟัส — ข้อติดยึดตั้งแต่ต้น ต้นแขน-ปลายขาอ่อนแรง และหัวใจเต้นผิดจังหวะ

Contractures appear before significant weakness
Heart block and atrial arrhythmias can cause sudden death
inv: ECG/Holter, echocardiography

case.exam: Elbow and ankle contractures, rigid spine, weak biceps and ankle dorsiflexors.
case.tests: ECG: slow atrial rhythm with first-degree block; EMD variant.
case.q: What intervention may be life-saving?

det.patho: EDMD results from variants in genes for nuclear envelope proteins: emerin (EMD, X-linked), lamin A/C (LMNA, usually autosomal dominant), and less often FHL1 and others. Defective nuclear lamina mechanics and gene regulation damage skeletal and cardiac muscle. The cardiac conduction system is particularly vulnerable.
det.clinical: Elbow, heel-cord and posterior neck contractures (rigid spine) develop early in childhood, often before notable weakness. Weakness and wasting follow a humero-peroneal distribution and later become more widespread. Cardiac disease includes atrial standstill, conduction block, atrial and ventricular arrhythmias and dilated cardiomyopathy, typically from the late teens or 20s. LMNA disease may also include lipodystrophy and has a high risk of sudden death.
det.diagnosis: The clinical triad suggests the diagnosis, and genetic testing for EMD, LMNA and related genes confirms it. CK is normal or moderately raised. ECG, Holter monitoring, echocardiography and cardiac MRI are essential at diagnosis and regularly thereafter. Muscle MRI may show characteristic involvement patterns, and emerin immunostaining is absent in X-linked cases.
det.treatment: Cardiac management is the priority: pacemaker for conduction disease, and an ICD for LMNA patients at high arrhythmic risk even without severe heart failure. Anticoagulation is often needed for atrial standstill or fibrillation because of stroke risk. Physiotherapy and surgical release may help contractures, and respiratory function needs monitoring. Female EMD carriers need cardiac screening.
det.prognosis: Survival depends largely on cardiac management; sudden cardiac death is the main threat, whereas muscle weakness progresses slowly.
pearls: Contractures before weakness plus a slow pulse in a young man: think EDMD.
A pacemaker alone may not prevent sudden death in LMNA disease — ICD is often needed.

Normal neurological examination between attacks

case.exam: Normal; during an attack recorded on phone video the movements vary in direction and stop when distracted.

det.patho: Most reported cases are functional, arising from altered attention and emotional processing rather than structural damage. Rarely, stress triggers attacks in genetic paroxysmal dyskinesias (e.g. PNKD). Data are limited to case descriptions.
det.clinical: Attacks are linked to emotional triggers and may be dramatic. Between attacks examination is normal. Functional features and coexisting functional symptoms support the diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: Positive functional signs, normal MRI and metabolic tests, and absent epileptic activity support a functional diagnosis. Family history and specific triggers (coffee, alcohol, sudden movement) suggest a paroxysmal dyskinesia.
det.treatment: For functional cases: clear explanation, specialist physiotherapy and CBT. For genetic paroxysmal dyskinesias: carbamazepine (PKD) or clonazepam (PNKD) and trigger avoidance.
det.prognosis: Functional cases may improve with early diagnosis and therapy; paroxysmal dyskinesias tend to lessen with age.
pearls: Episodic ballism with emotional triggers and normal MRI is usually functional.
Check glucose in any ballism.
Diagnose functional disorders on positive signs, not exclusion alone.

det.patho: Encephalitis is inflammation of brain parenchyma with neurological dysfunction. Infectious causes include viruses (HSV, VZV, enteroviruses, JE, dengue, rabies), bacteria and parasites; autoimmune causes include antibodies against neuronal surface proteins such as NMDA receptor and LGI1. Many cases remain without an identified cause despite testing. HSV encephalitis can be followed by NMDA receptor autoimmune encephalitis weeks later.
det.clinical: Most patients have fever, headache and altered behaviour or consciousness, with seizures in about half. Focal signs reflect the regions involved. Autoimmune encephalitis often begins with psychiatric symptoms, short-term memory loss, sleep change and movement disorders. Early complications include status epilepticus, raised pressure, hyponatraemia and autonomic instability.
det.diagnosis: Consensus criteria require altered mental status plus supportive features such as fever, seizures, focal signs, CSF pleocytosis, MRI parenchymal changes or EEG abnormality. CSF PCR and antibodies, MRI and EEG are core tests. Early HSV PCR may be negative in the first days; repeat if suspicion remains high. Consider metabolic, toxic and vascular mimics.
det.treatment: Empiric IV aciclovir should be started immediately in suspected encephalitis and continued until HSV is excluded (often 14–21 days if confirmed). Add antibiotics if bacterial meningitis is possible and doxycycline when rickettsial infection is likely. Autoimmune encephalitis is treated with steroids, IVIG or plasma exchange, followed by rituximab or cyclophosphamide if needed, and tumour removal when present. Seizures, raised pressure and complications need intensive supportive care.
det.prognosis: Outcome ranges from full recovery to death or severe disability; delayed treatment in HSV encephalitis worsens prognosis, while many autoimmune cases recover substantially over months.
pearls: Do not wait for imaging or LP to give aciclovir in suspected encephalitis.
Relapse after HSV encephalitis with new movements or psychiatric change: test for NMDA receptor antibodies.
Faciobrachial dystonic seizures and hyponatraemia point to LGI1 encephalitis.

Modern sporadic cases are rare; many may represent autoimmune encephalitis

CSF: mild pleocytosis; screen for anti-NMDA receptor and anti-D2 receptor antibodies

case.story: After a sore throat she became extremely sleepy, then developed episodes of eyes rolling up and became slow.
case.exam: Somnolent but rousable, bradykinesia, oculogyric crises, emotional lability.

case.q: What syndrome is this, and what treatment is used today?

det.patho: The epidemic cause was never established; influenza was suspected but not proven. Pathology showed inflammation of midbrain and basal ganglia, especially the substantia nigra. Some modern cases are associated with antibodies against dopamine D2 receptors, suggesting autoimmune mechanisms.
det.clinical: During the epidemic, patients had fever, lethargy, ophthalmoplegia and movement disorders. Survivors often developed postencephalitic parkinsonism years later, with oculogyric crises and behavioural changes. Modern cases present as somnolence, parkinsonism and psychiatric features in young people.
det.diagnosis: There are no definitive tests; diagnosis is clinical, after excluding infectious and autoimmune encephalitides. Antibody testing (anti-NMDAR, anti-D2R) and MRI are part of evaluation.
det.treatment: Immunotherapy (corticosteroids, IVIG, plasma exchange) is used in modern autoimmune-associated cases. Levodopa improves parkinsonism, though historical patients developed fluctuations and dyskinesia. Supportive care is essential.
det.prognosis: Historically high mortality and frequent chronic disability; outcome of modern autoimmune cases is better with immunotherapy.
pearls: Somnolence plus oculogyric crises plus parkinsonism: think encephalitis lethargica-like syndrome.
Check anti-D2 receptor antibodies in children with basal ganglia encephalitis.
The 1916–1930 epidemic left many with postencephalitic parkinsonism.
det.thd: Encephalitis lethargica หรือโรค von Economo เป็นโรคสมองอักเสบที่ระบาดช่วงปี 1916–1930 มีอาการง่วงหลับมาก ตาเหลือกขึ้น และต่อมามีพาร์กินสันหลังสมองอักเสบ สาเหตุยังไม่ทราบ ปัจจุบันพบน้อยมากและบางรายเกี่ยวกับภูมิคุ้มกันต่อ dopamine D2 receptor รักษาด้วยยากดภูมิคุ้มกันและ levodopa

det.patho: This is a syndromic label for disease affecting several levels of the nervous system at once. Infections can invade meninges and spread along roots and the cord, while immune mechanisms after infection may attack both central myelin and peripheral nerve or roots. The pattern is a clue that narrows aetiology.
det.clinical: Patients have combinations of confusion, seizures, cranial neuropathies, myelopathy with sensory level and sphincter disturbance, and radicular pain or areflexia. Reflexes may be paradoxically absent despite cord involvement because of root disease. Systemic features (rash, fever) point to infection.
det.diagnosis: MRI of brain, spine and roots plus CSF analysis is essential. Search for treatable infections (HSV-2, CMV, VZV, syphilis, Lyme, TB) and immune antibodies. EMG can show combined demyelinating or axonal root involvement.
det.treatment: Treat the infection where identified, e.g. aciclovir, ganciclovir, penicillin or ceftriaxone. Immune-mediated forms receive high-dose steroids followed by plasma exchange or IVIG if needed. Supportive care includes bladder management and rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: Variable, depending on cause and speed of treatment.
pearls: Sensory level with absent reflexes: think cord + roots, not just spinal shock.
Always test CSF for herpes viruses and syphilis.
MOG and GFAP antibodies can produce combined central and peripheral disease.

formal: Inflammation affecting both brain and spinal cord, either post-infectious (ADEM), autoimmune or viral, causing multifocal deficits, encephalopathy and often demyelinating lesions on MRI.

det.patho: Inflammation spans brain and spinal cord via direct viral infection of neurons or glia, immune-mediated demyelination after infection (ADEM, MOGAD), antibody-mediated astrocytopathy (NMOSD) or cytotoxic T-cell responses against intracellular onconeural antigens. The pathology ranges from perivenous demyelination to neuronal loss depending on mechanism.
det.clinical: Presentation combines altered consciousness or behaviour, seizures, cranial nerve or brainstem features with paraparesis, sensory level and sphincter dysfunction. Infectious causes often bring fever and meningism. ADEM is most frequent in children after an infection; paraneoplastic encephalomyelitis in adults with cancer (often anti-Hu) evolves subacutely and may include sensory neuronopathy. PERM, an encephalomyelitis with stiffness, myoclonus and brainstem signs, is linked to glycine-receptor antibodies.
det.diagnosis: Image the whole neuraxis, perform CSF analysis and send paired serum and CSF for infectious and autoimmune testing. Treat presumed HSV or bacterial infection empirically until excluded. MOG and AQP4 antibodies distinguish demyelinating syndromes; onconeural antibodies and tumour screening are needed in adults. Avoid calling a case ADEM in an adult without good evidence, since MS, NMOSD and infection are common mimics.
det.treatment: Treat infection specifically where identified (acyclovir for HSV, ganciclovir for CMV). Immune-mediated forms receive high-dose IV methylprednisolone, then IVIG or plasma exchange if there is inadequate response; relapsing NMOSD or MOGAD require maintenance therapy. Paraneoplastic forms need tumour treatment and immunotherapy. Supportive care includes seizure control, bladder care and rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: ADEM in children usually recovers well; viral and paraneoplastic forms often leave significant disability.
pearls: Encephalopathy is required for ADEM; isolated multifocal lesions without it point elsewhere.
Always test MOG and AQP4 antibodies in post-infectious encephalomyelitis.
Japanese encephalitis is an important infectious cause of encephalomyelitis in Thailand.
det.thd: Encephalomyelitis คือการอักเสบของทั้งสมองและไขสันหลัง สาเหตุมีทั้งติดเชื้อไวรัส เช่น Japanese encephalitis หรือ HSV ภาวะหลังติดเชื้อ (ADEM) โรคภูมิคุ้มกัน เช่น MOGAD, NMOSD และ paraneoplastic ผู้ป่วยมีซึมสับสน ชัก ร่วมกับขาอ่อนแรง มีระดับความรู้สึก และปัสสาวะผิดปกติ ต้องทำ MRI ทั้งสมองและไขสันหลัง ตรวจ CSF และ antibody รักษาตามสาเหตุ เช่น ยาต้านไวรัส หรือ steroid ขนาดสูง IVIG และ plasma exchange

det.patho: Encephalomyopathy describes combined brain and muscle disease. The commonest causes are defects of oxidative phosphorylation from mtDNA or nuclear gene variants; tissues with high energy demand, such as cortex and muscle, fail first. Heteroplasmy explains variable severity within families.
det.clinical: Presentations range from childhood Leigh syndrome to adult MELAS and MERRF. Brain features include seizures, migraine-like headache, stroke-like episodes, ataxia, cognitive decline and psychiatric symptoms. Muscle features include exercise intolerance, ptosis, ophthalmoplegia and weakness. Systemic clues such as diabetes, deafness, cardiomyopathy and short stature are very helpful.
det.diagnosis: Lactate in blood or CSF and an MRS lactate peak support the diagnosis but are neither sensitive nor specific. Genetic testing is now the main route; urine epithelium or muscle gives higher yield for m.3243A>G than blood. Muscle biopsy remains useful when genetic tests are negative.
det.treatment: Management is supportive and multidisciplinary. Avoid valproate in POLG disease and use caution with other mitochondrial toxins. Arginine or citrulline is commonly used for MELAS stroke-like episodes despite limited evidence. Treat seizures aggressively, correct dehydration and avoid prolonged fasting. Supplements such as coenzyme Q10 are widely used but evidence is weak, except in primary CoQ10 deficiency.
det.prognosis: Course depends on the specific disorder; most are progressive with episodic setbacks.
pearls: Stroke-like lesions crossing vascular territories in a young person: think mitochondrial.
Test urine rather than blood for m.3243A>G heteroplasmy.
Avoid valproate until POLG disease is excluded.

det.patho: Encephalopathy means global brain dysfunction. Mechanisms include impaired neuronal energy supply (hypoxia, hypoglycaemia), toxin or drug effects on neurotransmission, inflammatory cytokines in sepsis, osmotic shifts, and direct infection or immune attack. The ascending arousal system and widespread cortical networks are particularly vulnerable.
det.clinical: This is a syndrome rather than a single disease. Presentations range from subtle inattention to coma. Hypoactive forms are easily missed. Metabolic causes are often accompanied by asterixis and myoclonus, while focal deficits suggest structural disease. Older age, dementia and polypharmacy increase vulnerability.
det.diagnosis: Systematic screening for metabolic, toxic, infective, structural and epileptic causes is needed. EEG helps exclude non-convulsive status. MRI may show specific patterns (e.g. PRES, Wernicke, hypoglycaemia, CJD). Lumbar puncture is important if fever or unclear cause.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: correct glucose and electrolytes, give thiamine before glucose in at-risk patients, stop offending drugs and treat infection promptly. Dialysis may be needed for uraemia or dialysable toxins, and lactulose with rifaximin for hepatic encephalopathy. Supportive care includes delirium prevention measures, a calm well-lit environment, family presence and avoiding sedatives and anticholinergics where possible. Seizures or non-convulsive status need antiseizure treatment guided by EEG.
det.prognosis: Depends on the cause; reversible metabolic causes recover, hypoxic and some infective causes leave lasting damage.
pearls: Give thiamine before glucose in malnourished or alcoholic patients.
Check drug doses against kidney function in confused elderly patients.
EEG in unexplained encephalopathy to find non-convulsive status.

formal: Congenital myasthenic syndrome from COLQ mutations that remove acetylcholinesterase from the synaptic cleft, causing prolonged endplate currents, repetitive compound muscle action potentials and fatigable weakness.
simple: An inherited problem where the enzyme that clears the nerve signal chemical at the muscle junction is missing, causing weakness that tires easily.

case.story: Floppy at birth and slow to walk; she tires quickly, her head drops by afternoon, and pyridostigmine made her weaker.
case.exam: Mild ptosis, neck flexor and proximal weakness, slowly reacting pupils.
case.tests: Single stimulus produces a repetitive CMAP; RNS decrement; AChR antibodies negative; biallelic COLQ variants.

det.patho: COLQ encodes the collagen tail anchoring acetylcholinesterase to the basal lamina. Without it, acetylcholine persists in the synaptic cleft, causing prolonged endplate potentials, desensitisation and endplate myopathy from calcium overload.
det.clinical: Severity varies from life-threatening neonatal disease to milder childhood weakness. Axial and proximal muscles are often involved, and scoliosis can develop. Ocular muscles may be relatively spared. Fatigue and respiratory crises can occur.
det.diagnosis: Repetitive CMAP after single stimuli, decrement on repetitive stimulation, negative antibodies and lack of response or worsening with pyridostigmine suggest the diagnosis; COLQ testing confirms.
det.treatment: Beta-2 agonists (salbutamol) or ephedrine are the main treatment. Avoid cholinesterase inhibitors. Supportive respiratory care, physiotherapy and scoliosis management as needed.
det.prognosis: Variable; many improve with beta-agonist therapy but some have significant lifelong disability.
pearls: Repetitive CMAP: think COLQ deficiency or slow channel syndrome.
Pyridostigmine makes it worse.
Salbutamol is the main therapy.

qx.stem: A 16-year-old boy from Phrae had bilateral ptosis and delayed milestones from infancy and now has scoliosis and generalised fatigable weakness. The pupillary light reflex is sluggish. Edrophonium produced no improvement. A single stimulus of the ulnar nerve gives a repetitive CMAP, and low-rate stimulation shows a decrement. The family has no history of weakness and his parents are healthy.
qx.q: Which statement best fits his diagnosis and management?
opts: Dominant slow channel syndrome; use fluoxetine
Recessive COLQ-related deficiency; avoid pyridostigmine and use ephedrine or salbutamol
Autoimmune myasthenia gravis; treat with thymectomy
Presynaptic CMS; increase pyridostigmine
Lambert–Eaton syndrome; search for lung cancer
qx.why: A repetitive CMAP with a decrement, a slowed pupillary light response, scoliosis, early onset and no benefit from edrophonium in an unaffected family suggests the recessive COLQ form of end-plate acetylcholinesterase deficiency, in which acetylcholine lingers in the synaptic cleft. Cholinesterase inhibitors add nothing or are harmful, while ephedrine and salbutamol help. Slow channel syndrome is dominant and shows the same repetitive CMAP but a normal pupil response and no recessive pattern.

name: Endocarditis
formal: Infection of the heart valves that causes neurological complications through septic emboli, mycotic aneurysms, cerebral abscess, haemorrhage and ischaemic stroke.
simple: An infection of the heart's inner lining or valves that can send clots or germs to the brain and cause strokes.
th: การติดเชื้อที่ลิ้นหัวใจ ทำให้เกิดลิ่มเชื้อหลุดไปอุดหลอดเลือดสมอง หลอดเลือดโป่งพองจากเชื้อ ฝีในสมอง และเลือดออกในสมอง
tempoNote: Acute (e.g. Staphylococcus aureus) over days or subacute (viridans streptococci) over weeks
feat: Fever, new murmur, embolic phenomena; neurological events in a large minority
Embolic ischaemic stroke, often multiple and in different territories
Infectious (mycotic) aneurysms that bleed; intracerebral or subarachnoid haemorrhage
Meningitis, brain abscess and encephalopathy
Risk groups: prosthetic valves, rheumatic heart disease, IV drug use, haemodialysis
inv: Three sets of blood cultures before antibiotics
Transthoracic then transoesophageal echocardiography
MRI brain (often shows silent emboli and microbleeds) and CTA/DSA for aneurysms
Modified Duke (2023 ESC/Duke-ISCVID) criteria

case.who: 41-year-old man from Surat Thani with rheumatic mitral disease
case.story: Three weeks of fevers and weight loss, then sudden aphasia and right arm weakness.
case.exam: Temperature 38.4 C, pansystolic murmur, splinter haemorrhages, expressive aphasia, right arm weakness.
case.tests: MRI: multiple small acute infarcts in both hemispheres; blood cultures grow Streptococcus mitis; TOE shows a 12 mm mitral vegetation.
case.q: Why is thrombolysis contraindicated here?
case.a: Stroke from septic emboli of infective endocarditis carries high haemorrhage risk; thrombolysis is not given, though thrombectomy may be considered for large-vessel occlusion.

read.where: Chapter 8 Stroke and Cerebrovascular Diseases — Endocarditis
Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — Infective Endocarditis
Chapter 6: What caused this transient or persisting ischemic event?

det.patho: Bacteria adhere to damaged endocardium or prosthetic material and form friable vegetations. Fragments embolise to the brain, causing infarcts, abscesses and septic arteritis. Bacterial invasion of the arterial wall weakens it into infectious aneurysms. Immune complex mechanisms add encephalopathy and glomerulonephritis.
det.clinical: Neurological complications occur in roughly 25-35% of cases, sometimes as the very first sign of the illness. Embolic stroke is commonest, usually in the MCA territory. Haemorrhage may come from aneurysm rupture, haemorrhagic transformation of infarcts or septic arteritis. Encephalopathy, meningitis and seizures also occur. S. aureus endocarditis has the highest rate of CNS complications.
det.diagnosis: Any patient with stroke and fever, murmur or bacteraemia needs blood cultures and echocardiography. TOE is more sensitive for vegetations and abscesses. MRI often reveals multiple clinically silent emboli and microbleeds, which can support the diagnosis. Vascular imaging looks for infectious aneurysms, especially before cardiac surgery or anticoagulation.
det.treatment: Prolonged intravenous antibiotics tailored to the organism are the core. IV thrombolysis is avoided; mechanical thrombectomy may be considered for large-vessel occlusion. Anticoagulation is usually held or modified after haemorrhage. Timing of valve surgery after stroke is decided by the heart team; small ischaemic strokes need not delay urgent surgery, while haemorrhage often prompts a delay. Aneurysms may be treated endovascularly or surgically if they enlarge or bleed.
det.prognosis: Neurological complications increase mortality, particularly haemorrhage and S. aureus infection.
pearls: Fever plus stroke: get blood cultures before any antibiotic.
No IV thrombolysis for endocarditis-related stroke.
Multiple territory infarcts with microbleeds on SWI are suggestive.
det.thd: Infective endocarditis ทำให้เกิดภาวะแทรกซ้อนทางสมองได้บ่อย เช่น ลิ่มเชื้อหลุดไปอุดหลอดเลือดสมองหลายตำแหน่ง หลอดเลือดโป่งพองจากเชื้อที่แตกได้ ฝีในสมอง และเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ ผู้ป่วยที่มีไข้ร่วมกับ stroke ต้องเจาะเลือดเพาะเชื้อและทำ echocardiography ห้ามให้ยาละลายลิ่มเลือดทางหลอดเลือดดำ การรักษาหลักคือยาปฏิชีวนะนานหลายสัปดาห์และพิจารณาผ่าตัดลิ้นหัวใจ

name: Endocrine myopathies
formal: Muscle weakness, usually proximal, caused by hormone imbalance such as thyroid disease, Cushing syndrome, steroid excess, hyperparathyroidism or acromegaly, typically with normal or mildly raised CK.
simple: Muscle weakness caused by hormone problems such as an overactive or underactive thyroid or too much steroid.
more: Diagnosed by hormone assay such as TSH, cortisol or calcium with EMG and CK, which are often normal or mildly raised. Weakness improves on correcting the hormone abnormality, usually over months, and myopathy may present before other signs.
th: โรคกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง (มักเป็นต้นแขนขา) จากความผิดปกติของฮอร์โมน เช่น ไทรอยด์ cortisol พาราไทรอยด์ วิตามินดี หรือ growth hormone
tempoNote: Develops over weeks to months; improves after hormonal correction
feat: Symmetric proximal weakness, usually painless (myalgia and cramps in hypothyroidism)
Hypothyroid: raised CK, slow-relaxing reflexes, muscle hypertrophy (Hoffmann syndrome)
Hyperthyroid: normal CK, wasting, sometimes periodic paralysis or bulbar weakness
Cushing/steroids: normal CK, thighs most affected
Hyperparathyroidism/osteomalacia: bone pain, brisk reflexes, waddling gait
inv: TSH, free T4, cortisol tests, calcium, phosphate, PTH, 25-OH vitamin D, IGF-1
CK and potassium
EMG mostly to exclude other disease

case.story: Months of fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance and muscle aches; cannot get up from the floor after praying.
case.exam: Puffy face, dry skin, enlarged firm thigh muscles, hip flexor weakness, ankle jerks with delayed relaxation phase.
case.tests: CK 1,900 U/L, TSH 85 mIU/L, free T4 low; EMG mildly myopathic.
case.q: What is the cause of the raised CK and weakness?
case.a: Hypothyroid myopathy; thyroxine replacement should normalise CK and strength over months.

read.where: Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Endocrine Myopathies
Myopathies of Systemic Disease and Toxic Myopathies
18: Myopathies Associated with Systemic Disorders and Aging
Chapter 18 Thyroid Disease and the Nervous System

det.patho: Thyroid hormone, cortisol, PTH, vitamin D and growth hormone each regulate muscle metabolism and protein turnover. Hypothyroidism slows glycogen breakdown and mitochondrial function and leaks CK; thyrotoxicosis accelerates protein catabolism; glucocorticoid excess causes type 2 fibre atrophy; vitamin D and calcium disorders impair excitation-contraction coupling. Most changes are functional rather than destructive, so they reverse.
det.clinical: This heading covers several conditions sharing proximal weakness of endocrine origin. Hypothyroid myopathy causes cramps, stiffness, raised CK and occasionally rhabdomyolysis. Thyrotoxic myopathy causes wasting with normal CK and may coexist with myasthenia or periodic paralysis. Steroid myopathy causes painless thigh weakness, and osteomalacia causes bone pain with a waddling gait.
det.diagnosis: Endocrine causes should be screened in any new proximal myopathy because they are common and reversible. CK helps: raised in hypothyroidism, normal in steroid excess and hyperthyroidism. EMG and biopsy are non-specific and used mainly to exclude other myopathies.
det.treatment: Correct the underlying hormonal disorder: thyroxine or antithyroid drugs, reduce steroid exposure, parathyroidectomy, vitamin D and calcium repletion. Physiotherapy aids recovery. Avoid statins until hypothyroidism is treated.
det.prognosis: Usually good with recovery over weeks to months after correction.
pearls: Check TSH in every patient with unexplained raised CK.
Normal CK does not exclude an endocrine myopathy.
Brisk reflexes with proximal weakness suggests osteomalacia or hyperparathyroidism.
det.thd: Endocrine myopathy คือกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงจากความผิดปกติของฮอร์โมน เช่น ไทรอยด์ต่ำหรือสูง cortisol เกิน พาราไทรอยด์สูง หรือขาดวิตามินดี อาการมักเป็นต้นแขนขาอ่อนแรง ไทรอยด์ต่ำมักมี CK สูง ส่วน steroid และไทรอยด์สูงมักมี CK ปกติ ควรตรวจฮอร์โมนในผู้ป่วยกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงทุกราย เพราะรักษาให้หายได้

name: Endolymphatic hydrops
formal: Distension of the endolymphatic space of the inner ear, underlying Meniere disease, causing episodic vertigo, fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness.
simple: Too much fluid pressure in the inner ear, causing spinning attacks, hearing loss, ringing and a feeling of fullness in the ear.
th: ภาวะน้ำในหูชั้นในส่วน endolymph ขยายตัว เป็นพยาธิสภาพของโรค Ménière ทำให้เวียนศีรษะเป็นพัก ๆ การได้ยินเสียงต่ำลดลงแบบขึ้นลง เสียงในหู และหูอื้อ
tempoNote: Attacks last 20 minutes to 12 hours, recurring over years with gradual hearing decline
feat: Episodic spontaneous vertigo with nausea
Fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss
Tinnitus and aural fullness in the affected ear
Secondary hydrops can follow trauma, infection or otosclerosis
inv: Pure tone audiometry during and between attacks
Gadolinium-enhanced inner-ear MRI (delayed) to visualise hydrops
Electrocochleography; VEMP; exclude vestibular schwannoma on MRI

case.story: Several episodes of vertigo lasting 3 hours each, with roaring in the left ear and muffled hearing that improves afterwards.
case.exam: Between attacks normal, mild left low-frequency hearing loss on tuning fork testing.
case.tests: Audiogram shows left low-frequency sensorineural loss; delayed gadolinium MRI shows endolymphatic hydrops; no schwannoma.
case.q: What is the clinical diagnosis and first-line management?
case.a: Definite Ménière disease; salt restriction, betahistine (evidence limited), vestibular suppressants during attacks, and intratympanic steroids if refractory.

read.where: Chapter 23 Neuro-Otology: Dizziness, Balance and Hearing — Ménière’s Disease

det.patho: Excess endolymph distends the cochlear duct and saccule, possibly from impaired resorption in the endolymphatic sac. Membrane ruptures or pressure changes are thought to cause attacks. Hydrops is a histological and imaging finding; not everyone with hydrops has symptoms.
det.clinical: Classic Ménière disease includes recurrent vertigo, fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and fullness. Over time, hearing loss becomes permanent and vertigo attacks may diminish. Drop attacks (Tumarkin crises) can occur. Bilateral disease develops in a minority.
det.diagnosis: Bárány Society criteria for Ménière disease use clinical features plus audiometry. Delayed contrast MRI can visualise hydrops but is not required. Exclude retrocochlear lesions such as vestibular schwannoma.
det.treatment: Lifestyle measures (salt restriction, caffeine moderation), betahistine (limited evidence), diuretics, and acute vestibular suppressants. Intratympanic steroids or gentamicin for refractory cases; endolymphatic sac surgery or labyrinthectomy are later options. Hearing aids and tinnitus management.
det.prognosis: Vertigo often decreases over years, but hearing loss tends to progress.
pearls: Endolymphatic hydrops is the pathology; Ménière disease is the clinical syndrome.
Low-frequency fluctuating hearing loss is characteristic.
Always exclude vestibular schwannoma in asymmetric hearing loss.
det.thd: Endolymphatic hydrops คือภาวะน้ำ endolymph ในหูชั้นในเพิ่มขึ้น เป็นพยาธิสภาพของโรค Ménière ผู้ป่วยมีเวียนศีรษะบ้านหมุนเป็นพัก ๆ ครั้งละหลายชั่วโมง การได้ยินเสียงต่ำลดลงแบบขึ้นลง เสียงในหู และหูอื้อ ตรวจ audiogram และ MRI ฉีดสารทึบรังสีแบบหน่วงเวลา รักษาด้วยการลดเกลือ ยาบรรเทาเวียน และฉีดยาเข้าหูชั้นกลางในรายดื้อการรักษา
