name: Essential tremor
formal: Common bilateral postural and kinetic tremor of the arms, sometimes head and voice, familial in many cases, slowly progressive, improved by alcohol, propranolol and primidone.
simple: A common condition causing shaking of the hands, especially when doing tasks, which often runs in families and can be treated.
more: Slowly progressive bilateral postural and action tremor of hands, 4-12 Hz, often familial, improving with alcohol, treated with propranolol or primidone. Common postural and kinetic tremor, mostly of the hands, slowly progressive, often familial, improved by alcohol and responsive to propranolol or primidone.
th: มือสั่นขณะใช้งานหรือยกมือค้าง ทั้งสองข้าง มักมีคนในครอบครัวเป็น ดื่มแอลกอฮอล์แล้วดีขึ้น
feat: Bilateral postural and kinetic hand tremor (often with head or voice tremor)
No bradykinesia or rigidity
Family history and alcohol responsiveness common
inv: Clinical; thyroid function and drug review
DAT scan normal if parkinsonism is a question

case.story: Shaky hands for 10 years; worse when writing on the board or drinking from a cup. A glass of wine helps.
case.exam: Bilateral postural tremor and tremor on finger-nose testing, mild 'no-no' head tremor, normal tone and finger taps.
case.tests: TSH normal.
case.q: Which examination finding most clearly separates this from Parkinson’s disease?
case.a: Absence of bradykinesia (no decrement) — plus the tremor is postural/kinetic rather than at rest.

qx.stem: A 72-year-old man who has had bilateral hand tremor for 30 years can no longer drink soup or sign documents. Tremor is postural and kinetic, worse on the right, absent at rest, and his father had the same problem. Propranolol caused bradycardia and primidone made him too drowsy. He has atrial fibrillation on apixaban and refuses any procedure that involves opening the skull.
qx.q: Which option best fits his wishes and medical situation?
opts: Unilateral MR-guided focused ultrasound thalamotomy of the left ventral intermediate nucleus
Bilateral VIM deep brain stimulation in a single stage
Start levodopa for presumed tremor-dominant Parkinson's disease
Botulinum toxin into both forearm flexors and extensors as definitive therapy
Add clonazepam and haloperidol
qx.why: When drugs fail, essential tremor can be treated with VIM DBS or with incisionless MR-guided focused ultrasound, which suits a patient who refuses burr holes; it is done unilaterally on the dominant side first, with staged contralateral treatment now possible in selected cases. Anticoagulation is usually paused around either procedure. Levodopa does not help ET, toxin has a limited role because of hand weakness, and haloperidol has no place.

src.where: Case 78 A stimulating treatment for essential tremor

qx.stem: A 58-year-old teacher from Lampang has had tremor in both hands for ten years while holding a cup or writing, with mild head nodding. His father had a similar tremor, the tremor improves a little with a glass of wine, and there is no rest tremor, bradykinesia or rigidity. Tremor impairs handwriting and he has no cardiac or airway disease.
qx.q: Which is an appropriate first-line medication?
opts: Levodopa
Trihexyphenidyl
Propranolol or primidone
Clonazepam as monotherapy
Tetrabenazine
qx.why: Bilateral postural and kinetic arm tremor, a family history and alcohol responsiveness without parkinsonian signs indicate essential tremor, whose first-line drugs are propranolol and primidone (topiramate as an alternative). Levodopa and anticholinergics are for parkinsonism, tetrabenazine for hyperkinetic disorders such as chorea, and benzodiazepines are not recommended as monotherapy. Refractory disabling tremor may benefit from focused ultrasound or thalamic deep brain stimulation.

ddx.pt: Rest tremor, bradykinesia, asymmetric
Irregular, position-specific, with dystonic posturing and a sensory trick
Fine, fast, caused by thyrotoxicosis, caffeine or drugs

aN: classical essential tremor | et | benign essential tremor | familial tremor

det.patho: Essential tremor is thought to arise from abnormal oscillation in cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuits; pathology studies describe Purkinje cell changes in some brains. It is among the most frequent movement disorders, rising steeply with age, and about half of patients report an affected relative, consistent with autosomal dominant transmission of uncertain genes.
det.clinical: The tremor is bilateral (mildly asymmetric is allowed), affects the hands and forearms during posture and action, and is present for at least three years by definition. It may also involve the head, voice or legs and typically worsens with stress, caffeine and fatigue; many patients notice temporary improvement with alcohol. The 2018 consensus introduced 'ET plus' for patients with soft additional signs such as impaired tandem gait, questionable dystonic posturing or mild memory change. Isolated head or voice tremor, sudden onset, task-specific tremor or rest tremor should prompt reconsideration.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical: isolated bilateral upper-limb action tremor of three years or more, without other neurological signs. Watch the patient pour water or draw an Archimedes spiral to judge severity and axis. Check thyroid function and review drugs (valproate, lithium, beta-agonists, amiodarone, SSRIs). Copper studies are needed in young patients. DAT SPECT is normal and is useful only when distinguishing from tremor-dominant parkinsonism.
det.treatment: Treat when tremor interferes with daily life. Propranolol (avoid in asthma) and primidone are first-line, either alone or combined; topiramate and gabapentin are second-line options. Weighted cutlery, wrist weights and occupational therapy help. For disabling, drug-resistant tremor, options are thalamic (VIM) deep brain stimulation or MR-guided focused ultrasound thalamotomy, which is usually done on one side.
det.prognosis: It progresses slowly over decades and does not shorten life, though severe tremor can cause real disability and social embarrassment.
pearls: Tremor that is worse at the end of a finger-nose movement is kinetic/intention and fits ET; true rest tremor does not.
Spiral drawing shows a fixed tremor axis in ET; a variable, irregular pattern hints at dystonic tremor.
Primidone can make some patients feel sick and drowsy after the first dose — start very low.
det.thd: Essential tremor เป็นภาวะมือสั่นทั้งสองข้างขณะยกมือค้างหรือขณะใช้งาน เกิดจากวงจร cerebellum-thalamus-cortex ทำงานผิดจังหวะ มักมีคนในครอบครัวเป็นและดีขึ้นชั่วคราวเมื่อดื่มแอลกอฮอล์ วินิจฉัยทางคลินิกโดยไม่มีอาการเคลื่อนไหวช้าหรือเกร็ง ควรตรวจไทรอยด์และทบทวนยาที่ทำให้สั่น ยาหลักคือ propranolol หรือ primidone ถ้าไม่ได้ผลพิจารณา DBS หรือ focused ultrasound

name: ETF-QO deficiency
formal: Multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency caused by ETFDH mutations, the commonest cause of riboflavin-responsive lipid storage myopathy with proximal weakness and episodic vomiting.
simple: An inherited energy-metabolism defect causing muscle weakness and episodes of illness, which often improves with vitamin B2.
more: Biopsy shows lipid vacuoles; high-dose riboflavin and CoQ10 give dramatic improvement.
th: ภาวะพร่องเอนไซม์ ETF-QO จากยีน ETFDH ทำให้ไขมันสะสมในกล้ามเนื้อ อ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขา และตอบสนองดีมากต่อวิตามิน B2
tempoNote: Late-onset form fluctuates: weeks of worsening weakness, often triggered by fasting, infection or exercise
feat: Proximal and neck-extensor weakness with exercise intolerance, often in teens or young adults
Bouts of vomiting, lethargy or hypoglycaemia during fasting or illness
Masticatory or swallowing weakness may appear; some have muscle pain
Strikingly fast recovery after riboflavin is started
inv: Plasma acylcarnitines: raised short-, medium- and long-chain species together
Urine organic acids: glutaric, ethylmalonic and dicarboxylic acids, best caught during a crisis
Muscle biopsy: lipid droplets in type 1 fibres (oil red O)
ETFDH gene testing confirms

case.who: 19-year-old female university student from Nakhon Ratchasima
case.story: Two months of difficulty climbing stairs and holding her head up, worse after skipping meals during exams; two episodes of vomiting.
case.exam: Neck extensor and hip flexor weakness grade 4-/5, reflexes preserved, no sensory signs.
case.tests: CK 1,200 U/L; acylcarnitines show broad elevation of C4 to C18; biopsy shows lipid storage.
case.q: Which vitamin should be started before genetic results return?
case.a: Riboflavin — likely late-onset MADD from ETFDH (ETF-QO) deficiency; avoid fasting and add carnitine if low.

det.patho: ETF-QO, the product of ETFDH, passes electrons from many flavin-dependent dehydrogenases into the respiratory chain. Partial loss blocks fatty-acid oxidation and some amino-acid breakdown at once, so lipid accumulates in oxidative fibres. Many late-onset variants impair protein folding that can be partly rescued by extra FAD, which explains riboflavin responsiveness. Inheritance is autosomal recessive and the late-onset form appears especially common in East and Southeast Asia.
det.clinical: Neonatal forms are severe with acidosis and hypoglycaemia, but the neurologist usually meets the late-onset form: fluctuating proximal and neck weakness, fatigue and myalgia that worsen with fasting or illness. Episodic vomiting, encephalopathy or liver dysfunction may accompany crises. Bulbar or respiratory involvement can occur and should not be missed. A sensory neuropathy is reported in some patients.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in any lipid storage myopathy or unexplained fluctuating proximal weakness. Acylcarnitine profiling and urine organic acids are the key screening tests, though they may normalise between crises. Biopsy shows lipid excess and sometimes reduced CoQ10. ETFDH sequencing confirms; check free carnitine, glucose and liver function.
det.treatment: Start riboflavin (commonly 100–400 mg/day in adults) promptly; most patients improve within weeks. Avoid prolonged fasting, give frequent meals with carbohydrate cover during illness, and replace carnitine if deficient; CoQ10 is often added. Treat crises with intravenous glucose and avoid drugs that impair fat oxidation such as valproate.
det.prognosis: Late-onset riboflavin-responsive cases usually regain near-normal strength if treated early; neonatal forms carry high mortality.
pearls: Lipid storage myopathy in an Asian young adult: try riboflavin before anything else.
Head drop plus fasting-related vomiting is a useful clue.
Acylcarnitines may be normal between attacks; repeat during illness.
det.thd: ETF-QO deficiency เกิดจากยีน ETFDH ทำให้เผาผลาญไขมันไม่ได้ ไขมันจึงสะสมในกล้ามเนื้อ ผู้ป่วยวัยรุ่นหรือผู้ใหญ่ตอนต้นมีอ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขาและคอตก เป็นมากขึ้นเมื่ออดอาหารหรือเจ็บป่วย ตรวจ acylcarnitine และ urine organic acid ช่วยคัดกรอง ให้ riboflavin ขนาดสูงแล้วอาการมักดีขึ้นชัดเจน

ddx.pt: Episodic myoglobinuria after exertion with normal strength between attacks; no lipid-storage weakness
Also proximal and axial weakness, but vacuoles contain glycogen and acid alpha-glucosidase is low
Inflammatory infiltrates on biopsy and no fasting-linked metabolic crises

aN: etfdh deficiency | late onset madd | riboflavin responsive madd | rr madd | glutaric aciduria type ii etfdh

name: Exaggerated startle syndromes
formal: Disorders with excessive startle responses to unexpected stimuli, including hyperekplexia (GLRA1 mutations), startle epilepsy and functional startle, sometimes with stiffness and falls.
simple: Conditions where a surprise sound or touch triggers a very strong jump or stiffening, sometimes causing falls.
more: Diagnosis by clinical triad of startle, stiffness and falls with a positive nose-tap sign; genetic testing for GLRA1, SLC6A5 and GLRB. Clonazepam is first-line treatment and Vigevano manoeuvre can abort infant attacks; refractory cases may need valproate.
th: กลุ่มโรคที่สะดุ้งตกใจมากเกินต่อสิ่งกระตุ้นที่ไม่คาดคิด เช่น hyperekplexia จากยีน GLRA1 ลมชักที่กระตุ้นด้วยการตกใจ และแบบ functional
tempoNote: Hereditary hyperekplexia shows stiffness from birth; startle-triggered falls persist through life
feat: Excessive startle to unexpected noise, touch or movement, not habituating with repetition
Neonatal generalised stiffness that disappears in sleep (hereditary hyperekplexia)
Brief generalised stiffness after startle causing unprotected falls ('falls like a log'), with preserved consciousness
Positive nose-tap sign: tapping the nose provokes a persistent startle
Risk of apnoea and sudden death in infants; inguinal hernia common
inv: Genetic testing: GLRA1, SLC6A5, GLRB
EMG/neurophysiology: exaggerated brainstem startle reflex without habituation
EEG normal between events (distinguishes from startle epilepsy); MRI to exclude brainstem lesion in acquired cases

case.story: Since birth he becomes rigid when handled and has had two blue spells after being startled by a loud noise.
case.exam: Generalised hypertonia while awake, relaxes in sleep; tapping the tip of the nose causes repeated jerks and stiffening.
case.tests: EEG normal; GLRA1 pathogenic variant.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and how can parents abort a stiffness episode?
case.a: Hereditary hyperekplexia; give clonazepam, and use the Vigevano manoeuvre (flexing head and legs towards the trunk) to stop prolonged stiffness.

read.where: Chapter 21 - Abnormal Movements in Neurological Autoimmune Disorders

det.patho: Hereditary hyperekplexia results from defective glycinergic inhibition in the brainstem and spinal cord, caused by variants in the glycine receptor (GLRA1, GLRB) or the glycine transporter (SLC6A5). Without this inhibition the startle reflex is excessive and fails to habituate. Acquired startle syndromes arise from brainstem lesions, autoimmune disease or functional mechanisms; startle epilepsy arises from cortical lesions.
det.clinical: Infants show hypertonia in wakefulness, exaggerated startle and risk of apnoea; stiffness improves after the first year but excessive startle and falls continue. Adults may sustain injuries from unprotected falls. Startle epilepsy usually occurs in patients with cortical lesions and gives true seizures. Functional startle shows variable, inconsistent responses.
det.diagnosis: The triad of neonatal stiffness, excessive startle and startle-induced falls suggests hereditary hyperekplexia; confirm by genetic testing. Neurophysiology documents an exaggerated, non-habituating startle response. EEG helps separate startle epilepsy.
det.treatment: Clonazepam is first-line and very effective, as it enhances GABAergic inhibition. The Vigevano manoeuvre can abort prolonged infant stiffness and apnoea. Levetiracetam or valproate may be added in refractory cases. Startle epilepsy needs antiseizure drugs and sometimes surgery; functional startle needs physiotherapy and psychological support.
det.prognosis: Hereditary forms improve after infancy but excessive startle persists; prognosis is good with treatment.
pearls: Stiff neonate that relaxes in sleep + nose-tap startle = hyperekplexia.
Teach parents the Vigevano manoeuvre.
Clonazepam is the drug of choice.
det.thd: Exaggerated startle syndromes คือกลุ่มโรคที่ตกใจมากเกินต่อสิ่งกระตุ้นทั่วไป ชนิดพันธุกรรมคือ hyperekplexia จากยีน GLRA1 ทำให้ทารกตัวแข็งตอนตื่นแต่คลายตอนหลับ สะดุ้งมากเมื่อเคาะจมูก และอาจหยุดหายใจ ผู้ใหญ่ล้มตัวแข็งเมื่อตกใจแต่ยังรู้สึกตัว รักษาด้วย clonazepam และสอนผู้ปกครองทำ Vigevano manoeuvre ต้องแยกจาก startle epilepsy และ functional startle

name: Excessive fragmentary sleep myoclonus
formal: Benign electrophysiological finding of brief muscle twitches during non-REM sleep, with small amplitude and asynchronous EMG bursts, mostly incidental and not requiring treatment.
simple: Tiny muscle twitches during sleep that are usually harmless and found by chance.
th: การกระตุกเล็ก ๆ ของกล้ามเนื้อจำนวนมากระหว่างหลับ non-REM ที่เห็นใน PSG ส่วนใหญ่เป็นสิ่งที่พบโดยบังเอิญและไม่ต้องรักษา
tempoNote: Persistent finding across nights; usually discovered on polysomnography
feat: Tiny twitches of fingers, toes or mouth corners, often invisible to the bed partner
Brief, scattered, asynchronous EMG potentials in many muscles during NREM sleep
Frequently found with sleep apnoea, periodic limb movements or other sleep disorders
More common in middle-aged and older men
inv: Polysomnography with multiple-muscle EMG; defined by a sustained high rate of very short potentials in NREM sleep
Search for co-existing obstructive sleep apnoea or neuropathy

case.who: 58-year-old man, government officer from Khon Kaen
case.story: Referred for snoring and daytime sleepiness; wife notices nothing else at night.
case.exam: Obese, neck circumference large; neurological examination normal.
case.tests: PSG: AHI 32/h and many brief asynchronous EMG twitches in limbs throughout NREM sleep.
case.q: Do the twitches need specific treatment?
case.a: No — excessive fragmentary myoclonus is usually incidental; treat the obstructive sleep apnoea.

read.where: Chapter 4: Coma And Other States Of Altered Awareness In The Intensive Care Unit
Chapter 62: Neuromuscular Disease in the Neuroscience Intensive Care Unit

det.patho: The generator is unknown; a brainstem or subcortical origin of the brief discharges has been proposed. The EMG bursts are very short (usually under 150 ms) and lack cortical correlates. It may reflect sleep fragmentation or arousal instability and is common in apnoea.
det.clinical: This is mainly an electrophysiological label rather than a disease. Most people are unaware of the movements, which are small and scattered. Some have co-existing sleepiness or insomnia, but a causal link is unproven. It should not be confused with clinically disruptive myoclonus.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is made only on polysomnography by counting short EMG potentials over a prolonged period of NREM sleep. Exclude periodic limb movements, apnoea-related arousals and REM sleep behaviour disorder. Consider neuropathy or neurodegenerative disease if other signs exist.
det.treatment: No specific treatment is usually required. Treat associated conditions such as sleep apnoea. Clonazepam has been tried rarely when sleep is disrupted, with little evidence.
det.prognosis: Benign; it does not progress to a neurological disease on its own.
pearls: EFM is a PSG finding; the patient seldom complains of it.
Look for sleep apnoea whenever it is reported.
Do not treat a number on a report; treat symptoms.
det.thd: Excessive fragmentary sleep myoclonus คือการกระตุกเล็ก ๆ กระจายหลายกล้ามเนื้อระหว่างหลับ non-REM ที่เห็นจาก PSG มักไม่มีใครสังเกตเห็น พบร่วมกับภาวะหยุดหายใจขณะหลับได้บ่อย ส่วนใหญ่ไม่ต้องรักษา ให้มองหาและรักษาโรคการนอนที่พบร่วม

name: Exertional headache
formal: Primary headache provoked by sustained physical exercise, throbbing and bilateral, lasting minutes to hours, but secondary causes such as subarachnoid haemorrhage or cardiac cephalalgia must be excluded.
simple: A headache that starts during or after hard exercise, usually harmless but sometimes a sign of a more serious problem.
th: ปวดศีรษะที่เกิดจากการออกแรงหรือออกกำลังกาย ปวดตุบๆ สองข้าง นานไม่เกิน 48 ชั่วโมง ต้องแยกจากเลือดออกใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมองก่อน
tempoNote: Each episode lasts minutes to up to 48 hours, triggered only by sustained exertion
feat: Pulsating, bilateral headache brought on by and during sustained exercise
Commoner in hot weather or at altitude; often in young adults
No other cause found after investigation
First episode, sudden severe onset or neurological signs mandate exclusion of SAH, RCVS or dissection
Can overlap with migraine triggered by exercise
inv: First or atypical episode: CT brain and, if negative, lumbar puncture or CTA
MRI with MRA or CTA to exclude aneurysm, dissection, RCVS and posterior fossa lesions
Consider cardiac ischaemia (cardiac cephalalgia) in older patients with vascular risk

case.story: Three times in a month, a throbbing whole-head pain built up during evening training sessions and lasted about 4 hours; no thunderclap onset.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination and blood pressure.
case.tests: MRI brain with MRA and venography normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what can be offered?
case.a: Primary exercise headache; gradual warm-up, hydration and pre-exercise indometacin or a beta-blocker for frequent episodes.

det.patho: The mechanism is unclear; venous distension and transient rises in intracranial pressure during exertion are proposed, along with trigeminovascular activation as in migraine. Raised internal jugular venous reflux has been suggested in some studies.
det.clinical: Headache develops during or just after sustained exercise, is throbbing and bilateral and lasts minutes to up to two days. It may last months and then remit. The main task is to exclude secondary causes, which are more likely with older age, sudden onset, vomiting, altered consciousness or focal signs. Cardiac cephalalgia is exertional head pain from myocardial ischaemia relieved by rest or nitrates.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 criteria require headache brought on only by strenuous exercise, lasting less than 48 hours, with no other cause identified. The first episode needs imaging, ideally with vascular imaging, and LP if SAH is a concern.
det.treatment: Avoiding sudden strenuous exertion and building up with warm-up helps. Indometacin taken before exercise is commonly effective. Propranolol is an option for frequent episodes. Treat underlying migraine if present.
det.prognosis: Benign once secondary causes are excluded; tends to remit over months to years.
pearls: First exercise headache is SAH until proven otherwise.
Indometacin before exercise is the usual preventive.
Exertional headache with chest symptoms in an older patient: think cardiac cephalalgia.
det.thd: Exertional headache หรือ primary exercise headache คือปวดศีรษะตุบๆ ทั้งสองข้างที่เกิดเฉพาะตอนออกกำลังกายหนัก นานไม่เกิน 48 ชั่วโมง ครั้งแรกต้องตรวจหาสาเหตุอันตราย เช่น subarachnoid haemorrhage, RCVS และหลอดเลือดฉีกขาด ถ้าผลตรวจปกติถือว่าเป็นชนิดไม่ร้ายแรง ป้องกันด้วยการ warm-up และรับประทาน indometacin ก่อนออกกำลัง

name: Exploding head syndrome
formal: Benign parasomnia with perception of a loud bang or explosion at sleep-wake transitions, without pain, thought to arise from brainstem dysregulation of auditory sleep-wake transition.
simple: Hearing a sudden loud bang or explosion in the head while falling asleep or waking up, without pain and without danger.
th: ภาวะ parasomnia ที่ไม่อันตราย ผู้ป่วยได้ยินเสียงดังระเบิดในหัวขณะกำลังหลับหรือตื่น โดยไม่มีอาการปวด
tempoNote: Brief attacks lasting a second or less, clustering over days or weeks then remitting
feat: Sudden sensation of a loud bang, explosion or crash inside the head at sleep onset or on waking
Painless; may be accompanied by a flash of light or a myoclonic jerk
Causes fright, tachycardia and fear of stroke or brain haemorrhage
Benign and often self-limiting; more common with stress and sleep deprivation
Classified as a parasomnia in ICSD-3
inv: Clinical diagnosis; no tests needed in typical cases
Polysomnography or EEG only if atypical or seizures suspected
Neuroimaging only if pain or focal symptoms accompany attacks

case.who: 39-year-old office worker from Bangkok during a stressful audit period
case.story: Several times a week, just as she drifts off, she hears a gunshot-like bang inside her head and wakes with her heart racing; no pain follows.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination.
case.tests: None required; she has no headache, aura or nocturnal confusion.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the management?
case.a: Exploding head syndrome; explanation and reassurance, improving sleep and stress, and clomipramine only if very frequent and distressing.

read.where: Chapter 29 Disorders of Sleep — Other Forms of Parasomnia

det.patho: The mechanism is unknown. A favoured explanation is delayed or uncoordinated shutdown of auditory brainstem reticular neurons during the transition into sleep, producing a burst of perceived sound. Similar abrupt sensory phenomena occur as hypnic jerks. It is not associated with structural or epileptic brain disease.
det.clinical: Patients hear a sudden very loud noise — explosion, gunshot or door slam — lasting a moment, usually when falling asleep. Some see a flash of light or feel an electric sensation. It is frightening but painless and leaves no deficit. Episodes cluster over periods of stress or sleep loss and may disappear for months.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical based on the brief painless noise at sleep–wake transitions. Absence of pain distinguishes it from thunderclap and hypnic headaches. Investigations are reserved for atypical features such as pain, prolonged symptoms, confusion or neurological deficits.
det.treatment: Explanation and reassurance are usually enough and often reduce frequency. Address sleep deprivation, irregular schedules and stress. Clomipramine, topiramate, nifedipine and calcium channel blockers have been reported in small case series for severe, frequent attacks.
det.prognosis: Benign; many patients improve after reassurance and the condition often remits spontaneously.
pearls: Loud bang at sleep onset without pain: exploding head syndrome, not a haemorrhage.
Reassurance is the main treatment.
Any pain with the event should redirect toward headache disorders.
det.thd: Exploding head syndrome เป็น parasomnia ที่ไม่อันตราย ผู้ป่วยได้ยินเสียงดังคล้ายระเบิดหรือปืนในหัวขณะกำลังหลับหรือเพิ่งตื่นเพียงชั่วครู่ โดยไม่มีอาการปวด อาจเห็นแสงแวบร่วมด้วย ทำให้ตกใจกลัวว่าเป็นโรคสมอง การวินิจฉัยเป็นทางคลินิก การรักษาหลักคืออธิบายและให้ความมั่นใจ ปรับการนอนและลดความเครียด

name: Extradural haematoma
formal: Collection of blood between skull and dura, typically from middle meningeal artery tear after temporal bone fracture, with lucid interval, rapid deterioration and a biconvex lentiform CT appearance.
simple: Bleeding between the skull and the brain's outer covering after a head injury, which can quickly press on the brain and needs urgent surgery.
th: เลือดออกระหว่างกะโหลกศีรษะกับเยื่อดูรา มักจากหลอดเลือด middle meningeal ฉีกขาดจากกะโหลกขมับแตก อาจมีช่วงรู้สึกตัวดีก่อนทรุดลง
tempoNote: Deterioration over minutes to hours after head injury
feat: Head injury, often with temporal skull fracture, in young adults
Brief loss of consciousness, a lucid interval, then rapid decline (in a minority)
Headache, vomiting, ipsilateral dilated pupil and contralateral hemiparesis as herniation develops
Biconvex (lentiform) hyperdensity that does not cross suture lines on CT
Surgical emergency with excellent outcome if evacuated early
inv: Urgent non-contrast CT head with bone windows
Coagulation profile, platelets and group and crossmatch
CT cervical spine as part of trauma work-up

case.who: 22-year-old motorcycle rider from Nakhon Ratchasima without a helmet
case.story: Struck the left side of his head, was briefly knocked out, then talked normally in the emergency room; 2 hours later he became drowsy and vomited.
case.exam: GCS dropped to 9, left pupil dilated and sluggish, right-sided weakness.
case.tests: CT: left temporal biconvex hyperdense collection with temporal bone fracture and midline shift.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and immediate management?
case.a: Acute extradural haematoma with transtentorial herniation; emergency craniotomy and evacuation.

read.where: Chapter 28 Disorders of Consciousness and Intensive Care Neurology — Extradural Haematoma

det.patho: Most extradural haematomas follow a temporal or parietal fracture tearing the middle meningeal artery, so blood strips the dura from the inner table under arterial pressure. Venous sources (dural sinus, diploic veins) cause slower collections, including in the posterior fossa. The dura's tight attachment at sutures limits spread and creates the lens shape.
det.clinical: The classic lucid interval occurs in only a minority; many patients are unconscious from the outset or never lose consciousness. Expanding haematoma causes headache, vomiting, drowsiness and uncal herniation with a fixed dilated ipsilateral pupil and contralateral weakness. Posterior fossa extradural haematoma can cause sudden respiratory arrest. Children may present with pallor and falling haemoglobin.
det.diagnosis: Non-contrast CT is diagnostic: a biconvex hyperdense collection limited by sutures, often with an overlying fracture. Swirl sign of mixed density suggests active bleeding. Repeat CT is needed if the patient worsens.
det.treatment: Symptomatic or large haematomas (commonly over 30 mL, thickness over 15 mm or midline shift over 5 mm) need urgent craniotomy. Small, asymptomatic collections may be observed with serial CT in a neurosurgical setting. Correct coagulopathy, manage airway and ICP, and treat associated injuries. Burr-hole decompression may be lifesaving where neurosurgery is unavailable.
det.prognosis: Very good if treated before deep coma; mortality rises sharply with delayed surgery and bilateral fixed pupils.
pearls: A talking patient after head injury can still die from an extradural haematoma.
Biconvex, does not cross sutures: extradural; crescentic, crosses sutures: subdural.
Posterior fossa EDH can kill quickly via brainstem compression.
det.thd: Extradural haematoma คือเลือดออกระหว่างกะโหลกกับเยื่อดูรา มักเกิดจากกะโหลกขมับแตกทำให้หลอดเลือด middle meningeal ฉีกขาด ผู้ป่วยบางรายรู้สึกตัวดีช่วงหนึ่งก่อนซึมลงอย่างรวดเร็ว รูม่านตาข้างเดียวกันขยายและแขนขาด้านตรงข้ามอ่อนแรง CT พบก้อนเลือดรูปเลนส์นูนสองด้าน ต้องผ่าตัดเอาเลือดออกด่วน ผลการรักษาดีถ้าผ่าตัดทัน

name: Extrapyramidal diseases
formal: Disorders of the basal ganglia and associated pathways, including parkinsonism, dystonia, chorea, tics and tremor, with disturbed tone, posture and involuntary movement without paralysis.
simple: Illnesses of deep brain areas that control movement, causing slowness, stiffness or unwanted movements rather than weakness.
th: กลุ่มโรคของ basal ganglia ทำให้มีการเคลื่อนไหวช้าหรือเกินปกติ เช่น พาร์กินสัน dystonia chorea tic และ tremor โดยไม่มีอัมพาต
tempoNote: Most degenerative causes are chronic; drug-induced or vascular causes can be acute
feat: Two broad families: hypokinetic (parkinsonism) and hyperkinetic (chorea, dystonia, tics, myoclonus, tremor)
Strength and reflexes largely preserved; the problem is speed, tone and involuntary movement
Movements often worsen with stress and lessen in sleep
Causes include degeneration, drugs, vascular lesions, metabolic, genetic and autoimmune disease
inv: Careful drug history (antipsychotics, antiemetics, valproate) first
MRI brain; copper studies in anyone under 50; thyroid, glucose and calcium
Dopamine transporter imaging or genetics in selected cases

case.story: Three months of slowness and stiffness after starting flunarizine for dizziness.
case.exam: Symmetric bradykinesia and rigidity, mild postural tremor, no weakness.
case.tests: MRI normal; serum copper normal.
case.q: Which extrapyramidal category is this, and what is the first step?
case.a: Drug-induced parkinsonism (hypokinetic); stop flunarizine and reassess over months.

read.where: 27 - Functional (psychogenic) movement disorders: Phenomenology, diagnosis, and treatment
Chapter 8: Rating Scales in Movement Disorders

det.patho: The term is historical: it contrasts motor pathways outside the pyramidal tract, chiefly basal ganglia circuits with thalamus and cortex. Loss of nigral dopamine produces hypokinesia, whereas striatal or subthalamic dysfunction tends to release excess movement. Cerebellar disorders are usually classed separately even though they also affect movement.
det.clinical: This entry is an umbrella heading, not a single disease. Clinically one first names the phenomenology (parkinsonism, tremor, dystonia, chorea, ballism, tics, myoclonus), then the tempo and distribution, then searches for a cause. Drug-induced syndromes are common and reversible.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical and relies on phenomenology; video review helps. Exclude drugs, Wilson disease in younger people, structural lesions, thyroid and metabolic causes. Genetic panels, DaT-SPECT and autoimmune testing are targeted by the pattern.
det.treatment: Treat the cause where possible and the symptom otherwise: dopaminergic drugs for parkinsonism, botulinum toxin for focal dystonia, VMAT2 inhibitors for chorea or tardive dyskinesia, and deep brain stimulation in selected disorders. Physiotherapy and fall prevention matter in all.
det.prognosis: Depends entirely on the specific disorder.
pearls: Name the movement before naming the disease.
Always review medications first.
Under 50 with any movement disorder: check for Wilson disease.
det.thd: Extrapyramidal diseases เป็นชื่อรวมของโรคที่เกิดจาก basal ganglia แบ่งเป็นกลุ่มเคลื่อนไหวช้า (parkinsonism) และกลุ่มเคลื่อนไหวเกิน (chorea, dystonia, tic, myoclonus, tremor) ไม่มีอ่อนแรงจริง ควรระบุชนิดการเคลื่อนไหวก่อน แล้วค้นหาสาเหตุ โดยเริ่มจากยาที่ใช้และโรค Wilson ในคนอายุน้อย

name: Extrapyramidal rigidity
formal: Increased resistance throughout the range of passive movement (lead-pipe or cogwheel) from basal ganglia dysfunction, as in Parkinson disease, independent of movement speed.
simple: A steady stiffness in the muscles when someone moves your limb, typical of Parkinson disease.
th: ความตึงแข็งชนิดต้านเท่ากันตลอดช่วงการเคลื่อนไหว (lead-pipe) ที่พบในพาร์กินสันและโรคกลุ่มพาร์กินสัน ไม่ขึ้นกับความเร็วของการเหยียดงอ
tempoNote: Sign that develops with the underlying disorder; abrupt with neuroleptic malignant syndrome
feat: Equal resistance in flexors and extensors through the whole range (lead-pipe)
Ratchety catches when tremor is superimposed (cogwheeling)
Independent of speed of passive movement, unlike spasticity
Increases with activation of the opposite limb (Froment manoeuvre)
Often asymmetric in Parkinson disease; axial in PSP; dystonic or fever-linked in toxic states
inv: Bedside comparison with spasticity and paratonia using slow and fast passive movement
Search for cause: drug history, MRI, DaT-SPECT when doubtful
CK, temperature and autonomic signs if neuroleptic malignant syndrome is possible

case.story: His right arm has felt stiff for a year, his handwriting has become small, and his wife notes he swings that arm less when he walks.
case.exam: Right wrist shows smooth resistance at all speeds, increased when he opens and closes the left fist; reflexes normal and plantars flexor.
case.tests: No investigation is needed for the sign itself; DaT-SPECT shows reduced left putamen uptake.
case.q: How do you tell this from spasticity at the bedside?
case.a: Rigidity is speed-independent and affects agonist and antagonist alike, without clasp-knife release or hyperreflexia; it is boosted by activation.

read.where: 8 Overview of Parkinsonism and Approach to Differential Diagnosis
1 - Clinical overview and phenomenology of movement disorders

det.patho: Rigidity results from loss of basal ganglia modulation of brainstem and spinal circuits, which raises tonic stretch-reflex gain at long latency in both agonist and antagonist muscles. In contrast with spasticity, the short-latency reflex is normal. Dopaminergic depletion or blockade is the main mechanism, with additional contributions from other basal ganglia disorders.
det.clinical: Examiners feel a constant plastic resistance when passively moving the wrist, elbow or neck. Tremor adds cogwheel catches. Rigidity affects posture, causing flexed trunk and limbs, and axial rigidity of the neck is typical in PSP. It is found in Parkinson disease, atypical parkinsonism, drug-induced parkinsonism, Wilson disease and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
det.diagnosis: Test with relaxed limbs and varied speeds, compare both sides and use reinforcement by contralateral movement. Neck rigidity and a fever or altered consciousness suggest toxic or infectious causes. Imaging and DaT-SPECT are used for the underlying disorder, while CK is raised in neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
det.treatment: Treat the cause. Levodopa is most effective for rigidity in Parkinson disease, with dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors and amantadine as adjuncts. Stop dopamine antagonists, and in neuroleptic malignant syndrome give cooling, fluids, dantrolene or bromocriptine in intensive care. Physiotherapy keeps range of motion.
det.prognosis: Depends on the underlying disorder; rigidity in Parkinson disease usually responds well to levodopa.
pearls: Speed-independent resistance plus an activation effect means rigidity, not spasticity.
Sudden severe rigidity with fever after a drug change: think neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
Neck rigidity with early falls points to PSP.
det.thd: Extrapyramidal rigidity คือแรงต้านที่สม่ำเสมอเมื่อผู้ตรวจขยับแขนขาแบบ passive เหมือนบิดท่อตะกั่ว (lead-pipe) ทั้งกล้ามเนื้อเหยียดและงอ ไม่ขึ้นกับความเร็ว ถ้ามีอาการสั่นร่วมจะรู้สึกสะดุดเป็นจังหวะ (cogwheeling) และจะชัดขึ้นเมื่อให้ผู้ป่วยขยับแขนอีกข้าง ต่างจาก spasticity ที่ขึ้นกับความเร็วและมีรีเฟล็กซ์ไวร่วมด้วย พบในพาร์กินสัน ยาต้านโดปามีน Wilson และ NMS การรักษาตามสาเหตุ ในพาร์กินสันใช้ levodopa ได้ผลดี

name: Fabry disease
formal: X-linked lysosomal alpha-galactosidase A deficiency with acral neuropathic pain, angiokeratomas, corneal opacities, renal and cardiac disease and early-onset stroke.
simple: An inherited condition where a fatty substance builds up in cells, causing burning hand and foot pain, and kidney, heart and stroke problems.
more: Diagnose with leucocyte alpha-galactosidase A enzyme activity in men and GLA sequencing in women; plasma lyso-Gb3 and MRI showing pulvinar T1 hyperintensity help. Treat with agalsidase enzyme replacement or migalastat; control pain with carbamazepine.
th: โรค lysosomal storage X-linked — ปวดแสบร้อนมือเท้าตั้งแต่เด็ก, angiokeratoma, ไตเสื่อม, หัวใจหนา, stroke อายุน้อย รักษาด้วย ERT ได้
tempoNote: Painful crises from childhood; organ damage accumulates through adult life
feat: Burning hand and foot pain and episodic pain crises with fever, heat or exercise (small-fibre neuropathy)
Reduced sweating, heat intolerance, gastrointestinal cramps
Angiokeratomas (bathing-trunk area), whorled corneal opacities (cornea verticillata)
Proteinuria and renal failure, left ventricular hypertrophy, young stroke (posterior circulation, dolichoectasia)
Women heterozygotes can be significantly affected
inv: Males: α-galactosidase A enzyme activity (dried blood spot or leukocytes)
Females: GLA gene sequencing (enzyme often normal); plasma lyso-Gb3
Urine protein, eGFR, echo/cardiac MRI, ECG, brain MRI, slit-lamp exam

case.story: Burning hands and feet since childhood, worse with fever and hot weather; barely sweats; now admitted with sudden vertigo and ataxia.
case.exam: Clusters of dark red papules around the umbilicus and thighs; right limb ataxia; corneal whorls on slit lamp.
case.tests: MRI: acute right cerebellar infarct, white-matter lesions and dilated basilar artery; proteinuria 1.2 g/day; low α-Gal A activity; GLA variant.
case.q: Which other organs need staging, and what disease-specific therapy exists?
case.a: Kidney, heart (LVH, arrhythmia) and eyes. Enzyme replacement (agalsidase alfa/beta, pegunigalsidase) or oral migalastat for amenable variants; plus standard stroke prevention.

read.where: Section 3 Hereditary and Genetic Conditions and Malformations
Chapter 17 Neurologic Complications of Electrolyte Disturbances

det.patho: Pathogenic GLA variants reduce α-galactosidase A, so globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) and lyso-Gb3 accumulate in vascular endothelium, smooth muscle, dorsal root ganglia, kidney podocytes and cardiomyocytes. Inheritance is X-linked; hemizygous males with classic variants are most severe, but heterozygous females show variable disease due to X-inactivation. Late-onset variants may affect mainly the heart or kidney.
det.clinical: Classic males present in childhood with acroparaesthesia, pain crises triggered by fever, heat or exertion, hypohidrosis and gastrointestinal symptoms. Angiokeratomas and corneal whorls appear early. In adulthood proteinuria progresses to renal failure, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with arrhythmia develops, and strokes or TIAs occur at young age, often posterior circulation with vertebrobasilar dolichoectasia. Hearing loss and depression are common.
det.diagnosis: In males, low α-Gal A enzyme activity is diagnostic and gene testing confirms the variant. In females enzyme activity can be normal, so GLA sequencing is required; lyso-Gb3 helps assess pathogenicity of uncertain variants. Brain MRI may show white-matter lesions and pulvinar T1 hyperintensity. Fabry should be screened in young cryptogenic stroke, unexplained LVH and unexplained proteinuria. Cascade testing of relatives is essential.
det.treatment: Disease-specific options are enzyme replacement therapy (agalsidase alfa, agalsidase beta, pegunigalsidase alfa) and the oral chaperone migalastat for amenable variants; earlier treatment gives better outcomes. Adjunctive care includes ACE inhibitors/ARBs for proteinuria, antiplatelets and risk-factor control for stroke prevention, cardiac rhythm monitoring, and neuropathic pain treatment (carbamazepine, gabapentinoids). Avoid triggers such as overheating.
det.prognosis: Untreated classic males have reduced life expectancy due to renal, cardiac and cerebrovascular disease; treatment slows organ decline, particularly if started before irreversible damage.
pearls: Childhood burning hands and feet with heat intolerance and poor sweating: look for angiokeratomas.
Women are not just carriers — test the gene, not the enzyme.
Consider Fabry in young stroke with a dilated basilar artery or proteinuria.
det.thd: Fabry disease เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมแบบ X-linked ที่ขาดเอนไซม์ α-galactosidase A ทำให้ Gb3 สะสมในหลอดเลือด เส้นประสาท ไต และหัวใจ ผู้ป่วยปวดแสบร้อนมือเท้าตั้งแต่เด็ก เหงื่อออกน้อย มี angiokeratoma และ cornea verticillata ต่อมามีโปรตีนรั่วในปัสสาวะ หัวใจหนา และ stroke อายุน้อย ผู้ชายวินิจฉัยด้วยระดับเอนไซม์ ผู้หญิงต้องตรวจยีน รักษาด้วย enzyme replacement หรือ migalastat ร่วมกับดูแลไต หัวใจ และป้องกัน stroke

qx.stem: A 31-year-old man has a left thalamic and right cerebellar infarct. He has had burning pain in his hands and feet since childhood that worsens with fever, cannot sweat during football, and has small dark-red papules around the umbilicus. Urinalysis shows proteinuria and ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy. MRI also shows a dilated basilar artery.
qx.q: What is the most useful first diagnostic test?
opts: Serum ferritin and transferrin saturation
Very long chain fatty acids
Leukocyte alpha-galactosidase A enzyme activity
Serum lactate and mitochondrial DNA analysis
Antiphospholipid antibody panel
qx.why: Acroparesthesia, hypohidrosis, angiokeratomas, kidney and cardiac involvement with posterior-circulation stroke and basilar dolichoectasia suggest Fabry disease, an X-linked deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A. In men, low enzyme activity is diagnostic and GLA sequencing confirms it; women often have normal enzyme activity and need genetic testing. Enzyme replacement or migalastat for amenable variants is available.

name: Facial palsy
formal: Weakness of facial muscles from lesion of the facial nerve or its pathway; lower motor neuron types affect the whole face (Bell palsy, Ramsay Hunt), upper motor neuron types spare the forehead.
simple: Weakness or drooping of one side of the face because the nerve or brain pathways controlling it are damaged.
th: อัมพาตใบหน้า แบบ LMN อ่อนแรงทั้งซีก (เช่น Bell's palsy) ส่วนแบบ UMN หน้าผากไม่อ่อนแรง (เช่น stroke)
tempoNote: Bell palsy evolves over 48–72 hours; slowly progressive palsy suggests tumour
feat: A sign/syndrome with many causes rather than one disease
LMN: whole half of face weak, including forehead; poor eye closure, Bell phenomenon
UMN: lower face weak with forehead relatively spared
Associated clues: hyperacusis, taste loss, vesicles (Ramsay Hunt), parotid mass, bilateral palsy (GBS, Lyme, sarcoid)
Bell palsy is the commonest cause but a diagnosis of exclusion
inv: Clinical exam including ear, parotid and other cranial nerves
Blood glucose; HIV and other tests in bilateral or recurrent cases
MRI with contrast if atypical, progressive, recurrent or no recovery by 3 months
Neurophysiology (ENoG) for prognosis in complete palsy

case.story: Woke up unable to close her right eye; drink dribbles from the right mouth corner. Mild ache behind the right ear the day before.
case.exam: Right complete LMN facial weakness including forehead, Bell phenomenon, no vesicles, other cranial nerves normal, no limb signs.
case.tests: Glucose normal; no imaging needed at presentation.
case.q: Why is this LMN and what treatment improves outcome?
case.a: Forehead involvement shows a peripheral facial nerve lesion (Bell palsy); prednisolone within 72 hours plus eye protection improves recovery.

read.where: Chapter 13 Cranial Nerve Disorders — Facial Nerve (VII)
17. Lower Brainstem and Cranial Nerve Dysfunction

det.patho: The facial nerve leaves the pons, crosses the cerebellopontine angle and runs a long bony course through the temporal bone before supplying facial muscles via the parotid. Lesions anywhere along this path cause LMN weakness, while lesions above the facial nucleus spare the forehead because its supply is bilateral. Inflammation within the narrow labyrinthine segment is thought to underlie Bell palsy.
det.clinical: This is a sign rather than a disease. Acute LMN palsy with ear pain is usually Bell palsy, but vesicles suggest herpes zoster, bilateral palsy suggests GBS, sarcoidosis or Lyme disease, and gradual progression points to tumour. Involvement of taste, tearing and hearing helps localise the lesion within the temporal bone. Brain stem lesions add sixth nerve or limb signs.
det.diagnosis: Decide UMN versus LMN by forehead function, then examine ear, parotid, other cranial nerves and limbs. Investigations are targeted: glucose, serology and CSF for bilateral cases, MRI for atypical features or poor recovery. ENoG within the first two weeks predicts outcome in complete palsy.
det.treatment: For Bell palsy, start oral prednisolone within 72 hours; antivirals may be added in severe palsy but evidence is modest. For Ramsay Hunt syndrome, steroids plus antivirals are standard. Eye protection with lubricants, taping at night and urgent ophthalmology for exposure keratitis are essential. Treat specific causes such as GBS or tumours accordingly.
det.prognosis: About 70–85% of Bell palsy recovers fully; incomplete palsy and early recovery predict good outcome; Ramsay Hunt recovers less well.
pearls: Forehead weakness = LMN; forehead sparing = UMN (usually).
Bilateral facial palsy is rarely Bell palsy – think GBS, sarcoid, Lyme, HIV.
Always protect the cornea.
det.thd: Facial palsy คืออาการใบหน้าอ่อนแรง แยกเป็นแบบ LMN ซึ่งอ่อนแรงทั้งซีกรวมหน้าผาก เช่น Bell's palsy และ Ramsay Hunt กับแบบ UMN ที่หน้าผากยังย่นได้ เช่น stroke ต้องตรวจหู ต่อมน้ำลาย และเส้นประสาทสมองอื่นเพื่อหาสาเหตุ Bell's palsy รักษาด้วย prednisolone ภายใน 72 ชั่วโมง และต้องป้องกันกระจกตาเสมอ

name: Facial-onset sensory motor neuronopathy (FOSMN)
formal: Rare slowly progressive disorder starting with perioral and facial numbness, then bulbar and limb weakness, with abnormal blink reflexes, resembling a motor neuron disease with trigeminal sensory involvement.
simple: A rare disease that starts with numbness around the face, followed by weakness of the face, throat and limbs.
ab: Facial onset sensory and motor neuronopathy
th: โรคหายากที่เริ่มด้วยชารอบปากและใบหน้า แล้วลามลงคอ แขน พร้อมกลืนลำบากและกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงลีบคล้าย ALS
tempoNote: Very slow progression over years to decades, spreading downward from face to neck, arms and trunk
feat: Starts with numbness or burning in the trigeminal territory, often perioral and spreading outwards
Later bulbar weakness, tongue fasciculation, neck and shoulder wasting
Sensory loss spreads in a descending, cape-like pattern
Blink reflex R1/R2 absent or delayed; denervation in cranial and cervical muscles
TDP-43 pathology reported; sometimes a positive family history or ALS-linked variants
inv: Blink reflex and facial nerve studies; EMG of bulbar and limb muscles
Nerve conduction: reduced sensory potentials in upper limbs
MRI brainstem; CSF and antibodies to exclude Sjögren, sarcoid and infiltration
Genetic testing for ALS-related genes in selected cases

case.story: Five years of numb lips and cheeks, now choking on water and his shoulders look thin.
case.exam: Reduced facial pinprick in both trigeminal territories, absent corneal reflexes, tongue fasciculation, wasting of deltoids, reflexes reduced in arms.
case.tests: Blink reflex absent bilaterally; EMG chronic denervation in tongue and C5–C6 muscles; anti-Ro negative; MRI normal.
case.q: What is the syndrome and how does it differ from typical ALS?
case.a: FOSMN; early facial sensory loss and much slower course distinguish it from ALS.

read.where: Chapter 15 Disorders of the Motor Cells: The Motor Neuron Diseases — Other Forms

det.patho: FOSMN is a rare neurodegenerative disorder affecting the trigeminal sensory nucleus and ganglion and lower motor neurons in a rostral-to-caudal sequence. Autopsy studies show TDP-43 inclusions, placing it close to the ALS spectrum, and some patients carry ALS-associated gene variants. An immune contribution has been proposed because a few respond to immunotherapy.
det.clinical: Facial numbness or paraesthesia, typically starting around the mouth, precedes motor symptoms by months to years. Dysphagia, dysarthria and weakness of neck and shoulders follow, with sensory loss creeping down the upper body. Upper motor neuron signs are mild or absent. Many survive more than a decade, though respiratory and bulbar failure can eventually occur.
det.diagnosis: Characteristic features are facial-onset sensory loss with abnormal blink reflexes and subsequent lower motor neuron findings. Exclude Sjögren syndrome, sarcoidosis, Kennedy disease, leptomeningeal infiltration and brainstem lesions. Nerve conduction often shows reduced upper limb sensory potentials. There are no specific biomarkers.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy is established. Trials of IVIG or other immunotherapy are sometimes offered, with limited and inconsistent benefit. Care follows MND principles: swallowing assessment, gastrostomy, non-invasive ventilation, physiotherapy and palliative input. Riluzole has been used empirically without proven effect.
det.prognosis: Slow progression over years; disability is mainly from bulbar and respiratory involvement.
pearls: Face numb first, then bulbar weakness: think FOSMN.
An absent blink reflex is a useful neurophysiological marker.
Course is much slower than ALS; counsel accordingly.
det.thd: FOSMN เป็นโรคหายากที่เริ่มด้วยอาการชารอบปากและใบหน้า แล้วค่อยๆ มีกลืนลำบาก พูดไม่ชัด และกล้ามเนื้อคอและไหล่ลีบ คล้าย ALS แต่มีความผิดปกติด้านรับความรู้สึกและดำเนินโรคช้ากว่ามาก ตรวจ blink reflex ผิดปกติและ EMG พบ denervation ต้องแยก Sjögren และ sarcoidosis ยังไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ ดูแลแบบประคับประคองเหมือน MND

name: Faciomandibular myoclonus
formal: Rhythmic or irregular jerks of the facial and jaw muscles, as in propriospinal or brainstem myoclonus, or symptomatic of anti-IgLON5 disease, brainstem lesions and the like.
simple: Quick jerks of the face and jaw muscles that the person cannot control.
th: การกระตุกของกล้ามเนื้อขากรรไกรและใบหน้าเป็นพัก ๆ มักเกิดขณะหลับ ทำให้กัดลิ้นหรือมีเสียงกระทบฟัน
tempoNote: Recurrent nightly jerks over months or years
feat: Sudden brief jaw-closing jerks, often in NREM sleep, sometimes with tongue biting or bleeding
Bed partner hears a click or tap of the teeth
May co-exist with sleep bruxism or other sleep disorders
Similar jaw or facial jerks can occur with brainstem lesions, Whipple disease or rare autoimmune encephalopathies
inv: Video polysomnography with masseter and orbicularis oris EMG
EEG to exclude nocturnal seizures; MRI brainstem if jerks occur awake or with other signs

case.story: Wakes several times a month with a bitten tongue and blood on the pillow; no limb jerks or incontinence.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination; small scars on the lateral tongue.
case.tests: Video-PSG: brief masseter bursts with jaw closure in stage N2 sleep without EEG epileptiform activity.
case.q: What nocturnal condition must be excluded first?
case.a: Nocturnal epileptic seizures; with a normal EEG this fits sleep-related faciomandibular myoclonus.

read.where: Chapter 29 Disorders of Sleep — Sleep-Related Movement Disorders

det.patho: The mechanism is uncertain; a brainstem generator activating trigeminal motor nuclei during sleep is suspected. Symptomatic jaw myoclonus arises from lesions of the pons or medulla, from Whipple disease (myorhythmia) or, rarely, autoimmune and neurodegenerative disease.
det.clinical: The primary sleep form is benign but distressing because of tongue biting. Symptomatic forms often occur also while awake and come with other brainstem signs. Distinguish from rhythmic bruxism, which is a run of chewing-like contractions.
det.diagnosis: Video-PSG with masseter EMG captures brief jerks rather than rhythmic bruxing. EEG helps exclude epilepsy. Brain MRI and, if suggestive, tests for Whipple disease or autoimmune antibodies should be done when red flags exist.
det.treatment: Reassurance and a dental guard to protect the tongue are often enough; clonazepam at night can reduce jerks. Treat any symptomatic cause directly, for example antibiotics in Whipple disease.
det.prognosis: Primary sleep-related form is benign; symptomatic forms follow their cause.
pearls: Tongue biting at night is not always epilepsy.
Ask whether jerks also happen awake: that points to a symptomatic cause.
Oculomasticatory myorhythmia is nearly diagnostic of Whipple disease.
det.thd: Faciomandibular myoclonus คือการกระตุกของขากรรไกรเป็นจังหวะสั้น ๆ มักเกิดขณะหลับ ทำให้กัดลิ้น ต้องแยกจากชักกลางคืนด้วย video-PSG และ EEG ชนิดที่เกิดขณะหลับอย่างเดียวมักไม่อันตราย ใช้ที่ครอบฟันหรือ clonazepam ได้ ถ้ามีขณะตื่นหรืออาการก้านสมองร่วม ให้หาสาเหตุ

Rhythmic oculo-masticatory movements with weight loss, diarrhoea and supranuclear gaze problems
Abnormal sleep behaviours with stridor, bulbar dysfunction and gait problems in older adults

name: Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD)
formal: Autosomal dominant dystrophy from D4Z4 repeat contraction with DUX4 derepression, causing facial, scapular and humeral weakness, scapular winging and asymmetric progression, often with retinal vasculopathy.
simple: An inherited muscle disease that weakens the face, shoulders and upper arms, usually starting in teens or adulthood.
more: Diagnosis rests on 4q35 D4Z4 repeat contraction testing; CK is normal or mildly raised, and MRI shows asymmetric fatty replacement with STIR signal. Care is supportive with scapular fixation in selected patients; hearing and retinal screening is advised.
th: กล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมทางพันธุกรรม — หน้า สะบัก ต้นแขนอ่อนแรงแบบไม่เท่ากันสองข้าง สะบักยกเวลายกแขน
feat: Facial weakness: cannot whistle or bury eyelashes
Asymmetric scapular winging that rides up when the arms are raised
Biceps/triceps wasting with relatively preserved forearm ('Popeye arm')
Abdominal weakness (Beevor sign) and later foot drop
inv: Genetic testing: D4Z4 repeat contraction on 4q35 (FSHD1) or SMCHD1-related hypomethylation (FSHD2)
CK normal to modestly raised
Audiology and retinal screening in early-onset cases

case.story: Cannot lift his right arm above shoulder level to put things on a shelf; friends say his smile looks flat.
case.exam: Weak eye closure, asymmetric winging worse on the right, umbilicus moves up on sitting up.
case.tests: CK 380 U/L; genetic test: shortened D4Z4 array on a permissive 4qA allele.
case.q: Name the abdominal sign and what it implies.
case.a: Beevor sign — lower abdominal muscles weaker than upper; common in FSHD.

qx.stem: A 34-year-old rubber-plantation worker from Surat Thani cannot whistle or drink through a straw and has struggled to hang washing for years. Examination shows asymmetric facial weakness, high-riding winged scapulae with a 'poly-hill' shoulder outline, weak lower abdominal muscles with a positive Beevor sign and a right foot drop. Deltoids are relatively spared. CK is 410 U/L. His mother has milder shoulder weakness.
qx.q: Which genetic test is most appropriate first?
opts: CTG repeat sizing in DMPK
Dystrophin gene deletion and duplication analysis
SMN1 copy-number testing
Mitochondrial DNA sequencing from blood
Sizing of the D4Z4 repeat array on chromosome 4q35 with haplotype analysis
qx.why: Asymmetric face, scapular-fixator, abdominal and peroneal weakness with deltoid sparing and dominant inheritance is classic FSHD. Most cases (FSHD1) have a contracted D4Z4 array on a permissive 4qA allele that allows DUX4 expression; if this is normal, FSHD2 (D4Z4 hypomethylation, usually SMCHD1 variants) is tested next. Patients should also have hearing and retinal screening and respiratory review. Myotonic dystrophy and dystrophinopathies do not produce this pattern.

ddx.pt: Symmetric, face spared, often higher CK
Early respiratory weakness, paraspinal involvement
Older onset, finger flexors and quadriceps

det.patho: FSHD results from inappropriate expression of the DUX4 gene in skeletal muscle, which is toxic to muscle cells. In FSHD1 (about 95%) the D4Z4 macrosatellite array on chromosome 4q35 is contracted to 1–10 units on a permissive 4qA haplotype that supplies a polyadenylation signal; in FSHD2, variants in SMCHD1 (or DNMT3B, LRIF1) cause D4Z4 hypomethylation. Inheritance in FSHD1 is autosomal dominant with variable penetrance, and de novo cases occur. It is among the most common muscular dystrophies.
det.clinical: Onset is usually in the teens or twenties with facial weakness (difficulty whistling, drinking through a straw, incomplete eye closure) and scapular fixator weakness that causes winging, a high-riding scapula on arm abduction and difficulty lifting arms overhead. Asymmetry is a hallmark. Later involvement includes biceps and triceps with sparing of deltoid and forearm, abdominal weakness with Beevor sign and lumbar lordosis, and foot drop. Early-onset severe forms have hearing loss and retinal vasculopathy (Coats-like). Cardiac and respiratory involvement are uncommon but can occur in severe cases.
det.diagnosis: Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis: measurement of D4Z4 repeat size and 4qA haplotype for FSHD1, and methylation analysis plus SMCHD1 sequencing for FSHD2. CK is normal or mildly raised, and EMG is myopathic. Muscle MRI shows asymmetric, selective involvement and can direct testing. Biopsy is seldom required and may show inflammation, causing confusion with myositis. Consider Pompe disease, LGMDs, scapuloperoneal syndromes, myasthenia and IBM in the differential.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying treatment yet; DUX4-targeted therapies are in trials. Care includes physiotherapy and aerobic exercise, ankle-foot orthoses for foot drop, scapular fixation surgery in selected patients with good deltoid strength, eye protection for incomplete closure, and pain management. Screen hearing and retina in early-onset cases, check respiratory function in severe or early-onset disease, and offer genetic counselling.
det.prognosis: Progression is slow and variable; most remain ambulant, though about one in five eventually need a wheelchair. Life expectancy is usually normal.
pearls: Asymmetric scapular winging plus facial weakness = FSHD.
Beevor sign (umbilicus moves upward on sitting up) is common in FSHD.
Deltoid and forearm are relatively spared, giving the 'Popeye arm' appearance.
det.thd: FSHD เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมทางพันธุกรรมจากยีน DUX4 ที่ถูกแสดงออกผิดปกติในกล้ามเนื้อ ชนิด FSHD1 เกิดจาก D4Z4 บนโครโมโซม 4q35 สั้นลง ส่วน FSHD2 เกิดจากยีน SMCHD1 อาการเริ่มวัยรุ่นหรือวัยหนุ่มสาว ใบหน้าอ่อนแรง ผิวปากไม่ได้ หลับตาไม่สนิท สะบักยกและกางเวลายกแขน มักไม่เท่ากันสองข้าง และต่อมามีกล้ามเนื้อท้องอ่อนแรง (Beevor sign) และเท้าตก วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจพันธุกรรม ยังไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ การดูแลเน้นกายภาพบำบัด อุปกรณ์ช่วยเท้าตก และคำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

name: Fahr’s disease
formal: Primary familial brain calcification with symmetrical calcium deposits in basal ganglia, dentate and cortex, causing parkinsonism, dystonia, cognitive decline and psychiatric symptoms; SLC20A2 and others implicated.
simple: A condition where calcium builds up in deep parts of the brain, leading to movement problems, memory loss and mood changes.
more: Familial or sporadic Fahr disease with bilateral calcification of basal ganglia, dentate and thalamus, causing parkinsonism, dementia and psychiatric features; genes include SLC20A2, PDGFB and XPR1.
th: โรคหินปูนสะสมในสมองทั้งสองข้างโดยไม่มีสาเหตุทางเมตาบอลิก ทำให้เกิดพาร์กินสัน dystonia สมองเสื่อม และอาการทางจิต
tempoNote: Calcification accumulates for years; symptoms often begin in 30s–50s, many carriers remain asymptomatic
feat: Symmetric calcification of globus pallidus, dentate nuclei, thalamus and subcortical white matter
Parkinsonism, dystonia, chorea or ataxia
Cognitive decline, depression, psychosis or mood change
Headache, seizures or migraine-like episodes in some
Many relatives have calcification on CT without any symptoms
inv: CT brain: the most sensitive way to show calcium
Calcium, phosphate, PTH, vitamin D and magnesium to exclude hypoparathyroidism and mimics
Genetic testing: SLC20A2, PDGFRB, PDGFB, XPR1 (dominant); MYORG, JAM2 (recessive)

case.story: Two years of slowness, mood swings and paranoid ideas; his mother had 'calcium in the brain' on a CT.
case.exam: Symmetric bradykinesia, mild dysarthria, impaired executive tests.
case.tests: CT: dense bilateral pallidal, dentate and thalamic calcification; calcium, phosphate and PTH normal.
case.q: Which metabolic cause must be excluded before calling this primary?
case.a: Hypoparathyroidism or pseudohypoparathyroidism — check calcium, phosphate and PTH; with normal tests and family history it is primary familial brain calcification.

det.patho: Most known genes affect phosphate handling across the brain vasculature or the integrity of the neurovascular unit, leading to calcium-phosphate deposits around small vessels. Dominant forms (SLC20A2 most common) show reduced penetrance; recessive forms (MYORG, JAM2) are often more severe. The term Fahr disease is still used but primary familial brain calcification is preferred.
det.clinical: Presentations range from none to a combined movement, cognitive and psychiatric syndrome. Parkinsonism is the commonest motor feature, often poorly levodopa-responsive. Psychiatric symptoms may come first. The extent of calcification correlates only loosely with symptoms.
det.diagnosis: Bilateral calcification on CT plus progressive neurological symptoms, after excluding parathyroid, infectious (e.g. congenital infection, HIV), toxic and mitochondrial causes. Genetic testing confirms the familial form and helps counselling.
det.treatment: There is no proven therapy to remove calcium. Treat symptoms: trial of levodopa, antipsychotics with caution, antiseizure drugs, and cognitive support. Correct any metabolic abnormality if found.
det.prognosis: Variable; slowly progressive in symptomatic patients, while many carriers stay well.
pearls: Always check calcium, phosphate and PTH before calling it primary.
CT shows calcium far better than MRI.
Mild pallidal calcification in the elderly is normal.
det.thd: Fahr’s disease หรือ primary familial brain calcification คือภาวะหินปูนสะสมในสมองทั้งสองข้าง บริเวณ basal ganglia, dentate และ thalamus ทำให้มีพาร์กินสัน อาการทางจิต และความจำเสื่อม ต้องตรวจแคลเซียม ฟอสเฟต และ PTH เพื่อแยกภาวะพาราไทรอยด์ต่ำก่อน การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคองตามอาการ

name: Familial adult myoclonic epilepsy (FAME)
formal: Autosomal dominant epilepsy from intronic TTTCA repeat expansions with adult-onset cortical tremor, myoclonus and infrequent generalised seizures, a form of cortical tremor with epilepsy.
simple: An inherited condition of fine shaking, jerks and occasional seizures that begins in adulthood.
more: Autosomal dominant cortical tremor and myoclonic epilepsy (also FAME) with adult onset tremulous myoclonus, infrequent seizures and photosensitivity, linked to intronic repeat expansions. Autosomal dominant syndrome of fine postural tremor-like cortical myoclonus, infrequent seizures and photosensitivity, with giant SEPs, now largely overlapping with FAME.
ab: Familial cortical myoclonic tremor with epilepsy
merged: Familial cortical myoclonic tremor with epilepsy
th: ลมชักถ่ายทอดแบบยีนเด่น เริ่มในวัยผู้ใหญ่ มีมือสั่นจาก cortex ร่วมกับกระตุกและชักนาน ๆ ครั้ง จากการขยายตัวของซ้ำ TTTCA
tempoNote: Cortical tremor usually starts in the 20s–40s, slowly worsens with age; seizures are infrequent
feat: Fine, irregular 'tremor' of the hands that is actually rhythmic cortical myoclonus, worse with posture and action
Infrequent generalised tonic-clonic seizures, often triggered by sleep deprivation or photic stimulation
Autosomal dominant family history, often misdiagnosed as essential tremor
Photosensitivity and giant somatosensory evoked potentials
Mild cerebellar signs or cognitive change with ageing in some families
inv: EEG: generalised spike-wave and photoparoxysmal response
SEP: giant cortical responses; long-latency (C) reflexes; jerk-locked back-averaging
Genetic testing for intronic TTTCA/TTTTA repeat expansions (SAMD12, STARD7, MARCHF6 and others) — needs long-read or repeat-primed PCR

case.story: Shaky hands for ten years, diagnosed as essential tremor; propranolol does not help. Two convulsions after night shifts. Her mother and uncle have shaky hands too.
case.exam: Irregular jerky postural 'tremor' of both hands, myoclonus on finger-nose test; no ataxia.
case.tests: EEG photoparoxysmal response; giant SEP; repeat expansion in SAMD12.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and what drug helps both features?
case.a: FAME (cortical tremor with epilepsy); valproate, levetiracetam or clonazepam reduce both myoclonus and seizures.

read.where: 5 Electrophysiological Approaches to the Movement Disorder Patient

det.patho: FAME is caused by expansions of non-coding pentanucleotide repeats (TTTTA with inserted TTTCA) in introns of several genes, especially SAMD12 in Asian families. The inserted TTTCA motif appears pathogenic regardless of host gene. Cortical hyperexcitability produces rhythmic myoclonus, and cerebellar Purkinje cell pathology has been described.
det.clinical: Most patients present in adulthood with tremulous hand movements resembling tremor, sometimes with jerks of the voice or legs. Seizures are typically rare, generalised and provoked. Longer repeats are associated with earlier onset (anticipation), and older patients may show progression or mild cognitive changes.
det.diagnosis: Suspect FAME in familial 'tremor' that does not respond to tremor drugs, especially with seizures or photosensitivity. Neurophysiology demonstrating cortical myoclonus is helpful. Genetic confirmation requires repeat-expansion testing, which standard exome sequencing may miss.
det.treatment: Valproate, levetiracetam, clonazepam, perampanel and brivaracetam help myoclonus and seizures. Avoid sodium-channel blockers such as carbamazepine and lamotrigine where possible. Lifestyle advice on sleep and light triggers is useful.
det.prognosis: Generally benign with treatment, though tremor may progress slowly in old age.
pearls: Familial 'essential tremor' with seizures: think FAME.
Giant SEP and jerky irregular tremor point to cortical myoclonus.
Repeat-expansion testing is needed; exome may be negative.
det.thd: FAME เป็นโรคลมชักถ่ายทอดแบบยีนเด่น เกิดจากการขยายตัวของซ้ำ TTTCA ในอินทรอน (มักที่ SAMD12 ในคนเอเชีย) ผู้ป่วยวัยผู้ใหญ่มีมือสั่นไม่สม่ำเสมอซึ่งแท้จริงเป็นการกระตุกจาก cortex มักถูกวินิจฉัยผิดเป็น essential tremor และมีชักนาน ๆ ครั้งเมื่ออดนอน ตรวจพบ giant SEP และไวต่อแสง รักษาด้วย valproate, levetiracetam หรือ clonazepam

name: Familial amyloid polyneuropathy (FAP)
formal: Autosomal dominant transthyretin amyloidosis with length-dependent sensorimotor and autonomic neuropathy, carpal tunnel syndrome and cardiac involvement; treatable with silencers or stabilisers.
simple: An inherited disease where an abnormal protein builds up in nerves, causing numbness, weakness and problems with blood pressure and digestion.
more: Confirm with TTR gene sequencing and tissue biopsy with Congo red apple-green birefringence; scintigraphy detects cardiac involvement. Liver transplantation, tafamidis, patisiran, vutrisiran or inotersen treat the disease.
th: เส้นประสาทเสื่อมจาก amyloid ของ transthyretin ที่กลายพันธุ์ — ชาปวดปลายเท้า ระบบอัตโนมัติเสีย หัวใจหนา รักษาได้ด้วย TTR silencer/stabiliser
tempoNote: Adult onset (20s–70s depending on variant); progresses over years
feat: Length-dependent painful sensory neuropathy beginning with small fibres, later motor weakness
Autonomic failure: orthostatic hypotension, diarrhoea/constipation, erectile dysfunction, weight loss
Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, often years before
Cardiomyopathy (thick ventricular walls, conduction disease); vitreous opacities, nephropathy
inv: NCS/EMG: axonal sensorimotor neuropathy; small-fibre and autonomic testing
TTR gene sequencing (e.g. Val30Met, Ala97Ser — the latter frequent in Taiwan/Asia)
Tissue for amyloid (fat pad, salivary gland, nerve) with typing; echocardiogram, NT-proBNP, cardiac MRI or scintigraphy

case.story: Two years of burning feet, then lightheadedness on standing, alternating diarrhoea and 10 kg weight loss; carpal tunnel surgery on both hands 5 years ago.
case.exam: Distal pin and temperature loss to knees, mild toe weakness, absent ankle jerks, postural BP fall 35 mmHg.
case.tests: NCS: axonal neuropathy; echo: LV wall 15 mm; fat pad Congo red positive; TTR variant confirmed; free light chains normal.
case.q: Why exclude AL amyloidosis, and what treatments are available?
case.a: AL is treated by chemotherapy against the plasma cell clone, so light chains must be checked. For ATTRv neuropathy, TTR gene silencers (patisiran, vutrisiran, inotersen, eplontersen) or the stabiliser tafamidis slow progression.

det.patho: Point mutations in TTR destabilise the transthyretin tetramer, which dissociates into monomers that misfold and deposit as amyloid in nerve, dorsal root ganglia, autonomic ganglia, heart, kidney and eye. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with variable penetrance; the liver produces almost all circulating TTR. Endemic early-onset Val30Met clusters exist in Portugal, Sweden and Japan, while Asian populations show other variants and later onset.
det.clinical: Typical disease starts with painful small-fibre symptoms in the feet, progressing upward and later to motor weakness and gait failure. Autonomic dysfunction is early and prominent. Carpal tunnel syndrome, unexplained weight loss, heart failure with thick ventricles, and vitreous opacities are important clues. Late-onset forms in men over 50 may lack family history and mimic CIDP or idiopathic axonal neuropathy.
det.diagnosis: Suspect ATTRv in progressive axonal neuropathy with autonomic failure, carpal tunnel or cardiac thickening. TTR genetic testing is the key test; tissue biopsy with Congo red and mass spectrometry typing confirms amyloid. Always exclude AL amyloid with serum and urine immunofixation and free light chains. Staging includes NCS, autonomic tests, echocardiography, cardiac MRI or bone scintigraphy, renal and eye assessment.
det.treatment: Disease-modifying options include TTR silencers—siRNA (patisiran, vutrisiran) and antisense oligonucleotides (inotersen, eplontersen)—and the tetramer stabiliser tafamidis (diflunisal off-label); liver transplantation is now rarely used. Supportive care covers neuropathic pain, orthostatic hypotension, gastrointestinal symptoms, nutrition, pacing for conduction disease and heart failure. Inotersen requires platelet and renal monitoring; silencers require vitamin A supplementation. Offer genetic counselling and screen carriers.
det.prognosis: Untreated, death occurs about 7–12 years after onset from cachexia, cardiac disease or infection; early treatment considerably slows progression.
pearls: Neuropathy plus autonomic failure plus bilateral carpal tunnel = test TTR.
Exclude AL amyloid with free light chains before labelling ATTR.
Late-onset sporadic-looking cases are common; family history is often absent.
det.thd: FAP หรือ ATTRv amyloidosis เกิดจาก mutation ของยีน TTR ทำให้ transthyretin พับผิดรูปและสะสมเป็น amyloid ที่เส้นประสาท หัวใจ ไต และตา ผู้ป่วยชาแสบร้อนปลายเท้า ความดันตกเมื่อยืน ท้องเสียสลับท้องผูก น้ำหนักลด มี carpal tunnel ทั้งสองข้าง และหัวใจห้องล่างหนา วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีน TTR และชิ้นเนื้อย้อม Congo red ต้องแยก AL amyloid เสมอ รักษาด้วย TTR silencer หรือ tafamidis

qx.stem: A 58-year-old man from Chiang Mai has progressive burning feet, carpal tunnel syndrome, orthostatic dizziness and diarrhoea. Biopsy and genetic testing confirm hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis with polyneuropathy. The team reviews disease-modifying options.
qx.q: Which of the following lowers hepatic transthyretin production by RNA interference?
opts: Tafamidis
Vutrisiran
Diflunisal
Eplontersen
Intravenous immunoglobulin
qx.why: Gene silencers reduce circulating transthyretin by 85% to 90%: vutrisiran and patisiran are small interfering RNAs, whereas inotersen and eplontersen are antisense oligonucleotides. Tafamidis and diflunisal stabilise the tetramer instead. Amyloid neuropathy should be suspected when a progressive neuropathy comes with autonomic failure, carpal tunnel syndrome, cardiomyopathy or weight loss, and it is treatable.

name: Primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency with ataxia (ARCA2/COQ8A)
formal: Autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxia with coenzyme Q10 deficiency (ADCK3/COQ8A and others), with cerebellar atrophy, seizures, cognitive impairment and exercise intolerance.
simple: An inherited balance disorder caused by low levels of a cell energy molecule called coenzyme Q10.
more: Muscle biopsy CoQ10 level and genetic testing confirm it. High-dose oral CoQ10 may improve symptoms, especially if started early.
th: ataxia ยีนด้อยจากการสร้าง coenzyme Q10 บกพร่อง (COQ8A) — เริ่มวัยเด็ก สมองน้อยฝ่อ ชัก กระตุก เหนื่อยง่าย อาจดีขึ้นบางส่วนด้วย CoQ10 ขนาดสูง
tempoNote: Onset usually in childhood or adolescence, very slowly progressive; some adults remain ambulant
feat: Childhood-onset cerebellar dysarthria with gait and limb ataxia that worsens slowly
Myoclonus, tremor or dystonia; seizures in some
Mild intellectual disability or cognitive slowing
Exercise intolerance or muscle fatigue
Neuropathy usually absent
inv: MRI: cerebellar atrophy (sometimes marked); occasional stroke-like cortical lesions
Serum lactate may be mildly raised; plasma CoQ10 is unreliable (diet and lipids affect it)
Muscle or fibroblast CoQ10 measurement when available
COQ8A gene testing within a recessive-ataxia panel or exome

case.story: Unsteady since age 5, slowly worse; quick jerks of the hands, tires early in football, two seizures last year.
case.exam: Gait and limb ataxia, action myoclonus, normal reflexes and sensation, mild learning difficulty.
case.tests: MRI: cerebellar atrophy; lactate 2.6 mmol/L; NCS normal; exome finds biallelic COQ8A variants.
case.q: What treatment is worth trying and what response should you expect?
case.a: High-dose oral coenzyme Q10 — some patients improve modestly or stabilise, but response is variable and partial.

read.where: Review: Autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxias for which treatment is available; Table 3 (autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxia type 2)
Chapter 24 Cerebellar Ataxias and Related Conditions — Inherited Ataxia Syndromes

det.patho: Coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone) carries electrons in the respiratory chain and acts as an antioxidant. COQ8A (formerly ADCK3/CABC1) encodes a regulatory kinase-like protein needed for CoQ10 biosynthesis; biallelic variants reduce CoQ10 in tissues and cause the recessive ataxia ARCA2 (also called SCAR9). Other primary CoQ10 genes (e.g. COQ2, COQ4, PDSS2) give multisystem, renal or infantile phenotypes. Deficiency is called primary when a biosynthesis gene is faulty and secondary when tissue CoQ10 falls because of another disorder — for example ARSACS, AOA1, ETFDH-related multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency or mtDNA depletion; the distinction matters because primary forms are the ones most likely to respond to supplementation. Low CoQ10 slows the hand-over of electrons from complex I and complex II onward to complex III and increases oxidative stress, to which Purkinje cells seem especially vulnerable.
det.clinical: Most patients have a childhood-onset, very slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, often with myoclonus, tremor, dystonia, epilepsy, mild cognitive impairment and exercise intolerance, sometimes with a mildly raised CK. Neuropathy is not a feature, which helps distinguish it from many other recessive ataxias. Stroke-like episodes and adult onset are described. The wider primary CoQ10 family looks different: COQ2, COQ6 and PDSS2 variants cause infantile encephalomyopathy with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (sometimes with deafness, optic atrophy or retinopathy), COQ4 a severe neonatal multisystem illness, while an isolated lipid-storage myopathy with myoglobinuria usually reflects secondary deficiency.
det.diagnosis: Suspect in a recessive ataxia with cerebellar atrophy, no neuropathy, and extra features such as myoclonus or seizures. Muscle CoQ10 is more informative than plasma; lactate may be up but is often normal. Muscle biopsy may look nearly normal, yet combined complex I+III and II+III activities (the CoQ-dependent steps) are reduced, and fibroblast CoQ10 or biosynthesis assays can confirm a primary defect. Genetic testing (panel or exome) usually provides the answer. In any child with encephalopathy plus steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome, measure CoQ10 and test the CoQ genes urgently.
det.treatment: Oral CoQ10 is reasonable in all patients, typically in high doses (for example 5–30 mg/kg/day of ubiquinone, divided with meals); benefits are inconsistent, from no change to modest improvement. Timing matters: in infantile COQ2 disease, supplementation reversed much of the neurological picture but not kidney damage that was already established, so supplements should start once the disorder is suspected, without waiting for genetic proof. Treat seizures and myoclonus with standard drugs, avoiding valproate if mitochondrial dysfunction is uncertain. Rehabilitation and genetic counselling apply, and asymptomatic affected siblings may be candidates for early supplementation.
det.prognosis: Slow progression; many patients remain ambulant into adulthood.
pearls: Childhood ataxia + cerebellar atrophy + myoclonus/seizures + no neuropathy: think COQ8A.
Plasma CoQ10 is a poor diagnostic test; rely on genetics or muscle.
Always offer a CoQ10 trial — it is one of the few potentially treatable recessive ataxias.
Primary (biosynthesis gene) deficiency responds better than secondary deficiency; encephalopathy + steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome = test CoQ10 genes.
det.thd: ARCA2 เกิดจากยีน COQ8A ทำให้สร้าง coenzyme Q10 ได้น้อย ผู้ป่วยเริ่มเดินเซในวัยเด็กและแย่ลงช้า ๆ มีสมองน้อยฝ่อ อาจมีกระตุก ชัก สติปัญญาบกพร่องเล็กน้อย และเหนื่อยง่าย แต่มักไม่มีเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเสื่อม วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีน ร่วมกับวัด CoQ10 ในกล้ามเนื้อหรือ fibroblast ต้องแยกภาวะพร่องปฐมภูมิ (ยีนสร้าง CoQ10) จากทุติยภูมิ (เช่น ARSACS, AOA1) เพราะชนิดปฐมภูมิตอบสนองต่อการเสริมดีกว่า ควรลองให้ CoQ10 ขนาดสูงโดยเร็วเพราะบางรายดีขึ้น และในเด็กที่มีอาการสมองร่วมกับ nephrotic syndrome ที่ไม่ตอบสนองต่อสเตียรอยด์ต้องนึกถึงโรคกลุ่มนี้
