formal: Primary familial brain calcification with symmetrical calcium deposits in basal ganglia, dentate and cortex, causing parkinsonism, dystonia, cognitive decline and psychiatric symptoms; SLC20A2 and others implicated.
simple: A condition where calcium builds up in deep parts of the brain, leading to movement problems, memory loss and mood changes.
th: หินปูนในสมองชนิดถ่ายทอดในครอบครัวที่มี dystonia เด่น เป็นส่วนหนึ่งของกลุ่ม primary familial brain calcification
tempoNote: Slowly progressive over years; onset variable between families
feat: Focal or segmental dystonia (cranial, cervical, limb) with symmetric basal ganglia calcification
Often accompanied later by parkinsonism, dysarthria or cognitive change
Dominant inheritance pattern in most families

case.story: Neck twisting to the right for a year; her brother has a similar tremor and both had abnormal CT scans.
case.exam: Cervical dystonia with head tremor, mild bilateral bradykinesia.
case.tests: CT: bilateral pallidal and dentate calcification; PTH and calcium normal; SLC20A2 variant found.
case.q: How should the dystonia be treated?
case.a: Botulinum toxin for cervical dystonia as in other causes; offer family genetic counselling.

det.patho: This historical label refers to families with brain calcification in whom dystonia dominates. The underlying genes are the same as in primary familial brain calcification, chiefly SLC20A2 and PDGFB/PDGFRB, which disturb phosphate transport or pericyte support of the blood-brain barrier.
det.clinical: Dystonia may be focal, segmental or generalised and is frequently combined with parkinsonism. Some family members carry calcification without symptoms. Cognitive and psychiatric features often appear with time.
det.diagnosis: Confirm calcification on CT, exclude metabolic and acquired causes, and seek a genetic diagnosis. A careful family examination often finds affected relatives.
det.treatment: Symptomatic: botulinum toxin for focal dystonia, anticholinergics or levodopa trials, and physiotherapy. Deep brain stimulation is rarely reported and of uncertain benefit.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; severity varies widely even within one family.
pearls: Treat it as part of primary familial brain calcification.
Screen relatives with history and CT only when results will change care.
Exclude hypoparathyroidism before labelling.

formal: Inherited tendency to frequent painful muscle cramps, often benign and of autosomal dominant pattern, sometimes with fasciculations, after exclusion of metabolic and neuropathic causes.
simple: An inherited tendency to get frequent painful muscle cramps.

Multiple family members across generations

case.story: Painful calf and thigh cramps during runs since age 15; his father and sister have the same problem.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination, a few fasciculations in calves.
case.tests: CK mildly raised after exercise; EMG normal apart from cramp discharges.
case.q: What must be excluded before calling it familial cramps?
case.a: Neuromyotonia, metabolic myopathy and motor neuron disease.

det.patho: Inherited motor nerve hyperexcitability is presumed; specific genes are known for some families, but many remain unexplained. Cramp discharges originate in distal motor axons.
det.clinical: Onset in adolescence or early adulthood with frequent cramps, often exercise-related. Neurological examination is normal. Some members may show fasciculations or mild CK elevation. The condition is benign.
det.diagnosis: A diagnosis of exclusion based on family history and normal examination. EMG distinguishes cramps from neuromyotonia and myopathy; forearm exercise testing excludes glycogenoses when contractures are suspected.
det.treatment: Stretching, hydration and conditioning. Membrane stabilisers such as mexiletine or carbamazepine, or gabapentinoids, are options when cramps are frequent. Avoid quinine.
det.prognosis: Benign and non-progressive, though symptoms persist.
pearls: A strong family history with normal examination supports a benign cramp disorder.
Exclude metabolic myopathy if cramps occur early in exercise.
Membrane stabilisers may reduce frequency.

name: Familial dyskinesia and facial myokimia
formal: Autosomal dominant ADCY5-related disorder with early-onset chorea, dystonia and myoclonus, especially orofacial, with facial myokimia and nocturnal exacerbations.
simple: An inherited condition with writhing and jerking movements from early life, and fine rippling of the facial muscles.

Perioral and periorbital facial twitching (myokymia) that worsens with stress, anxiety and drowsiness

case.who: 9-year-old girl from Khon Kaen, referred by the paediatrician
case.story: She has had jerky movements of her face and arms since toddlerhood. Her mother notes that twitching around the eyes and mouth increases when she is anxious or sleepy, and that movements continue at night. Seizures have not occurred.
case.exam: Intermittent orofacial chorea and perioral twitching, dystonic posturing of the hands when walking, mild axial hypotonia; cognition near normal.
case.tests: MRI brain and EEG normal. Gene panel shows a heterozygous pathogenic ADCY5 variant not found in parents.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what does the treatment depend on?
case.a: ADCY5-related dyskinesia with facial myokymia. No curative drug exists; trial of tetrabenazine, clonazepam, acetazolamide or trihexyphenidyl, cardiac review and genetic counselling.

read.where: Scoping Review on ADCY5-Related Movement Disorders

det.patho: ADCY5 encodes adenylyl cyclase 5, an enzyme abundant in striatal medium spiny neurons that couples dopamine D1 and adenosine A2A receptors to cAMP. Gain-of-function variants cause excess cAMP signalling and hyperkinetic movement. Inheritance is mostly autosomal dominant with many de novo variants, and a few recessive cases are reported.
det.clinical: The phenotype ranges from mild, non-progressive facial myokymia and chorea in adults to severe infantile hypotonia with developmental delay. Movements can be fluctuating, and brief paroxysmal attacks on a continuous background are common. Characteristic aggravators are emotion, drowsiness and awakening, and sleep may not abolish them. Mild or atypical cases are often mistaken for cerebral palsy, tics or epilepsy for years.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is genetic and is suspected from early-onset mixed hyperkinesia with facial twitching and nocturnal worsening. Normal MRI and EEG reduce other possibilities such as dyskinetic cerebral palsy, myoclonus-dystonia, PNKD, PRRT2 disorders and GLUT1 deficiency. Genetic counselling is recommended for families.
det.treatment: Management is symptomatic and multidisciplinary. Tetrabenazine, clonazepam, acetazolamide, trihexyphenidyl or levodopa may be tried, each with variable benefit, and caffeine is reported to help some patients. Pallidal deep brain stimulation has been used in severe cases. Cardiac and psychiatric review and developmental support are needed.
det.prognosis: Often non-progressive or slowly progressive with a normal life span; severity varies widely, and some patients plateau or improve in adult life.
pearls: Dyskinesia that persists in sleep without EEG change should prompt ADCY5 testing.
Facial myokymia (periocular, perioral) plus chorea in a child is a strong clue.
Look for the de novo variant and counsel the family.

det.patho: Episodic ataxias are channelopathies. EA1 results from KCNA1 potassium channel variants causing neuronal hyperexcitability, including peripheral nerve myokymia. EA2 results from loss-of-function CACNA1A variants of the P/Q-type calcium channel in Purkinje cells, impairing cerebellar output. At least eight types are described, many rare.
det.clinical: Attacks are stereotyped and provoked by exertion, emotion, caffeine or alcohol. EA1 attacks last seconds to minutes and may come many times a day. EA2 attacks last hours, with vertigo and vomiting, and a slowly progressive interictal ataxia develops in some. EA2 is allelic with familial hemiplegic migraine type 1 and SCA6, so families may show overlapping features.
det.diagnosis: Suspect with recurrent, stereotyped, reversible ataxia and a dominant family history. Examine between attacks for myokymia (EA1) or nystagmus (EA2). Genetic testing confirms the subtype. Exclude structural, metabolic (e.g. pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency, Hartnup) and demyelinating causes of episodic ataxia.
det.treatment: Acetazolamide reduces attacks in many EA2 and some EA1 patients; 4-aminopyridine is effective in EA2. Carbamazepine or other sodium-channel drugs may help EA1. Avoid identified triggers.
det.prognosis: Not life-threatening; some develop mild permanent ataxia over decades.
pearls: Interictal downbeat nystagmus points to EA2.
Twitching of the eyelids or hands between attacks suggests EA1.
Acetazolamide response is a useful clinical clue.
det.thd: Familial periodic ataxia หรือ episodic ataxia เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมยีนเด่นของ ion channel ทำให้เดินเซเป็นพัก ๆ EA1 จากยีน KCNA1 เป็นสั้น ๆ ไม่กี่นาทีและมีกล้ามเนื้อกระตุกเล็ก ๆ ส่วน EA2 จาก CACNA1A เป็นหลายชั่วโมงร่วมกับเวียนหัวและมี downbeat nystagmus ระหว่างช่วงปกติ วินิจฉัยด้วยตรวจยีน รักษาด้วย acetazolamide หรือ 4-aminopyridine

name: Fanconi syndrome
formal: Generalised proximal renal tubular dysfunction causing phosphate, glucose and amino acid wasting; hypophosphataemic osteomalacia and proximal myopathy, and may accompany mitochondrial and metabolic diseases.
simple: A kidney problem that loses salts, sugar and minerals in the urine, weakening bones and muscles.
th: ภาวะท่อไตส่วนต้นทำงานผิดปกติทั่วไป สูญเสียฟอสเฟต กลูโคส และกรดอะมิโนทางปัสสาวะ ทำให้กระดูกอ่อน (osteomalacia) และกล้ามเนื้อต้นแขนขาอ่อนแรง
tempoNote: Develops over months; acquired forms may follow drug exposure
feat: Renal disorder, not primarily neurological; relevant because it causes myopathy
Hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, normal-gap metabolic acidosis, glycosuria with normal glucose
Bone pain, fractures and proximal weakness from osteomalacia
Acquired causes: tenofovir, ifosfamide, myeloma light chains, heavy metals; inherited: cystinosis, Wilson, mitochondrial disease
Hypokalaemic paralysis can occur
inv: Serum phosphate, potassium, bicarbonate; urine glucose, protein, amino acids, phosphate excretion
Alkaline phosphatase, vitamin D, PTH; bone imaging for pseudofractures
Screen for paraprotein; review drugs

case.who: 45-year-old man on HIV treatment attending a Bangkok hospital clinic
case.story: Hip and rib pain for months, now struggles to get up from a chair; on a tenofovir disoproxil-containing regimen for years.
case.exam: Waddling gait, proximal leg weakness grade 4, tender ribs, reflexes brisk.
case.tests: Phosphate 0.5 mmol/L, potassium 3.0 mmol/L, bicarbonate 17 mmol/L; glycosuria with normal blood glucose; ALP raised; pelvic X-ray shows pseudofractures.
case.q: What is causing his weakness and what should change?
case.a: Tenofovir-induced Fanconi syndrome with hypophosphataemic osteomalacia; switch antiretroviral, replace phosphate, potassium and vitamin D.

det.patho: Fanconi syndrome is generalised failure of proximal tubular reabsorption, so phosphate, glucose, amino acids, bicarbonate, uric acid and potassium are lost in urine. The proximal tubule is energy-intensive and vulnerable to mitochondrial toxins and metabolic diseases. Chronic phosphate loss produces osteomalacia, which with hypokalaemia explains the muscle weakness.
det.clinical: This is a renal disorder; the neurological relevance is proximal myopathy and bone pain from osteomalacia, and occasionally hypokalaemic weakness. Children with inherited forms show rickets and growth failure. Adults often have a drug cause or a light chain disorder. Polyuria and dehydration may accompany it.
det.diagnosis: Look for glycosuria with normal blood glucose, low serum phosphate with high urinary phosphate excretion, aminoaciduria and normal-anion-gap acidosis. Identify the cause through drug review, paraprotein testing and, in children, metabolic or genetic testing. Imaging shows Looser zones in osteomalacia.
det.treatment: Remove or treat the cause, such as stopping tenofovir disoproxil or ifosfamide, or treating myeloma. Replace phosphate, potassium, bicarbonate and active vitamin D as needed. Cysteamine treats cystinosis. Muscle strength improves as bone and electrolytes recover.
det.prognosis: Drug-induced forms often improve after withdrawal; inherited forms depend on the underlying disease.
pearls: Glycosuria with normal blood glucose suggests proximal tubulopathy.
Tenofovir disoproxil is a common acquired cause in HIV clinics.
Proximal weakness plus bone pain and brisk reflexes: think osteomalacia.
det.thd: Fanconi syndrome เป็นโรคของท่อไตส่วนต้น ไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาทโดยตรง ทำให้เสียฟอสเฟต โพแทสเซียม กลูโคส และกรดอะมิโนทางปัสสาวะ จึงเกิดกระดูกอ่อนและกล้ามเนื้อต้นขาอ่อนแรง สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยในผู้ใหญ่คือยา เช่น tenofovir และ light chain จาก myeloma การรักษาคือหยุดสาเหตุและให้ฟอสเฟต โพแทสเซียม และวิตามินดี

ddx.pt: Low phosphate from refeeding or other causes without generalised tubular leak
Osteomalacia with low calcium and high PTH but no glycosuria or aminoaciduria
High calcium and PTH; phosphate low but tubular function otherwise normal

name: Fast channel syndrome
formal: Congenital myasthenic syndrome from CHRNE mutations causing rapid acetylcholine receptor channel closure, with reduced endplate response and fatigable weakness from infancy.
simple: An inherited form of muscle weakness from birth where signals from nerve to muscle do not work properly.
th: congenital myasthenic syndrome ที่ช่อง acetylcholine receptor ปิดเร็วเกินไป (เช่นจาก CHRNE) ทำให้อ่อนแรงล้าง่าย ตอบสนองต่อ pyridostigmine และ 3,4-DAP
tempoNote: Neonatal or infant onset; lifelong fatigable weakness with crises during infections
feat: Neonatal hypotonia, weak cry and suck, ptosis, ophthalmoparesis
Fatigable limb and bulbar weakness; apnoeic episodes with infections
Recessive; usually a missense variant combined with a null allele in an AChR subunit gene
Decrement on repetitive stimulation; no repetitive CMAP
Improves with pyridostigmine and 3,4-diaminopyridine; quinidine and fluoxetine harmful
inv: Repetitive nerve stimulation (decrement); single-fibre EMG
AChR and MuSK antibodies negative
Genetic testing of CHRNE, CHRNA1, CHRND

case.who: 6-month-old girl in a paediatric ward in Hat Yai
case.story: Weak suck since birth, droopy eyes, two episodes of apnoea with colds requiring ventilation.
case.exam: Bilateral ptosis, limited eye movements, weak cry, generalised hypotonia worse late in the day.
case.tests: RNS 3 Hz shows decrement; antibodies negative; CHRNE missense plus null variant identified.
case.q: Which drug class should be avoided here even though it helps slow-channel syndrome?
case.a: Fast-channel CMS; avoid quinidine/fluoxetine (open-channel blockers) and treat with pyridostigmine plus 3,4-DAP.

read.where: Chapter 17 Disorders of the Neuromuscular Junction — Congenital Myasthenic Syndromes

det.patho: Kinetic variants in AChR subunits reduce acetylcholine affinity or channel gating efficiency, so channels open briefly and close abnormally fast. The resulting endplate current is small and short, and the safety margin of transmission is lost. It is autosomal recessive, often with a kinetic variant on one allele and a null variant on the other.
det.clinical: It presents from birth or early infancy with feeding difficulty, ptosis and eye movement limitation. Weakness is fatigable and may cause life-threatening apnoea during infection or fever. Severity ranges from mild to severe. Unlike slow-channel syndrome, there is no repetitive CMAP and inheritance is recessive.
det.diagnosis: Decrement on RNS with negative antibodies in an infant suggests a CMS. Absence of a repetitive CMAP after a single stimulus helps separate it from slow-channel and acetylcholinesterase deficiency. Genetic testing is required to identify the kinetic variant, which guides treatment.
det.treatment: Pyridostigmine and 3,4-diaminopyridine increase acetylcholine release and receptor activation, improving strength. Quinidine and fluoxetine, used for slow-channel syndrome, are contraindicated. Families should have plans for apnoeic crises and early treatment of infections.
det.prognosis: Variable; severe forms risk early respiratory death, others improve with therapy and survive to adulthood.
pearls: Know the genotype before choosing CMS treatment – fast and slow channel need opposite drugs.
Episodic apnoea with infections is a red flag for CMS in infants.
Repetitive CMAP points to slow-channel or AChE deficiency, not fast-channel.
det.thd: Fast channel syndrome เป็น congenital myasthenic syndrome แบบด้อย เกิดจากความผิดปกติของ acetylcholine receptor ที่ทำให้ช่องปิดเร็วเกินไป สัญญาณประสาทส่งไปกล้ามเนื้อไม่พอ เด็กจึงมีหนังตาตก ดูดนมไม่ดี อ่อนแรงล้าง่าย และหยุดหายใจเมื่อติดเชื้อ รักษาด้วย pyridostigmine และ 3,4-DAP ห้ามใช้ quinidine หรือ fluoxetine

name: Fatal familial insomnia
formal: Autosomal dominant prion disease (D178N with M129 on PRNP) with progressive insomnia, dysautonomia, myoclonus, ataxia and dementia, and thalamic degeneration, death in 12 to 18 months.
simple: A rare inherited brain disease that causes worsening inability to sleep, then confusion and loss of body control, leading to death.
th: โรคพรีออนทางพันธุกรรมแบบถ่ายทอดเด่น (PRNP D178N-129M) ทำลายธาลามัส ทำให้นอนไม่หลับรุนแรงขึ้นเรื่อย ๆ ระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติทำงานเกิน เดินเซ และสมองเสื่อม
tempoNote: Usually starts in midlife; survival about 12–18 months on average, with a range from months to several years
feat: Intractable, progressive insomnia with dream-enacting confusional episodes
Sympathetic overactivity: sweating, fever, tachycardia, hypertension, weight loss
Ataxia, dysarthria, myoclonus and later cognitive decline
Autosomal dominant family history, which may be hidden or mislabelled
Methionine homozygosity at codon 129 gives a more classic insomnia course than heterozygosity
inv: Polysomnography: reduced sleep spindles and slow-wave sleep, loss of normal sleep architecture
FDG-PET: thalamic hypometabolism, often before any MRI change
PRNP sequencing (D178N with codon 129 genotype) after genetic counselling
CSF RT-QuIC and 14-3-3 are less sensitive than in sporadic CJD; MRI and EEG often unremarkable

case.story: Eight months of worsening sleeplessness, sleeping 2 hours a night despite sedatives, with sweats, 8 kg weight loss and episodes where he speaks and gestures as if acting out a dream. His mother died at 55 after a similar illness.
case.exam: Heart rate 110/min, blood pressure 160/95, temperature 37.8 °C, unsteady wide-based gait and intermittent myoclonic jerks, slowed attention.
case.tests: MRI brain normal; EEG slow without periodic complexes; PSG shows almost no spindles; FDG-PET shows bilateral thalamic hypometabolism.
case.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis, and what should be done for relatives?
case.a: PRNP sequencing (D178N with methionine at 129); offer pre-test genetic counselling to at-risk relatives and respect the right not to know.

read.where: Chapter 11 Cognitive Impairment and Dementia — Inherited Prion Diseases

det.patho: A missense change at PRNP codon 178 (aspartate to asparagine) coupled in cis with methionine at codon 129 produces a misfolded prion protein that accumulates chiefly in the anterior ventral and dorsomedial thalamic nuclei and inferior olives. Thalamo-cortical and limbic circuits that generate sleep and regulate autonomic output are disrupted. A sporadic form without the mutation also exists, and prion disease is transmissible only through specific exposures, not casual contact.
det.clinical: Typical onset is in the fifth decade with insomnia, loss of sleep-related circadian cues, and autonomic overactivity such as sweating, tachycardia and fever. Dream-like confusion, ataxia, dysarthria, myoclonus and cognitive deterioration follow, ending in akinetic, mute states. Phenotypic variation depends on codon 129 genotype: heterozygotes lean towards earlier cerebellar and cognitive features and longer survival. The family history may be absent, hidden or labelled as another dementia.
det.diagnosis: Consider it when severe, progressive insomnia with dysautonomia and ataxia occurs, especially with a relative affected. Polysomnography and FDG-PET are the most informative non-genetic tests, while MRI is often normal and CSF markers can be negative. PRNP sequencing confirms the diagnosis, so counselling before testing is essential given the implications for relatives. Autoimmune encephalitis and Morvan syndrome must be excluded because they are treatable.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying treatment, and sedative-hypnotics fail to restore normal sleep. Management is palliative, with symptom control for dysautonomia, myoclonus, nutrition and safety, together with psychological and family support. Prion-specific infection control precautions apply to instruments and tissue. Presymptomatic carriers should be offered counselling and research trial opportunities.
det.prognosis: Invariably fatal, typically within about one to two years of onset.
pearls: Insomnia plus dysautonomia plus ataxia plus a family history suggests FFI.
Thalamic hypometabolism on PET may appear when MRI and CSF markers are normal.
Test CASPR2 and IgLON5 antibodies, since Morvan syndrome and anti-IgLON5 disease can be treated.
det.thd: Fatal familial insomnia เป็นโรคพรีออนทางพันธุกรรมที่ถ่ายทอดแบบ autosomal dominant จากการกลายพันธุ์ PRNP D178N ร่วมกับ methionine ที่ codon 129 โปรตีนพรีออนที่ผิดรูปทำลายธาลามัส ผู้ป่วยนอนไม่หลับรุนแรงและต่อเนื่อง เหงื่อออก ชีพจรเร็ว ความดันสูง เดินเซ กระตุก และสมองเสื่อมลงเรื่อย ๆ การตรวจ polysomnography และ FDG-PET ช่วยได้ ส่วน MRI อาจปกติ ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน PRNP หลังให้คำปรึกษา ยังไม่มียารักษาโรคโดยตรง ดูแลแบบประคับประคองและให้คำปรึกษาแก่ญาติ

qx.stem: A 52-year-old man from Lopburi has had six months of progressive total insomnia, sweating, tachycardia and hypertension at night, and dream-like confusional episodes that he enacts. He is now ataxic with myoclonus. His father died at 50 of an unexplained illness with sleeplessness. Polysomnography shows almost no sleep spindles or slow-wave sleep. MRI is normal and FDG-PET shows bilateral thalamic hypometabolism.
qx.q: What is the most likely genetic basis?
opts: CAG expansion in HTT
PRNP D178N mutation with methionine at codon 129
SNCA multiplication
C9orf72 repeat expansion
NOTCH3 mutation
qx.why: Fatal familial insomnia is an autosomal dominant prion disease with selective thalamic degeneration and autonomic overactivity, caused by the PRNP D178N mutation coupled with methionine at codon 129 on the same allele. Hallmark findings are intractable insomnia, loss of sleep architecture, dysautonomia and later ataxia, with a normal MRI. The other genes cause Huntington's disease, familial Parkinson's disease, FTD-ALS and CADASIL.

name: Fazio–Londe disease
formal: Rare progressive bulbar palsy of childhood from SLC52A3 or SLC52A2 mutations, a riboflavin transporter deficiency presenting with facial weakness, dysphagia and respiratory failure, treatable with riboflavin.
simple: A rare inherited childhood illness causing weakness of the face and throat muscles, helped by vitamin B2.
more: Typically begins in childhood or adolescence; diagnose by SLC52A2 or SLC52A3 testing with an acylcarnitine profile and blood flavin studies. High-dose oral riboflavin improves outcome, and early treatment is critical for ventilation and swallowing.
th: โรคอัมพาตกล้ามเนื้อหลอดอาหารและใบหน้าแบบก้าวหน้าในเด็ก จากยีน SLC52A3 หรือ SLC52A2 ที่ขนส่ง riboflavin รักษาได้ด้วย riboflavin ขนาดสูง
tempoNote: Onset in infancy or childhood, progressing over months to years; sometimes stepwise after infections
feat: Progressive bulbar palsy in a child: facial weakness, dysphagia, dysarthria, tongue wasting
Respiratory insufficiency and diaphragm weakness are common
Without hearing loss; with sensorineural deafness the same gene spectrum is called Brown–Vialetto–Van Laere syndrome
Sensory neuronopathy, optic atrophy and limb weakness may develop
Treatable: high-dose oral riboflavin can stabilise or improve
inv: Genetic testing for SLC52A2 and SLC52A3
Plasma acylcarnitine profile (may resemble MADD) and flavin levels
Nerve conduction studies and EMG: sensory neuronopathy and denervation
Audiometry, respiratory function and swallow assessment

case.story: Over eight months her speech became nasal, she chokes on rice and her smile has flattened; recent chest infection worsened her breathing.
case.exam: Bilateral facial weakness, wasted fasciculating tongue, weak palate, mild neck flexor weakness, absent reflexes; hearing normal.
case.tests: EMG shows denervation in bulbar muscles; acylcarnitine profile abnormal; SLC52A3 biallelic variants.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the urgent treatment?
case.a: Fazio–Londe disease due to riboflavin transporter deficiency; start high-dose oral riboflavin immediately and support breathing and swallowing.

read.where: Chapter 15 Disorders of the Motor Cells: The Motor Neuron Diseases — Rare Forms of Spinal Muscular Atrophy and Differential Diagnosis
17. Lower Brainstem and Cranial Nerve Dysfunction
Chapter 27: Brown Vialetto Van Laere [BVVL] Syndrome

det.patho: Riboflavin is the precursor of FAD and FMN, cofactors for mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation and the respiratory chain. Biallelic variants in SLC52A2 or SLC52A3, which encode riboflavin transporters, reduce cellular uptake. Motor neurons in brainstem nuclei and anterior horns, dorsal root ganglia, auditory and optic pathways are particularly vulnerable. Fazio–Londe disease and Brown–Vialetto–Van Laere syndrome are now viewed as one disease spectrum.
det.clinical: Children present with progressive facial and bulbar weakness, often followed by respiratory failure and neck and upper limb weakness. Hearing loss is the defining addition in Brown–Vialetto–Van Laere syndrome, but some cases historically called Fazio–Londe have later developed it. Sensory ataxia, optic atrophy and nystagmus can develop. Infections may trigger sudden deterioration.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in any child with progressive bulbar palsy, especially with deafness or sensory neuronopathy. Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis; acylcarnitine abnormalities are supportive but may be normal. EMG shows denervation, and nerve conduction studies often reveal reduced sensory amplitudes. Exclude myasthenia, brainstem tumours and other motor neuron disorders with MRI and antibody testing.
det.treatment: Begin high-dose oral riboflavin on clinical suspicion alone, without waiting for genetic results, since delay leads to irreversible loss. Doses are given in divided form and continued lifelong. Respiratory support, gastrostomy, speech therapy and hearing aids or cochlear implants address complications. Monitor response clinically and with acylcarnitines.
det.prognosis: Untreated, it often leads to respiratory failure and death in childhood; early riboflavin treatment stabilises or improves many patients.
pearls: Progressive bulbar palsy in a child: give riboflavin first, then confirm genetics.
Check hearing — deafness points to Brown–Vialetto–Van Laere on the same spectrum.
A normal acylcarnitine profile does not exclude the disease.
det.thd: Fazio–Londe disease คือโรคอัมพาตกล้ามเนื้อใบหน้า ลิ้น และการกลืนแบบค่อยๆ เป็นมากขึ้นในเด็ก เกิดจากยีน SLC52A2 หรือ SLC52A3 ที่ขนส่ง riboflavin ผิดปกติ เป็นกลุ่มเดียวกับ Brown–Vialetto–Van Laere ซึ่งมีหูหนวกร่วมด้วย ผู้ป่วยอาจหายใจล้มเหลว การรักษาสำคัญคือให้ riboflavin ขนาดสูงทันทีที่สงสัย ร่วมกับดูแลการหายใจและการกลืน

name: Febrile infection-related epilepsy syndrome (FIRES)
formal: Catastrophic epileptic encephalopathy with refractory status epilepticus after a febrile illness in a previously healthy child or adult, with poor outcome and probable inflammatory pathogenesis.
simple: A severe condition in which previously healthy children develop non-stop seizures after a fever, often with lasting brain damage.
th: ภาวะชักต่อเนื่องดื้อยารุนแรงที่เกิดหลังไข้ในคนที่เคยปกติ มักเป็นเด็กวัยเรียน เชื่อว่ากลไกเป็นการอักเสบ และพยากรณ์โรคไม่ดี
tempoNote: Febrile illness 1–14 days before explosive onset of seizures that escalate to refractory status within days
feat: Previously healthy child or young adult with a non-specific febrile illness, then rapidly escalating seizures
Refractory or super-refractory status epilepticus lasting weeks, often needing anaesthetic coma
Fever may have resolved by seizure onset (preceding fever 24 h to 2 weeks)
No identifiable infectious, autoimmune antibody, structural or metabolic cause
Survivors usually have drug-resistant epilepsy and cognitive impairment
inv: CSF: normal or mild pleocytosis, raised cytokines (IL-6) in research; PCR and autoimmune antibody panels negative
Continuous EEG monitoring: multifocal seizures, often perisylvian or temporal onset
MRI: often normal early, later T2 signal in hippocampi, claustrum and perisylvian cortex; atrophy later
Exclude infectious, toxic, metabolic and genetic causes

case.story: Had fever and sore throat for 5 days, recovered, then 2 days later developed clusters of focal seizures that became continuous despite benzodiazepines, levetiracetam and phenytoin.
case.exam: Intubated on midazolam infusion; no focal infectious signs.
case.tests: CSF 6 cells, normal glucose, negative viral PCR and neuronal antibodies; MRI shows bilateral claustrum T2 signal.
case.q: What syndrome is this, and which therapies are used besides anaesthetics?
case.a: FIRES; early ketogenic diet and immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG), with anakinra (IL-1 blockade) or tocilizumab (IL-6 blockade) for refractory cases.

read.where: Chapter 39: Status Epilepticus and Acute Seizures
Chapter 9 - Seizures and Antibodies Against Surface Antigens

det.patho: FIRES is regarded as the form of NORSE in which a febrile illness comes first. Evidence points to an innate immune-mediated process with excess cytokines (IL-1, IL-6) rather than direct infection or classic antibody-mediated autoimmunity. Genetic predisposition is suspected but unproven.
det.clinical: Most affected are school-age children, but adults also develop it. After a febrile illness, focal seizures quickly evolve into refractory status epilepticus requiring prolonged intensive care. The acute phase lasts weeks, and survivors enter a chronic phase with drug-resistant focal epilepsy without a silent period.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical according to international consensus definitions, after a thorough search for infectious, autoimmune, metabolic, toxic and genetic causes. Continuous EEG is essential. Brain biopsy is seldom informative.
det.treatment: Conventional antiseizure medicines and anaesthetic infusions are used, but early ketogenic diet and immunotherapy (methylprednisolone, IVIG, plasma exchange) are recommended. Anakinra or tocilizumab should be considered early in refractory cases based on consensus recommendations. Avoid prolonged deep anaesthetic coma when possible, and consider cannabidiol, vagus nerve stimulation and other adjuncts in the chronic phase.
det.prognosis: Mortality is about 10%, and most survivors have chronic epilepsy and cognitive deficits.
pearls: Fever days before refractory status in a healthy child: think FIRES.
Start ketogenic diet and anti-cytokine therapy early.
Claustrum sign on MRI is a suggestive clue.
det.thd: FIRES คือภาวะชักต่อเนื่องดื้อยารุนแรงที่เกิดภายในไม่กี่วันหลังมีไข้ในคนที่เคยปกติ ส่วนใหญ่เป็นเด็กวัยเรียน เชื่อว่าเกิดจากการอักเสบของระบบภูมิคุ้มกันแบบ innate ตรวจไม่พบเชื้อหรือแอนติบอดี ต้องเฝ้าดู EEG ต่อเนื่อง รักษาด้วยยากันชัก ยาสลบ อาหาร ketogenic และภูมิคุ้มกันบำบัด เช่น steroid, IVIG, anakinra หรือ tocilizumab ผู้รอดชีวิตมักเป็นลมชักเรื้อรังและสติปัญญาบกพร่อง

name: Femoral neuropathy
formal: Injury of the femoral nerve from diabetic infarct, retroperitoneal haematoma, hip surgery or pelvic compression, causing quadriceps weakness, absent knee jerk and anteromedial thigh sensory loss.
simple: Damage to the nerve in the front of the thigh, causing a weak knee that gives way and numbness in the front of the thigh.
th: เส้นประสาท femoral เสีย ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อ quadriceps อ่อนแรง reflex เข่าหาย และชาด้านหน้าต้นขาและด้านในขา
tempoNote: Acute after surgery or haematoma; subacute with diabetes or tumour
feat: Weak knee extension (quadriceps), knee buckling especially on stairs
Absent or reduced knee jerk
Numbness over anterior thigh and medial leg (saphenous branch)
Hip flexion is weak only when the lesion lies above the level of the inguinal ligament (iliacus branch)
Causes: retroperitoneal haematoma on anticoagulants, hip or pelvic surgery, lithotomy position, femoral catheterisation, diabetes
inv: NCS/EMG: confirm femoral denervation and spare adductors (obturator) and paraspinals
CT abdomen/pelvis urgently if anticoagulated (iliopsoas haematoma)
MRI of lumbar plexus if plexopathy or radiculopathy is suspected

case.who: 71-year-old woman from Nonthaburi on warfarin for atrial fibrillation
case.story: Developed severe right groin pain over a day, then could not straighten the right knee to stand.
case.exam: Right hip held flexed, weak hip flexion and knee extension, absent right knee jerk, numb anterior thigh; adductors strong.
case.tests: INR 5.2; CT shows a large right iliopsoas haematoma.
case.q: Why are the adductors spared, and what is the emergency?
case.a: The haematoma compresses the femoral nerve within the iliopsoas, sparing the obturator nerve; reverse anticoagulation and consider drainage.

3. Common Mononeuropathies of the Lower Extremities

det.patho: The femoral nerve forms from the L2–L4 roots within psoas, runs between psoas and iliacus, and goes beneath the inguinal ligament to supply the quadriceps and the skin of the anterior thigh and medial leg. It is vulnerable to compression in the iliopsoas compartment, stretch during hip surgery or lithotomy positioning, retractor injury during pelvic surgery and ischaemia in diabetes.
det.clinical: Patients describe the knee giving way, especially on stairs or downhill. Pain is prominent with haematoma. Sensory loss affects the anterior thigh and medial lower leg. Weak hip flexion means the lesion is located above the inguinal ligament. Adductor sparing separates femoral neuropathy from L3–L4 radiculopathy and lumbar plexopathy.
det.diagnosis: Clinical localisation is confirmed by EMG showing denervation in quadriceps with normal adductors, tibialis anterior and paraspinals. Femoral motor conduction and saphenous sensory responses help grade axonal loss. Imaging looks for haematoma, abscess or tumour, and urgently so in anticoagulated patients.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: reverse anticoagulation and consider drainage of a compressive haematoma, remove compressive positioning, manage diabetes. Physiotherapy and a knee-extension brace prevent falls. Neuropathic pain agents for painful cases. Surgical exploration is reserved for transection or failure of recovery after a penetrating or operative injury.
det.prognosis: Most compressive and stretch injuries recover over months; severe axonal lesions recover incompletely.
pearls: Femoral neuropathy spares adductors; L3–L4 radiculopathy does not.
Anticoagulated patient with groin pain and weak knee: iliopsoas haematoma.
Lithotomy positioning in long surgeries is a classic cause.
det.thd: Femoral neuropathy คือเส้นประสาท femoral เสีย ทำให้เหยียดเข่าไม่มีแรง เข่าทรุดเวลาลงบันได reflex เข่าหาย และชาด้านหน้าต้นขา สาเหตุที่สำคัญคือเลือดออกใน iliopsoas ในผู้ที่ใช้ยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือด การผ่าตัดสะโพกหรืออุ้งเชิงกราน และเบาหวาน จุดแยกจาก L3–L4 radiculopathy คือกล้ามเนื้อ adductor ปกติ

name: Fingerprint body myopathy
formal: Rare myopathy with distinctive fingerprint-like inclusions on electron microscopy, with variable proximal weakness, sometimes with cardiomyopathy, and unclear genetic basis.
simple: A very rare muscle disease named for the fingerprint-like patterns seen in muscle under an electron microscope.
more: Electron microscopy of biopsy is diagnostic; management is supportive.
th: โรคกล้ามเนื้อพบน้อย ที่พบโครงสร้างลายนิ้วมือในเส้นใยกล้ามเนื้อจากกล้องจุลทรรศน์อิเล็กตรอน อ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขาเล็กน้อยและดำเนินช้า
tempoNote: Usually congenital or childhood onset, static or very slowly progressive
feat: Mild hypotonia or proximal weakness from early life
Very slow progression or non-progressive course
Normal or mildly raised CK
Some reports describe cognitive delay or cardiac involvement
inv: Muscle biopsy with electron microscopy showing fingerprint-like lamellar inclusions
EMG: myopathic pattern or normal
Gene panel for congenital myopathies; no single gene established

case.story: Always slower at running and cannot climb ropes; condition unchanged over years.
case.exam: Mild symmetrical hip and shoulder girdle weakness, normal reflexes, no contractures.
case.tests: CK normal; biopsy EM shows subsarcolemmal fingerprint bodies; congenital myopathy panel negative.
case.q: Is the biopsy finding specific?
case.a: No — fingerprint bodies occur in other myopathies (e.g. myotonic dystrophy, IBM); the label is descriptive.

read.where: Section IV: General Principles of Therapy

det.patho: Fingerprint bodies are concentric lamellar structures seen on electron microscopy. They are not specific and appear in several myopathies. A distinct congenital myopathy with predominant fingerprint bodies was described in a few families, but its genetic cause remains unclear.
det.clinical: Described patients have early-onset mild weakness and hypotonia with a benign course. Evidence comes from small case reports, so the full clinical spectrum, including cardiac and cognitive features, is uncertain. Many current patients would receive a gene-based diagnosis instead.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires electron microscopy showing abundant fingerprint bodies and exclusion of other myopathies. Next-generation sequencing for congenital myopathies is recommended. Cardiac screening is reasonable.
det.treatment: Supportive: physiotherapy, monitoring of respiratory function and spine, and cardiac review if symptomatic.
det.prognosis: Generally favourable with slow or no progression in reported cases.
pearls: Fingerprint bodies are a finding, not a gene.
Seek a molecular diagnosis in congenital myopathy.
Check the heart in any unclassified myopathy.
det.thd: Fingerprint body myopathy เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้อที่พบน้อยมาก วินิจฉัยจากกล้องจุลทรรศน์อิเล็กตรอนที่เห็นโครงสร้างคล้ายลายนิ้วมือ อาการอ่อนแรงเล็กน้อยตั้งแต่เด็กและดำเนินโรคช้า ลักษณะนี้ไม่จำเพาะ ยังไม่ทราบยีนที่ชัดเจน การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง

Adult-onset distal and cardiac involvement with protein aggregates

name: Fixed dystonia
formal: Dystonic posture of limbs with rapid onset and no relaxation, usually of functional origin, often after minor injury and painful, with an associated complex regional pain syndrome.
simple: A twisted posture of a limb that does not relax, often appearing after a minor injury and usually functional in origin.
th: ท่าบิดเกร็งที่ค้างตลอดไม่คลายแม้พัก มักเกิดหลังบาดเจ็บเล็กน้อยและมีปวด ส่วนใหญ่เป็นกลไก functional
tempoNote: Rapid onset over hours to days, then often persistent for years
feat: Fixed posture of hand (clenched fist) or foot (inversion), present at rest and in sleep
Rapid onset after minor peripheral injury or surgery
Pain, often with CRPS features (swelling, colour and temperature change)
Other functional signs and inconsistency; poor response to botulinum toxin
Young women predominate
inv: Clinical diagnosis using positive functional features
MRI brain and spine normal; exclude structural or genetic causes if atypical
Examination under anaesthesia may show posture resolves (contracture vs active)

case.story: After a wrist sprain six months ago, her fingers curled into a tight fist within days and have stayed so; burning pain.
case.exam: Fixed fist posture, skin cool and shiny, inconsistent weakness of the arm, normal reflexes.
case.tests: MRI brain and cervical spine normal.
case.q: What is the likely mechanism and treatment approach?
case.a: Functional fixed dystonia with CRPS features; explain the diagnosis and give specialised physiotherapy with psychological support.

read.where: 27 - Functional (psychogenic) movement disorders: Phenomenology, diagnosis, and treatment

det.patho: Most fixed dystonia is now understood as functional, involving altered attention, expectation and sense of agency after injury or pain. Prolonged immobility then leads to secondary contracture and disuse. A minority have structural or genetic causes.
det.clinical: Onset is abrupt, often after trivial injury, with a posture that stays fixed and is painful. Spread to other limbs and fluctuations can occur. Contrast with organic dystonia, which usually begins as action-induced and mobile.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, with positive signs and inconsistency. Normal imaging and the absence of other neurological signs support it. Examination under sedation distinguishes active posture from fixed contracture.
det.treatment: Explain the diagnosis clearly. Multidisciplinary rehabilitation with physiotherapy based on movement retraining, pain management and psychological therapy is central. Avoid repeated surgery, immobilisation and escalating invasive pain treatments.
det.prognosis: Often chronic; earlier diagnosis and rehabilitation improve outcomes.
pearls: Organic dystonia starts mobile; fixed from day one suggests functional.
Minor injury plus CRPS features plus fixed posture is a classic triad.
Avoid immobilisation and surgery.
det.thd: Fixed dystonia คือท่าบิดเกร็งที่ค้างตลอด เกิดเร็วหลังบาดเจ็บเล็กน้อยและมีปวดร่วม ส่วนใหญ่เป็นกลไก functional มักมีลักษณะ CRPS ร่วม การรักษาคืออธิบายโรค ทำกายภาพบำบัดเฉพาะทาง และดูแลด้านจิตใจ หลีกเลี่ยงการใส่เฝือกนานหรือผ่าตัดซ้ำ

Broader category; fixed dystonia is its typical form

name: Flail arm/leg syndrome
formal: Regional variants of motor neuron disease with progressive proximal arm (Vulpian–Bernhardt) or leg weakness and atrophy and slower progression than classic ALS.
simple: A slowly progressing form of motor neuron disease where weakness mainly affects one arm or one leg.
th: ALS รูปแบบเฉพาะที่ แขนสองข้างส่วนต้นหรือขาส่วนปลายอ่อนแรงลีบเด่น ดำเนินโรคช้ากว่า ALS ทั่วไป
tempoNote: Progresses over years, often remaining confined to the arms or legs for 12 months or longer
feat: Flail arm: symmetric proximal arm weakness and wasting, 'man-in-a-barrel' appearance, strong male predominance
Flail leg: distal leg weakness starting asymmetrically, foot drop progressing to both legs
Reflexes may be reduced; upper motor neuron signs mild or delayed
Bulbar and respiratory function spared for longer than in classic ALS
Survival longer than typical limb-onset ALS
inv: EMG showing widespread denervation including clinically normal regions
Nerve conduction to exclude multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block
MRI cervical or lumbosacral spine; anti-GM1, CK, androgen receptor testing in men with bulbar signs

case.story: Eighteen months of difficulty lifting tools above shoulder height on both sides; legs and speech normal.
case.exam: Bilateral deltoid, spinati and biceps wasting with fasciculations, arms hang limply, hands relatively preserved, brisk knee jerks.
case.tests: EMG: active and chronic denervation in cervical and thoracic paraspinal muscles; no conduction block; MRI spine mild spondylosis.
case.q: What MND variant is this and what does it mean for prognosis?
case.a: Flail arm syndrome; progression is usually slower than classic ALS with longer survival.

det.patho: These are regional phenotypes of ALS in which degeneration starts in and remains confined to one body region for a prolonged period. Pathology is typically TDP-43 related as in other ALS forms. Why degeneration stays regional for so long is not understood.
det.clinical: Flail arm syndrome affects mostly men and starts with symmetrical proximal arm weakness, leaving the arms hanging beside the trunk. Flail leg syndrome begins distally in the legs and may be confused with neuropathy. In both, spread to bulbar and respiratory muscles is delayed, but eventually occurs in many patients. Upper motor neuron signs can be subtle.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on clinical pattern and EMG evidence of widespread lower motor neuron involvement. Gold Coast criteria allow diagnosis of ALS when progressive lower motor neuron disease involves two regions. Exclude MMN, cervical radiculomyelopathy, brachial neuritis, inclusion body myositis and Kennedy disease. MRI and nerve conduction with careful search for block are essential.
det.treatment: Management follows ALS guidance: riluzole, multidisciplinary care, splinting, physiotherapy and assistive devices. Tofersen is used in SOD1 carriers. Respiratory and nutritional surveillance continue because spread can occur. Discuss prognosis honestly but note the slower course.
det.prognosis: Median survival is longer than classic ALS, often several years beyond.
pearls: Man-in-a-barrel arms with preserved legs and speech: flail arm syndrome.
Always search hard for conduction block before calling it MND.
Strong male predominance in flail arm syndrome.
det.thd: Flail arm/leg syndrome เป็น ALS ชนิดที่จำกัดอยู่ที่ส่วนใดส่วนหนึ่งนาน เช่น แขนส่วนต้นสองข้างลีบอ่อนแรงจนแขนห้อย หรือขาส่วนปลายอ่อนแรง ส่วนการกลืนและการหายใจมักยังดีนาน พบในผู้ชายมากกว่า วินิจฉัยด้วย EMG และต้องแยก MMN และโรคกระดูกคอ การรักษาเหมือน ALS และพยากรณ์โรคดีกว่า ALS ทั่วไป

name: Focal aware seizures (auras)
formal: Focal seizures with preserved awareness giving sensory, autonomic, psychic or motor symptoms, such as rising epigastric sensation or deja vu, often from mesial temporal onset.
simple: Short seizures where the person stays awake but has odd feelings, smells, sights or movements, often a warning of a bigger seizure.
th: การชักเฉพาะที่ที่ยังรู้ตัวดี มีอาการรับความรู้สึก อัตโนมัติ จิตใจ หรือการเคลื่อนไหว เช่น รู้สึกจุกลิ้นปี่ลอยขึ้น หรือ déjà vu
tempoNote: Brief stereotyped episodes lasting seconds to a couple of minutes
feat: Awareness and memory of the event are preserved
Mesial temporal: rising epigastric sensation, fear, déjà vu, smell or taste illusions
Occipital: simple coloured lights or shapes; parietal: tingling or distortion of body image; frontal: motor jerks or posturing
Stereotyped in each patient; may progress to impaired awareness or bilateral tonic-clonic seizures
Symptoms are 'positive' and spread over seconds, unlike TIA
inv: EEG often normal on scalp; prolonged or ambulatory video-EEG for frequent events
MRI epilepsy protocol to find a focal lesion (hippocampal sclerosis, dysplasia, tumour, cavernoma)
ECG and other tests to exclude mimics when symptoms are atypical

case.story: Several times a month he gets a sudden rising feeling from his stomach with a sense of having lived the moment before, lasting 30 seconds; he stays fully aware.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination.
case.tests: MRI shows right hippocampal atrophy with high T2 signal; EEG right temporal sharp waves.
case.q: What seizure type is this, and what lesion is likely?
case.a: Focal aware seizures from the right mesial temporal lobe due to hippocampal sclerosis.

read.where: Section V: Antiepileptic Drugs and Diet

det.patho: Focal aware seizures arise from an epileptogenic area of one hemisphere, with symptoms reflecting the cortex involved. Because the discharge does not spread enough to disturb awareness networks, consciousness is retained. Common substrates are hippocampal sclerosis, cortical dysplasia, low-grade tumours, cavernomas and post-stroke scars.
det.clinical: The term 'aura' describes a focal aware seizure that may precede a larger seizure. Symptoms are stereotyped and brief; patients may struggle to describe psychic or visceral sensations. Some patients have only auras for years before progressing. Ictal fear, autonomic changes and language disturbance can be mistaken for panic or psychiatric illness.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is mainly clinical; scalp EEG during an aura is often normal because the discharge is deep or small. MRI is key to identify a cause. Distinguish from migraine aura, TIA, panic attacks and functional episodes by duration, march and stereotypy.
det.treatment: Antiseizure drugs for focal epilepsy (lamotrigine, levetiracetam, carbamazepine, lacosamide) are used when auras are disabling or progress to larger seizures. Drug-resistant focal epilepsy with a lesion should be referred for surgery. Auras that remain isolated may not always require treatment.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause; lesional temporal lobe epilepsy may become drug-resistant but often responds to surgery.
pearls: Ask about rising epigastric sensations and déjà vu in every patient with convulsions.
A normal EEG does not exclude focal aware seizures.
Seizure symptoms march in seconds; migraine auras over minutes.
det.thd: Focal aware seizure หรือ aura คือการชักเฉพาะที่ที่ผู้ป่วยยังรู้ตัวและจำได้ อาการขึ้นกับสมองส่วนที่เริ่มชัก เช่น กลีบขมับด้านในจะรู้สึกจุกลิ้นปี่ลอยขึ้น กลัว หรือ déjà vu อาการซ้ำแบบเดิมทุกครั้งและเป็นเพียงไม่กี่วินาที อาจลามเป็นชักที่ไม่รู้ตัวหรือชักเกร็งกระตุกทั้งตัว EEG บนหนังศีรษะมักปกติ ควรตรวจ MRI หาสาเหตุ รักษาด้วยยากันชักชนิด focal และพิจารณาผ่าตัดเมื่อดื้อยา

name: Focal cortical myoclonus
formal: Brief jerks confined to one body part from a discrete sensorimotor cortical focus, with giant SEPs and EEG correlates, as in epilepsia partialis continua.
simple: Quick jerks of one body part caused by a small overactive area on the brain surface.
th: การกระตุกเฉพาะส่วนของร่างกายที่เกิดจากจุดผิดปกติใน cortex บริเวณ sensorimotor เช่นใน epilepsia partialis continua
tempoNote: Jerks may come in bursts or be near-continuous for hours to years (EPC)
feat: Brief jerks restricted to one hand, face or limb, often distal and worse with action or touch
May be continuous (epilepsia partialis continua) and persist in sleep
Caused by a focal cortical lesion: stroke, tumour, Rasmussen encephalitis, cortical dysplasia, non-ketotic hyperglycaemia
Often with mild weakness or sensory change in the same limb
Associated with giant SEPs and EEG transients over the contralateral sensorimotor cortex
inv: EEG with EMG and jerk-locked back-averaging
SEP and long-latency reflexes
MRI with contrast; glucose (non-ketotic hyperglycaemia), antibodies or biopsy for Rasmussen

case.who: 62-year-old man from Nakhon Ratchasima with poorly controlled diabetes
case.story: For 2 days, continuous twitching of his left hand and face, persisting even during sleep.
case.exam: Rhythmic jerks of left hand and face, mild left arm weakness.
case.tests: Glucose 520 mg/dL without ketones; EEG right central spikes; MRI normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the key treatment?
case.a: Epilepsia partialis continua due to non-ketotic hyperglycaemia; correct glucose and hydration — antiseizure drugs work poorly until glucose is normal.

read.where: Chapter 21 - Abnormal Movements in Neurological Autoimmune Disorders

det.patho: A lesion or hyperexcitable area in primary sensorimotor cortex generates discharges that travel down corticospinal pathways, producing jerks in the matching body part. Loss of local inhibition leads to enhanced reflex responses to touch and movement. Causes include vascular, neoplastic, inflammatory, metabolic and developmental disorders.
det.clinical: Jerks typically affect the hand or face, sometimes spreading in a Jacksonian pattern. Epilepsia partialis continua is a form of focal status epilepticus lasting hours to years. In children progressive hemiparesis and cognitive decline with EPC suggest Rasmussen encephalitis; in adults, stroke, tumour and hyperglycaemia are common.
det.diagnosis: Clinical observation and neurophysiology confirm cortical origin, while MRI and blood tests seek the cause. EEG correlates may not be seen on scalp recordings, so back-averaging can help.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying cause. Levetiracetam, valproate, clonazepam, perampanel or brivaracetam help cortical myoclonus; EPC often responds poorly to drugs. Immunotherapy or hemispherotomy is used in Rasmussen encephalitis, and focal resection for dysplasia.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause; metabolic EPC often resolves fully, whereas Rasmussen encephalitis leads to permanent hemiparesis.
pearls: Continuous hand or face jerks persisting in sleep: think EPC.
Check glucose: non-ketotic hyperglycaemia is a reversible cause.
EPC with progressive hemiparesis in a child suggests Rasmussen encephalitis.
det.thd: Focal cortical myoclonus คือการกระตุกเฉพาะที่ เช่น มือหรือใบหน้า เกิดจากรอยโรคใน cortex บริเวณ sensorimotor ด้านตรงข้าม ถ้ากระตุกต่อเนื่องนานเรียกว่า epilepsia partialis continua สาเหตุได้แก่ stroke เนื้องอก Rasmussen encephalitis และน้ำตาลสูงแบบไม่มี ketone ตรวจ EEG, SEP และ MRI รักษาสาเหตุร่วมกับยากันชัก เช่น levetiracetam และ clonazepam

name: Focal epilepsy
formal: Epilepsy with seizures originating in one hemisphere, causing semiology based on the network involved and often due to structural lesions such as hippocampal sclerosis or cortical dysplasia.
simple: Epilepsy where seizures start in one area of the brain, causing symptoms that depend on where it begins.
th: โรคลมชักที่จุดกำเนิดอยู่ในเครือข่ายสมองซีกเดียว อาการชักขึ้นกับตำแหน่งที่เริ่ม อาจรู้ตัว เหม่อไม่รู้ตัว หรือลามเป็นชักเกร็งกระตุกทั้งตัว มักมีรอยโรคในสมองเป็นสาเหตุ
tempoNote: Stereotyped attacks lasting seconds to a couple of minutes, recurring over months to years; onset at any age, with a second peak in older adults from stroke and degeneration
feat: Attacks begin the same way each time, and the first symptom (aura) points to the lobe of onset
Focal aware seizures keep awareness; focal impaired-awareness seizures cause staring, automatisms and amnesia
May spread to a focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizure; post-ictal Todd paresis or dysphasia lateralises
Underlying causes: hippocampal sclerosis, cortical dysplasia, tumour, stroke, trauma, infection (e.g. neurocysticercosis), autoimmune
About a third become drug-resistant after two appropriate drugs fail
inv: Eyewitness account or phone video of the event — the single most useful diagnostic item
EEG (routine, sleep-deprived or prolonged): focal epileptiform discharges support the diagnosis; a normal EEG does not exclude it
Epilepsy-protocol MRI (thin coronal hippocampal cuts, 3D T1, FLAIR) to find a structural cause
Video-EEG telemetry when the diagnosis is unclear or before surgery; add PET/SPECT, neuropsychology as needed

case.story: For two years he has had spells of a rising feeling in his stomach and a familiar 'dream-like' sense, then stares and picks at his shirt for a minute; twice it ended in a whole-body convulsion.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination between events.
case.tests: EEG: left anterior temporal sharp waves. MRI: small, bright, shrunken left hippocampus on FLAIR.
case.q: What is the epilepsy type, and what should happen if two suitable medicines fail?
case.a: Focal epilepsy from left mesial temporal (hippocampal) sclerosis; after two failed tolerated drugs, refer early for presurgical evaluation.

read.where: Section IV: General Principles of Therapy
7 EEG and Semiology in Focal Epilepsy

det.patho: A focal seizure arises when a hyperexcitable cortical network escapes surrounding inhibition, then recruits connected regions; spread through thalamocortical and commissural pathways turns it bilateral. Common substrates include hippocampal sclerosis, focal cortical dysplasia, low-grade developmental tumours, cavernomas, gliotic scars from stroke or trauma, and infections — neurocysticercosis and tuberculoma matter in South-East Asia. Somatic or germline variants (e.g. mTOR pathway genes, DEPDC5) explain some non-lesional cases.
det.clinical: The ILAE 2017 scheme labels seizures by onset (focal), awareness (aware or impaired), and first feature (motor or non-motor), plus whether they evolve to bilateral tonic-clonic. Temporal seizures bring epigastric rising, déjà vu, fear, oral and manual automatisms and post-ictal confusion; frontal seizures are brief, nocturnal and hypermotor; parietal ones produce sensory symptoms; occipital ones bring coloured circles or visual loss. Lateralising clues include dystonic posturing of the contralateral hand, ictal speech preservation in non-dominant onset and post-ictal aphasia in dominant onset. Comorbid depression, memory trouble and SUDEP risk deserve attention.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical; epilepsy is defined by two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, or one with a high recurrence risk (for example an epileptogenic lesion or epileptiform EEG). Routine EEG captures interictal discharges in only about a third to a half, rising with repeats and sleep. MRI should follow an epilepsy protocol, read by someone used to subtle dysplasia. Exclude provoked causes (glucose, sodium, alcohol, drugs) and mimics such as syncope, functional seizures, TIA, migraine aura and parasomnia.
det.treatment: Start an antiseizure medicine after a second seizure, or after the first if recurrence risk is high; lamotrigine and levetiracetam are common first choices, with carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, lacosamide or zonisamide as alternatives. Match the drug to comorbidities, pregnancy plans and interactions, and counsel on driving, work and water safety. Drug resistance is declared once two appropriate, tolerated drugs have failed; such patients should be evaluated for resective surgery, laser ablation, or neuromodulation (VNS, DBS, RNS) and dietary therapy. Valproate is avoided in women who could become pregnant.
det.prognosis: Around two-thirds become seizure-free on medication; in selected drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy, surgery achieves lasting freedom in roughly 60–70%.
pearls: Ask what happens first — the aura is the seizure's address.
Two failed appropriate drugs = drug-resistant: refer for surgery assessment rather than trying drug after drug.
Post-ictal dysphasia suggests dominant-hemisphere onset; ictal speech preserved suggests non-dominant.
In Thailand, consider neurocysticercosis and tuberculoma in new focal seizures with a ring or calcified lesion.
det.thd: Focal epilepsy คือโรคลมชักที่จุดเริ่มอยู่ในสมองส่วนใดส่วนหนึ่ง อาการแรก (aura) บอกตำแหน่ง เช่น รู้สึกจุกลิ้นปี่ขึ้นมา เดจาวู แล้วเหม่อทำปากขมุบขมิบ อาจลามเป็นชักทั้งตัว สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยคือ hippocampal sclerosis, cortical dysplasia, เนื้องอก, stroke หรือพยาธิตืดหมูในสมอง วินิจฉัยจากประวัติผู้เห็นเหตุการณ์ EEG และ MRI แบบ epilepsy protocol รักษาด้วยยากันชัก เช่น lamotrigine, levetiracetam ถ้าล้มเหลว 2 ตัวควรประเมินผ่าตัด

qx.stem: A 27-year-old Thai rice farmer has focal impaired awareness seizures from a calcified right frontal granuloma. He lives far from the provincial hospital, and his doctor prefers carbamazepine because it is cheap and on the national essential drug list. He has no drug allergies and normal liver and kidney function.
qx.q: What should be done before the first dose?
opts: Measure baseline serum sodium only
Test for HLA-A*31:01 because it predicts carbamazepine toxicity in Southeast Asians
Do nothing extra, as serious skin reactions are equally rare in all ethnic groups
Genotype HLA-B*15:02 and avoid carbamazepine if it is present
Start at full dose with a short prednisolone course to prevent rash
qx.why: HLA-B*15:02 is common in Thai and Han Chinese people and strongly predicts carbamazepine-induced Stevens–Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis, so testing before starting is recommended (and covered in Thailand). Carriers should also generally avoid oxcarbazepine and, where possible, phenytoin. HLA-A*31:01 matters more in European and Japanese patients and is linked mainly to DRESS. Steroid cover does not prevent these reactions.

qx.stem: A 25-year-old nurse has been seizure-free for two years on lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily for focal epilepsy. Three months ago she started a combined ethinylestradiol–levonorgestrel pill taken 21 days on, 7 days off. She now has breakthrough focal seizures during the weeks she takes active pills, and dizziness and diplopia during the pill-free week.
qx.q: What best explains this pattern?
opts: The progestin component inhibits lamotrigine absorption
Lamotrigine induces the metabolism of the contraceptive, causing hormonal fluctuation
Estrogen in the pill speeds up lamotrigine glucuronidation, so levels fall on active pills and rebound in the pill-free week
Catamenial seizures from progesterone withdrawal
Poor adherence on working shifts
qx.why: Ethinylestradiol induces UGT enzymes and can cut lamotrigine levels by about half. Levels then recover during the hormone-free interval, which causes toxicity. Options include checking levels and raising the dose, using a continuous regimen, or switching to an IUD or progestin-only method. Lamotrigine itself has little effect on the estrogen component, so the reverse interaction is not the explanation.

qx.stem: A 79-year-old retired civil servant had a left MCA infarct 10 months ago and has now had two unprovoked focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures. He takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation, amlodipine and simvastatin. His eGFR is 48 mL/min/1.73 m² and he lives alone. MRI shows only the old infarct.
qx.q: Which antiseizure medication is the best first choice?
opts: Phenytoin
Carbamazepine
Phenobarbital
Lamotrigine with slow titration
Valproate
qx.why: In older adults with focal (often post-stroke) epilepsy, lamotrigine is well tolerated and was the preferred first-line focal drug in SANAD II. Levetiracetam with a renally adjusted dose is another option. Enzyme inducers such as phenytoin, carbamazepine and phenobarbital lower warfarin and statin levels, harm bone, and cause sedation or falls. Valproate interacts with warfarin and can cause tremor, parkinsonism and cognitive slowing in older people.

qx.stem: A 38-year-old woman with drug-resistant left frontal focal epilepsy has declined intracranial evaluation. She takes lamotrigine and clobazam, and her ECG shows a normal QT interval. Her neurologist proposes adding cenobamate.
qx.q: Which counseling point about cenobamate is correct?
opts: It must be titrated slowly from a low dose over several weeks to reduce the risk of DRESS
It prolongs the QT interval, so it should be avoided with any QT-prolonging drug
It has no effect on hormonal contraception
It usually lowers clobazam levels, so the clobazam dose should be increased
It can be loaded quickly because serious hypersensitivity has never been reported
qx.why: DRESS occurred with early fast titration, so cenobamate is started at 12.5 mg/day and increased every two weeks. It shortens the QT interval and is contraindicated in familial short-QT syndrome. It inhibits CYP2C19, which raises clobazam (and phenytoin) exposure and causes sedation, and it induces other pathways, lowering lamotrigine levels and making hormonal contraception less effective.

qx.stem: A 29-year-old woman with focal impaired awareness seizures and a normal MRI is referred as 'drug-resistant'. Carbamazepine was stopped after 10 days because of a widespread rash. She then took levetiracetam 1,500 mg twice daily for a year with good adherence (confirmed by levels) and still has three seizures a month.
qx.q: How should her status be classified?
opts: Drug-resistant, because two medications have been tried
Drug-resistant, because her seizures are monthly
Not yet drug-resistant; the carbamazepine trial does not count toward efficacy, so another appropriate drug should be tried while early presurgical referral is considered
Not drug-resistant, because she must fail at least five medications
Pseudo-resistant, because levetiracetam is inappropriate for focal seizures
qx.why: The ILAE defines drug resistance as failure of two tolerated, appropriately chosen and adequately dosed medication schedules to achieve sustained seizure freedom. A drug stopped early because of an allergic reaction tells you nothing about efficacy. Levetiracetam is appropriate for focal seizures. The chance of seizure freedom drops sharply with each failed drug, so referral should not be delayed once resistance is confirmed.

qx.stem: During video-EEG monitoring, a 26-year-old man whose focal epilepsy has a normal MRI has a typical seizure that lasts 40 seconds. The technologist injects technetium-99m ECD 75 seconds after clinical onset. The subtracted ictal–interictal SPECT coregistered to MRI shows hyperperfusion in the right parietal and posterior temporal regions, while EEG and semiology pointed to a right frontal origin.
qx.q: What is the most likely reason for this discordance?
opts: The tracer was injected too late, so the scan shows spread or postictal changes rather than the onset zone
SPECT cannot detect frontal seizures
The interictal scan was performed during a seizure
ECD is a metabolic rather than a perfusion tracer
The MRI coregistration always shifts results backward
qx.why: Perfusion tracers lock into the brain within about a minute of injection and show blood flow at that moment. Injection late in or after a short seizure therefore shows propagation or postictal hypoperfusion instead of the onset region. Ideally injection happens within seconds of onset, which an automated injector and trained staff make possible. SISCOM (ictal SPECT with interictal subtraction, coregistered to the MRI) is useful for frontal lobe epilepsy when timing is good.

Long, waxing–waning events with eyes closed and side-to-side movements; normal EEG during a captured attack
Negative symptoms (loss of power, speech, vision) without march, automatisms or impaired awareness

name: Focal impaired awareness seizures
formal: Focal seizures with impaired consciousness, typically temporal, with staring, automatisms, post-ictal confusion and often a preceding aura.
simple: Seizures starting in one part of the brain in which the person is not fully aware, may stare or make repeated movements, and then feels confused.
th: การชักเฉพาะที่ที่ความรู้ตัวบกพร่อง ส่วนใหญ่จากกลีบขมับ มีเหม่อ ทำท่าซ้ำ ๆ อัตโนมัติ สับสนหลังชัก และมักมี aura นำ
tempoNote: Episodes last about 30 seconds to 2 minutes, followed by minutes of post-ictal confusion
feat: Behavioural arrest and staring with reduced responsiveness and amnesia for the event
Oral and manual automatisms (lip-smacking, chewing, fumbling); contralateral dystonic arm posturing in temporal onset
Often preceded by an aura (focal aware seizure)
Post-ictal confusion, aphasia if dominant hemisphere, fatigue
Frontal lobe onset: brief, often nocturnal, hypermotor episodes with quick recovery
inv: EEG; prolonged video-EEG to capture events and localise onset
MRI epilepsy protocol (hippocampal sclerosis, dysplasia, tumour)
Neuropsychology; PET or SPECT in presurgical evaluation

case.who: 34-year-old female teacher from Nakhon Si Thammarat
case.story: Students notice she stops mid-lesson, stares, smacks her lips and fiddles with chalk for a minute, then is confused and cannot recall the episode.
case.exam: Normal; history of prolonged febrile seizures in childhood.
case.tests: EEG left anterior temporal spikes; MRI left hippocampal sclerosis.
case.q: What seizure type is this, and what option exists if two drugs fail?
case.a: Focal impaired awareness seizures from left mesial temporal lobe epilepsy; refer for epilepsy surgery (anterior temporal lobectomy or laser ablation).

read.where: 7 EEG and Semiology in Focal Epilepsy

det.patho: Seizure activity spreads from a focal onset into networks supporting awareness, including limbic structures and bilateral fronto-parietal and thalamic regions. Mesial temporal sclerosis is the commonest substrate in adults; frontal lobe and neocortical lesions are other causes. Childhood prolonged febrile seizures are a risk factor for hippocampal sclerosis.
det.clinical: Witnesses describe staring, unresponsiveness and automatisms; the patient often only knows of missing time. Seizures may progress to bilateral tonic-clonic activity. Lateralising signs include post-ictal aphasia (dominant hemisphere) and unilateral dystonic posturing (contralateral). Driving and safety restrictions apply because awareness is lost.
det.diagnosis: Based on eyewitness and video descriptions supported by EEG and MRI. Distinguish from absence seizures, syncope, TGA, functional seizures and parasomnias. Video-EEG monitoring confirms the diagnosis and localisation, particularly for surgery.
det.treatment: First-line focal antiseizure drugs include lamotrigine, levetiracetam, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine and lacosamide; newer options include cenobamate. Drug-resistant mesial temporal lobe epilepsy has excellent surgical outcomes. Neuromodulation (VNS, responsive neurostimulation, DBS) is an option when surgery is not possible.
det.prognosis: About half become seizure-free on medication; temporal lobe surgery achieves seizure freedom in about 60–70% of selected patients.
pearls: Staring + automatisms + post-ictal confusion in an adult = focal impaired awareness seizure, not absence.
Post-ictal aphasia suggests dominant hemisphere onset.
Early referral for surgery in drug-resistant mesial temporal lobe epilepsy.
det.thd: Focal impaired awareness seizure คือการชักเฉพาะที่ที่ผู้ป่วยไม่รู้ตัวระหว่างชัก มักเกิดจากกลีบขมับ ผู้ป่วยเหม่อ ไม่ตอบสนอง ทำปากหรือมือซ้ำ ๆ แล้วสับสนหลังชักและจำเหตุการณ์ไม่ได้ มักมี aura นำ สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยคือ hippocampal sclerosis วินิจฉัยด้วยประวัติ EEG และ MRI รักษาด้วยยากันชักชนิด focal และถ้าดื้อยาควรส่งผ่าตัดซึ่งได้ผลดี

Hours of repetitive questioning with preserved identity and no automatisms

aN: complex partial seizure | cps | fias | focal dyscognitive seizure | temporal lobe seizure

name: Focal mononeuropathy
formal: Damage to a single peripheral nerve by compression, trauma, ischaemia or entrapment, causing weakness and sensory loss in that nerve's territory.
simple: Damage to one single nerve, causing weakness or numbness in the area that nerve supplies.
th: ความเสียหายของเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเส้นเดียวจากการกดทับ บาดเจ็บ หรือขาดเลือด ทำให้อ่อนแรงและชาเฉพาะบริเวณของเส้นนั้น
tempoNote: Acute with trauma or ischaemia; chronic with entrapment
feat: Weakness and sensory loss confined to one nerve territory
Common sites: median at wrist, ulnar at elbow, radial at spiral groove, peroneal at fibular head
Tinel sign and provocative tests support entrapment
Underlying risk: diabetes, hypothyroidism, pregnancy, repetitive work, weight loss, prolonged immobility
Multiple mononeuropathies suggest vasculitis or hereditary pressure palsies
inv: NCS/EMG to localise, grade (demyelinating versus axonal) and exclude polyneuropathy
Nerve ultrasound to show swelling or compressive cause
Glucose, TSH; check for HNPP if recurrent pressure palsies

case.story: After sleeping in a squatting position following heavy weight loss from illness, he woke with a dropped right foot.
case.exam: Weak ankle dorsiflexion and eversion with preserved inversion and plantar flexion; numb dorsum of the foot; ankle jerk present.
case.tests: NCS: conduction block across the right fibular head.
case.q: Where is the lesion and is recovery likely?
case.a: Common fibular (peroneal) mononeuropathy at the fibular head; demyelinating conduction block predicts good recovery over weeks to months.

read.where: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves — Focal and Compressive Neuropathies
4. Approach to the Evaluation of Mononeuropathy Multiplex
Companion to Peripheral Neuropathy: chapters (see text)

det.patho: Focal nerve injury results from compression or entrapment, stretch, laceration, ischaemia, infiltration or inflammation. Mild compression causes focal demyelination and conduction block, while more severe injury causes axonal degeneration requiring regrowth at about 1 mm per day. Systemic conditions such as diabetes make nerves more vulnerable.
det.clinical: The pattern of weakness and sensory loss maps onto a single nerve's motor branches and cutaneous territory. Identifying which muscles are spared is as important as which are weak, because it separates nerve from root or plexus lesions. Pain may be prominent in entrapment or ischaemic lesions.
det.diagnosis: Careful examination localises the lesion; NCS/EMG confirms the site, severity and pathophysiology, and checks for a generalised neuropathy. Ultrasound or MRI identifies compressive masses, ganglia or nerve swelling. Recurrent or multiple lesions call for tests for HNPP, vasculitis, leprosy (relevant in Thailand) and diabetes.
det.treatment: Remove or relieve the cause: splinting, activity modification, corticosteroid injection or surgical decompression for entrapments; padding and positioning for pressure palsies. Physiotherapy and orthoses such as an ankle-foot orthosis maintain function. Lacerations may need nerve repair or grafting.
det.prognosis: Conduction block lesions often recover within weeks to months; axonal lesions are slower and less complete, depending on distance to target muscle.
pearls: Check muscles supplied by neighbouring nerves and roots to confirm a single-nerve lesion.
Recurrent pressure palsies point to HNPP.
Thickened nerves with sensory loss in Thailand: think leprosy.
det.thd: Focal mononeuropathy คือเส้นประสาทเส้นเดียวเสียจากการถูกกดทับ บาดเจ็บ หรือขาดเลือด ผู้ป่วยมีอ่อนแรงและชาเฉพาะบริเวณที่เส้นนั้นเลี้ยง เช่น carpal tunnel syndrome หรือเท้าตกจาก peroneal nerve การตรวจ NCS/EMG ช่วยหาตำแหน่งและความรุนแรง ถ้าเป็นหลายเส้นหรือเป็นซ้ำต้องหาโรคพื้นฐาน เช่น vasculitis, HNPP หรือโรคเรื้อน
