name: Focal motor seizures
formal: Seizures with localised clonic or tonic motor activity from the contralateral primary motor cortex, which may march (Jacksonian) and may be followed by transient Todd paralysis.
simple: Seizures causing jerking or stiffening of one part of the body, which may spread to nearby areas.
th: อาการชักเฉพาะที่ซึ่งเห็นเป็นการกระตุกหรือเกร็งของแขนขาหรือใบหน้าซีกตรงข้ามกับรอยโรคที่ motor cortex อาจลามเป็น Jacksonian march และตามด้วยอ่อนแรงชั่วคราว (Todd paralysis)
tempoNote: Seconds to a few minutes per attack; Todd weakness can last minutes to 1–2 days
feat: Rhythmic jerking or stiffening of the face, hand or leg on one side, often with preserved awareness at onset
Spread along the motor homunculus (thumb to hand to face) — the Jacksonian march
Head and eye turning away from the irritable hemisphere (versive onset) in frontal seizures
Post-ictal weakness of the same limb (Todd paralysis) that clears within hours
Can spread to become a bilateral tonic-clonic convulsion
inv: MRI brain with epilepsy protocol to find a structural cause (tumour, stroke, cortical dysplasia, cavernoma)
EEG: contralateral central or frontal spikes, though scalp EEG may be normal in brief simple seizures
Glucose, sodium and calcium — non-ketotic hyperglycaemia classically triggers focal motor seizures

case.who: 58-year-old man, rice farmer from Suphan Buri, with poorly controlled diabetes
case.story: Three episodes today of twitching starting in the left thumb, spreading to the arm and left side of the face over 30 seconds, fully aware throughout.
case.exam: After the attack the left hand is weak for two hours; no meningism.
case.tests: Capillary glucose 520 mg/dL, serum ketones negative; MRI shows no infarct.
case.q: What is the seizure type and the likely metabolic trigger?
case.a: Focal motor (Jacksonian) seizures with Todd paralysis, driven by non-ketotic hyperglycaemia; correct glucose and fluids — they often stop as glucose falls.

read.where: Chapter 10 Epilepsy and Related Disorders — Focal Seizures

det.patho: A hyperexcitable patch of the primary motor cortex or its connected premotor network discharges synchronously, producing movements in the matching body part on the opposite side. Spread through adjacent cortex explains the march, and post-ictal neuronal exhaustion or inhibition explains Todd weakness. Any cortical lesion can be the source; in adults stroke, tumour and trauma dominate, while in children dysplasia and genetic causes are common.
det.clinical: Attacks are stereotyped and brief; clonic jerking is most typical, but tonic posturing, versive turning or speech arrest occur depending on the region. Awareness is usually kept unless the seizure spreads beyond motor areas. Clusters, increasing frequency or prolonged attacks may herald status epilepticus. A new focal motor seizure in an adult is a structural lesion until shown otherwise.
det.diagnosis: History from a witness and video on a phone are central. MRI with thin-section and FLAIR sequences is required; CT is a first step in the emergency room but misses small lesions. EEG supports lateralisation but a normal record does not exclude the diagnosis. Check metabolic triggers (glucose, sodium, calcium, magnesium) and, when the context fits, autoimmune or infectious causes.
det.treatment: Treat the cause where possible and start an antiseizure medication suited to focal epilepsy, such as levetiracetam, lamotrigine, lacosamide or carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine. Seizures lasting over 5 minutes are managed as status epilepticus. Drug-resistant cases with a defined focus should be referred for surgical evaluation. Hyperglycaemia-related seizures often respond poorly to drugs until glucose is corrected.
det.prognosis: Depends on the underlying lesion; many patients achieve control with one drug, while lesional drug-resistant cases may become seizure-free after surgery.
pearls: Todd paralysis lasting over 48 hours should prompt a search for a new lesion such as stroke.
Focal motor seizures with high glucose and no ketones: think non-ketotic hyperglycaemia.
Phenytoin is often ineffective in hyperglycaemia-related seizures.
det.thd: Focal motor seizure คืออาการชักที่เริ่มจาก motor cortex ทำให้แขนขาหรือใบหน้าซีกตรงข้ามกระตุกหรือเกร็ง บางรายลามเป็นลำดับจากมือไปแขนและหน้า และอาจอ่อนแรงชั่วคราวหลังชัก ในผู้ใหญ่ต้องหาสาเหตุเชิงโครงสร้างด้วย MRI และตรวจน้ำตาลกับเกลือแร่เสมอ รักษาด้วยยากันชักสำหรับชักเฉพาะที่ร่วมกับแก้สาเหตุ

ddx.pt: Continuous focal jerking for hours to days rather than discrete attacks
Negative symptoms from the start; Todd weakness follows visible jerking
Variable, asynchronous movements with eyes closed and no post-ictal deficit

aN: focal motor seizure | focal clonic seizure | jacksonian seizure | partial motor seizure | focal tonic seizure

name: Focal myoclonus
formal: Brief jerks restricted to a body part from cortical, brainstem, spinal or peripheral causes such as stroke, tumour, spinal cord lesion or nerve injury.
simple: Quick jerks in just one part of the body, caused by a lesion in the nervous system.
th: การกระตุกสั้นๆ ของกล้ามเนื้อเฉพาะส่วนของร่างกาย จากรอยโรคที่เปลือกสมอง ก้านสมอง ไขสันหลัง หรือเส้นประสาทส่วนปลาย
tempoNote: Depends on cause; may persist for long periods
feat: Brief shock-like jerks confined to one limb, the face or a few spinal segments
Cortical focal myoclonus: distal, stimulus-sensitive, action-induced; may merge with EPC
Spinal segmental myoclonus: rhythmic jerks of muscles of one or a few segments, persists in sleep
Peripheral myoclonus from nerve or root lesions, e.g. hemifacial spasm-like
Causes: stroke, tumour, demyelination, myelitis, trauma, infection, post-surgical
inv: Surface EMG burst duration and distribution; back-averaged EEG for cortical origin
MRI of the relevant brain or spinal cord level
Metabolic screen (glucose, renal, hepatic) and drug review

case.who: 45-year-old woman from Songkhla two months after herpes zoster at the T8 level
case.story: Constant rhythmic twitching of the left lower abdominal wall muscles, even at night.
case.exam: Rhythmic jerks about 1–2 per second of left T8–T10 abdominal muscles, persistent during light sleep; mild sensory loss at T8.
case.tests: MRI thoracic cord shows a T2 lesion at T8 consistent with post-zoster myelitis.
case.q: What type of myoclonus is this?
case.a: Spinal segmental focal myoclonus from post-herpetic myelitis.

read.where: 18 - Myoclonus: Phenomenology, etiology, physiology, and treatment

det.patho: Focal myoclonus arises from abnormal discharges at any level of the neuraxis. Cortical myoclonus reflects hyperexcitable sensorimotor cortex; spinal segmental myoclonus reflects loss of inhibitory interneurons with rhythmic firing of anterior horn cells; peripheral myoclonus results from ectopic discharges in damaged nerves or roots.
det.clinical: Cortical forms affect distal limbs or face, are brief, irregular and often triggered by touch or movement. Spinal segmental forms are slower, rhythmic and persist during sleep. Peripheral forms are restricted to a nerve territory. Associated signs such as sensory level, weakness or seizures help localisation.
det.diagnosis: Neurophysiology classifies myoclonus by burst duration and pattern, and back-averaging can show a cortical potential preceding cortical jerks. Imaging targets the level suggested clinically. Functional jerks should be considered when variable, distractible and with long, variable latencies.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying lesion. Cortical myoclonus responds to levetiracetam, valproate, clonazepam or piracetam. Spinal segmental myoclonus may respond to clonazepam, levetiracetam or carbamazepine. Botulinum toxin can help focal peripheral or segmental forms.
det.prognosis: Varies with cause; symptomatic relief is often achievable even when the lesion persists.
pearls: Jerks that persist in sleep suggest a spinal or peripheral generator.
Stimulus-sensitive distal jerks point to cortical myoclonus.
Image the spinal cord when jerks map to dermatomal segments.
det.thd: Focal myoclonus คือการกระตุกสั้นๆ เฉพาะส่วนของร่างกาย อาจมาจากเปลือกสมอง ไขสันหลัง หรือเส้นประสาทส่วนปลาย การกระตุกที่ยังมีขณะหลับมักมาจากไขสันหลัง การตรวจ EMG และ EEG ช่วยแยกชนิด และ MRI หารอยโรค รักษาสาเหตุร่วมกับยา เช่น levetiracetam, clonazepam หรือ botulinum toxin

Axial jerks spreading up and down from a thoracic generator, often functional

name: Focal myositis
formal: Localised benign inflammatory pseudotumour of one muscle, often the calf, presenting with a painful swelling and raised CK, with biopsy showing inflammatory changes.
simple: Inflammation in one muscle, which causes a lump and pain, usually in the calf.
more: MRI and biopsy exclude tumour; it often resolves spontaneously or with steroids.
th: การอักเสบเฉพาะที่ของกล้ามเนื้อมัดเดียว มักที่น่อง เป็นก้อนบวมเจ็บ ไม่ร้ายแรงและหายได้เอง
tempoNote: Develops over days to weeks; often resolves spontaneously within months
feat: Painful or painless enlarging swelling of a single muscle, often lower leg
No systemic myositis; strength elsewhere normal
CK normal or mildly raised
MRI: oedema confined to one muscle; can mimic sarcoma
Some cases linked to denervation such as radiculopathy
inv: MRI with contrast
Biopsy to exclude tumour and infection; shows inflammatory infiltrate
EMG of the limb to look for underlying radiculopathy

case.story: Three weeks of a firm, aching lump in the left calf without fever or trauma; worried about cancer.
case.exam: Tender firm swelling of left medial gastrocnemius, no skin redness, normal strength elsewhere, left ankle reflex reduced.
case.tests: CK 410 U/L; MRI shows oedema limited to medial gastrocnemius without a mass; EMG shows chronic S1 radiculopathy; biopsy shows lymphocytic infiltrates.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and does it need long-term immunosuppression?
case.a: Focal myositis, possibly related to S1 radiculopathy; it usually resolves spontaneously and rarely needs steroids.

det.patho: Focal myositis is a localised inflammatory process within one muscle, of unclear cause. A proportion of cases occur in muscles affected by chronic denervation, suggesting that denervation can trigger local inflammation. Some show features of IgG4-related disease or are early presentations of systemic myositis.
det.clinical: A single muscle, often in the calf or thigh, becomes swollen over weeks, with or without pain. Systemic symptoms are absent. Most cases regress over weeks to months, and recurrence is uncommon. A small minority progress to polymyositis.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows oedema and enhancement limited to one muscle. Biopsy is often required to exclude sarcoma, lymphoma or infection and shows inflammatory infiltrates with fibre damage. EMG may reveal coexisting radiculopathy or neuropathy.
det.treatment: Observation is reasonable for mild cases. Corticosteroids or NSAIDs are used for persistent pain or swelling. Treat any underlying denervating cause. Follow up to ensure resolution and exclude progression.
det.prognosis: Generally benign, with spontaneous resolution in most.
pearls: A focal swollen muscle is often biopsied to exclude a tumour.
Look for radiculopathy in the same myotome.
Most cases resolve without treatment.
det.thd: Focal myositis คือการอักเสบของกล้ามเนื้อเพียงมัดเดียว มักที่น่องหรือต้นขา เป็นก้อนบวมเจ็บ ไม่มีอาการทั่วร่างกาย MRI พบการอักเสบจำกัดเฉพาะที่ อาจต้องตัดชิ้นเนื้อเพื่อแยกจากเนื้องอกหรือการติดเชื้อ บางรายสัมพันธ์กับ radiculopathy ส่วนใหญ่หายเองได้ และใช้ steroid เฉพาะในรายที่มีอาการมาก

name: Focal neuropathies
formal: Isolated peripheral nerve disorders, such as median, ulnar, radial, fibular nerve lesions, mainly from compression or trauma, and diagnosed with nerve conduction studies.
simple: Problems affecting single nerves, such as pinched nerves, causing numbness or weakness in a specific area.

feat: Weakness and sensory loss in the territory of one nerve
Causes: compression, trauma, ischaemia (diabetes, vasculitis), tumour, injection injury
Multiple mononeuropathies imply systemic disease (mononeuritis multiplex)
Pain prominent in vasculitic and diabetic lesions
Electrodiagnosis localises and grades severity

Ultrasound or MRI neurography for structural causes

case.who: 64-year-old man from Phrae with poorly controlled diabetes
case.story: Sudden painful foot drop over two days without trauma or prolonged squatting.
case.exam: Weak ankle dorsiflexion and eversion, inversion preserved, numb dorsum of foot.

det.patho: Focal nerve injury results from compression, stretch, laceration, ischaemia, infiltration or radiation. Pathology ranges from focal demyelination to axonal transection, with prognosis depending on which predominates.
det.clinical: Presentation depends on the nerve involved. Painless lesions suggest compression; painful lesions suggest ischaemia or inflammation. Multiple lesions over time indicate a systemic disorder.
det.diagnosis: Careful examination distinguishing nerve, plexus and root, then electrodiagnosis. Imaging finds masses or entrapment. Blood tests for diabetes, vasculitis and other systemic causes when appropriate.
det.treatment: Treat the cause; protect and splint; decompress or repair surgically when appropriate; immunotherapy for vasculitis. Physiotherapy maintains joint mobility.
det.prognosis: Demyelinating lesions recover quickly; axonal lesions slowly and sometimes incompletely.
pearls: Fibular palsy spares ankle inversion; L5 root lesion does not.
Painful acute mononeuropathy: think vasculitis or diabetic infarction.
Multiple mononeuropathies need systemic work-up.
det.thd: Focal neuropathy คือรอยโรคที่เส้นประสาทเส้นเดียว จากการกด บาดเจ็บ ขาดเลือด หรือเนื้องอก อาการชาและอ่อนแรงตามเส้นนั้น ต้องแยกจากรากประสาทและ plexus ด้วยการตรวจร่างกายและ NCS/EMG ถ้าเป็นหลายเส้นให้นึกถึง vasculitis หรือเบาหวาน รักษาตามสาเหตุ

name: Focal segmental myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus affecting adjacent muscles from a spinal cord lesion, giving rhythmic segmental jerks, often continuous, as in spinal myoclonus due to myelopathy.
simple: Rhythmic jerks of a few muscles of the trunk or limb caused by damage in the spinal cord.
th: การกระตุกเป็นจังหวะของกล้ามเนื้อที่เลี้ยงด้วยไขสันหลังเพียง 1–2 ระดับ เกิดจากรอยโรคของไขสันหลัง
tempoNote: Follows the spinal lesion; jerks are often continuous for weeks to years
feat: Rhythmic or semi-rhythmic jerks (about 1–3 Hz) confined to muscles of one or two cord segments
Continues during sleep and is little affected by stimuli
Arm, trunk or leg involvement depending on segment
May come with other cord signs or be isolated
inv: MRI spine with contrast for myelitis, tumour, syrinx, trauma or ischaemia
EMG: synchronous bursts in segmental muscles

case.story: Constant rhythmic twitching of the left abdominal wall for two months, present even at night; recent shingles on the same side.
case.exam: Rhythmic jerks of left lower abdominal muscles about 2/s; segmental sensory changes at T10.
case.tests: MRI thoracic spine: T2 lesion at T10; CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis with VZV DNA positive.
case.q: Where is the generator of this myoclonus?
case.a: The spinal cord segment (T10) — segmental spinal myoclonus from VZV myelitis.

det.patho: Loss of inhibitory interneurons in a cord segment allows anterior horn cells to fire rhythmically. Causes include myelitis (viral, autoimmune), tumours, syringomyelia, trauma, ischaemia, cervical spondylosis and post-procedure injury.
det.clinical: Jerks are limited to a myotomal distribution, persist in sleep and are relatively unaffected by voluntary action. Associated sensory, motor or sphincter signs help localise the lesion.
det.diagnosis: Spinal MRI is essential; EMG shows rhythmic synchronous bursts in a segmental pattern. Investigate the cause according to the lesion seen.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying lesion. Symptomatic options include clonazepam, levetiracetam and botulinum toxin for focal involvement.
det.prognosis: Depends on the cause; myoclonus can persist even after the lesion improves.
pearls: Persistent in sleep and segmental: look at the cord.
MRI spine before labelling as functional.
Levetiracetam and clonazepam are first symptomatic choices.
det.thd: Focal segmental myoclonus คือการกระตุกเป็นจังหวะเฉพาะกล้ามเนื้อของไขสันหลัง 1–2 ระดับ เกิดแม้ขณะหลับ สาเหตุคือรอยโรคไขสันหลัง เช่น การอักเสบ เนื้องอก หรือบาดเจ็บ ต้องทำ MRI ไขสันหลัง รักษาสาเหตุร่วมกับ clonazepam หรือ levetiracetam

name: Focal seizure
formal: Seizure arising from a network within one hemisphere, with motor, sensory, autonomic or cognitive features, with or without impaired awareness and with possible evolution to bilateral tonic-clonic.
simple: A seizure that begins in one area of the brain and causes symptoms depending on where it starts.
th: อาการชักที่เริ่มจากเครือข่ายสมองซีกเดียว อาจเป็นอาการด้านการเคลื่อนไหว ความรู้สึก อัตโนมัติ หรือความคิด มีหรือไม่มีการรับรู้ตัวลดลง และอาจลามเป็นชักเกร็งกระตุกทั้งตัว
tempoNote: Usually 30 seconds to 2–3 minutes, recurrent; post-ictal confusion common when awareness is impaired
feat: Onset within one hemisphere; symptoms reflect the lobe involved (motor, sensory, visual, autonomic, emotional)
Classified by awareness: focal aware vs focal impaired awareness (older term complex partial)
Auras such as epigastric rising, déjà vu or a smell are focal aware seizures
Automatisms (lip smacking, fumbling) with staring suggest temporal lobe origin
Can spread to focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizure
inv: MRI with epilepsy protocol (hippocampi, cortical dysplasia, tumours, vascular lesions)
EEG, including sleep-deprived or prolonged video-EEG when routine EEG is unrevealing
Blood glucose, electrolytes and, if new-onset with psychiatric or memory change, autoimmune encephalitis screen

case.story: For two years she has brief spells of a rising stomach feeling and a sense of familiarity; recently colleagues saw her stare, chew and fumble with papers for a minute without responding.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination between attacks.
case.tests: EEG shows left anterior temporal sharp waves; MRI shows left hippocampal atrophy with high T2 signal.
case.q: How would you classify the episodes and what is the likely underlying pathology?
case.a: Focal aware seizures (auras) progressing to focal impaired awareness seizures from the left mesial temporal lobe, due to hippocampal sclerosis.

read.where: Chapter 10 Epilepsy and Related Disorders — Seizure Classification; Focal Seizures
Section V: Antiepileptic Drugs and Diet

det.patho: Focal seizures arise when a local cortical or limbic network becomes hypersynchronous because of structural damage, abnormal development, inflammation or genetic channel dysfunction. Clinical expression depends on the symptomatogenic zone that the discharge reaches, which may differ from where it starts. Spread to the opposite hemisphere via callosal or subcortical pathways yields a bilateral tonic-clonic seizure.
det.clinical: The 2017 ILAE scheme separates focal seizures by awareness and then by first prominent feature: motor (automatisms, clonic, tonic, hyperkinetic) or non-motor (sensory, autonomic, cognitive, emotional, behaviour arrest). Temporal seizures typically last 1–2 minutes with automatisms and post-ictal confusion; frontal seizures are brief, nocturnal and hyperkinetic; occipital seizures produce coloured visual phenomena. Elderly patients often have subtle focal impaired awareness seizures misread as confusion or transient amnesia.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, built on a careful description of the first symptom and the witness account. MRI identifies the cause in a large proportion; EEG interictal epileptiform discharges help localise but are absent in many routine recordings. Video-EEG remains the reference test for uncertain events and for surgical work-up. Exclude syncope, TIA, migraine aura, sleep disorders and functional seizures.
det.treatment: First-line options include lamotrigine and levetiracetam, with lacosamide, oxcarbazepine, carbamazepine, zonisamide and others as alternatives; choice is guided by age, sex, pregnancy plans and comorbidity. Failure of two appropriate drugs defines drug-resistant epilepsy and warrants referral to an epilepsy surgery centre. Advise on driving, safety and seizure first aid.
det.prognosis: About two thirds become seizure-free with medication; lesional drug-resistant focal epilepsy has good surgical outcomes, especially mesial temporal sclerosis.
pearls: Ask what happened first — the earliest symptom localises best.
An aura is itself a focal aware seizure.
Carbamazepine and other sodium-channel drugs can worsen generalised epilepsies misdiagnosed as focal.
det.thd: Focal seizure คือชักที่เริ่มจากสมองซีกเดียว แสดงอาการตามตำแหน่ง เช่น ความรู้สึกแปลกในท้อง เดจาวู ตาค้างและเคี้ยวปาก หรือแขนกระตุก แบ่งตามการรับรู้ตัวว่ายังรู้ตัวหรือไม่ วินิจฉัยจากประวัติร่วมกับ MRI และ EEG รักษาด้วยยากันชัก และถ้าดื้อยาสองตัวควรประเมินผ่าตัด

name: Foeral alcohol syndrome
formal: Prenatal alcohol exposure syndrome with growth restriction, facial dysmorphism (smooth philtrum, thin upper lip), microcephaly and neurodevelopmental disability.
simple: A lifelong condition from alcohol drunk during pregnancy, causing small size, facial changes, and learning and behaviour problems.
th: ความผิดปกติของทารกจากมารดาดื่มแอลกอฮอล์ระหว่างตั้งครรภ์ มีการเจริญเติบโตช้า หน้าตาจำเพาะ ศีรษะเล็ก และปัญหาพัฒนาการ
tempoNote: Present from birth; neurodevelopmental and behavioural effects are lifelong
feat: Name is a misspelling of fetal alcohol syndrome in the source list
Facial features: short palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, thin upper lip
Prenatal or postnatal growth deficiency and microcephaly
Intellectual disability, ADHD-like behaviour, poor executive function, seizures in some
Part of the broader fetal alcohol spectrum disorder; many affected children lack facial features
inv: Clinical diagnosis with standard criteria (facial measurements, growth, head size, neurodevelopment)
Confirm maternal alcohol history where possible
Genetic testing (chromosomal microarray) to exclude mimicking syndromes
MRI brain may show corpus callosum anomalies or small brain

case.who: 5-year-old boy in foster care in Chon Buri
case.story: Mother drank heavily during pregnancy; he was small at birth, speaks late and is very hyperactive at kindergarten.
case.exam: Weight and head circumference below 3rd centile, short palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, thin upper lip; clumsy fine motor skills.
case.tests: Microarray normal; MRI shows a thin corpus callosum; developmental assessment shows global delay.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the main management aims?
case.a: Fetal alcohol syndrome; early developmental and educational support, management of ADHD symptoms and support for the caregiving family.

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Other Neurological Complications of Alcohol Abuse
Chapter 9: Congenital Disorders of the Brain and Spine

det.patho: Alcohol and its metabolites cross the placenta and disrupt neuronal proliferation and migration, increase apoptosis and impair midline facial development. First-trimester exposure drives the facial features, while exposure throughout pregnancy affects brain growth and function. There is no known safe threshold for alcohol in pregnancy, and genetic susceptibility modifies the effect.
det.clinical: The full syndrome combines characteristic facial features, growth deficiency and central nervous system abnormalities. Neurodevelopmental problems include learning disability, poor memory, attention problems, impulsivity, poor social judgement and motor clumsiness. Seizures, hearing and visual problems and heart defects may occur. Many children with significant exposure have neurodevelopmental deficits without facial features.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis uses established criteria such as the updated Hoyme or Canadian guidelines, combining facial measurements, growth, head circumference and neurodevelopmental testing. Confirmed maternal drinking is required for some categories. Exclude genetic syndromes with overlapping features, such as Williams or 22q11 deletion, with microarray testing.
det.treatment: There is no cure; early diagnosis allows early intervention. Management includes special education, speech and occupational therapy, behavioural support and medication for ADHD symptoms. Stable caregiving and support for the family improve outcomes. Prevention through counselling and screening of pregnant women is the most effective strategy.
det.prognosis: Disabilities are lifelong, with high risk of school failure and social problems; early support improves adaptive function.
pearls: The face may normalise in adolescence; look at childhood photographs.
Most affected children do not have the full facial phenotype.
No amount of alcohol in pregnancy is known to be safe.
det.thd: Fetal alcohol syndrome (ในรายการสะกดเป็น Foeral) เกิดจากมารดาดื่มแอลกอฮอล์ขณะตั้งครรภ์ ทารกตัวเล็ก ศีรษะเล็ก หน้าตาจำเพาะคือตาสั้น ร่องเหนือริมฝีปากเรียบ ริมฝีปากบนบาง และมีปัญหาพัฒนาการ สมาธิ และพฤติกรรม หลายรายไม่มีลักษณะใบหน้าแต่มีปัญหาสมอง การวินิจฉัยเป็นทางคลินิกร่วมกับประวัติการดื่ม การดูแลคือกระตุ้นพัฒนาการ การศึกษาพิเศษ และป้องกันโดยงดดื่มขณะตั้งครรภ์

name: Folate (vitamin B9) deficiency
formal: Deficiency causing megaloblastic anaemia, neuropathy, myelopathy, cognitive impairment and neural tube defects in pregnancy; frequently induced by antiepileptic drugs and malabsorption.
simple: Too little folate (vitamin B9), which can cause anaemia, nerve problems and, in pregnancy, spinal defects in the baby.
more: Check serum and red cell folate with homocysteine and MMA to separate from B12 deficiency; folic acid alone can worsen subacute combined degeneration if B12 deficiency is missed. Periconceptual supplementation prevents neural tube defects.
th: ขาดโฟเลตทำให้โลหิตจางชนิดเม็ดเลือดแดงใหญ่ ปลายประสาทอักเสบเล็กน้อย ซึมเศร้า ความจำถดถอย และเพิ่มความเสี่ยงท่อประสาทของทารก สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยคือสุรา ยากันชัก การดูดซึมผิดปกติ และตั้งครรภ์
tempoNote: Body stores last months, so symptoms develop over months of poor intake, malabsorption or drug effect; cerebral folate deficiency in children evolves over months to years
feat: Macrocytic anaemia with glossitis, fatigue and sometimes thrombocytopenia or leukopenia, usually more prominent than neurological signs
Mild distal sensory neuropathy; myelopathy is far less typical than in B12 deficiency
Low mood, apathy and slowed thinking, especially in older people
Causes: alcohol, poor diet, pregnancy, coeliac and other malabsorption, phenytoin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, valproate, methotrexate, trimethoprim

When the mother is deficient, neural tube defects become more likely; in children, cerebral folate deficiency causes progressive encephalopathy with seizures, ataxia and calcification of the occipital lobes and basal ganglia
inv: Complete blood count with MCV and blood film (hypersegmented neutrophils); serum folate for recent intake and red-cell folate for stores
B12, methylmalonic acid and homocysteine: homocysteine is raised in both deficiencies, methylmalonic acid only in B12 deficiency
Coeliac serology and review of medications; for suspected cerebral folate deficiency, CSF 5-methyltetrahydrofolate with serum folate normal, and FOLR1 or folate receptor antibody testing

case.who: 52-year-old man with alcohol use disorder, Khon Kaen
case.story: Several months of tiredness, a sore smooth tongue, and numb toes. Meals are irregular and mostly rice with spirits. He has become low and forgetful.
case.exam: Pale, glossitis, mild distal pinprick loss in the feet, reflexes preserved, normal Romberg.
case.tests: Haemoglobin 8.2 g/dL, MCV 112 fL, hypersegmented neutrophils; serum folate very low; B12 normal; homocysteine high, methylmalonic acid normal.
case.q: Why is the B12 result critical before giving folic acid?
case.a: Folic acid can correct the anaemia of B12 deficiency and let the nerve and cord damage progress unseen. Confirm B12 is adequate (or replace it), then give oral folic acid with nutrition and alcohol counselling.

read.where: Chapter 31: Epilepsy in the Setting of Inherited Metabolic and Mitochondrial Disorders — Cerebral Folate Deficiency
Section V: Antiepileptic Drugs and Diet

det.patho: Folate, in the form of tetrahydrofolate derivatives, carries one-carbon units for synthesis of purines, thymidylate and methionine, so deficiency impairs DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells and raises homocysteine. In the nervous system folate is actively concentrated and CSF levels exceed blood levels, which makes the brain depend on specific transport through the choroid plexus folate receptor. Primary cerebral folate deficiency may result from FOLR1 variants or from autoantibodies to the receptor, and secondary forms accompany mitochondrial disease, Rett syndrome and malabsorption.
det.clinical: Adults present with fatigue, pallor, sore tongue and macrocytosis; neurological effects are usually mild, with a distal sensory neuropathy, mood disturbance and cognitive slowing, and occasionally a myelopathy. Antiseizure drugs that induce liver enzymes or interfere with folate absorption are a recognised cause, and valproate and carbamazepine in pregnancy increase neural tube defect risk. In infants and children, cerebral folate deficiency produces slowly progressive encephalopathy with intractable seizures, ataxia and sometimes calcification on imaging. Methylene-tetrahydrofolate reductase deficiency, the commonest inborn error of folate metabolism, causes microcephaly, infantile spasms and high homocysteine.
det.diagnosis: Measure folate, preferably red-cell folate, together with B12, homocysteine and methylmalonic acid so that the two deficiencies are separated. Check for alcohol, drugs and malabsorption as causes. When a child has unexplained encephalopathy and seizures, analyse CSF neurotransmitters and 5-methyltetrahydrofolate, since a low CSF value with a normal blood level suggests cerebral deficiency. Normal amino and organic acids help to exclude other treatable causes.
det.treatment: In adults, replace with oral folic acid (usually 1–5 mg daily) after confirming adequate B12 status or replacing B12 at the same time, and correct diet, alcohol use and underlying malabsorption. Women of child-bearing potential who take antiseizure medication should take at least 0.4 mg daily and often more by local guidance, as folic acid is not harmful to seizure control at ordinary doses. Cerebral folate deficiency is treated with folinic acid, which crosses the blood–brain barrier better than folic acid, and a lactose-free diet is considered when receptor antibodies are suspected. MTHFR deficiency responds to betaine, folate and methionine.
det.prognosis: Haematological and mood symptoms recover quickly in adults; neuropathy improves slowly. Outcome in cerebral folate deficiency remains guarded despite treatment.
pearls: Never treat macrocytic anaemia with folic acid alone before B12 has been checked.
Homocysteine high with normal methylmalonic acid points to folate, not B12.
Folinic acid, not folic acid, is the drug for the brain in cerebral folate deficiency.
det.thd: โฟเลตจำเป็นต่อการสร้างดีเอ็นเอและเมทไธโอนีน ผู้ขาดมักมีโลหิตจางชนิดเม็ดเลือดแดงใหญ่ ลิ้นอักเสบ ปลายประสาทเสื่อมเล็กน้อย ซึมเศร้า และความจำช้าลง สาเหตุสำคัญคือสุรา อาหารไม่พอ ตั้งครรภ์ และยากันชักบางชนิด การตรวจควรวัดโฟเลต B12 homocysteine และ methylmalonic acid ก่อนให้ folic acid เสมอเพราะ folate อาจบังโลหิตจางจากการขาด B12 ส่วนเด็กที่ขาดโฟเลตในสมองมีอาการชักและสมองเสื่อม ต้องตรวจ CSF 5-MTHF และรักษาด้วย folinic acid

formal: Urinary retention in young women from failed urethral sphincter relaxation, associated with polycystic ovaries and abnormal sphincter EMG with complex repetitive discharges.
simple: A condition in which young women cannot empty their bladder because the outlet muscle does not relax.

Retention may follow surgery, childbirth or opioid exposure
Pain or difficulty on catheter removal (gripping sensation)
Neurological examination is otherwise normal

case.exam: Normal saddle sensation, anal tone and limb examination.

det.patho: The urethral sphincter fails to relax, possibly due to abnormal myotonia-like electrical activity that inhibits bladder afferents and detrusor contraction. An association with polycystic ovaries was reported but is not consistent. It is not a central neurological disease.
det.clinical: Note: this is a urological sphincter disorder, not a primary neurological disease, but neurologists see it when retention raises fear of cord disease. Retention is typically painless with large volumes. Recurrent urinary infections and difficulty with catheter removal are common.
det.diagnosis: Exclude neurological causes with examination and MRI. Urodynamics and sphincter EMG showing the characteristic discharges support the diagnosis; increased sphincter volume on ultrasound may be found.
det.treatment: Clean intermittent self-catheterisation is the first step. Sacral neuromodulation restores voiding in a good proportion. Avoid opioids where possible.
det.prognosis: Chronic in many, but neuromodulation gives lasting benefit in responders.
pearls: Young woman with painless retention and normal neurology: think Fowler.
Sphincter EMG is the key test.
Not functional: it has an objective electrophysiological signature.

name: Fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS)
formal: Late-onset neurodegeneration in FMR1 premutation carriers with intention tremor, cerebellar ataxia, parkinsonism, cognitive decline and MRI middle cerebellar peduncle T2 hyperintensity.
simple: An inherited disease in older carriers of a gene change on the X chromosome, causing shaking, unsteadiness and memory decline.
more: Diagnosis by FMR1 CGG repeat of 55 to 200; MRI middle cerebellar peduncle sign, with male predominance and variable penetrance in women. Treatment is symptomatic, with genetic counselling for risk of fragile X syndrome in descendants, especially grandchildren.
th: อาการสั่นขณะทำงานและเดินเซในผู้ชายสูงอายุที่เป็นพาหะ FMR1 premutation มักมีหลานเป็น fragile X MRI พบ MCP sign
tempoNote: Onset usually after 50, slowly progressive over years to decades
feat: Action/intention tremor followed by gait ataxia in an older man
Executive dysfunction, memory problems, apathy or anxiety; later dementia
Mild parkinsonism, peripheral neuropathy and autonomic symptoms (bladder, erectile)
Family clue: grandchild with intellectual disability/autism (fragile X) or daughter with early menopause
inv: FMR1 CGG repeat analysis: premutation 55–200 repeats
MRI: bright T2 change within the middle cerebellar peduncles (MCP sign), splenium change, cerebral and cerebellar atrophy
Nerve conduction for neuropathy; neuropsychology

case.story: Over 4 years his hands shake when drinking and he now walks with a broad base; he forgets appointments. His grandson has autism and developmental delay.
case.exam: Bilateral kinetic and intention tremor, gait ataxia, reduced ankle reflexes and distal vibration loss, mild bradykinesia.
case.tests: MRI: bilateral MCP T2 hyperintensity and mild atrophy; FMR1: 95 CGG repeats.
case.q: What genetic counselling issue arises for his family?
case.a: FXTAS; his daughters are obligate premutation carriers, at risk of primary ovarian insufficiency and of having children with full-mutation fragile X syndrome.

read.where: Chapter 27 Hereditary and Acquired Cerebellar Ataxias

det.patho: Premutation-sized CGG repeats (55–200) in FMR1 raise FMR1 mRNA levels, producing RNA toxicity, sequestration of RNA-binding proteins and repeat-associated non-AUG (FMRpolyG) translation. Pathology shows eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions in neurons and astrocytes. Penetrance increases with age and is much higher in men; carrier frequency is roughly 1 in 400–800 men.
det.clinical: Tremor usually precedes ataxia by a few years. Cognitive decline is frontal-executive in type and may progress to dementia, with apathy, disinhibition and depression. Neuropathy, autonomic dysfunction and mild parkinsonism are common. Women carriers develop FXTAS less often and more mildly, but have risks of ovarian insufficiency and mood disorders.
det.diagnosis: Consider FMR1 testing in anyone over 50 with unexplained late-onset cerebellar ataxia or action tremor plus cognitive change, especially with a relevant family history. Diagnostic criteria combine the premutation with clinical (tremor, ataxia) and radiological (MCP sign, white-matter change) features. Exclude MSA, SCAs, alcohol-related ataxia and vascular disease.
det.treatment: Management is symptomatic: propranolol or primidone for tremor, physiotherapy for gait and falls, treat neuropathy pain, mood and bladder problems, and cognitive support. Thalamic DBS has been used for disabling tremor but may worsen ataxia. Genetic counselling for the wider family is a central part of care.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; median survival after motor onset is around two decades, with increasing dependence.
pearls: Late-onset tremor plus ataxia in a man: ask about grandchildren with intellectual disability.
The MCP sign on T2 MRI is the radiological clue.
Premutation range is 55–200 CGG repeats; full mutation >200 causes fragile X syndrome.
det.thd: FXTAS เกิดในผู้ที่เป็นพาหะ FMR1 premutation (CGG 55–200 ซ้ำ) มักเป็นชายอายุเกิน 50 ปี มีมือสั่นขณะใช้งาน เดินเซ ความจำและการตัดสินใจถดถอย อาจมีปลายประสาทเสื่อม MRI พบ T2 hyperintensity ที่ middle cerebellar peduncle ประวัติครอบครัวมีหลานเป็น fragile X ช่วยมาก การรักษาเป็นการบรรเทาอาการและให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรมแก่ครอบครัว

Examination shows mild parkinsonism and reduced vibration sense in the feet. MRI shows T2 hyperintensity in both middle cerebellar peduncles and in the corpus callosum splenium. His daughter had early menopause at 36, and her son has an intellectual disability.

The MCP sign also occurs in MSA-C, but the family history is the key. Splenial hyperintensity is a supportive feature, and genetic counselling is essential for the wider family.

name: Fragile-X syndrome
formal: X-linked FMR1 full-mutation disorder (CGG greater than 200) with intellectual disability, autism spectrum features, macro-orchidism, long face and large ears; commonest inherited cause of intellectual disability.
simple: A common inherited condition causing learning difficulties and behaviour differences, with typical facial features.
th: โรคทางพันธุกรรมแบบ X-linked จากการขยายซ้ำ CGG ในยีน FMR1 เป็นสาเหตุทางพันธุกรรมที่พบบ่อยที่สุดของภาวะบกพร่องทางสติปัญญาและออทิซึม
tempoNote: Present from early childhood; stable or slowly improving behaviour into adulthood
feat: Developmental delay, language delay and intellectual disability, usually moderate in boys
Hyperactivity, anxiety, gaze avoidance, hand flapping and sensory over-reactivity
Long face, prominent ears, high palate, joint laxity and enlarged testes after puberty
Seizures in a minority, commonly focal and remitting in childhood
Premutation carriers (55–200 CGG repeats) risk FXTAS in later life and premature ovarian insufficiency
inv: FMR1 CGG repeat sizing with methylation analysis (PCR with Southern blot or methylation PCR)
Chromosomal microarray as part of first-tier developmental delay work-up
Cascade testing and genetic counselling for the mother and relatives
EEG if seizures

case.story: He speaks only a few words, avoids eye contact, flaps his hands and has meltdowns in crowded markets. A maternal uncle attended a special school.
case.exam: Long face, large soft ears, hyperextensible finger joints, flat feet, poor eye contact, no focal deficit.
case.tests: Microarray normal; FMR1 shows about 400 CGG repeats with abnormal methylation. His mother carries a premutation.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and what should the family be told?
case.a: Fragile-X syndrome. Mother and relatives need counselling and testing; female premutation carriers have a high risk of expansion in offspring, and older male carriers need to know about FXTAS.

det.patho: A CGG expansion above 200 in the 5' untranslated region of FMR1 triggers hypermethylation and silencing of the gene, removing the protein FMRP which regulates synaptic translation. The unstable premutation expands to full mutation when passed through females, and the risk rises with the repeat size. Prevalence is roughly 1 in 4000–7000 males.
det.clinical: Affected boys are usually brought at two to three years because speech lags, they are overactive, and they show habits such as hand biting, flapping and turning away from faces. Physical features become more obvious after puberty. Females with the full mutation range from normal to moderate disability, and anxiety and learning problems are frequent. Seizures and recurrent otitis are common comorbidities. Many affected boys also meet criteria for autism spectrum disorder.
det.diagnosis: Target FMR1 repeat analysis in any child with unexplained developmental delay, autism or a family history, alongside microarray. Methylation status distinguishes full mutation from premutation and mosaicism. Positive results lead to cascade testing and offering prenatal counselling. The test is also appropriate for adults with tremor, ataxia or ovarian insufficiency and suspected premutation disease.
det.treatment: There is no cure. Management combines early intervention, speech and occupational therapy, educational support and treatment of attention deficit, anxiety and aggression with standard medications. Seizures are treated with usual anti-seizure drugs. Targeted agents have been trialled but none has altered the course. Counselling about inheritance is central.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is near normal; most affected men need lifelong support. Behaviour often improves in adulthood.
pearls: Consider FMR1 testing in any boy with intellectual disability and autistic features.
Mothers of affected boys are premutation carriers, so counsel the whole maternal family.
FXTAS can appear in grandfathers of affected children.
det.thd: Fragile-X syndrome เกิดจากการซ้ำของ CGG ในยีน FMR1 เกิน 200 ครั้งบนโครโมโซม X ทำให้ไม่สร้างโปรตีน FMRP เด็กชายมักพูดช้า ซนมาก กระพือมือ หลบสายตา หน้ายาว หูใหญ่ ข้อหลวม และอัณฑะโตหลังวัยรุ่น การวินิจฉัยใช้การตรวจ FMR1 พร้อมวิเคราะห์ methylation การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง ได้แก่ การกระตุ้นพัฒนาการ ฝึกพูด และยารักษาอาการร่วม ที่สำคัญคือให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรมแก่มารดาและญาติ เพราะผู้เป็นพาหะมีความเสี่ยงต่อ FXTAS และรังไข่ล้มเหลวก่อนวัย

name: Freezing
formal: Brief episodic inability to initiate or continue stepping, with feet feeling glued to the floor, in parkinsonism and related disorders; triggers include turning, doorways and cueing helps.
simple: Sudden moments when the feet seem stuck to the floor and walking cannot start or continue, common in Parkinson disease.
th: Freezing (freezing of gait) คือภาวะที่เท้าติดพื้นชั่วคราวทั้งที่ตั้งใจจะก้าว พบบ่อยใน Parkinson disease ระยะท้ายและโรค parkinsonism อื่น ๆ เช่น PSP, vascular parkinsonism และ NPH มักเกิดตอนเริ่มเดิน เลี้ยว ผ่านประตูหรือที่แคบ เป็นสาเหตุสำคัญของการหกล้ม ต้องแยกให้ได้ว่าเกิดช่วง OFF หรือ ON และรักษาด้วยการปรับยา การใช้ cue และกายภาพบำบัด
tempoNote: Individual episodes last seconds to under a minute; the problem usually appears years into Parkinson disease, but within 1–2 years of onset in progressive supranuclear palsy or vascular parkinsonism
feat: Sudden, brief inability to start or continue stepping; the feet feel glued, the knees may tremble, and stride becomes tiny and shuffling before the block
Typical triggers are gait initiation (start hesitation), turning, doorways and narrow passages, approaching a target, crowds, stress and carrying out a second task while walking
May be mostly OFF-related and levodopa-responsive, or ON-related and levodopa-resistant; some patients rock side to side without leaving the floor (the 'slipping clutch' pattern)
Visual lines on the floor, counting, rhythmic sound or stepping over an object can release the block, an effect called paradoxical kinesia
Related freezing of speech, eyelid opening apraxia and freezing of the hands occur; it is one of the largest causes of falls and fractures in parkinsonism
inv: Provoke it in the clinic with a 360-degree turn, narrow doorway and dual task; use a freezing questionnaire (FOG-Q) and video, and compare ON and OFF state
Review of levodopa timing and dose, and of drugs that worsen gait such as sedatives and some antipsychotics
MRI brain when vascular disease, hydrocephalus or midbrain atrophy is suspected; orthostatic blood pressure; vision, neuropathy and frailty checks

case.who: 72-year-old man from Nonthaburi with 10 years of Parkinson disease
case.story: He gets stuck at doorways and when turning in the kitchen, especially in the hour before his next levodopa dose; he has fallen twice this month. He can walk easily when he follows the tiles on the corridor floor.
case.exam: Freezing during a full turn and in a narrow doorway, shuffling steps with reduced arm swing, improved when stepping over a line on the floor.
case.tests: No new investigations are needed; a diary links the freezing to OFF periods.
case.q: What management helps this type of freezing?
case.a: Reduce OFF time by adjusting levodopa (more frequent doses, a COMT or MAO-B inhibitor), and teach cueing strategies and turning techniques with a physiotherapist; deep brain stimulation is an option for fluctuating patients, though freezing in the ON state responds poorly.

det.patho: Freezing arises from a failure of the normal automatic scaling and sequencing of steps, which probably involves dysfunction of basal ganglia and mesencephalic locomotor region circuits, frontal executive control and the cholinergic and noradrenergic systems. Patients rely more on conscious attention and external cues, so competing demands (turning, narrow spaces, dual tasks) overload the system and gait stops. Because levodopa-resistant freezing is common, non-dopaminergic pathways are clearly involved.
det.clinical: Freezing is a leading cause of falls in Parkinson disease and often lowers confidence and independence. Its subtypes are start hesitation, turning hesitation, hesitation when approaching a target and freezing in tight places; episodes vary with the day, stress and medication state. It also occurs in progressive supranuclear palsy, vascular and lower-body parkinsonism, normal pressure hydrocephalus and frontal gait disorders, in which it may be the earliest sign. Treat freezing as a symptom to be localised to OFF, ON or independent of medication.
det.diagnosis: Document the pattern by watching the patient start, turn, pass a door and perform a second task, and ask a family member to video them at home. Time the episodes against levodopa doses using a diary or by comparing the examination in ON and OFF states. Imaging is for atypical settings, such as early falls (PSP), vascular risk (white-matter disease) or dilated ventricles (NPH). Evaluate balance and orthostatic hypotension as contributors to falls.
det.treatment: For OFF-related freezing, optimise dopaminergic therapy: split doses, add a dopamine agonist, COMT inhibitor or MAO-B inhibitor, or use apomorphine or an infusion therapy for refractory fluctuations. ON-related freezing may improve when the dose is lowered. Cueing devices (laser canes, floor markings, a metronome), step-over strategies, turning techniques and balance training from a physiotherapist are the most effective non-drug measures, together with a home safety review. Subthalamic DBS improves OFF freezing but not always the ON type; amantadine and methylphenidate have been tried with mixed results.
det.prognosis: Freezing tends to increase over time in Parkinson disease; early physiotherapy and medication timing reduce falls but cannot always remove it.
pearls: Ask whether the freezing occurs when the levodopa has worn off; if it does, the first step is to fix the OFF period.
A visual line on the floor can release a freezing patient, so a cane with a laser line may be a useful prescription.
Early freezing and falls with poor levodopa response suggest PSP or vascular parkinsonism, not typical Parkinson disease.

name: Friedreich’s ataxia
formal: Autosomal recessive GAA expansion in FXN with frataxin deficiency causing early-onset progressive gait and limb ataxia, areflexia, dorsal column loss, scoliosis, cardiomyopathy and diabetes.
simple: An inherited disease starting in childhood or teens causing worsening clumsiness, loss of balance and often heart disease.
more: Diagnose by FXN GAA repeat expansion testing; nerve conduction shows absent sensory responses and MRI shows cervical cord atrophy. Idebenone has uncertain benefit and omaveloxolone is approved; monitor for cardiomyopathy, diabetes and scoliosis. Autosomal recessive spinocerebellar and sensory ataxia from GAA expansions in FXN, causing frataxin deficiency, areflexia, cardiomyopathy, scoliosis and diabetes. Diagnosed by FXN repeat expansion testing; ECG and echo monitor the heart. Omaveloxolone is approved for treatment; otherwise supportive; typically wheelchair use within 10-15 years and cardiac cause of death. Autosomal recessive GAA expansion in FXN causing frataxin deficiency, with progressive gait and limb ataxia, areflexia, sensory neuronopathy, cardiomyopathy, and diabetes. Diagnosed by FXN repeat testing; omaveloxolone is approved; treat cardiac disease and diabetes; wheelchair dependence is common within about 15 years.
th: โรคเดินเซทางพันธุกรรมแบบด้อยที่พบบ่อยที่สุด — เซ + reflex หาย + Babinski + cardiomyopathy เริ่มในวัยรุ่น
tempoNote: Usually starts before 25; steady progression over years; late-onset forms exist
feat: Progressive gait and limb ataxia beginning in childhood or adolescence
Absent ankle and knee jerks with extensor plantars; loss of vibration and position sense
Dysarthria, scoliosis, pes cavus, square-wave jerks
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and diabetes are common non-neurological features
inv: FXN gene test: biallelic GAA repeat expansion (rarely one expansion plus a point variant)
NCS: absent or reduced sensory potentials (sensory neuronopathy)
ECG and echocardiogram; HbA1c; spine X-ray for scoliosis

case.story: Clumsy in sport since age 11, now falls frequently and his handwriting has deteriorated; parents are first cousins.
case.exam: Broad-based ataxic gait, positive Romberg, absent reflexes in legs, bilateral Babinski, pes cavus, mild thoracic scoliosis.
case.tests: Sural SNAPs absent; ECG shows widespread T inversion and echo shows concentric LV hypertrophy.
case.q: Which genetic test confirms the diagnosis, and what drug is now approved?
case.a: GAA repeat expansion in FXN on both alleles. Omaveloxolone is approved for patients aged 16 and over; cardiac follow-up is lifelong.

read.where: Chapter 74: Cerebellar Disorders and Ataxias: Inherited Disorders

det.patho: Most patients carry an expanded GAA trinucleotide repeat in intron 1 of FXN on both alleles, which silences the gene and reduces frataxin, a mitochondrial protein involved in iron–sulfur cluster assembly. Mitochondrial iron overload and oxidative stress damage dorsal root ganglia, spinocerebellar tracts, corticospinal tracts, dentate nucleus and heart. Shorter repeats on the smaller allele generally predict later onset and milder course.
det.clinical: Gait ataxia is the usual first sign, followed by limb ataxia, dysarthria and loss of proprioception, so Romberg is positive. Reflexes vanish early yet plantars become extensor, a classic combination. Scoliosis, pes cavus, optic atrophy, hearing loss and diabetes accumulate; many patients need a wheelchair 10–20 years after onset. Late-onset and retained-reflex variants occur and are easily missed.
det.diagnosis: Genetic testing for the FXN GAA expansion is diagnostic and should be requested in any young patient with progressive ataxia and areflexia. NCS show a sensory neuronopathy with preserved motor conduction. MRI often shows cervical cord thinning with relatively little cerebellar atrophy early on. Always measure vitamin E, and consider other recessive ataxias if testing is negative.
det.treatment: Omaveloxolone, an Nrf2 activator, has regulatory approval for patients 16 years and older and modestly slows decline; liver enzymes and lipids need monitoring. Supportive care includes physiotherapy, orthoses, scoliosis surgery when indicated, speech therapy and diabetes management. Regular cardiac review with ECG and echo is essential, treating heart failure and arrhythmia promptly.
det.prognosis: Disability progresses over decades; cardiomyopathy is the leading cause of death, often in middle age. Later onset generally means slower course.
pearls: Areflexia with upgoing toes in a teenager with ataxia = Friedreich until proven otherwise.
Cerebellar atrophy is usually mild early; the spinal cord is the thin structure on MRI.
Screen the heart at diagnosis even if the patient has no cardiac symptoms.

qx.stem: A 14-year-old boy from Nakhon Ratchasima becomes ataxic and areflexic after a septic illness and later develops esotropia. Sensory nerve action potentials are absent in the limbs, motor conduction and needle EMG are normal, and serology is negative. IVIG and plasma exchange do not help, and a cardiologist later finds cardiomyopathy.
qx.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis?

det.patho: The frontal lobes, especially prefrontal cortex and their loops through striatum and thalamus, support executive control, motivation and social behaviour. Damage to cortex or to frontal-subcortical circuits produces the syndrome, so subcortical lesions can mimic frontal cortex damage.
det.clinical: Three overlapping profiles are recognised: dysexecutive (dorsolateral), disinhibited (orbitofrontal) and apathetic (medial). Patients often lack insight, so history from relatives is essential. Release signs, perseveration, environmental dependency and frontal gait disorder may accompany behavioural change. Memory may appear poor because of inattention rather than true amnesia.
det.diagnosis: This is a syndrome; the task is finding the cause. MRI identifies tumours, infarcts, contusions, hydrocephalus and frontal atrophy. FDG-PET may show frontal hypometabolism in early bvFTD. Psychiatric disorders such as late-onset mania or depression can mimic frontal syndromes and need consideration.
det.treatment: Treatment targets the cause: surgery for tumours, shunting for hydrocephalus, rehabilitation after trauma or stroke. Behavioural management, structured routines and carer education are central. SSRIs may reduce disinhibition and compulsions in FTD; antipsychotics are used sparingly. Address driving and financial safety early.
det.prognosis: Depends entirely on the cause, from full recovery after meningioma removal to progressive decline in FTD.
pearls: Patients with frontal syndromes typically underestimate their problems; interview the family.
Always image before diagnosing bvFTD; frontal meningiomas can be large and silent.
Medial frontal damage gives apathy; orbitofrontal damage gives disinhibition.
det.thd: Frontal lobe syndrome คือกลุ่มอาการจากสมองส่วนหน้าทำงานผิดปกติ ผู้ป่วยวางแผนไม่ได้ เฉยเมย หรือทำตัวไม่เหมาะสม บุคลิกเปลี่ยน และมักไม่รู้ตัวว่าผิดปกติ สาเหตุมีทั้งเนื้องอก stroke อุบัติเหตุ โพรงน้ำในสมองขยาย และ frontotemporal dementia ต้องทำ MRI หาสาเหตุที่รักษาได้ก่อนเสมอ

name: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD)
formal: Neurodegenerative dementia with early behavioural change, disinhibition, apathy, or language impairment from frontal and temporal degeneration, often with tau, TDP-43 or FUS pathology and genetic forms (MAPT, GRN, C9orf72).
simple: A brain disease that mainly harms the front and sides of the brain, causing changes in personality, behaviour or language.
th: กลุ่มโรคสมองเสื่อมจากสมองส่วนหน้าและขมับฝ่อ พบได้ก่อนอายุ 65 ปี แบ่งเป็น bvFTD (บุคลิกภาพเปลี่ยน), svPPA (ลืมความหมายคำ), nfvPPA (พูดติดขัด ไวยากรณ์ผิด) และ FTD-MND บางรายถ่ายทอดทางพันธุกรรม (MAPT, GRN, C9orf72)

svPPA: fluent speech but loss of word meaning and object knowledge, surface dyslexia; anterior temporal (usually left) atrophy
nfvPPA: effortful, halting speech with grammatical errors and/or apraxia of speech; left inferior frontal/insular atrophy
FTD-MND: behavioural or language FTD with fasciculations, wasting and bulbar weakness
Family history in about a third; parkinsonism, psychosis or corticobasal features in some genetic forms

Neuropsychology and speech-language assessment to define the syndrome
EMG if any motor neuron signs; CSF or plasma Alzheimer biomarkers to exclude frontal-variant AD
Genetic testing (C9orf72 repeat, GRN, MAPT) when family history or early onset; plasma progranulin low in GRN carriers

case.tests: MRI: bilateral frontal and anterior temporal atrophy; EMG: active denervation in three regions; C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat expansion positive.
case.q: Which FTD syndrome and genetic cause are present?
case.a: Behavioural variant FTD with motor neuron disease (FTD-ALS) due to a C9orf72 expansion; offer genetic counselling to relatives.

det.patho: Frontotemporal lobar degeneration is pathologically split by the abnormal protein: tau (about 40%, including Pick, PSP and CBD pathology), TDP-43 (about 50%) and FUS (under 10%). svPPA is nearly always TDP-43 type C, nfvPPA usually tau, and FTD-MND usually TDP-43. Genetic forms are mostly autosomal dominant: C9orf72 repeat expansions (commonest; FTD and/or ALS), GRN loss-of-function (TDP-43 type A, asymmetric atrophy) and MAPT mutations (tau, often with parkinsonism).
det.clinical: bvFTD presents with personality change that families often first attribute to stress or psychiatric illness; insight is poor and caregiver burden high. The language variants present with word-finding or speech problems and may stay language-predominant for years before behaviour changes. A third phenotype, right temporal variant, produces prosopagnosia and loss of empathy. C9orf72 carriers may have psychosis, slow progression and thalamic or cerebellar atrophy; GRN carriers asymmetric frontoparietal atrophy with white-matter lesions; MAPT carriers early temporal atrophy and parkinsonism.
det.diagnosis: Rascovsky criteria for possible bvFTD need three of six features (disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, perseverative or compulsive behaviour, hyperorality, executive-predominant profile); probable bvFTD adds functional decline and typical imaging. PPA variants follow the Gorno-Tempini criteria. Exclude frontal-variant Alzheimer's, late-onset psychiatric illness, the slowly progressive 'phenocopy' syndrome, and treatable mimics such as frontal tumours, syphilis, HIV and spontaneous intracranial hypotension with brain sagging. Biomarkers (CSF or plasma Alzheimer markers, neurofilament light) help distinguish neurodegenerative from psychiatric causes.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy is approved; gene-targeted treatments for GRN and C9orf72 are in trials. SSRIs or trazodone can reduce disinhibition, compulsions and eating problems; antipsychotics only cautiously for severe agitation. Cholinesterase inhibitors do not help and may worsen behaviour. Speech therapy, caregiver education and support, financial and legal planning, and safety measures (driving, money) are essential; screen for dysphagia and MND.
det.prognosis: Median survival is roughly 7–10 years from symptom onset, shorter (about 2–3 years) with motor neuron disease and longer in svPPA.
pearls: Middle-aged person, new personality change, no insight — think bvFTD before a psychiatric label.
Check for fasciculations: FTD and ALS lie on one spectrum, especially with C9orf72.
Cholinesterase inhibitors do not help FTD.
A 'bvFTD' with normal MRI and no progression may be a phenocopy or SIH with brain sagging.
det.thd: FTD เป็นสมองเสื่อมที่สมองกลีบหน้าและขมับฝ่อ มักเริ่มอายุ 45–65 ปี แบ่งเป็น bvFTD ที่บุคลิกภาพเปลี่ยน ขาดยั้งคิด เฉยเมย ไม่เห็นใจผู้อื่น ชอบกินหวาน, svPPA ที่ลืมความหมายของคำ, nfvPPA ที่พูดติดขัดผิดไวยากรณ์ และ FTD-MND ที่มีกล้ามเนื้อลีบเต้นร่วมด้วย ประมาณหนึ่งในสามถ่ายทอดทางพันธุกรรม (C9orf72, GRN, MAPT) วินิจฉัยด้วยอาการ MRI/PET และแยก Alzheimer รักษาตามอาการด้วย SSRI/trazodone และช่วยเหลือผู้ดูแล ยา cholinesterase inhibitor ไม่ช่วย

det.patho: FTLD is a pathological label for neuronal loss in frontal and temporal lobes with inclusions of tau, TDP-43 or FET proteins. Hereditary cases arise mainly from C9orf72 repeat expansions, GRN loss-of-function and MAPT variants. Clinical syndrome predicts pathology only partly.
det.clinical: Behavioural variant FTD is most frequent, followed by the primary progressive aphasias. Motor neuron disease develops in a subset, especially with C9orf72. Psychiatric misdiagnosis is common early.
det.diagnosis: Use consensus criteria for bvFTD and PPA plus supportive imaging. Exclude Alzheimer disease with biomarkers, psychiatric disease and treatable mimics. Offer genetic testing when family history or early onset.
det.treatment: No approved disease-modifying therapy; GRN and C9orf72-targeted therapies are in trials. Manage behaviour with SSRIs or trazodone, support carers, address safety and finances, and refer to speech therapy for aphasia.
det.prognosis: Survival typically 6–10 years from onset; shorter with ALS overlap.
pearls: Midlife personality change without memory loss: think bvFTD.
Examine for fasciculations in every FTD patient.
Normal early MRI does not exclude FTD; consider FDG-PET.

det.patho: ALS and FTD share TDP-43 proteinopathy and overlapping genetics, forming a clinicopathological continuum. The C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat expansion is the commonest known genetic cause of both disorders, acting through RNA foci, dipeptide repeat proteins and loss of function. TBK1, SQSTM1, VCP, UBQLN2 and others also contribute.
det.clinical: Roughly 10–15% of ALS patients meet criteria for FTD and many more have milder executive or behavioural impairment. Conversely a proportion of bvFTD patients develop motor neuron disease. Behavioural symptoms may cause poor compliance with ventilation and feeding decisions. Disease progression and survival are typically worse than ALS alone.
det.diagnosis: Combine FTD criteria (behaviour or language) with ALS criteria using EMG. Screen all ALS patients with brief tools such as ECAS and examine all bvFTD patients for fasciculation and wasting. Imaging supports frontotemporal involvement. Offer genetic testing with counselling, especially with a family history.
det.treatment: Riluzole and multidisciplinary ALS care apply; tofersen only for SOD1 carriers, who rarely have FTD. Behavioural symptoms may respond to SSRIs or trazodone; avoid cholinesterase inhibitors which can worsen behaviour. Early advance care planning is crucial before capacity declines. Carer support and safety measures are central.
det.prognosis: Median survival is shorter than ALS without dementia, often 2–3 years from onset.
pearls: Screen ALS patients for cognition; examine FTD patients for fasciculations.
Late-onset psychosis with family history of ALS: test C9orf72.
Plan decisions on gastrostomy and ventilation early, while capacity remains.

det.patho: Functional dystonia arises from abnormal brain network function involving attention, prediction and self-agency, often after injury or pain. Structural brain imaging is normal. Psychological stressors may contribute but are not required for diagnosis.
det.clinical: Typically a young woman with a fixed painful limb posture after trivial trauma. Spread and fluctuations occur. Organic dystonia usually starts as action-induced and mobile, which contrasts with functional dystonia.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is based on positive features (rapid onset, fixed posture, inconsistency, other functional signs), not just exclusion. Investigations are normal. Atypical features call for genetic or metabolic tests.
det.treatment: Provide a clear, positive explanation. Specialised physiotherapy, CBT and pain management are key. Avoid immobilisation and unnecessary procedures.
det.prognosis: Often chronic; better with early diagnosis and engagement.
pearls: Fixed from the start points to functional.
Look for other positive functional signs.
Botulinum toxin failure is common.

det.patho: FMD is understood as a disorder of voluntary movement control in which abnormal attention, sense of agency and predictions about movement result in genuine involuntary-feeling movements. Functional imaging shows altered activity in the temporoparietal junction, limbic and prefrontal networks. Triggers include physical injury, pain, infection, panic or stress, and predisposing factors include earlier psychiatric illness, adverse experience and personality factors, but psychological stress is not required for the diagnosis in current classification.
det.clinical: Functional movement disorder accounts for a large fraction of patients in movement clinics, with tremor, dystonia, jerks, gait disorder and parkinsonism-like slowing being the main forms. Onset is typically sudden, often after trauma or illness, and the course fluctuates with attention. Fixed dystonia, often with pain and a complex regional pain syndrome, is a recognised pattern. Patients frequently have other functional symptoms and common comorbidities of depression, anxiety and chronic pain. A discrepancy between severe disability and the objective signs, or a response to distraction, are typical.
det.diagnosis: Make a positive diagnosis from the history and examination: inconsistency, distractibility, entrainment, coactivation, collapsing weakness, Hoover sign, midline splitting and unusual dynamics. Laboratory-supported criteria use neurophysiology (for tremor, myoclonus) to document features that organic movements cannot mimic. Co-existence with organic disease is possible and should not prevent the diagnosis. Tests should be limited to mimics suggested by the picture, since repeated investigation reinforces illness beliefs.
det.treatment: Delivery of the diagnosis is itself the first treatment: describe it as a real, common problem of the brain's functioning that can improve, and avoid the term 'all in the mind'. Specialised physiotherapy and occupational therapy based on retraining of automatic movement are the best-supported treatments; cognitive-behavioural therapy and other psychotherapies help when anxiety, depression or trauma contribute. Treat comorbid pain and sleep problems, stop unneeded drugs and avoid repeated imaging and botulinum toxin or surgery. Short inpatient programmes may help severe disability.
det.prognosis: Outcomes vary: many patients improve with early diagnosis and therapy, but long-standing or fixed dystonia and persistent disability carry a more guarded outlook.
pearls: Make the diagnosis on positive signs such as entrainment, not by exclusion.
Tremor is the commonest functional movement disorder, and tapping with the other hand is the quickest bedside test.
A clear, kind explanation and specialist physiotherapy are treatments in their own right.

det.patho: Functional movement disorders reflect abnormal brain control of voluntary movement — altered attention, prediction and sense of agency — rather than structural damage or feigning. The jerks are generated through voluntary motor pathways but experienced as involuntary, which is why a readiness potential can precede them. Physical triggers and illness beliefs often play a role; psychological stress is common but not required.
det.clinical: Onset is often sudden with rapid maximum severity. Jerks may be axial, multifocal or limb-limited and are frequently accompanied by other functional symptoms such as weakness or non-epileptic attacks. Fatigue, pain and anxiety are common comorbidities. Positive clinical signs rather than exclusion should drive the diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on positive features: inconsistency, distractibility, suggestibility and entrainment. Neurophysiology increases confidence — longer and variable EMG bursts, variable latency to stimuli and a Bereitschaftspotential on back-averaging. Organic myoclonus (cortical, subcortical, spinal) should be considered, and the two can coexist.
det.treatment: Explain the diagnosis clearly and positively as a real, potentially reversible problem of brain function. Specialist physiotherapy for functional movement disorders and psychological therapy (often CBT-based) are the main treatments. Avoid unnecessary drugs and repeated investigations; treat comorbid depression, anxiety and pain.
det.prognosis: Outcome is variable; short duration and acceptance of the diagnosis predict improvement, while long-standing symptoms often persist.
pearls: Bereitschaftspotential before a jerk = voluntary motor preparation, supporting functional origin.
Many adult 'propriospinal myoclonus' cases are functional.
Make the diagnosis on positive signs, not just normal tests.

det.patho: FND reflects a problem of how the brain works, not of its structure: altered attention, prediction and sense of agency disrupt voluntary movement and perception, so symptoms are genuine and not feigned. Predisposing factors include anxiety, depression, prior adverse experiences and other functional disorders, but many patients have none; triggers such as injury, illness, pain or a panic attack are common. It ranks among the commonest reasons for neurology outpatient referral.
det.clinical: Presentations include functional limb weakness, tremor, dystonia, gait disorders, sensory loss, speech and swallowing symptoms, visual loss, cognitive complaints and dissociative (non-epileptic) seizures. Symptoms often start abruptly, fluctuate and are worse when the person is attending to them. Fatigue, pain, poor sleep and dissociation frequently coexist. Structural neurological disease may also be present, so careful assessment is needed in every case.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is made on positive clinical features, not by exclusion alone: Hoover sign and hip abductor sign for leg weakness, drift without pronation, entrainment and distractibility of tremor, a dragging monoplegic gait, and for dissociative seizures features like prolonged duration, eyes closed, fluctuating course and recall of the event. Video-EEG of a typical attack is the gold standard for dissociative seizures. Let the history steer which investigations are done, and normal results should be presented as supportive, not as the basis of the diagnosis. Avoid labelling based on psychological history alone.
det.treatment: Explain the diagnosis clearly and confidently, naming it, describing the positive signs and emphasising that it is common, real and potentially reversible. Specialist physiotherapy using movement retraining and attention redirection is effective for motor symptoms; psychological therapy (e.g. CBT-based) helps dissociative seizures and coexisting anxiety or depression. Speech and occupational therapy address specific symptoms. Withdraw unnecessary antiseizure medication when seizures are confirmed as dissociative, and avoid repeated tests or invasive procedures.
det.prognosis: Outcomes vary; shorter symptom duration, acceptance of the diagnosis and early access to targeted therapy predict improvement, while long-standing symptoms are harder to reverse.
pearls: FND is a positive diagnosis — document the signs that show it.
Up to a fifth of patients with dissociative seizures also have epilepsy.
How the diagnosis is explained strongly influences the outcome.

det.patho: Functional seizures are now understood as a disorder of brain network function, where predictive processing, emotion regulation and attention interact with dissociation to produce attacks that are real and not willed. Predisposing factors include childhood adversity and trauma, anxiety, depression and prior illness experience, while triggers may be stress, panic or physical symptoms. They are the seizure form of functional neurological disorder in DSM-5-TR and dissociative neurological symptom disorder in ICD-11.
det.clinical: Attacks are typically long, fluctuating and asynchronous with closed eyes, or are long limp episodes without movement. Patients may recall the event, cry afterwards or describe fear and panic-like symptoms beforehand. Injury, tongue biting at the side and incontinence occur but are less common than in epilepsy. Many patients are misdiagnosed with refractory epilepsy for years and receive multiple drugs or ICU treatment for apparent status epilepticus.
det.diagnosis: The ILAE graded approach rates certainty from possible (witness history) through probable (clinician sees an event or video) to documented (video-EEG of a typical attack with no epileptiform activity). No single sign is perfect, so a combination of semiology, video and EEG is used, and a normal EEG between attacks never rules epilepsy out. Coexisting epilepsy must be considered, especially in patients with intellectual disability or a past brain injury. Frontal lobe hypermotor seizures, syncope and panic attacks are the main pitfalls.
det.treatment: A clear, non-blaming explanation of the diagnosis as a common, treatable brain condition is the first step and alone reduces attacks in some. Antiseizure medicines are withdrawn when epilepsy is excluded. Psychological therapy based on CBT, with treatment of comorbid depression, anxiety and PTSD, is the main intervention; the CODES trial showed improved secondary outcomes though not attack frequency at 12 months. An individual emergency plan and family education reduce unnecessary benzodiazepines and intubation.
det.prognosis: Many patients have fewer attacks after diagnosis and therapy, but full remission occurs in only a minority, and disability and unemployment often persist.
pearls: Closed eyes that resist opening during a convulsive event strongly suggest a functional seizure.
Video-EEG of a typical event is the diagnostic gold standard; home video is a valuable aid.
Patients with functional seizures may also have epilepsy, so look for both.

det.patho: Functional tics are thought to arise from learned or modelled behaviours in the context of stress and altered attention. Surges were seen during the COVID-19 pandemic related to social media exposure.
det.clinical: Onset is sudden with complex movements and phrases, often in teenage girls. They lack the stereotyped evolution of primary tics. Some patients have pre-existing mild tics.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis relies on history: age and abruptness of onset, complexity, lack of urge, and exposure to similar content. Exclude neurodevelopmental tic disorders.
det.treatment: Explain the diagnosis, reduce social media triggers, and provide behavioural therapy and treatment of comorbid anxiety or depression. Antipsychotics used for tics are usually unhelpful.
det.prognosis: Many improve over months with appropriate support.
pearls: Adolescent onset with complex tics from day one suggests functional tics.
Ask about online content exposure.
Avoid tic medications unless clearly needed.

name: Fungal myositis
formal: Rare invasive muscle infection by fungi such as Candida or Aspergillus, usually in immunosuppressed patients, causing focal pain, swelling and abscess or necrosis.
simple: A rare muscle infection caused by fungi, mostly seen in people with weak immune systems.
more: Diagnosis by MRI, muscle biopsy and fungal culture. Treated with antifungal drugs and surgical drainage; prognosis depends on the underlying immune status.
th: การติดเชื้อราในกล้ามเนื้อซึ่งพบน้อย มักในผู้ป่วยภูมิคุ้มกันต่ำ ทำให้ปวด บวม เป็นฝีหรือเนื้อตาย
tempoNote: Days to weeks of localised pain and swelling, often amid systemic fungal infection
feat: Immunosuppressed host: neutropenia, transplant, haematological cancer, high-dose steroids
Focal painful swollen muscle(s) with fever not responding to antibacterials
Disseminated candidiasis may produce multiple muscle nodules and skin lesions
Aspergillus, Fusarium or Mucorales can cause necrosis and vascular invasion
inv: MRI or CT of the affected muscle: oedema, abscess
Biopsy or aspiration with fungal stains, culture and histology
Blood cultures, beta-D-glucan, galactomannan

case.who: 26-year-old man receiving chemotherapy for AML, Bangkok
case.story: Persistent fever during neutropenia despite broad-spectrum antibiotics; now painful swollen right thigh and small skin nodules.
case.exam: Tender firm right quadriceps, multiple erythematous papules on trunk.
case.tests: MRI: multiple intramuscular abscesses; biopsy shows yeasts and pseudohyphae, culture Candida tropicalis.
case.q: What is the treatment?
case.a: Disseminated candidiasis with fungal myositis; an echinocandin then azole per susceptibility, drainage where possible, and recovery of neutrophils.

det.patho: Fungi reach muscle by haematogenous spread or direct extension from skin or adjacent tissue. Candida tends to form microabscesses, whereas moulds such as Aspergillus and Mucorales invade vessels, causing infarction and necrosis. Defective neutrophil function is the main risk factor.
det.clinical: Patients present with focal muscle pain, swelling and fever, often in the setting of disseminated fungal infection. Skin lesions and organ involvement elsewhere are common. Weakness is localised to the affected muscle.
det.diagnosis: Imaging defines extent and guides biopsy; tissue diagnosis with fungal staining and culture is essential. Serum fungal biomarkers support invasive infection. Differentiation from bacterial pyomyositis and tumour infiltration matters.
det.treatment: Systemic antifungal therapy is chosen by organism: an echinocandin or fluconazole for Candida, voriconazole for Aspergillus and liposomal amphotericin B for Mucorales. Abscesses need drainage and necrotic muscle needs debridement, sometimes repeatedly. Reducing immunosuppression and recovery of neutrophil counts are major determinants of cure. Remove infected central lines and look for other sites of dissemination such as eyes and heart valves.
det.prognosis: Prognosis depends on immune recovery; mortality is high in disseminated mould infection.
pearls: Persistent neutropenic fever + muscle pain + skin nodules: think disseminated Candida.
Biopsy for culture — do not rely on blood cultures alone.
Mould myositis is a surgical as well as medical emergency.
det.thd: Fungal myositis คือการติดเชื้อราในกล้ามเนื้อ พบน้อยและเกือบทั้งหมดอยู่ในผู้ป่วยภูมิต่ำ เช่น เม็ดเลือดขาวต่ำจากเคมีบำบัด ผู้ป่วยมีไข้ไม่ลง ปวดบวมกล้ามเนื้อเฉพาะที่ อาจมีผื่นตุ่ม ยืนยันด้วย MRI และตัดชิ้นเนื้อเพาะเชื้อ รักษาด้วยยาต้านเชื้อราที่เหมาะกับชนิดเชื้อร่วมกับระบายหนอง

Diffuse symmetric proximal weakness with raised CK, not focal abscesses
Diffuse muscle breakdown from drugs or exertion; no focal infection
