name: Fungal neurological infections
formal: CNS infections by fungi such as Cryptococcus, Aspergillus, Candida, Mucorales and Histoplasma, causing chronic meningitis, abscess or vasculopathy, mostly in immunocompromised people.
simple: Infections of the brain or its coverings caused by fungi, usually in people with weakened immune systems.
th: การติดเชื้อราในระบบประสาท (neuromycoses) แบ่งตามเชื้อ ภูมิคุ้มกันของผู้ป่วย และกลุ่มอาการ ควรสงสัยเมื่อมีอาการกึ่งเฉียบพลัน-เรื้อรัง ประวัติเดินทางหรือสัมผัสสิ่งแวดล้อม แม้ผลตรวจปกติ
tempoNote: Usually weeks to months; rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis and angioinvasive mould disease in neutropenia can move over days
feat: Think of it in subacute or chronic CNS illness that fails to respond to antibacterial or antiviral treatment; immunosuppression helps but is not required
Five syndromes: meningitis or meningoencephalitis, abscess or mass, ventriculitis, stroke from angioinvasion, and skull-base or orbital apex disease from the sinuses

Host and exposure decide the organism: HIV (Cryptococcus, Talaromyces, Histoplasma), neutropenia or transplant (Aspergillus, Mucorales, Candida, Scedosporium, Fusarium), diabetes and DKA (Mucorales), travel to endemic regions (Coccidioides, Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Paracoccidioides)
Normal CSF, absent fever, normal CRP and negative blood tests do not exclude it
One page per organism: Cryptococcus neoformans (pathogen), Aspergillus species (pathogen), Mucorales (pathogen), Talaromyces marneffei (pathogen) and others listed in the detail
inv: Opening pressure, cells, protein, glucose; CSF and serum CrAg; fungal smear and culture of adequate CSF volume
Serum and CSF beta-D-glucan and galactomannan: low serum sensitivity, so a negative serum result never rules disease out; CSF values are more informative
Contrast MRI of brain (and sinuses or spine as needed); ring-enhancing masses, haemorrhagic or wedge infarcts, leptomeningeal enhancement
Tissue (biopsy, aspirate) with histology, culture, and PCR or 18S sequencing when the course keeps worsening without a diagnosis

case.who: 52-year-old woman, rice farmer from Phayao, on prednisolone for years for rheumatoid arthritis
case.story: Six weeks of worsening headache, then right hand weakness and a seizure; chest radiograph earlier showed a nodule that was not followed up.
case.exam: Afebrile, right hemiparesis, no neck stiffness; skin has several small nodules on the forearms.
case.tests: MRI: two ring-enhancing frontal lesions with restricted diffusion; CSF 40 lymphocytes, protein 1.1 g/L; serum CrAg positive, beta-D-glucan negative; skin biopsy later shows yeasts.
case.q: Which organism fits best, and why does a negative beta-D-glucan not argue against it?
case.a: Cryptococcus: the cell wall of this yeast does not give a beta-D-glucan signal, so a negative result is expected; confirm with CrAg, culture and tissue, then start amphotericin-based therapy and reduce steroids if possible.

Part III: Fungal Pathogens: Pathogenesis, Pathology, Diagnosis and Treatment
Chapter 45 Fungal Infections of the Central Nervous System
Infectious Diseases of the Nervous System

det.patho: Fungi reach the nervous system by crossing the blood-brain barrier (via transcytosis of endothelium, between their junctions, or hidden inside carrier immune cells), or they spread directly from sinuses, ears or neurosurgical wounds. Yeasts such as Cryptococcus favour meninges and perivascular spaces. Moulds (Aspergillus, Mucorales, Fusarium, Scedosporium) invade vessels and cause thrombosis, haemorrhage and abscess. Dimorphic endemic fungi (Histoplasma, Coccidioides, Blastomyces, Paracoccidioides, Talaromyces) are tied to place and soil; Talaromyces marneffei is typical of northern Thailand and HIV.
det.clinical: Most cases evolve over weeks as chronic meningitis with hydrocephalus and cranial neuropathies, or as one or several enhancing masses, and the picture is easily mistaken for tuberculosis or tumour. Mould infection in neutropenic patients can produce sudden strokes and seizures. Sinus pain, orbital apex syndrome or cavernous sinus thrombosis should prompt thought of mucormycosis or aspergillosis. A history of travel (even years earlier), caves, pigeon droppings, near-drowning or spinal procedures can point to the organism.
det.diagnosis: Start from three questions: who is the host, where have they been, and which syndrome is this. Serum markers (galactomannan, beta-D-glucan) miss many CNS infections; CSF versions, CrAg, specific antigens (Histoplasma, Coccidioides, Blastomyces), PCR and tissue are more useful. Normal imaging, CSF or inflammatory markers never exclude disease. When the patient deteriorates without a diagnosis, brain or meningeal biopsy is often the quickest route to an answer.
det.treatment: No single drug covers everything. In a deteriorating patient with an unclear organism, liposomal amphotericin B is started early while tissue is sought; then therapy is matched: amphotericin plus flucytosine and fluconazole for Cryptococcus, voriconazole for Aspergillus and many rare moulds, amphotericin with surgical debridement for Mucorales, itraconazole step-down for most endemic fungi, and high-dose fluconazole for Coccidioides. Steroids are not used routinely. Reduce immunosuppression, drain or resect accessible lesions, and monitor drug levels and organ toxicity.
det.prognosis: Mortality and disability are high and depend on organism, host and the delay to treatment; moulds in the immunocompromised and delayed cryptococcosis fare worst.
pearls: Subacute or chronic CNS disease unresponsive to antibacterials and antivirals: ask about travel, soil, caves, birds and procedures, and think fungal.
A negative serum beta-D-glucan or galactomannan does not exclude CNS fungal disease; Cryptococcus, Mucorales and Blastomyces do not give a beta-D-glucan signal.

Organism pages: Cryptococcus neoformans (pathogen), Cryptococcus gattii (pathogen), Aspergillus species (pathogen), Candida species (pathogen), Mucorales (pathogen), Histoplasma capsulatum (pathogen), Coccidioides species (pathogen), Blastomyces (pathogen), Talaromyces marneffei (pathogen), Scedosporium and Lomentospora (pathogen), Fusarium species (pathogen), Dematiaceous moulds (pathogen), Sporothrix species (pathogen), Paracoccidioides (pathogen).
det.thd: Neuromycoses คือการติดเชื้อราในระบบประสาท ควรนึกถึงเมื่อผู้ป่วยมีอาการกึ่งเฉียบพลันถึงเรื้อรังที่ไม่ตอบสนองต่อยาต้านแบคทีเรียหรือไวรัส โดยพิจารณาจากเชื้อ ภูมิคุ้มกันของผู้ป่วย ประวัติเดินทางหรือสัมผัสสิ่งแวดล้อม และกลุ่มอาการ เช่น เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ ฝีหรือก้อน หรือสมองขาดเลือดจากเชื้อรุกล้ำหลอดเลือด ผลเลือดหรือ CSF ปกติไม่ได้ตัดโรคออก ควรตรวจ CrAg ตรวจหา antigen เฉพาะเชื้อ และตัดชิ้นเนื้อเมื่อโรคแย่ลงโดยไม่ทราบสาเหตุ การรักษาเลือกยาตามเชื้อ เช่น amphotericin B, flucytosine, fluconazole, voriconazole หรือ itraconazole ร่วมกับผ่าตัดเมื่อทำได้ และเลี่ยง steroid

qx.stem: A 48-year-old farmer from Buriram has had three months of progressive headache and cranial neuropathies. CSF cell count, glucose and protein are only mildly abnormal, serum beta-D-glucan and galactomannan are negative, and he is not immunosuppressed. Antibacterial and antiviral treatment have failed and MRI shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions.
qx.q: Which statement about his work-up is most accurate?
opts: Negative serum fungal markers and a bland CSF exclude neuromycosis
Taking a detailed exposure history and considering brain biopsy are appropriate if he keeps deteriorating
Immunosuppression is required before fungal infection can be considered
Fungal infection is impossible with ring-enhancing lesions
Corticosteroids should be started routinely while awaiting results
qx.why: Serum markers have poor negative predictive value, CSF may be near-normal in neuromycoses, and immunosuppression is not a prerequisite. Exposure history and early tissue diagnosis (biopsy) are advised when the course worsens without a diagnosis, and corticosteroids should not be used routinely.

name: Fungal spinal infections
formal: Spinal infections such as vertebral osteomyelitis or epidural abscess by Aspergillus, Candida or Coccidioides, often after surgery or in immunosuppression, causing back pain, radiculopathy or myelopathy.
simple: Infection of the spine or its coverings by a fungus, causing back pain and sometimes weakness or numbness in the legs.
th: การติดเชื้อราที่กระดูกสันหลังหรือช่อง epidural เช่น Aspergillus หรือ Candida มักในผู้ป่วยภูมิต่ำหรือหลังผ่าตัด ปวดหลัง รากประสาทหรือไขสันหลังถูกกด

feat: Slowly progressive back pain with little or no fever
Risk factors: immunosuppression, injection drug use, central lines, spinal surgery, diabetes
Radiculopathy or myelopathy when abscess or bony collapse compress neural tissue
Geographic fungi: Coccidioides, Blastomyces, Histoplasma, Talaromyces in Southeast Asia
Often mistaken for TB or tumour
inv: MRI spine with gadolinium
CT-guided biopsy for histology and fungal culture
Beta-D-glucan, galactomannan; serology for endemic fungi

case.who: 57-year-old woman from Phrae, 6 months after kidney transplant
case.story: Two months of mid-back pain, now with burning pain around the chest and weak legs.
case.exam: Tender T7, mild paraparesis, sensory level T8.
case.tests: MRI: T6–T7 spondylodiscitis with epidural phlegmon; biopsy: septate hyphae, Aspergillus fumigatus.
case.q: What treatment is required?
case.a: Voriconazole plus surgical debridement and decompression, reducing immunosuppression where possible.

det.patho: Fungi reach the spine through blood, contiguous spread from lungs, or direct inoculation at surgery. Aspergillus and Candida are the commonest in immunosuppressed and post-operative patients; endemic dimorphic fungi affect people in specific regions. Infection destroys vertebrae and disc and may extend to the epidural space.
det.clinical: Pain is the leading complaint with few systemic signs, delaying diagnosis. Neurological deficits arise from abscess or vertebral collapse. Multiple contiguous levels and paraspinal abscesses may occur.
det.diagnosis: MRI changes overlap heavily with tuberculous and bacterial infection, so imaging alone cannot name the organism. Image-guided or open biopsy with fungal stains, culture and histology is essential before committing to months of therapy. Serum beta-D-glucan and galactomannan support invasive candidiasis or aspergillosis, and serology helps for endemic dimorphic fungi. Always send samples for mycobacterial culture and histology for tumour at the same time.
det.treatment: Antifungal therapy is prolonged, often 6–12 months, and chosen by organism: voriconazole for Aspergillus, fluconazole or an echinocandin for Candida, and amphotericin-based induction for endemic moulds. Surgery is needed for cord compression, spinal instability, large abscesses or failure of medical therapy. Reduce immunosuppression where feasible and remove infected hardware if possible. Follow clinical status, inflammatory markers and MRI to judge response.
det.prognosis: Generally guarded due to the underlying immunosuppression; early surgery improves neurological outcomes.
pearls: 'Culture-negative' spondylodiscitis in the immunosuppressed — ask the lab for fungal studies.
Endemic Talaromyces marneffei in HIV in Southeast Asia can involve bone.
Treatment lasts months, not weeks.
det.thd: Fungal spinal infection คือการติดเชื้อราที่กระดูกสันหลังหรือหมอนรองกระดูก เช่น Aspergillus, Candida พบในผู้ป่วยภูมิต่ำหรือหลังผ่าตัด อาการปวดหลังเรื้อรัง ไข้ไม่เด่น อาจกดรากประสาทหรือไขสันหลัง ต้องตัดชิ้นเนื้อเพาะเชื้อเพื่อแยกจากวัณโรคและแบคทีเรีย รักษาด้วยยาต้านเชื้อรานานหลายเดือนร่วมกับผ่าตัด

th: ความผิดปกติของการเดินจากระบบประสาท กล้ามเนื้อ หรือกระดูก แยกตามรูปแบบ เช่น spastic ataxic parkinsonian steppage หรือ frontal

case.exam: Wide-based, magnetic gait with start hesitation; mild cognitive impairment.

19 - Gait disorders: Pathophysiology and clinical syndromes

det.patho: Walking requires intact motor, sensory, cerebellar and higher control systems. Disorders of any of these produce characteristic patterns. Multifactorial gait disorders are common in older people.
det.clinical: This is a heading, not a single disease. Observation of gait often localises the lesion: spastic suggests corticospinal, ataxic suggests cerebellar or sensory, shuffling suggests basal ganglia. Falls and fear of falling add disability.
det.diagnosis: Observe gait, turning, tandem walking and Romberg; then target investigations according to the pattern. Consider multiple contributing causes in the elderly.
det.treatment: Treat the cause, provide physiotherapy, walking aids and fall prevention. Address vision, medications and footwear.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause; many are improved by targeted treatment.
pearls: Watch the patient walk into the room.
Romberg positive points to sensory ataxia.
Gait plus incontinence plus cognitive decline suggests NPH.
det.thd: Gait disorders คือความผิดปกติของการเดิน ใช้รูปแบบการเดินช่วยบอกตำแหน่งรอยโรค เช่น spastic ataxic parkinsonian steppage frontal ตรวจ Romberg และเดินต่อส้นเท้า แล้วส่งตรวจตามรูปแบบที่พบ รักษาสาเหตุ ร่วมกับกายภาพบำบัดและป้องกันการหกล้ม

name: Gangliocytomas
formal: Rare benign, well-differentiated tumours of mature ganglion cells, commonly in the temporal lobe, presenting with long-standing epilepsy in young people.
simple: Rare slow-growing non-cancerous brain tumours made of nerve cells, often causing seizures.
th: เนื้องอกชนิดเซลล์ประสาทที่เจริญเต็มที่ เกรด 1 พบน้อยกว่า ganglioglioma มาก พบที่ temporal lobe ในเด็กและวัยหนุ่มสาว มักทำให้ชักเรื้อรัง อาจพบที่ cerebellum (Lhermitte-Duclos) หรือ pituitary ผ่าตัดแล้วหายดี
tempoNote: Years of focal seizures; cerebellar dysplastic form causes slowly progressive headache and ataxia
feat: Rare, well-differentiated tumour of mature ganglion cells in children and young adults, mostly in the temporal lobe
Long history of drug-resistant focal seizures; deficit uncommon
Cerebellar variant (dysplastic gangliocytoma, Lhermitte-Duclos disease) produces headache, ataxia and hydrocephalus and is linked with Cowden syndrome (PTEN)
Sellar and hypothalamic gangliocytomas can mimic pituitary adenoma and may secrete growth hormone or other hormones
Always CNS WHO grade 1; malignant transformation is not known
inv: MRI: solid or cystic cortical mass with or without a dural tail; cerebellar lesion shows striated or tiger-stripe folial thickening
Histology: large neoplastic neuronal cells in a non-neoplastic glial stroma; no neoplastic glial component, unlike ganglioglioma
For Lhermitte-Duclos, PTEN testing and screening for Cowden syndrome (thyroid, breast, endometrial, colon)
Presurgical epilepsy work-up for temporal tumours; pituitary hormone testing for sellar lesions

case.story: A decade of auras of fear followed by confused staring, 1-2 episodes monthly despite carbamazepine and levetiracetam.
case.exam: Normal examination apart from mild naming difficulty.
case.tests: MRI shows a 2 cm cortical lesion in the left mesial temporal region with a dural tail. Selective resection: gangliocytoma, grade 1, no glial neoplastic component, synaptophysin positive.
case.q: How does gangliocytoma differ from ganglioglioma and what is the follow-up?
case.a: Gangliocytoma has only neuronal neoplastic cells and does not transform; ganglioglioma also has a neoplastic glial part. Complete resection with epilepsy surgery gives similar seizure outcomes, and radiotherapy is not needed.

det.patho: Gangliocytoma consists of large, mature but dysplastic ganglion cells in a stroma of non-neoplastic glia and may show perivascular lymphocytes. It always corresponds to grade 1. The cerebellar form is dysplastic cerebellar gangliocytoma (Lhermitte-Duclos disease), which results from hypertrophic granule cell neurons and is associated with PTEN hamartoma tumour syndrome. Lesions of the pituitary may contain adenoma elements and be hormonally active.
det.clinical: Most patients are children or young adults with seizures that persist despite medication. Because the tumour is slow-growing, deficits are unusual. The cerebellar form can obstruct the fourth ventricle and cause hydrocephalus. The tumour is closely allied to ganglioglioma clinically and radiologically, which explains why they are considered together.
det.diagnosis: The imaging is nonspecific; a cortical solid or cystic lesion with minimal oedema is common, and a dural tail can suggest meningioma. Diagnosis rests on neuropathology demonstrating neoplastic neurons with synaptophysin and neurofilament expression, without a neoplastic glial component. In cerebellar lesions, the characteristic folial pattern on MRI plus PTEN germline analysis is useful.
det.treatment: Complete excision, with epilepsy surgery principles, is the treatment; outcome is similar to grade 1 ganglioglioma. Radiotherapy is not required. In Lhermitte-Duclos disease surgery is for mass effect or hydrocephalus, and long-term surveillance for Cowden-associated cancers is recommended. Sellar tumours are managed as pituitary lesions with endocrine assessment.
det.prognosis: Excellent after resection; recurrence is rare and malignant change has not been described.
pearls: Only ganglion cells are neoplastic in gangliocytoma; if a neoplastic glial component is present, it is a ganglioglioma.
Lhermitte-Duclos disease should prompt PTEN testing and Cowden syndrome screening.
A dural tail on a cortical temporal mass does not exclude gangliocytoma.
det.thd: Gangliocytoma เป็นเนื้องอกเกรด 1 ที่ประกอบด้วยเซลล์ประสาทที่เจริญแล้ว พบน้อยกว่า ganglioglioma มาก มักอยู่ที่ temporal lobe ผู้ป่วยชักเรื้อรังและดื้อยา อาจพบที่ cerebellum ในรูปแบบ Lhermitte-Duclos ซึ่งสัมพันธ์กับ Cowden syndrome การรักษาคือผ่าตัดเอาออกให้หมดและประเมินโรคลมชัก ไม่ต้องฉายรังสีและโอกาสเปลี่ยนเป็นมะเร็งแทบไม่มี

ddx.pt: Mixed neuronal and glial neoplasm; the glial part can become anaplastic
Intracortical bubbly lesion, floating neurons in mucin, no ganglion cell tumour

name: Gangliogliomas
formal: Low-grade glioneuronal tumours with neoplastic neurons and glia, typically temporal, causing drug-resistant epilepsy in children and young adults, with BRAF V600E mutation in many.
simple: Slow-growing brain tumours made of both nerve and support cells, usually causing seizures in young people.
th: เนื้องอกชนิดเซลล์ประสาทปนเซลล์เกลีย เกรด 1 พบบ่อยที่ temporal lobe ในเด็กและวัยหนุ่มสาว ทำให้ชักดื้อยามานาน การผ่าตัดเอาออกให้หมดทำให้ผู้ป่วยส่วนใหญ่หายชัก
tempoNote: Seizures for several years, sometimes more than a decade, before diagnosis; anaplastic forms and brainstem or spinal tumours have shorter histories
feat: Most frequent tumour of the low-grade epilepsy-associated tumour (LEAT) group; the temporal lobe is involved in about 80 percent
Focal seizures with or without impaired awareness in 85-97 percent, pharmacoresistant in the majority, with a mean seizure history of 10-15 years
Neurological deficits are uncommon in supratentorial tumours; brainstem and spinal gangliogliomas present with deficits or raised pressure
Imaging: cystic mass with enhancing mural nodule in about 40 percent, cortical location, little oedema, calcification on CT in a third to half
Mostly CNS WHO grade 1; BRAF V600E is present in a large share and is a therapeutic target
inv: MRI with epilepsy protocol: T2/FLAIR-bright cortical mass, often cystic with nodule; CT for calcification
Presurgical epilepsy evaluation: video-EEG, neuropsychology, sometimes PET or invasive monitoring to define epileptogenic zone and associated cortical dysplasia
Histology: mixed neoplastic ganglion cells and glial cells with CD34 positivity; BRAF V600E immunostain
Follow-up MRI at 1-2 year intervals after surgery

case.who: 19-year-old woman, a university student from Phayao
case.story: Since age 9, brief episodes of rising epigastric feeling then staring and lip-smacking, 2-3 per month despite two antiseizure drugs.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination; neuropsychology shows mild verbal memory weakness.
case.tests: MRI shows a cystic left anterior temporal lesion with a small enhancing nodule; video-EEG localises seizure onset to the same region. Lesionectomy with amygdalohippocampectomy: ganglioglioma, CNS WHO grade 1, BRAF V600E-positive, with adjacent focal cortical dysplasia.
case.q: What is the likelihood of seizure freedom after complete resection and is radiotherapy needed?
case.a: About 80-85% become seizure free. Radiotherapy is not indicated after resection of grade 1 tumours; it is considered only for anaplastic (grade 3) disease or inoperable recurrence.

det.patho: Gangliogliomas contain neoplastic ganglion cells and neoplastic glia, usually astrocytic. Most are CNS WHO grade 1; anaplastic change affects the glial component. BRAF V600E mutation is found in a substantial proportion and CD34-positive cells are common. They are often accompanied by cortical dysplasia. The temporal lobe predominates, but the tumour can arise anywhere including the brainstem and spinal cord. Papillary glioneuronal tumour is a related variant.
det.clinical: Seizures begin in childhood or early adult life and are usually refractory to drug therapy; long duration is the hallmark. Brainstem and spinal gangliogliomas present with focal deficit and raised pressure over a short period. Rarely, malignant transformation of the glial component produces a rapid decline. Cognitive function and quality of life depend on seizure control.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows a cortical mass, solid or cystic with a nodule; enhancement is variable. MRI cannot separate anaplastic from non-anaplastic tumours. Presurgical epilepsy evaluation is mandatory to decide whether additional perilesional tissue should be removed. Pathology identifies ganglion cells, CD34 positivity and BRAF V600E, and separates the tumour from DNET and pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma.
det.treatment: Complete resection is the treatment, achieved in about three-quarters of supratentorial tumours, with extended resection of epileptogenic cortex as needed; seizure freedom follows in 80-85 percent. Residual tumour is often stable, so re-operation is rarely required. Radiotherapy and chemotherapy are reserved for anaplastic tumours and inoperable recurrences. BRAF/MEK inhibitors (dabrafenib plus trametinib, vemurafenib) have produced responses in BRAF V600E-mutated recurrent tumours. Early surgery is favoured for drug-resistant epilepsy.
det.prognosis: Recurrence-free survival at 7.5 years was 97 percent in the source series; malignant transformation occurs in 2-9 percent, and spinal tumours recur more often.
pearls: Temporal cystic mass with mural nodule and years of drug-resistant seizures in a young person: ganglioglioma.
Do not treat with radiotherapy after complete resection of a grade 1 tumour.
BRAF V600E testing identifies candidates for targeted therapy at recurrence.
det.thd: Ganglioglioma เป็นเนื้องอกที่มีทั้งเซลล์ประสาทและเซลล์เกลีย เกรด 1 พบบ่อยที่ temporal lobe ในเด็กและวัยรุ่น ผู้ป่วยมักชักมานานหลายปีและดื้อต่อยากันชัก MRI พบถุงน้ำพร้อมก้อนที่ enhance การผ่าตัดเอาออกให้หมดร่วมกับการประเมินโรคลมชักก่อนผ่าตัดทำให้ผู้ป่วยกว่า 80% หายชัก ไม่ต้องฉายรังสีหากเป็นเกรด 1 และถ้ากลับเป็นซ้ำที่มี BRAF V600E อาจใช้ยา dabrafenib ร่วมกับ trametinib

name: Gardner’s syndrome
formal: Variant of familial adenomatous polyposis with colonic polyps, osteomas, soft tissue tumours and CNS tumours such as medulloblastoma, from APC mutations.
simple: An inherited condition with many bowel polyps, bone growths and a higher risk of some tumours, including in the brain.
th: รูปแบบหนึ่งของ familial adenomatous polyposis จากยีน APC มีติ่งเนื้อลำไส้ใหญ่จำนวนมาก osteoma เนื้องอกเนื้อเยื่ออ่อน และเสี่ยง medulloblastoma
tempoNote: Polyps appear in the teens; colon cancer almost certain by 40 without colectomy
feat: Hundreds to thousands of colonic adenomas from adolescence
Osteomas of skull and jaw, dental anomalies, epidermoid cysts
Desmoid tumours, especially after abdominal surgery
Pigmented retinal fundus lesions (CHRPE) on fundoscopy
Brain tumours, mainly medulloblastoma (FAP-associated Turcot syndrome)
inv: Colonoscopy and APC genetic testing
Fundoscopy for CHRPE; dental and skull imaging for osteomas
MRI brain for headache, ataxia or other neurological symptoms

case.story: Morning headaches and vomiting for a month; he had a hard lump on his forehead removed as a child, and his father died of colon cancer at 38.
case.exam: Papilloedema, truncal ataxia, bony swelling of the mandible.
case.tests: MRI shows a midline cerebellar mass; colonoscopy finds hundreds of polyps.
case.q: What genetic syndrome links these findings?
case.a: Gardner’s syndrome (APC-related FAP) with medulloblastoma, the brain-tumour pattern of Turcot syndrome.

det.patho: Germline APC loss-of-function variants activate Wnt/beta-catenin signalling after a second somatic hit, producing adenomas and extracolonic tumours. Gardner’s is now regarded as FAP with prominent extracolonic features rather than a separate disease. Medulloblastomas in these patients are typically of the WNT subgroup.
det.clinical: Gastrointestinal polyposis dominates, with near-certain colorectal cancer if untreated. Extracolonic features include osteomas, supernumerary teeth, epidermoid cysts, desmoid tumours, thyroid cancer and hepatoblastoma in children. Neurologically, the main risk is medulloblastoma in childhood or young adulthood; mismatch-repair-related Turcot syndrome instead causes gliomas.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on polyposis plus extracolonic features and APC genetic testing. CHRPE is a helpful bedside clue. Any brain tumour in a young patient with polyposis or a family history of early colon cancer should prompt genetic evaluation.
det.treatment: Prophylactic colectomy, lifelong upper endoscopic surveillance, and management of desmoids and osteomas. Medulloblastoma is treated with standard surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy; WNT-type tumours have a favourable outlook. Family cascade testing is essential.
det.prognosis: Desmoid tumours and upper gastrointestinal cancers become leading causes of death after colectomy.
pearls: Polyposis plus brain tumour = Turcot: APC links to medulloblastoma, mismatch repair genes to glioma.
CHRPE on fundoscopy is a quick clue to FAP.
Osteomas of the skull or jaw in a young person deserve a family history of colon cancer.
det.thd: Gardner’s syndrome คือ FAP จากยีน APC ที่มีอาการนอกลำไส้ชัด เช่น osteoma ของกะโหลกและขากรรไกร desmoid tumour และฟันเกิน ความเสี่ยงหลักคือมะเร็งลำไส้ใหญ่ตั้งแต่อายุน้อย ด้านระบบประสาทเสี่ยง medulloblastoma ซึ่งเป็นรูปแบบหนึ่งของ Turcot syndrome การดูแลคือผ่าตัดลำไส้ใหญ่ป้องกันและตรวจคัดกรองในครอบครัว

name: Gaucher disease
formal: Autosomal recessive glucocerebrosidase deficiency; neuronopathic types (II, III) cause oculomotor apraxia, seizures, myoclonus and bulbar signs, with hepatosplenomegaly and bone disease.
simple: An inherited fat-storage disease causing an enlarged liver and spleen, and in some forms damaging the brain.
more: Diagnosis by low leukocyte beta-glucosidase activity and GBA1 gene sequencing; elevated chitotriosidase and lyso-Gb1. Enzyme replacement or substrate reduction treat visceral disease but do not cross the blood-brain barrier.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมยีนด้อยจากขาดเอนไซม์ glucocerebrosidase ทำให้ม้ามตับโตและโรคกระดูก ชนิดที่ 2 และ 3 มีอาการทางประสาท เช่น กลอกตาแนวนอนผิดปกติ ชัก myoclonus
tempoNote: Type 2 fatal in infancy; type 3 progresses over years to decades; type 1 non-neuronopathic
feat: Hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, anaemia and bone pain or crises
Slow or absent horizontal saccades (supranuclear gaze palsy) — early sign of neuronopathic types
Type 2: infantile bulbar failure, opisthotonus, rapid death; type 3: progressive myoclonic epilepsy, ataxia, cognitive decline
GBA1 heterozygous and homozygous variants increase Parkinson disease and DLB risk
inv: Leukocyte or dried blood spot beta-glucocerebrosidase activity (low)
GBA1 sequencing; plasma lyso-Gb1 (glucosylsphingosine) for diagnosis and monitoring
CBC, liver/spleen volume, bone MRI or DEXA; EEG and saccade assessment in neuronopathic suspicion

case.story: Large spleen noted at 3 years; now has jerks of the arms, falls and declining school performance.
case.exam: Splenomegaly 8 cm, absent horizontal saccades with head thrust to look sideways, action myoclonus, mild ataxia.
case.tests: Platelets 70,000; leukocyte glucocerebrosidase markedly low; GBA1 L444P homozygous.
case.q: Which type is this and will enzyme replacement treat the neurological disease?
case.a: Type 3 neuronopathic Gaucher disease; ERT helps the spleen, blood counts and bones, but the infused enzyme cannot reach the brain.

read.where: Chapter 28 Progressive Myoclonic Epilepsies — Neuronopathic Gaucher Disease

det.patho: Biallelic GBA1 variants reduce lysosomal glucocerebrosidase, so glucosylceramide and its toxic derivative glucosylsphingosine build up in macrophages (Gaucher cells) of spleen, liver and marrow. In neuronopathic forms the residual activity is very low and neurons are injured directly, with brainstem oculomotor nuclei particularly affected. L444P is a common neuronopathic allele in Asian populations, whereas N370S protects against brain disease.
det.clinical: Type 1 (commonest overall) causes cytopenias, organomegaly and bone disease without primary brain involvement, though Parkinson disease risk rises. Type 2 begins in early infancy with stridor, swallowing failure, retroflexion and death usually by 2 years. Type 3 is chronic neuronopathic: horizontal saccade failure, myoclonic seizures, ataxia, learning decline, with variable visceral disease; a cardiac-valve calcification subtype exists.
det.diagnosis: Low glucocerebrosidase activity in leukocytes or fibroblasts confirms the diagnosis; GBA1 genotyping predicts phenotype and allows family testing. Lyso-Gb1 is a sensitive biomarker for diagnosis and follow-up. Bone marrow showing Gaucher cells is no longer required but may be found when lymphoma is being investigated.
det.treatment: Enzyme replacement therapy (imiglucerase, velaglucerase, taliglucerase) or substrate reduction (eliglustat for type 1) controls visceral and haematological disease. Neither reliably treats brain involvement; high-dose ERT in type 3 helps systemic disease, and brain-penetrant agents and gene therapy are in trials. Supportive care includes antiseizure drugs for myoclonic epilepsy, orthopaedic care and genetic counselling.
det.prognosis: Type 1 has near-normal life expectancy on treatment; type 2 is fatal in infancy; type 3 varies widely, with survival into adulthood common.
pearls: Horizontal saccade failure + splenomegaly = neuronopathic Gaucher; vertical gaze palsy points to NPC.
Among common genetic risks for Parkinson disease, GBA1 variants are the strongest.
Infused enzyme stays outside the brain, so ERT leaves neuronopathic disease untreated.
det.thd: Gaucher disease เกิดจากขาดเอนไซม์ glucocerebrosidase ทำให้สารไขมันสะสมในเซลล์ macrophage ตับม้ามโต เกล็ดเลือดต่ำ และปวดกระดูก ชนิดที่ 2 และ 3 มีอาการทางสมอง เช่น กลอกตาแนวนอนไม่ได้ ชักกระตุก และเดินเซ วินิจฉัยด้วยการวัดเอนไซม์และตรวจยีน GBA1 การให้เอนไซม์ทดแทนช่วยอาการทางกายแต่ไม่ช่วยสมอง

name: Gelsolin-related amyloidosis
formal: Hereditary amyloidosis from gelsolin gene mutations (Finnish type), with corneal lattice dystrophy, progressive cranial neuropathy, cutis laxa and mild peripheral neuropathy.
simple: An inherited disease where abnormal protein builds up, causing facial nerve weakness, loose skin and eye changes.
more: Autosomal dominant (GSN, D187N/Y); first seen with corneal lattice dystrophy in adults. Management is supportive, including facial reanimation and eye care; life expectancy is near normal.
th: amyloidosis ทางพันธุกรรมจากยีน gelsolin ทำให้กระจกตาขุ่นแบบ lattice เส้นประสาทใบหน้าอ่อนแรงทั้งสองข้าง และผิวหนังหย่อน
tempoNote: Corneal signs in the 20s–30s, cranial neuropathy from the 40s, slowly progressive
feat: Lattice corneal dystrophy as the earliest sign, with dry eyes and glare
Slowly progressive bilateral facial weakness starting in the upper face
Loose, sagging skin (cutis laxa) giving a prematurely aged face
Mild distal sensory neuropathy and bulbar involvement later
Autosomal dominant; founder effect in Finland but reported worldwide
inv: Slit-lamp examination for lattice lines
Nerve conduction and blink reflex: facial nerve axonal loss
Tissue biopsy (skin) with Congo red and typing; GSN gene testing

case.story: Years of gritty eyes and poor night vision, now cannot close his eyes fully or whistle; his mother had a similar droopy face.
case.exam: Bilateral lower motor neuron facial weakness worse in the forehead, lax skin of face and neck, reduced vibration at toes.
case.tests: Slit lamp shows lattice corneal dystrophy; GSN p.D214N (traditionally D187N) variant.
case.q: What connects his eyes, face and skin?
case.a: Hereditary gelsolin amyloidosis.

det.patho: A dominant GSN variant makes plasma gelsolin susceptible to abnormal cleavage, releasing amyloidogenic fragments that deposit in cornea, nerves, skin and blood vessel walls. Cranial nerve branches, particularly the facial nerve, are affected early.
det.clinical: The triad is corneal lattice dystrophy, cranial neuropathy (facial nerve first, upper branches before lower) and cutis laxa. Bulbar weakness, mild peripheral neuropathy, renal involvement and cardiac conduction disease may follow. Homozygotes have a severe early form.
det.diagnosis: Ophthalmological examination provides an early clue. Biopsy with Congo red and mass spectrometry typing confirms gelsolin amyloid. Gene testing confirms the variant and enables family screening.
det.treatment: No specific disease-modifying therapy is approved. Management includes eye lubrication and corneal care, plastic surgery for facial ptosis and lax skin, and monitoring for renal and cardiac complications.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive with near-normal life expectancy in heterozygotes; quality of life affected by facial and eye problems.
pearls: Bilateral facial palsy plus corneal lattice dystrophy is pathognomonic.
Forehead branches are affected before lower face.
Ask an ophthalmologist to look at the cornea in unexplained cranial neuropathy.
det.thd: Gelsolin amyloidosis เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมเด่น เกิดจากโปรตีน gelsolin ผิดปกติแล้วสะสมเป็น amyloid ที่กระจกตา เส้นประสาทสมอง และผิวหนัง อาการแรกคือกระจกตาขุ่นแบบ lattice ต่อมาใบหน้าอ่อนแรงทั้งสองข้างเริ่มจากหน้าผาก และผิวหนังหย่อน วินิจฉัยจากตรวจตา ชิ้นเนื้อ และยีน GSN รักษาตามอาการ

name: General paralysis
formal: Tertiary neurosyphilis (general paralysis of the insane) with progressive dementia, psychosis, tremor, dysarthria, Argyll Robertson pupils and frontal atrophy, treated with penicillin.
simple: A late brain infection from untreated syphilis causing memory loss, personality change and weakness.

tempoNote: Appears 10–30 years after infection with progressive course over months to years
feat: Personality change, poor judgement, mania, grandiosity or depression
Progressive memory and executive decline
Dysarthria with tremor of tongue, lips and hands
Pupillary abnormalities including Argyll Robertson pupils; seizures
Higher frequency and faster course in people with HIV

CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein, reactive CSF VDRL
MRI brain: frontotemporal atrophy, sometimes mesial temporal signal change

case.who: 52-year-old male truck driver from Nakhon Sawan
case.story: Over six months he has become grandiose, spending large sums, and forgetful of routes. A genital ulcer decades earlier was never treated.
case.exam: Disinhibited, dysarthric with tremulous speech, small irregular pupils reacting to accommodation but not light, brisk reflexes.
case.tests: Serum TPHA positive, RPR 1:64; CSF 25 lymphocytes/µL, protein raised, CSF VDRL reactive; HIV negative.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and treatment?
case.a: General paralysis due to neurosyphilis. Treat with IV aqueous penicillin G 18–24 million units a day for 10–14 days, then follow serology and CSF.

det.patho: Chronic Treponema pallidum infection of the cerebral cortex produces a meningo-encephalitis with perivascular lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates, neuronal loss and gliosis, predominantly in the frontal and temporal lobes. It follows untreated infection by a decade or more. Syphilis incidence has risen again in many countries, including among people with HIV.
det.clinical: Early features are psychiatric and cognitive: irritability, apathy, mania or psychosis, then dementia with dysarthria, tremor, hyperreflexia and seizures. Pupil abnormalities and optic atrophy may coexist. Neurosyphilis can occur at any stage, so meningitis, ocular and otic syphilis and stroke from meningovascular disease must be recognised too. Always consider it in any dementia of unclear cause in a patient with risk exposure.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis combines positive serum treponemal and non-treponemal tests with abnormal CSF, preferably reactive CSF VDRL, pleocytosis or raised protein. A negative CSF VDRL does not exclude disease, so a CSF treponemal test and the clinical context guide interpretation. MRI helps exclude alternatives. Screen all patients for HIV.
det.treatment: First-line is IV aqueous crystalline penicillin G for 10–14 days, or procaine penicillin with probenecid when admission is impractical. Ceftriaxone is an option for those who cannot take penicillin, with desensitisation preferred for pregnancy. Warn about the Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction. Repeat CSF at about six months and treat contacts. Psychiatric symptoms need supportive therapy.
det.prognosis: Treatment arrests progression and many improve, but established dementia may not fully recover. Untreated disease is fatal within a few years.
pearls: Test syphilis serology in every unexplained dementia or psychosis.
Argyll Robertson pupils: accommodation present, light reaction absent.
A normal serum RPR can occur in late disease, so rely on treponemal tests.
det.thd: General paralysis คือภาวะสมองอักเสบเรื้อรังจากซิฟิลิสที่ไม่ได้รับการรักษา มักเกิดหลายปีถึงหลายสิบปีหลังติดเชื้อ ผู้ป่วยมีพฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน คิดยิ่งใหญ่หรือซึมเศร้า ความจำเสื่อม พูดไม่ชัด มือสั่น และรูม่านตาแบบ Argyll Robertson วินิจฉัยด้วยเลือด TPHA/RPR และน้ำไขสันหลัง (VDRL ให้ผลบวก เซลล์เพิ่ม) รักษาด้วย penicillin G ทางหลอดเลือดดำ 10–14 วัน ตรวจติดตามน้ำไขสันหลังและตรวจ HIV ร่วมด้วยเสมอ

name: Generalised convulsive status epilepticus
formal: Prolonged or repeated generalised tonic-clonic seizures without recovery, lasting over 5 minutes, a medical emergency needing benzodiazepines then second-line antiseizure drugs.
simple: A medical emergency where a convulsion lasts more than five minutes, or repeats without the person waking up in between.
more: Prolonged or repeated generalised tonic-clonic seizures without recovery between them, a medical emergency requiring benzodiazepines and antiseizure drugs.
th: ภาวะชักเกร็งกระตุกทั้งตัวนานเกิน 5 นาทีหรือชักซ้ำโดยไม่ฟื้นระหว่างครั้ง เป็นภาวะฉุกเฉิน ต้องให้ benzodiazepine ทันทีแล้วตามด้วยยากันชักทางหลอดเลือด

feat: Continuous bilateral tonic-clonic activity over 5 minutes, or serial seizures without regaining consciousness
Systemic stress: hypoxia, acidosis, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, aspiration
Overt jerking may fade to subtle twitching while electrical status continues
Common causes: antiseizure drug withdrawal, stroke, alcohol, CNS infection, metabolic disturbance, autoimmune encephalitis

CT then MRI brain; lumbar puncture when infection is possible (after imaging)

case.who: 40-year-old man with known epilepsy from Samut Prakan
case.story: Stopped valproate two weeks ago; brought in by ambulance after 15 minutes of continuous generalised jerking.
case.exam: Unresponsive, ongoing bilateral clonic movements, SpO2 88% on air, temperature 38.2 °C.
case.tests: Glucose 140 mg/dL, lactate 8 mmol/L, CK later 6,000 U/L.
case.q: Outline the first 30 minutes of drug treatment.
case.a: Airway, oxygen, glucose check; IV lorazepam or diazepam (or IM midazolam) once and repeat once; then IV levetiracetam, fosphenytoin or valproate; if still seizing, intubate and start anaesthetic infusion with EEG monitoring.

det.patho: Status arises when seizure-terminating mechanisms fail: GABA-A receptors are internalised during prolonged seizures, explaining benzodiazepine resistance, while NMDA and AMPA receptors increase, sustaining excitation. Ongoing seizures cause excitotoxic neuronal death, especially in hippocampus, and systemic complications. The ILAE operational times are t1 = 5 minutes to treat and t2 = 30 minutes for likely long-term consequences.
det.clinical: It is the most common neurological emergency in many emergency departments. Early phase shows overt convulsions with tachycardia, hypertension and hyperthermia; later, motor activity dwindles into subtle twitches (electromechanical dissociation). Established status persists after benzodiazepine and a second-line drug; refractory and super-refractory stages follow. Mortality relates mainly to the cause and age.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, but EEG is required when consciousness does not return, when movements are subtle, or when paralysed or anaesthetised. Look urgently for reversible causes: hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia, alcohol withdrawal, thiamine deficiency, drug toxicity, infection, stroke and autoimmune encephalitis. Exclude functional seizures in atypical, prolonged events without physiological derangement.
det.treatment: Stage 1 (5–20 minutes): adequate dose benzodiazepine — IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg, IV diazepam, or IM/buccal/intranasal midazolam — repeated once. Stage 2: IV levetiracetam (about 60 mg/kg, max 4.5 g), fosphenytoin (20 mg PE/kg) or valproate (40 mg/kg, max 3 g), which are similarly effective (ESETT). Stage 3: intubation and anaesthetic infusion (midazolam, propofol or thiopental) with continuous EEG; give thiamine before glucose when alcohol or malnutrition is likely. Treat the cause and complications.
det.prognosis: Overall mortality is roughly 10–20%, much higher with anoxic or acute symptomatic causes and in the elderly; drug-withdrawal status in known epilepsy has the best outcome.
pearls: Under-dosing benzodiazepines is the commonest treatment error.
Stopped jerking but not waking = think non-convulsive status and get EEG.
Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate are equivalent second-line choices.

qx.stem: A 34-year-old motorcycle taxi driver with known epilepsy who stopped his medicines a week ago arrives in the emergency room convulsing. He received 10 mg midazolam intramuscularly from paramedics and a further 4 mg lorazepam intravenously 5 minutes ago, yet generalised tonic–clonic activity continues at minute 15. Glucose is 112 mg/dL.
qx.q: Which is the most appropriate next treatment?
opts: A third dose of intravenous lorazepam
Oral levetiracetam via nasogastric tube
Immediate propofol infusion without a second-line agent
Intravenous magnesium sulphate

qx.why: Seizures continuing after two adequate benzodiazepine doses define established status epilepticus. The ESETT trial showed similar efficacy of IV levetiracetam (~60 mg/kg), fosphenytoin (~20 mg PE/kg) and valproate (~40 mg/kg), so any one is appropriate, chosen by comorbidity. Further benzodiazepines add respiratory risk with little gain, and anaesthetic infusions are reserved for refractory status.

det.patho: Generalised seizures originate at some point within, and rapidly engage, bilaterally distributed networks, centred on thalamocortical circuits. Absence seizures reflect oscillation of thalamic T-type calcium channel-driven rhythms, which is why ethosuximide works. Most generalised epilepsies are polygenic, while some have single-gene causes (e.g. SCN1A, SLC2A1).
det.clinical: The idiopathic generalised group comprises childhood and juvenile absence epilepsies, juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, and a syndrome in which only tonic-clonic attacks occur. Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (Lennox–Gastaut, Dravet) feature tonic, atonic and atypical absences. A seizure that looks generalised may be secondarily generalised from a focus, so asking about warning symptoms is vital.
det.diagnosis: Classify the seizure type, then the epilepsy type and syndrome, then the cause. EEG generalised discharges support the diagnosis; sleep-deprived EEG increases the yield. Imaging is reserved for atypical features, focal signs or poor response. Distinguish from syncope, cardiac arrhythmia and functional events.
det.treatment: Valproate is the most effective broad-spectrum drug but should be avoided in women who could become pregnant unless no alternative works (teratogenicity). Levetiracetam and lamotrigine are common alternatives; ethosuximide is first-line for childhood absence. Avoid sodium-channel blockers (carbamazepine, phenytoin, oxcarbazepine) and gabapentin/pregabalin/vigabatrin, which may worsen absence and myoclonus. Counsel on sleep, alcohol and photic triggers.
det.prognosis: Childhood absence often remits; juvenile myoclonic epilepsy responds well but usually needs lifelong treatment; epileptic encephalopathies have poor prognosis.
pearls: Ask about morning jerks in every adolescent with a first tonic-clonic seizure.
Carbamazepine can aggravate absence and myoclonic seizures.
Valproate is highly effective but restricted in women of childbearing potential.

name: Generalized cortical myoclonus
formal: Widespread myoclonic jerks of cortical origin, as in progressive myoclonic epilepsy, post-anoxic and metabolic states, with EEG spike correlate and giant SEPs.
simple: Widespread sudden jerks of the body arising from overactive brain surface, seen in some epilepsies and brain injuries.
th: การกระตุกสั้น ๆ แบบไฟช็อตที่เกิดจากเปลือกสมองกระจายทั่วร่างกาย พบใน progressive myoclonic epilepsy ภายหลังสมองขาดออกซิเจน และภาวะเมตาบอลิก มีคลื่น spike ที่ EEG สัมพันธ์และ SEP ขนาดใหญ่
tempoNote: Subacute in metabolic or post-hypoxic states; chronic progressive in PME
feat: Very brief (<50 ms) jerks, multifocal, often stimulus- and action-sensitive
Distal and facial muscles favoured (largest cortical representation)
Action myoclonus disrupts reaching, eating and walking; often with negative myoclonus
Causes: PME (Unverricht–Lundborg, Lafora, MERRF), post-hypoxic (Lance–Adams), uraemia, CJD, drugs

case.story: Survived a cardiac arrest two months ago; now alert but cannot drink a cup of water because his arms jerk whenever he moves.
case.exam: Multifocal action-induced jerks of arms and face, worsened by touch, with drops when standing (negative myoclonus).
case.tests: SEPs show giant cortical potentials; EEG-EMG back-averaging confirms a preceding cortical discharge.
case.q: What syndrome is this and which drugs help?
case.a: Lance–Adams syndrome (chronic post-hypoxic cortical action myoclonus); levetiracetam, valproate, clonazepam or piracetam, often in combination.

read.where: Chapter 18 Myoclonus — Multifocal and generalized cortical myoclonus

det.patho: Hyperexcitable sensorimotor cortex fires brief discharges that travel down the corticospinal tract, giving short jerks in muscles with large cortical maps. Loss of inhibitory interneurons, often GABAergic, underlies most forms; in generalised forms the discharge spreads transcallosally and intrahemispherically. Sensory input reaches the excitable cortex quickly, explaining reflex sensitivity and giant SEPs.
det.clinical: Jerks are triggered by movement intention, touch, sound or light and impair function more than at rest. Patients with PME show progressive action myoclonus, generalised seizures and, depending on cause, ataxia or dementia. In acute post-anoxic coma, generalised myoclonus is a different entity with poorer prognosis than Lance–Adams. Metabolic causes (renal, liver failure, hyponatraemia) and drugs (gabapentin, pregabalin, cefepime, opioids, lithium) are frequent in hospital.
det.diagnosis: Confirm the cortical origin with short EMG bursts, an EEG correlate on back-averaging, giant SEPs and an enhanced C-reflex. Then search for a cause: metabolic panel, drug review, MRI, and when progressive, genetic testing for PME and enzyme studies. EEG background slowing indicates encephalopathy.
det.treatment: Remove the cause where possible (stop offending drugs, correct metabolic state). Effective drugs include levetiracetam, valproate, clonazepam, piracetam and brivaracetam; perampanel and zonisamide are used in PME. Avoid phenytoin, carbamazepine, lamotrigine (in some PMEs) and gabapentinoids, which can worsen myoclonus. Physical therapy addresses falls from negative myoclonus.
det.prognosis: Metabolic and drug-related forms resolve with correction; post-hypoxic chronic action myoclonus often improves partly; PME causes are progressive.
pearls: Giant SEPs and a back-averaged cortical spike define cortical myoclonus.
Cefepime, gabapentin and pregabalin are common hospital culprits in renal failure.
Levetiracetam and valproate are the backbone; sodium-channel blockers may worsen it.

case.q: What is the likely cause and management?

read.where: 18 - Myoclonus: Phenomenology, etiology, physiology, and treatment

det.patho: Myoclonus can be generated by cortex, subcortical structures (brainstem reticular formation, basal ganglia) or spinal cord; the source shapes the pattern. Cortical forms are brief, distal and stimulus-sensitive; brainstem reticular forms spread up and down the brainstem to produce axial jerks; spinal forms are segmental. Toxic-metabolic states lower inhibitory control across several levels at once.
det.clinical: The most common cause in hospitals is toxic or metabolic: renal and hepatic failure, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, opioids, antibiotics, antidepressants and lithium. Post-hypoxic myoclonus may be acute (in coma) or chronic (Lance–Adams). Neurodegenerative causes include CJD, Alzheimer disease (late), dementia with Lewy bodies and corticobasal syndrome. Epileptic causes include JME and progressive myoclonic epilepsies.
det.diagnosis: Characterise distribution, triggers, rest vs action, and associated signs, then classify anatomically with EEG-EMG, back-averaging and SEPs. The cause is often revealed by bloods and drug charts; MRI, EEG and CSF (including RT-QuIC) for suspected CJD; genetic testing for PME.
det.treatment: Treat the cause first. Symptomatic drugs depend on origin: cortical myoclonus responds to levetiracetam, valproate, clonazepam and piracetam; subcortical forms to clonazepam; spinal forms to clonazepam or levetiracetam. Withdraw drugs that provoke myoclonus.
det.prognosis: Toxic-metabolic myoclonus usually resolves with correction; prognosis otherwise follows the underlying disease.
pearls: Asterixis is negative myoclonus — classically hepatic, renal or CO2 retention.
Always review the drug chart: opioids, cefepime, lithium, SSRIs, gabapentinoids.
Rapid dementia plus myoclonus: think CJD.

name: Generalized primary dystonia

case.q: What is the diagnosis and what is the most effective treatment if oral drugs fail?

read.where: 11 - Dystonia: Phenomenology, classification, etiology, pathology, biochemistry, and genetics

det.patho: Generalised isolated dystonia reflects network dysfunction in basal ganglia–thalamo–cortical and cerebellar circuits with loss of surround inhibition and abnormal plasticity, without neurodegeneration. TOR1A encodes torsinA, an AAA+ ATPase in the nuclear envelope and endoplasmic reticulum; the common in-frame GAG deletion is dominant with roughly 30% penetrance, and onset after the late twenties is uncommon in carriers. Other genes include THAP1 (more cranial and laryngeal involvement), KMT2B (childhood onset with prominent oromandibular and laryngeal features) and GNAL (mostly adult cervical onset).
det.clinical: Onset is usually in a leg or arm between about 6 and 15 years, first only during a specific action such as walking forwards. Over time it appears with other movements and at rest, spreading to the trunk and other limbs to produce fixed-looking twisting postures. Speech and swallowing are generally spared in TOR1A, whereas prominent laryngeal or oromandibular features point to THAP1 or KMT2B. Any additional sign such as spasticity, ataxia, cognitive decline or neuropathy argues for a combined or acquired dystonia and needs a broader work-up.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, using the axis I (phenotype) and axis II (aetiology) classification. Every child with dystonia should have a levodopa trial to catch dopa-responsive dystonia, and copper studies for Wilson disease. MRI should be normal; abnormalities suggest a secondary cause. Genetic testing starts with TOR1A and moves to a panel or exome; a normal result cannot rule out primary dystonia because many genes are still unknown.
det.treatment: Oral options include high-dose trihexyphenidyl (often well tolerated in children), baclofen, clonazepam and tetrabenazine, with botulinum toxin for the most disabling focal components. Bilateral GPi deep brain stimulation is the most effective therapy for isolated generalised dystonia, particularly TOR1A, with gains building over months. Physiotherapy prevents contractures, and schools should be helped to adapt writing tasks. Rarely, dystonic storm requires intensive care, sedation and urgent DBS adjustment or placement.
det.prognosis: Spread usually stops after about 5 years; with DBS many TOR1A patients regain substantial function, though fixed skeletal deformity limits benefit if surgery is delayed.
pearls: Always try levodopa in childhood dystonia before calling it primary.
Leg-onset dystonia in a child tends to generalise; adult-onset dystonia usually stays focal.
TOR1A dystonia responds better to pallidal DBS than most secondary dystonias.

det.patho: Geniospasm is a familial movement disorder with rhythmic or myoclonic activity of the mentalis muscle. Linkage to chromosome 9q has been reported in some families, but the gene and mechanism remain uncertain. A brain stem generator is presumed.
det.clinical: Onset is in infancy or childhood with episodes of chin quivering lasting seconds to hours, often triggered by stress or emotion. Frequency tends to decrease with age. Some patients bite their tongues at night. There are no other neurological signs.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical, relying on the characteristic chin movement and dominant family history. Video recording is helpful. Investigation is unnecessary unless there are atypical features such as other abnormal movements.
det.treatment: Reassurance is usually enough. Botulinum toxin injections into the mentalis are effective for troublesome cases. Medication is rarely needed.
det.prognosis: Benign, with tendency to improve over time.
pearls: Familial chin quivering triggered by emotion in a child is geniospasm.
Botulinum toxin is the most effective treatment.
No investigation is needed in typical cases.

name: Gerhardt’s syndrome
formal: Bilateral vocal cord paralysis due to recurrent laryngeal nerve dysfunction, with vocal cords in the median position, causing stridor and dyspnoea.
simple: Weakness of both vocal cords that can make breathing noisy and difficult.
th: Gerhardt’s syndrome คือภาวะเส้นเสียงสองข้างอ่อนแรงหรือเปิดไม่ได้ (vocal cord abductor paresis) ทำให้เกิดเสียง stridor ตอนหายใจเข้าและกรนเสียงสูง โดยเฉพาะตอนนอนหลับ พบบ่อยใน multiple system atrophy อาจทำให้ทางเดินหายใจอุดกั้นเฉียบพลันและเสียชีวิตขณะหลับ ต้องตรวจส่องกล่องเสียงทั้งตอนตื่นและตอนหลับ และพิจารณา CPAP หรือเจาะคอ
tempoNote: Snoring and stridor progress over one to three years in most patients, with some showing sudden deterioration over days
feat: Loud, high-pitched, often metallic or croup-like snoring that begins in sleep, followed by inspiratory stridor while awake, especially during speech
Both vocal folds fail to open on inspiration and may move paradoxically (close on breathing in); movement is worse during sleep and may be near midline

In multiple system atrophy it can be the first or only sign and often appears around the time bladder symptoms begin; other causes include bilateral recurrent laryngeal injury, Chiari and brainstem disease
Sudden death during sleep, from airway obstruction or central dysregulation of breathing, is the major danger
Accompanying dysphagia and aspiration are frequent; adductor muscle overactivity (laryngeal dystonia) may contribute
inv: Fibre-optic laryngoscopy while awake and during drug-induced sleep (sleep endoscopy), with staging of vocal fold mobility and posterior glottis patency
Overnight oximetry or polysomnography with audio; the proportion of the night with oxygen saturation below 90% guides intervention
Swallow assessment, brain and craniocervical MRI, and autonomic testing when MSA is suspected
Laryngeal EMG in selected cases to separate abductor denervation from adductor overactivity

case.who: 58-year-old woman from Songkhla with a 3-year history of parkinsonism and urinary urgency
case.story: Her husband reports very loud, high-pitched snoring that has worsened over a year; lately she makes a harsh noise when she talks and breathes in.
case.exam: Inspiratory stridor louder over the neck than chest, suprasternal retraction, orthostatic blood pressure fall, slowed movements with symmetrical rigidity.
case.tests: Awake laryngoscopy shows restricted abduction of both vocal folds; sleep endoscopy shows inspiratory adduction with a slit-like posterior glottis; overnight oximetry shows 25% of the night under 90%.
case.q: What is the cause of the stridor and what should be arranged?
case.a: Vocal cord abductor paresis in probable multiple system atrophy. The oximetry and sleep findings mark a high risk of sudden death, so arrange nocturnal CPAP and an early decision on tracheostomy, with swallowing review.

read.where: 7. Movement Disorder Emergencies of the Upper Aerodigestive Tract

det.patho: In MSA the posterior cricoarytenoid, the only muscle that opens the glottis, shows selective neurogenic atrophy, probably from loss of ambiguus neurons. Abduction is both weak and delayed, so the negative pressure of inspiration may collapse the larynx before it opens, producing paradoxical closure. Increased adductor tone from pyramidal and extrapyramidal degeneration (a dystonia-like effect), sleep, and aspiration-triggered laryngeal narrowing all add to the obstruction. Other causes of bilateral paralysis include thyroid surgery, trauma and brainstem malformation.
det.clinical: Early disease shows only snoring in sleep, the later stage adds daytime inspiratory stridor and visible retraction above the sternum, and advanced disease causes respiratory distress. The progression may be slow over 1 to 3 years or rapid, with severe worsening over days that can follow an infection or secretions. Stridor can be misdiagnosed as steroid-resistant asthma. Gerhardt first attributed the syndrome to paralysis of the abductors; subsequent EMG studies have found overactive adductors in some patients, which responds to botulinum toxin.
det.diagnosis: Flexible laryngoscopy both awake and during induced sleep is the definitive test, because the abnormal movement may be seen only when asleep. Severity staging runs from normal to midline fixation. The pitch and character of the snoring, the daytime stridor and the lack of change with posture help to separate it from obstructive sleep apnoea. Awareness of timing is critical, since overnight oximetry can underestimate severity if sleep is light. Evaluate for MSA and other causes with MRI and autonomic tests.
det.treatment: Moderate disease can be treated with nocturnal CPAP, which often splints the airway, but it needs monitoring. Tracheostomy is the most reliable option and is indicated for severe fixed obstruction, for advanced glottic narrowing with a slit-like posterior glottis, or when sleep oximetry shows a large proportion of the night with desaturation. Botulinum toxin to overactive adductors, and arytenoidectomy or cordotomy, are alternatives. In an acute obstruction, humidified oxygen, steroids and an expert airway team are used; intubation may be difficult because the cords lie near the midline, and cricothyroidotomy may be required.
det.prognosis: VCAP is a serious marker in MSA, and sudden nocturnal death occurs, especially in those with rapid progression. Tracheostomy prevents this death but does not alter the underlying disease, whose median survival is under a decade.
pearls: Loud high-pitched snoring in MSA is a laryngeal problem until proved otherwise.
Daytime stridor is an ominous sign.
Look at the vocal folds while awake and in sleep.
det.thd: Gerhardt’s syndrome คือภาวะเส้นเสียงสองข้างเปิดไม่ได้ ทำให้หายใจเข้าแล้วมีเสียง stridor ผู้ป่วย multiple system atrophy มักมีเสียงกรนดังแหลมก่อน ต่อมาหายใจเสียงดังตอนพูดและตอนตื่น เสี่ยงเสียชีวิตขณะหลับ ต้องส่องกล่องเสียงทั้งตอนตื่นและหลับ ตรวจวัดออกซิเจนทั้งคืน ให้ CPAP หรือเจาะคอเมื่อทางเดินหายใจแคบมาก และระวังการใส่ท่อช่วยหายใจที่ยากเพราะเส้นเสียงอยู่ใกล้แนวกลาง

qx.stem: A 62-year-old man with 4 years of parkinsonism, orthostatic hypotension and urinary retention has a year of loud, high-pitched snoring. Now he makes a harsh inspiratory noise when talking in the daytime. Laryngoscopy awake shows restricted abduction of both vocal folds; with propofol sleep it shows inspiratory closure to a slit. Overnight oximetry shows 30% of the night with saturation below 90%.
qx.q: What is the most important implication?
opts: This is simple obstructive sleep apnoea and weight loss is enough
It is anxiety-related stridor requiring a benzodiazepine
Vocal cord abductor paresis in probable multiple system atrophy carries a risk of sudden nocturnal death, so CPAP and an early decision about tracheostomy are needed
The vocal folds should be injected with botulinum toxin into the abductors
The condition will resolve if levodopa is increased
qx.why: Stridor with paradoxical vocal fold closure and nocturnal desaturation in a patient with MSA features is bilateral abductor paresis (Gerhardt-type). Daytime stridor and marked nocturnal desaturation signal danger of sudden death, and management centres on CPAP, tracheostomy when the airway narrowing or desaturation burden is high, and botulinum toxin to overactive adductors (not abductors). Obstructive apnoea does not cause daytime stridor with paradoxical cord movement, and levodopa does not treat it.

name: Germ cell tumours (GCTs)
formal: Intracranial tumours from primordial germ cells in midline sites (pineal, suprasellar), including germinomas and non-germinomatous types, with raised AFP or beta-hCG, causing Parinaud syndrome, diabetes insipidus.
simple: Brain tumours in the middle of the head that start from early reproductive cells, often in children and teenagers.
th: เนื้องอกจากเซลล์สืบพันธุ์ปฐมภูมิในสมอง แบ่งเป็น germinoma และ non-germinomatous (teratoma, yolk sac, embryonal carcinoma, choriocarcinoma, mixed) พบที่ pineal และ suprasellar ในเด็กและวัยรุ่น ใช้ AFP, beta-hCG แยกชนิดและวางแผนการรักษา
tempoNote: Weeks to months of hydrocephalus, visual or endocrine symptoms; non-germinomatous tumours (choriocarcinoma, yolk sac) progress faster and may bleed
feat: Peak 10-20 years; about 10 times more common in Asian populations than Western series; pineal location in males, suprasellar in females
Pineal tumours cause hydrocephalus and Parinaud syndrome; suprasellar tumours cause diabetes insipidus, field loss and hypopituitarism
Basal ganglia or thalamic GCTs cause progressive hemiparesis, cognitive decline and hemiatrophy and are often mistaken for stroke or demyelination
Neonatal and infant teratomas are the commonest congenital brain tumours and present with macrocephaly
About 10 percent have CSF dissemination at presentation, higher in non-germinomatous disease
inv: MRI brain and spine with contrast; CT for calcification and fat (teratoma) and haemorrhage (choriocarcinoma)
Serum and CSF AFP and beta-hCG (CSF level higher than serum); placental alkaline phosphatase and c-KIT immunostaining
Biopsy when markers are normal or equivocal; for marker-positive tumours (AFP above 10 ng/mL or beta-hCG above 100 IU/L) treatment can start without biopsy in several protocols
Pituitary and visual assessment; CSF cytology after neuraxial imaging

case.story: Weeks of progressive left arm weakness and clumsiness with falling school grades; initially treated as a stroke.
case.exam: Mild left hemiparesis, hemiatrophy of left hand, impaired attention.
case.tests: MRI shows a heterogeneous right basal ganglia mass with peri-lesional atrophy and haemorrhage; serum AFP 230 ng/mL and beta-hCG 120 IU/L; biopsy not required. Diagnosis: mixed germ cell tumour with yolk sac and germinoma components.
case.q: How does the marker profile change treatment compared with pure germinoma?
case.a: Elevated AFP or high beta-hCG indicates non-germinomatous disease: intensive platinum-based chemotherapy followed by focal or craniospinal radiotherapy and second-look surgery for residual disease, whereas pure germinoma is cured with chemotherapy plus reduced-dose radiotherapy.

det.patho: Intracranial germ cell tumours are thought to arise from primordial germ cells that mismigrate along the midline during embryogenesis. WHO divides them into germinoma, teratoma (mature, immature, with malignant transformation), yolk sac tumour, embryonal carcinoma, choriocarcinoma and mixed tumours. Germinoma and teratoma tend to occur in pure form; mixed tumours have at least one primitive element, the commonest combination being germinoma with teratoma. Marker expression (AFP in yolk sac and embryonal carcinoma, beta-hCG in choriocarcinoma and syncytiotrophoblasts) correlates with histology.
det.clinical: Site determines presentation: pineal (hydrocephalus, Parinaud), suprasellar (visual loss, diabetes insipidus, hypopituitarism, delayed puberty) or basal ganglia (slowly progressive hemiparesis). Choriocarcinoma may produce precocious puberty and bleed. The source underlines that bifocal pineal plus suprasellar germinoma is almost pathognomonic and that overt diabetes insipidus at presentation favours germinoma over craniopharyngioma and optic pathway glioma.
det.diagnosis: CT and MRI identify the lesion and its relation to vessels and ventricles; teratoma shows calcification and fat, choriocarcinoma haemorrhage. Marker studies of serum and CSF often define the subtype and dictate therapy. Histology is required when markers are negative. Tissue can be obtained during shunting or endoscopic third ventriculostomy. Whole-spine MRI and CSF cytology complete staging.
det.treatment: Germinoma is treated with platinum-based chemotherapy and reduced-dose whole-ventricular irradiation with boost. Non-germinomatous GCTs are seldom cured by radiotherapy alone, so high-dose combination chemotherapy (cisplatin or carboplatin with etoposide and ifosfamide or bleomycin) is combined with focal or craniospinal irradiation (30-54 Gy) and second-look surgery to remove residual mature teratoma. Mature teratoma is resected. Radiosurgery may be used for small residual masses. Late effects include hormonal deficiency, cognitive and growth problems.
det.prognosis: Pure germinoma has five-year survival above 90 percent; non-germinomatous tumours reach about 70-80 percent with modern therapy, but choriocarcinoma and embryonal carcinoma do worse.
pearls: Always measure AFP and beta-hCG in serum and CSF before surgery in a midline paediatric tumour.
Basal ganglia germ cell tumours can mimic stroke or demyelination in a child.
Residual mature teratoma after chemotherapy needs resection to prevent growing teratoma syndrome.
det.thd: Germ cell tumour ในสมองเกิดจากเซลล์สืบพันธุ์ปฐมภูมิที่หลงอยู่แนวกลาง พบบ่อยในเด็กและวัยรุ่นเอเชีย แบ่งเป็น germinoma และ non-germinomatous ซึ่งมี AFP หรือ beta-hCG สูง ผู้ป่วยมีน้ำคั่งสมอง ตามัว เบาจืด หรืออ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกค่อย ๆ เป็น การตรวจ marker และชิ้นเนื้อแยกชนิด germinoma ใช้เคมีบำบัดและรังสีขนาดต่ำ ส่วน non-germinomatous ต้องใช้เคมีบำบัดเข้มข้น รังสี และผ่าตัดก้อนที่เหลือ

name: Germinomas
formal: Most common intracranial germ cell tumour, radiosensitive, in pineal or suprasellar regions, presenting with Parinaud syndrome, diabetes insipidus and hydrocephalus, with excellent prognosis.
simple: A type of brain tumour in the middle of the head, mostly in young people, that responds very well to treatment.
th: เนื้องอก germ cell ชนิดที่พบบ่อยที่สุดของสมอง พบบริเวณ pineal และ suprasellar ในเด็กและวัยรุ่น ทำให้ตามัว เบาจืด และ Parinaud syndrome ไวต่อรังสีและเคมีบำบัดมาก หายขาดได้มากกว่า 90%
tempoNote: Weeks to months of polyuria and visual loss (suprasellar) or headache, vomiting and upgaze palsy (pineal); diabetes insipidus can precede imaging changes by months
feat: Peak at 10-20 years, males predominate in the pineal region; suprasellar tumours are more common in females
Pineal tumours cause obstructive hydrocephalus and Parinaud syndrome (upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus, light-near dissociation)
Suprasellar tumours produce diabetes insipidus, bitemporal field loss, hypopituitarism, delayed puberty or growth failure
Bifocal disease (pineal plus suprasellar) is nearly specific, and basal ganglia germinomas present with progressive hemiparesis and cognitive decline
About 10 percent have CSF dissemination at diagnosis
inv: MRI of brain and whole spine with contrast: homogeneously enhancing midline mass with little oedema, ventricular wall deposits
Serum and CSF AFP and beta-hCG: AFP normal and beta-hCG low (below about 50-100 IU/L) in pure germinoma; higher values suggest a non-germinomatous component
CSF cytology (after neuraxial imaging), PLAP and placental alkaline phosphatase; biopsy by endoscopic or stereotactic approach is advised when markers are normal
Pituitary function tests, visual fields and osmolality for suprasellar tumours

case.story: Four months of drinking and urinating large volumes, then blurred vision; he is shorter than his classmates and has not started puberty.
case.exam: Bitemporal field loss, polyuria, and delayed puberty; no papilloedema.
case.tests: MRI shows an enhancing mass thickening the infundibulum and a second lesion in the pineal region. Serum and CSF AFP normal, beta-hCG 12 IU/L; endoscopic biopsy: germinoma, c-KIT positive. Spine MRI normal.
case.q: What treatment is used and what is the expected outcome?
case.a: Platinum-based chemotherapy followed by reduced-dose whole-ventricular irradiation with a boost, giving cure rates above 90%; hormone replacement (desmopressin, hydrocortisone, thyroxine, sex steroids) is long-term.

read.where: Chapter 13 Tumors of the Pineal Region

det.patho: Germinoma is the CNS counterpart of testicular seminoma. It consists of large primitive germ cells with clear cytoplasm in lobules, surrounded by lymphocytes and sometimes granulomas. Cells express OCT4, c-KIT, PLAP and D2-40 and carry KIT or RAS pathway mutations. A small subset has syncytiotrophoblast giant cells producing low-level beta-hCG. Pure germinoma is one of two main subtypes of CNS germ cell tumour, the other being non-germinomatous tumours (teratoma, yolk sac, embryonal carcinoma, choriocarcinoma, mixed).
det.clinical: Presentation depends on location: suprasellar tumours often begin with diabetes insipidus months before visual loss and endocrine failure; pineal tumours with hydrocephalus and Parinaud syndrome; basal ganglia tumours with insidious hemiparesis, cognitive decline and hemiatrophy. Dissemination along the ventricular and subarachnoid surfaces occurs in about 10 percent at diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows an enhancing midline mass; double lesions (pineal and suprasellar) are almost specific. Serum and CSF markers are measured before surgery: normal AFP with beta-hCG under the threshold supports germinoma, and markers above threshold lead to non-germinomatous treatment without biopsy in some protocols. If markers are normal, histologic diagnosis is needed, often at the time of a third ventriculostomy or by endoscopic biopsy. Whole-spine MRI and CSF cytology stage the disease.
det.treatment: Germinoma is highly radiosensitive and chemosensitive. Historically craniospinal irradiation to above 40 Gy gave high cure rates but caused substantial late toxicity. Current protocols give platinum-based chemotherapy (carboplatin plus etoposide) followed by whole-ventricular radiotherapy at 18-24 Gy with a boost to 30-40 Gy, or focal radiotherapy in selected localised cases, maintaining 5-year survival above 90 percent. Disseminated germinoma still receives craniospinal irradiation. Non-germinomatous tumours need higher-dose combination chemotherapy and radiation, and second-look surgery for residual mass.
det.prognosis: Five-year survival is over 90 percent for localised germinoma; long-term hormone replacement and neuropsychological follow-up are required.
pearls: Child or teen with polyuria and visual loss: think germinoma before craniopharyngioma, and measure AFP and beta-hCG.
Pineal plus suprasellar bifocal tumour is almost pathognomonic.
Low-dose, response-adapted radiotherapy after chemotherapy preserves cure while reducing late damage.
det.thd: Germinoma เป็นเนื้องอก germ cell ชนิดที่พบบ่อยที่สุดในสมอง พบบริเวณ pineal และ suprasellar ในเด็กและวัยรุ่น ทำให้น้ำคั่งสมอง Parinaud syndrome ตามัว ปัสสาวะมากจากเบาจืด และฮอร์โมนต่ำ การวินิจฉัยใช้ MRI วัด AFP และ beta-hCG ในเลือดและน้ำไขสันหลัง และชิ้นเนื้อเมื่อ marker ปกติ การรักษาคือเคมีบำบัดตามด้วยฉายรังสีขนาดต่ำที่ช่องสมอง ซึ่งหายขาดได้มากกว่า 90% แต่ต้องให้ฮอร์โมนทดแทนระยะยาว

qx.stem: A 14-year-old boy from Udon Thani has six months of excessive thirst and passing large volumes of urine, and recently cannot look upward. MRI shows enhancing masses in the pineal region and the pituitary stalk with hydrocephalus. Serum and CSF alpha-fetoprotein are normal and CSF beta-hCG is slightly raised.
qx.q: Which diagnosis is most likely, and what outcome should be expected?
opts: Pure germinoma, highly curable with chemotherapy followed by reduced-dose radiotherapy
Yolk sac tumour, requiring intensive chemotherapy and high-dose radiation
Pineoblastoma, with frequent spinal spread and a poor outlook
Langerhans cell histiocytosis, treated with steroids alone
Craniopharyngioma, treated by surgery alone
qx.why: Bifocal pineal and suprasellar tumours with diabetes insipidus and normal AFP point to germinoma; a mild beta-hCG rise from syncytiotrophoblastic cells is allowed. Germinoma is very sensitive to treatment and cure rates exceed 90% with chemotherapy and reduced-dose ventricular radiotherapy. A raised AFP would suggest a yolk sac component and a nongerminomatous tumour with a poorer prognosis.

name: Gerstmann syndrome
formal: Dominant angular gyrus lesion syndrome of finger agnosia, left-right disorientation, agraphia and acalculia, typically from left parietal infarct or tumour.
simple: A set of four problems, finger recognition, telling left from right, writing and calculating, caused by damage in one part of the brain.
th: กลุ่มอาการจากรอยโรคที่ angular gyrus ข้างซีกสมองเด่น ประกอบด้วย finger agnosia, สับสนซ้ายขวา, เขียนไม่ได้ และคำนวณไม่ได้
tempoNote: Sudden with infarcts; gradual with tumours or neurodegeneration
feat: Core elements: finger agnosia, left-right disorientation, acalculia and agraphia (some lists replace agraphia with constructional apraxia)
Lesion centred on the dominant (usually left) inferior parietal lobule, angular gyrus and the white matter beneath it
Often accompanied by alexia, anomia or a right lower visual field defect
The full tetrad without aphasia is uncommon; partial forms are the rule
Developmental form in children with learning difficulties is described
inv: MRI brain with DWI: left angular gyrus or parietal lesion
Vascular work-up for an inferior division MCA infarct: ECG and monitoring for atrial fibrillation, vessel imaging, echocardiography
Bedside battery: finger naming, crossed left-right commands, dictated writing, serial and written arithmetic

case.who: 61-year-old accountant from Nakhon Si Thammarat with atrial fibrillation not on anticoagulation
case.story: Suddenly could not add up figures at work, and his signature looked wrong.
case.exam: Cannot name or point to fingers on command, confuses right and left, makes spelling errors when writing, fails simple subtraction; speech fluent with mild anomia.
case.tests: MRI: acute infarct of left angular gyrus; ECG atrial fibrillation.
case.q: Name the syndrome and the likely mechanism.
case.a: Gerstmann syndrome from a cardioembolic left parietal infarct.

20 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Cerebral Hemispheres

det.patho: The angular gyrus sits at the junction of parietal, temporal and occipital association cortex in the dominant hemisphere, a hub for number sense, body schema and written language. A lesion there, or in the connections beneath it, disturbs these functions together. Common causes are inferior-division MCA infarcts, tumours and posterior cortical degeneration. Whether the tetrad reflects a true unitary cortical module or simply neighbouring functions is still debated.
det.clinical: Patients cannot say which finger is touched, cannot follow commands that require telling right from left, make errors in writing despite intact motor control, and cannot do calculation on paper. Because language centres are close by, many also have alexia or anomia, and a right inferior quadrantanopia may be found. Insight is variable, and daily tasks such as banking, handling money and filling forms become the first complaints. Elements can appear gradually in posterior cortical atrophy and Alzheimer disease.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical and anatomical, backed by imaging of the dominant parietal lobe. Aphasia must be accounted for, because it alone can impair finger naming and left-right commands, so test fingers and sides in ways that do not depend on fluent language. Look for the underlying cause as for any focal lesion: stroke investigation, tumour imaging or a neurodegenerative evaluation.
det.treatment: Treat the cause, for instance anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation after a cardioembolic stroke. Occupational and cognitive therapy target writing and calculation, and compensatory strategies such as calculators, typed communication and checklists help people return to work. Neurodegenerative causes are managed as the underlying disease.
det.prognosis: Stroke-related deficits often improve over weeks to months; progressive causes worsen over time.
pearls: Finger agnosia, right-left confusion, acalculia and agraphia point to the dominant angular gyrus.
Test finger naming separately from general naming so aphasia is not blamed or missed.
Partial Gerstmann features can be an early sign of posterior cortical atrophy.
det.thd: Gerstmann syndrome เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ angular gyrus ของสมองซีกเด่น มีอาการหลักคือบอกชื่อนิ้วไม่ได้ สับสนซ้ายขวา เขียนไม่ได้ และคิดเลขไม่ได้ (บางตำราใช้ constructional apraxia แทนการเขียน) มักพบร่วมกับ aphasia หรืออ่านไม่ได้ สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยคือ stroke ของ MCA และเนื้องอก วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจร่างกายและ MRI การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุร่วมกับการฟื้นฟูการรู้คิด
