name: Gerstmann–Sträussler–Scheinker syndrome (GSS)
formal: Autosomal dominant prion disease (commonly P102L) with slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, parkinsonism, and dementia, with multicentric amyloid plaques, lasting several years.
simple: A rare inherited brain disease causing slowly worsening unsteadiness, then memory loss, due to abnormal proteins in the brain.
th: GSS เป็นโรคพรีออนทางพันธุกรรมแบบ autosomal dominant (พบบ่อยที่สุดคือ P102L) เริ่มด้วยเดินเซและพาร์กินสันค่อยเป็นค่อยไป ต่อมาจึงสมองเสื่อม ดำเนินโรคหลายปี พบ amyloid plaque ในสมอง และ RT-QuIC หรือ MRI DWI มักไม่ช่วย ต้องตรวจยีน PRNP
tempoNote: Usually progresses over several years (mean about 5, range from months to 15 or more), far slower than sporadic CJD; a few mutation carriers run a fast CJD-like course
feat: Slowly worsening ataxia, dysarthria and gait failure, often with parkinsonism, and cognitive decline later; onset ranges from the teens to the 70s, typically around 40
Autosomal dominant; at least 24 PRNP mutations, P102L the commonest, plus stop-codon variants and insertions of six or more octapeptide repeats
Early burning leg dysaesthesia and reduced ankle reflexes are reported in P102L families
Often mislabelled as MSA, Parkinson disease, a spinocerebellar ataxia, Alzheimer disease or Huntington disease
Large multicentric PrP amyloid (kuru-type) plaques and amyloid angiopathy at autopsy
inv: PRNP sequencing after genetic counselling is the definitive test; octapeptide repeat changes may be missed on routine panels
MRI usually shows atrophy (cerebellar, later cortical) rather than restricted diffusion
CSF RT-QuIC is often negative and surrogate CSF markers are positive in only about 40–75%; EEG rarely shows periodic complexes
Exclude repeat-expansion ataxias, MSA, and immune or nutritional ataxia

case.who: 51-year-old woman, school canteen cook from Phrae
case.story: Two years of progressive imbalance and clumsy speech, then slowness and forgetfulness; her brother was told he had 'multiple system atrophy' and died at 54.
case.exam: Gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, mild rigidity, brisk reflexes in the arms with reduced ankle jerks, MoCA 20/30.
case.tests: MRI cerebellar and mild cortical atrophy with no restricted diffusion; CSF RT-QuIC negative; SCA panel negative; PRNP shows P102L.
case.q: Which test settles the diagnosis, and what should be offered to relatives?
case.a: PRNP sequencing confirms GSS. Relatives should receive genetic counselling before any predictive testing is done, and carriers can be told about preimplantation genetic diagnosis.

det.patho: GSS is caused by dominant PRNP mutations, of which P102L is most common, along with stop-codon changes and large octapeptide repeat insertions. The mutant protein is processed into truncated PrP fragments that aggregate into large extracellular amyloid plaques, called kuru-type plaques, in the cerebellum and cortex, with or without vacuolation; the group is sometimes described as dominantly inherited PrP cerebral amyloidosis. Stop-codon variants add tau tangles and amyloid angiopathy and may give AD- or FTD-like syndromes. First described in an Austrian family by Gerstmann and colleagues, the name was formalised in 1980.
det.clinical: Typical GSS starts with progressive ataxia and dysarthria, then parkinsonism, pyramidal signs and behavioural change, with cognitive impairment later. Duration ranges from a few months to 15 years or more, and the clinical picture varies even within a single family. Some carriers present with psychosis or an AD- or FTD-like illness, and a few with a rapidly progressive sCJD-like illness. Stop-codon variants add chronic diarrhoea, dysautonomia and sensory neuropathy to early cognitive decline. Because the family history is often wrongly labelled, the first diagnosis is frequently MSA, Parkinson disease or a hereditary ataxia.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis depends on detecting a disease-causing PRNP variant when the clinical syndrome fits; neuropathology alone is not enough to prove the genetic cause. Standard prion tests are unreliable in this slow form: RT-QuIC is often negative, surrogate CSF markers are positive in only about 40–75%, EEG periodic complexes are absent and MRI shows atrophy instead of restricted diffusion. Ask the laboratory specifically to look for octapeptide repeat insertions or deletions, which can escape routine panels. Genetic counselling should precede testing, and results affect relatives at 50% risk.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying treatment; management is symptomatic, with physiotherapy, speech and swallowing therapy, and cautious treatment of parkinsonism or mood symptoms. Offer genetic counselling to relatives, discuss preimplantation genetic diagnosis, and provide palliative support as disease advances. PrPC-lowering therapies such as antisense oligonucleotides are the most promising research direction. Patients are not a contact infection risk, but neurosurgical tissue handling follows prion precautions.
det.prognosis: Longest of the prion diseases, mean about 5 years and sometimes over a decade; always fatal.
pearls: A negative RT-QuIC and a normal diffusion MRI do not argue against GSS.
Think of GSS when 'MSA', 'SCA' or 'young Parkinson disease' runs in an autosomal dominant pattern with dementia late.
Kuru-type amyloid plaques are the pathological hallmark, found only sparsely in sCJD.
det.thd: GSS เป็นโรคพรีออนทางพันธุกรรมจากการกลายพันธุ์ของยีน PRNP โดยพบ P102L บ่อยที่สุด ผู้ป่วยมักเริ่มด้วยเดินเซ พูดไม่ชัด และพาร์กินสัน ต่อมาจึงสมองเสื่อม ใช้เวลาหลายปี จึงมักถูกวินิจฉัยผิดเป็น MSA หรือ SCA การตรวจ RT-QuIC และ MRI DWI มักไม่ช่วย ต้องตรวจยีน PRNP เพื่อยืนยัน หลังให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม ยังไม่มียารักษาให้หาย จึงดูแลตามอาการ

qx.stem: A 48-year-old man has three years of progressive imbalance and slurred speech, followed by slowing and forgetfulness. His mother and maternal uncle died in their fifties of an illness called multiple system atrophy. MRI shows cerebellar atrophy without restricted diffusion, and CSF RT-QuIC is negative twice.
qx.q: What should be done next?
opts: Conclude that prion disease is excluded because the RT-QuIC is negative
Start high-dose methylprednisolone for presumed autoimmune cerebellitis
Perform a brain biopsy to look for spongiform change
Offer genetic counselling and send PRNP sequencing, including a request to look for octapeptide repeat changes
Repeat the lumbar puncture monthly until the RT-QuIC becomes positive
qx.why: A dominant family pattern, slow ataxia and dementia later fit GSS, in which RT-QuIC is often negative and MRI diffusion is normal. The definitive test is PRNP sequencing after counselling, noting that some panels miss repeat insertions. Biopsy, steroids and repeated lumbar punctures are not indicated.

name: Giant axonal neuropathy
formal: Autosomal recessive childhood sensorimotor neuropathy from GAN gene mutations, with enlarged axons filled by neurofilaments, kinky hair, ataxia and CNS involvement.
simple: An inherited disease where nerves swell with protein clumps, causing weak legs, clumsiness and tightly curled hair in children.
more: Diagnosis by nerve biopsy showing giant axons and GAN genetic testing; MRI shows white matter changes. No cure; supportive care, and death usually occurs in the second or third decade.
th: โรคเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายทางพันธุกรรมแบบ autosomal recessive จากยีน GAN ในเด็ก มีผมหยิกงอ เดินเซ และมีความผิดปกติของสมองส่วน white matter ร่วม
tempoNote: Onset in early childhood, relentlessly progressive through adolescence
feat: Child with clumsy gait from about 3 years, distal weakness, areflexia and sensory loss
Tightly curled, coarse, pale hair in most (not all) patients
CNS signs: cerebellar ataxia, nystagmus, pyramidal signs, later cognitive decline
Foot deformity, scoliosis and wheelchair dependence by the teens
Consanguinity often present
inv: Nerve conduction: axonal sensorimotor neuropathy
MRI brain: symmetric periventricular and cerebellar white matter T2 hyperintensity
GAN gene sequencing and deletion analysis confirms; nerve biopsy (giant neurofilament-packed axons) rarely needed now

case.who: 6-year-old girl from Yala, parents are first cousins
case.story: Trips often and walks on the outer feet; teacher notes she cannot run. Her hair has been very curly since infancy, unlike her siblings.
case.exam: Kinky pale hair, pes cavus, distal wasting, absent reflexes, mild ataxia and nystagmus, extensor plantars.
case.tests: NCS axonal sensorimotor neuropathy; MRI shows cerebellar and periventricular white-matter change; homozygous GAN variant.
case.q: What unifying diagnosis links hair, nerves and white matter?
case.a: Giant axonal neuropathy (gigaxonin deficiency causing intermediate filament aggregation).

read.where: Companion to Peripheral Neuropathy: chapters (see text)

det.patho: Biallelic GAN variants abolish gigaxonin, a ubiquitin-ligase adaptor needed to degrade intermediate filaments. Neurofilaments and other intermediate filaments (vimentin, keratin, GFAP) accumulate, swelling axons into giant segments and altering hair structure. Both peripheral nerves and central white-matter tracts are affected, so this is a combined central and peripheral axonopathy.
det.clinical: Typical onset is around age 3–5 with gait difficulty and distal weakness that progress steadily. CNS involvement emerges over time with ataxia, nystagmus, dysarthria, spasticity and seizures in some, and cognitive decline in the second decade. Milder late-onset forms resembling CMT2 without curly hair are recognised. Most patients lose walking in adolescence and develop respiratory weakness later.
det.diagnosis: Suspect in a child with axonal neuropathy plus CNS signs, particularly with kinky hair or consanguinity. Brain MRI showing white-matter signal change supports it. Confirmation is genetic (sequencing plus copy-number analysis of GAN). Nerve biopsy showing giant axons filled with neurofilaments is classic but rarely needed.
det.treatment: Management is supportive: orthoses, physiotherapy, scoliosis surgery, nutrition and respiratory monitoring. An intrathecal AAV9 gene-transfer trial has been conducted at the US NIH with early safety data, but no therapy is approved. Families need genetic counselling and carrier testing.
det.prognosis: Progressive; most become wheelchair-dependent in the teens, with death often in the second or third decade, though milder forms survive longer.
pearls: Curly hair plus neuropathy in a child: think GAN.
Central white-matter change on MRI distinguishes it from ordinary CMT2.
Giant axons can also occur in toxic hexacarbon (glue-sniffing) neuropathy.
det.thd: Giant axonal neuropathy เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมแบบ autosomal recessive จากยีน GAN ทำให้ intermediate filament สะสมจนแอกซอนบวมโต เด็กเริ่มเดินลำบากราว 3–5 ขวบ มีอ่อนแรงปลายแขนขา reflex หาย ผมหยิกงอ และต่อมามีอาการของสมองน้อยและ white matter ผิดปกติ วินิจฉัยด้วย NCS, MRI และตรวจยีน การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง และมีการศึกษา gene therapy

name: Giant-cell arteritis (GCA)
formal: Large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis in people over 50 causing new headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness and visual loss from ischaemic optic neuropathy, with raised ESR; urgent steroids needed.
simple: Inflammation of blood vessels in older adults causing headache, jaw pain and a risk of sudden blindness if not treated quickly.
more: Giant cell arteritis: granulomatous vasculitis of cranial arteries in people over 50, with headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, visual loss risk and raised ESR; treated with steroids. Granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis in people over 50 involving temporal and cranial arteries, with headache, jaw claudication, visual loss and raised inflammatory markers. Diagnosis by ESR, CRP and temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound. Immediate high-dose steroids protect vision; tocilizumab is a steroid-sparing option; often associated with polymyalgia rheumatica.
th: หลอดเลือดแดงใหญ่และกลางอักเสบแบบ granuloma ในผู้สูงอายุเกิน 50 ปี ปวดศีรษะใหม่ ปวดกรามเวลาเคี้ยว ตามัวฉับพลันจาก AAION ESR/CRP สูง ต้องให้ steroid ทันที (พบน้อยในคนไทย)
tempoNote: Headache and systemic symptoms build over weeks; visual loss can occur suddenly at any time without treatment
feat: New persistent headache in someone over 50, with scalp tenderness and tender thickened temporal arteries
Jaw claudication (most specific symptom), fever, weight loss, fatigue, polymyalgia symptoms
Transient visual loss or diplopia preceding sudden permanent blindness from arteritic AION
Posterior circulation strokes; arm claudication or aortic involvement in large-vessel GCA
inv: ESR and CRP (both normal in very few), platelets often raised
Temporal artery ultrasound (halo sign) or temporal artery biopsy (≥ 1.5 cm, within 2 weeks of starting steroids)
Fundoscopy (chalk-white swollen disc) ± fluorescein angiography; PET-CT or CT/MR angiography for large vessels

case.story: Four weeks of right temporal headache, pain in the jaw when chewing sticky rice, and aching shoulders; this morning she lost vision in the right eye for 10 minutes.
case.exam: Tender, pulseless right temporal artery; visual acuity normal; fundi normal.
case.tests: ESR 98 mm/h, CRP 85 mg/L, platelets 520 × 10⁹/L; ultrasound halo sign in both temporal arteries.
case.q: What is the immediate management?
case.a: Probable GCA with threatened vision: start high-dose glucocorticoid now (IV methylprednisolone then oral prednisolone), arrange biopsy or confirm with ultrasound without delaying treatment.

det.patho: GCA is a granulomatous vasculitis of large and medium arteries, especially branches of the external carotid, ophthalmic and posterior ciliary arteries, vertebral arteries and the aorta. Dendritic cells in the adventitia activate CD4 T cells and macrophages, causing intimal hyperplasia and luminal occlusion. It affects people over 50, peaks in the 70s, is most common in Northern Europeans, and is uncommon in Thai and other Asian populations.
det.clinical: New headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, systemic symptoms and polymyalgia rheumatica are typical; some present only with fever of unknown origin or large-vessel disease. Visual loss arises from arteritic AION or central retinal artery occlusion, is often preceded by amaurosis fugax or diplopia, and can involve the second eye within days. Vertebrobasilar strokes are a rare but serious complication.
det.diagnosis: Use clinical features, raised inflammatory markers and vascular evidence. Temporal artery ultrasound is now first-line in fast-track pathways and biopsy remains valuable (skip lesions mean adequate length matters). Large-vessel imaging (PET-CT, CT or MR angiography) detects aortitis. The ACR/EULAR 2022 criteria classify the disease. Start treatment before results return when vision is at risk.
det.treatment: Begin glucocorticoids at once: prednisolone 40–60 mg/day, or IV methylprednisolone (typically 500–1000 mg daily for 3 days) for visual symptoms, followed by slow tapering over 12–18 months. Tocilizumab reduces relapse and cumulative steroid exposure, and upadacitinib has recently gained approval; methotrexate is an alternative steroid-sparing agent. Provide bone protection, gastric protection, glucose and blood pressure monitoring, and educate about urgent return if vision changes.
det.prognosis: With prompt treatment, new visual loss is rare, but established blindness rarely recovers; relapses during tapering are common and aortic aneurysm may develop years later.
pearls: New headache over 50 → ESR and CRP the same day.
Jaw claudication and diplopia are strong predictors; treat first, biopsy later.
Normal ESR does not completely exclude GCA; check CRP too.
In Thailand GCA is uncommon, but missing it costs vision.
det.thd: Giant cell arteritis เป็นหลอดเลือดแดงอักเสบแบบ granuloma ในผู้อายุเกิน 50 ปี อาการคือปวดศีรษะใหม่ หนังศีรษะเจ็บ ปวดกรามเวลาเคี้ยว ปวดไหล่และสะโพก ไข้ น้ำหนักลด และตามัวชั่วคราวก่อนตาบอดถาวรจาก AAION ESR และ CRP สูง ยืนยันด้วย ultrasound พบ halo sign หรือตัดชิ้นเนื้อหลอดเลือดขมับ ต้องให้ steroid ขนาดสูงทันทีโดยไม่ต้องรอผล และพิจารณา tocilizumab เพื่อลด steroid แม้พบน้อยในคนไทยแต่ห้ามพลาด

qx.stem: A 74-year-old woman from Lamphun has a new temporal headache, jaw claudication, an ESR of 92 mm/h and abrupt painless visual loss in the left eye. The left optic disc is chalky white and swollen.
qx.q: What is the best next step?
opts: Wait for the biopsy result before any steroid
Start aspirin alone
Obtain brain MRI and decide after the result
Start high-dose glucocorticoid at once and arrange temporal artery ultrasound or biopsy, because a negative biopsy occurs in a substantial minority
Start methotrexate monotherapy
qx.why: Giant-cell arteritis with arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy threatens the other eye within days, so treatment should not wait. The hypoechoic halo on superficial temporal artery ultrasound and a biopsy of at least 2 cm support the diagnosis, but about 40% of patients with GCA have a negative biopsy. Glucocorticoids are tapered slowly, with tocilizumab or other agents to reduce relapses.

qx.stem: A 74-year-old woman from Khon Kaen has had two weeks of temporal headache, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication, and this morning lost vision in the left eye with a pale swollen disc. ESR is 96 mm/h and CRP is high. Temporal artery biopsy can be arranged in four days.
qx.q: What is the correct next step?
opts: Start high-dose glucocorticoids immediately, including intravenous methylprednisolone for visual loss, and arrange biopsy without waiting
Wait for biopsy results before giving any steroid
Start tocilizumab alone and withhold steroids
Give aspirin only and repeat ESR in a week
Refer for optic nerve sheath fenestration
qx.why: Visual loss from arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy is an emergency because the other eye can be lost within days, so high-dose steroids are started at once and biopsy is arranged soon, as histology stays positive for a while after starting therapy. Tocilizumab, shown in the GiACTA trial to improve sustained remission when combined with a steroid taper, is an adjunct to reduce steroid exposure and is not a substitute in the acute phase. Aspirin alone and surgery do not treat the vasculitis.

name: Gillespie syndrome
formal: Rare disorder with partial aniridia, congenital hypotonia, cerebellar ataxia and intellectual disability, caused by ITPR1 mutations.
simple: A rare inherited condition with an abnormal iris in the eye, floppy muscles from birth, and balance and learning problems.
ab: Aniridia, cerebellar ataxia and mental deficiency
th: โรคพันธุกรรมหายากจากยีน ITPR1 มีม่านตาหายบางส่วน กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนปวกเปียกแต่กำเนิด เดินเซจากสมองน้อย และพัฒนาการช้า
tempoNote: Signs present from infancy; ataxia is non-progressive or very slowly progressive
feat: Partial aniridia with scalloped pupillary edge; fixed dilated-looking pupils noticed in infancy
Congenital hypotonia, delayed motor milestones and non-progressive cerebellar ataxia
Variable intellectual disability
Cerebellar (vermis) hypoplasia or atrophy on MRI
Caused by de novo dominant or biallelic ITPR1 variants; PAX6 is normal
inv: Ophthalmic examination documenting iris hypoplasia
MRI brain: cerebellar atrophy or hypoplasia
Genetic testing: ITPR1 (and PAX6 to exclude classic aniridia)

case.story: Parents noticed his pupils looked large and did not react from birth; he sits but cannot walk and wobbles when sitting unsupported.
case.exam: Bilateral partial aniridia, nystagmus, truncal titubation, hypotonia, reflexes normal.
case.tests: MRI shows small cerebellar vermis; exome shows de novo ITPR1 variant; PAX6 normal.
case.q: Which syndrome links the eye and cerebellar findings?
case.a: Gillespie syndrome from ITPR1 — partial aniridia with congenital cerebellar ataxia.

det.patho: ITPR1 encodes the IP3 receptor (type 1 isoform), a calcium release channel abundant in Purkinje cells. Variants that disrupt channel function impair intracellular calcium signalling, affecting cerebellar development and the formation of the iris sphincter. Other ITPR1 variants cause spinocerebellar ataxias 15 and 29, so this is one end of an ITPR1 spectrum.
det.clinical: Infants present with apparently large, unreactive pupils due to partial absence of the iris, followed by hypotonia and delayed motor milestones. Ataxia and nystagmus become obvious when the child starts sitting and walking. Cognitive impairment ranges from mild to moderate. The course is largely static, with some motor gains through childhood.
det.diagnosis: Iris findings combined with congenital ataxia should prompt ITPR1 testing. PAX6 analysis helps exclude classic aniridia, which lacks ataxia and has foveal hypoplasia. MRI shows cerebellar hypoplasia or atrophy, most marked in the vermis.
det.treatment: There is no specific therapy. Management includes physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy, special education, and protection of the eyes from glare with tinted lenses. Genetic counselling clarifies recurrence risk, which is low for de novo cases.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy appears normal; most patients achieve walking with support and need lifelong educational help.
pearls: Large non-reactive pupils in a floppy infant: examine the iris and think Gillespie syndrome.
The same gene causes adult SCA15 and childhood SCA29.
Classic PAX6 aniridia does not cause cerebellar ataxia.
det.thd: Gillespie syndrome เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมหายากจากยีน ITPR1 เด็กมีม่านตาหายบางส่วนทำให้รูม่านตาดูโตและไม่ตอบสนองต่อแสง ร่วมกับกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนปวกเปียก เดินเซจากสมองน้อยฝ่อ และพัฒนาการช้า อาการไม่ค่อยลุกลาม การวินิจฉัยใช้การตรวจตา MRI และตรวจยีน การดูแลคือกายภาพบำบัด การศึกษาพิเศษ และให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

name: Glaucoma
formal: Optic neuropathy with raised intraocular pressure or vulnerability causing progressive optic disc cupping and peripheral visual field loss.
simple: An eye disease where pressure damages the optic nerve and gradually reduces side vision.
th: โรคเส้นประสาทตาเสื่อมที่มักสัมพันธ์กับความดันลูกตาสูง ทำให้ขั้วประสาทตาเว้าลึกขึ้นและลานสายตาด้านข้างเสียไปเรื่อยๆ
tempoNote: Open-angle disease is silent and slowly progressive over years; acute angle closure is an emergency over hours
feat: Painless gradual peripheral field loss (arcuate, nasal step) with central acuity kept until late
Optic disc cupping with thinned neuroretinal rim, often asymmetric between eyes
Acute angle closure: red painful eye, haloes, fixed mid-dilated pupil, headache and vomiting
Risk factors: age, family history, myopia (open angle) or hyperopia and Asian ethnicity (angle closure), steroid use
An ophthalmological rather than neurological disease, but a common mimic of neurological visual loss
inv: Intraocular pressure, gonioscopy and dilated disc examination by ophthalmology
Automated perimetry and OCT of the retinal nerve fibre layer
Neuroimaging if pallor exceeds cupping, field loss respects the vertical meridian or acuity falls early

case.story: Referred to the neurology clinic for 'bumping into door frames' on the left side for a year; no headache, no other symptoms.
case.exam: Acuity 6/9 both eyes, large cup-to-disc ratios with pink rims, no RAPD on the right, mild RAPD left; no other neurological signs.
case.tests: IOP 30 and 34 mmHg; perimetry shows arcuate defects not respecting the vertical meridian; OCT shows thin superior and inferior rims.
case.q: Is a pituitary lesion likely, and what is the diagnosis?
case.a: No — arcuate defects with cupped but pink discs and high IOP indicate primary open-angle glaucoma.

det.patho: Glaucoma is a progressive loss of retinal ganglion cells and their axons at the lamina cribrosa, producing excavation of the optic disc. Raised intraocular pressure is the main modifiable risk factor, but vascular dysregulation and structural susceptibility explain disease at normal pressure. Angle-closure glaucoma, relatively common in East and Southeast Asia, results from obstruction of aqueous outflow by the iris.
det.clinical: This is primarily an eye disease. Open-angle glaucoma is asymptomatic until advanced peripheral loss, then causes tunnel vision. Acute angle closure produces a painful red eye, blurred vision with haloes, a mid-dilated unreactive pupil and nausea, and may present to emergency departments as headache. Neurologists meet it when assessing optic atrophy, unexplained field defects or eye pain.
det.diagnosis: Ophthalmological assessment combines IOP, gonioscopy, disc appearance, perimetry and OCT. Features suggesting a neurological rather than glaucomatous cause include disc pallor out of proportion to cupping, reduced acuity or colour vision early, young age and hemianopic field patterns. Normal-tension glaucoma should be diagnosed only after other causes are excluded, and imaging may be needed to rule out compression.
det.treatment: Lowering IOP slows progression: prostaglandin analogue, beta-blocker, alpha-agonist or carbonic anhydrase inhibitor drops, laser trabeculoplasty or surgery. Acute angle closure needs urgent IOP reduction (topical agents plus systemic acetazolamide) and laser iridotomy. Topiramate and anticholinergic drugs can precipitate angle closure, which matters when neurologists prescribe them.
det.prognosis: Treated open-angle glaucoma usually progresses slowly; untreated or late-detected disease can cause blindness, and acute angle closure can destroy vision in days.
pearls: Pallor more than cupping should make you think of a compressive lesion, not glaucoma.
Topiramate can trigger bilateral acute angle closure in the first weeks.
Acute angle closure can masquerade as migraine or subarachnoid haemorrhage.
det.thd: Glaucoma เป็นโรคตาที่เส้นประสาทตาถูกทำลายช้าๆ มักสัมพันธ์กับความดันลูกตาสูง ขั้วประสาทตาจะเว้าลึกและลานสายตาด้านข้างเสียโดยไม่รู้ตัว ส่วนชนิด angle closure เฉียบพลันจะมีตาแดงปวดและปวดศีรษะ อาจสับสนกับโรคทางประสาท ถ้าขั้วประสาทตาซีดมากกว่าเว้าหรือการมองเห็นตรงกลางเสียเร็ว ควรหาสาเหตุจากการกดทับ การรักษาคือลดความดันลูกตาด้วยยาหยอด เลเซอร์ หรือผ่าตัด

name: Glomus tumours
formal: Paragangliomas of the glomus bodies in the jugular bulb or middle ear (glomus jugulare, tympanicum) causing pulsatile tinnitus, hearing loss and lower cranial neuropathies.
simple: Slow-growing tumours near the ear and base of the skull, causing hearing loss, a pulsing sound and sometimes swallowing problems.
th: เนื้องอก paraganglioma ที่ jugular bulb หรือหูชั้นกลาง ทำให้มีเสียงดังในหูตามจังหวะชีพจร หูตึง และเส้นประสาทสมอง IX–XII อ่อนแรง
tempoNote: Very slow growth over years
feat: Pulsatile tinnitus, often the first symptom
Conductive hearing loss and a red retrotympanic mass
Jugular foramen syndrome: dysphagia, hoarseness, shoulder weakness (IX, X, XI) and later XII
Commoner in women; may be multiple or familial (SDH gene variants)
Rarely catecholamine-secreting
inv: MRI with contrast: salt-and-pepper appearance; CT temporal bone for bone erosion
Catheter or CT angiography for feeding vessels
Plasma or urine metanephrines; genetic testing for SDHx

case.story: Hears a whooshing sound in the left ear in time with her heartbeat for a year; now hoarse and coughing when drinking.
case.exam: Reddish pulsating mass behind the left eardrum, left palatal weakness, weak left trapezius.
case.tests: MRI shows an enhancing left jugular foramen mass with flow voids; CT shows erosion of the jugular plate.
case.q: What is the lesion and which test checks for secretion?
case.a: Glomus jugulare paraganglioma; plasma metanephrines.

det.patho: Paragangliomas arise from neural crest-derived chemoreceptor cells along the jugular bulb (glomus jugulare) or the tympanic plexus on the cochlear promontory (glomus tympanicum). Germline variants in succinate dehydrogenase subunit genes explain many familial and multifocal cases.
det.clinical: Pulsatile tinnitus and hearing loss are typical. Jugular tumours cause lower cranial nerve palsies, sometimes with facial palsy. Large lesions can compress the brainstem. Secreting tumours cause hypertension and palpitations.
det.diagnosis: Otoscopy may show a vascular mass. MRI and CT define extent; angiography helps planning and embolisation. Biochemical screening for catecholamines and genetic testing are recommended.
det.treatment: Options include observation for small asymptomatic tumours in elderly patients, surgical excision after embolisation, and stereotactic radiosurgery or fractionated radiotherapy, which provides good control with less cranial nerve risk. Alpha blockade precedes surgery in secreting tumours.
det.prognosis: Generally benign with good long-term control; morbidity mainly from cranial nerve deficits.
pearls: Pulsatile tinnitus with a red mass behind the eardrum suggests glomus tumour.
Do not biopsy the middle ear mass blindly: it bleeds.
Offer SDH genetic testing, especially if multiple or young.
det.thd: Glomus tumour เป็น paraganglioma ที่ jugular bulb หรือหูชั้นกลาง โตช้า อาการเด่นคือได้ยินเสียงในหูตามจังหวะชีพจร หูตึง และเส้นประสาทสมอง IX–XI อ่อนแรง ทำให้กลืนลำบากและเสียงแหบ ตรวจด้วย MRI CT และ metanephrines รักษาด้วยผ่าตัดหรือรังสีศัลยกรรม และควรตรวจยีน SDH

name: Glossopharyngeal neuralgia
formal: Paroxysmal severe lancinating pain in the throat, tonsil and ear provoked by swallowing, often from vascular compression, sometimes with syncope; treated with carbamazepine.
simple: Sudden attacks of severe stabbing pain in the throat or ear, often set off by swallowing or talking.
th: ปวดแปลบรุนแรงเป็นพักๆ ที่คอ ทอนซิล และหู กระตุ้นด้วยการกลืน พูด หรือไอ บางรายเป็นลมหมดสติร่วม
tempoNote: Paroxysms of seconds, in bouts over weeks to months with remissions
feat: Electric, stabbing pain in the tonsil fossa, base of tongue and ear
Triggers: swallowing, chewing, talking, coughing, yawning
Can cause bradycardia and syncope through vagal reflex
Much rarer than trigeminal neuralgia; may coexist
Usually unilateral; often left-sided
inv: MRI brain with high-resolution sequences of the posterior fossa for vascular loop or mass
ENT examination to exclude oropharyngeal or tonsillar cancer
ECG or Holter if syncope is reported

case.story: Lightning pain in the left throat and ear when swallowing rice; once fainted during an attack.
case.exam: Normal cranial nerves; no oropharyngeal mass.
case.tests: MRI shows the posterior inferior cerebellar artery contacting the left IX/X root entry; ENT endoscopy normal.
case.q: What is the first-line drug and the surgical option?
case.a: Carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine; microvascular decompression if refractory.

read.where: Chapter 13 Cranial Nerve Disorders — Glossopharyngeal Nerve (IX)
Chapter 13 Cranial Nerve Disorders — Glossopharyngeal Neuralgia
12 Cranial Nerves IX and X (The Glossopharyngeal and Vagus Nerves)

det.patho: Most cases are classical, with neurovascular compression of the glossopharyngeal and upper vagal rootlets, causing focal demyelination and ephaptic transmission. Secondary causes include tumours, Eagle syndrome (elongated styloid), multiple sclerosis and infection.
det.clinical: Attacks of brief, severe pain affect the throat and ear, triggered by swallowing or talking. Patients may avoid eating and lose weight. Vagal involvement can cause bradycardia, hypotension and syncope. Between attacks examination is normal in classical cases.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis follows the ICHD-3 clinical criteria. Imaging excludes structural lesions and shows vascular contact. Topical anaesthesia of the tonsil fossa abolishing attacks supports the diagnosis. Exclude oropharyngeal malignancy.
det.treatment: Sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine) are first-line; gabapentinoids or lamotrigine are alternatives. Refractory cases benefit from microvascular decompression or rhizotomy of IX and upper X rootlets. Pacemaker support is occasionally needed for syncope.
det.prognosis: Most respond to drugs or surgery; remissions are common but recurrence possible.
pearls: Pain triggered by swallowing points to IX rather than V.
Syncope with pain attacks is a clue to glossopharyngeal neuralgia.
Always look for oropharyngeal cancer in secondary forms.
det.thd: Glossopharyngeal neuralgia คือปวดแปลบรุนแรงที่คอ ทอนซิล และหู เป็นวินาที กระตุ้นด้วยการกลืนหรือพูด บางรายหัวใจเต้นช้าและหมดสติ มักเกิดจากหลอดเลือดกดรากประสาท IX ต้องทำ MRI และตรวจหู คอ จมูก เพื่อแยกเนื้องอก รักษาด้วย carbamazepine หรือ oxcarbazepine ถ้าไม่ได้ผลพิจารณาผ่าตัด microvascular decompression

name: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
formal: X-linked enzyme deficiency causing haemolysis after oxidant drugs or fava beans; neurologically relevant for neonatal kernicterus and drug avoidance.
simple: An inherited enzyme shortage in which red blood cells break down after certain foods or medicines.
th: ภาวะพร่องเอนไซม์ G6PD ถ่ายทอดทางโครโมโซม X ทำให้เม็ดเลือดแดงแตกเมื่อได้ยาบางชนิดหรือถั่วปากอ้า ความสำคัญทางระบบประสาทคือ kernicterus ในทารกและการเลือกยา
tempoNote: Lifelong enzyme deficiency with acute haemolytic episodes triggered by drugs, infection or fava beans
feat: Haematological, not a primary neurological disease
Very common in Thailand (roughly 1 in 8–10 Thai men), X-linked
Acute haemolysis after oxidant drugs (primaquine, dapsone, rasburicase, nitrofurantoin), infections or fava beans
Neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia risk: kernicterus with choreoathetosis, gaze palsy and deafness
Neurologically relevant drugs: methylene blue (for ifosfamide encephalopathy) can trigger haemolysis
inv: G6PD enzyme assay (may be falsely normal during acute haemolysis; repeat after recovery)
Blood film (bite and blister cells, Heinz bodies), reticulocytes, bilirubin, LDH
Neonatal bilirubin monitoring; MRI pallidal T2 signal in suspected kernicterus

case.who: 5-day-old male infant at a provincial hospital in Sakon Nakhon
case.story: Became deeply jaundiced on day 3; poor feeding and high-pitched cry developed before he was transferred.
case.exam: Lethargic, arching (retrocollis and opisthotonus), setting-sun eyes.
case.tests: Serum bilirubin 32 mg/dL; G6PD screening deficient; later MRI shows bilateral globus pallidus signal change.
case.q: What neurological complication has occurred and how could it have been prevented?
case.a: Acute bilirubin encephalopathy progressing to kernicterus due to G6PD deficiency; neonatal screening with early phototherapy or exchange transfusion.

det.patho: G6PD generates NADPH in red cells, which keeps glutathione reduced and protects against oxidative damage. When the enzyme is deficient, oxidant drugs, infections or fava bean compounds overwhelm this defence, damaging haemoglobin and membranes and causing haemolysis. In neonates, impaired bilirubin conjugation plus haemolysis can raise unconjugated bilirubin enough to enter the brain and injure the globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, brainstem auditory and oculomotor nuclei.
det.clinical: Most affected people are well until exposed to a trigger, then develop dark urine, jaundice, pallor and fatigue within days. Thai variants such as Viangchan and Mahidol are mostly class II–III with moderate deficiency. Neurological relevance lies in neonatal kernicterus, which produces dyskinetic cerebral palsy, upgaze palsy, sensorineural hearing loss and dental enamel dysplasia. Females can be affected through skewed X inactivation.
det.diagnosis: Quantitative or qualitative enzyme assays confirm deficiency, but results may be falsely normal during haemolysis because young cells have more enzyme. Neonatal screening is widely practised in Thailand. Kernicterus is diagnosed clinically, supported by abnormal auditory brainstem responses and pallidal signal change on MRI.
det.treatment: Avoid known oxidant drugs and fava beans, and treat haemolysis supportively with transfusion if severe. Check G6PD status before prescribing primaquine, dapsone, rasburicase or methylene blue. Neonatal jaundice is treated with phototherapy and exchange transfusion by bilirubin thresholds. Established kernicterus is managed with therapy for dystonia, hearing aids or cochlear implants.
det.prognosis: With avoidance of triggers, life expectancy is normal; kernicterus causes permanent disability.
pearls: Very common in Thai men — check status before giving oxidant drugs.
Methylene blue for ifosfamide encephalopathy or methaemoglobinaemia can cause haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
Kernicterus triad: dyskinesia, upgaze palsy and hearing loss.
det.thd: ภาวะพร่องเอนไซม์ G6PD พบบ่อยในคนไทย ถ่ายทอดทางโครโมโซม X ทำให้เม็ดเลือดแดงแตกเมื่อได้รับยาบางชนิด ติดเชื้อ หรือกินถั่วปากอ้า ไม่ใช่โรคทางระบบประสาทโดยตรง แต่สำคัญเพราะทำให้ทารกตัวเหลืองมากจนเกิด kernicterus ซึ่งทำให้มีการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติ มองขึ้นไม่ได้ และหูหนวก และต้องระวังยาบางตัว เช่น methylene blue การป้องกันคือคัดกรองทารกและหลีกเลี่ยงยาที่กระตุ้น

name: GLUT1 deficiency syndrome
formal: SLC2A1-related impaired glucose transport across the blood-brain barrier with infantile seizures, low CSF glucose, developmental delay, movement disorders and microcephaly, treated with ketogenic diet.
simple: An inherited condition where the brain cannot get enough sugar, causing seizures and developmental delay, helped by a special high-fat diet.
more: Diagnosis by CSF glucose below 40 mg/dL with low CSF-to-blood glucose ratio and normal blood glucose; confirm by SLC2A1 sequencing or erythrocyte 3-OMG uptake. Ketogenic diet should be started early; avoid phenobarbital and valproate.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมจากยีน SLC2A1 ทำให้ขนส่งกลูโคสผ่าน blood-brain barrier ไม่ได้ เกิดชักในวัยทารก น้ำตาลในน้ำไขสันหลังต่ำ พัฒนาการช้า ความผิดปกติของการเคลื่อนไหว รักษาด้วย ketogenic diet
tempoNote: Onset in infancy or childhood; paroxysmal events worse before meals and with fasting or exercise
feat: Infantile-onset drug-resistant seizures, or early-onset absence epilepsy before age 4
Paroxysmal exercise-induced dyskinesia, ataxia or alternating hemiplegia-like episodes
Developmental delay, acquired microcephaly, complex movement disorder
Symptoms worse with fasting and better after meals
Milder adult forms present with paroxysmal exercise-induced dyskinesia alone
inv: Fasting lumbar puncture with simultaneous blood glucose: CSF glucose usually <40 mg/dL, CSF:blood ratio <0.45 (often <0.5), low CSF lactate
SLC2A1 sequencing and deletion analysis
EEG may improve after glucose or feeding

case.story: Absence-like spells since 6 months, worse before breakfast; clumsy walking and episodes of leg twisting after playing.
case.exam: Small head circumference, mild ataxia, dysarthria.
case.tests: Fasting CSF glucose 30 mg/dL with blood glucose 90 mg/dL; CSF lactate low; SLC2A1 pathogenic variant.
case.q: What treatment should start immediately and which drugs should be avoided?
case.a: GLUT1 deficiency syndrome: start a ketogenic diet as early as possible; avoid phenobarbital, valproate and other GLUT1 inhibitors (also caffeine).

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Inherited Disorders of Metabolism Associated with Epilepsy
Multiple Choice Questions for Part I

det.patho: Heterozygous (often de novo) SLC2A1 variants reduce the GLUT1 transporter in endothelium of the blood–brain barrier, so the brain is energy-starved despite normal blood glucose. The developing brain, with high glucose demand, is most vulnerable, explaining infantile onset and acquired microcephaly. Ketone bodies enter the brain via a different transporter and supply alternative fuel.
det.clinical: The classic phenotype is infantile epilepsy with developmental delay, microcephaly and a mixed movement disorder of ataxia, dystonia and chorea. Non-classic forms include early-onset absence epilepsy, paroxysmal exertion-induced dyskinesia, and episodic ataxia or weakness; adult diagnosis is increasingly recognised. Symptoms fluctuate with fasting, illness and exertion.
det.diagnosis: Lumbar puncture after 4–6 hours of fasting, with blood glucose drawn just before, shows hypoglycorrhachia with low or normal lactate and a reduced CSF/blood glucose ratio. Genetic testing confirms most cases; a small subset have normal sequencing and need functional assays. Consider it in any early-onset absence epilepsy or paroxysmal exercise-induced dyskinesia.
det.treatment: A ketogenic diet (classic or modified Atkins) is the treatment of choice, controlling seizures and improving movement disorder; it should be continued at least through childhood and often for life. Antiseizure drugs add little; avoid phenobarbital, valproate, diazepam in high doses, methylxanthines and alcohol. Triheptanoin has shown benefit for paroxysmal movement disorders in some studies.
det.prognosis: Early diet therapy improves seizures and movement disorder, but cognitive outcome is variable and linked to age at treatment start.
pearls: Absence epilepsy starting before age 4 — check for GLUT1 deficiency.
Interpret CSF glucose only with a simultaneous fasting blood glucose.
Ketogenic diet is the disease-specific treatment.
det.thd: GLUT1 deficiency syndrome เกิดจากยีน SLC2A1 ทำให้กลูโคสผ่านเข้าสมองได้น้อย สมองขาดพลังงานแม้น้ำตาลในเลือดปกติ เด็กชักตั้งแต่ขวบปีแรกหรือ absence ก่อนอายุ 4 ปี พัฒนาการช้า เดินเซ และมีการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติเมื่อออกแรงหรืออดอาหาร ตรวจพบน้ำตาลในน้ำไขสันหลังต่ำ รักษาหลักด้วย ketogenic diet และหลีกเลี่ยง phenobarbital กับ valproate

name: Glutaric aciduria
formal: Autosomal recessive organic acidopathy (type 1, GCDH) with macrocephaly and acute striatal injury, causing dystonia after catabolic stress, and frontotemporal atrophy on MRI.
simple: An inherited metabolic disease in which a build-up of acids can damage the brain, causing stiffness and twisting movements in children.
th: กลุ่มโรค organic aciduria แบบ autosomal recessive (ส่วนใหญ่หมายถึง type 1 จาก GCDH) ทำให้หัวโตและเกิด striatal injury หลังเจ็บป่วยจนเกิด dystonia
tempoNote: Acute encephalopathic crisis in infancy (usually 3–36 months) leaves a permanent chronic movement disorder; some have insidious onset
feat: Macrocephaly from birth or early infancy, often the only sign before a crisis
Sudden dystonia and loss of motor skills after fever, vaccination reaction or poor feeding
Wide Sylvian fissures (frontotemporal hypoplasia) and subdural collections that mimic abuse
Glutaric aciduria type 2 (MADD) is a different disorder of fatty acid and amino acid oxidation
inv: Urine organic acids (glutaric and 3-hydroxyglutaric acid) and plasma glutarylcarnitine (C5DC)
GCDH sequencing; enzyme assay if needed; low excretors may have near-normal urine glutarate
MRI: open opercula, striatal T2/DWI change after crisis

case.story: Large head noted at well-baby visits; after a three-day diarrhoeal illness he stopped sitting and developed twisting of arms and neck.
case.exam: Head circumference above 98th centile, generalised dystonia, poor head control, alert and tracking.
case.tests: Urine 3-hydroxyglutaric acid markedly raised; MRI wide Sylvian fissures and bilateral putaminal restricted diffusion.
case.q: Which metabolic disease is this and how could the injury have been prevented?
case.a: Glutaric aciduria type 1; newborn screening plus lysine-restricted diet, carnitine and an emergency sick-day regimen.

det.patho: The term usually means type 1, caused by recessive GCDH variants that block lysine, hydroxylysine and tryptophan breakdown. Glutaric and 3-hydroxyglutaric acid are trapped in the brain and are thought to injure the striatum during catabolic stress, when lysine flux rises. Type 2 (MADD) is caused by defects in electron transfer flavoprotein or its dehydrogenase and is clinically distinct; a type 3 entity is mostly biochemical and benign.
det.clinical: Untreated infants are often normal apart from macrocephaly until an intercurrent illness triggers encephalopathy with acute striatal necrosis, leaving severe generalised dystonia with relatively preserved intellect. Some children have an insidious onset without a crisis. Subdural haematomas and retinal haemorrhages can occur and may be wrongly attributed to non-accidental injury. Adolescents and adults diagnosed late may have white-matter disease or subependymal nodules.
det.diagnosis: Many countries include C5DC on newborn screening. Urine organic acids and plasma acylcarnitines are diagnostic in high excretors; low excretors need GCDH sequencing or enzyme testing. MRI patterns of wide opercula and striatal injury are highly suggestive. Thailand's expanded newborn screening programme is growing, so check whether the child was screened.
det.treatment: Lifelong lysine-restricted, arginine-enriched diet with carnitine supplements, guided by a metabolic team, prevents most crises if started early. During illness, an emergency regimen of high-calorie fluids with glucose, reduced protein and extra carnitine should start without delay. Established dystonia is treated with trihexyphenidyl, baclofen, botulinum toxin and sometimes pallidal DBS, with modest benefit.
det.prognosis: Children diagnosed by screening and treated well usually escape striatal injury; once a crisis has occurred, dystonia is permanent and disability often severe.
pearls: Macrocephaly plus open Sylvian fissures in an infant: send urine organic acids.
Subdural haematoma in GA1 can be mistaken for child abuse.
The window of striatal vulnerability is mainly the first three years.
det.thd: Glutaric aciduria ส่วนใหญ่หมายถึง type 1 จากยีน GCDH ทำให้สลาย lysine ไม่ได้ เด็กมีศีรษะโตตั้งแต่เล็ก เมื่อเจ็บป่วยหรือขาดอาหารจะเกิด striatal injury เฉียบพลันจนเกิด dystonia ถาวร ตรวจพบ glutaric และ 3-hydroxyglutaric acid ในปัสสาวะ และ MRI เห็นร่อง Sylvian กว้าง การคัดกรองทารกแรกเกิด อาหารจำกัด lysine, carnitine และแผนรักษาฉุกเฉินช่วยป้องกันได้

name: Glutaric aciduria type I
formal: Autosomal recessive GCDH deficiency causing macrocephaly, acute striatal injury with dystonic-dyskinetic cerebral palsy after a febrile or catabolic crisis, with bilateral basal ganglia lesions.
simple: An inherited metabolic disease in which a crisis during infancy damages the brain and causes severe dystonia.
more: Urine glutaric and 3-hydroxyglutaric acid are raised; newborn screening exists. Low-lysine diet, carnitine and emergency treatment prevent damage if started early.
th: โรคพันธุกรรม autosomal recessive จากการขาดเอนไซม์ glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase (GCDH) ทำให้ศีรษะโตตั้งแต่แรกเกิด และเกิด dystonia รุนแรงหลังมีไข้หรือภาวะ catabolic เพราะ striatum ถูกทำลาย การคัดกรองทารกแรกเกิดและให้อาหารจำกัด lysine ช่วยป้องกันได้
tempoNote: Acute encephalopathic crisis between 3 and 36 months, often with fever, followed by fixed dystonic-dyskinetic state; insidious form in some
feat: Macrocephaly or megalencephaly at birth with otherwise normal early neurology
Acute crisis with somnolence, irritability, sweating, seizures and then dystonia after fever or fasting
Progressive dystonia and choreoathetosis; often misdiagnosed as dyskinetic cerebral palsy
Insidious type: hypotonia, mild developmental delay and later dyskinesias without a crisis
Subdural haematoma or retinal haemorrhage in infancy can mimic non-accidental injury
inv: Newborn screening and urine organic acids: glutaric and 3-hydroxyglutaric acid; plasma glutarylcarnitine (C5DC)
GCDH gene sequencing for confirmation and counselling
MRI: widened Sylvian fissures, frontotemporal atrophy and bilateral striatal lesions after a crisis
Blood gas, glucose, ammonia and lactate during a crisis

case.who: 11-month-old boy, referred from a district hospital in Nakhon Ratchasima
case.story: Born with a head circumference above the 97th centile. After three days of fever and vomiting he became drowsy, sweaty and irritable, then lost head control and developed stiff, twisting limbs.
case.exam: Macrocephaly, dystonic posturing and orofacial dyskinesia, hypotonic trunk, no focal weakness.
case.tests: Urine organic acids show raised 3-hydroxyglutaric and glutaric acid; MRI shows wide Sylvian fissures and bilateral T2 hyperintensity of putamen and caudate; GCDH biallelic variants.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the single most important action in future illnesses?
case.a: Glutaric aciduria type I. Begin an emergency regimen at the first sign of fever or illness: high-glucose intravenous fluids, carnitine and stopping protein intake, plus ongoing lysine restriction and carnitine; this prevents further striatal injury.

det.patho: GCDH deficiency blocks the lysine, hydroxylysine and tryptophan degradation pathway, and glutaric and 3-hydroxyglutaric acids accumulate. These metabolites are neurotoxic and, under a catabolic stress, damage the striatum of a developing brain. The disease is autosomal recessive and often detected by newborn screening.
det.clinical: Infants have macrocephaly and may look normal until a febrile or catabolic illness triggers the acute crisis in the first three years. Without treatment, two-thirds suffer sudden injury with severe dystonia, and others show a slowly progressive picture of hypotonia and dyskinesia. Subdural bleeding and retinal haemorrhage may be present and have led to mistaken child-abuse allegations. After the window of vulnerability, new injury is rare.
det.diagnosis: Urine organic acids, plasma glutarylcarnitine and GCDH genotyping confirm the disease; some low-excretor patients require enzyme or gene studies. MRI shows frontotemporal atrophy and striatal injury. Exclude cerebral palsy, mitochondrial and other organic acidaemias, Wilson disease, Huntington disease in the juvenile form and trauma.
det.treatment: Early lysine-restricted diet or tryptophan-reduced formula and L-carnitine supplementation, plus emergency treatment of intercurrent illness with high-calorie intravenous fluids, are the cornerstone. Dystonia is treated with baclofen, trihexyphenidyl, benzodiazepines, botulinum toxin and sometimes deep brain stimulation. Early treatment before any crisis protects the majority of children.
det.prognosis: Outstanding when started before neurological injury; once striatal damage has occurred, motor disability is permanent.
pearls: Macrocephaly plus dystonic cerebral palsy equals glutaric aciduria until proven otherwise.
A fever in an undiagnosed infant is the trigger: emergency regimen early.
Subdural haematoma may be the first sign, consider the metabolic cause.
det.thd: Glutaric aciduria type I เกิดจากขาดเอนไซม์ GCDH ทำให้สารพิษสะสมและทำลายส่วน striatum ของสมองเมื่อเด็กมีไข้หรืออดอาหาร ทารกมักศีรษะโตและเกิด dystonia รุนแรง ควรสงสัยในเด็กที่เหมือน cerebral palsy ร่วมกับหัวโต การตรวจใช้ organic acid ในปัสสาวะ ตรวจยีน และ MRI การรักษาคือจำกัด lysine ให้ carnitine และให้สารน้ำน้ำตาลเร็วเมื่อเจ็บป่วย

Mitochondrial disease with elevated lactate, brainstem and basal ganglia lesions and respiratory chain defects

name: Gluten encephalopathy
formal: Neurological manifestations of gluten sensitivity, including gluten ataxia, neuropathy and cognitive or white-matter involvement, with anti-gliadin antibodies, improving on a gluten-free diet.
simple: Nervous system problems such as unsteadiness or numbness linked to gluten sensitivity.
th: อาการทางระบบประสาทจากภาวะไวต่อกลูเตน เช่น เดินเซ ปลายประสาทอักเสบ ปวดศีรษะ และความจำไม่ดี ร่วมกับรอยโรคเนื้อสมองสีขาว ดีขึ้นเมื่องดกลูเตน
tempoNote: Slowly progressive over months to years; may stabilise on a strict gluten-free diet
feat: Recurrent headaches and cognitive slowing ('brain fog') with white-matter hyperintensities on MRI
Often coexists with gluten ataxia (gait and limb ataxia) or sensory neuropathy
Gut symptoms may be absent; many patients have no classic coeliac complaints
Serology: anti-gliadin, transglutaminase-2 or -6 antibodies
Improvement or stabilisation with strict gluten-free diet
inv: Serology: tissue transglutaminase IgA (with total IgA), endomysial, deamidated gliadin; anti-TG6 where available
Duodenal biopsy for villous atrophy
MRI brain: white-matter lesions; cerebellar atrophy or MR spectroscopy changes in ataxia
Exclude B12, vitamin E, copper deficiency and other causes

case.who: 45-year-old woman from Phuket who bakes bread for a living
case.story: Two years of daily headaches, poor concentration and unsteady walking; occasional bloating.
case.exam: Mild gait ataxia and heel-shin dysmetria; reduced vibration at the ankles.
case.tests: Anti-tTG IgA raised; duodenal biopsy shows villous atrophy; MRI shows scattered white-matter lesions.
case.q: What unifying diagnosis links her symptoms, and what is the treatment?
case.a: Neurological gluten sensitivity (gluten encephalopathy with ataxia and neuropathy) in coeliac disease; strict gluten-free diet with antibody monitoring.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Gluten Sensitivity
Chapter 13 Other Neurologic Disorders Associated with Gastrointestinal Disease

det.patho: Gluten sensitivity is an immune-mediated condition in genetically susceptible people (HLA-DQ2/DQ8). Neurological involvement is thought to involve antibodies against transglutaminase isoforms (TG2 in gut, TG6 in brain) and cross-reactive immune responses, with possible contributions from micronutrient deficiency. The concept of 'gluten encephalopathy' with white-matter lesions is less well established than gluten ataxia, and evidence comes largely from case series.
det.clinical: Patients present with chronic headache, cognitive complaints, and sometimes ataxia, neuropathy, myoclonus or epilepsy with occipital calcifications. Gastrointestinal symptoms are often minimal. The neurological picture can precede diagnosis of coeliac disease by years.
det.diagnosis: Check coeliac serology (tTG-IgA with total IgA, endomysial antibody, DGP) before any dietary change, then duodenal biopsy if positive. Anti-gliadin antibodies are sensitive but non-specific; anti-TG6 supports neurological involvement but is not widely available. Exclude other causes of white-matter disease, ataxia and neuropathy.
det.treatment: A strict lifelong gluten-free diet with dietitian support is the main treatment; repeat serology to confirm adherence. Correct vitamin and mineral deficiencies. Immunotherapy (IVIG, mycophenolate) has been tried in refractory gluten ataxia, but evidence is limited.
det.prognosis: Headache and white-matter lesions may improve on diet; established cerebellar loss usually stabilises rather than reverses.
pearls: Test serology before patients start avoiding gluten, or results become falsely negative.
Unexplained sporadic ataxia deserves coeliac serology.
Coeliac disease is less common in Thailand than in Europe, so confirm with biopsy and consider other causes.
det.thd: Gluten encephalopathy คืออาการทางสมองจากภาวะไวต่อกลูเตน (โปรตีนในข้าวสาลี) ผู้ป่วยอาจปวดศีรษะเรื้อรัง ความคิดช้า เดินเซ หรือชาปลายมือปลายเท้า โดยอาจไม่มีอาการท้องเสีย ตรวจเลือดหา anti-tTG และตัดชิ้นเนื้อลำไส้เล็ก MRI อาจพบรอยโรคเนื้อสมองสีขาว การรักษาหลักคืองดกลูเตนอย่างเคร่งครัดตลอดชีวิต

ddx.pt: The underlying enteropathy; neurological forms can occur with or without obvious gut disease
Malabsorption-related deficiency causing myelopathy, neuropathy and cognitive change; check levels
Relapsing course, ovoid periventricular lesions and CSF oligoclonal bands

aN: gluten ataxia | gluten sensitivity neuropathy | neurological gluten sensitivity | celiac encephalopathy

name: Glycerol kinase deficiency (GKD)
formal: X-linked recessive deficiency of glycerol kinase from Xp21 deletions, often a contiguous gene syndrome with DMD and adrenal hypoplasia, with hyperglyceroluria.
simple: An inherited enzyme deficiency that raises glycerol in blood and urine, sometimes coming with other genes missing next to it.
more: Isolated cases may be symptom-free; complex forms cause adrenal failure, developmental delay and dystrophinopathy. Diagnosed by urine organic acids and chromosomal microarray; treat any adrenal insufficiency.
th: ภาวะขาดเอนไซม์ glycerol kinase ที่ถ่ายทอดทาง X มักเป็นส่วนหนึ่งของ deletion บริเวณ Xp21 ร่วมกับ DMD และ adrenal hypoplasia
tempoNote: Isolated form often asymptomatic; contiguous gene form presents in infancy
feat: Raised plasma and urine glycerol; falsely high triglycerides on routine tests
Isolated adult form often found incidentally
Juvenile form: episodic vomiting, acidosis, hypoglycaemia, stupor
Contiguous Xp21 deletion: with congenital adrenal hypoplasia (NR0B1/DAX1) and Duchenne dystrophy
Boys affected; intellectual disability in larger deletions
inv: Plasma glycerol and urine organic acids (glyceroluria)
Triglycerides measured with glycerol blank (true value normal)
Cortisol, ACTH, electrolytes; CK
Chromosomal microarray for Xp21 deletion; GK gene testing

case.who: 3-week-old boy in a NICU in Khon Kaen
case.story: Poor feeding, vomiting and weight loss; dehydration with low sodium.
case.exam: Lethargic, dehydrated, darker skin, no ambiguous genitalia, hypotonic.
case.tests: Sodium 122, potassium 7.0, cortisol low with high ACTH; CK 8,000 U/L; triglycerides 'very high' on routine assay; microarray shows Xp21 deletion including NR0B1, GK and DMD.
case.q: Which three conditions does this deletion combine?
case.a: Glycerol kinase deficiency, congenital adrenal hypoplasia and Duchenne muscular dystrophy (Xp21 contiguous gene syndrome).

det.patho: Glycerol kinase phosphorylates glycerol so it can enter glycolysis or gluconeogenesis. The GK gene lies in Xp21 next to NR0B1 (DAX1) and DMD, so deletions often remove several genes. The isolated enzyme defect causes high glycerol, which interferes with laboratory triglyceride assays.
det.clinical: The isolated form is usually benign and detected through pseudohypertriglyceridaemia. The juvenile form presents with episodes of vomiting, acidosis and altered consciousness. In the contiguous gene syndrome, adrenal crisis in infancy dominates early, followed later by Duchenne weakness and sometimes intellectual disability. It is not a primary neurological disease, though weakness and encephalopathy can occur.
det.diagnosis: Very high triglycerides with clear plasma is a clue; glycerol-blanked assays reveal normal true triglycerides. Urine organic acids show glyceroluria. Microarray defines the extent of any Xp21 deletion. Check cortisol and CK in affected boys.
det.treatment: Isolated GKD needs avoidance of unnecessary lipid-lowering drugs and sometimes a low-fat diet. Adrenal hypoplasia requires glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement with stress dosing. Muscular dystrophy is managed as DMD. Genetic counselling for carrier mothers is important.
det.prognosis: Isolated form is benign; contiguous gene syndrome depends on adrenal and muscle disease.
pearls: Pseudohypertriglyceridaemia can be due to glycerol – ask for a glycerol-blanked assay.
Infant with adrenal crisis and high CK: think Xp21 deletion.
Do not start statins for 'triglycerides' in GKD.
det.thd: Glycerol kinase deficiency เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมทาง X ทำให้ glycerol ในเลือดสูง และผลไตรกลีเซอไรด์สูงเกินจริง รูปแบบเดี่ยวมักไม่มีอาการ แต่ถ้าเป็นการขาดหายของยีนบริเวณ Xp21 จะมีต่อมหมวกไตทำงานไม่พอและ Duchenne muscular dystrophy ร่วมด้วย ไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาทโดยตรง วินิจฉัยด้วยระดับ glycerol และ microarray รักษาตามโรคร่วม

ddx.pt: Isolated DMD without adrenal crisis or hyperglycerolaemia
Other causes such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia (ambiguous genitalia in girls)
Hypoglycaemia with hepatomegaly and raised lipids from true hypertriglyceridaemia

aN: gkd | glycerol kinase deficiency | hyperglycerolemia | glyceroluria | gk deficiency | xp21 contiguous gene deletion syndrome

name: Glycogen and lipid storage disorders
formal: Inherited metabolic myopathies from defects in glycogen or fatty acid metabolism, causing exercise intolerance, rhabdomyolysis, or progressive weakness with variable cardiac involvement.
simple: Inherited conditions where the body cannot use stored sugar or fat properly, leading to muscle pain, weakness or tiredness.
th: กลุ่มโรคกล้ามเนื้อจากความบกพร่องของการใช้ glycogen หรือไขมันเป็นพลังงาน ทำให้ทนการออกกำลังไม่ได้ กล้ามเนื้อสลาย หรืออ่อนแรงต่อเนื่อง
tempoNote: Exercise- or fasting-induced episodes, or slowly progressive weakness in some
feat: Two patterns: dynamic (episodic exercise intolerance, rhabdomyolysis) and static (fixed weakness)
Glycogen defects: symptoms in short intense exercise, cramps, second wind (McArdle)
Lipid defects: symptoms in prolonged exercise, fasting, fever or cold; no cramps typically (CPT2)
Static weakness: Pompe disease, debrancher deficiency, lipid storage myopathies
Myoglobinuria and acute kidney injury in severe episodes
inv: CK between and during episodes
Forearm exercise test (lactate/ammonia); acylcarnitine profile; urine organic acids
Dried blood spot acid alpha-glucosidase for Pompe
Muscle biopsy (glycogen, lipid stains) and gene panels

case.story: During a long march in hot weather after skipping breakfast, developed aching muscles and cola-coloured urine; similar milder episode with a fever last year.
case.exam: Tender thighs, normal strength between attacks, no cramps during short sprints.
case.tests: CK 85,000 U/L during episode, normal at rest; acylcarnitines suggest CPT2 deficiency; CPT2 variant confirmed.
case.q: Which group of metabolic myopathy does this pattern suggest compared with McArdle disease?
case.a: Lipid (fatty acid oxidation) disorder – CPT2 deficiency – triggered by prolonged exercise and fasting rather than short intense effort.

read.where: Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Glycogenoses and Lipid Storage Disorders

det.patho: Muscle relies on glycogen for short bursts of intense activity and on fatty acid oxidation for sustained exercise and fasting. Enzyme defects in either pathway cause energy failure, leading to contracture, necrosis or progressive fibre damage with storage of glycogen or lipid. Most are autosomal recessive.
det.clinical: This is a grouping rather than a single disease. Dynamic presentations include exercise intolerance, myalgia, cramps and recurrent rhabdomyolysis. Static presentations include limb-girdle weakness with respiratory involvement (Pompe) or slowly progressive weakness in lipid storage myopathies. Cardiomyopathy and hypoglycaemia occur in some.
det.diagnosis: The trigger history guides testing: brief intense exercise points to glycogen defects and prolonged exercise or fasting to lipid defects. Forearm exercise testing, acylcarnitines and blood spot enzyme assays are first-line, followed by gene panels. Biopsy shows glycogen or lipid accumulation in some disorders but can be normal between attacks in CPT2.
det.treatment: Management is disorder-specific: enzyme replacement for Pompe, pre-exercise sucrose and aerobic training for McArdle, avoidance of fasting and high-carbohydrate intake during illness for CPT2, riboflavin for riboflavin-responsive MADD and carnitine for primary carnitine deficiency. Rhabdomyolysis is treated with IV fluids.
det.prognosis: Most episodic disorders have a good outlook if triggers are avoided; storage myopathies may progress.
pearls: Short sprint problem = glycogen; long march or fasting problem = lipid.
Second-wind phenomenon is diagnostic of McArdle disease.
Riboflavin-responsive MADD is a treatable lipid storage myopathy.
det.thd: กลุ่มโรคนี้เกิดจากกล้ามเนื้อใช้ glycogen หรือไขมันเป็นพลังงานไม่ได้ ถ้าเป็นโรค glycogen จะมีอาการเมื่อออกแรงหนักช่วงสั้น เป็นตะคริว ส่วนโรคไขมันจะมีอาการเมื่อออกแรงนานหรืออดอาหาร ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อสลายและปัสสาวะสีเข้ม บางโรคทำให้อ่อนแรงเรื้อรัง เช่น Pompe การวินิจฉัยใช้ CK acylcarnitine เอนไซม์และยีน รักษาตามชนิดโรค

ddx.pt: Cramps in the first minutes of exercise and second wind
Prolonged exercise, fasting or fever triggers; normal between attacks
Progressive limb-girdle and respiratory weakness without episodes

aN: metabolic myopathies glycogen and lipid | glycogenoses and lipid storage myopathies | muscle energy metabolism disorders | inherited metabolic myopathies

name: Glycogen storage diseases (GSD)
formal: Inherited enzyme defects of glycogen metabolism, such as Pompe, McArdle and Cori diseases, causing exercise-induced cramps, myoglobinuria, or progressive proximal myopathy and cardiomyopathy.
simple: Inherited conditions where the body cannot use stored sugar properly, causing weakness, muscle cramps or heart problems.
th: กลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่ใช้หรือสร้าง glycogen ผิดปกติ ส่งผลต่อตับ (น้ำตาลต่ำ ตับโต) หรือกล้ามเนื้อ (ตะคริว ปัสสาวะสีเข้ม หรืออ่อนแรง)
tempoNote: Hepatic forms in infancy; muscle forms from childhood to adulthood
feat: Hepatic GSDs (I, III, VI, IX): fasting hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly, growth delay
Muscle-energy GSDs (V McArdle, VII Tarui): exercise cramps, myoglobinuria
Muscle-structural GSDs (II Pompe, III, IV): progressive limb and respiratory weakness
Pompe infantile form: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and macroglossia
Most autosomal recessive (some IX forms X-linked)
inv: Glucose, lactate, uric acid, lipids, liver enzymes, CK
Dried blood spot acid alpha-glucosidase (Pompe)
Non-ischaemic forearm exercise test
Gene panel; muscle or liver biopsy where needed

case.story: Gradual difficulty climbing stairs and morning headaches over 4 years; now breathless lying flat.
case.exam: Proximal hip and trunk weakness, mild scapular winging, weak diaphragm with paradoxical breathing supine.
case.tests: CK 650 U/L; FVC 55% sitting, 38% supine; low acid alpha-glucosidase on dried blood spot; GAA variants.
case.q: Which GSD is this and why is the supine FVC important?
case.a: Late-onset Pompe disease (GSD II); diaphragm weakness causes nocturnal hypoventilation – start enzyme replacement and NIV.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Glycogen Storage Diseases

det.patho: Each GSD results from a defect in an enzyme of glycogen synthesis, breakdown or lysosomal degradation. Liver forms impair release of glucose, while muscle forms either block energy supply during exercise or cause glycogen accumulation that disrupts fibres. Pompe disease is a lysosomal disorder from acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency.
det.clinical: Presentations follow the tissue involved. Infants with liver forms have hypoglycaemia and big livers. McArdle disease causes cramps and myoglobinuria in brief intense exercise with a second wind. Pompe disease ranges from infantile cardiomyopathy and hypotonia to adult limb-girdle weakness with early respiratory failure. Debrancher and brancher deficiencies may cause myopathy, cardiomyopathy or adult polyglucosan body disease.
det.diagnosis: Biochemical and enzyme tests target the likely type. The forearm exercise test shows flat lactate with normal ammonia in glycolytic defects. Blood spot enzyme activity screens for Pompe disease, confirmed by GAA genetics. Gene panels are now standard for most types.
det.treatment: Hepatic GSDs are managed with frequent feeds and uncooked cornstarch. Pompe disease is treated with enzyme replacement (alglucosidase alfa, avalglucosidase alfa or cipaglucosidase alfa with miglustat) plus respiratory support. McArdle disease benefits from aerobic training and pre-exercise sucrose. Avoid statins and extreme exercise in muscle forms.
det.prognosis: Varies by type; treated hepatic and McArdle forms have good outcomes, while untreated infantile Pompe is fatal in infancy.
pearls: Disproportionate diaphragm weakness in an adult myopathy: test for Pompe.
Second wind = McArdle.
Dried blood spot GAA testing is quick and cheap.
det.thd: Glycogen storage disease เป็นกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่สร้างหรือย่อย glycogen ไม่ได้ ชนิดที่เป็นที่ตับทำให้น้ำตาลต่ำและตับโต ชนิดที่เป็นที่กล้ามเนื้อทำให้ตะคริวและปัสสาวะสีเข้มหลังออกแรง (McArdle) หรืออ่อนแรงและหายใจไม่พอ (Pompe) วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจเอนไซม์และยีน Pompe รักษาด้วย enzyme replacement therapy

ddx.pt: Lipid accumulation on biopsy; fasting-related crises; acylcarnitine abnormal
Ophthalmoplegia, raised lactate, ragged-red fibres
Similar weakness but no early respiratory involvement and normal GAA

aN: gsd | glycogen storage diseases | glycogenoses | pompe disease gsd ii | mcardle disease gsd v | cori disease gsd iii

name: GM1-gangliosidosis
formal: Autosomal recessive beta-galactosidase deficiency with lysosomal ganglioside storage, causing infantile developmental regression, hepatosplenomegaly, cherry-red macula or later dystonia and ataxia.
simple: An inherited disease where a fatty substance builds up in brain cells, causing loss of skills in babies or movement problems later.
more: Diagnosis by reduced leukocyte beta-galactosidase and GLB1 sequencing; skeletal dysplasia and coarse features are common in infantile type. No disease-modifying therapy exists, with supportive care; juvenile and adult forms have slower progression.
th: โรคสะสมไขมันในไลโซโซมจากการขาด beta-galactosidase (GLB1) ชนิดทารกมีพัฒนาการถดถอย ตับม้ามโต cherry-red spot ส่วนชนิดผู้ใหญ่มี dystonia
tempoNote: Infantile form progresses over months with death by early childhood; juvenile form over years; adult form over decades
feat: Infantile (type I): hypotonia, poor responsiveness, then spasticity, seizures and regression; coarse face and skeletal dysostosis resemble Hurler syndrome
Cherry-red macular spot in about half of infantile patients, with hepatosplenomegaly, startle response and oedema in some
Late-infantile or juvenile (type II): onset in early childhood with ataxia, regression, spasticity and seizures; survival to adolescence or beyond
Adult (type III): slowly progressive generalised or oromandibular dystonia, parkinsonism, and short stature, with little or no organomegaly
Autosomal recessive, GLB1 variants; allelic Morquio B has skeletal disease with little brain involvement
inv: Beta-galactosidase activity in leukocytes, fibroblasts or serum (markedly reduced); neuraminidase and other enzymes to rule out galactosialidosis
GLB1 sequencing for confirmation, carrier testing and prenatal diagnosis; urine oligosaccharides and keratan sulfate
MRI: delayed myelination or white matter change in infants; T2 putaminal hyperintensity in adult type; skeletal survey with vertebral beaking
Ophthalmic examination for cherry-red spot

case.story: He was floppy from early on and recently stopped lifting his head or smiling. His parents noticed he startles to noise and has frequent chest infections. Both parents are from the same village.
case.exam: Hypotonia with brisk reflexes, exaggerated startle, coarse facial features, liver edge 3 cm below costal margin; fundus shows a cherry-red spot.
case.tests: Urine glycosaminoglycans normal; leukocyte beta-galactosidase activity severely reduced; hexosaminidase normal; X-ray shows beaking of vertebral bodies.
case.q: How do you separate this from Tay–Sachs disease and Hurler syndrome?
case.a: GM1 gangliosidosis has a cherry-red spot like Tay–Sachs, but with organomegaly and bone changes and reduced beta-galactosidase rather than hexosaminidase; Hurler lacks a cherry-red spot and shows mucopolysacchariduria.

read.where: Progressive Encephalopathies With Onset Before Age 2
Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Lysosomal Storage Disorders

det.patho: Lysosomal beta-galactosidase removes terminal galactose from GM1 ganglioside, keratan sulfate and glycoproteins. When GLB1 variants reduce its activity, GM1 ganglioside accumulates in neurons and causes membrane distortion, neuronal loss and secondary inflammation, while keratan sulfate and oligosaccharides build up in visceral organs and cartilage. Residual enzyme activity predicts the phenotype: nearly none gives the infantile form, a little gives juvenile and adult disease.
det.clinical: Infantile disease begins in the first year with weak sucking, hypotonia and delayed milestones, then loss of skills, spasticity, blindness and seizures. A coarse facial appearance, joint stiffness, hepatosplenomegaly and a cherry-red spot overlap with Hurler syndrome and other storage disorders. Juvenile disease shows regression and ataxia in childhood. The adult form is more insidious, with dystonia of the face or limbs, dysarthria, mild parkinsonism and short stature.
det.diagnosis: Enzyme assay showing deficient beta-galactosidase in leukocytes or fibroblasts is the confirmatory test, with GLB1 sequencing to complete diagnosis and enable family counselling. Normal urinary glycosaminoglycans plus a cherry-red spot favour GM1 over mucopolysaccharidosis. MRI findings and radiographs add support but are not specific, and a cherry-red spot does not appear in all cases.
det.treatment: There is no approved disease-modifying therapy, so management is supportive: anticonvulsants for seizures, spasticity and dystonia care, feeding support with gastrostomy, respiratory care and physiotherapy. Substrate reduction (miglustat) and gene therapy have been explored in trials and should be considered only in research settings. Genetic counselling and prenatal testing are important for affected families.
det.prognosis: Infantile disease is fatal in early childhood; juvenile disease shortens life to adolescence or early adulthood; adult disease progresses slowly over decades.
pearls: Cherry-red spot plus organomegaly and coarse features points to GM1 gangliosidosis, not Tay–Sachs.
Normal urinary GAGs separates it from Hurler syndrome.
The adult type presents as dystonia with putaminal MRI change, so think of it in unexplained young-onset dystonia.
det.thd: GM1-gangliosidosis เกิดจากการขาด beta-galactosidase จากยีน GLB1 ทำให้สะสม GM1 ganglioside ในสมองและอวัยวะอื่น ถ่ายทอดแบบ autosomal recessive ชนิดทารกมีกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง พัฒนาการถดถอย ชัก หน้าหยาบ ตับม้ามโต และพบ cherry-red spot ราวครึ่งหนึ่ง ชนิดผู้ใหญ่พบ dystonia และ parkinsonism ช้า ๆ วินิจฉัยด้วยการวัดกิจกรรมเอนไซม์และตรวจยีน GLB1 การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง ได้แก่ ยากันชัก ดูแลการกลืน การหายใจ และให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

files.chapter: Progressive Encephalopathies With Onset Before Age 2

ddx.pt: No organomegaly or bone dysostosis; hexosaminidase A deficiency
Massive hepatosplenomegaly, lung infiltrates and sphingomyelinase deficiency

aN: gm1 gangliosidosis | beta galactosidase deficiency | glb1 disease | landing disease | adult gm1 dystonia

name: GM2-gangliosidosis
formal: Hexosaminidase deficiency (Tay-Sachs, Sandhoff) with lysosomal GM2 storage, causing infantile regression, hyperacusis, cherry-red macula and seizures, with later-onset ataxia and motor neuron features.
simple: An inherited disease where a fatty substance builds up in brain cells, causing loss of skills, seizures and weakness.
more: Diagnosis by hexosaminidase A (Tay-Sachs) or A and B (Sandhoff) deficiency and HEXA or HEXB mutations; carrier screening in Ashkenazi Jewish communities reduces incidence. No proven therapy exists; infantile forms are fatal by early childhood.
th: โรคสะสมไขมัน GM2 ในไลโซโซมจากขาดเอนไซม์ hexosaminidase (Tay-Sachs, Sandhoff) ทารกมีพัฒนาการถดถอย ตกใจง่ายต่อเสียง cherry-red spot และชัก ส่วนชนิดเริ่มช้ามี ataxia และอาการคล้ายโรคเซลล์ประสาทสั่งการ
tempoNote: Infantile: regression from 3–6 months; juvenile and adult forms progress over years
feat: Infantile: hypotonia, loss of milestones from about 6 months, exaggerated startle to sound, macrocephaly
Cherry-red spot at the macula; blindness and seizures follow
Sandhoff adds hepatosplenomegaly and bony changes in some
Late-onset Tay–Sachs: proximal leg weakness and wasting (lower motor neuron), cerebellar ataxia, psychosis
inv: Hexosaminidase A activity (Tay–Sachs: A low, B normal or raised) and total hex A+B (Sandhoff: both low)
HEXA or HEXB gene sequencing (GM2 activator deficiency needs GM2A testing — enzyme normal)
MRI: thalamic T2 changes in infants; marked cerebellar atrophy in late-onset forms; EMG for anterior horn involvement

case.story: Smiled and sat at 6 months but now no longer holds his head; startles violently to every door slam.
case.exam: Hypotonia, brisk reflexes, poor visual fixation, bilateral cherry-red spots, liver and spleen slightly enlarged.
case.tests: Hexosaminidase A and B both markedly reduced; HEXB biallelic variants.
case.q: Which disease is this and how does it differ biochemically from Tay–Sachs?
case.a: Infantile Sandhoff disease; both hex A and hex B are deficient (beta subunit), whereas Tay–Sachs affects only hex A (alpha subunit).

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Lysosomal Storage Disorders

det.patho: Hexosaminidase A (alpha-beta heterodimer, HEXA and HEXB) with its GM2 activator protein breaks down GM2 ganglioside in neuronal lysosomes. Deficiency of the alpha subunit (Tay–Sachs), beta subunit (Sandhoff) or activator causes storage and neuronal death; residual activity determines age of onset. Tay–Sachs is classically frequent in Ashkenazi Jewish, French-Canadian and some other founder populations, but cases occur worldwide.
det.clinical: Infantile forms show normal early months, then regression, startle (hyperacusis), cherry-red spots, macrocephaly, seizures and death in early childhood. Juvenile forms present at 2–10 years with ataxia, dementia and spasticity. Late-onset (adult) forms are often missed: slowly progressive proximal leg weakness with fasciculations, cerebellar ataxia, dysarthria and psychiatric illness.
det.diagnosis: Enzyme assay in leukocytes or serum is the first test, followed by gene confirmation. Pseudodeficiency alleles can cause falsely low assays, so genetics is essential. MRI marked cerebellar atrophy plus lower motor neuron signs in a young adult should prompt hex A testing. Carrier screening and prenatal diagnosis are available.
det.treatment: There is no proven disease-modifying therapy; substrate reduction (miglustat, venglustat) and gene therapy are experimental. Care focuses on seizures, feeding (gastrostomy), respiratory support and palliative care in infants. In late-onset forms, manage psychiatric symptoms cautiously — some antipsychotics and tricyclics may worsen the disease. Genetic counselling is key.
det.prognosis: Infantile forms are fatal usually by 3–5 years; late-onset forms progress slowly over decades.
pearls: Infant with exaggerated startle and cherry-red spot: Tay–Sachs or Sandhoff.
Organomegaly favours Sandhoff over Tay–Sachs.
Young adult with LMN weakness, ataxia and psychosis: test hexosaminidase A.
det.thd: GM2-gangliosidosis เกิดจากขาดเอนไซม์ hexosaminidase ทำให้ไขมัน GM2 สะสมในเซลล์ประสาท ชนิดทารก (Tay-Sachs, Sandhoff) มีพัฒนาการถดถอยหลัง 6 เดือน ตกใจเสียงมาก cherry-red spot ชัก และเสียชีวิตในวัยเด็ก ชนิดผู้ใหญ่มีอ่อนแรงแบบ LMN เดินเซ และอาการทางจิต วินิจฉัยด้วยการวัดเอนไซม์และตรวจยีน ยังไม่มีการรักษาจำเพาะ

ddx.pt: Coarse features, dysostosis, beta-galactosidase deficiency
Infantile regression and myoclonus without startle or cherry-red spot
Mimicked by late-onset Tay–Sachs; check hex A in young atypical MND with ataxia
