name: Goodpasture syndrome
formal: Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease causing pulmonary haemorrhage and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis; neurological involvement is uncommon, but it appears in differentials with vasculitis.
simple: An autoimmune disease in which antibodies attack the kidneys and lungs, causing blood in the urine and coughing blood.
more: Diagnosed with anti-GBM antibodies and kidney biopsy. Treated with plasma exchange, steroids and cyclophosphamide; early treatment is essential to save the kidneys.
th: โรคภูมิต่อต้าน glomerular basement membrane ทำให้เลือดออกในปอดและไตวายเร็ว มีผลต่อระบบประสาทไม่บ่อย
tempoNote: Renal failure develops over days to weeks
feat: Primarily a kidney and lung disease, not a neurological disorder
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary haemorrhage (haemoptysis)
Neurological effects are mostly secondary: uraemic encephalopathy, hypertensive PRES, seizures
Rare reports of CNS vasculitis or cerebral haemorrhage
Up to a third are double-positive for ANCA, with vasculitic features
inv: Serum anti-GBM antibody, ANCA
Renal biopsy: linear IgG along the glomerular basement membrane
MRI brain if seizures or encephalopathy (look for PRES)
Chest imaging and diffusing capacity for lung haemorrhage

case.who: 24-year-old male welder from Samut Prakan who smokes
case.story: Coughing blood and passing little urine for a week; then a generalised seizure and blurred vision.
case.exam: BP 200/120, drowsy, cortical visual blurring, no focal weakness.
case.tests: Creatinine 7.8 mg/dL, anti-GBM strongly positive; MRI shows bilateral parieto-occipital vasogenic oedema.
case.q: How does the renal disease explain the neurological event?
case.a: Severe hypertension and renal failure from anti-GBM disease caused PRES; neurological involvement is secondary.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Neurological Involvement in Systemic Vasculitides and Related Disorders

det.patho: Autoantibodies target the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes. Smoking, inhaled hydrocarbons and infections may expose the antigen. The nervous system lacks this target in significant amounts, so neurological problems arise mainly from hypertension, uraemia, electrolyte disturbance and treatment side-effects.
det.clinical: Patients present with rapidly progressive kidney failure, often with haemoptysis. Seizures, encephalopathy and visual disturbance usually reflect PRES or uraemia. Double-positive anti-GBM and ANCA patients can have systemic vasculitis, including neuropathy. This entry is in the lexicon for completeness; it is not a primary neurological disease.
det.diagnosis: Anti-GBM antibodies and renal biopsy confirm the disease. In a patient with neurological symptoms, MRI distinguishes PRES from vasculitic infarcts or haemorrhage, and blood tests check urea, sodium, calcium and magnesium.
det.treatment: Urgent plasma exchange, high-dose glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide remove antibodies and stop their production; dialysis supports renal failure. Neurological complications are managed by controlling blood pressure, correcting metabolic disturbance and treating seizures.
det.prognosis: Patient survival is good with prompt treatment, but renal recovery is unlikely if dialysis-dependent at presentation; relapse is uncommon except in double-positive cases.
pearls: Neurological symptoms in anti-GBM disease are usually PRES or uraemia, not vasculitis.
Check ANCA too: double-positive disease behaves like vasculitis.
Pulmonary haemorrhage plus kidney failure is an emergency for plasma exchange.
det.thd: Goodpasture syndrome หรือ anti-GBM disease เป็นโรคภูมิต้านตนเองที่ทำลายไตและปอด ทำให้ไตวายเร็วและไอเป็นเลือด ไม่ใช่โรคทางระบบประสาทโดยตรง อาการทางสมองที่พบมักเป็นผลรอง เช่น PRES จากความดันสูง หรือสมองทำงานผิดปกติจากของเสียคั่ง รักษาด้วย plasma exchange, steroid และ cyclophosphamide ร่วมกับคุมความดันและแก้ไขเกลือแร่

name: Grade 3 oligodendrogliomas
formal: Anaplastic IDH-mutant, 1p/19q-codeleted gliomas with increased mitoses, vascular proliferation and a worse prognosis than grade 2, treated with surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy.
simple: A fast-growing type of brain tumour from support cells that responds fairly well to radiation and chemotherapy.
ab: Oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted, CNS WHO grade 3
th: oligodendroglioma เกรด 3 (anaplastic) ที่มี IDH mutation และ 1p/19q codeletion เติบโตเร็วกว่าเกรด 2 ต้องรักษาด้วยฉายรังสีร่วมกับ PCV หรือ temozolomide ตอบสนองดีและอยู่รอดนานกว่า glioma ชนิดอื่นที่เกรดเดียวกัน
tempoNote: Months of headache, seizure or deficit, often after years of lower-grade disease
feat: Mean age in the 40s to 50s, frontal or temporal predominance, often arising from a grade 2 oligodendroglioma
Seizures, headache, personality change, aphasia or hemiparesis, with faster progression than grade 2
Imaging shows patchy enhancement, mass effect, calcification and sometimes cystic degeneration or spread across the midline
Histology adds anaplastic features (mitoses, microvascular proliferation, necrosis); molecular criteria remain IDH mutation plus 1p/19q codeletion
CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion identifies a more aggressive subset with shorter survival
inv: MRI with contrast, perfusion and spectroscopy; CT for calcification
Integrated pathology: IDH1/2, 1p/19q, TERT promoter, CDKN2A/B, MGMT
Spinal MRI and CSF if symptoms suggest leptomeningeal spread
Baseline neurocognitive testing before radiotherapy

case.who: 52-year-old woman, a rice-mill owner from Phitsanulok
case.story: A grade 2 right frontal oligodendroglioma was resected 6 years ago and she was observed; now 5 weeks of headaches and mild left leg weakness.
case.exam: Left leg grade 4/5 with brisk reflexes; no papilloedema.
case.tests: MRI shows new nodular enhancement within the old cavity margin with oedema. Re-resection: oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant, 1p/19q-codeleted, mitoses and microvascular proliferation, CNS WHO grade 3.
case.q: What is the standard adjuvant plan and its main long-term risks?
case.a: Radiotherapy (about 59.4 Gy) followed by PCV chemotherapy (RTOG 9402/EORTC 26951), or temozolomide if PCV is not tolerated. Risks include myelosuppression, neuropathy, pulmonary fibrosis and delayed cognitive effects of radiation.

det.patho: Grade 3 (anaplastic) oligodendroglioma carries the IDH mutation and 1p/19q codeletion of its lower-grade counterpart with added anaplastic features. TERT promoter mutation and CIC/FUBP1 changes are common; CDKN2A/B deletion and high proliferation predict poorer outcome. Many tumours arise by progression from a grade 2 lesion, others are grade 3 at presentation. Under older rules grade III oligodendrogliomas and oligoastrocytomas were treated alike.
det.clinical: Headache, seizure and progressive focal deficit over months are typical, in a patient who may have a history of earlier grade 2 tumour. Peritumoral oedema and enhancement are more prominent than at grade 2. Leptomeningeal spread may occur and often responds to systemic therapy. Gliomatosis cerebri-like infiltration is seen in a minority.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows enhancement and mass effect, but only tissue can define grade and molecular type. Correct classification relies on demonstrating IDH and 1p/19q status; histology alone is unreliable. Early postoperative MRI documents residual disease. Spinal MRI and CSF cytology are indicated if leptomeningeal disease is suspected.
det.treatment: Standard of care is maximal safe resection, then radiotherapy (about 59.4 Gy in 33 fractions) with PCV (procarbazine, lomustine, vincristine), which prolonged overall survival by several years in codeleted tumours in RTOG 9402 and EORTC 26951 (long-term follow-up). Temozolomide is used when PCV is poorly tolerated, with CODEL comparing radiotherapy plus temozolomide with radiotherapy plus PCV. Chemotherapy first with radiotherapy held for relapse was tested in the NOA-04 trial. At recurrence consider re-resection, re-irradiation or alkylator rechallenge. Seizure management and steroids are supportive.
det.prognosis: Median survival in 1p/19q-codeleted grade 3 oligodendroglioma exceeds 12-14 years with radiotherapy plus PCV; non-codeleted tumours do much worse.
pearls: Codeleted grade 3 tumours treated with radiotherapy plus PCV had median survival of more than a decade.
Recurrence of a grade 2 tumour with new enhancement should prompt re-biopsy rather than assumption of radiation change.
Rely on molecular result, not on a round-cell appearance, to call a tumour oligodendroglioma.
det.thd: Grade 3 oligodendroglioma เป็น oligodendroglioma ที่มีลักษณะ anaplastic ผู้ป่วยมักอายุ 40-50 ปี มีปวดศีรษะ ชัก หรืออ่อนแรงเพิ่มขึ้นภายในไม่กี่เดือน การวินิจฉัยต้องมี IDH mutation และ 1p/19q codeletion การรักษาคือผ่าตัด ฉายรังสี แล้วให้ PCV หรือ temozolomide ผู้ที่มี codeletion มักอยู่รอดนานกว่า 10 ปี และต้องติดตาม MRI สม่ำเสมอ

name: Gradenigo syndrome
formal: Petrous apicitis from otitis media causing the triad of retro-orbital pain, abducens palsy and ear discharge, with risk of meningitis and venous thrombosis.
simple: A complication of ear infection that causes pain behind the eye, double vision and ear discharge.
th: การอักเสบติดเชื้อของปลายกระดูก petrous จากหูชั้นกลางอักเสบ ทำให้มีหูน้ำหนวก ปวดหลังตาหรือใบหน้า และเส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 6 อ่อนแรง อาจลุกลามเป็นเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบหรือหลอดเลือดดำอุดตัน
tempoNote: Days to weeks after otitis media or mastoiditis
feat: Horizontal diplopia from ipsilateral abducens palsy
Deep retro-orbital or facial pain from trigeminal ganglion irritation
Ear discharge or recent otitis media and mastoid tenderness
Facial weakness or hearing loss may be present with extension
Fever, headache, papilloedema or meningism indicate intracranial spread
inv: High-resolution CT temporal bone showing mastoid and petrous apex opacification and bone erosion
MRI with contrast and MR venography for apical enhancement, meningeal spread, abscess and sinus thrombosis
Ear swab and blood cultures; inflammatory markers
Lumbar puncture only after imaging if meningitis is suspected

case.story: After two weeks of left ear discharge and treatment with oral amoxicillin, she developed severe pain behind the left eye and double vision on looking left.
case.exam: Febrile, left abduction deficit, left otorrhoea, tender mastoid; no neck stiffness.
case.tests: CT shows left mastoid opacification with petrous apex erosion; MRI with contrast shows apical enhancement and no sinus thrombosis; culture grows Pseudomonas.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and treatment?
case.a: Gradenigo syndrome (petrous apicitis). Admit for intravenous antipseudomonal antibiotics for weeks, ENT drainage by mastoidectomy or tympanostomy tube, and monitor for intracranial complications.

read.where: Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — Focal Central Nervous System Infection
8 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System
Chapter 94: Neuro-ophthalmology: Extraocular Muscles and Cranial Nerves III, IV, and VI

det.patho: The abducens nerve crosses the petrous apex beneath the petroclinoid ligament in Dorello’s canal, adjacent to the trigeminal ganglion. Infection of the middle ear and mastoid spreads to the pneumatised petrous apex and inflames the nerve, producing the classic triad. Complications include meningitis, epidural or brain abscess, and thrombosis of the inferior petrosal and sigmoid sinuses.
det.clinical: Patients, usually children or young adults, have persistent otorrhoea or recent otitis media, deep pain in the eye or face, and diplopia from VI palsy. The full triad is not always present, particularly after antibiotic use, and facial paresis or hearing loss may be added. Fever, vomiting, papilloedema or altered consciousness warn of intracranial extension.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is by temporal bone CT and MRI with venography, alongside culture. Mimics include other causes of VI palsy such as raised pressure, tumours of the skull base, Tolosa–Hunt syndrome, closed head injury, and skull base osteomyelitis. Cerebrospinal fluid should be examined only when imaging allows.
det.treatment: Treatment combines prolonged intravenous antibiotics tailored to culture (covering Pseudomonas, Staphylococcus and anaerobes) with surgical drainage of the mastoid or petrous apex when response is poor. Anticoagulation is considered for associated venous sinus thrombosis. Corticosteroids are controversial and only used with specialist advice.
det.prognosis: Good with early antibiotics and drainage; the VI palsy usually recovers in weeks to months, and delay risks meningitis and permanent nerve damage.
pearls: Ear infection plus VI palsy plus deep facial pain is petrous apicitis until imaged.
Partial antibiotic treatment can mask the triad.
Always look for sinus thrombosis and intracranial spread.
det.thd: Gradenigo syndrome คือการติดเชื้อที่ปลายกระดูก petrous จากหูชั้นกลางอักเสบ ทำให้หูน้ำหนวก ปวดลึกหลังตา และตาเหลือกไม่ได้จาก CN VI palsy ตรวจ CT กระดูก temporal และ MRI พร้อมดู venous sinus การรักษาคือให้ยาปฏิชีวนะทางหลอดเลือดดำนาน ร่วมกับการระบายหนองโดยแพทย์หูคอจมูกเมื่อจำเป็น

name: Graft versus host disease (GvHD)
formal: Immune complication of allogeneic stem cell transplant in which donor T cells attack host tissues, with neuromuscular manifestations such as myositis, myasthenia, neuropathy and cerebrovascular events.
simple: A complication of bone marrow transplants where the donor's immune cells attack the patient's body, sometimes causing muscle or nerve problems.
th: ภาวะแทรกซ้อนหลังปลูกถ่ายไขกระดูกจากผู้อื่น T cell ของผู้ให้โจมตีเนื้อเยื่อผู้รับ อาจเกิด myositis, neuropathy, myasthenia ได้
tempoNote: Neuromuscular complications usually in chronic GvHD, months to years after transplant
feat: Systemic chronic GvHD: skin sclerosis, dry eyes and mouth, liver and lung involvement
Polymyositis-like proximal weakness, often with myalgia
Fasciitis causing joint contractures and restricted movement
Immune neuropathies (GBS- or CIDP-like) and myasthenia gravis
Often appears when immunosuppression is tapered
inv: CK, EMG and muscle or fascia biopsy
Nerve conduction studies for neuropathy pattern
AChR antibodies if fatigable weakness

case.who: 35-year-old woman from Bangkok, 14 months after allogeneic stem cell transplant for AML
case.story: Cyclosporin was tapered three months ago; now difficulty climbing stairs and tight forearm skin.
case.exam: Proximal weakness, skin thickening of forearms with groove sign, dry mouth.
case.tests: CK 2,400 U/L; EMG myopathic; biopsy shows inflammatory myopathy.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the plan?
case.a: Chronic GvHD myositis with fasciitis; escalate immunosuppression with corticosteroids and transplant team input.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Complications Related to Specific Allograft Transplantation
Chapter 9: Neurological complications of cell therapies in haematological malignancies
Chapter 16 - Autoimmune and Inflammatory Encephalopathies as Complications of Cancer

det.patho: Donor T cells recognise host antigens and, in chronic GvHD, both T- and B-cell autoimmunity and fibrosis develop. Muscle, fascia, nerve and the neuromuscular junction can be targeted, producing autoimmune syndromes analogous to idiopathic ones. Direct central nervous system GvHD is rare and controversial.
det.clinical: Neuromuscular involvement includes myositis, fasciitis, immune neuropathies and myasthenia gravis, typically arising during taper of immunosuppression. Other causes of weakness after transplant (steroid myopathy, drug neuropathy, infection, relapse) must be excluded.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis combines clinical features of chronic GvHD with neuromuscular tests and biopsy. NIH consensus criteria define chronic GvHD. Antibody tests support myasthenia.
det.treatment: Systemic corticosteroids with calcineurin inhibitors are first-line; ruxolitinib, belumosudil, ibrutinib and extracorporeal photopheresis are used for steroid-refractory chronic GvHD. IVIG or plasma exchange for neuropathies; standard therapy for myasthenia.
det.prognosis: Myositis generally responds to immunosuppression; overall prognosis depends on GvHD extent and infections.
pearls: New weakness after immunosuppression taper in a transplant patient: think GvHD myositis or myasthenia.
Steroid myopathy is a common confounder; CK is normal in steroid myopathy.
Fasciitis restricts joint motion more than weakness does.
det.thd: GvHD คือภาวะที่ T cell จากผู้ให้ไขกระดูกโจมตีเนื้อเยื่อของผู้รับ ในระยะเรื้อรังอาจเกิด myositis fasciitis neuropathy หรือ myasthenia มักเกิดตอนลดยากดภูมิ วินิจฉัยด้วย CK EMG และชิ้นเนื้อ ต้องแยกจาก steroid myopathy และยาที่เป็นพิษ รักษาด้วยยากดภูมิคุ้มกันร่วมกับทีมปลูกถ่าย

name: Gram-negative meningitis
formal: Bacterial meningitis due to Gram-negative bacilli such as E. coli, Klebsiella and Pseudomonas, in neonates, after neurosurgery, trauma or immunosuppression, with high mortality.
simple: A serious infection of the brain's coverings by a particular group of bacteria, mostly in newborns or after head surgery.
th: เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบจากแบคทีเรียแกรมลบ เช่น E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter พบในทารกแรกเกิด ผู้ป่วยหลังผ่าตัดสมอง ศีรษะบาดเจ็บ หรือภูมิคุ้มกันต่ำ ตายสูงและต้องรักษานาน
tempoNote: Acute over hours to 2 days; neonates may show non-specific illness first

det.patho: Enteric bacilli reach the CSF through bacteraemia from the urinary, biliary or intestinal tract, by direct spread from skull fracture or surgery, or by neonatal acquisition at birth. The K1 capsule of E. coli resists complement killing and favours invasion of the blood-brain barrier in newborns. Resistant strains arise from hospital antibiotic pressure. In strongyloidiasis, steroids allow the larval cycle to accelerate, creating mucosal breaks that spill bacteria into the circulation.
det.clinical: The illness resembles any acute bacterial meningitis but typically strikes people who are already sick, so fever and confusion may be mistaken for sepsis from the original focus. Neonates look unwell without meningism. Ventriculitis, hydrocephalus and abscess are frequent and prolong recovery. In the context of Thailand, ask about recent steroids, cough with eosinophilia and abdominal symptoms to uncover Strongyloides.
det.diagnosis: Obtain CSF for cell count, biochemistry, Gram stain and culture with susceptibility to the full panel including cephalosporins and carbapenems. Blood cultures and imaging are done early because ventriculitis and abscess are common. Search for the source organ, a persistent CSF leak, a recent device, or Strongyloides in stool, sputum or by serology. Report ESBL or carbapenemase production to the laboratory-driven regimen.
det.treatment: Third-generation cephalosporins (ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, ceftazidime) are used for susceptible isolates; ESBL producers need meropenem 2 g every 8 hours; Pseudomonas needs ceftazidime, cefepime or meropenem; carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter may need colistin plus a second agent and intraventricular dosing. Treat for at least 21 days, with 2 weeks after the first sterile CSF as a minimum, and remove devices. Treat strongyloidiasis with ivermectin, repeating it in disseminated disease, and taper steroids. Dexamethasone is not routinely given in Gram-negative disease.
det.prognosis: Mortality ranges from 15 to 40 per cent, higher with resistant bacteria and in neonates, with high rates of hydrocephalus and neurodevelopmental sequelae.
pearls: Gram-negative meningitis without a hospital or neurosurgical link in an Isan farmer on steroids should prompt a Strongyloides search.
Penetration of CSF matters: use meningitis doses of carbapenems and consider intraventricular therapy in drug-resistant infection.
Neonatal E. coli meningitis often needs 3 weeks of therapy.

det.patho: GPA is a necrotising small-vessel vasculitis with granulomatous inflammation, strongly linked to PR3-ANCA. Neurological disease arises by three routes: vasculitis of nerve or brain vessels, contiguous granulomatous invasion from sinuses and orbits, and remote granulomas in meninges or brain.
det.clinical: Peripheral neuropathy is the commonest neurological manifestation. Cranial neuropathies, especially optic, abducens, facial and vestibulocochlear, reflect skull base and orbital disease. Hypertrophic pachymeningitis presents with chronic headache and can be the sole feature in limited GPA. CNS vasculitis causing stroke or haemorrhage is uncommon.
det.diagnosis: ANCA testing is positive in most generalised cases but less often in limited disease. Biopsy of an accessible lesion confirms granulomatous vasculitis. Contrast MRI identifies dural, orbital and pituitary involvement. Infections such as tuberculosis and fungal disease, and lymphoma, are key mimics.
det.treatment: Induction uses glucocorticoids combined with rituximab or cyclophosphamide; avacopan is now used as a steroid-sparing option. Plasma exchange is reserved for selected severe renal or pulmonary disease. Maintenance is typically rituximab for 18 months or longer, or azathioprine. Prophylaxis against Pneumocystis is needed.
det.prognosis: Remission is achieved in most patients, but relapses are common; nerve and cranial deficits may persist.
pearls: Chronic sinus disease plus cranial palsies or pachymeningitis: check PR3-ANCA.
Limited GPA may be ANCA negative; biopsy if suspicion remains.
Thailand-relevant mimics: TB and fungal skull base infection must be excluded.

qx.why: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis causes granulomatous inflammation with fibrinoid necrosis in the upper airway, lung and kidney, usually with c-ANCA/PR3. Neurological manifestations include cranial neuritis (the acoustic nerve is the commonest), mononeuritis multiplex, pachymeningitis, intracranial vasculitis and thrombosis. Treatment is high-dose steroids with rituximab or cyclophosphamide, and ANCA-negative asthma with eosinophilia points to EGPA instead.

det.patho: Granulomatous inflammation infiltrates the anterior and/or posterior pituitary and stalk. It is either primary (idiopathic, a rare variant of autoimmune hypophysitis) or secondary to systemic granulomatous disease such as sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, GPA, syphilis or Langerhans cell histiocytosis, or to rupture of a Rathke cleft cyst. Epidemiology is poorly defined because cases are rare and often diagnosed only at surgery.
det.clinical: Headache is common and often more prominent than in adenoma. Anterior hormone deficits and diabetes insipidus occur together more often than with adenoma; hyperprolactinaemia from stalk compression is frequent. Chiasmal compression causes field loss, and lateral spread can affect cavernous sinus nerves. Systemic features (lung, skin, eye, kidney, sinus) suggest a secondary cause.
det.diagnosis: MRI typically shows homogeneous enlargement, thickened stalk, and absence of the normal posterior pituitary bright signal. Evaluate every axis and water balance. Search for systemic disease with chest CT, ACE, ANCA, TB testing and, if available, FDG-PET. Tissue diagnosis is needed when the cause remains uncertain, because lymphoma, germinoma and metastasis can look similar.
det.treatment: Replace hormones, giving glucocorticoid first, plus desmopressin for diabetes insipidus. High-dose glucocorticoids are first-line for non-infectious granulomatous disease, adding methotrexate or another steroid-sparing drug for sarcoid or relapse; GPA needs rituximab or cyclophosphamide regimens. Infection must be excluded or treated before immunosuppression. Surgery is for diagnosis or progressive visual loss.
det.prognosis: Mass effect often improves, but hormone deficits, especially diabetes insipidus, frequently remain permanent.
pearls: Diabetes insipidus with a pituitary mass suggests inflammation, infiltration or metastasis rather than adenoma.
Exclude TB before steroids in Thai patients.
Germinoma can mimic hypophysitis in young patients; check beta-hCG.

det.patho: Non-caseating granulomas of epithelioid macrophages and giant cells form within muscle, most often as a manifestation of sarcoidosis. Similar histology occurs with tuberculosis, fungal or parasitic infection, Crohn disease, graft-versus-host disease, and thymoma-associated myositis. Muscle granulomas are found in many sarcoid patients on biopsy, but symptomatic disease affects only a small percentage.
det.clinical: Three patterns are recognised: a chronic proximal myopathy (most common symptomatic form), palpable nodular myositis, and an uncommon acute polymyositis-like illness. Some chronic cases show IBM-like distribution or overlap with myasthenia. Cardiac and respiratory muscle involvement must be considered. Systemic sarcoid signs may be absent at presentation.
det.diagnosis: Muscle biopsy, ideally guided by MRI or PET, shows granulomas; special stains and cultures exclude infection before calling it sarcoid. Staging includes chest imaging, ACE, calcium, eye examination and cardiac MRI or ECG. EMG supports a myopathy but cannot show granulomas. Granulomas alone in an otherwise typical IBM biopsy should raise caution about diagnosis.
det.treatment: Corticosteroids are the first-line agent; methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate serve as steroid-sparing options, and TNF inhibitors such as infliximab for refractory sarcoid. Chronic forms respond less well than nodular or acute forms. Physiotherapy helps preserve function. Treat any infectious cause specifically.
det.prognosis: Acute and nodular forms often respond; the chronic atrophic form tends to stabilise rather than fully recover.
pearls: Granulomas in muscle are common in sarcoid, but symptomatic myopathy is rare.
Always exclude TB and fungi on biopsy before immunosuppression.
Nodules on MRI or PET are good biopsy targets.

case.story: Six weeks of drooping eyelids and double vision, then trouble lifting his arms and two fainting spells.

det.patho: Two overlapping entities share the histology of granulomas and multinucleated giant cells: sarcoid granulomatous myositis and a thymoma-related paraneoplastic myositis, frequently accompanied by myasthenia gravis and giant cell myocarditis. The thymoma form is linked to antibodies against striational antigens such as titin, ryanodine receptor and Kv1.4. Similar inflammation is reported with immune checkpoint inhibitors. Mechanisms beyond T-cell–driven granulomatous inflammation are not well established.
det.clinical: Presentation is proximal, axial or bulbar weakness with or without myalgia, often alongside ocular myasthenic signs. Cardiac involvement may be the first or most dangerous feature, causing conduction block, ventricular arrhythmia or heart failure. Sarcoid-associated disease tends to be slower and multisystem. Respiratory weakness can develop.
det.diagnosis: Biopsy demonstrating granulomas with giant cells is required, with exclusion of mycobacterial and fungal infection. Look for thymoma with CT, test AChR and striational antibodies, and screen the heart in every case. EMG may show both myopathy and decrement. Consider checkpoint inhibitor exposure.
det.treatment: High-dose corticosteroids are first-line, often combined with IVIG or plasma exchange if myasthenic or cardiac involvement is severe, and steroid-sparing agents later. Thymectomy is indicated for thymoma. Cardiac disease may need pacemaker or defibrillator and cardiology-led immunosuppression. Checkpoint inhibitor cases require drug withdrawal and aggressive immunotherapy.
det.prognosis: Muscle often responds to treatment; prognosis is largely determined by myocarditis and thymoma stage.
pearls: Myasthenia + high CK + heart block: think thymoma-associated giant cell myositis/myocarditis.
Screen the heart in every patient with this biopsy finding.
Checkpoint inhibitors can produce the same triad of myositis, myocarditis and myasthenia.

det.patho: Stimulating IgG autoantibodies against the TSH receptor drive thyroid hormone overproduction and goitre. The same receptor on orbital fibroblasts underlies thyroid eye disease, with inflammation and expansion of extraocular muscles and fat. Thyroid hormone increases Na/K-ATPase activity, which in genetically susceptible people (for example KCNJ18 variants) shifts potassium into cells and causes periodic paralysis.
det.clinical: This is an endocrine disease with important neurological manifestations. Neurological features include tremor, hyperreflexia, anxiety, proximal myopathy, rarely chorea, and in the elderly apathetic thyrotoxicosis with cognitive slowing. Thyroid eye disease causes restrictive ophthalmopathy that typically limits elevation and abduction, and compressive optic neuropathy at the orbital apex can threaten vision. Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis attacks follow carbohydrate loads, alcohol or rest after exercise.
det.diagnosis: Suppressed TSH with high free hormones confirms thyrotoxicosis; TRAb or a diffuse uptake scan identifies Graves. In ophthalmoplegia, forced duction and orbital imaging show restriction from enlarged muscle bellies with tendon sparing. Coexisting myasthenia should be considered if ptosis rather than lid retraction is present. Hypokalaemic paralysis in a thyrotoxic patient needs prompt potassium and thyroid testing.
det.treatment: Antithyroid drugs (methimazole; propylthiouracil in early pregnancy), radioiodine or thyroidectomy control hyperthyroidism, with beta-blockers for symptoms. Active moderate-to-severe eye disease is treated with IV methylprednisolone pulses, and teprotumumab or other agents where available; sight-threatening optic neuropathy needs urgent steroids and orbital decompression. Periodic paralysis resolves with euthyroidism; meanwhile use cautious potassium and propranolol. Smoking cessation reduces eye disease progression.
det.prognosis: Neuromuscular manifestations resolve once euthyroidism is achieved; eye disease often follows its own course and may leave diplopia or proptosis.
pearls: Restrictive diplopia with lid retraction: thyroid eye disease; with ptosis, check for myasthenia too.
Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis can occur when thyrotoxic symptoms are subtle.
Radioiodine can worsen eye disease; steroid cover is used in at-risk patients.
det.thd: Graves’ disease เป็นไทรอยด์เป็นพิษจาก antibody ต่อ TSH receptor มีผลต่อระบบประสาทหลายแบบ เช่น มือสั่น reflex ไว กล้ามเนื้อต้นแขนขาอ่อนแรง thyroid eye disease ที่ทำให้ตาโปนเห็นภาพซ้อนและอาจกดเส้นประสาทตา และอัมพาตเป็นพักๆ จากโพแทสเซียมต่ำ ซึ่งพบบ่อยในชายหนุ่มเอเชีย วินิจฉัยด้วย TSH ต่ำ free T4 สูงและ TRAb การรักษาคือคุมไทรอยด์ ให้ beta-blocker และรักษาอาการตาตามความรุนแรง

name: Grisel’s syndrome
formal: Non-traumatic atlantoaxial subluxation after pharyngeal or head and neck infection or surgery, causing painful torticollis and risk of cord compression.
simple: A neck problem after a throat infection or surgery in which the top two neck bones slip, causing a painful tilted neck.
th: ข้อ atlantoaxial เคลื่อนโดยไม่มีอุบัติเหตุ หลังติดเชื้อหรือผ่าตัดบริเวณคอหอยและศีรษะ ทำให้คอเอียงเจ็บและเสี่ยงกดไขสันหลัง
tempoNote: Develops days to a couple of weeks after pharyngeal infection or ENT surgery
feat: Mostly children after tonsillitis, pharyngitis, retropharyngeal abscess, otitis or adenotonsillectomy
Painful torticollis ('cock-robin' head tilt and rotation) with restricted neck movement
Muscle spasm on the side of the long sternocleidomastoid, unlike muscular torticollis
Neurological deficit (myelopathy) uncommon but serious
A musculoskeletal-infective condition, not a dystonia
inv: CT cervical spine with dynamic rotation views to show C1–C2 rotatory subluxation
MRI for ligament inflammation, abscess and cord compression
Inflammatory markers; ENT assessment

case.story: Five days after adenotonsillectomy he developed neck pain and held his head tilted to the left and turned to the right; unable to straighten it.
case.exam: Fixed cock-robin posture, tender upper neck, no limb weakness or sensory level.
case.tests: CT shows atlantoaxial rotatory subluxation (Fielding type I); MRI shows prevertebral oedema but no abscess.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the first-line treatment?
case.a: Grisel's syndrome; antibiotics, anti-inflammatories, muscle relaxants and immobilisation or halter traction with a collar.

det.patho: Inflammation from the pharynx spreads via the pharyngovertebral venous plexus and lymphatics to the atlantoaxial ligaments, causing laxity and spasm of the prevertebral muscles. The child's naturally lax ligaments and horizontally oriented facets make rotatory subluxation easier. Hyperaemic decalcification of C1 and C2 attachments has also been proposed.
det.clinical: Painful torticollis usually begins within one to two weeks after a head and neck infection or surgery. The head is tilted to one side and rotated to the other with slight flexion. Neck pain, fever and dysphagia can coexist. Neurological signs, from radicular pain to quadriparesis, are rare but delayed diagnosis increases the risk of fixed deformity. It is a spine-infection disorder rather than primary neurological disease.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis needs clinical suspicion and imaging: CT with 3D reconstruction and dynamic rotation demonstrates fixed C1–C2 rotation and the Fielding–Hawkins type. MRI evaluates ligaments, abscesses and the cord. Plain films are often hard to interpret. Exclude trauma, congenital anomalies (Down syndrome, Klippel–Feil) and posterior fossa tumours presenting with head tilt.
det.treatment: Early cases respond to treating the infection plus analgesia, muscle relaxants and immobilisation in a soft or rigid collar; halter traction or manipulation under anaesthesia is used if reduction fails. Delayed or unstable cases with neurological deficit may need halo immobilisation or C1–C2 fusion. Close follow-up imaging confirms maintained reduction.
det.prognosis: Most children recover fully if treated within weeks; delayed diagnosis can lead to irreducible fixation requiring surgery.
pearls: New torticollis after tonsillectomy should prompt CT of C1–C2.
Spasm is in the sternocleidomastoid on the long side, unlike muscular torticollis.
Down syndrome children are at higher risk because of ligament laxity.
det.thd: Grisel’s syndrome คือข้อ C1–C2 เคลื่อนแบบหมุนโดยไม่มีอุบัติเหตุ เกิดหลังติดเชื้อคอหอยหรือผ่าตัดต่อมทอนซิล/ต่อมอดีนอยด์ มักพบในเด็ก มีปวดคอและคอเอียงค้าง เสี่ยงกดไขสันหลังถ้าวินิจฉัยช้า ตรวจด้วย CT แบบหมุนคอและ MRI รักษาด้วยยาปฏิชีวนะ ยาแก้ปวด ใส่ collar หรือดึงคอ และผ่าตัดเชื่อมกระดูกถ้าแก้ไม่ได้ ไม่ใช่ dystonia

name: GTP cyclohydrolase I (GTPCH I) deficiency
formal: GCH1 deficiency causing dopa-responsive dystonia (Segawa disease) with childhood-onset limb dystonia with diurnal variation, parkinsonism and an excellent response to low-dose levodopa.
simple: An inherited condition in children causing stiff, twisted legs that are worse in the evening and respond very well to levodopa.
more: CSF biopterin and neopterin are low and genetics confirm it; dominant with reduced penetrance. Lifelong low-dose levodopa gives marked and sustained benefit.
th: ภาวะขาดเอนไซม์ GTP cyclohydrolase I (GCH1) ที่ทำให้เกิด dopa-responsive dystonia ในเด็ก อาการแย่ลงช่วงเย็น และตอบสนองดีมากต่อ levodopa ขนาดต่ำ
tempoNote: Childhood onset, slowly progressive with diurnal fluctuation; adult-onset parkinsonism variants exist
feat: Foot or leg dystonia beginning around 6–8 years, girls more often affected
Symptoms mild in the morning, worse by evening, improved by sleep
Later parkinsonism; brisk reflexes and apparent extensor plantar (striatal toe) may mislead
Dramatic, lasting response to low-dose levodopa without long-term dyskinesia
Recessive (biallelic) form causes severe infantile encephalopathy with hyperphenylalaninaemia
inv: Therapeutic levodopa trial is the most practical test
GCH1 sequencing and copy-number analysis
CSF neopterin and biopterin low, HVA low; phenylalanine loading test abnormal
DAT-SPECT normal (unlike juvenile Parkinson disease)

case.story: Walks on tiptoe with an inturned right foot by afternoon; mornings she can play normally. Her father has had mild hand tremor since his 30s.
case.exam: Right foot equinovarus on walking, mild bradykinesia of right hand, brisk knee jerks, intelligence normal.
case.tests: MRI normal; levodopa/carbidopa 100/25 mg twice daily abolishes symptoms within a week; GCH1 heterozygous variant.
case.q: Diagnosis, and why must children with dystonia receive a levodopa trial?
case.a: Dopa-responsive dystonia from GTPCH I deficiency; it is treatable with small doses and misdiagnosis as cerebral palsy deprives children of a near-cure.

det.patho: GTPCH I catalyses the first step in tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) synthesis. BH4 is an obligatory cofactor for tyrosine hydroxylase, so its deficiency limits dopamine production in nigrostriatal terminals while neurons survive. Heterozygous variants act dominantly with reduced and female-biased penetrance, while biallelic variants cause severe infantile BH4 deficiency with monoamine and phenylalanine abnormalities. GCH1 carriers also have a modestly increased risk of Parkinson disease in later life.
det.clinical: Classic Segawa disease begins in childhood with leg dystonia causing toe-walking or inversion, worse as the day goes on. Over years it generalises and parkinsonism emerges, and untreated adults may have marked postural dystonia. Adult-onset presentations include focal dystonia (writer's cramp, cervical) or levodopa-responsive parkinsonism. Recessive disease presents in infancy with hypotonia, oculogyric crises, developmental delay and autonomic signs.
det.diagnosis: A sustained response to levodopa supports the diagnosis, ideally confirmed by GCH1 testing (including deletions). CSF pterins and HVA are low; the phenylalanine loading test detects impaired BH4 synthesis. Normal DAT-SPECT distinguishes it from degenerative juvenile parkinsonism. Neonatal hyperphenylalaninaemia screening detects recessive but not dominant forms.
det.treatment: Levodopa with a decarboxylase inhibitor at low doses (often 1–5 mg/kg/day, many adults on 100–300 mg/day) gives sustained benefit lasting decades, with dyskinesia uncommon if titrated slowly. Recessive forms need BH4 supplementation, levodopa, 5-hydroxytryptophan and sometimes folinic acid in a metabolic centre. Anticholinergics are second line. Genetic counselling is offered to the family.
det.prognosis: Excellent with treatment; most patients have a normal life without progression of disability.
pearls: Every child with unexplained dystonia deserves a levodopa trial.
The 'striatal toe' can mimic a Babinski sign.
Response persists without motor fluctuations, unlike early-onset Parkinson disease.
det.thd: GTPCH I deficiency เป็นสาเหตุหลักของ dopa-responsive dystonia (Segawa) ยีน GCH1 ทำให้สร้าง BH4 ได้น้อย จึงสร้าง dopamine ไม่พอ เด็กมี dystonia ที่ขา อาการเป็นมากตอนเย็นและดีขึ้นหลังนอน ตอบสนองดีมากต่อ levodopa ขนาดต่ำโดยแทบไม่มี dyskinesia DAT-SPECT ปกติ เด็กทุกรายที่มี dystonia จึงควรลองให้ levodopa ส่วนชนิด recessive รุนแรงในทารกต้องรักษาด้วย BH4 และสารสื่อประสาทเสริม

name: Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS)
formal: Acute immune-mediated demyelinating or axonal polyneuropathy often after infection, with ascending weakness, areflexia, albuminocytologic dissociation, treated with IVIG or plasma exchange.
simple: A sudden immune illness, often after an infection, in which the nerves are attacked, causing weakness that spreads upward.
more: Use nerve conduction, CSF protein and, when needed, anti-ganglioside antibodies; monitor forced vital capacity and autonomic function. Recovery is typically good, with 5 to 10 percent mortality and some residual deficits, and relapses are rare.
th: เส้นประสาทอักเสบเฉียบพลันหลังติดเชื้อ — แขนขาอ่อนแรงลามขึ้นทั้งสองข้าง รีเฟล็กซ์หาย อาจหายใจไม่ไหว
tempoNote: Progresses to nadir within 4 weeks (usually 2)
feat: Symmetric ascending weakness with areflexia
Preceding diarrhoeal or respiratory infection 1–4 weeks earlier
Facial diplegia, dysautonomia, back or limb pain
Risk of respiratory failure — monitor vital capacity, not just SpO2
inv: Nerve conduction studies: demyelinating or axonal pattern (may be normal early)
CSF: albuminocytological dissociation (often after the first week)
Serial FVC/NIF; ECG and BP monitoring
Anti-ganglioside antibodies (e.g. GQ1b in Miller Fisher)

case.story: Diarrhoea 2 weeks ago; now 4 days of tingling feet and progressive leg then arm weakness; cannot climb stairs.
case.exam: Proximal and distal weakness MRC 3–4/5, absent reflexes, mild glove-and-stocking sensory loss, bilateral facial weakness.
case.tests: CSF protein 1.2 g/L, cells 2/µL; NCS: prolonged distal latencies and conduction block.
case.q: Which bedside measure decides ICU admission?
case.a: Serial forced vital capacity (e.g. < 20 mL/kg or falling quickly), plus bulbar weakness and autonomic instability; treat with IVIG or plasma exchange.

qx.stem: A 41-year-old rubber tapper from Trang develops tingling feet and then leg and arm weakness over six days after a diarrhoeal illness. Today he cannot walk unaided, has bilateral facial weakness, a weak cough and areflexia. Single-breath count is 14, forced vital capacity 1.6 L (about 35% predicted). Nerve conduction shows reduced motor amplitudes.
qx.q: What should be done next?
opts: Discharge with outpatient IVIG in one week
Admit to an ICU or monitored bed for possible intubation and start IVIG 2 g/kg (or plasma exchange)
Start high-dose oral prednisolone
Repeat nerve conduction in two weeks before treating
Give pyridostigmine for presumed myasthenia gravis
qx.why: Rapid progression, bulbar and facial weakness and FVC below about 20 mL/kg or a falling single-breath count predict respiratory failure, so monitored care is needed; the EGRIS score helps estimate ventilation risk. IVIG or plasma exchange should be started within two weeks of onset in patients who cannot walk. Steroids do not help GBS, and early neurophysiology can be non-diagnostic, so treatment should not wait for a repeat study.

qx.stem: A 46-year-old man from Ayutthaya is admitted with five days of ascending leg weakness and numb hands. He is areflexic, can barely lift his arms, and has mild facial weakness. Forced vital capacity is 2.3 L (about 28 mL/kg) and was 3.4 L yesterday, with new difficulty counting to 20 in one breath.
qx.q: Which monitoring finding most strongly mandates transfer to a high-dependency or intensive care unit?
opts: Mild distal paraesthesia
Absent ankle reflexes
Raised CSF protein
A falling vital capacity (more than 30 percent decline or approaching 20 mL/kg), bulbar weakness or autonomic instability
Normal nerve conduction studies
qx.why: An acute monophasic ascending areflexic paralysis reaching nadir within four weeks is GBS. Respiratory failure is the major early threat, so a rapidly declining vital capacity, a single-breath count under about 20, weak neck flexion, bulbar dysfunction or dysautonomia warrant intensive monitoring and early ventilation. Areflexia and CSF protein support diagnosis but do not themselves signal respiratory risk. IVIG or plasma exchange is given in parallel.

qx.q: Which acute immunotherapy decision is correct?
opts: IVIG 2 g/kg over five days or plasma exchange, which are equally effective; corticosteroids are not helpful
Intravenous methylprednisolone alone for three days
A second IVIG course in anyone not improving by day 14

qx.why: In GBS patients who cannot walk 10 metres unaided, IVIG and plasma exchange are equally beneficial, with IVIG preferred for convenience; plasma exchange works best within a week and IVIG within two weeks. Corticosteroids did not help in trials, and combination or repeat courses add adverse effects without added benefit. Monitor vital capacity, bulbar function and autonomic stability; the Erasmus scores estimate respiratory risk and outcome.

det.patho: An acute immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy, frequently triggered by infection (Campylobacter jejuni, CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma, Zika, influenza) through molecular mimicry. In the demyelinating form (AIDP) macrophages strip myelin; in axonal forms (AMAN, AMSAN), antibodies against gangliosides such as GM1 and GD1a attack the nodal axolemma. Axonal variants are relatively more frequent in Asia, and anti-GQ1b antibodies define the Miller Fisher spectrum.
det.clinical: Weakness typically starts in the legs and ascends over days, with areflexia, distal paraesthesia and often back or limb pain; nadir is reached within 4 weeks, usually by 2. Facial and bulbar weakness, respiratory failure (in about a quarter) and autonomic dysfunction — arrhythmias, BP swings, ileus, urinary retention — cause most deaths. Variants include Miller Fisher syndrome (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia), pharyngeal–cervical–brachial weakness, paraparetic GBS and Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis. Reflexes may be preserved early or in AMAN.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by CSF albuminocytological dissociation (often normal in week one) and nerve conduction studies, which may need repeating to classify demyelinating or axonal subtype. CSF cell counts above 50/µL should prompt reconsideration (HIV, Lyme, lymphoma, polio-like infections). Anti-GQ1b supports Miller Fisher; other ganglioside antibodies are of limited routine value. Exclude spinal cord compression, myelitis, myasthenia, botulism, hypokalaemia, porphyria, tick paralysis and critical illness neuropathy.
det.treatment: IVIG 2 g/kg total, split over 5 days, or plasma exchange (about five exchanges) within 2–4 weeks of onset are equally effective for patients who cannot walk unaided; combining them adds nothing and corticosteroids alone are ineffective. Monitor FVC and NIF regularly, intubating early for FVC below 20 mL/kg, inability to lift the head or cough, or rapid decline; EGRIS helps predict ventilation need. Provide DVT prophylaxis, pain management (gabapentinoids, opioids cautiously), cardiac monitoring, bowel and bladder care and early rehabilitation. Treatment-related fluctuations within 8 weeks may justify re-treatment; a third deterioration raises the possibility of acute-onset CIDP.
det.prognosis: About four in five patients walk independently at 6 months, but mortality remains around 3–7% and many have residual fatigue or weakness; mEGOS estimates outcome.
pearls: Measure vital capacity, not oxygen saturation, to judge respiratory risk.
Normal CSF protein in the first week does not exclude GBS.
Three or more treatment-related fluctuations or deterioration after 8 weeks suggests acute-onset CIDP.
Dilated unreactive pupils point away from GBS toward botulism.
det.thd: GBS คือภาวะเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายและรากประสาทอักเสบเฉียบพลันจากภูมิคุ้มกัน มักเกิดหลังติดเชื้อ เช่น ท้องเสียจาก Campylobacter อาการคืออ่อนแรงลามขึ้นจากขาทั้งสองข้าง รีเฟล็กซ์หาย ปวดหลัง อาจมีหน้าอ่อนแรง กลืนลำบาก หายใจล้มเหลว และระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติแปรปรวน วินิจฉัยทางคลินิกร่วมกับน้ำไขสันหลังที่โปรตีนสูงแต่เซลล์ปกติ และการตรวจ NCS รักษาด้วย IVIG 2 g/kg แบ่งให้ 5 วัน หรือ plasma exchange และเฝ้าดู vital capacity อย่างใกล้ชิด

name: H-IBM with frontotemporal dementia
formal: Hereditary inclusion body myopathy with frontotemporal dementia, usually with Paget disease of bone, due to VCP gene variants (multisystem proteinopathy).
simple: An inherited disease causing muscle weakness along with memory and behaviour changes.
more: Autosomal dominant VCP; muscle biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles and TDP-43 pathology. No disease-modifying therapy; supportive and symptomatic management with family counselling.
ab: Inclusion body myopathy with Paget disease and FTD
th: โรคพันธุกรรมจากยีน VCP ที่มี inclusion body myopathy ร่วมกับ frontotemporal dementia และมักมีโรค Paget ของกระดูก (multisystem proteinopathy)
tempoNote: Myopathy typically begins in the 30s–40s, Paget disease similar age, dementia later in the 50s
feat: Adult-onset proximal and sometimes scapular or distal weakness, often asymmetric
Paget disease of bone in about half: bone pain, raised alkaline phosphatase
Behavioural or language-variant frontotemporal dementia in about a third
Some develop ALS-like motor neuron disease or parkinsonism
Autosomal dominant family history with variable combinations

Muscle biopsy: rimmed vacuoles, TDP-43 and ubiquitin inclusions
VCP gene sequencing; alkaline phosphatase and bone scan; neuropsychology and MRI

case.who: 48-year-old woman, shop owner from Nakhon Pathom
case.story: Difficulty lifting goods onto shelves for four years; recently apathetic and making odd purchases. Her brother had bone pain and 'muscle disease'.
case.exam: Scapular winging, proximal arm and hip weakness, disinhibited behaviour, frontal assessment battery 9/18.
case.tests: CK 420 U/L; ALP raised; bone scan shows pelvic Paget lesions; biopsy rimmed vacuoles; VCP R155H.
case.q: Which genetic multisystem disorder links muscle, bone and brain?

det.patho: VCP (p97) is an ATPase that helps extract ubiquitinated proteins for proteasomal degradation and supports autophagy. Dominant missense variants disturb protein quality control, leading to TDP-43 and ubiquitin-positive inclusions in muscle, neurons and osteoclast abnormalities. Similar multisystem pictures occur with HNRNPA2B1, HNRNPA1, SQSTM1 and MATR3 variants.
det.clinical: Myopathy is the most frequent feature, often with scapuloperoneal or limb-girdle pattern and sometimes respiratory or cardiac involvement. Paget disease may be asymptomatic or cause bone pain and fractures. Dementia is usually behavioural variant FTD with apathy, disinhibition and language problems, appearing about a decade after weakness. Penetrance is high, but individuals in the same family may express only one or two features.
det.diagnosis: Consider it in adult myopathy with rimmed vacuoles plus Paget disease or FTD in the patient or family. Biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles and TDP-43 aggregates, overlapping with sporadic IBM. VCP gene testing confirms. Screen for bone disease (ALP, skeletal scintigraphy) and assess cognition.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying therapy. Bisphosphonates treat Paget disease, physiotherapy and orthoses support mobility, and respiratory and cardiac function should be monitored. Behavioural symptoms are managed with caregiver education and, cautiously, SSRIs. Predictive testing and family counselling follow genetic confirmation.
det.prognosis: Progressive; death usually occurs in the 50s–60s from respiratory failure or complications of dementia.
pearls: Myopathy plus Paget disease plus FTD: test VCP.
Rimmed vacuoles are not specific to sporadic IBM.
Ask about bone pain and raised ALP in any family myopathy.

ddx.pt: Sporadic after 50, finger flexor and quadriceps weakness; no bone or dementia component
No Paget disease or FTD; other gene defects
C9orf72 most commonly; neurogenic rather than myopathic weakness

aN: ibmpfd | vcp multisystem proteinopathy | msp1 | inclusion body myopathy with paget disease and ftd | vcp disease

name: H-IBM with Paget disease
formal: Autosomal dominant VCP-related multisystem proteinopathy combining inclusion body myopathy, early Paget disease of bone and sometimes frontotemporal dementia.
simple: An inherited condition where muscle weakness occurs together with bone disease called Paget disease.
more: VCP gene testing confirms it; high alkaline phosphatase indicates Paget. Bisphosphonates treat the bone disease, but the muscle and brain components have no cure.
ab: inclusion body myopathy with Paget disease and frontotemporal dementia
th: โรคพันธุกรรมยีนเด่นจากยีน VCP ทำให้กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงแบบ inclusion body myopathy โรคกระดูก Paget และบางรายมีสมองเสื่อมแบบ frontotemporal หรือ ALS
tempoNote: Weakness usually begins in the 30s–50s and progresses over 10–20 years
feat: Adult-onset proximal and/or distal weakness, often with scapular winging (limb-girdle or scapuloperoneal pattern)
Paget disease of bone in about half: bone pain, raised alkaline phosphatase, often before 50
Frontotemporal dementia in about a third, typically later than muscle onset
Some develop ALS, parkinsonism or Charcot-Marie-Tooth-like neuropathy
Autosomal dominant family history with variable features between relatives
inv: CK normal to moderately raised; EMG myopathic, sometimes mixed
Serum alkaline phosphatase, skeletal X-rays or bone scan for Paget lesions
Muscle biopsy: rimmed vacuoles, TDP-43 and ubiquitin inclusions
VCP gene testing (confirmatory); cognitive and behavioural assessment

case.story: Four years of difficulty raising his arms and climbing stairs; his mother had 'bone disease' and became disinhibited before death.
case.exam: Scapular winging, proximal arm and hip weakness, mild ankle dorsiflexion weakness; reflexes reduced.
case.tests: CK 600 U/L; ALP 420 U/L; bone scan shows pelvic Paget lesions; biopsy with rimmed vacuoles.
case.q: Which gene ties together myopathy, bone disease and family dementia?
case.a: VCP — multisystem proteinopathy (IBMPFD); treat Paget with bisphosphonate and monitor for FTD and ALS.

det.patho: Heterozygous missense variants in VCP (valosin-containing protein), an ATPase that unfolds ubiquitinated proteins for degradation and autophagy, impair protein quality control. The result is a multisystem proteinopathy with TDP-43 aggregates in muscle and brain and abnormal osteoclast activity in bone. Penetrance is high but expression of each component varies even within families. Similar multisystem pictures occur with HNRNPA2B1, HNRNPA1 and SQSTM1 variants.
det.clinical: Muscle weakness is the most frequent and usually first feature, appearing in mid-adulthood with proximal and sometimes distal or scapular involvement; respiratory and cardiac muscles may be affected late. Paget disease often presents earlier than the sporadic form, with bone pain or deformity. Frontotemporal dementia (behavioural or language variants) appears in later decades. Motor neuron disease, parkinsonism and neuropathy are less common features.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it when myopathy coexists with raised alkaline phosphatase, early Paget disease or a family history of dementia or ALS. Muscle biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles and TDP-43 inclusions with mild inflammation, overlapping with sporadic IBM. Genetic testing of VCP confirms the diagnosis; multigene myopathy or ALS-FTD panels often include it.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy is approved; experimental VCP inhibitors are under study. Bisphosphonates control Paget disease and bone pain. Supportive care includes physiotherapy, orthoses, respiratory monitoring, behavioural management for FTD and multidisciplinary ALS care when relevant. Offer genetic counselling to relatives.
det.prognosis: Progressive; death commonly occurs 15–20 years after onset from respiratory failure or dementia-related complications.
pearls: Myopathy + high ALP + family dementia = think VCP.
Biopsy can look like IBM; age, pattern and family history separate them.
Steroids do not help the myopathy.
det.thd: โรคนี้เกิดจากยีน VCP ถ่ายทอดแบบยีนเด่น ผู้ป่วยวัยกลางคนมีกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขาหรือสะบักบาน ร่วมกับโรคกระดูก Paget (ALP สูง ปวดกระดูก) และบางรายมีสมองเสื่อมแบบ frontotemporal หรือ ALS ตามมา ชิ้นเนื้อกล้ามเนื้อพบ rimmed vacuoles ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน ยังไม่มียารักษาให้หายขาด ใช้ bisphosphonate รักษากระดูกและดูแลแบบสหสาขา

name: Haemangioblastomas (HBO)
formal: Highly vascular benign tumours of the cerebellum, brainstem or spinal cord, sporadic or associated with von Hippel–Lindau disease, sometimes with polycythaemia and cystic changes.
simple: Slow-growing blood-vessel-rich tumours in the back of the brain or spinal cord, sometimes linked to an inherited syndrome.
th: เนื้องอกหลอดเลือดเกรด 1 ที่โตช้า พบที่ cerebellum ไขสันหลัง และจอตา ทั้งแบบเกิดเองและแบบที่สัมพันธ์กับ von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) มักมีถุงน้ำ การผ่าตัดเอา nodule ออกให้หมดรักษาหายได้ และมียา belzutifan สำหรับ VHL
tempoNote: Months of headache and ataxia; spinal tumours cause gradual sensory loss with syrinx; retinal lesions may be asymptomatic for years until exudation
feat: Cerebellar tumour (about three-quarters of CNS lesions) causing headache, vomiting, truncal and limb ataxia, and hydrocephalus; cyst plus enhancing mural nodule
Spinal cord and medulla tumours cause dissociated sensory loss, pain and myelopathy with syringomyelia
Polycythaemia from tumour erythropoietin in a minority of patients
Retinal haemangioblastoma gives floaters, flashes and visual loss from exudation or detachment; often the first VHL feature at a mean age of 25
In VHL: multiple, recurrent lesions plus renal cell carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma, pancreatic cysts and neuroendocrine tumours, endolymphatic sac tumours and epididymal cystadenomas
inv: Contrast MRI of brain and entire spine: intensely enhancing nodule with flow voids, with or without non-enhancing cyst; angiography only for planning embolisation
Ophthalmology with dilated fundoscopy and fluorescein angiography
VHL gene sequencing and deletion analysis; screening MRI of brain and spine every 1-2 years, abdominal imaging, plasma metanephrines, audiology
Full blood count (polycythaemia) and EPO; renal imaging for RCC surveillance

case.story: Four months of daily headache, vomiting and unsteady gait; his father died from kidney cancer at 41 and his brother had a retinal operation.
case.exam: Papilloedema, bilateral dysmetria and wide-based gait; haemoglobin 18.2 g/dL.
case.tests: MRI shows a large cystic right cerebellar mass with a 1.5 cm enhancing mural nodule, plus two small enhancing nodules in the cervical cord; VHL gene deletion identified. Retinal examination shows two peripheral angiomas.
case.q: How should the cerebellar tumour be treated and what systemic drug is now approved for multiple VHL lesions?
case.a: Microsurgical removal of the solid nodule in one piece with feeder coagulation, which also resolves the cyst. Belzutifan, an HIF-2 alpha inhibitor, is approved for VHL-associated CNS haemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours.

det.patho: Haemangioblastoma is a benign (CNS WHO grade 1) vascular tumour composed of neoplastic stromal cells with vacuolated lipid-rich cytoplasm and a dense capillary network. The cell of origin is uncertain. Loss of VHL function, germline in VHL disease and somatic in sporadic tumours, stabilises HIF and drives VEGF and EPO production, explaining intense vascularity, peritumoural cysts and secondary polycythaemia. In the source about a quarter to a half of tumours occur with VHL disease.
det.clinical: Sporadic tumours are usually solitary and found in the fourth to fifth decade, while VHL tumours are multiple, appear at about 30 years and recur. Cerebellar lesions give headache, ataxia and hydrocephalus; brainstem and cord lesions give bulbar or sensory dysfunction with syrinx. Retinal angiomas threaten sight through exudation. VHL causes premature death from renal cell carcinoma and CNS haemangioblastoma, and early surveillance changes outcome.
det.diagnosis: MRI of the whole neuraxis finds all nodules, however small, because they maintain cysts and are the source of recurrence. A solid red nodule in the wall of a cyst is typical. Histology shows clear stromal cells that are inhibin and brachyury-negative and may be confused with metastatic renal cell carcinoma. Anyone with a haemangioblastoma needs VHL genetic evaluation and family screening.
det.treatment: Microsurgical removal of the solid nodule is the treatment of choice and often cures sporadic tumours; subtotal removal and cyst drainage alone should be avoided. Preoperative embolisation can help large, brainstem or spinal tumours. Stereotactic radiosurgery (about 15-18 Gy to the margin) controls small lesions but responds slowly and does not always stop cyst growth. Belzutifan, an oral HIF-2 alpha inhibitor, achieves responses in VHL haemangioblastomas and is a standard systemic option from 2021 onwards. Retinal lesions are treated with laser or cryotherapy. Screening for RCC and phaeochromocytoma is lifelong.
det.prognosis: Sporadic tumours have excellent outcomes after complete excision; VHL patients have a mean age at death of around 40-50 years in older series, improving with surveillance and new drugs.
pearls: Cystic cerebellar mass with an enhancing nodule in an adult: haemangioblastoma; the nodule, not the cyst, must be removed.
Raised haemoglobin with a cerebellar lesion suggests tumour erythropoietin.
Multiple or young-onset lesions need VHL testing; belzutifan is now available for VHL disease.
det.thd: Haemangioblastoma เป็นเนื้องอกหลอดเลือดเกรด 1 พบที่ cerebellum ไขสันหลัง และจอตา บางรายเป็นส่วนหนึ่งของ von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) ซึ่งมีหลายก้อนและเกิดซ้ำร่วมกับมะเร็งไตและ phaeochromocytoma อาการคือปวดศีรษะ เดินเซ หรือชาไขสันหลัง ลักษณะ MRI คือถุงน้ำพร้อมก้อนที่ enhance ชัด การผ่าตัดเอาก้อนออกทั้งชิ้นรักษาได้ ในผู้ป่วย VHL ใช้ยา belzutifan ได้ ต้องตรวจยีน VHL และติดตามอวัยวะอื่นตลอดชีวิต

name: Haematogenous osteomyelitis
formal: Bone infection spread via blood, in the spine causing vertebral osteomyelitis with back pain, fever and risk of epidural abscess and cord compression.
simple: A bone infection that has travelled through the blood, in the spine causing back pain and fever.
th: การติดเชื้อกระดูกที่แพร่ทางเลือด ในกระดูกสันหลังทำให้ปวดหลัง มีไข้ และอาจเกิดฝีใน epidural กดไขสันหลังได้
tempoNote: Back pain for weeks before diagnosis is typical in adults
feat: Long bones in children, vertebrae in adults
Persistent back pain, local tenderness, fever in about half
Source: skin, urinary tract, endocarditis, IV lines, injection drug use
Neurological deficits from epidural extension or collapse
inv: MRI spine with gadolinium
Blood cultures, CRP/ESR

case.story: Six weeks of lower back pain after a fistula infection; recently, pain radiates down both legs.
case.exam: Lumbar tenderness, normal strength, reduced ankle reflexes.
case.tests: CRP 95 mg/L; MRI L3–L4 discitis with endplate destruction; blood cultures MRSA.
case.q: What treatment?
case.a: IV vancomycin (or alternative) for 6 weeks with monitoring; surgery if deficit, abscess or instability.

det.patho: Bacteria in the blood lodge in the vascular metaphysis in children or the vertebral endplate in adults. Infection spreads into the disc and neighbouring vertebra, and can extend into paraspinal tissue or the epidural space. S. aureus predominates; Gram-negatives follow urinary sources.
det.clinical: The spine involvement presents with insidious back pain and focal tenderness. Fever is inconsistent. Neurological involvement indicates epidural abscess or instability and is an emergency.
det.diagnosis: MRI is the most sensitive test. Blood cultures identify the organism in a significant proportion; otherwise biopsy before antibiotics if stable. Evaluate for endocarditis.
det.treatment: Targeted antibiotics are given for about 6 weeks, initially intravenous; switching to well-absorbed oral agents is acceptable once the patient is stable. Surgery is indicated for epidural abscess with neurological deficit, spinal instability, uncontrolled sepsis or failure of medical therapy. Treat the source, such as an infected dialysis access or endocarditis. Track clinical response and CRP rather than repeating MRI early, as imaging lags behind healing.
det.prognosis: Most recover with appropriate therapy; neurological deficit worsens outlook.
pearls: Dialysis or diabetic patient with new back pain: consider vertebral osteomyelitis.
S. aureus bacteraemia and back pain = MRI.
Obtain cultures before antibiotics if neurologically intact.
det.thd: Haematogenous osteomyelitis คือการติดเชื้อกระดูกที่มาทางเลือด ในผู้ใหญ่มักเป็นที่กระดูกสันหลัง ทำให้ปวดหลังเรื้อรัง กดเจ็บ อาจไม่มีไข้ ถ้าลามเป็นฝีใน epidural จะกดไขสันหลังหรือรากประสาท ตรวจด้วย MRI และเพาะเชื้อจากเลือด รักษาด้วยยาปฏิชีวนะราว 6 สัปดาห์และผ่าตัดเมื่อมีอาการทางประสาท

name: Haemolytic disease of the newborn
formal: Fetal or neonatal haemolysis from maternal alloantibodies such as anti-D, causing hyperbilirubinaemia; severe cases lead to kernicterus with athetosis, deafness and gaze palsy.
simple: Breakdown of a baby's red blood cells from the mother's antibodies, which can cause severe jaundice and brain damage.
ab: Haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
th: ภาวะเม็ดเลือดแดงของทารกแตกจาก antibody ของมารดา (เช่น anti-D) ทำให้ bilirubin สูง รายรุนแรงเกิด kernicterus ซึ่งทำให้มี athetosis หูหนวก และกลอกตาขึ้นไม่ได้
tempoNote: Haemolysis and jaundice in the first days of life; kernicterus leaves a lifelong movement disorder
feat: Primarily a haematological and neonatal disease; neurological harm comes from bilirubin encephalopathy
Early jaundice (first 24 hours), anaemia, hydrops in severe fetal cases
Acute bilirubin encephalopathy: lethargy, hypotonia then hypertonia, retrocollis, high-pitched cry
Chronic kernicterus: dyskinetic (athetoid) cerebral palsy, sensorineural hearing loss/auditory neuropathy, upgaze palsy, dental enamel dysplasia
inv: Maternal and infant blood groups, direct antiglobulin test, bilirubin trend against hour-specific nomogram

MRI: bilateral globus pallidus and subthalamic T2 hyperintensity in kernicterus

case.story: Born at home to a Rh-negative mother whose previous baby was also jaundiced; deeply yellow on day 2 and treated late. Now cannot sit independently and does not respond to speech.
case.exam: Writhing athetoid limb movements, preserved social smile, limited upgaze, dental enamel defects.
case.tests: ABR absent waves with present cochlear microphonics; MRI bilateral globus pallidus T2 hyperintensity.
case.q: What caused his cerebral palsy?
case.a: Kernicterus from Rh haemolytic disease of the newborn, producing dyskinetic CP, auditory neuropathy and upgaze palsy.

det.patho: Maternal IgG against fetal red-cell antigens (RhD, other Rh antigens, Kell, or ABO in group O mothers) crosses the placenta and destroys fetal erythrocytes. After birth, the immature liver cannot conjugate the bilirubin load, and unconjugated bilirubin crosses the blood–brain barrier, especially with prematurity, acidosis, sepsis or low albumin. Bilirubin is toxic to the globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, hippocampus, oculomotor and auditory brainstem nuclei and cerebellar Purkinje cells.
det.clinical: This is not a primary neurological disease; neurology becomes involved through bilirubin-induced neurological dysfunction. Acute encephalopathy progresses from poor feeding and lethargy to hypertonia with arching and retrocollis, fever and seizures. Survivors of severe exposure develop chronic kernicterus: dyskinetic cerebral palsy with athetosis and dystonia, auditory neuropathy, vertical gaze palsy and dental dysplasia, often with relatively preserved intelligence. ABO disease is usually milder than Rh disease.
det.diagnosis: Antenatal screening for maternal antibodies and fetal anaemia monitoring (middle cerebral artery Doppler) identifies at-risk pregnancies. After birth, a positive direct antiglobulin test with rising bilirubin confirms immune haemolysis. In a child with dyskinetic CP, a history of severe neonatal jaundice plus pallidal T2 signal and abnormal ABR strongly support kernicterus. Rule out G6PD deficiency, common in Thailand, which also causes severe neonatal jaundice.
det.treatment: Prevention relies on anti-D immunoglobulin for RhD-negative mothers and intrauterine transfusion for severe fetal anaemia. Neonatal management uses intensive phototherapy, exchange transfusion at threshold bilirubin levels, and IVIG in selected immune haemolysis. Established kernicterus is managed with multidisciplinary CP care: anticholinergics, botulinum toxin, sometimes DBS, cochlear implants or hearing support for auditory neuropathy, and communication aids.
det.prognosis: With modern prevention and treatment, kernicterus is rare; once established, the movement disorder and hearing loss are permanent.
pearls: Dyskinetic CP with upgaze palsy and hearing loss: ask about neonatal jaundice.
Kernicterus targets the globus pallidus, whereas hypoxia targets putamen and thalamus.
In Thai neonates, G6PD deficiency is an important non-immune cause of dangerous hyperbilirubinaemia.
det.thd: Haemolytic disease of the newborn เกิดจาก antibody ของแม่ทำลายเม็ดเลือดแดงทารก เช่น Rh หรือ ABO ทำให้ทารกตัวเหลืองมากตั้งแต่วันแรก ถ้า bilirubin สูงมากจะเข้าสมองเกิด kernicterus ทำลาย globus pallidus และนิวเคลียสก้านสมอง ผลระยะยาวคือ cerebral palsy ชนิด athetoid หูหนวกแบบ auditory neuropathy และกลอกตาขึ้นไม่ได้ ป้องกันด้วย anti-D และรักษาด้วย phototherapy หรือ exchange transfusion

name: Haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)
formal: Life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome with fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly and high ferritin, with CNS involvement causing seizures, encephalopathy and cranial nerve palsies.
simple: A dangerous overreaction of the immune system causing fever, low blood counts and organ damage, sometimes involving the brain.
th: กลุ่มอาการภูมิคุ้มกันทำงานเกินอย่างรุนแรงที่อาจถึงชีวิต มีไข้ เม็ดเลือดต่ำ ตับม้ามโต ferritin สูงมาก และอาจมีอาการทางสมอง เช่น ชัก ซึม หรือเส้นประสาทสมองพิการ

feat: Persistent fever, splenomegaly, cytopenias in two or more lines
Very high ferritin, high triglycerides, low fibrinogen, raised soluble CD25
CNS: seizures, encephalopathy, ataxia, cranial nerve palsies, irritability in infants
Primary (familial, e.g. PRF1, UNC13D) in children; secondary to EBV, other infections, lymphoma or autoimmune disease in adults

Bone marrow showing haemophagocytosis (supportive, not required)
MRI brain (multifocal white matter or leptomeningeal lesions) and CSF (pleocytosis, high protein)
EBV PCR, lymphoma work-up (PET-CT), genetic testing in children

case.story: Two weeks of high fever after an EBV-like illness, then confusion and a generalised seizure.
case.exam: Drowsy, splenomegaly, petechiae, left sixth nerve palsy.
case.tests: Hb 7.8, platelets 30,000, ferritin 18,000 ng/mL, triglycerides 400 mg/dL, fibrinogen 1.0 g/L; CSF protein 1.2 g/L with mild lymphocytosis; EBV DNA high.
case.q: What syndrome links the fever, cytopenias and neurological picture?
case.a: EBV-associated secondary HLH with CNS involvement; urgent HLH-directed treatment with dexamethasone and etoposide, with haematology input.

det.patho: Defective cytotoxic lymphocyte killing (genetically, or overwhelmed by an infectious or malignant trigger) leaves activated T cells and macrophages unchecked, producing a cytokine storm with interferon-gamma central. Macrophages engulf blood cells and infiltrate organs, including the meninges and brain parenchyma. CNS-HLH may result from direct infiltration, cytokine toxicity, haemorrhage or PRES.
det.clinical: Systemic features dominate: fever, organomegaly, cytopenias, liver dysfunction and coagulopathy. Neurological involvement occurs in a large share of children and a smaller share of adults, presenting with seizures, altered consciousness, ataxia, meningism or cranial nerve deficits. Isolated CNS-HLH can mimic encephalitis or demyelination, especially in familial forms.
det.diagnosis: HLH-2004 criteria (5 of 8 features or a molecular diagnosis) and the HScore help estimate probability. Ferritin above 10,000 ng/mL is highly suggestive in adults but not specific. MRI and CSF assess CNS involvement. Always seek the trigger: EBV and other infections, lymphoma, autoimmune disease (macrophage activation syndrome) and immune effector cell therapy.
det.treatment: Treatment is a haematological emergency: dexamethasone with etoposide (HLH-94/2004-based protocols), and intrathecal methotrexate with hydrocortisone for CNS disease. Anakinra, emapalumab and ruxolitinib are used in selected or refractory cases. Treat the trigger (antivirals, rituximab for EBV, lymphoma therapy). Familial HLH requires haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation.
det.prognosis: Mortality remains high, especially with malignancy-associated HLH; CNS involvement predicts neurological sequelae.
pearls: Fever + cytopenias + ferritin in the thousands + encephalopathy: think HLH.
In adults, always look for lymphoma.
CNS disease needs intrathecal therapy as part of the protocol.
det.thd: HLH คือภาวะภูมิคุ้มกันทำงานเกินอย่างรุนแรง ผู้ป่วยมีไข้สูง ตับม้ามโต เม็ดเลือดต่ำ ferritin สูงมาก และอาจมีชัก ซึม หรือเส้นประสาทสมองพิการ สาเหตุในผู้ใหญ่มักเป็น EBV หรือมะเร็งต่อมน้ำเหลือง ในเด็กมักเป็นพันธุกรรม รักษาเร่งด่วนด้วย dexamethasone etoposide และรักษาสาเหตุร่วมกับทีมโลหิตวิทยา

qx.stem: A 41-year-old man with fever for ten days develops confusion and seizures. Ferritin is 18,000 ng/mL, triglycerides are high, fibrinogen is low, there is pancytopenia and splenomegaly. MRI shows multifocal white matter lesions and leptomeningeal enhancement.
qx.q: Which element is most important in management?
opts: Antiepileptic drugs and observation only
Empirical IVIG alone
Splenectomy
Intrathecal antibiotics
Searching for a trigger such as lymphoma or infection while starting HLH-directed immunosuppression, including agents with CNS penetration
qx.why: CNS involvement in HLH is a marker of severe disease and requires prompt immunosuppression, typically dexamethasone with etoposide or alternatives such as ruxolitinib or emapalumab depending on cause, together with trigger treatment. Supportive care or IVIG alone is inadequate, and splenectomy has no role in acute disease.

name: Haemorrhage after thrombolysis
formal: Symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage after intravenous thrombolysis for stroke, occurring in a small percentage, causing neurological worsening and requiring emergency CT.
simple: Bleeding in the brain as a complication of clot-busting treatment for stroke, which can worsen symptoms.
th: เลือดออกในสมองที่มีอาการหลังให้ยาละลายลิ่มเลือดรักษา ischaemic stroke ทำให้อาการแย่ลงและต้องหยุดยาและแก้ฤทธิ์ยาเร่งด่วน
tempoNote: Usually within the first 24–36 hours after alteplase or tenecteplase
feat: Neurological worsening, headache, vomiting or reduced consciousness during or after thrombolysis
Occurs in a few per cent of treated patients; most haemorrhagic transformation is asymptomatic
Risk increases with large infarct, high NIHSS, older age, hyperglycaemia, uncontrolled BP, many microbleeds
Parenchymal haematoma type 2 carries the worst outcome
Also orolingual angioedema and systemic bleeding as other complications
inv: Stop infusion and do urgent non-contrast CT
Fibrinogen, platelets, PT/INR, aPTT, group and crossmatch
Classify by ECASS/Heidelberg categories

case.who: 76-year-old woman from Saraburi given alteplase 2 hours after left MCA stroke
case.story: Thirty minutes after the infusion ended, she vomited and became drowsy.
case.exam: GCS fell from 14 to 9, BP 196/104, worsened right hemiplegia.
case.tests: CT shows a large left frontal parenchymal haematoma with mass effect; fibrinogen 120 mg/dL.
case.q: What are the immediate steps?
case.a: Symptomatic ICH after thrombolysis: give cryoprecipitate (and consider tranexamic acid), lower BP, involve neurosurgery and manage ICP.

read.where: Chapter 8 Stroke and Cerebrovascular Diseases — Reperfusion Therapies for Acute Ischaemic Stroke
Chapter 8 Stroke and Cerebrovascular Diseases — Management of Acute Intracerebral Haemorrhage

det.patho: Ischaemia damages the blood-brain barrier and microvasculature; reperfusion and plasmin-mediated fibrinolysis allow blood to leak into infarcted tissue. Thrombolytic agents also deplete fibrinogen, impairing clot formation. Larger infarcts, older age, prior antithrombotics, hyperglycaemia and hypertension enlarge this risk.
det.clinical: Symptomatic haemorrhage manifests as new headache, nausea, worsening deficit or falling consciousness, mostly within 24 hours. Asymptomatic petechial haemorrhagic transformation is far commoner and generally benign. Remote haemorrhages outside the infarct suggest amyloid angiopathy.
det.diagnosis: Any neurological worsening during or after thrombolysis triggers stopping the infusion and urgent CT. Symptomatic ICH is defined in trials by haemorrhage plus a set increase in NIHSS (e.g. 4 points); definitions vary between SITS-MOST, ECASS and NINDS. Coagulation tests including fibrinogen guide reversal.
det.treatment: Stop the thrombolytic, give cryoprecipitate to raise fibrinogen and consider tranexamic acid or aminocaproic acid. Platelets are considered when antiplatelet effect is relevant, though evidence is weak. Control blood pressure, manage raised ICP and involve neurosurgery for selected haematomas. Antithrombotics are withheld initially. Prevention relies on careful selection, BP below 185/110 before and 180/105 after treatment, and glucose control.
det.prognosis: Symptomatic parenchymal haemorrhage carries high mortality, around half in many series.
pearls: Neurological worsening on thrombolysis: stop the infusion first, then scan.
Check fibrinogen; cryoprecipitate is the main reversal tool.
Strict post-thrombolysis BP control reduces haemorrhage risk.
det.thd: เลือดออกในสมองหลังให้ยาละลายลิ่มเลือดพบได้ไม่บ่อยแต่รุนแรง ผู้ป่วยมีอาการแย่ลง ปวดศีรษะ อาเจียน หรือซึมลง ต้องหยุดยาทันทีและทำ CT ด่วน ตรวจ fibrinogen และการแข็งตัวของเลือด รักษาด้วย cryoprecipitate ร่วมกับ tranexamic acid คุมความดันโลหิต และปรึกษาศัลยแพทย์ระบบประสาท การป้องกันคือเลือกผู้ป่วยให้เหมาะสมและคุมความดันอย่างเคร่งครัด

qx.stem: A 70-year-old woman is 40 minutes into an alteplase infusion for a right MCA stroke when she develops severe headache, vomiting and a fall in GCS from 14 to 10. BP is 205/110 mmHg. The infusion is stopped and an urgent CT shows a large right hemispheric haematoma.
qx.q: Which is the most appropriate pharmacological step after stopping the infusion?
opts: Give cryoprecipitate (to raise fibrinogen) and consider tranexamic acid, check fibrinogen, and lower BP
Give protamine sulfate
Restart alteplase at half dose
Give idarucizumab 5 g IV
Give IV vitamin K and wait for the INR
qx.why: Symptomatic haemorrhage after alteplase reflects fibrinogen depletion and plasmin activity, so guidelines suggest cryoprecipitate (about 10 units, more if fibrinogen remains under 1.5 g/L) and an antifibrinolytic such as tranexamic acid, with BP control and neurosurgical review. Protamine reverses heparin, idarucizumab reverses dabigatran, and vitamin K does not address thrombolytic-induced coagulopathy.

name: Haemorrhagic stroke
formal: Stroke due to intracerebral or subarachnoid haemorrhage, most often from hypertensive small-vessel disease, aneurysm or amyloid angiopathy, causing sudden deficits and high mortality.
simple: A stroke caused by bleeding in or around the brain, usually causing sudden headache and weakness.
th: stroke จากเลือดออกในเนื้อสมองหรือใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมอง สาเหตุบ่อยคือความดันสูง หลอดเลือดโป่งพอง และ amyloid angiopathy
tempoNote: Sudden onset with early worsening over hours as haematoma expands
feat: Sudden focal deficit, often with headache, vomiting and reduced consciousness
Two main forms: intracerebral haemorrhage (ICH) and subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH)
Deep ICH (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum) points to hypertensive arteriopathy
Lobar ICH in the elderly suggests cerebral amyloid angiopathy
Haematoma expansion in the first hours drives early deterioration
inv: Urgent non-contrast CT
CTA for spot sign, aneurysm, AVM or venous thrombosis
Coagulation profile, platelets, glucose; MRI later for underlying cause

case.who: 54-year-old man from Udon Thani, a heavy drinker not taking his antihypertensives
case.story: Collapsed while at a funeral ceremony with sudden right-sided weakness and headache.
case.exam: BP 220/130, GCS 12, right hemiplegia, left gaze deviation.
case.tests: CT: 35 mL left putaminal haematoma with small intraventricular extension.
case.q: What is the cause and what are the first treatment priorities?
case.a: Hypertensive deep ICH; lower systolic BP towards 140 mmHg, reverse any coagulopathy, neurosurgical review and stroke unit care.
