det.patho: Haemorrhagic stroke covers spontaneous bleeding into brain tissue or subarachnoid space. ICH arises mainly from rupture of small penetrating arteries damaged by chronic hypertension or from amyloid-laden cortical vessels; SAH is mostly due to ruptured saccular aneurysms. Secondary causes include AVMs, cavernomas, tumours, anticoagulants, venous thrombosis and drugs such as methamfetamine.
det.clinical: Onset is abrupt, frequently during activity. Headache and vomiting are more common than in ischaemic stroke, and consciousness may fall as the haematoma enlarges or hydrocephalus develops. SAH typically gives a thunderclap headache with meningism. Haemorrhagic stroke makes up a larger share of strokes in Asia, including Thailand, than in Western populations.
det.diagnosis: CT confirms haemorrhage within minutes. Location and patient age guide the search for a cause: CTA for vascular lesions, MRI with SWI for amyloid angiopathy, cavernoma or tumour, and DSA when a vascular malformation is suspected. Scores such as ICH score help communication but should not lead to early withdrawal of care.
det.treatment: Acute care bundles combine intensive BP lowering (targeting about 140 mmHg systolic, avoiding sharp drops), rapid anticoagulant reversal, glucose and temperature control and early stroke unit care. Surgery is considered for cerebellar haemorrhage with compression or hydrocephalus and for selected lobar clots; minimally invasive evacuation is an evolving option. SAH needs early aneurysm securing and nimodipine.
det.prognosis: Mortality is higher than for ischaemic stroke, around 40% at one month for ICH; survivors often recover more than initially expected.
pearls: You cannot tell bleed from clot at the bedside; scan first.
Deep bleed with hypertension is typical; lobar bleed in the elderly suggests amyloid angiopathy.
Avoid early do-not-resuscitate decisions; they worsen outcomes.
det.thd: Haemorrhagic stroke คือ stroke จากเลือดออกในเนื้อสมองหรือใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมอง สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยคือความดันโลหิตสูง หลอดเลือดโป่งพองแตก และ amyloid angiopathy ผู้ป่วยมีอาการอ่อนแรงเฉียบพลัน ปวดศีรษะ อาเจียน และซึมลง CT ยืนยันได้ทันที การรักษาคือลดความดันอย่างระมัดระวัง แก้ฤทธิ์ยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือด และพิจารณาผ่าตัดในบางราย

name: Harlequin syndrome
formal: Unilateral facial flushing and sweating with contralateral anhidrosis from sympathetic dysfunction, often with Horner or Adie pupil, and benign or following surgery or lesions.
simple: A rare condition where one side of the face flushes and sweats while the other stays pale and dry.
th: ใบหน้าแดงและมีเหงื่อออกครึ่งซีกเมื่อร้อนหรือออกกำลัง ขณะที่อีกซีกไม่มีเหงื่อและซีด เพราะเส้นประสาท sympathetic ฝั่งที่ซีดเสีย
tempoNote: Asymmetry appears episodically with heat, exercise or emotion; the underlying deficit is usually permanent
feat: Sharp midline demarcation: one side flushed and sweaty, the other pale and dry
The pale, anhidrotic side is the abnormal side
May coexist with Horner syndrome or tonic (Adie) pupil on the same or opposite side
Usually idiopathic and benign; secondary cases after neck or chest surgery, sympathetic blocks, tumours or carotid dissection
inv: Clinical observation after exercise or heat; thermoregulatory sweat test or starch-iodine test
Pupil examination for Horner or tonic pupil
MRI head, neck and upper chest, plus CT chest, if acquired, painful or with other signs

case.story: After jogging, the right half of her face turns bright red and sweaty while the left stays pale and dry; otherwise well.
case.exam: Mild left ptosis with smaller left pupil in dim light; no other neurological signs.
case.tests: Starch-iodine test shows left facial anhidrosis; MRI of neck and chest apex normal.
case.q: Which side is abnormal, and what pathway is affected?
case.a: The pale, dry left side — loss of left-sided sympathetic sudomotor and vasomotor supply, i.e. idiopathic Harlequin syndrome with partial Horner.

read.where: 8 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System

det.patho: Facial sweating and flushing depend on preganglionic sympathetic fibres leaving the upper thoracic cord (around T2–T3) and synapsing in the superior cervical ganglion. Interruption on one side causes loss of flushing and sweating there, and the intact side appears exaggerated by contrast. Pupillary fibres (around T1) may be spared, explaining why Horner signs are absent in many cases.
det.clinical: Patients usually notice the striking red-and-white face during exercise, heat or emotion and worry about the flushed side. Most cases are idiopathic and stable. Secondary forms follow thoracic surgery, internal jugular cannulation, sympathetic blocks, superior mediastinal tumours, brainstem lesions or carotid dissection. It belongs to a spectrum of autonomic neuropathies that includes Adie and Ross syndromes.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, confirmed by sweat testing that shows anhidrosis on the pale side. Examine pupils and other sweating territories. Imaging of the cervicothoracic sympathetic chain is needed for acquired, painful or progressive cases, or when Horner signs are present. Autonomic function testing helps if widespread dysautonomia is suspected.
det.treatment: Idiopathic cases need reassurance only. If cosmetically troublesome, contralateral sympathectomy has been used but is rarely justified, and it may cause compensatory sweating elsewhere. Secondary causes are treated directly. Advise patients about heat intolerance if large areas are anhidrotic.
det.prognosis: Idiopathic Harlequin syndrome is benign and usually non-progressive.
pearls: The pale side is the diseased side.
Look for associated Horner or Adie pupils.
New onset after neck or chest surgery is usually iatrogenic.
det.thd: Harlequin syndrome คือใบหน้าแดงและมีเหงื่อครึ่งซีกเมื่อร้อนหรือออกกำลัง ส่วนอีกซีกซีดและไม่มีเหงื่อ ซีกที่ผิดปกติคือซีกที่ซีด เพราะเส้นประสาท sympathetic ฝั่งนั้นเสีย อาจพบร่วมกับ Horner หรือ Adie pupil ส่วนใหญ่ไม่ทราบสาเหตุและไม่อันตราย แต่ถ้าเกิดหลังผ่าตัดหรือมีอาการอื่นควรตรวจภาพบริเวณคอและทรวงอก

name: Hartnup disease
formal: Autosomal recessive neutral amino acid transport defect (SLC6A19) causing pellagra-like rash, intermittent cerebellar ataxia, psychiatric symptoms and aminoaciduria; responds to nicotinamide.
simple: An inherited problem absorbing some amino acids, causing sun-sensitive rashes, unsteadiness and mood changes.
th: โรคยีนด้อยที่ลำไส้และไตดูดกลับกรดอะมิโนกลาง (รวม tryptophan) ไม่ได้ ทำให้ผื่นแบบ pellagra เมื่อโดนแดด เดินเซเป็นพัก ๆ และอาการทางจิต ตอบสนองต่อ nicotinamide
tempoNote: Attacks triggered by sunlight, fever, poor diet or stress; normal between episodes
feat: Photosensitive scaly red rash on exposed skin resembling pellagra
Episodes of cerebellar ataxia, nystagmus and tremor lasting days to weeks
Mood change, anxiety, delirium or psychosis during attacks
Many people found by screening never have symptoms; diet determines expression
inv: Urine amino acids: large excess of neutral amino acids (alanine, serine, threonine, tryptophan, etc.) with normal plasma levels
Urine indican and indole derivatives raised from gut bacterial breakdown of unabsorbed tryptophan
SLC6A19 gene testing

case.story: After a school camp in strong sun he developed a red scaly rash on face and arms, then three days of staggering gait and irritability; similar but milder episode last year.
case.exam: Photodistributed dermatitis, broad-based gait, horizontal nystagmus, otherwise normal.
case.tests: Urine shows marked neutral aminoaciduria; plasma amino acids normal; MRI normal.
case.q: Why does the boy develop pellagra-like features, and what treatment helps?
case.a: Tryptophan is lost in urine and poorly absorbed, so niacin synthesis falls; oral nicotinamide, a high-protein diet and sun protection.

read.where: Chapter 24 Cerebellar Ataxias and Related Conditions — Other Metabolic Causes of Ataxia

det.patho: Biallelic SLC6A19 variants disable the B0AT1 transporter that absorbs neutral amino acids in the small intestine and reabsorbs them in the proximal tubule. Loss of tryptophan reduces endogenous nicotinamide (NAD) production, which underlies the skin and nervous system features when dietary niacin is marginal. Incidence on newborn screening is about 1 in 30,000, but most are symptom-free.
det.clinical: Symptoms appear in childhood, usually triggered by sun exposure, fever, poor diet or drugs. Attacks combine pellagra-like dermatitis with reversible cerebellar ataxia and psychiatric symptoms; intelligence is usually normal. Some adults remain asymptomatic throughout life.
det.diagnosis: A characteristic urinary amino acid pattern with normal plasma levels is the key; only the neutral amino acids are lost, unlike generalised Fanconi syndrome. Genetic testing confirms. Rule out dietary pellagra and other causes of episodic ataxia.
det.treatment: Oral nicotinamide during and between symptomatic periods, an adequate protein diet, and strict sun protection. Avoid fasting and treat infections promptly. Tryptophan ethyl ester has been tried experimentally.
det.prognosis: Generally good with nutrition and nicotinamide; attacks become less frequent with age.
pearls: Pellagra-like rash + intermittent ataxia in a well-fed child: check urine amino acids.
Plasma amino acids are normal; the defect is transport, not metabolism.
Most screened cases never become ill; disease reflects diet and environment.
det.thd: Hartnup disease เกิดจากยีน SLC6A19 ทำให้ลำไส้และไตดูดกรดอะมิโนกลางไม่ได้ โดยเฉพาะ tryptophan ซึ่งเป็นสารตั้งต้นของ niacin เด็กจึงมีผื่นแบบ pellagra เมื่อโดนแดด เดินเซและอารมณ์แปรปรวนเป็นช่วง ๆ ตรวจปัสสาวะพบกรดอะมิโนกลางสูงแต่ในเลือดปกติ รักษาด้วย nicotinamide อาหารโปรตีนเพียงพอ และป้องกันแสงแดด

name: Hashimoto’s encephalopathy
formal: Steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis (SREAT) and anti-thyroid antibodies, with seizures, myoclonus, stroke-like episodes and cognitive decline.
simple: A rare immune brain condition linked to thyroid antibodies, causing confusion, seizures and memory problems that improve with steroids.
more: Hashimoto encephalopathy or SREAT with confusion, seizures and anti-thyroid antibodies, dramatically responding to steroids.
ab: steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis
th: สมองเสื่อมหรือสับสนที่ตอบสนองต่อ steroid ในผู้ที่มีแอนติบอดีต่อต่อมไทรอยด์ (anti-TPO) — เป็นการวินิจฉัยแบบตัดโรคอื่นออก
tempoNote: Either relapsing stroke-like or seizure episodes, or a diffuse progressive course over weeks to months
feat: Fluctuating confusion, cognitive decline, psychosis or reduced consciousness
Tremor, myoclonus, ataxia and seizures are common
Stroke-like focal episodes in a relapsing form
Raised anti-TPO or anti-thyroglobulin antibodies; thyroid function may be normal
Marked improvement with corticosteroids
inv: Anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies, TSH and free T4
Comprehensive neuronal antibody panel (serum and CSF) to exclude a defined autoimmune encephalitis
CSF: raised protein, mild or no pleocytosis; EEG: diffuse slowing, sometimes triphasic or epileptiform discharges
MRI often normal or with nonspecific white matter change; DWI to exclude CJD

case.story: Six weeks of worsening forgetfulness, episodes of confusion and jerks of both hands; one generalised seizure.
case.exam: Inattentive, MMSE 19/30, multifocal myoclonus, postural tremor, unsteady tandem gait; no focal weakness.
case.tests: TSH 6.2, free T4 normal, anti-TPO 1450 IU/mL. CSF protein 78 mg/dL, 2 cells. Neuronal antibody panel negative. MRI DWI normal; EEG diffuse slowing. RT-QuIC negative.
case.q: Why is this label reached only after excluding other causes, and what response is expected?
case.a: Anti-TPO antibodies are common in healthy people and are not pathogenic in the brain, so prion disease, infections, metabolic causes and antibody-defined encephalitis must be ruled out first; SREAT typically improves strikingly with corticosteroids.

read.where: Chapter 57 Seizures and General Medical Disorders

det.patho: The mechanism is uncertain; anti-thyroid antibodies are viewed as a marker of an autoimmune tendency rather than the cause, because they occur in up to 10–20% of healthy adults and do not bind the brain in a relevant way. Proposed mechanisms include cerebral vasculitis, immune-complex deposition or unidentified neuronal antibodies. Many historical cases would now be reclassified as defined antibody-mediated encephalitides.
det.clinical: Two patterns are described: a vasculitic type with recurrent stroke-like events and a diffuse progressive type with cognitive decline, psychiatric symptoms and confusion. Myoclonus, tremor, seizures and fluctuating consciousness are frequent across both. Women are affected more often, and thyroid status may be euthyroid, hypothyroid or occasionally hyperthyroid.
det.diagnosis: It is a diagnosis of exclusion: compatible encephalopathy, raised thyroid antibodies, no known neuronal antibodies and no alternative cause, plus steroid responsiveness. Mandatory exclusions include infection, prion disease, metabolic and toxic causes, non-convulsive status and defined autoimmune encephalitis. CSF protein rise and diffuse EEG slowing support but do not confirm it.
det.treatment: High-dose corticosteroids are the mainstay, often IV methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisolone tapered over months. IVIG or plasma exchange are used if steroids fail or are contraindicated, and azathioprine, mycophenolate or rituximab may be needed for relapse. Correct thyroid dysfunction, but thyroid hormone alone does not resolve the encephalopathy.
det.prognosis: Most patients improve substantially with steroids, but relapses occur, and lack of steroid response should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis.
pearls: Anti-TPO alone is common and nonspecific; never stop the workup there.
Exclude CJD before giving the label to a patient with myoclonus and dementia.
Steroid responsiveness is part of the definition.
det.thd: Hashimoto encephalopathy หรือ SREAT คือภาวะสมองทำงานผิดปกติที่ตอบสนองต่อ steroid ในผู้ที่มี anti-TPO สูง ผู้ป่วยมีสับสน ความจำเสื่อม ชัก กระตุก มือสั่น หรืออาการคล้ายอัมพาตเป็นพัก ๆ แอนติบอดีไทรอยด์เป็นเพียงตัวบ่งชี้ ไม่ใช่ตัวก่อโรค จึงต้องแยก CJD การติดเชื้อ ภาวะเมตาบอลิก และ autoimmune encephalitis ชนิดอื่นก่อน รักษาด้วย steroid ขนาดสูงแล้วค่อย ๆ ลด

qx.stem: A 51-year-old woman from Lampang develops two weeks of fluctuating confusion, tremor and multifocal myoclonus, then focal status epilepticus needing midazolam infusion. She is euthyroid on levothyroxine. Anti-TPO antibodies are 1,800 IU/mL. MRI is normal; CSF shows protein 0.85 g/L with 3 cells/µL. EEG shows diffuse slowing without periodic complexes. Infection screens are negative.
qx.q: Which approach is most appropriate?
opts: Diagnose Hashimoto encephalopathy on the anti-TPO titre alone and stop further testing
Avoid immunotherapy until CSF RT-QuIC is reported
Send serum and CSF neural antibody panels, check RT-QuIC, and start IV methylprednisolone without waiting
Treat with antiseizure drugs only because thyroid antibodies are common in healthy people
Increase the levothyroxine dose to suppress the antibodies
qx.why: Steroid-responsive encephalopathy with autoimmune thyroiditis (SREAT) is a diagnosis of exclusion; anti-TPO is present in up to 10–20% of healthy adults and is not pathogenic. Current practice is to test for specific neural antibodies (NMDAR, LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-A/B, GAD65 and others) and exclude CJD, while starting high-dose steroids early because delay worsens outcome. Thyroid hormone dose does not influence the encephalopathy.

qx.stem: A 57-year-old woman from Chiang Mai has three weeks of confusion, myoclonic jerks and one seizure, with stroke-like episodes of left arm weakness that resolved. She is euthyroid, anti-TPO antibody titre is very high, EEG shows generalised slowing, CSF protein is 90 mg/dL and brain MRI is largely normal.
qx.q: Which statement about this diagnosis is correct?
opts: The anti-TPO antibody is itself pathogenic and the titre correlates with severity
It is a steroid-responsive encephalopathy with thyroid autoimmunity (SREAT) that is a diagnosis of exclusion
MRI is almost always markedly abnormal
The patient must be hypothyroid at presentation
Only patients with a goitre are affected
qx.why: Hashimoto's encephalopathy (SREAT) presents with confusion, seizures, myoclonus, stroke-like episodes and psychiatric features in a euthyroid or mildly abnormal patient with high anti-TPO titres, normal or non-specific MRI, EEG slowing and raised CSF protein. Anti-TPO is common in healthy people and the titre does not track severity, so autoimmune encephalitis, infection and prion disease must be excluded.

qx.stem: The patient above has had infectious, metabolic, autoimmune encephalitis antibody and prion work-ups, all negative. Her team asks about treatment.
qx.q: What is the first-line treatment?
opts: Plasma exchange alone
Intravenous immunoglobulin as sole therapy because it lowers anti-TPO titres
Corticosteroids, such as intravenous methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisolone, with immunosuppressants or rituximab for steroid-resistant disease
Radioactive iodine
Levothyroxine at high dose only
qx.why: Most patients respond to corticosteroids (IV methylprednisolone 500 to 1,000 mg daily, then oral prednisolone about 1 to 2 mg/kg), with azathioprine, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide or rituximab for those who relapse or fail to respond. name: Hashimoto’s thyroiditis
formal: Autoimmune thyroiditis with anti-TPO antibodies causing hypothyroidism, with neuromuscular complications such as myopathy, carpal tunnel and neuropathy, and association with encephalopathy.
simple: An autoimmune thyroid disease causing an underactive thyroid, which can cause tiredness, weakness and slowed thinking.

feat: Endocrine disease: goitre, fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, menstrual change

case.exam: Diffuse firm goitre, puffy face, proximal weakness 4/5, delayed relaxation of ankle jerks, positive Tinel sign at both wrists.

det.patho: T cells and antibodies against thyroid peroxidase and thyroglobulin cause lymphocytic infiltration and gradual destruction of thyroid follicles. It is the commonest cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions and is several times more common in women. Neurological effects arise mostly from hormone deficiency (glycosaminoglycan deposition, slowed muscle metabolism), with a separate autoimmune association with encephalopathy.
det.clinical: This is a thyroid disease; neurologists meet it through its complications. Hypothyroid myopathy produces proximal weakness, myalgia, cramps, muscle enlargement and sometimes very high CK; myoedema can be seen on percussion. Entrapment neuropathies, especially carpal tunnel, and a length-dependent sensory neuropathy occur. Cognitive slowing, depression and ataxia may develop, and severe deficiency leads to myxoedema coma.
det.diagnosis: Raised TSH with low free T4 confirms overt hypothyroidism; anti-TPO identifies the autoimmune cause. Always check TSH in unexplained myopathy with raised CK before biopsy. Electrophysiology confirms entrapment or neuropathy. Thyroid antibodies are common in healthy people, so their presence does not prove Hashimoto encephalopathy in an encephalopathic patient.
det.treatment: Levothyroxine replacement, starting low in older or cardiac patients, titrated to TSH. Myopathy and neuropathy typically improve over months; carpal tunnel may still need surgery. Myxoedema coma needs ICU care with IV thyroid hormone and hydrocortisone. Statins can aggravate hypothyroid myopathy, so correct thyroid status first.
det.prognosis: Excellent with replacement; neuromuscular complications usually recover over 3–12 months.
pearls: Check TSH in every patient with raised CK and proximal weakness.
Delayed relaxation of the ankle jerk is a classic bedside clue.
Positive anti-TPO is common in the population; do not over-attribute encephalopathy to it.
det.thd: Hashimoto’s thyroiditis คือไทรอยด์อักเสบเรื้อรังจากภูมิคุ้มกัน เป็นสาเหตุหลักของไทรอยด์ทำงานต่ำ ผลต่อระบบประสาทเกิดจากการขาดฮอร์โมน เช่น กล้ามเนื้อต้นแขนขาอ่อนแรงและ CK สูง ตะคริว carpal tunnel ปลายประสาทชา และความคิดช้า และยังสัมพันธ์กับ Hashimoto encephalopathy วินิจฉัยด้วย TSH, FT4 และ anti-TPO รักษาด้วย levothyroxine ซึ่งอาการกล้ามเนื้อมักดีขึ้นภายในหลายเดือน

name: Haw river syndrome
formal: Autosomal dominant dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy variant (ATN1 CAG expansion) in African-American families with ataxia, chorea, dementia, seizures and basal ganglia calcification.
simple: A rare inherited brain disease with unsteadiness, jerky movements and memory loss, first described in one family.
th: รูปแบบหนึ่งของ DRPLA ที่ถ่ายทอดแบบยีนเด่นจากการขยายตัวของ CAG ใน ATN1 รายงานในครอบครัวชาวแอฟริกันอเมริกัน มี ataxia chorea สมองเสื่อม ชัก และหินปูนที่ basal ganglia

feat: Progressive cerebellar ataxia with chorea and dementia
Seizures reported, but myoclonic epilepsy less prominent than in juvenile DRPLA
Basal ganglia calcification and white matter demyelination; neuroaxonal dystrophy at pathology
Single large African-American kindred from North Carolina; autosomal dominant with anticipation
inv: ATN1 CAG repeat testing (same mutation as DRPLA)
MRI: cerebellar and brainstem atrophy, white matter changes; CT for calcification
Exclude Huntington disease and HDL2 (also relevant in African ancestry)

case.who: 34-year-old man (invented teaching case) with African ancestry, family history of 'shaking and memory loss' in father and aunt
case.story: Five years of unsteady walking and fidgety movements, now forgetting work tasks; one generalised seizure.
case.exam: Gait ataxia, generalised chorea, dysarthria, frontal executive impairment.
case.tests: HTT normal; ATN1 CAG expansion confirmed; CT shows basal ganglia calcification.
case.q: What is the relationship between this syndrome and DRPLA?
case.a: Haw River syndrome is the same ATN1 CAG expansion as DRPLA, described as a distinct phenotype in one family; it is now regarded as a variant of DRPLA.

det.patho: An expanded CAG repeat in ATN1 (atrophin-1) produces a polyglutamine protein that accumulates in neuronal nuclei and disrupts transcription, as in other polyglutamine diseases. Larger repeats give earlier and more severe disease, with anticipation particularly via paternal transmission. The original kindred also showed basal ganglia calcification, neuroaxonal dystrophy and demyelination that were less typical of Japanese DRPLA.
det.clinical: Described in a single extended African-American family in North Carolina in the 1990s, with adult-onset ataxia, chorea, seizures and dementia progressing to death after many years. Seizures were present but myoclonic epilepsy was not prominent. Little is known beyond that kindred and its later recognition as DRPLA.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is by ATN1 repeat testing in a patient with ataxia, chorea and dementia and a dominant family history. Huntington disease and HDL2 must be excluded, particularly in people of African ancestry. Imaging supports but does not confirm.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy exists. Symptomatic care includes antiseizure drugs, tetrabenazine or antipsychotics for chorea where appropriate, physiotherapy, speech therapy, and support for cognitive and behavioural decline. Genetic counselling for relatives is essential.
det.prognosis: Progressive over years to decades; outcomes are largely extrapolated from the original family and DRPLA cohorts.
pearls: Haw River syndrome = DRPLA genotype (ATN1 CAG) with a distinctive family phenotype.
Ataxia + chorea + dementia with dominant inheritance: test HTT, ATN1, JPH3 and SCA17.
Calcification in the basal ganglia was a notable feature of the original kindred.

name: Head tremor
formal: Rhythmic oscillation of the head, either yes-yes or no-no, from essential tremor, dystonic tremor or cervical dystonia, and sometimes from cerebellar lesions.
simple: A rhythmic shaking or nodding of the head that the person cannot control.
th: การสั่นของศีรษะเป็นจังหวะ แบบพยักหน้าหรือส่ายหน้า มักเกิดจาก essential tremor, dystonic tremor หรือ cervical dystonia และบางครั้งจากรอยโรคสมองน้อย
tempoNote: Usually insidious and slowly progressive; abrupt onset suggests a structural or drug cause
feat: A sign rather than a disease: rhythmic horizontal ('no-no') or vertical ('yes-yes') head oscillation
Essential tremor: regular, often with arm and voice tremor, more common in older women
Dystonic head tremor: irregular, jerky, directional, with null point, sensory trick and head turning or tilt
Cerebellar titubation: slow truncal and head oscillation with other cerebellar signs
Usually disappears when lying with the head supported, except in dystonia sometimes
inv: Clinical examination with head in neutral and in different positions; look for subtle cervical dystonia
Accelerometry/EMG in uncertain cases
MRI if cerebellar signs, rapid onset or young age; thyroid and drug review

case.story: Head shakes 'no-no' for three years, worse when she is nervous; no family history of tremor.
case.exam: Irregular horizontal head tremor that lessens when she touches her chin, slight head turn to the right with hypertrophied left sternocleidomastoid; minimal arm tremor.
case.tests: Thyroid normal; EMG shows irregular bursts; MRI normal.
case.q: Is this essential tremor or something else?
case.a: Dystonic head tremor from cervical dystonia — irregular, with a sensory trick and abnormal head posture; botulinum toxin is the best treatment.

read.where: 8 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System

det.patho: Head tremor arises from oscillation in networks linking the cerebellum, brainstem and basal ganglia. In essential tremor, cerebello-thalamo-cortical dysfunction is central, whereas dystonic head tremor reflects abnormal sensorimotor integration in cervical dystonia. Cerebellar titubation results from midline cerebellar (vermis) or outflow lesions.
det.clinical: Isolated head tremor in a middle-aged woman is more often dystonic than essential. Clues to dystonia include irregularity, directionality, a null point where tremor stops, a sensory trick and abnormal posture or muscle hypertrophy. Essential tremor head tremor usually accompanies arm tremor and may be 'yes-yes' or 'no-no'. Titubation occurs with cerebellar disease such as MS, stroke or degeneration, accompanied by gait ataxia. Functional head tremor varies with distraction and entrainment.
det.diagnosis: Careful observation in different head positions, while speaking and while distracted, separates most causes. Palpation of neck muscles and the search for subtle cervical dystonia are essential. Drug-induced and enhanced physiological tremor (valproate, lithium, thyroxine excess) should be excluded. Neurophysiology and MRI are used when the pattern is unclear or other signs are present.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin to the relevant cervical muscles is first-line for dystonic head tremor and helps essential head tremor too. Propranolol and primidone have modest effect on head tremor in essential tremor. Treat cerebellar causes where possible. DBS or focused ultrasound is reserved for disabling refractory cases, with bilateral procedures more relevant for midline tremor.
det.prognosis: Usually slowly progressive or stable; mostly a social rather than disabling problem.
pearls: Isolated head tremor in a woman: look hard for cervical dystonia.
A null point or sensory trick strongly favours dystonic tremor.
Botulinum toxin works better than oral drugs for head tremor.
det.thd: Head tremor เป็นอาการไม่ใช่โรค คือศีรษะสั่นเป็นจังหวะแบบพยักหน้าหรือส่ายหน้า สาเหตุบ่อยคือ essential tremor และ dystonic tremor จาก cervical dystonia ถ้าสั่นไม่สม่ำเสมอ มีท่าคอเอียง หรือหยุดสั่นเมื่อแตะคาง ให้นึกถึง dystonia ถ้ามีเดินเซร่วมให้นึกถึงโรคสมองน้อย การรักษาที่ได้ผลดีคือ botulinum toxin ส่วนยา propranolol หรือ primidone ช่วยได้บ้าง

formal: Pain in the head, either primary (migraine, tension-type, cluster) or secondary to conditions such as haemorrhage, meningitis, giant-cell arteritis, tumour or raised pressure; red flags guide investigation.
simple: Pain felt anywhere in the head, most often harmless, but sometimes a sign of a serious illness.

det.patho: Pain arises from pain-sensitive structures: meninges, large intracranial vessels, venous sinuses, cranial nerves and extracranial tissues. Primary headaches involve activation and sensitisation of the trigeminovascular system and central pain networks, while secondary headaches reflect traction, inflammation, raised pressure or vessel injury.
det.clinical: The history is the main diagnostic tool: onset speed, pattern over time, triggers, accompanying features and family history. Most patients have migraine or tension-type headache. Red flags help pick the minority with secondary causes. Analgesic overuse often turns episodic headache into daily headache.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 provides operational criteria for each headache type. Neuroimaging is not needed for typical primary headache with a normal examination. Thunderclap headache needs CT and LP if CT is negative beyond about 6 hours. Older new-onset headache needs ESR, CRP and temporal artery assessment.
det.treatment: Treatment depends on diagnosis. Primary headaches are managed with acute medication limits, lifestyle factors and preventives (e.g. propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate, CGRP-pathway drugs). Secondary headaches require treatment of the cause. Patient education and headache diaries are useful in all.
det.prognosis: Most primary headaches are manageable; secondary headache outcome depends on the cause.
pearls: Change in pattern is a red flag even in a known migraineur.
Analgesic use on 10–15 or more days per month risks medication-overuse headache.
Examine the fundi in every headache patient.

det.patho: Primary headaches arise from dysfunction of the trigeminovascular system and its brainstem and hypothalamic modulators, with CGRP and PACAP as key mediators. Secondary headaches result from traction, inflammation or compression of pain-sensing tissues, namely meninges, large vessels and venous sinuses. The brain parenchyma itself is insensitive to pain.
det.clinical: Most patients have migraine or tension-type headache. Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias have short unilateral attacks with autonomic features. Secondary headaches present with new, changing or atypical patterns and red flags: systemic symptoms, neurological deficit, sudden onset, older age, positional or Valsalva triggers, pregnancy, immunosuppression or papilloedema.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 provides operational criteria. Diagnosis is clinical in most primary headaches; investigations follow red flags. Medication overuse should be sought in every frequent headache. Neuroimaging in typical migraine with normal examination is rarely helpful.
det.treatment: Acute therapy ranges from NSAIDs and triptans to gepants and lasmiditan for migraine, oxygen and injectable sumatriptan for cluster headache. Preventive drugs include beta-blockers, topiramate, amitriptyline, candesartan, CGRP-targeted antibodies and onabotulinumtoxinA. Secondary headaches require treatment of the cause. Lifestyle, sleep and comorbidity management support all.
det.prognosis: Primary headaches are usually manageable but may be lifelong; secondary headache outcome follows the underlying disease.
pearls: Use SNNOOP10 red flags to decide who needs urgent work-up.
Always look at the fundi.

det.patho: Reduced cardiac output, blood stasis in a dilated or akinetic ventricle and frequent atrial fibrillation predispose to embolism. Chronic low cerebral perfusion, microemboli and shared vascular risk factors contribute to brain atrophy and cognitive decline. Neurohormonal activation and treatment can cause electrolyte disturbances.
det.clinical: Neurological presentations include embolic stroke, transient ischaemic attacks, syncope, delirium during decompensation and slowly progressive cognitive impairment that affects self-care and medication adherence. Depression and sleep-disordered breathing are also common. This entry is not a neurological disease but a systemic condition with neurological effects.
det.diagnosis: In stroke patients, echocardiography and rhythm monitoring identify cardiac sources. Cognitive screening is worthwhile in heart failure clinics because impairment affects self-management. Delirium should prompt checks for hyponatraemia, hypoperfusion, infection and drug effects.
det.treatment: Optimise guideline-directed heart failure therapy. Anticoagulate for atrial fibrillation or LV thrombus; anticoagulation in sinus rhythm without thrombus is not routinely recommended. Manage vascular risk factors and screen for sleep apnoea. Involve family support for cognitive impairment.
det.prognosis: Stroke and cognitive impairment worsen survival and quality of life in heart failure.
pearls: Check echo for LV thrombus after anterior MI with stroke.
Cognitive impairment in heart failure undermines adherence; screen for it.

name: Heat stroke
formal: Hyperthermia above 40 C with CNS dysfunction, including delirium, seizures and coma, from environmental heat or exertion, and cerebellar injury in survivors.
simple: A life-threatening overheating of the body that causes confusion, seizures or collapse.
th: ภาวะร่างกายร้อนเกิน 40 องศาเซลเซียสร่วมกับสมองทำงานผิดปกติ เช่น สับสน ชัก โคม่า จากอากาศร้อนหรือออกแรงหนัก ผู้รอดชีวิตอาจมี cerebellar ataxia
tempoNote: Develops over hours; neurological sequelae may persist
feat: Core temperature above about 40 C with confusion, delirium, seizures or coma
Exertional type in soldiers, athletes, labourers; classic type in elderly during heatwaves
Sweating may persist in exertional cases; skin hot
Multi-organ injury: rhabdomyolysis, renal failure, liver injury, DIC
Survivors may have persistent cerebellar syndrome from Purkinje cell loss
inv: Rectal or oesophageal core temperature
CK, renal and liver function, coagulation, glucose, electrolytes
CT or MRI brain if coma persists after cooling; later MRI may show cerebellar atrophy

case.story: Collapsed during a midday training run in April, then became combative and had a seizure.
case.exam: Rectal temperature 41.8 C, GCS 8, tachycardia, hot moist skin.
case.tests: CK 18,000 U/L, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, platelets low; CT brain normal.
case.q: What is the single most important treatment?
case.a: Immediate rapid cooling, ideally cold-water immersion, aiming to bring core temperature below about 39 C within 30 minutes.

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Heat Stroke

det.patho: When heat gain exceeds heat loss, core temperature rises beyond the range at which cells tolerate it. Direct thermal injury, gut endotoxin leak and a systemic inflammatory response lead to multi-organ failure. Cerebellar Purkinje cells are particularly vulnerable, explaining persistent ataxia in survivors.
det.clinical: Neurological dysfunction is the defining feature: confusion, irritability, ataxia, seizures and coma. Exertional heat stroke affects young, fit individuals and is common in hot climates such as Thailand's hot season. Classic heat stroke affects elderly people, those on anticholinergic or diuretic drugs and the chronically ill. Delayed complications include rhabdomyolysis, renal failure, liver failure and DIC.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical: hyperthermia plus CNS dysfunction in a heat-exposed person. Core temperature must be measured, as skin or oral readings underestimate it. Infections such as meningitis or cerebral malaria, drug-induced hyperthermia syndromes and thyroid storm should be considered.
det.treatment: Cool first, transport second: cold-water immersion is the most effective method for exertional heat stroke; evaporative cooling and ice packs are used otherwise. Stop active cooling around 38.5–39 C to avoid overshoot. Support airway and circulation, treat seizures with benzodiazepines, and manage rhabdomyolysis and DIC. Antipyretics such as paracetamol do not help.
det.prognosis: Mortality relates to duration of hyperthermia; rapid cooling makes survival likely, but some survivors are left with ataxia or cognitive deficits.
pearls: Antipyretics do not work in heat stroke; physical cooling does.
Measure core temperature; a normal oral reading does not exclude heat stroke.
Persistent ataxia after heat stroke reflects cerebellar Purkinje cell injury.
det.thd: Heat stroke คือภาวะที่ร่างกายร้อนเกิน 40 องศาร่วมกับสมองทำงานผิดปกติ เช่น สับสน ชัก หรือหมดสติ พบในทหารหรือนักกีฬาที่ออกกำลังกลางแดด และผู้สูงอายุช่วงอากาศร้อน การรักษาที่สำคัญที่สุดคือทำให้ตัวเย็นลงอย่างรวดเร็ว เช่น แช่น้ำเย็น ยาลดไข้ไม่ช่วย ผู้รอดชีวิตบางรายมีเดินเซถาวรจาก cerebellum เสียหาย

name: Heavy metal poisoning
formal: Toxicity from lead, mercury, arsenic, thallium or manganese, causing neuropathy, encephalopathy, ataxia, tremor or parkinsonism depending on the metal, treated by removal of source and chelation.
simple: Illness from exposure to metals such as lead or mercury, which can damage nerves and the brain.
more: Neurotoxicity from lead, mercury, arsenic, manganese or thallium, producing encephalopathy, peripheral neuropathy, tremor or parkinsonism depending on the agent and exposure.
ab: Lead, mercury, arsenic and thallium poisoning
th: พิษจากโลหะหนัก เช่น ตะกั่ว ปรอท สารหนู แทลเลียม หรือแมงกานีส ทำให้เกิด neuropathy, encephalopathy, ataxia, tremor หรือ parkinsonism ตามชนิดโลหะ
tempoNote: Acute poisoning (arsenic, thallium) evolves over days; occupational or environmental exposure over months to years
feat: Arsenic and thallium: painful sensorimotor neuropathy after GI upset; Mees lines (arsenic) or alopecia (thallium)
Lead: encephalopathy in children; wrist/finger extensor (radial) weakness, anaemia and colic in adults
Organic mercury: visual field constriction, ataxia, paraesthesia, tremor (Minamata pattern)
Manganese: parkinsonism with dystonia and cock-walk gait, early psychiatric symptoms
Clues: occupation, traditional remedies, contaminated water, other affected household members
inv: Blood lead; 24-hour urine arsenic or mercury (speciated); urine thallium; whole-blood manganese
Nerve conduction (axonal or early demyelinating-like pattern in arsenic)
FBC with basophilic stippling, renal and liver function; MRI pallidal T1 hyperintensity in manganese

case.who: 41-year-old man from Nakhon Si Thammarat, works in a tin-mining area
case.story: Three weeks after vomiting and diarrhoea he developed burning feet and then weakness; his wife had similar GI symptoms.
case.exam: Distal symmetric weakness and sensory loss, absent ankle jerks, hyperkeratosis of palms, white transverse nail bands.
case.tests: NCS axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy; 24-hour urine arsenic markedly raised; well water contaminated.
case.q: Which metal and which classic sign on the nails supports it?
case.a: Arsenic poisoning; Mees lines. Remove the source and chelate (e.g. DMSA or dimercaprol).

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System
Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Neurological Disorders Associated with Exposure to Toxic Substances

det.patho: Metals injure the nervous system by binding sulfhydryl groups, disrupting mitochondrial energy production, generating oxidative stress and interfering with neurotransmission. Arsenic and thallium cause length-dependent axonal degeneration; lead impairs haem synthesis and damages motor axons and the developing brain; methylmercury targets the cerebellar granule cells and visual cortex; manganese accumulates in the globus pallidus. Each metal has a characteristic exposure source and target pattern.
det.clinical: Acute arsenic or thallium poisoning causes GI illness followed within 1–3 weeks by severe painful neuropathy that can mimic GBS, with skin changes, Mees lines or alopecia. Chronic lead exposure in adults produces motor neuropathy with wrist drop, abdominal colic, anaemia and gout, whereas children develop cognitive impairment and acute encephalopathy. Mercury causes tremor, erethism (irritability, shyness), ataxia and visual field constriction. Manganese, from welding, mining or ephedrone use, causes levodopa-resistant parkinsonism with dystonia.
det.diagnosis: Exposure history is crucial: occupation, hobbies, folk or Ayurvedic medicines, cosmetics, contaminated water and homicidal intent. Measure the relevant metal in the appropriate sample (blood for lead and manganese, urine for arsenic, mercury and thallium), avoiding spurious organic arsenic from seafood. NCS define the neuropathy. In Thailand, arsenic contamination has been documented in former mining districts in the south.
det.treatment: Removing the patient from the source is the most important step. Chelation is used according to toxicology advice: DMSA (succimer) or dimercaprol for lead and arsenic, with EDTA for severe lead encephalopathy; DMPS or DMSA for mercury; Prussian blue for thallium; EDTA has limited benefit for manganese. Supportive care, rehabilitation and neuropathic pain treatment follow. Notify occupational health and screen co-exposed people.
det.prognosis: Recovery is slow and often incomplete for neuropathy and manganism; early removal and chelation improve outcome, and childhood lead damage to cognition is largely permanent.
pearls: GBS-like neuropathy after a GI illness with skin or nail changes: check urine arsenic or thallium.
Wrist drop with anaemia and basophilic stippling: think lead.
Manganism looks like parkinsonism but responds poorly to levodopa.
det.thd: Heavy metal poisoning คือพิษจากโลหะหนัก แต่ละชนิดให้อาการต่างกัน สารหนูและแทลเลียมทำให้ปลายประสาทอักเสบปวดแสบหลังท้องเสีย ตะกั่วทำให้ข้อมือตกและซีดในผู้ใหญ่และสมองเสื่อมในเด็ก ปรอททำให้สั่น เดินเซ ลานสายตาแคบ แมงกานีสทำให้ parkinsonism ต้องซักประวัติอาชีพ ยาสมุนไพร และน้ำดื่ม แล้วตรวจระดับโลหะในเลือดหรือปัสสาวะ รักษาโดยหยุดการสัมผัสและให้ยาขับโลหะ

name: Heller’s disease
formal: Childhood disintegrative disorder, with severe regression in language, social and motor skills after normal development for at least 2 years, often with seizures.
simple: A rare condition where a child who developed normally for years suddenly loses language, social and other skills.
th: Childhood disintegrative disorder คือภาวะที่เด็กพัฒนาการปกติอย่างน้อย 2 ปี แล้วถดถอยรุนแรงด้านภาษา สังคม และการเคลื่อนไหว มักมีชักร่วม ปัจจุบันจัดอยู่ใน autism spectrum disorder
tempoNote: Regression over weeks to months, usually between 3 and 4 years (range 2–10), then a plateau
feat: At least 2 years of normal development before marked loss of language, social, play, toilet and motor skills
Autistic behaviours emerge after regression
Seizures or epileptiform EEG in a substantial minority
Historical label; DSM-5 (2013) folds it into autism spectrum disorder
inv: EEG including sleep (exclude Landau–Kleffner and electrical status epilepticus in sleep)
MRI brain; metabolic and genetic screen for neurodegenerative causes (NCL, leukodystrophies, MECP2)
Hearing and developmental assessment

case.story: Spoke in short sentences and was toilet trained at 2½; over three months she stopped talking, lost interest in playing and became incontinent.
case.exam: No eye contact, repetitive hand flapping, normal head size and motor examination.
case.tests: MRI normal; sleep EEG shows occasional spikes without ESES; metabolic and genetic screens normal so far.
case.q: What must be excluded before accepting this diagnosis?
case.a: Treatable or progressive causes: Landau–Kleffner/ESES, neurometabolic and neurodegenerative disorders, hearing loss and Rett syndrome; if all negative, childhood disintegrative disorder (now autism spectrum).

det.patho: The cause is unknown; it is regarded as a rare, severe regressive form within the autism spectrum rather than a single disease. Proposed contributors include genetic factors and early epileptic or inflammatory brain dysfunction, but no consistent pathology has been shown. Some historical cases later proved to be neurodegenerative disorders, which is why careful work-up matters.
det.clinical: Heller described it in 1908. After normal development to at least age 2, children lose skills in at least two domains over weeks to months, often with anxiety and agitation at onset. After regression, a plateau with severe intellectual disability and autistic features usually follows; continued decline suggests another diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: It is a diagnosis of exclusion based on history of normal development and documented regression. Sleep EEG, MRI, hearing tests, metabolic screening and genetic testing (including chromosomal microarray and exome) should be done. Under DSM-5 such children are diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder with a note on regression.
det.treatment: There is no specific treatment. Management follows autism care: intensive behavioural and developmental therapy, speech and occupational therapy, special education and family support. Treat seizures and behaviour problems symptomatically.
det.prognosis: Usually poorer than typical autism, with severe persisting disability.
pearls: Regression after age 2 with seizures: always do a sleep EEG.
Ongoing deterioration after the plateau argues for a neurodegenerative disease.
The term is historical; DSM-5 uses autism spectrum disorder.
det.thd: Heller’s disease หรือ childhood disintegrative disorder คือเด็กที่พัฒนาการปกติอย่างน้อย 2 ปี แล้วสูญเสียทักษะด้านภาษา สังคม และการขับถ่ายอย่างรวดเร็ว มีพฤติกรรมแบบออทิสติกและอาจชัก ต้องตรวจ EEG ขณะหลับ MRI และตรวจเมตาบอลิกหรือพันธุกรรมเพื่อแยกโรคที่รักษาได้หรือโรคสมองเสื่อมในเด็ก ปัจจุบันรวมอยู่ใน autism spectrum disorder

name: Hemiathetosis
formal: Slow, writhing involuntary movements of one side of the body from contralateral basal ganglia lesions, often following stroke or perinatal injury.
simple: Slow, twisting involuntary movements on one side of the body, usually from damage in the brain.
th: การเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติแบบช้า บิดไปมา ที่แขนขาข้างเดียว จากรอยโรคของ basal ganglia หรือ thalamus ด้านตรงข้าม
tempoNote: Often delayed after stroke or perinatal injury, then persistent
feat: Slow, writhing, sinuous movements, mostly of the hand and fingers, on one side
Often follows hemiparesis from stroke or perinatal brain injury
Pseudoathetosis from loss of position sense (thalamic or parietal lesions) looks similar
May blend with hemidystonia or hemichorea
Worse with action and attempted posture, absent in sleep
inv: MRI brain: contralateral putamen, thalamus or parietal lesion
Test joint position sense with eyes closed to detect pseudoathetosis
Glucose and autoimmune screen if no structural cause

case.who: 15-year-old girl from Nan with mild left hemiplegia since birth
case.story: Over the last two years her left fingers make slow writhing movements when she tries to write or hold things.
case.exam: Mild left spastic hemiparesis; continuous slow twisting finger movements worse on action; proprioception intact.
case.tests: MRI shows an old right periventricular and putaminal porencephalic lesion.
case.q: What movement disorder is this and its likely cause?
case.a: Hemiathetosis secondary to perinatal right basal ganglia injury.

det.patho: Athetosis is thought to arise from damage to the striatum or thalamus that disrupts basal ganglia output and causes unstable posture control. Pseudoathetosis is different, resulting from loss of proprioceptive feedback rather than a basal ganglia lesion.
det.clinical: Movements are slow, continuous and writhing, often involving finger extension-flexion and wrist rotation, and are increased by voluntary action. Hemiathetosis usually appears after a hemiparetic insult, sometimes with a delay. Distinguishing true athetosis from pseudoathetosis requires testing position sense with eyes closed; pseudoathetosis worsens markedly with eye closure.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, guided by MRI to identify the lesion. If no structural lesion is found, consider hyperglycaemia, autoimmune causes and drug effects. Video recording helps classification over time.
det.treatment: Treatment is often unsatisfying. Options include anticholinergics, tetrabenazine, clonazepam or botulinum toxin for focal components. Rehabilitation and adaptive devices help function. Deep brain stimulation has been tried in selected cases.
det.prognosis: Usually persistent, though severity may plateau.
pearls: Close the patient's eyes: pseudoathetosis worsens, true athetosis does not.
Athetosis often coexists with dystonia and chorea; describe what you see.
Perinatal injury can produce delayed hemiathetosis in adolescence.
det.thd: Hemiathetosis คือการเคลื่อนไหวช้าๆ บิดไปมาของมือและนิ้วข้างเดียว จากรอยโรคที่ basal ganglia หรือ thalamus ด้านตรงข้าม มักเกิดหลัง stroke หรือการบาดเจ็บของสมองแรกเกิด ต้องแยกจาก pseudoathetosis ที่เกิดจากการเสียความรู้สึกตำแหน่งข้อ โดยให้ผู้ป่วยหลับตา การรักษามักได้ผลจำกัด ใช้ยาหรือ botulinum toxin ร่วมกับการฟื้นฟู

name: Hemiballism
formal: Violent proximal flinging movements of one side of the body from contralateral subthalamic nucleus or connected lesions, classically stroke, often resolving with time.
simple: Wild flinging movements of an arm and leg on one side, usually after a small stroke deep in the brain.
more: Spectrum of unilateral hyperkinetic movements, from irregular flinging to chorea, due to lesions of the subthalamic nucleus or striatum, including non-ketotic hyperglycaemia.
th: การเหวี่ยงแขนขาข้างเดียวแรง ๆ อย่างควบคุมไม่ได้ มักเกิดเฉียบพลันจาก stroke ที่ subthalamic nucleus หรือ basal ganglia ด้านตรงข้าม หรือจากน้ำตาลสูง
tempoNote: Sudden onset with a stroke; usually lessens to hemichorea over weeks to months
feat: Large-amplitude, flinging, proximal movements of one arm and leg, continuous while awake
Sudden onset in an older person with vascular risk factors
Lesion contralateral: subthalamic nucleus, striatum, thalamus or their connections
Often merges with distal hemichorea; may cause injury, exhaustion and rhabdomyolysis
Little or no weakness in pure subthalamic strokes
inv: Capillary glucose and HbA1c at once — nonketotic hyperglycaemia is a key treatable cause
MRI with DWI (small STN or striatal infarct/haemorrhage); CT may miss small lesions
CT/MRI T1 striatal hyperintensity in diabetic striatopathy
Stroke work-up: ECG, lipids, vascular imaging

case.who: 73-year-old man who has both hypertension and diabetes from Phitsanulok
case.story: Woke up with his left arm and leg flinging wildly; he hit the bedside table repeatedly.
case.exam: Continuous large proximal throwing movements of left limbs, with distal writhing; strength near-normal; no visual field defect.
case.tests: Glucose 142 mg/dL; MRI DWI: small acute infarct in the right subthalamic nucleus.
case.q: Which drug class is most effective for the movements, and what is the expected course?
case.a: Vascular hemiballism from a right STN infarct: an antidopaminergic (haloperidol, risperidone or tetrabenazine) controls it; most improve over weeks, so taper later; plus secondary stroke prevention.

det.patho: Damage to the subthalamic nucleus or its pallidal connections reduces excitatory drive to the internal globus pallidus, releasing thalamocortical activity and producing large involuntary movements on the opposite side. Small-vessel ischaemia or haemorrhage is the main cause in older adults; non-ketotic hyperglycaemia, tumours, demyelination, infections (toxoplasmosis in HIV) and drugs are others. Most vascular lesions are actually in the striatum or thalamus rather than the STN itself.
det.clinical: Onset is abrupt, often on waking. Movements are violent and proximal, absent in sleep, and can lead to bruising, falls, fatigue and dehydration. Hemichorea and hemiballism lie on a continuum, and ballism tends to downgrade to distal chorea as the lesion matures. Rarely, it persists for months.
det.diagnosis: Check glucose first, then MRI with DWI and T1 sequences. Diabetic striatopathy shows T1 hyperintensity of the putamen with high glucose, usually in older Asian women. In younger patients consider HIV-related lesions, autoimmune disease and drugs. EEG if seizures are possible.
det.treatment: Protect the limbs and patient from injury and treat the cause (stroke prevention, glucose correction). Dopamine-receptor blockers (haloperidol, risperidone) or VMAT2 depleters (tetrabenazine) are effective; add clonazepam or topiramate if needed. Taper after weeks to months because of spontaneous improvement. Refractory persistent cases may benefit from GPi or thalamic surgery.
det.prognosis: Usually good — most vascular hemiballism improves substantially within weeks to a few months.
pearls: Acute one-sided flinging in an elderly diabetic: check glucose before ordering the MRI.
Lesion is contralateral, classically subthalamic nucleus, but striatal lesions are more common.
Many cases settle; avoid long-term dopamine blockers when possible.
det.thd: Hemiballism คือแขนขาข้างหนึ่งเหวี่ยงแรงและต่อเนื่อง มักเกิดเฉียบพลันจาก stroke ขนาดเล็กที่ subthalamic nucleus หรือ striatum ด้านตรงข้าม หรือจากน้ำตาลในเลือดสูงแบบ non-ketotic ต้องตรวจน้ำตาลทันทีและทำ MRI รักษาด้วยยาต้านโดปามีนเช่น haloperidol หรือ tetrabenazine ป้องกันบาดเจ็บ และป้องกัน stroke ซ้ำ ส่วนใหญ่อาการดีขึ้นในไม่กี่สัปดาห์

Variable, distractible movements without a corresponding lesion

name: Hemichorea
formal: Unilateral irregular, flowing involuntary movements from contralateral striatal or subthalamic lesion, often due to stroke, hyperglycaemia or lupus.
simple: Irregular, flowing involuntary movements on one side of the body.
more: MRI may show striatal hyperintensity on T1 with putaminal lesions in hyperglycaemic hemichorea; CT may be hyperdense. Treat the underlying cause (glucose control); dopamine blockers such as haloperidol or tetrabenazine are used and prognosis is usually good.
th: Hemichorea คือการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติเร็ว ไม่เป็นแบบแผน ไหลลื่น ที่ครึ่งซีกของร่างกาย จากรอยโรคด้านตรงข้ามของ striatum หรือ subthalamic nucleus สาเหตุสำคัญคือหลอดเลือดสมอง น้ำตาลในเลือดสูงแบบ non-ketotic และโรค lupus หรือ antiphospholipid อยู่ใน spectrum เดียวกับ hemiballismus มักดีขึ้นเมื่อแก้สาเหตุและใช้ยาต้านโดพามีนหรือ tetrabenazine
tempoNote: Starts over hours to days; many cases settle within weeks to a year, and the hyperglycaemic type may clear within days of glucose control
feat: Irregular, flowing, non-patterned movements of one arm, leg and sometimes the face, appearing in the limbs on the side opposite the lesion
Large proximal flinging (hemiballismus) in the same patient at the onset, with smaller distal movements as recovery begins
Commonest causes: striatal or subthalamic stroke, and non-ketotic hyperglycaemia, especially in older Asian women with poorly controlled diabetes
Other causes: lupus and antiphospholipid antibodies, tumour or infection in the basal ganglia, demyelination, thyrotoxicosis, drugs and Sydenham's chorea
Dopamine drugs worsen it, dopamine blockers and depleters improve it; most cases are self-limited
inv: Glucose and HbA1c at once; ketones and osmolality if glucose is very high
MRI brain; T1 hyperintensity of the putamen in hyperglycaemia, infarct or mass in other causes; CT may show putaminal density
ANA, antiphospholipid antibodies, thyroid function and HIV test in young or atypical cases
Stroke work-up when the onset is abrupt

case.who: 58-year-old woman from Kalasin with long-standing hypertension and diabetes
case.story: Over three days the right arm and leg began to move on their own in a restless, flowing way, and the face grimaced on that side; sleep stopped the movements.
case.exam: Alert; continuous irregular chorea of the right arm, leg and face, with the odd wider flinging movement at the shoulder; power full; reflexes symmetric.
case.tests: Glucose 28 mmol/L without ketones; MRI T1 hyperintensity of the left putamen with no infarct on diffusion imaging.
case.q: What is the cause and what treatment should be given first?
case.a: Hemichorea from hyperglycaemia. Lower the glucose steadily with insulin and treat the precipitant; add a low-dose dopamine blocker or tetrabenazine only if the movements remain troublesome, since most settle within days to weeks.

read.where: Ablative lesions of the thalamus, pallidum, and subthalamic nucleus

det.patho: Hemichorea and hemiballismus appear to be two ends of the same disorder of basal ganglia output. A lesion in the subthalamic nucleus, striatum or its connections reduces pallidal inhibition of the thalamus, which then drives the motor cortex excessively. Modern imaging has shown that stroke affects the subthalamic nucleus directly in only a minority of cases, and that hyperglycaemic hemichorea involves mainly the putamen and globus pallidus. In the diabetic form, pathology shows gliosis with reactive astrocytes rather than clear infarction.
det.clinical: The patient is alert, with movements that disappear in sleep and rise with action, stress or excitement. Hemichorea is lower in amplitude and more distal than hemiballismus, and the two coexist or follow each other in the same patient. Most cases are in older people, and in Asian patients the hyperglycaemic type is common. After a stroke, the movements may be delayed until strength recovers. Bilateral disease is rare.
det.diagnosis: Check glucose first, then image with MRI. Take a history of stroke risk, infection and drugs (levodopa, anticonvulsants, contraceptives, stimulants). In young patients look for lupus, antiphospholipid syndrome, thyrotoxicosis, polycythaemia and pregnancy. Sydenham's chorea should be considered in children. Distinguish from functional movements, which vary with distraction.
det.treatment: Correct the cause: lower glucose, treat infection or tumour, give antithrombotic therapy and risk-factor control for stroke, and reduce dopaminergic drugs. Mild cases need only protection of the limb and reassurance. When treatment is needed, dopamine blockers such as haloperidol and risperidone, or tetrabenazine, work in most patients; valproate, clonazepam and other options help some. Treat for about 3 months and then taper. Pallidotomy, thalamotomy or deep brain stimulation are reserved for rare, severe, persistent cases.
det.prognosis: Usually benign; most patients improve within weeks to months and many of the hyperglycaemic cases within days. The long-term risk relates to the underlying vascular disease.
pearls: Check glucose and imaging; the cure is often in the blood test.
Hemichorea and hemiballism are one spectrum.
Levodopa can provoke or worsen it.
det.thd: Hemichorea คือการเคลื่อนไหวเร็วผิดแบบแผนและไหลลื่นที่ครึ่งซีกของร่างกาย มักเกิดจากรอยโรคด้านตรงข้ามของ striatum ที่พบบ่อยคือหลอดเลือดสมองและน้ำตาลในเลือดสูงแบบ non-ketotic โดยเฉพาะผู้สูงอายุหญิงเอเชีย ตรวจน้ำตาลและทำ MRI ทันที แก้สาเหตุ ลดยากลุ่มโดพามีน ถ้าอาการรบกวนมากใช้ haloperidol, risperidone หรือ tetrabenazine ส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นในไม่กี่สัปดาห์ถึงไม่กี่เดือน

name: Hemicord syndrome
formal: Brown-Séquard syndrome of cord hemisection, with ipsilateral weakness and loss of proprioception and vibration, and contralateral loss of pain and temperature below the lesion.
simple: Damage to one half of the spinal cord causing weakness on one side and loss of pain sensation on the other.
th: รอยโรคครึ่งซีกของไขสันหลัง ทำให้อ่อนแรงและเสีย proprioception ข้างเดียวกัน แต่เสียความรู้สึกเจ็บและอุณหภูมิด้านตรงข้าม
tempoNote: Acute with trauma, haemorrhage or infarct; subacute or gradual with demyelination, tumour or disc
feat: Ipsilateral weakness and upper motor neuron signs below the lesion
Same-side loss of vibration and position sense
Contralateral loss of pain and temperature beginning one or two segments below
Ipsilateral segmental band of complete sensory loss or radicular pain at the level
Pure forms are rare; partial hemicord patterns are common in MS, NMOSD, trauma and compression
inv: MRI spine with contrast at the clinically estimated level
CSF studies and AQP4/MOG antibodies if inflammatory
CT spine in penetrating or blunt trauma
MRI brain to look for demyelination elsewhere

case.story: Stabbed in the back during a fight; on arrival cannot move his right leg.
case.exam: Right leg weak with extensor plantar, right-sided loss of vibration and position sense; left-sided loss of pinprick and cold below T8.
case.tests: CT shows knife track near T6; MRI shows right-sided cord contusion at T6.
case.q: Name the syndrome and explain the crossed sensory findings.
case.a: Hemicord (Brown–Séquard) syndrome; dorsal columns and corticospinal fibres are ipsilateral, while spinothalamic fibres have already crossed.

det.patho: The lateral corticospinal tract and dorsal columns stay on the same side until the medulla, but pain and temperature fibres cross within a segment or two through the ventral white commissure. A lesion confined to one half of the cord therefore produces ipsilateral motor and proprioceptive loss with contralateral spinothalamic loss. Root and dorsal horn damage at the lesion level adds a narrow ipsilateral band of total anaesthesia.
det.clinical: The classic cause is a penetrating injury, but in practice the pattern is usually incomplete and arises from multiple sclerosis, NMOSD, disc herniation, extramedullary tumours, haematoma, radiation myelopathy or spinal cord herniation through a dural defect. Bladder function is often relatively spared compared with complete lesions. Partial forms may show only crossed pain loss with mild ipsilateral weakness.
det.diagnosis: Careful sensory testing on both sides localises the level and side of the lesion. MRI is the key test and guides further work-up, such as CSF and antibody testing for inflammation or contrast imaging for tumour. Idiopathic spinal cord herniation shows a ventral kink of the thoracic cord on MRI and is easily missed.
det.treatment: Treatment follows the cause: surgical exploration and stabilisation for trauma or compression, high-dose steroids and disease-modifying therapy for demyelination, and repair of dural defects in cord herniation. Rehabilitation focuses on gait, spasticity and sensory protection of the analgesic side.
det.prognosis: Among incomplete cord syndromes it carries one of the better outlooks; most traumatic cases regain walking ability.
pearls: Weakness and proprioceptive loss on one side, pain loss on the other: think cord hemisection.
The contralateral pain level lies a segment or two below the true lesion level.
In middle-aged patients with slowly progressive thoracic hemicord, consider idiopathic spinal cord herniation.
det.thd: Hemicord syndrome หรือ Brown–Séquard syndrome เกิดจากรอยโรคครึ่งซีกของไขสันหลัง ทำให้ข้างเดียวกันอ่อนแรงและเสียความรู้สึกตำแหน่งและการสั่น ส่วนด้านตรงข้ามเสียความรู้สึกเจ็บและอุณหภูมิ เพราะ spinothalamic tract ข้ามฝั่งไปแล้ว สาเหตุมีทั้งการบาดเจ็บ ปลอกประสาทอักเสบ หรือก้อนกดทับ ตรวจ MRI และรักษาตามสาเหตุ

name: Hemidystonia
formal: Dystonia affecting the arm and leg on one side, commonly secondary to a contralateral basal ganglia or thalamic lesion from stroke, trauma, perinatal injury or tumour.
simple: Twisting, abnormal postures of the arm and leg on one side of the body, usually from a brain injury on the opposite side.
more: MRI to look for contralateral lesions is essential. Treat with anticholinergics, baclofen, botulinum toxin or deep brain stimulation; onset may be delayed months after the injury. Dystonia affecting one half of the body, usually symptomatic of contralateral basal ganglia or thalamic lesions, such as stroke, trauma or perinatal injury.
th: dystonia ที่แขนและขาข้างเดียวกัน มักเป็นผลจากรอยโรคที่ basal ganglia หรือ thalamus ด้านตรงข้าม เช่น stroke อุบัติเหตุ หรือการบาดเจ็บแรกเกิด
tempoNote: Often delayed weeks to years after the causal lesion
feat: Sustained twisting postures of arm and leg on one side
Almost always secondary to a structural contralateral lesion, especially putamen or thalamus
Causes: stroke, perinatal injury, trauma, encephalitis, tumour, AVM, demyelination
Delayed onset after the insult is common
May combine with hemiparesis, hemiathetosis or tremor
inv: MRI brain for contralateral basal ganglia or thalamic lesion
If MRI is normal, consider Wilson disease, NBIA, genetic dystonias and functional dystonia
Copper studies in under 50s

case.who: 38-year-old man from Phayao two years after a left thalamic haemorrhage
case.story: His right hand gradually curled and the right foot turned inward on walking.
case.exam: Right arm flexion-pronation dystonia, right foot inversion dystonia, mild right sensory loss.
case.tests: MRI shows old haemosiderin-lined left thalamic cavity.
case.q: What is this and what treatment helps most?
case.a: Post-thalamic hemidystonia; botulinum toxin injections for the most disabling muscles plus physiotherapy.

det.patho: Hemidystonia results from contralateral lesions of the basal ganglia (particularly putamen), thalamus or their connections. Abnormal output from damaged circuits and maladaptive plasticity make opposing muscles fire together. Thalamic lesions often give dystonia mixed with sensory loss and pseudoathetosis.
det.clinical: Postures are often flexion-pronation of the arm and inversion of the foot, initially action-induced and later fixed. Onset is frequently delayed, sometimes years after the insult. Associated hemiparesis or sensory deficits reflect the original lesion. Progressive hemidystonia without a lesion suggests corticobasal syndrome or other degenerative disease.
det.diagnosis: MRI is essential; the vast majority have a demonstrable structural lesion. When none is found, look for metabolic, degenerative, genetic or functional causes. EMG is occasionally used to plan botulinum toxin injection.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin for focal components is the most effective treatment. Oral options include trihexyphenidyl, baclofen and clonazepam, with modest benefit. Deep brain stimulation (GPi or thalamic targets) helps some patients but less than in isolated dystonia. Physiotherapy, splinting and contracture prevention are important.
det.prognosis: Usually persistent; disability depends on extent and response to injections.
pearls: Hemidystonia almost always means a structural lesion: image the brain.
No lesion plus progressive course: consider corticobasal syndrome.
Botulinum toxin is the first practical step.
det.thd: Hemidystonia คือ dystonia ของแขนและขาข้างเดียวกัน เกือบทั้งหมดเกิดจากรอยโรคที่ basal ganglia หรือ thalamus ด้านตรงข้าม เช่น stroke หรืออุบัติเหตุ อาการอาจเกิดช้าหลังรอยโรคหลายเดือนหรือหลายปี ต้องทำ MRI ทุกราย ถ้าไม่พบรอยโรคให้นึกถึง corticobasal syndrome หรือ Wilson disease รักษาด้วย botulinum toxin ยารับประทาน และกายภาพบำบัด

name: Hemifacial spasm
formal: Unilateral involuntary twitching of facial muscles, usually from vascular compression of the facial nerve at the root exit zone, treated with botulinum toxin or microvascular decompression.
simple: Repeated twitching of the muscles on one side of the face, often caused by a blood vessel pressing on a nerve.
th: หน้ากระตุกข้างเดียวเป็นพัก ๆ เริ่มรอบตาแล้วลามลงมุมปาก ส่วนใหญ่จากหลอดเลือดกดเส้นประสาทที่ 7 รักษาด้วย botulinum toxin หรือ microvascular decompression
tempoNote: Brief twitches occurring in bursts many times a day; slowly worsens over years, persists in sleep
feat: One-sided clonic twitching beginning around the eye, spreading over years to cheek and mouth
Tonic contractions closing the eye and pulling the mouth; may continue during sleep
Babinski-2 (other Babinski) sign: eyebrow rises as the eye closes
Mild facial weakness or none; usually aged 40–60, more common in women and Asians
inv: MRI with high-resolution posterior fossa sequences (CISS/FIESTA) and MRA for vascular loop and to exclude tumour
EMG: lateral spread response (optional; useful intraoperatively)
Blood pressure check — association with hypertension

case.story: For 3 years her left eye twitches shut, and now the left corner of her mouth pulls up too; it continues when she sleeps according to her husband.
case.exam: Synchronous twitches of left orbicularis oculi and oris, left eyebrow rises as the eye closes; facial strength normal.
case.tests: MRI/MRA: left AICA loop touching the facial nerve root exit zone; no mass.
case.q: What are the two main treatment options?
case.a: Primary hemifacial spasm: botulinum toxin injections every 3–4 months, or microvascular decompression surgery for a durable cure.

det.patho: Most cases result from pulsatile compression of the facial nerve root exit zone by a vascular loop (AICA, PICA or vertebral artery). Ectopic excitation and ephaptic transmission at the damaged segment, plus facial nucleus hyperexcitability, produce synchronous contractions. Secondary causes include CPA tumours, AVMs, demyelination and previous facial nerve injury.
det.clinical: Typical HFS starts in the lower lid and spreads downward; atypical HFS starts in the lower face and spreads upward. Spasms are worsened by stress, fatigue and voluntary facial movements, and persist in sleep. It is usually unilateral; bilateral cases are rare and asynchronous. Social embarrassment and visual interference are the main burdens.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical. Every patient should have MRI with thin-slice cisternal sequences to identify the offending vessel and exclude a tumour. The other Babinski sign helps separate HFS from functional facial spasm. Differentiate from blepharospasm, facial myokymia, tics, focal seizures and synkinesis.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin injection into orbicularis oculi (and lower face muscles if needed) helps the majority; repeat every 3–4 months. Carbamazepine, clonazepam or gabapentin give modest benefit. Microvascular decompression is curative in most, with risks of hearing loss and facial weakness; it suits younger, fit patients wanting a lasting solution.
det.prognosis: Spontaneous remission is rare; long-term control with toxin or surgery is good.
pearls: Spasms persisting during sleep favour HFS over blepharospasm or functional spasm.
Babinski-2 sign: frontalis rises while the eye closes.
Image every patient to look for a CPA lesion.
det.thd: Hemifacial spasm คือกล้ามเนื้อใบหน้าข้างเดียวกระตุก มักเริ่มที่เปลือกตาล่างแล้วลามลงมาที่ปาก และเป็นได้ขณะหลับ เกิดจากหลอดเลือดกดเส้นประสาทที่ 7 บริเวณที่ออกจากก้านสมอง ควรทำ MRI/MRA ทุกรายเพื่อแยกเนื้องอก รักษาด้วยฉีด botulinum toxin ทุก 3–4 เดือน หรือผ่าตัด microvascular decompression

qx.stem: A 61-year-old market vendor from Udon Thani has had two years of twitching that began under the right eye and now pulls the right corner of the mouth upward. The twitches continue in sleep according to her husband. During a spasm the right eyebrow rises while the eye closes. The left face is normal, and there is no facial weakness or hearing loss.
qx.q: Which statement about her condition is most accurate?
opts: It is a focal cranial dystonia and should be treated like blepharospasm with bilateral injections
It is a facial tic and responds best to behavioural therapy
Carbamazepine is the treatment of choice and usually abolishes the spasms
MRI is unnecessary because the cause is always idiopathic
MRI should look for a vascular loop compressing the facial nerve root exit zone; botulinum toxin is first-line
qx.why: Unilateral spasms that start around the eye, spread down the face, persist in sleep and include the 'other Babinski sign' (brow elevation with eye closure) are typical of hemifacial spasm, usually from an artery pressing on the facial nerve at the brainstem. Local botulinum toxin is first-line, and microvascular decompression is the curative option for suitable patients; blepharospasm is bilateral and tics are suppressible with an urge.

name: Hemiparkinsonism
formal: Parkinsonian features limited to one side of the body, typically early Parkinson disease, but also from contralateral lesion or in hemiparkinsonism-hemiatrophy syndrome.
simple: Parkinson-like slowness and tremor affecting just one side of the body.
th: parkinsonism ที่เป็นข้างเดียวของร่างกาย มักเป็นระยะแรกของ Parkinson disease แต่อาจเกิดจากรอยโรคฝั่งตรงข้ามหรือกลุ่มอาการ hemiparkinsonism-hemiatrophy
tempoNote: Gradual in Parkinson disease; subacute or sudden with structural lesions; HPHA usually slowly progressive from young adulthood
feat: Bradykinesia and rigidity, with or without rest tremor, limited to one arm and leg
Most often the first stage of idiopathic Parkinson disease, which later becomes bilateral but asymmetric
Remaining strictly unilateral for years raises suspicion of a structural lesion or HPHA
HPHA: body hemiatrophy on the affected side, often with dystonia and early onset
Apraxia, alien limb or cortical sensory loss suggest corticobasal syndrome
inv: MRI brain for tumour, infarct, haemorrhage, abscess or hemiatrophy of the opposite hemisphere
DAT-SPECT if diagnosis remains unclear
Levodopa trial; drug history

case.who: 52-year-old male rubber tapper from Surat Thani
case.story: For two years his left arm swings less and his left leg drags; handwriting is fine because he is right-handed. Had a difficult birth according to his mother.
case.exam: Left-sided rigidity and bradykinesia with dystonic foot posturing; left arm and leg visibly smaller in girth and length.
case.tests: MRI shows mild right hemispheric atrophy; DAT-SPECT reduced in right striatum; modest levodopa response.
case.q: What syndrome explains unilateral parkinsonism with a smaller limb on the same side?
case.a: Hemiparkinsonism-hemiatrophy syndrome, possibly related to early-life injury to the contralateral hemisphere.

det.patho: Unilateral parkinsonism reflects dopaminergic deficit or basal ganglia circuit damage in the contralateral hemisphere. In Parkinson disease, nigral degeneration is asymmetric from the start. Structural causes include tumours, infarcts, haemorrhage, abscess (toxoplasma in HIV) and trauma. Hemiparkinsonism-hemiatrophy syndrome is thought to stem from early-life injury to one hemisphere, with later decompensation of the dopaminergic system.
det.clinical: Most people presenting with one-sided slowness, stiffness or tremor have Parkinson disease, which becomes bilateral within a few years while remaining asymmetric. Persistent strict laterality, abrupt onset, early dystonia, hemiatrophy or cortical signs should prompt reconsideration. HPHA typically presents in early to mid adulthood with dystonia and parkinsonism on the smaller side. Corticobasal syndrome causes asymmetric akinetic-rigid parkinsonism with apraxia and dystonic limb.
det.diagnosis: Neurological examination should check for limb size discrepancy, cortical signs and pyramidal signs. MRI is mandatory when features are atypical. DAT-SPECT is abnormal in Parkinson disease and HPHA but normal in many functional, drug-induced or essential tremor mimics. A levodopa trial helps both diagnosis and treatment.
det.treatment: Treatment follows the cause: dopaminergic therapy for Parkinson disease, surgical or medical management of structural lesions, and levodopa plus symptomatic dystonia treatment for HPHA (response is often partial). Physiotherapy addresses gait and limb use. DBS has been reported in selected HPHA patients.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause; Parkinson disease follows its usual course, HPHA tends to progress slowly, and structural causes may resolve with treatment.
pearls: Unilateral Parkinson features persisting more than several years without spread warrant MRI.
Compare limb size — hemiatrophy is easy to miss.
In people with HIV, consider toxoplasma abscess in the basal ganglia.
det.thd: Hemiparkinsonism คือ parkinsonism ข้างเดียว ส่วนใหญ่เป็นระยะแรกของ Parkinson’s disease ซึ่งต่อมาจะเป็นสองข้าง แต่ถ้าเป็นข้างเดียวนานหลายปี เกิดฉับพลัน หรือมีแขนขาข้างนั้นเล็กลง ต้องคิดถึงรอยโรคในสมองฝั่งตรงข้ามหรือกลุ่มอาการ hemiparkinsonism-hemiatrophy ควรทำ MRI และอาจทำ DAT-SPECT การรักษาตามสาเหตุและลองให้ levodopa

name: Hepatic encephalopathy
formal: Reversible neuropsychiatric syndrome of liver failure or portosystemic shunting, with asterixis, confusion, personality change and coma, linked to hyperammonaemia and treated with lactulose.
simple: Confusion, sleepiness and a flapping tremor caused by a failing liver that cannot clear toxins from the blood.
more: Diagnosis supported by raised blood ammonia, EEG triphasic waves, MRI pallidal T1 hyperintensity and psychometric tests; grade by West Haven criteria. Rifaximin is added to lactulose for recurrence, with precipitants (infection, bleeding.
th: สมองทำงานผิดปกติจากตับวายหรือมีทางลัดเลือด portosystemic สับสน ง่วงซึม มี asterixis มักมีตัวกระตุ้น เช่น เลือดออกทางเดินอาหาร ติดเชื้อ ท้องผูก รักษาด้วย lactulose และ rifaximin
tempoNote: Overt episodes develop over hours to days after a trigger and clear with treatment; covert disease is a persistent low-grade cognitive slowing; acute liver failure can progress to coma and brain swelling within days
feat: Fluctuating inattention, disturbed sleep–wake rhythm (daytime sleepiness, night wakefulness) and personality change
Asterixis on outstretched wrists, slowed speech and, in deeper grades, stupor and coma (West Haven 1–4)
Usually set off by a precipitant: GI bleeding, infection or SBP, constipation, dehydration or diuretics, hypokalaemia, sedatives
Stigmata of chronic liver disease, jaundice or ascites; occasionally a shunt with near-normal liver tests
Covert form: normal bedside exam but poor attention, slowed reactions and accident-prone driving
inv: Exclude mimics first: glucose, sodium, renal function, infection screen, CT head after falls (subdural), thiamine status by clinical judgement
Venous ammonia: a normal value makes HE unlikely, but the level does not track grade well; useful in acute liver failure
EEG: slowing with triphasic waves; MRI may show symmetric T1 brightness of the globus pallidus (manganese)
Covert HE: psychometric testing (PHES, Stroop app, animal naming)

case.who: 58-year-old man from Khon Kaen with hepatitis B cirrhosis
case.story: Family say he has slept all day and been muddled at night for 2 days; stools have become black since yesterday.
case.exam: Drowsy but rousable, disorientated to date, coarse flapping tremor of both hands, spider naevi, mild ascites, no focal signs.
case.tests: Hb 8.2 g/dL (from 11), Na 132 mmol/L, glucose 6 mmol/L, ammonia raised; CT head unremarkable.
case.q: What is the grade and the most likely trigger, and what are the first treatment steps?
case.a: West Haven grade 2 hepatic encephalopathy triggered by upper GI bleeding; resuscitate, arrange endoscopy, give lactulose titrated to 2–3 soft stools daily and look for infection.
