det.patho: When the liver fails or blood bypasses it through shunts, gut-derived ammonia and other neurotoxins reach the brain. Astrocytes detoxify ammonia into glutamine, which draws in water and disturbs neurotransmission; inflammation, altered GABAergic tone and manganese deposition add to the picture. In acute liver failure, astrocyte swelling can cause dangerous cerebral oedema, whereas in cirrhosis the brain stays mostly low-grade and reversible. Sarcopenia matters because muscle is a major site of ammonia clearance.
det.clinical: Overt HE ranges from subtle confusion and reversed sleep pattern (grade 1–2) to somnolence and coma (grade 3–4); asterixis is common in middle grades and disappears in coma. Most episodes follow an identifiable trigger, and recurrence is common once one episode has occurred. Covert HE has no obvious signs but impairs driving, work and quality of life and predicts overt episodes. Focal deficits, seizures or a persistent movement disorder should prompt a search for another cause, including acquired hepatocerebral degeneration, a parkinsonian–ataxic syndrome seen with long-standing shunting.
det.diagnosis: It is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion in someone with liver disease or a shunt. Check glucose, electrolytes, renal function, cultures and paracentesis if ascites, and image the head if there was a fall, a focal sign or anticoagulation. Ammonia is most helpful when normal (argues strongly against HE) and in acute liver failure, where very high levels predict brain swelling; it must be taken from free-flowing venous blood and analysed quickly. EEG triphasic waves are supportive but not specific; psychometric tests are used to detect covert HE.
det.treatment: Treat the precipitant and protect the airway in grade 3–4. Lactulose (oral or by enema) is first line, titrated to two or three soft stools a day; avoid over-purging, which causes dehydration and hypernatraemia. Rifaximin 550 mg twice daily is added to lactulose to prevent recurrence after a further episode; L-ornithine L-aspartate and polyethylene glycol are alternatives in some guidelines. Avoid benzodiazepines and opioids, correct potassium, do not restrict protein (aim 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day with a late-evening snack), and consider shunt embolisation or liver transplant referral for recurrent disease.
det.prognosis: Episodes usually reverse, but a first overt episode marks advanced liver disease with poor survival without transplantation; some patients keep residual cognitive deficits.
pearls: A normal ammonia should make you look hard for another cause of confusion.
Always ask: what tipped this patient over? Bleeding, infection, constipation, drugs and electrolytes are the usual culprits.
Give thiamine in any malnourished drinker with confusion — Wernicke and HE often coexist.
Pallidal T1 hyperintensity reflects manganese and liver disease, not acute HE severity.
det.thd: Hepatic encephalopathy เกิดจากตับไม่สามารถกำจัด ammonia และสารพิษจากลำไส้ ทำให้ astrocyte บวมและการสื่อประสาทผิดปกติ ผู้ป่วยสับสน ง่วงกลางวันตื่นกลางคืน มี asterixis จนถึงโคม่า มักมีตัวกระตุ้น เช่น เลือดออกทางเดินอาหาร ติดเชื้อ ท้องผูก ยานอนหลับ วินิจฉัยโดยแยกสาเหตุอื่นก่อน ระดับ ammonia ปกติช่วยบอกว่าไม่น่าใช่ รักษาด้วยการแก้ตัวกระตุ้น ให้ lactulose จนถ่ายนิ่ม 2–3 ครั้งต่อวัน และเพิ่ม rifaximin เพื่อป้องกันการกลับเป็นซ้ำ ไม่ควรจำกัดโปรตีน

qx.stem: A 59-year-old man with hepatitis B cirrhosis is admitted with melaena and becomes sleepy and confused with asterixis. EEG shows diffuse slowing with frequent bilaterally synchronous blunt triphasic waves at 1.5–2 Hz, maximal frontally with an anterior-to-posterior lag, waxing and waning with arousal; there is no evolution in frequency or field.
qx.q: What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Load intravenous phenytoin for non-convulsive status
Start a midazolam infusion
Order urgent MRI before any treatment
Give flumazenil and start haloperidol
Treat the precipitant and start lactulose with rifaximin
qx.why: Blunt triphasic waves at about 2 Hz with anterior-posterior lag, changing with arousal and without evolution, favour metabolic encephalopathy; with asterixis and GI bleeding this is hepatic encephalopathy. Management is correcting the precipitant and reducing ammonia. If doubt remains, continuous EEG or a cautious benzodiazepine trial with clinical improvement can clarify, but empiric anaesthetic infusions are not indicated.

name: Hepatitis C
formal: Chronic hepatitis C virus infection with neurological complications including cryoglobulinaemic neuropathy, mononeuritis multiplex, stroke, cognitive slowing and treatment-related neuropathy.
simple: A viral liver infection that can also affect nerves, causing numbness, weakness and tiredness.
th: การติดเชื้อไวรัสตับอักเสบซีเรื้อรัง มีภาวะแทรกซ้อนทางประสาทเช่น cryoglobulinaemic neuropathy, mononeuritis multiplex, stroke และปัญหาการรู้คิด

feat: Primarily a liver infection; neurological features are extrahepatic
Mixed cryoglobulinaemia causing painful sensory or sensorimotor neuropathy and mononeuritis multiplex
Palpable purpura, arthralgia and glomerulonephritis with cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis

case.who: 55-year-old man from Khon Kaen with past injecting drug use
case.story: Burning feet for a year, then sudden right wrist drop and purple spots on his legs.
case.exam: Palpable purpura of the shins, right radial neuropathy, glove-and-stocking sensory loss.
case.tests: HCV RNA positive; type II cryoglobulins present; C4 very low; NCS shows axonal polyneuropathy plus right radial mononeuropathy.
case.q: What links the neuropathy to his infection, and what treatment is needed?
case.a: HCV-associated cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis; direct-acting antivirals, with rituximab for severe vasculitic neuropathy.

det.patho: HCV infects B cells chronically, driving clonal expansion and production of cryoglobulins (IgM rheumatoid factor complexed with IgG). These deposit in small vessels, activating complement and causing vasculitis of skin, kidney and vasa nervorum. Low-level CNS infection and systemic inflammation may contribute to fatigue and cognitive symptoms.
det.clinical: Peripheral neuropathy is the main neurological manifestation, often painful and distal, with superimposed mononeuropathies. Purpura, arthralgia and Raynaud phenomenon suggest cryoglobulinaemia. CNS complications such as stroke or encephalopathy from vasculitis are rare. This is an infectious disease with neurological complications rather than a primary neurological disease.
det.diagnosis: Confirm active infection with HCV RNA. Cryoglobulin testing needs blood kept at 37 C until clotted; low C4 is a helpful surrogate. Electrodiagnostic studies define neuropathy type; biopsy shows vasculitis. Exclude diabetes, alcohol and other causes common in this group.
det.treatment: Direct-acting antivirals (e.g. sofosbuvir/velpatasvir) cure most infections and often improve cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis. Severe or progressive vasculitic neuropathy is treated additionally with rituximab, with plasma exchange for life-threatening disease. Neuropathic pain treatment and rehabilitation support recovery.
det.prognosis: Viral cure improves most extrahepatic disease, though established axonal damage may recover partially.
pearls: Purpura plus neuropathy plus low C4: test for cryoglobulins and HCV.
Keep cryoglobulin samples warm or the test will be falsely negative.
Antiviral cure is the foundation of treatment for HCV vasculitis.
det.thd: Hepatitis C เป็นการติดเชื้อไวรัสที่ตับ ไม่ใช่โรคทางระบบประสาทโดยตรง แต่ทำให้เกิด cryoglobulinaemia ซึ่งเป็น vasculitis ของหลอดเลือดเล็ก ทำให้เส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเสีย ปวดแสบปวดร้อน และเส้นประสาทหลายเส้นเสีย ร่วมกับจ้ำเลือดที่ขา วินิจฉัยด้วย HCV RNA และ cryoglobulin รักษาด้วยยาต้านไวรัส direct-acting antivirals และใช้ rituximab ในรายรุนแรง

name: Hepatopathy
formal: Liver disease within neurological or metabolic disorders, for example Wilson disease, POLG Alpers syndrome and mitochondrial depletion syndromes, with raised enzymes and hepatic failure.
simple: Liver damage that occurs together with certain inherited brain or muscle diseases.
more: Liver function tests and imaging with targeted genetic testing; treatment depends on cause, including chelation for Wilson disease.
th: ความผิดปกติของตับที่พบร่วมกับโรคทางประสาทหรือเมตาบอลิก เช่น Wilson disease, POLG/Alpers และ mitochondrial depletion syndromes
tempoNote: Can be acute liver failure (POLG with valproate, Wilson fulminant), or chronic cirrhosis with neurological decline
feat: A descriptive term, not a single disease: liver dysfunction as part of a neurological or metabolic syndrome
Wilson disease: hepatitis or cirrhosis with tremor, dystonia, dysarthria and psychiatric change
POLG (Alpers–Huttenlocher): refractory seizures with liver failure, often triggered by valproate
Also: mitochondrial DNA depletion, urea cycle and fatty acid oxidation defects, Niemann–Pick C, acquired hepatocerebral degeneration
Liver failure itself causes encephalopathy, asterixis and parkinsonism (manganese deposition)
inv: Liver enzymes, albumin, INR, ammonia, ultrasound
Ceruloplasmin, 24-hour urine copper, slit-lamp for Kayser–Fleischer rings
Lactate, POLG and mitochondrial gene testing; MRI brain (pallidal T1 hyperintensity in chronic liver disease)

case.story: Jaundice and tiredness for two months; now her handwriting has deteriorated and she drools.
case.exam: Mild jaundice, spleen tip palpable, wing-beating tremor, dysarthria, fixed smile.
case.tests: ALT 140, low ceruloplasmin, urine copper markedly raised, Kayser–Fleischer rings on slit lamp; MRI T2 putaminal change.
case.q: Which disease links her liver and neurological findings?
case.a: Wilson disease presenting with hepatopathy and neurological involvement.

det.patho: This entry describes a category rather than one disease. Several genetic disorders damage liver and brain together: copper accumulation in Wilson disease, defective mitochondrial DNA replication in POLG and other depletion syndromes, lysosomal cholesterol trafficking failure in Niemann–Pick C, and urea cycle defects with hyperammonaemia. Conversely, chronic liver failure or portosystemic shunting exposes the brain to ammonia and manganese.
det.clinical: Presentations range from neonatal liver failure with hypotonia (mitochondrial depletion), to childhood seizures with hepatic failure (Alpers), to adolescent hepatitis with movement disorder (Wilson). Adults with cirrhosis may develop hepatic encephalopathy, myelopathy or acquired hepatocerebral degeneration with parkinsonism and ataxia. Valproate-induced liver failure in a child with seizures should immediately raise POLG disease.
det.diagnosis: Approach starts with liver tests and imaging, then targeted metabolic studies: copper indices, lactate and pyruvate, ammonia, amino and organic acids, acylcarnitines and oxysterols. Genetic panels or exome sequencing identify POLG, DGUOK, MPV17 and others. Brain MRI patterns (putaminal T2 in Wilson, pallidal T1 in cirrhosis, cortical lesions in Alpers) narrow the field.
det.treatment: Management depends on the cause: chelation (penicillamine or trientine) and zinc for Wilson, avoidance of valproate in suspected mitochondrial disease, dietary and ammonia-scavenger therapy for urea cycle defects, and lactulose and rifaximin for hepatic encephalopathy. Liver transplantation is considered for Wilson-related acute failure and selected acquired hepatocerebral degeneration, but is generally contraindicated in POLG disease with neurological involvement.
det.prognosis: Highly variable: Wilson disease does well with early treatment, whereas Alpers and mitochondrial depletion syndromes usually carry a poor outlook.
pearls: Never give valproate to a child with unexplained seizures and liver dysfunction.
Every young person with liver disease and a movement disorder needs Wilson screening.
Pallidal T1 hyperintensity on MRI suggests chronic liver disease with manganese deposition.
det.thd: Hepatopathy ในที่นี้หมายถึงความผิดปกติของตับที่พบร่วมกับโรคทางประสาท ไม่ใช่โรคเดียว ตัวอย่างสำคัญคือ Wilson disease ที่มีตับอักเสบร่วมกับสั่นและ dystonia, POLG/Alpers ที่มีชักรุนแรงและตับวายโดยเฉพาะหลังได้ valproate และโรคตับเรื้อรังที่ทำให้เกิด encephalopathy หรือ parkinsonism การตรวจเริ่มจาก liver function, ceruloplasmin, ทองแดงในปัสสาวะ และตรวจยีน การรักษาตามสาเหตุ

name: Hereditary ataxias
formal: Genetically determined progressive cerebellar syndromes, either autosomal dominant (spinocerebellar ataxias), recessive (Friedreich, AT) or X-linked, with gait ataxia, dysarthria and variable extracerebellar signs.
simple: Inherited conditions that gradually cause problems with balance, coordination and speech.
more: Genetic panels cover repeat expansions and point mutations; MRI shows cerebellar atrophy, sometimes with pontine change. Care is mainly supportive rehabilitation, with specific therapy for treatable causes such as vitamin E and CoQ10 deficiency. Group of genetic cerebellar disorders, including spinocerebellar ataxias, Friedreich ataxia and episodic ataxias, with progressive gait and limb incoordination and dysarthria.
ab: SCA, Friedreich and other hereditary ataxias
th: กลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่ทำให้สมองน้อยเสื่อมค่อยเป็นค่อยไป ได้แก่ autosomal dominant (SCA), recessive (Friedreich, AT) และ X-linked มีเดินเซ พูดไม่ชัด และอาการอื่นนอกสมองน้อย
tempoNote: Most progress over years to decades; episodic ataxias cause attacks lasting minutes to hours
feat: Progressive gait ataxia, limb incoordination, dysarthria and nystagmus
Dominant: SCA1/2/3/6/7 and DRPLA; SCA3 (Machado–Joseph) and SCA2 are common in Thai and other Asian families
Recessive: Friedreich ataxia (rare in East Asia), AOA1/2, ataxia-telangiectasia, AVED, RFC1-CANVAS
X-linked: FXTAS in older male premutation carriers
Extracerebellar signs (neuropathy, retinopathy, parkinsonism, spasticity, slow saccades) guide gene choice
inv: MRI: cerebellar (± brainstem) atrophy pattern
Repeat-expansion panel (SCA1/2/3/6/7/12/17, DRPLA, FXN, RFC1, FGF14-GAA SCA27B) then NGS panel or exome/genome
Exclude treatable acquired causes: vitamin E, B12, thyroid, anti-GAD, coeliac, alcohol, drugs
NCS, eye examination, alpha-fetoprotein, albumin, cholesterol where recessive disease suspected

case.story: Unsteady for four years, now uses a stick; her father and two aunts became wheelchair-bound in their 50s.
case.exam: Gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, bulging eyes, gaze-evoked nystagmus, brisk knees with mild spasticity, faciolingual fasciculations.
case.tests: MRI pontocerebellar atrophy; ATXN3 CAG expansion 72 repeats.
case.q: Which hereditary ataxia, and how is it inherited?
case.a: SCA3, also called Machado–Joseph disease; autosomal dominant with anticipation.

read.where: Chapter 24 Cerebellar Ataxias and Related Conditions — Inherited Ataxia Syndromes
19 - Gait disorders: Pathophysiology and clinical syndromes

det.patho: Hereditary ataxias arise from repeat expansions (polyglutamine CAG repeats in many SCAs, intronic GAA in Friedreich and SCA27B, pentanucleotide in RFC1), point mutations affecting ion channels, DNA repair, mitochondrial function or lipid metabolism. Cerebellar Purkinje cells and their connections degenerate, often with brainstem, spinal tract or peripheral nerve involvement. Repeat expansions show anticipation in several dominant forms.
det.clinical: The core syndrome is slowly progressive ataxia of gait, limbs, speech and eye movements. Dominant SCAs typically begin in adult life and each has characteristic extras: slow saccades in SCA2, dystonia or parkinsonism and bulging eyes in SCA3, pure late-onset ataxia in SCA6, retinal degeneration in SCA7. Recessive ataxias usually start before 25 and are often accompanied by neuropathy, oculomotor apraxia or systemic signs. Episodic ataxias cause attacks with interictal myokymia or nystagmus.
det.diagnosis: Take a three-generation family history and consider consanguinity, but note that de novo, reduced penetrance or recessive forms may appear sporadic. MRI defines the atrophy pattern. Repeat-expansion testing is still needed because short-read exome misses most expansions; long-read genome sequencing is increasingly used. Treatable mimics must be excluded in every patient.
det.treatment: Omaveloxolone is approved for Friedreich ataxia in patients aged 16 and older; for other forms, management is supportive. Coordination-focused physiotherapy improves function, and speech, swallowing, falls and mood need attention. Specific treatments exist for AVED (vitamin E), cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis (chenodeoxycholic acid), episodic ataxia type 2 (acetazolamide, 4-aminopyridine) and SCA27B (4-aminopyridine). Genetic counselling and predictive testing are offered to families.
det.prognosis: Progressive; most dominant SCAs lead to wheelchair use 10–20 years after onset, with shortened lifespan in SCA1, SCA2 and SCA3; SCA6 is slower.
pearls: Always look for a treatable acquired or metabolic cause before labelling an ataxia degenerative.
SCA3 is the most common dominant ataxia worldwide and frequent in Thailand.
Exome sequencing does not detect most repeat expansions — order them specifically.
det.thd: Hereditary ataxias เป็นกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่สมองน้อยเสื่อม ทำให้เดินเซ พูดไม่ชัด และตากระตุก แบ่งเป็นแบบ autosomal dominant (SCA โดย SCA3 พบบ่อยในไทย), recessive (Friedreich, AT, AOA, CANVAS) และ X-linked (FXTAS) วินิจฉัยด้วยประวัติครอบครัว MRI และตรวจ repeat expansion ร่วมกับ gene panel ต้องตัดสาเหตุที่รักษาได้ เช่น ขาดวิตามิน E หรือ B12 ก่อน การรักษาส่วนใหญ่เป็นกายภาพบำบัด ยกเว้น Friedreich ที่มี omaveloxolone

name: Hereditary essential myoclonus
formal: Autosomal dominant non-progressive myoclonus with onset in childhood or teens, often with dystonia, due to SGCE mutation and alcohol-responsive (myoclonus-dystonia).
simple: An inherited condition of sudden muscle jerks that begins early in life and may improve with alcohol.

feat: Fast, lightning-like jerks of the neck, shoulders and arms, worse with action and posture
Mild dystonia (for example torticollis or writer's cramp) in about half
Jerks often melt away for an hour or so after a drink of alcohol
Anxiety, depression and obsessive-compulsive traits are common companions
Normal cognition, no ataxia and no seizures; examination otherwise clean
inv: SGCE gene testing (paternally expressed, so the mutation is usually inherited from the father)

MRI brain normal; exclude Wilson disease and other causes in young patients

case.story: Since age 8 her arms jerk when she writes or holds a glass, spilling drinks. Her father had similar jerks that he says ease after beer.
case.exam: Irregular brief jerks of both arms and neck on posture, mild right torticollis, normal gait and reflexes.
case.tests: EEG normal; MRI normal; heterozygous SGCE frameshift variant.
case.q: What is the condition and which features steer away from progressive myoclonic epilepsy?
case.a: Myoclonus-dystonia (SGCE); no seizures, no cognitive decline, normal EEG and a static course argue against a progressive myoclonic epilepsy.

read.where: Chapter 9 Movement Disorders — Hereditary Essential Myoclonus
11 - Dystonia: Phenomenology, classification, etiology, pathology, biochemistry, and genetics

det.patho: Most familial cases carry loss-of-function variants in SGCE, which encodes epsilon-sarcoglycan; the gene is maternally imprinted, so disease shows almost only when the faulty copy comes from the father. The myoclonus is thought to arise from cerebello-thalamo-cortical and basal ganglia network dysfunction rather than cortical hyperexcitability. A minority of SGCE-negative families carry variants in other genes such as KCTD17.
det.clinical: Onset is usually in the first two decades with jerks predominantly of the upper body, brought out by action, posture or stress. Dystonia, when present, tends to be focal or segmental and mild. Psychiatric comorbidity, including anxiety, panic, OCD and alcohol misuse, is frequent and sometimes more disabling than the movements. Life expectancy and intellect are normal.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis rests on the clinical pattern plus SGCE testing; family history may be absent because of imprinting. Electrophysiology shows short subcortical bursts without cortical correlates. Exclude acquired causes and progressive myoclonic syndromes when there are seizures, cognitive change or ataxia. Normal imaging is expected.
det.treatment: Clonazepam, levetiracetam, zonisamide or trihexyphenidyl can reduce jerks; sodium oxybate has been used off-label for alcohol-responsive cases. Patients should be warned not to self-medicate with alcohol. Botulinum toxin helps focal dystonia. Bilateral pallidal (GPi) deep brain stimulation gives substantial benefit for both myoclonus and dystonia in refractory patients.
det.prognosis: The course is benign and largely static, though social and psychiatric burden can be considerable.
pearls: Young person with upper-body jerks that settle after alcohol: think SGCE myoclonus-dystonia.
Paternal transmission pattern reflects maternal imprinting of SGCE.
GPi DBS works well when drugs fail.
det.thd: Hereditary essential myoclonus หรือ myoclonus-dystonia ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจากยีน SGCE ซึ่งแสดงผลเมื่อได้รับยีนผิดปกติจากพ่อ ผู้ป่วยมีอาการกระตุกเร็วที่คอ ไหล่ และแขนตั้งแต่วัยเด็ก มัก dystonia เล็กน้อยร่วม และอาการดีขึ้นชั่วคราวหลังดื่มแอลกอฮอล์ วินิจฉัยด้วยลักษณะทางคลินิกและตรวจยีน รักษาด้วย clonazepam หรือ GPi DBS ในรายดื้อยา

name: Hereditary hyperekplexia
formal: Genetic startle disease (GLRA1, SLC6A5) with exaggerated startle, neonatal stiffness and falls; treated with clonazepam, and Vigevano manoeuvre for apnoea.
simple: An inherited condition in which a sudden noise or touch causes extreme startle and stiffening, sometimes causing falls.
th: โรคสะดุ้งเกินปกติจากพันธุกรรม ทารกแข็งเกร็งตั้งแต่แรกเกิด สะดุ้งแรงและล้มแข็งทื่อเมื่อถูกกระตุ้น ตอบสนองดีต่อ clonazepam
tempoNote: Present from birth; stiffness eases during infancy but exaggerated startle persists for life
feat: Newborn stiffness when handled that disappears in sleep
Excessive, non-habituating startle to tapping the nose or sudden noise
Falls 'like a log' with arms held stiff, without loss of consciousness
Risk of apnoea and sudden infant death during stiffening spells
Hip dislocation, hernias and nocturnal jerks may occur

case.story: Since birth he becomes rigid when picked up and once turned blue during a stiffening episode after a loud noise.
case.exam: Tapping the nose bridge gives a vigorous startle each time without habituation; tone normal during sleep.
case.tests: EEG normal during a spell; homozygous GLRA1 variant.
case.q: What bedside manoeuvre can abort a dangerous stiffening episode?
case.a: Hereditary hyperekplexia; flexing the head and legs toward the trunk (Vigevano manoeuvre) breaks the spasm, and clonazepam is the drug of choice.

read.where: Hyperekplexia: a rare neurological condition with a treatable solution (case report)
1 - Clinical overview and phenomenology of movement disorders

det.patho: Glycine is the main inhibitory transmitter in brainstem and spinal cord. Variants in the glycine receptor alpha-1 or beta subunits (GLRA1, GLRB) or the presynaptic glycine transporter GlyT2 (SLC6A5) reduce inhibition, so brainstem startle circuits fire excessively and motor neurones are released from restraint. Inheritance may be dominant or recessive depending on gene and variant.
det.clinical: The major form shows neonatal hypertonia, exaggerated startle and stiff falls; the minor form has only excessive startle without stiffness. Stiffness subsides during the first years but startle and falls continue, causing injuries and fear of walking in crowds. Neonatal apnoeic spells can be life-threatening. Development is usually normal.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in a stiff newborn with a reproducible nose-tap startle and a normal EEG. Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis. Exclude neonatal seizures, metabolic encephalopathy and hypocalcaemia. EMG can document the abnormal startle pattern.
det.treatment: Clonazepam, which enhances GABA-A inhibition, reduces stiffness and falls in most patients. Parents are taught the Vigevano manoeuvre for apnoeic spasms and may use apnoea monitoring in infancy. Levetiracetam or other agents have been tried when clonazepam is insufficient. Offer genetic counselling.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is normal once the infant period is passed, though injuries from falls are common.
pearls: Repeated nose-tap startle with no habituation in a stiff newborn = hyperekplexia.
Folding the infant's head and legs toward the chest aborts dangerous spasms.
Clonazepam is first-line.
det.thd: Hereditary hyperekplexia เกิดจากความผิดปกติของระบบ glycine ซึ่งเป็นสารยับยั้งในก้านสมองและไขสันหลัง ทารกจะตัวแข็งเมื่ออุ้มและสะดุ้งรุนแรงทุกครั้งที่เคาะจมูก อาจหยุดหายใจได้ ต่อมาโตขึ้นยังสะดุ้งและล้มแข็งทื่อ EEG ปกติและยืนยันด้วยยีน GLRA1 หรือ SLC6A5 รักษาด้วย clonazepam และสอนผู้ปกครองทำ Vigevano manoeuvre

name: Hereditary inclusion body myopathies
formal: Group of inherited vacuolar myopathies resembling inclusion body myositis but without inflammation, including GNE myopathy, sparing the quadriceps and presenting with distal weakness.
simple: A family of inherited muscle diseases with slowly worsening weakness and tiny holes seen in muscle fibres.
more: Most are autosomal recessive (GNE) or dominant (VCP, MYH2, desmin). Muscle biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles; no proven cure, with supportive care and physiotherapy.
th: กลุ่มโรคกล้ามเนื้อทางพันธุกรรมที่ชิ้นเนื้อพบ rimmed vacuole คล้าย IBM แต่ไม่มีการอักเสบ เช่น GNE myopathy ที่ไม่กระทบกล้ามเนื้อ quadriceps
tempoNote: Onset in young adults (GNE) or mid-life (VCP); slowly progressive
feat: GNE myopathy (recessive): foot drop from tibialis anterior weakness in 20s, quadriceps spared
VCP disease (dominant): myopathy plus Paget's bone disease and FTD
Rimmed vacuoles with little or no inflammation on biopsy
CK normal to moderately raised
Slow progression; many need wheelchair 10–20 years after onset (GNE)
inv: CK; EMG (myopathic, may show irritability)
Muscle MRI: quadriceps sparing in GNE
Gene testing: GNE, VCP, HNRNPA2B1, others
Alkaline phosphatase and cognitive screen in VCP disease

case.story: Tripping over her toes for 3 years, now hand grip weakening; no family history.
case.exam: Bilateral foot drop, weak hamstrings and hip adductors, strong quadriceps, mild finger flexor weakness, normal sensation.
case.tests: CK 520 U/L; MRI thighs shows fatty change in hamstrings and adductors with spared quadriceps; biopsy rimmed vacuoles without inflammation; biallelic GNE variants.
case.q: Which MRI finding is the key clue?
case.a: Quadriceps sparing – GNE myopathy (hereditary inclusion body myopathy).

read.where: 19: A Quick Glance at the Therapeutic Approaches for Neuromuscular Disorders

det.patho: Hereditary inclusion body myopathies are genetic disorders sharing rimmed vacuoles and protein aggregates on biopsy without the inflammation of sporadic IBM. GNE myopathy results from impaired sialic acid synthesis, causing hyposialylation of muscle glycoproteins. VCP and related genes affect protein degradation and autophagy, producing multisystem proteinopathy.
det.clinical: GNE myopathy begins in early adulthood with foot drop and later involves hamstrings, hip muscles and hands while sparing the quadriceps. Multisystem proteinopathy from VCP presents in mid-life with limb-girdle or scapuloperoneal weakness, Paget disease and frontotemporal dementia in varying combinations. Progression is slow.
det.diagnosis: MRI patterns and age help: quadriceps sparing strongly suggests GNE. Biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles without significant inflammation. Genetic testing confirms. Screen VCP families for bone and cognitive involvement.
det.treatment: There is no approved disease-modifying therapy; sialic acid supplementation trials in GNE gave mixed results. Physiotherapy, ankle-foot orthoses and mobility aids are central. Manage Paget disease and dementia in VCP disease.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; many lose ambulation within 10–20 years in GNE myopathy.
pearls: Young adult with foot drop and strong quadriceps: GNE myopathy.
Myopathy plus Paget disease or FTD: VCP.
Rimmed vacuoles are not unique to sporadic IBM.
det.thd: Hereditary inclusion body myopathy เป็นกลุ่มโรคกล้ามเนื้อทางพันธุกรรมที่ชิ้นเนื้อพบ rimmed vacuole แต่ไม่มีการอักเสบ ที่สำคัญคือ GNE myopathy ซึ่งเริ่มในวัยหนุ่มสาวด้วยเท้าตก แต่กล้ามเนื้อ quadriceps ไม่อ่อนแรง และ VCP disease ที่มีโรคกระดูก Paget และสมองเสื่อม วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI ชิ้นเนื้อ และตรวจยีน ยังไม่มียาเฉพาะ

name: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies (HNPP)
formal: PMP22 deletion causing recurrent focal neuropathies at compression sites, such as peroneal and ulnar, after minor pressure, with tomaculous changes on nerve biopsy.
simple: An inherited condition in which nerves are very sensitive to pressure, causing episodes of numbness and weakness.
more: Diagnose by PMP22 deletion testing; nerve conduction shows diffuse mild slowing with prolonged distal latencies and conduction block at entrapment sites. Management is avoiding compression and splinting; most episodes resolve over weeks to months.
ab: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies
th: เส้นประสาทไวต่อการกดทับทางพันธุกรรม (PMP22 หาย) — ชา/อ่อนแรงซ้ำ ๆ หลังนั่งไขว่ห้างหรือนอนทับแขน หายเองได้
feat: Recurrent painless mononeuropathies at compression sites (peroneal, ulnar, radial, brachial plexus) after minor pressure
Most episodes recover over days to months
Autosomal dominant; relatives may have mild background neuropathy
inv: NCS: focal slowing at entrapment sites plus mild diffuse slowing even in unaffected nerves
PMP22 deletion (17p11.2)

case.story: Foot drop after kneeling on guard duty; last year a weak wrist after sleeping on his arm, which recovered. His mother has 'carpal tunnel' in both hands.
case.exam: Right peroneal palsy, reduced ankle jerks bilaterally.
case.tests: Conduction block at the fibular head plus prolonged distal latencies in median and ulnar nerves; PMP22 deletion.
case.q: What advice prevents further episodes?
case.a: Avoid prolonged pressure or stretching of nerves (crossing legs, kneeling, leaning on elbows) and take care during anaesthesia positioning.

qx.stem: A 21-year-old army conscript in Kanchanaburi develops a painless right foot drop after hours of squatting during training. Two years earlier he woke with a left wrist drop after sleeping on his arm, which recovered over three months. Reflexes are reduced at the ankles. Nerve conduction studies show focal slowing across the fibular head and both wrists plus mild diffuse sensory slowing in clinically unaffected nerves.
qx.q: Which investigation would best establish the diagnosis?
opts: Anti-GM1 antibodies
PMP22 duplication analysis
Sural nerve biopsy
PMP22 deletion analysis on chromosome 17p11.2
MPZ sequencing
qx.why: Recurrent painless compression mononeuropathies on a background of multifocal slowing at entrapment sites suggest HNPP, usually due to a 1.5-Mb deletion including PMP22. The reciprocal duplication causes CMT1A, which gives uniform slowing. Biopsy (tomacula) is no longer needed when genetic testing is available. Counselling covers avoiding prolonged pressure and caution with neurotoxic chemotherapy such as vincristine.

qx.stem: A 24-year-old rice farmer from Roi Et wakes with a foot drop after sitting cross-legged for 2 hours, recovering over six weeks. He has had two earlier episodes of wrist drop after leaning on his elbow. His father had similar episodes. Nerve conduction shows prolonged distal latencies at common entrapment sites and generalised mild slowing.
qx.q: What genetic abnormality is expected?
opts: PMP22 gene duplication
PMP22 deletion
MFN2 mutation
GJB1 mutation
SH3TC2 mutation
qx.why: Recurrent pressure palsies with focal slowing at compression sites reflect PMP22 deletion, which causes tomaculous (sausage-shaped) myelin. PMP22 duplication causes CMT1A with uniform slowing, MFN2 causes axonal CMT2A, GJB1 causes CMTX1, and SH3TC2 causes a recessive demyelinating form.

files.chapter: Chapter 43: Hereditary Neuropathy with Pressure Palsy (HNPP)

ddx.pt: Progressive symmetric distal weakness; PMP22 duplication
Not related to pressure, raised CSF protein, steroid/IVIG responsive
Severe pain at onset

nN: hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies hnpp
aN: hnpp | hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies | tomaculous neuropathy | pmp22 deletion | pressure palsy neuropathy

det.patho: HNPP is usually caused by a heterozygous 1.4 Mb deletion of chromosome 17p11.2 that includes PMP22 — the reciprocal of the duplication in CMT1A; point mutations account for a minority. Reduced PMP22 dosage destabilises myelin and junctions, producing focal sausage-like myelin thickenings (tomacula) and nerves that tolerate pressure or stretch poorly. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with variable penetrance, and many carriers are unaware.
det.clinical: Typical patients have repeated painless focal palsies after trivial compression — peroneal palsy after crossing legs, ulnar palsy after leaning, radial palsy after sleeping on the arm, or brachial plexus palsy after carrying a backpack. Episodes usually recover over days to weeks, though recovery can be incomplete. Some develop a mild length-dependent polyneuropathy, recurrent carpal tunnel-like symptoms, or no symptoms at all. Pes cavus and reduced ankle reflexes may be found.
det.diagnosis: NCS characteristically show prolonged distal motor latencies, slowing at usual entrapment sites, and mild generalised sensory abnormalities even in clinically unaffected nerves — finding these in a patient with a single palsy is a strong clue. Genetic testing for the PMP22 deletion (MLPA or similar) confirms the diagnosis and avoids biopsy. Family members may need testing and counselling.
det.treatment: There is no specific therapy. Education is central: avoid prolonged leg crossing, kneeling, leaning on elbows, tight straps and repetitive wrist flexion, and use padding. Inform anaesthetists to pad and position limbs carefully. Orthoses and physiotherapy aid recovery from palsies, and surgical decompression of entrapments is generally avoided unless clearly indicated. Neurotoxic drugs such as vincristine should be used with caution.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is normal and most episodes resolve, but accumulating residual deficits occur in some people over time.
pearls: Recurrent pressure palsies + diffuse NCS abnormalities = PMP22 deletion.
Deletion causes HNPP; duplication causes CMT1A.
Think HNPP before operating on a young patient with multiple entrapments.
det.thd: HNPP เป็นโรคเส้นประสาททางพันธุกรรม (PMP22 deletion) ทำให้เยื่อหุ้มเส้นประสาทไม่แข็งแรงและไวต่อการกดทับ ผู้ป่วยมีอ่อนแรง/ชาไม่ปวดซ้ำ ๆ หลังนั่งไขว่ห้าง นอนทับแขน หรือวางศอกนาน ส่วนใหญ่หายเองในไม่กี่สัปดาห์ NCS พบความผิดปกติกระจายทั่วไปแม้ในเส้นที่ไม่มีอาการ ยืนยันด้วยตรวจยีน ไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ เน้นการหลีกเลี่ยงการกดทับและแจ้งวิสัญญีแพทย์เรื่องการจัดท่า

name: Hereditary optic neuropathy
formal: Inherited optic nerve disease, including Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (mitochondrial) and dominant optic atrophy (OPA1), causing painless visual loss and optic disc pallor.
simple: An inherited disease of the optic nerve that gradually causes loss of vision.
th: กลุ่มโรคเส้นประสาทตาเสื่อมจากพันธุกรรม เช่น LHON และ dominant optic atrophy ทำให้ตามัวแบบไม่เจ็บและขั้วประสาทตาซีด
tempoNote: LHON: subacute painless loss in one eye then the other over weeks; DOA: insidious childhood decline
feat: Painless, bilateral central or centrocaecal scotomas with colour vision loss
LHON: young men, sequential eyes within weeks to months; disc may look hyperaemic early
DOA: slow childhood visual decline with temporal disc pallor and family history
Pupil responses relatively preserved in LHON despite poor acuity
Some carry extra-ocular features (deafness, neuropathy, ataxia) — 'plus' syndromes
inv: mtDNA testing for the three common LHON variants (m.11778, m.3460, m.14484) and OPA1 testing
OCT: early RNFL swelling in LHON, then thinning; temporal thinning in DOA
MRI orbits and brain to exclude compression or inflammation
Visual fields and B12, folate and toxin screen to exclude acquired optic neuropathy

case.who: 22-year-old male rubber-plantation worker from Surat Thani
case.story: Painless blurring in the right eye, then the left eye six weeks later. He smokes and drinks; his maternal uncle went blind young.
case.exam: VA 6/60 both eyes, central scotomas, mildly swollen-looking discs that do not leak on angiography, no RAPD.
case.tests: MRI orbits normal; mtDNA m.11778G>A homoplasmic.
case.q: Which inheritance pattern and which treatment option should be discussed?
case.a: LHON — maternal (mitochondrial) inheritance; discuss idebenone, stopping smoking and alcohol, and low-vision support.

read.where: Chapter 38: Congenital Diseases of the Optic Nerve

det.patho: LHON is caused by mtDNA variants in complex I subunits, impairing energy supply to retinal ganglion cells, especially the small papillomacular fibres. Penetrance is incomplete and male-biased; smoking and heavy alcohol increase the risk of conversion. Dominant optic atrophy usually results from OPA1 variants affecting mitochondrial fusion, causing slow ganglion cell loss from childhood.
det.clinical: LHON typically presents in the teens to thirties with painless subacute visual loss in one eye, with the fellow eye affected within months, leaving dense central scotomas. DOA causes insidious bilateral loss in the first decade, often noticed at school screening, with blue-yellow colour defects. Both may be accompanied by systemic or neurological features in 'plus' phenotypes, and an MS-like illness can occur with LHON (Harding disease).
det.diagnosis: Consider it in any painless bilateral optic neuropathy without an obvious acquired cause. Test for common LHON mtDNA variants and OPA1, with broader panels if negative. OCT and visual fields document the pattern. Imaging and blood tests are needed to exclude compressive, inflammatory, nutritional and toxic causes.
det.treatment: Idebenone is approved in some regions for LHON and is most useful if started early. Gene therapy for the m.11778 variant has been trialled with modest results. Advise avoidance of tobacco, alcohol excess and mitochondrial-toxic drugs. Low-vision rehabilitation, driving advice and genetic counselling apply to all forms.
det.prognosis: Most LHON patients remain legally blind, though some (especially m.14484) recover partially; DOA usually progresses slowly with moderate impairment.
pearls: Young man, painless sequential optic neuropathy, maternal relatives affected: LHON.
Early LHON discs can look swollen but do not leak on fluorescein.
Stop smoking and heavy drinking in carriers.
det.thd: Hereditary optic neuropathy คือโรคเส้นประสาทตาเสื่อมจากพันธุกรรม ที่พบบ่อยคือ LHON ซึ่งถ่ายทอดทางแม่ (mitochondrial DNA) ผู้ชายวัยหนุ่มตามัวตรงกลางทีละข้างโดยไม่เจ็บ และ dominant optic atrophy (OPA1) ที่ตามัวช้า ๆ ตั้งแต่เด็ก วินิจฉัยด้วยตรวจยีนและ OCT หลังแยกสาเหตุอื่นด้วย MRI และเลือด รักษาด้วย idebenone ในบางราย งดบุหรี่และสุรา และฟื้นฟูการมองเห็น

name: Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy
formal: Inherited neuropathies with predominant loss of pain and temperature sensation, ulcers, mutilation and autonomic dysfunction, such as HSAN types I to V.
simple: Inherited nerve diseases where people cannot feel pain or temperature properly, leading to injuries and sores.
more: Heterogeneous inherited neuropathies marked by sensory loss, ulceration and autonomic failure, classified HSAN I to VIII based on genes such as SPTLC1 and RETREG1. Diagnosis by genetic testing and nerve studies; inheritance mostly autosomal recessive except HSAN I. Care focuses on foot protection, wound care and managing autonomic symptoms.
th: กลุ่มโรคเส้นประสาทจากพันธุกรรมที่สูญเสียความรู้สึกเจ็บและร้อนเย็น เกิดแผลเรื้อรัง นิ้วกุด และระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติผิดปกติ
tempoNote: Congenital in recessive types; adolescent or adult onset with slow progression in HSAN I
feat: Impaired pain and temperature sensation, leading to painless injuries and burns
Foot ulcers, osteomyelitis, Charcot joints and acral mutilation
Autonomic features: anhidrosis, fever spikes, postural hypotension, GI dysmotility
HSAN I (dominant, adult) may have shooting pains and mild distal weakness
Some types have intellectual disability, absent tears or self-mutilation
inv: Nerve conduction: reduced or absent sensory potentials; motor often spared
Genetic panel (SPTLC1, RAB7, NTRK1, NGF, ELP1, SCN9A, RETREG1 and others)
Autonomic tests, sweat testing and skin biopsy for small-fibre density
X-ray or MRI of feet for silent fractures and osteomyelitis

case.story: Recurrent painless ulcers under both big toes for five years; her mother lost toes to infection.
case.exam: Loss of pinprick and temperature to the mid-shin, preserved power, absent ankle jerks, deep plantar ulcer.
case.tests: Sural SNAPs absent; HbA1c normal; SPTLC1 variant found.
case.q: Which HSAN type is this and what is the main focus of care?
case.a: HSAN I (dominant, SPTLC1); foot protection, wound care and infection control, with L-serine studied as a potential therapy.

read.where: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves — Hereditary Sensory Neuropathy

det.patho: These disorders affect development or survival of small sensory and autonomic neurones. HSAN I (SPTLC1/2) produces toxic deoxysphingolipids; HSAN III (ELP1) is familial dysautonomia; HSAN IV and V involve the NGF–TrkA pathway that small fibres need to develop. Many other genes have been identified, and classification is now partly gene-based.
det.clinical: Dominant HSAN I appears in adolescence or adulthood with distal sensory loss, lancinating pains and foot ulcers. Recessive congenital forms show insensitivity to pain from infancy, with self-injury, unrecognised fractures and anhidrosis causing hyperthermia (HSAN IV). Familial dysautonomia brings feeding problems, absent tears and blood pressure crises. Course and severity vary widely by gene.
det.diagnosis: Distinguish from acquired causes such as diabetes, leprosy, amyloidosis and syringomyelia. Nerve conduction shows sensory axonal loss; skin biopsy confirms small-fibre loss. A family history, early onset or mutilating complications point to a genetic cause, confirmed by gene panels or exome sequencing.
det.treatment: No cure exists. Care centres on daily foot inspection, protective footwear, early wound management and orthopaedic care of joints. Treat orthostatic hypotension, temperature instability and GI symptoms. Oral L-serine lowers deoxysphingolipids in HSAN I and has been studied as disease-modifying therapy; carbamazepine or gabapentinoids help shooting pain.
det.prognosis: Morbidity comes mainly from infection and amputation; life expectancy depends on type, being reduced in severe congenital forms.
pearls: Painless toe ulcers with a family history: think HSAN, not just diabetes.
Anhidrosis plus pain insensitivity in a child: HSAN IV (NTRK1).
Always exclude leprosy in endemic areas.
det.thd: Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy เป็นกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่เส้นประสาทรับความรู้สึกเจ็บและอุณหภูมิเสียไป ร่วมกับระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติผิดปกติ ผู้ป่วยเกิดแผลที่เท้าโดยไม่เจ็บ กระดูกหักโดยไม่รู้ตัว และอาจไม่มีเหงื่อ วินิจฉัยด้วย NCS ตรวจยีน และแยกเบาหวาน เรื้อน amyloid ออก การดูแลเน้นป้องกันแผล รักษาการติดเชื้อ และคุมอาการระบบอัตโนมัติ

qx.stem: A 40-year-old man from Lampang has had years of burning and shooting pains in his feet, painless ulcers on his fingertips and toes, and a deformed, shortened toe after osteomyelitis. His mother and uncle had a similar problem. Examination shows reduced pain and temperature sensation in a stocking distribution with preserved power, and a heterozygous SPTLC1 variant is found.
qx.q: Which mechanism best explains this neuropathy?
opts: Impaired copper transport
Accumulation of phytanic acid
Antibodies against myelin-associated glycoprotein
Abnormal serine palmitoyltransferase using alanine to create neurotoxic deoxysphingolipids
Deletion of the PMP22 gene
qx.why: A length-dependent small-fibre predominant sensory neuropathy with ulcerating mutilation and dominant inheritance suggests HSAN type 1, caused by SPTLC1 or SPTLC2 mutations that shift substrate specificity of serine palmitoyltransferase so that alanine and glycine form neurotoxic deoxysphingolipids. Oral L-serine supplementation is being studied. PMP22 deletion causes HNPP and phytanic acid accumulation causes Refsum disease.

name: Hereditary sensory neuropathy (HSN)
formal: Inherited neuropathies with predominant loss of pain and temperature sensation, ulcers, mutilation and autonomic dysfunction, such as HSAN types I to V.
simple: Inherited nerve diseases where people cannot feel pain or temperature properly, leading to injuries and sores.
th: กลุ่มโรคเส้นประสาทพันธุกรรมที่เสียการรับรู้ความเจ็บปวดและอุณหภูมิเป็นหลัก ทำให้เกิดแผลเรื้อรัง กระดูกถูกทำลาย และระบบอัตโนมัติผิดปกติ
tempoNote: Congenital forms from birth; HSAN1 begins in young adulthood and progresses slowly
feat: Painless injuries, burns and chronic foot ulcers
Osteomyelitis, Charcot joints and acral mutilation (digit loss)
Shooting pains in HSAN1 despite sensory loss
Variable autonomic involvement: anhidrosis (HSAN4), dysautonomic crises (HSAN3)
Distal motor weakness in some types
inv: Nerve conduction: reduced or absent sensory responses
Gene panel: SPTLC1/2, RAB7A, NTRK1, ELP1, SCN9A, others
Foot X-ray or MRI for osteomyelitis

case.story: Recurrent painless ulcers under both big toes for 8 years; amputation of one toe; father had similar ulcers.
case.exam: Loss of pain and temperature to knees, mild vibration loss, absent ankle jerks, mild toe weakness, deep ulcer under left hallux.
case.tests: Sural responses absent; HbA1c normal; leprosy smear negative; SPTLC1 variant.
case.q: Which acquired disease is the key mimic in Thailand?
case.a: Leprosy; but symmetric distal pattern and family history favour HSAN1.

read.where: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves — Hereditary Sensory Neuropathy

det.patho: Genes involved affect sphingolipid metabolism (SPTLC1/2 causing neurotoxic deoxysphingolipids), axonal transport, nerve growth factor signalling (NTRK1, NGF) and sodium channels (SCN9A). Loss of small sensory and autonomic fibres leads to insensitivity and impaired protective reflexes.
det.clinical: HSAN1 (dominant) presents in adolescence or adulthood with distal sensory loss, ulcers and lancinating pains. Congenital recessive types (HSAN2–5) present in childhood with insensitivity to pain, self-injury and autonomic features. Bone and joint destruction follows repeated unnoticed injury.
det.diagnosis: A symmetric distal small-fibre-predominant neuropathy with ulcers and family history suggests HSAN. Exclude leprosy, diabetes, amyloidosis and alcohol. Genetic testing confirms the subtype.
det.treatment: No cure; foot care, protective footwear, early ulcer treatment and infection control are critical. L-serine supplementation reduced toxic deoxysphingolipids in SPTLC1 cases and showed slower progression in a trial. Pain management for lancinating pains.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; major morbidity from ulcers, infections and amputations.
pearls: Painless ulcers with family history: HSAN; in Thailand exclude leprosy first.
L-serine is a targeted therapy option for SPTLC1 disease.
Prevention through foot care is the most effective intervention.
det.thd: HSAN เป็นโรคเส้นประสาทพันธุกรรมที่เสียการรับรู้ความเจ็บและอุณหภูมิ ทำให้มีแผลเรื้อรังที่เท้า กระดูกติดเชื้อ และนิ้วถูกทำลาย บางชนิดมีระบบอัตโนมัติผิดปกติ ต้องแยกจากโรคเรื้อนและเบาหวาน ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน การรักษาหลักคือดูแลเท้าและป้องกันแผล ชนิด SPTLC1 อาจใช้ L-serine

name: Hereditary spastic ataxia
formal: Autosomal recessive disorder with spastic ataxia, such as ARSACS (SACS), with early-onset ataxia, spasticity, peripheral neuropathy and retinal striation.
simple: An inherited condition with both stiff legs and unsteady balance, usually starting in childhood.
th: กลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่มีทั้งเดินเซจาก cerebellum และขาเกร็งร่วมกัน เช่น ARSACS ที่เริ่มในเด็กเล็ก มีปลายประสาทเสื่อมและลายเส้นที่จอตา
tempoNote: Early childhood onset in ARSACS with slow progression; dominant SPAX forms start later
feat: Gait ataxia combined with leg spasticity and extensor plantars
Peripheral neuropathy with distal wasting and pes cavus over time
Hypermyelinated retinal nerve fibres visible as striations (ARSACS)
Dysarthria, nystagmus and saccadic pursuit
Slow progression; many need walking aids by middle age
inv: MRI: superior vermian atrophy, linear pontine T2 hypointensities, thick middle cerebellar peduncles
OCT showing thickened peripapillary RNFL
Nerve conduction: mixed axonal-demyelinating neuropathy
Gene testing: SACS and spastic ataxia panels (e.g., VAMP1, KIF1C)

case.story: Clumsy since he started walking and now trips more; parents are first cousins.
case.exam: Ataxic gait, brisk knee jerks with absent ankle jerks, extensor plantars, saccadic pursuit, striated yellow fibres around the discs.
case.tests: MRI: pontine linear stripes and vermian atrophy; biallelic SACS variants.
case.q: Which imaging sign is characteristic of this disorder?
case.a: ARSACS; linear T2-hypointense stripes in the pons together with superior vermis atrophy and thickened retinal nerve fibre layer.

read.where: 1 - Clinical overview and phenomenology of movement disorders

det.patho: Spastic ataxias are a clinical grouping in which both cerebellar and corticospinal pathways degenerate. ARSACS, the best-known recessive example, results from biallelic SACS variants encoding sacsin, a protein involved in mitochondrial dynamics and neurofilament organisation. Other forms (SPAX types) are linked to genes such as VAMP1, KIF1C and AFG3L2.
det.clinical: Children with ARSACS walk late or unsteadily, then develop progressive spastic ataxia, distal amyotrophy and neuropathy; reflexes may be brisk at the knee yet absent at the ankle. Retinal striations are a helpful clue but not universal. Adult-onset and atypical presentations occur, including predominant neuropathy or spastic paraparesis. Cognition is usually preserved.
det.diagnosis: Combine examination findings with MRI clues (pontine stripes, peduncle thickening) and OCT. Nerve studies support it. Genetic panels or exome sequencing confirm the cause. Exclude Friedreich ataxia, vitamin E deficiency, B12 deficiency and structural cervical lesions.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy exists. Physiotherapy, stretching and orthoses address spasticity and contractures; baclofen or botulinum toxin may help focal stiffness. Monitor for foot deformity and scoliosis. Provide genetic counselling for families.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; many become wheelchair-dependent in their 40s, with near-normal life expectancy.
pearls: Ataxia + spasticity + neuropathy in a child: think ARSACS.
Look for retinal striations and pontine stripes.
Knee jerks brisk but ankle jerks lost reflects combined upper and lower motor neurone involvement.
det.thd: Hereditary spastic ataxia คือกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่มีทั้งอาการเดินเซและขาเกร็ง ตัวอย่างสำคัญคือ ARSACS จากยีน SACS เด็กเริ่มเดินเซตั้งแต่เล็ก มีเส้นประสาทปลายเสื่อมและเส้นใยประสาทจอตาหนาเป็นริ้ว MRI พบลายเส้นในพอนส์ วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีน การรักษาเป็นกายภาพบำบัดและลดเกร็ง

ddx.pt: Absent reflexes, cardiomyopathy and diabetes; no retinal striations
Pure spasticity predominates with little cerebellar ataxia
The prototype itself; confirm with SACS testing

aN: spastic ataxia | arsacs | sacs related ataxia | charlevoix saguenay spastic ataxia | spax

name: Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP)
formal: Heritable upper motor neuron disorders with progressive lower limb spasticity and weakness from corticospinal tract axonopathy, pure or complicated, with many genes (SPG4 commonest).
simple: Inherited conditions that gradually make the legs stiff and weak because of damage to nerve fibres from the brain.
more: Diagnosis uses MRI to exclude structural causes, and a gene panel including SPG4 (SPAST), SPG3A and SPG11; thin corpus callosum is typical of SPG11. Treat symptomatically with baclofen, tizanidine, botulinum toxin and physiotherapy. Hereditary spastic paraplegias with length-dependent corticospinal degeneration causing progressive lower limb spasticity and weakness.
th: ขาเกร็งแข็งและเดินลำบากค่อยเป็นค่อยไปจากพันธุกรรม — corticospinal tract ยาวเสื่อม แขนมักปกติ
tempoNote: Any age from childhood to late adulthood; very slow progression over decades
feat: Spasticity in the legs out of proportion to weakness; scissoring, toe-walking gait
Brisk leg reflexes, extensor plantars, often mild vibration loss at the ankles
Urinary urgency is common; arms usually spared
'Complicated' forms add neuropathy, ataxia, cognitive decline, thin corpus callosum or epilepsy
inv: MRI brain and whole spine to exclude compression, demyelination and leukodystrophy
B12, copper, HTLV-1, VLCFA (adrenomyeloneuropathy) to exclude acquired or treatable mimics
Gene panel or exome (SPAST, ATL1, REEP1, SPG7, SPG11 and others)

case.story: Since his twenties he has tripped over curbs; legs feel stiff rather than weak. His mother walked with a stiff gait in later life.
case.exam: Spastic paraparesis with mild hip flexor weakness, ankle clonus, bilateral Babinski, reduced vibration at the toes; normal arms and speech.
case.tests: MRI brain and spine normal; B12, copper and HTLV-1 negative; SPAST pathogenic variant.
case.q: What is the role of spinal MRI when a family history is clear?
case.a: Still essential — structural lesions and treatable myelopathies must be excluded before attributing spastic paraparesis to HSP.

read.where: Chapter 14 Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders

det.patho: HSP is a group of over 80 genetic disorders that cause length-dependent degeneration of the longest corticospinal axons and, to a lesser extent, the dorsal columns. Implicated genes affect axonal transport, membrane shaping of the endoplasmic reticulum, lipid metabolism and mitochondrial function. SPAST (SPG4) mutations are the most frequent dominant cause; SPG11 and SPG7 are common recessive causes.
det.clinical: Pure forms present with slowly progressive leg stiffness and gait difficulty; walking deteriorates more because of tone than weakness. Onset age varies widely even within a family. Complicated forms add features such as cerebellar ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, cognitive decline, optic atrophy, amyotrophy of the hands or a thin corpus callosum. Bladder urgency is common; rapid progression or sensory level should prompt a search for another cause.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis needs a compatible syndrome, family history or genetic confirmation, and exclusion of mimics. MRI of brain and spine is mandatory to rule out compressive myelopathy, MS, leukodystrophy and spinal dural fistula. Bloods for B12, copper, HTLV-1, VLCFA and syphilis address acquired and treatable causes. Next-generation sequencing panels identify a cause in perhaps half of familial cases.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying therapy. Management targets spasticity with stretching, physiotherapy, oral baclofen or tizanidine, botulinum toxin to selected muscles and intrathecal baclofen for severe cases. Ankle-foot orthoses, walking aids, bladder antimuscarinics and genetic counselling complete care.
det.prognosis: Pure forms usually allow independent walking for decades with normal lifespan; complicated forms carry more disability.
pearls: Stiffness greater than weakness in the legs is the HSP signature.
Thin corpus callosum on MRI suggests SPG11 or SPG15.
Always exclude B12, copper and adrenomyeloneuropathy — treatable or important mimics.
det.thd: HSP เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมที่ทำให้ corticospinal tract ส่วนที่ยาวที่สุดเสื่อม ผู้ป่วยมีขาเกร็งแข็ง เดินลากขา reflex ไว Babinski บวก แต่แขนมักปกติ แบ่งเป็นชนิด pure และ complicated ต้องทำ MRI สมองและไขสันหลัง และตรวจ B12, copper, HTLV-1, VLCFA เพื่อแยกโรคที่รักษาได้ ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน การรักษาเน้นลดเกร็งและกายภาพบำบัด

name: Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE)
formal: Necrotising temporal and orbitofrontal encephalitis from HSV-1 with fever, seizures, aphasia and behavioural change; diagnosed by CSF PCR and MRI and treated promptly with aciclovir.
simple: A serious brain infection from the cold sore virus, causing fever, confusion and seizures, treated urgently with antiviral medicine.
th: สมองอักเสบจากเชื้อเริม — ไข้ สับสน พฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน ชัก กระทบสมองกลีบขมับ ให้ acyclovir ทันที
feat: Fever with confusion, behavioural change, dysphasia
Focal seizures, olfactory or gustatory hallucinations
Can trigger later anti-NMDAR encephalitis
inv: MRI: asymmetric medial temporal/insular/orbitofrontal T2 change
CSF lymphocytes, red cells; HSV PCR (repeat if early negative)
EEG: temporal periodic discharges

case.story: Two days of fever and headache, now talking nonsense and smelling burning rubber.
case.exam: Temp 38.7 °C, fluent dysphasia, no neck stiffness.
case.tests: MRI: left medial temporal FLAIR hyperintensity; CSF WBC 85 (lymphocytes), HSV-1 PCR positive.
case.q: When should acyclovir be started?
case.a: Immediately on suspicion — before results return.

read.where: Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — Herpes Simplex Encephalitis

qx.stem: A 63-year-old retired teacher from Nakhon Pathom has two days of fever, odd behaviour and a smell of burning rubber that nobody else notices, then a focal seizure. MRI shows right mesial temporal and insular FLAIR signal. CSF taken on day 2 has 85 lymphocytes/µL, protein 0.9 g/L and normal glucose; HSV PCR is negative. IV acyclovir was started on admission.
qx.q: What should be done next?
opts: Stop acyclovir because the PCR has excluded HSV
Switch to oral valacyclovir and discharge with follow-up
Keep acyclovir going and perform a second lumbar puncture with HSV PCR in 3–7 days
Start high-dose methylprednisolone for presumed autoimmune encephalitis
Arrange brain biopsy of the right temporal lobe this week
qx.why: HSV PCR can be falsely negative in the first 72 hours, so with a typical clinical and MRI picture acyclovir continues and CSF PCR is repeated; treatment usually runs 14–21 days. Stopping on one early negative PCR is a classic pitfall. Oral valacyclovir does not reach adequate CSF levels for initial therapy, biopsy is now rarely needed, and anti-NMDAR encephalitis may follow HSE weeks later but is not the first concern here.

qx.stem: A 45-year-old man in Bangkok has three days of fever, an odd smell sensation, and then a generalised seizure with confusion. CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with moderately raised red cells. MRI shows swelling and T2/FLAIR hyperintensity with restricted diffusion in the right medial temporal lobe, insula and orbitofrontal cortex, and the putamen is spared.
qx.q: What is the right action?
opts: Await HSV PCR before treating
Start high-dose corticosteroids for autoimmune encephalitis
Prescribe oral valaciclovir alone
Observe, as imaging is non-specific
Start intravenous aciclovir immediately and confirm by CSF HSV PCR
qx.why: Limbic and temporal involvement with sparing of the basal ganglia is typical of HSV-1 encephalitis, a treatable emergency where delay worsens outcome. Intravenous aciclovir should begin on suspicion; CSF PCR can be falsely negative early in the illness, within about three days and can be repeated. Anti-NMDAR and other autoimmune encephalitides must be considered later if relapse occurs.

det.patho: HSV-1, either from primary infection or reactivation in the trigeminal ganglion, reaches the orbitofrontal and medial temporal lobes and causes asymmetric haemorrhagic necrotising encephalitis. Worldwide, HSV-1 tops the list of sporadic fatal viral encephalitis worldwide, occurring at any age without seasonality. Defects in innate TLR3 signalling predispose some children; HSV-2 causes neonatal encephalitis and adult meningitis more often.
det.clinical: Most patients have fever and headache with altered behaviour, confusion, memory problems, dysphasia or personality change developing over days. Focal seizures, olfactory or taste hallucinations and hemiparesis may occur. Neck stiffness is often absent. About a quarter of patients develop anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis weeks after HSE, presenting as a relapse with movement disorders or psychiatric change and negative viral PCR.
det.diagnosis: CSF typically shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis with raised protein and often red cells; a normal early CSF does not exclude it. HSV PCR is highly sensitive and specific but can be falsely negative during the first three days, so repeat it if suspicion remains. MRI is the most sensitive imaging test, showing T2/FLAIR and diffusion change in the medial temporal lobe, insula and cingulate, often bilateral but asymmetric. EEG may show lateralised periodic discharges over the temporal lobe.
det.treatment: Give IV acyclovir at 10 mg/kg per dose, 8-hourly (adjusted for renal function) as soon as encephalitis is suspected, and continue for 14–21 days in confirmed cases. Maintain hydration to avoid crystal nephropathy. Treat seizures and raised intracranial pressure; corticosteroids are not routinely recommended. Monitor for post-HSE autoimmune encephalitis and test NMDAR antibodies if new symptoms appear after initial improvement.
det.prognosis: Untreated mortality exceeds 70%; with acyclovir it falls to around 10–20%, but many survivors have memory, behavioural or language deficits, especially if treatment is delayed.
pearls: Fever plus confusion means acyclovir now — every hour of delay worsens outcome.
Early negative HSV PCR does not rule it out; repeat the LP.
New chorea or psychiatric change weeks after HSE suggests NMDAR encephalitis, not viral relapse.
det.thd: HSE เป็นสมองอักเสบจากเชื้อ HSV-1 ที่ทำลายสมองกลีบขมับด้านในและส่วนหน้าล่าง ผู้ป่วยมีไข้ ปวดศีรษะ สับสน พฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน พูดผิดปกติ หรือชัก บางรายได้กลิ่นแปลก ๆ MRI เห็นรอยโรคที่ medial temporal และ insula น้ำไขสันหลังมี lymphocyte และส่ง HSV PCR (ถ้าลบในช่วงแรกควรเจาะซ้ำ) ต้องให้ acyclovir ทางหลอดเลือดทันทีที่สงสัย 14–21 วัน หลังหายอาจเกิด anti-NMDAR encephalitis ตามมาได้

name: Herpes simplex virus 2 vasculitis
formal: HSV-2 related central nervous system infection that is associated with Mollaret meningitis and rare vasculopathy causing stroke or myelitis.
simple: A rare complication of the genital herpes virus that inflames blood vessels in the brain or spinal cord.
th: การติดเชื้อ HSV-2 ในระบบประสาท ที่พบบ่อยคือเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบซ้ำแบบ Mollaret ส่วนน้อยทำให้หลอดเลือดอักเสบจน stroke หรือไขสันหลังอักเสบ
tempoNote: Meningitis attacks recur over years; vasculopathy and myelitis are acute or subacute
feat: Most common CNS presentation: aseptic meningitis, often recurrent (Mollaret)
Sacral radiculitis with urinary retention (Elsberg syndrome)
Myelitis, particularly in immunocompromised patients
Rare vasculopathy causing ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke
Genital lesions may be absent at the time of neurological illness
inv: CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis; HSV-2 PCR (may be negative later in attacks)
MRI brain and spine; vessel imaging (CTA/MRA or DSA) if stroke
HIV test; serology for HSV-2

case.who: 29-year-old woman from Pattaya with 3 previous episodes of meningitis, each resolving in a week
case.story: Another attack of severe headache, fever and neck stiffness.
case.exam: Neck stiffness, no focal signs, no rash.
case.tests: CSF: 420 lymphocytes, normal glucose, HSV-2 PCR positive.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and how might recurrences be reduced?
case.a: Recurrent HSV-2 (Mollaret) meningitis; acyclovir/valacyclovir for attacks, with suppressive therapy as an option although evidence is mixed.

read.where: Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — Mollaret’s Meningitis

det.patho: HSV-2 establishes latency in sacral dorsal root ganglia after genital infection. Reactivation can seed the meninges, roots or cord. Rarely the virus or the immune response injures vessel walls, producing a vasculopathy similar to that seen with VZV. Immunosuppression increases the risk of myelitis and severe disease.
det.clinical: Recurrent lymphocytic meningitis lasting days and resolving spontaneously is typical. Sacral radiculitis causes urinary retention, constipation and perineal numbness. Myelitis may be necrotising in HIV. Stroke from vasculitis is rare and mainly in case reports; evidence for this entity is limited.
det.diagnosis: CSF PCR for HSV-2 is the key test; repeat if early CSF is negative and suspicion remains. Imaging identifies cord, root or vascular involvement. In stroke with lymphocytic CSF, VZV, syphilis and TB are commoner causes and should also be tested.
det.treatment: Acyclovir intravenously for myelitis, vasculopathy or severe illness, and oral valacyclovir for uncomplicated meningitis. Suppressive valacyclovir for recurrent meningitis is used by some, but a trial suggested no reduction and possibly rebound after stopping. Steroids are sometimes added for vasculopathy by analogy with VZV.
det.prognosis: Meningitis is benign; myelitis and vasculopathy may leave deficits.
pearls: Recurrent lymphocytic meningitis in a young adult: send HSV-2 PCR.
Urinary retention with meningitis suggests sacral radiculitis (Elsberg).
HSV-2 vasculitis is rare; check VZV and syphilis in any infective vasculopathy.
det.thd: HSV-2 ในระบบประสาทที่พบบ่อยที่สุดคือเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบแบบหายเองและเป็นซ้ำ (Mollaret) บางรายมีรากประสาทส่วนก้นอักเสบทำให้ปัสสาวะไม่ออก หรือไขสันหลังอักเสบ การที่ HSV-2 ทำให้หลอดเลือดสมองอักเสบจน stroke พบได้น้อยมาก วินิจฉัยด้วย CSF PCR และรักษาด้วย acyclovir หรือ valacyclovir

ddx.pt: Recurrent benign lymphocytic meningitis, mostly due to HSV-2
Usually HSV-1 temporal lobe encephalitis with confusion and seizures
Broader group including VZV, syphilis, TB and fungi

name: High-grade glioma
formal: Aggressive diffuse gliomas of WHO grade 3 or 4, including glioblastoma and anaplastic astrocytoma, with rapid growth, contrast enhancement and poor prognosis.
simple: Fast-growing brain tumours that spread into nearby tissue and are difficult to treat.
th: กลุ่ม glioma เกรด 3-4 ที่เติบโตเร็วและแทรกซึม เช่น glioblastoma IDH-wildtype การรักษาหลักคือผ่าตัด ฉายรังสีร่วมกับ temozolomide และอาจใช้ tumour-treating fields พยากรณ์โรคยังไม่ดี
tempoNote: Weeks to a few months of progressive headache, deficit, seizure or personality change
feat: Subacute onset of focal weakness, language or visual field loss, seizures or personality change, with symptoms that improve temporarily on dexamethasone
Raised pressure signs (headache worse in the morning, vomiting, papilloedema) from mass effect and oedema
Imaging shows irregular ring enhancement around a necrotic core with surrounding oedema; corpus callosum crossing gives a butterfly pattern

WHO CNS5 divides adult tumours into astrocytoma IDH-mutant grade 3-4 and glioblastoma IDH-wildtype grade 4, and children into paediatric-type high-grade gliomas such as H3 K27-altered diffuse midline glioma
Recurrence is the rule, usually next to the original site, and treatment effect (pseudoprogression, radionecrosis) can mimic it
inv: MRI with gadolinium, diffusion, perfusion and spectroscopy; compare with CT only when MRI is unavailable
Tissue diagnosis with IDH, MGMT promoter methylation, TERT promoter, EGFR, CDKN2A/B, +7/-10, H3 K27M and BRAF V600E
Biopsy rather than resection for deep, bilateral or callosal lesions of the basal ganglia and thalamus
Follow-up MRI every 2-3 months with RANO criteria; PET or amino-acid PET and perfusion for equivocal enhancement

case.who: 63-year-old man, retired civil servant from Bangkok
case.story: Six weeks of progressive left-sided weakness and morning headache; he now drops objects with his left hand.
case.exam: Left hemiparesis grade 4/5 with a drift, mild left visual inattention, mild papilloedema.
case.tests: MRI shows a 4 cm right parietal ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis and oedema. Resection: glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, TERT promoter mutated, MGMT promoter methylated, CNS WHO grade 4.
case.q: What is the standard post-operative regimen and what does MGMT methylation predict?
case.a: Radiotherapy 60 Gy in 30 fractions with daily temozolomide, then six or more adjuvant temozolomide cycles; tumour-treating fields can be added. MGMT promoter methylation predicts a better response to temozolomide.

det.patho: High-grade gliomas are infiltrating astrocytic tumours with mitoses, microvascular proliferation and necrosis. The two broad paths are primary glioblastoma arising de novo in older adults with IDH-wildtype biology (TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification, chromosome 7 gain and 10 loss, CDKN2A/B loss) and secondary grade 3-4 astrocytoma evolving from IDH-mutant low-grade tumours. MGMT promoter methylation silences a DNA repair enzyme and predicts sensitivity to alkylating agents.
det.clinical: Presentation is a rapidly progressive focal syndrome on a background of headache or seizure, localisation depending on the lobe. Response to dexamethasone is typical because oedema accounts for much of the deficit. Treatment-related change in the first months after radiotherapy can look like progression. Venous thromboembolism, steroid myopathy and hyperglycaemia, and cognitive decline are common complications.
det.diagnosis: MRI features strongly suggest the diagnosis but cannot replace tissue; metastasis, lymphoma, abscess and tumefactive demyelination mimic it. Spectroscopy (raised choline, low NAA) and perfusion help. Resection or biopsy provides histology and the molecular profile that determines classification, treatment and trial eligibility. Differentiating true progression from pseudoprogression may need amino-acid PET, serial MRI or re-resection.
det.treatment: Maximal safe resection (with fluorescence guidance such as 5-ALA and mapping) is followed by radiotherapy 60 Gy in 30 fractions with concurrent temozolomide, then adjuvant temozolomide; the Stupp protocol raised median survival from about 12 to about 15 months. Adding tumour-treating fields to maintenance temozolomide extended median survival to about 21 months in the EF-14 trial. Older patients receive hypofractionated radiotherapy (40 Gy in 15 fractions) with temozolomide, or temozolomide alone if MGMT is methylated. At recurrence options include re-resection, re-irradiation, lomustine, bevacizumab for oedema and symptoms, and clinical trials; local wafers of carmustine used in the book's era are now seldom used.
det.prognosis: Median survival of glioblastoma is about 15-21 months with full treatment; age and performance status are the strongest predictors, along with MGMT methylation and extent of resection.
pearls: Ring-enhancing mass with necrosis crossing the corpus callosum is glioblastoma until proved otherwise, but send for biopsy to rule out lymphoma and metastasis.
Enhancement growing within 12 weeks of chemoradiation can be pseudoprogression; avoid abandoning effective therapy too early.
MGMT methylation is prognostic and predicts temozolomide benefit, especially in elderly patients.
det.thd: High-grade glioma คือ glioma เกรด 3-4 โดยชนิดที่พบบ่อยที่สุดคือ glioblastoma IDH-wildtype ผู้ป่วยมีอาการอ่อนแรง ชัก หรือปวดศีรษะที่เป็นมากขึ้นภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์ MRI พบก้อน enhance เป็นวงรอบเนื้อตายและบวม การวินิจฉัยต้องใช้ชิ้นเนื้อและตรวจ MGMT, IDH, TERT การรักษาคือผ่าตัด ฉายรังสีร่วมกับ temozolomide แล้วให้ temozolomide ต่อ อาจเพิ่ม tumour-treating fields พยากรณ์โรคส่วนใหญ่ยังต่ำกว่า 2 ปี

ddx.pt: Round, well-demarcated, multiple lesions at the grey-white junction with disproportionate oedema and a known primary
Homogeneous enhancement, restricted diffusion, periventricular or callosal location; avoid steroids before biopsy
Open-ring enhancement, mild mass effect, other white-matter lesions and fast steroid response

aN: hgg | glioblastoma | gbm | grade 4 astrocytoma | anaplastic astrocytoma | malignant glioma

name: Hindbrain malformation
formal: Congenital cerebellar and brainstem malformations such as Chiari, Dandy-Walker and Joubert, with hydrocephalus, ataxia, developmental delay and respiratory irregularity.
simple: A birth defect of the back part of the brain that can cause balance problems, delay or fluid build-up.
th: กลุ่มความผิดปกติแต่กำเนิดของสมองน้อยและก้านสมอง เช่น Chiari, Dandy–Walker และ Joubert ทำให้มีน้ำในโพรงสมอง เดินเซ พัฒนาการช้า และหายใจผิดปกติ
tempoNote: Congenital; presents in fetal life, infancy or, for Chiari I, often in adolescence or adulthood
feat: Umbrella term for malformations of the cerebellum, pons and medulla
Includes Chiari malformations, Dandy–Walker malformation, Joubert syndrome, rhombencephalosynapsis and pontocerebellar hypoplasia
Presentations: hydrocephalus, hypotonia, ataxia, nystagmus, developmental delay, apnoea or abnormal breathing
Lower cranial nerve dysfunction with swallowing difficulty and stridor in severe forms
Many are detected on fetal ultrasound or MRI
inv: MRI brain with sagittal views of the posterior fossa and craniocervical junction
Spine MRI for syrinx or spina bifida in Chiari II
Genetic testing (exome, ciliopathy panels) for Joubert and pontocerebellar hypoplasia
Eye, renal and liver screening in ciliopathies

case.who: 3-month-old girl at a Bangkok children's hospital
case.story: Head circumference crossing centiles upward; parents notice poor head control and episodes of fast breathing.
case.exam: Bulging fontanelle, hypotonia, nystagmus.
case.tests: MRI shows a cystic dilated fourth ventricle continuous with an enlarged posterior fossa, hypoplastic upturned vermis and hydrocephalus.
case.q: What malformation is this and what is the immediate concern?
case.a: Dandy–Walker malformation, a hindbrain malformation; hydrocephalus needs neurosurgical CSF diversion.

det.patho: The hindbrain develops from the rhombencephalon under tight genetic control of patterning, cell migration and primary cilium signalling. Defects in these processes produce hypoplasia, dysplasia or abnormal folding of the cerebellum and brainstem. Some malformations, such as Chiari I, reflect a small posterior fossa rather than primary neural defects. Environmental insults like prematurity-related cerebellar haemorrhage can produce disruptive lesions that look similar.
det.clinical: Infants may have hypotonia, nystagmus, abnormal eye movements, feeding difficulty, apnoea or hyperpnoea, and macrocephaly from hydrocephalus. Older children show ataxia, developmental delay and learning difficulties. Chiari I often presents later with cough headache, syrinx symptoms or lower cranial nerve signs. Associated features in other organs (kidney, liver, retina) point to ciliopathies.
det.diagnosis: MRI is the cornerstone, with attention to vermis size and rotation, fourth ventricle shape, brainstem configuration and cerebellar tonsil position. Specific patterns, such as the molar tooth sign or tonsillar descent, define subtypes. Genetic testing identifies many causes and informs recurrence risk. Screening of other organs is guided by the subtype.
det.treatment: Management depends on the malformation: CSF shunting or endoscopic third ventriculostomy for hydrocephalus, posterior fossa decompression for symptomatic Chiari I, and multidisciplinary developmental support. Respiratory monitoring is important when breathing control is affected. Genetic counselling is offered to families.
det.prognosis: Outcome varies widely, from normal intelligence in isolated mild malformations to severe disability in pontocerebellar hypoplasia.
pearls: Look at the midline sagittal MRI: vermis, fourth ventricle and tonsils tell most of the story.
Abnormal breathing patterns in a hypotonic infant suggest Joubert syndrome.
A large posterior fossa cyst is not always Dandy–Walker; check the vermis.
det.thd: Hindbrain malformation เป็นกลุ่มความผิดปกติแต่กำเนิดของสมองน้อยและก้านสมอง เช่น Chiari, Dandy–Walker และ Joubert อาการได้แก่หัวโตจากน้ำในโพรงสมอง กล้ามเนื้ออ่อน ตากระตุก เดินเซ พัฒนาการช้า และหายใจผิดปกติ การวินิจฉัยใช้ MRI ดูสมองน้อยและโพรงสมองที่สี่ ร่วมกับตรวจยีน การรักษาตามชนิด เช่นการผ่าตัดระบายน้ำในโพรงสมองและการกระตุ้นพัฒนาการ
