name: Hippocampal sclerosis
formal: Neuronal loss and gliosis of hippocampus, the commonest pathology in drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy, with T2 hyperintensity and atrophy on MRI, treatable by temporal lobectomy.
simple: Scarring and shrinkage of a memory-related brain region, a common cause of seizures that do not respond to medicine.
th: การสูญเสียเซลล์ประสาทและเกิดพังผืดเกลียในฮิปโปแคมปัส เป็นพยาธิสภาพที่พบบ่อยที่สุดในโรคลมชักกลีบขมับดื้อยา MRI เห็นฮิปโปแคมปัสฝ่อและสัญญาณ T2 สูง รักษาได้ด้วยการผ่าตัด
tempoNote: Often follows childhood complex febrile seizures; seizures start in later childhood or adolescence after a latent period
feat: Focal seizures with rising epigastric aura, déjà vu or fear, then staring, oral and hand automatisms
Contralateral dystonic hand posturing and post-ictal dysphasia (if dominant side)
History of prolonged febrile seizure or early brain insult in many
Frequently drug resistant; memory complaints common
In the elderly, hippocampal sclerosis of ageing (often with TDP-43) causes amnestic dementia — a separate context
inv: 3T MRI with coronal T2/FLAIR perpendicular to the hippocampus: atrophy, high signal, loss of internal architecture
Video-EEG: ipsilateral anterior temporal interictal and ictal discharges
Neuropsychology, fMRI/Wada for language and memory; PET when MRI uncertain

case.story: Had a 40-minute febrile seizure at 18 months; since age 12 has monthly attacks of a rising stomach sensation then lip smacking and fumbling, uncontrolled by three drugs.
case.exam: Normal; mild verbal memory difficulty.
case.tests: MRI shows a small bright left hippocampus; video-EEG captures left temporal onset seizures.
case.q: What is the most effective treatment now?
case.a: Drug-resistant left mesial temporal epilepsy due to a sclerotic hippocampus; anterior temporal lobectomy (or selective amygdalohippocampectomy / laser ablation) after full pre-surgical evaluation.

read.where: Chapter 10 Epilepsy and Related Disorders — Epilepsy Surgery

det.patho: Selective neuronal loss and gliosis affect CA1 and CA4 most, with dentate granule cell dispersion and mossy-fibre sprouting creating recurrent excitatory circuits. The ILAE classifies patterns (types 1–3); type 1 carries the best surgical outcome. Whether early prolonged febrile seizures cause the sclerosis or reflect a predisposed hippocampus remains debated.
det.clinical: Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy typically begins in late childhood or adolescence after a silent interval. Seizures have stereotyped auras, behavioural arrest, oral and manual automatisms and post-ictal confusion; secondary generalisation is infrequent on treatment. Verbal memory decline accompanies dominant-side disease. Hippocampal sclerosis may coexist with another lesion (dual pathology).
det.diagnosis: High-resolution MRI with dedicated hippocampal sequences is the key test; visual review by an experienced reader and volumetry improve detection. Concordant video-EEG, neuropsychology and, if needed, FDG-PET support surgical candidacy. Bilateral sclerosis or discordant data may need intracranial EEG.
det.treatment: Antiseizure drugs for focal epilepsy are tried first, but once two drugs fail, early surgical referral is advised. Anterior temporal lobectomy gives seizure freedom in roughly 60–80% and is superior to continued medical therapy in randomised trials. Selective amygdalohippocampectomy and MRI-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy are less invasive alternatives with somewhat lower seizure-free rates; neuromodulation is an option when resection is unsuitable.
det.prognosis: Excellent after surgery in well-selected patients; untreated drug-resistant cases carry risks of memory decline, injury and SUDEP.
pearls: Commonest lesion in adult drug-resistant focal epilepsy and the most surgically curable.
Ask about prolonged febrile seizures in infancy.
Refer to surgery after two failed appropriate drugs, not after ten years.
det.thd: Hippocampal sclerosis คือการตายของเซลล์ประสาทและพังผืดในฮิปโปแคมปัส ทำให้เกิดโรคลมชักกลีบขมับส่วนใน มีอาการนำเช่นรู้สึกแปลกในท้อง แล้วเหม่อ เคี้ยวปาก มักดื้อยา MRI เห็นฮิปโปแคมปัสเล็กและสว่างใน T2/FLAIR การผ่าตัดกลีบขมับส่วนหน้าช่วยให้หายชักได้มากกว่าครึ่ง

qx.stem: A 31-year-old man had a prolonged febrile seizure at 18 months and since age 12 has had rising epigastric auras followed by staring and lip smacking. His referral brain MRI from a 1.5 T scanner, using standard axial slices, was called normal. Video-EEG localizes his seizures to the left temporal lobe.
qx.q: Which imaging approach and finding would best confirm the most likely pathology?
opts: Contrast CT showing left temporal enhancement
3 T epilepsy-protocol MRI with thin coronal slices angled perpendicular to the hippocampus, showing left hippocampal shrinkage, high T2/FLAIR signal and loss of internal structure
MR angiography showing a left temporal vascular malformation
Diffusion imaging showing restricted diffusion in the left cortex
Standard axial MRI repeated with gadolinium
qx.why: Hippocampal sclerosis is most often missed on non-dedicated scans. An epilepsy protocol (such as HARNESS-MRI) with high-resolution 3D T1 and coronal T2/FLAIR angled perpendicular to the hippocampal long axis shows the classic triad: volume loss, increased signal and blurred internal layering, sometimes with atrophy of the same-side fornix or mammillary body. CT is insensitive and diffusion restriction suggests an acute process.

qx.stem: A 42-year-old lawyer has drug-resistant left (dominant) mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with concordant MRI hippocampal sclerosis, EEG and PET. She is very worried about word-finding problems after surgery and asks about options other than standard anterior temporal lobectomy.
qx.q: Which statement about MRI-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) of the left mesial temporal structures is most accurate compared with anterior temporal lobectomy?
opts: It gives higher seizure-freedom rates than lobectomy
It needs a large craniotomy and a longer hospital stay
It tends to spare naming and object recognition better, at the cost of somewhat lower seizure-freedom rates
It is only suitable for neocortical lesions
It cannot be followed by later resection if it fails
qx.why: Stereotactic laser ablation through a small skull opening spares lateral temporal neocortex and white matter tracts, so naming and recognition decline are less common than after open lobectomy. Seizure freedom is generally somewhat lower than with lobectomy, which remains the most effective option for hippocampal sclerosis. A repeat ablation or open resection can still be done if seizures continue. Selective amygdalohippocampectomy sits between the two.

name: Hirayama’s disease
formal: Juvenile asymmetric distal upper limb amyotrophy of the hand and forearm in young males, from forward displacement of the cervical dura on flexion, with benign self-limited course.
simple: A condition in young men causing slow wasting and weakness of one or both hands and forearms, usually stopping after a few years.
more: Diagnosis is usually clinical with MRI showing cervical flexion cord compression and forward displacement of the posterior dura; cervical collar is the mainstay. EMG shows chronic denervation in C7 to T1 myotomes and progression stops after 2 to 5 years.
ab: juvenile muscular atrophy of the distal upper extremity
th: กล้ามเนื้อปลายแขนลีบข้างเดียวในชายวัยรุ่น — จากไขสันหลังส่วนคอถูกกดเวลาก้มคอ มักหยุดลุกลามเอง
tempoNote: Insidious onset in teens/early 20s; progresses for a few years then usually plateaus
feat: Young man (often Asian) with unilateral or asymmetric hand and forearm wasting
Oblique amyotrophy: forearm wasted but brachioradialis preserved
Weakness worse in the cold (cold paresis); minipolymyoclonus of the fingers
No sensory loss, no UMN signs in the legs
inv: Cervical MRI in neutral AND full flexion with contrast: forward shift of the posterior dura with an enlarged epidural venous plexus; lower cervical cord atrophy
EMG: chronic denervation in C7–T1 myotomes, normal sensory studies

case.story: Over 18 months his right hand became weak and thin; it gets much worse in an air-conditioned room. Writing is now slow.
case.exam: Wasting of right intrinsic hand muscles and ulnar forearm with sparing of brachioradialis, fine finger tremor on extension, normal reflexes and sensation.
case.tests: Neutral MRI: mild cord flattening at C5–C6; flexion MRI: posterior dura moves forward with a crescent of epidural enhancement.
case.q: What simple measure is advised early?
case.a: A cervical collar to prevent neck flexion — it can halt progression; surgery is reserved for selected progressive cases.

qx.stem: A 19-year-old male engineering student from Chiang Rai has two years of painless wasting of the right hand and forearm with sparing of the brachioradialis, worse in cold weather, and no sensory loss. EMG shows chronic denervation in C7–T1 myotomes with normal sensory responses. Neutral-position cervical MRI shows only mild flattening of the lower cervical cord.
qx.q: Which imaging study is most likely to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
opts: Brachial plexus MR neurography
Contrast MRI of the brain
Cervical MRI performed in full neck flexion
CT myelography in the neutral position
Spinal angiography
qx.why: Juvenile asymmetric distal upper limb amyotrophy with cold paresis is Hirayama disease. Flexion MRI shows forward displacement of the posterior dura with a crescent-shaped dorsal epidural space full of engorged venous plexus compressing the lower cervical cord, which may be missed in neutral position. Treatment is a cervical collar to limit flexion during the progressive phase; plexus imaging, brain MRI and angiography do not show the dynamic compression.

det.patho: During growth spurts, the dural sac may be relatively short compared with the vertebral column, so neck flexion pulls the posterior dura forward and compresses the lower cervical cord. Repeated flexion causes chronic ischaemic damage to the anterior horns at C7–T1, with an enlarged posterior epidural venous plexus visible on flexion. It predominantly affects young men and is reported most often in Asia.
det.clinical: Onset is between the mid-teens and early twenties with insidious weakness and wasting of the hand and ulnar forearm, usually on one side or asymmetric. Brachioradialis is typically spared, giving 'oblique amyotrophy'. Cold paresis, irregular finger tremor and mild contralateral involvement are common. There are no sensory or pyramidal signs, and the disease progresses for a few years before stabilising.
det.diagnosis: Cervical MRI in neutral position may show only lower cord atrophy or flattening; MRI in full flexion with contrast shows anterior shift of the posterior dura and an enhancing epidural crescent. EMG shows chronic denervation in C7–T1 myotomes with normal sensory studies. Exclude ALS, MMN, syringomyelia, spinal cord tumours and thoracic outlet syndrome.
det.treatment: Avoiding repeated neck flexion with a cervical collar during the active phase may stop progression. Surgery (duraplasty or anterior decompression and fusion) is reserved for progressive cases despite collar therapy. Hand therapy and occupational adaptation support function.
det.prognosis: The disease usually becomes self-limiting within about 5 years, leaving stable focal weakness.
pearls: Young man + unilateral hand/forearm wasting + spared brachioradialis + cold paresis = Hirayama.
A neutral-position MRI can be nearly normal — request flexion MRI.
det.thd: Hirayama disease พบในชายวัยรุ่น เกิดจากเมื่อก้มคอ เยื่อหุ้มไขสันหลังด้านหลังเลื่อนมากดไขสันหลังส่วนคอล่าง ทำให้เซลล์ประสาทสั่งการระดับ C7–T1 เสื่อม มีอาการกล้ามเนื้อมือและปลายแขนลีบข้างเดียว โดย brachioradialis ยังดี และอ่อนแรงมากขึ้นเมื่ออากาศเย็น การวินิจฉัยต้องทำ MRI ท่าก้มคอร่วมกับฉีดสารทึบรังสี การรักษาคือใส่ปลอกคอเพื่อลดการก้มคอ และโรคมักหยุดลุกลามเองภายในไม่กี่ปี

name: Histone mutant gliomas
formal: Diffuse midline glioma H3 K27-altered and diffuse hemispheric glioma H3 G34-mutant, aggressive tumours of children and young adults, such as diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma.
simple: Aggressive brain tumours in children and young adults caused by a specific gene change, often in the brainstem.
th: glioma ที่มีการกลายพันธุ์ของ histone H3 โดยเฉพาะ diffuse midline glioma H3 K27-altered (เดิม DIPG) ที่ pons ของเด็ก และ diffuse hemispheric glioma H3 G34-mutant พยากรณ์โรคไม่ดี ฉายรังสีเป็นการรักษาหลัก และมียา ONC201 (dordaviprone) สำหรับ H3 K27M ที่กลับเป็นซ้ำ
tempoNote: Weeks of cranial nerve palsies, ataxia and long-tract signs in a child with pontine tumour; hemispheric G34 tumours present over weeks to months
feat: Diffuse midline glioma H3 K27-altered arises in the pons (diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma), thalamus or spinal cord, peak at 5-10 years
The classic pontine triad is cranial nerve palsies (especially VI and VII), cerebellar signs and long-tract signs, evolving over weeks
Hydrocephalus is uncommon at presentation and bulbar failure appears as the tumour progresses
Diffuse hemispheric glioma H3 G34-mutant occurs in adolescents and young adults and presents with seizures, headache or focal signs
Both are CNS WHO grade 4 regardless of histology
inv: MRI: expansile non-enhancing or mildly enhancing T2-bright pons occupying more than half of the cross section and encasing the basilar artery
Stereotactic biopsy is now accepted and recommended in specialist centres for molecular testing (H3 K27M, ACVR1, TP53, PDGFRA, EGFR)
Immunohistochemistry for H3 K27M and loss of H3 K27me3; H3 G34R/V by sequencing for hemispheric tumours
Spinal MRI at progression, because roughly one in three patients develop leptomeningeal spread

case.story: Three weeks of double vision, a drooping left mouth corner and unsteady walking that has worsened each week.
case.exam: Left sixth and seventh palsy, dysarthria, bilateral dysmetria and a brisk left plantar response.
case.tests: MRI shows an expanded pons with hyperintense T2 signal engulfing the basilar artery, no enhancement and mild hydrocephalus. Stereotactic biopsy: diffuse glioma, H3 K27M-mutant, ACVR1 mutation, CNS WHO grade 4.
case.q: What is the standard first-line treatment and what drug is available at progression?
case.a: Palliative focal radiotherapy (54 Gy, given as 30 fractions across about six weeks) is standard; chemotherapy adds nothing proven. At progression, ONC201 (dordaviprone) is approved for H3 K27M-mutant diffuse midline glioma, and re-irradiation or trial entry may be offered.

det.patho: Histone H3 gene mutations alter chromatin regulation. In diffuse midline glioma a K27M substitution (H3F3A or HIST1H3B/C) reduces H3 K27 trimethylation and drives a stem-like gliomagenesis, frequently with ACVR1, TP53 and PDGFRA changes. WHO CNS5 names the entity diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27-altered, grade 4; it includes pontine, thalamic and spinal tumours and replaces the older anatomical term DIPG. H3 G34R/V mutations define diffuse hemispheric glioma with a different biology and MGMT often methylated.
det.clinical: The pontine tumour is the prototype: a few weeks of squint, face weakness, gait ataxia and swallowing trouble, often followed by rapid decline. Even with radiotherapy improvement lasts a few months and most children die within 1-2 years. Thalamic and spinal tumours present with hemiparesis, movement disorder or myelopathy. Rapid steroid dependence and bulbar failure require palliative planning.
det.diagnosis: Classic MRI features of a diffuse intrinsic pontine tumour were once enough for diagnosis. Biopsy is now advised in experienced centres for molecular typing and trial eligibility, because the risk is low (about 1 percent permanent deficit). Immunostaining for H3 K27M and loss of K27me3, with ACVR1 and TP53 status, confirms. Alternative diagnoses include other pontine gliomas, demyelination and brainstem encephalitis.
det.treatment: Radiotherapy 54 Gy in 30 fractions remains standard; hyperfractionation, radiosensitisers and many chemotherapy regimens tried in decades past (as the source book describes) did not improve survival. ONC201 (dordaviprone), an imipridone that antagonises DRD2 and activates ClpP, gained accelerated approval in 2025 for recurrent H3 K27M-mutant diffuse midline glioma, and the phase 3 ACTION trial tests it upfront. Re-irradiation, convection-enhanced delivery and CAR-T cell trials are used selectively. Dexamethasone should be limited to the minimum dose needed, and hydrocephalus is treated only if symptomatic.
det.prognosis: Median survival for DIPG is 9-12 months; more than 90 percent die within two years. Hemispheric G34 tumours fare somewhat better (about 1-2 years) with alkylator treatment.
pearls: Pontine tumour with cranial nerve palsies, ataxia and long-tract signs over weeks in a child: DIPG; hydrocephalus is a late feature.
Biopsy for H3 K27M now matters because ONC201 and trials are molecularly selected.
H3 K27-altered midline glioma is grade 4 even when histology looks low grade.
det.thd: Histone mutant glioma เช่น diffuse midline glioma H3 K27-altered (DIPG) พบที่ pons ในเด็ก ทำให้เกิดอัมพาตเส้นประสาทสมอง เดินเซ และอ่อนแรงภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์ MRI พบ pons ขยายโตและชิ้นเนื้อพบ H3 K27M การฉายรังสี 54 Gy ช่วยบรรเทาอาการได้หลายเดือน เคมีบำบัดแบบเดิมไม่ช่วยยืดชีวิต ยา ONC201 (dordaviprone) ได้รับอนุมัติสำหรับ H3 K27M ที่กลับเป็นซ้ำ ส่วน H3 G34-mutant เกิดที่ซีกสมองในวัยรุ่น

qx.stem: A 7-year-old girl from Ubon Ratchathani has a six-week history of double vision, drooling and unsteady walking. Examination shows left sixth and seventh nerve palsies, bilateral long-tract signs and ataxia. MRI shows an expansile, poorly marginated T2-bright lesion occupying more than half of the pons with little enhancement. A stereotactic biopsy confirms an H3 K27M mutation.
qx.q: Which statement about management is most accurate?
opts: Gross total resection is the treatment of choice and offers cure
Focal radiotherapy is the standard first treatment, and dordaviprone (ONC201) is an approved option at progression
Temozolomide with radiotherapy doubles median survival
Observation is advised because most such tumours are grade 1
Craniospinal irradiation is curative in most cases
qx.why: Diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27-altered, is CNS WHO grade 4 and not resectable in the pons; focal radiotherapy gives temporary relief but median survival is still about a year. Dordaviprone (ONC201) received accelerated approval in 2025 for progressive H3 K27M-mutant diffuse midline glioma. Temozolomide adds no survival benefit and craniospinal treatment is not standard.

name: HIV infection
formal: Chronic retroviral infection of CD4 cells that causes progressive immunodeficiency and can directly injure brain, cord and nerve, or permit opportunistic CNS infections and lymphoma.
simple: A virus that weakens the immune system over time and can also affect the brain, spinal cord and nerves, directly or by allowing other infections.
more: Acquired immunodeficiency from HIV, with neurological disease from direct viral effects, opportunistic infections such as toxoplasmosis, cryptococcus and PML, lymphoma, and neuropathy. Infection with HIV causing severe CD4 depletion and opportunistic neurological disease including toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis, PML, CNS lymphoma, HIV dementia and neuropathy.

feat: Seroconversion illness may cause aseptic meningitis, GBS or Bell palsy
Low CD4 (<200) brings toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis, PML, TB and CNS lymphoma
Distal painful sensory neuropathy is the commonest neurological complication
HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder and vacuolar myelopathy in advanced disease
IRIS can unmask or worsen CNS infections after starting ART
inv: HIV serology, CD4 count and viral load (plasma and, when needed, CSF)
MRI brain with contrast for focal lesions; serum and CSF cryptococcal antigen
CSF analysis with PCR for JC virus, EBV, CMV, TB and syphilis tests

case.who: 34-year-old man from Chiang Rai, newly diagnosed HIV
case.story: Two weeks of worsening headache and fever, then confusion and right-sided weakness.
case.exam: Drowsy, right hemiparesis, no neck stiffness.
case.tests: CD4 45 cells/µL; MRI: multiple ring-enhancing lesions in basal ganglia; Toxoplasma IgG positive.
case.q: What is the first step, and when should a brain biopsy be considered?
case.a: Empirical anti-toxoplasma therapy (e.g., pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine or co-trimoxazole); biopsy if no clinical or radiological improvement in 10–14 days, to exclude lymphoma.

23. Neuropathies Associated With HIV Infection and Antiretroviral Therapy

det.patho: HIV infects CD4 T cells and monocyte-macrophages; infected macrophages and microglia carry the virus into the CNS early. Neurological disease arises through direct viral and inflammatory injury (neurocognitive disorder, vacuolar myelopathy, neuropathy), opportunistic infections and tumours from immunodeficiency, and drug toxicity. Thailand still has a significant HIV burden, with cryptococcal meningitis and toxoplasmosis common at presentation.
det.clinical: Primary infection may cause aseptic meningitis or acute neuropathy. In chronic infection the CD4 count predicts risk: below 200 toxoplasmosis and PCNSL, below 100 cryptococcus, CMV and PML. Distal sensory polyneuropathy from HIV or older nucleoside drugs is common even with good control. Mild cognitive impairment persists in some well-treated patients.
det.diagnosis: Every patient with unexplained neurological disease, especially meningitis, myelopathy or stroke in the young, should be tested for HIV. CD4 count frames the differential. Imaging and CSF analysis with antigen and PCR tests identify opportunistic infections; serum cryptococcal antigen screening is recommended when CD4 is under 100.
det.treatment: Antiretroviral therapy (usually dolutegravir-based) is lifelong and transforms prognosis. ART start is delayed by 4–6 weeks in cryptococcal meningitis and by a few weeks in TB meningitis to limit IRIS, but otherwise begun promptly. Treat opportunistic infections specifically and give prophylaxis (co-trimoxazole) when CD4 is low. Check drug interactions with antiepileptics.
det.prognosis: With sustained viral suppression life expectancy approaches normal; untreated advanced disease carries high mortality from CNS infections.
pearls: Test for HIV in any unexplained meningitis, myelopathy or young stroke.
Delay ART for several weeks in cryptococcal meningitis.
Ring lesions at low CD4 = treat toxoplasma first, biopsy if no response.

det.patho: HIV-1 is a lentivirus that uses CD4 and chemokine co-receptors to enter cells. It integrates into host DNA, depleting CD4 T cells over years. In the CNS it infects microglia and perivascular macrophages but not neurons; neuronal injury occurs through viral proteins, cytokines and chronic inflammation.
det.clinical: This entry is the virus itself. Neurological complications appear at every stage: seroconversion syndromes, chronic HIV-related disorders, and opportunistic infections and tumours with severe immunodeficiency. ART-related toxicity and IRIS add to the spectrum.
det.diagnosis: Fourth-generation antigen/antibody assays with confirmatory testing establish infection. Viral load and CD4 count stage disease. Measure CSF HIV RNA when CNS escape is suspected.
det.treatment: Lifelong ART, now usually integrase inhibitor-based (e.g. dolutegravir with two NRTIs), started as soon as possible. Opportunistic infection prophylaxis by CD4 count. Prevention includes PrEP and treatment as prevention.
det.prognosis: With ART, life expectancy approaches normal; neurological morbidity has fallen sharply.
pearls: Test for HIV in any unexplained neurological syndrome in a young adult.
CD4 count tells which opportunistic infections are possible.
Untreated HIV CNS involvement starts at seroconversion.

det.patho: HIV enters the brain within infected monocytes; perivascular macrophages and microglia produce viral proteins and inflammatory mediators that injure synapses and white matter. Neurons themselves are rarely infected. Pathology shows multinucleated giant cells, microglial nodules and white matter pallor.
det.clinical: HAD is the severe end of HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND), which also includes asymptomatic impairment and mild neurocognitive disorder. The picture is subcortical: slowed thinking, apathy, executive problems and motor slowing; aphasia and agnosia are not typical. Untreated, it advances to mutism, incontinence and paraparesis. It is now uncommon in people on effective ART.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires cognitive impairment interfering with daily life, attributable to HIV after excluding other causes. MRI and CSF are needed to rule out opportunistic infections and lymphoma. Measure CSF viral load to detect CSF escape. Screen for depression, substance use and metabolic contributors.
det.treatment: Effective ART is the cornerstone; regimen choice should account for resistance testing and CSF escape. Cognitive and functional support, treatment of depression and caregiver education are important. No adjunctive neuroprotective drug has proven benefit.
det.prognosis: Many patients improve or stabilise after ART; untreated, it progresses to death within months.
pearls: Subcortical slowing in untreated HIV: think HAD, but first exclude PML and infection.
Check CSF viral load if cognition worsens despite suppressed plasma virus.
Apathy may be mistaken for depression.
det.thd: HIV-associated dementia คือภาวะสมองเสื่อมรุนแรงจาก HIV ที่ไม่ได้รักษา ไวรัสเข้าสู่สมองผ่านเซลล์ macrophage และ microglia ทำให้คิดช้า เฉยเมย ความจำลดลง และเคลื่อนไหวช้า MRI พบสมองฝ่อและเนื้อขาวผิดปกติแบบสมมาตร ต้องแยกเชื้อฉวยโอกาสเช่น PML และซิฟิลิส รักษาหลักคือยาต้านไวรัสที่มีประสิทธิภาพ

case.exam: Proximal weakness 4/5 in hips and shoulders, normal reflexes and sensation.

det.patho: HIV can provoke an immune-mediated inflammatory myopathy in which CD8 T cells and macrophages surround and invade muscle fibres that upregulate MHC class I. The virus is found in infiltrating cells rather than inside muscle fibres themselves. Other mechanisms in people with HIV include mitochondrial toxicity from older NRTIs, wasting, nemaline rod myopathy and secondary infection.
det.clinical: Patients present with symmetric proximal weakness and myalgia over weeks to months, with variable CK elevation. Dysphagia and respiratory involvement are uncommon. In long-standing HIV an inclusion body myositis-like picture with finger flexor and quadriceps weakness may appear. Pyomyositis should be considered when pain is focal with fever.
det.diagnosis: CK, EMG and muscle MRI confirm a myopathy and guide biopsy. Biopsy separates inflammatory, mitochondrial-toxic and nemaline rod patterns. Exclude hypothyroidism, statin toxicity (boosted ART raises statin levels), other drugs and infection. Myositis antibodies are usually negative.
det.treatment: Ensure effective ART with suppressed viral load and withdraw toxic drugs. Inflammatory forms usually respond to corticosteroids, with monitoring for opportunistic infection. IVIG is an alternative when steroids are risky or ineffective. IBM-like disease responds poorly and is managed with physiotherapy and assistive devices.
det.prognosis: Most respond to treatment; IBM-like forms progress.
pearls: Biopsy is key: inflammation vs mitochondrial toxicity.
Check ART-statin interactions (e.g. boosted protease inhibitors raise statin levels).
IVIG is useful when steroids are risky.
det.thd: HIV-associated myopathy คือโรคกล้ามเนื้อในผู้ติดเชื้อ HIV อาจเกิดจากภูมิคุ้มกันอักเสบคล้าย polymyositis จากยา เช่น zidovudine หรือภาวะผอมแห้ง ผู้ป่วยอ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขา CK สูง ตัดชิ้นเนื้อกล้ามเนื้อเพื่อแยกชนิด รักษาด้วยยาต้านไวรัส steroid หรือ IVIG และหยุดยาที่เป็นพิษ

det.patho: HIV enters the brain early via infected monocytes and persists in perivascular macrophages and microglia. Viral proteins and chronic inflammatory mediators damage synapses in fronto-striatal circuits, giving a subcortical pattern. With modern ART, the severe form is uncommon, but milder impairment remains, probably reflecting legacy injury, vascular and metabolic comorbidity, and low-level CNS inflammation.
det.clinical: HAND is classified (Frascati) into asymptomatic neurocognitive impairment, mild neurocognitive disorder and HIV-associated dementia, according to test performance and effect on daily activities. Typical complaints are slowness, poor attention and executive difficulty with apathy, rather than prominent amnesia or aphasia. Motor signs and slow saccades favour HIV over primary degenerative causes. CSF viral escape can present as a newer, more rapid decline despite suppressed plasma virus.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires documented impairment in at least two cognitive domains and exclusion of confounders: opportunistic infections, syphilis, depression, substance use, metabolic causes and other dementias. MRI and CSF are essential to exclude PML, toxoplasmosis, cryptococcosis and lymphoma. Measure CSF and plasma HIV RNA together; a CSF level higher than plasma suggests escape, and resistance testing of CSF virus guides regimen change.
det.treatment: Effective ART is the cornerstone; begin promptly in the untreated patient and maximise adherence. For CSF escape, change regimen based on resistance testing, considering drugs with better CNS penetration. Treat vascular risk factors, depression and sleep problems, and review neurotoxic drugs. Occupational therapy, cognitive strategies and adherence support (pill boxes, family involvement) are practical gains.
det.prognosis: HIV-associated dementia often stabilises or improves partially with ART; milder forms tend to remain stable over years.
pearls: Subcortical pattern: slow, apathetic, poor attention — not an aphasic or purely amnestic picture.
Always exclude OIs and syphilis before labelling HAND.
Paired CSF/plasma viral load uncovers CSF escape.

qx.stem: A 45-year-old tour guide in Chiang Rai has taken antiretroviral therapy for 10 years with an undetectable plasma viral load and a CD4 count of 480 cells/mm³. Over five months he has become slow, forgetful and unsteady. MRI shows diffuse symmetric white matter hyperintensities without enhancement; CSF cryptococcal antigen and JC virus PCR are negative, but CSF HIV RNA is 2,800 copies/mL.
qx.q: What should be done next?
opts: Reassure him, since an undetectable plasma viral load excludes HIV brain disease
Start high-dose steroids for presumed IRIS
Perform genotypic resistance testing on CSF virus and adjust antiretroviral therapy accordingly
Stop all antiretrovirals to reduce drug neurotoxicity
Start empirical toxoplasma treatment
qx.why: Detectable HIV RNA in CSF despite plasma suppression, with new cognitive decline, is symptomatic CSF viral escape, a recognised cause of HAND in the treatment era. CSF genotype often reveals resistance, and switching to a fully active regimen usually improves symptoms. JCV and cryptococcal tests are negative and the MRI does not suggest IRIS, toxoplasmosis or PML, while stopping therapy would be harmful.

qx.stem: A 54-year-old woman from Khon Kaen, HIV positive for 15 years and virally suppressed, complains of slowed thinking. Neuropsychological testing shows impairment of at least two cognitive domains by more than one standard deviation, and she says she needs help with paperwork and managing medicines. Normal ageing
Mild neurocognitive disorder (MND)
HIV-associated dementia (HAD)
Depression only

th: ระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติเสื่อมในผู้ติดเชื้อ HIV ทำให้ความดันตกเมื่อลุกยืน เหงื่อผิดปกติ ท้องเสียหรือท้องผูก และกระเพาะปัสสาวะผิดปกติ มักถูกมองข้ามหรือโทษว่าเป็นผลข้างเคียงของยา

case.who: 53-year-old woman, 15 years on ART, Chiang Mai
case.story: Several months of dizziness on standing, nausea after meals and urinary urgency. Her clinic notes attribute each symptom to tenofovir or her blood-pressure pill; burning feet for years.
case.exam: BP 134/82 lying, 96/62 at 3 minutes standing with pulse rising only from 78 to 82; reduced pinprick and absent ankle jerks.
case.tests: CD4 520, viral load undetectable; HbA1c 5.4%, morning cortisol normal; tilt and Valsalva show impaired adrenergic and cardiovagal responses.
case.q: Why did the diagnosis go unrecognised, and what can be done at the bedside?
case.a: Single autonomic symptoms are non-specific and are attributed to drugs or organ disease. Check postural vitals, review and slow down BP-lowering drugs, add fluids and compression, and treat gastroparesis or bladder symptoms directly.

read.where: Autonomic neuropathy in HIV is unrecognized and associated with medical morbidity

det.patho: Autonomic fibres are affected by the same processes that injure sensory nerves in HIV: chronic immune activation, viral protein toxicity and, in people exposed to older dideoxynucleoside drugs, mitochondrial injury. Laboratory studies in treated cohorts find abnormal autonomic scores in a majority of patients, often with no complaint. Higher scores track with a higher burden of comorbid illness. Some authors even suggest that HIV lipodystrophy may reflect selective sympathetic involvement.
det.clinical: Symptoms are scattered across several organ systems: dizziness on standing, nausea and bowel change, urinary and sexual dysfunction, dry eyes or mouth, and sweating or foot colour change. When only one or two appear, they are readily put down to medication or to organ disease. In a clinic review, most patients with laboratory-proven autonomic neuropathy who voiced such symptoms received no specific diagnosis, and the autonomic cause was considered only once. The typical patient is older, has long-standing HIV, distal polyneuropathy and other illnesses, though CD4 may now be normal on ART.
det.diagnosis: Start with orthostatic vital signs, reading both blood pressure and the pulse response, since a fixed rate suggests a neurogenic cause. Formal testing (deep breathing, Valsalva, tilt, sweat testing) allows a composite severity score, and a score of about 3 or more on its 0–10 scale is commonly used for neuropathy. Before attributing symptoms to HIV, remove contributors: dehydration, adrenal insufficiency, diabetes, alcohol, B12 deficiency, hepatitis C and drugs such as antihypertensives, antidepressants and opioids. Distal nerve examination and conduction studies support the association.
det.treatment: No HIV-specific therapy has been shown to reverse the condition, so management is supportive. Keep viral suppression, avoid neurotoxic nucleoside agents, and review every drug that lowers blood pressure or slows the gut, titrating antihypertensives slowly. For orthostatic hypotension use fluids, salt if no contraindication, waist-high compression and staged posture changes, then midodrine or fludrocortisone, watching for supine hypertension. Consider a prokinetic for gastroparesis and standard bladder or sexual-function measures.
det.prognosis: Cross-sectional data link autonomic neuropathy to higher predicted mortality in a veterans-based risk index, though whether it is an independent cause remains unproven. Symptoms often fluctuate and partly respond to supportive care.
pearls: Autonomic symptoms in a person with HIV are usually attributed to drugs; ask about them directly.
Older patient + distal polyneuropathy + comorbidity is the high-risk profile.
Do orthostatic vitals with pulse, and always exclude adrenal insufficiency and diabetes first.
det.thd: ระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติเสื่อมพบได้บ่อยในผู้ติดเชื้อ HIV โดยเฉพาะผู้สูงอายุที่มีปลายประสาทอักเสบร่วมและโรคประจำตัวอื่น อาการมีหลายระบบ เช่น หน้ามืดเมื่อลุกยืน คลื่นไส้หลังอาหาร ท้องเสียหรือท้องผูก ปัสสาวะผิดปกติ และเหงื่อผิดปกติ จึงมักถูกมองว่าเป็นผลข้างเคียงของยา ควรวัดความดันและชีพจรท่านอนกับท่ายืน แยกภาวะขาดน้ำ ต่อมหมวกไตทำงานน้อย เบาหวานและยาที่เป็นสาเหตุ การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง ได้แก่ ปรับยาลดความดัน เพิ่มน้ำและเกลือ ใส่ถุงน่อง และใช้ midodrine หรือ fludrocortisone เมื่อจำเป็น

ddx.pt: Long-standing hyperglycaemia with retinopathy or nephropathy; HIV patients may have both, so check glucose
Subacute, severe, multi-domain failure with antibodies or an underlying cancer
Autonomic failure with parkinsonism, cerebellar signs or stridor, no distal neuropathy

aN: hiv autonomic neuropathy | hiv dysautonomia | autonomic dysfunction in hiv

name: HIV-related inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy
formal: HIV-associated acute or chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy, often at seroconversion or with CD4 recovery, with CSF pleocytosis in contrast to typical GBS.
simple: An immune-driven nerve condition in people with HIV that causes weakness and loss of reflexes.
more: Nerve studies show demyelination; CSF has raised cells. Treated with IVIG or plasma exchange, with steroids in chronic forms, along with antiretroviral therapy.
th: เส้นประสาทอักเสบแบบ demyelinating ทั้งเฉียบพลันและเรื้อรังในผู้ติดเชื้อ HIV มักเกิดช่วงติดเชื้อใหม่หรือภูมิฟื้นตัว และ CSF มีเซลล์สูง
tempoNote: AIDP-like form over days (seroconversion or IRIS); CIDP-like form over more than 8 weeks
feat: Occurs early in HIV infection (often at seroconversion) or with immune recovery after starting ART
Clinically like GBS or CIDP: symmetric weakness and areflexia
CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis (often 10–50 cells/µL) with raised protein — unlike typical GBS
CD4 count usually relatively preserved
Must be distinguished from CMV polyradiculopathy in advanced AIDS
inv: HIV serology and viral load in any GBS/CIDP with CSF pleocytosis; CD4 count
NCS: demyelinating features as in AIDP or CIDP
CSF CMV PCR, syphilis serology, cytology for lymphoma when CD4 is low

case.story: Three weeks after a febrile illness with rash and sore throat, his legs became weak over a week and he now cannot walk.
case.exam: Symmetric weakness 3/5 in legs and 4/5 in arms, areflexia, mild distal sensory loss; small cervical nodes.
case.tests: CSF protein 1.0 g/L with 30 lymphocytes/µL; NCS demyelinating; HIV antigen/antibody positive, viral load very high, CD4 520.
case.q: Why does the CSF finding matter and how is he managed?
case.a: Pleocytosis in a GBS-like illness should prompt HIV testing; this is seroconversion-associated AIDP, treated with IVIG or plasma exchange and early ART.

det.patho: Immune dysregulation in early HIV infection, before profound CD4 depletion, or during immune reconstitution, triggers an autoimmune attack on peripheral myelin similar to GBS or CIDP. Direct viral infection of nerves is not the main mechanism. HIV-associated lymphocytosis explains the CSF pleocytosis.
det.clinical: The acute form resembles AIDP, often around seroconversion with fever, rash and lymphadenopathy, or after ART initiation as part of IRIS. The chronic form resembles CIDP with progressive or relapsing weakness. Facial weakness and respiratory involvement can occur. In advanced AIDS, a subacute flaccid paraparesis with sphincter loss more likely reflects CMV polyradiculopathy or lymphomatous infiltration.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis combines a GBS or CIDP clinical and electrophysiological picture with confirmed HIV infection. CSF shows raised protein with mild lymphocytic pleocytosis. Exclude CMV (PCR), syphilis, lymphoma and drug toxicity. Routine HIV testing is recommended in all GBS/CIDP patients with CSF pleocytosis or risk factors.
det.treatment: Acute forms are treated as GBS with IVIG or plasma exchange; chronic forms respond to IVIG, plasma exchange or corticosteroids (with care regarding infection risk). Start or optimise ART in coordination with an HIV physician, considering IRIS. Supportive measures follow standard GBS practice.
det.prognosis: Generally similar to non-HIV GBS or CIDP when CD4 count is preserved, with good recovery in most.
pearls: GBS with CSF pleocytosis: test for HIV.
Relatively high CD4 favours inflammatory demyelinating neuropathy; very low CD4 favours CMV polyradiculopathy.
IRIS after starting ART can unmask or trigger this neuropathy.
det.thd: HIV-related inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy คือเส้นประสาทอักเสบแบบ GBS หรือ CIDP ในผู้ติดเชื้อ HIV มักเกิดช่วงติดเชื้อใหม่หรือหลังเริ่มยาต้านไวรัส ลักษณะสำคัญคือ CSF มีเซลล์ lymphocyte สูงกว่า GBS ทั่วไป และ CD4 ยังไม่ต่ำมาก รักษาด้วย IVIG หรือ plasma exchange ร่วมกับยาต้านไวรัส และต้องแยกจาก CMV polyradiculopathy ในผู้ที่ CD4 ต่ำ

ddx.pt: Typical GBS has CSF cells usually below 10/µL and negative HIV test
Low CD4, cauda equina syndrome with neutrophilic CSF and CMV PCR positive
Painful length-dependent axonal sensory neuropathy without weakness

aN: hiv associated gbs | hiv associated cidp | hiv inflammatory demyelinating neuropathy | hiv aidp

name: HIV-related multiple mononeuropathies
formal: Vasculitic multiple mononeuropathy in HIV, either from immune reconstitution or CMV or other infection, producing stepwise multifocal nerve deficits.
simple: Several separate nerves become damaged in people with HIV, causing patchy weakness and numbness.
more: Nerve biopsy and CMV testing guide therapy; treatments include ganciclovir for CMV, immunotherapy for vasculitis and antiretroviral therapy.
th: เส้นประสาทหลายเส้นเสียแบบเป็นขั้นในผู้ติดเชื้อ HIV จาก vasculitis ช่วงแรกหรือจาก CMV ในระยะ CD4 ต่ำ
tempoNote: Stepwise accumulation of nerve deficits over weeks
feat: Sequential painful mononeuropathies (e.g. peroneal, ulnar, facial)
Early HIV (CD4 above 200): self-limited immune vasculitis
Advanced HIV (CD4 below 50): rapidly progressive CMV-related multifocal neuropathy
Can also occur with immune reconstitution, hepatitis C cryoglobulinaemia or lymphoma
Asymmetric sensory and motor deficits, distinct from symmetric distal HIV neuropathy
inv: CD4 count and HIV viral load
NCS/EMG: multifocal axonal neuropathy
CMV PCR in blood/CSF; HCV and cryoglobulins
Nerve biopsy: vasculitis or CMV inclusions

case.who: 36-year-old man from Chiang Rai with newly diagnosed HIV, CD4 22
case.story: Over three weeks developed left foot drop, then right hand numbness and weakness, with pain.
case.exam: Left peroneal and right ulnar deficits, retinal white patches with haemorrhage on fundoscopy.
case.tests: NCS: multifocal axonal mononeuropathies; CMV DNA high in blood; CMV retinitis confirmed.
case.q: What is the cause and treatment?
case.a: CMV-related multiple mononeuropathy in advanced HIV; ganciclovir then valganciclovir with ART.

read.where: Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — HIV-Associated Peripheral Neuropathy

det.patho: In early HIV, immune-complex or T-cell mediated vasculitis of epineurial vessels causes ischaemic nerve infarcts. In advanced immunosuppression, CMV infects nerves and vessels directly. Other contributors include HCV cryoglobulinaemia, lymphomatous infiltration and diffuse infiltrative lymphocytosis syndrome.
det.clinical: Patients develop asymmetric, often painful deficits in individual nerves, including cranial nerves. Early-stage disease is often limited and may resolve. Advanced-stage CMV disease progresses rapidly to confluent weakness and may accompany retinitis or polyradiculopathy. Since effective ART, this condition is uncommon.
det.diagnosis: CD4 count is the first discriminator. NCS confirm multifocal axonal involvement. CMV PCR in blood and CSF and fundoscopy for retinitis are key in low CD4 patients. Nerve biopsy may be needed if diagnosis is unclear, particularly to show vasculitis or lymphoma.
det.treatment: For CMV, start ganciclovir or foscarnet promptly, followed by maintenance and ART. Immune vasculitis in early HIV may improve spontaneously or with ART; corticosteroids or IVIG are sometimes used. Treat HCV if cryoglobulinaemia is responsible. Neuropathic pain management is part of care.
det.prognosis: Early-stage disease often improves; CMV-related disease is serious and recovers incompletely.
pearls: CD4 count separates benign vasculitic from dangerous CMV-related forms.
Look in the fundi for CMV retinitis.
Asymmetric stepwise deficits are not typical HIV distal neuropathy.
det.thd: ในผู้ติดเชื้อ HIV อาจเกิดเส้นประสาทหลายเส้นเสียแบบเป็นขั้น ในระยะแรกที่ CD4 ยังสูงมักเกิดจาก vasculitis และหายได้เอง ส่วนในระยะที่ CD4 ต่ำมากมักเกิดจาก CMV ซึ่งลุกลามเร็วและรุนแรง ต้องตรวจ CD4, NCS, CMV PCR และตรวจจอประสาทตา รักษาด้วย ganciclovir ร่วมกับยาต้านไวรัส HIV

ddx.pt: Symmetric painful feet, length-dependent, much more common
CMV cauda equina syndrome with leg weakness and sphincter loss
General pattern; consider vasculitis, diabetes and leprosy too

aN: hiv mononeuritis multiplex | hiv associated vasculitic neuropathy | mononeuropathy multiplex in hiv | cmv mononeuritis multiplex

name: HIV-related progressive polyradiculopathy
formal: CMV-related cauda equina syndrome in advanced HIV, with rapidly progressive flaccid paraparesis, sphincter dysfunction and neutrophilic CSF pleocytosis.
simple: A fast-worsening leg weakness and bladder problem from infection of lower spinal nerve roots in advanced HIV.
more: MRI shows root enhancement; CSF PCR confirms CMV. Prompt ganciclovir or foscarnet with antiretroviral therapy is needed to prevent permanent damage.
th: รากประสาทส่วน cauda equina อักเสบจากเชื้อ CMV ในผู้ป่วย HIV ระยะท้าย ขาอ่อนแรงแบบอ่อนปวกเปียกเร็ว ปัสสาวะไม่ออก CSF มี neutrophil สูง
tempoNote: Progresses over days to weeks; delay leads to permanent paralysis
feat: Advanced HIV with CD4 usually <50 cells/µL
Low back and radicular pain, then ascending flaccid paraparesis
Early urinary retention and saddle anaesthesia; areflexic legs
Often accompanies CMV retinitis or colitis
inv: MRI lumbosacral spine with gadolinium: thickened, enhancing cauda equina roots
CSF: neutrophilic pleocytosis, high protein, low glucose; CMV PCR positive
Ophthalmology for CMV retinitis; CD4 and viral load

case.who: 36-year-old man from Phayao, HIV untreated, CD4 18
case.story: One week of back pain then progressive leg weakness and urinary retention.
case.exam: Flaccid legs 2/5, absent knee and ankle jerks, saddle numbness.
case.tests: MRI: diffuse cauda equina enhancement; CSF 600 cells (70% neutrophils), protein 2.5 g/L, glucose low; CMV PCR positive.
case.q: Treatment?
case.a: IV ganciclovir (or foscarnet) induction promptly, then ART once stable.

det.patho: Cytomegalovirus infects nerve roots, especially of the cauda equina, causing necrotising inflammation in profound immunosuppression. Neutrophilic CSF response is characteristic. Lymphomatous infiltration and syphilis are other causes of polyradiculopathy in HIV.
det.clinical: Low back and radicular pain is followed within days to weeks by ascending flaccid paraparesis with areflexia. Urinary retention and saddle anaesthesia appear early, unlike GBS. The arms are usually spared. Patients often have other CMV disease such as retinitis or colitis.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows thickened enhancing roots. CSF neutrophilic pleocytosis with CMV PCR positive is diagnostic. Examine for CMV retinitis.
det.treatment: Start IV ganciclovir (or foscarnet if resistance or cytopenia) on clinical suspicion alone, before PCR returns. Induction is followed by maintenance therapy until CD4 recovery on ART. ART should be started or optimised once antiviral therapy is under way, watching for IRIS. Bladder care, thromboprophylaxis and rehabilitation are important.
det.prognosis: Recovery is incomplete and depends on early treatment; untreated disease is fatal.
pearls: Neutrophilic CSF with cauda equina syndrome in AIDS = CMV.
Start ganciclovir on suspicion.
Look in the eyes for CMV retinitis.
det.thd: HIV-related progressive polyradiculopathy เกิดจาก CMV ติดรากประสาท cauda equina ในผู้ป่วย HIV ที่ CD4 ต่ำมาก ผู้ป่วยปวดหลัง ขาอ่อนแรงปวกเปียกอย่างรวดเร็ว และปัสสาวะไม่ออก CSF มี neutrophil สูงและ CMV PCR บวก รักษาทันทีด้วย ganciclovir หรือ foscarnet ร่วมกับยาต้านไวรัส HIV

files.chapter: Infectious Diseases of the Nervous System

ddx.pt: Lymphocytic or acellular CSF and less early sphincter involvement
Compressive cause, e.g. disc or tumour
Lymphoma can infiltrate roots in HIV; cytology positive

aN: cmv polyradiculopathy | hiv progressive lumbosacral polyradiculopathy | cmv polyradiculitis | hiv cauda equina syndrome

name: HIV-related sensory neuropathy
formal: Distal symmetric sensory polyneuropathy, the commonest HIV neurological complication, with painful burning feet from HIV itself or from antiretroviral toxicity.
simple: Burning, painful or numb feet and hands in people with HIV.
more: Diagnosed clinically with nerve studies or skin biopsy. Stopping neurotoxic drugs, antiretroviral therapy, and neuropathic pain agents such as gabapentin help.
th: ปลายประสาทรับความรู้สึกเสื่อมแบบสมมาตร พบบ่อยที่สุดในผู้ติดเชื้อ HIV ปวดแสบร้อนเท้า จากตัวไวรัสหรือยาต้านไวรัสรุ่นเก่า
tempoNote: Gradual over months to years
feat: Burning, numb feet; length-dependent; ankle reflexes reduced
Commonest neurological complication of HIV
Risk: older age, height, low CD4 nadir, old 'd-drugs' (stavudine, didanosine)
Weakness is mild or absent
inv: NCS: axonal sensory neuropathy (may be normal if small fibres only)
Skin biopsy for small fibre density
Exclude B12, diabetes, alcohol, syphilis, isoniazid without pyridoxine

case.who: 52-year-old man from Chonburi treated with stavudine-containing ART years ago
case.story: Burning feet worse at night for several years.
case.exam: Stocking pinprick loss, reduced vibration at toes, absent ankle jerks, normal strength.
case.tests: NCS: reduced sural amplitudes; B12 and HbA1c normal.
case.q: Management?
case.a: HIV sensory neuropathy with prior NRTI toxicity; neuropathic pain drugs and foot care; avoid further neurotoxic drugs.

read.where: 23. Neuropathies Associated With HIV Infection and Antiretroviral Therapy

det.patho: Distal axonal degeneration begins in the longest sensory fibres. HIV does not infect neurons directly; injury is driven by activated macrophages and viral proteins acting in dorsal root ganglia and nerves. Older dideoxynucleoside drugs (stavudine, didanosine) add mitochondrial toxicity. Risk rises with age, height and low CD4 nadir.
det.clinical: Numbness, tingling and burning start in the toes and spread slowly upward; the hands become involved later. Pain, especially at night, is the main disability. Examination shows reduced pinprick and vibration distally with absent ankle jerks, while strength is preserved. Many patients have signs without symptoms.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by reduced sural responses on NCS or reduced fibre density on skin biopsy. Exclude diabetes, B12 deficiency, alcohol, syphilis, hepatitis C and isoniazid toxicity. Weakness, asymmetry or rapid progression suggest another process such as inflammatory neuropathy or CMV.
det.treatment: Avoid neurotoxic drugs and give pyridoxine with isoniazid. Evidence for gabapentinoids, duloxetine and tricyclics in HIV neuropathy is weak, though they are often tried. The high-concentration capsaicin patch has the best trial support. Foot care and treatment of coexisting causes complete management.
det.prognosis: Tends to persist even with ART; progression slows.
pearls: Ask about past stavudine or didanosine.
Give pyridoxine with isoniazid in HIV.
Capsaicin 8% patch has trial support in HIV neuropathy.
det.thd: HIV-related sensory neuropathy คือปลายประสาทเสื่อมแบบสมมาตรที่พบบ่อยที่สุดในผู้ติดเชื้อ HIV ปวดแสบร้อนและชาเท้า เกิดจากตัวไวรัสหรือยาต้านไวรัสรุ่นเก่า เช่น stavudine วินิจฉัยทางคลินิกร่วมกับ NCS หรือ skin biopsy รักษาด้วยยาลดปวดประสาทและหลีกเลี่ยงยาที่เป็นพิษต่อเส้นประสาท

ddx.pt: Same clinical entity under another label
Weakness, areflexia and demyelinating NCS
Rapid onset, normal NCS

aN: hiv dsp | distal symmetric polyneuropathy in hiv | hiv painful neuropathy | toxic nrti neuropathy | hiv sn

name: HIV-related vacuolar myelopathy
formal: Spinal cord degeneration in advanced AIDS with vacuolation of the posterior and lateral columns, giving spastic paraparesis, sensory ataxia and bladder dysfunction, resembling B12 deficiency.
simple: Damage to the spinal cord in advanced HIV that causes stiff, weak legs, poor balance and bladder trouble.
more: Progressive myelopathy in advanced HIV infection with spastic paraparesis, sensory ataxia and bladder dysfunction.
th: ไขสันหลังเสื่อมจากเอชไอวี (vacuolar myelopathy) พบในผู้ป่วยระยะท้ายที่ไม่ได้รับ ART ขาเกร็งอ่อนแรง สูญเสียการรับรู้ตำแหน่ง ปัสสาวะผิดปกติ คล้ายขาดวิตามิน B12 เป็นการวินิจฉัยแบบตัดโรคอื่นออก
tempoNote: Slowly progressive over months to years in advanced untreated HIV
feat: Painless spastic paraparesis without a clear sensory level, developing over months
Posterior column signs: reduced vibration and joint position sense with sensory ataxia and positive Romberg
Urinary urgency or incontinence and erectile dysfunction
Reflexes may be brisk at the knees but ankle jerks are lost when a distal sensory neuropathy coexists
Usually with other markers of advanced HIV (HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder, neuropathy); now rare where ART is widely used
inv: MRI spine: normal or mild thoracic cord atrophy and T2 signal in the dorsal columns; excludes compression, abscess, lymphoma and TB
B12, folate, methylmalonic acid, copper, zinc, and syphilis and HTLV-1 serology
CSF to exclude CMV, VZV, HSV, TB and lymphoma; HIV RNA in CSF
Somatosensory evoked potentials may show prolonged central conduction

case.who: 41-year-old man from Phayao, HIV diagnosed late, CD4 38 cells/µL, not on ART
case.story: Eight months of stiff legs, tripping in the dark and urgency of micturition.
case.exam: Spastic paraparesis, absent vibration at the toes, sensory ataxia, extensor plantar responses, no sensory level.
case.tests: MRI shows mild thoracic cord thinning without compression; B12, copper, syphilis and HTLV-1 normal; CSF acellular.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what treatment can be offered?
case.a: HIV-associated vacuolar myelopathy (diagnosis of exclusion); start effective ART, give symptomatic spasticity and bladder management, and rehabilitation.

read.where: Chapter 19 Human Immunodeficiency Virus - Spinal Cord Disease, HIV-Associated Myelopathy
Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — HIV-Related Vacuolar Myelopathy
Chapter 43 HIV and Other Retroviral Infections of the Nervous System
23. Neuropathies Associated With HIV Infection and Antiretroviral Therapy

det.patho: Pathologically there is vacuolation of myelin in the posterior and lateral columns, most marked in the thoracic cord with macrophage infiltration, resembling B12 deficiency. HIV itself is not found in proportion to the injury, and activated macrophages appear to drive myelin damage. Altered methylation, with low S-adenosylmethionine in the CSF, has been proposed. The condition arises in advanced AIDS and became uncommon after combination antiretroviral therapy.
det.clinical: Patients describe slowly worsening leg stiffness, weakness and unsteady walking, then bladder and bowel dysfunction. Examination shows spastic paraparesis, posterior column loss and sensory ataxia, often combined with painful sensory neuropathy and cognitive slowing. The course is chronic, and the lack of back pain or a sensory level distinguishes it from compressive and infective lesions.
det.diagnosis: It is a diagnosis of exclusion. MRI excludes compression, lymphoma, epidural abscess and TB; serology and levels exclude syphilis, HTLV-1, B12, copper and folate deficiencies. CSF excludes CMV, VZV, HSV and tuberculosis. MRI is normal or shows mild atrophy and dorsal column signal, which is non-specific. Evoked potentials can support dorsal column dysfunction.
det.treatment: Treatment is to start or optimise ART and suppress viral load. There is no proven specific therapy: L-methionine and IV immunoglobulin did not help in small trials. Management includes baclofen or tizanidine for spasticity, anticholinergics or intermittent catheterisation for bladder dysfunction, physiotherapy, and fall prevention. Replace B12 or copper if low, because deficiency can coexist with HIV.
det.prognosis: Often stable or slowly progressive; ART can halt or improve some patients, but established deficits usually persist.
pearls: Spastic paraparesis plus proprioceptive loss in advanced HIV: check B12, copper, syphilis and HTLV-1 before labelling it vacuolar myelopathy.
A sensory level, back pain or rapid course means compression, TB, lymphoma or infectious myelitis, not vacuolar myelopathy.
The pathology looks like B12 deficiency even when B12 is normal.
det.thd: Vacuolar myelopathy จากเอชไอวีพบในผู้ป่วยระยะท้ายที่ CD4 ต่ำและไม่ได้รับ ART ผู้ป่วยมีขาเกร็งอ่อนแรง เดินเซ สูญเสียการรับรู้ตำแหน่ง และปัสสาวะราด คล้ายโรคขาดวิตามิน B12 MRI มักปกติหรือไขสันหลังฝ่อเล็กน้อย ต้องตัดสาเหตุอื่นออก เช่น กดทับไขสันหลัง วัณโรค ซิฟิลิส HTLV-1 และขาด B12 หรือทองแดง การรักษาหลักคือ ART ร่วมกับยาลดเกร็งและกายภาพบำบัด

23. Neuropathies Associated With HIV Infection and Antiretroviral Therapy

ddx.pt: Similar dorsal and lateral column degeneration from low B12; macrocytosis, raised methylmalonic acid, responds to B12
Slow spastic paraparesis with positive HTLV-1 serology and CSF antibodies
Low copper and caeruloplasmin, anaemia and neutropenia, often after zinc excess or bariatric surgery

aN: vacuolar myelopathy hiv infection | vacuolar myelopathy | hiv infection | hiv myelopathy | aids associated myelopathy | hiv vm

name: HIV/AIDS basal ganglia calcification
formal: Bilateral basal ganglia calcification in children with HIV, often with encephalopathy, probably from vascular injury and mineral deposition, seen on CT as symmetric dense deposits.
simple: Calcium deposits in deep brain areas, seen on scans of some children with HIV, often linked to developmental problems.
th: หินปูนเกาะที่ basal ganglia ทั้งสองข้างในเด็กที่ติดเชื้อ HIV มักร่วมกับภาวะสมองผิดปกติ เห็นชัดใน CT
tempoNote: Develops over months to years in perinatally infected children
feat: Perinatal HIV infection with progressive encephalopathy, developmental delay
Symmetric basal ganglia (and frontal white matter) calcification on CT
Microcephaly, spasticity, cognitive impairment
Less frequent with early ART
inv: CT brain (calcification), MRI (atrophy)
HIV viral load, CD4; exclude congenital CMV, toxoplasma, parathyroid disorders

case.who: 5-year-old boy from Khon Kaen with perinatal HIV, ART started late
case.story: Loss of motor milestones and slow speech development.
case.exam: Microcephaly, spastic legs, brisk reflexes.
case.tests: CT: bilateral symmetric basal ganglia calcification and cerebral atrophy.
case.q: Cause and management?
case.a: HIV encephalopathy with basal ganglia calcification; optimise ART, rehabilitation.

det.patho: The calcification probably results from a mineralising microangiopathy of small vessels in the basal ganglia and adjacent white matter. It is linked to HIV infection of the developing brain and chronic inflammation. The exact mechanism is not fully established.
det.clinical: It is seen mainly in children with perinatally acquired HIV and encephalopathy. Features include developmental arrest or regression, acquired microcephaly, spasticity and cognitive impairment. It is now uncommon where ART is started in infancy.
det.diagnosis: CT shows symmetric basal ganglia calcification, sometimes with frontal white-matter calcification and atrophy. Other causes must be excluded: congenital CMV and toxoplasmosis, hypoparathyroidism, mitochondrial and genetic disorders. HIV viral load and CD4 count define disease control.
det.treatment: There is no treatment for the calcification itself. Effective ART may stabilise or improve encephalopathy. Physiotherapy, developmental support and seizure treatment are provided as needed. Prevention is by early infant diagnosis and ART.
det.prognosis: Depends on ART timing; established deficits often persist.
pearls: Basal ganglia calcification in a child: think HIV, CMV, toxoplasma and parathyroid.
Early ART prevents HIV encephalopathy.
CT is better than MRI to see calcium.

name: Hodgkin’s disease
formal: Lymphoma with Reed-Sternberg cells; neurological involvement includes spinal cord compression, paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, limbic encephalitis and neuropathy.
simple: A cancer of the lymph glands that can press on the spinal cord or trigger immune attacks on the brain and nerves.
th: มะเร็งต่อมน้ำเหลืองชนิด Hodgkin ที่มีเซลล์ Reed-Sternberg อาจกดไขสันหลัง หรือทำให้เกิดกลุ่มอาการ paraneoplastic เช่น cerebellar degeneration จาก anti-Tr และ limbic encephalitis
tempoNote: Neurological complications usually evolve over weeks; may precede lymphoma diagnosis
feat: Painless lymphadenopathy, fever, night sweats and weight loss; alcohol-induced node pain
Epidural spread causing back pain and cord compression
Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration with anti-Tr (DNER) antibodies
Limbic encephalitis (e.g., mGluR5, 'Ophelia syndrome') and neuropathy
Treatment-related: radiation myelopathy, chemotherapy neuropathy, PML/VZV in immunosuppression
inv: Excisional lymph node biopsy; PET-CT staging
MRI spine for compression; MRI brain
Paraneoplastic antibody panel (DNER/Tr, mGluR5) and CSF

case.story: Three weeks of rapidly worsening unsteadiness and slurred speech; she has had night sweats and itching for months.
case.exam: Severe gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, downbeat nystagmus; supraclavicular lymph node 2 cm.
case.tests: MRI brain normal; CSF mild pleocytosis; anti-Tr (DNER) positive; node biopsy shows classical Hodgkin lymphoma.
case.q: What is the neurological syndrome, and what drives its treatment?
case.a: Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration with anti-Tr; treating the lymphoma (plus immunotherapy) offers the best chance of improvement.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Proliferative Conditions

det.patho: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma is a B-cell neoplasm in which few malignant Reed-Sternberg cells sit within an inflammatory background. Neurological disease arises from local spread (epidural or bony compression), immune-mediated paraneoplastic syndromes, immunosuppression-related infections and treatment toxicity. Direct parenchymal brain invasion is rare.
det.clinical: Spinal cord compression from epidural deposits is the classic structural complication. Paraneoplastic anti-Tr cerebellar degeneration typically affects young men and may precede the lymphoma diagnosis. Limbic encephalitis with mGluR5 antibodies causes memory loss and psychiatric change. Survivors may later have radiation-related vasculopathy, myelopathy or plexopathy.
det.diagnosis: Neurological symptoms in a patient with lymphoma require imaging for compression and metastasis and CSF analysis. In a new paraneoplastic syndrome with anti-Tr or mGluR5, perform PET-CT to look for Hodgkin lymphoma. Tissue diagnosis is by excisional biopsy.
det.treatment: Treat the lymphoma with chemotherapy (e.g., ABVD or escalated BEACOPP, now often with brentuximab or checkpoint inhibitors in selected settings) and radiotherapy. Cord compression needs urgent steroids and radiotherapy or surgery. Paraneoplastic syndromes are treated by tumour control plus steroids, IVIG or plasma exchange.
det.prognosis: Hodgkin lymphoma is highly curable; anti-Tr and mGluR5 syndromes recover better than most paraneoplastic disorders.
pearls: Young adult with subacute cerebellar ataxia: check anti-Tr and look for Hodgkin.
mGluR5 encephalitis ('Ophelia syndrome') signals Hodgkin lymphoma.
Checkpoint inhibitor therapy can itself trigger immune neurological complications.
det.thd: Hodgkin’s disease หรือ Hodgkin lymphoma เป็นมะเร็งต่อมน้ำเหลืองที่รักษาหายได้สูง ผลต่อระบบประสาทได้แก่ ก้อนกดไขสันหลัง กลุ่มอาการ paraneoplastic เช่น cerebellar degeneration จาก anti-Tr และ limbic encephalitis จาก mGluR5 รวมถึงผลแทรกซ้อนจากยาเคมีและรังสี วินิจฉัยด้วยชิ้นเนื้อต่อมน้ำเหลืองและ PET-CT รักษามะเร็งเป็นหลักร่วมกับภูมิคุ้มกันบำบัดสำหรับกลุ่ม paraneoplastic

name: Holmes tremor
formal: Rest, postural and kinetic tremor of low frequency (under 4.5 Hz) from midbrain lesions affecting the cerebello-thalamic and nigrostriatal pathways, often after stroke or trauma.
simple: A slow, large, shaking tremor of the arm, present at rest and with movement, usually after damage to the midbrain.
more: Coarse low-frequency proximal rest, postural and intention tremor from midbrain lesions affecting the dentato-rubro-thalamic pathway and nigrostriatal fibres (Holmes tremor). Historical term for the large proximal wing-beating tremor due to lesions of the superior cerebellar peduncle (brachium conjunctivum) or red nucleus. Holmes tremor: slow, large-amplitude rest, postural and intention tremor from lesions of the cerebellothalamic and nigrostriatal pathways, often after stroke or trauma.
th: tremor ความถี่ต่ำ (ต่ำกว่า 4.5 Hz) ที่มีทั้งขณะพัก ขณะยกค้าง และขณะเคลื่อนไหว จากรอยโรคที่ midbrain/thalamus ที่ทำลายทั้งทาง cerebellar และ nigrostriatal
tempoNote: Appears weeks to months (up to 2 years) after the causal lesion
feat: Irregular, low-frequency (under 4.5 Hz) tremor combining rest, postural and intention components
Proximal and distal arm, coarse and disabling
Delay between lesion and tremor onset is typical
Causes: midbrain/thalamic stroke or haemorrhage, trauma, demyelination, AVM, toxoplasma abscess
May coexist with ataxia, ocular palsy (third nerve) or hemiparesis
inv: MRI brain: lesion of midbrain tegmentum, red nucleus region, thalamus or cerebellar outflow
DAT SPECT may show nigrostriatal deficit, supporting levodopa trial
HIV test and toxoplasma serology where relevant

case.who: 47-year-old man from Lopburi 8 months after a right midbrain haemorrhage
case.story: Left arm developed a coarse shaking at rest that becomes violent when reaching for a cup.
case.exam: Left arm 3 Hz tremor at rest, worse with posture and intention; right partial third nerve palsy.
case.tests: MRI shows old right midbrain tegmental haemosiderin.
case.q: Name the tremor and a first-line drug to try.
case.a: Holmes tremor; trial of levodopa, then consider thalamic (Vim) DBS if refractory.

read.where: 2.5 Clinical Presentation of HOD (criteria and 5 cases in the pooled series)

det.patho: The tremor requires combined damage to the cerebellothalamic (dentatorubrothalamic) pathway and the nigrostriatal dopaminergic system, typically where they converge in the midbrain or thalamus. The delay before onset suggests secondary reorganisation of networks after the lesion.
det.clinical: The tremor is slow, irregular and large in amplitude, present at rest but worse with posture and goal-directed movement. It is usually unilateral, contralateral to the lesion. Associated signs depend on the lesion and include ataxia, ocular motor palsies and hemiparesis.
det.diagnosis: Movement Disorder Society criteria require rest and intention tremor, low frequency, and a delay between lesion and onset in most cases. MRI confirms the causative lesion. Neurophysiology can document frequency and pattern.
det.treatment: Levodopa helps a proportion of patients; dopamine agonists, anticholinergics, levetiracetam and clonazepam are alternatives. Deep brain stimulation aimed at the thalamic Vim nucleus, sometimes combined with GPi, or focused lesioning can reduce disabling tremor. Treat the underlying cause, such as toxoplasmosis in HIV.
det.prognosis: Often persistent and disabling; partial benefit from treatment is common.
pearls: Rest plus intention tremor, slow, after a midbrain lesion: Holmes tremor.
Try levodopa first; dopaminergic deficit is part of the mechanism.
Look for an accompanying third nerve palsy.
det.thd: Holmes tremor เป็น tremor ความถี่ต่ำ มีทั้งขณะพัก ขณะยกแขนค้าง และขณะเอื้อมหยิบของ เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ midbrain หรือ thalamus ที่ทำลายทั้งทาง cerebellum และ dopamine มักเกิดหลังรอยโรคหลายเดือน สาเหตุ เช่น stroke, อุบัติเหตุ, MS รักษาด้วย levodopa เป็นอันดับแรก และพิจารณา DBS ในรายที่ไม่ตอบสนอง

qx.stem: A 55-year-old man from Phrae had a left thalamic haemorrhage three months ago. Now he has a coarse, low-frequency tremor of the right arm at rest, on posture and worst on reaching a target, with mild right hemisensory loss. He has no parkinsonian bradykinesia.
qx.q: What best describes this tremor?
opts: Orthostatic tremor
Physiological tremor
Holmes tremor, a rest, postural and intention tremor that appears weeks to months after a midbrain-thalamic-cerebellar lesion
Primary writing tremor
Cerebellar tremor with only intention component
qx.why: Holmes (rubral or midbrain) tremor is a slow, coarse tremor present at rest, with posture and on action, appearing after a delay following lesions of the cerebellothalamic and nigrostriatal pathways. A purely intention tremor suggests cerebellar outflow disease, and orthostatic tremor occurs on standing. Treatment includes levodopa, anticholinergics or antiepileptics in trial, and deep brain stimulation in refractory cases.

name: Holmes–Adie syndrome (HAS)
formal: Tonic pupil with absent or reduced tendon reflexes, from damage to ciliary ganglion and dorsal root ganglion neurons; usually young women, benign, with sectoral iris palsy and light-near dissociation.
simple: A harmless condition with one large, slowly reacting pupil and reduced knee and ankle reflexes.
th: รูม่านตาแบบ tonic ร่วมกับรีเฟล็กซ์เอ็นลดลงหรือหาย จากความเสียหายของ ciliary ganglion และ dorsal root ganglion พบบ่อยในหญิงอายุน้อยและไม่อันตราย
tempoNote: Pupil change noticed suddenly; the condition is then lifelong and slowly evolves (pupil becomes smaller over years)
feat: Unilateral (later often bilateral) dilated pupil with poor light reaction
Slow, sustained constriction to near effort and slow redilation (light-near dissociation)
Segmental iris sphincter palsy with vermiform movements on slit lamp
Reduced or absent knee and ankle reflexes
Blurred near vision or photophobia; mostly women aged 20–40
inv: Slit-lamp examination for sectoral palsy
Dilute pilocarpine 0.1% (or 0.125%): tonic pupil constricts (cholinergic denervation supersensitivity)
Reflex examination; consider syphilis serology and autonomic screen if atypical or bilateral

case.story: A colleague noticed her right pupil was larger; she has some blur when reading her phone and is dazzled outdoors.
case.exam: Right pupil 6 mm, minimal light response, slow constriction on near gaze; no ptosis or ophthalmoplegia; ankle jerks absent bilaterally.
case.tests: Right pupil constricts briskly to dilute pilocarpine; syphilis serology negative.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and why is urgent imaging not needed?
case.a: Holmes–Adie syndrome; normal eye movements and lids with denervation supersensitivity exclude a compressive third nerve palsy.

read.where: Chapter 22 Neuro-Ophthalmology — Abnormalities of the Pupil

det.patho: Injury to the ciliary ganglion and the nerves leaving it, presumed viral or inflammatory, denervates the iris sphincter and ciliary muscle. Aberrant regeneration of fibres destined for the ciliary muscle (which vastly outnumber sphincter fibres) explains why near response is relatively preserved while light response is lost. Loss of large dorsal root ganglion neurons explains the areflexia.
det.clinical: Most patients are young women who notice anisocoria or blurred near vision. The tonic pupil is larger initially but may become smaller than the other over years ('little old Adie'). The second eye becomes involved in a proportion. Some develop reduced sweating, linking it to Ross syndrome. The condition is benign but often causes alarm.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical: poor light response, tonic near response, sectoral palsy on slit lamp, and supersensitivity to dilute pilocarpine. Normal extraocular movements and lids distinguish it from third nerve palsy. Bilateral tonic pupils warrant consideration of syphilis, diabetes, Sjögren syndrome, amyloid and other autonomic neuropathies.
det.treatment: Reassurance is usually sufficient. Reading glasses help accommodation problems, and tinted lenses help photophobia. Low-dose pilocarpine drops can improve cosmetic and near-vision symptoms in some patients.
det.prognosis: Benign; the pupil tends to constrict over time and the second eye may become involved.
pearls: Dilated pupil with normal lids and eye movements: think Adie, not aneurysm.
Check the knee and ankle jerks in every patient with anisocoria.
Dilute pilocarpine constricts an Adie pupil but not a pharmacologically blocked one.
det.thd: Holmes-Adie syndrome คือรูม่านตาข้างหนึ่งโตแบบ tonic ตอบสนองต่อแสงน้อย แต่หดช้า ๆ เมื่อมองใกล้ ร่วมกับรีเฟล็กซ์เอ็นหาย เกิดจากความเสียหายของ ciliary ganglion มักพบในหญิงอายุ 20-40 ปี ทดสอบด้วย pilocarpine เจือจางแล้วรูม่านตาหด การกลอกตาและหนังตาปกติจึงไม่ใช่ third nerve palsy ไม่อันตราย รักษาด้วยแว่นอ่านหนังสือหรือแว่นกันแดด

name: Horizontal gaze palsy
formal: Loss of conjugate eye movement to one side from a lesion of the PPRF or abducens nucleus in the pons, or the frontal eye field; may be isolated or part of a brainstem syndrome.
simple: Inability to move both eyes together toward one side, caused by damage in the brainstem or brain.
th: การกลอกตาสองข้างไปด้านใดด้านหนึ่งไม่ได้ จากรอยโรคที่ PPRF หรือ abducens nucleus ใน pons หรือ frontal eye field
tempoNote: Acute in stroke, subacute in demyelination or tumour, chronic in congenital or degenerative causes
feat: Both eyes fail to move to one side; no diplopia because the eyes stay aligned
Frontal lesion: eyes deviate toward the lesion, overcome by doll's head manoeuvre
Pontine lesion: eyes deviate away from the lesion; abducens nucleus lesions not overcome by vestibulo-ocular reflex
Seizure focus can drive the eyes away from the irritated hemisphere
May combine with INO (one-and-a-half syndrome) or facial palsy
inv: Bedside: saccades, pursuit and oculocephalic reflex to localise supranuclear vs nuclear
MRI brain with diffusion-weighted imaging
EEG if seizure-related deviation suspected

case.story: Sudden dizziness and inability to look to the right, along with a weak left side.
case.exam: Neither eye moves to the right on command or with doll's head manoeuvre, right lower motor neuron facial palsy, left hemiparesis.
case.tests: MRI DWI: acute infarct in right dorsal pons involving abducens nucleus and facial colliculus.
case.q: Why does the vestibulo-ocular reflex fail to overcome this gaze palsy?
case.a: The lesion involves the abducens nucleus itself, the final common pathway for horizontal gaze, so reflex eye movements are also lost (pontine Foville-type syndrome).

read.where: Chapter 22 Neuro-Ophthalmology — Central Disorders of Eye Movements

det.patho: Horizontal saccades are generated by the PPRF (paramedian pontine reticular formation), driving the ipsilateral abducens nucleus. Abducens interneurons send signals via the contralateral MLF to the medial rectus subnucleus. Frontal eye fields drive contralateral gaze. Lesions at different levels produce distinctive patterns: PPRF lesions abolish saccades but may spare vestibular movements; abducens nucleus lesions abolish all ipsilateral horizontal movements.
det.clinical: Acute hemispheric strokes cause transient deviation toward the lesion with contralateral hemiparesis. Pontine strokes cause gaze palsy away from the lesion, often with ipsilateral facial palsy and contralateral hemiparesis. Demyelination, tumours, Wernicke encephalopathy and congenital disorders (Möbius, horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis) are other causes.
det.diagnosis: Test saccades, pursuit and doll's head responses: supranuclear palsies are overcome by reflexes. Look for associated signs (facial palsy, INO, hemiparesis). MRI with DWI is the key investigation; consider thiamine deficiency in at-risk patients.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: acute stroke pathways, immunotherapy for demyelination, thiamine for Wernicke, tumour management. Gaze palsies from hemispheric stroke usually recover within days to weeks.
det.prognosis: Frontal gaze palsies recover quickly; nuclear pontine palsies may persist.
pearls: Eyes look toward a hemispheric stroke but away from a pontine one.
Doll's head eye movements overcome supranuclear but not nuclear palsies.
Gaze palsy with ipsilateral LMN facial weakness localises to the dorsal pons.
det.thd: Horizontal gaze palsy คือการกลอกตาสองข้างไปด้านหนึ่งไม่ได้ ถ้ารอยโรคอยู่ที่ frontal ตาจะเบนไปทางรอยโรคและ doll's eye ยังทำได้ ถ้าอยู่ที่ pons (PPRF หรือ abducens nucleus) ตาจะเบนออกจากรอยโรค และรอยโรคที่ abducens nucleus ทำให้ reflex หายด้วย สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยคือ stroke, MS, เนื้องอก และ Wernicke ตรวจด้วย MRI และรักษาตามสาเหตุ

name: Horner syndrome
formal: Oculosympathetic palsy with ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis from a lesion along the three-neuron sympathetic pathway; causes include carotid dissection, Pancoast tumour and lateral medullary stroke.
simple: A drooping eyelid, small pupil and reduced sweating on one side of the face, from damage to nerves that run from brain to eye.
th: ภาวะระบบประสาท sympathetic ไปตาเสีย ทำให้หนังตาตกเล็กน้อย รูม่านตาเล็ก และเหงื่อออกน้อยด้านเดียวกัน จากรอยโรคในเส้นทาง 3 neuron
tempoNote: Acute painful onset suggests carotid dissection; chronic may be congenital or benign
feat: Mild ptosis (1–2 mm), miosis, apparent enophthalmos and reverse ptosis of lower lid
Anisocoria greater in the dark; dilation lag
Anhidrosis depends on the level: absent or limited with postganglionic lesions
Central (lateral medulla, cord), preganglionic (lung apex, neck) or postganglionic (carotid, cavernous sinus) causes
Painful acute Horner: carotid dissection until proven otherwise
inv: Apraclonidine or cocaine eye drops to confirm
Urgent CTA or MRA head and neck for painful or acute cases
MRI brain and cervical cord; chest imaging for Pancoast tumour
In children without history: neuroblastoma screening (imaging, urine catecholamines)

case.who: 44-year-old man from Bangkok who had a traditional neck massage two days before
case.story: Severe right neck pain and right-sided headache, then his wife noticed the right eyelid drooping.
case.exam: Right ptosis 2 mm, right pupil smaller with dilation lag in dim light, normal facial sweating.
case.tests: CTA shows right internal carotid dissection.
case.q: Why is facial sweating spared?
case.a: Dissection injures the postganglionic third-order fibres on the ICA; the sudomotor supply to most facial skin follows the external carotid branches instead.
