det.patho: The oculosympathetic pathway has three neurons: hypothalamus to the C8–T2 cord (first order), cord to the superior cervical ganglion via the lung apex (second order), and ganglion along the internal carotid to the eye (third order). Damage at any level reduces sympathetic tone to the dilator pupillae and Müller muscle.
det.clinical: Ptosis is mild and pupillary asymmetry is most obvious in dim light. Central lesions come with brainstem or cord signs (e.g. lateral medullary syndrome). Preganglionic lesions include Pancoast tumour, neck trauma and surgery. Postganglionic lesions include carotid dissection, cavernous sinus disease and cluster headache. Congenital Horner causes iris heterochromia.
det.diagnosis: Pharmacological testing confirms the diagnosis: apraclonidine reverses the anisocoria by dilating the hypersensitive Horner pupil, while cocaine fails to dilate it. Hydroxyamfetamine distinguishes postganglionic lesions but is rarely available. Imaging is chosen by clinical localisation; acute painful Horner requires urgent vascular imaging.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: antithrombotic therapy for dissection, oncological management for apical lung tumours, and so on. The ptosis itself rarely needs treatment; topical apraclonidine or surgery can be used for cosmetic concerns.
det.prognosis: Depends on the cause; Horner signs may persist after the underlying lesion is treated.
pearls: Painful acute Horner equals carotid dissection until proven otherwise.
Anisocoria worse in the dark points to the small pupil as abnormal.
Horner plus hand weakness and arm pain: Pancoast tumour.
det.thd: Horner syndrome เกิดจากเส้นประสาท sympathetic ที่ไปตาเสีย ทำให้หนังตาตกเล็กน้อย รูม่านตาเล็ก และเหงื่อออกน้อยด้านเดียวกัน รอยโรคอาจอยู่ที่ก้านสมอง ไขสันหลัง ยอดปอด หรือหลอดเลือด carotid ถ้าเกิดเฉียบพลันร่วมกับปวดคอหรือปวดศีรษะต้องคิดถึง carotid dissection และทำ CTA ด่วน การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ

qx.stem: A 44-year-old woman from Phuket develops a right droopy eyelid and a small right pupil that dilates poorly in the dark, after three days of right-sided neck pain and headache. Right facial sweating is normal. Apraclonidine 0.5% dilates the right pupil and reverses the ptosis.
qx.q: Which test should be done urgently?
opts: Tensilon test for myasthenia
CT or MR angiography of the neck and head to look for carotid dissection
Lumbar puncture for cell count
Skull radiograph
Visual evoked potentials
qx.why: Apraclonidine reversal confirms Horner syndrome, and painful neck or head pain with a postganglionic pattern (sparing of facial sweating) suggests internal carotid artery dissection, which risks stroke and needs prompt vascular imaging and antithrombotic therapy. Myasthenia does not cause miosis, and lumbar puncture or evoked potentials are not first-line here.

qx.stem: A 58-year-old man from Pathum Thani has a mild left ptosis and a miotic left pupil that dilates slowly in the dark. Apraclonidine 0.5 percent drops are instilled in both eyes. Forty-five minutes later the left pupil has become larger than the right, and the ptosis is reduced.
qx.q: What does this reversal of anisocoria indicate?
opts: Denervation supersensitivity in the left pupil, supporting a diagnosis of Horner syndrome
A normal physiological anisocoria
An Adie tonic pupil
A third nerve palsy
Pharmacological pupil dilatation from atropine
qx.why: Apraclonidine is a weak alpha-1 agonist that has little effect on a normal pupil but dilates a sympathetically denervated pupil because of receptor supersensitivity, so reversal of anisocoria supports Horner syndrome (it may be falsely negative in acute cases). The test does not localise the lesion; hydroxyamphetamine testing, where available, or imaging directed by the clinical context does that. Atropine or third nerve palsy give a large, poorly reactive pupil, and an Adie pupil constricts to dilute pilocarpine.

qx.stem: A 40-year-old woman from Bangkok has an unexplained left ptosis, with the left pupil 1.5 mm smaller than the right in the dark and a slowed dilation lag. The clinic has apraclonidine 0.5% eye drops available but no cocaine or hydroxyamphetamine.
qx.q: What response would confirm Horner syndrome after instillation of apraclonidine?
opts: Both pupils constrict equally and the left lid droops further
The left pupil dilates, the anisocoria reverses and the ptotic lid lifts, owing to denervation supersensitivity
The left pupil fails to dilate while the right pupil dilates
No change in either pupil, which shows a preganglionic lesion
Both pupils dilate equally with no change in the lids
qx.why: Apraclonidine is a weak alpha-1 agonist that has little effect on a normal pupil but dilates a pupil with up-regulated post-synaptic receptors after sympathetic denervation, so a reversal of the anisocoria confirms Horner syndrome. Cocaine blocks noradrenaline re-uptake and fails to dilate a Horner pupil, and hydroxyamphetamine, which releases transmitter from intact post-ganglionic terminals, helps tell pre- from post-ganglionic lesions. Apraclonidine can give false negatives in very recent lesions.

det.patho: HTLV-1 is a deltaretrovirus that persists by clonal expansion of infected CD4 T cells rather than by free virions, so spread needs cell-rich fluids: prolonged breastfeeding, sex, transfused cellular blood products, shared needles and organ transplantation. Only about 1–4% of carriers ever develop HAM/TSP, and the main predictor is a high proviral load, with host HLA type and the vigour of the cytotoxic response also mattering. Infected T cells migrate into the cord, where viral protein (Tax) expression attracts virus-specific CD8 cells and a CXCL10-driven inflammatory loop; the bystander damage falls mostly on the lateral and posterior columns of the lower thoracic cord, which eventually atrophies. The same virus causes adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma, uveitis, infective dermatitis and a predisposition to Strongyloides hyperinfection.
det.clinical: Onset is usually in the fourth to sixth decade, after a latency of years, and women are affected more often. Stiff, heavy legs with slowly mounting spastic weakness (often more proximal), early urinary urgency, frequency or retention, constipation and erectile failure, and burning low back or leg pain dominate, while objective sensory loss is slight — perhaps reduced vibration at the ankles. Arms become involved late and mildly, and bulbar muscles are spared; a few develop cerebellar signs, peripheral neuropathy or a steroid-resistant inflammatory myositis. Most worsen steadily over decades, but about one in five progresses quickly over the first two years. Endemic regions include southern Japan, the Caribbean, South America, sub-Saharan Africa, Iran, Melanesia and central Australia; in Thailand the infection is rare, so ask about birthplace, migration, transfusion and partners.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in any slowly progressive myelopathy with prominent bladder symptoms and few sensory signs. Screen serum and CSF with ELISA or chemiluminescence and confirm by western blot, line immunoassay or proviral DNA PCR (which also separates HTLV-1 from HTLV-2); the WHO and later graded criteria rank cases as definite, probable or possible depending on CSF evidence and exclusion of mimics. CSF typically shows a mild lymphocytosis, raised protein, intrathecal HTLV-1 antibody and specific oligoclonal bands, and a CSF/blood proviral load ratio above 1 together with high CSF neopterin or CXCL10 indicates active inflammation and a faster course. Spine MRI usually shows thoracic atrophy, sometimes swelling and T2 signal early, and brain MRI may show non-specific white matter lesions that can mislead toward MS. Exclude compression, B12 and copper deficiency, HIV and syphilis myelopathy, primary progressive MS and hereditary spastic paraplegia.
det.treatment: There is no proven antiviral therapy — zidovudine and lamivudine have not changed the course. Consensus favours corticosteroids for active or rapidly progressive disease (for example pulsed IV methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisolone tapering to a low maintenance dose) and low-dose oral prednisolone for slower progressors, always after excluding or treating Strongyloides with ivermectin. Interferon-alpha is licensed in Japan, and the anti-CCR4 antibody mogamulizumab is under evaluation as it reduces infected cell numbers. Symptomatic care is essential: baclofen, tizanidine or botulinum toxin for spasticity, antimuscarinics and intermittent catheterisation for the bladder, neuropathic pain treatment, physiotherapy and mobility aids. Counsel carriers about transmission (avoiding or shortening breastfeeding, barrier contraception, no blood or organ donation) and screen for adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma.
det.prognosis: The course is usually slowly progressive: many need a stick within about 10 years and a wheelchair after two decades, while rapid progressors may lose walking within a few years; life expectancy is mainly reduced by ATL, infections and immobility.
pearls: Spastic paraparesis with early bladder symptoms, back pain and few sensory signs: test HTLV-1 in serum and CSF.
Screen for Strongyloides before any steroid — hyperinfection can be fatal.
A CSF/blood proviral load ratio above 1 and high CSF CXCL10 or neopterin mark active disease likely to respond to steroids.
Check for adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma in carriers with lymphocytosis, flower cells, hypercalcaemia or skin lesions.

det.patho: HTLV-1 is a deltaretrovirus that integrates into CD4 T cells and spreads mainly cell-to-cell. A high proviral load and strong immune response lead to perivascular inflammation in the thoracic cord (HAM/TSP), whereas clonal expansion of infected cells leads to ATL. Global prevalence is in the millions, concentrated in endemic clusters.
det.clinical: Only a small percentage of carriers develop HAM/TSP, typically women in midlife. It begins with leg stiffness, back pain, urinary urgency and constipation, progressing over years; sensory loss is mild. Rapid progressors exist. Other associations include uveitis, myositis, Sjögren-like features and severe strongyloidiasis.
det.diagnosis: Requires a compatible myelopathy plus HTLV-1 antibodies in serum and CSF, after excluding other causes. CSF may show mild lymphocytosis, oligoclonal bands and high proviral load; CSF neopterin and CXCL10 indicate activity. MRI often shows thoracic cord atrophy.
det.treatment: There is no antiviral cure. Corticosteroids (pulsed or oral) are used to slow active inflammatory progression; interferon-alpha has some evidence, and mogamulizumab is being studied. Symptomatic care includes baclofen, tizanidine, bladder management and physiotherapy. Prevention involves screening blood donors and advising against breastfeeding by carrier mothers where safe alternatives exist.
det.prognosis: HAM/TSP progresses slowly; many patients need walking aids within a decade.
pearls: Slow spastic paraparesis with bladder symptoms in someone from an endemic area: test HTLV-1.
Screen for strongyloides before steroids.
Breastfeeding is the main mother-to-child route.

det.patho: Herpesviruses reach the cord by different routes: VZV spreads from reactivated dorsal root ganglia, HSV-2 travels along sacral roots, and CMV spreads by blood in severe immunosuppression. det.patho: A pathogenic variant in the X-linked IDS gene removes iduronate-2-sulfatase, so dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate accumulate within lysosomes of many tissues. Storage in the CNS damages neurons, causing cognitive decline, while storage in meninges and arachnoid granulations impairs CSF absorption. Males are affected; rare symptomatic females have been described.
det.clinical: Features appear in early childhood: coarse face, large head, recurrent otitis and airway obstruction, joint stiffness, hernias and organomegaly. Neurological complications include communicating hydrocephalus, cervical stenosis with cord compression, carpal tunnel syndrome and, in the severe form, regression and behavioural problems from about age 2–4. Attenuated patients live to adulthood with relatively preserved intellect.
det.diagnosis: Elevated urinary GAGs prompt measurement of IDS enzyme activity in plasma or leukocytes, with genetic confirmation. Imaging evaluates ventricles, craniocervical junction and spine. Differentiate from other MPS types, mucolipidosis, and oligosaccharidoses by enzyme assays.
det.treatment: Weekly intravenous enzyme replacement with idursulfase improves walking, respiratory function and organ size, but cerebral disease is not reliably reached. Newer brain-penetrant enzymes and gene therapy, and haematopoietic stem cell transplant in selected cases, are being studied. Care also covers shunting for hydrocephalus, surgical decompression for cord compression or carpal tunnel, anaesthesia planning, and hearing and cardiac support.
det.prognosis: The severe form usually leads to death in the teens; attenuated patients can survive into adult life, depending on airway and cardiac disease.
pearls: X-linked MPS with clear corneas distinguishes Hunter from Hurler.
Chronic hydrocephalus and carpal tunnel in a child suggests MPS.

det.patho: A CAG repeat expansion in HTT on chromosome 4 produces huntingtin with a long polyglutamine tract that is toxic to neurons, especially medium spiny neurons of the caudate and putamen. Inheritance is autosomal dominant; 36–39 repeats show reduced penetrance and 40 or more are fully penetrant. Larger repeats give earlier onset, and repeats tend to expand through the father, explaining anticipation and juvenile (Westphal) cases.
det.clinical: Onset is usually in the 30s–50s with a combination of motor, cognitive and psychiatric change, any of which may come first. Early motor signs are fidgety restlessness, slowed saccade initiation and motor impersistence, evolving to chorea, dystonia, dysarthria, dysphagia and gait instability. Psychiatric features include depression, irritability, apathy, obsessive behaviour and a high suicide risk. Cognitive decline affects speed, planning and multitasking before memory. Juvenile HD often presents with rigidity, bradykinesia and seizures rather than chorea.
det.diagnosis: Confirm with genetic testing for HTT CAG repeat length in a symptomatic person; predictive testing of at-risk relatives must follow a formal counselling protocol. MRI shows caudate atrophy with enlarged frontal horns, but this is supportive, not diagnostic. Where testing is negative, consider phenocopies: C9orf72 expansion, HDL2, SCA17, neuroacanthocytosis, Wilson disease, and acquired chorea from drugs, thyroid disease, lupus or polycythaemia.
det.treatment: No therapy slows the disease yet; antisense and other huntingtin-lowering strategies remain under study. Chorea that causes harm or distress can be treated with tetrabenazine or deutetrabenazine/valbenazine (watch for depression) or with antipsychotics, which also help agitation. Treat depression and irritability actively and screen for suicidality. Speech and swallow therapy, nutritional support (high calorie needs), physiotherapy, social care and genetic counselling for the family are essential.
det.prognosis: Death typically occurs 15–20 years after motor onset, usually from aspiration, falls or complications of immobility.
pearls: Motor impersistence — inability to sustain a grip or tongue protrusion — is often more reliable than chorea itself.
Always ask about suicidal thoughts; risk peaks around diagnosis and when independence is lost.
A negative family history does not exclude HD: misattributed paternity, early parental death or intermediate-allele expansion can hide it.
det.thd: Huntington's disease เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมแบบยีนเด่นจากการขยายของ CAG repeat ในยีน HTT ทำให้เซลล์ใน caudate และ putamen ตาย อาการมีสามด้านคือ การเคลื่อนไหวกระตุกแบบ chorea ความผิดปกติทางจิตใจ เช่น ซึมเศร้า หงุดหงิด และความคิดช้าลงจนสมองเสื่อม วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีน (40 repeats ขึ้นไปแสดงโรคแน่นอน) โดยต้องให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม การรักษาเป็นการบรรเทาอาการ เช่น tetrabenazine และดูแลด้านจิตเวชและครอบครัว

name: Huntington’s disease look like-2 disease
formal: Phenocopy of Huntington disease with chorea, psychiatric and cognitive features but a negative huntingtin test; causes include HDL1 to 4 and other genetic disorders.
simple: A condition that looks like Huntington disease but is caused by a different gene or cause.
th: กลุ่มโรคที่อาการเหมือน Huntington (chorea, จิตเวช, สมองเสื่อม) แต่ตรวจยีน HTT ปกติ เช่น HDL1–4, C9orf72, SCA17 และ neuroacanthocytosis
tempoNote: Progressive over years, typically adult onset
feat: Chorea with psychiatric change and cognitive decline resembling Huntington disease
Negative HTT CAG repeat test
Ancestry, onset age and extra features (ataxia, neuropathy, seizures, acanthocytes) give clues
Family history may suggest dominant or recessive inheritance
inv: Genetic testing in tiers: C9orf72, JPH3 (HDL2), TBP (SCA17), PRNP (HDL1), ATXN2/3, DRPLA
Blood film for acanthocytes, CK, ferritin and copper studies
MRI: caudate atrophy, iron deposits or other patterns

case.story: Two years of fidgety movements, irritability and declining work performance; his mother had a 'nervous' illness.
case.exam: Generalised chorea, motor impersistence, mild ataxia, dysexecutive cognition.
case.tests: HTT CAG repeats normal; TBP gene expanded.
case.q: What does a negative HTT test with this picture prompt, and what diagnosis was made here?
case.a: Search for HD phenocopies; here SCA17 (TBP expansion), which often adds ataxia and dementia.

det.patho: Huntington disease phenocopies are a genetically diverse group. The best-defined include C9orf72 expansions (most frequent in Europeans), HDL2 (JPH3, mainly African ancestry), SCA17 (TBP, sometimes called HDL4), HDL1 (PRNP octapeptide insertions) and DRPLA, plus neuroacanthocytosis, brain iron disorders and Wilson disease. A substantial share remain genetically unexplained.
det.clinical: Patients show chorea, psychiatric and cognitive disturbance much like HD, but additional signs (ataxia, seizures, parkinsonism, neuropathy, early dementia) and different inheritance patterns help. Disease course is usually progressive. This name in the lexicon refers to the phenocopy concept rather than a single distinct disease.
det.diagnosis: When HTT testing is negative, review history for drugs and autoimmune or metabolic causes, then pursue tiered genetic tests guided by ancestry and associated features. Blood smear, CK, copper studies and MRI narrow options. Exome or genome sequencing may be needed.
det.treatment: Management mirrors HD: tetrabenazine or deutetrabenazine, or antipsychotics for chorea; treat depression, psychosis and irritability; multidisciplinary rehabilitation and genetic counselling. Treat specific causes when found (e.g., Wilson disease).
det.prognosis: Depends on underlying cause; most genetic forms progress over years.
pearls: Negative HTT test does not end the work-up: think C9orf72, SCA17, HDL2.
Acanthocytes and high CK point toward neuroacanthocytosis.
Always exclude treatable causes such as Wilson disease and autoimmune chorea.
det.thd: Huntington disease phenocopy คือกลุ่มโรคที่อาการเหมือน Huntington ทั้ง chorea อาการทางจิต และสมองเสื่อม แต่ยีน HTT ปกติ สาเหตุได้แก่ C9orf72, SCA17, HDL2, HDL1 และ neuroacanthocytosis การวินิจฉัยใช้ประวัติครอบครัว เชื้อชาติ ลักษณะร่วม และตรวจยีนเป็นขั้น รักษาตามอาการเหมือน Huntington และแก้สาเหตุที่รักษาได้

name: Huntington’s disease-like 2 (HDL2)
formal: Autosomal dominant triplet repeat disorder from a CTG/CAG expansion in JPH3, resembling Huntington disease with chorea, dementia and acanthocytes; almost exclusively in people of African ancestry.
simple: An inherited disease that closely mimics Huntington disease, with movement problems and dementia, mostly seen in people of African descent.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมยีนเด่นจากการขยายของ CTG/CAG ในยีน JPH3 อาการเหมือน Huntington เกือบทั้งหมด พบเกือบเฉพาะในคนเชื้อสายแอฟริกัน
tempoNote: Adult onset (around 40) with progression over 10–20 years
feat: Chorea, dystonia or parkinsonism with progressive dementia
Psychiatric symptoms: depression, apathy, irritability
Acanthocytes in some patients
Dominant family history in people of African ancestry
inv: JPH3 repeat expansion testing after negative HTT
MRI: caudate and cortical atrophy like HD
Blood film for acanthocytes

case.who: 41-year-old South African man working in Bangkok
case.story: Three years of involuntary movements and forgetfulness; father and aunt had similar illness.
case.exam: Chorea, dysarthria, slowed saccades, impaired executive function.
case.tests: HTT normal; JPH3 CTG expansion 48 repeats; MRI caudate atrophy.
case.q: What clue in his background prompted this test?
case.a: African ancestry with an HD-like illness and normal HTT — HDL2 is the main phenocopy in this population.

read.where: Chapter 9 Movement Disorders — Differential Diagnosis of Huntington’s Disease

det.patho: HDL2 results from an expanded CTG/CAG repeat in JPH3, encoding junctophilin-3. Pathogenic alleles are about 40 or more repeats. Toxicity likely involves RNA foci and polyglutamine-containing protein from the antisense strand, giving intranuclear inclusions similar to HD. The expansion traces to an African founder.
det.clinical: Onset is typically in the fourth decade with chorea, dystonia or parkinsonism (rigidity increases as disease advances), psychiatric change and dementia. It is essentially indistinguishable from HD at the bedside. Seizures are uncommon. Juvenile forms are rare.
det.diagnosis: Test for JPH3 expansion in patients of African ancestry with an HD-like syndrome and negative HTT. MRI shows caudate and cortical atrophy. Acanthocytes may be present in a minority.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy. Chorea and psychiatric symptoms are managed as in HD (VMAT2 inhibitors, antipsychotics, antidepressants). Provide genetic counselling, rehabilitation and long-term care planning.
det.prognosis: Progressive with death about 10–20 years after onset.
pearls: HD picture + African ancestry + negative HTT = test JPH3.
Parkinsonism tends to dominate later stages.
Acanthocytes do not exclude HDL2.
det.thd: HDL2 เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมยีนเด่นจากการขยายของ repeat ในยีน JPH3 พบเกือบเฉพาะคนเชื้อสายแอฟริกัน อาการเหมือน Huntington คือ chorea อาการทางจิต และสมองเสื่อมที่ค่อย ๆ แย่ลง วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีน JPH3 หลังตรวจ HTT ปกติ รักษาตามอาการและให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

Recessive, with lip biting, neuropathy, seizures and high CK

name: Hurler-Scheie syndrome
formal: Intermediate form of mucopolysaccharidosis I from alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency, with corneal clouding, joint stiffness, valvular disease and carpal tunnel syndrome, but milder or absent intellectual impairment.
simple: An inherited enzyme disorder that causes joint stiffness, cloudy eyes and heart problems, milder than the severe infant form.
th: mucopolysaccharidosis type I ชนิดกลาง จากขาดเอนไซม์ alpha-L-iduronidase ทำให้กระจกตาขุ่น ข้อติด ลิ้นหัวใจผิดปกติ และ carpal tunnel
tempoNote: Onset in childhood; progressive over decades
feat: Coarse facial features, short stature and joint stiffness
Corneal clouding and hearing loss
Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome in childhood
Cervical cord compression from dural thickening and odontoid dysplasia
Intelligence normal or mildly impaired; cardiac valve disease
inv: Urine glycosaminoglycans raised (dermatan and heparan sulphate)
Alpha-L-iduronidase enzyme assay low; IDUA gene testing
MRI cervical spine and nerve conduction for neurological complications

case.story: Stiff fingers that cannot fully straighten, hand numbness at night, cloudy eyes and short stature.
case.exam: Claw hands, positive Tinel at wrists, corneal clouding, mild hepatomegaly, normal cognition.
case.tests: Urine GAGs high; IDUA activity low; NCS shows bilateral severe median slowing at wrist.
case.q: Which neurological complications need surveillance?
case.a: Carpal tunnel syndrome and cervical cord compression; also hydrocephalus and hearing loss.

det.patho: Deficiency of alpha-L-iduronidase leads to lysosomal accumulation of dermatan and heparan sulphate in connective tissue, cornea, heart valves, ligaments and meninges. Thickened flexor retinaculum and dura explain entrapment and cord compression.
det.clinical: Hurler-Scheie lies between severe Hurler (with intellectual disability) and mild Scheie. Patients have skeletal dysplasia, joint contractures, corneal clouding, cardiac valve disease and airway problems. Neurological issues include carpal tunnel syndrome, cervical myelopathy and communicating hydrocephalus.
det.diagnosis: Urinary GAGs, enzyme activity in leucocytes or dried blood spots and IDUA sequencing confirm the diagnosis. Newborn screening for MPS I is expanding. Children with carpal tunnel should be screened for MPS.
det.treatment: Enzyme replacement therapy with laronidase improves somatic features but not the central nervous system. Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is preferred in severe Hurler before age 2. Carpal tunnel release and cervical decompression as needed; cardiology and airway management.
det.prognosis: Survival into adulthood is common; morbidity from cardiopulmonary and skeletal complications.
pearls: Carpal tunnel in a child is MPS until proven otherwise.
Corneal clouding separates MPS I from MPS II.
Anaesthesia is high-risk because of airway narrowing.
det.thd: Hurler-Scheie เป็น MPS I ชนิดกลาง จากขาดเอนไซม์ alpha-L-iduronidase ทำให้ GAGs สะสม ผู้ป่วยตัวเตี้ย ข้อติด กระจกตาขุ่น ลิ้นหัวใจผิดปกติ ทางระบบประสาทพบ carpal tunnel ตั้งแต่เด็กและไขสันหลังส่วนคอถูกกด สติปัญญามักปกติ วินิจฉัยด้วย urine GAGs และวัดเอนไซม์ รักษาด้วย enzyme replacement และผ่าตัดตามภาวะแทรกซ้อน

name: Hydrocephalic parkinsonism
formal: Gait disorder with bradykinesia and rigidity predominantly in the legs in patients with hydrocephalus, due to ventricular enlargement compressing frontal-subcortical pathways; may improve after shunting.
simple: Slow, shuffling walking and stiffness caused by fluid build-up in the brain, which can improve after the fluid is drained.
th: parkinsonism ที่เกิดจากโพรงสมองขยาย เด่นที่ขา เดินช้าก้าวสั้น อาจดีขึ้นหลังทำ shunt
tempoNote: Gradual in normal pressure hydrocephalus; subacute in obstructive hydrocephalus or shunt failure
feat: Lower-body predominant slowness with short, shuffling, broad-based steps and freezing
Upper limbs relatively spared; arm swing often preserved
Rest tremor uncommon; poor or absent levodopa response
May accompany urinary urgency and cognitive slowing (NPH triad)
Can appear after shunt malfunction with upgaze palsy in obstructive cases
inv: MRI: ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy, high Evans index, DESH, narrow callosal angle
CSF tap test or lumbar drainage with timed gait assessment
DAT-SPECT usually normal or mildly reduced

case.story: One year of slow shuffling walk and a few falls; recently needs to rush to the toilet. Levodopa trial gave no benefit.
case.exam: Broad-based magnetic gait with start hesitation, normal arm swing, mild bradykinesia of legs only, MoCA 22.
case.tests: MRI: enlarged ventricles with narrow callosal angle and tight high-convexity sulci; gait speed improves after 40 mL tap.
case.q: What treatment is suggested by the tap test?
case.a: Ventriculoperitoneal shunt for idiopathic NPH, which may improve the parkinsonian gait.

det.patho: Enlarged ventricles stretch and compress periventricular fibres linking frontal cortex, basal ganglia and brainstem locomotor centres, and may reduce striatal blood flow. The nigrostriatal dopamine system is usually intact, explaining poor levodopa response. Causes include idiopathic NPH, obstructive hydrocephalus (e.g., aqueductal stenosis) and shunt failure.
det.clinical: The gait is slow, wide-based and shuffling with freezing and postural instability, while the arms move fairly normally. Urinary urgency and executive slowing are common companions. In obstructive hydrocephalus or shunt failure, onset may be subacute with headache, upgaze palsy and decreased alertness, sometimes with an acute akinetic-rigid state.
det.diagnosis: MRI or CT shows ventriculomegaly with features favouring NPH. Supplementary tests (CSF tap or extended lumbar drainage) predict shunt response. DAT imaging is usually normal or only mildly abnormal, helping separate it from degenerative parkinsonism. Shunt series and CT are needed when shunt failure is suspected.
det.treatment: CSF diversion (VP shunt or endoscopic third ventriculostomy in obstructive hydrocephalus) is the definitive treatment. Levodopa can be tried but rarely helps; it may help after shunt revision in acute cases. Physiotherapy and fall prevention are important.
det.prognosis: Gait often improves after shunting in well-selected patients; longstanding disease or comorbid vascular change limits benefit.
pearls: Lower-body parkinsonism with preserved arm swing and no levodopa response: image the ventricles.
Acute parkinsonism in a shunted patient may signal shunt failure.
A positive tap test supports shunting but a negative one does not exclude benefit.
det.thd: Hydrocephalic parkinsonism คือ parkinsonism ที่เกิดจากโพรงสมองขยาย เช่น NPH หรือ shunt อุดตัน ผู้ป่วยเดินช้า ก้าวสั้น ขากว้าง ติดขัดตอนเริ่มเดิน แต่แขนแกว่งปกติ ตอบสนอง levodopa น้อย MRI พบโพรงสมองโตไม่สัมพันธ์กับสมองฝ่อ และอาการดีขึ้นหลังเจาะระบายน้ำไขสันหลัง รักษาด้วยการทำ shunt

ddx.pt: Lower-body parkinsonism with extensive white-matter infarcts rather than disproportionate ventricles
Vertical gaze palsy, early falls and midbrain atrophy
The commonest underlying cause; same work-up

name: Hydrocephalus
formal: Excess CSF within the ventricles from obstructed flow, impaired absorption or rarely overproduction, producing raised pressure, headache, vomiting and papilloedema, or gait and cognitive decline in normal pressure form.
simple: A build-up of fluid inside the brain that raises pressure and can cause headache, vomiting and problems with walking or thinking.
ab: น้ำคั่งในโพรงสมอง
th: น้ำไขสันหลังคั่งในโพรงสมองจากการอุดตันทางไหลหรือการดูดซึมบกพร่อง แบบเฉียบพลันมีปวดศีรษะ อาเจียน ซึม ตาเหลือกลงไม่ขึ้น อาจถึงชีวิต แบบเรื้อรังมีเดินลำบาก ความจำเสื่อม รักษาด้วยระบายน้ำ shunt หรือ ETV
tempoNote: Acute (hours–days) with obstruction or haemorrhage; subacute with meningitis; chronic over months in normal-pressure or slowly compensated forms
feat: Acute raised pressure: headache worse lying or on waking, vomiting, drowsiness, papilloedema, sixth nerve palsy
Dorsal midbrain signs: impaired upgaze, light–near dissociation, lid retraction (setting-sun eyes in infants)
Infants: enlarging head circumference, bulging fontanelle, split sutures
Causes: posterior fossa or third-ventricle tumours, colloid cyst, aqueductal stenosis, SAH, IVH, bacterial/TB/cryptococcal meningitis, neurocysticercosis
Shunted patients: any headache, drowsiness or vomiting is shunt failure until proven otherwise
inv: Urgent CT: enlarged ventricles (temporal horns, rounded third ventricle), periventricular lucency from transependymal flow
MRI with CSF flow or thin T2 sequences to locate the obstruction (aqueduct, fourth ventricle outlets)
LP is dangerous in obstructive hydrocephalus with a mass; in communicating forms CSF studies identify infection or blood
Shunt series X-ray and comparison with previous scans for suspected malfunction

case.who: 24-year-old male construction worker from Nakhon Ratchasima
case.story: Three weeks of fever and headache treated with antibiotics at a district hospital; now vomiting and drowsy.
case.exam: GCS 12, neck stiffness, bilateral sixth nerve palsies, blurred disc margins.
case.tests: CT: dilated lateral and third ventricles with periventricular lucency and basal meningeal enhancement. CSF via EVD: lymphocytes 220, protein 2.4 g/L, glucose ratio 0.25; Xpert MTB/RIF positive.
case.q: Why has he deteriorated and what are the immediate steps?
case.a: Communicating hydrocephalus from tuberculous meningitis; urgent CSF diversion (external ventricular drain, then shunt if persistent) plus anti-TB therapy with dexamethasone.

read.where: Chapter 28 Disorders of Consciousness and Intensive Care Neurology
18. Disorders of Cranial Volume and Shape

det.patho: CSF is mainly made by the choroid plexus at around 500 mL per day and absorbed through arachnoid granulations and perivascular/lymphatic routes. Obstruction within the ventricular system (aqueduct, foramina of Monro, fourth-ventricle outlets) causes non-communicating hydrocephalus; scarring of the basal cisterns or granulations after haemorrhage or meningitis causes communicating hydrocephalus. Overproduction from choroid plexus papilloma is rare. Rising ventricular pressure stretches periventricular white matter and, in the acute setting, compresses the brainstem.
det.clinical: Acute hydrocephalus produces headache, vomiting, declining consciousness, sixth nerve palsy and Parinaud features and can progress quickly to herniation. In infants, head growth crosses centiles and the fontanelle bulges. Chronic or compensated forms present with gait disturbance, cognitive slowing, urinary symptoms and visual loss from chronic papilloedema. In Thailand, tuberculous and cryptococcal meningitis and neurocysticercosis are important acquired causes, along with SAH and tumours.
det.diagnosis: CT or MRI confirms enlarged ventricles; signs of active hydrocephalus include dilated temporal horns, a ballooned third ventricle, effaced sulci and periventricular oedema, unlike atrophy where sulci are wide. MRI identifies the level of block and the cause. Evans' index above 0.3 indicates ventriculomegaly but is non-specific. Fundoscopy and, in shunted patients, comparison with baseline scans are essential since ventricles may not enlarge in some shunt failures.
det.treatment: Acute symptomatic hydrocephalus needs urgent neurosurgical CSF diversion — an external ventricular drain, then a permanent ventriculoperitoneal (or ventriculoatrial) shunt if needed. Endoscopic third ventriculostomy avoids hardware in obstructive forms such as aqueductal stenosis or posterior fossa tumours. Treat the cause (tumour resection, meningitis therapy). Acetazolamide is only a temporising option in selected cases. Shunts can block, become infected, disconnect or over-drain (causing low-pressure headache or subdural collections), so patients and families need clear warning signs.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause and speed of treatment; promptly treated acute hydrocephalus can recover fully, while delayed treatment risks blindness, cognitive damage or death.
pearls: Never do an LP before imaging when hydrocephalus or mass effect is possible.
Upgaze palsy and drowsiness in a patient with meningitis or SAH — scan for hydrocephalus.
In a shunted patient, unexplained headache or vomiting is shunt malfunction until excluded.
det.thd: Hydrocephalus คือภาวะน้ำไขสันหลังคั่งในโพรงสมอง จากการอุดตันทางไหล (เช่น เนื้องอก aqueductal stenosis) หรือการดูดซึมผิดปกติหลังเลือดออกหรือเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ เช่น วัณโรค แบบเฉียบพลันมีปวดศีรษะ อาเจียน ซึม ตาเหลือกขึ้นไม่ได้ เส้นประสาทคู่ที่ 6 อ่อนแรง ต้องรีบระบายน้ำด้วย EVD ตามด้วย VP shunt หรือ ETV ผู้ป่วยที่มี shunt แล้วปวดศีรษะอาเจียนต้องนึกถึง shunt อุดตันก่อนเสมอ ห้ามเจาะหลังก่อนทำภาพถ่ายสมอง

name: Hydrogen sulphide poisoning
formal: Toxic gas exposure inhibiting cytochrome oxidase, causing rapid loss of consciousness, seizures, respiratory failure and, in survivors, basal ganglia damage and parkinsonism or cognitive sequelae.
simple: Poisoning by a rotten-egg smelling gas that can cause sudden collapse, seizures and lasting brain damage.
th: พิษจากก๊าซไข่เน่าซึ่งยับยั้ง cytochrome oxidase ทำให้หมดสติเฉียบพลัน ชัก หยุดหายใจ และผู้รอดชีวิตอาจมีความเสียหายที่ basal ganglia เกิด parkinsonism หรือปัญหาความคิด
tempoNote: Collapse within seconds at high concentrations; sequelae may become evident days to weeks later
feat: Exposure in sewers, septic tanks, wells, fish holds, farm manure pits, oil and gas or tannery work
Rotten-egg smell at low levels; olfactory paralysis at high levels so the smell disappears
'Knockdown': abrupt collapse, seizures, apnoea; multiple victims including rescuers
Eye and airway irritation, pulmonary oedema, arrhythmias, lactic acidosis
Survivors: memory and executive deficits, parkinsonism, dystonia, ataxia
inv: Clinical diagnosis from scene history; arterial blood gas with lactate, ECG, troponin, chest X-ray
Exclude co-exposure: carboxyhaemoglobin, cyanide, methaemoglobin
MRI in survivors: basal ganglia and cortical lesions similar to hypoxic injury

case.who: Two workers, aged 35 and 41, from Samut Sakhon
case.story: One collapsed while cleaning a fish-sauce fermentation tank; the second collapsed trying to pull him out. Both were rescued by firemen with breathing apparatus.
case.exam: One is comatose with seizures; the other is drowsy with red eyes and cough.
case.tests: Lactate 12 mmol/L; carboxyhaemoglobin normal. Months later the first worker has bradykinesia and poor memory; MRI shows bilateral globus pallidus lesions.
case.q: What toxic exposure explains this and why did the rescuer collapse?
case.a: Hydrogen sulphide; it is heavy and accumulates in confined spaces, and high concentrations paralyse smell and cause rapid unconsciousness, so untrained rescuers become victims.

det.patho: Hydrogen sulphide reversibly inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase, blocking oxidative phosphorylation much like cyanide, and it also irritates mucosa and lungs. Neurons in the brainstem respiratory centres fail quickly, causing apnoea. Survivors show injury in metabolically active areas — basal ganglia, cortex, hippocampus — from combined direct toxicity and hypoxia.
det.clinical: Low concentrations cause eye irritation, headache, nausea and cough; higher levels cause olfactory fatigue then collapse, seizures and respiratory arrest within breaths. Clusters with would-be rescuers are typical. Long-term effects include memory impairment, personality change, parkinsonism, dystonia and neuropathy-like complaints.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, built on the setting, odour reports and multiple casualties. Blood sulphide or urinary thiosulphate levels are not available in time and are rarely needed. Work-up looks for complications (acidosis, pulmonary oedema, myocardial injury) and co-exposures. Later MRI and neuropsychology document sequelae.
det.treatment: Rescue only with self-contained breathing apparatus; remove the victim to fresh air, give 100% oxygen and supportive ICU care including seizure control. Nitrite therapy (to form sulphmethaemoglobin) has been used but evidence is limited and it may worsen hypotension; hydroxocobalamin is being studied. Hyperbaric oxygen is unproven. Long-term rehabilitation and occupational safety measures follow.
det.prognosis: Patients who recover quickly after short exposure usually do well; prolonged unconsciousness predicts persistent cognitive and movement sequelae.
pearls: Several people collapsing in a confined space = think H2S until proved otherwise.
Loss of the rotten-egg smell means a dangerous concentration, not safety.
Survivors can develop delayed parkinsonism from pallidal injury.
det.thd: พิษก๊าซไข่เน่า (H2S) พบในงานลอกท่อ ถังหมักปลา บ่อน้ำเสีย และฟาร์ม ก๊าซยับยั้ง cytochrome oxidase ทำให้หมดสติ ชัก และหยุดหายใจภายในไม่กี่วินาที ผู้ช่วยเหลือที่ไม่มีเครื่องช่วยหายใจมักหมดสติตาม รักษาด้วยนำออกสู่อากาศบริสุทธิ์ ให้ออกซิเจน และดูแลแบบประคับประคอง ผู้รอดชีวิตอาจมีความจำเสื่อมหรือ parkinsonism จากรอยโรคที่ basal ganglia

name: Hyperacute stroke
formal: Earliest phase of ischaemic stroke, within roughly six hours of onset, when thrombolysis or thrombectomy can salvage penumbra; imaging may show early ischaemic change or a hyperdense vessel.
simple: The very first hours after a stroke begins, when urgent treatment can save the most brain tissue.
ab: Acute ischaemic stroke in the treatment window
th: ระยะแรกสุดของ ischaemic stroke ภายในประมาณ 6 ชั่วโมง (หรือนานกว่าในบางราย) ที่ยังให้ยาละลายลิ่มเลือดหรือทำ thrombectomy เพื่อรักษา penumbra ได้
tempoNote: Minutes to hours from onset; every minute of delay loses brain tissue
feat: Sudden focal deficit with known last-known-well time
Window for IV thrombolysis generally up to 4.5 hours; beyond with advanced imaging selection
Mechanical clot retrieval for LVO, in selected patients out to a day from onset
Early CT may be normal or show subtle loss of grey-white differentiation and hyperdense artery
Stroke mimics: hypoglycaemia, seizure with Todd paresis, migraine aura, functional
inv: Capillary glucose immediately
Non-contrast CT plus CTA (and CT perfusion when relevant)
Do not delay treatment for most blood tests unless anticoagulant use or bleeding disorder suspected

case.who: 65-year-old woman from Nakhon Pathom who collapsed at the market at 09:10
case.story: Arrived at a stroke centre at 10:00 with right weakness and inability to speak.
case.exam: NIHSS 18: global aphasia, right hemiplegia, left gaze deviation; glucose 118 mg/dL.
case.tests: CT ASPECTS 9; CTA left M1 occlusion.
case.q: What treatments are indicated?
case.a: IV thrombolysis (alteplase or tenecteplase) followed by mechanical thrombectomy without delay.

det.patho: Arterial occlusion produces an ischaemic core that is irreversibly damaged and a surrounding penumbra that is dysfunctional but salvageable if flow returns. Penumbra survival depends on collateral circulation and time; with poor collaterals core grows quickly.
det.clinical: The hyperacute phase is defined by treatment opportunity rather than symptoms. Recognition by the public (FAST or BE-FAST campaigns) and pre-hospital notification shorten delays. Wake-up and unknown-onset strokes can still be treated if imaging suggests tissue is salvageable.
det.diagnosis: Rapid clinical assessment with NIHSS, glucose check and immediate brain imaging. CTA identifies large-vessel occlusion; perfusion or MRI DWI-FLAIR mismatch selects patients outside standard windows. Stroke mimics are common but thrombolysis of mimics carries low risk.
det.treatment: IV thrombolysis with alteplase or tenecteplase within 4.5 hours in eligible patients, and in selected later or unknown-onset cases with imaging evidence. Mechanical thrombectomy for anterior circulation LVO up to 24 hours with imaging selection, including large-core patients per recent trials, and for basilar occlusion. BP must be below 185/110 before thrombolysis. Stroke unit care follows.
det.prognosis: Outcomes depend on time to reperfusion; earlier treatment yields more patients free of disability.
pearls: Time is brain: aim for door-to-needle under 60 minutes, ideally under 30.
Check glucose before calling it a stroke.
Do not wait for blood tests unless anticoagulation or coagulopathy is suspected.
det.thd: Hyperacute stroke คือระยะแรกสุดของสมองขาดเลือดที่ยังสามารถเปิดหลอดเลือดได้ ด้วยยาละลายลิ่มเลือดภายใน 4.5 ชั่วโมง และ thrombectomy ในรายที่หลอดเลือดใหญ่อุดตันจนถึง 24 ชั่วโมงในผู้ป่วยที่คัดเลือก ต้องตรวจน้ำตาลและทำ CT ทันที การรักษาเร็วช่วยรักษาเนื้อสมองส่วน penumbra และลดความพิการ

name: Hyperekplexias
formal: Startle disorders, usually hereditary from glycine receptor or transporter mutations, with exaggerated startle, stiffening and falls to unexpected stimuli, and neonatal stiffness; treated with clonazepam.
simple: Conditions in which a sudden noise or touch causes an exaggerated startle and stiffening, sometimes with falls.
th: Hyperekplexia คือกลุ่มโรคที่มีการสะดุ้งตกใจ (startle) มากเกินไปและไม่ชินต่อสิ่งกระตุ้นซ้ำ ตามด้วยการเกร็งทั้งตัวจนล้มโดยไม่มีการป้องกันตัว ทารกแรกเกิดตัวแข็ง (stiff baby) ชนิดพันธุกรรมพบจากยีน GLRA1, GLRB และ SLC6A5 ที่เกี่ยวกับ glycine ตอบสนองดีต่อ clonazepam ส่วนชนิด symptomatic เกิดหลังรอยโรคที่ก้านสมอง
tempoNote: Hereditary forms are present from birth with neonatal stiffness; attacks are episodic and triggered by unexpected stimuli, and the startle persists through life; symptomatic forms follow brainstem injury
feat: Startle that is larger than normal and does not habituate with repetition, in response to unexpected noise, touch or visual stimuli
A major form with prolonged tonic stiffening and falls without protective reflexes (like a falling tree), and a minor form with a simple brief startle jerk
Neonatal hypertonia relieved by sleep, with risk of apnoea; Vigevano manoeuvre (forced flexion of head and legs towards the trunk) can terminate attacks in infants
Hereditary forms: GLRA1 (autosomal dominant or recessive), GLRB and SLC6A5 (glycine transporter 2); a nose-tap test gives a head-retraction response
Symptomatic startle syndromes result from brainstem stroke, encephalitis, hypoxia, multiple sclerosis, stiff-person spectrum or paraneoplastic disease, and may include startle epilepsy
inv: Clinical test: tapping the nose or glabella elicits exaggerated, non-habituating head retraction and a startle response
Genetic testing for GLRA1, GLRB, SLC6A5 and associated genes (GPHN, ARHGEF9); MRI brainstem for symptomatic causes
EMG startle studies and video-EEG to exclude startle-induced epileptic seizures; consider anti-glycine receptor antibodies in adults with PERM

case.story: Since childhood she falls rigidly when someone surprises her, and has bruises on her face from falling; her son was a stiff baby and had apnoeic episodes.
case.exam: Brisk, non-habituating response to nose tapping, mild stiffness; otherwise normal.
case.tests: EEG normal; heterozygous GLRA1 variant in both mother and son.
case.q: Which medicine usually helps and why?
case.a: Clonazepam; by enhancing GABA-A inhibition it compensates for the deficient glycinergic inhibition.

det.patho: Hyperekplexia is a disorder of brainstem startle circuitry in which glycinergic inhibition is deficient. Pathogenic variants in the alpha-1 (GLRA1) or beta (GLRB) subunits of the postsynaptic glycine receptor, the presynaptic glycine transporter 2 (SLC6A5) or the gephyrin gene reduce inhibition of motor neurons in the pontomedullary reticular formation, so a normal startle reflex becomes exaggerated and fails to habituate. Symptomatic cases involve lesions of the same circuits.
det.clinical: Affected infants are hypertonic and startle to handling, with attacks of stiffness that can stop breathing, so neonatal apnoea is a risk and is part of the reason for early recognition. In later life the startle response persists, and patients fall rigidly. Gait is cautious and daytime anxiety about falls limits activity. A mild exaggerated startle in anxious individuals or in culture-specific startle syndromes (for example the jumping Frenchmen of Maine) must be distinguished from true hyperekplexia. Neonatal symptoms may be mistaken for epilepsy.
det.diagnosis: The nose-tap response and the history of neonatal stiffness suggest the diagnosis, which is confirmed by finding variants in GLRA1, GLRB or SLC6A5. EMG recordings show short latency, non-habituating responses spreading up and down the brainstem and spinal cord. Exclude epilepsy with video-EEG and symptomatic causes with MRI of the brainstem and autoimmune and paraneoplastic testing in adults. Evaluation of a sleep-related movement disorder may be needed.
det.treatment: Teach parents and caregivers the Vigevano manoeuvre for infants and to place infants on their back safely. Clonazepam (low starting dose, titrated carefully) is first-line and can be life-changing, with valproate, levetiracetam, piracetam or phenobarbital as alternatives. Protective measures include helmets in adults who fall. Treat symptomatic causes and use immunotherapy when autoimmune.
det.prognosis: Hereditary hyperekplexia has an excellent outlook if apnoea is avoided in infancy; startle persists lifelong but is controlled by clonazepam, and falls are the main hazard.
pearls: A stiff baby who stiffens with nose tapping needs GLRA1 testing.
Teach the family the Vigevano manoeuvre; it can stop an apnoeic attack.
Clonazepam is the first-line drug; avoid misdiagnosing as epilepsy.
det.thd: Hyperekplexia คือภาวะที่สะดุ้งตกใจเกินปกติและไม่ชินต่อสิ่งกระตุ้นซ้ำ แล้วเกร็งทั้งตัวล้มลงโดยไม่มีการป้องกัน ชนิดพันธุกรรมเกิดจากยีนของระบบ glycine เช่น GLRA1, GLRB และ SLC6A5 ทารกอาจตัวแข็งและหยุดหายใจ ซึ่งแก้ได้ด้วย Vigevano manoeuvre การเคาะที่จมูกแล้วหัวสะดุ้งถอยเป็นการตรวจที่ช่วยวินิจฉัย การรักษาหลักคือ clonazepam และต้องแยกจากโรคลมชักและโรค stiff-person

name: Hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES)
formal: Persistent eosinophilia with end-organ damage, which can cause neuropathy, mononeuritis, myopathy, encephalopathy and cardiac thrombosis.
simple: A condition where very high levels of one type of white blood cell damage organs such as nerves and heart.
more: Diagnosed by sustained eosinophil count over 1500 with organ involvement after excluding other causes; treated with steroids, hydroxyurea or imatinib or mepolizumab.
th: eosinophil สูงต่อเนื่องร่วมกับอวัยวะเสียหาย ทางระบบประสาททำให้เกิด neuropathy, mononeuritis, สมองขาดเลือดจากลิ่มเลือดหัวใจ และ encephalopathy
tempoNote: Weeks to months of eosinophilia; strokes can be sudden
feat: Eosinophil count above 1.5 × 10⁹/L on two occasions with organ damage
Sensory or sensorimotor neuropathy, sometimes mononeuritis multiplex
Embolic strokes from endomyocardial fibrosis and ventricular thrombus
Watershed infarcts and encephalopathy
Cardiac, skin and lung involvement
inv: FBC with eosinophil count; peripheral smear
Echocardiogram or cardiac MRI for endomyocardial disease
MRI brain for border-zone infarcts; NCS/EMG for neuropathy
Bone marrow, FIP1L1-PDGFRA, T-cell clonality; stool for parasites

case.story: Weeks of fatigue, cough and burning feet, then sudden confusion and right hand weakness.
case.exam: Mild right hand weakness, distal sensory loss in feet, skin rash.
case.tests: Eosinophils 9.8 × 10⁹/L; MRI shows multiple small bilateral border-zone infarcts; echo shows apical LV thrombus; strongyloides negative.
case.q: What mechanism explains the strokes?
case.a: Cardioembolism from eosinophilic endomyocardial disease plus local vascular injury.

read.where: Section 6 Systemic Disorders That Also Involve the Cerebrovascular System

det.patho: Eosinophils release cytotoxic granule proteins causing endothelial and tissue damage. HES can be primary (clonal myeloid neoplasm, e.g. FIP1L1-PDGFRA), secondary (reactive to parasites, drugs, T-cell lymphoma) or idiopathic. Cardiac thrombi cause embolic strokes.
det.clinical: Neurological complications include stroke (embolic and border-zone), encephalopathy and peripheral neuropathy. Systemic disease affects heart, lungs, skin and gut. In Thailand, parasitic infection (Strongyloides) must be excluded before steroids.
det.diagnosis: Requires persistent hypereosinophilia and organ damage with exclusion of secondary causes. Work-up includes parasites, drugs, haematological studies and cardiac imaging.
det.treatment: Corticosteroids are first-line for idiopathic HES (after empirical ivermectin when Strongyloides risk exists). Imatinib for PDGFRA-rearranged disease; mepolizumab is approved for HES. Anticoagulation for cardiac thrombi.
det.prognosis: Improved with targeted therapy; cardiac involvement drives mortality.
pearls: Treat or exclude Strongyloides before giving steroids for eosinophilia.
Bilateral border-zone infarcts with eosinophilia suggest HES.
PDGFRA-rearranged HES responds dramatically to imatinib.
det.thd: HES คือ eosinophil สูงต่อเนื่องและทำลายอวัยวะ ทางระบบประสาทเกิดเส้นประสาทเสื่อม สมองขาดเลือดจากลิ่มเลือดในหัวใจ และสับสน ต้องหาสาเหตุ เช่น พยาธิ ยา และโรคเลือด ก่อนให้ steroid ควรรักษาหรือแยก Strongyloides รักษาด้วย steroid imatinib หรือ mepolizumab ตามชนิด

name: Hyperferritinemia-cataract syndrome (OMIM 600886)
formal: Autosomal dominant disorder from mutations in the iron-responsive element of the L-ferritin gene, causing high serum ferritin without iron overload and early bilateral cataracts.
simple: An inherited condition with very high blood ferritin without too much iron and cataracts at a young age.
more: Distinguished from iron overload by normal transferrin saturation; genetic test confirms. Treat cataracts surgically; venesection is not helpful and can cause anaemia.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมยีนเด่นของยีน L-ferritin ทำให้ ferritin ในเลือดสูงโดยไม่มีเหล็กเกิน และต้อกระจกตั้งแต่อายุน้อย ไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาท
tempoNote: Lifelong; cataracts appear in childhood or early adulthood
feat: Persistently high serum ferritin with normal transferrin saturation
Bilateral early-onset cataracts with a distinctive 'sunflower' or breadcrumb pattern
No iron overload, no neurological disease
Dominant family history of cataract and high ferritin
inv: Ferritin, transferrin saturation, liver iron (MRI if needed)
FTL gene IRE sequencing
Slit-lamp eye examination of patient and relatives

case.story: Referred for 'iron overload' after ferritin 1,400 µg/L on a check-up; he had cataract surgery at 25.
case.exam: Well, no liver enlargement or skin pigmentation; neurological exam normal.
case.tests: Transferrin saturation 25%; MRI liver iron normal; FTL IRE variant.
case.q: Why should venesection be avoided?
case.a: There is no iron overload; venesection would only cause iron-deficiency anaemia while ferritin stays high.

det.patho: Point mutations or deletions in the iron-responsive element of the FTL 5'-UTR stop iron regulatory proteins from repressing translation, so L-ferritin is produced constitutively regardless of iron stores. Excess ferritin crystallises in the lens, causing cataracts. Body iron metabolism is otherwise normal.
det.clinical: Patients are usually healthy apart from early bilateral cataracts and a high ferritin found incidentally. This is not a neurological disorder; it is included in the lexicon because it is a differential of high ferritin and of FTL-related disease. Misdiagnosis as haemochromatosis is the main hazard.
det.diagnosis: High ferritin with normal transferrin saturation and no tissue iron overload should prompt this diagnosis, particularly with family cataracts. Confirm by FTL IRE sequencing. Exclude inflammation, liver disease and metabolic syndrome as causes of hyperferritinaemia.
det.treatment: Cataract surgery as needed. No iron-lowering therapy is indicated, and venesection is harmful. Offer family screening and counselling.
det.prognosis: Normal life expectancy; visual outcome is good after cataract surgery.
pearls: High ferritin + normal transferrin saturation + young cataracts = HHCS.
Do not bleed these patients.
Different FTL mutation causes neuroferritinopathy — do not confuse the two.
det.thd: Hyperferritinemia-cataract syndrome เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมยีนเด่นของยีน L-ferritin ส่วนควบคุมเหล็ก ทำให้ร่างกายสร้าง ferritin มากเกินโดยไม่มีเหล็กเกิน ผู้ป่วยมี ferritin สูงแต่ transferrin saturation ปกติ และต้อกระจกตั้งแต่อายุน้อย ไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาท วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีน ไม่ควรเจาะเลือดออกเพื่อลดเหล็ก

name: Hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis (hyperPP)
formal: Autosomal dominant sodium or calcium channel muscle disease with episodes of flaccid weakness during raised serum potassium, often triggered by rest after exercise or potassium intake, with myotonia.
simple: An inherited condition causing attacks of muscle weakness when blood potassium rises, often after rest following exercise.
th: อ่อนแรงเป็นพัก ๆ สั้น ๆ เริ่มในวัยเด็ก กระตุ้นด้วยการพักหลังออกกำลังหรือกินอาหารโพแทสเซียมสูง — โรค SCN4A
tempoNote: Attacks last minutes to a few hours, often daily; onset in first decade
feat: Brief attacks of flaccid limb weakness, frequently in the morning or during rest after exercise
Provoked by potassium-rich food, fasting, cold, stress; eased by mild exercise or carbohydrate
Serum potassium high or high-normal in attacks (can be normal)
Mild myotonia or paramyotonia (eyelid lag), and later a fixed proximal myopathy in some
inv: Potassium during an attack; ECG
Long exercise test: post-exercise fall in CMAP amplitude; EMG may show myotonia
SCN4A genetic testing; exclude secondary hyperkalaemia (renal, adrenal, drugs)

case.story: Several times a week, after resting following football, his legs go weak for 30–60 minutes; eating bananas seems to bring attacks on. His father had similar episodes as a child.
case.exam: Between attacks strength is normal; lid lag after looking down; mild grip myotonia.
case.tests: K 5.6 mmol/L during an attack; long exercise test shows a 45% CMAP decline; SCN4A variant confirmed.
case.q: What are the first-line measures?
case.a: Frequent carbohydrate-rich low-potassium meals, avoiding fasting and cold, mild exercise at onset, inhaled salbutamol to abort attacks, and a thiazide or acetazolamide for prevention.

read.where: 37: Approach to Electrodiagnostic Studies in the Intensive Care Unit

det.patho: Gain-of-function mutations in SCN4A, the skeletal-muscle sodium channel, impair inactivation so that a modest rise in extracellular potassium leaves the membrane persistently depolarised and inexcitable. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with high penetrance. The same gene causes paramyotonia congenita and some potassium-aggravated myotonias, and phenotypes overlap.
det.clinical: Attacks begin in infancy or childhood and are typically short and frequent. Weakness affects limbs more than face, rarely the respiratory muscles. Rest after exercise, fasting, cold, potassium intake and anaesthesia provoke attacks, while light activity can abort them. Myotonia, paramyotonia of the eyelids, and a slowly progressive fixed proximal weakness in middle age may accompany the disorder.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the clinical pattern, potassium during attacks (raised in many but not all), exclusion of secondary hyperkalaemia, and genetic confirmation of SCN4A. The long exercise test (prolonged exercise then serial CMAPs) shows a delayed decrement; EMG often reveals myotonic discharges between attacks. Provocative potassium loading is no longer recommended outside specialist settings.
det.treatment: Lifestyle: frequent carbohydrate-rich meals, avoid potassium-rich foods, fasting, cold and strenuous exercise followed by rest. Acute attacks may resolve with light exercise, glucose, or inhaled beta-agonist. Preventive therapy uses kaliuretic diuretics (thiazides) or carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide, dichlorphenamide). Anaesthetists must be informed—avoid potassium-containing fluids and depolarising relaxants and keep the patient warm.
det.prognosis: Attacks often lessen after middle age, but a permanent proximal myopathy can develop. Life expectancy is normal.
pearls: Short, frequent attacks in childhood favour hyperPP; long attacks in adolescence favour hypoPP.
Potassium can be normal in an attack — the name reflects sensitivity, not always the level.
Ask about anaesthesia: suxamethonium and potassium-rich fluids can provoke severe weakness.
det.thd: HyperPP เกิดจาก mutation ของยีน SCN4A (sodium channel ของกล้ามเนื้อ) ถ่ายทอดแบบเด่น ผู้ป่วยอ่อนแรงเป็นพัก ๆ สั้น ๆ ตั้งแต่เด็ก มักเกิดขณะพักหลังออกกำลังหรือหลังกินอาหารโพแทสเซียมสูง ระหว่างอาการโพแทสเซียมสูงหรือปกติ อาจมี myotonia ร่วม วินิจฉัยด้วย long exercise test และตรวจยีน รักษาโดยกินคาร์โบไฮเดรตบ่อย หลีกเลี่ยงโพแทสเซียม ใช้ thiazide หรือ acetazolamide ป้องกัน

formal: Movement disorders with excess involuntary movement, including chorea, dystonia, tremor, tics, myoclonus and athetosis, from dysfunction of basal ganglia circuits.
simple: A group of conditions in which the body makes too many unwanted movements, such as jerks, twists, tremors or tics.
th: กลุ่มความผิดปกติของการเคลื่อนไหวที่มีการเคลื่อนไหวเกินโดยไม่ตั้งใจ เช่น chorea, dystonia, tremor, tics, myoclonus จากวงจร basal ganglia ผิดปกติ
tempoNote: Depends on cause: acute (drugs, stroke, metabolic) to chronic (genetic, degenerative)
feat: Chorea: flowing, random, dance-like movements
Dystonia: sustained or patterned twisting postures
Tremor: rhythmic oscillation; myoclonus: sudden shock-like jerks
Tics: brief suppressible movements with premonitory urge; also stereotypies and athetosis
Classify by phenomenology first, then search for cause
inv: Video recording to classify phenomenology
Basic labs: glucose, electrolytes, thyroid, liver, copper/ceruloplasmin, drug history
MRI brain; genetic or antibody tests guided by phenotype
Neurophysiology for myoclonus and tremor characterisation

case.who: 68-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes from Nan
case.story: Sudden onset of flinging movements of the left arm and leg over two days.
case.exam: Left hemichorea-hemiballism; otherwise alert.
case.tests: Glucose 520 mg/dL; non-ketotic; CT shows right putaminal hyperdensity, MRI T1 hyperintense.
case.q: What type of hyperkinetic syndrome is this and what is the cause?
case.a: Hemichorea-hemiballism from non-ketotic hyperglycaemia (diabetic striatopathy); correcting glucose usually resolves it.

read.where: 6 - Medical treatment of the motor features of Parkinson disease

det.patho: Hyperkinetic disorders reflect imbalance of basal ganglia output, typically reduced inhibition from the internal globus pallidus and subthalamic nucleus to the thalamus, releasing excessive cortical motor activity. Cerebellar and cortical networks contribute to tremor and myoclonus. Causes range from genetic, degenerative and structural to drugs, metabolic, autoimmune and functional.
det.clinical: This is a syndrome group, not a single disease. The first step is naming the movement: chorea, ballism, athetosis, dystonia, tremor, myoclonus, tics or stereotypies; mixed forms are common. Tempo, age, distribution and associated features (cognition, neuropathy, systemic disease) then guide the search for cause.
det.diagnosis: Careful observation and video, drug history (dopamine blockers, levodopa, anticonvulsants, stimulants) and metabolic screening come first. MRI detects structural, vascular or deposition patterns. Genetic, antibody, neurophysiological and functional assessment follow as indicated.
det.treatment: Treat the cause where possible (stop offending drug, correct glucose, treat autoimmune disease). Symptomatic options depend on phenomenology: VMAT2 inhibitors for chorea, anticholinergics or botulinum toxin for dystonia, beta-blockers or primidone for tremor, levetiracetam or clonazepam for myoclonus. DBS for refractory dystonia and tremor.
det.prognosis: Highly variable: from fully reversible metabolic chorea to progressive neurodegeneration.
pearls: Name the movement before chasing the cause.
Always check glucose and drug history in new chorea.
Videos are invaluable for review and second opinion.
det.thd: Hyperkinetic syndromes คือกลุ่มความผิดปกติที่มีการเคลื่อนไหวเกินโดยไม่ตั้งใจ ได้แก่ chorea dystonia tremor myoclonus tics และ stereotypy เกิดจากวงจร basal ganglia ยับยั้งไม่พอ ขั้นแรกคือบอกชนิดการเคลื่อนไหวให้ได้ แล้วค้นหาสาเหตุ เช่น ยา น้ำตาลสูง พันธุกรรม หรือภูมิคุ้มกัน รักษาที่สาเหตุและใช้ยาตามชนิดของการเคลื่อนไหว

The opposite category: too little movement, bradykinesia and rigidity
Stereotyped episodes with altered awareness or EEG change

name: Hyperosmolar non-ketotic state (HONK)
formal: Hyperglycaemic emergency in type 2 diabetes with severe dehydration, serum osmolality above 320 and minimal ketosis, causing confusion, seizures, focal deficits and coma.
simple: A dangerous complication of diabetes with very high blood sugar and dehydration that can cause confusion, seizures and coma.
th: ภาวะน้ำตาลสูงวิกฤตในเบาหวานชนิดที่ 2 มีขาดน้ำรุนแรง osmolality เกิน 320 และคีโตนน้อย ทำให้สับสน ชัก อาการทางระบบประสาทเฉพาะที่ และหมดสติ
tempoNote: Evolves over several days of polyuria and poor intake
feat: Older patient with type 2 diabetes (sometimes undiagnosed), infection or drug trigger, profound dehydration
Glucose usually >600 mg/dL (33 mmol/L), effective osmolality >320 mOsm/kg, little ketosis or acidosis
Confusion to coma roughly proportional to osmolality
Focal motor seizures, epilepsia partialis continua, transient hemiparesis, aphasia
Hemichorea-hemiballism with striatal T1 hyperintensity on the contralateral side
inv: Glucose, sodium (corrected), urea, creatinine, calculated osmolality, ketones, venous gas
Infection screen (cultures, urine, chest X-ray), ECG and troponin
CT/MRI if focal signs persist; T1 bright putamen in hyperglycaemic hemichorea

case.who: 72-year-old woman from Phrae with type 2 diabetes on glipizide
case.story: One week of urinary infection, drinking little; now confused with twitching of the right face and hand.
case.exam: Dry, GCS 11, right focal clonic seizures, mild right arm weakness.
case.tests: Glucose 980 mg/dL, Na 148 mmol/L, osmolality 360 mOsm/kg, ketones trace, pH 7.33.
case.q: What is the metabolic emergency and how should the seizures be managed?
case.a: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state; cautious fluid resuscitation and insulin to lower glucose and osmolality gradually, treat infection — seizures usually stop as the metabolic state corrects; avoid relying on phenytoin.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Diabetes Mellitus

det.patho: Relative insulin deficiency allows hyperglycaemia without ketogenesis (enough insulin remains to suppress lipolysis). Osmotic diuresis produces severe water and electrolyte loss, and rising osmolality shrinks brain cells. Focal cortical irritability may reflect GABA depletion from altered metabolism in hyperglycaemia; striatal dysfunction underlies hemichorea.
det.clinical: Typically older adults with type 2 diabetes develop several days of polyuria, thirst and weakness, then drowsiness. Neurological features include delirium, coma, focal seizures (sometimes the presenting sign), transient focal deficits mimicking stroke and movement disorders. Complications include thrombosis, rhabdomyolysis, and cerebral oedema or osmotic demyelination if correction is too fast.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on marked hyperglycaemia, effective osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg, and absence of significant ketoacidosis; mixed DKA–HHS states occur. Look for the precipitant, commonly infection, myocardial infarction, stroke, steroids or thiazides. Imaging is needed if focal deficits do not resolve.
det.treatment: Restore volume with isotonic saline first, aiming for a gradual fall in osmolality (about 3–8 mOsm/kg per hour) and in sodium no faster than 10 mmol/L per day. Start low-dose insulin once fluids are running and glucose stops falling with fluids alone; replace potassium. Give prophylactic anticoagulation and treat the trigger. Seizures respond to metabolic correction; if drugs are needed use benzodiazepines or levetiracetam — phenytoin may impair insulin release and is often ineffective.
det.prognosis: Mortality is higher than DKA (around 5–20%), mainly from age, comorbidity and the precipitant.
pearls: Focal seizures + very high glucose + no ketones = non-ketotic hyperglycaemia.
Correct osmolality slowly to avoid cerebral oedema and osmotic demyelination.
Hemichorea with T1-bright putamen in an elderly diabetic is often hyperglycaemic.
det.thd: HONK หรือ HHS คือภาวะน้ำตาลในเลือดสูงมากในเบาหวานชนิดที่ 2 ร่วมกับขาดน้ำรุนแรงและ osmolality สูงโดยมีคีโตนน้อย ผู้ป่วยซึม สับสน ชักเฉพาะที่ อ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกชั่วคราว หรือมี hemichorea รักษาด้วยการให้สารน้ำและอินซูลินโดยลดน้ำตาลและ osmolality อย่างช้า ๆ ร่วมกับรักษาสาเหตุกระตุ้น อาการชักมักหายเมื่อแก้ภาวะเมตาบอลิก

name: Hypertensive encephalopathy
formal: Acute encephalopathy from severe hypertension exceeding cerebral autoregulation, with headache, visual loss, seizures and confusion, and vasogenic oedema on MRI, as in PRES.
simple: Brain swelling caused by extremely high blood pressure, leading to headache, vision problems, seizures and confusion.
th: ภาวะสมองบวมทำงานผิดปกติจากความดันโลหิตสูงขึ้นเฉียบพลันเกินขีด autoregulation มีปวดศีรษะ สับสน ชัก ตามัว จอตามีเลือดออก/papilloedema อาการดีขึ้นเมื่อลดความดันลงอย่างควบคุม มักพบลักษณะ PRES บน MRI
tempoNote: Develops over hours to 1–2 days with a sharp BP surge; reversible within days if BP is lowered promptly
feat: Very high BP (typically > 180/120 mmHg, or a sharp rise from baseline in young or pregnant patients)
Severe headache, nausea, vomiting and progressive confusion or drowsiness
Visual blurring or cortical blindness; seizures
Grade III–IV hypertensive retinopathy: flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, papilloedema
Other target organ damage: acute kidney injury, heart failure, microangiopathic haemolysis
inv: MRI FLAIR: symmetric parieto-occipital vasogenic oedema (PRES pattern); exclude haemorrhage and infarction
Fundoscopy for retinopathy and papilloedema
Renal function, urinalysis, troponin, ECG, blood film for schistocytes
Search for causes: renal disease, phaeochromocytoma, drug withdrawal, pre-eclampsia, stimulants

case.who: 39-year-old construction worker from Khon Kaen who stopped his BP pills 6 months ago
case.story: Two days of pounding headache and vomiting; this evening he became confused and had a generalised seizure at home.
case.exam: BP 230/140, drowsy but rousable, no focal weakness; fundi show flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and bilateral disc swelling.
case.tests: Creatinine 2.6 mg/dL, proteinuria 3+; CT no haemorrhage; MRI FLAIR bilateral occipital subcortical oedema without diffusion restriction.
case.q: How fast should BP be lowered and with which drugs?
case.a: IV titratable agent (nicardipine or labetalol infusion) reducing mean arterial pressure by no more than about 20–25% in the first hour, then gradually toward 160/100 over the next 2–6 h.

read.where: Chapter 10 Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, cardiac arrests and cardiac encephalopathy
Chapter 31 An unusual PRESentation of stroke
PRES in the setting of COPD: proposed pathogenesis
Chapter 16: Neurologic Manifestations Of Acute Hepatic Failure

det.patho: Cerebral autoregulation keeps flow constant over a range of pressures; when BP rises abruptly above the upper limit (lower in previously normotensive people), forced dilatation of arterioles leads to hyperperfusion, endothelial injury and blood–brain barrier breakdown with vasogenic oedema, predominantly in the posterior circulation, which has less sympathetic innervation. Chronic hypertension shifts the curve rightwards, so long-standing hypertensives tolerate higher pressures — but also tolerate rapid reduction poorly.
det.clinical: Headache, vomiting and blurred vision progress over hours to confusion, lethargy, seizures and occasionally coma. Focal signs are usually mild; prominent focal deficits should raise suspicion of haemorrhage or infarction. Retinopathy with papilloedema confirms malignant-phase hypertension. In pregnancy, eclampsia is the obstetric counterpart and can occur at lower absolute BP levels.
det.diagnosis: It is a clinical diagnosis of encephalopathy with severe hypertension that improves after BP reduction. MRI usually shows the PRES pattern (parieto-occipital, sometimes frontal, cerebellar or brainstem oedema). Exclude stroke, CVT, infection, intoxication and metabolic encephalopathies. Investigate end-organ damage and secondary causes of hypertension, particularly in young patients.
det.treatment: Admit to a monitored bed and use IV titratable drugs (nicardipine, clevidipine, labetalol; avoid sublingual nifedipine). Lower the MAP by no more than about 20–25% in the first hour, then towards 160/100–110 over the next hours, and normalise over 24–48 h; overly rapid falls risk watershed infarction. Treat seizures with benzodiazepine then levetiracetam or similar. In eclampsia, give magnesium sulphate and plan delivery. Afterwards, establish a durable oral regimen and address adherence.
det.prognosis: Usually fully reversible with prompt treatment; delayed or excessive BP correction can leave infarction or haemorrhage.
pearls: Encephalopathy + very high BP + papilloedema/retinal haemorrhages = treat as hypertensive emergency.
Lower BP in a controlled way: about 25% in the first hour, not to normal.
Prominent focal deficits suggest stroke, not simple hypertensive encephalopathy.
det.thd: Hypertensive encephalopathy เกิดจากความดันโลหิตสูงขึ้นเฉียบพลันเกินความสามารถ autoregulation ของสมอง ทำให้เกิดสมองบวมแบบ vasogenic โดยเฉพาะบริเวณท้ายทอย ผู้ป่วยปวดศีรษะ อาเจียน สับสน ตามัว และชัก ตรวจพบ papilloedema และเลือดออกที่จอตา MRI มักเป็นแบบ PRES รักษาด้วยยาลดความดันทางหลอดเลือดดำ (nicardipine, labetalol) โดยลด MAP ไม่เกิน 20–25% ในชั่วโมงแรก แล้วค่อย ๆ ลดต่อ

name: Hyperthermic catatonia
formal: Catatonia with fever and autonomic instability, overlapping with neuroleptic malignant syndrome and lethal catatonia; features stupor, rigidity and tachycardia and needs urgent benzodiazepines or ECT.
simple: A serious state of immobility or agitation with high fever and unstable vital signs, needing urgent hospital treatment.
th: Hyperthermic catatonia (malignant catatonia) คือ catatonia ที่มีไข้สูงและระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติรวน ผู้ป่วยอาจนิ่งแข็งหรือกระวนกระวายมาก มีชีพจรเร็ว ความดันแกว่ง เหงื่อออก CK สูง ต้องแยกจาก NMS และการติดเชื้อสมอง รักษาด้วย lorazepam และ ECT เร็วที่สุด และหลีกเลี่ยงยาต้านโรคจิต
tempoNote: Fever and autonomic change develop over one to several days, sometimes after an excited phase; delay of more than a few days sharply raises the risk of death
feat: Catatonic stupor with mutism and posturing, or intense excitement and agitation, with rising fever up to 40–42 °C
Autonomic instability: tachycardia, labile or high blood pressure, profuse sweating, fast breathing and pale or bluish skin
Muscle rigidity in about four of five patients, clouded consciousness and refusal of food and fluid
Raised CK and white count, low serum iron and sometimes abnormal liver tests; imaging and CSF are usually non-diagnostic
Underlying cause is a psychosis or mood disorder in most, an infection, encephalitis or metabolic disease in some, and antipsychotic exposure in the NMS-like form
inv: CK, renal function, electrolytes, iron, liver enzymes, full blood count, blood and urine cultures
EEG, MRI and CSF with autoimmune antibody panel to exclude encephalitis or non-convulsive status
Thyroid, adrenal and toxicology tests; ECG and coagulation screen; leg imaging for thrombosis

case.who: 31-year-old man from Nakhon Pathom with recurrent depression and psychotic features
case.story: He stopped eating and talking for four days, lay rigid with open eyes, and on the fifth day developed high fever and drenching sweats; a relative had given him an extra dose of his antipsychotic.
case.exam: Temperature 40.0 °C, pulse 128, blood pressure 165/105 mmHg, lead-pipe rigidity, mutism, negativism and staring; pupils reactive, no meningism.
case.tests: CK 5,600 U/L, white count 15,000/µL, low serum iron; blood cultures, CT brain, EEG and CSF normal.
case.q: What is the working diagnosis and the most effective treatment?
case.a: Malignant (hyperthermic) catatonia, with NMS overlap because of antipsychotic exposure. Give intensive supportive care and scheduled intravenous lorazepam, stop the antipsychotic, and arrange ECT promptly if the temperature and rigidity do not fall within a day or two.

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System

det.patho: Malignant catatonia is thought to result from reduced dopaminergic activity in frontal-subcortical circuits, mainly the motor, anterior cingulate and lateral orbitofrontal loops. Hypodopaminergia in the motor loop would produce rigidity, in the cingulate loop mutism, akinesia and autonomic and heat-regulation failure through hypothalamic projections. Baseline low dopamine tone and stress sensitivity may predispose, and dopamine receptor blockers worsen the state. Some authors regard neuroleptic malignant syndrome as the drug-triggered counterpart of this same syndrome.
det.clinical: The classical excited form passes through an acute phase of motor excitement with progressive hyperthermia into exhaustion and stupor; a second form is stuporous from the start. Fever, autonomic instability, rigidity, altered consciousness and catatonic signs coexist, and about one in five cases occurring on antipsychotics are indistinguishable from NMS. The syndrome has many triggers, including infections, metabolic and endocrine disease, tumours and seizures. Without treatment it may lead to cardiovascular collapse, kidney failure, thromboembolism and death.
det.diagnosis: Diagnose by combining catatonic signs with fever and autonomic features after other causes have been excluded. A careful history for psychiatric disorder and drug exposure is needed, together with the laboratory evaluation listed above. A positive CK and leucocytosis are supportive but non-specific. Lorazepam response may be partial. Exclude central nervous system infection, NMS, serotonin syndrome, thyroid storm, heat stroke and anticholinergic toxicity.
det.treatment: Admit to intensive care for fluid replacement, cooling, monitoring and prophylaxis against venous thrombosis, and give lorazepam intravenously. If benzodiazepines do not rapidly reverse the process, proceed to ECT within a day or two, since bilateral ECT once or twice daily for a series of treatments is effective and delay worsens outcomes. Dantrolene and bromocriptine have been tried alone or with ECT but evidence is anecdotal. Corticosteroids are a reserve option. Antipsychotics should be withheld whenever the diagnosis is suspected, and the underlying medical condition must be corrected.
det.prognosis: Recent series show mortality around one in ten, much lower than in the pre-antipsychotic era, thanks to earlier recognition and ECT. Response is poor if coma or a temperature above 41 °C is already present.
pearls: Fever plus catatonic signs is malignant catatonia until proven otherwise; do not wait for cultures to give lorazepam.
ECT is the definitive treatment; delay costs lives.
Never give antipsychotics for the agitation.
det.thd: Hyperthermic catatonia หรือ malignant catatonia คือ catatonia ที่มีไข้สูง ชีพจรเร็ว ความดันแกว่ง เหงื่อออกมาก กล้ามเนื้อแข็ง และ CK สูง ผู้ป่วยอาจกระวนกระวายสุดขีดหรือนิ่งเฉยไม่พูด ต้องแยกการติดเชื้อสมอง NMS และ serotonin syndrome ออก การรักษาคือดูแลในไอซียู ให้น้ำ ลดไข้ ป้องกันลิ่มเลือด ให้ lorazepam ทางหลอดเลือดดำ และทำ ECT โดยเร็วถ้าไม่ตอบสนองภายใน 1–2 วัน ห้ามใช้ยาต้านโรคจิต
