name: Hypnic headache
formal: Rare primary headache of older adults that wakes patients from sleep at consistent times with moderate pain lasting 15 to 240 minutes; responds to caffeine or lithium.
simple: A rare headache in older people that wakes them from sleep at the same time each night.
more: Rare primary headache that wakes patients from sleep at a fixed time, similar to hypnic headache, usually in older adults and often responsive to caffeine or lithium.
th: ปวดศีรษะปฐมภูมิที่หายาก พบในผู้สูงอายุ ปลุกให้ตื่นจากการนอนในเวลาใกล้เคียงกันทุกคืน ปวดนาน 15 นาทีถึง 4 ชั่วโมง ตอบสนองต่อคาเฟอีนหรือ lithium
tempoNote: Attacks on 10 or more nights a month for over 3 months; onset usually after 50
feat: Wakes the patient from sleep, often at the same time each night
Mild to moderate, usually bilateral dull pain lasting 15 minutes to 4 hours
No prominent autonomic features or restlessness (unlike cluster headache)
Mostly over 50, slightly more often women
May also occur during daytime naps
inv: MRI brain to exclude structural lesions, especially pituitary or posterior fossa
Nocturnal blood pressure monitoring; sleep study if apnoea suspected
Review evening medications and nocturnal hypoglycaemia

case.story: For four months she is woken at 2 a.m. almost every night by a dull whole-head ache lasting an hour; she gets up and makes coffee.
case.exam: Normal; no ptosis, tearing or nasal congestion.
case.tests: MRI brain normal; overnight oximetry and BP normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and simple first treatment?
case.a: Hypnic headache; a cup of coffee or caffeine tablet at bedtime, with lithium or melatonin as alternatives.

det.patho: The mechanism is unknown; links to the hypothalamic circadian pacemaker and REM sleep have been proposed, and MRI studies suggest reduced hypothalamic grey matter. The responses to caffeine, lithium and melatonin, which influence circadian systems, support this idea.
det.clinical: Attacks occur only from sleep at a consistent time and are usually less severe than cluster headache. Patients typically get up and move around or eat. Mild autonomic symptoms or nausea may occur. Several attacks per night are possible.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 criteria: recurrent attacks developing only during sleep, on at least 10 days monthly for over three months, lasting 15 minutes to 4 hours after waking, without cranial autonomic symptoms or restlessness. Secondary causes such as nocturnal hypertension, hypoglycaemia, sleep apnoea, intracranial lesions and medication overuse must be excluded.
det.treatment: Caffeine at bedtime (coffee or 100–200 mg tablet) is first-line and rarely disturbs sleep in these patients. Lithium is effective but needs careful monitoring in the elderly; indomethacin, melatonin and flunarizine are alternatives.
det.prognosis: Benign; may remit spontaneously after months to years.
pearls: An older adult woken at the same hour nightly by headache — think hypnic.
Bedtime coffee is paradoxically the treatment.
Check blood pressure and oxygenation at night before diagnosing.
det.thd: Hypnic headache เป็นปวดศีรษะปฐมภูมิในผู้สูงอายุที่ตื่นขึ้นมาเพราะปวดหัวเวลาเดิมทุกคืน ปวดตื้อทั้งศีรษะนาน 15 นาทีถึง 4 ชั่วโมง ไม่มีน้ำตาไหลหรือกระสับกระส่ายแบบ cluster คาดว่าเกี่ยวกับ hypothalamus ต้องตัดสาเหตุอื่น เช่น ความดันสูงกลางคืน หยุดหายใจขณะหลับ หรือก้อนในสมอง รักษาด้วยการดื่มกาแฟก่อนนอน หรือ lithium

name: Hypokalaemic periodic paralysis (hypoPP)
formal: Channelopathy from calcium or sodium channel mutations causing episodes of flaccid weakness with low serum potassium, often after carbohydrate meals or rest following exercise; treated with potassium and acetazolamide.
simple: An inherited condition causing attacks of muscle weakness when blood potassium is low, often after carbohydrate-rich meals or rest after exercise.
th: อัมพาตเป็นพัก ๆ จากโพแทสเซียมต่ำ — ตื่นมาขยับแขนขาไม่ได้หลังมื้อแป้งหรือออกกำลังกาย หายในไม่กี่ชั่วโมง
tempoNote: Attacks last hours to a day, often on waking
feat: Flaccid weakness of limbs, sparing face and breathing, with low potassium during the attack
Triggers: carbohydrate-rich meals, rest after exercise, stress, cold
Primary form begins in the first two decades; adult first attacks suggest thyrotoxicosis or secondary causes
Late fixed proximal myopathy can develop
inv: Potassium during the attack; ECG (U waves, arrhythmia)
Thyroid function; urine potassium to exclude renal loss
Long exercise test on NCS; CACNA1S / SCN4A genetics

case.story: Woke at 5 a.m. unable to lift his arms or legs after a large rice-and-sweets dinner; normal the day before. Recent weight loss and tremor.
case.exam: Symmetric flaccid quadriparesis, absent reflexes, normal sensation and cranial nerves, fine tremor, tachycardia.
case.tests: K 1.9 mmol/L; ECG U waves; TSH suppressed, free T4 high.
case.q: How does this change long-term treatment?
case.a: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis — attacks stop once the patient is euthyroid; beta-blockers help meanwhile. Give potassium cautiously to avoid rebound hyperkalaemia.

ddx.pt: Days not hours, sensory symptoms, normal potassium

det.patho: Primary hypoPP is an autosomal dominant channelopathy, mostly from CACNA1S (calcium channel) and less often SCN4A (sodium channel) variants that create an abnormal leak current through the voltage-sensor region. When serum potassium falls, affected fibres depolarise paradoxically, sodium channels inactivate and the membrane becomes inexcitable. Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis, frequent in Asian men, reflects thyroid hormone driving Na/K-ATPase activity with a genetic susceptibility (e.g. KCNJ18), shifting potassium into cells.
det.clinical: Attacks of flaccid weakness usually begin on waking or after rest following exertion or a carbohydrate load, and can persist anywhere between several hours and a day or longer. Proximal limbs are hit hardest; bulbar, ocular and respiratory muscles are generally spared, although severe hypokalaemia can threaten cardiac rhythm. Reflexes drop during the episode and sensation is normal. Primary forms start in childhood or adolescence, with attack frequency often waning after mid-life while a permanent proximal myopathy may emerge. A first attack in an adult man, especially with weight loss, tremor or palpitations, should prompt a thyroid screen.
det.diagnosis: Document a low potassium during an attack, since values between attacks are normal in primary disease. Check thyroid function, and measure urinary potassium and acid–base status to exclude renal or gastrointestinal loss (secondary hypokalaemic paralysis). The long exercise test on nerve conduction shows a delayed decline in CMAP amplitude in many patients, though a normal result does not exclude the diagnosis. Genetic testing of CACNA1S and SCN4A confirms primary disease; distinguish from Andersen–Tawil syndrome (KCNJ2) by looking for arrhythmia and dysmorphic features.
det.treatment: During an attack, give oral potassium chloride in modest repeated doses with ECG and potassium monitoring; reserve IV potassium for patients who cannot swallow or have arrhythmia, using non-glucose diluent. Overcorrection is common because potassium returns from cells as the attack resolves. Prevention includes avoiding high-carbohydrate meals and abrupt rest after strenuous exercise, plus carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide or dichlorphenamide) or potassium-sparing diuretics. In thyrotoxic paralysis, non-selective beta-blockade (propranolol) helps acutely and restoring euthyroidism stops attacks; acetazolamide is not useful there.
det.prognosis: Attacks are rarely fatal when potassium and rhythm are watched, but a fixed proximal myopathy can accumulate over decades. Thyrotoxic attacks cease once thyroid function is normal.
pearls: Normal potassium between attacks does not exclude hypoPP — test during the episode.
Adult Asian man with first attack: think thyrotoxicosis first.
Beware rebound hyperkalaemia after aggressive potassium replacement.
SCN4A-related hypoPP may worsen with acetazolamide; genotype guides choice.

det.patho: Potassium sets the resting membrane potential of muscle and heart. Low extracellular potassium hyperpolarises some fibres but paradoxically depolarises others with channel defects, making them inexcitable; high potassium depolarises membranes and inactivates sodium channels. Losses (gut, kidney), shifts (insulin, catecholamines, thyroid hormone) and reduced excretion (renal failure, drugs) are the main mechanisms.
det.clinical: This is a metabolic disorder with neuromuscular effects. Hypokalaemia causes generalised weakness, cramps, myalgia and rhabdomyolysis when severe, and can affect respiratory muscles. Hyperkalaemia causes weakness and life-threatening arrhythmias. In Thailand, distal renal tubular acidosis and thyrotoxic periodic paralysis are important causes of hypokalaemic paralysis.
det.diagnosis: Measure serum potassium urgently in any acute flaccid weakness with normal sensation. Urine potassium distinguishes renal loss from shift or gut loss. Check acid–base status, magnesium, thyroid function and CK. ECG assesses cardiac risk.
det.treatment: Replace potassium orally or IV with cardiac monitoring, and correct magnesium. In shift-related paralysis, give smaller amounts to avoid rebound and treat the cause, such as hyperthyroidism. Hyperkalaemia needs calcium gluconate for cardiac protection, insulin-glucose, beta-agonists and potassium removal.
det.prognosis: Excellent when corrected promptly; arrhythmia is the main risk.
pearls: Check potassium before diagnosing GBS in acute flaccid weakness.
Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis is common in young Asian men.
In shift disorders, rebound hyperkalaemia follows aggressive replacement.
det.thd: ความผิดปกติของโพแทสเซียมเป็นภาวะเกลือแร่ ไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาทโดยตรง แต่ทำให้กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงแบบอ่อนปวกเปียก โพแทสเซียมต่ำอาจทำให้อัมพาตทั้งตัวและกล้ามเนื้อสลาย ส่วนโพแทสเซียมสูงทำให้หัวใจเต้นผิดจังหวะ สาเหตุสำคัญในไทยคือท้องเสีย RTA และ thyrotoxic periodic paralysis ต้องตรวจโพแทสเซียมและ ECG ทุกครั้งในผู้ป่วยอ่อนแรงเฉียบพลัน

det.patho: Severe potassium depletion hyperpolarises and then destabilises muscle membranes, impairs glycogen synthesis and reduces exercise-induced vasodilation, causing ischaemic muscle injury. Total-body potassium loss distinguishes this from transcellular shifts in periodic paralysis. Renal (diuretics, RTA, aldosteronism, Gitelman/Bartter) or gastrointestinal losses are typical causes.
det.clinical: Weakness develops over days, often proximal, with myalgia and cramps; severe cases involve respiratory muscles. Rhabdomyolysis may complicate it, especially with exercise. Cardiac arrhythmias and paralytic ileus are dangerous accompaniments. In Thailand, distal RTA (including Sjögren-related) and diuretic or herbal licorice use are notable causes.
det.diagnosis: Confirm low potassium and measure CK, magnesium and acid-base status. A urine potassium above about 20 mmol/day (or high TTKG) during hypokalaemia indicates renal loss. Workup includes renin, aldosterone, urine pH and autoimmune tests. Persistent weakness after correction warrants EMG or biopsy for another myopathy.
det.treatment: Replace potassium with cardiac monitoring; oral when possible, intravenous at controlled rates when severe. Correct magnesium. In RTA, potassium should be restored before bicarbonate to avoid worsening hypokalaemia. Treat the underlying cause and manage rhabdomyolysis with fluids.
det.prognosis: Usually fully reversible within days to weeks once potassium is restored.
pearls: Profound weakness with K < 2.5 and high CK: check urine K and acid-base.
In distal RTA, give potassium before alkali.
Always check magnesium — hypokalaemia will not correct without it.

det.patho: Dominant missense variants in SCN4A, the skeletal muscle sodium channel, usually neutralise arginines in the voltage sensor. This creates an abnormal 'gating pore' leak current that depolarises the fibre when extracellular potassium falls, making the membrane inexcitable. HypoPP2 accounts for roughly 10–20% of familial hypoPP, the remainder mostly being CACNA1S (type 1).
det.clinical: Episodes of weakness lasting hours occur after carbohydrate loads or rest following exercise, often on waking. Attacks may be shorter and associated with myalgia more often than in type 1, and penetrance is reduced in women. Between attacks strength is normal early on, but a progressive proximal myopathy can develop after middle age even in patients with few attacks.
det.diagnosis: Document low potassium during an attack and exclude secondary hypokalaemia (diuretics, renal tubular acidosis, hyperaldosteronism, GI loss) and thyrotoxicosis. The long exercise test supports a periodic paralysis, and genetic testing for SCN4A, CACNA1S and KCNJ2 confirms the type. ECG excludes Andersen–Tawil syndrome.
det.treatment: Acute attacks are treated with oral potassium chloride in repeated small doses, monitoring for rebound hyperkalaemia; IV potassium in mannitol rather than dextrose if needed. Prevention includes avoiding high-carbohydrate meals and strenuous exercise followed by rest. Dichlorphenamide is approved for primary periodic paralyses; acetazolamide may help some but can worsen SCN4A cases, so potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, eplerenone, triamterene) are alternatives.
det.prognosis: Attacks often lessen with age, but permanent proximal weakness may accumulate.
pearls: Never give potassium in glucose solution during an attack.
Gene type matters: SCN4A hypoPP may worsen with acetazolamide.
Always check thyroid function in a young man with hypokalaemic paralysis.

det.patho: Hypokinesia results from reduced dopaminergic drive to the striatum or downstream damage in basal ganglia circuits, which increases inhibitory output from the globus pallidus internus to the thalamus and brainstem. In Parkinson disease, alpha-synuclein pathology causes nigral neuron loss; atypical syndromes involve tau (PSP, CBD) or alpha-synuclein in glia (MSA). Dopamine receptor blockade, vascular lesions and toxins produce secondary parkinsonism.
det.clinical: Parkinsonism is defined by bradykinesia together with rest tremor, rigidity or both. Parkinson disease is the commonest cause, followed by drug-induced parkinsonism, which is frequent in Thailand due to flunarizine, cinnarizine, metoclopramide and antipsychotics. Atypical parkinsonisms (MSA, PSP, CBD, DLB) present with red flags and progress faster. Other causes include vascular disease, NPH, Wilson disease, toxins (manganese, carbon monoxide) and structural lesions.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, guided by MDS criteria with supportive features, exclusion criteria and red flags. A medication review is essential. MRI helps detect vascular, structural and atypical patterns. DAT-SPECT differentiates degenerative presynaptic parkinsonism from drug-induced, functional and essential tremor mimics, while cardiac MIBG and skin alpha-synuclein seed assays are emerging adjuncts.
det.treatment: Treatment depends on the cause: levodopa, dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors and advanced therapies for Parkinson disease; withdrawal of offending drugs for drug-induced forms; levodopa trials in atypical and vascular parkinsonism, often with limited response. Physiotherapy, exercise, speech therapy and falls prevention apply to all. Avoid dopamine-blocking antiemetics and antipsychotics; quetiapine or clozapine are safer if needed.
det.prognosis: Parkinson disease has a long course with good early drug response; atypical forms lead to severe disability within about 5–10 years; drug-induced forms usually resolve within months of stopping the drug.
pearls: Ask about flunarizine and metoclopramide in every new parkinsonism.
Bradykinesia means decrement in speed and amplitude, not just slowness.
Poor levodopa response plus early falls or autonomic failure: think atypical.

det.patho: Primary hypophysitis is autoimmune infiltration of the pituitary, most often lymphocytic, with granulomatous, xanthomatous and IgG4-related forms. Secondary hypophysitis complicates systemic diseases (sarcoidosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, tuberculosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis) or drugs, especially anti-CTLA-4 and anti-PD-1 checkpoint inhibitors. Inflammation enlarges the gland and then may lead to fibrosis and atrophy.
det.clinical: Headache and hypopituitarism are the main features; ACTH and TSH deficits appear earlier than in adenomas, and diabetes insipidus points to infundibular involvement. Large lesions compress the chiasm, and cavernous sinus extension can cause diplopia. Checkpoint-inhibitor hypophysitis presents with fatigue, headache and low cortisol, often with only mild enlargement. Lymphocytic hypophysitis classically affects women in late pregnancy or after delivery.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows a symmetric, homogeneously enhancing gland with a thick stalk, with the posterior pituitary bright spot no longer visible. Complete pituitary hormone testing is mandatory, interpreting cortisol carefully in pregnancy. Systemic screening (IgG4, ACE, ANCA, chest CT, CSF where indicated) looks for secondary causes. Biopsy is reserved for atypical, progressive or diagnostic-uncertain cases.
det.treatment: Hormone replacement is the cornerstone: hydrocortisone first, then levothyroxine, desmopressin for diabetes insipidus and sex hormones as needed. Glucocorticoids at higher doses are used for compressive symptoms or active inflammation, with azathioprine, rituximab or other agents for refractory or IgG4 disease. Surgery is reserved for progressive visual loss or diagnostic doubt. Checkpoint-inhibitor cases usually continue cancer therapy with lifelong cortisol replacement.
det.prognosis: Enlargement often regresses, but ACTH deficiency is frequently permanent; recurrence occurs in some primary cases.
pearls: A pituitary mass in a peripartum woman is hypophysitis until proven otherwise.
Diabetes insipidus with a pituitary mass argues against a simple adenoma.
Give hydrocortisone before thyroxine in any hypopituitarism.
det.thd: Hypophysitis คือการอักเสบของต่อมใต้สมอง ชนิด lymphocytic พบบ่อยในหญิงช่วงตั้งครรภ์หรือหลังคลอด และอาจเกิดจากยา checkpoint inhibitor, IgG4 หรือ sarcoidosis อาการคือปวดศีรษะ อ่อนเพลีย โซเดียมต่ำ ปัสสาวะมาก และลานสายตาเสีย MRI เห็นต่อมโตสม่ำเสมอและก้านหนา ต้องตรวจฮอร์โมนทุกตัว รักษาด้วยการให้ hydrocortisone ก่อน thyroxine และใช้ steroid ขนาดสูงถ้ามีการกดทับ

name: Hypothyroid myopathy
formal: Proximal weakness, cramps, delayed reflex relaxation, and mounding with raised CK in hypothyroidism, from impaired glycogenolysis and mitochondrial function.
simple: Muscle weakness, cramps, and aching caused by an underactive thyroid.
more: Thyroid function tests confirm the cause; thyroxine replacement normalises strength over months.
th: กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง ปวด ตะคริว และ CK สูงจากภาวะไทรอยด์ต่ำ — รักษาไทรอยด์แล้วดีขึ้น
tempoNote: Develops over weeks to months as hypothyroidism worsens
feat: Proximal weakness, muscle aches, cramps and stiffness, worse in cold
Slow relaxation phase of tendon reflexes ('hung-up' ankle jerk)
Muscle mounding (myoedema) when percussed
Occasional muscle enlargement (Hoffmann syndrome in adults)
Systemic signs: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin, bradycardia
inv: TSH and free T4
CK often raised, sometimes many times normal
EMG: normal or mildly myopathic; nerve studies may show coexisting carpal tunnel or neuropathy

case.who: 50-year-old woman with prior radioactive iodine for Graves
case.story: Missed follow-up; over 4 months tired, cold, gaining weight, with aching thighs and painful cramps climbing stairs.
case.exam: Puffy face, dry skin, HR 54; mild hip flexor weakness; ankle jerks contract briskly but relax very slowly; tapping the deltoid raises a ridge.
case.tests: TSH 86 mIU/L, free T4 low; CK 2,400 U/L.
case.q: Does she need a muscle biopsy?
case.a: Usually no — replace thyroid hormone and recheck CK and strength; biopsy is reserved for failure to improve once euthyroid.

det.patho: Thyroid hormone deficiency slows muscle metabolism: reduced mitochondrial oxidative capacity, impaired glycogen breakdown and slowed calcium reuptake by the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Slow calcium handling explains delayed relaxation of reflexes and myoedema. Membrane leakiness raises CK.
det.clinical: Most patients have aches, cramps, fatigue and mild proximal weakness rather than severe paralysis. Delayed reflex relaxation is a classic sign. Rarely there is marked muscle hypertrophy with stiffness (Hoffmann syndrome), or rhabdomyolysis, especially with exercise or statins. Carpal tunnel syndrome and a mild sensorimotor neuropathy may coexist.
det.diagnosis: High TSH with low free T4 explains the picture; CK may be strikingly high and can trigger an unnecessary myositis work-up. Always check TSH in any unexplained raised CK or myopathy. EMG and biopsy are needed only when weakness persists after correction.
det.treatment: Levothyroxine replacement, started cautiously in older patients or those with heart disease, resolves the myopathy. Hold or review statins until euthyroid. Symptoms and CK improve over weeks to months.
det.prognosis: Very good; weakness and CK normalise with adequate replacement, though recovery may take several months.
pearls: Check TSH before labelling a high CK as myositis.
Slow-relaxing ankle jerk is a bedside clue to hypothyroidism.
Hypothyroidism amplifies statin muscle toxicity.
det.thd: Hypothyroid myopathy เกิดจากภาวะไทรอยด์ต่ำ ทำให้ปวดกล้ามเนื้อ ตะคริว อ่อนแรงต้นขา และ CK สูงได้มาก ลักษณะเด่นคือ reflex คลายตัวช้า และเคาะกล้ามเนื้อแล้วนูน (myoedema) วินิจฉัยด้วย TSH สูงและ free T4 ต่ำ การรักษาคือให้ levothyroxine ซึ่งทำให้อาการและ CK กลับปกติในหลายสัปดาห์ถึงเดือน

name: Hypothyroidism
formal: Thyroid hormone deficiency with neuromuscular manifestations including myopathy, carpal tunnel syndrome, polyneuropathy, myoedema, and delayed relaxation of reflexes.
simple: An underactive thyroid gland, which can cause tiredness, weakness, muscle pain, and nerve compression.
more: Diagnosed by high TSH with low free T4; levothyroxine replacement usually reverses neuromuscular complications.
th: ภาวะขาดฮอร์โมนไทรอยด์ ทำให้กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง carpal tunnel เส้นประสาทเสื่อม reflex คลายช้า และอาจซึม สับสน
tempoNote: Symptoms evolve over months
feat: Slow relaxation of tendon reflexes (hung-up ankle jerks)
Proximal myopathy with cramps and raised CK
Carpal tunnel syndrome and mild sensory polyneuropathy
Myoedema: mounding of muscle on percussion
Cognitive slowing, ataxia, and rarely myxoedema coma
inv: TSH and free T4
CK (often raised)
NCS if neuropathy or entrapment suspected

case.story: Tiredness, weight gain, cold intolerance, muscle aches and tingling fingers at night over 6 months.
case.exam: Dry skin, hoarse voice, mild proximal weakness, delayed relaxation of ankle jerks, positive Phalen.
case.tests: TSH 78 mIU/L, free T4 low, CK 1,100 U/L.
case.q: What unifies the neuromuscular findings?
case.a: Primary hypothyroidism causing myopathy and carpal tunnel; treat with levothyroxine.

det.patho: Thyroid hormone deficiency slows muscle metabolism and calcium reuptake, impairing relaxation, and reduces glycogenolysis and mitochondrial function. Mucopolysaccharide deposition causes soft tissue swelling and nerve entrapment.
det.clinical: Neuromuscular features include myalgia, cramps, proximal weakness, slowed reflex relaxation, carpal tunnel syndrome and sensory neuropathy. Central features include cognitive slowing, depression, ataxia and in severe cases myxoedema coma with hypothermia and hyponatraemia.
det.diagnosis: TSH with free T4 confirms primary hypothyroidism. CK is often raised. Exclude other causes when features persist after treatment.
det.treatment: Levothyroxine replacement; start low in elderly or cardiac patients. Myxoedema coma is an emergency requiring intravenous thyroid hormone and steroids. Treat entrapments if they persist after euthyroidism.
det.prognosis: Neuromuscular features usually resolve over months on replacement.
pearls: Delayed relaxation of ankle reflexes is a classic bedside clue.
Raised CK can be due to hypothyroidism alone.
Hypothyroidism increases statin myopathy risk.
det.thd: Hypothyroidism ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อทำงานช้า อ่อนแรง เป็นตะคริว CK สูง reflex คลายช้า และมี carpal tunnel จากเนื้อเยื่อบวม บางรายสมองช้า ซึม วินิจฉัยด้วย TSH และ free T4 รักษาด้วย levothyroxine อาการทางกล้ามเนื้อและเส้นประสาทมักดีขึ้นภายในหลายเดือน

qx.stem: A 68-year-old woman from Surat Thani has several months of apathy, somnolence, cold intolerance, weight gain and, in recent weeks, paranoid delusions and hallucinations. TSH is 85 mIU/L and free T4 is very low. There is no focal neurological deficit.
qx.q: Which diagnosis best accounts for her psychosis?
opts: Alzheimer disease with psychosis
Primary psychotic disorder
Dementia with Lewy bodies
Severe hypothyroidism (myxoedema madness), which usually improves with careful thyroid replacement
Frontotemporal dementia
qx.why: Overt hypothyroidism can cause slowed thinking, apathy and somnolence, and in severe cases confusion, delirium or psychosis (myxoedema madness), which generally improves with thyroid hormone replacement started cautiously, especially in older people with heart disease. Other dementias would not explain the biochemistry or the subacute course. Thyroid function should be checked in every cognitive or psychiatric presentation.

name: Hypoxic ischaemic encephalopathy (HIE)
formal: Brain injury from inadequate oxygen and blood flow, classically after cardiac arrest or perinatal asphyxia, causing coma, seizures, myoclonus and watershed or deep grey matter infarction.
simple: Brain damage from a lack of oxygen and blood flow, for example after a cardiac arrest or a difficult birth.
th: สมองบาดเจ็บจากขาดออกซิเจนและเลือดไปเลี้ยง เช่น หลังหัวใจหยุดเต้น หรือขาดออกซิเจนแรกเกิด ทำให้โคม่า ชัก myoclonus
tempoNote: Injury occurs over minutes; evolution of oedema and prognosis over 72 hours or more
feat: Coma after cardiac arrest, hanging, drowning or perinatal asphyxia
Selective vulnerability: cortex (layers 3, 5), hippocampus, basal ganglia, cerebellar Purkinje cells, watershed zones
Early myoclonus, status myoclonus, seizures
Survivors may have Lance-Adams action myoclonus, amnesia, or disorders of consciousness
Neonatal form graded by Sarnat stages
inv: Neurological exam after sedation wears off; pupillary and corneal reflexes
EEG (background, reactivity, burst suppression with identical bursts)
SSEP N20 responses; serum NSE at 48–72 hours
CT (loss of grey-white differentiation) and MRI DWI at 2–5 days

case.who: 54-year-old man from Nonthaburi resuscitated after 25 minutes of cardiac arrest from ventricular fibrillation
case.story: Comatose on day 4 despite sedation being stopped 48 hours earlier.
case.exam: No pupillary or corneal reflexes, generalised myoclonic jerks.
case.tests: EEG suppressed background with periodic discharges; bilateral absent N20; NSE 110 µg/L; MRI diffuse cortical diffusion restriction.
case.q: What does the combination of findings indicate?
case.a: Severe HIE with a very poor prognosis; multimodal predictors of poor outcome are concordant.

read.where: Chapter 28 Disorders of Consciousness and Intensive Care Neurology — Hypoxic–Ischaemic Brain Injury

det.patho: Global hypoperfusion or hypoxaemia depletes ATP, causing excitotoxic glutamate release, calcium influx and neuronal death. Reperfusion adds free radical injury and inflammation. Neurons in specific cortical layers, hippocampus CA1, basal ganglia and Purkinje cells are most vulnerable; watershed regions suffer in hypotension.
det.clinical: Adults present in coma after cardiac arrest. Early myoclonus may reflect severe injury but is not always fatal. Outcome ranges from full recovery to unresponsive wakefulness or death. Neonatal HIE presents with encephalopathy, seizures and hypotonia after a sentinel perinatal event. Long-term survivors may have action myoclonus, memory deficits and spasticity.
det.diagnosis: Prognostication should be multimodal and delayed until at least 72 hours after return of circulation and sedation clearance. Poor-outcome predictors include bilaterally absent pupillary and corneal reflexes, bilaterally absent N20, high NSE, highly malignant EEG patterns, and diffuse injury on CT/MRI. Exclude confounders: sedation, hypothermia, metabolic disturbance, and non-convulsive status.
det.treatment: Post-arrest care focuses on temperature control (active prevention of fever; targeted hypothermia remains debated in adults), maintaining adequate BP and oxygenation, glucose control and treating seizures. Therapeutic hypothermia for 72 hours is standard for moderate to severe neonatal HIE in term infants. Rehabilitation for survivors; levetiracetam, clonazepam or piracetam for Lance-Adams myoclonus.
det.prognosis: Highly variable; prognosis depends on duration of arrest and concordance of multimodal tests.
pearls: Do not prognosticate before 72 hours, and never from one test alone.
Early myoclonus is not automatically a death sentence; check EEG.
Lance-Adams action myoclonus emerges in awake survivors.
det.thd: Hypoxic ischaemic encephalopathy คือสมองบาดเจ็บจากขาดออกซิเจนและเลือด เช่น หลังหัวใจหยุดเต้นหรือขาดออกซิเจนแรกเกิด ผู้ป่วยมักโคม่า ชัก หรือมี myoclonus การพยากรณ์โรคต้องรออย่างน้อย 72 ชั่วโมงและใช้หลายวิธีร่วมกัน เช่น การตรวจร่างกาย EEG SSEP NSE และ MRI การรักษาคือควบคุมอุณหภูมิ ความดัน ออกซิเจน และรักษาการชัก ส่วนทารกแรกเกิดใช้ therapeutic hypothermia

qx.stem: A term girl with moderate-to-severe encephalopathy after placental abruption is started on therapeutic hypothermia within 4 hours. Serial EEG recordings are reviewed with the family at 72 hours, at the end of cooling.
qx.q: Which EEG finding at this time most strongly predicts death or severe disability?
opts: Continuous mixed-frequency activity with emerging sleep–wake cycling
Occasional sharp transients over the frontal regions during quiet sleep
Mild excess of discontinuity that improved from day 1 to day 3
Persistently low-voltage or burst-suppression background with no state change or reactivity
Brief rhythmic delta bursts over the temporal regions in active sleep
qx.why: In cooled neonates, a background that remains severely suppressed or burst-suppressed without cycling or reactivity beyond 48–72 hours carries a poor prognosis. Early recovery of continuity and sleep–wake cycling predicts favourable outcome. Frontal sharp transients and temporal rhythmic delta in sleep are normal maturational features in term and near-term infants.

qx.stem: A 61-year-old man from Samut Prakan remains comatose 72 hours after an out-of-hospital ventricular fibrillation arrest and temperature management with normothermia. He has had no sedation for 24 hours. The motor score is 1, pupillary and corneal reflexes are absent, bilateral N20 somatosensory potentials are absent and MRI at day 3 shows diffuse cortical diffusion restriction.
qx.q: What is the correct interpretation?
opts: The prognosis is good, since MRI abnormalities are always reversible
Two or more concordant poor-outcome predictors support a very likely poor neurological outcome, which should be discussed with the family while still treating as a multimodal decision
One absent pupillary reflex is sufficient on its own to withdraw care
Prognosis cannot be estimated until 3 weeks have passed
EEG should be ignored in all cases
qx.why: Current European and North American recommendations advise a multimodal approach after 72 hours, free of sedation and confounders: two or more concordant predictors, such as absent pupillary and corneal reflexes, bilaterally absent N20, high NSE, malignant EEG patterns or extensive diffusion restriction, indicate a poor outcome with a low false-positive rate. No single test should be used alone, and families should be counselled that it is a probability.

name: Hysterical hyperekplexia
formal: Functional startle disorder with exaggerated, non-habituating startle responses and abnormal posturing that lack the features of genetic hyperekplexia and are inconsistent with distraction.
simple: A psychologically driven, exaggerated startle reaction to sudden stimuli that is not due to structural brain disease.
th: การสะดุ้งตกใจที่มากผิดปกติแบบ functional ไม่ลดลงเมื่อถูกกระตุ้นซ้ำและมีท่าทางแปลก โดยไม่มีลักษณะของ hereditary hyperekplexia และเปลี่ยนไปเมื่อเบี่ยงความสนใจ
tempoNote: Episodes triggered by sudden stimuli; onset often abrupt in adulthood, sometimes after a physical or emotional event
feat: Exaggerated, variable startle to noise or touch with dramatic, prolonged or elaborate responses
Latency of response longer than true brainstem startle and inconsistent pattern between trials
Poor or absent habituation; reduced with distraction
No neonatal stiffness, no family history, no falls with injury like hereditary forms
Often coexists with other functional symptoms, pain or anxiety
inv: Polymyography of startle: long and variable latency, no rostrocaudal brainstem pattern, no blink-first sequence
MRI brainstem usually normal; consider GLRA1 testing only if neonatal or familial features
Exclude stiff-person spectrum (anti-GAD, anti-glycine receptor antibodies) when stiffness is present

case.story: Since a road accident a year ago she jumps violently, screams and sometimes falls to her knees whenever a phone rings or someone touches her shoulder.
case.exam: Startle to a hand clap is delayed and theatrical with arm flinging; repeated claps do not reduce it, but it disappears while she counts backwards.
case.tests: EMG startle study: variable latency over 100 ms without orderly brainstem spread; anti-GAD and glycine receptor antibodies negative.
case.q: Is this hyperekplexia and how should it be explained to her?
case.a: Functional (psychogenic) startle disorder; explain it as a real, treatable brain-function problem and refer for specialist physiotherapy and CBT.

det.patho: Functional movement disorders arise from abnormal attention, expectation and sense of agency over movement rather than structural damage. In functional startle, the normal brainstem reflex is followed or replaced by a learned, voluntary-appearing pattern generated by higher brain networks. Precipitating physical events, anxiety and prior experiences of startle-related trauma are common contributors.
det.clinical: Patients describe uncontrollable dramatic jumps, cries, flailing or collapses in response to unexpected sounds or touch. Responses vary in form and duration, sometimes with posturing or prolonged shaking. They often worsen in medical settings and with attention, and improve when the person is engaged in a task. Many have other functional symptoms such as functional tremor or dissociative seizures.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis relies on positive clinical signs — variability, distractibility, lack of habituation and incongruent features — rather than only exclusion. Startle neurophysiology helps: true reticular startle has short latency (about 50–100 ms in proximal muscles) and an ordered spread, whereas functional responses are delayed and inconsistent. Exclude hereditary hyperekplexia, glycine receptor antibody disease and brainstem pathology when features suggest them.
det.treatment: Explain the diagnosis clearly and without stigma, emphasising that symptoms are real and reversible. Specialist physiotherapy for functional movement disorders, CBT and treatment of comorbid anxiety, depression or PTSD form the core. Avoid unnecessary drugs such as high-dose clonazepam unless for anxiety. Follow-up should reinforce self-management techniques.
det.prognosis: Variable; better outcomes with short duration, acceptance of the diagnosis and engagement with rehabilitation.
pearls: A true startle is fast and stereotyped; a functional startle is slow and variable.
Lack of habituation alone does not prove an organic cause.
Check glycine receptor antibodies when startle comes with stiffness.
det.thd: Hysterical hyperekplexia หรือ functional startle คืออาการสะดุ้งตกใจรุนแรงผิดปกติจากการทำงานของสมองแบบ functional ไม่ใช่จากโรคพันธุกรรม การสะดุ้งจะช้า ไม่สม่ำเสมอ และลดลงเมื่อเบี่ยงความสนใจ ต่างจาก hereditary hyperekplexia ที่เริ่มตั้งแต่แรกเกิดและตอบสนองเร็วคงที่ การตรวจ EMG ช่วยแยก รักษาด้วยการอธิบายโรคอย่างเข้าใจ กายภาพบำบัดเฉพาะทาง และ CBT

ddx.pt: Neonatal stiffness, nose-tap startle, injurious falls; GLRA1/SLC6A5 variants
Brainstem lesion, hypoxic injury or stiff-person spectrum with abnormal antibodies or MRI
Startle triggers true seizures with EEG changes, usually with a structural lesion

name: Iatrogenic Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease
formal: Prion disease transmitted by medical procedures, such as contaminated neurosurgical instruments, dura mater grafts or human growth hormone, with long incubation before progressive dementia and ataxia.
simple: A rare form of CJD passed on by contaminated medical equipment or tissue products, appearing years after exposure.
th: iCJD เป็นโรคพรีออนที่ติดต่อจากหัตถการทางการแพทย์ เช่น ฮอร์โมนการเจริญเติบโตจากต่อมใต้สมองศพ การปลูกถ่าย dura mater กระจกตา และเครื่องมือผ่าตัดสมอง ระยะฟักตัวนานหลายปีถึงหลายสิบปี แล้วจึงมีเดินเซและสมองเสื่อมเร็ว
tempoNote: Incubation of about 1.5 to over 30 years (mean about 12 for dura, 17 for growth hormone, 1.6 for neurosurgical instruments); after symptoms start, decline over months
feat: Exposure history: cadaveric dura mater graft (mostly Lyodura), pituitary-derived growth hormone or gonadotrophin, corneal transplant, or neurosurgery or depth electrodes with contaminated instruments
Peripheral routes (growth hormone) usually start with cerebellar ataxia; dura grafts give cerebellar and visual signs with dementia; direct brain exposure has a short incubation
Rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, visual, pyramidal and extrapyramidal signs resembling sCJD
About 400 cases to date; 253 from growth hormone (France, UK, USA), more than 240 from dura grafts (Japan about 156)
Dura exposures ended after a sodium hydroxide step was added in 1987, but cases from remote exposure still appear; the lymphoreticular system is not involved
inv: MRI DWI/FLAIR: cortical ribboning and basal ganglia signal in many, but some growth-hormone cases show deep-nuclei or cerebellar signal or only atrophy
CSF RT-QuIC and 14-3-3; in a series of 23 cases the sensitivity of CSF markers, MRI and EEG was similar to sCJD
PRNP sequencing excludes a genetic cause; codon 129 genotype is recorded
Exposure tracing and notification of public-health authorities, with quarantine or destruction of instruments

case.story: More than three decades ago he had a craniotomy abroad with a cadaveric dural graft. Now 10 weeks of clumsy hands, falls, blurred vision and word-finding trouble.
case.exam: Gait and limb ataxia, right lower visual field defect, startle myoclonus, impaired recall; no family history.
case.tests: MRI DWI shows cortical ribboning and caudate restriction with matching ADC; CSF RT-QuIC positive; PRNP wild type; tonsil biopsy not needed.
case.q: What is the likely mechanism, and which two actions follow?
case.a: Iatrogenic CJD from a contaminated dura graft with a very long incubation; notify infection control and public health, and manage neurosurgical equipment under prion rules (single-use or destroy).

read.where: Chapter 95 Prion Diseases — Acquired Prion Disease: Iatrogenic Prion Disease, Table of iatrogenic cases and prion decontamination
CJD board tutorial — iatrogenic causes and spectrum table
Chapter 11 Cognitive Impairment and Dementia — Acquired Prion Diseases

det.patho: Misfolded prions on contaminated instruments, tissue grafts or hormone preparations seed conversion of the recipient's PrPC. Prions bind strongly to metal and survive ordinary sterilisation, and human prions are harder to inactivate than the animal strains used in many disinfection studies. The route determines the incubation: direct brain contact gives about 1.5 years, dura grafts about 12 years and peripheral growth hormone about 17 years, with long tails to 30–40 years especially in codon 129 heterozygotes.
det.clinical: Growth-hormone recipients typically begin with cerebellar ataxia and later develop dementia, whereas dura graft recipients show ataxia, visual disturbance and dementia, and neurosurgical or depth-electrode cases show visual and cognitive changes early. Myoclonus, pyramidal and extrapyramidal signs and akinetic mutism follow as in sCJD. Cases from corneal transplants and from instruments are few. The number of new iCJD cases is falling, but remote exposures from decades earlier continue to surface, and contamination of instruments still occurs despite WHO guidance.
det.diagnosis: Use the same RT-QuIC-based approach as for sCJD, adding an exposure history (graft, hormone injections, neurosurgery) and PRNP sequencing. PrPSc is not found in the lymphoreticular system, so tonsil biopsy is not useful. Diagnostic yield of CSF biomarkers, MRI and EEG resembles sCJD, but growth-hormone cases may show atrophy, cerebellar or deep nuclear signal instead of cortical ribboning. Definite diagnosis relies on neuropathology.
det.treatment: Treatment is symptomatic and palliative as for other prion diseases. Prevention depends on decontamination: WHO-preferred methods include steam sterilisation at 132 °C for at least 30 minutes in a gravity-displacement autoclave, but because even that may be inadequate, single-use instruments or incineration of exposed equipment is recommended. Trace and counsel people who shared exposure to the same batch or instrument set, and notify surveillance.
det.prognosis: Fatal within months to about 1 year after symptom onset in most; the disease is now rare because recombinant growth hormone and synthetic dural substitutes replaced cadaveric products.
pearls: A young-ish patient with ataxia-first CJD should be asked about neurosurgery, dural grafts and childhood hormone injections.
Incubation can exceed 30 years, so a graft decades ago is still relevant.
Tonsil biopsy is positive in vCJD but not in iatrogenic or sporadic disease.

qx.stem: A 45-year-old man received injections of growth hormone prepared from cadaveric pituitary glands as a child for short stature. He now has three months of gait ataxia and dysarthria followed by memory loss and myoclonus. CSF RT-QuIC is positive, PRNP is wild type and he has no family history.
qx.q: Which statement about his illness is most accurate?
opts: Tonsil biopsy will show abnormal prion protein, as in variant CJD
A PRNP mutation is required for this form and the negative gene test makes the diagnosis unlikely
Peripheral exposure to growth hormone typically presents with cerebellar signs, and the incubation can last on average more than a decade
He is a risk to household contacts through coughing and shared meals
Incubation is always under two years, so the exposure in childhood is irrelevant
qx.why: Growth-hormone-related iatrogenic CJD usually starts with cerebellar dysfunction after a mean incubation of about 17 years (range roughly 5–30 or more). The lymphoreticular system is generally not involved in iatrogenic disease, so tonsil biopsy is not helpful; no mutation is involved, and prions are not transmitted by casual contact. Surveillance and prion precautions for instruments are still needed.

name: ICCA syndrome
formal: Familial syndrome linking infantile convulsions with later paroxysmal choreoathetosis, autosomal dominant, from PRRT2 mutation; benign infantile seizures respond well to carbamazepine.
simple: An inherited condition in which a baby has seizures and later in childhood or adulthood has episodes of writhing movements.
th: กลุ่มอาการทางพันธุกรรมยีนเด่น PRRT2 ที่มีชักในขวบปีแรกซึ่งหายเองได้ แล้วต่อมาในวัยเด็กหรือวัยรุ่นเกิดอาการกระตุกบิดเกร็งสั้น ๆ เมื่อขยับตัวทันที ตอบสนองดีต่อ carbamazepine ขนาดต่ำ
tempoNote: Clusters of afebrile infant seizures at 3–12 months that remit by age 2; brief movement-triggered attacks start years later, usually in late childhood or teens
feat: Afebrile focal seizures, often in clusters, in an otherwise normal infant, with normal development afterwards
Later brief (seconds, under a minute) attacks of dystonia or chorea set off by a sudden movement such as standing up or starting to run
Awareness kept during the dyskinetic attacks; many attacks a day are possible
Strong family history across generations (dominant, incomplete penetrance); relatives may have only seizures or only dyskinesia
Other PRRT2 relatives can have hemiplegic migraine or episodic ataxia
inv: Interictal EEG and brain MRI are typically normal
PRRT2 testing (a common single-base duplication accounts for many families); 16p11.2 deletions also include PRRT2
Home video of attacks helps separate dyskinesia from seizures or functional events

case.story: For a year he freezes and twists his right arm for about 10 seconds whenever he jumps up from his desk or starts a sprint, many times a day. His mother says he had several seizures at 6 months that stopped without long treatment.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination between attacks; an attack is provoked by asking him to rise quickly, showing right arm dystonia with full awareness.
case.tests: EEG and MRI brain normal; his father had the same attacks as a teenager.
case.q: What is the likely gene and the first-line treatment?
case.a: PRRT2 (ICCA syndrome: infantile seizures followed by paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia); low-dose carbamazepine usually stops attacks.

read.where: Chapter 24 Paroxysmal dyskinesias: Paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia (p925)

det.patho: PRRT2 encodes a presynaptic protein that interacts with the vesicle-release machinery and modulates sodium channel availability; loss of function leaves neurons more excitable. In infancy the excess excitability shows up in cortex as seizures, while in later childhood it seems to affect basal ganglia and cerebellar circuits, giving movement-triggered dyskinesia. It is dominantly inherited but incompletely penetrant, so carriers may be unaffected.
det.clinical: Seizures begin in the middle of the first year, often as clusters of focal events with or without bilateral spread, and stop by early childhood whatever the treatment. Years later, around 5–15 years of age, sudden movements trigger short dystonic or choreic attacks, sometimes preceded by a tingling aura; consciousness is intact. Some family members have only one component, and the same variant can also cause hemiplegic migraine or episodic ataxia. Attack frequency usually falls in adulthood.
det.diagnosis: The history is characteristic: a normal infant with self-remitting seizures, then kinesigenic attacks with a normal examination and normal EEG and MRI between episodes. Video of an attack is very helpful. Confirm with PRRT2 sequencing and copy-number analysis; a negative result does not exclude the clinical diagnosis, as other genes (for example TMEM151A) occasionally cause similar pictures. Rule out functional events and frontal lobe seizures when the trigger is unclear.
det.treatment: Infant seizures respond readily to sodium channel blockers and are usually treated only briefly. For kinesigenic dyskinesia, low-dose carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine typically abolishes attacks; lamotrigine or other sodium channel agents are alternatives if not tolerated. Patients can learn to avoid abrupt starts. Offer genetic counselling to the family.
det.prognosis: Excellent: infant seizures remit and dyskinesia responds to treatment and tends to lessen with age; development is normal.
pearls: Infant seizures that stopped plus teenage attacks on sudden standing: think PRRT2.
Dramatic response to a small dose of carbamazepine supports kinesigenic dyskinesia.
Normal EEG during or between attacks does not mean the events are functional.
det.thd: ICCA syndrome เกิดจากยีน PRRT2 ถ่ายทอดแบบยีนเด่น เด็กมีชักเป็นชุดช่วงอายุ 3–12 เดือนแล้วหายเอง พัฒนาการปกติ ต่อมาในวัยเด็กโตหรือวัยรุ่นจะมีอาการบิดเกร็งหรือกระตุกสั้น ๆ ไม่กี่วินาทีเมื่อเปลี่ยนท่าทันที โดยยังรู้สึกตัวดี EEG และ MRI ปกติ ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน และรักษาด้วย carbamazepine ขนาดต่ำซึ่งได้ผลดีมาก

name: Ideational/conceptual apraxia
formal: Apraxia from failure of the concept of an action, so patients misuse objects and cannot sequence multi-step tasks, due to dominant parietal or diffuse lesions as in Alzheimer disease.
simple: Loss of understanding of how to use objects or plan a sequence of actions, even though muscles work normally.
more: Failure to conceive or sequence the actions of an object use despite intact motor function, with lesion of the left parietal or temporal region; seen in Alzheimer disease.
th: ภาวะที่ผู้ป่วยไม่เข้าใจแนวคิดของการใช้สิ่งของหรือเรียงลำดับขั้นตอนการทำงานผิด แม้กล้ามเนื้อปกติ พบในรอยโรคสมองซีกเด่นส่วน parietal หรือ Alzheimer
tempoNote: Acute after stroke; progressive in Alzheimer and corticobasal degeneration
feat: Uses objects for the wrong purpose (e.g. tries to write with a comb)
Cannot sequence multi-step tasks (making tea, lighting a candle) in the right order
Strength, sensation and coordination adequate to perform the movement
Often coexists with aphasia and ideomotor apraxia
Causes marked disability in daily living (dressing, cooking, hygiene)
inv: Bedside: ask patient to demonstrate a multi-step task with real objects and to match tools to actions
Language assessment to exclude comprehension failure
MRI brain for left parietal/temporal stroke or atrophy pattern

case.story: Temple staff notice he puts toothpaste on his comb and tries to light incense by pressing it on the matchbox.
case.exam: Understands commands, good strength; when given tea, cup and kettle he pours water before opening the lid and stirs with a spoon handle.
case.tests: MRI shows bilateral parietal and hippocampal atrophy, worse on the left.
case.q: Which apraxia is this and how does it differ from ideomotor apraxia?
case.a: Ideational/conceptual apraxia — knowledge and sequence of action are lost; in ideomotor apraxia the patient knows what to do but the spatial/temporal execution of the gesture is faulty, especially to command.

det.patho: Skilled tool use depends on stored knowledge of what objects are for and how actions are sequenced, which relies largely on left parietal and temporal cortex and their frontal connections. Damage to these semantic-action systems disrupts the concept of the action rather than its motor execution. Terminology varies: some authors separate conceptual apraxia (wrong tool or action knowledge) from ideational apraxia (wrong sequence).
det.clinical: Patients misuse objects, pick the wrong tool, or perform steps of a familiar task in the wrong order, even though they can move normally. Errors appear with real objects, distinguishing it from purely gestural deficits. It is seen after left hemisphere stroke and in moderate Alzheimer disease, corticobasal degeneration and some semantic dementias. It greatly impairs activities of daily living and home safety.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical: observe real multi-step tasks, tool selection and tool-action matching after confirming adequate comprehension, strength and sensation. Apraxia batteries quantify it. Imaging identifies the lesion or atrophy pattern.
det.treatment: Treat the cause. Occupational therapy using strategy training, errorless learning and environmental adaptation helps; simplify tasks and supervise for safety (stoves, sharp objects). Carer education is essential.
det.prognosis: Partial recovery is possible after stroke; in neurodegenerative disease it worsens.
pearls: Test with real objects and multi-step tasks, not just pantomime.
Wrong tool or wrong order = ideational; right idea, clumsy gesture = ideomotor.
Exclude aphasic comprehension failure before calling it apraxia.
det.thd: Ideational/conceptual apraxia คือภาวะที่ผู้ป่วยไม่รู้ว่าสิ่งของใช้ทำอะไร หรือเรียงขั้นตอนงานผิด เช่น ใช้หวีแปรงฟัน รินน้ำก่อนเปิดฝากาน้ำ ทั้งที่แขนขาแข็งแรงและเข้าใจคำสั่ง พบในรอยโรคสมองซีกซ้ายส่วน parietal และใน Alzheimer หรือ corticobasal degeneration ตรวจโดยให้ทำงานหลายขั้นตอนด้วยของจริง การรักษาคือแก้สาเหตุ กิจกรรมบำบัด และดูแลความปลอดภัย

name: Ideomotor apraxia
formal: Apraxia with impaired performance of skilled movements to command or imitation, with intact object use in context, due to dominant parietal or premotor lesions or the corpus callosum.
simple: Difficulty carrying out learned gestures, such as waving goodbye, on request even though the person understands and has normal strength.
th: ความบกพร่องในการทำท่าทางที่เรียนรู้มาตามคำสั่งหรือเลียนแบบ ทั้งที่เข้าใจคำสั่ง กำลังและความรู้สึกปกติ และมักใช้วัตถุจริงได้ดีกว่า มักเกิดจากรอยโรคสมองซีกเด่นส่วน parietal หรือ premotor
tempoNote: Acute after stroke; subacute or progressive when caused by tumour, corticobasal degeneration or Alzheimer disease
feat: Poor performance of skilled gestures to command (waving goodbye, saluting, pretending to brush teeth)
Errors in the timing, sequencing and spatial orientation of movements, or using a body part as the object
Imitation is also poor, though performance often improves with real objects in daily life
Not explained by weakness, sensory loss, ataxia or failure to understand the instruction
Bilateral deficit from a left hemisphere lesion; a callosal lesion may spare the right hand and affect only the left
inv: Bedside testing of gestures to command, imitation and real object use, with comprehension checked first
MRI brain for left parietal, premotor or supplementary motor area lesion, white matter tract or callosal infarct
Formal neuropsychological assessment when the cause is degenerative

case.story: After a left parietal infarct, he can hold a toothbrush correctly but cannot show the examiner how he brushes his teeth on command. His family notices clumsy gestures when asked to wave or salute.
case.exam: Fluent speech and good comprehension, mild right arm weakness (4+/5), normal sensation. Pantomime of tools is poor, with hand used as the tool, and improves with the real object.
case.tests: MRI shows a subacute infarct involving the supramarginal gyrus and adjacent left inferior parietal cortex; swallowing and vision are normal.
case.q: How can apraxia be distinguished from weakness or aphasia in this patient?
case.a: Strength is only mildly reduced and comprehension is intact, so the failure to perform learned gestures to command and imitation reflects ideomotor apraxia.

det.patho: Ideomotor apraxia reflects disruption of motor programming for learned skilled movement. The left parietal cortex stores movement representations that are conveyed through the supplementary motor and premotor areas to the primary motor cortex. Lesions of the parietal association cortex, supplementary motor area or the connecting white matter, including the corpus callosum, impair planning without affecting basic motor function.
det.clinical: Patients carry out gestures poorly when asked, make spatial and temporal errors and may use a body part as the tool. They often do better with real objects in natural settings, so the deficit may be missed in daily life. A left supplementary motor area infarct causes more severe impairment in the contralateral limbs, but even the unaffected-side limb performs poorly. Callosal lesions disconnect language and motor areas and can produce left hand apraxia. Associated aphasia, hemiparesis and neglect are frequent.
det.diagnosis: Check that language comprehension and basic strength are sufficient, then ask the patient to show symbolic and tool-use gestures to command and by imitation, and compare with performance when real objects are provided. Brain imaging identifies the responsible lesion in stroke, tumour or degenerative disease. Formal batteries are used in research and in rehabilitation planning.
det.treatment: Treatment targets the cause, for example secondary prevention after stroke, and rehabilitation. Occupational therapy uses gesture and strategy training, error-reduction, and use of real objects and cues in functional tasks. Caregivers should be taught that the difficulty is not due to lack of effort. Evidence for specific drug therapy is lacking.
det.prognosis: Often improves in the weeks to months after stroke; progressive causes tend to worsen.
pearls: Test with real objects and with pantomime; apraxia often shows only in pantomime.
Left-hemisphere lesions cause bilateral limb apraxia; callosal lesions may affect only the left hand.
Apraxia in only one limb with rigidity or myoclonus suggests corticobasal syndrome.
det.thd: Ideomotor apraxia คือการทำท่าทางที่เรียนรู้มาตามคำสั่งหรือเลียนแบบได้ไม่ดี ทั้งที่เข้าใจคำสั่งและกำลังกล้ามเนื้อปกติ มักเกิดจากรอยโรคส่วน parietal หรือ premotor ซีกซ้าย รวมถึง supplementary motor area และ corpus callosum ตรวจโดยให้ทำท่าทาง เช่น โบกมือลา แล้วเปรียบเทียบกับการใช้วัตถุจริง การรักษาคือแก้สาเหตุและทำกิจกรรมบำบัดแบบฝึกท่าทางและใช้สิ่งของช่วย

name: IDH-mutant diffuse glioma
formal: WHO-defined astrocytoma or oligodendroglioma with IDH1 or IDH2 mutation, typically young adults, with favourable prognosis; oligodendroglioma also has 1p19q codeletion.
simple: A slow-growing type of brain tumour in younger adults that carries a particular genetic change and has a better outlook.
more: Diffuse glioma family with IDH mutation, including astrocytomas with ATRX and TP53 changes and 1p19q-codeleted oligodendrogliomas, associated with longer survival than IDH-wildtype tumours.
th: กลุ่ม glioma ผู้ใหญ่ที่มี IDH1/2 mutation ประกอบด้วย astrocytoma IDH-mutant (เกรด 2-4) และ oligodendroglioma ที่มี 1p/19q codeletion (เกรด 2-3) ปัจจุบันมียา vorasidenib สำหรับเกรด 2 ที่เหลือหลังผ่าตัด
tempoNote: Grade 2 lesions behave over years with seizures as the main event; grade 3 and 4 progress over weeks to months
feat: Young to middle-aged adults (typically 25-50 years) with a first seizure and normal examination
Frontal and temporal lobes are favoured; oligodendrogliomas are cortical and calcified, astrocytomas more white-matter based
The IDH mutation creates 2-hydroxyglutarate, detectable by MR spectroscopy, and gives a better prognosis than IDH-wildtype glioma at the same grade
ATRX loss with TP53 mutation defines the astrocytoma branch; 1p/19q codeletion with TERT promoter mutation defines the oligodendroglioma branch
A T2-FLAIR mismatch sign (homogeneous T2 bright mass with a dark FLAIR rim) is very specific for IDH-mutant astrocytoma without codeletion
inv: MRI with contrast, spectroscopy for 2-hydroxyglutarate, and perfusion to guide biopsy
IDH1 R132H immunohistochemistry plus sequencing of IDH1/2 when the stain is negative in a patient under 55
ATRX, p53, 1p/19q (FISH or methylation array), CDKN2A/B, TERT promoter and MGMT
DNA methylation classification where available to resolve borderline cases

case.story: A single generalised seizure at night; examination later is normal, and she wants to continue night shifts.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination.
case.tests: MRI: non-enhancing right frontal mass, T2 homogeneous bright with a dark FLAIR rim. Resection with small residual: IDH1 R132H-mutant, ATRX lost, 1p/19q intact, CNS WHO grade 2.
case.q: What non-surgical treatment can she start now, and what should be explained before long-term use?
case.a: Vorasidenib 40 mg daily can delay progression in residual IDH-mutant grade 2 glioma. Counsel on liver enzyme monitoring, contraception and treatment duration; radiotherapy and chemotherapy are deferred until progression.

det.patho: A mutation in IDH1 (codon R132) or IDH2 makes the enzyme produce 2-hydroxyglutarate, which blocks histone and DNA demethylation and creates a hypermethylated state. IDH-mutant gliomas split into astrocytoma (ATRX loss, TP53 mutation) and oligodendroglioma (1p/19q codeletion, TERT promoter mutation, retained ATRX), according to WHO CNS5. The two share a better outlook than IDH-wildtype glioma, but astrocytomas have a shorter survival than oligodendrogliomas and may reach grade 4 through CDKN2A/B loss.
det.clinical: Seizures and a normal examination are typical at diagnosis. Cognitive change and fatigue may appear later and with treatment. Tumours grow slowly, are often large when found, and may transform with new enhancement. Frontal oligodendrogliomas can spread through the callosum or cause leptomeningeal seeding late in the course.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is by tissue with an integrated report. Immunostain for IDH1 R132H detects most IDH mutations; negative stain in a young patient needs sequencing. 1p/19q codeletion confirms oligodendroglioma, while loss of ATRX in the absence of codeletion points to astrocytoma. MRI features (calcification, T2-FLAIR mismatch) are supportive only. CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion upgrades astrocytomas to grade 4.
det.treatment: Resection to the safe maximum comes first. For grade 2 disease with residual tumour and no high-risk features, vorasidenib is now approved on the strength of the INDIGO trial and delays the need for radiotherapy and chemotherapy; dose is 40 mg daily with liver tests. Higher-grade or high-risk tumours receive radiotherapy plus PCV or temozolomide; oligodendroglioma shows the largest benefit from radiotherapy plus PCV. Seizure control, rehabilitation and cognitive assessment are part of ongoing care.
det.prognosis: Median survival ranges from about 10-15 years for grade 2 oligodendroglioma and 8-12 years for grade 2 astrocytoma to 3-5 years or less for grade 4 astrocytoma.
pearls: IDH1 R132H immunostain is a quick screen; negative in a patient under 55 means sequence IDH1/2.
1p/19q codeletion plus IDH mutation = oligodendroglioma; ATRX loss without codeletion = astrocytoma.
Vorasidenib is for residual or recurrent grade 2 only, not for glioblastoma.

simple: The most common and aggressive primary brain cancer in adults, which is hard to treat.

inv: MRI with contrast: irregular thick ring enhancement around necrosis with extensive FLAIR signal; perfusion shows high rCBV
Maximal safe resection or biopsy for histology plus molecular profile (IDH, TERT promoter, EGFR amplification, +7/−10, MGMT promoter methylation)
Body imaging only if metastasis is a realistic alternative

case.who: 61-year-old male tuk-tuk driver from Chiang Mai
case.story: Six weeks of worsening morning headache, then he started misjudging turns and his family noticed he was slow to answer.
case.exam: Left homonymous hemianopia, mild left hemiparesis, flattened affect.
case.tests: MRI: 5-cm right temporoparietal mass with irregular rim enhancement, central necrosis and wide oedema. Resection: IDH-wildtype, TERT promoter mutated, MGMT promoter methylated.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the standard post-operative treatment?
case.a: Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype (CNS WHO grade 4); radiotherapy 60 Gy in 30 fractions with daily temozolomide, then 6 cycles of adjuvant temozolomide (Stupp protocol); MGMT methylation predicts better response.

det.patho: Under WHO CNS5 (2021), an adult IDH-wildtype diffuse astrocytic glioma is graded 4 as glioblastoma if it shows necrosis or microvascular proliferation, or if it carries TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification or gain of chromosome 7 with loss of 10 — even when histology looks lower grade. Tumours arise from glial progenitors and infiltrate along white-matter tracts far beyond the enhancing rim. MGMT promoter methylation silences a DNA repair enzyme and makes tumour cells more vulnerable to temozolomide.
det.clinical: Presentation depends on location: headache from raised pressure, cognitive slowing, personality change, hemiparesis, aphasia or field cuts, and seizures. The course is weeks to months. Steroid-responsive oedema often causes early improvement. Venous thromboembolism, fatigue and steroid side effects are common through treatment.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows a heterogeneous, ring-enhancing mass with necrosis and surrounding T2/FLAIR signal; perfusion and spectroscopy help separate it from abscess, lymphoma and demyelination. Histology and molecular testing are needed for the integrated diagnosis. After chemoradiation, new enhancement within 12 weeks may be pseudoprogression rather than true progression; RANO criteria and perfusion imaging guide interpretation.
det.treatment: Standard care for fit patients is maximal safe resection followed by radiotherapy (60 Gy in 30 fractions) with concurrent daily temozolomide and then six adjuvant temozolomide cycles; tumour-treating fields can be added. Older or frailer patients receive short-course radiotherapy (e.g. 40 Gy in 15 fractions) with or without temozolomide, or temozolomide alone if MGMT is methylated. Dexamethasone controls oedema at the lowest effective dose; antiseizure medicine (often levetiracetam) only after seizures. At recurrence, options include re-resection, re-irradiation, lomustine or bevacizumab (which improves symptoms and progression-free time but not overall survival), and trials; early palliative care is important.
det.prognosis: Median survival is about 15–18 months with standard therapy and longer with MGMT methylation; long-term survival beyond 5 years is under 10%.
pearls: In adults, an IDH-wildtype astrocytoma with TERT, EGFR or +7/−10 is glioblastoma even without necrosis.
MGMT promoter methylation is the key predictive marker for temozolomide benefit.
New enhancement soon after chemoradiation may be pseudoprogression — don't stop treatment too early.
det.thd: Glioblastoma ชนิด IDH-wildtype เป็นมะเร็งสมองปฐมภูมิที่พบบ่อยและรุนแรงที่สุดในผู้ใหญ่ อาการปวดศีรษะ บุคลิกเปลี่ยน อ่อนแรง หรือชัก ภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์ MRI เป็นก้อนขอบจับสีไม่สม่ำเสมอ ตรงกลางตาย บวมรอบมาก วินิจฉัยจากพยาธิวิทยาร่วมกับ molecular marker (IDH, TERT, EGFR, MGMT) รักษาด้วยผ่าตัดเอาออกให้มากที่สุดอย่างปลอดภัย ตามด้วยฉายรังสีร่วม temozolomide (Stupp) MGMT methylation พยากรณ์ดีกว่า มัธยฐานการรอดชีวิตราว 15–18 เดือน

qx.stem: A 58-year-old school director from Phitsanulok presented with three weeks of word-finding difficulty. MRI showed a ring-enhancing left temporal mass with central necrosis. After gross total resection, the tumour is IDH-wildtype with MGMT promoter methylation and EGFR amplification. He completed 60 Gy radiotherapy with daily temozolomide and has a Karnofsky score of 90.
qx.q: Which addition to maintenance temozolomide has shown an overall survival benefit in a phase 3 trial?
opts: Lomustine with procarbazine and vincristine
Prophylactic craniospinal radiotherapy
Tumour-treating fields applied with scalp arrays for most of each day
Vorasidenib
Low-dose dexamethasone for one year
qx.why: In EF-14, adding tumour-treating fields to maintenance temozolomide improved both progression-free and overall survival in newly diagnosed glioblastoma, so it is offered to fit patients after chemoradiation. Vorasidenib applies only to IDH-mutant tumours, PCV is used for oligodendroglioma, craniospinal radiotherapy has no place here, and steroids should be tapered rather than continued.

qx.stem: A 63-year-old rice farmer from Roi Et has had six weeks of worsening headache and left-hand clumsiness. MRI shows a heterogeneous right frontal mass with a thick, irregular, nodular enhancing rim around a necrotic centre. The tumour extends across the genu of the corpus callosum, with extensive surrounding T2/FLAIR hyperintensity. Perfusion imaging shows markedly raised relative cerebral blood volume in the rim.
qx.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis and the most appropriate next step?
opts: Cerebral abscess; start empirical antibiotics and aspirate in a week
Tumefactive demyelination; give pulse methylprednisolone and repeat MRI
Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype; plan maximal safe resection with tissue for molecular testing, then chemoradiation
Solitary metastasis; resect without further work-up
Subacute infarct; start antiplatelet therapy
qx.why: A thick irregular enhancing rim with central necrosis, callosal crossing and high rCBV is the classic picture of glioblastoma, which WHO CNS5 defines as an IDH-wildtype astrocytic tumour. Tissue is needed for IDH, MGMT and TERT testing before temozolomide-based chemoradiation. An abscess has a thin smooth rim with restricted diffusion centrally, and demyelination typically shows an open-ring enhancement with low perfusion.

ddx.pt: Known or occult primary, often multiple, at the grey–white junction with smaller tumour-to-oedema ratio
Homogeneous periventricular enhancement, little necrosis in immunocompetent patients, rapid steroid response
Smooth thin capsule with central diffusion restriction, fever and infection source

name: Idiopathic axonal neuropathy (IAN)
formal: Slowly progressive, mainly sensory distal axonal neuropathy in older people, with no identified cause after exhaustive work-up, diagnosed by exclusion.
simple: A slowly worsening nerve problem causing numbness and tingling in the feet, with no cause found.
more: Distal, mostly sensory length-dependent axonal polyneuropathy of unknown cause in older adults, slowly progressive, with normal evaluation for secondary causes.
th: เส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเสื่อมแบบ axonal ในผู้สูงอายุ ส่วนใหญ่เป็นด้านรับความรู้สึก หาสาเหตุไม่พบ
tempoNote: Slowly progressive over years
feat: Onset after 50 with distal sensory symptoms
Mild distal motor weakness in some
Absent ankle reflexes
Slow progression, rarely severe disability
Associated with metabolic syndrome in many
inv: Comprehensive screen for causes: glucose tolerance, B12, paraprotein, TSH, renal, liver
NCS: axonal length-dependent pattern
Consider genetic testing if family history or foot deformity

case.story: Numb feet and mild unsteadiness for 6 years, slowly worse.
case.exam: Absent ankle jerks, stocking sensory loss to mid-calf, mild toe extensor weakness.
case.tests: Extensive work-up normal; NCS shows axonal sensorimotor neuropathy.
case.q: What advice regarding prognosis?
case.a: Usually slow progression with low risk of severe disability; manage symptoms and review periodically.

read.where: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves — Idiopathic Axonal Neuropathy

det.patho: Idiopathic by definition. Contributors may include prediabetes, dyslipidaemia, obesity and age-related axonal vulnerability.
det.clinical: Slowly ascending distal sensory loss, often with pain and mild motor signs. Rapid progression or asymmetry should prompt reconsideration.
det.diagnosis: Requires thorough exclusion of known causes and an axonal length-dependent pattern on NCS. Repeat testing for paraprotein and glucose over time can uncover a cause.
det.treatment: Neuropathic pain medication, foot care, exercise and management of metabolic risk factors.
det.prognosis: Benign course in most; disability is uncommon.
pearls: Repeat the work-up if the course changes.
Metabolic syndrome components are common and modifiable.
Family history and foot deformities suggest a hereditary neuropathy.
det.thd: IAN คือเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเสื่อมชนิด axonal ในผู้สูงอายุที่หาสาเหตุไม่พบหลังตรวจครบ อาการชาปลายเท้าลามขึ้นช้าๆ อาจอ่อนแรงเล็กน้อย การรักษาคือคุมปัจจัยเมตาบอลิก ใช้ยาลดปวด ดูแลเท้า และติดตามเป็นระยะ

Family history, pes cavus and onset earlier in life

name: Idiopathic choreic syndromes
formal: Choreic disorders with no secondary cause, including benign hereditary chorea and senile chorea, as well as unexplained sporadic chorea, after genetic and metabolic exclusion.
simple: Jerky, dance-like movements for which doctors cannot find a clear cause.
th: chorea ที่หาสาเหตุไม่ได้ รวมถึง benign hereditary chorea และ senile chorea หลังตรวจสาเหตุทางพันธุกรรมและเมตาบอลิกครบแล้ว
tempoNote: Benign hereditary chorea starts in childhood and is static or improves; senile chorea begins late in life and is slowly progressive
feat: Chorea without cognitive or psychiatric decline and without an identifiable secondary cause
Benign hereditary chorea: early childhood onset, non-progressive, often with hypotonia, thyroid and lung problems (NKX2-1)
Senile chorea: late-onset generalised or orofacial chorea; diagnosis increasingly shrinking as HD and vascular causes are found
Label applies only after exclusion of Huntington disease, drugs, autoimmune, metabolic and structural causes
inv: HTT CAG repeat (even with negative family history), then NKX2-1, ADCY5, PDE10A and HD-like genes
Glucose, thyroid, calcium, polycythaemia, antiphospholipid and lupus antibodies, acanthocytes, autoimmune encephalitis panel if subacute
MRI brain (striatal hyperintensity in non-ketotic hyperglycaemia, infarcts, caudate atrophy)

case.who: 78-year-old woman from Phra Nakhon Si Ayutthaya
case.story: Gradual onset of restless, fidgety movements of face and hands over two years; memory normal; no family history; not on any dopaminergic or antipsychotic drug.
case.exam: Mild generalised chorea, normal saccades, MoCA 27/30.
case.tests: HbA1c, thyroid, calcium, FBC, antiphospholipid antibodies normal; MRI mild small-vessel change; HTT 18/20 repeats.
case.q: What label fits after full work-up, and what must still be borne in mind?
case.a: Idiopathic (senile) chorea; other causes must be excluded first, and the label should be reconsidered if cognition or behaviour changes.

det.patho: The term describes chorea without a demonstrated structural, metabolic, drug, autoimmune or genetic cause. As genetic testing improves, many former idiopathic cases are reclassified: benign hereditary chorea to NKX2-1, ADCY5 and other genes, and some senile chorea to Huntington disease with reduced penetrance alleles or late vascular lesions. Mechanistically, chorea reflects reduced activity of the indirect striatal pathway, causing disinhibition of thalamocortical motor output.
det.clinical: Benign hereditary chorea presents in infancy or early childhood with chorea, delayed walking and falls, often stable or improving in adulthood, with hypothyroidism and respiratory problems in brain–lung–thyroid syndrome. Senile chorea begins after 60 with mild orofacial or limb chorea without dementia or family history. Sporadic idiopathic chorea in adults should prompt periodic reassessment because evolving signs may reveal a specific diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: This is strictly a diagnosis of exclusion. Workup includes HTT repeat testing, drug review (including oral contraceptives, levodopa, antiepileptics), metabolic tests, thyroid, polycythaemia, autoimmune screens, peripheral smear for acanthocytes and MRI. Gene panels are appropriate for childhood onset. Elderly patients with sudden hemichorea should be assessed for stroke or hyperglycaemia.
det.treatment: Treat only if chorea is functionally or socially troublesome. Tetrabenazine or deutetrabenazine, or low-dose antipsychotics, reduce chorea; levodopa has been reported helpful in some NKX2-1 cases. Address falls and provide education. Reassess periodically for emerging features.
det.prognosis: Benign hereditary chorea often improves; senile chorea usually progresses slowly without major disability.
pearls: Test HTT even without a family history before calling chorea idiopathic.
Hemichorea with hyperglycaemia is a reversible cause, common in elderly Asian women.
Benign hereditary chorea: think brain–lung–thyroid (NKX2-1).
det.thd: Idiopathic choreic syndromes คือ chorea ที่ตรวจครบแล้วหาสาเหตุไม่ได้ เช่น benign hereditary chorea ที่เริ่มในเด็กและไม่แย่ลง และ senile chorea ที่เกิดในผู้สูงอายุโดยไม่มีสมองเสื่อม ต้องตรวจยีน HTT ยา เมตาบอลิก ไทรอยด์ ภูมิคุ้มกัน และ MRI ก่อนจะให้การวินิจฉัยนี้ รักษาด้วย tetrabenazine หรือยาต้านโดปามีนเมื่ออาการรบกวน และติดตามซ้ำเพราะอาจพบสาเหตุภายหลัง

ddx.pt: CAG expansion in HTT, cognitive and psychiatric decline, family history (may be hidden)
Subacute onset with antiphospholipid, lupus or neuronal antibodies
Childhood onset non-progressive chorea, often NKX2-1 variant with thyroid and lung involvement
