name: Idiopathic copper toxicosis syndromes
formal: Copper overload disorders without a Wilson gene defect, such as Indian childhood cirrhosis and Tyrolean copper toxicosis, with hepatic copper accumulation and liver failure from environmental and genetic factors.
simple: Rare conditions in which too much copper builds up in the liver in children, causing liver damage.
more: Liver copper is high but ceruloplasmin is often normal. Treat with copper chelation like penicillamine and avoid copper-rich water and utensils.
th: ภาวะทองแดงสะสมในตับที่ไม่ได้เกิดจากยีน Wilson เช่น Indian childhood cirrhosis และ Tyrolean copper toxicosis ทำให้ตับวาย โดยเกิดจากสิ่งแวดล้อมร่วมกับพันธุกรรม
tempoNote: Infants and young children; liver disease progresses over months to cirrhosis
feat: Primarily a paediatric liver disease, not a neurological disorder; neurological involvement is uncommon and mainly from hepatic encephalopathy
Presents in babies and toddlers with hepatomegaly, jaundice and progressive cirrhosis
Copper-contaminated milk (brass or copper vessels) or water plus suspected recessive susceptibility
Kayser–Fleischer rings absent and ceruloplasmin normal or high, unlike Wilson disease
inv: Liver biopsy: very high hepatic copper, Mallory–Denk bodies, pericellular fibrosis
Ceruloplasmin, serum and urine copper; ATP7B testing to exclude Wilson disease
Exposure history for copper-containing vessels and water supply

case.who: 2-year-old boy from a migrant family in Tak province
case.story: Swelling of the abdomen and yellow eyes for two months; milk is boiled and stored in a brass pot inherited from grandparents.
case.exam: Firm hepatomegaly, jaundice, mild ascites, irritable but neurologically non-focal.
case.tests: Ceruloplasmin normal; liver biopsy shows marked copper deposition with Mallory bodies; ATP7B negative.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and the immediate intervention?
case.a: Idiopathic (Indian-childhood-type) copper toxicosis; stop copper exposure and start chelation such as penicillamine, with liver transplant evaluation if failing.

det.patho: These disorders combine excessive copper intake in infancy with an impaired, probably genetically determined, hepatic copper handling unrelated to ATP7B. Copper accumulates in hepatocytes, causing oxidative injury, Mallory–Denk body formation and rapid fibrosis. The genetic basis remains unknown; some families suggest autosomal recessive inheritance.
det.clinical: This is a hepatic, not primarily neurological, disease. Children aged 6 months to 5 years present with hepatomegaly, jaundice, abdominal distension and features of liver failure. Neurological signs, if present, reflect hepatic encephalopathy rather than basal ganglia copper deposition. Since public health measures discouraged copper vessels, new cases are rare.
det.diagnosis: Liver biopsy with quantitative copper measurement confirms marked overload. Unlike Wilson disease, ceruloplasmin is normal or raised, KF rings are absent and ATP7B is normal. Exposure history is key. Other infant liver diseases (biliary atresia, metabolic and infectious hepatitis) must be excluded.
det.treatment: Remove the copper source and start chelation with penicillamine (or trientine) under paediatric hepatology care. Early chelation may reverse liver disease, but advanced cirrhosis may require liver transplantation. Prevention through community education about copper and brass utensils is essential.
det.prognosis: Untreated disease is usually fatal within months; early chelation markedly improves survival.
pearls: Normal ceruloplasmin and absent KF rings separate this from Wilson disease.
Ask about brass or copper milk vessels in infants with cirrhosis.
Neurological features here are usually due to liver failure, not copper in the brain.
det.thd: Idiopathic copper toxicosis syndromes คือภาวะทองแดงสะสมในตับของเด็กเล็กที่ไม่ได้เกิดจากยีน Wilson เช่น Indian childhood cirrhosis มักสัมพันธ์กับการต้มหรือเก็บนมในภาชนะทองเหลืองหรือทองแดงร่วมกับปัจจัยทางพันธุกรรม เด็กมีตับโต ตัวเหลือง และตับแข็ง ceruloplasmin ปกติและไม่มี KF ring เป็นโรคตับมากกว่าโรคประสาท รักษาโดยหยุดแหล่งทองแดงและให้ยาขับทองแดง

ddx.pt: Older children and adults, low ceruloplasmin, KF rings, ATP7B variants
The best-known regional form; this entry is the broader non-Wilsonian category
Copper deficiency (not excess) with kinky hair, seizures and low serum copper

name: Idiopathic cranial dystonias
formal: Primary focal dystonias of cranial muscles, such as blepharospasm, oromandibular dystonia and Meige syndrome, of unknown origin and usually in middle age.
simple: Involuntary muscle spasms of the eyes, face or jaw that start without a clear cause.
th: dystonia ชนิด focal หรือ segmental ของกล้ามเนื้อบริเวณศีรษะ เช่น blepharospasm, oromandibular dystonia และ Meige syndrome ไม่ทราบสาเหตุ มักเริ่มในวัยกลางคน
tempoNote: Onset usually in the 50s–60s, gradual worsening over a few years then stabilisation
feat: Blepharospasm: increased blinking progressing to forced eyelid closure, worse in bright light
Oromandibular dystonia: jaw opening or closing, lip pursing, tongue protrusion, trouble chewing or speaking
Meige syndrome: combination of blepharospasm and oromandibular dystonia
Sensory tricks (touching the eyebrow, humming, chewing gum) temporarily relieve spasms
Women more often affected; may spread to neck or larynx
inv: Clinical diagnosis; review drugs (neuroleptics, metoclopramide, levodopa) for tardive or drug-induced dystonia
MRI brain if young, unilateral or with other signs
Eye examination for dry eye or blepharitis as triggers or mimics

case.who: 61-year-old female rice seller from Chai Nat
case.story: For a year her eyes squeeze shut in sunlight and while riding her motorbike; recently her jaw clenches when talking. Pressing a finger beside her eye helps.
case.exam: Frequent forceful bilateral blinks and eyelid spasm, jaw-closing dystonia with lip pursing; no ptosis, normal eye movements.
case.tests: No dopamine-blocking drugs; MRI normal.
case.q: Name the syndrome and first-line treatment.
case.a: Meige syndrome (idiopathic cranial dystonia); botulinum toxin injections into the orbicularis oculi and jaw muscles.

read.where: Ablative lesions of the thalamus, pallidum, and subthalamic nucleus

det.patho: Cranial dystonias are thought to stem from abnormal sensorimotor integration and plasticity in basal ganglia, cerebellar and brainstem circuits controlling blink and orofacial movements. Brainstem blink reflex recovery is abnormally enhanced. A few genes (for example GNAL, THAP1, ANO3) occasionally underlie familial cranial-cervical dystonia, but most cases are sporadic with environmental triggers such as dry eye.
det.clinical: Blepharospasm starts with eye irritation or excessive blinking and progresses to involuntary closure that can cause functional blindness and dangerous driving. Oromandibular dystonia affects jaw opening or closure, tongue and lips, causing problems with chewing, swallowing and speech, and may lead to dental damage. Symptoms are worse with stress and fatigue and improve with sensory tricks, sleep and relaxation. Spread to the neck or larynx occurs in a proportion.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical and depends on recognising patterned, task-sensitive spasms and sensory tricks. Exclude drug-induced and tardive dystonia, and structural lesions in atypical cases. Differentiate from hemifacial spasm, tics, apraxia of eyelid opening, ptosis and functional facial spasm. Apraxia of lid opening may coexist and requires pretarsal injections.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin injections every 3–4 months are first-line and effective in most patients with blepharospasm; jaw-opening or closing dystonia also responds with careful muscle selection. Oral agents (trihexyphenidyl, clonazepam, baclofen) give modest help. Tinted lenses, lubricating drops and sensory tricks are useful adjuncts. Refractory cases may consider myectomy or pallidal DBS.
det.prognosis: Usually chronic and lifelong, but botulinum toxin keeps most patients functional; spontaneous remission is uncommon.
pearls: Bright light worsens blepharospasm; a sensory trick improves it.
Blepharospasm is bilateral; hemifacial spasm is unilateral.
Always exclude a dopamine-blocking drug in orofacial dystonia.
det.thd: Idiopathic cranial dystonias คือ dystonia ของกล้ามเนื้อใบหน้าและขากรรไกร เช่น blepharospasm ที่ตาหลับเองเมื่อเจอแสง และ oromandibular dystonia ที่ขากรรไกรอ้าหรือหุบเอง เมื่อเป็นร่วมกันเรียก Meige syndrome พบบ่อยในหญิงวัยกลางคน อาการดีขึ้นเมื่อใช้ sensory trick ต้องแยกจาก hemifacial spasm และยาที่ทำให้เกิด tardive dystonia การรักษาหลักคือฉีด botulinum toxin ทุก 3–4 เดือน

name: Idiopathic hypersomnia
formal: Chronic excessive daytime sleepiness with long unrefreshing sleep, sleep inertia and no cataplexy, with normal sleep apnoea testing and mean sleep latency below eight minutes.
simple: Constant, heavy daytime sleepiness despite long nights of sleep, without a clear cause.
more: Chronic daytime sleepiness with long unrefreshing sleep, sleep inertia and no cataplexy, without another cause; diagnosed after excluding narcolepsy and sleep apnoea.
ab: Idiopathic hypersomnia with long sleep time
th: ภาวะง่วงนอนมากเรื้อรังทั้งที่นอนนาน ตื่นยากและงัวเงียมากตอนเช้า งีบนานแต่ไม่สดชื่น ไม่มี cataplexy และไม่มีสาเหตุอื่น เช่น OSA หรืออดนอน
tempoNote: Onset usually in adolescence or young adulthood, persisting for years; must last at least 3 months for diagnosis
feat: Constant daytime sleepiness despite long night sleep, often more than 10–11 hours
Severe sleep inertia (sleep drunkenness): very hard to wake, confused or irritable for a long time after waking
Long naps that are not refreshing, unlike the short refreshing naps of narcolepsy
No cataplexy; fewer than two SOREMPs
Cognitive fog, headaches and autonomic complaints are common; more frequent in women
inv: PSG to exclude OSA and other causes, then MSLT: average latency to sleep of 8 min or under with fewer than two SOREMPs
Alternatively total 24-hour sleep time of 660 minutes or more on prolonged PSG or actigraphy
Two weeks of actigraphy and sleep diary before testing to exclude insufficient sleep
Screen for depression, hypothyroidism and sedating medicines

case.story: Since high school she sleeps 11 hours a night, needs three alarms and her mother to wake her, and feels drunk for an hour afterwards; a 2-hour nap leaves her no fresher. She has never had weakness with laughter.
case.exam: Normal; BMI 21.
case.tests: Actigraphy shows ample sleep; PSG AHI 2; MSLT mean latency 6 minutes with no SOREMPs.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what treatment is approved for it?
case.a: Idiopathic hypersomnia; low-sodium oxybate is approved for IH, and modafinil, pitolisant or other stimulants are commonly used.

read.where: Chapter 29 Disorders of Sleep — Primary (Idiopathic) Hypersomnia
Etiology and pathogenesis of Parkinson disease

det.patho: The cause is unknown; orexin levels are normal. Proposed mechanisms include an endogenous enhancer of GABA-A receptor activity, abnormal circadian timing and a raised homeostatic sleep need. Family clustering suggests a genetic contribution in some patients.
det.clinical: Patients describe sleepiness that never lets up, very long sleep periods and prolonged sleep inertia that can make them late for work or aggressive when woken. Naps tend to be long and unrefreshing. Symptoms usually start between the teens and early thirties and are chronic, though some patients improve. There is no cataplexy, and hypnagogic hallucinations or sleep paralysis, if present, do not change the diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: ICSD-3-TR requires daily sleepiness for at least 3 months, absence of cataplexy, fewer than two SOREMPs, and either MSLT mean latency of 8 minutes or less or 24-hour total sleep of at least 660 minutes. Insufficient sleep must be excluded by diary and actigraphy, and OSA, depression, medicines and circadian disorders must be ruled out. The MSLT is less reliable than in narcolepsy and may need repeating.
det.treatment: Low-sodium oxybate is the only approved drug for idiopathic hypersomnia in several countries. Modafinil or armodafinil is often tried first, with pitolisant, solriamfetol, methylphenidate or amphetamines as alternatives used off label. Responses are less complete than in narcolepsy, and sleep inertia is particularly hard to treat. Regular sleep, scheduled naps only if helpful, and workplace adjustments are useful.
det.prognosis: Usually lifelong, though spontaneous improvement occurs in a minority.
pearls: Refreshing short naps point to narcolepsy, long unrefreshing naps to idiopathic hypersomnia.
Always rule out insufficient sleep with actigraphy before calling sleepiness idiopathic.
A 24-hour sleep time of 11 hours or more can make the diagnosis even when the MSLT is normal.
det.thd: Idiopathic hypersomnia คือง่วงมากเรื้อรังทั้งที่นอนนานกว่า 10–11 ชั่วโมง ตื่นยากและงัวเงียนาน งีบนานแต่ไม่สดชื่น ไม่มี cataplexy การวินิจฉัยต้องตัด OSA และการอดนอนก่อน แล้วตรวจ MSLT พบ sleep latency 8 นาทีหรือน้อยกว่าโดย SOREMP น้อยกว่า 2 ครั้ง หรือนอนรวมใน 24 ชั่วโมงอย่างน้อย 660 นาที การรักษาใช้ low-sodium oxybate, modafinil, pitolisant หรือยากระตุ้นอื่น

qx.stem: A 27-year-old woman from Nakhon Si Thammarat sleeps 11–12 hours nightly, takes 2-hour naps that leave her groggy, and needs an hour to feel awake each morning. She has no cataplexy. Two weeks of actigraphy confirm long sleep. PSG shows AHI 1; the following MSLT shows mean sleep latency 7 minutes with one SOREMP.
qx.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Narcolepsy type 2
Insufficient sleep syndrome
Idiopathic hypersomnia
Delayed sleep–wake phase disorder
Kleine–Levin syndrome
qx.why: Chronic sleepiness with long unrefreshing sleep, severe sleep inertia, no cataplexy, a mean latency of 8 minutes or less and fewer than two SOREMPs fits idiopathic hypersomnia. Narcolepsy type 2 needs two or more SOREMPs. Actigraphy excludes insufficient sleep, and the continuous rather than episodic course argues against Kleine–Levin syndrome.

qx.stem: A 22-year-old woman from Songkhla sleeps 11 to 12 hours every night but wakes unrefreshed with marked difficulty becoming alert for an hour or more. Naps of one to two hours leave her no better. She has no cataplexy. MSLT shows a 6-minute mean latency and a single SOREMP, after documented adequate sleep and no interfering drugs.
qx.q: Which feature best separates this disorder from narcolepsy type 2?
opts: Sleepiness that is worse after meals
Sleep paralysis on waking
A short mean sleep latency on the MSLT
Rapid improvement with sleep extension
Long unrefreshing sleep, severe sleep inertia and no more than one REM-onset nap
qx.why: Idiopathic hypersomnia is characterised by prolonged sleep time, severe sleep inertia, unrefreshing naps and an MSLT showing at most one REM-onset nap. A short MSLT latency is shared with narcolepsy, and improvement with sleep extension would instead suggest insufficient sleep. Sleep paralysis can occur in either condition.

ddx.pt: Cataplexy or two or more SOREMPs; short naps are refreshing
Sleepiness resolves when sleep is extended on holidays or by diary-guided extension
Snoring and witnessed apnoeas with raised AHI on sleep testing

name: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy
formal: Autoimmune muscle diseases including dermatomyositis, polymyositis, necrotizing myopathy and inclusion body myositis, causing proximal weakness with raised CK.
simple: A group of conditions where the immune system attacks muscles, causing weakness and sometimes skin rashes.
more: Diagnosis by CK, EMG, MRI, antibodies and biopsy; treat with steroids, immunosuppressants or IVIG; screen for cancer in dermatomyositis. Heterogeneous autoimmune muscle diseases, including dermatomyositis, polymyositis, necrotising myopathy and inclusion body myositis, with proximal weakness and raised creatine kinase.
th: กลุ่มโรคกล้ามเนื้ออักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกัน ได้แก่ dermatomyositis, immune-mediated necrotising myopathy, antisynthetase syndrome, overlap myositis และ inclusion body myositis มีอ่อนแรงต้นแขนขาและ CK สูง
tempoNote: Weeks to months in DM, IMNM and antisynthetase; years in inclusion body myositis
feat: Symmetric proximal weakness (neck flexors, hips, shoulders); IBM instead targets quadriceps and finger flexors
Skin: heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, shawl sign in dermatomyositis; mechanic's hands in antisynthetase
Interstitial lung disease, arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, dysphagia
Raised CK (very high in IMNM; normal in some DM and IBM)
Cancer association in adult dermatomyositis (TIF1-gamma, NXP2)
inv: CK, myositis-specific and associated antibody panel
EMG with fibrillations and small polyphasic units; muscle MRI (STIR oedema) to guide biopsy
Muscle biopsy for subtype; HRCT chest and lung function
Cancer screening for dermatomyositis and IMNM with HMGCR antibody

case.story: Two months of difficulty combing her hair and getting up from the floor, with a purplish rash on her eyelids and knuckles.
case.exam: Heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, neck flexor and proximal limb weakness 3+/5, reflexes preserved.
case.tests: CK 2,800 U/L; anti-TIF1-gamma positive; MRI thigh muscle oedema; biopsy perifascicular atrophy.
case.q: What subtype is this and what additional screening is mandatory?
case.a: Dermatomyositis (IIM subtype); TIF1-gamma carries high cancer risk, so screen thoroughly (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, gynaecological, breast, nasopharynx in Thai/Asian patients).

det.patho: IIM is an umbrella for immune-driven muscle diseases with distinct mechanisms: complement-mediated microangiopathy and interferon signature in dermatomyositis, antibody-mediated fibre necrosis in IMNM (SRP, HMGCR), autoimmunity against tRNA synthetases with lung disease in antisynthetase syndrome, and combined cytotoxic T-cell and degenerative pathology in IBM. 'Polymyositis' as a separate entity is now considered rare and often a misclassification. Myositis-specific antibodies define clinically useful subgroups.
det.clinical: Most forms cause subacute symmetric proximal weakness with dysphagia in a third; extra-muscular involvement (skin, lung, joints, heart) varies by antibody. IBM affects patients over 45 with asymmetric quadriceps and deep finger flexor weakness. Clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis shows skin disease without weakness, and anti-MDA5 forms may have rapidly progressive lung disease. Cancer risk is highest in the first three years after DM diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: Combine clinical pattern, CK, EMG, MRI, autoantibodies and biopsy; EULAR/ACR 2017 classification criteria help. Antibody results often predict histology and complications. Exclude drugs (statins, checkpoint inhibitors), hypothyroidism, muscular dystrophies (e.g. dysferlin, FSHD with inflammation) and metabolic myopathies. Screen lungs with HRCT and the heart with ECG and troponin.
det.treatment: High-dose corticosteroids plus early steroid-sparing agent (methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate) for DM, antisynthetase and overlap disease; IVIG is effective in DM (proven in trial) and IMNM. Rituximab, tacrolimus or cyclophosphamide are used for refractory disease or ILD. IBM does not respond to immunotherapy, so management is supportive. Exercise therapy is safe and helpful.
det.prognosis: Most non-IBM patients improve with treatment, though many have chronic disease; outcomes are worse with cancer, severe ILD or late treatment.
pearls: Polymyositis is a diagnosis of exclusion; look for IBM, IMNM or dystrophy first.
Myositis antibodies predict lung disease and cancer risk.
Steroid-unresponsive 'polymyositis' in an older patient is often IBM.
det.thd: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy เป็นกลุ่มโรคกล้ามเนื้ออักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกัน มี dermatomyositis, IMNM, antisynthetase syndrome, overlap myositis และ IBM ส่วนใหญ่อ่อนแรงต้นแขนขาภายในสัปดาห์ถึงเดือน CK สูง อาจมีผื่น ปอดอักเสบ และกลืนลำบาก วินิจฉัยด้วย CK, EMG, MRI, antibody และชิ้นเนื้อ รักษาด้วยสเตียรอยด์ร่วมกับยากดภูมิหรือ IVIG ยกเว้น IBM ที่ไม่ตอบสนอง และต้องคัดกรองมะเร็งใน dermatomyositis

ddx.pt: Raised CK with high TSH; no rash or inflammatory biopsy
Male, family history, calf hypertrophy, slower course; dystrophin abnormal
Fatigable ocular-bulbar weakness, normal CK

aN: idiopathic inflammatory myopathies | iim | myositis | autoimmune myositis

name: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH)
formal: Raised intracranial pressure with normal imaging and CSF content, typical in overweight young women, causing headache, papilloedema and visual loss; treated with weight loss, acetazolamide or shunting.
simple: High pressure around the brain with no tumour, causing headaches and risk to vision, most often in young women with obesity.
th: ความดันในกะโหลกสูงโดยไม่มีก้อน — มักเป็นหญิงน้ำหนักเกิน ปวดศีรษะ ตามัวชั่วขณะ จอประสาทตาบวม
feat: Daily headache, transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus
Bilateral papilloedema; sixth nerve palsy may occur (false-localising)
Typically women of childbearing age with recent weight gain
Threat is permanent visual field loss
inv: MRI with MR venography to exclude mass and venous sinus thrombosis
Lumbar puncture in lateral decubitus: raised opening pressure, normal CSF contents
Formal visual fields and OCT

case.story: Three months of headache and brief greying of vision on standing; hears a whooshing in her ears.
case.exam: Bilateral papilloedema, enlarged blind spots, mild left abduction deficit.
case.tests: MRI/MRV normal apart from empty sella; LP opening pressure 38 cmH2O, normal cell count and protein.
case.q: What is the most important outcome to protect?
case.a: Vision — treat with weight loss and acetazolamide and monitor fields; escalate urgently if fields deteriorate.

qx.stem: A 27-year-old woman from Pathum Thani with BMI 36 kg/m² has two months of daily headache, pulsatile tinnitus and brief visual greying on bending. She has bilateral papilloedema and an enlarged blind spot, with visual acuity 6/6 and mild peripheral field loss. MRI with MR venography shows an empty sella and bilateral transverse sinus stenosis without thrombosis. Opening pressure is 34 cmH2O with normal CSF.
qx.q: Which initial management plan is most appropriate?
opts: Urgent optic nerve sheath fenestration before any medical therapy
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for one month
Repeated weekly lumbar punctures as the main treatment
Acetazolamide plus a structured weight-loss programme (GLP-1 receptor agonists or bariatric referral as options), with close field monitoring
Anticoagulation for presumed venous sinus thrombosis
qx.why: Without fulminant visual loss, IIH is treated with acetazolamide and weight reduction of about 5–15%; GLP-1 receptor agonists and bariatric surgery are increasingly used, and IIH:WT supported surgery for sustained weight loss. Surgical or venous sinus stenting options are for progressive visual loss despite medical therapy. Transverse sinus stenosis is typical of IIH rather than thrombosis, steroids are avoided because of weight gain and rebound, and serial LPs are not a long-term treatment.

qx.stem: A 27-year-old woman from Bangkok with BMI 38 has had three months of daily headaches and pulsatile tinnitus. Visual acuity is normal, but she has bilateral papilloedema and enlarged blind spots on perimetry. MRI and MR venography are normal, and lumbar puncture opening pressure is 38 cm CSF with normal CSF contents.
qx.q: Which is the best initial management?
opts: Immediate bilateral optic nerve sheath fenestration
Weight loss programme with acetazolamide and serial visual field monitoring
Repeated daily lumbar punctures
Oral prednisolone for six months
Observation only without medication
qx.why: Modified Dandy criteria are met. For IIH with mild visual loss, weight reduction (including bariatric surgery when appropriate) plus acetazolamide with perimetry and fundus follow-up is first-line. Surgery (optic nerve sheath fenestration or a CSF shunt) is reserved for rapidly progressive or refractory visual loss, steroids cause weight gain, and repeated punctures give only transient relief.

qx.stem: A 12-year-old overweight girl from Bangkok has had three months of morning headaches and brief visual obscurations, and now has a left sixth nerve palsy. Both optic discs are swollen. MRI and MR venography are normal, and lumbar puncture shows an opening pressure of 36 cm of water with normal CSF.
qx.q: Which plan fits current management?
opts: Dexamethasone and urgent craniotomy
Repeat daily lumbar punctures indefinitely without any medication
Therapeutic CSF removal to about half the opening pressure, acetazolamide, removal of triggers, weight reduction and serial visual field testing
Immediate lumboperitoneal shunt for all children
Observation alone, because vision is not yet affected
qx.why: Papilloedema or a sixth nerve palsy with raised pressure, normal CSF and normal imaging establishes idiopathic intracranial hypertension, in which the real danger is insidious loss of peripheral vision. One lumbar puncture with a closing pressure around half the opening value often relieves symptoms, and acetazolamide is the usual drug, with topiramate as a substitute. Triggers such as tetracyclines and vitamin A are removed. Shunting or optic nerve sheath fenestration is kept for progressive visual loss.

qx.stem: A 24-year-old obese woman from Nakhon Pathom has daily headaches and brief bilateral visual blackouts on standing. Visual acuity is 6/6 and colour vision is normal in both eyes. Both optic discs are swollen with blurred margins.
qx.q: What visual field finding is expected early, and how should vision be followed?
opts: A dense central scotoma with early loss of acuity and colour vision
Bitemporal hemianopia
Homonymous hemianopia
Enlarged blind spots with preserved central acuity, followed by serial perimetry because central vision is spared until late
An altitudinal field defect with a pale disc
qx.why: In papilloedema from raised pressure, acuity and critical fusion frequency usually stay normal for a long time, and the typical early field change is an enlarged blind spot, later peripheral constriction. Because central vision is lost last, serial perimetry rather than acuity must be used to monitor. Central scotomas with early acuity loss suggest optic neuritis, bitemporal defects suggest a chiasmal lesion, and altitudinal loss with a pale disc suggests ischaemia.

qx.stem: A 33-year-old woman from Bangkok with BMI 38 has headache, pulsatile tinnitus and Frisen grade 3 papilloedema. MRI is normal apart from bilateral transverse sinus stenosis, and the opening pressure is 38 cm CSF. Despite 6 months of maximal acetazolamide and weight loss her visual field defects are worsening.
qx.q: What should be done next?
opts: Continue the same treatment for another year
Start long-term high-dose steroids
Reassure, as papilloedema alone does not threaten vision
Repeated serial lumbar punctures as the long-term plan
Urgent referral for a surgical or interventional procedure such as optic nerve sheath fenestration, CSF diversion, or venous sinus stenting after manometry shows a significant pressure gradient
qx.why: Progressive visual field loss despite maximal medical therapy in IIH is an indication for urgent intervention to protect vision. Options include optic nerve sheath fenestration, CSF shunting, or venous sinus stenting when there is a haemodynamically significant stenosis with a pressure gradient across it. Waiting risks permanent blindness, steroids can worsen weight and are not recommended long term, and serial lumbar punctures are only a temporising measure.

ichd.title: Headache attributed to idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH)

ddx.pt: Venous filling defect on MRV
Disc drusen or crowded discs without true oedema; normal pressure
Normal fundi and pressure

aN: iih | idiopathic intracranial hypertension | pseudotumor cerebri | benign intracranial hypertension | pseudotumour cerebri

det.patho: IIH is raised intracranial pressure with normal brain parenchyma on imaging and normal CSF contents, diagnosed only after secondary causes such as cerebral venous thrombosis are excluded. Its mechanism is still debated; current models combine reduced CSF outflow, a self-sustaining loop in which high pressure narrows the transverse sinuses and the resulting venous hypertension further impairs drainage, and an obesity-linked metabolic state with androgen excess and heightened cortisol activation within fat tissue. The typical patient is a woman of child-bearing age with obesity, often after recent weight gain, and incidence is climbing with population obesity. A similar syndrome can follow tetracyclines, vitamin A derivatives, growth hormone, steroid withdrawal and some endocrine disorders. In men, children, older adults and slim patients, look harder for a secondary cause.
det.clinical: Headache is the commonest complaint and varies in pattern — often daily, sometimes worse lying flat or on straining, and frequently migraine-like. Brief visual obscurations on standing or bending, whooshing pulse-synchronous tinnitus, horizontal diplopia from abducens palsy and neck, back or radicular pain complete the picture. Papilloedema is usually bilateral but may be asymmetric; field loss begins with blind-spot enlargement and inferonasal defects while central acuity falls late, so a patient can read the chart well yet be losing field. Fulminant IIH, with rapid visual decline over less than about four weeks, is a neuro-ophthalmic emergency. Men and patients with untreated sleep apnoea carry a higher risk of visual loss, and headache often continues after the pressure is controlled.
det.diagnosis: Revised (Friedman) criteria require papilloedema, a normal neurological examination apart from cranial nerve palsy (usually the sixth), normal MRI parenchyma without hydrocephalus or mass, normal CSF composition, and lumbar opening pressure of at least 25 cmH2O in adults (28 in children) measured lying on the side with legs relaxed. Without papilloedema, the diagnosis needs a sixth nerve palsy, or at least three of four MRI signs (empty sella, flattened posterior globe, distended optic nerve sheath, transverse sinus stenosis). MRI with MR venography (or CT venography) is mandatory to exclude venous sinus thrombosis, and a single pressure reading can mislead in either direction. Record baseline perimetry, acuity, fundus photographs and OCT of the retinal nerve fibre layer to guide follow-up. Confirm true papilloedema and exclude disc drusen or other pseudopapilloedema with OCT, ultrasound or autofluorescence before committing the patient to the label.
det.treatment: Weight reduction is the only disease-modifying approach: loss of about 5–15% of body weight usually induces remission, bariatric surgery beat a community weight programme in a randomised trial, and GLP-1 receptor agonists are increasingly used. Acetazolamide, titrated as tolerated, is the usual first drug and improves papilloedema in mild visual loss; topiramate is an alternative that also helps weight and headache. Visual function dictates urgency — worsening fields or fulminant disease need prompt CSF shunting, optic nerve sheath fenestration or transverse sinus stenting in selected patients, with a lumbar drain as a temporary bridge. Serial lumbar punctures are not a long-term strategy. Manage headache as its own problem with migraine preventives and avoidance of medication overuse; opioids are unhelpful.
det.prognosis: With weight loss and close monitoring most patients stabilise, but permanent field loss affects a minority and relapse often follows weight regain; chronic headache frequently outlasts the papilloedema.
pearls: Always do MRI with MRV before calling it idiopathic.
Sixth nerve palsy in raised ICP is a false-localising sign.
Vision, not headache, is what you are protecting.
Field loss comes first — follow perimetry and OCT, not just Snellen acuity.
det.thd: ความดันในกะโหลกศีรษะสูงโดยไม่พบก้อน โพรงน้ำไม่ขยาย และไม่มีลิ่มเลือดในหลอดเลือดดำ พบบ่อยในหญิงวัยเจริญพันธุ์ที่น้ำหนักเกินหรือน้ำหนักเพิ่มเร็ว อาการคือปวดศีรษะ ตามัวชั่ววินาที ได้ยินเสียงฟู่ตามชีพจร และ papilloedema วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI+MRV ปกติ และเจาะหลังพบ opening pressure ≥25 cmH2O โดยน้ำไขสันหลังปกติ รักษาด้วยการลดน้ำหนักประมาณ 5–15% (อาจใช้ยากลุ่ม GLP-1 receptor agonist หรือผ่าตัดลดน้ำหนัก) ร่วมกับ acetazolamide หรือ topiramate เฝ้าติดตาม visual field และ OCT เป็นระยะเพราะลานสายตาเสียก่อนสายตาส่วนกลาง ถ้าการมองเห็นแย่ลงเร็วต้องผ่าตัดระบายน้ำไขสันหลัง ทำ optic nerve sheath fenestration หรือใส่ stent ที่ transverse sinus

name: Idiopathic late onset cerebellar ataxia (ILOCA)
formal: Sporadic progressive cerebellar ataxia starting after about age 40 with no family history and no identified cause, after excluding genetic, toxic, immune, vitamin and paraneoplastic causes.
simple: A balance and coordination problem beginning in later life with no known cause, in someone without a family history.
more: MRI shows cerebellar atrophy. Some cases are probable MSA-C or have genetic causes, so search carefully; treatment is supportive. Progressive cerebellar ataxia developing after age 40 with no identified genetic or acquired cause, often sporadic and including undiagnosed cases later classified as MSA-C.
ab: Sporadic adult-onset ataxia of unknown aetiology
th: สมองน้อยเสื่อมแบบค่อยเป็นค่อยไปที่เริ่มหลังอายุราว 40 ปี ไม่มีประวัติครอบครัวและหาสาเหตุไม่พบหลังตัดสาเหตุพันธุกรรม พิษ ภูมิคุ้มกัน วิตามิน และ paraneoplastic
tempoNote: Slowly progressive over many years, much slower than MSA-C
feat: Gait ataxia followed by limb ataxia, dysarthria and nystagmus after age 40
No family history and no clear secondary cause
No early autonomic failure, parkinsonism or rapid progression (which would suggest MSA-C)
A shrinking diagnosis: RFC1 (CANVAS) and FGF14 GAA (SCA27B) expansions explain many former cases
inv: MRI: cerebellar atrophy without brainstem 'hot cross bun' sign
Screen vitamin E, B12, thyroid, anti-GAD, anti-gliadin/TTG, paraneoplastic antibodies, alcohol history
Genetic testing: RFC1, FGF14-GAA, SCA panel, FXTAS; NCS and vestibular testing
Autonomic tests to watch for MSA conversion

case.who: 63-year-old male retired policeman from Nakhon Sawan
case.story: Unsteady walking for five years, gradually needing a stick; no family history; drinks rarely.
case.exam: Gait and mild limb ataxia, scanning dysarthria, gaze-evoked nystagmus; normal BP lying and standing, no parkinsonism.
case.tests: MRI pure cerebellar atrophy; vitamin, thyroid, antibody and SCA/RFC1/FGF14 tests negative; autonomic function normal.
case.q: What working diagnosis fits, and what should be monitored?
case.a: Idiopathic late-onset cerebellar ataxia; monitor for autonomic failure suggesting MSA-C and repeat genetic testing as panels expand.

read.where: Chapter 24 Cerebellar Ataxias and Related Conditions — Late-Onset Cerebellar Degenerations

det.patho: ILOCA is a heterogeneous category of sporadic cerebellar degeneration of unknown cause. Pathology, where available, shows Purkinje cell loss with variable olivary involvement. A proportion later turns out to be MSA-C, and modern genetics has found RFC1 and FGF14 repeat expansions or recessive variants in a significant minority.
det.clinical: Patients develop slowly progressive gait ataxia in middle or later life, then limb incoordination, dysarthria and eye movement abnormalities. Disability accrues over decades rather than years. The emergence of autonomic failure, parkinsonism or REM sleep behaviour disorder within the first few years should trigger reconsideration of MSA. Mild neuropathy or vestibular loss suggests CANVAS.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires excluding acquired causes (alcohol, drugs such as phenytoin, vitamin deficiencies, hypothyroidism, gluten, anti-GAD, paraneoplastic, superficial siderosis) and known genetic forms. MRI shows cerebellar atrophy without brainstem involvement in most. Autonomic testing and follow-up are important. The label should be re-evaluated over time.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy exists. Intensive coordination-focused physiotherapy, gait aids, falls prevention and speech therapy help. Treat any identified contributing factor, and consider 4-aminopyridine if SCA27B is later confirmed. Support for mood and fatigue is part of care.
det.prognosis: Slow progression; many remain ambulant with aids for over 10 years, unlike MSA-C.
pearls: ILOCA is a diagnosis of exclusion that should be revisited.
Early autonomic failure turns ILOCA into probable MSA-C.
Test RFC1 and FGF14 expansions — they are not detected by exome.
det.thd: ILOCA คือภาวะสมองน้อยเสื่อมที่เริ่มหลังอายุ 40 ปี ไม่มีประวัติครอบครัวและหาสาเหตุไม่พบ ผู้ป่วยเดินเซช้าๆ หลายปี พูดไม่ชัด ตากระตุก ต้องตัดสาเหตุ เช่น สุรา ยา วิตามินขาด ไทรอยด์ ภูมิคุ้มกัน มะเร็ง และพันธุกรรม (RFC1, FGF14, SCA) ก่อน ถ้ามีระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติเสียเร็วให้นึกถึง MSA-C การรักษาเป็นกายภาพบำบัดและป้องกันการล้ม

Sensory neuronopathy, chronic cough and bilateral vestibular loss; RFC1 expansion
Positive repeat expansion, often with family history

case.exam: Patchy sensory loss in the saphenous and superficial fibular territories; strength normal.

det.diagnosis: Nerve biopsy is required, showing perineurial inflammation without vasculitis or granulomas typical of other causes. Exclude leprosy carefully in endemic regions.
det.treatment: Corticosteroids are commonly used with good response in many reports; data are limited to case series.
det.prognosis: Often responds to steroids; relapses possible.

In Thailand exclude leprosy before calling it idiopathic.
Distinct from optic perineuritis, which affects the optic nerve sheath.

name: Idiopathic recurring stupor
formal: Rare recurrent episodes of unexplained stupor with elevated endogenous benzodiazepine-like activity, reversed by flumazenil, with normal EEG and structural imaging.
simple: Repeated episodes of unexplained drowsiness and unresponsiveness that may be caused by natural sedative-like substances in the body.
th: ภาวะซึมลึกเป็นพักๆ ซ้ำๆ ที่หาสาเหตุไม่ได้ สัมพันธ์กับสารคล้าย benzodiazepine ในร่างกายและตอบสนองต่อ flumazenil
tempoNote: Attacks last hours to a few days and recur at irregular intervals, with normal function between attacks
feat: Recurrent episodes of stupor or coma lasting hours to days in middle-aged or older adults
Normal between episodes; no structural, metabolic or toxic cause found
EEG during attacks shows fast (beta) activity, as seen with benzodiazepine effect
Prompt but temporary awakening after intravenous flumazenil
Many reported cases were later attributed to covert benzodiazepine intake; the concept is controversial

Comprehensive toxicology including benzodiazepine screening by mass spectrometry
EEG during an episode

case.who: 66-year-old man brought to an emergency department in Nakhon Ratchasima
case.story: Third episode in a year of being found deeply drowsy for about a day; recovers fully each time. Family denies sedative use.
case.exam: Stuporous, rousable only to pain, normal pupils and brainstem reflexes, no focal signs.
case.tests: Glucose, ammonia, sodium, creatinine normal; CT and MRI normal; EEG shows diffuse beta activity; standard urine drug screen negative.
case.q: Which bedside test helps and what must still be excluded?

det.patho: The original hypothesis proposed accumulation of an endogenous benzodiazepine-like ligand (endozepine) acting at GABA-A receptors. Later work found that many patients labelled with this condition had ingested exogenous benzodiazepines that routine assays missed, so the existence of a primary endozepine disorder remains uncertain. It is best viewed as a rare and contested diagnosis of exclusion.
det.clinical: Patients, usually adult men, have recurrent attacks of unexplained drowsiness progressing to stupor that last from hours to several days and end spontaneously. Between attacks they are well. There are no focal signs, and brainstem reflexes are preserved. Attacks may cluster or occur months apart.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis requires exclusion of metabolic, structural, epileptic and toxic causes. EEG during an attack shows widespread fast activity, and flumazenil reverses the stupor transiently. Benzodiazepine-like activity has been measured in plasma or CSF in research laboratories, but sensitive mass-spectrometry screening for commercial benzodiazepines and newer designer agents is essential before accepting the label.
det.treatment: Acute attacks can be shortened with flumazenil under monitoring, although sedation may return when it wears off. Supportive care and airway protection are needed during deep stupor. Oral flumazenil was tried in older reports. If covert drug use is found, this becomes a safeguarding and toxicology issue rather than a neurological one.
det.prognosis: Individual attacks resolve without lasting damage; the long-term course is poorly documented.
pearls: Beta-rich EEG plus a flumazenil response points to a benzodiazepine effect, endogenous or not.
Order mass-spectrometry toxicology; standard urine immunoassays miss several benzodiazepines.
Treat this as a diagnosis of exclusion with known controversy.

name: Idiopathic scoliosis
formal: Lateral spinal curvature of unknown cause, usually in adolescent girls, defined by Cobb angle above 10 degrees; neurological screening is needed to exclude syringomyelia and other spinal causes.
simple: A sideways curve of the spine appearing in childhood or teens without a known cause.
th: กระดูกสันหลังคดด้านข้างโดยไม่ทราบสาเหตุ มักพบในเด็กหญิงวัยรุ่น Cobb angle มากกว่า 10 องศา ต้องตรวจระบบประสาทเพื่อแยก syrinx หรือ Chiari
tempoNote: Develops and progresses mainly during growth spurts; usually stabilises after skeletal maturity unless the curve is large
feat: Orthopaedic condition; neurological relevance is excluding secondary (neuromuscular or syringomyelic) scoliosis
Typically right thoracic curve in an adolescent girl, painless
Detected by shoulder or waist asymmetry and rib hump on Adams forward bend test
Red flags for a neurological cause: left thoracic curve, pain, rapid progression, abnormal reflexes (asymmetric abdominal reflexes), cavus foot, early onset
Managed with observation, bracing or surgery depending on curve size and growth remaining
inv: Standing full-length spine radiographs with Cobb angle and skeletal maturity (Risser)
MRI whole spine and craniocervical junction if red flags
Neurological examination including abdominal reflexes

case.story: School screening found uneven shoulders; no pain. Her mother had similar curvature.
case.exam: Rib hump on forward bending, right thoracic curve; neurological examination normal including symmetric abdominal reflexes.
case.tests: X-ray shows right thoracic Cobb angle 28°, Risser 1.
case.q: Is MRI required and what is the treatment?

det.patho: The cause is multifactorial and incompletely understood, involving genetic susceptibility (e.g. LBX1, GPR126 loci), asymmetric spinal growth, and possibly subtle abnormalities of proprioceptive and vestibular control. Curve progression is driven by asymmetric loading during rapid growth. By definition, no underlying neuromuscular or congenital vertebral cause is present.
det.clinical: Most cases are adolescent onset in girls, with painless asymmetry of shoulders, waist or scapulae. Large curves cause cosmetic concern, back pain in adulthood and, above 70–80 degrees, restrictive lung disease. Neurologists are consulted when red flags suggest a secondary cause, such as syringomyelia, Chiari malformation, tethered cord or spinal tumour.
det.diagnosis: Standing radiographs measure the Cobb angle; a curve of at least 10 degrees with rotation defines scoliosis. MRI of the whole neuraxis is indicated for atypical curves (left thoracic, short angular), rapid progression, pain, neurological signs, early onset under 10 years, or before surgery in some centres. Asymmetric abdominal reflexes are a classic clue to a syrinx.
det.treatment: Small curves are observed with serial radiographs. Bracing is used for moderate curves (roughly 20–40 degrees) in growing children and reduces progression to surgery. Spinal fusion or growth-friendly techniques are reserved for severe or progressive curves. Exercise programmes may supplement care.
det.prognosis: Most curves stay mild; curves above 50 degrees at maturity can continue to progress slowly in adulthood.
pearls: Left thoracic curve or absent abdominal reflexes: image for syrinx.
Painful scoliosis is not idiopathic until proved otherwise.
Check the feet for cavus deformity suggesting a neurological cause.
det.thd: Idiopathic scoliosis คือกระดูกสันหลังคดด้านข้างโดยไม่ทราบสาเหตุ พบมากในเด็กหญิงวัยรุ่น มักคดไปทางขวาที่ระดับอก ไม่ปวด เป็นโรคทางกระดูก แต่แพทย์ระบบประสาทต้องช่วยแยกสาเหตุ เช่น syrinx, Chiari หรือโรคกล้ามเนื้อ ถ้ามีสัญญาณเตือน เช่น คดไปทางซ้าย ปวด คดเร็ว หรือ abdominal reflex ไม่เท่ากัน ควรทำ MRI การรักษาคือติดตาม ใส่เสื้อเกราะ หรือผ่าตัดตามขนาดความคด

name: Idiopathic torsion dystonia
formal: Primary generalised dystonia, often DYT1 (TOR1A) mutation, with childhood onset limb dystonia that spreads, especially in Ashkenazi Jewish families, without other neurological features.
simple: An inherited condition in which muscles twist the body into abnormal postures, usually starting in childhood.

feat: Older historical term for isolated (primary) torsion dystonia, largely overlapping Generalized primary dystonia
Limb-onset twisting in childhood, spreading to trunk and other limbs
Normal cognition, reflexes, sensation and MRI
TOR1A GAG deletion with about 30% penetrance; founder effect in Ashkenazi Jews but occurs in all populations including Thai
Adult-onset ITD is usually focal or segmental and rarely generalises

case.story: Left arm twists behind her back when she writes on the board; over 18 months her neck and trunk started arching during walking.
case.exam: Action-induced dystonia of left arm, truncal and mild cervical dystonia; neurological examination otherwise normal.
case.tests: MRI, ceruloplasmin and levodopa trial negative; TOR1A ΔGAG positive; father is an unaffected carrier.

det.patho: Idiopathic torsion dystonia is the classic name for isolated dystonia without structural or neurodegenerative cause. TOR1A encodes torsinA, involved in nuclear envelope and ER function; the GAG deletion disturbs neurodevelopment of motor circuits, particularly cerebello-thalamo-cortical and striatal pathways, during a critical childhood window. Neuropathology is essentially normal, and the disorder is functional at network level.
det.clinical: Onset is commonly in a leg or arm around age 9–12, initially action-specific, then generalising within about 5 years in many. Cranial and laryngeal muscles are less involved than in THAP1 or KMT2B dystonia. Adult-onset idiopathic dystonia usually remains focal (cervical, blepharospasm, writer's cramp). Absence of any other neurological sign is part of the definition.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical with exclusion of secondary causes. Key steps are a levodopa trial, copper studies, MRI and genetic testing. Consider combined dystonias (myoclonus dystonia, dystonia-parkinsonism) if additional features appear. Normal DAT-SPECT supports isolated dystonia.
det.treatment: Trihexyphenidyl in gradually increasing doses is the main oral therapy in children; baclofen, clonazepam and tetrabenazine are alternatives. Botulinum toxin targets the most disabling regions. Bilateral GPi DBS gives large and sustained improvements in TOR1A dystonia and should be offered before fixed deformity develops. Rehabilitation and educational support are important.
det.prognosis: Disease stabilises after spread; with DBS many patients achieve independent function into adulthood.
pearls: Younger onset and leg involvement predict generalisation.
Unaffected parents can carry TOR1A because penetrance is low.
Earlier DBS before contractures gives better results.
det.thd: Idiopathic torsion dystonia เป็นชื่อดั้งเดิมของ dystonia ชนิด primary/isolated ที่มักเกิดจากยีน TOR1A (DYT1) เด็กเริ่มมีแขนหรือขาบิดขณะใช้งานแล้วลามไปลำตัว แต่สติปัญญาและการตรวจอื่นปกติ ยีนนี้ penetrance ต่ำ พ่อแม่อาจเป็นพาหะโดยไม่มีอาการ ต้องลอง levodopa และตรวจ Wilson ก่อน การรักษาใช้ trihexyphenidyl, botulinum toxin และ DBS ที่ GPi ซึ่งได้ผลดีมาก

name: Imipramine akathisia
formal: Akathisia induced by imipramine or other tricyclic antidepressants, with inner restlessness and inability to sit still, probably from altered dopaminergic and serotonergic transmission.
simple: Intense restlessness and inability to stay still caused by a tricyclic antidepressant medicine.
th: อาการกระสับกระส่ายนั่งไม่ติดที่ที่เกิดจากยา imipramine หรือยาต้านเศร้ากลุ่ม tricyclic พบไม่บ่อยและมักดีขึ้นเมื่อลดหรือหยุดยา
tempoNote: Usually within days to weeks of starting imipramine or raising the dose
feat: Inner restlessness and an urge to keep moving that began after imipramine was started or increased
Shifting weight, crossing and uncrossing legs, pacing; worse when asked to sit still
Not tied to the evening or to lying down, unlike restless legs syndrome
May be mistaken for worsening anxiety or agitated depression
Less common than with antipsychotics or SSRIs, but well described with tricyclics
inv: Medication timeline: start date, dose changes and co-prescribed dopamine blockers or SSRIs
Barnes Akathisia Rating Scale to quantify and follow
Ferritin and renal function if restless legs is a competing explanation

case.story: Started imipramine 75 mg at night for chronic pain and low mood; ten days later she cannot sit through meetings and feels driven to walk.
case.exam: Rocks and shifts in the chair, marches on the spot when standing; no rigidity, tremor or clonus.
case.tests: Ferritin normal; no other new drugs.
case.q: What has happened and what is the first step?
case.a: Tricyclic-induced akathisia; reduce or stop imipramine, and consider propranolol or mirtazapine-style alternatives if needed.

det.patho: Akathisia is thought to arise from reduced dopaminergic drive in mesocortical and striatal circuits, with serotonin acting through 5-HT2 receptors to inhibit dopamine release. Imipramine strongly blocks serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake, which may tip this balance. Noradrenergic overactivity likely contributes, explaining the benefit of beta-blockers.
det.clinical: The subjective feeling of inner tension is the core; objective fidgeting, rocking or pacing follows. Symptoms often appear soon after a dose increase and can be mistaken for agitation, prompting further dose rises that worsen it. Severe akathisia is distressing and has been linked to impulsive self-harm, so it must be asked about directly.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, based on new restlessness clearly related to drug exposure. Distinguish it from restless legs syndrome, anxiety, hyperthyroidism, serotonin toxicity and withdrawal states. Rating scales help document severity and response.
det.treatment: Lower the dose or stop the tricyclic where possible. Low-dose propranolol is the usual first symptomatic choice; benzodiazepines can help briefly, and low-dose mirtazapine has supportive evidence. Avoid adding dopamine-blocking drugs.
det.prognosis: Acute drug-induced akathisia usually settles within days to weeks after the offending drug is reduced.
pearls: Restlessness after an antidepressant dose rise is akathisia until shown otherwise.
Ask about suicidal thoughts; akathisia can drive impulsive acts.
Propranolol helps; anticholinergics are less useful than in other drug-induced movement disorders.
det.thd: Imipramine akathisia คืออาการกระสับกระส่าย อยากขยับตัวตลอดเวลาหลังเริ่มหรือเพิ่มยา imipramine คาดว่าเกิดจาก serotonin ไปลดการทำงานของ dopamine และ noradrenaline เพิ่มขึ้น ต่างจาก RLS ตรงที่ไม่สัมพันธ์กับช่วงเย็นหรือการนอน การรักษาคือลดหรือหยุดยา และใช้ propranolol ขนาดต่ำได้ ควรถามเรื่องความคิดทำร้ายตัวเองเสมอ

simple: Confusion, speech trouble and seizures that can occur after certain cancer immune cell treatments.

Immune effector cell neurotoxicity after CAR T therapy with encephalopathy, aphasia, tremor and seizures, often following cytokine release syndrome; managed with steroids and supportive care. Reversible severe encephalopathy after CAR T therapy or T-cell engagers with cytokine release, aphasia, seizures and cerebral oedema.

Inattention, confusion, drowsiness progressing to stupor in severe grades

case.who: 58-year-old woman with relapsed large B-cell lymphoma at a Bangkok transplant centre
case.story: Received CD19 CAR-T cells; fever and hypotension on day 2 settled with tocilizumab. On day 6 she wrote her name poorly and struggled to name objects.
case.exam: Alert but cannot name a pen or count back from 100 by tens; ICE score 6/10; mild postural tremor, no focal weakness.
case.tests: CT brain normal; EEG shows generalised slowing without seizures; CSF not taken.

det.patho: After T-cell redirecting therapy, activated immune cells release cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-1 that disrupt the blood-brain barrier and activate brain endothelium and pericytes, raising cytokine levels in the CSF. Myeloid cells amplify this response. Some CD19 expression on brain mural cells has been proposed as an on-target contributor. Risk rises with high tumour burden, early severe CRS, high CAR-T expansion and certain CD28-based products.
det.clinical: Symptoms typically appear after CRS has begun or even as it fades, though they can occur alone. The first signs are often subtle: impaired writing, reduced verbal output or attention. Severe cases bring depressed consciousness, seizures, motor weakness and, rarely, fulminant oedema. Separate syndromes exist: delayed parkinsonism and cranial nerve palsies after BCMA-directed CAR-T, and late encephalopathy linked to haemophagocytic states, so a new neurological change weeks later still needs evaluation.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, based on timing after immune effector therapy and the ICE assessment (orientation, naming, following commands, writing, attention). Grade 1–4 is assigned by the worst of ICE score, consciousness, seizures, motor signs and oedema. Exclude infection, metabolic disturbance, drugs, stroke and haemorrhage with bloods, imaging and, when platelets allow, CSF. EEG is valuable because non-convulsive seizures are common in drowsy patients.
det.treatment: Grade 1 is managed with supportive care, aspiration precautions and frequent reassessment. From grade 2, corticosteroids are the mainstay (dexamethasone, escalating to high-dose methylprednisolone for grade 3–4); anakinra is used for steroid-refractory cases. Tocilizumab treats CRS but barely enters the CNS and is not given for isolated ICANS. Levetiracetam prophylaxis is widely used; seizures and status are treated with standard protocols, and oedema needs ICU care with osmotherapy.
det.prognosis: Most cases resolve fully within days to a few weeks; deaths are uncommon and mainly from cerebral oedema or refractory seizures.
pearls: Ask the patient to write a sentence daily: dysgraphia is an early warning.
Tocilizumab is for CRS; steroids are for ICANS.
A drowsy post-CAR-T patient needs an EEG to exclude non-convulsive status.
det.thd: ICANS คือภาวะพิษต่อสมองหลังรักษามะเร็งด้วย CAR-T หรือยา bispecific เกิดจาก cytokine ที่ทำให้ blood-brain barrier รั่ว อาการเริ่มด้วยเขียนหนังสือผิด พูดติดขัด สับสน แล้วอาจซึม ชัก หรือสมองบวม ประเมินด้วย ICE score และ EEG ต้องแยกการติดเชื้อและเลือดออก รักษาด้วย dexamethasone ตั้งแต่ grade 2 ขึ้นไป ส่วน tocilizumab ใช้กับ CRS เป็นหลัก ส่วนใหญ่หายได้ภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์

qx.stem: On day 6 after CD19 CAR-T infusion for relapsed large B-cell lymphoma, a 52-year-old Bangkok bank clerk who had fever on day 2 now cannot name a pen or write a sentence. His ICE score is 4/10, he is drowsy but rousable, and there is no seizure. CRP and ferritin are high; CT is normal.
qx.q: What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Dexamethasone, with tocilizumab reserved for concurrent cytokine release syndrome, plus neurological monitoring
Observe only, since grade 1 ICANS resolves without treatment
Start levetiracetam and discharge
Plasma exchange for presumed antibody-mediated encephalopathy
High-dose cytarabine to reduce the CAR-T cell burden
qx.why: An ICE score of 3 to 6 indicates grade 2 ICANS, for which corticosteroids are first line, and escalation is needed if it worsens. Tocilizumab treats cytokine release syndrome but does not reliably penetrate the CNS or prevent ICANS when given alone. Seizure prophylaxis alone does not treat the encephalopathy, and the other options have no role.

name: Immune mediated necrotising myopathy
formal: Autoimmune myopathy with anti-SRP or anti-HMGCR antibodies and necrotic muscle fibres with little inflammation, causing subacute proximal weakness and very high creatine kinase; may follow statin use.
simple: A muscle disease in which the immune system damages muscle, causing weakness and often linked to statin medicines.
more: Immune-mediated myopathy with subacute proximal weakness, very high CK and necrotic fibres without much inflammation; anti-SRP or anti-HMGCR antibodies, may follow statins.
th: กล้ามเนื้ออักเสบแบบเนื้อตายจากภูมิคุ้มกัน — อ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขารุนแรง CK สูงมาก สัมพันธ์ยาสแตติน (HMGCR) หรือ anti-SRP
feat: Weeks to months of severe symmetric proximal weakness; dysphagia common
No rash; weakness continues after stopping a statin (unlike toxic statin myopathy)
Anti-SRP: severe, cardiac involvement; anti-HMGCR: statin exposure, also in young statin-naive patients
inv: CK very high (often thousands to tens of thousands)
Anti-HMGCR and anti-SRP antibodies
Biopsy: scattered necrotic fibres with little inflammation; MRI oedema
Cancer screening

case.story: Three months of rising difficulty standing from a chair; the statin was stopped 6 weeks ago without improvement.
case.exam: Hip flexors and deltoids 3/5, neck flexors weak, no rash, reflexes normal.
case.tests: CK 9,800 U/L; anti-HMGCR positive; biopsy: necrotic fibres with minimal inflammation.
case.q: What treatment is usually needed?
case.a: Immunotherapy — steroids plus a steroid-sparing agent and often IVIG; stopping the statin alone is not enough.

qx.stem: A 66-year-old woman from Bangkok has taken atorvastatin 40 mg for four years. Over three months she develops symmetric proximal leg and arm weakness without rash. Atorvastatin was stopped two months ago but she continues to weaken and CK remains 8,400 U/L. MRI thigh shows diffuse muscle oedema; biopsy shows scattered necrotic fibres with little inflammation.
qx.q: Which investigation would best establish the diagnosis?
opts: Anti-Jo-1 antibody
Anti-Mi-2 antibody
Anti-HMGCR antibody
Acid maltase (GAA) enzyme activity
Anti-MDA5 antibody
qx.why: Statin-associated self-limited myopathy improves within weeks of stopping the drug; persistent weakness and high CK with a necrotising biopsy suggest anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotising myopathy. It requires immunotherapy, often IVIG early plus steroids and a steroid-sparing agent, and statins should not be restarted. Jo-1, Mi-2 and MDA5 are associated with antisynthetase syndrome and dermatomyositis, and Pompe disease does not follow statin exposure.

ddx.pt: Endomysial inflammation around non-necrotic fibres; diagnosis of exclusion
Skin signs, perifascicular atrophy

aN: necrotising autoimmune myopathy nam | nam | necrotising autoimmune myopathy | imnm | necrotizing autoimmune myopathy | anti hmgcr myopathy | anti srp myopathy | statin myopathy autoimmune

det.patho: IMNM is an autoimmune myopathy in which antibodies (anti-SRP or anti-HMGCR) and complement target muscle fibres, causing widespread necrosis with little lymphocytic infiltration. Anti-HMGCR disease is linked to statin exposure in older adults, although it also occurs in statin-naive younger patients; HLA-DRB1*11:01 increases risk. A seronegative form shows the strongest cancer association. It is classified alongside dermatomyositis, antisynthetase syndrome and inclusion body myositis.
det.clinical: Symmetric proximal weakness develops over weeks to months, often severe, with neck flexor weakness, dysphagia and myalgia. Extramuscular features are uncommon, though anti-SRP disease may involve the heart and lungs and is often more aggressive. Younger patients, especially children with anti-HMGCR disease, may present slowly and resemble limb-girdle dystrophy. Unlike self-limited statin myotoxicity, weakness and high CK persist after stopping the statin.
det.diagnosis: CK is typically very high. Test anti-SRP and anti-HMGCR antibodies; a positive HMGCR antibody with a typical picture may make biopsy unnecessary. Biopsy shows scattered necrotic and regenerating fibres, sparse inflammation and sarcolemmal complement deposition. Muscle MRI shows oedema and helps choose a biopsy site. Screen for cancer, especially in seronegative and anti-HMGCR cases, and assess cardiac and pulmonary function.
det.treatment: Start early, combined immunotherapy: corticosteroids plus a steroid-sparing agent (methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate), with IVIG frequently added and effective, particularly for anti-HMGCR disease. Rituximab is used in refractory or anti-SRP disease. Stop the statin and avoid re-exposure; PCSK9 inhibitors or ezetimibe are lipid-lowering alternatives. Physiotherapy and swallowing therapy support recovery.
det.prognosis: Many patients improve, but relapses on tapering and residual weakness are common; younger patients and those with anti-SRP antibodies tend to do worse.
pearls: Persistent weakness with very high CK after stopping a statin = test anti-HMGCR.
Necrosis with little inflammation on biopsy does not mean non-immune.
Children with slow anti-HMGCR myopathy may be misdiagnosed as LGMD.
det.thd: IMNM เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้ออักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกันที่ทำให้เซลล์กล้ามเนื้อตายเป็นจำนวนมาก โดยมีเซลล์อักเสบน้อย สัมพันธ์กับแอนติบอดี anti-HMGCR (มักมีประวัติใช้ยาสแตติน) หรือ anti-SRP ผู้ป่วยอ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขารุนแรงภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์ถึงเดือน CK สูงมาก และอาการไม่ดีขึ้นแม้หยุดยาสแตติน การวินิจฉัยใช้การตรวจแอนติบอดี MRI และชิ้นเนื้อ ร่วมกับตรวจคัดกรองมะเร็ง การรักษาคือสเตียรอยด์ร่วมกับยากดภูมิ และมักให้ IVIG ร่วมด้วย ส่วนรายที่ดื้อยาใช้ rituximab

name: Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS)
formal: Paradoxical worsening of an infection or onset of inflammation after antiretroviral recovery of the immune system in HIV, such as with cryptococcal meningitis, TB or PML.
simple: A worsening of infection symptoms when the immune system recovers after starting HIV treatment.
th: อาการแย่ลงอย่างขัดแย้งหลังเริ่มยาต้านไวรัส HIV เมื่อภูมิคุ้มกันฟื้นตัว เกิดการอักเสบต่อเชื้อเดิม เช่น cryptococcus วัณโรค หรือ PML
tempoNote: Usually within 1–3 months after ART starts
feat: Worsening of known infection (paradoxical) or appearance of a hidden one (unmasking) after ART
Low baseline CD4 with rapid viral load fall
Cryptococcal meningitis, TB meningitis, PML most important in CNS
Culture often negative, with brisk inflammation
inv: CD4 rise and viral load fall
CSF culture to exclude treatment failure or new infection
MRI: enhancement and oedema around lesions

case.who: 30-year-old man from Kanchanaburi treated for cryptococcal meningitis
case.story: Five weeks after starting ART he develops headache, fever and seizures.
case.exam: Neck stiffness, papilloedema.
case.tests: CD4 rose 30 to 140; CSF culture negative, cells up; MRI meningeal enhancement.
case.q: What is happening?
case.a: Cryptococcal IRIS; continue ART, therapeutic LP and consider corticosteroids for severe disease.

det.patho: When ART restores immunity, recovering T cells respond vigorously to antigens of pathogens already present, producing harmful inflammation. Risk is highest with very low baseline CD4 and rapid fall in viral load. In the CNS this inflammation causes oedema, raised pressure and new or enlarging lesions.
det.clinical: Paradoxical IRIS is worsening of a known treated infection; unmasking IRIS reveals an unrecognised one. It usually appears within the first 1–3 months of ART, with fever, headache, seizures or new deficits. Cryptococcal, tuberculous and PML-related CNS IRIS carry substantial mortality.
det.diagnosis: IRIS is a diagnosis of exclusion based on timing after ART, evidence of immune recovery and absence of treatment failure, drug resistance, poor adherence or a new infection. CSF cultures are usually negative in paradoxical cryptococcal IRIS. MRI may show enhancement and oedema around lesions.
det.treatment: Continue ART in most cases. Corticosteroids for TB-IRIS and severe PML-IRIS; for cryptococcal IRIS, control pressure and consider steroids only for severe life-threatening inflammation. Prevent by delaying ART after cryptococcal and TB meningitis.
det.prognosis: Varies; CNS IRIS can be fatal but many recover.
pearls: Worsening after ART with negative cultures = IRIS.
Delay ART 4–6 weeks in cryptococcal meningitis.
Prednisone reduces TB-IRIS risk in high-risk patients.
det.thd: IRIS คือภาวะอาการแย่ลงหลังเริ่มยาต้านไวรัส HIV เมื่อภูมิคุ้มกันฟื้นตัวแล้วเกิดการอักเสบต่อเชื้อเดิม เช่น cryptococcus วัณโรค หรือ PML มักเกิดใน 1–3 เดือนแรก ต้องแยกจากเชื้อดื้อยาหรือเชื้อใหม่ รักษาโดยให้ยาต้านไวรัสต่อ ใช้ steroid ในบางชนิด และป้องกันด้วยการเลื่อนเวลาเริ่มยาในเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ

name: Immune-mediated encephalitis
formal: Brain inflammation due to autoimmune or paraneoplastic mechanisms, such as anti-NMDA receptor or LGI1 antibodies, with seizures, memory loss, psychiatric change and movement disorders.
simple: The immune system attacking the brain, causing confusion, seizures and memory or behaviour changes.
th: สมองอักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกันต่อต้านตนเองหรือจากมะเร็ง เช่น anti-NMDAR หรือ LGI1 มีความจำเสื่อมเร็ว ชัก อาการทางจิต และการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์
tempoNote: Evolves over days to under 3 months; some antibody types relapse
feat: Rapid loss of recent memory, confusion or personality change over weeks
New seizures, often drug resistant; faciobrachial dystonic seizures point to LGI1
Psychosis, agitation, catatonia, then dyskinesias and dysautonomia in anti-NMDAR encephalitis
Sleep disturbance, reduced consciousness, hypoventilation in severe cases
Possible underlying tumour (ovarian teratoma, small-cell lung cancer, thymoma) or immune checkpoint inhibitor exposure
inv: MRI with FLAIR (mesial temporal or multifocal change; may be normal, especially in NMDAR)
CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis, oligoclonal bands; send antibodies in both serum and CSF
EEG: slowing, seizures, extreme delta brush in NMDAR encephalitis
Tumour screening by CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, pelvic ultrasound or MRI, testicular ultrasound, and FDG-PET when needed

case.who: 22-year-old female university student from Chiang Mai
case.story: After a flu-like illness she became anxious, sleepless and paranoid over 10 days, was admitted to psychiatry, then had a generalised seizure.
case.exam: Fluctuating responsiveness, orofacial dyskinesia, labile blood pressure and heart rate; no meningism.
case.tests: MRI normal; CSF 35 lymphocytes, protein mildly raised, HSV PCR negative; EEG with extreme delta brush; pelvic ultrasound shows an ovarian cyst.
case.q: Which antibody should be sent and what treatment is urgent?
case.a: NMDAR antibodies in CSF; start first-line immunotherapy (IV methylprednisolone with IVIG or plasma exchange) and remove the ovarian teratoma.

read.where: Immunological diseases of the nervous system: Autoimmune Encephalitis (p126)
Chapter 9 - Seizures and Antibodies Against Surface Antigens
Considerations about the diagnosis of antibody-negative autoimmune encephalitis

det.patho: Antibodies against neuronal surface proteins (NMDAR, LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, AMPA, GABA-A, DPPX) alter receptor function or number and are directly pathogenic, so damage is often reversible. Antibodies to intracellular antigens (Hu, Ma2, CV2, amphiphysin, GAD65) mark T-cell–mediated neuronal destruction and are more often paraneoplastic and less treatable. Triggers include tumours, preceding HSV encephalitis (post-HSV NMDAR encephalitis) and immune checkpoint inhibitors.
det.clinical: Presentation depends on the antibody: anti-NMDAR affects mainly young women and children with psychiatric onset then seizures, dyskinesia, reduced consciousness and autonomic instability; LGI1 affects older men with faciobrachial dystonic seizures, amnesia and hyponatraemia; CASPR2 causes neuromyotonia, pain and insomnia; GABA-B gives severe seizures with small-cell lung cancer. Paediatric cases may start with behaviour change or movement disorder. Many patients initially land in psychiatry.
det.diagnosis: Consensus criteria allow a possible diagnosis when subacute memory, mental status or psychiatric change is accompanied by new focal signs, unexplained seizures, CSF pleocytosis or suggestive MRI, after reasonable exclusion of alternatives. Test antibodies in both CSF and serum because some (NMDAR) are more reliable in CSF and others (LGI1) in serum. Infection, especially HSV, must be excluded first. Antibody-negative cases can still be treated when the picture is convincing; be cautious with low-titre serum-only results, which can be false positives.
det.treatment: Start immunotherapy early, as delay worsens outcome: high-dose IV methylprednisolone, IVIG 2 g/kg or plasma exchange, often in combination. If response is poor after about two weeks, escalate to rituximab or cyclophosphamide. Remove any tumour found. Treat seizures, agitation and dysautonomia supportively; some need ICU care for months. Steroid-sparing maintenance may be needed for relapsing forms.
det.prognosis: Surface antibody syndromes usually improve substantially, though recovery may take 1–2 years and memory deficits can persist; intracellular-antibody paraneoplastic forms carry a poorer outlook.
pearls: New psychosis with seizures, dyskinesia or autonomic swings in a young woman: send CSF NMDAR antibodies and image the ovaries.
Brief arm and face jerks dozens of times a day in an older man: LGI1 until proven otherwise; check sodium.
A normal MRI does not exclude autoimmune encephalitis.
det.thd: Immune-mediated encephalitis คือสมองอักเสบจากแอนติบอดีต่อเซลล์ประสาท เช่น NMDAR หรือ LGI1 อาการเกิดภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์ ได้แก่ ความจำเสื่อม พฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน ชัก และการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติ ตรวจ MRI, CSF, EEG และแอนติบอดีทั้งในเลือดและน้ำไขสันหลัง พร้อมหามะเร็งซ่อนเร้น รักษาด้วย steroid, IVIG หรือ plasma exchange ตั้งแต่เนิ่น ๆ และ rituximab ถ้าไม่ตอบสนอง ส่วนใหญ่ฟื้นตัวได้ดีถ้ารักษาเร็ว

name: Immune-mediated neurological diseases
formal: Neurological disorders from immune attack on the nervous system, such as multiple sclerosis, myasthenia gravis, Guillain-Barre syndrome, autoimmune encephalitis and CIDP.
simple: Conditions in which the body's own immune system damages the brain, nerves or muscles.
th: กลุ่มโรคที่ระบบภูมิคุ้มกันทำลายระบบประสาท เช่น MS, NMOSD, myasthenia gravis, GBS, CIDP และ autoimmune encephalitis
tempoNote: Variable: acute monophasic (GBS), relapsing (MS, NMOSD), chronic (CIDP, MG)
feat: Umbrella term covering CNS, PNS, NMJ and muscle autoimmunity
CNS: MS, NMOSD, MOGAD, autoimmune encephalitis, neurosarcoidosis, CNS vasculitis
PNS: GBS, CIDP, MMN, nodopathies, vasculitic neuropathy; NMJ: myasthenia, LEMS; muscle: inflammatory myopathies
Paraneoplastic and immune checkpoint inhibitor-related syndromes
Responsive to immunotherapy, so early recognition prevents disability
inv: Syndrome-specific antibodies tested in serum and/or CSF
MRI, CSF analysis and neurophysiology according to the level of the nervous system involved
Tumour screening when paraneoplastic disease is possible

case.story: Over three weeks she developed memory loss, odd behaviour and two focal seizures with an episode of fear.
case.exam: Disorientated, poor short-term recall, no focal weakness.
case.tests: MRI bilateral mesial temporal FLAIR hyperintensity; CSF 12 lymphocytes/µL; LGI1 antibodies positive; serum sodium 128.
case.q: Which immune-mediated neurological disease is this and how is it treated?
case.a: LGI1 antibody autoimmune limbic encephalitis; treat with IV methylprednisolone and/or IVIG, adding second-line therapy if needed.

det.patho: Loss of immune tolerance leads to antibody-, T-cell- or complement-mediated injury of neural targets such as myelin proteins, ion channels, receptors, synaptic proteins and nodal proteins. Triggers include infections, tumours expressing neural antigens and drugs such as immune checkpoint inhibitors. Genetic background shapes susceptibility. This entry is a category, not a single disease.
det.clinical: Presentations range from encephalitis, myelitis and optic neuritis to neuropathies, myasthenic weakness and myositis. Course may be acute monophasic, relapsing–remitting or chronic progressive. Clues are subacute evolution, inflammatory CSF or MRI, coexisting autoimmunity or cancer, and steroid responsiveness.
det.diagnosis: Localise the syndrome, then use targeted antibody panels, MRI, CSF and neurophysiology. Use published criteria (e.g. McDonald for MS, Graus for autoimmune encephalitis, EAN/PNS for CIDP). Exclude infection, malignancy and metabolic disease. Treat antibody results in clinical context, as false positives occur.
det.treatment: Acute therapy uses corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange. Long-term immunotherapy includes disease-modifying therapies for MS, rituximab, complement inhibitors, FcRn blockers, anti-IL-6R therapy and conventional immunosuppressants. Tumour removal is essential in paraneoplastic disorders. Rehabilitation and infection prevention accompany immunotherapy.
det.prognosis: Variable; many conditions respond well to timely immunotherapy, whereas delayed treatment risks permanent deficit.
pearls: Subacute onset plus inflammatory CSF or MRI should raise suspicion of an immune-mediated cause.
Antibodies to cell-surface antigens usually respond better to immunotherapy than those to intracellular antigens.
Ask about checkpoint inhibitor therapy in any cancer patient with new neurological symptoms.
det.thd: Immune-mediated neurological diseases เป็นชื่อกลุ่มโรคที่ภูมิคุ้มกันโจมตีระบบประสาท ครอบคลุมสมอง ไขสันหลัง เส้นประสาท รอยต่อประสาทกล้ามเนื้อ และกล้ามเนื้อ เช่น MS, NMOSD, autoimmune encephalitis, GBS, CIDP และ myasthenia gravis อาการมักเป็นแบบกึ่งเฉียบพลันหรือกำเริบเป็นพัก ๆ วินิจฉัยด้วย antibody, MRI, CSF และการตรวจไฟฟ้าประสาท ส่วนใหญ่ตอบสนองต่อ steroid, IVIG, plasma exchange และยากดภูมิ

name: Immunoglobulin G4-related disease (IgG4-RD)
formal: Fibro-inflammatory disease with IgG4-positive plasma cells, causing hypertrophic pachymeningitis, hypophysitis, orbital pseudotumour and cranial neuropathies; responds to steroids and rituximab.
simple: An immune condition causing swollen, scarred tissues that can affect the brain coverings, pituitary, eye sockets and nerves.
th: โรคพังผืดอักเสบที่มี plasma cell ชนิด IgG4 ทำให้เยื่อหุ้มสมองหนา hypophysitis ก้อนหลังตา และเส้นประสาทสมองผิดปกติ ตอบสนองดีต่อ steroid และ rituximab
tempoNote: Indolent over months
feat: Middle-aged or older men; multi-organ (pancreas, salivary, lacrimal, retroperitoneum)
Hypertrophic pachymeningitis with headache and cranial neuropathies
Hypophysitis with diabetes insipidus or hypopituitarism
Orbital pseudotumour, proptosis
Serum IgG4 often raised but not specific

case.story: Months of headache and double vision, past history of 'autoimmune pancreatitis'.
case.exam: Left VI palsy, reduced left vision.
case.tests: MRI: diffuse dural thickening with enhancement; serum IgG4 high; dural biopsy IgG4+ plasma cells.
case.q: Treatment?
case.a: IgG4-related pachymeningitis; glucocorticoids, with rituximab or inebilizumab for relapse.

det.patho: IgG4-RD is an immune-mediated fibroinflammatory disorder in which B cells, plasmablasts and CD4 cytotoxic T cells drive dense infiltration and fibrosis. IgG4 itself is probably a marker rather than the cause. Lesions form tumour-like masses in many organs.
det.clinical: It mainly affects middle-aged and older men and often involves several organs over time. Neurological manifestations include hypertrophic pachymeningitis with headache and cranial neuropathies, hypophysitis with diabetes insipidus, orbital masses and perineural spread along trigeminal branches. History of pancreatitis, sialadenitis or retroperitoneal fibrosis is a clue.
det.diagnosis: The 2019 ACR/EULAR classification criteria combine clinical, imaging, serological and histological features. Serum IgG4 is often raised but is neither sensitive nor specific. Biopsy showing lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate, storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis with many IgG4-positive cells is key. Exclude lymphoma, GPA, sarcoidosis and infection.
det.treatment: Glucocorticoids induce remission in most patients. Rituximab is used for relapse or steroid sparing. Inebilizumab, an anti-CD19 antibody, gained approval in 2025 for reducing flares. Early treatment matters because fibrotic damage does not reverse.
det.prognosis: Responds well but relapses are frequent.
pearls: Pachymeningitis + hypophysitis + pancreatitis history = IgG4-RD.
Serum IgG4 is neither sensitive nor specific; biopsy is key.
Steroid responsiveness is typical.
det.thd: IgG4-related disease เป็นโรคอักเสบเรื้อรังที่มี plasma cell ชนิด IgG4 และพังผืด กระทบหลายอวัยวะ ทางระบบประสาททำให้เยื่อหุ้มสมองหนา ต่อมใต้สมองอักเสบ และก้อนหลังตา วินิจฉัยด้วยการตัดชิ้นเนื้อ รักษาด้วย steroid และ rituximab
