name: Impulsive behavior disorders
formal: Impulse control disorders such as pathological gambling, compulsive shopping, hypersexuality and binge eating, frequently dopamine agonist related in Parkinson disease.
simple: Strong urges to do things like gamble, shop or overeat that are hard to resist, often triggered by Parkinson treatment.
more: Screen at each visit and lower or stop the dopamine agonist; cognitive behavioural therapy can help. Symptoms usually improve after the drug is adjusted.
th: พฤติกรรมควบคุมแรงกระตุ้นผิดปกติ เช่น พนัน ช้อปปิ้ง พฤติกรรมทางเพศ หรือกินมากผิดปกติ มักสัมพันธ์กับยา dopamine agonist ในผู้ป่วย Parkinson
tempoNote: Usually develops months after starting or increasing a dopamine agonist
feat: Pathological gambling, compulsive shopping, hypersexuality and binge eating
Related behaviours: punding, hobbyism and dopamine dysregulation syndrome (compulsive overuse of levodopa)
Risk factors: dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole, rotigotine), younger age, male sex, prior addiction or impulsivity, depression
Patients often hide symptoms; spouses report debts or behaviour change
Also seen with agonists used for restless legs and prolactinoma
inv: Direct questioning of patient and carer at every visit; QUIP questionnaire
Medication review including levodopa equivalent and agonist dose
Assess mood, cognition and financial or legal harm

case.who: 54-year-old male civil servant from Chonburi with Parkinson disease
case.story: Pramipexole increased six months ago; his wife discovers he has spent family savings on online lotteries and stays up all night buying tools he never uses.
case.exam: Good motor control, mildly elated, no dyskinesia; denies a problem.
case.tests: QUIP positive for gambling and buying.
case.q: What is the problem and what is the management priority?
case.a: Dopamine agonist-induced impulse control disorder; taper the agonist (replace with levodopa if needed), watching for agonist withdrawal syndrome, and involve the family.

read.where: Chapter 9 Movement Disorders — Medical Treatment of Parkinson’s Disease
11 Non-motor Symptom Management in Parkinson’s Disease

det.patho: Dopamine agonists, particularly those preferring D3 receptors abundant in the ventral striatum, overstimulate the mesolimbic reward system, increasing reward sensitivity and decreasing response to negative outcomes. Individual vulnerability includes genetic variation in dopamine and opioid systems, premorbid impulsivity and younger disease onset. Levodopa and amantadine carry smaller risks, and DBS may unmask or relieve symptoms.
det.clinical: Up to about one in six PD patients on agonists develops at least one ICD, with cumulative risk rising over years of exposure. Behaviours escalate gradually and cause financial, marital and legal harm, and patients often lack insight or feel ashamed. Punding involves repetitive purposeless handling of objects; dopamine dysregulation syndrome involves craving extra levodopa. ICDs can also appear in restless legs syndrome patients on agonists.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on history from both patient and carer, ideally with screening questionnaires such as QUIP-RS. Ask specifically about money, internet use, sex and eating, since patients rarely volunteer them. Assess comorbid depression, anxiety and cognitive change. Warn and document before prescribing agonists.
det.treatment: The most effective step is to reduce or stop the dopamine agonist, compensating motor control with levodopa. Taper gradually to avoid dopamine agonist withdrawal syndrome (anxiety, pain, dysphoria). CBT and family involvement help; safeguards such as handing over financial control may be needed. Evidence for drugs like naltrexone or amantadine is weak; clozapine or quetiapine are sometimes used for severe cases.
det.prognosis: Most ICDs improve or resolve within months of reducing agonist therapy, although some persist and agonist withdrawal can be difficult.
pearls: Ask the spouse — patients often hide gambling or spending.
Warn every patient started on a dopamine agonist and document it.
Taper agonists slowly; abrupt withdrawal causes a distressing syndrome.
det.thd: Impulsive behavior disorders คือพฤติกรรมควบคุมแรงกระตุ้นไม่ได้ เช่น เล่นพนัน ซื้อของ พฤติกรรมทางเพศ หรือกินมาก พบบ่อยในผู้ป่วย Parkinson ที่ใช้ dopamine agonist อย่าง pramipexole หรือ ropinirole ผู้ป่วยมักไม่เล่า จึงต้องถามคนในครอบครัวทุกครั้งที่ติดตาม การรักษาหลักคือลดหรือหยุด agonist อย่างช้าๆ แล้วใช้ levodopa แทน ร่วมกับ CBT และการดูแลด้านการเงิน

name: Inclusion body myositis (IBM)
formal: Late-onset inflammatory myopathy with asymmetric weakness of finger flexors and quadriceps, rimmed vacuoles, endomysial inflammation, and poor response to immunotherapy.
simple: A slowly progressing muscle disease in older people, causing weak grip and thigh muscles and falls.
more: Diagnose from biopsy with rimmed vacuoles, p62 or TDP-43 aggregates, and positive anti-cN1A antibodies; CK is mildly raised and EMG shows mixed myopathic and neurogenic changes. Dysphagia is frequent; supportive care and exercise are the main management.
th: กล้ามเนื้ออักเสบเรื้อรังในผู้สูงอายุ — นิ้วมือกำไม่แน่นและต้นขาอ่อนแรง ไม่ตอบสนองต่อสเตียรอยด์
feat: Over 50, slowly progressive, often asymmetric
Weak deep finger flexors and quadriceps (falls, knees giving way)
Dysphagia common
Poor response to immunosuppression
inv: CK normal to mildly raised
Anti-cN1A antibody
Biopsy: endomysial inflammation, rimmed vacuoles, protein aggregates
Muscle MRI: forearm flexor and quadriceps involvement

case.story: Three years of falls on stairs and difficulty gripping a golf club.
case.exam: Wasted forearms with weak finger flexors, quadriceps 3/5, knee jerks reduced, sensation normal.
case.tests: CK 600 U/L; biopsy: rimmed vacuoles with endomysial CD8 T cells.
case.q: Which two muscle groups give the diagnosis away at the bedside?
case.a: Deep finger flexors and quadriceps.

read.where: บทที่ 6 IIM หน้า 104–136 (แนวทางวินิจฉัย แผนภูมิ 6.1 หน้า 106; MSA ตารางที่ 6.1 หน้า 107; พยาธิวิทยา ตารางที่ 6.2–6.3 หน้า 108–109)

qx.stem: A 68-year-old man from Lopburi has 4 years of progressive difficulty gripping and standing from low chairs and choking on solids. Examination shows weak finger flexors and quadriceps with asymmetrical atrophy. CK is 700 U/L, and a trial of prednisolone for six months did not help.
qx.q: Which histological features are expected?
opts: Perifascicular atrophy and capillary loss
Ragged-red fibres and COX-negative fibres only
Central nuclei in type 1 fibres
Grouped fibre atrophy only
Rimmed vacuoles with endomysial inflammatory cells invading non-necrotic fibres
qx.why: IBM is characterised by finger flexor and quadriceps weakness, dysphagia, age over 45 and unresponsiveness to immunosuppression, with biopsy showing endomysial inflammation, rimmed vacuoles and protein aggregates. Perifascicular atrophy is typical of dermatomyositis. Ragged-red fibres point to mitochondrial disease and central nuclei to centronuclear myopathy.

qx.stem: A 67-year-old man from Sakon Nakhon has had seven years of difficulty climbing stairs, falls from knee buckling, weak grip with a floppy handshake and recent choking on rice. Quadriceps and finger flexors are weakest, and CK is 650 U/L. A trial of prednisolone gave no benefit.
qx.q: Which biopsy and serological findings support the diagnosis?
opts: Rimmed vacuoles, endomysial CD8-positive T cells invading non-necrotic fibres and anti-cN1A antibodies
Perifascicular atrophy only
Nemaline rods
Ragged blue fibres with PAS-positive glycogen only
Type 2 fibre atrophy with negative antibodies
qx.why: The selective weakness of quadriceps and finger flexors, dysphagia, slow progression and steroid resistance are typical of sporadic inclusion body myositis. Histology shows rimmed vacuoles, protein inclusions and CD8-positive cells invading non-necrotic fibres, and anti-cN1A antibodies support it. Perifascicular atrophy characterises dermatomyositis, and nemaline rods a congenital myopathy.

ddx.pt: Symmetric proximal, much higher CK, responds to steroids
UMN signs and fasciculations; neurogenic EMG
Myotonia, ptosis, cataracts, family history

aN: ibm | inclusion body myositis | sibm | sporadic inclusion body myositis

det.patho: An older-adult myopathy with slow progression, combining cytotoxic CD8 T-cell inflammation with degenerative features — rimmed vacuoles, protein aggregates (TDP-43, p62) and mitochondrial abnormalities. Antibodies against cytosolic 5′-nucleotidase 1A (cN1A) are found in a proportion of patients. IBM is the commonest acquired myopathy after age 50, more frequent in men, and does not respond to standard immunotherapy, suggesting the degenerative process is not simply driven by inflammation.
det.clinical: Weakness develops over years, typically asymmetric, with selective involvement of deep finger flexors (weak grip, difficulty turning keys) and quadriceps (knees buckling, falls on stairs). Ankle dorsiflexors and facial muscles may be involved, and dysphagia affects over half. Wasting of the medial forearm and thigh is a visual clue. Sensation is normal, but a mild neuropathy can coexist, causing confusion with motor neuron disease.
det.diagnosis: CK is normal or moderately raised (usually under 15 times the upper limit). EMG shows myopathic and often neurogenic-looking units with fibrillations. Muscle MRI or ultrasound highlights selective flexor digitorum profundus and quadriceps involvement with relative rectus femoris sparing. Biopsy shows endomysial inflammation invading non-necrotic fibres, rimmed vacuoles, protein aggregates and mitochondrial changes; anti-cN1A is supportive but not specific (also seen in Sjögren and SLE). The ENMC 2011 criteria are commonly used.
det.treatment: No drug has proven effective; corticosteroids and conventional immunosuppressants do not halt progression. Management centres on physiotherapy and safe exercise, falls prevention with knee-ankle orthoses and walking aids, occupational therapy for grip, and swallowing assessment with dilatation or cricopharyngeal myotomy for severe dysphagia. IVIG may help dysphagia in some reports. Patients should be offered clinical trials where available.
det.prognosis: Slow progression over years; many need a walking aid within 10–15 years, but life expectancy is near normal unless dysphagia causes aspiration.
pearls: Older man, weak finger flexors and quadriceps, poor steroid response = IBM.
Steroid-refractory polymyositis should prompt reconsideration of IBM.
det.thd: IBM เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้ออักเสบเรื้อรังในผู้ที่อายุเกิน 50 ปี มีทั้งการอักเสบจาก CD8 T cell และการเสื่อมที่พบ rimmed vacuoles ในชิ้นเนื้อ อาการค่อย ๆ อ่อนแรงหลายปีแบบไม่เท่ากันสองข้าง เด่นที่กล้ามเนื้องอนิ้วมือ (กำไม่แน่น) และ quadriceps (เข่าทรุด หกล้ม) และกลืนลำบาก CK สูงเล็กน้อย ตรวจแอนติบอดี anti-cN1A, MRI กล้ามเนื้อ และตัดชิ้นเนื้อช่วยยืนยัน โรคนี้ไม่ตอบสนองต่อสเตียรอยด์และยากดภูมิ การรักษาเน้นกายภาพบำบัด อุปกรณ์ช่วยเดิน และดูแลการกลืน

name: Index subcortical dementia
formal: Dementia from basal ganglia, thalamus and white matter disease, with slowed thinking, apathy, executive dysfunction and movement abnormalities, as in Parkinson, Huntington disease and HIV.
simple: Memory and thinking problems with slowed thinking and mood change, caused by damage to deep brain structures.
th: ภาวะสมองเสื่อมจากโรคของ basal ganglia, thalamus และ white matter มีความคิดช้า เฉื่อยชา executive function เสีย และมีความผิดปกติของการเคลื่อนไหว เช่น ใน Parkinson, Huntington และ HIV
tempoNote: Usually gradual; stepwise or subacute when vascular, infective or toxic-metabolic
feat: A descriptive syndrome, not one disease (the entry is a lexicon index term)
Slowed thinking, inattention, apathy, mood change and poor planning and sequencing; memory loss is of the retrieval type and improves with cues
Cortical signs such as aphasia, agnosia and ideomotor apraxia are typically absent
Motor companions: parkinsonian or apraxic gait, falls, dysarthria, chorea, urinary urgency
Causes: small-vessel disease and Binswanger disease, HIV, Whipple disease, PSP, Parkinson and Huntington disease, NPH, MS, Wilson disease
inv: Neuropsychology weighted to processing speed and executive tasks (trail making, fluency, digit symbol)
MRI: leukoaraiosis and lacunes, basal ganglia or midbrain change, ventriculomegaly
Reversible-cause screen: HIV, syphilis, B12, thyroid, calcium, copper studies, and Whipple PCR in the right setting

case.who: 67-year-old retired teacher from Khon Kaen with long-standing hypertension and diabetes
case.story: Family says she is slow to answer, has lost interest in cooking and has fallen twice in a year; she needs a long time to recall a name but gets it when given the first syllable.
case.exam: Short-stepped gait with poor turning, brisk reflexes, impaired trail making, normal naming and comprehension.
case.tests: MRI shows extensive confluent periventricular white-matter change and lacunes; B12, thyroid and HIV tests are normal.
case.q: What cognitive pattern is this and what is the most likely substrate?
case.a: Subcortical (frontal-subcortical) dementia from small-vessel disease; treat vascular risk, especially blood pressure.

read.where: Chapter 80: Nondegenerative Dementias and Encephalopathies — Vascular Dementia (Binswanger disease)

det.patho: The syndrome reflects interruption of frontal-subcortical circuits running through the basal ganglia, thalamus and deep white matter, which supports attention, speed and executive control. Damage can come from ischaemia, degeneration of deep nuclei, demyelination or infection. Because the cortex is relatively spared, naming, comprehension and praxis stay intact. Small-vessel disease is the commonest cause in practice.
det.clinical: Relatives describe slowness, forgetfulness that is helped by prompts, apathy or depression, and trouble with multistep tasks. Gait disturbance and urinary symptoms often arrive early in vascular forms, whereas chorea or parkinsonism leads in the basal ganglia diseases. Vascular forms may progress in steps or gradually from accumulated microinfarcts. Patients can look unmotivated, so depression and apathy must be distinguished.
det.diagnosis: Use a bedside cognitive screen that includes executive items, then formal neuropsychology that separates speed and executive failure from cortical amnesia. MRI shows white-matter hyperintensity and lacunes, deep nuclei changes or hydrocephalus. Because many causes are reversible or treatable, screen for HIV, syphilis, B12 deficiency, thyroid and metabolic disease, and consider Whipple disease when there are gaze abnormalities, myoclonus or gut symptoms.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: antiretroviral therapy for HIV, penicillin for neurosyphilis (it halts but may not reverse the damage), antibiotics for Whipple disease, shunting for NPH in selected patients, and strict blood-pressure and vascular risk control for small-vessel disease. Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine have not been shown to help vascular dementia in trials, though some patients with coexisting Alzheimer pathology benefit. Treat depression, review sedatives, and add physiotherapy for gait and falls.
det.prognosis: Depends on the cause: treatable infective and metabolic forms can improve, whereas vascular and degenerative forms progress slowly.
pearls: Slow but correct answers suggest a subcortical pattern.
Cued recall helps subcortical, not hippocampal, memory deficits.
Look for the motor sign: it usually names the disease.
det.thd: Subcortical dementia เป็นลักษณะอาการ ไม่ใช่โรคเดี่ยว เกิดจากความเสียหายของวงจร frontal-subcortical ผู้ป่วยคิดช้า เฉื่อยชา วางแผนไม่ได้ ซึมเศร้า ความจำดีขึ้นเมื่อมีตัวช่วยจำ แต่พูดและเข้าใจภาษาปกติ มักมีเดินผิดปกติหรือ parkinsonism ร่วมด้วย สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยคือโรคหลอดเลือดสมองขนาดเล็ก รวมทั้ง HIV, PSP, Huntington และ NPH ควรตรวจหาสาเหตุที่รักษาได้ และควบคุมความดันโลหิตและปัจจัยเสี่ยงหลอดเลือด

ddx.pt: Cortical amnesia that does not improve with cueing, with early aphasia or agnosia
Disinhibition, loss of empathy and hyperorality outweigh the slowing
Gait, urinary and cognitive triad with ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy, partly reversible by shunting

name: Index systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid antibody
formal: Systemic autoimmune disease with antiphospholipid antibodies, causing stroke, seizures, chorea, myelitis, cognitive dysfunction and cerebral venous thrombosis through vasculopathy and thrombosis.
simple: An immune disease that can lead to strokes, seizures and thinking problems, in part through blood clots in brain vessels.
th: โรค SLE ที่มี antiphospholipid antibody ทำให้เกิด stroke ชัก chorea ไขสันหลังอักเสบ ปัญหาการรู้คิด และหลอดเลือดดำในสมองอุดตัน
tempoNote: Thrombotic events are sudden; cognitive and inflammatory features evolve over weeks to years
feat: Index-style entry combining SLE and antiphospholipid antibodies (aPL)
aPL increase arterial and venous thrombosis: stroke, TIA, CVT, retinal occlusion
Chorea, seizures and transverse myelitis are associated with aPL in SLE
Cognitive dysfunction and white matter lesions; Libman-Sacks endocarditis may embolise
Recurrent pregnancy loss and thrombocytopenia are clues
inv: ANA, anti-dsDNA, complement; lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I (repeat at 12 weeks)
MRI brain/spine; MRV for CVT
Echocardiography for valve vegetations

case.who: 26-year-old woman from Phuket with SLE and two miscarriages
case.story: Sudden left arm weakness and slurred speech; months earlier she had brief jerky movements of the right side.
case.exam: Left hemiparesis, livedo reticularis, mild right-sided choreiform movements.
case.tests: Lupus anticoagulant and anti-beta2GPI positive (persisting at 12 weeks); MRI right MCA infarct; echo mitral thickening.
case.q: What is the cause and long-term treatment?
case.a: Stroke from antiphospholipid syndrome secondary to SLE; long-term warfarin (DOACs are not recommended in high-risk APS).

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Antiphospholipid Syndrome

det.patho: Antiphospholipid antibodies bind phospholipid-protein complexes such as beta2-glycoprotein I on endothelium, platelets and monocytes, promoting thrombosis and complement activation. In SLE, these thrombotic mechanisms coexist with immune-complex, antibody-mediated and cytokine-driven CNS injury, so neurological events can be thrombotic, inflammatory or both.
det.clinical: Neurological manifestations include ischaemic stroke and TIA, cerebral venous thrombosis, seizures, chorea, myelitis, migraine-like headaches and cognitive impairment. Livedo, thrombocytopenia, valvular disease and obstetric history suggest aPL involvement. The odd lexicon name reflects an index entry; the clinical concept is SLE with aPL.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on persistent laboratory aPL (two tests at least 12 weeks apart) plus thrombotic or obstetric events, and on SLE classification criteria. 2023 ACR/EULAR APS criteria weight clinical and laboratory domains. Imaging classifies the neurological event, and inflammatory markers help separate active lupus from thrombosis.
det.treatment: Thrombotic APS is treated with long-term vitamin K antagonists; DOACs are avoided, especially in arterial or triple-positive disease. Inflammatory neuropsychiatric lupus needs glucocorticoids and immunosuppression (cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate, rituximab). Hydroxychloroquine is used in most SLE patients. Seizures and chorea are treated symptomatically.
det.prognosis: Recurrence risk is substantial without anticoagulation; neurological involvement worsens long-term outcome in SLE.
pearls: Young stroke with miscarriages and livedo: check aPL.
Avoid DOACs in arterial or triple-positive APS.
Repeat aPL testing at 12 weeks to confirm persistence.
det.thd: ผู้ป่วย SLE ที่มี antiphospholipid antibody เสี่ยงต่อลิ่มเลือดทั้งหลอดเลือดแดงและดำ ทำให้เกิด stroke หลอดเลือดดำในสมองอุดตัน ชัก chorea และไขสันหลังอักเสบ ต้องตรวจ lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin และ anti-beta2GPI ซ้ำห่าง 12 สัปดาห์ การรักษาคือ warfarin ระยะยาวสำหรับเหตุการณ์ลิ่มเลือด และยากดภูมิสำหรับการอักเสบของ lupus

ddx.pt: Inflammatory lupus CNS disease without aPL-mediated thrombosis
APS without features of SLE
Microangiopathic haemolysis with schistocytes, low ADAMTS13

aN: sle with antiphospholipid antibodies | lupus with aps | neuro lupus with apl | secondary antiphospholipid syndrome

name: Indian childhood cirrhosis
formal: Infantile copper-associated liver disease of rural India with progressive cirrhosis and marked hepatic copper deposits, linked to copper-contaminated milk in brass vessels with a genetic susceptibility.
simple: A fatal childhood liver disease from too much copper in the diet seen in rural India, historically.
more: Liver biopsy shows copper and Mallory bodies. Early chelation (penicillamine) and stopping copper exposure help; it is now rare after public health changes.
th: โรคตับแข็งในเด็กเล็กชนบทอินเดียจากทองแดงสะสมในตับมาก สัมพันธ์กับนมที่เก็บในภาชนะทองเหลืองร่วมกับปัจจัยพันธุกรรม
tempoNote: Begins between about 6 months and 3 years, progressing to cirrhosis over months
feat: A paediatric liver disease, not a neurological disease; included for copper-disorder differential
Insidious onset with abdominal distension, irritability and hepatomegaly with a sharp, leafy edge
Progressive jaundice, ascites and liver failure if untreated
Copper-contaminated milk from brass or copper utensils; familial clustering
Now rare after public education; similar cases in other regions are grouped as idiopathic copper toxicosis
inv: Liver biopsy: very high copper, orcein-positive copper-associated protein, Mallory–Denk bodies, pericellular fibrosis
Ceruloplasmin normal or raised; serum and urinary copper raised
Exclude Wilson disease and other infant liver diseases

case.who: 18-month-old girl born in a rural Indian community, now living in Bangkok
case.story: Abdomen enlarging and poor feeding for three months; family has used a brass pot to boil milk since birth.
case.exam: Firm hepatomegaly with sharp edge, mild jaundice, no neurological signs.
case.tests: Ceruloplasmin normal; liver biopsy shows dense copper deposits, Mallory bodies and micronodular cirrhosis.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the two key treatment steps?
case.a: Indian childhood cirrhosis; stop copper exposure and begin penicillamine chelation, with transplant referral if decompensated.

det.patho: Excess copper intake from milk heated or stored in copper or brass vessels, together with a presumed inherited weakness in hepatic copper handling, leads to massive hepatocellular copper accumulation. Copper generates oxidative stress, Mallory–Denk bodies, necrosis and pericellular fibrosis that evolves rapidly to micronodular cirrhosis. The responsible gene is unknown.
det.clinical: This is a liver disease of infancy with minimal primary neurological involvement. Early stages show irritability, poor appetite and hepatomegaly; intermediate stages bring jaundice and pruritus; late stages cause ascites, bleeding and hepatic encephalopathy. Without treatment death usually occurs within months of the onset of jaundice.
det.diagnosis: Liver biopsy is diagnostic, showing marked copper excess and characteristic histology. Laboratory copper indices differ from Wilson disease, with normal ceruloplasmin and no KF rings. A detailed feeding and utensil history supports the diagnosis. Infectious, metabolic and biliary causes must be excluded.
det.treatment: Remove the copper source immediately. Chelation with D-penicillamine started in early stages can produce remission and survival. Advanced decompensated cirrhosis may need liver transplantation. Prevention through community education led to near-disappearance of the disease in India.
det.prognosis: Formerly almost uniformly fatal; early chelation has transformed survival, but late-stage disease remains grave.
pearls: Infant cirrhosis with normal ceruloplasmin: ask about copper or brass vessels.
Not Wilson disease — the age and copper indices differ.
Its disappearance after changing utensil use shows the role of environment.
det.thd: Indian childhood cirrhosis เป็นโรคตับแข็งในเด็กเล็กที่เคยพบมากในชนบทอินเดีย เกิดจากทองแดงสะสมในตับมากจากการต้มหรือเก็บนมในภาชนะทองเหลือง ร่วมกับปัจจัยพันธุกรรม เด็กมีตับโต ตัวเหลือง และตับแข็งเร็ว ceruloplasmin ปกติต่างจาก Wilson วินิจฉัยด้วยชิ้นเนื้อตับ รักษาโดยหยุดแหล่งทองแดงและให้ penicillamine เป็นโรคตับ ไม่ใช่โรคทางประสาทโดยตรง

name: PLA2G6-associated neurodegeneration (PLAN)
formal: Autosomal recessive PLA2G6-related disorder with onset in infancy of psychomotor regression, hypotonia, optic atrophy and cerebellar atrophy, with axonal spheroids on biopsy.
simple: An inherited disease starting in infancy in which a child loses skills and develops weak muscles, vision problems and later stiffness.
more: Diagnosed by PLA2G6 testing; MRI shows cerebellar atrophy with iron accumulation in the globus pallidus and a characteristic clock-hand sign in the thin cord. Biopsy of skin or conjunctiva shows spheroids; prognosis is poor and care is supportive. Infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy, PLA2G6-associated, with early psychomotor regression, hypotonia, tetraparesis, visual failure and cerebellar atrophy; iron accumulation in globus pallidus later. Infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy from PLA2G6 mutation with psychomotor regression, hypotonia, optic atrophy and cerebellar atrophy with iron deposition. Autosomal recessive PLA2G6 disorder (infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy, NBIA) with regression, hypotonia, optic atrophy, cerebellar atrophy and iron deposition; also adult dystonia-parkinsonism. Neuroaxonal dystrophy beginning at 2 to 3 years with psychomotor regression, ataxia, optic atrophy and seizures, with axonal spheroids on biopsy, often PLA2G6-related. PLA2G6-associated neurodegeneration (infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy and related) with brain iron accumulation, psychomotor regression, hypotonia, spasticity and optic atrophy, with early childhood onset. MRI shows cerebellar atrophy and pallidal iron; autosomal recessive PLA2G6 mutations. No cure and treatment is supportive. Infantile or late-onset neurodegeneration with axonal spheroids, PLA2G6 mutation, developmental regression, hypotonia, optic atrophy and iron accumulation. Nerve or skin biopsy shows axonal spheroids; MRI shows cerebellar atrophy with T2 hypointensity in the globus pallidus and cerebellar cortex hyperintensity. Autosomal recessive, with no cure; treatment is supportive with seizure and spasticity control. Childhood or adolescent onset neuroaxonal dystrophy with progressive dystonia, parkinsonism, cognitive decline and iron accumulation, as in PLA2G6-associated neurodegeneration. Rare autosomal recessive neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation from PLA2G6 or related variants, with childhood onset dystonia, spasticity, cognitive loss and cerebellar atrophy first reported in Pakistan. MRI shows iron in the globus pallidus and cerebellar atrophy. Care is supportive, and the disease is progressive.

det.patho: PLA2G6 encodes a calcium-independent phospholipase A2 that remodels membrane phospholipids. Biallelic loss disrupts membrane homeostasis and mitochondrial function in neurons, leading to swollen distal axons (spheroids) in central and peripheral nervous system and, in some, brain iron deposition. It is classified within both neuroaxonal dystrophies and NBIA (type 2).
det.clinical: Classic infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy begins with regression and hypotonia between 6 months and 3 years, followed by spasticity, optic atrophy, cognitive decline and sometimes seizures. Atypical neuroaxonal dystrophy starts later in childhood with gait instability, ataxia, speech delay and behavioural problems. Adult onset (PARK14) causes levodopa-responsive dystonia-parkinsonism with early dyskinesias and cognitive and psychiatric features.
det.diagnosis: MRI showing cerebellar atrophy with abnormal cortical signal in a regressing infant suggests the diagnosis; pallidal iron may appear only later. Neurophysiology shows denervation and axonal neuropathy. Confirmation is by finding biallelic PLA2G6 variants on a panel or exome. Exclude metabolic and lysosomal causes of regression in parallel.
det.treatment: There is no curative treatment. Supportive care includes physiotherapy, management of spasticity and dystonia, seizure control, nutrition and gastrostomy, and palliative planning in infantile cases. Adult-onset parkinsonism responds to levodopa but troublesome dyskinesias appear early. Deuterated polyunsaturated fatty acids have been investigated for INAD without proven benefit.
det.prognosis: Infantile form progresses to severe disability with death often in the first decade; adult-onset forms progress over many years.
pearls: Infant regression + floppy + optic atrophy + cerebellar atrophy on MRI: think PLAN.
Absent reflexes with upgoing toes in a regressing toddler implies combined central and peripheral axonal disease.
PLA2G6 also causes young-onset dystonia-parkinsonism (PARK14) in adults.
det.thd: PLA2G6-associated neurodegeneration เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมยีนด้อย ทำให้ปลายแอกซอนบวม (spheroid) ในระบบประสาท เด็กอายุ 6 เดือนถึง 3 ปีมีพัฒนาการถดถอย ตัวอ่อน ตาฝ่อ และสมองน้อยฝ่อ ต่อมาเกร็งทั้งตัว รูปแบบผู้ใหญ่มาด้วย dystonia-parkinsonism วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI และตรวจยีน PLA2G6 การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง

name: Infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (Haltia-Santavuori disease)
formal: Santavuori-Haltia disease, a CLN1 PPT1-related lysosomal storage disorder with onset before 2 years of microcephaly, myoclonus, visual failure and flat EEG, with granular osmiophilic deposits.
simple: An inherited childhood disease causing loss of skills, seizures, blindness and early death, from build-up of waste material in brain cells.
more: Infantile NCL (CLN1, PPT1 deficiency) with developmental regression at 6 to 24 months, microcephaly, myoclonus, visual failure, flat EEG and granular osmiophilic deposits.

Slowing of head growth, ending in microcephaly

case.story: Sat at 7 months but has stopped babbling and no longer reaches for toys; frequent jerks of arms and repetitive hand movements.
case.exam: Head circumference falling to 3rd centile, axial hypotonia, does not fix or follow, optic pallor, multifocal myoclonus.
case.tests: EEG low-amplitude background; ERG markedly reduced; PPT1 activity absent; homozygous PPT1 variant.
case.q: Which neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis is this?

det.patho: Biallelic PPT1 variants abolish palmitoyl-protein thioesterase 1, a lysosomal enzyme that removes fatty acid chains from proteins. Undegraded material forms granular osmiophilic deposits in neurons, which undergo rapid and widespread loss, especially in the cortex. The disease was first described in Finland, where a founder variant is common, but occurs worldwide.
det.clinical: After normal early development, infants develop irritability, sleep problems, hypotonia and loss of skills before age 2. Microcephaly, blindness, myoclonus and seizures follow, and children become vegetative by about age 3. Hand-knitting movements can mimic Rett syndrome. Later-onset CLN1 variants present with slower courses in childhood or adulthood.
det.diagnosis: Enzyme assay of PPT1 is rapid and reliable, with gene sequencing for confirmation. EEG shows progressive loss of amplitude to isoelectric, ERG becomes extinguished, and MRI shows atrophy with thalamic T2 hypointensity and white-matter change. Electron microscopy shows granular osmiophilic deposits but is now rarely necessary.
det.treatment: There is no approved disease-modifying therapy; enzyme replacement and gene therapy remain experimental. Care is palliative and supportive: seizure and myoclonus control (valproate, levetiracetam, benzodiazepines; avoid drugs worsening myoclonus), nutrition via gastrostomy, management of spasticity, sleep and pain. Families need genetic counselling and prenatal or preimplantation options.
det.prognosis: Death usually occurs between 8 and 13 years after a long vegetative phase; later-onset variants live longer.
pearls: Infant regression with blindness, myoclonus and a flattening EEG: test PPT1.
INCL differs from CLN2, for which enzyme replacement exists.
Hand stereotypies can mislead toward Rett syndrome.
det.thd: Infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (CLN1) เกิดจากยีน PPT1 ทำให้สารสะสมในไลโซโซมของเซลล์ประสาท เด็กพัฒนาการปกติช่วงแรกแล้วถดถอยก่อนอายุ 2 ปี ศีรษะเล็กลง ตาบอด กระตุก myoclonus และ EEG แบนลงเรื่อยๆ วินิจฉัยด้วยการวัดเอนไซม์ PPT1 และตรวจยีน ยังไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ ดูแลแบบประคับประคองและให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

name: Infantile onset spinocerebellar ataxia (IOSCA)
formal: Finnish autosomal recessive disorder from C10orf2 (Twinkle) variants with infantile ataxia, athetosis, ophthalmoplegia, sensory neuropathy, deafness and epilepsy.
simple: An inherited childhood disease causing worsening balance, abnormal movements, deafness and nerve damage beginning in infancy.
more: Confirmed by genetic testing and MRI showing cerebellar atrophy. Treatment is supportive, and affected individuals often lose mobility in adolescence.

case.story: Walked at 12 months but by 20 months started falling and now cannot stand unsupported; he writhes his hands and does not turn to soft sounds.
case.exam: Truncal ataxia, athetoid hand movements, absent reflexes, limited upgaze.

det.patho: TWNK encodes Twinkle, the helicase that unwinds mitochondrial DNA during replication. Recessive loss of function causes mtDNA depletion in neurons, especially in sensory ganglia, cerebellum and auditory pathways. Dominant TWNK variants cause a different disease, adult progressive external ophthalmoplegia with mtDNA deletions.
det.clinical: Infants develop normally, then from about the second year develop ataxia, athetosis and hypotonia with areflexia. During childhood ophthalmoplegia, hearing loss and sensory neuropathy accumulate; girls have hypergonadotropic hypogonadism. In the teenage years an epileptic encephalopathy with recurrent status epilepticus may develop and is the main threat to life. Most patients lose independent walking by adolescence.
det.diagnosis: Consider it in a toddler with progressive ataxia, sensory neuropathy and deafness. Genetic testing of TWNK, usually within an ataxia or mitochondrial panel or exome, confirms it. Lactate can be normal; mtDNA copy number in tissue supports depletion. Exclude treatable ataxias such as vitamin E deficiency.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying treatment exists. Supportive care includes physiotherapy, hearing aids or cochlear implants, hormone replacement, and nutritional support. Seizures are treated with standard agents other than valproate, with early aggressive management of status epilepticus. Genetic counselling is essential.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive disability; survival into adulthood is possible but severe epilepsy can be fatal in adolescence.
pearls: Toddler ataxia + deafness + absent sensory potentials + ophthalmoplegia: think mtDNA depletion such as TWNK.
Avoid valproate in suspected mitochondrial DNA maintenance disorders.
Recessive TWNK gives IOSCA; dominant TWNK gives adult PEO.

det.patho: Biallelic GAA variants abolish lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase, so glycogen accumulates in lysosomes of cardiac, skeletal and smooth muscle and in motor neurons. Lysosomal swelling and autophagic dysfunction destroy muscle fibres. Infantile forms have almost no residual enzyme activity, which explains early cardiac involvement.
det.clinical: Within the first months infants show hypotonia, weakness, macroglossia, feeding problems and respiratory difficulty. Cardiomegaly with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy leads to heart failure. Without treatment, death from heart and respiratory failure typically follows before the first birthday. Treated survivors may develop residual myopathy, ptosis, hearing loss and speech problems.
det.diagnosis: The combination of floppy infant, cardiomegaly and high CK is highly suggestive. Enzyme activity on dried blood spots is the first test, confirmed by gene sequencing. CRIM status predicts antibody response to enzyme therapy. Newborn screening programmes, increasingly adopted in Asia, allow presymptomatic diagnosis.
det.treatment: Recombinant enzyme replacement therapy (alglucosidase alfa or avalglucosidase alfa) should start as early as possible, ideally within days of diagnosis. CRIM-negative infants receive immune tolerance induction with rituximab, methotrexate and IVIG. Supportive care includes cardiac management, ventilatory support, feeding and physiotherapy. Gene therapies are in clinical trials.
det.prognosis: Untreated, most die in infancy; with early enzyme replacement many survive and walk, although residual weakness is common.
pearls: Floppy baby plus big heart plus big tongue: test GAA activity.
A short PR with giant QRS voltage on ECG is a strong clue.
Raised AST/ALT may be muscle-derived — check CK before a liver work-up.

det.patho: Septic emboli lodge at distal branch points or in the vasa vasorum and inflame the arterial wall from the adventitia inward, destroying the media and internal elastic lamina. The result is a fragile pseudoaneurysm rather than a true aneurysm. Some form at the site of a previous embolic occlusion, and bacteria may also reach the wall through the lumen in vessels without vasa vasorum. Healing with antibiotics produces fibrosis, but weakened walls can still rupture weeks to months after bacteriological cure.
det.clinical: They occur in a few per cent of patients with endocarditis, but many are never detected because they heal. Rupture produces lobar haemorrhage or subarachnoid blood over the convexity, often with focal deficits rather than the thunderclap and basal SAH of saccular aneurysms. Headache or a small warning leak may precede rupture by hours to days. Some cases come to attention only as an unexplained lobar bleed, which should prompt blood cultures and echocardiography.
det.diagnosis: Brain MRI with susceptibility imaging and vessel imaging are part of the evaluation of endocarditis with neurological symptoms. CTA and MRA detect larger aneurysms well, but catheter angiography remains the reference for small distal lesions and for treatment planning; all four vessels should be studied because multiple lesions are common. If an aneurysm is the first sign of illness, a thorough search for the infection and the organism is needed.
det.treatment: All patients receive prolonged pathogen-directed antibiotics. Unruptured lesions are followed with serial vascular imaging and treated if they enlarge or fail to shrink, whereas ruptured aneurysms are usually occluded, endovascularly when distal and in non-eloquent territory (often with parent artery occlusion) or surgically when there is a large haematoma or an eloquent parent vessel. Endovascular treatment is favoured before urgent valve surgery because it allows early cardiac surgery with heparinisation. After intracranial haemorrhage, the 2023 ESC endocarditis guideline generally advises delaying valve surgery for about four weeks unless the cardiac situation demands earlier operation. Anticoagulation and thrombolysis are avoided in septic embolism, while thrombectomy can be considered for large-vessel occlusion.
det.prognosis: Mortality is high after rupture, historically far higher than for intact aneurysms, so early detection and treatment of enlarging or ruptured lesions matters.
pearls: A distal MCA branch aneurysm with lobar haemorrhage in a febrile patient means endocarditis until proven otherwise.
A negative CTA does not exclude a small distal infectious aneurysm; get catheter angiography if haemorrhage is unexplained.
Rupture can occur after antibiotics are finished, so follow unresolved aneurysms with imaging.
det.thd: หลอดเลือดสมองโป่งพองจากการติดเชื้อมักเกิดจากลิ่มเชื้อของ infective endocarditis ทำลายผนังหลอดเลือดแขนงปลายของ MCA เป็น pseudoaneurysm ที่เปราะ อาจมีหลายจุด และแตกทำให้เลือดออกในเนื้อสมองหรือ SAH บริเวณ convexity CTA หรือ MRA อาจไม่เห็นก้อนเล็ก จึงต้องทำ catheter angiography เมื่อสงสัย รักษาด้วยยาปฏิชีวนะนาน ติดตามภาพหลอดเลือด และอุดหลอดเลือดด้วย endovascular หรือผ่าตัดเมื่อแตกหรือโตขึ้น โดยหลีกเลี่ยงยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือดและยาละลายลิ่มเลือด

qx.stem: A 41-year-old man on day 9 of IV penicillin for viridans streptococcal aortic valve endocarditis develops a sudden headache and right arm weakness. CT shows a left frontal lobar haemorrhage with a thin layer of convexity subarachnoid blood. CT angiography is reported as normal.
qx.q: What is the next best investigation?
opts: Repeat CT angiography after antibiotics are finished
Lumbar puncture for xanthochromia
Catheter angiography of all four vessels
Transcranial Doppler
No further imaging, as CTA excluded an aneurysm
qx.why: Infectious aneurysms are often small, distal and multiple, and CTA or MRA can miss lesions under about 5 mm. A lobar haemorrhage in endocarditis therefore needs catheter angiography of all vessels to find a lesion that may need occlusion before valve surgery. Lumbar puncture and Doppler do not answer the question.

name: Infective endocarditis
formal: Infection of heart valves producing septic emboli to the brain, with ischaemic stroke, mycotic aneurysm, abscess, meningitis and haemorrhage as neurological complications.
simple: An infection of the heart valves that can send clots or germs to the brain and cause strokes or abscesses.
th: การติดเชื้อที่ลิ้นหัวใจ — ก้อน vegetation หลุดไปอุดหลอดเลือดสมอง ทำให้ stroke หลายจุด ฝีในสมอง เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ และ mycotic aneurysm แตก ห้ามให้ tPA ตอบด้วย antibiotic และพิจารณาผ่าตัดลิ้น
tempoNote: Embolic events are sudden, on a background of fever and malaise over days to weeks; most occur before or in the first 2 weeks of antibiotics
feat: Fever, new murmur, anaemia and raised CRP in a patient with stroke or encephalopathy
Multiple small infarcts in several territories, cortical microbleeds or convexity SAH
Mycotic (infectious) aneurysms on distal MCA branches that may bleed
Brain abscess, meningitis or toxic encephalopathy
Risk groups: injecting drug use, prosthetic valve, rheumatic heart disease, haemodialysis, recent dental or line infection
inv: Three sets of blood cultures before antibiotics
Transthoracic then transoesophageal echocardiography (TOE more sensitive for small vegetations and abscess)
MRI with SWI: scattered infarcts and microbleeds; CTA or catheter angiography for mycotic aneurysm
Modified Duke (2023 Duke-ISCVID) criteria

case.who: 41-year-old man with rheumatic mitral disease, rice farmer, Surin
case.story: Two weeks of evening fevers and weight loss, then sudden inability to speak this morning.
case.exam: Temp 38.6°C, pansystolic murmur, splinter haemorrhages; global aphasia with right facial weakness.
case.tests: CT: left frontal hypodensity; MRI: further tiny infarcts in both hemispheres; blood cultures grow viridans streptococci; TOE: 12 mm mitral vegetation.
case.q: Should he receive IV thrombolysis, and what should happen next?
case.a: No — thrombolysis is contraindicated in IE because of bleeding risk; start IV antibiotics, screen for mycotic aneurysm and refer early to cardiac surgery given a large vegetation with embolism.

read.where: Chapter 6: What caused this transient or persisting ischemic event?

det.patho: Bacteria (most often Staphylococcus aureus, streptococci or enterococci) colonise damaged or prosthetic valves and form friable vegetations of fibrin, platelets and organisms. Pieces break off and reach the brain in roughly 20–40% of cases, causing infarcts that may turn haemorrhagic, abscesses and meningitis. Septic emboli lodging in distal arteries infect the vessel wall and create mycotic aneurysms. Rheumatic heart disease remains an important substrate in Thailand.
det.clinical: Neurological complications are often the presenting feature and include ischaemic stroke, encephalopathy, intracranial haemorrhage, abscess and meningitis; many more patients have silent lesions on MRI. Embolic risk is highest with S. aureus, mitral vegetations and vegetations larger than 10 mm, and drops sharply after the first week of effective antibiotics. Haemorrhage can arise from haemorrhagic transformation, rupture of a mycotic aneurysm or septic arteritis.
det.diagnosis: Any stroke with fever, a murmur or a raised inflammatory picture deserves blood cultures before antibiotics and echocardiography. Brain MRI with susceptibility imaging reveals clinically silent emboli and microbleeds, which count as a vascular phenomenon. Angiography is indicated for haemorrhage or when mycotic aneurysms are suspected. Culture-negative cases need serology (Bartonella, Coxiella) and consideration of NBTE.
det.treatment: Prolonged pathogen-directed intravenous antibiotics are the basis of care. IV thrombolysis is contraindicated; mechanical thrombectomy can be considered for large-vessel occlusion in experienced centres. Anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy are generally not started for the embolism itself; interrupt existing anticoagulation if bleeding occurs. Early valve surgery is advised for heart failure, uncontrolled infection or persistent large vegetations, and can usually proceed after ischaemic stroke without major haemorrhage. Mycotic aneurysms that bleed or enlarge are treated endovascularly or surgically.
det.prognosis: Neurological complications roughly double in-hospital mortality; outcome depends on organism, haemorrhage and timely surgery.
pearls: Stroke + fever = blood cultures and echo before giving any thrombolytic.
Embolic risk falls rapidly once appropriate antibiotics start.
Distal branch aneurysm in a febrile patient is mycotic until proved otherwise.
det.thd: Infective endocarditis คือการติดเชื้อที่ลิ้นหัวใจ ก้อน vegetation อาจหลุดไปอุดหลอดเลือดสมองทำให้ stroke หลายตำแหน่ง ฝีในสมอง เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ หรือหลอดเลือดโป่งพองจากการติดเชื้อ (mycotic aneurysm) แตก ควรสงสัยเมื่อผู้ป่วย stroke มีไข้ เสียงฟู่ที่หัวใจ ตรวจด้วย blood culture และ echocardiography ห้ามให้ยาละลายลิ่มเลือด รักษาด้วยยาปฏิชีวนะทางหลอดเลือดและพิจารณาผ่าตัดลิ้นหัวใจ

name: Infective vasculitis
formal: Inflammation of cerebral blood vessels caused by infection such as VZV, syphilis, tuberculosis or fungi, leading to ischaemic stroke or aneurysm and cranial neuropathy.
simple: Brain blood vessel inflammation caused by an infection, which can lead to stroke.
th: หลอดเลือดสมองอักเสบจากการติดเชื้อ เช่น VZV ซิฟิลิส วัณโรค หรือเชื้อรา ทำให้เกิด stroke หรือหลอดเลือดโป่งพอง และมักมีความผิดปกติของน้ำไขสันหลัง
tempoNote: Weeks to months; strokes may be preceded by headache or meningitis
feat: Stroke in a young or immunocompromised patient with meningitis or a known infection
VZV vasculopathy: weeks to months after zoster (including ophthalmicus) or without rash
Meningovascular syphilis: subacute prodrome then stroke, often deep territories
TB meningitis: basal exudate engulfing perforators, giving basal ganglia and internal capsule infarcts
Fungi (Aspergillus, Mucor) and bacterial meningitis can cause arteritis and thrombosis
inv: CSF: cell count, protein, VDRL, VZV PCR and anti-VZV IgG index, TB PCR/culture, fungal antigens
Serum treponemal tests, HIV
MRI with vessel wall imaging; CTA/MRA or DSA showing segmental stenoses

case.who: 52-year-old woman from Lamphun who had shingles over the left forehead six weeks earlier
case.story: Sudden right arm and face weakness with difficulty speaking.
case.exam: Healed zoster scars in the left V1 distribution; right face-arm weakness, non-fluent speech.
case.tests: MRI: left MCA territory infarct; MRA focal stenosis of left M1; CSF 18 lymphocytes, anti-VZV IgG intrathecal synthesis.
case.q: What is the stroke mechanism and treatment?
case.a: VZV vasculopathy after herpes zoster ophthalmicus; IV acyclovir with a short course of steroids, plus antiplatelet therapy.

read.where: Chapter 8 Stroke and Cerebrovascular Diseases — Cerebral Vasculitis

det.patho: Pathogens injure vessels by direct invasion of the wall (VZV, fungi), by immune-mediated inflammation (syphilis), or by inflammatory exudate bathing the basal cerebral arteries (TB, bacterial meningitis). The result is luminal narrowing, thrombosis or aneurysm formation.
det.clinical: Presentations include ischaemic stroke, TIA, haemorrhage from aneurysm rupture, encephalopathy and seizures. Headache, fever, cranial neuropathies and meningism point toward infection. In Thailand, TB, syphilis, VZV, cryptococcus and HIV-related infections are the leading considerations.
det.diagnosis: CSF analysis is central: pleocytosis and raised protein are typical, and pathogen-specific tests (PCR, antibody indices, antigens, cultures) define the cause. VZV vasculopathy is best diagnosed by intrathecal anti-VZV IgG, as PCR is often negative. Vessel wall MRI shows concentric enhancement. Biopsy is rarely needed.
det.treatment: Treat the infection: acyclovir for VZV, intravenous penicillin for neurosyphilis, four-drug anti-TB therapy with dexamethasone for TB meningitis, antifungals for fungal arteritis. Corticosteroids are used adjunctively in VZV and TB. Antiplatelets are commonly given for ischaemic events; anticoagulation is generally avoided where aneurysms exist.
det.prognosis: Outcome depends on pathogen and speed of treatment; deficits from established infarcts often persist.
pearls: Young stroke with abnormal CSF: think infective vasculitis before primary angiitis.
Ask about zoster in the previous year, including facial zoster.
Always test syphilis and HIV in unexplained young stroke.
det.thd: Infective vasculitis คือหลอดเลือดสมองอักเสบจากการติดเชื้อ เช่น VZV ซิฟิลิส วัณโรค และเชื้อรา ทำให้เกิด stroke ในคนอายุน้อยหรือภูมิคุ้มกันต่ำ น้ำไขสันหลังมักผิดปกติ ต้องตรวจหาเชื้อเฉพาะ เช่น anti-VZV IgG, VDRL, TB PCR การรักษาคือยาฆ่าเชื้อตามสาเหตุ บางชนิดให้ steroid ร่วม และให้ยาต้านเกล็ดเลือด

name: Infiltrative optic neuropathy
formal: Visual loss from optic nerve infiltration by lymphoma, leukaemia, carcinoma, sarcoidosis or granuloma, with optic disc swelling or pallor, often with a sluggish course.
simple: Loss of vision caused by cancer cells or inflammatory tissue growing into the optic nerve.
th: การมองเห็นเสียจากการแทรกซึมเส้นประสาทตาโดยมะเร็งต่อมน้ำเหลือง ลิวคีเมีย มะเร็งแพร่กระจาย sarcoidosis หรือ granuloma มีขั้วประสาทตาบวมหรือซีดและดำเนินโรคค่อยเป็นค่อยไป
tempoNote: Visual loss over weeks, sometimes stepwise; can be acute in leukaemic infiltration
feat: Progressive painless (or mildly painful) monocular or bilateral visual loss with RAPD
Optic disc swelling with haemorrhages, or pallor if retrobulbar
Poor or transient response to steroids, then relapse
Known cancer, leukaemia relapse, systemic sarcoidosis or tuberculosis in the history
Other cranial neuropathies suggest leptomeningeal spread
inv: MRI orbits and brain with contrast: thickened, enhancing nerve or perineural sheath
Lumbar puncture with cytology and flow cytometry (repeat if negative)
Chest CT, ACE, PET-CT; blood film and marrow for haematological malignancy
Optic nerve sheath biopsy in selected cases

case.who: 58-year-old man from Udon Thani treated for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma a year ago
case.story: Painless blurring of the left eye over three weeks, now only counting fingers.
case.exam: Left RAPD, swollen left disc with peripapillary haemorrhages, right eye normal; mild left facial numbness.
case.tests: MRI enhancing thickened left optic nerve and trigeminal nerve; CSF flow cytometry shows clonal B cells.
case.q: What causes his visual loss and what treatment is required?
case.a: Lymphomatous infiltrative optic neuropathy with CNS relapse; urgent high-dose methotrexate-based chemotherapy and/or orbital radiotherapy.

read.where: Chapter 22 Neuro-Ophthalmology — Tumours Affecting the Optic Nerve
Chapter 22 Neuro-Ophthalmology — Compressive or Infiltrative Optic Neuropathy

det.patho: Malignant cells or granulomas infiltrate the optic nerve parenchyma, sheath or subarachnoid space around it, compressing axons and disturbing their blood supply. Haematological malignancies (leukaemia, lymphoma), metastatic carcinoma (breast, lung), sarcoidosis, tuberculosis and IgG4 disease are the main causes. Infiltration of the prelaminar nerve produces dramatic disc swelling, whereas retrobulbar disease causes a normal disc initially.
det.clinical: Visual loss typically progresses over days to weeks, often without the pain on eye movement of optic neuritis. A partial or temporary response to corticosteroids may falsely reassure. Other features include additional cranial neuropathies, headache, proptosis or systemic symptoms. In leukaemia, optic infiltration is an emergency signalling CNS relapse.
det.diagnosis: Contrast MRI of orbits and brain is the key study, showing nerve enlargement, sheath enhancement or meningeal disease. CSF cytology and flow cytometry may require large volumes and repeated taps. Systemic staging includes chest imaging and PET-CT, and bone marrow examination for haematological disease. Optic nerve sheath biopsy is considered when vision is already poor and diagnosis remains uncertain.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying disease urgently: intrathecal or systemic chemotherapy for leukaemia and lymphoma, orbital radiotherapy to preserve vision, corticosteroids and steroid-sparing immunosuppression (or TNF inhibitors) for sarcoidosis, and antituberculous therapy for TB. Delay in treatment usually leads to permanent vision loss. Coordinate with haematology or oncology.
det.prognosis: Visual recovery is possible if treated early, but the systemic prognosis depends on the underlying malignancy or granulomatous disease.
pearls: Atypical optic neuritis (older age, no pain, steroid dependence) needs imaging and CSF for infiltration.
Optic disc swelling in a leukaemia patient is an oncological emergency.
Steroid response does not exclude lymphoma.
det.thd: Infiltrative optic neuropathy คือการที่มะเร็ง เช่น lymphoma หรือ leukaemia หรือโรค granuloma อย่าง sarcoidosis และวัณโรค แทรกเข้าเส้นประสาทตา ทำให้ตามัวลงเรื่อยๆ ภายในหลายสัปดาห์ ขั้วประสาทตาบวมหรือซีด มักไม่ปวดตาเหมือน optic neuritis และอาจดีขึ้นชั่วคราวด้วย steroid ต้องทำ MRI, เจาะน้ำไขสันหลังหาเซลล์มะเร็ง และตรวจทั่วร่างกาย การรักษาคือรักษาโรคต้นเหตุโดยเร็ว เช่น เคมีบำบัดหรือฉายรังสี

name: Inflammatory bowel disease
formal: Chronic inflammatory gut disease, Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis, with extra-intestinal neurological associations such as peripheral neuropathy, stroke, venous thrombosis and demyelination.
simple: Long-term gut inflammation, such as Crohn disease, that can also be linked to nerve problems and blood clots.
more: Neurological syndromes include natalizumab progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy and demyelination during anti-TNF therapy. Evaluate for B12 and copper deficiency or vasculitis; treat the gut disease and associated thromboembolism risk.
th: โรคลำไส้อักเสบเรื้อรัง Crohn และ ulcerative colitis ซึ่งไม่ใช่โรคทางระบบประสาท แต่สัมพันธ์กับ neuropathy, ลิ่มเลือดในหลอดเลือดสมอง, ภาวะขาดวิตามิน และผลข้างเคียงของยา
tempoNote: Chronic relapsing gut disease; neurological events are acute or chronic
feat: A gastrointestinal disease; listed for its neurological associations
Peripheral neuropathy (axonal or demyelinating) and B12 deficiency after ileal disease or resection
Prothrombotic state: cerebral venous thrombosis and arterial stroke during flares
Higher rates of demyelinating disease, especially with anti-TNF therapy
Drug-related: metronidazole neuropathy, PML with natalizumab, PRES with ciclosporin
inv: B12, folate, copper, vitamin E; NCS
MRI/MRV for stroke or CVT
Review IBD medications for neurotoxicity

case.who: 28-year-old woman from Bangkok with active ulcerative colitis
case.story: Severe progressive headache for 4 days, then a seizure during a flare with bloody diarrhoea.
case.exam: Drowsy, bilateral papilloedema, mild left leg weakness.
case.tests: MRV shows superior sagittal sinus thrombosis with right parasagittal venous infarct.
case.q: What links her colitis to the neurological event?
case.a: Active IBD creates a prothrombotic state causing cerebral venous thrombosis; anticoagulation with heparin is indicated.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Inflammatory Bowel Disease
Section 6 Systemic Disorders That Also Involve the Cerebrovascular System
Chapter 13 Other Neurologic Disorders Associated with Gastrointestinal Disease
Chapter 7: Unusual causes of ischemic stroke and transient ischemic attack

det.patho: Neurological involvement arises from several mechanisms: immune-mediated nerve injury, malabsorption of B12 and other nutrients, a hypercoagulable state with raised fibrinogen, platelets and factor VIII during flares, and toxicity or immunosuppression from treatment.
det.clinical: Peripheral neuropathy is relatively common, sometimes with sensory-predominant small-fibre features. Venous and arterial thrombosis, including CVT, occur more often during active disease. Patients on anti-TNF agents may develop demyelination or neuropathy, and those on natalizumab or vedolizumab have different PML risks. This entry is a gastroenterological disease with neurological complications.
det.diagnosis: Evaluate deficiencies, drug history and disease activity. MRI with venography is used for headache or focal signs. NCS characterise neuropathy. Demyelinating lesions require MS-style assessment and review of biologic therapy.
det.treatment: Correct deficiencies, adjust or stop neurotoxic drugs, and control IBD activity. CVT and arterial thrombosis are treated with anticoagulation and antithrombotic prophylaxis is used during admissions for flares. Demyelination on anti-TNF therapy often prompts switching agents.
det.prognosis: Most neurological complications respond to treating the cause; CVT outcomes are usually good with anticoagulation.
pearls: IBD flare plus headache: think venous sinus thrombosis.
Ileal resection years earlier: check B12.
New neuro deficit on anti-TNF therapy: consider drug-induced demyelination.
det.thd: Inflammatory bowel disease เป็นโรคลำไส้อักเสบเรื้อรัง ไม่ใช่โรคทางระบบประสาทโดยตรง แต่สัมพันธ์กับเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเสื่อม การขาดวิตามินบี 12 ลิ่มเลือดในหลอดเลือดดำสมองช่วงที่โรคกำเริบ และผลข้างเคียงจากยา เช่น anti-TNF หรือ metronidazole การรักษาคือแก้ไขสาเหตุและคุมโรคลำไส้

name: Inflammatory disease of orbit
formal: Idiopathic orbital inflammation, or orbital pseudotumour, causing painful proptosis, diplopia and ophthalmoplegia, responsive to corticosteroids; differential includes IgG4 disease and thyroid orbitopathy.
simple: Painful swelling inside the eye socket that causes a bulging eye and double vision, usually improving with steroids.
th: การอักเสบของเนื้อเยื่อในเบ้าตาที่ไม่ทราบสาเหตุ ทำให้ปวด ตาโปน เห็นภาพซ้อน และกลอกตาไม่ได้ ตอบสนองดีต่อ steroid
tempoNote: Develops over hours to days; may relapse
feat: Acute orbital pain, worse on eye movement
Proptosis, lid swelling, conjunctival injection, chemosis
Diplopia and restricted movements (myositis often involves one muscle including tendon)
Optic nerve involvement can reduce vision
Usually unilateral; bilateral in children or systemic disease

Blood: ESR, CRP, thyroid antibodies, ANCA, IgG4, ACE

case.story: Three days of severe left eye pain, worse when looking to the right, and double vision.
case.exam: Mild proptosis, red swollen lids, painful restricted adduction, normal vision and pupils.
case.tests: MRI: enlarged enhancing left medial rectus including its tendon; thyroid tests normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and expected response to treatment?
case.a: Idiopathic orbital myositis; rapid improvement within 48 hours on oral corticosteroids.

read.where: 8 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System

det.patho: Idiopathic orbital inflammation is a non-infectious, non-neoplastic inflammatory process of unknown cause, with polymorphous lymphocytic infiltrates and variable fibrosis. It can involve extraocular muscles, lacrimal gland, orbital fat, apex or diffusely. A subset represents IgG4-related disease or systemic vasculitis.
det.clinical: Presents acutely with pain, swelling, redness and diplopia. Orbital myositis typically affects a single rectus muscle with tendon involvement. Apical involvement can mimic optic neuropathy. Recurrence and contralateral involvement occur, and chronic sclerosing forms respond poorly to steroids.
det.diagnosis: It is a diagnosis of exclusion: imaging, blood tests for thyroid disease, vasculitis, sarcoidosis and IgG4-related disease, and exclusion of infection (orbital cellulitis) and tumour. Biopsy is recommended for atypical, recurrent or steroid-resistant disease.
det.treatment: High-dose oral corticosteroids produce rapid relief and are tapered over weeks. Steroid-sparing agents (methotrexate, mycophenolate), rituximab or low-dose orbital radiotherapy are used for recurrent or refractory cases. Treat any identified systemic cause.
det.prognosis: Most respond well; recurrence affects a substantial minority.
pearls: Tendon involvement favours orbital myositis; tendon sparing favours thyroid eye disease.
Dramatic steroid response is typical, but steroids can also shrink lymphoma.
Fever and sinusitis suggest orbital cellulitis, not pseudotumour.
det.thd: Inflammatory disease of orbit หรือ orbital pseudotumour คือการอักเสบในเบ้าตาที่ไม่ใช่การติดเชื้อหรือมะเร็ง ผู้ป่วยปวดตามากโดยเฉพาะเวลากลอกตา ตาโปน หนังตาบวม เห็นภาพซ้อน MRI พบกล้ามเนื้อตาหรือเนื้อเยื่อเบ้าตาบวมและ enhance ต้องแยก thyroid eye disease, cellulitis, lymphoma และ IgG4 disease ตอบสนองเร็วต่อ steroid รายที่ไม่ตรงแบบควรตัดชิ้นเนื้อ

name: Inflammatory myopathy
formal: Acquired muscle disease with inflammatory infiltrates, such as dermatomyositis, polymyositis or inclusion body myositis, giving progressive proximal weakness with raised CK.
simple: A muscle disease with inflammation that causes weakness, usually of the shoulders and hips.
more: Group of immune-mediated muscle diseases such as polymyositis, dermatomyositis and inclusion body myositis causing proximal weakness, elevated CK and inflammatory infiltrates. Check myositis-specific antibodies (anti-Jo-1, Mi-2, TIF1-gamma, SRP, NT5c1A), EMG with irritable myopathy, MRI and biopsy. Treat PM and DM with steroids plus methotrexate or azathioprine and IVIG; IBM is resistant and screen for malignancy in DM.
th: โรคกล้ามเนื้อที่ชิ้นเนื้อพบการอักเสบ ทั้งจากภูมิคุ้มกัน (เช่น dermatomyositis, IBM) และจากสาเหตุรอง เช่น ติดเชื้อ ยา หรือ immune checkpoint inhibitor
tempoNote: Most develop over weeks to months; infectious and drug-induced forms may be acute
feat: Proximal symmetric weakness with myalgia in some; neck flexor weakness and dysphagia
Raised CK in most; irritable myopathic EMG
Includes idiopathic forms and secondary forms: viral (HIV, HTLV-1), parasitic, drugs, checkpoint inhibitors
Skin rash, ILD, arthritis or myocarditis point to specific subtypes
Inflammatory infiltrates on biopsy distinguish it from dystrophies and toxic myopathies
inv: CK, myositis-specific antibodies (Jo-1, Mi-2, TIF1-gamma, NXP2, MDA5, SRP, HMGCR, cN1A)
EMG, muscle MRI, then biopsy of an affected muscle
Drug history (statins, checkpoint inhibitors), HIV and parasite serology if relevant
HRCT chest, ECG/troponin, cancer screen as indicated

case.story: Receiving pembrolizumab for lung cancer; three weeks after the second dose he has droopy eyelids, aching thighs and cannot climb steps.
case.exam: Bilateral ptosis, neck flexor weakness 3/5, proximal limb weakness 4-/5.
case.tests: CK 6,500 U/L, troponin raised; EMG myopathic with fibrillations; AChR antibody negative.
case.q: What is this and what must be checked urgently?
case.a: Immune checkpoint inhibitor myositis, often overlapping with myasthenia and myocarditis; stop the drug, screen the heart and give high-dose steroids.

read.where: Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Inflammatory Myopathies

det.patho: Inflammatory myopathies comprise the idiopathic immune myopathies plus secondary forms in which inflammation is triggered by infection (HIV, HTLV-1, Toxoplasma, Trichinella, bacteria causing pyomyositis), drugs (statins, checkpoint inhibitors, D-penicillamine) or systemic autoimmune disease (overlap). Mechanisms range from complement-mediated capillary damage to cytotoxic T-cell attack and antibody-driven necrosis. Biopsy pattern and serology together define the subtype.
det.clinical: Patients usually describe subacute difficulty rising, climbing stairs and lifting arms; neck flexor and pharyngeal weakness are common. Muscle pain is more frequent in infective, drug and necrotising forms. Systemic clues include rash, ILD, Raynaud phenomenon, arthritis and myocarditis. Checkpoint-inhibitor myositis characteristically adds ocular and bulbar weakness and myocarditis within weeks of starting treatment.
det.diagnosis: Start with CK, EMG and MRI to confirm an active myopathy and pick a biopsy site; send a myositis antibody panel. Biopsy distinguishes DM, IMNM, IBM, overlap and infection-related patterns. Review drugs and exposures; test thyroid function and electrolytes. Muscular dystrophies with secondary inflammation (dysferlinopathy, FSHD) are frequent mimics.
det.treatment: Immune forms are treated with corticosteroids plus steroid-sparing agents, IVIG or rituximab depending on subtype. Secondary forms need the cause removed: stop statins or checkpoint inhibitors, treat infection, add immunotherapy as needed. IBM is managed supportively. Monitor strength, CK, swallowing and lung function, and plan bone protection on long-term steroids.
det.prognosis: Variable; most immune non-IBM forms are controllable, checkpoint myositis with myocarditis carries substantial mortality, and IBM progresses slowly.
pearls: Checkpoint-inhibitor myositis + ptosis: screen urgently for myocarditis.
A dystrophy can show inflammation on biopsy; correlate with history and pattern.
Normal CK does not exclude dermatomyositis or IBM.
det.thd: Inflammatory myopathy คือโรคกล้ามเนื้อที่มีการอักเสบ ครอบคลุมทั้งโรคจากภูมิคุ้มกัน เช่น dermatomyositis, IMNM, IBM และโรคที่มีสาเหตุรอง เช่น ติดเชื้อ ยา statin หรือ immune checkpoint inhibitor ผู้ป่วยอ่อนแรงต้นแขนขา อาจปวดกล้ามเนื้อ CK สูง ตรวจ EMG, MRI, antibody และชิ้นเนื้อเพื่อแยกชนิด รักษาด้วยการหยุดสาเหตุและให้สเตียรอยด์หรือยากดภูมิ ส่วน IBM รักษาแบบประคับประคอง

ddx.pt: Weakness that worsens with steroid dose; normal CK and no inflammation on biopsy
Proximal weakness with reduced reflexes, autonomic symptoms; CK normal; incremental CMAP
Proximal weakness with weight loss and tremor; CK often normal; TSH suppressed

name: Inflammatory neuropathies
formal: Immune-mediated nerve diseases such as Guillain-Barre syndrome and CIDP, with demyelination causing weakness, areflexia and sensory loss, treatable with IVIG, plasma exchange or steroids.
simple: Conditions in which the immune system attacks nerves, causing weakness and numbness.
th: กลุ่มโรคเส้นประสาทอักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกัน ทั้งเฉียบพลัน (GBS) และเรื้อรัง (CIDP, MMN) ทำให้อ่อนแรง รีเฟล็กซ์หาย และชา รักษาได้
tempoNote: Acute (GBS, nadir < 4 weeks), subacute (4–8 weeks), chronic (CIDP > 8 weeks)
feat: Acute: Guillain–Barré syndrome and variants (AIDP, AMAN, Miller Fisher)
Chronic: CIDP and variants, MMN, anti-MAG neuropathy, autoimmune nodopathies
Vasculitic neuropathy presents as painful mononeuritis multiplex
Areflexia, weakness and sensory loss; asymmetric pure motor pattern in MMN
Treatable with IVIG, plasma exchange, steroids or rituximab depending on the type
inv: NCS/EMG to classify demyelinating versus axonal and focal versus diffuse
CSF protein and cells; serum immunofixation; ganglioside, MAG and nodal antibodies
Nerve imaging (ultrasound/MRI) and nerve biopsy for suspected vasculitis

case.story: Over three months, painless weakness has developed in her right hand then left wrist, with no numbness.
case.exam: Asymmetric weakness in radial and ulnar territories, fasciculations, reduced reflexes in affected arms; sensation normal.
case.tests: NCS: motor conduction block in right ulnar and left radial nerves with normal sensory responses; anti-GM1 IgM positive.
case.q: Which inflammatory neuropathy is this and which drug should be avoided?
case.a: Multifocal motor neuropathy; treat with IVIG and avoid corticosteroids, which can worsen it.

det.patho: Immune responses directed at myelin, Schwann cells, nodal proteins or axonal gangliosides cause demyelination or axonal injury. In GBS, molecular mimicry after infection is the main mechanism; CIDP involves macrophage and T-cell driven demyelination; MMN involves IgM anti-GM1 antibodies and complement; nodopathies are mainly IgG4-mediated. Vasculitic neuropathy results from ischaemia due to inflammation of nerve vessels.
det.clinical: GBS causes rapidly ascending weakness over days to weeks with possible respiratory and autonomic failure. CIDP progresses over more than 8 weeks with proximal and distal weakness and sensory involvement. MMN causes slowly progressive asymmetric, mainly upper-limb motor weakness. Vasculitic neuropathy produces painful, stepwise mononeuropathies. Each has distinct treatment implications.
det.diagnosis: Tempo and pattern guide the differential; NCS classifies demyelinating versus axonal processes. CSF protein is often high in GBS and CIDP. Antibody tests (gangliosides, MAG, nodal proteins) and serum immunofixation refine diagnosis. Current EAN/PNS guidelines (2021 CIDP, 2023 GBS) provide diagnostic criteria; nerve biopsy is reserved for suspected vasculitis or uncertain cases.
det.treatment: GBS is treated with IVIG or plasma exchange plus intensive supportive care. CIDP responds to IVIG, corticosteroids or plasma exchange, and FcRn blockers are emerging maintenance options. MMN responds to IVIG; steroids should be avoided. Nodopathies and anti-MAG neuropathy respond best to rituximab. Vasculitic neuropathy requires corticosteroids with cyclophosphamide or rituximab.
det.prognosis: Most inflammatory neuropathies improve with prompt treatment, though axonal loss leads to residual weakness.
pearls: Classify by tempo (acute vs chronic) and pattern (symmetric vs multifocal, motor vs sensory).
Conduction block without sensory involvement suggests MMN.
Painful stepwise mononeuropathies suggest vasculitis — consider nerve biopsy.
det.thd: Inflammatory neuropathies คือกลุ่มโรคเส้นประสาทอักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกัน แบ่งเป็นเฉียบพลัน เช่น GBS และเรื้อรัง เช่น CIDP, MMN, anti-MAG และ nodopathy รวมถึง vasculitic neuropathy อาการคืออ่อนแรง รีเฟล็กซ์หาย และชา ตามรูปแบบของแต่ละโรค การตรวจ NCS ช่วยแยกชนิด รักษาด้วย IVIG, plasma exchange, steroid หรือ rituximab ตามชนิด ส่วน MMN ห้ามใช้ steroid

name: Infratentorial haemorrhage
formal: Bleeding in the posterior fossa, such as cerebellar or brainstem haemorrhage, causing vomiting, ataxia, coma and risk of hydrocephalus and herniation; may need surgical decompression.
simple: Bleeding in the lower part of the brain, around the cerebellum or brainstem, which can quickly become life-threatening.
th: เลือดออกในโพรงสมองส่วนหลัง เช่น cerebellum หรือก้านสมอง ทำให้อาเจียน เดินเซ โคม่า และเสี่ยงโพรงน้ำในสมองอุดตันและสมองเคลื่อน
tempoNote: Sudden onset; cerebellar haematomas may deteriorate over hours
feat: Cerebellar: sudden vertigo, vomiting, headache, inability to stand, ipsilateral ataxia, gaze palsy
Pontine: rapid coma, pinpoint reactive pupils, quadriplegia, hyperthermia, ocular bobbing
Compression of the fourth ventricle causes obstructive hydrocephalus
Main cause is hypertension; also AVM, cavernoma, anticoagulants
Deterioration may be rapid, needing neurosurgical decompression
inv: Urgent CT brain
CTA for vascular malformation, especially in young or normotensive patients
Coagulation profile; MRI later for cavernoma

case.story: Sudden occipital headache, vertigo and repeated vomiting; cannot stand.
case.exam: Alert initially, right limb ataxia, right gaze palsy, BP 210/115; two hours later GCS drops to 10.
case.tests: CT: 4 cm right cerebellar haematoma with fourth ventricle effacement and hydrocephalus.
case.q: What is the definitive management?
case.a: Emergency suboccipital decompression and haematoma evacuation, not external ventricular drain alone.

read.where: Chapter 8 Stroke and Cerebrovascular Diseases — Clinical Syndromes of Intracranial Haemorrhage
22 Posterior circulation stroke and vestibular syndromes

det.patho: Hypertensive arteriopathy of perforating branches from the basilar artery and of the superior cerebellar and PICA branches causes most cases. The tight posterior fossa means small haematomas can compress the brainstem and fourth ventricle, causing hydrocephalus and herniation.
det.clinical: Cerebellar haemorrhage typically presents with abrupt vertigo, vomiting and inability to walk, sometimes misdiagnosed as a peripheral vestibular problem. Brainstem compression causes falling consciousness, gaze palsies and respiratory irregularity. Pontine haemorrhage often causes immediate coma with pinpoint pupils.
det.diagnosis: CT makes the diagnosis. Haematoma volume, diameter (over 3 cm), fourth ventricle compression and hydrocephalus guide surgical decisions. Vascular imaging is used if the patient is young, normotensive or the location is atypical.
det.treatment: Cerebellar haemorrhage causing neurological deterioration, brainstem compression or hydrocephalus warrants surgical evacuation. Ventricular drainage alone risks upward herniation. Pontine haemorrhages are managed medically. General ICH measures apply: BP lowering, anticoagulant reversal and close monitoring.
det.prognosis: Cerebellar haemorrhage can have good outcomes with timely surgery; large pontine haemorrhages are frequently fatal.
pearls: Vertigo with inability to stand plus hypertension: CT before calling it labyrinthitis.
Cerebellar haematoma over 3 cm or hydrocephalus: neurosurgery now.
Pinpoint pupils plus coma: pontine haemorrhage or opioids.
det.thd: Infratentorial haemorrhage คือเลือดออกใน cerebellum หรือก้านสมอง มักเกิดจากความดันโลหิตสูง ผู้ป่วยเวียนศีรษะ อาเจียน ยืนไม่ได้ และอาจซึมลงอย่างรวดเร็วจากการกดก้านสมองหรือโพรงน้ำในสมองอุดตัน CT วินิจฉัยได้ทันที ถ้าก้อนเลือดใน cerebellum ใหญ่กว่า 3 เซนติเมตรหรือมี hydrocephalus ต้องผ่าตัดด่วน

name: Inherited Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (iCJD)
formal: Genetic prion disease caused by PRNP mutations, with CJD-like rapid dementia, myoclonus and ataxia, with autosomal dominant inheritance.
simple: A rare inherited form of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease that runs in families and causes fast-progressing dementia.
th: โรค prion ทางพันธุกรรมจากการกลายพันธุ์ของยีน PRNP มีสมองเสื่อมเร็ว myoclonus และเดินเซคล้าย CJD ถ่ายทอดแบบ autosomal dominant
tempoNote: Onset usually earlier than sporadic CJD and the course is often longer; pace depends on the mutation
feat: Rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus, ataxia, visual or behavioural symptoms
Family history may be absent or misattributed because of reduced penetrance and misdiagnosis in relatives
E200K (the most frequent worldwide), V210I and V180I (the latter common in Japan and East Asia, slower and milder); insertional repeat mutations cause a slower, earlier dementia
Makes up roughly 10–15% of human prion disease, with autosomal dominant transmission
The same D178N mutation produces fatal familial insomnia if M129 is on the mutant allele and an fCJD picture if V129 is
inv: MRI DWI: cortical ribboning and striatal restricted diffusion (may be atypical in V180I)
CSF RT-QuIC (usually positive in E200K, sometimes negative in V180I), 14-3-3 and total tau
EEG: periodic sharp-wave complexes are seen mainly with E200K
PRNP sequencing with codon 129 genotyping after counselling

case.who: 58-year-old woman from Nakhon Pathom whose mother died of 'rapid dementia' at 60
case.story: Three months of memory decline, visual blurring and clumsiness, then startle jerks.
case.exam: Disoriented, cerebellar ataxia of gait, myoclonus, brisk reflexes.
case.tests: MRI DWI: cortical ribbon restriction; RT-QuIC positive; PRNP shows E200K.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what should be offered to the family?
case.a: Genetic CJD (E200K); offer genetic counselling, with predictive testing only with proper counselling and consent.

read.where: Chapter 116: Prion Disorders: Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease and Related Disorders — Familial CJD

det.patho: Pathogenic variants in the prion protein gene PRNP make the protein prone to adopt the infectious conformation, and transmission follows an autosomal dominant pattern with nearly complete penetrance in most families. The codon 129 polymorphism (methionine or valine) modifies the phenotype, as does the particular mutation. Many carriers have no known family history because of reduced penetrance, misdiagnosis or non-paternity.
det.clinical: Features resemble sporadic CJD with dementia, myoclonus, cerebellar and visual signs, pyramidal and extrapyramidal signs, and finally akinetic mutism. Compared with sporadic disease, familial CJD usually starts earlier and lasts longer, and apart from E200K periodic EEG complexes are often absent. Subtypes such as V180I may have a slow dementia with atypical MRI and negative RT-QuIC. Other mutations produce the GSS or fatal familial insomnia phenotypes.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in rapidly progressive dementia with a family history, young onset or atypical features. Combine the clinical syndrome with MRI, CSF RT-QuIC and EEG, and send PRNP sequencing in every suspected case because the family history is unreliable. Genetic confirmation allows precise counselling. Exclude autoimmune, paraneoplastic and infectious mimics.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying treatment exists; manage myoclonus, agitation, swallowing and end-of-life care. Offer genetic counselling to at-risk relatives, with predictive testing only through a structured protocol that includes psychological support, and discuss reproductive options. Standard infection-control precautions apply to blood and body fluids, while neurosurgical and tissue procedures need prion-specific sterilisation or disposable instruments. Antisense-oligonucleotide and antibody therapies directed at PrP are under investigation.
det.prognosis: Invariably fatal, generally within months to a few years depending on the mutation.
pearls: Send PRNP in every suspected CJD: many genetic cases have no known family history.
V180I CJD is common in East Asia and may have negative RT-QuIC and atypical MRI.
Genetic prion disease is still infectious tissue for surgical purposes.
det.thd: Inherited CJD เกิดจากการกลายพันธุ์ของยีน PRNP ถ่ายทอดแบบ autosomal dominant คิดเป็น 10-15% ของโรคพรีออนในคน ผู้ป่วยมีสมองเสื่อมเร็ว กล้ามเนื้อกระตุก เดินเซ และตามัว ประวัติครอบครัวอาจไม่ชัด การกลายพันธุ์ที่พบบ่อยคือ E200K และ V180I ซึ่งพบในเอเชียตะวันออก ตรวจ MRI RT-QuIC และยีน PRNP ยังไม่มียารักษาโรค แต่ควรให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุศาสตร์แก่ญาติและป้องกันการแพร่เชื้อจากการผ่าตัด
