name: Inherited muscle disorders
formal: Genetic myopathies, including muscular dystrophies, congenital and metabolic myopathies and channelopathies, with progressive weakness and often elevated creatine kinase.
simple: Inherited conditions that weaken and waste muscles over time.
th: กลุ่มโรคกล้ามเนื้อทางพันธุกรรม ได้แก่ muscular dystrophy, congenital myopathy, metabolic myopathy และ channelopathy มีอ่อนแรงค่อยเป็นค่อยไปและ CK มักสูง
tempoNote: Most progress over years; metabolic myopathies and channelopathies cause episodic symptoms
feat: An umbrella category: dystrophies (DMD/BMD, LGMD, FSHD, DM1/2, OPMD), congenital myopathies, metabolic (Pompe, McArdle), mitochondrial and channelopathies
Pattern of weakness (limb-girdle, facioscapulohumeral, distal, ocular-bulbar) guides diagnosis
Associated clues: calf hypertrophy, myotonia, cataract, cardiomyopathy, contractures, exercise intolerance, rhabdomyolysis
Family history with dominant, recessive, X-linked or maternal inheritance
inv: CK (very high in DMD and many LGMDs; normal in many congenital myopathies)
EMG (myopathic, myotonic discharges), muscle MRI pattern
Genetic testing: targeted (DMD MLPA, DMPK repeats, FSHD D4Z4) or NGS panel/exome; biopsy when genetics inconclusive
Cardiac (ECG, echo, Holter) and respiratory (FVC, sleep study) surveillance; dried blood spot GAA for Pompe

case.story: Falls often, struggles to climb stairs and rises from the floor by pushing on his thighs.
case.exam: Gowers sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, waddling gait, normal sensation and reflexes reduced at the knees.
case.tests: CK 18,000 U/L; MLPA shows DMD exon 45–50 deletion.
case.q: Which inherited muscle disorder, and which organ needs regular monitoring besides skeletal muscle?
case.a: Duchenne muscular dystrophy; the heart (cardiomyopathy) and breathing (restrictive respiratory failure).

read.where: Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Muscular Dystrophies
Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Genetic Muscle Diseases

det.patho: Inherited muscle disorders arise from variants in genes for sarcolemmal and extracellular matrix proteins (dystrophin, sarcoglycans, collagen VI), sarcomere and Z-disc proteins, nuclear envelope proteins, glycogen and lipid enzymes, mitochondrial components and ion channels. The result may be fibre necrosis and fibrosis (dystrophies), structural abnormality without necrosis (congenital myopathies), energy failure (metabolic) or excitability disorders (channelopathies).
det.clinical: Presentation ranges from neonatal hypotonia to adult-onset weakness. Distribution of weakness, age at onset, rate of progression, and associated features such as myotonia, contractures, cardiomyopathy, ptosis, or exercise-induced pain and myoglobinuria help define the group. Respiratory and cardiac complications often determine prognosis, sometimes more than limb weakness.
det.diagnosis: Clinical pattern recognition is followed by CK, EMG and muscle MRI to localise and refine, then targeted genetic tests or NGS panels. Muscle biopsy with immunohistochemistry remains useful when genetics is uncertain. Variants of uncertain significance need careful interpretation and family segregation. Acquired myopathies such as inflammatory, toxic or endocrine forms should be excluded.
det.treatment: Disease-specific therapies are increasing: corticosteroids (prednisolone or deflazacort, vamorolone) and exon-skipping or gene therapies for DMD, enzyme replacement for Pompe disease, and drugs for channelopathies. Multidisciplinary care covers physiotherapy, orthoses, cardiac medication, non-invasive ventilation, scoliosis surgery and nutrition. Genetic counselling and carrier testing (e.g. DMD in mothers) are key, and anaesthetic precautions apply in RYR1-related disorders.
det.prognosis: Highly variable, from normal lifespan to early death; cardiorespiratory care has improved survival significantly.
pearls: Very high CK in a boy with falls: think Duchenne first.
Always screen the heart and lungs in genetic myopathies.
Normal CK does not exclude a congenital or metabolic myopathy.
det.thd: Inherited muscle disorders เป็นกลุ่มโรคกล้ามเนื้อทางพันธุกรรม ได้แก่ muscular dystrophy, congenital myopathy, metabolic myopathy, mitochondrial และ channelopathy ผู้ป่วยมีอ่อนแรงตามรูปแบบเฉพาะ บางโรคมี CK สูงมาก การวินิจฉัยใช้ลักษณะอาการ CK, EMG, MRI กล้ามเนื้อ และตรวจยีน การดูแลเน้นหัวใจและการหายใจ ร่วมกับกายภาพบำบัด และมียาเฉพาะในบางโรค เช่น DMD และ Pompe

name: Inherited neuromyotonia and paroxysmal ataxia
formal: Episodic ataxia type 1, from KCNA1 mutation, with brief ataxia attacks lasting seconds to minutes, interictal myokymia and neuromyotonia, triggered by startle or exercise.
simple: An inherited condition with short attacks of unsteadiness and muscle twitching, set off by sudden movement or fright.
th: โรคทางพันธุกรรมจากยีน KCNA1 ที่มีทั้งกล้ามเนื้อกระตุกตึงต่อเนื่อง (neuromyotonia/myokymia) และ ataxia เป็นช่วงสั้น ๆ
tempoNote: Brief ataxic attacks on a background of continuous muscle activity, from childhood
feat: Continuous muscle twitching, stiffness, cramps and delayed relaxation (neuromyotonia)
Paroxysmal ataxia lasting seconds to minutes provoked by startle or exertion
Some patients have only neuromyotonia without ataxia
Autosomal dominant; childhood onset
Hand and calf hypertrophy, joint contractures in some
inv: EMG: myokymic and neuromyotonic discharges persisting after nerve block
VGKC-complex antibodies (CASPR2, LGI1) negative – excludes acquired Isaacs syndrome
KCNA1 sequencing

case.story: Since childhood his muscles ripple constantly and stiffen after playing football; occasionally sways and slurs for a minute when he stands quickly.
case.exam: Visible undulating muscle movements in calves and hands, bulky calves, slow hand opening after grip, otherwise normal between episodes.
case.tests: EMG shows doublet and multiplet neuromyotonic discharges; CASPR2 negative; KCNA1 variant shared with father.
case.q: How does this differ from Isaacs' syndrome?
case.a: Inherited KCNA1 channelopathy (EA1 spectrum) – childhood onset, family history, episodic ataxia and negative antibodies; Isaacs is acquired autoimmune.

read.where: Chapter 24 Cerebellar Ataxias and Related Conditions — Genetic Forms of Episodic Ataxia
23 Genetics of episodic and progressive vestibulocerebellar syndromes

det.patho: Kv1.1 potassium channels, encoded by KCNA1, stabilise the membrane at juxtaparanodes of peripheral axons and at cerebellar basket cell terminals. Pathogenic variants reduce potassium current, so peripheral axons fire spontaneously (neuromyotonia) and cerebellar inhibition is disturbed during sudden movement. It is the same genetic disorder as episodic ataxia type 1, with variable expression.
det.clinical: Patients have continuous muscle activity from childhood, sometimes the dominant feature, with stiffness, cramps and muscle enlargement. Brief ataxic attacks occur with sudden movement or emotion. Expression varies within families, from isolated neuromyotonia to classic EA1. Epilepsy is an occasional association.
det.diagnosis: EMG demonstrates spontaneous repetitive motor unit discharges of peripheral origin. Negative VGKC-complex antibodies and childhood onset with family history point to the inherited form. KCNA1 testing confirms.
det.treatment: Sodium channel blockers such as carbamazepine, phenytoin or lamotrigine reduce neuromyotonia and often the ataxic attacks. Acetazolamide helps some. Avoid triggers where possible.
det.prognosis: Not usually progressive; symptoms often lessen with age.
pearls: Neuromyotonia from childhood with a family history: KCNA1, not Isaacs.
Same gene, two faces: peripheral hyperexcitability and paroxysmal ataxia.
Carbamazepine usually helps both.

Chapter 44: Hereditary Motor Sensory Neuropathies (HMSN)/Charcot-Marie-Tooth Disease (CMT)

det.patho: More than 100 genes cause inherited neuropathies, affecting myelin structure (PMP22, MPZ), Schwann cell–axon interaction (GJB1), axonal transport and mitochondrial dynamics (MFN2, NEFL), and aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases. PMP22 duplication (CMT1A) accounts for most demyelinating cases, and its deletion causes HNPP. Long axons are most vulnerable, producing length-dependent distal weakness.
det.clinical: Most patients develop slowly worsening distal leg weakness and high-arched feet during childhood or adolescence, with hand involvement later. Sensory loss is often greater on examination than patients report. Some forms add hearing loss, optic atrophy, vocal cord paresis or pyramidal signs. HNPP causes recurrent painless pressure palsies at entrapment sites.
det.diagnosis: Clinical pattern, family history and NCS (demyelinating vs axonal vs intermediate) guide genetic testing, beginning with PMP22 copy number when conduction is uniformly slow. Panels or exome identify other genes. Exclude acquired treatable neuropathies (CIDP, paraproteinaemic, toxic, nutritional) and remember that amyloid neuropathy (TTR) is a treatable inherited neuropathy.
det.treatment: CMT still lacks a licensed disease-modifying drug; trials target PMP22 expression. Care includes physiotherapy, ankle–foot orthoses, foot surgery and hand therapy, plus avoidance of neurotoxic drugs (notably vincristine). Weight control and exercise help preserve function. Genetic counselling informs family planning. Hereditary TTR amyloid neuropathy, by contrast, has disease-modifying drugs (tafamidis, patisiran, vutrisiran, inotersen, eplontersen).
det.prognosis: Most CMT patients keep walking throughout life with aids; life expectancy is usually normal.
pearls: Uniform slowing suggests inherited demyelination; patchy slowing suggests acquired.
Look at the parents' feet.
Vincristine can cause catastrophic weakness in undiagnosed CMT1A.
det.thd: Inherited neuropathy คือโรคเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายทางพันธุกรรม ที่พบบ่อยคือ CMT โดยเฉพาะ CMT1A จาก PMP22 duplication ผู้ป่วยมีเท้าโก่ง นิ้วเท้างอ ปลายขาลีบ เท้าตก reflex หาย และอาการค่อยเป็นค่อยไปตั้งแต่เด็ก NCS ช่วยแยกชนิด demyelinating หรือ axonal แล้วตรวจยีน การรักษาเป็นกายภาพ อุปกรณ์พยุงข้อเท้า ผ่าตัดเท้า และหลีกเลี่ยงยาที่เป็นพิษต่อเส้นประสาท เช่น vincristine

name: Inherited peripheral nerve diseases
formal: Genetic disorders of peripheral nerves such as CMT, HNPP and familial amyloid neuropathy, causing slowly progressive weakness and sensory loss, often with foot deformities.
simple: Inherited conditions that damage nerves in the arms and legs, causing weakness and numbness.
ab: CMT, HNPP and familial amyloid neuropathy
th: กลุ่มโรคเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายทางพันธุกรรม เช่น CMT, HNPP และ familial amyloid neuropathy ทำให้อ่อนแรงและชาค่อยเป็นค่อยไป มักมีเท้าผิดรูป

case.story: Two years of burning feet, diarrhoea alternating with constipation, erectile dysfunction and 10 kg weight loss; bilateral carpal tunnel surgery last year.
case.exam: Distal pain and temperature loss, absent ankle jerks, orthostatic hypotension.
case.tests: Axonal sensorimotor neuropathy; echocardiography shows thick ventricles; TTR A97S variant; fat pad Congo red positive.
case.q: Which inherited neuropathy is treatable here?
case.a: Hereditary TTR amyloid polyneuropathy (A97S is common in Thai and Taiwanese patients); TTR stabiliser or silencer therapy.

det.patho: These disorders result from mutations affecting myelin, axonal transport, mitochondrial function, sensory neuron survival or systemic protein misfolding (TTR). Demyelinating forms slow conduction uniformly; axonal forms reduce amplitudes. HNPP is caused by PMP22 deletion, making nerves vulnerable to compression. TTR variants destabilise the transthyretin tetramer, producing amyloid fibrils in nerves and heart.
det.clinical: Clinical spectrum includes slowly progressive distal weakness and deformity (CMT), recurrent focal palsies (HNPP), painless mutilating ulcers (HSAN), pure distal motor weakness (dHMN), and rapidly progressive painful autonomic neuropathy with cardiac involvement (TTR). Age of onset, inheritance pattern and associated systemic features guide classification. Some inherited neuropathies, such as porphyria and Fabry disease, have systemic and treatable aspects.
det.diagnosis: The approach combines clinical phenotype, family history, NCS pattern and targeted or panel genetic testing. Look for red flags of treatable acquired neuropathy that mimic inherited forms. Consider TTR testing in any adult with progressive idiopathic axonal neuropathy, especially with autonomic or cardiac features, carpal tunnel syndrome or a family history. Skin biopsy, tissue Congo red staining and cardiac imaging (bone scintigraphy) support amyloidosis.
det.treatment: Supportive care (orthoses, physiotherapy, surgery, foot care and pain management) is the mainstay for most forms. HNPP patients should avoid prolonged compression. TTR amyloid polyneuropathy has disease-modifying drugs (tafamidis, patisiran, vutrisiran, inotersen, eplontersen) and liver transplantation in selected cases. Genetic counselling for families is essential.
det.prognosis: CMT and HNPP have normal life expectancy; untreated TTR amyloidosis is fatal within about 10 years, but treatment slows progression.
pearls: Recurrent pressure palsies: test for PMP22 deletion (HNPP).
Adult axonal neuropathy plus autonomic failure and cardiomyopathy: think TTR amyloid.
TTR A97S is a common variant in Thai patients.
det.thd: Inherited peripheral nerve diseases เป็นกลุ่มใหญ่ของโรคเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายทางพันธุกรรม ได้แก่ CMT, HNPP ที่เส้นประสาทถูกกดง่าย, HSAN ที่ไม่รู้สึกเจ็บจนเกิดแผล และ TTR amyloidosis ที่มีปลายประสาทอักเสบปวดแสบ ระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติเสีย และหัวใจหนา ซึ่งในไทยพบ A97S บ่อย การวินิจฉัยใช้ NCS และตรวจยีน ส่วนใหญ่รักษาแบบประคับประคอง แต่ TTR amyloidosis มียาเฉพาะ

name: Inherited prion diseases
formal: Genetic prion disorders from PRNP mutation, including familial CJD, Gerstmann-Straussler-Scheinker disease and fatal familial insomnia, with rapidly progressive dementia and ataxia.
simple: Rare inherited brain diseases from faulty prion protein that cause dementia, imbalance and sleep problems.
th: โรคพรีออนทางพันธุกรรมเกิดจากการกลายพันธุ์ของยีน PRNP แบบ autosomal dominant คิดเป็นราว 15% ของโรคพรีออน แบ่งเดิมเป็น genetic CJD, GSS และ FFI แต่ผู้ป่วยเกือบครึ่งไม่มีประวัติครอบครัว จึงควรตรวจยีน PRNP และให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรมในผู้ป่วยทุกราย
tempoNote: Genetic CJD often runs months, FFI about 18 months, GSS and octapeptide-insertion or stop-codon variants years (up to 15 or more); onset usually in the 40s–60s
feat: Autosomal dominant PRNP variants: more than 60 reported, with five (E200K, V210I, V180I, P102L, D178N) causing about 85% of cases
Three historical phenotypes: genetic CJD (E200K, V210I and others; sCJD-like), GSS (P102L; slow ataxia) and FFI (D178N with 129M; insomnia and dysautonomia); several variants fit none of them
Penetrance varies: near 100% for most, but about 10% for V210I, 1% for V180I and 0.1% for M232R, which also occur in healthy people
No family history in about 47% of genetic cases (misdiagnosis, low penetrance, early death or, rarely, de novo variants)
Codon 129 changes the phenotype of D178N (129M gives FFI, 129V gives genetic CJD) and the speed of decline
inv: PRNP sequencing from blood, saliva or a buccal swab, with codon 129 genotype, after genetic counselling; octapeptide repeat changes may be missed on gene panels
MRI, RT-QuIC and CSF markers behave like sCJD in fast variants (E200K, V210I) but are often negative in GSS, FFI, stop-codon and 5–7 repeat insertions
FDG-PET thalamic and cingulate hypometabolism and polysomnography in FFI

case.story: Eight months of severe insomnia, drenching sweats, weight loss and episodes of confusion, then unsteady gait. His father died after years of 'sleeplessness'.
case.exam: Inattentive, dysarthric, myoclonic jerks, tachycardia with hypertension, ataxic gait.
case.tests: Polysomnography shows near-absent sleep spindles and slow-wave sleep; FDG-PET thalamic hypometabolism; MRI normal; PRNP D178N with 129 MM.
case.q: Which inherited prion disease is this, and what is offered to his children?
case.a: Fatal familial insomnia; offer genetic counselling before predictive testing, with preimplantation genetic diagnosis as a reproductive option.

det.patho: Dominant PRNP variants (point mutations, octapeptide repeat insertions, deletions, stop codons) make the mutant protein prone to misfolding and conversion to PrPSc; small amounts form throughout life and are cleared until adult ageing weakens clearance, after which conversion accelerates exponentially. Missense variants at E200K, V210I and others cause CJD, P102L and others cause GSS with plaques, and D178N on a 129M allele causes thalamic degeneration in FFI. Octapeptide insertions of two to four repeats act like CJD, five to seven give a long course, and eight or more give GSS.
det.clinical: Most variants begin in the 40s–60s, younger than sCJD. Genetic CJD resembles sporadic CJD, often with overlapping MRI and EEG; E200K is the commonest pathogenic variant worldwide. GSS is a slowly progressive ataxia and parkinsonism, and FFI starts with insomnia and autonomic overactivity. Stop-codon variants have early cognitive change, chronic diarrhoea, neuropathy and long durations, sometimes resembling AD or FTD. Phenotype varies even within a family.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis needs a pathogenic PRNP variant in a compatible syndrome; neuropathology alone cannot prove a genetic cause. Offer sequencing to every patient with prion disease, because phenotypes overlap and family history is absent in nearly half. Variants with low penetrance (V210I, V180I, M232R) must be interpreted cautiously, since many carriers are healthy. RT-QuIC and 14-3-3 are positive in fast variants but frequently negative in slow ones, so an uninformative result should not stop the work-up.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying treatment exists; manage symptoms and provide palliative care. Genetic counselling is essential, including preimplantation genetic diagnosis, and diagnosing a dominant fatal disease can distress both the patient and relatives. Research includes PrPC-lowering antisense oligonucleotides and doxycycline prophylaxis in FFI carriers. Handle neurosurgical instruments under prion rules.
det.prognosis: Varies from months (E200K genetic CJD) through about 18 months (FFI) to over a decade (GSS); always fatal in symptomatic patients.
pearls: Nearly half of genetic cases have no known family history, so test every case.
D178N produces FFI with codon 129 methionine and genetic CJD with valine.
Be cautious with V210I, V180I and M232R: low penetrance means a positive result does not prove the cause.
det.thd: โรคพรีออนทางพันธุกรรมเกิดจากการกลายพันธุ์แบบ autosomal dominant ของยีน PRNP แบ่งเดิมเป็น genetic CJD, GSS และ FFI ซึ่งแต่ละแบบมีอาการนำต่างกัน และตำแหน่ง codon 129 มีผลต่อรูปแบบโรค ผู้ป่วยเกือบครึ่งไม่มีประวัติครอบครัว จึงควรตรวจ PRNP ทุกราย การตรวจ RT-QuIC และ MRI อาจไม่ช่วยในชนิดที่ดำเนินช้า ยังไม่มียารักษา ควรให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรมและพิจารณา PGD

name: Initiation tremor
formal: Tremor that appears at the start of voluntary movement, as in Holmes tremor or primary orthostatic tremor variants, due to cerebellar outflow disturbance or other basal ganglia lesions.
simple: A tremor that shows up at the start of a movement and often settles once the movement is under way.
th: อาการสั่นที่เกิดตอนเริ่มเคลื่อนไหว เป็นคำบรรยายลักษณะ ไม่ใช่โรคเฉพาะ อาจพบใน Holmes tremor, orthostatic tremor บางแบบ หรือรอยโรคในทางออกของสมองน้อยและ basal ganglia
tempoNote: Depends on cause; usually persistent once established
feat: A descriptive, non-standard term rather than a recognised disease entity
Tremor burst at the start of a voluntary movement or when assuming a posture, which may settle as movement continues
Contexts: Holmes (rubral) tremor after midbrain/thalamic lesions, orthostatic tremor on standing, task-specific tremors, re-emergent tremor of Parkinson disease (after a latency)
Classify using the MDS tremor axes (clinical features plus aetiology)
inv: Careful clinical classification: rest, posture, kinetic, task-specific, position-specific
Surface EMG/accelerometry for frequency and latency (e.g. 13–18 Hz in orthostatic tremor)
MRI for structural midbrain, thalamic or cerebellar lesions; DAT-SPECT if parkinsonism suspected

case.story: Six months after a pontine-midbrain haemorrhage his right arm shakes coarsely as soon as he reaches for a glass and also at rest.
case.exam: Slow (about 3–4 Hz) large-amplitude tremor at rest, worse on posture and movement onset, with ataxia of the right arm.
case.tests: MRI old haemorrhage in the left midbrain tegmentum; DAT-SPECT reduced on the left.
case.q: How should this tremor be classified?
case.a: Holmes tremor from a midbrain lesion — the initiation component is part of a rest-postural-kinetic tremor; levodopa may help.

det.patho: Tremor that appears as a movement starts reflects instability in the circuits that launch and stabilise voluntary action, particularly cerebello-thalamo-cortical and nigrostriatal pathways. Lesions of the dentato-rubro-thalamic tract combined with nigrostriatal damage produce Holmes tremor. Other initiation-related tremors relate to postural loading (orthostatic tremor) or specific tasks (primary writing tremor).
det.clinical: Clinically, the term describes when tremor appears rather than defining a disease. It is important to note whether tremor persists through the movement, whether it also occurs at rest or posture, and whether it is task- or position-specific. Re-emergent tremor in Parkinson disease starts after a delay once a posture is held. Associated signs (ataxia, parkinsonism, dystonia) point to the underlying syndrome.
det.diagnosis: Use the MDS consensus approach: define the tremor syndrome by its activation conditions, distribution and frequency, then look for aetiology. Neurophysiology clarifies frequency and burst patterns. Imaging is indicated if the history suggests a structural lesion or if signs are unilateral. Medication and toxic causes should be excluded.
det.treatment: Treatment is that of the underlying tremor syndrome: levodopa, anticholinergics or levetiracetam for Holmes tremor; clonazepam or gabapentin for orthostatic tremor; propranolol or primidone for essential tremor; botulinum toxin for task-specific forms. Thalamic DBS or focused ultrasound may help disabling refractory tremors.
det.prognosis: Determined by the cause; lesional tremors are often persistent but can partly respond to therapy.
pearls: Describe tremor by its activation condition, then name the syndrome.
Rest plus postural plus kinetic tremor after a midbrain lesion: Holmes tremor.
Re-emergent tremor in Parkinson disease can be mistaken for essential tremor.
det.thd: Initiation tremor เป็นคำบรรยายลักษณะการสั่นที่เกิดเมื่อเริ่มเคลื่อนไหว ไม่ใช่โรคเฉพาะ อาจพบใน Holmes tremor จากรอยโรคที่ midbrain หรือ thalamus, orthostatic tremor หรือ tremor เฉพาะงาน ควรจำแนกตามแนวทาง MDS ว่าเกิดขณะพัก ท่าทาง หรือเคลื่อนไหว แล้วหาสาเหตุด้วย MRI หรือ EMG การรักษาตามชนิดของ tremor

name: Insomnia
formal: Chronic difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep with daytime impairment; may be primary or secondary to psychiatric, medical or neurological disease, medicines or sleep disorders.
simple: Ongoing trouble falling or staying asleep that affects how a person feels and functions in the daytime.
th: นอนหลับยาก หลับไม่ต่อเนื่อง หรือตื่นเช้ากว่าที่ต้องการ อย่างน้อย 3 คืนต่อสัปดาห์ร่วมกับผลเสียในเวลากลางวัน ถ้าเป็นนานเกิน 3 เดือนเรียก chronic insomnia การรักษาหลักคือ CBT-I
tempoNote: Short-term insomnia lasts under 3 months, often after a stressor; chronic insomnia disorder needs symptoms at least 3 nights a week for 3 months or more
feat: Trouble getting to sleep, staying asleep or waking too early despite adequate opportunity and a suitable bedroom
Daytime consequences: fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, worry about sleep, errors at work
Conditioned arousal in bed, clock-watching and spending long periods awake in bed keep the problem going
Frequently comorbid with depression, anxiety, pain, menopause, nocturia, RLS, sleep apnoea and stimulant or alcohol use
More common in women and older adults; affects about one adult in ten as a chronic disorder
inv: Clinical diagnosis from history and a 2-week sleep diary; screen with the Insomnia Severity Index
Actigraphy when timing or total sleep is uncertain or a circadian disorder is suspected
Polysomnography only if sleep apnoea, PLMD, parasomnia or treatment failure is suspected; not for routine insomnia
Look for causes: depression and anxiety scales, thyroid function, ferritin if RLS symptoms, medicine and substance review

case.story: For 8 months she has lain awake for over an hour most nights and wakes at 3 am thinking about work; she naps after lunch and drinks four cups of coffee a day.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination; she is tense but not depressed on screening; BMI 23, no snoring reported.
case.tests: Sleep diary shows 8.5 h in bed with about 5.5 h of sleep; Insomnia Severity Index 19; TSH normal.
case.q: What is the first-line treatment?
case.a: Chronic insomnia disorder; CBT-I with stimulus control, sleep restriction to about 6 h in bed, cognitive work and caffeine reduction, with a short medicine course only as an adjunct.

det.patho: Insomnia is best understood as a state of hyperarousal, with raised cognitive, autonomic and cortical activity at night. Predisposing traits, a precipitating stressor and perpetuating habits such as long time in bed, napping and anxious monitoring combine to make it chronic. Twin studies show moderate heritability, and insomnia predicts later depression, hypertension and reduced quality of life.
det.clinical: Patients describe difficulty with sleep onset, maintenance or early waking, often in a mixed pattern, plus daytime fatigue and low mood rather than true sleepiness. Many report sleeping better away from home, a clue to conditioned arousal. Some underestimate how much they sleep, a feature formerly called paradoxical insomnia. Red flags are loud snoring, leg urges, dream enactment, a shifted but otherwise normal sleep period, or new insomnia with neurological decline.
det.diagnosis: ICSD-3-TR chronic insomnia disorder requires a sleep complaint with daytime impairment at least 3 nights a week for 3 months, not explained by poor opportunity or another sleep disorder; short-term insomnia covers under 3 months. A sleep diary is the key tool and polysomnography is reserved for suspected other disorders. Screen for depression, anxiety, pain, nocturia, medicines, alcohol and caffeine. Excess daytime sleepiness on the Epworth scale should prompt a search for another diagnosis.
det.treatment: CBT-I is first line for adults of all ages, including digital programmes, and combines stimulus control, sleep restriction, relaxation, cognitive therapy and sleep education. When medicines are needed, options include the dual orexin receptor antagonists suvorexant, lemborexant and daridorexant, low-dose doxepin for sleep maintenance, Z-drugs for short courses, and melatonin-receptor agonists for sleep onset. Benzodiazepines and Z-drugs carry falls, dependence and complex sleep behaviour risks, especially in older people. Treat comorbid depression, pain and sleep apnoea in parallel.
det.prognosis: Chronic insomnia often persists for years without treatment, but CBT-I gives durable benefit that outlasts medicine.
pearls: Time in bed much longer than sleep time is the habit most worth correcting, and sleep restriction does exactly that.
Insomnia with real daytime sleepiness is a clue to a second disorder such as OSA or a circadian problem.
DORAs block orexin signalling and have less rebound and dependence than benzodiazepines.
det.thd: Insomnia คือนอนหลับยาก หลับไม่ต่อเนื่อง หรือตื่นเร็ว ร่วมกับผลเสียตอนกลางวัน เป็นอย่างน้อย 3 คืนต่อสัปดาห์ ถ้านานเกิน 3 เดือนเรียก chronic insomnia กลไกหลักคือภาวะตื่นตัวมากเกินและพฤติกรรมที่ทำให้เรื้อรัง เช่น นอนอยู่บนเตียงนานเกินไป การวินิจฉัยใช้ประวัติและ sleep diary ส่วน PSG ใช้เมื่อสงสัยโรคอื่น การรักษาหลักคือ CBT-I ส่วนยาเช่น DORA หรือ Z-drug ใช้เสริมระยะสั้น

qx.stem: A 58-year-old bank manager from Bangkok has had difficulty falling and staying asleep at least four nights a week for two years, spends 9 hours in bed trying to sleep and worries about the next day. He has no snoring, restless legs or depression, and a physical examination is normal. He asks for a sleeping pill.
qx.q: Which is the recommended first-line treatment?
opts: Zolpidem nightly
Diphenhydramine
Alprazolam
Melatonin 10 mg
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia
qx.why: Current guidelines recommend cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, with stimulus control and sleep restriction, as first-line treatment for chronic insomnia, with benefit that persists after treatment ends. Hypnotics are for short, carefully chosen use, and antihistamines and benzodiazepines carry more risk than benefit. Melatonin has little effect on primary chronic insomnia.

qx.stem: A 76-year-old woman from Lampang with mild cognitive impairment and two falls in the past year has chronic sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia. A structured behavioural programme gave partial benefit. She was previously prescribed lorazepam and diphenhydramine, which her daughter wants stopped.
qx.q: Which pharmacological option is most suitable if medication is needed?
opts: Triazolam
Amitriptyline
A dual orexin receptor antagonist at the lowest dose
Zopiclone 7.5 mg
Diazepam
qx.why: Dual orexin receptor antagonists such as suvorexant, lemborexant and daridorexant improve sleep with less impact on gait, cognition and falls than benzodiazepines or Z-drugs, and are suitable for short- to medium-term use in older adults. Benzodiazepines, Z-drugs and tricyclics increase falls, confusion and next-day impairment, and are on potentially inappropriate medication lists.

name: Insulin neuritis
formal: Acute painful small fibre neuropathy with autonomic features after rapid glycaemic correction in poorly controlled diabetes, such as treatment-induced neuropathy of diabetes.
simple: Severe nerve pain and autonomic symptoms that can follow a sudden fall in blood sugar after starting diabetes treatment.
ab: Acute painful neuropathy of rapid glycaemic control
th: ปวดแสบร้อนรุนแรงจากเส้นประสาทเล็กหลังคุมน้ำตาลลดลงอย่างรวดเร็วในผู้ป่วยเบาหวานที่คุมไม่ดีมานาน
tempoNote: Starts within 2–8 weeks of a rapid HbA1c fall
feat: Severe burning pain and allodynia, often widespread
Autonomic symptoms: orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction
Triggered by HbA1c drop of more than 2% over 3 months
Often coexists with worsening retinopathy
Also reported in type 1 diabetes and eating disorders with insulin restriction
inv: Serial HbA1c
NCS often normal; skin biopsy shows small fibre loss
Autonomic testing; eye examination for retinopathy

case.who: 26-year-old woman from Bangkok with type 1 diabetes
case.story: HbA1c dropped from 13% to 7% over 10 weeks after starting an insulin pump; then severe burning legs and dizziness on standing.
case.exam: Allodynia over legs and trunk, postural BP drop of 30 mmHg.
case.tests: NCS normal; skin biopsy shows reduced intraepidermal nerve fibres; eye exam shows worsened retinopathy.
case.q: Should glycaemic control be relaxed?
case.a: No; maintain control while treating pain and autonomic symptoms.

read.where: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves — Endocrine Disorders

det.patho: Rapid reduction of glucose may cause endoneurial ischaemia via arteriovenous shunting, microvascular steal or neovascularisation of nerve. Small fibres are most vulnerable.
det.clinical: Acute severe pain within weeks of aggressive glucose lowering, frequently with autonomic dysfunction and retinopathy worsening. Pain may be widespread, involving the trunk.
det.diagnosis: Clinical criteria: compatible symptoms within 8 weeks of HbA1c fall of more than 2% over 3 months. Skin biopsy and autonomic testing support.
det.treatment: Pain control with gabapentinoids, duloxetine or tricyclics; may need opioids briefly. Manage orthostatic hypotension. Avoid abrupt glucose lowering in high-risk patients.
det.prognosis: Pain and autonomic symptoms often improve over 12–24 months, especially in type 1 diabetes.
pearls: Ask about recent rapid HbA1c drops in new painful neuropathy.
Retinopathy may worsen in parallel.
Prevention: gradual glycaemic correction in long-standing poor control.
det.thd: Insulin neuritis หรือ TIND เกิดหลังคุมน้ำตาลลดลงเร็วเกินไปในผู้ป่วยที่คุมไม่ดีมานาน ปวดแสบร้อนรุนแรงและมีอาการระบบอัตโนมัติ เช่น ความดันตกเวลาลุกยืน NCS มักปกติ แต่ skin biopsy ผิดปกติ รักษาด้วยยาลดปวดและควบคุมน้ำตาลต่อ อาการมักดีขึ้นใน 1–2 ปี ป้องกันโดยลดน้ำตาลอย่างค่อยเป็นค่อยไป

name: Intention tremor
formal: Tremor on goal-directed movement that increases toward the target, characteristic of cerebellar outflow lesions in the dentate-rubro-thalamic pathway, seen in multiple sclerosis, stroke and toxins.
simple: A tremor that gets worse as the hand approaches a target, such as touching the nose, usually from cerebellar damage.
th: tremor ที่เกิดขณะเคลื่อนไหวไปยังเป้าหมาย และสั่นมากขึ้นเมื่อใกล้เป้า พบในรอยโรคของ cerebellum และทางออก dentato-rubro-thalamic
tempoNote: Depends on cause: acute with stroke, progressive in degeneration or MS
feat: Tremor amplitude increases as the limb approaches a target (finger-nose test)
Low frequency, usually under 5 Hz, proximal and distal
Accompanied by dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia and ataxia
Causes: MS, stroke, tumour, alcohol, drugs (lithium, phenytoin), SCA, Wilson disease
May have a postural and titubation component
inv: MRI brain with attention to cerebellum and superior cerebellar peduncle
Drug levels (phenytoin, lithium), thyroid, alcohol history
Genetic testing for SCA when familial and progressive

case.who: 30-year-old woman from Phrae with multiple sclerosis diagnosed 4 years ago
case.story: Her right hand shakes when she brings a spoon to her mouth, spilling food.
case.exam: Right arm tremor increasing near the target, dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia; rest tremor absent.
case.tests: MRI: demyelinating plaque in right superior cerebellar peduncle.
case.q: What type of tremor is this?
case.a: Cerebellar intention tremor from an MS lesion in the cerebellar outflow.

read.where: 1 - Clinical overview and phenomenology of movement disorders

det.patho: The cerebellum predicts and corrects movement trajectories. Lesions of the dentate nucleus or its outflow through the superior cerebellar peduncle to red nucleus and thalamus disrupt feedforward control, so corrective movements overshoot and oscillate as accuracy demands rise near the target.
det.clinical: The tremor is absent at rest, emerges during reaching, and worsens near the goal. It is usually accompanied by other cerebellar signs. Severe outflow lesions can make limbs nearly useless. Head and trunk titubation may coexist.
det.diagnosis: Clinical observation during finger-nose and heel-shin testing is diagnostic. MRI identifies structural causes. Drug and toxin history, thyroid function and, in young patients, copper studies are checked. Progressive cases with family history need genetic testing.
det.treatment: Medications are of limited benefit; options include propranolol, primidone, topiramate, clonazepam or levetiracetam. Weighted utensils and wrist weights help function. Thalamic DBS or focused ultrasound may reduce tremor in selected patients, particularly MS, though ataxia persists. Address the cause where possible.
det.prognosis: Often persistent; drug-induced cases resolve after the offending drug is stopped.
pearls: Intention tremor grows as the finger approaches the nose; rest tremor fades with action.
Check phenytoin and lithium levels in new cerebellar tremor.
Superior cerebellar peduncle lesions cause severe outflow tremor.
det.thd: Intention tremor คือการสั่นขณะเคลื่อนไหวเข้าหาเป้าหมายและสั่นมากขึ้นเมื่อใกล้เป้า พบร่วมกับอาการอื่นของ cerebellum เช่น dysmetria เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ cerebellum หรือทางออกไป thalamus สาเหตุ เช่น MS, stroke, เหล้า และยา phenytoin หรือ lithium การรักษาด้วยยาได้ผลจำกัด อาจพิจารณา DBS ในบางราย

name: Intermittent ataxias
formal: Episodic ataxia syndromes with attacks of incoordination between normal intervals, due to channelopathies or metabolic disorders; episodic ataxia types 1 and 2 are common.
simple: Conditions in which attacks of poor balance and coordination come and go.
th: กลุ่มภาวะที่มีอาการเดินเซเป็นพัก ๆ แล้วกลับเป็นปกติระหว่างครั้ง สาเหตุจาก channelopathy เช่น EA1, EA2 หรือโรคเมตาบอลิกที่ถูกกระตุ้นด้วยการเจ็บป่วยหรือโปรตีน
tempoNote: Attacks last seconds to hours (channelopathies) or days (metabolic); normal or near normal between
feat: Recurrent attacks of imbalance, slurred speech and limb incoordination
Triggers: sudden movement, startle, exercise, emotion, caffeine, fever or protein load
EA1: brief attacks (minutes) with interictal myokymia; EA2: longer attacks (hours) with interictal nystagmus
Metabolic types: attacks with vomiting, drowsiness or encephalopathy during illness
inv: Interictal exam for nystagmus or myokymia; EMG for neuromyotonic discharges (EA1)
Gene panel (KCNA1, CACNA1A, SLC1A3 and others)
During attacks in children: glucose, ammonia, lactate, amino acids, urine organic acids

case.story: Since age 9 has had attacks of staggering, vertigo and vomiting lasting 2–6 hours, brought on by exercise or stress; her mother had similar attacks.
case.exam: Between attacks: downbeat nystagmus on lateral gaze, mild gait ataxia.
case.tests: MRI mild vermian atrophy; CACNA1A truncating variant.
case.q: Which subtype is this and what drug reduces attacks?
case.a: Episodic ataxia type 2; acetazolamide (or 4-aminopyridine) usually lessens attack frequency.

read.where: Chapter 24 Cerebellar Ataxias and Related Conditions — Genetic Forms of Episodic Ataxia

det.patho: Most hereditary episodic ataxias arise from ion channel or transporter defects: KCNA1 (potassium channel, EA1), CACNA1A (P/Q calcium channel, EA2), SLC1A3 (glutamate transporter, EA6) and others. Abnormal excitability of cerebellar circuits produces transient dysfunction. Metabolic forms reflect energy failure or toxic metabolite build-up when intake or catabolism changes.
det.clinical: EA1 begins in childhood with brief attacks provoked by startle or movement and continuous fine muscle rippling. EA2 attacks last longer, are often accompanied by vertigo and vomiting, and many develop permanent nystagmus and slowly progressive ataxia; migraine and epilepsy are associated. Metabolic causes (MSUD, PDH deficiency, urea cycle defects, Hartnup) present in infancy or childhood with attacks during infection.
det.diagnosis: History of triggers, duration and interictal signs guides testing. Genetic panels confirm channelopathies. In children, blood and urine metabolic tests taken during an attack are critical. MRI excludes structural or demyelinating causes. Consider functional disorders and migraine but do not accept them before excluding treatable causes.
det.treatment: Acetazolamide helps many with EA2 and some with EA1; 4-aminopyridine reduces EA2 attacks. Carbamazepine may help EA1. Avoid identified triggers. Metabolic forms require disease-specific measures such as protein restriction, thiamine or ketogenic diet.
det.prognosis: Variable; channelopathies are lifelong but often controllable, while some metabolic forms risk permanent damage if attacks are not treated.
pearls: Minutes + myokymia = EA1; hours + interictal nystagmus = EA2.
Acetazolamide responsiveness is a clue to a channelopathy.
Test blood and urine during the attack in a child; metabolic markers may normalise between.
det.thd: Intermittent ataxias คือกลุ่มโรคที่มีเดินเซเป็นพัก ๆ แล้วหายกลับปกติ ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจาก channelopathy เช่น EA1 อาการสั้นเป็นนาทีร่วมกับกล้ามเนื้อกระตุกเป็นระลอก และ EA2 อาการเป็นชั่วโมงพร้อมเวียนศีรษะและตากระตุกระหว่างครั้ง อีกกลุ่มคือโรคเมตาบอลิกที่ถูกกระตุ้นจากไข้หรือโปรตีน วินิจฉัยด้วยประวัติ ตรวจยีน และตรวจเมตาบอลิกขณะมีอาการ acetazolamide ช่วยลดอาการใน EA2

ddx.pt: Vertigo attacks with migraine features; no interictal cerebellar signs or channel variant
Paroxysmal ataxia can occur, but MRI shows demyelinating lesions
Ataxia with encephalopathy during illness or protein load; abnormal metabolic tests during attack

aN: episodic ataxias | paroxysmal ataxia | ea | recurrent ataxia

name: Intermittent metabolic ataxias
formal: Episodic ataxia from inborn errors of metabolism, such as maple syrup urine disease, pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency, urea cycle defects and Hartnup disease, triggered by illness or protein load.
simple: Attacks of unsteady walking caused by inherited metabolic disorders, often brought on by infection or a high-protein meal.
th: อาการเดินเซเป็นพัก ๆ จากโรคพันธุกรรมเมตาบอลิซึม เช่น MSUD, PDH deficiency, urea cycle defect, Hartnup โดยมักเกิดเมื่อติดเชื้อ อดอาหาร หรือกินโปรตีนมาก
tempoNote: Attacks over hours to days during catabolic stress, with recovery between
feat: Ataxia accompanied by vomiting, drowsiness, confusion or irritability
Triggered by infection, fasting, surgery or high-protein meals
Possible developmental delay, failure to thrive or prior neonatal illness
Family history of unexplained infant deaths or consanguinity
inv: During attack: glucose, ammonia, blood gas, lactate/pyruvate, ketones
Plasma amino acids, acylcarnitines, urine organic acids and amino acids
Targeted gene panel or exome

case.story: Third episode of staggering and sleepiness, each during a febrile illness; between episodes he is normal but a slow talker.
case.exam: Truncal ataxia, drowsy but rousable, no meningism.
case.tests: Ammonia 210 µmol/L, normal glucose; plasma glutamine high, citrulline low; urine orotic acid raised.
case.q: What class of disorder is likely, and what emergency measures are needed?
case.a: Urea cycle defect (likely OTC deficiency); stop protein, give IV glucose to halt catabolism, and use nitrogen scavengers or dialysis if ammonia keeps rising.

read.where: Chapter 24 Cerebellar Ataxias and Related Conditions — Other Metabolic Causes of Ataxia

det.patho: Inborn errors that limit amino acid breakdown, ammonia disposal or pyruvate oxidation leave the brain vulnerable when demand rises. During catabolism, toxic metabolites (leucine, ammonia) or energy deficit (lactate rise) disturb cerebellar and cortical function. Hartnup disease produces attacks through secondary niacin deficiency.
det.clinical: Partial (intermediate) forms of MSUD, OTC deficiency, PDH deficiency and others may spare the neonate and present later as recurrent ataxia with encephalopathy during illness. Between attacks children may be normal or show subtle delay. Severe attacks risk cerebral oedema, coma and death.
det.diagnosis: Samples must be collected during the episode: ammonia, lactate, glucose, plasma amino acids, acylcarnitines and urine organic acids. Normal results between attacks do not exclude the disorder. Confirmation is by enzyme or genetic testing.
det.treatment: Emergency care stops protein briefly, provides high-calorie glucose infusion to reverse catabolism, corrects acidosis and lowers toxic metabolites (scavengers, haemodialysis). Long term: disease-specific diet, cofactors (thiamine for some MSUD and PDH cases), ketogenic diet in PDH deficiency, and sick-day plans.
det.prognosis: Good when recognised early and attacks are prevented; repeated severe crises cause cumulative brain injury.
pearls: Ataxia + vomiting + drowsiness during a fever in a toddler: check ammonia, glucose and lactate immediately.
Metabolic samples drawn after recovery are often normal.
Give glucose, not just saline, to stop catabolism.
det.thd: อาการเดินเซเป็นพัก ๆ จากโรคเมตาบอลิกพันธุกรรมพบในเด็ก เช่น MSUD โรคของวงจรยูเรีย และ PDH deficiency มักเกิดเมื่อมีไข้ อดอาหาร หรือกินโปรตีนมาก มักมีอาเจียนและซึมร่วมด้วย ต้องเจาะเลือดตรวจแอมโมเนีย น้ำตาล แลคเตต และกรดอะมิโนขณะมีอาการ รักษาฉุกเฉินด้วยการหยุดโปรตีนชั่วคราวและให้กลูโคสทางหลอดเลือด

name: Internal carotid artery (ICA) disease
formal: Stenosis or occlusion of the ICA, usually atherosclerotic at the bifurcation, causing amaurosis fugax, TIA or hemispheric stroke; also dissection, treated with endarterectomy or stenting.
simple: Narrowing or blockage of the main neck artery to the brain, which can cause temporary vision loss or stroke.
more: Stenosis, occlusion or dissection of the internal carotid artery causing amaurosis fugax, TIA or stroke through emboli or haemodynamic failure.
th: โรคหลอดเลือดแดงคาโรติดภายใน (ICA) มักเกิดจากหินปูน atherosclerosis ที่ตำแหน่งแยกของหลอดเลือด ทำให้ตามัวข้างเดียวชั่วคราว (amaurosis fugax), TIA หรือเนื้อสมองตาย ตรวจด้วย duplex, CTA หรือ MRA วัดความตีบแบบ NASCET ถ้าตีบ 70–99% และมีอาการ ควรผ่าตัด endarterectomy ภายใน 2 สัปดาห์ ร่วมกับยาต้านเกล็ดเลือด สแตติน และคุมปัจจัยเสี่ยง
tempoNote: Plaque grows over years and is silent; symptoms are sudden, and the recurrence risk is highest in the first days to two weeks after a TIA or minor stroke
feat: Amaurosis fugax: painless, curtain-like monocular visual loss lasting minutes; retinal infarction and ocular ischaemic syndrome in severe chronic disease
Hemispheric TIA or stroke: contralateral weakness or numbness, aphasia (dominant hemisphere) or neglect, often with stereotyped recurrent attacks in tight stenosis
Border-zone (watershed) infarcts and limb-shaking TIAs from haemodynamic failure when the stenosis or occlusion is severe and collaterals are poor
Asymptomatic stenosis: stroke risk of roughly 1–2% a year on older medical treatment (lower with current therapy), and a marker of coronary disease
Non-atherosclerotic causes include dissection, fibromuscular dysplasia, radiation arteriopathy, carotid web and Takayasu arteritis, usually in younger patients
inv: Carotid duplex ultrasound first; confirm with CT angiography or MR angiography, with measurement of stenosis by NASCET method; catheter angiography only when non-invasive tests disagree
Brain MRI with DWI, vascular risk work-up (lipids, glucose or HbA1c), ECG and prolonged rhythm monitoring because atrial fibrillation often coexists
Plaque features (ulceration, intraplaque haemorrhage, soft plaque) and cerebral perfusion or cerebrovascular reserve studies in selected patients

case.who: 67-year-old man, a retired bus driver from Songkhla, with diabetes and 30 pack-years
case.story: Three episodes of painless left monocular blindness lasting a few minutes this week, then 20 minutes of right hand clumsiness and word-finding difficulty yesterday.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination now, left carotid bruit, blood pressure 158/92.
case.tests: CT angiography shows 82% stenosis at the origin of the left ICA with an ulcerated plaque; MRI shows small left frontal and parietal DWI lesions; ECG sinus rhythm.
case.q: What is the best next step?
case.a: Symptomatic severe left ICA stenosis. Start dual antiplatelet therapy for the first weeks, a high-intensity statin and blood pressure control, and refer for carotid endarterectomy within two weeks of the event (stenting is an alternative in selected patients).

read.where: Chapter 80 Stroke – General Information and Physiology — Carotid artery stenosis (symptomatic and asymptomatic)
Chapter 8 Stroke and Cerebrovascular Diseases — Anterior Circulation
Chapter 4: Which arterial territory is involved?

det.patho: Atherosclerotic plaque forms at the carotid bifurcation and proximal ICA where flow is disturbed. Plaque rupture or intraplaque haemorrhage releases emboli into the ophthalmic and middle cerebral arteries, which is the commonest mechanism, whereas tight stenosis or occlusion can reduce flow and cause watershed ischaemia when collaterals fail. Carotid stenosis above 50% is present in a small but significant proportion of men and women over 65, and the lesion usually coexists with coronary and peripheral disease.
det.clinical: Symptomatic disease presents as amaurosis fugax, TIA or stroke. After a TIA the early recurrence risk is high, so urgent assessment is important. A carotid bruit is not a reliable guide to the degree of stenosis. Chronic occlusion may cause limb-shaking TIAs or ocular ischaemia. Asymptomatic stenosis is found on screening and carries a low annual stroke risk, which should be weighed against perioperative risk.
det.diagnosis: Duplex ultrasound is the usual first test and CT or MR angiography confirms the degree of narrowing and shows the arch and intracranial vessels; the methods should agree, and if two non-invasive tests disagree, catheter angiography is considered. Stenosis is graded by NASCET criteria (distal ICA as reference). Near-occlusion with a collapsed distal vessel behaves differently from simple severe stenosis. A full stroke work-up should look for coexisting cardiac sources.
det.treatment: Best medical therapy includes antiplatelet treatment (aspirin, clopidogrel, or short-term dual therapy after minor stroke or high-risk TIA), a high-intensity statin, blood pressure and glucose control, smoking cessation and exercise. For symptomatic stenosis of 70–99%, and for selected patients with 50–69%, carotid endarterectomy by a surgeon whose complication rate is low is recommended ideally within two weeks, since benefit falls with delay; carotid stenting is a reasonable alternative for younger patients or those with a difficult neck, with a slightly higher periprocedural stroke risk in older patients. For asymptomatic stenosis above 60–70%, the older trials (ACAS, ACST) showed modest benefit of endarterectomy over medical treatment in suitable patients, whereas modern intensive medical therapy lowers the absolute stroke risk, so intervention is individualised.
det.prognosis: Risk of recurrent stroke is highest in the first weeks and falls sharply after revascularisation and with intensive medical therapy.
pearls: Amaurosis fugax is a carotid TIA: work it up urgently.
Endarterectomy benefit is largest in the first two weeks after symptoms.
A bruit neither confirms nor excludes significant stenosis; image the vessel.
det.thd: ICA disease ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจาก atherosclerosis ที่ carotid bifurcation ทำให้ตามัวชั่วคราวข้างเดียว (amaurosis fugax) TIA หรือเนื้อสมองตายด้านตรงข้าม วินิจฉัยด้วย duplex และ CTA/MRA ระดับความตีบวัดแบบ NASCET ถ้าตีบ 70–99% และมีอาการ ควรทำ carotid endarterectomy ภายใน 2 สัปดาห์ (หรือใส่ stent ในบางราย) พร้อมยาต้านเกล็ดเลือด สแตตินขนาดสูง และควบคุมความดัน เบาหวาน และหยุดสูบบุหรี่ ส่วนที่ตีบแต่ไม่มีอาการ ใช้ยาเป็นหลักและเลือกผ่าตัดเฉพาะรายเสี่ยงสูง

name: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO)
formal: Impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye on lateral gaze, with nystagmus of the abducting eye, from MLF lesions; commonly multiple sclerosis in young adults and brainstem stroke in older patients.
simple: Poor inward movement of one eye when looking sideways, caused by damage in a brainstem pathway.

feat: Weak or slow adduction of the ipsilateral eye (same side as the MLF lesion)
Dissociated abducting nystagmus of the opposite eye
Convergence often preserved (lesion below midbrain)
Bilateral INO in young adults: typically MS; unilateral in older adults: often brainstem infarct
Can be part of one-and-a-half syndrome with PPRF or abducens nucleus involvement
inv: MRI brain with thin brainstem slices (FLAIR, DWI)
If MRI negative: consider myasthenia (pseudo-INO), Wernicke, tumour, trauma
CSF oligoclonal bands if demyelination suspected

case.story: Three days of horizontal double vision when looking to either side.
case.exam: Bilateral slowed adduction, nystagmus of each abducting eye, convergence intact; brisk reflexes.
case.tests: MRI: bilateral pontine MLF lesions plus periventricular ovoid lesions; CSF oligoclonal bands.
case.q: What is the localisation and likely disease?
case.a: Bilateral MLF lesions (bilateral INO) due to multiple sclerosis.

det.patho: The MLF links the abducens nucleus interneurons on one side to the medial rectus subnucleus of the contralateral oculomotor nucleus. A lesion interrupts this signal, so the ipsilateral eye fails to adduct in horizontal gaze while the abducting eye overshoots with nystagmus, partly due to adaptive increased innervation.
det.clinical: Patients may complain of horizontal diplopia, blurred vision or oscillopsia, but mild INO may only show as slowed adducting saccades. Bilateral INO can give exotropia (WEBINO) if the lesion is rostral. Skew deviation can accompany it. Demyelination and stroke account for most cases; trauma, tumours, infection and Wernicke are less common.
det.diagnosis: Look for adduction lag with fast horizontal saccades, which is more sensitive than slow pursuit. MRI targets the dorsomedial pons and midbrain. Myasthenia can produce a pseudo-INO and should be considered when MRI is normal or ptosis fluctuates.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: MS relapse management and disease-modifying therapy, secondary stroke prevention, thiamine for Wernicke. Diplopia may be eased by occlusion or prisms. Recovery often occurs spontaneously over weeks to months, especially in demyelination.
det.prognosis: Most INO from demyelination improves substantially; ischaemic INO also often recovers.
pearls: Test fast saccades: subtle INO shows as a lagging adducting eye.
Young bilateral INO: MS; older unilateral INO: stroke.
Normal MRI with variable INO: check for myasthenia.
det.thd: INO เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ medial longitudinal fasciculus ในก้านสมอง ทำให้ตาข้างเดียวกับรอยโรคหุบเข้าไม่ได้หรือช้าเวลามองด้านข้าง และตาอีกข้างที่กางออกมี nystagmus ในคนอายุน้อยมักเกิดจาก MS ส่วนผู้สูงอายุมักเป็น stroke ต้องทำ MRI ก้านสมอง และนึกถึง myasthenia gravis ถ้า MRI ปกติ อาการมักดีขึ้นเองในหลายสัปดาห์

name: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia of abduction
formal: Posterior or Lutz INO with weakness of abduction, rather than adduction, due to dysfunction of the contralateral side or lesions of paramedian pontine fibres, a variant of internuclear ophthalmoplegia.
simple: A rare eye movement problem in which the eye cannot move outward properly, due to damage to a brainstem pathway.

case.who: 42-year-old woman with known MS from Chiang Mai
case.story: New horizontal diplopia when looking to the left over several days.
case.exam: Left eye abducts poorly on voluntary leftward saccades but abducts fully on rapid head turning; adduction intact.
case.tests: MRI shows new enhancing lesion in the right paramedian pons.
case.q: Why is this not a left sixth nerve palsy?
case.a: Vestibular-driven abduction is preserved, implying a supranuclear (prenuclear) lesion — a posterior INO of Lutz.

det.patho: The proposed mechanism is interruption of descending pathways from the contralateral PPRF or premotor neurons to the abducens nucleus motoneurons, sparing the vestibular inputs. Its existence as a clean anatomical entity is debated, and some cases may represent partial nuclear or fascicular lesions or myasthenia.
det.clinical: Patients have horizontal diplopia with impaired abduction during voluntary gaze but not during reflex head turning. It has been reported with brainstem demyelination and stroke. Because so few well-studied cases exist, its localising value is limited.
det.diagnosis: Requires demonstration that voluntary abduction is impaired while vestibulo-ocular abduction is intact, supported by brainstem MRI. Myasthenia should be excluded by antibody testing and fatigability assessment.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying lesion (MS relapse management, stroke care). Prisms or occlusion help diplopia while recovery occurs.
det.prognosis: Depends on the cause; demyelinating lesions often improve.
pearls: Always test vestibulo-ocular reflex when abduction is weak.
Posterior INO is rare; consider myasthenia first.
Classic INO is an adduction failure — know the difference.
det.thd: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia of abduction หรือ posterior INO (Lutz) เป็นภาวะพบน้อยที่ตากลอกออกได้ไม่ดีเมื่อสั่งให้มอง แต่กลอกออกได้เมื่อหมุนศีรษะ (VOR) แสดงว่ารอยโรคอยู่เหนือ abducens nucleus ใน pons ยังมีข้อถกเถียงว่าเป็น entity จริงหรือไม่ ต้องแยก sixth nerve palsy และ myasthenia ตรวจ MRI และรักษาตามสาเหตุ

name: Interstitial lung disease (ILD)
formal: Diffuse parenchymal lung disease commonly associated with antisynthetase syndrome and other inflammatory myopathies, causing dyspnoea and restrictive physiology.
simple: Scarring or inflammation of the lungs, often seen alongside autoimmune muscle disease, causing breathlessness.
more: Diagnosed with HRCT and lung function tests; treated with steroids and immunosuppressants such as mycophenolate; strongly affects prognosis in myositis.
th: โรคเนื้อปอดอักเสบหรือพังผืดแบบกระจาย พบร่วมกับ inflammatory myopathy โดยเฉพาะ antisynthetase syndrome และ anti-MDA5 dermatomyositis
tempoNote: Chronic in most antisynthetase cases; rapidly progressive over weeks in anti-MDA5 disease
feat: Lung disease, not neurological; relevant as a major complication of myositis
Exertional dyspnoea, dry cough, bibasal fine crackles
May precede, accompany or follow muscle weakness
Antisynthetase syndrome: myositis, ILD, arthritis, mechanic's hands, Raynaud, fever
Anti-MDA5 DM: little muscle weakness but rapidly progressive ILD, skin ulcers
inv: High-resolution CT chest
Pulmonary function: restrictive pattern, reduced DLCO
Myositis antibodies: Jo-1, PL-7, PL-12, MDA5, Ro52
CK; separate respiratory muscle weakness (low MIP) from lung disease

case.story: Two months of breathlessness walking to the market, dry cough, joint pains and cracked rough skin on her fingers; mild thigh weakness.
case.exam: Fine bibasal crackles, hyperkeratotic fissured radial fingertips, hip flexor weakness grade 4.
case.tests: CK 1,400 U/L; HRCT shows NSIP pattern; anti-Jo-1 positive; FVC 62% and DLCO reduced.
case.q: What syndrome links lung and muscle here?
case.a: Antisynthetase syndrome with ILD; treat with steroids plus a steroid-sparing agent (e.g., mycophenolate, tacrolimus or rituximab).

det.patho: ILD in myositis results from immune-mediated alveolar and interstitial inflammation, often in a non-specific interstitial pneumonia or organising pneumonia pattern. Antisynthetase antibodies target tRNA synthetase enzymes, while anti-MDA5 antibodies associate with vasculopathy and rapidly progressive alveolar damage. The same autoimmune process affects muscle, skin and joints.
det.clinical: This is a lung disease; neurologists meet it as a key extramuscular feature of inflammatory myopathy and the main cause of death. Patients report breathlessness and cough, sometimes before any weakness. Anti-MDA5 dermatomyositis, common in East Asia, can cause minimal weakness yet fatal ILD within weeks. Breathlessness in myositis can also reflect respiratory muscle weakness, cardiomyopathy or drug pneumonitis.
det.diagnosis: HRCT and pulmonary function testing define the ILD. Myositis-specific antibodies predict risk and phenotype. Measure respiratory muscle strength to distinguish ventilatory weakness from parenchymal disease. Exclude infection before escalating immunosuppression.
det.treatment: Glucocorticoids with steroid-sparing agents (mycophenolate, azathioprine, tacrolimus) are standard; rituximab or cyclophosphamide are used in severe disease. Rapidly progressive anti-MDA5 ILD often needs combined intensive immunosuppression. Antifibrotics are considered for progressive fibrosis. Co-manage with pulmonology.
det.prognosis: Chronic antisynthetase ILD often stabilises with treatment; anti-MDA5 RP-ILD carries high early mortality.
pearls: Ask every myositis patient about breathlessness and get HRCT.
Mechanic's hands plus ILD: antisynthetase syndrome.
Anti-MDA5 can have little weakness but deadly lungs.
det.thd: ILD เป็นโรคของเนื้อปอด ไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาท แต่เป็นภาวะแทรกซ้อนสำคัญของ inflammatory myopathy โดยเฉพาะ antisynthetase syndrome (anti-Jo-1) และ anti-MDA5 dermatomyositis ผู้ป่วยมีเหนื่อยง่าย ไอแห้ง ฟังได้ crackles วินิจฉัยด้วย HRCT และ PFT ต้องแยกจากการหายใจอ่อนแรงจากกล้ามเนื้อ รักษาด้วย steroid ร่วมกับยากดภูมิ และดูแลร่วมกับแพทย์โรคปอด

name: Intracerebral haemorrhage (ICH)
formal: Haemorrhagic stroke from rupture of a vessel in the parenchyma, most often hypertensive deep bleed or amyloid lobar bleed, with sudden headache, deficit and reduced consciousness.
simple: A stroke caused by bleeding inside the brain, often linked to high blood pressure.
more: Focal collection of blood within the brain parenchyma, typically from hypertensive vasculopathy, amyloid angiopathy, trauma or vascular malformation, with sudden deficit and mass effect.
th: เลือดออกในเนื้อสมอง — อาการคล้ายสมองขาดเลือด แต่มักปวดศีรษะ อาเจียน ซึมลงเร็ว ต้องแยกด้วย CT

feat: Sudden focal deficit with headache, vomiting and early drop in consciousness
Very high blood pressure at presentation is common
Deep (putamen, thalamus, pons, cerebellum) sites suggest hypertensive arteriolopathy; lobar sites in the elderly suggest amyloid angiopathy
inv: Non-contrast CT (hyperdense clot); CTA spot sign predicts expansion

case.q: Name the likely mechanism and two immediate management priorities.

qx.stem: A 72-year-old man on warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve arrives 2 hours after sudden right hemiparesis. CT shows a 22 mL left putaminal haemorrhage without intraventricular extension. BP is 196/104 mmHg, INR 3.1, glucose 13 mmol/L and temperature 38.1 °C.
qx.q: Which set of early measures is most appropriate?
opts: Fresh frozen plasma alone and lower systolic pressure below 100 mmHg
Four-factor PCC with IV vitamin K, lower systolic pressure to about 140 mmHg smoothly, and treat hyperglycaemia and fever as a care bundle
Hold warfarin only and recheck INR tomorrow
Platelet transfusion and desmopressin
Immediate surgical evacuation before reversal
qx.why: Warfarin-associated ICH needs rapid INR correction with four-factor PCC plus IV vitamin K, which acts faster and with less volume than plasma. The INTERACT3 care bundle (early SBP target below 140 mmHg, glucose control, antipyrexia and fast reversal) improved functional outcome. Excessive BP drops are avoided, platelets are not indicated, and deep small haematomas do not routinely need surgery; anticoagulation for the valve is revisited later.

qx.stem: An 80-year-old woman taking apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation, last dose 3 hours ago, presents with headache and left hemiparesis. CT shows a 30 mL right lobar haemorrhage. Her GCS is 14 and BP is 170/90 mmHg.
qx.q: Which reversal strategy is most appropriate?
opts: Idarucizumab 5 g IV
Protamine sulfate
Vitamin K 10 mg IV alone
Andexanet alfa where available, or four-factor PCC if it is not
No reversal, because apixaban has a short half-life
qx.why: For a factor Xa inhibitor taken within the last day or so, guidelines support andexanet alfa, which in ANNEXA-I improved haemostatic efficacy at the cost of more thrombotic events, or four-factor PCC (around 50 IU/kg) when it is unavailable or not chosen. Idarucizumab reverses only dabigatran, protamine reverses heparin, and vitamin K has no effect on DOACs. Waiting allows haematoma expansion in the first hours.

det.patho: Rupture of a small penetrating artery bleeds into brain parenchyma; chronic hypertension damages deep perforators (lipohyalinosis, arteriolosclerosis), whereas amyloid angiopathy weakens cortical and leptomeningeal vessels in older people. Other causes include anticoagulants, vascular malformations, cavernomas, tumours, venous thrombosis, sympathomimetic drugs such as amphetamine or cocaine, and haemorrhagic transformation of infarcts. ICH makes up a larger share of strokes in Asian populations than in Western ones. Injury comes in two waves: mass effect and haematoma growth in the first hours (about a third expand, mostly within 6 hours), then perihaematomal oedema and inflammation from blood breakdown products over days.
det.clinical: Onset is sudden with a focal deficit, often accompanied by headache, vomiting, very high BP and progressive drowsiness, though small bleeds are clinically indistinguishable from infarction. Site predicts the syndrome: putamen (hemiplegia, gaze toward lesion), thalamus (sensory loss, downward gaze deviation, small unreactive pupils), lobar (seizures, cortical signs), pons (coma, pinpoint pupils, quadriplegia), cerebellum (vertigo, ataxia, inability to stand, gaze palsy). Cerebellar haematomas can rapidly compress the brainstem or block the fourth ventricle. Deterioration in the first day usually reflects expansion, intraventricular extension or hydrocephalus, so frequent GCS checks are essential.
det.diagnosis: Non-contrast CT confirms the bleed; estimate volume with ABC/2 and look for ventricular blood and hydrocephalus. A spot sign on CTA, or swirl and blend signs on plain CT, marks risk of expansion. Check coagulation, platelets, renal function and timing of the last anticoagulant dose. In young or normotensive patients and in lobar or unusually placed bleeds, look for an underlying lesion with CTA, MRI with SWI (microbleed pattern, siderosis, cavernoma, tumour) and catheter angiography when doubt remains; the DIAGRAM score helps decide who needs angiography. The ICH score helps communicate severity but should not by itself justify early withdrawal of care, and do-not-resuscitate decisions are best deferred for at least a day.
det.treatment: Start a bundle within the first hour: lower systolic BP early and smoothly toward about 140 mmHg (target range 130–150, avoiding big swings), correct glucose and fever, and reverse anticoagulation at once; this combined approach improved functional outcome in a large trial. Reversal: vitamin K plus four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate for warfarin, idarucizumab for dabigatran, and andexanet alfa or PCC for factor Xa inhibitors (andexanet limits expansion better but carries a thrombotic signal). Platelet transfusion is not helpful for antiplatelet-associated ICH unless surgery is planned, and tranexamic acid is not established. Cerebellar haematomas over about 3 cm or with brainstem compression or hydrocephalus need evacuation; external ventricular drainage treats obstructive hydrocephalus, and minimally invasive evacuation of moderate lobar haematomas within 24 hours improved outcome in a recent trial. Treat seizures if they occur (no routine prophylaxis), use intermittent pneumatic compression early, and later restarting an antiplatelet is reasonably safe, whereas resuming anticoagulation for AF is an individual decision weighing ischaemic benefit against rebleeding (higher with CAA), with appendage occlusion as an alternative.
det.prognosis: Thirty-day mortality is around 40%; volume, GCS, age, intraventricular blood and infratentorial site predict poor outcome, but early pessimism can become self-fulfilling.
pearls: Deep bleed + hypertension = arteriolopathy; lobar bleed in the elderly = think CAA.
Cerebellar haemorrhage is a neurosurgical emergency even if the patient looks well.
Do not give platelets routinely for antiplatelet-related ICH.
Haematoma growth is the main modifiable target: early BP lowering plus rapid reversal, ideally in the first hour.
det.thd: เลือดออกในเนื้อสมองจากหลอดเลือดเล็กแตก สาเหตุหลักคือความดันสูง (ตำแหน่งลึก เช่น putamen, thalamus, pons, cerebellum) และ CAA ในผู้สูงอายุ (ตำแหน่ง lobar) อาการคล้าย stroke ตีบแต่มักปวดศีรษะ อาเจียน ความดันสูงมาก และซึมลง วินิจฉัยด้วย CT ประเมินปริมาตรด้วย ABC/2 และหา spot sign การรักษาเป็นชุดภายในชั่วโมงแรก คือลดความดันซิสโตลิกไปประมาณ 140 แก้ฤทธิ์ยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือดทันที (vitamin K+PCC, idarucizumab, andexanet หรือ PCC) คุมน้ำตาลและไข้ ส่งศัลยแพทย์เมื่อเลือดออกใน cerebellum ขนาดใหญ่หรือมี hydrocephalus และไม่ควรตัดสินใจหยุดการรักษาเร็วเกินไป

name: Intracranial epidural abscess
formal: Collection of pus between dura and skull, from sinusitis, otitis, trauma or surgery, causing fever, headache and subtle focal signs; needs drainage and antibiotics.
simple: A pocket of pus between the skull and the brain's outer covering, usually after a sinus or ear infection or surgery.
th: หนองระหว่างกะโหลกกับเยื่อดูรา มักลามจากไซนัสหน้าผาก หูชั้นกลาง/กกหู หรือหลังผ่าตัดเปิดกะโหลก โตช้า อาการน้อย (ไข้ ปวดศีรษะ หน้าผากบวม) จึงวินิจฉัยช้า รักษาด้วยการระบายหนองร่วมกับยาปฏิชีวนะ ห้ามเจาะหลัง
tempoNote: Slowly enlarging collection; symptoms often present for weeks or months, and postoperative cases may appear months to years after craniotomy
feat: Source: frontal sinusitis, otitis or mastoiditis, recent sinus, ear or cranial surgery, compound skull fracture, rarely dental infection
Few symptoms because the dura is tightly stuck to the skull: fever, dull localised headache, skull tenderness, nausea and lethargy
Pott puffy tumour (subperiosteal forehead abscess) and periorbital swelling in sinus-related cases; wound infection in postoperative cases
Focal deficits and seizures are uncommon and suggest spread to subdural empyema, brain abscess, meningitis or venous sinus thrombosis
Petrous apex involvement may give retro-orbital pain with sixth nerve palsy (Gradenigo pattern)
inv: Contrast MRI with DWI is preferred: lentiform extra-axial collection with thick enhancing displaced dura and restricted diffusion; CT shows bone erosion and the sinus or mastoid source
Always look for a coexisting subdural empyema or parenchymal abscess on the same scan
Cultures of surgical pus (aerobic and anaerobic) are far more useful than blood cultures; CRP to follow response
Lumbar puncture is contraindicated: low yield and risk of herniation

case.story: Three weeks of nasal blockage treated with two antibiotic courses, then a week of frontal headache, low fever and a soft swelling over the forehead.
case.exam: Fluctuant tender swelling above the right eyebrow, puffy right upper eyelid, alert with no focal signs and no neck stiffness.
case.tests: CRP 120 mg/L; contrast MRI shows frontal sinus pus, a subperiosteal collection and a 1.5 cm lentiform enhancing epidural collection with DWI restriction behind the frontal bone; no subdural or parenchymal pus.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the definitive management?
case.a: Frontal epidural abscess with Pott puffy tumour from sinusitis; combined ENT sinus drainage and neurosurgical drainage of the epidural pus, then IV ceftriaxone plus metronidazole adjusted to cultures for several weeks, with no lumbar puncture.

det.patho: Inside the skull the dura doubles as the periosteum of the inner table, so the epidural space is only potential and opens when infection, trauma or surgery separates them. Infection reaches it directly through eroded bone, through valveless emissary veins or along a craniotomy flap. Because the pus must strip the dura from bone it enlarges slowly, which explains the indolent course. Spread through the dura or by venous thrombosis produces subdural empyema, meningitis, brain abscess or sinus thrombosis.
det.clinical: Sinus-related cases are typical of adolescents and young men, with fever, frontal headache, forehead swelling and periorbital oedema. Postoperative cases present with wound infection or encephalopathy and may show few systemic signs. Many patients have symptoms for weeks before diagnosis. Sudden seizures, meningism or falling consciousness usually indicate a complication rather than the epidural abscess itself.
det.diagnosis: MRI with diffusion is more sensitive than CT for small collections and distinguishes pus from sterile postoperative fluid or chronic haematoma. The epidural collection is lens-shaped, may cross the midline but not sutures, and has a thick, irregular enhancing dural rim. CT of sinuses and temporal bone defines the source. Microbiology comes from surgical pus; organisms include streptococci (notably the S. anginosus group), anaerobes and staphylococci, with S. aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci and Gram-negative bacilli after surgery.
det.treatment: Treatment combines drainage (burr hole, craniotomy or craniectomy, with removal of infected bone or bone flap) with treatment of the source by ENT or dental surgery. Empirical therapy follows brain abscess principles: ceftriaxone or cefotaxime plus metronidazole for community cases, and vancomycin with meropenem (or cefepime plus metronidazole) after neurosurgery. Courses of about 6 weeks are typical, with oral step-down after an initial IV phase considered in stable, well-drained patients, as allowed by the 2024 ESCMID brain abscess guideline. Small collections without mass effect have occasionally been managed with antibiotics alone under close imaging follow-up.
det.prognosis: Outcome is usually excellent with drainage and antibiotics; delay leads to complications and permanent deficits, and late mortality after surgery reflects comorbidity more than the infection.
pearls: Forehead swelling in a teenager with sinusitis is a Pott puffy tumour until proven otherwise: image the brain.
An epidural abscess often coexists with subdural empyema; look for the more dangerous lesion on every scan.
Do not perform lumbar puncture: the CSF adds little and herniation is a real risk.
det.thd: ฝีชั้นนอกดูราในกะโหลกมักลามจากไซนัสหน้าผาก หูชั้นกลางหรือกกหู หรือเกิดหลังผ่าตัดเปิดกะโหลก โตช้าจึงมีอาการน้อย เช่น ไข้ ปวดศีรษะเฉพาะที่ หน้าผากบวม (Pott puffy tumour) ตรวจด้วย MRI ฉีดสีร่วมกับ DWI และต้องหา subdural empyema หรือฝีในสมองร่วมด้วย รักษาโดยระบายหนองและจัดการต้นเหตุ ให้ ceftriaxone ร่วมกับ metronidazole (หลังผ่าตัดใช้ vancomycin ร่วมกับ meropenem) นานประมาณ 6 สัปดาห์ และห้ามเจาะหลัง

qx.stem: A 15-year-old boy from Sakon Nakhon has had two weeks of sinusitis and now a soft, tender swelling of the forehead with low-grade fever. He is alert with no focal signs or neck stiffness. Contrast MRI shows frontal sinus opacification, a subperiosteal collection and a lens-shaped enhancing collection with restricted diffusion between the frontal bone and dura.
qx.q: Which step should be avoided?
opts: Lumbar puncture to obtain CSF culture
Surgical drainage of the epidural collection
Endoscopic drainage of the frontal sinus
IV ceftriaxone with metronidazole
Checking the scan carefully for subdural empyema
qx.why: Lumbar puncture adds little in intracranial epidural abscess because CSF findings are nonspecific and cultures usually negative, and it carries a risk of herniation. Management is drainage of the collection and the sinus source, with empirical ceftriaxone and metronidazole adjusted to pus cultures. A coexisting subdural empyema must always be sought.

det.patho: Bleeding arises from torn bridging veins (subdural), meningeal arteries (extradural), ruptured aneurysms (subarachnoid), small penetrating or cortical arteries (intraparenchymal) or extension into the ventricles. Expanding blood raises intracranial pressure and distorts brain structures; blood products cause oedema and irritate the cortex.
det.clinical: Clinical features depend on compartment and speed: thunderclap headache in SAH, lucid interval in extradural, fluctuating confusion in chronic subdural, focal deficits in intraparenchymal haemorrhage. Elderly anticoagulated patients may have subtle presentations after minor trauma.
det.diagnosis: CT defines the compartment and size. Shape helps: lens-shaped extradural, crescentic subdural, sulcal or cisternal SAH. Vascular imaging is guided by pattern and age. Coagulation tests are mandatory.
det.treatment: Management depends on the type: surgical evacuation for large extra-axial collections, aneurysm securing and nimodipine for SAH, BP control and reversal of anticoagulation for ICH, and ventricular drainage for hydrocephalus. General measures include airway protection, seizure treatment and ICP management.
det.prognosis: Highly variable by type, size and patient factors.
pearls: Name the compartment first; management follows from it.
Anticoagulated elderly patient with minor head trauma: low threshold for CT.
Reverse anticoagulants as fast as possible.
det.thd: Intracranial haemorrhage เป็นคำรวมของเลือดออกในกะโหลกศีรษะทุกชนิด ได้แก่ extradural, subdural, subarachnoid, ในเนื้อสมอง และในโพรงสมอง สาเหตุมีทั้งอุบัติเหตุ ความดันสูง หลอดเลือดโป่งพอง และยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือด CT แยกชนิดได้ การรักษาขึ้นกับชนิดและขนาด เช่น ผ่าตัด แก้ฤทธิ์ยา และคุมความดัน

name: Intradural extramedullary (ID-EM) tumours
formal: Spinal tumours inside the dura but outside the cord, such as meningioma and schwannoma, causing slowly progressive radicular pain and myelopathy; usually resectable.
simple: Slow-growing tumours near the spinal cord that press on nerves or the cord, usually removable by surgery.
th: เนื้องอกในช่องไขสันหลังที่อยู่ภายในเยื่อดูราแต่นอกเนื้อไขสันหลัง เช่น meningioma และ schwannoma ทำให้ปวดตามรากประสาทและไขสันหลังถูกกดช้า ๆ
tempoNote: Slowly progressive over months to years
feat: Radicular pain, often nocturnal, as the first symptom
Progressive myelopathy with Brown-Séquard pattern
Schwannomas: dumbbell-shaped; meningiomas: dural-based
Usually benign and resectable
inv: MRI spine with gadolinium

case.story: Nocturnal pain radiating around his right chest for a year, now leg stiffness.
case.exam: Right leg weakness with brisk reflexes, left-sided pain and temperature loss below T8.
case.tests: MRI: intradural extramedullary T6 schwannoma displacing the cord.
case.q: Treatment?
case.a: Surgical resection.

det.patho: These tumours arise from nerve sheath cells (schwannoma, neurofibroma) or arachnoid cap cells (meningioma) inside the dura but outside the cord. They grow slowly and push the cord aside while compressing nearby roots. Multiple tumours suggest NF1, NF2 or schwannomatosis.
det.clinical: Radicular pain, often worse at night or lying down, typically precedes cord signs. Compression from one side produces an asymmetric or Brown-Séquard pattern. Because growth is slow, considerable compression can exist before weakness or sphincter changes appear.
det.diagnosis: MRI with contrast places the tumour inside the dura but outside the cord, with widened CSF space above and below. Meningiomas are dural-based with a tail; schwannomas may be dumbbell-shaped through a foramen. Histology after resection confirms the type.
det.treatment: Microsurgical resection is the standard and is usually curative. Small asymptomatic tumours can be observed with MRI. Radiosurgery is an option for residual or recurrent lesions or poor surgical candidates. Genetic evaluation is offered for multiple tumours.
det.prognosis: Excellent after complete resection.
pearls: Night-time radicular pain: image for spinal tumour.
Multiple schwannomas suggest NF2 or schwannomatosis.
Brown-Séquard pattern suggests extramedullary compression.
det.thd: ID-EM tumour คือเนื้องอกในช่องไขสันหลังภายในเยื่อดูราแต่นอกเนื้อไขสันหลัง เช่น meningioma หรือ schwannoma อาการเริ่มด้วยปวดตามรากประสาทโดยเฉพาะกลางคืน ต่อมาไขสันหลังถูกกดทำให้อ่อนแรงและชา ตรวจด้วย MRI รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัดซึ่งผลดี
