name: Intradural spinal tumours
formal: Tumours within the dural sac of the spine, either extramedullary such as meningioma and schwannoma, or intramedullary such as ependymoma and astrocytoma, causing pain and myelopathy.
simple: Growths inside the spinal canal that can press on the spinal cord and nerve roots.
th: เนื้องอกภายในเยื่อดูราของไขสันหลัง แบ่งเป็นนอกเนื้อไขสันหลัง (meningioma, schwannoma) และในเนื้อไขสันหลัง (ependymoma, astrocytoma) ทำให้ปวดและไขสันหลังทำงานผิดปกติ
tempoNote: Gradual over months to years
feat: Back pain or radicular pain, often worse lying down
Extramedullary: radicular then long-tract signs; intramedullary: central cord, dissociated sensory loss, sacral sparing
Common: meningioma, schwannoma, ependymoma, astrocytoma, haemangioblastoma
Associations: NF1, NF2, von Hippel–Lindau
inv: MRI spine with gadolinium
Brain MRI if NF or VHL suspected

case.story: Neck pain and numbness in both hands for a year.
case.exam: Cape-like pain and temperature loss, weak hands, brisk leg reflexes.
case.tests: MRI: C4–C6 intramedullary enhancing lesion with syrinx, consistent with ependymoma.
case.q: Treatment?
case.a: Surgical resection; radiotherapy for incomplete removal.

det.patho: Intradural tumours are classified by their relation to the cord. Extramedullary tumours such as meningioma and schwannoma compress the cord from outside. Intramedullary tumours such as ependymoma, astrocytoma and haemangioblastoma expand the cord from within and often cause a syrinx.
det.clinical: Extramedullary tumours tend to cause radicular pain and asymmetric long-tract signs. Intramedullary tumours produce central cord features with dysaesthesia, dissociated sensory loss and sacral sparing. Symptoms usually progress over months to years.
det.diagnosis: Contrast MRI defines location, extent and associated syrinx. Imaging pattern suggests histology, but biopsy or resection is needed for confirmation. Brain MRI is performed when NF or von Hippel–Lindau disease is suspected.
det.treatment: Surgery is the mainstay, aiming at gross total resection when it can be done safely. Adjuvant radiotherapy is used depending on histology and extent of removal. Rehabilitation and long-term MRI surveillance follow.
det.prognosis: Depends on histology; benign extramedullary tumours do best.
pearls: Sacral sparing suggests intramedullary lesion.
Tumour-associated syrinx is common in ependymoma.
Always contrast-enhance an unexplained syrinx.
det.thd: Intradural spinal tumour คือเนื้องอกภายในเยื่อดูราของไขสันหลัง ชนิดนอกเนื้อไขสันหลัง เช่น meningioma และ schwannoma ทำให้ปวดตามรากประสาทก่อน ชนิดในเนื้อไขสันหลัง เช่น ependymoma และ astrocytoma ทำให้ชาแบบ central cord ตรวจ MRI รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัด

name: Intramedullary spinal tumours
formal: Tumours arising within the cord, most often ependymoma or astrocytoma, and haemangioblastoma, causing pain, dissociated sensory loss and myelopathy; treated by microsurgical resection.
simple: Tumours that grow inside the spinal cord, causing pain, numbness and weakness.
th: เนื้องอกที่เกิดภายในเนื้อไขสันหลัง ส่วนใหญ่เป็น ependymoma, astrocytoma และ haemangioblastoma ทำให้ปวด เสียความรู้สึกแบบแยกส่วน และไขสันหลังเสื่อมช้าๆ
tempoNote: Usually progresses over months to years; faster with high-grade tumours or haemorrhage
feat: Constitute a small fraction of spinal tumours; ependymoma commonest in adults, astrocytoma in children
Local back or neck pain, often worse at night
Dissociated (suspended) sensory loss from central cord involvement and sacral sparing
Slowly progressive weakness, spasticity and later sphincter dysfunction
Associated syrinx or cysts; haemangioblastoma linked to VHL, ependymoma to NF2

Spinal angiography for haemangioblastoma
Biopsy or resection with histology and molecular profiling

case.story: A year of neck pain at night and burning in both arms; recently drops cups and stumbles.
case.exam: Cape-like loss of pain and temperature over shoulders, hand wasting, brisk leg reflexes, extensor plantars.
case.tests: MRI shows a centrally located enhancing C4–C6 intramedullary mass with cysts at both poles and a haemosiderin cap.
case.q: What is the likely tumour and the treatment?
case.a: Intramedullary ependymoma; microsurgical gross total resection with neurophysiological monitoring.

det.patho: These tumours arise from glial, ependymal or vascular elements inside the cord. Ependymomas grow centrally and displace tracts, often with a cleavage plane; astrocytomas infiltrate eccentrically without a clear border; haemangioblastomas are highly vascular nodules, often dorsal, with extensive cysts or syrinx. Expansion compresses crossing spinothalamic fibres first, then long tracts.
det.clinical: Pain is the commonest initial symptom, followed by sensory disturbance and progressive weakness. Central lesions produce suspended pain and temperature loss, segmental wasting and later spasticity below the level. Sacral sensation is often spared until late. Children may present with scoliosis, torticollis or gait regression.
det.diagnosis: MRI with contrast characterises the lesion: central, symmetrical expansion with haemosiderin cap suggests ependymoma; eccentric poorly defined lesion suggests astrocytoma; an enhancing nodule with large cyst and flow voids suggests haemangioblastoma. Screening for NF2 or VHL is appropriate when lesions are multiple or the patient is young. Histology confirms the diagnosis.
det.treatment: Microsurgical resection with intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring is the main treatment, aiming for gross total removal of ependymomas and haemangioblastomas. Infiltrative astrocytomas are debulked or biopsied and treated with radiotherapy and sometimes chemotherapy. Belzutifan is an option for VHL-associated haemangioblastomas.
det.prognosis: Preoperative neurological status predicts outcome; ependymomas and haemangioblastomas have favourable long-term control after complete resection.
pearls: Night-time spinal pain plus suspended sensory loss: image the cord with contrast.
A haemosiderin cap points to ependymoma.
Operate before deficits become severe — function rarely recovers beyond the preoperative level.
det.thd: Intramedullary spinal tumours คือเนื้องอกที่เกิดภายในเนื้อไขสันหลัง ที่พบบ่อยคือ ependymoma, astrocytoma และ haemangioblastoma ผู้ป่วยปวดหลังหรือคอตอนกลางคืน เสียความรู้สึกเจ็บและร้อนเย็นแบบแยกส่วน กล้ามเนื้อลีบ และอ่อนแรงช้าๆ การวินิจฉัยใช้ MRI ฉีดสี การรักษาหลักคือผ่าตัดโดยมีการเฝ้าระวังการทำงานของระบบประสาทระหว่างผ่าตัด และฉายรังสีในเนื้องอกที่ผ่าออกไม่หมด

th: มะเร็งต่อมน้ำเหลือง B cell ชนิดที่เซลล์มะเร็งอยู่ภายในหลอดเลือดเล็ก ทำให้สมองขาดเลือดหลายจุด สมองเสื่อมเร็ว วินิจฉัยยากมักต้องตัดชิ้นเนื้อ

feat: Multifocal strokes, rapidly progressive dementia or encephalopathy, seizures

MRI may mimic vasculitis or small-vessel disease

case.story: Two months of fever, weight loss and progressive confusion with episodes of left then right arm weakness.
case.exam: Disoriented, bilateral pyramidal signs, no lymph nodes.
case.tests: LDH 1,100 U/L, sIL-2R very high; MRI multiple DWI lesions in different territories; random skin biopsy shows large B cells inside dermal capillaries.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and treatment?
case.a: Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma; R-CHOP-based chemotherapy with CNS-directed high-dose methotrexate.

det.patho: Malignant large B cells lack surface adhesion molecules needed to leave vessels, so they proliferate within capillaries and small vessels, occluding them. The brain, skin, marrow and lungs are commonly involved. The result is ischaemia in many small territories.
det.clinical: Neurological forms present with multifocal stroke-like episodes, subacute encephalopathy, rapidly progressive dementia, seizures, myelopathy or neuropathy. Systemic symptoms such as fever and night sweats are common. An Asian variant features haemophagocytosis, hepatosplenomegaly and cytopenias.
det.diagnosis: Clinical suspicion is critical; markers like raised LDH and soluble IL-2 receptor are useful. Random deep skin biopsies from normal-appearing skin give a diagnosis in many patients. Brain biopsy may be required. Imaging findings are non-specific and can mimic vasculitis, PML or small-vessel disease.
det.treatment: Rituximab-containing chemotherapy (R-CHOP) is standard, with CNS-directed high-dose methotrexate for CNS disease or prophylaxis. Autologous transplant is considered in fit patients. Steroids before biopsy can obscure diagnosis but may be needed for oedema.
det.prognosis: Historically poor; rituximab-era therapy has improved survival considerably, but CNS involvement still carries higher risk.
pearls: Unexplained multifocal strokes plus fever plus high LDH: think intravascular lymphoma.
Random skin biopsy is a simple high-yield test.
Mimics CNS vasculitis on imaging and angiography.
det.thd: Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma เป็นมะเร็งต่อมน้ำเหลืองที่เซลล์มะเร็งอยู่ภายในหลอดเลือดเล็ก ไม่เป็นก้อน ทำให้สมองขาดเลือดหลายจุด สับสน สมองเสื่อมเร็ว ร่วมกับไข้และ LDH สูง วินิจฉัยด้วยการตัดชิ้นเนื้อผิวหนังแบบสุ่มหรือชิ้นเนื้อสมอง รักษาด้วยเคมีบำบัดสูตรที่มี rituximab และ methotrexate ขนาดสูง

name: Intraventricular haemorrhage
formal: Blood within the cerebral ventricles from germinal matrix bleeding in premature infants or extension of intracerebral or subarachnoid haemorrhage, risking hydrocephalus.
simple: Bleeding into the brain's fluid-filled chambers, which can block fluid flow and cause hydrocephalus.
th: เลือดออกในโพรงสมอง (IVH) ในทารกคลอดก่อนกำหนดเกิดจากเลือดออกที่ germinal matrix ตัดสินระดับด้วยอัลตราซาวด์ตาม Papile grade I–IV และเสี่ยงต่อ hydrocephalus ใน 1–3 สัปดาห์ ส่วนในผู้ใหญ่มักลามมาจาก ICH หรือ SAH ถ้าเป็น IVH ล้วนต้องหา AVM, moyamoya หรือหลอดเลือดโป่งพอง รักษา hydrocephalus ด้วยการระบายน้ำไขสันหลัง
tempoNote: Preterm IVH occurs mostly within the first 3 to 4 days of life, with post-haemorrhagic hydrocephalus 1–3 weeks later; adult IVH is sudden
feat: Preterm infants: germinal matrix haemorrhage in about a fifth of very-low-birth-weight infants, graded I to IV by the Papile system; often clinically silent and found on screening ultrasound
Symptomatic neonatal IVH: sudden fall in haematocrit, apnoea and bradycardia, tense fontanelle, seizures, abnormal tone or posturing, bulging scalp veins
Post-haemorrhagic hydrocephalus develops in as many as half of infants with grade III–IV bleeds, usually 1–3 weeks later
Adults: usually extension of a thalamic, caudate or putaminal ICH or of aneurysmal SAH; primary IVH suggests a vascular lesion (AVM, moyamoya, aneurysm), coagulopathy or a tumour
Adult outcome relates to ventricular blood volume and to hydrocephalus; blood in the ventricles raises the risk of obstructive hydrocephalus and impaired consciousness
inv: Neonates: cranial ultrasound through the anterior fontanelle at days 3–7 and again at 4–6 weeks in infants under 32 weeks; MRI at term-equivalent age for white-matter injury
Adults: non-contrast CT, CT angiography then digital subtraction angiography for primary IVH, coagulation tests and drug history
Serial imaging and head circumference for ventricular enlargement; ICP or external ventricular drain monitoring when hydrocephalus is present

case.who: Preterm boy born at 27 weeks, 980 g, in a provincial hospital in Chiang Mai
case.story: On day 3 of ventilation he has an unexplained drop in haemoglobin, a bulging fontanelle and a run of apnoea.
case.exam: Reduced tone, tense anterior fontanelle, sluggish pupils.
case.tests: Cranial ultrasound: bilateral germinal matrix haemorrhages with blood and dilated ventricles, and a right periventricular echodense area; haematocrit has fallen 12 points.
case.q: How is this graded and what is the main complication to watch for?
case.a: Papile grade IV (IVH with parenchymal haemorrhage, a venous infarct) on the right. Watch head circumference and ultrasound for post-haemorrhagic hydrocephalus over the next 1–3 weeks and involve paediatric neurosurgery if it progresses.

read.where: Chapter 84 Intracerebral Hemorrhage — Neonatal periventricular-intraventricular hemorrhage

det.patho: In premature infants the germinal matrix beneath the ependyma is a richly vascularised, poorly supported tissue whose capillaries rupture when cerebral blood flow fluctuates, for example with hypotension, respiratory distress or rapid volume changes; most bleeds occur in the first days of life, with a second peak on days 3–4. In adults, blood usually enters the ventricle from an adjacent parenchymal haemorrhage or SAH, rarely from a malformation, aneurysm or coagulopathy. Intraventricular blood can obstruct the foramina and aqueduct and later inflame the arachnoid granulations, causing hydrocephalus.
det.clinical: Neonatal IVH is clinically silent in most, but large bleeds cause catastrophic deterioration with apnoea, bradycardia, seizures, a tense fontanelle and a fall in haematocrit. Severity is linked to gestational age: the younger the infant, the more often grade III or IV haemorrhage is seen. Adults present with headache, vomiting and decreased consciousness together with signs of the primary bleed; confusion and abnormal posture reflect hydrocephalus. Post-haemorrhagic hydrocephalus can be transient or progressive and evolve for weeks.
det.diagnosis: Cranial ultrasound grades neonatal IVH (I germinal matrix only; II blood in ventricles of normal size; III intraventricular blood with dilated ventricles; IV with parenchymal haemorrhage) and is repeated to detect ventricular enlargement. MRI at term age shows white matter injury. In adults, CT is diagnostic and CT angiography screens for aneurysm, AVM or other vascular causes; when primary IVH has no clear source, catheter angiography is done. Check coagulation and platelets.
det.treatment: Neonatal care aims to prevent the bleed through preterm birth avoidance, antenatal corticosteroids, delayed cord clamping, transfer to a level III unit and stable haemodynamics, and later to treat hydrocephalus. Temporising measures include serial lumbar punctures or reservoir drainage, and a ventriculoperitoneal shunt is placed when the infant is large enough and CSF protein and blood have cleared. In adults, an external ventricular drain relieves acute hydrocephalus. Intraventricular alteplase (CLEAR III) accelerated clot clearance and cut mortality but did not improve the proportion with good functional outcome, so it is not routine; the underlying cause is treated.
det.prognosis: Severe neonatal IVH (grade III–IV) carries high mortality, hydrocephalus and later cerebral palsy and developmental impairment; large ventricular blood volume worsens adult outcome.
pearls: A sudden fall in haematocrit with a bulging fontanelle in a preterm baby is IVH until proven otherwise.
Primary IVH in an adult needs angiography to look for a vascular source.
Watch for hydrocephalus 1–3 weeks after any significant IVH.
det.thd: IVH ในทารกคลอดก่อนกำหนดเกิดจากหลอดเลือดเปราะบางที่ germinal matrix แตก ส่วนใหญ่เกิดใน 3–4 วันแรก ตรวจด้วยอัลตราซาวด์ผ่านกระหม่อมและแบ่งระดับ Papile I–IV ทารกอาจไม่มีอาการ หรือมี Hct ลดลง หยุดหายใจ กระหม่อมตึง ชัก ภายหลัง 1–3 สัปดาห์อาจเกิด hydrocephalus ในผู้ใหญ่ IVH มักลามมาจาก ICH หรือ SAH และถ้าเป็นแบบปฐมภูมิต้องหา AVM, moyamoya หรือ aneurysm การรักษาคือแก้ต้นเหตุและระบายน้ำไขสันหลังเมื่อมี hydrocephalus

ddx.pt: A parenchymal bleed that may extend into the ventricles
Aneurysmal blood can reflux into the ventricles; the cisterns are filled with blood
A cause of primary IVH in East Asian adults, with characteristic collaterals on angiography

name: Intrinsic cord tumours
formal: Tumours originating within the spinal cord, especially ependymoma, astrocytoma and haemangioblastoma, causing pain, segmental sensory loss and myelopathy.
simple: Tumours growing inside the spinal cord itself, causing back pain, numbness and weakness.
th: เนื้องอกที่เกิดจากเนื้อไขสันหลังเอง โดยเฉพาะ ependymoma, astrocytoma และ haemangioblastoma ทำให้ปวด เสียความรู้สึกเป็นปล้อง และไขสันหลังเสื่อม
tempoNote: Gradual progression over months to years in most cases
feat: Same group as intramedullary spinal tumours; term emphasises origin within cord tissue
Segmental pain and sensory loss with long tract signs below
Ependymoma (adults), pilocytic and diffuse astrocytoma (children, young adults), haemangioblastoma (VHL)
Diffuse midline glioma H3 K27-altered can arise in the cord and progress rapidly
Rare: gangliogliomas, lymphoma, intramedullary metastases
inv: Contrast MRI of the whole spine and brain
Histology including molecular markers (H3 K27M, BRAF, NF2)
Genetic testing if VHL or NF2 suspected

case.story: Four months of back pain and progressive stiffness of the legs; teachers notice he walks oddly.
case.exam: Spastic paraparesis, sensory level around T6, brisk reflexes, mild scoliosis.
case.tests: MRI shows an eccentric, poorly marginated T2-hyperintense thoracic cord lesion with patchy enhancement spanning four segments; biopsy shows pilocytic astrocytoma with BRAF fusion.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and treatment approach?
case.a: Intrinsic cord tumour — pilocytic astrocytoma; maximal safe resection, with MEK/BRAF-targeted therapy or radiotherapy for residual progressive tumour.

read.where: Chapter 20 Neuro-Oncology — Primary Spinal Cord Tumours

det.patho: Intrinsic cord tumours originate from glial, ependymal or vascular cells within the cord. Molecular drivers include NF2 loss in ependymoma, BRAF alterations in pilocytic astrocytoma, H3 K27 alterations in diffuse midline glioma and VHL loss in haemangioblastoma. Their growth expands the cord and disrupts both segmental grey matter and long tracts.
det.clinical: Pain, often nocturnal and localised, is usually first, followed by paraesthesia, segmental weakness and spasticity. Children may present with scoliosis or gait regression. High-grade tumours progress quickly, sometimes over weeks. Bladder dysfunction is usually late.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows cord expansion with enhancing tumour, cysts and oedema; imaging features suggest the type but tissue is needed. Inflammatory myelitis, sarcoidosis and vascular malformations are important mimics; repeat imaging after steroids can mislead because lymphoma and demyelination shrink. Molecular classification refines prognosis.
det.treatment: Surgery aims for safe maximal resection with neuromonitoring. Radiotherapy is used for residual or high-grade tumours. Targeted drugs such as MEK or BRAF inhibitors for paediatric low-grade gliomas and belzutifan for VHL tumours are expanding options. Rehabilitation and bladder management are integral.
det.prognosis: Low-grade circumscribed tumours often have long survival after resection; diffuse midline glioma is usually fatal within a few years.
pearls: Avoid steroids before tissue diagnosis if lymphoma is possible.
In a child, painful scoliosis can be the presenting clue to a cord tumour.
Eccentric infiltrative lesion = astrocytoma; central circumscribed = ependymoma.
det.thd: Intrinsic cord tumours คือเนื้องอกที่เกิดจากเนื้อไขสันหลังเอง ได้แก่ ependymoma ในผู้ใหญ่ astrocytoma ในเด็กและคนหนุ่มสาว และ haemangioblastoma ที่สัมพันธ์กับ VHL ผู้ป่วยปวดหลังตอนกลางคืน ชาเป็นปล้อง และขาเกร็งอ่อนแรงช้าๆ การวินิจฉัยต้องใช้ MRI ฉีดสีและผลชิ้นเนื้อร่วมกับ molecular markers การรักษาคือผ่าตัด ฉายรังสี และยามุ่งเป้าในบางชนิด

ddx.pt: Central, well-circumscribed adult tumour with haemosiderin cap
Enhancing dorsal nodule with large cyst; VHL association
Faster onset and improvement with immunotherapy; no mass on follow-up

name: Ipsiversive seizures
formal: Focal seizures with head and eye version toward the side of the epileptic focus, an uncommon pattern in semiology compared with contraversive turning; lateralising value is debated.
simple: Seizures in which the head and eyes turn toward the same side as the seizure's starting point.
th: ลักษณะของชักชนิด focal ที่ศีรษะและตาหันไปด้านเดียวกับจุดกำเนิดชัก พบน้อยกว่าการหันไปด้านตรงข้าม และใช้บอกข้างของรอยโรคได้ไม่แน่นอน
tempoNote: Seconds, as one phase of a focal seizure
feat: Head and eyes turn toward the same side as the seizure focus
Often early, gentle, non-forced turning, unlike the forced tonic version of contraversive seizures
May appear in temporal lobe seizures or after a seizure has spread bilaterally
A semiological sign within a focal seizure rather than a separate disease
inv: Video-EEG to time the head turn relative to ictal onset and spread
MRI with an epilepsy protocol to find the underlying lesion

case.who: 29-year-old woman from Songkhla with drug-resistant epilepsy
case.story: Her seizures begin with a rising stomach feeling, then she stares, smacks her lips and slowly turns her head to the left.
case.exam: Normal interictal examination.
case.tests: Video-EEG: left temporal ictal onset with leftward non-forced head turn early in the seizure; MRI shows left hippocampal sclerosis.
case.q: Does the leftward head turn mean a right-sided focus?
case.a: No; early non-forced head turning is often ipsiversive and the focus here is left temporal. Only forced, sustained version late in the seizure reliably points to the opposite hemisphere.

det.patho: Head and eye turning is produced by activation of cortical eye fields and their brainstem connections. When a seizure activates the frontal eye field strongly, the head is driven to the opposite side; ipsilateral turning may reflect neglect from the involved hemisphere, activation of other areas, or spread to the opposite hemisphere.
det.clinical: This is a semiological description, not a disease. Ipsiversive turning is usually early, mild and non-forced and is common in temporal lobe seizures; it can also occur late, after bilateral spread, when the head swings back toward the side of origin. Observers often misreport the direction, so video is important.
det.diagnosis: Interpret head turning together with other signs: forced, sustained version shortly before bilateral tonic-clonic activity points contralateral; early, non-forced turning tends to point ipsilateral. Video-EEG confirms timing and onset, and MRI and other presurgical tests define the focus.
det.treatment: Treatment is that of the underlying focal epilepsy: appropriate antiseizure medication and, in drug-resistant cases, presurgical evaluation for resection, ablation or neuromodulation.
det.prognosis: Depends on the cause and drug responsiveness of the underlying epilepsy.
pearls: Forced late version = contralateral focus; gentle early turning is often ipsilateral.
Never lateralise on head turning alone; combine with dystonic posturing, automatisms and EEG.
Ask for a home video: witnesses frequently mistake the direction.
det.thd: Ipsiversive seizure คือการชักแบบ focal ที่ศีรษะและตาหันไปด้านเดียวกับจุดกำเนิดชัก มักเป็นการหันเบา ๆ ช่วงต้นของชัก โดยเฉพาะในชักจากสมองกลีบขมับ ต่างจากการหันอย่างรุนแรงช่วงท้ายซึ่งชี้ไปสมองด้านตรงข้าม จึงต้องแปลผลร่วมกับอาการอื่นและ video-EEG การรักษาคือรักษาโรคลมชักที่เป็นสาเหตุ

ddx.pt: The umbrella term; forced contraversive version is the form with good lateralising value
Turning away from the focus, typically frontal eye field origin, more reliable for lateralisation
Side-to-side head shaking, eyes closed, fluctuating course and normal ictal EEG

name: Iris hamartomas
formal: Lisch nodules, benign pigmented iris hamartomas that are a diagnostic criterion for neurofibromatosis type 1 and appear in childhood.
simple: Small harmless bumps on the coloured part of the eye that are a sign of neurofibromatosis type 1.
th: ตุ่มเม็ดสีเล็ก ๆ บนผิวม่านตา (Lisch nodules) ซึ่งเป็น hamartoma ไม่ทำให้ตามัว แต่เป็นเครื่องชี้สำคัญของ neurofibromatosis type 1 และพบเกือบทุกคนเมื่อเป็นผู้ใหญ่
tempoNote: Absent in infancy, appear from late childhood and multiply through the second and third decades; they stay stable and harmless for life
feat: Tiny dome-shaped tan to brown nodules on the iris surface, usually in both eyes, visible only with a slit lamp in most patients
No symptoms: acuity, pupils and intraocular pressure are normal, so the finding is picked up by examination rather than complaint
Uncommon before about age 5 but present in the great majority of adults with NF1, which makes the count useful for screening relatives
Part of the NF1 diagnostic criteria (two or more nodules count as one criterion) alongside café-au-lait macules, axillary or groin freckling and neurofibromas
The same eye examination should look for optic nerve glioma, choroidal freckling and eyelid plexiform neurofibroma
inv: Slit-lamp examination of both irides; infrared or OCT imaging of the choroid can show NF1-related patches that supplement the nodule count
Skin survey for café-au-lait macules and freckling, and a family history, to see whether NF1 criteria are met
Annual ophthalmology review in a child with NF1 (acuity, colour vision, discs, fields as age allows); MRI only for visual or endocrine signs; NF1 gene testing when the picture is incomplete

case.who: 9-year-old boy from Nakhon Ratchasima, referred from the paediatric clinic
case.story: Brought in because of many brown skin patches that appeared in the first years of life. His mother has similar patches and a few soft lumps on her arms. He has no visual complaint and does well at school apart from some difficulty with reading.
case.exam: Seven café-au-lait macules larger than 5 mm and axillary freckling. Visual acuity 6/6 in both eyes, no relative afferent pupillary defect, discs normal. Slit lamp shows several small tan nodules on the surface of each iris.
case.tests: Slit-lamp findings satisfy the iris criterion; with the skin signs he meets NF1 criteria and the mother is confirmed on examination. OCT of the retinal nerve fibre layer is normal.
case.q: Do the iris nodules need treatment, and what should the ophthalmologist keep watching?
case.a: No. They are benign and never affect sight. The follow-up target is the optic pathway: yearly checks of acuity, colour vision and discs, with MRI only if vision, proptosis or early puberty raise suspicion of an optic pathway glioma.

det.patho: Lisch nodules are melanocytic hamartomas of the iris stroma, formed by aggregates of pigmented cells in people who carry a heterozygous loss of NF1, the gene for neurofibromin. Neurofibromin restrains RAS signalling, so cells that lose both copies proliferate. NF1 affects roughly 1 in 3,000 people, is autosomal dominant, and about half of cases arise from new variants.
det.clinical: The nodules do not interfere with vision and are discovered when the eye is examined for NF1. They are rare in infancy, begin to appear in the school years, and are seen in almost every adult with the disease, which is why an ophthalmic examination of a parent can settle whether a family is affected. In the child the more important eye problems are optic pathway glioma, which presents before age 7 in most cases, and an eyelid or orbital plexiform neurofibroma. Choroidal abnormalities seen on infrared imaging are a further ocular marker of NF1.
det.diagnosis: Identify the nodules with a slit lamp, where they appear as raised, dome-like, translucent tan lesions, in contrast to flat iris naevi that lie within the stroma. The clinical criteria for NF1 (café-au-lait macules, freckling, neurofibromas, optic glioma, bony dysplasia, Lisch nodules, affected relative) are met when two are present, and the 2021 revision also allows a pathogenic NF1 variant or choroidal abnormalities on OCT to count. Genetic testing helps in young children who have only pigmentary signs. Iris melanoma and other pigmented lesions should be separated by their solitary, growing character.
det.treatment: The nodules themselves need no treatment. Management is that of NF1: annual clinical review, ophthalmology surveillance in childhood, blood pressure checks, scoliosis and learning assessment, and genetic counselling. Optic pathway glioma is treated only when vision or the lesion progresses, usually with chemotherapy, while radiotherapy is avoided in these children because of a high risk of second tumours. Selumetinib, a MEK inhibitor, is available for children with symptomatic inoperable plexiform neurofibromas.
det.prognosis: The finding itself is benign for life. Outcome depends on other NF1 complications, notably optic glioma, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour and learning disability.
pearls: More than 90% of adults with NF1 have Lisch nodules, so examining a parent can confirm the diagnosis in a child.
Lisch nodules are harmless; the real eye task in a child with NF1 is looking for optic pathway glioma.
A single growing iris lesion with pupil distortion is not a Lisch nodule; think melanoma or iris naevus.
det.thd: Iris hamartoma หรือ Lisch nodule คือตุ่มสีน้ำตาลเล็ก ๆ บนผิวม่านตาที่ตรวจเห็นด้วย slit lamp ไม่ทำให้ตามัวและไม่ต้องรักษา แต่ถือเป็นเกณฑ์วินิจฉัยหนึ่งของ NF1 ซึ่งเกิดจากยีน NF1 ผิดปกติ พบได้ในผู้ใหญ่ที่เป็นโรคนี้เกือบทุกคน ในเด็กที่เป็น NF1 ควรตรวจตาทุกปีเพื่อหา optic pathway glioma และให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรมแก่ครอบครัว

ddx.pt: The disease that the nodules point to; confirm with skin signs, neurofibromas or the NF1 gene
Cataract, schwannomas and meningiomas, with no Lisch nodules and few or no café-au-lait spots
A solitary, enlarging, vascularised iris mass with distorted pupil, unlike multiple small stable nodules

aN: lisch nodules | iris lisch nodules | pigmented iris hamartomas

name: Iron akathisia
formal: Akathisia related to iron deficiency, overlapping with restless legs syndrome and responding to iron replacement; low ferritin is linked to reduced dopamine function.
simple: Inner restlessness and the need to move, linked to low iron stores and improved by iron treatment.
th: อาการกระวนกระวายนั่งไม่ติดที่สัมพันธ์กับภาวะขาดธาตุเหล็ก ซ้อนทับกับ restless legs syndrome และดีขึ้นเมื่อให้ธาตุเหล็ก
tempoNote: Gradual, fluctuating restlessness that tracks iron status
feat: Inner urge to move with pacing, rocking or shifting position
Worse in the evening and at rest; may involve the whole body, not just the legs
Low ferritin, often from menstruation, pregnancy, GI blood loss or blood donation
May coexist with or unmask antipsychotic-related akathisia
inv: Ferritin and transferrin saturation; aim ferritin above about 75 µg/L in symptomatic patients
Full blood count and search for the source of iron loss
Medication review for dopamine blockers, antiemetics and SSRIs

case.story: Several months of evening restlessness; she cannot sit through TV and walks around the house. Heavy periods for a year. On no psychiatric drugs.
case.exam: Fidgety, crosses and uncrosses legs, normal neurological examination.
case.tests: Hb 10.4 g/dL, ferritin 9 µg/L, transferrin saturation 8%.
case.q: What is the likely cause of her restlessness and first step in treatment?
case.a: Restlessness linked to iron deficiency (RLS/akathisia spectrum); replace iron (IV if ferritin fails to rise) and treat menorrhagia.

det.patho: Iron is a cofactor for tyrosine hydroxylase and is needed for dopamine receptor and transporter function. Brain iron deficiency, shown in autopsy and MRI studies of RLS, reduces striatal dopaminergic signalling and may lower the threshold for akathisia. The concept of a distinct iron akathisia rests on case reports and overlap with RLS rather than large studies.
det.clinical: Patients describe an unpleasant inner restlessness and urge to move that is relieved by walking. Unlike classic RLS, the arms and trunk may be involved and sensory complaints are less specific. Iron deficiency also worsens antipsychotic-induced akathisia, so a patient on these drugs may have two contributing factors. Pregnancy, heavy menstrual loss, renal failure and frequent blood donation are common settings.
det.diagnosis: This is a clinical diagnosis supported by low ferritin or low transferrin saturation and improvement after iron repletion. Ferritin is an acute-phase protein, so values in the normal range can hide deficiency during inflammation. Exclude drug causes, hyperthyroidism, anxiety and peripheral neuropathy.
det.treatment: Treat the cause of iron loss and replete iron: oral iron on alternate days with vitamin C, or IV iron (for example ferric carboxymaltose) when oral iron is not tolerated, absorption is poor or symptoms are severe. Recheck ferritin after about 3 months. If a dopamine blocker is involved, reduce or switch it; propranolol or mirtazapine may help residual akathisia.
det.prognosis: Symptoms often improve within weeks to months of iron repletion; recurrence follows renewed iron loss.
pearls: Check ferritin in any patient with akathisia or RLS before adding drugs.
A ferritin of 40 may still be too low for someone with restless symptoms.
Dopamine agonists given for RLS can cause augmentation; iron is the safer first step.
det.thd: Iron akathisia คือภาวะกระวนกระวายอยากขยับตัวที่สัมพันธ์กับการขาดธาตุเหล็ก กลไกคือเหล็กจำเป็นต่อการสร้างและทำงานของ dopamine อาการคล้ายและซ้อนทับกับ RLS แต่อาจเป็นทั้งตัว วินิจฉัยโดยดู ferritin และ transferrin saturation ร่วมกับตัดสาเหตุจากยา รักษาโดยหาสาเหตุการเสียเลือดและให้ธาตุเหล็กทางปากหรือทางหลอดเลือด

ddx.pt: Urge confined mainly to legs with sensory discomfort and relief by moving; overlaps strongly
Follows starting or increasing a dopamine blocker; iron normal
Lifelong pattern from childhood with inattention, not new-onset evening restlessness

aN: iron deficiency akathisia | iron related restlessness | low ferritin akathisia

name: Iron deficiency
formal: Reduced body iron stores, linked to restless legs syndrome, akathisia, breath-holding spells, pica and cognitive effects in children; ferritin below 50 is relevant in RLS.
simple: Not having enough iron in the body, which can cause tiredness and is linked to restless legs.
th: ภาวะร่างกายขาดธาตุเหล็ก เป็นโรคทางเลือดแต่สัมพันธ์กับ RLS, akathisia, breath-holding spells และพัฒนาการด้านความคิดในเด็ก
tempoNote: Develops over months; neurological effects improve with repletion
feat: Fatigue, pallor, pica (including ice craving) and hair loss
Restless legs syndrome and akathisia-like restlessness
Breath-holding spells and poorer attention or development in young children
Severe anaemia can contribute to stroke risk, especially in children and with venous sinus thrombosis
Causes: menstrual and GI blood loss, pregnancy, poor intake, malabsorption, hookworm
inv: Ferritin (low below about 30 µg/L; for RLS target above 75), transferrin saturation
Full blood count: microcytic hypochromic anaemia, raised platelets
Find the cause: stool occult blood, endoscopy in adults, coeliac serology, stool for parasites

case.story: Several episodes of crying, then going silent, turning blue and briefly limp after being scolded. Drinks large volumes of cow's milk and eats little else.
case.exam: Pale but developmentally normal; neurological examination normal.
case.tests: Hb 8.2 g/dL, MCV 58 fL, ferritin 4 µg/L; EEG not required.
case.q: What links his spells to the blood result and what is the management?
case.a: Cyanotic breath-holding spells worsened by iron deficiency; oral iron and limiting milk intake reduce the spells.

read.where: Chapter 11: Neurological complications of red blood cell disorders

det.patho: Iron is needed for haemoglobin, myelination, energy metabolism and monoamine synthesis. In the brain, iron deficiency reduces dopamine signalling in the striatum and impairs myelination during early development. Anaemia also alters autonomic responses, which may explain the link with breath-holding spells.
det.clinical: Iron deficiency is a systemic, mainly haematological condition, not a primary neurological disease. Its neurological associations include RLS and akathisia in adults, breath-holding spells and developmental or attention problems in infants and toddlers, and fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance at all ages. Severe anaemia with thrombocytosis has been associated with childhood stroke and cerebral venous thrombosis.
det.diagnosis: Low ferritin is the most specific single test, but it rises with inflammation, so transferrin saturation below about 20% is a useful companion. Anaemia is a late feature; low iron stores can exist with normal haemoglobin. In adults, especially men and postmenopausal women, unexplained iron deficiency warrants GI investigation.
det.treatment: Oral iron (for example ferrous sulfate once daily or on alternate days) is first line, with dietary advice and treatment of the cause. IV iron is used for intolerance, malabsorption, chronic kidney disease, pregnancy in later stages or when rapid repletion is needed for RLS. In toddlers, limit cow's milk to about 500 mL per day. Recheck indices after 2–3 months.
det.prognosis: Haematological and most neurological symptoms reverse with repletion; developmental effects of prolonged deficiency in infancy may be partly permanent.
pearls: Measure ferritin in every patient with RLS.
Breath-holding spells often lessen when iron is replaced, even without anaemia.
Unexplained iron deficiency in an adult man is GI cancer until proven otherwise.
det.thd: Iron deficiency เป็นภาวะทางเลือดและโภชนาการ ไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาทโดยตรง แต่เกี่ยวข้องกับ RLS, akathisia, breath-holding spells และปัญหาพัฒนาการในเด็ก เพราะเหล็กจำเป็นต่อการสร้าง dopamine และ myelin วินิจฉัยด้วย ferritin และ transferrin saturation แล้วหาสาเหตุของการเสียเลือด รักษาด้วยธาตุเหล็กทางปากหรือทางหลอดเลือด

ddx.pt: A neurological consequence of low iron; may be primary with normal ferritin
Spells without a provoking cry or upset, with postictal state and EEG changes
Behavioural diagnosis; iron deficiency may worsen attention but is not the cause

name: Isaacs’ syndrome
formal: Acquired peripheral nerve hyperexcitability with muscle stiffness, fasciculation, myokymia and cramps, from VGKC complex antibodies (CASPR2), sometimes with thymoma; responds to immunotherapy.
simple: A condition in which overactive nerves cause constant muscle twitching, stiffness and cramps.
more: Diagnose with EMG showing neuromyotonic, myokymic or doublet discharges that persist during sleep and nerve block, with anti-CASPR2 or LGI1 antibodies. Treat with carbamazepine, phenytoin, plasma exchange or IVIG. Acquired peripheral nerve hyperexcitability syndrome with continuous muscle fibre activity, myokymia, cramps and delayed relaxation, often autoimmune (CASPR2 or LGI1 antibodies). Neuromyotonic discharges on EMG; test for CASPR2 antibodies and thymoma. Treat with carbamazepine or phenytoin, and immunotherapy for autoimmune cases. Peripheral nerve hyperexcitability (Isaacs syndrome) with continuous muscle fibre activity, stiffness, myokymia, cramps and delayed relaxation, from VGKC complex (CASPR2) antibodies. Detect with EMG showing myokymic and neuromyotonic discharges, with CASPR2 and LGI1 antibodies, and search for thymoma or other tumour. Treat with carbamazepine or phenytoin, with plasma exchange or IVIG for severe cases; Morvan syndrome combines CNS features.

det.patho: Acquired neuromyotonia arises from hyperexcitability of motor axons, usually distal. Antibodies against proteins of the voltage-gated potassium channel complex — chiefly CASPR2 at the juxtaparanode — reduce potassium currents, so axons fire repetitively and spontaneously. A paraneoplastic origin, especially thymoma, is found in a substantial minority. Combined central involvement (Morvan syndrome) indicates a broader autoimmune process.
det.clinical: Patients describe continuous twitching, rippling, stiffness, cramps and slow relaxation after a grip; symptoms persist during sleep. Hyperhidrosis and other autonomic features are common, and neuropathic pain or paraesthesia may occur. Insomnia, agitation, hallucinations, dysautonomia and weight loss suggest Morvan syndrome. A coexisting myasthenia gravis raises suspicion of thymoma.
det.diagnosis: EMG shows myokymic and neuromyotonic discharges (high-frequency bursts with decrementing amplitude), and after-discharges following nerve stimulation. Test for CASPR2 and LGI1 antibodies with cell-based assays; many patients remain seronegative. Image the chest for thymoma and screen for other tumours, such as lung cancer. Distinguish from cramp-fasciculation syndrome, stiff-person syndrome and hereditary forms (e.g. KCNA1).
det.treatment: Symptomatic control uses sodium-channel blocking drugs such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin or lamotrigine. Plasma exchange, IVIG, corticosteroids and rituximab are used for antibody-positive or disabling disease. Remove a thymoma if present. Morvan syndrome often needs more aggressive immunotherapy.
det.prognosis: Non-paraneoplastic disease often improves with treatment and may remit; outcome in paraneoplastic cases depends on the tumour.
pearls: Twitching that continues during sleep and after nerve block points to peripheral nerve hyperexcitability.
Thymoma links Isaacs, Morvan and myasthenia gravis — image the chest.

simple: Eye problems caused by poor blood flow to the eye, from temporary vision loss to permanent damage.
ab: Amaurosis fugax and retinal artery occlusion

feat: Amaurosis fugax: brief monocular visual loss from emboli or low flow
Central or branch retinal artery occlusion: sudden painless loss, retinal whitening, cherry-red spot, visible emboli

case.who: 68-year-old retired farmer from Ubon Ratchathani with diabetes and smoking history
case.story: A curtain closed over the left eye for 10 minutes yesterday; this morning he woke with a persistent dark field and a mild ache around that eye.
case.exam: Left acuity counting fingers, RAPD, retinal whitening with a cherry-red spot and a bright embolus at an arteriolar bifurcation; left carotid bruit.
case.tests: ESR normal; CTA shows 90% left internal carotid stenosis; MRI DWI shows small left hemispheric infarcts.
case.q: How should this be triaged and managed?
case.a: Treat it as stroke: immediate stroke pathway, antithrombotic and statin therapy, and urgent carotid revascularisation planning.

det.patho: The retina has high metabolic demand and no collateral circulation, so interrupted arterial flow causes infarction within about an hour and a half. Emboli from carotid plaques, the heart or aortic arch lodge at arteriolar bifurcations. Large-artery inflammation (giant-cell arteritis) or failure of low-flow perfusion of the optic nerve head causes ischaemic optic neuropathy. In ocular ischaemic syndrome, tight carotid stenosis reduces ophthalmic artery pressure, leading to retinal and anterior-segment hypoxia with neovascularisation.
det.clinical: Transient monocular loss lasting minutes suggests carotid or embolic disease, while a persistent painless loss with cherry-red macula suggests retinal artery occlusion. Branch occlusions cause sector field loss and recover better than central occlusion. Optic neuropathy causes altitudinal loss with disc swelling. In ocular ischaemic syndrome, patients describe dull periocular pain relieved by lying down, slow visual loss and prolonged recovery from bright light. Many patients have asymptomatic cerebral infarcts or coronary disease.
det.diagnosis: Examine acuity, pupils and fundus, and check inflammatory markers urgently in older patients. Imaging of the cervical vessels and heart looks for the embolic source. Fluorescein angiography and OCT clarify the retinal findings. Differentiate from retinal vein occlusion, retinal detachment, optic neuritis and vitreous haemorrhage. Work-up in younger patients includes vasculitis, thrombophilia, dissection, migraine and drugs.
det.treatment: Treat acute retinal artery occlusion as stroke: arrange immediate transfer to a stroke-capable centre because thrombolysis is considered within very early time windows in some protocols, though evidence is mixed. Ocular massage or lowering of IOP has uncertain benefit. Secondary prevention includes antiplatelets, statin, blood pressure and diabetes control, anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation, and carotid endarterectomy or stenting for symptomatic high-grade stenosis. Arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy is treated with high-dose corticosteroid at once, and ocular ischaemic syndrome with revascularisation plus management of rubeosis (panretinal photocoagulation, anti-VEGF).
det.prognosis: Poor for central retinal artery occlusion; branch occlusions often recover; the main danger is stroke and cardiac death in the following years.
pearls: Retinal artery occlusion is a stroke of the eye: refer to stroke services immediately.
Check ESR and CRP in every older patient with acute ischaemic visual loss.
Look for emboli at retinal arteriole bifurcations.
det.thd: Ischaemic ocular syndromes คือกลุ่มโรคที่จอตาหรือเส้นประสาทตาขาดเลือด ได้แก่ amaurosis fugax, retinal artery occlusion, ischaemic optic neuropathy และ ocular ischaemic syndrome จากหลอดเลือด carotid ตีบมาก ผู้ป่วยตามัวหรือมองไม่เห็นข้างเดียวแบบไม่เจ็บ ต้องถือเป็นภาวะ stroke ส่งต่อแผนก stroke ทันที ตรวจ ESR/CRP ในผู้สูงอายุเพื่อหา GCA ตรวจหลอดเลือด carotid และหัวใจ และป้องกันการเกิด stroke ซ้ำด้วยยาต้านเกล็ดเลือด statin ควบคุมความดันและเบาหวาน

qx.stem: A 68-year-old man with hypertension and smoking history notices painless, sudden, near-complete loss of vision in his left eye 2 hours ago. Fundoscopy shows a pale, oedematous retina with a cherry-red spot and a bright refractile plaque at a branch point of a retinal arteriole. He has no other neurological deficit.
qx.q: What is the most appropriate approach?
opts: Routine ophthalmology clinic follow-up in 2 weeks
Ocular massage at home and topical eye drops only
Oral prednisolone for presumed giant cell arteritis without further tests
Manage it as an acute ischaemic stroke: emergency stroke-centre assessment, vascular and cardiac work-up, and secondary prevention
Observation, because retinal infarction carries no risk for later cerebral stroke
qx.why: Central retinal artery occlusion is a form of acute ischaemic stroke with a high short-term risk of cerebral infarction and myocardial events, and a cholesterol embolus implicates a proximal arterial source such as the carotid. It warrants emergency stroke evaluation, where time-sensitive reperfusion options may be considered, followed by carotid imaging, cardiac monitoring and preventive therapy. ESR and CRP should still be checked in older patients, but empirical steroids without testing are not the default.

det.patho: Interrupted arterial flow causes energy failure in neurons within minutes, leading to excitotoxicity, oedema and cell death in the core; surrounding penumbra survives temporarily on collateral flow. Thrombus arises in situ on atheroma, embolises from heart or arteries, or small penetrating arteries become occluded by lipohyalinosis.
det.clinical: Clinical syndromes follow territories: MCA (contralateral weakness, aphasia or neglect), ACA (leg weakness, abulia), PCA (hemianopia), vertebrobasilar (vertigo, diplopia, ataxia, crossed signs), and lacunar syndromes. Early neurological deterioration may come from infarct growth, oedema or haemorrhagic transformation.
det.diagnosis: Brain imaging excludes haemorrhage; CTA identifies large-vessel occlusion; MRI DWI confirms infarction and helps with uncertain diagnoses. Aetiological work-up includes vascular imaging, cardiac monitoring for AF, echocardiography and risk factor tests, with extended testing in young patients.
det.treatment: Acute: thrombolysis and thrombectomy for eligible patients, stroke unit care, swallow screening, early mobilisation and prevention of complications. Secondary prevention: antiplatelets (short dual antiplatelet therapy for minor stroke or high-risk TIA), anticoagulation for AF, statins, BP control, carotid revascularisation where indicated, and lifestyle change.
det.prognosis: Outcome depends on severity, age and reperfusion; recurrence risk is highest early and falls with prevention.
pearls: Treat first, refine aetiology later; time to reperfusion matters most.
Classify mechanism because secondary prevention depends on it.
Stroke unit care benefits all stroke subtypes.

qx.stem: A 58-year-old man with diabetes develops sudden dense left face, arm and leg weakness, numbness of the whole left half of the body plus a left homonymous visual field defect. Language and attention are preserved, and there is no gaze deviation. MRI shows a slender infarct along the back part of the right internal capsule extending into the lateral thalamus and the start of the optic radiation.
qx.q: Which artery was most likely occluded?
opts: Recurrent artery of Heubner
Anterior choroidal artery
Artery of Percheron
Upper-division branch of the MCA
Callosomarginal branch of the anterior cerebral artery
qx.why: The anterior choroidal artery, a small branch of the supraclinoid internal carotid artery, supplies the capsular posterior limb, parts of the thalamus and the optic tract or radiation, giving the triad of hemiparesis, hemisensory loss and hemianopia without cortical signs. Heubner's artery supplies the caudate head and anterior limb, Percheron's artery causes bilateral paramedian thalamic infarcts, and cortical MCA or ACA branches would produce neglect, language or leg-predominant deficits.

qx.stem: A 76-year-old woman has a right frontal cortical infarct. Holter monitoring shows paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and carotid duplex shows a 60% right internal carotid stenosis with an irregular plaque. Echocardiography is otherwise normal, and there is no small-vessel lesion on MRI.
qx.q: Using the TOAST scheme, how should this stroke be classified?
opts: Large-artery atherosclerosis
Cardioembolism
Small-vessel occlusion
Stroke of undetermined cause, because two or more plausible causes were found
Stroke of other determined cause
qx.why: TOAST places a stroke in the undetermined category not only when the work-up is negative but also when two competing mechanisms are identified, as here with atrial fibrillation and a relevant ipsilateral stenosis. Phenotypic systems such as ASCOD instead grade each mechanism separately. Treatment still addresses both: anticoagulation for AF and assessment of the carotid lesion.

name: Isolated sleep paralysis
formal: Brief inability to move or speak on falling asleep or waking, with full awareness, from REM atonia intruding into wakefulness; not accompanied by narcolepsy.
simple: Being unable to move or speak for a short time when falling asleep or waking up, while fully aware.

feat: Fully conscious but unable to move limbs, trunk or speak at sleep onset or on waking
Eye movements and breathing preserved, though chest pressure is often felt
Frequently accompanied by frightening hallucinations of an intruder or presence
Common: lifetime prevalence around 8%, higher in students and with shift work, stress and supine sleep
No daytime sleepiness or cataplexy (otherwise consider narcolepsy)

PSG and MSLT only if narcolepsy features are present

case.exam: Normal; sleeps 5 hours on exam nights; no daytime sleep attacks or cataplexy.
case.tests: None needed.
case.q: What is happening and how is it managed?
case.a: Isolated sleep paralysis from REM atonia persisting into wakefulness; explanation, regular adequate sleep and avoiding sleeping on her back.

det.patho: During REM sleep, brainstem circuits in the sublaterodorsal nucleus and ventromedial medulla inhibit spinal motor neurons, causing atonia. In sleep paralysis, the cortex wakes while this REM atonia persists, producing a dissociated state of awareness without movement. Dream imagery from REM can intrude simultaneously, giving vivid hallucinations. Sleep deprivation and fragmented sleep favour these state dissociations.
det.clinical: Episodes occur on falling asleep or waking and last seconds to minutes, ending spontaneously or with touch or sound. People feel awake but cannot move, with intense fear, a sensed presence, chest pressure or out-of-body experiences. Cultural interpretations, such as phi am in Thailand, shape the experience. Isolated cases have no other sleep disorder features.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is based on the typical history. Ask specifically about daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, hypnagogic hallucinations and disturbed nocturnal sleep, which suggest narcolepsy. Distinguish from nocturnal seizures, periodic paralysis and panic attacks. Testing is reserved for atypical cases.
det.treatment: Reassurance and education are central, as understanding reduces fear. Maintain regular adequate sleep, reduce stress and avoid sleeping supine. For frequent distressing episodes, CBT-based approaches or REM-suppressing antidepressants such as SSRIs or clomipramine may be used.
det.prognosis: Benign; episodes often lessen with improved sleep habits.
pearls: Sleep paralysis alone is common and benign; with sleepiness and cataplexy it signals narcolepsy.
Explaining the REM atonia mechanism is therapeutic in itself.
Phi am in Thai culture describes the same experience.
det.thd: Isolated sleep paralysis หรือที่คนไทยเรียกว่าผีอำ คือภาวะที่รู้สึกตัวแต่ขยับตัวหรือพูดไม่ได้ชั่วครู่ขณะกำลังหลับหรือเพิ่งตื่น อาจเห็นหรือรู้สึกว่ามีอะไรมาทับหน้าอก เกิดจากการที่กล้ามเนื้อยังอ่อนแรงแบบช่วง REM ขณะสมองตื่นแล้ว พบบ่อยเมื่ออดนอนหรือเครียด ถ้าไม่มีง่วงนอนกลางวันหรือ cataplexy ก็ไม่ใช่ narcolepsy การรักษาคืออธิบายให้เข้าใจและนอนให้พอ

name: Isolated thalamic degeneration (pure thalamic atrophy)
formal: Rare degenerative disease with neuronal loss limited to thalamic nuclei, causing cognitive decline, ataxia and sleep disturbance, sometimes with familial or prion-like mechanisms such as fatal insomnia.
simple: A rare brain condition in which only the thalamus shrinks, causing memory problems and balance and sleep trouble.
more: Diagnosis is by imaging or pathology. No treatment, and prion testing should be considered when sleep failure and dysautonomia are present.
th: โรคเสื่อมที่พบน้อยมาก เซลล์ประสาทตายเฉพาะใน thalamus ทำให้สมองเสื่อม นอนไม่หลับ และระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติผิดปกติ หลายรายเป็นโรคพรีออน เช่น fatal familial insomnia
tempoNote: Progressive over months to a few years
feat: Progressive cognitive decline with apathy, attention and memory impairment
Severe insomnia, loss of normal sleep architecture and dream-enactment
Dysautonomia: sweating, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia
Ataxia, myoclonus or dysarthria in some cases
Many reported cases proved to be fatal familial insomnia (PRNP D178N-129M) or sporadic fatal insomnia
inv: MRI often normal or shows thalamic atrophy; FDG-PET thalamic hypometabolism is a sensitive clue
Polysomnography: loss of sleep spindles and slow-wave sleep
PRNP gene sequencing; CSF RT-QuIC (lower sensitivity in fatal insomnia)
Exclude bilateral thalamic infarcts, gliomatosis, Wernicke encephalopathy and autoimmune encephalitis

case.story: Eight months of near-total inability to sleep, sweating, weight loss and poor memory; his father died of a similar illness.
case.exam: Inattentive, mild ataxia, myoclonic jerks, tachycardia and fluctuating blood pressure.
case.tests: MRI unremarkable; FDG-PET shows bilateral thalamic hypometabolism; PRNP D178N variant.
case.q: What is the best label for this thalamic degeneration?
case.a: Fatal familial insomnia — the main identifiable cause of isolated thalamic degeneration.

det.patho: Neuronal loss and gliosis are concentrated in the anterior and mediodorsal thalamic nuclei, with relative sparing of cortex. Older reports described familial and sporadic cases before prion genetics; many are now recognised as fatal familial insomnia or sporadic fatal insomnia, both prion diseases. Whether a non-prion isolated thalamic degeneration exists as a separate entity is uncertain.
det.clinical: Patients develop insomnia, autonomic overactivity, apathy, attention and memory failure, and later ataxia, myoclonus and dysarthria. Because thalamic nuclei relay to frontal cortex, the dementia often looks frontal-subcortical. Mean disease duration is around one to two years in prion cases.
det.diagnosis: Structural MRI is often unrevealing; FDG-PET showing thalamic hypometabolism, polysomnography and PRNP testing are the most useful tests. CSF RT-QuIC and 14-3-3 are less sensitive here than in sporadic CJD. Neuropathology remains definitive.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying treatment exists. Supportive care addresses sleep, autonomic instability, nutrition and family counselling; sedatives give little restorative sleep. Genetic counselling is important when a PRNP variant is found.
det.prognosis: Relentlessly progressive and fatal, typically within 1–3 years.
pearls: Insomnia + dysautonomia + dementia = check PRNP.
Normal MRI does not exclude it; FDG-PET shows thalamic hypometabolism.
RT-QuIC can be negative in fatal insomnia.
det.thd: Isolated thalamic degeneration เป็นโรคที่เซลล์ประสาทใน thalamus เสื่อมลงเฉพาะที่ ผู้ป่วยนอนไม่หลับรุนแรง เหงื่อออก หัวใจเต้นเร็ว ความจำและสมาธิแย่ลง ต่อมาอาจเดินเซและกระตุก หลายรายเป็นโรคพรีออน fatal familial insomnia MRI มักปกติ แต่ FDG-PET พบ thalamus ทำงานลดลง ควรตรวจยีน PRNP ไม่มีการรักษาเฉพาะ

name: Isolated vertigo
formal: Vertigo as the only symptom without other neurological signs; causes include BPPV, vestibular neuritis, Meniere disease, and rarely posterior circulation stroke.
simple: A spinning sensation that is the only symptom, often from a problem in the inner ear.
th: อาการบ้านหมุนเป็นอาการเดียวโดยไม่มีอาการทางระบบประสาทอื่น ส่วนใหญ่เป็นโรคหูชั้นใน เช่น BPPV, vestibular neuritis แต่บางครั้งเป็น stroke ใน posterior circulation
tempoNote: Single prolonged episode (acute vestibular syndrome) or brief recurrent spells
feat: Vertigo without diplopia, dysarthria, weakness or numbness
Peripheral causes are commonest: vestibular neuritis, BPPV, Ménière
Small cerebellar or brainstem strokes may present as isolated vertigo
HINTS exam (head impulse, nystagmus, test of skew) separates central from peripheral in prolonged vertigo
Severe imbalance (unable to sit or walk) suggests central cause
inv: HINTS plus hearing assessment by a trained examiner
MRI with DWI (may be falsely negative in first 48 hours for small strokes)
Dix-Hallpike for positional episodes

case.story: Continuous vertigo with vomiting for 10 hours; no other symptoms.
case.exam: Direction-changing gaze-evoked nystagmus, normal head impulse test bilaterally, small skew deviation; cannot walk unaided.
case.tests: Initial CT normal; MRI DWI at 48 hours shows right inferior cerebellar (PICA) infarct.
case.q: Which bedside findings pointed to a central cause?
case.a: Normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus and skew deviation (central HINTS), plus severe gait ataxia.

read.where: Chapter 23 Neuro-Otology: Dizziness, Balance and Hearing — Clinical Disorders

det.patho: Vertigo results from asymmetric vestibular input from the labyrinth, vestibular nerve, vestibular nuclei or their cerebellar connections. Small infarcts in the PICA or AICA territory, including the nodulus, can mimic peripheral vestibulopathy; AICA strokes may also damage the labyrinth, causing hearing loss.
det.clinical: Separating patients into acute prolonged vertigo, triggered episodic vertigo and spontaneous episodic vertigo guides the approach. In prolonged vertigo, a central cause is suggested by a normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, skew deviation, severe truncal ataxia or new hearing loss (AICA). Vascular risk factors raise suspicion but cannot exclude stroke in younger patients.
det.diagnosis: HINTS performed by trained clinicians is more sensitive for stroke than early MRI. MRI with DWI is used when central features or doubt exist; repeat imaging may be needed. Audiometry, Dix-Hallpike and roll tests address peripheral causes.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: repositioning for BPPV, short-term vestibular suppressants and early rehabilitation for vestibular neuritis (steroids are optional), and stroke pathway management including thrombolysis when indicated for central causes. Avoid prolonged vestibular suppressants.
det.prognosis: Peripheral causes usually recover well; missed posterior circulation stroke risks recurrence and fatal cerebellar swelling.
pearls: A normal head impulse test in acute continuous vertigo is a worrying sign.
Early MRI can miss small posterior fossa strokes.
Inability to walk unaided favours a central lesion.
det.thd: Isolated vertigo คืออาการบ้านหมุนเป็นอาการเดียวโดยไม่มีอาการทางระบบประสาทอื่น ส่วนใหญ่มาจากหูชั้นใน เช่น vestibular neuritis หรือ BPPV แต่ stroke เล็กๆ ใน cerebellum หรือก้านสมองก็ทำให้เกิดอาการนี้ได้ การตรวจ HINTS ช่วยแยก ถ้า head impulse ปกติ nystagmus เปลี่ยนทิศ หรือมี skew deviation ให้คิดถึง stroke และทำ MRI

name: Primary angiitis of the CNS (PACNS)
formal: Primary angiitis of the CNS, a rare vasculitis restricted to brain and spinal cord vessels, causing headaches, stroke and cognitive change, confirmed by biopsy.
simple: Rare inflammation of blood vessels in the brain and spinal cord without disease elsewhere in the body.
more: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system, an inflammatory vasculitis confined to cerebral vessels, with headache, strokes and cognitive change; diagnosed by angiography or biopsy.
th: หลอดเลือดอักเสบชนิดหายากที่จำกัดเฉพาะหลอดเลือดในสมองและไขสันหลัง ทำให้ปวดศีรษะ stroke หลายตำแหน่ง และความคิดความจำเปลี่ยนแปลง ยืนยันด้วยการตัดชิ้นเนื้อ
tempoNote: Insidious headache and cognitive change over weeks to months, punctuated by stroke-like events
feat: Chronic progressive headache with cognitive decline or encephalopathy
Recurrent strokes in different territories, often small and bilateral
Seizures, focal deficits; spinal cord involvement less often
No systemic features: normal ESR/CRP is common
Two main forms: small-vessel (biopsy positive, angiography often normal) and medium/large-vessel (angiography positive)
inv: MRI: multiple infarcts of different ages, white matter lesions, leptomeningeal enhancement, microbleeds; rarely normal
CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis and raised protein in most (normal CSF argues against)
Angiography (DSA preferred): beading, stenoses in multiple vessels; low specificity
Brain and leptomeningeal biopsy of a lesional area: gold standard; also excludes lymphoma and infection

case.story: Three months of daily headache, forgetfulness and two episodes of transient right-sided weakness and word-finding difficulty.
case.exam: MoCA 21/30, mild right pronator drift; no rash or systemic signs.
case.tests: MRI: multiple small infarcts of different ages bilaterally and leptomeningeal enhancement; CSF 30 lymphocytes, protein 1.1 g/L; ESR normal; infection screen negative; DSA normal; brain-leptomeningeal biopsy shows granulomatous vasculitis.
case.q: Why was biopsy needed despite the normal angiogram?
case.a: Small-vessel PACNS is often angiographically normal; biopsy confirms vasculitis and excludes mimics such as lymphoma and infection before long-term immunosuppression.

det.patho: PACNS is an idiopathic inflammatory disease of cerebral and spinal cord vessels without systemic vasculitis. Histology shows granulomatous, lymphocytic or necrotising patterns; amyloid-beta-related angiitis (ABRA) is a variant associated with cerebral amyloid angiopathy. Its rarity (a few cases per million per year) and similarity to mimics make diagnosis difficult.
det.clinical: The typical patient is middle-aged with subacute headache, cognitive decline, and multifocal stroke-like episodes. Small-vessel disease often presents with encephalopathy, seizures, and enhancing lesions, while medium-vessel disease presents with infarcts. Some patients have tumour-like mass lesions. Thunderclap headache is unusual and favours RCVS.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis needs exclusion of systemic vasculitis, infection (VZV, TB, syphilis, fungi, HIV), malignancy (lymphoma), RCVS and other vasculopathies. Supportive findings are inflammatory CSF and abnormal MRI; angiography alone is non-specific and can be falsely positive in RCVS and atherosclerosis. Biopsy of a lesional area including leptomeninges is the gold standard but can be falsely negative due to patchy involvement. High-resolution vessel wall MRI may help show concentric enhancement.
det.treatment: Induction therapy is high-dose glucocorticoids (IV methylprednisolone then oral prednisolone) with cyclophosphamide for severe or progressive disease. Maintenance uses azathioprine, mycophenolate or methotrexate for 2–3 years. Rituximab and TNF inhibitors are options in refractory disease. Antiplatelet therapy is often used for ischaemic events. Monitoring uses clinical status and MRI.
det.prognosis: With treatment many patients stabilise or improve, but relapses occur in about a quarter and residual disability is common.
pearls: Normal CSF makes PACNS unlikely; thunderclap headache favours RCVS.
Beaded angiography is not specific for vasculitis.
Biopsy also catches lymphoma and infection, which change treatment.
det.thd: PACNS คือหลอดเลือดอักเสบชนิดหายากที่เกิดเฉพาะในสมองและไขสันหลังโดยไม่มีอวัยวะอื่นเกี่ยวข้อง อาการคือปวดศีรษะเรื้อรัง ความจำเสื่อม และ stroke เล็ก ๆ หลายตำแหน่ง น้ำไขสันหลังมักพบเซลล์และโปรตีนสูง ภาพหลอดเลือดอาจปกติในชนิดหลอดเลือดเล็ก จึงต้องยืนยันด้วยการตัดชิ้นเนื้อสมองและเยื่อหุ้มสมอง ต้องแยก RCVS การติดเชื้อ และ lymphoma ออก รักษาด้วย steroid ร่วมกับ cyclophosphamide แล้วตามด้วยยากดภูมิระยะยาว

qx.stem: A 19-year-old woman from Chiang Mai has weeks of headache, then fever, drowsiness and a seizure. MRI shows a right pontine infarct and focal left posterior cerebral artery stenosis. CSF shows mild pleocytosis. Viral, autoimmune and drug screens are negative, and the team is separating primary CNS vasculitis from RCVS.
qx.q: Which vessel-wall MRI pattern favours vasculitis over RCVS?
opts: No wall enhancement, with reversal in three months
Eccentric enhancement with an intimal flap
Eccentric plaque with a peripheral non-enhancing rim
Fusiform dilatation without wall enhancement
Concentric vessel wall enhancement, whereas RCVS shows no wall enhancement and reverses within about three months
qx.why: Isolated CNS angiitis is an uncommon small-to-medium vessel inflammation with multiterritory infarcts, CSF pleocytosis and a diagnosis that may need cortical-meningeal biopsy. High-resolution vessel-wall imaging helps: vasculitis gives concentric enhancement, dissection an eccentric wall enhancement with an intimal flap, atherosclerosis an eccentric enhancing plaque, and RCVS no enhancement with reversibility. Pseudovasculitis such as RCVS and infection must be excluded.

qx.stem: A 45-year-old woman from Lampang has subacute headache, cognitive decline and recurrent small infarcts in different territories. CSF has 18 lymphocytes and protein 90 mg/dL, systemic markers and ANCA are negative, and CT angiography is normal. MRI shows enhancing lesions in the right frontal region. Infectious and malignant causes have been excluded.
qx.q: Which investigation is the diagnostic gold standard?
opts: Repeat CT angiography
Brain and leptomeningeal biopsy sampling the radiologically abnormal area
Serum ESR
Transthoracic echocardiogram
EEG
qx.why: Primary CNS vasculitis has no pathognomonic clinical picture, and angiography has low specificity and can be normal when small vessels are involved. Biopsy of an abnormal area (including dura, leptomeninges, cortex and white matter) shows transmural vascular inflammation and also reveals mimics such as infection; it has a sensitivity of roughly 50 to 70 percent because the disease is segmental, so a negative result does not exclude it.

qx.stem: The woman above has biopsy-proven granulomatous vasculitis. She is started on pulse methylprednisolone.
qx.q: What is the usual induction and maintenance strategy?
opts: Glucocorticoids with cyclophosphamide for induction, then azathioprine, methotrexate or mycophenolate for maintenance
Aspirin alone for life
Interferon beta
High-dose antibiotics for 6 weeks
Statins alone
qx.why: Induction of remission usually combines glucocorticoids (about 1 mg/kg tapered over months) with cyclophosphamide for 3 to 6 months in severe disease, and maintenance uses azathioprine, methotrexate or mycophenolate, with Pneumocystis prophylaxis and monitoring. About 80 percent improve; non-response should lead to re-checking the diagnosis, and rituximab is a limited-evidence rescue option.

name: Isometric tremor
formal: Tremor from voluntary muscle contraction against a rigid object, such as in primary orthostatic tremor or functional tremor, without movement.
simple: A shaking that occurs when muscles tighten against something without moving, such as gripping a bar.
th: tremor ที่เกิดขณะกล้ามเนื้อหดตัวต้านวัตถุที่ไม่ขยับ เช่น กำมือแน่นหรือยืนนิ่ง พบใน orthostatic tremor และ tremor แบบอื่น
tempoNote: A descriptive tremor type; time course depends on the cause
feat: Appears when pushing against a fixed object, making a fist or bearing weight
Disappears when the limb relaxes or moves freely
Classic example: primary orthostatic tremor in the legs on standing
Also seen in enhanced physiological, essential, dystonic and functional tremor
inv: Surface EMG or accelerometry: frequency and coherence (13–18 Hz in orthostatic tremor)
Thyroid function and medication review for enhanced physiological tremor
Neuroimaging only if other neurological signs are present

case.story: Notices her hand shakes only while gripping a heavy shopping bag or pushing a stuck door; no tremor when writing or holding a cup.
case.exam: Fine 8–10 Hz tremor while squeezing the examiner's fingers; none at rest or on finger-nose testing.
case.tests: TSH low; free T4 raised.
case.q: What tremor type is this and what is the likely cause?
case.a: Isometric tremor from enhanced physiological tremor due to hyperthyroidism.

det.patho: Isometric tremor is one of the action tremors in the consensus tremor classification, defined by muscle contraction without change in limb position. It reflects oscillation in central circuits, peripheral stretch-reflex loops or both, depending on the cause. Orthostatic tremor has a very high frequency that suggests a central brainstem or cerebellar oscillator.
det.clinical: This is a tremor descriptor, not a disease. Patients notice shaking when holding a heavy object, pressing down or standing still. The key is the context: if the legs shake and feel unsteady only when standing, consider orthostatic tremor; if the hands shake with effort and also with posture, enhanced physiological or essential tremor is more likely.
det.diagnosis: Observe the limb at rest, in posture, during movement and during sustained contraction. In the legs, auscultation of the thigh with a stethoscope may reveal a helicopter-like sound in orthostatic tremor. Surface EMG confirms frequency and coherence. Look for causes of enhanced physiological tremor: thyroid disease, caffeine, beta-agonists, valproate, lithium, anxiety and withdrawal states.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying condition. Enhanced physiological tremor responds to removing triggers and sometimes propranolol. Orthostatic tremor may improve with clonazepam, gabapentin or primidone, and selected cases with deep brain stimulation. Functional tremor is managed with explanation and physiotherapy.
det.prognosis: Depends on the cause; physiological forms resolve when the trigger is removed, while orthostatic tremor tends to be chronic.
pearls: Ask what the patient is doing when the tremor appears; effort without movement points here.
Legs shaking only on standing: listen to the thigh for a fast regular tremor.
Always check thyroid function in a new action tremor.
det.thd: Isometric tremor คือ tremor ที่เกิดเมื่อกล้ามเนื้อออกแรงต้านสิ่งที่ไม่ขยับ เช่น กำมือ ถือของหนัก หรือยืนนิ่ง เป็นคำบรรยายชนิด tremor ไม่ใช่โรค ตัวอย่างสำคัญคือ orthostatic tremor ที่ขาสั่นความถี่สูงเมื่อยืน วินิจฉัยด้วยการสังเกตและ surface EMG ร่วมกับหาสาเหตุ เช่น ไทรอยด์เป็นพิษหรือยา แล้วรักษาตามสาเหตุ

Mainly postural and kinetic arm tremor, often familial
Variable frequency, entrainment and distractibility

name: Isovaleric acidaemia (IVA)
formal: Autosomal recessive organic aciduria from isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, with sweaty-feet odour, vomiting, lethargy and coma, triggered by illness or protein load.
simple: An inherited condition in which the body cannot break down part of protein, causing vomiting and drowsiness and a sweaty-feet smell.
th: โรคกรดอินทรีย์คั่งแบบยีนด้อยจากขาดเอนไซม์ isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase ทำให้มีกลิ่นเหมือนถุงเท้าเหม็น อาเจียน ซึม และโคม่า เมื่อเจ็บป่วยหรือได้โปรตีนมาก
tempoNote: Neonatal crisis in the first days, or recurrent decompensations later in childhood
feat: Distinctive odour of sweaty feet during crises
Neonatal poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy progressing to coma
Chronic intermittent form: recurrent episodes with infection or protein load, developmental delay
Pancytopenia and pancreatitis can accompany crises
inv: Blood gas: high anion gap metabolic acidosis, ketosis, sometimes hyperammonaemia and hypoglycaemia
Acylcarnitines: raised C5 (isovalerylcarnitine); urine isovalerylglycine
IVD gene testing; newborn screening detects many cases

case.who: 5-day-old girl in a provincial hospital in Nakhon Sawan
case.story: Fed well at first, then stopped feeding, vomited and became floppy; nurses notice a strong cheesy, foot-like smell.
case.exam: Lethargic, hypotonic, rapid breathing.
case.tests: pH 7.12, anion gap 28, ammonia 180 µmol/L; acylcarnitines show high C5; urine isovalerylglycine raised.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and long-term therapy?
case.a: Isovaleric acidaemia; leucine-restricted diet with glycine and carnitine supplements, plus emergency plans for illness.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Isovaleric Acidaemia

det.patho: IVD catalyses a step in leucine breakdown. When it is deficient, isovaleryl-CoA builds up and is diverted into isovaleric acid, isovalerylglycine and isovalerylcarnitine. Isovaleric acid is toxic to brain and bone marrow and has the characteristic smell. Some mild genotypes found on screening may never cause symptoms.
det.clinical: About half present acutely in the first two weeks with vomiting, lethargy, seizures and coma; the rest have a chronic intermittent course with episodes during infections and variable learning difficulty. Basal ganglia injury and cerebellar haemorrhage have been described after severe crises.
det.diagnosis: Raised C5 acylcarnitine on newborn screening or crisis testing, with high urine isovalerylglycine, is diagnostic. Note that C5 can be falsely raised by pivalate-containing antibiotics. Confirm by gene testing.
det.treatment: Acute: stop protein, give high-dose IV glucose with insulin if needed, correct acidosis, and give glycine and L-carnitine to promote excretion; dialysis for severe hyperammonaemia. Long term: modest leucine restriction, glycine and carnitine supplements, and an emergency regimen for illness.
det.prognosis: Early-detected patients often develop normally; survivors of severe neonatal crises may have intellectual disability.
pearls: Sweaty-feet odour + neonatal acidosis = IVA.
Glycine conjugation is the key detox route; supplement glycine.
Pivmecillinam and other pivalate drugs can mimic raised C5 on screening.
det.thd: Isovaleric acidaemia เกิดจากขาดเอนไซม์ในการย่อย leucine ทำให้ isovaleric acid คั่ง ผู้ป่วยมีกลิ่นเหมือนเท้าอับ ทารกแรกเกิดดูดนมไม่ดี อาเจียน ซึมจนโคม่า หรือบางรายเป็นซ้ำเมื่อป่วย ตรวจพบภาวะเลือดเป็นกรดและ C5 acylcarnitine สูง รักษาด้วยการจำกัด leucine เสริม glycine และ carnitine และมีแผนฉุกเฉินเมื่อเจ็บป่วย

name: Jacksonian motor partial seizures
formal: Focal motor seizures with march of clonic jerking from a distal body part up the limb, caused by a lesion in the contralateral primary motor cortex; may be followed by Todd paralysis.
simple: Seizures starting with jerking in one hand or foot that spreads up the limb as the seizure moves across the brain.
th: ชักชนิด focal motor ที่กระตุกเริ่มจากส่วนปลาย เช่น นิ้วมือหรือมุมปาก แล้วลามขึ้นไปตามแขนตาม homunculus ของ motor cortex ด้านตรงข้าม หลังชักอาจมีแขนขาอ่อนแรงชั่วคราว (Todd paralysis)
tempoNote: Seconds to a few minutes per seizure; the march spreads over seconds
feat: Clonic jerking that starts in one hand, foot or the face and spreads to neighbouring body parts
Awareness usually preserved unless the seizure spreads widely
May evolve to a bilateral tonic-clonic seizure
Postictal weakness of the involved limb lasting minutes to hours
Usually signals a structural lesion near the primary motor cortex
inv: MRI brain with contrast to look for tumour, infarct, cavernoma, abscess or cortical dysplasia
EEG: focal spikes over the central region (scalp EEG can be normal)
Glucose and sodium: non-ketotic hyperglycaemia can cause focal motor seizures

case.who: 63-year-old man from Udon Thani with hypertension
case.story: Three episodes of jerking that begin in his left thumb, spread to the wrist, elbow and left face within half a minute; he stays aware. His left arm is weak for an hour afterwards.
case.exam: Mild left pronator drift; otherwise normal.
case.tests: MRI shows an enhancing mass in the right precentral gyrus; capillary glucose normal.
case.q: Where is the lesion and what is the postictal weakness called?
case.a: Right primary motor cortex (hand area); the transient weakness is Todd paralysis.

det.patho: The seizure discharge starts in a small part of the primary motor cortex and spreads along adjacent cortex, so jerking follows the somatotopic map, typically hand to arm to face. Common causes are tumours, vascular lesions, cavernous malformations, cortical dysplasia, infection (including neurocysticercosis and tuberculoma), and metabolic triggers such as hyperglycaemia.
det.clinical: Jerking usually begins distally, for example in the thumb or the corner of the mouth, and marches proximally over seconds. Consciousness is typically spared. Sensory equivalents (a spreading tingling) arise from the postcentral gyrus. After the seizure, weakness of the affected limb can last minutes to a day and must not be mistaken for a stroke.
det.diagnosis: The history of a spreading clonic seizure is itself localising. MRI is mandatory to find a lesion; scalp EEG may miss a small focus. Check glucose and electrolytes. In the acute setting with postictal weakness, stroke imaging may be needed to separate Todd paralysis from infarction.
det.treatment: Start a focal antiseizure medication such as levetiracetam, lamotrigine or carbamazepine, and treat the cause (resection, antimicrobial therapy, correction of hyperglycaemia). Surgery near eloquent cortex requires mapping to protect motor function.
det.prognosis: Depends on the underlying lesion; seizures from resectable lesions often stop after surgery.
pearls: A spreading march over seconds is epileptic; over minutes suggests migraine aura.
New Jacksonian seizures in an adult need contrast MRI to look for tumour.
Check glucose: non-ketotic hyperglycaemia is a classic reversible cause of focal motor seizures.
det.thd: Jacksonian seizure คือชักชนิด focal motor ที่เริ่มกระตุกจากนิ้วหรือมุมปาก แล้วลามไปตามแขนขาด้านเดียวกันภายในไม่กี่วินาที ผู้ป่วยมักยังรู้สึกตัว เกิดจากรอยโรคใน primary motor cortex ด้านตรงข้าม เช่น เนื้องอก หลอดเลือดผิดปกติ หรือการติดเชื้อ หลังชักอาจมีแขนขาอ่อนแรงชั่วคราว ต้องตรวจ MRI และน้ำตาลในเลือด รักษาด้วยยากันชักและแก้ไขสาเหตุ
