name: Jansky-Bieschowsky disease (late infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis)
formal: Late infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis CLN2 with seizures, ataxia and regression between ages 2 and 4, caused by TPP1 deficiency; treated with cerliponase alfa enzyme replacement.
simple: An inherited childhood disease causing seizures, loss of skills and vision, from a faulty enzyme in brain cells.
th: โรค CLN2 หรือ late infantile NCL จากการขาดเอนไซม์ TPP1 เด็กอายุ 2–4 ปีเริ่มชัก เดินเซ เสียทักษะที่เคยทำได้ ตามด้วยตามัว มีการรักษาด้วยเอนไซม์ cerliponase alfa ฉีดเข้าโพรงสมอง
tempoNote: Onset with language delay and seizures at 2–4 years, then rapid loss of motor, language and vision over a few years
feat: Language delay or stagnation followed by seizures (myoclonic, atonic, tonic-clonic) at 2–4 years, usually drug-resistant
Severe ataxia and myoclonus, with later loss of walking
Visual failure with macular degeneration and optic atrophy
Loss of previously acquired speech, motor and cognitive skills
Autosomal recessive inheritance with TPP1 (CLN2) variants; sibling cases may be known
inv: TPP1 enzyme activity in leukocytes or dried blood spot as the first-line diagnostic test
TPP1 (CLN2) gene sequencing to confirm
EEG with photoparoxysmal response to slow flashes, and MRI with progressive cerebellar and cerebral atrophy

case.story: She was speaking short sentences until a few months ago, but now stopped talking. She has had three generalised seizures and falls often.
case.exam: Truncal and limb ataxia, myoclonic jerks, few words, optic fundi with early macular changes.
case.tests: EEG shows spikes in posterior regions on slow flash stimulation; MRI shows cerebellar atrophy; leukocyte TPP1 activity very low; biallelic CLN2 variants.
case.q: What disease-specific therapy exists, and how is it given?
case.a: Cerliponase alfa, a recombinant TPP1 enzyme infused every two weeks into the ventricles through an implanted reservoir, which slows loss of motor and language function.

read.where: Chapter 28 Progressive Myoclonic Epilepsies: Neuronal Ceroid Lipofuscinoses

det.patho: Classic late infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (CLN2) results from deficiency of tripeptidyl peptidase 1 (TPP1), a lysosomal enzyme encoded by CLN2 on chromosome 11p15. Autofluorescent lipopigments (ceroid and lipofuscin) accumulate in neurons, retina and some other tissues. Progressive neuronal loss in the cerebral cortex and cerebellum underlies the clinical decline.
det.clinical: Development is typically normal until language delay at about 2 to 3 years, followed by seizures that are myoclonic, atonic, tonic and generalised and are often refractory to drugs. Severe ataxia, myoclonus and dementia follow. Visual failure and macular degeneration may occur early or late. Children lose walking and speech and become dependent within a few years. In the older literature, ophthalmic changes were reported before visual symptoms.
det.diagnosis: Suspect CLN2 in any child with language delay and new seizures at ages 2 to 4. Measure TPP1 activity in leucocytes or dried blood spots, then confirm with CLN2 sequencing. EEG shows posterior spikes at low flash frequencies, and MRI shows cerebellar and later cerebral atrophy. Electron microscopy of skin or conjunctival biopsy for curvilinear profiles is now seldom needed.
det.treatment: Cerliponase alfa, an enzyme replacement given by intraventricular infusion every two weeks through a reservoir, slows motor and language decline and is the first disease-specific therapy; it needs early diagnosis for the best results. Care includes anti-seizure drugs, management of spasticity and dystonia, gastrostomy feeding, respiratory care and palliative support. Genetic counselling is essential.
det.prognosis: Untreated disease progresses to death in late childhood or adolescence; early enzyme replacement can preserve function for longer.
pearls: Language stagnation plus seizures at 2–4 years should prompt a TPP1 enzyme test.
A photoparoxysmal response at slow flash rates on EEG is a classic clue.
Treatment is most effective if started before substantial loss of function.
det.thd: CLN2 หรือ Jansky-Bielschowsky disease เป็นโรค lysosomal จากขาดเอนไซม์ TPP1 ถ่ายทอดแบบยีนด้อย เด็กอายุ 2–4 ปีพัฒนาการด้านภาษาชะงัก ชักควบคุมยาก เดินเซ เสียทักษะ และสูญเสียการมองเห็น ตรวจกิจกรรมเอนไซม์ TPP1 ในเม็ดเลือดขาวแล้วยืนยันด้วยยีน CLN2 EEG พบ photoparoxysmal response ที่ความถี่ช้า รักษาด้วย cerliponase alfa ฉีดเข้าโพรงสมองทุก 2 สัปดาห์ ร่วมกับดูแลอาการชัก ให้อาหาร และการดูแลแบบประคับประคอง

simple: A brain infection spread by mosquitoes in Asia that causes fever, seizures and confusion.
more: Mosquito-borne flavivirus encephalitis in Asia, with fever, seizures, parkinsonism and flaccid paralysis; vaccine preventable and often leaves persistent deficits.

case.who: 9-year-old boy from Surin, rice-farming family who keep pigs; vaccination history uncertain

case.exam: GCS 10, mask-like face, cogwheel rigidity of both arms, coarse tremor, no rash.
case.tests: CSF WBC 80 (90% lymphocytes), protein 0.7 g/L, glucose normal; CSF JEV IgM positive; MRI bilateral thalamic T2 hyperintensities.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what can be offered beyond supportive care?
case.a: Japanese encephalitis; there is no antiviral — treat seizures and raised pressure, support airway and nutrition, rehabilitate, and ensure household children are vaccinated.

Chapter 3 - Pathogenesis and Disease Mechanisms in Neuronal Antibody-Mediated Encephalitis

det.patho: Japanese encephalitis virus is a flavivirus cycling between Culex mosquitoes (notably C. tritaeniorhynchus, breeding in rice paddies), pigs and wading birds; humans are dead-end hosts. Most infections are silent — fewer than 1 in 100 cause encephalitis. The virus targets neurons of the thalamus, basal ganglia, substantia nigra, brainstem and anterior horns, explaining the movement disorder and flaccid paralysis.
det.clinical: After a 5–15-day incubation, fever and headache are followed by reduced consciousness, seizures (frequent in children, sometimes status) and focal signs. Parkinsonism, dystonia and a 'mask' face are classic. A poliomyelitis-like flaccid paralysis can occur with or without encephalitis. Long-term sequelae include cognitive impairment, behavioural problems, epilepsy and motor disability.
det.diagnosis: The standard test is JEV IgM capture ELISA in CSF (more specific) and serum; antibodies may not appear until day 7–10, so repeat if early tests are negative. Dengue or recent vaccination can cause cross-reactive results. Thalamic lesions on MRI in a febrile encephalopathy from an endemic area strongly support the diagnosis. Treat empirically for HSV until it is excluded.
det.treatment: No specific antiviral exists; corticosteroids, interferon and IVIG have not proved beneficial. Care focuses on airway protection, seizure control, managing intracranial pressure, fluids, nutrition and preventing complications, followed by long rehabilitation. Prevention works: Thailand includes live attenuated JE vaccine in the national childhood schedule, and travellers to rural Asia should be vaccinated.
det.prognosis: Around 20–30% of encephalitic patients die and up to half of survivors have lasting neurological or psychiatric sequelae.
pearls: Fever + encephalopathy + parkinsonism + bilateral thalamic lesions in rural Asia: JE.
Positive JEV IgM may cross-react with dengue — interpret with history.
Acute flaccid paralysis in a febrile child in Asia can be JE, not only polio or enterovirus.
det.thd: Japanese encephalitis เกิดจากไวรัสในกลุ่ม flavivirus ที่ยุงรำคาญซึ่งเพาะพันธุ์ในนาข้าวนำมาจากหมูและนก ผู้ติดเชื้อส่วนใหญ่ไม่มีอาการ แต่บางรายมีไข้สูง ซึม ชัก มีอาการคล้ายพาร์กินสัน หรืออ่อนแรงแบบอัมพาตปวกเปียก MRI มักพบ thalamus ทั้งสองข้างผิดปกติ วินิจฉัยด้วย JEV IgM ใน CSF ไม่มียาต้านไวรัสเฉพาะ รักษาแบบประคับประคองและฟื้นฟู การป้องกันด้วยวัคซีนในแผนสร้างเสริมภูมิคุ้มกันของไทยสำคัญที่สุด

name: Jaw tremor
formal: Rhythmic tremor of the jaw, from Parkinson disease, essential tremor, drug-induced causes such as antipsychotics (rabbit syndrome), dystonic tremor or functional movement disorder.
simple: A shaking of the jaw, which can occur with Parkinson disease or as a drug side effect.
th: การสั่นเป็นจังหวะของขากรรไกร พบใน Parkinson's disease, essential tremor, dystonic tremor, ยาต้านจิต (rabbit syndrome) หรือ functional
tempoNote: Usually gradual; acute onset suggests drug exposure
feat: Rest jaw tremor at 4–6 Hz strongly suggests Parkinson's disease
Postural or speech-related jaw tremor occurs in essential tremor, often with head and voice tremor
Jerky, irregular jaw tremor with jaw-opening or closing posture suggests oromandibular dystonia
Perioral rabbit-like movements after antipsychotic exposure (rabbit syndrome)
inv: Careful drug history (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, valproate)
Examine at rest with mouth slightly open, during speech and with sustained jaw opening

case.story: Wife notices his chin shakes while he watches TV and his teeth chatter; for a year his right hand has been slow.
case.exam: Rest tremor of the jaw that settles when he talks, right-sided bradykinesia and cogwheel rigidity, reduced arm swing.
case.tests: Brain MRI unremarkable.
case.q: What does the jaw tremor indicate?
case.a: Rest jaw tremor is a typical feature of Parkinson's disease; levodopa trial is appropriate.

det.patho: Jaw tremor reflects the same oscillatory mechanisms as limb tremor: basal ganglia-thalamocortical rhythm in parkinsonism, cerebello-thalamic oscillation in essential tremor, and abnormal motor programmes in dystonia. Dopamine receptor blockers can produce a perioral tremor through striatal D2 blockade.
det.clinical: This is a sign with several causes rather than a disease. In parkinsonism the tremor is at rest, may involve the lips and chin, and lessens on voluntary movement. In essential tremor it appears with posture or speech, usually late in the course and alongside arm, head or voice tremor. Dystonic jaw tremor is irregular and accompanied by sustained deviation or opening. Rabbit syndrome is a rhythmic perioral tremor about 5 Hz that does not involve the tongue.
det.diagnosis: Watch the jaw at rest with lips gently apart, during speech and during holding the mouth open. Look for parkinsonian signs, dystonic postures, head and voice tremor. Drug exposure is the key history item. DaT imaging can separate degenerative parkinsonism from essential or drug-induced tremor when the picture is mixed.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: levodopa for Parkinson's disease, propranolol or primidone for essential tremor, botulinum toxin for dystonic jaw tremor, and withdrawal of the offending drug plus anticholinergics for rabbit syndrome. Dental and speech therapy input helps functional problems.
det.prognosis: Follows the underlying condition; drug-induced forms usually improve after withdrawal.
pearls: Jaw tremor at rest is far more common in Parkinson's than in essential tremor.
Rabbit syndrome spares the tongue, unlike tardive dyskinesia.
Jaw tremor alone without other signs deserves a drug review first.

det.patho: JC virus variants carrying mutations in the VP1 capsid gene gain tropism for cerebellar granule neurons. Infection causes neuronal loss and cerebellar atrophy rather than the demyelination of classic PML. It occurs in severe cellular immunosuppression.
det.clinical: Patients develop subacute progressive gait and limb ataxia with dysarthria. It may occur alone or alongside classic PML lesions. Settings include HIV, haematological cancer, transplantation and immunomodulatory drugs.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows cerebellar atrophy, sometimes with no white-matter lesions. JCV PCR in CSF supports the diagnosis, although sensitivity is imperfect. Exclude paraneoplastic, toxic and nutritional causes of cerebellar degeneration.
det.treatment: Treatment relies on restoring immunity through ART or withdrawing immunosuppressive drugs. No antiviral agent is proven effective. Immune checkpoint inhibitors have been tried in PML with mixed results. Watch for IRIS after immune recovery.
det.prognosis: Variable; deficits often persist.
pearls: Progressive ataxia in immunosuppressed patient = test CSF for JCV.
Atrophy without lesions does not exclude JC virus.
Immune reconstitution is the only treatment.

formal: Stiff-person-like syndrome with painful spasms and prominent startle-induced jerks, often with brainstem involvement and glycine receptor antibodies, as in PERM.
simple: A rare condition with muscle stiffness, painful spasms and sudden jerks, often set off by noise or touch.

case.story: Over two months his back and legs became stiff and painful; any sudden noise makes his whole body jerk and he falls. He now has double vision and choking on liquids.
case.exam: Rigid trunk, stimulus-sensitive jerks on tapping the lip or limbs, gaze-evoked nystagmus, brisk reflexes.

det.patho: The term was used for patients with stiffness plus marked jerking and brainstem involvement and today sits within the stiff-person spectrum, overlapping PERM. Glycine receptor antibodies reduce inhibitory glycinergic transmission in brainstem and spinal cord, causing excessive motor activity and startle. Some cases have GAD65, DPPX or amphiphysin antibodies or an underlying tumour.
det.clinical: Stiffness and spasms resemble classic SPS, but sudden jerks triggered by sound, touch or emotion dominate. Brainstem features (ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus, dysphagia), sensory symptoms and autonomic instability suggest progression to PERM, which can be life threatening through respiratory failure. DPPX cases often begin with diarrhoea and weight loss.
det.diagnosis: Base the diagnosis on clinical features, EMG evidence of continuous motor unit firing with stimulus-sensitive reflexes, and antibody testing in serum and CSF. CSF may show mild pleocytosis. Screen for thymoma, lymphoma and other cancers. Exclude tetanus, strychnine exposure and structural brainstem or cord lesions.
det.treatment: Treat early with immunotherapy: IV methylprednisolone, IVIG or plasma exchange, then rituximab or other agents for maintenance; remove any tumour. Symptomatic treatment includes benzodiazepines (diazepam, clonazepam), baclofen and levetiracetam or other agents for myoclonus. Severe cases may need ICU care.
det.prognosis: Many GlyR-positive patients improve substantially with immunotherapy; relapses occur and untreated PERM can be fatal.
pearls: Stiffness plus startle jerks plus brainstem signs: test GlyR antibodies, not just GAD65.
This is an immunotherapy-responsive syndrome; do not label it functional.
Always look for thymoma or lymphoma.

det.patho: Joubert syndrome and related disorders are ciliopathies, caused by biallelic variants in genes whose products build or maintain the primary cilium and its transition zone. Failure of ciliary signalling alters cerebellar and brainstem development, producing vermis hypoplasia and absent decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles and corticospinal tracts, the basis of the molar tooth sign. Retina, kidney and liver also depend on cilia, which explains the multisystem expression.
det.clinical: Infants are hypotonic with abnormal breathing patterns, followed by delayed motor and language milestones, gait ataxia and abnormal eye movements, including oculomotor apraxia and nystagmus. Intellectual outcome varies from normal to severe disability. Some children have retinal dystrophy, coloboma, polydactyly, renal cysts with progressive nephronophthisis leading to kidney failure, and liver fibrosis with portal hypertension. Breathing irregularities usually fade by early childhood, while renal and hepatic disease can emerge years later.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on clinical signs and the molar tooth sign on MRI, with confirmation by gene panel or exome. The molar tooth sign is best seen on axial images at the isthmus level, and it also appears in related disorders. Because the subtypes carry different organ risks, genetic confirmation allows tailored surveillance. Exclude Dandy–Walker spectrum, pontocerebellar hypoplasia and other cerebellar malformations.
det.treatment: No cure exists; care is multidisciplinary. Monitor breathing in infancy, give physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy, and manage vision with low-vision support. Yearly kidney function, urine concentration and liver tests detect organ disease early, with nephrology care and transplant planning when needed and avoidance of nephrotoxic drugs. Offer genetic counselling to the family because recurrence risk is 25% in each pregnancy.
det.prognosis: Variable. Severe respiratory or renal and hepatic involvement limits survival in some, whereas many children survive into adulthood with developmental disability.
pearls: Hypotonic infant with episodic panting and apnoea plus abnormal eye movements: image the brainstem for the molar tooth sign.
Screen kidney, liver and retina for life, as the gene predicts organ risk.
The molar tooth sign is a shape in the midbrain, not a single disease: confirm with genetics.

formal: Combined lesion of cranial nerves IX, X and XI at the jugular foramen, causing dysphagia, hoarseness and shoulder weakness; typically from glomus tumours or skull base disease.
simple: Damage to three cranial nerves leaving the skull, causing trouble swallowing, hoarse voice and weak shoulder.

det.patho: The jugular foramen transmits cranial nerves IX, X and XI with the internal jugular vein. Lesions here include paragangliomas, schwannomas, meningiomas, metastases, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, skull base osteomyelitis, trauma and jugular vein thrombosis. Involvement of XII or the sympathetic chain indicates extension beyond the foramen.
det.clinical: Patients present with dysphagia, hoarseness and shoulder weakness on one side. Pulsatile tinnitus or conductive hearing loss suggests glomus tumour. Headache, otalgia and other cranial neuropathies may coexist.
det.diagnosis: MRI and CT of the skull base define the lesion. Laryngoscopy confirms vocal cord palsy. Catecholamine testing may be needed for functional paragangliomas, and biopsy is required for suspected malignancy.
det.treatment: Treatment targets the cause: surgery, radiosurgery or radiotherapy for tumours, antibiotics for skull base osteomyelitis. Speech and swallowing therapy, vocal cord medialisation and feeding support help symptoms.
det.prognosis: Depends on the lesion; glomus tumours grow slowly and are often controlled with radiosurgery.
pearls: IX + X + XI on one side = jugular foramen.
Pulsatile tinnitus points to a glomus jugulare tumour.
In Thailand, consider nasopharyngeal carcinoma in lower cranial nerve palsies.
det.thd: Jugular foramen syndrome หรือ Vernet syndrome คือเส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 9, 10, 11 เสียพร้อมกันจากรอยโรคที่ jugular foramen ทำให้กลืนลำบาก สำลัก เสียงแหบ และยักไหล่อ่อนแรงข้างเดียว สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยคือ glomus jugulare tumour ซึ่งมักมีเสียงหึ่งเต้นตามชีพจรในหู และในไทยควรคิดถึงมะเร็งโพรงหลังจมูก วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI และ CT ฐานกะโหลก รักษาตามสาเหตุ

qx.stem: A 46-year-old woman from Lampang reports six months of a pulsatile whooshing sound in the right ear, hoarseness and choking on thin fluids. Examination shows a reddish mass behind the intact right tympanic membrane, a lower palate on the right with the uvula pulled to the left, an immobile right vocal cord and a weak right trapezius. Tongue movement is normal and there is no Horner syndrome.
qx.q: Which lesion is most likely, and which statement about work-up is correct?
opts: Vestibular schwannoma; confirm with audiometry and proceed to stereotactic biopsy
Glomus jugulare paraganglioma; obtain contrast MRI and CT of the skull base and avoid blind biopsy of the vascular mass
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma; the first step is endoscopic biopsy of the tympanic mass
Facial nerve schwannoma; MRI of the internal acoustic meatus is sufficient
Cholesteatoma; surgical exploration of the middle ear is the next step
qx.why: Pulsatile tinnitus with a vascular retrotympanic mass and IX, X and XI palsy with a spared hypoglossal nerve localises to the jugular foramen and typically reflects a glomus jugulare tumour. Imaging, often with angiography or functional studies for catecholamine secretion, comes before any tissue sampling because of bleeding risk. A vestibular schwannoma involves the internal acoustic meatus and the VIII nerve, and a cholesteatoma does not paralyse the lower cranial nerves.

qx.stem: A 17-year-old female university student drops her toothbrush most mornings from sudden arm jerks and had a convulsion after an all-night exam revision. A clinic started carbamazepine and the jerks became more frequent. EEG shows generalised 4–6 Hz polyspike-and-wave with a photoparoxysmal response.

opts: Increase carbamazepine to a higher dose
Switch to valproate as first choice
Add phenytoin
Stop all medicines; this syndrome remits by age 20

qx.why: Morning myoclonus, tonic–clonic seizures after sleep deprivation and fast generalised polyspike-wave indicate juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. Sodium-channel drugs like carbamazepine and phenytoin can worsen myoclonus. Valproate is highly effective but should be avoided where possible in women who could become pregnant; levetiracetam is a good alternative. Remission is uncommon, so treatment is usually long-term.

qx.stem: A 16-year-old schoolgirl drops her toothbrush most mornings because of brief arm jerks, and last week had a convulsion after an all-night study session. Examination is normal. EEG shows generalized 4–5 Hz polyspike-and-wave discharges that increase with photic stimulation. She is not sexually active but may be in the future.
qx.q: Which is the most appropriate first antiseizure medication?
opts: Sodium valproate, as it is the most effective drug for this syndrome
Carbamazepine, titrated slowly
Levetiracetam
Oxcarbazepine
Gabapentin
qx.why: This is juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. Current regulatory guidance (EMA, MHRA 2024) says valproate should not be started in girls or women who could become pregnant unless no other option works, because of major malformation and neurodevelopmental risks. Levetiracetam (or lamotrigine, which may worsen myoclonus) is preferred. Sodium-channel drugs such as carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine, and gabapentin, can aggravate myoclonic and absence seizures.

qx.stem: A 23-year-old accountant has had no myoclonic jerks or convulsions for four years on levetiracetam. She was diagnosed at age 15 after morning jerks and two tonic-clonic seizures, and her EEG then showed generalized polyspike-wave with photosensitivity. A recent EEG still shows brief generalized polyspikes. She asks to stop treatment.
qx.q: Which advice is most accurate?
opts: Relapse after stopping is likely in this syndrome; long-term treatment is usually advised, with the choice of drug reviewed for pregnancy planning
She can safely stop because four seizure-free years guarantees remission
Taper over one week and resume only if two convulsions occur
Switching to carbamazepine would allow eventual withdrawal
Persistent EEG discharges have no bearing on relapse risk
qx.why: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy usually lasts for life, and most patients relapse after withdrawal, especially with ongoing epileptiform discharges or photosensitivity. Teen onset and generalized polyspikes add to the risk. Any withdrawal should be slow, done with full understanding of the risk, and paired with advice on sleep and driving. Carbamazepine can worsen myoclonic seizures.

det.patho: JME is a common idiopathic generalised epilepsy with complex polygenic inheritance; first-degree relatives often have generalised epilepsies. Imaging and network studies suggest altered thalamo-frontal connectivity, though routine MRI is normal. Onset is usually between 12 and 18 years, and it accounts for roughly 5–10% of all epilepsies.
det.clinical: The hallmark is brief bilateral myoclonic jerks of the arms, mostly within an hour or two of waking, with preserved awareness; patients often regard them as clumsiness. Most patients also have generalised tonic-clonic seizures, often provoked by lack of sleep, alcohol or stress, and some have absence seizures. Photosensitivity is common. Because the jerks go unreported, the diagnosis is frequently missed until the first convulsion — direct questioning about morning jerks is essential.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by EEG showing generalised 4–6 Hz polyspike-and-wave discharges on a normal background, often triggered by photic stimulation or sleep deprivation. A sleep-deprived EEG improves yield. MRI is normal and is not required in a typical case. Focal-looking EEG asymmetries are common and should not redirect the diagnosis to focal epilepsy if the clinical picture fits.
det.treatment: Broad-spectrum antiseizure medication is used: valproate is the most effective but should be avoided in women and girls who could become pregnant because of teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risks; levetiracetam and lamotrigine (which can sometimes worsen myoclonus) are common alternatives, with topiramate or perampanel as further options. Carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, gabapentin and pregabalin may aggravate myoclonic and absence seizures. Counsel about regular sleep, alcohol limits and driving regulations.
det.prognosis: Seizures are usually well controlled with treatment, but the condition is typically lifelong, with high relapse rates after drug withdrawal.
pearls: Always ask a teenager with a first convulsion whether they drop things or jerk in the morning.
Sodium-channel blockers can make JME worse.
Plan contraception and pregnancy counselling before choosing a drug for a young woman.

simple: An inherited childhood disease that first causes loss of vision, followed by seizures and loss of skills.

det.patho: Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses are lysosomal storage disorders in which autofluorescent lipopigment (ceroid and lipofuscin) accumulates in brain, retina and some visceral tissues. CLN3 encodes battenin, a lysosomal membrane protein whose function is incompletely understood. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
det.clinical: Children are normal, then lose vision between 4 and 7 years, which often prompts treatment for refractive error before the diagnosis is made. Seizures and dementia follow in the next years with myoclonus, fast hesitant speech and psychiatric symptoms. Loss of walking occurs in the second decade because of parkinsonism and spasticity, and death is usually in the late teens to twenties.
det.diagnosis: Consider CLN3 in any school-age child with fast visual loss and a retinopathy out of proportion to refractive error. A blood film with vacuolated lymphocytes, a flat or markedly reduced ERG and homozygous CLN3 variants confirm it. Because some forms of NCL now have specific treatment, genetic confirmation is important to separate them. Electron microscopy of skin shows fingerprint inclusions if genetics is unavailable.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy is approved for CLN3 disease. Management is supportive: low-vision services and school adaptation, antiseizure drugs (levetiracetam, valproate and lamotrigine are common choices), treatment of psychiatric symptoms and parkinsonism, physiotherapy, swallowing care and palliative planning. Cerliponase alfa is only for CLN2, so confirm the subtype before counselling the family.
det.prognosis: Relentless progression with survival into the late teens or twenties.
pearls: School-age child going blind with a normal-looking eye: think NCL and look at the blood film.
Early blindness with later dementia suggests CLN3, early seizures with later blindness CLN2.
CLN2 is the only NCL with enzyme replacement; genotype matters.

name: Juvenile neuronopathic Gaucher’s disease
formal: Neuronopathic Gaucher disease with onset in childhood, causing supranuclear gaze palsy, myoclonic seizures and ataxia, plus organomegaly, from glucocerebrosidase deficiency.
simple: An inherited enzyme disorder in children that affects the brain, causing abnormal eye movements, seizures and balance problems.

det.patho: Recessive GBA1 variants reduce glucocerebrosidase, so glucosylceramide and glucosylsphingosine build up in macrophages (Gaucher cells) of spleen, liver and marrow. In type 3, residual enzyme is low enough for neurons to be affected, especially brainstem saccade generators, but higher than in the fatal infantile type 2. Certain genotypes such as L444P homozygosity predict neuronopathic disease and are common in Asia.
det.clinical: Children present with organomegaly and cytopenias, then show a horizontal saccade initiation defect that may be the only neurological sign for years. Others develop progressive myoclonic epilepsy, ataxia, spasticity and cognitive impairment. Severity varies widely, even within one genotype; some adults have only the eye movement sign.
det.diagnosis: Confirm low glucocerebrosidase activity and GBA1 variants. Look specifically at horizontal saccades, since this sign defines neuronopathic disease. Biomarkers (lyso-Gb1) track visceral burden. EEG, MRI and neuropsychology document CNS involvement.
det.treatment: Enzyme replacement (imiglucerase and related agents) reverses visceral, haematological and much of the bone disease but has little effect on the brain. Substrate reduction agents that penetrate the brain and other approaches (chaperones, gene therapy) are being studied. Treat seizures with standard agents and provide educational and rehabilitation support; HSCT is rarely used now.
det.prognosis: Variable; many survive into adulthood with treatment, but those with progressive myoclonic epilepsy decline.
pearls: Splenomegaly + head thrusts to look sideways: Gaucher type 3.
Enzyme therapy treats the body, not the brain.
Carrying one GBA1 variant is a frequent inherited risk for Parkinson disease.

Sleep benefit and slow progression in PRKN (parkin) disease
Pyramidal signs, gaze palsy, dementia or systemic signs point to complex causes
Treatable mimics: Wilson's disease, dopa-responsive dystonia
inv: Ceruloplasmin in serum, urinary copper over 24 h, and a slit-lamp check for Kayser–Fleischer rings
Brain MRI: normal in PRKN; abnormal in Wilson, NBIA, Kufor-Rakeb
Genetic panel (PRKN, PINK1, DJ1, ATP13A2, PLA2G6, FBXO7, GCH1, TH)
DaT-SPECT shows presynaptic loss in degenerative forms, normal in DRD

case.who: 17-year-old boy from Khon Kaen, parents are first cousins
case.story: Two years of right foot turning in while walking, slow handwriting and stiffness; symptoms milder after sleep.
case.exam: Right foot dystonia, bradykinesia and rigidity, brisk reflexes, no gaze palsy, no Kayser–Fleischer rings.
case.tests: Ceruloplasmin normal; MRI normal; genetic testing shows homozygous PRKN exon deletion.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what treatment issue is expected?
case.a: PRKN-related juvenile parkinsonism; good levodopa response but early dyskinesia, so start low and consider agonists.

det.patho: Most cases in consanguineous or recessive families are due to biallelic variants in PRKN, PINK1 or DJ1, genes that work in mitochondrial quality control (mitophagy). Nigral neuron loss occurs, often without Lewy bodies in PRKN disease. Complex forms come from ATP13A2 (Kufor-Rakeb), PLA2G6, FBXO7 and other genes, and secondary causes include Wilson's disease, juvenile Huntington's disease and drugs.
det.clinical: Isolated juvenile parkinsonism usually begins with dystonia of a foot or leg, slowness and stiffness, sometimes with sleep benefit. Tremor is less common than in late-onset Parkinson's disease, and cognition is usually preserved. Additional pyramidal signs, supranuclear gaze palsy, cognitive decline, seizures or psychiatric features suggest a complex genetic form or a metabolic disorder.
det.diagnosis: Exclude treatable causes first: copper studies and slit lamp for Wilson's disease, and a levodopa trial with consideration of GCH1 or TH testing for dopa-responsive dystonia. MRI helps detect iron deposition, basal ganglia lesions or atrophy. DaT-SPECT distinguishes degenerative presynaptic loss from DRD. Gene panels or exome sequencing now give a molecular diagnosis in many families.
det.treatment: Levodopa works very well but motor fluctuations and dyskinesia appear early, so lower doses, dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors or amantadine are often used. Deep brain stimulation is effective in selected PRKN patients. Copper chelation or zinc is essential for Wilson's disease. Genetic counselling and psychosocial support for a young patient are important.
det.prognosis: PRKN and PINK1 forms progress slowly with long survival; complex forms progress faster with more disability.
pearls: In every young patient with parkinsonism, rule out Wilson's disease.
Foot dystonia as the first sign in a teenager suggests PRKN or DRD.
Early dyskinesia with small levodopa doses is typical of PRKN disease.
det.thd: Juvenile parkinsonism คือ parkinsonism ที่เริ่มก่อนอายุ 21 ปี สาเหตุหลักคือยีนแบบ recessive เช่น PRKN และ PINK1 ผู้ป่วยมักมี dystonia ที่เท้า เคลื่อนไหวช้า ตอบสนองต่อ levodopa ดีแต่มี dyskinesia เร็ว ต้องตัด Wilson's disease และ dopa-responsive dystonia ก่อนเสมอ วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจทองแดง MRI DaT-SPECT และตรวจยีน

name: Juvenile segmental SMA
formal: Focal lower motor neuron disease affecting one limb with asymmetric wasting, usually self-limited, as in monomelic amyotrophy (Hirayama or Sobue).
simple: A rare condition where muscles of one arm or leg waste away in young people and then the disease stops on its own.
more: EMG shows anterior horn cell loss in a segment; MRI may show cord flexion changes. A neck collar may help; typically plateaus within 1-5 years.
ab: Juvenile muscular atrophy of the distal upper extremity
th: โรคกล้ามเนื้อแขนข้างเดียวลีบอ่อนแรงในชายวัยรุ่น ดำเนินโรคช้าแล้วหยุดเอง เช่น Hirayama disease
tempoNote: Insidious progression for 1–5 years, then spontaneous arrest
feat: Young men 15–25 years, mostly in Asia including Thailand
Unilateral or asymmetric wasting of hand and forearm with oblique amyotrophy sparing brachioradialis
Cold paresis: weakness worse in cold; tremulous finger movements
No sensory loss, no pyramidal signs, reflexes normal or slightly reduced
Leg forms exist (monomelic leg amyotrophy) but are rarer
inv: EMG: chronic denervation in C7–T1 myotomes, normal sensory potentials
Flexion cervical MRI: forward shift of posterior dura and lower cervical cord flattening
Exclude MMN (conduction block) and syrinx or tumour

case.who: 19-year-old male vocational student from Nakhon Pathom
case.story: Two years of slowly worsening weakness and thinning of the right hand; symptoms worse in air-conditioned classrooms.
case.exam: Wasting of right intrinsic hand muscles and ulnar forearm, brachioradialis spared, no sensory loss, reflexes normal.
case.tests: EMG chronic denervation in right C8–T1 muscles; neck-flexion MRI shows anterior displacement of the posterior dura with cord flattening at C5–C7.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the key management advice?
case.a: Hirayama disease (juvenile segmental SMA); avoid repeated neck flexion, use a cervical collar during the progressive phase.

read.where: Chapter 15 Disorders of the Motor Cells: The Motor Neuron Diseases — Flail Arm/Leg Syndrome and Hirayama’s Disease
Chapter 9: Hirayama Disease and Other Focal Amyotrophies

det.patho: The leading theory is that repeated neck flexion causes forward displacement of the lower cervical dura, compressing the cord and causing chronic microcirculatory ischaemia of anterior horn cells. A tight dural sac relative to vertebral growth during adolescence may explain the age range and arrest after growth ends. Other forms without dural shift probably have different causes.
det.clinical: Typical patients are adolescent males with insidious unilateral hand weakness and forearm wasting, sparing brachioradialis to give an oblique pattern. Weakness worsens with cold and fine finger tremor is common. The condition progresses for a few years and then plateaus. Upper motor neuron and sensory signs are absent.
det.diagnosis: EMG shows chronic neurogenic change limited to lower cervical myotomes with normal sensory responses. Neutral MRI may show only cord atrophy; flexion MRI demonstrates dural shift and epidural venous engorgement. Nerve conduction excludes MMN and ulnar neuropathy. ALS should be considered if signs spread or upper motor neuron features emerge.
det.treatment: Avoiding sustained neck flexion and wearing a cervical collar during the active phase may halt progression. Surgery such as duraplasty or anterior decompression is reserved for selected progressive cases. Hand therapy and occupational adaptation help function.
det.prognosis: Benign; progression stops within about five years, leaving stable focal weakness.
pearls: Young Asian male, unilateral hand wasting, sparing brachioradialis: Hirayama.
Order flexion MRI; neutral MRI can miss it.
Cold paresis is a characteristic symptom.
det.thd: Juvenile segmental SMA หรือ Hirayama disease พบในชายวัยรุ่น โดยเฉพาะในเอเชีย มีกล้ามเนื้อมือและแขนข้างเดียวลีบอ่อนแรงช้าๆ ไม่มีอาการชา และหยุดลุกลามเองภายในไม่กี่ปี สาเหตุเชื่อว่าเกิดจากการก้มคอทำให้เยื่อหุ้มไขสันหลังกดไขสันหลังส่วนคอ ตรวจ MRI ท่าก้มคอและ EMG การรักษาคือเลี่ยงการก้มคอและใส่ collar ช่วงที่โรคยังลุกลาม

name: Juvenile-onset Huntington’s disease
formal: Huntington disease with onset before age 20, with rigidity, bradykinesia, seizures and cognitive decline rather than chorea, associated with CAG repeats over 60.
simple: Huntington disease that starts in childhood or teens, causing stiffness, seizures and learning decline.
more: Huntington disease starting in childhood or adolescence, with rigidity, dystonia, seizures and cognitive decline rather than chorea, associated with large CAG repeat expansions inherited paternally.
th: โรคฮันติงตันที่เริ่มก่อนอายุ 20 ปี พบอาการเกร็ง เคลื่อนไหวช้า ชัก และเรียนแย่ลงมากกว่าอาการกระตุกแบบ chorea
tempoNote: Onset before age 20; progression faster than in adult-onset disease
feat: Falling school performance and behaviour change as early features
Rigidity, bradykinesia and dystonia in place of chorea (Westphal variant)
Seizures in a substantial proportion, especially with onset in early childhood
Dysarthria, drooling, dysphagia, slow saccades and gait difficulty
Large CAG expansion (often above 60) usually inherited from the father
inv: HTT CAG repeat analysis, with careful counselling and diagnostic-only testing in minors
MRI: caudate and putamen atrophy with enlarged frontal horns
EEG if seizures; copper studies and slit lamp to exclude Wilson disease
Metabolic and mitochondrial screen when family history is unclear

case.story: Over two years his grades fell, he became irritable, his movements slowed, and recently he had two generalised seizures. His father developed involuntary movements in his 30s.
case.exam: Rigid limbs, slow movements, dystonic foot posture, slow saccades, no chorea.
case.tests: HTT CAG repeat of 78; MRI shows caudate atrophy; copper studies normal.
case.q: Why does this child have such a different picture from his father?
case.a: Juvenile HD. Paternal transmission tends to lengthen the CAG repeat, and a very long repeat produces an akinetic-rigid picture with seizures rather than chorea.

read.where: 12 The Many Faces of Parkinsonism: A Review of the Parkinson Look-alike Syndromes

det.patho: Juvenile HD arises from an expanded CAG repeat in HTT, producing a polyglutamine-rich mutant huntingtin that damages striatal medium spiny neurons. Longer repeats mean earlier onset (an inverse relationship), and repeats above about 60 usually cause onset before 20. Anticipation is strongest with paternal inheritance because of instability in spermatogenesis. Around 5–10% of HD begins in childhood or adolescence.
det.clinical: Children present with school failure, behavioural and psychiatric change, and motor signs that are rigid and dystonic rather than choreic. Seizures, tremor, ataxia and dysarthria are common, particularly with younger onset. Teenagers may show a mixed picture with chorea. Progress is quicker than in adults and swallowing problems, weight loss and falls appear early. Ask for family history, which may be hidden or unrecognised in a parent.
det.diagnosis: Confirm by HTT repeat testing in symptomatic children, with genetic counselling and psychological support. MRI shows striatal atrophy but may be normal early. The differential is wide and includes Wilson disease, NBIA, mitochondrial disease, metabolic disorders and DRPLA, so targeted tests are often needed. Predictive testing in asymptomatic minors is not offered.
det.treatment: No therapy slows disease. Treat symptoms: anti-seizure medicines, baclofen or botulinum toxin for dystonia and rigidity, and levodopa trials in rigid forms. Support behaviour, school and mood problems and arrange swallowing, nutritional and palliative planning. Family counselling and cascade risk assessment are essential.
det.prognosis: Survival is typically 10–15 years from onset, shorter than in adult-onset disease.
pearls: Rigidity plus seizures in a child with a paternal family history suggests juvenile HD.
Exclude Wilson disease first because it is treatable.
Paternal transmission drives repeat expansion.
det.thd: Juvenile Huntington’s disease คือโรคฮันติงตันที่เริ่มก่อนอายุ 20 ปี เกิดจากการซ้ำของ CAG ในยีน HTT จำนวนมาก (มักเกิน 60) และมักได้รับจากพ่อ เด็กจะเรียนแย่ลง พฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน แข็งเกร็ง เคลื่อนไหวช้า มีท่าเกร็งผิดปกติและชัก มากกว่ากระตุกแบบ chorea MRI พบ caudate ฝ่อ การวินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีน HTT ต้องแยกโรค Wilson ที่รักษาได้ก่อน การรักษาเป็นตามอาการ เช่น ยากันชัก baclofen และให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม โรคดำเนินเร็วกว่าชนิดผู้ใหญ่

name: Kallmann syndrome
formal: Genetic disorder with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and anosmia from failed migration of GnRH neurons; may include mirror movements, renal agenesis and hearing loss.
simple: An inherited condition causing absent sense of smell and delayed puberty.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมที่มี hypogonadotropic hypogonadism ร่วมกับไม่ได้กลิ่น จากการเคลื่อนย้ายของเซลล์ GnRH ผิดปกติ อาจมี mirror movements
tempoNote: Congenital; usually recognised at absent or delayed puberty
feat: Delayed or absent puberty, small testes, primary amenorrhoea
Anosmia or hyposmia from absent or small olfactory bulbs
Mirror movements (bimanual synkinesia), especially with ANOS1 (KAL1)
Unilateral renal agenesis, cleft lip/palate, dental agenesis, hearing loss in some
inv: Low testosterone or oestradiol with low or inappropriately normal LH and FSH
Smell testing (UPSIT or similar)
MRI of olfactory bulbs and sulci, pituitary imaging
Genetic testing (ANOS1, FGFR1, CHD7, PROKR2 and others); renal ultrasound

case.who: 17-year-old boy brought to an endocrine clinic in Chiang Mai
case.story: No signs of puberty; he has never been able to smell food. When he writes with his right hand, his left hand copies the movement.
case.exam: Prepubertal genitalia, no facial hair, mirror movements of both hands, otherwise normal neurology.
case.tests: LH and FSH low, testosterone very low; MRI shows absent olfactory bulbs; renal ultrasound shows a single kidney.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what explains the mirror movements?
case.a: Kallmann syndrome (likely X-linked ANOS1); abnormal crossing of the corticospinal tract gives mirror movements.

det.patho: GnRH neurons originate in the olfactory placode and migrate along olfactory nerve fibres into the forebrain. Variants in ANOS1, FGFR1, PROKR2, CHD7 and other genes disrupt this journey, giving both GnRH deficiency and olfactory bulb hypoplasia. Inheritance can be X-linked, dominant or recessive, and oligogenic cases are recognised.
det.clinical: It is mainly an endocrine and developmental disorder with neurological features. Boys may have micropenis or cryptorchidism at birth; most cases are recognised in adolescence because puberty fails. Anosmia is often unnoticed by the patient. Mirror movements, sensorineural deafness, eye movement abnormalities and cerebellar signs occur in some genetic subtypes, and CHD7 overlaps with CHARGE syndrome.
det.diagnosis: Biochemistry shows low sex steroids with low or inappropriately normal gonadotropins and otherwise normal pituitary function. Formal smell testing and MRI of the olfactory system confirm the olfactory component. Pituitary and hypothalamic lesions must be excluded. Genetic testing helps counselling but is negative in a proportion.
det.treatment: Sex steroid replacement induces puberty and maintains bone and sexual health; gonadotropins or pulsatile GnRH are used when fertility is desired. Anosmia has no treatment, so smoke and gas alarms are advised. Bone density monitoring and psychological support are part of care. Some patients recover reproductive function later in life.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is normal; fertility is often achievable with treatment.
pearls: Delayed puberty plus inability to smell: ask about mirror movements and check the kidneys.
Normal pituitary MRI with absent olfactory bulbs is the imaging signature.
Mirror movements reflect abnormal ipsilateral corticospinal projections.
det.thd: Kallmann syndrome เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมที่เซลล์ GnRH เคลื่อนย้ายจากบริเวณจมูกไปสมองไม่สำเร็จ จึงมีภาวะไม่เข้าสู่วัยหนุ่มสาวร่วมกับไม่ได้กลิ่น บางรายมี mirror movements ไตข้างเดียว หรือหูตึง วินิจฉัยด้วยฮอร์โมน การทดสอบกลิ่น MRI olfactory bulb และตรวจยีน รักษาด้วยฮอร์โมนเพศและ gonadotropin เมื่อต้องการมีบุตร

name: Kanner’s disease
formal: Early infantile autism as originally described by Kanner, a neurodevelopmental disorder with impaired social interaction, language delay and repetitive behaviours.
simple: The original name for classic autism, a developmental condition affecting communication, social interaction and behaviour.
th: ออทิสซึมแบบคลาสสิกที่ Kanner บรรยายไว้ เป็นโรคพัฒนาการทางระบบประสาทที่มีปัญหาการสื่อสารและปฏิสัมพันธ์ทางสังคม พูดช้า และพฤติกรรมซ้ำๆ
tempoNote: Signs appear in the first 2–3 years of life and persist; some children show regression of language around 18–24 months
feat: Historical eponym; now part of autism spectrum disorder (DSM-5-TR, ICD-11)
Impaired social communication: poor eye contact, lack of shared attention, delayed or unusual language
Restricted, repetitive behaviours: stereotypies, insistence on sameness, intense interests, sensory sensitivities
Intellectual disability and epilepsy are common companions
Genetic causes found in a minority: fragile X, tuberous sclerosis, copy-number variants
inv: Developmental assessment with validated tools (e.g. M-CHAT screening, ADOS)
Hearing test in every child with speech delay
Chromosomal microarray, FMR1 testing; exome if dysmorphic or intellectual disability
EEG only if seizures or regression

case.story: Has no words, does not respond to his name, lines up toy cars for hours and screams if the route to grandma's house changes.
case.exam: Poor eye contact, no pointing, hand flapping, normal growth and no dysmorphism, normal neurological examination.
case.tests: Hearing normal; microarray and FMR1 normal; M-CHAT high risk, ADOS consistent with autism.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what treatment has the strongest evidence?
case.a: Autism spectrum disorder (classic Kanner type); early intensive behavioural and developmental intervention with speech therapy.

read.where: Section IV: General Principles of Therapy

det.patho: Autism has high heritability, involving many common variants plus rare de novo variants and copy-number changes in genes for synaptic function, chromatin regulation and neuronal development. Altered cortical connectivity and synaptic balance are thought to underlie the social and sensory features. Environmental factors such as prematurity and prenatal valproate exposure add risk, while vaccines do not.
det.clinical: Leo Kanner described children with profound social aloofness, language abnormalities and insistence on sameness in 1943. Today the condition is diagnosed along a spectrum, with specifiers for intellectual and language impairment. Signs include delayed speech, echolalia, lack of pointing and shared attention, repetitive play and sensory sensitivities. Epilepsy affects a sizeable minority, peaking in early childhood and adolescence.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, using DSM-5-TR criteria supported by structured assessments such as ADOS-2. Every child should have hearing and vision assessed. Genetic testing with microarray and fragile X testing is recommended, with exome sequencing increasingly offered. Neurological examination looks for macrocephaly, skin signs of tuberous sclerosis and regression suggesting other disorders.
det.treatment: Early intensive behavioural and developmental intervention, speech and occupational therapy and parent training improve outcomes. Medications treat associated problems: risperidone or aripiprazole for severe irritability, melatonin for sleep, and stimulants for ADHD symptoms. Seizures are treated with standard antiseizure medication. Families benefit from social and educational support.
det.prognosis: Outcome ranges from independent adult life to lifelong dependence; early language and nonverbal IQ are the best predictors.
pearls: Test hearing in any child with speech delay before diagnosing autism.
Regression of hand use in a girl suggests Rett rather than autism.
Fragile X testing is part of the routine work-up.
det.thd: Kanner’s disease หรือออทิสซึมแบบคลาสสิก ปัจจุบันจัดอยู่ใน autism spectrum disorder เป็นโรคพัฒนาการทางระบบประสาทที่มีปัญหาการสื่อสารและปฏิสัมพันธ์ทางสังคม พูดช้า และพฤติกรรมซ้ำๆ หรือยึดติดกับสิ่งเดิม การวินิจฉัยเป็นทางคลินิก ต้องตรวจการได้ยินและส่งตรวจพันธุกรรมพื้นฐาน การรักษาสำคัญคือการกระตุ้นพัฒนาการแบบเข้มข้นตั้งแต่เนิ่นๆ และใช้ยารักษาอาการร่วม

name: Katayama syndrome
formal: Acute schistosomiasis with fever, urticaria and eosinophilia occurring several weeks after exposure, sometimes with encephalopathy or cord involvement from egg migration.
simple: A feverish illness caused by schistosome worms in people newly infected, which can rarely affect the brain or spinal cord.
th: ระยะเฉียบพลันของโรคพยาธิใบไม้เลือด schistosomiasis มีไข้ ผื่นลมพิษ eosinophil สูง หลังสัมผัสน้ำจืดหลายสัปดาห์ บางรายมีอาการทางสมองหรือไขสันหลัง
tempoNote: Begins about 2–8 weeks after freshwater exposure and lasts days to weeks
feat: Fever, urticaria, cough, myalgia, diarrhoea and headache weeks after freshwater swimming in endemic areas
Marked eosinophilia
Neurological involvement is uncommon: encephalopathy, focal deficits or myelitis from egg deposition or immune reaction
Typically seen in non-immune travellers; Thailand is not a major endemic area but Mekong-region exposure (S. mekongi) matters
Treat with praziquantel plus corticosteroids when neurological or severe
inv: Blood count with eosinophils; schistosomal serology (may be negative early, repeat later)
Stool or urine for eggs (often negative in the acute phase)
MRI brain or spine if neurological signs; CSF may show eosinophils
Chest imaging for pulmonary infiltrates

case.who: 34-year-old Thai volunteer returning to Ubon Ratchathani after three months in Laos near the Mekong
case.story: Four weeks after swimming in the river he developed fever, itchy hives and cough; now has leg numbness and urinary hesitancy.
case.exam: Febrile, urticarial rash, mild paraparesis with a sensory level at T10 and brisk reflexes.
case.tests: Eosinophils 4,500/µL; MRI shows swollen conus with patchy enhancement; schistosoma serology positive on repeat.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what treatment combination is used?
case.a: Acute schistosomiasis (Katayama syndrome) with myelopathy; corticosteroids together with praziquantel, often repeated after a few weeks.

read.where: Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — Schistosomiasis (Bilharzia)

det.patho: When cercariae penetrate the skin and mature into egg-laying worms, a strong immune response to schistosomal antigens produces a serum-sickness-like illness with circulating immune complexes. Neurological disease can result from ectopic egg deposition in the brain or cord with granulomatous inflammation, or from eosinophil-mediated vasculitis. S. mansoni and S. haematobium favour the spinal cord, S. japonicum the brain; S. mekongi is the species of the lower Mekong.
det.clinical: Most patients have systemic features — fever, urticaria, dry cough, abdominal pain and diarrhoea — beginning weeks after exposure. A minority develop headache, confusion, seizures, focal deficits or a myelitis, particularly of the conus and cauda equina. Symptoms may worsen briefly after starting praziquantel. Travellers to sub-Saharan Africa and the Mekong region are the classic patients.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis combines exposure history, eosinophilia and serology, accepting that eggs and antibodies may be absent at first. Repeat serology after several weeks increases yield. MRI of the spine in neuroschistosomiasis shows cord swelling with heterogeneous enhancement. Exclude other eosinophilic CNS infections, which in Thailand include angiostrongyliasis and gnathostomiasis.
det.treatment: Corticosteroids are given to dampen the immune response, especially with neurological involvement. Praziquantel kills adult worms but is less effective against immature stages, so a repeat course after several weeks is common practice. Steroid cover reduces post-treatment worsening. Spinal disease needs rehabilitation and bladder care.
det.prognosis: Systemic illness usually resolves; neurological recovery is better with early combined treatment, while delayed treatment of myelitis may leave lasting deficits.
pearls: Fever, urticaria and eosinophilia after freshwater exposure: think acute schistosomiasis.
Negative early serology does not exclude it — repeat later.
Give steroids with praziquantel when the nervous system is involved.
det.thd: Katayama syndrome คือระยะเฉียบพลันของโรคพยาธิใบไม้เลือด เกิดหลังลงแหล่งน้ำจืดในพื้นที่ระบาดประมาณ 2–8 สัปดาห์ มีไข้ ผื่นลมพิษ ไอ และ eosinophil สูง บางรายมีอาการทางสมองหรือไขสันหลังอักเสบ การตรวจเลือดหา antibody อาจลบในระยะแรก ต้องตรวจซ้ำ การรักษาใช้ steroid ร่วมกับ praziquantel และมักให้ซ้ำอีกรอบ

aN: acute schistosomiasis | katayama fever | acute schistosomiasis syndrome | toxemic schistosomiasis

name: Kearns–Sayre syndrome
formal: Mitochondrial disorder from large mtDNA deletion with onset before age 20: progressive external ophthalmoplegia, pigmentary retinopathy and cardiac conduction block, often with ataxia and raised CSF protein.
simple: A mitochondrial disease with drooping eyelids, restricted eye movement, retinal changes and heart rhythm problems.
more: Diagnose from the clinical triad, muscle biopsy with ragged red fibres, and a large single mtDNA deletion in muscle. Monitor ECG and pacemaker as needed, and screen for diabetes, hypoparathyroidism and short stature; prognosis is poor.
th: กลอกตาไม่ได้ + จอประสาทตาเสื่อมแบบมีเม็ดสี + หัวใจนำไฟฟ้าผิดปกติ เริ่มก่อนอายุ 20 ปี — เสี่ยงหัวใจหยุดเต้น
tempoNote: Onset in childhood or teens; multisystem progression over years
feat: Progressive ptosis and ophthalmoplegia beginning before age 20
Salt-and-pepper pigmentary retinopathy, usually with only mild visual loss
Cardiac conduction block that can progress suddenly to complete heart block
Cerebellar ataxia, raised CSF protein, short stature, hearing loss
Endocrine problems: diabetes, hypoparathyroidism, delayed puberty
inv: ECG and Holter repeatedly; electrophysiology study if any conduction change
Fundoscopy; CSF protein (often >1 g/L); serum lactate
Muscle mtDNA analysis for a large single deletion; biopsy shows ragged-red fibres
MRI brain: symmetric T2 change in subcortical white matter, basal ganglia and brainstem

case.story: Droopy eyelids since age 12, now clumsy when walking; fainted twice at school this month.
case.exam: Short stature, bilateral ptosis and near-complete ophthalmoplegia, pigmentary retinopathy, mild limb ataxia.
case.tests: ECG: bifascicular block; Holter shows intermittent complete heart block. CSF protein 1.4 g/L. Muscle shows a 5 kb mtDNA deletion.
case.q: What is the most urgent management step?
case.a: Prophylactic permanent pacemaker (or ICD as advised by cardiology) — sudden death from heart block is the main preventable risk.

det.patho: KSS is caused by a large single mtDNA deletion (classically about 5 kb) that is almost always sporadic, arising during early embryonic development. The deleted mtDNA is spread widely through tissues, which explains the multisystem nature. Pearson syndrome (marrow and pancreas failure in infancy) can evolve into KSS in survivors.
det.clinical: The defining triad is onset before 20, PEO and pigmentary retinopathy, with at least one of heart block, cerebellar ataxia or CSF protein above 1 g/L. Many also have deafness, short stature, diabetes, hypoparathyroidism, renal tubular disease and cognitive decline. Syncope in a young person with ptosis is a red flag for advancing conduction disease.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the clinical criteria plus detection of a large mtDNA deletion, best in muscle (blood may also show it in KSS more often than in CPEO). Serial ECG and Holter are mandatory. Low CSF folate is common and is worth measuring because it is treatable.
det.treatment: Early pacemaker or ICD prevents sudden death and should be considered even for lesser blocks. Replace calcium, vitamin D and hormones as needed; manage diabetes and hearing. Folinic acid is given when CSF folate is low. Coenzyme Q10 is often used but evidence is weak.
det.prognosis: Progressive, with death often in early to mid adulthood from cardiac or multisystem failure; pacing has improved survival.
pearls: Triad: under 20, PEO, pigmentary retinopathy; plus heart block, ataxia or CSF protein >1 g/L.
Sporadic deletion: recurrence risk for siblings is low.
Check CSF folate — cerebral folate deficiency responds to folinic acid.
det.thd: Kearns–Sayre syndrome เกิดจาก mtDNA deletion ขนาดใหญ่ที่มักไม่ถ่ายทอด เริ่มก่อนอายุ 20 ปี มีหนังตาตก กลอกตาไม่ได้ จอประสาทตาเสื่อมแบบมีเม็ดสี และอาจมี heart block เดินเซ หรือโปรตีนในน้ำไขสันหลังสูง สิ่งสำคัญที่สุดคือตรวจ ECG/Holter และใส่ pacemaker แต่เนิ่น ๆ เพื่อป้องกันเสียชีวิตเฉียบพลัน

ddx.pt: Onset after 20 without retinopathy or the full multisystem picture
Myotonia, distal weakness, cataract and CTG expansion; ophthalmoplegia uncommon
Fatigable fluctuating ptosis and diplopia without retinopathy or heart block

aN: kss | kearns sayre syndrome | oculocraniosomatic syndrome

name: Kennedy’s disease
formal: X-linked spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy from an androgen receptor CAG expansion, with proximal weakness, fasciculations, bulbar signs, gynaecomastia and sensory neuropathy in men.
simple: An inherited disease in men that causes slowly worsening muscle weakness, twitching and swallowing problems.
more: Diagnosed by AR gene CAG repeat testing (more than 38 repeats); CK is raised and EMG shows chronic denervation with reduced sensory action potentials. Management is supportive; the disease is slowly progressive and lifespan is near normal.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมยีน AR ในผู้ชาย — อ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขาและกล้ามเนื้อพูด/กลืน เต้นรอบปาก เต้านมโต
feat: Adult men; slowly progressive proximal and bulbar weakness
Perioral and chin fasciculations on pursing the lips; cramps; postural tremor
Gynaecomastia, reduced fertility, diabetes (androgen insensitivity)
Mild sensory neuropathy (reduced sensory potentials) — unusual for a motor neuron disease
inv: Genetic test: expanded CAG tract in the AR gene (androgen receptor)
CK often moderately raised; EMG neurogenic; sensory potentials reduced

case.story: Ten years of thigh cramps and slow decline climbing stairs; recently nasal speech; breast enlargement for years.
case.exam: Proximal weakness, twitching of the chin when whistling, tongue wasting, reduced reflexes, mild distal vibration loss, gynaecomastia.
case.tests: CK 1,100 U/L; sural SNAP absent; AR CAG repeat 47.
case.q: Which two findings argue strongly against ALS?
case.a: Sensory nerve involvement and signs of androgen insensitivity (gynaecomastia), together with an X-linked family pattern and very slow course.

read.where: Chapter 14 Spinal muscular atrophy (X-linked SBMA), pp. 157–176

qx.stem: A 45-year-old man from Buriram has 6 years of proximal weakness, perioral twitching, tremor of the hands and cramps. He has gynaecomastia and reduced sensation in the feet. Reflexes are reduced, upper motor neuron signs are absent, and CK is 800 U/L. His maternal uncle had a similar illness.
qx.q: Which genetic test confirms the diagnosis?
opts: Androgen receptor gene CAG repeat expansion
SMN1 deletion analysis
C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat expansion
DMPK CTG repeat
PMP22 duplication
qx.why: The combination of bulbar and proximal lower motor neuron weakness, gynaecomastia, sensory neuropathy and X-linked pattern identifies spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy, from an expanded CAG triplet in the androgen receptor gene. SMN1 testing is for SMA, C9orf72 for ALS-FTD, DMPK for myotonic dystrophy type 1 and PMP22 duplication for CMT1A.

qx.stem: A 46-year-old house painter from Lampang has had painful cramps for 30 years, with recent twitching in the arms. His strength is normal but his tongue and perioral muscles fasciculate. CK is 643 U/L. Sural and median sensory potentials are absent, and needle EMG shows widespread chronic denervation with fasciculations.
qx.q: Which test should be sent next?
opts: SMN1 deletion testing
Androgen receptor gene CAG repeat analysis
CLCN1 chloride channel gene sequencing
Anti-GM1 IgM antibodies
Muscle biopsy looking for myotonia
qx.why: Cramps, perioral and tongue fasciculations and chronic denervation with absent sensory potentials in a man suggest spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy, an X-linked polyglutamine disorder; an androgen receptor gene expansion of 40 or more CAG triplets is pathogenic and confirms it. The sensory ganglionopathy is part of the disease, and weakness may appear late, so the diagnosis can be made before significant weakness. There is no disease-modifying treatment.

ddx.pt: UMN signs, faster progression, normal sensory studies
No sensory or endocrine features; SMN1 deletion
Fatigable bulbar weakness without wasting or fasciculation

aN: sbma | spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy | x linked bulbospinal neuronopathy | kennedy disease

det.patho: Spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy is X-linked and caused by an expanded CAG repeat (generally 38 or more) in the androgen receptor gene. The mutant receptor, when bound by testosterone, enters the nucleus, misfolds and aggregates, damaging lower motor neurons, dorsal root ganglion cells and muscle. Partial loss of receptor function produces signs of androgen insensitivity. Female carriers are usually asymptomatic because of lower androgen levels.
det.clinical: Men develop symptoms in their 30s to 50s, often preceded by years of cramps, tremor or gynaecomastia. Proximal limb weakness, facial and tongue weakness with chin fasciculations on lip pursing, dysarthria and dysphagia progress slowly. Laryngospasm episodes may occur. Reduced sensation and absent sensory responses, gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy, reduced fertility, and metabolic abnormalities (diabetes, fatty liver, dyslipidaemia) complete the picture.
det.diagnosis: Genetic testing for the AR CAG repeat is diagnostic. Supportive findings are a raised CK (often moderately high), neurogenic EMG with fasciculations, and sensory nerve responses that are small or unrecordable. It is frequently misdiagnosed as ALS; the absence of UMN signs, sensory involvement, endocrine signs and X-linked family history should prompt testing.
det.treatment: There is no proven disease-modifying therapy in most countries; androgen-reduction strategies have been studied with limited benefit. Management is supportive with speech and swallowing therapy, physiotherapy, respiratory monitoring, treatment of diabetes and dyslipidaemia, and genetic counselling. Testosterone supplementation should be avoided.
det.prognosis: it advances slowly and survival is close to normal, though late aspiration pneumonia can occur.
pearls: Gynaecomastia plus bulbar and limb LMN signs in a man = test the androgen receptor gene.
Absent sensory potentials in a 'motor neuron disease' argue against ALS.
Daughters of an affected man are obligate carriers; his sons are unaffected.
det.thd: Kennedy's disease เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมแบบ X-linked จากการขยายตัวของ CAG repeat ในยีน androgen receptor พบในผู้ชายวัยกลางคน มีอาการอ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขาและกล้ามเนื้อพูดกลืน คางและริมฝีปากเต้น ร่วมกับเต้านมโตและมีบุตรยาก ตรวจพบการรับความรู้สึกเสียและ SNAP ลดลง ซึ่งช่วยแยกจาก ALS การวินิจฉัยใช้การตรวจยีน ยังไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ การดูแลเป็นแบบประคับประคอง และโรคดำเนินไปช้า

name: Kinetic tremor
formal: Tremor during voluntary movement, including intention and action components, from cerebellar disease, drug effects or essential tremor.
simple: A tremor that occurs while moving a body part, such as reaching or writing.
th: tremor ที่เกิดระหว่างการเคลื่อนไหวโดยตั้งใจ รวมทั้งแบบ intention พบใน essential tremor โรคสมองน้อย และจากยา
tempoNote: A tremor descriptor; course follows the cause
feat: Simple kinetic tremor: same amplitude throughout the movement (typical of essential tremor)
Intention tremor: amplitude grows as the target approaches (cerebellar outflow)
Spills drinks, shaky handwriting, trouble with buttons and spoons
Cerebellar causes bring dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, ataxic gait
inv: Bedside: finger–nose, spiral drawing, pouring water
Thyroid function, drug review (valproate, lithium, amiodarone, beta-agonists)
MRI brain when cerebellar signs or other deficits are present

case.story: Over six months her hand shakes when she brings a spoon to her mouth, and she now staggers; she has had a previous episode of blurred vision in one eye.
case.exam: Coarse right-hand tremor worsening near the target on finger–nose testing, dysmetria, ataxic gait, internuclear ophthalmoplegia.
case.tests: MRI shows periventricular and cerebellar peduncle lesions; CSF oligoclonal bands present.
case.q: What type of tremor is this and where is the lesion?
case.a: Kinetic tremor with an intention component from cerebellar outflow (superior cerebellar peduncle) involvement in multiple sclerosis.

det.patho: Kinetic tremor arises from oscillation in cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuits. Damage to the dentate nucleus or its outflow through the superior cerebellar peduncle produces the large, slow intention tremor, while essential tremor involves a more diffuse functional disturbance of the same network. Drugs and thyroid excess enhance normal physiological oscillation.
det.clinical: This is a tremor type, not a disease. Simple kinetic tremor is seen in essential tremor and enhanced physiological tremor. Intention tremor, usually 3–5 Hz, points to cerebellar disease such as multiple sclerosis, stroke, tumour, alcohol-related degeneration or hereditary ataxia. Task-specific kinetic tremor, such as primary writing tremor, appears only during one action.
det.diagnosis: Examine the limb during goal-directed movement and note whether amplitude rises near the target. Look for accompanying ataxia, nystagmus or dysarthria. Spiral drawing and handwriting samples document severity. Investigations depend on the context: metabolic and drug screen in all, MRI if cerebellar or other signs are present.
det.treatment: Treat the cause and remove aggravating drugs. Essential tremor responds to propranolol, primidone and, in refractory cases, thalamic DBS or focused ultrasound. Cerebellar intention tremor responds poorly to drugs; weighted utensils, occupational therapy and in selected cases thalamic DBS may help.
det.prognosis: Variable; cerebellar intention tremor is often disabling and treatment-resistant.
pearls: Kinetic tremor that worsens near the target means cerebellar outflow until proved otherwise.
Essential tremor is mainly postural and kinetic, not intention tremor, early on.
Weighted cutlery is a cheap and useful aid.
det.thd: Kinetic tremor คือ tremor ที่เกิดขณะเคลื่อนไหว แบ่งเป็น simple kinetic ที่สั่นเท่ากันตลอด (เช่น essential tremor) และ intention tremor ที่สั่นมากขึ้นเมื่อใกล้เป้าหมาย ซึ่งบอกรอยโรคที่สมองน้อยหรือทางออกของสมองน้อย ต้องตรวจหาอาการสมองน้อยอื่น ๆ ทบทวนยาและไทรอยด์ ทำ MRI เมื่อมีอาการร่วม การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ

ddx.pt: Bilateral postural plus simple kinetic tremor, family history, alcohol response
Intention component with dysmetria and other cerebellar signs
Rest, postural and kinetic tremor together after a midbrain or thalamic lesion

aN: action tremor during movement | intention tremor terminal kinetic | simple kinetic tremor

name: Kleine–Levin syndrome
formal: Rare disorder of recurrent episodes of hypersomnia lasting days to weeks with cognitive change, hyperphagia and hypersexuality in adolescent boys; thought to involve hypothalamic dysfunction.
simple: A rare condition in which teenagers have repeated bouts of extreme sleepiness, strange behaviour and overeating.
th: โรคพบน้อยที่มีช่วงหลับนานมากผิดปกติเป็นพัก ๆ ครั้งละหลายวันถึงหลายสัปดาห์ ร่วมกับความคิดสับสน รู้สึกไม่จริง กินมาก หรือพฤติกรรมทางเพศเพิ่ม ระหว่างช่วงปกติดี มักพบในวัยรุ่นชาย
tempoNote: Each episode lasts days to weeks, with several recurrences a year; the illness usually burns out after about a decade or less
feat: Recurrent episodes of severe hypersomnia, sleeping up to 16–20 hours a day
During episodes: cognitive slowing, derealisation, apathy, irritability, sometimes hyperphagia or hypersexuality
Normal alertness, behaviour and cognition between episodes
Onset mainly in adolescence, more often in boys; first episode often after an infection or alcohol
Episodes recur at least once every 18 months, often several times a year
inv: Clinical diagnosis; MRI brain and EEG to exclude structural, epileptic and inflammatory causes
EEG during episodes may show diffuse slowing
Exclude encephalitis, substance use, psychiatric disorders and metabolic causes during the first episode
Functional imaging may show thalamic and frontotemporal hypoperfusion (research use)

case.story: After a flu-like illness he slept 18 hours a day for 10 days, ate large amounts when awake and felt as if in a dream; he then returned to normal. A second identical episode happened 4 months later.
case.exam: During the episode he is drowsy, slow and apathetic but without focal signs; between episodes normal.
case.tests: MRI brain normal; EEG mild diffuse slowing during the episode, normal afterwards; CSF normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and is there any preventive treatment?
case.a: Kleine–Levin syndrome; supportive care during episodes, and lithium may reduce the frequency and length of episodes.

read.where: Chapter 29 Disorders of Sleep — Recurrent Hypersomnia
17 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Hypothalamus and Pituitary Gland

det.patho: The cause is unknown; a post-infectious or autoimmune process affecting the hypothalamus and thalamus is suspected, and HLA associations have been explored. Functional imaging during and between episodes shows hypometabolism or hypoperfusion in thalamus, hypothalamus and association cortex. Familial clustering occurs and a related menstrual-associated form exists in women.
det.clinical: The core feature is recurrent hypersomnia with altered cognition and a sense of unreality. Hyperphagia and hypersexuality are classic but not present in everyone. Episodes start abruptly, last around 1–3 weeks and end with a brief period of insomnia or elation. Between episodes the patient is normal, though some develop mild lasting cognitive or mood problems.
det.diagnosis: ICSD-3-TR requires at least two recurrent episodes of excessive sleepiness and sleep duration lasting 2 days to 5 weeks, recurring at least once every 18 months, with normal function between and at least one of cognitive dysfunction, altered perception, eating disorder or disinhibition. The first episode needs a full work-up to exclude encephalitis, structural lesions, epilepsy and toxins. PSG and MSLT are not required and may be hard to perform during episodes.
det.treatment: There is no proven curative therapy. During episodes, keep the patient safe at home under supervision and avoid driving and alcohol. Lithium has the best evidence for reducing episode frequency, while stimulants can increase wakefulness but do not correct the cognitive change. Valproate or carbamazepine are alternatives reported in small series.
det.prognosis: Episodes usually become less frequent and milder and stop after a median of about a decade; early onset and male sex predict a longer course.
pearls: Recurrent hypersomnia with normal intervals in a teenage boy is the clue to Kleine–Levin syndrome.
Derealisation and apathy are more common than the textbook hyperphagia and hypersexuality.
Infection or alcohol often triggers episodes.
det.thd: Kleine–Levin syndrome พบน้อย มักเป็นในวัยรุ่นชาย มีช่วงหลับนานมาก 16–20 ชั่วโมงต่อวันครั้งละหลายวันถึงหลายสัปดาห์ ร่วมกับสับสน รู้สึกเหมือนไม่จริง เฉยชา บางรายกินมากหรือมีพฤติกรรมทางเพศเพิ่ม ระหว่างช่วงจะปกติดี ต้องตรวจตัดโรคสมองอักเสบและสาเหตุอื่นในครั้งแรก ยังไม่มีการรักษาที่หายขาด lithium อาจช่วยลดความถี่ และโรคมักหายเองในเวลาหลายปี

qx.stem: A 15-year-old boy from Lopburi has had three episodes in 18 months, each beginning after a febrile illness, in which he slept about 18 hours a day for 1–2 weeks, felt that the world seemed unreal, and ate large amounts when awake. Between episodes he is a normal, high-achieving student. MRI, CSF and inter-episode EEG are normal.
qx.q: Which medicine has the best evidence for reducing the frequency of episodes?
opts: Lithium
Modafinil
Sodium oxybate
Clonazepam
Fluoxetine
qx.why: In Kleine–Levin syndrome, lithium is the medicine with the most supportive data for reducing episode frequency and duration. Modafinil or other stimulants may improve alertness during an episode but do not prevent recurrences or correct the derealisation. Oxybate, clonazepam and fluoxetine have no established preventive role.

qx.stem: A 16-year-old boy from Nonthaburi has had four episodes over 14 months, each lasting about ten days. During episodes he sleeps 18 hours a day, eats ravenously, feels unreal and speaks slowly; between episodes he is normal and performs well at school. MRI, EEG and drug screening are unremarkable. His parents ask what to expect.
qx.q: Which statement is correct?
opts: Modafinil taken daily prevents further episodes
Episodes recur for years but the disorder usually fades, and lithium may reduce episodes in some patients
The MSLT will show multiple sleep-onset REM periods and low hypocretin
Temporal lobe epilepsy is the usual underlying cause
Lifelong antipsychotic treatment is needed
qx.why: Kleine–Levin syndrome is recurrent hypersomnia with cognitive and behavioural change and normal function between episodes; episodes are discontinuous and tend to lessen over about a decade. Treatment is largely supportive, with stimulants used during episodes and lithium considered for prevention in selected patients. It is not a narcolepsy-type MSLT picture and is not explained by epilepsy.
