ddx.pt: Constant long sleep and sleep inertia without symptom-free intervals
Fever, seizures, focal signs, CSF pleocytosis and persistent abnormalities
Mood episodes with prominent mania or depression rather than primary hypersomnia with derealisation

aN: kls | recurrent hypersomnia | periodic hypersomnia | sleeping beauty syndrome

name: Klinefelter’s disease
formal: Sex chromosome disorder, 47,XXY, with hypogonadism, tall stature and learning difficulties; associated with tremor, epilepsy and an increased risk of cerebral venous disease.
simple: A genetic condition in males with an extra X chromosome, causing small testes, tall height and learning problems.
th: ความผิดปกติโครโมโซมเพศ 47,XXY ในเพศชาย มีอัณฑะเล็ก ฮอร์โมนเพศชายต่ำ ตัวสูง ปัญหาการเรียนรู้และภาษา และพบสั่น ชัก และหลอดเลือดดำอุดตันได้บ่อยขึ้น
tempoNote: Present from conception; features emerge across childhood, puberty and adulthood
feat: Tall stature with long legs, small firm testes, gynaecomastia (about 30% moderate to severe) and sparse body hair; almost all are infertile
Language-based learning difficulty and reading problems; verbal IQ typically 10–20 points below that of relatives, with attention problems and social anxiety
Motor immaturity in childhood: clumsiness, poor handwriting, mildly reduced strength and coordination
Postural and action tremor resembling essential tremor
Higher rates of epilepsy and venous thromboembolism, including cerebral venous thrombosis; adults risk osteoporosis, metabolic syndrome and (reported) early-onset Alzheimer disease
inv: Karyotype or chromosomal microarray on blood (47,XXY, mosaic forms, or 48,XXYY and other variants with more neurological features)
LH and FSH (raised) and testosterone (low or low-normal)
Bone density, glucose, lipids and thrombosis risk review in adults

case.who: 24-year-old man from Chonburi sent for tremor
case.story: Trembling hands since adolescence, trouble in reading at school, and no children after 3 years of marriage.
case.exam: Height 188 cm, long legs, bilateral gynaecomastia, testes 4 mL; postural tremor of both hands, normal tone and reflexes.
case.tests: Karyotype 47,XXY; testosterone low with raised FSH and LH.
case.q: What single test explains the tremor, the testes and the learning history?
case.a: Karyotype: Klinefelter syndrome. Offer testosterone replacement and fertility counselling.

det.patho: A supernumerary X chromosome arises from non-disjunction (maternal or paternal meiosis) in about 1 in 600–1000 males. Testicular failure causes low testosterone and raised gonadotrophins, while altered gene dosage on the X affects cognition and language lateralisation, and neuroimaging has shown reduced leftward asymmetry in temporal-parietal regions. Mosaic karyotypes give milder disease.
det.clinical: Many are diagnosed late. Children show speech delay, reading disability and motor clumsiness; adolescence brings incomplete virilisation. Adults have tall stature, gynaecomastia and infertility, and increased rates of anxiety, depression and attention difficulties. Neurological features include tremor, epilepsy and cerebral venous thrombosis, and the risk of leg ulcers, osteoporosis and breast cancer is higher than normal.
det.diagnosis: A peripheral blood karyotype or microarray confirms the diagnosis; hormone profiling shows hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism. Consider it in tall young men with tremor, learning difficulty, hypogonadism, unexplained venous thrombosis or infertility. Other X or Y aneuploidy variants (XXYY, XXXY) have more severe cognitive and neurological involvement.
det.treatment: Testosterone replacement started at puberty supports virilisation, bone density and wellbeing, and is monitored for haematocrit and thrombotic risk. Speech and language therapy, educational support and psychological care help the neurodevelopmental profile. Assisted reproduction with testicular sperm extraction has produced pregnancies in selected cases. Treat tremor and seizures as in others, and review bone and metabolic health.
det.prognosis: Normal or near-normal life expectancy with good support; quality of life depends on early recognition and educational help.
pearls: Tall young man with tremor and small testes: ask for a karyotype.
Remember Klinefelter in unexplained venous thrombosis in men, particularly on testosterone.
Kennedy disease is the other classic neuro diagnosis with gynaecomastia.
det.thd: Klinefelter syndrome คือภาวะโครโมโซม 47,XXY ในผู้ชาย ตัวสูง ขายาว อัณฑะเล็ก เต้านมโต มีบุตรยาก ฮอร์โมนเพศชายต่ำ เด็กมักมีปัญหาด้านภาษา การอ่าน และความคล่องแคล่วของกล้ามเนื้อ ในทางระบบประสาทพบมือสั่น ชัก และหลอดเลือดดำสมองอุดตันได้บ่อยขึ้น วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจโครโมโซม รักษาด้วยฮอร์โมนเทสโทสเตอโรน การสนับสนุนด้านการเรียนรู้ และให้คำปรึกษาเรื่องการมีบุตร

name: Klippel–Feil syndrome
formal: Congenital fusion of cervical vertebrae causing a short neck, low hairline and limited motion, with risk of cord compression, Chiari malformation and mirror movements.
simple: A condition from birth in which neck bones are fused, giving a short neck and limited motion.
th: ความผิดปกติแต่กำเนิดที่กระดูกสันหลังส่วนคอเชื่อมติดกัน ทำให้คอสั้น ไรผมต่ำ และขยับคอได้น้อย เสี่ยงไขสันหลังถูกกด Chiari และหูหนวก
tempoNote: Congenital; neurological complications may arise in adolescence or adulthood, sometimes acutely after minor trauma
feat: Classic triad (present in a minority): short neck, low posterior hairline, limited neck movement
Two or more neck vertebrae are fused from birth because segmentation failed
Hypermobile segments next to fused levels lead to instability, early spondylosis and myelopathy
Associations: Sprengel deformity, scoliosis, Chiari malformation, syringomyelia, deafness, renal and cardiac anomalies, mirror movements
Genetic forms: GDF6, GDF3, MEOX1, MYO18B
inv: Cervical X-rays with flexion–extension views; CT for bony anatomy
MRI cervical spine and craniocervical junction
Hearing test, renal ultrasound, echocardiography

case.story: Since childhood has had a short stiff neck; after a minor motorbike fall he has tingling in both hands and electric shocks down his back on neck flexion.
case.exam: Short neck, low hairline, restricted neck movement, hyperreflexia in all limbs, mirror movements of the hands.
case.tests: CT shows fusion of C2–C3 and C5–C6 with hypermobile C3–C4; MRI shows cord signal change at C3–C4.
case.q: Why did a minor injury cause myelopathy?
case.a: Klippel–Feil syndrome concentrates motion at the unfused segment, causing instability; needs surgical stabilisation and avoidance of contact sports.

read.where: Chapter 14 Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders — Craniocervical Junction Anomalies

det.patho: Klippel–Feil syndrome arises when the cervical somites do not segment properly during weeks 3 to 8 of gestation. The fused vertebrae concentrate movement at adjacent open segments, which degenerate early or become unstable. Associated anomalies reflect concurrent developmental disruption of other mesodermal and neural crest structures.
det.clinical: Many patients are asymptomatic and diagnosed incidentally. Symptoms include neck pain, restricted movement, radiculopathy and myelopathy, which may occur acutely after minor trauma. Mirror movements, hearing loss, scoliosis, Sprengel shoulder and renal anomalies are frequent companions. Craniocervical junction anomalies may cause lower cranial nerve or brainstem signs.
det.diagnosis: Plain radiographs show fused vertebrae; flexion–extension films evaluate instability at adjacent levels. CT defines bony anatomy and MRI shows cord compression, Chiari malformation and syrinx. Systemic screening includes renal ultrasound, hearing tests and cardiac evaluation.
det.treatment: Asymptomatic patients need education and avoidance of high-risk contact sports when unstable segments exist. Symptomatic instability or cord compression requires surgical decompression and fusion. Associated Chiari or syrinx is managed on its own merits. Hearing aids and orthopaedic care address other features.
det.prognosis: Usually good if instability is recognised; neurological injury after trauma is the main risk.
pearls: Short stiff neck plus mirror movements: think Klippel–Feil.
The danger lies at the mobile segments next to the fusion.
Screen kidneys and hearing in every patient.
det.thd: Klippel–Feil syndrome คือกระดูกสันหลังส่วนคอเชื่อมติดกันแต่กำเนิด ทำให้คอสั้น ไรผมต่ำ ขยับคอได้น้อย ระดับที่ไม่เชื่อมจะรับแรงมากจนเสื่อมหรือไม่มั่นคง เสี่ยงไขสันหลังถูกกดแม้บาดเจ็บเล็กน้อย มักพบร่วมกับ Chiari, syrinx, หูหนวก ไตผิดปกติ และ mirror movements การวินิจฉัยใช้ภาพรังสี CT และ MRI การรักษาคือหลีกเลี่ยงกีฬาปะทะและผ่าตัดเชื่อมกระดูกเมื่อไม่มั่นคงหรือกดไขสันหลัง

name: Klüver–Bucy syndrome
formal: Bilateral anterior temporal lobe lesion syndrome with visual agnosia, hyperorality, hypersexuality, placidity and memory loss; seen after herpes encephalitis, trauma or frontotemporal dementia.
simple: Behaviour changes with a compulsion to put objects in the mouth and loss of fear, caused by damage to both temporal lobes.
th: กลุ่มอาการจากรอยโรคสมองกลีบขมับส่วนหน้าทั้งสองข้าง ทำให้เอาของเข้าปาก มองเห็นแต่ไม่รู้จัก เฉื่อยชาไม่กลัว กินมาก และพฤติกรรมทางเพศผิดปกติ
tempoNote: Acute or subacute after encephalitis or trauma; gradual in frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer disease
feat: Hyperorality: puts objects, even inedible ones, into the mouth
Placidity with loss of fear and emotional reactivity
Visual agnosia ('psychic blindness') and hypermetamorphosis (compulsion to touch everything seen)
Hyperphagia or dietary change and altered or increased sexual behaviour
Usually amnesia from hippocampal involvement; partial forms are far more common than the full syndrome
inv: MRI brain: bilateral anterior/medial temporal lesions (encephalitis, contusion, atrophy)
CSF with HSV PCR and autoimmune antibodies when acute
EEG for seizures; neuropsychological assessment

case.who: 34-year-old man from Surat Thani, 6 weeks after HSV encephalitis
case.story: He chews tissues and soap, eats constantly, makes sexual remarks to nurses and shows no fear when a dog barks at him.
case.exam: Placid, amnestic for new events, cannot name familiar objects by sight but can by touch.
case.tests: MRI shows bilateral medial and anterior temporal gliosis.
case.q: Which syndrome is this and where are the lesions?
case.a: Klüver–Bucy syndrome from bilateral anterior temporal (amygdala) damage after herpes simplex encephalitis.

det.patho: The syndrome follows bilateral damage to the anterior temporal lobes, particularly the amygdala and connected temporal neocortex, which link sensory input with emotional and motivational value. Loss of this linkage produces inappropriate approach behaviour, absent fear and indiscriminate oral exploration. It was first described in monkeys after bilateral temporal lobectomy.
det.clinical: Full Klüver–Bucy syndrome is rare; partial forms with hyperorality, placidity and hyperphagia are more common. Causes include herpes simplex and autoimmune encephalitis, traumatic brain injury, bilateral temporal infarcts, hypoxia, frontotemporal dementia, advanced Alzheimer disease and, in children, other encephalitides. Amnesia and aphasia often coexist.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, based on at least several of the core behaviours, with MRI confirming bilateral temporal involvement. Investigate acute cases for encephalitis with CSF PCR and antibody testing. EEG detects temporal seizures.
det.treatment: Treat the cause promptly (aciclovir, immunotherapy). Behavioural management, supervised eating and environmental safety are key. SSRIs, carbamazepine, antipsychotics or leuprolide have been used for hypersexuality and agitation with variable success.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause; post-encephalitic cases may partially improve, while degenerative cases worsen.
pearls: Hyperorality after encephalitis — think bilateral temporal (amygdala) damage.
Most cases are partial; do not wait for all features.
HSV encephalitis is the classic acquired cause in adults.
det.thd: Klüver–Bucy syndrome เกิดจากรอยโรคสมองกลีบขมับส่วนหน้า โดยเฉพาะ amygdala ทั้งสองข้าง ผู้ป่วยหยิบของเข้าปาก กินไม่หยุด ไม่กลัวสิ่งใด มองเห็นแต่ไม่รู้ว่าเป็นอะไร และพฤติกรรมทางเพศผิดปกติ สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยคือสมองอักเสบจาก herpes simplex การบาดเจ็บศีรษะ และ frontotemporal dementia การรักษาคือแก้สาเหตุและจัดการพฤติกรรม

name: Korsakoff syndrome
formal: Amnestic syndrome from thiamine deficiency with severe anterograde amnesia, retrograde loss and confabulation, with damage to the mammillary bodies and thalamus; follows Wernicke encephalopathy.
simple: Severe memory loss, often with made-up stories to fill gaps, caused by a lack of vitamin B1, usually in heavy drinkers.
th: กลุ่มอาการความจำเสื่อมเรื้อรังจากการขาดวิตามิน B1 จำเรื่องใหม่ไม่ได้อย่างรุนแรง แต่งเรื่อง และขาดความตระหนักรู้ มักตามหลัง Wernicke's encephalopathy ที่ไม่ได้รับ thiamine เพียงพอ
tempoNote: Emerges as the confusion of Wernicke encephalopathy clears over days to weeks, then usually stable; partial improvement may continue for months to a year with abstinence and nutrition
feat: Severe anterograde amnesia with temporally graded retrograde loss (older memories better kept)
Confabulation, especially early, with apathy and poor insight; immediate recall and attention relatively preserved
Residual nystagmus, gait ataxia or peripheral neuropathy from preceding Wernicke encephalopathy
Settings: alcohol use disorder, bariatric surgery, hyperemesis gravidarum, cancer, refeeding and prolonged vomiting
inv: Thiamine (whole blood or erythrocyte) taken before treatment if possible, but never delay thiamine for the test
MRI: mammillary body atrophy and medial thalamic or periaqueductal changes; excludes stroke, tumour or herpes encephalitis
Neuropsychological testing showing memory loss out of proportion to other domains

case.who: 52-year-old unemployed man from Suphan Buri with long-standing heavy rice-whisky use
case.story: He was admitted a month ago with confusion and unsteady walking and received a single 100 mg thiamine dose; the confusion cleared, but he cannot remember any staff names or what he ate an hour ago and tells visitors he went fishing this morning.
case.exam: Alert with fluent speech, digit span normal, recalls 0 of 3 words at 5 minutes; mild horizontal nystagmus and wide-based gait; reduced ankle reflexes.
case.tests: MRI shows atrophic mammillary bodies; LFTs show raised GGT; no other cause found.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what lesson does the initial treatment teach?
case.a: Korsakoff syndrome after under-treated Wernicke encephalopathy; suspected Wernicke needs high-dose IV thiamine (for example 500 mg three times daily), and he still needs thiamine, abstinence support and cognitive rehabilitation.

read.where: 10.4 Amnestic Disorders and Mild Cognitive Impairment
Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Chronic Disorders Associated with Prolonged Alcohol Abuse
Chapter 15 Neurologic Manifestations of Nutritional Disorders

det.patho: Thiamine is a cofactor for enzymes of glucose metabolism; deficiency causes energy failure, glutamate excitotoxicity and blood-brain barrier breakdown in regions with high turnover. Damage to the mammillary bodies, mammillothalamic tract and anterior and medial thalamic nuclei disconnects the memory circuit. Alcohol worsens the deficiency through poor intake, reduced absorption and impaired storage.
det.clinical: Most cases follow an episode of Wernicke encephalopathy, which is often missed because the classic triad is incomplete. As the acute confusion settles, a dense inability to form new memories becomes obvious, with retrograde loss spanning years and older memories better kept. Confabulation fills gaps, while patients lack insight and show apathy. Other cognitive skills are relatively preserved, unlike in global dementia.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical in a patient at risk, supported by MRI and neuropsychological testing. Caine criteria (two of dietary deficiency, eye signs, cerebellar signs and altered mental state or memory impairment) improve recognition of the preceding Wernicke stage. Exclude other amnestic causes such as herpes encephalitis, bilateral thalamic or posterior cerebral artery strokes, anoxia, tumours near the third ventricle and limbic encephalitis.
det.treatment: Give high-dose parenteral thiamine whenever Wernicke encephalopathy is suspected, commonly 500 mg IV three times daily for several days followed by oral supplementation, and do not delay glucose in hypoglycaemia. Correct magnesium, which is needed for thiamine function. In established Korsakoff syndrome, thiamine continues, but the main work is abstinence support, nutrition, structured routines, errorless learning and supported living. Cholinesterase inhibitors lack controlled evidence.
det.prognosis: About a quarter improve substantially, many partially, and a significant minority need long-term care; continued drinking predicts a worse outcome.
pearls: Korsakoff syndrome is largely a preventable consequence of under-treated Wernicke encephalopathy.
Confabulation with preserved attention and immediate recall points to Korsakoff rather than delirium.
Older textbook thiamine doses of 100 mg are too low; current practice uses high-dose IV thiamine.
det.thd: Korsakoff syndrome เป็นความจำเสื่อมเรื้อรังจากขาดวิตามิน B1 มักตามหลัง Wernicke encephalopathy ที่ได้ thiamine ไม่พอ ผู้ป่วยจำเรื่องใหม่ไม่ได้ แต่งเรื่องขึ้นมาเติม และไม่รู้ตัวว่าผิดปกติ แต่ความตั้งใจและการจำทันทียังดี MRI อาจพบ mammillary body ฝ่อ การป้องกันคือให้ thiamine ขนาดสูงทางหลอดเลือดดำทันทีที่สงสัย Wernicke ส่วนการดูแลระยะยาวคือหยุดสุรา โภชนาการ และฟื้นฟูความจำ

qx.stem: A 45-year-old woman from Songkhla had sleeve gastrectomy 3 months ago and has vomited daily since. She is admitted with confusion, unsteady gait and horizontal nystagmus, and receives intravenous fluids with glucose. Within days the confusion clears, but she cannot recall any new information after a few minutes and describes a shopping trip she could not have taken.
qx.q: Which statement about this condition is correct?
opts: It could have been prevented by early high-dose parenteral thiamine
It occurs only in people who drink alcohol
Attention and digit span are severely impaired
MRI typically shows hippocampal sclerosis
Cholinesterase inhibitors are the proven treatment
qx.why: She developed Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency after bariatric surgery and vomiting, with glucose given without enough thiamine, followed by Korsakoff syndrome with dense anterograde amnesia and confabulation. Early high-dose IV thiamine is the key preventive step. Alcohol is the commonest but not the only cause, attention is relatively spared, MRI may show mammillary body atrophy, and cholinesterase inhibitors lack evidence.

name: Krabbe disease (globoid cell leukodystrophy)
formal: Autosomal recessive lysosomal disorder from galactocerebrosidase deficiency, causing demyelination, irritability, spasticity, seizures and blindness; globoid cells on pathology.
simple: An inherited disease in which the brain's nerve coating breaks down, causing irritability, stiffness and seizures.
more: Diagnosed by low galactocerebrosidase activity in leucocytes and GALC mutations; MRI shows symmetric periventricular white matter and optic nerve change, with slowed nerve conduction. Early stem cell transplant helps if given before symptoms. Galactosylceramide lipidosis with globoid cell leucodystrophy: infant irritability, stiffness, seizures and optic atrophy, from GALC enzyme deficiency; later-onset forms exist. Autosomal recessive lysosomal disease from galactocerebrosidase deficiency, causing demyelination with irritability, spasticity, seizures and optic atrophy, usually in infancy.
th: โรคสะสมไลโซโซมยีนด้อยจากการขาดเอนไซม์ galactocerebrosidase (GALC) ทำให้ไมอีลินในสมองและเส้นประสาทถูกทำลาย ทารกหงุดหงิด เกร็ง ชัก และตาบอด ส่วนชนิดเริ่มช้ามีขาเกร็งอ่อนแรง
tempoNote: Infantile form starts at 3–6 months with rapid decline; late-onset forms progress slowly over years
feat: Infant with extreme irritability, feeding difficulty, unexplained fevers and stiffening
Rapid loss of milestones, opisthotonus, seizures and optic atrophy
Peripheral demyelinating neuropathy, so reflexes may be reduced despite spasticity
Later-onset forms (child to adult) with spastic paraparesis, ataxia or visual loss and slow course
inv: GALC enzyme activity in leucocytes and GALC gene testing
Psychosine level in dried blood spot (high in infantile disease; used in newborn screening)
MRI: symmetric periventricular and cerebellar white matter, corticospinal tract signal; enlarged optic nerves; CT thalamic hyperdensity
Raised CSF protein and slowed nerve conduction

case.story: Previously well, he has cried inconsolably for a month, feeds poorly, has unexplained low fevers and now stiffens his whole body when touched.
case.exam: Hypertonic, fisted hands, poor visual tracking, depressed ankle jerks.
case.tests: CSF protein 1.4 g/L; MRI shows symmetric white matter change involving the dentate region; leucocyte GALC activity very low; psychosine markedly high.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and why is the timing of transplant important?
case.a: Infantile Krabbe disease; haematopoietic stem cell transplant helps only if done before symptoms (ideally in the first weeks of life), so this symptomatic infant needs supportive and palliative care.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism: Adult-Onset Inherited Leukodystrophies — Krabbe Disease (p994)
Progressive Encephalopathies With Onset Before Age 2

det.patho: Biallelic GALC variants reduce galactocerebrosidase, so galactosylceramide and the toxic lipid psychosine accumulate in myelin-forming cells. Psychosine kills oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells, causing central and peripheral demyelination; macrophages engulf the debris and become multinucleated globoid cells.
det.clinical: Most cases are infantile, with irritability, hypersensitivity to stimuli, feeding failure and fever without infection, then spasticity, seizures, blindness and a decerebrate state within months. Later-infantile and juvenile forms show regression, gait disturbance and vision loss. Adult-onset disease can present as slowly progressive spastic paraparesis, sometimes resembling hereditary spastic paraplegia, with relatively selective corticospinal tract involvement on MRI.
det.diagnosis: Low GALC activity plus pathogenic GALC variants confirms it; pseudodeficiency alleles make enzyme results alone unreliable. Psychosine helps separate infantile disease from benign low activity, and some newborn screening programmes use it. MRI, raised CSF protein and slowed conduction support the diagnosis.
det.treatment: Haematopoietic stem cell transplant (usually cord blood) before symptoms in early infancy improves survival and development, though motor problems often remain. Once infantile symptoms appear, transplant offers little and care focuses on comfort, seizure and spasticity control and feeding. Gene therapy and combined approaches are in trials. Transplant may be considered in mildly affected later-onset patients.
det.prognosis: Untreated infantile disease is usually fatal by about 2 years; later-onset forms progress more slowly, with survival into adulthood.
pearls: Irritable stiff infant with high CSF protein and reduced reflexes: think Krabbe.
Transplant works only before symptoms; this is the rationale for newborn screening.
Adult Krabbe can mimic hereditary spastic paraplegia.
det.thd: Krabbe disease เกิดจากการขาดเอนไซม์ GALC ทำให้สาร psychosine สะสมและทำลายเซลล์สร้างไมอีลินทั้งในสมองและเส้นประสาทส่วนปลาย ทารกอายุ 3–6 เดือนจะร้องกวนมาก กินไม่ได้ มีไข้ไม่ทราบสาเหตุ ตัวเกร็ง ชัก และตาบอด ตรวจเอนไซม์ GALC ยีน psychosine และ MRI ยืนยัน การปลูกถ่ายเซลล์ต้นกำเนิดได้ผลเฉพาะเมื่อทำก่อนมีอาการ

name: Kufor-Rakeb disease
formal: Autosomal recessive ATP13A2-related juvenile parkinsonism with pyramidal signs, supranuclear gaze palsy and dementia, a PARK9 disorder.
simple: An inherited form of Parkinson disease that starts in teens or twenties, with dementia and eye movement trouble.
more: Diagnosis by ATP13A2 mutation testing; MRI shows generalised or pallidal-pyramidal atrophy and iron accumulation in some. Usually levodopa-responsive at first with early motor complications; patients may show visual hallucinations.
th: parkinsonism วัยเยาว์แบบ autosomal recessive จากยีน ATP13A2 ร่วมกับ pyramidal signs, supranuclear gaze palsy และสมองเสื่อม
tempoNote: Onset in adolescence or early adulthood, then steady progression over years
feat: Juvenile levodopa-responsive akinetic-rigid parkinsonism
Spasticity and extensor plantars
Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy
Facial-faucial-finger mini-myoclonus, hallucinations and cognitive decline
Early levodopa-induced dyskinesia and hallucinations
inv: ATP13A2 sequencing and deletion analysis
MRI: generalised atrophy; iron deposition in basal ganglia in some
DaT-SPECT shows presynaptic dopaminergic loss

case.story: Slowness and stiffness for two years, falling grades at school and recent visual hallucinations.
case.exam: Bradykinesia, rigidity, brisk reflexes with extensor plantars, limited upgaze, small jerks of fingers and face.
case.tests: Copper studies normal; MRI shows diffuse atrophy; homozygous ATP13A2 variant.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and why is levodopa tricky here?
case.a: Kufor-Rakeb disease (PARK9); initial levodopa response is good but dyskinesias and hallucinations come early.

read.where: 12 The Many Faces of Parkinsonism: A Review of the Parkinson Look-alike Syndromes

det.patho: ATP13A2 encodes a lysosomal P5-type ATPase that transports polyamines and supports lysosomal and mitochondrial health. Loss of function leads to lysosomal dysfunction, alpha-synuclein handling problems and neuronal death. Allelic disease includes a form of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis and complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia.
det.clinical: First described in a Jordanian family, it is very rare and has since been reported in several ethnic groups. Typical onset is between 10 and 20 years with parkinsonism, pyramidal signs, supranuclear upgaze palsy, mini-myoclonus and cognitive or psychiatric decline. Phenotypes vary, and some patients look like juvenile parkinsonism alone.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in juvenile parkinsonism with pyramidal signs, gaze palsy or dementia, especially with consanguinity. Exclude Wilson's disease and other treatable causes. Genetic testing confirms biallelic ATP13A2 variants. MRI findings are non-specific.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying therapy. Levodopa helps early motor symptoms but dyskinesia and psychosis limit doses; amantadine and atypical antipsychotics such as clozapine or quetiapine may help. Physiotherapy, educational support, and genetic counselling are important.
det.prognosis: Progressive with loss of independence over years to decades; data on survival are limited.
pearls: Juvenile parkinsonism plus pyramidal signs plus gaze palsy: think ATP13A2.
Early drug-induced hallucinations limit levodopa dosing.
ATP13A2 is a lysosomal gene, linking parkinsonism with lysosomal storage biology.
det.thd: Kufor-Rakeb disease (PARK9) เป็น parkinsonism วัยรุ่นแบบ recessive จากยีน ATP13A2 ที่ทำงานในไลโซโซม ผู้ป่วยมีอาการ parkinsonism ร่วมกับ pyramidal signs มองขึ้นลำบาก กระตุกเล็ก ๆ และสมองเสื่อม ตอบสนอง levodopa ช่วงแรกแต่มี dyskinesia และประสาทหลอนเร็ว วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีนหลังตัดโรค Wilson รักษาตามอาการ

det.patho: Kufs disease is a group of adult NCLs caused by several genes affecting lysosomal function, with lipopigment storage confined largely to the brain. Recessive forms involve CLN6, CLN5, CTSF and homozygous GRN variants; the dominant form (Parry disease) involves DNAJC5. Heterozygous GRN variants cause frontotemporal dementia instead, showing that dose matters.
det.clinical: Type A presents as progressive myoclonic epilepsy with later dementia and ataxia; type B presents with dementia, behavioural change and motor features such as facial dyskinesia or parkinsonism. Onset is typically in early to mid adulthood. Retinal involvement and blindness are absent, which made the diagnosis historically difficult.
det.diagnosis: Consider it in young adults with progressive myoclonic epilepsy or unexplained early dementia with ataxia or movement disorder. Genetic testing is now the main route; storage material in skin or rectal biopsy is inconsistent in adults. Exclude other progressive myoclonic epilepsies, mitochondrial disease and prion disease.
det.treatment: No specific therapy exists. Myoclonus and seizures respond partly to valproate, levetiracetam, clonazepam, perampanel or brivaracetam; avoid phenytoin, carbamazepine and other sodium channel blockers that can worsen myoclonus. Support for cognition, behaviour and mobility is needed.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive, with death often 10 or more years after onset.
pearls: Adult progressive myoclonic epilepsy with normal vision: include Kufs disease.
Kufs is genetically diverse; use a panel, not a single gene test.
Avoid sodium channel blockers when myoclonus dominates.

det.patho: Viral or bacterial inflammation of the membranous labyrinth damages both cochlear and vestibular end organs. Viral cases follow upper respiratory infection, while bacteria spread from otitis media or meningitis. Bacterial invasion causes suppurative destruction and permanent loss.
det.clinical: Patients present with acute vertigo, nausea and imbalance along with hearing loss and tinnitus in one ear. Symptoms are worst in the first days and improve over weeks as central compensation develops. Hearing may recover partly or not at all.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical, supported by audiometry. Because AICA territory stroke can produce vertigo with hearing loss, HINTS plus hearing assessment is needed, and MRI is performed in patients with vascular risk or atypical signs. CT temporal bone helps in suspected bacterial disease.
det.treatment: Use vestibular suppressants and antiemetics for only a few days, then encourage early mobilisation and vestibular rehabilitation. Oral or intratympanic steroids are offered for sudden sensorineural hearing loss. Bacterial labyrinthitis requires antibiotics and urgent ENT management.
det.prognosis: Vertigo improves over weeks; hearing loss may be permanent.
pearls: Vertigo + hearing loss can be AICA stroke — check HINTS plus.
Bacterial labyrinthitis complicating otitis media needs urgent ENT care.
Avoid prolonged vestibular suppressants.

det.patho: Most lacunes arise from disease of single deep perforating arterioles 40–800 µm wide — lenticulostriate, thalamoperforating and paramedian pontine branches. Chronic hypertension drives lipohyalinosis and fibrinoid change in the smallest vessels, while larger perforators are blocked by microatheroma at their origin or by parent-artery plaque (branch atheromatous disease, which tends to give larger, elongated infarcts and more progression). Lacunar stroke accounts for about a quarter of ischaemic strokes and is especially common in Asian populations. Embolism is an uncommon cause but must be considered when no small vessel risk factors exist.
det.clinical: C. Miller Fisher described the core syndromes. Pure motor hemiparesis is the commonest; the weakness involves face, arm and leg proportionately because fibres are tightly packed in the capsule or pons. Pure sensory stroke from VPL/VPM thalamic infarcts gives hemibody numbness or paraesthesia, sometimes followed months later by central post-stroke pain. Sensorimotor stroke combines both from thalamocapsular lesions. Ataxic hemiparesis pairs pyramidal weakness, usually leg-predominant, with same-sided limb incoordination that clearly exceeds the weakness. Dysarthria–clumsy hand shows marked slurring, facial weakness and a fine-motor clumsy hand with little power loss. Other recognised lacunar presentations include hemichorea-hemiballism from subthalamic or striatal infarcts and isolated dysarthria. Early fluctuation and worsening in the first days is common and does not change the diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: Clinical syndromes are only about 70–80% predictive: a small cortical infarct or an embolic deep infarct can produce an identical picture, so imaging is essential. DWI-MRI confirms a single small deep lesion and shows co-existing markers of small vessel disease (white matter hyperintensities, old lacunes, microbleeds). Deep infarcts larger than 15–20 mm, especially striatocapsular comma-shaped ones, suggest MCA stem occlusion or embolism rather than a true lacune. Still perform vascular and cardiac work-up, because carotid stenosis or AF changes management even when the infarct looks lacunar.
det.treatment: Acute: eligible patients receive IV thrombolysis (alteplase or tenecteplase) within 4.5 h; lacunar syndromes benefit as much as other subtypes. Minor stroke (NIHSS ≤ 3–5) or fluctuating syndromes: short dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus clopidogrel for about 21 days) then single antiplatelet; cilostazol is a reasonable long-term option in Asian patients. Secondary prevention centres on blood pressure (target generally < 130/80 mmHg), statin, diabetes control, stopping smoking and exercise. Avoid long-term dual antiplatelets, which raised bleeding without reducing recurrence in small vessel stroke.
det.prognosis: Early mortality is low and functional recovery is often good, but recurrence (~2–4%/year) and cumulative cognitive decline make it a marker of progressive small vessel disease.
pearls: Pure motor hemiparesis = face, arm, leg equal, with nothing cortical; it is the most frequent lacunar syndrome.
Ataxic hemiparesis: ataxia far worse than the weakness, on the same side.
A fluctuating hemiparesis over hours (capsular warning syndrome) predicts a capsular infarct — treat early and aggressively.
Lacunar syndrome does not equal lacunar mechanism: always image and screen for embolic and large artery sources.

det.patho: Lacunar infarcts arise from occlusion of single penetrating arterioles (lenticulostriate, thalamoperforating, pontine paramedian), usually from lipohyalinosis or microatheroma at the origin of the perforator. Branch atheromatous disease at the parent artery can produce larger, progressive lacunar-type infarcts.
det.clinical: The classic syndromes are pure motor, pure sensory, sensorimotor, ataxic hemiparesis and dysarthria-clumsy hand. Fluctuating, repeated episodes of hemiparesis (capsular warning syndrome) predict infarction. Accumulating lacunes contribute to vascular cognitive impairment and gait disturbance.
det.diagnosis: Clinical syndrome predicts a lacunar lesion in most but not all cases; MRI confirms. Investigations should still exclude cardioembolic and large-artery sources because about one in five lacunar syndromes have a non-lacunar cause.
det.treatment: Acute treatment is as for other ischaemic strokes, including thrombolysis. Secondary prevention relies on BP control, antiplatelets (short-term dual therapy for minor stroke), statins and diabetes care. Cilostazol is used in some Asian practice for small-vessel stroke prevention.
det.prognosis: Short-term outcome is relatively good, but recurrence, cognitive decline and dementia risk are increased.
pearls: No cortical signs, equal face-arm-leg weakness: think lacune.
Capsular warning syndrome: repeated stereotyped hemiparesis that may culminate in infarction.
Still look for embolic sources; not every lacunar syndrome is a lacune.

qx.why: Ataxic hemiparesis, a well-known lacunar syndrome, is caused by small-vessel infarcts in the basis pontis or internal capsule (or corona radiata), where corticospinal and corticopontocerebellar fibres run together. The absence of cortical signs makes a cortical localisation unlikely.

det.patho: Laforin (EPM2A) and malin (NHLRC1) work together to keep glycogen properly branched and soluble. Loss of either lets poorly branched glycogen precipitate as insoluble polyglucosan (Lafora bodies) in neurons, muscle, liver and sweat glands, triggering neurotoxicity and inflammation.
det.clinical: A previously normal adolescent develops occipital seizures with visual phenomena, myoclonus and generalised tonic-clonic seizures. Within a few years cognitive decline, behavioural change and ataxia appear, leading to a vegetative state. NHLRC1 cases may progress slightly more slowly than EPM2A cases.
det.diagnosis: Genetic testing confirms it. Axillary skin biopsy showing Lafora bodies in duct cells is a quick supportive test, but samples must be from the duct, not apocrine glands, to avoid false positives. EEG background slowing and photosensitivity in a teenager with decline are strong clues.
det.treatment: There is no cure; seizures are treated with valproate, levetiracetam, clobazam, perampanel and others, avoiding phenytoin and carbamazepine. Metformin has been used off-label with limited evidence. Antisense oligonucleotides targeting glycogen synthase and enzyme-based glycogen degradation are in development. Palliative care and family support are central.
det.prognosis: Death usually occurs around 10 years after onset.
pearls: Teenager with visual seizures, myoclonus and falling grades: think Lafora.
Axillary skin biopsy can show Lafora bodies.
A slowed EEG background separates PME from JME.

case.tests: CK 300 U/L; NCS normal; MRI shows fatty change in anterior leg compartments; heterozygous MYH7 variant.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what extra screening is needed?
case.a: Laing distal myopathy; screen heart with ECG and echo because MYH7 is also a cardiomyopathy gene.

det.patho: Heterozygous variants in MYH7, which encodes the slow beta-myosin heavy chain, mostly cluster in the rod region and disturb thick filament assembly. Slow-twitch type 1 fibres are affected, explaining early weakness of tibialis anterior and long toe extensors. The same gene causes hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathy and myosin storage myopathy.
det.clinical: Onset is usually in childhood with foot drop and a hanging big toe. Finger extensors, especially of the third and fourth fingers, and neck flexors become weak later. Progression is slow and most patients remain ambulant. Some families show proximal involvement or cardiomyopathy, so phenotype varies.
det.diagnosis: Distal anterior leg weakness with normal sensation and a myopathic EMG raises suspicion; muscle MRI pattern supports it. Genetic testing for MYH7 confirms the diagnosis and may reveal de novo variants. Nerve conduction studies exclude neuropathy causes of foot drop.
det.treatment: Management is supportive: ankle-foot orthoses, physiotherapy, and occupational aids for hand weakness. Cardiac review at diagnosis and periodically is sensible. Genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance is needed.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; life expectancy usually normal unless cardiomyopathy develops.
pearls: Childhood foot drop with normal nerves and a hanging big toe: think MYH7.
Distal myopathy genes often also affect the heart; check it.
Muscle MRI pattern is a useful guide before gene testing.
det.thd: Laing distal myopathy เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้อถ่ายทอดแบบ dominant จากยีน MYH7 เริ่มตั้งแต่วัยเด็กด้วยปลายเท้าตก นิ้วโป้งเท้ากระดกไม่ได้ ต่อมานิ้วมือเหยียดอ่อนแรง โรคดำเนินช้ามาก CK ปกติหรือสูงเล็กน้อย วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI กล้ามเนื้อและการตรวจยีน รักษาแบบประคับประคองด้วยอุปกรณ์พยุงข้อเท้าและตรวจหัวใจ

simple: An immune disease causing muscle weakness and dry mouth, often linked to lung cancer.

Autonomic features: dry mouth, constipation, erectile dysfunction
Reduced reflexes that transiently improve after brief exercise (facilitation)
About half are paraneoplastic (small-cell lung cancer)

Low CMAP amplitudes with >100% increment after 10 s exercise or high-rate stimulation

qx.stem: A 63-year-old male taxi driver from Chachoengsao who has smoked 40 pack-years has three months of difficulty getting out of the car, dry mouth and erectile dysfunction. Hip flexors are weak, but strength and the absent knee jerks improve briefly after 10 seconds of maximal contraction. P/Q-type VGCC antibodies are strongly positive. Repetitive nerve stimulation shows low CMAP amplitudes with a 180% increment after brief exercise. CT chest shows a hilar mass with mediastinal nodes.
qx.q: Besides treatment of the tumour, which drug is first-line for his neuromuscular symptoms?
opts: Pyridostigmine as the only treatment
Eculizumab
Amifampridine (3,4-diaminopyridine)
Efgartigimod
Intrathecal baclofen
qx.why: Proximal weakness, autonomic symptoms and areflexia with post-exercise facilitation and an increment of 100% or more indicate LEMS, here almost certainly from small-cell lung cancer (DELTA-P score high). Amifampridine blocks presynaptic potassium channels, prolongs depolarisation and increases acetylcholine release, so it is the first-line symptomatic drug; pyridostigmine adds only a modest effect. Treating the cancer often improves LEMS. Complement and FcRn inhibitors are used in myasthenia gravis, not LEMS.

qx.stem: A 60-year-old woman from Nakhon Sawan, an ex-smoker, has three months of difficulty rising from a low chair and climbing stairs, a dry mouth and constipation. Hip flexors are weak, knee and ankle jerks are absent at rest but appear after ten seconds of maximal contraction, and she has mild bilateral ptosis. The referring doctor suspects myasthenia gravis.
qx.q: Which test best supports the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Repetitive nerve stimulation showing low CMAPs that increase by more than 100% after brief exercise
Single-fibre EMG showing increased jitter
Serum AChR binding antibody
Muscle biopsy of the quadriceps
Serum creatine kinase
qx.why: Proximal leg weakness, autonomic symptoms and areflexia with post-exercise facilitation of reflexes indicate LEMS. The electrodiagnostic hallmark is low resting CMAP amplitudes with a marked (>100%) increment after 10 s of exercise or high-frequency stimulation; P/Q-type VGCC antibodies support it. Jitter is abnormal in any junction disorder and is not specific. Because about half of cases have small-cell lung cancer, CT or PET of the chest follows, and amifampridine is the symptomatic drug.

qx.stem: A 63-year-old man who has smoked for 40 years presents with 3 months of thigh weakness, dry mouth and absent knee reflexes. Strength improves transiently after a 10-second maximal contraction. Baseline CMAP of the abductor digiti minimi is 2.1 mV, and after brief exercise it rises to 5.4 mV.
qx.q: Which electrodiagnostic abnormality is characteristic?
opts: Decrement of 10% at 3 Hz that repairs after exercise but with a normal baseline CMAP
Incremental response of more than 100% after brief exercise or at 20–50 Hz stimulation, with low baseline CMAP
Myotonic discharges on needle examination
Spontaneous fibrillations and positive sharp waves confined to one root territory
Conduction block across the elbow
qx.why: In LEMS presynaptic calcium channel antibodies cause reduced acetylcholine release, so the resting CMAP is small and facilitates dramatically, by more than 100%, after brief maximal exercise or high-frequency stimulation. Decrement with repair characterises postsynaptic myasthenia gravis, which has a normal baseline CMAP. The smoking history should prompt a search for small-cell lung cancer.

qx.stem: A 62-year-old man who has smoked for 40 pack-years has progressive thigh weakness, a dry mouth and erectile dysfunction. Knee and ankle reflexes are absent, but briefly return after he contracts the muscle for ten seconds. Strength improves transiently with repeated effort.
qx.q: Which investigation is most diagnostic of the neuromuscular junction disorder, and which search must follow?
opts: Single-fibre EMG only, then colonoscopy
Edrophonium test, then thyroid ultrasound
Repetitive nerve stimulation showing low resting CMAP with post-exercise or high-frequency increment, then chest CT/PET for small cell lung cancer
Muscle biopsy, then bone marrow
Serum CK, then lumbar puncture
qx.why: Proximal weakness, autonomic dryness, areflexia and facilitation after exertion describe LEMS, caused by P/Q-type calcium channel antibodies. Low resting CMAP amplitudes with an increment of more than 100 percent after brief exercise or fast stimulation is diagnostic, and about half of cases are paraneoplastic, mostly small cell lung cancer, so cancer screening is mandatory in a smoker.

qx.stem: A 64-year-old man was ventilated for respiratory failure and found to have fatigable proximal weakness, reduced reflexes that enhance after sustained contraction, and dry mouth. AChR antibodies are negative but voltage-gated calcium channel antibodies are positive. CT chest reveals a hilar mass, and biopsy shows small cell carcinoma.
qx.q: Which symptomatic drug is most effective for the weakness?
opts: 3,4-Diaminopyridine (amifampridine), a potassium channel blocker that prolongs presynaptic depolarisation
Mexiletine
Edaravone
Dantrolene
Neostigmine alone
qx.why: Paraneoplastic LEMS is treated by treating the cancer and by symptomatic therapy with amifampridine, which blocks presynaptic potassium channels and increases acetylcholine release; immunotherapy (IVIG, steroids) can add benefit. Pyridostigmine alone is weak in LEMS, and the other drugs act on sodium channels, free radicals or muscle calcium release.

qx.stem: A 58-year-old smoker from Rayong has proximal leg weakness, dry mouth and absent knee jerks that briefly return after exercise. Resting hand CMAP (compound muscle action potential) amplitude is 1.2 mV (low) with normal conduction velocity.
qx.q: Which motor nerve stimulation result best supports Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome?
opts: A progressive 20% decrement at 3 Hz with no change after exercise
Normal baseline CMAP with a 10% decrement at 3 Hz only
Temporal dispersion and conduction block in multiple nerves
Fibrillation potentials and complex repetitive discharges
A CMAP amplitude increment of about 100% or more (at least roughly 60% in newer series) after brief maximal exercise or high-rate stimulation
qx.why: In LEMS a presynaptic calcium channel defect lowers resting CMAP amplitude, and brief exercise or fast stimulation increases the quantal release and makes the CMAP jump, classically by 100% or more, with some studies accepting about 60%. Myasthenia gravis shows a decrement at slow rates and a small post-exercise change. Conduction block and dispersion indicate demyelinating neuropathy. Look for small-cell lung cancer in smokers.

qx.stem: A 63-year-old man from Samut Sakhon who smokes 40 cigarettes a day has proximal leg weakness, dry mouth, erectile dysfunction and absent ankle jerks that return briefly after sustained contraction. Repetitive stimulation at 50 Hz shows an increment of 180 percent and antibodies against P/Q channels (VGCC) are present.
qx.q: Which action should accompany symptomatic therapy with amifampridine?
opts: Immediate thymectomy
A search for small cell lung cancer with chest CT and, if negative, PET-CT with repeat surveillance
Edrophonium test followed by lifelong pyridostigmine monotherapy
High-dose plasma exchange before any other test
Long-term high-dose prednisolone as the only therapy
qx.why: LEMS in an older smoker is paraneoplastic until proven otherwise, most often from small cell lung cancer, so cancer screening with imaging and follow-up is essential. Amifampridine (3,4-diaminopyridine) treats the presynaptic release defect; pyridostigmine alone is poorly effective, thymectomy treats myasthenia gravis, and immunotherapy is added if needed after tumour treatment and symptomatic therapy.

qx.stem: A 66-year-old man who smokes 30 cigarettes a day presents with difficulty rising from a chair, a dry mouth and impotence. Ankle jerks are absent but briefly return after 10 seconds of maximal contraction. A median nerve CMAP is 1.6 mV at rest and 4.1 mV after 10 seconds of voluntary exercise; low-rate stimulation shows a decrement.
qx.q: What should be done next?
opts: Plan thymectomy for thymoma-associated myasthenia
Give edrophonium to confirm the diagnosis and start pyridostigmine alone
Start rituximab immediately without further tests
Test for voltage-gated calcium channel antibodies and start a search for small cell lung cancer with chest CT and PET-CT
Reassure, as an increment of 150% is a normal finding
qx.why: A low resting CMAP that increases by more than 100% after brief exercise, with proximal weakness, areflexia and autonomic features, is diagnostic of a presynaptic disorder, most often LEMS, which is paraneoplastic in about half of cases, usually small cell lung cancer. VGCC (and SOX1) antibodies and thorough cancer screening, repeated if negative, are the priority; 3,4-diaminopyridine then provides symptomatic benefit. Pyridostigmine alone gives little benefit and thymectomy does not apply.

det.patho: Autoantibodies to the presynaptic P/Q calcium channel (VGCC) reduce calcium entry into motor and autonomic nerve terminals, so fewer acetylcholine quanta are released. Repeated activation lets calcium accumulate, temporarily boosting release — the basis of facilitation. About half of cases are paraneoplastic, nearly always small-cell lung cancer; the rest are autoimmune, often in younger patients with HLA-B8-DR3.
det.clinical: Proximal leg weakness with difficulty rising and climbing stairs is the presenting complaint in most; ocular and bulbar symptoms are milder than in MG. Autonomic features — dry mouth, constipation, erectile dysfunction, orthostatic symptoms — are characteristic. Reflexes are reduced or absent but may return briefly after sustained contraction. Paraneoplastic cases may also have cerebellar ataxia, and symptoms may precede detection of the tumour by months or years.
det.diagnosis: VGCC antibodies are positive in most cases. Electrodiagnosis shows low resting CMAP amplitudes, decrement at low-rate stimulation and an increment of more than 100% after 10 seconds of maximal exercise or 50 Hz stimulation (60% is often used as a sensitive cut-off). The DELTA-P score estimates the likelihood of underlying SCLC. Screen with CT chest and FDG-PET, repeating periodically for at least two years if negative.
det.treatment: Treating the tumour often improves LEMS. Amifampridine (3,4-diaminopyridine) is the first-line symptomatic drug, blocking potassium channels to prolong depolarisation; pyridostigmine adds little. Immunotherapy with prednisolone and azathioprine is used for persistent weakness, and IVIG or plasma exchange for severe disability. Avoid neuromuscular-blocking drugs and agents that impair transmission, and anticipate prolonged paralysis after anaesthesia.
det.prognosis: Prognosis is determined by the cancer in paraneoplastic cases; non-tumour LEMS is chronic but usually controllable.
pearls: Proximal leg weakness + dry mouth + low reflexes that improve after exercise = LEMS.
Look for small-cell lung cancer repeatedly, not just once.
Increment after brief exercise is the electrophysiological signature.
det.thd: LEMS เกิดจากแอนติบอดีต่อช่องแคลเซียมชนิด P/Q ที่ปลายประสาท ทำให้หลั่ง acetylcholine ได้น้อย ครึ่งหนึ่งสัมพันธ์กับมะเร็งปอดชนิด small cell อาการคือต้นขาอ่อนแรง ลุกจากเก้าอี้ลำบาก ปากแห้ง ท้องผูก รีเฟล็กซ์ลดลงแต่กลับมาชั่วคราวหลังเกร็งกล้ามเนื้อ วินิจฉัยด้วยแอนติบอดี VGCC และ EMG ที่ CMAP ต่ำแต่เพิ่มขึ้นมากกว่า 100% หลังออกแรง 10 วินาที ต้องค้นหามะเร็งปอดซ้ำเป็นระยะ รักษาด้วยการรักษามะเร็ง ยา amifampridine และยากดภูมิคุ้มกัน

name: Lance–Adams syndrome
formal: Chronic post-hypoxic action myoclonus, often with intention myoclonus and ataxia, after cardiac arrest or asphyxia, usually with preserved intellect.

det.patho: Hypoxia injures cortical inhibitory interneurons, cerebellar Purkinje cells and possibly brainstem serotonergic pathways. The loss of inhibition leaves sensorimotor cortex hyperexcitable, producing cortical reflex myoclonus set off by movement and sensory input. This contrasts with the generalised myoclonic status of comatose survivors with severe global brain injury.
det.clinical: Patients regain consciousness with fairly good cognition, then develop action myoclonus as they try to move. Negative myoclonus of the legs destabilises standing and walking. Ataxia, dysarthria and seizures can coexist. Intensive-care teams distinguish this from acute post-anoxic myoclonus status, which appears while the patient is still comatose and predicts a poor outcome. Symptoms often improve partly during the first year.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, in a conscious survivor with action-induced jerks after a hypoxic event. Neurophysiology (back-averaging, giant SEPs) confirms a cortical origin. Screen for drug toxicity, renal and hepatic failure and electrolyte problems, and use MRI to exclude other lesions.
det.treatment: Combine antimyoclonic drugs: levetiracetam, valproate, clonazepam, piracetam, and sometimes zonisamide or perampanel. Sodium channel blockers such as phenytoin and carbamazepine can worsen myoclonus. Physiotherapy and walking aids are central, and deep brain stimulation has been tried in refractory cases.
det.prognosis: Many improve partly over a year; disability is dominated by action myoclonus rather than cognition.
pearls: Lance–Adams occurs in awake survivors; acute myoclonic status occurs in coma.
Action myoclonus with falls from negative myoclonus after cardiac arrest.
Piracetam and levetiracetam are useful first choices.
det.thd: Lance–Adams syndrome คือกล้ามเนื้อกระตุกเวลาเคลื่อนไหวเรื้อรังหลังสมองขาดออกซิเจน เช่น หลังหัวใจหยุดเต้น ผู้ป่วยรู้ตัวดีแต่ยกแขนหรือเดินแล้วกระตุกรุนแรง ขาอาจทรุดจาก negative myoclonus เกิดจากเปลือกสมองและซีรีเบลลัมสูญเสียการยับยั้ง ตรวจ EEG-EMG เพื่อยืนยัน รักษาด้วย levetiracetam, valproate, clonazepam หรือ piracetam และหลีกเลี่ยง phenytoin กับ carbamazepine

det.patho: Large vessel vasculitis comprises giant cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis: granulomatous arterial inflammation that targets the aortic trunk and the big vessels arising from it, with intimal hyperplasia, stenosis, occlusion or aneurysm. It is mediated by T cells and macrophages driven by interleukin-6 and interferon-gamma pathways. In the Chapel Hill classification they are defined by size of vessel affected.
det.clinical: The picture includes constitutional symptoms and polymyalgia, and then vascular insufficiency. Giant cell arteritis causes headache, jaw claudication and sudden, often irreversible visual loss from anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, and can cause stroke in vertebrobasilar territory. Takayasu arteritis presents with low-flow symptoms, subclavian steal, claudication, hypertension from renal artery stenosis and coronary involvement. Both can be complicated by aneurysm.
det.diagnosis: ESR and CRP are usually raised. Giant cell arteritis is diagnosed by ultrasound or biopsy of the temporal artery, which should not delay treatment. Takayasu arteritis is diagnosed by angiography or PET showing characteristic arterial lesions in a young patient. Mimics include atherosclerosis, fibromuscular dysplasia, infection (syphilis, tuberculosis), IgG4 disease and other vasculitides.
det.treatment: For suspected giant cell arteritis with visual symptoms, give immediate high-dose glucocorticoid, intravenous methylprednisolone 500–1000 mg daily for up to 3 days then oral prednisolone with tapering, and use tocilizumab as steroid-sparing therapy. Takayasu arteritis is treated with steroid plus methotrexate, azathioprine, or biologic agents (tocilizumab, TNF inhibitors), with surgery or stenting only in quiescent disease. Low-dose aspirin and risk-factor control are standard.
det.prognosis: Visual loss from GCA is often permanent if treatment is delayed; Takayasu has relapsing course but outcome has improved with biologics.
pearls: Treat suspected GCA with steroids before the biopsy result if vision is at risk.
Unequal arm blood pressures in a young woman should prompt vascular imaging.
Normal ESR does not exclude GCA.
det.thd: Large vessel vasculitis ได้แก่ giant cell arteritis ในผู้สูงอายุ ทำให้ปวดศีรษะ ปวดกรามเวลาเคี้ยว และตาบอดเฉียบพลัน และ Takayasu arteritis ในหญิงอายุน้อย ทำให้ชีพจรแขนไม่เท่ากัน เวียนศีรษะ หน้ามืด และ stroke ตรวจ ESR/CRP ดูภาพหลอดเลือดด้วย CTA/MRA/PET หรือตรวจ temporal artery การรักษาคือสเตียรอยด์ขนาดสูงทันที ร่วมกับยากดภูมิคุ้มกัน เช่น methotrexate หรือ tocilizumab

Pain and temperature sensation may be spared, and neuropathic pain is variable
Causes: B12 or copper deficiency, diabetes, paraproteinaemia including anti-MAG, CIDP, Sjögren syndrome, paraneoplastic anti-Hu, platinum chemotherapy, pyridoxine excess, HIV and hereditary ataxias
inv: Nerve conduction: reduced sensory amplitudes in nerve disease, with or without demyelinating features; normal studies do not exclude a lesion in the dorsal roots proximal to the ganglion
Quantitative sensory testing of vibration, somatosensory evoked potentials, and MRI of the spine and roots when conduction is normal
B12, copper, glucose, serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation, anti-MAG, anti-Hu and anti-Ro/La; CSF protein; HIV test

case.who: 49-year-old woman, a nurse in Hat Yai
case.story: Four months of unsteady walking that is worse in the bathroom at night, numbness of the hands and trouble buttoning clothes. She is not weak and has no pain. No drugs or alcohol.
case.exam: Normal strength, absent ankle and knee jerks, vibration lost to the knees and wrists, impaired joint position of the toes and fingers, finger pseudoathetosis, wide-based gait and positive Romberg.
case.tests: Sensory conduction studies are normal; SSEP shows prolonged central latencies; CSF protein 98 mg/dL; lumbar MRI shows thickened enhancing dorsal roots; anti-Hu, anti-Ro and B12 are negative.
case.q: Why can the nerve conduction study be normal, and what treatment is suggested?
case.a: The lesion lies in the dorsal roots proximal to the ganglion, so the peripheral sensory axons are intact. Chronic immune sensory polyradiculopathy is treated with immunotherapy (IVIG or corticosteroids), judged by clinical response.

read.where: Companion to Peripheral Neuropathy, Chapter 6: Sensory Ataxia with Normal Nerve Conduction—Chronic Inflammatory Sensory Polyradiculopathy (CISP)
Companion to Peripheral Neuropathy, Chapter 46: A Weak, and Numb Patient with Tremor—Antimyelin-Associated Glycoprotein Polyneuropathy

det.patho: Large myelinated fibres carry vibration, proprioception and the afferent limb of the stretch reflex, so damage anywhere from the nerve to the dorsal root ganglion and root removes position sense and tendon reflexes. The injury may be demyelinating (CIDP, anti-MAG), axonal (diabetes, toxic, deficiency) or neuronal (ganglionopathy from Sjögren syndrome, platinum toxicity or paraneoplastic anti-Hu). Where the lesion lies determines whether nerve conduction is abnormal.
det.clinical: Patients describe walking on cotton wool, dropping objects and needing to look at their feet to place them. Examination shows reduced vibration and proprioception, pseudoathetosis, sensory ataxia and absent reflexes with preserved power. Asymmetric onset and early involvement of the arms and face suggest a ganglionopathy. Anti-MAG neuropathy gives a distal sensory loss with a disabling postural and intention tremor in a man in later life. Autonomic, small-fibre and motor features show which other populations of fibres are affected.
det.diagnosis: Document the pattern with the bedside examination, then conduction studies to separate neuropathy from sensory neuronopathy and from a lesion proximal to the ganglion. A normal conduction study with sensory ataxia should prompt root imaging, SSEPs and CSF. Screen for B12 and copper, paraprotein and immunofixation, anti-MAG and neuronal antibodies, Sjögren markers, HIV, diabetes and drug or toxin exposure, and consider cancer search if a paraneoplastic picture emerges. Nerve or root biopsy is kept for cases not otherwise explained.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: replace B12 or copper, stop pyridoxine or platinum drugs when feasible, optimise glycaemia, and treat Sjögren syndrome or malignancy as appropriate. Immune-mediated forms such as CIDP and chronic immune sensory polyradiculopathy are treated with IVIG, corticosteroids or plasma exchange and monitored by clinical response. Anti-MAG neuropathy responds only modestly to IVIG, and rituximab is used in selected progressing cases. Physiotherapy, gait aids, visual cues, home safety and treatment of tremor reduce disability.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause: deficiency and immune forms may improve with treatment; ganglionopathies and paraneoplastic forms often leave lasting disability because neurons are lost.
pearls: Sensory ataxia with areflexia and preserved strength is the large-fibre syndrome.
A normal sensory nerve study does not exclude a proximal (root) lesion; image the roots and check CSF.
Asymmetric, rapid onset and face or arm involvement point to ganglionopathy, which carries different causes.
det.thd: Large-fibre neuropathy คือโรคที่เส้นใยประสาทขนาดใหญ่เสีย ทำให้ไม่รู้สึกสั่นสะเทือนและตำแหน่งข้อ เดินเซโดยเฉพาะในที่มืด ยืนหลับตาแล้วล้ม (Romberg บวก) และ reflex หาย แต่กำลังกล้ามเนื้อมักปกติ สาเหตุได้แก่ ขาด B12 หรือทองแดง เบาหวาน paraprotein anti-MAG CIDP Sjögren และ paraneoplastic เมื่อ NCS ปกติแต่มี sensory ataxia ให้ทำ MRI ราก ตรวจ SSEP และน้ำไขสันหลัง การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ และกลุ่มภูมิคุ้มกันตอบสนองต่อ IVIG หรือสเตียรอยด์

name: Laryngo-pharyngeal dystonia
formal: Focal dystonia of the laryngeal and pharyngeal muscles, causing spasmodic dysphonia or dysphagia, often task-specific, or drug-induced.
simple: Involuntary muscle spasms in the voice box or throat, affecting speech or swallowing.
th: focal dystonia ของกล้ามเนื้อกล่องเสียงและคอหอย ทำให้เสียงขาดหรือเสียงหายใจปน และกลืนลำบาก มักเป็นเฉพาะงาน
tempoNote: Gradual onset in adulthood, then plateaus; acute forms from dopamine blockers
feat: Strained, strangled voice with breaks (adductor type) or breathy whispery breaks (abductor type)
Task-specific: speech affected, but laughing, singing or whispering may be normal
Pharyngeal involvement gives dysphagia and choking
May be part of segmental dystonia (Meige, cranial-cervical)
Acute laryngeal dystonia from antipsychotics or antiemetics can cause stridor
inv: Laryngoscopy (fibreoptic) during speech by ENT/voice specialist
Drug history; MRI only if atypical or with other signs
Gene testing (e.g. THAP1) in young onset or familial cases

case.story: Two years of a choked, broken voice when talking on the phone, yet her singing at karaoke sounds normal; stress makes it worse.
case.exam: Strained voice with frequent breaks on vowels; normal neurological examination otherwise.
case.tests: Laryngoscopy shows irregular hyperadduction of vocal folds during speech, normal structure.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the treatment of choice?
case.a: Adductor laryngeal dystonia (spasmodic dysphonia); botulinum toxin injection into thyroarytenoid muscles.

det.patho: Like other focal dystonias, it involves abnormal sensorimotor integration and reduced inhibition in the basal ganglia-cerebellar-cortical network controlling the larynx. It is task-specific because the network for speech differs from that for laughter or singing. Drug-induced acute forms arise from sudden D2 blockade.
det.clinical: Adductor spasmodic dysphonia is the commonest form; abductor and mixed types are less frequent. Pharyngeal dystonia causes swallowing difficulty and may coexist with oromandibular or cervical dystonia. Voice tremor often accompanies it. Acute laryngeal dystonia after haloperidol or metoclopramide is an emergency because of airway risk.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical with laryngoscopic confirmation by a voice specialist. Speech tasks loaded with voiced or voiceless sounds help separate adductor from abductor types. Structural lesions, muscle tension dysphonia and functional dysphonia are the main alternatives. Drug review is essential.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin injection into the affected laryngeal muscles is first line and is repeated every few months. Voice therapy supports technique. Oral drugs help little; surgical options exist in specialised centres. Acute drug-induced laryngeal dystonia is treated with IV anticholinergic (benztropine or diphenhydramine) and airway support.
det.prognosis: Chronic but non-progressive in most; good functional control with regular botulinum toxin.
pearls: A broken speaking voice with normal singing suggests laryngeal dystonia.
Stridor after an antiemetic or antipsychotic: think acute laryngeal dystonia.
Botulinum toxin works for months and needs repeat injections.
det.thd: Laryngo-pharyngeal dystonia คือ dystonia เฉพาะที่ของกล้ามเนื้อกล่องเสียงและคอหอย ทำให้เสียงขาดเป็นช่วง ๆ หรือกลืนลำบาก มักเป็นเฉพาะเวลาพูด แต่ร้องเพลงหรือหัวเราะได้ปกติ วินิจฉัยด้วยการส่องกล่องเสียงขณะพูด รักษาด้วย botulinum toxin และฝึกเสียง ถ้าเกิดเฉียบพลันหลังยาต้านจิตหรือยาแก้อาเจียนต้องให้ยา anticholinergic ทันทีเพราะอาจอุดทางเดินหายใจ

name: Late onset Huntington’s disease
formal: Huntington disease beginning after age 50 with milder chorea and slower decline, often with smaller CAG expansions and no family history.
simple: Huntington disease that starts late in life and tends to progress more slowly.
th: Huntington's disease ที่เริ่มหลังอายุ 50–60 ปี chorea ไม่รุนแรงและดำเนินโรคช้า CAG repeat มักไม่ยาวมาก และอาจไม่มีประวัติครอบครัว
tempoNote: Insidious onset late in life with slow progression
feat: Chorea is the main feature; gait unsteadiness and falls
Cognitive and psychiatric changes milder than in midlife onset
Family history often missing (early parental death, misdiagnosis, reduced penetrance alleles)
Often mislabelled as senile chorea or vascular chorea
inv: HTT CAG repeat testing with pre-test counselling (often 36–44 repeats)
MRI: caudate atrophy; excludes vascular lesions
Exclude other chorea causes: hyperglycaemia, thyroid, drugs, polycythaemia, autoimmune

case.story: Daughter notes two years of fidgety movements of hands and face and some unsteadiness; no known family neurological disease, father died young in an accident.
case.exam: Generalised mild chorea, motor impersistence of tongue, slow saccades, MoCA 25/30.
case.tests: Glucose, thyroid and blood count normal; MRI shows caudate atrophy; HTT CAG 40 repeats.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and does a negative family history exclude it?
case.a: Late onset Huntington's disease; no — family history is often absent in late-onset cases.

det.patho: A CAG expansion in HTT produces mutant huntingtin with a polyglutamine tract that damages striatal medium spiny neurons and later the cortex. Age at onset correlates inversely with repeat length, so late onset usually reflects shorter expansions in the reduced-penetrance (36–39) or low full-penetrance range, modified by DNA repair gene variants.
det.clinical: Late onset accounts for about a tenth of HD. Chorea and gait problems dominate, and cognitive and behavioural changes tend to be milder and slower. Because parents may have died before symptoms or been misdiagnosed, many patients have no family history. Disease duration from onset is often shorter in calendar years because of age-related comorbidity.
det.diagnosis: Any adult with progressive chorea warrants HTT testing after counselling, regardless of age or family history. Reduced-penetrance results need careful interpretation. Exclude acquired chorea, especially non-ketotic hyperglycaemia, thyroid disease, drugs, stroke and polycythaemia. MRI may show caudate atrophy.
det.treatment: Chorea can be treated with tetrabenazine or deutetrabenazine (watching for depression and parkinsonism) or with antipsychotics. Fall prevention, swallowing assessment and management of mood are central. Genetic counselling for children and grandchildren is important even though the patient is elderly.
det.prognosis: Progression is usually slower than in midlife onset; death is often from comorbid illness.
pearls: No family history does not rule out HD, especially in older adults.
Test HTT before labelling chorea as senile.
A late-onset diagnosis has major implications for younger relatives.
det.thd: Late onset Huntington's disease คือ HD ที่เริ่มหลังอายุ 50–60 ปี มัก CAG repeat ไม่ยาวมาก อาการหลักคือ chorea และเดินเซ ความจำและอารมณ์เปลี่ยนน้อยกว่าแบบอายุน้อย และมักไม่มีประวัติครอบครัว จึงควรตรวจยีน HTT ก่อนสรุปว่าเป็น senile chorea รักษาด้วย tetrabenazine หรือยาต้านจิตและให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรมแก่ญาติ

name: Late-onset cerebellar degenerations
formal: Sporadic or hereditary cerebellar atrophy starting after age 40, such as MSA-C, alcohol-related, autoimmune or SAOA, causing progressive ataxia.
simple: Gradual loss of balance and coordination in older age due to degeneration of the cerebellum.
th: กลุ่มโรคสมองน้อยฝ่อที่เริ่มหลังอายุ 40 ทั้งแบบพันธุกรรม (เช่น SCA27B, CANVAS) และแบบเกิดเอง (MSA-C, แอลกอฮอล์, ภูมิคุ้มกัน, SAOA) ทำให้เดินเซลุกลาม
tempoNote: Gradual progression over years; subacute (weeks–months) course suggests paraneoplastic or immune cause
feat: Progressive gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria and nystagmus starting after about 40
Autonomic failure and parkinsonism point to MSA-C
Neuropathy plus vestibular loss and cough suggests CANVAS (RFC1)
Downbeat nystagmus and episodic symptoms suggest SCA27B (FGF14)
Gait-predominant ataxia with alcohol excess: alcoholic cerebellar degeneration
inv: MRI: vermis or pancerebellar atrophy, 'hot cross bun' or middle cerebellar peduncle signal in MSA
Vitamin E, B12, thyroid, anti-gliadin/transglutaminase, GAD and onconeural antibodies
Nerve conduction, vestibular testing, autonomic testing
Genetic tests: RFC1, FGF14 GAA repeat, SCA panel, FXTAS (FMR1)

case.story: Four years of slowly worsening unsteadiness and numb feet; dry cough for 15 years; falls in the dark.
case.exam: Wide-based gait, mild dysarthria, broken smooth pursuit, bilateral positive head impulse test, reduced vibration sense and absent ankle jerks.
case.tests: MRI mild vermian atrophy; NCS sensory neuronopathy; biallelic RFC1 AAGGG expansion.
case.q: What syndrome is this and why test head impulses?
case.a: CANVAS from RFC1 expansions; bilateral vestibular loss is a defining component and explains worse balance in the dark.

read.where: Chapter 24 Cerebellar Ataxias and Related Conditions — Acquired Ataxia Syndromes

det.patho: This is a heterogeneous grouping: neurodegenerative (MSA-C, sporadic adult-onset ataxia of unknown cause), genetic (repeat expansions in RFC1, FGF14, FMR1 premutation, late-onset SCAs, Friedreich with late onset), toxic-nutritional (alcohol, vitamin E or B1 deficiency, drugs such as phenytoin) and immune (gluten, GAD, paraneoplastic). Recent discovery of the FGF14 GAA expansion (SCA27B) and RFC1 repeats explained a large fraction of previously 'idiopathic' late-onset ataxia.
det.clinical: All share progressive imbalance beginning in middle or later life. The tempo matters: weeks to months suggests immune, paraneoplastic or prion disease; years suggests degenerative or genetic causes. Accompanying features guide diagnosis: autonomic failure and RBD (MSA), neuropathy and vestibular loss (CANVAS), downbeat nystagmus and episodic worsening (SCA27B), tremor and premutation family history (FXTAS).
det.diagnosis: MRI first, then a metabolic and immune screen (B12, vitamin E, thyroid, coeliac and GAD antibodies, onconeural antibodies when subacute). Electrophysiology and vestibular testing detect neuropathy and bilateral vestibulopathy. Genetic testing for RFC1, FGF14, FMR1 and common SCAs is now first-tier in late-onset sporadic ataxia, even without family history. Reassess regularly, as MSA features may emerge later.
det.treatment: Remove toxins (alcohol, offending drugs) and replace deficient vitamins. Immune ataxias may respond to gluten-free diet or immunotherapy. 4-aminopyridine can improve SCA27B and downbeat nystagmus; riluzole has modest evidence in some ataxias. Physiotherapy focused on balance and coordination improves function; manage autonomic symptoms in MSA.
det.prognosis: Varies by cause: MSA progresses within a decade, genetic forms usually slowly, and treatable forms may stabilise or improve.
pearls: Late onset does not exclude genetics: test RFC1 and FGF14.
Subacute ataxia over weeks is paraneoplastic or immune until proven otherwise.
Ask about cough (CANVAS), urinary/erectile symptoms (MSA) and alcohol.
det.thd: Late-onset cerebellar degenerations คือกลุ่มโรคสมองน้อยฝ่อที่เริ่มหลังอายุ 40 มีทั้ง MSA-C, ภาวะจากแอลกอฮอล์หรือขาดวิตามิน, ภูมิคุ้มกัน และพันธุกรรม เช่น RFC1 (CANVAS) และ FGF14 (SCA27B) ผู้ป่วยเดินเซ พูดไม่ชัด ลุกลามช้า ๆ ถ้าแย่ลงเร็วภายในสัปดาห์ถึงเดือนให้นึกถึง paraneoplastic ตรวจ MRI เลือดหาสาเหตุที่รักษาได้ และตรวจยีน รักษาตามสาเหตุร่วมกับกายภาพบำบัด

name: Late-onset nemaline myopathy
formal: Adult-onset myopathy with nemaline rods, sometimes associated with monoclonal gammopathy or HIV, causing rapidly progressive proximal and axial weakness.
simple: A form of muscle disease starting in adulthood, with rod-like structures in muscle, causing weakness that can progress quickly.
more: Screen for monoclonal gammopathy; treat the underlying clone, for example with chemotherapy and stem cell transplantation.
th: โรคกล้ามเนื้อมี nemaline rods เริ่มในผู้ใหญ่แบบเป็นเอง มักสัมพันธ์กับ monoclonal gammopathy — ค่อนข้างรักษาได้
tempoNote: Weakness develops over months (sometimes weeks) after age 40
feat: Progressive proximal and axial weakness — prominent neck extensor weakness ('dropped head')
Respiratory muscle involvement and dysphagia may occur early
Normal or mildly raised CK; no family history
Associated monoclonal gammopathy in about half; also HIV
inv: Serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation and free light chains; HIV test
EMG: myopathic, often with fibrillations; pulmonary function tests
Muscle biopsy: nemaline rods on Gomori trichrome / electron microscopy without inflammation

case.story: Six months of difficulty keeping his head up while driving a tuk-tuk, then trouble rising from a squat and breathlessness lying flat.
case.exam: Severe neck extensor weakness, symmetric hip and shoulder weakness, mild facial weakness, normal sensation and reflexes.
case.tests: CK 280 U/L; IgG-kappa paraprotein; FVC 55% predicted; biopsy shows many fibres with nemaline rods.
case.q: Why does the paraprotein matter for treatment?
case.a: SLONM with MGUS often responds to clone-directed therapy — high-dose melphalan with autologous stem-cell transplant or daratumumab-based regimens — and IVIG; untreated it can cause respiratory failure.

read.where: Review: Monoclonal gammopathy of clinical significance (Table 1); Management of MGCS
Review: Diagnosis — mimics of inflammatory myopathy and lack of response to glucocorticoids
Chapters 41–42 Congenital Nemaline Myopathy Types 1 and 2 (genetic forms for comparison)
Chapter 14 Muscle and Myotonic Diseases (congenital myopathies; HIV-associated rod myopathy)

det.patho: Nemaline rods are aggregates of Z-disc material, mainly α-actinin, within muscle fibres. In the sporadic late-onset form the cause is probably acquired and immune-related, as about half of patients carry a monoclonal protein and response to clone-directed therapy suggests a pathogenic role. HIV and other inflammatory states are also associated. When a paraprotein is present, SLONM fits the modern idea of a monoclonal gammopathy of clinical significance: the clone is small and not malignant, yet its product damages an organ, which is the rationale for treating the clone. This acquired disorder should be kept separate from congenital nemaline myopathy, in which variants in thin-filament genes (NEB most often, also ACTA1, TPM2, TPM3, TNNT1 and others) produce rods from infancy.
det.clinical: Patients over 40 develop subacute weakness of proximal limbs, neck and trunk; head drop and camptocormia are typical. Bulbar, facial and respiratory muscles can be involved, sometimes leading to ventilatory failure as the first presentation, so orthopnoea or morning headache deserve direct questions. Course without treatment is relentless, and patients with a paraprotein tend to progress faster. Unlike the congenital forms, there is no lifelong slender build, long face, high-arched palate or delayed motor milestones, and the family history is negative. Myalgia and skin or lung involvement are absent, which helps separate it from inflammatory myopathies.
det.diagnosis: SLONM should be considered in any adult with new progressive axial and proximal myopathy, especially with head drop or respiratory weakness. Serum and urine immunofixation and free light chains are mandatory, and an HIV test should be done. Biopsy shows rods in a variable proportion of fibres with little inflammation; EMG is myopathic, often irritable, and muscle MRI often highlights paraspinal and posterior thigh involvement. Myositis-specific antibodies are negative, and a 'polymyositis' that fails to respond to glucocorticoids should prompt re-review of the biopsy with trichrome staining or electron microscopy. Because MGUS is common in older adults, the biopsy rather than the paraprotein makes the diagnosis; HIV-associated rod myopathy may have a high CK and necrotic fibres. Exclude congenital nemaline myopathy, myositis, MG, Pompe disease and ALS.
det.treatment: Patients with a monoclonal protein have the best responses to autologous stem-cell transplantation after high-dose chemotherapy or modern anti-plasma-cell therapy (for example daratumumab-based regimens), and deeper suppression of the paraprotein tends to bring better muscle recovery, so haematology should be involved from the start. IVIG can stabilise or improve some patients and is often used as a bridge. Patients without a paraprotein may respond to immunotherapy but evidence is limited; corticosteroids alone rarely help. Respiratory monitoring (FVC, nocturnal oximetry or blood gases) and non-invasive ventilation are essential, together with swallowing assessment and physiotherapy.
det.prognosis: Untreated, many die from respiratory failure within a few years; with clone-directed treatment a substantial proportion improve or stabilise.
pearls: Dropped head plus a paraprotein in a middle-aged adult: think SLONM and biopsy.
A treatable myopathy hiding behind 'MGUS' — always check immunofixation in unexplained adult myopathy.
Rods can be missed on routine H&E; ask for trichrome staining or EM.
Seronegative 'polymyositis' with axial weakness that ignores steroids: re-examine the biopsy for rods and check immunofixation.
det.thd: SLONM เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้อที่เริ่มหลังอายุ 40 ปี กล้ามเนื้อคอ ลำตัว และต้นแขนขาอ่อนแรงในหลายเดือน มักคอตก และอาจหายใจล้มเหลว ประมาณครึ่งหนึ่งพบ monoclonal gammopathy ซึ่งถือเป็น monoclonal gammopathy of clinical significance ตัดชิ้นเนื้อพบ nemaline rods โดยไม่มีการอักเสบ ต่างจาก nemaline myopathy แต่กำเนิดที่เป็นตั้งแต่เด็กและมีรูปร่างผอมยาว วินิจฉัยต้องตรวจ immunofixation และ HIV ทุกราย ถ้าวินิจฉัยว่าเป็น myositis แต่ไม่ตอบสนองต่อสเตียรอยด์ให้ทบทวนชิ้นเนื้อ ผู้ที่มี paraprotein ตอบสนองดีต่อการรักษาที่มุ่ง plasma cell clone เช่น เคมีบำบัดร่วม stem-cell transplant หรือ daratumumab ร่วมกับ IVIG และต้องติดตามการหายใจใกล้ชิด
