name: Lateral orbitofrontal syndrome
formal: Frontal lobe syndrome from lateral orbitofrontal damage with disinhibition, impulsivity, irritability and loss of social judgement, as in frontotemporal dementia or traumatic brain injury.
simple: Impulsive, rude and socially inappropriate behaviour caused by damage to the lower part of the frontal lobes.
th: กลุ่มอาการ frontal lobe จากรอยโรคที่ orbitofrontal ด้านข้าง ทำให้ขาดการยับยั้ง หุนหันพลันแล่น หงุดหงิด และเสียวิจารณญาณทางสังคม
tempoNote: Course depends on cause: abrupt after trauma or stroke, insidious in dementia or tumour
feat: Disinhibition, tactlessness and socially inappropriate jokes or acts
Impulsivity, irritability and emotional lability
Poor insight; preserved memory and standard IQ tests
Utilisation or imitation behaviour, hyperorality and anosmia in some
Causes: traumatic brain injury, frontotemporal dementia, olfactory groove meningioma, ACA aneurysm rupture
inv: MRI brain for contusion, tumour, atrophy or infarct
Neuropsychology: social cognition and inhibition tasks (bedside Go/No-Go)
Collateral history; FDG-PET if neurodegeneration suspected

case.story: Wife reports a year of rude remarks to colleagues, reckless spending and eating sweets constantly; he has also lost his sense of smell.
case.exam: Overfamiliar, jocular, impulsive on Go/No-Go; memory and orientation normal; anosmic both sides.
case.tests: MRI shows a large olfactory groove meningioma compressing both orbitofrontal regions.
case.q: Which frontal syndrome is this and why is the cause important?
case.a: Orbitofrontal (disinhibited) syndrome from olfactory groove meningioma; the tumour is removable, so behaviour may improve.

det.patho: The orbitofrontal cortex links emotion, reward and social rules with behaviour through connections with the amygdala, hypothalamus and caudate. Damage removes top-down inhibition, so drives and impulses are expressed without regard to context. The syndrome is part of the classic division of prefrontal syndromes into dorsolateral (executive), medial (apathetic) and orbital (disinhibited).
det.clinical: This is a clinical syndrome rather than a single disease. Family members describe a personality change: rudeness, poor social judgement, impulsive spending or sexual behaviour, and emotional lability. Patients usually lack insight and perform well on formal memory and IQ tests, which can delay diagnosis. Anosmia suggests a basal frontal lesion.
det.diagnosis: Collateral history is essential. MRI identifies trauma, tumours such as olfactory groove meningioma, infarcts or atrophy. Bedside tests (Go/No-Go, Luria sequence, social cognition tasks) may be abnormal, though standard screens like MMSE can be normal. When imaging is non-diagnostic and the course is progressive, consider bvFTD and psychiatric illness.
det.treatment: Treat the cause, such as resecting a meningioma. For persistent behaviour, use structured environment, caregiver education and behavioural strategies; SSRIs or trazodone may reduce disinhibition and compulsions in FTD, and antipsychotics are reserved for severe agitation. Address safety issues: driving, finances and employment.
det.prognosis: Variable: may improve after removal of a compressive lesion or recovery from trauma; progressive in neurodegenerative causes.
pearls: New personality change in midlife with anosmia: image the frontal base.
Normal MMSE does not exclude a frontal syndrome.
Orbitofrontal: disinhibited; medial: apathetic; dorsolateral: dysexecutive.
det.thd: Lateral orbitofrontal syndrome คือกลุ่มอาการจากรอยโรคที่สมองส่วนหน้าด้านฐาน ทำให้ขาดการยับยั้งตนเอง พูดจาไม่เหมาะสม หุนหัน และหงุดหงิด แต่ความจำและ IQ ปกติ สาเหตุได้แก่ บาดเจ็บศีรษะ bvFTD และเนื้องอก เช่น olfactory groove meningioma วินิจฉัยจากประวัติจากญาติและ MRI แล้วรักษาตามสาเหตุร่วมกับการจัดการพฤติกรรม

Orbitofrontal contusions are classic after head injury
Medial frontal lesions give apathy and akinesia rather than disinhibition

name: LCAD deficiency
formal: Rare long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase defect of fatty acid oxidation causing hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy, and myopathy with rhabdomyolysis.
simple: A very rare inherited defect in breaking down fats for energy, leading to low blood sugar and muscle breakdown.
more: Acylcarnitine analysis and enzyme or gene tests; avoid fasting, use a low-fat diet with medium-chain triglycerides.
th: ภาวะขาดเอนไซม์ long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase ในการเผาผลาญกรดไขมัน มีรายงานน้อยมาก และผู้ป่วยในอดีตส่วนใหญ่แท้จริงเป็น VLCAD deficiency
tempoNote: Crises with fasting or illness in infancy; adult muscle presentations reported rarely
feat: Historically described fatty acid oxidation defect with hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy and rhabdomyolysis
Most older 'LCAD' cases were reclassified as VLCAD deficiency after the VLCAD enzyme was found (1992)
True ACADL deficiency in humans is extremely rare; its clinical picture is uncertain
Fasting, infection and prolonged exercise are the usual triggers in long-chain FAO defects
Treat clinically as a long-chain fatty acid oxidation disorder
inv: Glucose, ketones, CK, ammonia, liver enzymes during crises
Plasma acylcarnitine profile
Gene panel for FAO disorders (ACADVL, ACADL, HADHA/B, CPT2)

case.who: 8-month-old boy in a hospital in Nakhon Ratchasima
case.story: After two days of vomiting with gastroenteritis he became floppy and drowsy.
case.exam: Lethargic, hepatomegaly, hypotonia, tachycardia.
case.tests: Glucose 1.8 mmol/L with low ketones, CK 9,000 U/L; acylcarnitines show raised long-chain species; panel finds ACADVL variants (not ACADL).
case.q: Why should a historical 'LCAD deficiency' label be re-examined today?
case.a: Most cases labelled LCAD were actually VLCAD deficiency; modern acylcarnitine and gene testing clarify the true defect.

det.patho: LCAD was the enzyme first blamed for a long-chain fatty acid oxidation defect, but later work showed most patients lacked VLCAD instead. ACADL is expressed mainly in lung and has limited roles in human muscle fatty acid oxidation. Confirmed human ACADL deficiency is exceedingly rare, and its consequences are not well defined.
det.clinical: The historical clinical picture is that of a long-chain FAO disorder: hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, liver dysfunction, cardiomyopathy and rhabdomyolysis triggered by fasting or illness. Because true cases are so scarce, it is unclear which features belong to genuine ACADL deficiency. Clinicians should treat the label with caution.
det.diagnosis: Acylcarnitine profiling with gene panel testing establishes which enzyme is defective. ACADVL variants are found in most patients with long-chain patterns. Enzyme studies in fibroblasts can resolve uncertain cases.
det.treatment: Management follows long-chain FAO principles: avoid fasting, provide frequent high-carbohydrate feeds, restrict long-chain fat, supplement medium-chain triglycerides or triheptanoin, and give IV glucose early in illness. Treat rhabdomyolysis with fluids.
det.prognosis: Uncertain for true ACADL deficiency; good for treated long-chain FAO disorders if crises are prevented.
pearls: 'LCAD deficiency' in older literature usually means VLCAD deficiency.
Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with high CK points to a fatty acid oxidation defect.
IV glucose early in intercurrent illness prevents crises.
det.thd: LCAD deficiency เป็นชื่อเดิมของโรคพร่องการเผาผลาญกรดไขมันสายยาว แต่ภายหลังพบว่าผู้ป่วยส่วนใหญ่ที่เคยวินิจฉัยว่า LCAD แท้จริงเป็น VLCAD deficiency ภาวะขาด ACADL จริงในมนุษย์พบน้อยมากและยังไม่ทราบลักษณะทางคลินิกชัดเจน อาการแบบโรคกลุ่มนี้คือน้ำตาลต่ำโดยไม่มีคีโตน หัวใจผิดปกติ และกล้ามเนื้อสลายเมื่ออดอาหารหรือเจ็บป่วย วินิจฉัยด้วย acylcarnitine และตรวจยีน

name: Lead poisoning
formal: Toxic exposure producing encephalopathy in children and motor neuropathy (wrist drop) in adults, anaemia with basophilic stippling, and abdominal pain; treated with chelation.
simple: Harm to nerves and brain from lead exposure, causing weakness, abdominal pain, learning problems and anaemia.
more: Lead-induced toxicity causing encephalopathy, motor neuropathy with wrist drop, anaemia, abdominal colic and cognitive impairment, treated with chelation.

tempoNote: Usually weeks to months of ongoing exposure
feat: Adults: motor-predominant neuropathy, classically bilateral wrist and finger drop (radial territory) with little sensory loss
Abdominal colic, constipation, fatigue, arthralgia; blue-grey gum line
Microcytic anaemia with basophilic stippling of red cells

Hypertension, gout and renal impairment with chronic exposure

case.who: 34-year-old man working at a car-battery recycling shop
case.story: Three months of cramping abdominal pain and constipation; for two weeks he cannot lift his wrists to ride his motorbike.
case.exam: Bilateral wrist and finger extensor weakness, brachioradialis spared on one side, normal sensation; grey line along gingival margin; pale.
case.tests: Hb 9.8 g/dL, microcytic with basophilic stippling; blood lead 92 µg/dL; NCS: low radial CMAPs, normal sensory responses.
case.q: What is the treatment?
case.a: Remove from exposure, report as occupational disease, and chelate (succimer orally, or CaNa2EDTA ± dimercaprol for very high levels or encephalopathy) with toxicology input.

det.patho: Lead substitutes for calcium and zinc, inhibits haem synthesis enzymes (ALA dehydratase, ferrochelatase) and damages mitochondria and endothelium. Peripheral nerves develop motor axonal (with some demyelinating) damage, while in children the immature blood–brain barrier allows cerebral oedema and lasting cognitive harm. Common sources are batteries, paint, smelting, traditional medicines, ceramic glazes and contaminated cosmetics.
det.clinical: Adults present with fatigue, abdominal colic, joint pains and a motor neuropathy favouring the most-used muscles, most famously radial wrist drop. Sensation is usually spared. Children show developmental delay, behavioural change and, at high levels, encephalopathy with seizures and coma. Anaemia, hypertension and renal impairment add to the picture.
det.diagnosis: Blood lead level confirms exposure; there is no safe threshold in children. Supporting findings are microcytic anaemia with basophilic stippling and raised zinc protoporphyrin. Electrodiagnosis shows motor axonal involvement. Search for the source and test co-workers or family.
det.treatment: Remove the source first. Chelation is guided by blood level and symptoms: oral succimer (DMSA) for moderate levels, and parenteral CaNa2EDTA (preceded by dimercaprol in encephalopathy) for severe toxicity. Correct iron deficiency, which increases lead absorption. Use splints and physiotherapy for wrist drop.
det.prognosis: Adult neuropathy generally improves after exposure ends; childhood cognitive effects are often permanent.
pearls: Bilateral wrist drop with colic and anaemia = lead until proved otherwise.
Ask about occupation, hobbies and traditional remedies.
Porphyria shares colic plus motor neuropathy — check both lead and urine PBG.
det.thd: พิษตะกั่วในผู้ใหญ่ทำให้เกิด motor neuropathy โดยเฉพาะข้อมือตกทั้งสองข้าง ร่วมกับปวดท้อง ท้องผูก โลหิตจางที่มี basophilic stippling และเส้นสีเทาที่เหงือก ในเด็กทำให้พัฒนาการและสติปัญญาเสียได้ถาวร วินิจฉัยด้วยระดับตะกั่วในเลือด รักษาโดยหยุดการสัมผัสและให้ยาขับโลหะ เช่น succimer หรือ EDTA

name: Leber’s hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON)
formal: Maternally inherited mitochondrial optic neuropathy from mtDNA point mutations, causing subacute painless bilateral central vision loss mainly in young men, with disc hyperaemia.
simple: An inherited eye nerve disease that causes sudden, painless loss of central vision, mostly in young men.
more: Diagnosis by MT-ND4 (11778), MT-ND1 (3460) or MT-ND6 (14484) mutation testing; OCT shows retinal nerve fibre swelling and later atrophy. Idebenone is used and gene therapy is under development; spontaneous recovery occurs in some (14484). Mitochondrial inherited optic atrophy from mtDNA mutations (11778, 3460, 14484), causing painless subacute central vision loss in young men, with telangiectatic microangiopathy.
th: ตามัวไม่เจ็บตาจากความผิดปกติของ DNA ไมโทคอนเดรีย ถ่ายทอดทางแม่ พบในชายหนุ่ม ตาข้างหนึ่งมัวก่อนแล้วอีกข้างตามภายในสัปดาห์ถึงเดือน มี central scotoma
tempoNote: Painless loss in one eye over weeks, the second eye follows within weeks to months; vision then plateaus, with partial recovery in some
feat: Young man (peak late teens to 30s) with painless subacute central vision loss in one eye then the other
Dense central or centrocaecal scotoma, poor colour vision, acuity often 6/60 or worse
Acute disc looks hyperaemic with swollen-appearing nerve fibre layer and peripapillary telangiectatic vessels but does not leak on fluorescein
Relatively preserved pupil reactions for the degree of visual loss
Maternal family history in many; smoking and heavy alcohol increase penetrance
inv: mtDNA testing for the three common primary point variants (11778, 3460 and 14484), then whole mitochondrial genome if negative
OCT: early RNFL thickening, later temporal thinning; visual fields show central scotomas
MRI orbits/brain to exclude compressive or inflammatory causes (usually normal or mild nerve T2 signal)
ECG for pre-excitation; consider neurological review for 'LHON plus' features

case.story: Six weeks ago a smudge appeared in the centre of his right eye's vision; this week the left eye has the same blur. No pain. His maternal uncle 'went blind young'. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day.
case.exam: Acuity 3/60 right, 6/36 left; central scotomas both eyes; left disc hyperaemic with tortuous small vessels around it; weak right RAPD only.
case.tests: MRI orbits and brain normal; AQP4 and MOG antibodies negative; mtDNA m.11778G>A homoplasmic.
case.q: Diagnosis, and what advice and treatment would you offer?
case.a: LHON; stop smoking and limit alcohol, offer idebenone early, and genetic counselling for maternal relatives.

det.patho: LHON is caused by mtDNA point variants in complex I subunit genes; three variants account for about 90% of cases. Retinal ganglion cells, with their long unmyelinated intraocular axons and high energy demand, are particularly vulnerable, and the small papillomacular fibres fail first. Penetrance is incomplete and strongly male biased, so many carriers never lose vision; smoking and alcohol are modifiable risk factors.
det.clinical: Typically a young man loses central vision painlessly in one eye, followed by the second eye usually within months; simultaneous onset occurs in some. Acuity falls to counting fingers or worse in many, and the nadir is reached within months. The m.14484T>C variant carries the best chance of spontaneous improvement. A minority have 'LHON plus' with dystonia, tremor, MS-like illness (Harding disease) or cardiac pre-excitation.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in any bilateral sequential painless central loss in a young adult, especially with a maternal family history. Confirm by mtDNA testing of blood. MRI excludes compression and helps distinguish demyelinating optic neuritis, which can coexist (Harding disease). Look for toxic and nutritional causes because they produce a similar central field defect.
det.treatment: Idebenone (a short-chain quinone that bypasses complex I) is licensed in Europe for patients within about five years of onset and may improve the chance of recovery when started early. Gene therapy with intravitreal MT-ND4 (lenadogene nolparvovec) has trial data for m.11778G>A but is not widely available. All patients and at-risk relatives should avoid smoking and heavy alcohol; provide low-vision aids and counselling.
det.prognosis: Most patients remain legally blind, though partial recovery of central islands can occur, best with m.14484T>C and young onset.
pearls: Young man, painless sequential central scotomas, pseudo-oedematous disc that does not leak: LHON.
Inheritance is maternal; affected men do not transmit it.
Tell carriers to stop smoking — it is the main changeable risk.
det.thd: LHON เป็นโรคตามัวจากยีนในไมโทคอนเดรียที่ถ่ายทอดทางแม่ มักเป็นชายหนุ่ม ตามัวตรงกลางโดยไม่เจ็บตา ข้างหนึ่งก่อนแล้วอีกข้างตามภายในสัปดาห์ถึงเดือน ขั้วประสาทตาดูบวมแดงแต่ไม่รั่วสี ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจ mtDNA รักษาด้วย idebenone หากเริ่มเร็ว แนะนำให้งดบุหรี่และสุรา และให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรมแก่ญาติฝั่งแม่

name: Leg tremor
formal: Rhythmic shaking of the leg, from orthostatic tremor, Parkinson disease, essential tremor, cerebellar lesions or functional disorders; orthostatic tremor appears on standing.
simple: Shaking of the leg or legs, often on standing, with various possible causes.
th: การสั่นเป็นจังหวะของขา จาก orthostatic tremor (สั่นเมื่อยืน) Parkinson's disease, essential tremor, โรคสมองน้อย หรือ functional

Tremor and unsteadiness only on standing that vanish on walking or sitting suggests orthostatic tremor
Postural leg tremor occurs in advanced essential tremor

case.story: For three years she feels her legs quiver and she is afraid of falling when standing in a queue at the market; walking or sitting brings relief.
case.exam: Fine visible ripple of thigh muscles on standing, palpable buzzing; none sitting; gait almost normal.

read.where: 4 - Parkinsonism: Clinical features and differential diagnosis

det.patho: Leg tremor shares mechanisms with tremor elsewhere: basal ganglia rest tremor, cerebellar outflow tremor, and in orthostatic tremor a central high-frequency oscillator thought to involve the brainstem and cerebellum. Peripheral neuropathy can also add tremor to the legs.
det.clinical: This is a symptom with several causes. Patients may describe shaking, quivering or a sense of instability rather than a visible tremor. Orthostatic tremor typically affects older women, with fear of falling while standing still. Parkinsonian rest tremor of a foot is common early in PD. Functional leg tremor may start abruptly and change with attention.
det.diagnosis: Watch the legs at rest seated, while standing still, while walking and during heel-shin testing. Palpate or auscultate thigh muscles while standing. Surface EMG confirms orthostatic tremor by its high frequency. Look for parkinsonian, cerebellar or neuropathic signs and review drugs.
det.treatment: Treat by cause: dopaminergic therapy for PD; clonazepam, gabapentin or primidone for orthostatic tremor; beta blockers or primidone for essential tremor; physiotherapy for functional tremor. Walking aids, a perching stool and avoidance of prolonged standing help orthostatic tremor.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause; orthostatic tremor is chronic and may slowly worsen.
pearls: Feeling unsteady standing still but fine walking: orthostatic tremor.
A foot rest tremor can be the first sign of Parkinson's.
Listen to the thigh: a helicopter sound means a fast orthostatic tremor.

name: Leigh syndrome
formal: Subacute necrotising encephalomyelopathy of mitochondrial or nuclear gene origin, with infant regression, hypotonia, dystonia, brainstem signs and basal ganglia lesions with lactic acidosis.
simple: A severe inherited mitochondrial disease of children causing loss of skills, weak muscles, movement problems and breathing trouble.
more: Diagnose by MRI showing symmetric basal ganglia and brainstem lesions, raised lactate, and genetic testing (SURF1, MT-ATP6, PDHA1 and others). Care is supportive; biotin, thiamine or ketogenic diet help selected defects; prognosis is poor. Subacute necrotising encephalomyelopathy from mitochondrial or nuclear gene defects, with infantile regression, dystonia, brainstem dysfunction and symmetrical basal ganglia lesions.

feat: Onset usually before 2 years with developmental regression, hypotonia and feeding problems
Brainstem signs: abnormal breathing, nystagmus, ophthalmoparesis, swallowing problems
Dystonia, ataxia and pyramidal signs
Decompensation with febrile illness; lactic acidosis
Optic atrophy, neuropathy, cardiomyopathy in some genetic types

case.story: Sitting at 7 months, but after a febrile illness he stopped sitting and has trouble swallowing and irregular breathing.
case.exam: Hypotonia, dystonic posturing of arms, nystagmus, intermittent hyperventilation.
case.tests: Blood lactate 6 mmol/L, CSF lactate raised; MRI shows bilateral symmetric putaminal and brainstem lesions; SURF1 biallelic variants.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and which treatable mimic must be covered?

det.patho: Leigh syndrome results from defects in mitochondrial energy production caused by more than 100 different genes in mitochondrial or nuclear DNA, including respiratory chain subunits, assembly factors and the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex. Energy failure in metabolically active regions produces focal necrosis, spongiform change, gliosis and capillary proliferation in the basal ganglia and brainstem.
det.clinical: Typical onset is in infancy with regression, hypotonia, feeding difficulty, vomiting and failure to thrive, often after an infection. Brainstem involvement gives breathing irregularities, eye movement disorders and dysphagia; respiratory failure is a common cause of death. Later-onset and adult forms exist with dystonia, ataxia or optic neuropathy.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis combines a compatible clinical course, typical bilateral symmetrical lesions on MRI and evidence of mitochondrial dysfunction such as raised lactate. Genetic testing (mtDNA plus exome or genome) gives a molecular diagnosis in most; muscle biopsy for respiratory chain analysis is now used less often. Lactate can be normal, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis.
det.treatment: No cure exists. Avoid fasting and treat infections promptly; avoid valproate and propofol in many cases. Mitochondrial supplements (coenzyme Q10, riboflavin, carnitine) are commonly used despite limited evidence. Specific treatable forms require biotin and thiamine (SLC19A3), ketogenic diet (PDH deficiency) or CoQ10 (primary CoQ10 defects). Multidisciplinary palliative care is often needed.
det.prognosis: Most infantile cases are fatal within a few years, often from respiratory failure; later-onset forms may survive longer.
pearls: Symmetric basal ganglia and brainstem lesions in a regressing infant: think Leigh.
Give biotin and thiamine empirically while awaiting genes.
Normal lactate does not exclude a mitochondrial disorder.
det.thd: Leigh syndrome เป็นโรคไมโทคอนเดรียในเด็กเล็กจากยีนหลายชนิด ทำให้พัฒนาการถดถอยหลังติดเชื้อ ตัวอ่อน กลืนลำบาก หายใจผิดปกติ และ dystonia MRI พบรอยโรคสมมาตรที่ basal ganglia และก้านสมอง lactate มักสูง วินิจฉัยยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง แต่ต้องให้ biotin และ thiamine ไว้ก่อนเผื่อเป็นชนิดที่รักษาได้

One cause of Leigh picture; normal lactate/pyruvate ratio, ketogenic diet helps

name: Length-dependent polyneuropathy
formal: Polyneuropathy with distal onset and progressive proximal spread, most often axonal from diabetes, alcohol or toxins, causing stocking glove sensory loss and ankle areflexia.
simple: Nerve damage that begins in the toes and feet and moves upward, causing numbness, tingling and weakness.
more: Look for diabetes, B12, thyroid, alcohol, paraprotein or inherited causes; treat the cause and manage pain with duloxetine or gabapentinoids.
th: เส้นประสาทเสื่อมเริ่มที่ปลายสุดของเส้นยาวที่สุด จากเท้าลามขึ้นและมือในแบบถุงมือถุงเท้า สาเหตุหลักคือเบาหวาน สุรา และสารพิษ
tempoNote: Usually slowly progressive over months to years
feat: Starts in toes, reaches knees before fingers become involved
Ankle reflexes lost first
Sensory symptoms predominate; distal weakness later
Common causes: diabetes, alcohol, B12 deficiency, drugs, hypothyroidism, uraemia, HIV
Hereditary causes suggested by foot deformity and family history
inv: HbA1c or OGTT, B12, TSH, renal function, SPEP/immunofixation
NCS: axonal length-dependent pattern
Further tests guided by history (HIV, genetic)

case.who: 52-year-old man from Phetchabun drinking spirits daily
case.story: Burning numb feet over a year, now tingling fingertips.
case.exam: Sensory loss to knees and wrists, absent ankle jerks, mild toe weakness.
case.tests: HbA1c 6.0%, B12 low-normal, NCS axonal sensorimotor neuropathy.
case.q: Why did the hands become involved only now?
case.a: Sensory loss reaching the knees means the longest fibres lost equal length to finger axons; classic length-dependent progression.

det.patho: Longest axons have the highest metabolic and transport demands, so systemic insults first impair their distal ends. Degeneration proceeds proximally, producing the stocking-glove pattern.
det.clinical: Gradual distal sensory symptoms, then weakness of toe extensors and intrinsic foot muscles. Fingers become involved when leg symptoms reach about knee level. Pain varies by cause.
det.diagnosis: A typical pattern with targeted tests identifies most causes; diabetes is the leading one. NCS confirms axonal involvement and excludes demyelination. Atypical features (asymmetry, proximal weakness, rapid course) need broader work-up.
det.treatment: Correct the cause; neuropathic pain treatment; foot care, balance training and orthotics as needed.
det.prognosis: Depends on the cause; progression slows when the cause is controlled.
pearls: Hands are involved when leg sensory loss reaches the knees.
Asymmetry or proximal weakness breaks the length-dependent rule.
Screen glucose, B12, TSH and paraprotein in every case.
det.thd: Length-dependent polyneuropathy เสื่อมจากปลายเส้นประสาทที่ยาวที่สุด เริ่มที่นิ้วเท้า ลามขึ้นถึงเข่าแล้วจึงเริ่มที่ปลายนิ้วมือ สาเหตุหลักคือเบาหวาน สุรา ขาด B12 ยา และไทรอยด์ ตรวจเลือดหาสาเหตุร่วมกับ NCS รักษาที่สาเหตุและบรรเทาอาการ

name: Lennox–Gastaut syndrome
formal: Severe childhood epileptic encephalopathy with multiple seizure types including tonic seizures, slow spike-wave on EEG, intellectual disability and poor response to treatment.
simple: A severe childhood epilepsy with several seizure types, learning problems and difficult control.
more: EEG shows slow spike-wave with generalised paroxysmal fast activity during sleep; MRI and genetic panel investigate cause (tuberous sclerosis, prior West syndrome). Valproate, lamotrigine, rufinamide, clobazam and cannabidiol.
ab: childhood epileptic encephalopathy with slow spike-wave
th: เด็กมีชักหลายแบบ โดยเฉพาะชักเกร็งตอนหลับและล้มลงทันที ร่วมกับปัญญาอ่อน EEG เป็น slow spike-wave <2.5 Hz — ดื้อยามาก
tempoNote: Onset usually 18 months to 8 years; daily multiple seizure types persisting into adulthood
feat: Several seizure types at once: tonic (especially in sleep), atypical absences, atonic drops, myoclonic and tonic-clonic
Sudden falls causing facial and dental injuries; many children wear helmets
Intellectual disability and behaviour problems that worsen over time
Frequent non-convulsive status with fluctuating responsiveness
Often follows infantile spasms or has a structural or genetic cause
inv: Sleep EEG: slow spike-and-wave below 2.5 Hz while awake and bursts of generalised paroxysmal fast activity (about 10 Hz) during sleep
Video-EEG to document tonic seizures and separate them from behavioural events
MRI brain and genetic testing (panel or exome) to find a cause

case.story: Had spasms as an infant. Now drops suddenly several times a day, has split his lip twice, stares with slow fading responsiveness, and stiffens briefly many times at night.
case.exam: Moderate intellectual disability, healed facial scars, wears a soft helmet; no focal deficit.
case.tests: EEG: 2 Hz generalised slow spike-wave awake; runs of 10 Hz fast activity during sleep with axial stiffening.
case.q: Which drug should be avoided because it may worsen atypical absences and drops, and what surgical option helps drop attacks?
case.a: Carbamazepine (and other sodium-channel drugs can aggravate some seizures); corpus callosotomy is effective for drop attacks, VNS is an alternative.

read.where: 10 Electro-Clinical Syndromes by Age of Onset—Childhood, Adolescence, and Adult

det.patho: LGS is a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy in which diffuse cortical–subcortical network dysfunction produces generalised discharges regardless of the initial cause. Causes include hypoxic–ischaemic injury, malformations, tuberous sclerosis, prior infantile spasms and many single-gene or chromosomal disorders; in a minority none is found. It accounts for a small percentage of childhood epilepsy but a large share of refractory cases.
det.clinical: Diagnosis rests on a triad: multiple drug-resistant seizure types including tonic seizures, a characteristic EEG, and cognitive impairment, which may not be present at first. Tonic seizures in sleep can be missed unless specifically sought. Atonic and tonic drops cause injury, and episodes of non-convulsive status may look like lethargy or worsened behaviour. In adulthood tonic seizures remain while slow spike-wave may become less obvious.
det.diagnosis: Sleep and wake EEG, ideally with video, should show slow spike-wave and generalised paroxysmal fast activity; documenting tonic seizures is central. Early in the course features may be incomplete, so repeat EEG over time. Cause should be pursued with MRI and genetic testing since some causes have specific therapy.
det.treatment: Valproate is a usual first drug, with lamotrigine, clobazam, rufinamide, topiramate and felbamate as add-ons; fenfluramine and cannabidiol have trial evidence for drop seizures. Carbamazepine and other sodium-channel agents can worsen atypical absences or myoclonus, and benzodiazepines given IV may provoke tonic status. Non-drug options include ketogenic diet, vagus nerve stimulation, corpus callosotomy for drops and resective surgery for a clear focal lesion. Goals are to reduce injurious seizures and sedation rather than achieve complete freedom.
det.prognosis: Seizure freedom is uncommon, most patients have lifelong intellectual disability and need support, and premature mortality including SUDEP is increased.
pearls: Tonic seizures in sleep plus slow spike-wave = LGS; record sleep.
Helmets and callosotomy target the injurious drop attacks.
IV benzodiazepines can paradoxically trigger tonic status in LGS.
det.thd: LGS เป็น developmental and epileptic encephalopathy ในเด็กอายุราว 1.5–8 ปี มีชักหลายแบบโดยเฉพาะชักเกร็งตอนหลับ ล้มฟุบ และเหม่อแบบ atypical absence ร่วมกับปัญญาอ่อน EEG เป็น slow spike-wave <2.5 Hz และ fast activity ตอนหลับ สาเหตุหลากหลายและมักต่อมาจาก West syndrome รักษายากด้วย valproate, lamotrigine, clobazam, rufinamide, cannabidiol หรือ fenfluramine อาจใช้อาหารคีโต VNS หรือผ่าตัด corpus callosotomy

qx.stem: A 9-year-old girl with intellectual disability, formerly treated for infantile spasms, has daily drop attacks with facial injuries, frequent nocturnal stiffening of the trunk and staring spells with slow onset. Waking EEG shows diffuse 1.5–2 Hz sharp-and-slow-wave complexes on a slow background; sleep shows runs of generalised 10–20 Hz rhythmic fast activity. She remains uncontrolled on valproate and lamotrigine.
qx.q: Which add-on medication has randomised trial evidence for reducing drop seizures in this syndrome?
opts: Carbamazepine
Ethosuximide
Gabapentin
Pregabalin
Cannabidiol (or clobazam, rufinamide, fenfluramine)
qx.why: Tonic seizures in sleep, atypical absences, drops, slow spike-wave below 2.5 Hz and generalised paroxysmal fast activity in sleep characterise Lennox–Gastaut syndrome. Cannabidiol, clobazam, rufinamide, fenfluramine and felbamate have controlled-trial evidence for drop seizures. Carbamazepine and gabapentin may aggravate generalised seizure types, and ethosuximide does not address tonic or atonic seizures.

src.where: 10 Electro-Clinical Syndromes by Age of Onset—Childhood, Adolescence, and Adult

qx.stem: An 8-year-old girl with Lennox–Gastaut syndrome has had 60% fewer tonic seizures since starting a 4:1 ketogenic diet 9 months ago. She also takes topiramate. Her mother notices pink urine and the child cries with left flank pain. Ultrasound shows a 5 mm stone in the left renal pelvis without hydronephrosis.
qx.q: What is the best management?
opts: Stop the ketogenic diet permanently
Add acetazolamide
Restrict fluids to keep ketosis high
Continue the diet, increase fluids, and start oral potassium citrate, with urology input as needed
Switch topiramate to zonisamide
qx.why: Kidney stones affect a small but important minority of children on the diet, especially when combined with carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as topiramate or zonisamide. Because the diet is working, it is usually continued, with more fluids and potassium citrate to alkalinize the urine and raise urinary citrate. Acetazolamide and zonisamide carry the same stone risk, and fluid restriction makes stones worse.

qx.stem: A 24-year-old man with Lennox–Gastaut syndrome and moderate intellectual disability lives with his parents and takes valproate and clobazam. Highly purified cannabidiol is added and his drop attacks fall by half, but within a month he becomes very drowsy and drools. ALT has risen to four-fold the normal ceiling while bilirubin stays normal.
qx.q: What is the most likely explanation, and the best adjustment?
opts: Valproate toxicity from cannabidiol; double the valproate dose
Cannabidiol raises the active clobazam metabolite and adds to valproate-related liver enzyme rise; lower the clobazam dose and monitor liver tests closely
Nonconvulsive status from cannabidiol; give IV lorazepam
Cannabidiol-induced hypothyroidism; start levothyroxine
Expected tolerance; make no changes
qx.why: Cannabidiol inhibits CYP2C19 and raises N-desmethylclobazam, which causes sleepiness and drooling, so the clobazam dose is usually lowered. Transaminase rises with cannabidiol are much more common with valproate co-therapy. Doses are adjusted and the drug stopped if ALT stays above 3 times normal with symptoms or rising bilirubin. In people with intellectual disability, a change in behavior or alertness should first prompt a medication review.

qx.stem: An 8-year-old boy from Rayong has developmental delay, nocturnal tonic seizures, atonic drop attacks and atypical absences. The EEG shows slow spike-wave at 2 Hz in wakefulness and bursts of generalised paroxysmal fast activity in sleep. He takes valproate and lamotrigine, and a physician proposes a third drug.
qx.q: Which drug is most likely to worsen his seizures?
opts: Rufinamide
Clobazam
Cannabidiol
Carbamazepine
Valproate at a higher dose
qx.why: The picture is Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, in which sodium channel blockers such as carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine can aggravate atypical absences, atonic and myoclonic seizures. Rufinamide, clobazam and cannabidiol (and fenfluramine, felbamate and cenobamate in selected cases) have evidence in LGS, and valproate is a standard first-line drug. Intravenous benzodiazepines should also be used with care because they may precipitate tonic status.

name: Leprosy
formal: Chronic mycobacterial infection (Mycobacterium leprae) causing a granulomatous mononeuropathy multiplex with thickened nerves, hypoaesthetic skin patches and neuropathic ulcers.
simple: A long-term bacterial infection that damages skin and nerves, causing numb patches and weakness.
more: Diagnose by skin smear for acid-fast bacilli, slit-skin test or nerve biopsy, with thickened greater auricular, ulnar and peroneal nerves. Treat with multidrug therapy (dapsone, rifampicin, clofazimine) and prednisolone for reactions. Leprosy from Mycobacterium leprae causing hypoaesthetic skin lesions and thickened peripheral nerves with sensory loss, mononeuritis multiplex and deformity.
th: โรคเรื้อนต่อระบบประสาท — ผื่นชา เส้นประสาทโตคลำได้ เส้นประสาทเสียหลายเส้น แผลไม่หาย
tempoNote: Indolent; acute worsening during lepra reactions
feat: Hypopigmented or erythematous skin patches with loss of temperature and pain sensation
Palpably thickened nerves: ulnar at elbow, greater auricular, common peroneal, superficial radial
Mononeuritis multiplex with claw hand, foot drop, lagophthalmos; painless ulcers
Pure neuritic form has no skin lesions
inv: Slit-skin smear and skin biopsy (acid-fast bacilli)
Nerve ultrasound or MRI: thickened nerves; nerve biopsy in pure neuritic cases
NCS: multifocal sensory > motor axonal loss

case.story: A pale numb patch on his forearm for a year; now his little and ring fingers curl and he burned his hand without noticing.
case.exam: Anaesthetic hypopigmented patch, thickened tender ulnar nerve at the elbow, ulnar claw hand, thickened great auricular nerve.
case.tests: Skin biopsy: granulomas with acid-fast bacilli.
case.q: Which treatment is added if the nerve becomes acutely painful and weak during therapy?
case.a: Corticosteroids for the lepra (reversal) reaction, alongside multidrug therapy (rifampicin, dapsone, clofazimine).

ddx.pt: Systemic inflammation, no anaesthetic skin patches or thickened nerves
Single compressive lesion without skin changes
Recurrent painless palsies with family history

aN: hansen disease | leprous neuropathy | pure neuritic leprosy | lepra reaction

det.patho: Mycobacterium leprae has a tropism for Schwann cells and multiplies best in cooler tissues, explaining involvement of superficial nerves and skin. The host immune response shapes the disease spectrum: strong cell-mediated immunity gives tuberculoid (paucibacillary) disease with few lesions and granulomatous nerve damage, while weak immunity gives lepromatous (multibacillary) disease with many bacilli and diffuse involvement. Immune reactions (type 1 reversal, type 2 erythema nodosum leprosum) cause acute nerve inflammation and much of the permanent disability. Transmission is via respiratory droplets after prolonged contact.
det.clinical: Hypopigmented or reddish skin patches with reduced temperature, pain and touch sensation are typical, often with loss of sweating and hair. Peripheral nerves become thickened and sometimes tender, especially the ulnar, median, common peroneal, posterior tibial, great auricular and superficial radial nerves. The neuropathy is a mononeuritis multiplex that can coalesce into a symmetric distal pattern, preferentially in cool body regions. Complications include claw hand, foot drop, facial weakness with lagophthalmos, painless ulcers, burns and bone resorption. Pure neuritic leprosy, common in India, lacks skin lesions.
det.diagnosis: WHO cardinal signs are loss of sensation in a skin patch, thickened peripheral nerve with sensory or motor loss, and acid-fast bacilli on slit-skin smear or biopsy. Skin biopsy shows granulomas around nerves; smears are often negative in paucibacillary disease. NCS show multifocal, sensory-predominant axonal changes, and ultrasound demonstrates focal nerve enlargement. Nerve biopsy or PCR is helpful in pure neuritic cases. Exclude other causes of thickened nerves such as CIDP, CMT and amyloidosis.
det.treatment: WHO multidrug therapy combines rifampicin, dapsone and clofazimine, now recommended for both paucibacillary (6 months) and multibacillary (12 months) disease. Type 1 reactions and acute neuritis need prompt oral corticosteroids for several months; ENL may require steroids, thalidomide (with strict precautions) or clofazimine. Disability prevention includes self-care education, protective footwear, eye care and reconstructive surgery. Contacts should be screened and may receive single-dose rifampicin prophylaxis.
det.prognosis: Infection is curable with MDT, but nerve damage present at diagnosis often persists. Early recognition and steroid treatment of reactions prevent much of the disability.
pearls: Palpate the great auricular and ulnar nerves in any unexplained mononeuritis multiplex in an endemic area.
Acute painful nerve during therapy = reaction, treat with steroids, continue MDT.
Pure neuritic leprosy has no skin lesions — nerve biopsy may be needed.
det.thd: โรคเรื้อนเกิดจากเชื้อ M. leprae ซึ่งชอบ Schwann cell และบริเวณที่อุณหภูมิต่ำ ทำให้มีผื่นสีจางที่ชา เส้นประสาทโตคลำได้ (ulnar, great auricular, peroneal) และเส้นประสาทเสียหลายเส้น เช่น มือกรงเล็บ เท้าตก หลับตาไม่สนิท วินิจฉัยจาก cardinal signs ของ WHO, slit-skin smear และ skin/nerve biopsy รักษาด้วย MDT (rifampicin, dapsone, clofazimine) และให้ steroid เมื่อมี lepra reaction เพื่อป้องกันความพิการถาวร

name: Lesch–Nyhan syndrome
formal: X-linked recessive HPRT deficiency, with hyperuricaemia, choreoathetosis and dystonia, intellectual disability and compulsive self-injury, usually boys.
simple: An inherited disorder in boys causing movement problems, learning difficulty and self-injury, due to an enzyme deficiency.
more: Diagnosis by low HPRT enzyme activity and HPRT1 gene analysis, with urinary uric acid raised. Allopurinol controls hyperuricaemia but not neurological features; manage self-injury with protective devices, dental extraction, and behavioural therapy.
th: โรคพันธุกรรม X-linked จากขาดเอนไซม์ HPRT ทำให้กรดยูริกสูง dystonia ร่วม choreoathetosis พัฒนาการช้า และทำร้ายตัวเอง พบในเด็กชาย
tempoNote: Hypotonia and delay from early infancy; dystonia by age 1; self-injury from age 2–3
feat: Boys with motor delay and hypotonia, then severe generalised dystonia with chorea or ballism
Compulsive self-biting of lips, fingers and tongue
Orange crystals in nappies, uric acid stones, gout and renal failure
Intellectual disability, often less severe than motor disability suggests
Partial deficiency variants: hyperuricaemia with milder neurological signs
inv: Serum and urine uric acid (urate/creatinine ratio raised)
HPRT enzyme activity in red cells or fibroblasts
HPRT1 gene analysis; carrier testing for mothers
Renal ultrasound for stones

case.story: Cannot sit unsupported; mother found orange sand in his nappies as a baby. Recently bites his lower lip until it bleeds.
case.exam: Generalised dystonia with choreic movements, brisk reflexes, scarred lips and fingertips.
case.tests: Serum uric acid 11 mg/dL, high urine urate/creatinine ratio; HPRT activity absent; HPRT1 pathogenic variant.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and does allopurinol help the neurological features?
case.a: Lesch–Nyhan syndrome; allopurinol prevents gout and kidney damage but does not improve dystonia or self-injury.

det.patho: Loss of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase stops purine recycling, so purines are broken down to uric acid in excess. The cause of the neurological syndrome is not fully understood but involves a marked deficit of basal ganglia dopamine pathways that develops early in life. The gene is on the X chromosome, so affected individuals are almost always male.
det.clinical: Infants are hypotonic and delayed; by the first year severe dystonia emerges, often with superimposed chorea and ballism, and most never walk. Self-injury begins in early childhood and is compulsive, painful and distressing to the child, who often asks for restraints. Hyperuricaemia causes kidney stones, renal failure and later gout. Milder HPRT deficiency produces variants with less motor disability and no self-injury.
det.diagnosis: Raised uric acid in a boy with dystonia or developmental delay should prompt enzyme and HPRT1 gene testing. Uric acid may be normal in serum because of renal clearance, so urine urate/creatinine ratio is useful. Prenatal and carrier testing are available. Cerebral palsy is the commonest misdiagnosis.
det.treatment: Allopurinol (or febuxostat) with hydration prevents urate nephropathy but not neurological disease. Self-injury is managed with protective devices, dental guards or extraction, behavioural strategies and sometimes medications such as gabapentin or benzodiazepines. Dystonia is treated with baclofen, benzodiazepines and in selected cases pallidal DBS. Care involves a multidisciplinary team.
det.prognosis: Most patients survive into the second or third decade; renal failure, aspiration and sudden death are causes of mortality.
pearls: Orange crystals in the nappy of a delayed boy: check uric acid.
Self-injury is involuntary; restraints are often requested by the patient.
Many children labelled with dystonic cerebral palsy deserve a uric acid test.
det.thd: Lesch–Nyhan syndrome เป็นโรคพันธุกรรม X-linked จากการขาดเอนไซม์ HPRT พบในเด็กชาย ทำให้กรดยูริกสูง เกิดนิ่วและไตวาย ร่วมกับ dystonia รุนแรง พัฒนาการช้า และกัดริมฝีปากหรือนิ้วตัวเองโดยควบคุมไม่ได้ วินิจฉัยด้วยระดับยูริก การวัดเอนไซม์และยีน HPRT1 ยา allopurinol ช่วยเรื่องไตและข้อแต่ไม่ช่วยอาการทางระบบประสาท

Acute striatal injury after illness with macrocephaly, abnormal urine organic acids

name: Lethal catatonia (LC)
formal: Severe catatonia with high fever, autonomic instability, agitation or stupor and delirium, with high mortality unless treated early by benzodiazepines or ECT.
simple: A life-threatening form of catatonia with fever, rigid or agitated behaviour and unstable vital signs.

Classic course: a prodrome of insomnia, anorexia and mood lability, then intense motor excitement, then stuporous exhaustion with extreme fever and circulatory failure
Younger adults, with women in the majority of modern series, and an association with mood disorders, schizophrenia and periodic catatonia
Raised CK and white count, low serum iron and raised transaminases are the commonest laboratory clues
Mortality was about three-quarters before antipsychotics, near 60% in the mid-twentieth century, and fell to under 10% in series published after 1986

Review of recent antipsychotic exposure to decide how far the picture resembles NMS
Continuous ECG and coagulation screen; leg Doppler or D-dimer for thrombosis

case.who: 22-year-old woman, a university student from Surin, with a first episode of acute psychosis
case.story: She slept little for a week, tore at her clothes and struck the walls, then declined all food and water; three days later she is limp and barely responsive with a high fever.
case.exam: Temperature 41.0 °C, pulse 140, blood pressure falling to 90/50 mmHg, bluish extremities, mutism, mild rigidity; pupils equal and reactive.
case.tests: CK 9,000 U/L, creatinine rising, white count raised; CT, EEG and CSF normal; lorazepam over 24 hours gives only brief improvement.
case.q: What is the right next step?
case.a: Lethal (malignant) catatonia after an excited phase, with a poor benzodiazepine response and a temperature already above 41 °C. Move to ECT without delay, continue intensive support and avoid antipsychotics.

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System

det.patho: The syndrome is believed to reflect profound hypodopaminergia in frontal-subcortical loops, which would explain rigidity, akinesia, mutism and loss of temperature control through hypothalamic pathways. Autopsy series in the pre-antipsychotic era were often unrevealing, and many deaths were from the consequences of immobility, such as venous thrombosis with pulmonary embolism, and infection. The French school favoured an encephalitic origin involving the hypothalamus, whereas German authors regarded it as a psychiatric syndrome with no specific brain lesion.
det.clinical: Stauder gave the lethal form its name in 1934, though cases were recorded from the early nineteenth century as acute delirious mania or Bell's mania. The excitement phase includes tearing at clothing, striking objects and refusing food and drink, with fever, rapid pulse, sweating and bluish skin. Later the patient lapses into stupor, with rigidity in most and flaccidity in some. In modern practice about two-thirds begin with excitement and one-third are stuporous from the outset, a shift toward the stuporous form that probably reflects antipsychotic-related cases.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis combines catatonic features, hyperthermia without infection and autonomic instability, supported by raised CK, white count and transaminases and low serum iron. It is a syndrome with many triggers, so the evaluation must include encephalitis, epilepsy, metabolic, endocrine, infectious and toxic causes. Distinguish from NMS by the antipsychotic timeline and by whether fever appeared during the excited phase.
det.treatment: Intensive supportive care addresses fluids, cooling, nutrition, renal protection and thrombosis prophylaxis. A benzodiazepine, usually lorazepam, can be tried for hours, but if the response is not brisk the book argued for ECT immediately rather than waiting five days. ECT once or twice daily, or on alternate days, for 5 to 15 sessions, is usually effective if started within about five days of the onset of fever, and a delay beyond that or coma and temperature above 41 °C predict a poor response. Adjuncts include dantrolene and bromocriptine, and corticosteroids if ECT is unavailable. Antipsychotics are contraindicated while the condition is active.
det.prognosis: From mortality above 75% in the pre-antipsychotic era the figure dropped to roughly 9% in reports after 1986. Residual catatonia and relapse can follow, and the underlying mental disorder needs long-term care.
pearls: The best prognostic factor is how fast ECT is given after fever begins.
Fever in an excited psychotic patient who refuses fluids should never be called just infection.
Many deaths come from pulmonary embolism or infection; prevent them.
det.thd: Lethal catatonia คือ catatonia ชนิดรุนแรงที่ทำให้เสียชีวิตได้ เริ่มจากนอนไม่หลับ กินน้อย แล้วกระวนกระวายรุนแรง มีไข้สูง เหงื่อออก ชีพจรเร็ว ก่อนจะซึมและแข็งเกร็ง ในอดีตเสียชีวิตสูงมากแต่ปัจจุบันลดลงเหลือราว 1 ใน 10 ด้วยการดูแลในไอซียู ให้ lorazepam และทำ ECT เร็วโดยไม่ต้องรอหลายวัน ควรหลีกเลี่ยงยาต้านโรคจิต และป้องกันลิ่มเลือดอุดตันและการติดเชื้อ

qx.stem: A 24-year-old woman from Nakhon Ratchasima was brought in after a week of insomnia, shouting and refusing fluids. She is now stuporous with temperature 41.2 °C, pulse 142, blood pressure 80/50 mmHg, rigidity and bluish extremities. CK is 11,000 U/L. Cultures, CT and CSF are unremarkable. Lorazepam over 24 hours has given only brief benefit.
qx.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive treatment now?
opts: Increase the antipsychotic dose
Continue lorazepam alone for five more days
Start high-dose corticosteroids and wait
Arrange ECT urgently together with intensive care support
Give antibiotics for presumed meningitis and defer other treatment
qx.why: A rapidly rising fever, autonomic instability, stupor and catatonic features after an excited phase are lethal (malignant) catatonia. When benzodiazepines do not rapidly reverse it, ECT should be given without waiting, because results are far worse when coma or temperatures above 41 °C are established and when treatment is delayed beyond a few days of fever. Antipsychotics can worsen the illness, steroids are only a reserve, and a negative infection work-up argues against meningitis.

name: Leucoencephalopathy
formal: Disease of cerebral white matter from toxic, ischaemic, inflammatory, infectious, metabolic or genetic causes, such as PML, PRES, chemotherapy toxicity and CADASIL.
simple: Damage to the brain's white matter, which can be caused by many things and affects thinking and movement.
th: โรคของเนื้อสมองส่วนสีขาวจากหลายสาเหตุ เช่น ยาและสารพิษ ขาดเลือด อักเสบ ติดเชื้อ เมตาบอลิก หรือพันธุกรรม เช่น PML, PRES, พิษเคมีบำบัด, leukodystrophy
tempoNote: Acute (PRES, toxic), subacute (PML), or chronic (genetic, small vessel)
feat: Descriptive imaging-clinical term, not a single disease
Cognitive slowing, apathy, gait disturbance, spasticity, urinary symptoms
Toxic: chemotherapy (methotrexate), heroin vapour, carbon monoxide, radiation
Infective: PML (JC virus), HIV; inflammatory: MS, ADEM
Vascular and genetic: small vessel disease, CADASIL, leukodystrophies (ALD, MLD, vanishing white matter)
inv: MRI pattern recognition (symmetry, location, diffusion restriction, enhancement)
Drug and exposure history; HIV and JC virus PCR in CSF
Metabolic/genetic tests (VLCFA, arylsulfatase A, NOTCH3) when suggested

case.who: 38-year-old man from Bangkok with HIV not on treatment, CD4 40
case.story: Six weeks of progressive right arm clumsiness and word-finding difficulty.
case.exam: Right hemiparesis and expressive aphasia, no fever or headache.
case.tests: MRI: asymmetric left frontoparietal subcortical white matter T2 lesion involving U-fibres, no mass effect or enhancement; CSF JC virus PCR positive.
case.q: What type of leucoencephalopathy is this?
case.a: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) due to JC virus; start ART.

det.patho: White matter consists of myelinated axons supported by oligodendrocytes and a vulnerable end-artery blood supply. Damage can target myelin, oligodendrocytes, axons or the microvasculature, through toxins, infection, autoimmunity, ischaemia, metabolic defects or genetic disorders of myelin.
det.clinical: Predominant white matter disease produces slowed processing, inattention, apathy, executive dysfunction and gait disorders more than aphasia or amnesia. Progressive spastic paraparesis, ataxia and urinary symptoms are common. Tempo, age and exposures narrow the differential.
det.diagnosis: MRI pattern recognition is the main tool: periventricular and confluent (small vessel), anterior temporal (CADASIL), parieto-occipital vasogenic (PRES), posterior with enhancing rim (X-ALD), asymmetric subcortical (PML). Targeted laboratory, CSF and genetic tests follow.
det.treatment: Management depends on cause: remove toxins, control BP in PRES, restore immunity in PML, immunotherapy for inflammatory conditions, haematopoietic stem cell transplant for early cerebral ALD, and vascular risk control for small vessel disease. Supportive rehabilitation is needed for all.
det.prognosis: Ranges from full reversal (PRES, some toxic forms) to relentless progression (many genetic forms).
pearls: Leucoencephalopathy is a pattern: always ask why.
Asymmetric non-enhancing lesions in an immunosuppressed patient: PML.
Ask about drugs, chemotherapy, heroin inhalation and carbon monoxide exposure.
det.thd: Leucoencephalopathy คือความผิดปกติของเนื้อสมองส่วนสีขาว เป็นรูปแบบจากภาพ MRI ไม่ใช่โรคเดียว สาเหตุมีหลายกลุ่ม เช่น สารพิษหรือเคมีบำบัด การติดเชื้อ JC virus (PML) PRES การอักเสบ หลอดเลือดเล็ก และโรคพันธุกรรม leukodystrophy ผู้ป่วยมักคิดช้า เฉยเมย เดินผิดปกติ การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ

name: Leukodystrophy
formal: Heritable disorder primarily affecting brain white matter with progressive spasticity, ataxia, cognitive decline and symmetrical MRI myelin changes; examples include MLD, Krabbe, ALD and Alexander.
simple: A genetic disease in which the brain's white matter breaks down, causing progressive weakness, stiffness and loss of skills.
more: Diagnosed by MRI pattern, enzyme tests and gene panels. Transplantation or gene therapy may help in selected types; most care is supportive. Group of inherited diseases of myelin, such as metachromatic leucodystrophy, Krabbe disease, adrenoleukodystrophy and Alexander disease, with progressive motor and cognitive regression.
th: กลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่ทำลาย white matter ของสมอง ทำให้เกร็ง เดินเซ ความคิดถดถอย และ MRI เห็นความผิดปกติของ myelin แบบสมมาตร
tempoNote: Usually progressive; some forms have stepwise worsening after illness or head injury
feat: Spasticity, ataxia, cognitive and behavioural decline, seizures
Infantile forms: regression, irritability, macrocephaly (Alexander, Canavan)
Adult forms: psychiatric change, dementia, spastic paraparesis (ALD, MLD, CSF1R)
Peripheral neuropathy in MLD and Krabbe; adrenal insufficiency in X-ALD
Symmetrical confluent white matter signal change on MRI
inv: MRI pattern recognition (frontal vs posterior, U-fibres, contrast, cysts)
Arylsulfatase A and galactocerebrosidase activities, very long chain fatty acids
Leukodystrophy gene panel or exome/genome
Nerve conduction, adrenal function, ophthalmology

case.story: Previously well; over six months school performance dropped, he became inattentive and now his handwriting and vision are worse. Skin looks tanned.
case.exam: Hyperactive reflexes, homonymous visual field defect, mild spastic gait.
case.tests: MRI: symmetric posterior periventricular white matter lesions with enhancing rim; raised VLCFA; low morning cortisol.
case.q: Which leukodystrophy is this and what is the time-critical treatment?
case.a: Cerebral X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy; early haematopoietic stem cell transplant (or gene therapy) plus steroid replacement.

det.patho: Leukodystrophies are inherited disorders in which white matter glia (oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, microglia) or myelin itself are primarily affected. Mechanisms include lysosomal storage (MLD, Krabbe), peroxisomal lipid accumulation (X-ALD), astrocyte dysfunction (Alexander disease), hypomyelination (Pelizaeus–Merzbacher) and microglial failure (CSF1R-related).
det.clinical: Childhood forms present with regression, spasticity, ataxia and seizures; some show macrocephaly or neuropathy. Adult forms tend to start with psychiatric symptoms, executive dysfunction, spastic paraparesis or ataxia and are often misdiagnosed as MS or psychiatric disease. Systemic clues include adrenal failure, gallbladder abnormalities and tendon xanthomas.
det.diagnosis: MRI pattern analysis is the key first step and directs biochemical tests: VLCFA, lysosomal enzyme activities, sterols and others. Next-generation sequencing panels or exome/genome sequencing now give a diagnosis in most. Acquired causes such as MS, small vessel disease, toxic leukoencephalopathy and PML must be excluded.
det.treatment: Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation or gene therapy can halt progression in early cerebral X-ALD, MLD and Krabbe disease, which makes early diagnosis and newborn or family screening valuable. Other forms are managed supportively with spasticity treatment, seizure control, nutrition and rehabilitation. Adrenal replacement is required in X-ALD.
det.prognosis: Most are progressive; infantile forms often fatal in childhood, adult forms progress over years.
pearls: Read the MRI pattern first; it narrows the list more than any single blood test.
Test adrenal function in any boy with a leukodystrophy.
Transplant works only before significant symptoms; screen siblings.
det.thd: Leukodystrophy คือกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่ทำลาย white matter ของสมอง เด็กจะมีพัฒนาการถดถอย เกร็ง ชัก ส่วนผู้ใหญ่มักเริ่มด้วยอาการทางจิตหรือขาเกร็ง วินิจฉัยด้วยรูปแบบ MRI ร่วมกับการตรวจ VLCFA เอนไซม์ไลโซโซมและยีน บางชนิด เช่น X-ALD และ MLD รักษาได้ด้วยการปลูกถ่ายไขกระดูกหรือยีนบำบัดหากวินิจฉัยเร็ว

name: Leukodystrophy and tubulopathy
formal: Mitochondrial disease combining white matter degeneration with renal tubular dysfunction, as in some respiratory chain defects such as BCS1L and FARS2-related disorders.
simple: An inherited disease that damages the brain's white matter and also the kidney tubules.
more: Lactate, MRI and kidney function testing with genetic confirmation. Treatment is supportive and prognosis is variable.
th: โรคไมโทคอนเดรียที่มีทั้ง white matter เสื่อมและการทำงานของท่อไตผิดปกติ เช่น ในความผิดปกติของ respiratory chain จากยีน BCS1L
tempoNote: Usually infantile onset with progressive course and crises during illness
feat: Infant with hypotonia, developmental regression, seizures or spasticity
Proximal tubulopathy: glycosuria, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, metabolic acidosis (Fanconi-type)
Lactic acidosis, poor growth, liver involvement in some
Leukoencephalopathy on MRI, sometimes with basal ganglia or brainstem lesions
inv: Blood and CSF lactate; urine amino acids, glucose, phosphate and bicarbonate
MRI with spectroscopy (lactate peak)
Exome or genome sequencing including mtDNA; respiratory chain enzymes if needed

case.story: Poor weight gain since birth, now losing head control after a cold; frequent rickets-like bone changes noted on X-ray.
case.exam: Hypotonia, brisk reflexes, poor visual tracking.
case.tests: Lactate 5.5 mmol/L, glycosuria with normal blood glucose, generalised aminoaciduria, low phosphate; MRI diffuse white matter T2 hyperintensity; biallelic BCS1L variants.
case.q: What combination does this represent and why does it matter?
case.a: Mitochondrial leukodystrophy with renal Fanconi tubulopathy; it points to a respiratory chain defect and the renal losses need replacement.

det.patho: Defects in respiratory chain assembly (for example BCS1L for complex III) or mitochondrial translation (for example FARS2 and other aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases) limit ATP production. Highly energy-dependent tissues are hit: the proximal renal tubule, which needs ATP for reabsorption, and myelinating glia. This is a descriptive grouping rather than one disease, and the number of reported patients for each gene is small.
det.clinical: Presentation is mostly in infancy with failure to thrive, hypotonia, regression and seizures, alongside a proximal tubulopathy causing acidosis, rickets and electrolyte loss. Liver dysfunction, hearing loss and cardiomyopathy occur in some genetic types; the GRACILE syndrome of BCS1L is a severe neonatal variant. Decompensation often follows infection.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it when a child with a white matter disorder also has urinary losses of glucose, amino acids, phosphate or bicarbonate. Lactate and MR spectroscopy support a mitochondrial cause. Exome or genome sequencing with mtDNA analysis usually provides the diagnosis; tissue enzyme studies are used when results are uncertain.
det.treatment: There is no curative therapy. Care includes correcting acidosis and electrolyte and phosphate losses, vitamin D, nutrition, seizure control and avoidance of mitochondrial toxins such as valproate. Supplements (coenzyme Q10, riboflavin, carnitine) are often given with limited evidence. Genetic counselling is offered.
det.prognosis: Generally poor, with many severe infantile forms fatal in early childhood; milder courses are reported for some genes.
pearls: White matter disease plus glycosuria with normal glucose: test for mitochondrial disease.
Check urine for tubular losses in any infant with suspected mitochondrial leukoencephalopathy.
Avoid valproate in suspected mitochondrial disorders.

name: Leukoencephalopathy (CARASAL)
formal: CARASAL is an adult-onset hereditary small vessel disorder of the brain due to a heterozygous CTSA variant with autosomal dominant inheritance, presenting with lacunar strokes, migraine, hard-to-control hypertension and confluent white matter changes.
simple: A rare inherited disease of small brain vessels causing strokes and white matter damage.
more: Caused by CTSA mutation, with MRI showing white matter lesions, microbleeds and strokes; diagnosis by genetic testing and skin biopsy shows nonspecific changes. Cathepsin A deficiency is distinct from galactosialidosis.

feat: Autosomal dominant inheritance (heterozygous CTSA variant, first described in European families) — not recessive
Ischaemic and haemorrhagic strokes, migraine-like headache
Treatment-resistant hypertension, dry mouth and dry eyes reported
Cognitive decline and gait problems with extensive white matter disease
Brainstem, thalamic and basal ganglia involvement on MRI

Genetic testing: small vessel disease panel including CTSA, NOTCH3, HTRA1, COL4A1

case.who: 44-year-old woman from Bangkok whose mother had early dementia and strokes
case.story: Recurrent headaches, two small strokes in 3 years and difficult-to-control blood pressure; complains of dry mouth.
case.exam: Mild dysarthria, brisk reflexes, slowed executive tasks.
case.tests: MRI: extensive confluent white matter changes involving pons and thalami; NOTCH3 negative; small vessel gene panel identifies pathogenic CTSA variant.
case.q: Which monogenic small-vessel disease is this?
case.a: CARASAL — the cathepsin A (CTSA) related small vessel disease.

det.patho: CARASAL is caused by a heterozygous variant in CTSA, encoding cathepsin A, a lysosomal enzyme. The variant appears to act through toxic or regulatory effects rather than causing the recessive lysosomal storage disease galactosialidosis. Pathology shows small-vessel arteriopathy with fibrosis and loss of smooth muscle cells. Knowledge comes from a small number of families, so the full spectrum is not well defined.
det.clinical: Onset is usually in mid adulthood with strokes (ischaemic and occasionally haemorrhagic), headache, cognitive decline and gait disorder. Hypertension is often marked and resistant. Sicca symptoms have been described. Progression is slow but leads to disability.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in adults with familial or unexplained extensive small-vessel disease, particularly with brainstem involvement and negative NOTCH3 testing. Diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing. Imaging can resemble CADASIL, but anterior temporal involvement is less typical.
det.treatment: No specific therapy exists. Management mirrors other monogenic small-vessel diseases: control blood pressure, manage stroke risk factors, cautious use of antithrombotics given haemorrhage risk, and rehabilitation. Genetic counselling for relatives is important.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive with accumulation of disability; long-term data are limited.
pearls: Familial small-vessel disease with negative NOTCH3: think HTRA1, COL4A1, CTSA.
Extensive brainstem white matter disease is a clue to CARASAL.
The lexicon's original entry said recessive; reported families show dominant inheritance.
det.thd: CARASAL เป็นโรคหลอดเลือดสมองขนาดเล็กทางพันธุกรรมที่พบน้อยมาก เกิดจากยีน CTSA ถ่ายทอดแบบ autosomal dominant ผู้ป่วยวัยกลางคนมี stroke ปวดศีรษะ ความดันสูงคุมยาก และความจำเสื่อม MRI พบ white matter ผิดปกติกว้างขวางรวมถึงก้านสมอง วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีน ยังไม่มีการรักษาเฉพาะ ใช้การคุมความดันและป้องกัน stroke

name: Levodopa-induced chorea
formal: Chorea occurring at peak dose of levodopa in Parkinson disease from pulsatile stimulation of denervated striatal dopamine receptors.
simple: Dancing, flowing involuntary movements that appear when a Parkinson drug is at its strongest effect.
more: Treat by reducing the single dose, splitting doses, adding amantadine or advanced therapies such as deep brain stimulation.

feat: Flowing writhing movements of head, trunk and limbs about 1–2 hours after a dose
Coincides with the best motor 'on' state
Risk: young onset, long disease, higher levodopa dose, female sex, lower body weight
Often unnoticed or preferred by the patient over being 'off'

case.who: 59-year-old teacher from Chiang Rai with Parkinson's disease for 9 years
case.story: Takes levodopa 200 mg five times daily; about an hour after each dose his trunk and arms sway and twist, which embarrasses him at school.
case.exam: At peak: generalised chorea with good mobility; before the next dose: slow and rigid.
case.tests: Patient diary confirms dyskinesia only at peak-dose times.
case.q: What is the movement disorder and two options to manage it?
case.a: Peak-dose levodopa-induced chorea; smaller more frequent doses and amantadine, with DBS for refractory cases.

read.where: Chapter 9 Movement Disorders — Medical Treatment of Parkinson’s Disease

det.patho: With progressive nigral loss, the striatum loses its ability to buffer dopamine, so oral levodopa produces surges and troughs of synaptic dopamine. Pulsatile stimulation drives maladaptive plasticity in striatal D1 pathways, with changes in glutamatergic signalling and serotonergic terminals releasing dopamine unregulated. The result is excessive output through the direct pathway at peak levels.
det.clinical: It is the commonest form of levodopa-induced dyskinesia, affecting about half of patients after 5 years of therapy. Movements are choreic and sometimes dystonic, involve the neck, trunk and limbs, and match the 'on' period. Mild chorea is often well tolerated; severe chorea can cause falls, weight loss and social distress.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, by relating the timing of movements to doses. Home diaries, video and wearable sensors help. It must be separated from diphasic dyskinesias and off-period dystonia because the management differs, and from chorea of other causes when the history is unclear.
det.treatment: Reduce individual levodopa doses and give them more often, or add a long-acting agent while lowering levodopa. Amantadine (immediate or extended release) reduces dyskinesia. Continuous delivery (levodopa–carbidopa intestinal gel, subcutaneous foslevodopa or apomorphine infusion) and DBS of STN or GPi are effective for advanced cases. Clozapine is sometimes used.
det.prognosis: Tends to persist and worsen with disease progression, but device-aided therapies give good control.
pearls: Ask whether the movements occur when the patient is at their best: that is peak dose.
Many patients prefer to be on with mild chorea than off.
Amantadine is the main oral anti-dyskinetic drug.

name: Levodopa-induced dyskinesias
formal: Involuntary choreic or dystonic movements complicating long-term levodopa therapy in Parkinson disease, usually at peak dose, but also biphasic or off-period dystonia.
simple: Involuntary writhing or jerking movements that develop after years of Parkinson treatment with levodopa.
more: Managed by dose fractionation, amantadine, avoiding dopamine peaks, continuous infusions or deep brain stimulation.
th: การเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติแบบ chorea หรือ dystonia ที่เกิดจากการใช้ levodopa ระยะยาวใน Parkinson's disease ทั้งแบบ peak-dose, biphasic และ off-period dystonia

feat: Peak-dose: chorea or dystonia during best 'on' time
Diphasic: repetitive leg movements or dystonia at onset and wearing off of a dose
Off-period dystonia: painful foot cramping, often early morning
Accompanied by motor fluctuations (wearing off, delayed on)
inv: Symptom diary with dose times; clinic video at different phases
Wearable motion sensors where available
Check other contributing drugs (agonists, MAO-B and COMT inhibitors)

case.who: 52-year-old woman from Khon Kaen with young-onset Parkinson's disease for 7 years
case.story: Her legs kick and twist for 15 minutes as each dose starts and again as it wears off; at peak she feels good. Early mornings bring painful toe curling.
case.exam: Observed at dose onset: stereotyped leg movements; at peak: near normal.
case.tests: Diary shows clear timing at beginning and end of doses.
case.q: What types of dyskinesia does she have and how does management differ from peak-dose type?
case.a: Diphasic dyskinesia plus early-morning off dystonia; needs more continuous dopaminergic stimulation (higher or longer-acting doses, infusion or DBS), not dose reduction.

det.patho: Loss of presynaptic dopamine storage plus pulsatile oral levodopa leads to sensitised postsynaptic signalling in the striatum, abnormal corticostriatal plasticity and altered glutamate and serotonin activity. Dyskinesia threshold falls as disease progresses, so smaller doses trigger it. Young age at onset and disease severity matter more than cumulative exposure alone.
det.clinical: Three timing patterns are recognised. Peak-dose dyskinesia is most common, usually choreic. Diphasic dyskinesia shows up as each dose takes effect and again as it fades, often as repetitive leg movements, and is more disabling. Off-period dystonia occurs when levels are low, commonly as painful foot inversion in the morning. Patients often have fluctuations at the same time.
det.diagnosis: Careful timing in relation to doses is the key to classification; diaries, videos and sensors help. Separate dyskinesias from tremor, akathisia and functional movements. Review all dopaminergic drugs. Classification guides therapy because the treatments are different.
det.treatment: Peak-dose: smaller and more frequent levodopa doses, reduce add-on drugs, add amantadine. Diphasic: paradoxically needs more sustained dopaminergic levels, using longer-acting drugs or infusions. Off dystonia: bedtime long-acting preparations, early morning dose, botulinum toxin for focal dystonia. Device-aided therapies (DBS, intestinal gel, subcutaneous foslevodopa or apomorphine) treat refractory cases.
det.prognosis: Common and long-lasting, but most patients can be helped with timing changes or device therapies.
pearls: Always ask when the movements occur relative to the dose.
Diphasic dyskinesia worsens if you simply cut the dose.
Delaying levodopa does not prevent dyskinesia in the long run; dose matters more.
det.thd: Levodopa-induced dyskinesias คือการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติจากการใช้ levodopa ระยะยาวใน Parkinson's disease แบ่งตามเวลาเป็น peak-dose, diphasic และ off-period dystonia การแยกชนิดสำคัญเพราะการรักษาต่างกัน peak-dose ให้ลดขนาดต่อครั้งและใช้ amantadine ส่วน diphasic ต้องทำให้ระดับยาคงที่ขึ้น รายรุนแรงใช้ DBS หรือยาให้ต่อเนื่อง

qx.stem: A 68-year-old woman with 11 years of PD has disabling writhing movements of the neck and limbs that peak about an hour after each levodopa dose and interfere with eating. Reducing levodopa brings back rigidity and 'off' periods. She is not a surgical candidate because of cognitive impairment, and her eGFR is 70 mL/min.
qx.q: Which drug is most appropriate to add for her dyskinesia?
opts: Amantadine (immediate- or extended-release)
Haloperidol
Pramipexole
Trihexyphenidyl
Selegiline
qx.why: Amantadine, an NMDA antagonist, reduces peak-dose dyskinesia, and extended-release formulations have trial evidence for both dyskinesia and 'off' time. Dose must be adjusted for renal function and watched for hallucinations, livedo reticularis and ankle oedema, which matters in a cognitively impaired patient. Antipsychotics worsen parkinsonism, anticholinergics worsen cognition, and agonists or MAO-B inhibitors increase dopaminergic stimulation.

name: Levodopa-induced myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus following levodopa therapy in Parkinson disease, usually at peak dose or at night, benign and responsive to dose reduction.
simple: Muscle jerks triggered by levodopa medicine in people with Parkinson disease.
more: Myoclonus induced by levodopa in parkinsonism, often from drug peak dose or neuroplasticity, usually mild and reversible with dose reduction.
th: myoclonus ที่เกิดจาก levodopa ในผู้ป่วย Parkinson's disease มักช่วงระดับยาสูงสุดหรือตอนกลางคืน ไม่อันตรายและดีขึ้นเมื่อลดยา
tempoNote: Intermittent, often during sleep or at peak dose, after long-term therapy
feat: Brief, shock-like jerks of limbs, often during sleep or drowsiness
Peak-dose association; usually not disabling
Often accompanied by vivid dreams or hallucinations
More common with cognitive impairment or dementia with Lewy bodies
inv: Clinical: relation to doses and sleep
Exclude metabolic causes (renal, hepatic, electrolytes) and other drugs (opioids, SSRIs, amantadine)
EEG/polysomnography if seizures or REM sleep behaviour disorder are questioned

case.who: 74-year-old man from Phrae with Parkinson's disease for 12 years
case.story: Wife says his arms and legs jerk several times an hour during his evening nap and in bed; he also reports vivid dreams. His evening levodopa dose was recently increased.
case.exam: Mild cognitive slowing; occasional multifocal jerks while drowsy; no asterixis.
case.tests: Renal and liver function, electrolytes normal.
case.q: What most likely explains the jerks, and what is the first step?
case.a: Levodopa-induced myoclonus; reduce the evening dose and check other contributing drugs.

det.patho: The mechanism is not well established. Excess dopaminergic and possibly serotonergic stimulation, given that levodopa is also taken up by serotonergic neurons, may increase brainstem or cortical excitability. Methysergide and serotonin antagonists reduced it in older studies, supporting a serotonergic role.
det.clinical: Jerks are typically brief, multifocal and occur during sleep or at rest when drug levels are high. They are usually mild and rarely disabling. They frequently coexist with vivid dreams, hallucinations or cognitive decline and may herald dopaminergic psychosis. Asterixis and confusion suggest a metabolic cause instead.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, based on timing with doses and improvement after reduction. Exclude renal or hepatic failure, hyponatraemia and drugs such as opioids, SSRIs, gabapentin and amantadine. Distinguish from REM sleep behaviour disorder, periodic limb movements, hypnic jerks and seizures.
det.treatment: Reduce the dose, especially the evening dose, or simplify the drug regimen. If myoclonus persists and treatment is needed, clonazepam is commonly used. Address coexisting hallucinations with drug reduction and quetiapine, clozapine or pimavanserin where available.
det.prognosis: Benign and usually responsive to dose reduction.
pearls: Night jerks in a PD patient on high evening doses: think of levodopa first.
Myoclonus with hallucinations is a warning of dopaminergic toxicity.
Check renal function before blaming the drug.
det.thd: Levodopa-induced myoclonus คืออาการกระตุกสั้น ๆ ของแขนขาที่เกิดจาก levodopa มักเกิดตอนนอนหรือช่วงระดับยาสูง พบบ่อยในผู้ป่วยที่มีความจำเสื่อมหรือฝันชัด ไม่อันตราย วินิจฉัยจากเวลาที่สัมพันธ์กับยาหลังตัดสาเหตุทางเมตาบอลิกและยาอื่น รักษาโดยลดยาโดยเฉพาะมื้อเย็น หรือใช้ clonazepam

name: Levodopa-responsive parkinsonism
formal: Parkinsonian syndrome in which levodopa gives sustained improvement of motor signs, supporting a nigrostriatal dopamine deficit as in Parkinson disease.
simple: Parkinson-like symptoms that improve clearly with levodopa treatment.
more: Response supports a diagnosis of Parkinson disease; evaluate also for genetic forms in young patients. Long-term use can cause motor fluctuations and dyskinesia. A good levodopa response supports Parkinson disease; if lost early, consider atypical causes. Treat with levodopa titration and adjuncts.
th: parkinsonism ที่ดีขึ้นชัดและต่อเนื่องเมื่อให้ levodopa บ่งว่ามีการขาด dopamine ในทาง nigrostriatal เช่น Parkinson's disease
tempoNote: Descriptor of treatment response; course follows the underlying disease
feat: Clear and sustained improvement (often >30% in motor scores) in bradykinesia and rigidity
Strongly supports Parkinson's disease; also in DRD, PRKN and other genetic forms
Early in MSA or PSP, partial response can occur but usually fades
Development of levodopa dyskinesia also supports a presynaptic dopamine deficit
inv: Formal levodopa trial (up to about 1000 mg/day for 1–3 months) or acute challenge with MDS-UPDRS
DaT-SPECT if diagnosis is uncertain
MRI to look for atypical parkinsonism features

case.story: One-year history of slowness in the left hand and a shuffling walk; unclear whether this is Parkinson's or vascular.
case.exam: Left-predominant bradykinesia, rigidity and rest tremor.
case.tests: After 2 months of levodopa 300 mg/day, MDS-UPDRS part III improved from 34 to 16, sustained at follow-up; MRI shows no vascular lesions.
case.q: What does this response imply?
case.a: Levodopa-responsive parkinsonism, strongly supportive of Parkinson's disease rather than vascular or atypical parkinsonism.
