det.patho: A good levodopa response means postsynaptic striatal machinery is intact and the problem is mainly presynaptic dopamine deficiency. This is the case in Parkinson's disease, dopa-responsive dystonia (impaired synthesis) and recessive genetic parkinsonism. In MSA and PSP striatal neurons themselves degenerate, so response is weak or short-lived.
det.clinical: This is a description of treatment response, not a disease. Patients typically improve in bradykinesia and rigidity; tremor and gait respond more variably, while postural instability, freezing at late stage and speech respond less. A clear response, motor fluctuations and dyskinesia count as supportive criteria for Parkinson's disease.
det.diagnosis: The response should be tested at an adequate dose and duration and measured objectively, preferably with MDS-UPDRS part III or video before and after. Lack of response to at least about 600–1000 mg/day for long enough is a red flag for atypical parkinsonism. Acute challenge tests are used in some centres, for example before DBS.
det.treatment: Continue levodopa at the lowest effective dose, combining with other agents as needed. Response may be sustained for many years in Parkinson's disease, though complications develop. In atypical parkinsonism with partial response, continue a trial dose as long as it helps.
det.prognosis: Sustained response predicts a typical PD course and better long-term function than poorly responsive syndromes.
pearls: No convincing response to adequate levodopa should make you rethink a PD diagnosis.
Use objective scoring; patient impression alone can mislead.
Dyskinesia on levodopa supports a presynaptic disorder.
det.thd: Levodopa-responsive parkinsonism หมายถึง parkinsonism ที่ดีขึ้นชัดและต่อเนื่องเมื่อให้ levodopa เป็นลักษณะการตอบสนองต่อยา ไม่ใช่โรค บ่งว่าปัญหาอยู่ที่การขาด dopamine ก่อน synapse เช่น Parkinson's disease, DRD และ parkinsonism จากยีน ถ้าไม่ตอบสนองต่อยาขนาดเพียงพอให้นึกถึง MSA, PSP หรือ vascular parkinsonism ควรประเมินด้วย MDS-UPDRS ก่อนและหลังให้ยา

det.patho: Misfolded alpha-synuclein aggregates into Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites, spreading in a roughly predictable sequence from peripheral autonomic and olfactory systems and lower brainstem to midbrain, limbic regions and neocortex. Alzheimer co-pathology is frequent and worsens cognition. Biological definitions based on synuclein seed assays are now being proposed alongside clinical categories.
det.clinical: Lewy body disease covers PD, PDD and DLB, which are viewed as points on one spectrum distinguished largely by the timing of dementia relative to parkinsonism. Non-motor features such as RBD, constipation, hyposmia and depression may precede motor signs by years. Fluctuating attention, hallucinations, autonomic failure and antipsychotic sensitivity are characteristic of cortical involvement.
det.diagnosis: Clinical consensus criteria exist for PD and DLB. Supportive biomarkers include reduced DaT-SPECT uptake, low cardiac MIBG uptake, polysomnographic REM sleep without atonia, and positive synuclein seed amplification in CSF or skin. Neuropathology remains the reference standard.
det.treatment: Motor symptoms respond to levodopa, though less in DLB. Cholinesterase inhibitors (rivastigmine, donepezil) help cognition and hallucinations. Avoid typical antipsychotics; low-dose quetiapine or clozapine are used cautiously. Treat orthostatic hypotension, constipation and RBD (melatonin, clonazepam). Disease-modifying therapies are under trial.
det.prognosis: Progressive; DLB generally shortens life more than PD, with median survival of several years after diagnosis.
pearls: Dream enactment years before parkinsonism is a strong clue to a synucleinopathy.
One-year rule: dementia first or within a year of parkinsonism suggests DLB.
Neuroleptic sensitivity can be life-threatening.
det.thd: Lewy body disease คือกลุ่มโรคที่มี alpha-synuclein สะสมเป็น Lewy bodies ได้แก่ Parkinson's disease, PDD และ DLB อาการมีทั้ง parkinsonism ความจำเปลี่ยนแปลงขึ้นลง เห็นภาพหลอน ละเมอตามฝัน ท้องผูก และความดันตกเมื่อลุกยืน วินิจฉัยจากเกณฑ์ทางคลินิกร่วมกับ DaT-SPECT หรือ alpha-synuclein SAA รักษาตามอาการด้วย levodopa และ cholinesterase inhibitor และต้องหลีกเลี่ยงยาต้านจิตกลุ่มเก่า

name: LHON and dystonia
formal: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy plus dystonia, from mitochondrial DNA variants (for example m.14459G>A), with subacute visual loss and childhood dystonia with basal ganglia lesions.
simple: An inherited mitochondrial disease combining sudden vision loss with dystonia.
more: Genetic testing of mtDNA confirms; maternal inheritance. Idebenone may help vision; dystonia is treated symptomatically.
ab: Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy with dystonia
th: ภาวะ Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy ร่วมกับ dystonia จากความผิดปกติของ mtDNA เช่น m.14459G>A ทำให้ตามัวกึ่งเฉียบพลันและ dystonia ในเด็ก

feat: Painless subacute central visual loss, one eye then the other
Generalised or segmental dystonia from childhood, sometimes with spasticity and dysarthria
Symmetric putaminal (striatal) necrosis on MRI

case.story: Gradually twisting neck and right arm for two years; over two months his vision has become blurred in both eyes. A maternal uncle went blind at 20.
case.exam: Visual acuity 6/60 both eyes, central scotomas, temporal disc pallor; cervical and right arm dystonia.
case.tests: MRI shows bilateral putaminal lesions; mtDNA m.14459G>A homoplasmic.
case.q: What is the syndrome and the inheritance?
case.a: LHON plus dystonia from an MT-ND6 complex I variant; maternal (mitochondrial) inheritance.

det.patho: Certain mtDNA variants, notably in complex I genes such as MT-ND6 and MT-ND1, impair oxidative phosphorylation. Retinal ganglion cells and striatal neurons are particularly vulnerable, giving optic neuropathy and bilateral striatal necrosis. Heteroplasmy levels, nuclear modifiers and environmental factors such as smoking influence which features appear.
det.clinical: Within one maternal pedigree, members may have pure LHON, pure dystonia, or both. Dystonia often starts in childhood and may be generalised with dysarthria and spasticity; visual loss is the LHON pattern of painless subacute central loss. Some children show Leigh-like regression, so the spectrum overlaps.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it with dystonia plus striatal necrosis on MRI or optic atrophy, especially with maternal relatives affected. Targeted testing for common LHON variants is often negative, so full mtDNA sequencing is needed. Exclude Wilson's disease, organic acidurias and other causes of striatal necrosis.
det.treatment: There is no curative therapy. Idebenone is used for LHON visual loss in some countries, with modest benefit when started early. Dystonia is managed with anticholinergics, baclofen, botulinum toxin and sometimes DBS, though response is variable. Advise avoidance of smoking and excess alcohol, and provide low-vision support and genetic counselling.
det.prognosis: Variable; dystonia often persists and visual recovery is limited, though some LHON variants recover partly.
pearls: Childhood dystonia with putaminal necrosis: ask about maternal relatives with blindness.
Common LHON variant screening may miss it; request full mtDNA sequencing.
Mitochondrial variants can produce different syndromes in members of one family.
det.thd: LHON and dystonia เป็นโรคจาก mtDNA เช่น m.14459G>A ที่ทำให้ตามัวกึ่งเฉียบพลันแบบ LHON ร่วมกับ dystonia ตั้งแต่เด็ก MRI พบรอยโรคที่ putamen ทั้งสองข้าง ถ่ายทอดทางแม่ และสมาชิกในครอบครัวอาจมีอาการต่างกัน วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจ mtDNA ทั้งหมด รักษาตามอาการ เช่น ยาและ botulinum toxin สำหรับ dystonia และ idebenone สำหรับสายตาในบางราย

det.patho: LGMDs are genetic myopathies caused by mutations in proteins of the sarcolemma (sarcoglycans, dysferlin), sarcomere (titin), enzymes (calpain-3), and glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan (FKRP and others). The 2018 classification names them LGMD R (recessive) or D (dominant) with a number and the protein, and requires description in at least two unrelated families with independent walking achieved. Recessive forms are far more common, especially in populations with consanguinity. Prevalence of individual subtypes varies by region.
det.clinical: Weakness of hip and shoulder girdle muscles develops in childhood to adulthood and progresses slowly, with facial muscles usually spared. Subtype clues include scapular winging and early Achilles contractures (calpainopathy), calf or anterior tibial onset with very high CK (dysferlinopathy), a Duchenne-like course (sarcoglycanopathies), and cardiomyopathy or respiratory failure (FKRP, sarcoglycans). Cognitive development is normal.
det.diagnosis: CK level, muscle MRI pattern and EMG help narrow the differential. Genetic testing with multigene panels or exome sequencing is now the first-line test; biopsy with immunostaining and western blotting is used when genetics is inconclusive. Exclude dystrophinopathy, Pompe disease (enzyme assay), myositis, FSHD and myotonic dystrophy. Baseline and periodic cardiac and respiratory assessment are required.
det.treatment: There is no approved disease-modifying therapy, though gene therapy trials are ongoing for some sarcoglycanopathies and other subtypes. Care is supportive: physiotherapy, contracture management, mobility aids, cardiac and respiratory monitoring with timely ventilation, and genetic counselling. Corticosteroids are not helpful in dysferlinopathy.
det.prognosis: Highly variable by subtype, from near-normal life expectancy with mild disability to early loss of ambulation and cardiorespiratory failure.
pearls: Dysferlinopathy with inflammation on biopsy is often mistaken for polymyositis.
Always exclude Pompe disease — it is treatable.
FKRP-related LGMD needs cardiac and respiratory screening even when limbs are mildly affected.
det.thd: LGMD เป็นกลุ่มโรคกล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมทางพันธุกรรมหลายยีน ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อรอบสะโพกและไหล่อ่อนแรงช้าๆ ทั้งในชายและหญิง ส่วนใหญ่ถ่ายทอดแบบยีนด้อย แต่ละชนิดมีลักษณะเฉพาะ เช่น calpainopathy มีสะบักยื่นและข้อเท้าติด ส่วน dysferlinopathy มีน่องอ่อนแรงและ CK สูงมาก การวินิจฉัยใช้ MRI กล้ามเนื้อและตรวจยีนแบบ panel ต้องตัดโรค Pompe ซึ่งรักษาได้ออกก่อน ปัจจุบันยังไม่มียาเฉพาะ จึงเน้นกายภาพบำบัด และเฝ้าระวังหัวใจกับการหายใจ

name: Limb-kinetic apraxia
formal: Apraxia with loss of fine, precise finger and hand movements in the limb contralateral to a premotor or parietal lesion, without weakness, sensory loss or ataxia.
simple: Clumsiness of fine hand and finger movements despite normal strength, from brain damage.
more: Loss of fine, skilled movement of a limb, especially the hand, without weakness, sensory loss or true cerebellar signs, from lesions of premotor or frontal circuits, seen in corticobasal syndrome. It is a feature of frontal or corticobasal disease. Occupational therapy is helpful; treat the underlying disorder.
th: apraxia ที่สูญเสียการเคลื่อนไหวละเอียดของนิ้วและมือด้านตรงข้ามรอยโรค premotor หรือ parietal โดยไม่มีอ่อนแรง ชา หรือ ataxia
tempoNote: Gradual in degenerative disease (e.g. corticobasal syndrome); sudden after stroke
feat: Clumsy, slow, coarse finger movements such as buttoning, coin rotation and finger tapping
Affects one hand, contralateral to the lesion
Not explained by weakness, sensory loss, ataxia or parkinsonism alone
Present for both imitation and spontaneous use, unlike ideomotor apraxia
Common early sign in corticobasal syndrome
inv: Bedside: coin rotation, finger tapping, picking up small objects
MRI: asymmetric frontoparietal atrophy or focal lesion
FDG-PET or amyloid/tau biomarkers when degenerative

case.story: Over a year she can no longer thread a needle or fasten buttons with her right hand, though her strength feels normal.
case.exam: Normal power and sensation; right hand coin rotation slow and clumsy, mild rigidity, myoclonic jerks of right fingers.
case.tests: MRI shows left frontoparietal atrophy; FDG-PET asymmetric hypometabolism.
case.q: What is the cortical sign and the likely syndrome?
case.a: Limb-kinetic apraxia of the right hand as part of corticobasal syndrome.

det.patho: Skilled fine finger control depends on premotor and primary motor cortex and their parietal inputs. Damage here, often in corticobasal degeneration, focal stroke or tumour, disrupts the motor programmes for individual finger movements while leaving basic strength intact. Some authors regard it as a mild cortical motor deficit rather than a true apraxia.
det.clinical: This is a sign rather than a disease. Patients describe a hand that feels awkward or does not obey for fine tasks. Movements are coarse and fragmented regardless of whether the task is imitated, pantomimed or done with a real object. It is usually unilateral and appears early in corticobasal syndrome.
det.diagnosis: Diagnose it when fine motor clumsiness exceeds what weakness, sensory loss, ataxia or bradykinesia could produce. Coin rotation between thumb and fingers is a sensitive test. Imaging looks for a contralateral frontoparietal lesion or atrophy. Separating it from ideomotor apraxia and bradykinesia can be difficult.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying cause. Occupational therapy, adaptive tools and practice of specific tasks help function. There is no drug therapy for the apraxia itself.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause: may improve after stroke, progressive in degenerative disease.
pearls: Coin rotation is a quick bedside screen for limb-kinetic apraxia.
Unilateral clumsy hand with myoclonus and rigidity: think corticobasal syndrome.
Strength may be normal when the hand is useless.
det.thd: Limb-kinetic apraxia คือการสูญเสียการเคลื่อนไหวละเอียดของนิ้วมือด้านตรงข้ามรอยโรคที่ premotor หรือ parietal cortex โดยกำลังและความรู้สึกปกติ เช่น ติดกระดุมหรือหมุนเหรียญไม่ได้ เป็นอาการไม่ใช่โรค พบบ่อยใน corticobasal syndrome หรือหลังโรคหลอดเลือดสมอง ตรวจด้วยการหมุนเหรียญและ MRI รักษาตามสาเหตุร่วมกับกิจกรรมบำบัด

name: Limbic encephalitis
formal: Inflammation of limbic structures, autoimmune or paraneoplastic (LGI1, GABA-B, anti-Hu), with amnesia, seizures, psychiatric change and mesial temporal MRI hyperintensity.
simple: Brain inflammation in memory areas, causing confusion, memory loss and seizures.
th: การอักเสบของระบบ limbic จากภูมิคุ้มกันหรือมะเร็ง ทำให้ความจำระยะสั้นเสีย ชักจากสมองกลีบขมับ และพฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน MRI พบ mesial temporal สัญญาณสูง
tempoNote: Develops over days to weeks, by definition within about 3 months
feat: Rapid short-term memory loss with repetitive questioning
Temporal lobe seizures (déjà vu, epigastric rising, pilomotor seizures), often frequent
Mood, behaviour and sleep change; confusion
Clues to antibody: hyponatraemia and faciobrachial dystonic seizures (LGI1), smoking history (GABA-B, Hu), testicular mass (Ma2)
inv: MRI FLAIR: bilateral or unilateral mesial temporal hyperintensity
CSF: mild pleocytosis or oligoclonal bands; HSV PCR to exclude infection
Neural antibodies in serum and CSF (LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, AMPA, Hu, Ma2, GAD65)
EEG for temporal seizures; CT chest and FDG-PET for tumour

case.story: For six weeks he asks the same questions repeatedly and has brief episodes of grimacing with arm jerking many times a day.
case.exam: Disoriented in time, cannot recall 3 words at 5 minutes; brief right face and arm dystonic jerks observed.
case.tests: Serum sodium 126; MRI shows left mesial temporal FLAIR signal; LGI1 antibodies positive in serum.
case.q: What treatment should start, and why urgently?
case.a: Immunotherapy (IV methylprednisolone with or without IVIG); early treatment of LGI1 encephalitis controls seizures and improves long-term memory outcome.

det.patho: Inflammation targets the hippocampus, amygdala and related limbic cortex. Surface antibodies (LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, AMPA) are pathogenic and the disease is often reversible; intracellular antibodies (Hu, Ma2) signal T-cell mediated paraneoplastic damage, mainly with small-cell lung and testicular cancer. GAD65-associated cases are often chronic and drug resistant.
det.clinical: Subacute amnesia, seizures and psychiatric features are the core. LGI1 cases, typically older men, may show faciobrachial dystonic seizures before memory problems and frequent hyponatraemia. GABA-B cases present with prominent seizures and often a lung tumour. Paraneoplastic cases may have other neurological involvement such as sensory neuronopathy or brainstem signs.
det.diagnosis: Criteria require subacute memory deficit, seizures or psychiatric symptoms plus bilateral mesial temporal MRI abnormality, and either CSF pleocytosis or temporal EEG abnormality, after excluding other causes. Antibodies refine the diagnosis but are not required. Always exclude HSV and other infections, and look for a tumour; repeat cancer screening over time if an onconeural antibody is found.
det.treatment: First-line therapy is IV methylprednisolone, IVIG or plasma exchange, given early; rituximab or cyclophosphamide is used if response is inadequate. Tumour treatment is key in paraneoplastic cases. Antiseizure drugs help, but in LGI1 the seizures often respond better to immunotherapy. Correct hyponatraemia carefully.
det.prognosis: Surface antibody forms often improve markedly though residual memory deficit and hippocampal atrophy are common; onconeural forms usually stabilise at best.
pearls: Older man with amnesia, low sodium and brief face-arm jerks: LGI1.
Treat as HSV encephalitis until PCR is negative.
Mesial temporal FLAIR change can evolve into hippocampal sclerosis.
det.thd: Limbic encephalitis คือการอักเสบของ hippocampus และ amygdala จากภูมิคุ้มกันหรือมะเร็ง ผู้ป่วยความจำระยะสั้นเสียภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์ มีชักจากสมองกลีบขมับ และพฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน MRI พบสัญญาณสูงที่ mesial temporal ตรวจ CSF แอนติบอดี เช่น LGI1 และหามะเร็ง ต้องแยกการติดเชื้อ HSV ก่อน รักษาด้วย steroid, IVIG หรือ plasma exchange โดยเร็ว

name: Lip tremor
formal: Rhythmic perioral tremor, as in rabbit syndrome from antipsychotics or Parkinson disease, with 3 to 7 Hz oscillation of the lip.
simple: A shaking of the lips, often as a side effect of certain medicines or in Parkinson disease.
th: การสั่นเป็นจังหวะของริมฝีปาก ความถี่ประมาณ 3–7 Hz พบใน rabbit syndrome จากยาต้านจิต และใน Parkinson's disease
tempoNote: Gradual; drug-induced form appears after months of antipsychotic therapy
feat: Rapid vertical movements of the lips like a rabbit chewing, tongue spared
Occurs at rest; may lessen with speaking
Drug-induced: antipsychotics, metoclopramide; often with parkinsonism
Parkinson's disease: rest tremor of lips and jaw
Essential tremor occasionally involves lips with voice tremor
inv: Medication history; examine for parkinsonism
DaT-SPECT if uncertain between drug-induced and degenerative parkinsonism

case.who: 45-year-old man with schizophrenia from Srithanya Hospital outpatient clinic, Nonthaburi
case.story: On haloperidol for a year; family notices his lips quiver constantly as if nibbling.
case.exam: 5 Hz rhythmic vertical lip movements, tongue still, mild bradykinesia, no choreic orolingual movements.
case.tests: None needed; diagnosis clinical.
case.q: What is this and how does it differ from tardive dyskinesia in management?
case.a: Rabbit syndrome (drug-induced perioral tremor); responds to anticholinergics and switching to a lower-potency antipsychotic, whereas anticholinergics may worsen TD.

read.where: 17 - The tardive syndromes: Phenomenology, concepts on pathophysiology and treatment, and other neuroleptic-­induced syndromes

det.patho: Lip tremor is a parkinsonian-type tremor arising from basal ganglia dysfunction, through D2 receptor blockade in drug-induced cases or nigral degeneration in Parkinson's disease. Its frequency and response to anticholinergics support a parkinsonian mechanism rather than a tardive one.
det.clinical: This is a sign rather than a disease. Rabbit syndrome is the classic drug-induced form, appearing after months or years of antipsychotic use and often accompanied by other parkinsonian features. In Parkinson's disease, lip tremor accompanies jaw and limb rest tremor. Essential and dystonic tremors may rarely involve the lips.
det.diagnosis: Observe at rest and during speech. Regular, rhythmic vertical movements of the lips with sparing of the tongue suggest rabbit syndrome or parkinsonian tremor, whereas tardive dyskinesia is irregular and involves the tongue. Drug history is essential; DaT imaging may help when parkinsonism persists after withdrawal.
det.treatment: For drug-induced forms, reduce or switch to an antipsychotic with lower D2 affinity (clozapine, quetiapine) and use anticholinergics such as trihexyphenidyl. For Parkinson's disease, dopaminergic therapy is used. Botulinum toxin is rarely needed.
det.prognosis: Drug-induced forms usually improve after medication change; degenerative forms follow PD course.
pearls: Rabbit syndrome spares the tongue; TD involves it.
Anticholinergics help rabbit syndrome but can aggravate TD.
Lip tremor in a drug-naive older adult deserves assessment for Parkinson's.
det.thd: Lip tremor คือริมฝีปากสั่นเป็นจังหวะ เป็นอาการไม่ใช่โรค รูปแบบที่สำคัญคือ rabbit syndrome จากยาต้านจิต ซึ่งริมฝีปากขยับเร็วคล้ายกระต่ายแต่ลิ้นไม่ขยับ ต่างจาก tardive dyskinesia และพบได้ใน Parkinson's disease วินิจฉัยจากการสังเกตและประวัติยา รักษาด้วยการปรับยาต้านจิตและให้ยา anticholinergic

name: Lipid metabolism disorders
formal: Inherited or acquired defects of fat transport or oxidation, such as carnitine or CPT II deficiency and ETF defects, producing myopathy, rhabdomyolysis and hypoglycaemia.
simple: Problems with how the body uses fat for energy, which can cause weakness, muscle breakdown and low blood sugar.
more: Diagnose by acylcarnitines, enzyme and genetic testing; treat with avoiding fasting, carnitine, riboflavin or diet changes as appropriate.
th: ความผิดปกติของการขนส่งหรือการเผาผลาญไขมันแต่กำเนิดหรือภายหลัง เช่น CPT II หรือ carnitine deficiency ทำให้เกิด myopathy, rhabdomyolysis และน้ำตาลต่ำ
tempoNote: Episodes triggered by fasting, exercise, fever or cold; some forms give fixed weakness
feat: Exercise- or fasting-induced myalgia and rhabdomyolysis with dark urine (CPT II, VLCAD)
Fixed proximal weakness with lipid storage on biopsy (carnitine deficiency, MADD)
Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and encephalopathy in infancy
Cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia in some types
Normal between attacks in the episodic forms
inv: Plasma acylcarnitine profile (ideally during or after an episode); free and total carnitine
CK during attacks; urine organic acids
Muscle biopsy: lipid droplets on oil red O in storage forms
Gene testing (CPT2, ACADVL, SLC22A5, ETFDH, HADHA/B)

case.story: Third episode of severe muscle pain and cola-coloured urine after a long march without breakfast; no cramps during the exercise itself.
case.exam: Tender thighs, mild proximal weakness.
case.tests: CK 85,000 U/L, myoglobinuria, creatinine rising; between attacks CK normal; acylcarnitine profile raised long-chain species; CPT2 common variant.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the preventive advice?
case.a: CPT II deficiency, a lipid metabolism disorder; avoid fasting and prolonged exertion, carbohydrate intake before exercise, hydrate and treat rhabdomyolysis early.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Fatty Acid Oxidation Defects
14 Specific dietary management of certain neurological disorders

det.patho: Long-chain fatty acids enter mitochondria through the carnitine shuttle (OCTN2 transporter, CPT I, translocase, CPT II) and then undergo beta-oxidation. Defects at any step limit energy supply when glucose is scarce, such as during fasting, prolonged exercise or fever. Muscle may accumulate lipid or break down, and liver may fail to make ketones.
det.clinical: Presentations follow age. Infants show hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, liver dysfunction and sudden death risk. Children and adults show exercise intolerance, myalgia and recurrent rhabdomyolysis, typically after prolonged rather than brief exertion. Storage forms such as primary carnitine deficiency and riboflavin-responsive MADD cause progressive proximal weakness, sometimes with cardiomyopathy.
det.diagnosis: Acylcarnitine profiling is the main screen, with carnitine levels and urine organic acids. Newborn screening detects many disorders. Biopsy shows lipid accumulation in storage disorders but may be normal in CPT II deficiency. Genetic testing confirms the specific defect.
det.treatment: Avoid fasting, use frequent carbohydrate-rich meals, extra carbohydrate during illness or exercise, and medium-chain triglyceride supplements for long-chain defects. Carnitine replacement is effective in primary carnitine deficiency, and riboflavin can be dramatic in late-onset MADD. Where available, triheptanoin is used in disorders of long-chain fatty acid oxidation. Treat rhabdomyolysis with fluids to prevent renal failure.
det.prognosis: Good for adult episodic forms with prevention; infantile forms carry risk of early death without diagnosis.
pearls: Rhabdomyolysis after prolonged effort or fasting points to fat metabolism; after brief effort to glycogen.
Draw an acylcarnitine profile during the acute episode.
Always try riboflavin in lipid storage myopathy.
det.thd: Lipid metabolism disorders คือกลุ่มโรคที่ร่างกายขนส่งหรือเผาผลาญไขมันไม่ได้ เช่น CPT II deficiency และ carnitine deficiency ผู้ป่วยมีกล้ามเนื้อสลายและปัสสาวะสีโค้กหลังอดอาหารหรือออกกำลังนาน หรือมีกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงต่อเนื่อง ในทารกอาจน้ำตาลต่ำ วินิจฉัยด้วย acylcarnitine profile ชิ้นเนื้อและยีน รักษาโดยหลีกเลี่ยงการอดอาหาร เสริม carnitine หรือ riboflavin ตามชนิด

name: Lipid storage disorders
formal: Inherited metabolic disorders with accumulation of lipids in lysosomes, including Gaucher, Niemann-Pick, Tay-Sachs and Fabry diseases, with neurological regression and organomegaly.
simple: Inherited conditions where fatty substances build up in the body's cells and damage the brain and organs.
th: กลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่ไขมันสะสมในไลโซโซม เช่น Gaucher, Niemann-Pick, Tay-Sachs, Fabry, Krabbe, MLD ทำให้พัฒนาการถดถอย ตับม้ามโต หรือปวดปลายประสาท
tempoNote: Infantile forms regress over months; juvenile and adult forms progress over years
feat: Loss of acquired milestones, seizures, spasticity or ataxia in infants and children
Hepatosplenomegaly (Gaucher, Niemann-Pick) or none (Tay-Sachs, Krabbe)
Eye clues: cherry-red spot, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, corneal clouding
Adult forms: psychiatric illness, dementia, movement disorder or painful small-fibre neuropathy (Fabry)
inv: Leukocyte or dried blood spot enzyme assays (glucocerebrosidase, hexosaminidase, sphingomyelinase, alpha-galactosidase, galactocerebrosidase, arylsulfatase A)
Biomarkers: chitotriosidase, lyso-Gb1, lyso-Gb3, oxysterols
MRI white matter or atrophy patterns, nerve conduction, ophthalmology exam; gene confirmation

case.story: Developed normally until 5 months, now no longer sits, startles excessively to sounds and has had two seizures.
case.exam: Axial hypotonia with brisk reflexes, macrocephaly, bilateral cherry-red spots, no organomegaly.
case.tests: Hexosaminidase A activity almost absent; HEXA biallelic variants.
case.q: Which lipid storage disorder is this and why is the liver normal?
case.a: Tay–Sachs disease (GM2 gangliosidosis); ganglioside accumulates mainly in neurons, so there is no visceral enlargement.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Lysosomal Storage Disorders

det.patho: Each disorder results from deficiency of a lysosomal enzyme or transporter that degrades a lipid (glucocerebroside, sphingomyelin, gangliosides, globotriaosylceramide, sulfatides) or from cholesterol trafficking failure (NPC). Accumulated lipid damages neurons, myelin-producing cells, macrophages and blood vessels depending on where the substrate is normally turned over. Most are autosomal recessive; Fabry is X-linked.
det.clinical: Infantile forms cause rapid neurological regression; juvenile forms bring ataxia, dystonia, seizures and cognitive decline; adult forms may present to psychiatrists or as dementia, ataxia or neuropathy. Visceral involvement points to Gaucher or Niemann-Pick; demyelinating neuropathy with leukodystrophy suggests Krabbe or MLD; acroparaesthesia, angiokeratoma and stroke suggest Fabry.
det.diagnosis: Choose enzyme tests based on clinical clues, or use multiplex dried blood spot panels. Confirm with gene testing and use biomarkers for monitoring. MRI and eye examination direct the search. Pseudodeficiency alleles (e.g. arylsulfatase A) can mislead, so correlate with urine sulfatides or genotype.
det.treatment: Disease-specific therapies exist for some: enzyme replacement (Gaucher type 1, Fabry, ASMD), substrate reduction (miglustat, eliglustat), migalastat chaperone for amenable Fabry variants, gene therapy for presymptomatic MLD, haematopoietic stem cell transplant for early Krabbe. Many neuronopathic forms remain untreatable, and supportive care and genetic counselling are central.
det.prognosis: Ranges from death in early childhood (Tay-Sachs, infantile Krabbe) to near-normal survival with treatment (Gaucher type 1).
pearls: Organomegaly + neurological regression: think Gaucher or Niemann-Pick; regression without organomegaly: Tay-Sachs, Krabbe, MLD.
Cherry-red spot: Tay-Sachs, Sandhoff, Niemann-Pick A, sialidosis.
Newborn and presymptomatic diagnosis matters because transplant and gene therapy work best early.
det.thd: Lipid storage disorders คือกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่ขาดเอนไซม์ในไลโซโซมทำให้ไขมันสะสมในเซลล์ประสาท ไมอีลิน หรืออวัยวะภายใน เด็กเล็กมีพัฒนาการถดถอย ชัก ตับม้ามโตในบางชนิด ผู้ใหญ่อาจมาด้วยโรคจิต สมองเสื่อม หรือปวดปลายประสาท ตรวจวินิจฉัยด้วยการวัดเอนไซม์และตรวจยีน บางโรครักษาได้ด้วยเอนไซม์ทดแทน ยาลดสารตั้งต้น หรือปลูกถ่ายไขกระดูก

formal: Myopathies with excessive lipid droplets in muscle fibres, e.g. primary carnitine deficiency, neutral lipid storage disease or multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency.
simple: Muscle diseases where fat builds up inside muscle fibres, causing weakness.

ab: Neutral lipid storage disease with myopathy

Biopsy: excess lipid droplets in type 1 fibres

case.exam: Neck extensor weakness, proximal limb weakness grade 3–4, no ptosis, reflexes reduced.
case.tests: CK 1,100 U/L; acylcarnitines show raised short-, medium- and long-chain species; biopsy shows lipid droplets in type 1 fibres; ETFDH variants.
case.q: What is the treatment and what response is expected?
case.a: Riboflavin-responsive MADD (lipid storage myopathy); high-dose riboflavin (with carnitine and CoQ10) often produces dramatic improvement within weeks.

read.where: Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Glycogenoses and Lipid Storage Disorders

det.patho: Defects in carnitine transport, electron transfer from acyl-CoA dehydrogenases, or triglyceride breakdown lead to accumulation of lipid droplets in muscle fibres, especially oxidative type 1 fibres. Energy production from fatty acids fails, causing weakness that worsens with metabolic stress. All are autosomal recessive.
det.clinical: Patients present at any age with subacute or fluctuating proximal and axial weakness, sometimes with episodic metabolic crises, vomiting or encephalopathy. Neck extensor weakness and exercise intolerance are common. Cardiomyopathy and liver involvement occur in some forms. Riboflavin-responsive MADD from ETFDH is the most frequent cause in southern China and Southeast Asia.
det.diagnosis: Biochemical tests (carnitine levels, acylcarnitines, organic acids) are central, preferably during symptoms. A blood smear showing lipid vacuoles in granulocytes suggests neutral lipid storage disease. Biopsy confirms lipid accumulation, and genetic testing identifies the specific gene.
det.treatment: Riboflavin is effective in ETFDH-related MADD; carnitine replaces deficiency in primary carnitine deficiency; NLSD has no specific therapy but needs cardiac monitoring. Avoid fasting and treat intercurrent illness promptly with carbohydrate. Exercise should be moderate.
det.prognosis: Excellent in treatable forms; NLSD-M may progress with cardiomyopathy.
pearls: Always check acylcarnitines in an unexplained proximal or dropped-head myopathy.
Riboflavin-responsive MADD is common in Asia and highly treatable.
Jordans' anomaly on a blood film points to neutral lipid storage disease.
det.thd: Lipid storage myopathy คือกลุ่มโรคกล้ามเนื้อที่ใช้ไขมันเป็นพลังงานไม่ได้ จึงมีไขมันสะสมในกล้ามเนื้อ ทำให้อ่อนแรงต้นแขนขาและคอตก โดยเฉพาะหลังเจ็บป่วยหรืออดอาหาร สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยในเอเชียคือ MADD จากยีน ETFDH ซึ่งตอบสนองต่อ riboflavin ดีมาก วินิจฉัยด้วย acylcarnitine ชิ้นเนื้อ และตรวจยีน

name: Lithium catatonia
formal: Catatonia or toxicity associated with lithium treatment, with stupor, rigidity, tremor and confusion, particularly at high serum levels or with neuroleptics; requires lithium withdrawal.
simple: Stupor, stiffness or confusion occurring during lithium treatment, usually linked to toxic drug levels.
th: catatonia หรืออาการพิษที่สัมพันธ์กับการรักษาด้วย lithium มีภาวะไม่ตอบสนอง แข็งเกร็ง สั่น และสับสน มักเกิดเมื่อระดับยาสูงหรือใช้ร่วมกับยาต้านจิต
tempoNote: Develops over days, often after dose increase, dehydration or interacting drugs
feat: Stupor, mutism, posturing, rigidity and waxy flexibility
Coarse tremor, myoclonus, ataxia, dysarthria, confusion
Triggers: dehydration, renal impairment, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, thiazides
Overlap with neuroleptic malignant syndrome when combined with antipsychotics
Neurotoxicity possible even at therapeutic serum levels
inv: Serum lithium level, creatinine, sodium, calcium, TSH
CK, temperature monitoring (exclude NMS)
EEG (diffuse slowing, triphasic waves)
Bush–Francis Catatonia Rating Scale

case.who: 48-year-old woman with bipolar disorder from Nakhon Sawan
case.story: Started ibuprofen for back pain a week ago; became withdrawn, stopped eating and now lies still and does not speak.
case.exam: Mute, staring, rigid limbs with posturing, coarse tremor, multifocal myoclonus; temperature 37.4 °C.
case.tests: Lithium 2.4 mmol/L, creatinine raised; CK mildly elevated; EEG generalised slowing.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the immediate management?
case.a: Lithium toxicity with catatonia; stop lithium and NSAID, IV fluids, consider haemodialysis, and lorazepam for catatonia.

det.patho: Lithium affects second-messenger signalling, dopamine and glutamate systems, and accumulates in the brain more slowly than in serum. Toxicity alters cortical and cerebellar function, and in combination with dopamine blockers may push the basal ganglia toward catatonic or NMS-like states. Brain levels can remain high after serum levels fall.
det.clinical: Patients often present with a mixture of catatonia and toxic encephalopathy: stupor, mutism, rigidity, tremor, myoclonus, ataxia and confusion. Chronic toxicity in a patient on long-term therapy is more neurologically dangerous than acute overdose at the same serum level. Persistent cerebellar damage (SILENT syndrome) may follow severe toxicity.
det.diagnosis: Measure lithium levels, renal function, sodium and thyroid function. Neurotoxicity can occur at therapeutic levels, so clinical findings matter more than the number. Exclude NMS, serotonin syndrome, non-convulsive status epilepticus and infection. EEG helps detect encephalopathy and seizures.
det.treatment: Stop lithium and interacting drugs, restore fluids and electrolytes, and use haemodialysis for severe toxicity, renal failure or marked neurological signs. Benzodiazepines (lorazepam) treat catatonia; ECT is reserved for refractory cases after lithium is cleared. Avoid antipsychotics during the acute phase. Re-evaluate the need for lithium and the safe dose afterward.
det.prognosis: Most recover fully with prompt treatment; a minority have lasting cerebellar dysfunction.
pearls: Stupor plus coarse tremor and myoclonus in a lithium patient: check the level and renal function.
NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and thiazides are common precipitants.
A therapeutic serum level does not exclude neurotoxicity.

name: Liver disease/failure chorea
formal: Acquired hepatocerebral degeneration, chorea with ataxia, parkinsonism and dementia in chronic liver disease, with manganese deposition in pallidum on MRI.
simple: Involuntary movements and thinking problems caused by chronic liver failure.
th: chorea ร่วมกับ ataxia, parkinsonism และสมองเสื่อมในผู้ป่วยโรคตับเรื้อรัง พบการสะสม manganese ที่ globus pallidus ใน MRI
tempoNote: Usually develops gradually after repeated hepatic encephalopathy or portosystemic shunting
feat: Orofacial and limb chorea, often with ataxia, dysarthria and action tremor
Parkinsonism and asterixis; cognitive slowing
Background of cirrhosis or portosystemic shunt, often repeated encephalopathy
Bilateral pallidal T1 hyperintensity on MRI (manganese)
inv: Liver function, ammonia, ultrasound for shunts
MRI: T1 hyperintense globus pallidus; exclude other causes of chorea
Copper studies to exclude Wilson's disease in younger patients

case.who: 58-year-old man from Udon Thani with hepatitis B cirrhosis
case.story: Several admissions for hepatic encephalopathy; over six months he has developed writhing movements of the mouth and hands and an unsteady walk.
case.exam: Orofacial and limb chorea, mild ataxia, slow speech, asterixis.
case.tests: Ammonia moderately raised; MRI shows symmetric T1 bright globus pallidus; ceruloplasmin normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the definitive treatment?
case.a: Acquired hepatocerebral degeneration with chorea; liver transplantation may reverse it, while lactulose/rifaximin and symptomatic drugs help partly.

det.patho: Reduced hepatic clearance and portosystemic shunting allow manganese and ammonia to reach the brain. Manganese accumulates in the globus pallidus and other basal ganglia, while ammonia causes astrocyte swelling and Alzheimer type II glia. Neuronal loss and spongy change develop in the cortex, basal ganglia and cerebellum in chronic cases.
det.clinical: Acquired hepatocerebral degeneration usually appears after repeated episodes of hepatic encephalopathy, although some patients never have overt episodes. Chorea, especially orofacial, may coexist with ataxia, parkinsonism, tremor and cognitive decline. Signs persist between encephalopathic episodes, unlike simple hepatic encephalopathy.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on chronic liver disease or a shunt, compatible movement disorder and pallidal T1 hyperintensity, after excluding Wilson's disease, drug-induced chorea, Huntington's disease and structural lesions. Ammonia levels correlate imperfectly with severity.
det.treatment: Treat hepatic encephalopathy with lactulose and rifaximin and correct precipitants. Closure of portosystemic shunts can help. Liver transplantation may substantially improve or reverse the syndrome. Chorea can be reduced with tetrabenazine or low-dose antipsychotics used carefully; parkinsonism responds poorly to levodopa.
det.prognosis: Without transplantation symptoms usually persist or progress, and overall prognosis is that of the liver disease.
pearls: Bright globus pallidus on T1 in a cirrhotic patient is manganese deposition.
Persistent chorea between encephalopathic episodes suggests acquired hepatocerebral degeneration.
Always exclude Wilson's disease in younger patients with liver disease and movement disorder.
det.thd: Liver disease/failure chorea หรือ acquired hepatocerebral degeneration เป็นภาวะที่ผู้ป่วยตับแข็งหรือมี portosystemic shunt มี chorea ร่วมกับเดินเซ parkinsonism และความคิดช้า เกิดจาก manganese และ ammonia สะสมในสมอง MRI พบ globus pallidus สว่างใน T1 ต้องตัด Wilson's disease รักษาด้วย lactulose rifaximin ยาควบคุม chorea และการปลูกถ่ายตับอาจทำให้ดีขึ้น

name: Locked-in syndrome
formal: Quadriplegia with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movement, from bilateral ventral pontine lesions such as basilar artery occlusion, central pontine myelinolysis or ALS.
simple: A state in which a person is awake and aware but cannot move or speak, apart from the eyes.
th: ผู้ป่วยรู้สึกตัวดีแต่ขยับแขนขาและพูดไม่ได้ ยังกลอกตาขึ้นลงและกะพริบตาได้ เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ ventral pons ทั้งสองข้าง
tempoNote: Usually abrupt from basilar occlusion or pontine haemorrhage; can evolve over days in osmotic demyelination or develop in severe neuropathy
feat: Tetraplegia and anarthria with preserved consciousness and cognition
Communication only through vertical eye movements and blinking
Horizontal gaze often lost because of pontine involvement
Causes: basilar artery occlusion, pontine haemorrhage, osmotic demyelination, trauma; functional mimics from severe GBS
Easily mistaken for coma or vegetative state
inv: Urgent CT angiography or MRI with MR angiography for basilar occlusion
EEG shows reactive near-normal background, unlike coma
Sodium history and MRI pons for osmotic demyelination
Nerve conduction studies if a peripheral cause (GBS, botulism) is possible

case.who: 58-year-old hypertensive man admitted to a stroke unit in Phitsanulok
case.story: Had two days of dizziness and slurred speech, then collapsed; nurses think he is in coma.
case.exam: Eyes open, cannot move limbs or speak, but looks up and blinks twice when asked; horizontal gaze absent; bilateral extensor plantars.
case.tests: CTA shows basilar artery occlusion; MRI shows bilateral ventral pontine infarction.
case.q: What is his conscious state and how should the team communicate?
case.a: Locked-in syndrome — fully aware; set up a yes/no blink code and later an eye-gaze communication system, and consider reperfusion if within the window.

read.where: Chapter 28 Disorders of Consciousness and Intensive Care Neurology — Locked-In Syndrome
Chapter 29: The Neurologist And End-Of-Life Care In The Intensive Care Unit

det.patho: A bilateral lesion of the ventral pons interrupts corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres, so voluntary limb, facial and bulbar movement are lost. The reticular activating system in the dorsal tegmentum is spared, preserving arousal, and vertical eye movements controlled from the midbrain remain. Basilar artery thrombosis is the most frequent cause.
det.clinical: Classic locked-in syndrome preserves vertical gaze and blinking; incomplete forms retain some other movement, and total locked-in syndrome has no eye movement at all. Patients are fully aware and can feel pain, so staff must talk to them and provide analgesia. Prodromal vertigo, dysarthria or fluctuating hemiparesis often precede basilar occlusion. Aspiration and respiratory complications are major early threats.
det.diagnosis: Ask every apparently comatose patient with open eyes to look up and down and to blink on command. MRI confirms the pontine lesion and angiography identifies basilar occlusion. EEG shows a reactive background, and evoked potentials or brain-computer interface testing help in uncertain cases. Fulminant neuropathy, botulism and neuromuscular blockade must be considered when imaging is normal.
det.treatment: Basilar occlusion is treated urgently with thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy where possible, as recent trials support benefit. Supportive care covers airway protection, often tracheostomy, gastrostomy, pressure care and thromboprophylaxis. Early establishment of a communication code and later eye-tracking devices is essential. Rehabilitation can restore some head and finger movement.
det.prognosis: Early mortality is high, mostly from respiratory complications, but long-term survivors can live for decades, and many report acceptable quality of life.
pearls: Always test vertical eye movement and blinking to command in an apparently comatose patient.
Patients hear and understand everything — speak to them, not about them.
Prodromal brainstem symptoms before collapse should prompt immediate basilar imaging.
det.thd: Locked-in syndrome คือผู้ป่วยรู้สึกตัวและคิดได้ปกติ แต่ขยับแขนขา หน้า และพูดไม่ได้ เหลือเพียงกลอกตาขึ้นลงและกะพริบตา เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ ventral pons ทั้งสองข้าง ส่วนใหญ่จาก basilar artery อุดตัน มักถูกเข้าใจผิดว่าโคม่า ต้องทดสอบให้มองขึ้นลงหรือกะพริบตาตามคำสั่ง การรักษาคือเปิดหลอดเลือดอย่างเร่งด่วนและสร้างระบบสื่อสารด้วยตา

Bilateral thalamic lesions

name: Logopenic aphasia (LPA)
formal: Primary progressive aphasia variant with word-finding pauses and impaired sentence repetition, usually from Alzheimer pathology involving the left temporoparietal junction.
simple: A form of language decline with trouble finding words and repeating sentences, often due to Alzheimer disease.
th: ภาวะภาษาเสื่อมแบบก้าวหน้าชนิด logopenic พูดหยุดเพื่อหาคำบ่อย พูดซ้ำประโยคยาวไม่ได้ มักเกิดจากพยาธิสภาพ Alzheimer ที่สมองซีกซ้ายส่วนขมับ-ข้างขม่อม
tempoNote: Insidious onset, usually age 55–70, progressing over years to broader dementia
feat: Slow speech with frequent word-finding pauses but grammar largely intact
Poor repetition of sentences and phrases (phonological working memory loss), single words better
Phonological paraphasias (sound errors) without motor speech apraxia
Single-word comprehension and object knowledge relatively spared
Episodic memory and other Alzheimer features emerge over time
inv: Language assessment: naming, sentence repetition, comprehension, motor speech
MRI: left posterior temporal and inferior parietal atrophy
FDG-PET left temporoparietal hypometabolism; amyloid PET or CSF/plasma AD biomarkers usually positive

case.story: Two years of stopping mid-sentence to search for words; colleagues finish his sentences. He still runs meetings and remembers events.
case.exam: Fluent grammar but many pauses, fails to repeat 'no ifs, ands or buts', occasional sound errors, good word comprehension.
case.tests: MRI left temporoparietal atrophy; CSF low Abeta42/40 and high p-tau.
case.q: Which PPA variant is this and what pathology underlies it?
case.a: Logopenic variant PPA, usually due to Alzheimer disease pathology.

read.where: Chapter 11 Cognitive Impairment and Dementia — Frontotemporal Dementia
Case 11 Progressive aphasia complicated by intracerebral bleeding

det.patho: Logopenic aphasia reflects degeneration of the left posterior superior/middle temporal gyrus and inferior parietal lobule, which support phonological short-term memory and lexical retrieval. Most patients have Alzheimer pathology (amyloid plaques and tau tangles); a minority have FTLD-TDP or other proteinopathies. It was defined in the 2011 consensus classification of primary progressive aphasia.
det.clinical: Patients present with hesitant speech, frequent pauses for words, and sound-based errors, with relatively preserved grammar and articulation. Repetition of long sentences is disproportionately poor. Over several years memory, calculation, praxis and visuospatial skills decline, and the picture merges with Alzheimer dementia. Some develop myoclonus or seizures.
det.diagnosis: Diagnose PPA first (language the leading and dominant deficit), then apply the 2011 criteria: impaired single-word retrieval and sentence repetition, plus supportive features. Imaging shows left temporoparietal involvement. Alzheimer biomarkers (CSF, amyloid/tau PET, plasma p-tau217) are positive in most and determine eligibility for anti-amyloid therapy.
det.treatment: Speech and language therapy with word-retrieval strategies and communication aids helps maintain function. Cholinesterase inhibitors are often tried given the Alzheimer pathology, though evidence is limited. Anti-amyloid antibodies may be considered in biomarker-confirmed early disease where available. Plan for progression and support carers.
det.prognosis: Progresses to global dementia over several years, often faster than amnestic Alzheimer disease in some series.
pearls: Poor sentence repetition with spared grammar = logopenic.
Logopenic is the PPA variant most likely to be Alzheimer disease.
Check AD biomarkers — they change management.
det.thd: Logopenic aphasia เป็นภาวะภาษาเสื่อมแบบก้าวหน้า ผู้ป่วยพูดหยุดหาคำบ่อย พูดซ้ำประโยคยาวไม่ได้ แต่ไวยากรณ์และความเข้าใจคำเดี่ยวยังดี เกิดจากสมองซีกซ้ายส่วนขมับและข้างขม่อมเสื่อม ส่วนใหญ่มีพยาธิสภาพ Alzheimer ตรวจ MRI, PET และ biomarker ของ Alzheimer การรักษาคืออรรถบำบัด ยา cholinesterase inhibitor และวางแผนดูแลระยะยาว

name: Long-chain HAD deficiency
formal: Defect in mitochondrial trifunctional protein (HADHA/HADHB), causing hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy, rhabdomyolysis, and peripheral neuropathy with retinopathy.
simple: An inherited problem burning fat for energy, causing weak muscles, nerve damage, and low blood sugar.
more: Raised hydroxyacylcarnitines; treat with avoidance of fasting, a low-long-chain-fat diet, and medium-chain triglycerides; triheptanoin has been used.
th: ความผิดปกติของ mitochondrial trifunctional protein (HADHA/HADHB) ทำให้น้ำตาลต่ำแบบไม่มีคีโตน cardiomyopathy กล้ามเนื้อสลาย และ neuropathy ร่วมกับ retinopathy
tempoNote: Acute metabolic crises in infancy; chronic neuropathy and retinopathy in survivors
feat: Infant hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, liver dysfunction, cardiomyopathy, sudden death
Recurrent rhabdomyolysis with fever or exercise in older children
Progressive sensorimotor axonal neuropathy (especially in MTP deficiency)
Pigmentary retinopathy with progressive visual loss (especially LCHAD)
Mothers carrying an affected fetus may develop AFLP or HELLP syndrome
inv: Acylcarnitine profile (raised long-chain 3-hydroxy acylcarnitines); newborn screening
HADHA/HADHB gene testing (common HADHA c.1528G>C in LCHAD)
CK, echocardiogram, NCS, ophthalmology

case.who: 6-year-old girl from Nan diagnosed by newborn screening
case.story: On a low-fat diet with MCT oil; recently weaker in the legs and tripping, with episodes of dark urine during fevers.
case.exam: Distal weakness and areflexia in legs, pigmentary changes in fundi.
case.tests: NCS: length-dependent axonal sensorimotor neuropathy; CK 20,000 during febrile illness; HADHA homozygous c.1528G>C.
case.q: Which disorder explains the neuropathy, retinopathy and rhabdomyolysis?
case.a: LCHAD (mitochondrial trifunctional protein) deficiency.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Fatty Acid Oxidation Defects

det.patho: Mitochondrial trifunctional protein carries out the last three steps of long-chain beta-oxidation; LCHAD is one of its activities. Biallelic HADHA or HADHB variants cause energy failure and accumulation of toxic long-chain 3-hydroxy fatty acids, which may damage the retina and peripheral nerves. Heterozygous mothers can be overwhelmed by fetal metabolites, causing acute fatty liver of pregnancy.
det.clinical: Severe forms present in infancy with hypoglycaemia, liver failure, cardiomyopathy and sudden death. Milder forms show recurrent rhabdomyolysis triggered by illness or exertion. Survivors develop a progressive axonal neuropathy and pigmentary retinopathy that continue despite metabolic control. A mother with pregnancy complications (AFLP, HELLP) can be the earliest hint in a family.
det.diagnosis: Newborn screening by acylcarnitine profile identifies most cases in screened populations. Confirmation is by gene testing or enzyme assay in fibroblasts. Echocardiography, ophthalmology and nerve conduction studies define organ involvement.
det.treatment: Avoid fasting, use a low long-chain fat diet with MCT supplementation and extra carbohydrates during illness, and treat crises urgently with IV glucose. Triheptanoin is an option in long-chain FAOD. Docosahexaenoic acid has been used to protect the retina with limited evidence. Monitor heart, eyes and nerves; give physiotherapy and orthoses for neuropathy.
det.prognosis: Early diagnosis has improved survival, but neuropathy and retinopathy often progress.
pearls: Neuropathy plus retinopathy plus rhabdomyolysis in a child: think LCHAD/MTP.
Ask the mother about fatty liver or HELLP syndrome in pregnancy.
MCT oil bypasses the long-chain defect.
det.thd: Long-chain HAD deficiency หรือ LCHAD/MTP deficiency เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมของการเผาผลาญไขมันสายยาว ทารกอาจมีน้ำตาลต่ำ ตับและหัวใจผิดปกติ ส่วนเด็กโตมีกล้ามเนื้อสลาย เส้นประสาทเสื่อม และจอประสาทตาเสื่อม แม่ที่ตั้งครรภ์อาจเกิด AFLP หรือ HELLP วินิจฉัยด้วย acylcarnitine และยีน HADHA/HADHB รักษาด้วยอาหารไขมันต่ำร่วม MCT และหลีกเลี่ยงการอดอาหาร

name: Long-QT syndrome
formal: Inherited or acquired cardiac channelopathy with delayed repolarisation, leading to torsades de pointes, syncope and seizure-like events; commonly misdiagnosed as epilepsy.
simple: A heart rhythm condition that can cause fainting or seizure-like episodes and sudden cardiac arrest.

Electrolytes including potassium, magnesium and calcium; medication review
Holter, exercise testing and genetic testing (KCNQ1, KCNH2, SCN5A) via cardiology

case.who: 17-year-old girl from Phuket labelled as having epilepsy
case.story: Three episodes of sudden collapse with jerks lasting under a minute, each when her alarm clock rang or the phone woke her; she recovers quickly. Her cousin died suddenly while sleeping.
case.exam: Normal.
case.tests: Interictal EEG normal; ECG shows QTc 520 ms with notched T waves.
case.q: What is the real diagnosis and what is the danger of the current label?
case.a: Congenital long-QT syndrome (likely LQT2, triggered by auditory startle) with convulsive syncope; continuing to treat as epilepsy leaves her at risk of sudden cardiac death.

read.where: Chapter 6 Neurologic Manifestations of Infective Endocarditis

det.patho: Delayed ventricular repolarisation, from loss of potassium current (KCNQ1, KCNH2) or persistent sodium current (SCN5A), predisposes to early afterdepolarisations and torsades de pointes. Acquired long QT results from drugs (macrolides, fluoroquinolones, antipsychotics, methadone, domperidone, ondansetron and others), electrolyte deficits, bradycardia and structural heart disease. KCNH2 is also expressed in the brain, and some patients have true seizures as well.
det.clinical: This is a cardiac disorder, included because it mimics epilepsy. Torsades causes abrupt loss of consciousness, often with stiffening and jerks as the brain becomes hypoperfused, followed by quick recovery; if sustained, it degenerates into ventricular fibrillation and sudden death. A family history of unexplained death, drowning or epilepsy and event triggers such as exercise, noise or sleep are clues.
det.diagnosis: Obtain an ECG in every patient with a first convulsive event or suspected seizure. Measure QTc manually; diagnostic scoring combines QTc, T-wave morphology, symptoms and family history. Look for and correct hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and offending drugs. Cardiology confirms with ambulatory monitoring, exercise testing and genetic testing, and screens relatives.
det.treatment: Avoid QT-prolonging drugs (including some antiseizure and psychiatric medications) and correct electrolytes. Beta-blockers, especially nadolol or propranolol, are first line in congenital LQTS. High-risk patients may receive an implantable defibrillator or left cardiac sympathetic denervation. Acute torsades is treated with IV magnesium and correction of the cause.
det.prognosis: With diagnosis and beta-blockers, risk of sudden death falls considerably; untreated symptomatic patients have high mortality.
pearls: Every new seizure-like event deserves a 12-lead ECG.
Collapse with jerks triggered by an alarm clock or swimming: think long QT, not epilepsy.
Check QT before adding drugs that prolong it, and correct magnesium and potassium.
det.thd: Long-QT syndrome เป็นความผิดปกติของช่องไอออนในหัวใจ ทำให้เกิดหัวใจเต้นผิดจังหวะแบบ torsades de pointes ผู้ป่วยหมดสติทันทีและอาจกระตุกสั้น ๆ คล้ายชัก จึงถูกวินิจฉัยผิดเป็นโรคลมชักได้ ตัวกระตุ้นเช่นการออกกำลังกาย เสียงดัง หรือขณะนอน ควรตรวจ ECG ในทุกรายที่มีอาการคล้ายชักครั้งแรก รักษาด้วย beta-blocker หลีกเลี่ยงยาที่ทำให้ QT ยาว และส่งพบแพทย์โรคหัวใจ

name: Spontaneous intracranial hypotension (SIH)
formal: Headaches from reduced CSF volume, such as spontaneous intracranial hypotension or post-lumbar puncture, worse on standing and eased by lying flat, with meningeal enhancement on MRI.
simple: Headaches that worsen on standing and ease on lying down, from low spinal fluid pressure.
ab: ปวดศีรษะจากความดันน้ำไขสันหลังต่ำ
th: ปวดศีรษะจากน้ำไขสันหลังรั่วที่ไขสันหลังโดยไม่มีสาเหตุชัดเจน ปวดมากเมื่อลุกยืนและดีขึ้นเมื่อนอนราบ MRI พบเยื่อดูราจับสีหนา สมองย้อยลง อาจมีเลือดคั่งใต้ดูรา รักษาด้วย epidural blood patch
tempoNote: Often begins abruptly or within a day (sometimes after a cough, strain or minor trauma); untreated it can persist for months, and orthostatic features may fade with time
feat: Orthostatic headache — worse within minutes to hours of being upright and eased by lying flat
Neck or interscapular pain, nausea, muffled hearing, tinnitus, dizziness
Peak age 30–50, women more often; association with connective tissue disorders (joint hypermobility, Marfan)
Complications: bilateral subdural collections, sagging-brain behavioural syndrome mimicking bvFTD, superficial siderosis, reduced consciousness
Similar picture after dural puncture, but SIH has no obvious procedure
inv: Contrast MRI brain: diffuse smooth pachymeningeal enhancement, subdural fluid, venous engorgement, pituitary enlargement, brain sagging (Bern score)
Whole-spine heavily T2-weighted MRI for extradural CSF collections
Dynamic CT myelography or digital subtraction myelography (lateral decubitus for CSF-venous fistula) to localise the leak
Lumbar opening pressure is often normal; LP is not required for diagnosis

case.story: After a hard sneezing fit 3 weeks ago she developed a headache that starts 20 minutes after sitting up and vanishes after lying down for 15 minutes. Her ears feel blocked when upright.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination; joint hypermobility.
case.tests: MRI: diffuse smooth dural enhancement, thin bilateral subdural collections, flattened pons and low-lying cerebellar tonsils. Spinal MRI: ventral extradural fluid collection from T2 to T8.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the usual first intervention?
case.a: Spontaneous intracranial hypotension from a spinal CSF leak; after brief conservative measures, an epidural blood patch (large-volume non-targeted, or targeted if the leak is localised), with myelography and surgery if it fails.

read.where: Chapter 50 Headache attributed to non-vascular intracranial disorder
Chapter 21 Headache — Headache Caused by Disturbance of Intracranial Pressure

det.patho: CSF escapes from the spinal canal through a ventral dural tear (often caused by a calcified disc spicule), a lateral tear at a nerve-root sleeve or meningeal diverticulum, or a direct CSF-to-epidural-vein fistula. Loss of volume, rather than low measured pressure, lets the brain sag when upright, stretching pain-sensitive meninges and bridging veins, with compensatory venous and meningeal engorgement (Monro–Kellie doctrine). Connective tissue weakness predisposes.
det.clinical: The hallmark is headache that develops on sitting or standing and settles on lying flat, but over months this pattern may blur into daily headache or only late-day headache. Hearing change, tinnitus, neck pain, nausea and cranial nerve palsies (especially sixth) occur. Severe brain sagging produces a frontotemporal-type behavioural syndrome, daytime sleepiness, gait problems or even coma, and long-standing ventral leaks cause superficial siderosis with deafness and ataxia. Rebound intracranial hypertension can appear after successful treatment.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 requires headache attributed to low CSF pressure (opening pressure below 60 mm CSF) and/or imaging evidence of a CSF leak, with no recent dural puncture explaining it. Brain MRI is abnormal in most but can be normal, especially with CSF-venous fistulas. Spinal imaging decides leak type: extradural fluid indicates a dural tear, while fistulas need specialised decubitus myelography or photon-counting CT. Avoid misdiagnosing tonsillar descent as Chiari I malformation.
det.treatment: Initial bed rest, hydration, caffeine and analgesia help some, but many need an epidural blood patch — non-targeted large-volume lumbar or thoracic patches are commonly first, then targeted patches or fibrin glue once the leak is found. Persistent ventral or lateral tears may need surgical repair; CSF-venous fistulas respond well to transvenous embolisation or surgical ligation. Subdural collections usually resolve when the leak is sealed — draining them alone risks worsening the sagging. Warn about rebound high-pressure headache, which often responds to acetazolamide.
det.prognosis: Most patients improve with patching or leak repair, but a proportion have persistent or recurrent leaks needing several procedures.
pearls: Ask 'Is it better lying flat?' — the key question in any new daily headache.
Pachymeningeal enhancement + sagging + subdural fluid = intracranial hypotension pattern.
Never decompress a 'Chiari' with brain sagging and dural enhancement — seal the leak instead.
Normal opening pressure does not exclude SIH.
det.thd: SIH คือภาวะน้ำไขสันหลังรั่วจากช่องไขสันหลังเองโดยไม่มีการเจาะหลังนำมาก่อน ทำให้สมองย้อยลงเมื่อลุกขึ้น อาการเด่นคือปวดศีรษะเมื่อนั่งหรือยืนและหายเมื่อนอนราบ อาจมีปวดคอ หูอื้อ เสียงในหู MRI พบเยื่อดูราจับสีหนา สมองย้อย และเลือด/น้ำคั่งใต้ดูรา ความดันน้ำไขสันหลังอาจปกติ ตรวจหาจุดรั่วด้วย MRI ไขสันหลังหรือ myelography รักษาด้วย epidural blood patch ถ้าไม่หายพิจารณาผ่าตัดซ่อมหรืออุดหลอดเลือดดำในกรณี CSF-venous fistula

qx.stem: A 39-year-old male badminton coach from Khon Kaen has three weeks of headache that comes on within minutes of standing and settles when lying down, with neck stiffness and muffled hearing. There was no lumbar puncture or trauma. MRI shows diffuse smooth pachymeningeal enhancement, venous sinus engorgement and brain sagging. Spinal MRI shows no extradural fluid collection.
qx.q: If conservative measures fail, what should be done next?
opts: Targeted or non-targeted epidural blood patch, with dynamic CT/digital subtraction myelography in lateral decubitus position to look for a CSF-venous fistula if symptoms persist
Ventriculoperitoneal shunt
Repeated lumbar punctures to measure opening pressure
Long-term topiramate as for chronic migraine
Dural biopsy for suspected pachymeningitis
qx.why: Orthostatic headache with pachymeningeal enhancement, venous distension and brain sag indicate spontaneous intracranial hypotension; the Bern score estimates the likelihood of a leak. A blood patch is the usual first intervention. When spinal MRI shows no epidural collection, a CSF-venous fistula is common and is best found with decubitus dynamic myelography, then treated by transvenous embolisation or surgery. Lumbar punctures worsen the leak, and biopsy is unnecessary for this typical pattern.

name: Low-grade gliomas
formal: Slow-growing gliomas (WHO grade 1 or 2) such as pilocytic astrocytoma and diffuse astrocytoma, often presenting with seizures, with variable behaviour.
simple: Slow-growing brain tumours that often cause seizures and may progress over years.
th: เนื้องอก glioma ที่โตช้า (WHO grade 1–2) มักทำให้ชักก่อนแล้วตรวจร่างกายปกติ ต้องจัดกลุ่มตามชีววิทยา (IDH, 1p/19q) การรักษาคือผ่าตัดให้มากที่สุดเท่าที่ปลอดภัย แล้วพิจารณารังสีและเคมีบำบัดหรือยา vorasidenib
tempoNote: Seizures or subtle cognitive change for months to years; slow growth, with risk of progression to higher grade over years
feat: Seizures are the presenting symptom in a large majority, often with a normal neurological examination
Cortical, temporal and insular tumours are the most epileptogenic; oligodendroglial tumours especially
Young adults are most often affected; deficits and raised pressure appear later
T2/FLAIR hyperintense, usually non-enhancing mass with little oedema; calcification suggests oligodendroglioma
Behaviour is variable: some stay stable for years, others transform to a higher grade
inv: MRI with and without contrast, with spectroscopy or perfusion when the lesion is ambiguous
Tissue diagnosis with IDH mutation, 1p/19q codeletion, ATRX, TP53 and CDKN2A testing (WHO 2021 classification)
Video-EEG for tumour-related epilepsy before surgery, and neuropsychology for baseline function

case.story: Three episodes of a rising stomach sensation and sudden loss of words lasting a minute, followed by a generalised convulsion once. She is otherwise well.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination.
case.tests: MRI shows a non-enhancing left temporal FLAIR hyperintense lesion; video-EEG shows left temporal interictal spikes; biopsy shows IDH-mutant astrocytoma, grade 2.
case.q: What are the treatment priorities, and why is earlier surgery relevant for seizures?
case.a: Maximal safe resection with adjuvant therapy according to risk, and antiseizure treatment; shorter epilepsy duration before surgery is linked to better seizure freedom.

det.patho: Low-grade gliomas are infiltrating glial tumours with slow growth, now classified molecularly: IDH-mutant astrocytoma, IDH-mutant 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendroglioma, and circumscribed paediatric tumours such as pilocytic astrocytoma. Their epileptogenicity arises from an interplay of cortical location, the tumour's effects on adjacent cortex, glutamate and chloride dysregulation, and a peritumoral environment. Slow growth gives time for network remodelling without major tissue destruction.
det.clinical: More than 80% of patients with a low-grade glioma have seizures, which may be focal with preserved awareness, focal impaired awareness or secondarily generalised. Young patients commonly have normal examinations at diagnosis. Tumours in the temporal and insular regions often cause limbic seizures, while tumours in eloquent cortex may produce subtle language or executive change. Up to half of tumour-related epilepsies become drug-resistant, and growth or transformation can bring headache, deficits and worsening seizures.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows a diffusely infiltrating, mostly non-enhancing T2/FLAIR lesion. Final diagnosis needs tissue with integrated molecular testing under the WHO 2021 system, since IDH status and 1p/19q codeletion determine behaviour and treatment. Video-EEG with ictal recording is recommended before surgery to define the epileptogenic zone, which can extend beyond the visible lesion. Rapid growth, contrast enhancement or new deficits should prompt re-imaging for progression.
det.treatment: Maximal safe resection, guided by awake mapping where needed, is the cornerstone. Higher-risk patients receive radiotherapy with chemotherapy (PCV or temozolomide), and the IDH inhibitor vorasidenib has been shown to delay progression in grade 2 IDH-mutant glioma after surgery. Antiseizure drugs without strong enzyme induction, such as levetiracetam, lamotrigine or lacosamide, are preferred to avoid interactions with chemotherapy. Early resection of epileptogenic tumours and extending resection into epileptogenic cortex improve seizure freedom.
det.prognosis: Median survival ranges from many years in oligodendroglioma to shorter in IDH-mutant astrocytoma, with progression to higher grade over time.
pearls: New adult-onset focal seizures with a normal examination still need MRI.
Molecular markers now define diagnosis and prognosis, not histology alone.
Choose antiseizure drugs with few chemotherapy interactions.
det.thd: Low-grade glioma เป็นเนื้องอก glia ที่โตช้า พบบ่อยในคนอายุน้อยและมักเริ่มด้วยอาการชักโดยตรวจร่างกายปกติ MRI พบรอยโรค T2/FLAIR สูงและมักไม่ติดสารทึบแสง การวินิจฉัยต้องใช้ชิ้นเนื้อและตรวจ IDH กับ 1p/19q การรักษาคือผ่าตัดให้มากที่สุดเท่าที่ปลอดภัย แล้วพิจารณารังสีและเคมีบำบัดหรือยา vorasidenib ใน IDH-mutant grade 2 ควรเลือกยากันชักที่ไม่รบกวนเคมีบำบัด เช่น levetiracetam

Cortical malformation with transmantle sign and no mass effect
Cystic and solid temporal tumour in children and young adults, often with calcification

name: Low-grade glioneuronal tumours
formal: Group of low-grade neuroepithelial tumours, such as DNET and ganglioglioma, typically in children and young adults with temporal lobe epilepsy and indolent course.
simple: Slow-growing brain tumours made of mixed cell types, often causing seizures in young people.
th: กลุ่มเนื้องอกเกรดต่ำที่ประกอบด้วยเซลล์ประสาทและ/หรือเซลล์เกลีย เช่น ganglioglioma, DNET, desmoplastic infantile ganglioglioma และ PLNTY เป็นสาเหตุสำคัญของโรคลมชักดื้อยาในเด็กและคนหนุ่มสาว ผ่าตัดแล้วหายชักได้มาก
tempoNote: Seizure history of years before diagnosis; infantile desmoplastic variants present within months with a rapidly enlarging head
feat: Group name for low-grade epilepsy-associated tumours (LEAT): ganglioglioma, gangliocytoma, DNET, desmoplastic infantile ganglioglioma/astrocytoma, central neurocytoma, cerebellar liponeurocytoma, papillary glioneuronal tumour, PLNTY
About 6 percent of surgically treated intracranial tumours in the source series; the temporal lobe is the usual site
Typical story: focal drug-resistant epilepsy starting in childhood, with a normal examination
Desmoplastic infantile tumours present in the first year with a bulging fontanelle, sunset eyes and large head circumference
Many carry MAPK-pathway alterations (BRAF V600E, FGFR1, FGFR2/3 fusions), which allow targeted treatment
inv: High-resolution MRI with epilepsy protocol (FLAIR, T2, volumetrics) looking for cortical mass, pseudocysts and associated cortical dysplasia
Video-EEG and neuropsychological evaluation; invasive EEG in selected patients
Pathology with CD34, synaptophysin, NeuN, BRAF V600E and molecular panels; DNA methylation profiling for ambiguous cases
Post-operative MRI and long-term seizure diary

case.story: Since age 5, nocturnal focal seizures with right arm clonic movement, 3-4 per week, unresponsive to valproate and levetiracetam.
case.exam: Normal examination; school performance slipping.
case.tests: MRI shows a well-circumscribed non-enhancing cortical lesion in the left precentral region with cystic components. Resection with intraoperative mapping: ganglioglioma, grade 1, BRAF V600E positive.
case.q: Why is early surgery recommended for these tumours despite their benign behaviour?
case.a: Because long-standing seizures impair cognition and development, and complete resection with the epileptogenic zone gives seizure freedom in 80-85% and avoids lifelong medicines.

det.patho: Low-grade glioneuronal tumours share neuronal (and sometimes glial) differentiation, slow growth and a strong tendency to cause epilepsy. The group includes ganglioglioma, gangliocytoma, desmoplastic infantile ganglioglioma/astrocytoma, DNET, central neurocytoma, cerebellar liponeurocytoma and the newer entities PLNTY (a polymorphous, low-grade neuroepithelial tumour seen in young people) and diffuse glioneuronal tumour with oligodendroglioma-like features and nuclear clusters (DGONC). Most are CNS WHO grade 1 and many harbour alterations in the MAPK pathway such as BRAF V600E or FGFR family changes.
det.clinical: Children and young adults have seizures that are focal in onset and refractory, often with a normal examination. Tumours in infants can cause head enlargement, and infratentorial and spinal tumours cause deficits. Cognitive and behavioural effects result from the seizures. Malignant change is uncommon and associated with ganglioglioma and a few other types.
det.diagnosis: MRI of the cortex combined with EEG localises the epileptogenic zone. Histology plus immunohistochemistry (CD34, BRAF V600E, synaptophysin) identifies the entity. Associated cortical dysplasia (focal cortical dysplasia type IIIb) is common and affects surgical planning. Molecular profiling is increasingly used because overlapping features lead to misclassification.
det.treatment: Surgery aims at complete tumour resection and, when indicated, removal of the surrounding epileptogenic cortex; seizure freedom occurs in about 80-85 percent. Surgery should not be delayed after failure of two appropriate antiseizure drugs. Observation is reasonable for small, asymptomatic lesions. Adjuvant therapy is withheld except for anaplastic or inoperable tumours; BRAF and MEK inhibitors are options for BRAF-mutant recurrences.
det.prognosis: Excellent: low recurrence and mortality, and good quality of life when seizures are controlled.
pearls: Drug-resistant focal epilepsy with a temporal cortical lesion in a young person: LEAT until proved otherwise.
Complete resection plus epileptogenic cortex removal gives the best seizure outcomes; delay costs cognition.
Immunostain for CD34 and BRAF V600E points toward ganglioglioma and PXA.
det.thd: Low-grade glioneuronal tumours คือกลุ่มเนื้องอกเกรดต่ำที่มีเซลล์ประสาทและเซลล์เกลีย เช่น ganglioglioma, DNET, DIG และ PLNTY ผู้ป่วยมักเป็นเด็กหรือวัยรุ่นที่ชักเฉพาะที่เรื้อรังและดื้อต่อยากันชัก MRI พบรอยโรคที่เปลือกสมอง และชิ้นเนื้อย้อม CD34 หรือ BRAF V600E การผ่าตัดเอาก้อนและบริเวณที่เป็นต้นกำเนิดชักออกให้หมดทำให้ผู้ป่วยกว่า 80% หายชัก โดยทั่วไปไม่ต้องใช้รังสีหรือเคมีบำบัด

name: Lower extremity neuropathy
formal: Peripheral nerve disorder affecting the lower limb, such as sciatic, peroneal, tibial, femoral or lateral femoral cutaneous lesions, causing focal weakness, sensory loss and often pain.
simple: Damage to a nerve in the leg that causes weakness, numbness or pain, for example foot drop.
more: Localised by examination and electrodiagnostic studies, with imaging for compressive or mass causes. Treatment targets the cause, such as decompression, bracing or physiotherapy.
th: ความผิดปกติของเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายที่ขา เช่น sciatic, peroneal, tibial, femoral หรือ lateral femoral cutaneous ทำให้อ่อนแรง ชา และปวดเฉพาะที่
tempoNote: Acute after compression, injury or injection; chronic with entrapment
feat: Common peroneal at fibular head: foot drop, sensory loss on dorsum of foot, inversion preserved
Sciatic: foot drop plus weak plantar flexion and knee flexion, absent ankle jerk
Femoral: weak knee extension, absent knee jerk, anterior thigh numbness
Lateral femoral cutaneous (meralgia paraesthetica): burning outer thigh, no weakness
Tibial at tarsal tunnel: sole burning and numbness
inv: NCS/EMG to localise and grade, including paraspinal muscles to exclude radiculopathy
Nerve ultrasound or MRI to find compression, mass or haematoma
Glucose/HbA1c and vasculitis screen when multiple nerves or pain

case.who: 30-year-old male rice farmer from Sakon Nakhon
case.story: After a long day squatting to plant rice and recent 8 kg weight loss, he woke up with a floppy right foot.
case.exam: Weak ankle dorsiflexion and eversion, normal inversion and plantar flexion, numb first web space and dorsum of foot, normal reflexes.
case.tests: NCS: conduction block in the peroneal nerve across the fibular head; EMG normal in tibialis posterior and paraspinals.
case.q: Where is the lesion and what is the management?
case.a: Common peroneal neuropathy at the fibular head from squatting and weight loss; avoid squatting and leg crossing, ankle-foot orthosis, expect recovery in weeks to months.

det.patho: Leg nerves are vulnerable where they are superficial or tethered, such as the common peroneal nerve winding around the fibular neck and the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve under the inguinal ligament. Compression, stretch, haematoma, injection injury, diabetes, vasculitis and tumours can damage them. Mild injury causes demyelinating conduction block that recovers quickly; axonal loss recovers slowly.
det.clinical: This is an umbrella term, not a single disease. The key is to recognise the nerve territory and separate it from root or plexus disease. Foot drop is the commonest presentation; checking inversion (tibial nerve, L5) and the ankle jerk distinguishes peroneal, sciatic and L5 causes. Pain suggests vasculitis, diabetes or a mass lesion.
det.diagnosis: Detailed muscle-by-muscle examination and sensory mapping localise the lesion. NCS and EMG confirm localisation, show demyelinating or axonal injury and give prognosis. Ultrasound and MRI identify compressive lesions such as ganglion cysts or tumours. Multiple mononeuropathies require a vasculitis and diabetes work-up.
det.treatment: Remove the cause: avoid crossing legs, squatting or tight casts; decompress or excise masses; treat diabetes. Ankle-foot orthoses prevent falls while recovering. Neuropathic pain can be treated with gabapentinoids, duloxetine or amitriptyline. Surgery is considered for persistent entrapment or nerve injury without recovery after 3–6 months.
det.prognosis: Compressive conduction block usually recovers within weeks to months; severe axonal injury recovers slowly and incompletely.
pearls: Foot drop with weak inversion is L5 or sciatic, not peroneal.
Weight loss and squatting are classic peroneal risks in agricultural workers.
Meralgia paraesthetica never causes weakness or reflex loss.
det.thd: Lower extremity neuropathy เป็นคำรวมของโรคเส้นประสาทเดี่ยวที่ขา เช่น peroneal ที่หัวกระดูก fibula ทำให้ปลายเท้าตก sciatic femoral และ meralgia paraesthetica การวินิจฉัยใช้การตรวจกล้ามเนื้อทีละมัด เช่น การบิดเท้าเข้า (inversion) เพื่อแยกจาก L5 radiculopathy ร่วมกับ NCS/EMG และภาพถ่าย รักษาโดยกำจัดสาเหตุการกดทับ ใส่อุปกรณ์พยุงข้อเท้า และผ่าตัดในบางราย

ddx.pt: Commonest leg mononeuropathy; inversion spared unlike L5 radiculopathy
Several nerve territories in one leg, often painful, paraspinal EMG normal

name: Lower motor neuron lesions
formal: Damage to anterior horn cells or peripheral axons, with weakness, atrophy, fasciculations and hypotonia, areflexia; causes include ALS, polyneuropathy and radiculopathy.
simple: Damage to the nerves that connect the spinal cord to muscles, causing weak, thin muscles and twitching.
th: กลุ่มอาการจากความเสียหายของเซลล์ประสาทสั่งการส่วนล่างหรือแอกซอน ได้แก่ อ่อนแรง กล้ามเนื้อลีบ กระตุกเป็นมัด (fasciculation) กล้ามเนื้อตึงน้อยลงและรีเฟลกซ์ลดหรือหายไป ใช้ตำแหน่งแยกว่ามาจาก anterior horn, root, plexus หรือ nerve
tempoNote: Depends on cause: hours to days for trauma or Guillain-Barre, weeks to months for motor neuron disease and compressive roots, years for inherited forms
feat: Weakness in a segmental, root, nerve or distal pattern, with early wasting of the affected muscles
Fasciculations (visible twitches) and cramps, most informative when found in clinically weak or wasted muscle
Reduced tone and depressed or absent tendon reflexes in the affected segment
No spasticity and no Babinski response unless an upper motor neuron lesion coexists
Sensory loss points to root, plexus or nerve; a pure motor picture points to anterior horn cell, motor neuropathy or neuromuscular junction
inv: Nerve conduction studies and needle EMG to place the lesion and to show active denervation with reinnervation
MRI of the spine or plexus when a root, cord or plexus lesion is suspected
Targeted blood tests and genetics (CK, glucose, antibodies, SMN1 or androgen receptor testing) guided by the pattern

case.story: Eight months of cramps and a weak right hand: he drops his keys and cannot press the car horn firmly. His wife has noticed twitching in his thigh at night.
case.exam: Wasting of right thenar and first dorsal interosseous, fasciculations in both arms and a thigh, reduced reflexes in the right arm, brisk knee jerks, normal sensation.
case.tests: EMG shows widespread active denervation with large chronic motor units in cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions; sensory nerve action potentials are normal; no conduction block.
case.q: Are upper motor neuron signs also present, and which mimics must be excluded before settling on a diagnosis?
case.a: The brisk knee jerks mean upper motor neuron signs coexist, so this is more than a pure LMN syndrome and fits amyotrophic lateral sclerosis; mimics to exclude include multifocal motor neuropathy, cervical root or cord disease, Kennedy disease and adult SMA.
