det.patho: A lower motor neuron lesion interrupts the final common pathway from the anterior horn cell through the root, plexus and peripheral nerve to the muscle. Denervated muscle fibres lose trophic input and atrophy, while unstable surviving motor units discharge spontaneously and appear as fasciculations. Loss of the efferent limb of the stretch reflex explains the hypotonia and areflexia.
det.clinical: The key bedside task is to decide where along the pathway the lesion sits. Anterior horn disease gives asymmetric, painless weakness with fasciculation and no sensory loss, and often spreads between segments. Root lesions follow a dermatomal and myotomal pattern with pain, while plexus lesions cross root and nerve territories. Peripheral nerve lesions follow one nerve or a distal length-dependent pattern with sensory symptoms. Upper motor neuron signs appearing alongside lower motor neuron signs in the same region are the hallmark of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
det.diagnosis: Start with the pattern of weakness, reflexes and sensation, then use EMG and nerve conduction studies to separate neuronopathy, radiculopathy, plexopathy, neuropathy and muscle disease. Normal sensory potentials with widespread denervation suggest a motor neuron disorder, whereas conduction block on motor studies suggests multifocal motor neuropathy. MRI of the relevant segment and targeted blood or genetic tests complete the work-up. The El Escorial and related criteria are used for motor neuron disease and require exclusion of mimics.
det.treatment: Management follows the cause: surgical or conservative treatment for compressive root and nerve lesions, immunotherapy for conduction-block neuropathies and Guillain-Barre syndrome, and riluzole or other disease-modifying options plus multidisciplinary care in motor neuron disease. Supportive measures include physiotherapy, orthoses for foot or wrist drop, cramp management and monitoring of breathing and swallowing. Early recognition of treatable mimics is the main therapeutic goal.
det.prognosis: Varies widely from full recovery after a compressed nerve is released to relentless progression in motor neuron disease.
pearls: Fasciculations in strong, normal-looking muscle are usually benign; in weak, wasted muscle they are pathological.
A pure LMN picture with asymmetric hand weakness and conduction block is multifocal motor neuropathy until proved otherwise, because it is treatable.
Brisk reflexes in a wasted limb are a clue to ALS rather than neuropathy.
det.thd: Lower motor neuron lesion คือความเสียหายตั้งแต่เซลล์ประสาทสั่งการใน anterior horn ผ่าน root, plexus จนถึงเส้นประสาทส่วนปลาย ทำให้กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง ลีบ กระตุกเป็นมัด และรีเฟลกซ์ลดลง ต่างจาก upper motor neuron ที่เกร็งและรีเฟลกซ์ไว การตรวจ EMG และ nerve conduction ช่วยบอกตำแหน่งและแยกโรคที่รักษาได้ เช่น multifocal motor neuropathy ออกจาก ALS การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ ร่วมกับกายภาพบำบัดและการดูแลการหายใจและการกลืน

name: Lower-half/lower-body parkinsonism
formal: Gait disorder with parkinsonism mainly in the legs and relatively preserved arms, usually from vascular disease or normal pressure hydrocephalus, with poor levodopa response.
simple: Shuffling, short-stepped walking with stiff legs but a relatively normal upper body, often from small vessel disease.
more: Vascular parkinsonism with gait freezing, short shuffling steps and postural instability but relatively preserved arm function, usually from subcortical small-vessel ischaemia. MRI shows widespread white matter lesions or lacunes. Response to levodopa is poor; manage vascular risk factors and use physiotherapy.
th: parkinsonism ที่เด่นที่ขา เดินซอยเท้า ก้าวสั้น ฐานกว้าง แต่แขนค่อนข้างปกติ มักเกิดจากโรคหลอดเลือดสมองเล็กหรือ NPH และตอบสนองต่อ levodopa ไม่ดี
tempoNote: Insidious progression, sometimes with stepwise worsening
feat: Short-stepped, broad-based, shuffling gait with start hesitation and freezing
Arm swing and upper-limb dexterity relatively preserved
Rest tremor usually absent
Often coexisting cognitive slowing and urinary urgency
Poor or modest levodopa response
inv: MRI: extensive white matter disease, lacunes, or ventriculomegaly
DAT SPECT usually normal or only mildly abnormal
CSF tap test if NPH is considered

case.who: 76-year-old retired policeman from Nakhon Si Thammarat with hypertension and diabetes
case.story: Two years of slow shuffling walking and frequent near-falls; hands work normally.
case.exam: Short steps, wide base, freezing at doorways, normal arm swing, no rest tremor, mild leg rigidity.
case.tests: MRI: extensive confluent white matter lesions and basal ganglia lacunes; levodopa trial gives little benefit.
case.q: What is the diagnosis?
case.a: Lower-body (vascular) parkinsonism due to cerebral small vessel disease.

det.patho: Damage to frontal-subcortical white matter and basal ganglia circuits controlling gait, usually from small vessel disease, disconnects motor planning regions from brainstem locomotor centres. Nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons are largely spared, explaining the poor levodopa response.
det.clinical: Patients have a frontal-type gait disorder resembling parkinsonism but confined to the legs. They may have pseudobulbar features, pyramidal signs, urinary urgency and executive dysfunction. Onset may be insidious or follow a stroke. Falls are frequent.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by MRI evidence of substantial cerebrovascular disease. Normal DAT imaging supports a non-degenerative cause. NPH should be considered when ventricles look larger than the degree of atrophy would explain. A levodopa trial is worthwhile because some patients have mixed pathology.
det.treatment: Levodopa trial (adequate dose for several weeks) is reasonable. Physiotherapy with gait training and cueing, fall prevention and walking aids are central. Vascular risk factor control may slow progression. Shunting is considered if NPH is confirmed.
det.prognosis: Gradual progression with increasing falls and dependency; partial improvement with rehabilitation.
pearls: Legs worse than arms, no tremor, poor levodopa response: think vascular parkinsonism.
Look for ventriculomegaly; NPH is the treatable mimic.
Always try levodopa properly before concluding non-response.
det.thd: Lower-body parkinsonism คือ parkinsonism ที่เด่นที่ขา เดินซอยเท้า ก้าวสั้น ขาติด แต่แขนเคลื่อนไหวค่อนข้างปกติและไม่มีอาการสั่นขณะพัก มักเกิดจากหลอดเลือดสมองเล็กเสื่อม หรือ NPH ตอบสนองต่อ levodopa ไม่ดี การรักษาคือทดลอง levodopa กายภาพบำบัด ป้องกันการหกล้ม และคุมปัจจัยเสี่ยงหลอดเลือด

name: Lowe’s syndrome
formal: X-linked oculocerebrorenal syndrome from OCRL mutation, with congenital cataracts, hypotonia, intellectual disability and renal tubular dysfunction.
simple: An inherited disorder in boys causing cataracts, weak muscles, learning problems and kidney trouble.
th: โรค oculocerebrorenal ที่ถ่ายทอดทางโครโมโซม X จากยีน OCRL ในเด็กชาย มีต้อกระจกแต่กำเนิด กล้ามเนื้อตึงตัวต่ำ พัฒนาการช้า และไตเสีย Fanconi
tempoNote: Present from birth; kidney tubular disease and neurological problems evolve through childhood
feat: Bilateral congenital cataracts in a boy, often with glaucoma
Marked neonatal hypotonia with absent tendon reflexes and delayed motor milestones
Intellectual disability with tantrums and stereotyped behaviour
Renal Fanconi syndrome with low-molecular-weight proteinuria, aminoaciduria, phosphate loss and rickets
X-linked inheritance; carrier mothers show lens opacities
inv: Urine for low-molecular-weight proteins, amino acids, phosphate and calcium; bicarbonate and phosphate in serum
Slit-lamp examination of the boy and his mother
OCRL sequencing; MRI may show periventricular cysts or white matter change

case.story: Born with dense cataracts, floppy, not sitting; referred for poor growth and bone deformity.
case.exam: Cloudy lenses, generalised hypotonia, absent knee jerks, rachitic wrist widening.
case.tests: Urine shows proteinuria with generalised aminoaciduria, low serum phosphate, alkaline phosphatase raised; OCRL hemizygous variant.
case.q: Which two organs explain the combination, and how is it inherited?
case.a: Lens, brain and kidney tubules via OCRL deficiency (Lowe syndrome); X-linked recessive, so the mother is likely a carrier.

det.patho: OCRL encodes an inositol polyphosphate 5-phosphatase that regulates phosphoinositide metabolism, vesicle trafficking and actin dynamics. Its loss disturbs lens development, endocytosis in proximal renal tubule cells and neuronal function. The condition is X-linked recessive and affects mainly males.
det.clinical: Cataracts are noted at birth and glaucoma may follow. Infants are very hypotonic with poor reflexes, then show developmental delay, seizures in some and behavioural difficulty. Tubular acidosis, phosphate wasting and rickets evolve over the first years, and kidney function slowly deteriorates. Dent disease 2 is a milder allelic disorder with renal but little eye or brain involvement.
det.diagnosis: Suspect in a hypotonic boy with congenital cataracts. Supporting findings are tubular proteinuria and generalised aminoaciduria; confirmation is by OCRL testing or reduced enzyme activity in fibroblasts. Check the mother by slit lamp and genetic testing for counselling. Exclude peroxisomal, mitochondrial and congenital infection causes.
det.treatment: Care is multidisciplinary: early cataract surgery with glaucoma control, replacement of bicarbonate, phosphate and vitamin D to treat acidosis and rickets, and physical, speech and behavioural therapy. Antiseizure treatment is used when required. Monitor kidney function and plan for progression to renal replacement therapy in adulthood.
det.prognosis: Survival is shortened, commonly into the third or fourth decade, mainly because of kidney failure or infection; the degree of cognitive impairment differs between patients.
pearls: Cataracts plus hypotonia in a boy should prompt urine amino acid testing.
Check the mother's lenses for carrier detection.
Renal Fanconi in the context of brain and eye disease equals OCRL until shown otherwise.
det.thd: Lowe syndrome หรือ oculocerebrorenal syndrome เกิดจากยีน OCRL บนโครโมโซม X ในเด็กชาย มีต้อกระจกตั้งแต่เกิด กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง พัฒนาการช้า และไตเสียแบบ Fanconi ทำให้รั่วโปรตีนและกรดอะมิโน กระดูกอ่อน ตรวจปัสสาวะ ตรวจตา และยีน OCRL รักษาตามอาการ ผ่าตัดต้อ เสริมฟอสเฟตและวิตามินดี และให้คำปรึกษาครอบครัว

name: Lumbar arachnoiditis
formal: Inflammation or scarring of the lumbar arachnoid membrane, after surgery, infection or contrast, causing chronic pain, radiculopathy and cauda equina symptoms with clumped nerve roots on MRI.
simple: Scarring around the nerves of the lower spine that causes chronic back and leg pain and weakness.
th: การอักเสบและพังผืดของเยื่ออะแร็กนอยด์บริเวณเอว หลังผ่าตัด ติดเชื้อ หรือฉีดสาร ทำให้ปวดเรื้อรังและรากประสาทจับกลุ่มกันใน MRI
tempoNote: Develops months to years after the insult (surgery, infection, intrathecal agents, haemorrhage) and then persists
feat: Constant burning low back and leg pain, often in several root territories and worse with activity
Patchy sensory loss, reflex changes and weakness affecting more than one lumbosacral root
Bladder, bowel or sexual dysfunction in more severe scarring
History of repeated spine surgery, epidural or intrathecal procedures, old myelography with oil contrast, meningitis or SAH
inv: MRI lumbar spine: roots clumped centrally or stuck to the dural wall ('empty sac'), or an intrathecal soft-tissue mass
CT may show intradural calcification in the ossifying form
EMG/NCS to document multiple chronic radiculopathies and exclude other neuropathy

case.story: After three lumbar operations over ten years he has unremitting burning pain in both legs and new urinary hesitancy.
case.exam: Reduced pinprick in L4–S1 patches on both sides, absent ankle jerks, mild bilateral foot weakness.
case.tests: MRI: no recurrent disc; nerve roots glued to the thecal sac wall giving an empty-looking sac.
case.q: What is the likely cause of his symptoms, and is more surgery likely to help?
case.a: Chronic adhesive lumbar arachnoiditis; further decompression rarely helps, so management focuses on pain control and rehabilitation.

det.patho: An inflammatory reaction in the arachnoid around the cauda equina leads to fibrin deposition and collagen scarring that bind roots to one another and to the dura. Triggers include surgery, blood in the subarachnoid space, infection (including tuberculosis), and older oil-based contrast or certain intrathecal drugs. Scarring impairs root blood supply and CSF flow, and may lead to syringomyelia above the lesion.
det.clinical: Patients describe constant burning or electric leg pain, sometimes with cramps and muscle twitching, that is poorly linked to any single disc level. Neurological signs are typically multi-root and asymmetric. Sphincter problems indicate more extensive involvement. The course is chronic and usually stable rather than relentlessly progressive, though a minority worsen.
det.diagnosis: MRI is the key test: central clumping of roots, peripheral adhesion to the dura or a mass of matted roots filling the sac. Contrast helps separate it from tumour or active infection. CSF is not needed in most cases but can exclude infection or malignancy if the picture is atypical. Neurophysiology supports chronic multilevel root damage.
det.treatment: There is no cure; care is multidisciplinary pain management with neuropathic agents (gabapentinoids, duloxetine, tricyclics), physiotherapy and psychological support. Spinal cord stimulation is used in selected patients. Repeat decompressive surgery or adhesiolysis has disappointing results and may worsen scarring. Treat any associated syrinx or active infection specifically.
det.prognosis: Usually a lifelong pain condition with variable disability; neurological deficits generally remain stable.
pearls: Failed back syndrome with multi-root burning pain: look for clumped roots on MRI.
More surgery is rarely the answer.
Ask about past meningitis, SAH, TB or intrathecal procedures.
det.thd: Lumbar arachnoiditis คือพังผืดของเยื่ออะแร็กนอยด์ที่รัดรากประสาทบริเวณเอว มักตามหลังผ่าตัดหลายครั้ง ติดเชื้อ เลือดออก หรือสารที่ฉีดเข้าช่องไขสันหลัง ผู้ป่วยปวดแสบร้อนที่ขาเรื้อรังหลายรากประสาท บางรายมีปัญหาปัสสาวะ MRI เห็นรากประสาทจับกลุ่มหรือติดผนัง dura การรักษาเน้นควบคุมปวดและฟื้นฟู การผ่าตัดซ้ำมักไม่ช่วย

name: Lumbar disc disease
formal: Degenerative lumbar disc herniation or degeneration with radiculopathy or cauda equina syndrome, causing back pain, sciatica, weakness and sphincter disturbance.
simple: Wear or bulging of discs in the lower back that can press on nerves and cause back and leg pain.
th: หมอนรองกระดูกเอวเคลื่อน (lumbar disc herniation) มักเกิดที่ L4–5 และ L5–S1 กดรากประสาทที่ผ่านลงมา ทำให้ปวดหลังร้าวลงขา (sciatica) ชา และอ่อนแรงตามราก ตรวจ straight leg raise และ crossed SLR ส่วนใหญ่หายได้ภายใน 6–12 สัปดาห์ ผ่าตัดเมื่อปวดรุนแรงนานเกินไป อ่อนแรงมากขึ้น หรือ cauda equina syndrome ซึ่งเป็นภาวะฉุกเฉิน
tempoNote: Often acute after lifting; most radicular pain improves over weeks to three months
feat: Most herniations are posterolateral at L4–5 or L5–S1 and compress the traversing root one level below the disc (L4–5 disc compresses L5; L5–S1 disc compresses S1); far-lateral discs compress the exiting root instead (L4 at L4–5)
Leg pain usually exceeds back pain and follows a dermatome; true sciatica below the knee is highly sensitive for a clinically relevant disc, so its absence makes a disc herniation unlikely
Straight leg raise reproduces leg pain below 60° (sensitive but not specific); a crossed SLR is much more specific; femoral stretch test points to the upper lumbar roots
Motor, sensory and reflex deficit in the affected root; weakness is often milder than the patient's complaint of pain
A massive central herniation can cause cauda equina syndrome: urinary retention or overflow, saddle anaesthesia, bilateral leg symptoms and sexual and bowel dysfunction
inv: MRI lumbar spine for severe or progressive deficit, red flags, or persistent radicular pain beyond about 6 weeks; image only if the result would change management
Emergency MRI for suspected cauda equina syndrome, with bladder scan for post-void residual
EMG for uncertain level or to separate root from plexus or peripheral lesions; CT or myelography when MRI is contraindicated

case.who: 36-year-old male dock worker from Laem Chabang
case.story: He felt a pop in the back while lifting a sack, followed by severe pain from the right buttock down the back of the leg to the outer foot; coughing worsens it.
case.exam: Right SLR positive at 40 degrees with crossed SLR positive; weak plantarflexion and absent ankle jerk, numbness of the lateral foot; normal saddle sensation and anal tone.
case.tests: MRI shows a large right paracentral L5–S1 extrusion compressing S1, with no cauda equina compression; post-void residual 30 mL.
case.q: Is urgent surgery needed and what counselling is appropriate?
case.a: S1 radiculopathy from L5–S1 disc extrusion without cauda equina features. Initial conservative care with analgesia, staying active and physiotherapy; surgery if disabling pain persists after about 6–12 weeks or weakness progresses, and immediate review if bladder or saddle symptoms appear.

det.patho: Degeneration of the annulus (desiccation, fissures, tears) allows the nucleus pulposus to protrude or extrude into the canal, most often posterolaterally, since the midline part of the posterior longitudinal ligament is the thickest and strongest. The herniation compresses the root as it passes through the lateral recess on its way to the foramen of the next level down, and inflammatory mediators from disc material cause chemical radiculitis. Herniated fragments often shrink spontaneously through resorption. Large central herniations compress several roots of the cauda equina.
det.clinical: Sciatica radiates from the buttock into the leg below the knee, worse with sitting, coughing or straining, and associated with paraesthesia in the root dermatome. Nerve root tension signs and the neurological findings by root (L5: foot dorsiflexion and great toe extension weakness, dorsum numbness; S1: plantarflexion weakness, absent ankle jerk, lateral foot numbness) establish the level. Bladder symptoms such as frequency, nocturia or retention can occur and may be the only complaint in a few patients. Cauda equina syndrome is rare but must always be asked about, and a thorough examination of saddle sensation and anal tone is mandatory in a patient with severe or bilateral symptoms.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is mainly clinical, with MRI used for severe or progressive deficit, red flags or persistent symptoms and interpreted alongside the findings because asymptomatic herniations occur. Reduced ankle jerk and weak plantarflexion indicate S1; weak dorsiflexion and great toe extension indicate L5. Straight leg raise is sensitive but unspecific, while crossed SLR and a matching dermatomal sensory loss increase confidence. Consider other causes if sciatica is absent, if there are systemic features, or if pain is present at rest and at night.
det.treatment: Avoid bed rest. Use analgesics (paracetamol, short courses of NSAIDs), activity as tolerated, physiotherapy and, for persistent radicular pain, neuropathic agents or epidural steroid injection for short-term relief. Randomised trials show that surgical discectomy speeds recovery compared with prolonged conservative care, but long-term results are similar, so surgery is offered when radicular pain remains severe after about 6–12 weeks, for progressive weakness or intolerable pain, and as an emergency for cauda equina syndrome, ideally decompressed urgently, no later than 24–48 hours from onset. Recurrence at the same level occurs in about 6% of surgical patients.
det.prognosis: Most radicular symptoms improve within 3 months; back pain responds less well to surgery than leg pain.
pearls: Ask every sciatica patient about bladder, bowel and saddle sensation.
Without sciatica, a disc herniation is an unlikely cause of leg symptoms; consider stenosis, hip or vascular disease.
Crossed straight leg raise is the most specific bedside sign of a disc herniation.
det.thd: หมอนรองกระดูกเอวเคลื่อนมักเกิดที่ L4–5 หรือ L5–S1 และกดรากประสาทที่ผ่านลงไปที่ระดับถัดลงมา (เช่น L5–S1 กดราก S1) ผู้ป่วยปวดหลังร้าวลงขาต่ำกว่าเข่า ชา และกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงตามราก ตรวจ SLR และ crossed SLR ใช้ MRI เมื่ออาการรุนแรงหรือไม่ดีขึ้นภายใน 6–12 สัปดาห์ ผู้ป่วยส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นด้วยการรักษาแบบไม่ผ่าตัด ผ่าตัด discectomy เมื่ออาการปวดรุนแรงนานหรืออ่อนแรงมากขึ้น และต้องผ่าตัดด่วนในภาวะ cauda equina syndrome

qx.stem: A 39-year-old construction worker from Rayong has had right sciatica for 2 weeks. This morning he noticed numbness around the anus and genitals, and he has not passed urine for 10 hours. The bladder scan shows 900 mL, the anal tone is reduced, and both ankle jerks are absent.
qx.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Oral NSAIDs and review in 6 weeks
Lumbar epidural steroid injection
Nerve conduction studies before any imaging
Urgent MRI of the lumbar spine and emergency decompression if a large central disc is confirmed
Bed rest and gabapentin for one week
qx.why: Saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention and reduced anal tone indicate cauda equina syndrome, usually from a large central disc herniation. Emergency MRI and decompression, ideally before retention becomes long-standing, give the best chance of bladder recovery. Conservative care and injections are for uncomplicated radiculopathy only.

name: Lumbar spine degenerative disease
formal: Age-related degeneration of lumbar discs, facets and ligaments causing spinal stenosis, radiculopathy and neurogenic claudication, with back pain and leg symptoms on walking.
simple: Wear and tear in the lower spine that can narrow the canal and cause pain, numbness or weakness in the legs.
th: กระดูกสันหลังส่วนเอวเสื่อม ทำให้ช่องไขสันหลังแคบ ปวดหลัง ปวดร้าวลงขา และเดินแล้วขาหนักต้องหยุดพัก
tempoNote: Gradual over years
feat: Neurogenic claudication: leg pain or heaviness on walking or standing, relieved by sitting or bending forward
Back pain, often mechanical
Often few signs at rest
Degenerative spondylolisthesis, commonly at L4–L5
Can cause multiple root involvement
inv: MRI lumbar spine
Standing flexion-extension X-rays for instability
ABI to exclude vascular claudication

case.story: Cannot walk to the market without sitting down because both legs feel heavy and numb.
case.exam: Normal foot pulses, mild bilateral ankle reflex loss.
case.tests: MRI shows severe L4–L5 central stenosis with grade 1 spondylolisthesis.
case.q: What treatment can be offered?
case.a: Physiotherapy and analgesia; decompression if function is significantly limited.

det.patho: Disc degeneration, facet arthropathy and ligamentum flavum hypertrophy reduce canal and foraminal space. Standing extension narrows the canal further and impairs nerve root blood flow.
det.clinical: Neurogenic claudication is typical; patients lean forward when walking. Radicular pain and sensory symptoms may be present. Examination is often normal at rest.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows stenosis; correlation with symptoms is essential. Exclude vascular claudication and hip disease.
det.treatment: Conservative: physiotherapy, weight loss, analgesics. Decompressive laminectomy (with fusion for instability) improves walking in selected patients.
det.prognosis: Many remain stable; surgery improves leg symptoms in most selected patients.
pearls: Uphill walking is easier than downhill in neurogenic claudication.
Cycling is tolerated better than walking because of flexed posture.
Check pulses to separate vascular claudication.
det.thd: กระดูกเอวเสื่อมทำให้ช่องไขสันหลังแคบ เดินแล้วขาหนัก ชา ต้องนั่งหรือก้มตัวจึงดีขึ้น เรียก neurogenic claudication ต้องแยกจากหลอดเลือดแดงตีบ ตรวจ MRI ยืนยัน รักษาแบบกายภาพบำบัดก่อน ผ่าตัดคลายเมื่ออาการจำกัดการใช้ชีวิต

name: Lumbosacral monoradiculopathies
formal: Single lumbosacral nerve root lesions, usually from disc herniation, producing radicular leg pain with dermatomal sensory and myotomal motor loss, for example L5 foot drop or S1 absent ankle reflex.
simple: A pinched nerve in the lower back causing leg pain, numbness, and weakness.
more: MRI and EMG confirm. Most improve with conservative care; surgery for severe or progressive deficits or cauda equina.
th: Lumbosacral monoradiculopathy คือรากประสาทเอวหรือกระเบนเหน็บถูกกดเพียงรากเดียว โดยมากจากหมอนรองกระดูกหรือรูรากประสาทตีบ มีปวดแนว dermatome ชา และอ่อนแรงตามรากนั้น เช่น L5 มีเท้าตกและ SLR positive, S1 ไม่มี ankle jerk และกล้ามเนื้อน่องอ่อนแรง การตรวจ EMG ที่มีกล้ามเนื้อกระดูกสันหลังและ sensory nerve action potential ปกติช่วยยืนยันตำแหน่ง
tempoNote: Usually acute or subacute with radicular pain; recovery over weeks to months
feat: L3 or L4: anterior thigh pain, quadriceps weakness, reduced knee jerk, medial leg numbness; femoral stretch test positive
L5: pain to the dorsum of the foot, weakness of ankle dorsiflexion, toe extension, inversion and hip abduction (foot drop with a Trendelenburg gait), reflexes largely preserved
S1: pain along the posterior leg to the lateral foot, plantarflexion weakness, absent or reduced ankle jerk, lateral foot numbness
Straight leg raise tenses mainly L5 and S1; crossed SLR is specific; a positive femoral stretch test points to L2–L4
Causes: disc herniation, lateral recess or foraminal stenosis, synovial cyst, tumour, infection, diabetic radiculopathy and herpes zoster
inv: MRI lumbar spine to match the level of compression with the clinical root, interpreted with caution because of high rates of asymptomatic findings
Needle EMG with paraspinal sampling shows denervation in a myotomal pattern after 2–3 weeks, with normal sensory nerve action potentials (the dorsal root ganglion is spared)
Glucose or HbA1c, ESR and CRP if infection, diabetes or malignancy is in question

case.story: Three weeks of pain from the right buttock down the lateral leg to the dorsum of the foot, with the foot slapping and catching on kerbs.
case.exam: Weak right ankle dorsiflexion (3/5), great toe extension (3/5), inversion (4/5) and hip abduction (4/5); numb dorsum of the foot; ankle and knee jerks present; SLR positive at 50 degrees.
case.tests: MRI shows an L4–5 right foraminal disc protrusion compressing L5; EMG shows active denervation in tibialis anterior, tibialis posterior, gluteus medius and L5 paraspinals; sural sensory response normal.
case.q: How does this differ from a common fibular neuropathy and what is the plan?
case.a: L5 radiculopathy: inversion and hip abduction weakness, back-radiating pain and paraspinal denervation distinguish it from fibular neuropathy at the knee. Conservative care for 6–12 weeks; decompression if weakness progresses or pain remains disabling.

read.where: Chapter 66 Lumbar and Thoracic Intervertebral Disc Herniation / Radiculopathy — Nerve root syndromes; Physical findings in radiculopathy

det.patho: A single root is compressed in the lateral recess or foramen, most often by a posterolateral disc herniation, an osteophyte or a facet hypertrophy; far-lateral discs affect the exiting root. Compression leads to ischaemia, demyelination and, if severe, axonal loss; inflammation around the root produces the typical radicular pain. Sensory nerve action potentials stay normal even when the dermatome is numb, since the damage lies proximal to the dorsal root ganglion.
det.clinical: Pain and sensory symptoms in a dermatome are accompanied by weakness and reflex change in muscles supplied by the root. In series of patients referred for radiating leg pain, motor loss, sensory loss and reflex change were each found in only a half or less, so a normal examination does not exclude a root lesion. Straight leg raise or femoral stretch signs and paraspinal tenderness support the diagnosis. Associated bladder symptoms or bilateral signs should prompt consideration of cauda equina.
det.diagnosis: Localise clinically using myotomal weakness, reflexes and sensory distribution, and use MRI to confirm a concordant lesion. EMG helps in uncertain cases: a root pattern requires abnormalities in muscles of one root supplied by different peripheral nerves plus paraspinal denervation, with normal sensory potentials. Reduced ankle jerk and weak plantarflexion indicate S1; ankle inversion and hip abduction weakness distinguish L5 from peroneal neuropathy. Rule out diabetic radiculopathy, zoster, tumour and infection when the picture is atypical.
det.treatment: Conservative management is usual: analgesia and NSAIDs, remaining active, physiotherapy, neuropathic agents and epidural steroid injection for persistent pain. Surgery (microdiscectomy, decompression of a lateral recess or foramen) is considered for progressive or severe motor deficit, persistent disabling pain beyond roughly 6–12 weeks, or cauda equina syndrome. Foot drop from L5 compression with severe weakness warrants earlier surgical discussion. Treat the underlying cause in non-compressive radiculopathy.
det.prognosis: Most patients improve over weeks to months; severe motor weakness may recover slowly or incompletely.
pearls: Ankle inversion and hip abduction weakness locate a foot drop to L5, not the fibular nerve.
A normal sural sensory response with a numb foot supports a root (pre-ganglionic) lesion.
Disc compresses the traversing root: L4–5 disc, L5 root; far-lateral disc, exiting L4 root.
det.thd: Lumbosacral monoradiculopathy คือรากประสาทเอวหรือกระเบนเหน็บถูกกดเพียงรากเดียว ส่วนใหญ่จากหมอนรองกระดูกหรือรูรากประสาทแคบ ผู้ป่วยปวดตามแนว dermatome ชา และอ่อนแรงตามรากนั้น L5 มีเท้าตก ข้อเท้าพลิกเข้าด้านในและสะโพกกางออกได้น้อย S1 ไม่มี ankle jerk และกดปลายเท้าลงได้น้อย EMG แสดงการเสียเส้นประสาทของกล้ามเนื้อที่รากเดียวกันและกล้ามเนื้อกระดูกสันหลัง โดย sensory potentials ปกติ รักษาเบื้องต้นแบบอนุรักษ์ และผ่าตัดเมื่อไม่ดีขึ้น

name: Lumbosacral plexopathy
formal: Disorder of the lumbosacral plexus from diabetes, tumour, haematoma, radiation, trauma or inflammation, with leg pain and multi-root weakness and sensory loss.
simple: Damage to the network of nerves in the lower back and pelvis, causing leg pain, weakness and numbness.
more: MRI or CT of pelvis and EMG localise the lesion; treatment is directed to the cause, such as immunotherapy for diabetic amyotrophy. Lesions of the lumbosacral plexus due to diabetes, tumour, haematoma, radiation, or trauma causing multi-root leg weakness, pain, and sensory loss. MRI of the pelvis and EMG localise it. Treat the cause; immunotherapy for inflammatory forms; recovery varies.
th: โรคของ lumbosacral plexus จากเบาหวาน มะเร็ง เลือดออก รังสีรักษา อุบัติเหตุ หรือการอักเสบ ทำให้ปวดขาและอ่อนแรงชาหลายรากประสาท
tempoNote: Acute with haematoma or trauma; subacute with diabetes or tumour; delayed after radiation
feat: Leg weakness and sensory loss spanning several roots and nerves but sparing paraspinal muscles
Lumbar plexus: hip flexion, adduction and knee extension weak; anterior thigh numbness
Sacral plexus: hip extension/abduction, hamstrings and foot muscles weak; posterior leg numbness
Pain prominent in tumour, haematoma and diabetic forms; painless progressive weakness after radiation
Causes: diabetes (radiculoplexus neuropathy), cervical or colorectal cancer, retroperitoneal haematoma, pelvic fracture, obstetric injury, radiation
inv: EMG/NCS: multinerve denervation with normal paraspinals; low sensory potentials indicate post-ganglionic lesion
MRI pelvis and lumbosacral plexus; CT if haematoma suspected
PET-CT for suspected malignancy; glucose, coagulation

case.who: 53-year-old woman from Lampang treated with pelvic radiation for cervical cancer 2 years ago
case.story: Severe right buttock and leg pain for 2 months, then progressive right leg weakness.
case.exam: Weak right hip extension, knee flexion and ankle movements, absent right ankle jerk, sensory loss in sciatic territory.
case.tests: EMG: denervation in L5–S1 sciatic and gluteal muscles, paraspinals normal; sural SNAP absent; MRI pelvis shows enhancing mass infiltrating the right sacral plexus.
case.q: Recurrence or radiation plexopathy?
case.a: Painful course with a mass favours tumour recurrence infiltrating the sacral plexus; radiation plexopathy is usually painless with myokymia.

read.where: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves — Plexopathies

det.patho: The lumbar plexus (L1–L4) lies within psoas and the sacral plexus (L4–S4) on the posterior pelvic wall. Lesions arise from compression (haematoma, tumour, pregnancy), infiltration, microvasculitis (diabetic and non-diabetic radiculoplexus neuropathy), radiation fibrosis and trauma. Postganglionic location means sensory nerve action potentials are lost.
det.clinical: Patients have weakness and sensory loss crossing nerve and root boundaries in one leg. Pain is severe in malignant infiltration and haematoma. Radiation plexopathy tends to be painless, slowly progressive and often bilateral. Obstetric plexopathy causes foot drop after prolonged labour.
det.diagnosis: EMG demonstrates multinerve involvement with spared paraspinals, distinguishing plexus from root lesions. Absent SNAPs support a plexus location. MRI with gadolinium is the key imaging test; PET-CT helps with malignancy. Myokymic discharges suggest radiation injury.
det.treatment: Treatment targets the cause: tumour therapy, haematoma management and reversal of anticoagulation, diabetic glucose control with pain management, and immunotherapy considered for inflammatory forms. Physiotherapy, orthoses and neuropathic pain agents support function.
det.prognosis: Variable: diabetic and obstetric forms often recover; malignant and radiation plexopathies tend to progress.
pearls: Normal paraspinal EMG plus absent SNAPs: plexus, not root.
Painful plexopathy after cancer: tumour; painless with myokymia: radiation.
Anticoagulated patient with acute plexopathy: look for retroperitoneal haematoma.
det.thd: Lumbosacral plexopathy คือรอยโรคของร่างแหประสาทส่วนเอวและก้นกบ ทำให้ขาข้างหนึ่งอ่อนแรงและชาข้ามหลายเส้นประสาท สาเหตุสำคัญคือเบาหวาน มะเร็งลุกลาม เลือดออกหลังช่องท้อง รังสีรักษา และการคลอด EMG พบความผิดปกติหลายเส้นแต่กล้ามเนื้อข้างกระดูกสันหลังปกติ MRI ช่วยหาสาเหตุ การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ

name: Lumbosacral polyradiculopathy
formal: Disease of multiple lumbosacral nerve roots causing leg weakness, sensory loss and areflexia; causes include stenosis, infection, inflammation, infiltration or compressive cauda equina disease.
simple: Several nerves at the base of the spine are damaged, causing weakness, numbness or pain in the legs.
more: Multiple nerve root involvement, for example from cauda equina syndrome, stenosis, carcinomatous or infectious meningitis, and diabetic or inflammatory causes. MRI with contrast and CSF analysis are key; management depends on cause, with urgent decompression for cauda equina.
th: โรคของรากประสาทระดับเอวและก้นกบหลายราก ทำให้ขาอ่อนแรง ชา และ reflex หาย สาเหตุมีทั้งกระดูกสันหลังตีบ ติดเชื้อ อักเสบ และมะเร็งแทรกซึม
tempoNote: Acute in disc or infection, subacute in CMV or malignancy, chronic in stenosis or arachnoiditis
feat: Asymmetric leg weakness, sensory loss and areflexia in multiple root distributions
Radicular pain in back and legs
Sphincter and saddle sensory disturbance when sacral roots are involved
Upper limbs and cranial nerves spared unless meningeal process is widespread
Causes: lumbar canal stenosis, diabetes, CMV/HSV, TB, leptomeningeal metastases, lymphoma, GBS variants, arachnoiditis
inv: MRI lumbosacral spine with gadolinium: compression, nerve root enhancement, clumping
CSF: cells, protein, glucose, cytology, flow cytometry, PCR (CMV, HSV, VZV), TB tests
EMG: multi-myotomal denervation including paraspinals
HIV test, glucose, ESR

case.who: 36-year-old man with advanced HIV from Chiang Rai (CD4 30)
case.story: Ten days of low back pain, progressive leg weakness and urinary retention.
case.exam: Flaccid asymmetric leg weakness, absent knee and ankle jerks, saddle anaesthesia, normal arms.
case.tests: MRI: enhancement and thickening of cauda equina roots; CSF neutrophilic pleocytosis, low glucose, CMV PCR positive.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and treatment?
case.a: CMV lumbosacral polyradiculopathy in AIDS; IV ganciclovir (± foscarnet) and antiretroviral therapy.

read.where: Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — Cytomegalovirus Infection

det.patho: The lumbosacral roots run within the thecal sac as the cauda equina and can be damaged by compression, inflammation, infection or infiltration. Bathed in CSF, they are vulnerable to meningeal disease, for example carcinomatous or lymphomatous infiltration and opportunistic viral infection. Ischaemia from microvasculitis contributes in diabetic radiculoplexus neuropathy.
det.clinical: This is a syndrome with many causes rather than one disease. Patients have asymmetric lower-motor-neuron leg weakness, radicular pain, areflexia and variable sphincter involvement, with sparing of the arms. Rapid progression with sphincter failure in an immunosuppressed patient suggests CMV; subacute progression with weight loss suggests malignancy; chronic neurogenic claudication suggests canal stenosis.
det.diagnosis: Contrast MRI of the lumbosacral spine is the key test, showing compression, root enhancement or clumping. CSF analysis (with repeated cytology and PCR) identifies infection or malignancy. EMG confirms multilevel root involvement. Nerve root biopsy is occasionally needed for infiltrative causes.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: decompression for stenosis or disc, antiviral therapy for CMV or HSV, antituberculous drugs for TB, intrathecal or systemic therapy and radiotherapy for leptomeningeal malignancy, immunotherapy for inflammatory forms. Manage pain, bladder and bowel dysfunction, and provide rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause and speed of treatment; infectious and compressive forms may recover well if treated early.
pearls: Leg-only areflexic weakness with sphincter loss: image the cauda equina urgently.
In advanced HIV with polyradiculopathy, start CMV treatment before PCR returns.
Repeat CSF cytology if malignancy is suspected; one negative sample is not enough.
det.thd: Lumbosacral polyradiculopathy คือโรคของรากประสาทเอวและก้นกบหลายรากพร้อมกัน ทำให้ขาอ่อนแรงไม่เท่ากัน ปวดร้าว reflex หาย และอาจมีปัญหาการขับถ่าย สาเหตุมีหลายอย่าง เช่น กระดูกสันหลังตีบ เบาหวาน CMV ในผู้ป่วย HIV วัณโรค และมะเร็งแทรกซึมเยื่อหุ้ม วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI ฉีดสี การตรวจน้ำไขสันหลัง และ EMG รักษาตามสาเหตุ

name: Lumbosacral radiculoplexopathy
formal: Lesion involving lumbosacral roots and plexus with asymmetric leg pain, weakness and wasting; seen in diabetic amyotrophy, malignant infiltration, radiation, or retroperitoneal haematoma.
simple: Damage to the nerve roots and nerve network in the lower back and pelvis, causing painful leg weakness and wasting, often in diabetes or cancer.
th: ความผิดปกติของรากประสาทและข่ายประสาทเอว-กระเบนเหน็บ ปวดต้นขาหรือสะโพกมากแล้วตามด้วยกล้ามเนื้อต้นขาอ่อนแรงลีบข้างเดียวก่อน สาเหตุสำคัญคือ diabetic amyotrophy มะเร็งลุกลาม และเลือดออกหลังช่องท้อง
tempoNote: Inflammatory/diabetic forms evolve over weeks to months then slowly recover; malignant and radiation forms progress; haematoma is acute
feat: Severe deep pain in hip, buttock or anterior thigh, often first, then weakness
Proximal leg weakness and wasting (quadriceps, iliopsoas, hip adductors), knee jerk lost; later distal spread and the other leg
Weight loss is common in diabetic and non-diabetic inflammatory forms
Sensory loss in the thigh and leg not confined to one nerve or root
Malignant: progressive painful deficit with known pelvic cancer; radiation: painless, slowly progressive, with myokymia
inv: EMG/NCS: axonal changes in multiple roots and plexus territories, paraspinal denervation and distal involvement on both sides
MRI lumbar spine and lumbosacral plexus (with contrast) to exclude disc, tumour, haematoma; CT abdomen if bleeding suspected
HbA1c, ESR/CRP; CSF protein often raised
Nerve biopsy (cutaneous nerve) shows microvasculitis in diabetic and non-diabetic LRPN, reserved for atypical cases

case.who: 62-year-old man from Nakhon Ratchasima with type 2 diabetes
case.story: Six weeks ago severe burning pain began in his right thigh, keeping him awake; now he cannot climb onto the bus. He has lost 8 kg.
case.exam: Wasted right quadriceps, hip flexion 3/5, knee extension 3/5, mild weakness of ankle dorsiflexion, absent right knee jerk, reduced sensation over anterior thigh and medial leg; mild weakness also in left hip flexion.
case.tests: HbA1c 7.6%; MRI lumbar spine: mild degenerative change only; EMG: denervation in quadriceps, adductors, tibialis anterior and lumbar paraspinals bilaterally (right > left).
case.q: What is this syndrome and how is it managed?
case.a: Diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy (diabetic amyotrophy); pain control, physiotherapy and glucose control, with slow spontaneous recovery; immunotherapy is debated.

read.where: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves

det.patho: Diabetic and non-diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy are caused by an inflammatory microvasculitis of epineurial vessels producing ischaemic axonal injury across roots, plexus and peripheral nerves. Other causes include tumour infiltration (cervical, colorectal, prostate cancer, lymphoma), radiation, retroperitoneal haematoma (often on anticoagulation), psoas abscess, and trauma or surgery.
det.clinical: Diabetic LRPN typically affects older patients with relatively mild, often recently diagnosed type 2 diabetes, starting with intense unilateral thigh pain and progressing to wasting and weakness, with spread to the other side in most. Weight loss is common. Neoplastic plexopathy causes progressive pain with a palpable mass or lymphoedema, whereas radiation plexopathy is slower, usually painless, often bilateral and may show myokymic discharges. Retroperitoneal haematoma presents acutely with groin pain and femoral deficits.
det.diagnosis: Electrodiagnosis confirms a multifocal axonal process across roots and plexus. MRI of the spine and plexus excludes compressive lesions and shows nerve enlargement or enhancement in inflammatory forms. Blood tests identify diabetes and inflammatory markers; CSF protein is often high. Biopsy is reserved for unclear cases or when considering immunotherapy.
det.treatment: Management of diabetic LRPN centres on pain control (neuropathic agents, sometimes opioids short term), physiotherapy and orthoses, and glucose control. Corticosteroids or IVIG may reduce pain but have not proved to speed motor recovery in a controlled trial. Malignant plexopathy needs oncological treatment and pain management; haematoma may need reversal of anticoagulation or drainage.
det.prognosis: Diabetic and idiopathic forms improve over months to years, often with residual weakness; malignant forms progress.
pearls: Severe thigh pain then quadriceps wasting and weight loss in a diabetic: diabetic amyotrophy.
Check paraspinals and hip adductors on EMG to separate plexus/root disease from femoral neuropathy.
Acute groin pain and femoral deficit on anticoagulation: retroperitoneal haematoma.
det.thd: Lumbosacral radiculoplexopathy คือรอยโรคที่รากประสาทและข่ายประสาทบริเวณเอว ทำให้ปวดสะโพกหรือต้นขาอย่างมากแล้วตามด้วยกล้ามเนื้อต้นขาอ่อนแรงและลีบ มักเริ่มข้างเดียวแล้วลามไปอีกข้าง สาเหตุบ่อยในผู้สูงอายุเบาหวานคือ diabetic amyotrophy จากหลอดเลือดเล็กอักเสบ สาเหตุอื่นคือมะเร็งลุกลาม รังสีรักษา และเลือดออกหลังช่องท้อง ตรวจ EMG และ MRI รักษาตามสาเหตุ ควบคุมปวดและทำกายภาพ อาการมักค่อย ๆ ฟื้นในหลายเดือน

name: Lung carcinoma
formal: Primary pulmonary malignancy with neurological relevance through brain and spinal metastases, paraneoplastic syndromes (Lambert-Eaton, limbic encephalitis), Pancoast brachial plexopathy and Horner syndrome.
simple: Cancer that starts in the lungs and can spread to the brain or cause nerve problems elsewhere in the body.
th: มะเร็งปอดปฐมภูมิซึ่งสำคัญทางประสาทวิทยาเพราะแพร่กระจายไปสมองและไขสันหลัง ทำให้เกิด paraneoplastic syndrome, Pancoast plexopathy และ Horner syndrome
tempoNote: Neurological complications develop over weeks to months; some precede the cancer diagnosis
feat: Brain metastases: headache, seizures, focal deficits; spinal cord compression from vertebral metastases
Paraneoplastic (mostly SCLC): LEMS, limbic encephalitis, cerebellar degeneration, sensory neuronopathy
Pancoast tumour: shoulder pain, C8/T1 weakness and Horner syndrome
Leptomeningeal disease, SIADH hyponatraemia and recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy
Treatment toxicity: checkpoint inhibitor neurotoxicity, radiation necrosis
inv: CT chest or PET-CT; MRI brain with contrast for staging
Onconeural antibodies (anti-Hu, VGCC, SOX1, CRMP5, GABA-B, amphiphysin)
MRI spine for back pain with neurological signs; CSF cytology for leptomeningeal disease

case.story: Three months of proximal leg weakness that improves briefly after exertion, dry mouth and erectile dysfunction.
case.exam: Proximal weakness, absent reflexes that reappear after brief contraction, mild ptosis.
case.tests: Repetitive nerve stimulation: low CMAP with >100% increment after exercise; VGCC antibodies positive; CT chest shows hilar mass, biopsy small cell carcinoma.
case.q: What is the neurological syndrome and how is it linked?
case.a: Paraneoplastic Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome from small cell lung carcinoma; treat the tumour plus 3,4-diaminopyridine.

read.where: Chapter 26 Metastatic Disease and the Nervous System

det.patho: Lung cancer is a non-neurological malignancy that affects the nervous system by direct spread, haematogenous metastasis, local invasion of the brachial plexus and sympathetic chain, and immune cross-reactivity. Small cell carcinoma, a neuroendocrine tumour, expresses neuronal antigens and is the commonest cause of paraneoplastic neurological syndromes. Targeted drugs and checkpoint inhibitors have added treatment-related neurological complications.
det.clinical: Lung cancer is the most frequent source of brain metastases and a major cause of epidural spinal cord compression. Neurological syndromes may precede tumour detection, especially paraneoplastic ones: LEMS, anti-Hu encephalomyelitis and sensory neuronopathy, cerebellar degeneration and limbic encephalitis. Apical tumours cause Pancoast syndrome with lower trunk plexopathy and Horner syndrome.
det.diagnosis: In a smoker with a new neurological syndrome, search for lung cancer with CT chest or PET-CT, and test onconeural antibodies when a paraneoplastic picture is suspected. Contrast MRI identifies brain and spinal metastases. If initial screening is negative in a high-risk paraneoplastic syndrome, repeat cancer screening periodically.
det.treatment: Treatment combines oncological therapy (surgery, chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, radiotherapy including stereotactic radiosurgery for brain metastases) with neurological management. Paraneoplastic syndromes improve most with tumour control; immunotherapy is added for some. Spinal cord compression requires urgent steroids and radiotherapy or surgery.
det.prognosis: Outlook depends on stage and tumour type; targeted therapies have improved survival even with brain metastases.
pearls: A new neurological syndrome in a smoker warrants a chest CT.
Shoulder pain plus Horner syndrome and hand weakness: Pancoast tumour.
LEMS should prompt a search for SCLC for at least two years.
det.thd: Lung carcinoma เป็นมะเร็งปอด ไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาทโดยตรง แต่สำคัญเพราะแพร่กระจายไปสมองและกดไขสันหลังบ่อย และเป็นสาเหตุหลักของ paraneoplastic syndrome เช่น LEMS และ limbic encephalitis รวมถึง Pancoast tumour ที่ทำให้ปวดไหล่ มืออ่อนแรง และ Horner syndrome ในผู้สูบบุหรี่ที่มีอาการทางระบบประสาทใหม่ควรตรวจ CT ทรวงอก รักษาที่ตัวมะเร็งร่วมกับการรักษาทางระบบประสาท

name: LVO syndromes
formal: Acute ischaemic stroke from large vessel occlusion (ICA, M1 MCA, basilar) with severe deficits such as hemiplegia, aphasia or neglect; candidates for urgent endovascular thrombectomy.
simple: Strokes caused by a blockage in a major brain artery, producing severe sudden weakness or speech problems and needing urgent clot removal.
th: ischaemic stroke จากหลอดเลือดใหญ่อุดตัน (ICA, M1 MCA, basilar) ทำให้อาการรุนแรง เช่น อัมพาตครึ่งซีก aphasia neglect เหมาะกับการทำ thrombectomy
tempoNote: Minutes to hours; fast core growth in poor collateral patients
feat: Severe deficits: hemiplegia, gaze deviation, aphasia or neglect, typically NIHSS 6 or more
Cortical signs (gaze deviation, aphasia, neglect) strongly predict LVO
Basilar occlusion: coma, quadriparesis, ocular motor signs, sometimes fluctuating prodrome
Pre-hospital scales (RACE, VAN, FAST-ED) help triage to thrombectomy centres
Main causes: cardioembolism, large-artery atherosclerosis (intracranial atherosclerosis common in Asia), dissection
inv: CT + CTA from arch to vertex; CT perfusion or MRI for late window selection
Glucose; do not delay for other labs unless anticoagulation suspected
ECG/cardiac monitoring after reperfusion

case.who: 71-year-old man from Chiang Mai found at 07:00, last seen well at 22:00 the night before
case.story: Unable to speak and right side not moving on awakening.
case.exam: Global aphasia, right hemiplegia, left gaze deviation; NIHSS 20.
case.tests: CT ASPECTS 8; CTA left ICA terminus occlusion; CT perfusion shows small core with large mismatch.
case.q: Is he a thrombectomy candidate despite being beyond 6 hours?
case.a: Yes — imaging-selected late-window LVO; mechanical thrombectomy up to 24 hours is indicated.

read.where: Chapter 8 Stroke and Cerebrovascular Diseases — Ischaemic Stroke Due to Large-Vessel Occlusion

det.patho: Occlusion of the ICA, proximal MCA, or basilar artery cuts flow to large regions. Collateral circulation through leptomeningeal vessels determines how long the penumbra survives. Fast progressors with poor collaterals lose tissue rapidly; slow progressors may still have salvageable tissue many hours later.
det.clinical: LVO causes about a third of ischaemic strokes but a large share of stroke disability and death. Anterior LVO causes cortical syndromes; basilar occlusion causes coma, quadriplegia, pupillary abnormalities and locked-in states. Intracranial atherosclerotic occlusions, common in Thai and other Asian patients, may need angioplasty or stenting during thrombectomy.
det.diagnosis: CTA is the key test and should be done with the first CT. CT perfusion or MRI helps select late-window and wake-up patients. Clinical scales predict LVO but cannot replace vessel imaging.
det.treatment: IV thrombolysis for eligible patients, without delaying transfer for thrombectomy. Mechanical thrombectomy is standard for anterior circulation LVO within 6 hours, and up to 24 hours with imaging selection; recent trials extended benefit to large-core infarcts and to basilar occlusion. Post-procedure care includes BP management, monitoring for haemorrhage and malignant oedema, and secondary prevention by mechanism.
det.prognosis: Successful early reperfusion greatly increases the chance of independence; untreated LVO has poor outcomes.
pearls: Gaze deviation plus aphasia or neglect: assume LVO and get CTA.
Do not wait to see if thrombolysis works before arranging thrombectomy.
Intracranial atherosclerotic occlusion is common in Asian patients and may need rescue stenting.
det.thd: LVO syndromes คือ ischaemic stroke จากหลอดเลือดใหญ่อุดตัน เช่น ICA, M1 MCA หรือ basilar ผู้ป่วยมีอาการรุนแรง เช่น อัมพาตครึ่งซีก ตาเหลือบไปด้านหนึ่ง aphasia หรือ neglect ต้องทำ CT ร่วมกับ CTA ทันที การรักษาคือยาละลายลิ่มเลือดร่วมกับ mechanical thrombectomy ภายใน 6 ชั่วโมงและนานถึง 24 ชั่วโมงในผู้ป่วยที่คัดเลือกด้วยภาพ

name: Lyme disease
formal: Tick-borne infection by Borrelia burgdorferi causing erythema migrans, then lymphocytic meningitis, cranial neuritis (especially facial palsy) and radiculoneuritis; later arthritis and encephalopathy.
simple: An infection from tick bites that can cause a rash, facial weakness, meningitis and nerve pain if untreated.
more: Confirm with serum and CSF Lyme antibodies by two-tier ELISA and immunoblot, with CSF showing lymphocytosis and intrathecal antibody. Treat neuroborreliosis with IV ceftriaxone or oral doxycycline, with usually good recovery but facial palsy may persist.
th: โรคติดเชื้อ Borrelia จากเห็บ — อาจทำให้ใบหน้าเบี้ยว ปวดร้าวตามรากประสาท และเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ พบในผู้ที่เดินทางจากพื้นที่ระบาด
tempoNote: Early neurological disease weeks to months after the tick bite; late forms over months to years
feat: Expanding red rash (erythema migrans) at the bite site in many, though often missed
Facial nerve palsy, sometimes bilateral
Painful radiculitis with severe, often nocturnal, dermatomal pain (Bannwarth syndrome)
Lymphocytic meningitis with headache and mild neck stiffness
Others: carditis with AV block, arthritis; rare encephalomyelitis
inv: Serology: two-tier ELISA then immunoblot (or two EIAs)
CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein; CSF/serum Borrelia antibody index
ECG for heart block; MRI if myelitis or encephalitis suspected

case.who: 29-year-old Thai woman returning from hiking in central Europe
case.story: Three weeks after the trip, a ring-shaped rash on her thigh faded; now severe burning pain wraps around her left chest at night, and her right face droops.
case.exam: Right lower motor neuron facial palsy, band of hyperaesthesia over left T6–T7, mild meningism.
case.tests: CSF: 140 lymphocytes, protein 1.1 g/L, positive intrathecal Borrelia antibody index; serum immunoblot positive.
case.q: What is the treatment?
case.a: Oral doxycycline for 14–21 days (or IV ceftriaxone); oral therapy is as effective as IV for neuroborreliosis without parenchymal involvement.

read.where: Chapter 39 Spirochetal Infections of the Nervous System

det.patho: Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato is transmitted by Ixodes ticks and spreads from the skin through blood to meninges, roots and cranial nerves. Neurological disease reflects both direct infection and the immune response. Species differ by region: European strains (B. garinii) favour painful meningoradiculitis, while North American strains more often cause meningitis and facial palsy.
det.clinical: Early disseminated neuroborreliosis brings lymphocytic meningitis, cranial neuropathies (especially facial) and painful radiculoneuritis, sometimes with limb weakness. Late manifestations include chronic encephalomyelitis and a distal sensory neuropathy linked to acrodermatitis. Lyme is not endemic in Thailand, so travel history to North America or Europe is essential.
det.diagnosis: In a compatible case, serology plus CSF showing lymphocytic pleocytosis and intrathecal antibody production confirms neuroborreliosis. Serology can be negative early and stays positive long after cure, so it must be read with the clinical picture. PCR of CSF has low sensitivity. Think of HIV, syphilis, sarcoidosis and VZV in the differential.
det.treatment: Doxycycline orally for 14–21 days or ceftriaxone IV for 14–21 days are effective; parenchymal CNS disease is often treated IV. Steroids for facial palsy remain debated. Persisting fatigue or pain afterwards ('post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome') does not respond to prolonged antibiotics.
det.prognosis: Most recover well after treatment; facial palsy usually resolves, and late complications are prevented by timely therapy.
pearls: Facial palsy plus CSF lymphocytes in a traveller: test for Lyme.
Bannwarth: severe night-time radicular pain + facial palsy + lymphocytic CSF.
Antibodies persist after cure — do not treat a positive test without disease.
det.thd: Lyme disease เกิดจากเชื้อ Borrelia ที่เห็บ Ixodes นำมา ไม่พบเป็นโรคประจำถิ่นในไทย จึงต้องถามประวัติเดินทางไปยุโรปหรืออเมริกาเหนือ อาการทางประสาท ได้แก่ หน้าเบี้ยว ปวดแสบตามรากประสาทมากตอนกลางคืน และเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบชนิด lymphocytic วินิจฉัยด้วย serology และตรวจน้ำไขสันหลัง รักษาด้วย doxycycline หรือ ceftriaxone 2–3 สัปดาห์ ส่วนใหญ่หายดี

name: Lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus
formal: Rodent-borne arenavirus causing aseptic meningitis or meningoencephalitis, and congenital infection with chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and microcephaly; transmitted via mouse excreta.
simple: A virus carried by mice that can cause meningitis, and can harm the brain and eyes of an unborn baby.
th: ไวรัส arenavirus ที่ติดจากหนูบ้านหรือหนูแฮมสเตอร์ ทำให้ไข้แบบสองระยะแล้วตามด้วยเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบแบบ aseptic ที่ลิมโฟไซต์สูงมาก บางรายเป็นสมองอักเสบ การติดเชื้อในครรภ์ทำให้ hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis และหินปูนรอบโพรงสมอง
tempoNote: Flu-like phase 1-3 weeks after exposure, a few days of improvement, then meningitis or encephalitis
feat: Exposure to house mice, pet hamsters or guinea pigs, rodent-infested storage, laboratory work, or receipt of an organ from an infected donor
Biphasic illness: fever, myalgia, headache and vomiting, a short remission, then meningism or encephalitis
Extra-neural clues: orchitis, parotitis, arthritis, alopecia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and raised transaminases
About a third of infections are silent; meningitis is usually self-limited but recovery can be slow
Congenital infection: chorioretinitis, microcephaly or macrocephaly with hydrocephalus and periventricular calcification
inv: CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis that can reach several thousand cells, mildly raised protein, normal or low glucose
LCMV IgM and paired IgG serology; RT-PCR on CSF or blood through a reference laboratory
Full blood count and liver tests; MRI if encephalitic; fundoscopy and cranial imaging in suspected congenital infection

case.who: 27-year-old woman working in a rice-mill warehouse in Suphan Buri
case.story: Four days of fever and muscle aches settled, then five days later she developed severe headache, vomiting and neck stiffness; mice infest the storehouse.
case.exam: Neck stiffness, alert and oriented, tender swollen right parotid, no rash or focal signs.
case.tests: CSF 1,100 cells/µL (95% lymphocytes), protein 1.0 g/L, glucose slightly low; Gram stain, culture, cryptococcal antigen and Xpert negative; white count 3,200, platelets 110,000; LCMV IgM positive.
case.q: What is the likely cause and what is the treatment?
case.a: LCMV meningitis; supportive care, as there is no proven antiviral, with rodent control at the workplace and advice to avoid infection during pregnancy.

det.patho: LCMV is an Old World arenavirus maintained in house mice, which carry it lifelong and shed it in urine, saliva and droppings. Humans inhale contaminated dust or aerosols or are exposed through bites and contaminated food; person-to-person spread occurs only via pregnancy or transplantation. Disease in the CNS is largely immune mediated, driven by cytotoxic T cells attacking infected meningeal and choroid cells. In the fetus the virus injures the developing brain and retina.
det.clinical: Many infections are subclinical or a febrile flu-like illness. A minority progress after a brief remission to meningitis with intense headache and photophobia, and occasionally to meningoencephalitis, myelitis or hydrocephalus. Orchitis, parotitis or arthritis in a patient with lymphocytic meningitis are useful pointers. Organ transplant recipients infected through a donor develop fulminant multisystem disease with high mortality, and congenital infection mimics CMV or toxoplasmosis.
det.diagnosis: Ask about rodents at home, at work and as pets. CSF lymphocyte counts can be strikingly high and glucose may be low, which can raise false concern for TB or fungal infection. Serology (IgM, or rising IgG) and RT-PCR confirm it; testing usually requires a reference laboratory. In congenital cases maternal and infant serology plus imaging and eye examination are used once CMV, Toxoplasma and Zika have been considered.
det.treatment: Treatment is supportive with analgesia, antiemetics and hydration, and occasionally CSF diversion for hydrocephalus. Ribavirin has been used for severe or transplant-associated infection with reduction of immunosuppression, without proof of benefit. Prevention relies on rodent control, safe handling of pet rodents, especially during pregnancy, and donor screening when an unexplained encephalitis is present.
det.prognosis: Acquired meningitis almost always recovers fully, sometimes slowly; congenital infection often leaves severe neurodevelopmental disability or visual loss.
pearls: Lymphocytic meningitis after a biphasic illness plus parotitis or orchitis: think mumps and LCMV, and ask about mice.
Very high CSF lymphocyte counts and low glucose can occur in LCMV, a benign mimic of TB meningitis.
Congenital LCMV is an under-recognised cause of hydrocephalus with periventricular calcification and chorioretinitis.
det.thd: LCMV เป็น arenavirus ที่หนูบ้านเป็นแหล่งรังโรค ติดต่อทางฝุ่นหรือละอองที่ปนปัสสาวะหรือน้ำลายหนู ผู้ป่วยมักมีไข้ปวดเมื่อยก่อน ดีขึ้นช่วงสั้น แล้วเกิดเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบที่ลิมโฟไซต์ในน้ำไขสันหลังสูงมาก อาจมีอัณฑะอักเสบหรือต่อมน้ำลายอักเสบร่วม วินิจฉัยด้วย serology หรือ RT-PCR รักษาตามอาการเพราะยังไม่มียาต้านไวรัสที่พิสูจน์ได้ หญิงตั้งครรภ์ควรหลีกเลี่ยงหนู เพราะทำให้ทารกมี hydrocephalus และ chorioretinitis

name: Lymphocytic hypophysitis
formal: Autoimmune lymphocytic infiltration of the pituitary, often peripartum, causing headache, hypopituitarism and a mass-like enlargement mimicking adenoma; also associated with checkpoint inhibitors.
simple: Inflammation of the pituitary gland, often around pregnancy, causing headaches and low hormone levels.
th: การอักเสบแบบภูมิต้านตนเองของต่อมใต้สมองจาก lymphocyte มักพบในหญิงช่วงตั้งครรภ์หรือหลังคลอด ทำให้ปวดศีรษะ ฮอร์โมนต่อมใต้สมองต่ำ และก้อนคล้าย adenoma
tempoNote: Weeks to months; may resolve spontaneously or leave permanent deficits
feat: Headache, often severe, in late pregnancy or postpartum
ACTH deficiency early (risk of adrenal crisis), then TSH and gonadotropin loss
Visual field defect if the gland enlarges upward
Diabetes insipidus when the infundibulum or posterior lobe is involved
Checkpoint inhibitor therapy (ipilimumab, anti-PD-1) is a major modern cause
inv: Morning cortisol, ACTH, TSH/fT4, prolactin, LH/FSH, sex steroids, sodium and urine osmolality
Pituitary MRI: symmetric enlargement, thickened stalk, homogeneous enhancement, loss of posterior bright spot
Visual fields
Biopsy only when diagnosis unclear

case.story: Severe frontal headache for 3 weeks, fatigue, nausea, and she could not breastfeed well.
case.exam: BP 90/60 mmHg, mild bitemporal field cut.
case.tests: Morning cortisol low, fT4 low with low TSH, sodium 128 mmol/L; MRI shows symmetric pituitary enlargement with thick stalk and uniform enhancement.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the first treatment?
case.a: Lymphocytic hypophysitis; replace glucocorticoid first (before thyroxine), consider higher-dose steroid for mass effect.

det.patho: Lymphocytes and plasma cells infiltrate the anterior pituitary, the stalk or the posterior lobe, causing enlargement followed by fibrosis and atrophy. The autoimmune basis is supported by association with other autoimmune diseases and anti-pituitary antibodies, although these tests are not reliable diagnostically. Immune checkpoint inhibitors trigger a related hypophysitis, especially with CTLA-4 blockade.
det.clinical: This is mainly an endocrine disorder of the pituitary, encountered by neurologists because of headache and visual field loss. Women in late pregnancy or the postpartum period are classically affected. ACTH deficiency is common and early, unlike in pituitary adenomas where growth hormone and gonadotropins fail first. Infundibulo-neurohypophysitis presents with diabetes insipidus.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows symmetric gland enlargement, a thickened but midline stalk, homogeneous enhancement and sometimes a dural tail; posterior bright spot may be lost. Endocrine testing documents the pattern of deficiency. Exclude adenoma, germinoma, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, sarcoidosis, IgG4-related disease and metastasis; biopsy is reserved for uncertain or progressive cases.
det.treatment: Replace hormones, giving glucocorticoids before thyroxine to avoid adrenal crisis, and desmopressin for diabetes insipidus. Higher-dose glucocorticoids may shrink the mass when there is compression; azathioprine or rituximab are options in refractory cases. Surgery is reserved for visual threat not responding to medical therapy. Checkpoint inhibitor cases usually need long-term cortisol replacement but can continue cancer therapy.
det.prognosis: The mass often regresses, but hormone deficiencies, especially ACTH, frequently persist.
pearls: Pituitary mass in pregnancy or postpartum with early ACTH loss: think hypophysitis, not adenoma.
Always give hydrocortisone before thyroxine.
New headache and fatigue on ipilimumab: check cortisol and pituitary MRI.
det.thd: Lymphocytic hypophysitis เป็นการอักเสบแบบภูมิต้านตนเองของต่อมใต้สมอง ไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาทโดยตรง แต่ทำให้ปวดศีรษะและลานสายตาแคบ มักพบในหญิงตั้งครรภ์ช่วงปลายหรือหลังคลอด และในผู้ป่วยที่ได้ยา immune checkpoint inhibitor มักขาด cortisol ก่อน MRI เห็นต่อมใต้สมองโตสมมาตรและก้านหนา รักษาด้วยการให้ hydrocortisone ก่อนฮอร์โมนไทรอยด์และ steroid ขนาดสูงเมื่อกดทับ

name: Lymphoma
formal: Lymphoid malignancy affecting the CNS as primary CNS lymphoma (enhancing periventricular lesions, steroid-responsive) or secondary leptomeningeal or nerve involvement.
simple: A cancer of lymphocytes that can involve the brain, spinal cord or nerves, causing headaches, confusion or weakness.
th: มะเร็งต่อมน้ำเหลืองที่ระบบประสาท ทั้งชนิดปฐมภูมิในสมอง (PCNSL ซึ่งเป็น diffuse large B-cell lymphoma) และชนิดแพร่กระจายมาที่เยื่อหุ้มสมองหรือเส้นประสาท ภาพ MRI พบก้อน enhance สม่ำเสมอรอบโพรงสมอง การรักษาหลักคือ high-dose methotrexate และควรเลี่ยงสเตียรอยด์ก่อนตัดชิ้นเนื้อ
tempoNote: Weeks to a few months of cognitive and focal decline; leptomeningeal and nerve involvement may be more indolent
feat: Primary CNS lymphoma: subacute personality or cognitive change, focal deficit, headache, seizures (less frequent than in glioma) and visual blurring from vitreous or uveal disease
Median age about 60 years in immunocompetent adults; HIV and transplant recipients develop EBV-driven lymphoma at a younger age
Imaging shows one or several homogeneously enhancing deep masses near ventricles or callosum, with restricted diffusion and moderate oedema; ring enhancement is common in immunosuppressed patients
Steroids shrink or even eliminate lesions within days to weeks, which can make the biopsy non-diagnostic (ghost tumour)
Secondary involvement: leptomeningeal lymphomatous meningitis with cranial nerve palsies and radiculopathy, and neurolymphomatosis of peripheral nerves
inv: Contrast MRI with diffusion; thallium-SPECT/FDG-PET in HIV patients; CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, testis examination and bone marrow only to exclude systemic disease

case.story: Five weeks of slowly worsening memory, flat affect and unsteady walking; she was given dexamethasone by a local clinic and felt briefly better.
case.exam: Disoriented to date, apathy, mild right hemiparesis and gait ataxia.
case.tests: MRI shows two homogeneously enhancing periventricular and callosal lesions with restricted diffusion; CT chest-abdomen normal; HIV negative. Stereotactic biopsy: diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, CD20 positive.
case.q: What is the backbone of first-line treatment and what is the major late toxicity of whole-brain irradiation?
case.a: A combination built on methotrexate in high doses (3-8 g/m2 per dose) with rituximab and cytarabine, followed by consolidation with autologous stem cell transplant or reduced-dose whole-brain radiotherapy; whole-brain radiation after 60 years causes leukoencephalopathy and dementia.

det.patho: More than 95 percent of primary CNS lymphomas are diffuse large B-cell lymphomas of the activated B-cell type, characterised by CD20, BCL6 and MUM1 expression, MYD88 and CD79B mutations, and angiocentric growth along vessels. EBV drives tumours in HIV and transplant patients. Lymphoma cells infiltrate the neuropil diffusely, spread along white-matter tracts and the ventricular wall, and can invade the CSF and eye. Systemic lymphomas secondarily affect the nervous system by leptomeningeal, parenchymal, epidural or peripheral nerve involvement.
det.clinical: PCNSL produces a rapidly evolving frontal-type syndrome or focal deficits, headache and ataxia; seizures are less frequent than in glioma. Uveitis-like visual symptoms suggest ocular lymphoma. In AIDS, lymphoma and toxoplasmosis are the key differential for ring-enhancing lesions. Corticosteroids can transiently shrink the tumour in about 15-25 percent, falsely suggesting inflammation. Without treatment, survival is measured in weeks to months.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows homogeneous enhancement and restricted diffusion; CSF cytology is positive in fewer than a quarter of cases and flow cytometry or IGH PCR can help, but stereotactic biopsy remains the diagnostic standard. Resection offers no benefit. Steroids should be withheld until biopsy unless life-threatening oedema requires them; osmotic therapy can be used meanwhile. Staging includes the eye, CSF, testes in men and body imaging to exclude systemic lymphoma.
det.treatment: First-line therapy is high-dose methotrexate (3.5-8 g/m2) in combination with cytarabine, thiotepa and rituximab (MATRix) or other regimens; consolidation with autologous stem-cell transplant (IELSG43) or reduced-dose whole-brain irradiation improves disease control. Elderly or frail patients receive methotrexate-based therapy with procarbazine or maintenance. Whole-brain radiotherapy alone produces temporary responses and neurotoxicity in older adults, so radiation is reserved for failure or residual disease. Relapse is treated with high-dose chemotherapy, ibrutinib or other BTK inhibitors, lenalidomide, or CD19 CAR-T cell therapy in trials. Intrathecal chemotherapy is used for leptomeningeal disease. In HIV-associated lymphoma, antiretroviral therapy accompanies treatment.
det.prognosis: Median survival is 2-3 months untreated, about 12 months with radiotherapy alone, and 4 years or more with modern methotrexate-based programmes and consolidation; older age and poor performance predict worse outcome.
pearls: Homogeneously enhancing deep lesions with restricted diffusion in a middle-aged or older adult: PCNSL until biopsied.
Do not give steroids before biopsy; a vanishing lesion after dexamethasone is a clue.
High-dose methotrexate is the cornerstone; whole-brain radiation alone is no longer first-line.
det.thd: Lymphoma ในระบบประสาท ส่วนใหญ่เป็นชนิด primary CNS lymphoma (diffuse large B-cell lymphoma) ผู้ป่วยมีความจำเสื่อม อ่อนแรง หรือเดินเซภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์ MRI พบก้อน enhance สม่ำเสมอใกล้โพรงสมองและ corpus callosum การตัดชิ้นเนื้อสำคัญที่สุด และควรเลี่ยงสเตียรอยด์ก่อนตัดเพราะก้อนอาจหายชั่วคราว การรักษาคือ high-dose methotrexate ร่วมกับยาอื่นและ consolidation ด้วย autologous stem cell transplant หรือรังสีขนาดต่ำ

simple: Genetic diseases where cells cannot break down certain substances, which build up and cause developmental and nerve problems.
more: Inherited enzyme or transporter defects of lysosomes causing accumulation of undegraded substrate, producing neurodegeneration, organomegaly, dysmorphism and developmental regression. Diagnose by enzyme assays in leukocytes or fibroblasts, urinary oligosaccharides or glycosaminoglycans, and genetic testing. Enzyme replacement, haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, substrate reduction and chaperones are available for selected disorders.

case.story: Clumsy since adolescence, falling school grades, now cataplexy-like falls when laughing and difficulty looking down.
case.exam: Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy (downgaze), ataxia, dysarthria, mild dystonia, spleen tip palpable.
case.tests: Oxysterols raised; NPC1 biallelic variants.
case.q: Which lysosomal disorder is this and which treatment is approved?
case.a: Niemann–Pick disease type C; miglustat (and arimoclomol/levacetylleucine where available) plus supportive care.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Lysosomal Storage Disorders

det.patho: Over 70 disorders are caused by deficiency of a lysosomal enzyme, an activator protein or a membrane transporter, leading to accumulation of sphingolipids, glycosaminoglycans, glycoproteins or cholesterol. Storage disrupts autophagy, calcium homeostasis and inflammation, causing cell death. Inheritance is mostly autosomal recessive; Fabry, Hunter and Danon are X-linked.
det.clinical: Infantile forms present with regression, seizures and visceral enlargement; later-onset forms may show only ataxia, dystonia, psychosis, dementia or neuropathy. Key clues include cherry-red spot, supranuclear gaze palsy, organomegaly, skeletal dysplasia, angiokeratomas and small-fibre neuropathy. GBA variants also raise the risk of Parkinson's disease.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis uses clinical clues to select enzyme assays and biomarkers, followed by gene confirmation; broad gene panels and exome sequencing are now common first-line tests. Newborn screening exists for several disorders in some countries. MRI, ophthalmic examination and abdominal imaging support diagnosis.
det.treatment: Enzyme replacement therapy works for systemic features of Gaucher, Fabry, Pompe and several MPS types, but poorly crosses the blood-brain barrier. Substrate reduction therapy (eliglustat, miglustat), haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (e.g. Hurler, MLD, Krabbe) and gene therapies are available for selected disorders. Others rely on supportive care: seizure control, nutrition and rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: Ranges from death in early childhood to near-normal lifespan depending on the disorder and treatment.
pearls: Cherry-red spot plus regression: think sphingolipid storage.
Downgaze palsy in a young adult with ataxia or psychosis: test for NPC.
Early diagnosis matters because transplant and gene therapy work best before symptoms.

case.story: Unsteady walking for three years and slurred speech; his mother and uncle used wheelchairs from their 40s.
case.exam: Ataxic gait, dysarthria, gaze-evoked nystagmus with limited upgaze, staring eyes from lid retraction, brisk reflexes, facial fasciculations.
case.tests: MRI: pontocerebellar atrophy; ATXN3 CAG 72 repeats.
case.q: What is the diagnosis?
case.a: Machado–Joseph disease (SCA3), the commonest dominant ataxia in many Asian populations including Thailand.

read.where: Chapter 24 Cerebellar Ataxias and Related Conditions — Inherited Ataxia Syndromes

det.patho: An expanded CAG repeat in ATXN3 encodes a long polyglutamine tract in ataxin-3, a deubiquitinating enzyme. The mutant protein forms nuclear inclusions and disturbs protein quality control and transcription, causing loss of neurons in the dentate nucleus, pons, substantia nigra, spinal cord and dorsal root ganglia. Longer repeats give earlier onset, and paternal transmission may produce anticipation.
det.clinical: It is the commonest autosomal dominant ataxia worldwide and in many Asian countries. Phenotypes vary with repeat length: young-onset patients show prominent spasticity and dystonia, middle-onset show pure ataxia with ophthalmoparesis, and late-onset show neuropathy and amyotrophy; some present with levodopa-responsive parkinsonism. Lid retraction, facial fasciculations and diplopia are clues.
det.diagnosis: Genetic testing for the ATXN3 repeat confirms the diagnosis. MRI shows pontine and cerebellar atrophy, less marked than in SCA2 or MSA. Exclude acquired ataxias and test other SCA genes if negative. Predictive testing of relatives requires formal counselling.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy is approved, though antisense oligonucleotide trials are under way. Physiotherapy and balance training help, along with speech and swallow therapy. Treat spasticity, dystonia, restless legs, sleep disorders and depression; levodopa helps parkinsonian features. Genetic counselling is essential.
det.prognosis: Progressive, with wheelchair use often 10–15 years after onset and survival around 20 years.
pearls: Ataxia plus bulging eyes and facial fasciculations: think SCA3.
SCA3 is the commonest dominant ataxia in Thailand and much of Asia.
Parkinsonism in an ataxia family can be SCA3 or SCA2.

case.who: 41-year-old nurse from Songkhla seen in a neuromuscular clinic
case.story: Two years of widespread muscle aches, tiredness and poor concentration; a private clinic biopsied her left deltoid.
case.exam: Normal power, reflexes and sensation; diffuse muscle tenderness.
case.tests: CK, ESR and thyroid normal; EMG normal; deltoid biopsy shows a small cluster of PAS-positive macrophages in the fascia.
case.q: How should this biopsy finding be interpreted?
case.a: Macrophagic myofasciitis — a local tattoo of previous aluminium-adjuvanted vaccination; it does not prove a cause for her symptoms, so continue evaluating for other treatable causes.

read.where: Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Other Rare Inflammatory Myopathies

det.patho: Aluminium salts used as vaccine adjuvants are taken up by macrophages at the injection site, and in some people these macrophages persist in the epimysium and perimysium for years. The resulting lesion is well documented histologically. A proposed mechanism by which persistent aluminium causes systemic disease via translocation to the brain has been put forward by some groups, but has not been confirmed by independent epidemiological or experimental work.
det.clinical: Reported patients have widespread myalgia, arthralgia, chronic fatigue and sometimes cognitive complaints, overlapping with chronic fatigue syndrome and fibromyalgia. Objective weakness is unusual. Because only the deltoid lesion is specific and that lesion may be found in people without symptoms, the clinical entity remains disputed. Some authors include it under the controversial ASIA concept.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is histological: aggregates of large PAS-positive macrophages containing aluminium inclusions in fascia and adjacent muscle at a vaccinated site. Clinicians should still evaluate for treatable causes of myalgia and fatigue, such as hypothyroidism, polymyalgia rheumatica, myositis, metabolic myopathy and depression. Biopsy of a non-vaccinated muscle helps judge whether there is a genuine myopathy.
det.treatment: There is no proven specific treatment. Management is symptomatic, with graded activity, sleep and mood care, and pain management. Vaccination decisions should be individualised and based on the strong evidence for vaccine benefit, since no causal link to systemic illness has been established.
det.prognosis: Symptoms often persist for a long time but are not known to be progressive or life-threatening.
pearls: Biopsy the deltoid and you may find old vaccine adjuvant — always ask where the patient was vaccinated.
A histological marker is not proof of a disease mechanism.
Keep looking for treatable causes of chronic myalgia.
