case.story: Over a few weeks the centre of vision in his right eye has become blurred and door frames look bent; he now sees pictures of flowers that are not there.
case.exam: Right acuity 6/60, no RAPD, normal visual fields peripherally, macular haemorrhage on fundoscopy.
case.tests: OCT: subretinal fluid with choroidal neovascular membrane.
case.q: Is this a neurological problem, and what explains the flowers?
case.a: No — neovascular AMD (an eye disease); the visual hallucinations are Charles Bonnet syndrome from visual loss, not dementia or psychosis.

read.where: Chapter 36: Hereditary Diseases of the Retina
Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves

det.patho: AMD results from degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium, Bruch membrane and photoreceptors at the macula. Complement dysregulation (CFH variants), oxidative stress, smoking and age drive drusen formation. In neovascular disease, VEGF-driven vessels grow from the choroid beneath the retina, leaking fluid and blood.
det.clinical: This is an ophthalmological, not neurological, disease, but it is a common reason for visual complaints in older patients seen by neurologists. Central blur and distortion with preserved navigation vision are typical. Sudden worsening suggests neovascular change or haemorrhage. Visual hallucinations can lead to misdiagnosis of dementia.
det.diagnosis: Fundoscopy and OCT confirm. Neurologists should recognise that a normal pupil response, distortion on Amsler grid and macular changes point to retinal rather than optic nerve disease. Colour vision is less affected than in optic neuropathy.
det.treatment: Neovascular AMD is treated with intravitreal anti-VEGF agents (e.g. aflibercept, ranibizumab, faricimab), which preserve vision when started early. Dry AMD may benefit from antioxidant supplements (AREDS2 formula) in intermediate disease; complement inhibitors are approved in some regions for geographic atrophy. Low-vision aids and smoking cessation help.
det.prognosis: Untreated neovascular AMD leads to severe central loss; with prompt anti-VEGF therapy many maintain reading vision.
pearls: Wavy lines and central blur with a normal pupil: think macula.
Visual hallucinations with insight in an AMD patient are Charles Bonnet syndrome.
AMD is not neurological — refer urgently to ophthalmology when vision worsens quickly.

formal: Multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (glutaric aciduria type II), disorder of electron transfer flavoprotein pathway causing lipid storage myopathy and metabolic decompensation.
simple: An inherited disorder that stops the body using fats and proteins for energy, causing weakness and episodes of illness.

ab: Multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (as used here)

case.story: Muscle aches and exercise intolerance for a year; after a febrile illness he could not raise his head and vomited repeatedly.
case.exam: Drowsy but rousable, neck extensor and proximal weakness, hepatomegaly.
case.tests: Glucose 2.5 mmol/L, ammonia raised, CK 2,500 U/L; acylcarnitines show multiple chain lengths raised; ETFDH variants found.
case.q: What is the acute and long-term treatment?
case.a: MADD: IV glucose and avoid fasting acutely, then riboflavin with carnitine and CoQ10, and a fat-moderated diet.

det.patho: Electron transfer flavoprotein (ETF) and its oxidoreductase (ETF-QO) carry electrons from multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenases into the respiratory chain. Defects block oxidation of fatty acids and several amino acids, causing lipid accumulation in muscle and toxic organic acids. Some ETFDH variants impair flavin binding, explaining riboflavin responsiveness.
det.clinical: As defined here, MAD deficiency means MADD. Severe neonatal forms present with acidosis, hypoglycaemia and sometimes congenital anomalies. Late-onset forms in children and adults present with fluctuating proximal weakness, dropped head and episodes of metabolic decompensation after fasting or illness. Users should be aware that 'MAD deficiency' more often refers to myoadenylate deaminase deficiency in muscle literature.
det.diagnosis: Acylcarnitines and urine organic acids, ideally during an episode, show a characteristic multi-chain pattern. Biopsy reveals lipid storage. Genetic testing of ETFA, ETFB and ETFDH confirms. Clarify which 'MAD' is meant when reading referral letters.
det.treatment: Riboflavin is first-line for late-onset forms, often combined with carnitine and coenzyme Q10. Avoid fasting, treat illness promptly with carbohydrate, and moderate dietary fat and protein. Severe neonatal forms require intensive metabolic care.
det.prognosis: Late-onset riboflavin-responsive forms have an excellent outlook; neonatal forms are often fatal.
pearls: Check what 'MAD' means: MADD versus myoadenylate deaminase deficiency.
Dropped head with lipid storage: give riboflavin.
Acylcarnitines are best collected during symptoms.

name: Magnesium deficiency
formal: Hypomagnesaemia causing neuromuscular hyperexcitability: tremor, tetany, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, seizures and arrhythmias; often with hypocalcaemia and hypokalaemia, due to alcohol, diuretics or PPIs.
simple: Low magnesium in the blood, causing muscle cramps, twitching, tremor and sometimes seizures.
th: แมกนีเซียมในเลือดต่ำทำให้ระบบประสาทและกล้ามเนื้อไวเกิน มีมือสั่น เกร็ง (tetany) รีเฟล็กซ์ไว กระตุก ชัก และหัวใจเต้นผิดจังหวะ มักพบร่วมกับแคลเซียมและโพแทสเซียมต่ำ จากสุรา ยาขับปัสสาวะ หรือ PPI
tempoNote: Develops over days to weeks; acute seizures or arrhythmia when severe
feat: Tremor, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm, positive Chvostek and Trousseau signs
Hyperreflexia, myoclonus, and generalised seizures
Confusion, agitation, and occasionally ataxia with vertical (often downbeat) nystagmus
Torsades de pointes and other arrhythmias
Refractory hypocalcaemia and hypokalaemia that will not correct until magnesium is replaced
inv: Serum magnesium, calcium (ionised), potassium, phosphate and PTH
ECG for QT prolongation and arrhythmia
Urinary magnesium (fractional excretion) to separate renal from gut loss

case.who: 61-year-old man from Ayutthaya on long-term omeprazole and a thiazide
case.story: One week of hand cramps, shaking and confusion, then a generalised seizure.
case.exam: Coarse tremor, positive Chvostek sign, brisk reflexes, multifocal jerks.
case.tests: Magnesium 0.3 mmol/L, calcium 1.7 mmol/L, potassium 2.9 mmol/L; ECG QTc 510 ms.
case.q: Why does his calcium fail to improve with calcium infusion alone?
case.a: Severe hypomagnesaemia blocks PTH release and action; IV magnesium sulfate must be given first, then calcium and potassium correct; stop the PPI.

read.where: Other Deficiency States Associated with Neurological Manifestations: Magnesium Deficiency (p956)

det.patho: Magnesium stabilises excitable membranes and blocks NMDA receptor channels at rest; deficiency lowers the threshold for nerve and muscle firing and enhances cortical excitability. Low magnesium also impairs PTH secretion and action, causing hypocalcaemia, and promotes renal potassium loss. Causes include alcohol use, malnutrition, diarrhoea, long-term proton pump inhibitors, loop and thiazide diuretics, aminoglycosides, cisplatin, calcineurin inhibitors, amphotericin and refeeding.
det.clinical: Mild deficiency is often silent. As levels fall below about 0.5 mmol/L, neuromuscular irritability, tremor, myoclonus, tetany and seizures appear, along with confusion or psychosis. A cerebellar picture with nystagmus is described. Cardiac arrhythmias, particularly torsades, are the most dangerous complication.
det.diagnosis: Measure serum magnesium in anyone with tetany, unexplained seizures, refractory hypocalcaemia or hypokalaemia, or arrhythmia; serum levels may underestimate total body deficit. Urinary magnesium distinguishes renal wasting from gut losses. Review medications, alcohol intake and nutritional status.
det.treatment: Severe or symptomatic deficiency (seizures, arrhythmia, tetany) is treated with IV magnesium sulfate, for example 1–2 g over 5–15 minutes for torsades or seizures, then a slower infusion; reduce doses in renal impairment and monitor reflexes and levels. Mild deficiency is replaced orally, though diarrhoea limits dosing. Correct potassium and calcium after magnesium, address the cause and give thiamine in alcohol-related cases.
det.prognosis: Neurological features usually resolve fully with correction.
pearls: Hypocalcaemia or hypokalaemia that will not correct: check magnesium.
Long-term PPI use is a common, overlooked cause.
In alcohol-related presentations, think magnesium and thiamine together.
det.thd: ภาวะแมกนีเซียมต่ำทำให้เส้นประสาทและกล้ามเนื้อไวต่อการกระตุ้น ผู้ป่วยมีมือสั่น ตะคริว เกร็ง กระตุก ชัก สับสน และหัวใจเต้นผิดจังหวะ มักพบร่วมกับแคลเซียมและโพแทสเซียมต่ำซึ่งจะแก้ไม่ขึ้นจนกว่าจะให้แมกนีเซียม สาเหตุพบบ่อยคือสุรา ท้องเสีย ยาขับปัสสาวะ และ PPI ระยะยาว รักษาด้วย magnesium sulfate ทางหลอดเลือดเมื่อมีอาการรุนแรง และแก้ไขสาเหตุ

name: Magnesium disorders
formal: Altered serum magnesium: hypomagnesaemia causes tetany, tremor, cramps and seizures while hypermagnesaemia causes areflexia and weakness.
simple: Too little or too much magnesium in the blood, causing cramps, tremor or weakness.
more: Check renal function, drugs and calcium and potassium; replace magnesium or treat toxicity with calcium and dialysis.
th: ภาวะแมกนีเซียมในเลือดผิดปกติ — ต่ำทำให้กล้ามเนื้อเกร็งกระตุก สั่น และชัก ส่วนสูงทำให้รีเฟล็กซ์หายและอ่อนแรงจนหายใจไม่พอ
tempoNote: Symptoms appear over hours to days as the level drifts; severe toxicity after IV magnesium can evolve within an hour
feat: Low Mg: tremor, cramps, carpopedal spasm, positive Chvostek or Trousseau sign, nystagmus and seizures
Low Mg drags potassium and calcium down with it, so they stay low until magnesium is replaced
High Mg: loss of deep tendon reflexes first, then flaccid weakness, drowsiness and respiratory depression
Cardiac clues: long QT and torsades with deficiency; bradycardia, hypotension and heart block with excess
Usual settings: PPIs, diuretics, alcohol, diarrhoea, cisplatin (low); renal failure, eclampsia infusion, laxatives (high)
inv: Serum magnesium together with calcium, potassium, phosphate and creatinine
ECG for QT prolongation or conduction block
Urinary magnesium excretion to separate renal wasting from gut loss when the cause is unclear

case.who: 58-year-old man from Khon Kaen on long-term omeprazole and a thiazide
case.story: Two weeks of hand cramps, shaky hands and pins and needles around the mouth; this morning he had a generalised seizure.
case.exam: Fine tremor, brisk reflexes, tapping in front of the ear makes the lip twitch, wrist spasm when a BP cuff is inflated.
case.tests: Mg 0.35 mmol/L, corrected Ca 1.85 mmol/L, K 2.9 mmol/L; QTc 510 ms.
case.q: Why will calcium and potassium replacement alone fail here?
case.a: PPI-related hypomagnesaemia — low magnesium blocks PTH release and causes renal potassium loss; give IV magnesium first and stop the PPI.

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Magnesium Deficiency

det.patho: Magnesium stabilises excitable membranes and is a cofactor for ATP-dependent pumps. When it falls, nerve and muscle fire too easily, NMDA channels lose their magnesium block, and PTH secretion and action are impaired, so calcium also drops; renal potassium wasting follows. Excess magnesium competes with calcium at the presynaptic terminal, cutting acetylcholine release and depressing the heart and brain.
det.clinical: Deficiency is common in hospital and often silent until it is severe; neuromuscular irritability, tremor, vertical nystagmus, confusion and seizures are typical, and reversible cerebellar or posterior MRI changes have been described. Torsades de pointes is the feared cardiac event. Excess is nearly always iatrogenic or renal: obstetric infusions for pre-eclampsia, magnesium-containing laxatives or enemas in kidney failure. Reflex loss is the earliest bedside warning, followed by paralysis, apnoea and cardiac arrest at very high levels.
det.diagnosis: Measure serum magnesium in anyone with unexplained tetany, seizures, arrhythmia, resistant hypokalaemia or hypocalcaemia. Serum values underestimate total body stores, so a low-normal level in a high-risk patient may still mean deficiency. A fractional excretion above about 2–4% in the face of low serum magnesium points to renal wasting. In suspected toxicity, check reflexes, respiratory rate and the level together.
det.treatment: Symptomatic deficiency is treated with IV magnesium sulfate (for example 2 g over 10–15 minutes for seizures or torsades, then a slower infusion), followed by oral repletion; correct potassium and calcium afterwards and remove the cause such as a PPI. Use lower doses and close monitoring in renal impairment. For toxicity, stop all magnesium, give IV calcium gluconate or chloride to antagonise its effect, support breathing, and use fluids with loop diuretics or haemodialysis when renal function is poor.
det.prognosis: Both states reverse fully with timely correction; deaths come from arrhythmia or respiratory arrest when the problem is missed.
pearls: Hypokalaemia or hypocalcaemia that will not correct: check and replace magnesium.
In women on magnesium infusion, lost patellar reflexes are the cue to stop and check the level.
Long-term PPI use is a frequently missed cause of severe hypomagnesaemia.
det.thd: ภาวะแมกนีเซียมต่ำทำให้เส้นประสาทและกล้ามเนื้อไวต่อการกระตุ้น เกิดตะคริว มือจีบเกร็ง สั่น และชัก มักพบร่วมกับโพแทสเซียมและแคลเซียมต่ำซึ่งจะแก้ไม่ขึ้นจนกว่าจะให้แมกนีเซียม สาเหตุพบบ่อยคือยา PPI ยาขับปัสสาวะ สุรา และท้องเสีย ส่วนแมกนีเซียมสูงมักเกิดจากการให้ยาทางหลอดเลือดหรือไตวาย ทำให้รีเฟล็กซ์หาย อ่อนแรง และหยุดหายใจ แก้ด้วย calcium gluconate และการฟอกไต

name: Malformations of cortical development (MCDs)
formal: Group of developmental disorders of neuronal proliferation, migration or organisation, including lissencephaly, heterotopia, polymicrogyria and focal cortical dysplasia; cause of drug-resistant epilepsy and developmental delay.
simple: Conditions in which the brain surface forms abnormally before birth, often causing seizures and developmental delay.
th: กลุ่มความผิดปกติแต่กำเนิดของการสร้าง การเคลื่อนที่ หรือการจัดเรียงเซลล์ประสาทในเปลือกสมอง เป็นสาเหตุสำคัญของโรคลมชักดื้อยาและพัฒนาการช้า
tempoNote: Present from before birth; seizures may start in infancy or only in adulthood (e.g. small focal cortical dysplasia or heterotopia)
feat: Seizures, often focal and drug-resistant; infantile spasms with the more severe forms
Developmental delay or intellectual disability, ranging from none to profound
Microcephaly or macrocephaly, hypotonia or spasticity, depending on the subtype
Subtypes: focal cortical dysplasia, hemimegalencephaly, heterotopia, lissencephaly, polymicrogyria, schizencephaly
May be part of a syndrome (e.g. tuberous sclerosis, congenital CMV, tubulinopathy)
inv: High-resolution epilepsy-protocol MRI (3T, thin T1/FLAIR); subtle dysplasia is easily missed on routine scans
EEG and video-EEG to tie the lesion to the seizures
Genetic testing (panel or exome) and congenital infection screen in diffuse or bilateral forms
For surgery candidates: PET, MEG or SEEG to map the epileptogenic zone

case.story: Daily brief episodes of staring with lip smacking since age 8 despite three antiseizure drugs; school grades are dropping.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination.
case.tests: Routine MRI reported normal; a 3T epilepsy-protocol MRI shows blurred grey-white junction with a funnel-shaped FLAIR signal in the right frontal lobe.
case.q: What lesion is this and what is the next management step?
case.a: Focal cortical dysplasia type II (transmantle sign); refer for epilepsy surgery work-up, as resection offers a good chance of seizure freedom.

det.patho: Cortical development proceeds through proliferation of progenitors, migration of neurons from the ventricular zone and organisation into six layers. Faults at each step give recognisable patterns: too few or too many cells (micro- or hemimegalencephaly, focal dysplasia type II via mTOR pathway variants), stalled migration (lissencephaly, heterotopia via LIS1, DCX, tubulin genes) or disordered late organisation (polymicrogyria, schizencephaly). Causes include germline and somatic variants, congenital infection such as CMV, and fetal vascular insults.
det.clinical: Presentation depends on extent: diffuse lissencephaly causes severe delay, spasms and early death, whereas a small bottom-of-sulcus dysplasia may cause only focal seizures beginning in childhood or adult life. Bilateral perisylvian polymicrogyria gives pseudobulbar palsy with oromotor problems. Periventricular nodular heterotopia, often FLNA-related in females, may present with seizures in an otherwise normal adult and can be linked to cardiovascular and connective tissue issues. Focal dysplasia is the most common lesion in children having epilepsy surgery.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is radiological, so MRI quality matters: use an epilepsy protocol and re-read 'normal' scans with EEG findings in mind; post-processing (morphometry) can reveal subtle dysplasia. Classify the pattern, then look for a cause with genetic testing, CMV testing on neonatal samples and family history. Histology after resection subtypes focal dysplasia (ILAE classification).
det.treatment: Seizures are treated with antiseizure medicines, but many are refractory; after failure of two appropriate drugs, refer early for presurgical evaluation. Focal resection, hemispherotomy, or laser ablation can be curative for focal lesions. Everolimus or other mTOR inhibitors help tuberous sclerosis and are being studied in other mTORopathies. Vigabatrin or ACTH/steroids for infantile spasms, ketogenic diet and neuromodulation are options; developmental and family support matter as much.
det.prognosis: Very variable: well-localised dysplasias often do well after surgery, while diffuse malformations carry lifelong disability and refractory epilepsy.
pearls: Drug-resistant focal epilepsy with a 'normal' MRI — repeat at 3T with an epilepsy protocol.
The transmantle sign tapering toward the ventricle suggests focal cortical dysplasia type IIb.
Periventricular heterotopia in a woman: think FLNA and ask about valve and aortic disease.
det.thd: Malformations of cortical development คือความผิดปกติแต่กำเนิดของเปลือกสมอง เกิดจากเซลล์ประสาทแบ่งตัว เคลื่อนที่ หรือจัดเรียงผิดพลาด เช่น focal cortical dysplasia, heterotopia, lissencephaly และ polymicrogyria ผู้ป่วยมักชักดื้อยาและอาจมีพัฒนาการช้า การวินิจฉัยต้องใช้ MRI แบบเฉพาะสำหรับโรคลมชัก ร่วมกับ EEG และตรวจยีน หากชักดื้อยาและรอยโรคเฉพาะที่ ควรส่งประเมินผ่าตัดเร็ว

name: Malignant brachial plexopathy
formal: Brachial plexus infiltration by tumour (breast, lung, lymphoma) producing painful, progressive lower-trunk predominant weakness and sensory loss, often with Horner syndrome.
simple: Cancer invading the nerve network in the shoulder, causing pain, weakness and numbness in the arm and hand.
th: มะเร็งลุกลามเข้า brachial plexus เช่น มะเร็งเต้านม ปอด lymphoma ทำให้ปวดมาก อ่อนแรงและชาแขนส่วน lower trunk และ Horner syndrome
tempoNote: Progressive over weeks to months
feat: Severe shoulder and arm pain, often first
Lower trunk involvement: hand weakness, medial arm and forearm numbness
Horner syndrome is common
History of breast or lung cancer or lymphoma
Distinguish from radiation plexopathy
inv: MRI brachial plexus with contrast
PET-CT for recurrence
EMG/NCS: lower trunk axonal lesion; myokymia suggests radiation instead

case.who: 55-year-old woman from Nakhon Sawan treated for breast cancer 4 years ago
case.story: Three months of severe left shoulder pain radiating to the little finger and increasing hand weakness.
case.exam: Left Horner syndrome, weakness of hand intrinsics and finger flexors, medial forearm numbness.
case.tests: MRI shows a mass encasing the lower trunk; PET-CT avid; EMG no myokymia.
case.q: Recurrent tumour or radiation plexopathy?
case.a: Recurrent tumour: severe pain, lower trunk, Horner, mass on imaging, no myokymia.

det.patho: Tumours invade the plexus directly (apical lung) or via lymph node spread (breast, lymphoma). The lower trunk is close to axillary nodes and the lung apex.
det.clinical: Pain is the dominant early feature, followed by lower-trunk deficits and Horner syndrome. Lymphoedema can coexist.
det.diagnosis: MRI and PET-CT identify tumour; biopsy may be needed. EMG localises and helps distinguish radiation injury.
det.treatment: Oncological therapy (radiotherapy, chemotherapy, targeted agents) and aggressive pain management including neuropathic drugs and interventional procedures.
det.prognosis: Reflects advanced cancer; pain control is central to quality of life.
pearls: Painful lower-trunk plexopathy with Horner syndrome: tumour.
Painless upper-trunk plexopathy with myokymia: radiation.
PET-CT helps when MRI is equivocal.
det.thd: มะเร็งลุกลามเข้า brachial plexus มักเป็นมะเร็งเต้านม ปอด และ lymphoma ทำให้ปวดไหล่และแขนมาก ตามด้วยมืออ่อนแรงชาด้านใน และ Horner syndrome ต้องแยกจาก radiation plexopathy ซึ่งมักไม่ปวดและมี myokymia ตรวจด้วย MRI และ PET-CT รักษามะเร็งร่วมกับคุมปวด

name: Malignant hyperthermia
formal: Pharmacogenetic hypermetabolic crisis of skeletal muscle, mostly from RYR1 variants, triggered by volatile anaesthetics or succinylcholine, causing hyperthermia, rigidity and rhabdomyolysis.
simple: A dangerous reaction to certain anaesthetic drugs where muscles overheat and stiffen, caused by an inherited tendency.
more: Treat with immediate dantrolene, cooling and stopping triggers; test with caffeine-halothane contracture or genetics. Autosomal dominant; relatives need counselling.
th: ภาวะกล้ามเนื้อเผาผลาญพลังงานเกินแบบเฉียบพลันในผู้มีพันธุกรรมไว เมื่อได้ยาดมสลบชนิดระเหยหรือ succinylcholine ทำให้ CO2 ในลมหายใจออกสูง กล้ามเนื้อแข็ง ไข้สูง และกล้ามเนื้อสลาย ต้องให้ dantrolene ทันที
tempoNote: Crisis develops within minutes to a few hours of trigger exposure during or just after anaesthesia; between exposures the person is usually well
feat: Unexplained climb in end-tidal CO2 despite raised ventilation is often the first warning
Masseter spasm after succinylcholine, then generalised rigidity and tachycardia
Temperature rise is frequently a late sign; mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis
Hyperkalaemia, arrhythmia, myoglobinuria and very high CK as muscle breaks down
Autosomal dominant susceptibility (mostly RYR1, less often CACNA1S or STAC3); patients look normal between events
inv: Arterial blood gas, potassium, CK, myoglobin, coagulation and renal function during the crisis
After recovery: genetic testing of RYR1 and CACNA1S in the patient and relatives
In vitro caffeine-halothane contracture test on fresh muscle when genetics is inconclusive

case.who: 19-year-old man at a provincial hospital in Khon Kaen
case.story: During appendicectomy under sevoflurane, the anaesthetist sees end-tidal CO2 rise from 38 to 70 mmHg within 15 minutes despite doubling minute ventilation.
case.exam: Jaw remains tight, heart rate 150, limbs rigid, skin hot; core temperature climbing by about 1 °C every 10 minutes.
case.tests: pH 7.08, PaCO2 85 mmHg, K 6.8 mmol/L; CK the next day above 40,000 U/L with dark urine.
case.q: What must be done in the operating room right now?
case.a: Malignant hyperthermia: stop volatile agents, hyperventilate with 100% oxygen, give IV dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg repeated until controlled, cool and treat hyperkalaemia; later refer for RYR1 testing and family counselling.

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Malignant Hyperthermia
Chapter 36 Abnormalities of Thermal Regulation and the Nervous System

det.patho: Abnormal ryanodine receptor or dihydropyridine receptor channels let calcium leak uncontrollably from the sarcoplasmic reticulum when exposed to halogenated volatile agents or succinylcholine. The resulting sustained contraction and ATP consumption generate heat, CO2 and lactate and finally rupture muscle membranes. Susceptibility is inherited dominantly with variable penetrance, so a previous uneventful anaesthetic does not exclude risk.
det.clinical: The crisis can begin at induction or be delayed until late in the case or recovery room. Early clues are hypercarbia, tachycardia and masseter rigidity; hyperthermia, arrhythmia, rhabdomyolysis, renal failure and disseminated intravascular coagulation follow if untreated. Some RYR1 carriers also have exertional rhabdomyolysis or heat stroke, and congenital myopathies such as central core disease carry the same risk.
det.diagnosis: It is a bedside clinical diagnosis made during anaesthesia; treatment should never wait for tests. Clinical grading scales help retrospectively. Afterwards, a pathogenic RYR1 or CACNA1S variant confirms susceptibility, whereas a negative genetic result needs a contracture test on muscle from a specialised centre. Exclude sepsis, thyroid storm, phaeochromocytoma, inadequate anaesthesia and equipment faults.
det.treatment: Stop triggers, change to non-triggering anaesthesia (total IV), give 100% oxygen with high ventilation and IV dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg, repeating until signs settle (some need more than 10 mg/kg in total). Treat hyperkalaemia without calcium channel blockers, cool actively, maintain urine output and monitor in ICU for at least a day because recrudescence occurs. Susceptible people should carry an alert card; future anaesthesia uses trigger-free techniques, while local and most IV agents are safe.
det.prognosis: Mortality has fallen to a few percent where dantrolene is available promptly; delay sharply increases death and organ damage.
pearls: Rising end-tidal CO2 that ventilation cannot correct is the earliest and most reliable sign.
Every theatre that uses volatile agents must stock dantrolene.
Ask about family anaesthetic deaths before any general anaesthetic.
det.thd: Malignant hyperthermia เกิดจากช่องปล่อยแคลเซียมในกล้ามเนื้อผิดปกติทางพันธุกรรม (ส่วนใหญ่ยีน RYR1) เมื่อได้ยาดมสลบชนิดระเหยหรือ succinylcholine กล้ามเนื้อจะหดตัวไม่หยุด สัญญาณแรกคือ end-tidal CO2 สูงขึ้นเรื่อย ๆ ตามด้วยกรามแข็ง หัวใจเต้นเร็ว ไข้สูง โพแทสเซียมสูง และกล้ามเนื้อสลาย การรักษาคือหยุดยากระตุ้นและให้ dantrolene ทางหลอดเลือดดำทันที พร้อมลดอุณหภูมิ หลังหายแล้วควรตรวจยีนและแนะนำญาติ

det.patho: When most of the MCA territory dies, cytotoxic oedema develops in the first hours, followed by vasogenic oedema as the blood-brain barrier breaks down. The swollen hemisphere has no room in the rigid skull, so intracranial pressure rises, perfusion falls in the surviving tissue and brain shifts across the midline or through the tentorium. Young brains without atrophy have less spare space and decompensate earlier.
det.clinical: Patients start with a full hemispheric syndrome and a high NIHSS (often above 15–20 for dominant lesions). Over the next one to five days drowsiness deepens, vomiting may appear, and the ipsilateral pupil eventually enlarges. Deterioration often happens at night or at weekends, so staff need clear escalation rules. Survivors almost always have severe hemiparesis; dominant-side lesions leave significant aphasia.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical-radiological: a large MCA infarct plus decreasing consciousness and imaging mass effect. Predictors include early CT hypodensity in more than half the territory, additional ACA or PCA involvement, ICA terminus occlusion and large diffusion lesion volume. Repeat imaging when the patient worsens to exclude haemorrhagic transformation or hydrocephalus. Communicate early with neurosurgery once a high-risk infarct is recognised.
det.treatment: Give reperfusion therapy (IV thrombolysis, thrombectomy) when eligible, because restoring flow is the best prevention. Supportive care: head of bed about 30 degrees, normothermia, normoglycaemia, normal sodium, avoid hypotonic fluids; osmotherapy (mannitol or hypertonic saline) and brief hyperventilation only bridge to definitive care. Decompressive hemicraniectomy within 48 hours reduces death substantially in patients up to 60 years, and trials also show benefit beyond 60 at the cost of more survivors with severe disability. Decisions must reflect patient values; steroids are not helpful.
det.prognosis: Surgery roughly halves mortality, but many survivors remain dependent (mRS 4); outcome is better in younger patients and non-dominant lesions.
pearls: A large MCA stroke that gets sleepier on day 1–2 is swelling until proven otherwise; call neurosurgery early.
Do not wait for a blown pupil before discussing hemicraniectomy.
Osmotherapy buys time but does not change the outcome of malignant oedema.
det.thd: Malignant MCA infarction คือสมองขาดเลือดบริเวณ MCA ขนาดใหญ่ที่บวมมากขึ้นในวันที่ 2–5 จนเกิด herniation ผู้ป่วยอัมพาตครึ่งซีกรุนแรงแล้วซึมลงเรื่อย ๆ CT พบรอยขาดเลือดกว้างและเส้นกลางเลื่อน การรักษาที่ได้ผลคือผ่าตัดเปิดกะโหลก (decompressive hemicraniectomy) ภายใน 48 ชั่วโมงในผู้ป่วยที่เหมาะสม ร่วมกับดูแลประคับประคองใน ICU และพูดคุยเป้าหมายการรักษากับครอบครัว

det.patho: Melanocytes arise from the neural crest, which may explain the tumour's strong affinity for nervous tissue. Melanoma spreads haematogenously and tends to bleed because the deposits are highly vascular. Primary CNS melanocytic tumours arise from leptomeningeal melanocytes; neurocutaneous melanosis is a mosaic NRAS-driven disorder with large congenital naevi and meningeal melanocytes.
det.clinical: Brain metastases develop in a substantial share of patients with advanced melanoma and may be the first sign of relapse. Typical presentations are headache, seizure, focal weakness, cognitive change or sudden haemorrhage. Leptomeningeal involvement causes multiple cranial nerve palsies, hydrocephalus and back or limb pain. In Thailand acral and mucosal melanomas are relatively common, so look at soles, nails and mucosa.
det.diagnosis: Contrast MRI is the key study; melanin and blood both shorten T1, making lesions bright before contrast. Systemic staging helps choose between biopsy sites. Tissue confirms melanoma (S100, SOX10, HMB-45, Melan-A) and mutational status. Exclude abscess or primary brain tumour when there is no known cancer.
det.treatment: Management is multidisciplinary. Stereotactic radiosurgery treats a limited number of lesions; surgery is used for large symptomatic or bleeding lesions. Combination immune checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1 plus anti-CTLA-4) and, for BRAF V600-mutant tumours, BRAF plus MEK inhibitors achieve meaningful intracranial responses. Steroids reduce oedema but may blunt immunotherapy; levetiracetam is used for seizures.
det.prognosis: Previously survival was a few months; with modern immunotherapy a subset of asymptomatic patients achieve durable intracranial control.
pearls: Haemorrhagic brain metastases: think melanoma, renal cell, thyroid and choriocarcinoma.
T1-bright lesions before contrast suggest melanin or blood.
Examine soles, nails and mucosa in Thai patients with unknown primary.

name: Manganese poisoning
formal: Chronic exposure to manganese (mining, welding, parenteral nutrition) causing basal ganglia deposition with T1 pallidal hyperintensity and a levodopa-poor parkinsonism with dystonia and psychiatric features.
simple: Poisoning from too much manganese, for example in welders, causing movement problems like Parkinson disease and mood changes.
more: Excess manganese exposure causing basal ganglia deposition with T1 pallidal hyperintensity and a levodopa-poor parkinsonism with dystonia and psychiatric features.
th: ภาวะพิษแมงกานีสสะสมที่ globus pallidus จากงานเชื่อมโลหะ เหมือง สารอาหารทางหลอดเลือด หรือยาเสพติดที่ผลิตด้วย permanganate ทำให้ parkinsonism ที่ไม่ค่อยตอบสนองต่อ levodopa ร่วมกับ dystonia และอาการทางจิต
tempoNote: Develops over months to years of exposure; often keeps progressing for years even after exposure stops
feat: Symmetric parkinsonism with early gait and balance problems and little rest tremor
Characteristic high-stepping, tiptoe 'cock-walk' gait and dystonia, with falls backwards
Hypophonic, slurred speech; facial grimacing
Psychiatric prodrome: irritability, compulsive behaviour, hallucinations ('manganese madness')
Poor or short-lived response to levodopa
inv: MRI: symmetric T1 hyperintensity of the globus pallidus (also seen in liver failure and parenteral nutrition)
Whole-blood manganese (reflects recent exposure only); liver function tests
DAT-SPECT usually normal or near-normal, unlike Parkinson disease
Consider SLC30A10 or SLC39A14 testing in children or with polycythaemia and liver disease

case.who: 44-year-old welder from a shipyard in Chonburi
case.story: Over two years he has become slow and irritable, falls backwards and walks on his toes; a trial of levodopa did nothing.
case.exam: Symmetric bradykinesia and rigidity, facial grimacing, dystonic toe-walking gait with poor postural reflexes, no rest tremor.
case.tests: Bright globus pallidus on T1 MRI bilaterally; blood manganese raised; DAT-SPECT normal.
case.q: Why is levodopa failing here?
case.a: Manganese damages the pallidum downstream of the nigral dopamine neurons, so presynaptic dopamine replacement helps little; remove exposure and consider chelation.

det.patho: Inhaled manganese fumes reach the brain directly, and ingested or infused manganese accumulates when biliary excretion fails. It concentrates in the globus pallidus, striatum and substantia nigra pars reticulata and causes oxidative and mitochondrial injury, sparing the nigrostriatal dopaminergic terminals to a large degree. Inherited forms from SLC30A10 or SLC39A14 transporter defects cause childhood dystonia with hypermanganesaemia.
det.clinical: Classic occupational cases occur in miners, smelters and welders; recreational injection of homemade methcathinone (ephedrone) prepared with permanganate and long-term parenteral nutrition are other sources. Behavioural change may precede motor signs. The motor picture combines symmetric parkinsonism, dystonia, dysarthria and a distinctive gait, and symptoms can continue to worsen after removal from exposure.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on an exposure history, compatible clinical features and pallidal T1 hyperintensity. Blood and urine levels fluctuate and correlate poorly with brain burden; MRI signal fades months after exposure ends while symptoms may persist. Exclude liver disease, Wilson disease and atypical parkinsonism.
det.treatment: Stop exposure first, including adjusting manganese in parenteral nutrition. Chelation with calcium disodium EDTA lowers blood levels but neurological benefit is inconsistent; para-aminosalicylic acid has been reported helpful in small series. Levodopa can be tried but rarely helps much. Inherited transporter forms respond to chelation plus iron supplementation if started early.
det.prognosis: Established neurological deficits are usually permanent and may progress slowly despite cessation of exposure.
pearls: Bright pallidum on T1 + parkinsonism: ask about welding, mining, parenteral nutrition, liver disease and drug use.
Cock-walk gait and early backward falls with little tremor suggest manganism over Parkinson disease.
Normal DAT-SPECT helps separate it from degenerative parkinsonism.

det.patho: Bipolar disorder is a highly heritable disorder of mood regulation involving frontolimbic circuits, circadian rhythm and many genes of small effect. Secondary mania arises when lesions or drugs disrupt orbitofrontal, basotemporal, caudate or thalamic links, usually on the right side, often in people with a family history or pre-existing brain atrophy. Corticosteroids, dopaminergic drugs, antidepressants and stimulants can precipitate mania in susceptible patients.
det.clinical: Primary bipolar I disorder has at least one manic episode; bipolar II has hypomania with major depression. Secondary mania after stroke or head injury looks very like primary mania, with high mood, pressured speech and grandiosity, but tends to occur later in life and with fewer prior mood episodes. Red flags for a neurological cause are first onset after about 50, confusion, focal signs, seizures, headache or a new drug. Lithium toxicity can present to neurology with coarse tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, myoclonus and confusion, sometimes leaving permanent cerebellar damage.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis uses DSM-5-TR criteria, with secondary or drug-induced labels used when a cause is clear. A careful history from relatives, drug review and toxicology come first. Brain MRI, HIV and syphilis serology, thyroid tests and, where encephalitis is possible, EEG and CSF with antibodies are indicated in late or atypical onset. Distinguish mania from delirium, frontal disinhibition and agitation from akathisia.
det.treatment: Acute mania is treated with lithium, valproate or an atypical antipsychotic (quetiapine, olanzapine, risperidone, aripiprazole), with removal of the precipitant in secondary cases. Valproate is avoided in women who could become pregnant because of teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risk unless no alternative works. Lithium needs level, renal and thyroid monitoring and is risky with dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and thiazides. Bipolar depression responds to quetiapine, lurasidone, cariprazine or lamotrigine rather than antidepressants alone.
det.prognosis: Primary bipolar disorder is relapsing and lifelong, but maintenance treatment cuts relapse and suicide; secondary mania often settles over weeks to months once the cause is treated.
pearls: A first manic episode in an older adult is a neurological work-up until proven otherwise.
Right-sided thalamic, caudate and orbitofrontal lesions are the classic substrates of post-stroke mania.
Coarse tremor, ataxia and confusion in a patient on lithium need an urgent level, even if the dose has not changed.

name: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD)

simple: An inherited disorder in which the body cannot process certain amino acids, causing sweet-smelling urine, poor feeding and brain damage if untreated.

feat: Healthy at birth, then poor feeding, lethargy and vomiting by days 4–7
Sweet burnt-sugar odour of urine, sweat or earwax
Alternating hypertonia and hypotonia, 'fencing' or bicycling movements, seizures, coma
Leucine-driven cerebral oedema during crises; later dystonia, learning and psychiatric problems if control is poor

det.patho: Biallelic variants in subunits of the mitochondrial branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex block oxidation of leucine, isoleucine and valine. Leucine and its ketoacid cross into the brain, competing with other amino acids for transport and depleting neurotransmitter precursors, while osmotic shifts cause intramyelinic oedema. Severity depends on residual enzyme activity; a few forms respond to thiamine.
det.clinical: Classic MSUD presents with neonatal encephalopathy that progresses to coma and death without treatment. Intermediate and intermittent variants show developmental delay or recurrent ataxia and encephalopathy with infections, surgery or catabolism. Even treated patients carry risks of attention, mood and anxiety disorders, and acute leucine spikes may cause brain swelling at any age.
det.diagnosis: Alloisoleucine on plasma amino acids is pathognomonic. Newborn screening catches most classic cases, but the baby may already be unwell before results return. Genetic testing confirms the subtype and helps family planning. Exclude sepsis and other inborn errors in any neonate who deteriorates after an initial well period.
det.treatment: Acute crises need anabolism: high glucose (with insulin if needed), lipids and a branched-chain-free formula, isoleucine and valine supplements, and management of cerebral oedema; dialysis removes leucine fastest. Long-term care is a lifelong leucine-restricted diet with frequent level monitoring and a written sick-day plan. A trial of thiamine is reasonable. Liver transplantation effectively cures the metabolic defect and is increasingly used; the explanted liver can serve as a domino graft.
det.prognosis: With newborn screening and good metabolic control, many achieve normal or near-normal intelligence; delayed diagnosis or repeated crises leave lasting disability.
pearls: Well baby for a few days, then encephalopathy with ketosis and sweet odour: think MSUD.
Alloisoleucine is the diagnostic marker.
Restricted diffusion in myelinated tracts on neonatal MRI is a strong imaging clue.
det.thd: MSUD เป็นโรคยีนด้อยที่ร่างกายย่อยกรดอะมิโนสายกิ่งไม่ได้ ทำให้ leucine คั่งและเป็นพิษต่อสมอง ทารกแข็งแรงช่วงแรกแล้วเริ่มซึม ดูดนมไม่ดี เกร็ง ชัก และปัสสาวะมีกลิ่นหวานเหมือนน้ำเชื่อม ตรวจพบ alloisoleucine ในเลือดเป็นตัวยืนยัน รักษาภาวะวิกฤตด้วยกลูโคสพลังงานสูง สูตรนมไม่มีกรดอะมิโนสายกิ่ง และฟอกเลือดถ้าจำเป็น ระยะยาวคุมอาหารตลอดชีวิตหรือพิจารณาปลูกถ่ายตับ

name: Marchiafava–Bignami syndrome
formal: Demyelination and necrosis of the corpus callosum, classically in chronic alcoholism, presenting with confusion, dementia, seizures, apraxia or disconnection signs; MRI shows callosal lesions.
simple: A rare brain disease, mostly in heavy drinkers, damaging the bundle of fibres joining the two hemispheres and causing confusion and dementia.
more: Diagnosis by MRI showing T2 or DWI hyperintensity with swelling of corpus callosum; treat with high-dose thiamine, B-complex vitamins and nutrition support, plus steroids sometimes. Prognosis varies from death to recovery.
th: การเสื่อมของปลอกประสาทและเนื้อตายที่คอร์ปัส คัลโลซัม พบในผู้ดื่มสุราเรื้อรังหรือขาดสารอาหาร ทำให้สับสน ซึม ชัก และอาการสมองสองซีกขาดการเชื่อมต่อ
tempoNote: Acute form with coma and seizures over days; subacute or chronic forms with progressive confusion and disconnection over weeks to months
feat: Long-standing heavy drinking or malnutrition (rarely diabetes or other causes)
Acute confusion, drowsiness to coma, seizures, dysarthria and gait disturbance
Interhemispheric disconnection: left-hand apraxia, alien hand, inability to name objects in the left hand
Often coexists with Wernicke encephalopathy or osmotic demyelination
inv: MRI: swollen T2/FLAIR-bright corpus callosum (body and splenium), restricted diffusion acutely, later thinning or cysts
Thiamine level if available, glucose, sodium, liver function and alcohol history
EEG if seizures or fluctuating consciousness

case.who: 52-year-old man from Ubon Ratchathani, drinking local rice spirit daily for 25 years
case.story: Brought in after three days of increasing confusion, slurred speech and two seizures; he has eaten little for weeks.
case.exam: Drowsy and disoriented, unable to carry out commands with the left hand, mild ataxia, no meningism.
case.tests: MRI shows swollen high-T2 signal throughout the corpus callosum with restricted diffusion; sodium 136 mmol/L.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what should be given immediately?
case.a: Marchiafava–Bignami disease; give high-dose IV thiamine with B vitamins and nutrition at once, since early treatment improves outcome.

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Alcohol Abuse

det.patho: The cause is not fully settled; most cases occur with chronic alcohol use and malnutrition, and thiamine and other B-vitamin deficiency are thought central, possibly with osmotic and cytotoxic oedema. Pathology shows demyelination and necrosis of the middle layers of the corpus callosum, sometimes extending into adjacent white matter. It was first reported in Italian men who drank red wine, but any alcohol and some non-alcoholic malnourished patients can be affected.
det.clinical: Two broad pictures are described: type A with coma, seizures and whole-callosum involvement, and type B with partial lesions, milder confusion and better outcomes. Chronic cases show dementia, personality change and slowly emerging disconnection signs such as left-hand ideomotor apraxia or tactile anomia. Gait disorder, dysarthria and primitive reflexes are frequent. Because symptoms overlap with intoxication, withdrawal and Wernicke disease, it is easily missed without MRI.
det.diagnosis: MRI is the key test: symmetrical swelling and T2/FLAIR hyperintensity of the callosal body or splenium, often with diffusion restriction in the acute phase, evolving to atrophy and cavitation. Lateral cortical involvement suggests a worse outlook. Exclude reversible splenial lesion syndrome (seen with infection, antiseizure drugs, hypoglycaemia), demyelinating disease, lymphoma and infarction by clinical context and follow-up imaging.
det.treatment: Give parenteral thiamine promptly at high dose (as for Wernicke encephalopathy), plus folate and B-complex, and correct nutrition and electrolytes carefully. Corticosteroids have been used in some reports without proven benefit. Treat seizures and alcohol withdrawal, and arrange rehabilitation and support for abstinence.
det.prognosis: Ranges from death or severe disability in the comatose type to good recovery when treated early; outcomes have improved with prompt thiamine.
pearls: Malnourished drinker with confusion and a bright, swollen corpus callosum on MRI — treat with thiamine now.
Left-hand apraxia or tactile naming failure points to callosal disconnection.
A small isolated splenial lesion in a febrile or seizing patient is more often a transient cytotoxic lesion than MBD.
det.thd: Marchiafava–Bignami คือโรคที่คอร์ปัส คัลโลซัมเสื่อมและตาย มักพบในผู้ดื่มสุราเรื้อรังร่วมกับขาดสารอาหารโดยเฉพาะวิตามินบี ผู้ป่วยมีอาการสับสน ซึม ชัก พูดไม่ชัด และอาการสมองสองซีกขาดการเชื่อมต่อ เช่น มือซ้ายทำตามสั่งไม่ได้ MRI พบคอร์ปัส คัลโลซัมบวมและสัญญาณสูง ควรให้ thiamine ขนาดสูงทางหลอดเลือดทันทีร่วมกับวิตามินและอาหาร

Follows rapid sodium correction; pontine and extrapontine lesions

name: Marin–Amat syndrome
formal: Inverse jaw-winking phenomenon, where mouth opening causes ipsilateral eyelid closure, usually after facial nerve palsy from aberrant regeneration.
simple: After facial weakness, the eye closes when the person opens their mouth because nerves have regrown in the wrong pattern.
th: เปลือกตาปิดเองข้างเดียวกันเมื่ออ้าปาก มักเกิดหลังอัมพาตเส้นประสาทใบหน้าจากการงอกใหม่ผิดทาง
tempoNote: Appears months after facial palsy and persists
feat: Involuntary ipsilateral eyelid closure on mouth opening or chewing
Follows peripheral facial palsy, often Bell's palsy
Other synkinesis may coexist
Opposite of Marcus Gunn jaw-winking, in which the lid elevates
Not a disease itself but a sequel of aberrant facial nerve regeneration
inv: Clinical diagnosis
Facial EMG or blink reflex studies if uncertain

case.story: Right Bell's palsy a year ago, mostly recovered; now her right eye closes whenever she opens her mouth to eat.
case.exam: Mild residual right facial weakness; right eye narrows with jaw opening.
case.tests: None required.
case.q: What causes this?
case.a: Aberrant regeneration of facial nerve fibres (Marin–Amat syndrome).

det.patho: After facial nerve injury regenerating axons misroute, so fibres intended for lower-face muscles reach orbicularis oculi. Movements of the mouth therefore also close the eye. Trigeminal involvement is not required, despite the jaw-movement trigger.
det.clinical: Eyelid narrowing or closure occurs with mouth opening, chewing or smiling, interfering with eating and vision. Often accompanied by other facial synkinesis.
det.diagnosis: Clinical, based on history of facial palsy and observed synkinesis.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin to orbicularis oculi, facial retraining physiotherapy; selective neurolysis or myectomy in refractory cases.
det.prognosis: Persistent but manageable with treatment.
pearls: Lid closes on jaw opening = inverse Marcus Gunn = Marin–Amat.
It follows facial palsy, not congenital trigeminal-oculomotor miswiring.
Botulinum toxin is effective.
det.thd: Marin–Amat syndrome คือเปลือกตาปิดเองเมื่ออ้าปาก มักเกิดหลังอัมพาตใบหน้า เช่น Bell’s palsy เพราะใยประสาทใบหน้างอกใหม่ผิดทาง ต่างจาก Marcus Gunn ที่เปลือกตายกขึ้น วินิจฉัยจากอาการ รักษาด้วย botulinum toxin และกายภาพใบหน้า

ddx.pt: Spontaneous involuntary contractions, not tied to jaw movement
Bilateral involuntary eye closure
The preceding cause; acute facial weakness

name: Maternal phenylketonuria syndrome
formal: Fetal damage from uncontrolled maternal hyperphenylalaninaemia in pregnancy, causing microcephaly, intellectual disability, congenital heart disease and growth restriction.
simple: Harm to a baby when a mother with phenylketonuria does not keep her diet controlled in pregnancy, causing a small head and learning problems.
th: ความผิดปกติของทารกจากมารดาเป็น PKU และระดับ phenylalanine สูงระหว่างตั้งครรภ์ ทำให้ทารกศีรษะเล็ก บกพร่องทางสติปัญญา และหัวใจพิการ
tempoNote: Damage occurs in utero; effects are present at birth and permanent
feat: Affected child does not have PKU; injury comes from high maternal phenylalanine crossing the placenta
Microcephaly, intellectual disability, growth restriction
Congenital heart disease (especially with poor control in early pregnancy)
Facial features overlapping fetal alcohol syndrome
Fully preventable by strict maternal phenylalanine control before conception and throughout pregnancy
inv: Maternal plasma phenylalanine level and history of PKU or newborn screening
Infant echocardiography and head circumference
Developmental assessment

case.who: Newborn girl at a Bangkok tertiary hospital
case.story: Mother was diagnosed with PKU as a child but stopped her diet in her teens; pregnancy was unplanned.
case.exam: Head circumference below 3rd centile, low birth weight, smooth philtrum, cardiac murmur.
case.tests: Mother's phenylalanine 1,200 µmol/L in pregnancy; infant has a ventricular septal defect; infant's own newborn PKU screen normal.
case.q: Why is the baby affected if she does not have PKU?
case.a: Maternal phenylketonuria syndrome — high maternal phenylalanine is teratogenic; prevented by restarting diet before conception.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Maternal Phenylketonuria Syndrome

det.patho: Phenylalanine is actively transported across the placenta, so fetal levels exceed maternal levels. High concentrations impair neuronal growth, myelination and heart development. The risk is dose-dependent, and harm is greatest when maternal levels are high during organogenesis in the first trimester.
det.clinical: Infants are born small, with microcephaly and often dysmorphic facial features; congenital heart defects occur in a proportion. Development is globally delayed and intellectual disability is common. The children themselves usually have normal phenylalanine metabolism, being heterozygous carriers.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis depends on identifying maternal PKU or hyperphenylalaninaemia, sometimes in women who were lost to follow-up after childhood. Measuring maternal phenylalanine is advised when a baby has unexplained microcephaly and heart defects. The infant's newborn screen is usually normal.
det.treatment: Prevention is the key: women with PKU should resume a phenylalanine-restricted diet and reach target levels (commonly 120–360 µmol/L) before conception and maintain them through pregnancy. Sapropterin can help responsive women. Once a child is affected, management is supportive, with cardiac care and developmental services.
det.prognosis: Damage is permanent, but good maternal control from preconception leads to normal outcomes in most pregnancies.
pearls: Microcephaly in a newborn with normal PKU screening — ask about maternal PKU.
Control must be achieved before conception, not after pregnancy is detected.
Women diagnosed with PKU in childhood need lifelong follow-up and pre-pregnancy counselling.
det.thd: Maternal phenylketonuria syndrome เกิดจากมารดาเป็นโรค PKU และควบคุมระดับ phenylalanine ไม่ดีขณะตั้งครรภ์ สารนี้ผ่านรกไปทำลายสมองและหัวใจของทารก ทารกจึงศีรษะเล็ก บกพร่องทางสติปัญญา และหัวใจพิการ ทั้งที่ตัวทารกเองไม่ได้เป็น PKU ป้องกันได้โดยให้มารดากลับมาคุมอาหารให้ระดับ phenylalanine ต่ำก่อนตั้งครรภ์และตลอดการตั้งครรภ์

Intellectual disability in boys without microcephaly; large ears, FMR1
Typical facial features and heart defects with trisomy 21 on karyotype

name: May White syndrome
formal: Rare syndrome of progressive myoclonic epilepsy with ataxia and sensorineural hearing loss, often with lipomas, associated with mitochondrial tRNA mutations.
simple: A rare inherited condition causing jerky muscle movements, seizures, poor balance, deafness and fatty lumps under the skin.
th: กลุ่มอาการหายากที่ถ่ายทอดทางมารดา มีอาการกระตุกแบบ myoclonus ชัก เดินเซ และหูหนวกประสาท อาจมีก้อนไขมันใต้ผิวหนัง สัมพันธ์กับความผิดปกติของ mitochondrial tRNA
tempoNote: Onset usually in childhood to early adulthood with slow progression over years
feat: Action myoclonus and generalised seizures
Progressive cerebellar ataxia
Bilateral sensorineural hearing loss
Sometimes multiple lipomas, short stature or myopathy; affected relatives on the maternal side
inv: Mitochondrial DNA testing (blood, urine sediment or muscle) for tRNA variants, including MERRF-type changes
Serum and CSF lactate; audiometry; EEG
Muscle biopsy for ragged-red or COX-negative fibres if blood testing is negative

case.story: Jerky hands that spill her drinks since her teens, two convulsions, and worsening hearing; her mother and maternal uncle are deaf and unsteady.
case.exam: Action myoclonus, mild limb ataxia, bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, soft lumps on the neck.
case.tests: Resting lactate mildly raised; EEG generalised spike-wave; mtDNA testing shows a pathogenic tRNA variant.
case.q: What inheritance pattern does the family history suggest, and which antiseizure drug should be avoided?
case.a: Maternal (mitochondrial) inheritance; avoid valproate and prefer levetiracetam for myoclonus and seizures.

det.patho: The name comes from a 1968 report of a family with myoclonus, ataxia and deafness. Later molecular work on similar maternally inherited families found mitochondrial tRNA variants (for example in tRNA-Ser(UCN) and tRNA-Lys), which impair mitochondrial protein synthesis and energy production in cortex, cerebellum, cochlea and muscle. Whether it is a distinct entity or simply a MERRF-like phenotype is uncertain.
det.clinical: Reported patients develop action myoclonus, generalised seizures, cerebellar ataxia and progressive hearing loss, sometimes with lipomas, myopathy or cardiomyopathy. Severity varies within families because of heteroplasmy, so some relatives have only deafness or diabetes. Course is slowly progressive; cognitive decline may appear later.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in a progressive myoclonic epilepsy with deafness and a maternal family history. Test mtDNA, ideally from urine or muscle when blood heteroplasmy is low, and check lactate, hearing, ECG and glucose. Muscle histology may show ragged-red fibres. Exclude other progressive myoclonic epilepsies and acquired causes.
det.treatment: No disease-specific therapy exists. Levetiracetam, clonazepam, piracetam or zonisamide help myoclonus; avoid valproate, which can worsen mitochondrial function. Hearing aids or cochlear implants, physiotherapy, cardiac and diabetes screening, and genetic counselling for the maternal line are recommended.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive disability; limited data because very few families are reported.
pearls: Myoclonus + ataxia + deafness + maternal transmission: test mitochondrial DNA.
Treat it like MERRF clinically — avoid valproate.
det.thd: May-White syndrome เป็นกลุ่มอาการหายากที่ถ่ายทอดทางมารดา มี myoclonus ชัก เดินเซ และหูหนวกประสาท บางรายมีก้อนไขมันใต้ผิวหนัง เกิดจากความผิดปกติของ mitochondrial tRNA และหลายท่านมองว่าเป็นส่วนหนึ่งของ MERRF การวินิจฉัยอาศัยตรวจ mtDNA และ lactate ไม่มีการรักษาจำเพาะ ใช้ levetiracetam หรือ clonazepam คุมอาการกระตุก และหลีกเลี่ยง valproate

ddx.pt: Overlapping or identical picture; May-White is often now regarded as part of the MERRF spectrum
Recessive PME with stimulus-sensitive myoclonus, no deafness or lactic acidosis
Teenage PME with occipital seizures and rapid dementia; Lafora bodies on skin biopsy

aN: may white syndrome | familial myoclonus ataxia deafness | myoclonus ataxia deafness syndrome

name: MCA infarction
formal: Ischaemic stroke in the middle cerebral artery territory causing contralateral face and arm predominant weakness, sensory loss, aphasia (dominant) or neglect (non-dominant) and gaze deviation.
simple: A stroke from a blocked main brain artery, causing weakness on one side of the body, with speech or attention problems.
th: สมองขาดเลือดในเขต middle cerebral artery ทำให้อ่อนแรงและชาซีกตรงข้ามโดยเด่นที่หน้าและแขน พูดไม่ได้ (ซีกเด่น) หรือ neglect (ซีกไม่เด่น) และตามองไปด้านรอยโรค
tempoNote: Sudden onset; deficits may fluctuate in the first hours with large-vessel occlusion
feat: Contralateral face and arm weaker than leg, with cortical sensory loss
Dominant hemisphere: aphasia (Broca with superior division, Wernicke with inferior division); non-dominant: neglect, anosognosia
Eyes deviated towards the lesion and contralateral homonymous field defect
Deep (lenticulostriate) infarcts give pure motor or striatocapsular syndromes without cortical signs
Causes: cardioembolism, carotid or intracranial atherosclerosis (common in Asians), dissection
inv: Non-contrast CT immediately, ASPECTS scoring; CT angiography for large-vessel occlusion
MRI DWI to confirm extent; perfusion imaging for late-window selection
ECG and prolonged rhythm monitoring, echocardiography, carotid imaging
Glucose, lipids, HbA1c; young patients: thrombophilia and vasculitis screen as indicated

case.who: 71-year-old woman from Khon Kaen with irregular pulse
case.story: Daughter saw her suddenly drop her rice bowl and stop speaking 90 minutes ago.
case.exam: Global aphasia, right face and arm plegia, mild right leg weakness, gaze to the left, right hemianopia; NIHSS 18.
case.tests: CT: no bleed, ASPECTS 8; CTA: left M1 occlusion; ECG atrial fibrillation.
case.q: What treatment should be given now?
case.a: IV thrombolysis (alteplase or tenecteplase) and immediate mechanical thrombectomy; then anticoagulation for AF timed by infarct size.

Chapter 8 Stroke and Cerebrovascular Diseases — Anterior Circulation

Chapter 5: What is the role of imaging in acute stroke?
Chapter 19: Chemotherapy Emboli as an Iatrogenic Cause of Ischaemic Stroke Arising from a Misplaced Central Venous Access Line

det.patho: The MCA supplies most of the lateral hemisphere and, through lenticulostriate branches, the basal ganglia and internal capsule. Emboli from the heart or carotid commonly lodge in the M1 or its divisions, while intracranial atherosclerosis at M1 is a frequent cause in Thai and other Asian patients. Collateral flow from ACA and PCA leptomeningeal vessels largely determines how much tissue survives.
det.clinical: Complete stem occlusion produces the full syndrome: hemiplegia, hemisensory loss, hemianopia, gaze deviation and aphasia or neglect. Superior-division occlusion gives arm-face weakness and non-fluent aphasia; inferior-division occlusion may present with fluent aphasia or confusion and little weakness, which is easy to misread as delirium. Deep perforator infarcts cause capsular or striatocapsular syndromes. Early neurological worsening may come from clot extension, haemorrhagic transformation or oedema.
det.diagnosis: Rapid assessment with NIHSS, CT and CTA identifies occlusion and excludes haemorrhage. ASPECTS on CT estimates early ischaemic change; perfusion or DWI-FLAIR mismatch helps select patients outside standard time windows. Etiological work-up follows TOAST categories: cardiac rhythm, echo, vessel imaging and risk factors. Mimics include seizure, hypoglycaemia, migraine aura and functional weakness.
det.treatment: IV thrombolysis within 4.5 hours of last known well (or later with imaging selection) and thrombectomy for proximal occlusions up to 24 hours in selected patients, including those with large cores per recent trials. Stroke-unit care covers swallowing, blood pressure, glucose, fever and early mobilisation. Secondary prevention depends on cause: anticoagulation for AF, antiplatelets and high-intensity statin for atherosclerosis, carotid revascularisation for symptomatic stenosis.
det.prognosis: Outcome depends on infarct size, age, collateral status and speed of reperfusion; successful thrombectomy markedly increases independence.
pearls: Gaze deviation plus cortical signs suggest large-vessel occlusion; send for CTA.
Fluent aphasia without weakness can look like confusion; check language carefully.
Arm weaker than leg points to MCA; leg weaker than arm points to ACA.
det.thd: MCA infarction คือสมองขาดเลือดในเขต middle cerebral artery พบบ่อยที่สุด ผู้ป่วยอ่อนแรงและชาซีกตรงข้ามโดยเด่นที่หน้าและแขน ตามองไปด้านรอยโรค ถ้าเป็นซีกเด่นจะพูดไม่ได้ ซีกไม่เด่นจะ neglect ตรวจ CT และ CTA ทันที รักษาด้วยยาละลายลิ่มเลือดและการลากลิ่มเลือดถ้าเข้าเกณฑ์ แล้วป้องกันซ้ำตามสาเหตุ

Small deep infarct: pure motor or sensory deficit without aphasia, neglect or field loss

name: MCAD deficiency
formal: Autosomal recessive medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (ACADM), a fatty-acid oxidation disorder causing fasting-induced hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and encephalopathy.
simple: An inherited problem burning fats for energy, so going without food can cause low blood sugar and illness, mainly in children.
more: Newborn screening finds elevated octanoylcarnitine; treated by avoiding fasting and giving sugars in illness. With prevention outlook is excellent.
th: โรคยีนด้อยที่เผาผลาญกรดไขมันสายกลางไม่ได้ เมื่ออดอาหารหรือป่วยจะน้ำตาลต่ำโดยไม่มีคีโตน ซึม ชัก และอาจเสียชีวิตเฉียบพลัน ป้องกันได้ด้วยการไม่อดอาหารนาน
tempoNote: Normal between crises; each crisis evolves over hours during fasting, vomiting or fever, most often between 3 months and 2 years
feat: Lethargy, vomiting then seizures or coma after a long fast or a gastroenteritis
Hypoglycaemia with absent or very low ketones; hepatomegaly and raised transaminases
A first crisis can be fatal, and some infant deaths are explained only afterwards
Entirely well between episodes; many screen-detected infants never decompensate
Adult presentations occur after surgery, binge alcohol or prolonged starvation
inv: Plasma acylcarnitines: octanoylcarnitine (C8) high with raised C6 and C10:1, the newborn screening hallmark
Urine organic acids in illness: dicarboxylic aciduria plus hexanoyl- and suberylglycine with disproportionately low ketones
ACADM sequencing; critical blood and urine drawn at the time of low glucose

case.story: Vomited for two days with a cold, ate nothing overnight, and was found unrousable at dawn after a short generalised seizure.
case.exam: Drowsy, liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin, no focal deficit.
case.tests: Glucose 1.6 mmol/L, urine ketones negative, ammonia mildly raised; acylcarnitines show a marked C8 peak.
case.q: What does the missing ketone response indicate, and how is recurrence prevented?
case.a: A fatty acid oxidation defect (MCAD deficiency). Avoid prolonged fasting, start glucose drinks early in any illness and use IV dextrose when oral intake fails, guided by a written emergency plan.

det.patho: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase performs an early step in mitochondrial beta-oxidation of C6–C12 fatty acids. After glycogen is used up in a fast, the liver cannot make ketones or fuel gluconeogenesis, so glucose drops while toxic medium-chain metabolites build up. One variant (c.985A>G) accounts for most northern European cases; it is rare in Asian populations, where other ACADM variants predominate. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
det.clinical: The usual first crisis follows an infection or skipped feeds in infancy, though some present as sudden death or, rarely, in adulthood. Sequence is vomiting, drowsiness, seizures, coma and a Reye-like liver picture. Severe episodes may leave cognitive or motor sequelae, while a child kept out of fasting develops normally. Examiners ask about timing of the last meal and family history of unexplained infant death.
det.diagnosis: Tandem mass spectrometry newborn screening detects nearly all affected infants; acylcarnitines and genetic testing confirm. In an unscreened child with unexplained hypoglycaemia, take blood and urine before dextrose where this does not delay rescue. Post-mortem blood spot or bile acylcarnitines can clarify unexplained deaths. Hyperinsulinism and other fatty acid oxidation defects are the main mimics.
det.treatment: Management is preventive: fasting limits suited to age, a bedtime starch snack in some, and a sick-day plan with early glucose drinks and IV 10% dextrose if vomiting. Patients carry an emergency letter for the emergency department. Carnitine supplementation is used variably and evidence is limited. Medium-chain triglyceride formulas are avoided.
det.prognosis: Excellent once diagnosed and protected from fasting; harm comes almost entirely from the first unrecognised crisis.
pearls: Hypoglycaemia with no ketones in a child points to fatty acid oxidation disorder or hyperinsulinism.
Draw the critical sample before correcting glucose if that can be done safely.
A written sick-day letter is the most protective single measure.

det.patho: Autosomal recessive loss of muscle glycogen phosphorylase (PYGM) blocks the breakdown of muscle glycogen, so fibres cannot use their own carbohydrate stores during the first minutes of intense or isometric effort. Energy failure leads to painful contracture and fibre necrosis. As blood-borne glucose and free fatty acids reach muscle after several minutes, exercise capacity improves — the second wind. It is the commonest muscle glycogenosis; p.R50X (R49X) is frequent in Europeans, while other variants dominate in Asian populations.
det.clinical: Symptoms usually date from childhood but diagnosis is often delayed into adulthood after labels of laziness or poor fitness. Patients describe early fatigue, tachycardia, cramps and muscle locking with sprinting, lifting or carrying, and pigmenturia after heavy exertion. Slowing down briefly and then resuming allows them to continue at a better level. About a quarter develop fixed proximal weakness with age. Severe rhabdomyolysis can cause acute kidney injury, and compartment syndrome is a rare complication.
det.diagnosis: Baseline CK is raised in nearly all patients even between episodes. A non-ischaemic forearm exercise test shows a flat lactate curve with an exaggerated ammonia rise. A 12-minute cycle test demonstrates the second wind as a fall in heart rate at constant workload. PYGM sequencing is the confirmatory test and has largely replaced biopsy, which shows subsarcolemmal glycogen and absent phosphorylase staining. Exclude other glycolytic defects (e.g. PFK deficiency, with haemolysis and no second wind).
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying therapy. Regular supervised moderate aerobic training improves capacity and reduces attacks, while avoiding sudden maximal or static effort. A small sucrose drink a few minutes before planned exercise boosts tolerance, but chronic high sugar intake promotes weight gain and is not advised. Treat rhabdomyolysis with fluids and renal monitoring; warn patients about dark urine. Statins may aggravate symptoms, and anaesthetists should be informed although the malignant hyperthermia link is uncertain.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is normal; quality of life depends largely on staying active and avoiding severe rhabdomyolysis. Some fixed weakness may appear in later life.
pearls: Second wind is virtually specific for McArdle among metabolic myopathies.
Raised resting CK plus exercise-triggered pigmenturia in a young adult: think McArdle.
Forearm test: flat lactate, brisk ammonia.

det.patho: The XK gene encodes a membrane protein linked to the Kell glycoprotein on red cells and expressed in brain and muscle; it is now known to act as a lipid scramblase partner of VPS13A. Loss of XK causes striatal neurodegeneration, myopathy and red cell shape change. Large deletions can also remove neighbouring genes, causing chronic granulomatous disease or Duchenne dystrophy in the same patient.
det.clinical: Most affected males present in mid-adulthood with a choreiform movement disorder, behavioural change and seizures, along with neuromuscular signs and raised CK that may have been noticed for years as unexplained 'liver enzyme' elevations. Heterozygous women are usually asymptomatic but occasionally develop mild features. Cardiac involvement is common and can be fatal.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in a man with chorea plus raised CK, areflexia or cardiomyopathy. Request extended red cell phenotyping for Kell and Kx; acanthocytes support but their absence does not exclude. XK sequencing and deletion analysis confirm, and should prompt evaluation for contiguous gene syndromes.
det.treatment: Management is symptomatic: VMAT2 inhibitors or antipsychotics for chorea, antiseizure drugs, psychiatric care and regular cardiac surveillance with treatment of heart failure or arrhythmia. Transfusion planning is essential because of anti-Kx alloimmunisation risk. Offer genetic counselling to maternal relatives.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive over decades; cardiomyopathy and sudden death limit survival in some.
pearls: Chorea + high CK + absent reflexes in a man: request Kell/Kx typing.
Look for cardiomyopathy in every patient.
Only Kx-negative blood is safe for transfusion.

det.patho: Measles virus spreads systemically and transiently suppresses immunity. The acute post-infectious form is an autoimmune demyelinating reaction without virus in the brain. Inclusion body encephalitis is direct viral infection of neurons in people who cannot mount a cellular response. SSPE results from a mutated, poorly assembled virus persisting in neurons for years, usually after infection before age two; resurgence of measles where vaccine coverage has dropped has brought all three forms back.
det.clinical: Post-infectious encephalomyelitis affects roughly 1 per 1000 cases and behaves like ADEM, with mortality around 10–20% and frequent sequelae. Inclusion body encephalitis presents with relentless focal seizures, altered consciousness and focal deficits in transplant, leukaemia or HIV patients and is often fatal. SSPE progresses through behavioural, myoclonic, rigid and vegetative stages over months to years and may also affect the retina (macular chorioretinitis). Primary measles itself can also cause febrile seizures and simple encephalopathy.
det.diagnosis: Timing relative to the rash and the immune state of the patient point to the form. MRI and CSF support inflammation; measles IgM confirms recent infection, PCR of CSF or brain tissue confirms inclusion body disease, and a raised CSF to serum measles antibody ratio with periodic EEG supports SSPE. Exclude HSV and other viral encephalitides, and consider brain biopsy in an immunocompromised patient with unexplained refractory seizures.
det.treatment: There is no proven antiviral; ribavirin has been tried in severe and immunocompromised cases with uncertain benefit. The post-infectious form is treated like ADEM with intravenous methylprednisolone, then IVIG or plasma exchange if poor response. Give vitamin A to all children with measles, control seizures and provide intensive supportive care. For SSPE, isoprinosine and intraventricular interferon may slow progression in some patients but none is curative. Prevention through two doses of MMR vaccine is the effective strategy.
det.prognosis: The post-infectious form often leaves deficits; inclusion body encephalitis and SSPE are usually fatal.
pearls: Ask about measles at an early age in any child with unexplained cognitive decline and periodic jerks.
An immunocompromised child with epilepsia partialis continua during a measles outbreak may have inclusion body encephalitis even without a rash.
Vaccination prevents all three forms; vaccine-strain SSPE has not been convincingly shown.
det.thd: หัดทำให้เกิดโรคสมองได้ 3 แบบ คือ สมองอักเสบหลังติดเชื้อซึ่งเป็นปฏิกิริยาภูมิคุ้มกันคล้าย ADEM ในช่วง 1–2 สัปดาห์หลังผื่น, สมองอักเสบจากไวรัสโดยตรงในผู้ภูมิคุ้มกันต่ำซึ่งชักไม่หยุด และ SSPE ซึ่งเกิดหลังหลายปี วินิจฉัยด้วยช่วงเวลา MRI น้ำไขสันหลัง และ serology หัด รักษาแบบประคับประคอง ให้ vitamin A และใช้ steroid ในแบบหลังติดเชื้อ การฉีดวัคซีน MMR ป้องกันได้ทั้งหมด

det.patho: The median nerve passes under the flexor retinaculum with nine tendons; any increase in tunnel content or decrease in space raises pressure, causing ischaemia and focal demyelination, then axonal loss. Risk factors include diabetes, hypothyroidism, pregnancy, rheumatoid arthritis, obesity, repetitive wrist use and amyloidosis.
det.clinical: Carpal tunnel syndrome presents with intermittent, often nocturnal, paraesthesia in median-innervated fingers, progressing to constant numbness and thenar weakness. Proximal median lesions (pronator region, anterior interosseous branch) are rare and produce different patterns.
det.diagnosis: Clinical features plus conduction studies confirm the site and severity. Ultrasound is a useful adjunct. Bilateral cases in men or older adults should prompt consideration of ATTR amyloidosis, and systemic risk factors should be checked.
det.treatment: Wrist splinting in neutral at night and corticosteroid injection for mild-moderate disease; surgical decompression (open or endoscopic) for severe disease, axon loss or failed conservative care. Manage contributing conditions.
det.prognosis: Surgery relieves symptoms in most patients; long-standing thenar wasting may not fully recover.
pearls: Sparing of thenar skin sensation localises to the carpal tunnel.
Bilateral carpal tunnel can precede cardiac ATTR amyloidosis by years.
Night splints are an effective first step.

det.patho: Medium vessel vasculitides inflame the walls of named visceral arteries, causing necrosis, thrombosis and small aneurysms. PAN may be idiopathic or triggered by hepatitis B; deficiency of adenosine deaminase 2 (DADA2) is a genetic PAN-like cause of early strokes. Kawasaki disease is a childhood immune response, probably to an infectious trigger, with a predilection for coronary arteries.
det.clinical: Systemic features dominate: fever, myalgia, weight loss, skin nodules or ulcers, renal hypertension and gut ischaemia. Nerve infarcts appear as sudden painful deficits in individual nerves, which may coalesce into an asymmetric polyneuropathy. Strokes, often lacunar, occur in a minority of PAN and are characteristic of DADA2 in children and young adults. Kawasaki disease may be complicated by aseptic meningitis, irritability or facial palsy.
det.diagnosis: Tissue diagnosis is preferred: combined nerve and muscle biopsy of an affected region gives the highest yield. Angiography showing microaneurysms supports PAN when biopsy is unhelpful. Check ANCA, hepatitis serology, cryoglobulins and complement to classify the vasculitis; consider ADA2 activity in early-onset cases. Infections such as endocarditis must be excluded.
det.treatment: Idiopathic PAN with severe organ or nerve involvement is treated with high-dose glucocorticoids plus cyclophosphamide, followed by maintenance azathioprine or methotrexate. HBV-related PAN needs antivirals with a short course of steroids, sometimes plasma exchange. DADA2 responds to TNF inhibitors rather than standard immunosuppression. Kawasaki disease is treated with IVIG and aspirin.
det.prognosis: Treated PAN has good survival, and relapse is less frequent than in ANCA disease; nerve recovery is slow and often incomplete.
pearls: Painful foot drop plus systemic symptoms: think vasculitic mononeuritis multiplex.
PAN is ANCA negative and spares the lung.
Strokes in a child with livedo and fevers: test ADA2.
det.thd: Medium vessel vasculitis คือการอักเสบของหลอดเลือดแดงขนาดกลาง เช่น polyarteritis nodosa และ Kawasaki อาการทางระบบประสาทที่พบบ่อยคือเส้นประสาทหลายเส้นขาดเลือดทีละเส้น (mononeuritis multiplex) ปวดและอ่อนแรงทันที ร่วมกับไข้ น้ำหนักลด ความดันสูง ยืนยันด้วยการตัดชิ้นเนื้อเส้นประสาทและกล้ามเนื้อ รักษาด้วยสเตียรอยด์ร่วม cyclophosphamide และถ้าสัมพันธ์กับไวรัสตับอักเสบบีต้องให้ยาต้านไวรัส
