name: Medulloblastoma
formal: Malignant embryonal posterior fossa tumour of childhood, arising in cerebellar vermis, with hydrocephalus, ataxia and vomiting; molecular groups include WNT, SHH, group 3 and 4, with CSF seeding.
simple: A fast-growing brain cancer in children arising in the back of the brain, causing poor balance, headaches and vomiting.
th: เนื้องอกตัวอ่อนที่เกิดจาก cerebellum พบบ่อยที่สุดในเด็ก ทำให้น้ำคั่งสมอง อาเจียน และเดินเซ จัดเป็น 4 กลุ่มทางโมเลกุล (WNT, SHH, Group 3, Group 4) การรักษาคือผ่าตัด ฉายรังสีทั่วระบบประสาท และเคมีบำบัด
tempoNote: Weeks (often 1-3 months) of headache, vomiting and clumsiness with rapid worsening as hydrocephalus develops
feat: Most children are 3-10 years old with morning headache, vomiting, papilloedema, unsteady gait and truncal ataxia from a midline vermian tumour
Adults (about 1 in 4 cases is over 15) more often have lateral hemispheric tumours with limb ataxia and a longer prodrome
Diplopia from sixth nerve palsy, nystagmus and head tilt appear when hydrocephalus or brainstem involvement develops
Leptomeningeal spread is present at diagnosis in about a third, and drop metastases can cause back or radicular pain
Post-operative cerebellar mutism (posterior fossa syndrome) appears about 2-3 days after resection in up to a quarter and recovers over weeks to months
inv: CT: hyperdense midline vermian mass with hydrocephalus; MRI: restricted diffusion, avid enhancement in most, relation to the fourth ventricle floor
Contrast MRI of the entire spine before surgery, and CSF cytology about 2 weeks after surgery
Histological types: classic, large cell/anaplastic, desmoplastic/nodular and the extensively nodular form; WHO CNS5 groups WNT-activated, SHH-activated (TP53-mutant or wildtype), non-WNT/non-SHH
Molecular tests: CTNNB1 (WNT), PTCH1/SUFU/SMO (SHH), MYC and MYCN amplification, isochromosome 17q, TP53; germline testing for Gorlin, Li-Fraumeni and APC (Turcot) in selected patients

case.story: Two months of morning headaches and vomiting, then a drunken gait and a few days of double vision.
case.exam: Papilloedema, bilateral sixth nerve palsies, truncal ataxia and mild dysmetria.
case.tests: CT shows a hyperdense midline mass in the fourth ventricle with hydrocephalus; MRI shows restricted diffusion and no spinal deposits. Near-total resection after steroids: classic medulloblastoma, WNT-activated, CTNNB1-mutated, CNS WHO grade 4. CSF cytology negative.
case.q: What post-operative treatment is used and why does the molecular group matter?
case.a: Craniospinal radiotherapy (about 23.4 Gy for standard risk, with a boost to the tumour bed) plus chemotherapy such as vincristine, cisplatin and CCNU. WNT tumours have survival above 90%, so trials test de-escalation; group 3 with MYC amplification and TP53-mutant SHH tumours have a worse outlook.

read.where: Chapter 20 Neuro-Oncology — Primitive Neuroepithelial Tumours and Medulloblastomas

det.patho: Medulloblastoma is a small-blue-cell embryonal tumour of the cerebellum, thought to arise from external granular layer precursors (SHH group) or rhombic lip cells (WNT and others). Histological variants include classic (more than 70 percent), desmoplastic/nodular (10-20 percent, SHH-related), extensive nodularity and large cell/anaplastic. WHO CNS5 classifies WNT-activated, SHH-activated and non-WNT/non-SHH groups (groups 3 and 4), with MYC amplification, isochromosome 17q, TP53 mutation and metastasis as high-risk features. Hereditary syndromes include Gorlin syndrome (PTCH1), Li-Fraumeni (TP53) and Turcot syndrome (APC).
det.clinical: Children develop a rapid sequence of raised pressure and cerebellar dysfunction; infants may show lethargy and macrocephaly. Metastasis along the CSF produces spinal pain, weakness and cranial neuropathies. Adults often have a milder, longer story with lateral cerebellar tumours. Mutism and mood change can follow surgery. Late effects of treatment include hearing loss, endocrine deficits, neurocognitive decline, and second tumours.
det.diagnosis: Hyperdensity on plain CT and diffusion restriction on MRI favour medulloblastoma. Spinal MRI is needed pre-operatively, and CSF cytology after two weeks. Pathology and molecular testing assign group and risk. Post-operative MRI within 72 hours quantifies residual tumour (less than 1.5 cm squared defined near-total resection in the source). Atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumour is excluded by INI1 staining, particularly in infants.
det.treatment: Initial management of hydrocephalus is by steroids and early surgery; CSF diversion is used only if the child is unstable. Maximal safe resection is followed by risk-adapted craniospinal radiotherapy (23.4 Gy for standard-risk, 36 Gy for high-risk) with a boost to 54-55.8 Gy to the posterior fossa and chemotherapy (vincristine, cisplatin, lomustine or cyclophosphamide). Children under about 3 years receive intensive chemotherapy to avoid or defer radiotherapy. WNT-activated trials explore reduced therapy, and SHH inhibitors such as vismodegib are not used in children because they stunt growth. Treat cerebellar mutism with rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: Overall five-year survival is about 70-85 percent in standard-risk disease and 60-70 percent in high-risk; WNT exceeds 90 percent and MYC-amplified group 3 is below 50 percent.
pearls: Hyperdense midline posterior fossa mass with hydrocephalus in a child: medulloblastoma; image the whole spine.
Wait 2 weeks after surgery before reading spinal MRI or CSF for staging because artefacts persist.
Basal cell naevus (Gorlin) patients should avoid radiotherapy-induced basal cell carcinomas where possible.
det.thd: Medulloblastoma เป็นเนื้องอกตัวอ่อนของ cerebellum พบบ่อยในเด็กอายุ 3-10 ปี อาการคือปวดศีรษะตอนเช้า อาเจียน และเดินเซจากน้ำคั่งสมอง CT พบก้อนเข้มที่ vermis MRI ต้องตรวจทั้งไขสันหลังก่อนผ่าตัดเพราะอาจกระจายในน้ำไขสันหลัง การรักษาคือผ่าตัด ฉายรังสีทั่วสมองและไขสันหลัง และเคมีบำบัด การจัดกลุ่ม WNT, SHH, Group 3 และ Group 4 ช่วยบอกพยากรณ์โรค กลุ่ม WNT รักษาหายได้มากกว่า 90%

qx.stem: A 10-year-old girl from Surat Thani has truncal ataxia and vomiting. MRI shows an enhancing mass of the fourth ventricle extending into the left cerebellopontine angle, with no spinal deposits, and CSF cytology is negative after gross total resection. Pathology shows classic histology with nuclear beta-catenin staining, a CTNNB1 mutation and monosomy 6.
qx.q: What does this molecular profile mean for her care?
opts: The subgroup has the poorest outlook and needs high-dose chemotherapy with stem-cell rescue
It suggests Li-Fraumeni syndrome and radiotherapy should be avoided
The SHH subgroup is likely and a smoothened inhibitor is first-line
It indicates group 3 disease with MYC amplification
It is the WNT-activated subgroup with an excellent prognosis, and trials are testing reduced-intensity therapy
qx.why: WNT-activated medulloblastoma, marked by CTNNB1 mutation, nuclear beta-catenin and monosomy 6, has long-term survival above 90% in children, so current trials study lower-dose craniospinal radiotherapy to limit late effects. Group 3 with MYC amplification carries the worst prognosis, and SHH tumours with TP53 mutation may signal Li-Fraumeni syndrome; smoothened inhibitors are limited to skeletally mature SHH patients in trials.

qx.stem: A 6-year-old boy from Songkhla has had two months of morning vomiting and an unsteady gait. CT shows a midline, hyperdense mass in the fourth ventricle with obstructive hydrocephalus. MRI shows the mass is dark on ADC with restricted diffusion and enhances moderately; the entire neuraxis is to be imaged next.
qx.q: Why is spinal MRI with contrast part of the staging work-up?
opts: The tumour commonly seeds the CSF and forms drop metastases along the spinal subarachnoid space
It is needed to look for a syrinx that causes the gait ataxia
Spinal imaging predicts the risk of postoperative mutism
To exclude a coexisting spinal meningioma
To confirm the tumour arose from the cerebellar tonsil
qx.why: Medulloblastoma is a dense embryonal tumour with restricted diffusion that spreads through the CSF, so a contrast-enhanced spine MRI (ideally before surgery, to avoid postoperative blood confusing the picture) and CSF cytology define M-stage. Molecular grouping (WNT, SHH, group 3, group 4) is now integral to WHO CNS5 diagnosis. Syrinx or meningioma are not the reason for staging.

ddx.pt: Fills the fourth ventricle floor, calcified and heterogeneous, with extension through foramina; spread less often
Cyst with enhancing mural nodule, hemispheric, no restricted diffusion
Infant under 3 years, INI1 (SMARCB1) loss, aggressive and often with cranial extension

name: Meige’s syndrome (Breughel’s syndrome)
formal: Cranial dystonia combining blepharospasm with oromandibular dystonia, usually in older adults, with sensory tricks and response to botulinum toxin.
simple: A movement disorder causing involuntary eye squeezing together with jaw and mouth spasms.
more: Usually an idiopathic disorder, sometimes secondary to dopamine blockers; treat with botulinum toxin injections to orbicularis oculi, with oral trihexyphenidyl, clonazepam or tetrabenazine as alternatives. Rarely DBS is used for refractory cases. Combination of blepharospasm and oromandibular dystonia, a segmental cranial dystonia named after a painting.
th: dystonia บริเวณใบหน้าที่มีทั้งหนังตากระตุกปิด (blepharospasm) และกรามหรือปากเกร็งผิดท่า (oromandibular dystonia) พบในผู้สูงอายุ รักษาหลักด้วย botulinum toxin
tempoNote: Usually begins in the 50s–60s with blinking, spreads to jaw and mouth over months to a few years, then stabilises
feat: Excessive blinking progressing to forced, sustained eyelid closure (functional blindness at worst)
Jaw opening or closing, lip pursing, tongue protrusion or grimacing; may affect speech and chewing
Sensory tricks: touching the eyebrow, humming, chewing gum or talking may ease spasms
Worse with bright light, stress and fatigue; dry, gritty eyes common
More common in women; may also spread to neck or larynx
inv: Clinical diagnosis; review all drugs (dopamine blockers suggest tardive cause)
MRI brain if onset is young, asymmetric or with other neurological signs
Ophthalmology to exclude ocular surface disease driving reflex blinking

case.story: For a year her eyes keep squeezing shut when she watches TV or walks in sunlight; recently her jaw pulls open while speaking. Pressing a finger near her temple helps.
case.exam: Frequent forceful bilateral eyelid closure, involuntary jaw opening with lip retraction, otherwise normal neurological examination; no antipsychotic exposure.
case.tests: MRI brain normal; ocular surface mildly dry.
case.q: What is the first-line treatment?
case.a: Meige (blepharospasm with oromandibular dystonia); botulinum toxin injections to orbicularis oculi and the relevant jaw muscles, repeated about every 3 months.

read.where: Ablative lesions of the thalamus, pallidum, and subthalamic nucleus

det.patho: Meige syndrome is an adult-onset segmental cranial dystonia thought to arise from abnormal basal ganglia–cerebellar–cortical network function with reduced inhibition in brainstem reflex circuits (for example an enhanced blink reflex recovery). Most cases are idiopathic; secondary forms follow dopamine blockers, brainstem or basal ganglia lesions, and occasionally neurodegenerative disease.
det.clinical: Onset is usually with blepharospasm, followed by spread to lower face, jaw, tongue or neck within a few years. Patients often report light sensitivity and that spasms vanish when they sleep or with a trick. Severe cases cause effective blindness, difficulty eating and social withdrawal; mood and anxiety symptoms are frequent.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, based on pattern, sensory tricks and normal examination otherwise. Distinguish from hemifacial spasm (unilateral, synchronous upper and lower face), facial tics, apraxia of lid opening and functional facial spasm. Check drug history and examine for parkinsonism or other neurological signs.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin is first line for both eyelid and jaw components; jaw injections require care to avoid swallowing problems. Oral options include anticholinergics, clonazepam, baclofen and tetrabenazine, with modest benefit. Tinted lenses help photophobia; refractory eyelid cases may benefit from myectomy, and bilateral pallidal deep brain stimulation helps selected severe patients.
det.prognosis: Chronic but usually non-progressive after the first few years; spontaneous remission is uncommon.
pearls: Bilateral blepharospasm plus jaw dystonia = Meige; unilateral twitching = hemifacial spasm.
Always ask about antipsychotics and antiemetics such as metoclopramide.
Sensory tricks strongly support dystonia over a functional disorder.
det.thd: Meige syndrome เป็น dystonia บริเวณศีรษะและใบหน้า มีหนังตากระตุกปิดทั้งสองข้างร่วมกับกรามหรือปากเกร็งผิดท่า พบในผู้สูงอายุ มักแย่ลงเมื่อเจอแสงจ้าหรือเครียด และดีขึ้นเมื่อแตะใบหน้าหรือพูด วินิจฉัยจากอาการ ต้องถามประวัติยาต้านโดพามีน รักษาหลักด้วยการฉีด botulinum toxin ทุก 3 เดือน รายดื้อการรักษาอาจทำ DBS

name: Melkersson–Rosenthal syndrome
formal: Rare granulomatous disorder with recurrent orofacial swelling, relapsing facial palsy and fissured tongue.
simple: A rare condition with repeated swelling of the lips and face, facial weakness and a furrowed tongue.
th: โรคหายากชนิด granuloma ที่มีริมฝีปากหรือใบหน้าบวมเป็น ๆ หาย ๆ ร่วมกับใบหน้าอัมพาตที่กลับเป็นซ้ำ และลิ้นมีร่อง
tempoNote: Begins in adolescence or early adulthood; swelling and facial palsy recur, and swelling may become permanent
feat: Recurrent painless swelling of the lips or face, eventually persistent
Recurrent peripheral facial palsy, on the same or alternating sides
Fissured (furrowed) tongue
Full triad present in only a minority; mono- and oligosymptomatic forms common
Occasionally headache or other cranial nerve involvement
inv: Biopsy of swollen lip: non-caseating granulomas
Exclude Crohn disease, sarcoidosis and TB (ACE, chest imaging, GI symptoms)
Allergy history and patch testing in orofacial granulomatosis
MRI if facial palsy is atypical or progressive

case.story: Third episode of right facial weakness in four years; her upper lip swells for days at a time.
case.exam: Right lower motor neuron facial palsy, swollen upper lip, deeply fissured tongue.
case.tests: Lip biopsy non-caseating granulomas; ACE normal; chest X-ray clear; no bowel symptoms.
case.q: Which syndrome explains recurrent facial palsy here?
case.a: Melkersson–Rosenthal syndrome.

read.where: Chapter 10 Cranial Nerve VII (The Facial Nerve)

det.patho: The cause is unknown; proposed contributors include genetic predisposition, delayed hypersensitivity to food or dental allergens, infection and immune dysregulation. Biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas with lymphoedema. It overlaps with orofacial granulomatosis and can be the first manifestation of Crohn disease or sarcoidosis in some patients.
det.clinical: Most patients first notice symptoms as teenagers or young adults. Orofacial swelling, especially of the upper lip, is the commonest feature; facial palsy is recurrent and lower motor neuron in type, and the tongue is fissured. The classic triad is uncommon. Swelling may become firm and permanent over time.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by granulomas on lip biopsy. Exclude Crohn disease, sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, angioedema and foreign-body reactions. Recurrent facial palsy should also prompt consideration of diabetes, Lyme disease and structural lesions of the facial nerve.
det.treatment: There is no proven cure. Intralesional or systemic corticosteroids reduce swelling and are used for acute facial palsy. Other options reported include clofazimine, tetracyclines, dapsone, methotrexate and TNF inhibitors, and surgical lip reduction in severe chronic cases. Facial nerve decompression has been tried for frequent recurrences, but evidence is limited.
det.prognosis: Chronic relapsing course; facial palsy usually recovers, though repeated episodes can leave residual weakness.
pearls: Recurrent facial palsy plus lip swelling plus fissured tongue: Melkersson–Rosenthal.
Look for Crohn disease and sarcoidosis behind orofacial granulomas.
A single Bell palsy needs no work-up for this; a second episode with lip swelling does.
det.thd: Melkersson–Rosenthal syndrome เป็นโรคหายาก มีริมฝีปากหรือใบหน้าบวมเป็น ๆ หาย ๆ ใบหน้าอัมพาตแบบ LMN ที่กลับเป็นซ้ำ และลิ้นมีร่อง แต่ส่วนน้อยที่มีครบสามอาการ ตัดชิ้นเนื้อริมฝีปากพบ granuloma และต้องแยก Crohn และ sarcoidosis รักษาด้วย steroid และยาต้านการอักเสบอื่น ๆ โรคมักเป็นเรื้อรัง

Facial palsy (often bilateral) with parotid swelling, uveitis and hilar nodes

name: Membranous lipodystrophy
formal: Nasu-Hakola disease, a recessive disorder from TYROBP or TREM2 mutations with polycystic bone lesions, fractures, and presenile frontal dementia with white matter change.
simple: A rare inherited disease causing bone cysts and fractures in adulthood followed by early dementia.
more: Diagnosis with imaging and genetic testing; no specific treatment is available. Course is progressive and care is supportive.
ab: Polycystic lipomembranous osteodysplasia with sclerosing leukoencephalopathy
th: ชื่อเรียกอีกแบบของโรค Nasu-Hakola โรคยีนด้อยจาก TREM2 หรือ TYROBP มีถุงน้ำในกระดูกข้อมือข้อเท้าและกระดูกหักง่ายในวัยหนุ่มสาว ตามด้วยสมองเสื่อมแบบ frontal ก่อนวัย
tempoNote: Bone pain and fractures in the 20s, personality change and dementia from the 30s, death usually before 50
feat: Ankle and wrist pain with cystic bone lesions and fractures after minor trauma in young adults
Then frontal-type personality change: disinhibition, euphoria, loss of insight
Progressive dementia, seizures, upper motor neuron signs and eventual mutism
Autosomal recessive; most reported families from Finland and Japan
inv: Skeletal X-rays: multiple cystic radiolucent lesions in carpal, tarsal and long-bone ends
MRI brain: frontal white matter change, thin corpus callosum, basal ganglia calcification on CT
TREM2 or TYROBP sequencing

case.story: Broke his wrist twice after trivial falls in his 20s; now his family reports tactless jokes, overspending and neglect of work.
case.exam: Disinhibited, poor planning, brisk reflexes with extensor plantar responses, tender ankles.
case.tests: X-rays show multiple cysts in carpal and tarsal bones; MRI frontal leukoencephalopathy; biallelic TREM2 variants.
case.q: What combination links his fractures and behaviour?
case.a: Nasu-Hakola disease (membranous lipodystrophy): microglial and osteoclast TREM2–DAP12 signalling failure causes both bone cysts and leukoencephalopathy with frontal dementia.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Adult-Onset Inherited Leukodystrophies

det.patho: TREM2 and its adaptor TYROBP (DAP12) form a receptor complex on microglia and osteoclasts. Loss of either impairs microglial clearance and support of myelin and alters osteoclast development, leading to sclerosing leukoencephalopathy and membranous lipid-filled cysts in bone marrow fat. The 'membranous lipodystrophy' name comes from the characteristic membranous structures seen in adipose tissue.
det.clinical: The disease runs in stages: a latent phase, a bone phase with pain and pathological fractures, an early neuropsychiatric phase with frontal-lobe syndrome, and a late phase of profound dementia, seizures and immobility. Some patients have little bone disease, so absence of fractures does not rule it out.
det.diagnosis: Combine skeletal survey, brain imaging and genetic testing in young adults with early-onset frontal dementia, especially if bone cysts or family history are present. Bone biopsy shows membranocystic lesions. Exclude other leukodystrophies and early-onset FTD genes.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy exists. Care is supportive: orthopaedic management of fractures, antiseizure drugs, behavioural and psychiatric support, and planning for long-term care. Genetic counselling for siblings is important.
det.prognosis: Relentlessly progressive; most patients die in their forties or fifties.
pearls: Young-onset frontal dementia + fractures/bone cysts = Nasu-Hakola.
TREM2 variants in heterozygous form are a risk factor for Alzheimer disease; biallelic loss causes this disease.
Same disease appears in this lexicon under the name Nasu-Hakola disease.
det.thd: Membranous lipodystrophy คือโรค Nasu-Hakola เป็นโรคยีนด้อยจาก TREM2 หรือ TYROBP ซึ่งทำงานใน microglia และ osteoclast ผู้ป่วยวัย 20 ปีมีถุงน้ำในกระดูกข้อมือข้อเท้าและกระดูกหักง่าย ต่อมาวัย 30 ปีมีบุคลิกภาพเปลี่ยนแบบ frontal และสมองเสื่อมเร็ว MRI พบความผิดปกติของเนื้อสมองขาว ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน ไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ ดูแลแบบประคับประคอง

name: Meningiomas
formal: Common extra-axial, usually benign, dural-based tumours from arachnoid cap cells, with dural tail enhancement; present with seizures, focal deficits or cranial nerve compression; associated with NF2 and radiation.
simple: Usually slow-growing, non-cancerous tumours of the brain or spinal cord coverings that press on the brain and cause headaches, seizures or weakness.
ab: เนื้องอกเยื่อหุ้มสมอง
th: เนื้องอกนอกเนื้อสมองที่เกิดจากเซลล์เยื่อหุ้มสมองชั้น arachnoid พบบ่อยที่สุดในผู้ใหญ่ ส่วนใหญ่โตช้าและไม่ร้าย พบมากในหญิงวัยกลางคน อาการขึ้นกับตำแหน่ง เช่น ชัก อ่อนแรง ตามัว หรือบังเอิญพบ
tempoNote: Grows slowly over years; often found incidentally; symptoms creep in over months, but seizures may be the first abrupt event
feat: Commonest primary intracranial tumour; women outnumber men about 2–3 : 1, incidence rises with age
Many are asymptomatic and found on scans done for other reasons
Symptoms by site: seizures and focal deficits (convexity/parasagittal), anosmia and frontal change (olfactory groove), visual loss (sphenoid/optic sheath), cranial neuropathies (skull base)
Risk factors: prior cranial irradiation, NF2, long-term high-dose progestogens (e.g. cyproterone acetate)
Most are WHO grade 1; grade 2 and 3 recur more and can invade brain
inv: MRI with contrast: extra-axial, dural-based, avidly and uniformly enhancing mass with a dural tail and CSF cleft
CT: calcification and adjacent hyperostosis
Histology with WHO CNS5 grading (mitoses, brain invasion, TERT promoter mutation or CDKN2A/B deletion → grade 3)
Visual fields and acuity for anterior skull base and optic sheath tumours

case.who: 52-year-old female government clerk from Nakhon Si Thammarat
case.story: First-ever convulsion at home. Her family says she has been forgetful and less tidy for a year. She took high-dose cyproterone for hirsutism for over ten years.
case.exam: Mild left pronator drift and left-sided brisk reflexes.
case.tests: MRI: 4-cm homogeneously enhancing right frontal convexity mass with a dural tail and surrounding oedema; CT shows hyperostosis of the overlying bone.
case.q: What is the likely tumour and which drug exposure is relevant?
case.a: Convexity meningioma; long-term cyproterone acetate raises meningioma risk and should be stopped — some regress afterwards. Symptomatic lesions are usually resected.

det.patho: Meningiomas arise from arachnoid cap cells. About half carry NF2 loss; others have TRAF7, KLF4, AKT1, SMO or POLR2A mutations, which tend to cluster at the skull base. The WHO CNS5 (2021) system grades them 1–3 by histology and, for grade 3, TERT promoter mutation or homozygous CDKN2A/B deletion; DNA methylation profiling refines prognosis. Hormone receptors (progesterone) explain the female predominance and the link with progestogen therapy.
det.clinical: Most are slow-growing and remain asymptomatic for years. Symptoms reflect compression: seizures, hemiparesis or personality change from convexity and falx tumours; Foster Kennedy-type pictures from olfactory groove tumours; proptosis and visual loss from spheno-orbital tumours; diplopia or facial numbness from cavernous sinus lesions; and cord compression from spinal meningiomas (typically thoracic in women). Peritumoral oedema can be large despite benign histology.
det.diagnosis: Imaging is usually characteristic, but dural metastases, lymphoma, solitary fibrous tumour, sarcoid and IgG4 disease can look similar. Tissue confirms grade when resected. For incidental tumours, a repeat MRI at 6–12 months establishes growth rate; calcification and lack of oedema predict slow growth.
det.treatment: Small asymptomatic tumours can be watched with serial MRI. Symptomatic or growing tumours are resected aiming for removal of the tumour with its dural attachment and involved bone (Simpson grading). Stereotactic radiosurgery suits small lesions or residual tumour near critical structures; fractionated radiotherapy follows incomplete resection of grade 2 or any grade 3 tumour. Stop progestogens such as cyproterone when possible. Antiseizure medication is used for those who have had seizures; drug therapy for refractory tumours is investigational.
det.prognosis: Grade 1 tumours have excellent survival with recurrence mainly after incomplete resection; grade 2 and especially grade 3 recur frequently and shorten survival.
pearls: Dural tail + CSF cleft + hyperostosis = extra-axial meningioma pattern.
Ask about cyproterone and other progestogens — stopping them can shrink some tumours.
A small, calcified, oedema-free incidental meningioma can usually be watched.

det.patho: Pathogens reach the subarachnoid space through the bloodstream, adjacent infection or a breach in the skull, then multiply in CSF where host defences are weak. The inflammatory response, not just the organism, injures vessels, cranial nerves and brain, causing oedema, infarction and hydrocephalus. Non-infectious causes include drugs, autoimmune disease and malignant infiltration.
det.clinical: Fewer than half of adults with bacterial disease show all three of fever, a stiff neck and confusion together, but almost all have at least one of headache, fever, neck stiffness or confusion. Viral meningitis is usually milder with a clear sensorium. Subacute forms (tuberculosis, cryptococcus) present with weeks of headache, cranial neuropathies and drowsiness. Infants and the elderly may present only with irritability, poor feeding or confusion.
det.diagnosis: CSF analysis defines the type: neutrophilic with low glucose in bacterial, lymphocytic with normal glucose in viral, lymphocytic with low glucose and high protein in TB or fungal disease. Gram stain, culture, multiplex PCR, cryptococcal antigen and TB tests narrow the cause. Neck signs (Kernig, Brudzinski) are insensitive, so a negative result never rules meningitis out.
det.treatment: Suspected bacterial meningitis is an emergency: take blood cultures and start empirical antibiotics within an hour, adjusting for age and risk (e.g. ceftriaxone plus vancomycin, adding ampicillin for listeria in older or immunocompromised patients). Adjunctive dexamethasone reduces deafness and death in pneumococcal disease. Viral meningitis is supportive, with acyclovir if HSV encephalitis cannot be excluded. TB and fungal meningitis need specific long courses.
det.prognosis: Viral meningitis usually resolves fully; bacterial meningitis still carries significant mortality and long-term deficits such as hearing loss.
pearls: Never delay antibiotics for a CT scan.
Low CSF glucose with lymphocytes: think TB, fungus or malignancy.
Request a hearing test after bacterial meningitis.
det.thd: Meningitis คือการอักเสบของเยื่อหุ้มสมอง เกิดจากแบคทีเรีย ไวรัส วัณโรค เชื้อรา หรือสาเหตุที่ไม่ใช่เชื้อ อาการเด่นคือไข้ ปวดศีรษะ คอแข็ง และกลัวแสง การเจาะน้ำไขสันหลังช่วยแยกชนิด ถ้าสงสัยแบคทีเรียต้องเจาะเลือดเพาะเชื้อและให้ยาปฏิชีวนะทันทีพร้อม dexamethasone โดยไม่ต้องรอ CT

name: Meningococcal meningitis
formal: Acute bacterial meningitis due to Neisseria meningitidis with fever, neck stiffness, petechial or purpuric rash and meningococcaemia; risk of shock, deafness and epidemic spread.
simple: A dangerous bacterial infection of the brain coverings causing fever, stiff neck and a purple rash, needing urgent antibiotics.

tempoNote: Hyperacute: hours from the first fever to shock in the fulminant form; meningitis alone evolves over 1 to 2 days
feat: Abrupt fever, headache, vomiting and neck stiffness in a child, adolescent or young adult; alertness is often better preserved than in pneumococcal disease
Non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash on trunk and legs (sparing nail beds), sometimes preceded by a pink macular rash; absent in a minority
Meningococcaemia in roughly 10 to 20 per cent: shock, DIC, purpura fulminans with limb gangrene and adrenal haemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome)
Early warning signs in sepsis: cold hands and feet, leg pain, abnormal skin colour, rapid breathing
Epidemic setting: dormitories, military camps, pilgrimage (Hajj/Umrah) and the African meningitis belt; asplenia and complement deficiency predispose
Late complications: sensorineural hearing loss, skin or limb necrosis, arthritis, cranial nerve palsy

Serogrouping by the public health laboratory; complement studies after recurrent or serogroup W/Y/non-groupable disease

case.who: 19-year-old conscript at a training camp in Lop Buri
case.story: Woke with severe headache and vomiting, then spots appeared on his thighs within hours; he is now very drowsy and his hands are cold.
case.exam: BP 82/48, pulse 132, capillary refill 5 s, non-blanching purpura on legs and flanks, marked neck stiffness.
case.tests: Platelets 48,000, INR 1.9, lactate 5.8 mmol/L; Gram-negative diplococci on a skin scraping.
case.q: What is the order of priorities, and what should his barracks mates receive?
case.a: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV at once without waiting for the lumbar puncture, then fluid resuscitation, vasopressors and ICU care for meningococcal septic shock; notify public health and give close contacts a single dose of ciprofloxacin 500 mg (or rifampicin for 2 days, or ceftriaxone IM), with vaccination where the serogroup is vaccine-preventable.

det.patho: Meningococci colonise the nasopharynx of up to a tenth of healthy young people and only occasionally invade; capsular serogroups A, B, C, W and Y cause nearly all disease. Invasion across the mucosa is favoured by recent viral infection, smoke exposure, crowding and deficiency of the terminal complement components or of the spleen. Endotoxin and outer membrane vesicles trigger cytokine storm, endothelial injury and microvascular thrombosis, producing purpura and shock; the meninges are then seeded from the blood. Humans are the only reservoir, so cases cluster in close contacts.
det.clinical: The commonest form is meningitis with or without a rash; about one in five has fulminant septicaemia in which the patient may deteriorate from well to moribund within a day, with little meningism. Children under five and teenagers are most affected, but older adults and the immunocompromised also fall ill. Rash is a late sign in some patients, so cold peripheries, severe limb pain and a mottled or pale skin in a febrile child are earlier cues. Outbreaks occur in military recruits, schools, pilgrims and, in Africa, dry-season epidemics.
det.diagnosis: Start antibiotics the moment meningococcal disease is suspected, then document it by blood culture, blood/CSF PCR and a Gram stain of CSF or a skin lesion scraping. Non-culture methods remain positive after antibiotics, which matters because the organism is fragile and cultures are often sterile once treatment begins. A petechial rash with fever in a child with systemic upset is treated as meningococcal disease until proven otherwise. Notify public health the same day; serogroup determines vaccine use for contacts.
det.treatment: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (adult) or an equivalent weight-based dose in children is first choice, with benzylpenicillin acceptable when the isolate is sensitive; duration is 5 to 7 days for uncomplicated meningococcal meningitis. Septic shock needs early fluid and vasopressors, correction of coagulopathy and intensive care; current guidance favours ceftriaxone over older penicillin-based schedules. Dexamethasone is given with meningitis in most guidelines but has uncertain benefit for meningococcal disease alone. Close contacts get a single dose of ciprofloxacin, or rifampicin or ceftriaxone, within 24 hours, and vaccination (MenACWY, MenB) is added according to serogroup, outbreak or travel.
det.prognosis: Mortality is about 5 to 10 per cent for meningitis and up to 40 per cent or more for fulminant septicaemia; around one in ten survivors has deafness, scarring or amputations.
pearls: A febrile patient with purpura is a medical emergency; give ceftriaxone before imaging or a lumbar puncture.
Chemoprophylaxis for household and kissing contacts should be given within 24 hours; the index patient also needs eradication therapy if treated with penicillin alone.
Pilgrims returning from Mecca and recruits living in crowded barracks are the Thai groups at the highest practical risk; MenACWY vaccination is required for Hajj.

qx.stem: A 19-year-old university student in Bangkok has laboratory-confirmed meningococcal meningitis. His roommate, who shared his room and utensils, has no symptoms. Local health authorities need to decide on prophylaxis.

No prophylaxis unless the contact develops fever

qx.why: The risk to household contacts is hundreds of times that of the general population, so WHO strongly recommends a single dose of ceftriaxone or ciprofloxacin for close contacts of confirmed cases, guided by local susceptibility, with rifampicin as an alternative. det.patho: Pathogens or immune processes inflame the meninges and the underlying brain together, producing cerebral oedema, vasculitis, infarction and neuronal dysfunction. Viruses (HSV, VZV, enteroviruses, Japanese encephalitis, dengue), bacteria (pneumococcus, S. suis, Listeria, TB), rickettsiae (scrub typhus), fungi (Cryptococcus) and parasites (Angiostrongylus, Naegleria) are all possible; the mix depends on age, immune state and geography.
det.clinical: Most patients have fever, headache and meningism plus encephalopathy, seizures or focal signs; the elderly and immunocompromised may have little fever or neck stiffness. Movement disorders and flaccid paralysis suggest Japanese encephalitis; hearing loss after raw pork suggests S. suis; eosinophilic CSF after eating snails suggests Angiostrongylus. Complications include raised intracranial pressure, hydrocephalus, status epilepticus, SIADH and stroke.
det.diagnosis: Lumbar puncture is central; image first if there is reduced consciousness, focal deficit, papilloedema or new seizures, but never delay empirical treatment for the scan. CSF patterns separate bacterial (neutrophils, low glucose), viral (lymphocytes, normal glucose) and TB/fungal (lymphocytes, high protein, low glucose) causes. MRI localises parenchymal involvement, for example mesial temporal in HSV or thalamic in Japanese encephalitis. A persistently negative infectious work-up should prompt autoimmune antibody testing.
det.treatment: Give empirical therapy immediately: ceftriaxone (plus vancomycin where resistant pneumococcus is a concern and ampicillin for Listeria risk), IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours, and doxycycline when rickettsial infection is possible; add dexamethasone for suspected bacterial meningitis. Narrow treatment once results return. Manage seizures, intracranial pressure, fluids and sodium, and involve ICU early for deteriorating patients. Specific regimens apply for TB, cryptococcus and parasites.
det.prognosis: Depends on organism and speed of treatment; delays in aciclovir or antibiotics clearly worsen survival and cognitive outcome.
pearls: Fever plus altered mental state: start aciclovir and antibiotics before imaging or LP results.
In Thailand, ask about raw pork, pigs, rice fields, snails and travel to the forest.
A normal early HSV PCR does not exclude HSE; repeat if suspicion stays high.

name: Meningovascular syphilis
formal: Form of neurosyphilis from endarteritis of small and medium arteries months to years after infection, causing strokes in young adults with prodromal headache and cranial neuropathies.
simple: Syphilis infection affecting the brain coverings and blood vessels, which can cause strokes in younger people.

feat: Ischaemic stroke in a young or middle-aged adult, most often in the MCA territory or deep perforators (internal capsule, basal ganglia, pons)
Prodromal headache, vertigo, irritability, insomnia or memory change before the stroke; many have some cognitive impairment
Cranial nerve palsies, meningism or eye involvement (uveitis, optic neuritis) from the accompanying meningitis
Spinal form: anterior spinal artery infarction or meningomyelitis
Frequently coexists with HIV; a resurgence of syphilis is seen in Thailand, notably in MSM networks

HIV test (with CD4 and viral load if positive) and screening for other sexually transmitted infections

case.story: Three weeks of headache, poor sleep and irritability, then woke unable to use his right arm and leg properly, with slurred words.

case.q: What is the diagnosis and treatment?

det.patho: Treponema pallidum invades the CSF early in infection, and persistent meningeal infection inflames the arteries crossing the subarachnoid space. Two patterns occur: Heubner arteritis of medium and large vessels with adventitial inflammation, medial thinning and intimal proliferation, and endarteritis of small vessels. The narrowed vessels thrombose, causing infarcts of brain or cord. Aneurysm, intracerebral haemorrhage and dissection are uncommon vascular complications.
det.clinical: Meningovascular syphilis belongs to early neurosyphilis and appears months to years after infection, earlier and more often in HIV. Strokes are typically subcortical or MCA territory, sometimes recurrent or in several territories, and are often preceded by a prodrome of headache, dizziness and personality change. Cognitive impairment can be prominent enough to resemble general paresis. Eye and ear involvement can accompany it and need the same treatment.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in any young stroke with few vascular risk factors and request syphilis serology routinely. Lumbar puncture is indicated in every patient with neurological signs and positive serology. A reactive CSF-VDRL confirms neurosyphilis, but a negative test does not exclude it; pleocytosis and raised protein support it, while a negative CSF FTA-ABS or TPPA argues against it. Imaging shows deep or cortical infarcts and focal arterial stenosis, sometimes with vessel-wall enhancement.
det.treatment: Following CDC 2021 STI guidance, give IV aqueous crystalline penicillin G as 3-4 MU by vein 4-hourly or by continuous infusion (a daily total of 18-24 MU) for 10-14 days; alternatives are procaine penicillin 2.4 MU IM daily with probenecid, or once-daily IV ceftriaxone at 1-2 g, each given for 10-14 days, and some add benzathine penicillin weekly for up to three weeks afterwards. Warn about the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction. Secondary stroke prevention uses antiplatelet therapy and risk factor control; anticoagulation has no specific role. Follow serum RPR at 3, 6, 12 and 24 months; current CDC guidance no longer requires repeat lumbar puncture when the serum response is adequate and HIV, if present, is treated.
det.prognosis: Meningeal symptoms resolve with treatment, but established infarcts leave residual deficits; early treatment prevents further strokes.
pearls: Request syphilis serology and an HIV test in every young adult with unexplained stroke.
Benzathine penicillin does not reach treponemicidal CSF levels; neurosyphilis needs IV penicillin G (or an approved alternative).
Ocular syphilis and otosyphilis are treated as neurosyphilis even if the CSF is normal.
det.thd: Meningovascular syphilis คือซิฟิลิสระบบประสาทที่ทำให้หลอดเลือดสมองอักเสบตีบจนเกิด stroke ในคนอายุน้อย มักมีปวดศีรษะ เวียนศีรษะ หรือบุคลิกเปลี่ยนนำมาหลายวันถึงสัปดาห์ และพบร่วมกับ HIV บ่อย ตรวจ RPR/VDRL และ TPHA ในเลือด เจาะน้ำไขสันหลังดูเซลล์ โปรตีน และ CSF-VDRL รักษาด้วย aqueous penicillin G 18-24 ล้านยูนิตต่อวันทางหลอดเลือดดำ 10-14 วัน ร่วมกับยาต้านเกล็ดเลือด ติดตาม RPR และตรวจรักษาคู่นอน

name: Menkes’ disease
formal: X-linked copper transport defect (ATP7A) causing infantile seizures, hypotonia, kinky hair, neurodegeneration, connective tissue abnormalities and low serum copper and ceruloplasmin.
simple: An inherited problem of copper handling in baby boys causing seizures, brittle kinky hair and severe developmental problems.
more: X-linked ATP7A defect of copper transport causing infantile seizures, hypotonia, developmental regression, kinky hair, connective tissue problems and early death. Low serum copper and ceruloplasmin; early copper-histidinate injections can help in some. Prognosis is poor and most affected children die in early childhood.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมถ่ายทอดทางโครโมโซม X จากยีน ATP7A ทำให้ขนส่งทองแดงผิดปกติ ทารกชายมีชัก ตัวอ่อนปวกเปียก ผมหยิกเปราะ พัฒนาการถดถอย และทองแดงกับ ceruloplasmin ในเลือดต่ำ
tempoNote: Normal at birth or near-normal; decline begins at 2–3 months with seizures and loss of skills
feat: Boy aged 2–3 months with hypotonia, poor feeding, loss of milestones and seizures (often infantile spasms)
Sparse, short, twisted, colourless hair (pili torti); pudgy cheeks and sagging skin
Hypothermia, failure to thrive and bladder diverticula
Tortuous intracranial arteries and subdural haematomas that can be mistaken for abuse
Milder allelic forms: occipital horn syndrome and an ATP7A distal motor neuropathy
inv: Low serum copper and ceruloplasmin (interpret against age norms; neonates are normally low)
Plasma catecholamines: raised DOPA:DHPG ratio is an early sensitive marker
Hair microscopy for pili torti; MRI/MRA for tortuous vessels, white matter change and subdural collections
ATP7A sequencing and deletion analysis

case.story: Feeding poorly and floppy for a month, with repeated clusters of jerks; his mother's brother died in infancy of 'brain disease'.
case.exam: Hypotonic, no social smile, short wiry pale hair that breaks easily, low temperature.
case.tests: Copper 2 µmol/L and ceruloplasmin 40 mg/L (low for age); MRA shows corkscrew intracranial arteries.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and what treatment works best if started early?
case.a: Menkes disease (ATP7A); subcutaneous copper histidinate, ideally begun in the first weeks of life.

det.patho: ATP7A is a copper-transporting ATPase that moves dietary copper out of gut cells and delivers it to copper-dependent enzymes. When it fails, copper is trapped in the intestine and kidney, and the brain becomes deficient. Loss of cytochrome c oxidase, dopamine beta-hydroxylase, lysyl oxidase and tyrosinase activity explains neurodegeneration, autonomic features, fragile vessels and connective tissue, and hair hypopigmentation. Inheritance is X-linked recessive; about a third arise de novo.
det.clinical: Classic Menkes disease presents in male infants at 6–12 weeks with hypotonia, seizures, developmental arrest, temperature instability and characteristic hair. Bone changes (wormian bones, metaphyseal spurs) and subdural bleeding can mimic non-accidental injury. Occipital horn syndrome presents later with connective tissue problems and mild cognitive impairment, and a distal motor neuropathy form appears in adults. Carrier females are usually healthy but may show patchy hair changes.
det.diagnosis: Combine low serum copper and ceruloplasmin (beyond the first weeks of life) with an abnormal plasma neurochemical pattern and confirm with ATP7A genetic testing. Hair microscopy, MRA and skeletal survey support the diagnosis. Prenatal and newborn diagnosis is possible when the family variant is known, which is important because early treatment changes outcome.
det.treatment: Subcutaneous copper histidinate is the main treatment and works best when started within about the first month in babies who retain some ATP7A function; it is supplied through specialist or compassionate-use programmes and is approved in some countries. Otherwise care is supportive: antiseizure drugs, nutrition and gastrostomy, physiotherapy and management of bladder and vascular complications. Gene therapy approaches are in development.
det.prognosis: Untreated classic disease usually leads to death by about 3 years; early-treated infants can survive longer and some develop near-normally.
pearls: Infant boy with seizures, hypotonia and odd wiry hair: check copper and ceruloplasmin.
In Menkes disease, subdural haematoma and metaphyseal spurs may be misread as non-accidental injury.
Menkes = too little copper reaching the brain; Wilson = copper overload.
det.thd: Menkes disease เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมยีน ATP7A ถ่ายทอดทางโครโมโซม X ทำให้ทองแดงไม่ถูกส่งไปยังสมองและเอนไซม์สำคัญ ทารกชายอายุ 2–3 เดือนมีชัก ตัวอ่อน พัฒนาการถดถอย อุณหภูมิกายต่ำ และผมหยิกเปราะสีซีด ตรวจพบทองแดงและ ceruloplasmin ต่ำ หลอดเลือดสมองคดเคี้ยว ยืนยันด้วยยีน การรักษาหลักคือฉีด copper histidinate ใต้ผิวหนังให้เร็วที่สุดหลังเกิด

qx.stem: A 3-week-old boy from Songkhla is hypotonic with unstable temperature and sparse, pale, wiry scalp hair. His maternal uncle died in infancy with seizures and brittle hair. Serum copper and ceruloplasmin are low, but the laboratory warns that these values are unreliable at this age, and sequencing shows a hemizygous ATP7A pathogenic variant.
qx.q: Which treatment has been shown to improve neurodevelopmental outcome and survival only when started very early?
opts: Subcutaneous copper histidinate injections, started in the first weeks of life (before about 28 days)
Oral penicillamine to chelate the accumulated copper
Oral zinc acetate for several months
Intravenous copper sulfate given only after seizures begin
Daily high-dose vitamin B12 injections
qx.why: Menkes disease is an X-linked ATP7A copper transport defect: copper is poorly absorbed from the gut and trapped in other tissues, so brain enzymes that need copper fail. Because serum copper and ceruloplasmin are normally low in the first two months, genetic testing is the reliable test early on. Parenteral copper histidinate started before about 28 days of age improves outcome, though many infants remain significantly affected. Chelators and zinc lower copper and would worsen the disease.

name: Mercury neurotoxicity
formal: Toxicity from inorganic or organic mercury causing tremor, erethism, ataxia, paraesthesias, visual field constriction and, in infants, acrodynia or developmental harm (Minamata disease).
simple: Nerve damage from mercury poisoning, causing tremor, mood changes, numbness and poor coordination.
th: พิษปรอทต่อระบบประสาท ไอปรอททำให้มือสั่นและอารมณ์เปลี่ยน ปรอทอินทรีย์ทำให้ชารอบปาก เดินเซ ลานสายตาแคบ และเป็นอันตรายต่อทารกในครรภ์ ปรอทอนินทรีย์ในครีมหน้าขาวทำลายไต
tempoNote: Builds over weeks to months of exposure; methylmercury effects can appear after a latent period of weeks
feat: Vapour: fine intention tremor, gingivitis, irritability, shyness and insomnia (erethism)
Methylmercury: perioral and distal paraesthesia, ataxia, dysarthria, concentric field constriction, hearing loss
Inorganic salts, e.g. cosmetic creams: nephrotic-range proteinuria with sensory complaints
Children: acrodynia with painful pink hands and feet, sweating, hypertension
Prenatal exposure gives cerebral palsy-like disability and developmental delay
inv: Whole blood mercury for methylmercury; 24-hour or creatinine-corrected urine mercury for elemental and inorganic forms
Hair segments can time methylmercury exposure
Urine protein, renal function, visual fields and nerve conduction; MRI for calcarine or cerebellar atrophy

case.story: A year of an unlabelled whitening cream bought online; now tingling hands, poor sleep, irritability and puffy legs.
case.exam: Fine postural tremor, reduced pinprick in the hands and feet, pitting ankle oedema.
case.tests: Urine mercury markedly high, heavy proteinuria; the cream tests positive for mercury.
case.q: What is the source, and what is the first step?
case.a: Inorganic mercury from a cosmetic. Stop the product, screen close contacts, and discuss chelation (DMSA or DMPS) with a poison centre.

det.patho: Mercury binds thiol groups, impairing enzymes, microtubules and synaptic transmission. Vapour and methylmercury enter the brain readily, while inorganic salts concentrate in the kidney. Methylmercury favours calcarine cortex, cerebellar granule cells and dorsal root ganglia, which accounts for field loss, ataxia and numbness, and it crosses the placenta.
det.clinical: Exposures include amalgam handling, artisanal gold mining, heated broken thermometers, contaminated fish, traditional remedies and illicit skin-lightening creams. The chemical form shapes the picture: tremor and personality change after vapour, sensory-cerebellar-visual loss after organic exposure, renal disease after inorganic salts. A heavy acute inhalation also causes chemical pneumonitis. Ask about household members and hobbies.
det.diagnosis: Rely on a careful exposure history, then choose the specimen matching the suspected form and read it against reference ranges, bearing in mind that fish eaters have mild elevations. Test the product itself when a cosmetic is suspected. MRI can show calcarine and cerebellar atrophy in long-standing organic poisoning, and conduction studies assess neuropathy.
det.treatment: Eliminating the source comes first. Oral DMSA or DMPS lowers body burden in elemental and inorganic poisoning; established methylmercury brain injury is largely unresponsive, and dimercaprol is avoided in organic mercury because it may shift mercury to the brain. Supportive care covers kidney monitoring and rehabilitation, and public health reporting of the source.
det.prognosis: Vapour and inorganic toxicity often recover over months; methylmercury injury to the adult brain and the fetus is mostly permanent.
pearls: Ask about whitening creams, folk medicines and small-scale gold mining.
Blood for methylmercury, urine for elemental or inorganic mercury.
Field constriction plus ataxia plus perioral numbness suggests organic mercury.
det.thd: พิษปรอทมีหลายรูปแบบ ไอปรอทจากงานอุตสาหกรรมหรือเหมืองทองทำให้มือสั่น หงุดหงิด นอนไม่หลับ ปรอทอนินทรีย์ในครีมหน้าขาวทำให้ไตรั่วและชา ส่วน methylmercury จากปลาปนเปื้อนทำให้ชารอบปาก เดินเซ ลานสายตาแคบ และทำอันตรายต่อทารกในครรภ์ ตรวจระดับปรอทในเลือดหรือปัสสาวะตามชนิด รักษาโดยหยุดแหล่งสัมผัสและพิจารณายาขับโลหะ

name: Metabolic encephalopathy
formal: Diffuse brain dysfunction from systemic metabolic derangement such as hepatic, uraemic, hypoglycaemic or electrolyte disturbance, causing fluctuating consciousness, asterixis and myoclonus.
simple: Brain dysfunction caused by a body chemistry problem such as liver or kidney failure, leading to confusion and drowsiness.
ab: Acute confusional state of metabolic origin
th: ภาวะสมองทำงานผิดปกติทั่วไปจากความผิดปกติของระบบเมตาบอลิซึมในร่างกาย เช่น ตับวาย ไตวาย น้ำตาลหรือเกลือแร่ผิดปกติ ทำให้ระดับความรู้สึกตัวขึ้นลง สับสน asterixis และ myoclonus
tempoNote: Develops over hours to days and fluctuates; reverses if the underlying derangement is corrected promptly
feat: Fluctuating attention and arousal with disorientation; hypoactive or agitated delirium
Asterixis, multifocal myoclonus and tremor; focal signs are uncommon (except hypoglycaemia)
Pupils usually remain reactive even in deep coma
Seizures with hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia or uraemia
Signs of the systemic cause: jaundice, uraemic fetor, dehydration, sepsis
inv: Glucose at the bedside, sodium, calcium, magnesium, urea, creatinine, liver tests, ammonia, blood gas, thyroid function
EEG: diffuse slowing, triphasic waves; excludes non-convulsive status
CT or MRI to exclude structural lesions; drug levels and toxicology

case.who: 72-year-old woman with diabetes and CKD from Ratchaburi

case.exam: Drowsy but rousable, inattentive, bilateral asterixis, multifocal jerks, pupils reactive, no focal weakness.

case.q: What is the likely cause and how fast should sodium be corrected?

det.patho: Neurons depend on stable glucose, oxygen, osmolality, electrolytes and clearance of toxins. Derangements impair neurotransmission and cerebral energy metabolism diffusely, giving global dysfunction rather than focal deficits. Ammonia, uraemic toxins, drugs and inflammatory mediators often act together, especially in elderly people with limited brain reserve.
det.clinical: The core picture is delirium: inattention, fluctuating arousal, disorganised thinking and perceptual changes. Motor signs such as asterixis and myoclonus are typical and help distinguish it from primary psychiatric illness. Hypoglycaemia can cause focal deficits mimicking stroke, and severe hyponatraemia or hypocalcaemia may present with seizures.
det.diagnosis: Approach systematically: check glucose immediately, then electrolytes, renal and hepatic function, blood gas, thyroid, drugs and infection. Image the brain when the cause is unclear, there are focal signs, or the patient has had a fall or anticoagulation. EEG helps exclude non-convulsive status epilepticus and supports a metabolic pattern.
det.treatment: Correct the underlying derangement at a safe rate, give IV thiamine to at-risk patients before glucose, review and stop deliriogenic drugs, and adjust renally cleared medicines. Supportive delirium care includes orientation, sleep hygiene, mobilisation and avoiding restraints. Protect the airway in deep coma.
det.prognosis: Usually reversible when the cause is corrected, though older patients may recover slowly and some are left with cognitive decline.
pearls: Check glucose in every confused patient before anything else.
Asterixis and multifocal myoclonus point to a metabolic cause rather than a structural one.
Reactive pupils in coma favour metabolic over structural brainstem causes.
det.thd: Metabolic encephalopathy คือภาวะสมองทำงานผิดปกติทั่วไปจากความผิดปกติในร่างกาย เช่น น้ำตาลต่ำหรือสูง โซเดียมต่ำ ตับวาย ไตวาย หรือยา ผู้ป่วยสับสน ระดับความรู้สึกตัวขึ้นลง มี asterixis และ myoclonus โดยรูม่านตายังตอบสนองต่อแสง ต้องเจาะน้ำตาลก่อนเสมอ ตรวจเกลือแร่ ตับ ไต และ EEG รักษาโดยแก้สาเหตุอย่างปลอดภัย และให้ thiamine ในผู้มีความเสี่ยง

name: Metabolic muscle diseases
formal: Inherited disorders of glycogen, lipid or purine metabolism affecting muscle energy supply, with exercise intolerance, cramps, recurrent myoglobinuria or fixed weakness.
simple: Inherited problems in how muscles make energy, causing tiring, cramps and sometimes muscle breakdown with exercise.
more: Investigate with forearm exercise test, CK, acylcarnitine profile, lactate, muscle biopsy and gene panels; avoid fasting and strenuous exercise. Treatment depends on the defect: carbohydrate loading, carnitine, or enzyme replacement where available.

feat: Glycogen disorders: pain and cramps in the first minutes of intense exercise, second wind (McArdle)
Fatty acid oxidation disorders: rhabdomyolysis after prolonged exercise, fasting, cold or fever (CPT II)
Mitochondrial myopathies: fatigue, ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, lactic acidosis, multisystem features
Pompe disease: progressive limb-girdle and respiratory weakness rather than episodes
Normal examination between attacks in many patients

Non-ischaemic forearm exercise test (lactate and ammonia)

case.who: 19-year-old military conscript at a hospital in Lop Buri
case.story: After a long march in the heat with little food he developed aching thighs and dark urine; similar milder episodes followed fevers in childhood. Short sprints never troubled him.
case.exam: Tender thighs, mild proximal weakness, otherwise normal.
case.tests: CK 95,000 U/L, creatinine rising; between attacks CK normal; acylcarnitine shows raised long-chain species; CPT2 variant.
case.q: Which category of metabolic myopathy fits prolonged-exercise and fasting triggers?
case.a: A fatty acid oxidation defect — CPT II deficiency.

det.patho: Muscle uses glycogen for brief intense work, fatty acids for prolonged low-intensity work and fasting, and mitochondria for oxidative phosphorylation of both. Defects in glycogenolysis or glycolysis (McArdle, Tarui), fatty acid transport and oxidation (CPT II, VLCAD, MADD, carnitine disorders), purine nucleotide cycling (myoadenylate deaminase) or the respiratory chain lead to energy shortfall when demand rises. Some disorders, like Pompe and debrancher deficiency, cause storage and progressive weakness.
det.clinical: The pattern of exercise intolerance points to the pathway: early pain with intense exercise in glycogenoses, late or post-exercise problems with fasting or infection in lipid disorders, and limited endurance with multisystem features in mitochondrial disease. Recurrent rhabdomyolysis risks acute kidney injury. Fixed proximal or respiratory weakness suggests Pompe, debrancher deficiency or lipid storage myopathies.
det.diagnosis: Take a careful history of triggers and timing. Basic tests include CK, lactate, acylcarnitines, urine organic acids and a forearm exercise test (flat lactate rise in glycogenoses, flat ammonia in myoadenylate deaminase deficiency). Gene panels now often precede biopsy, but biopsy with histochemistry and enzyme analysis remains useful. Avoid testing during an acute attack except to measure CK and acylcarnitines.
det.treatment: Management depends on the defect: pre-exercise sucrose and moderate aerobic training in McArdle; frequent carbohydrate, avoidance of fasting and medium-chain triglycerides in some fat oxidation disorders; riboflavin for responsive MADD; enzyme replacement for Pompe. Rhabdomyolysis needs prompt IV fluids and renal monitoring. Patients should carry an emergency letter.
det.prognosis: Generally good with trigger avoidance, except progressive forms (Pompe, some mitochondrial disease).
pearls: Short intense exercise triggers: glycogen; long exercise, fasting or fever: fat.
Second wind after 10 minutes of walking is characteristic of McArdle disease.
Collect acylcarnitines during the attack when possible.
det.thd: Metabolic muscle diseases เป็นกลุ่มโรคกล้ามเนื้อทางพันธุกรรมที่สร้างพลังงานไม่พอ แบ่งเป็นความผิดปกติของไกลโคเจน ไขมัน และไมโทคอนเดรีย ผู้ป่วยมีตะคริว เหนื่อยง่าย และกล้ามเนื้อสลายเมื่อออกกำลัง อดอาหาร หรือมีไข้ ตรวจ CK, acylcarnitine, forearm exercise test, ชิ้นเนื้อ และยีน การรักษาขึ้นกับชนิด เช่น หลีกเลี่ยงการอดอาหาร กินน้ำตาลก่อนออกกำลังใน McArdle และ enzyme replacement ใน Pompe

formal: Myoclonus resulting from systemic metabolic disturbance such as uraemia, hepatic failure, hypoxia or hyponatraemia, often multifocal with asterixis.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks caused by body chemistry problems such as kidney or liver failure.
th: myoclonus ที่เกิดจากความผิดปกติทางเมตาบอลิซึม เช่น ไตวาย ตับวาย ขาดออกซิเจน โซเดียมต่ำ หรือยาสะสม มักกระตุกหลายตำแหน่งร่วมกับ asterixis และหายเมื่อแก้สาเหตุ
tempoNote: Appears with the metabolic derangement over hours to days and resolves as it is corrected
feat: Multifocal, irregular jerks of face and limbs, often worse with action or stimulation
Negative myoclonus (asterixis) with outstretched hands
Accompanied by encephalopathy of varying depth
Common triggers: renal failure with drug accumulation (gabapentinoids, opioids, cefepime), hepatic failure, hyponatraemia, hyperglycaemia
inv: Electrolytes, renal and liver function, glucose, ammonia, calcium, magnesium
Drug review and levels where available
EEG to exclude non-convulsive status; neurophysiology can show cortical origin

case.story: Started pregabalin for neuropathic pain at a full dose; within days he became confused with jerking of arms and face.
case.exam: Drowsy, multifocal myoclonus, bilateral asterixis, no focal deficit.
case.tests: Urea and creatinine at usual dialysis levels; EEG generalised slowing without seizures.
case.q: What is driving the jerks?
case.a: Metabolic/toxic myoclonus from pregabalin accumulation in renal failure; stop the drug and arrange extra dialysis.

read.where: Chapter 9 Movement Disorders — Metabolic Causes of Myoclonus

det.patho: Metabolic derangements reduce cortical inhibition and alter brainstem reticular excitability, producing cortical or reticular reflex myoclonus. Accumulated drugs and toxins (uraemic solutes, ammonia, gabapentinoids, opioid metabolites, beta-lactams, lithium) add to this. Asterixis reflects brief lapses of postural muscle activity from the same network dysfunction.
det.clinical: Myoclonus is usually multifocal, bilateral and stimulus-sensitive, and appears alongside confusion. In uraemia it may be severe and include startle; in hepatic failure asterixis dominates. Serotonin syndrome and lithium toxicity cause myoclonus with other characteristic signs.
det.diagnosis: Identify the metabolic and drug causes with laboratory testing and a careful medication list. EEG excludes non-convulsive seizures and may show triphasic waves. Imaging is needed if focal signs, trauma or unexplained course.
det.treatment: Correct the metabolic disturbance and stop or reduce offending drugs; dialysis clears many renally excreted agents. Symptomatic options include clonazepam or levetiracetam (dose-adjusted for renal function) if jerks are disabling. Avoid adding further sedatives that accumulate.
det.prognosis: Usually resolves fully with correction of the cause.
pearls: New myoclonus in renal failure: check the drug chart for gabapentinoids, opioids and cefepime.
Asterixis is negative myoclonus.
Myoclonus + encephalopathy + reversible cause = metabolic until proven otherwise.
det.thd: Metabolic myoclonus คืออาการกล้ามเนื้อกระตุกหลายตำแหน่งจากความผิดปกติทางเมตาบอลิซึม เช่น ไตวาย ตับวาย โซเดียมต่ำ หรือยาสะสมในผู้ป่วยไตวาย เช่น pregabalin หรือ cefepime มักพบร่วมกับสับสนและ asterixis ตรวจเลือดหาสาเหตุและทบทวนยา ทำ EEG เพื่อแยกชักแบบไม่เกร็ง รักษาโดยแก้สาเหตุหรือหยุดยา ส่วนใหญ่หายสนิท

name: Metabolic neuropathies
formal: Peripheral neuropathies caused by metabolic disease such as diabetes, uraemia, hypothyroidism or porphyria, usually length-dependent axonal sensorimotor.
simple: Nerve damage in the hands and feet caused by body chemistry problems such as diabetes or kidney failure.
more: Nerve conduction shows axonal sensorimotor neuropathy, and treatment relies on addressing the underlying disorder, including glycaemic control and dialysis. Check B12, thyroid and monoclonal protein; pain is managed symptomatically.
th: เส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเสื่อมจากโรคเมตาบอลิก เช่น เบาหวาน ไตวาย ไทรอยด์ต่ำ และ porphyria ส่วนใหญ่เป็นแบบ axonal เริ่มจากปลายเท้า ยกเว้น porphyria ที่เกิดเป็นช่วงเฉียบพลัน
tempoNote: Mostly slow over months to years; porphyria and hereditary tyrosinaemia produce acute attacks over hours to days
feat: Distal symmetric sensory or sensorimotor neuropathy is the usual pattern, with burning feet and loss of ankle jerks
Diabetes: also autonomic, radiculoplexus and focal neuropathies; uraemia: restless legs and distal polyneuropathy
Hypothyroidism: entrapment (carpal tunnel) and mild axonal polyneuropathy
Acute intermittent porphyria: severe abdominal pain, then proximal-predominant motor neuropathy, psychiatric and autonomic features
Hereditary tyrosinaemia type 1: attacks of painful dysaesthesia with axial stiffness, weakness and sometimes respiratory failure
inv: HbA1c or OGTT, renal and liver function, TSH, B12 and a toxic and drug review
Urine porphobilinogen (and delta-aminolevulinic acid) during an attack
Nerve conduction studies: axonal sensorimotor pattern; skin biopsy for pure small-fibre disease
Plasma tyrosine and succinylacetone in children with attacks and liver or renal disease

case.who: 60-year-old man on haemodialysis from Ubon Ratchathani
case.story: Over a year he has burning feet, restless legs at night and weak toe extension; diabetes was excluded.
case.exam: Stocking sensory loss, absent ankle jerks and mild toe weakness.
case.tests: NCS shows an axonal sensorimotor neuropathy; dialysis adequacy borderline.
case.q: What would most improve this neuropathy?
case.a: Kidney transplantation is the most effective treatment; more intensive dialysis helps less.

read.where: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves — Metabolic Neuropathies

det.patho: Metabolic disturbances impair axonal energy supply, the endoneurial microvasculature and Schwann cell function. Hyperglycaemia causes oxidative stress and microvascular damage, uraemic toxins disturb axonal membranes, and haem precursors in porphyria are directly neurotoxic. In hereditary tyrosinaemia type 1, succinylacetone accumulation inhibits haem synthesis and produces porphyria-like crises.
det.clinical: Most metabolic neuropathies are length-dependent, starting in the feet and rising over years. Acute intermittent porphyria behaves differently: attacks follow drugs (barbiturates, many antiepileptics), fasting, infection or hormonal change, begin with abdominal pain and are followed by a motor neuropathy that is proximal and arm-dominant with reduced or absent reflexes. About half the patients have central features such as confusion and seizures, and ninety percent of gene carriers never have an attack. Children with tyrosinaemia type 1 have attacks of pain and stiffness, usually with infection.
det.diagnosis: Treat each as a systematic search: glucose, renal, thyroid and B12 first, with nerve conduction studies to confirm an axonal pattern. Suspect porphyria in any unexplained abdominal pain with psychiatric or neuropathic features and send urine PBG during the attack, since values may be normal between attacks; molecular testing is definitive. Tyrosinaemia is confirmed by raised blood tyrosine and succinylacetone with enzyme or gene studies, and many newborn programmes screen for it.
det.treatment: Correct the metabolic cause: glycaemic control, adequate dialysis or transplantation for uraemia, thyroid replacement and vitamin replacement. For porphyria, stop trigger drugs, give intravenous glucose (for example 10 percent dextrose) and haem arginate or hemin, with analgesia and monitoring of respiratory function. Tyrosinaemia is treated with a tyrosine- and phenylalanine-restricted diet and nitisinone, with liver transplantation as definitive therapy. Neuropathic pain is treated symptomatically with duloxetine, gabapentinoids or tricyclics.
det.prognosis: Neuropathy often stabilises with metabolic control, and transplant improves uraemic neuropathy; porphyric motor neuropathy may recover slowly over months.
pearls: Porphyria can mimic Guillain–Barré syndrome with abdominal pain: check urine PBG.
Diabetes causes many neuropathy patterns, not only distal symmetric.
Uraemic neuropathy improves with transplantation more than with dialysis.
det.thd: Metabolic neuropathy คือเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเสื่อมจากภาวะเมตาบอลิก เช่น เบาหวาน ไตวาย ไทรอยด์ต่ำ และ porphyria มักเป็นแบบ axonal ชาและแสบที่ปลายเท้าก่อน ส่วน acute intermittent porphyria มีปวดท้องรุนแรง ต่อมาอ่อนแรงของแขนขาส่วนต้น และอาจมีอาการทางจิต วินิจฉัยด้วยตรวจน้ำตาล ไต ไทรอยด์ NCS และ urine PBG ช่วงโรคกำเริบ รักษาที่สาเหตุ เช่น คุมน้ำตาล ปลูกถ่ายไต หรือให้ glucose ทางหลอดเลือดและ hemin ใน porphyria

name: Metabolic syndrome
formal: Cluster of central obesity, hypertension, dyslipidaemia and impaired glucose tolerance that increases risk of stroke, diabetes and cardiovascular disease; also linked to neuropathy and cognitive decline.
simple: A group of conditions, including belly fat, high blood pressure and raised sugar and cholesterol, that raise the risk of heart disease and stroke.
more: Diagnosis from waist, blood pressure, lipids and glucose measurements. Treat with lifestyle change, weight loss and drugs for each component.
th: กลุ่มภาวะอ้วนลงพุง ความดันสูง ไขมันผิดปกติ และน้ำตาลสูง ซึ่งเพิ่มความเสี่ยง stroke เบาหวาน โรคหัวใจ และสัมพันธ์กับปลายประสาทเสื่อมและความจำเสื่อม
tempoNote: Develops silently over years; neurological consequences appear late
feat: Not a neurological disease itself but a cluster of vascular risk factors
Any three of: large waist, high triglycerides, low HDL, raised blood pressure, raised fasting glucose
Raises risk of ischaemic stroke, especially small vessel disease and lacunes
Associated with small-fibre and length-dependent neuropathy even before diabetes
Linked to vascular cognitive impairment and possibly Alzheimer pathology
inv: Waist circumference (Asian cut-offs: ≥90 cm men, ≥80 cm women) and blood pressure
Fasting glucose or HbA1c, lipid profile
In patients with neuropathy: NCS, consider skin biopsy for small fibre loss

case.story: Two years of burning feet at night; recently mild forgetfulness noticed by his wife.
case.exam: Waist 104 cm, BP 150/95; reduced pinprick below the ankles, ankle reflexes present.
case.tests: Fasting glucose 112 mg/dL, triglycerides 260, HDL 34; NCS normal; MRI scattered white matter hyperintensities.
case.q: What unifying condition is present and what is the main intervention?
case.a: Metabolic syndrome with small fibre neuropathy and small vessel disease; lifestyle change with weight loss and exercise plus control of each risk factor.

read.where: Part III: Prevention, Complications, and Recovery - Rehabilitation

det.patho: Visceral adiposity drives insulin resistance, chronic low-grade inflammation and endothelial dysfunction. These changes accelerate atherosclerosis in large arteries and arteriolosclerosis in small brain vessels. In nerves, dyslipidaemia and hyperglycaemia both injure small fibres through oxidative and metabolic stress, which is why neuropathy may appear before diabetes.
det.clinical: Patients are usually asymptomatic until a complication appears. Neurologically relevant consequences include ischaemic stroke and TIA, lacunar syndromes, gradual executive slowing from small vessel disease, painful small fibre neuropathy and obstructive sleep apnoea. It is a common background in Thai stroke clinics. This entry describes a risk-factor cluster rather than a primary neurological disorder.
det.diagnosis: Harmonised criteria use three of five components with ethnicity-specific waist cut-offs. In a neurology clinic, screen glucose, lipids, blood pressure and waist in any patient with stroke, unexplained neuropathy or cognitive decline. Look for sleep apnoea and fatty liver as associated features.
det.treatment: Lifestyle change is the foundation: weight loss of 5–10%, regular aerobic and resistance exercise, Mediterranean-style or reduced-carbohydrate diet, alcohol and smoking cessation. Treat each component to target with antihypertensives, statins and glucose-lowering drugs; GLP-1 receptor agonists help weight and cardiovascular risk. Neuropathic pain can be managed with standard agents such as duloxetine or pregabalin.
det.prognosis: Risk of stroke and cardiovascular events roughly doubles, but sustained risk-factor control reduces it.
pearls: Check metabolic risk in idiopathic small fibre neuropathy before calling it idiopathic.
Asian waist cut-offs are lower than Western ones.
Lifestyle intervention is the single most effective treatment.
det.thd: Metabolic syndrome คือกลุ่มปัจจัยเสี่ยง ได้แก่ อ้วนลงพุง ความดันสูง ไตรกลีเซอไรด์สูง HDL ต่ำ และน้ำตาลสูง ไม่ใช่โรคทางระบบประสาทโดยตรง แต่เพิ่มความเสี่ยง stroke หลอดเลือดสมองเล็กเสื่อม ความจำเสื่อม และปลายประสาทเส้นเล็กอักเสบ การรักษาหลักคือปรับพฤติกรรม ลดน้ำหนัก ออกกำลังกาย และควบคุมแต่ละปัจจัยให้ได้เป้าหมาย

name: Metachromatic leukodystrophy
formal: Autosomal recessive arylsulfatase A deficiency causing sulfatide accumulation, with progressive demyelination, motor regression, ataxia, neuropathy and dementia; late-infantile, juvenile and adult forms.
simple: An inherited lysosomal disease that gradually destroys myelin in the brain and nerves, causing loss of movement and thinking skills.
more: Diagnosed by low leucocyte arylsulfatase A activity and ARSA mutations, with raised urinary sulfatides; MRI shows confluent periventricular T2 hyperintensity with a tigroid pattern. Stem cell transplant in early disease; gene therapy for late-infantile.
th: โรคยีนด้อยจากการขาดเอนไซม์ arylsulfatase A ทำให้ sulfatide สะสมในปลอกประสาททั้งในสมองและเส้นประสาทส่วนปลาย เด็กมีพัฒนาการถดถอย เดินไม่ได้ ส่วนผู้ใหญ่มีอาการทางจิตและสมองเสื่อม
tempoNote: Late-infantile onset before 30 months with rapid decline; juvenile (2.5–16 years) slower; adult form over years to decades
feat: Late-infantile: toddler loses walking, becomes hypotonic then spastic, with absent reflexes from neuropathy
Juvenile: school difficulties, behaviour change, gait disorder
Adult: psychiatric symptoms or frontal dementia often long before motor signs
Combined central and peripheral demyelination: spasticity with depressed reflexes
Optic atrophy, seizures and gallbladder disease can occur
inv: MRI: symmetric confluent periventricular white matter T2 hyperintensity with 'tigroid' stripes, U-fibres spared early
Leucocyte arylsulfatase A activity (beware pseudodeficiency alleles) plus urine sulfatides
Nerve conduction: uniform demyelinating slowing
ARSA sequencing; PSAP (saposin B) testing if enzyme is normal

case.story: Walked at 13 months but over the past 4 months has started falling, now cannot stand, and has become irritable.
case.exam: Hypotonia with absent ankle and knee jerks, extensor plantars, mild optic pallor.
case.tests: MRI confluent periventricular white matter change with tigroid pattern; NCS demyelinating; low arylsulfatase A and high urine sulfatides.
case.q: Why is testing her baby brother urgent?
case.a: Late-infantile MLD; ex vivo gene therapy or transplantation works only before symptoms, so a presymptomatic sibling should be tested immediately.

Progressive Encephalopathies With Onset After Age 2

det.patho: Arylsulfatase A, assisted by saposin B, breaks down sulfatides in lysosomes. Deficiency causes sulfatide build-up in oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells, leading to myelin breakdown in the brain and peripheral nerves; metachromatic granules are seen on tissue staining. Genotype correlates with residual activity and age at onset.
det.clinical: Late-infantile MLD causes motor regression in the second year, followed by spastic quadriparesis, blindness, seizures and loss of all skills within a few years. Juvenile forms begin with cognitive or behavioural problems and gait disturbance. Adult MLD presents with psychosis, personality change or dementia and is often misdiagnosed as a psychiatric disorder.
det.diagnosis: Low enzyme activity must be combined with raised urinary sulfatides or two pathogenic ARSA variants, because pseudodeficiency is common in healthy people. Normal enzyme with typical findings suggests saposin B deficiency. MRI pattern and demyelinating neuropathy are strong supportive clues. Newborn screening programmes are being introduced in some countries.
det.treatment: Ex vivo lentiviral gene therapy (atidarsagene autotemcel) is approved in Europe and the USA for presymptomatic late-infantile and pre- or early-symptomatic early juvenile children. Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation may stabilise early juvenile or adult disease with minimal symptoms. Established disease receives supportive care: spasticity treatment, nutrition and gastrostomy, seizure control and palliative care.
det.prognosis: Late-infantile disease is usually fatal within several years without treatment; juvenile and adult forms progress more slowly. Early gene therapy can preserve motor and cognitive function.
pearls: Spasticity with absent reflexes in a regressing toddler: think MLD or Krabbe.
Low ARSA activity alone is not diagnostic — check urine sulfatides or genetics.
Treatment windows close at symptom onset; screen siblings early.
det.thd: Metachromatic leukodystrophy เกิดจากการขาดเอนไซม์ arylsulfatase A ทำให้ sulfatide สะสมและทำลายปลอกประสาททั้งในสมองและเส้นประสาทส่วนปลาย เด็กเล็กเดินได้แล้วกลับเดินไม่ได้ เกร็งแต่รีเฟล็กซ์หาย ผู้ใหญ่มีอาการทางจิตและสมองเสื่อม MRI พบ white matter ผิดปกติแบบลายเสือ ยืนยันด้วยเอนไซม์ sulfatide ในปัสสาวะ และยีน ARSA การให้ยีนบำบัดหรือปลูกถ่ายไขกระดูกได้ผลเมื่อทำก่อนมีอาการ

name: Metastatic spinal cord tumours
formal: Epidural or intradural spread of cancer (lung, breast, prostate) causing back pain, myelopathy and cord compression; an oncological emergency needing steroids, radiotherapy or surgery.
simple: Cancer that has spread to the spine and presses on the spinal cord, causing back pain, leg weakness and numbness.
th: มะเร็งแพร่กระจายมาที่กระดูกสันหลังหรือช่องเหนือเยื่อหุ้มไขสันหลังจนกดไขสันหลัง ทำให้ปวดหลังแล้วตามด้วยขาอ่อนแรง ชา และกลั้นปัสสาวะไม่ได้ เป็นภาวะฉุกเฉินทางมะเร็ง

feat: New or progressive back pain, often thoracic, worse lying flat or at night, in a person with cancer
Band-like radicular pain, then leg weakness, sensory level and sphincter disturbance
Commonest primaries: lung, breast, prostate, kidney, myeloma and lymphoma
Up to a fifth present with cord compression as the first sign of cancer

case.who: 61-year-old man, ex-smoker, from Nakhon Si Thammarat
case.story: Two months of mid-back pain that wakes him at night; since yesterday both legs feel heavy and he has had difficulty passing urine.
case.exam: Tender T6 spinous process, bilateral leg weakness 4/5, brisk reflexes, sensory level at T7, palpable bladder.
case.tests: Whole-spine MRI shows T6 vertebral body metastasis with epidural tumour compressing the cord; CT chest a hilar mass.
case.q: What should happen within the next 24 hours?
case.a: Metastatic cord compression: start high-dose dexamethasone, consult spinal surgery and radiation oncology urgently, and obtain tissue diagnosis if feasible.

read.where: Chapter 20 Neuro-Oncology — Metastatic Spinal Cord Tumours

det.patho: Most metastases reach the vertebral body haematogenously and grow into the epidural space or cause vertebral collapse with retropulsed bone. Compression causes venous congestion, vasogenic oedema and finally ischaemic cord infarction. Intramedullary and leptomeningeal spread are less common routes.
det.clinical: Pain precedes neurological deficits in most patients, often by weeks, providing a window for diagnosis. Thoracic spine is most commonly involved, followed by lumbar and cervical levels. Once weakness appears it can progress quickly; patients who are still walking at treatment usually remain ambulant, whereas paraplegic patients rarely recover walking.
det.diagnosis: Any cancer patient with new spinal pain, especially thoracic or nocturnal, should have MRI of the whole spine urgently, ideally before deficits appear. MRI defines the extent, number of levels, and degree of compression. Biopsy is needed when no primary is known; myeloma and lymphoma should be considered because they respond well to non-surgical treatment.
det.treatment: Give dexamethasone promptly (commonly 16 mg daily, then tapered) for patients with deficits. Decompressive surgery with stabilisation followed by radiotherapy benefits selected patients with good performance status and a single level, especially with instability. Others receive radiotherapy (including stereotactic body radiotherapy) and systemic therapy for chemosensitive tumours. Include analgesia, thromboprophylaxis, bladder and bowel care and rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: Survival depends on tumour type and systemic disease; neurological outcome depends mostly on pre-treatment function and speed of treatment.
pearls: Cancer + new thoracic back pain = whole-spine MRI, do not wait for weakness.
Pre-treatment ambulation is the best predictor of post-treatment ambulation.
Sensory level may be several segments below the true lesion; image the whole spine.
det.thd: มะเร็งแพร่กระจายมาที่กระดูกสันหลังแล้วกดไขสันหลัง พบบ่อยจากมะเร็งปอด เต้านม ต่อมลูกหมาก ไต และ myeloma ผู้ป่วยมักปวดหลังก่อนหลายสัปดาห์โดยเฉพาะตอนกลางคืน จากนั้นขาอ่อนแรง มีระดับการชา และปัสสาวะลำบาก ต้องทำ MRI ทั้งไขสันหลังอย่างเร่งด่วน ให้ dexamethasone และปรึกษาศัลยกรรมกระดูกสันหลังกับรังสีรักษาทันที ผู้ที่ยังเดินได้ตอนเริ่มรักษามีโอกาสเดินได้ต่อสูง
