name: Methyl bromide-induced myoclonus
formal: Toxic action myoclonus and ataxia after inhalational exposure to the fumigant methyl bromide, with seizures and encephalopathy; resembles Lance-Adams syndrome.
simple: Jerking muscle movements and poor balance caused by breathing in a pesticide gas called methyl bromide.
th: อาการกระตุกแบบ myoclonus เดินเซ และชักจากการสูดดมสารรมควันกำจัดแมลง methyl bromide มักเกิดหลังสัมผัสหลายชั่วโมงถึงหลายวัน

feat: Exposure in fumigation of grain, soil, warehouses or shipping containers, sometimes through leaks
Action and stimulus-sensitive myoclonus with cerebellar ataxia, dysarthria and tremor
Seizures, confusion, visual disturbance and, in severe cases, coma

case.story: Helped fumigate a rice store without a respirator; two days later developed jerking of his arms whenever he reached for something and walked unsteadily.
case.exam: Multifocal action myoclonus, intention tremor, wide-based gait, normal strength.
case.tests: Serum bromide mildly raised; MRI shows bilateral dentate nucleus T2 hyperintensity; EEG shows spikes time-locked to jerks.
case.q: What is the mechanism of the movement disorder, and how is it treated?
case.a: Toxic cortical (and cerebellar) myoclonus from methyl bromide; remove exposure and treat with levetiracetam, valproate or clonazepam.

det.patho: Methyl bromide is a volatile alkylating fumigant that is absorbed through the lungs and skin. It methylates sulfhydryl groups of proteins and glutathione, disturbing neuronal metabolism, especially in the cerebellum, brainstem and cortex. Individual susceptibility varies, possibly depending on glutathione S-transferase activity. Its agricultural use is now restricted under ozone protection rules but continues for quarantine fumigation.
det.clinical: After a latent period, patients develop headache, nausea and visual blurring, followed by action myoclonus, ataxia, tremor and seizures; severe exposure causes status epilepticus, pulmonary oedema and death. Chronic or repeated low-level exposure causes a subacute cerebellar and myoclonic syndrome with neuropathy and mood change. Residual myoclonus and cognitive or psychiatric problems may persist for months or permanently.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the exposure history plus a compatible syndrome; bromide levels support but do not exclude it. MRI may show symmetrical dentate, brainstem or callosal lesions. Neurophysiology confirms cortical myoclonus. Rule out hypoxic injury, other toxins and metabolic encephalopathies.
det.treatment: Remove the person from exposure, decontaminate skin and clothes, and provide supportive and intensive care as needed. Treat myoclonus and seizures with levetiracetam, valproate, clonazepam or piracetam. N-acetylcysteine has been used as an antidote in case reports, but evidence is limited. Report the case to occupational health so co-workers can be checked.
det.prognosis: Mild cases recover over weeks to months; severe poisoning can leave persistent myoclonus, ataxia or cognitive impairment, or be fatal.
pearls: New action myoclonus and ataxia in a fumigation worker: ask about methyl bromide.
Symptoms are often delayed, so the link to exposure is easily missed.
det.thd: Methyl bromide เป็นสารรมควันกำจัดแมลงในโกดังและสินค้า การสูดดมทำให้เกิด myoclonus เมื่อเคลื่อนไหว เดินเซ สั่น และชัก มักเริ่มหลังสัมผัสหลายชั่วโมงถึงหลายวัน การวินิจฉัยอาศัยประวัติการทำงาน ระดับ bromide และ MRI ที่อาจพบรอยโรคที่ dentate nucleus รักษาโดยให้พ้นจากสาร ดูแลประคับประคอง และใช้ยา levetiracetam หรือ clonazepam คุมอาการกระตุก

name: Methylmalonic acidaemia (MMA)
formal: Inherited disorder of methylmalonyl-CoA mutase or cobalamin metabolism, causing recurrent ketoacidosis, hyperammonaemia, encephalopathy, basal ganglia infarction and developmental delay.
simple: An inherited condition where the body cannot break down some proteins, leading to acid build-up, vomiting, lethargy and brain damage.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมเมตาบอลิซึมที่ขาดเอนไซม์ methylmalonyl-CoA mutase หรือความผิดปกติของ cobalamin ทำให้เลือดเป็นกรด แอมโมเนียสูง ซึมชัก มี basal ganglia infarct และพัฒนาการช้า
tempoNote: Neonatal crisis or recurrent decompensations triggered by illness or protein load, on a background of chronic complications
feat: Neonate: poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, coma after protein feeding begins
Ketoacidosis with high anion gap, hyperammonaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia
Metabolic stroke of the globus pallidus causing acute dystonia
Long-term: developmental delay, chronic kidney disease, pancreatitis, optic atrophy
Some cobalamin-responsive forms (cblA, cblB) are milder
inv: Blood gas, ammonia, lactate, glucose, ketones in any crisis
Urine organic acids: very high methylmalonic acid, methylcitrate
Plasma acylcarnitines (raised propionylcarnitine C3), plasma B12 and homocysteine
Molecular testing (MMUT, MMAA, MMAB, MCEE); newborn screening where available

case.who: 4-day-old girl born in Nakhon Si Thammarat
case.story: Fed well for two days, then became floppy, vomited and breathed fast.
case.exam: Lethargic, hypotonic, tachypnoeic; no focal signs.
case.tests: pH 7.08, anion gap 28, ammonia 420 µmol/L, urine ketones strongly positive; urine organic acids show massive methylmalonic acid.
case.q: What is the emergency management?
case.a: Stop protein, give high-rate IV glucose with insulin as needed, carnitine, IM hydroxocobalamin trial, ammonia scavengers and early haemodialysis for severe hyperammonaemia.

det.patho: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA in the breakdown of certain amino acids, odd-chain fatty acids and cholesterol, using adenosylcobalamin as cofactor. Defects in the enzyme (mut0 or mut-) or in cofactor synthesis (cblA, cblB) cause accumulation of toxic organic acids that inhibit mitochondrial energy production and the urea cycle. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
det.clinical: Severe forms present in the first days of life with encephalopathy; milder ones present later with recurrent vomiting, failure to thrive or decompensation during infection. Bilateral globus pallidus necrosis may follow a crisis and leave a movement disorder. Chronic complications include intellectual disability, renal tubular and glomerular disease, cardiomyopathy and optic neuropathy. Combined MMA and homocystinuria (cblC) is a separate group with retinopathy and microangiopathy.
det.diagnosis: Suspect in any child with metabolic acidosis and hyperammonaemia. Urine organic acids and plasma acylcarnitines confirm; homocysteine distinguishes isolated from combined forms. Genetic testing identifies the subtype and B12 responsiveness, and enzyme studies may be used. Newborn screening by tandem mass spectrometry detects many cases early.
det.treatment: Acute crisis: stop protein briefly, give calories as IV glucose, correct acidosis, carnitine, hydroxocobalamin, and haemodialysis when ammonia is very high; carglumic acid can lower ammonia. Long term: restricted natural protein with special formula, carnitine, metronidazole cycles to reduce gut propionate, and an emergency plan for intercurrent illness. Liver or combined liver-kidney transplantation reduces crises in severe mut0 disease but does not fully prevent neurological complications.
det.prognosis: B12-responsive forms do best; severe mutase deficiency carries risk of early death, cognitive impairment and renal failure.
pearls: Acidosis plus high ammonia in a sick neonate: send urine organic acids.
Bilateral pallidal infarcts after a crisis suggest organic acidaemia.
Always try hydroxocobalamin; responsiveness changes prognosis.
det.thd: Methylmalonic acidaemia เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมยีนด้อยที่ย่อยกรดอะมิโนบางชนิดไม่ได้ ทารกมีอาการหลังเริ่มกินนมไม่กี่วัน ซึม อาเจียน หายใจหอบ เลือดเป็นกรดและแอมโมเนียสูง อาจเกิด basal ganglia infarct วินิจฉัยด้วย urine organic acids และ acylcarnitine รักษาภาวะวิกฤตด้วยงดโปรตีน ให้กลูโคส carnitine วิตามิน B12 และฟอกเลือดถ้าแอมโมเนียสูงมาก ระยะยาวจำกัดโปรตีนและบางรายต้องปลูกถ่ายตับ

name: Methylphenidate akathisia
formal: Drug-induced motor restlessness and inability to stay still related to stimulant methylphenidate, a form of medication-induced movement disorder.
simple: Inner restlessness and an urge to keep moving caused by the medicine methylphenidate.
th: อาการกระสับกระส่ายนั่งไม่ติดจากยากระตุ้น methylphenidate เป็นความผิดปกติการเคลื่อนไหวจากยาที่พบไม่บ่อย
tempoNote: Usually within days of starting or increasing the dose; settles after reduction
feat: Inner restlessness and fidgeting that worsens after methylphenidate is started or increased
Hard to separate from the hyperactivity being treated; worsening rather than improvement is the clue
Often with insomnia, irritability, appetite loss, tics or stereotypies
Risk rises when combined with antipsychotics (e.g. risperidone) or SSRIs
inv: Timeline of dose changes and co-medications; parent and teacher reports
Rating with Barnes Akathisia Rating Scale where feasible
Heart rate and blood pressure; ECG if cardiac symptoms

case.who: 9-year-old boy from Khon Kaen with ADHD
case.story: Methylphenidate was raised from 10 to 30 mg/day; teacher reports he now cannot stay in his seat at all and says his legs 'feel itchy inside'.
case.exam: Constant shifting, crossing and uncrossing legs, mild motor tics of the eyes; no chorea or dystonia.
case.tests: Normal growth parameters for age; HR 108/min; no further tests required.
case.q: What is happening and what is the next step?
case.a: Stimulant-related akathisia; lower the dose or switch to a non-stimulant such as atomoxetine or guanfacine.

det.patho: Methylphenidate blocks dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake. Excess noradrenergic tone and altered dopaminergic signalling in mesocortical and striatal circuits are thought to drive akathisia, mirroring the noradrenergic component of antipsychotic akathisia. Evidence comes mainly from case reports and small series.
det.clinical: Symptoms are subjective restlessness with visible fidgeting, pacing or rocking, often in the hours after a dose. Children may be unable to describe the inner urge, so a sudden behavioural deterioration after a dose increase should prompt the question. Other stimulant effects such as insomnia, anxiety and tics may accompany it.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical and time-linked. Distinguish from rebound hyperactivity at dose wear-off, from emerging tics, and from akathisia caused by concurrent antipsychotics. A drug-holiday or dose reduction trial is often diagnostic.
det.treatment: Reduce or divide the dose, move to an extended-release form, or switch to a non-stimulant. Propranolol or clonidine have been used in small reports. Reassess any added antipsychotic.
det.prognosis: Reversible once the dose is adjusted.
pearls: Worsening restlessness after a stimulant increase is not always 'more ADHD'.
Ask children whether their body feels like it has to keep moving.
Stimulant plus antipsychotic combinations raise akathisia risk.
det.thd: Methylphenidate akathisia คืออาการกระสับกระส่ายนั่งไม่ติดหลังเริ่มหรือเพิ่มยา methylphenidate ในเด็กสมาธิสั้นอาจแยกยากจากอาการเดิม จุดสังเกตคืออาการแย่ลงหลังปรับยา การวินิจฉัยใช้ประวัติและการลองลดยา การรักษาคือลดขนาด เปลี่ยนรูปแบบยา หรือเปลี่ยนเป็นยาที่ไม่ใช่ stimulant

ddx.pt: Baseline hyperactivity without the subjective inner urge or dose-linked worsening
Tics with premonitory urge, suppressible, present before the drug

name: MGUS neuropathy
formal: Peripheral neuropathy associated with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance, often IgM with anti-MAG antibodies causing distal demyelinating sensory ataxic neuropathy and tremor.
simple: Nerve damage associated with an abnormal protein in the blood that is not cancer, causing numbness and unsteadiness.
more: Serum immunofixation, anti-MAG antibodies, and nerve conduction studies; rituximab for IgM; IVIG or steroids in IgG or IgA forms.
ab: monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance neuropathy
th: เส้นประสาทเสื่อมร่วมกับ MGUS — โปรตีนโมโนโคลนอลปริมาณน้อยโดยยังไม่เป็นมะเร็ง ชนิด IgM มักเป็น anti-MAG ชนิด IgG/IgA อาจคล้าย CIDP
feat: MGUS = M-protein < 30 g/L, marrow plasma cells < 10%, no myeloma-related organ damage
IgM type: distal demyelinating, often anti-MAG
IgG/IgA type: either CIDP-like (treat as CIDP) or slowly progressive axonal (often no treatment)
Becomes commoner with age, so the link to the neuropathy may be coincidental
inv: Immunofixation, free light chains, haematology review to exclude myeloma/lymphoma
Repeat M-protein measurement every 6–12 months

case.exam: Stocking loss of pinprick to mid-shin, reduced ankle jerks, normal strength.

det.patho: MGUS is a premalignant clonal plasma-cell or B-cell disorder present in about 3% of people over 50 and more in older age. When neuropathy and MGUS coexist the link may be causal (IgM with anti-MAG or anti-ganglioside activity) or coincidental. IgM MGUS can evolve, at a low yearly rate, into Waldenström macroglobulinaemia or lymphoma, and non-IgM MGUS to myeloma or AL amyloidosis, at roughly 1% per year overall.
det.clinical: IgM MGUS usually produces a distal demyelinating, sensory-predominant neuropathy with ataxia. IgG or IgA MGUS is associated with either a CIDP-like syndrome with proximal weakness or a slowly progressive axonal neuropathy indistinguishable from idiopathic neuropathy of the elderly. New pain, autonomic symptoms or systemic features should prompt a search for amyloid or malignancy.
det.diagnosis: MGUS requires an M-protein below 30 g/L, fewer than 10% clonal marrow plasma cells and no end-organ damage (no hypercalcaemia, renal failure, anaemia or bone lesions) or lymphoma features. Characterise the neuropathy carefully with NCS, test anti-MAG when IgM, and exclude other causes such as diabetes, B12 deficiency and alcohol. Haematological follow-up with periodic M-protein levels and blood counts is advised.
det.treatment: CIDP-like IgG/IgA MGUS neuropathy is treated like CIDP with IVIG, steroids or plasma exchange. IgM anti-MAG disease is managed as anti-MAG neuropathy. Mild axonal neuropathy needs symptomatic treatment (neuropathic pain agents, foot care) rather than immunotherapy.
det.prognosis: Most patients have slowly progressive disability; the main long-term risk is haematological transformation, which needs lifelong surveillance.
pearls: MGUS is common in older adults — finding it does not prove it caused the neuropathy.
Check the M-protein isotype: IgM points to anti-MAG; IgG/IgA with demyelination points to a CIDP-like disorder.
det.thd: MGUS คือภาวะที่มีโปรตีนโมโนโคลนอลปริมาณน้อยในเลือด โดยยังไม่เข้าเกณฑ์มะเร็ง พบได้บ่อยในผู้สูงอายุ จึงอาจเกี่ยวข้องหรือไม่เกี่ยวข้องกับเส้นประสาทเสื่อมก็ได้ ชนิด IgM มักเป็น anti-MAG ทำให้ชาและเดินเซ ส่วนชนิด IgG/IgA อาจคล้าย CIDP หรือเป็นแบบแอกซอนช้าๆ การรักษาแบบ CIDP ใช้ IVIG หรือสเตียรอยด์ ส่วนแบบแอกซอนรักษาตามอาการ และต้องติดตามระดับโปรตีนเพราะมีโอกาสกลายเป็นมะเร็งเม็ดเลือดประมาณ 1% ต่อปี

name: Microangiopathy
formal: Small-vessel endothelial injury with thrombosis, hemolysis and ischaemia, as in thrombotic microangiopathy, CNS cerebral small vessel disease or diabetic microangiopathy.
simple: Damage to the smallest blood vessels, leading to clots and poor blood supply to organs.
more: Management depends on type, such as plasma exchange for TTP and complement inhibitors for atypical HUS; control of diabetes and hypertension for chronic forms.
th: ความผิดปกติของหลอดเลือดขนาดเล็กจากผนังหลอดเลือดถูกทำลาย มีลิ่มเลือดอุดตันและเม็ดเลือดแดงแตก เช่น TTP หรือหลอดเลือดสมองเล็กเสื่อมและภาวะแทรกซ้อนของเบาหวาน
tempoNote: Thrombotic microangiopathies are acute emergencies; small vessel and diabetic microangiopathy are chronic
feat: Umbrella term rather than a single disease
Thrombotic microangiopathy: haemolysis with schistocytes, low platelets, organ ischaemia (brain, kidney)
Neurological TMA features: fluctuating confusion, headache, seizures, transient focal deficits, small infarcts
Chronic cerebral small vessel disease: lacunes, white matter disease, microbleeds
Diabetic microangiopathy underlies retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy

ADAMTS13 activity (<10% = TTP); complement studies and stool STEC testing for HUS
MRI: small multifocal infarcts or PRES pattern in TMA; white matter hyperintensities in chronic SVD

case.story: Three days of headache and episodes of word-finding difficulty lasting minutes, with bruises on her legs.
case.exam: Drowsy but rousable, petechiae, fluctuating mild right arm weakness.
case.tests: Hb 7.5, platelets 18,000, schistocytes on film, LDH 1,800; creatinine mildly raised; ADAMTS13 activity <5%.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the urgent treatment?
case.a: Immune TTP; urgent plasma exchange with steroids, plus caplacizumab and rituximab where available; avoid platelet transfusion unless bleeding.

det.patho: In thrombotic microangiopathy, endothelial injury leads to platelet-rich microthrombi in arterioles and capillaries; red cells are fragmented as they pass. Causes include ADAMTS13 deficiency (TTP), complement dysregulation (atypical HUS), Shiga toxin, drugs, malignancy, pregnancy and malignant hypertension. Chronic microangiopathies such as hypertensive arteriolosclerosis and diabetic microvascular disease cause wall thickening and luminal narrowing over years.
det.clinical: Acute TMA affecting the brain causes fluctuating neurological symptoms that may be subtle, together with anaemia, bruising and kidney injury. Seizures and coma indicate severe disease. Chronic microangiopathy manifests as lacunar strokes, slow cognitive decline, gait change and, systemically, retinopathy and kidney disease. Susac syndrome is a rare autoimmune microangiopathy of brain, retina and inner ear.
det.diagnosis: The combination of microangiopathic haemolysis and thrombocytopenia defines TMA; ADAMTS13 activity separates TTP from other causes, and the PLASMIC score helps while results are pending. MRI may show small scattered infarcts or PRES. For chronic forms, MRI markers of small vessel disease and fundoscopy for retinopathy are key.
det.treatment: TTP requires emergency plasma exchange, steroids, rituximab and caplacizumab; atypical HUS is treated with complement C5 inhibitors (eculizumab, ravulizumab). Treat triggers such as drugs, infection or hypertension. Chronic microangiopathy is managed by strict control of blood pressure, glucose and lipids, smoking cessation and antiplatelet therapy after ischaemic events.
det.prognosis: Untreated TTP is often fatal, but modern therapy brings survival above 90%; chronic forms progress slowly with risk-factor control.
pearls: Confusion plus low platelets plus schistocytes: TTP until proved otherwise.
Do not wait for ADAMTS13 results to start plasma exchange when suspicion is high.
Microangiopathy is a mechanism; always name the underlying cause.
det.thd: Microangiopathy หมายถึงโรคของหลอดเลือดขนาดเล็ก แบ่งเป็นแบบเฉียบพลัน เช่น TTP และ HUS ที่มีลิ่มเลือดเล็ก ๆ อุดตัน เม็ดเลือดแดงแตก เกล็ดเลือดต่ำ และอาการทางสมองเป็น ๆ หาย ๆ ต้องรีบทำ plasma exchange และแบบเรื้อรัง เช่น หลอดเลือดสมองเล็กเสื่อมจากความดันหรือเบาหวาน ซึ่งรักษาด้วยการควบคุมปัจจัยเสี่ยง

case.story: Tingling feet and hands and unsteady walking for 3 months.

det.patho: Vitamins and trace elements serve as cofactors for myelin synthesis, energy metabolism and antioxidant defence. Deficiencies lead to axonal degeneration, demyelination of long tracts or neuronal injury depending on the nutrient.
det.clinical: Syndromes overlap: myeloneuropathy (B12, copper, folate), encephalopathy (thiamine, niacin), ataxia (vitamin E), optic neuropathy (B12, copper, thiamine). Multiple deficiencies often coexist in malabsorption.
det.diagnosis: Measure relevant levels and functional markers. Look for the underlying cause and test for several deficiencies together.
det.treatment: Replace deficient nutrients, using parenteral routes when absorption is impaired. Give thiamine before glucose in at-risk patients. Correct the underlying cause and provide nutritional support.
det.prognosis: Better with early treatment; long-standing deficits may persist.
pearls: Thiamine before glucose in malnourished or alcoholic patients.
Normal B12 with myelopathy: check copper.
Malabsorption usually means more than one deficiency.
det.thd: การขาดวิตามินและแร่ธาตุทำให้เกิดโรคระบบประสาทหลายแบบ เช่น ขาด B12 และทองแดงทำให้ไขสันหลังและเส้นประสาทเสื่อม ขาด thiamine ทำให้ Wernicke encephalopathy ขาดวิตามิน E ทำให้เดินเซ ปัจจัยเสี่ยงคือสุรา ผ่าตัดกระเพาะ ลำไส้ดูดซึมผิดปกติ ตรวจระดับสารหลายชนิดพร้อมกันและให้ทดแทน

name: Microscopic polyangiitis
formal: ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis (usually MPO-ANCA) with necrotising glomerulonephritis, pulmonary haemorrhage and mononeuritis multiplex or, less often, CNS involvement.
simple: An inflammatory disease of small blood vessels that can damage kidneys, lungs and nerves.
more: Diagnose with MPO-ANCA, urine sediment, and biopsy of kidney or nerve; treat with high-dose steroids plus cyclophosphamide or rituximab, and plasma exchange in severe cases. Relapse is common; maintenance with azathioprine or rituximab.

feat: Older adults (often 50–70); fever, weight loss, arthralgia
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary haemorrhage or fibrosis

No granulomas, so no sinus or orbital masses (unlike GPA)

inv: MPO-ANCA (p-ANCA) positive in most

det.patho: ANCA directed against myeloperoxidase activate primed neutrophils, which adhere to and damage small vessel walls through degranulation and neutrophil extracellular traps; complement C5a amplifies the process. Necrotising inflammation of the vasa nervorum produces nerve infarction. Certain drugs (hydralazine, propylthiouracil) and silica exposure can induce MPO-ANCA vasculitis.
det.clinical: Kidney involvement is the most common and often decides outcome. Peripheral neuropathy occurs in a sizeable minority, usually as sudden painful deficits in single nerves that accumulate. Lung involvement ranges from alveolar haemorrhage to interstitial fibrosis. CNS disease is uncommon but includes strokes, intracerebral bleeding and hypertrophic pachymeningitis.
det.diagnosis: ACR/EULAR 2022 classification criteria weight MPO-ANCA, pauci-immune glomerulonephritis and absence of eosinophilia or granulomas. Biopsy of an affected organ confirms; nerve plus muscle biopsy is useful when neuropathy is prominent. Exclude infection (endocarditis, hepatitis) and drug causes, which can also produce ANCA.
det.treatment: Induction uses glucocorticoids with rituximab or cyclophosphamide; avacopan (C5a receptor blocker) allows a faster steroid taper. Plasma exchange is reserved for selected patients with severe kidney failure or lung haemorrhage. Maintenance with rituximab every six months (or azathioprine) continues for at least two years. Provide Pneumocystis prophylaxis and bone protection.
det.prognosis: Most patients achieve remission, but relapses occur and residual neuropathic pain or weakness is common.
pearls: Mononeuritis multiplex plus active urine sediment: check ANCA.
MPA lacks granulomas; ENT and orbit are spared.
Avacopan is a steroid-sparing option in ANCA vasculitis.

name: Migraine
formal: Primary headache disorder of recurrent unilateral pulsating attacks with nausea, photophobia and phonophobia, with or without aura, from trigeminovascular activation and cortical spreading depression.
simple: A common condition causing repeated severe throbbing headaches, often with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound.
th: ไมเกรน — ปวดศีรษะตุบ ๆ ข้างเดียว คลื่นไส้ กลัวแสงเสียง เป็นซ้ำ ๆ 4–72 ชั่วโมง
tempoNote: Attacks of 4–72 h, recurrent
feat: Unilateral, pulsating, moderate–severe headache worsened by activity
Nausea, photophobia and phonophobia
Aura in a third: spreading visual or sensory symptoms over 5–60 min
Triggers: sleep change, menstruation, fasting, stress
inv: Clinical diagnosis; imaging only for red flags (SNOOP4)

case.exam: Normal, including fundi.
case.tests: None needed.
case.q: What features of the visual aura distinguish it from a TIA?

ddx.pt: Bilateral pressing, mild–moderate, no nausea
Strictly orbital, 15–180 min, restless, autonomic signs

det.patho: Migraine is a genetically influenced brain disorder of sensory processing. Activation of the trigeminovascular system releases CGRP and other neuropeptides, sensitising meningeal nociceptors and central pain pathways; aura corresponds to cortical spreading depolarisation. The hypothalamus and brainstem probably drive the premonitory phase. It affects roughly 15% of people, with a threefold female predominance during reproductive years.
det.clinical: Attacks can include a premonitory phase (yawning, food cravings, neck stiffness), aura in about a third, the headache phase and a postdrome of fatigue. Aura is typically visual (scintillating zigzags or scotoma), sometimes sensory or speech-related, developing gradually and lasting 5–60 minutes. Chronic migraine means headache on half or more of the days in a month (15+) with migraine features on at least eight; medication overuse often drives this. Red flags (SNOOP4) include systemic symptoms, neurological deficit, sudden onset, onset after 50, positional or Valsalva-triggered pain, and a change in pattern. Recognised variants include vestibular, hemiplegic and brainstem-aura forms of migraine.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis follows ICHD-3 clinical criteria: at least five attacks of 4–72 hours with two of unilateral, pulsating, moderate-severe or activity-worsened pain, plus nausea or photophobia and phonophobia. A headache diary clarifies frequency and medication use. Neuroimaging is not needed with a typical history and normal examination; image when red flags are present or the aura is atypical (motor weakness, prolonged, or always on the same side). First-ever aura after 50 should be evaluated as possible TIA.
det.treatment: For acute attacks, give an NSAID or paracetamol early, with an antiemetic, and use a triptan for moderate-severe attacks; gepants and lasmiditan are alternatives when triptans are contraindicated. Limit acute treatment to fewer than 10–15 days a month to avoid medication-overuse headache. Prevention is offered for frequent or disabling attacks: propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate, candesartan, flunarizine or valproate (not in people who could become pregnant), and for refractory cases CGRP monoclonal antibodies, gepants or onabotulinumtoxinA for chronic migraine. Regular sleep, meals, exercise and treatment of comorbid anxiety, depression or sleep disorders support any drug plan.
det.prognosis: Migraine often eases after menopause and with age, but it remains a leading cause of disability in young adults; migraine with aura carries a small increase in ischaemic stroke risk, enhanced by smoking and oestrogen-containing contraception.
pearls: Aura spreads over minutes (march); TIA symptoms appear all at once.
Ask about painkiller days per month in every patient with frequent headache.
Combined oestrogen contraception should be avoided in migraine with aura.
det.thd: ไมเกรนเป็นโรคของสมองที่ไวต่อสิ่งกระตุ้น เกี่ยวข้องกับระบบ trigeminovascular และสาร CGRP อาการคือปวดศีรษะตุบ ๆ ข้างเดียว 4–72 ชั่วโมง คลื่นไส้ กลัวแสงเสียง บางรายมี aura เห็นแสงซิกแซกค่อย ๆ ขยายก่อนปวด วินิจฉัยจากประวัติตามเกณฑ์ ICHD-3 ส่งภาพสมองเมื่อมี red flags การรักษาเฉียบพลันใช้ NSAID หรือ triptan ไม่ควรกินยาแก้ปวดเกิน 10–15 วันต่อเดือน ถ้าเป็นบ่อยให้ยาป้องกัน เช่น propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate หรือยากลุ่ม CGRP

name: Mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI)
formal: Head injury with brief altered consciousness, amnesia or GCS 13 to 15, causing concussion symptoms such as headache, dizziness, cognitive slowing; most recover within weeks.
simple: A mild head injury, often called concussion, causing headache, dizziness and trouble concentrating.
th: mTBI คือการบาดเจ็บที่ศีรษะระดับ GCS 13–15 ซึ่งมักมีอาการชั่วคราว เช่น มึนงง ปวดศีรษะ ความจำช่วงเกิดเหตุหาย ผู้ป่วยส่วนใหญ่หายภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์ สิ่งสำคัญคือแยกผู้ที่ต้องทำ CT (เช่น อาเจียนซ้ำ ชัก อายุมาก กินยากันเลือด) ออกจากผู้ที่ดูแลที่บ้านได้ และให้คำแนะนำการกลับไปเรียน ทำงาน และออกกำลังอย่างค่อยเป็นค่อยไป
tempoNote: Symptoms begin at impact or within hours; most settle within days to a month, a minority persist
feat: GCS 13–15 with a brief period of confusion, amnesia for the event, or loss of consciousness for less than 30 minutes; post-traumatic amnesia under 24 hours
Headache, dizziness, nausea, light and noise sensitivity, slowed thinking, poor concentration, fatigue, irritability, anxiety and sleep disturbance
Concussion is the low-severity end of mTBI with normal structural imaging; mTBI can also include small contusions, subarachnoid blood or a fracture visible on CT

Red flags for intracranial bleeding: GCS below 15 two hours after injury, repeated vomiting, worsening headache, seizure, focal signs, suspected skull fracture, age over 65 and anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy
Delayed bleeds, especially subdural, can appear days to weeks later in older and anticoagulated patients
inv: Clinical decision rules for CT (Canadian CT Head Rule for adults, PECARN for children, or New Orleans criteria); use a low threshold in older or anticoagulated patients
Serum GFAP and UCH-L1, where available, help to decide who can safely skip CT; they do not diagnose concussion
MRI with susceptibility-weighted imaging for persistent symptoms or an unexplained deficit; cervical spine, vestibular and oculomotor screening

case.story: His bike skidded on a wet road at about 30 km/h; he was wearing a helmet, was dazed for a few minutes and cannot remember the crash. He vomited twice at the roadside and now has a headache and nausea.
case.exam: GCS 15, scalp bruise on the right temple, oriented, no focal deficit, mildly unsteady on tandem walking.
case.tests: He takes no anticoagulant. Under a decision rule, repeated vomiting and a dangerous mechanism indicate CT, which shows no intracranial lesion.
case.q: What is the disposition and what advice should be given?
case.a: Mild TBI with a normal CT. He can go home with a responsible adult and written red-flag advice, relative rest for 24–48 hours, then gradual return to activity; he must not ride until symptoms resolve and review is needed if drowsiness, repeated vomiting, worsening headache or weakness occurs.

Chapter 25 Restorative Neurology, Rehabilitation and Brain Injury — Mild Traumatic Brain Injury, Sports Concussion and Minor Head Injury
27 Fits, faints, funny turns, and falls in the differential diagnosis of the dizzy patient

det.patho: Rapid acceleration, deceleration and rotation stretch axons and trigger an ionic and neurotransmitter flux with an energy mismatch and reduced cerebral blood flow. Most of the clinical picture reflects temporary functional disturbance, so routine imaging is normal in concussion even though microscopic axonal injury may exist. In mTBI proper there can be small contusions, subarachnoid haemorrhage or a fracture visible on CT, which is why mTBI and concussion are not interchangeable terms.
det.clinical: Road traffic collisions (especially motorcycle crashes), falls, assault and sport are the leading causes. Symptoms cluster into physical, cognitive, emotional and sleep domains, appear immediately or within hours, and often go unreported. Loss of consciousness is not required and a direct blow is not essential. Risk of slower recovery rises with previous concussions, migraine, anxiety or depression, female sex in some data, and high initial symptom load. Children can show irritability, listlessness, balance changes or altered feeding and sleep.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical and depends on a plausible mechanism and an acute change in orientation, memory, balance, reaction or symptoms in a patient with GCS 13–15. No single test confirms it; symptom checklists, balance and oculomotor examination are used, and the diagnosis is best made within 24 hours. Decide on CT with a validated rule, remembering that a normal CT excludes surgical lesions, not concussion. Look for cervical spine and facial injuries and for conditions that raise bleeding risk.
det.treatment: Remove the patient from risk, observe for the first hours, and give written red-flag advice with a responsible adult. Current consensus advocates a short period of relative rest of 24 to 48 hours followed by early, gradual, symptom-limited activity rather than prolonged bed rest. Return to school or work comes before return to contact sport and driving. Treat headache without overusing analgesics, address sleep and mood, and refer for vestibular, cervical or graded aerobic exercise therapy if symptoms persist beyond a few weeks. Promote helmets and road safety.
det.prognosis: Most adults recover within one to four weeks; a minority have symptoms for months, and the risk is higher after repeated injuries.
pearls: Concussion is a clinical diagnosis with normal imaging; mTBI is a broader category that includes small CT lesions.
Anticoagulated or elderly patients need a lower threshold for CT and a period of observation.
Advise a staged return: learn, work, exercise, and only then contact sport or riding.
det.thd: mTBI คือการบาดเจ็บศีรษะที่ GCS 13–15 อาจมีหมดสติสั้น ๆ หรือจำเหตุการณ์ไม่ได้ ส่วน concussion เป็นกลุ่มย่อยที่ภาพรังสีปกติ วินิจฉัยจากประวัติและตรวจร่างกาย ใช้กฎการสั่ง CT (เช่น Canadian CT Head Rule) และระวังเป็นพิเศษในผู้สูงอายุหรือผู้ที่กินยากันเลือด ผู้ป่วยส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นใน 1–4 สัปดาห์ แนะนำพักสั้น ๆ 24–48 ชั่วโมงแล้วค่อย ๆ กลับสู่กิจกรรม และให้ย้ำสัญญาณอันตรายก่อนกลับบ้าน

name: Miller Fisher syndrome
formal: Variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia, associated with anti-GQ1b antibodies after infection.
simple: A variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome causing weak eye movements, poor balance and absent reflexes.
more: Anti-GQ1b IgG is positive in most cases; CSF shows albuminocytologic dissociation. Prognosis is excellent with spontaneous recovery over weeks to months, and IVIG is used in severe cases; Bickerstaff encephalitis is the central overlap variant.
th: GBS ชนิดหนึ่ง — กลอกตาไม่ได้ เดินเซ รีเฟล็กซ์หาย สัมพันธ์แอนติบอดี GQ1b พยากรณ์ดี
feat: Triad: external ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia
Often follows a respiratory or gastrointestinal infection
May overlap with GBS limb weakness or Bickerstaff encephalitis (drowsiness, upgoing plantars)
Usually recovers well over weeks to months
inv: Anti-GQ1b IgG (and GT1a)
CSF albuminocytological dissociation (may be delayed)
MRI brain to exclude a brainstem lesion

case.exam: Bilateral ophthalmoparesis, mild ptosis, truncal and limb ataxia, absent reflexes, normal power.
case.tests: MRI brain normal; anti-GQ1b IgG positive.
case.q: Why are the eye muscles particularly vulnerable to this antibody?

aN: mfs | fisher syndrome | anti gq1b syndrome | ophthalmoplegia ataxia areflexia

det.patho: After an infection (often respiratory, sometimes Campylobacter or Haemophilus influenzae), cross-reactive IgG is produced against GQ1b and GT1a. GQ1b is concentrated in the paranodal regions of the nerves to the extraocular muscles and in muscle spindle afferents and dorsal root ganglion neurons, explaining ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia. Antibody binding at nerve terminals may also contribute. It accounts for a larger share of GBS spectrum disorders in East Asia.
det.clinical: Diplopia is usually the first symptom, followed within days by unsteady gait. Ptosis, facial or bulbar weakness and pupillary abnormalities may accompany it. Overlap with limb-weakness GBS or with Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis (drowsiness, hyperreflexia) occurs and these form one anti-GQ1b spectrum. Incomplete forms include acute ophthalmoparesis without ataxia or acute ataxic neuropathy. Respiratory failure is uncommon unless it overlaps with GBS.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical, supported by anti-GQ1b IgG in most cases. CSF protein may be normal in the first week. Nerve conduction may show reduced sensory amplitudes or be normal. MRI brain is important to exclude brainstem stroke, Wernicke encephalopathy or tumour. Also consider botulism, myasthenia and diphtheria.
det.treatment: Pure MFS usually recovers well without immunotherapy; IVIG has not been proven to change outcome, though many clinicians treat severe or overlapping cases. Monitor for evolving limb or respiratory weakness, which would prompt standard GBS treatment. Supportive care includes prism or patch for diplopia, fall prevention and physiotherapy.
det.prognosis: Most patients recover fully over 3–6 months; recurrence is uncommon.
pearls: Ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + areflexia after infection: send anti-GQ1b and get an MRI brain.
Drowsiness or extensor plantars suggests Bickerstaff encephalitis on the same spectrum.
det.thd: Miller Fisher syndrome เป็น GBS ชนิดหนึ่ง เกิดหลังการติดเชื้อ ร่างกายสร้างแอนติบอดีต่อ GQ1b ซึ่งพบมากที่เส้นประสาทกลอกตา จึงมีอาการเห็นภาพซ้อน กลอกตาไม่ได้ เดินเซ และรีเฟล็กซ์หาย การวินิจฉัยอาศัยอาการและตรวจ anti-GQ1b ควรทำ MRI สมองเพื่อแยกโรคก้านสมอง ส่วนใหญ่หายเองได้ดีภายในไม่กี่เดือน แต่ต้องเฝ้าระวังกรณีที่มีแขนขาอ่อนแรงหรือหายใจลำบากร่วมด้วย

name: Minamata disease
formal: Methylmercury poisoning from contaminated fish, causing cerebellar ataxia, constriction of visual fields, sensory disturbance, dysarthria and hearing loss, with fetal exposure producing congenital disease.
simple: A mercury poisoning from eating contaminated fish that causes clumsiness, numbness, tunnel vision and hearing loss.
more: Diagnosed from exposure history and blood or hair mercury levels. Chelation is of limited use; prevention by avoiding exposure is key and damage is mostly permanent.
th: พิษปรอทอินทรีย์ (methylmercury) จากการกินปลาที่ปนเปื้อน ทำให้เดินเซ ลานสายตาแคบ ชาปลายมือปลายเท้าและรอบปาก พูดไม่ชัด และหูตึง
tempoNote: Symptoms appear weeks to months after exposure; congenital form evident in infancy; deficits largely permanent
feat: Distal and perioral paraesthesia as early symptom
Cerebellar ataxia, dysarthria, intention tremor
Concentric constriction of visual fields (calcarine cortex damage)
Hearing loss, cognitive and psychiatric change
Congenital form: cerebral palsy-like picture in children of exposed mothers
inv: Blood and hair mercury levels (hair segments reflect timing of exposure)
MRI: atrophy of calcarine cortex, cerebellar vermis and hemispheres
Visual field testing, audiometry, nerve conduction
Environmental investigation of food source

case.who: 52-year-old fisherman's wife from a river community downstream of an illegal gold mine in the north
case.story: Over months she has developed numb lips and fingertips, clumsy walking, slurred speech and 'tunnel vision'. The family eats river fish daily.
case.exam: Perioral and glove-stocking sensory loss, dysarthria, limb and gait ataxia, concentric field constriction, mild hearing loss.
case.tests: Blood and hair mercury markedly elevated; MRI shows calcarine and cerebellar atrophy.
case.q: Which toxin and which classic triad of signs fit?
case.a: Methylmercury (Minamata disease) — sensory disturbance, ataxia and constricted visual fields (Hunter–Russell).

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Neurological Disorders Associated with Exposure to Toxic Substances

det.patho: Methylmercury is absorbed efficiently from the gut, crosses the blood-brain barrier and placenta, and binds sulfhydryl groups, disrupting protein synthesis and microtubules. Neurons in the calcarine cortex, cerebellar granule layer and dorsal root ganglia are particularly vulnerable. It accumulates up the aquatic food chain, so large fish carry the highest load.
det.clinical: The disease was first recognised in Minamata, Japan, after industrial discharge. Adult cases show paraesthesia, ataxia, visual field constriction, dysarthria and hearing loss. Fetal exposure causes severe developmental disability even when mothers are mildly affected. Lower-level chronic exposure may produce subtle cognitive and sensory effects.
det.diagnosis: History of fish consumption from a contaminated source plus characteristic signs; confirmed by blood and hair mercury levels. Note that inorganic and elemental mercury cause different syndromes (tremor, erethism, nephropathy). Exclude other causes of ataxia and neuropathy.
det.treatment: Stop exposure. Chelating agents (DMSA, DMPS) increase mercury excretion but have limited effect on established neurological damage. Rehabilitation and supportive care are central. Prevention through control of industrial and mining discharges is essential.
det.prognosis: Neurological deficits are usually permanent; severe exposure can be fatal.
pearls: Ataxia plus tunnel vision plus perioral numbness: think methylmercury.
Hair mercury gives a timeline of exposure.
Organic mercury hits the brain; inorganic mercury affects kidneys and causes tremor and mood change.
det.thd: Minamata disease คือพิษปรอทอินทรีย์ (methylmercury) จากการกินปลาที่ปนเปื้อน สารนี้ทำลายสมองส่วน calcarine สมองน้อย และปมประสาทรับความรู้สึก ทำให้ชารอบปากและปลายมือปลายเท้า เดินเซ พูดไม่ชัด ลานสายตาแคบ และหูตึง ทารกในครรภ์ได้รับผลรุนแรง วินิจฉัยจากประวัติและระดับปรอทในเลือดและเส้นผม การรักษาคือหยุดการสัมผัส ยาขับโลหะช่วยได้จำกัด

det.patho: After motor neuron loss, surviving neurons reinnervate orphaned fibres, creating giant motor units. When these few large units fire irregularly during weak contraction, each discharge produces a visible jerk of a finger. Some cases have a cortical myoclonic component, but most are explained by peripheral motor unit enlargement.
det.clinical: This is a clinical sign rather than a disease. It is best seen with fingers spread and arms outstretched, appearing as fine, arrhythmic twitches. It indicates chronic denervation and reinnervation and should prompt evaluation for a lower motor neuron disorder.
det.diagnosis: Distinguish from tremor (rhythmic), fasciculation (at rest, single unit, no voluntary effort needed) and cortical myoclonus (larger jerks, stimulus-sensitive). EMG confirms neurogenic changes.
det.treatment: No specific treatment for the sign; manage the underlying disease. In SMA, disease-modifying therapies (nusinersen, risdiplam, onasemnogene abeparvovec) are available.
det.prognosis: Depends entirely on the underlying condition.
pearls: Irregular finger twitching in a weak, wasted patient suggests chronic reinnervation.
Common in SMA type 2–3; may be mistaken for tremor.
Not a disease — always look for the motor neuron or nerve cause.
det.thd: Minipolymyoclonus คืออาการนิ้วมือกระตุกเล็ก ๆ ไม่เป็นจังหวะเวลาเหยียดมือ เป็น sign ไม่ใช่โรค เกิดจาก motor unit ขนาดใหญ่ที่เกิดขึ้นหลังเซลล์ประสาทสั่งการตายและมีการงอกเส้นประสาทใหม่ พบบ่อยใน SMA และ ALS แยกจากอาการสั่นด้วยความไม่สม่ำเสมอและผล EMG ต้องหาและรักษาโรคต้นเหตุ

name: Mitochondrial ataxia syndromes
formal: Ataxia syndromes arising from mitochondrial DNA or nuclear POLG-related defects, often with neuropathy, epilepsy, ophthalmoplegia and, sometimes, NARP or SANDO phenotypes.
simple: Inherited energy-production problems that cause poor balance and clumsiness along with other nerve problems.
th: กลุ่มโรคเดินเซจากความผิดปกติของไมโทคอนเดรีย ทั้ง mtDNA และยีนในนิวเคลียส เช่น POLG มักมีเส้นประสาทเสื่อม ชัก หนังตาตกกลอกตาไม่ได้ ร่วมด้วย

Ptosis with PEO (SANDO = sensory ataxic neuropathy, dysarthria, ophthalmoplegia)
Epilepsy, including occipital focal seizures and epilepsia partialis continua in POLG disease
Other organ clues: deafness, diabetes, retinopathy (NARP), myopathy, liver failure with valproate
inv: Genetic testing: POLG and other nuclear genes (TWNK, SPG7), mtDNA sequencing (e.g. m.8993T>G in NARP)
Nerve conduction studies for axonal sensory neuronopathy; MRI for cerebellar, thalamic or olivary signal change

case.exam: Bilateral ptosis, limited eye movements without diplopia, absent reflexes, loss of joint position sense, positive Romberg, mild limb dysmetria.

case.q: Which antiseizure drug is contraindicated and why?

det.patho: Defects in mtDNA itself or in nuclear genes that maintain it reduce oxidative phosphorylation in high-energy tissues. POLG, the mitochondrial DNA polymerase, is the commonest nuclear cause: its variants lead to multiple mtDNA deletions or depletion, damaging dorsal root ganglia, cerebellar and thalamic neurons and extraocular muscles. Primary mtDNA variants such as m.8993T>G (NARP) or MERRF-type tRNA changes also cause ataxia; heteroplasmy explains variable expression.
det.clinical: Phenotypes include MIRAS/SANDO (POLG), NARP, MERRF, Kearns–Sayre and Leigh-spectrum disease, and they overlap. A combination of ataxia with sensory neuronopathy, ophthalmoplegia, epilepsy, migraine-like headache, deafness or myopathy should raise suspicion. POLG disease can present abruptly with status epilepticus or stroke-like episodes in adults. Cognitive decline and psychiatric symptoms may develop.
det.diagnosis: First-line testing is now usually a nuclear gene panel or exome together with mtDNA sequencing from blood; urine or muscle samples improve detection of heteroplasmic mtDNA variants. NCS showing a non-length-dependent sensory neuronopathy is a strong clue. MRI may show cerebellar atrophy and bilateral thalamic, olivary or occipital lesions. Lactate and muscle biopsy are supportive but can be normal.
det.treatment: There is no proven disease-modifying therapy; care is supportive and preventive. Avoid valproate and use caution with other mitochondrial toxins; treat seizures early and aggressively because status epilepticus drives decline. Provide physiotherapy, eyelid surgery for disabling ptosis, hearing aids, cardiac and diabetes screening, and genetic counselling. Coenzyme Q10 and other supplements are widely used but evidence is weak; nucleoside therapy is in trials for some depletion syndromes.
det.prognosis: Highly variable; many remain ambulant for years, but POLG-related epilepsy and liver involvement can be life-threatening.
pearls: Ataxia + sensory neuronopathy + ophthalmoplegia = think POLG (SANDO).
Never give valproate to a patient with possible POLG disease.
A normal blood mtDNA test does not rule out a heteroplasmic variant; test urine or muscle.
det.thd: Mitochondrial ataxia syndromes คือกลุ่มโรคเดินเซจากไมโทคอนเดรียสร้างพลังงานไม่พอ เกิดได้จาก mtDNA หรือยีนนิวเคลียสโดยเฉพาะ POLG ผู้ป่วยมักมีเดินเซ เสียการรับรู้ตำแหน่งข้อ หนังตาตก กลอกตาไม่ได้ ชัก และอาจหูหนวกหรือเบาหวานร่วม การวินิจฉัยใช้การตรวจยีน NCS และ MRI ไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ ต้องดูแลประคับประคองและห้ามใช้ valproate

name: Mitochondrial cytopathy
formal: General term for disease from impaired oxidative phosphorylation, affecting high-energy tissues such as brain, muscle, heart and eye, with variable multisystem presentations.
simple: An illness where the cell's energy factories do not work properly, affecting organs such as brain and muscle.
th: คำเรียกรวมของโรคที่ไมโทคอนเดรียสร้างพลังงานผิดปกติ กระทบอวัยวะที่ใช้พลังงานมาก เช่น สมอง กล้ามเนื้อ หัวใจ ตา และหู
tempoNote: Any age; slowly progressive, with stepwise worsening during illness or stroke-like episodes
feat: Multisystem involvement across organs that do not seem connected
Ptosis and ophthalmoplegia, exercise intolerance, myopathy
Seizures, stroke-like episodes, ataxia, migraine-like headache, cognitive decline
Deafness, diabetes, short stature, cardiomyopathy, retinopathy, GI dysmotility
Maternal inheritance (mtDNA) or Mendelian inheritance (nuclear genes)
inv: Blood and CSF lactate (normal values do not exclude)
Serum GDF-15 and FGF-21 as supportive biomarkers
Blood/urine mtDNA testing (m.3243A>G), then nuclear gene panel or exome/genome
Muscle biopsy: ragged-red and COX-negative fibres; ECG, echo, audiogram, HbA1c

case.story: Diabetes since 24, hearing aids since 26, and now an episode of headache and confusion with right homonymous field loss. Her mother is deaf and diabetic.
case.exam: Short stature, bilateral sensorineural deafness, right homonymous hemianopia.
case.tests: MRI: left occipital cortical lesion crossing arterial territories; lactate raised; m.3243A>G in urine sediment at high level.
case.q: What unifying diagnosis links the stroke-like event, deafness and maternal diabetes?
case.a: Mitochondrial cytopathy — MELAS spectrum due to m.3243A>G.

det.patho: Mitochondria produce ATP through five respiratory chain complexes encoded by both mtDNA and nuclear genes. Pathogenic variants in mtDNA are often heteroplasmic, so the proportion of mutant copies in each tissue influences severity. Nuclear gene defects affect respiratory chain subunits, assembly factors, mtDNA maintenance (POLG, TWNK) or translation. Tissues with high energy demand fail first.
det.clinical: The term is a broad umbrella. Recognisable syndromes include MELAS, MERRF, Kearns–Sayre, CPEO, Leigh syndrome, NARP, LHON and POLG-related disease, but many patients do not fit neatly. Red flags are a combination of seemingly unrelated features: ptosis plus deafness plus diabetes, or epilepsy plus myopathy plus cardiomyopathy. Symptoms often worsen during infection, fasting or with certain drugs.
det.diagnosis: Genetic testing is now the first step: specific mtDNA variants in blood or urine, then whole mtDNA sequencing and nuclear exome or genome. Muscle biopsy remains useful when blood results are negative, providing histology, respiratory chain enzymes and tissue mtDNA. Supportive tests include lactate, GDF-15, MR spectroscopy lactate peak, ECG and echocardiography.
det.treatment: There is no cure. Care is multidisciplinary: cardiac surveillance and pacing, hearing aids or cochlear implants, diabetes treatment, seizure control (avoid valproate in POLG disease), and exercise programmes. L-arginine is used in MELAS stroke-like episodes in some centres. Supplements such as coenzyme Q10 are widely used but evidence is limited except in primary CoQ10 deficiency. Avoid prolonged fasting and mitochondrial-toxic drugs.
det.prognosis: Extremely variable, from mild lifelong ptosis to fatal infantile disease.
pearls: Think mitochondrial when three unrelated organ systems are affected.
Urine sediment is better than blood for detecting m.3243A>G in adults.
Never give valproate to a patient with suspected POLG disease.
det.thd: Mitochondrial cytopathy เป็นคำรวมของโรคที่ไมโทคอนเดรียสร้างพลังงานไม่ได้ เกิดจากยีนใน mtDNA (ถ่ายทอดทางแม่) หรือยีนในนิวเคลียส อวัยวะที่ใช้พลังงานมากจะผิดปกติ เช่น สมอง กล้ามเนื้อ หัวใจ ตา หู และตับอ่อน ควรสงสัยเมื่อมีหลายระบบผิดปกติพร้อมกัน วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีนในเลือดหรือปัสสาวะ และชิ้นเนื้อกล้ามเนื้อ การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคองและเฝ้าระวังภาวะแทรกซ้อน

det.patho: Defects in respiratory chain complexes reduce ATP production. Mitochondrial DNA mutations show heteroplasmy, explaining variable severity and tissue distribution, while nuclear gene defects affect mtDNA maintenance, complex assembly or other mitochondrial functions.
det.clinical: Any organ can be involved, with neurological, muscular, ophthalmic, auditory, cardiac, endocrine and gastrointestinal features. Childhood forms are often severe (Leigh syndrome); adult forms include PEO, MELAS and myopathy. Metabolic stress (infection, fasting) can trigger decompensation.
det.diagnosis: Clinical suspicion with multisystem involvement, lactate and imaging, then genetic testing. Muscle biopsy remains helpful when genetics is inconclusive. Exclude mimics such as myasthenia and inflammatory disease.
det.treatment: Mostly supportive: treat seizures (avoid valproate in POLG), cardiac conduction disease, diabetes, hearing loss. L-arginine or citrulline is used in MELAS stroke-like episodes. Exercise training helps myopathy. Idebenone is used in LHON. Avoid mitochondrial toxins.
det.prognosis: Highly variable from mild to fatal; childhood-onset forms are generally more severe.
pearls: Valproate can cause fatal liver failure in POLG disease.
Stroke-like lesions crossing vascular territories suggest MELAS.
mtDNA mutation load is often higher in urine or muscle than blood.

det.patho: Defects in the respiratory chain, from mitochondrial DNA mutations or nuclear genes, impair ATP production in tissues with high energy demand such as cortex and muscle. Heteroplasmy, the varying proportion of mutant mtDNA among cells, explains why severity differs widely even within one family. Stroke-like episodes probably reflect neuronal energy failure and hyperexcitability rather than arterial occlusion.
det.clinical: Presentations range from childhood to adulthood. MELAS features stroke-like episodes with headache, vomiting and seizures; MERRF combines myoclonus, seizures, ataxia and myopathy; Kearns-Sayre syndrome includes progressive external ophthalmoplegia, retinopathy and cardiac conduction block. Overlap is common, and many patients have diabetes, deafness, short stature or gastrointestinal dysmotility. Cumulative episodes lead to cognitive decline.
det.diagnosis: Clinical pattern guides targeted mtDNA testing; urine or muscle is more sensitive than blood for some variants. If targeted tests are negative, whole mtDNA sequencing and nuclear gene panels or exome are used. Lactate can be normal between episodes. Muscle biopsy remains helpful when genetics is inconclusive.
det.treatment: There is no cure. Supportive care includes treatment of seizures (avoid valproate, especially in POLG disease), L-arginine or citrulline for stroke-like episodes, coenzyme Q10 and other supplements (limited evidence), and avoidance of fasting and mitochondrial toxins. Screen and manage cardiac conduction disease (pacemaker), diabetes, hearing loss and swallowing. Genetic counselling must explain maternal transmission and reproductive options.
det.prognosis: Variable and generally progressive; stroke-like episodes, epilepsy and cardiac complications drive disability and mortality.
pearls: Stroke-like lesion crossing vascular territories in a young person: think MELAS.
Ask about deafness and diabetes in the mother.
Avoid valproate in suspected mitochondrial disease.

det.patho: Failure of oxidative phosphorylation leaves neurons, especially in metabolically active deep grey nuclei and brainstem, unable to meet energy demand during stress. Gene defects include respiratory chain subunits and assembly factors, pyruvate dehydrogenase, coenzyme Q10 synthesis, mtDNA maintenance (POLG) and mtDNA point mutations such as m.8993T>G. Lesions show spongiform necrosis, capillary proliferation and gliosis.
det.clinical: Leigh syndrome usually starts before age two with regression, hypotonia, feeding problems and brainstem signs, then progresses stepwise with each illness. POLG-related disease (Alpers) combines refractory focal seizures with liver failure. Older children and adults may have MELAS-type episodes, ataxia, neuropathy or optic atrophy. Cardiomyopathy, renal tubulopathy and hearing loss can accompany it.
det.diagnosis: MRI patterns and raised lactate (CSF more reliable than blood) raise suspicion, but normal lactate does not exclude it. Genome or exome sequencing with mtDNA analysis is now the first-line test; muscle biopsy and respiratory chain enzyme assays are used when genetics is inconclusive. Exclude treatable mimics: thiamine transporter defects, biotinidase deficiency, pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency (ketogenic diet), and CoQ10 deficiency.
det.treatment: Mostly supportive: nutrition, avoidance of prolonged fasting, prompt treatment of infections and acidosis, seizure control without valproate in POLG. A vitamin cocktail (thiamine, riboflavin, CoQ10, biotin) is often tried; specific benefit exists only in certain defects. Ketogenic diet helps PDH deficiency. Several gene and drug therapies are in trials.
det.prognosis: Leigh syndrome is often fatal in childhood, usually from respiratory failure; milder genotypes survive into adolescence or adulthood.
pearls: Regression after fever with symmetric brainstem lesions: Leigh syndrome.
Always give biotin and thiamine early; some mimics are fully treatable.
Valproate can cause fatal liver failure in POLG disease.

19: A Quick Glance at the Therapeutic Approaches for Neuromuscular Disorders

det.patho: Defects in oxidative phosphorylation, from mitochondrial DNA variants or nuclear genes that maintain mtDNA, reduce ATP production in high-energy tissues. Muscle fibres compensate by proliferating abnormal mitochondria (ragged-red fibres). Heteroplasmy, the proportion of mutant mtDNA in each tissue, explains variable severity even within a family.
det.clinical: Presentations range from isolated PEO to limb myopathy, exercise intolerance, rhabdomyolysis, and multisystem syndromes such as Kearns–Sayre, MELAS and MERRF. Adults often present in midlife with ptosis that has progressed unnoticed. Infantile forms (e.g. TK2 deficiency) may cause severe weakness and respiratory failure.
det.diagnosis: Genetic testing increasingly comes first: blood or urine for common point variants, nuclear gene panels or exome, and muscle tissue for deletions. Biopsy remains useful for histochemistry and mtDNA analysis. Exclude myasthenia, OPMD and thyroid eye disease in ptosis/ophthalmoplegia.
det.treatment: Care is largely supportive: aerobic and resistance exercise training, ptosis surgery (conservative, to protect the cornea), pacemaker for conduction disease, management of diabetes, hearing aids and nutrition. Avoid valproate in POLG disease and be cautious with drugs that impair mitochondrial function (some aminoglycosides, linezolid). Coenzyme Q10 is specifically indicated in primary CoQ10 deficiency; nucleoside therapy for TK2 deficiency has shown benefit and is becoming available.
det.prognosis: Highly variable; isolated PEO is compatible with normal lifespan, whereas multisystem and infantile forms carry significant morbidity.
pearls: Symmetric ophthalmoplegia without diplopia favours mitochondrial disease over myasthenia.
Do an ECG in every patient with PEO.
Normal CK does not exclude a mitochondrial myopathy.
det.thd: Mitochondrial myopathy คือโรคกล้ามเนื้อจากไมโทคอนเดรียสร้างพลังงานไม่พอ ผู้ป่วยมีหนังตาตกและกลอกตาได้น้อยทั้งสองข้างช้า ๆ มักไม่เห็นภาพซ้อน เหนื่อยง่ายเมื่อออกแรง และกล้ามเนื้อต้นแขนต้นขาอ่อนแรง อาจมีหูตึง เบาหวาน หรือหัวใจนำไฟฟ้าผิดปกติ ตรวจพบ lactate สูง ชิ้นเนื้อกล้ามเนื้อพบ ragged-red fibre และยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน การรักษาส่วนใหญ่เป็นแบบประคับประคองร่วมกับการออกกำลังกาย

Chapter 49: Ischemic Stroke: Uncommon and Special Situations

det.patho: Most cases stem from the m.3243A>G point change in the mitochondrial tRNA-Leu gene, inherited through the mother with variable heteroplasmy. Faulty oxidative phosphorylation causes an energy crisis in neurons and in the smooth muscle and endothelium of small vessels, and nitric oxide depletion may impair vasodilatation. Stroke-like lesions are thought to be metabolic and partly vascular rather than embolic or atherothrombotic.
det.clinical: Typical onset is in childhood or early adult life, although first episodes after 40 are recognised. Attacks begin with headache, vomiting or seizures and leave a cortical deficit that may improve over weeks; recurrent attacks cause cumulative cognitive and visual loss. The same mutation can produce only diabetes and deafness (MIDD) in relatives, so family history must be taken across the maternal line. Look for cardiomyopathy, WPW, renal tubular problems, gut dysmotility and short stature.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it when a young person has a stroke with cortical, non-territorial lesions and normal vessels. MRI and MRS (lactate doublet) support it; serum lactate is raised in most but not all. Genetic confirmation is key, and urine sediment gives higher yield than blood. Exclude encephalitis, venous thrombosis, vasculitis, PRES and status-related cortical change.
det.treatment: During an attack, give IV L-arginine where available and treat seizures aggressively, since status worsens the energy failure. Avoid valproate, which can precipitate liver failure and worsen mitochondrial function; take care with metformin and prolonged propofol. Long-term care includes L-arginine or citrulline prophylaxis (evidence moderate), cardiac and diabetes surveillance, hearing aids or cochlear implants, and genetic counselling for maternal relatives.
det.prognosis: Course is progressive with accumulating disability; many patients develop dementia, and median survival after first stroke-like event is limited to roughly a decade or two.
pearls: Cortical lesion not respecting arterial borders plus normal MRA in a young patient: think MELAS.
Blood can miss the mutation; send urine or muscle.
Do not use valproate for MELAS seizures.
det.thd: MELAS เป็นโรคไมโทคอนเดรียถ่ายทอดทางแม่ ส่วนใหญ่จาก m.3243A>G ทำให้สมองขาดพลังงานเป็นพัก ๆ ผู้ป่วยมีอาการคล้ายอัมพาตเฉียบพลันร่วมกับปวดศีรษะ อาเจียน และชัก รอยโรคใน MRI ไม่ตรงกับเขตหลอดเลือด และมี lactate สูง ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีนจากปัสสาวะหรือกล้ามเนื้อ รักษาด้วย L-arginine คุมชัก และหลีกเลี่ยง valproate

det.patho: Biallelic TYMP variants abolish thymidine phosphorylase, so thymidine and deoxyuridine accumulate in plasma and tissues. The skewed nucleoside pools disturb mitochondrial DNA maintenance, producing depletion, multiple deletions and point mutations, with the gut's smooth muscle and peripheral nerves hit hardest. Inheritance is autosomal recessive, and a few MNGIE-like cases come from POLG or RRM2B variants instead.
det.clinical: Gastrointestinal failure usually leads and dominates, with recurrent pseudo-obstruction, diverticula, perforation and relentless weight loss. Ptosis, ophthalmoparesis, hearing loss and a sensorimotor neuropathy accumulate over the years. The leukoencephalopathy is often clinically silent and intellect is typically intact, which helps separate it from leukodystrophies. Delay to diagnosis of many years is common because the picture is read as a psychiatric or functional bowel disorder.
det.diagnosis: Gut dysmotility with cachexia, ophthalmoplegia, neuropathy and diffuse white matter change on MRI is highly suggestive. A very high plasma thymidine and deoxyuridine with near-absent enzyme activity confirms the diagnosis, and TYMP sequencing defines the genotype. Nerve conduction often looks demyelinating, so do not stop at a CIDP label. Muscle biopsy is supportive but not required.
det.treatment: Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can restore enzyme activity but carries substantial mortality, particularly once nutrition is poor, so referral should be early. Orthotopic liver transplantation is an emerging alternative that normalises metabolites with perhaps lower risk, and enzyme replacement via carrier red cells has been explored. Supportive care includes parenteral nutrition, decompression of pseudo-obstruction, pain control and avoiding mitochondrially toxic drugs such as valproate and linezolid.
det.prognosis: Untreated disease is progressive and usually fatal in the fourth or fifth decade from malnutrition, perforation or sepsis. Successful transplantation can stabilise the biochemistry and symptoms.
pearls: Young adult labelled anorexia nervosa plus ptosis and neuropathy: think MNGIE and send plasma thymidine.
Demyelinating NCS with ophthalmoplegia and gut failure is not CIDP.
The white matter looks alarming on MRI but cognition is usually spared.

det.patho: The mitochondrial trifunctional protein catalyses the last three steps of long-chain fatty acid beta-oxidation. Deficiency causes energy failure during fasting and accumulation of toxic long-chain hydroxyacyl metabolites that damage muscle, retina and nerve.
det.clinical: Severe neonatal forms present with cardiomyopathy and hypoglycaemia. Later-onset forms have exercise or illness-triggered rhabdomyolysis and a progressive neuropathy that is characteristic of MTP compared with other oxidation defects.

det.treatment: Avoid fasting, use high-carbohydrate low long-chain fat diet supplemented with MCT or triheptanoin; emergency glucose during illness; manage rhabdomyolysis with fluids.
det.prognosis: Neonatal forms have high mortality; neuropathy and retinopathy often progress despite treatment.

simple: An autoimmune disease with features of several others like lupus and scleroderma, including joint pain, rashes and muscle weakness.

th: โรคภูมิคุ้มกันแบบซ้อนทับที่มี anti-U1 RNP สูง มีลักษณะของ SLE, scleroderma และ myositis ร่วมกัน ระบบประสาทที่พบเด่นคือ trigeminal sensory neuropathy และ aseptic meningitis
tempoNote: Systemic disease over years; neurological complications appear subacutely
feat: Systemic rheumatic disease: Raynaud phenomenon, puffy hands, arthritis, myositis, pulmonary hypertension
Trigeminal sensory neuropathy: facial numbness, often bilateral and slowly progressive
Aseptic meningitis, sometimes provoked by NSAIDs such as ibuprofen
Inflammatory myositis with raised CK; occasional peripheral neuropathy
Headache, and rarely CNS vasculitis or seizures
inv: High-titre anti-U1 RNP; ANA speckled pattern
CK, EMG; MRI with contrast for trigeminal nerves and meninges
CSF if meningitic; echocardiography and lung function

case.story: Fingers turn white in cold water at the market; puffy hands and joint pain for two years; now numbness spreading over both cheeks.
case.exam: Sclerodactyly-like puffy fingers, reduced pinprick in the V2–V3 territory bilaterally with intact jaw power, mild proximal weakness.
case.tests: ANA 1:1280 speckled, anti-U1 RNP strongly positive, anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm negative; CK 900 U/L.
case.q: What explains the facial numbness?
case.a: Trigeminal sensory neuropathy associated with mixed connective tissue disease.

read.where: Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System

det.patho: MCTD is defined by high-titre antibodies to U1 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein with overlapping features of lupus, systemic sclerosis and polymyositis. Whether it is a distinct disease or an overlap that may evolve into a defined CTD is still debated. Neurological involvement occurs in a minority and is thought to involve immune-mediated ganglionopathy or vasculopathy; the mechanisms are not fully established.
det.clinical: Systemic features dominate: Raynaud phenomenon, swollen hands, arthritis, myositis, oesophageal dysmotility and lung disease, with pulmonary hypertension as the main cause of death. The best-known neurological manifestation is trigeminal sensory neuropathy, slowly progressive and usually painless. Aseptic meningitis (including NSAID-induced), myositis, headache and less often polyneuropathy or myelitis also occur.
det.diagnosis: Classification relies on anti-U1 RNP positivity plus clinical criteria (e.g. Alarcón-Segovia or Kasukawa). Neurological features prompt MRI, CSF, EMG and nerve conduction as appropriate. Exclude lupus by anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm, and infection in meningitis. Trigeminal numbness with motor involvement or progression should prompt imaging to exclude tumour.
det.treatment: Managed with rheumatology: hydroxychloroquine, low-dose glucocorticoids and immunosuppressants (methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate) according to organ involvement. Myositis responds to steroids; trigeminal neuropathy responds poorly and is managed symptomatically. Avoid ibuprofen if it has triggered meningitis. Screen for pulmonary hypertension regularly.
det.prognosis: Variable; many have a mild course, while pulmonary hypertension and ILD determine survival.
pearls: Bilateral painless facial numbness: test anti-U1 RNP and anti-Ro/La.
Ibuprofen-induced aseptic meningitis is a recognised trap in MCTD and lupus.
Puffy hands plus Raynaud plus high anti-RNP is the classic triad.
det.thd: Mixed connective tissue disease เป็นโรคภูมิคุ้มกันที่มี anti-U1 RNP สูง มีลักษณะผสมของ SLE, scleroderma และ myositis เช่น นิ้วซีดเมื่อเย็น มือบวม ปวดข้อ และกล้ามเนื้ออักเสบ อาการทางระบบประสาทที่สำคัญคือหน้าชาจาก trigeminal sensory neuropathy และเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบปลอดเชื้อซึ่งอาจเกิดจาก ibuprofen รักษาร่วมกับแพทย์โรคข้อด้วย hydroxychloroquine สเตียรอยด์ และยากดภูมิ

Isolated facial numbness; MCTD and Sjögren are common causes, so screen serology

name: Miyoshi distal myopathy
formal: Autosomal recessive dysferlinopathy (DYSF) with early distal posterior calf weakness, markedly raised CK and inflammatory features on biopsy.
simple: An inherited muscle disease that begins with weak calf muscles in young adults.
more: Genetic testing of DYSF or dysferlin protein studies; no specific therapy, so physiotherapy and avoiding eccentric exercise.
th: กล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมทางพันธุกรรมยีนด้อยจากยีน DYSF เริ่มที่น่องด้านหลังในวัยหนุ่มสาว เขย่งเท้าไม่ได้ CK สูงมาก มักถูกวินิจฉัยผิดเป็น polymyositis
tempoNote: Onset in late teens to 30s with calf weakness; slow progression to proximal muscles over decades
feat: Early inability to stand or walk on tiptoes; calf atrophy (gastrocnemius and soleus)
Often athletic before onset; symptoms may begin after strenuous activity
CK very high (often 10–100 times normal), sometimes found before symptoms
Later spread to thighs and hip girdle; forearm flexors may be involved
Heart and breathing usually spared
inv: CK; muscle MRI showing posterior calf (medial gastrocnemius, soleus) fatty change
Muscle biopsy: dystrophic or inflammatory-looking changes with absent dysferlin on immunostaining/immunoblot
DYSF sequencing; ANO5 if dysferlin normal (Miyoshi type 3)

case.story: Over a year he cannot run fast or push off on tiptoe; a clinic found CK 9,000 U/L and treated 'myositis' with steroids without benefit.
case.exam: Bilateral calf wasting, cannot stand on toes, mild hip extensor weakness, normal reflexes elsewhere.
case.tests: MRI fatty change in posterior calves; biopsy with mild inflammation; dysferlin absent; biallelic DYSF variants.
case.q: Why did steroids fail?
case.a: Miyoshi distal myopathy (dysferlinopathy) mimics inflammatory myopathy on biopsy but is genetic and does not respond to immunosuppression.

det.patho: Dysferlin is involved in repairing the sarcolemma after contraction-induced damage. Without it, membrane tears are resealed poorly, leading to necrosis, inflammation and fibrosis. Eccentric load on the calves explains the distal predominance, and inflammatory infiltrates on biopsy reflect secondary immune activation.
det.clinical: Typically a previously fit young adult develops calf weakness and wasting, difficulty climbing stairs or running, and later proximal involvement. Some show calf swelling initially. Wheelchair use may be needed decades after onset. The same mutation in one family may cause Miyoshi or limb-girdle presentations.
det.diagnosis: High CK with posterior calf weakness in a young adult should raise suspicion. Absent dysferlin on biopsy or blood monocyte assay supports it, and genetic testing confirms. Steroid-unresponsive 'polymyositis' with very high CK should prompt dysferlin testing.
det.treatment: There is no approved disease-modifying therapy; steroids are not helpful and may worsen strength. Physiotherapy with moderate, non-eccentric exercise, orthoses for foot drop and avoidance of over-exertion are advised. Gene therapy approaches are in trials.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; life expectancy is near normal because cardiac and respiratory muscles are usually spared.
pearls: Can't walk on toes + CK in thousands in a young adult = think dysferlin.
Inflammation on biopsy does not mean myositis.
Distal posterior calf pattern contrasts with anterior compartment involvement in other distal myopathies.
det.thd: Miyoshi distal myopathy เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมจากยีน DYSF ถ่ายทอดแบบยีนด้อย ผู้ป่วยวัยหนุ่มสาวที่เคยแข็งแรงเริ่มเขย่งเท้าไม่ได้ น่องลีบ CK สูงมาก ชิ้นเนื้ออาจมีการอักเสบจึงถูกวินิจฉัยผิดเป็น polymyositis แต่ไม่ตอบสนองต่อสเตียรอยด์ ยืนยันด้วยการไม่พบโปรตีน dysferlin และตรวจยีน การรักษาเป็นกายภาพบำบัดและอุปกรณ์ช่วย

ddx.pt: Same gene with proximal-onset limb-girdle pattern
Proximal weakness responding to steroids; dysferlin preserved
Over 50, quadriceps and finger flexor weakness, CK only mildly raised

name: MOG-associated optic neuritis (MOG-ON)
formal: Optic neuritis in MOG antibody-associated disease, often bilateral with marked disc swelling, long optic nerve involvement, steroid-responsive but relapsing.
simple: Inflammation of the optic nerve linked to an antibody against MOG, causing vision loss and eye pain.
th: เส้นประสาทตาอักเสบในโรค MOGAD มักเป็นสองข้าง ขั้วประสาทตาบวมมาก ปวดตามาก ตอบสนองดีต่อสเตียรอยด์ แต่กลับเป็นซ้ำได้โดยเฉพาะเมื่อลดยาเร็ว
tempoNote: Visual loss evolves over days; recovery over weeks; relapses occur in about half, often when steroids are tapered
feat: Often bilateral simultaneous or sequential visual loss with severe pain on eye movement
Prominent optic disc swelling in most cases
Very poor nadir acuity but usually good recovery
Steroid dependence: relapse soon after stopping or tapering steroids
Occurs in children and adults; may accompany ADEM or myelitis
inv: Serum MOG-IgG by live cell-based assay (titre matters; low positives need caution)
MRI orbits: long-segment anterior optic nerve enhancement with perineural sheath enhancement
MRI brain and spine; AQP4-IgG to exclude NMOSD; OCT

case.story: Painful blurred vision in both eyes over four days after a flu-like illness; she had a similar episode in one eye a year ago that recovered after steroids.
case.exam: Acuity counting fingers both eyes, marked bilateral disc swelling, no RAPD because both eyes affected.
case.tests: MRI long anterior optic nerve enhancement with perineural spread; serum MOG-IgG positive (high titre), AQP4-IgG negative.
case.q: What treatment plan reduces the chance of another relapse?
case.a: MOG-associated optic neuritis; IV methylprednisolone then a slow oral steroid taper, and consider maintenance therapy (e.g. IVIG, azathioprine or mycophenolate) because this is a relapse.

det.patho: Antibodies against myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein, on the outer myelin surface, are associated with an inflammatory demyelinating disorder distinct from MS and AQP4 NMOSD. Lesions show perivenous demyelination with relative axonal preservation, which may explain the better recovery. Triggers such as infections or vaccination precede some attacks.
det.clinical: Optic neuritis is the commonest adult presentation of MOGAD. Bilateral involvement, severe disc oedema and steroid responsiveness are typical. Children more often present with ADEM. Relapses usually involve the optic nerve again; cumulative damage can occur with repeated attacks.
det.diagnosis: The 2023 international MOGAD criteria require a core clinical event, positive MOG-IgG by cell-based assay, supportive features if titre is low or unknown, and exclusion of better explanations such as MS. Test early and in serum; titres may fall in remission. Do not test indiscriminately, as low-titre false positives occur.
det.treatment: Acute attacks: IV methylprednisolone, followed by an oral taper over weeks to months; plasma exchange for severe steroid-refractory attacks. Long-term immunotherapy is generally reserved for relapsing patients; IVIG, azathioprine, mycophenolate and rituximab are used, and MS disease-modifying drugs are avoided as they may worsen it. Clinical trials of FcRn and IL-6 receptor blockade are under way.
det.prognosis: Visual recovery is usually good after a single attack, but relapses are common and some patients accumulate deficit.
pearls: Bilateral optic neuritis with swollen discs: test MOG-IgG and AQP4-IgG.
Relapse on steroid taper is characteristic.
Perineural enhancement on orbital MRI is a useful clue.
det.thd: MOG-ON คือเส้นประสาทตาอักเสบในโรค MOGAD ซึ่งมีแอนติบอดีต่อ MOG ผู้ป่วยมักตามัวทั้งสองข้าง ปวดตามาก ขั้วประสาทตาบวมชัด MRI พบเส้นประสาทตาอักเสบยาวด้านหน้าและเยื่อหุ้มรอบเส้นประสาท ยืนยันด้วย MOG-IgG แบบ cell-based assay ตอบสนองดีต่อสเตียรอยด์และมองเห็นกลับมาดี แต่กลับเป็นซ้ำบ่อยเมื่อลดยาเร็ว รายที่เป็นซ้ำควรให้ยากดภูมิระยะยาว

AQP4-IgG positive, posterior/chiasmal involvement and poorer recovery

name: Mohr-Tranebjaerg syndrome
formal: X-linked deafness-dystonia-optic neuronopathy syndrome from TIMM8A mutations, with childhood sensorineural deafness, then dystonia, visual loss and cognitive decline.
simple: A rare X-linked condition causing early deafness, followed by movement problems, vision loss and dementia.
more: Diagnosis by TIMM8A sequencing; MRI is often normal early, and females are mildly affected carriers. Some have contiguous gene deletion with BTK deficiency; therapy is supportive, with hearing aids or cochlear implants and symptomatic dystonia treatment. X-linked Mohr-Tranebjaerg syndrome from TIMM8A mutations, with progressive sensorineural deafness, dystonia, visual impairment and cognitive decline, with a mitochondrial import defect. Genetic testing of TIMM8A confirms it. Treatment is supportive with hearing aids or cochlear implants; dystonia and cognitive decline progress over years. Rare X-linked disorder (Mohr–Tranebjaerg, DDON) with progressive sensorineural deafness, dystonia, visual loss and cognitive decline from TIMM8A mutations.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมถ่ายทอดทางโครโมโซม X จากยีน TIMM8A เด็กชายหูหนวกตั้งแต่เล็ก ต่อมามี dystonia ตามัวจากเส้นประสาทตาเสื่อม และสมองเสื่อม
tempoNote: Hearing loss in early childhood, dystonia in adolescence, visual decline in early adulthood, dementia later
feat: Progressive sensorineural (auditory neuropathy) deafness from early childhood in boys
Dystonia or other movement disorders starting in adolescence
Progressive visual loss from optic atrophy in the 20s–30s
Behavioural problems, psychosis and dementia later
Contiguous deletion with BTK may add X-linked agammaglobulinaemia
inv: Audiology with auditory brainstem responses
Ophthalmology with OCT and visual fields; MRI brain (often normal or shows atrophy)
TIMM8A sequencing and deletion testing; immunoglobulins if deletion extends to BTK

case.story: Deaf since age 3 and uses hearing aids; over the last year his neck twists and his writing hand cramps; his maternal cousin has similar deafness.
case.exam: Cervical dystonia and writer's cramp, mild pallor of both optic discs, bilateral severe hearing loss.
case.tests: Auditory brainstem responses absent; TIMM8A deletion; immunoglobulins normal.
case.q: Which other relatives should be offered testing?
case.a: Mohr-Tranebjaerg syndrome is X-linked: his mother and maternal female relatives may be carriers; male maternal relatives may be affected.
