det.patho: TIMM8A encodes DDP1, part of the inner mitochondrial membrane protein import machinery. Loss of function impairs mitochondrial protein import, causing selective degeneration of cochlear and auditory nerve neurons, striatal neurons and retinal ganglion cells. It is considered a mitochondrial disease of nuclear (X-linked) origin.
det.clinical: Prelingual or early childhood deafness is the first sign and often the only one for years. Movement disorders (dystonia, ataxia, spasticity) follow in adolescence, with optic atrophy and visual loss in early adulthood and progressive psychiatric and cognitive decline. Carrier females can have mild hearing loss or focal dystonia.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in boys with sensorineural deafness who later develop dystonia or optic atrophy, especially with an X-linked pedigree. Genetic testing confirms. Check immunoglobulins because contiguous deletions may cause agammaglobulinaemia.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy. Cochlear implantation can help when the auditory nerve is functional, though benefit is variable in auditory neuropathy. Dystonia is treated with botulinum toxin, oral agents and, in selected cases, pallidal DBS. Low-vision support, psychiatric care and genetic counselling are essential.
det.prognosis: Progressive over decades with severe disability; lifespan varies.
pearls: Deaf boy who later develops dystonia: test TIMM8A.
Check for agammaglobulinaemia from BTK co-deletion.
Carrier mothers may have mild deafness or focal dystonia.
det.thd: Mohr-Tranebjaerg syndrome เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมถ่ายทอดทางโครโมโซม X จากยีน TIMM8A ซึ่งเกี่ยวกับการนำโปรตีนเข้าไมโทคอนเดรีย เด็กชายหูหนวกตั้งแต่เล็ก วัยรุ่นเริ่มมี dystonia วัยผู้ใหญ่ตอนต้นตามัวจากเส้นประสาทตาฝ่อ และต่อมามีสมองเสื่อม ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน ไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ รักษาตามอาการ เช่น เครื่องช่วยฟัง botulinum toxin และให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

name: Mollaret’s meningitis
formal: Recurrent benign aseptic lymphocytic meningitis with large Mollaret cells in CSF, often caused by herpes simplex virus type 2 reactivation, with self-limited attacks.
simple: Repeated attacks of viral meningitis that go away by themselves, often caused by a herpes virus.
th: เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบชนิดไม่มีหนองที่เป็นซ้ำหลายครั้ง แต่ละครั้งหายเองภายในไม่กี่วัน ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจากไวรัสเริม HSV-2 กลับมาแสดงอาการ
tempoNote: Attacks last 2–5 days and resolve fully; recur at intervals of weeks to years, usually ceasing over several years
feat: Recurrent episodes of headache, fever, neck stiffness and photophobia
Complete recovery between attacks
Most often young or middle-aged women
Genital herpes lesions usually absent during attacks
Transient neurological symptoms occur in a minority
inv: CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis (early neutrophils possible), normal or mildly low glucose, raised protein; large monocytes (Mollaret cells)
CSF HSV-2 PCR (positive in most, best early in attack)
MRI brain and spine to exclude epidermoid or dermoid cyst; autoimmune screen

case.story: Third admission in two years with sudden headache, fever and neck stiffness; each time she recovered in a few days on empirical antibiotics.
case.exam: Neck stiffness, normal mental state, no rash or ulcers.
case.tests: CSF 250 cells (mostly lymphocytes), glucose normal, protein mildly raised; HSV-2 PCR positive; MRI normal.
case.q: Is long-term suppressive antiviral therapy proven to prevent attacks?
case.a: Mollaret's (HSV-2) recurrent meningitis; evidence for valaciclovir suppression is weak, and a trial found no reduction in recurrences, so decisions are individualised.

read.where: Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — Mollaret’s Meningitis

det.patho: Most cases are due to reactivation of HSV-2 from sacral dorsal root ganglia with viral spread to the meninges; HSV-1, EBV and other viruses are occasional causes. 'Mollaret cells' are activated monocytes and are not specific. Some recurrent aseptic meningitis is caused instead by leaking epidermoid cysts, drugs (NSAIDs, IVIG, antibiotics) or systemic inflammatory disease.
det.clinical: Each attack resembles acute viral meningitis and resolves without sequelae. Attacks recur over years, often with decreasing frequency. Fewer than half recall genital herpes. Persistent deficits, seizures or encephalopathy should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: Confirm lymphocytic meningitis during an attack and send HSV PCR. Exclude bacterial and tuberculous meningitis, drug-induced aseptic meningitis, Behçet disease, sarcoidosis, VKH, SLE and intracranial cysts with MRI and clinical review.
det.treatment: Attacks are self-limited; supportive care with analgesia is enough for most, and IV aciclovir is often given during the acute episode though benefit is unproven. Suppressive valaciclovir has not been shown to prevent attacks and recurrences may rise after stopping. Counsel about HSV-2 transmission.
det.prognosis: Benign; attacks usually wane over several years without lasting damage.
pearls: Recurrent lymphocytic meningitis with full recovery: send CSF HSV-2 PCR.
Image to exclude an epidermoid cyst.
Mollaret cells are suggestive but not diagnostic.
det.thd: Mollaret's meningitis คือเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบแบบไม่มีหนองที่เป็นซ้ำ ๆ แต่ละครั้งปวดศีรษะ ไข้ คอแข็ง และหายเองใน 2–5 วัน ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจากไวรัส HSV-2 น้ำไขสันหลังพบเซลล์ lymphocyte และอาจเห็น Mollaret cell ตรวจ PCR หา HSV-2 และทำ MRI เพื่อแยกถุงน้ำ epidermoid การรักษาส่วนใหญ่เป็นแบบประคับประคอง ยาต้านไวรัสระยะยาวยังไม่พิสูจน์ว่าป้องกันได้

name: Monge’s disease
formal: Chronic mountain sickness: excessive erythrocytosis with hypoxaemia and pulmonary hypertension at high altitude, causing headache, dizziness and cognitive slowing.
simple: A long-term illness in people living at high altitude where too many red blood cells cause headache, tiredness and dizziness.
th: ภาวะป่วยเรื้อรังจากการอยู่ที่สูงนาน ๆ ร่างกายสร้างเม็ดเลือดแดงมากเกินไป ร่วมกับขาดออกซิเจนและความดันปอดสูง ทำให้ปวดศีรษะ มึนงง และคิดช้า ไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาทโดยตรง
tempoNote: Develops after years of living above about 2,500 m; improves after moving to low altitude
feat: Long-term high-altitude residents with haemoglobin about 21 g/dL or more in men, 19 g/dL or more in women
Headache, dizziness, tinnitus, poor sleep, fatigue and slowed thinking
Cyanosis, plethora, dilated veins and burning paraesthesias of hands and feet
Pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure in advanced cases
Resolves on descent to low altitude and recurs on return
inv: Haemoglobin/haematocrit and pulse oximetry (scored with the Qinghai CMS score)
Echocardiography for pulmonary hypertension
Exclude other causes of polycythaemia (lung disease, sleep apnoea, JAK2 mutation)

case.who: 48-year-old Thai engineer who has worked 6 years at a mine in the Bolivian Andes
case.story: Daily headaches, insomnia, burning feet and poor concentration; colleagues say his face is dark red.
case.exam: Plethoric, cyanosed lips, SpO2 82% at altitude; no focal neurological signs.
case.tests: Hb 23 g/dL; JAK2 negative; echo shows moderate pulmonary hypertension.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the definitive treatment?
case.a: Chronic mountain sickness (Monge disease); relocation to low altitude, with acetazolamide or phlebotomy as temporising measures.

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Altitude Medicine

det.patho: Chronic hypoxia at altitude drives erythropoietin production; in susceptible people ventilatory drive is blunted, so hypoxaemia worsens and erythrocytosis becomes excessive. High blood viscosity, hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and relative hypoventilation produce symptoms. Andean populations are more affected than Tibetans, who have genetic adaptations (EPAS1, EGLN1). It is not primarily a neurological disease, though its symptoms are often neurological.
det.clinical: Symptoms include headache, dizziness, breathlessness, sleep disturbance, palpitations, tinnitus, paraesthesias and cognitive slowing. Signs are plethora, cyanosis and dilated veins, progressing to cor pulmonale. Thrombosis, including cerebral venous and arterial events, may be more likely with very high haematocrit.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis uses the international (Qinghai) consensus: excessive erythrocytosis in a high-altitude resident, a symptom score, and exclusion of chronic lung disease and other secondary causes. Echocardiography assesses pulmonary pressures.
det.treatment: Definitive treatment is moving to low altitude, which reverses the condition over weeks to months. Acetazolamide stimulates ventilation and lowers haematocrit; isovolaemic phlebotomy relieves symptoms short term. Treat coexistent sleep-disordered breathing and avoid smoking.
det.prognosis: Good after descent; progressive pulmonary hypertension and heart failure if exposure continues.
pearls: Not a disease of Thailand's lowlands — ask about long stays at high altitude.
Cure is descent; acetazolamide and phlebotomy only buy time.
Distinguish from acute mountain sickness, which occurs within hours to days of ascent.
det.thd: Monge’s disease หรือ chronic mountain sickness เกิดในคนที่อาศัยบนที่สูงมากเป็นเวลาหลายปี ร่างกายขาดออกซิเจนเรื้อรังจนสร้างเม็ดเลือดแดงมากเกิน เลือดข้น ความดันในปอดสูง ทำให้ปวดศีรษะ มึนงง นอนไม่หลับ แสบร้อนปลายมือเท้า และคิดช้า วินิจฉัยจากค่าฮีโมโกลบินสูงและตัดสาเหตุอื่น การรักษาที่ได้ผลคือย้ายลงมาอยู่ที่ต่ำ

ddx.pt: Snoring, witnessed apnoeas and daytime sleepiness; can cause secondary erythrocytosis at any altitude
Headache and cognitive slowing with raised carboxyhaemoglobin; pulse oximetry falsely normal
Opposite haematology; also causes fatigue, headache and poor concentration

aN: chronic mountain sickness | cms | high altitude polycythemia | monge disease | excessive erythrocytosis of altitude

name: Monoamine disorders
formal: Inherited disorders of dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin synthesis or metabolism, such as tyrosine hydroxylase or AADC deficiency, with hypotonia, oculogyric crises, dystonia and autonomic features.
simple: Inherited disorders of brain chemicals such as dopamine and serotonin, causing floppiness, abnormal movements and developmental delay in infants.
more: Diagnosed by CSF neurotransmitter metabolites and genetics. Treatment with levodopa, dopamine agonists or gene therapy depends on type.
th: กลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่ขาดการสร้างหรือขนส่งโดปามีนและเซโรโทนิน ทำให้เด็กอ่อนแรง กล้ามเนื้อเกร็งบิด ตาเหลือกขึ้นเป็นพัก ๆ และมีอาการระบบอัตโนมัติ
tempoNote: Constant developmental problems with fluctuating dystonia and episodic oculogyric crises
feat: Low tone, weak head control and delayed milestones in infancy
Oculogyric crises: upward gaze lasting minutes to hours, often mistaken for seizures
Dystonia, rigidity or poverty of movement, worse late in the day in some types
Autonomic clues: ptosis, sweating, blocked nose, temperature swings, low glucose
BH4 defects may also show high phenylalanine on newborn screening
inv: CSF neurotransmitter metabolites (HVA, 5-HIAA, 3-OMD) and pterins from a carefully handled sample
Dried blood spot or plasma 3-O-methyldopa and AADC enzyme activity
Plasma phenylalanine, urine pterins, then gene panel (DDC, TH, GCH1, PTS, SPR, QDPR, SLC6A3, SLC18A2)

case.who: 8-month-old boy of mixed Thai-Taiwanese parentage, living in Bangkok
case.story: He has been floppy since birth and cannot hold up his head. Several times a week his eyes roll upward for an hour while he sweats and cries; EEG during one spell was normal.
case.exam: Axial hypotonia, dystonic limb posturing, ptosis and a stuffy nose.
case.tests: CSF shows low HVA and 5-HIAA with high 3-OMD; blood spot 3-OMD raised; homozygous DDC splice variant.
case.q: Name the disorder and the treatment options.
case.a: AADC deficiency; dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors and pyridoxine help partly, and putaminal AAV gene therapy (eladocagene exuparvovec) is licensed in several countries.

read.where: 11 - Dystonia: Phenomenology, classification, etiology, pathology, biochemistry, and genetics

det.patho: Dopamine and serotonin come from tyrosine and tryptophan through hydroxylase steps that need tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), then a decarboxylase step by AADC that needs pyridoxal phosphate. Faults in the enzymes, in BH4 production or recycling, or in dopamine transport and vesicle loading deplete brain monoamines. AADC deficiency is notably common in Taiwanese and southern Chinese people because of a founder splice variant.
det.clinical: Severity ranges from a profound infantile encephalopathy with hypotonia, oculogyric crises and autonomic failure to milder childhood dystonia-parkinsonism. Symptoms that improve after sleep point to a dopamine disorder. BH4 defects add seizures and high phenylalanine, while dopamine transporter deficiency produces progressive infantile parkinsonism-dystonia. Board teaching links GTP cyclohydrolase 1 to the rate-limiting step of catecholamine synthesis.
det.diagnosis: Lumbar puncture with strictly standardised sample handling gives the metabolite pattern that separates the enzymes. Blood 3-O-methyldopa is a practical screen for AADC deficiency, and phenylalanine with urine pterins sorts BH4 defects. Gene sequencing confirms. Rule out epilepsy and cerebral palsy, which these children are often mislabelled with.
det.treatment: Treatment follows the defect: levodopa/carbidopa for tyrosine hydroxylase and GTPCH deficiency; BH4, levodopa and 5-hydroxytryptophan for BH4 disorders; dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors, anticholinergics and pyridoxine for AADC deficiency. Gene therapy for AADC deficiency is approved in Europe and the USA. Starting early gives the best motor gains.
det.prognosis: Variable; mild forms do very well on levodopa while severe infantile forms leave major disability, although gene therapy has improved motor milestones.
pearls: Oculogyric crises with a normal EEG: think neurotransmitter disease.
Diurnal fluctuation and dopa response point to a dopamine deficit.
CSF must be collected and frozen by protocol or results are unreliable.
det.thd: Monoamine disorders คือกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่สร้างหรือขนส่งโดปามีนและเซโรโทนินบกพร่อง เช่น AADC deficiency, tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency และ BH4 deficiency เด็กจะอ่อนแรง พัฒนาการช้า ตาเหลือกขึ้น (oculogyric crisis) มีอาการเกร็งบิดและอาการระบบอัตโนมัติ ตรวจน้ำไขสันหลังหาสารสื่อประสาท ตรวจ 3-OMD และยีนเพื่อยืนยัน รักษาตามชนิดด้วย levodopa, BH4, dopamine agonist หรือ gene therapy ใน AADC deficiency

files.chapter: 11 - Dystonia: Phenomenology, classification, etiology, pathology, biochemistry, and genetics

ddx.pt: GCH1 deficiency starting later in childhood with leg dystonia and marked levodopa response
Fixed motor disorder after a perinatal insult; no oculogyric crises or diurnal swing
Oculogyric crisis after dopamine-blocking drugs, resolving with anticholinergics

aN: neurotransmitter disorders | inborn errors of monoamine metabolism | aadc deficiency | tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency | bh4 deficiency

name: Monoballism
formal: Violent flinging movements of a single limb caused by a basal ganglia lesion, typically contralateral subthalamic nucleus stroke; a restricted form of hemiballism.
simple: Wild flinging movements of just one limb, usually from a small stroke in a deep brain area.
th: การเคลื่อนไหวแบบเหวี่ยงแรงของแขนหรือขาข้างเดียว เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ basal ganglia มักเป็น stroke ที่ subthalamic nucleus ด้านตรงข้าม เป็นรูปแบบจำกัดของ hemiballism
tempoNote: Abrupt onset with stroke; usually lessens over weeks to months
feat: Large-amplitude, irregular, flinging movements of one limb, usually the proximal arm
Contralateral to a lesion of subthalamic nucleus, striatum or thalamus
Movements persist at rest, worsen with stress, disappear in sleep
Commonly elderly with vascular risk factors; also non-ketotic hyperglycaemia
May evolve into chorea as it improves
inv: Blood glucose and HbA1c urgently (hyperglycaemic striatopathy)
MRI brain with DWI; CT may show striatal hyperdensity in hyperglycaemia
Consider toxoplasmosis or other lesions in immunocompromised patients

case.who: 74-year-old woman from Suphan Buri with poorly controlled diabetes
case.story: Since yesterday her left arm suddenly throws itself outward many times a minute; she has bruised it on furniture.
case.exam: Violent proximal flinging of left arm only; strength normal; no sensory loss.
case.tests: Glucose 520 mg/dL, no ketones; CT shows right putaminal hyperdensity; MRI T1 hyperintense right putamen without restricted diffusion.
case.q: What is the cause and treatment?
case.a: Non-ketotic hyperglycaemic striatopathy with monoballism; correct glucose gradually, add haloperidol or tetrabenazine if movements are disabling.

read.where: Movement Disorders — Huntington’s Disease and Other Choreas

det.patho: The subthalamic nucleus normally drives the internal globus pallidus to restrain unwanted movement. Damage to the nucleus or its connections reduces pallidal inhibition of the thalamus, releasing large involuntary movements on the opposite side. Partial or somatotopically restricted lesions confine the movement to one limb. Striatal lesions, often from hyperglycaemia, produce a similar network disturbance.
det.clinical: Monoballism appears suddenly, usually in the arm, with wild throwing or kicking movements that may cause injury and exhaustion. It is often a transitional state: hemiballism may shrink to one limb or become chorea as the lesion recovers. Elderly Asian women with uncontrolled type 2 diabetes are a well-recognised group with hyperglycaemic striatopathy. Other causes include small haemorrhage, tumour, demyelination, toxoplasmosis in HIV, and drugs.
det.diagnosis: Clinical observation identifies ballism; imaging locates the lesion. Check glucose in every patient, since striatal T1 hyperintensity with hyperglycaemia is diagnostic. Diffusion-weighted MRI shows small infarcts in the subthalamic nucleus or striatum. In young patients, look for lupus, antiphospholipid syndrome, HIV and drug exposure.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: glucose correction often resolves hyperglycaemic cases within days to weeks. Symptomatic options include dopamine receptor blockers (haloperidol, risperidone) or VMAT2 inhibitors (tetrabenazine); topiramate or benzodiazepines may help. Pad the limb to prevent injury. Persistent disabling cases may respond to pallidotomy or deep brain stimulation.
det.prognosis: Most vascular and hyperglycaemic cases improve markedly within weeks to months.
pearls: Sudden flinging limb in an elderly diabetic: check glucose and look for bright putamen on CT.
Ballism and chorea are a spectrum; ballism often settles into chorea.
Movements are contralateral to the lesion.
det.thd: Monoballism คือการเหวี่ยงแขนหรือขาข้างเดียวอย่างรุนแรงโดยควบคุมไม่ได้ เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ subthalamic nucleus หรือ striatum ด้านตรงข้าม สาเหตุหลักคือ stroke และน้ำตาลในเลือดสูงแบบไม่มีคีโตน ควรตรวจน้ำตาลและ CT/MRI ทุกราย รักษาสาเหตุร่วมกับยาเช่น haloperidol หรือ tetrabenazine ส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นในไม่กี่สัปดาห์

ddx.pt: Same mechanism involving both arm and leg on one side
Smaller, flowing, distal movements rather than violent proximal flinging
Distractible, variable movements with inconsistent features and no lesion

aN: monoballismus | single limb ballism | brachial ballism | focal ballism | ballism of one limb

name: Monoclonal gammopathy
formal: Presence of a clonal plasma cell paraprotein, such as MGUS, associated with demyelinating neuropathy (anti-MAG IgM), POEMS, amyloidosis and other neuropathies.
simple: A blood condition where abnormal immune cells make one abnormal protein, which can sometimes cause nerve damage.
th: การพบโปรตีน monoclonal (paraprotein) จากเซลล์พลาสมาโคลนเดียว เช่น MGUS ซึ่งอาจสัมพันธ์กับปลายประสาทอักเสบ เช่น anti-MAG, POEMS และ amyloidosis
tempoNote: Paraprotein is often found incidentally; associated neuropathies usually progress over months to years
feat: A laboratory finding rather than a neurological disease; common in older adults (about 3% over 50)
IgM paraprotein: distal, sensory-predominant demyelinating neuropathy with ataxia and tremor (often anti-MAG)
IgG or IgA lambda with demyelinating neuropathy, oedema, skin change or organomegaly: think POEMS
Painful small fibre and autonomic neuropathy with carpal tunnel syndrome, weight loss or heart failure: think AL amyloidosis
inv: Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and serum free light chains (electrophoresis alone misses small bands)
Nerve conduction studies to classify demyelinating versus axonal pattern
Anti-MAG antibodies for IgM; VEGF, skeletal survey or PET-CT for POEMS; tissue biopsy for amyloid
Haematology review: blood count, calcium, creatinine, bone marrow when indicated

case.story: Two years of numb, tingling feet that slowly reached the ankles; now unsteady in the dark and has a fine hand tremor.
case.exam: Absent ankle jerks, reduced vibration and joint position to knees, positive Romberg, mild toe extensor weakness.
case.tests: NCS: symmetric demyelination with very prolonged distal motor latencies; IgM kappa paraprotein 6 g/L; anti-MAG strongly positive.
case.q: What is the neuropathy, and what treatment has the best evidence?
case.a: Anti-MAG IgM paraproteinaemic neuropathy; rituximab is used for progressive disabling disease, with haematology follow-up for Waldenström transformation.

read.where: 5. CASE PRESENTATIONS ILLUSTRATING THE DIAGNOSTIC METHOD

det.patho: A single clone of plasma cells or B cells secretes an immunoglobulin or light chain. The paraprotein may harm nerves directly as an antibody against myelin glycolipids or proteins (IgM anti-MAG, anti-ganglioside), by depositing as amyloid, or indirectly through cytokines such as VEGF in POEMS. In many patients with IgG or IgA MGUS the gammopathy is coincidental and the neuropathy has another cause.
det.clinical: The neurologist's task is to decide whether the paraprotein is causal. IgM-associated neuropathy is slowly progressive, distal and sensory with gait ataxia. POEMS presents as a severe, often painful demyelinating-axonal neuropathy that looks like treatment-resistant CIDP. AL amyloid produces burning pain, autonomic failure, carpal tunnel syndrome and organ involvement. Myeloma, Waldenström macroglobulinaemia, cryoglobulinaemia and lymphoma can also underlie the gammopathy.
det.diagnosis: Screen every adult with unexplained chronic neuropathy using electrophoresis plus immunofixation and free light chains. Classify the neuropathy by NCS and match the pattern to the isotype and light chain. Perform targeted tests (anti-MAG, VEGF, skeletal imaging, biopsy for amyloid) and refer to haematology to stage the clone. A careful search for other causes remains essential, because coincidental MGUS is common.
det.treatment: Treatment depends on mechanism. Anti-MAG neuropathy that is disabling may respond to rituximab; IVIG gives short-lived benefit in some. POEMS is treated by targeting the plasma cell clone with radiotherapy for isolated lesions or systemic therapy such as lenalidomide-dexamethasone and autologous stem cell transplant. AL amyloidosis needs clone-directed chemotherapy (for example daratumumab-based regimens) plus symptomatic and organ support. MGUS without neuropathy needs only periodic haematological monitoring.
det.prognosis: Anti-MAG neuropathy progresses slowly; POEMS and AL amyloidosis carry significant morbidity, improved by early clone-directed therapy.
pearls: Always order immunofixation, not just protein electrophoresis, when screening neuropathy.
CIDP that fails IVIG and steroids with a lambda light chain: check VEGF for POEMS.
IgM MGUS can evolve into Waldenström macroglobulinaemia; keep monitoring.
det.thd: Monoclonal gammopathy คือการพบโปรตีนจากเซลล์พลาสมาโคลนเดียวในเลือด ไม่ใช่โรคทางประสาทโดยตรง แต่บางชนิดทำให้ปลายประสาทเสื่อม เช่น IgM anti-MAG ทำให้ชาและเดินเซ, POEMS ทำให้ปลายประสาทอักเสบรุนแรงร่วมกับ VEGF สูง และ AL amyloidosis ทำให้ปวดแสบร้อนและระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติเสีย การตรวจต้องทำ immunofixation และ free light chain ร่วมกับ NCS แล้วรักษาตามกลไก ร่วมกับทีมโลหิตวิทยา

name: Monomelic polyneuropathies
formal: Asymmetric sensorimotor neuropathy confined to one limb, such as monomelic amyotrophy or focal neuropathy of a limb, usually with a slow or self-limiting course.
simple: Nerve disease affecting only one arm or leg.
more: Workup includes EMG and MRI; treatment depends on cause, with immunotherapy for immune cases.
th: โรคเส้นประสาทที่จำกัดอยู่แขนหรือขาข้างเดียว ไม่สมมาตร เช่น monomelic amyotrophy หรือ ischaemic monomelic neuropathy
tempoNote: Course varies: self-limiting progression over a few years in monomelic amyotrophy, acute after vascular access surgery
feat: Weakness and sensory changes confined to one limb
Causes: Hirayama disease, ischaemic monomelic neuropathy after AV fistula, MMN, focal CIDP, nerve tumour
Pattern does not follow a single nerve or root
Pain prominent in ischaemic forms
Requires search for structural, vascular and immune causes
inv: EMG/NCS including contralateral limb
MRI plexus and spine; nerve ultrasound
Vascular assessment if after vascular procedure

case.who: 62-year-old woman from Khon Kaen with diabetes and kidney failure
case.story: Hours after creation of a left brachiocephalic AV fistula, severe burning pain and weakness of the left hand.
case.exam: Warm hand with palpable radial pulse, weakness of all hand muscles, sensory loss in median, ulnar and radial territories.
case.tests: NCS shows distal axonal loss in all three nerves.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and urgent step?
case.a: Ischaemic monomelic neuropathy; urgent fistula ligation or banding.

read.where: Chapter 11: Neurologic Manifestations Of Acute Bacterial Infections And Sepsis
Chapter 9: Hirayama Disease and Other Focal Amyotrophies

det.patho: Mechanisms include ischaemia (diversion of blood by fistula), anterior horn cell injury from dynamic cord compression (Hirayama), immune-mediated demyelination (MMN, focal CIDP) and nerve tumours.
det.clinical: Limb-restricted weakness and sensory symptoms that cross nerve and root territories. Timing and pain are important clues.
det.diagnosis: Electrodiagnosis defines nerves involved and whether demyelinating or axonal; imaging finds structural causes; immune studies for MMN/CIDP.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: fistula ligation for ischaemic neuropathy, cervical collar for Hirayama, IVIG for MMN, steroids/IVIG for focal CIDP.
det.prognosis: Variable; prompt treatment improves ischaemic and immune forms.
pearls: Pain and weakness right after AV fistula creation suggests ischaemic monomelic neuropathy.
Distal nerve damage with a warm hand and pulse is typical.
Hirayama disease is painless and sensory-sparing.
det.thd: Monomelic neuropathy คืออาการเส้นประสาทผิดปกติที่จำกัดอยู่แขนหรือขาข้างเดียว สาเหตุเช่น ischaemic monomelic neuropathy หลังทำ AV fistula, Hirayama, MMN และ CIDP แบบเฉพาะที่ ต้องตรวจ EMG และภาพถ่ายเพื่อหาสาเหตุ รักษาตามสาเหตุ

ddx.pt: Young men, painless forearm-hand wasting without sensory loss
Conduction block, pure motor
Severe shoulder pain then patchy weakness

aN: monomelic neuropathy | single limb neuropathy | monomelic amyotrophy | limb restricted neuropathy

name: Mononeuropathy
formal: Focal injury of a single peripheral nerve by compression, entrapment, trauma, ischaemia or infiltration, with deficits in its distribution.
simple: Damage to a single nerve, causing numbness, weakness or pain in the area it supplies.
more: Electrodiagnosis localises the lesion; entrapments are managed with splinting, injection or surgery. Focal disorders of a single peripheral nerve from entrapment, compression, trauma, or ischaemia, such as median at the wrist or peroneal at the fibular head. Nerve conduction studies and ultrasound locate the lesion; splinting, avoiding compression, steroid injection, or surgical decompression depending on cause.
th: เส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเส้นเดียวบาดเจ็บจากการกดทับ การติดกับ ภยันตราย ขาดเลือด หรือมีสิ่งแทรกซึม ทำให้อ่อนแรงและชาในบริเวณของเส้นประสาทนั้น
tempoNote: Acute with trauma, compression or infarction; chronic and fluctuating with entrapment
feat: Weakness, numbness or pain limited to one nerve's territory
Commonest: median at wrist, ulnar at elbow, common peroneal at fibular head, radial at spiral groove
Tinel sign and provocation tests at the entrapment site
Predisposing conditions: diabetes, hypothyroidism, pregnancy, HNPP, leprosy (Thailand)
Multiple simultaneous mononeuropathies imply mononeuritis multiplex
inv: NCS/EMG: localise the lesion, demyelinating versus axonal, severity
Nerve ultrasound: swelling at entrapment site, masses, continuity after trauma
Glucose, TSH; consider leprosy skin exam and slit smear
MRI for proximal lesions or suspected tumour

case.story: After squatting for many hours during a long tapping shift, he woke with his right foot slapping when walking.
case.exam: Weak right ankle dorsiflexion and eversion, inversion preserved, numb dorsum of foot, ankle reflex normal.
case.tests: NCS: conduction block of the peroneal nerve across the fibular head.
case.q: Where is the lesion and what is the outlook?
case.a: Common peroneal mononeuropathy at the fibular head from compression; avoid squatting and leg crossing, ankle-foot orthosis; recovery expected over weeks to months.

read.where: Chapter 2 Entrapment Neuropathies of the Upper Extremity; Chapter 3 Common Mononeuropathies of the Lower Extremities
Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves — Focal and Compressive Neuropathies
Companion to Peripheral Neuropathy: chapters (see text)

det.patho: Focal compression first causes ischaemia and paranodal demyelination, giving conduction block that recovers quickly once pressure is relieved. Prolonged or severe injury leads to axonal loss with Wallerian degeneration, and recovery then depends on regrowth of around 1 mm per day. Laceration or stretch can disrupt the whole nerve. Diabetes and other metabolic states make nerves more vulnerable to pressure.
det.clinical: Patterns match nerve anatomy: carpal tunnel causes nocturnal hand tingling and thenar wasting; ulnar neuropathy gives weakness of intrinsic hand muscles and little-finger numbness; peroneal palsy causes foot drop with preserved inversion; radial palsy gives wrist drop with spared triceps. Pain may spread beyond the nerve territory, which can mislead. In Thailand, leprosy should be remembered for thickened nerves with skin patches.
det.diagnosis: Careful examination of muscles supplied above and below candidate sites localises the lesion. Electrodiagnosis confirms the site and grades severity; ultrasound adds structural detail and is increasingly used. Look for underlying systemic causes when lesions are atypical, bilateral or recurrent. Distinguish from radiculopathy, plexopathy and motor neuron disease.
det.treatment: Remove the cause: avoid pressure positions, splints (wrist splint for carpal tunnel, elbow padding for ulnar), local steroid injection for some entrapments. Surgical decompression helps moderate to severe or progressive entrapment. Traumatic transection needs early surgical repair. Ankle-foot orthoses and physiotherapy support function during recovery.
det.prognosis: Demyelinating compressive lesions usually recover fully; severe axonal loss recovers slowly and incompletely.
pearls: Foot drop with preserved inversion = peroneal; weak inversion suggests L5 or sciatic.
Wrist drop with preserved triceps localises to the spiral groove.
Recurrent pressure palsies: think HNPP.
det.thd: Mononeuropathy คือเส้นประสาทเส้นเดียวผิดปกติ มักเกิดจากการกดทับ เช่น carpal tunnel ที่ข้อมือ ulnar ที่ข้อศอก หรือ peroneal ที่หัวกระดูก fibula ผู้ป่วยชาและอ่อนแรงเฉพาะบริเวณเส้นประสาทนั้น ตรวจ NCS และอัลตราซาวด์เพื่อหาตำแหน่ง รักษาด้วยหลีกเลี่ยงการกดทับ ใส่เฝือกอ่อน ฉีดยา หรือผ่าตัดคลายการกดทับ

ddx.pt: Dermatomal pain, myotomal weakness across several nerves and reflex change; e.g. L5 also weakens inversion
Several nerves affected in sequence, often vasculitic
Recurrent pressure palsies with family history; PMP22 deletion

aN: mononeuropathies | focal neuropathy | single nerve palsy | entrapment neuropathy | compression neuropathy

name: Monoradiculopathies
formal: Disorder of a single spinal nerve root, usually from disc herniation or foraminal stenosis, producing dermatomal pain or sensory loss, myotomal weakness and reduced reflex.
simple: Pinching or irritation of one nerve root near the spine, causing pain, numbness or weakness in the area that nerve supplies.
more: Confirmed by MRI and EMG; most cases improve with conservative care, while persistent deficits or cord compromise may need steroid injection or surgical decompression.
th: รอยโรคของรากประสาทไขสันหลังเส้นเดียว มักจากหมอนรองกระดูกหรือรูรากประสาทแคบ ทำให้ปวดร้าว ชาตาม dermatome และอ่อนแรงตาม myotome
tempoNote: Disc herniation is acute; foraminal stenosis is chronic
feat: Radiating pain along the dermatome
Sensory loss and paraesthesia in the dermatome
Myotomal weakness and reduced reflex
Commonest in C6, C7, L5 and S1
Non-compressive causes: diabetes, herpes zoster, infection, tumour
inv: MRI of the relevant spinal level
EMG with paraspinals
Glucose and infection screen in non-compressive cases

case.story: Burning pain along the right chest wall followed a week later by blisters in the same band.
case.exam: Vesicular rash in a T6 dermatome; allodynia.
case.tests: None needed.
case.q: What is the cause of this monoradiculopathy?
case.a: Herpes zoster (shingles) affecting the T6 dorsal root ganglion.

read.where: Chapter 14 Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders — Degenerative Disease of the Spine

det.patho: Most result from mechanical compression by disc or osteophyte, but inflammation (herpes zoster), ischaemia (diabetes), infiltration (tumour) and infection also damage single roots.
det.clinical: Pain is usually the leading complaint; motor and reflex findings help confirm the level. Thoracic radiculopathy causes band-like pain mimicking visceral disease.
det.diagnosis: Clinical localisation, MRI and EMG. Sensory potentials remain normal because the lesion is pre-ganglionic (except zoster which affects the ganglion).
det.treatment: Treat the cause; analgesia and physiotherapy; antivirals for zoster; surgery for persistent compressive deficits.
det.prognosis: Usually favourable for compressive forms.
pearls: Thoracic band pain may be radicular, not cardiac or abdominal.
Diabetic truncal radiculopathy can cause abdominal wall bulging.
Zoster pain may precede rash by days.
det.thd: Monoradiculopathy คือรากประสาทเส้นเดียวผิดปกติ ปวดร้าว ชา และอ่อนแรงตามรากนั้น ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจากหมอนรองกระดูก แต่ก็เกิดจากงูสวัด เบาหวาน เนื้องอก หรือติดเชื้อ ตรวจ MRI และ EMG รักษาตามสาเหตุ

name: Mood disorders
formal: Psychiatric conditions including major depression and bipolar disorder, with persistent disturbance of affect; common comorbidities of epilepsy, stroke, Parkinson disease and dementia.
simple: Conditions such as depression and bipolar disorder where mood is persistently very low or very high.
more: Psychiatric conditions of mood, such as depression and bipolar disorder, that frequently coexist with and complicate neurological disease including stroke, Parkinson disease and epilepsy.
th: ภาวะซึมเศร้าและอารมณ์ผิดปกติที่พบบ่อยในผู้ป่วยโรคระบบประสาท เช่น หลัง stroke ประมาณหนึ่งในสาม ในโรคลมชัก พาร์กินสัน และ MS ทำให้การฟื้นตัวแย่ลง คัดกรองด้วย PHQ-9 และรักษาด้วย SSRI ร่วมกับจิตบำบัด
tempoNote: Post-stroke depression peaks in the first months but can start at any time in the first years; in epilepsy and Parkinson disease, mood symptoms may precede the neurological diagnosis or fluctuate around seizures and OFF periods
feat: Depressed mood or loss of interest for at least 2 weeks, with sleep, appetite, energy, concentration and guilt changes; somatic items overlap with neurological symptoms, so the mood items carry more weight
Post-stroke depression affects roughly one in three survivors, is linked to prior depression, disability, aphasia and social isolation, and worsens recovery, cognition and survival
In epilepsy, depression is the commonest comorbidity, suicide risk is several times higher, and some drugs (levetiracetam, perampanel, topiramate, barbiturates) can cause irritability or low mood
In Parkinson disease, depression, anxiety and apathy may appear before motor signs; mood can dip with OFF periods
Look for related syndromes that are not depression: apathy, pathological crying (pseudobulbar affect), catastrophic reaction and post-stroke anxiety
inv: Screen with PHQ-9 (or PHQ-2 first) or HADS, adapted for aphasia with observer tools when needed; ask directly about suicidal thoughts
Check TSH, B12, sodium, calcium, glucose and review drugs (antiseizure medicines, beta-blockers, steroids, interferon)
MRI or EEG only for atypical, late-onset or rapidly changing presentations (new lesion, autoimmune encephalitis, non-convulsive seizures)

case.who: 63-year-old retired teacher from Chachoengsao, 3 months after a left frontal ischaemic stroke
case.story: His right arm has recovered well, but he has stopped going to physiotherapy, sleeps badly, eats little and tells his wife he is a burden; he cries when talking about his grandchildren but not at random moments.
case.exam: Mild right pronator drift and non-fluent but understandable speech; he looks sad and answers slowly; no new focal signs.
case.tests: PHQ-9 is 17 with a positive item on thoughts of being better off dead; sodium, TSH and B12 are normal; repeat CT shows only the old infarct.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what should be started?
case.a: Post-stroke major depression with passive suicidal ideation; assess safety, start an SSRI such as sertraline or escitalopram with sodium monitoring, add psychological support and keep him in rehabilitation.

det.patho: Mood disorders in neurological disease arise from both lesion biology and reaction to disability. After stroke, damage to frontal-subcortical circuits and monoamine pathways, inflammation and loss of function all contribute; early studies linked left anterior lesions with depression, but later meta-analyses show the lesion side is a weak predictor. In epilepsy the link is two-way, since depression raises the risk of later seizures, and shared limbic dysfunction is suspected. In Parkinson disease, serotonergic, noradrenergic and dopaminergic loss underlie depression and apathy.
det.clinical: Post-stroke depression usually appears in the first months and is often missed because flat affect, fatigue and slowing are blamed on the stroke. Epilepsy-related mood change may be peri-ictal (a dysphoric prodrome or postictal low mood lasting days) or interictal, and suicidality must be asked about at every visit. Parkinson disease depression is often mixed with anxiety, apathy and sleep problems and may fluctuate with OFF periods. Mania after a neurological lesion is rare but is classically linked with right-sided or orbitofrontal damage. Untreated depression reduces adherence and rehabilitation effort and is associated with higher mortality.
det.diagnosis: DSM-5-TR major depressive disorder criteria apply, but when the mood change is judged to be a direct physiological effect of the illness DSM-5-TR codes it as a depressive disorder attributed to that illness. Validated screens (PHQ-9, HADS, NDDI-E for epilepsy, GDS for older adults) improve detection, and observer scales help when aphasia or cognitive impairment limits self-report. Exclude delirium, hypothyroidism, drug effects and apathy, which lacks sadness. Separate pathological crying, which comes in brief bursts out of proportion to mood.
det.treatment: SSRIs (sertraline, escitalopram, citalopram) are first line in stroke, epilepsy and Parkinson disease; at usual doses they do not meaningfully raise seizure risk, while bupropion at high dose, clomipramine and maprotiline are best avoided in epilepsy. Watch for hyponatraemia, bleeding with antithrombotics, falls and QT effects with citalopram. Large trials found that routine fluoxetine does not improve motor recovery after stroke and increases fractures, so it is not given for that purpose. Cognitive behavioural therapy, behavioural activation, exercise and caregiver support add benefit; in epilepsy, review drugs that worsen mood, and in Parkinson disease optimise dopaminergic therapy and consider venlafaxine or nortriptyline when SSRIs fail.
det.prognosis: Many patients respond to treatment, but recurrence is common and untreated depression predicts worse function, cognition and survival in neurological disease.
pearls: Ask about suicide in every patient with epilepsy and depression; the risk is several times that of the general population.
Fluoxetine is for depression after stroke, not for motor recovery.
Apathy without sadness and pathological crying without sustained low mood are separate syndromes with different treatments.
det.thd: ภาวะซึมเศร้าพบบ่อยมากในโรคระบบประสาท หลัง stroke พบประมาณหนึ่งในสาม ในโรคลมชักเป็นโรคร่วมที่พบมากที่สุดและเพิ่มความเสี่ยงฆ่าตัวตาย ในพาร์กินสันอาจเกิดก่อนอาการทางการเคลื่อนไหว ควรคัดกรองด้วย PHQ-9 หรือ HADS และถามเรื่องความคิดฆ่าตัวตายเสมอ การรักษาหลักคือ SSRI เช่น sertraline หรือ escitalopram ร่วมกับจิตบำบัด โดยติดตามระดับโซเดียม และไม่ใช้ fluoxetine เพื่อช่วยฟื้นกำลังกล้ามเนื้อหลัง stroke

qx.stem: A 66-year-old male retired civil servant from Lopburi is 2 months out from a left middle cerebral artery infarct with moderate right hemiparesis. His daughter asks whether he should take fluoxetine because she read that it helps arm recovery. He has no depressive symptoms; PHQ-9 is 3.
qx.q: What is the most appropriate advice?
opts: Start fluoxetine 20 mg daily for 6 months to improve motor recovery
Start fluoxetine only if he also has aphasia
Start citalopram as a safer motor-recovery drug
Start amitriptyline at night to aid recovery
Do not start fluoxetine for motor recovery; continue rehabilitation and screen for depression over time
qx.why: Large randomised trials found that routine fluoxetine after stroke does not improve functional or motor outcome and increases fractures and hyponatraemia. Antidepressants are indicated when depression is present, which affects about one in three survivors, so repeated screening is sensible. No other antidepressant has proven benefit for motor recovery.

name: Morvan syndrome
formal: Autoimmune syndrome with peripheral nerve hyperexcitability, autonomic dysfunction, insomnia and encephalopathy, linked to CASPR2 antibodies and sometimes thymoma.
simple: An autoimmune condition causing muscle twitching and cramps, severe insomnia, sweating and confusion.
th: โรคจากแอนติบอดีต่อ CASPR2 — กล้ามเนื้อกระตุกเป็นคลื่น ปวดแสบร้อน นอนไม่หลับรุนแรง สับสน และระบบอัตโนมัติแปรปรวน มักสัมพันธ์กับ thymoma
tempoNote: Builds over weeks to months; CASPR2 disease overall can be slowly progressive or fluctuating
feat: Peripheral nerve hyperexcitability: myokymia, cramps, fasciculation and stiffness
Severe insomnia with agitated dream enactment (agrypnia excitata), confusion and hallucinations
Dysautonomia: drenching sweats, tachycardia, blood pressure swings, weight loss
Neuropathic pain, burning or itching in the limbs
Mostly men over 50; thymoma (often malignant) in a sizeable minority
inv: CASPR2 IgG by cell-based assay (serum more sensitive than CSF); LGI1 may coexist in Morvan syndrome
EMG: myokymic and neuromyotonic discharges, after-discharges following nerve stimulation
CT or MRI chest for thymoma; polysomnography shows loss of normal sleep architecture
Sodium (can fall), MRI brain usually normal, CSF often bland

case.story: Three months of worm-like twitching in both calves, burning feet and nightly sweats soaking the bed. His wife says he has barely slept for weeks and talks and gestures as if working on the boat at night.
case.exam: Continuous rippling of calf and thigh muscles, slow relaxation after grip, resting heart rate 118, fluctuating attention, no weakness.
case.tests: EMG: myokymic doublets and neuromyotonic discharges. Serum CASPR2 strongly positive. CT chest: 6 cm anterior mediastinal mass.
case.q: What is the syndrome, and which treatment step is essential besides immunotherapy?
case.a: Morvan syndrome from CASPR2 autoimmunity; resection of the thymoma is central, combined with steroids, IVIG or PLEX and symptomatic relief of hyperexcitability.

det.patho: CASPR2 (contactin-associated protein-like 2) clusters Kv1 potassium channels at juxtaparanodes of myelinated axons and is also expressed in brain. Mostly IgG4 antibodies disturb its interaction with contactin-2, lowering potassium channel function and causing spontaneous repetitive firing of peripheral nerves. Morvan syndrome is the most severe phenotype and is strongly tied to thymoma, where faulty T-cell selection may explain combined antibodies.
det.clinical: CASPR2 antibodies produce a spectrum: isolated neuromyotonia, painful neuropathy, limbic encephalitis, cerebellar ataxia, episodic ataxia-like attacks, or the full Morvan picture. Morvan syndrome combines nerve hyperexcitability, insomnia with dream-like behaviour, hallucinations, autonomic storms and weight loss. Severe cases risk arrhythmia and sudden death. Ask about myasthenia, as thymoma-related autoimmunity can overlap.
det.diagnosis: Confirm CASPR2 IgG by cell-based assay, interpreting low-titre serum-only positives cautiously because false positives occur. EMG documents peripheral hyperexcitability, and sleep studies show disorganised sleep without normal cycling. Image the chest for thymoma in every patient. Exclude prion disease, delirium tremens, thyrotoxicosis and drug toxicity.
det.treatment: Treat the tumour where present, then give corticosteroids with IVIG or plasma exchange; rituximab is used for refractory or relapsing disease. Sodium-channel blockers such as carbamazepine or phenytoin reduce cramps and myokymia, and neuropathic pain agents help discomfort. Monitor cardiac rhythm and autonomic parameters in severe cases.
det.prognosis: Many patients improve substantially with tumour removal and immunotherapy, but relapse may herald tumour recurrence; untreated Morvan syndrome can be fatal.
pearls: Twitching muscles plus profound insomnia and sweating: test CASPR2 and image the mediastinum.
LGI1 = mostly CNS; CASPR2 = peripheral nerve plus variable CNS.
Thymoma recurrence can present as a neurological relapse.
det.thd: Morvan syndrome เกิดจากแอนติบอดีต่อ CASPR2 ซึ่งทำให้เส้นประสาทส่วนปลายทำงานเกิน จึงมีกล้ามเนื้อกระตุกเป็นคลื่น ตะคริว ปวดแสบร้อน ร่วมกับนอนไม่หลับรุนแรง ละเมอทำงาน สับสน และเหงื่อออกมาก ใจสั่น พบ thymoma ได้บ่อย ต้องตรวจ CT ทรวงอกทุกราย รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัดเนื้องอก steroid IVIG หรือ PLEX และยาลดการกระตุกของเส้นประสาท

qx.stem: A 57-year-old man from Ayutthaya has four months of near-total insomnia with vivid dream-like behaviour and talking in light sleep, soaking night sweats, a 9-kg weight loss and constant rippling of his calf and thigh muscles. He is intermittently confused and has burning pain in the feet. Needle EMG shows myokymic and neuromyotonic discharges. Serum CASPR2-IgG is positive.
qx.q: Which investigation is most important next?
opts: CT or MRI of the chest to look for a thymoma
Testicular ultrasound for a germ-cell tumour
Pelvic MRI for an ovarian teratoma
Bone-marrow biopsy for multiple myeloma
No tumour search, because CASPR2 disease is never paraneoplastic
qx.why: Peripheral nerve hyperexcitability with severe insomnia (agrypnia), autonomic overactivity, encephalopathy and neuropathic pain is Morvan syndrome, usually with CASPR2 (often plus LGI1) antibodies. It is the CASPR2 phenotype most strongly linked to thymoma, often malignant, so chest imaging is essential; treatment combines tumour removal with immunotherapy. Ovarian teratoma is the classic association of anti-NMDAR encephalitis and testicular tumours of anti-Ma2 (KLHL11) disease.

simple: Gradual loss of the nerve cells controlling muscles, leading to weakness, wasting and stiffness.

Fasciculations, cramps, weight loss; sensation and eye movements preserved

det.patho: Motor neuron disease is a group of neurodegenerative disorders where cortical and spinal or bulbar motor neurons die. Most cases show TDP-43 cytoplasmic aggregates; inherited forms involve C9orf72, SOD1, TARDBP, FUS and others. Mechanisms include impaired RNA processing, protein clearance failure, excitotoxicity and neuroinflammation.
det.clinical: Presentations vary with which neurons fail first: limb onset with asymmetric weakness, bulbar onset with speech and swallowing problems, or rarely respiratory onset. Combination of wasting and hyperreflexia is the classic finding. Sensory, sphincter and eye movement functions are largely spared. Cognitive or behavioural change occurs in up to half.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by EMG showing denervation in multiple regions; Gold Coast criteria simplify this. Exclude mimics: cervical myelopathy, MMN, Kennedy disease, inclusion body myositis, myasthenia and structural lesions. Neurofilament light levels in blood or CSF are raised and assist prognosis. Genetic testing is offered when family history or young onset is present.
det.treatment: Riluzole modestly prolongs survival; edaravone has limited evidence and variable access. Tofersen treats SOD1-related ALS. Non-invasive ventilation improves survival and quality of life, and gastrostomy should be placed before vital capacity falls too low. Multidisciplinary clinics, symptom control and early palliative planning are core.
det.prognosis: Median survival is 2–4 years from symptom onset, with about 10% living beyond 10 years.
pearls: Wasted muscles with brisk reflexes and normal sensation: think MND.
Always exclude conduction block and cervical cord compression.
NIV prolongs survival more than any current drug.
det.thd: MND คือกลุ่มโรคที่เซลล์ประสาทสั่งการทั้งบนและล่างเสื่อม ตัวอย่างหลักคือ ALS ผู้ป่วยมีกล้ามเนื้อลีบ เต้นระริก อ่อนแรง แต่รีเฟล็กซ์ไว และไม่ชา บางรายเริ่มจากกลืนและพูดลำบาก วินิจฉัยด้วยอาการและ EMG ร่วมกับตัดโรคที่รักษาได้ การรักษาคือ riluzole การช่วยหายใจแบบ NIV การใส่สายอาหาร และการดูแลแบบสหสาขา

det.patho: Degeneration affects upper motor neurons of the motor cortex together with lower motor neurons of the bulbar nuclei and spinal cord. Around 97% of cases show cytoplasmic TDP-43 aggregates; about 10% are familial, with C9orf72 expansion the commonest cause, then SOD1, TARDBP and FUS. Disease appears to spread through connected neuronal networks.
det.clinical: Onset is focal, often in a hand, foot or the bulbar muscles, then spreads to contiguous regions. Weight loss, cramps and fatigue are common. Respiratory muscle weakness causes orthopnoea, morning headache and poor sleep. Cognitive and behavioural change ranges from mild executive dysfunction to frank FTD.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis relies on progressive UMN and LMN signs supported by EMG and exclusion of mimics. Gold Coast criteria require progressive motor impairment with LMN signs in two regions, or with both UMN and LMN signs within a single region. Investigations should exclude myelopathy, MMN, myasthenia, Kennedy disease, IBM and metabolic causes. Neurofilament light is supportive and prognostic.
det.treatment: Riluzole extends survival by a few months. Tofersen, an antisense oligonucleotide, is approved for SOD1-ALS. Multidisciplinary clinics provide NIV, gastrostomy, speech aids, physiotherapy and symptom drugs for saliva, cramps, spasticity and emotional lability. Early advance care planning and palliative involvement are essential.
det.prognosis: Median survival 2–4 years; younger onset, limb onset and slower early decline predict longer survival.
pearls: Wasting plus hyperreflexia without sensory loss is the classic combination.
Ask about orthopnoea and morning headache at every visit.
Exclude MMN and cervical myelopathy before giving the diagnosis.
det.thd: Motor neuron disease ส่วนใหญ่คือ ALS เกิดจากเซลล์ประสาทสั่งการทั้งบนและล่างเสื่อม ทำให้อ่อนแรง กล้ามเนื้อลีบ เต้นระริก รีเฟล็กซ์ไว และอาจกลืนพูดลำบาก โดยไม่ชา วินิจฉัยด้วยอาการ EMG และตัดโรคเลียนแบบที่รักษาได้ การรักษามี riluzole tofersen สำหรับ SOD1 การใช้ NIV และใส่สายอาหาร ร่วมกับการดูแลแบบประคับประคอง

Toxic: lead (wrist drop), dapsone
Must be separated from motor neuron disease
inv: NCS/EMG: conduction block, motor axonal loss, normal sensory responses
Anti-GM1 antibodies
Heavy metal screen; genetic panel for HMN

case.story: Gradual weakness of right finger extension and left grip over 3 years, worse in cold.
case.exam: Asymmetric weakness in radial and ulnar territories, minimal wasting, reflexes reduced, no sensory loss, no UMN signs.
case.tests: Motor conduction block in right radial and left ulnar nerves; sensory normal; anti-GM1 IgM positive.
case.q: Diagnosis and treatment?
case.a: Multifocal motor neuropathy; IVIG.

det.patho: Selective motor axon or motor nerve myelin involvement results from immune attack on motor nerve antigens (GM1 in MMN), genetic defects in motor axon maintenance (HMN) or toxins with motor predilection.
det.clinical: Pure or predominantly motor weakness with wasting and cramps. Pattern (asymmetric nerve territories versus length-dependent) and tempo differentiate causes.
det.diagnosis: Electrodiagnosis is central; antibodies, toxicology and genetics guide aetiology. Exclude motor neuron disease.
det.treatment: IVIG for MMN (steroids ineffective or harmful); remove toxin; supportive orthotics for HMN.
det.prognosis: MMN responds to IVIG; HMN is slowly progressive.
pearls: Steroids can worsen MMN.
Lower motor neuron weakness in nerve rather than myotome territories suggests MMN.
Look for pes cavus and family history in HMN.
det.thd: Motor neuropathy คือโรคเส้นประสาทที่เสียใยประสาทสั่งการเป็นหลัก อ่อนแรงและลีบโดยไม่ค่อยชา เช่น MMN ที่อ่อนแรงไม่สมมาตรตามเส้นประสาทและมี conduction block, HMN แบบพันธุกรรม และพิษตะกั่ว ต้องแยกจาก ALS ด้วย EMG MMN รักษาด้วย IVIG

name: Motor tics
formal: Sudden, brief, repetitive stereotyped movements, such as blinking or head jerks, preceded by premonitory urge and temporarily suppressible; core feature of Tourette syndrome.
simple: Quick, repeated, involuntary movements such as eye blinking or head jerking that a person can sometimes hold back briefly.
th: การเคลื่อนไหวสั้น ๆ ซ้ำ ๆ แบบเดิม เช่น กะพริบตา สะบัดคอ ยักไหล่ มักมีความรู้สึกอยากทำนำมาก่อนและกลั้นได้ชั่วคราว เป็นลักษณะหลักของ Tourette syndrome
tempoNote: Begins in childhood, usually age 4–8; individual tics are momentary but the disorder waxes and wanes over months and often eases by early adulthood
feat: Brief, patterned movements that repeat in the same way: blinking, grimacing, head jerks, shoulder shrugs
An inner urge or itch-like sensation precedes the tic and is relieved once it is done
Can be held back for a while at the cost of rising discomfort; worse with stress, excitement or fatigue
Tics wax and wane and change their repertoire over months; they often persist in light sleep
Frequently accompanied by ADHD, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, anxiety or learning problems
inv: Diagnosis is clinical from history and observation (home video is helpful)
Neurological examination should otherwise be normal; imaging and EEG only for atypical features
Consider ASO titre/streptococcal history, thyroid and drug review only when onset or course is unusual

case.who: 9-year-old boy brought to a paediatric neurology clinic in Nakhon Ratchasima
case.story: For a year he has blinked hard and jerked his head to the right many times a day; his teacher says it worsens before tests, and he can stop it briefly when asked.
case.exam: Several rapid eye-blink and neck-jerk movements during the visit; he says he feels a 'tight' feeling in his neck beforehand. Rest of the examination is normal.
case.tests: No investigations needed; parent's phone video confirms the same stereotyped movements at home.
case.q: Which features separate these from myoclonus or seizures?
case.a: Motor tics: premonitory urge, temporary suppressibility and stereotyped repetition with preserved awareness. Education and behavioural therapy (CBIT) come first; medication only if tics impair function.

det.patho: Tics are thought to arise from faulty gating within cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loops, with excess dopaminergic signalling in the striatum and altered inhibitory interneuron function. Twin and family studies show strong heritability, but it is polygenic with many small-effect variants. Transient tics are very common in school-age children, affecting perhaps one in five at some point.
det.clinical: Simple motor tics involve one muscle group in a fast jerk (clonic) or a sustained posture (dystonic or tonic). Complex motor tics combine several movements in sequence, such as touching, jumping or copying gestures. They usually start in the face and move downwards, peak in severity around 10–12 years and lessen in most by late adolescence. Duration over one year without vocal tics defines persistent motor tic disorder; with vocal tics it becomes Tourette syndrome.
det.diagnosis: DSM-5 groups tic disorders by type and duration: provisional (under one year), persistent motor or vocal (over one year) and Tourette syndrome. Onset must be before 18 and not due to drugs or another illness. Look for features that suggest secondary tics: onset in adulthood, abnormal neurological signs, regression or exposure to stimulants and dopamine blockers. Screening for ADHD and OCD matters because they often drive disability more than the tics themselves.
det.treatment: Explanation and reassurance are often enough. Comprehensive Behavioural Intervention for Tics (habit reversal training) is first-line when treatment is needed. Alpha-2 agonists (clonidine, guanfacine) help mild cases with ADHD; aripiprazole or other dopamine-modulating drugs are used for severe tics, and botulinum toxin for a single troublesome tic. Deep brain stimulation is reserved for refractory adults in specialist centres.
det.prognosis: Most childhood tics improve markedly by adulthood; a minority persist and a small group remain severe.
pearls: Ask about the premonitory urge — it is the most useful feature separating tics from other jerks.
Tics are typically less obvious in clinic than at home; a video is worth more than an examination.
Treat the comorbid ADHD or OCD — it is often what impairs school and social life.
det.thd: Motor tics คือการเคลื่อนไหวสั้นและซ้ำแบบเดิม เช่น กะพริบตาหรือสะบัดคอ มักมีความรู้สึกอยากทำนำมาก่อนและกลั้นได้ชั่วคราว เกิดจากวงจร basal ganglia–cortex ที่ควบคุมการยับยั้งผิดปกติ พบบ่อยในเด็กวัยเรียนและมักดีขึ้นเมื่อโต การวินิจฉัยอาศัยประวัติและการสังเกตเป็นหลัก การรักษาเริ่มที่อธิบายให้ครอบครัวเข้าใจและฝึก behavioural therapy (CBIT) ใช้ยาเช่น clonidine หรือ aripiprazole เมื่ออาการรบกวนชีวิตประจำวัน

name: Moyamoya disease
formal: Progressive steno-occlusive disease of distal ICA and proximal circle of Willis vessels, with fragile collaterals giving the puff of smoke angiographic appearance; causes ischaemic or haemorrhagic strokes.
simple: A disease where brain arteries narrow and tiny fragile vessels form to compensate, causing strokes in children and adults.
more: Diagnosis by MRA or catheter angiography; RNF213 variants are a susceptibility locus in East Asians. Treat with revascularisation (STA-MCA bypass or indirect synangiosis); children present with TIAs on crying or hyperventilation, so avoid hypocapnia.
ab: spontaneous occlusion of the circle of Willis
th: หลอดเลือดแดง ICA ส่วนปลายและแขนงต้นของ ACA/MCA ตีบตันแบบค่อยเป็นค่อยไปทั้งสองข้าง เกิดเส้นเลือดฝอยข้างเคียงคล้าย 'กลุ่มควัน' พบมากในเอเชียตะวันออก (RNF213) เด็กมาด้วย TIA/stroke ผู้ใหญ่มักมาด้วยเลือดออก
tempoNote: Progressive arteriopathy over years; children have repeated TIAs triggered by crying or hyperventilation, adults may present suddenly with haemorrhage
feat: Bimodal onset: children around 5 years and adults in their 30s–40s; female predominance
Children: recurrent TIAs or strokes provoked by crying, blowing, hot food or exercise (hyperventilation), alternating sides
Adults: intraventricular, deep or subarachnoid haemorrhage from fragile collaterals, as well as ischaemia
Headache, seizures, involuntary movements (chorea) and cognitive decline
Moyamoya syndrome: same angiogram secondary to sickle cell, Down syndrome, NF1, radiation, thyroid disease
inv: MRI/MRA: stenosis of terminal ICA, ACA and MCA; flow voids in basal ganglia; FLAIR 'ivy sign'
Catheter angiography: Suzuki staging and external carotid collaterals (pre-surgical planning)
Perfusion imaging (SPECT, CT/MR perfusion with acetazolamide challenge) for haemodynamic reserve
Screen for associated conditions (thyroid, sickle cell, NF1); RNF213 variant testing in familial cases

case.story: While blowing up balloons at a birthday party and again while crying, her right arm went limp for ten minutes; last month a similar episode affected the left leg.
case.exam: Normal between attacks except a mild left pronator drift.
case.tests: MRI: small cortical infarct in the right frontal lobe and FLAIR hyperintense sulci (ivy sign); MRA: bilateral severe stenosis of distal ICAs with basal collateral networks.
case.q: Why do attacks follow blowing or crying, and what treatment is offered?
case.a: Hyperventilation lowers CO2 and constricts vessels, dropping flow beyond the stenoses; aspirin and surgical revascularisation (indirect bypass such as EDAS in children) are recommended.

read.where: Chapter 14 Stroke in children and young adults
Chapter 33 A case of moya moya
Section 7 Non-Inflammatory Disorders of the Arterial Wall
Chapter 7: Unusual causes of ischemic stroke and transient ischemic attack

det.patho: A non-inflammatory, non-atherosclerotic occlusive vasculopathy affecting the terminal ICAs and proximal circle of Willis, with intimal fibrocellular thickening and thin media. Reduced flow drives growth of fragile lenticulostriate and thalamoperforating collaterals (the angiographic 'puff of smoke'), plus transdural collaterals. The RNF213 p.R4810K founder variant is strongly linked in Japanese, Korean and Chinese patients and also occurs in Thailand. Microaneurysms on stressed collaterals explain adult haemorrhage.
det.clinical: Paediatric disease usually presents with ischaemia — TIAs, strokes, cognitive impairment and headaches — and attacks are classically triggered by hyperventilation. Adults present either with ischaemic events or with haemorrhage (intraventricular or basal ganglia), which carries higher mortality. Unilateral involvement can progress to bilateral disease, especially in children. Pregnancy and dehydration may destabilise patients.
det.diagnosis: Angiography or high-quality MRA showing stenosis/occlusion of the terminal ICA and proximal ACA/MCA with abnormal collateral networks establishes the diagnosis; Suzuki stages I–VI describe progression. 'Moyamoya disease' implies no associated cause; when an underlying condition is present the term moyamoya syndrome is used. Vessel wall MRI helps distinguish it from atherosclerosis (concentric, non-enhancing narrowing with small outer diameter) and vasculitis. Perfusion studies with vasodilatory challenge identify those at risk who need revascularisation.
det.treatment: Revascularisation is the mainstay for symptomatic ischaemic disease: direct bypass (superficial temporal to MCA anastomosis) in adults, indirect procedures (EDAS, EDAMS, pial synangiosis, multiple burr holes) particularly in children, or combined approaches. In haemorrhagic adult moyamoya, direct bypass reduces rebleeding. Aspirin is commonly given for ischaemic presentations. Avoid hyperventilation, dehydration and hypotension, especially during anaesthesia. Thrombolysis is used with caution because of fragile collaterals.
det.prognosis: Untreated paediatric disease frequently progresses with accumulating deficits and cognitive decline; successful revascularisation substantially lowers future stroke risk.
pearls: Child with TIAs when crying, blowing or eating hot noodles: think moyamoya.
Adult moyamoya often presents with intraventricular haemorrhage.
Avoid hypocapnia and hypotension during anaesthesia in moyamoya patients.
det.thd: Moyamoya disease คือหลอดเลือด ICA ส่วนปลายและต้น ACA/MCA ตีบตันทั้งสองข้างอย่างช้า ๆ ทำให้เกิดหลอดเลือดข้างเคียงเล็ก ๆ คล้ายกลุ่มควัน พบบ่อยในเอเชียตะวันออกและสัมพันธ์กับยีน RNF213 เด็กมักมี TIA หรือ stroke เวลาร้องไห้หรือเป่าลูกโป่ง ผู้ใหญ่อาจมาด้วยเลือดออกในสมอง วินิจฉัยด้วย MRA/angiography รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัด revascularisation (direct/indirect bypass) และหลีกเลี่ยงภาวะหายใจเร็วหรือความดันต่ำ

qx.stem: A 9-year-old girl has recurrent transient left weakness when she cries or blows on hot food. MRA shows progressive stenosis of both distal internal carotid arteries and proximal anterior and middle cerebral arteries, with a fine network of collaterals at the base. FLAIR shows 'ivy' sign over the hemispheres.
qx.q: What is the best strategy for stroke prevention?
opts: Warfarin with INR 2–3 lifelong
Intracranial stenting of the carotid termini
Intravenous immunoglobulin monthly
Observation until the first infarct
Surgical revascularisation (direct or indirect bypass) in addition to antiplatelet therapy and avoidance of hyperventilation
qx.why: Moyamoya with haemodynamic insufficiency benefits from bypass surgery, which reduces the risk of stroke compared with medical therapy. Triggers such as crying, hyperventilation and dehydration should be avoided. The 'ivy' sign reflects slow leptomeningeal collateral flow. Stenting and warfarin are not proven, and IVIG is not indicated.

qx.stem: A 8-year-old girl has repeated episodes of right-hand weakness triggered by crying and blowing on hot noodles. MRI shows small infarcts in the left frontal watershed zone and, on FLAIR, linear bright sulcal signal over the hemispheres. MR angiography shows tapering of both distal internal carotid arteries and proximal anterior and middle cerebral arteries, with a tangle of fine collateral vessels around the basal ganglia region.
qx.q: What is the most appropriate approach?
opts: Long-term anticoagulation alone with no surgery
Intravenous thrombolysis whenever symptoms recur
Reassurance; this is benign vasospasm
Encourage hyperventilation to improve cerebral perfusion
Perfusion assessment and surgical revascularisation, with antiplatelet therapy and avoidance of hyperventilation and dehydration
qx.why: Progressive bilateral stenosis of the terminal internal carotids with basal moyamoya collaterals and an ivy sign in a child with hyperventilation-triggered TIAs defines moyamoya disease. Hyperventilation lowers CO2 and reduces perfusion in a maximally dilated vascular bed, so crying provokes ischaemia. Direct or indirect bypass is the established treatment for symptomatic haemodynamic compromise.

qx.stem: A 7-year-old girl has repeated brief episodes of right arm weakness when she plays the recorder or cries hard. Between episodes she is normal. MRI shows small left frontal watershed infarcts and the 'ivy sign' on FLAIR. Angiography shows bilateral narrowing of the distal internal carotid arteries with a basal network of fine collateral vessels.
qx.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
opts: Long-term warfarin
Monthly transfusion to keep haemoglobin S below 30%
High-dose corticosteroids for presumed vasculitis
Carotid stenting of the narrowed segments
Surgical revascularisation, such as indirect EDAS, with peri-operative antiplatelet therapy and avoidance of hyperventilation and dehydration
qx.why: Hyperventilation-induced TIAs in a child, ivy sign and bilateral distal ICA stenosis with collaterals indicate moyamoya. Symptomatic children benefit from revascularisation, often indirect techniques like EDAS, while hypocapnia and hypotension are avoided because they lower cerebral blood flow. Transfusion is the approach for sickle-cell vasculopathy, which should be excluded, and stenting or steroids do not address the progressive arteriopathy.

name: MtDNA depletion syndrome
formal: Group of disorders with reduced mitochondrial DNA copy number from nuclear gene defects such as TK2, POLG, and DGUOK, causing myopathic, hepatocerebral, or encephalomyopathic phenotypes.
simple: Inherited conditions where cells have too few mitochondrial DNA copies, causing weakness, liver or brain disease.
more: Muscle biopsy with mtDNA quantification and gene panels; nucleoside therapy for TK2 deficiency; otherwise supportive; severity ranges widely.
th: กลุ่มโรคที่จำนวน DNA ของไมโทคอนเดรียลดลงจากยีนในนิวเคลียส เช่น TK2, POLG, DGUOK ทำให้เกิดโรคกล้ามเนื้อ ตับ และสมองในเด็ก
tempoNote: Infant or toddler onset is typical, with fast decline; TK2 can also present in adults
feat: Myopathic form (TK2): hypotonia, rapidly progressive weakness, respiratory failure, raised CK
Hepatocerebral form (DGUOK, MPV17, POLG): liver failure, hypoglycaemia, developmental regression
Encephalomyopathic form (SUCLA2, SUCLG1, RRM2B): hypotonia, deafness, dystonia, methylmalonic aciduria
POLG (Alpers–Huttenlocher): refractory epilepsy and liver failure, valproate-sensitive
Autosomal recessive inheritance
inv: Lactate, liver function, CK, urine organic acids (methylmalonic acid in SUCLA2/SUCLG1)
Muscle or liver biopsy with quantitative mtDNA copy number
Nuclear gene panel or exome
EEG and MRI when seizures or regression occur

case.who: 18-month-old girl at a children's hospital in Bangkok
case.story: Walked at 12 months but over 4 months has stopped walking, cannot lift her head and has frequent chest infections.
case.exam: Generalised weakness, facial weakness, absent reflexes, normal cognition, weak cough.
case.tests: CK 1,200 U/L; muscle biopsy COX-deficient fibres with mtDNA copy number 15% of normal; biallelic TK2 variants.
case.q: Why is the genetic subtype especially important here?
case.a: TK2-related mtDNA depletion has a specific nucleoside therapy (doxecitine/doxribtimine), now approved in some regions.

det.patho: Nuclear genes maintain the mtDNA pool by supplying nucleotides (TK2, DGUOK, RRM2B, SUCLA2, SUCLG1) or replicating mtDNA (POLG, TWNK). Their loss leads to a reduced number of mtDNA copies in affected tissues, so too few respiratory chain subunits are made. Which tissue is affected depends on the gene and on tissue-specific nucleotide supply.
det.clinical: Presentation is grouped as myopathic, hepatocerebral, encephalomyopathic or neurogastrointestinal. Onset is usually in infancy with rapid decline, although TK2 deficiency can appear later in childhood or adult life with progressive myopathy, ophthalmoplegia and respiratory weakness. Liver failure can be precipitated by valproate in POLG disease.
det.diagnosis: Measure mtDNA copy number in the affected tissue (muscle or liver); depletion below roughly 30–40% of age-matched controls is supportive. Confirmation requires biallelic variants in a known gene through panel or exome sequencing. Biochemical clues include high lactate, methylmalonic aciduria and raised CK in TK2.
det.treatment: For TK2 deficiency, oral pyrimidine nucleoside therapy has shown survival and motor benefits and has gained regulatory approval in some regions. Liver transplantation is considered for isolated DGUOK hepatic disease without neurological involvement. Otherwise care is supportive with ventilation, nutrition, seizure control and avoidance of valproate.
det.prognosis: Often poor in infantile forms; late-onset TK2 and treated cases can have a slower course.
pearls: Infant with rapid weakness and high CK but no SMN1 deletion: consider TK2.
Methylmalonic aciduria plus deafness and dystonia suggests SUCLA2.
Valproate can trigger fatal liver failure in POLG disease.
det.thd: MtDNA depletion syndrome เกิดจากยีนในนิวเคลียส เช่น TK2, POLG, DGUOK ที่ทำให้จำนวน DNA ของไมโทคอนเดรียลดลง มีหลายรูปแบบ เช่น แบบกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงเร็วและหายใจล้มเหลว แบบตับวายร่วมกับสมอง และแบบชักดื้อยา วินิจฉัยด้วยการวัดจำนวน mtDNA ในชิ้นเนื้อและตรวจยีน TK2 deficiency มีการรักษาด้วย nucleoside therapy ห้ามใช้ valproate ในโรคจาก POLG

name: Muckle–Wells syndrome
formal: Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome from NLRP3 mutation with recurrent fever, urticaria, sensorineural deafness and amyloidosis; aseptic meningitis and papilloedema may occur.
simple: An inherited inflammatory condition causing recurrent fever, rash, joint pain and hearing loss.
th: โรคอักเสบจากระบบภูมิคุ้มกันแต่กำเนิด (autoinflammatory) จากยีน NLRP3 มีไข้เป็นพัก ๆ ผื่นลมพิษ หูตึงประสาทรับเสียง ปวดข้อ และเสี่ยง amyloidosis อาจมีเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบปลอดเชื้อ
tempoNote: Attacks of fever and rash last one to three days and recur often; hearing loss and amyloidosis accumulate over years
feat: Recurrent fever with a non-itchy urticaria-like rash, conjunctivitis and joint pain, often triggered by cold or stress
Progressive bilateral sensorineural hearing loss starting in childhood or adolescence
Headache, chronic aseptic meningitis and occasionally papilloedema
Raised CRP and SAA during attacks; renal AA amyloidosis with proteinuria if untreated
Autosomal dominant or de novo gain-of-function NLRP3 variants
inv: CRP, ESR and serum amyloid A during and between attacks; urine protein for amyloidosis
NLRP3 genetic testing (somatic mosaicism possible if germline test is negative)
Audiometry; lumbar puncture shows mild neutrophilic or lymphocytic pleocytosis if meningitis suspected
MRI may show cochlear or meningeal enhancement

case.who: 22-year-old woman seen in the rheumatology and neurology clinics of a university hospital in Bangkok
case.story: Since childhood she has had flares of fever, hives and sore knees after cold weather or air-conditioning; now she needs hearing aids and has daily headaches.
case.exam: Pink urticarial plaques on the trunk, bilateral sensorineural deafness, mild papilloedema; no focal deficit.
case.tests: CRP 85 mg/L, SAA high; CSF 40 white cells with normal glucose and sterile cultures; urine protein 0.8 g/day; heterozygous NLRP3 variant.
case.q: What is the unifying diagnosis and the targeted therapy?
case.a: Muckle–Wells syndrome (CAPS): IL-1 blockade with anakinra or canakinumab controls inflammation, may stabilise hearing and prevents amyloidosis.

det.patho: Gain-of-function NLRP3 variants make the inflammasome overactive, so caspase-1 releases excess interleukin-1 beta with little or no trigger. The resulting systemic inflammation produces fever, rash and acute phase response, while chronic inflammation in the cochlea and meninges causes deafness and aseptic meningitis. Persistently high serum amyloid A deposits as AA amyloid, mostly in the kidney.
det.clinical: Episodes of fever, urticaria-like rash, conjunctivitis, arthralgia and fatigue begin in infancy or childhood. Sensorineural hearing loss typically appears in adolescence and progresses. Neurological involvement includes chronic headache, aseptic meningitis and raised intracranial pressure; it is milder than in the neonatal-onset form (NOMID/CINCA), which adds cognitive impairment and bony overgrowth. Amyloid nephropathy develops in a substantial minority without treatment.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis combines raised inflammatory markers with at least two typical features (urticaria, cold or stress triggers, deafness, eye inflammation, musculoskeletal symptoms, neurological symptoms) and is confirmed by NLRP3 testing. A negative germline test does not exclude it because somatic mosaic variants occur. Exclude chronic urticaria, Schnitzler syndrome in adults, infections and other autoinflammatory fevers.
det.treatment: IL-1 blockade is the standard: anakinra daily, rilonacept, or canakinumab every 4–8 weeks. It usually abolishes attacks within days, normalises CRP and SAA, and may halt or partly reverse hearing loss if started early. Monitor hearing, renal function and inflammatory markers; adjust dose until SAA is normal.
det.prognosis: With early IL-1 blockade outlook is good; untreated, progressive deafness and renal amyloidosis cause major disability.
pearls: Urticaria plus sensorineural deafness plus periodic fever should make you think of NLRP3.
Chronic aseptic meningitis in a young person with a rash may be autoinflammatory, not infectious.
Measure SAA to monitor treatment and amyloid risk.
det.thd: Muckle–Wells syndrome เป็นโรค autoinflammatory จากยีน NLRP3 ที่ทำงานมากเกิน ทำให้หลั่ง IL-1 มากผิดปกติ ผู้ป่วยมีไข้เป็นพัก ๆ ผื่นคล้ายลมพิษ ปวดข้อ หูตึงประสาทรับเสียงที่แย่ลงเรื่อย ๆ และอาจมีเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบปลอดเชื้อ การวินิจฉัยใช้ค่าการอักเสบร่วมกับการตรวจยีน การรักษาด้วยยายับยั้ง IL-1 เช่น anakinra หรือ canakinumab ได้ผลดีและป้องกันภาวะ amyloidosis ที่ไต

Hearing loss with encephalopathy and branch retinal artery occlusions, no urticaria or periodic fever
Oral and genital ulcers, uveitis and brainstem lesions rather than urticaria and deafness
