name: Multi-infarct dementia
formal: Vascular cognitive impairment from multiple cortical or subcortical infarcts, with stepwise decline, focal signs, pseudobulbar features and executive dysfunction.
simple: Memory and thinking decline caused by a series of small strokes that damage the brain over time.
th: สมองเสื่อมจากหลอดเลือดที่เกิดจาก infarct หลายตำแหน่งทั้งเปลือกสมองและใต้เปลือก อาการแย่ลงเป็นขั้นบันได มีอาการทางระบบประสาทเฉพาะที่ และ executive function บกพร่อง
tempoNote: Stepwise decline with each new stroke, sometimes with plateaus
feat: Stepwise cognitive decline linked to clinical strokes
Focal signs: hemiparesis, field defects, aphasia, extensor plantars
Pseudobulbar features: dysarthria, dysphagia, emotional lability
Executive slowing and gait disorder more than early amnesia
Vascular risk factors: hypertension, AF, diabetes, smoking
inv: MRI: multiple cortical and subcortical infarcts, white matter disease
Cognitive testing (MoCA, Thai version) with executive focus
Vascular work-up: ECG/Holter, carotid imaging, lipids, glucose
B12, TSH, syphilis serology to exclude reversible contributors

case.who: 72-year-old retired rice merchant from Ayutthaya with AF not on anticoagulation
case.story: Over three years, after each of three small strokes, he became noticeably slower, now needs help with money and gets lost.
case.exam: Mild left hemiparesis, right extensor plantar, slowed speech, small-step gait, emotional lability.
case.tests: MoCA 17/30 with poor executive items; MRI: right MCA cortical infarct, left thalamic and several lacunar infarcts.
case.q: What type of dementia and what is the main preventive step?
case.a: Multi-infarct (vascular) dementia; anticoagulate for AF and control vascular risk to prevent further steps.

det.patho: Repeated infarcts, typically from cardioembolism or large-artery disease, destroy cortical and subcortical tissue and disconnect frontal-subcortical networks. Once the cumulative volume or strategic location of damage passes a threshold, cognitive reserve is overwhelmed. Many patients also harbour small vessel disease and Alzheimer pathology, which add to the deficit.
det.clinical: The classic course is abrupt worsening with each stroke followed by partial recovery or plateau. Cognitive impairment emphasises slowed processing, executive dysfunction, attention problems and apathy; memory retrieval is affected more than storage. Focal neurological signs, gait disturbance, urinary urgency and pseudobulbar affect are common. Depression frequently coexists.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on dementia with clinical or imaging evidence of cerebrovascular disease sufficient to explain it, using criteria such as VASCOG or VICCCS. Hachinski ischaemic score features (abrupt onset, stepwise course, focal signs) support it. MRI shows multiple infarcts; cognitive testing should include executive tasks. Consider mixed disease if memory loss dominates.
det.treatment: Secondary prevention is central: anticoagulation for AF, antiplatelets, statins, blood pressure control and lifestyle change. Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine give modest benefit in vascular dementia and are reasonable when Alzheimer co-pathology is likely. Rehabilitation, treatment of depression and support for carers improve daily function.
det.prognosis: Survival is shorter than in Alzheimer disease, mainly from further cardiovascular events; preventing new strokes slows decline.
pearls: Stepwise decline with focal signs suggests multi-infarct dementia.
Executive dysfunction and slowing dominate over memory loss.
Mixed vascular and Alzheimer pathology is the rule in older people.
det.thd: Multi-infarct dementia คือสมองเสื่อมจากหลอดเลือดที่เกิดจากสมองขาดเลือดหลายครั้ง อาการแย่ลงเป็นขั้นบันไดหลังแต่ละ stroke มีอ่อนแรงเฉพาะที่ คิดช้า วางแผนไม่ได้ และอารมณ์แปรปรวน MRI พบ infarct หลายตำแหน่ง การรักษาสำคัญคือป้องกัน stroke ซ้ำ เช่น ยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือดใน AF ควบคุมความดัน น้ำตาล และไขมัน

name: Multi/minicore myopathy
formal: Congenital myopathy with multiple small cores on oxidative stains, due to SEPN1 or RYR1 mutations, with axial weakness, scoliosis, rigid spine, and respiratory failure.
simple: An inherited muscle disease with weak trunk and neck muscles, scoliosis, and breathing problems.
more: Biopsy shows minicores; genetic confirmation; supportive care, including ventilation monitoring, scoliosis surgery. Congenital myopathy with multifocal cores lacking oxidative activity on biopsy, mostly from RYR1 or SEPN1 variants; hypotonia, proximal weakness, scoliosis and respiratory involvement. Diagnosis by muscle biopsy with oxidative stains and genetic testing (RYR1, SEPN1). Inheritance varies; care is supportive with respiratory and orthopaedic monitoring; RYR1 cases carry malignant hyperthermia risk.
th: โรคกล้ามเนื้อแต่กำเนิดที่ชิ้นเนื้อมี core เล็ก ๆ หลายจุด จากยีน SELENON (SEPN1) หรือ RYR1 ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อแกนลำตัวอ่อนแรง กระดูกสันหลังคดแข็ง และหายใจล้มเหลว
tempoNote: Present from birth or early childhood; slowly progressive or static limb weakness while respiratory and spinal problems worsen
feat: Hypotonia, delayed motor milestones and axial weakness with neck flexor weakness, high-arched palate and long narrow face
Rigid spine, progressive scoliosis and respiratory insufficiency often out of proportion to limb weakness (typical for SELENON)
RYR1 forms may add ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, hand and hip girdle involvement or arthrogryposis
Most patients keep walking; four phenotypes: classic (about 75%), antenatal with arthrogryposis, moderate with hand involvement, and ophthalmoplegic
Autosomal recessive; malignant hyperthermia susceptibility is a concern in RYR1-related disease
inv: Muscle biopsy with oxidative enzyme stains: multiple small zones with sarcomeric disorganisation and no oxidative activity that do not run the full fibre length; type 1 predominance
Gene testing: SELENON, RYR1 and a congenital myopathy panel or exome (finds a cause in about half)
Pulmonary function sitting and lying, overnight oximetry or polysomnography, echocardiography for right heart strain
Muscle MRI pattern, spine radiographs; CK normal or mildly increased

case.story: He was a floppy infant who walked at 20 months. His school noticed his neck looks stiff and he tires on stairs. He now snores and is often sleepy in class. His spine has started to bend sideways.
case.exam: Long narrow face, high palate, weak neck flexors, rigid spine with mild scoliosis, reduced reflexes, no fasciculations, intact cognition.
case.tests: CK 180 U/L; vital capacity 45% predicted and falls when supine; biopsy shows multiple small cores in both fibre types; SELENON biallelic variants.
case.q: Which complications dominate follow-up and what anaesthetic precaution should be recorded?
case.a: Restrictive respiratory failure (nocturnal hypoventilation) and scoliosis dominate; start non-invasive ventilation as indicated. Malignant hyperthermia precautions are required for RYR1 cases and prudent when the gene is unknown.

read.where: 7: Molecular Diagnostic Procedures and Genetics in Neuromuscular Disorders

det.patho: Multiminicore disease is one of the core myopathies, defined by foci in which sarcomeric structure collapses and oxidative enzymes are absent. Two main genes explain many cases: SELENON, coding for selenoprotein N in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and RYR1, coding for the ryanodine receptor calcium release channel. Defective redox and calcium handling impair excitation-contraction coupling in both fibre types, with early involvement of axial and diaphragm muscles in SELENON disease.
det.clinical: The classic form presents at birth or in the first years with hypotonia, delayed milestones and weak neck flexors. Over time, scoliosis and spinal rigidity develop, and breathing muscles weaken more than limbs, leading to nocturnal hypoventilation and, in some, cor pulmonale. Most children walk, although stamina is limited. RYR1 disease adds ophthalmoplegia, hand weakness or an antenatal arthrogrypotic presentation. Cognition is normal and cardiac muscle is usually spared.
det.diagnosis: Muscle biopsy remains central: multiple short, poorly delimited cores lacking oxidative activity in both fibre types, with type 1 predominance, differentiate it from central core disease with its single long core. Muscle MRI patterns (selective involvement of sartorius and adductor magnus) help to point to SELENON. Genetic testing resolves a diagnosis in about half of patients. Exclude SMA, congenital muscular dystrophy with rigid spine, Pompe disease and myasthenic syndromes.
det.treatment: Care is supportive and anticipatory: screening for respiratory failure with sleep studies and vital capacity, early non-invasive ventilation and airway clearance, spine surveillance and scoliosis surgery planning, nutrition and physiotherapy. Alert anaesthetists to malignant hyperthermia risk in RYR1-related and unclassified cases: avoid volatile agents and succinylcholine and have dantrolene available. Salbutamol has been tried for symptoms in some core myopathies but is not curative.
det.prognosis: Limb strength is stable or slowly progressive, but respiratory failure and scoliosis determine outcome, so survival is good with early ventilatory support.
pearls: Respiratory failure out of proportion to limb weakness plus a rigid spine suggests SELENON myopathy.
Record malignant hyperthermia risk when RYR1 is involved or the gene is unknown.
Check oxidative stains on the biopsy: cores are invisible on routine haematoxylin and eosin.
det.thd: Multi/minicore myopathy เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้อแต่กำเนิดที่ชิ้นเนื้อพบ core เล็ก ๆ หลายจุดไม่มีกิจกรรมออกซิเดทีฟ เกิดจากยีน SELENON หรือ RYR1 เด็กมักตัวอ่อนปวกเปียก คอและลำตัวอ่อนแรง กระดูกสันหลังคดและแข็ง และมีปัญหาการหายใจมากเกินกว่ากำลังแขนขา ส่วนใหญ่ยังเดินได้ วินิจฉัยด้วยชิ้นเนื้อ ตรวจยีน และประเมินปอดด้วย spirometry และ sleep study การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง ใช้เครื่องช่วยหายใจแบบไม่รุกล้ำเมื่อจำเป็น ดูแลกระดูกสันหลัง และระวังภาวะ malignant hyperthermia ในผู้ที่มี RYR1

name: Multibacillary leprosy
formal: Leprosy with many skin lesions and high bacillary load (lepromatous, borderline types), causing symmetrical nerve thickening, sensory loss and neuropathy; treated with multidrug therapy.
simple: A more widespread form of leprosy with many bacteria, causing skin patches and numbness from nerve damage.
th: โรคเรื้อนชนิดเชื้อมาก มีรอยโรคผิวหนังหลายแห่ง เส้นประสาทโตหลายเส้นทั้งสองข้าง ชาแบบสมมาตรเริ่มที่ส่วนปลายเย็น รักษาด้วยยาสามขนานนาน 12 เดือน
tempoNote: Years of slow progression after a long incubation (often 3–10 years); type 2 reactions and neuritis can strike abruptly during or after treatment
feat: Many skin lesions (more than five) or diffuse infiltration with nodules, loss of eyebrows, thickened earlobes and leonine face
Symmetric loss of temperature and pain sensation in the cooler areas first: hands, feet, ears, nose, with later glove-and-stocking spread
Palpably enlarged nerves: ulnar at the elbow, common peroneal at the fibular head, great auricular, radial cutaneous
Claw hand, foot drop, lagophthalmos, painless burns and ulcers, Charcot joints, sweat loss from sudomotor involvement
Type 2 reaction (erythema nodosum leprosum) with fever, tender red nodules, neuritis, iritis and arthritis; type 1 reaction with swollen skin lesions and acute nerve pain
inv: Slit-skin smear with Ziehl–Neelsen stain for bacillary index; skin or nerve biopsy with Fite stain; PCR for Mycobacterium leprae where available
Nerve conduction: patchy multifocal axonal or mixed loss resembling mononeuritis multiplex; ultrasound can show nerve enlargement
Baseline voluntary muscle and sensory testing, eye examination, and screening for coexisting HIV, TB and diabetes

case.story: Two years of numb hands and feet with a blistering burn on his fingers that he did not feel. Facial skin has become thick, and his eyebrows have thinned. His left foot drags.
case.exam: Diffuse shiny infiltration of the face, madarosis, enlarged ulnar and common peroneal nerves on both sides, glove-and-stocking loss of pinprick and warmth, claw ulnar hand on the right, left foot drop.
case.tests: Slit-skin smear positive with high bacillary index, biopsy with abundant acid-fast bacilli in globi; nerve conduction shows multifocal axonal sensory and motor loss.
case.q: What treatment and which complication must be watched during it?
case.a: WHO multidrug therapy with rifampicin, dapsone and clofazimine for 12 months. Watch for type 1 and type 2 reactions with nerve pain or new weakness, which need prompt prednisolone (and thalidomide or other agents for ENL), and teach daily care of insensate hands and feet.

read.where: Companion to Peripheral Neuropathy, Chapter 68: Characteristic Sudomotor Abnormalities in Lepromatous Leprosy
Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — Leprosy (Hansen’s Disease)
Chapter 22 Neurologic Disorders Associated with Bone and Joint Disease

det.patho: Mycobacterium leprae multiplies slowly in Schwann cells and macrophages and prefers cool tissues, so skin, nasal mucosa, peripheral nerves and testes are affected. The clinical form depends on cell-mediated immunity: lepromatous disease reflects poor immunity, abundant bacilli and a muted granulomatous reaction, while tuberculoid disease reflects strong immunity and few organisms. Transmission is probably by respiratory droplets, and most people are not susceptible.
det.clinical: Multibacillary disease shows many skin lesions, nodules, symmetric nerve involvement and ultimately widespread anaesthesia of cool regions. The nerves are damaged in a multifocal fashion and may mimic mononeuritis multiplex, while sudomotor fibres are also lost so the skin is dry and anhidrotic in patches. Injury from insensate hands and feet leads to burns, ulcers, bone resorption and Charcot joints. Lepra reactions are major sources of new disability, and they occur before, during or after treatment. Leprosy remains a differential for sensory neuropathy with skin lesions in Thailand, particularly in people from or travelling to endemic areas.
det.diagnosis: The cardinal signs are a definite skin patch with sensory loss, enlarged peripheral nerve, and bacilli on smear or biopsy. A single cardinal sign in the right setting is enough to treat. Slit-skin smears give the bacillary index and classification; biopsy with Fite staining and PCR add certainty. Thermoregulatory sweat testing and nerve conduction show the pattern of nerve and sudomotor loss. Look for HIV, TB, diabetes and thyroid disease, and test household contacts.
det.treatment: WHO recommends rifampicin, dapsone and clofazimine as multidrug therapy for multibacillary disease for 12 months, usually dispensed through the national leprosy programme. Reactions are managed with prednisolone for neuritis and type 1 reaction, and with prednisolone, clofazimine or thalidomide for erythema nodosum leprosum, avoiding thalidomide in women who could become pregnant. Nerve function should be tested regularly, and patients need education in foot and hand care, protective footwear, splints, physiotherapy and surgical correction of deformities. Offer chemoprophylaxis and examination to close contacts.
det.prognosis: Bacterial cure is expected with full treatment. Disability depends on how early nerves are protected; established nerve damage often does not recover, and reactions can recur for years.
pearls: Sensory loss in cool body parts with enlarged nerves is leprosy until proved otherwise.
New nerve pain or weakness on treatment is a reaction, not drug failure: give steroids promptly.
Sural or other nerve biopsy may be the first place the diagnosis is made when skin signs are subtle.
det.thd: โรคเรื้อนชนิดเชื้อมาก (multibacillary) เกิดจากเชื้อ Mycobacterium leprae ที่ชอบเติบโตในที่เย็น เช่น มือ เท้า หู จมูก ผู้ป่วยมีผื่นหรือตุ่มนูนที่ผิวหนังหลายแห่ง เส้นประสาทโตทั้งสองข้าง ชาแบบถุงมือถุงเท้า อ่อนแรงจนมือเป็นง่ามและเท้าตก และมีแผลที่ไม่รู้สึกเจ็บ วินิจฉัยด้วย slit-skin smear และตัดชิ้นเนื้อ รักษาด้วยยา rifampicin dapsone และ clofazimine นาน 12 เดือน และต้องเฝ้าระวัง lepra reaction ที่ทำให้เส้นประสาทอักเสบเฉียบพลัน

name: Multifocal cortical myoclonus
formal: Cortical myoclonus affecting multiple body parts with sensorimotor cortex hyperexcitability and giant SEPs, seen in encephalopathy, post-hypoxia and progressive myoclonic epilepsies.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks in several parts of the body that arise from overactive brain cortex.
th: อาการกระตุกสั้น ๆ คล้ายไฟช็อตหลายตำแหน่งที่มาจากเปลือกสมองส่วนรับความรู้สึกและสั่งการที่ไวเกิน มักเกิดเมื่อเคลื่อนไหวหรือถูกกระตุ้น พบในภาวะสมองเสื่อมจากเมตาบอลิก หลังขาดออกซิเจน และ PME
tempoNote: Acute with metabolic, drug or post-hypoxic causes; chronic and progressive in degenerative and genetic disorders
feat: Very brief (<50 ms) irregular jerks of distal limbs and face, often in many body parts at different times
Brought out by action, posture, touch or sudden noise (reflex myoclonus); may coexist with negative myoclonus
Interferes with writing, eating and walking more than at rest
Causes: renal or hepatic failure, drugs (e.g. opioids, gabapentinoids, cefepime), post-hypoxia, CJD, PMEs
inv: Metabolic screen (urea, liver tests, glucose, sodium, calcium, magnesium), drug review and drug levels
EEG with EMG; jerk-locked back-averaging and giant SEPs or enhanced long-latency reflexes confirm cortical origin
MRI brain; further tests (genetics, CSF RT-QuIC) depending on tempo

case.who: 71-year-old woman from Ratchaburi with chronic kidney disease
case.story: Started pregabalin for shingles pain five days ago; now her hands jerk so much she cannot drink from a cup and she is mildly confused.
case.exam: Multifocal jerks of arms and face worsened by reaching, flapping negative myoclonus with arms outstretched, no focal weakness.
case.tests: eGFR 18; EEG shows diffuse slowing with occasional spikes preceding jerks.
case.q: What is the most likely cause and the first step in management?
case.a: Drug-induced multifocal cortical myoclonus from pregabalin accumulating in renal failure; stop or reduce the drug and treat the metabolic state.

read.where: 18 - Myoclonus — Multifocal and generalized cortical myoclonus

det.patho: Hyperexcitable sensorimotor cortex fires abnormal discharges that travel quickly down the corticospinal tract, giving very short jerks. Loss of cortical inhibition, often involving GABAergic interneurons, explains enlarged ('giant') somatosensory evoked potentials and exaggerated cortical reflexes to touch or stretch. Diffuse insults such as uraemia, drug toxicity or hypoxia affect many cortical areas, so jerks appear in many parts of the body.
det.clinical: Jerks are shock-like, irregular and usually most obvious in the fingers, hands and face, and they increase with voluntary movement or stimulation. Negative myoclonus (asterixis) often accompanies metabolic forms and can make the person drop objects or buckle at the knees. In chronic disorders, action myoclonus can be more disabling than weakness. Associated features such as seizures, dementia, ataxia or confusion point to the cause.
det.diagnosis: Clinical observation identifies myoclonus; neurophysiology defines its cortical origin with a short-latency EEG transient before each jerk, giant SEPs and short EMG bursts. Look first for reversible causes: renal and liver failure, electrolytes, drugs and toxins. When none is found, the age and tempo guide investigation toward CJD, autoimmune encephalitis, neurodegenerative disease or PMEs.
det.treatment: Correct the metabolic problem and stop the offending drug where possible. Levetiracetam, valproate, clonazepam and piracetam are effective for cortical myoclonus and are often combined; perampanel and zonisamide are alternatives. Avoid phenytoin, carbamazepine and other sodium-channel drugs in PMEs because they can worsen myoclonus.
det.prognosis: Metabolic and drug-induced forms usually resolve quickly once the cause is reversed; degenerative and genetic forms persist or progress.
pearls: Multifocal jerks in a renal patient: review the drug chart (gabapentinoids, cefepime, opioids) first.
Giant SEPs are the neurophysiological signature of cortical reflex myoclonus.
Do not reach for carbamazepine or phenytoin for myoclonus.
det.thd: Multifocal cortical myoclonus คืออาการกระตุกเร็วหลายตำแหน่งจากเปลือกสมองที่ไวเกิน มักเกิดเมื่อเคลื่อนไหวหรือถูกสัมผัส สาเหตุบ่อยคือไตวาย ตับวาย ยาเช่น pregabalin หรือ cefepime ภาวะหลังขาดออกซิเจน และโรคพันธุกรรมกลุ่ม PME ตรวจยืนยันด้วย EEG-EMG และ SEP ขนาดใหญ่ การรักษาคือแก้สาเหตุ หยุดยาที่เป็นต้นเหตุ และใช้ levetiracetam, valproate หรือ clonazepam

name: Multifocal motor acquired motor axonopathy
formal: Immune-mediated pure motor neuropathy with conduction block, asymmetric distal weakness, and anti-GM1 antibodies in some patients.
simple: An immune condition causing slowly worsening weakness in the hands or feet without numbness.
more: Nerve conduction shows motor conduction block; IVIG is first-line, whereas steroids and plasma exchange are ineffective or harmful.
ab: Axonal variant of multifocal motor neuropathy
th: โรคเส้นประสาทสั่งการแบบหลายตำแหน่งที่คล้าย MMN แต่เป็นชนิด axonal ไม่มี conduction block อ่อนแรงและลีบไม่สมมาตรที่ปลายแขนขา โดยไม่มีอาการชา
tempoNote: Slowly progressive over months to years in individual nerve territories
feat: Asymmetric distal weakness and wasting in the distribution of individual nerves, often arms first
Pure motor picture: sensation intact and sensory conduction studies normal
Reflexes reduced or preserved; no upper motor neuron signs
Cramps and fasciculations are possible
Unlike classic MMN, no conduction block on nerve conduction
inv: NCS: low motor amplitudes in a multifocal pattern, normal sensory studies, no conduction block
EMG: denervation and reinnervation in affected territories
Anti-GM1 IgM antibodies (sometimes positive); CSF protein
MRI brachial plexus may show nerve enlargement

case.story: Two years of weakness of his right hand grip, then left foot drop, without numbness.
case.exam: Wasting of right first dorsal interosseous, weak finger extension and left ankle dorsiflexion, normal sensation, reflexes reduced in the left ankle, no Babinski.
case.tests: NCS: reduced ulnar and peroneal motor amplitudes without conduction block; sensory studies normal; anti-GM1 IgM weakly positive.
case.q: What is this and how does management differ from motor neuron disease?
case.a: A multifocal acquired motor axonopathy (axonal MMN-like neuropathy); it is potentially treatable, so a trial of IVIG is reasonable, whereas ALS is not immune-responsive.

det.patho: The term (multifocal acquired motor axonopathy) was proposed for patients with an MMN-like clinical picture whose nerve conduction shows axonal loss without demonstrable conduction block. It is thought to sit within the MMN spectrum, with conduction block either very distal, proximal beyond reach, or already progressed to axonal degeneration. Anti-GM1 IgM is found in a minority. Because few cases have been reported, its nosology, frequency and pathology remain uncertain. The entry name in this lexicon is non-standard; the published label is 'multifocal acquired motor axonopathy'.
det.clinical: Patients present with slowly progressive, asymmetric lower motor neuron weakness in the territories of single nerves, without sensory symptoms. Upper limbs are often affected first. There are no upper motor neuron or bulbar signs, which separates it from ALS. Progression is generally slow.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis needs a multifocal pure motor neuropathy pattern on NCS with normal sensory responses and no conduction block, after careful search for proximal blocks with root stimulation or MRI of the plexus. Exclude ALS, PMA, Hirayama disease, multiple entrapments and vasculitic neuropathy. Anti-GM1 and nerve imaging (enlarged nerves) support an immune neuropathy.
det.treatment: IVIG is the usual trial; responses are reported but appear less consistent than in classic MMN, and some patients do not improve. Steroids and plasma exchange are not recommended, as in MMN they may worsen weakness. Supportive measures include splints and occupational therapy.
det.prognosis: Generally slow progression; response to IVIG is variable and the long-term course is not well characterised.
pearls: Pure motor, asymmetric, nerve-territory weakness without block can still be an immune neuropathy.
Search for proximal conduction block before calling it axonal.
Do not use steroids: IVIG is the treatment of choice in the MMN spectrum.

det.patho: MMN is an immune neuropathy of motor axons in which IgM antibodies, often against GM1, bind at or near the nodes and activate complement, causing focal conduction block. Why motor fibres are selectively targeted is uncertain; motor and sensory axons differ in ganglioside composition and ion-channel properties. Ongoing block leads to secondary axonal loss over years. It affects men more often, usually with onset between 20 and 50.
det.clinical: Weakness begins in one hand or forearm, following the territory of an individual nerve (often radial, ulnar or median), and spreads slowly to other nerves over years. Strength may be lost well before obvious wasting. Cramps, fasciculations and cold-worsened weakness are common, reflexes are variable, and sensation stays normal. There are no bulbar or upper motor neuron signs, and legs are affected less than arms.
det.diagnosis: The core finding is motor conduction block at sites away from common entrapment points, with normal sensory conduction through the same segment; the 2021 EAN/PNS guideline defines definite and probable block. IgM anti-GM1 is present in roughly half. Nerve ultrasound or MRI of the brachial plexus may show focal enlargement. CSF protein is normal or only mildly raised. The main mimic is lower motor neuron-predominant ALS; also exclude Lewis–Sumner syndrome and HNPP.
det.treatment: IVIG is first-line: a loading course of 2 g/kg followed by individualised maintenance infusions (intravenous or subcutaneous) at the lowest effective dose and interval. Corticosteroids and plasma exchange are generally ineffective and may worsen weakness. Cyclophosphamide is rarely used because of toxicity. Complement-targeted agents are under clinical study. Track grip strength and functional scores to adjust dosing.
det.prognosis: Most patients improve with IVIG, but many need long-term infusions and slow axonal loss can still accumulate. Life expectancy is normal.
pearls: Asymmetric hand weakness with no sensory loss and no UMN signs: look for conduction block before diagnosing ALS.
Steroids can make MMN worse — unlike CIDP.
A negative anti-GM1 test does not exclude MMN.

det.patho: Multifocal myoclonus reflects widespread hyperexcitability of the cortex, brainstem reticular formation or both. Metabolic toxins, drugs and hypoxia lower GABAergic inhibition and alter serotonergic transmission, so small groups of neurons discharge abruptly and unpredictably. In prion and other neurodegenerative disease, neuronal loss and network disruption give a similar unstable output.
det.clinical: Jerks are arrhythmic, brief and appear in different places from moment to moment, and may worsen with startle, light touch or voluntary movement. They are usually part of an encephalopathy, with confusion, drowsiness and sometimes seizures. Severe hypoxia produces multifocal myoclonus along with obtundation and sometimes focal signs. Drug toxicity from reduced renal clearance is a very common and reversible cause.
det.diagnosis: Start from the bedside: list every drug, check renal and liver function, electrolytes, glucose and calcium, and look for asterixis. EEG excludes non-convulsive status and shows diffuse slowing in metabolic causes, whereas periodic complexes raise the possibility of CJD. MRI with diffusion imaging and CSF tests are used when the course is subacute, progressive or unexplained.
det.treatment: Remove the cause: stop or reduce the offending drug, dialyse, correct electrolytes, treat hepatic encephalopathy and treat hypoxia. Symptomatic drugs include levetiracetam, valproate, clonazepam and piracetam for cortical myoclonus; benzodiazepines are used cautiously in encephalopathic patients. Lamotrigine and carbamazepine can worsen myoclonus in some epilepsy syndromes and should be reviewed. Palliative and supportive care are the approach in prion disease.
det.prognosis: Reversible causes usually clear in days after correction; prognosis in hypoxic or prion myoclonus is poor.
pearls: Read the drug chart first: gabapentinoids, opioids, cefepime and lithium accumulate in renal failure.
Myoclonus with rapidly progressive dementia: think CJD.
Asterixis is negative myoclonus and travels with the positive kind in metabolic encephalopathy.

det.patho: Multifocal neuropathies result from patchy injury to individual nerves. Mechanisms include ischaemic infarction in vasculitis, immune attack at nodes or myelin in MMN and MADSAM, inherited myelin fragility in HNPP, and infiltration by granulomas, lymphoma or Mycobacterium leprae. When enough nerves are involved the deficits merge and may look symmetrical.
det.clinical: The temporal pattern is the best clue: painful stepwise deficits point to vasculitis; slow painless motor loss to MMN; sensory and motor multifocal loss with upper-limb onset to MADSAM; recurrent short palsies after pressure to HNPP. Skin, systemic symptoms and nerve thickening should be sought. Leprosy remains an important cause in Thailand.
det.diagnosis: Careful electrodiagnosis documents asymmetric involvement and separates axonal from demyelinating processes. Conduction block outside entrapment sites supports MMN or MADSAM. Laboratory screening for vasculitis, infection and paraproteins guides the next step; nerve biopsy is used for suspected vasculitis or infiltration. Ultrasound shows focal enlargement in immune neuropathies.
det.treatment: Treatment depends on cause: IVIG for MMN; IVIG or steroids for MADSAM; steroids with cyclophosphamide or rituximab for vasculitis; multidrug therapy for leprosy; avoidance of pressure and protective padding for HNPP. Supportive physiotherapy and orthoses help in all forms.
det.prognosis: Variable; immune and vasculitic forms improve with timely treatment but residual axonal loss is common.
pearls: Asymmetric, stepwise and painful: vasculitic mononeuritis multiplex.
Pure motor with conduction block: MMN; steroids can worsen it.
Feel for thickened nerves and look at the skin for leprosy.

det.patho: Electron transfer flavoprotein (ETF) and its dehydrogenase (ETF-QO, ETFDH) collect electrons from several acyl-CoA dehydrogenases and pass them to the respiratory chain. Loss of this step blocks fatty acid oxidation and the breakdown of some amino acids and choline. Many ETFDH variants destabilise a flavin-binding protein, which is why extra riboflavin (the FAD precursor) can restore activity.
det.clinical: Severe neonatal forms present with acidosis, hypoglycaemia and multi-organ involvement, sometimes with congenital anomalies. The late-onset form is a common, under-recognised cause of treatable lipid storage myopathy in Asian adults: fluctuating proximal, neck and sometimes bulbar weakness, exercise intolerance, and episodes of metabolic decompensation. Some patients have sensory neuropathy.
det.diagnosis: An acylcarnitine profile showing elevations across chain lengths and characteristic urine organic acids strongly suggest MADD, but results may normalise between attacks. Muscle biopsy shows lipid droplets in type 1 fibres. Genetic testing of ETFDH, ETFA and ETFB confirms; if negative, consider riboflavin transporter defects and FAD synthesis disorders.
det.treatment: Give riboflavin (commonly 100–400 mg/day), often with carnitine and coenzyme Q10, and avoid fasting with a high-carbohydrate, lower-fat diet. During illness provide IV glucose to prevent catabolism. Responsive patients often regain strength within weeks. Non-responsive severe forms need specialised metabolic care; ketone body supplementation has been tried.
det.prognosis: Late-onset riboflavin-responsive forms have an excellent outlook with treatment; neonatal forms are often fatal.
pearls: Treatable cause of neck extensor weakness: think late-onset MADD.
Acylcarnitines can be normal between attacks — repeat during illness.
Riboflavin is cheap and safe; start while awaiting genetics.

formal: Involvement of two or more cranial nerves from skull base disease, carcinomatous or infectious meningitis, cavernous sinus lesions, sarcoidosis, Lyme or Tolosa-Hunt syndrome.

th: เส้นประสาทสมองเสียตั้งแต่สองเส้นขึ้นไป สาเหตุสำคัญคือโรคที่ฐานกะโหลก มะเร็งหลังโพรงจมูก เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบจากมะเร็งหรือติดเชื้อ cavernous sinus และ GBS
tempoNote: Acute in GBS variants and stroke; subacute in meningitis and inflammation; chronic in skull-base tumours
feat: Two or more cranial nerves affected, simultaneously or sequentially
Pattern localises: III/IV/V1/VI cavernous sinus; IX/X/XI jugular foramen; V/VI petrous apex
Headache or facial pain suggests skull base infiltration, Tolosa–Hunt or meningitis
Serous otitis, nasal bleeding or neck nodes in a Thai adult: nasopharyngeal carcinoma
Other causes: TB/fungal/carcinomatous meningitis, sarcoidosis, GBS variants, diabetes, VZV, vasculitis, IgG4
inv: MRI brain and skull base with fat-suppressed contrast; CT for bone erosion
Nasopharyngoscopy and biopsy; EBV DNA
CSF: cells, protein, cytology, TB/fungal tests; serum glucose, ACE, ANCA, IgG4
Nerve conduction and ganglioside antibodies if GBS variant suspected

case.story: Four months of right ear blockage, then double vision and right facial numbness; now hoarse voice.
case.exam: Right VI palsy, reduced sensation in V2–V3, right palatal droop and vocal cord weakness, firm upper neck node.
case.tests: MRI: nasopharyngeal mass invading clivus and petrous apex; biopsy undifferentiated carcinoma; plasma EBV DNA raised.
case.q: Why is this cause particularly important in Thailand?
case.a: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is common in Southern China and Southeast Asia and often presents with skull-base cranial neuropathies; look at the nasopharynx in any adult with multiple lower and abducens palsies.

read.where: Chapter 13 Cranial Nerve Disorders — Multiple Cranial Neuropathies
Skull base syndromes: anatomy, step approach, foramen syndromes
17. Lower Brainstem and Cranial Nerve Dysfunction

det.patho: Multiple cranial nerves fail together when a process involves a shared anatomical space (cavernous sinus, skull base foramina, brainstem, subarachnoid space) or when a systemic disease attacks nerves diffusely. Neoplastic causes (nasopharyngeal carcinoma, metastases, lymphoma, meningioma, chordoma) are the most frequent in series, followed by vascular, infectious, inflammatory and immune-mediated causes. Diabetes can cause sequential palsies but should not be assumed when more than one nerve fails.
det.clinical: Presentation varies by site: ophthalmoplegia with periorbital pain (cavernous sinus), facial numbness with abducens palsy (petrous apex), dysphagia, hoarseness and shoulder weakness (jugular foramen), or bilateral facial palsy (GBS, Lyme, sarcoid, leukaemia). Accompanying meningism, fever, weight loss or other root deficits point to meningeal disease. Ascertain whether nerves are on one side or both, which helps distinguish local from diffuse processes.
det.diagnosis: Contrast MRI focused on the skull base is the key test, supplemented by CT for bone. Nasopharyngoscopy is essential in Southeast Asia. CSF analysis (often repeated) addresses infection, malignancy and inflammation; serology and imaging search for systemic disease. Biopsy of an accessible lesion is frequently required, and a normal first MRI should be repeated if deficits progress.
det.treatment: Treatment targets the cause: radiotherapy and chemotherapy for nasopharyngeal carcinoma, anti-infective therapy for meningitis, immunotherapy for sarcoid, vasculitis and Tolosa–Hunt, IVIG for GBS variants. Symptomatic care includes eye protection, prisms for diplopia and swallowing assessment. Avoid blind steroids before excluding lymphoma and infection.
det.prognosis: Determined by cause; malignant infiltration carries a poor outlook, whereas immune and some infectious causes recover well.
pearls: More than one cranial nerve palsy is never 'just diabetes' until imaging is clear.
In Thai adults, examine the nasopharynx and neck nodes.
Steroid response in painful ophthalmoplegia does not prove Tolosa–Hunt; lymphoma also responds.
det.thd: Multiple cranial neuropathies คือเส้นประสาทสมองเสียตั้งแต่สองเส้นขึ้นไป ตำแหน่งที่เสียช่วยบอกจุดรอยโรค เช่น cavernous sinus หรือ jugular foramen สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยคือมะเร็ง โดยเฉพาะมะเร็งหลังโพรงจมูกในคนไทย รองลงมาคือเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบจากวัณโรค เชื้อรา หรือมะเร็ง และโรคภูมิคุ้มกัน ตรวจ MRI ฐานกะโหลกที่ฉีดสี ส่องหลังโพรงจมูก และตรวจ CSF รักษาตามสาเหตุและอย่าให้สเตียรอยด์ก่อนวินิจฉัย

Known cancer, multifocal cranial and spinal root signs; CSF cytology
Painful ophthalmoplegia from granulomatous cavernous sinus inflammation; steroid-responsive, diagnosis of exclusion

aN: mcns | multiple cranial neuropathies | mcn | multiple cranial nerve palsies | polyneuritis cranialis | cranial polyneuropathy

name: Multiple sclerosis (MS)
formal: Chronic immune-mediated demyelinating and neurodegenerative CNS disease with relapsing-remitting or progressive course, optic neuritis, myelitis and brainstem syndromes with periventricular lesions.
simple: A long-term disease where the immune system attacks the covering of nerves in the brain and spinal cord, causing vision, strength and balance problems.
more: Diagnose with MRI brain and spine (McDonald criteria), CSF oligoclonal bands and evoked potentials. Use high-dose steroids for relapses and disease-modifying therapy such as interferon, ocrelizumab, natalizumab or fingolimod to reduce relapses.
th: ปลอกประสาทในสมองและไขสันหลังอักเสบเป็นพัก ๆ — อาการเกิดซ้ำต่างตำแหน่ง ต่างเวลา พบมากในหญิงวัยหนุ่มสาว
tempoNote: Relapses evolve over days and recover over weeks; progressive forms advance over years
feat: Attacks separated in time and space: optic neuritis, partial myelitis, brainstem syndromes
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (often bilateral in young adults)
Lhermitte phenomenon and Uhthoff phenomenon (worse with heat)
Fatigue and bladder urgency
inv: MRI brain and spine: periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial and cord lesions; gadolinium enhancement
CSF-specific oligoclonal bands
Visual evoked potentials; exclude mimics (AQP4-IgG, MOG-IgG, B12)

case.story: Painful blurred vision in the right eye 2 years ago that recovered; now 5 days of numbness rising to the waist and electric shocks down the spine on neck flexion.
case.exam: Right RAPD and pale right disc, T6 sensory level to vibration, brisk leg reflexes.
case.tests: MRI: ovoid periventricular lesions perpendicular to the ventricles, short-segment cervical cord lesion; CSF oligoclonal bands positive.
case.q: Which two MRI/CSF findings establish dissemination in time and space?
case.a: Lesions in ≥2 typical CNS regions (space) plus either new/enhancing lesions or CSF-specific oligoclonal bands (time) — McDonald criteria.

read.where: Chapter 19 Multiple Sclerosis and Demyelinating Diseases
8 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System

qx.stem: A 29-year-old pharmacist in Phitsanulok develops tingling of the left arm and trunk over five days, followed by horizontal diplopia from a right internuclear ophthalmoplegia. MRI shows a right medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion plus one ovoid periventricular lesion perpendicular to the lateral ventricle; none enhance. Spinal MRI is normal and there has been no earlier episode.
qx.q: Under the 2024 revision of the McDonald criteria, which additional result would allow a diagnosis of MS at this point?
opts: A serum neurofilament light level above the age-adjusted reference
Oligoclonal bands restricted to the CSF, or a raised CSF kappa free light chain index
Matching oligoclonal bands present in both serum and CSF
Symptoms that persist for more than four weeks despite corticosteroids
A serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level below 20 ng/mL
qx.why: She has a typical attack and MRI dissemination in space (infratentorial plus periventricular). In the 2024 McDonald revision, CSF-specific oligoclonal bands or an elevated kappa free light chain index can complete the diagnosis in place of dissemination in time. A mirror (serum = CSF) band pattern reflects systemic inflammation, not intrathecal synthesis. NfL and vitamin D are not diagnostic, and symptom duration says nothing about dissemination.

src.where: Case 4 New-Onset Right-Sided Numbness and Double Vision

qx.stem: A 24-year-old woman from Nakhon Si Thammarat had a brainstem relapse eight months ago and now a severe myelitis leaving her needing a cane (EDSS 4.5). MRI shows nine gadolinium-enhancing lesions, including two in the cord. She has no plans for pregnancy within two years. Anti-JCV antibody index is 0.18 (negative); hepatitis B and tuberculosis screening are negative.
qx.q: Which long-term treatment strategy is most appropriate?
opts: Start a high-efficacy therapy now, such as natalizumab or an anti-CD20 antibody
Begin interferon beta-1a and escalate only if another relapse occurs
Start teriflunomide because it is oral and well tolerated
Give monthly pulses of IV methylprednisolone without a disease-modifying drug
Observe off treatment and repeat MRI in six months
qx.why: Two disabling relapses within a year with many enhancing lesions define highly active MS, where early high-efficacy therapy (anti-CD20 such as ocrelizumab or ofatumumab, or natalizumab when JCV-negative) gives better long-term disability outcomes than an escalation approach. Moderate-efficacy oral or injectable drugs leave her exposed to further damage. Pulsed steroids treat relapses but do not modify the course.

ddx.pt: Severe optic neuritis and longitudinally extensive myelitis (≥3 segments); AQP4-IgG positive

aN: ms | multiple sclerosis | disseminated sclerosis | rrms | relapsing remitting ms

det.patho: An immune-mediated disease in which autoreactive T and B cells cross the blood–brain barrier and cause focal inflammatory demyelination with axonal injury, alongside a slower compartmentalised process (smouldering lesions, microglial activation) that drives progression. Risk is shaped by genetics (HLA-DRB1*15:01), Epstein–Barr virus infection, low vitamin D, smoking and obesity in youth. It is commoner in women and at higher latitudes, and less common in Thailand than in Western countries.
det.clinical: Most patients start with relapsing-remitting disease: optic neuritis with painful eye movement, partial myelitis, brainstem syndromes such as INO, or cerebellar symptoms, evolving over days and recovering over weeks. Fatigue, heat sensitivity, Lhermitte sign, bladder urgency, depression and cognitive slowing are common. Many later enter secondary progressive MS; about one in ten has primary progressive disease from onset, often as a spastic paraparesis. Red flags for another diagnosis include fever, encephalopathy, peripheral neuropathy and very extensive cord lesions.
det.diagnosis: The McDonald criteria (2017, with later revisions recognising optic nerve lesions and central vein sign) require dissemination in space and time with no better explanation. MRI shows ovoid periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial and spinal cord lesions; new enhancing lesions or CSF-specific oligoclonal bands satisfy dissemination in time. In Asian patients, test for AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG before diagnosing MS. Exclude B12 deficiency, sarcoidosis, vasculitis, infection and small vessel disease.
det.treatment: Relapses that impair function are treated with high-dose methylprednisolone (typically 1 g IV per day over 3–5 days), with plasma exchange for severe steroid-unresponsive attacks. Disease-modifying therapies range from moderate efficacy (interferons, glatiramer, teriflunomide, dimethyl fumarate) to high efficacy (S1P modulators, natalizumab, anti-CD20 antibodies such as ocrelizumab, alemtuzumab, cladribine); early high-efficacy treatment is increasingly favoured. Ocrelizumab is approved for primary progressive MS. Monitor for PML, infections and lymphopenia, and address spasticity, bladder, fatigue, mood and rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: Disease course is highly variable; early effective therapy has substantially reduced long-term disability, and life expectancy is only modestly reduced.
pearls: Bilateral INO in a young adult is MS until proven otherwise.
Always test AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG in suspected MS — some MS drugs worsen NMOSD.
Oligoclonal bands can substitute for dissemination in time under McDonald 2017.
det.thd: MS เป็นโรคภูมิคุ้มกันทำลายปลอกประสาทในสมอง ไขสันหลัง และเส้นประสาทตา เกิดเป็นครั้ง ๆ ต่างตำแหน่งต่างเวลา พบในหญิงวัยหนุ่มสาวมากกว่า อาการเช่น optic neuritis, myelitis บางส่วน, INO, ชา และอ่อนเพลีย วินิจฉัยตาม McDonald criteria ด้วย MRI และ oligoclonal bands ในน้ำไขสันหลัง และในคนเอเชียต้องตรวจ AQP4-IgG และ MOG-IgG แยกก่อนเสมอ รักษาอาการกำเริบด้วย methylprednisolone ขนาดสูง และป้องกันระยะยาวด้วยยาปรับภูมิคุ้มกัน (DMT) โดยปัจจุบันนิยมเริ่มยาประสิทธิภาพสูงเร็ว

name: Multiple sclerosis chorea
formal: Rare chorea in multiple sclerosis from demyelinating lesions of the basal ganglia or thalamus, usually transient.
simple: Uncommon involuntary dance-like movements in a person with multiple sclerosis.
th: อาการ chorea ที่พบได้น้อยในผู้ป่วย multiple sclerosis จากรอยโรคปลอกประสาทอักเสบบริเวณ basal ganglia หรือ thalamus มักเป็นชั่วคราว
tempoNote: Appears over days with a relapse and usually fades over weeks as the lesion resolves
feat: Involuntary flowing, irregular movements, often of one side (hemichorea) during an MS relapse
Other relapse signs may coexist: sensory loss, weakness, ataxia
Responsible lesion in the subthalamic region, striatum, thalamus or their connections
Usually transient; improves with relapse treatment
Rare overall; other causes of chorea must be excluded
inv: MRI brain with gadolinium looking for an active deep grey matter or subthalamic lesion
Glucose, thyroid function, pregnancy test, drug review, antiphospholipid and lupus serology
CSF oligoclonal bands if MS not yet established

case.who: 29-year-old woman with known relapsing MS seen at a neurology clinic in Chiang Mai
case.story: Over four days her left arm and leg started making restless, dance-like movements she cannot stop, along with numbness of the left side.
case.exam: Left hemichorea, left hemisensory loss, brisk left reflexes; no fever.
case.tests: MRI: new gadolinium-enhancing lesion in the right thalamus and subthalamic area; glucose and thyroid normal.
case.q: How should this be managed?
case.a: Chorea from an active MS lesion: treat the relapse with high-dose methylprednisolone, add a short course of tetrabenazine or low-dose antipsychotic if disabling, and review disease-modifying therapy.

det.patho: MS plaques typically lie in white matter, but lesions in the thalamus, subthalamic nucleus or pallido-thalamic connections can disinhibit thalamocortical output and produce chorea or ballism. Inflammation is usually short-lived, which explains why the movement disorder fades. The exact anatomy in many reported cases is debated, and causation is not always proven.
det.clinical: It is reported mainly as single cases or small series, mostly hemichorea or hemiballism during a relapse, occasionally paroxysmal. It may be the first sign of MS. Paroxysmal tonic spasms are a more common MS-related movement phenomenon and should not be confused with chorea.
det.diagnosis: A new, appropriately placed active lesion supports the link, but because chorea in MS is uncommon, look for other causes: hyperglycaemia, thyrotoxicosis, pregnancy, oral contraceptives, lupus and antiphospholipid syndrome, and drugs. MRI with contrast and a basic chorea screen are sufficient in most.
det.treatment: Manage the relapse with intravenous methylprednisolone or plasma exchange if severe. Symptomatic options include VMAT2 inhibitors (tetrabenazine), low-dose antipsychotics or benzodiazepines while waiting for resolution. Optimise long-term disease-modifying therapy.
det.prognosis: Usually resolves within weeks to months; persistent chorea is rare.
pearls: Chorea in a young woman with MS still needs a lupus and pregnancy check.
Brief stereotyped painful spasms in MS are paroxysmal tonic spasms, not chorea.
Deep grey matter lesions are increasingly recognised in MS; they explain rare movement disorders.
det.thd: Chorea ใน multiple sclerosis พบน้อย เกิดจากรอยโรคอักเสบที่ thalamus หรือบริเวณ subthalamic nucleus ทำให้แขนขาข้างหนึ่งเคลื่อนไหวเองแบบไหลไปมาในช่วงที่โรคกำเริบ ควรตรวจ MRI หารอยโรคใหม่ และตัดสาเหตุอื่นของ chorea เช่น น้ำตาลสูง ไทรอยด์เป็นพิษ ตั้งครรภ์ หรือ SLE การรักษาคือให้ steroid ขนาดสูงสำหรับการกำเริบ และใช้ยา tetrabenazine ชั่วคราวถ้าอาการมาก ส่วนใหญ่หายภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์

ddx.pt: Most often from stroke or non-ketotic hyperglycaemia in older people
Chorea with antiphospholipid antibodies, rash, arthritis or renal disease
Child or adolescent after streptococcal infection, with emotional lability

aN: ms related chorea | chorea in multiple sclerosis | demyelinating chorea | ms hemichorea

name: Multiple sclerosis-associated optic neuritis (MS-ON)
formal: Typically unilateral, painful subacute visual loss from optic nerve demyelination with colour desaturation and relative afferent pupillary defect, often the first MS manifestation.
simple: Painful loss of vision in one eye from nerve inflammation, often an early sign of multiple sclerosis.
th: ประสาทตาอักเสบจากการสูญเสียปลอกประสาทที่สัมพันธ์กับ multiple sclerosis ตามัวข้างเดียวภายในไม่กี่วัน ปวดเมื่อกลอกตา เห็นสีซีดลง และมี RAPD มักฟื้นตัวเองได้ดี
tempoNote: Vision falls over several days, reaches a nadir within about two weeks and starts recovering within a month
feat: Unilateral visual loss developing over hours to days, usually in a young adult woman
Pain around the eye that worsens with eye movement
Reduced colour vision, central scotoma and relative afferent pupillary defect
Optic disc normal (retrobulbar) in most; mild swelling in a third
Spontaneous recovery begins within weeks; Uhthoff phenomenon may follow
inv: MRI orbits with fat-suppressed contrast and MRI brain for white matter lesions predicting MS
Aquaporin-4 and MOG antibodies to exclude NMOSD and MOGAD
OCT: retinal nerve fibre layer swelling acutely, thinning later; visual evoked potentials if diagnosis unclear
CSF oligoclonal bands to support MS diagnosis

case.story: Over three days the vision in her right eye became misty with a grey patch in the centre; moving the eye hurts. She had a week of tingling in her legs a year ago.
case.exam: Right acuity 6/36, red desaturation, right RAPD, normal-looking disc; left eye normal.
case.tests: MRI: enhancing right intraorbital optic nerve and three periventricular ovoid lesions; AQP4 and MOG antibodies negative; CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands.
case.q: Will steroids change her final vision, and what else should be discussed?
case.a: MS-associated optic neuritis: IV methylprednisolone speeds recovery but does not change final acuity; with brain lesions and OCBs she likely meets MS criteria, so start disease-modifying therapy.

det.patho: Autoreactive T cells and antibodies target myelin of the optic nerve, producing inflammation, conduction block and variable axonal loss. Recovery of vision reflects resolution of inflammation and remyelination, while residual deficits mirror axonal and ganglion cell loss measurable by OCT. It is the first clinical event of MS in about a fifth of patients and occurs at some point in about half.
det.clinical: Typical features are a woman aged 20–45, unilateral subacute visual loss, pain on eye movement, central scotoma and colour loss, with a normal or mildly swollen disc. Red flags for atypical optic neuritis include no pain, severe loss to no perception of light, bilateral simultaneous onset, marked disc swelling with haemorrhage, no recovery by three weeks and steroid dependence.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by MRI showing optic nerve enhancement and, importantly, brain lesions that predict MS risk. Under the 2024 revised McDonald criteria the optic nerve can count as a lesion site, and OCT asymmetry or VEP changes can support dissemination. Test AQP4 and MOG antibodies in all, and consider infections, sarcoidosis, compression and Leber hereditary optic neuropathy when features are atypical.
det.treatment: High-dose IV methylprednisolone (1 g per day, given for three to five days) or an equivalent high oral dose hastens recovery but does not change the final visual outcome; plasma exchange is used for severe steroid-unresponsive loss. When MRI or CSF indicate MS, early disease-modifying therapy reduces further relapses. Avoid oral low-dose prednisolone alone.
det.prognosis: Most recover to 6/12 or better within months, though subtle colour, contrast and motion deficits often remain.
pearls: Pain with eye movement plus RAPD in a young woman is typical; painless profound loss is not.
The baseline brain MRI is the strongest predictor of later MS.
Steroids improve speed, not the final level, of visual recovery.
det.thd: MS-ON คือประสาทตาอักเสบชนิดทั่วไปที่สัมพันธ์กับ MS ผู้ป่วยหญิงอายุน้อยมีตามัวข้างเดียวภายในไม่กี่วัน ปวดเมื่อกลอกตา สีซีดลง และพบ RAPD ส่วนใหญ่จานประสาทตาปกติ ควรตรวจ MRI ตาและสมอง และ AQP4/MOG antibody เพื่อแยก NMOSD และ MOGAD การให้ methylprednisolone ทางหลอดเลือดดำช่วยให้หายเร็วขึ้นแต่ไม่เปลี่ยนผลสุดท้าย ถ้า MRI สมองมีรอยโรคควรเริ่มยาปรับการดำเนินโรค MS

Marked disc swelling, bilateral, long anterior nerve and perineural enhancement, steroid dependent
Older patient, painless sudden loss on waking, swollen disc and altitudinal field defect

name: Multiple system atrophy (MSA)
formal: Sporadic alpha-synucleinopathy with autonomic failure, poorly levodopa-responsive parkinsonism (MSA-P) or cerebellar ataxia (MSA-C), pyramidal signs and glial cytoplasmic inclusions.
simple: A progressive brain disease causing stiffness, slow movement, poor balance and blood pressure and bladder problems.
more: MRI shows hot cross bun sign (pons), putaminal slit sign and cerebellar atrophy; autonomic testing, orthostatic hypotension and urodynamics help. Treat with fludrocortisone, midodrine and droxidopa, and levodopa trial; survival is about 6 to 9 years. Neurodegeneration of inferior olives, pons and cerebellum causing progressive ataxia; sporadic form is multiple system atrophy with cerebellar predominance, also familial SCAs. MRI shows the hot cross bun sign and atrophy of cerebellum, middle cerebellar peduncles and pons; autonomic testing is needed. Sporadic cases have the MSA-C phenotype; consider SCA genetic testing for familial cases, and treatment is symptomatic. Neurodegenerative cerebellar syndrome with loss of inferior olive, pontine nuclei and Purkinje cells, a pattern of multiple system atrophy or hereditary ataxias. Neuropathological diagnosis of loss of olivary, pontine and cerebellar neurons; MRI shows the hot cross bun sign in MSA-C. Genetic testing for SCA mutations and autonomic tests help differentiate; treatment is supportive. Old term for late-onset cerebellar atrophy with olivopontocerebellar involvement, now part of multiple system atrophy-cerebellar type. Parkinsonian variant of multiple system atrophy with neuronal loss and gliosis in putamen and substantia nigra, causing akinetic-rigid syndrome with poor levodopa response and autonomic failure. MRI shows reduced putaminal volume with T2 hypointensity of the posterolateral putamen and rim of hyperintensity; autonomic testing is helpful. Treat with levodopa trial (may produce orofacial dystonia), droxidopa, and supportive care. Historical name for multiple system atrophy with prominent autonomic failure, parkinsonism and cerebellar signs, caused by alpha-synuclein glial inclusions. Multiple system atrophy with prominent autonomic failure including orthostatic hypotension, urinary dysfunction and parkinsonian or cerebellar signs; an older term, now MSA. Autonomic testing and MRI help diagnosis. Treat orthostatic hypotension with fludrocortisone, midodrine and droxidopa; no cure. Alternative term for multiple system atrophy, an alpha-synucleinopathy with parkinsonism, cerebellar ataxia and autonomic failure. Multiple system atrophy, characterised by glial cytoplasmic inclusions of alpha-synuclein in oligodendrocytes, producing parkinsonism, cerebellar ataxia and autonomic failure. Diagnosed by clinical criteria and MRI; no disease-modifying therapy. Treat orthostatic hypotension and urinary symptoms; survival is about 6 to 10 years.
th: โรคเสื่อมหลายระบบ — พาร์กินสันหรือเดินเซ ร่วมกับระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติล้มเหลวเร็ว เช่น ความดันตกเมื่อยืน ปัสสาวะลำบาก
feat: Early, severe autonomic failure: orthostatic hypotension, urinary retention/incontinence, erectile dysfunction
Parkinsonism with poor levodopa response (MSA-P) or cerebellar ataxia (MSA-C)
Stridor, antecollis, cold dusky hands
Rapid progression
inv: Lying/standing BP, bladder ultrasound for residual volume
MRI: pontine 'hot cross bun', putaminal rim, middle cerebellar peduncle atrophy

case.story: Faints on standing, urinary urgency, and over 18 months became unsteady and slow.
case.exam: BP drops from 140/85 lying to 95/60 standing without a rise in pulse, wide-based ataxic gait, symmetric rigidity, inspiratory stridor at night.
case.tests: MRI: cruciform pontine hyperintensity.
case.q: Why does the pulse not rise when the BP falls?
case.a: Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension — the autonomic baroreflex pathway is failing.

qx.stem: A 58-year-old woman developed urinary urgency with incomplete emptying, then symmetric slowness and a quiet, strained voice over three years. Levodopa 900 mg/day gave little benefit but caused facial dystonia. She faints when standing (BP falls from 136/82 to 98/64 mmHg after 3 minutes) and her husband reports snoring with high-pitched inspiratory noises at night. She already uses a wheelchair outdoors.
qx.q: Which finding would most strongly support MSA under the 2022 MDS criteria?
opts: Hyposmia on a 16-item smell test
Abnormal DaT-SPECT with asymmetric putaminal loss
Midbrain atrophy with 'hummingbird' sign
Positive amyloid PET
MRI showing putaminal and pontine/middle cerebellar peduncle atrophy with a 'hot cross bun' sign
qx.why: Early autonomic failure (urogenital and orthostatic), poorly levodopa-responsive parkinsonism, levodopa-induced craniocervical dystonia, inspiratory stridor and early loss of mobility are MSA red flags. The 2022 MDS criteria require an MRI marker such as putaminal, pontine or middle cerebellar peduncle atrophy or hot cross bun sign for 'clinically established' MSA. Abnormal DaT-SPECT and hyposmia occur in PD too, midbrain atrophy suggests PSP, and nocturnal stridor needs urgent ENT and sleep assessment for CPAP or tracheostomy.

qx.stem: A 63-year-old man from Nakhon Sawan has had two years of fainting on standing, difficulty emptying his bladder and a wife who reports that he shouts and flails in his sleep. His gait is wide-based, his speech is slurred and there is mild limb ataxia. A trial of levodopa 600 mg daily produced almost no improvement.
qx.q: Which MRI finding would best support the leading diagnosis?
opts: Bilateral T2 hypointense globus pallidus with a central hyperintense spot
Cruciform T2 hyperintensity in the pons with middle cerebellar peduncle atrophy
Midbrain atrophy with preserved pons (hummingbird sign)
Bilateral mesial temporal atrophy with enlarged temporal horns
Cortical ribboning with restricted diffusion in the cingulate gyri
qx.why: Early severe autonomic failure, cerebellar signs, REM sleep behaviour problems and poor levodopa response define the cerebellar subtype of MSA, whose imaging signature is the pontine hot-cross-bun sign with middle cerebellar peduncle atrophy and putaminal slit-like change. The hummingbird sign belongs to PSP, the pallidal eye-of-the-tiger to PKAN, and cortical ribboning to prion disease.

qx.stem: A 63-year-old man from Nakhon Sawan has two years of parkinsonism with orthostatic faintness and urinary hesitancy. His doctor wants a simple test that favours multiple system atrophy over Parkinson’s disease.
qx.q: Which finding is the most specific?
opts: An elevated post-void residual urine volume
Mild constipation
Loss of smell
Reduced dopamine transporter uptake
A rest tremor that responds to levodopa
qx.why: Neurogenic bladder with incomplete emptying and a raised post-void residual is the most specific bladder sign for MSA versus PD, though not versus PSP. Severe early autonomic failure, stridor, antecollis, cold cyanotic hands, cerebellar signs and the pontine hot-cross-bun sign also support MSA. Constipation, anosmia and DaT loss occur in PD as well, and a good sustained levodopa response argues against MSA.

qx.stem: A 63-year-old man from Nakhon Ratchasima has poorly levodopa-responsive parkinsonism, symptomatic orthostatic hypotension and urinary retention. His wife reports REM sleep behaviour disorder and, over the past three months, loud high-pitched inspiratory noises through the night with gasping. He sleeps poorly and is increasingly short of breath.
qx.q: What is the best next step?
opts: Reassure; snoring is common in Parkinson's disease
Add a benzodiazepine to calm the night-time behaviour
Increase levodopa at bedtime
Start a diuretic for orthostatic hypotension only
Video-polysomnography with laryngoscopy, then CPAP and consideration of tracheostomy for severe stridor
qx.why: Nocturnal stridor from vocal cord abductor weakness or laryngeal dystonia is a feature of multiple system atrophy, and it carries a risk of sudden death during sleep. Assessment with video-polysomnography and laryngoscopy guides therapy: CPAP is first-line, and tracheostomy is considered when stridor is severe or persists. Benzodiazepines and sedation can worsen airway obstruction.

det.patho: MSA is an alpha-synucleinopathy in which the protein accumulates mainly inside oligodendrocytes as glial cytoplasmic inclusions, leading to neuronal loss in the striatonigral system, the olivopontocerebellar circuits and central autonomic nuclei. Degeneration of brainstem and spinal autonomic neurons causes preganglionic autonomic failure. Onset is usually in the sixth decade and the disease is sporadic.
det.clinical: Patients present with parkinsonism (MSA-P, commoner in Western series) or cerebellar ataxia (MSA-C, relatively commoner in East Asia), together with prominent autonomic failure. Urinary urgency, incomplete emptying and erectile dysfunction often precede motor symptoms by years; symptomatic orthostatic hypotension can cause syncope. Other clues are night-time inspiratory stridor, sleep apnoea, disproportionate antecollis, Pisa syndrome, jerky postural tremor, cold violaceous hands and emotional incontinence. Levodopa responsiveness is poor or transient and may provoke facial dystonia. Progression is noticeably faster than in PD, with walking aids needed within a few years.
det.diagnosis: The 2022 MDS criteria define clinically established and clinically probable MSA based on autonomic dysfunction plus parkinsonism and/or cerebellar syndrome, supported by MRI markers and red flags. Document orthostatic hypotension (a fall of at least 20/10 mmHg, ideally with a blunted heart-rate rise) and measure post-void residual volume. MRI may show putaminal atrophy with a hypointense rim and hyperintense lateral margin, pontine cruciform hyperintensity, and middle cerebellar peduncle or pontine atrophy. Cardiac MIBG uptake is usually preserved, unlike PD and DLB. Exclude fragile X tremor-ataxia syndrome, SCAs and other secondary ataxias in MSA-C.
det.treatment: Treatment is supportive. For orthostatic hypotension use non-drug measures first (fluids, salt, head-up tilt at night, compression garments) then midodrine, fludrocortisone or droxidopa. Bladder symptoms need urodynamic assessment; clean intermittent catheterisation is often required because of high residual volumes. A levodopa trial is worth doing, and CPAP or tracheostomy may be needed for stridor. Botulinum toxin, physiotherapy, speech and swallowing therapy and palliative care input are central.
det.prognosis: Median survival is about 7–10 years from symptom onset; sudden death at night, aspiration and infections are major causes of mortality.
pearls: Early urogenital and orthostatic failure in a patient with parkinsonism or ataxia: think MSA.
Nocturnal stridor is a red flag for sudden death — refer for airway assessment.
A normal cardiac MIBG scan favours MSA over PD/DLB because MSA is a preganglionic failure.
det.thd: MSA เป็นโรคเสื่อมจาก alpha-synuclein ที่สะสมในเซลล์ oligodendrocyte ทำให้มีอาการพาร์กินสัน (MSA-P) หรือเดินเซ (MSA-C) ร่วมกับระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติล้มเหลวตั้งแต่ต้น เช่น ความดันตกเมื่อลุกยืน ปัสสาวะค้าง หย่อนสมรรถภาพทางเพศ เสียงหายใจดังตอนนอน MRI อาจเห็น hot cross bun sign ตอบสนองต่อ levodopa ไม่ดี การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง เช่น แก้ความดันตก สวนปัสสาวะเป็นระยะ และดูแลทางเดินหายใจ

name: Mononeuritis multiplex (multiplex mononeuropathy)
formal: Mononeuritis multiplex, with asymmetric involvement of separate nerves, often due to vasculitis, diabetes, leprosy, or infections.
simple: Several different nerves are damaged one after another, causing patchy weakness and numbness.
more: Nerve and muscle biopsy, and vasculitis work-up; treat with immunosuppression for vasculitis. Involvement of multiple individual peripheral nerves, mononeuritis multiplex, from vasculitis, diabetes, leprosy, or sarcoidosis, with asymmetric patchy weakness and sensory loss.
th: เส้นประสาทหลายเส้นเสียทีละเส้นแบบไม่สมมาตร ในเวลาต่างกัน มักปวดมาก สาเหตุสำคัญคือ vasculitis เบาหวาน และโรคเรื้อน ต้องหาสาเหตุและรักษาเร็ว
tempoNote: Each nerve fails over hours to days, often painfully; new nerves join over weeks to months, and overlap can later mimic a symmetric polyneuropathy
feat: Stepwise, asymmetric deficits in named nerves, e.g. foot drop on one side then wrist drop or ulnar numbness on the other
Deep burning or aching pain at the onset of each new nerve lesion
The peroneal, tibial, ulnar and radial nerves are affected most often; cranial nerves less often
Systemic clues: weight loss, fever, rash or purpura, sinus or lung disease, renal involvement, asthma
Confluent late stage can look like a distal symmetrical neuropathy unless the history is taken carefully
inv: NCS/EMG: patchy axonal loss in individual nerves with side-to-side asymmetry; look for pseudo-conduction block early after infarction
Blood: ESR, CRP, ANCA, ANA, complement, cryoglobulins, hepatitis B and C, HIV, HbA1c, urine protein and sediment, eosinophil count
Combined nerve (superficial peroneal or sural) and muscle biopsy to show vessel-wall inflammation; skin smear or nerve biopsy if leprosy suspected

case.who: 61-year-old man, rice farmer from Roi Et
case.story: Two months of weight loss and night sweats; three weeks ago his right foot suddenly dropped with burning pain along the shin, and last week he could not straighten his left wrist.
case.exam: Right foot drop with numb dorsum of foot, left wrist and finger drop with numbness over the first web space, normal reflexes elsewhere; palpable purpura on both shins.
case.tests: ESR 98 mm/h, creatinine 2.1 mg/dL with haematuria, MPO-ANCA positive; NCS shows absent right superficial peroneal and reduced left radial sensory potentials.
case.q: What pattern is this, and what is the likely cause?
case.a: Mononeuritis multiplex from systemic vasculitis (microscopic polyangiitis); needs urgent steroids plus cyclophosphamide or rituximab.

det.patho: Most cases result from ischaemia: inflammation of epineurial arterioles (vasculitis) blocks supply to a nerve segment, usually in the watershed zone of the mid-arm or mid-thigh, so axons die at that level. Primary systemic vasculitides (polyarteritis nodosa, ANCA-associated vasculitis), connective tissue disease, cryoglobulinaemia from hepatitis C, and diabetes are the commonest causes; non-systemic nerve vasculitis is confined to nerve and muscle. Leprosy, HIV, Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, lymphoma infiltration and multiple compressions (HNPP) are non-vasculitic causes.
det.clinical: The hallmark is sequential involvement of separate nerves, typically beginning with abrupt painful weakness in one territory. Asymmetry and the timeline are the key historical clues; once many nerves are affected the picture blurs into an asymmetric distal neuropathy. Constitutional symptoms, rash, renal or pulmonary disease point to a systemic vasculitis that may itself be life threatening. In Thailand, leprosy must be considered when there are thickened nerves and hypopigmented, anaesthetic skin patches.
det.diagnosis: Map each deficit clinically and with nerve conduction studies to confirm multiple separate axonal lesions. A broad blood and urine screen looks for systemic vasculitis, infection, diabetes and paraproteins. Definite vasculitic neuropathy requires biopsy showing vessel-wall inflammation with damage; combined nerve and muscle biopsy raises the yield, but a negative biopsy does not exclude it because lesions are patchy. Ultrasound may reveal focal nerve enlargement in leprosy or inflammatory neuropathies.
det.treatment: Treat the cause. Systemic or severe vasculitic neuropathy is an emergency: high-dose corticosteroids (often IV methylprednisolone pulses) combined with cyclophosphamide or rituximab for induction, then maintenance with azathioprine, methotrexate or rituximab. Non-systemic nerve vasculitis may respond to steroids alone, with a second agent if it relapses. Leprosy needs multidrug therapy and management of reactions; diabetic cases need glycaemic control. Neuropathic pain treatment, splints and physiotherapy run in parallel.
det.prognosis: Axonal regrowth is slow, so recovery takes months to years and is often incomplete; relapses occur in a substantial minority of vasculitic cases.
pearls: Painful foot drop plus a new wrist drop in a sick patient: think vasculitis and act within days.
Ask about the order in which nerves failed; the timeline separates multiplex from length-dependent neuropathy.
Check urine for blood and protein — kidney involvement changes urgency and treatment.
In Thailand, feel for thickened nerves and look for anaesthetic skin patches (leprosy).
det.thd: Mononeuritis multiplex คือเส้นประสาทหลายเส้นเสียแยกกันทีละเส้นแบบไม่สมมาตร มักปวดแสบร้อนตอนเริ่ม เช่น เท้าตกข้างหนึ่งแล้วตามด้วยข้อมืออีกข้างตก สาเหตุส่วนใหญ่คือหลอดเลือดอักเสบที่เลี้ยงเส้นประสาท รองลงมาคือเบาหวาน โรคเรื้อน และไวรัสตับอักเสบซี ตรวจ NCS ยืนยัน ตรวจเลือดหา ANCA ANA cryoglobulin และปัสสาวะ ยืนยันด้วยตัดชิ้นเนื้อเส้นประสาทและกล้ามเนื้อ รักษาด้วย steroid ร่วมกับ cyclophosphamide หรือ rituximab ในรายที่เป็น vasculitis

name: Multisystem mitochondrial disorders
formal: Mitochondrial diseases affecting several organs, such as brain, muscle, heart, eye, ear and endocrine glands, from mtDNA or nuclear DNA mutations.
simple: Energy-production diseases of the cell that affect many organs of the body at once.
th: โรคไมโตคอนเดรียที่กระทบหลายอวัยวะพร้อมกัน เช่น สมอง กล้ามเนื้อ หัวใจ ตา หู และต่อมไร้ท่อ จากความผิดปกติของ mtDNA หรือยีนในนิวเคลียส อาการแตกต่างกันแม้ในครอบครัวเดียวกัน
tempoNote: Usually slowly progressive over years, punctuated by acute episodes (stroke-like events, metabolic crises) often triggered by illness or fasting
feat: Combinations of seizures, myoclonus, ataxia, stroke-like episodes, migraine and dementia
Myopathy with exercise intolerance, ptosis and progressive external ophthalmoplegia
Sensorineural deafness, optic atrophy or pigmentary retinopathy, short stature and diabetes
Cardiac conduction defects or cardiomyopathy; gastrointestinal dysmotility
Maternal inheritance with variable heteroplasmy, so severity differs even within one family

case.story: A few years of falling grades, jerks of both hands when reaching for objects, and unsteady walking. A generalised seizure last month occurred while watching flickering television. His mother has deafness and diabetes.
case.exam: Short stature, action myoclonus, ataxia, mild proximal weakness, sensorineural hearing loss.
case.tests: Lactate raised; muscle biopsy shows ragged-red fibres; mtDNA testing shows the m.8344A>G mutation at high heteroplasmy in muscle.
case.q: What syndrome fits and which drug should be avoided for the seizures?

det.patho: Mitochondrial disorders result from impaired oxidative phosphorylation, caused by variants in mitochondrial DNA or in nuclear genes controlling mitochondrial function. mtDNA variants are maternally inherited and exist as a mixture of mutant and normal copies (heteroplasmy), and the severity of disease generally tracks the mutant load in a given tissue. Tissues with high energy demand, including brain, muscle, heart, retina, cochlea and endocrine organs, are most vulnerable.
det.clinical: Multisystem features are the clue. Classic syndromes include MERRF (myoclonus, epilepsy, ataxia and ragged-red fibres), MELAS (stroke-like episodes and lactic acidosis), Kearns–Sayre syndrome, Leigh syndrome and chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia. Onset can occur in childhood or adulthood, with insidious school decline, seizures or myoclonus as the presenting problem. Photic stimulation can trigger seizures, and action myoclonus can disrupt hand use. Clinical heterogeneity is marked even within a family.
det.diagnosis: Think of this group whenever several organ systems are involved and no other unifying cause emerges. Check serum lactate, perform MRI, and obtain muscle biopsy with histochemistry (ragged-red and COX-negative fibres). Targeted mtDNA analysis, mtDNA sequencing in muscle and nuclear gene panels, including POLG, are used to confirm. Screening of hearing, eyes, heart, glucose and kidneys identifies treatable complications.
det.treatment: No cure exists. Management is supportive and organ-specific: seizure control, cardiac pacing, hearing aids, diabetes care and nutrition. Valproate and other mitochondrial toxins such as certain aminoglycosides should be avoided. Coenzyme Q10 and other supplements are widely used with limited evidence, and arginine or citrulline are used for stroke-like episodes in MELAS. Genetic counselling covers maternal transmission and heteroplasmy.
det.prognosis: Progressive in most, with prognosis determined by the syndrome, mutation load and heart, brain and metabolic involvement.
pearls: Short stature, deafness, diabetes and a neurological disease in a maternal line suggest a mitochondrial disorder.
Avoid valproate in suspected mitochondrial disease, especially POLG.
Blood mtDNA can be falsely negative; test muscle or urinary sediment.
det.thd: โรคไมโตคอนเดรียหลายระบบเกิดจากการสร้างพลังงานของเซลล์บกพร่อง จากความผิดปกติของ mtDNA ที่ถ่ายทอดทางแม่หรือยีนในนิวเคลียส ทำให้ระบบที่ใช้พลังงานมากเสียหาย เช่น สมอง กล้ามเนื้อ หัวใจ ตา และหู ตัวอย่างคือ MERRF ที่มี myoclonus ชัก เดินเซ และ ragged-red fibres ตรวจ lactate MRI ตัดชิ้นเนื้อกล้ามเนื้อและยีน รักษาแบบประคับประคองและหลีกเลี่ยง valproate

det.patho: Reduced absorptive surface, bypassed duodenum or mucosal damage impairs uptake of several micronutrients. Vomiting and poor intake add to deficits.
det.clinical: Neurological complications appear in phases: acute (thiamine), intermediate (B12, copper, vitamin E) and chronic. Neuropathy, myelopathy and encephalopathy are common.
det.diagnosis: Test a broad panel and repeat periodically; treat empirically when Wernicke encephalopathy is suspected.
det.treatment: Replace each deficiency, often parenterally; long-term supplementation after bariatric surgery; gluten-free diet in coeliac disease.
det.prognosis: Early treatment yields good recovery; delayed treatment leaves deficits.
pearls: Persistent vomiting after bariatric surgery: give thiamine.

Lifelong supplementation is needed after malabsorptive procedures.

name: Munchausen syndrome
formal: Factitious disorder in which a person deliberately feigns or induces illness to assume the sick role without external gain; can present with neurological symptoms such as seizures or weakness.
simple: A mental health condition in which someone makes up or causes illness so as to receive medical care.
more: Diagnosis requires excluding real disease and finding inconsistent history. Management is supportive psychiatric care; confrontation is often unhelpful.
th: โรคทางจิตเวชที่ผู้ป่วยแกล้งทำหรือทำให้ตนเองเจ็บป่วยโดยตั้งใจเพื่อให้ได้บทบาทผู้ป่วย โดยไม่มีผลประโยชน์ภายนอก อาจแสดงเป็นอาการทางระบบประสาท เช่น ชักหรืออ่อนแรง

feat: Not a neurological disease: a psychiatric factitious disorder in which symptoms or signs are deliberately produced
Dramatic but inconsistent history; many prior admissions, procedures and hospitals
Neurological presentations: 'seizures', paralysis, coma, or induced hypoglycaemia or drug toxicity
Distinct from functional disorder (not deliberate) and malingering (external gain such as money)

case.story: Fourth admission this year with 'status epilepticus'; she knows medical terms well and asks for more procedures. Other hospitals report negative work-ups.
case.exam: During an event her eyes are forcibly closed and she resists eye opening; no injury, oxygen saturation stable.
case.tests: Video-EEG during typical events shows normal background rhythm; insulin is high with suppressed C-peptide at an episode of 'unexplained' hypoglycaemia.
case.q: What feature separates factitious disorder from functional seizures?
case.a: Deliberate production of symptoms (here, injected insulin) to gain the sick role; functional seizures are not consciously produced.
