det.patho: Factitious disorder imposed on self is a psychiatric condition in which a person knowingly fabricates, exaggerates or induces illness, with the main motive being to occupy the patient role rather than to obtain external rewards. Childhood illness, abuse, healthcare employment and personality disorders are commonly reported associations, but the underlying mechanism is poorly understood. The eponymous 'Munchausen' label is usually kept for the most severe, chronic, wandering cases.
det.clinical: Patients may feign seizures, weakness, sensory loss or coma, tamper with tests, or harm themselves with insulin, anticoagulants or infections. They often accept invasive procedures readily, and the story changes when checked. Symptoms may escalate when discharge approaches. Factitious disorder imposed on another (on a child, formerly 'by proxy') is a form of abuse and requires safeguarding.
det.diagnosis: It is a diagnosis of evidence, not exclusion: genuine disease must be properly excluded, and deception needs to be documented (inconsistent records, lab evidence of induced illness, direct observation). Video-EEG is decisive for apparent seizures. Distinguish it from functional disorders and malingering, and consider comorbid real illness. Involve psychiatry and record findings carefully and factually.
det.treatment: Management focuses on preventing harm from unnecessary tests and treatment, with one coordinating clinician. A non-confrontational, supportive discussion that allows the patient to save face is preferred; direct accusation usually leads to self-discharge. Psychiatric treatment of comorbidities and psychotherapy may help, though engagement is often poor. Safeguarding procedures apply if others, especially children, are at risk.
det.prognosis: Often chronic with poor engagement; some patients improve when a trusting long-term relationship is established.
pearls: Intentional symptom production + no external gain = factitious; external gain = malingering; not intentional = functional.
Unexplained hypoglycaemia with high insulin and low C-peptide means exogenous insulin.
Always keep looking for real disease; factitious and genuine illness can coexist.
det.thd: Munchausen syndrome ไม่ใช่โรคทางระบบประสาทแต่เป็นโรคทางจิตเวชชนิด factitious disorder ผู้ป่วยตั้งใจแกล้งหรือทำให้ตนเองป่วย เช่น แกล้งชัก แกล้งอ่อนแรง หรือฉีดอินซูลินเอง เพื่อให้ได้รับการดูแลแบบผู้ป่วย โดยไม่มีผลประโยชน์อื่น ต่างจาก functional disorder ที่ไม่ได้ตั้งใจ และ malingering ที่หวังผลประโยชน์ การดูแลต้องยืนยันด้วยหลักฐาน หลีกเลี่ยงหัตถการเกินจำเป็น และส่งจิตแพทย์แบบไม่เผชิญหน้า

name: Muscle-specific kinase myasthenia gravis (MuSK MG)
formal: Autoimmune myasthenia with anti-MuSK antibodies, prominent bulbar, facial, neck and respiratory weakness, muscle atrophy and poor response to cholinesterase inhibitors.
simple: A type of myasthenia gravis causing weakness of the face, throat and neck, often responding poorly to usual medicines.
th: myasthenia gravis ชนิดที่มี anti-MuSK พบเด่นในผู้หญิงวัยหนุ่มสาว อ่อนแรงที่ใบหน้า กลืน คอ และการหายใจมาก ลิ้นและใบหน้าอาจลีบ ตอบสนองต่อ pyridostigmine ไม่ดี แต่ตอบสนองดีต่อ rituximab
tempoNote: Weeks to months to bulbar and respiratory weakness; crises are more frequent than in AChR MG
feat: Predominant facial, bulbar, neck extensor and respiratory weakness; limbs and eyes less affected
Tongue and facial muscle atrophy with chronic disease
Poor response or intolerance (cramps, fasciculations) to cholinesterase inhibitors
Thymoma is not associated and thymectomy is not beneficial
Women aged 20–40 most often affected
inv: Anti-MuSK antibodies (cell-based assay if radioimmunoassay negative) in AChR-negative patients
Single-fibre EMG of facial or neck muscles; RNS from limbs may be normal
Lung function (FVC/NIF) and swallowing assessment

case.story: Three months of nasal speech, choking on rice and a head that drops forward by evening; pyridostigmine made her cramp without benefit.
case.exam: Bilateral facial weakness, tongue atrophy with furrows, weak neck extensors, mild ptosis, limbs nearly normal.
case.tests: AChR antibodies negative, anti-MuSK positive; facial single-fibre EMG shows increased jitter; CT chest normal thymus.
case.q: Which treatment is especially effective, and which commonly used treatment is not?
case.a: Rituximab works particularly well in MuSK MG; thymectomy offers no benefit and pyridostigmine is often poorly tolerated.

read.where: Chapter 17 Disorders of the Neuromuscular Junction — Muscle-Specific Kinase Myasthenia Gravis

det.patho: IgG4 antibodies against muscle-specific kinase block the agrin–LRP4–MuSK signalling that clusters acetylcholine receptors, leading to loss of postsynaptic receptor density without complement-mediated damage. Being IgG4, they do not fix complement, so complement inhibitors do not help. It accounts for a minority (around 5–8%) of MG and up to a third or more of AChR-negative generalised disease; prevalence is reported to vary by region.
det.clinical: Onset is often abrupt with bulbar symptoms, neck extensor ('dropped head') weakness and respiratory compromise; myasthenic crisis is more common than in AChR MG. Ocular involvement is usually milder and pure ocular disease is rare. Chronic disease leads to fixed weakness and atrophy of facial and tongue muscles. Cholinesterase inhibitors may provoke cramps, fasciculations and cholinergic worsening.
det.diagnosis: Test anti-MuSK in AChR-negative patients with a compatible picture; cell-based assays improve sensitivity. Limb repetitive stimulation is often normal, so examine facial muscles and use single-fibre EMG. Exclude motor neuron disease, brainstem lesions and myopathies. CT of the mediastinum is usually normal and does not need intervention.
det.treatment: Corticosteroids and plasma exchange (often more effective than IVIG acutely) are mainstays; steroid-sparing agents follow. Early rituximab yields high remission rates and is favoured for moderate to severe disease. FcRn inhibitors (e.g. efgartigimod, rozanolixizumab) have shown benefit in MuSK MG; complement inhibitors are not indicated. Pyridostigmine at low dose only if tolerated; thymectomy not recommended.
det.prognosis: With rituximab and modern therapy most achieve good control, but residual bulbar and facial weakness is more frequent than in AChR MG.
pearls: AChR-negative, bulbar and neck predominant, worse on pyridostigmine: check MuSK.
MuSK antibodies are IgG4: complement inhibitors and thymectomy do not help.
Rituximab is particularly effective; plasma exchange is preferred for crises.
det.thd: MuSK myasthenia gravis คือ myasthenia ที่เกิดจาก anti-MuSK ชนิด IgG4 พบมากในผู้หญิงอายุน้อย อ่อนแรงที่ใบหน้า กลืน คอตก และการหายใจเด่น อาจมีลิ้นและใบหน้าลีบ ตรวจ RNS ที่แขนขามักปกติต้องตรวจกล้ามเนื้อใบหน้าหรือ single-fibre EMG ไม่ค่อยตอบสนองต่อ pyridostigmine และไม่มีประโยชน์จาก thymectomy รักษาด้วยสเตียรอยด์ plasma exchange และ rituximab ซึ่งได้ผลดี

qx.stem: A 34-year-old woman from Roi Et has four months of nasal speech, difficulty swallowing and a drooping head by evening, with little limb weakness. AChR antibodies are negative and MuSK-IgG is positive. Pyridostigmine 60 mg caused cramps and fasciculations without benefit. She stabilised after plasma exchange but relapses as prednisolone is reduced below 20 mg.
qx.q: Which long-term treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Thymectomy to induce remission
Increase pyridostigmine to 120 mg every three hours
Eculizumab as the preferred complement inhibitor
Rituximab as an early steroid-sparing therapy
Stop prednisolone and use acetazolamide
qx.why: MuSK MG is IgG4 mediated, bulbar and neck predominant, and often responds poorly or adversely to pyridostigmine. Rituximab gives durable remission in many patients and is recommended early when steroids cannot be tapered; FcRn blockers such as rozanolixizumab are also options. Complement inhibitors target complement-fixing AChR antibodies and are not used for MuSK MG, and thymectomy has no proven benefit in MuSK disease.

qx.stem: A 55-year-old woman from Kanchanaburi has had two months of double vision, slurred speech, swallowing difficulty and a head that drops forward, then needed intubation for hypercapnic respiratory failure. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies are negative. Tongue wasting is noted and pyridostigmine caused cramps and fasciculations without benefit.
qx.q: Which statement about the likely diagnosis and treatment is correct?
opts: Thymectomy is the key curative step
Anticholinesterases are the most effective treatment
Early rituximab with corticosteroids and plasma exchange or IVIG for crisis is effective, and MuSK antibodies should be requested
Mexiletine is the drug of choice
The antibody-negative form never needs immunotherapy
qx.why: Bulbar and neck-extensor weakness, crisis and tongue atrophy with negative AChR antibodies suggest MuSK myasthenia gravis, confirmed by anti-MuSK antibodies. These patients often react badly to cholinesterase inhibitors, derive little benefit from thymectomy, and respond well to B-cell depletion with rituximab together with steroids, with PLEX or IVIG during crisis.

name: Muscle–eye–brain disease (MEB)
formal: Congenital muscular dystrophy with cobblestone lissencephaly, eye malformations and severe developmental delay, from defective alpha-dystroglycan glycosylation (POMGNT1).
simple: A severe inherited condition from birth that affects muscle, eyes and brain.
more: Autosomal recessive; MRI shows brain malformation and CK is high; care is supportive, with limited survival in severe cases.
th: congenital muscular dystrophy ชนิด dystroglycanopathy ที่มีสมองผิดปกติแบบ cobblestone lissencephaly ความผิดปกติของตา และพัฒนาการล่าช้ารุนแรง จากความบกพร่องของ glycosylation ของ alpha-dystroglycan (เช่น POMGNT1)
tempoNote: Present from birth or early infancy; static to slowly progressive course
feat: Neonatal hypotonia and weakness with high CK
Severe myopia, glaucoma, cataract, retinal and optic nerve abnormalities and erratic eye movements
Cobblestone lissencephaly, brainstem hypoplasia, hydrocephalus and cerebellar cysts
Severe developmental delay and intellectual disability, with seizures in some
Contractures and limited motor skills; many never walk independently
inv: Serum CK, typically elevated
MRI brain showing cobblestone cortex, brainstem and cerebellar involvement, hydrocephalus
Genetic testing: POMGNT1, POMT1, POMT2 and other dystroglycanopathy genes
Ophthalmological examination and ERG; muscle biopsy with alpha-dystroglycan staining if genetics unavailable

case.story: She is floppy, feeds poorly and does not follow objects. Parents are first cousins. A brother died in infancy with similar problems.
case.exam: Marked hypotonia, weak antigravity movements, large head, high myopia and bilateral buphthalmos.
case.tests: CK about 10 times normal; MRI shows cobblestone cortex and brainstem hypoplasia with enlarged ventricles; POMGNT1 biallelic variant found.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what supportive care is needed?
case.a: Muscle–eye–brain disease, an alpha-dystroglycanopathy. Care is supportive: feeding and respiratory support, seizure control, ophthalmic management of glaucoma, physiotherapy and genetic counselling.

det.patho: Variants in genes that glycosylate alpha-dystroglycan (POMGNT1 in the classic form; POMT1, POMT2, FKRP and others) break the link between muscle and brain basement membranes and the extracellular matrix. Neurons in the developing cortex then overmigrate through gaps in the pial membrane, causing cobblestone lissencephaly. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
det.clinical: Newborns are hypotonic and weak, with eye anomalies such as congenital myopia, glaucoma, cataract and retinal hypoplasia. Brain MRI shows migration defects, brainstem and cerebellar hypoplasia and hydrocephalus. Development is severely delayed and seizures occur in some, while contractures and respiratory weakness can appear. The condition lies between Walker-Warburg and Fukuyama in severity.
det.diagnosis: Elevated CK, MRI pattern and ophthalmological findings narrow the diagnosis, and genetic testing confirms it. Biopsy shows reduced glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan. Exclude Walker-Warburg, Fukuyama CMD, other CMD types, congenital myotonic dystrophy and mitochondrial disorders.
det.treatment: Treatment is supportive and multidisciplinary: respiratory and feeding support, anti-seizure medication, shunting of hydrocephalus when needed, physiotherapy and orthopaedic care, ophthalmic management of glaucoma and myopia, and genetic counselling for family planning. No disease-modifying therapy exists, although clinical trials are underway.
det.prognosis: Severe disability with reduced life expectancy, although survival into childhood and beyond occurs with good supportive care.
pearls: Hypotonic infant with high CK, eye anomalies and cobblestone MRI is a dystroglycanopathy.
POMGNT1 is the classic gene for MEB.
Severity ranks Walker-Warburg > MEB > Fukuyama in most series.
det.thd: Muscle–eye–brain disease เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้อสลายตัวแต่กำเนิดชนิด dystroglycanopathy ทำให้เด็กตัวอ่อน CK สูง ตามีความผิดปกติ เช่น สายตาสั้นมาก ต้อหิน และสมองมี cobblestone lissencephaly พัฒนาการล่าช้ามาก วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI และตรวจยีน POMGNT1 การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง ได้แก่ ช่วยหายใจ ให้อาหาร ควบคุมชัก ดูแลตา กายภาพบำบัด และให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

Fukutin-related, common in Japan, with milder eye involvement and cortical dysgenesis
Broader group; merosin-deficient CMD shows white-matter changes with a normal cortex

name: Muscular dystrophy
formal: Group of inherited primary muscle diseases with progressive degeneration and weakness, raised CK and dystrophic biopsy changes; caused by mutations in genes for muscle structural or membrane proteins.
simple: Inherited conditions in which muscles gradually break down and become weaker over time.
more: Diagnosis by CK, biopsy and genetic testing; patterns include Duchenne, limb-girdle, myotonic and facioscapulohumeral. Care is supportive with steroids, respiratory and cardiac care; some have gene-targeted therapy. Inherited progressive myopathies with muscle fibre degeneration, elevated CK and dystrophic biopsy, including Duchenne, Becker, limb-girdle and facioscapulohumeral types. Diagnosed by CK, EMG, muscle imaging, biopsy with dystrophin, sarcoglycan or merosin immunostaining, and genetic testing. Corticosteroids help Duchenne; management is supportive with cardiac and respiratory surveillance and physiotherapy.
th: กลุ่มโรคกล้ามเนื้อทางพันธุกรรมที่ใยกล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมและถูกแทนที่ด้วยพังผืดและไขมัน ทำให้อ่อนแรงมากขึ้นเรื่อย ๆ CK สูง เช่น Duchenne, Becker, limb-girdle, FSHD และ myotonic dystrophy
tempoNote: Progressive over years to decades; onset ranges from birth to late adulthood depending on type
feat: Progressive weakness with a pattern typical of each type: proximal limb-girdle, facial-scapular, distal or ocular-pharyngeal
Calf hypertrophy, Gowers sign and toe walking in dystrophinopathies
Contractures, scoliosis and respiratory weakness as disease advances
Cardiomyopathy or conduction block in dystrophinopathy, Emery–Dreifuss, some LGMD and myotonic dystrophy
CK often markedly raised (very high in Duchenne), but may be near normal in FSHD and myotonic dystrophy
inv: CK; EMG to confirm myopathic pattern and detect myotonia
Genetic testing first-line: MLPA/sequencing of DMD, D4Z4 sizing for FSHD, repeat testing for DM1/DM2, NGS panels for LGMD
Muscle MRI pattern and biopsy with immunostaining when genetics is unrevealing
ECG, echocardiography or cardiac MRI and pulmonary function at diagnosis and regularly

case.who: 5-year-old boy brought to a district hospital in Udon Thani
case.story: He falls often, cannot keep up with classmates and climbs stairs one at a time; his maternal uncle used a wheelchair from age 11.
case.exam: Waddling gait, enlarged firm calves, Gowers sign, proximal weakness; reflexes reduced at the knees.
case.tests: CK 18,000 U/L; MLPA shows deletion of DMD exons 48–50.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the key early treatments?
case.a: Duchenne muscular dystrophy, one of the muscular dystrophies: start corticosteroids (prednisolone or deflazacort; vamorolone where available), arrange cardiac and respiratory surveillance, physiotherapy against contractures, and offer genetic counselling to the mother.

det.patho: Muscular dystrophies are caused by variants in genes for the dystrophin–glycoprotein complex, sarcolemmal repair proteins (dysferlin), nuclear envelope proteins, extracellular matrix (collagen VI, laminin alpha-2) and RNA-processing defects (myotonic dystrophy, FSHD). The common end point is repeated fibre necrosis and incomplete regeneration, with replacement by fat and fibrous tissue. Depending on the gene, transmission is X-linked, dominant or recessive.
det.clinical: Duchenne starts in early childhood and causes loss of walking by early teens without treatment; Becker is milder and later. Limb-girdle dystrophies affect hip and shoulder girdles from childhood to adulthood. FSHD gives asymmetric facial, scapular and foot dorsiflexor weakness; myotonic dystrophy adds myotonia, cataract and multisystem features; oculopharyngeal dystrophy presents late with ptosis and dysphagia. Cardiac and respiratory complications largely determine survival.
det.diagnosis: Pattern recognition guides targeted genetic testing, which has replaced biopsy as the first step in most. CK, EMG and muscle MRI help define the pattern and choose the panel. Biopsy with immunohistochemistry or western blot remains useful for variants of uncertain significance. Exclude acquired treatable myopathies and Pompe disease (dried blood spot enzyme assay).
det.treatment: Management is multidisciplinary: physiotherapy, orthoses, scoliosis surgery, respiratory support and cardiac protection (ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid antagonists; devices for conduction disease). Corticosteroids are standard in Duchenne; exon-skipping oligonucleotides, givinostat and micro-dystrophin gene therapy are approved in some countries for selected patients. Avoid succinylcholine and be careful with volatile anaesthetics in dystrophinopathies.
det.prognosis: Highly variable by type: Duchenne survival now commonly reaches the 30s with ventilatory and cardiac care, while many adult-onset forms have near-normal lifespan.
pearls: A very high CK in a young boy with Gowers sign is Duchenne until proven otherwise.
Screen the heart in every dystrophy — cardiomyopathy may outpace limb weakness.
Female dystrophin carriers can develop cardiomyopathy and need follow-up.
det.thd: Muscular dystrophy เป็นกลุ่มโรคกล้ามเนื้อทางพันธุกรรมที่ใยกล้ามเนื้อถูกทำลายซ้ำ ๆ และถูกแทนที่ด้วยไขมันและพังผืด ทำให้อ่อนแรงมากขึ้นตามเวลา ตัวอย่างเช่น Duchenne, Becker, LGMD, FSHD และ myotonic dystrophy การวินิจฉัยปัจจุบันใช้การตรวจยีนเป็นหลัก ร่วมกับ CK, EMG และ MRI กล้ามเนื้อ การดูแลต้องทำร่วมกันหลายสาขา เช่น กายภาพบำบัด ดูแลหัวใจและการหายใจ และใช้ steroid ใน Duchenne

name: Muscular dystrophy (MDC) 1C
formal: Congenital muscular dystrophy from FKRP mutations causing alpha-dystroglycan hypoglycosylation, with proximal weakness, calf hypertrophy and respiratory or cardiac involvement.
simple: An inherited muscle disease from early life causing weakness, large calves and breathing trouble.
more: Autosomal recessive; very high CK; monitor respiration and heart; management supportive.
th: congenital muscular dystrophy จากยีน FKRP ทำให้ alpha-dystroglycan มีน้ำตาลไม่ครบ อ่อนแรงต้นแขนขา น่องโต และหายใจ/หัวใจอ่อนแรง
tempoNote: Onset at birth or early infancy; progressive over childhood
feat: Hypotonia and weakness from birth or first months; walking often never achieved
Calf and thigh muscle hypertrophy, sometimes tongue hypertrophy
Respiratory insufficiency and dilated cardiomyopathy
Very high CK; intellect usually normal (brain involvement in some)
Same gene as the milder LGMD R9 (formerly 2I)
inv: CK often 10–50 times normal
Muscle biopsy: dystrophic with reduced glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan
FKRP sequencing
Spirometry, echocardiogram and ECG at diagnosis and regularly

case.story: Weak since infancy, sat at 10 months, has never walked independently; prominent calves.
case.exam: Proximal weakness, calf hypertrophy, mild contractures, normal speech and cognition.
case.tests: CK 9,500 U/L; biopsy reduced alpha-dystroglycan glycosylation; FKRP compound heterozygous variants; echo LV ejection fraction 48%.
case.q: Which surveillance is essential besides physiotherapy?
case.a: Regular cardiac and respiratory monitoring — FKRP disorders cause cardiomyopathy and respiratory failure.

read.where: Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Genetic Muscle Diseases

det.patho: FKRP adds ribitol phosphate to the glycan chain of alpha-dystroglycan. Severe biallelic loss-of-function variants produce MDC1C, whereas the common founder variant c.826C>A in homozygous form gives the milder limb-girdle phenotype. Defective glycosylation disrupts binding to laminin, making the sarcolemma fragile.
det.clinical: Infants show hypotonia and weakness, with muscle hypertrophy despite weakness. Motor milestones are limited; many never walk. Respiratory muscle weakness and dilated cardiomyopathy may develop in childhood. Some patients have structural brain changes or learning difficulties, linking them to the wider dystroglycanopathy spectrum.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in a hypotonic infant with very high CK and muscle hypertrophy. Biopsy demonstrates reduced glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan with normal dystrophin. Genetic confirmation in FKRP is required; MRI brain checks for malformations.
det.treatment: No approved disease-modifying therapy; ribitol supplementation and gene therapy are in clinical trials. Supportive care includes physiotherapy, splints, scoliosis management, non-invasive ventilation, and heart failure therapy. Corticosteroids are not standard.
det.prognosis: Variable; cardiorespiratory failure determines survival, often limiting life to adolescence or early adulthood in severe forms.
pearls: Muscle hypertrophy plus very high CK in a girl: consider FKRP, not just DMD.
The same gene causes both congenital and limb-girdle phenotypes.
Echocardiography belongs in routine follow-up.
det.thd: MDC1C เป็น congenital muscular dystrophy จากยีน FKRP ทำให้ alpha-dystroglycan มีน้ำตาลไม่สมบูรณ์ เด็กอ่อนแรงตั้งแต่เกิด กล้ามเนื้อน่องโต CK สูงมาก และอาจมีหัวใจโตและหายใจไม่พอ ยีนเดียวกันทำให้เกิด LGMD R9 แบบเบาได้ วินิจฉัยด้วยชิ้นเนื้อและตรวจยีน การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง เน้นติดตามหัวใจและการหายใจ

name: Musicians occupational cramps
formal: Task-specific focal dystonia in musicians affecting hands or embouchure, with loss of motor control during playing but normal other activities.
simple: Involuntary cramping or curling of the hand or lips that only occurs when playing a musical instrument.
th: dystonia เฉพาะที่ที่เกิดเฉพาะเวลาเล่นดนตรี เช่น นิ้วม้วนงอเวลาเล่นเปียโนหรือกีตาร์ หรือริมฝีปากควบคุมไม่ได้เวลาเป่าเครื่องเป่า ขณะทำกิจกรรมอื่นเป็นปกติ
tempoNote: Develops gradually over months in experienced players and tends to persist; usually remains confined to the playing task
feat: Loss of fine control of fingers (curling, extension, sticking) or lip/embouchure during playing only
Usually painless, starting as reduced accuracy in fast passages
Typically affects highly trained professionals after years of intensive practice; men more often
Sensory tricks (changing grip, wearing a glove) may help briefly
Neurological examination otherwise normal
inv: Clinical diagnosis by watching the person play the instrument (video recording)
Imaging and blood tests only if signs spread or atypical features suggest secondary dystonia
Nerve conduction studies if ulnar neuropathy or entrapment is suspected

case.who: 34-year-old classical guitarist with an orchestra in Bangkok
case.story: For eight months his right middle and ring fingers curl into the palm during fast arpeggios; writing, eating and typing are normal.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination; when he plays, the two fingers flex involuntarily within seconds and the wrist extends to compensate.
case.tests: MRI brain and nerve conduction normal.
case.q: What is this and what options exist?
case.a: Musician's focal task-specific dystonia: EMG-guided botulinum toxin to the overactive finger flexors and specialised retraining are the main options; outcome is variable.

read.where: 11 - Dystonia: Phenomenology, classification, etiology, pathology, biochemistry, and genetics

det.patho: Task-specific dystonia arises from maladaptive plasticity: years of repetitive, highly precise practice combined with genetic susceptibility blur the cortical representation of individual fingers and weaken surround inhibition. Sensorimotor integration, not muscle or nerve, is the core problem. Perfectionism and anxiety may contribute but do not cause it.
det.clinical: Pianists and guitarists usually develop finger flexion, string players right-hand or left-hand problems, and brass and woodwind players embouchure dystonia affecting lips, jaw or tongue. Early complaints are subtle loss of speed or evenness. Spread to other tasks occurs in a minority, and some develop tremor or writer's cramp.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical and requires seeing the patient perform the task. Exclude overuse syndromes with pain, nerve entrapment, joint disease and early parkinsonism. Spread beyond the task, onset in childhood or other signs prompt evaluation for secondary or genetic dystonia.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin injections into selected muscles with EMG or ultrasound guidance are the main treatment for hand dystonia; embouchure dystonia responds less well. Retraining programmes, technique adaptation and instrument modification help some. Trihexyphenidyl is occasionally tried; deep brain stimulation or thalamotomy is reserved for very selected cases.
det.prognosis: Many players cannot fully return to professional performance, though a proportion regain useful function with combined therapy.
pearls: Always ask the patient to bring the instrument to clinic.
Painless loss of control in one task points to dystonia, not overuse injury.
Rest alone rarely cures it.

more: Diagnose with repetitive nerve stimulation showing decrement, single-fibre EMG with increased jitter, and antibody testing; CT chest for thymoma. qx.stem: A 27-year-old woman from Songkhla has fluctuating ptosis and diplopia that worsens in the evening. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies are negative, and 3 Hz repetitive stimulation of the abductor digiti minimi and trapezius shows no decrement. Her symptoms remain restricted to the eyes and face.
qx.q: Which test has the highest sensitivity for demonstrating a transmission defect in this ocular and facial presentation?
opts: Needle EMG of the paraspinal muscles
Sensory nerve conduction studies of the upper limbs
Median F-wave studies
Motor unit number estimation of the thenar muscles
Single-fibre EMG of a facial muscle, such as orbicularis oculi or frontalis, showing increased jitter
qx.why: Single-fibre EMG detects increased jitter and blocking and is the most sensitive electrophysiological test for myasthenia, especially in ocular disease where repetitive stimulation is often normal. The rest are tests of nerve or anterior horn function, so they would be expected to be normal. A normal jitter in a symptomatic facial muscle makes MG unlikely.

qx.stem: A 34-year-old woman from Phuket has fatigable ptosis and diplopia. AChR antibody is negative and 3 Hz repetitive nerve stimulation of the hand and face muscles is normal. A neuromuscular transmission defect is still suspected.
qx.q: Which test is the most sensitive electrodiagnostic study to confirm it?
opts: Routine needle EMG of motor unit shape alone
Single-fibre EMG showing increased jitter with blocking in a clinically weak muscle
Sural sensory nerve action potential
H-reflex latency
Minimum F-wave latency
qx.why: Jitter is the variability of the interval between two muscle fibres of one motor unit, and it is a sensitive measure of neuromuscular transmission, abnormal early when routine conduction studies and repetitive stimulation are normal. Increased jitter with blocking is sensitive but not specific, so it supports the diagnosis only in the right clinical context. Needle EMG, sensory and reflex studies do not test the junction directly.

qx.stem: A 32-year-old woman has had intermittent double vision for four months. AChR, MuSK and LRP4 antibodies are negative and repetitive nerve stimulation of the facial and trapezius muscles is normal. Single-fibre EMG of a clinically weak frontalis muscle, performed with good quality potentials with rise time under 300 microseconds, shows normal jitter in 20 fibre pairs and no blocking.
qx.q: How should the single-fibre EMG result be interpreted?
opts: It proves seronegative myasthenia, because repetitive stimulation was also normal
It is uninterpretable, because single-fibre EMG is only useful when antibodies are positive
Normal jitter in a clinically weak muscle makes a neuromuscular junction disorder very unlikely, so another cause should be sought
It confirms ocular myasthenia, which spares jitter in the face
It shows reinnervation, which is the usual finding in myasthenia
qx.why: Single-fibre EMG is the most sensitive test of neuromuscular transmission, so normal jitter in a muscle that is clinically weak effectively excludes an NMJ disorder; abnormal jitter, in contrast, is not specific, because reinnervation or any neuropathic or myopathic disease can increase it. This patient needs a different explanation for the diplopia, such as thyroid eye disease, microvascular cranial neuropathy or a mass lesion. Normal jitter does not prove myasthenia.

aN: mg | myasthenia gravis | myasthenia | achr myasthenia | generalised myasthenia | ocular myasthenia gravis

det.patho: Autoantibodies against postsynaptic proteins at the neuromuscular junction — the acetylcholine receptor in about 85% of generalised cases, MuSK or LRP4 in a minority — reduce the safety factor of transmission. AChR antibodies are complement-fixing IgG1/3, whereas MuSK antibodies are IgG4 and do not activate complement. The thymus is central: thymic hyperplasia in early-onset disease and thymoma in about 10–15%. Incidence peaks in young women and in older men.
det.clinical: Fatigable weakness is the core feature: ptosis and diplopia that worsen through the day, then bulbar weakness (nasal speech, chewing fatigue, dysphagia), neck flexor and proximal limb weakness. About half start with ocular symptoms and most of those generalise within two years. MuSK-MG favours bulbar, neck and respiratory muscles with tongue atrophy. Myasthenic crisis — respiratory or severe bulbar failure — is often precipitated by infection, surgery, pregnancy or drugs such as aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, magnesium and beta-blockers.
det.diagnosis: Antibody testing comes first (AChR, then MuSK and LRP4 if negative); about half of purely ocular cases are seronegative. Repetitive nerve stimulation at 3 Hz shows a decrement above 10%, and single-fibre EMG jitter is the most sensitive test but not specific. The ice pack test supports ocular MG at the bedside. Image the chest for thymoma and check thyroid function. Exclude LEMS, botulism, mitochondrial myopathy, thyroid eye disease and brainstem lesions.
det.treatment: Pyridostigmine relieves symptoms. Most generalised patients need immunotherapy: prednisolone (start low and increase slowly to avoid early worsening) plus azathioprine or mycophenolate to spare steroids. Thymectomy benefits AChR-positive generalised patients aged roughly 18–65 and is mandatory for thymoma. Refractory disease options include rituximab (especially MuSK-MG), complement inhibitors (eculizumab, ravulizumab, zilucoplan) and FcRn blockers (efgartigimod, rozanolixizumab). Crisis is treated with ventilatory support and IVIG or plasma exchange, with temporary withdrawal of pyridostigmine if intubated.
det.prognosis: With modern therapy most patients achieve minimal manifestations and near-normal life expectancy; crisis mortality is now low.
pearls: Pupils are never involved in MG; if they are, think of a third nerve lesion or botulism.
High-dose steroids can transiently worsen MG — start low or admit.
Know the drugs to avoid: aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, IV magnesium, some beta-blockers.
det.thd: MG เป็นโรคภูมิคุ้มกันสร้างแอนติบอดีต่อ acetylcholine receptor (หรือ MuSK, LRP4) ที่รอยต่อเส้นประสาทกับกล้ามเนื้อ อาการเด่นคืออ่อนแรงที่แย่ลงเมื่อใช้งานหรือช่วงเย็น เช่น หนังตาตก เห็นภาพซ้อน เสียงขึ้นจมูก กลืนลำบาก แต่รูม่านตาและความรู้สึกปกติ วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจแอนติบอดี RNS ที่พบ decrement และ CT ทรวงอกหา thymoma รักษาด้วย pyridostigmine สเตียรอยด์ ยากดภูมิ ผ่าตัด thymectomy และยาใหม่ เช่น complement inhibitor หรือ FcRn blocker ส่วน crisis ให้ IVIG หรือ plasma exchange

more: Repetitive nerve stimulation, antibodies (VGCC, AChR) and drug history differentiate them. Treat the cause with 3,4-diaminopyridine, immunotherapy or withdrawal of the drug.

feat: Fatigable or fluctuating weakness, ptosis, diplopia or bulbar weakness
LEMS: proximal leg weakness, reduced reflexes that improve after effort, dry mouth
Botulism and neurotoxic snakebite (cobra, krait): rapid descending paralysis with ptosis

case.story: Shared home-canned bamboo shoots at a village festival; 24 hours later he and four relatives developed double vision, dry mouth and difficulty swallowing.

read.where: Chapter 17 Disorders of the Neuromuscular Junction — Lambert–Eaton and Congenital Myasthenic Syndromes

det.patho: Neuromuscular transmission can fail presynaptically (LEMS antibodies to P/Q calcium channels, botulinum toxin cleaving SNARE proteins, magnesium, krait beta-bungarotoxin), synaptically (acetylcholinesterase deficiency, organophosphate excess) or postsynaptically (AChR blockade by cobra alpha-toxins, drugs such as aminoglycosides, genetic receptor defects). This lexicon entry is an umbrella for MG mimics, not a single disease.
det.clinical: All produce weakness that worsens with use, but patterns differ. LEMS favours proximal legs with autonomic dysfunction and reflexes that return after brief exercise. Botulism and snake envenoming cause rapid ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, bulbar and respiratory paralysis; pupils are often affected in botulism. Drug-induced worsening may unmask latent MG. Congenital myasthenic syndromes start early with family history and episodic crises.
det.diagnosis: History (food, wound, snakebite, drugs, cancer, family) is decisive. Serology for AChR, MuSK and VGCC, plus RNS with pre- and post-exercise testing, separates pre- from postsynaptic defects. Single-fibre EMG is sensitive but not specific. Genetic testing defines congenital forms, and cancer screening is required in LEMS.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: amifampridine (3,4-diaminopyridine) and tumour treatment for LEMS, antitoxin for botulism, antivenom and airway support for neurotoxic snakebite, withdrawal of the offending drug. Congenital forms need gene-tailored therapy (pyridostigmine, salbutamol, ephedrine, fluoxetine or quinidine depending on subtype), as some worsen with cholinesterase inhibitors. Monitor respiratory function closely in acute forms.
det.prognosis: Toxin- and drug-related forms recover fully with supportive care; LEMS prognosis depends on associated cancer; congenital forms vary by gene.
pearls: Post-exercise increment over 100% means a presynaptic disorder.
In Thailand, consider snakebite and botulism in any acute ptosis with bulbar weakness.
Some congenital myasthenic syndromes get worse with pyridostigmine; get the gene first.
det.thd: Myasthenia gravis-like syndrome เป็นกลุ่มโรครอยต่อประสาทกล้ามเนื้อที่อ่อนแรงแบบล้าคล้าย MG ได้แก่ LEMS ที่สัมพันธ์กับมะเร็งปอด botulism จากหน่อไม้ปี๊บ งูเห่าหรืองูสามเหลี่ยมกัด ยาบางชนิด และ congenital myasthenic syndrome แยกจากประวัติ antibody และ RNS โดยเฉพาะการเพิ่มของ CMAP หลังออกแรงในโรคที่ presynaptic รักษาตามสาเหตุ เช่น 3,4-DAP, antitoxin, antivenom หรือหยุดยา และเฝ้าระวังการหายใจ

name: Myasthenic crisis
formal: Life-threatening exacerbation of myasthenia gravis with respiratory or bulbar failure needing ventilation, often precipitated by infection or drugs; treated with IVIG or plasma exchange.
simple: A dangerous worsening of myasthenia gravis in which breathing or swallowing muscles become too weak.
th: ภาวะกำเริบรุนแรงของ myasthenia gravis จนหายใจหรือกลืนไม่ได้ ต้องใส่ท่อช่วยหายใจ มักมีตัวกระตุ้นจากติดเชื้อหรือยา

feat: Increasing dysphagia, nasal speech, weak cough and pooling of secretions
Breathlessness, use of accessory muscles and paradoxical abdominal breathing; cannot count aloud to 20 on a single breath
Neck flexor weakness that parallels diaphragm weakness
Triggers: infection, surgery, pregnancy, steroid start, drugs (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, magnesium, beta-blockers, checkpoint inhibitors)
inv: Serial bedside FVC and maximal inspiratory pressure; arterial blood gas changes are late
Search for infection: CBC, CXR, cultures; electrolytes including Mg and K
AChR/MuSK antibody status if not known; CT chest for thymoma

case.who: 34-year-old woman with known AChR-positive MG from Surat Thani
case.story: Three days after starting levofloxacin for a urinary infection she can no longer swallow water and feels short of breath.
case.exam: Bilateral ptosis, weak neck flexion, staccato speech, single-breath count 9.
case.tests: FVC 14 mL/kg falling to 11 mL/kg within 4 hours; PaCO2 still normal.
case.q: What are the immediate priorities?
case.a: ICU admission and elective intubation, stop the fluoroquinolone, hold pyridostigmine while intubated, and start plasma exchange or IVIG (total 2 g/kg, divided across several days).

read.where: Chapter 17 Disorders of the Neuromuscular Junction — Myasthenic Crisis

det.patho: Crisis occurs when neuromuscular transmission fails in respiratory and bulbar muscles, usually because a trigger increases antibody-mediated damage or adds a pharmacological block. Infection is the commonest precipitant. Excess cholinesterase inhibitor (cholinergic crisis) is now uncommon and is distinguished by muscarinic features.
det.clinical: About 15–20% of people with MG have a crisis at some point, often within the first two years. Bulbar weakness may lead to aspiration even before ventilatory failure. Patients can look deceptively calm because hypercapnia appears late. MuSK-positive patients are prone to bulbar and respiratory crises.
det.diagnosis: It is a clinical diagnosis in a patient with known or suspected MG whose ventilation or airway protection fails. Track FVC (concern below 20 mL/kg) and negative inspiratory force (weaker than −30 cmH2O), along with the trend. Look for triggers and exclude other causes of respiratory failure. A first presentation in crisis requires confirming MG with antibodies and neurophysiology.
det.treatment: Secure the airway early in ICU; non-invasive ventilation can avoid intubation if hypercapnia is absent. Plasma exchange and IVIG are equally effective for most patients, with plasma exchange possibly faster. Start or increase corticosteroids cautiously as they may transiently worsen weakness, and plan long-term immunotherapy (azathioprine, mycophenolate, rituximab for MuSK, complement or FcRn inhibitors for refractory AChR disease). Treat infection and avoid drugs that worsen MG.
det.prognosis: With modern ICU care mortality is below 5%; most patients are extubated within two weeks.
pearls: Measure FVC; oxygen saturation stays normal until late.
Ask what new drug was started this week.
Neck flexor weakness tracks diaphragmatic weakness.
det.thd: Myasthenic crisis คือ myasthenia gravis กำเริบจนกล้ามเนื้อหายใจและกลืนอ่อนแรง ต้องใช้เครื่องช่วยหายใจ มักมีตัวกระตุ้นเช่นติดเชื้อ ผ่าตัด หรือยาบางชนิด ติดตาม FVC ทุกไม่กี่ชั่วโมง เพราะออกซิเจนในเลือดลดลงช้า รักษาด้วย plasma exchange หรือ IVIG ร่วมกับหาตัวกระตุ้นและวางแผนยากดภูมิคุ้มกันระยะยาว

case.who: 38-year-old woman presenting to the emergency department of a regional hospital in Songkhla
case.story: Over five days she developed numbness rising from the feet to the umbilicus, weak legs and urinary retention; she had persistent hiccups and vomiting two weeks earlier.
case.exam: Paraparesis grade 3, sensory level at T10, brisk reflexes and bilateral extensor plantars.
case.tests: MRI: T2 lesion from C6 to T9, central cord; CSF 30 white cells; AQP4-IgG positive.
case.q: What is the cause of this myelitis and the acute treatment?

det.patho: Inflammation of the cord may be autoimmune demyelinating (MS, NMOSD, MOGAD, ADEM), systemic inflammatory (sarcoidosis, lupus, Sjögren), direct infection (viruses, tuberculosis, syphilis, schistosomiasis), post-infectious or paraneoplastic. Cytokine-mediated injury and demyelination block conduction across the affected segments, and severe lesions cause axonal loss and necrosis. In Thailand, NMOSD accounts for a relatively larger share of myelitis than in Western populations.
det.clinical: Patients develop motor, sensory and autonomic dysfunction below the lesion over hours to days. MS myelitis tends to be partial, asymmetric and short, with mild deficits. NMOSD causes severe, longitudinally extensive lesions often with optic neuritis or area postrema syndrome; MOGAD frequently affects the conus with prominent bladder problems. Infectious myelitis may show anterior horn involvement (acute flaccid myelitis) or radicular pain (herpes zoster).
det.diagnosis: The first priority is to exclude compression with urgent MRI. Then confirm inflammation (gadolinium enhancement, CSF pleocytosis or raised IgG index) and determine cause with brain MRI, serology and CSF studies. Lesion length, position and enhancement pattern guide the differential. If none is found after full work-up, the label idiopathic transverse myelitis is used, but re-testing antibodies later may reveal a cause.
det.treatment: First-line acute therapy is IV methylprednisolone 1 g per day over three to five days; add plasma exchange early in severe cases or poor response. Treat infections specifically (aciclovir for HSV/VZV, antituberculous therapy). Long-term immunotherapy depends on the cause: MS disease-modifying drugs, or for NMOSD rituximab, inebilizumab, eculizumab/ravulizumab, satralizumab. Rehabilitation, bladder care and thromboprophylaxis are essential.
det.prognosis: About a third recover well, a third partially and a third remain severely disabled; rapid onset, complete paralysis and spinal shock predict worse outcome.
pearls: Image the whole spine urgently; treat compression before thinking about inflammation.
A lesion longer than three segments means test AQP4 and MOG antibodies.
Unexplained hiccups or vomiting before myelitis point to NMOSD.
det.thd: Myelitis คือไขสันหลังอักเสบ ทำให้ขาหรือแขนอ่อนแรง ชาใต้ระดับรอยโรค และปัสสาวะลำบาก ภายในชั่วโมงถึงไม่กี่สัปดาห์ สาเหตุได้แก่ MS, NMOSD, MOGAD, การติดเชื้อ และโรคภูมิคุ้มกันทั่วร่างกาย ต้องทำ MRI ไขสันหลังด่วนเพื่อแยกการกดทับก่อน แล้วตรวจน้ำไขสันหลังและ AQP4/MOG antibody การรักษาเฉียบพลันใช้ methylprednisolone ขนาดสูงและ plasma exchange ในรายรุนแรง ตามด้วยการรักษาระยะยาวตามสาเหตุและฟื้นฟูสมรรถภาพ

name: Myeloneuropathy
formal: Combined spinal cord and peripheral nerve disorder with spastic gait and neuropathy, seen in B12 or copper deficiency, HIV, HTLV-1 and nitrous oxide toxicity.
simple: A condition where both the spinal cord and the nerves in the limbs are damaged, causing stiff, weak and numb legs.
ab: Spinal cord and peripheral nerve syndrome
th: ภาวะที่มีทั้งไขสันหลังและเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายผิดปกติพร้อมกัน ทำให้เดินเกร็งเซร่วมกับชาปลายมือปลายเท้า พบในการขาดวิตามิน B12 ขาดทองแดง ใช้ไนตรัสออกไซด์ HIV และ HTLV-1
tempoNote: Usually evolves over weeks to months; nitrous oxide abuse can produce it over a few weeks
feat: Spastic or ataxic gait with impaired vibration and proprioception (dorsal columns)
Distal sensory loss and paraesthesiae from accompanying polyneuropathy
Mixed reflexes: depressed ankle jerks with brisk knees and extensor plantars
Positive Romberg sign; Lhermitte sign possible
Causes: B12, copper or folate deficiency, nitrous oxide, HIV, HTLV-1, adrenomyeloneuropathy, hereditary syndromes
inv: B12, methylmalonic acid, homocysteine, folate, serum copper and caeruloplasmin, zinc, full blood count
MRI spine: dorsal column T2 signal ('inverted V') in B12, copper and nitrous oxide myelopathy
Nerve conduction studies to confirm neuropathy
HIV, HTLV-1 serology; very long chain fatty acids in men; ask about nitrous oxide and zinc use

case.who: 23-year-old man admitted to a university hospital in Bangkok
case.story: Over a month his feet and hands became numb and he started stumbling in the dark; he admits inhaling 'whipped cream gas' balloons most weekends.
case.exam: Sensory ataxic gait, loss of joint position at the toes, absent ankle jerks, brisk knee jerks, extensor plantars, positive Romberg.
case.tests: B12 low-normal but homocysteine and methylmalonic acid high; MRI dorsal column T2 hyperintensity C2–C6; NCS axonal sensorimotor neuropathy.
case.q: What is the mechanism and the management?
case.a: Nitrous oxide myeloneuropathy: N2O inactivates B12. Stop exposure completely and give parenteral hydroxocobalamin; recovery depends on prompt treatment.

Chapter 125: Neurologic Complications of Nutritional Disorders

det.patho: Many nutritional and toxic disorders injure long tracts and long peripheral axons together because both depend on the same metabolic supply. B12 deficiency (or N2O-induced inactivation) impairs methylation and myelin maintenance, producing dorsal and lateral column degeneration plus axonal neuropathy. Copper deficiency, often from excess zinc or bariatric surgery, gives an almost identical picture. Infectious causes (HIV vacuolar myelopathy, HTLV-1) and inherited ones (adrenomyeloneuropathy, some hereditary spastic paraplegias) also combine both.
det.clinical: Patients report numb, clumsy feet and unsteadiness, worse in the dark, followed by stiffness of the legs. Examination finds spastic legs with absent ankle jerks. Anaemia, cytopenia, cognitive change or optic neuropathy may accompany nutritional causes. Thailand has seen rising nitrous oxide-related cases among young adults.
det.diagnosis: Measure B12 together with functional markers (methylmalonic acid, homocysteine), because serum B12 may be normal in nitrous oxide toxicity. Check copper, caeruloplasmin and zinc, and viral serology. MRI may show posterior column signal; nerve conduction defines the neuropathy. Consider genetic testing when acquired causes are excluded.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: intramuscular hydroxocobalamin or cyanocobalamin for B12 deficiency (with full stop of nitrous oxide), oral or IV copper replacement and removal of zinc sources, antiretroviral therapy for HIV. Physiotherapy and gait aids support recovery. Symptomatic treatment of spasticity and neuropathic pain as needed.
det.prognosis: Nutritional and toxic forms improve with prompt treatment, but long-standing deficits may only partly recover; inherited and HTLV-1 forms progress slowly.
pearls: Brisk knees with absent ankles plus loss of joint position: think myeloneuropathy.
Normal B12 does not exclude nitrous oxide toxicity — check homocysteine or MMA.
Copper deficiency mimics B12 deficiency; ask about zinc supplements and gastric surgery.
det.thd: Myeloneuropathy คือภาวะที่ไขสันหลังและเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเสียพร้อมกัน ผู้ป่วยชาปลายเท้า เดินเซโดยเฉพาะในที่มืด ขาเกร็ง รีเฟล็กซ์เข่าไวแต่ข้อเท้าหาย สาเหตุสำคัญคือขาดวิตามิน B12 การสูดไนตรัสออกไซด์ ขาดทองแดง HIV และ HTLV-1 ควรตรวจ B12 ร่วมกับ homocysteine หรือ methylmalonic acid ระดับทองแดง และ MRI ไขสันหลัง การรักษาคือแก้สาเหตุโดยเร็ว เช่น ฉีด B12 และหยุดสารที่สัมผัส

name: Myelopathy
formal: Disorder of the spinal cord with upper motor neuron signs, sensory level and sphincter disturbance, caused by compression (spondylosis), inflammation, vascular, infective or metabolic disease.
simple: Damage to the spinal cord causing weakness, numbness and bladder or bowel problems.
more: Investigate with MRI of the spine, CSF analysis (oligoclonal bands, AQP4 and MOG antibodies), B12, copper, HIV and syphilis serology, and urgent decompression for compressive lesions. Prognosis depends on the cause and the severity at presentation.
th: กลุ่มอาการจากไขสันหลังผิดปกติ มีอ่อนแรงแบบ upper motor neuron ระดับการรับความรู้สึก และปัสสาวะอุจจาระผิดปกติ สาเหตุได้ทั้งการกดทับ อักเสบ หลอดเลือด ติดเชื้อ และเมตาบอลิก
tempoNote: Minutes to hours suggests vascular or traumatic cause; hours to weeks suggests inflammatory or infective; months to years suggests compressive, degenerative or metabolic
feat: A syndrome, not a single disease: spastic weakness with brisk reflexes and extensor plantars below the lesion
A sensory level on the trunk, or a dissociated loss (pain versus vibration) by tract
Urgency, retention or constipation, and erectile dysfunction
Normal cranial nerves and cognition; arms spared in thoracic lesions
Back or neck pain and radicular pain at the lesion level in compressive disease
inv: Urgent MRI of the whole spine (gadolinium) for any acute or subacute cord syndrome
CSF: cells, protein, oligoclonal bands, infection studies; serum AQP4 and MOG antibodies
Blood: B12, methylmalonic acid, copper, HIV, syphilis, HTLV-1 serology
Brain MRI and visual evoked potentials if demyelination is suspected

case.story: Eight months of stiff legs and dropping things; recently needs to rush to the toilet and his hands feel clumsy when buttoning.
case.exam: Spastic gait, hyperreflexia in all limbs, Hoffmann sign, bilateral extensor plantars, wasting of intrinsic hand muscles, reduced vibration in feet.
case.tests: MRI cervical spine: multilevel spondylotic narrowing at C4–C6 with T2 cord signal change.
case.q: What is the cause, and what is the definitive treatment?
case.a: Degenerative cervical (spondylotic) myelopathy; surgical decompression is advised for moderate or progressive disease.

read.where: Chapter 28 Neurologic Complications of Chemotherapy and Radiation Therapy

det.patho: The cord carries descending corticospinal tracts, ascending dorsal column and spinothalamic tracts, and autonomic pathways in a narrow space, so small lesions produce disproportionate deficits. Causes include extrinsic compression (spondylosis, disc, tumour, abscess, haematoma), inflammation (MS, NMOSD, MOGAD, sarcoid, connective tissue disease), ischaemia or fistula, infection (HTLV-1, HIV, syphilis, schistosomiasis, tuberculosis), metabolic deficiency (B12, copper, nitrous oxide), radiation and hereditary degeneration.
det.clinical: Patterns help localise: complete transverse, Brown-Séquard, central cord, anterior cord, and posterior column syndromes. Acute lesions may first cause flaccid areflexic weakness (spinal shock). Tempo is the most useful clue to cause: sudden onset suggests infarct or haemorrhage; evolution over days suggests inflammation or abscess; slow progression suggests spondylosis, tumour or metabolic disease. Pain, fever and red flags such as cancer history demand emergency imaging.
det.diagnosis: Image first: MRI of the entire spine identifies compression that needs surgery. Lesion length (longitudinally extensive versus short), position in the axial plane and enhancement guide the differential. CSF, antibody tests, metabolic and infectious serology then refine the cause. Consider spinal angiography for an unexplained progressive cord lesion with flow voids, which may be a dural arteriovenous fistula.
det.treatment: Compression from tumour, abscess or haematoma is a surgical or oncological emergency; give dexamethasone for malignant cord compression and arrange decompression or radiotherapy. Inflammatory myelitis is treated with high-dose methylprednisolone and escalation to plasma exchange. Replace B12 or copper promptly in deficiency. Rehabilitation, bladder and bowel programmes, spasticity treatment, and prevention of pressure sores and thrombosis apply to all.
det.prognosis: Depends on the cause and the severity at nadir; early decompression and treatment improve recovery.
pearls: Any new cord syndrome is an MRI emergency until compression is excluded.
Normal MRI with a myelopathy: think B12, copper, nitrous oxide, HTLV-1 and hereditary causes.
Arm sparing with a sensory level on the trunk localises to the thoracic cord or below.
det.thd: Myelopathy คือกลุ่มอาการจากไขสันหลัง ผู้ป่วยมีขาเกร็งอ่อนแรง reflex ไว มีระดับการรับความรู้สึกที่ลำตัว และปัสสาวะผิดปกติ สาเหตุมีทั้งการกดทับ การอักเสบ หลอดเลือด ติดเชื้อ และขาดวิตามิน ต้องทำ MRI ไขสันหลังทั้งหมดอย่างเร่งด่วนเพื่อหาการกดทับ แล้วตรวจน้ำไขสันหลังและเลือดตามความเหมาะสม รักษาตามสาเหตุร่วมกับการฟื้นฟู

name: Myoadenylate deaminase (MAD) deficiency
formal: Common metabolic myopathy from AMPD1 variants with exercise intolerance and cramps, though often asymptomatic, and absent histochemical activity.
simple: An enzyme shortage in muscle that can cause tiredness or cramps with exercise, though many people have no symptoms.
more: Diagnosed by absent AMPD1 staining or genetic testing; the ischaemic forearm test shows low ammonia rise; reassurance and graded exercise.
th: ภาวะพร่องเอนไซม์ AMP deaminase ในกล้ามเนื้อจากยีน AMPD1 พบบ่อยแต่ส่วนใหญ่ไม่มีอาการ บางรายเป็นตะคริวหรือปวดกล้ามเนื้อหลังออกกำลัง
tempoNote: Exercise-related cramps or myalgia; many carriers never have symptoms
feat: Most common enzyme defect found on muscle biopsy (homozygous in about 1–2% of Europeans; less in Asians)
Exertional myalgia, cramps and early fatigue in some
Normal strength and usually normal CK
Often coincidental finding alongside another neuromuscular disease
No myoglobinuria in isolated cases
inv: Forearm exercise test: normal lactate rise but absent ammonia rise
Muscle biopsy: absent myoadenylate deaminase histochemical stain
AMPD1 genotyping (common c.34C>T nonsense variant)
Exclude other metabolic myopathies (McArdle, CPT II)

case.story: Gets aching thigh cramps after long marches, which settle with rest; never dark urine.
case.exam: Normal strength, bulk and reflexes.
case.tests: CK normal; forearm test: lactate rises normally, ammonia does not; AMPD1 homozygous c.34C>T.
case.q: How certain is it that this explains his symptoms?
case.a: MAD deficiency is consistent but often asymptomatic, so other causes should be excluded; management is reassurance and graded training.

det.patho: AMP deaminase converts AMP to IMP in the purine nucleotide cycle, which supports energy balance during intense muscle activity. Biallelic AMPD1 loss removes this step, yet most individuals compensate fully, which is why the clinical significance remains debated. Secondary deficiency can occur in other neuromuscular diseases.
det.clinical: Symptomatic patients report exercise-induced cramps, pain or fatigue with normal examination. Many people with the genotype have no complaints, and some studies suggest no overall excess of symptoms. It is not a cause of fixed weakness. When found with another muscle disease it may modify symptoms.
det.diagnosis: A normal lactate rise with flat ammonia response on the forearm exercise test, or absent histochemical stain, suggests the diagnosis; genotyping confirms. Because the defect is common, always look for an alternative explanation before attributing symptoms to it. Exclude glycogen and lipid storage disorders, mitochondrial myopathy and endocrine causes.
det.treatment: No specific therapy is proven. Reassurance, graded conditioning exercise and avoidance of extreme exertion are advised. Ribose supplementation has been tried with inconsistent benefit.
det.prognosis: Benign, non-progressive.
pearls: A common genotype with uncertain penetrance: do not stop the search for another cause.
Forearm test: lactate up, ammonia flat.
Normal strength and CK are the rule.
det.thd: MAD deficiency คือการขาดเอนไซม์ AMP deaminase ในกล้ามเนื้อจากยีน AMPD1 พบได้บ่อยแต่ส่วนใหญ่ไม่มีอาการ บางคนมีตะคริวหรือปวดเมื่อยหลังออกกำลัง ตรวจร่างกายและ CK ปกติ การทดสอบ forearm exercise พบ ammonia ไม่ขึ้น ยืนยันด้วยยีน การรักษาคือให้ความมั่นใจและฝึกออกกำลังแบบค่อยเป็นค่อยไป และควรหาสาเหตุอื่นเสมอ

ddx.pt: No lactate rise but exaggerated ammonia rise on forearm test; second-wind and myoglobinuria

name: Myocardial infarction (MI)
formal: Acute heart muscle necrosis from coronary occlusion; neurologically relevant as a cause of cardioembolic stroke, hypoxic brain injury and syncope.
simple: A heart attack, when blood flow to part of the heart is blocked; it can lead to stroke or brain injury.
th: กล้ามเนื้อหัวใจตายเฉียบพลันจากหลอดเลือดหัวใจอุดตัน สำคัญทางประสาทวิทยาเพราะเป็นต้นเหตุ cardioembolic stroke สมองขาดออกซิเจน และหมดสติ
tempoNote: Stroke risk highest in the first weeks to months after MI, especially with LV thrombus
feat: Not a neurological disease; important cause and companion of neurological events
Left ventricular thrombus after large anterior MI can embolise to the brain
Cardiac arrest from MI causes hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury
Arrhythmia or hypotension can present as syncope or watershed infarcts
Thrombolysis, antithrombotics and PCI carry intracranial bleeding and procedural stroke risk
inv: ECG and troponin in stroke patients with chest pain or ECG changes
Echocardiography (or cardiac MRI) for LV thrombus and wall motion
Brain CT/MRI for neurological symptoms around MI

case.story: Two weeks after a large anterior STEMI treated with late PCI, he suddenly could not move his left arm.
case.exam: Left face and arm weakness, left neglect.
case.tests: MRI: right MCA cortical infarct; echo: apical akinesia with LV thrombus.
case.q: Mechanism and secondary prevention?
case.a: Cardioembolic stroke from LV thrombus; anticoagulation (warfarin or a DOAC) for about three months with repeat echo, alongside antiplatelet therapy as cardiology advises.

det.patho: Coronary plaque rupture and thrombosis cause myocardial necrosis. Akinetic segments, especially after anterior MI, slow blood flow and allow mural thrombus to form within days. Arrhythmias, pump failure and cardiac arrest reduce cerebral perfusion, and treatments add bleeding risk. Stroke and MI share the same atherosclerotic risk factors.
det.clinical: Neurological complications include embolic stroke (often MCA territory), hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy after arrest, watershed infarcts from low output, delirium and intracranial haemorrhage after fibrinolytics. Conversely, acute stroke can cause troponin rise and ECG changes, and true MI may occur in the days after stroke. This entry is included for its relevance to neurology.
det.diagnosis: MI is diagnosed by symptoms, ECG changes and troponin dynamics. In stroke patients, raised troponin requires distinguishing true coronary events from stroke-related myocardial injury, with cardiology input. Echocardiography detects LV thrombus; cardiac MRI is more sensitive.
det.treatment: MI management (reperfusion, dual antiplatelet therapy, statin, beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor) is directed by cardiology. For LV thrombus, anticoagulation for roughly three months is typical. Acute ischaemic stroke shortly after MI requires individual decisions on thrombolysis because of possible pericarditis or rupture after recent large MI. Shared vascular risk-factor control prevents both.
det.prognosis: Stroke after MI is linked to higher mortality; most events occur within the first month.
pearls: Large anterior MI plus new stroke: look for LV thrombus.
Troponin may rise after stroke itself; interpret with ECG and echo.
Recent MI is a relative caution, not an absolute bar, for stroke thrombolysis.
det.thd: Myocardial infarction คือกล้ามเนื้อหัวใจตายเฉียบพลัน ไม่ใช่โรคทางระบบประสาท แต่เป็นสาเหตุสำคัญของ stroke จากลิ่มเลือดในหัวใจห้องล่างซ้าย สมองขาดออกซิเจนหลังหัวใจหยุดเต้น และหมดสติจากหัวใจเต้นผิดจังหวะ ผู้ป่วย stroke หลัง MI ควรทำ echo หาลิ่มเลือด และให้ยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือดถ้าพบ

name: Myocarditis
formal: Inflammation of heart muscle, relevant to neurology as a source of cardioembolic stroke and association with myopathies, Duchenne and some autoimmune diseases.
simple: Inflammation of the heart muscle, which can cause strokes if clots form.
th: กล้ามเนื้อหัวใจอักเสบ สำคัญทางประสาทวิทยาเพราะทำให้เกิด cardioembolic stroke และพบร่วมกับโรคกล้ามเนื้อบางชนิด เช่น myositis จาก immune checkpoint inhibitor และ dystrophy

feat: Not a primary neurological disease but overlaps with neuromuscular disorders
Chest pain, dyspnoea, palpitations, heart failure or sudden death

Inflammatory myopathies (e.g. anti-SRP, anti-mitochondrial antibodies) and dystrophies can involve the heart
Embolic stroke from LV dysfunction or arrhythmia
inv: Troponin, ECG, echocardiography; cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement

case.who: 67-year-old man from Phuket on pembrolizumab for lung cancer
case.story: Three weeks after the second dose he developed drooping eyelids, double vision, neck and arm weakness and breathlessness.
case.exam: Bilateral ptosis, ophthalmoparesis, neck flexor and proximal weakness.
case.tests: CK 6,000 U/L, troponin markedly raised, ECG new conduction delay, AChR antibody positive; MRI heart shows myocardial enhancement.
case.q: What is the syndrome and why is it urgent?
case.a: Immune checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis-myositis-myasthenia overlap; high mortality from arrhythmia and respiratory failure, so stop the drug and give high-dose steroids with escalation (IVIG, plasma exchange, abatacept).

det.patho: Myocardial inflammation follows viral infection, autoimmune disease, drugs (notably immune checkpoint inhibitors) or, rarely, vaccination. Inflammatory cells damage myocytes and the conduction system, causing dysfunction and arrhythmia. Shared antigens between heart and skeletal muscle explain overlap with myositis.
det.clinical: Presentations range from mild chest pain to fulminant heart failure. For neurologists, the key settings are patients with inflammatory myopathy or ICI-related neuromuscular syndromes, where cardiac involvement may be silent but lethal, and young stroke patients with LV dysfunction. Dystrophies cause chronic cardiomyopathy that can show inflammatory flares. This entry describes a cardiac condition relevant to neurology.
det.diagnosis: Troponin, ECG and echocardiography are first-line; cardiac MRI using Lake Louise criteria is the main non-invasive test, and biopsy is reserved for severe cases. In any myositis or ICI neuromuscular syndrome, check troponin and ECG at baseline and during follow-up. Troponin T may be raised from skeletal muscle injury; troponin I is more cardiac-specific.
det.treatment: Supportive heart failure and arrhythmia care with cardiology. Immune-mediated myocarditis (ICI, giant cell, myositis-associated) is treated with high-dose steroids and further immunosuppression. Stroke prevention may require anticoagulation when there is LV thrombus or severe dysfunction.
det.prognosis: Viral myocarditis often resolves; ICI myocarditis and giant cell myocarditis carry high mortality.
pearls: Ptosis plus high CK plus troponin on immunotherapy: ICI overlap syndrome.
Use troponin I to separate cardiac from skeletal muscle injury.
Screen the heart in every new inflammatory myopathy.
det.thd: Myocarditis คือกล้ามเนื้อหัวใจอักเสบ ไม่ใช่โรคทางระบบประสาทโดยตรง แต่สำคัญเพราะทำให้เกิด stroke จากลิ่มเลือดในหัวใจ และพบร่วมกับ myositis โดยเฉพาะจากยา immune checkpoint inhibitor ที่มีกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง หนังตาตก และหัวใจอักเสบพร้อมกัน ตรวจ troponin ECG echo และ cardiac MRI รักษาด้วยสเตียรอยด์และยากดภูมิในรายที่เกิดจากภูมิคุ้มกัน

name: Myoclonic encephalopathy
formal: Disorder with myoclonus and encephalopathy from metabolic, toxic, post-hypoxic or neurodegenerative causes, or opsoclonus-myoclonus in childhood.
simple: A brain condition with muscle jerks and reduced alertness caused by various illnesses or poisons.
th: ภาวะสมองทำงานผิดปกติร่วมกับการกระตุกแบบ myoclonus จากเมตาบอลิก ยา การขาดออกซิเจน หรือโรคเสื่อม ในเด็กเล็กอาจเป็นกลุ่ม opsoclonus–myoclonus
tempoNote: Most causes evolve over hours to weeks; degenerative and prion causes progress over weeks to months
feat: Altered consciousness, confusion or irritability with multifocal or generalised myoclonic jerks
Adult causes: uraemia, liver failure, hypoxia, drugs, serotonin toxicity, Hashimoto encephalopathy, CJD
Childhood form (Kinsbourne): opsoclonus, myoclonus, ataxia and irritability, often with neuroblastoma
Seizures and asterixis may coexist
Course depends entirely on the cause
inv: Metabolic panel, ammonia, drug levels, thyroid function and antibodies
EEG to exclude non-convulsive status and identify periodic patterns
MRI brain, CSF including 14-3-3/RT-QuIC and autoimmune panel when indicated
In children: urine catecholamines, chest and abdominal imaging for neuroblastoma

case.who: 18-month-old girl admitted to a children's hospital in Bangkok
case.story: After a cold two weeks ago she became irritable, stopped walking and has jerky arms and wild darting eye movements.
case.exam: Chaotic multidirectional saccades (opsoclonus), truncal ataxia, multifocal limb myoclonus, very irritable.
case.tests: MRI brain normal; urine VMA mildly raised; chest MRI shows a posterior mediastinal mass.
case.q: What syndrome is this and what is the treatment approach?
case.a: Opsoclonus–myoclonus (myoclonic encephalopathy of infancy) associated with neuroblastoma: tumour resection plus immunotherapy (corticosteroids or ACTH, IVIG, often rituximab) to improve long-term neurodevelopment.

det.patho: This is a descriptive umbrella rather than one disease. In adults, metabolic toxins, drugs and hypoxic or prion injury cause cortical and reticular hyperexcitability. In infants, Kinsbourne's myoclonic encephalopathy is an immune-mediated cerebellar and brainstem disorder, paraneoplastic with neuroblastoma in about half and otherwise post-infectious.
det.clinical: Adults present with confusion or reduced consciousness plus irregular jerks, sometimes stimulus-sensitive. Children with opsoclonus–myoclonus develop sleep disturbance, irritability, ataxia and opsoclonus over days to weeks. Other important causes include post-hypoxic myoclonus, autoimmune encephalitis, serotonin syndrome and progressive myoclonus epilepsies.
det.diagnosis: Work-up aims at the cause: metabolic and drug screen, EEG, MRI and CSF analysis. In children, actively search for neuroblastoma with urine catecholamines and MRI or MIBG scanning, repeating if initially negative. Autoimmune and prion tests are reserved for suggestive cases.
det.treatment: Correct metabolic causes and remove toxic drugs. Symptomatic myoclonus control with levetiracetam, clonazepam or valproate. Immune causes need immunotherapy: steroids, IVIG, plasma exchange and rituximab; tumours are removed. Prion disease is managed supportively.
det.prognosis: Metabolic and drug causes generally recover; childhood opsoclonus–myoclonus often leaves cognitive and behavioural sequelae despite treatment.
pearls: In a toddler with jerks and darting eyes, look for neuroblastoma.
Check EEG to avoid missing non-convulsive status.
Treat the cause — anticonvulsants alone rarely fix the encephalopathy.

simple: A kind of epilepsy in which the main seizures are sudden muscle jerks.

Triggers: sleep deprivation, alcohol, flashing lights

det.patho: Myoclonic seizures arise from brief synchronous discharges in thalamocortical networks. Most idiopathic forms have polygenic susceptibility with occasional single-gene causes, whereas progressive myoclonic epilepsies result from defined genetic disorders of lysosomes, mitochondria or neuronal proteins (e.g. CSTB, EPM2A/NHLRC1, CLN genes, MT-TK).
det.clinical: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy begins in adolescence with morning jerks, often later complicated by tonic-clonic seizures. Infancy-onset myoclonic epilepsy and epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures (Doose) occur in younger children. Progressive myoclonic epilepsies present in childhood or youth with increasing action myoclonus, seizures, ataxia and cognitive decline. Myoclonus may also occur in developmental and epileptic encephalopathies such as Dravet syndrome.
det.diagnosis: History of jerks on waking and a generalised polyspike-wave EEG make the diagnosis in idiopathic forms; ask specifically, because patients may not mention jerks. Background slowing, progressive neurological signs, or failure to respond to treatment should prompt investigation for a PME. Distinguish from non-epileptic myoclonus, hypnic jerks and functional events.
det.treatment: Valproate is very effective but should be avoided in women and girls who could become pregnant unless other options fail, under current regulatory guidance. Levetiracetam is a common first choice; brivaracetam, topiramate, zonisamide, clonazepam and perampanel are alternatives. Carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, gabapentin, pregabalin and vigabatrin can aggravate myoclonus. Lifestyle advice about sleep and alcohol is important.
det.prognosis: Idiopathic forms usually respond well but often need long-term treatment; progressive forms have a poor long-term outlook.
pearls: Always ask a teenager with a first convulsion about morning jerks.
Sodium-channel blockers can worsen myoclonic epilepsies.
Slowing background EEG plus progression means think PME, not JME.

det.patho: About 80% of cases carry m.8344A>G in the mitochondrial tRNA-Lys gene; other tRNA variants account for the rest. Impaired mitochondrial translation reduces respiratory chain function, especially complexes I and IV, in brain, muscle and other energy-hungry tissues. Ragged-red fibres reflect compensatory mitochondrial proliferation under the muscle membrane. Heteroplasmy level and tissue distribution explain variable severity within a family.
det.clinical: The core features are myoclonus, generalised epilepsy, ataxia and ragged-red fibres. Many patients also have myopathy, neuropathy, deafness, optic atrophy, dementia, lipomas and cardiac involvement. Some carriers show only partial features such as deafness, lipomas or diabetes, and overlap with MELAS or Leigh syndrome occurs. It is classed among the progressive myoclonic epilepsies.
det.diagnosis: Suspect MERRF in progressive myoclonus with seizures plus multisystem or maternal-family clues. Targeted testing for m.8344A>G and full mtDNA sequencing, preferably in urine or muscle, is usually diagnostic. Lactate, EEG (generalised discharges, photosensitivity, giant SEPs) and muscle histology support it. Screen the heart, hearing, eyes and endocrine function.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying therapy. Levetiracetam is preferred for myoclonus and seizures, often with clonazepam, zonisamide or piracetam; avoid valproate. Exercise programmes, hearing aids, cardiac monitoring, surgery for disfiguring lipomas and genetic counselling for maternal relatives are part of care. Supplements such as coenzyme Q10 and L-carnitine are used without strong evidence.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; severity correlates roughly with heteroplasmy level, and some patients live into later adulthood.
pearls: Myoclonus + ataxia + neck lipomas: think MERRF.
Blood heteroplasmy can be low; test urine sediment or muscle.
Avoid valproate in all mitochondrial epilepsies.

det.patho: A myoclonic seizure results from a short, synchronous cortical discharge, usually generalised through thalamocortical circuits, that activates motor pathways for a few tens of milliseconds. The jerk is the motor expression of a polyspike on EEG. Focal myoclonic seizures are less common and arise from a localised cortical region.
det.clinical: In the 2017 ILAE seizure classification, myoclonic seizures are a generalised motor type, with related types including myoclonic-atonic and myoclonic-tonic-clonic seizures. Jerks are typically bilateral and symmetrical, often clustered after waking, and provoked by sleep loss or photic stimuli. Patients often call them 'clumsiness' or 'nerves', so they are underreported. Their presence helps classify the epilepsy syndrome and choose medication.
det.diagnosis: Ask directly about early-morning jerks. Confirm with EEG showing generalised polyspike-wave, ideally capturing a jerk with video and EMG. Separate from physiological hypnic jerks, non-epileptic myoclonus (subcortical, spinal), tics and functional jerks. Identify the underlying syndrome because prognosis and treatment depend on it.
det.treatment: Levetiracetam, valproate (with caution in females of reproductive potential), brivaracetam, topiramate, zonisamide, clonazepam and perampanel are effective. Avoid carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, gabapentinoids and vigabatrin, and be aware that lamotrigine can worsen myoclonus in some people. Advise regular sleep and moderation of alcohol.
det.prognosis: Depends on the syndrome; myoclonic seizures in JME are usually well controlled.
pearls: Myoclonic seizures keep awareness — do not exclude them because the patient remembers the event.
'Clumsy in the morning' is often myoclonus.

det.patho: Most cases have a genetic basis, usually polygenic, and in a minority a single gene is found, such as SLC2A1, SCN1A, SCN1B, SCN2A, STX1B, CHD2 or SYNGAP1. Seizures arise from generalised thalamocortical discharges; the 'atonic' component reflects a brief silent period in muscle activity following the myoclonic burst. In the 2022 ILAE classification it is a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (EMAtS).
det.clinical: Typically a normally developing toddler suddenly begins to have myoclonic-atonic drops and other generalised seizures, with an initial period of very frequent seizures. Some children have non-convulsive status with drooling, ataxia and apathy. Development may slow during the active phase. About half or more become seizure-free with normal or near-normal cognition, while others have persistent epilepsy and intellectual disability.
det.diagnosis: Video-EEG documenting myoclonic-atonic seizures is ideal. Absence of tonic seizures early, normal prior development and normal MRI help distinguish it from Lennox–Gastaut syndrome. Check GLUT1 deficiency because it is treatable, and use a gene panel for others.
det.treatment: Valproate is often first choice in young children; levetiracetam, ethosuximide (for absences), lamotrigine, topiramate, clobazam and rufinamide are also used. The ketogenic diet is particularly effective and should be started early if seizures persist. Carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin and vigabatrin can worsen seizures. Helmets protect against facial injury.
det.prognosis: Variable: many achieve remission within a few years, but prolonged non-convulsive status or tonic seizures predict poorer cognitive outcome.
pearls: Healthy toddler + sudden drop attacks + normal MRI: think Doose and test for GLUT1.
The ketogenic diet works well here; consider it early.
