det.patho: SGCE encodes epsilon-sarcoglycan, expressed in the brain including cerebellar Purkinje cells and the basal ganglia. Loss of function is thought to disrupt cerebello-thalamo-cortical and striatal circuits, producing subcortical myoclonus and dystonia. Because the maternal copy is silenced by imprinting, penetrance is high on paternal transmission and low on maternal.
det.clinical: Onset is usually before 20 with jerks of the neck, trunk and arms, plus dystonia in about half. Legs and gait are spared in most. Symptoms often improve dramatically with alcohol, which may lead to dependence, and psychiatric features are common. The disorder is not progressive in most patients.
det.diagnosis: Clinical pattern, family history with paternal transmission and alcohol responsiveness strongly suggest it; SGCE testing confirms the diagnosis in a portion of typical cases. Normal EEG and absence of cortical myoclonus markers separate it from epilepsy. Other genes can produce similar phenotypes.
det.treatment: Clonazepam, zonisamide, levetiracetam and sodium oxybate (where available) can help jerks; botulinum toxin is used for focal dystonia. Bilateral GPi deep brain stimulation markedly improves jerks as well as dystonic postures in severe cases. Address anxiety, depression and alcohol use.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is normal; disability is usually mild to moderate, and severe cases respond well to DBS.
pearls: Alcohol-responsive jerks in a teenager plus a parent with similar jerks: think SGCE.
Imprinting explains skipped generations through female carriers.
Ask about alcohol use and mood — they are part of the syndrome.
det.thd: Myoclonus dystonia (DYT11) เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมจากยีน SGCE เริ่มในวัยเด็กหรือวัยรุ่น มีการกระตุกเร็วของคอ ไหล่ และแขน ร่วมกับ dystonia เล็กน้อย และอาการดีขึ้นชัดเมื่อดื่มแอลกอฮอล์ ยีนนี้มี imprinting ทำให้แสดงอาการเมื่อได้รับจากพ่อ ผู้ป่วยมักมีความวิตกกังวลหรือซึมเศร้าร่วม การรักษาด้วย clonazepam หรือ zonisamide และในรายรุนแรงการผ่าตัด DBS ที่ GPi ได้ผลดีมาก

ddx.pt: Rhythmic oscillation rather than shock-like jerks, usually later onset
Morning myoclonus with generalised spike-wave on EEG and generalised seizures
Flowing chorea from early childhood, NKX2-1 variants, thyroid or lung involvement

aN: myoclonic dystonia | myoclonus dystonia syndrome | dyt11 | dyt sgce | hereditary essential myoclonus

name: Myofacial pain syndrome (MPS)
formal: Regional musculoskeletal pain disorder with trigger points and taut bands, causing local and referred pain and restricted motion.
simple: A common muscle pain problem with tender knots that can send pain to other areas.
more: Diagnosis is clinical; treated with physiotherapy, stretching, trigger point injection and analgesics.
th: ปวดกล้ามเนื้อเฉพาะที่จาก trigger point และ taut band ทำให้ปวดเฉพาะที่และปวดร้าวไปตำแหน่งอื่น เช่น ศีรษะหรือใบหน้า เป็นโรคระบบกล้ามเนื้อกระดูก ไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาท
tempoNote: Often follows overuse, posture strain or minor injury; may persist for months
feat: Regional aching pain in neck, shoulder, jaw or back muscles
Palpable taut band with an exquisitely tender trigger point that reproduces familiar pain
Referred pain patterns, e.g. trapezius to temple, sternocleidomastoid to forehead or ear
Local twitch response on snapping palpation; restricted range of motion
Normal neurological examination — no weakness, reflex or sensory change
inv: Clinical diagnosis by palpation
Blood tests (CK, ESR, thyroid) only if weakness or systemic features suggest another disorder
Imaging of the neck or shoulder only for red flags or radicular signs

case.story: Aching right neck and shoulder for three months with headache around the right temple by evening; works long hours on a laptop.
case.exam: Firm band in the right upper trapezius; pressing it reproduces the temple pain; neurological exam normal.
case.tests: None required.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and first-line management?
case.a: Myofascial pain syndrome; ergonomics, stretching and physiotherapy, with trigger point injection or dry needling if needed.

read.where: Progressive Encephalopathies With Onset Before Age 2

det.patho: Trigger points are thought to be areas of sustained sarcomere contraction from excessive acetylcholine release at motor end plates, causing local ischaemia and release of sensitising substances. Peripheral and central sensitisation then produce referred pain. The concept remains debated and diagnostic reliability is modest.
det.clinical: Patients describe deep aching, sometimes burning pain in a regional pattern. Head and neck muscles (trapezius, sternocleidomastoid, masseter, temporalis, suboccipitals) commonly refer pain to the head and face and may aggravate tension-type headache or temporomandibular disorder. This is a musculoskeletal condition, not a neurological disease, but it frequently reaches headache clinics.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on finding a taut band, a tender spot within it and pressure that reproduces the usual pain, with a normal neurological examination. Exclude radiculopathy, shoulder pathology, inflammatory myopathy, polymyalgia rheumatica and fibromyalgia, which is more widespread.
det.treatment: Correct posture and ergonomics, stretching and strengthening exercises, heat and manual therapy. Trigger point injection with local anaesthetic or dry needling can provide short-term relief. NSAIDs, low-dose amitriptyline and treatment of sleep disturbance may help chronic cases.
det.prognosis: Most improve with physical therapy; recurrence is common if provoking factors persist.
pearls: Pressing the trigger point should reproduce the patient’s own pain.
Neurological findings point away from MPS.
Neck muscle trigger points can drive temporal or frontal headaches.
det.thd: Myofascial pain syndrome เป็นภาวะปวดกล้ามเนื้อเฉพาะส่วนที่มี trigger point อยู่ในแถบกล้ามเนื้อแข็ง กดแล้วเจ็บมากและปวดร้าวไปตำแหน่งอื่น เช่น จากบ่าไปขมับ เป็นโรคของระบบกล้ามเนื้อกระดูก ไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาท ตรวจระบบประสาทปกติ รักษาด้วยปรับท่าทาง ยืดกล้ามเนื้อ กายภาพบำบัด และฉีดยาชาหรือฝังเข็มแห้งที่ trigger point

files.chapter: Progressive Encephalopathies With Onset Before Age 2

ddx.pt: Bilateral band-like headache; pericranial tenderness may overlap with MPS
Proximal weakness with raised CK, not focal tender bands
Brief electric facial pain triggered by light touch, not muscle palpation

aN: mps | myofacial pain syndrome | myofascial pain syndrome | myofascial trigger point pain | trigger point syndrome | regional myofascial pain

name: Myofibrillar myopathy (MFM)
formal: Group of genetic myopathies caused by mutations in DES, MYOT, CRYAB, FLNC, and others, with myofibrillar disorganisation, Z-disc dissolution, desmin accumulation, and cardiomyopathy.
simple: An inherited muscle disease where the internal muscle fibres break down, causing slowly progressive weakness and often heart problems.
more: Biopsy shows desmin-positive aggregates; gene panel; monitor cardiac and respiratory function; no specific therapy. Genetically heterogeneous muscle diseases (desmin, myotilin, BAG3) with myofibrillar disorganisation and protein aggregates on biopsy, causing distal or proximal weakness, cardiomyopathy and neuropathy.
th: กลุ่มโรคกล้ามเนื้อทางพันธุกรรมที่ Z-disc ของ sarcomere สลายตัวและมีโปรตีนอย่าง desmin สะสม จากยีน DES, MYOT, CRYAB, FLNC, BAG3 ทำให้อ่อนแรงส่วนปลายหรือต้นแขนขาร่วมกับโรคหัวใจ
tempoNote: Usually adult onset (30s–50s) with slow progression over years; BAG3 forms start in childhood and progress quickly
feat: Slowly progressive weakness, often distal legs first, later proximal and axial
Cardiomyopathy and conduction disorders (especially DES, CRYAB, FLNC)
Respiratory muscle weakness may be early
Associated features: cataract (CRYAB), peripheral neuropathy (MYOT, BAG3), rigid spine
CK normal or mildly raised
inv: Neuromuscular gene panel or exome covering DES, MYOT, CRYAB, FLNC, BAG3, ZASP (LDB3) and others
Muscle biopsy: myofibrillar disarray with desmin-, myotilin- and alpha-B crystallin-positive aggregates, rimmed vacuoles
EMG with myopathic units and often myotonic or complex repetitive discharges
ECG, Holter, echocardiography; spirometry

case.who: 45-year-old man referred to a neuromuscular clinic in Khon Kaen
case.story: For five years he has tripped on stairs and now has trouble rising from a squat; he recently fainted and needed a pacemaker for complete heart block.
case.exam: Weak ankle dorsiflexion and toe extension, mild hip flexor weakness, normal sensation.
case.tests: CK 450 U/L; EMG myopathic with complex repetitive discharges; biopsy shows desmin-positive aggregates; heterozygous DES variant.
case.q: Why is cardiac screening essential for his relatives?
case.a: Desmin-related myofibrillar myopathy is autosomal dominant and causes conduction block and cardiomyopathy that can be fatal; at-risk family members need genetic testing and cardiac surveillance.

det.patho: The Z-disc anchors sarcomeres and links them to the cytoskeleton. Variants in its proteins or chaperones (desmin, myotilin, alpha-B crystallin, filamin C, BAG3, ZASP) destabilise the Z-disc, leading to myofibrillar breakdown and accumulation of misfolded proteins that overwhelm protein-clearance systems. Most are autosomal dominant; some are recessive or de novo.
det.clinical: Weakness is commonly distal in the legs at onset but may be proximal or scapuloperoneal. Cardiac involvement (arrhythmia, conduction block, dilated, restrictive or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy) may precede, accompany or dominate the myopathy. Respiratory failure and dysphagia can appear. BAG3 variants cause a severe childhood form with neuropathy and rigid spine.
det.diagnosis: Suspect MFM in adult distal myopathy with cardiac disease or respiratory weakness. Biopsy shows characteristic aggregates and amorphous material best seen on trichrome and electron microscopy. Genetic testing identifies the gene in many but not all cases. Muscle MRI patterns differ between genes and can focus testing.
det.treatment: No disease-specific therapy exists. Management includes cardiology follow-up with pacemaker or defibrillator implantation when indicated, heart failure therapy, respiratory monitoring and non-invasive ventilation, physiotherapy and orthoses for foot drop. Genetic counselling for families.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive with variable disability; cardiac and respiratory complications are the main causes of death.
pearls: Distal myopathy plus heart block: think desmin or filamin C.
Complex repetitive or myotonic discharges on EMG are common clues.
Rimmed vacuoles are not only IBM — they occur in MFM too.
det.thd: Myofibrillar myopathy เป็นกลุ่มโรคกล้ามเนื้อทางพันธุกรรมที่โปรตีนโครงสร้างของ Z-disc ผิดปกติ ทำให้ myofibril แตกและมีโปรตีน เช่น desmin สะสม ผู้ป่วยวัยผู้ใหญ่อ่อนแรงปลายขาก่อนแล้วลามขึ้น และมักมีโรคหัวใจ เช่น heart block หรือ cardiomyopathy การวินิจฉัยใช้ชิ้นเนื้อกล้ามเนื้อร่วมกับการตรวจยีน ยังไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ การดูแลเน้นติดตามหัวใจ ใส่เครื่องกระตุ้นหัวใจเมื่อจำเป็น และดูแลการหายใจ

ddx.pt: Older age, finger flexor and quadriceps weakness, rimmed vacuoles with inflammation, no cardiac block
Broader group; MFM genes are one subset
Early contractures, humeroperoneal weakness and conduction block (EMD, LMNA)

aN: mfm | myofibrillar myopathy | myofibrillar myopathies | desminopathy | myotilinopathy | protein aggregate myopathy

name: Myopathies associated with malignancy
formal: Muscle diseases accompanying cancer, such as paraneoplastic dermatomyositis, necrotising myopathy or steroid and cachectic myopathy, with proximal weakness.
simple: Muscle weakness linked to cancer, either from the cancer itself or its treatment.
th: โรคกล้ามเนื้อที่พบร่วมกับมะเร็ง เช่น dermatomyositis แบบ paraneoplastic, necrotising myopathy, หรือกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงจาก steroid และภาวะผอมแห้งจากมะเร็ง ทำให้ต้นแขนต้นขาอ่อนแรง
tempoNote: Paraneoplastic inflammatory forms evolve over weeks to months, often within a few years before or after cancer diagnosis; cachectic and drug-related forms build up gradually
feat: Proximal symmetric weakness, often with dysphagia
Dermatomyositis skin signs (heliotrope rash, Gottron papules), especially with anti-TIF1-gamma or anti-NXP2
Necrotising myopathy with very high CK, sometimes HMGCR- or antibody-negative, linked to cancer
Cachexia, corticosteroid use and immune checkpoint inhibitor myositis as other mechanisms
Checkpoint inhibitor myositis may overlap with myasthenia and myocarditis
inv: CK, myositis-specific antibodies (TIF1-gamma, NXP2, HMGCR, SRP), troponin and ECG
EMG, muscle MRI and biopsy to define inflammatory versus necrotising versus atrophic change
Cancer screening: CT chest-abdomen-pelvis, mammography, gynaecological and GI assessment; PET-CT if high risk
In Southeast Asia, nasopharyngeal examination and EBV serology for nasopharyngeal carcinoma

case.who: 52-year-old man admitted to a regional hospital in Nakhon Si Thammarat
case.story: For six weeks he has had a violet rash on his eyelids, trouble lifting his arms and choking on rice; he also has nasal stuffiness and blood-stained nasal discharge.
case.exam: Heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, neck flexor and proximal weakness grade 4-, nasal voice.
case.tests: CK 3,200 U/L; anti-TIF1-gamma positive; endoscopy and biopsy show nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
case.q: Why must cancer screening be pursued in this myositis?
case.a: Paraneoplastic dermatomyositis with TIF1-gamma carries a high cancer risk; in Southeast Asia nasopharyngeal carcinoma is a classic association. Treat the tumour plus steroids and IVIG for the myositis.

det.patho: Tumours expressing antigens shared with regenerating muscle may trigger autoimmunity, most clearly in dermatomyositis with anti-TIF1-gamma or anti-NXP2 antibodies and in a proportion of immune-mediated necrotising myopathies. Immune checkpoint inhibitors unmask T-cell myositis. Non-immune mechanisms include cancer cachexia (type 2 fibre atrophy), corticosteroid myopathy and direct tumour infiltration.
det.clinical: Paraneoplastic dermatomyositis presents with rash, proximal weakness and dysphagia, often severe and refractory. Cancers include ovary, lung, breast, stomach, colorectal and, in Asian populations, nasopharynx. Checkpoint inhibitor myositis develops in the first weeks to months of treatment, frequently with ptosis, diplopia and myocarditis, and can be fatal. Cachectic myopathy is painless with wasting and normal CK.
det.diagnosis: Characterise the myopathy with CK, antibodies, EMG, MRI and biopsy, then screen for cancer according to antibody risk (2023 IMACS recommendations give risk-stratified screening). Repeat screening for at least three years in high-risk antibody groups. In checkpoint inhibitor cases, check troponin, ECG and acetylcholine receptor antibodies urgently.
det.treatment: Treat the cancer whenever possible, as this often improves the myopathy. Immunotherapy (corticosteroids, IVIG, methotrexate or other steroid-sparing agents) is used for inflammatory forms; IVIG is useful when immunosuppression conflicts with chemotherapy. Checkpoint inhibitor myositis requires stopping the drug and high-dose steroids, with escalation (IVIG, plasma exchange, abatacept or others) if myocarditis or myasthenic features. Nutrition and rehabilitation address cachexia.
det.prognosis: Outcome depends largely on the cancer; paraneoplastic myositis may remit after successful tumour treatment.
pearls: Adult dermatomyositis with TIF1-gamma antibodies means a careful cancer search.
In Thailand and southern China, look in the nasopharynx.
Checkpoint inhibitor myositis plus ptosis: check troponin the same day.
det.thd: Myopathies associated with malignancy คือโรคกล้ามเนื้อที่พบร่วมกับมะเร็ง ที่สำคัญคือ dermatomyositis และ necrotising myopathy แบบ paraneoplastic รวมถึงกล้ามเนื้ออักเสบจากยา immune checkpoint inhibitor และกล้ามเนื้อลีบจากภาวะผอมแห้งหรือ steroid ผู้ป่วยมีต้นแขนต้นขาอ่อนแรงและกลืนลำบาก ควรตรวจ antibody เช่น anti-TIF1-gamma และค้นหามะเร็ง ซึ่งในคนไทยต้องนึกถึงมะเร็งโพรงหลังจมูก การรักษาคือรักษามะเร็งร่วมกับ steroid หรือ IVIG

ddx.pt: Same disease without an underlying tumour; still needs screening
Paraneoplastic proximal weakness with areflexia, autonomic symptoms and incremental CMAP
Normal CK, hip flexor weakness during high-dose corticosteroids

aN: paraneoplastic myopathy | cancer associated myositis | cancer associated myopathy | paraneoplastic dermatomyositis | cancer associated necrotising myopathy

name: Myopathy
formal: Primary disease of skeletal muscle causing proximal weakness with raised CK and myopathic EMG; causes include inherited, inflammatory, endocrine, toxic and metabolic.
simple: A disease of the muscles themselves that leads to weakness, usually of the hips and shoulders.
more: Evaluation with CK, EMG, MRI, biopsy and genetics. Treatment depends on cause: steroids for inflammatory, stop statins or correct hormones for acquired forms. Heterogeneous group of primary muscle disorders causing weakness, including inherited, inflammatory, metabolic, toxic and endocrine causes. Evaluate with CK, EMG, MRI, biopsy and genetics; treatment depends on the cause.
th: โรคของกล้ามเนื้อลายโดยตรง ทำให้ต้นแขนต้นขาอ่อนแรง มักมี CK สูงและ EMG แบบ myopathic สาเหตุมีทั้งพันธุกรรม อักเสบ ต่อมไร้ท่อ ยาหรือสารพิษ และเมตาบอลิก
tempoNote: Acute (rhabdomyolysis, critical illness), subacute (inflammatory, toxic, endocrine) or chronic (inherited dystrophies and congenital myopathies)
feat: Symmetric proximal weakness: trouble rising from a chair, climbing stairs, lifting arms
Sensation normal; reflexes preserved until weakness is advanced
Possible myalgia, cramps, myoglobinuria, contractures or muscle hypertrophy depending on cause
Some patterns are distinctive: ptosis/ophthalmoplegia, distal, facial-scapular, finger flexor and quadriceps
Extra-muscular clues: rash, cataract, cardiomyopathy, respiratory weakness
inv: CK, TSH, electrolytes (K, Ca, phosphate), vitamin D, renal and liver function, drug history (statins, steroids, alcohol)
EMG/NCS to confirm myopathy and look for irritability or myotonia
Myositis antibody panel; muscle MRI to guide biopsy
Muscle biopsy and genetic panel; forearm exercise test or acylcarnitines for metabolic myopathies

case.who: 60-year-old woman with hypertension and dyslipidaemia seen at a district hospital in Ratchaburi
case.story: Three months after her atorvastatin dose was doubled, she struggled to rise from the floor and to climb the stairs to her house; stopping the statin did not help.
case.exam: Symmetric hip and shoulder girdle weakness grade 4-, no rash, normal sensation and reflexes.
case.tests: CK 6,500 U/L; EMG irritable myopathy; anti-HMGCR antibodies strongly positive; MRI thigh oedema.
case.q: Why did stopping the statin not resolve her myopathy?
case.a: This is anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotising myopathy, an autoimmune myopathy that persists after statin withdrawal and needs immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG, methotrexate).

det.patho: Myopathies arise from structural gene defects (dystrophies, congenital myopathies), ion channel disorders, metabolic defects of glycogen, lipid or mitochondrial energy production, immune attack (inflammatory myopathies), endocrine disturbance (thyroid, adrenal, parathyroid) and toxins or drugs (statins, alcohol, steroids, colchicine, chloroquine). The final pathway is loss of functional contractile tissue or failure of excitation–contraction coupling.
det.clinical: Most cause proximal symmetric weakness without sensory loss. Tempo, family history, triggers (exercise, fasting, drugs), and patterns such as ocular, distal or asymmetric involvement narrow the differential. Episodic weakness suggests channelopathies or metabolic myopathy; dark urine after exertion suggests rhabdomyolysis. Cardiac and respiratory involvement must be sought in every case.
det.diagnosis: A structured approach combines the pattern of weakness with CK, EMG, MRI and targeted tests. High CK favours necrotising, inflammatory or dystrophic processes; normal CK occurs in steroid, congenital and some mitochondrial myopathies. Antibodies, biopsy and genetic panels confirm specific diagnoses. Always exclude hypothyroidism, hypokalaemia and drug causes.
det.treatment: Treatment depends on cause: immunotherapy for inflammatory myopathies, withdrawal of offending drugs, hormone correction, enzyme replacement for Pompe disease and dietary measures for some metabolic myopathies. Supportive care includes physiotherapy, respiratory and cardiac monitoring and orthotics. Anaesthetic precautions matter in RYR1-related and dystrophic disorders.
det.prognosis: Acquired myopathies often improve with treatment; inherited forms usually progress slowly.
pearls: Weakness with normal sensation and preserved reflexes — think muscle or junction.
Normal CK does not exclude myopathy.
A statin myopathy that persists after stopping the drug needs HMGCR testing.
det.thd: Myopathy คือโรคของกล้ามเนื้อลายเอง ผู้ป่วยมักอ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขาสองข้างเท่ากัน ลุกจากเก้าอี้หรือขึ้นบันไดลำบาก ความรู้สึกปกติ สาเหตุมีหลายกลุ่ม ได้แก่ พันธุกรรม การอักเสบ ต่อมไร้ท่อ ยาเช่น statin และ steroid และโรคเมตาบอลิก การตรวจ CK, EMG, MRI กล้ามเนื้อ antibody ชิ้นเนื้อ และยีนช่วยหาสาเหตุ การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ เช่น immunotherapy หยุดยา หรือแก้ฮอร์โมน

ddx.pt: Fatigable weakness with ptosis and diplopia, normal CK
Neurogenic EMG, fasciculations and reduced reflexes
Proximal weakness with areflexia, dry mouth and post-exercise facilitation

aN: myopathies | primary muscle disease | muscle disease | myopathic weakness

name: Myorhythmia (mobile spasms)
formal: Slow, rhythmic 1 to 4 Hz repetitive movements of face, limbs or palate, often from brainstem lesions; seen in Whipple disease with oculomasticatory myorhythmia.
simple: Slow repeating rhythmic movements, often of the jaw or limbs, usually from a brainstem problem.
th: การเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติเป็นจังหวะช้า 1–4 ครั้งต่อวินาทีของใบหน้า ลิ้น ขากรรไกร หรือแขนขา มักเกิดจากรอยโรคก้านสมอง ลักษณะเฉพาะคือ oculomasticatory myorhythmia ใน Whipple disease
tempoNote: Emerges weeks to months after a brainstem lesion or with an evolving inflammatory disease; persists at rest and during sleep
feat: Slow (about 1–4 Hz), rhythmic, repetitive movements, less sinusoidal than tremor
Affects face, jaw, tongue, palate, eyes or limbs; present at rest and often in sleep
Oculomasticatory myorhythmia: pendular vergence eye movements with synchronous jaw contractions — virtually diagnostic of Whipple disease
Other causes: brainstem stroke, anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, drugs, neurodegeneration, toxins
inv: MRI brain (brainstem, thalamus, hypothalamus); video recording of movements; EMG for frequency
Whipple work-up: Tropheryma whipplei PCR on CSF, duodenal biopsy (PAS-positive macrophages), blood or saliva
Autoimmune encephalitis antibodies when context fits

case.story: Eight months of weight loss, diarrhoea and joint pains, now forgetful and sleepy with odd rhythmic chewing movements.
case.exam: Slow convergent-divergent eye oscillations in time with jaw contractions, vertical gaze palsy, mild cognitive impairment.
case.tests: Duodenal biopsy: PAS-positive foamy macrophages; T. whipplei PCR positive in CSF.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the usual treatment?
case.a: CNS Whipple disease with oculomasticatory myorhythmia; IV ceftriaxone for about 2 weeks then prolonged oral co-trimoxazole (or doxycycline with hydroxychloroquine).

det.patho: Myorhythmia is thought to arise from disrupted brainstem and diencephalic circuits, particularly involving the dentato-rubro-olivary pathway and tegmentum, generating slow oscillation. In Whipple disease, Tropheryma whipplei infects the hypothalamus, brainstem and other deep structures. The mechanism is incompletely understood, and the term 'mobile spasm' is an older label.
det.clinical: Movements are slow and rhythmic, repeat at a fixed rate, and can affect the eyes, face, jaw, tongue, palate or limbs. Patients may also have gaze palsy, cognitive change, hypersomnia or hypothalamic signs. Whipple disease often begins with weight loss, arthralgia and diarrhoea, though isolated CNS disease occurs. In anti-NMDA encephalitis, orofacial myorhythmia may appear during the hyperkinetic phase.
det.diagnosis: Recognise the movement on video and confirm its slow frequency with EMG. MRI looks for brainstem or diencephalic lesions. Always test for Whipple disease with PCR and biopsies because it is curable yet lethal when overlooked; check autoimmune encephalitis antibodies and drug history.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: for Whipple disease, a CNS-penetrating regimen such as IV ceftriaxone followed by a year of co-trimoxazole, or doxycycline with hydroxychloroquine, with monitoring for relapse. Immunotherapy for autoimmune encephalitis. Symptomatic options for the movement itself include clonazepam, levetiracetam or other agents, with limited evidence.
det.prognosis: Depends on the cause; treated Whipple disease can improve but relapses and residual deficits are common.
pearls: Eyes converge-diverge in time with chewing = oculomasticatory myorhythmia = Whipple disease until proved otherwise.
Myorhythmia is slower than most tremors and persists in sleep.
det.thd: Myorhythmia คือการเคลื่อนไหวเป็นจังหวะช้าราว 1–4 ครั้งต่อวินาทีของใบหน้า ขากรรไกร ลิ้น ตา หรือแขนขา มักเกิดจากรอยโรคก้านสมอง รูปแบบที่ตาเคลื่อนเข้าออกพร้อมการขบกราม (oculomasticatory myorhythmia) แทบบ่งชี้ Whipple disease ต้องตรวจ PCR หาเชื้อ T. whipplei และตัดชิ้นเนื้อลำไส้ รักษาด้วย ceftriaxone ตามด้วย co-trimoxazole นาน ส่วนสาเหตุอื่นเช่น anti-NMDA encephalitis และ stroke รักษาตามสาเหตุ

det.patho: MYH7 encodes slow beta-myosin heavy chain, expressed in type 1 skeletal fibres and heart. Variants near the tail region impair myosin filament assembly, so abnormal myosin accumulates beneath the sarcolemma as hyaline bodies. Other MYH7 variants cause Laing distal myopathy or cardiomyopathy, forming a spectrum.
det.clinical: Weakness may begin in childhood or adulthood, typically with scapuloperoneal or proximal pattern and slow progression. Some develop respiratory weakness; cardiomyopathy is variable but should be checked. Families may show wide variability in severity.
det.diagnosis: Biopsy demonstrates hyaline bodies that stain for slow myosin; they can be patchy. Muscle MRI may show a selective pattern. MYH7 sequencing confirms the diagnosis and allows cascade testing.
det.treatment: No disease-specific therapy exists. Physiotherapy, ankle-foot orthoses, scapular support, and respiratory and cardiac surveillance are the mainstays. Genetic counselling for dominant inheritance.
det.prognosis: Usually slowly progressive with preserved walking for many years; respiratory or cardiac involvement determines risk.
pearls: Hyaline bodies in type 1 fibres point to MYH7.
MYH7 links skeletal myopathy and cardiomyopathy — always screen the heart.
Scapuloperoneal weakness has a broad differential including FSHD.

det.patho: Inflammatory myopathies are autoimmune diseases with distinct mechanisms. Dermatomyositis involves type I interferon-driven injury to capillaries and perifascicular fibres. Necrotising myopathy is mediated by autoantibodies and complement against fibres. Antisynthetase syndrome targets tRNA synthetases with lung involvement. IBM combines cytotoxic T-cell inflammation with degenerative protein aggregation.
det.clinical: Most patients present with subacute symmetric proximal weakness and sometimes dysphagia, myalgia or respiratory symptoms. Extramuscular features define subtypes: skin rash, interstitial lung disease, arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, cardiac involvement. Polymyositis as a separate entity is now rarely diagnosed after better classification. Cancer risk is highest in dermatomyositis within three years of diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: Combine clinical pattern, CK, EMG, antibodies, muscle MRI and biopsy. Antibodies such as anti-Jo-1, anti-Mi-2, anti-TIF1-gamma, anti-NXP2, anti-MDA5, anti-HMGCR, anti-SRP and anti-cN1A guide subtype and prognosis. Screen lungs and for cancer according to subtype. Exclude drug-induced, endocrine, infective and genetic myopathies.
det.treatment: First-line therapy is corticosteroids plus a steroid-sparing agent (methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate). IVIG has proven benefit in dermatomyositis and is valuable in necrotising myopathy; rituximab, tacrolimus or cyclophosphamide are used for refractory or lung-dominant disease. IBM does not respond to immunotherapy; management is exercise, mobility aids and dysphagia care. Monitor bone health and glucose on steroids.
det.prognosis: Most dermatomyositis and antisynthetase patients improve; lung disease, cancer and anti-MDA5 rapidly progressive ILD carry worse outcomes; IBM progresses slowly.
pearls: Classify by antibody — it predicts lung, skin and cancer risk.
Steroid-unresponsive 'polymyositis' over 50: reconsider IBM.
Anti-MDA5 dermatomyositis can cause rapidly fatal lung disease with little weakness.

det.patho: Myotonia results from muscle membrane hyperexcitability: reduced chloride conductance (CLCN1, or missplicing in myotonic dystrophy) or impaired inactivation of sodium channels (SCN4A) lets the fibre fire repeated action potentials after voluntary activity stops. Potassium accumulating in T-tubules adds to depolarisation. Drugs such as some statins, fibrates and chloroquine can rarely induce it.
det.clinical: Patients describe stiffness, slowness to release objects, trouble starting movement and sometimes falls when startled. In DM1 myotonia is mild compared with weakness and systemic involvement; in myotonia congenita it is the main complaint, often with muscle hypertrophy. Paradoxical myotonia, worsening with repetition and cold, is typical of paramyotonia congenita.
det.diagnosis: Elicit grip, eyelid and percussion myotonia clinically. EMG confirms myotonic discharges and helps distinguish from neuromyotonia and pseudomyotonia. Genetic testing defines the cause; clinical and systemic features (cataract, cardiac conduction, frontal balding, family history) guide which test first.
det.treatment: Mexiletine is the best-established treatment for disabling myotonia; ECG screening is required before use. Alternatives include lamotrigine, carbamazepine and others. Avoid depolarising relaxants (succinylcholine) and be cautious with anaesthesia; avoid triggers such as cold in paramyotonia.
det.prognosis: Non-dystrophic myotonias do not shorten life; outlook in myotonic dystrophy depends on cardiac and respiratory involvement.
pearls: Warm-up suggests chloride channel myotonia; worsening with repetition suggests paramyotonia.
Ask a DM1 patient to grip and release your hand — the slow release is often unnoticed by them.
Check the ECG before starting mexiletine.
det.thd: Myotonia คือการที่กล้ามเนื้อคลายตัวช้าหลังเกร็งหรือถูกเคาะ เกิดจาก ion channel ของเยื่อหุ้มกล้ามเนื้อผิดปกติ เช่น chloride channel (CLCN1) หรือ sodium channel (SCN4A) พบใน myotonic dystrophy และ myotonia congenita อาการมักดีขึ้นเมื่อขยับซ้ำ ๆ EMG พบ myotonic discharge ที่มีเสียงขึ้นลงเฉพาะตัว การวินิจฉัยสาเหตุใช้การตรวจยีน การรักษาอาการใช้ mexiletine และควรหลีกเลี่ยง succinylcholine

det.patho: Loss-of-function variants in CLCN1 reduce the resting chloride conductance of the muscle membrane. Without this electrical buffer, potassium accumulating in the T-tubules after activity depolarises the fibre and triggers repetitive self-sustaining discharges, so relaxation is delayed. Dominant (Thomsen) and recessive (Becker) forms exist; the recessive form is more common and more severe.
det.clinical: Stiffness is most noticeable at the start of movement after rest — rising from a chair, starting to run, releasing a grip — and lessens with repeated contractions (warm-up). Muscles are often hypertrophied, giving an athletic build. Becker patients may have brief transient weakness when first moving and mild fixed distal weakness later. Cold, pregnancy and emotional startle can worsen stiffness. There are no systemic features, which separates it from myotonic dystrophy.
det.diagnosis: Grip and percussion myotonia on examination with warm-up favour the diagnosis. Needle EMG shows abundant myotonic discharges in many muscles. The short exercise test, ideally with cooling, displays a characteristic CMAP pattern that helps separate chloride from sodium channel myotonia. CLCN1 sequencing confirms the diagnosis; CK is normal or slightly raised. Check ECG and eyes only if myotonic dystrophy is still in question.
det.treatment: Many patients need no drugs and learn to warm up. When stiffness limits function, mexiletine is the best-supported option (with baseline ECG); alternatives include lamotrigine, carbamazepine or other sodium-channel blockers. Depolarising muscle relaxants such as suxamethonium can cause severe masseter spasm and must be avoided; some drugs like beta-agonists may aggravate myotonia.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is normal and the disorder is usually stable. Recessive forms may develop mild distal weakness over time.
pearls: Warm-up = chloride channel (CLCN1); worsening with repetition = sodium channel (paramyotonia).
Hypertrophied muscles without cataract or cardiac block distinguish it from DM1.
Flag suxamethonium risk on the anaesthetic record.

8 - Cramps, Muscle Stiffness, and Exercise Intolerance

det.patho: Heterozygous gain-of-function variants in SCN4A, which encodes the sodium channel of skeletal muscle, impair fast inactivation and leave a persistent sodium current. After voluntary contraction, muscle fibres re-fire repeatedly. Raised extracellular potassium depolarises the membrane further, which explains potassium sensitivity. The condition belongs to the potassium-aggravated myotonias.
det.clinical: Stiffness starts in the second decade, though cramps in toes, fingers and eyelids may appear in childhood, especially when tired or cold. Severity swings from day to day, and a bad day may follow exercise or potassium intake rather than occurring at once. Muscles of limbs, trunk and the extraocular muscles can be affected, but strength is preserved and there are no true attacks of paralysis.
det.diagnosis: Clinical history is suggestive, and EMG shows myotonic discharges on needle insertion and voluntary contraction. Mild reduction of CMAP amplitude can follow cooling or potassium loading. Gene sequencing of SCN4A confirms it, and testing relatives may be helpful. Distinguish from CLCN1 myotonia congenita, paramyotonia and DM1/DM2 using the pattern of provocation, weakness and multisystem features.
det.treatment: Treatment is needed only if symptoms interfere with life. Mexiletine, which blocks sodium channels, is the drug with the best evidence; acetazolamide is an alternative, especially if potassium sensitivity dominates. Lamotrigine or ranolazine may be used when mexiletine is not tolerated. Advise reduction of high-potassium foods in some patients, and warn anaesthetists, because depolarising relaxants such as suxamethonium can cause severe spasm in sodium channel myotonias.
det.prognosis: Benign, non-progressive course with normal life expectancy; symptoms can be controlled with drugs and lifestyle.
pearls: Delayed stiffness after exercise plus potassium sensitivity: think SCN4A.
Examine on several days, because myotonia fluctuates.
Avoid suxamethonium and flag the diagnosis to anaesthetists.

case.story: Stiff and muscular since toddlerhood, cannot run, and became blue and rigid after drinking a large glass of orange juice.

det.patho: Severe SCN4A gain-of-function variants cause markedly impaired sodium channel inactivation, leading to continuous electrical instability of the muscle membrane. Potassium further depolarises the membrane and worsens stiffness. Myotonia permanens is the extreme end of the potassium-aggravated myotonia spectrum.
det.clinical: Children show persistent, generalised stiffness that interferes with movement and breathing, with marked muscle hypertrophy. Respiratory crises triggered by potassium or exercise can be life-threatening. Severe neonatal episodic laryngospasm, related to SCN4A, is a recognised early-life manifestation in some families.
det.diagnosis: EMG demonstrates continuous myotonic activity. Genetic testing of SCN4A confirms. Differentiate from other continuous muscle activity syndromes (Schwartz–Jampel, neuromyotonia, stiff-person spectrum) by clinical features and EMG pattern.
det.treatment: Mexiletine is usually highly effective; carbamazepine or other sodium channel blockers are alternatives. Avoid potassium-rich foods and suxamethonium. Provide an emergency plan for respiratory crises.
det.prognosis: Good with treatment, though untreated respiratory crises can be dangerous.
pearls: Constant myotonia with hypertrophy and respiratory crises: myotonia permanens.
Neonatal laryngospasm can be an SCN4A channelopathy — sodium channel blockers may help.
Avoid potassium loads in all potassium-aggravated myotonias.

det.patho: Both types are caused by expanded repeats transcribed into RNA that accumulates in nuclear foci and sequesters splicing regulators (MBNL proteins). Many genes then express fetal splice isoforms, including the chloride channel (causing myotonia) and insulin receptor. In DM1 the CTG repeat expands across generations, especially through the mother, producing anticipation.
det.clinical: DM1 ranges from congenital (severe hypotonia, respiratory failure, intellectual disability) through childhood and classic adult forms to mild late-onset cataract. Systemic features often matter more than weakness: arrhythmia, respiratory failure, dysphagia, daytime sleepiness, diabetes. DM2 is milder, more proximal and painful, and often diagnosed late.
det.diagnosis: Clinical recognition plus genetic testing; EMG supports. In DM1 repeat size broadly correlates with severity and onset. DM2 can be missed on EMG and requires specific CNBP testing. Screen systematically for cardiac, respiratory, ocular and endocrine complications.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy yet; antisense oligonucleotide and other trials are under way. Management follows consensus care guidelines: annual ECG, pacemaker or ICD when indicated, non-invasive ventilation, cataract surgery, glucose control, modafinil for hypersomnolence, mexiletine for troublesome myotonia (after cardiac assessment). Anaesthesia carries risk of prolonged respiratory depression. Genetic counselling, especially for women at risk of having a congenitally affected child.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is reduced in DM1, mainly from respiratory and cardiac causes; DM2 has a better outlook.
pearls: Ask about cataract at a young age and a floppy baby in the family.
Anticipation through maternal transmission causes congenital DM1.
Every DM patient needs regular ECG — conduction disease can be silent.

det.patho: An unstable CTG expansion in the 3' untranslated region of DMPK produces toxic RNA that binds MBNL splicing factors, leaving many transcripts in fetal splicing patterns. Mis-splicing of CLCN1 gives myotonia, of the insulin receptor gives insulin resistance, and of cardiac sodium channels contributes to conduction disease. Repeat length increases in successive generations.
det.clinical: Classic adult DM1 combines distal and facial weakness, myotonia, cataract and multisystem features. Childhood-onset forms present mainly with learning and behavioural problems. Congenital DM1, almost always maternally transmitted, causes neonatal hypotonia, respiratory failure and clubfeet. Late-onset forms may have only cataract.
det.diagnosis: The clinical pattern is often recognisable at the bedside; genetic testing for the DMPK repeat confirms. EMG with myotonic discharges supports but is not required when genetic testing is available. Systematic screening of heart, lungs, eyes, endocrine and GI systems is essential at diagnosis.
det.treatment: Care is multidisciplinary under international consensus guidance. Key steps are annual ECG, referral for electrophysiology when conduction is abnormal, pacemaker or ICD as indicated, non-invasive ventilation, cataract surgery, diabetes management, and modafinil for sleepiness. Mexiletine helps disabling myotonia but needs cardiac clearance. Anaesthetic precautions for sedatives and opioids. Gene-targeted therapies are in trials.
det.prognosis: Reduced life expectancy, mostly from respiratory failure and cardiac arrhythmia.
pearls: Handshake that will not let go plus ptosis and baldness: DM1.
Unexplained heart block in a young adult: check for myotonia.
Women with DM1 risk having a baby with congenital DM1.

det.patho: An autosomal dominant disorder caused by CTG repeat expansion within the non-coding 3′ end of the DMPK gene (chromosome 19). The mutant RNA forms nuclear foci that sequester MBNL splicing regulators, causing mis-splicing of many transcripts, such as the muscle chloride channel (myotonia) and insulin receptor (insulin resistance). Repeat size tends to grow across generations (anticipation), especially via maternal transmission, and larger expansions cause earlier, more severe disease, including congenital DM1.
det.clinical: Adult-onset DM1 causes distal limb weakness (finger flexors, ankle dorsiflexors), facial, jaw and neck flexor weakness with ptosis, temporal wasting and frontal balding producing a 'hatchet face', and grip or percussion myotonia. Multisystem features include early cataracts, cardiac conduction disease and arrhythmias, insulin resistance, hypogonadism, excessive daytime sleepiness, apathy, gastrointestinal dysmotility and respiratory muscle weakness. Congenital DM1 presents with neonatal hypotonia, respiratory failure and intellectual disability.
det.diagnosis: Genetic testing for the DMPK CTG expansion is definitive (normal under about 35 repeats; disease usually above 50). EMG shows myotonic discharges with myopathic units, which may be used if genetics is delayed. CK is normal or mildly raised. Baseline assessment includes ECG and Holter, echocardiography, slit-lamp examination, glucose and HbA1c, thyroid and gonadal function, pulmonary function tests and a sleep evaluation.
det.treatment: Management is multidisciplinary and largely supportive. Annual ECG screening, with electrophysiology study and pacemaker or ICD when conduction disease or arrhythmia is found, is the main life-saving intervention. Mexiletine can relieve troublesome myotonia (with cardiac screening), modafinil helps sleepiness, and NIV treats respiratory failure. Provide cataract surgery, orthoses, diabetes care and genetic counselling. Anaesthesia carries risk because of sensitivity to sedatives and respiratory weakness.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is reduced, mainly from respiratory failure and sudden cardiac death; severity correlates loosely with repeat length.
pearls: Distal weakness + myotonia + ptosis + early cataracts = DM1.
The heart, not the muscles, often determines survival — screen ECG yearly.
Anaesthesia is hazardous: sensitivity to opioids and sedatives.

case.story: Several years of aching thighs, trouble rising from low chairs and squatting at the market; had cataract surgery at 45. Her brother has similar thigh weakness.
case.exam: Mild hip-flexor and neck-flexor weakness, subtle grip myotonia after repeated effort, normal face.

case.q: Name two key differences from DM1.
case.a: DM2 is proximal rather than distal/facial weakness, has no congenital form or clear anticipation, and is generally milder with pain as a prominent symptom.

det.patho: DM2 is caused by an expanded CCTG tetranucleotide repeat in intron 1 of CNBP. Like DM1, expanded RNA accumulates in nuclear foci and sequesters splicing regulators (MBNL), so muscle-chloride-channel and insulin-receptor transcripts are mis-spliced, producing myotonia and insulin resistance. Repeat size correlates poorly with severity and anticipation is minimal.
det.clinical: Presentation is in adulthood with proximal weakness, myalgia, stiffness and fatigue. Myotonia may be subtle and missed on bedside testing. Multisystem features—cataract, diabetes, testicular failure, hyperhidrosis and cardiac conduction disease—are common but less severe than in DM1; cognitive involvement is mild. Many patients spend years with diagnoses such as fibromyalgia or seronegative myositis.
det.diagnosis: Suspect DM2 with proximal weakness plus pain, early cataract, or myotonic discharges on EMG. Genetic testing for the CNBP expansion is diagnostic; standard PCR may miss it, so repeat-primed or Southern methods are used. Muscle biopsy is nonspecific but may show type 2 fibre atrophy and nuclear clumps. Screen heart, eyes, glucose and endocrine function at diagnosis.
det.treatment: Management is supportive: exercise and physiotherapy, pain control (NSAIDs, gabapentinoids), and mexiletine for disabling myotonia after cardiac assessment. Annual ECG with Holter or electrophysiology for conduction disease, cataract surgery when needed, and diabetes management. Statins may worsen muscle symptoms. Inform anaesthetists given sensitivity to sedatives and possible arrhythmia.
det.prognosis: Most patients remain ambulant into old age; lifespan is near normal unless significant cardiac disease occurs.
pearls: Proximal weakness with muscle pain and early cataract in a middle-aged adult: test for DM2.
Myotonia may only be found on EMG — sample many muscles.
DM2 has no congenital form, unlike DM1.

case.story: Stiff when starting to march or climb stairs; the stiffness eases after a few steps. Muscular since childhood.
case.exam: Athletic build, grip myotonia that improves with repetition, no weakness, no cataract.

det.patho: Myotonia results from muscle membrane hyperexcitability. Reduced chloride conductance (CLCN1) or impaired sodium channel inactivation (SCN4A) causes repetitive firing after a voluntary contraction ends. In the myotonic dystrophies, the chloride channel is mis-spliced as part of a toxic RNA disorder.
det.clinical: The group divides into nondystrophic myotonias (myotonia congenita, paramyotonia congenita, sodium channel myotonias) and myotonic dystrophies. Nondystrophic forms cause stiffness, pain and sometimes transient weakness but no progressive dystrophy. Dystrophic forms add weakness, cataract, cardiac, endocrine and cognitive features. Triggers such as cold, potassium and rest help distinguish subtypes.
det.diagnosis: Clinical myotonia is confirmed by EMG. Exercise and cooling tests distinguish chloride from sodium channel disease. Genetic testing establishes the diagnosis. Always consider myotonic dystrophy first in adults, because of its cardiac implications.
det.treatment: Mexiletine is first-line for disabling nondystrophic myotonia; lamotrigine, carbamazepine or acetazolamide are alternatives. Myotonic dystrophy management focuses on systemic complications. Avoid depolarising muscle relaxants in all forms.
det.prognosis: Nondystrophic myotonias have normal life expectancy; myotonic dystrophies carry cardiac and respiratory risks.
pearls: Warm-up phenomenon: chloride channel; worse with repetition and cold: paramyotonia.

Mexiletine helps but needs an ECG first.

simple: An inner ear problem causing attacks of spinning dizziness, ringing in the ear and hearing loss that comes and goes.
ab: น้ำในหูไม่เท่ากัน
th: โรคน้ำในหูไม่เท่ากัน มีเวียนศีรษะบ้านหมุนเป็นพัก ๆ ครั้งละ 20 นาทีถึง 12 ชั่วโมง ร่วมกับหูอื้อ เสียงในหู และการได้ยินเสียงต่ำลดลงข้างเดียวที่ค่อย ๆ แย่ลง
tempoNote: Spells last 20 minutes to 12 hours, recurring in clusters over months; hearing gradually worsens and vertigo tends to burn out after years
feat: Recurrent spontaneous rotational vertigo lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours, often with vomiting
Fluctuating unilateral sensorineural hearing loss affecting low-to-mid frequencies
Aural fullness and roaring tinnitus in the affected ear, often heralding the attack
Horizontal-torsional nystagmus during attacks; normal neurological examination between them
In late disease, abrupt falls with no vertigo and no loss of consciousness (Tumarkin drop attacks)
inv: Pure-tone audiometry, ideally repeated, to document low-frequency SNHL on the symptomatic side
Video head impulse and caloric testing (calorics may be reduced while vHIT is normal)
MRI with gadolinium of internal auditory meatus to exclude vestibular schwannoma; delayed-contrast inner-ear MRI can show hydrops
Syphilis serology and autoimmune screen when bilateral or atypical

case.story: Over the past year she has had five attacks of spinning vertigo lasting 2–4 hours with vomiting; before each, her left ear feels blocked and roars. Her left ear hearing seems to come and go.
case.exam: Between attacks: normal neurology, negative head impulse test, Weber lateralises to the right.
case.tests: Audiogram: left low-frequency SNHL of 35 dB; caloric paresis 40% left; MRI IAM normal.
case.q: Does she meet criteria for definite Ménière's, and what first-line measures would you advise?
case.a: Yes — two or more 20 min–12 h spells, documented low-frequency SNHL and fluctuating aural symptoms in the same ear; advise salt reduction, betahistine and vestibular sedatives only for attacks.

read.where: Chapter 23 Neuro-Otology: Dizziness, Balance and Hearing

det.patho: Ménière's disease is associated with endolymphatic hydrops — excess endolymph distending the cochlear duct and saccule — though hydrops is also found in asymptomatic ears, so it is a marker rather than a complete explanation. Proposed contributors include impaired endolymph resorption, genetic susceptibility, autoimmunity, allergy and vascular factors. Peak onset is in the 40s to 60s and with time both ears become involved in perhaps a quarter to a third.
det.clinical: Attacks begin with ear fullness, tinnitus or muffled hearing, followed by spinning vertigo lasting hours, nausea and vomiting, and then exhaustion. Hearing fluctuates early but progressively declines, flattening across frequencies. Some develop Tumarkin otolithic crises. Vertigo often lessens after 5–10 years as vestibular function is lost, leaving hearing loss and imbalance.
det.diagnosis: The Bárány Society/AAO-HNS criteria require at least two spontaneous episodes of vertigo lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours, audiometrically confirmed low-to-mid frequency SNHL in one ear on at least one occasion, and fluctuating aural symptoms in that ear, not better explained by another disorder. Exclude vestibular schwannoma with MRI, and consider vestibular migraine, which overlaps greatly and may coexist. Delayed gadolinium inner-ear MRI can demonstrate hydrops in specialist centres.
det.treatment: Acute attacks are managed with short-term vestibular suppressants and antiemetics. Prevention includes salt and caffeine reduction and betahistine (though trial evidence is weak), with diuretics as an alternative. For persistent disabling vertigo, intratympanic steroid is tried before intratympanic gentamicin; endolymphatic sac surgery, vestibular nerve section or labyrinthectomy are reserved for refractory cases. Hearing aids and vestibular rehabilitation help long-term disability.
det.prognosis: Vertigo controls in most with stepwise treatment, but progressive hearing loss in the affected ear is common.
pearls: Vertigo for hours + fluctuating low-tone hearing loss + aural fullness in one ear = Ménière's.
A single vertigo spell with hearing loss is not Ménière's — consider labyrinthitis or AICA stroke.
Always image the IAM to exclude a schwannoma.
The two conditions overlap — Ménière's and vestibular migraine can coexist, so treat both when both sets of criteria are satisfied.
det.thd: โรคน้ำในหูไม่เท่ากัน (Ménière’s disease) สัมพันธ์กับน้ำ endolymph ในหูชั้นในมากเกิน ทำให้เวียนศีรษะบ้านหมุนเป็นพัก ๆ ครั้งละ 20 นาทีถึง 12 ชั่วโมง ร่วมกับหูอื้อ เสียงในหู และการได้ยินเสียงต่ำลดลงข้างเดียว การได้ยินแย่ลงตามเวลา วินิจฉัยจากอาการร่วมกับ audiogram และทำ MRI เพื่อแยกเนื้องอกเส้นประสาทหู รักษาด้วยลดเกลือ betahistine ยาแก้เวียนช่วงสั้น ๆ และฉีดยาเข้าหูชั้นกลางในรายที่ดื้อต่อการรักษา

name: Möbius syndrome
formal: Congenital facial diplegia with abducens palsy from brainstem cranial nerve nuclei hypoplasia, causing expressionless face, inability to abduct eyes and sometimes limb anomalies.
simple: A rare condition from birth where facial muscles and eye movements to the side are weak, giving a face with little expression.
th: อัมพาตใบหน้าสองข้างแต่กำเนิดร่วมกับกลอกตาออกด้านข้างไม่ได้ จากนิวเคลียสประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 6 และ 7 ในก้านสมองเจริญไม่ดี
tempoNote: Present from birth and non-progressive
feat: Bilateral (sometimes unilateral) congenital facial palsy: mask-like face, incomplete eye closure, poor suck
Horizontal gaze limitation from abducens or gaze centre involvement; vertical movements spared
Other cranial nerves (XII, IX, X) may be involved: tongue hypoplasia, dysphagia
Limb anomalies: talipes, Poland anomaly, digital defects
Mostly sporadic; linked to prenatal misoprostol exposure and vascular disruption; rare PLXND1/REV3L variants
inv: MRI brain: flattened floor of the fourth ventricle, absent facial colliculi, brainstem calcification
Ophthalmology and orthoptic assessment
Feeding and speech assessment; hearing test

case.who: Newborn boy at a district hospital in Mae Hong Son
case.story: Cannot suck well; mother notices he never smiles and his eyes do not close fully in sleep. She took tablets to try to end the pregnancy early on.
case.exam: Expressionless face with bilateral lower motor neuron facial weakness, eyes cannot abduct, club foot.
case.tests: MRI shows flattened floor of the fourth ventricle with absent facial colliculi.
case.q: What is the syndrome and what prenatal exposure is associated?
case.a: Möbius syndrome; misoprostol exposure in early pregnancy is a recognised association.

read.where: Chapter 13 Cranial Nerve Disorders — Facial Nerve (VII)

det.patho: Möbius syndrome results from failed development or early destruction of brainstem nuclei and fibres, particularly the facial and abducens nuclei. A vascular disruption hypothesis proposes that transient ischaemia in the subclavian or basilar territory during early gestation injures the developing brainstem and limbs. Misoprostol and other early-pregnancy insults are linked, and rare genetic forms have been identified.
det.clinical: Infants have a mask-like face, poor suck, drooling and incomplete eye closure. Horizontal gaze is limited, but convergence and vertical gaze are often preserved. Additional cranial nerve palsies, limb and chest wall anomalies and mild developmental or autistic features may be present. Speech articulation problems and social difficulties arise from lack of facial expression.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical: congenital, non-progressive facial weakness with limited abduction. MRI may show brainstem hypoplasia and calcifications. Neuromuscular disorders such as congenital myotonic dystrophy and congenital myasthenia should be excluded when weakness is generalised.
det.treatment: Management includes feeding support, eye protection with lubricants, strabismus surgery, speech therapy and orthopaedic correction of limb anomalies. Facial reanimation surgery using free gracilis muscle transfer ('smile surgery') can restore a smile. Psychosocial support helps with social interaction.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is normal; functional outcome depends on associated anomalies and feeding in infancy.
pearls: Facial diplegia plus abduction failure from birth: Möbius syndrome.
Ask about misoprostol use in early pregnancy.
Lack of facial expression is often misread as low intelligence.
det.thd: Möbius syndrome คือภาวะอัมพาตใบหน้าสองข้างแต่กำเนิดร่วมกับกลอกตาออกด้านข้างไม่ได้ จากนิวเคลียสของเส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 6 และ 7 ในก้านสมองเจริญไม่ดี ทารกหน้านิ่งไม่ยิ้ม ดูดนมลำบาก หลับตาไม่สนิท และอาจมีความผิดปกติของแขนขา สัมพันธ์กับการใช้ยา misoprostol ช่วงต้นการตั้งครรภ์ การรักษาเป็นการดูแลการกินอาหาร ป้องกันกระจกตา ฝึกพูด และผ่าตัดช่วยให้ยิ้มได้

name: Narcolepsy
formal: Chronic hypersomnia disorder with excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy (type 1) from hypocretin loss, hypnagogic hallucinations, sleep paralysis and short REM latency; associated with HLA-DQB1*06:02.
simple: A sleep disorder with overwhelming daytime sleepiness and sometimes sudden muscle weakness triggered by emotion.
th: โรคง่วงนอนกลางวันมากผิดปกติเรื้อรังจากการสูญเสียเซลล์ hypocretin (orexin) ในไฮโปทาลามัส type 1 มี cataplexy (กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงทันทีเมื่อหัวเราะหรือตกใจ) ร่วมกับฝันขณะเคลิ้มหลับและผีอำ
tempoNote: Usually starts in the teens or twenties (peak around 15 and a smaller one around 35); sleepiness is lifelong, cataplexy may appear months to years after the sleepiness
feat: Daily irrepressible sleepiness with short, refreshing naps and dreaming during naps
Cataplexy (type 1): brief bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by laughter, joking or surprise, with preserved awareness
Hypnagogic or hypnopompic hallucinations and sleep paralysis
Fragmented night sleep, automatic behaviours, weight gain; sometimes RBD
Strong link with HLA-DQB1*06:02; onset may follow H1N1 infection or vaccination
inv: Overnight polysomnography followed by MSLT: mean sleep latency ≤ 8 minutes with ≥ 2 sleep-onset REM periods (a nocturnal SOREMP can count)
CSF hypocretin-1 ≤ 110 pg/mL confirms type 1 (useful when on antidepressants or MSLT unreliable)
Two weeks of actigraphy or sleep diary before testing; withdraw REM-suppressing drugs if possible
HLA typing is supportive only — its absence makes type 1 unlikely

case.who: 19-year-old male university student from Khon Kaen
case.story: Falls asleep in lectures and once on his motorbike at a red light. When friends make him laugh his knees buckle and his jaw drops for a few seconds, but he hears everything. He sometimes cannot move on waking.
case.exam: Normal; during a joke in clinic his face sags briefly and neck tone drops.
case.tests: Polysomnography: no apnoea, SOREMP at night; MSLT mean latency 3 minutes with 4 SOREMPs.
case.q: Which type of narcolepsy is this and what medicines could help?
case.a: Narcolepsy type 1 (cataplexy present); treat sleepiness with modafinil, pitolisant or solriamfetol, and cataplexy with sodium oxybate, pitolisant or an SNRI such as venlafaxine; advise not to ride until controlled.

det.patho: Type 1 narcolepsy results from selective loss of hypocretin (orexin)-producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus, very likely through T-cell–mediated autoimmunity in HLA-DQB1*06:02 carriers. Hypocretin normally stabilises wakefulness and suppresses REM sleep, so its absence lets REM phenomena (atonia, dreaming) intrude into wake. The cause of type 2, with normal hypocretin, is less clear and the diagnosis is less stable over time.
det.clinical: Excessive daytime sleepiness is the core symptom and the first to appear; naps are short and restoring. Cataplexy ranges from facial slackening and head drops to full collapse, lasting seconds to two minutes, with intact consciousness and absent reflexes during attacks; children may show persistent facial hypotonia and tongue thrusting near onset. Sleep paralysis and vivid sleep-onset hallucinations are common but non-specific. Disrupted night sleep, obesity, depression and accidents are frequent, and diagnosis is often delayed by years.
det.diagnosis: ICSD-3 type 1 needs daily sleepiness for at least 3 months plus either cataplexy with a positive MSLT or low CSF hypocretin-1. Type 2 needs a positive MSLT without cataplexy and with normal or unmeasured hypocretin. Insufficient sleep, shift work, sedating drugs, OSA and recent antidepressant withdrawal can all produce false-positive MSLTs, so prepare carefully. Secondary narcolepsy occurs with hypothalamic tumours, sarcoid, NMOSD and anti-Ma2 encephalitis.
det.treatment: Scheduled naps and regular sleep help. Wake-promoting options include modafinil or armodafinil, pitolisant (an H3 inverse agonist that also reduces cataplexy), solriamfetol, and methylphenidate or amphetamines. Sodium oxybate (and low-sodium oxybate) improves sleepiness, cataplexy and night sleep; venlafaxine, SSRIs or clomipramine suppress cataplexy, but stopping them abruptly can cause rebound status cataplecticus. Orexin-2 receptor agonists are in advanced trials. Counsel on driving, school and work adjustments; modafinil reduces hormonal contraceptive efficacy.
det.prognosis: Lifelong but usually non-progressive; most achieve useful function with treatment, although sleepiness rarely disappears completely.
pearls: Cataplexy = emotion-triggered weakness with full awareness — ask about laughter.
Low CSF hypocretin is the most specific test for type 1.
Suddenly stopping an antidepressant used for cataplexy can trigger repeated attacks.
det.thd: Narcolepsy เป็นโรคง่วงนอนมากผิดปกติจากเซลล์สร้าง hypocretin ในไฮโปทาลามัสถูกทำลาย (น่าจะจากภูมิคุ้มกัน สัมพันธ์กับ HLA-DQB1*06:02) อาการเด่นคือหลับง่ายกลางวัน งีบแล้วสดชื่น type 1 มี cataplexy คือกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงทันทีเมื่อหัวเราะแต่ยังรู้สึกตัว ร่วมกับผีอำและเห็นภาพหลอนตอนเคลิ้มหลับ วินิจฉัยด้วย PSG + MSLT หรือวัด hypocretin ในน้ำไขสันหลัง รักษาด้วยการงีบตามเวลา modafinil, pitolisant, solriamfetol และ sodium oxybate

qx.stem: A 24-year-old woman who works in a Bangkok call centre has had two years of daily irresistible sleep attacks that refresh her briefly, plus vivid dream-like images when falling asleep. She has never had muscle weakness with laughter. A two-week sleep diary with actigraphy shows 8 hours of sleep nightly; she took no antidepressants. Polysomnography shows a REM latency of 9 minutes and no apnoea, and the next-day multiple sleep latency test has a mean latency of 5 minutes with 3 sleep-onset REM periods. CSF hypocretin has not been measured.
qx.q: Which diagnosis does she meet?
opts: Idiopathic hypersomnia
Narcolepsy type 1
Narcolepsy type 2
Insufficient sleep syndrome
Delayed sleep–wake phase disorder
qx.why: The criteria need daily sleepiness for over 3 months and an MSLT mean latency not above 8 minutes, together with at least two REM-onset naps or night-time REM onsets; a REM latency of 15 minutes or less on the preceding night counts as one. Without cataplexy and without a low CSF hypocretin-1 (110 pg/mL or less), the diagnosis is type 2 rather than type 1. Idiopathic hypersomnia does not reach that count, and documented adequate sleep argues against insufficient sleep.

qx.stem: A 19-year-old university student from Chiang Mai has had sleepiness since age 15. Over the past year he has also dropped his tray and slumped to the floor with laughter, remaining fully awake and aware. Lumbar puncture shows CSF hypocretin-1 below 110 pg/mL. Modafinil improved his alertness but not the collapses, and he asks for one drug that would address both.
qx.q: Which treatment best covers both excessive sleepiness and cataplexy?
opts: Sodium oxybate taken at bedtime and again during the night
Methylphenidate three times daily
Modafinil at a higher dose
Zolpidem at bedtime
Fluoxetine as the only agent
qx.why: Sodium oxybate consolidates night sleep and reduces both daytime sleepiness and cataplexy; pitolisant is another option that treats both. Higher-dose modafinil and methylphenidate treat sleepiness but not cataplexy. Zolpidem has no effect on either, and an SSRI alone would not treat the sleepiness. Oxybate must not be combined with alcohol or other sedatives and requires monitoring for respiratory depression.

ddx.pt: Long unrefreshing sleep, severe sleep inertia, no cataplexy and fewer than 2 SOREMPs
Snoring, witnessed apnoeas, obesity; polysomnography shows apnoea–hypopnoea index raised
Loss of consciousness with pallor; cataplexy keeps awareness and is triggered by emotion

name: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
formal: Epithelial tumour of the nasopharynx associated with EBV, spreading through the skull base to cause multiple cranial neuropathies, headache and cervical nodes.
simple: A cancer at the back of the nose that can invade the skull base and damage nerves of the face and eyes.
th: มะเร็งโพรงหลังจมูกสัมพันธ์กับ EBV พบบ่อยในเอเชียตะวันออกเฉียงใต้ ลุกลามฐานกะโหลกทำให้เส้นประสาทสมองหลายเส้นเสีย ปวดศีรษะ และต่อมน้ำเหลืองคอโต
tempoNote: Symptoms evolve over weeks to months
feat: Neck lump, unilateral serous otitis media, epistaxis or nasal obstruction
Cranial neuropathies: VI and V commonly; IX–XII with parapharyngeal spread
Headache from skull base erosion
Common in southern China and Southeast Asia including Thailand
Late radiation complications: lower cranial neuropathies, temporal lobe necrosis, carotid stenosis
inv: Nasoendoscopy with biopsy
MRI nasopharynx and skull base
Plasma EBV DNA

case.story: Blocked left ear, then left facial numbness and diplopia over 2 months.
case.exam: Left VI palsy, V2 numbness, left serous otitis, firm upper neck node.
case.tests: Nasoendoscopy shows a mass in the fossa of Rosenmüller; biopsy undifferentiated carcinoma; EBV DNA high.
case.q: How does this spread to the cranial nerves?
case.a: Through foramen lacerum and ovale to the cavernous sinus and skull base.

det.patho: Undifferentiated non-keratinising carcinoma associated with EBV, genetic susceptibility and dietary factors (salted fish). It spreads superiorly through skull base foramina and laterally to the parapharyngeal space.
det.clinical: Presenting features include neck mass, ear and nasal symptoms, and cranial neuropathies. Late effects of radiotherapy are a major neurological issue in survivors.
det.diagnosis: Endoscopic biopsy confirms; MRI stages local extent; EBV DNA aids diagnosis and monitoring.
det.treatment: Radiotherapy (IMRT) with concurrent chemotherapy for locally advanced disease; induction chemotherapy in high-risk cases; immunotherapy for recurrent or metastatic disease.
det.prognosis: Good for early-stage disease; cranial nerve involvement indicates advanced stage but remains curable.
pearls: Unexplained cranial neuropathy in a Thai adult: look at the nasopharynx.
Unilateral serous otitis media in adults is a red flag.
Delayed lower cranial neuropathies years after radiotherapy are often radiation-induced.
det.thd: มะเร็งโพรงหลังจมูกพบบ่อยในไทย สัมพันธ์กับ EBV อาการคือก้อนที่คอ หูอื้อข้างเดียว เลือดกำเดา และเส้นประสาทสมองเสีย เช่น VI และ V จากการลุกลามฐานกะโหลก วินิจฉัยด้วยการส่องกล้องตัดชิ้นเนื้อ MRI และ EBV DNA รักษาด้วยรังสีร่วมเคมีบำบัด ผู้รอดชีวิตอาจมีผลแทรกซ้อนทางประสาทจากรังสีภายหลัง

name: Nasu-Hakola disease
formal: Polycystic lipomembranous osteodysplasia with sclerosing leukoencephalopathy from TREM2 or TYROBP mutations, causing bone cysts and presenile frontal dementia.
simple: A rare inherited disease causing bone cysts and an early dementia with personality change.
ab: Polycystic lipomembranous osteodysplasia with sclerosing leukoencephalopathy
th: โรคพันธุกรรมแบบด้อยจากยีน TREM2 หรือ TYROBP ทำให้มีถุงน้ำในกระดูกและกระดูกหักง่ายในวัยหนุ่มสาว ตามด้วยภาวะสมองเสื่อมแบบ frontal และ leukoencephalopathy ก่อนวัยอันควร
tempoNote: Bone symptoms start in the 20s; dementia emerges in the 30s and progresses to death usually by the late 40s
feat: Ankle and wrist pain and pathological fractures from multiple bone cysts in young adulthood
Frontal-type personality change, disinhibition and euphoria from the fourth decade
Progressive dementia, seizures and upper motor neuron signs
Leukoencephalopathy with basal ganglia calcification and thin corpus callosum
Autosomal recessive; most cases described from Finland and Japan
inv: X-rays of hands, wrists, ankles and feet: symmetric cystic lesions
MRI brain: white matter change, frontal atrophy; CT for basal ganglia calcification
Genetic testing of TREM2 and TYROBP
EEG for seizures

case.who: 32-year-old man referred to a memory clinic in Bangkok
case.story: He broke his wrist and ankle after minor falls in his 20s; now his family says he is reckless, jokes inappropriately and has lost his job. His parents are first cousins.
case.exam: Disinhibition, poor planning, brisk reflexes and bilateral grasp reflexes.
case.tests: X-rays show multiple cysts in the carpal and tarsal bones; MRI bifrontal atrophy and white matter change; CT basal ganglia calcification; homozygous TREM2 variant.
case.q: What links the bone cysts and the frontal dementia?
case.a: Nasu–Hakola disease (PLOSL) from TREM2/TYROBP loss, affecting microglia and osteoclasts; management is supportive with seizure control and family counselling.

det.patho: TREM2 and its adaptor TYROBP (DAP12) form a receptor complex on microglia and osteoclasts. Loss of function impairs microglial clearance and survival and osteoclast development, producing a primary microgliopathy with frontal white matter demyelination and axonal loss and abnormal bone remodelling with cyst formation. It is very rare, and phenotypes without bone disease have been reported.
det.clinical: Classic course passes through a latent phase, an osseous phase of bone pain and fractures in early adulthood, an early neuropsychiatric phase of frontal lobe syndrome in the 30s and a late phase of severe dementia and immobility. Seizures, myoclonus and pyramidal signs occur. Heterozygous TREM2 variants raise Alzheimer disease risk but do not cause PLOSL.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in young-onset frontal dementia with a history of fractures or bone pain, especially with consanguinity. Skeletal radiographs, brain imaging and genetic testing confirm. Exclude other leukoencephalopathies and frontotemporal dementia genes.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying treatment exists. Care includes orthopaedic management, antiseizure medication, behavioural support, safety planning and genetic counselling for siblings. Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, considered for CSF1R disease, remains experimental for PLOSL.
det.prognosis: Progressive, with death usually in the fifth decade.
pearls: Young-onset frontal dementia plus old wrist or ankle fractures: X-ray the bones.
PLOSL is a microgliopathy, linked conceptually to CSF1R leukoencephalopathy.
Heterozygous TREM2 variants are an Alzheimer risk factor, a separate issue.
det.thd: Nasu-Hakola disease (PLOSL) เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมแบบด้อยจากยีน TREM2 หรือ TYROBP ซึ่งสำคัญต่อ microglia และ osteoclast ผู้ป่วยมีถุงน้ำในกระดูกข้อมือข้อเท้าและกระดูกหักง่ายในวัย 20 ปี ต่อมาในวัย 30 ปีมีพฤติกรรมเปลี่ยนแบบ frontal และสมองเสื่อม ร่วมกับชักและ leukoencephalopathy การวินิจฉัยใช้ภาพรังสีกระดูก MRI สมอง และการตรวจยีน ยังไม่มีการรักษาเฉพาะ เน้นดูแลประคับประคองและให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

Wider group including CSF1R-related leukoencephalopathy, which shares microglial pathology

name: Neck flexion dystonia
formal: Anterocollis, a cervical dystonia pattern with forward neck flexion, seen in idiopathic dystonia, multiple system atrophy, Parkinson disease and myopathy, such as the dropped head syndrome.
simple: Abnormal forward bending of the neck so the chin drops toward the chest.
more: Distinguish from neck extensor myopathy and parkinsonian syndromes. Botulinum toxin to the longus colli and sternocleidomastoid has mixed results; collars and physiotherapy help.
th: cervical dystonia แบบก้มคอไปด้านหน้า พบใน dystonia ปฐมภูมิ multiple system atrophy, Parkinson’s disease และต้องแยกจากกล้ามเนื้อเหยียดคออ่อนแรง (dropped head syndrome)
tempoNote: Develops over months and usually persists; in parkinsonian syndromes it tends to progress with the underlying disease
feat: Forward flexion of the neck (anterocollis) or of the head on the neck (anterocaput)
Patient can often not fully extend the neck actively because flexors pull against it
Neck pain and difficulty looking ahead, eating and walking
May accompany parkinsonism (MSA in particular), or be idiopathic or drug-induced
Sensory tricks may help in primary dystonia
inv: Careful examination to separate flexor overactivity from extensor weakness
EMG of neck muscles (longus colli, sternocleidomastoid, extensors) and CK
MRI cervical spine and neck muscles; brain MRI and DAT imaging if parkinsonism suspected

case.who: 63-year-old woman attending a movement clinic in Chiang Rai
case.story: For two years she has had increasing stiffness and slowness, falls and dizziness on standing; over six months her head has dropped forward so she sees only the floor.
case.exam: Marked anterocollis that can be passively corrected only partly, symmetric akinetic-rigid syndrome, cerebellar dysarthria, orthostatic BP fall 35/15 mmHg.
case.tests: MRI: putaminal atrophy and pontine 'hot cross bun' sign; neck extensor EMG normal; CK normal.
case.q: What is the likely cause of her head drop?
case.a: Disproportionate anterocollis typical of multiple system atrophy; botulinum toxin may give modest benefit, along with physiotherapy and collar support.

det.patho: Overactivity of neck flexors (longus colli, longus capitis, scalenes, bilateral sternocleidomastoid) produces anterocollis, while in parkinsonian disorders a combination of axial dystonia, rigidity and focal extensor myopathy may contribute. The relative role of dystonia versus weakness varies between patients and is not fully understood.
det.clinical: Anterocollis is an uncommon form of cervical dystonia in isolation. It is classically disproportionate in MSA and also occurs in Parkinson disease and dopamine-blocking drug exposure. Patients develop neck pain, dysphagia and visual field restriction. It must be separated from dropped head syndrome due to neck extensor weakness in myasthenia, ALS, inflammatory or focal myopathy.
det.diagnosis: Clinically assess whether the head can be raised passively and whether extensors are weak. EMG and MRI of neck muscles help: extensor myopathy shows myopathic EMG and fatty change, dystonia shows sustained flexor activity. Screen for parkinsonism and autonomic failure.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin targeting deep flexors (longus colli via ultrasound or CT guidance, sternocleidomastoid, scalenes) helps some, though results are less reliable than in torticollis. Physiotherapy, collars and management of the underlying parkinsonian disorder are important; DBS benefit is uncertain.
det.prognosis: Often refractory and disabling, especially when part of a neurodegenerative disease.
pearls: Separate a pulling neck (dystonia) from a falling neck (extensor weakness).
Severe anterocollis in a parkinsonian patient points towards MSA.
Deep neck flexors need image-guided botulinum injection.
det.thd: Neck flexion dystonia หรือ anterocollis คือ cervical dystonia ที่ทำให้คอก้มไปด้านหน้า พบได้ใน dystonia ปฐมภูมิ Parkinson’s disease และเด่นใน multiple system atrophy ต้องแยกจาก dropped head syndrome ที่เกิดจากกล้ามเนื้อเหยียดคออ่อนแรง เช่น myasthenia หรือ ALS โดยตรวจร่างกาย EMG และ MRI กล้ามเนื้อคอ การรักษาด้วยการฉีด botulinum toxin ที่กล้ามเนื้อก้มคอส่วนลึกได้ผลไม่แน่นอน ร่วมกับกายภาพบำบัดและอุปกรณ์พยุงคอ

name: Necrotising myelopathy
formal: Acute or subacute spinal cord necrosis, as in paraneoplastic, infective, post-radiation or vascular causes, with severe and often irreversible paraplegia.
simple: Severe damage and death of tissue in the spinal cord, causing sudden leg weakness and loss of feeling.
th: ภาวะไขสันหลังตายแบบเฉียบพลันหรือกึ่งเฉียบพลัน จากสาเหตุ paraneoplastic การติดเชื้อ รังสีรักษา หรือหลอดเลือด ทำให้อัมพาตครึ่งล่างรุนแรงและมักไม่ฟื้น
tempoNote: Deficit builds over days to weeks and often ascends; vascular (fistula) forms may worsen stepwise over months
feat: Rapidly progressive, often ascending paraplegia with sensory level and sphincter failure
Flaccid areflexic legs later as grey matter is destroyed
Causes: paraneoplastic (lymphoma, lung cancer), severe NMOSD, viral infection (HSV, VZV, CMV), radiation, spinal dural arteriovenous fistula
MRI shows long swollen cord lesion with later atrophy or cavitation
Poor recovery in most
inv: MRI whole spine with contrast; spinal angiography if flow voids suggest a dural fistula
CSF cells, protein, viral PCR, cytology and flow cytometry
AQP4-IgG, MOG-IgG and paraneoplastic antibodies
CT chest-abdomen-pelvis or PET-CT for an occult tumour

case.who: 58-year-old male smoker admitted to a tertiary hospital in Ubon Ratchathani
case.story: Over three weeks his legs became weak, then completely paralysed, with numbness rising to the chest and urinary retention.
case.exam: Flaccid paraplegia, absent leg reflexes, sensory level T4, loss of anal tone.
case.tests: MRI: swollen cord with T2 signal from T1 to the conus; CSF protein 1.8 g/L, mild pleocytosis, negative viral PCR; AQP4 and MOG negative; CT chest shows a hilar mass (small cell carcinoma).
case.q: What is the probable diagnosis and expected outcome?
case.a: Paraneoplastic necrotising myelopathy; treat the cancer and give immunotherapy, but neurological recovery is usually poor.

read.where: Chapter 25 Neurologic Manifestations of Hematologic Disorders

det.patho: Necrosis of both grey and white matter over several segments may follow intense immune attack (paraneoplastic or severe NMOSD), direct viral invasion in immunocompromised hosts, delayed radiation injury, or venous hypertension from a spinal dural arteriovenous fistula (Foix–Alajouanine). The term describes pathology rather than a single cause, and older paraneoplastic reports predate antibody testing, so some may have been NMOSD.
det.clinical: Weakness and sensory loss rise over days to weeks, leading to complete paraplegia with bladder and bowel failure. Upper motor neuron signs give way to flaccidity and areflexia as anterior horn cells die. Radiation myelopathy appears months to years after radiotherapy within the field. Dural fistula causes stepwise progressive myelopathy that worsens with exercise or standing.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows long T2 lesions with cord swelling, often enhancing; later atrophy. Investigations must rapidly exclude treatable causes: AQP4 and MOG antibodies, viral PCR, and dural fistula (flow voids, angiography). CSF often has high protein with modest cells. A cancer search is required when no other cause emerges.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: immunotherapy (steroids, plasma exchange) for immune forms, antivirals for viral infection, endovascular or surgical closure of dural fistula, and cancer treatment for paraneoplastic disease. Supportive care includes thromboprophylaxis, bladder and bowel management, pressure care and rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: Severe permanent paraplegia is common; dural fistula and some immune forms may partly recover with early treatment.
pearls: Always look for a dural AV fistula in progressive myelopathy with flow voids — it is treatable.
Test AQP4 before calling a necrotising myelopathy paraneoplastic.
Flaccid legs after a spastic phase mean grey matter necrosis.
det.thd: Necrotising myelopathy คือภาวะไขสันหลังตายหลายปล้อง เกิดจาก paraneoplastic, NMOSD รุนแรง การติดเชื้อไวรัส รังสีรักษา หรือ spinal dural AV fistula ผู้ป่วยขาอ่อนแรงลามขึ้นจนเป็นอัมพาต ชาและปัสสาวะไม่ได้ภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์ MRI พบรอยโรคยาวและไขสันหลังบวม ต้องตรวจหาสาเหตุที่รักษาได้ เช่น AQP4 antibody ไวรัส และ AV fistula รวมทั้งค้นหามะเร็ง ผลการฟื้นตัวมักไม่ดี
