name: Necrotizing myopathy
formal: Myopathy with prominent muscle fibre necrosis and little inflammation, including immune-mediated forms with anti-SRP or anti-HMGCR antibodies and statin or paraneoplastic forms.
simple: A muscle disease where muscle fibres die, causing marked weakness, often linked to statin drugs or immune antibodies.
more: CK is very high; check anti-SRP and anti-HMGCR antibodies; immunotherapy with steroids, IVIG, and others is required.
th: โรคกล้ามเนื้อที่ใยกล้ามเนื้อตายเด่นแต่มีการอักเสบน้อย ส่วนใหญ่เป็นแบบภูมิคุ้มกัน (anti-SRP, anti-HMGCR) สัมพันธ์กับ statin หรือมะเร็ง CK สูงมากและต้องรักษาด้วย immunotherapy
tempoNote: Weakness usually develops over weeks to months; some HMGCR cases are slowly progressive over years and resemble a dystrophy
feat: Symmetric proximal weakness, sometimes severe, with neck flexor and dysphagia involvement
Very high CK, often above 5,000–10,000 U/L
Anti-SRP: rapid severe weakness, possible cardiac and lung involvement; anti-HMGCR: often statin-exposed adults
Little or no rash; myalgia in some
Seronegative cases carry higher cancer risk
inv: CK and myositis antibodies (SRP, HMGCR)
MRI thighs showing muscle oedema to choose a biopsy site
Muscle biopsy: scattered necrotic and regenerating fibres, sparse inflammation, MHC-I and complement deposition
Cancer screening, especially in seronegative and HMGCR-positive patients; cardiac and lung assessment

case.who: 47-year-old woman, a rubber farmer from Surat Thani
case.story: Over two months she became unable to climb into her truck or lift a basket; now she chokes on food. She has never taken a statin.
case.exam: Grade 3 hip and shoulder weakness, weak neck flexors, no rash, normal sensation.
case.tests: CK 14,000 U/L; anti-SRP strongly positive; MRI widespread thigh oedema; biopsy many necrotic fibres with minimal inflammation.
case.q: How should this be treated?
case.a: Anti-SRP immune-mediated necrotising myopathy: high-dose corticosteroids with an early steroid-sparing agent (methotrexate) and often rituximab; IVIG for severe weakness or dysphagia.

read.where: Chapter 32 Drug-Induced Disorders of the Nervous System

det.patho: IMNM is an antibody-associated myopathy: anti-SRP or anti-HMGCR antibodies activate complement on the sarcolemma and cause fibre necrosis with macrophage clearance rather than lymphocyte infiltration. Statin exposure is the main trigger for anti-HMGCR, while anti-SRP has no clear trigger. Non-immune necrotising myopathy also follows toxins, drugs and critical illness.
det.clinical: Most patients present with subacute proximal weakness and very high CK; dysphagia, neck weakness and respiratory involvement occur in severe cases. Anti-SRP disease tends to be more aggressive with muscle atrophy. HMGCR disease in young people may mimic limb-girdle dystrophy. Myocarditis and interstitial lung disease are less common than in antisynthetase syndrome but occur.
det.diagnosis: The 2017 ENMC criteria require high CK, proximal weakness and either positive SRP/HMGCR antibodies or a biopsy showing necrosis without major inflammation. Exclude hypothyroidism, toxic myopathies, dystrophies (dysferlinopathy, FKRP) and metabolic myopathies. Screen for cancer according to antibody status.
det.treatment: Start high-dose corticosteroids with an early second agent (methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate). IVIG is effective, and may be used first-line in HMGCR disease; rituximab is particularly useful in anti-SRP. Stop statins permanently in HMGCR disease. Monitor strength and CK; relapses are frequent when tapering.
det.prognosis: Many improve, but a proportion have persistent weakness, especially anti-SRP and those treated late.
pearls: Very high CK with little inflammation on biopsy suggests IMNM.
Statin myopathy that persists after stopping the statin needs anti-HMGCR testing.
Seronegative necrotising myopathy deserves a cancer search.
det.thd: Necrotizing myopathy คือโรคกล้ามเนื้อที่ใยกล้ามเนื้อตายเป็นหลักแต่มีการอักเสบน้อย ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจากภูมิคุ้มกันที่มี anti-SRP หรือ anti-HMGCR (สัมพันธ์กับ statin) ผู้ป่วยอ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขาภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์ถึงเดือน CK สูงมาก การวินิจฉัยใช้ antibody และชิ้นเนื้อกล้ามเนื้อ การรักษาคือ steroid ขนาดสูงร่วมกับยากดภูมิตัวที่สอง IVIG หรือ rituximab และต้องหยุด statin ถาวรในกลุ่ม HMGCR

qx.stem: A 66-year-old woman from Nonthaburi on atorvastatin for 2 years has 3 months of proximal weakness that persists 6 months after stopping the drug. CK is 6,200 U/L. Biopsy shows necrotic and regenerating fibres with little inflammation.
qx.q: Which antibody should be sought, and how does it affect therapy?
opts: Anti-Jo-1; add cyclophosphamide
Anti-Mi-2; no treatment is needed
Anti-AChR; thymectomy
Anti-HMGCR; immunotherapy with steroids and an additional agent such as IVIG or methotrexate is often needed
Anti-GM1; plasma exchange
qx.why: Persistent statin-associated immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy is associated with anti-HMGCR antibodies and usually requires immunotherapy, often combination, because the weakness does not resolve with drug withdrawal. The other antibodies relate to antisynthetase syndrome, dermatomyositis, myasthenia and multifocal motor neuropathy, none of which fit this biopsy and history.

name: Necrotizing vasculitis/vasculopathy
formal: Inflammatory destruction of vessel walls causing ischaemic neuropathy or myopathy, as in polyarteritis nodosa or ANCA vasculitis.
simple: Inflammation of blood vessels cutting off blood supply to nerves and muscles, leading to pain and weakness.
more: Diagnosed by biopsy and serology; treated with steroids and cyclophosphamide or rituximab.
th: การอักเสบที่ทำลายผนังหลอดเลือดจนเกิดเนื้อตาย ทำให้เส้นประสาทหรือกล้ามเนื้อขาดเลือด เช่น polyarteritis nodosa หรือ ANCA vasculitis
tempoNote: Weeks to months, with sudden painful nerve infarcts
feat: Histological term: inflammation with fibrinoid necrosis of vessel walls
Neuropathy: painful mononeuritis multiplex or asymmetric sensorimotor axonal neuropathy
Muscle involvement: myalgia, weakness, sometimes raised CK
Systemic (PAN, ANCA, cryoglobulin, connective tissue disease) or non-systemic (nerve-only) forms
Diabetic radiculoplexus neuropathy has microvasculitis
inv: Nerve (superficial peroneal or sural) plus muscle biopsy: transmural inflammation with necrosis
ESR, CRP, ANCA, hepatitis B/C, cryoglobulins, complement, ANA, HIV
NCS/EMG: asymmetric axonal loss
Urinalysis and renal function to detect systemic involvement

case.story: Painful numbness started in the right foot, followed within weeks by left foot drop and right hand weakness; no fever or weight loss.
case.exam: Asymmetric distal weakness and sensory loss in multiple nerve territories.
case.tests: ESR 60; ANCA, hepatitis serology and cryoglobulins negative; urinalysis normal; superficial peroneal nerve and peroneus brevis biopsy: necrotising vasculitis with axonal loss.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and treatment?
case.a: Non-systemic vasculitic neuropathy; glucocorticoids, adding cyclophosphamide, rituximab or methotrexate if progressive or severe.

read.where: Chapter 36: Mononeuritis Multiplex: Vasculitis (Systemic, Nonsystemic) Neuropathies

det.patho: Immune complexes, ANCA-activated neutrophils or T-cell responses attack arterial walls, producing fibrinoid necrosis, thrombosis and occlusion. Nerves are vulnerable because their blood supply has watershed regions in the mid-arm and mid-thigh. Muscle shares vessels with nerve, so combined biopsy increases yield.
det.clinical: Most patients present with painful, asymmetric neuropathy that accumulates over weeks, often starting in the legs. Systemic forms add fever, weight loss, skin lesions, kidney or lung disease. Non-systemic vasculitic neuropathy is limited to nerve and muscle and has a milder course. CNS involvement is uncommon.
det.diagnosis: Definite diagnosis requires biopsy showing vessel wall inflammation with necrosis; supportive features include haemosiderin, asymmetric fibre loss and Wallerian degeneration. Serology classifies systemic causes. Exclude infection (hepatitis B, C, HIV) and drug causes before immunosuppression.
det.treatment: Glucocorticoids are first-line; cyclophosphamide or rituximab is added for systemic vasculitis or progressive neuropathy. Infection-associated forms need antiviral therapy with limited immunosuppression. Neuropathic pain treatment and rehabilitation are important.
det.prognosis: Most patients stabilise with treatment, but axonal deficits recover slowly and relapses occur.
pearls: Painful asymmetric neuropathy evolving over weeks: biopsy nerve and muscle together.
Non-systemic vasculitic neuropathy has normal blood tests in many patients.
Check hepatitis B and C before giving immunosuppression.
det.thd: Necrotizing vasculitis คือการอักเสบที่ทำลายผนังหลอดเลือดจนเนื้อตาย ทำให้เส้นประสาทและกล้ามเนื้อขาดเลือด ผู้ป่วยปวด ชา และอ่อนแรงแบบไม่สมมาตรทีละเส้น อาจเป็นทั้งระบบหรือเฉพาะเส้นประสาท วินิจฉัยด้วยการตัดชิ้นเนื้อเส้นประสาทร่วมกล้ามเนื้อและตรวจเลือดหาสาเหตุ รักษาด้วยสเตียรอยด์ร่วม cyclophosphamide หรือ rituximab

name: Negative myoclonus
formal: Brief lapses of muscle tone causing sudden postural loss without prior contraction, such as asterixis, from epileptic or non-epileptic cortical mechanisms.
simple: Sudden brief loss of muscle strength causing a limb to drop or the body to sag.
th: การเสียแรงตึงตัวของกล้ามเนื้อแบบสั้น ๆ ทำให้ท่าทางตกลงชั่วขณะ เช่น asterixis ในภาวะตับวายหรือไตวาย เกิดได้ทั้งจากกลไกลมชักและไม่ใช่ลมชัก
tempoNote: Usually appears over hours to days with a metabolic or drug cause; epileptic forms are episodic
feat: Brief (50–200 ms) silent pauses in muscle activity causing a sudden drop of an outstretched limb, then recovery
Asterixis: flapping of the hands with wrists extended; can be seen at the tongue, feet or neck
Bilateral asterixis = metabolic encephalopathy (liver, kidney, CO2 retention) or drugs; unilateral = focal lesion (thalamus, midbrain, parietal)
Postural lapses in the legs can cause falls or a bouncy gait (e.g. post-hypoxic)
inv: Ammonia, liver tests, urea, blood gas (CO2), electrolytes, drug levels (valproate, phenytoin, carbamazepine, gabapentinoids)
MRI if unilateral or with focal signs
EEG-EMG: EMG silent period, with or without preceding EEG spike in epileptic negative myoclonus

case.who: 63-year-old man from Kanchanaburi with hepatitis B cirrhosis
case.story: Constipated for four days after a small upper GI bleed; today drowsy and reversing day and night.
case.exam: Arms outstretched with wrists extended show irregular flapping; jaundice, ascites.
case.tests: Ammonia raised; sodium and glucose normal; no focal lesion on CT.
case.q: What sign is this and what is the immediate management?
case.a: Asterixis (negative myoclonus) from hepatic encephalopathy; treat precipitants and give lactulose, adding rifaximin.

det.patho: Negative myoclonus is an interruption of ongoing muscle activity. Metabolic and drug causes disturb cortical and subcortical motor control circuits so that sustained posture cannot be maintained. In epileptic negative myoclonus, a cortical spike is followed by an inhibitory period that silences the muscle. Unilateral asterixis results from structural damage in the contralateral thalamus, internal capsule, midbrain or parietal cortex.
det.clinical: This is a sign rather than a disease. Asterixis is most often seen in hepatic, renal or respiratory failure and with drug toxicity, alongside confusion. Epileptic negative myoclonus occurs in some childhood epilepsies such as atypical self-limited focal epilepsy. Post-hypoxic and other cortical myoclonus syndromes combine positive and negative jerks, giving unsteady stance and falls.
det.diagnosis: Ask the patient to hold the arms out with wrists extended and fingers spread for at least 30 seconds; look for irregular lapses. Lateralised asterixis demands imaging. EEG-EMG polygraphy confirms the silent period and whether a cortical discharge precedes it. Search for metabolic and drug causes first.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: lactulose and rifaximin for hepatic encephalopathy, dialysis for uraemia, ventilation for CO2 retention, withdraw or reduce culprit drugs. Epileptic negative myoclonus may respond to ethosuximide, levetiracetam, valproate or benzodiazepines, and some drugs such as carbamazepine can provoke it in children.
det.prognosis: Metabolic asterixis resolves as the encephalopathy improves; persistent forms reflect the underlying disorder.
pearls: Unilateral asterixis is a focal sign; image the contralateral thalamus and midbrain.
Asterixis is not specific to liver disease: check urea, CO2 and drugs.
det.thd: Negative myoclonus คือการเสียแรงตึงตัวของกล้ามเนื้อชั่วขณะทำให้มือหรือขาตกลงแล้วกลับขึ้นมา ตัวอย่างที่รู้จักดีคือ asterixis หรือมือกระพือในภาวะตับวาย ไตวาย คาร์บอนไดออกไซด์คั่ง และพิษยา ถ้าเกิดข้างเดียวให้คิดถึงรอยโรคที่ทาลามัสหรือก้านสมอง การรักษาคือแก้สาเหตุ เช่น ให้ lactulose ในภาวะตับวาย หรือหยุดยาที่เป็นสาเหตุ

name: Nelson’s syndrome
formal: Enlargement of an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma after bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing disease, causing hyperpigmentation, headaches and visual field defects.
simple: Growth of a pituitary tumour after removal of the adrenal glands, causing darker skin, headaches and vision problems.
th: การโตขึ้นของเนื้องอกต่อมใต้สมองที่สร้าง ACTH หลังผ่าตัดต่อมหมวกไตทั้งสองข้างเพื่อรักษา Cushing disease ทำให้ผิวคล้ำ ปวดศีรษะ และลานสายตาผิดปกติ

Headache and an enlarging sellar mass on MRI
Bitemporal field defects with chiasmal compression

Risk is highest when adrenalectomy was done young or with residual tumour visible

Pituitary MRI with contrast

case.story: Had both adrenal glands removed eight years ago for Cushing disease; now her skin and gums have darkened and she bumps into doorframes.
case.exam: Diffuse hyperpigmentation, bitemporal hemianopia.
case.tests: ACTH markedly raised; MRI shows a 2.5 cm sellar mass invading the right cavernous sinus.

det.patho: Removing both adrenals eliminates cortisol negative feedback on a corticotroph adenoma, allowing unchecked growth and very high ACTH secretion. Excess ACTH and related peptides stimulate melanocytes, causing pigmentation. Some tumours become aggressive, and a few carry somatic USP8 or other mutations.
det.clinical: Patients present with progressive pigmentation, headache and visual loss, sometimes cranial nerve palsies from cavernous sinus extension. Because it is now called corticotroph tumour progression, guidelines recommend surveillance rather than waiting for symptoms. Neurological relevance lies in mass effect on the chiasm and cranial nerves.
det.diagnosis: Rising ACTH with an enlarging or newly visible pituitary tumour on MRI after bilateral adrenalectomy confirms it. Regular ACTH and MRI surveillance (for example yearly at first) is recommended after adrenalectomy.
det.treatment: Transsphenoidal surgery is first-line; radiotherapy or stereotactic radiosurgery treats residual or invasive tumour. Pasireotide and cabergoline have partial effects; temozolomide is used for aggressive tumours. Patients also need lifelong glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement.
det.prognosis: Usually controllable with surgery and radiation, but aggressive or carcinomatous cases carry a poor outlook.
pearls: Darkening skin after bilateral adrenalectomy = check ACTH and pituitary MRI.
Field defects mean chiasmal compression — test visual fields formally.
Surveillance after adrenalectomy prevents late presentation.
det.thd: Nelson’s syndrome คือเนื้องอกต่อมใต้สมองที่สร้าง ACTH โตขึ้นหลังผ่าตัดต่อมหมวกไตทั้งสองข้างเพื่อรักษา Cushing disease เพราะไม่มี cortisol กดการทำงาน ทำให้ ACTH สูงมาก ผิวคล้ำ ปวดศีรษะ และลานสายตาด้านข้างหายจากการกดทับ optic chiasm วินิจฉัยด้วย ACTH และ MRI ต่อมใต้สมอง รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัดผ่านโพรงจมูกและรังสีรักษา

name: Nemaline myopathy
formal: Congenital myopathy with rod-shaped nemaline bodies on biopsy, hypotonia, facial and proximal weakness and respiratory involvement; NEB, ACTA1 and TPM mutations.
simple: An inherited muscle disease present from birth, with floppiness and weakness, including the face and breathing muscles.
more: Muscle biopsy with Gomori trichrome stain shows rods on a background of normal fibres; CK is usually normal. Genetics clarifies the subtype; management is supportive with respiratory and nutritional care, and severity is mostly determined by the age of onset.

feat: Floppy infant or late-walking child with long, expressionless face and high-arched palate
Weakness of face, neck flexors and proximal (sometimes distal) limbs; reflexes reduced
Breathing muscles disproportionately weak compared with the limbs, giving nocturnal hypoventilation
Feeding difficulty, scoliosis and joint contractures in severe forms
Wide range: lethal neonatal form to mild childhood or late-onset variants

Muscle biopsy: rod bodies on modified Gomori trichrome, confirmed by electron microscopy
Gene panel or exome: NEB (commonest recessive), ACTA1 (often de novo dominant), TPM2/TPM3, KLHL40 and others

case.exam: Narrow elongated face, open mouth, weak neck flexion, mild proximal weakness, absent knee jerks, no fatigability.

case.a: Nemaline myopathy (likely NEB); nocturnal respiratory failure — needs regular sleep studies and possible non-invasive ventilation.

det.patho: Variants in genes for thin-filament proteins (nebulin, skeletal alpha-actin, tropomyosins, troponin) or their regulators disturb sarcomere assembly. Z-disc material accumulates as rod-shaped inclusions, and force generation per fibre is reduced. Rods are a marker of the disease process rather than the direct cause of weakness, and their number correlates poorly with severity.
det.clinical: Most cases are typical congenital forms with hypotonia, facial and bulbar weakness and slowly progressive or static course. Severe neonatal forms present with absent movements, arthrogryposis and respiratory failure, often from ACTA1 or KLHL40 variants. Childhood and adult-onset forms can show distal or neck-extensor weakness. Breathing problems may be silent while limb strength is reasonable, so nocturnal hypoventilation is easily missed.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in a child with congenital hypotonia, facial weakness and normal CK. Biopsy with Gomori trichrome and electron microscopy shows rods; sampling may need more than one stain or site. Genetic testing via a neuromuscular panel or exome confirms the subtype and allows counselling. Adult-onset rods with paraprotein should raise sporadic late-onset nemaline myopathy, which is an acquired, treatable entity.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy is approved; trials of tyrosine and troponin activators have been small. Care centres on respiratory surveillance and non-invasive ventilation, airway clearance, nutrition (sometimes gastrostomy), scoliosis monitoring and physiotherapy. Anaesthetists should be informed about respiratory weakness. Genetic counselling depends on inheritance pattern.
det.prognosis: Severe neonatal forms are often fatal in infancy; typical forms usually survive into adulthood with stable or slowly worsening weakness, with respiratory failure the main threat.
pearls: Normal CK does not exclude a congenital myopathy; biopsy and genetics settle it.
Check breathing at night even in ambulant patients.
Adult-onset rods with a monoclonal protein: think sporadic late-onset nemaline myopathy, which may respond to treatment.
det.thd: Nemaline myopathy เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้อแต่กำเนิดจากยีนของ thin filament เช่น NEB และ ACTA1 เด็กมักตัวอ่อนปวกเปียกตั้งแต่เกิด หน้ายาวไม่มีแรง ต้นแขนขาและคออ่อนแรง กล้ามเนื้อหายใจอ่อนแรงทำให้หายใจไม่พอตอนกลางคืน CK มักปกติ ชิ้นเนื้อพบ rod bodies และยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคองโดยเน้นการดูแลการหายใจและโภชนาการ

simple: A serious seizure disorder in newborns with muscle jerks and developmental problems.

det.patho: Early myoclonic encephalopathy was defined as a neonatal epileptic encephalopathy with erratic myoclonus and burst-suppression, overlapping with Ohtahara syndrome. In the 2022 ILAE classification both are grouped as early infantile developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (EIDEE). Many cases have metabolic causes, especially glycine encephalopathy, while others result from variants in genes such as KCNQ2, SCN2A, STXBP1 or ERBB4, or from structural lesions.
det.clinical: Babies present within days with fragmentary myoclonus, focal seizures and later tonic spasms, along with marked hypotonia, poor feeding and apnoea. Hiccups and breathing problems suggest glycine encephalopathy. Development is severely impaired and many infants die in the first year; survivors often evolve to infantile spasms.
det.diagnosis: Diagnose from clinical features and burst-suppression EEG. A rapid metabolic work-up is essential, including paired CSF and plasma glycine, and vitamin trials. MRI and genetic testing follow. Exclude acute provoked causes such as hypoxic-ischaemic injury, hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia and infection.
det.treatment: Give trials of pyridoxine, then pyridoxal phosphate, folinic acid and biotin as indicated. Antiseizure medicines (phenobarbital, levetiracetam, topiramate, benzodiazepines) usually have limited effect. In glycine encephalopathy, sodium benzoate lowers glycine and dextromethorphan or ketamine block NMDA receptors. Precision therapy can help some genetic causes (e.g. sodium channel blockers in KCNQ2 or SCN2A gain-of-function). Palliative care discussions are often appropriate.
det.prognosis: Generally poor: high early mortality and severe developmental disability in survivors.
pearls: Erratic neonatal myoclonus + burst-suppression: test glycine and trial pyridoxine/PLP.
Hiccups and apnoea in a floppy seizing neonate suggest nonketotic hyperglycinaemia.
det.thd: Neonatal myoclonic epilepsy หรือ early myoclonic encephalopathy (ปัจจุบันจัดอยู่ใน EIDEE) คือโรคลมชักรุนแรงที่เริ่มในทารกแรกเกิด มีการกระตุกกระจัดกระจาย ตัวอ่อน ดูดนมไม่ได้ EEG แบบ burst-suppression สาเหตุสำคัญคือ glycine encephalopathy และโรคพันธุกรรมหรือเมตาบอลิกอื่น ต้องตรวจเมตาบอลิกเร่งด่วนและลองให้ pyridoxine และ PLP พยากรณ์โรคส่วนใหญ่ไม่ดี

name: Neonatal pyridoxine deficiency
formal: Pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (ALDH7A1) causing intractable neonatal seizures that respond to pyridoxine, with developmental risk if untreated.
simple: A rare condition where newborns have seizures that only stop with vitamin B6.

case.exam: Irritable then lethargic between seizures; no dysmorphism.

det.patho: Biallelic ALDH7A1 variants impair antiquitin, an enzyme in lysine breakdown. Upstream metabolites (alpha-AASA and P6C) accumulate, and P6C binds and inactivates pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP), the biologically active vitamin B6 that is needed for GABA synthesis and many neurotransmitter enzymes. The result is a functional B6 deficiency in the brain. The entry name 'deficiency' is historical: dietary B6 intake is normal; true nutritional deficiency is separate and rare.
det.clinical: Classic cases have refractory seizures in the first days of life, sometimes preceded by fetal seizures, with encephalopathy and irritability. Seizure types are mixed and EEG may show burst-suppression or multifocal discharges. Late-onset forms present up to early childhood. Even with treatment, many children have learning or developmental problems, especially if treatment was delayed.
det.diagnosis: Any neonate or infant with drug-resistant seizures should have a pyridoxine trial and biomarker testing (urine alpha-AASA/P6C). Give IV pyridoxine 100 mg under EEG and cardiorespiratory monitoring; apnoea and hypotonia can follow, so be ready to support breathing. If there is no response, continue oral pyridoxine for several days, and consider PLP for PNPO deficiency. Confirm with ALDH7A1 testing; newborn screening is being piloted.
det.treatment: Maintain lifelong oral pyridoxine (commonly about 15–30 mg/kg/day in infants, adjusted by specialists). Add 'triple therapy' with a lysine-restricted diet and arginine supplementation, which lowers toxic metabolites and may improve cognition. Antiseizure drugs can often be stopped. Monitor for pyridoxine-induced neuropathy at high doses.
det.prognosis: Seizure control is usually excellent; neurodevelopmental outcome is better with early treatment but many still have some delay.
pearls: Refractory neonatal seizures: give a pyridoxine trial, ideally with EEG running and the ventilator ready.
Send alpha-AASA before or soon after pyridoxine — it stays raised on treatment.
No response to pyridoxine? Try PLP for PNPO deficiency.

name: Neoplastic parkinsonism
formal: Parkinsonism secondary to tumours, particularly frontal, basal ganglia or midbrain lesions, or paraneoplastic processes.
simple: Stiffness, slowness and tremor caused by a tumour in the brain.
th: parkinsonism ที่เกิดจากเนื้องอกกดหรือแทรกบริเวณ basal ganglia, frontal lobe หรือ midbrain หรือจากกลไก paraneoplastic
tempoNote: Evolves over weeks to months, usually faster than idiopathic Parkinson disease
feat: Parkinsonism often unilateral and rapidly progressive, with little or no rest tremor
Accompanying signs: headache, seizures, hemiparesis, frontal release or gaze palsy
Poor or absent levodopa response in most cases
Tumours include frontal meningioma, glioma, lymphoma, metastases or midbrain lesions; paraneoplastic forms with anti-Ma2 or CRMP5
inv: MRI brain with contrast in any atypical, asymmetric or rapidly worsening parkinsonism
If MRI is unremarkable but course is subacute: paraneoplastic antibody panel and CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or PET
Biopsy or tissue diagnosis guided by imaging

case.story: Over 4 months his right hand became slow and stiff and his speech quieter. His wife says he has become apathetic and has headaches in the morning.
case.exam: Right-sided bradykinesia and rigidity without tremor, grasp reflex on the right, mild right pronator drift.
case.tests: MRI shows a large left frontal convexity meningioma compressing the frontal lobe and displacing the basal ganglia.
case.q: Which features should have prompted imaging, and what is the treatment?
case.a: Rapid course, frontal signs, pyramidal drift and headache; surgical resection often improves the parkinsonism.

det.patho: Tumours can produce parkinsonism by directly invading the striatum or substantia nigra, compressing these structures or their frontal connections, or distorting the midbrain. Mass effect on the frontal lobe can impair motor programming. Rarely, immune responses against tumour antigens (paraneoplastic) target basal ganglia or brainstem neurons.
det.clinical: Presentation is often asymmetric akinetic-rigid parkinsonism without the classic tremor, developing over weeks to months. Clues are headache, seizures, cognitive or behavioural change, pyramidal signs, gaze palsy or papilloedema. Paraneoplastic cases, such as anti-Ma2 encephalitis, may combine parkinsonism with hypersomnia and vertical gaze palsy.
det.diagnosis: Neuroimaging is the key step; contrast MRI identifies most lesions. Any atypical parkinsonism (rapid course, early falls, unilateral rigidity with focal signs, no levodopa response) deserves imaging. When structural imaging is negative but the course is subacute, test for onconeural antibodies and screen for occult cancer.
det.treatment: Treat the tumour: surgery, radiotherapy or chemotherapy as appropriate; parkinsonism may improve after decompression. Levodopa can be tried but response is often limited. Paraneoplastic cases need tumour treatment plus immunotherapy.
det.prognosis: Depends on tumour type; benign extra-axial tumours often have good recovery of motor function after removal.
pearls: Asymmetric parkinsonism plus headache or focal signs: image before diagnosing PD.
Frontal meningiomas can mimic PD and are curable.
Paraneoplastic parkinsonism with vertical gaze palsy and sleepiness suggests anti-Ma2.

det.patho: Behçet disease is a variable-vessel vasculitis that can hit both arteries and veins of any size; it is commonest along the old Silk Road and is seen in Thailand. Neutrophil-rich and lymphocytic perivenular inflammation drives parenchymal neuro-Behçet, while thrombosis of dural sinuses reflects inflamed vein walls rather than classic thrombophilia. HLA-B51 is the strongest genetic association, and nervous system involvement occurs in roughly 5–10% of patients, usually a few years after the first ulcers.
det.clinical: Parenchymal disease is the main form: a subacute brainstem or diencephalic syndrome with headache, cranial nerve palsies, ataxia, hemiparesis or behavioural change, sometimes with fever. It can follow a single-attack, relapsing-remitting or secondary progressive course; spinal cord and hemispheric lesions are less frequent. The non-parenchymal form presents with intracranial hypertension from venous sinus thrombosis and carries a better outlook. Isolated headache is common in Behçet but alone does not mean neurological involvement.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on established systemic Behçet disease (international criteria based on oral and genital ulcers, eye, skin and pathergy findings) plus a compatible neurological syndrome, typical MRI and inflammatory CSF. Large brainstem lesions extending upward into the thalamus with oedema, and later brainstem atrophy, are suggestive. Exclude infection (TB, Listeria, syphilis), MS, sarcoidosis and lymphoma; neurological onset before systemic features occurs in a minority and makes diagnosis difficult.
det.treatment: Acute parenchymal attacks are treated with intravenous methylprednisolone followed by an oral taper. Maintenance immunosuppression is needed: azathioprine for milder disease, and anti-TNF agents (infliximab or adalimumab) for severe, relapsing or progressive disease. Ciclosporin should be avoided because it can provoke neuro-Behçet. Venous thrombosis is treated with steroids, and anticoagulation is often used after excluding pulmonary artery aneurysms.
det.prognosis: Single-attack disease may recover well, but progressive parenchymal disease causes cumulative disability; venous thrombosis forms generally do better.
pearls: Brainstem-diencephalic lesion + neutrophilic CSF + mouth ulcers: think neuro-Behçet.
Avoid ciclosporin in Behçet patients with nervous system disease.
Before anticoagulating Behçet CVT, check for pulmonary artery aneurysm.

feat: Chorea with prominent orofacial dyskinesia and 'feeding dystonia' (tongue pushes food out), plus self-biting of the lips and tongue, which is a strong clue; vocal tics, grunting and dysarthria are common
Personality change, psychiatric illness and cognitive decline resembling Huntington disease; parkinsonism may develop later

McLeod syndrome (X-linked XK) adds cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia, haemolysis and weak Kell antigen expression, in men; carrier women may have mild features

Other acanthocytosis syndromes in the differential include abetalipoproteinaemia and hypobetalipoproteinaemia (low lipids, retinitis pigmentosa, malabsorption of vitamin E) and the pantothenate kinase-associated HARP syndrome

case.story: Three years of fidgety movements, biting his lips and tongue until they bleed and pushing food out of his mouth with his tongue. He recently had a generalised seizure, and his family say he is irritable; his parents and sister are well.

case.tests: CK 1,800 U/L; fresh blood film shows about 15% acanthocytes; HTT repeat normal; MRI caudate atrophy.
case.q: Which gene is suspected, and which simple measure protects the patient?

det.patho: Chorea-acanthocytosis is an autosomal recessive disease with loss-of-function variants in VPS13A, which encodes chorein, a lipid-transfer protein involved in intracellular trafficking; red-cell membrane abnormalities lead to spiky acanthocytes, while striatal neurons degenerate. McLeod syndrome is X-linked and due to variants in XK, affecting the Kell blood group system, with similar striatal degeneration plus muscle and heart involvement. Recent work links chorein to actin and membrane signalling pathways, but treatments targeting the mechanism are still experimental.
det.clinical: Chorea-acanthocytosis is the second most common inherited chorea after Huntington disease in some populations. The movement disorder begins with orofacial dyskinesia and chorea, then adds dystonia and later parkinsonism, together with unusual self-injury (biting of tongue and lips), tics and dysarthria. Seizures, behavioural change and cognitive impairment are frequent and may be the presenting problem. Muscle involvement is shown by a raised CK and often a neurogenic or myopathic process, and areflexia reflects axonal neuropathy. McLeod syndrome tends to present later and carries a risk of dilated cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia and haemolysis that needs cardiac follow-up.
det.diagnosis: Look for acanthocytes on several fresh blood films, using saline dilution or a coverslip to improve the yield, since the percentage can vary and the absence of cells on one smear does not exclude the disease. A raised CK, a caudate atrophy on MRI and the clinical picture direct the work-up, and the diagnosis is confirmed by VPS13A sequencing, absent chorein on Western blot or XK testing with Kell typing. Because the presentation resembles Huntington disease, exclude HTT expansion and consider HDL2 and other genetic choreas; a fasting lipid profile and vitamin E help in the other acanthocytosis syndromes.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying therapy. Treat chorea and dyskinesia with a VMAT2 inhibitor (tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine or valbenazine) or a low dose of an atypical antipsychotic such as olanzapine, being careful with mood. Use mouth guards or dental protection against self-biting, and botulinum toxin for dystonia such as tongue or jaw dystonia. Treat seizures with standard antiseizure drugs, assess swallowing and nutrition, and for McLeod syndrome arrange cardiology follow-up. Pallidal (GPi) deep brain stimulation has been tried for refractory chorea and dystonia with encouraging results.
det.prognosis: Progression is steady, and many patients lose independent walking and speech over 10–20 years; death often follows complications of dysphagia, seizures, or cardiac disease in McLeod syndrome.
pearls: Self-biting of the lips and tongue in a young adult with chorea suggests chorea-acanthocytosis.
A high CK and absent reflexes in a Huntington-like patient should lead to a blood film and VPS13A testing.
A single negative blood film does not exclude acanthocytes; repeat with dilution.

det.patho: Heterozygous loss-of-function variants in CSF1R impair signalling that maintains microglia, leading to a primary microgliopathy with axonal swellings (spheroids), myelin loss and pigmented macrophages. Historically separate names, hereditary diffuse leukoencephalopathy with spheroids and pigmentary orthochromatic leukodystrophy, are now grouped as one entity. The term differs from infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy (PLA2G6), a childhood disorder.
det.clinical: Most present between 30 and 60 with psychiatric or behavioural change, then cognitive decline, motor slowing and spasticity. Women tend to present earlier. Some show seizures or a corticobasal-like syndrome. Penetrance is incomplete, so a negative family history does not exclude it.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in a young or middle-aged adult with frontal-predominant leukoencephalopathy and dementia, especially with callosal thinning, persistent diffusion restriction and CT calcifications. Genetic testing for CSF1R confirms; pathology shows spheroids but biopsy is rarely needed now. Exclude vascular, inflammatory and other genetic leukodystrophies, including adult ALD, metachromatic leukodystrophy and AARS2.
det.treatment: No drug therapy is proven. Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, which replaces microglia, has stabilised some patients when done early, but its role is still being defined. Supportive care includes treatment of behaviour and mood, seizure control, physiotherapy and planning for care needs. Genetic counselling for relatives is important.
det.prognosis: Median survival is around 6–10 years from onset without transplantation.
pearls: Dementia plus frontal white matter disease plus dotted calcifications on CT: test CSF1R.
Persistent diffusion-restricting spots in white matter over months are characteristic.
Avoid confusing it with infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy, a different paediatric disease.
det.thd: โรคนี้เป็น leukodystrophy ในผู้ใหญ่ ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจากยีน CSF1R ทำให้ microglia ผิดปกติและมี axonal spheroid ผู้ป่วยวัยกลางคนมีบุคลิกเปลี่ยน สมองเสื่อม และเดินช้า MRI เห็นเนื้อขาวผิดปกติด้านหน้าและ corpus callosum บาง ส่วน CT อาจเห็นหินปูนจุดเล็ก ๆ ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน การปลูกถ่ายไขกระดูกช่วงต้นอาจชะลอโรค

det.patho: Neuroblastoma arises from sympathetic neuroblasts derived from the neural crest and ranges from undifferentiated small round cell tumour to the benign ganglioneuroma; the peripheral neuroblastic tumour spectrum also includes ganglioneuroblastoma intermixed or nodular. MYCN amplification, ALK mutation or amplification, segmental chromosomal gains and losses (1p, 11q, 17q) and age at diagnosis define risk. Metastases go to bone marrow, cortical bone including the orbit and skull, liver and lymph nodes; CNS parenchymal metastases are rare and tend to be dural-based.
det.clinical: Presentation depends on the primary site and spread. Abdominal masses, bone pain and cytopenias are common; paraspinal tumours enter the canal through the foramina and produce back pain, then paraparesis and sphincter loss. Orbital deposits give proptosis with periorbital bruising. Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome often appears in children with localised, low-risk tumours and carries long-term cognitive and behavioural sequelae even after tumour removal. Infants under 18 months may have spontaneous regression, including stage 4S disease.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis uses biopsy or bone marrow histology plus raised urinary catecholamine metabolites. MIBG scan stages the disease and monitors response. Whole-spine MRI is mandatory for suspected cord compression. Risk classification (INRG) uses age, stage, histology, MYCN and genomic profile and determines whether observation, chemotherapy, or intensive therapy is chosen. Raised intracranial pressure from skull metastasis or cord compression requires immediate imaging.
det.treatment: Neuroblastoma-associated cord compression is treated mostly with chemotherapy and steroids, as the small round-cell tumour is chemosensitive; surgery is considered when neurological loss progresses or chemotherapy does not act fast enough, and radiotherapy is reserved for progressive deficits. Low-risk tumours need surgery or observation. High-risk disease uses induction chemotherapy, surgery, myeloablative chemotherapy with autologous stem cell rescue, radiotherapy, and maintenance with anti-GD2 antibody (dinutuximab, naxitamab) and isotretinoin; ALK inhibitors (lorlatinib) are used in ALK-driven relapse. Opsoclonus-myoclonus needs immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG, rituximab) alongside tumour treatment.
det.prognosis: Survival exceeds 90 percent in low- and intermediate-risk disease and is about 50-60 percent in high-risk disease; intraspinal neuroblastoma had around 70 percent five-year survival in the source series.
pearls: A child who refuses to walk, with back pain and a flank mass, needs urgent spine MRI and urine catecholamines.
Opsoclonus-myoclonus in a toddler should prompt a search for neuroblastoma, but the tumour may be tiny.
MYCN amplification defines high risk irrespective of stage.

case.exam: Facial angiofibromas, several ash-leaf macules, shagreen patch on the lower back.

det.patho: Most neurocutaneous syndromes result from loss of tumour suppressor genes that regulate cell growth (RAS-MAPK in NF1, mTOR in TSC, hypoxia signalling in VHL, merlin in NF2-related schwannomatosis). Because skin and nervous system share ectodermal origin, both show lesions. Sturge–Weber results from a somatic mosaic activating GNAQ variant affecting capillary development.
det.clinical: Each syndrome has typical skin signs and neurological features: NF1 with neurofibromas, optic gliomas and learning difficulties; TSC with epilepsy, autism and SEGA; Sturge–Weber with seizures, hemiparesis and glaucoma; VHL with haemangioblastomas, renal cancer and phaeochromocytoma. Severity varies even within families.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on consensus clinical criteria supported by genetic testing. Imaging defines nervous system involvement; systemic surveillance (kidney, eye, heart, adrenal) follows syndrome-specific guidelines.
det.treatment: Management is multidisciplinary: antiseizure drugs and epilepsy surgery, MEK inhibitors for plexiform neurofibromas, mTOR inhibitors in TSC, belzutifan for VHL tumours, laser and glaucoma care in Sturge–Weber. Genetic counselling and lifelong surveillance are essential.
det.prognosis: Variable; many live normal lifespans, but malignancy, epilepsy and organ complications drive morbidity.
pearls: Always look at the skin in a child with epilepsy or developmental delay.
Wood's lamp reveals ash-leaf macules.
Targeted drugs now exist for NF1, TSC and VHL tumours.
det.thd: Neurocutaneous syndromes หรือ phakomatoses คือกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่มีความผิดปกติของผิวหนังร่วมกับระบบประสาท เช่น NF1 (café-au-lait และ neurofibroma), tuberous sclerosis (ด่างขาวรูปใบไม้ angiofibroma และลมชัก), Sturge–Weber (ปานแดงที่หน้าและลมชัก) และ VHL (haemangioblastoma) การวินิจฉัยใช้เกณฑ์ทางคลินิก ภาพ MRI และการตรวจยีน การดูแลต้องเป็นทีมสหสาขาและเฝ้าระวังตลอดชีวิต

name: Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA)
formal: Group of genetic disorders (PKAN, PLA2G6, BPAN) with basal ganglia iron deposition on MRI, causing dystonia, parkinsonism, spasticity and cognitive decline.
simple: Inherited diseases where iron builds up in the brain, causing stiffness, abnormal postures and decline in movement and thinking.
more: MRI (eye-of-the-tiger sign in PKAN; cerebellar atrophy in PLA2G6) with T2* sequences showing iron; genetic testing. Treatment is symptomatic; deferiprone has been trialled in PKAN, and BPAN is X-linked dominant (WDR45) with early epilepsy.
th: NBIA เป็นกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่มีธาตุเหล็กสะสมใน basal ganglia (globus pallidus, substantia nigra) ทำให้เกิด dystonia, parkinsonism, spasticity และสมองเสื่อม ชนิดสำคัญคือ PKAN (PANK2), PLAN (PLA2G6), MPAN (C19orf12) และ BPAN (WDR45) ใช้ MRI ที่เห็นเหล็ก (T2*/SWI) และตรวจยีนช่วยวินิจฉัย การรักษาเน้นอาการ รวมทั้งยา botulinum toxin และ DBS ที่ GPi
tempoNote: Classic PKAN and infantile PLAN start in early childhood; atypical PKAN, MPAN, BPAN and adult forms begin in adolescence to adulthood; all progress over years with plateaus and rapid declines
feat: Progressive dystonia (often oromandibular and with gait toe-walking), parkinsonism, spasticity, dysarthria and swallowing difficulty
Cognitive decline and psychiatric symptoms, with pigmentary retinopathy in PKAN, optic atrophy in MPAN and PLAN and seizures in BPAN
PKAN: 'eye-of-the-tiger' sign (bright spot within dark pallidum) on T2 MRI; PLAN: early hypotonia, cerebellar atrophy and axonal neuropathy; MPAN: spastic paraparesis and motor neuron signs
BPAN (WDR45, X-linked dominant): childhood epilepsy and developmental delay, then adult-onset dystonia-parkinsonism and dementia
Other iron-related genetic disorders to remember: neuroferritinopathy (FTL), aceruloplasminaemia (CP), Kufor–Rakeb disease (ATP13A2) and fatty acid hydroxylase-associated neurodegeneration (FA2H)
inv: MRI with T2*/SWI: iron in the pallidum and nigra; the pattern points to the subtype, with cerebellar atrophy in PLAN
Genetic panel (PANK2, PLA2G6, C19orf12, WDR45, COASY, FA2H, FTL, CP, ATP13A2)
Ceruloplasmin and copper (aceruloplasminaemia, exclude Wilson disease), ferritin, fundoscopy or ERG, nerve conduction, acanthocyte film and EEG when seizures occur

case.story: Over two years his walking has become stiff with toe-walking, his speech is slurred and his jaw pulls open when he talks. His parents are cousins.
case.exam: Oromandibular and limb dystonia, spasticity with brisk reflexes, mild rigidity, pigmentary retinopathy.
case.tests: MRI: low T2 signal in both globi pallidi with a central bright spot; biallelic PANK2 variants confirmed.
case.q: What is the condition and which options help severe dystonia?
case.a: Pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN); manage with anticholinergics, baclofen, botulinum toxin and, for severe dystonia, pallidal deep brain stimulation; iron chelation reduces pallidal iron but did not improve clinical outcome in a trial.

det.patho: NBIA disorders have in common neurodegeneration plus excess iron in the pallidum and nigra, but the genes involved affect different pathways: coenzyme A synthesis (PANK2, COASY), phospholipid metabolism (PLA2G6, FA2H), mitochondrial membrane and autophagy pathways (C19orf12, WDR45) and iron metabolism (FTL, CP). The old name Hallervorden–Spatz disease was dropped in favour of NBIA, partly because of the historical misconduct of the physician for whom it was named. It remains unclear whether iron drives the cell injury or merely follows it.
det.clinical: Classic PKAN starts before 6 years with gait problems and dystonia that progress to loss of walking in a decade, with dysarthria and oromandibular dystonia; atypical PKAN begins later with speech problems, psychiatric features and parkinsonism. Infantile PLAN causes developmental regression with hypotonia, then spasticity; later onset PLAN is a dystonia-parkinsonism that responds to levodopa. MPAN and BPAN usually combine spasticity or epilepsy with later dystonia and parkinsonism. Retinopathy or optic atrophy, neuropathy and seizures give clues to the subtype.
det.diagnosis: MRI of the brain with iron-sensitive sequences is the first step: an eye-of-the-tiger appearance (pallidal low signal with a central bright spot) suggests PKAN, cerebellar atrophy with thin cerebellar cortex suggests PLAN, and pallidal and nigral low signal with a thin white band in the substantia nigra suggests BPAN. Confirmation is by gene panel or exome sequencing. Exclude Wilson disease, neuroferritinopathy, aceruloplasminaemia (low ceruloplasmin and diabetes, anaemia) and other mimics with blood tests. Not every NBIA patient shows iron on early MRI.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy has been proven. Deferiprone lowered pallidal iron in a randomised trial in PKAN but did not give a clear clinical benefit, so it is not standard. Treat dystonia with anticholinergics, baclofen (oral or intrathecal), benzodiazepines and botulinum toxin; pallidal deep brain stimulation improves dystonia and quality of life in many children and adults, and a levodopa trial is worthwhile for parkinsonism in PLAN and BPAN. Provide multidisciplinary care for feeding, respiratory complications, seizures and psychiatric symptoms; genetic counselling is essential.
det.prognosis: Classic PKAN and infantile PLAN progress over one to two decades; atypical and adult forms are slower but cause serious disability.
pearls: Eye-of-the-tiger on T2 MRI points to PKAN.
Always check ceruloplasmin and copper in a young person with dystonia and basal ganglia changes.
Pallidal deep brain stimulation can help dystonia in PKAN, while iron chelation is still investigational.
det.thd: NBIA คือกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่มีเหล็กสะสมใน basal ganglia ทำให้เกิด dystonia, parkinsonism, spasticity และสมองเสื่อมที่ค่อย ๆ แย่ลง ชนิดสำคัญคือ PKAN จากยีน PANK2 ที่เห็น eye-of-the-tiger sign บน MRI, PLAN, MPAN และ BPAN ควรตรวจ MRI ชนิดไวต่อเหล็ก ตรวจยีน และตรวจ ceruloplasmin เพื่อแยก Wilson disease ยังไม่มียาที่เปลี่ยนการดำเนินโรค การรักษาเน้นลดอาการ ใช้ botulinum toxin ยาคลายกล้ามเนื้อ และ DBS ที่ GPi ในรายรุนแรง

name: Neuroepithelial tumours
formal: Group of primary CNS tumours from neuroepithelial cells, including gliomas, ependymomas, embryonal and choroid plexus tumours.
simple: Brain tumours arising from the brain's own supporting and nerve cells.
th: กลุ่มเนื้องอกปฐมภูมิของระบบประสาทส่วนกลางที่เกิดจากเซลล์ neuroepithelial ได้แก่ glioma, ependymoma, embryonal tumour และ choroid plexus tumour

feat: An umbrella category, not one disease
Seizures are often the first sign, especially from temporal cortical tumours such as dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumour (DNET), ganglioglioma and pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma
Other presentations: focal deficit, raised intracranial pressure, cognitive or personality change

case.story: Three years of drug-resistant focal seizures with an epigastric rising feeling, then loss of awareness; school performance is normal.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination.
case.tests: MRI shows a cortical, multinodular, microcystic lesion in the right temporal lobe without enhancement or oedema; resection confirms a low-grade glioneuronal tumour with adjacent cortical dysplasia.
case.q: Which tumour type typically behaves this way, and what is the best treatment?
case.a: Dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumour (a WHO grade I epilepsy-associated tumour); surgical resection often cures the seizures.

det.patho: These tumours arise from glial or neuronal precursor cells, and their genetics now define the entity more than the microscope does. Diffuse gliomas in adults are separated by IDH status (mutant astrocytoma or oligodendroglioma with 1p/19q codeletion versus IDH-wildtype glioblastoma), and paediatric tumours by markers such as H3 K27M, BRAF and MYC or WNT pathway changes. Low-grade epilepsy-associated tumours arise in cortex, frequently with adjacent focal cortical dysplasia. Most cases are sporadic, with rare predisposition syndromes such as NF1, tuberous sclerosis and Li-Fraumeni.
det.clinical: Presentation depends on location and growth rate. Cortical tumours cause seizures, deep or frontal tumours cause cognitive and behavioural change, and posterior fossa or ventricular tumours cause headache, vomiting and hydrocephalus. Slow-growing lesions in young people are often found after years of epilepsy, whereas glioblastoma produces progressive deficits over weeks. Papilloedema, morning headache or a new seizure at any adult age warrants imaging.
det.diagnosis: MRI with contrast is the first test, but enhancement alone does not predict grade. Definitive diagnosis needs tissue, reported with an integrated diagnosis that includes molecular findings. Neuropathology of epilepsy surgery specimens shows, for example, multinodular cortex with floating neurons in DNET, a cystic lesion with a mural nodule in pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma, and white-matter oligodendroglioma with the classic perinuclear clearing. Staging of the neuraxis is needed for tumours that spread through CSF.
det.treatment: Maximal safe resection is the first step for most tumours and cures many low-grade glioneuronal lesions. Adjuvant radiotherapy and temozolomide follow for glioblastoma; IDH-mutant gliomas receive radiotherapy with chemotherapy according to grade, and the IDH inhibitor vorasidenib is now an option for selected grade 2 disease. Embryonal tumours are treated with multimodal protocols and ependymoma with surgery and radiotherapy. Antiseizure medication, corticosteroids for oedema and rehabilitation support all patients.
det.prognosis: Ranges from cure after resection of grade I tumours to median survival of about 15 months for IDH-wildtype glioblastoma.
pearls: Molecular markers now outweigh histology in classification.
A first seizure in an adult warrants MRI.
Use the specific tumour name, not the umbrella term, for management decisions.
det.thd: Neuroepithelial tumours เป็นกลุ่มเนื้องอกสมองและไขสันหลังที่เกิดจากเซลล์ glia หรือ neuron ได้แก่ glioma, ependymoma, embryonal tumour และ choroid plexus tumour ผู้ป่วยอาจมาด้วยอาการชัก อ่อนแรง ปวดศีรษะจากความดันในกะโหลกสูง หรือพฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน ตรวจ MRI พร้อมสารทึบรังสี แล้วยืนยันด้วยชิ้นเนื้อและผลโมเลกุล เช่น IDH และ 1p/19q การรักษาคือผ่าตัดให้มากที่สุดเท่าที่ปลอดภัย แล้วให้รังสีรักษาและเคมีบำบัดตามชนิดและเกรด

feat: Adult-onset chorea or dystonia, often asymmetric at first
Prominent orofacial dystonia with dysarthria and dysphagia; action-specific facial dystonia

Relatives affected in a pattern that suggests autosomal dominant transmission

case.exam: Oromandibular dystonia on speaking, choreiform right arm, mild bradykinesia, normal eye movements.
case.tests: Serum ferritin 8 ng/mL without anaemia; MRI shows low T2 signal and cystic change in both putamina.

det.patho: Dominant variants in FTL, encoding ferritin light chain, alter the C-terminus so ferritin shells leak iron. Free iron promotes oxidative damage and ferritin aggregates form inclusions in neurons and glia, especially in basal ganglia. Most reported families share a founder insertion from northern England, but cases occur worldwide.
det.clinical: Begins in mid-adulthood with focal chorea or dystonia, frequently with characteristic orofacial and lingual involvement leading to speech and swallowing difficulties. Over years it spreads, and parkinsonism, cerebellar features and subcortical cognitive impairment may appear. Psychiatric symptoms can occur.
det.diagnosis: Suspect with an adult-onset movement disorder, dominant family history and basal ganglia iron on MRI (susceptibility or T2*). Cystic necrosis of the pallidum and putamen is a late clue. Low serum ferritin is supportive but not universal. Confirm with FTL sequencing.
det.treatment: No therapy has proven disease-modifying; iron chelation has not shown meaningful benefit and may worsen systemic iron status. Symptomatic options include botulinum toxin for focal dystonia, tetrabenazine for chorea and anticholinergics; levodopa is generally unhelpful. Speech, swallowing and genetic counselling support are important.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive, with disability from dysphagia and dysarthria after many years.
pearls: Basal ganglia iron in an adult with dominant chorea or dystonia: test FTL.
Low serum ferritin despite brain iron overload is a useful clue.
Late MRI shows cystic cavitation of the putamen and pallidum.
det.thd: Neuroferritinopathy เกิดจากยีน FTL แบบเด่น ทำให้ ferritin ผิดรูปและเหล็กสะสมใน basal ganglia ผู้ป่วยวัยกลางคนมี chorea หรือ dystonia โดยเฉพาะบริเวณปากและลิ้น พูดและกลืนลำบาก ต่อมาอาจมี parkinsonism และความคิดถดถอย MRI พบเหล็กสะสมและโพรง cyst ใน putamen ferritin ในเลือดมักต่ำ ยืนยันด้วยตรวจยีน รักษาตามอาการ

feat: Cutaneous neurofibromas are soft, violaceous skin nodules that begin at puberty and increase with age and pregnancy
Subcutaneous and nodular nerve tumours are firm, may be tender or tingle on percussion (Tinel sign) and cause sensory or motor deficit in the nerve territory

Plexiform neurofibromas are diffuse, intrafascicular, often congenital tumours of nerve roots and plexuses that disfigure, compress structures and carry a 8-13 percent lifetime risk of malignant transformation

case.who: 15-year-old girl from Nan with known NF1
case.story: A soft swelling on the left neck and shoulder present since infancy has enlarged over two years and causes aching and left arm clumsiness.
case.exam: Multiple café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, a boggy left supraclavicular mass, mild left finger flexion weakness; no recent rapid growth.
case.tests: MRI shows a large plexiform neurofibroma infiltrating the left brachial plexus roots and trunks with target sign; FDG-PET shows low uptake; volumetric MRI confirms steady growth.
case.q: What treatment can shrink an inoperable symptomatic plexiform neurofibroma and which finding would raise concern for malignancy?
case.a: A MEK inhibitor: selumetinib (children aged 2 years or more) or mirdametinib; surgery is limited by infiltration. Rapid growth, intense pain and increasing FDG avidity suggest malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour and need biopsy.

det.patho: Neurofibromas are benign nerve sheath tumours composed of neoplastic Schwann cells with loss of both NF1 alleles, together with fibroblasts, perineurial-like cells, mast cells and collagen, with axons running through the tumour (intrafascicular growth). Loss of neurofibromin leaves RAS signalling unchecked, which explains the efficacy of MEK inhibitors. NF1 affects about 1 in 3,000-4,000 people, half de novo. WHO recognises localized, diffuse and plexiform types; atypical neurofibromatous neoplasm of uncertain biologic potential (ANNUBP) is an intermediate lesion with CDKN2A loss.
det.clinical: Cutaneous tumours are often cosmetic and itchy. Deeper nerve and plexiform tumours cause pain, weakness, scoliosis and disfigurement, or compress the airway and spinal cord. Plexiform tumours of the orbit and face lead to asymmetry and visual problems. Malignant transformation to MPNST is the major cause of mortality in adult NF1, presenting as rapid enlargement and pain.
det.diagnosis: MRI features are suggestive; target sign is frequent. Neurofibroma must be distinguished from schwannoma (extrafascicular, encapsulated) and from MPNST, for which no single imaging sign is reliable. FDG-PET with SUV above about 3.5 raises suspicion, and biopsy of the avid region follows. Genetic testing helps in atypical cases. For NF1 patients, annual clinical review and symptom-triggered MRI are recommended.
det.treatment: Asymptomatic tumours are observed. Symptomatic discrete tumours are excised when they can be separated safely. For inoperable symptomatic plexiform neurofibromas selumetinib (approved for children aged 2 and over in 2020) and mirdametinib (approved 2025 for children and adults) produce volume reduction in about 70 percent and functional benefit. Radiotherapy is avoided because it increases the risk of malignant transformation. MPNST requires wide surgical excision, often with radiotherapy and chemotherapy, and has a poor prognosis.
det.prognosis: Benign neurofibromas follow a stable or slowly progressive course; MPNST has a five-year survival of about 40-50 percent when completely resected and less when metastatic.
pearls: Target sign on MRI favours neurofibroma or schwannoma, but rapid growth or intense pain in NF1 warrants FDG-PET and biopsy for MPNST.
Plexiform neurofibroma is nearly pathognomonic of NF1 and may be congenital.
MEK inhibitors, not radiotherapy, are the targeted option for inoperable plexiform tumours.
det.thd: Neurofibroma เป็นเนื้องอกของเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายที่ไม่ร้ายแรงจาก Schwann cell ที่ขาด neurofibromin พบได้เดี่ยว ๆ หรือหลายก้อนใน NF1 ชนิด plexiform มีความเสี่ยงกลายเป็น MPNST ประมาณ 8-13% ถ้าก้อนโตเร็ว ปวดมาก หรือ FDG-PET สูงต้องตัดชิ้นเนื้อ ก้อน plexiform ที่ผ่าตัดไม่ได้ใช้ยา selumetinib หรือ mirdametinib ได้ และควรเลี่ยงการฉายรังสี

det.patho: NF1 results from loss of neurofibromin, a RAS-GTPase activating protein, causing RAS/MAPK overactivity. NF2-related schwannomatosis results from loss of merlin, a tumour suppressor controlling contact inhibition. Other schwannomatoses involve SMARCB1 or LZTR1. Around half of NF1 and NF2 cases are new mutations, and mosaicism is common in NF2.
det.clinical: NF1 (about 1 in 3,000) is mainly cutaneous and neurodevelopmental, with optic gliomas, scoliosis, tibial dysplasia, hypertension and vasculopathy. NF2-related schwannomatosis (about 1 in 25,000–60,000) causes progressive deafness, balance loss and multiple CNS tumours. Schwannomatosis presents with chronic pain from peripheral schwannomas. The term was revised in 2022 to replace NF2 with NF2-related schwannomatosis.
det.diagnosis: Use the 2021 revised international criteria, which incorporate genetic findings, choroidal abnormalities and mosaic forms. MRI defines tumour burden. Rapid growth or new pain in a plexiform neurofibroma suggests malignant transformation and needs PET-CT and biopsy.
det.treatment: Care is surveillance-based and multidisciplinary. MEK inhibitors (selumetinib, mirdametinib) shrink symptomatic plexiform neurofibromas. Bevacizumab can slow vestibular schwannoma growth and preserve hearing in NF2; surgery and radiosurgery are used selectively, with radiation used cautiously in NF1. Pain management is central in schwannomatosis.
det.prognosis: NF1 shortens life expectancy by roughly 10–15 years, mostly through malignancy; NF2 severity depends on age at onset and tumour load.
pearls: In NF1 the café-au-lait criterion needs at least six spots, sized by age (5 mm in children, 15 mm in adults).
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas mean NF2-related schwannomatosis.
New pain or rapid growth of a neurofibroma = think MPNST.

det.patho: NF1 is inherited as a dominant trait and results from inactivating variants in NF1, which encodes neurofibromin, a negative regulator of RAS. Half of cases are de novo; penetrance is essentially complete but expression varies even within families. Tumours arise after a second hit in the remaining allele, especially in Schwann cells. Birth incidence is around 1 in 2,500–3,000.
det.clinical: Skin features dominate in childhood, while neurofibromas increase through adolescence and pregnancy. Plexiform neurofibromas can be disfiguring and painful, and carry a lifetime risk of malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour of about 10%. Optic pathway gliomas occur in about 15% of children, usually indolent. Cognitive and behavioural difficulties are the commonest cause of reduced quality of life; adults face increased risks of gliomas, breast cancer, GIST and vasculopathy.
det.diagnosis: The revised 2021 criteria require two or more features: café-au-lait macules, freckling, neurofibromas, optic glioma, Lisch nodules or choroidal anomalies, a distinctive osseous lesion, a heterozygous NF1 variant, or one feature plus an affected parent. Legius syndrome (SPRED1) causes café-au-lait macules and freckling without tumours and is the main genetic mimic.
det.treatment: Care is surveillance-based and multidisciplinary. The MEK inhibitor selumetinib is approved for symptomatic inoperable plexiform neurofibromas in children (and increasingly in adults), and MEK inhibitors are used for progressive optic gliomas along with chemotherapy. Surgery removes troublesome cutaneous or plexiform lesions; MPNST needs wide excision. Learning support, BP monitoring and earlier breast screening in women are important.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is reduced by around 10–15 years, chiefly from malignancy and vascular disease.
pearls: Multiple café-au-lait patches plus freckles in the armpit or groin: NF1.
New pain or rapid growth in a plexiform neurofibroma suggests malignant change.
Annual eye examination in children screens for optic pathway glioma.
det.thd: Neurofibromatosis type 1 เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมถ่ายทอดแบบเด่นจากยีน NF1 ผู้ป่วยมีปานสีกาแฟใส่นมหลายจุด กระที่รักแร้หรือขาหนีบ ก้อน neurofibroma ที่ผิวหนัง และ Lisch nodules ที่ม่านตา เด็กเสี่ยงเนื้องอกเส้นประสาทตาและปัญหาการเรียนรู้ ผู้ใหญ่เสี่ยงเนื้องอกร้ายของปลอกประสาทและมะเร็งเต้านม การดูแลเน้นการติดตามตา ความดัน และก้อนที่โตเร็วหรือปวด ยา selumetinib ใช้รักษา plexiform neurofibroma

det.patho: Heterozygous pathogenic variants in NF2 on chromosome 22 inactivate merlin, a tumour suppressor regulating contact inhibition. A second hit in Schwann or meningeal cells produces tumours. About half of cases are new mutations and many of these are mosaic, giving milder or segmental disease. Truncating variants tend to cause severe disease; missense and splice variants are milder.
det.clinical: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are the hallmark. Other features include meningiomas (including optic sheath), spinal ependymomas, nerve root and peripheral schwannomas, mononeuropathies and cataracts. The 2022 nomenclature renamed it NF2-related schwannomatosis to separate it from NF1 and from SMARCB1/LZTR1 schwannomatosis.
det.diagnosis: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas, or an identified NF2 variant in two anatomically distinct tumours, establish the diagnosis; revised criteria also accept combinations of a unilateral vestibular schwannoma or first-degree relative with other NF2-type tumours. Gene testing in blood detects most non-mosaic cases. Lifelong MRI surveillance of brain and spine is required.
det.treatment: Management is in specialist centres: observation of slow tumours, microsurgery or stereotactic radiosurgery balanced against hearing preservation (radiation carries a small malignancy risk in NF2). Bevacizumab can shrink growing vestibular schwannomas and improve hearing in some. Hearing rehabilitation includes hearing aids, cochlear or auditory brainstem implants and early sign-language support.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is reduced, especially with early onset, but has improved with specialist care.
pearls: Vestibular schwannoma under 30 years old: test for NF2.
NF2 has few café-au-lait spots — do not confuse with NF1.
Avoid radiation where possible in younger NF2 patients.
det.thd: NF2 หรือ NF2-related schwannomatosis เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมยีนเด่นจากยีน NF2 ทำให้เกิด vestibular schwannoma ทั้งสองข้าง ร่วมกับ meningioma, ependymoma และต้อกระจกตั้งแต่อายุน้อย ผู้ป่วยหูอื้อ หูหนวก และเดินเซ วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI สมองและไขสันหลังร่วมกับตรวจยีน รักษาโดยทีมเฉพาะทาง ผ่าตัด ฉายรังสีบางราย หรือใช้ bevacizumab และฟื้นฟูการได้ยิน

det.patho: A fibrous band running from a cervical rib or long C7 transverse process to the first rib angulates the plexus lower trunk. T1 fibres are most affected, explaining preferential thenar wasting (APB is mainly T1) and medial forearm sensory loss. Injury is postganglionic, so sensory nerve action potentials fall.
det.clinical: True neurogenic TOS is uncommon. Patients notice hand muscles gradually thinning and weakening over months or years, often with aching of the arm and paraesthesia on the ulnar side. Vascular TOS (arterial or venous compression) is a separate entity with different features. Many referrals labelled TOS lack objective deficits and are not neurogenic.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis relies on the characteristic electrodiagnostic pattern: reduced median motor and ulnar or medial antebrachial cutaneous sensory responses with normal median sensory response, plus denervation in C8/T1 muscles. Imaging identifies the rib or band. Provocative manoeuvres (Adson, Roos) are unreliable.
det.treatment: Surgical division of the band and resection of the cervical rib, usually via a supraclavicular approach, stops progression and relieves pain. Wasting improves little after long-standing deficits. Physiotherapy is used for mild or uncertain cases.
det.prognosis: Pain and sensory symptoms usually improve after surgery; muscle wasting often persists.
pearls: Thenar wasting with a normal median SNAP: think lower trunk lesion, not carpal tunnel.
Medial antebrachial cutaneous SNAP is a sensitive marker.
Most 'TOS' referrals are non-neurogenic; insist on objective findings.

name: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)
formal: Life-threatening reaction to dopamine antagonists with fever, lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability, altered consciousness and raised CK; treatment is stopping drug and supportive care.
simple: A dangerous reaction to certain psychiatric or anti-nausea medicines, causing high fever, severe stiffness and confusion.

det.patho: Abrupt central D2 blockade in hypothalamus and striatum disturbs thermoregulation and causes rigidity, while sympathetic overactivity drives autonomic instability; muscle breakdown adds heat and CK. Risk factors are high-potency or depot drugs, rapid escalation, parenteral route, dehydration, agitation, restraint and previous NMS. Withdrawal of levodopa in Parkinson disease produces a similar picture.
det.clinical: Onset is usually within days of a new drug or dose increase but can occur at any time. Mental change and rigidity often come first, followed by fever and autonomic swings. Complications include rhabdomyolysis with renal failure, DIC, aspiration pneumonia, venous thrombosis and cardiac arrhythmia. Atypical NMS with second-generation drugs may have less rigidity or lower fever.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by high CK and leucocytosis; international expert consensus criteria list exposure, hyperthermia, rigidity, mental change, CK rise and autonomic features. Exclude sepsis, meningitis/encephalitis, serotonin syndrome, malignant hyperthermia, anticholinergic toxicity, heat stroke, thyroid storm and non-convulsive status.
det.treatment: Stop the culprit drug (or restart dopaminergic therapy in PD), move to monitored care, cool actively, hydrate and correct electrolytes, and prevent thrombosis. Benzodiazepines (lorazepam) are useful early. In moderate-severe cases add bromocriptine or amantadine and dantrolene for extreme hyperthermia. ECT is effective for refractory cases or overlapping catatonia. Wait at least two weeks after recovery before cautious rechallenge with a low-potency agent.
det.prognosis: Mortality is now around 5–10% with early recognition; most recover over 1–2 weeks (longer after depot drugs).
pearls: Rigidity + fever + confusion after a dopamine blocker = NMS until proven otherwise.
Clonus and hyperreflexia point to serotonin syndrome instead.
Abrupt stop of levodopa in PD can cause the same syndrome.

det.patho: Blockade of dopamine D2 receptors in mesocortical and striatal pathways is the main mechanism, with possible serotonergic and noradrenergic contributions. High-potency first-generation agents carry the most risk, but aripiprazole, lurasidone and others among newer drugs also cause it. Metoclopramide and prochlorperazine can trigger it acutely.
det.clinical: The core is subjective restlessness with objective movement, mostly of the legs. Patients may describe vague anxiety or irritability, so it is easily misread as worsening psychosis, leading to further dose increases. Tardive and chronic forms persist despite stable or reduced dosing.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, based on temporal relation to a dopamine blocker and the combination of inner restlessness with repetitive movements. Distinguish from agitation, anxiety, restless legs and tardive dyskinesia. Use a rating scale to follow response.
det.treatment: First reduce the dose or switch to an agent with lower risk (for example quetiapine or clozapine). Low-dose propranolol, mirtazapine and benzodiazepines have the best evidence; anticholinergics help mainly when parkinsonism coexists. Avoid rapid escalation of antipsychotics in agitated patients without considering akathisia.
det.prognosis: Acute akathisia usually resolves within days to weeks of drug adjustment; chronic or tardive akathisia may persist.
pearls: New agitation after starting an antipsychotic: ask about inner restlessness before increasing the dose.
Propranolol is a useful first drug if not contraindicated.
Metoclopramide in the emergency room is a common trigger.

det.patho: This is a classification heading covering diseases of the lower motor neuron, roots and plexus, peripheral nerves, the neuromuscular junction and skeletal muscle. Causes span genetic, autoimmune, toxic, metabolic, infectious and degenerative mechanisms.
det.clinical: Not a specific disease. Clinical localisation within the motor unit is the first task: distribution of weakness, presence of sensory loss, reflexes, fatigability, fasciculations, cramps and myotonia. Tempo and family history narrow the differential. Respiratory, bulbar and cardiac involvement determine urgency.
det.diagnosis: A stepwise approach uses history and examination to localise, then CK, NCS/EMG and targeted antibody or genetic testing. Muscle MRI helps choose a biopsy site and recognise patterns of genetic myopathy. Many disorders now have specific treatments, so a precise diagnosis matters.
det.treatment: Depends on the cause: immunotherapy for autoimmune neuropathies, myasthenia and myositis; gene-based therapy for SMA; enzyme replacement for Pompe disease; supportive and rehabilitation care for others. Multidisciplinary clinics handle respiratory support, nutrition, orthotics and cardiac surveillance.
det.prognosis: Highly variable according to the specific diagnosis.
pearls: Localise first: neuron, nerve, junction or muscle.
Measure vital capacity in any acute weakness.
Normal CK does not exclude myopathy; high CK does not exclude neurogenic disease.

det.patho: Transmission can fail presynaptically (reduced acetylcholine release, as in LEMS with calcium channel antibodies, botulinum toxin, some congenital forms), synaptically (acetylcholinesterase deficiency) or postsynaptically (antibodies to AChR, MuSK or LRP4, or receptor gene defects). The safety margin of transmission falls, so repeated firing produces failure of some fibres and fatigable weakness.
det.clinical: Fatigability and fluctuation are hallmarks. MG commonly begins with ptosis and diplopia and may generalise; LEMS favours proximal legs with autonomic symptoms and reduced reflexes; botulism gives rapid descending weakness with pupillary involvement. Congenital myasthenic syndromes start in infancy or childhood with a family history.
det.diagnosis: Antibody testing, repetitive nerve stimulation and single-fibre EMG localise to the NMJ and define the subtype. The ice-pack test helps with ptosis at the bedside. det.treatment: MG: pyridostigmine, steroids and steroid-sparing agents, thymectomy, and newer complement and FcRn inhibitors for refractory generalised disease; IVIG or plasma exchange for crisis. det.prognosis: Most autoimmune NMJ disorders are well controlled with modern therapy; outcome in paraneoplastic LEMS depends on the tumour.
pearls: Fatigable weakness with normal sensation localises to the NMJ.

det.patho: An antibody-mediated astrocytopathy: IgG against aquaporin-4 water channels on astrocyte end-feet activates complement, destroys astrocytes and causes secondary demyelination and necrosis. Lesions cluster in AQP4-rich regions — optic nerves, central spinal cord, area postrema and periependymal areas. It is much more common in women and has a relatively higher share of demyelinating disease in East and Southeast Asian populations; it frequently coexists with other autoimmune conditions, notably Sjögren syndrome and lupus.
det.clinical: Core syndromes are severe optic neuritis (often bilateral or involving the chiasm), longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, area postrema syndrome with intractable hiccups or vomiting, acute brainstem syndromes, diencephalic syndromes with hypersomnolence, and symptomatic cerebral lesions. Attacks are typically more severe and recover less than in MS, so disability accumulates with each relapse. Painful tonic spasms after myelitis are characteristic. A progressive course independent of relapses is unusual.
det.diagnosis: The 2015 IPND criteria require one core clinical characteristic with positive AQP4-IgG (cell-based assay preferred), or stricter clinical and MRI requirements when seronegative. MRI typically shows a central cord lesion spanning three or more vertebral segments, and long posterior optic nerve or chiasmal lesions. CSF may show neutrophils or eosinophils with pleocytosis; oligoclonal bands are usually absent. Test MOG-IgG in seronegative cases, and avoid labelling as MS.
det.treatment: Acute attacks need high-dose IV methylprednisolone, with early plasma exchange for severe or steroid-unresponsive attacks. Long-term relapse prevention is essential after the first attack: rituximab, azathioprine and mycophenolate are widely used, and approved targeted agents include eculizumab and ravulizumab (complement), inebilizumab (anti-CD19) and satralizumab (IL-6 receptor). Several MS drugs, including interferon-beta, natalizumab and fingolimod, can worsen NMOSD and should be avoided.
det.prognosis: Untreated disease leads to blindness or paraplegia in many patients; effective preventive therapy has greatly reduced relapses and mortality.
pearls: Intractable hiccups and vomiting with myelitis or optic neuritis = area postrema syndrome.
Long central cord lesion (≥3 segments) argues for NMOSD over MS.
Interferon-beta and natalizumab can harm patients with NMOSD.
det.thd: NMOSD เกิดจากแอนติบอดีต่อ aquaporin-4 บนเซลล์ astrocyte ทำให้เซลล์ถูกทำลายผ่าน complement พบมากในหญิงเอเชีย ตำแหน่งที่เป็นคือเส้นประสาทตา ไขสันหลังยาว ≥3 ปล้อง และ area postrema (สะอึกและอาเจียนไม่หยุด) การกำเริบแต่ละครั้งมักรุนแรงและหายไม่สมบูรณ์ วินิจฉัยด้วย AQP4-IgG แบบ cell-based assay และ MRI รักษาครั้งกำเริบด้วย methylprednisolone และ plasma exchange ป้องกันระยะยาวด้วย rituximab, azathioprine หรือยาใหม่ เช่น eculizumab, inebilizumab, satralizumab และห้ามใช้ยา MS บางตัว เช่น interferon-beta

name: Neuromyotonic syndromes
formal: Peripheral nerve hyperexcitability syndromes including Isaacs syndrome and Morvan syndrome, with myokymia, cramps, stiffness and autoimmune CASPR2 or LGI1 antibodies.
simple: Conditions where nerves fire too much, causing constant muscle twitching, stiffness and cramps.
th: กลุ่มโรคเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายไวเกิน ได้แก่ Isaacs และ Morvan syndrome กล้ามเนื้อกระเพื่อม (myokymia) ตะคริว ตึงแข็ง เหงื่อออกมาก และสัมพันธ์กับ CASPR2/LGI1 antibody และ thymoma
tempoNote: Develops over weeks to months; can be chronic and fluctuating
feat: Continuous rippling of muscles (myokymia), cramps, stiffness and delayed relaxation after grip
Excess sweating and other autonomic symptoms
Morvan syndrome adds insomnia, confusion, hallucinations and dysautonomia
Associated with thymoma, myasthenia gravis and occasionally lung cancer
Some forms are hereditary (KCNA1 episodic ataxia type 1, HINT1 neuropathy)
inv: EMG: myokymic and neuromyotonic discharges (high-frequency, decrementing) persisting in sleep
CASPR2 and LGI1 antibodies, AChR antibodies
CT chest for thymoma; sodium, calcium and magnesium
Polysomnography and EEG in suspected Morvan syndrome

case.story: Three months of constant muscle twitching, stiffness and drenching sweats; recently sleeps only two hours a night and talks to people who are not there.
case.exam: Undulating myokymia over calves and thighs, slow hand opening after grip, tachycardia, intact strength.
case.tests: EMG neuromyotonic discharges; CASPR2 antibody positive; CT anterior mediastinal mass.
case.q: Name the syndrome and the next definitive step.
case.a: Morvan syndrome (CASPR2, thymoma-associated); resect the thymoma and give immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG or plasma exchange, then rituximab if needed).

read.where: Chapter 21 - Abnormal Movements in Neurological Autoimmune Disorders
