det.patho: Motor nerve membranes become hyperexcitable, usually because antibodies against CASPR2 (and less often LGI1) disrupt Kv1 potassium channel complexes at juxtaparanodes. Spontaneous repetitive firing arises along the axon, producing continuous muscle activity that persists in sleep and under general anaesthesia but stops with curare. Paraneoplastic forms link to thymoma; genetic channelopathies cause rarer inherited forms.
det.clinical: Isaacs syndrome (acquired neuromyotonia) presents with myokymia, cramps, pseudomyotonia, stiffness and hyperhidrosis; weakness is not prominent. Morvan syndrome combines this with severe insomnia (agrypnia), encephalopathy, hallucinations and autonomic instability, and can be fatal. Cramp-fasciculation syndrome lies at the milder end. Neuropathic pain and paraesthesia are frequent with CASPR2.
det.diagnosis: EMG demonstrating myokymic and neuromyotonic discharges confirms peripheral nerve hyperexcitability. Antibody testing (CASPR2, LGI1) and chest imaging for thymoma are essential; AChR antibodies often coexist. In Morvan syndrome, sleep studies show loss of normal sleep architecture. Exclude electrolyte disturbance, drugs (e.g. gold), and radiation-related myokymia.
det.treatment: Symptomatic therapy uses sodium-channel blockers (carbamazepine, phenytoin, oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine) or mexiletine. Immunotherapy—corticosteroids, plasma exchange, IVIG, and rituximab for refractory cases—is indicated for antibody-positive or disabling disease. Thymoma resection is central to paraneoplastic forms. Morvan syndrome may need ICU-level autonomic management.
det.prognosis: Non-paraneoplastic Isaacs syndrome often improves or remits; outcome in paraneoplastic and Morvan cases depends on tumour control.
pearls: Continuous activity that persists during sleep localises to peripheral nerve.
Myokymia + insomnia + hallucinations = Morvan; look for thymoma.
CASPR2 antibodies link the mild (cramp-fasciculation) and severe (Morvan) ends.
det.thd: Neuromyotonic syndromes คือกลุ่มโรคปลายประสาทไวเกิน ได้แก่ Isaacs syndrome ที่มีกล้ามเนื้อกระเพื่อมตลอดเวลา ตะคริว ตึง และเหงื่อออกมาก และ Morvan syndrome ที่มีนอนไม่หลับ ประสาทหลอน และระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติผิดปกติร่วม มักเกิดจาก CASPR2 antibody และสัมพันธ์กับ thymoma ตรวจ EMG พบ neuromyotonic discharges และทำ CT ทรวงอก รักษาด้วยยากลุ่ม carbamazepine ร่วมกับยากดภูมิ และผ่าตัด thymoma

name: Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis
formal: Group of lysosomal storage disorders (Batten disease) with progressive visual loss, seizures, myoclonus and dementia, with lipopigment accumulation; CLN genes.
simple: Inherited childhood diseases that cause seizures, vision loss and loss of skills (Batten disease).
th: กลุ่มโรคสะสมในไลโซโซมแบบถ่ายทอดทางพันธุกรรม (ยีน CLN) ทำให้เด็กมีชัก กระตุก สายตาบอด และพัฒนาการถดถอยจนสมองเสื่อม
tempoNote: Relentless decline over years; age of first symptoms (infancy, toddler, school age, adult) depends on the CLN gene
feat: A previously normal child who starts losing skills, with seizures, myoclonus and falling school performance
Visual failure from retinal degeneration; in the juvenile (CLN3) form, blindness at age 5–8 is often the first sign
Late-infantile CLN2: new seizures at 2–4 years after mild speech delay, then rapid motor and cognitive regression
Ataxia, spasticity, parkinsonism and behavioural or psychiatric change as the disease advances
Adult (Kufs) forms present with progressive myoclonic epilepsy or dementia, usually without blindness
inv: Enzyme activity in leukocytes or dried blood spot: PPT1 (CLN1) and TPP1 (CLN2)
Gene panel or exome for CLN genes; blood film for vacuolated lymphocytes (CLN3)
EEG (photoparoxysmal response at slow flash rates in CLN2); ERG reduced or extinguished
MRI shows cerebral and cerebellar atrophy; electron microscopy of skin or lymphocytes shows typical storage inclusions

case.story: Spoke few words at 2 and then had her first afebrile seizure at 3; within months she had daily jerks, unsteady walking and lost words she had learned.
case.exam: Multifocal myoclonus, truncal ataxia, poor visual fixation; no organomegaly.
case.tests: EEG shows spikes driven by 1–2 Hz photic stimulation; MRI cerebellar atrophy; TPP1 activity absent in leukocytes.
case.q: Which NCL is this, and what specific treatment exists?
case.a: CLN2 (late-infantile NCL from TPP1 deficiency); intraventricular cerliponase alfa enzyme replacement slows motor and language loss.

read.where: Chapter 28 Progressive Myoclonic Epilepsies — Neuronal Ceroid Lipofuscinoses
18 - Myoclonus: Phenomenology, etiology, physiology, and treatment

det.patho: The NCLs are at least 13 genetically distinct disorders (CLN1–CLN14) sharing accumulation of autofluorescent lipopigment within lysosomes of neurons and other cells. Some genes encode lysosomal enzymes (PPT1, TPP1, cathepsin D) and others membrane or trafficking proteins (CLN3, CLN6, CLN8). Neurons in the cortex, cerebellum and retina die progressively, producing brain atrophy. Almost all are autosomal recessive; one adult form (CLN4, DNAJC5) is dominant.
det.clinical: Classic childhood forms are named by onset: infantile CLN1 (developmental arrest, microcephaly and myoclonus before 2), late-infantile CLN2 (seizures at 2–4, then fast regression), and juvenile CLN3 (vision loss at school age, then seizures, cognitive and behavioural decline and parkinsonian features in adolescence). Variant late-infantile forms (CLN5, CLN6, CLN7, CLN8) overlap clinically. Adult Kufs disease shows progressive myoclonic epilepsy or dementia with motor signs. Death typically occurs in childhood or early adulthood depending on the subtype.
det.diagnosis: Suspect NCL in any child with new epilepsy plus regression or unexplained visual loss with retinal change. Enzyme assays for PPT1 and TPP1 are fast and widely available; genetic testing defines the subtype and enables family counselling. Supporting clues include vacuolated lymphocytes (CLN3), a slow-flash photoparoxysmal EEG response (CLN2), an abnormal ERG and storage material on electron microscopy. Early testing matters because CLN2 now has disease-specific therapy.
det.treatment: Cerliponase alfa, a recombinant TPP1 given into the ventricles every two weeks through a reservoir, is approved for CLN2 and slows loss of walking and language, especially when begun early. Other forms have no approved disease-modifying treatment; gene therapy and small-molecule trials are ongoing. Management is otherwise supportive: broad-spectrum anti-seizure drugs (valproate, levetiracetam, clobazam; avoid carbamazepine and phenytoin that may worsen myoclonus), feeding support, mobility aids and palliative care. Genetic counselling and cascade testing are essential.
det.prognosis: Progressive in all forms; survival ranges from early childhood (CLN1, CLN2 untreated) to the 20s–30s (CLN3), and is longer in adult forms.
pearls: School-age child going blind, then seizures and dementia: test for CLN3 (look for vacuolated lymphocytes).
Toddler with first seizures and regression: check TPP1 early, because CLN2 has enzyme replacement.
NCL is a leading cause of progressive myoclonic epilepsy in childhood.
det.thd: Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (Batten disease) เป็นกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่มีการสะสมสารไขมันเม็ดสีในไลโซโซมของเซลล์ประสาท ทำให้เด็กที่เคยปกติมีชัก กระตุก ตาบอด และพัฒนาการถดถอย อายุที่เริ่มเป็นขึ้นกับยีน เช่น CLN2 เริ่มชักอายุ 2–4 ปี ส่วน CLN3 เริ่มด้วยตามัวตอนวัยเรียน วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจเอนไซม์ PPT1/TPP1 และตรวจยีน CLN2 รักษาได้ด้วย cerliponase alfa ฉีดเข้าโพรงสมอง ส่วนชนิดอื่นรักษาตามอาการ

name: Neuronal intranuclear inclusion body disease
formal: Neurodegenerative disease (NOTCH2NLC GGC repeat expansions) with eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions, dementia, parkinsonism, neuropathy and DWI corticomedullary junction hyperintensity.
simple: A rare brain disease with abnormal clumps inside nerve cell nuclei, causing dementia, tremor and nerve problems.
th: โรคเสื่อมจาก GGC repeat expansion ในยีน NOTCH2NLC มี inclusion ในนิวเคลียส ทำให้สมองเสื่อม parkinsonism neuropathy และ MRI DWI สูงที่รอยต่อเนื้อเทาเนื้อขาว
tempoNote: Slowly progressive over years, sometimes punctuated by acute encephalitic episodes
feat: Adult-onset cognitive decline, often with leukoencephalopathy
Episodic encephalopathy, stroke-like episodes, headache or seizures
Peripheral neuropathy, tremor, parkinsonism or ataxia; bladder and pupillary autonomic dysfunction
Juvenile and infantile forms exist; family history may be dominant
inv: MRI: DWI curvilinear hyperintensity along the corticomedullary junction plus white matter changes
Skin biopsy: p62/ubiquitin-positive intranuclear inclusions in fibroblasts, adipocytes, sweat gland cells
Genetic testing for NOTCH2NLC GGC repeat expansion (long-read or repeat-primed PCR)
NCS: mild demyelinating-range or mixed neuropathy

case.story: Two years of forgetfulness and urinary urgency, then an episode of confusion, fever-free headache and vomiting lasting 4 days.
case.exam: Mild dysexecutive syndrome, postural tremor, miotic pupils, reduced ankle reflexes.
case.tests: MRI FLAIR leukoencephalopathy with ribbon-like DWI high signal at the grey-white junction in frontal lobes; skin biopsy shows intranuclear inclusions.
case.q: Which gene test confirms the diagnosis?
case.a: NOTCH2NLC GGC repeat expansion — neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease.

det.patho: Expanded GGC repeats in the 5' region of NOTCH2NLC lead to toxic polyglycine-containing protein and RNA effects, producing eosinophilic hyaline intranuclear inclusions in neurons, glia and many somatic cells. The disease has been recognised mainly in East Asian populations, including Japan, China and Taiwan, but occurs elsewhere.
det.clinical: Adult forms present with dementia, autonomic failure, neuropathy, tremor or parkinsonism, and episodic encephalopathy with fever-like or stroke-like attacks. Repeat size may influence phenotype: some carriers present with essential tremor-like illness, neuropathy, or leukoencephalopathy. Many patients were previously labelled as unexplained leukoencephalopathy.
det.diagnosis: The DWI corticomedullary junction sign is a strong clue though not universal or entirely specific. Skin biopsy with p62 or ubiquitin staining is minimally invasive and sensitive. Genetic confirmation of the GGC expansion is now the standard test where available.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy exists. Management is symptomatic: antiseizure drugs, treatment of tremor or parkinsonism, bladder management, and supportive care for encephalitic episodes, which sometimes appear to respond to steroids though evidence is limited.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive over years to decades; course is variable.
pearls: Ribbon of DWI hyperintensity at the grey-white junction in an older adult with leukoencephalopathy: think NIID.
Skin biopsy can make the diagnosis without brain tissue.
Miosis and bladder dysfunction are useful autonomic clues.
det.thd: Neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease (NIID) เกิดจาก GGC repeat expansion ในยีน NOTCH2NLC พบมากในเอเชียตะวันออก ผู้ป่วยผู้ใหญ่มีสมองเสื่อม เส้นประสาทเสื่อม สั่น ปัสสาวะผิดปกติ และอาจมีภาวะสับสนเป็นพัก ๆ MRI พบ DWI สูงเป็นแนวโค้งตามรอยต่อ grey-white matter ตัดชิ้นเนื้อผิวหนังพบ intranuclear inclusion ยืนยันด้วยตรวจยีน ยังไม่มีการรักษาเฉพาะ

name: Neuropathic pain
formal: Pain arising from lesion or disease of the somatosensory nervous system, with burning, shooting character, allodynia and hyperalgesia, as in diabetic neuropathy and post-herpetic neuralgia.
simple: Burning or shooting pain caused by damaged nerves.
th: อาการปวดที่เกิดจากรอยโรคหรือโรคของระบบรับความรู้สึก somatosensory ลักษณะแสบร้อน แปลบ allodynia เช่นจากเบาหวานหรืองูสวัด
tempoNote: Defined as persistent pain; may begin acutely after nerve injury or zoster
feat: Burning, electric, shooting or stabbing pain in a neuroanatomically plausible distribution
Allodynia (pain from light touch) and hyperalgesia, alongside sensory loss in the same area
Peripheral causes: diabetic neuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia, radiculopathy, trigeminal neuralgia
Central causes: post-stroke (thalamic) pain, spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis
Often worse at night; sleep and mood disturbance common
inv: Clinical grading using history, sensory examination and screening tools (DN4, painDETECT)
NCS for large-fibre neuropathy; skin biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fibre density in small-fibre disease
Tests for cause: glucose/HbA1c, B12, MRI of spine or brain as indicated

case.story: Three months after shingles on her left chest wall she still has burning pain and cannot bear her blouse touching the skin.
case.exam: Healed scars in a T5 dermatome, reduced pinprick but marked allodynia to cotton wool in the same band.
case.tests: None required.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and first-line drug options?
case.a: Postherpetic neuralgia (neuropathic pain); pregabalin/gabapentin, amitriptyline or duloxetine, plus topical lidocaine.

23. Neuropathies Associated With HIV Infection and Antiretroviral Therapy

det.patho: Damage to sensory neurons leads to ectopic firing, altered ion channel expression (notably sodium channels), loss of inhibitory control and central sensitisation in the dorsal horn and higher centres. Central lesions in spinothalamic pathways or thalamus cause pain through disinhibition of pain-processing networks.
det.clinical: Pain is described with positive sensory terms and accompanied by negative signs such as numbness. Distribution follows nerves, roots, a dermatome or a central pathway. It is common in diabetes, after zoster, after nerve injury and after stroke. Psychological and sleep comorbidities greatly affect disability.
det.diagnosis: The grading system asks whether the pain has a plausible neuroanatomic distribution and history of a relevant lesion, with confirmation by sensory signs and tests. Screening questionnaires help non-specialists. Look for the underlying cause and treatable contributors.
det.treatment: First-line agents are gabapentinoids, tricyclic antidepressants and SNRIs (duloxetine, venlafaxine); topical lidocaine and high-concentration capsaicin suit localised pain. Tramadol and stronger opioids are reserved as second or third line given modest benefit and harm. Carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine are specific for trigeminal neuralgia. Combine with physical therapy, sleep and mood management; neuromodulation for refractory cases.
det.prognosis: Often chronic; partial pain reduction (30–50 percent) is a realistic goal, and some causes such as postherpetic neuralgia can improve over time.
pearls: Pain with numbness in the same territory strongly suggests a neuropathic mechanism.
Start low, go slow, and give each drug an adequate trial before switching.
Opioids are not first line for neuropathic pain.
det.thd: Neuropathic pain คืออาการปวดจากรอยโรคของระบบประสาทรับความรู้สึก ลักษณะแสบร้อน แปลบเหมือนไฟช็อต และเจ็บจากการสัมผัสเบา ๆ (allodynia) มักพบในเบาหวาน หลังงูสวัด รากประสาทถูกกด หรือหลังโรคหลอดเลือดสมอง วินิจฉัยจากประวัติและการตรวจความรู้สึก ยาหลักคือ gabapentinoid, tricyclic และ SNRI ร่วมกับยาทาเฉพาะที่ และการดูแลการนอนและอารมณ์

det.patho: Weak or imbalanced trunk muscles cannot maintain spinal alignment, leading to collapse into a long curve.
det.clinical: Sitting imbalance, pain, pressure sores and respiratory compromise.
det.diagnosis: Radiographs measure curves; investigate for underlying neuromuscular disease.
det.treatment: Seating supports; bracing has limited effect; spinal fusion for progressive curves. Steroids in Duchenne and SMA therapies reduce scoliosis incidence.

name: Neuropathic tremor syndrome
formal: Postural and action tremor associated with demyelinating neuropathy, as in CIDP, anti-MAG neuropathy and Charcot-Marie-Tooth (Roussy-Levy), thought to arise from sensory afferent loss.
simple: A shaking of the hands that occurs in people with certain nerve diseases.
th: อาการสั่นขณะยกแขนหรือเคลื่อนไหวที่พบร่วมกับโรคเส้นประสาทชนิด demyelinating เช่น CIDP, anti-MAG และ CMT
tempoNote: Develops with or after the neuropathy; may fluctuate with neuropathy activity
feat: Postural and kinetic tremor of the hands, often coarse and irregular
Occurs with demyelinating neuropathy: IgM paraproteinaemic (anti-MAG), CIDP, CMT1 (Roussy-Levy)
Accompanied by sensory ataxia, areflexia and distal weakness or numbness
Severity does not correlate tightly with weakness; may be disabling
inv: NCS: demyelinating features (slow conduction, prolonged distal latencies)
Serum and urine immunofixation and anti-MAG antibodies
Genetic testing (PMP22 duplication) if familial
Accelerometry or EMG tremor analysis if needed

case.story: Two years of numb feet and unsteadiness, now a shaky hand tremor that makes drinking soup difficult.
case.exam: Postural and action tremor of both hands, positive Romberg, absent ankle reflexes, distal sensory loss, mild toe weakness.
case.tests: NCS shows markedly prolonged distal motor latencies; IgM kappa paraprotein and high anti-MAG titre.
case.q: What is the tremor mechanism and underlying diagnosis?
case.a: Neuropathic tremor due to anti-MAG demyelinating neuropathy — abnormal proprioceptive feedback with cerebellar mis-correction.

det.patho: The tremor probably arises from mismatch between distorted, slowed proprioceptive afferent input from demyelinated nerves and central (cerebellar) motor control, producing oscillation. Imaging and physiology studies suggest cerebellar involvement in compensating for abnormal feedback.
det.clinical: Typically a postural and action tremor of the upper limbs, frequency often lower than essential tremor, with sensory ataxia and areflexia. It is common in IgM paraprotein neuropathies and less so in CIDP or hereditary demyelinating neuropathy. Tremor may persist even when neuropathy treatment improves strength.
det.diagnosis: Identify the tremor clinically and confirm a demyelinating neuropathy with NCS; search for paraprotein, anti-MAG antibodies and genetic causes. Exclude coexisting essential tremor, drug-induced tremor and cerebellar disease.
det.treatment: Treat the neuropathy (immunotherapy for CIDP, rituximab for anti-MAG), though tremor response is inconsistent. Symptomatic options include propranolol, primidone or gabapentin with modest benefit; refractory cases have been treated with thalamic DBS. Occupational therapy and weighted utensils help.
det.prognosis: Variable; often persistent and can be the most disabling feature.
pearls: Tremor plus areflexia and sensory ataxia: get NCS before diagnosing essential tremor.
IgM paraprotein neuropathy is the classic setting.

det.patho: MADSAM is an immune-mediated demyelinating neuropathy classified as a multifocal variant of CIDP in the 2021 EAN/PNS guideline. Inflammation targets discrete nerve segments, causing persistent conduction block in both motor and sensory fibres rather than diffuse length-dependent involvement. Specific antibodies are usually absent, and the trigger is unknown.
det.clinical: Patients develop asymmetric weakness and sensory loss in the territories of individual nerves, most often starting in the arm (median or ulnar) and spreading over months or years to other limbs. Pain is usually mild, and reflexes are reduced in affected limbs. Cranial neuropathies occasionally occur. The pattern can mimic multiple entrapments, but deficits appear at non-compression sites.
det.diagnosis: Electrodiagnosis shows multifocal demyelinating features — conduction block, temporal dispersion and focal slowing — in motor nerves, with abnormal sensory conduction in the same segments, meeting CIDP criteria for a multifocal pattern. CSF protein is often raised. MRI or ultrasound may show focal nerve or plexus thickening and enhancement. Exclude MMN (normal sensory studies), vasculitis (axonal, painful), HNPP, paraproteinaemia and lymphoma infiltration.
det.treatment: First-line options are IVIG (a 2 g/kg loading course, followed by maintenance infusions) or corticosteroids, and plasma exchange in selected patients. Unlike MMN, steroids are generally effective. Response should be judged with objective strength and disability measures, and the maintenance dose tapered to the lowest effective level. Refractory cases may receive rituximab or other immunosuppressants.
det.prognosis: Most patients respond to immunotherapy, though fewer reach complete remission than in typical CIDP. Long-standing conduction block with axonal loss leaves residual deficits.
pearls: Asymmetric sensory plus motor multifocal demyelination = MADSAM; pure motor = MMN.

Chapter 7 Occupational, Biologic, and Environmental Toxic Neuropathies (Arsenic)

det.patho: Inorganic trivalent arsenic binds sulfhydryl groups and disrupts pyruvate dehydrogenase and other enzymes, impairing energy production in long axons. The result is a dying-back axonopathy with secondary changes. Exposure sources include contaminated ground water, mining, pesticides, some traditional remedies and deliberate poisoning. Large-diameter sensory and motor fibres bear the brunt, and the metalloid also injures gut, skin, marrow, liver and kidney, so the neuropathy is one part of a multisystem illness. Worldwide on the order of a hundred million people drink groundwater with unsafe arsenic levels, with the heaviest burden in South and Southeast Asia, and contaminated herbal, Ayurvedic or homeopathic preparations remain a recurring source.
det.clinical: Acute poisoning starts with GI upset and cardiovascular instability; the neuropathy follows after roughly one to four weeks and keeps advancing for weeks even without further exposure, sometimes to bifacial and respiratory weakness, closely mimicking GBS. Chronic low-level exposure causes a slowly developing painful sensorimotor neuropathy in a glove-and-stocking pattern with characteristic skin changes, and increases risk of skin, lung and bladder cancer. Systemic clues include gingival and skin melanosis, palmar–plantar hyperkeratosis, transient leucopenia or pancytopenia with anaemia, raised transaminases, coarse tremor and QT prolongation. Neuropathy appearing at the same time in several members of one household or village, who share water or a remedy, is a powerful pointer to a toxin. Thailand's Ron Phibun district is a historically known endemic area.
det.diagnosis: Measure urine arsenic in a 24-hour collection, with speciation because seafood contains non-toxic organic arsenic; a high value proves exposure, but toxicity needs the matching clinical picture. Blood arsenic is cleared within hours, so a normal blood level does not exclude chronic poisoning; hair and nails reflect exposure over months. Studies done soon after acute exposure can meet demyelinating criteria (slowing, conduction block, dispersion, absent F waves), but early loss of the sural response — the opposite of the sural sparing typical of AIDP — is a clue, and repeat studies evolve into a severe dying-back axonal pattern. CSF protein may be raised without cells, so albuminocytological dissociation does not settle the question. Mees lines, basophilic stippling and skin changes are strong supporting clues, and testing the household water or remedy identifies the source.
det.treatment: Stop exposure and give supportive care, including cardiac monitoring for QT prolongation and torsades, hydration to keep urine output high, and respiratory monitoring in acute cases. Chelation with DMSA or DMPS (or intramuscular dimercaprol in severe acute cases) is most effective soon after exposure and has limited, debated benefit for established neuropathy; DMSA is generally preferred when chronic poisoning is treated, and dimercaprol can cause haemolysis in G6PD deficiency. Plasma exchange and IVIG do not alter the course. Treat pain and provide rehabilitation; notify public-health authorities, test family members sharing the same water, and arrange an arsenic-safe supply.
det.prognosis: Recovery is slow and often incomplete over months to years, depending on severity and duration of exposure; younger patients with milder deficits may recover fully within about a year once the source is removed.
pearls: GBS-like illness preceded by vomiting and diarrhoea: think heavy metals and check urine arsenic.
Mees lines appear weeks after exposure, so their position on the nail dates the poisoning.

'GBS' with an absent sural response, cytopenia and raised liver enzymes — or a second 'GBS' in the same home — means arsenic until proven otherwise.

det.patho: Inorganic lead binds sulfhydryl groups and disrupts haem synthesis enzymes (ALA dehydratase, ferrochelatase), which explains the anaemia and raised protoporphyrin. In nerves it damages axons and Schwann cells, with a preference for long motor fibres. Adults accumulate it mostly in bone, so stores can be released again during illness, pregnancy or bone turnover.
det.clinical: Adults present with a slowly evolving motor neuropathy, characteristically in radial-supplied extensors, sometimes in a pattern that resembles motor neuron disease. Sensory symptoms are minor. Gastrointestinal colic, fatigue, irritability, hypertension and nephropathy are common companions. Children exposed to lead develop cognitive and behavioural problems and, at high levels, encephalopathy with raised intracranial pressure.
det.diagnosis: A raised blood lead level confirms recent or ongoing exposure, while protoporphyrin levels and bone lead reflect longer accumulation. Basophilic stippling and microcytic anaemia support the diagnosis. Electrophysiology shows a motor-predominant axonal neuropathy. An exposure history must be taken actively because patients rarely volunteer occupational details.
det.treatment: The essential step is stopping exposure, which may require workplace changes and testing of co-workers or children at home. Chelation (for example oral succimer or parenteral calcium disodium EDTA, sometimes with dimercaprol in severe cases) is chosen according to blood level and symptoms, ideally with toxicology advice. Physiotherapy and wrist splints help function while axons regrow.
det.prognosis: Motor recovery usually occurs over months once exposure stops, though long-standing cases may leave residual weakness.
pearls: Bilateral wrist drop with abdominal colic: check blood lead.
Look at the blood film for basophilic stippling.
Ask about battery work, smelting, renovation of old paint and traditional medicines.
det.thd: พิษตะกั่วเรื้อรังทำให้เกิด neuropathy ที่เด่นด้าน motor โดยเฉพาะกล้ามเนื้อเหยียดข้อมือ (wrist drop) ทั้งสองข้าง ความรู้สึกมักปกติ ผู้ป่วยมักมีปวดท้องบิด ท้องผูก และซีดแบบ basophilic stippling ร่วมด้วย การวินิจฉัยใช้ระดับตะกั่วในเลือดและประวัติการสัมผัส เช่น งานรีไซเคิลแบตเตอรี่ การรักษาคือหยุดการสัมผัสและให้ยาขับโลหะ (chelation)

name: Neuropathy related to mercury
formal: Sensory neuropathy with ataxia, tremor, and erethism following inorganic or organic mercury exposure, with acrodynia in children.

Ataxia, tremor, dysarthria and constricted visual fields (methylmercury, Minamata pattern)
Erethism: irritability, shyness, insomnia, memory problems (inorganic or elemental vapour)

case.exam: Fine action tremor, reduced pinprick in gloves and stockings, brisk mood lability, normal strength.

det.patho: Mercury binds sulfhydryl groups and disrupts protein function, microtubules and oxidative defences. Methylmercury crosses the blood-brain barrier and damages cerebellar granule cells, visual cortex and dorsal root ganglia. Elemental vapour is absorbed through the lungs and oxidised to inorganic mercury that affects the brain and kidneys; inorganic salts mainly cause kidney and nerve injury.
det.clinical: Features depend on the form. Methylmercury produces distal and perioral paraesthesia, ataxia, dysarthria, hearing loss and concentric visual field constriction. Vapour exposure gives tremor and neuropsychiatric change. Chronic inorganic exposure from creams causes sensory symptoms, tremor and nephrotic syndrome; children may develop acrodynia.
det.diagnosis: Take a detailed exposure history (cosmetics, occupation, diet, home remedies). Measure blood mercury for organic exposure and urine for inorganic; interpret against reference ranges and timing. NCS and renal tests characterise damage.
det.treatment: Remove the source first. Chelation with DMSA (succimer) or DMPS is used for significant inorganic or elemental exposure, guided by a toxicologist; chelation is less effective for methylmercury. Supportive treatment for pain, tremor and renal disease. Notify public health when a commercial product is implicated.
det.prognosis: Recovery after removal of exposure is often partial; central damage from methylmercury tends to be permanent.
pearls: Ask about skin-lightening creams in a woman with neuropathy and proteinuria.
Blood for methylmercury, urine for inorganic mercury.
Concentric field loss plus ataxia recalls the Minamata outbreak.
det.thd: พิษปรอททำให้เกิดอาการทางระบบประสาทได้หลายแบบ ปรอทอินทรีย์ (methylmercury จากปลาที่ปนเปื้อน) ทำให้ชารอบปากและปลายมือเท้า เดินเซ ลานสายตาแคบ ส่วนไอปรอทหรือปรอทอนินทรีย์ (เช่นครีมหน้าขาว) ทำให้มือสั่น อารมณ์แปรปรวน นอนไม่หลับ และไตผิดปกติ ตรวจระดับปรอทในเลือดหรือปัสสาวะ หยุดแหล่งสัมผัสทันที และพิจารณายาขับโลหะร่วมกับผู้เชี่ยวชาญพิษวิทยา

det.patho: Nitrofurantoin and its metabolites accumulate when renal clearance falls and are thought to impair axonal energy metabolism, producing a dying-back axonopathy. Sensory fibres are usually affected first, followed by motor fibres in more severe cases. Susceptibility is greater in older adults and those with diabetes, anaemia or vitamin deficiency.
det.clinical: Symptoms begin as distal paraesthesias that may spread within days to weeks. In severe or unrecognised cases, a rapidly ascending flaccid weakness develops that can be confused with Guillain–Barré syndrome. The neuropathy can occur with short courses in renal failure or after months of low-dose prophylaxis.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis rests on temporal association with the drug, an axonal sensorimotor pattern on nerve conduction studies and exclusion of other causes. CSF is usually unremarkable, which helps separate it from GBS. Kidney function should be measured in anyone taking long-term nitrofurantoin.
det.treatment: Stop nitrofurantoin as soon as the neuropathy is suspected and do not rechallenge. Management is supportive with neuropathic pain medication, physiotherapy and falls prevention. Avoid the drug in significant renal impairment according to current prescribing guidance.

det.patho: Some organophosphates inhibit and then 'age' neuropathy target esterase in neurons, triggering a distal axonopathy of long motor and sensory axons in nerves and spinal tracts. This mechanism is separate from acetylcholinesterase inhibition, so delayed neuropathy can follow even mild cholinergic toxicity. The intermediate syndrome reflects persistent postsynaptic dysfunction at the neuromuscular junction.
det.clinical: Three phases are recognised: the acute cholinergic crisis, the intermediate syndrome with proximal and respiratory weakness, and the delayed neuropathy. The delayed phase begins with calf cramps and distal tingling and evolves into distal weakness, sometimes severe enough to cause foot and wrist drop. Upper motor neuron signs may become prominent months later and determine long-term disability.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, linking the timeline to a known exposure, supported by an axonal motor-predominant pattern on nerve conduction studies. Cholinesterase levels help in the acute phase but do not predict delayed neuropathy. Imaging and CSF are used mainly to exclude alternatives.
det.treatment: Acute poisoning is managed with decontamination, atropine titrated to secretions, oximes in line with local protocols, and ventilatory support. No antidote prevents or reverses the delayed neuropathy; treatment is rehabilitation, orthoses and spasticity management. Psychiatric follow-up is important after intentional ingestion.
det.prognosis: Peripheral recovery is slow and often incomplete; persistent spasticity and gait disability are common in severe cases.
pearls: Three phases: cholinergic crisis, intermediate syndrome, delayed neuropathy.
Calf cramps two to three weeks after poisoning herald the delayed neuropathy.
Watch respiratory function closely in the intermediate syndrome.

det.patho: Thalidomide likely damages dorsal root ganglion neurons and distal sensory axons, possibly through anti-angiogenic effects on nerve blood supply and interference with neurotrophic signalling. det.treatment: Early dose reduction or discontinuation is the main measure, in partnership with the treating oncologist or dermatologist. Neuropathic pain may respond to duloxetine, gabapentinoids or tricyclics. Foot care and balance training reduce injury and falls.

det.patho: Thallium behaves like potassium and enters cells through potassium transport mechanisms, where it disrupts mitochondrial function and sulfhydryl-dependent enzymes. Long axons and rapidly dividing hair follicles are especially vulnerable. It undergoes enterohepatic circulation, which prolongs toxicity.
det.clinical: Gastrointestinal illness is followed within days by a strikingly painful sensory neuropathy beginning in the feet. Motor weakness, autonomic disturbance, cranial nerve palsies and encephalopathy appear with heavier exposure. Hair falls out roughly two to three weeks after exposure, a sign that strongly points to the diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: Elevated 24-hour urine thallium confirms the diagnosis. Nerve conduction studies show axonal damage, which may be minimal in the first days. Clusters of cases or suspicious circumstances should prompt early testing.
det.treatment: Prussian blue (potassium ferric hexacyanoferrate) given orally binds thallium in the gut; haemodialysis or haemoperfusion helps in severe poisoning. Supportive care, pain control and rehabilitation are needed. Legal and public health authorities should be involved when poisoning is deliberate or environmental.
det.prognosis: Outcome depends on the dose and speed of treatment; survivors often recover partially, with residual neuropathy and sometimes cognitive problems.
pearls: Painful neuropathy plus alopecia two weeks later: think thallium.
Test urine, not just blood.
Several family members ill together suggests poisoning.

name: Neuropathy, ataxia, and retinitis pigmentosa (NARP)
formal: Maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder (m.8993T>G in MT-ATP6) with sensory neuropathy, ataxia, retinitis pigmentosa, seizures and developmental delay.
simple: An inherited energy-production disease causing nerve damage, poor balance and gradual vision loss.
th: โรคไมโทคอนเดรียที่ถ่ายทอดทางแม่ (MT-ATP6) ทำให้มีปลายประสาทรับความรู้สึกเสื่อม เดินเซ และจอประสาทตาเสื่อมชนิด retinitis pigmentosa
tempoNote: Onset in childhood or young adulthood with slow progression; may worsen stepwise with intercurrent illness
feat: Night blindness and constricted fields from pigmentary retinopathy
Sensory-predominant neuropathy causing numb feet and loss of ankle jerks; proximal weakness in some
Cerebellar and sensory ataxia
Seizures, learning difficulty or developmental delay; affected maternal relatives with variable signs
Higher mutant load in a sibling or child can produce Leigh syndrome (MILS)
inv: mtDNA testing for m.8993T>G or T>C in blood, urine epithelium or muscle, with heteroplasmy level
Electroretinogram and fundoscopy; nerve conduction studies
Blood and CSF lactate (may be normal); MRI for cerebellar atrophy or basal ganglia lesions

case.story: Trouble seeing at dusk since his teens and now stumbles on uneven ground; his younger brother died in infancy after developmental regression.
case.exam: Bone-spicule pigment in both retinas, absent ankle reflexes, reduced vibration at toes, heel-shin ataxia.
case.tests: NCS shows axonal sensory neuropathy; ERG markedly reduced; blood m.8993T>G at 82% heteroplasmy.
case.q: How does one mutation explain both his illness and his brother's death?
case.a: NARP from MT-ATP6; a higher proportion of the same maternally inherited variant causes maternally inherited Leigh syndrome in infancy.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Primary Mitochondrial Diseases

det.patho: NARP results from point variants at position 8993 of the mitochondrial genome, within MT-ATP6, which encodes a subunit of ATP synthase (complex V). Impaired ATP production hits energy-hungry tissues such as retina, peripheral sensory neurons and cerebellum. Severity tracks the proportion of mutant mtDNA (heteroplasmy): around 70–90% tends to give NARP, while higher loads give maternally inherited Leigh syndrome.
det.clinical: Typical onset is in childhood or early adult life with a combination of night blindness, sensory neuropathy and ataxia; not every feature is present in every patient. Additional problems include seizures, cognitive impairment, proximal weakness, hearing loss and cardiac conduction disease. Illness, fever or surgery may provoke stepwise deterioration. Maternal relatives may have isolated retinopathy, mild neuropathy or nothing at all.
det.diagnosis: Targeted testing for m.8993T>G/C is the first step when the triad is present or Leigh syndrome runs in the maternal line. Heteroplasmy can differ between tissues, so urine or muscle may be needed if blood is negative. ERG, NCS and MRI document organ involvement. Exclude other causes of retinopathy with neuropathy such as Refsum disease, abetalipoproteinaemia and vitamin E deficiency.
det.treatment: There is no cure. Care is supportive: low-vision aids, physiotherapy for ataxia, standard anti-seizure drugs, and cardiac and hearing surveillance. Mitochondrial supplements (coenzyme Q10, riboflavin and similar) are commonly tried but have little proof. Avoid prolonged fasting and treat infections promptly; genetic counselling should explain the unpredictable risk to offspring of women carrying the variant.
det.prognosis: Usually slowly progressive with survival into adulthood, but outcome varies widely with mutant load.
pearls: Retinitis pigmentosa plus sensory ataxia in a young adult: think NARP, Refsum and vitamin E deficiency.
NARP and maternally inherited Leigh syndrome are the same mutation at different heteroplasmy levels.
A negative blood test does not exclude mtDNA disease; test urine or muscle.
det.thd: NARP เป็นโรคไมโทคอนเดรียที่ถ่ายทอดทางแม่ เกิดจากการกลายพันธุ์ m.8993 ในยีน MT-ATP6 ทำให้สร้างพลังงานไม่พอ ผู้ป่วยมีปลายประสาทรับความรู้สึกเสื่อม เดินเซ และตาบอดกลางคืนจาก retinitis pigmentosa อาจมีชักหรือพัฒนาการช้า ถ้าสัดส่วนดีเอ็นเอผิดปกติสูงมากจะเป็น Leigh syndrome ในทารก วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจ mtDNA และรักษาตามอาการ

name: Neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus (NPSLE)
formal: Neuropsychiatric manifestations of lupus, including seizures, psychosis, stroke, myelitis, neuropathy and cognitive disorder, related to vasculopathy, antiphospholipid antibodies and autoantibodies.
simple: Lupus affecting the brain or nerves, causing seizures, mood or thinking changes, or strokes.
th: อาการทางระบบประสาทและจิตเวชในผู้ป่วย SLE เช่น ชัก โรคจิต stroke ไขสันหลังอักเสบ เส้นประสาทผิดปกติ และความจำถดถอย จากหลอดเลือดผิดปกติ antiphospholipid antibody และ autoantibody
tempoNote: Seizures, stroke and psychosis are acute; myelitis and confusional states subacute; cognitive dysfunction chronic and often fluctuating
feat: Usually young women with active or established SLE (rash, arthritis, nephritis, cytopenias)
Central syndromes: seizures, stroke or TIA, acute confusional state, psychosis, myelitis, aseptic meningitis, chorea
Headache, mood disorder and mild cognitive complaints are common but least specific
Peripheral syndromes: mononeuritis multiplex, polyneuropathy, cranial neuropathy, rarely GBS-like illness
Two drivers: inflammatory autoantibody-mediated injury vs thrombotic disease from antiphospholipid antibodies
inv: MRI brain/spine: infarcts, small white matter lesions, longitudinally extensive myelitis; often normal in psychosis
Serology: complement, anti-dsDNA, antiphospholipid panel (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2GPI)
CSF to exclude infection (immunosuppressed host); EEG for seizures or confusion
Rule out mimics: infection, PRES, drug effects (steroid psychosis), uraemia, electrolyte disturbance

case.story: Diagnosed with SLE two years ago, poorly adherent to treatment. Over a week she became suspicious, heard voices and then had a generalised seizure.
case.exam: Malar rash, oral ulcers, disoriented with paranoid ideas; no focal deficits; neck supple.
case.tests: Low C3/C4, high anti-dsDNA, positive anti-ribosomal P; MRI shows a few small white matter foci; CSF mild protein rise, cultures negative.
case.q: What must be excluded before attributing this to lupus, and how is it treated?
case.a: Exclude CNS infection, PRES, metabolic and drug causes; then treat inflammatory NPSLE with IV methylprednisolone plus cyclophosphamide or rituximab, with antiseizure and antipsychotic drugs as needed.

read.where: Cerebrovascular Disease — Vasculitis of the Central Nervous System: Noninfectious Cerebral Vasculitis
Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
Chapter 25 - Frequently Asked Questions on Autoimmune Encephalitis and Related Disorders
Chapter 50 Connective Tissue Diseases, Vasculitis, and the Nervous System
Section 6 Systemic Disorders That Also Involve the Cerebrovascular System

det.patho: Two broad mechanisms are recognised. Inflammatory disease follows leakage across a damaged blood-brain barrier, letting autoantibodies (anti-ribosomal P, anti-NR2 subsets of anti-dsDNA) and cytokines reach and act on neurons, producing diffuse syndromes such as psychosis and confusion. Ischaemic disease comes from antiphospholipid-related thrombosis, Libman-Sacks endocarditis and a non-inflammatory small-vessel vasculopathy; true vasculitis of brain vessels is uncommon. Accelerated atherosclerosis adds risk over time.
det.clinical: The ACR nomenclature lists 19 neuropsychiatric syndromes, 12 central and 7 peripheral. Serious events (seizures, stroke, myelitis, psychosis, acute confusion) often appear early in the disease and with general lupus activity, but stroke can occur when SLE is quiet. Cognitive dysfunction is frequent and usually mild-moderate. Up to half of neuropsychiatric events in lupus patients are due to something else, such as infection, drugs or metabolic disturbance.
det.diagnosis: Attribution is clinical: decide whether the event is due to SLE, a complication of treatment or an unrelated cause, using timing, lupus activity, serology and imaging. MRI, CSF and EEG are tailored to the syndrome; antiphospholipid testing must be repeated after 12 weeks for confirmation. Lupus myelitis needs MRI and AQP4 testing because NMOSD coexists with SLE. Attribution models (e.g. the SLICC and Italian models) help standardise this judgement.
det.treatment: Inflammatory syndromes are treated with high-dose glucocorticoids plus a second agent, usually IV cyclophosphamide, with rituximab or mycophenolate as alternatives; plasma exchange is used in refractory cases. Thrombotic events are treated as stroke plus long-term anticoagulation (warfarin) in antiphospholipid-positive patients. Hydroxychloroquine is continued in all, and symptomatic therapy covers seizures, psychosis and mood. Control vascular risk factors and minimise long-term steroid exposure.
det.prognosis: Many acute inflammatory syndromes respond well, but NPSLE increases mortality and long-term disability, especially with stroke or recurrent events.
pearls: In a lupus patient on immunosuppression with new CNS symptoms, rule out infection first.
Stroke in SLE is often antiphospholipid-mediated, not vasculitic: anticoagulate, not just immunosuppress.
Steroid-induced psychosis usually appears within weeks of a dose increase; lupus psychosis with active serology.

name: Neuropsychiatry catatonia
formal: Psychomotor syndrome with stupor, mutism, posturing, negativism and waxy flexibility, from psychiatric, autoimmune or medical causes, responsive to benzodiazepines or ECT.
simple: A condition where a person is unresponsive, still or mute, or shows odd repeated movements, which can improve with treatment.
th: กลุ่มอาการทางจิตประสาทที่มีการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติ เช่น นิ่งไม่พูด คงท่าแปลก ๆ ต่อต้าน เกิดได้ทั้งจากโรคจิตเวชและโรคทางกาย ตอบสนองดีต่อ lorazepam หรือ ECT
tempoNote: Usually builds over hours to days; can persist for weeks if unrecognised, and may recur with each mood episode
feat: Stupor or marked slowing with little response to the surroundings, often with mutism
Holding odd postures against gravity (posturing, catalepsy) and waxy resistance to passive movement
Negativism, staring, echolalia or echopraxia, grimacing and repetitive mannerisms
Refusal to eat or drink, leading to dehydration and weight loss
Underlying cause may be mood disorder, psychosis, autism, encephalitis, drugs or metabolic illness

Lorazepam challenge (e.g. 1–2 mg IV) — clear improvement within hours supports the diagnosis
Screen for medical causes: electrolytes, glucose, CK, thyroid, drug levels; EEG to exclude non-convulsive seizures

case.who: 24-year-old woman from Nakhon Pathom brought in by her mother
case.story: For four days she has stopped speaking and eating after two weeks of low mood and little sleep; she stands by the window for hours.
case.exam: Awake with open eyes but mute; her raised arm stays in the air for a minute; she resists being moved with equal force; afebrile, BP normal.
case.tests: Electrolytes, glucose, CK and TSH normal; EEG diffuse slowing without seizures; after lorazepam 2 mg IV she says a few words and drinks water.
case.q: What syndrome is present, and what is the next treatment step?
case.a: Catatonia, probably linked to a depressive episode; continue scheduled lorazepam and arrange ECT if response is incomplete, while still excluding autoimmune encephalitis.

read.where: 1 - Clinical overview and phenomenology of movement disorders

det.patho: Catatonia describes a cluster of motor and behavioural signs, not one illness, and is thought to reflect disturbed GABA-A, glutamate and dopamine signalling in frontal–basal ganglia motor circuits. Around half of cases occur with mood disorders, especially bipolar depression or mania, and a smaller share with schizophrenia; the rest arise from medical or neurological illness such as encephalitis, epilepsy, metabolic disturbance or drug withdrawal. The rapid benefit of benzodiazepines points to a GABA deficit, whereas antipsychotics can worsen it.
det.clinical: Patients may be stuporous and mute or, less often, excited and purposelessly overactive. Typical signs include staring, posturing, catalepsy, waxy flexibility, negativism, automatic obedience, echo phenomena and verbigeration. It is frequently missed in medical wards, where it may be labelled as depression, delirium or decreased consciousness. Complications include dehydration, pressure sores, aspiration, venous thromboembolism and contractures; a febrile autonomic form (malignant or lethal catatonia) is an emergency.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, based on the presence of several characteristic signs (DSM-5-TR requires three of twelve) and helped by a standard rating scale. A lorazepam challenge with clear improvement is strong support. Every first episode needs a medical work-up, as autoimmune encephalitis, non-convulsive seizures, hyponatraemia, hepatic or renal failure and drug toxicity can all present this way. Always ask about recent antipsychotics to distinguish NMS.
det.treatment: Lorazepam is first line, given regularly and titrated (often several milligrams per day) until signs resolve, then tapered slowly. ECT is highly effective when benzodiazepines fail or in malignant forms, and should not be delayed. Stop or avoid dopamine-blocking drugs during the acute phase. Supportive care includes fluids, nutrition, thromboprophylaxis, positioning and treatment of the underlying condition.
det.prognosis: Most patients respond fully to lorazepam or ECT, particularly those with mood disorders; chronic catatonia in schizophrenia or autism responds less well.
pearls: Arm stays where you place it, mute patient, eyes open: think catatonia and try lorazepam.
Antipsychotics can tip catatonia into an NMS-like malignant state; hold them initially.
First-episode catatonia in a young woman deserves NMDAR antibody testing.

name: Neuroretinitis
formal: Optic disc swelling with macular star exudates from optic nerve and retinal inflammation, often due to Bartonella henselae infection.
simple: Swelling of the optic nerve with a star-shaped pattern in the retina causing blurred vision, often from infection such as cat-scratch disease.
th: การอักเสบของขั้วประสาทตาและจอตา ทำให้ขั้วประสาทตาบวมร่วมกับไขมันรูปดาวที่ macula มักเกิดจากเชื้อ Bartonella henselae และไม่ใช่โรคนำไป MS
tempoNote: Visual loss over days; macular star appears a few days to two weeks after disc swelling, then resolves over months
feat: Usually painless unilateral blurring after a flu-like illness or lymphadenopathy, with the vision typically 20/200 to 20/40
Optic disc swelling with peripapillary subretinal fluid, then lipid exudates in Henle layer forming a macular star days later
Relative afferent pupillary defect and colour loss are present but eye movement is painless, unlike optic neuritis
Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch) is the leading cause; syphilis, Lyme, toxoplasma, TB, leptospirosis and viral infections are others, many cases remain idiopathic
Vitritis or retinal white spots may accompany it; systemic symptoms include fever and tender regional nodes

case.story: He had low-grade fever and a tender swelling in the left armpit two weeks after a scratch from a stray kitten. Then blurred vision developed in the left eye over three days, with no pain on eye movement.
case.exam: Left acuity 20/100, mild RAPD, reduced colour plates; disc swollen with early exudate beginning to fan out at the macula. Right eye normal.
case.tests: OCT shows subretinal fluid; Bartonella henselae IgM positive; syphilis serology negative; MRI orbits shows mild enhancement of the optic nerve head only.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and does he have MS?
case.a: Neuroretinitis due to Bartonella. It does not usually predict MS. Treat with doxycycline plus rifampicin for 4–6 weeks; steroid is sometimes added in severe cases.

read.where: Chapter 42: Acquired Inflammatory Diseases of the Optic Nerve

det.patho: Neuroretinitis is an inflammatory or infective disease of the optic nerve head with leakage from peripapillary capillaries. Fluid collects in the retina and lipid-rich exudate settles into the radial fibre layer of Henle around the fovea, which explains the star shape that appears only after the swelling subsides. Bartonella henselae from a cat flea, scratch or bite is responsible for most identified cases, with other infective agents far less common.
det.clinical: Patients are often young and present with unilateral, painless blurring that evolves over several days, sometimes preceded by fever, malaise or enlarged nodes. Acuity ranges from near normal to marked loss, colour vision is reduced, and the field shows a central or caecocentral defect. The macular star may be absent at the first visit, so a swollen disc with leakage warrants a second look a week later. Cat-scratch disease may also cause encephalopathy, which Fenichel notes as the commonest neurological complication.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is made by the fundus and OCT findings, and supported by serology or PCR for the likely agent. A typical picture in a patient with cat contact and a positive Bartonella result is enough, but all cases need syphilis serology and exposure-directed tests. MRI is optional; the risk of later multiple sclerosis is low, unlike typical optic neuritis. Differentiate from papilloedema, ischaemic neuropathy, hypertensive retinopathy and posterior uveitis.
det.treatment: Many cases recover without treatment, but antibiotics (doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, often with rifampicin, for 4 to 6 weeks) are commonly given for Bartonella, especially in severe or systemic disease, and speed recovery. Systemic corticosteroids are sometimes added at the ophthalmologist's discretion. Treat syphilis, toxoplasmosis or tuberculosis according to the specific infection.
det.prognosis: Usually good, with recovery over weeks to months and acuity returning near baseline, though some retain a mild field defect or colour loss.
pearls: Disc swelling with a macular star means neuroretinitis, not typical optic neuritis.
The star may appear only 1 to 2 weeks after onset, so re-examine.
Always ask about cats and send syphilis serology.

simple: A headache that starts suddenly and then continues every day without letting up.

feat: Patient recalls the exact day (sometimes the hour) the headache started
Daily and unremitting from the start, without previous escalating headache history
May have migraine-like or tension-type-like features
Onset sometimes follows an infection, stressful event or surgery
Often resistant to standard preventive treatments

case.story: Headache started on the morning after a viral fever two months ago and has not stopped a single day since; she had no prior headaches.
case.exam: Normal, including fundi; headache unchanged when lying or standing.
case.tests: MRI brain with contrast and MRV normal.

det.patho: The cause is unknown. Proposed mechanisms include post-infectious inflammation (raised CSF TNF-alpha in some), cervical joint hypermobility, and persistent central sensitisation after a trigger. It may represent a heterogeneous group rather than one disorder.
det.clinical: Onset is sudden in the sense of a clearly remembered day, though not thunderclap. The phenotype is usually migraine-like or tension-type-like and varies in severity. Two courses are described: self-limiting (resolving within months) and refractory (persisting for years). It affects young adults and teenagers more often.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 requires a distinct, remembered onset, continuous pain within 24 hours, duration over 3 months and no better explanation. Secondary NDPH mimics must be excluded: SIH, CVT, IIH, dissection, sphenoid sinusitis, meningitis, giant cell arteritis in older patients and medication overuse.
det.treatment: No preventive is specifically proven. Treatment follows the phenotype: amitriptyline, topiramate, gabapentin, propranolol or CGRP-targeted therapy for migraine-like cases; nerve blocks and onabotulinumtoxinA have been tried. Address sleep, mood and medication overuse.
det.prognosis: Some remit within a few months; others persist for years despite treatment.
pearls: Ask: do you remember the day it started? A clear date suggests NDPH.
Rule out SIH and CVT before labelling NDPH.
No prior headache history is part of the picture.
det.thd: NDPH คือปวดศีรษะที่เริ่มต้นในวันที่ผู้ป่วยจำได้ชัดเจน และปวดทุกวันต่อเนื่องตั้งแต่วันแรกนานเกิน 3 เดือน โดยไม่เคยปวดหัวบ่อยมาก่อน บางรายเริ่มหลังติดเชื้อหรือความเครียด ต้องตัดสาเหตุทุติยภูมิ เช่น ความดันน้ำไขสันหลังต่ำ หลอดเลือดดำในสมองอุดตัน หรือหลอดเลือดฉีกขาด การรักษาใช้ยาป้องกันตามลักษณะอาการ บางรายหายเองได้ แต่บางรายเป็นนานหลายปี

name: New-onset refractory status epilepticus (NORSE)
formal: Refractory status epilepticus without prior epilepsy and no clear structural or toxic cause; often autoimmune or cryptogenic, with FIRES as a childhood subtype after febrile illness.
simple: A serious state of continuous seizures in a previously healthy person that does not respond to usual medicines and has no obvious cause.
th: ภาวะชักต่อเนื่องดื้อยาที่เกิดครั้งแรกในคนไม่เคยเป็นลมชักและไม่พบสาเหตุโครงสร้าง ยา หรือเมตาบอลิกชัดเจน มักมีสาเหตุจากภูมิคุ้มกันหรือหาสาเหตุไม่พบ
tempoNote: Explosive onset over hours to days, often after a mild febrile illness; status lasts weeks to months in severe cases
feat: Healthy person with no epilepsy history develops repeated seizures that become status despite two anti-seizure drugs
Prodromal fever, headache, fatigue or behavioural change in many cases in the days before
Often needs anaesthetic coma; frequently becomes super-refractory
FIRES is the subtype preceded by fever 24 hours to 2 weeks before seizures, mostly in school-age children
inv: Continuous EEG; MRI brain (often normal early, later limbic or claustrum T2 signal)
CSF cell count, protein, oligoclonal bands, viral PCR; neuronal antibodies in serum and CSF
Toxicology, metabolic screen; tumour search (CT chest–abdomen–pelvis, pelvic imaging for teratoma)
Genetic and metabolic tests when no cause emerges, especially in children

case.story: Three days after a flu-like illness she became confused, then had clusters of focal seizures progressing to convulsive status that persisted after diazepam, levetiracetam and valproate.
case.exam: Intubated, on midazolam infusion; intermittent facial twitching; no meningism or rash.
case.tests: CSF 12 cells, protein mildly raised, viral PCR negative; MRI bilateral mesial temporal T2 hyperintensity; antibody panel and pelvic ultrasound pending.
case.q: What should start now rather than after the antibody results?
case.a: First-line immunotherapy (IV methylprednisolone with IVIG or plasma exchange) within 72 hours, with early escalation (e.g. anakinra or tocilizumab, ketogenic diet) if seizures persist.

Chapter 9 - Seizures and Antibodies Against Surface Antigens
Considerations about the diagnosis of antibody-negative autoimmune encephalitis

det.patho: NORSE is a clinical presentation rather than a single disease. Roughly half of adult cases are eventually explained, most often by autoimmune encephalitis (e.g. NMDAR, LGI1, GABA-A, GAD) or paraneoplastic disease, with fewer infectious or genetic causes. The remainder stay cryptogenic, and in these, and in FIRES, excessive innate immune signalling (IL-1, IL-6, chemokines) appears to drive ongoing seizures.
det.clinical: Most patients are previously healthy young adults or children. A short prodrome of fever, malaise or psychiatric change is followed by escalating focal or generalised seizures that fail first- and second-line treatment and frequently become super-refractory, needing prolonged anaesthesia. Complications include infection, cardiac arrhythmia, propofol infusion syndrome and critical illness weakness. Survivors commonly have drug-resistant epilepsy and cognitive or behavioural deficits.
det.diagnosis: By consensus definitions, NORSE is refractory status in someone without prior epilepsy or other relevant neurological disease and without an acute structural, toxic or metabolic cause found at presentation. Work-up runs in parallel: continuous EEG, MRI, CSF (including antibodies, PCR and metagenomics where available), serum antibodies, toxicology, and tumour screening. Persistent cryptogenic cases warrant genetic and metabolic testing. Repeat MRI may show evolving limbic, claustral or diffuse cortical changes.
det.treatment: Treat the status with standard benzodiazepine, second-line drug and anaesthetic stages. International consensus (2022) advises first-line immunotherapy (high-dose steroids, IVIG or plasma exchange) within 72 hours once infection is reasonably covered, and second-line therapy within about a week if no response: rituximab when an antibody-mediated cause is likely, anakinra or tocilizumab for cryptogenic NORSE and FIRES. The ketogenic diet is recommended early. Remove any tumour found and continue long-term anti-seizure medication.
det.prognosis: Mortality in adults is around 15–25%; most survivors develop chronic epilepsy, but good functional recovery is possible even after months of status.
pearls: NORSE is a syndrome label, not a diagnosis: keep looking for autoimmune, infectious and genetic causes.
Do not wait for antibody results to start immunotherapy.
Cryptogenic NORSE and FIRES may respond to anti-cytokine drugs (anakinra, tocilizumab) and the ketogenic diet.
det.thd: NORSE คือภาวะชักต่อเนื่องดื้อยาที่เกิดครั้งแรกในคนที่ไม่เคยเป็นลมชัก โดยไม่พบสาเหตุโครงสร้าง ยา หรือเมตาบอลิกตั้งแต่ต้น มักมีไข้หรืออาการคล้ายหวัดนำมาก่อน สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยคือสมองอักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกัน อีกครึ่งหนึ่งหาสาเหตุไม่พบ ส่วน FIRES คือชนิดที่มีไข้นำในเด็ก ต้องตรวจ EEG ต่อเนื่อง MRI น้ำไขสันหลัง และหาแอนติบอดีกับเนื้องอก ควรเริ่มยากดภูมิภายใน 72 ชั่วโมงโดยไม่ต้องรอผล และพิจารณา anakinra หรือ tocilizumab และอาหารคีโตเจนิกถ้ายังชักอยู่

qx.stem: A previously well 27-year-old nurse develops confusion and focal seizures that evolve into status epilepticus over two days and continue despite three antiseizure medicines and midazolam. She had no fever, toxin exposure or prior epilepsy. MRI shows bilateral mesial temporal FLAIR hyperintensity; CSF has 12 white cells/µL with normal glucose, and HSV PCR is negative.
qx.q: Besides continuing seizure control, which step should not be delayed?
opts: Wait for antibody panel results before any immunotherapy
Start empirical antituberculous therapy
Begin first-line immunotherapy (high-dose steroids, IVIG or plasma exchange) and screen for tumour
Perform temporal lobectomy
Discontinue all antiseizure medicines to allow an EEG baseline
qx.why: New-onset refractory status epilepticus without a clear cause is often autoimmune or cryptogenic, and early immunotherapy is associated with better outcomes, so it is started while antibody results are pending. Tumour screening (e.g. ovarian teratoma) is essential. Surgery and drug withdrawal are inappropriate, and nothing here suggests tuberculous meningitis.

name: Niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency
formal: Pellagra with dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia, along with neuropathy, ataxia and encephalopathy, seen in alcoholism, malnutrition and carcinoid.
simple: Lack of vitamin B3 causing skin rash, diarrhoea and confusion or memory problems.
th: ภาวะขาดไนอะซินหรือวิตามินบี 3 (pellagra) มีผื่นผิวหนังบริเวณที่โดนแดด ท้องเสีย และสับสนหรือสมองเสื่อม พบในผู้ติดสุราและขาดสารอาหาร
tempoNote: Develops over weeks to months of deficiency; encephalopathy can be acute in alcohol withdrawal settings
feat: Photosensitive symmetric dermatitis (Casal necklace on the neck, dorsal hands)
Diarrhoea, glossitis and stomatitis
Neuropsychiatric change: apathy, depression, confusion, delirium, dementia
Encephalopathy with rigidity, grasp/suck reflexes and myoclonus in alcohol-related cases, often without rash
Peripheral neuropathy and ataxia, often with other B-vitamin deficiencies
inv: Clinical diagnosis; urinary N-methylnicotinamide or blood NAD/NADP levels where available
Check thiamine, B6, B12, folate, zinc and nutrition status
Exclude Wernicke encephalopathy, hepatic encephalopathy and other causes of delirium
Response to niacin replacement supports the diagnosis

case.who: 57-year-old man from Roi Et with heavy rice-whisky drinking
case.story: Weeks of diarrhoea, poor appetite and increasing confusion; a sunburn-like rash on his hands and neck.
case.exam: Disoriented, paratonic rigidity, grasp reflexes; symmetric scaly hyperpigmented rash on sun-exposed skin; reduced ankle reflexes.
case.tests: Albumin low; CT brain mild atrophy; improves within days of nicotinamide.
case.q: What deficiency explains the rash, diarrhoea and confusion?
case.a: Niacin deficiency (pellagra); give nicotinamide with thiamine and other B vitamins.

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Vitamin B3, Niacin (Nicotinic Acid and Nicotinamide)
Chapter 33 Alcohol and the Nervous System

det.patho: Niacin (nicotinic acid and nicotinamide) is a precursor of NAD and NADP, essential for cellular energy and DNA repair; it can also be made from tryptophan. Deficiency arises from poor diet (especially maize-based), alcohol use, malabsorption, carcinoid syndrome (tryptophan diverted to serotonin), Hartnup disease and drugs such as isoniazid. Neurons in the cortex, basal ganglia and brainstem show chromatolysis.
det.clinical: The classic triad is dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia, but in alcoholic patients a 'pellagra encephalopathy' with confusion, rigidity, primitive reflexes and myoclonus can occur without skin changes. Psychiatric symptoms, insomnia and depression are common early. Neuropathy and myelopathy may coexist from combined deficiencies. Untreated, it can be fatal.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is largely clinical, supported by the setting and a prompt response to replacement; laboratory tests are not widely available. Screen for other vitamin deficiencies and alcohol-related disorders. Think of carcinoid syndrome or isoniazid use in non-drinkers.
det.treatment: Give nicotinamide (commonly about 300–500 mg/day in divided doses for several weeks) rather than nicotinic acid, which causes flushing. Replace thiamine first and other B vitamins and zinc, treat alcohol use and improve diet, and protect skin from sun. Mental status often improves within days.
det.prognosis: Good if treated early; delayed treatment may leave residual cognitive deficits, and untreated cases can die.
pearls: Confused malnourished drinker with rigidity and grasp reflexes but no rash — still consider pellagra.
Think of isoniazid and carcinoid in non-alcoholic pellagra.
Always give thiamine alongside.
det.thd: ภาวะขาดไนอะซิน (pellagra) พบในผู้ดื่มสุรา ขาดอาหาร หรือใช้ยา isoniazid อาการเด่นคือผื่นแพ้แดดบริเวณคอและหลังมือ ท้องเสีย และสับสนหรือสมองเสื่อม ในผู้ติดสุราอาจสับสน เกร็ง และมี grasp reflex โดยไม่มีผื่น วินิจฉัยทางคลินิกและดูการตอบสนองต่อการรักษา ให้ nicotinamide ร่วมกับ thiamine และวิตามินอื่น

name: Niemann–Pick disease type C
formal: Autosomal recessive NPC1 or NPC2 cholesterol trafficking defect with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, cerebellar ataxia, dystonia, cataplexy, splenomegaly and psychiatric features.
simple: An inherited disease where cholesterol builds up in cells, causing balance problems, eye movement problems and dementia.
more: Diagnosis by filipin staining of fibroblasts, oxysterol or lyso-sphingomyelin levels, and NPC1 or NPC2 sequencing; the gaze palsy is vertical saccades. Miglustat slows neurological progression, and arimoclomol and levacetylleucine are newer options. Autosomal recessive lysosomal lipid storage disorder from NPC1 or NPC2 variants with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, ataxia, dystonia, dementia, splenomegaly and neonatal cholestasis. Diagnosed by plasma oxysterols and genetic testing; filipin staining. Miglustat slows neurological progression, and the course is progressive. Autosomal recessive lysosomal cholesterol transport disorder (NPC1 or NPC2) with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, ataxia, dystonia, cognitive decline, gelastic cataplexy and hepatosplenomegaly.
th: โรคสะสมไขมันในไลโซโซมจากยีน NPC1/NPC2 — กลอกตาลงล่างไม่ได้ (vertical supranuclear gaze palsy) ร่วมกับ ataxia, dystonia, cataplexy, ม้ามโต และโรคจิตหรือสมองเสื่อม
tempoNote: Any age from infancy to adulthood; neurological course runs over years, faster with earlier onset
feat: Slow or absent vertical saccades, downward first, with preserved vestibulo-ocular reflex
Progressive cerebellar ataxia, dysarthria and dysphagia
Dystonia and gelastic cataplexy (collapse with laughter)
Psychosis, behavioural change or early cognitive decline in teens and adults
Splenomegaly (may be mild) or a history of prolonged neonatal jaundice
inv: Plasma oxysterols (cholestane-triol), lysosphingomyelin-509 or bile acid markers as screening
NPC1 and NPC2 gene sequencing (confirmatory)
Abdominal ultrasound for spleen size; video-oculography for saccade velocity
Filipin staining of cultured fibroblasts when genetics is inconclusive

case.story: Grades fell over two years, then auditory hallucinations; psychiatric drugs made her stiffer. Her legs give way when she laughs.
case.exam: Clumsy gait, mild limb dystonia, very slow downward saccades with full movement on doll's-head manoeuvre; spleen tip palpable.
case.tests: Ultrasound spleen 14 cm; plasma oxysterols raised; NPC1 biallelic pathogenic variants.
case.q: Which eye sign links her psychiatric illness to a neurometabolic disease?
case.a: Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy — with ataxia, cataplexy and splenomegaly it indicates Niemann–Pick type C.

det.patho: NPC1 (about 95%) or NPC2 variants impair export of unesterified cholesterol from late endosomes and lysosomes. Cholesterol and glycosphingolipids accumulate, damaging Purkinje cells, cortical neurons and the reticuloendothelial system. It is panethnic, with an estimated birth incidence of around 1 in 100,000, though adult cases are underdiagnosed.
det.clinical: Presentation depends on age: neonatal cholestasis or hepatosplenomegaly, childhood clumsiness and learning decline, or adolescent/adult psychiatric illness with ataxia, dystonia and dementia. Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy is the hallmark and is often present long before the patient notices it. Cataplexy, seizures, dysphagia and dysarthria accrue over time. Splenomegaly can be subtle or absent in adults.
det.diagnosis: Use a suspicion index: combinations of vertical gaze palsy, ataxia, cataplexy, psychosis and splenomegaly or prior neonatal jaundice. Screen with plasma oxysterols, lyso-SM-509 or bile acid metabolites, then confirm by NPC1/NPC2 genetics; filipin testing is now a second-line tool. MRI may be normal or show cerebellar and frontal atrophy.
det.treatment: Miglustat (substrate reduction) is approved in many countries and may slow neurological progression. In 2024 the FDA approved arimoclomol (used with miglustat) and levacetylleucine. Symptomatic care covers cataplexy, seizures, dystonia, dysphagia and psychosis; antipsychotics should be used cautiously because of parkinsonism. Swallowing assessment and gastrostomy planning are important.
det.prognosis: Earlier neurological onset predicts faster decline; adult-onset patients may live for decades after diagnosis.
pearls: Teen or adult psychosis + vertical saccade slowing + ataxia: think NPC.
Check vertical saccade speed, not just range, at the bedside.
Laughter-induced falls (gelastic cataplexy) are a classic clue.
det.thd: Niemann–Pick type C เกิดจากยีน NPC1 หรือ NPC2 ทำให้ cholesterol ค้างในไลโซโซม อาการเด่นคือกลอกตาขึ้นลงช้าหรือไม่ได้แต่ doll's eye ปกติ ร่วมกับเดินเซ dystonia ล้มเมื่อหัวเราะ (cataplexy) ม้ามโต และในวัยรุ่นหรือผู้ใหญ่มักเริ่มด้วยโรคจิตหรือความจำถดถอย ตรวจ oxysterol และยืนยันด้วยยีน รักษาด้วย miglustat และยาใหม่เช่น arimoclomol หรือ levacetylleucine

name: Niemann–Pick type A disease
formal: Infantile acid sphingomyelinase deficiency with hepatosplenomegaly, severe neurodegeneration, cherry-red macula and early death.
simple: A severe infant form of Niemann-Pick disease causing a swollen liver, loss of skills and early death.
th: โรคขาดเอนไซม์ acid sphingomyelinase ชนิดรุนแรงในทารก มีตับม้ามโต สมองเสื่อมถอยรวดเร็ว จุด cherry-red ที่ macula และเสียชีวิตเร็ว

Hypotonia, then psychomotor regression and loss of milestones
Cherry-red spot at the macula in about half

case.story: Large tummy since 3 months, poor weight gain; she used to sit but now cannot and no longer babbles.
case.exam: Massive hepatosplenomegaly, hypotonia, poor visual fixation, cherry-red spots at both maculae.
case.tests: Acid sphingomyelinase activity markedly reduced; SMPD1 biallelic variants; foamy histiocytes in marrow.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and is enzyme therapy helpful?
case.a: Niemann–Pick type A; olipudase alfa treats visceral disease in ASMD but cannot reach the brain, so neurological care is palliative.

det.patho: Biallelic SMPD1 variants with near-absent acid sphingomyelinase activity cause sphingomyelin and cholesterol to build up in lysosomes of macrophages, hepatocytes and neurons. Foamy lipid-laden cells infiltrate liver, spleen, lungs and marrow, while neuronal storage produces progressive neurodegeneration. Type B has residual activity and spares the brain; intermediate forms exist.
det.clinical: Infants appear normal at birth but develop hepatosplenomegaly, vomiting and failure to thrive in the first months. Neurological regression follows, with hypotonia, loss of milestones and later spasticity and blindness. Recurrent respiratory infections relate to interstitial lung infiltration. Most children die in early childhood.
det.diagnosis: Measure acid sphingomyelinase activity and confirm with SMPD1 sequencing. Lyso-sphingomyelin is a useful biomarker. Distinguish from Niemann–Pick type C, which has a different mechanism and is diagnosed with oxysterols or NPC1/NPC2 testing. Prenatal diagnosis is possible in subsequent pregnancies.
det.treatment: Olipudase alfa, a recombinant enzyme, is approved for non-CNS manifestations of ASMD, but it does not treat brain disease in type A. Care is supportive and palliative: nutrition, respiratory support, seizure and spasticity management. Genetic counselling and family planning support are essential.
det.prognosis: Death usually occurs by 2–3 years of age.
pearls: Cherry-red spot plus massive hepatosplenomegaly suggests Niemann–Pick A; without organomegaly, think Tay–Sachs.
Types A and B share the enzyme; type C is a separate disease.
Enzyme therapy helps the viscera, not the brain.
det.thd: Niemann–Pick type A เกิดจากยีน SMPD1 ทำให้ขาดเอนไซม์ acid sphingomyelinase เกือบทั้งหมด ไขมัน sphingomyelin สะสมในตับ ม้าม ปอด และเซลล์ประสาท ทารกมีตับม้ามโตมากตั้งแต่ไม่กี่เดือน แล้วพัฒนาการถดถอย ตาพบ cherry-red spot และมักเสียชีวิตภายใน 2–3 ปี วินิจฉัยด้วยการวัดเอนไซม์และตรวจยีน ยาเอนไซม์ทดแทนช่วยอาการทางกายแต่ไม่ช่วยสมอง การดูแลจึงเป็นแบบประคับประคอง

formal: Visceral acid sphingomyelinase deficiency with hepatosplenomegaly and lung disease, with little or no neurological involvement.
simple: A milder form of Niemann-Pick disease affecting mainly liver, spleen and lungs rather than the brain.
th: โรคขาดเอนไซม์ acid sphingomyelinase ชนิดที่กระทบอวัยวะภายในเป็นหลัก ตับม้ามโต ปอดเป็นโรคเนื้อปอด ไขมันผิดปกติ แต่ระบบประสาทแทบไม่เกี่ยว

feat: Hepatosplenomegaly found in childhood, with thrombocytopenia from hypersplenism
Interstitial lung disease causing breathlessness and reduced diffusion capacity

case.story: Known since childhood to have a large spleen; now short of breath on climbing stairs.
case.exam: Massive splenomegaly, liver edge 4 cm, normal neurological examination.
case.tests: Platelets 85,000; HDL low; CT shows reticulonodular lung change; ASM activity markedly low.
case.q: Why was this patient sent to neurology clinic and what is reassuring?
case.a: Niemann-Pick was suspected; type B (chronic visceral ASMD) spares the nervous system, and enzyme replacement with olipudase alfa now treats the visceral disease.

det.patho: Biallelic SMPD1 variants reduce acid sphingomyelinase activity; residual activity is enough to protect neurons but not macrophages, so sphingomyelin-laden foam cells accumulate in spleen, liver, lung and marrow. Type A and B now sit on one spectrum termed ASMD (chronic visceral, chronic neurovisceral, infantile neurovisceral).
det.clinical: Presentation is with splenomegaly, liver dysfunction, bleeding tendency and lung disease, often in childhood and sometimes only in adulthood. Growth delay and liver fibrosis may occur. This is not a primary neurological disease; neurology involvement, if any, is mild and seen in intermediate phenotypes.
det.diagnosis: Low ASM activity confirms ASMD; SMPD1 genotype helps predict phenotype (some alleles are protective for neurology). Lyso-sphingomyelin tracks disease burden. Bone marrow foam cells are supportive but not specific.
det.treatment: Olipudase alfa enzyme replacement is approved for non-CNS manifestations and improves spleen size and lung function. Supportive care covers lipids, bleeding risk and respiratory disease. Avoid splenectomy where possible because it may worsen lung disease.
det.prognosis: Many survive into adulthood; causes of death include liver failure, lung disease and bleeding.
pearls: Type B is a visceral disease; an abnormal neurological exam suggests another diagnosis or an intermediate form.
Niemann-Pick A/B (ASMD) and C (NPC1/NPC2) are biochemically different diseases.
Olipudase alfa stays outside the brain, so it would not help neurological forms.
det.thd: Niemann-Pick type B หรือ chronic visceral ASMD เกิดจากขาดเอนไซม์ acid sphingomyelinase บางส่วน ทำให้ sphingomyelin สะสมในตับ ม้าม ปอด ผู้ป่วยตับม้ามโต เกล็ดเลือดต่ำ เหนื่อยจากโรคเนื้อปอด และไขมันผิดปกติ แต่ระบบประสาทมักปกติ วินิจฉัยด้วยการวัดเอนไซม์และยีน SMPD1 ปัจจุบันมีเอนไซม์ทดแทน olipudase alfa

ddx.pt: Splenomegaly and cytopenias with bone crises; low glucocerebrosidase, not sphingomyelinase
Same enzyme deficiency but infantile neurodegeneration and death in early childhood
Cholesterol trafficking defect with vertical gaze palsy, ataxia and dementia
