name: Niemann–Pick type D disease
formal: Nova Scotia variant of Niemann-Pick type C, due to NPC1 mutation, with similar neurovisceral cholesterol storage disease.
simple: A form of Niemann-Pick type C found in a Nova Scotia population, with the same brain and eye movement problems.
th: ชื่อเดิมของ Niemann-Pick type C ที่พบในประชากรกลุ่มหนึ่งของ Nova Scotia แคนาดา เกิดจากยีน NPC1 ตัวเดียวกัน อาการเหมือน NPC คือดีซ่าน ตับม้ามโต เดินเซ กลอกตาขึ้นลงไม่ได้ สมองเสื่อม
tempoNote: Neonatal jaundice possible, neurological decline from childhood
feat: Historical label for a founder NPC1 variant in an Acadian population; now classed as NPC
Prolonged neonatal jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly
Childhood clumsiness, ataxia and vertical supranuclear gaze palsy
Gelastic cataplexy, dysphagia, seizures and cognitive decline later
inv: Plasma oxysterols, lyso-sphingomyelin-509 and bile acid biomarkers
NPC1 gene testing (founder variant)
Filipin staining of fibroblasts (now second-line)

case.who: 8-year-old girl whose family are Canadian expatriates working in Chon Buri
case.story: Had prolonged jaundice as a newborn; now falls often, school performance dropping, and she collapses briefly when laughing.
case.exam: Slow vertical saccades, mild ataxia, palpable spleen.
case.tests: Oxysterols raised; homozygous NPC1 founder variant.
case.q: What is the modern name for this disease and what drug is used?
case.a: Niemann-Pick disease type C (the old 'type D'); miglustat, and arimoclomol or levacetylleucine where available.

det.patho: The Nova Scotia form results from a homozygous NPC1 founder variant. NPC1 protein moves cholesterol out of late endosomes; its loss traps unesterified cholesterol and glycosphingolipids in lysosomes in liver, spleen and neurons, especially cerebellar Purkinje cells. Biochemically and genetically it is identical to NPC.
det.clinical: The course matches juvenile NPC: neonatal liver disease, then ataxia, dysarthria, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, cataplexy and dementia. The label 'type D' is obsolete but appears in older literature and lexicons.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis follows NPC guidelines: biomarker screening (oxysterols, lyso-SM-509, bile acids) then NPC1/NPC2 sequencing. Filipin testing is used if genetics is inconclusive.
det.treatment: As for NPC: miglustat to slow neurological progression; arimoclomol and N-acetyl-L-leucine (levacetylleucine) were approved in the US in 2024. Supportive care for dysphagia, seizures and cataplexy. Intrathecal cyclodextrin remains investigational.
det.prognosis: Progressive with death typically in adolescence or early adulthood, varying with onset age.
pearls: 'Type D' = NPC1 disease in the Nova Scotia population; treat and counsel as NPC.
Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy in a child is a strong pointer to NPC.
Niemann-Pick A/B and C/D are different diseases despite the shared name.
det.thd: Niemann-Pick type D เป็นชื่อเก่าของโรค Niemann-Pick type C ที่พบในประชากรกลุ่มหนึ่งใน Nova Scotia ประเทศแคนาดา เกิดจากยีน NPC1 ทำให้คอเลสเตอรอลคั่งในไลโซโซม ทารกมีดีซ่านนาน ต่อมาเด็กเดินเซ กลอกตาขึ้นลงช้า ล้มเมื่อหัวเราะ และสติปัญญาถดถอย วินิจฉัยและรักษาเหมือน NPC

ddx.pt: Same disease; 'type D' is only the historical label for the Nova Scotia founder form
Neuronopathic Gaucher has horizontal saccade palsy and low glucocerebrosidase
Liver disease plus movement disorder with Kayser-Fleischer rings and low caeruloplasmin

name: Niemann–Pick type E disease
formal: Historical, rarely used category of adult non-neuronopathic Niemann-Pick disease with sphingomyelin storage; no longer a distinct entity.
simple: An old name for a mild adult form of Niemann-Pick disease, no longer used as a separate type.
th: หมวดหมู่เก่าที่แทบไม่ใช้แล้ว หมายถึงผู้ใหญ่ที่มี sphingomyelin สะสมโดยไม่มีอาการทางประสาท ปัจจุบันไม่ถือเป็นโรคแยก มักจัดเป็น ASMD หรือ NPC ตามผลตรวจยีน
tempoNote: Historical adult-onset visceral label; no defined natural history
feat: Obsolete category from older classifications of Niemann-Pick disease
Described adults with foam cells and visceral sphingomyelin storage but no neurological disease
Patients today are reclassified by enzyme and gene testing
Not a neurological diagnosis to make in current practice
inv: Acid sphingomyelinase activity and SMPD1 genotype
NPC biomarkers and NPC1/NPC2 genes if ASM is normal

case.story: Splenomegaly discovered at a health check; an old haematology report from decades ago mentions 'Niemann-Pick type E'.
case.exam: Moderate splenomegaly, normal neurological examination.
case.tests: ASM activity reduced; SMPD1 variants consistent with chronic visceral ASMD.
case.q: How should the old label be handled?
case.a: Reclassify it as chronic visceral ASMD (type B spectrum); the 'type E' category is no longer used.

det.patho: Type E was proposed in the mid-twentieth century for adults with sphingomyelin storage in viscera and no nervous system signs, before the enzyme and genes were known. Its biochemical basis was never defined, and modern testing places such patients within ASMD or other lipidoses.
det.clinical: There is no distinct clinical syndrome. Reported cases had splenomegaly or foam cells in marrow. The term survives in older texts and lexicons, which is why it appears here.
det.diagnosis: If a patient carries this label, retest: ASM enzyme activity, SMPD1 sequencing, NPC biomarkers and genes, and glucocerebrosidase activity. Bone marrow foam cells alone are nonspecific.
det.treatment: Treatment depends on the reclassified diagnosis (e.g. olipudase alfa for ASMD). No therapy is directed at 'type E' as such.
det.prognosis: Not defined; depends on the true underlying disorder.
pearls: Niemann-Pick type E is a historical category, not a current diagnosis.
Modern classification: ASMD (old A/B) and NPC (old C/D).
Foam cells in marrow have many causes; confirm with enzyme and gene tests.
det.thd: Niemann-Pick type E เป็นหมวดหมู่เก่าที่ใช้เรียกผู้ใหญ่ที่มี sphingomyelin สะสมในอวัยวะภายในโดยไม่มีอาการทางประสาท ก่อนยุคที่ตรวจเอนไซม์และยีนได้ ปัจจุบันไม่ถือเป็นโรคแยก หากผู้ป่วยมีชื่อนี้ในประวัติ ควรตรวจเอนไซม์ ASM และยีนใหม่เพื่อจัดกลุ่มเป็น ASMD หรือ NPC และรักษาตามโรคจริง

ddx.pt: Most adults once labelled type E fit the chronic visceral ASMD spectrum
Adult psychiatric and cognitive presentation with gaze palsy; NPC genes
Splenomegaly with bone disease and Gaucher cells; low glucocerebrosidase

name: Nijmegen Breakage syndrome
formal: Autosomal recessive NBN mutation disorder with microcephaly, growth failure, immunodeficiency, radiosensitivity and lymphoid malignancy.
simple: An inherited condition with a small head, weak immunity, and high risk of cancers, sensitive to radiation.
more: Autosomal recessive NBN mutation disorder (misspelled Nijmegen) with microcephaly, growth failure, immunodeficiency, radiosensitivity and lymphoid malignancy.
th: โรคยีนด้อยจากยีน NBN ที่ซ่อม DNA ไม่ได้ ทำให้ศีรษะเล็กแต่กำเนิด ตัวเตี้ย ภูมิคุ้มกันบกพร่อง ไวต่อรังสี และเสี่ยงมะเร็งต่อมน้ำเหลืองสูง
tempoNote: Microcephaly is present from birth or early infancy; immune and cancer complications accrue through childhood
feat: Progressive microcephaly with a sloping forehead, prominent midface and receding chin
Growth failure and mild to moderate intellectual disability that becomes evident in childhood
Combined immunodeficiency with recurrent sinopulmonary infections
Very high risk of lymphoma and other cancers; marked sensitivity to ionising radiation
Unlike ataxia telangiectasia, ataxia and telangiectasia are absent, although the DNA-repair pathway (MRE11-RAD50-NBN, ATM) is shared
inv: NBN gene sequencing (a Slavic founder deletion, c.657del5, is common in Central and Eastern Europe)
Immunoglobulins, lymphocyte subsets and vaccine responses
Karyotype for rearrangements involving chromosomes 7 and 14; radiosensitivity assay
MRI brain (simplified gyral pattern, corpus callosum anomalies) and AFP, usually normal or only slightly raised

case.who: 6-year-old girl at a university hospital in Bangkok, born to unrelated parents
case.story: Small head since infancy, short stature, repeated pneumonia and sinusitis, and difficulty keeping up at school. She is walking steadily with no clumsiness.
case.exam: Microcephaly (below -4 SD), sloping forehead and receding chin, height below the 3rd centile, normal tone, no telangiectasia, no ataxia.
case.tests: Low IgG and IgA, reduced CD4 T cells; genetic analysis shows biallelic NBN variants.
case.q: Why is this not ataxia telangiectasia, and what tumour should be anticipated?
case.a: No ataxia or telangiectasia, but microcephaly with immunodeficiency; lymphoma risk is high and X-rays or CT should be minimised.

read.where: Chapter 24 Cerebellar Ataxias and Related Conditions — Ataxic Disorders Associated with Defective DNA Repair
Chapter 24 Cerebellar Ataxias and Related Conditions — Inherited Ataxia Syndromes

det.patho: NBN encodes nibrin, part of the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex that senses double-strand DNA breaks and activates ATM-dependent repair and cell-cycle checkpoints. Biallelic loss-of-function variants cause chromosomal instability, radiosensitivity, impaired V(D)J recombination (immunodeficiency) and defective neurogenesis, which explains microcephaly. Inheritance is autosomal recessive and heterozygous carriers have a modestly higher cancer risk.
det.clinical: Microcephaly is noticeable at birth or in infancy and progresses as the child grows, with a characteristic facial profile. Intellect is usually normal or mildly impaired in early life, with learning problems evolving. Recurrent respiratory and ear infections reflect antibody and T-cell dysfunction. Lymphoma often arises during childhood or adolescence, and ovarian failure is common in girls. Classical cerebellar ataxia is not expected, in contrast to AT and ATLD.
det.diagnosis: Consider it in any child with microcephaly, growth delay and immunodeficiency, particularly with lymphoma. Molecular confirmation by NBN testing is definitive. Immunological studies, cytogenetic analysis showing translocations involving chromosomes 7 and 14, and radiosensitivity assays support the diagnosis. Distinguish from AT, ATLD, Fanconi anaemia, Bloom syndrome and other primary microcephalies.
det.treatment: There is no cure. Management includes immunoglobulin replacement and antimicrobial prophylaxis for antibody deficiency, avoidance of ionising radiation wherever possible (use MRI or ultrasound), and tumour surveillance. Cancer treatment needs reduced-dose protocols because of chemo- and radiosensitivity. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is considered carefully for severe immunodeficiency or haematological malignancy, using reduced-intensity regimens. Educational support and genetic counselling are essential.
det.prognosis: Limited by malignancy and infection; many patients survive into early adulthood, but lymphoma is the major cause of death.
pearls: Microcephaly + immunodeficiency + lymphoma risk = NBS; ataxia is not a feature.
NBN, MRE11 (ATLD) and ATM (A-T) are a pathway; their syndromes overlap.
Avoid unnecessary CT and X-ray in suspected DNA-repair disorders.
det.thd: Nijmegen breakage syndrome เป็นโรคถ่ายทอดแบบ autosomal recessive จากยีน NBN ซึ่งทำหน้าที่ซ่อมแซม DNA เด็กมีศีรษะเล็กตั้งแต่แรกเกิด ตัวเตี้ย พัฒนาการหรือการเรียนช้าเล็กน้อย ติดเชื้อทางเดินหายใจซ้ำจากภูมิคุ้มกันบกพร่อง ไวต่อรังสี และมีโอกาสเป็นมะเร็งต่อมน้ำเหลืองสูง ต่างจาก ataxia telangiectasia ตรงที่ไม่มีอาการเดินเซหรือหลอดเลือดฝอยขยาย วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีน NBN รักษาแบบประคับประคอง หลีกเลี่ยงรังสี และติดตามการเกิดมะเร็ง

Milder AT-like ataxia from MRE11 mutations, without microcephaly
Isolated or syndromic microcephaly without the immunodeficiency, radiosensitivity and lymphoma risk

name: Nitrous oxide, neurotoxicity
formal: Recreational or occupational nitrous oxide inactivates vitamin B12, causing subacute combined degeneration with myeloneuropathy, paraesthesias, sensory ataxia and megaloblastosis.
simple: Nerve and spinal cord damage from repeated laughing gas use because it blocks vitamin B12.
th: การสูดก๊าซ nitrous oxide ทำให้ vitamin B12 ไม่ทำงาน เกิด subacute combined degeneration และ neuropathy
tempoNote: Weeks to months of frequent recreational use; occasionally after a single anaesthetic in someone already B12-deficient
feat: Young adult using balloons or canisters of 'laughing gas' at parties
Tingling hands and feet, then unsteady gait worse in the dark
Impaired vibration and proprioception, positive Romberg, mixed reflex picture
Lhermitte sign, bladder symptoms or psychiatric change in heavier use
Serum B12 may be normal despite functional deficiency
inv: Methylmalonic acid and homocysteine (raised) — more reliable than serum B12
MRI cervical spine: T2 hyperintensity of the dorsal columns (inverted V sign)
NCS: axonal sensorimotor neuropathy, sometimes motor-predominant
Full blood count (macrocytosis may be absent)

case.story: Inhales several canisters of nitrous oxide most weekends for six months; now has numb hands and keeps falling in the shower when she closes her eyes.
case.exam: Absent vibration to the iliac crests, impaired toe position sense, Romberg positive, knee jerks brisk, ankle jerks absent.
case.tests: B12 low-normal, homocysteine and methylmalonic acid raised; MRI shows dorsal column T2 signal from C2 to C6.
case.q: What is the mechanism and what is the treatment?
case.a: N2O oxidises cobalamin and blocks methionine synthase, producing subacute combined degeneration; stop exposure and give intensive B12 replacement.

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Neurological Disorders Associated with Exposure to Toxic Substances
Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Nitrous Oxide
Chapter 9: Neurological complications of cell therapies in haematological malignancies
Chapter 34 Neurologic Complications of Recreational Drugs
Chapter 27: Neurologic Complications Of Organ Transplantation

det.patho: Nitrous oxide irreversibly oxidises the cobalt ion in methylcobalamin, inactivating methionine synthase. Methionine and S-adenosylmethionine fall, impairing myelin methylation, while homocysteine accumulates. Heavy recreational use or exposure in a person with low B12 stores produces myelopathy and neuropathy.
det.clinical: Symptoms evolve over weeks: distal paraesthesias, sensory ataxia, falls, and sometimes weakness. Examination shows dorsal column loss with variable pyramidal signs and depressed ankle reflexes from coexisting neuropathy. Mood change, psychosis and, rarely, thromboembolism from hyperhomocysteinaemia may occur.
det.diagnosis: Ask directly about nitrous oxide use. Serum B12 can be normal, so measure methylmalonic acid and homocysteine. MRI often shows dorsal column hyperintensity in the cervical cord, and NCS documents the neuropathy.
det.treatment: Complete abstinence from nitrous oxide is essential. Give parenteral B12 (hydroxocobalamin or cyanocobalamin) frequently at first, then maintenance; some clinicians add methionine. Rehabilitation and harm-reduction counselling are part of care.
det.prognosis: Many improve over months, especially with early treatment; severe or delayed cases can leave persistent sensory ataxia.
pearls: Normal B12 does not exclude N2O toxicity — check MMA and homocysteine.
Continued use undermines any amount of B12 replacement.
Consider it in any young person with new sensory ataxia.
det.thd: การสูดก๊าซหัวเราะ (nitrous oxide) เป็นประจำทำให้ vitamin B12 ถูก oxidise จนใช้งานไม่ได้ เกิด subacute combined degeneration ของไขสันหลังร่วมกับ neuropathy ผู้ป่วยชาปลายมือปลายเท้า เดินเซโดยเฉพาะในที่มืด ระดับ B12 อาจปกติ ต้องตรวจ methylmalonic acid และ homocysteine MRI พบ T2 signal ที่ dorsal column การรักษาคือเลิกใช้ก๊าซและให้ B12 ฉีด

name: Nociplastic pain
formal: Chronic pain from altered nociceptive processing without clear tissue or nerve damage, as in fibromyalgia, with widespread pain, fatigue, sleep and mood disturbance.
simple: Long-lasting pain from a nervous system that is overly sensitive, without clear injury, as in fibromyalgia.
th: อาการปวดเรื้อรังจากการประมวลผลความเจ็บปวดที่ผิดปกติ โดยไม่มีหลักฐานการบาดเจ็บของเนื้อเยื่อหรือเส้นประสาท เช่น fibromyalgia
tempoNote: Pain persisting longer than 3 months, often fluctuating
feat: Widespread or regional pain without a structural or nerve lesion to explain it
Fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive complaints and mood symptoms
Hypersensitivity to touch, pressure, sound or light
Examples: fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome, some chronic low back pain and TMD
Not a neurological disease in the structural sense; neurological exam is normal
inv: Clinical criteria (e.g. widespread pain index and symptom severity score for fibromyalgia)
Limited tests to exclude mimics: thyroid function, CK, ESR/CRP, vitamin D
Avoid repeated imaging without new findings

case.story: Two years of aching all over her body, poor sleep, exhaustion and difficulty concentrating; several MRIs were normal.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination; widespread tenderness to light pressure.
case.tests: Normal thyroid tests, CK and inflammatory markers.
case.q: What pain mechanism is this, and what treatment has the best evidence?
case.a: Nociplastic pain (fibromyalgia); graded exercise, sleep and education, with amitriptyline or duloxetine as adjuncts.

read.where: Chapter 31 Pain in Neurological Disorders — Definitions and Taxonomy

det.patho: Proposed mechanisms include increased central amplification of sensory signals, reduced descending inhibition and altered brain network connectivity, with contributions from sleep disturbance, stress and genetic susceptibility. The term was introduced by IASP in 2017 as a third pain mechanism besides nociceptive and neuropathic.
det.clinical: Not a primary neurological disease. Patients describe diffuse pain with fatigue, sleep disturbance and cognitive fog; overlapping functional syndromes are common. It can coexist with nociceptive or neuropathic pain, for example in rheumatoid arthritis.
det.diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis based on pain features and absence of an adequate nociceptive or neuropathic explanation; it is not meant to be made purely by exclusion. Fibromyalgia criteria assist. Limited tests rule out thyroid, inflammatory and muscle disease.
det.treatment: Education and validation, graded aerobic exercise, sleep hygiene and cognitive behavioural approaches form the base. Drugs with modest benefit include amitriptyline, duloxetine, milnacipran and pregabalin; opioids should be avoided. Treat depression and anxiety.
det.prognosis: Usually chronic with fluctuations; function often improves with active self-management.
pearls: Normal examination and widespread pain with fatigue: think nociplastic, not neuropathic.
Exercise has the strongest evidence.
Avoid opioids; they often worsen sensitisation.
det.thd: Nociplastic pain คืออาการปวดเรื้อรังที่เกิดจากระบบประสาทส่วนกลางขยายสัญญาณความเจ็บปวดผิดปกติ โดยไม่พบการบาดเจ็บของเนื้อเยื่อหรือเส้นประสาท ตัวอย่างคือ fibromyalgia ผู้ป่วยปวดทั่วตัว อ่อนเพลีย นอนไม่หลับ สมาธิไม่ดี ตรวจระบบประสาทปกติ ไม่ใช่โรคทางระบบประสาทเชิงโครงสร้าง การรักษาหลักคือให้ความรู้ ออกกำลังกาย ปรับการนอน และยาเช่น amitriptyline หรือ duloxetine

Objective proximal weakness and raised CK
Positive signs of functional weakness or sensory loss; may coexist

name: Nocturnal epileptic seizures
formal: Seizures arising during sleep, often frontal lobe in origin, with brief stereotyped hypermotor, tonic or dystonic events clustering in NREM sleep, as in autosomal dominant nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy.
simple: Seizures that happen only or mostly during sleep, causing sudden movements or stiffening at night.
more: Video-EEG polysomnography helps diagnosis; carbamazepine is effective and genetic testing may show CHRNA4 variants.
th: อาการชักที่เกิดขณะหลับเป็นหลัก มักมาจากสมองกลีบหน้า (sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy) เป็นชุดสั้น ๆ มีท่าทางเคลื่อนไหวรุนแรงหรือเกร็ง เหมือนเดิมทุกครั้ง หลายครั้งต่อคืน และอาจสับสนกับ parasomnia
tempoNote: Brief events, often several in one night, arising mostly from light NREM sleep; usually begin in childhood or adolescence and persist into adulthood
feat: Brief (often under 2 minutes), highly stereotyped hypermotor, tonic or dystonic events arising from NREM sleep, mainly N2
Several events per night, at any time of night, often with abrupt onset and offset and quick return to sleep
Vocalisation, bicycling, thrashing or asymmetric posturing; awareness may be partly preserved
Familial forms (CHRNA4, CHRNB2, KCNT1, DEPDC5) and focal cortical dysplasia are important causes
Seizures in general are least likely in REM sleep and most likely in light NREM sleep
inv: Video-EEG or video-PSG with a full EEG montage to capture events
Scalp EEG may be normal or obscured by muscle artefact in frontal seizures; rely on video semiology
MRI brain with epilepsy protocol for focal cortical dysplasia
Genetic testing when there is a family history or early onset

case.story: Since age 14 his wife sees him wake abruptly 4–6 times a night, raise his arms and kick for 30 seconds, then go back to sleep; each event looks the same. His father had similar night attacks.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination.
case.tests: Video-PSG captures three identical hypermotor events from N2 sleep with little EEG change; MRI normal; CHRNA4 variant found.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and first-line drug?
case.a: Sleep-related hypermotor (formerly nocturnal frontal lobe) epilepsy, familial form; low-dose carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine is usually effective.

det.patho: Sleep, especially light NREM sleep, synchronises thalamocortical networks and lowers the threshold for focal seizures, while REM sleep is relatively protective. In sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy, seizures usually arise from frontal cortex but can start in insular, temporal or parietal areas. Familial forms result from variants in nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunits or mTOR pathway genes, and focal cortical dysplasia is a common structural cause.
det.clinical: Seizures are short, stereotyped and frequent, often clustering several times a night, with abrupt hyperkinetic movements, dystonic posturing or vocalisation. Patients may wake fully afterwards or recall the event, unlike NREM arousal disorders. Daytime seizures are uncommon but may occur. Many patients are misdiagnosed for years as having nightmares or parasomnias.
det.diagnosis: Video recording of several events is the key tool, because scalp EEG may be normal or hidden by muscle artefact. Video-EEG or video-PSG with a full montage helps show the sleep stage and any ictal change. Stereotypy, multiple events per night, onset from N2 and dystonic posturing favour epilepsy over parasomnia. MRI and genetic tests look for dysplasia and familial causes.
det.treatment: Carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine at low dose controls many patients, and other focal antiseizure medicines such as lacosamide or levetiracetam can be used. About a third are drug resistant; for them, presurgical evaluation can identify a resectable dysplasia, and surgery offers good outcomes. Treat sleep deprivation and coexisting OSA, which can worsen seizures.
det.prognosis: Usually lifelong but often well controlled; surgical cases with a clear lesion can become seizure free.
pearls: Several identical events per night, at any time of night, favour epilepsy over NREM parasomnia.
A normal scalp EEG does not exclude frontal seizures; trust the video semiology.
Nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy was renamed sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy because seizures relate to sleep, not time of day, and need not be frontal.
det.thd: อาการชักขณะหลับส่วนใหญ่เป็น sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy มักมาจากสมองกลีบหน้า เกิดช่วง NREM โดยเฉพาะ N2 เป็นชุดสั้น ๆ ไม่ถึง 2 นาที เหมือนเดิมทุกครั้ง และหลายครั้งต่อคืน ต่างจาก parasomnia ที่มักเกิดครั้งเดียวช่วงต้นคืน EEG ผิวหนังอาจปกติจึงต้องอาศัยวิดีโอ ยา carbamazepine ขนาดต่ำได้ผลดี ส่วนรายดื้อยาที่มี cortical dysplasia อาจผ่าตัดได้

qx.stem: A 19-year-old female student from Phuket has, since age 12, woken abruptly up to 8 times a night, sat up with arms raised and legs cycling for 20–40 seconds, then returned to sleep. Her roommate's videos show the same sequence each time. Daytime EEG and MRI are normal.
qx.q: Which feature most strongly favours epilepsy over a NREM arousal disorder?
opts: Onset in adolescence
Normal daytime EEG
Events from sleep with partial amnesia
Multiple brief, identical events in a single night
Normal MRI brain
qx.why: Highly stereotyped, brief events occurring several times a night are characteristic of sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy. NREM arousal disorders are more variable, longer, and usually occur once, early in the night. A normal scalp EEG and MRI do not exclude frontal seizures, so video-EEG or video-PSG is the next test.

qx.stem: A 22-year-old man from Nakhon Si Thammarat has had three to five brief episodes every night since age 12, each lasting 20 to 40 seconds with sudden arousal, thrashing, grunting and a dystonic posture, then immediate recovery with recall of being unable to stop. The movements are identical each time. His uncle has similar events. Interictal EEG is normal.
qx.q: Which feature most favours sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy over a NREM parasomnia?
opts: Amnesia for the whole episode
Occurrence only in the first hour of sleep
Stimuli such as touch ending the event
Dependence on sleep deprivation
Brief, stereotyped, clustered events at any time of night with retained awareness
qx.why: Sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy, including the autosomal dominant form, produces brief stereotyped hypermotor or dystonic events, often several per night, with preserved awareness and a family history. NREM arousal disorders are longer, variable, mostly early in the night and with amnesia. Normal routine EEG between events is common, and video-EEG helps; carbamazepine is usually effective.

ddx.pt: Longer, variable events early in the night from N3, usually one per night, childhood onset
Dream enactment in older adults from late-night REM sleep; REM without atonia on PSG
Events start after EEG-confirmed wakefulness, long duration, eyes closed and waxing–waning

aN: sleep related hypermotor epilepsy | she | nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy | nfle | sleep related epilepsy

name: Nocturnal myoclonus
formal: Periodic limb movements in sleep: repetitive stereotyped leg flexion movements at intervals of 20 to 40 seconds, often with restless legs syndrome.
simple: Repeated leg jerks during sleep that can disturb sleep.
th: การกระตุกงอขาเป็นจังหวะซ้ำ ๆ ทุก 20–40 วินาทีขณะหลับ (PLMS) ถ้าทำให้หลับไม่ดีหรือง่วงกลางวันโดยไม่มีสาเหตุอื่นเรียก PLMD มักพบร่วมกับ RLS
tempoNote: Movements recur in runs through the night, mainly in light NREM sleep; frequency rises with age and fluctuates with iron status and medicines
feat: Repetitive extension of the big toe with ankle, knee and sometimes hip flexion, like a triple flexion response
Movements every 5–90 seconds (typically 20–40) in runs of four or more, mostly in N1–N2 sleep
Usually unaware; bed partner reports kicking and tangled sheets
Found in most patients with RLS, and increased by antidepressants, antihistamines and dopamine blockers
Common incidental finding in older adults; also seen in narcolepsy, RBD and OSA
inv: PSG with anterior tibialis EMG: PLMS index above 15 per hour in adults or above 5 in children
Ferritin and transferrin saturation; treat iron deficiency
Look for RLS, OSA, narcolepsy and RBD before diagnosing PLMD

case.story: She feels unrefreshed and her husband sleeps in another room because she kicks every half minute; she has no leg discomfort in the evening and started sertraline 6 months ago.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination.
case.tests: PSG: PLMS index 48 per hour, many with arousals; AHI 3; ferritin 28 ng/mL.
case.q: What should be done first?
case.a: Periodic limb movement disorder likely aggravated by the SSRI and low iron; replace iron and consider switching the antidepressant (for example to bupropion) before adding a gabapentinoid.

det.patho: PLMS reflect rhythmic disinhibition of spinal motor circuits during sleep, under the influence of reduced dopaminergic and iron-dependent control. They share genetic risk variants with RLS such as MEIS1 and BTBD9. Each movement is accompanied by autonomic activation, with rises in heart rate and blood pressure.
det.clinical: Most people with PLMS have no symptoms, and the finding becomes more common with age. Periodic limb movement disorder is diagnosed only when frequent PLMS cause disturbed sleep or daytime impairment not explained by another condition. Antidepressants other than bupropion, sedating antihistamines and antipsychotics increase the movements. In children PLMD is associated with ADHD symptoms and low iron.
det.diagnosis: PSG is required; leg movements last 0.5–10 seconds and form a series of at least four separated by 5–90 seconds. A PLMS index over 15 per hour in adults or 5 in children supports PLMD when symptoms are present. RLS must be excluded by history, because when RLS is present the diagnosis is RLS, not PLMD. Respiratory-related leg movements should not be counted.
det.treatment: Treat only when the movements are clearly linked to symptoms. Correct iron deficiency, aiming for ferritin above 75 ng/mL, and reduce or switch provoking medicines. Gabapentin, pregabalin or gabapentin enacarbil are preferred when medicine is needed, in line with current RLS guidance that discourages long-term dopamine agonists because of augmentation. Clonazepam reduces arousals rather than the movements themselves.
det.prognosis: Benign, but often persistent; symptoms usually improve when iron and drug factors are corrected.
pearls: PLMS is a PSG finding; PLMD is a diagnosis of exclusion that requires symptoms and no RLS.
SSRIs and SNRIs commonly increase PLMS; bupropion does not.
Check ferritin in every patient with PLMS or RLS.
det.thd: Nocturnal myoclonus หรือ PLMS คือการกระตุกขาเป็นจังหวะทุก 20–40 วินาทีขณะหลับ ตรวจพบจาก PSG ถ้าทำให้หลับไม่ดีหรือง่วงกลางวันโดยไม่มี RLS หรือสาเหตุอื่นเรียก PLMD ยากลุ่ม SSRI และยาต้านฮิสตามีนทำให้เป็นมากขึ้น การรักษาคือเสริมธาตุเหล็กให้ ferritin สูงพอ ปรับยาที่กระตุ้น และใช้ gabapentinoid ถ้าจำเป็น

ddx.pt: Awake evening urge to move the legs relieved by walking; diagnosed clinically, PLMS commonly coexist
Complex dream enactment in REM sleep, not periodic leg jerks
Very brief non-periodic twitches of many body parts

aN: periodic limb movements in sleep | plms | periodic limb movement disorder | plmd | sleep myoclonus

name: Nocturnal paroxysmal dystonia
formal: Brief stereotyped dystonic or hyperkinetic attacks from NREM sleep, now generally recognised as a form of nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy.
simple: Short episodes of twisting or thrashing movements during sleep, usually from seizures in the frontal lobe.
more: Diagnosed with video-EEG; carbamazepine often abolishes attacks. Prognosis is generally benign. Nocturnal dystonic attacks from NREM sleep, now regarded as nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy responsive to carbamazepine. Nocturnal episodes of dystonic or choreic movements arising from NREM sleep, likely frontal lobe epilepsy mimic and responsive to carbamazepine. Old term for paroxysmal dystonic or hyperkinetic attacks arising from sleep, now largely recognised as nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy, often linked to CHRNA4 and related genes. Video-EEG confirms an epileptic basis; carbamazepine often works. Differentiate from parasomnias and from true paroxysmal dyskinesias. Abnormal involuntary movements arising from sleep, such as paroxysmal nocturnal dystonia, that are often frontal lobe seizures and appear in stereotyped episodes at night.
th: ชื่อเดิมของอาการเกร็งบิดหรือเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติเป็นพัก ๆ ที่เกิดจากการหลับช่วง NREM ปัจจุบันถือว่าส่วนใหญ่เป็นลมชักกลีบหน้าขณะหลับ
tempoNote: Short attacks (usually under 1–2 minutes) several times a night; rare long-lasting attacks up to an hour were described
feat: Historical term (1981) for sudden dystonic, choreic or ballistic movements arising from NREM sleep
Attacks are brief, stereotyped and may recur many times nightly, sometimes after a short arousal
Patient may be partly aware; no post-event confusion in many
Scalp EEG often unrevealing, which is why it was once thought to be a movement disorder
Short-attack form now regarded as sleep-related hypermotor (frontal lobe) epilepsy
inv: Video-polysomnography with full EEG montage to capture the attacks
MRI brain for frontal focal cortical dysplasia
Family history and genetic testing (e.g. CHRNA4) if relatives are affected

case.story: Her husband reports that several times a night she suddenly grimaces, twists her arms and swings her legs for about 40 seconds, then settles back to sleep; this has gone on since adolescence.
case.exam: Daytime neurological examination normal.
case.tests: Video-PSG records five similar attacks from N2; scalp EEG obscured by artefact; MRI normal.
case.q: How is this condition classified today, and what treatment usually works?
case.a: As sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy (formerly nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy); low-dose carbamazepine typically abolishes or reduces the attacks.

read.where: Chapter 16 Autosomal Dominant Focal Epilepsies — Autosomal Dominant Nocturnal Frontal Lobe Epilepsy

det.patho: The original description grouped sleep-onset dystonic attacks as a possible basal ganglia disorder because surface EEG showed no clear epileptic activity. Later depth-electrode recordings, carbamazepine response and familial cases with nicotinic receptor gene variants showed that most short attacks are frontal lobe seizures originating in mesial or orbital cortex. A small number of prolonged attacks remain of uncertain mechanism.
det.clinical: Attacks begin abruptly from NREM sleep with dystonic posturing, choreoathetosis or ballistic limb movements, often with vocalisation, and last seconds to a couple of minutes. They may occur several times a night for years. Daytime function is normal apart from tiredness. Clinicians now use the term mainly in a historical sense; in practice such patients are managed as sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on witness description, home video and video-polysomnography showing stereotyped events from NREM sleep. EEG may be normal or show only brief frontal rhythmic activity, so a normal study does not refute epilepsy. MRI looks for frontal dysplasia. Distinguish from NREM parasomnias, RBD, periodic limb movements and functional events.
det.treatment: Carbamazepine at bedtime is the classic and usually effective treatment; oxcarbazepine and other focal anti-seizure drugs are alternatives. Drug-resistant patients with a lesion are candidates for surgical evaluation. Treat coexisting sleep disorders that fragment sleep.
det.prognosis: Generally benign and non-progressive; most respond well to medication.
pearls: Nocturnal paroxysmal dystonia is an older name; think sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy.
Carbamazepine response was an early clue that the attacks are epileptic.
Stereotypy and clustering matter more than a normal scalp EEG.
det.thd: Nocturnal paroxysmal dystonia เป็นชื่อเรียกเดิมของอาการเกร็งบิดหรือแขนขาสะบัดเป็นพัก ๆ ที่เกิดจากการหลับช่วง NREM ครั้งละไม่กี่สิบวินาทีและเกิดได้หลายครั้งต่อคืน เดิมเข้าใจว่าเป็นโรคการเคลื่อนไหว แต่ปัจจุบันพบว่าส่วนใหญ่เป็นลมชักจากสมองกลีบหน้าขณะหลับ (sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy) วินิจฉัยด้วย video-polysomnography และ MRI รักษาด้วย carbamazepine ก่อนนอนมักได้ผลดี

ddx.pt: Confusional arousals and sleepwalking are longer, less stereotyped and fewer per night
Daytime attacks triggered by sudden movement, not sleep; PRRT2 variants
Arise from EEG-confirmed wakefulness, prolonged and fluctuating, with closed eyes

aN: paroxysmal hypnic dystonia | paroxysmal hypnic dyskinesia | hypnogenic paroxysmal dyskinesia | hypnogenic dyskinesias | npd | hypnogenic paroxysmal dystonia

name: Non-24-hour sleep–wake rhythm disorder
formal: Circadian rhythm disorder where the sleep-wake cycle drifts later each day, due to lack of light entrainment, typical in blind people, with insomnia and daytime sleepiness.
simple: A body clock problem where sleep time shifts later and later each day, common in people who are blind.
th: นาฬิกาชีวภาพไม่ถูกปรับด้วยแสง ทำให้เวลาหลับเลื่อนช้าลงทุกวัน เป็นรอบ ๆ ช่วงที่เวลาไม่ตรงจะนอนไม่หลับและง่วงกลางวัน พบมากในคนตาบอดสนิท
tempoNote: Chronic free-running rhythm; symptoms wax and wane in cycles of weeks as the internal clock moves in and out of phase with the day
feat: Sleep onset and wake times drift later each day, often by 30–60 minutes or more
Periods of insomnia and daytime sleepiness alternate with symptom-free weeks when the clock is aligned
Typical in totally blind people without light perception; rare in sighted people, where it may follow DSWPD, brain injury or psychiatric illness
Social and occupational impairment from unpredictable sleep
inv: Sleep diary and actigraphy for at least 14 days, often longer, showing a steady daily drift
Serial melatonin or urinary 6-sulphatoxymelatonin rhythm confirming a period longer than 24 hours
In sighted patients, MRI brain and psychiatric assessment if no obvious cause

case.who: 45-year-old totally blind massage therapist from Nakhon Ratchasima
case.story: Every few weeks he cannot sleep at night and dozes through his work shifts, then sleeps well for a while; his diary shows bedtime creeping later each day.
case.exam: No light perception in either eye after childhood glaucoma; otherwise normal.
case.tests: Six weeks of diary and actigraphy show sleep drifting about 45 minutes later each day.
case.q: Which treatment entrains the clock?
case.a: Free-running (non-24-h) circadian rhythm in total blindness; nightly timed melatonin or the melatonin agonist tasimelteon at a fixed hour before the desired bedtime.

det.patho: The human circadian clock runs slightly longer than 24 hours and needs daily light signals through retinal ganglion cells and the retinohypothalamic tract to stay aligned. Without light input, as in total blindness, the clock free-runs, drifting in and out of alignment with clock time. Many totally blind people are not entrained, and a proportion develop symptoms.
det.clinical: Symptoms come in cycles: when internal night falls during the day, the person has insomnia at night and sleepiness by day, and weeks later sleep becomes normal again. Sighted patients are often young men with DSWPD, late-night habits, traumatic brain injury or psychiatric disease. The pattern is easily missed unless sleep is charted over weeks.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires a history of cyclical insomnia or sleepiness and at least 14 days of diary or actigraphy showing a steady daily delay. Serial melatonin measurements can confirm a non-24-hour period. In blind patients, ask about light perception, because those with some perception are more likely to entrain.
det.treatment: Melatonin or tasimelteon given at the same clock time each evening, about an hour before desired bedtime, can entrain the clock in blind patients, though it may take weeks. Sighted patients also need bright light on waking, fixed wake times and strong social cues. Vitamin B12 has weak evidence. Hypnotics and stimulants treat only symptoms.
det.prognosis: Lifelong in totally blind people, but many entrain while melatonin or tasimelteon is taken regularly.
pearls: Cyclical insomnia in a blind patient is non-24-hour disorder until proven otherwise.
Keep melatonin at a fixed clock time, not at whatever time the patient feels sleepy.
det.thd: ภาวะ non-24 (free-running rhythm) เกิดเมื่อนาฬิกาชีวภาพไม่ได้รับสัญญาณแสง เช่น ในคนตาบอดสนิท ทำให้เวลาหลับเลื่อนช้าลงทุกวัน และมีช่วงนอนไม่หลับกับง่วงกลางวันสลับกับช่วงปกติเป็นรอบหลายสัปดาห์ วินิจฉัยด้วย sleep diary หรือ actigraphy อย่างน้อย 14 วัน การรักษาคือให้ melatonin หรือ tasimelteon เวลาเดิมทุกค่ำ และในคนที่มองเห็นให้รับแสงเช้าร่วมด้วย

name: Non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (NAION)
formal: Acute painless optic nerve head infarction, usually with crowded small cup-to-disc ratio, causing altitudinal visual loss with disc swelling; vascular risk factors.
simple: Sudden painless loss of part of vision in one eye from reduced blood flow to the optic nerve.
th: ขั้วประสาทตาขาดเลือดแบบไม่ใช่หลอดเลือดแดงอักเสบ ตามัวเฉียบพลันไม่เจ็บ มักสังเกตตอนตื่นนอน มีลานสายตาขาดครึ่งล่างหรือบน และขั้วประสาทตาบวม พบในผู้สูงอายุที่มีปัจจัยเสี่ยงหลอดเลือดและขั้วประสาทตาแออัด
tempoNote: Painless loss noticed on waking or over hours; may step down further over 1–2 weeks, then stabilises; disc swelling resolves into sectoral pallor over 6–8 weeks
feat: Sudden painless monocular visual loss, often discovered on waking, in a person over 50
Altitudinal (usually inferior) or arcuate field defect and an RAPD
Swollen, often segmentally, hyperaemic disc with flame haemorrhages; the other disc is small and crowded (cup-to-disc ratio near zero)
Vascular risk factors: hypertension, diabetes, sleep apnoea, nocturnal hypotension; also linked with PDE5 inhibitors and possibly semaglutide
No jaw claudication, headache or systemic symptoms (if present, think arteritic AION)
inv: Urgent ESR, CRP and platelets in every patient over 50 to exclude giant cell arteritis
Fundus photography, OCT of RNFL, and formal visual fields
Vascular risk screen: BP, HbA1c, lipids; ask about snoring and arrange sleep study
MRI orbits only if atypical (pain, progression after 2 weeks, young age)

case.story: Woke up and found the lower half of the world dark through his right eye. No pain, headache or jaw pain. He has diabetes, hypertension and loud snoring.
case.exam: Acuity 6/12 right; inferior altitudinal defect; right RAPD; right disc diffusely swollen with a splinter haemorrhage; left disc small with no cup.
case.tests: ESR 18 mm/h, CRP normal, platelets normal; HbA1c 8.4%; sleep study shows moderate OSA.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the key test you must not skip?
case.a: Non-arteritic AION; inflammatory markers (and a temporal artery biopsy if suspicious) to exclude giant cell arteritis.

read.where: Chapter 22 Neuro-Ophthalmology — Non-Arteritic Anterior Ischaemic Optic Neuropathy
Chapter 18: Differential Diagnosis of Visual Field Deficits at the Bedside

det.patho: NAION results from hypoperfusion of the optic nerve head supplied by the short posterior ciliary arteries. A small, crowded disc (the 'disc at risk') allows initial swelling to cause compartment-like compression and further ischaemia. Nocturnal hypotension, often aggravated by antihypertensive drugs taken at night, OSA and diabetes are major contributors. It is the commonest acute optic neuropathy in people over 50.
det.clinical: Patients notice painless monocular blurring or a shade, typically on waking. Field loss is usually inferior altitudinal; central acuity may be preserved or poor. Some deteriorate in a stepwise way over the first fortnight. The second eye is affected in about 15–20% over five years, and recurrence in the same eye is rare.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical: acute painless loss with disc oedema, RAPD and a crowded fellow disc. Every older patient needs ESR and CRP to rule out arteritic AION, which threatens both eyes within days. Atypical features — pain, bilateral simultaneous loss, progression beyond two weeks, normal-sized cups — warrant MRI and broader work-up. Diabetic papillopathy and optic disc drusen-associated ischaemia are related entities.
det.treatment: There is no proven treatment to restore vision: optic nerve sheath decompression was harmful and oral steroids and other neuroprotectants remain unproven. Management focuses on risk factor control, treating OSA, avoiding night-time dosing of antihypertensives where possible, and caution with PDE5 inhibitors. Recent data linking semaglutide with NAION should be discussed with patients at risk. Low-vision support and driving advice may be needed.
det.prognosis: Vision usually stabilises within two months; about 40% show modest improvement of acuity, but altitudinal field loss generally persists.
pearls: Painless, on waking, altitudinal, swollen disc, crowded fellow disc: NAION.
Always check ESR/CRP in over-50s — arteritic AION is the can't-miss mimic.
Look at the other eye's disc: a tiny cup supports the diagnosis.
det.thd: NAION คือขั้วประสาทตาขาดเลือดที่ไม่ได้เกิดจากหลอดเลือดแดงอักเสบ พบในผู้สูงอายุที่มีเบาหวาน ความดันสูง หรือหยุดหายใจขณะหลับ ตามัวข้างเดียวทันทีไม่เจ็บ มักรู้ตัวตอนตื่นนอน ลานสายตาหายครึ่งล่าง ขั้วประสาทตาบวม และตาอีกข้างมีขั้วประสาทตาเล็กแออัด ต้องตรวจ ESR CRP เพื่อแยก giant cell arteritis ทุกครั้ง ยังไม่มีการรักษาที่ช่วยให้กลับมาเห็นแน่นอน จึงเน้นควบคุมปัจจัยเสี่ยง

qx.stem: A 64-year-old man from Phitsanulok with hypertension, diabetes and obstructive sleep apnoea wakes with painless loss of the lower visual field in the right eye. There is sectoral disc swelling in that eye and a small cup in the left disc. ESR and CRP are normal and there are no jaw symptoms.
qx.q: What is the most accurate statement about treatment?
opts: Intravitreal anti-VEGF injection is established standard care
No therapy has been proven to improve visual outcome; manage vascular risk factors, sleep apnoea and medication triggers
Oral prednisolone for 6 weeks is proven to restore vision
Optic nerve sheath fenestration is the standard operation
Levodopa has proven benefit
qx.why: NAION is the commonest acute optic neuropathy in people over 50, linked to a crowded disc ('disc at risk'), vascular risk factors and sleep apnoea. Despite many trials, no treatment has proven benefit, so care focuses on excluding giant cell arteritis when suspected, controlling vascular risk, treating sleep apnoea and reviewing drugs such as phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors and amiodarone. Steroids, anti-VEGF agents and surgery lack convincing evidence.

name: Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE)
formal: Sterile fibrin and platelet vegetations on heart valves in cancer or hypercoagulable states, causing embolic multifocal infarcts.
simple: Sterile clots on the heart valves in people with cancer that can break off and cause strokes.
more: Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis with sterile fibrin vegetations on valves in cancer or hypercoagulable states, causing embolic multifocal infarcts.
th: ก้อน fibrin-เกล็ดเลือดบนลิ้นหัวใจที่ไม่มีเชื้อ พบในมะเร็ง (โดยเฉพาะ adenocarcinoma) และ SLE/APS — ทำให้ stroke หลายจุดทั้งสองซีกพร้อมกัน รักษาด้วย heparin และรักษาโรคต้นเหตุ
tempoNote: Repeated embolic strokes over days to weeks, often in someone with active cancer
feat: Multiple small infarcts in several arterial territories on both sides (the 'three-territory sign')
Active malignancy, especially mucin-producing adenocarcinoma of pancreas, lung, ovary or stomach
Also seen in SLE/APS, sepsis, burns and chronic wasting illness
No fever or positive cultures; murmur often absent
Coexisting DIC markers and venous thrombosis
inv: TOE: small sessile vegetations on mitral or aortic valves (TTE often misses them)
Repeated negative blood cultures
D-dimer (usually very high), fibrinogen, platelets; cancer screen (CT chest-abdomen-pelvis, tumour markers)
Antiphospholipid antibodies and ANA

case.story: Weight loss and abdominal discomfort for two months; over one week, sudden right hand clumsiness, then confusion and left visual loss.
case.exam: Afebrile, no murmur; right hand ataxia, left homonymous hemianopia, inattentive.
case.tests: MRI DWI: tiny infarcts in left MCA, right PCA and both cerebellar hemispheres; D-dimer 12 µg/mL; blood cultures negative ×3; TOE: 5 mm mitral leaflet vegetations; CT: pancreatic tail mass with liver lesions.
case.q: What anticoagulant is recommended and why not a DOAC or warfarin first?
case.a: NBTE with cancer-related hypercoagulability — low-molecular-weight or unfractionated heparin is preferred; warfarin and DOACs have been associated with recurrence in this setting.

det.patho: Sterile vegetations of platelets and fibrin settle on valves — most often the aortic, then the mitral, sometimes both — usually on leaflets that were structurally normal, where endothelial injury from circulating cytokines meets a hypercoagulable blood. In cancer, mucin from adenocarcinomas (pancreas, lung, ovary, stomach, colon, breast, prostate) binds selectins on platelets and endothelium, and tumour cells release tissue factor and cancer procoagulant, so NBTE is often regarded as a valvular expression of chronic, low-grade DIC; together NBTE and DIC account for much of the ischaemic stroke seen in cancer, with DIC dominating in leukaemia, lymphoma and breast cancer and NBTE in mucin-secreting tumours. In lupus and antiphospholipid syndrome, immune-complex and antibody-mediated endothelial damage produce the same lesion (Libman–Sacks endocarditis), and sepsis, burns and wasting illnesses are rarer substrates. The vegetations are small, friable and free of inflammatory cells, so fragments break off easily and shower many vascular beds.
det.clinical: Embolic stroke is the commonest presentation and may be the first sign of an occult cancer; systemic emboli occur in about half of patients and reach kidneys, spleen, limbs, bowel and coronary arteries. Brain infarcts are typically multiple, widely scattered and of varying size across both hemispheres and the anterior and posterior circulations, and the clinical picture is often a fluctuating or progressive encephalopathy with or without focal signs rather than a single clean stroke syndrome; TIAs sometimes come first. Patients are usually afebrile, murmurs are often absent and valvular dysfunction is unusual, which is why the diagnosis is missed. Clues include migratory superficial or deep vein thrombosis (Trousseau syndrome), weight loss, abnormal coagulation tests and, in lupus, other features of SLE or APS. Without anticoagulation, recurrent embolism within days to weeks is common.
det.diagnosis: Suspect NBTE when DWI shows acute infarcts in three or more territories at once, particularly with known or suspected cancer, lupus or a very high D-dimer (raised BNP and fibrinogen are also associated). Transoesophageal echocardiography is the key test because vegetations are usually under 1 cm and are often missed on transthoracic study; a normal TOE does not exclude micro-vegetations, and autopsy series still find lesions that imaging missed. Take at least three sets of blood cultures before antibiotics and consider serology for culture-negative organisms (Bartonella, Coxiella) to exclude infective endocarditis. When no cancer is known, look for one with CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis (and mammography or tumour markers as indicated), and check platelets, fibrinogen, PT/aPTT, a blood film for DIC, and antiphospholipid antibodies and ANA. Serial D-dimer can help track coagulopathy and response to anticoagulation, although cancer and its treatment raise it independently.
det.treatment: Acute reperfusion follows usual rules: thrombectomy is reasonable for a large vessel occlusion, whereas IV thrombolysis needs individual judgement because of cancer-related bleeding risk, thrombocytopenia or DIC. For secondary prevention, therapeutic anticoagulation with LMWH (or unfractionated heparin when bleeding risk is high or procedures are planned) is the preferred approach in cancer-associated NBTE, continued while the cancer is active or until bleeding or intolerance intervenes; recurrence has been reported after switching to warfarin, and trial data on DOACs in cancer-related stroke are small and inconclusive. Libman–Sacks endocarditis with antiphospholipid syndrome is generally managed with warfarin rather than a DOAC, alongside treatment of the lupus. Antiplatelet therapy alone is not adequate, and atrial fibrillation or conventional risk factors should still be sought and treated. Treating the underlying cancer is essential, and valve surgery is reserved for rare cases with large vegetations, recurrent emboli despite anticoagulation, or valve dysfunction in patients with a good outlook.
det.prognosis: Prognosis is mostly set by the underlying malignancy, which is often advanced, and many patients die within months; recurrent embolism is frequent if anticoagulation is stopped, while lupus-related disease carries a better outlook.
pearls: Multi-territory acute infarcts + cancer (or weight loss) + high D-dimer = ask for TOE and think NBTE.
Choose heparin (usually LMWH), not warfarin or a DOAC, in cancer-associated NBTE.
Stroke may unmask a hidden mucin-producing adenocarcinoma: screen for cancer when no cause is found.
A patchy, fluctuating encephalopathy in a cancer patient may be showers of emboli — check DWI before blaming metabolism or drugs.
det.thd: NBTE คือก้อน fibrin และเกล็ดเลือดบนลิ้นหัวใจ (มักเป็นลิ้น aortic หรือ mitral) ที่ไม่มีเชื้อโรค เกิดจากภาวะเลือดแข็งตัวง่ายในมะเร็ง โดยเฉพาะ adenocarcinoma ที่สร้าง mucin เช่น ตับอ่อน ปอด รังไข่ กระเพาะ หรือใน SLE/APS ก้อนเปราะหลุดง่าย ทำให้สมองขาดเลือดหลายจุดหลายเขตหลอดเลือดทั้งสองซีกพร้อมกัน บางรายมาด้วยสับสนเป็น ๆ หาย ๆ มากกว่าอ่อนแรงชัดเจน และมี emboli ไปไต ม้าม แขนขาได้ ผู้ป่วยมักไม่มีไข้ D-dimer สูงมาก ต้องตรวจ TOE เพราะก้อนเล็ก เพาะเชื้อในเลือดให้ผลลบ และค้นหามะเร็งที่ซ่อนอยู่ รักษาด้วย heparin (มักเป็น LMWH) ระยะยาวตราบที่มะเร็งยัง active ร่วมกับรักษามะเร็ง ส่วน Libman–Sacks ใน APS ใช้ warfarin การพยากรณ์โรคขึ้นกับมะเร็งเป็นหลัก

name: Non-convulsive status epilepticus (NCSE)
formal: Prolonged electrographic seizure activity without prominent convulsions, presenting with confusion, behavioural change or reduced consciousness, diagnosed by EEG.
simple: A long-lasting seizure state with no obvious shaking, causing confusion or drowsiness.
more: Prolonged seizure activity without prominent motor signs, causing confusion or altered consciousness and diagnosed by EEG.
th: ภาวะชักต่อเนื่องที่ไม่มีอาการเกร็งกระตุกชัดเจน แสดงเป็นสับสน พฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน หรือซึมลง ต้องอาศัย EEG ในการวินิจฉัย
tempoNote: Hours to days of altered mental state; may follow convulsive status or appear de novo
feat: Unexplained confusion, mutism, perseveration, odd behaviour or reduced consciousness
Subtle motor signs: eyelid or facial twitching, nystagmus-like eye jerks, automatisms
Common in ICU patients, the elderly, after convulsive status and with acute brain injury
Absence status in generalised epilepsy: patient walks and talks but is slowed and dazed
Precipitants include sepsis, drug withdrawal, and drugs such as cefepime, carbapenems or tramadol

case.story: Recovering from a left frontal haemorrhage, she was talking normally but on day 4 became quiet, staring and unable to follow commands; nurses noted occasional right eyelid flutter.
case.exam: Drowsy but opens eyes, mute, intermittent right facial twitching, no new limb weakness.
case.tests: Sodium and glucose normal; EEG shows rhythmic 2.5 Hz left frontal spike-wave evolving in frequency and field.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and next step?
case.a: Focal non-convulsive status after haemorrhage; give IV benzodiazepine under EEG then load a second-line drug such as levetiracetam or lacosamide.

Section IV: General Principles of Therapy
Chapter 9 - Seizures and Antibodies Against Surface Antigens

det.patho: NCSE reflects sustained seizure activity in cortical networks without enough motor-system recruitment to produce convulsions. It may arise from acute brain injury (stroke, haemorrhage, trauma, encephalitis, hypoxia), metabolic or drug-related causes, or decompensation of existing epilepsy. Prolonged activity can injure neurons, but the degree of harm varies greatly between forms.
det.clinical: Presentations span a wide range: absence status in idiopathic generalised epilepsy (dazed but interactive), focal status with impaired awareness (confusion, aphasia, automatisms), and NCSE in coma, which carries the worst outlook. Clues include fluctuating confusion without a clear cause, subtle twitching, sudden aphasia without a stroke, and failure to wake after a convulsion. Elderly patients, especially those on cephalosporins or after benzodiazepine withdrawal, are often missed.
det.diagnosis: EEG is mandatory. The Salzburg criteria accept epileptiform discharges above 2.5 Hz, or slower discharges with clear evolution, subtle ictal clinical signs or improvement after IV anti-seizure medication. Rhythmic patterns on the ictal–interictal continuum are harder to interpret and benefit from expert review and repeat or continuous EEG. Search for the underlying cause in parallel.
det.treatment: First give an IV benzodiazepine (lorazepam, diazepam or midazolam) if the patient can tolerate it, then a second-line agent such as levetiracetam, valproate, fosphenytoin or lacosamide. In non-comatose patients avoid rushing to anaesthetic coma because the risks may exceed the benefit; repeated non-anaesthetic drugs are often preferred. NCSE in coma is treated more aggressively, similar to refractory convulsive status. Correct the cause and stop provoking drugs.
det.prognosis: Depends mainly on the cause and level of consciousness: absence status does well, while NCSE in comatose patients after anoxia or major brain injury carries high mortality.
pearls: Unexplained confusion in hospital, especially after a stroke or convulsion: get an EEG.
Cefepime and carbapenems in renal impairment are classic triggers in the elderly.
Absence status may be worsened by carbamazepine, phenytoin or oxcarbazepine.

qx.stem: A 74-year-old woman from Ayutthaya with a left MCA infarct two years ago is brought in with 24 hours of fluctuating confusion and reduced speech. She has subtle twitching of the right corner of the mouth, no fever and no metabolic derangement. CT shows only the old infarct. She recently started cefepime for a urinary infection.
qx.q: Which investigation will most directly establish the diagnosis?
opts: Repeat CT brain in 24 hours
MRI brain with perfusion imaging
Urgent EEG, interpreted against criteria such as the Salzburg criteria
Lumbar puncture for cell count and protein
Serum ammonia and thyroid function only
qx.why: Fluctuating confusion with subtle motor signs after a cortical stroke, possibly lowered threshold from cefepime, should prompt urgent EEG for non-convulsive status epilepticus; the Salzburg consensus criteria guide interpretation, with a benzodiazepine trial if uncertain. Imaging and CSF exclude other causes but cannot confirm NCSE. Cefepime neurotoxicity itself can produce triphasic or periodic patterns, which EEG also helps clarify.

qx.stem: A 71-year-old woman with an old right parietal infarct is treated for a convulsive seizure; the jerking stops after lorazepam and fosphenytoin. Four hours later she remains drowsy, opens eyes only to pain and has subtle twitching of the left eyelid. CT shows no new lesion.
qx.q: What should be done next?
opts: Assume a prolonged postictal state and reassess the next morning
Discharge to the ward with neurological observations every 4 hours
Lumbar puncture before any further investigation
Continuous EEG monitoring to look for non-convulsive seizures
Start haloperidol for delirium
qx.why: Failure to return to baseline after controlled convulsive status is a common setting for non-convulsive status epilepticus, and subtle facial twitching raises the suspicion further. Continuous EEG is required, because a short routine study misses many intermittent seizures. Waiting for postictal recovery delays treatment, and antipsychotics may lower the seizure threshold.

name: Non-epileptic seizures
formal: Paroxysmal events resembling seizures without epileptiform EEG activity, either psychogenic (functional) or physiological such as syncope.
simple: Episodes that look like seizures but are not caused by abnormal electrical activity, often related to stress.
th: เหตุการณ์ที่คล้ายลมชักแต่ไม่ได้เกิดจากคลื่นไฟฟ้าสมองผิดปกติ อาจเป็นชนิด functional (จิตใจ) หรือจากสาเหตุทางกายเช่นเป็นลม (syncope)
tempoNote: Recurrent paroxysmal events; duration and triggers depend on the cause
feat: Umbrella term: functional (dissociative) seizures plus physiological mimics such as syncope, hypoglycaemia, sleep disorders, TIA and migraine
Functional seizures: long events with closed eyes, side-to-side head shaking, asynchronous movements, waxing and waning
Convulsive syncope: brief jerks lasting seconds after a clear postural or vasovagal trigger, with rapid recovery
Coexisting epilepsy in about 10–20% of patients with functional seizures
Often misdiagnosed as drug-resistant epilepsy for years
inv: Video-EEG capturing a typical event is the gold standard
ECG (and Holter or loop recorder if cardiac syncope suspected); glucose during events
Home smartphone video of events
Prolactin after an event (raised after most generalised tonic–clonic seizures, usually not after functional events)

case.who: 24-year-old female factory worker from Samut Prakan
case.story: Three years of 'drug-resistant seizures' up to weekly, lasting 10–20 minutes with flailing limbs and eyes tightly shut; she is on three anti-seizure drugs and has been intubated twice.
case.exam: Normal examination; resists eye opening during an observed event.
case.tests: Video-EEG records a typical event with normal alpha rhythm before, during and after; MRI normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and how should it be communicated?
case.a: Functional (dissociative) seizures; explain the diagnosis clearly as a real, common and treatable condition, taper unnecessary anti-seizure drugs and refer for psychological therapy.

Section IV: General Principles of Therapy

det.patho: This is a descriptive umbrella, not a single disease. Functional (dissociative) seizures arise from altered brain network function influencing attention, emotion and motor control, often with predisposing factors such as anxiety, trauma or other functional symptoms, though none may be found. Physiological non-epileptic events have organic causes, most often reflex or cardiac syncope, but also hypoglycaemia, sleep disorders, paroxysmal movement disorders and TIAs.
det.clinical: Up to a quarter of patients referred with refractory epilepsy have non-epileptic events. Features favouring functional seizures include long duration, fluctuating course, eyes closed, pelvic thrusting or side-to-side movements, ictal crying and memory of the event. Syncope is suggested by triggers (standing, pain, micturition), prodromal light-headedness, pallor and short duration. Exertional or supine collapse, palpitations or a family history of sudden death suggests cardiac syncope and needs urgent cardiology review.
det.diagnosis: Video-EEG recording of a typical event with no ictal EEG change and a matching semiology establishes functional seizures; home video adds valuable information. No single sign is perfectly reliable, so the full picture should be weighed. Basic tests include ECG in all patients with transient loss of consciousness and glucose testing where relevant. Do not diagnose functional seizures from an interictal normal EEG alone, since many epilepsy patients have one.
det.treatment: Management follows the cause. For functional seizures, a clear, non-judgmental explanation is the foundation, followed by psychological therapy (e.g. CBT-informed approaches), treatment of comorbid anxiety or depression, and gradual withdrawal of unneeded anti-seizure drugs where epilepsy is not present. Syncope is treated by trigger avoidance, hydration and counter-pressure manoeuvres or by cardiac intervention as needed. Mislabelled patients should have the epilepsy diagnosis formally reviewed.
det.prognosis: Variable; many functional-seizure patients improve after diagnosis, but a substantial proportion continue to have events, especially with long delays to diagnosis.
pearls: Eyes closed during an event strongly favours a functional seizure; epileptic seizures usually have eyes open.
Brief jerks during a faint are common and do not mean epilepsy.
Every patient with unexplained collapse needs an ECG.
det.thd: Non-epileptic seizures เป็นคำรวมของเหตุการณ์ที่ดูคล้ายลมชักแต่ไม่ได้เกิดจากไฟฟ้าสมองผิดปกติ แบ่งเป็นชนิด functional หรือ dissociative seizures และชนิดที่มีสาเหตุทางกาย เช่น เป็นลมหมดสติ (syncope) น้ำตาลต่ำ หรือความผิดปกติขณะหลับ ผู้ป่วยหลายรายถูกวินิจฉัยผิดว่าเป็นลมชักดื้อยา การวินิจฉัยที่ดีที่สุดคือ video-EEG ร่วมกับตรวจคลื่นหัวใจ การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ สำหรับชนิด functional ให้อธิบายโรคอย่างชัดเจน ทำจิตบำบัด และค่อย ๆ หยุดยากันชักที่ไม่จำเป็น

name: Non-germinomatous germ cell tumours (NGGCT)
formal: Malignant intracranial germ cell tumours (yolk sac, embryonal carcinoma, choriocarcinoma) in pineal or suprasellar regions with raised AFP or beta-HCG and hydrocephalus; Parinaud syndrome.
simple: Aggressive brain tumours from germ cells, usually near the pineal gland or pituitary, in young people.
th: germ cell tumour ชนิดร้ายในสมอง เช่น yolk sac tumour, embryonal carcinoma, choriocarcinoma ที่ pineal หรือ suprasellar มี AFP หรือ beta-hCG สูง
tempoNote: Weeks to a few months of progressive symptoms
feat: Children and adolescents; pineal or suprasellar location
Parinaud syndrome, hydrocephalus, diabetes insipidus, visual loss
Raised AFP (yolk sac) or markedly raised beta-hCG (choriocarcinoma)
Haemorrhage particularly in choriocarcinoma

case.story: Two months of headache and vomiting, with recent deepening of voice and pubic hair.
case.exam: Upgaze palsy, papilloedema, early pubertal features.
case.tests: MRI: heterogeneous pineal mass with hydrocephalus; serum AFP 380 ng/mL, beta-hCG 150 IU/L.
case.q: What tumour type does the marker profile indicate and how is it treated?
case.a: NGGCT (mixed with yolk sac elements); intensive platinum-based chemotherapy followed by radiotherapy and resection of residual tumour.

det.patho: NGGCTs arise from primordial germ cells that differentiate along embryonic or extra-embryonic lines. Yolk sac elements secrete AFP and choriocarcinoma secretes hCG; many tumours are mixed. They are more aggressive than germinomas and less radiosensitive.
det.clinical: Presentation is similar to germinoma but often more rapid. Pineal masses cause hydrocephalus and dorsal midbrain syndrome; suprasellar ones cause endocrine failure and visual loss. hCG-secreting tumours may cause precocious puberty.
det.diagnosis: Elevated AFP or high beta-hCG in serum or CSF with a midline mass establishes NGGCT without biopsy in many protocols. Staging includes spinal MRI and CSF cytology.
det.treatment: Platinum-based chemotherapy followed by craniospinal or focal radiotherapy, with second-look surgery for residual masses. Mature teratoma may remain after chemotherapy (growing teratoma syndrome) and needs resection.
det.prognosis: Survival is about 70–80% with modern combined therapy, lower for choriocarcinoma and high AFP.
pearls: High AFP or hCG in CSF can make the diagnosis without biopsy.
Growing mass with falling markers suggests growing teratoma syndrome.
Precocious puberty in a boy with a pineal mass suggests hCG secretion.

name: Non-progressive myoclonic encephalopathy
formal: Disorder with static encephalopathy and myoclonus, often following hypoxia or from neonatal causes, without neurodegeneration.
simple: A non-worsening brain condition with muscle jerks, often after oxygen deprivation or in childhood.
more: Disorders with static encephalopathy and myoclonus, often following hypoxia or from neonatal causes, without neurodegeneration.
th: ภาวะสมองบกพร่องคงที่ร่วมกับ myoclonus ในเด็ก มักเกิดจากการขาดออกซิเจนหรือโรคทางพันธุกรรม เช่น Angelman โดยไม่มีการเสื่อมต่อเนื่อง
tempoNote: Begins in infancy or early childhood; encephalopathy static, with episodes of myoclonic status
feat: Infant or young child with severe developmental delay and hypotonia
Recurrent or prolonged myoclonic status, often subtle and mistaken for tremor or jitteriness
Causes: Angelman syndrome, 4p deletion (Wolf-Hirschhorn), hypoxic-ischaemic injury, other genetic or structural causes
No progressive loss of skills apart from that caused by uncontrolled seizures
inv: Video EEG with polygraphy: continuous slow-wave or spike activity correlating with myoclonus
MRI brain for structural or hypoxic lesions
Genetic tests: chromosome microarray, UBE3A/methylation for Angelman, exome

case.story: Global developmental delay since infancy; for weeks she has had constant small jerks of her hands and face and seems more absent.
case.exam: Happy demeanour, frequent laughter, ataxic movements, microcephaly, continuous subtle multifocal myoclonus.
case.tests: EEG shows near-continuous rhythmic slow-wave and spike activity; methylation test confirms Angelman syndrome.
case.q: What is the epilepsy syndrome and which drugs are preferred?
case.a: Myoclonic status in a non-progressive encephalopathy (Angelman); valproate, levetiracetam, clobazam; avoid carbamazepine.

det.patho: Underlying genetic or acquired brain disorders produce cortical hyperexcitability that manifests as recurrent myoclonic status. Angelman syndrome (loss of maternal UBE3A) is the classic cause; others include 4p deletion, Rett syndrome and perinatal hypoxic injury. The encephalopathy itself is static.
det.clinical: It typically begins during infancy. Myoclonic status may last hours to days, producing apathy, drowsiness and worsening motor control; because jerks are small, they can go unrecognised. Absences and other seizure types occur.
det.diagnosis: Polygraphic video-EEG demonstrates the link between EEG discharges and jerks. Genetic and imaging tests define the cause. Lack of progressive decline distinguishes it from progressive myoclonus epilepsies.
det.treatment: Broad-spectrum antiseizure drugs such as valproate, levetiracetam, clobazam, and ethosuximide; steroids or ACTH have been used for status. Avoid drugs that aggravate myoclonus (carbamazepine, phenytoin, vigabatrin). Developmental and rehabilitation support is essential.
det.prognosis: Developmental outcome is generally poor and reflects both the underlying cause and the burden of myoclonic status.
pearls: Constant subtle jerks with a new loss of alertness in a delayed child: get video-EEG.
Angelman syndrome is the prototype cause.
Avoid sodium channel blockers that worsen myoclonus.

name: Non-systemic vasculitis
formal: Vasculitis restricted to the peripheral nerves (non-systemic vasculitic neuropathy), causing painful mononeuritis multiplex without other organ involvement.
simple: Inflammation of blood vessels supplying nerves only, causing painful patchy nerve damage.
th: หลอดเลือดอักเสบที่จำกัดเฉพาะเส้นประสาทส่วนปลาย ทำให้เกิด mononeuritis multiplex ที่ปวดมาก โดยไม่มีอวัยวะอื่นเกี่ยวข้อง
tempoNote: Stepwise painful nerve deficits over weeks to months; slower and more indolent than systemic vasculitic neuropathy
feat: Older adult with painful, stepwise, asymmetric sensorimotor deficits in individual nerves (peroneal, ulnar, tibial most often)
Over time deficits merge into an asymmetric or even symmetric distal pattern (overlapping mononeuropathies)
Burning or deep pain in the affected territory; foot drop or wrist drop is common
No fever, weight loss, renal, skin or lung involvement beyond mild constitutional symptoms
Variant: diabetic and non-diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy share the same microvasculitis
inv: NCS/EMG: asymmetric axonal loss; side-to-side amplitude differences; pseudo-conduction block early after infarction
Blood: ESR/CRP often normal or mildly raised; ANCA, cryoglobulins, hepatitis B/C, HIV, ANA negative
Biopsy of an affected sensory nerve (superficial peroneal or sural), ideally with an adjacent muscle such as peroneus brevis: transmural inflammation with vessel damage
Screen for systemic disease at diagnosis and periodically (urine, renal function, chest imaging)

case.story: Three months ago her right foot became numb and floppy; six weeks later her left hand went numb in the little fingers, with burning pain in both areas.
case.exam: Right foot drop with dorsum-of-foot sensory loss, left ulnar-distribution weakness and numbness; other nerves normal; no rash.
case.tests: NCS: absent right peroneal and left ulnar sensory responses with axonal motor loss; ESR 35, ANCA and cryoglobulins negative, hepatitis B/C negative; urine normal.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and how is it confirmed?
case.a: Painful mononeuritis multiplex without systemic vasculitis points to non-systemic vasculitic neuropathy; confirm by biopsying the superficial peroneal nerve together with nearby muscle.

read.where: Chapter 36: Mononeuritis Multiplex: Vasculitis (Systemic, Nonsystemic) Neuropathies

det.patho: An immune-mediated inflammation of small epineurial arteries and arterioles causes ischaemic infarction of nerve fascicles, which explains the patchy multifocal axonal loss. It is usually classed as a localised form of small-vessel vasculitis; why it stays confined to nerve is unknown. It is one of the commonest forms of vasculitic neuropathy seen in specialist practice, and only a small proportion later evolve into a systemic vasculitis.
det.clinical: Typical patients are in their 60s with painful, stepwise mononeuropathies that accumulate over months; the lower limbs are affected first and most. As more nerves are involved, the picture may look like a distal asymmetric polyneuropathy, so careful mapping of individual nerve territories matters. Constitutional symptoms are absent or mild. Some patients describe a relapsing course after treatment is stopped.
det.diagnosis: It is a diagnosis of exclusion that needs nerve biopsy evidence of vasculitis (definite) or strongly suggestive changes (probable). Electrodiagnosis shows asymmetric axonal involvement and guides which nerve to biopsy; adding muscle increases yield. Systemic vasculitis, diabetes, cryoglobulinaemia, infection (hepatitis, HIV, leprosy), sarcoidosis and lymphoma must be excluded. Serum inflammatory markers are frequently normal, so normal ESR does not rule it out.
det.treatment: Glucocorticoid monotherapy (prednisolone around 1 mg/kg/day with a slow taper) is first line for most patients. Rapidly progressive or severe disease, or failure of steroids, warrants adding cyclophosphamide, methotrexate or azathioprine; IVIG and rituximab are used in selected cases. Pain management, ankle-foot orthoses and physiotherapy are essential. Evidence comes mainly from retrospective series, so treatment duration is individualised (often 6–18 months).
det.prognosis: Most patients stabilise and partly recover, but relapse affects about a third and residual deficits and pain are common; mortality is low.
pearls: Painful stepwise mononeuritis multiplex without systemic disease: think nerve-only vasculitis and biopsy.
A normal ESR does not exclude non-systemic vasculitic neuropathy.
Biopsy an affected sensory nerve together with a muscle to raise the yield.
det.thd: Non-systemic vasculitic neuropathy คือหลอดเลือดอักเสบที่เกิดเฉพาะในเส้นประสาทส่วนปลาย ผู้ป่วยมักสูงอายุ มีอาการชาอ่อนแรงของเส้นประสาททีละเส้นร่วมกับปวดแสบร้อน เช่น เท้าตก โดยไม่มีอาการทางไตหรืออวัยวะอื่น ผลเลือดอักเสบอาจปกติ ต้องยืนยันด้วยการตัดชิ้นเนื้อเส้นประสาทและกล้ามเนื้อ รักษาด้วย steroid และเพิ่มยากดภูมิเช่น cyclophosphamide หรือ methotrexate ในรายรุนแรง

name: Nonaka distal myopathy
formal: Autosomal recessive GNE myopathy (distal myopathy with rimmed vacuoles) with tibialis anterior weakness in early adulthood and sparing of the quadriceps.
simple: An inherited muscle disease starting in young adults with foot drop that spreads slowly.
more: Biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles; GNE genetics; no approved therapy, supportive care.
th: โรคกล้ามเนื้อปลายแขนขาแบบยีนด้อยจากยีน GNE อ่อนแรงกล้ามเนื้อ tibialis anterior ในวัยหนุ่มสาว โดย quadriceps ยังแข็งแรง
tempoNote: Onset typically 20–40 years, slow progression; many lose walking 10–20 years after onset
feat: Foot drop and steppage gait from tibialis anterior weakness in young adults
Weakness spreads to hamstrings, hip adductors and hand muscles
Quadriceps characteristically spared until late
Autosomal recessive; frequent in Japan, Middle East and also reported in Thailand
inv: CK normal to mildly raised (usually under 5 times normal)
EMG myopathic, sometimes with mixed units
Muscle biopsy: rimmed vacuoles, small angular fibres, little inflammation
GNE gene sequencing confirms

case.story: Two years of tripping and slapping feet; now struggles to climb into a bus.
case.exam: Bilateral foot drop, weak hamstrings, strong quadriceps, normal sensation and reflexes except ankle jerks.
case.tests: CK 480 U/L; biopsy rimmed vacuoles; biallelic GNE variants.
case.q: Which muscle sparing pattern is the clue?
case.a: Quadriceps sparing with anterior tibial weakness — GNE myopathy (Nonaka).

det.patho: Biallelic variants in GNE impair the bifunctional enzyme that initiates sialic acid synthesis, causing hyposialylation of muscle glycoproteins. Fibres develop rimmed vacuoles and protein aggregates similar to sporadic IBM but without inflammation.
det.clinical: Begins in early adulthood with distal anterior leg weakness and gradual spread. The quadriceps are notably preserved, which is the opposite of sporadic IBM. Respiratory and cardiac involvement is uncommon but mild respiratory weakness may develop late.
det.diagnosis: Recognise the pattern clinically and on muscle MRI (anterior leg, hamstrings, adductors involved; quadriceps spared). CK is only mildly raised. Biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles; GNE genetic testing is definitive.
det.treatment: No approved disease-modifying therapy; sialic acid and ManNAc supplementation have been tested in trials with mixed results, and gene approaches are under study. Ankle-foot orthoses, physiotherapy and mobility aids remain the mainstay. Genetic counselling for the family.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; many patients need a wheelchair within one to two decades.
pearls: Young adult foot drop with spared quadriceps: test GNE.
Rimmed vacuoles do not always mean IBM.
CK is only modestly raised.
det.thd: Nonaka distal myopathy หรือ GNE myopathy เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้อทางพันธุกรรมแบบยีนด้อย เริ่มในวัยหนุ่มสาวด้วยเท้าตก จากกล้ามเนื้อ tibialis anterior อ่อนแรง ต่อมาลามไป hamstrings และมือ แต่ quadriceps ยังแข็งแรง CK สูงเล็กน้อย ชิ้นเนื้อพบ rimmed vacuoles ยืนยันด้วยยีน GNE ยังไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ ใช้กายอุปกรณ์และกายภาพบำบัด

qx.stem: A 32-year-old woman of Bangladeshi origin living in Bangkok has had six years of progressive weakness that spares the quadriceps, with distal leg and proximal arm involvement. CK is mildly raised, EMG shows an irritable myopathy with some neurogenic units, and biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles without inflammation or MHC-1 upregulation. Prednisolone and methotrexate gave no benefit.
qx.q: Which gene is most likely mutated?
opts: DYSF
GAA
VCP
GNE
CAPN3
qx.why: Distal-onset, quadriceps-sparing weakness in early adulthood with rimmed vacuoles and no inflammation is typical of GNE myopathy (Nonaka distal myopathy, hereditary inclusion body myopathy), an autosomal recessive disorder of sialic acid synthesis. Muscle MRI shows the short head of biceps femoris affected early, and cardiac and respiratory muscles are spared until late. It is often mislabelled as myositis, so the absence of an immunotherapy response is a clue.
