name: Nondystrophic myotonias and hereditary periodic paralysis
formal: Group of skeletal muscle ion channelopathies including myotonia congenita, paramyotonia and periodic paralyses, from CLCN1, SCN4A and CACNA1S mutations.
simple: Inherited muscle conditions causing stiffness or attacks of weakness due to faulty ion channels.
more: Genetics and EMG exercise tests; treat with mexiletine, acetazolamide or dichlorphenamide.
th: กลุ่มโรคช่องไอออนของกล้ามเนื้อลาย ได้แก่ myotonia congenita, paramyotonia congenita และ periodic paralysis จากยีน CLCN1, SCN4A, CACNA1S
tempoNote: Myotonia lifelong and stable; paralytic attacks episodic for hours to days; some develop fixed weakness later
feat: Muscle stiffness after rest that eases with repeated movement (warm-up) in myotonia congenita
Paradoxical myotonia worsened by exercise and cold in paramyotonia congenita
Episodes of flaccid weakness with low or high potassium, provoked by carbohydrate, rest after exercise or fasting
Muscle hypertrophy in some; later fixed proximal weakness in periodic paralysis
Andersen-Tawil adds arrhythmia and dysmorphism
inv: Potassium during an attack; thyroid function to exclude thyrotoxic periodic paralysis
EMG myotonic discharges; long and short exercise tests patterns
Genetic testing: CLCN1, SCN4A, CACNA1S, KCNJ2
ECG for long QT/U waves in Andersen-Tawil

case.story: Wakes after a rice-heavy dinner unable to move his legs for several hours; similar attacks since age 15. His father had the same.
case.exam: Between attacks normal strength; during attack flaccid weakness with absent reflexes.
case.tests: Potassium 2.4 mmol/L in the attack; thyroid normal; CACNA1S variant.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and preventive drug?
case.a: Familial hypokalaemic periodic paralysis; acetazolamide or dichlorphenamide and avoiding carbohydrate loads.

det.patho: Variants in chloride (CLCN1), sodium (SCN4A), calcium (CACNA1S) and potassium (KCNJ2) channel genes change muscle membrane excitability. Increased excitability leads to repetitive firing (myotonia); sustained depolarisation inactivates sodium channels and causes paralysis. In hypokalaemic periodic paralysis, gating-pore leak currents underlie the paradoxical depolarisation.
det.clinical: Myotonia congenita (recessive Becker or dominant Thomsen) shows stiffness with warm-up. Paramyotonia gives cold-sensitive eyelid and hand stiffness that worsens with repetition. Hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis features brief frequent attacks; hypokalaemic attacks are longer, often on waking. Permanent myopathy can develop in middle age.
det.diagnosis: Combine clinical history, potassium levels during attacks, EMG and exercise testing patterns, and genetic testing. Exclude secondary causes such as thyrotoxicosis, renal potassium loss and drugs.
det.treatment: Mexiletine is first-line for disabling myotonia; lamotrigine is an alternative. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide, dichlorphenamide) reduce attacks in periodic paralysis. Acute hypokalaemic attacks need oral potassium with careful monitoring; hyperkalaemic attacks may abort with carbohydrate or inhaled salbutamol. Inform anaesthetists of risks with depolarising agents.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy normal; quality of life depends on attack control and late myopathy.
pearls: Warm-up phenomenon suggests CLCN1 myotonia congenita.
Always check thyroid in a young man with hypokalaemic paralysis.
Andersen-Tawil: periodic paralysis plus arrhythmia and short stature.
det.thd: กลุ่มโรคช่องไอออนของกล้ามเนื้อลายประกอบด้วย myotonia congenita (กล้ามเนื้อแข็งเกร็งหลังพัก ดีขึ้นเมื่อขยับซ้ำ) paramyotonia congenita (แย่ลงเมื่อเย็นหรือขยับซ้ำ) และ periodic paralysis (อ่อนแรงเป็นพัก ๆ ร่วมกับโพแทสเซียมต่ำหรือสูง) วินิจฉัยด้วยระดับโพแทสเซียมขณะมีอาการ EMG exercise test และตรวจยีน รักษา myotonia ด้วย mexiletine และป้องกันการอ่อนแรงด้วย acetazolamide หรือ dichlorphenamide ต้องตรวจไทรอยด์เสมอ

Subcortical cognitive slowing
Arm swing and upper limbs relatively preserved (unlike Parkinson’s disease)

qx.stem: A 77-year-old former rubber planter in Trang has a year of short, shuffling, wide-based steps as if his feet stick to the floor, urinary urgency with occasional wetting, and slowed thinking. Arm swing and hand dexterity are relatively preserved. MRI shows ventricles disproportionately large for sulcal size, a tight high-convexity sulci pattern and widened Sylvian fissures (DESH).
qx.q: What should be done before deciding on surgery?
opts: Insert a ventriculoperitoneal shunt immediately without testing
Start levodopa and review in 6 months
Perform cisternography as the definitive test
Perform a high-volume lumbar tap test (or extended lumbar drainage) with gait measurement before and after
Start acetazolamide as long-term treatment
qx.why: Magnetic gait, urinary symptoms and cognitive slowing with DESH on MRI suggest idiopathic NPH. Removing about 30–50 mL of CSF, or several days of lumbar drainage, with timed gait testing predicts shunt response; a positive result supports a programmable VP shunt, while a negative tap does not fully exclude benefit. Cisternography has poor predictive value, acetazolamide is not an established therapy, and a levodopa trial mainly addresses coexisting parkinsonism.

qx.stem: A 74-year-old man from Chiang Rai has a magnetic gait, urinary incontinence and mild cognitive slowing. MRI shows enlarged ventricles with widened Sylvian fissures and tight high-convexity sulci. A DaT SPECT scan unexpectedly shows reduced striatal uptake.
qx.q: How should the DaT result be interpreted?
opts: It excludes NPH and confirms Parkinson’s disease
It proves a shunt will not help
It is normal in every case of NPH
Only CSF tau can decide whether to shunt
An abnormal DaT does not exclude NPH, since it is reported abnormal in about a third; the large-volume tap or drainage trial remains central
qx.why: NPH combines gait apraxia, urinary incontinence and cognitive decline with ventriculomegaly, and its imaging signature includes widened Sylvian fissures with crowded sulci at the vertex. Dopamine transporter scans can be abnormal in some NPH patients and sometimes normalise after shunting. A response to large-volume lumbar puncture or continuous drainage supports shunt surgery, though the best surgical technique is unsettled.

qx.stem: A 76-year-old man in Nonthaburi has a two-year history of a slow, wide-based, magnetic gait, followed by urinary urgency and mild forgetfulness. MRI shows enlarged lateral and third ventricles out of proportion to sulcal widening, with tight high-convexity sulci and widened Sylvian fissures, an acute callosal angle of about 70 degrees, and a flow void in the aqueduct. There is no obstruction.
qx.q: Which is the best next step?
opts: Start levodopa for presumed Parkinson disease
Reassure, as ventricular size reflects ageing atrophy
Perform a high-volume lumbar tap or external drainage trial with gait testing before and after, and consider shunting if improved
Immediate third ventriculostomy for obstructive hydrocephalus
Begin acetazolamide for idiopathic intracranial hypertension
qx.why: Disproportionate enlargement of the ventricles with tight high-convexity sulci and an acute callosal angle (the DESH pattern) supports idiopathic NPH, which is communicating hydrocephalus. A measured improvement in gait after CSF removal predicts a good shunt response. Atrophy would widen all sulci, and Parkinson disease does not explain this imaging.

det.patho: Communicating hydrocephalus in older adults in which CSF dynamics are disturbed while lumbar opening pressure remains normal or mildly raised. Idiopathic NPH probably reflects impaired CSF absorption and reduced intracranial compliance, often with coexisting small vessel disease; secondary NPH follows SAH, meningitis or head injury. Ventricular enlargement stretches periventricular fibres serving leg control, bladder and frontal circuits.
det.clinical: Gait disturbance comes first and dominates: broad-based, short, shuffling, 'magnetic' steps with poor turning and start hesitation, but arm swing and upper-limb movement are relatively preserved. Cognitive slowing, apathy and inattention follow, and urinary urgency progresses to incontinence. The full triad is present in only some patients. Comorbid Parkinson disease, vascular disease and Alzheimer pathology often coexist and limit shunt response.
det.diagnosis: Imaging shows ventriculomegaly (Evans index >0.3) with a disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space pattern: tight high-convexity sulci with widened Sylvian fissures (DESH), and a narrow callosal angle. Confirm likely shunt-responsiveness with a high-volume tap test (30–50 mL) or extended lumbar drainage, measuring gait speed and cognition before and after. A negative tap test does not exclude benefit. Exclude obstructive hydrocephalus and other causes of gait apraxia.
det.treatment: Ventriculoperitoneal (or lumboperitoneal) shunting with an adjustable valve is the definitive treatment. Gait improves most reliably; cognition and continence less so. Complications include over-drainage with subdural collections, infection and shunt blockage, so follow-up is needed. Physiotherapy and management of comorbidities support recovery.
det.prognosis: Most carefully selected patients improve after shunting, especially those with a short history and gait-led presentation; benefit may wane over years.
pearls: Gait first, then cognition, then bladder — reversed order argues against NPH.
Normal arm swing and no rest tremor separate NPH from Parkinson disease.
DESH on MRI predicts a good shunt response.
det.thd: NPH คือโพรงน้ำในสมองขยายในผู้สูงอายุโดยความดันน้ำไขสันหลังปกติหรือสูงเล็กน้อย อาการเด่นเรียงลำดับคือเดินลำบากแบบเท้าติดพื้น ก้าวสั้น ฐานกว้าง ตามด้วยคิดช้าและกลั้นปัสสาวะไม่อยู่ ส่วนแขนยังแกว่งปกติ ไม่สั่น MRI พบ Evans index >0.3 และ DESH การทำ tap test ระบายน้ำไขสันหลัง 30–50 มล. แล้วเดินดีขึ้นช่วยทำนายว่าจะตอบสนองต่อการผ่าตัดใส่ VP shunt

name: Norrie’s disease
formal: X-linked NDP mutation disorder with congenital blindness from retinal dysplasia, progressive deafness and intellectual disability.
simple: A rare inherited condition in boys causing blindness from birth, later hearing loss and learning problems.
th: โรคทางพันธุกรรมแบบ X-linked จากยีน NDP ทำให้ตาบอดแต่กำเนิดจากจอตาผิดรูป หูตึงแบบลุกลาม และบางรายมีพัฒนาการช้า

feat: Boys with bilateral congenital blindness, leukocoria from retinal dysplasia or detachment
Eyes may shrink (phthisis bulbi) over time
Progressive sensorineural hearing loss from childhood
Intellectual disability, autism or behavioural problems in some
Carrier females usually unaffected; peripheral vascular disease reported in adult males

case.who: 3-month-old boy at a university hospital in Bangkok
case.story: Parents noticed a white reflex in both pupils and that he does not follow faces; a maternal uncle has been blind since birth and became deaf as a teenager.
case.exam: Bilateral leukocoria, no fixation, roving eye movements.
case.tests: Ultrasound: bilateral retinal detachment with retrolental mass, no calcification; NDP pathogenic variant.
case.q: Which X-linked disorder fits, and what future problem needs monitoring?
case.a: Norrie disease; progressive hearing loss — serial audiology and early hearing aids or cochlear implants.

det.patho: NDP encodes norrin, a ligand that activates Wnt/beta-catenin signalling through the Frizzled-4 receptor, essential for vascular development of the retina and inner ear. Loss of norrin leads to failure of retinal vascularisation, retinal dysplasia and detachment, and progressive cochlear vascular damage. Related genes (FZD4, LRP5) cause familial exudative vitreoretinopathy.
det.clinical: Affected boys are blind from birth or soon after. Hearing loss usually develops in childhood or adolescence and progresses. Up to about half have developmental or behavioural problems, and some have seizures, particularly with larger deletions. Carrier females occasionally show mild retinal changes.
det.diagnosis: Clinical findings of bilateral congenital retinal detachment in a boy with X-linked family history, confirmed by NDP testing. Retinoblastoma must be excluded with imaging. Prenatal diagnosis is possible for at-risk pregnancies.
det.treatment: No treatment restores vision in established cases; early vitreoretinal surgery is attempted in selected infants with partial attachment. Hearing aids and cochlear implants are important. Developmental support and genetic counselling are needed.
det.prognosis: Blindness is permanent; hearing outcome depends on early intervention.
pearls: Blind boy who later becomes deaf: think Norrie disease.
Always exclude retinoblastoma in leukocoria.
Large deletions including MAOA/MAOB produce more severe neurological features.

name: Nosocomial meningitis
formal: Hospital-acquired meningitis, usually after neurosurgery, shunts or drains; caused by Gram-negative bacilli or staphylococci, with atypical presentation and need for broad empirical cover.
simple: A brain-lining infection caught during a hospital stay, often after brain surgery or a drain, and caused by hospital-type germs.
th: เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ/โพรงสมองอักเสบที่เกี่ยวข้องกับการรักษาในโรงพยาบาล มักหลังผ่าตัดสมองหรือใส่สายระบาย EVD และ shunt เชื้อก่อโรคต่างจากชุมชน ต้องคลุมเชื้อ staphylococci และแกรมลบดื้อยา
tempoNote: Days to weeks after neurosurgery or device placement; chronic low-grade shunt infection with Cutibacterium can smoulder for months
feat: Fever, falling consciousness, headache, vomiting or new seizures after craniotomy, EVD, lumbar drain, shunt or intrathecal pump
Neck stiffness is often absent or masked by sedation, surgery and blood in the CSF
Wound redness, CSF leak, shunt malfunction or abdominal pain/pseudocyst with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt

Organisms: coagulase-negative staphylococci and S. aureus most often; Gram-negative bacilli (Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas, Klebsiella) common with EVD and in ICUs; Cutibacterium acnes in indolent shunt infection
Risk factors: EVD duration beyond 1 to 2 weeks, frequent CSF sampling, leak, intraventricular haemorrhage, prior shunt infection, reoperation
inv: CSF from the drain, shunt reservoir or lumbar puncture: cell count, glucose, protein, lactate, Gram stain and culture, held for 14 days when Cutibacterium is possible
Interpret against the post-operative baseline: a rising count, falling glucose or CSF lactate above about 4 mmol/L supports infection, but counts can be normal in up to a fifth of shunt infections
Blood cultures; CT or MRI for hydrocephalus, ventriculitis, abscess or subdural empyema
Repeat CSF twice weekly until two sterile cultures confirm cure

case.who: 58-year-old man in a Bangkok neurosurgical ICU after surgery for a ruptured aneurysm
case.story: Day 11 with an external ventricular drain in place; new fever and a fall in alertness, with cloudy drain fluid.
case.exam: GCS drops from 13 to 10, no meningism, clean drain exit site.
case.tests: Drain CSF: 2,400 cells (85% neutrophils), glucose 1.0 mmol/L, lactate 7.2 mmol/L; Gram-negative coccobacilli later identified as carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii.
case.q: How is the infection treated and what is done with the drain?
case.a: Replace or remove the infected drain, start vancomycin plus an agent active against the isolate (meropenem or colistin-based therapy for resistant Acinetobacter), add intraventricular colistin or an aminoglycoside because IV drug penetration is poor, and continue for about 10 to 14 days after the first negative culture.

read.where: Chapter 35 Iatrogenic Infections of the Central Nervous System - shunts, external ventricular drains, diagnosis and treatment
Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — Specific Causes of Bacterial Meningitis
Part I: Introduction: An Insight into Central Nervous System (CNS) Infections

det.patho: Skin flora or hospital organisms enter the CSF along the catheter surface, through the wound, or from the abdomen in a ventriculoperitoneal shunt, and form biofilm on silicone that shields bacteria from antibiotics. Dural defects, CSF leak and blood in the ventricles favour infection, and each CSF sample from a drain adds a chance for contamination. The result is ventriculitis, meningitis, abscess or empyema, and often shunt blockage as the system clogs with debris.
det.clinical: Presentation is blunter than community meningitis because surgery, sedation and subarachnoid blood cause baseline fever, pleocytosis and neck stiffness. Clues are a new fever without another source, a drop in level of consciousness, a leaking wound and a drain that becomes cloudy or blocked. In children with shunts, irritability, vomiting and headache suggest shunt failure or infection. Most shunt infections declare themselves within six months of surgery, and EVD infections appear around the end of the first week.
det.diagnosis: There is no perfect test. A positive Gram stain and culture of CSF from the device is the standard, and sampling from the shunt reservoir has a higher yield than lumbar puncture. A cell count above 100 per microlitre with neutrophil predominance, low glucose and raised lactate supports infection when culture is negative or delayed, but the numbers must be read against the surgical baseline. Hold cultures for 14 days when Cutibacterium acnes is possible. MRI with diffusion imaging can show ventricular debris and ependymal enhancement not visible on CT.
det.treatment: Start intravenous vancomycin plus an antipseudomonal beta-lactam (cefepime, ceftazidime or meropenem), adjust to the isolate and remove or externalise the infected device; antibiotics alone fail more often than combined antibiotics and device removal. Add intraventricular vancomycin, colistin or an aminoglycoside for resistant organisms or slow clearance, using the dose per day in a standard reference. Continue treatment for about 10 to 14 days after the first sterile culture (longer for Gram-negatives and complicated infection), then reinsert the shunt once CSF is sterile. Prevention rests on short perioperative prophylaxis, minimal CSF sampling, avoiding routine EVD exchange, and consideration of antibiotic- or silver-impregnated catheters.
det.prognosis: Most patients recover with early device removal, but mortality remains 10 to 20 per cent, and shunt re-infection is frequent.
pearls: A normal CSF cell count does not exclude shunt infection.
Neck stiffness and Kernig's sign are unreliable in sedated post-operative patients; fever plus falling GCS is the cue.
Without removing the device, biofilm infections relapse.
det.thd: เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบจากการรักษาในโรงพยาบาลพบหลังผ่าตัดสมอง ใส่สายระบายน้ำไขสันหลังภายนอก (EVD) หรือ shunt เชื้อมักเป็น Staphylococcus และแกรมลบรวมถึง Acinetobacter อาการอาจไม่ชัด เช่น ไข้ ซึมลง หรือแผลรั่ว คอไม่แข็ง ควรส่งน้ำไขสันหลังจากสายหรือ reservoir เพาะเชื้อให้ครบ ให้ vancomycin ร่วมกับ cefepime หรือ meropenem นำอุปกรณ์ที่ติดเชื้อออกหรือเปลี่ยน และพิจารณายาฉีดเข้าโพรงสมองในเชื้อดื้อยา

name: NREM arousal disorders
formal: Parasomnias from slow wave sleep including sleepwalking, sleep terrors and confusional arousals, with partial arousal and amnesia, common in childhood.
simple: Sleep problems such as sleepwalking and night terrors in which a person partly wakes up and does not remember.
more: Diagnosed clinically and polysomnography if atypical. Treat triggers such as poor sleep and sleep apnoea; safety measures and sometimes clonazepam.
th: parasomnia จากการตื่นไม่สมบูรณ์ออกจากหลับลึก (N3) เช่น ละเมอเดิน sleep terror และ confusional arousal มักเกิดช่วงแรกของคืน ผู้ป่วยจำเหตุการณ์ไม่ได้ พบบ่อยในเด็ก
tempoNote: Episodes within 1–3 hours of sleep onset, lasting minutes; peak in childhood and usually fading by adolescence, with a minority persisting or starting in adults
feat: Confusional arousals, sleepwalking or sleep terrors arising from deep NREM sleep, mostly in the first 1–3 hours
Eyes open but glassy, hard to wake, and next day recall is patchy or absent
Sleep terrors: sudden scream, intense fear, tachycardia and sweating; the child cannot be comforted
Triggers: sleep deprivation, fever, stress, alcohol, Z-drugs, and arousal-causing disorders such as OSA and PLMS
Strong family history; often one event per night and not every night
inv: Diagnosis by history and home video in typical cases
Video-PSG with extended EEG if events are frequent, stereotyped, injurious, start in adulthood or suggest seizures
PSG can show arousals from N3 and look for OSA or periodic limb movements as triggers

case.story: About an hour after falling asleep he sits up screaming, sweating and staring, several nights a month; his parents cannot calm him and he remembers nothing next day. Episodes worsen after football camp with early starts.
case.exam: Normal; tonsils not enlarged; father sleepwalked as a child.
case.tests: None needed; home video shows a single 4-minute episode early in the night.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and management?
case.a: Sleep terrors, a NREM arousal disorder; reassure, ensure enough sleep and a safe room, avoid waking him during the event, and consider scheduled awakenings if frequent.

read.where: Chapter 29 Disorders of Sleep — Non-Rapid Eye Movement Parasomnias
Chapter 52: Violent parasomnias and sleep forensics

det.patho: The brain shows a dissociated state in which motor and limbic areas are partly awake while frontal and parietal association cortex remain in slow wave sleep. Anything that deepens slow wave sleep or fragments it, such as sleep loss, fever, OSA or periodic limb movements, raises the risk. Genetic susceptibility is strong and HLA-DQB1 variants have been associated.
det.clinical: Confusional arousals are slow, muddled awakenings; sleepwalking adds walking or complex behaviour; sleep terrors add a scream and autonomic storm. Events usually last a few minutes and occur once a night in the first third of sleep. Sleep-related eating and sexsomnia are recognised variants. Adult cases may cause injury or violence and raise forensic questions.
det.diagnosis: ICSD-3-TR criteria require recurrent incomplete awakenings from sleep, inappropriate or absent responsiveness, limited dream imagery and partial or complete amnesia. Typical childhood events need no testing. Video-PSG with extended EEG montage is used for atypical, frequent or dangerous events, and to look for OSA or PLMS. Distinguishing features from frontal lobe seizures are timing, variability, duration and number per night.
det.treatment: Management starts with reassurance, regular and sufficient sleep and a safe sleeping environment with locked doors and windows. Treat triggers such as OSA, RLS and periodic limb movements, and stop sedative hypnotics such as zolpidem. For frequent childhood events, waking the child shortly before the usual episode time each night can break the pattern. Clonazepam at bedtime is used for frequent or dangerous adult events; hypnosis and CBT approaches have supportive evidence.
det.prognosis: Most childhood cases resolve by adolescence; adult cases are more persistent but usually controllable.
pearls: First third of the night means N3, last third means REM; timing is the most useful history question.
Do not try to wake a child during a sleep terror; guide them back to bed.
New sleepwalking on zolpidem is a reason to stop the drug.
det.thd: NREM arousal disorders คือการตื่นไม่สมบูรณ์จากหลับลึก N3 ได้แก่ confusional arousal ละเมอเดิน และ sleep terror มักเกิดช่วงต้นคืน ผู้ป่วยตาเปิดแต่ปลุกยากและจำไม่ได้ ปัจจัยกระตุ้นคืออดนอน ไข้ ความเครียด ยา Z-drug และ OSA การวินิจฉัยใช้ประวัติและวิดีโอ ถ้าผิดแบบให้ตรวจ video-PSG การรักษาคือนอนให้พอ จัดห้องให้ปลอดภัย รักษาปัจจัยกระตุ้น และใช้ clonazepam ในผู้ใหญ่ที่เป็นบ่อยหรืออันตราย

qx.stem: A 35-year-old male bank manager from Chiang Rai was started on zolpidem for insomnia. Over the next month his wife twice found him walking outside the house at night, unresponsive, with no memory next morning. He sleepwalked as a child. He has no daytime sleepiness.
qx.q: Which action should come first?
opts: Add clonazepam to the zolpidem
Start levetiracetam for possible nocturnal seizures
Stop zolpidem and secure the home
Order an MSLT
Start a dopamine agonist at bedtime
qx.why: Zolpidem can trigger sleepwalking and other complex sleep behaviours in susceptible people, especially those with a childhood history. The first steps are to stop the drug and make the environment safe, then treat insomnia with CBT-I. Adding clonazepam is not the first move, and there is no feature of seizures or narcolepsy to justify antiseizure drugs or an MSLT.

qx.stem: A 28-year-old nurse from Pathum Thani wakes to find food scattered in the kitchen, with no memory of getting up. Her husband reports that she walks, eyes open, one hour after sleep onset and is hard to rouse. The episodes began after she started zolpidem 10 mg for insomnia and happen more after night duty. Examination and an awake EEG are normal.
qx.q: What is the best first step?
opts: Start clonazepam immediately
Begin levetiracetam for presumed nocturnal seizures
Start an antipsychotic at night
Stop zolpidem, regularise sleep, screen for sleep apnoea and secure the home
Order a lumbar puncture
qx.why: Sleepwalking is a disorder of arousal from slow-wave sleep occurring early in the night with amnesia, and sedative-hypnotics such as zolpidem, sleep deprivation and untreated sleep apnoea are classic triggers. Removing triggers and making the environment safe comes first; medicines are reserved for persistent or dangerous cases. Seizures, psychosis and CNS infection do not fit this picture.

name: Nucleoside neuropathies
formal: Painful distal axonal sensory neuropathy from nucleoside analogue antiretroviral and antiviral drugs (ddI, ddC, d4T), via mitochondrial toxicity.
simple: Nerve damage with burning and numbness in the feet, caused by some HIV drugs.
more: Withdraw the drug; symptom control with neuropathic pain medications; improvement may take months.
th: เส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเสื่อมแบบปวดจากยาต้านไวรัสกลุ่ม nucleoside รุ่นเก่า (ddI, ddC, d4T) ผ่านพิษต่อไมโทคอนเดรีย
tempoNote: Weeks to months after starting the drug; may worsen for a few weeks after stopping ('coasting')
feat: Burning, tingling and pain in the soles and toes, rising up the legs
Reduced pinprick and vibration distally, depressed ankle jerks
Onset linked to stavudine, didanosine or zalcitabine, especially at higher doses
Clinically similar to HIV-associated distal sensory polyneuropathy
inv: Drug history and timing; B12, glucose/HbA1c, TSH to exclude other causes
NCS: length-dependent axonal sensory neuropathy; may be normal in small-fibre-predominant disease
Serum lactate if hyperlactataemia from mitochondrial toxicity is suspected

case.who: 41-year-old woman from Phayao on an older antiretroviral regimen
case.story: Four months after starting a stavudine-containing regimen she has burning feet that wake her at night.
case.exam: Stocking hyperalgesia to the mid-calf, absent ankle jerks, normal strength.
case.tests: B12 and glucose normal; NCS reduced sural amplitudes.
case.q: What is the most useful intervention?
case.a: Switch stavudine to a non-neurotoxic agent (e.g. tenofovir-based regimen with dolutegravir) and treat pain with neuropathic agents.

det.patho: Dideoxynucleoside analogues inhibit mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma, depleting mitochondrial DNA in axons and dorsal root ganglia and causing distal axonal degeneration. Toxicity is dose-dependent and additive with other neurotoxins. Older age, height, existing neuropathy and concurrent isoniazid increase risk.
det.clinical: The picture is a painful, length-dependent sensory neuropathy beginning in the feet; motor involvement is minimal. Symptoms may continue to worsen for several weeks after the drug is stopped before improving. Because these drugs are now largely obsolete, new cases are rare but chronic sequelae persist in long-term survivors from the stavudine era, including in Thailand.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the temporal relationship to a neurotoxic NRTI and exclusion of other causes; it cannot be distinguished reliably from HIV-related neuropathy by tests. Nerve conduction confirms axonal sensory loss, and skin biopsy shows reduced intraepidermal fibre density. Check for lactic acidosis and pancreatitis with didanosine.
det.treatment: Withdraw the offending drug and use modern regimens without d-drugs. Treat pain with duloxetine, gabapentinoids, tricyclics or topical capsaicin, though trial evidence in HIV neuropathy is limited. Address coexisting contributors such as B12 deficiency, alcohol and isoniazid (give pyridoxine).
det.prognosis: Many improve partially over months after withdrawal, but persistent pain is common.
pearls: Expect 'coasting' — worsening for weeks after stopping the drug.
Modern regimens (tenofovir, dolutegravir) are not neurotoxic.
Always give pyridoxine with isoniazid in HIV–TB co-infection.
det.thd: Nucleoside neuropathy เกิดจากยาต้าน HIV รุ่นเก่าเช่น stavudine, didanosine ที่ยับยั้ง DNA polymerase ของไมโทคอนเดรีย ทำให้ปลายประสาทรับความรู้สึกเสื่อม ผู้ป่วยแสบร้อนปลายเท้า ปวดกลางคืน การวินิจฉัยอาศัยประวัติยาและตัดสาเหตุอื่น รักษาโดยเปลี่ยนยาเป็นสูตรใหม่และใช้ยาลดปวด neuropathic อาการอาจแย่ลงช่วงแรกหลังหยุดยา

name: Numb chin syndrome
formal: Mental neuropathy with numbness of the chin and lip from inferior alveolar or mental nerve involvement; an ominous sign of metastatic or haematological malignancy, or dental or mandibular disease.
simple: Numbness of the chin and lower lip from damage to a facial nerve, which can be an early warning of cancer spread.
th: อาการชาที่คางและริมฝีปากล่างจากเส้นประสาท mental หรือ inferior alveolar ถูกรบกวน เป็นสัญญาณเตือนของมะเร็งแพร่กระจายหรือมะเร็งเม็ดเลือด
tempoNote: Numbness develops over days to weeks
feat: Unilateral numbness of the chin and lower lip, sometimes with pain
Dental causes: extraction, implants, abscess, local anaesthetic injury
Malignant causes: mandibular metastasis (breast, lung, prostate), lymphoma, leukaemia, skull base or leptomeningeal spread
May be the first sign of cancer or of relapse
inv: Dental assessment and panoramic X-ray
CT or MRI of the mandible and skull base with contrast
If imaging negative: CSF cytology/flow cytometry, bone scan or PET, blood film

case.who: 52-year-old woman from Chonburi, breast cancer treated 4 years ago
case.story: Three weeks of numbness over the right side of her chin and lower lip without dental work.
case.exam: Light touch and pinprick are diminished only within the right mental nerve territory.
case.tests: Panoramic X-ray subtle; MRI shows enhancing lesion in the right mandibular body; bone scan multiple metastases.
case.q: What does this symptom signify here?
case.a: Numb chin syndrome from mandibular metastasis — a sign of systemic relapse requiring oncological staging.

read.where: Chapter 13 Cranial Nerve Disorders — Peripheral Vth Nerve Lesions
Numb chin and numb cheek syndromes

det.patho: Any process along the inferior alveolar nerve and its mental branch, from the skull base through the mandibular canal to the mental foramen, can cause chin numbness. Metastatic deposits in the mandible, infiltration of the nerve by lymphoma, or leptomeningeal involvement at the trigeminal root are the important malignant mechanisms.
det.clinical: It is a symptom pattern, not a disease. Benign dental causes are common, but without a clear dental reason it is a red flag. Breast cancer and lymphoma are the leading malignant causes; it often heralds progression.
det.diagnosis: Take a dental and oncology history. Image the mandible and skull base; if negative, consider CSF studies for leptomeningeal disease and systemic staging. Blood tests may reveal leukaemia.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: dental care for local disease, radiotherapy or systemic therapy for metastases, and intrathecal or systemic therapy for leptomeningeal disease. Symptomatic pain management may be needed.
det.prognosis: When due to malignancy, it often indicates advanced disease with limited survival.
pearls: Unexplained numb chin in an adult is cancer until proven otherwise.
Ask about breast cancer and lymphoma history.
Normal mandible imaging should prompt skull base and CSF evaluation.
det.thd: Numb chin syndrome คืออาการชาบริเวณคางและริมฝีปากล่างด้านหนึ่งจากเส้นประสาท mental หรือ inferior alveolar ถูกรบกวน อาจเกิดจากปัญหาฟันได้ แต่ถ้าไม่มีสาเหตุทางฟันชัดเจนต้องคิดถึงมะเร็งแพร่กระจายมาที่ขากรรไกรล่าง lymphoma หรือ leukaemia และมะเร็งลามเยื่อหุ้มสมอง ควรทำภาพถ่ายขากรรไกรและฐานกะโหลก ตรวจน้ำไขสันหลังถ้าจำเป็น และรักษาที่สาเหตุ

qx.stem: A 58-year-old teacher from Phitsanulok, treated for oestrogen receptor-positive breast cancer three years ago and in remission, notices that the left lower lip and chin have become numb over three weeks. Taste and tongue sensation are normal, her teeth are healthy and a dental radiograph shows no periapical disease. Examination shows reduced pinprick over the left chin and lower lip only.
qx.q: What should be done next?
opts: Reassurance and a trial of carbamazepine for neuropathic symptoms
Referral to a dentist for extraction of the nearest lower molar
Repeat examination in three months before any further tests
A nerve conduction study of the mental nerve to confirm the lesion
Urgent restaging with imaging of the mandible, skull base and body, as numb chin syndrome may herald metastatic relapse
qx.why: Mental neuropathy without a dental cause is a recognised warning sign of malignancy, most often bony metastasis or lymphoma, and in a patient with prior breast cancer it should trigger immediate re-evaluation with imaging such as mandibular MRI, bone scan or PET-CT, and consideration of leptomeningeal disease. Waiting, symptomatic drugs or dental procedures delay the diagnosis. Electrodiagnosis would not change management.

name: Nummular headache
formal: Primary headache with chronic focal pain in a small coin-shaped scalp area of 1-6 cm, with stable location and often paroxysmal exacerbations; benign, may respond to gabapentin or indomethacin.
simple: A long-lasting headache felt in one small round patch of the scalp, about the size of a coin.
th: ปวดศีรษะปฐมภูมิเฉพาะจุดเล็กรูปเหรียญบนหนังศีรษะขนาด 1–6 ซม. ตำแหน่งคงที่ ปวดเรื้อรังและอาจปวดแปลบเป็นพัก ๆ ไม่อันตราย
tempoNote: Continuous or intermittent pain lasting months to years
feat: Pain confined to a sharply outlined round or oval area 1–6 cm across
Usually parietal; shape and size stay the same over time
Mild to moderate pressure-like pain with occasional sharp exacerbations
Local allodynia or numbness over the patch
Middle-aged adults; more common in women
inv: Examination of the scalp and skull for local lesions
MRI or CT with bone windows to exclude skull or dural lesions
ESR/CRP in older patients if near the temporal region

case.story: For a year she has had a constant ache in a coin-sized spot on the top-right of her head, with sharp stabs a few times a week.
case.exam: Tender, mildly hypoaesthetic 3 cm round area at the right parietal scalp; otherwise normal.
case.tests: MRI with skull views normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and treatment options?
case.a: Nummular headache; gabapentin or local onabotulinumtoxinA, with local anaesthetic blocks for flares.

det.patho: Nummular headache is thought to be a localised neuralgia of terminal branches of scalp nerves, supported by the sensory changes in the affected area. Central mechanisms may also contribute. The cause in individual patients is usually unknown.
det.clinical: The key feature is the stable, coin-shaped painful area. Pain is often continuous with episodes of worsening and may be accompanied by dysaesthesia, tenderness or itch. Some patients have more than one patch. Spontaneous remissions occur.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 criteria require pain exclusively in a sharply defined area of fixed size and shape, round or elliptical, 1–6 cm in diameter, not explained by another disorder. Imaging excludes bone or dural lesions; skin examination excludes local dermatological causes.
det.treatment: Reassurance is important. Gabapentin is commonly used; NSAIDs, tricyclics and onabotulinumtoxinA injected into the patch have been reported to help, and local anaesthetic blocks can abort flares. Evidence comes from case series rather than trials.
det.prognosis: Benign, often chronic, with occasional spontaneous remission.
pearls: A fixed coin-sized painful patch is the defining feature.
Always image the skull beneath the patch.
Local botulinum toxin is a useful option in refractory cases.
det.thd: Nummular headache คือปวดศีรษะเฉพาะจุดรูปเหรียญบนหนังศีรษะขนาด 1–6 ซม. ตำแหน่งและขนาดคงที่ อาจมีปวดแปลบเป็นพัก ๆ และชาหรือแสบบริเวณนั้น คาดว่าเกิดจากปลายประสาทของหนังศีรษะ ต้องตรวจภาพกะโหลกและหนังศีรษะเพื่อแยกรอยโรค รักษาด้วย gabapentin หรือฉีด botulinum toxin เฉพาะที่

ddx.pt: Brief jabs that move around the head rather than a fixed patch
Skull or dural lesion beneath the painful area seen on imaging
Temporal tenderness in over-50s with systemic symptoms and raised ESR

aN: coin shaped headache | nummular cephalalgia | coin shaped cephalalgia | focal scalp headache

name: Nutritional and toxic optic neuropathies
formal: Bilateral symmetric painless visual loss with centrocaecal scotomas from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, or toxins such as methanol, ethambutol and tobacco; mitochondrial vulnerability of papillomacular fibres.
simple: Slowly worsening vision in both eyes caused by poor diet or poisons that damage the nerves carrying signals from the eyes.
th: ตามัวสองข้างแบบสมมาตร ไม่ปวด เห็นสีผิดปกติ มี centrocaecal scotoma จากขาด B12 โฟเลต ไทอามีน ทองแดง หรือสารพิษเช่น methanol และ ethambutol
tempoNote: Subacute in malnutrition, alcohol or tobacco related disease and drug toxicity; acute (hours to days) after methanol
feat: Gradual, painless, symmetric blur of central vision with desaturated colours in both eyes
Centrocaecal scotomas on field testing; peripheral fields are spared
Normal discs early, with temporal pallor later, and occasional splinter haemorrhages

Risk groups: heavy drinkers or smokers, vegans without supplements, bariatric surgery or small bowel resection, malabsorption such as Crohn disease, and people on ethambutol, linezolid, amiodarone or methotrexate
Often accompanied by distal numbness or gait imbalance when B12 or copper lack is the root cause
inv: Visual acuity, Ishihara plates, central fields and OCT, which also rules out macular disease
B12 with methylmalonic acid and homocysteine, folate, thiamine, copper, zinc, full blood count, renal function
Drug and toxin history, serum methanol and anion gap if suspected, MRI orbits and brain, and mtDNA studies when LHON is possible

case.who: 47-year-old woman who had gastric bypass two years ago, Bangkok
case.story: Over two months, vision in both eyes became cloudy, with reds looking brown. She stopped her vitamins soon after surgery. She also reports tingling in the feet.
case.exam: Acuity 6/18 in both eyes, severely reduced colour plates, bilateral central scotomas, normal discs apart from slight temporal pallor, absent vibration at the ankles.
case.tests: B12 very low with high methylmalonic acid, copper low-normal, MRI orbits normal, OCT shows early thinning of the papillomacular fibres.
case.q: What is the unifying diagnosis and the first-line management?
case.a: Nutritional optic neuropathy with B12 deficiency neuropathy after bariatric surgery. Replace B12 (parenteral at first), add a multivitamin and long-term supplementation, check copper, and recheck vision and fields.

read.where: Chapter 13: Workup for Optic Atrophy — Subacute Vision Loss

det.patho: Optic nerve fibres of the papillomacular bundle depend heavily on mitochondrial function, and a shortage of B-vitamins, copper or protein, or toxins that block the respiratory chain, impairs them first. Cyanide in tobacco smoke and formate produced from methanol add to this injury. Several hits usually coincide, for example poor diet with smoking and alcohol, or a TB drug in a malnourished patient, and the picture is common in developing regions.
det.clinical: Painless blurring evolves over weeks to months in both eyes, together with weak colour perception and small central or centrocaecal scotomas. The discs look normal at first or show subtle changes, then pale on the temporal side. Peripheral neuropathy, myelopathy or cognitive change often accompanies the visual loss if the underlying lesion is B12 or copper depletion. Nutritional forms may occur in clusters during famine or sanctions, and ethambutol loss most often arises after months of therapy.
det.diagnosis: Define the pattern of symmetric painless central loss with dyschromatopsia, then look for cause. Laboratory screen: B12, folate, copper, thiamine, with methylmalonic acid and homocysteine when B12 is borderline. MRI excludes a mass or demyelinating disease, OCT confirms papillomacular loss and excludes macular pathology, and unexplained cases deserve LHON testing because smoking and alcohol can unmask it.
det.treatment: Remove the toxin or offending drug at once, supply a full diet with a multivitamin, thiamine and folate, and replace B12. If B12 and folate are both deficient, correct B12 first or together to avoid worsening neurological damage. Injected B12 is useful where absorption is poor or follow-up is unreliable. Advise stopping tobacco and alcohol, manage co-existing neuropathy, and re-test vision regularly. Methanol poisoning is a medical emergency needing an alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor, bicarbonate and dialysis.
det.prognosis: Early treatment often brings substantial recovery; delay leaves permanent pallor and scotomas. Methanol and late nutritional cases do worse.
pearls: Disproportionate loss of colour vision plus centrocaecal scotomas is the signature.
Bariatric surgery, veganism and Crohn disease are modern routes to B12 optic neuropathy.
Unexplained bilateral central loss in a smoker or drinker can still be LHON, so test if no deficiency is found.
det.thd: ภาวะนี้เกิดจากการขาดวิตามิน (B12 โฟเลต ไทอามีน) หรือทองแดง หรือได้รับสารพิษ เช่น ethambutol และ methanol ทำให้เส้นประสาทตาทั้งสองข้างเสียเท่า ๆ กัน ผู้ป่วยมองมัว ไม่ปวด เห็นสีเพี้ยน และตรวจพบ centrocaecal scotoma การวินิจฉัยต้องตรวจเลือดหาสาเหตุ ทำ MRI เพื่อแยกก้อนกดทับ และคิดถึง LHON ถ้าไม่พบสาเหตุ รักษาโดยหยุดสารก่อโรค ให้วิตามินทดแทน และงดสุราและบุหรี่ ผู้ป่วยมักดีขึ้นถ้าวินิจฉัยเร็ว

ddx.pt: Sequential bilateral loss in a young male with a mtDNA variant, typically without a nutritional lead
Insidious loss from childhood with a family history, temporal pallor and tritanopia; stable over years
Usually one eye, painful eye movements, recovers over weeks, with demyelinating MRI changes

aN: toxic optic neuropathy | nutritional optic neuropathy | tobacco alcohol amblyopia | ethambutol optic neuropathy | methanol optic neuropathy

name: Obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD)
formal: Psychiatric disorder of intrusive obsessions and repetitive compulsions linked to cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuit dysfunction; associated with tics, Tourette syndrome and basal ganglia disease.
simple: A condition with unwanted repeated thoughts and rituals that a person feels driven to carry out, even though they know they are excessive.
more: Treat with high-dose SSRIs and exposure and response prevention; augment with antipsychotics, and consider DBS for refractory disease. Neuroimaging is usually normal; rule out secondary causes such as PANDAS and structural lesions.
th: โรคย้ำคิดย้ำทำ มีความคิดซ้ำที่ไม่ต้องการและการกระทำซ้ำเพื่อลดความกังวล เกี่ยวข้องกับวงจร cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical พบร่วมกับ tic และอาจเกิดจากรอยโรค basal ganglia หรือ PANS/PANDAS
tempoNote: Bimodal onset in childhood (often boys, tic-related) and early adulthood; usually chronic with waxing and waning; abrupt onset in a child suggests PANS/PANDAS
feat: Intrusive unwanted thoughts, urges or images (contamination, harm, symmetry, taboo themes) with anxiety, neutralised by repetitive actions or mental rituals
Insight ranges from good to absent; DSM-5-TR asks for insight and tic-related specifiers
Strong overlap with Tourette syndrome and chronic tics; secondary OCD follows basal ganglia damage (stroke, carbon monoxide, encephalitis lethargica, Sydenham chorea)
Late-onset rituals with loss of insight should raise bvFTD or other frontal-striatal disease
inv: Clinical diagnosis with Y-BOCS (or CY-BOCS in children) severity rating
Neurological examination for tics, chorea and frontal signs; MRI when onset is late, sudden, or with focal or cognitive signs
In abrupt childhood onset: throat swab, ASO and anti-DNase B, and assessment for PANS/PANDAS or Sydenham chorea

case.who: 16-year-old schoolboy from Phitsanulok with motor tics since age 7
case.story: Over the past year he has to touch door frames evenly on both sides and recheck his school bag until it feels just right, spending 2 hours a day; he knows this is excessive.
case.exam: Frequent eye blinking and shoulder shrugs; normal neurological examination otherwise; no chorea.
case.tests: Y-BOCS 24 (moderate to severe); thyroid function normal; MRI not needed.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the first-line treatment?
case.a: Tic-related OCD with Tourette syndrome; start exposure and response prevention, add an SSRI such as sertraline or fluvoxamine at adequate dose, and consider low-dose aripiprazole augmentation if response is partial.

read.where: Chapter 30 Neuropsychiatry — Obsessions, Compulsions and Impulsivity

det.patho: OCD is linked with hyperactivity and abnormal connectivity in orbitofrontal, anterior cingulate, striatal and thalamic loops, together with weaker inhibitory control. Genetic risk is moderate and overlaps with Tourette syndrome. Damage to the striatum from infarcts, hypoxia, carbon monoxide, post-streptococcal autoimmunity or encephalitis can produce secondary obsessions and compulsions, supporting a circuit model.
det.clinical: Symptoms cluster into contamination and washing, harm and checking, symmetry and ordering, and unacceptable taboo thoughts. Patients often hide symptoms for years. Tic-related OCD starts earlier, is more common in boys and features just-right and symmetry themes. Related disorders include body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding, trichotillomania and skin-picking. Depression and suicidality are frequent companions.
det.diagnosis: DSM-5-TR requires obsessions, compulsions or both that are time-consuming (more than about an hour a day) or impairing, not due to substances or another condition, with specifiers for insight and tics. Y-BOCS measures severity. Neurological work-up is reserved for late onset, sudden onset, neurological signs or cognitive decline. Distinguish compulsions from tics, stereotypies, punding in Parkinson disease and ruminations in depression.
det.treatment: Exposure and response prevention is first line, alone or with an SSRI at higher doses than for depression, given for at least 8–12 weeks before judging response; clomipramine is an alternative. Partial responders may receive low-dose antipsychotic augmentation (aripiprazole or risperidone), particularly when tics coexist. For severe refractory cases, deep TMS and DBS targeting the ventral capsule and ventral striatum are options in specialist centres. PANS/PANDAS management focuses on symptomatic therapy, with antibiotics or immunotherapy only in selected cases.
det.prognosis: Usually chronic, but most patients improve meaningfully with combined treatment; a proportion of childhood tic-related OCD lessens by adulthood.
pearls: Ask a patient with tics about obsessions and rituals; a large share have OCD.
New OCD in late life should prompt a search for frontal or striatal disease.
SSRIs for OCD need higher doses and longer trials than for depression.
det.thd: โรคย้ำคิดย้ำทำมีความคิดซ้ำที่ไม่ต้องการทำให้กังวล และต้องทำพฤติกรรมซ้ำเพื่อลดความกังวล เกี่ยวกับวงจรระหว่างสมองส่วนหน้าและ basal ganglia จึงพบบ่อยร่วมกับ tic และ Tourette และอาจเกิดหลังรอยโรค basal ganglia หรือ PANS/PANDAS ในเด็ก การรักษาหลักคือ exposure and response prevention ร่วมกับ SSRI ขนาดสูง รายที่ดื้อต่อการรักษาอาจใช้ยาต้านโรคจิตเสริมหรือ deep brain stimulation

ddx.pt: Complex tics can resemble compulsions but are driven by a sensory urge rather than an anxious thought
Overnight onset of OCD or food restriction in a child with anxiety, regression and urinary symptoms
Late-onset stereotyped rituals without anxiety or insight, with disinhibition and loss of empathy

aN: ocd | obsessive compulsive disorder | obsessional neurosis | tic related ocd

name: Obsessive–compulsive personality disorders (OCPD)
formal: Personality disorder marked by perfectionism, rigidity, orderliness and control, without true obsessions or compulsions, and ego-syntonic unlike OCD.
simple: A lasting personality style with extreme perfectionism and a need for order and control that interferes with relationships and flexibility.
th: ความผิดปกติทางบุคลิกภาพที่ยึดติดความสมบูรณ์แบบ ระเบียบ และการควบคุม โดยผู้ป่วยมักไม่รู้สึกว่าเป็นปัญหา ต่างจาก OCD ที่มีความคิดย้ำและพฤติกรรมย้ำทำจริง
tempoNote: Enduring trait pattern from early adulthood; stable over years
feat: Psychiatric personality disorder, not a neurological disease; listed here because it is often confused with OCD and tic-related behaviours
Perfectionism that delays finishing tasks, preoccupation with rules, lists and order
Rigid, stubborn, reluctant to delegate; excessive devotion to work; miserly or hoarding tendencies
Traits are ego-syntonic: the person sees them as correct, so distress usually falls on family or colleagues
No true intrusive obsessions or ritual compulsions, unlike OCD
inv: Clinical psychiatric assessment against DSM-5-TR or ICD-11 (anankastia trait domain) criteria
Screen for co-existing depression, anxiety and OCD
Neurological examination and imaging only if a late-onset change in personality suggests a brain disorder (e.g. frontotemporal dementia)

case.who: 38-year-old male accountant referred from a Bangkok district hospital
case.story: His wife says he rewrites every report many times, will not let staff help and becomes angry if household items are moved. He thinks his standards are simply correct.
case.exam: Neurologically normal; no tics, no ritualised checking, no intrusive unwanted thoughts on questioning.
case.tests: Not required; psychiatric interview confirms long-standing traits since university.
case.q: Is this OCD, and what features separate the two?
case.a: OCPD rather than OCD: the traits are lifelong and ego-syntonic, without intrusive obsessions or anxiety-relieving rituals; refer for psychotherapy.

read.where: Chapter 30 Neuropsychiatry — Personality Disorder and Personality Change

det.patho: OCPD is a psychiatric personality disorder with a mixture of heritable temperament and developmental influences. It is among the commonest personality disorders in community surveys. No structural brain lesion underlies it, and it is not a basal ganglia disorder in the neurological sense.
det.clinical: This is not a neurological disease; neurologists meet it mainly as a differential for OCD, tics or frontal-lobe personality change. People with OCPD are controlling, perfectionistic and inflexible, often to the detriment of productivity and relationships. Because they regard their behaviour as right, they rarely seek help for the traits themselves but may present with depression, anxiety or conflict at work. A new rigid or obsessive personality in mid or late life should prompt a search for frontotemporal dementia or other organic causes.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical by a psychiatrist or psychologist using DSM-5-TR criteria or the ICD-11 dimensional model, in which anankastia is a trait domain. The key distinction from OCD is the absence of intrusive obsessions and anxiety-reducing compulsions. Collateral history from family helps. Investigations are only needed when onset is late or other neurological signs are present.
det.treatment: Psychotherapy, particularly cognitive behavioural and schema-focused approaches, is the main treatment. Co-morbid depression, anxiety or OCD is treated in the usual way, often with SSRIs. There is no specific drug for the personality traits. Engagement may be difficult because the patient does not see the traits as a problem.
det.prognosis: Traits are long-standing but may soften with age and therapy; outcome is better when co-morbid mood disorders are treated.
pearls: Ego-syntonic perfectionism = OCPD; ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts with rituals = OCD.
OCPD and OCD can coexist in the same patient.
New obsessive rigidity after 50: consider bvFTD before calling it a personality disorder.
det.thd: OCPD เป็นความผิดปกติทางจิตเวชด้านบุคลิกภาพ ไม่ใช่โรคทางระบบประสาท ผู้ป่วยยึดติดความสมบูรณ์แบบ ระเบียบ กฎเกณฑ์ และต้องควบคุมทุกอย่าง โดยมองว่าตนเองถูกต้อง ต่างจาก OCD ที่มีความคิดย้ำซึ่งผู้ป่วยไม่ต้องการและต้องทำพฤติกรรมซ้ำเพื่อลดความกังวล วินิจฉัยโดยการซักประวัติทางจิตเวช และรักษาด้วยจิตบำบัดเป็นหลัก หากบุคลิกภาพเปลี่ยนแปลงตอนอายุมากควรนึกถึงโรคสมองเสื่อมกลุ่ม frontotemporal

ddx.pt: Unwanted intrusive thoughts and rituals that the patient recognises as excessive (ego-dystonic)
Emotional instability, impulsivity and unstable relationships rather than rigid control
Motor and vocal tics from childhood; obsessive-compulsive symptoms may coexist but tics define it

aN: ocpd | obsessive compulsive personality disorders | anankastic personality disorder | obsessional personality | compulsive personality disorder

name: Obstetrically related plexopathies
formal: Brachial or lumbosacral plexus injuries related to childbirth, such as Erb palsy from shoulder dystocia or maternal lumbosacral trunk compression.
simple: Nerve injury connected with childbirth, either in the baby (arm weakness) or in the mother (leg weakness).
more: Most recover spontaneously; severe infant cases may need microsurgical repair.
th: การบาดเจ็บของข่ายประสาทแขน (brachial plexus) ในทารกจากภาวะไหล่ติดขณะคลอด หรือข่ายประสาทเอว-กระเบนเหน็บ (lumbosacral plexus) ในมารดาจากศีรษะทารกกดเส้นประสาทขณะคลอด ทำให้เท้าตก
tempoNote: Deficit is noticed at or soon after delivery; most recover over weeks to months
feat: Maternal form: foot drop or leg weakness and numbness noticed after delivery, from compression of the lumbosacral trunk (L4–L5 fibres)
Risk factors: first pregnancy, cephalopelvic disproportion, short maternal stature and prolonged or difficult labour
Peroneal-innervated muscles are weakest, but hip abductors, hamstrings and tibialis posterior are also involved, unlike a fibular neck lesion
Neonatal form: Erb palsy (C5–C6) with arm adducted and internally rotated after shoulder dystocia or macrosomia
Klumpke pattern (C8–T1) gives a claw hand and possible Horner syndrome; Moro reflex is asymmetric
inv: Needle EMG and nerve conduction studies about 3 weeks after onset to separate plexus lesion, peroneal neuropathy and root injury
MRI of lumbosacral plexus or spine if the picture is atypical or the deficit is severe
In neonates: clinical grading, chest X-ray for phrenic involvement, and MRI or electrodiagnosis if no recovery

case.story: After a long second stage with forceps delivery of a 3.8 kg baby, she cannot lift her left foot and trips when walking to the bathroom. Back pain is minimal.
case.exam: Left foot drop, weak ankle inversion and hip abduction, patchy numbness on the top of the foot and outer lower leg, knee jerk preserved.
case.tests: EMG shows denervation in tibialis anterior, tibialis posterior and gluteus medius, with normal lumbar paraspinal muscles and a normal fibular nerve across the knee.
case.q: Why is this not a common peroneal neuropathy at the fibular head, and what is the expected outcome?
case.a: Muscles supplied by other nerves are also affected, indicating a lumbosacral trunk lesion from fetal head compression; most women recover fully within months.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Neurological Aspects of Pregnancy

det.patho: Obstetric plexopathy is a compressive or traction injury occurring during labour and delivery. In the mother, the lumbosacral trunk crosses the pelvic brim and can be squeezed between the fetal head and the pelvis, injuring L4–L5 fibres. In the infant, lateral traction on the neck during shoulder dystocia stretches or avulses the upper roots.
det.clinical: The maternal syndrome presents with foot drop and sensory loss soon after delivery and is often misread as a fibular neck neuropathy. Clues to the proximal location are weak ankle inversion and hip abduction and an abnormal lumbosacral trunk distribution. Contributing factors are a first pregnancy, a small mother with a large baby and a prolonged labour. In babies, Erb palsy is the usual pattern, and global palsy or Klumpke involvement carries a poorer outlook.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis rests on the history, a careful examination of muscles beyond the peroneal territory and electrodiagnosis, which shows denervation in tibialis posterior, gluteal and other muscles. Normal paraspinal muscles help to exclude radiculopathy, although they are not always abnormal in root lesions. Imaging excludes spinal haematoma, tumour or other compressive lesions when pain, bilateral signs or sphincter symptoms are present. Neonatal palsy is graded clinically with regular follow-up of biceps and deltoid recovery.
det.treatment: Treatment is supportive for the maternal form: ankle-foot orthosis, physiotherapy and fall precautions, with an expectation of spontaneous recovery. Neonates need early physiotherapy to preserve passive range of motion and prevent contracture, and referral to a brachial plexus team if there is no antigravity elbow flexion by about three months. Nerve grafts or transfers are options for infants without recovery. Counselling about future delivery planning is appropriate.
det.prognosis: Most maternal cases recover fully within weeks to months, and most neonatal Erb palsies improve spontaneously.
pearls: Foot drop after labour with weak inversion and hip abduction means lumbosacral trunk, not the fibular nerve.
Normal paraspinal EMG favours a plexus over a root lesion.
In neonates, failure of biceps recovery by three months is the signal to refer for surgery.
det.thd: Obstetric plexopathy คือการบาดเจ็บของข่ายประสาทจากการคลอด ในมารดาเกิดจากศีรษะทารกกด lumbosacral trunk (L4–L5) ทำให้เท้าตกหลังคลอด และอาจถูกวินิจฉัยผิดเป็นเส้นประสาท peroneal ส่วนในทารกพบ Erb palsy จากไหล่ติด การตรวจ EMG ช่วยบอกตำแหน่ง รักษาด้วยกายภาพบำบัดและอุปกรณ์พยุงข้อเท้า ส่วนใหญ่หายได้เอง ทารกที่ไม่ฟื้นภายใน 3 เดือนควรส่งต่อเพื่อพิจารณาผ่าตัด

ddx.pt: Weakness limited to tibialis anterior and peroneal muscles; hip abduction and ankle inversion are spared
Adult or neonatal traction injury; mechanism and level determine the pattern
Pain, weight loss and diabetes suggest inflammatory plexopathy; not clustered with labour

aN: obstetric brachial plexus palsy | neonatal brachial plexus palsy | erb palsy | klumpke palsy | maternal lumbosacral trunk palsy

name: Obstructive hydrocephalus
formal: Ventricular dilatation from blockage of CSF flow within the ventricular system, for example aqueduct stenosis or a posterior fossa mass, causing raised intracranial pressure.
simple: A build-up of fluid in the brain because a blockage stops it draining, causing headache, vomiting and drowsiness.
th: โพรงสมองขยายจากการอุดตันการไหลของน้ำไขสันหลังภายในระบบโพรงสมอง เช่น ท่อ aqueduct ตีบ หรือก้อนในโพสทีเรียฟอสซา ทำให้ความดันในกะโหลกสูง
tempoNote: Acute blockage (tumour, haemorrhage) causes deterioration over hours; slow obstruction (aqueduct stenosis) may present over years
feat: Headache, worse on waking or lying down, with vomiting
Drowsiness, papilloedema, sixth nerve palsy
Parinaud syndrome (upgaze palsy) with dorsal midbrain compression
In infants: enlarging head, bulging fontanelle, sunset eyes
Sudden deterioration and death possible (herniation)
inv: CT brain urgently: enlarged ventricles proximal to the block
MRI with contrast and CSF flow sequences to find the cause
Lumbar puncture is contraindicated until obstruction is excluded

case.story: Three weeks of morning headaches and vomiting, now unsteady walking and double vision.
case.exam: Bilateral papilloedema, left sixth nerve palsy, truncal ataxia.
case.tests: CT: mass in the fourth ventricle with dilated lateral and third ventricles.
case.q: What is the immediate concern and management?
case.a: Obstructive hydrocephalus from a posterior fossa tumour (e.g. medulloblastoma); urgent neurosurgical CSF diversion and tumour resection; do not perform lumbar puncture.

read.where: Chapter 28 Disorders of Consciousness and Intensive Care Neurology
Chapter 50: Headache attributed to non-vascular intracranial disorder

det.patho: Obstruction anywhere within the ventricular system — foramen of Monro, third ventricle, aqueduct of Sylvius or fourth ventricle outlets — causes ventricles upstream to dilate. Causes include tumours (colloid cyst, pineal and posterior fossa tumours), haemorrhage, cysts, infections with ependymitis, congenital aqueduct stenosis and Chiari or Dandy-Walker malformations. Raised intracranial pressure reduces cerebral perfusion and can cause herniation.
det.clinical: Acute obstruction produces headache, vomiting and rapidly declining consciousness; colloid cysts can cause sudden death. Slower obstruction gives chronic headaches, visual blurring, cognitive slowing, gait disturbance and endocrine changes. Children show increasing head size and developmental delay. Upward gaze palsy, sixth nerve palsy and papilloedema are classic signs.
det.diagnosis: CT is the first test and shows dilated ventricles proximal to the block with periventricular oedema. MRI defines the cause and site; CSF flow studies help in aqueduct stenosis. Lumbar puncture is contraindicated until a mass and obstruction have been excluded because of herniation risk.
det.treatment: Emergencies require external ventricular drainage. Definitive options include treating the cause (tumour resection), endoscopic third ventriculostomy (especially for aqueduct stenosis and posterior fossa lesions), or ventriculoperitoneal shunting. Steroids help with tumour-related oedema. Long-term follow-up for shunt failure is important.
det.prognosis: Outcome depends on cause and speed of treatment; prompt diversion usually reverses symptoms, but delayed treatment risks permanent visual and cognitive loss.
pearls: New headache with vomiting and papilloedema: image before any lumbar puncture.
Colloid cyst: positional headache and sudden collapse.
Shunt patients with headache and drowsiness need urgent shunt assessment.

name: Obstructive sleep apnoea/hypopnoea syndrome (OSAHS)
formal: Recurrent upper airway collapse in sleep causing hypoxaemia, fragmented sleep and daytime somnolence; risk factor for stroke, hypertension and arrhythmia; treated with CPAP.
simple: Breathing repeatedly stops or becomes shallow during sleep because the throat closes, leading to loud snoring and daytime tiredness.
th: ทางเดินหายใจส่วนบนตีบหรือปิดซ้ำ ๆ ขณะหลับ ทำให้ออกซิเจนต่ำ หลับไม่ต่อเนื่อง ง่วงกลางวัน และเพิ่มความเสี่ยงความดันสูง หัวใจเต้นผิดจังหวะ และ stroke รักษาหลักด้วย CPAP

feat: Loud habitual snoring, witnessed pauses, choking or gasping awakenings and unrefreshing sleep
Daytime sleepiness, morning headache, poor concentration, low mood and drowsy driving
Risk factors: obesity, large neck, retrognathia, enlarged tonsils, male sex, menopause, alcohol and sedatives
Linked with resistant hypertension, atrial fibrillation, heart failure and ischaemic stroke; very common after stroke
In children: snoring, mouth breathing, enuresis, hyperactivity and poor school performance, usually from adenotonsillar hypertrophy

Home sleep apnoea test for uncomplicated adults with high pretest probability; in-lab PSG if cardiopulmonary or neuromuscular disease, or a negative home test with strong suspicion

case.story: He snores loudly, his wife sees him stop breathing at night, and he has twice nodded off at traffic lights; he has hypertension on three drugs.
case.exam: BMI 33, neck 43 cm, crowded oropharynx, BP 162/96; neurological examination normal.
case.tests: Home sleep apnoea test: AHI 41 per hour, oxygen nadir 76%; Epworth score 15.
case.q: What is the best treatment and what advice about driving is needed?
case.a: Severe OSA; start CPAP with mask fitting and adherence follow-up, add weight management (including tirzepatide if obesity criteria are met), and advise no driving while sleepy until treatment works.

Chapter 51 Neurologic Aspects of Sleep Medicine

det.patho: During sleep the dilator muscles of the pharynx lose tone, and in an anatomically narrow airway this causes repeated partial or complete collapse. Each event produces intermittent hypoxia, large negative intrathoracic pressure swings and an arousal that ends the event and fragments sleep. These repeated surges in sympathetic activity and oxidative stress drive hypertension, arrhythmia and vascular injury. Phenotypes differ in airway anatomy, loop gain, arousal threshold and muscle responsiveness.
det.clinical: Snoring and witnessed apnoeas are the core history, with sleepiness, nocturia, morning headache and cognitive slowing. Women and older adults may present mainly with insomnia, fatigue or mood change. OSA is present in at least half of patients after stroke or TIA and impairs recovery. Examiners ask about craniofacial clues, overlap with COPD, and children with tonsillar enlargement, Down syndrome or neuromuscular weakness.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires an AHI of 5 or more with symptoms or comorbidity, or 15 or more regardless of symptoms. A home sleep apnoea test is suitable for adults with a high pretest probability and no major comorbidity, while attended PSG is used for complex patients and when a home test is negative but suspicion remains. Hypopnoea scoring rules (3% or 4% desaturation) change the AHI, so read the report method. Assess sleepiness, drowsy driving and cardiovascular risk at the same visit.
det.treatment: CPAP or auto-PAP is first line for moderate to severe disease, with humidification and mask fitting to improve adherence. Mandibular advancement devices suit mild to moderate OSA or CPAP intolerance, and positional therapy helps supine-dependent disease. Hypoglossal nerve stimulation is an option for CPAP-intolerant adults with moderate to severe OSA and no complete concentric palatal collapse. Weight loss is essential: tirzepatide is approved for moderate to severe OSA with obesity, and bariatric surgery can be curative. Residual sleepiness despite effective therapy may be treated with solriamfetol or pitolisant; avoid sedatives and alcohol.
det.prognosis: Untreated severe OSA raises cardiovascular events and road accidents; consistent CPAP use improves sleepiness, quality of life and blood pressure.
pearls: After a stroke or TIA, ask about snoring and sleepiness, because OSA is common and treatable.
Benzodiazepines can worsen apnoea; do not use them to treat the irritability or confusion of untreated OSA.
CPAP adherence is usually judged as at least 4 hours a night on 70% of nights.
det.thd: OSA เกิดจากทางเดินหายใจส่วนบนยุบตัวซ้ำ ๆ ขณะหลับ ทำให้ออกซิเจนต่ำและตื่นบ่อย ผู้ป่วยกรนดัง มีคนเห็นหยุดหายใจ ง่วงกลางวัน และเสี่ยงความดันสูง AF และ stroke การวินิจฉัยใช้ home sleep test หรือ PSG ดูค่า AHI การรักษาหลักคือ CPAP ร่วมกับลดน้ำหนัก (เช่น tirzepatide) ทางเลือกอื่นคือ oral appliance และ hypoglossal nerve stimulation

qx.stem: A 50-year-old woman from Bangkok with moderate OSA (AHI 28) could not tolerate CPAP despite trials of three masks and humidification. Her BMI is 29. Drug-induced sleep endoscopy shows anteroposterior collapse at the palate without complete concentric collapse.
qx.q: Which treatment is the most appropriate next option?
opts: Hypoglossal nerve stimulation
Nightly zolpidem to improve CPAP tolerance
Supplemental oxygen alone
Mirtazapine at bedtime
Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty as first choice regardless of anatomy
qx.why: Hypoglossal nerve stimulation is indicated for CPAP-intolerant adults with moderate to severe OSA, acceptable BMI and no complete concentric collapse on endoscopy. Oxygen alone does not treat the obstruction, mirtazapine does not improve OSA and can cause weight gain, and sedatives may worsen apnoea. A mandibular advancement device would also be a reasonable alternative.

qx.stem: A 40-year-old taxi driver from Samut Prakan with focal impaired-awareness seizures has had breakthrough events despite two appropriate antiseizure medications at adequate doses. He snores loudly, has morning headaches, a BMI of 34 and an Epworth score of 15. Seizures cluster after nights of poor sleep.
qx.q: What should be done next?
opts: Sleep study, and treat sleep apnoea if present
Add a third antiseizure medication immediately
Refer immediately for vagus nerve stimulation
Increase both drugs to maximum doses
Repeat the MRI under general anaesthesia
qx.why: Untreated obstructive sleep apnoea fragments sleep and can worsen seizure control, and treating it (for example with CPAP) can reduce seizure frequency in drug-resistant epilepsy. Sleepiness also raises driving risk. Escalation of drugs or neurostimulation is premature before addressing this reversible contributor.

name: Obturator neuropathy
formal: Injury to the obturator nerve (L2-4) from pelvic surgery, hernia, labour or tumour, causing weak hip adduction and sensory loss over the medial thigh.
simple: Damage to a nerve in the pelvis causing weakness pulling the leg inward and numbness on the inner thigh.
th: เส้นประสาท obturator (L2–4) บาดเจ็บ ทำให้หุบสะโพกอ่อนแรงและชาด้านในต้นขา
tempoNote: Acute after pelvic surgery or labour; gradual with tumour or entrapment
feat: Weak hip adduction causing a wide-based, circumducting gait
Numbness or pain over a palm-sized area of the medial thigh
Groin or medial thigh pain worse with hip extension in entrapment (athletes)

case.exam: Weak left hip adduction, numb patch on the medial thigh, normal knee jerk and quadriceps strength.
case.tests: EMG at 3 weeks: fibrillations in left adductor longus only; pelvic CT shows no haematoma.
case.q: Which nerve is injured and what is the outlook?

3. Common Mononeuropathies of the Lower Extremities

det.patho: The obturator nerve arises from L2–L4 within psoas, runs along the pelvic side wall and exits through the obturator canal to supply the adductors and medial thigh skin. Its course near pelvic lymph nodes and the ovary makes it vulnerable to surgical stretch, cautery, ligation or compression by masses. Entrapment by fascia at the canal occurs in athletes.
det.clinical: Isolated obturator neuropathy is uncommon. It presents with medial thigh numbness or pain and weak adduction that makes the leg swing outwards. In athletes, exercise-related medial thigh pain dominates. Bilateral lesions may follow difficult labour.
det.diagnosis: Examination confirms adductor weakness with preserved quadriceps and knee jerk. EMG localises the lesion and assesses axonal loss after about three weeks. Imaging is needed when no surgical or obstetric cause is evident, to exclude tumour, haematoma, endometriosis or hernia.
det.treatment: Most cases are managed conservatively with physiotherapy and gait training. Surgical exploration or repair is considered for transection recognised at operation, failed recovery or compressive lesions. Neurolysis can help chronic entrapment in athletes.
det.prognosis: Stretch and compression injuries usually recover over months; transection without repair carries a poorer outlook.
pearls: Medial thigh numbness plus weak adduction with a normal knee jerk points to the obturator nerve.
Pelvic node dissection is a classic setting.
Image the pelvis if there is no obvious surgical cause.
det.thd: Obturator neuropathy คือการบาดเจ็บของเส้นประสาท obturator (L2–4) มักเกิดหลังผ่าตัดในอุ้งเชิงกราน การคลอด หรือจากก้อนในอุ้งเชิงกราน ผู้ป่วยหุบสะโพกไม่มีแรง เดินขาแกว่งออกด้านข้าง และชาด้านในต้นขา โดยที่ knee jerk และ quadriceps ปกติ วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจร่างกาย EMG และภาพถ่ายอุ้งเชิงกราน ส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นด้วยกายภาพบำบัด

name: Occupational cramp
formal: Task-specific focal dystonia such as writer's cramp or musician's dystonia, with abnormal posturing triggered by a repetitive skilled movement; linked to impaired sensorimotor plasticity.
simple: Cramping or twisting of the hand or arm that occurs only during a repeated skilled task such as writing or playing an instrument.
th: focal dystonia ที่เกิดเฉพาะเวลาทำงานที่ใช้ทักษะซ้ำ ๆ เช่น เขียนหนังสือ เล่นดนตรี หรือพิมพ์ดีด ทำให้มือหรือนิ้วบิดเกร็งผิดท่า
tempoNote: Gradual onset over months in adult life; often static after the first few years
feat: Abnormal posture or loss of control of the hand only during one practised task (writing, playing an instrument, typing, golf putting)
Other actions with the same hand are normal at first; may spread to other tasks later
Excess co-contraction, wrist flexion, finger curling or extension, sometimes with dystonic tremor
Sensory tricks (changing pen grip, touching the hand) may help; pain is mild or absent
Neurological examination otherwise normal
inv: Clinical diagnosis by watching the patient perform the triggering task
Nerve conduction studies if numbness or wasting suggests ulnar or median entrapment
MRI or genetic tests only for atypical features (young onset with spread, other neurological signs)

case.who: 29-year-old female ranat (Thai xylophone) player from a music college in Bangkok
case.story: Over a year her right middle and ring fingers curl involuntarily only when playing fast passages; writing and eating are normal.
case.exam: Normal tone, power, reflexes and sensation; when playing, the fingers flex and the wrist deviates, easing when she holds the mallet differently.
case.tests: Nerve conduction studies normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the usual treatment?
case.a: Task-specific (musician’s) focal dystonia; EMG-guided botulinum toxin to the overactive forearm muscles plus specialised retraining.

read.where: 11 - Dystonia: Phenomenology, classification, etiology, pathology, biochemistry, and genetics

det.patho: Task-specific dystonia arises from maladaptive plasticity in sensorimotor networks after intense repetitive practice. Studies show reduced surround inhibition, abnormal sensory discrimination and blurred cortical hand maps. Genetic susceptibility contributes in some families, and high training load is a recognised risk factor in musicians.
det.clinical: Most patients first notice it between their twenties and forties. The first sign is often subtle loss of fine control, slowing or fatigue during the task, before a clear abnormal posture appears. Writer’s cramp may be simple (writing only) or progress to affect other tasks. Musicians’ dystonia is specific to the instrument and even to particular passages, and embouchure dystonia affects brass and wind players. Spread beyond the hand is uncommon.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical and depends on observing the task, as the examination at rest is normal. Look for mirror dystonia in the affected hand while the other hand performs the task. Exclude peripheral nerve lesions, joint disease and parkinsonism. Atypical features such as very young onset, spread or other signs should prompt imaging and genetic testing.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin injections into selected forearm or hand muscles, guided by EMG or ultrasound, are the most effective treatment, though benefit varies and weakness is a common side effect. Oral anticholinergics such as trihexyphenidyl help a minority. Retraining, ergonomic changes (thick pen, altered grip) and specialised musician rehabilitation are useful. Deep brain stimulation or thalamotomy is reserved for refractory severe cases in expert centres.
det.prognosis: Usually persistent; many writers adapt by switching hands, and only a proportion of professional musicians return to full performance.
pearls: Watch the task: the hand is normal at rest.
Mirror dystonia helps choose muscles for botulinum toxin.
Spread to the other hand occurs in some writers who switch hands.
det.thd: Occupational cramp คือ focal dystonia ที่เกิดเฉพาะขณะทำงานที่ฝึกซ้ำบ่อย ๆ เช่น เขียนหนังสือหรือเล่นดนตรี เกิดจากสมองส่วนควบคุมการเคลื่อนไหวและรับความรู้สึกปรับตัวผิดปกติ ตรวจร่างกายตอนพักจะปกติ ต้องดูขณะทำงานนั้นจึงเห็นนิ้วหรือข้อมือบิดเกร็ง การรักษาหลักคือฉีด botulinum toxin ร่วมกับฝึกและปรับอุปกรณ์
