name: Ocular ischaemic syndrome
formal: Chronic hypoperfusion of the eye from severe ipsilateral carotid stenosis or occlusion, causing visual loss, orbital pain, venous stasis retinopathy and neovascularisation.
simple: Reduced blood flow to the eye from a badly narrowed neck artery, causing vision loss and eye pain.
th: ตาขาดเลือดเรื้อรังจากหลอดเลือด carotid ข้างเดียวกันตีบมากหรืออุดตัน ทำให้ตามัวลง ปวดรอบตา หลอดเลือดดำจอตาขยาย และมีเส้นเลือดงอกใหม่ที่ม่านตา
tempoNote: Gradual loss over weeks to months; transient obscurations or sudden loss can occur
feat: Older patient with atherosclerotic risk factors and usually unilateral gradual visual loss (unilateral in about 80%)
Dull ache around the eye or brow, which may ease when lying down; amaurosis fugax and slow recovery after bright light
Fundus: dilated veins, narrowed arterioles, deep blot-type and flame-shaped retinal bleeds, soft exudates (cotton wool spots), occasionally disc swelling, retinal arterial pulsation
Anterior segment: episcleral injection, flare with few cells, iris atrophy and rubeosis; neovascular glaucoma, with intraocular pressure often normal or low because the ciliary body is underperfused
Caused by a stenosis of more than 90% or occlusion of the ipsilateral carotid; five-year mortality about 40%, mostly cardiac
inv: Carotid duplex, CT or MR angiography, or catheter angiography; echocardiography and ECG for associated heart disease
Fluorescein angiography: the choroid fills late and the dye takes longer to pass from artery to vein, with late leakage
Slit lamp with gonioscopy, intraocular pressure, dilated fundus examination; ESR and CRP for giant cell arteritis; lipids, glucose, renal function

case.who: 68-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension and type 2 diabetes, Lampang
case.story: A few months of progressive blur in the left eye with an ache above it. Vision is hazy in sunlight and takes a long time to recover. A previous retina clinic diagnosed diabetic retinopathy, but laser has not helped.
case.exam: Left acuity counting fingers, mid-dilated sluggish pupil, new iris vessels, dilated retinal veins with blot haemorrhages mainly in the mid-periphery, easily induced central retinal artery pulsation on gentle pressure.
case.tests: Carotid duplex shows that the left internal carotid artery is occluded; fluorescein angiography shows delayed choroidal filling; the right eye has only mild diabetic changes.
case.q: Why does the retinopathy look worse on the left, and is endarterectomy possible?
case.a: Chronic hypoperfusion on the side of the carotid occlusion aggravates retinal ischaemia and drives neovascularisation. Endarterectomy is not possible for a totally occluded carotid; treat the eye, optimise medical therapy, and discuss bypass options only in selected cases.

read.where: Chapter 13: Retinal vascular disease — Ocular ischaemic syndrome
Chapter 22 Neuro-Ophthalmology — Chronic Ocular Ischaemic Syndromes

det.patho: A stenosis exceeding 90% (or occlusion) of the ipsilateral internal or common carotid artery lowers perfusion pressure to the ophthalmic artery and its branches, so both the retinal and uveal circulations become ischaemic. Retinal hypoxia leads to the release of angiogenic factors and proliferative retinopathy, and the iris develops new vessels that close the angle. Under-perfusion of the ciliary body reduces aqueous production, which can keep pressure normal despite neovascular glaucoma.
det.clinical: Patients are typically older men with diabetes, hypertension and coronary disease. Symptoms include gradual visual decline, eye or brow ache, persistent after-images, a slow return of vision after bright light and amaurosis fugax. The signs range from subtle venous dilatation to dense haemorrhage and neovascular glaucoma. Because it mirrors diffuse vascular disease, patients are at high risk of stroke and cardiac events, and OIS may be the first sign of severe carotid disease.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis combines the picture of chronic ocular ischaemia with demonstration of high-grade carotid disease. Fluorescein angiography shows delayed choroidal filling and slow vessel transit; duplex ultrasound, CT angiography or MR angiography quantify the carotid. Look for retinal artery pulsation and compare the eyes. Differentiate from diabetic retinopathy, central retinal vein occlusion and hypertensive retinopathy, which are usually bilateral, and exclude giant cell arteritis.
det.treatment: Treat inflammation with topical steroid, control neovascular glaucoma medically or surgically, and treat proliferative disease with panretinal photocoagulation or intravitreal anti-VEGF. Carotid endarterectomy or stenting lowers stroke risk and may help neovascularisation if done early, whereas extracranial–intracranial bypass is sometimes considered when the carotid is totally occluded. Rises in pressure after revascularisation are a recognised risk. Lifelong antiplatelet and statin therapy, blood pressure and diabetes control, and smoking cessation are mandatory.
det.prognosis: Visual prognosis is generally poor, better in those with better acuity at presentation. Overall survival is limited by cardiovascular disease.
pearls: Unilateral diabetic-looking retinopathy with pain should raise suspicion of ipsilateral carotid disease.
Low or normal intraocular pressure does not rule out neovascular glaucoma in this condition.
Treat the eye and the vessel; the patient’s survival depends on the vessel.
det.thd: ภาวะตาขาดเลือดเรื้อรัง (OIS) เกิดจาก carotid ข้างเดียวกันตีบมากหรืออุดตัน พบในผู้สูงอายุที่มีเบาหวาน ความดันสูง และโรคหัวใจ ผู้ป่วยตามัวช้า ๆ ปวดบริเวณตาหรือคิ้ว และมองไม่เห็นนานเมื่อโดนแสงจ้า ตรวจพบหลอดเลือดดำจอตาขยาย เลือดออกเป็นจุด และเส้นเลือดงอกที่ม่านตา ความดันตาอาจไม่สูง ตรวจยืนยันด้วย fluorescein angiography และ carotid imaging การรักษาคือ laser หรือ anti-VEGF รักษาต้อหินจากหลอดเลือดงอก และพิจารณาผ่าตัดหรือใส่ขดลวด carotid ร่วมกับควบคุมปัจจัยเสี่ยง

name: Ocular myasthenia
formal: Myasthenia gravis limited to ptosis and diplopia, often AChR antibody positive, with possible generalization within two years.
simple: A form of myasthenia affecting only eye muscles, causing droopy eyelids and double vision.
more: Diagnosed by ice-pack test, antibodies and single-fibre EMG; treat with pyridostigmine or low-dose prednisolone.
th: myasthenia gravis ที่จำกัดอยู่เฉพาะกล้ามเนื้อตาและหนังตา ทำให้หนังตาตกและเห็นภาพซ้อนที่เป็นมากขึ้นตอนเย็น บางรายลุกลามเป็นชนิดทั่วร่างกายภายใน 2 ปี
tempoNote: Symptoms fluctuate through the day and worsen with fatigue; most generalisation happens within the first two years
feat: Drooping eyelid that varies in degree, often swapping sides, and worse late in the day
Double vision that does not fit a single nerve palsy; pupils always spared
Fatigable ptosis on sustained upgaze and Cogan lid-twitch sign
Orbicularis oculi weakness (cannot bury eyelashes) may accompany it
No limb, bulbar or breathing weakness at least two years from onset
inv: Ice-pack test: ptosis improves ≥2 mm after 2 minutes of cooling
AChR antibodies (positive in only about half of purely ocular cases); MuSK and LRP4 if negative
Single-fibre EMG of a facial muscle (most sensitive); repetitive stimulation often normal
CT or MRI chest for thymoma; thyroid function, as thyroid eye disease can coexist

case.who: 52-year-old man, rubber farmer from Surat Thani
case.story: For six weeks his right eyelid droops in the afternoon and he sees double while riding his motorbike; it is better on waking.
case.exam: Right ptosis that deepens after one minute of upgaze, variable left eye adduction weakness, normal pupils; limbs, speech and swallowing normal.
case.tests: Ice pack lifts the eyelid by 3 mm; AChR antibody positive; repetitive stimulation of limb nerves normal; CT chest no thymoma.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what should you warn him about?
case.a: Ocular myasthenia; he has a meaningful risk of generalised weakness in the next two years, so report trouble swallowing, speaking or breathing promptly.

det.patho: Antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor (or less often MuSK or LRP4) reduce the safety margin of neuromuscular transmission. Extraocular muscles are especially vulnerable because their motor units fire at high rates, have fewer junctional folds and express a different receptor isoform, so weakness shows there first. Roughly half of all myasthenia starts in the eyes and a substantial minority of these patients generalise, mostly within two years.
det.clinical: Ptosis and diplopia that fluctuate, worsen with use or bright light and improve with rest are the core picture. Any eye muscle pattern can be mimicked, including pseudo-internuclear ophthalmoplegia, but the pupil is never affected. Patients may tilt the head back or raise the brows to compensate. Ask carefully about subtle bulbar, neck or limb symptoms, as these redefine the case as generalised myasthenia.
det.diagnosis: Bedside clues include fatigable ptosis, Cogan lid twitch, enhanced ptosis when the other lid is lifted, and the ice-pack test. AChR antibody sensitivity is much lower than in generalised disease, so a negative result does not exclude it; single-fibre EMG of frontalis or orbicularis oculi is the most sensitive test. Brain and orbit imaging is advisable when signs are atypical. Look for thymoma and autoimmune thyroid disease.
det.treatment: Pyridostigmine improves ptosis more reliably than diplopia. Low-dose prednisolone, increased slowly to limit early worsening, often controls diplopia and may reduce generalisation; steroid-sparing agents such as azathioprine are added for long-term use. Prisms, occlusion or lid crutches help symptoms. Thymectomy is needed for thymoma; its role in non-thymomatous ocular MG is less established. Avoid drugs that impair the junction, such as aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones and magnesium.
det.prognosis: Most patients stay purely ocular if no spread occurs in the first two years, and many achieve good control with low-dose therapy.
pearls: Painless, pupil-sparing, variable diplopia with ptosis: test for myasthenia before imaging for aneurysm only if the pupil is normal.
Seronegative ocular MG is common; single-fibre EMG is the best confirmatory test.
Warn patients about generalisation and myasthenic crisis triggers.

Slow, symmetric, non-fluctuating ophthalmoplegia; patients seldom complain of diplopia

name: Oculomotor (IIIrd) nerve palsy
formal: Ptosis, ophthalmoplegia with eye down and out, and mydriasis from lesion of the third nerve; pupil-involving cases suggest compressive causes such as posterior communicating aneurysm, pupil-sparing suggests diabetic ischaemia.
simple: Damage to the third eye nerve causing a drooping eyelid, an eye turned down and outward, and often a large pupil.
th: อัมพาตเส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 3 ทำให้หนังตาตก ตามองลงและออกนอก และรูม่านตาขยาย หากรูม่านตาเกี่ยวข้องต้องรีบหา aneurysm ของ posterior communicating artery
tempoNote: Microvascular and aneurysmal palsies develop over hours to days; slowly progressive palsy over months suggests a tumour or other compressive lesion
feat: Ptosis with the eye resting down and out; diplopia (vertical and horizontal) when the lid is lifted
Weak adduction, elevation and depression; abduction and intorsion on down-gaze (IV) preserved
Dilated, poorly reactive pupil in compressive lesions; spared pupil typical of diabetic/hypertensive ischaemia
Headache or pain around the eye can occur with both aneurysm and microvascular causes
Accompanying signs localise: contralateral hemiparesis or tremor (midbrain), IV/V/VI involvement (cavernous sinus/orbital apex)
inv: Urgent CTA or MRA (or catheter angiography) for any pupil-involving or incomplete palsy, or patients under 50
MRI brain with contrast including cavernous sinus and orbits
Glucose/HbA1c, BP, lipids, ESR/CRP in older patients (GCA can cause it)
Consider ice-pack test/AChR antibodies if the pupil is spared and signs fluctuate

case.who: 52-year-old woman, market vendor from Suphan Buri
case.story: Two days of severe right frontal headache, then her right eyelid drooped and she saw double when she lifted it.
case.exam: Complete right ptosis; right eye down and out; cannot adduct, elevate or depress; right pupil 7 mm and unreactive; no other deficits; neck supple.
case.tests: CT brain no subarachnoid blood; CTA shows a 7 mm right posterior communicating artery aneurysm.
case.q: Why is the pupil important here and what is the next step?
case.a: Pupillomotor fibres run superficially and are compressed early by an aneurysm; urgent neurosurgical/endovascular treatment is needed before it ruptures.

read.where: Chapter 8 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System

det.patho: The oculomotor nerve leaves the midbrain, crosses the subarachnoid space next to the posterior communicating artery, then travels within the cavernous sinus wall before dividing into superior (levator, superior rectus) and inferior (medial and inferior recti, inferior oblique, pupil) branches. Pupillary fibres lie superficially and receive good collateral blood supply, so compression affects them early while ischaemia of the nerve's core tends to spare them. Common causes in adults are microvascular ischaemia, aneurysm, trauma, tumour and uncal herniation.
det.clinical: A complete palsy produces ptosis that may hide the diplopia, with the eye abducted and depressed. Microvascular palsies are often painful at onset, spare the pupil and recover within three months. Aneurysmal palsies usually involve the pupil and may precede rupture. Midbrain lesions give additional signs (Weber, Benedikt syndromes) and can cause bilateral ptosis because the levator subnucleus is single. Aberrant regeneration (lid elevation on adduction or down-gaze) implies a chronic compressive or traumatic cause, never a microvascular one.
det.diagnosis: Any pupil-involving, partial or painful third nerve palsy in a non-diabetic or younger patient needs emergency vascular imaging; CTA detects most aneurysms of 3 mm or more. A complete, pupil-sparing palsy in an older vascular patient may be observed, but many centres now image all cases with MRI and MRA. Check for GCA in the elderly and for myasthenia when signs fluctuate. Failure to improve by three months or new aberrant regeneration mandates imaging.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: coiling or clipping for aneurysm, tumour management, vascular risk control for microvascular palsy. Diplopia can be relieved with occlusion (patch or frosted lens) or prisms; occlusion is not needed while ptosis covers the eye. Strabismus or lid surgery is considered after at least 6 months of stability.
det.prognosis: Microvascular palsies usually resolve fully within 3–4 months; recovery after aneurysm treatment is common but may be incomplete with aberrant regeneration.
pearls: Painful pupil-involving III palsy = PComm aneurysm until proved otherwise.
Aberrant regeneration never follows a microvascular palsy.
Bilateral ptosis with a unilateral III palsy points to the midbrain nucleus.
A blown pupil in a drowsy patient is uncal herniation, a neurosurgical emergency.
det.thd: อัมพาตเส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 3 ทำให้หนังตาตก ตาเหล่ลงและออกด้านนอก มองเห็นภาพซ้อน และอาจมีรูม่านตาขยาย ถ้ารูม่านตาขยายมักเกิดจากการกดเบียด เช่น aneurysm ของ posterior communicating artery ต้องทำ CTA ด่วน ส่วนชนิดที่รูม่านตาปกติในผู้ป่วยเบาหวานหรือความดันสูงมักเกิดจากหลอดเลือดเล็กขาดเลือด และหายเองใน 3 เดือน รักษาตามสาเหตุและปิดตาหรือใช้ปริซึมแก้ภาพซ้อน

name: Oculomotor apraxia
formal: Impaired voluntary initiation of horizontal saccades with preserved reflex eye movements, compensated by head thrusts; congenital or associated with ataxia-telangiectasia and bilateral cortical lesions.
simple: Difficulty starting voluntary sideways eye movements, so the person turns the head to look at things.
more: Deficit of voluntary horizontal saccade initiation with intact reflexive eye movements, congenital or associated with ataxia-telangiectasia and bilateral cerebral lesions; head thrusts are typical. Impaired voluntary initiation of horizontal saccades with preserved reflex movements, compensated by head thrusts; congenital (Cogan) or acquired from bilateral frontoparietal lesions.
th: ความบกพร่องในการเริ่มกลอกตาแบบ saccade ในแนวนอนโดยสมัครใจ แต่ reflex ยังดี ผู้ป่วยชดเชยด้วยการสะบัดศีรษะ พบแต่กำเนิดหรือร่วมกับโรคสมอง
tempoNote: Congenital form noticed in infancy and improves with age; acquired forms follow the underlying disease
feat: Difficulty initiating voluntary horizontal saccades; vertical often spared in congenital form
Head thrusts that overshoot, with blinks, to drag the eyes to a new target
Reflex and random eye movements preserved
Infants may appear blind in the first months
Associated with Joubert syndrome, ataxia telangiectasia, AOA1/AOA2, Gaucher type 3 and others
inv: Observation: head thrusts during target change; doll's head and OKN testing
MRI brain (molar tooth sign in Joubert; cerebellar hypoplasia/atrophy)
AFP (raised in AT and AOA2), albumin and cholesterol (AOA1), immunoglobulins
Gene panel for ataxia syndromes and ciliopathies

case.who: 8-month-old boy at a children's hospital in Bangkok
case.story: Parents thought he was blind at 3 months; now he jerks his head sideways to look at toys.
case.exam: Head thrusts with blinks when shifting gaze horizontally, full movements with doll's head manoeuvre, mild truncal hypotonia.
case.tests: MRI shows molar tooth sign; genetic testing identifies biallelic CEP290 variants.
case.q: What is the eye movement disorder and which syndrome underlies it?
case.a: Congenital oculomotor apraxia as part of Joubert syndrome.

det.patho: Voluntary saccades depend on frontal and parietal eye fields projecting via the superior colliculus to brainstem burst generators, with cerebellar refinement. Congenital forms often reflect cerebellar vermis or brainstem malformation; acquired forms arise from bilateral frontoparietal lesions or degenerative disease. Reflexive saccades and vestibulo-ocular movements are spared, as they use different pathways.
det.clinical: Infants may seem visually inattentive, then develop characteristic head thrusts. The congenital idiopathic form (Cogan) typically improves through childhood. Oculomotor apraxia is a hallmark of several recessive ataxias and ciliopathies and appears in neurodegenerative conditions such as Gaucher disease type 3 and Niemann–Pick type C (where vertical saccades are affected).
det.diagnosis: Clinical observation is key. MRI and targeted tests define associated disorders. In older children with progressive ataxia, check AFP, albumin, cholesterol and immunoglobulins, and perform gene testing.
det.treatment: No specific treatment; the congenital form improves with age. Visual and developmental support is important. Treat or monitor the associated condition (e.g. renal and hepatic surveillance in Joubert, cancer surveillance in AT).
det.prognosis: Congenital idiopathic forms improve; outcome otherwise depends on the underlying disease.
pearls: Head thrusts to change gaze in an infant: oculomotor apraxia, not blindness.
Check AFP in a child with ataxia and oculomotor apraxia.
Molar tooth sign on MRI points to Joubert syndrome.
det.thd: Oculomotor apraxia คือการเริ่มกลอกตาตามสั่งในแนวนอนทำไม่ได้ แต่ reflex ยังปกติ เด็กจะสะบัดศีรษะพร้อมกระพริบตาเพื่อมองสิ่งใหม่ ในช่วงแรกอาจดูเหมือนตาบอด แบบแต่กำเนิดมักดีขึ้นเมื่อโต แต่อาจเป็นอาการของ Joubert syndrome, ataxia telangiectasia, AOA และ Gaucher ควรทำ MRI ตรวจ AFP และตรวจยีน

name: Oculopalatal tremor
formal: Pendular vertical ocular oscillations with synchronous palatal tremor following brainstem or cerebellar lesion, with hypertrophic olivary degeneration within the Guillain-Mollaret triangle.
simple: Rhythmic eye wobbling together with a rhythmic movement of the soft palate, usually after a stroke in the brainstem.
ab: Symptomatic palatal tremor with pendular nystagmus
th: การสั่นของเพดานอ่อนร่วมกับลูกตาแกว่งแนวตั้งในจังหวะเดียวกัน ที่เกิดตามหลังรอยโรคก้านสมองหรือ cerebellum จาก hypertrophic olivary degeneration
tempoNote: Appears weeks to months after a brainstem or cerebellar insult and usually persists
feat: Rhythmic soft palate movement at about 1–3 Hz, usually without ear click
Pendular nystagmus, often vertical or oblique, synchronised with the palate; oscillopsia
Develops several months after a pontine or midbrain haemorrhage, infarct, trauma or demyelination
Persists in sleep; associated ataxia and signs of the original lesion
inv: MRI: enlarged T2-bright inferior olive (hypertrophic olivary degeneration) and the original lesion in the dentato-rubro-olivary pathway
Video oculography to document the pendular nystagmus

case.who: 56-year-old man from Khon Kaen, 8 months after pontine haemorrhage
case.story: Recovered walking with a stick, but now complains that the world jumps up and down, worse when reading.
case.exam: Vertical pendular nystagmus at about 2 Hz, rhythmic soft palate elevation in the same rhythm, left limb ataxia.
case.tests: MRI shows old pontine haemosiderin and an enlarged hyperintense right inferior olive.
case.q: What has developed and why now?
case.a: Oculopalatal tremor from hypertrophic olivary degeneration, which typically appears months after a lesion of the Guillain-Mollaret triangle.

read.where: 2.5 Clinical Presentation of HOD (ocular myoclonus and nystagmus)

det.patho: A lesion interrupting the dentato-rubro-olivary pathway deafferents the inferior olive, which then enlarges and develops abnormal electrical coupling between neurons. The olive generates a slow rhythmic output that drives the palate and, via cerebellar connections, the eyes. MRI changes of the olive appear after about a month, peak at several months and may fade over years while the tremor continues.
det.clinical: Patients usually have a known pontine, midbrain or cerebellar lesion, most often haemorrhage, and develop the oscillation after a delay of weeks to months. The visual complaint of oscillopsia is the main disability; the palatal movement itself is rarely noticed. The nystagmus may be dissociated between the eyes. Ataxia, gaze palsy and other signs of the original lesion are common.
det.diagnosis: Look in the mouth for rhythmic palatal elevation when a patient has pendular nystagmus after a brainstem stroke. MRI showing an enlarged T2-hyperintense olive confirms the mechanism. Exclude progressive ataxia syndromes when no causal lesion is present.
det.treatment: Treatment targets oscillopsia. Gabapentin and memantine have the best evidence for reducing pendular nystagmus; clonazepam or other agents help some patients. Botulinum toxin and prisms are occasionally used. The palatal component rarely needs treatment.
det.prognosis: Usually persistent; drug therapy reduces but seldom abolishes the oscillation.
pearls: Pendular nystagmus after a pontine bleed: open the mouth and look at the palate.
The delay of months between lesion and tremor is characteristic.
Gabapentin or memantine are first choices for the eye oscillation.
det.thd: Oculopalatal tremor เกิดหลังรอยโรคที่ก้านสมองหรือ cerebellum ซึ่งตัดวงจร dentato-rubro-olivary ทำให้ inferior olive โตและปล่อยสัญญาณเป็นจังหวะ ผู้ป่วยมีเพดานอ่อนสั่นและลูกตาแกว่งแนวตั้งจังหวะเดียวกัน มักเริ่มหลายเดือนหลังเลือดออกในก้านสมอง อาการเด่นคือเห็นภาพสั่น MRI พบ olive โตและสัญญาณสูง รักษาด้วย gabapentin หรือ memantine เพื่อลดภาพสั่น

name: Oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy
formal: Late-onset autosomal dominant muscular dystrophy with ptosis, dysphagia and proximal limb weakness due to GCG repeat expansion in PABPN1; common in French Canadian families.
simple: An inherited muscle disease causing drooping eyelids and swallowing difficulty from midlife.
more: Diagnosed with GCG trinucleotide expansion (more than 10 repeats) in PABPN1; biopsy shows intranuclear filamentous inclusions and rimmed vacuoles. Treatment is cricopharyngeal myotomy for dysphagia and ptosis surgery; disease progresses slowly. Late-onset autosomal dominant muscular dystrophy with ptosis, dysphagia and limb weakness caused by GCG repeat expansion in PABPN1, with intranuclear inclusions. Late-onset autosomal dominant muscular dystrophy due to GCN expansions in PABPN1, with ptosis, dysphagia and proximal limb weakness, and intranuclear inclusions. Diagnosed by PABPN1 repeat testing. Treatment is eyelid surgery, cricopharyngeal myotomy for swallowing and supportive care; more common in French-Canadian and Bukhara Jewish populations.

feat: Onset after 40–50: slowly progressive bilateral ptosis and dysphagia
Later proximal limb weakness; ophthalmoparesis mild, diplopia rare
Autosomal dominant; patients tilt the head back to see
inv: PABPN1 GCN repeat expansion
CK normal or mildly raised; swallow assessment

case.story: Eyelids have drooped over 10 years; now chokes on solid food. His mother had the same.
case.exam: Bilateral ptosis with frontalis overactivity, mild upgaze limitation, mild hip weakness.
case.tests: PABPN1 expansion; no fatigability on sustained upgaze.
case.q: What helps the dysphagia?
case.a: Cricopharyngeal myotomy or dilatation after swallow assessment; ptosis surgery for the eyelids.

ddx.pt: Fatigable and fluctuating, antibody positive
Marked ophthalmoplegia, mitochondrial DNA changes, ragged-red fibres

det.patho: OPMD is usually autosomal dominant and caused by a short expansion of the GCN trinucleotide repeat in PABPN1, lengthening a polyalanine tract. The mutant protein forms intranuclear filamentous inclusions in muscle fibres and impairs RNA processing. Founder populations include French-Canadians and Bukhara Jews, but it occurs worldwide.
det.clinical: Bilateral ptosis and dysphagia begin after age 40–50 and progress slowly over years. Patients compensate by tilting the head back and contracting the frontalis. Mild ophthalmoparesis, tongue weakness, dysphonia and proximal limb weakness appear later; diplopia is uncommon. Aspiration pneumonia, weight loss and social isolation are the major complications.
det.diagnosis: Genetic testing for the PABPN1 repeat expansion confirms the diagnosis. CK is normal or mildly elevated, and muscle biopsy (rarely needed) shows rimmed vacuoles and intranuclear inclusions. Videofluoroscopy assesses swallowing safety. Distinguish from myasthenia gravis (fluctuation, antibodies), mitochondrial CPEO (marked ophthalmoplegia) and myotonic dystrophy.
det.treatment: Ptosis is managed with levator resection or frontalis sling surgery when vision is obscured. Dysphagia may improve with cricopharyngeal myotomy, dilatation or botulinum toxin, along with diet modification and speech therapy; gastrostomy is used in advanced disease. Physiotherapy addresses limb weakness. Genetic counselling is offered to families.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is usually close to normal, but severe dysphagia and aspiration can shorten survival if not managed.
pearls: Late-onset ptosis + dysphagia + family history = OPMD; check the PABPN1 repeat.
Lack of fatigability helps separate OPMD from ocular-bulbar myasthenia.
det.thd: OPMD เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมทางพันธุกรรมแบบยีนเด่น จากการขยายตัวของ repeat ในยีน PABPN1 มักเริ่มหลังอายุ 40–50 ปี ด้วยหนังตาตกสองข้างและกลืนลำบากที่ค่อยๆ เป็นมากขึ้น ผู้ป่วยมักเงยหน้าเพื่อมอง ต่อมาอาจมีต้นแขนต้นขาอ่อนแรง การวินิจฉัยใช้การตรวจยีน และต้องแยกจาก myasthenia gravis ที่อาการเปลี่ยนแปลงตามความล้า การรักษาคือผ่าตัดแก้หนังตาตก และผ่าตัดหรือขยายหูรูดหลอดอาหารเพื่อช่วยการกลืน

name: Off period dyskinesias
formal: Dystonic or choreic movements during the low levodopa state in Parkinson disease, often painful foot dystonia in early morning; related to fluctuating dopaminergic stimulation.
simple: Twisting or painful muscle spasms that occur in Parkinson disease when the medicine has worn off.
th: การเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติแบบ dystonia หรือ chorea ที่เกิดช่วงระดับ levodopa ต่ำในผู้ป่วยพาร์กินสัน มักเป็นเท้าบิดเกร็งเจ็บตอนเช้า
tempoNote: Recurs daily with the dose cycle in advanced Parkinson disease
feat: Occurs when levodopa effect is lowest: early morning before the first dose or at end-of-dose wearing-off
Mostly painful sustained dystonia (foot inversion, toe curling); occasionally other involuntary movements
Accompanied by other off features: slowness, rigidity, tremor, anxiety
Relieved within 30–60 minutes once the next dose takes effect
Distinct from peak-dose dyskinesia, which appears at highest drug levels
inv: Diary or home video linking movements to timing of doses
Observed levodopa challenge in clinic when timing is unclear

case.who: 63-year-old female teacher from Chiang Mai with Parkinson disease for 9 years
case.story: Wakes at 5 am with the left big toe pointing up and the foot twisting inward, very painful, settling about 40 minutes after her first levodopa tablet.
case.exam: In clinic during on-state: mild bradykinesia, no dyskinesia; video from home shows sustained foot inversion.
case.tests: Symptom diary confirms morning and end-of-dose episodes.
case.q: Which kind of dyskinesia is this and how would you manage it?
case.a: Off-period dystonia; extend dopaminergic cover overnight, e.g. controlled-release levodopa at bedtime, a long-acting agonist, a MAO-B or COMT inhibitor.

det.patho: Off-period dyskinesia reflects inadequate striatal dopamine when plasma levodopa falls, in a basal ganglia circuit already altered by pulsatile stimulation. Loss of presynaptic buffering in advanced disease makes the brain dependent on blood levels. The sustained dystonic form is the most frequent pattern.
det.clinical: Typical patients have had Parkinson disease for several years and other motor fluctuations. The classic picture is painful foot dystonia on waking or as a dose wears off, sometimes involving the leg, hand or neck. Patients may mistake it for cramp. It may also be the first sign of Parkinson disease in young-onset cases before treatment.
det.diagnosis: The key step is relating movements to dose timing using a diary, wearable sensor or home video. Clinic examination at a convenient time can miss it. Separate it from peak-dose and diphasic dyskinesias, because the management is opposite.
det.treatment: Aim for smoother and longer dopaminergic stimulation: shorten dose intervals, add a COMT or MAO-B inhibitor, add a long-acting dopamine agonist, or use bedtime controlled-release levodopa. Dispersible levodopa or apomorphine can rescue a morning attack. Botulinum toxin helps persistent focal foot dystonia. Device-aided therapy (DBS, levodopa intestinal gel, subcutaneous apomorphine or foslevodopa infusion) suits refractory fluctuations.
det.prognosis: Usually controllable with treatment adjustments, but tends to accompany progressive motor fluctuations.
pearls: Ask when the movement occurs: low drug level points to off-period dyskinesia.
Increasing dopaminergic cover improves off dystonia, unlike peak-dose dyskinesia.
Early-morning painful foot inversion in PD is the classic picture.
det.thd: Off period dyskinesia คือการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติที่เกิดช่วงยา levodopa หมดฤทธิ์ในผู้ป่วยพาร์กินสันระยะท้าย ส่วนใหญ่เป็น dystonia ของเท้าที่ปวดตอนตื่นนอนหรือก่อนมื้อยาถัดไป ต้องดูความสัมพันธ์กับเวลากินยาเพื่อแยกจาก peak-dose dyskinesia การรักษาคือเพิ่มความต่อเนื่องของ dopamine เช่น ปรับช่วงยา เพิ่ม COMT/MAO-B inhibitor หรือ agonist ออกฤทธิ์ยาว และพิจารณา DBS ในรายที่ดื้อ

name: Off-dystonia
formal: Painful dystonic posturing, typically of the foot, during wearing-off of levodopa in Parkinson disease or early morning; responds to improved dopaminergic coverage.
simple: Painful cramping or twisting of a foot or leg in Parkinson disease when the medicine wears off, often in the morning.
th: dystonia ที่ปวดและบิดเกร็ง มักเป็นที่เท้า ช่วงยา levodopa หมดฤทธิ์หรือตอนตื่นเช้าในผู้ป่วยพาร์กินสัน ตอบสนองดีเมื่อเพิ่ม dopaminergic
tempoNote: Episodes lasting minutes to an hour, recurring with low-drug periods
feat: Painful cramp-like foot inversion, toe flexion or big-toe extension when dopaminergic effect is low
Classically on waking before the first dose of the day
Usually on the side more affected by Parkinson disease
Can be an early or presenting feature in young-onset or genetic PD (e.g. PRKN)
Settles as the next dose of levodopa starts working
inv: Timing diary or video relating episodes to dose times
Trial of a rescue dose (dispersible levodopa) confirms dopaminergic responsiveness

case.who: 44-year-old male motorcycle taxi driver from Nonthaburi with young-onset PD
case.story: Every morning his right foot turns inward with clawing toes and severe pain, stopping him walking until 30 minutes after his first tablet.
case.exam: Mild right-sided rigidity and bradykinesia during on-state; no peak-dose chorea.
case.tests: Home video shows sustained right foot inversion at 6 am, resolving after dispersible levodopa.
case.q: How would you reduce these morning episodes?
case.a: Off-dystonia: give longer night-time cover (controlled-release levodopa or a long-acting agonist at night) or an early rescue dose; consider botulinum toxin if focal and persistent.

read.where: 10 Parkinson’s Disease: Advanced Disease, Motor Complications, and Management

det.patho: Low striatal dopamine during off periods drives prolonged simultaneous firing of opposing muscle groups, mostly in the lower limb. It is a manifestation of advancing nigrostriatal degeneration and pulsatile levodopa exposure. Young-onset and parkin-related Parkinson disease are especially prone to dystonia.
det.clinical: Patients describe a painful cramp, often mistaken for a musculoskeletal problem, that wakes them or appears as each dose fades. Big-toe dorsiflexion, foot inversion and claw toes are the usual patterns. The episodes can be the most disabling symptom despite modest parkinsonism. Similar dystonia may be the presenting feature before diagnosis in young-onset disease.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is based on the relation to drug timing. A rescue dose that relieves the dystonia supports it. Distinguish from diphasic dystonia and from neuropathic or musculoskeletal foot pain.
det.treatment: Increase continuous dopaminergic cover: bedtime controlled-release levodopa, long-acting dopamine agonists, COMT or MAO-B inhibitors, or a dispersible levodopa dose on waking. Botulinum toxin into tibialis posterior or toe flexors helps fixed focal patterns. Device-aided therapies and DBS are options for severe fluctuations.
det.prognosis: Usually improves with medication adjustment, though fluctuations tend to increase with disease progression.
pearls: Painful early-morning foot dystonia in a PD patient is off-dystonia until proved otherwise.
It may be the first sign of young-onset Parkinson disease.
Fix the dopamine gap rather than reducing levodopa.
det.thd: Off-dystonia คือเท้าหรือนิ้วเท้าบิดเกร็งและปวดในช่วงที่ยาพาร์กินสันหมดฤทธิ์ โดยเฉพาะตอนตื่นเช้า มักเป็นข้างที่โรคเด่นกว่าและพบบ่อยใน young-onset PD วินิจฉัยจากความสัมพันธ์กับเวลากินยา การรักษาคือให้ยาครอบคลุมช่วงกลางคืนและเช้า เช่น levodopa ออกฤทธิ์นานก่อนนอน หรือ agonist และพิจารณา botulinum toxin ถ้าเป็นเฉพาะที่

name: Olanzapine akathisia
formal: Drug-induced restlessness with inner urge to move after olanzapine, due to dopamine receptor blockade; managed by dose reduction, beta-blockers, benzodiazepines or anticholinergics.
simple: Feeling unable to sit still, caused as a side effect of the antipsychotic medicine olanzapine.
th: อาการกระสับกระส่ายต้องขยับตัวตลอดหลังได้ยา olanzapine จากการปิดกั้น dopamine receptor
tempoNote: Usually within days to weeks of starting or increasing the dose
feat: Subjective inner restlessness plus objective movements: rocking, marching on the spot, crossing legs
Dose-related and less frequent with olanzapine than with high-potency first-generation agents, but still clinically important
Easily mistaken for worsening psychosis or agitation, leading to inappropriate dose increases
Distress can be marked and is linked to non-adherence and, rarely, suicidal behaviour
inv: Barnes Akathisia Rating Scale at baseline and after changes
Review other contributing drugs (SSRIs, metoclopramide, other antipsychotics)
Ferritin if restless legs features are present

case.who: 26-year-old female university student from Phitsanulok with schizophrenia
case.story: Olanzapine raised to 20 mg two weeks ago. Ward staff note she is 'more agitated', pacing corridors all day and asking to go home.
case.exam: Rocks from foot to foot when standing, crosses and uncrosses legs when seated; mild cogwheeling at the right wrist; not responding to voices.
case.tests: Barnes scale global score 3 (moderate).
case.q: Should the antipsychotic dose be increased for agitation?
case.a: No — this is drug-induced akathisia; reduce the dose and consider propranolol or low-dose mirtazapine.

read.where: Chapter 9 Movement Disorders — Movement Disorders Associated with Dopamine Receptor Blockade or Dopamine Depletion

det.patho: Blockade of D2 receptors in mesocortical and striatal pathways, combined with relative noradrenergic overactivity and serotonergic influences, is believed to cause akathisia. Olanzapine's 5-HT2A antagonism lowers but does not abolish the risk. Rapid dose escalation and high plasma levels increase likelihood.
det.clinical: Acute akathisia combines an urge to move with semi-purposeful motor behaviour, usually worst when sitting or standing still. Patients may describe it as anxiety, irritability or 'wanting to jump out of my skin'. It may coexist with drug-induced parkinsonism. Chronic and tardive forms follow longer exposure.
det.diagnosis: Ask directly about the inner urge and observe for at least two minutes seated and standing. Use the temporal link to the drug change. Differentiate from psychotic agitation, anxiety, restless legs, and withdrawal states.
det.treatment: First reduce the dose or switch to an antipsychotic with lower akathisia liability (e.g. quetiapine or clozapine). Low-dose propranolol, mirtazapine 15 mg at night and short courses of benzodiazepines have the best supporting evidence. Anticholinergics help mainly if parkinsonism coexists.
det.prognosis: Usually resolves within days to weeks after adjustment; a minority become chronic.
pearls: New agitation after an antipsychotic increase: think akathisia before escalating.
Ask about the inner feeling; observation alone underdiagnoses it.
Propranolol and mirtazapine are first-line symptomatic options.
det.thd: Olanzapine akathisia คืออาการกระวนกระวายต้องขยับตัวตลอดหลังเริ่มหรือเพิ่มยา olanzapine เกิดจากการปิดกั้น dopamine receptor มักถูกเข้าใจผิดว่าเป็นอาการทางจิตกำเริบ การวินิจฉัยใช้การซักถามความรู้สึกภายในและสังเกตการเคลื่อนไหว ร่วมกับ Barnes scale การรักษาคือลดยา เปลี่ยนยา หรือให้ propranolol, mirtazapine หรือ benzodiazepine

name: Olfactory groove meningioma
formal: Slow-growing anterior skull base tumour causing anosmia, frontal lobe behaviour change and Foster Kennedy syndrome; often large at diagnosis.
simple: A slow-growing tumour under the front of the brain that can cause loss of smell and personality change.
th: เนื้องอกเยื่อหุ้มสมองที่ฐานกะโหลกด้านหน้า โตช้า ทำให้ไม่ได้กลิ่น บุคลิกเปลี่ยน และอาจเกิด Foster Kennedy syndrome
tempoNote: Grows over years; often large before symptoms are noticed
feat: Loss of smell, often unnoticed by the patient
Apathy, disinhibition, poor planning or memory change from frontal lobe compression
Visual loss: optic atrophy on one side and papilloedema on the other (Foster Kennedy)
Headache, seizures, urinary incontinence in large tumours
inv: Contrast MRI: midline dural-based enhancing mass over the cribriform plate with dural tail and frontal oedema
CT: hyperostosis or calcification of the skull base
Formal smell testing, visual acuity and fields, neuropsychology

case.story: Her family says she has become careless and indifferent over two years; she admits food tastes bland.
case.exam: Anosmia both sides, frontal release signs, left optic disc pale and right disc swollen.
case.tests: MRI: 6 cm enhancing midline anterior fossa mass with bifrontal oedema.
case.q: Which eponymous syndrome is present, and what is the treatment?
case.a: Foster Kennedy syndrome from an olfactory groove meningioma; surgical resection by an experienced skull-base team.

read.where: Chapter 13 Cranial Nerve Disorders — Other Causes of Olfactory Dysfunction
Skull base syndromes: anatomy, step approach, foramen syndromes

det.patho: Meningiomas arise from arachnoid cap cells; at the olfactory groove they grow from the dura over the cribriform plate and planum, displacing the frontal lobes and olfactory tracts. Most are WHO grade 1. Slow growth allows remarkable adaptation, so tumours often reach several centimetres.
det.clinical: The commonest complaints are behavioural change, headache and visual loss; anosmia is frequent but rarely volunteered. Large tumours can cause seizures, gait problems and incontinence. Foster Kennedy syndrome results from direct optic nerve compression on one side and raised pressure on the other, though it is uncommon.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows a homogeneously enhancing extra-axial midline mass with a dural tail, often with surrounding oedema; CT shows hyperostosis and helps surgical planning. Assessment of vascular encasement (anterior cerebral arteries) and invasion into sinuses guides approach. Biopsy is rarely needed before surgery.
det.treatment: Surgical removal, including involved dura and bone where safe, is the main treatment via bifrontal, unilateral subfrontal or endoscopic endonasal routes. Radiosurgery or fractionated radiotherapy is used for residual or recurrent tumour or in poor surgical candidates. Small asymptomatic tumours in older patients may be observed with serial imaging.
det.prognosis: Complete resection usually gives long-term control; behavioural symptoms often improve but anosmia rarely recovers.
pearls: Test smell in any patient with new personality change.
Foster Kennedy: optic atrophy one side, disc swelling the other.
A mass can masquerade as dementia; image before labelling FTD.
det.thd: Olfactory groove meningioma เป็นเนื้องอกเยื่อหุ้มสมองที่ฐานกะโหลกด้านหน้า โตช้ามากจนมีขนาดใหญ่ก่อนมีอาการ ผู้ป่วยไม่ได้กลิ่น บุคลิกเปลี่ยน เฉยเมย และอาจพบ Foster Kennedy syndrome คือ optic atrophy ข้างหนึ่งและ papilloedema อีกข้าง MRI เห็นก้อนติดสีที่เส้นกลาง รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัด และฉายรังสีเมื่อเหลือก้อนหรือกลับเป็นซ้ำ

Descriptive syndrome; imaging defines cause

name: Oligodendrogliomas
formal: Diffuse glioma with IDH mutation and 1p/19q codeletion, typically frontal, calcified and presenting with seizures; better chemosensitivity and prognosis than astrocytoma.
simple: A type of brain tumour, often in the frontal lobe, that commonly causes seizures and tends to grow slowly.
th: glioma ที่มี IDH mutation ร่วมกับ 1p/19q codeletion พบบ่อยที่ frontal lobe มักมีหินปูนและเริ่มด้วยอาการชัก ตอบสนองต่อการฉายรังสีร่วมกับ PCV หรือ temozolomide ดีกว่า astrocytoma ในกลุ่มเดียวกัน
tempoNote: Seizures for years before diagnosis; grade 3 tumours progress over months
feat: Peak in the fourth to fifth decade; frontal lobe in more than half, then temporal and parietal
Seizures are the commonest presentation, often for a long time before diagnosis, with a normal examination in many
Cortical or subcortical mass, calcified on CT in many, non-enhancing in grade 2 and with patchy enhancement in grade 3
WHO CNS5 definition: IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted, CNS WHO grade 2 or 3; the older mixed oligoastrocytoma is no longer used
Late leptomeningeal seeding occurs in a minority, so spinal MRI is done only when symptoms point there
inv: CT (calcification) and MRI (cortical thickening, T2-bright mass, little oedema)
Histology: round nuclei with perinuclear halos (fried-egg), delicate branching capillaries; IDH1/2 mutation and 1p/19q codeletion confirmed by FISH or methylation profiling
TERT promoter mutation, CIC and FUBP1 mutations, and MGMT status give supportive information
MRI follow-up every 3-6 months in the first years; spinal MRI and CSF cytology if leptomeningeal disease is suspected

case.story: Intermittent episodes of speech arrest and right hand twitching for 3 years that were attributed to stress, followed by a generalised seizure.
case.exam: Normal examination.
case.tests: CT shows a calcified left frontal lesion; MRI shows a non-enhancing cortical mass. Resection: IDH1-mutant, 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendroglioma, CNS WHO grade 2, residual tumour on post-operative MRI.
case.q: Which adjuvant approach has randomised evidence for improved survival in codeleted tumours?
case.a: Radiotherapy followed by PCV (RTOG 9802 for high-risk grade 2, RTOG 9402 and EORTC 26951 for grade 3) prolonged overall survival; vorasidenib is an option for residual grade 2 disease before radiotherapy is needed.

det.patho: Oligodendroglioma is an infiltrating glioma of uniform round cells with perinuclear clearing, a plexiform capillary network and calcification. Molecular criteria are IDH1/2 mutation plus whole-arm codeletion of 1p and 19q, usually with TERT promoter, CIC and FUBP1 mutation and retained ATRX. The book written before this classification used histology alone and described an oligoastrocytoma category; under WHO CNS5 these tumours are assigned by molecular result. CDKN2A/B loss marks progression to grade 3 and worse outcome.
det.clinical: A long history of seizures is the norm. Many patients have a normal examination at diagnosis, with deficits or raised pressure in higher grades. The frontal and temporal lobes are common; the tumour grows into the callosum and across the midline in grade 3. Leptomeningeal seeding occurs in up to about 30 percent in older series, though the outcome in these patients is not as grim as with other cancers.
det.diagnosis: CT may show a cortical calcified mass, and MRI the extent of infiltration. Diagnosis needs histology plus molecular proof that the tumour is IDH-mutant and carries the 1p/19q codeletion. Presence of the codeletion predicts chemosensitivity and better prognosis, although the absence of codeletion does not justify withholding chemotherapy in related tumours. Frozen sections are unreliable, so the surgeon may need preoperative biopsy or imaging impressions to plan resection.
det.treatment: Resection is safe in accessible lesions; extent matters less than in astrocytoma because these tumours respond so well to radiotherapy and chemotherapy. For grade 2 residual disease, vorasidenib (INDIGO) offers delay of radiotherapy, but high-risk patients receive radiotherapy (54 Gy) followed by PCV, which more than doubled survival in RTOG 9802. Grade 3 tumours receive radiotherapy plus PCV (RTOG 9402, EORTC 26951), with temozolomide as an alternative (CODEL). The book reports PCV regimens, response rates above 50 percent and the use of temozolomide at recurrence, consistent with later trials. PCV toxicity includes myelosuppression, neuropathy and pulmonary fibrosis.
det.prognosis: Median survival for codeleted grade 2 tumours exceeds 12-15 years; for grade 3 tumours with radiotherapy plus PCV it exceeds 14 years in codeleted cases.
pearls: IDH-mutant plus 1p/19q-codeleted is the only definition now; histology alone does not make an oligodendroglioma.
Codeleted tumours are the glioma group with the best chemotherapy response; PCV after radiotherapy extends survival.
Calcified cortical frontal mass with seizures for years: think oligodendroglioma.
det.thd: Oligodendroglioma คือ glioma ที่มี IDH mutation และ 1p/19q codeletion พบบ่อยที่ frontal lobe และมักมีหินปูนใน CT อาการสำคัญคือชักเรื้อรัง การวินิจฉัยตามระบบ WHO 2021 ต้องมีผล molecular ครบ การรักษาคือผ่าตัด ฉายรังสี และให้ PCV หรือ temozolomide ผู้ที่มี codeletion ตอบสนองดี อยู่รอดนานกว่า astrocytoma ส่วน vorasidenib ใช้ในเกรด 2 ที่ยังเหลือก้อนหลังผ่าตัด

name: One and a half syndrome
formal: Pontine lesion involving the PPRF or abducens nucleus and ipsilateral MLF, causing ipsilateral gaze palsy and internuclear ophthalmoplegia so only abduction of the contralateral eye remains.
simple: A brainstem problem leaving one eye unable to move sideways and the other able to move only outward.
th: รอยโรคใน pons ที่ PPRF หรือ abducens nucleus ร่วมกับ MLF ข้างเดียวกัน ทำให้มอง horizontal ไม่ได้ทั้งสองด้าน เหลือเพียงตาข้างตรงข้ามกลอกออกได้
tempoNote: Usually acute from stroke or demyelination
feat: Ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy ('one')
Ipsilateral INO ('half'): the ipsilateral eye cannot adduct
Only movement left: abduction of the contralateral eye, often with nystagmus
Vertical movements and convergence often preserved
Exotropia of the contralateral eye in acute phase (paralytic pontine exotropia)
With facial palsy forms 'eight-and-a-half' syndrome
inv: MRI brain with DWI and thin brainstem slices
Vascular risk work-up in older adults; MS work-up in young adults

case.story: Woke with double vision and difficulty looking to either side.
case.exam: Neither eye moves left; on right gaze only the right eye abducts with nystagmus; convergence intact; vertical movements normal.
case.tests: MRI: enhancing lesion in left dorsal pontine tegmentum plus periventricular lesions; CSF oligoclonal bands.
case.q: Where is the lesion and what is the likely cause?
case.a: Left dorsal pons (PPRF/abducens nucleus plus left MLF); multiple sclerosis.

read.where: Chapter 22 Neuro-Ophthalmology — One and a Half Syndrome

det.patho: A single lesion in the dorsal pontine tegmentum damages the abducens nucleus or PPRF (causing ipsilateral gaze palsy) and the adjacent ipsilateral MLF (blocking adduction of the ipsilateral eye on contralateral gaze). Only the pathway from the intact contralateral abducens nucleus to its own lateral rectus remains functional.
det.clinical: Patients present with diplopia or blurred vision and striking horizontal ophthalmoplegia. Young patients usually have MS; older patients usually have a pontine infarct or haemorrhage. Additional pontine signs (facial palsy, hemiparesis, ataxia) are common.
det.diagnosis: Bedside recognition localises the lesion precisely. MRI confirms and identifies the cause. Myasthenia and Miller Fisher syndrome can mimic it and should be considered if MRI is normal.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: stroke pathways, or high-dose steroids and disease-modifying therapy in MS. Temporary prisms or patching help diplopia.
det.prognosis: Often improves over weeks to months, especially in demyelination.
pearls: Only one eye can move, and only outward: one-and-a-half.
Add a facial palsy and it becomes 'eight-and-a-half'.
Young patient: MS; older patient: stroke.
det.thd: One and a half syndrome เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ pons ด้านหลังซึ่งทำลาย PPRF หรือ abducens nucleus ร่วมกับ MLF ข้างเดียวกัน ทำให้มองไปข้างรอยโรคไม่ได้ (หนึ่ง) และตาข้างรอยโรคกลอกเข้าไม่ได้ (ครึ่ง) เหลือเพียงตาข้างตรงข้ามกลอกออกได้ สาเหตุในคนอายุน้อยมักเป็น MS ผู้สูงอายุมักเป็น stroke ตรวจ MRI และรักษาตามสาเหตุ

name: Opioid toxicity
formal: Overdose causing coma, miosis and respiratory depression via mu receptor agonism; reversed by naloxone; chronic use may cause leukoencephalopathy and myoclonus.
simple: Too much opioid medicine or drug, causing deep drowsiness, tiny pupils and slow breathing that can be fatal.
th: ภาวะได้รับ opioid เกินขนาด ทำให้ซึมจนหมดสติ รูม่านตาเล็ก และหายใจช้า แก้ด้วย naloxone
tempoNote: Minutes to hours after use; delayed or prolonged with long-acting or slow-release drugs
feat: Triad: reduced consciousness, pinpoint pupils and slow, shallow breathing
Hypotension, bradycardia, hypothermia; aspiration and rhabdomyolysis from prolonged lying
Myoclonus, hyperalgesia or seizures (tramadol, pethidine) with high doses or renal failure
Rare delayed complications: hypoxic brain injury, toxic leukoencephalopathy after inhaled heroin, cerebellar injury in children
inv: Clinical diagnosis confirmed by response to naloxone; capillary glucose at once
Arterial blood gas, CK, renal function, paracetamol level; ECG
Urine drug screen (may miss synthetic opioids such as fentanyl)
MRI brain if coma persists despite reversal

case.who: 71-year-old woman in a Ratchaburi provincial hospital ward with cancer pain and chronic kidney disease
case.story: Morphine was increased yesterday; the nurse finds her very drowsy with a respiratory rate of 7 per minute.
case.exam: GCS 8, pupils 1 mm and reactive, multifocal twitching, no lateralising signs.
case.tests: Glucose 6.2 mmol/L; creatinine raised; blood gas shows respiratory acidosis.
case.q: What is the cause and what is the immediate treatment?
case.a: Opioid toxicity from accumulated morphine metabolites in renal failure; titrated IV naloxone with airway support, then review analgesic choice and dose.

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System

det.patho: Opioids act on mu receptors in brainstem respiratory centres, reducing the response to carbon dioxide and causing apnoea. Miosis results from stimulation of the Edinger-Westphal nucleus. Active metabolites (morphine-6-glucuronide, norpethidine) accumulate in renal failure and cause sedation or neuroexcitation. Hypoxia, hypotension and immobility account for most secondary neurological injury.
det.clinical: The patient is drowsy or comatose, with small pupils and slow breathing; pupils may dilate if hypoxic damage occurs or with co-ingestants. Long-acting opioids, transdermal patches and methadone cause recurrent toxicity after naloxone wears off. Tramadol can cause seizures and serotonin toxicity. Survivors may show hypoxic-ischaemic injury, compartment syndrome or plexus and nerve compression injuries.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in any patient with miosis and respiratory depression, and look for access to opioids, patches or injection marks. Response to naloxone confirms it, but a lack of response does not exclude mixed overdose. Check glucose, gases, CK and co-ingested drugs. Image the brain if focal signs or persistent coma.
det.treatment: Support airway and ventilation first. Give naloxone IV in small titrated doses (e.g. 0.04–0.4 mg increments, more in suspected high-potency opioids) to restore breathing rather than full wakefulness, avoiding abrupt withdrawal; an infusion may be needed for long-acting agents. Observe for recurrence for several hours. Address renal dosing, offer harm-reduction, naloxone take-home kits and referral for opioid use disorder treatment.
det.prognosis: Excellent if breathing is restored quickly; death or hypoxic brain injury follows delayed treatment.
pearls: Coma + pinpoint pupils: think opioid, but also pontine haemorrhage.
Naloxone wears off before many opioids; observe and re-dose.
In renal failure, avoid morphine and pethidine accumulation.
det.thd: Opioid toxicity คือภาวะได้รับยากลุ่ม opioid เกินขนาด ทำให้ซึมหรือหมดสติ รูม่านตาเล็กมาก และหายใจช้า เกิดจากยากระตุ้น mu receptor ที่ก้านสมอง ผู้ป่วยไตวายเสี่ยงสะสมยา การรักษาคือดูแลทางเดินหายใจและให้ naloxone ทีละน้อยจนหายใจดี ต้องเฝ้าระวังอาการกลับซ้ำเพราะ naloxone หมดฤทธิ์เร็ว ถ้าขาดออกซิเจนนานอาจเกิดสมองเสียหายถาวร

name: Opportunistic infections
formal: CNS infections in immunocompromised hosts such as HIV, with toxoplasmosis, cryptococcus, PML, CMV and TB; present with subacute focal deficits, headache or encephalopathy.
simple: Infections of the nervous system that mainly occur when the immune system is weak, such as in advanced HIV.

Focal lesions: toxoplasmosis (ring-enhancing, basal ganglia), PCNSL, TB abscess; PML (non-enhancing white matter)
Meningitis: cryptococcal (headache, high pressure, few signs) and tuberculous
Encephalitis or ventriculitis: CMV, VZV; myelitis and radiculitis also occur
Signs of inflammation may be muted in profound immunosuppression

MRI with contrast

case.exam: Drowsy, right hemiparesis, no neck stiffness.

det.patho: Loss of cell-mediated immunity, chiefly CD4 T-cell depletion in HIV, allows reactivation of latent organisms (Toxoplasma, JC virus, CMV, VZV, TB) or progression of newly acquired fungi such as Cryptococcus. Iatrogenic immunosuppression with transplant drugs, chemotherapy and biologics like natalizumab or rituximab creates similar risks. Immune reconstitution after ART can worsen inflammation (IRIS).
det.clinical: Presentation depends on the organism: focal deficits and seizures with mass lesions, headache and raised pressure with cryptococcal meningitis, progressive multifocal deficits without headache in PML, and cranial neuropathies with TB meningitis. Several infections may coexist. In Thailand, cryptococcal meningitis, toxoplasmosis and TB remain the commonest. Fever and meningism are often absent.
det.diagnosis: Know the immune status (CD4 count) because it narrows the list. MRI pattern guides the next step: enhancing masses, non-enhancing white matter lesions or meningeal disease. CSF studies, antigen tests and PCR identify most organisms; brain biopsy is reserved for lesions not responding to empirical treatment. Serum cryptococcal antigen screening in advanced HIV allows pre-emptive therapy.
det.treatment: Treat the specific organism, for example induction amphotericin with flucytosine for cryptococcal meningitis plus repeated CSF drainage for high pressure, and standard regimens for toxoplasmosis and TB. Timing of ART matters: it is delayed for several weeks in cryptococcal and TB meningitis to reduce IRIS mortality, but started early for most others. PML has no specific antiviral, and immune recovery is the treatment. Secondary prophylaxis continues until CD4 recovery.
det.prognosis: Variable: good with early treatment of toxoplasmosis, but cryptococcal and TB meningitis and PML still carry high mortality in advanced disease.
pearls: CD4 under 100 with ring-enhancing lesions: treat toxoplasmosis first, biopsy if no response.
Always measure opening pressure in cryptococcal meningitis.
Delay ART in cryptococcal and TB meningitis to avoid fatal IRIS.

name: Opsoclonus myoclonus syndrome (OMS)
formal: Chaotic multidirectional saccades with myoclonus, ataxia and irritability; paraneoplastic (neuroblastoma in children, breast or lung cancer in adults) or parainfectious and immune-mediated.
simple: A condition with rapid, random jerking eye movements and muscle jerks, often linked to an immune reaction to cancer.
more: Chaotic multidirectional saccades with myoclonus and ataxia, paraneoplastic (neuroblastoma, small cell lung or breast cancer) or post-infectious; probable cerebellar disinhibition. Childhood opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome, often paraneoplastic with neuroblastoma, with irritability and sleep disturbance; treated with immunotherapy and tumour removal. Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome in infancy with chaotic eye movements, myoclonus and ataxia, often paraneoplastic from neuroblastoma. Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome in infants with chaotic eye movements, myoclonus, ataxia and irritability, often paraneoplastic from neuroblastoma or post-infectious. Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome: chaotic saccades with myoclonus and ataxia, in children with neuroblastoma or post-infectious, and in adults paraneoplastic.
ab: Dancing eyes–dancing feet syndrome (myoclonic encephalopathy of infancy)
merged: Dancing eyes–dancing feet syndrome (myoclonic encephalopathy of infancy)
th: ตากระตุกไวทุกทิศทางอย่างไม่เป็นจังหวะ ร่วมกับกล้ามเนื้อกระตุกและเดินเซ — ในเด็กเล็กต้องหา neuroblastoma ในผู้ใหญ่เกิดหลังติดเชื้อหรือร่วมกับมะเร็ง
tempoNote: Develops over days to a few weeks; in children may relapse with infections or steroid tapering
feat: Opsoclonus: rapid, chaotic, multidirectional conjugate saccades without intersaccadic pause, persisting in sleep or eye closure
Action and resting myoclonus of trunk, limbs and head; truncal ataxia with refusal to walk
Irritability, sleep disturbance and behavioural regression in toddlers
Children aged 1–3 years: neuroblastoma in about half
Adults: post-infectious, or paraneoplastic with SCLC or breast/gynaecological cancer (anti-Ri, others)
inv: Children: MRI or CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, urine catecholamine metabolites (HVA, VMA), MIBG scan
Adults: paraneoplastic antibody panel (Ri, Hu, others), CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, mammography or PET
CSF: oligoclonal bands, B-cell expansion in children; infectious studies
MRI brain usually normal; exclude brainstem or cerebellar structural lesions

case.story: Two weeks after a cold he became irritable, stopped walking and could not hold his cup. His mother says his eyes 'shake in all directions'.
case.exam: Bursts of chaotic conjugate saccades in every direction, multifocal myoclonus of arms and head, unable to sit unsupported, crying constantly.
case.tests: MRI brain normal. Urine HVA and VMA mildly raised. CT abdomen: 2 cm right adrenal mass; MIBG avid.
case.q: What is the syndrome and what does treatment involve beyond tumour removal?
case.a: Neuroblastoma-associated opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome; resection treats the tumour, but the neurological syndrome needs sustained immunotherapy (ACTH or steroids with IVIG, often rituximab) to protect long-term development.

det.patho: OMS is thought to arise from immune disinhibition of brainstem omnipause neurons and their cerebellar control (fastigial nucleus), releasing saccadic burst neurons into chaotic firing. B-cell activation is prominent in paediatric cases, while in adults onconeural antibodies such as anti-Ri mark the immune response but no single target explains most cases. Tumours, especially neuroblastoma, and infections act as triggers.
det.clinical: In toddlers, irritability and loss of walking often come first, and opsoclonus may be intermittent and missed. Adults present with opsoclonus or ocular flutter, myoclonus, ataxia and sometimes encephalopathy; younger adults often have a post-infectious, benign course, while older patients more often harbour a cancer. Long-term behavioural, learning and sleep problems are frequent in children.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical; in children at least three of four features (opsoclonus, myoclonus/ataxia, behavioural or sleep disturbance, neuroblastoma) are used. Search for neuroblastoma thoroughly and repeat if the first screen is negative. In adults, perform a full paraneoplastic workup and tumour search. Ocular flutter (horizontal only) belongs to the same spectrum.
det.treatment: Children need early, adequately long immunotherapy: ACTH or high-dose corticosteroids with IVIG, plus rituximab for moderate to severe or relapsing cases, alongside tumour resection. Adults with post-infectious OMS often respond to steroids or IVIG, while paraneoplastic adults require tumour therapy and immunotherapy. Clonazepam or levetiracetam can reduce myoclonus symptomatically.
det.prognosis: Children frequently have residual cognitive and behavioural problems, worse with delayed or insufficient treatment; adults with idiopathic or post-infectious OMS usually recover well, whereas paraneoplastic adult cases fare worse.
pearls: Toddler who stops walking and is irritable with dancing eyes: search for neuroblastoma.
Opsoclonus continues with eyes closed and during sleep.
The tumour is usually low grade; the neurological outcome depends on immunotherapy.
det.thd: Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome คือตากระตุกเร็วอย่างไม่เป็นระเบียบทุกทิศทาง ร่วมกับกล้ามเนื้อกระตุกและเดินเซ ในเด็กเล็กประมาณครึ่งหนึ่งพบ neuroblastoma จึงต้องตรวจภาพช่องท้องทรวงอกและ urine HVA/VMA ส่วนผู้ใหญ่มักเกิดหลังติดเชื้อหรือร่วมกับมะเร็ง ต้องตรวจแอนติบอดีและหามะเร็ง รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัดเนื้องอกร่วมกับ ACTH หรือ steroid, IVIG และ rituximab

name: Optic atrophy plus syndrome
formal: Inherited optic atrophy with additional neurological features such as deafness, ataxia or neuropathy, as in OPA1 or mitochondrial disease.
simple: Inherited loss of the optic nerve that comes with other problems like deafness or poor coordination.
th: optic atrophy ทางพันธุกรรมที่มีอาการทางระบบประสาทอื่นร่วม เช่น หูหนวก เดินเซ หรือเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเสื่อม เช่น จากยีน OPA1 หรือโรคไมโทคอนเดรีย
tempoNote: Visual loss from childhood; extra-ocular features usually appear in adolescence or adult life
feat: Bilateral, slowly progressive visual loss from childhood with temporal or diffuse disc pallor and central or caecocentral scotomas
Plus features: sensorineural deafness, ataxia, axonal neuropathy, myopathy with ptosis or ophthalmoplegia
Some cases resemble multiple sclerosis or spastic paraparesis
Family history often dominant, but variable penetrance
inv: OCT showing retinal nerve fibre and ganglion cell layer thinning
Genetic testing: OPA1 first; panels including WFS1, OPA3, mtDNA (including LHON variants) and others
Audiometry, nerve conduction, MRI; muscle biopsy may show multiple mtDNA deletions

case.story: Poor vision since school that slowly worsened; now has hearing loss and unsteady walking. Her father also has poor vision.
case.exam: Acuity 6/36 both eyes, temporal disc pallor, bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, mild ataxia and reduced ankle reflexes.
case.tests: OCT shows thin nerve fibre layer; nerve conduction shows sensory axonal neuropathy; OPA1 pathogenic variant found.
case.q: What is the syndrome?
case.a: OPA1-related dominant optic atrophy plus, with deafness, ataxia and neuropathy.

det.patho: OPA1 encodes a mitochondrial inner membrane protein needed for fusion and maintenance of mitochondrial DNA. Retinal ganglion cells, with long unmyelinated axons and high energy needs, are the most vulnerable, but some variants (often missense in the GTPase domain) cause wider neurodegeneration and multiple mtDNA deletions. Similar syndromic pictures come from WFS1, OPA3 and primary mtDNA disease.
det.clinical: Optic atrophy usually starts in the first decade with slow decline. Up to about one in five OPA1 carriers develop plus features, most often deafness, followed by ataxia, axonal neuropathy, chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia and myopathy. A multiple sclerosis-like or spastic paraplegia picture is reported. Severity varies widely even within one family.
det.diagnosis: Combine OCT, colour vision and visual fields with assessment for hearing, neuropathy and muscle involvement. Genetic testing is the definitive step; testing of relatives clarifies inheritance. Exclude compressive, nutritional and inflammatory optic neuropathies.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying treatment is proven; idebenone is used off-label by some centres with uncertain benefit. Management includes low-vision aids, hearing aids or cochlear implants, physiotherapy and genetic counselling. Avoid smoking and heavy alcohol, which may add mitochondrial stress.
det.prognosis: Slow progression; most keep some navigational vision, but plus features add disability.
pearls: Childhood optic atrophy + deafness: test OPA1 and WFS1.
Temporal pallor with caecocentral scotoma suggests a mitochondrial optic neuropathy.
Ptosis and ophthalmoplegia in an optic atrophy family point to OPA1 with mtDNA deletions.
det.thd: Optic atrophy plus syndrome คือโรคประสาทตาฝ่อทางพันธุกรรม ส่วนใหญ่จากยีน OPA1 ที่เกี่ยวกับไมโทคอนเดรีย ผู้ป่วยสายตาค่อย ๆ แย่ลงตั้งแต่เด็ก และต่อมามีหูตึง เดินเซ เส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเสื่อม หรือหนังตาตก วินิจฉัยด้วย OCT และตรวจยีน ยังไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ ให้การดูแลด้านการมองเห็น การได้ยิน และให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

name: Optic neuritis
formal: Acute inflammatory optic neuropathy with painful subacute monocular visual loss, dyschromatopsia and RAPD; commonly first presentation of multiple sclerosis, also NMO and MOG disease.
simple: Inflammation of the eye nerve causing pain on eye movement and blurred, dull vision, often linked to multiple sclerosis.

th: เส้นประสาทตาอักเสบ ตามัวภายในไม่กี่วันร่วมกับปวดเวลากลอกตา สีจางลง และมี RAPD ชนิดทั่วไปสัมพันธ์กับ MS ส่วนชนิดผิดแบบต้องคิดถึง NMOSD และ MOGAD

Reduced colour saturation (red desaturation) and contrast, central or diffuse field loss
Relative afferent pupillary defect in the affected eye
Normal disc (retrobulbar) in two-thirds, mild swelling in the rest

case.exam: Acuity 6/24 left, 6/6 right; left RAPD; red desaturation and central scotoma on the left; normal fundi.
case.tests: MRI: enhancing intraorbital left optic nerve segment and three periventricular ovoid lesions; AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG negative; CSF oligoclonal bands positive.
case.q: What does this indicate and would you give steroids?
case.a: Typical demyelinating optic neuritis as a first MS event (likely meeting MS criteria); IV methylprednisolone speeds recovery but not the final outcome, and disease-modifying therapy should be discussed.

det.patho: Inflammatory demyelination of the optic nerve blocks conduction; the myelin is central-type, so the process mirrors MS plaques. In Western series most cases are MS-related, whereas in Thailand and other Asian populations a larger share is due to AQP4 (astrocytopathy) or MOG antibodies. Infections, sarcoidosis, autoimmune connective tissue disease and immune checkpoint inhibitors are rarer causes.
det.clinical: Typical optic neuritis affects women aged 20–45 with unilateral subacute loss and pain on eye movement, reaches a nadir within two weeks, and recovers substantially over months. Persistent deficits include reduced contrast, colour desaturation and Uhthoff's phenomenon (blurring with heat). Atypical forms are bilateral, painless, severe, slow to recover or relapse when steroids are stopped; these demand antibody testing and broader work-up.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by MRI showing optic nerve enhancement and by VEP. Long lesions reaching the chiasm favour NMOSD, while anterior lesions with perineural enhancement and disc swelling favour MOGAD. Brain lesions estimate future MS risk; CSF oligoclonal bands can substitute for dissemination in time under the 2017 McDonald criteria. Exclude compressive lesions, LHON, ischaemic and infiltrative optic neuropathies.
det.treatment: For typical ON, IV methylprednisolone 1 g a day, given for three to five days, hastens recovery but does not change the final acuity; oral low-dose prednisolone alone should be avoided. Severe or AQP4-positive attacks warrant early plasma exchange and then long-term immunosuppression (e.g. rituximab, inebilizumab, satralizumab, eculizumab). MOGAD attacks are treated with steroids and a slow taper. When MS criteria are met, start disease-modifying therapy.
det.prognosis: In typical ON over 90% regain 6/12 or better within a year; NMOSD-associated ON often leaves severe permanent loss.
pearls: Pain on eye movement plus RAPD plus red desaturation in a young adult: optic neuritis.
Check AQP4 and MOG antibodies before labelling it MS-related, especially in Asian patients.
No improvement by 3–4 weeks means re-think the diagnosis.
Avoid oral low-dose steroids alone for ON (higher relapse rate in the ONTT).

qx.stem: A 28-year-old woman from Chonburi had left optic neuritis 8 months ago. Visual acuity has recovered to 6/6 and she has no symptoms. A pattern-reversal visual evoked potential is performed.
qx.q: What result is most likely on the affected side?
opts: Normal P100 latency in nearly all patients by three months
Permanent absence of the response despite normal acuity
Reduced amplitude with normal latency
An equally delayed response from both eyes
Prolonged P100 latency with a preserved waveform and recovered amplitude, which often persists for years
qx.why: After optic neuritis the demyelinated optic nerve conducts slowly, so P100 latency stays prolonged even after acuity recovers, while amplitude and waveform recover. Normal latencies are found in only a small minority at three months and fewer than a quarter after two years. In acute severe neuritis, however, the P100 may be absent. Prolonged latency with an interocular difference suggests a prechiasmal lesion, whereas abnormality in both eyes suggests a bilateral lesion.

qx.stem: A 29-year-old woman from Chiang Mai has had three days of pain on eye movement and reduced vision in the left eye, 6/24 with a relative afferent pupillary defect and a normal disc. MRI shows three periventricular white matter lesions. A resident asks what intravenous corticosteroids will achieve.
qx.q: Which statement is most accurate?
opts: They restore normal vision in all patients regardless of timing
They prevent the development of multiple sclerosis
They are contraindicated because they worsen the final outcome
They are required to avoid permanent blindness in every case
They speed visual recovery but do not change the visual acuity outcome at six months
qx.why: In typical demyelinating optic neuritis, intravenous methylprednisolone hastens recovery without altering long-term visual acuity, and the MRI lesion count is the strongest predictor of later multiple sclerosis; steroids do not prevent it. Oral prednisolone alone at standard dose was associated with more recurrences in the classic trial. Recovery is good in most untreated patients, so steroids are used for speed and not to save the eye.

det.patho: AQP4-IgG targets the water channel on astrocyte endfeet, activating complement and causing astrocyte loss with secondary demyelination and axonal destruction. The optic nerve is highly vulnerable, so single attacks can leave permanent blindness. NMOSD is more common in East and Southeast Asia, and about nine in ten patients are women.
det.clinical: Optic neuritis is a common first attack of NMOSD. Compared with MS, attacks are more severe, more often bilateral or chiasmal, and recovery is poorer. Patients may also have myelitis, area postrema syndrome, brainstem or diencephalic episodes. Untreated disease relapses and accumulates disability with each attack.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis follows the 2015 international NMOSD criteria: a positive AQP4-IgG plus one core clinical syndrome after exclusion of alternatives. Cell-based assays are preferred. MRI typically shows a lesion longer than half the optic nerve or reaching the chiasm. Test MOG-IgG too, because seronegative cases and MOGAD need different management.
det.treatment: Treat attacks urgently with IV methylprednisolone (1 g/day, 3–5 doses); add plasma exchange early, especially when vision is severely affected, as delay worsens outcome. Long-term prevention is essential: options include rituximab, inebilizumab, satralizumab, tocilizumab, eculizumab or ravulizumab, with azathioprine or mycophenolate where resources are limited. Avoid MS drugs such as interferon-beta, natalizumab and fingolimod, which can worsen NMOSD.
det.prognosis: Without prevention many patients relapse and may become legally blind in one or both eyes; modern therapies greatly cut relapse rates.
pearls: Severe or bilateral optic neuritis in an Asian woman: test AQP4-IgG and do not wait for the result to give plasma exchange.
Ask about past hiccups or vomiting (area postrema attacks).
MS disease-modifying drugs can harm NMOSD patients.
det.thd: NMO-ON คือ optic neuritis ในโรค NMOSD ที่มี AQP4 antibody ทำลาย astrocyte อาการรุนแรง ตามัวมากจนเห็นแค่มือโบก อาจเป็นสองข้างหรือลามถึง chiasm และฟื้นตัวไม่ดี MRI พบรอยโรคยาวด้านหลังของเส้นประสาทตา ต้องตรวจ AQP4-IgG และ MOG-IgG รักษาเร่งด่วนด้วย methylprednisolone และ plasma exchange จากนั้นให้ยาป้องกันการกำเริบระยะยาว เช่น rituximab และห้ามใช้ยา MS บางชนิด

qx.stem: A 41-year-old woman from Songkhla has severe, rapid visual loss in the right eye to hand movements, with painful eye movements. MRI shows enhancement of a lengthy stretch of optic nerve reaching toward the chiasm. Brain MRI is otherwise normal. A colleague asks which feature distinguishes this from MS-related optic neuritis.
qx.q: Which feature most strongly suggests NMOSD-related optic neuritis?
opts: Mild visual loss with full recovery in two weeks
Short anterior optic nerve lesion confined to the orbit
Abnormal MRI with multiple periventricular ovoid lesions
Optic nerve involvement of more than half its length or the chiasm, with poor recovery and AQP4-IgG or MOG-IgG testing needed
Presence of oligoclonal bands as the only abnormality
qx.why: Optic neuritis from AQP4-IgG NMOSD tends to be severe, can be bilateral, involves a long posterior segment and the chiasm, and recovers poorly unless treated promptly, so antibody testing and early high-dose steroids or plasma exchange matter. In MS-related optic neuritis the lesion is shorter and the outcome is better. MOG-IgG disease also causes long anterior lesions with disc swelling, so both antibodies should be tested.
