name: Optic neuropathy
formal: Damage to the optic nerve from inflammation, ischaemia, compression, toxins or inheritance, causing visual loss, colour desaturation, RAPD and a visual field defect.
simple: Damage to the nerve connecting the eye to the brain, causing reduced vision and dull colours.
th: เส้นประสาทตาเสียหายจากการอักเสบ ขาดเลือด ถูกกดทับ สารพิษ หรือพันธุกรรม ทำให้ตามัว เห็นสีจางลง มี RAPD และลานสายตาผิดปกติ
tempoNote: Tempo is the main clue to cause: sudden (ischaemic), days (inflammatory), weeks–months (compressive, toxic, hereditary)
feat: Reduced acuity and colour vision (red desaturation) out of proportion to refractive error
Relative afferent pupillary defect in unilateral or asymmetric disease
Field defects: central or caecocentral scotoma, altitudinal defect, or generalised constriction
Disc swollen (anterior) or normal at first (retrobulbar), with pallor appearing after 4–6 weeks
Pain on eye movement suggests inflammation; painless sudden loss suggests ischaemia
inv: Visual acuity, colour plates, swinging flashlight test, formal perimetry and OCT of the nerve fibre layer
MRI orbits and brain with contrast: inflammation, compression, demyelination
Bloods by context: ESR/CRP (GCA), AQP4 and MOG antibodies, B12, syphilis, toxicology
Genetic testing for LHON or OPA1 in bilateral painless subacute loss

case.story: Has had slowly worsening vision in the right eye for eight months, noticed only when he covered the left eye.
case.exam: VA 6/24 right, red desaturation, right RAPD, temporal pallor of the right disc; left eye normal.
case.tests: MRI with contrast shows a right anterior clinoid meningioma compressing the optic nerve.
case.q: What feature of the history points to compression rather than inflammation or ischaemia?
case.a: The painless, slowly progressive course over months is typical of compressive optic neuropathy; refer for neurosurgical management.

det.patho: Optic neuropathy is an umbrella term for injury to the retinal ganglion cell axons forming the optic nerve. Causes include demyelination or autoimmune inflammation, ischaemia (arteritic or non-arteritic), compression or infiltration, toxic-nutritional injury (methanol, ethambutol, B12 deficiency), trauma and inherited mitochondrial dysfunction (LHON, OPA1). Whatever the mechanism, axonal loss ends in optic atrophy visible on fundoscopy and OCT.
det.clinical: This is a syndrome, not a single disease. The diagnostic task is to identify the cause from age, tempo, pain, laterality and disc appearance. Painful subacute loss in a young adult suggests optic neuritis; sudden painless loss in an older vasculopath suggests ischaemia; bilateral symmetric central scotomas suggest toxic, nutritional or hereditary disease; insidious unilateral loss suggests compression. Bilateral optic neuropathy may lack an RAPD.
det.diagnosis: Confirm an optic nerve problem (acuity, colour, RAPD, field pattern) and exclude retinal disease, which usually shows on fundoscopy or OCT. MRI of orbits with fat suppression and contrast is the core test. Age over 50 with sudden loss calls for ESR/CRP to exclude giant cell arteritis. Antibody tests (AQP4, MOG), nutritional and toxic screens and genetic tests are chosen by pattern.
det.treatment: Treatment depends on cause: steroids for inflammatory and arteritic disease, plasma exchange for severe NMOSD-related attacks, decompression or tumour treatment for compression, stopping the toxin and replacing vitamins for toxic-nutritional cases, and idebenone for LHON. Low-vision support helps those with permanent loss. Urgency is greatest for GCA, where the fellow eye is at risk.
det.prognosis: Highly variable: good in typical optic neuritis, poor in arteritic ischaemia and LHON; compressive loss may improve after early decompression.
pearls: Tempo plus pain separates most causes at the bedside.
Normal disc + RAPD + reduced colour = retrobulbar optic neuropathy until proven otherwise.
Sudden visual loss in anyone over 50: check ESR/CRP the same day.
det.thd: Optic neuropathy คือภาวะที่เส้นประสาทตาเสียหายจากหลายสาเหตุ ได้แก่ การอักเสบ ขาดเลือด ถูกกดทับ สารพิษหรือขาดวิตามิน และพันธุกรรม อาการคือตามัว เห็นสีจาง มี RAPD และลานสายตาผิดปกติ ใช้อายุ ความเร็วของอาการ อาการปวด และลักษณะ optic disc ช่วยหาสาเหตุ ตรวจ MRI และเลือดตามความเหมาะสม รักษาตามสาเหตุ และผู้ป่วยอายุเกิน 50 ที่ตามัวเฉียบพลันต้องรีบตรวจหา giant cell arteritis

name: Optic pathway glioma (OPG)
formal: Pilocytic astrocytoma of the optic nerve, chiasm or tract, usually in childhood and associated with NF1, causing visual loss, proptosis, precocious puberty or hypothalamic signs.
simple: A usually slow-growing tumour along the vision pathway in children that can affect sight and hormones.
more: Low-grade pilocytic astrocytomas of the optic pathway, linked to NF1, in children causing progressive visual loss, proptosis and optic atrophy. Pilocytic low-grade astrocytomas of optic nerve or chiasm, frequent in neurofibromatosis type 1, causing visual loss, proptosis and endocrine dysfunction.
th: เนื้องอก astrocyte เกรดต่ำ (ส่วนใหญ่ pilocytic) ของเส้นประสาทตา chiasm หรือ hypothalamus พบบ่อยในเด็กที่เป็น NF1 อาการคือตามัวลง ตาโปน อาการเหมือนวัยหนุ่มสาวก่อนวัย รักษาด้วยเคมีบำบัดหรือยา MEK inhibitor เมื่อการมองเห็นแย่ลง หลีกเลี่ยงการฉายรังสีใน NF1
tempoNote: Often indolent for years; in early childhood vision may decline over months, with occasional spontaneous stabilisation or regression
feat: Usually before age 6 years; about 15-20 percent of children with NF1 have an optic pathway glioma and many are asymptomatic
Unilateral tumours cause proptosis and monocular visual loss; chiasmatic-hypothalamic tumours cause field loss, optic atrophy, nystagmus (including seesaw), head nodding and diencephalic features
Precocious puberty, growth hormone excess or deficiency and the diencephalic syndrome (emaciation with euphoria) occur with hypothalamic involvement
Sporadic tumours behave more aggressively than NF1-associated tumours and more often progress
Almost all are pilocytic astrocytoma, CNS WHO grade 1, rarely higher grade
inv: MRI of orbits and brain with contrast: fusiform enlargement of the optic nerve or chiasm, kinking, cystic change; lesion enhances variably
Formal ophthalmic examination: acuity, colour vision, fields, fundus, and optical coherence tomography of the retinal nerve fibre layer
Endocrine screening (IGF-1, LH/FSH, bone age) for chiasmatic-hypothalamic tumours
Biopsy only if imaging is atypical or in a non-NF1 child; NF1 genetic and clinical criteria

case.who: 4-year-old girl from Sakon Nakhon with NF1
case.story: Mother noticed she holds toys close to her left eye; she has had many café-au-lait spots since infancy.
case.exam: Reduced left visual acuity with a relative afferent pupillary defect, pale left disc, mild proptosis, axillary freckling.
case.tests: MRI shows a fusiform enlargement of the left optic nerve and chiasm with mild enhancement. Serial OCT shows retinal nerve fibre layer thinning over 6 months.
case.q: When should treatment start, and which therapies are preferred?
case.a: When vision declines or there is progressive tumour growth: carboplatin with vincristine, or targeted MEK inhibitors such as selumetinib; radiotherapy is avoided in NF1 because of vasculopathy (moyamoya), cognitive and second tumour risk.

det.patho: OPG is a pilocytic astrocytoma (rarely diffuse astrocytoma) of the anterior visual pathway. In NF1, loss of neurofibromin in the tumour and a permissive microenvironment drive growth, whereas sporadic tumours carry KIAA1549::BRAF fusion. NF1-associated tumours commonly stabilise or regress after infancy, in contrast to sporadic ones. The tumour may extend along the optic radiations.
det.clinical: The usual presentation in NF1 is detection by MRI or visual screening; symptomatic children have decreased acuity, colour desaturation, field loss, nystagmus or proptosis. Hypothalamic involvement causes growth and puberty disorders, hydrocephalus (if the foramen of Monro is blocked) or the diencephalic syndrome. The source emphasises that vision outcome is the main concern; severe visual loss at diagnosis rarely recovers.
det.diagnosis: MRI with orbital sequences defines the extent (Dodge classification: optic nerve, chiasm, or hypothalamus). In a child with known NF1 and typical findings, no biopsy is needed. In sporadic tumours, biopsy confirms pilocytic histology and BRAF status. Visual function monitoring (acuity, fields, OCT) is the key surveillance; serial imaging supports clinical decisions, since MRI change and vision may be dissociated.
det.treatment: Observation is appropriate for asymptomatic tumours. Chemotherapy with carboplatin plus vincristine delays radiotherapy and stabilises vision in about 85 percent of children in older series. For progression, MEK inhibitors (selumetinib in NF1, trametinib with dabrafenib for BRAF V600E, tovorafenib for BRAF-altered relapse) are increasingly used. Radiotherapy has a role only for older children with sporadic progressive tumours. Surgery is restricted to unilateral blind eye with proptosis or to debulking for hydrocephalus. Endocrine replacement and visual rehabilitation are part of care.
det.prognosis: Overall survival is excellent (above 90 percent at 10 years); visual morbidity and endocrine sequelae drive disability.
pearls: Annual ophthalmological screening for NF1 children until about age 8 detects OPG.
Treat for visual decline, not for imaging growth alone.
Avoid radiotherapy in NF1 children because of moyamoya and malignancy.
det.thd: Optic pathway glioma เป็น pilocytic astrocytoma ของเส้นประสาทตา chiasm หรือ hypothalamus พบบ่อยในเด็ก NF1 อายุต่ำกว่า 6 ปี ทำให้ตามัว ตาโปน ตากระตุก และบางรายมีวัยเจริญพันธุ์ก่อนวัย รักษาเมื่อการมองเห็นลดลงหรือก้อนโตด้วยเคมีบำบัด carboplatin กับ vincristine หรือยา MEK inhibitor หลีกเลี่ยงรังสีในผู้ป่วย NF1 และควรตรวจตาเป็นประจำทุกปี

name: Optic perineuritis
formal: Inflammation of optic nerve sheath with eye pain, visual loss and ring enhancement around the nerve on MRI; responds well to corticosteroids, may follow infection or autoimmune disease.
simple: Swelling of the covering around the eye nerve causing pain and blurred vision, which usually improves with steroids.
th: การอักเสบของเยื่อหุ้มเส้นประสาทตา ทำให้ปวดตาและตามัว MRI พบการ enhance เป็นวงรอบเส้นประสาทตา ตอบสนองดีต่อ steroid
tempoNote: Develops over days to weeks; relapses if steroids are stopped quickly
feat: Eye pain, especially on movement, with visual loss often milder than in typical optic neuritis
Arcuate or paracentral field defects with relatively spared central acuity
Disc swelling common; older age group than MS optic neuritis
Causes: idiopathic orbital inflammation, MOGAD, sarcoidosis, GPA, IgG4 disease, syphilis, TB
inv: Fat-suppressed contrast MRI orbits: tram-track or doughnut enhancement of the sheath, nerve core spared
Serology: syphilis, MOG-IgG, ANCA, ACE, IgG4; chest imaging for sarcoid and TB
CSF if infection or meningeal disease suspected

case.story: Two weeks of aching pain behind the left eye with blurred lower field.
case.exam: Acuity 6/9 left, inferior arcuate defect, swollen left disc, mild left RAPD.
case.tests: MRI orbits shows ring-like enhancement of the left optic nerve sheath with a non-enhancing nerve; syphilis and MOG serology negative; ANCA negative.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and how does treatment differ from MS optic neuritis?
case.a: Idiopathic optic perineuritis; high-dose steroids with a slow taper over months, because rapid withdrawal leads to relapse.

read.where: Chapter 10 - Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis and Myelin Oligodendrocyte Glycoprotein Antibody-Associated Disease

det.patho: Inflammation affects the optic nerve sheath rather than the nerve itself, as a localised form of orbital inflammation or part of a systemic disease. Associated conditions include MOG antibody disease, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, sarcoidosis, IgG4-related disease, syphilis, TB and herpes zoster. The axons are compromised secondarily, explaining peripheral field loss.
det.clinical: The age at presentation is usually higher than in MS optic neuritis, and there is pain, disc swelling and peripheral field loss with preserved central acuity. Some have no visual loss at all and present like papilloedema with pain. Without adequate treatment it relapses and can cause severe damage. Systemic symptoms point to an underlying cause.
det.diagnosis: MRI with fat suppression and contrast is the key test, showing enhancement around the nerve, sometimes extending into orbital fat. A systematic search for infectious and inflammatory causes is required before labelling it idiopathic. Lumbar puncture helps when there is papilloedema, to rule out raised pressure. Biopsy is occasionally needed for atypical or steroid-resistant cases.
det.treatment: Idiopathic and most autoimmune cases respond quickly to high-dose corticosteroids, followed by a slow taper over months. Steroid-sparing agents (methotrexate, mycophenolate, rituximab) are used in relapsing disease or systemic vasculitis. Infectious causes such as syphilis need specific antimicrobial treatment and steroids only with cover.
det.prognosis: Generally good with prompt steroids; relapse risk is high with short courses.
pearls: Tram-track enhancement + pain + good central vision: think perineuritis.
Exclude syphilis before steroids.
Taper slowly; quick withdrawal invites relapse.
det.thd: Optic perineuritis คือการอักเสบของเยื่อหุ้มเส้นประสาทตา มักพบในผู้ใหญ่อายุมากกว่า optic neuritis จาก MS อาการคือปวดตา ลานสายตาส่วนรอบผิดปกติแต่สายตาตรงกลางยังดี MRI พบ enhance เป็นวงรอบเส้นประสาทตา ต้องหาสาเหตุ เช่น ซิฟิลิส MOGAD sarcoidosis หรือ vasculitis การรักษาคือ steroid ขนาดสูงแล้วลดช้า ๆ หลายเดือนเพื่อป้องกันการกลับเป็นซ้ำ

name: Orbicularis oculi cranial dystonias
formal: Benign essential blepharospasm, focal cranial dystonia with involuntary bilateral eyelid closure; may combine with oromandibular dystonia (Meige syndrome); treated with botulinum toxin.
simple: Involuntary squeezing shut of the eyelids caused by overactive eye muscles.
th: dystonia เฉพาะที่ของกล้ามเนื้อ orbicularis oculi ทำให้กะพริบตาถี่หรือหลับตาเองทั้งสองข้าง อาจร่วมกับ oromandibular dystonia เป็น Meige syndrome รักษาด้วย botulinum toxin
tempoNote: Gradual onset in mid to late adult life; fluctuates through the day
feat: Increased blinking progressing to forceful bilateral involuntary eye closure
Triggered by bright light, wind, reading, driving or stress; better with talking, singing or touching the brow (sensory tricks)
Gritty eyes and photophobia are common early symptoms
Can make the patient functionally blind despite normal vision
Commoner in women over 50; may spread to lower face, jaw or neck
inv: Clinical diagnosis; examine for spread to other regions and features of parkinsonism or PSP
Ophthalmic assessment for dry eye or blepharitis
Imaging only if unilateral, very young onset or other neurological signs

case.who: 62-year-old female market vendor from Suphan Buri
case.story: Two years of frequent blinking, now eyes clamp shut when she drives or goes into sunlight; she had to stop riding her motorcycle.
case.exam: Bilateral forceful eye closure with brow lowering, relieved when she presses her temple; rest of the examination normal.
case.tests: None needed; ophthalmologist confirms mild dry eye only.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the first-line treatment?
case.a: Benign essential blepharospasm (focal cranial dystonia); botulinum toxin injections into orbicularis oculi every 3–4 months.

det.patho: Blepharospasm is an adult-onset focal dystonia due to abnormal function of networks linking the basal ganglia, cerebellum, thalamus and sensorimotor cortex, with impaired inhibition of the blink reflex. Most cases are idiopathic; some are secondary to drugs (dopamine blockers, levodopa), brainstem or thalamic lesions, or neurodegenerative disease. A sensory component explains photophobia and ocular discomfort.
det.clinical: Onset is usually gradual with excess blinking and dry eye symptoms. Spasms then become sustained, causing involuntary eye closure that interferes with reading, driving and walking in public. Around a third spread to the lower face or jaw (Meige syndrome) or the neck. Apraxia of eyelid opening may coexist and limit response to treatment.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on observing bilateral synchronous involuntary eye closure with characteristic triggers and sensory tricks. Distinguish from hemifacial spasm, tics, ptosis, functional eyelid spasm and ocular surface disease. Look for drug causes and features of PSP or other parkinsonism.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin injected into the orbicularis oculi is highly effective, typically repeated every three months. Side effects include ptosis, diplopia and dry eye. Tinted (FL-41) glasses, lubricants and treating blepharitis help. Oral drugs (clonazepam, trihexyphenidyl) are second-line; myectomy is an option for refractory cases.
det.prognosis: Chronic, rarely remits, but most patients function well with regular botulinum toxin.
pearls: Bilateral and synchronous: blepharospasm; one-sided with cheek twitch: hemifacial spasm.
Patients often first see an ophthalmologist for dry eye.
Check for spread to jaw and neck (Meige).
det.thd: Orbicularis oculi cranial dystonia หรือ blepharospasm คือ dystonia ของกล้ามเนื้อรอบตา ทำให้กะพริบถี่และหลับตาเองสองข้าง โดนแสงหรือขับรถแล้วเป็นมากขึ้น ใช้นิ้วแตะขมับแล้วดีขึ้น พบบ่อยในหญิงวัยกลางคนขึ้นไป บางรายลามไปที่ปากและขากรรไกรเป็น Meige syndrome วินิจฉัยทางคลินิกและรักษาด้วยการฉีด botulinum toxin ทุก 3 เดือน

name: Orbital inflammatory syndromes
formal: Idiopathic or IgG4-related inflammation of orbital tissues causing pain, proptosis, diplopia and ophthalmoplegia; diagnosis of exclusion, responsive to steroids.
simple: Swelling and inflammation behind the eye that can cause pain, bulging of the eye and double vision.
th: กลุ่มโรคอักเสบในเบ้าตาที่ไม่ใช่การติดเชื้อหรือมะเร็ง เช่น idiopathic orbital inflammation (pseudotumour), IgG4-related disease และ Tolosa–Hunt ทำให้ปวดตา ตาโปน เห็นภาพซ้อน ตอบสนองดีต่อ steroid
tempoNote: Painful onset over days to a few weeks; relapses are common after steroid taper
feat: Orbital pain, eyelid swelling and redness, proptosis and diplopia, typically unilateral in adults
Restricted eye movements from extraocular muscle (myositis), lacrimal gland or diffuse orbital fat involvement
Apical involvement may cause optic neuropathy with visual loss and colour desaturation
Tolosa–Hunt pattern: painful ophthalmoplegia from cavernous sinus, superior orbital fissure or apex with mild or no proptosis
Rapid improvement of pain within days of corticosteroid, but it does not by itself prove the diagnosis
inv: MRI orbits with contrast and fat suppression, with sinuses and cavernous sinus
Blood tests: ANCA, IgG4, ACE, thyroid antibodies, ESR, CRP and infection screen to look for systemic disease
Biopsy when presentation is atypical, bilateral, steroid-resistant or relapsing, to exclude lymphoma and IgG4-related disease

case.story: Four days of severe pain around the right eye, redness and double vision when looking to the right. No fever, no sinus symptoms, no thyroid history.
case.exam: Mild right proptosis, lid swelling, injected conjunctiva over the lateral rectus, limited abduction and painful eye movements, normal acuity and colour vision.
case.tests: MRI shows enlargement and enhancement of the right lateral rectus including the tendon; ESR mildly raised, ANCA and IgG4 negative, TSH normal; pain and diplopia improve after high-dose prednisolone.
case.q: What distinguishes this from thyroid eye disease and what finding would prompt biopsy?
case.a: Acute painful onset with tendon involvement and normal thyroid tests favour idiopathic orbital myositis; failed steroid response, relapse or bilateral/atypical features would justify biopsy to exclude lymphoma, IgG4-related disease or vasculitis.

det.patho: Orbital inflammatory syndromes are non-infective, non-neoplastic inflammatory conditions that can involve any orbital structure, with a pleomorphic inflammatory infiltrate followed by reactive fibrosis. Idiopathic orbital inflammation, formerly pseudotumour, is a diagnosis of exclusion, while IgG4-related ophthalmic disease, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, sarcoidosis and Tolosa–Hunt syndrome are defined entities with specific features.
det.clinical: Idiopathic orbital inflammatory disease is usually unilateral in adults, though bilateral disease occurs in children and should prompt a search for systemic disease. It may involve muscles (myositis), the lacrimal gland, orbital fat, the sclera or the apex. Pain, proptosis, diplopia and lid swelling develop over days. Tolosa–Hunt syndrome produces a steroid-responsive painful ophthalmoplegia with variable pupillary and trigeminal involvement and a relapsing course. Symptoms of sinus disease or bilateral inflammation raise the possibility of granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
det.diagnosis: Infection, thyroid eye disease, tumour and vascular lesions must be excluded first. MRI with contrast and fat suppression characterises the pattern, and blood tests screen for ANCA vasculitis, IgG4 disease, sarcoidosis and infection. Biopsy is advised for atypical presentations, bilateral disease, poor steroid response or recurrence. Tolosa–Hunt syndrome remains a diagnosis of exclusion and needs thorough investigation of the cavernous sinus and skull base.
det.treatment: Systemic corticosteroids, for example prednisolone 1 mg/kg tapered over weeks, give a rapid response in most patients. Relapsing, steroid-dependent or IgG4-related disease is treated with steroid-sparing agents such as methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate or rituximab. Radiotherapy is a rarely used alternative. For vasculitis, cyclophosphamide or rituximab with steroids is used. Optic nerve compression requires urgent treatment.
det.prognosis: Most patients respond to treatment, but relapse and fibrosis occur in a substantial minority.
pearls: Pain is the main clue, in contrast to thyroid eye disease where it is usually minimal.
Do not diagnose by steroid response alone; biopsy atypical or relapsing cases.
Bilateral orbital inflammation suggests systemic disease such as IgG4 disease or GPA.
det.thd: โรคอักเสบในเบ้าตาไม่ใช่การติดเชื้อหรือมะเร็ง เช่น idiopathic orbital inflammation (pseudotumour), IgG4-related disease และ Tolosa–Hunt ผู้ป่วยปวดตา ตาโปน เปลือกตาบวม และเห็นภาพซ้อน ตรวจ MRI เบ้าตาและเลือดหาโรคร่วม เช่น ANCA และ IgG4 และตัดชิ้นเนื้อถ้าไม่ปกติหรือไม่ตอบสนอง รักษาด้วย prednisolone และใช้ยากดภูมิหรือ rituximab ในรายที่กำเริบ

name: Orbital pseudotumour
formal: Idiopathic non-infectious orbital inflammation with painful proptosis, ophthalmoplegia and chemosis, rapidly responsive to corticosteroids; excludes thyroid eye disease, lymphoma and infection.
simple: A non-cancerous swelling behind the eye causing pain, bulging and double vision, which usually responds to steroids.
th: การอักเสบของเบ้าตาที่ไม่ทราบสาเหตุและไม่ใช่การติดเชื้อ ทำให้ปวดตา ตาโปน กลอกตาลำบาก ตอบสนองดีต่อสเตียรอยด์
tempoNote: Hours to days to peak; may remit, recur or end in fibrosis
feat: Unilateral orbital pain, worse on eye movement, lid swelling, redness and chemosis
Proptosis with restricted movement and diplopia; the process may centre on one muscle (orbital myositis), the lacrimal gland, the apex or the whole orbit
Optic neuropathy (reduced acuity or colour vision, RAPD) when the apex is involved
Natural course varies: spontaneous remission, intermittent flares, or persistent inflammation that fibroses into a frozen orbit
Myositis involves the tendons of the enlarged muscle, unlike thyroid eye disease where tendons are spared
inv: MRI or CT orbits with contrast: ill-defined enhancing infiltrate of fat, lacrimal gland or muscles including their tendons
Exclusion screen: TFTs and TRAb, ANCA, ACE, serum IgG4, ANA, infection screen and imaging of sinuses
Biopsy for atypical, bilateral, recurrent, steroid-resistant or apical cases, to exclude lymphoma, IgG4-related disease and granulomatous disease

case.story: Two days of severe right eye pain on looking sideways, with red swollen lids and double vision. No fever or sinus symptoms.
case.exam: Mild proptosis, injection over the medial rectus, limited abduction and adduction, normal acuity, no RAPD, normal temperature.
case.tests: MRI shows an enlarged medial rectus including its tendon; thyroid tests and ANCA are negative. Pain and diplopia settle within three days of oral prednisolone.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and what scan feature separates it from thyroid eye disease?
case.a: Idiopathic orbital inflammation (orbital myositis type); tendon involvement points to inflammation rather than thyroid disease.

read.where: Chapter 3: Orbit — Non-infective inflammatory disease (idiopathic orbital inflammatory disease, orbital myositis)
8 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System

det.patho: Idiopathic orbital inflammatory disease is a non-specific inflammatory process in the orbit with polymorphous cellular infiltrate, and it can later fibrose. It is a diagnosis of exclusion; many cases once labelled pseudotumour are now recognised as IgG4-related disease, sarcoidosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis or lymphoma. Immune dysregulation is suspected but the trigger is unknown.
det.clinical: Typical patients have acute unilateral pain, lid swelling and redness with painful eye movements. Subtypes follow the anatomy: myositis (pain and diplopia on gaze toward the inflamed muscle), dacryoadenitis (S-shaped ptosis over the lacrimal gland), anterior, diffuse or apical disease, with optic nerve compression in the latter. Children, bilateral disease or systemic features raise the possibility of another cause. Relapse after steroid taper is common, particularly in myositis.
det.diagnosis: Rule out infection and an acute orbital inflammatory mimic first (orbital cellulitis, sinus disease, cavernous sinus thrombosis and carotid-cavernous fistula), then thyroid eye disease. MRI shows the distribution and tendon involvement. Biopsy should not be postponed when the picture is atypical, bilateral or fails to respond within about a week, since lymphoma and IgG4 disease can respond temporarily to steroids and then recur.
det.treatment: Mild disease can be observed or treated with NSAIDs. Moderate or severe disease, and any vision threat, receives oral prednisolone around 1 mg/kg daily with a slow taper over weeks to months, followed by steroid-sparing agents (methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate, rituximab) for relapsing or dependent cases. Low-dose orbital radiotherapy is reserved for refractory disease. Apical disease with optic neuropathy is an emergency requiring prompt high-dose steroid.
det.prognosis: Often good, but relapse is frequent; a minority progress to fibrosis and a frozen orbit with persistent diplopia and visual loss.
pearls: Painful proptosis with tendon involvement suggests inflammation; tendon-sparing suggests thyroid eye disease.
Steroid response does not exclude lymphoma.
Fever plus sinusitis: think orbital cellulitis first.
det.thd: Orbital pseudotumour หรือ idiopathic orbital inflammatory disease คือการอักเสบของเนื้อเยื่อในเบ้าตาที่ไม่ใช่การติดเชื้อและไม่ทราบสาเหตุ ผู้ป่วยปวดตา ตาแดง หนังตาบวม ตาโปน และเห็นภาพซ้อน โดยอาจอักเสบที่กล้ามเนื้อตา ต่อมน้ำตา หรือบริเวณ apex ตรวจ MRI ดูการอักเสบรวมถึงเอ็นกล้ามเนื้อ ต้องแยกโรคไทรอยด์ตา การติดเชื้อ IgG4 และมะเร็งต่อมน้ำเหลือง รักษาด้วยสเตียรอยด์ขนาดสูงแล้วค่อยลดช้า ๆ กลับเป็นซ้ำได้บ่อย อาจต้องใช้ยากดภูมิหรือตัดชิ้นเนื้อ

name: Organic acidurias
formal: Group of inherited metabolic diseases such as propionic, methylmalonic and glutaric aciduria with accumulation of organic acids, causing metabolic acidosis, encephalopathy, and basal ganglia injury.
simple: Inherited disorders in which the body cannot break down certain protein parts, causing acid build-up and brain injury.
more: Urine organic acid analysis and newborn screening diagnose them. Treat with protein restriction, carnitine and emergency fluids; early treatment improves outcome. Inherited disorders of amino acid or fatty acid catabolism, such as methylmalonic or propionic acidaemia, causing metabolic acidosis, encephalopathy and basal ganglia injury.
th: กลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่ย่อยกรดอะมิโนหรือกรดไขมันไม่สมบูรณ์จนกรดอินทรีย์คั่ง เช่น propionic, methylmalonic, isovaleric, glutaric aciduria ทำให้เลือดเป็นกรด สมองบวม และ basal ganglia เสียหาย
tempoNote: Neonatal crisis, intermittent decompensations, or slowly progressive neurological disease
feat: Newborn poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, hypotonia, seizures and coma after a symptom-free interval
Later crises triggered by infection, fasting or protein excess
Basal ganglia stroke-like injury causing dystonia (MMA, PA, GA1)
Macrocephaly with subdural collections in glutaric aciduria type 1
Long-term: cardiomyopathy (PA), renal failure and optic atrophy (MMA)
inv: Blood gas with anion gap, ketones, ammonia, lactate, glucose
Urine organic acids by GC-MS and plasma acylcarnitines (C3, C5, C5DC)
Newborn screening; MRI for basal ganglia and white matter changes; gene testing

case.who: 14-month-old boy from Nakhon Phanom with a large head
case.story: Normal development until a febrile gastroenteritis; within a day he became floppy and then developed twisting movements of the limbs that have persisted.
case.exam: Macrocephaly, generalised dystonia, poor head control.
case.tests: MRI: bilateral striatal necrosis and widened Sylvian fissures; urine glutaric and 3-hydroxyglutaric acid raised; C5DC high.
case.q: Which organic aciduria is this and could it have been prevented?
case.a: Glutaric aciduria type 1; newborn screening with lysine-restricted diet, carnitine and intensive sick-day treatment largely prevents striatal injury.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Organic Acidaemias
Section II: Epidemiology, Etiology, and Diagnosis

det.patho: Enzyme defects in intermediary metabolism (mostly in branched-chain amino acid, lysine or tryptophan breakdown) cause specific CoA esters and organic acids to accumulate. These inhibit the urea cycle, Krebs cycle and mitochondrial function, sequester carnitine and directly injure neurons. Vulnerable regions such as the striatum suffer infarct-like damage during crises.
det.clinical: Classic forms present in the neonate with encephalopathy and acidosis. Intermediate forms decompensate with illness during infancy or childhood. Cerebral organic acidurias (GA1, L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria, Canavan) may lack acidosis and present instead with movement disorders, macrocephaly or leukodystrophy. Multisystem complications include pancreatitis, cardiomyopathy and kidney disease.
det.diagnosis: Urine organic acid profile plus acylcarnitine profile identifies most disorders; confirm with enzyme or gene tests. Many are on expanded newborn screening programmes, including in Thailand. Samples during acute illness have the highest yield.
det.treatment: Emergency: stop protein for 24–48 hours, give high-energy IV glucose (with insulin if needed), correct acidosis, give L-carnitine, and use dialysis for severe hyperammonaemia; carglumic acid helps hyperammonaemia in PA and MMA. Long term: precursor-restricted diet, carnitine, cofactors (vitamin B12 for responsive MMA, riboflavin in some), and written emergency plans. Liver (or liver-kidney) transplant is an option for severe MMA and PA.
det.prognosis: Improved with screening and early care, but severe neonatal forms still carry significant mortality and neurological disability.
pearls: Neonatal encephalopathy + high anion gap acidosis + ketosis: send urine organic acids and acylcarnitines.
A child with sudden dystonia after a febrile illness: think GA1, MMA or PA.
Subdural haematomas in GA1 can be mistaken for non-accidental injury.
det.thd: Organic acidurias คือกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่ขาดเอนไซม์ย่อยกรดอะมิโนหรือกรดไขมัน จึงมีกรดอินทรีย์คั่ง ทารกดูดนมไม่ดี อาเจียน ซึม เลือดเป็นกรด หรือมีวิกฤตซ้ำเมื่อป่วย บางรายสมองส่วน basal ganglia เสียหายจนเกิด dystonia ตรวจปัสสาวะหากรดอินทรีย์และ acylcarnitine ในเลือด รักษาด้วยการหยุดโปรตีนชั่วคราว ให้กลูโคส carnitine และควบคุมอาหารระยะยาว

name: Organic solvents, neurological toxicity
formal: Chronic or acute exposure to toluene, n-hexane or related solvents causing encephalopathy, cerebellar ataxia, leukoencephalopathy and peripheral neuropathy.
simple: Nerve and brain damage caused by breathing or touching industrial solvents such as glue or paint thinner.
th: พิษต่อระบบประสาทจากตัวทำละลายอินทรีย์ เช่น toluene (ดมกาว/ทินเนอร์) และ n-hexane ทำให้สมองเสื่อม เดินเซ เนื้อขาวสมองผิดปกติ และปลายประสาทเสื่อม
tempoNote: Acute intoxication within minutes of inhalation; encephalopathy, ataxia and neuropathy develop over months to years of repeated exposure
feat: Acute exposure: euphoria, dizziness, slurred speech, ataxia, then drowsiness, seizures or coma
Chronic toluene inhalation: cognitive decline, cerebellar ataxia, tremor, hearing loss and optic neuropathy
n-Hexane or MnBK (methyl n-butyl ketone): subacute distal sensorimotor neuropathy that may worsen for weeks after exposure stops (coasting)
Ask about glue or thinner sniffing in teenagers and occupational exposure (shoe, paint, printing, cleaning industries)
inv: MRI brain: diffuse white matter T2 change, cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, and T2 hypointensity of thalami in chronic toluene use
Nerve conduction: axonal loss with some conduction slowing in hexacarbon neuropathy
Electrolytes and blood gas: toluene causes hypokalaemia and renal tubular acidosis
Urinary metabolites (hippuric acid for toluene, 2,5-hexanedione for n-hexane) if exposure is recent

case.who: 19-year-old man from an urban community in Bangkok
case.story: Has inhaled paint thinner daily for three years; family notices slow thinking, slurred speech and frequent falls.
case.exam: Broad-based ataxic gait, dysarthria, bilateral horizontal nystagmus, mild spasticity of legs, reduced hearing.
case.tests: MRI shows diffuse white matter hyperintensity and cerebellar atrophy; potassium 2.8 mmol/L with normal anion gap acidosis.
case.q: Which solvent is responsible, and what is the main treatment?
case.a: Toluene leukoencephalopathy; stop exposure (addiction treatment and social support), correct electrolytes and offer rehabilitation.

read.where: Chapter 7. Occupational, Biologic, and Environmental Toxic Neuropathies
Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System
Chapter 35 Neurotoxin Exposure in the Workplace

det.patho: Lipophilic solvents dissolve readily into myelin and neuronal membranes, causing acute depression of neuronal function. Chronic toluene exposure damages myelin, giving a leukoencephalopathy with cerebellar and brainstem involvement. n-Hexane and the related ketone MnBK are metabolised to 2,5-hexanedione, which cross-links neurofilaments and produces giant axonal swellings in long nerves. Trichloroethylene is linked to trigeminal sensory loss.
det.clinical: Acute intoxication resembles alcohol, with risk of arrhythmia and sudden death. Long-term inhalant use produces a combination of dementia, ataxia, pyramidal signs, eye movement abnormalities and deafness. Occupational exposure at lower doses causes subtler cognitive and mood symptoms, sometimes called chronic solvent encephalopathy, whose existence as a distinct entity is debated. Hexacarbon neuropathy begins in the feet and may progress for weeks after removal from exposure.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on a careful exposure history from patient and family, supported by typical MRI and nerve conduction findings. Metabolite levels help only for recent exposure. Exclude B12 deficiency, alcohol, inherited ataxias, demyelinating disease and other toxins. Workplace investigation and notification may be needed for occupational cases.
det.treatment: The essential step is ending exposure, with addiction and psychosocial treatment for inhalant users and occupational hygiene measures for workers. Correct potassium and acid-base disorders and monitor heart rhythm in acute toxicity. Rehabilitation, hearing support and treatment of neuropathic pain help function. There is no specific antidote.
det.prognosis: Neuropathy and mild cognitive effects often improve over months after exposure ends; established toluene leukoencephalopathy usually leaves permanent deficits.
pearls: Young person with ataxia, dementia, deafness and hypokalaemia: ask about thinner or glue sniffing.
Hexacarbon neuropathy can keep worsening for weeks after exposure stops; do not assume ongoing exposure.
Thalamic T2 hypointensity on MRI is a characteristic toluene clue.
det.thd: ตัวทำละลายอินทรีย์ เช่น toluene ในทินเนอร์และกาว หรือ n-hexane ในโรงงาน เป็นพิษต่อระบบประสาท การสูดดมเรื้อรังทำให้สมองเสื่อม เดินเซ หูตึง และเนื้อขาวสมองผิดปกติ ส่วน n-hexane ทำให้ปลายประสาทเสื่อมที่อาจแย่ต่ออีกหลายสัปดาห์หลังหยุดสัมผัส วินิจฉัยจากประวัติการสัมผัส MRI และ NCS รักษาโดยหยุดสัมผัส แก้เกลือแร่ และฟื้นฟู

name: Organophosphate poisoning
formal: Cholinesterase inhibition producing cholinergic crisis with muscarinic, nicotinic and CNS features and intermediate syndrome with proximal weakness.
simple: Poisoning by pesticides that overstimulates nerves, causing sweating, small pupils, weakness and breathing failure.
more: Treat with atropine, pralidoxime, decontamination and ventilatory support; delayed neuropathy can follow.
th: พิษยาฆ่าแมลงกลุ่ม organophosphate — มีอาการ cholinergic เฉียบพลัน, intermediate syndrome และ neuropathy ภายหลัง
tempoNote: Cholinergic crisis in minutes–hours; intermediate syndrome day 1–4; delayed neuropathy 2–3 weeks later
feat: Muscarinic excess: pinpoint pupils, sweating, salivation, bronchorrhoea, bradycardia, vomiting, diarrhoea
Nicotinic effects: fasciculations, then weakness; CNS: confusion, seizures, coma
Intermediate syndrome: neck flexor, proximal and respiratory muscle weakness 1–4 days later
OP-induced delayed neuropathy: distal motor-predominant axonal neuropathy with later spasticity
Garlic or solvent smell; history of farm work or self-poisoning
inv: Red-cell acetylcholinesterase (or plasma butyrylcholinesterase) activity — supportive, do not delay treatment

NCS/EMG weeks later if distal weakness develops

case.story: Drank an insecticide after a family argument; brought in drooling, vomiting and short of breath.
case.exam: Pupils 1 mm, wet crackles, HR 48, diffuse fasciculations; responsive to voice.
case.tests: Plasma cholinesterase markedly reduced; SpO2 88% on room air.
case.q: On day 3, after atropine is tapered, he cannot lift his head and breathing becomes shallow. What is this?
case.a: Intermediate syndrome — postsynaptic NMJ failure needing ventilatory support; atropine does not reverse it. Watch neck flexion and vital capacity daily.

det.patho: Organophosphorus insecticides (and the related military nerve agents) phosphorylate the active site of acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine builds up at muscarinic endings, autonomic ganglia, the neuromuscular junction and central synapses. Over minutes to days, depending on the compound, the enzyme–poison complex 'ages' into a permanent bond that oximes can no longer reverse; carbamates bind reversibly and do not age, which is why their toxicity is shorter. Intermediate syndrome reflects sustained postsynaptic nicotinic failure at the motor end-plate, whereas the delayed polyneuropathy (OPIDN) follows inhibition and ageing of neuropathy target esterase by certain compounds, triggering a central–peripheral distal axonopathy of the longest motor fibres and corticospinal tracts. Many products also contain solvents that add aspiration and CNS toxicity.
det.clinical: The acute cholinergic crisis appears within minutes to hours: miosis, salivation, lacrimation, sweating, bronchorrhoea and bronchospasm, vomiting, diarrhoea and urination, with bradycardia (though tachycardia and hypertension from nicotinic or hypoxic drive are common), then fasciculations, weakness, agitation, seizures and coma; most deaths are from respiratory failure. About 1–4 days later, often as muscarinic signs seem controlled, intermediate syndrome brings weakness of neck flexors, proximal limbs, cranial muscles and the diaphragm with sudden respiratory failure, but no sensory loss. Some 1–3 weeks after exposure to particular compounds, OPIDN starts with cramping calf pain and distal paraesthesia, then foot and hand weakness and foot drop; as peripheral nerves recover, spasticity, hyperreflexia and a spastic gait may be unmasked. In Thailand most severe cases follow deliberate ingestion or agricultural exposure, and some patients also have late neuropsychiatric problems.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the toxidrome plus exposure history (product container, farm work, smell of garlic or solvent); never delay atropine for laboratory confirmation. Red-cell acetylcholinesterase mirrors synaptic inhibition more closely than plasma butyrylcholinesterase, although the plasma assay is more widely available; both support the diagnosis and help track recovery but correlate imperfectly with severity. Watch for intermediate syndrome with serial neck-flexion strength, single-breath count, vital capacity and blood gases; repetitive nerve stimulation may show a decrement or repetitive CMAPs after single shocks. OPIDN is confirmed by NCS showing low motor amplitudes with denervation on EMG, and later corticospinal signs. Differentials include carbamate, paraquat or mixed pesticide poisoning, myasthenic crisis, GBS and botulism.
det.treatment: Resuscitate: secure the airway early (avoid succinylcholine, whose action is greatly prolonged), give oxygen, remove contaminated clothes and wash the skin, with staff wearing gloves. Give IV atropine 1–3 mg and double the dose every 5 minutes until the chest is clear on auscultation, heart rate exceeds about 80, systolic pressure exceeds about 80 mmHg, and the skin and axillae are dry, then maintain with an infusion of roughly 10–20% of the loading total per hour, titrating to avoid atropine toxicity (confusion, hyperthermia, absent bowel sounds). Pralidoxime may be added early, particularly for diethyl compounds, but trials have not shown a clear survival benefit; benzodiazepines treat seizures and agitation. Monitor in a high-dependency bed for at least several days for intermediate syndrome and ventilate promptly; OPIDN has no specific treatment, so rehabilitation, orthoses and spasticity care are the mainstays.
det.prognosis: Mortality depends on the compound, dose and speed of atropinisation and ventilation; highly toxic or fast-ageing compounds and large deliberate ingestions carry the highest risk. Intermediate syndrome resolves within about 1–3 weeks with ventilatory support; OPIDN recovers slowly and incompletely, and residual spasticity is common when the corticospinal tracts are involved.
pearls: Atropine endpoints are a dry chest, heart rate above 80 and adequate BP — not pupil size.
Neck flexion weakness after the crisis settles is the warning sign of intermediate syndrome.
Fasciculations plus pinpoint pupils plus wet lungs in a farm worker: treat for organophosphate poisoning immediately.
Do not use succinylcholine for intubation — paralysis may last hours.
det.thd: Organophosphate ยับยั้ง acetylcholinesterase ทำให้ acetylcholine คั่งที่ปลายประสาท muscarinic, nicotinic และในสมอง ระยะแรกภายในไม่กี่ชั่วโมงมีน้ำลายและเสมหะมาก รูม่านตาเล็ก เหงื่อออก อาเจียน ถ่ายเหลว หัวใจเต้นช้า กล้ามเนื้อเต้นระริก แล้วซึมหรือชัก ต้องดูแลทางเดินหายใจ ล้างตัว และให้ atropine 1–3 mg เพิ่มเป็นสองเท่าทุก 5 นาทีจนปอดแห้ง ชีพจรมากกว่า 80 และความดันดี แล้วต่อด้วยยาหยด อาจให้ pralidoxime ร่วม ห้ามใช้ succinylcholine ช่วงวันที่ 1–4 อาจเกิด intermediate syndrome คือคออ่อน แขนขาส่วนต้นอ่อน และหายใจล้มเหลวทันที ต้องเฝ้าดูกำลังกล้ามเนื้อคอและการหายใจ อีก 1–3 สัปดาห์ต่อมาบางรายเกิด OPIDN คือปลายประสาทสั่งการเสีย เท้าตก และอาจเกร็งภายหลัง

name: Orgasmic sex headache
formal: Primary headache of explosive onset at orgasm, lasting minutes to hours; must exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome; usually benign.
simple: A sudden severe headache at the moment of sexual climax, usually harmless but needing a check for serious causes.
ab: primary headache associated with sexual activity
th: ปวดศีรษะชนิดปฐมภูมิที่เกิดขึ้นทันทีรุนแรงขณะถึงจุดสุดยอด นานเป็นนาทีถึงชั่วโมง ต้องแยกเลือดออกใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมองและ RCVS ก่อนเสมอ
tempoNote: Explosive onset at or just before orgasm; attacks cluster over weeks to months then often remit
feat: Sudden severe bilateral or occipital headache at orgasm, peaking within seconds
A milder dull pre-orgasmic headache building with sexual excitement is the other subtype
Lasts from a minute to several hours; no focal deficits
More common in men; often comorbid with migraine or exertional headache
Bouts recur over weeks, then may disappear for months or years

case.story: For two weeks he has had a sudden severe pounding headache at orgasm on three occasions, each lasting about 40 minutes; he has a history of migraine.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination, BP 128/80.
case.tests: CT brain, CT angiography and later MRA after one week are normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and how can attacks be prevented?
case.a: Primary headache associated with sexual activity (orgasmic type); take indometacin 30–60 minutes beforehand or use a beta-blocker for preventive cover, and reassure once secondary causes are excluded.

read.where: Chapter 40: Primary cough headache, primary exertional headache, and

det.patho: The mechanism is uncertain. Abrupt rises in blood pressure and intracranial pressure at orgasm, abnormal cerebrovascular reactivity and trigeminovascular activation have all been proposed. Overlap with migraine, exertional headache and RCVS suggests a shared vascular sensitivity, and some patients with recurrent sexual headache turn out to have RCVS.
det.clinical: ICHD-3 recognises one entity with two presentations: a dull pre-orgasmic ache that intensifies with arousal, and an explosive orgasmic headache. Attacks typically come in bouts over weeks to a year; about half of patients have only one bout. Vomiting, prolonged confusion, neck stiffness or focal symptoms suggest a secondary cause.
det.diagnosis: This is a diagnosis made only after excluding SAH, RCVS, dissection and other secondary causes, especially after a first thunderclap attack. Neuroimaging with vascular studies is standard; LP is considered when CT is unrevealing. If several thunderclap attacks happen within a short period, RCVS should be suspected and angiography repeated.
det.treatment: Reassurance is important as many patients avoid sex or feel embarrassed. Indometacin (about 25–50 mg) taken 30–60 minutes before sexual activity is the most used preventive option; triptans before activity are an alternative in some. A daily beta-blocker such as propranolol is used for frequent attacks. Stop drugs that can trigger vasoconstriction (decongestants, serotonergic drugs, cannabis).
det.prognosis: Usually benign and self-limited, though bouts may recur.
pearls: The first explosive sex-related headache is SAH or RCVS until imaging says otherwise.
Repeated thunderclaps within days suggest RCVS, not primary sex headache.
Pre-emptive indometacin is the practical first-line option.
det.thd: Orgasmic sex headache เป็นปวดศีรษะปฐมภูมิที่ปวดทันทีรุนแรงขณะถึงจุดสุดยอด นานเป็นนาทีถึงหลายชั่วโมง มักเป็นช่วง ๆ แล้วหายไปเอง ครั้งแรกต้องแยกเลือดออกใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมอง RCVS และหลอดเลือดฉีกขาดด้วย CT, CTA หรือเจาะหลัง การป้องกันใช้ indometacin ก่อนมีเพศสัมพันธ์หรือ propranolol ทุกวันในรายเป็นบ่อย และควรให้คำแนะนำให้ผู้ป่วยสบายใจ

name: Orofacial apraxia
formal: Inability to perform voluntary mouth and face movements on command with preserved automatic movements, from left frontal or opercular lesions, often with Broca aphasia.
simple: Difficulty making face and mouth movements on request, such as blowing or sticking out the tongue, although they happen automatically.
th: ไม่สามารถทำท่าทางของปากและใบหน้าตามคำสั่งได้ เช่น เป่าลม แลบลิ้น ทั้งที่การเคลื่อนไหวอัตโนมัติยังทำได้ มักเกิดจากรอยโรค frontal-opercular ซีกซ้ายร่วมกับ Broca aphasia
tempoNote: Sudden after stroke; gradual in neurodegenerative disease such as non-fluent primary progressive aphasia
feat: Cannot blow out a match, lick lips, cough or click the tongue on command or imitation
Same movements occur normally when automatic (licking crumbs, spontaneous cough)
Strength and sensation of face and tongue are not sufficient to explain the failure
Often accompanies Broca aphasia and apraxia of speech
Seen after left frontal-opercular or insular infarcts and in non-fluent variant PPA and CBS
inv: Bedside testing of commanded versus automatic orofacial actions
MRI brain: left inferior frontal, opercular or insular lesion or focal atrophy
Speech and language assessment for aphasia and apraxia of speech

case.who: 67-year-old man from Ayutthaya admitted with acute stroke
case.story: Sudden difficulty speaking and right arm weakness this morning.
case.exam: Non-fluent effortful speech, right face and arm weakness; cannot blow out a match or protrude the tongue on request, but licks his lips spontaneously after drinking.
case.tests: MRI diffusion shows an acute left frontal operculum and insula infarct.
case.q: What higher-cortical sign is shown with the mouth movements?
case.a: Orofacial (buccofacial) apraxia from a left frontal-opercular infarct, accompanying Broca aphasia.

read.where: 9 - Atypical parkinsonism, parkinsonism-­plus syndromes and secondary parkinsonian disorders

det.patho: Learned skilled movements of the lips, tongue and face depend on a left-hemisphere network including the inferior frontal gyrus, operculum, insula and their connections with premotor cortex. Damage disrupts planning of voluntary orofacial gestures while the brainstem-driven automatic programmes remain intact. Left MCA infarction is the usual cause.
det.clinical: Patients struggle to produce mouth movements when asked, often groping, making the wrong movement or saying the action aloud instead (e.g. saying 'blow'). Imitation may be slightly better than verbal command. It frequently coexists with apraxia of speech and Broca aphasia, and may impair swallowing initiation. In neurodegenerative disease it can be an early sign of non-fluent PPA or corticobasal syndrome.
det.diagnosis: Ask the patient to perform actions such as blowing, sucking through a straw, coughing, clicking the tongue and showing teeth, first to command then by imitation. Confirm that facial weakness or poor comprehension does not explain the errors. MRI localises the lesion.
det.treatment: There is no specific drug treatment. Speech and language therapy addresses apraxia of speech and communication strategies, and dysphagia assessment ensures safe swallowing. Treat the cause, such as acute stroke management or support in progressive aphasia.
det.prognosis: Often improves after stroke over weeks to months; progresses in neurodegenerative causes.
pearls: Compare commanded and automatic mouth movements: the gap defines apraxia.
Orofacial apraxia strongly points to the left hemisphere.
Look for it in PNFA, where it is a useful bedside clue.
det.thd: Orofacial apraxia คือภาวะที่ผู้ป่วยทำท่าทางปากและใบหน้าตามคำสั่งไม่ได้ เช่น เป่าลมหรือแลบลิ้น แต่ทำได้เองโดยอัตโนมัติ เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ frontal operculum หรือ insula ซีกซ้าย มักพบร่วมกับ Broca aphasia หลังหลอดเลือดสมองตีบ หรือในโรคสมองเสื่อมแบบ PNFA วินิจฉัยจากการตรวจข้างเตียงและ MRI รักษาด้วยการฝึกพูดและดูแลการกลืน

name: Orofacial chorea
formal: Involuntary irregular movements of lips, tongue and jaw, as in Huntington disease or tardive dyskinesia, or after levodopa or neuroleptics.
simple: Irregular uncontrolled movements of the mouth, lips and tongue.
th: การเคลื่อนไหวไม่เป็นจังหวะและไม่สม่ำเสมอของริมฝีปาก ลิ้น และขากรรไกร พบใน Huntington disease, tardive dyskinesia หรือหลังได้ levodopa หรือยาต้านโรคจิต
tempoNote: Gradual in degenerative causes; subacute after drugs or metabolic triggers
feat: Brief, irregular, flowing movements of lips, cheeks, tongue and jaw; tongue cannot be kept protruded (motor impersistence)
Causes: tardive syndrome, levodopa, Huntington disease, chorea-acanthocytosis, Sydenham chorea, autoimmune, metabolic (hyperglycaemia, hyperthyroidism)
Associated limb chorea, dysarthria or dysphagia depending on cause
Tongue and lip biting with self-injury suggests chorea-acanthocytosis
inv: Drug history (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, levodopa)
Blood glucose, thyroid function, calcium, renal and liver tests; blood film for acanthocytes; CK
MRI brain; genetic testing (HTT CAG repeat) when family history or progressive course

case.story: Family notice grimacing and restless mouth movements for two years, and he has become irritable and forgetful; his mother died with similar movements.
case.exam: Irregular lip and jaw movements, motor impersistence of the tongue, mild chorea of the fingers, slow saccades.
case.tests: MRI shows caudate atrophy; HTT gene shows 44 CAG repeats.
case.q: What is the diagnosis?
case.a: Huntington disease presenting with orofacial chorea; counsel and treat chorea if disabling (e.g. tetrabenazine), with psychiatric support.

det.patho: Chorea arises when indirect pathway output from the striatum is reduced, disinhibiting thalamocortical drive. Causes include striatal neuronal loss (Huntington disease), dopamine receptor hypersensitivity (tardive and levodopa-induced), immune attack (Sydenham, autoimmune) and metabolic disturbance (non-ketotic hyperglycaemia). The orofacial region is often prominent because of its large cortical and striatal representation.
det.clinical: Movements are random and flow from one part to another, unlike the repetitive pattern of tardive dyskinesia. Patients may incorporate them into purposeful gestures. Speech and swallowing can be affected. Associated features such as cognitive or psychiatric change, neuropathy, seizures or systemic disease point to the cause.
det.diagnosis: Characterise the movement carefully on video, then look for drugs, metabolic causes and family history. Blood tests including glucose, thyroid function and blood film are quick and useful. Genetic testing for Huntington disease requires counselling. MRI may show caudate atrophy, striatal hyperintensity in hyperglycaemia or other lesions.
det.treatment: Remove or reduce the causative drug and correct metabolic causes. Symptomatic options include VMAT2 inhibitors (tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine, valbenazine) or antipsychotics, balanced against depression and parkinsonism. Speech and swallowing therapy and dental care are important. Treat autoimmune and infectious causes specifically.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause: drug and metabolic chorea often improve, while Huntington disease progresses.
pearls: Random flowing movements suggest chorea; stereotyped repetitive ones suggest tardive dyskinesia.
Lip and tongue biting: think chorea-acanthocytosis.
Always check glucose in an older patient with new facial and limb chorea.
det.thd: Orofacial chorea คือการเคลื่อนไหวของริมฝีปาก ลิ้น และขากรรไกรแบบไม่เป็นจังหวะและไม่ซ้ำรูปแบบ สาเหตุมีทั้ง Huntington disease ยาต้านโรคจิต levodopa โรคภูมิคุ้มกัน และน้ำตาลในเลือดสูง ควรซักประวัติยาและครอบครัว ตรวจเลือดหาสาเหตุทางเมตาบอลิก และ MRI การรักษาคือแก้สาเหตุและใช้ VMAT2 inhibitor หากอาการรบกวนชีวิต

name: Orofacial dyskinesia
formal: Involuntary repetitive lip smacking, tongue protrusion and chewing, as in tardive dyskinesia from dopamine blockers, edentulous states or levodopa.
simple: Uncontrolled chewing, lip-smacking or tongue movements, often a side effect of some medicines.
more: Review drug history and dental status; stop or reduce the neuroleptic and consider switching to clozapine or quetiapine. VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine) are effective in tardive forms; spontaneous orofacial dyskinesia occurs in older people.
th: การเคลื่อนไหวซ้ำ ๆ ที่ไม่ตั้งใจของปาก เช่น ดูดปาก แลบลิ้น เคี้ยว พบใน tardive dyskinesia จากยาต้าน dopamine ผู้สูงอายุไม่มีฟัน หรือจาก levodopa
tempoNote: Develops over months; tardive forms may persist for years after drug withdrawal
feat: Stereotyped repetitive chewing, lip pursing, lip smacking, tongue protrusion or rolling
Patient often unaware; worsens with distraction and stress, disappears in sleep
Commonest cause: tardive dyskinesia after antipsychotics or metoclopramide
Other causes: levodopa peak-dose dyskinesia, spontaneous dyskinesia of old age, edentulous state
Can impair speech, eating and denture fit
inv: Detailed drug history including antiemetics and prior antipsychotics
AIMS rating to grade severity and follow response
Dental assessment; glucose, thyroid and other tests only if features suggest chorea of another cause

case.who: 58-year-old woman from Nakhon Pathom with schizophrenia
case.story: Took haloperidol for many years; her sister notices constant chewing and lip smacking for six months.
case.exam: Repetitive lip pursing and tongue writhing that stop when she is asked to speak; no limb chorea.
case.tests: Glucose and thyroid function normal.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and how would you manage it?
case.a: Tardive orofacial dyskinesia; switch to clozapine or quetiapine with psychiatric input and consider a VMAT2 inhibitor (valbenazine or deutetrabenazine).

det.patho: Chronic dopamine receptor blockade leads to upregulation and supersensitivity of striatal D2 receptors and maladaptive plasticity, producing tardive dyskinesia. Older age, female sex, diabetes, mood disorder and longer exposure increase risk. Spontaneous oral dyskinesia occurs in elderly people without drug exposure, and loss of dental proprioception contributes in edentulous patients.
det.clinical: The movements are stereotyped and repetitive, mostly of lips, tongue and jaw, sometimes with trunk rocking or finger movements. Patients are frequently unconcerned while families are distressed. Severe cases affect speech, swallowing and cause dental and oral ulceration. Tardive dyskinesia can appear on dose reduction or drug withdrawal (withdrawal-emergent dyskinesia).
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, requiring at least a few months of dopamine blocker exposure for the tardive label. Exclude other causes of chorea and dystonia, including Huntington disease, Wilson disease and metabolic disorders, when the history does not fit. Record baseline and follow-up AIMS scores.
det.treatment: Review the need for the causative drug; stop metoclopramide and consider switching antipsychotics to clozapine or quetiapine. VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine, or tetrabenazine where available) have the best evidence. Clonazepam and ginkgo biloba have modest evidence. Avoid anticholinergics, which may worsen the movements, and fit dentures in edentulous patients.
det.prognosis: Many cases persist for years; improvement is more likely with early recognition and drug change.
pearls: Ask about metoclopramide, a common hidden cause.
Anticholinergics help dystonia but can worsen tardive dyskinesia.
Use AIMS regularly in patients on long-term antipsychotics.
det.thd: Orofacial dyskinesia คือการเคลื่อนไหวซ้ำ ๆ ของปาก ลิ้น และขากรรไกร สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยที่สุดคือ tardive dyskinesia จากยาต้านโรคจิตหรือ metoclopramide นอกจากนี้พบในผู้สูงอายุที่ไม่มีฟันและจาก levodopa ควรประเมินความจำเป็นของยา เปลี่ยนเป็น clozapine หรือ quetiapine และใช้ VMAT2 inhibitor ในรายที่มีอาการมาก หลีกเลี่ยงยา anticholinergic

name: Orofacial tremor
formal: Rhythmic movement of lips, jaw or tongue, for example rabbit syndrome from antipsychotics, or tremor in Parkinson disease.
simple: Rhythmic shaking of the lips, jaw or tongue.
th: การสั่นเป็นจังหวะของริมฝีปาก ขากรรไกร หรือลิ้น เช่น rabbit syndrome จากยาต้านโรคจิต หรืออาการสั่นในโรคพาร์กินสัน
tempoNote: Subacute after starting dopamine blockers; slowly progressive in Parkinson disease
feat: Regular rhythmic movement of the lips, chin or jaw, usually at rest, sometimes on posture or speaking
Rabbit syndrome: fast (about 5 Hz) vertical perioral tremor sparing the tongue, after antipsychotics
Parkinson disease: jaw and lip rest tremor with limb rest tremor and bradykinesia
Essential tremor may involve the jaw or voice in older patients; dystonic jaw tremor also occurs
inv: Drug history (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, valproate)
Look for limb tremor, bradykinesia and rigidity
DAT-SPECT when drug-induced and degenerative parkinsonism need separation

case.who: 45-year-old man from Rayong on risperidone for bipolar disorder
case.story: Three months after a dose increase, his lips tremble constantly, especially when he is sitting quietly.
case.exam: Fast regular vertical lip and chin tremor, tongue still, mild bilateral bradykinesia and rigidity.
case.tests: Not needed.
case.q: What is this tremor and how is it treated?
case.a: Rabbit syndrome, a drug-induced parkinsonian perioral tremor; reduce or change the antipsychotic, and an anticholinergic usually helps.

read.where: 17 - The tardive syndromes: Phenomenology, concepts on pathophysiology and treatment, and other neuroleptic-­induced syndromes

det.patho: Orofacial tremor is a descriptive term rather than a single disease. Drug-induced forms are parkinsonian, from striatal D2 blockade, while Parkinson disease tremor reflects altered basal ganglia-cerebellar-thalamic oscillation. Essential and dystonic tremors involve cerebellar network dysfunction.
det.clinical: Rest tremor of the lips and jaw is typical of Parkinson disease, often with other rest tremor. Rabbit syndrome appears after months of antipsychotic exposure and mimics a rabbit chewing, but without tongue involvement. Jaw tremor in essential tremor is usually postural or kinetic. Dystonic jaw tremor is irregular and accompanied by jaw posturing.
det.diagnosis: Classify the tremor by rhythm, frequency, context (rest, posture, speaking) and associated signs. Review drugs carefully. DAT-SPECT helps if it is unclear whether parkinsonism is drug-induced or degenerative.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: reduce or switch antipsychotics and use anticholinergics for rabbit syndrome; dopaminergic therapy for Parkinson disease; propranolol or primidone for essential tremor; botulinum toxin for dystonic jaw tremor. Supportive dental and speech care may help.
det.prognosis: Drug-induced tremor usually improves after stopping the drug; degenerative forms follow the underlying disease.
pearls: Tongue spared + fast perioral tremor + antipsychotic = rabbit syndrome.
Jaw rest tremor is a classic Parkinson disease feature, not essential tremor.
Rabbit syndrome improves with anticholinergics, unlike tardive dyskinesia.
det.thd: Orofacial tremor คือการสั่นเป็นจังหวะของริมฝีปาก คาง หรือขากรรไกร เป็นคำบรรยายอาการไม่ใช่โรคเดียว สาเหตุสำคัญคือ rabbit syndrome จากยาต้านโรคจิต ซึ่งริมฝีปากสั่นเร็วแต่ลิ้นไม่สั่น และการสั่นขณะพักของขากรรไกรในโรคพาร์กินสัน การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ เช่น ปรับยาต้านโรคจิตและให้ anticholinergic หรือให้ยาพาร์กินสัน

name: Orolingual dyskinesia
formal: Repetitive involuntary movements of tongue, lips and jaw, such as chewing, lip smacking and tongue protrusion, typical of tardive dyskinesia from dopamine blockers or edentulous states.
simple: Repeated involuntary tongue, lip and jaw movements such as chewing or smacking.
more: Treat by withdrawing the offending drug if feasible, with VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine) as first-line; may persist for years.
th: การเคลื่อนไหวซ้ำ ๆ ของลิ้น ริมฝีปาก และขากรรไกร เช่น เคี้ยว ดูดปาก แลบลิ้น ซึ่งเป็นลักษณะของ tardive dyskinesia หรือพบในผู้สูงอายุไม่มีฟัน
tempoNote: Gradual onset; tardive cases may persist long after the drug is stopped
feat: Tongue darting in and out ('fly-catcher'), tongue writhing within the mouth, lip smacking and chewing
Stereotyped, repetitive; can be suppressed briefly and vanishes in sleep
Usually after months of dopamine blockers (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine)
Also seen in edentulous elderly people and as levodopa dyskinesia
Can cause tongue ulcers, dysarthria and denture problems
inv: Medication history including antiemetics and over-the-counter remedies
Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale (AIMS) at baseline and follow-up
Tests for other chorea causes (glucose, thyroid, blood film) only if the history is atypical

case.story: Took metoclopramide daily for a year for dyspepsia; now has constant tongue movements and her dentures keep falling out.
case.exam: Tongue moves in and out and rolls in the mouth, lips smack; movements briefly stop when asked to hold the tongue still.
case.tests: Glucose and thyroid normal.
case.q: What caused this and what is the next step?
case.a: Tardive orolingual dyskinesia from metoclopramide; stop the drug and consider a VMAT2 inhibitor if movements persist.

det.patho: Most cases are tardive, reflecting dopamine receptor supersensitivity and striatal plasticity after long-term blockade. Risk rises with age, female sex, diabetes and longer exposure, and with metoclopramide in older adults. Loss of dental support alters oral sensory feedback and contributes in edentulous patients.
det.clinical: Movements centre on the tongue and lips and may extend to the jaw, face, trunk or limbs. They are repetitive and patterned rather than random. Patients often underestimate them, while families find them distressing or stigmatising. Withdrawal of the drug can transiently worsen movements.
det.diagnosis: Diagnose clinically using drug history and observation, recording AIMS. Separate from chorea of other causes, from oromandibular dystonia and from tremor syndromes. Investigate further if there is family history, rapid progression or systemic features.
det.treatment: Withdraw the dopamine blocker where possible, or switch to clozapine or quetiapine in psychiatric patients. VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine) are first-line pharmacological therapy, with tetrabenazine as an alternative. Avoid anticholinergics. Proper dentures and oral care help edentulous patients; DBS of the globus pallidus is for severe refractory cases.
det.prognosis: May persist for years; partial improvement is common after drug withdrawal and VMAT2 inhibitor treatment.
pearls: Fly-catcher tongue in an older patient: ask about metoclopramide.
Withdrawal may temporarily worsen the movements; warn the family.
VMAT2 inhibitors are first-line; anticholinergics can worsen it.
det.thd: Orolingual dyskinesia คือการเคลื่อนไหวซ้ำ ๆ ของลิ้นและริมฝีปาก เช่น แลบลิ้นเข้าออก ม้วนลิ้น ดูดปาก ส่วนใหญ่เป็น tardive dyskinesia จากยาต้าน dopamine เช่น ยาต้านโรคจิตหรือ metoclopramide พบในผู้สูงอายุที่ไม่มีฟันได้ด้วย การรักษาคือหยุดหรือเปลี่ยนยา ใช้ VMAT2 inhibitor และหลีกเลี่ยง anticholinergic อาการอาจอยู่นานหลายปี

case.story: His wife notices his chin and tongue shaking while he watches television; his right hand also trembles at rest.
case.exam: Rest tremor of the jaw, lips and tongue in the mouth, right hand rest tremor, bradykinesia and rigidity; no tongue wasting.
case.tests: None required; good response to a levodopa trial.
case.q: What is the cause of the tongue tremor?
case.a: Parkinson disease with orolingual rest tremor; treat with dopaminergic therapy.

det.patho: Orolingual tremor is a sign rather than a disease, produced by the same oscillating circuits as limb tremor. Parkinsonian rest tremor arises from basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical interaction; essential and dystonic tremor involve the cerebellothalamic network. Some drugs enhance physiological tremor or cause parkinsonism.
det.clinical: Rest tongue tremor visible inside the mouth, often with jaw tremor, is common in Parkinson disease. Essential tremor tends to cause tremor on protrusion and speech, usually with voice and hand tremor. Isolated tongue tremor may be dystonic or functional. Fasciculations are irregular flickers, not rhythmic, and suggest motor neuron disease.
det.diagnosis: Watch the tongue lying relaxed inside the mouth first, then when it is pushed out. Look for associated limb tremor, parkinsonism, dystonia or bulbar weakness. Review drugs and check thyroid function. EMG and imaging only if there are atypical features.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying disorder: dopaminergic therapy for Parkinson disease, propranolol or primidone for essential tremor, botulinum toxin for focal dystonic tremor, and drug reduction for drug-induced tremor. Speech therapy helps when articulation is affected.
det.prognosis: Follows the underlying condition; drug-induced forms often resolve.
pearls: Look at the tongue resting in the mouth first: fasciculations vs tremor.
Jaw and tongue rest tremor favours Parkinson disease.
Tremor only on protrusion favours action tremor syndromes.

formal: Focal cranial dystonia with involuntary jaw, lip and tongue contractions causing jaw opening, closing or deviation; worsened by speaking or eating, relieved by sensory tricks; treated with botulinum toxin.

case.exam: Jaw-opening and left-deviating dystonia during speech, mild blepharospasm; dental examination normal; no drug exposure.
case.tests: MRI brain and copper studies normal.

det.patho: OMD is a focal dystonia from abnormal basal ganglia-cerebellar-cortical network function with reduced inhibition in brainstem reflex circuits. Most adult cases are idiopathic; others follow dopamine blocker exposure, brain injury, or form part of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation, neuroacanthocytosis, Wilson disease or genetic dystonias. Peripheral trauma or dental procedures are reported but not proven triggers.
det.clinical: Patients have difficulty speaking, chewing and swallowing, with jaw pain, tooth wear, temporomandibular problems and weight loss. Embarrassment and social withdrawal are common. Some forms appear only during specific tasks such as speaking or eating. It may spread to adjacent regions, especially the eyelids and neck.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, based on patterned involuntary jaw movements, triggers and sensory tricks. Distinguish it from TMJ disorders, bruxism, tardive dyskinesia, hemimasticatory spasm and functional disorders. Young onset or other neurological signs require MRI, copper studies, blood film and genetic testing.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin is first-line: lateral pterygoid and digastric for jaw opening, masseter and temporalis for jaw closing. Dysphagia and dysarthria are possible side effects. Oral agents (anticholinergics, clonazepam, baclofen) help some patients. Bite splints and sensory tricks may assist, and DBS of the globus pallidus is considered in refractory cases.
det.prognosis: Chronic; most patients gain meaningful relief with regular botulinum toxin.
pearls: Jaw-closing dystonia is often misdiagnosed as a dental or TMJ problem.
Check the drug history: tardive jaw dystonia is common.
Young-onset OMD with tongue protrusion: think neuroacanthocytosis or PKAN.

name: Orthostatic hypotension (OH)
formal: Sustained fall in blood pressure of at least 20/10 mmHg within three minutes of standing, from autonomic failure, hypovolaemia or drugs; seen in Parkinson disease, MSA and neuropathy.
simple: A drop in blood pressure on standing up that causes dizziness or fainting.
th: ความดันโลหิตลดลงอย่างน้อย 20/10 mmHg ภายใน 3 นาทีหลังยืน เกิดจากระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติเสื่อม ภาวะขาดน้ำ หรือยา พบในโรคพาร์กินสัน MSA และ neuropathy
tempoNote: Symptoms episodic on standing; neurogenic forms chronic and progressive
feat: Light-headedness, blurred vision, neck and shoulder (coat-hanger) ache or fainting on standing, after meals, heat or exertion
Neurogenic OH: little or no rise in heart rate on standing, often with supine hypertension
Causes: PD, MSA, DLB, pure autonomic failure, diabetic and amyloid neuropathy, autoimmune ganglionopathy
Non-neurogenic: dehydration, blood loss, antihypertensives, alpha-blockers, nitrates, antidepressants
Major cause of falls and cognitive fluctuation in older people
inv: Lying (5 min) and standing BP and heart rate at 1 and 3 minutes; ΔHR/ΔSBP below 0.5 bpm/mmHg suggests neurogenic
Head-up tilt and autonomic function tests (Valsalva) when bedside test is unclear

Glucose, B12, renal tests; consider TTR genetic tests, ganglionic AChR antibodies, DAT scan or skin biopsy by context

case.who: 68-year-old man from Lopburi with type 2 diabetes

case.exam: BP lying 162/88, after 3 minutes standing 108/64 with heart rate rising only from 74 to 78; reduced ankle reflexes and stocking sensory loss.
case.tests: Autonomic tests show abnormal Valsalva response; HbA1c 9.1%.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the first management steps?
case.a: Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension from diabetic autonomic neuropathy with supine hypertension; review drugs, increase fluid and salt, compression garments, head-up sleeping, then midodrine or fludrocortisone if needed.

det.patho: On standing, about 500–1000 mL of blood pools in the legs and splanchnic circulation; normally baroreflex-triggered sympathetic vasoconstriction maintains pressure. In neurogenic OH, failure of noradrenaline release from central (MSA) or peripheral (PD, pure autonomic failure, neuropathy) sympathetic neurones prevents this response. Non-neurogenic OH comes from volume loss, drugs or cardiac pump failure with an intact reflex.
det.clinical: Symptoms range from vague fatigue and cognitive slowing to recurrent syncope, and are worse in the morning, after meals, in heat and after alcohol. Many patients are asymptomatic despite large falls. Supine hypertension coexists in about half of neurogenic cases, complicating treatment. OH may precede motor symptoms of synucleinopathies by years.
det.diagnosis: By consensus, OH means a sustained drop of at least 20/10 mmHg (systolic/diastolic) within 3 minutes of upright posture, active or on a tilt table (30/15 when supine hypertension is present). A small heart rate rise suggests neurogenic OH. Delayed OH beyond three minutes can occur in early disease. Look for the cause with history, neurological examination, autonomic testing and targeted blood tests.
det.treatment: Start by stopping or reducing culprit drugs and correcting volume. Non-drug measures include fluids 2–2.5 L daily, extra salt, bolus water drinking, compression garments or abdominal binders, slow rising, counter-manoeuvres, small low-carbohydrate meals and sleeping with the bed head elevated. Drugs include midodrine, fludrocortisone, droxidopa (where available) and pyridostigmine for milder cases. Treat supine hypertension with short-acting agents at night and avoid lying flat by day.
det.prognosis: Neurogenic OH is associated with falls, cognitive decline and higher mortality; prognosis depends largely on the underlying disease.
pearls: Measure heart rate too: a blunted rise points to a neurogenic cause.
Coat-hanger neck pain on standing is a hypoperfusion symptom.
Treat for symptoms and falls, not the BP number; watch for supine hypertension.
det.thd: Orthostatic hypotension คือความดันลดลงอย่างน้อย 20/10 mmHg ภายใน 3 นาทีหลังลุกยืน ทำให้หน้ามืด ตาลาย ปวดต้นคอ หรือหมดสติ สาเหตุจากระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติเสื่อม เช่น พาร์กินสัน MSA เบาหวาน หรือจากยาและภาวะขาดน้ำ ถ้าชีพจรไม่เพิ่มตอนยืนชวนนึกถึงสาเหตุทางระบบประสาท การรักษาเริ่มจากหยุดยาที่เป็นสาเหตุ ดื่มน้ำ เพิ่มเกลือ ใส่ถุงน่องรัด นอนหัวสูง แล้วจึงใช้ยา เช่น midodrine หรือ fludrocortisone

name: Orthostatic myoclonus
formal: Brief jerks of the legs and trunk on standing that improve on walking or sitting, causing unsteadiness; often cortical and seen in neurodegenerative disease.
simple: Sudden jerks in the legs when standing that make a person unsteady, easing when they sit.

feat: Shaky, jerky legs within seconds of standing still; relief when walking, leaning or sitting
Often described by patients as weak or wobbly legs rather than as jerks
Visible or palpable irregular twitches in thigh and calf muscles while standing
Frequently accompanies neurodegeneration such as MSA, Lewy body disease or Alzheimer disease
Commonly misread as orthostatic tremor, orthostatic hypotension or a fear-of-falling gait

det.patho: The generator is not fully settled; some patients show cortical features on back-averaging, while others seem to have a subcortical source. It appears to be a stance-specific failure of the postural control network rather than a disease in its own right. Most reported cases have an associated neurodegenerative or structural brain disorder.
det.clinical: The usual complaint is unsteadiness that starts soon after rising and improves with movement, so many patients are labelled as having gait apraxia or anxiety. Jerks may be subtle and are best felt with a hand on the thigh. Falls can occur. It is often discovered in patients already followed for parkinsonism, MSA or cognitive decline, and may even be the first sign.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on surface EMG while standing, showing brief arrhythmic bursts, often synchronous across muscles. Measure orthostatic blood pressure to separate it from hypotension, and look for features of a neurodegenerative disorder. Distinguishing it from orthostatic tremor matters because treatment and associations differ.
det.treatment: Evidence is limited to small series. Levetiracetam, clonazepam or other antimyoclonic drugs help some patients. Physiotherapy, walking aids and strategies such as shifting weight or leaning on a support are practical measures. Treat the associated disorder where possible.
det.prognosis: Course mostly follows the underlying neurodegenerative disease; the myoclonus itself may respond partially to drugs.
pearls: Leg wobble on standing that disappears on walking: think orthostatic tremor or orthostatic myoclonus and request standing EMG.
Orthostatic myoclonus is irregular and brief; orthostatic tremor is very fast and rhythmic.
Its presence should prompt a search for MSA, Lewy body disease or Alzheimer disease.

det.patho: Primary orthostatic tremor is thought to arise from a central oscillator in the brainstem or cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuit, as the 13–18 Hz rhythm is coherent across all leg, trunk and even arm muscles bearing weight. It is rare, sporadic and slightly more common in women.
det.clinical: The main complaint is unsteadiness rather than tremor, which worsens the longer the patient stands and resolves with walking or sitting. The upper limbs can show the same tremor when weight-bearing (e.g. pushing on a table). Some develop additional parkinsonism, cerebellar signs or cognitive change (OT plus), and slower 'pseudo-orthostatic' tremor occurs in other disorders.
det.diagnosis: Surface EMG showing high-frequency (13–18 Hz) synchronous bursts on standing confirms it. Bedside clues are palpable or audible thigh/calf tremor. Exclude orthostatic myoclonus, slower orthostatic tremor in parkinsonism, orthostatic hypotension, cerebellar disorders and functional gait disturbance.
det.treatment: Clonazepam is the most commonly used drug; gabapentin, primidone and perampanel are alternatives, and levodopa may help a subset. Responses are often partial. Walking aids, a seat stick and avoiding prolonged standing help daily life. Thalamic or spinal cord stimulation has been tried in refractory cases.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive and seldom disabling for walking, but quality of life is affected; a minority develop other neurological features.
pearls: Unsteady standing still, fine when walking: think orthostatic tremor.
Put a stethoscope on the thigh — a helicopter-like rumble is a clue.
Confirm with leg surface EMG: 13–18 Hz.

name: Oscillatory myoclonus

simple: Repeated rhythmic muscle jerks.

case.a: Each burst is brief and shock-like with gaps, generated by a brainstem focus; it is oscillatory brainstem myoclonus.
