det.patho: Oscillatory myoclonus is a descriptive term rather than a disease: a myoclonic generator fires repeatedly at a semi-regular rate. The source can be sensorimotor cortex, brainstem reticular structures or spinal segments. Lesions, metabolic stress or drugs that disinhibit these circuits allow self-sustaining bursts.
det.clinical: Patients show runs of rhythmic jerks that may be provoked by stimuli or action and then die away. Cortical forms affect distal limbs and are often multifocal; brainstem forms are axial and startle-sensitive; spinal forms stay segmental and may continue in sleep. Because the rhythm resembles tremor, misclassification is common.
det.diagnosis: Neurophysiology is the key step: short bursts (often 10–50 ms in cortical myoclonus) favour myoclonus, while longer, alternating or co-contracting bursts favour tremor. Back-averaging, giant SSEPs and the C-reflex point to a cortical source. Imaging and a search for metabolic, toxic and drug causes follow the localisation.
det.treatment: Treat the cause where possible. For cortical forms, levetiracetam, valproate, clonazepam or piracetam are used, often in combination. Brainstem and spinal forms respond more often to clonazepam; botulinum toxin is an option for focal segmental jerks. Avoid drugs that worsen myoclonus where possible.
det.prognosis: Depends on the cause; drug response is better in cortical than in spinal forms.
pearls: Rhythmicity does not prove tremor: short EMG bursts mean myoclonus.
Myoclonus persisting in sleep points to a spinal or brainstem source.
Cortical myoclonus responds to levetiracetam and valproate; phenytoin and carbamazepine may worsen it.
det.thd: Oscillatory myoclonus คือ myoclonus ที่เกิดซ้ำเป็นชุดอย่างค่อนข้างเป็นจังหวะจนดูคล้าย tremor ต้นกำเนิดอาจอยู่ที่ cortex ก้านสมอง หรือไขสันหลัง การแยกจาก tremor ใช้ EMG ที่เห็น burst สั้นมาก ควรค้นหาสาเหตุด้วย MRI และตรวจเมตาบอลิก รักษาตามต้นกำเนิด เช่น levetiracetam หรือ clonazepam

name: Osler-Rendu-Weber disease
formal: Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, an autosomal dominant vascular disorder (ENG, ACVRL1) with mucocutaneous telangiectasias, recurrent epistaxis and visceral arteriovenous malformations, causing stroke and brain abscess.
simple: An inherited disease with fragile abnormal blood vessels, causing nosebleeds and sometimes strokes or brain abscess.
more: Curacao criteria and genetic testing; screen for pulmonary and cerebral AVMs. Treat with embolisation, bevacizumab and iron replacement.
th: โรคหลอดเลือดถ่ายทอดแบบยีนเด่น มีเส้นเลือดฝอยขยายที่ผิวหนังและเยื่อบุ เลือดกำเดาไหลซ้ำ และ AVM ในปอด ตับ และสมอง ทำให้เกิด stroke และฝีในสมอง
tempoNote: Lifelong disorder; nosebleeds start in childhood, telangiectases increase with age; neurological events are sudden (stroke, abscess, haemorrhage)
feat: Recurrent spontaneous nosebleeds, often from childhood, causing iron deficiency anaemia
Red spots on lips, tongue, fingertips and nasal mucosa that blanch with pressure
Pulmonary AVMs: paradoxical embolism causing ischaemic stroke or brain abscess, plus hypoxaemia and clubbing
Cerebral AVMs or capillary malformations that may bleed; spinal AVMs are rare
Gastrointestinal bleeding and hepatic AVMs (high-output heart failure) in adults
inv: Curaçao criteria: epistaxis, telangiectases, visceral AVM, first-degree relative (≥3 = definite)
Genetic testing: ENG (HHT1), ACVRL1 (HHT2), SMAD4 (with juvenile polyposis)
Screen with transthoracic contrast (bubble) echocardiography for pulmonary AVM; CT chest if positive
Brain MRI screening for cerebral AVMs; CBC and iron studies

case.story: Lifelong nosebleeds, like her mother. One week of fever and headache followed by right arm weakness and a focal seizure.
case.exam: Telangiectases on lips and fingertips, clubbing, SpO2 91% on air, right arm weakness.
case.tests: MRI: ring-enhancing left frontal abscess; bubble echo shows late right-to-left shunt; CT chest: right lower lobe pulmonary AVM.
case.q: How did the brain abscess arise, and what prevents a recurrence?
case.a: HHT with a pulmonary AVM allows bacteria to bypass the lung filter (paradoxical spread); embolise the pulmonary AVM and give antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures.

read.where: Chapter 9: Congenital Disorders of the Brain and Spine

det.patho: HHT is inherited in a dominant pattern and disturbs TGF-β/BMP9 signalling in vessel walls (ENG, ACVRL1, less often SMAD4 or GDF2). Haploinsufficiency leads to fragile dilated vessels and direct artery-to-vein connections without capillaries. Small lesions form mucocutaneous telangiectases; larger ones form AVMs in lung, liver, brain and gut. Prevalence is about 1 in 5,000–8,000 worldwide.
det.clinical: Epistaxis is the commonest and often most troublesome feature. Neurological complications mostly arise from pulmonary AVMs: right-to-left shunting lets clots and bacteria reach the brain, causing ischaemic stroke, TIA and abscess, sometimes as the first presentation. Cerebral AVMs (more common with ENG variants) can rupture, and liver AVMs can produce portosystemic encephalopathy or heart failure. Migraine is more frequent in those with pulmonary AVMs.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis uses the Curaçao clinical criteria or a pathogenic variant on genetic testing. Once diagnosed, guidelines (second international HHT guidelines 2020) recommend screening for pulmonary AVMs with contrast echocardiography and for brain AVMs with MRI, including in children. Relatives should be offered genetic testing or screening. In anyone with cryptogenic brain abscess or stroke and a right-to-left shunt, look for telangiectases.
det.treatment: Pulmonary AVMs with feeding arteries large enough to treat are closed by transcatheter embolisation, which prevents stroke and abscess; antibiotic prophylaxis before dental or dirty procedures is advised for unscreened or treated patients. Brain AVMs are managed case by case (surgery, radiosurgery, embolisation or observation). Epistaxis and GI bleeding are treated with humidification, local therapy, tranexamic acid, iron and, for severe bleeding, systemic bevacizumab; pomalidomide has shown benefit in a recent trial. Antithrombotic drugs are not forbidden when clearly indicated.
det.prognosis: With screening and treatment of visceral AVMs, life expectancy approaches normal; untreated pulmonary AVMs carry a substantial risk of stroke and abscess.
pearls: Cryptogenic brain abscess: look for pulmonary AVM and HHT.
Ask about nosebleeds and family history in young stroke with a right-to-left shunt.
Bubble echo with late (after 3–4 beats) shunting suggests an intrapulmonary rather than cardiac shunt.
det.thd: Osler-Rendu-Weber หรือ HHT เป็นโรคหลอดเลือดถ่ายทอดทางพันธุกรรมแบบยีนเด่น ผู้ป่วยมีเลือดกำเดาไหลบ่อย มีจุดเส้นเลือดฝอยแดงที่ริมฝีปาก ลิ้น และนิ้ว และมี AVM ในปอด ตับ และสมอง AVM ในปอดทำให้ลิ่มเลือดหรือเชื้อโรคผ่านไปสมองได้จนเกิด stroke หรือฝีในสมอง วินิจฉัยด้วยเกณฑ์ Curaçao และตรวจยีน ควรตรวจคัดกรองด้วย bubble echo และ MRI สมอง รักษาด้วยการอุด AVM ในปอด ยาเช่น bevacizumab สำหรับเลือดออก และให้ยาปฏิชีวนะป้องกันก่อนทำฟัน

name: Osmotic demyelination
formal: Pontine and extrapontine demyelination after rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia, causing quadriparesis, dysarthria, locked-in state and parkinsonism.
simple: Brain damage after sodium levels in the blood are corrected too quickly, causing weakness and speech problems.
more: Central pontine or extrapontine myelinolysis from rapid sodium correction, causing quadriparesis, dysarthria, dysphagia and locked-in state.
th: การสูญเสีย myelin ที่ pons และนอก pons หลังแก้ภาวะโซเดียมต่ำเรื้อรังเร็วเกินไป ทำให้แขนขาอ่อนแรง พูดและกลืนลำบาก จนถึง locked-in หรือ parkinsonism
tempoNote: Signs appear 2–6 days after a too-rapid sodium rise, often after initial improvement in confusion
feat: Biphasic course: hyponatraemic encephalopathy improves, then new deficits appear a few days later
Dysarthria, dysphagia and spastic quadriparesis with pseudobulbar features
Severe cases reach a locked-in state with preserved vertical eye movements
Extrapontine lesions cause parkinsonism, dystonia, catatonia or behavioural change
High-risk background: alcohol use, malnutrition, liver disease or transplant, hypokalaemia, sodium under 105 mmol/L
inv: Review the sodium chart: rise above about 8–10 mmol/L in 24 hours (lower thresholds in high-risk patients)
MRI with DWI: central pontine T2 hyperintensity sparing the periphery (trident or bat-wing shape); striatal and thalamic lesions in extrapontine forms
MRI can be normal early; repeat after 1–2 weeks if suspicion persists

case.who: 49-year-old man from Khon Kaen with heavy rice-whisky use
case.story: Admitted confused with sodium 106 mmol/L after days of vomiting; sodium reached 124 within 24 hours with saline. He woke up, but four days later stopped speaking and could not swallow.
case.exam: Anarthria, spastic quadriparesis, brisk jaw jerk; follows commands with vertical eye movements.
case.tests: MRI shows symmetric central pontine T2/DWI hyperintensity.
case.q: What happened, and how could it have been prevented?
case.a: Osmotic demyelination from overcorrection; limit the rise to about 8 mmol/L per 24 hours in high-risk patients and relower promptly if exceeded.

read.where: Chapter 28 Disorders of Consciousness and Intensive Care Neurology — Hyponatraemia
9. Role of Electrodiagnosis in the Evaluation of Peripheral Neuropathies
Chapter 17 Neurologic Complications of Electrolyte Disturbances

det.patho: In chronic hyponatraemia brain cells shed organic osmolytes to avoid swelling. If serum sodium then rises quickly, cells cannot regain these osmolytes fast enough, they shrink, and oligodendrocytes in tightly packed grey-white regions such as the central pons are injured. Blood-brain barrier disruption and astrocyte loss also contribute. Malnutrition, alcohol, liver disease and hypokalaemia lower tolerance.
det.clinical: Most cases follow correction of hyponatraemia that has been present more than 48 hours. After an interval of a few days, patients develop dysarthria, dysphagia, behaviour change and progressive weakness, sometimes to a locked-in state. Extrapontine involvement of basal ganglia, thalamus and cortex gives movement disorders and neuropsychiatric features, which may appear late in survivors. Rare cases occur without hyponatraemia, for example in severe hyperglycaemia or after liver transplantation.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical-radiological: an appropriate sodium history plus typical MRI lesions. DWI may become positive before T2 changes, but early scans can be normal. Exclude brainstem stroke, Wernicke encephalopathy, demyelinating disease and central nervous system infection.
det.treatment: Prevention is the main treatment: in chronic hyponatraemia aim for a rise of roughly 4–8 mmol/L per 24 hours and keep under 8 in high-risk patients, checking sodium frequently. If the limit is exceeded, relower sodium with free water and desmopressin. Once established, care is supportive: airway, nutrition, prevention of complications and rehabilitation; levodopa may help parkinsonism. Plasma exchange and IVIG have only anecdotal support.
det.prognosis: Outcome is better than once thought: many survivors recover partly or fully over months, though some remain severely disabled.
pearls: Hyponatraemia improves, patient wakes, then deteriorates days later: suspect ODS.
Overcorrection is reversible if caught early: relower with desmopressin and dextrose water.
Alcohol, malnutrition, hypokalaemia and liver disease lower the safe correction rate.
det.thd: Osmotic demyelination syndrome เกิดจากการแก้โซเดียมต่ำเรื้อรังเร็วเกินไป ทำให้ oligodendrocyte ที่ pons และบริเวณอื่นบาดเจ็บ อาการมักเริ่ม 2–6 วันหลังแก้ไข มีพูดไม่ชัด กลืนลำบาก แขนขาอ่อนแรงจนถึง locked-in MRI เห็นรอยโรคกลาง pons การป้องกันสำคัญที่สุดคือเพิ่มโซเดียมไม่เกินประมาณ 8 mmol/L ใน 24 ชั่วโมงในกลุ่มเสี่ยง และลดกลับด้วย desmopressin เมื่อแก้เกิน ผู้ป่วยจำนวนไม่น้อยฟื้นตัวได้

qx.stem: A 48-year-old alcohol-dependent man with sodium 108 mmol/L is treated, and the sodium reaches 128 mmol/L in 24 hours. Four days later he becomes quadriparetic and dysarthric with pseudobulbar signs. MRI shows a T2 hyperintense, non-enhancing 'trident' lesion in the central pons sparing the periphery, with diffusion restriction.
qx.q: What is the best explanation?
opts: Basilar artery thrombosis
Central pontine myelinolysis from overly rapid sodium correction
Pontine glioma
Neuromyelitis optica
Pontine haemorrhage
qx.why: Osmotic demyelination follows rapid correction (more than 8–10 mmol/L per 24 hours, with lower limits in high-risk patients such as alcoholism and malnutrition) and shows a central pontine lesion sparing the periphery, often with a lag of days. Basilar thrombosis would present acutely with asymmetric territory involvement, and tumours or NMOSD would show enhancement or distribution differences.

qx.stem: A 46-year-old woman with chronic alcohol use and poor nutrition is admitted with serum sodium 106 mmol/L after weeks of vomiting. Treated with hypertonic saline, her sodium reaches 128 mmol/L within 20 hours. She improves, but on day 4 she develops dysarthria, dysphagia, spastic quadriparesis and slow vertical eye movements, and MRI later shows T2 hyperintensity in the central pons.
qx.q: What is the best preventive strategy for such a patient in the future?
opts: Correct hyponatraemia rapidly to normal in the first 6 hours
Avoid all treatment of severe hyponatraemia
Use vaptans routinely for faster correction
Give high-dose steroids with each sodium infusion
Limit correction to about 6-8 mmol/L in 24 hours in high-risk patients, check sodium every 2-4 hours and be ready to relower with desmopressin and hypotonic fluid if overcorrection occurs
qx.why: Rapid correction in patients with chronic hyponatraemia and risk factors such as alcohol use, malnutrition, hypokalaemia or liver disease causes osmotic demyelination, typically appearing several days later as a pontine syndrome. Recommended limits are no more than 8 mmol/L in 24 hours (6 in the highest risk), with frequent monitoring and rescue relowering if exceeded. Vaptans accelerate rise and steroids are not preventive.

name: Osteoid osteoma
formal: Benign bone tumour with a nidus, causing nocturnal pain relieved by NSAIDs; in the spine may cause painful scoliosis and radiculopathy.
simple: A small non-cancerous bone growth causing night pain that aspirin-like drugs relieve, sometimes in the spine.
th: เนื้องอกกระดูกชนิดไม่ร้ายมี nidus ทำให้ปวดตอนกลางคืนที่หายด้วย NSAIDs หากเกิดที่กระดูกสันหลังทำให้หลังคดเจ็บและปวดร้าวตามราก
tempoNote: Months of progressive, typically nocturnal pain
feat: Adolescents and young adults, males more often
Night pain dramatically relieved by aspirin or NSAIDs
Spinal lesions (usually posterior elements of lumbar spine) cause painful, stiff scoliosis concave to the tumour
May produce radicular pain mimicking disc herniation
Not a neurological disease itself; reaches neurology as back or radicular pain
inv: Thin-slice CT: small lucent nidus with surrounding sclerosis (best test)
MRI may show striking marrow and soft-tissue oedema that can mislead
Bone scintigraphy: intense focal uptake

case.who: 16-year-old boy from Udon Thani who plays football
case.story: Four months of right low back pain waking him at night, relieved within an hour by ibuprofen; recently pain into the right buttock.
case.exam: Painful scoliosis with paraspinal spasm; straight leg raise mildly limited; no neurological deficit.
case.tests: MRI shows oedema around the right L4 pedicle; CT reveals a 7-mm lucent nidus with sclerotic rim.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and how is it usually treated today?
case.a: Spinal osteoid osteoma; CT-guided radiofrequency ablation or surgical excision of the nidus, with care near neural structures.

read.where: Chapter 31 Pain in Neurological Disorders — Orthopaedic Conditions that may Present to a Neurologist

det.patho: Osteoid osteoma is a benign bone-forming tumour with a small (usually under 1.5 cm) highly vascular nidus that produces prostaglandins, explaining the inflammatory night pain and NSAID response. Reactive sclerosis forms around it. About one in ten arise in the spine, mainly posterior elements.
det.clinical: Persistent localised pain, worse at night and dramatically helped by NSAIDs, is typical. In the spine it causes muscle spasm and a painful, non-structural scoliosis, and sometimes radicular pain when near a foramen. Neurological deficits are uncommon.
det.diagnosis: CT is the most specific test, showing the lucent nidus. MRI may show extensive oedema that can be mistaken for infection or a malignant lesion, so correlate with CT. Bone scan is sensitive for localisation.
det.treatment: Percutaneous CT-guided radiofrequency or other thermal ablation is first-line for most accessible lesions; spinal lesions near the cord or roots may need open excision or special protection techniques. NSAIDs can control pain while awaiting treatment. Untreated lesions sometimes burn out over years.
det.prognosis: Excellent after complete nidus removal; scoliosis often resolves if treated early.
pearls: Night pain relieved by NSAIDs in a teenager: think osteoid osteoma.
Painful scoliosis in an adolescent needs imaging.
CT shows the nidus that MRI may hide.
det.thd: Osteoid osteoma เป็นเนื้องอกกระดูกชนิดไม่ร้ายในวัยรุ่น มี nidus ขนาดเล็กที่สร้าง prostaglandin ทำให้ปวดตอนกลางคืนและหายเร็วเมื่อกิน NSAIDs หากเกิดที่กระดูกสันหลังทำให้หลังคดและเกร็ง บางรายปวดร้าวตามราก แต่ไม่ใช่โรคทางระบบประสาทโดยตรง CT เห็น nidus ได้ดีที่สุด รักษาด้วย radiofrequency ablation หรือผ่าตัด

formal: Rare primary malignant bone tumour of the spine, causing pain and cord or root compression, often after radiation or in Paget disease.
simple: A rare cancer of the spine bone that may press on the nerves.
th: มะเร็งกระดูกชนิด osteosarcoma ที่กระดูกสันหลัง พบน้อย ทำให้ปวดและกดไขสันหลังหรือรากประสาท มักเกิดหลังฉายรังสีหรือใน Paget disease

feat: Persistent, progressive back pain, often worse at night

Primary spinal origin rare; secondary cases after radiotherapy or in Paget disease of older adults
Bone-forming mass with mineralised matrix on imaging

case.exam: Spastic paraparesis, sensory level at T9, local spinal tenderness.

case.q: What is the urgent priority and the overall treatment plan?

det.patho: Osteosarcoma is a malignant tumour producing osteoid. Primary spinal osteosarcoma is rare; secondary forms arise in irradiated bone or in Paget disease. Germline TP53 or RB1 variants predispose.
det.clinical: Night pain and local tenderness precede neurological signs. Cord or cauda equina compression, radiculopathy and pathological fracture follow. Systemic symptoms and lung metastases may be present at diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: Imaging shows an aggressive, matrix-forming lesion. Biopsy should be planned with the surgical team to avoid tract contamination. Staging includes chest CT and bone scan or PET.
det.treatment: Multidisciplinary sarcoma care with neoadjuvant and adjuvant chemotherapy and en bloc resection when possible; radiotherapy (often proton) for unresectable disease. Emergency decompression for cord compression.
det.prognosis: Worse than limb osteosarcoma because complete resection is difficult.
pearls: Night back pain in a young adult needs imaging.
Biopsy planning by the definitive surgeon avoids tract seeding.
Post-radiation sarcoma can appear many years after treatment.
det.thd: Osteosarcoma ที่กระดูกสันหลังพบได้น้อย อาจเกิดเองหรือเกิดตามหลังการฉายรังสีและ Paget disease ผู้ป่วยปวดหลังมากขึ้นเรื่อย ๆ โดยเฉพาะกลางคืน แล้วตามด้วยอาการกดไขสันหลังหรือรากประสาท CT พบรอยโรคที่สร้างกระดูก การรักษาคือเคมีบำบัดร่วมกับผ่าตัดเอาก้อนออกทั้งหมดถ้าทำได้ และผ่าตัดด่วนเมื่อมีการกดไขสันหลัง

name: Otosclerosis
formal: Bone remodelling of the otic capsule that fixes the stapes and causes progressive conductive hearing loss, tinnitus and paracusis; Schwartz sign on otoscopy.
simple: Abnormal bone growth in the middle ear that stops sound passing and gradually causes hearing loss.
th: โรคของกระดูกหูชั้นในที่มีการสร้างกระดูกใหม่ผิดปกติจนกระดูกโกลน (stapes) ยึดติด ทำให้หูตึงแบบการนำเสียงบกพร่องค่อย ๆ มากขึ้น เป็นโรคหู ไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาทโดยตรง
tempoNote: Slowly progressive over years, typically starting in the 20s–40s; may accelerate in pregnancy
feat: Progressive conductive hearing loss, often bilateral and asymmetric, in young to middle-aged adults
Tinnitus; some hear better in noisy places (paracusis of Willis)
Normal tympanic membrane; occasionally a reddish promontory blush (Schwartze sign)
Family history common; women affected more often and may worsen during pregnancy
Cochlear involvement adds sensorineural loss; vertigo is uncommon
inv: Tuning forks: Rinne negative on the affected side, Weber lateralising to that ear
Pure-tone audiogram with air-bone gap; bone-conduction dip near 2 kHz (Carhart notch); absent stapedial reflexes
High-resolution temporal bone CT: lucent focus anterior to the oval window (fissula ante fenestram)

case.story: Hearing in her left ear has slowly faded over three years and got worse after her pregnancy; her mother wore hearing aids from her 40s.
case.exam: Ear drums look normal; Rinne negative left, Weber lateralises left; cranial nerves otherwise normal.
case.tests: Audiogram: left conductive loss with Carhart notch; CT shows a small lucent focus in front of the oval window.
case.q: What is the cause, and what are the options?
case.a: Otosclerosis with stapes fixation; hearing aid or stapedotomy by an otologist.

read.where: Chapter 23 Neuro-Otology: Dizziness, Balance and Hearing — Aetiology of Hearing Loss

det.patho: Otosclerosis is a localised disorder of bone remodelling in the otic capsule, the dense bone surrounding the inner ear. Spongy, vascular new bone typically forms near the oval window and fixes the stapes footplate, blocking sound transmission. Genetic susceptibility (often autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance), hormonal factors and possibly measles virus have been implicated. Extension into the cochlea can damage hair cells and add sensorineural loss.
det.clinical: This is an ear disease rather than a neurological one, but it enters the neurology differential of hearing loss and tinnitus. Patients describe gradually worsening hearing, frequently in both ears, with tinnitus and sometimes better hearing in noise. Examination of the drum is usually normal. Vestibular symptoms are infrequent and should prompt consideration of other diagnoses.
det.diagnosis: Tuning fork tests and audiometry show a conductive pattern with absent acoustic reflexes. The Carhart notch is a typical but not specific clue. Temporal bone CT supports the diagnosis and evaluates cochlear involvement. A sensorineural or asymmetric loss with poor word recognition requires MRI to exclude a retrocochlear lesion.
det.treatment: Options include observation, hearing aids, or surgery (stapedotomy or stapedectomy), which closes the air-bone gap in most patients. Sodium fluoride or bisphosphonates have been used to slow cochlear progression, with modest evidence. Advanced mixed loss may need cochlear implantation.
det.prognosis: Hearing loss progresses slowly; surgical results are generally excellent in experienced hands.
pearls: Conductive loss with a normal ear drum in a young woman: think otosclerosis.
Carhart notch is a bone-conduction dip near 2 kHz that often improves after surgery.
Unilateral sensorineural loss is not otosclerosis until MRI excludes a schwannoma.
det.thd: Otosclerosis เป็นโรคของกระดูกรอบหูชั้นในที่สร้างกระดูกใหม่ผิดปกติจนกระดูกโกลนยึดติด ทำให้หูตึงแบบการนำเสียงบกพร่องค่อย ๆ มากขึ้น มักเริ่มในวัยหนุ่มสาว พบในผู้หญิงมากกว่าและอาจแย่ลงขณะตั้งครรภ์ ตรวจพบ Rinne ลบ แก้วหูปกติ audiogram มี air-bone gap และ Carhart notch รักษาด้วยเครื่องช่วยฟังหรือผ่าตัด stapedotomy เป็นโรคหู ไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาทโดยตรง

name: Otosyphilis
formal: Syphilitic involvement of cochlea and labyrinth causing sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and vertigo; part of neurosyphilis, treated with penicillin and steroids.
simple: Syphilis infection of the inner ear that causes hearing loss, ringing and dizziness.
th: ซิฟิลิสที่ลามเข้าหูชั้นในทำให้หูดับแบบประสาทรับเสียง เสียงในหู และเวียนศีรษะ รักษาเหมือน neurosyphilis ด้วย penicillin ทางหลอดเลือด
tempoNote: Hearing loss evolves over days to weeks, sometimes suddenly; may fluctuate; can occur at any stage of syphilis
feat: Sensorineural hearing loss, often bilateral or asymmetric, sometimes sudden
Tinnitus, vertigo and imbalance from vestibular involvement
May coexist with ocular syphilis or other neurosyphilis features, or be isolated
Higher risk in people living with HIV and in MSM (men who have sex with men)
Congenital late form causes fluctuating hearing loss in young adults
inv: Treponemal and non-treponemal serology (RPR/VDRL) plus HIV test
Audiometry and vestibular testing to document deficit and follow response
Lumbar puncture if there are other neurological or ocular signs; CSF may be normal in isolated otosyphilis
MRI of internal auditory canals to exclude other causes

case.story: Over two weeks both ears have become muffled with ringing and spinning dizziness; he had a painless genital sore three months ago.
case.exam: Bilateral sensorineural loss on tuning forks, abnormal head-impulse test both sides, faint palmar rash.
case.tests: RPR 1:64, TPHA positive; HIV negative; audiogram bilateral sensorineural loss; MRI normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and treatment?
case.a: Otosyphilis; treat as neurosyphilis with IV penicillin G for 10–14 days, often with a corticosteroid course.

read.where: Chapter 23 Neuro-Otology: Dizziness, Balance and Hearing — Sensorineural Hearing Loss

det.patho: Treponema pallidum spreads haematogenously to the temporal bone and inner ear, causing osteitis of the otic capsule, endolymphatic hydrops and inflammation of the cochlea, labyrinth and eighth nerve. It can occur in early or late acquired syphilis and as a late feature of congenital disease. Rising syphilis incidence has made it more common again.
det.clinical: Patients present with sensorineural hearing loss that may be sudden, progressive or fluctuating, often with tinnitus and vertigo. Bilateral involvement is a useful clue, but unilateral disease occurs. Look for skin rash, uveitis or other ocular involvement, and cranial or meningeal signs. Delay in treatment risks permanent deafness.
det.diagnosis: Serology in any unexplained sensorineural hearing loss is the essential step; a positive treponemal test with compatible symptoms is enough to treat. Current guidance treats otic syphilis like neurosyphilis; CSF examination is recommended when there are other neurological signs, but a normal CSF does not exclude it. Test for HIV and other sexually transmitted infections and notify contacts.
det.treatment: Treat with IV aqueous penicillin G (18–24 MU daily) for 10–14 days, as for neurosyphilis; ceftriaxone is an alternative in penicillin allergy when desensitisation is not possible. Corticosteroids are often added to limit inflammatory damage, although trial evidence is limited. Follow hearing and serological titres afterwards.
det.prognosis: Hearing improves in a proportion of patients, more often with early treatment; long-standing loss tends to persist.
pearls: Check syphilis serology in every sudden or bilateral sensorineural hearing loss.
Treat otosyphilis with the neurosyphilis regimen even if CSF is normal.
Test for HIV in all patients with syphilis.
det.thd: Otosyphilis คือซิฟิลิสที่ลามเข้าหูชั้นในและเส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 8 ทำให้หูดับแบบประสาทรับเสียง มีเสียงในหูและเวียนศีรษะ อาจเป็นทั้งสองข้างหรือเกิดเฉียบพลัน ควรตรวจ RPR/TPHA ในผู้ป่วยหูดับทุกราย รักษาเหมือน neurosyphilis ด้วย penicillin G ทางหลอดเลือด 10–14 วัน มักให้ steroid ร่วม รักษาเร็วมีโอกาสได้ยินดีขึ้น

name: Overlap myositis
formal: Inflammatory myopathy occurring with another connective tissue disease such as scleroderma or lupus; often anti-synthetase, PM-Scl or Ku antibodies.
simple: Muscle inflammation occurring together with another autoimmune disease.
th: กล้ามเนื้ออักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกันที่เกิดร่วมกับโรคเนื้อเยื่อเกี่ยวพัน เช่น systemic sclerosis, SLE, Sjögren หรือ MCTD มักพบ antibody เฉพาะ เช่น anti-synthetase, PM-Scl, Ku, U1-RNP
tempoNote: Proximal weakness evolves over weeks to months, usually with skin, joint or lung features alongside
feat: Symmetric proximal limb weakness with raised CK
Raynaud phenomenon, puffy hands, skin tightening or sclerodactyly
Interstitial lung disease, inflammatory arthritis and fissured 'mechanic's hands' in anti-synthetase cases
Dysphagia from striated or oesophageal smooth muscle involvement
Fever, fatigue and arthralgia during flares
inv: CK plus myositis-specific/associated antibodies (anti-synthetase including Jo-1, PM-Scl, Ku, U1-RNP) and ANA
HRCT chest with spirometry and DLCO to find interstitial lung disease
EMG and thigh MRI to confirm active myositis and choose a biopsy site
Muscle biopsy when unclear: inflammatory infiltrate, perifascicular change in anti-synthetase disease, perimysial fibrosis in scleroderma overlap

case.who: 41-year-old woman, garment worker in Samut Prakan
case.story: For three months she has struggled to stand up from a squat; her fingertips turn white in the cool air-conditioned factory, and she has a dry cough.
case.exam: Hip and shoulder girdle power 4-/5, rough cracked skin along the sides of the fingers, fine bibasal inspiratory crackles.
case.tests: CK 3,200 U/L; anti-Jo-1 positive; HRCT shows a basal non-specific interstitial pneumonia pattern.
case.q: Which myositis subgroup fits, and which organ will shape the treatment plan?
case.a: Anti-synthetase overlap myositis; the extent of interstitial lung disease largely decides how strongly to immunosuppress.

read.where: Myopathies Associated with Systemic Disorders and Aging — Myopathies Associated with Connective Tissue Diseases (Overlap Syndromes)

det.patho: Overlap myositis is an immune-mediated inflammatory myopathy occurring in someone who also has, or is developing, another connective tissue disease such as systemic sclerosis, lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren syndrome or mixed connective tissue disease. It is defined as much by the antibody profile as by the clinical partner disease: anti-aminoacyl tRNA synthetase, PM-Scl, Ku and U1-RNP are the typical clusters. In current classification a large share of cases once called polymyositis belong here, and the book chapter on systemic disorders notes that overlap is seen most often with scleroderma.
det.clinical: Weakness is proximal and symmetric, yet extramuscular disease frequently drives the presentation: interstitial lung disease, arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, fever and mechanic's hands. Anti-synthetase syndrome can start with lung disease while muscle is still quiet. PM-Scl overlap tends to bring scleroderma-like skin change and calcinosis, whereas Ku and U1-RNP groups lean toward arthralgia and pulmonary hypertension. Ask specifically about swallowing, exertional dyspnoea and palpitations, because oesophageal, lung and cardiac involvement carry the main long-term risk.
det.diagnosis: Combine clinical weakness and raised CK with EMG or MRI evidence of active myositis, then the antibody panel and the features of the partner connective tissue disease. Biopsy is most useful when the picture is atypical; scleroderma overlap may show perimysial fibrosis, type 2 fibre atrophy and vasculopathy, while anti-synthetase disease shows perifascicular necrosis. Baseline HRCT, spirometry with DLCO and echocardiography are recommended, even when the patient has no respiratory complaint. Malignancy risk is lower than in dermatomyositis, but age-appropriate screening remains reasonable.
det.treatment: Start glucocorticoids together with an early steroid-sparing drug such as methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate; mycophenolate is often preferred when lung disease is present, and methotrexate is avoided in significant ILD. Refractory or lung-dominant disease is managed with rituximab, a calcineurin inhibitor, IVIG or cyclophosphamide together with rheumatology and respiratory teams. Supervised exercise is safe and helps function. Monitor for steroid myopathy, infection, bone loss and pulmonary hypertension.
det.prognosis: Muscle weakness usually responds well to treatment. Long-term outcome is set mainly by interstitial lung disease, pulmonary hypertension and cardiac involvement.
pearls: Weakness plus Raynaud, puffy fingers and a cough: send the myositis antibody panel and image the lungs.
Anti-Jo-1 or other synthetase antibodies predict ILD, so lung status guides the intensity of therapy.
A scleroderma-type overlap often resists steroids less than expected for the skin but needs vigilance for oesophageal dysmotility and pulmonary hypertension.
det.thd: Overlap myositis คือกล้ามเนื้ออักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกันที่เกิดร่วมกับโรคเนื้อเยื่อเกี่ยวพัน เช่น scleroderma หรือ SLE ผู้ป่วยมักอ่อนแรงที่สะโพกและไหล่ ร่วมกับนิ้วซีดเขียวเมื่อเจอความเย็น ข้ออักเสบ หรือไอแห้งจากปอดอักเสบแทรกซ้อน การวินิจฉัยใช้ CK, antibody เช่น Jo-1 หรือ PM-Scl, EMG/MRI และ HRCT ปอด บางรายต้องตัดชิ้นเนื้อ การรักษาใช้ steroid ร่วมกับยากดภูมิ เช่น mycophenolate หรือ azathioprine และ rituximab ในรายดื้อยา ผลระยะยาวขึ้นกับพังผืดในปอดเป็นหลัก

name: Pachymeningitis
formal: Thickening and inflammation of the dura causing headache and cranial neuropathies, from IgG4-related disease, sarcoidosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, TB or infection.
simple: Inflammation of the thick outer covering of the brain causing headache and nerve problems.
th: เยื่อหุ้มสมองชั้น dura หนาตัวและอักเสบ ทำให้ปวดศีรษะเรื้อรังและเส้นประสาทสมองพิการ สาเหตุ เช่น IgG4-related disease, GPA, sarcoidosis หรือวัณโรค
tempoNote: Headache and cranial nerve deficits accumulate over weeks to months, sometimes with relapses
feat: Chronic, often severe headache that may be worse lying down
Multiple cranial neuropathies: vision loss, ophthalmoplegia, facial numbness, hearing loss
Spinal form causes radicular pain and myelopathy
Systemic clues: sinusitis, orbital masses, salivary or lacrimal swelling, renal disease
Seizures or venous sinus thrombosis in some cases
inv: MRI with gadolinium: smooth or nodular thickening and enhancement of the dura (dural tail, falx, tentorium)
Serum IgG4, ANCA (PR3/MPO), ACE, ESR/CRP, syphilis serology, TB tests
CSF: mild pleocytosis and raised protein; cultures and cytology
Dural (meningeal) biopsy is often needed to confirm the cause

case.story: Five months of headache and blocked nose, then double vision and loss of hearing in the left ear.
case.exam: Left sixth nerve palsy, left sensorineural hearing loss, nasal crusting.
case.tests: MRI diffuse thickened enhancing tentorium and convexity dura; c-ANCA/PR3 positive; urine shows microscopic haematuria.
case.q: What most likely underlies the pachymeningitis?
case.a: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis; treat with steroids plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide after excluding TB and malignancy.

read.where: Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — Syphilis
Chapter 18 - CNS Syndromes at the Frontier of Autoimmune Encephalitis
Chapter 6: Infectious and Noninfectious Inflammatory Diseases of the Brain

det.patho: The dura becomes thickened by chronic inflammation and fibrosis, either without a clear cause or secondary to autoimmune, infectious or neoplastic disease. Recent series show that IgG4-related disease and ANCA-associated vasculitis (mainly granulomatosis with polyangiitis) explain a large share of cases once called idiopathic. Other causes include sarcoidosis, rheumatoid arthritis, tuberculosis, syphilis, fungal infection, lymphoma and meningioma en plaque.
det.clinical: Headache is the most frequent symptom, followed by cranial neuropathies from compression or vascular compromise of nerves as they traverse the dura, particularly the optic, oculomotor, trigeminal and lower cranial nerves. Involvement near venous sinuses may cause thrombosis or raised pressure. The spinal type causes progressive cord compression. Look for sinus, orbit, ear, salivary and kidney disease that points to the underlying condition.
det.diagnosis: Contrast MRI shows linear or nodular dural thickening and enhancement; the leptomeninges are often spared. Blood tests target vasculitis, IgG4 disease, sarcoidosis and infection, and CSF may show mild inflammation. Biopsy of dura (or a more accessible organ) is frequently decisive, revealing storiform fibrosis with IgG4 plasma cells, necrotising granulomas or caseation. Always exclude infection before strong immunosuppression.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: antituberculous or antimicrobial therapy for infections; glucocorticoids for inflammatory forms, with rituximab favoured for IgG4-related and ANCA-associated disease and methotrexate or azathioprine as maintenance options. Idiopathic cases are usually treated with steroids followed by a steroid-sparing agent because relapse is common. Surgical decompression is reserved for compressive lesions. Follow with serial MRI and clinical review.
det.prognosis: Headache often improves with treatment, but established cranial nerve deficits, especially vision loss, may not recover; relapses are frequent when therapy is withdrawn.
pearls: Thick enhancing dura plus cranial neuropathies: check ANCA and IgG4 before calling it idiopathic.
Diffuse smooth dural enhancement with orthostatic headache suggests low CSF pressure instead.
Biopsy before high-dose immunosuppression whenever TB or lymphoma is possible.
det.thd: Pachymeningitis คือการอักเสบและหนาตัวของเยื่อดูรา ทำให้ปวดศีรษะเรื้อรังและเส้นประสาทสมองหลายเส้นพิการ สาเหตุสำคัญคือ IgG4-related disease, GPA, sarcoidosis วัณโรค และมะเร็ง ตรวจ MRI ฉีดสี พบ dura หนาและติดสี ตรวจเลือดหา ANCA และ IgG4 และมักต้องตัดชิ้นเนื้อยืนยัน รักษาตามสาเหตุ เช่น steroid ร่วมกับ rituximab หรือยารักษาวัณโรค

name: Paediatric-onset multiple sclerosis
formal: MS beginning before age 18, with a higher relapse rate than adult-onset but slower progression; needs distinction from ADEM and MOG disease.
simple: Multiple sclerosis that starts in childhood or teenage years.
th: MS ที่เริ่มก่อนอายุ 18 ปี กำเริบบ่อยกว่าผู้ใหญ่แต่ความพิการสะสมช้ากว่า ต้องแยกจาก ADEM และ MOGAD
tempoNote: Relapses develop over days and recover over weeks; relapse rate is roughly two to three times that of adults in the first years
feat: Most cases begin after puberty; under age 11 it is rare and MOGAD or ADEM is more likely
Relapsing course from the start (almost never primary progressive)
Optic neuritis, brainstem syndromes, partial myelitis or polysymptomatic first attacks
Large lesion load and early cognitive or school difficulties despite good physical recovery
inv: MRI brain and spine: ovoid periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial and cord lesions; black holes support MS over ADEM
CSF oligoclonal bands (present in most adolescents with MS)
Serum MOG-IgG and AQP4-IgG by cell-based assay before labelling MS
Exclude mimics: vitamin B12, infection, leukodystrophy and vasculitis as clinically indicated

case.story: Lost vision in her right eye with pain on eye movement two weeks ago; a year earlier had numb legs for a month that resolved.
case.exam: Right visual acuity 6/36, right RAPD, brisk reflexes in the legs.
case.tests: MRI: multiple periventricular and juxtacortical ovoid lesions, one enhancing; CSF oligoclonal bands positive; MOG and AQP4 antibodies negative.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and how is treatment approached differently from older practice?
case.a: Paediatric-onset relapsing MS; early use of highly effective therapy (for example fingolimod or an anti-CD20 agent) is increasingly favoured because of high inflammatory activity.

read.where: Chapter 10 - Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis and MOG Antibody-Associated Disease

det.patho: The immunology is the same as adult MS, with genetic risk (HLA-DRB1*15:01), low vitamin D, obesity and prior Epstein-Barr virus infection as key contributors. Children have more intense inflammation but greater capacity for repair, which explains frequent relapses with good early recovery. Exposure to the disease during brain development raises the risk of cognitive problems.
det.clinical: About 3–5% of all MS starts in childhood. Adolescents present like adults, whereas young children may present with ADEM-like encephalopathy before the course declares itself. Relapses are more frequent and lesion loads higher than in adults. Patients reach secondary progression around a decade later than adult-onset MS but at a younger age.
det.diagnosis: The 2017 McDonald criteria apply well to adolescents; after an ADEM-like onset, MS requires further non-encephalopathic attacks or new lesions. MOG and AQP4 antibody testing is mandatory, especially in younger children. Oligoclonal bands and typical MRI features support MS; atypical features prompt metabolic, infectious and genetic work-up.
det.treatment: Relapses are treated with intravenous methylprednisolone. Fingolimod has trial evidence in children, teriflunomide and dimethyl fumarate have paediatric data, and anti-CD20 therapies and natalizumab are widely used for active disease. Many experts now start a highly effective agent early. Care should include school support, cognitive monitoring, mental health care, vaccination review before immunotherapy, and vitamin D optimisation.
det.prognosis: Physical disability accrues slowly, but patients reach milestones at younger ages and cognitive impairment is relatively common.
pearls: In a child under 11 with demyelination, check MOG-IgG before calling it MS.
Primary progressive course in a child should prompt a search for a genetic or metabolic mimic.
Good recovery from relapses does not mean benign disease; monitor MRI and cognition.
det.thd: MS ในเด็กและวัยรุ่น (ก่อน 18 ปี) มีการอักเสบมากและกำเริบบ่อยกว่าผู้ใหญ่ แต่ฟื้นตัวดี ความพิการสะสมช้ากว่า ต้องแยกจาก ADEM, MOGAD และ NMOSD โดยตรวจ MOG-IgG และ AQP4-IgG ทุกราย การรักษาช่วงกำเริบใช้ steroid ทางหลอดเลือด และปัจจุบันนิยมเริ่มยา disease-modifying ที่มีประสิทธิภาพสูงตั้งแต่ต้น พร้อมดูแลเรื่องการเรียนและความคิดความจำ

name: Paget’s disease
formal: Disordered bone remodelling with bone enlargement causing deafness, spinal stenosis, cranial neuropathies and platybasia; raised alkaline phosphatase; treated with bisphosphonates.
simple: A bone disease in which bones grow too large and weak, which can squeeze nerves and cause deafness.
th: โรคกระดูกที่มีการสร้างและสลายผิดปกติ กระดูกโตและผิดรูป อาจทำให้หูตึง ไขสันหลังหรือเส้นประสาทถูกกด และ platybasia
tempoNote: Slow progression over years; often found incidentally
feat: Older adults; frequently asymptomatic with isolated raised alkaline phosphatase
Bone pain, enlarging skull, bowed long bones, warm skin over affected bone
Hearing loss (conductive and/or sensorineural) from temporal bone involvement
Spinal stenosis, myelopathy or radiculopathy; basilar invagination with lower cranial nerve and brainstem signs
Rare sarcomatous change: new severe pain in a known lesion
inv: Raised alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium and phosphate
Plain films: thickened cortex, coarse trabeculae, 'cotton wool' skull, picture-frame vertebra
Isotope bone scan to map extent; MRI/CT for spinal or skull-base compression

case.story: Hat no longer fits, hearing has declined over years, and for six months his legs feel stiff and clumsy.
case.exam: Frontal bossing, bilateral hearing loss, spastic paraparesis with brisk reflexes and upgoing toes, sensory level at T8.
case.tests: ALP 620 U/L; skull X-ray shows cotton-wool appearance; MRI shows an enlarged T7 vertebra narrowing the canal.
case.q: What unifies these findings and what is first-line medical therapy?
case.a: Paget disease of bone with skull and thoracic vertebral involvement causing cord compression; intravenous zoledronic acid, with surgical decompression if deficits do not improve.

read.where: Chapter 14 Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders — Management of Spinal Deformity
Chapter 14 Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders — Rheumatological Disorders Affecting the Spine and Spinal Cord
Chapter 22 Neurologic Disorders Associated with Bone and Joint Disease

det.patho: Paget disease is a focal bone-remodelling disorder in which overactive, abnormal osteoclasts trigger chaotic new bone formation. The resulting bone is larger, more vascular and mechanically weaker. Genetic susceptibility (notably SQSTM1 variants) and possibly environmental triggers contribute; incidence has fallen in recent decades.
det.clinical: Most patients are asymptomatic. Neurological complications arise from enlargement of skull and vertebrae: hearing loss, cranial nerve compression at foramina, basilar invagination with hydrocephalus or brainstem compression, and spinal stenosis or myelopathy. A vascular steal from hypervascular bone can occasionally produce myelopathy without severe compression.
det.diagnosis: A raised alkaline phosphatase with characteristic radiographs is usually diagnostic; bone scan shows the distribution. MRI or CT defines neural compression. Biopsy is reserved for suspected sarcoma or metastasis.
det.treatment: Bisphosphonates, particularly a single infusion of zoledronic acid, control disease activity and bone pain and may improve some neural compression syndromes. Surgery is needed for progressive cord compression or symptomatic basilar invagination, ideally after bisphosphonate to reduce bleeding. Hearing aids and analgesia help symptomatic care.
det.prognosis: Generally good with treatment; neurological deficits from compression may improve, and sarcomatous transformation is rare but grave.
pearls: Isolated high ALP in an older adult: think Paget.
Enlarging skull plus deafness plus myelopathy is a classic triad of complications.
Treat with bisphosphonate before spinal surgery to reduce vascularity.
det.thd: Paget disease of bone เป็นโรคที่ osteoclast ทำงานผิดปกติ ทำให้กระดูกใหญ่ขึ้น ผิดรูป และเปราะ พบในผู้สูงอายุ ส่วนใหญ่ไม่มีอาการและพบ ALP สูง ภาวะแทรกซ้อนทางระบบประสาทได้แก่ หูตึง เส้นประสาทสมองถูกกด basilar invagination และไขสันหลังหรือรากประสาทถูกกด รักษาด้วย bisphosphonate เช่น zoledronic acid และผ่าตัดเมื่อมีการกดไขสันหลัง

det.patho: The mechanism is incompletely understood. A leading idea holds that injured nerves, roots or dorsal horn neurons send abnormal afferent input that rewires spinal and supraspinal motor circuits and drives involuntary movement. Central sensitisation sustains the pain. The movements are therefore a secondary response to sensory injury rather than a primary basal ganglia disorder.
det.clinical: Pain usually comes first and dominates the picture. The toes move in slow irregular sequences that look semi-purposeful, present at rest and often reduced in sleep. A painless variant exists. In reviews of restless legs it is discussed as a related but distinct condition because the movements are continuous and the pain deep. Finger involvement in the arm is called painful arms and moving fingers.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, from the combination of limb pain and continuous toe movements. EMG may show semi-rhythmic bursts of muscle activity. Search for the underlying lesion with nerve conduction studies, lumbar or cord MRI and metabolic tests. Distinguish restless legs syndrome, akathisia and dystonia by the absence of an urge to move and by the character of the movement.
det.treatment: Treatment is often unsatisfying. Neuropathic pain agents such as gabapentin, pregabalin, duloxetine or tricyclics come first. Botulinum toxin, epidural or lumbar sympathetic blocks and spinal cord stimulation have helped selected patients. Treating the cause, for example glucose control in diabetes, is part of management.
det.prognosis: Often persistent and difficult to treat, but not life-threatening.
pearls: Pain first, then writhing toes: think PLMT.
Look for a nerve, root or cord lesion behind it.
Not an urge to move, which distinguishes it from RLS.

23. Neuropathies Associated With HIV Infection and Antiretroviral Therapy

det.patho: Damage to thinly myelinated A-delta and unmyelinated C fibres produces ectopic firing, altered sodium channel function and central sensitisation, which generate spontaneous pain. Causes include metabolic (diabetes, prediabetes), toxic (alcohol, chemotherapy), infectious (HIV, leprosy), immune (Sjögren syndrome, sarcoidosis, vasculitis), amyloid and genetic sodium channelopathies. Gain-of-function SCN9A variants cause erythromelalgia and paroxysmal extreme pain disorder.
det.clinical: Patients describe burning, tight, stabbing or icy pain, often with allodynia and worse at night, and it frequently begins in the feet. Examination may show only reduced pinprick or temperature sense, so patients can be told the 'nerves are normal'. Childhood syndromes include erythromelalgia with burning, red, warm hands and feet triggered by heat, exercise or standing, and paroxysmal extreme pain disorder with attacks of deep pain around the eyes, jaw and rectum, with flushing triggered by cold wind, emotion, eating or defecation. Chronic pain often brings anxiety, depression and sleep loss.
det.diagnosis: Take a careful history and search for treatable causes with the blood tests listed above; glucose intolerance is common even with a normal HbA1c. Normal NCS does not exclude the disease, and skin biopsy for fibre density or autonomic testing documents small-fibre loss. In young patients with familial attacks, a sodium channel gene panel is indicated, and screening for Fabry disease and amyloid is needed when systemic features are present.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying cause and give neuropathic pain drugs: duloxetine, pregabalin or gabapentin, or nortriptyline, with topical lidocaine or capsaicin 8% patches for focal pain. Combination of drugs from different classes works better than pushing one drug to toxicity. Erythromelalgia is helped by cooling (avoid ice immersion), and by sodium channel blockers such as mexiletine or carbamazepine in some, while PEPD often responds to carbamazepine. Address mood, sleep and function with a pain programme; opioids are not recommended for long-term use.
det.prognosis: Course follows the cause; metabolic and toxic forms can improve with control, while pain may persist despite treatment.
pearls: A normal NCS does not exclude a painful small-fibre neuropathy.
Rapidly progressive painful neuropathy with weight loss: think amyloid, vasculitis or cancer.
Burning red feet from childhood that cool water relieves: erythromelalgia and SCN9A.

det.patho: The term describes a syndrome rather than a disease. Pain arises from trigeminal (mainly V1) fibres and dura near the orbital apex, superior orbital fissure and cavernous sinus, where the ocular motor nerves run close together. Causes include idiopathic granulomatous inflammation (Tolosa-Hunt), aneurysm or carotid-cavernous fistula, microvascular ischaemia in diabetes, pituitary apoplexy, tumours (metastasis, lymphoma, meningioma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma), infection (mucormycosis, aspergillosis, herpes zoster, septic thrombosis) and ophthalmoplegic migraine-like neuropathy in children.
det.clinical: Localisation helps: involvement of several cranial nerves with V1 and Horner points to cavernous sinus; with visual loss to orbital apex; proptosis and chemosis to orbit or fistula. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is an important cause in South-East Asia and often affects the abducens and V2/V3. A painful pupil-sparing third nerve palsy in an older diabetic is often microvascular, but needs follow-up.
det.diagnosis: Neuroimaging is essential in nearly all cases: vascular imaging for aneurysm in third nerve palsies and MRI with contrast and fat suppression of the orbit and cavernous sinus. Blood tests look for diabetes, systemic inflammation, IgG4-related disease and vasculitis. Tolosa-Hunt is a diagnosis of exclusion that requires imaging evidence of granulomatous inflammation and steroid response, with repeat imaging to confirm resolution.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: endovascular treatment of aneurysm or fistula, surgery for apoplexy, glycaemic control for microvascular palsy, antifungal drugs and debridement for invasive fungal infection, oncological care for tumours. Tolosa-Hunt responds to prednisolone (around 1 mg/kg) with pain relief within 72 hours, though palsies recover more slowly; steroid-sparing agents are used for relapses.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause; ischaemic and inflammatory palsies usually recover over months, while neoplastic and fungal causes carry poor outcomes if diagnosed late.
pearls: Steroid response does not prove Tolosa-Hunt: lymphoma can respond too.
Diabetic with ketoacidosis, black nasal eschar and painful ophthalmoplegia: mucormycosis emergency.
In Thailand, think nasopharyngeal carcinoma in painful VI or multiple cranial neuropathies.

3. EVALUATION AND MANAGEMENT OF THE PATIENT WITH PERIPHERAL NEUROPATHY

det.patho: Damage to thinly myelinated A-delta and unmyelinated C fibres produces spontaneous ectopic firing and central sensitisation, leading to burning pain and allodynia. Autonomic small fibres are often involved. Mechanisms include metabolic injury, toxins, immune attack on dorsal root ganglia and gain-of-function sodium channel variants.
det.clinical: Pain usually starts in the feet and spreads upward; sensory examination may be subtle with only reduced pinprick or temperature. Patients may have dysautonomia. Patchy, face- or trunk-involving symptoms suggest a ganglionopathy rather than length-dependent axon loss. Large-fibre signs develop if a mixed neuropathy evolves.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis combines symptoms, small fibre signs and confirmation by skin biopsy or autonomic testing, while NCS excludes large-fibre involvement. A careful search for treatable causes is essential because about half have an identifiable cause, with glucose dysregulation the most common. Quantitative sensory testing can support but not prove the diagnosis.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying cause where possible. First-line pain drugs are duloxetine, pregabalin or gabapentin, and amitriptyline or nortriptyline; topical capsaicin 8% or lidocaine help localised pain. Combine with sleep, mood and exercise support; avoid long-term opioids. Immune-mediated forms may justify a trial of immunotherapy in specialist hands.
det.prognosis: Often chronic but stable; pain control rather than cure is the realistic goal in idiopathic cases.
pearls: Normal NCS does not exclude small fibre neuropathy.
Check an OGTT, not just fasting glucose.
Non-length-dependent pain suggests Sjögren or another immune ganglionopathy.

det.patho: Symptomatic palatal tremor results from lesions interrupting the dentate–red nucleus–inferior olive circuit (Guillain–Mollaret triangle), most often in the central tegmental tract or in the dentate nucleus. Deafferented inferior olive neurons enlarge, become electrically coupled and oscillate, driving rhythmic output through the cerebellum. Essential palatal tremor has no structural lesion and involves the tensor veli palatini; many cases are now considered functional.
det.clinical: Symptomatic tremor develops weeks to months after stroke, trauma, demyelination or tumour, usually with the levator veli palatini moving. Patients more often complain of oscillopsia from pendular nystagmus or of ataxia than of the palatal movement itself. Essential tremor causes an audible ear click from Eustachian tube opening. Progressive ataxia with palatal tremor suggests a degenerative cause such as adult Alexander disease.
det.diagnosis: Look at the palate with the mouth open at rest for at least a minute. MRI identifies the causal lesion and olivary T2 hyperintensity with later hypertrophy. Absence of a lesion with ear click, entrainment or distractibility suggests essential or functional forms.
det.treatment: Treatment is often unsatisfactory. Botulinum toxin to the tensor veli palatini relieves troublesome ear click. Gabapentin or memantine can reduce pendular nystagmus and oscillopsia. Clonazepam, valproate and other agents have inconsistent effects; functional cases benefit from physiotherapy-based approaches.
det.prognosis: Symptomatic palatal tremor usually persists for life; the olivary changes evolve to atrophy over years.
pearls: Oscillopsia after brainstem stroke: look at the palate.
Hypertrophic olivary degeneration is not a new tumour or infarct; it reflects deafferentation.
Ear click without a lesion suggests essential or functional palatal tremor.

case.story: Four years of start hesitation and freezing when walking, softer slurred speech and several backward falls; no family history; levodopa did not help.
case.exam: Gait freezing, postural instability, mild axial rigidity, slightly slowed vertical saccades, no ataxia or chorea.
case.tests: MRI shows mild midbrain and subthalamic atrophy; ATN1 and HTT repeat testing normal.
case.q: What pathology could explain this picture, and how is it best classified in life?

det.patho: Pallidoluysian atrophy describes degeneration of the globus pallidus and its reciprocally connected subthalamic nucleus. It occurs as part of dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy, caused by CAG expansion in ATN1, and also as a rare sporadic condition. Most sporadic 'pure' cases studied with modern methods show 4-repeat tau pathology and are considered a restricted variant of PSP. Knowledge comes largely from small autopsy series.
det.clinical: When part of DRPLA, the pallidoluysian component contributes chorea, dystonia and other involuntary movements alongside ataxia, myoclonus, seizures and dementia. The sporadic form usually begins in mid-to-late adult life with progressive gait disturbance, freezing, speech difficulty, dystonia or akinesia and eventually falls, with variable eye-movement involvement. There is no reliable clinical way to separate pure PLA from other PSP phenotypes during life.
det.diagnosis: Evaluate as for an atypical parkinsonian or hyperkinetic disorder: MRI for midbrain, subthalamic and cerebellar atrophy, and genetic testing for ATN1 and HTT repeat expansions when chorea, ataxia, seizures or family history are present. Sporadic cases are usually diagnosed clinically under the MDS PSP criteria (e.g. progressive gait freezing). Definite diagnosis of pure PLA requires neuropathology.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy exists. Management is symptomatic and multidisciplinary: trial of levodopa (usually minimal benefit), botulinum toxin for focal dystonia, physiotherapy for gait and falls, and speech and swallowing therapy. In DRPLA, anti-seizure drugs and treatment of chorea or psychiatric symptoms are added, with genetic counselling for relatives.
det.prognosis: Progressive disability over years; course resembles PSP in sporadic cases and DRPLA in genetic ones.
pearls: PLA is a pathological label, not a bedside diagnosis.
Pallidoluysian plus dentatorubral degeneration with dominant inheritance = DRPLA (ATN1).
Sporadic pure PLA sits within the PSP tauopathy spectrum.

name: Pallidoluysian dentate atrophy (PLDA)
formal: Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy, a CAG repeat disorder of ATN1 with progressive ataxia, choreoathetosis, myoclonic epilepsy and dementia, more frequent in Japan.
simple: A rare inherited brain disease with clumsiness, jerking movements, seizures and dementia, seen mostly in Japan.
more: Autosomal dominant with anticipation; confirm by ATN1 repeat testing. MRI shows brainstem and cerebellar atrophy; treat symptomatically.

Autosomal dominant with strong anticipation, especially on paternal transmission

case.who: 14-year-old boy from Bangkok whose father is of Japanese descent
case.story: Worsening school grades for two years, then frequent jerks of the arms and two generalised seizures; his father, 41, has had increasing unsteadiness and odd writhing movements.
case.exam: Boy: action myoclonus, mild ataxia, slowed thinking. Father: ataxic gait, choreoathetosis of hands, mild cognitive impairment.
case.tests: Boy's EEG shows generalised spike-wave with photosensitivity; MRI mild cerebellar and brainstem atrophy; ATN1 expanded allele in both, longer in the son.
case.q: What explains the different phenotypes and the son's earlier onset?
case.a: DRPLA (PLDA): larger CAG expansions, often after paternal transmission, cause earlier onset with progressive myoclonic epilepsy, while smaller adult expansions cause ataxia, chorea and dementia.

read.where: Chapter 28 Progressive Myoclonic Epilepsies — Dentatorubropallidoluysian Atrophy (DRPLA)

det.patho: This entry is the same disorder as dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy. An expanded CAG repeat in ATN1 produces a polyglutamine-containing atrophin-1 that accumulates in neuronal nuclei. Degeneration predominantly affects the dentate nucleus and its outflow to the red nucleus, together with the globus pallidus and subthalamic nucleus, with white matter changes in older patients. It is most frequent in Japan, but cases occur in other Asian, European and African-American families.
det.clinical: Phenotype depends on repeat size and age: large expansions present in childhood or adolescence as progressive myoclonic epilepsy with cognitive decline; intermediate sizes give a mixed picture; smaller expansions present after 40 with ataxia, choreoathetosis, dementia and psychiatric symptoms. Anticipation is marked, especially when inherited from the father, so a child may be severely affected before a parent is diagnosed.
det.diagnosis: Genetic testing for ATN1 CAG expansion confirms the diagnosis and should be considered in any dominant family with ataxia plus chorea, myoclonus, epilepsy or dementia, or in a juvenile PME with a dominant history. MRI shows cerebellar and brainstem atrophy and, in adults, confluent white matter T2 hyperintensities. Test for HTT, HDL2 and SCA17 when ATN1 is normal.
det.treatment: Treatment is symptomatic: broad-spectrum anti-seizure drugs (valproate, levetiracetam, clobazam, perampanel) for myoclonus and seizures, avoiding sodium-channel blockers that may worsen myoclonus; tetrabenazine or antipsychotics for disabling chorea; and rehabilitation, nutrition and psychiatric care. Genetic counselling covers anticipation and predictive testing. No disease-modifying therapy is approved; antisense approaches are in early development.
det.prognosis: Relentlessly progressive; juvenile-onset patients have the fastest decline.
pearls: PLDA and DRPLA are the same ATN1 polyglutamine disease.
Juvenile form looks like progressive myoclonic epilepsy; adult form looks like Huntington disease with ataxia.
Strong paternal anticipation can make the child present before the parent.
det.thd: Pallidoluysian dentate atrophy คือโรคเดียวกับ DRPLA เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมแบบยีนเด่นจาก CAG repeat ในยีน ATN1 พบมากในญี่ปุ่น ถ้าเริ่มเป็นในเด็กหรือวัยรุ่นจะมีลมชักกระตุกแบบ progressive myoclonic epilepsy ร่วมกับสติปัญญาถดถอย ถ้าเริ่มในผู้ใหญ่จะมีเดินเซ chorea และสมองเสื่อม คล้าย Huntington รุ่นลูกมักเป็นเร็วและรุนแรงกว่า โดยเฉพาะเมื่อได้รับยีนจากพ่อ วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีน ATN1 และรักษาตามอาการ

name: Pallidonigral atrophy (PNA)
formal: Rare degeneration of the globus pallidus and substantia nigra producing parkinsonism with poor levodopa response, sometimes with pyramidal signs, described pathologically.
simple: A rare brain degeneration affecting two movement centres, causing stiffness and slowness.
more: Diagnosis made at autopsy; treatments have limited effect and care is supportive.

feat: Akinetic-rigid parkinsonism with little or no levodopa response
Prominent gait freezing, speech and handwriting freezing in some reported cases
Pyramidal signs or dystonia may be present

case.story: Over four years his steps have become shorter, he freezes at doorways and his speech stutters; levodopa up to 1,000 mg/day did nothing.
case.exam: Severe gait freezing, mild axial rigidity, almost no limb bradykinesia, normal vertical saccades early on.
case.tests: MRI unremarkable; DAT-SPECT shows reduced striatal uptake.
case.q: Which pathological entity was historically linked to this picture, and how is it classified now?
case.a: Pallidonigral (pallido-nigro-luysian) atrophy; today most such cases are classed as PSP with progressive gait freezing.

det.patho: Pallidonigral atrophy is a historical pathological label describing neuronal loss and gliosis restricted to the pallidum and nigra. Many such brains show tau pathology, and the entity is now generally considered within the progressive supranuclear palsy spectrum. Familial forms reported in older literature lack a clear genetic basis.
det.clinical: Reported patients have levodopa-unresponsive parkinsonism with marked freezing of gait and speech, sometimes with dystonia or pyramidal signs. The clinical picture largely matches the PSP variant with progressive gait freezing. Because published cases are few and mostly old, firm clinical rules cannot be drawn.
det.diagnosis: There are no clinical criteria for PNA itself. In practice, apply the MDS PSP criteria and exclude structural, vascular, toxic and genetic causes of atypical parkinsonism. Definite confirmation requires neuropathology.
det.treatment: Treatment is symptomatic: a levodopa trial at adequate dose, physiotherapy with cueing strategies for freezing, speech and swallowing therapy, and fall prevention. No disease-modifying therapy exists.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive disability over many years; survival appears longer than in classic PSP.
pearls: Pure gait freezing with no levodopa response suggests a PSP-spectrum disorder.
PNA is a pathological, not a clinical, diagnosis.
Always try levodopa adequately before calling parkinsonism unresponsive.

det.patho: PNLA describes neuronal loss in the globus pallidus, substantia nigra and subthalamic (luysian) nucleus. In modern series most cases carry 4-repeat tau pathology and are regarded as a restricted, gait-dominant form of progressive supranuclear palsy. The cause of the regional selectivity is unknown.
det.clinical: The dominant picture is progressive freezing of gait and speech with poor response to levodopa, sometimes with dystonia, chorea or pyramidal signs. Patients may go years before developing the gaze palsy and cognitive features of classic PSP. Information on non-tau or familial cases is sparse.
det.diagnosis: Clinically it is approached as PSP with progressive gait freezing under the MDS criteria. MRI and DAT imaging support a degenerative parkinsonism and exclude other causes. Definite diagnosis needs autopsy.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy is proven. Try levodopa; amantadine sometimes helps freezing. Physiotherapy with visual and auditory cues, speech therapy, fall prevention and botulinum toxin for focal dystonia are the main measures.
det.prognosis: Course is often slower than Richardson syndrome, with longer survival.
pearls: Luysian refers to the subthalamic nucleus (Luys body).
Pure akinesia with gait freezing is a PSP variant until proved otherwise.
Do not confuse PNLA with DRPLA, a genetic repeat disorder.

det.patho: Davison first described the pallidopyramidal syndrome in 1954 as pathology of the pallidum, nigra and pyramidal tracts. Genetic studies have since explained many cases: biallelic FBXO7 (PARK15) variants are the classic cause, with ATP13A2 (PARK9) and PLA2G6 (PARK14) producing overlapping phenotypes. These genes affect mitochondrial quality control, lysosomal function and phospholipid metabolism.
det.clinical: Patients develop parkinsonism in late childhood to early adulthood together with pyramidal signs and dystonia. Levodopa helps at first, but dyskinesias and fluctuations appear early, and dose escalation is limited by psychiatric side effects in some. Additional features vary by gene, including cognitive decline, gaze palsy and myoclonus.
det.diagnosis: Young-onset parkinsonism with spasticity should prompt a multi-gene panel or exome. MRI helps detect iron or atrophy patterns; DAT imaging confirms presynaptic loss. Exclude Wilson disease, dopa-responsive dystonia and structural lesions.
det.treatment: Use levodopa at the lowest effective dose; amantadine may help dyskinesias. Treat spasticity and dystonia with physiotherapy, baclofen or botulinum toxin. Deep brain stimulation has limited and variable reported results. Genetic counselling is important for families.
det.prognosis: Progressive disability; outlook varies with the gene involved.
pearls: Parkinsonism plus Babinski signs in a young patient: think pallidopyramidal syndrome.
Early dyskinesia after levodopa is common in genetic juvenile parkinsonism.
Always exclude Wilson disease in parkinsonism under 40.

more: Historic name for pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN), with iron accumulation in the globus pallidus, dystonia, parkinsonism, retinopathy and an eye-of-the-tiger MRI sign. Diagnosis by MRI and PANK2 mutation testing; autosomal recessive with early dystonia and retinitis pigmentosa, and acanthocytes may be seen. Treatment is symptomatic, with botulinum toxin, intrathecal baclofen and deep brain stimulation. det.patho: Biallelic PANK2 mutations impair mitochondrial pantothenate kinase 2, the key enzyme for coenzyme A synthesis. CoA deficiency disrupts lipid metabolism and mitochondrial function, and iron accumulates in the globus pallidus with axonal spheroids. It accounts for roughly half of NBIA cases.
det.clinical: Classic PKAN starts in early childhood with gait problems and progresses rapidly to severe generalized dystonia, with characteristic oromandibular involvement, dysarthria and loss of ambulation within years. Retinopathy is common in classic disease. Atypical PKAN presents in adolescence with speech difficulty, neuropsychiatric change and parkinsonism, progressing more slowly. Status dystonicus is a dangerous complication.
det.diagnosis: MRI with T2/SWI showing the eye-of-the-tiger sign strongly suggests PKAN and is confirmed by PANK2 testing. Other NBIA disorders (PLAN, MPAN, BPAN, neuroferritinopathy, aceruloplasminemia) have different MRI patterns. Exclude Wilson disease in every child or young adult with dystonia.
det.treatment: Treatment is symptomatic: trihexyphenidyl, baclofen (oral or intrathecal), botulinum toxin for focal dystonia, and GPi DBS for severe generalized or status dystonicus. Iron chelation with deferiprone lowers pallidal iron but has not clearly changed progression. Feeding support (gastrostomy), physiotherapy, vision care and palliative care planning are important.
det.prognosis: Classic disease often leads to loss of walking within 10–15 years and shortened life; atypical disease is milder and slower.
pearls: Eye-of-the-tiger: dark pallidum with a bright centre on T2 — PKAN.
Severe jaw-opening dystonia with tongue biting in a child suggests PKAN.
Always check copper studies before labelling NBIA.
det.thd: PKAN เกิดจากยีน PANK2 แบบ autosomal recessive ทำให้มีเหล็กสะสมใน globus pallidus เด็กมีปัญหาการเดินแล้วตามด้วย dystonia ทั่วตัว เด่นที่ปากและขากรรไกร พูดไม่ชัด กัดลิ้น และอาจมีจอประสาทตาเสื่อม MRI พบ eye-of-the-tiger sign รักษาตามอาการด้วยยา botulinum toxin และ DBS ร่วมกับดูแลการกลืน ต้องตรวจแยก Wilson disease เสมอ

qx.stem: A 9-year-old boy from Songkhla has had two years of toe-walking, falls, and dystonic posturing of the feet and jaw, followed by dysarthria. His night vision is poor and fundoscopy shows pigmentary retinopathy. MRI T2 sequences show bilateral low-signal globus pallidus with a small central bright area.
qx.q: Which metabolic pathway is disrupted by the underlying gene defect?
opts: Phytanic acid alpha-oxidation
Copper export from hepatocytes
Lysosomal degradation of sulfatides
Mitochondrial complex I assembly
Coenzyme A biosynthesis via pantothenate kinase 2
qx.why: The eye-of-the-tiger sign with early dystonia and pigmentary retinopathy in childhood is classic PKAN, caused by biallelic PANK2 variants that impair the first step of coenzyme A synthesis and lead to iron accumulation in the globus pallidus. Phytanic acid defects cause Refsum disease, copper export failure causes Wilson disease, and sulfatide storage causes metachromatic leukodystrophy.

ddx.pt: Low ceruloplasmin, raised urinary copper, KF rings and liver disease; treatable with chelation
Adult onset, dominant inheritance, low serum ferritin, cystic basal ganglia change
Rigidity, seizures and cognitive decline with paternal HD history; HTT CAG expansion

aN: hallervorden spatz disease hsd | hsd | hallervorden spatz disease | pantothenate kinase associated neurodegeneration | harp syndrome | pkan | pank2 | nbia1 | hallervorden spatz syndrome | neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation type 1 | eye of the tiger

name: Pantothenate kinase-associated parkinsonism
formal: Atypical late-onset PANK2 disease with parkinsonism, gait freezing, speech disorder and psychiatric features; pallidal iron accumulation on MRI.
simple: A later-onset form of an inherited iron-storage brain disease causing stiffness, slowness and speech problems.
th: PKAN ชนิดเริ่มช้าจากยีน PANK2 มี parkinsonism เดินติด พูดผิดปกติ และอาการทางจิตเวช MRI เห็น eye-of-the-tiger จากเหล็กสะสมที่ globus pallidus
tempoNote: Typically starts in adolescence or early adulthood; slower progression than classic childhood PKAN
feat: Speech disturbance (palilalia, dysarthria, tachylalia) often an early feature
Parkinsonism with freezing of gait; dystonia milder than in classic PKAN
Psychiatric features: impulsivity, depression, emotional lability, obsessive behaviour
Slower course, with patients often ambulant 15 years or more after onset
inv: MRI T2/SWI: pallidal hypointensity with central hyperintensity (eye-of-the-tiger)
PANK2 gene testing (biallelic variants)
Peripheral blood smear for acanthocytes in some; exclude Wilson disease

case.story: Since 18 his speech has become rushed and repetitive and he has angry outbursts; now he freezes when turning.
case.exam: Palilalia, mild bradykinesia and rigidity, gait freezing, mild foot dystonia; eye movements normal.
case.tests: MRI shows bilateral eye-of-the-tiger sign; biallelic PANK2 variants.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and which MRI finding is characteristic?
case.a: Atypical (late-onset) PKAN; pallidal iron with a central bright spot — the eye-of-the-tiger sign.

det.patho: Biallelic PANK2 variants impair mitochondrial pantothenate kinase 2, the key enzyme for coenzyme A synthesis. Disturbed lipid and iron handling leads to iron deposition, axonal spheroids and gliosis in the globus pallidus. Residual enzyme activity in atypical cases probably explains the later onset and slower course.
det.clinical: Atypical PKAN appears in adolescence or adulthood with speech problems, psychiatric change and parkinsonism, including prominent freezing. Dystonia, spasticity and pigmentary retinopathy are less frequent than in childhood disease. Many patients remain walking for decades.
det.diagnosis: The MRI eye-of-the-tiger pattern is strongly suggestive, especially early; confirm with PANK2 sequencing. Other NBIA disorders (PLAN, MPAN, BPAN) and Wilson disease should be considered. The sign may fade in advanced disease as iron becomes uniform.
det.treatment: No therapy changes the course. Deferiprone iron chelation reduced pallidal iron in trials without a clear clinical benefit, and fosmetpantotenate failed. Symptomatic care includes levodopa trial, anticholinergics or botulinum toxin for dystonia, speech therapy, psychiatric care and GPi deep brain stimulation for disabling dystonia.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; long survival into adulthood is common.
pearls: Young adult with palilalia, impulsivity and freezing: check MRI for pallidal iron.
Eye-of-the-tiger is typical of PANK2 disease but not perfectly specific.
Exclude Wilson disease in any young person with a movement disorder.
det.thd: PKAN ชนิด atypical เกิดจากยีน PANK2 เริ่มอาการช่วงวัยรุ่นถึงผู้ใหญ่ตอนต้น มีการพูดผิดปกติ เช่น พูดซ้ำ พูดเร็ว อาการทางจิตเวช และ parkinsonism ที่เดินติดเด่น MRI เห็น eye-of-the-tiger จากเหล็กสะสมที่ globus pallidus ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน ยังไม่มียาที่หยุดโรค รักษาตามอาการ บางรายใช้ DBS สำหรับ dystonia โรคดำเนินช้ากว่าแบบเด็ก
