ddx.pt: Classic childhood form with early severe dystonia, retinopathy and rapid course
Low ceruloplasmin, Kayser–Fleischer rings, liver disease; treatable
PRKN or PINK1 forms lack pallidal iron and respond well to levodopa

aN: atypical pkan | late onset pkan | pank2 parkinsonism | adult onset pkan

name: Paraballism
formal: Bilateral ballistic flinging movements of both legs, usually from bilateral basal ganglia or subthalamic lesions, or less commonly spinal causes.
simple: Wild flinging movements of both legs, usually after damage to deep brain areas.
th: การเหวี่ยงขาทั้งสองข้างอย่างรุนแรงและไม่ตั้งใจ มักเกิดจากรอยโรคที่ basal ganglia หรือ subthalamic nucleus ทั้งสองข้าง พบได้ยากมาก
tempoNote: Usually sudden onset after a vascular or metabolic insult; may settle over weeks
feat: Large-amplitude, flinging, proximal movements of both legs
Arms spared or much less involved
Movements continuous while awake, disappear in sleep
Causes include bilateral subthalamic or striatal infarcts, non-ketotic hyperglycaemia and, rarely, spinal lesions
inv: Blood glucose and HbA1c (non-ketotic hyperglycaemia), sodium, calcium and thyroid tests
MRI brain with DWI for bilateral basal ganglia or subthalamic lesions; striatal T1 hyperintensity in hyperglycaemia
Spinal MRI if brain imaging is normal

case.who: 71-year-old woman from Suphan Buri with poorly controlled diabetes
case.story: For three days both legs have been kicking and flinging uncontrollably; she cannot sit in a chair.
case.exam: Violent proximal flinging of both legs, arms mildly choreic, alert and oriented.
case.tests: Glucose 520 mg/dL without ketones; MRI T1 shows bilateral putaminal hyperintensity.
case.q: What is the cause and first step in treatment?
case.a: Non-ketotic hyperglycaemic chorea-ballism; correct the glucose, add a dopamine blocker such as haloperidol or tetrabenazine if needed.

det.patho: Ballism results from reduced output of the subthalamic nucleus or its connections, which disinhibits thalamocortical motor drive. Paraballism requires bilateral involvement of the leg representation, which is unusual, explaining its rarity. Reported causes include bilateral infarcts or haemorrhages, hyperglycaemia, drugs and occasional spinal cord lesions.
det.clinical: Patients show violent, continuous flinging of both legs, often with exhaustion, injury and skin abrasions. Arms may be mildly affected. Most cases arise acutely in older people with vascular risk factors or metabolic disturbance.
det.diagnosis: Check glucose, electrolytes and drugs first, then image the brain with MRI including T1 (hyperglycaemic striatopathy) and DWI. If the brain is normal, image the spinal cord. Functional movement disorder is considered when signs are inconsistent.
det.treatment: Treat the cause, such as correcting hyperglycaemia. Symptomatic options include dopamine receptor blockers (haloperidol, risperidone) or VMAT2 inhibitors (tetrabenazine). Protect from injury with padding and maintain hydration and nutrition. Persistent severe cases occasionally need pallidal surgery.
det.prognosis: Vascular and metabolic forms often improve over weeks to months.
pearls: Check glucose in any elderly patient with new chorea or ballism.
Ballism is severe proximal chorea; treatment principles are the same.
Bright putamen on T1 in a diabetic suggests hyperglycaemic striatopathy.
det.thd: Paraballism คือการเหวี่ยงขาทั้งสองข้างอย่างรุนแรงจากรอยโรคที่ basal ganglia หรือ subthalamic nucleus ทั้งสองข้าง พบได้ยาก สาเหตุเช่น stroke ทั้งสองข้าง หรือน้ำตาลสูงแบบไม่มีคีโตน ควรตรวจน้ำตาลและทำ MRI รักษาสาเหตุและให้ยาต้าน dopamine หรือ tetrabenazine ส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นภายในสัปดาห์ถึงเดือน

ddx.pt: Ballism of one arm and leg from a contralateral subthalamic or striatal lesion
Smaller, flowing, distal movements; ballism is its severe proximal end
Variable, distractible, suggestible movements with inconsistent pattern

aN: bilateral leg ballism | paraballismus | lower limb ballism

name: Paramnesias
formal: Distortions of memory with false recognition or recall such as déjà vu, confabulation or reduplicative paramnesia; seen in temporal lobe epilepsy and frontal or right hemispheric lesions.
simple: Memory distortions in which a person believes a false memory or feels wrongly familiar with something.
th: ความผิดปกติของความจำที่จำผิดหรือรู้สึกคุ้นเคยผิด เช่น déjà vu การแต่งเรื่อง (confabulation) หรือเชื่อว่าสถานที่ถูกทำซ้ำ เป็นอาการ ไม่ใช่โรค พบในลมชักกลีบขมับและรอยโรคสมองกลีบหน้าหรือซีกขวา
tempoNote: Episodic when ictal (seconds); persistent when due to structural or degenerative brain disease
feat: A symptom group, not a disease: distorted familiarity or recall
Déjà vu or jamais vu as a brief aura of mesial temporal lobe seizures, often with fear or epigastric rising
Confabulation in Korsakoff syndrome, anterior communicating artery aneurysm rupture and frontal injury
Reduplicative paramnesia (belief that a place exists in two copies) after right hemisphere plus frontal damage
Occasional déjà vu without other features is normal, especially in young people
inv: EEG (sleep-deprived or prolonged) when experiences are frequent, stereotyped or followed by impaired awareness
MRI with hippocampal sequences for sclerosis, tumour or encephalitis
Cognitive screening; thiamine status and alcohol history when confabulation is present

case.story: For a year she has had sudden intense feelings that the current moment has happened before, lasting 20 seconds, with a rising stomach sensation; twice she then stared and smacked her lips.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination.
case.tests: Sleep EEG shows right anterior temporal sharp waves; MRI right hippocampal sclerosis.
case.q: Is her déjà vu normal?
case.a: No — stereotyped, frequent déjà vu with epigastric aura and later automatisms indicates focal seizures from the mesial temporal lobe.

read.where: Chapter 30 Neuropsychiatry — Pseudohallucinations, Déjà Vu, Depersonalisation and Derealisation
18 The Anatomic Localization of Lesions in the Thalamus

det.patho: Paramnesias reflect disturbance of the systems that tag memories as familiar or accurately sourced. Ictal déjà vu arises from discharges in the entorhinal and perirhinal cortex and hippocampus, which generate familiarity signals. Confabulation follows damage to ventromedial and orbitofrontal cortex or basal forebrain that impairs monitoring of retrieved memories. Reduplicative paramnesia and related misidentification syndromes usually need combined right hemisphere and frontal dysfunction.
det.clinical: This entry is a symptom category, not a neurological disease. Déjà vu is normal when rare and isolated, but should raise suspicion of epilepsy when frequent, stereotyped, accompanied by other aura symptoms or followed by loss of awareness. Confabulation ranges from provoked filling of memory gaps to spontaneous, fantastic stories. Reduplicative paramnesia is seen after stroke, trauma, tumour, encephalitis or in dementia, typically transiently.
det.diagnosis: Context determines work-up. Suspected ictal phenomena need EEG and epilepsy-protocol MRI; confabulation needs assessment for thiamine deficiency, frontal or basal forebrain lesions and broader cognitive testing. Psychiatric causes such as dissociation or psychosis should be considered when neurological tests are normal.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: anti-seizure drugs or surgery for temporal lobe epilepsy, urgent parenteral thiamine for Wernicke–Korsakoff, and rehabilitation after focal brain injury. Reassurance is enough for occasional benign déjà vu. Gentle reorientation is preferable to confrontation when patients confabulate or reduplicate.
det.prognosis: Depends on the underlying disorder; post-injury reduplication and confabulation often improve over weeks to months.
pearls: Déjà vu plus epigastric rising or fear, recurring the same way: think mesial temporal seizures.
Confabulation is not lying; it reflects frontal monitoring failure.
Reduplicative paramnesia points to right hemisphere plus frontal involvement.
det.thd: Paramnesia เป็นกลุ่มอาการความจำผิดเพี้ยน ไม่ใช่โรค ได้แก่ déjà vu (รู้สึกว่าเคยเกิดขึ้นแล้ว) confabulation (แต่งเรื่องเติมช่องว่างของความจำโดยไม่ตั้งใจ) และ reduplicative paramnesia (เชื่อว่าสถานที่มีซ้ำสองแห่ง) déjà vu ที่เกิดบ่อยแบบเดิมร่วมกับรู้สึกจุกลิ้นปี่หรือกลัว บ่งชี้ลมชักกลีบขมับ ส่วน confabulation พบใน Korsakoff และรอยโรคสมองกลีบหน้า การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ

ddx.pt: Recurrent stereotyped déjà vu auras with epigastric rising, fear, automatisms; EEG and MRI abnormalities
Severe anterograde amnesia with confabulation after thiamine deficiency, usually with alcohol use
Hours of anterograde amnesia with repetitive questions, no false memories, complete recovery

aN: paramnesia | deja vu | reduplicative paramnesia | confabulation | false recognition

name: Paramyotonia congenita
formal: Autosomal dominant SCN4A sodium channelopathy with cold-induced myotonia worsening with exercise, and episodic weakness; mexiletine helpful.
simple: An inherited muscle disease where muscles stiffen in the cold and with repeated use.
more: Cold provocation with EMG shows a drop in compound muscle amplitude; the common mutation is T1313M or R1448C in SCN4A. Avoid cold and potassium loading; mexiletine or acetazolamide reduces attacks. Sodium channel myotonia (SCN4A) with cold-induced myotonia that worsens with exercise and may cause episodes of weakness. Cooling EMG test and genetic testing; mexiletine is effective.
th: กล้ามเนื้อคลายช้าแบบที่แย่ลงเมื่อทำซ้ำและเมื่อเย็น — ใบหน้า มือ เปลือกตา (SCN4A)
feat: Paradoxical myotonia: stiffness increases with repeated action
Cold provokes stiffness and then weakness of face, eyelids and hands
Eyelid myotonia (slow opening after forced closure); may overlap with hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis
inv: EMG myotonia; cooling worsens findings
SCN4A genetic testing

case.story: In cold weather her face stiffens and she cannot open her eyes quickly after squeezing them shut; in winter her hands become weak.
case.exam: Eyelid myotonia increasing with repeated closures, mild grip myotonia that worsens with repetition.
case.tests: EMG myotonic discharges; SCN4A variant.
case.q: Which bedside feature separates this from myotonia congenita?
case.a: Worsening (not improving) with repetition, and cold sensitivity.

read.where: 36: Myotonic Muscle Disorders and Periodic Paralysis Syndromes

files.chapter: 36: Myotonic Muscle Disorders and Periodic Paralysis Syndromes
Chapter 1: Neuromuscular Disorders: A Clinical Approach

ddx.pt: Warm-up phenomenon, muscle hypertrophy
Episodes of flaccid weakness with high K; may overlap

aN: paramyotonia | eulenburg disease | scn4a myotonia | paradoxical myotonia

det.patho: Autosomal dominant gain-of-function variants in SCN4A stop the muscle Nav1.4 channel from inactivating quickly, particularly at low temperatures. Persistent inward sodium current produces repetitive firing (myotonia) and, with more sustained depolarisation, inexcitability and weakness. Some variants overlap with hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis.
det.clinical: Symptoms begin in infancy or childhood and mainly affect the face, eyelids, tongue and hands. Stiffness becomes worse rather than better with repeated movement (paradoxical myotonia) and is provoked by cold, leading to weakness that can last hours after rewarming. Eyelid myotonia after forced closure is a typical bedside sign. Some patients also have episodic flaccid weakness, particularly after potassium intake or rest following exercise.
det.diagnosis: Clinical history of cold sensitivity and paradoxical myotonia is very suggestive. EMG shows myotonic discharges; on short exercise testing with cooling, CMAP amplitude falls progressively, unlike chloride channel myotonia. SCN4A testing confirms the diagnosis. CK may be mildly elevated.
det.treatment: Keep the body and hands warm and avoid triggers such as cold water swimming. Mexiletine is effective for cold-induced stiffness; acetazolamide or thiazide-type diuretics may reduce weakness episodes in overlap patients. As with other myotonias, avoid depolarising muscle relaxants and monitor temperature during anaesthesia.
det.prognosis: The course is non-progressive and life expectancy is normal; quality of life is mainly affected in cold climates or occupations.
pearls: Paradoxical myotonia (worse with repetition) plus cold sensitivity = SCN4A.
Test eyelid opening after repeated forced closures.
Ask about episodic weakness: overlap with hyperPP is common.
det.thd: Paramyotonia congenita เกิดจากยีน SCN4A ทำให้ช่องโซเดียมของกล้ามเนื้อปิดไม่สนิทโดยเฉพาะเมื่อเย็น อาการเด่นคือใบหน้า เปลือกตา และมือแข็งเกร็งมากขึ้นเมื่อทำซ้ำหรือโดนอากาศเย็น ตามด้วยอ่อนแรงได้ ต่างจาก myotonia congenita ที่ดีขึ้นเมื่อทำซ้ำ ตรวจ EMG ร่วมกับทำให้กล้ามเนื้อเย็น และตรวจยีน SCN4A รักษาด้วยการรักษาความอบอุ่นและ mexiletine

name: Paraneoplastic autonomic neuropathy
formal: Autonomic neuropathy related to cancer, commonly anti-Hu or ganglionic AChR antibodies, causing gastroparesis, orthostatic hypotension and pseudo-obstruction.
simple: Nerve damage affecting automatic body functions caused by the immune response to a cancer.
more: Search for tumour, e.g. small cell lung cancer; treat tumour and immunotherapy; prognosis often poor.
th: ความผิดปกติของระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติจากมะเร็งผ่านกลไกภูมิคุ้มกัน มักสัมพันธ์กับ anti-Hu หรือ ganglionic AChR antibody ทำให้ความดันตกเมื่อยืน กระเพาะไม่บีบตัว และลำไส้อืดเทียม
tempoNote: Develops over weeks to a few months, often before the cancer is known
feat: Orthostatic hypotension with syncope, fixed heart rate
Gastroparesis, severe constipation or intestinal pseudo-obstruction
Dry eyes and mouth, urinary retention, erectile dysfunction, pupil abnormalities
Often accompanied by sensory ganglionopathy or encephalomyelitis in anti-Hu disease
Small-cell lung cancer is the commonest associated tumour; thymoma and others occur
inv: Paraneoplastic antibody panel: anti-Hu (ANNA-1), CRMP5, ganglionic AChR (gAChR) antibodies
Autonomic tests: tilt table, heart-rate variability, sudomotor testing; gastric emptying study
CT chest-abdomen-pelvis and FDG-PET for occult tumour

case.story: Over two months he has fainted on standing, vomits after meals and has had no bowel movement for a week despite laxatives.
case.exam: BP falls from 140/80 lying to 85/50 standing without heart-rate rise; distended abdomen; reduced vibration sense in the hands.
case.tests: Anti-Hu positive; CT shows a small hilar mass; biopsy small-cell carcinoma.
case.q: What is the unifying diagnosis?
case.a: Paraneoplastic autonomic neuropathy with sensory ganglionopathy from anti-Hu and small-cell lung cancer.

det.patho: An immune response directed at the tumour cross-reacts with neurons of autonomic ganglia and the enteric plexus. Anti-Hu is a marker of T-cell–mediated neuronal destruction, which is why damage is often irreversible. Antibodies to the ganglionic acetylcholine receptor, by contrast, are pathogenic and may be associated with tumours or be idiopathic.
det.clinical: Autonomic failure develops subacutely and may dominate or accompany other paraneoplastic syndromes such as sensory neuronopathy, limbic encephalitis or cerebellar ataxia. Gastrointestinal dysmotility, including pseudo-obstruction, is a classic and often missed manifestation. Symptoms usually precede detection of the tumour.
det.diagnosis: Subacute, severe autonomic failure in an adult, particularly with weight loss or smoking history, should prompt antibody testing and tumour search. Formal autonomic testing documents the extent of involvement. Exclude diabetes, amyloidosis, drug effects and other neuropathies; if the initial screen is negative, repeat tumour imaging periodically.
det.treatment: Treat the cancer promptly, which is the most effective intervention. Immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG, plasma exchange) is often tried, with modest effect in anti-Hu cases. Symptomatic management includes fludrocortisone, midodrine or droxidopa, compression garments, prokinetics, bowel regimens and nutritional support.
det.prognosis: Prognosis is usually poor and depends on the tumour; neurological recovery is limited.
pearls: Unexplained intestinal pseudo-obstruction in a smoker: test anti-Hu.
Fixed heart rate with orthostatic hypotension indicates autonomic failure, not dehydration.
Negative initial tumour search should be repeated, often with FDG-PET.
det.thd: Paraneoplastic autonomic neuropathy เป็นภาวะระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติเสียจากภูมิคุ้มกันที่ตอบสนองต่อมะเร็ง โดยเฉพาะมะเร็งปอดชนิดเซลล์เล็กร่วมกับ anti-Hu ผู้ป่วยมีความดันตกเมื่อยืน ท้องผูกรุนแรง ลำไส้อืดเทียม และกระเพาะไม่บีบตัว ควรตรวจ antibody และค้นหามะเร็งด้วย CT หรือ PET การรักษามะเร็งสำคัญที่สุด immunotherapy ได้ผลจำกัด และพยากรณ์โรคมักไม่ดี

Slow onset in long-standing diabetes with length-dependent neuropathy
Autonomic failure with painful small-fibre neuropathy, paraprotein, cardiac or renal disease

name: Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration (PCD)
formal: Subacute pancerebellar syndrome with Purkinje cell loss due to onconeural antibodies such as anti-Yo, Hu or Tr, associated with ovarian, breast, lung cancer or Hodgkin lymphoma.
simple: Rapidly worsening balance and coordination caused by the immune system attacking the cerebellum in response to a cancer.
th: สมองน้อยเสื่อมจากภูมิต้านทานที่สัมพันธ์กับมะเร็ง โดยเฉพาะ anti-Yo ในผู้หญิงที่มีมะเร็งรังไข่หรือเต้านม — เซรุนแรงภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์
tempoNote: Ataxia evolves rapidly over days to weeks and plateaus within about 3 months, often before the cancer is known
feat: Rapidly progressive pancerebellar syndrome: gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria
Downbeat nystagmus, oscillopsia and vertigo with nausea at onset
Patient often bedbound or chairbound within weeks
Anti-Yo (PCA-1): almost always women with ovarian, uterine, fallopian tube or breast cancer
Other antibodies: Tr/DNER (Hodgkin lymphoma), Hu, CV2, Ri, KLHL11, VGCC (small-cell lung cancer)
inv: Paraneoplastic panel: Yo (CDR2/CDR2L) by immunoblot confirmed with tissue immunohistochemistry
MRI brain: normal early, cerebellar atrophy later; exclude metastasis and stroke
CSF: early mild pleocytosis, raised protein, oligoclonal bands
Tumour search: mammography/breast MRI, pelvic ultrasound or CT, CA-125, then FDG-PET if negative

case.who: 57-year-old woman, rubber plantation owner in Surat Thani
case.story: Five weeks of dizziness and vomiting, then rapidly worsening imbalance; now she cannot sit without support and speech is slurred.
case.exam: Downbeat nystagmus, scanning dysarthria, severe limb and truncal ataxia, normal strength and sensation.
case.tests: MRI brain normal. CSF: 12 lymphocytes, protein 62 mg/dL, OCB positive. Anti-Yo strongly positive. Pelvic CT: complex left adnexal mass; CA-125 410 U/mL.
case.q: Why is urgent tumour treatment important even though the ataxia rarely improves?
case.a: Anti-Yo PCD reflects an occult gynaecological cancer, often small at diagnosis; early oncological treatment improves survival and may stabilise the neurological deficit, which results from rapid Purkinje cell loss.

read.where: Chapter 27 Paraneoplastic and Nonparaneoplastic Autoimmune Syndromes of the Nervous System

det.patho: Tumours express onconeural proteins such as CDR2/CDR2L, provoking an immune response that also attacks cerebellar Purkinje cells, which normally express these antigens. Because the targets are intracellular, cytotoxic T cells are the main effectors and Purkinje cell loss occurs quickly and irreversibly. The antibody serves as a diagnostic marker rather than the main cause of damage.
det.clinical: Onset is often heralded by dizziness, nausea and visual blurring, followed within weeks by severe pancerebellar ataxia. Neurological symptoms precede the cancer diagnosis in most patients. Mild extracerebellar signs (hyperreflexia, neuropathy) can occur, especially with other antibodies. Tr/DNER cases occur in younger patients with Hodgkin lymphoma and may have a better prognosis.
det.diagnosis: Updated PNS-Care criteria (2021) treat subacute cerebellar syndrome as a high-risk phenotype; a high-risk antibody plus cancer gives definite diagnosis. Confirm commercial line-blot Yo results with tissue-based assays because isolated weak blots can be false. Early MRI is normal, which helps distinguish from structural lesions. If the initial screen is negative, repeat tumour screening at intervals up to about 2 years.
det.treatment: Treat the tumour as the priority. Immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG, plasma exchange, cyclophosphamide or rituximab) is given early, but responses in anti-Yo PCD are modest because neurons are lost quickly. Rehabilitation, safety aids and symptomatic therapy for vertigo and nystagmus are important.
det.prognosis: Most anti-Yo patients remain severely disabled; survival depends mainly on the cancer, while Tr/DNER-associated cases can improve with lymphoma therapy.
pearls: Subacute severe ataxia in a middle-aged woman with normal MRI: think anti-Yo and look for ovarian or breast cancer.
Downbeat nystagmus is common in PCD.
Hodgkin lymphoma plus subacute ataxia points to Tr/DNER antibodies.

det.patho: Tumours expressing neuronal proteins trigger immunity that also attacks shared neural antigens. Antibodies against intracellular antigens (Hu, Ma2, CV2/CRMP5, amphiphysin) are markers of a cytotoxic T-cell attack that destroys neurons, which explains limited reversibility. Antibodies against surface receptors (NMDAR, AMPAR, GABA-B) are directly pathogenic and respond better to treatment. The 2021 PNS-Care criteria classify antibodies as high-risk (over 70% cancer association) or intermediate-risk.
det.clinical: Limbic encephalitis evolves over weeks with memory loss, temporal lobe seizures and psychiatric features; other forms involve the brainstem, diencephalon or cortex diffusely, or overlap with cerebellar degeneration and sensory neuronopathy (encephalomyelitis). Neurological symptoms precede the cancer diagnosis in most patients. Tumours include small-cell lung cancer (Hu, CRMP5, GABA-B), testicular germ-cell tumours (Ma2, KLHL11), thymoma and breast cancer.
det.diagnosis: Apply criteria for possible autoimmune encephalitis, then test serum and CSF for neuronal antibodies, using cell-based assays and confirming line-blot results. MRI, CSF and EEG support inflammation. The PNS-Care score combines phenotype, antibody risk and cancer finding to grade definite, probable or possible paraneoplastic syndrome. If the first tumour search is negative, repeat it every 4–6 months for about 2 years in high-risk cases.
det.treatment: Find and treat the cancer as soon as possible, as this offers the best chance of stabilising neurology. Immunotherapy (IV methylprednisolone, IVIG or plasma exchange, then cyclophosphamide or rituximab) is standard, recognising that intracellular-antibody syndromes rarely improve much while surface-antibody syndromes often do. Manage seizures and psychiatric symptoms. Patients on immune checkpoint inhibitors may develop or unmask similar syndromes.
det.prognosis: Poor with high-risk intracellular antibodies (frequent residual deficits and cancer-related death); better with surface antibodies and early tumour removal.
pearls: Limbic encephalitis plus sensory neuronopathy in a smoker: anti-Hu and small-cell lung cancer.
Young man with limbic plus hypothalamic or midbrain signs: anti-Ma2 and testicular tumour.
A negative first cancer search does not end screening in high-risk antibody syndromes.

det.patho: Tumours express proteins normally restricted to the nervous system, provoking an immune response that also targets neurons. Antibodies to intracellular antigens mark a cytotoxic T-cell process with irreversible neuronal loss, whereas antibodies to surface receptors and channels are often directly pathogenic and potentially reversible. Checkpoint inhibitor therapy can unmask or trigger such responses.
det.clinical: Syndromes can affect any level, from cortex to muscle, and often combine (e.g. encephalomyelitis with sensory neuronopathy). Onset is subacute, with rapid disability. The neurological syndrome typically comes first, and tumours may be small and localised. Recognition of high-risk phenotypes is the key clinical skill.
det.diagnosis: The 2021 updated criteria classify cases as definite, probable or possible using phenotype, antibody risk level, cancer and follow-up (PNS-Care score). Test both serum and CSF, and confirm positive line blots with a second method such as tissue immunohistochemistry. Exclude metastasis, infection, nutritional deficiency and treatment toxicity.
det.treatment: Early tumour treatment is central. Immunotherapy (corticosteroids, IVIG, plasma exchange, then rituximab or cyclophosphamide) is given promptly, with better results in surface-antibody syndromes. Symptomatic therapies such as 3,4-diaminopyridine for LEMS are used. In checkpoint-inhibitor cases, stop the drug and give steroids.
det.prognosis: Variable: surface-antibody syndromes often improve; intracellular-antibody syndromes usually leave fixed deficits.
pearls: The neurological syndrome often appears before the cancer is known.
A negative first tumour screen should be repeated for at least 2 years in high-risk cases.
Intracellular antibody = T-cell damage, poor recovery; surface antibody = better prognosis.

name: Paraneoplastic opsoclonus–myoclonus (POM)
formal: Opsoclonus-myoclonus with ataxia associated with neuroblastoma in children and breast, lung or other tumours in adults, with anti-Ri antibodies in some.

case.story: Over a week she stopped walking, became extremely irritable and her eyes are flicking constantly.
case.exam: Chaotic conjugate eye movements in all directions, jerky trunk and limb myoclonus, unable to sit unsupported.
case.tests: Urine HVA raised; MIBG shows a left adrenal mass — neuroblastoma.
case.q: What is the syndrome, and why must treatment go beyond tumour removal?
case.a: Paraneoplastic opsoclonus-myoclonus; the immune process persists, so steroids/ACTH, IVIG and often rituximab are needed to limit long-term cognitive and behavioural sequelae.

det.patho: An immune response against tumour antigens disrupts the brainstem and cerebellar circuits that control saccades, particularly omnipause neurons and their cerebellar input. In children, neuroblastoma-associated cases involve B-cell activation in CSF; adult cases may carry anti-Ri or other antibodies, though many have none.
det.clinical: Children present with acute ataxia, opsoclonus, myoclonus and marked irritability; the tumour is often low-stage. Adults show similar eye and limb features plus encephalopathy in some. Relapses with illness or steroid withdrawal are common, and children frequently have lasting learning and behavioural problems.
det.diagnosis: Opsoclonus is the key sign and should not be mistaken for nystagmus. In every child, screen thoroughly for neuroblastoma, repeating if initially negative. In adults, test antibodies and search for breast, lung and ovarian tumours. Exclude infection, toxins and other brainstem lesions.
det.treatment: Remove or treat the tumour. Immunotherapy is given early and sustained: corticosteroids or ACTH, IVIG, and rituximab in children, with slow tapering to prevent relapse. Adults receive steroids, IVIG or plasma exchange alongside tumour therapy. Clonazepam or levetiracetam may help myoclonus.
det.prognosis: Childhood neurological outcome is often incomplete despite good tumour prognosis; adult paraneoplastic cases do worse than idiopathic ones.
pearls: Toddler with ataxia and irritability: look at the eyes and test urine HVA/VMA.
Opsoclonus has no intersaccadic pause, unlike nystagmus or square-wave jerks.
In adult women, anti-Ri points to breast cancer.

case.story: Over four months, tingling feet spread to his knees and hands, and he now trips on steps; he has lost 7 kg.
case.exam: Distal weakness, absent ankle reflexes, glove-stocking sensory loss.
case.tests: NCS axonal sensorimotor neuropathy; CRMP5 antibody positive; CT shows mediastinal nodes; biopsy small-cell carcinoma.

det.patho: Mechanisms include T-cell and antibody-mediated attack on nerve (CRMP5, Hu), paraprotein deposition or binding, vasculitis, and direct infiltration by lymphoma. Several mechanisms may coexist, and nutritional and treatment-related factors add to damage in cancer patients.
det.clinical: Most present with a length-dependent sensorimotor neuropathy, but patterns range from mononeuritis multiplex to polyradiculoneuropathy. Pain, autonomic involvement or rapid progression should raise suspicion. In plasma cell disorders, look for organomegaly, skin change and oedema.
det.diagnosis: Characterise the neuropathy electrophysiologically, then search for paraproteins, antibodies and tumours. det.treatment: Treat the underlying malignancy, which offers the best chance of stabilisation. Immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG, plasma exchange) is tried when an immune mechanism is likely. Provide neuropathic pain treatment, physiotherapy and fall prevention.
det.prognosis: Variable; often stabilises with tumour control, but recovery of established axonal loss is limited.
pearls: Unexplained progressive neuropathy with weight loss: screen for paraproteins and cancer.
Demyelinating neuropathy plus lambda light chain: check VEGF for POEMS.
Rule out chemotherapy toxicity before calling a neuropathy paraneoplastic.

det.patho: Cytotoxic T cells directed at the Hu family of RNA-binding proteins destroy dorsal root ganglion neurons; anti-Hu antibodies are markers rather than the direct cause. Because the cell bodies die, both central and peripheral sensory axons degenerate, giving non-length-dependent loss and dorsal column changes.
det.clinical: Onset is subacute and often asymmetric, with numbness, burning pain and progressive sensory ataxia. Upper limbs and face may be involved early. Many patients also develop encephalomyelitis, autonomic neuropathy or cerebellar signs. The neurological syndrome precedes tumour diagnosis in most cases.
det.diagnosis: Suspect ganglionopathy when sensory loss is patchy, proximal or arm-predominant with widespread areflexia and preserved strength; NCS confirms diffuse sensory loss with normal motor responses. Anti-Hu with a compatible phenotype is a high-risk combination. Exclude Sjögren syndrome, cisplatin, pyridoxine excess and hereditary causes.
det.treatment: Find and treat the tumour quickly; this offers the best chance of halting progression. Immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG, plasma exchange, cyclophosphamide) rarely produces improvement but may help stabilisation. Provide neuropathic pain therapy, rehabilitation for sensory ataxia and safety measures.
det.prognosis: Most patients are left with severe disability; survival depends mainly on the cancer.
pearls: Non-length-dependent sensory loss with normal power = ganglionopathy.
Pseudoathetosis is a sign of severe proprioceptive loss, not a basal ganglia disorder.
Anti-Hu in a smoker means small-cell lung cancer until proven otherwise.

name: Paraneoplastic stiff man syndrome
formal: Stiff-person variant with progressive rigidity and spasms associated with anti-amphiphysin antibodies and breast or lung cancer.
simple: A rare condition of muscle stiffness and spasms triggered by the body's immune response to cancer.
th: กลุ่มอาการกล้ามเนื้อแข็งเกร็งและกระตุกเจ็บที่สัมพันธ์กับมะเร็ง โดยเฉพาะ anti-amphiphysin ร่วมกับมะเร็งเต้านมหรือมะเร็งปอด

Amphiphysin form often begins in the neck and arms rather than the lower back

case.story: Three months of a stiff, painful neck and arms with violent spasms when startled; she can barely lift her arms to comb her hair.

case.tests: EMG continuous motor unit activity; amphiphysin antibody strongly positive; breast biopsy invasive ductal carcinoma.
case.q: What is the most important step beyond symptomatic drugs?

det.patho: Amphiphysin is a presynaptic protein needed for endocytosis of synaptic vesicles in inhibitory GABAergic and glycinergic neurons. Antibodies, together with T-cell responses, reduce inhibition in the spinal cord and brainstem, leading to excessive motor neuron firing. Amphiphysin is a high-risk paraneoplastic antibody under the 2021 criteria; most patients have breast cancer or small-cell lung cancer. GAD65 antibodies are only rarely paraneoplastic.
det.clinical: Rigidity and spasms resemble classic SPS but tend to be asymmetric, involve the neck and upper limbs earlier and progress faster. Patients may develop additional paraneoplastic features such as sensory neuronopathy, myelitis or encephalitis. Spasms can be severe enough to cause fractures, falls and respiratory or autonomic crises. Neurological symptoms often precede the cancer diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: Clinical stiffness with continuous motor unit activity and a positive amphiphysin antibody establishes the diagnosis; CSF may show inflammation or intrathecal antibody synthesis. Search immediately for breast and lung cancer, repeating screening if negative. Consider other stiffness causes: spinal lesions, tetanus, neuromyotonia, dystonia and drug-induced rigidity.
det.treatment: Cancer treatment is central and may improve stiffness. Symptomatic relief uses GABAergic drugs (diazepam, clonazepam, baclofen, including intrathecal baclofen in severe cases). Immunotherapy with IVIG, steroids, plasma exchange or rituximab is commonly used, with variable response. Avoid sudden withdrawal of benzodiazepines or baclofen, which can trigger dangerous spasms.
det.prognosis: Variable; outcome depends heavily on cancer control, and many have residual stiffness.
pearls: Stiff-person picture in a woman with neck and arm stiffness: check amphiphysin and examine the breasts.
GAD65 SPS is usually not paraneoplastic; amphiphysin SPS usually is.
Abrupt baclofen or benzodiazepine withdrawal can be life-threatening.
det.thd: Paraneoplastic stiff man syndrome เป็นกลุ่มอาการกล้ามเนื้อแข็งเกร็งและกระตุกเจ็บที่สัมพันธ์กับมะเร็ง ส่วนใหญ่พบ anti-amphiphysin ร่วมกับมะเร็งเต้านมหรือมะเร็งปอดชนิดเซลล์เล็ก มักเริ่มที่คอและแขน และเป็นเร็วกว่า SPS แบบคลาสสิกที่สัมพันธ์กับ GAD65 ตรวจ EMG พบ motor unit ทำงานตลอดเวลา การรักษาที่สำคัญคือรักษามะเร็ง ร่วมกับ diazepam หรือ baclofen และยาปรับภูมิคุ้มกันเช่น IVIG

name: Paraneoplastic syndrome
formal: Remote effects of malignancy on the nervous system or other organs from immune mechanisms or secreted factors, with antibodies such as Hu, Yo, Ri and CV2.
simple: Symptoms caused not by a tumour itself but by the body's immune response to it.
more: Test for onconeural antibodies (anti-Hu, Yo, Ri, CV2/CRMP5, amphiphysin, Ma2) and screen for tumour with CT, PET and mammography. Treat the tumour and give immunotherapy, but prognosis is poor; neurological syndromes often precede detection of the cancer.

feat: Broad umbrella term covering neurological, endocrine, dermatological and haematological remote effects of cancer
Neurological forms are mainly immune-mediated with onconeural antibodies

Symptoms can be the first sign of an occult tumour

case.story: Over a month he has become confused and weak; family notes weight loss and a chronic cough.
case.exam: Drowsy but no focal signs; proximal weakness that improves briefly after sustained effort.
case.tests: Sodium 118 mmol/L with inappropriate urine concentration; VGCC antibodies positive; CT shows a central lung mass.
case.q: Which two paraneoplastic processes are present?

read.where: Chapter 16 - Autoimmune and Inflammatory Encephalopathies as Complications of Cancer
Chapter 27 Paraneoplastic and Nonparaneoplastic Autoimmune Syndromes of the Nervous System

det.patho: Paraneoplastic effects arise either from substances secreted by the tumour (hormones, cytokines) or from immune responses against tumour antigens that cross-react with normal tissue. In the nervous system the immune route predominates. The term excludes direct invasion, metastasis, infection, metabolic effects of treatment and nutritional deficiency.
det.clinical: Neurological syndromes include encephalitis, cerebellar degeneration, opsoclonus-myoclonus, myelitis, sensory neuronopathy, autonomic neuropathy, LEMS and dermatomyositis. Non-neurological examples (SIADH, hypercalcaemia, Cushing syndrome) can still present with confusion or weakness. Recognising the pattern often leads to earlier cancer diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: Base the diagnosis on a compatible syndrome, antibody results and cancer detection, applying the 2021 PNS criteria for neurological cases. Exclude metastases, infection and treatment effects. Repeat tumour surveillance if the first search is negative.
det.treatment: Treat the tumour as the primary measure. Immunotherapy is added for immune-mediated neurological syndromes; metabolic syndromes need targeted correction (fluid restriction or tolvaptan for SIADH, bisphosphonates for hypercalcaemia). Supportive and rehabilitative care are important.
det.prognosis: Depends on the tumour and syndrome type; early tumour control gives the best outcome.
pearls: Paraneoplastic means remote effect, not metastasis.
No tumour generates more paraneoplastic syndromes than SCLC.
Always check sodium and calcium in a cancer patient with new confusion.
det.thd: Paraneoplastic syndrome คือผลทางไกลของมะเร็งที่ไม่ใช่การลุกลามโดยตรง เกิดจากสารที่ก้อนหลั่งหรือภูมิคุ้มกันที่โจมตีเนื้อเยื่อปกติ ในระบบประสาทพบ encephalitis, cerebellar degeneration, sensory neuronopathy, LEMS ส่วนที่ไม่ใช่ระบบประสาทเช่น SIADH และแคลเซียมสูง การวินิจฉัยใช้อาการ antibody และการค้นหามะเร็ง รักษามะเร็งเป็นหลักร่วมกับ immunotherapy

case.who: 66-year-old woman from Lampang with breast cancer treated five years ago

det.patho: Paraplegia arises when motor pathways to both legs are interrupted, most often in the thoracic or lumbar cord, conus or cauda equina. Upper motor neuron lesions produce spasticity and hyperreflexia after an initial period of spinal shock, whereas root lesions produce flaccid areflexia. Bilateral medial frontal lesions affecting the leg area of motor cortex are an uncommon cerebral cause.
det.clinical: Acute paraplegia may follow trauma, spinal cord infarction, epidural haematoma or abscess, or malignant compression. Subacute causes include transverse myelitis, NMOSD and B12 deficiency. Chronic progressive forms are seen in HTLV-1 myelopathy (common in parts of the tropics), hereditary spastic paraplegia, spondylosis, tumours and dural arteriovenous fistula. Complications include bladder retention, pressure ulcers and venous thromboembolism.
det.diagnosis: Examination determines upper versus lower motor neuron pattern and the sensory level. Emergency MRI of the whole spine is the key test for compressive and structural causes. If MRI is unrevealing, CSF analysis, antibody testing, metabolic screens and neurophysiology follow. Consider brain imaging when there are cortical signs.
det.treatment: Compressive lesions are emergencies: dexamethasone and urgent oncological or surgical management for metastases, and surgery plus antibiotics for abscess. Inflammatory myelitis needs high-dose steroids and plasma exchange. Supportive care includes bladder management, thromboprophylaxis, skin care, spasticity treatment and rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause, severity and time to treatment; ability to walk at presentation best predicts outcome in cord compression.
pearls: Back pain plus leg weakness in a cancer patient = cord compression until proved otherwise.
Early spinal shock can make a cord lesion look flaccid like GBS — check for a sensory level.
Image the whole spine; multiple metastatic levels are common.
det.thd: Paraplegia คือภาวะขาทั้งสองข้างอ่อนแรงหรือเป็นอัมพาต เป็นกลุ่มอาการไม่ใช่โรคเดียว ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจากรอยโรคไขสันหลังส่วนอกหรือเอว หรือ cauda equina บางครั้งจากสมองส่วน parasagittal สาเหตุสำคัญได้แก่ อุบัติเหตุ มะเร็งแพร่กดไขสันหลัง ฝี ไขสันหลังอักเสบ ขาด B12 และ HTLV-1 ต้องทำ MRI กระดูกสันหลังทั้งหมดอย่างเร่งด่วน และรักษาตามสาเหตุร่วมกับดูแลกระเพาะปัสสาวะและฟื้นฟู

name: Paraproteinaemic neuropathy
formal: Neuropathy occurring with a monoclonal immunoglobulin (M-protein) produced by a clonal plasma-cell or B-cell population — most often MGUS, sometimes myeloma, Waldenström macroglobulinaemia, lymphoma, AL amyloidosis, cryoglobulinaemia or POEMS; mechanisms include antibody binding to nerve antigens and deposition of immunoglobulin or amyloid.
simple: Nerve damage that comes with an abnormal single type of antibody protein in the blood, made by an overgrown family of blood cells; sometimes that family is a cancer, so it must be looked for.
th: เส้นประสาทเสื่อมที่พบร่วมกับโปรตีนโมโนโคลนอลในเลือด — ต้องตรวจหาโรคเม็ดเลือดชนิด plasma cell/B cell ที่ซ่อนอยู่
feat: Usually a slowly progressive distal sensory-predominant polyneuropathy in older adults
Three clinical patterns: distal demyelinating (often IgM/anti-MAG), CIDP-like (often IgG/IgA), or length-dependent axonal
The neuropathy may appear years before the blood disorder declares itself
Red flags for malignancy: weight loss, bone pain, organomegaly, anaemia, renal failure, autonomic failure
inv: Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation (more sensitive than electrophoresis alone) and serum free light chains
Urine protein electrophoresis/immunofixation
NCS to define demyelinating vs axonal pattern
Haematology referral: bone marrow, skeletal survey; anti-MAG if IgM; VEGF if POEMS suspected; fat pad biopsy for amyloid

case.exam: Stocking sensory loss, reduced vibration at the knees, absent ankle jerks, mild toe extensor weakness.

det.patho: A clone of plasma cells or B cells secretes a single immunoglobulin (M-protein). Nerve injury can arise because the M-protein acts as an autoantibody (anti-MAG, anti-ganglioside), because light chains form amyloid deposits, because cryoglobulins cause vasculitis, through cytokines such as VEGF in POEMS, or through direct infiltration. In many older patients with an IgG or IgA band the M-protein is incidental, since MGUS is common in the elderly. IgM gammopathies are proportionally more often truly linked to neuropathy.
det.clinical: Most patients have a slowly worsening distal sensory or sensorimotor neuropathy. Three main patterns guide work-up: distal acquired demyelinating (typical of IgM/anti-MAG), CIDP-like with proximal weakness, and length-dependent axonal. Red flags for a serious underlying disorder include weight loss, bone pain, organomegaly, autonomic failure, painful small-fibre neuropathy, rapid progression, renal impairment and skin changes.
det.diagnosis: Screen any unexplained neuropathy with serum electrophoresis plus immunofixation and serum free light chains; electrophoresis alone misses small bands. Characterise the neuropathy with NCS. Then tailor tests: anti-MAG for IgM, VEGF and bone imaging for lambda bands with demyelination, fat pad or nerve biopsy for amyloid, cryoglobulins and hepatitis C for vasculitic pictures. Refer to haematology for marrow examination and staging.
det.treatment: Treatment depends on the mechanism. CIDP-like IgG/IgA cases are treated as CIDP. Anti-MAG disease is treated with rituximab when disabling. Malignant causes (myeloma, Waldenström, AL amyloid, POEMS) require haematological therapy directed at the clone. Slow axonal neuropathy with an incidental MGUS usually needs only symptomatic care and monitoring.
det.prognosis: Outlook depends on the underlying disorder, ranging from a benign course with MGUS to serious systemic disease with amyloidosis or POEMS.
pearls: Immunofixation and free light chains are more sensitive than SPEP — order them together.
A lambda paraprotein with a demyelinating neuropathy is POEMS until proven otherwise.
An IgG MGUS in an elderly patient may be a bystander; do not over-attribute.
det.thd: Paraproteinaemic neuropathy คือเส้นประสาทเสื่อมที่พบร่วมกับโปรตีนโมโนโคลนอลในเลือด ซึ่งสร้างจากกลุ่มเซลล์พลาสมาหรือ B cell ที่เจริญผิดปกติ กลไกมีหลายแบบ เช่น โปรตีนทำหน้าที่เป็นแอนติบอดีต่อเส้นประสาท หรือสะสมเป็นอะไมลอยด์ ควรตรวจ immunofixation และ free light chain ในผู้ป่วยเส้นประสาทเสื่อมที่ไม่ทราบสาเหตุ และส่งปรึกษาโลหิตวิทยาเพื่อหาโรคมะเร็ง การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ เช่น แบบคล้าย CIDP รักษาเหมือน CIDP ส่วนแบบที่เป็นมะเร็งต้องรักษาตัวโรคเลือด

name: Parasagittal meningioma
formal: Meningioma along the superior sagittal sinus causing focal seizures and contralateral leg weakness from parasagittal motor cortex involvement.
simple: A slow-growing brain-lining tumour near the midline that can cause seizures and leg weakness.
th: เนื้องอกเยื่อหุ้มสมองตามแนว superior sagittal sinus ทำให้ชักเฉพาะที่และขาอ่อนแรงด้านตรงข้าม หรือขาอ่อนแรงทั้งสองข้างคล้ายรอยโรคไขสันหลัง
tempoNote: Slow growth over years; symptoms creep in gradually or appear as a first seizure
feat: Focal motor seizures starting in the foot or leg
Progressive contralateral leg weakness; bilateral leg weakness with large or bilateral tumours mimicking spinal cord disease
Urinary urgency or incontinence and apathy from mesial frontal involvement
Headache and raised intracranial pressure if the sagittal sinus becomes occluded
More common in middle-aged women
inv: MRI with contrast: extra-axial dural-based enhancing mass with dural tail
MR or CT venography to assess sagittal sinus invasion and patency
EEG if seizures; histology with WHO grading after surgery

case.story: A year of right foot dragging and recent urinary urgency, initially investigated with lumbar spine MRI; last week her right leg jerked rhythmically for two minutes.
case.exam: Right leg weakness with brisk knee jerk and upgoing right toe; arms normal.
case.tests: Normal spine MRI; brain MRI shows a 4 cm homogeneously enhancing dural-based mass along the left falx at the vertex, middle third of the sagittal sinus partly invaded.
case.q: Why was her lesion missed initially and what is the treatment plan?
case.a: Leg-predominant UMN weakness can come from the parasagittal motor strip; treat with resection preserving the patent sinus, with radiosurgery for residual tumour.

det.patho: Meningiomas arise from arachnoid cap cells; parasagittal ones attach to the lateral wall of the superior sagittal sinus and adjacent convexity dura, while falcine tumours arise from the falx itself. Common drivers include NF2 loss, and in benign skull-base or convexity tumours TRAF7, KLF4, AKT1 or SMO variants; TERT promoter mutation and CDKN2A/B deletion mark aggressive disease. They are mostly WHO grade 1, slow growing and more common in women, and risk rises with prior radiation.
det.clinical: Tumours compress the paracentral lobule (leg motor and sensory cortex), causing focal motor or sensory seizures in the leg and progressive leg weakness. Bilateral or large lesions give paraparesis and bladder symptoms that mislead clinicians toward spinal cord disease. Anterior-third tumours cause personality change and apathy, and posterior ones visual or sensory symptoms. Sinus occlusion can produce raised intracranial pressure.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows an extra-axial, dural-based, avidly enhancing mass with a dural tail, CSF cleft and possible hyperostosis. Venous imaging determines whether the sinus is patent, partly or fully occluded, which guides surgery. Differential includes dural metastasis, haemangiopericytoma (solitary fibrous tumour), lymphoma and granulomatous disease. Grade is assigned histologically and molecularly.
det.treatment: Small asymptomatic tumours can be watched with serial MRI. Symptomatic or growing tumours are resected; surgeons generally avoid sacrificing a patent sinus and leave sinus-invading tissue for radiosurgery or radiotherapy. Higher-grade tumours receive adjuvant radiotherapy. Anti-seizure medication controls seizures, and perioperative venous infarction is a key surgical risk.
det.prognosis: Usually good for grade 1 tumours, but sinus invasion increases recurrence because complete removal is harder.
pearls: UMN leg weakness with normal spine imaging: image the brain vertex.
Jacksonian march starting in the foot points to the paracentral lobule.
Sinus patency, not tumour size alone, shapes the surgical strategy.
det.thd: Parasagittal meningioma เป็นเนื้องอกเยื่อหุ้มสมองที่เกาะตามแนว superior sagittal sinus กดเปลือกสมองส่วนที่ควบคุมขา ทำให้ชักเฉพาะที่เริ่มจากเท้าและขาอ่อนแรงด้านตรงข้าม ถ้าเป็นสองข้างจะมีขาอ่อนแรงสองข้างและปัสสาวะผิดปกติคล้ายโรคไขสันหลัง วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI สมองร่วมกับตรวจหลอดเลือดดำว่าเนื้องอกลุกลาม sinus หรือไม่ รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัดโดยรักษา sinus ที่ยังเปิดอยู่ และใช้ radiosurgery กับส่วนที่เหลือ

name: Parasitic neurological infections
formal: CNS infection by helminths or protozoa such as neurocysticercosis, toxoplasmosis, malaria and schistosomiasis, producing seizures, mass lesions and meningitis.
simple: Nervous system infections caused by parasites, such as tapeworm cysts in the brain.
th: การติดเชื้อปรสิตในระบบประสาท เช่น พยาธิตืดหมู พยาธิหอยโข่ง พยาธิตัวจี๊ด มาลาเรียขึ้นสมอง และ toxoplasma ทำให้ชัก ก้อนในสมอง เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ หรือไขสันหลังอักเสบ
tempoNote: Hours in cerebral malaria, days to weeks in eosinophilic meningitis and gnathostomiasis, months to years in neurocysticercosis
feat: Neurocysticercosis: leading cause of acquired epilepsy in endemic areas; cystic, enhancing or calcified lesions
Angiostrongylus cantonensis (raw snails): severe headache, limb paraesthesia and eosinophilic meningitis
Gnathostoma spinigerum (raw fish, frogs): root pain then myelitis, or haemorrhagic tracks in brain with subarachnoid or intracerebral bleeding
Cerebral malaria with coma and seizures; toxoplasmosis with ring lesions in advanced HIV
Naegleria fowleri: fulminant meningoencephalitis after freshwater exposure
inv: MRI or CT for cysts, calcification, ring lesions, haemorrhagic tracks and cord swelling
CSF with eosinophil percentage (above 10% favours helminths) and xanthochromia in gnathostomiasis; wet mount for amoebae
Serology or immunoblot for cysticercus, Gnathostoma, Angiostrongylus, Toxoplasma; malaria smear or rapid test

case.who: 34-year-old male construction worker from Nakhon Ratchasima
case.story: Ten days after a party with raw apple snails he developed severe headache, neck stiffness and burning legs.
case.exam: Mild neck stiffness, alert, no focal deficit, hyperaesthesia over the legs.
case.tests: Blood eosinophils 18%; CSF pressure 32 cmH2O, 450 cells with 40% eosinophils, normal glucose; CT brain normal.
case.q: Which parasite is likely, and what is the treatment approach?
case.a: Angiostrongylus cantonensis eosinophilic meningitis. Treat with repeated therapeutic lumbar puncture and analgesia; add a short corticosteroid course for headache, with antihelminthics decided case by case.

det.patho: Parasites reach the nervous system by blood spread (Plasmodium, Toxoplasma, cysticerci), nasal or skin entry (Naegleria) or migration through tissue (Angiostrongylus, Gnathostoma). Damage arises from mass effect, inflammation around dying parasites, vascular occlusion, and mechanical tearing of vessels and parenchyma by migrating larvae. Dietary habits with raw freshwater animals drive the local epidemiology in Thailand.
det.clinical: Presentation follows the organism: seizures and headache in neurocysticercosis, eosinophilic meningitis from snails, and in gnathostomiasis a sudden radicular pain that evolves to paraparesis with sphincter loss, or abrupt haemorrhagic stroke-like events. Migratory swellings in the skin may precede or be absent. Cerebral malaria is a medical emergency with fever and coma, and Naegleria progresses in days.
det.diagnosis: Combine exposure history, eosinophilia, CSF analysis and imaging, then confirm with organism-specific serology; immunoblot is the reference for gnathostomiasis. MRI in cerebrospinal gnathostomiasis shows cord enlargement with diffuse signal change and haemorrhagic tracts in brain with nodular enhancement. Exclude bacterial, tuberculous and fungal meningitis, and always test for HIV.
det.treatment: Treat the specific parasite: albendazole with or without praziquantel and steroids for neurocysticercosis, artesunate for severe malaria, pyrimethamine-based therapy for toxoplasmosis, and albendazole (or ivermectin) for gnathostomiasis, with steroids considered case by case. Eosinophilic meningitis is managed by analgesia and serial lumbar punctures. Control seizures and raised pressure, and counsel on thorough cooking of snails, fish and frogs.
det.prognosis: Variable: eosinophilic meningitis usually resolves, whereas cerebral gnathostomiasis with haemorrhage and myelitis carries high mortality or lasting disability, and untreated cerebral malaria and amoebic infection are often fatal.
pearls: CSF eosinophilia plus raw snail or fish exposure is parasitic until proven otherwise.
Xanthochromic CSF with eosinophils suggests Gnathostoma.
Give steroids before antihelminthics when many cysts or heavy inflammation are expected.
det.thd: ปรสิตเข้าสู่ระบบประสาทได้หลายทาง เช่น พยาธิตืดหมูทำให้ชักและมีถุงน้ำในสมอง พยาธิหอยโข่งทำให้เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบชนิด eosinophil สูง ส่วนพยาธิตัวจี๊ดทำให้ปวดรากประสาท ไขสันหลังอักเสบ หรือเลือดออกในสมอง ตรวจเลือดดู eosinophil เจาะน้ำไขสันหลัง ทำ MRI และตรวจ serology ยืนยัน รักษาตามชนิดของพยาธิ ควบคุมอาการชักและความดันในกะโหลก และป้องกันโดยไม่กินอาหารดิบ

name: Parasomnias
formal: Abnormal sleep behaviours, either NREM (sleepwalking, night terrors) or REM (REM sleep behaviour disorder, nightmares), reflecting incomplete state dissociation.
simple: Unusual behaviours during sleep such as sleepwalking, talking or acting out dreams.
th: กลุ่มพฤติกรรมผิดปกติขณะหลับ แบ่งเป็นช่วง NREM เช่น ละเมอเดิน night terror และช่วง REM เช่น REM sleep behaviour disorder และฝันร้าย
tempoNote: Recurrent nocturnal events; NREM forms peak in childhood, RBD in older adults
feat: NREM disorders of arousal: confusional arousals, sleepwalking, sleep terrors, sleep-related eating; early-night (first-third) timing
REM parasomnias: REM sleep behaviour disorder, nightmare disorder, recurrent isolated sleep paralysis; later in the night
Other: exploding head syndrome, sleep-related hallucinations, enuresis
Triggers: sleep deprivation, fever, alcohol, sedatives (e.g. Z-drugs), sleep apnoea
Key mimic: sleep-related hypermotor (frontal lobe) epilepsy
inv: Detailed history from bed partner and home video
Video-polysomnography with extended EEG montage when diagnosis uncertain or behaviour dangerous
Look for triggers such as sleep apnoea or periodic limb movements

case.story: About an hour after falling asleep, he sits up screaming, sweating and wide-eyed, does not recognise his parents and remembers nothing the next morning; worse when he has fever.
case.exam: Normal; large tonsils, snores.
case.tests: Video-PSG shows arousals from slow-wave sleep and moderate obstructive sleep apnoea.
case.q: Which parasomnia and what treatment may help?
case.a: Sleep terrors (NREM disorder of arousal) triggered by sleep apnoea; reassurance, safety and adenotonsillectomy to reduce arousals.

read.where: Chapter 52: Violent parasomnias and sleep forensics

det.patho: Parasomnias reflect incomplete transitions between wake, NREM and REM sleep, so that features of different states occur together. In NREM disorders of arousal, motor and limbic regions activate while the frontal cortex remains in deep sleep, producing complex behaviour without awareness or memory. In RBD, loss of REM atonia from brainstem pathology lets dream content be acted out, often heralding Parkinson disease, DLB or MSA.
det.clinical: NREM parasomnias usually begin in childhood, often run in families and arise during the first hours of sleep with confusion and amnesia. Sleep terrors involve screaming and autonomic arousal; sleepwalking can lead to injury. RBD affects mainly older men, with vocal and violent movements linked to vivid dreams, mostly in the later hours of sleep, when REM periods lengthen. Nightmare disorder causes awakening with recall of distressing dreams.
det.diagnosis: History from witnesses and home video often suffice for typical childhood NREM parasomnias. Video-polysomnography is indicated for adults, injurious behaviour, suspected RBD or possible epilepsy; RBD requires REM sleep without atonia. Stereotyped, frequent, brief events suggest sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy. Identify triggers like apnoea, medications and sleep deprivation.
det.treatment: Make the environment safe and reduce triggers. Childhood NREM parasomnias usually need only reassurance and regular sleep; scheduled awakenings or clonazepam are options for frequent events. RBD is treated with melatonin or clonazepam and bedroom safety, plus counselling about future neurodegeneration risk. Nightmare disorder responds to imagery rehearsal therapy or prazosin in PTSD.
det.prognosis: Childhood NREM parasomnias usually fade by adolescence; idiopathic RBD carries a high long-term risk of synucleinopathy.
pearls: Early-night events point to NREM parasomnia; late-night events to REM sleep.
New dream enactment in an older adult is a prodrome of synucleinopathy.
Many brief stereotyped nightly events suggest epilepsy, not parasomnia.
det.thd: Parasomnias คือกลุ่มพฤติกรรมผิดปกติขณะหลับ แบ่งเป็นช่วง NREM เช่น ละเมอเดิน ตื่นมากรีดร้อง และกินขณะหลับ ซึ่งมักเกิดช่วงต้นคืนในเด็ก และช่วง REM เช่น REM sleep behaviour disorder ที่ผู้สูงอายุแสดงท่าทางตามความฝัน ซึ่งอาจเป็นสัญญาณเริ่มต้นของ Parkinson การวินิจฉัยใช้ประวัติ วิดีโอ และ video-polysomnography การรักษาคือดูแลความปลอดภัย แก้ปัจจัยกระตุ้น และใช้ยาเมื่อจำเป็น

name: Parathyroid disorders
formal: Hyper- or hypoparathyroidism causing calcium disturbance, with neuromuscular irritability, tetany, seizures, basal ganglia calcification and proximal myopathy.
simple: Problems with the glands controlling calcium, which can cause muscle cramps, weakness and seizures.
more: Check serum calcium, phosphate, PTH and vitamin D, with CT or MRI showing basal ganglia calcification. Neuromuscular signs improve with correction of calcium: calcium and calcitriol for hypoparathyroidism, parathyroidectomy for primary hyperparathyroidism.
th: ภาวะพาราไทรอยด์ทำงานมากหรือน้อยเกินไปทำให้แคลเซียมผิดปกติ มีชา เกร็ง (tetany) ชัก หินปูนในปมประสาทฐาน หรือกล้ามเนื้อต้นแขนขาอ่อนแรง
tempoNote: Chronic insidious symptoms; acute tetany, seizures or confusion when calcium falls or rises sharply
feat: Endocrine disorders with neurological effects, not primary neurological diseases
Hypocalcaemia: perioral and finger tingling, carpopedal spasm, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, seizures, laryngospasm
Chronic hypoparathyroidism: basal ganglia calcification, parkinsonism or chorea, raised intracranial pressure, cataracts
Hypercalcaemia (hyperparathyroidism): fatigue, depression, confusion, proximal weakness with brisk reflexes
Post-thyroidectomy is the commonest cause of hypoparathyroidism
inv: Serum calcium (adjusted or ionised), phosphate, magnesium, PTH, 25-OH vitamin D, creatinine
ECG for QT change; CT brain for basal ganglia calcification
EMG/CK if myopathy suspected; neck ultrasound or sestamibi scan to locate an adenoma

case.story: Total thyroidectomy for goitre 8 years ago; now has hand cramps, tingling around the mouth, a recent generalised seizure and a slight tremor and slowness.
case.exam: Positive Chvostek and Trousseau signs, mild bradykinesia, bilateral cataracts.
case.tests: Calcium 1.6 mmol/L, phosphate high, PTH undetectable; CT shows symmetric calcification of the basal ganglia and dentate nuclei; QTc prolonged.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and how should it be treated?
case.a: Post-surgical hypoparathyroidism with secondary basal ganglia calcification; IV calcium gluconate for symptomatic hypocalcaemia, then oral calcium with calcitriol (and magnesium if low).

Myopathies of Systemic Disease and Toxic Myopathies

det.patho: PTH controls serum calcium through bone, kidney and vitamin D activation. Low ionised calcium increases nerve membrane excitability, producing paraesthesia, tetany and seizures; long-standing high phosphate with low calcium favours calcium deposition in the basal ganglia, dentate nuclei and lens. Excess PTH and calcium reduce neuromuscular excitability and cause a type 2 fibre myopathy and neuropsychiatric slowing. Pseudohypoparathyroidism reflects end-organ PTH resistance (GNAS).
det.clinical: This entry is an endocrine group with neurological consequences rather than a neurological disease. Hypoparathyroidism (post-surgical, autoimmune, genetic such as 22q11 deletion) gives tetany, laryngospasm, seizures, cognitive or psychiatric symptoms, movement disorders from calcification and occasionally papilloedema. Primary hyperparathyroidism is often found incidentally but can cause fatigue, depression, poor concentration and proximal weakness, rarely with brisk reflexes resembling motor neuron disease. Severe hypercalcaemia leads to confusion and coma.
det.diagnosis: Measure calcium with paired PTH: low calcium with low or inappropriately normal PTH means hypoparathyroidism; high calcium with high-normal or raised PTH means hyperparathyroidism; low calcium with high PTH suggests vitamin D deficiency, renal disease or pseudohypoparathyroidism. Always check magnesium. Imaging (CT for calcification, neck imaging for adenomas) follows the biochemistry.
det.treatment: Symptomatic hypocalcaemia needs IV calcium gluconate with cardiac monitoring and correction of magnesium; chronic hypoparathyroidism uses oral calcium plus calcitriol (or alfacalcidol), aiming for low-normal calcium to protect the kidneys, and recombinant PTH analogues such as palopegteriparatide in difficult cases. Primary hyperparathyroidism is treated by parathyroidectomy when criteria are met; cinacalcet is an option for non-surgical patients. Neuromuscular and seizure symptoms usually improve with correction, while established calcification does not regress.
det.prognosis: Tetany, seizures and myopathy usually resolve with correction; basal ganglia calcification and related movement disorders tend to persist.
pearls: New seizures years after thyroid surgery: check calcium and PTH.
Brain calcification with low calcium and low PTH is hypoparathyroidism, not Fahr disease.
Correct magnesium, or calcium will not normalise.
det.thd: ความผิดปกติของต่อมพาราไทรอยด์ทำให้ระดับแคลเซียมในเลือดผิดปกติ ภาวะพาราไทรอยด์ต่ำ (พบบ่อยหลังผ่าตัดไทรอยด์) ทำให้แคลเซียมต่ำ มีชารอบปาก มือจีบเกร็ง ชัก และในระยะยาวมีหินปูนในปมประสาทฐานจนเกิดพาร์กินสันหรือ chorea ส่วนภาวะพาราไทรอยด์เกินทำให้แคลเซียมสูง อ่อนเพลีย ซึมเศร้า สับสน และกล้ามเนื้อต้นแขนขาอ่อนแรง วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจแคลเซียม ฟอสเฟต แมกนีเซียม และ PTH รักษาด้วยการแก้ไขแคลเซียม ให้ calcitriol หรือผ่าตัดต่อมพาราไทรอยด์

name: Parathyroid-induced myopathy
formal: Proximal muscle weakness and wasting from primary hyperparathyroidism or vitamin D deficiency osteomalacia, with normal CK, reversible after treatment.
simple: Muscle weakness in the thighs and hips caused by an overactive parathyroid gland or low vitamin D.
th: กล้ามเนื้อต้นแขนขาอ่อนแรงและฝ่อจาก hyperparathyroidism หรือขาดวิตามินดี (osteomalacia) CK มักปกติ และดีขึ้นหลังรักษาสาเหตุ
tempoNote: Gradual over months; improves over weeks to months after correction
feat: Proximal leg weakness, waddling gait, difficulty rising
Bone pain, fractures, fatigue; brisk reflexes may be preserved
CK normal or slightly raised
Associated with primary or secondary hyperparathyroidism (CKD) and vitamin D deficiency
Hypercalcaemia symptoms (thirst, constipation, confusion) in primary disease

CK; EMG normal or mildly myopathic

case.who: 58-year-old Muslim woman from Pattani who wears full covering and rarely goes outdoors
case.story: One year of difficulty standing from the floor during prayer, aching hips and a waddling gait.
case.exam: Proximal leg weakness MRC 4-/5, tender pelvis and ribs, normal reflexes and sensation.
case.tests: CK normal; calcium low-normal, phosphate low, ALP high, PTH elevated, 25-OH vitamin D very low.
case.q: What is the cause of her weakness and its treatment?
case.a: Osteomalacic myopathy from vitamin D deficiency with secondary hyperparathyroidism — vitamin D and calcium replacement.

det.patho: Vitamin D acts on muscle through its receptor, supporting calcium handling and fibre function; deficiency produces type 2 fibre atrophy. Excess PTH promotes muscle protein breakdown and alters calcium flux. The resulting myopathy is non-inflammatory and non-necrotic, explaining the normal CK.
det.clinical: Patients describe proximal leg weakness and fatigue, often with bone pain from osteomalacia. Primary hyperparathyroidism may cause weakness with hypercalcaemic symptoms; a classic but now rare neuromuscular syndrome includes brisk reflexes and tongue fasciculations that mimic motor neuron disease. Risk groups include those with little sun exposure, malabsorption, CKD and anticonvulsant use.
det.diagnosis: Bone biochemistry is the key: raised ALP and PTH with low vitamin D or high calcium. CK is usually normal and EMG may be normal or show short polyphasic units. Biopsy, rarely needed, shows type 2 fibre atrophy. Exclude other endocrine and drug-induced myopathies.
det.treatment: Replace vitamin D and calcium in deficiency, with monitoring of calcium. Primary hyperparathyroidism is treated by parathyroidectomy when indicated. In CKD, manage secondary hyperparathyroidism with active vitamin D, phosphate binders or calcimimetics. Physiotherapy aids recovery.
det.prognosis: Usually reversible over weeks to months after correction.
pearls: Proximal weakness with normal CK and high ALP: check vitamin D and PTH.
Covered clothing and indoor life are common risk factors even in sunny countries.
Hyperparathyroidism can mimic motor neuron disease.
det.thd: Parathyroid-induced myopathy คือกล้ามเนื้อต้นขาอ่อนแรงจาก hyperparathyroidism หรือขาดวิตามินดี (osteomalacia) ผู้ป่วยเดินโยกเยก ลุกจากพื้นลำบาก ปวดกระดูก CK มักปกติ ตรวจพบ ALP และ PTH สูง วิตามินดีต่ำ การรักษาคือให้วิตามินดีและแคลเซียม หรือผ่าตัดต่อมพาราไทรอยด์ อาการมักดีขึ้นภายในไม่กี่เดือน

name: Parenchymal CNS tuberculosis
formal: Tuberculoma or abscess of brain or spinal cord from Mycobacterium tuberculosis, causing focal deficits and seizures with ring-enhancing lesions.
simple: Tuberculosis forming lumps within the brain or spinal cord, causing weakness or seizures.
th: วัณโรคในเนื้อสมองและไขสันหลัง ได้แก่ tuberculoma, ฝีวัณโรค, tuberculous encephalopathy ในเด็ก และ tuberculoma ในไขสันหลัง มักมาด้วยชักหรืออาการเฉพาะที่ และอาจเกิดหรือโตขึ้นระหว่างรักษา (paradoxical reaction)

feat: Forms: tuberculoma (single, multiple or hundreds of lesions), tuberculous abscess, a diffuse encephalopathy in young children, and intramedullary tuberculoma of the cord
Seizures, headache and focal deficits; systemic symptoms and an abnormal chest film are absent in many patients
Coexists with tuberculous meningitis in a sizeable minority; meningitis adds basal exudate, hydrocephalus and lenticulostriate infarcts
Paradoxical reaction: lesions appear or grow on correct therapy for pulmonary, miliary or meningeal TB, without drug resistance
Intramedullary tuberculoma gives a subacute compressive myelopathy that may need early decompression

Look for TB elsewhere: chest CT, sputum or gastric aspirate Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra and culture, lymph node aspirate; HIV test
CSF (if safe) for cells, glucose, Xpert Ultra and culture when meningitis may coexist

case.who: 22-year-old woman from Mae Sot treated for tuberculous meningitis, HIV negative
case.story: Her headache and fever resolved in the first month of four-drug therapy with dexamethasone, but in week 9 she develops new right-hand clumsiness and a focal seizure.
case.exam: Alert, mild right hemiparesis, no papilloedema; adherence confirmed by her village health volunteer.
case.tests: Repeat MRI shows three new ring-enhancing lesions in the left basal ganglia and frontal lobe with oedema; the original isolate was fully drug susceptible; sputum is now smear negative.
case.q: What explains the deterioration and how should treatment change?
case.a: Paradoxical tuberculoma formation; keep the same anti-TB drugs, restart or increase corticosteroids, add an antiseizure medicine, and consider thalidomide or a TNF blocker only if steroid-refractory lesions threaten function.

Chapter 40 Tuberculosis of the Central Nervous System
Chapter 6: Infectious and Noninfectious Inflammatory Diseases of the Brain
Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System

det.patho: Haematogenous bacilli lodge in brain or cord and form caseating granulomas; if a focus lies next to the pia or ependyma and ruptures, meningitis follows, while a deep focus enlarges as a tuberculoma. When the caseous core softens and fills with bacilli the lesion becomes an abscess. Paradoxical enlargement reflects a recovering immune response to dying mycobacteria rather than treatment failure. Tuberculous encephalopathy in children is a diffuse, probably immune and multifactorial white matter injury with few bacilli in the brain.
det.clinical: Most patients present with seizures or a slowly progressive deficit, and in endemic regions tuberculomas used to account for a large share of intracranial masses. Lesions in the posterior fossa cause ataxia, cranial nerve signs and hydrocephalus. Cord tuberculoma mimics an intramedullary tumour with sensory level and sphincter change over weeks. Deterioration during therapy has several causes besides paradoxical reaction: poor adherence, resistance, infarction, hydrocephalus and hyponatraemia must each be sought.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is usually presumptive, built on typical MRI plus proof of TB elsewhere or in CSF; Xpert Ultra and culture of any accessible tissue are the main microbiological tools. A solid caseating tuberculoma is dark on T2 with a lipid peak on spectroscopy, whereas an abscess has a bright fluid core with diffusion restriction. When the picture is atypical and no systemic TB is found, biopsy prevents treating a glioma, lymphoma or fungal lesion as tuberculosis. Drug susceptibility testing is essential because rifampicin resistance changes the regimen and prognosis.
det.treatment: Standard drug-susceptible CNS TB therapy is 2 months of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol followed by isoniazid and rifampicin to complete about 12 months; many clinicians extend it until lesions have largely resolved. Corticosteroids reduce perilesional oedema and are restarted for paradoxical reactions, and thalidomide or infliximab have been used in steroid-refractory, function-threatening lesions. Surgery is reserved for diagnostic biopsy, abscess drainage, obstructive hydrocephalus or cord compression. In HIV, ART is started after the first weeks of TB therapy rather than immediately, with close watch for IRIS.
det.prognosis: Most tuberculomas shrink and calcify with treatment over 6-18 months; residual epilepsy is the commonest sequel, and outcome is worse with coexisting meningitis, HIV or drug resistance.
pearls: New lesions on treatment with adherent therapy and a susceptible isolate are usually paradoxical, not failure: do not switch drugs.
Residual enhancement can persist for months after cure; do not prolong therapy indefinitely on imaging alone.
A T2-hypointense ring lesion with a lipid peak in a Thai patient favours tuberculoma over cysticercus or abscess.

name: Parinaud’s syndrome
formal: Dorsal midbrain syndrome with vertical gaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus, light-near dissociation and Collier sign, typically from pineal region tumour or hydrocephalus.
simple: Trouble looking upward with abnormal pupils, caused by pressure on the back of the midbrain.
more: Dorsal midbrain syndrome with impaired upgaze, convergence-retraction nystagmus, light-near dissociation and lid retraction, from pineal tumour, hydrocephalus or midbrain stroke.
th: กลุ่มอาการ midbrain ด้านหลัง มีมองขึ้นไม่ได้ convergence-retraction nystagmus รูม่านตาตอบสนองต่อการมองใกล้แต่ไม่ตอบสนองต่อแสง และหนังตาบนหดรั้ง มักเกิดจากเนื้องอกบริเวณ pineal หรือโพรงน้ำในสมองขยาย
tempoNote: Subacute with tumours or shunt failure; abrupt with midbrain stroke or haemorrhage
feat: Impaired upgaze (saccades first), often with preserved vertical doll's head movements early
Convergence-retraction nystagmus on attempted upward saccades (best seen with downward-moving OKN drum)
Light-near dissociation: mid-dilated pupils that constrict to near but poorly to light
Lid retraction in primary gaze (Collier sign); skew deviation or downgaze palsy in larger lesions
Headache, vomiting and papilloedema when aqueductal compression causes hydrocephalus

Pineal tumour markers in serum/CSF (AFP, β-hCG) and CSF cytology in young patients

Consider MS, Whipple disease or neurosyphilis when imaging shows inflammatory lesions

case.story: Six weeks of morning headaches and vomiting, then trouble looking up at the board in class.
case.exam: Upgaze limited, eyes jerk back into the orbits on attempted upward look, pupils react to near not light, eyelids retracted, bilateral papilloedema.
case.tests: MRI shows a 3 cm enhancing pineal mass with obstructive hydrocephalus; serum β-hCG mildly raised.
case.q: Which structure is compressed, and what is the first management step?
case.a: The dorsal midbrain (posterior commissure and pretectum) by a pineal germ cell tumour; relieve hydrocephalus (endoscopic third ventriculostomy with biopsy) then treat the tumour.

det.patho: The vertical gaze centre (riMLF and interstitial nucleus of Cajal) lies in the rostral midbrain, and upgaze pathways cross in the posterior commissure. Pressure or damage here, plus disruption of the pretectal pupillary fibres, gives the classic signs. Causes depend on age: pineal tumours and aqueductal stenosis in children and young adults, hydrocephalus and shunt failure at any age, midbrain or thalamic stroke and haemorrhage in older adults, and rarely MS, infection or trauma.
det.clinical: Upward saccades fail first, while upward pursuit and vestibulo-ocular movements may be relatively preserved early (a supranuclear pattern). Attempted upgaze produces convergence and globe retraction rather than true nystagmus. Lid retraction (Collier sign) and light-near dissociation are useful clues. In children with hydrocephalus a 'setting sun' downward deviation is a related sign. Accompanying signs (ataxia, hearing loss, endocrine change) depend on the lesion.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical and localising; MRI with contrast identifies the cause. Pineal region tumours need serum and CSF AFP and β-hCG because germ cell tumours may be treated without surgery. In shunted patients, new upgaze palsy suggests shunt failure even if ventricles look little changed.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: CSF diversion for hydrocephalus (often endoscopic third ventriculostomy), tumour-specific therapy (germinomas respond readily to both radiotherapy and chemotherapy) and standard stroke care for vascular causes. Prisms or occlusion help diplopia. Signs may improve after decompression, though light-near dissociation can persist.
det.prognosis: Depends on the cause; gaze signs often improve after relief of hydrocephalus or tumour treatment.
pearls: Upgaze palsy + lid retraction + light-near dissociation = dorsal midbrain; image for pineal mass or hydrocephalus.
Use a downward-moving OKN drum to provoke convergence-retraction nystagmus.
New upgaze limitation in a shunted child is shunt failure until proved otherwise.
det.thd: Parinaud syndrome หรือ dorsal midbrain syndrome เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ midbrain ด้านหลังบริเวณ posterior commissure ผู้ป่วยมองขึ้นไม่ได้ ตากระตุกหดเข้าเบ้าเมื่อพยายามมองขึ้น รูม่านตาหดเมื่อมองใกล้แต่ไม่หดต่อแสง และหนังตาบนหดรั้ง ในเด็กและวัยรุ่นมักเกิดจากเนื้องอก pineal หรือโพรงน้ำในสมองขยาย ส่วนผู้สูงอายุมักเกิดจาก stroke ตรวจ MRI และ tumour marker แล้วรักษาตามสาเหตุ เช่น ระบายน้ำไขสันหลังและรักษาเนื้องอก

qx.stem: A 19-year-old Thai student has headache and trouble looking up. Examination shows upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus on attempted upgaze, light-near dissociation of the pupils and bilateral lid retraction. MRI reveals a pineal region mass.
qx.q: Where is the responsible lesion?
opts: Ventral pons
Dorsal midbrain at the posterior commissure and rostral interstitial nucleus
Lateral medulla
Cerebral peduncle
Occipital pole
qx.why: The dorsal midbrain syndrome results from compression or infarction of the posterior commissure, pretectum and rostral interstitial nucleus of the MLF. Pineal tumours and hydrocephalus are typical causes in the young, and the normal near response with poor light reaction reflects pretectal damage.

name: Parkin disease
formal: Autosomal recessive early-onset Parkinson disease from PRKN mutations, with dystonia, slow progression, good levodopa response and usually no Lewy bodies.
simple: An inherited form of Parkinson disease starting in young adults, caused by a change in the parkin gene.
th: โรคพาร์กินสันเริ่มอายุน้อยถ่ายทอดแบบยีนด้อยจากยีน PRKN มี dystonia ที่เท้า ดำเนินโรคช้า ตอบสนอง levodopa ดีมาก และมักไม่มี Lewy body
tempoNote: Onset usually before 40 (often before 30); very slow progression over decades
feat: Young-onset, often symmetric parkinsonism

Excellent, sustained levodopa response but early dyskinesias at low doses
Diurnal fluctuation and sleep benefit in some

PRKN gene testing including copy-number (exon deletion/duplication) analysis
Copper studies and MRI to exclude Wilson disease and structural causes

case.story: Since age 22 her right foot turns inward when walking; now both hands are slow and her handwriting is small. Her older brother has similar symptoms.
case.exam: Symmetric bradykinesia and rigidity, foot dystonia on walking, brisk reflexes, no cognitive problems.
case.tests: DAT-SPECT reduced; compound heterozygous PRKN exon deletion and point variant; ceruloplasmin normal.
case.q: What clinical course do you expect on levodopa?
case.a: Excellent long-lasting response at low dose, but early dyskinesia; slow progression overall.

det.patho: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in PRKN, encoding the E3 ubiquitin ligase parkin, disrupt PINK1–parkin mitophagy so damaged mitochondria accumulate in dopaminergic neurons. Exon deletions and duplications are frequent, so sequencing alone can miss them. Neuropathology typically shows nigral loss without Lewy bodies. PRKN is the commonest cause of autosomal recessive early-onset Parkinson disease.
det.clinical: Onset is usually in the 20s or 30s, sometimes in the teens. Lower-limb dystonia, symmetrical signs and hyperreflexia are typical. Progression is slow and dementia is rare, although motor complications and psychiatric symptoms are common. Single heterozygous variants are not a clear cause of disease.
det.diagnosis: Consider genetic testing in Parkinson disease starting before 40–50 years or with an affected sibling or consanguinity. Use methods that detect copy-number changes as well as point variants. DAT imaging confirms a presynaptic deficit; exclude Wilson disease and dopa-responsive dystonia.
det.treatment: Levodopa and dopamine agonists are effective at modest doses; start low because dyskinesias appear early. Amantadine helps dyskinesia. Subthalamic deep brain stimulation gives durable benefit and patients are often good candidates given preserved cognition. Address mood, impulse control and family genetic counselling.
det.prognosis: Slow progression with long survival; many remain independent for decades.
pearls: Young-onset Parkinson with foot dystonia and a sibling affected: test PRKN including deletions.
Parkin disease usually lacks Lewy bodies despite nigral loss.
Good DBS candidates because cognition is usually preserved.
det.thd: Parkin disease คือโรคพาร์กินสันชนิดเริ่มอายุน้อยจากยีน PRKN ถ่ายทอดแบบยีนด้อย มักเริ่มก่อนอายุ 40 มี dystonia ที่เท้า reflex ไว ดำเนินโรคช้ามาก ตอบสนอง levodopa ดีแต่เกิด dyskinesia เร็ว พยาธิสภาพมักไม่มี Lewy body ตรวจยีนต้องรวมการหา exon deletion ด้วย รักษาด้วยยาขนาดต่ำและ DBS ได้ผลดี
