name: Parkinsonian rigidity
formal: Lead-pipe or cogwheel increased resistance to passive movement of limbs, a cardinal sign of parkinsonism from nigrostriatal dopamine loss.
simple: Stiffness of the arms and legs when someone moves them, a typical sign of Parkinson disease.
th: อาการแข็งเกร็งแบบ parkinsonism ต้านการเคลื่อนไหวเท่ากันตลอดช่วงและไม่ขึ้นกับความเร็ว อาจมีลักษณะ cogwheel เมื่อมีสั่นร่วม พบใน Parkinson disease และ parkinsonism ชนิดอื่น รวมทั้งจากยา
tempoNote: Gradual over months to years in degenerative causes; days to weeks after dopamine blocker or toxin exposure
feat: Even resistance through the whole range of passive movement, unrelated to how fast the limb is moved (lead-pipe)
Ratchet or cogwheel feel when tremor is present
Enhanced by contralateral activation such as opposite arm movement (Froment)
Asymmetric early in Parkinson disease; neck and trunk predominance in PSP
Acute, symmetric rigidity after neuroleptics, MPTP-type toxins or manganese suggests secondary causes
inv: Bedside tone testing with distraction and activation; review drug list for dopamine blockers
MRI for vascular, toxic or atypical parkinsonism patterns; DAT-SPECT when drug-induced or functional disease is in doubt

case.story: Two years of a slow, quiet voice, smaller handwriting and a stiff right arm; her husband notes less arm swing.
case.exam: Lead-pipe resistance in the right arm, cogwheeling at the wrist, rigidity increases while the left hand taps; bradykinesia and a pill-rolling rest tremor.
case.tests: MRI normal; no dopamine-blocking drugs; clear improvement on a levodopa trial.
case.q: What distinguishes this tone abnormality from spasticity?
case.a: Parkinsonian rigidity is uniform in both directions and speed-independent, with no clasp-knife catch or hyperreflexia; it reflects basal ganglia dysfunction as in Parkinson disease.

det.patho: Loss of dopaminergic drive to the striatum alters basal ganglia output so that both agonist and antagonist muscles remain tonically active and stretch reflexes in long latency pathways are exaggerated. The resistance therefore persists in both flexion and extension. Neurodegeneration, drugs, toxins, vascular lesions and metabolic injury can all produce it.
det.clinical: Patients describe stiffness, aching shoulders, and slowed turning in bed. Rigidity usually appears with bradykinesia and tremor but can predominate, notably in axial form in progressive supranuclear palsy. Toxic parkinsonism from manganese, carbon monoxide, MPTP or neuroleptics tends to be symmetric and less responsive to levodopa. Marked rigidity with fever and confusion needs urgent exclusion of neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
det.diagnosis: Examine tone slowly in the relaxed limb, then repeat with distraction to expose rigidity that is initially hidden. Separate it from spasticity (velocity-dependent), paratonia (variable, oppositional) and dystonia. Obtain a drug and exposure history, MRI when atypical, and consider DAT imaging when drug-induced or functional parkinsonism is suspected.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: withdraw offending dopamine blockers, remove toxin exposure, and for Parkinson disease use levodopa, dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors or amantadine as appropriate. Physiotherapy keeps range and reduces falls. Atypical forms respond poorly, so rehabilitation and goals-of-care planning matter. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome needs stopping the drug, cooling, fluids and ICU support.
det.prognosis: Depends on the cause: levodopa-responsive in Parkinson disease, often reversible in drug-induced forms, and persistent in atypical or toxic disease.
pearls: Tone that is the same at slow and fast speeds is rigidity, not spasticity.
Activation by moving the other limb brings out subtle rigidity.
Symmetric, levodopa-resistant rigidity should prompt a hunt for drugs or toxins.
det.thd: Parkinsonian rigidity คืออาการแข็งเกร็งที่ต้านการเคลื่อนไหวเท่ากันตลอดช่วงและไม่ขึ้นกับความเร็ว ต่างจาก spasticity ที่มี clasp-knife และรีเฟล็กซ์ไว เกิดจากการขาดโดพามีนในปมประสาทฐานสมอง พบใน Parkinson disease และ parkinsonism จากยาหรือสารพิษ ตรวจโดยจับขยับแขนขาแบบผ่อนคลายและให้ผู้ป่วยขยับแขนอีกข้างเพื่อกระตุ้น รักษาตามสาเหตุ เช่น หยุดยาที่ปิดกั้นโดพามีนหรือให้ levodopa

name: Parkinsonian-dementia syndromes
formal: Disorders combining parkinsonism and cognitive decline, including Parkinson disease dementia, dementia with Lewy bodies, PSP and corticobasal degeneration.
simple: Illnesses that cause both movement slowness or stiffness and memory or thinking problems.

feat: Bradykinesia and rigidity combined with cognitive decline
Dementia within a year of parkinsonism suggests DLB; later dementia suggests Parkinson disease dementia
Early falls and vertical gaze limitation suggest PSP; asymmetric apraxia and alien limb suggest CBD
Visual hallucinations, fluctuating attention and REM sleep behaviour disorder suggest Lewy body disease
Treatable mimics: normal pressure hydrocephalus, vascular disease, drug effects, Wilson disease

DaT-SPECT, cardiac MIBG and FDG-PET to support Lewy body disease or atypical parkinsonism

case.story: Over a year he has seen children playing in the house, his alertness swings from day to day, and he now walks slowly with short steps. His wife says he shouts and moves in his sleep.
case.exam: Mild symmetric bradykinesia and rigidity, poor intersecting pentagon copying, fluctuating attention, no gaze palsy.
case.tests: MRI mild generalised atrophy with relative preservation of the medial temporal lobes; DaT-SPECT shows reduced striatal uptake.
case.q: Which disorder is most likely and what drug caution applies?
case.a: Dementia with Lewy bodies. Avoid typical antipsychotics because of severe sensitivity; a cholinesterase inhibitor may help cognition and hallucinations.

read.where: Chapter 20: The Lewy Body Dementias: Dementia with Lewy Bodies and Related Syndromes

det.patho: These syndromes share degeneration of basal ganglia and cortical circuits but differ in the underlying protein: alpha-synuclein in Lewy body disease and multiple system atrophy, and tau in PSP and CBD. Mixed Alzheimer co-pathology is frequent in the Lewy body disorders and shapes the cognitive course. Classification relies on clinical phenotype because biomarkers are still evolving.
det.clinical: Core clinical task is separating Lewy body disease from tauopathies. DLB shows fluctuating cognition, well-formed visual hallucinations, RBD and parkinsonism; PSP presents with early postural instability, falls, slowed vertical saccades and frontal dysexecutive features; CBD gives asymmetric rigidity, apraxia and cortical sensory loss. Orthostatic hypotension and constipation point towards synucleinopathy. Levodopa response is partial in DLB and poor in PSP and CBD.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis uses consensus clinical criteria, the one-year rule for DLB versus PDD, and supportive tests such as abnormal DaT-SPECT, REM sleep without atonia, and midbrain atrophy on MRI. Alpha-synuclein seed amplification assays in CSF are increasingly used for Lewy body disease. Always exclude reversible causes and obtain collateral history for sleep and drug reactions.
det.treatment: Management is symptomatic: cholinesterase inhibitors (rivastigmine, donepezil) for cognition and hallucinations in Lewy body disease, low-dose levodopa for motor symptoms, and clonazepam or melatonin for RBD. Avoid dopamine antagonists and anticholinergics; low-dose quetiapine or clozapine can be used for troublesome psychosis. PSP and CBD have no disease-modifying treatment, so physiotherapy, swallowing assessment and palliative planning are crucial.
det.prognosis: These conditions progress, with survival of about 5–8 years from diagnosis in DLB and PSP. Falls, dysphagia and aspiration pneumonia are major causes of death.
pearls: One-year rule: dementia before or within a year of motor onset points to DLB.
Severe neuroleptic sensitivity is a warning sign of Lewy body disease.
Early falls with vertical gaze limitation suggest PSP, not Parkinson disease.

case.story: Over three months she has become slow, shuffles and drools; she has taken flunarizine nightly for dizziness for a year, prescribed at a clinic.
case.exam: Symmetric bradykinesia and rigidity, mild bilateral postural-rest tremor, no gaze palsy or ataxia.
case.tests: MRI brain shows only mild small-vessel change.
case.q: What is the first step in management?

8 Overview of Parkinsonism and Approach to Differential Diagnosis

det.patho: Parkinsonism reflects failure of the nigrostriatal dopamine system or its downstream basal ganglia circuits. The lesion may be presynaptic loss of dopamine neurons (Parkinson disease, MSA, PSP), postsynaptic receptor blockade (drugs), or structural damage to striatum and its connections (vascular, hydrocephalus, toxins such as manganese or carbon monoxide). Parkinson disease accounts for most cases in older adults.
det.clinical: The core is bradykinesia, which clinicians must show as progressive slowing and shrinking of repeated movements, not simple slowness. Rest tremor, cogwheel or lead-pipe rigidity, stooped posture, shuffling gait and hypomimia complete the picture. Red flags for an atypical cause include rapid progression, falls in the first years, early dementia or hallucinations, marked autonomic failure, cerebellar signs, gaze palsy, pyramidal signs and symmetric lower-body predominance.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, followed by a cause-directed work-up. Take a thorough drug history, image the brain with MRI, and check copper studies in younger patients. DaT-SPECT separates presynaptic degenerative disease from drug-induced, psychogenic and essential-tremor syndromes but does not distinguish PD from MSA or PSP. A supervised levodopa trial up to adequate doses helps define levodopa responsiveness.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: withdraw offending drugs, shunt selected hydrocephalus, chelate in Wilson disease. For degenerative parkinsonism, levodopa remains the most effective symptomatic drug; dopamine agonists and MAO-B inhibitors are alternatives in milder or younger patients. Physiotherapy, fall prevention and speech therapy matter in every subtype. Avoid typical antipsychotics and metoclopramide; quetiapine or clozapine are preferred if an antipsychotic is needed.
det.prognosis: Depends entirely on the cause; drug-induced parkinsonism usually settles over weeks to months, though some unmask latent PD, while atypical syndromes progress faster than PD.
pearls: Without decremental bradykinesia, it is not parkinsonism.
In Thailand, always ask about flunarizine, cinnarizine, metoclopramide and antipsychotics.
Poor response to levodopa above 1000 mg/day should make you rethink the diagnosis.
det.thd: Parkinsonism คือกลุ่มอาการที่มีการเคลื่อนไหวช้าลงและลดขนาดลงเมื่อทำซ้ำ ร่วมกับสั่นขณะพักหรือแข็งเกร็ง สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยคือโรคพาร์กินสัน แต่ต้องแยกจากยาที่ต้านโดปามีน (เช่น flunarizine, metoclopramide) โรคหลอดเลือดสมอง และโรคพาร์กินสันเทียมเช่น PSP หรือ MSA การตรวจที่ช่วยคือ MRI สมอง และ DaT-SPECT การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ เช่น หยุดยา หรือให้ levodopa ในโรคเสื่อม

name: Parkinsonism–dementia complex of Guam (PDC)
formal: Western Pacific tauopathy with parkinsonism and dementia, linked to ALS-parkinsonism-dementia complex, with neurofibrillary tangles; possible environmental cycad toxin link.
simple: A rare illness on the island of Guam causing Parkinson-like symptoms and dementia.
th: โรคเสื่อมเฉพาะถิ่นของชาวชามอร์โรบนเกาะกวม มีพาร์กินโซนิซึมร่วมกับสมองเสื่อม พยาธิสภาพเป็น tau tangle และพบร่วมกับ ALS ในชุมชนเดียวกัน
tempoNote: Insidious onset in mid to late adult life, steadily progressive over several years
feat: Akinetic-rigid parkinsonism, often symmetric, with little tremor
Progressive dementia with apathy and slowness of thought
Occurs in clusters with ALS in Chamorro families on Guam; similar foci in Kii peninsula (Japan) and West Papua
Pigmentary retinopathy is described in many affected and at-risk villagers
Incidence has fallen sharply since the mid-twentieth century
inv: MRI: frontotemporal atrophy; exclude vascular and structural causes
Neuropathology (research setting): widespread neurofibrillary tangles with little amyloid plaque
Genetic testing to exclude MAPT, C9orf72 and other familial FTD-parkinsonism genes in non-endemic patients

case.who: 63-year-old Chamorro man, visiting relatives in Bangkok, seen at a university neurology clinic
case.story: Two years of slowness, stiffness and growing forgetfulness; an uncle on Guam had ALS.
case.exam: Symmetric bradykinesia and rigidity, mild apathy and executive impairment, no gaze palsy.
case.tests: MRI shows frontal and temporal atrophy; minimal response to levodopa.
case.q: What endemic disorder fits his origin and family history?
case.a: Parkinsonism–dementia complex of Guam, part of the Western Pacific ALS-PDC focus.

det.patho: PDC is a tauopathy with dense neurofibrillary tangles in cortex, hippocampus, basal ganglia and brainstem, frequently with coexisting TDP-43 and some synuclein pathology. The cause is unresolved: proposed factors include cycad seed toxins (such as BMAA and sterol glucosides), low calcium and magnesium in soil and water, and genetic susceptibility. The fall in incidence as the island westernised supports an environmental contribution.
det.clinical: Patients develop a slowly worsening akinetic-rigid syndrome together with dementia, usually after age 50. ALS, PDC and mixed forms can appear in the same families, and some people have only cognitive decline. Death typically follows within about a decade from complications of immobility and dysphagia.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the combination of origin from an endemic focus and the clinical picture, after exclusion of other causes of parkinsonism with dementia. Imaging is supportive but non-specific. Outside endemic regions, a patient with a similar phenotype should be investigated for genetic tauopathies and atypical parkinsonian syndromes rather than given this label.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy exists. Levodopa gives limited and usually transient benefit. Management is supportive: physiotherapy, swallowing assessment, caregiver support and palliative planning.
det.prognosis: Progressive and fatal, usually over 5–10 years.
pearls: The classic example of a geographically clustered neurodegenerative disease, linked historically to cycad flour.
Pathology is tau, not Lewy bodies, explaining poor levodopa response.
ALS and PDC are now viewed as ends of one Western Pacific disease spectrum.
det.thd: Parkinsonism–dementia complex of Guam เป็นโรคเสื่อมเฉพาะถิ่นของชาวชามอร์โรบนเกาะกวม ผู้ป่วยมีอาการเคลื่อนไหวช้าแข็งเกร็งร่วมกับสมองเสื่อม และพบ ALS ในครอบครัวเดียวกันได้ พยาธิสภาพเด่นคือ neurofibrillary tangle (tauopathy) สาเหตุยังไม่ชัดเจน สงสัยสารพิษจากเมล็ดปรงร่วมกับพันธุกรรม ตอบสนองต่อ levodopa น้อย รักษาแบบประคับประคอง

name: Parkinson’s disease (PD)
formal: Neurodegenerative synucleinopathy with nigrostriatal dopamine loss causing bradykinesia, rest tremor and rigidity, with non-motor symptoms; levodopa-responsive.
simple: A brain disease causing slowness, stiffness and tremor because cells that make dopamine are lost.
more: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by DAT-SPECT showing reduced striatal uptake; MRI excludes secondary causes. Treat with levodopa, dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors, COMT inhibitors and amantadine; DBS for motor fluctuations; LRRK2. Historical term for Parkinson disease, meaning shaking palsy, referring to rest tremor with rigidity and bradykinesia. Sporadic Parkinson disease with bradykinesia, rest tremor, rigidity and postural instability from loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra with Lewy body pathology, responsive to levodopa. Diagnosis is clinical with levodopa response, and DaT scan if unclear. Treat with levodopa, dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors and deep brain stimulation in selected patients.
th: โรคพาร์กินสัน — เคลื่อนไหวช้า สั่นขณะพัก แข็งเกร็ง เริ่มข้างเดียว ตอบสนองดีต่อยาเลโวโดปา
feat: Bradykinesia with decrement plus rest tremor and/or rigidity
Asymmetric onset that stays asymmetric
Prodrome: hyposmia, constipation, REM sleep behaviour disorder, depression
Clear, sustained levodopa response; later motor fluctuations and dyskinesia
inv: Clinical diagnosis (MDS criteria)
Dopamine transporter SPECT if uncertain (vs essential or drug-induced tremor)
MRI to look for atypical features if red flags

case.story: Two years of a shaking right hand at rest, smaller handwriting and slowness doing up buttons; his wife says he shouts and kicks in his sleep.
case.exam: Right pill-rolling rest tremor, decrementing finger taps on the right, cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist, reduced arm swing.
case.tests: None required; marked improvement on levodopa.
case.q: Which sleep symptom is a prodromal clue?
case.a: REM sleep behaviour disorder (dream enactment) — a synucleinopathy marker.

qx.stem: A 64-year-old woman has asymmetric rest tremor and bradykinesia of the right hand for two years, with clear benefit from levodopa and mild peak-dose dyskinesia. She had constipation and dream-enactment behaviour for many years before. A research clinic reports a positive CSF α-synuclein seed amplification assay (SAA). Her son asks whether the test rules out every other parkinsonian disorder.
qx.q: How should the SAA result be interpreted?
opts: A positive SAA confirms Parkinson's disease and excludes MSA and DLB
A positive SAA indicates PSP pathology
The test detects misfolded α-synuclein with high sensitivity in Lewy body disease, but it is also positive in DLB and many MSA cases, so the clinical picture still defines the syndrome
SAA is only useful after death on brain tissue
A positive SAA means she will develop dementia within one year
qx.why: α-Synuclein SAA in CSF (and increasingly skin) detects seeding activity with sensitivity around 90% in PD and high specificity against controls and tauopathies such as PSP and CBD. It is also positive in DLB, pure autonomic failure and a proportion of MSA, so it marks synuclein pathology rather than a specific syndrome. Her levodopa response, dyskinesia and prodromal features meet clinically established PD under the 2015 MDS criteria.

src.where: Case 39 Levodopa responsive parkinsonism: is it Parkinson's disease?

qx.stem: A 57-year-old school principal has had PD for nine years. He now has five daily 'off' periods with severe tremor and freezing, and troublesome dyskinesia when 'on', despite optimised levodopa, entacapone and a dopamine agonist. A levodopa challenge improves his MDS-UPDRS part III from 48 to 18. Cognition is normal on testing, he has no untreated depression, and MRI shows only mild small-vessel change.
qx.q: Which is the most appropriate recommendation?
opts: He is unsuitable for surgery because DBS works only for tremor
Refer for bilateral STN or GPi deep brain stimulation
Add a second dopamine agonist and review in a year
Stop levodopa and start rasagiline monotherapy
He should wait until falls and dementia develop before surgery
qx.why: Good candidates have idiopathic PD with disabling motor fluctuations or dyskinesia, a strong levodopa response (over about 30% improvement), intact cognition, controlled psychiatric symptoms and acceptable surgical risk. DBS improves 'off' time, tremor and dyskinesia but not levodopa-unresponsive features such as freezing in the 'on' state, falls or dementia, which is why surgery should not be delayed until those develop. Device-aided alternatives include subcutaneous levodopa infusion and levodopa–carbidopa intestinal gel.

src.where: Case 99 Patient selection for deep brain stimulation for idiopathic Parkinson's disease

qx.stem: A 64-year-old man from Phitsanulok has had Parkinson's disease for six years and takes levodopa plus pramipexole. Last week he fell asleep at the wheel with no warning and drove into a ditch, escaping with bruises. He reports daytime dozing and has an Epworth score of 17. He snores.
qx.q: What is the best management?
opts: Increase the evening levodopa dose
Add zolpidem at night
Add a second dopamine agonist
Reassure that dozing is a normal part of ageing
Advise him to stop driving, reduce or replace the dopamine agonist, and screen for sleep apnoea
qx.why: Dopamine agonists, and to a lesser extent levodopa, can cause sudden-onset sleep and daytime somnolence in Parkinson's disease. Safety comes first with driving cessation, then reducing or switching the agonist. Coexisting sleep apnoea and nocturnal problems should be evaluated, and wake-promoting agents are considered only afterwards.

src.where: Chapter 25 Sleep dysfunction in Parkinson disease

qx.stem: A 68-year-old woman from Ayutthaya has Parkinson's disease with a good daytime response to immediate-release levodopa. She wakes at around 4 a.m. every night with rigidity, painful foot dystonia and inability to turn in bed, and then cannot sleep again. Bladder diary and polysomnography reveal no other cause.
qx.q: Which is the most appropriate change?
opts: Add a hypnotic benzodiazepine
Start an antipsychotic
Add a bedtime long-acting dopaminergic option such as extended-release levodopa or a rotigotine patch
Stop all dopaminergic drugs at night
Start amitriptyline
qx.why: Early-morning wearing-off with nocturnal akinesia and painful dystonia is a motor cause of insomnia in Parkinson's disease. Providing continuous nocturnal dopaminergic stimulation, with a long-acting levodopa preparation or a transdermal agonist, treats the cause. Sedatives do not address the motor symptoms and increase fall and confusion risk; antipsychotics worsen parkinsonism.

ddx.pt: Bilateral postural/action tremor, no bradykinesia, alcohol responsive

Symmetric, dopamine blocker exposure, normal DAT scan
Lower-body gait disorder with incontinence and ventriculomegaly

aN: pd | parkinson disease | paralysis agitans | idiopathic pd | idiopathic parkinson disease | ipd

det.patho: Misfolded alpha-synuclein aggregates into Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites, and pigmented dopaminergic cells of the substantia nigra pars compacta die off, starving the dorsal putamen of dopamine. Pathology probably begins years earlier in the olfactory bulb and lower brainstem (and possibly the gut), which explains the non-motor prodrome. Most cases are sporadic; monogenic forms (LRRK2, SNCA, PRKN, PINK1) and GBA variants as a risk factor account for a minority. Age is the dominant risk factor, with a modest male excess.
det.clinical: Motor onset is typically one-sided, with slowness and fatiguing of repetitive movements, a 4–6 Hz resting tremor and lead-pipe or cogwheel rigidity. Patients describe small handwriting, a quiet voice, reduced facial expression and a shuffling gait with less arm swing. Non-motor problems — smell loss, constipation, dream enactment, mood change, pain, urinary urgency and later orthostasis and cognitive decline — often matter more for quality of life. After some years on levodopa, wearing-off, peak-dose dyskinesia and freezing of gait appear. Red flags pointing elsewhere include early falls, early dementia, early severe autonomic failure, rapid progression, symmetric onset and a poor drug response.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, built on the 2015 MDS criteria: establish parkinsonism (bradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity), then weigh supportive features against absolute exclusions and red flags. A convincing, sustained response to dopaminergic therapy strongly supports the diagnosis. DAT SPECT shows presynaptic dopaminergic loss but cannot separate PD from MSA or PSP; it is mainly useful against essential tremor, dystonic tremor and drug-induced parkinsonism. Routine MRI is normal; order it if atypical signs are present. Skin biopsy or CSF seed amplification assays for alpha-synuclein are emerging biomarkers, mostly in research or specialist use.
det.treatment: Start symptomatic treatment when symptoms impair function; levodopa with a decarboxylase inhibitor is the most effective drug, while dopamine agonists and MAO-B inhibitors are alternatives in younger or milder patients. Warn every patient on agonists about impulse control disorders and sudden sleep attacks. Fluctuations are managed by fractionating levodopa, adding COMT or MAO-B inhibitors, amantadine for dyskinesia, and rescue apomorphine or inhaled levodopa. Advanced options include deep brain stimulation (STN or GPi) and continuous levodopa or apomorphine infusion. Exercise, physiotherapy, speech therapy and treatment of non-motor symptoms are integral; avoid typical antipsychotics and metoclopramide, and never stop levodopa abruptly.
det.prognosis: Progression is slow over 10–20 years, with life expectancy only modestly reduced; falls, dementia and dysphagia drive late disability and death.
pearls: Tremor that is absent when the hands are held out but returns after a few seconds (re-emergent tremor) is still a Parkinsonian rest tremor.
Abrupt levodopa withdrawal can cause a hyperpyrexic crisis resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
Strictly symmetric onset, early falls or no levodopa benefit should make you rethink the diagnosis.
det.thd: โรคพาร์กินสันเกิดจากเซลล์สร้างโดปามีนใน substantia nigra ตายลงพร้อมการสะสมของโปรตีน alpha-synuclein อาการหลักคือเคลื่อนไหวช้าที่เริ่มข้างเดียว ร่วมกับสั่นขณะพักหรือเกร็ง และมีอาการนำ เช่น จมูกไม่ได้กลิ่น ท้องผูก ละเมอตามความฝัน การวินิจฉัยใช้อาการทางคลินิกตามเกณฑ์ MDS ส่วน DAT scan ช่วยเมื่อแยกจาก essential tremor หรือยาที่ทำให้เกิดอาการ ยาหลักคือ levodopa และเมื่อโรคก้าวหน้าอาจใช้ DBS หรือยาแบบให้ต่อเนื่อง

name: Parkinson’s disease dementia (PDD)
formal: Dementia developing after at least a year of established Parkinson disease, with attention and executive deficits, hallucinations and Lewy body pathology.
simple: Memory and thinking decline that develops in someone who has had Parkinson disease for some time.
th: ภาวะสมองเสื่อมที่เกิดขึ้นในผู้ป่วยพาร์กินสันหลังมีอาการทางการเคลื่อนไหวมาแล้วอย่างน้อย 1 ปี เด่นด้านสมาธิ การบริหารจัดการ และมิติสัมพันธ์ มักมีประสาทหลอนร่วม
tempoNote: Develops gradually, typically many years into established Parkinson disease
feat: Dementia appearing at least one year after motor PD onset (the one-year rule separates it from DLB)
Impaired attention, executive function and visuospatial skills; memory retrieval more than storage
Visual hallucinations, delusions, apathy and daytime sleepiness are common
Fluctuating alertness and REM sleep behaviour disorder often coexist
Affects up to about 80% of people living 15–20 years with PD
inv: MoCA rather than MMSE to capture executive and visuospatial deficits
Bloods (B12, thyroid, calcium, glucose) and drug review for anticholinergics and dopamine agonists
MRI to exclude vascular or structural contributors

case.who: 76-year-old retired civil servant from Khon Kaen with PD for 9 years
case.story: Over the past year he gets lost in his own village, cannot handle his pension paperwork and sees small children in the house at night.
case.exam: Moderate parkinsonism; MoCA 17/30 with poor clock drawing, trail-making and cube copy; recall improves with cues.
case.tests: MRI shows mild global atrophy; routine bloods normal; he takes trihexyphenidyl.
case.q: What two management steps come first?
case.a: Withdraw trihexyphenidyl, then start a cholinesterase inhibitor such as rivastigmine for PD dementia.

9 - Atypical parkinsonism, parkinsonism-­plus syndromes and secondary parkinsonian disorders

det.patho: PDD results from spread of alpha-synuclein Lewy pathology into limbic and neocortical regions, often accompanied by Alzheimer-type amyloid and tau changes. Cholinergic cell loss in the basal forebrain (Meynert nucleus) is marked, which explains the response to cholinesterase inhibitors. Risk factors include older age, longer disease duration, postural-instability-gait phenotype, hallucinations, RBD and GBA variants.
det.clinical: The cognitive profile is mainly dysexecutive and visuospatial with slow processing, while language is relatively spared. Neuropsychiatric problems, especially visual hallucinations and delusions, are frequent and are aggravated by dopaminergic and anticholinergic drugs. Falls, dysphagia and autonomic failure often increase at the same stage, and caregiver burden rises steeply.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis follows the Movement Disorder Society clinical criteria: established PD plus cognitive decline in more than one domain that impairs daily function. The MoCA is a practical screening tool. Exclude delirium, depression, metabolic causes and drug toxicity before labelling dementia. Imaging is mainly to rule out other pathology.
det.treatment: Rivastigmine (oral or patch) has the best evidence; donepezil is an alternative and memantine may be added. Simplify the drug regimen by removing anticholinergics, amantadine and agonists before reducing levodopa. For distressing psychosis, quetiapine, clozapine with monitoring, or pimavanserin where available are used; avoid typical antipsychotics. Support caregivers and plan care early.
det.prognosis: PDD marks advanced disease, with increased nursing-home placement and reduced survival over the following years.
pearls: One-year rule: dementia after a year of motor PD is PDD; earlier is DLB.
Remove anticholinergics first; they are a common reversible cause of confusion.
Rivastigmine helps cognition and may reduce hallucinations and falls.

qx.stem: A 72-year-old former civil engineer from Nakhon Pathom has had Parkinson's disease for nine years. His son reports that he now loses track of his tablets, cannot follow the plot of a TV drama and gets lost on the way to the market. MMSE in a busy clinic is 28/30, and the referring doctor feels dementia is unlikely.
qx.q: Which assessment step should come next?
opts: Use a test weighted towards executive, attention and visuospatial domains, such as MoCA or formal neuropsychology, plus a functional history
Reassure the family, as an MMSE of 28 excludes dementia
Order amyloid PET to look for coexisting Alzheimer's disease
Increase levodopa and recheck the MMSE in three months
Arrange an EEG to exclude non-convulsive status
qx.why: Dementia in Parkinson's disease mainly affects attention, executive function and visuospatial skills, which the MMSE samples poorly, so a near-normal score can hide real impairment; MoCA (or a domain-based battery) and evidence of loss of independence establish the diagnosis. Amyloid imaging and EEG are not first-line, and raising levodopa does not treat cognitive decline. If PDD is confirmed, rivastigmine or donepezil is reasonable.

name: Parkinson’s disease with mild cognitive impairment (PD-MCI)
formal: Cognitive decline in Parkinson disease not interfering with daily function, with executive or visuospatial deficits; risk factor for later dementia.
simple: Mild thinking and memory problems in a person with Parkinson disease that do not yet affect daily life.
ab: Parkinson’s disease with mild cognitive impairment
th: ผู้ป่วยพาร์กินสันที่มีความสามารถทางสติปัญญาลดลงจากเดิม โดยยังทำกิจวัตรประจำวันได้เอง เป็นปัจจัยเสี่ยงสำคัญต่อการเกิดสมองเสื่อมในอนาคต
tempoNote: Gradual decline; may be present at diagnosis or appear years later
feat: Subjective or informant-reported cognitive decline in someone with established PD
Deficits in attention, executive function or visuospatial ability most often
Independence in daily activities preserved apart from minor inefficiencies
Present in roughly a quarter to a third of non-demented PD patients
Posterior-cortical deficits (e.g. figure copying, naming) predict faster progression to dementia
inv: MoCA or a PD-specific scale for screening; formal neuropsychology for classification
Screen for depression, sleep disturbance and drug-related cognitive effects
Bloods for reversible contributors (B12, thyroid)

case.who: 64-year-old accountant from Bangkok with PD for 4 years
case.story: He makes more errors on spreadsheets and finds it hard to juggle tasks, but still works and drives.
case.exam: Mild right-predominant parkinsonism; MoCA 24/30 losing points on trail-making, fluency and delayed recall.
case.tests: Neuropsychology shows deficits in two executive tests; MRI unremarkable.
case.q: How would you classify his cognition and what would you advise?
case.a: PD-MCI (multi-domain-level testing showing executive impairment); advise exercise, sleep and mood optimisation and regular cognitive follow-up.

det.patho: PD-MCI reflects early dysfunction of frontostriatal dopamine circuits and, in some patients, early cortical Lewy and cholinergic pathology. Two broad patterns are described: a dopamine-related executive profile that may fluctuate with medication, and a posterior-cortical profile linked to higher dementia risk. Older age, more severe motor disease, RBD and GBA variants increase risk.
det.clinical: Patients or families notice slower thinking, poor multitasking, word-finding pauses or misplacing items, yet daily activities are largely maintained. Anxiety, apathy and depression often coexist and can magnify complaints. Some patients remain stable or even revert, but many progress to dementia over the following years.
det.diagnosis: The MDS criteria require PD, gradual cognitive decline reported by patient, informant or clinician, deficits on formal testing, and no significant functional impact. Level I diagnosis uses a scale or limited testing; Level II uses at least two tests in each of five domains. Exclude delirium, depression and medication effects.
det.treatment: No drug is proven to prevent progression or to improve PD-MCI reliably. Regular aerobic exercise, cognitive engagement, good sleep and treating depression are recommended. Minimise anticholinergics and sedatives. Re-evaluate cognition periodically and discuss future planning while capacity is intact.
det.prognosis: PD-MCI roughly multiplies the risk of later dementia several-fold, though a minority stay stable.
pearls: The difference from PDD is function, not test score.
Poor pentagon copying and naming are warning signs of faster decline.
Exercise is the most practical intervention to recommend.
det.thd: PD-MCI คือผู้ป่วยพาร์กินสันที่มีความจำหรือความคิดลดลงจากเดิมเมื่อทดสอบ แต่ยังทำกิจวัตรประจำวันได้เอง มักบกพร่องด้านการบริหารจัดการและสมาธิ วินิจฉัยตามเกณฑ์ MDS โดยใช้ MoCA หรือแบบทดสอบทางประสาทจิตวิทยา ยังไม่มียาที่ป้องกันการลุกลามได้ แนะนำการออกกำลังกาย นอนหลับดี รักษาภาวะซึมเศร้า และติดตามเป็นระยะเพราะเสี่ยงต่อ PDD

det.patho: Primary paroxysmal movement disorders are mostly channelopathies or synaptopathies. PRRT2 regulates synaptic vesicle release and neuronal excitability; PNKD (MR-1) influences dopamine release through effects on enzymes handling oxidative stress; SLC2A1 encodes the brain glucose transporter GLUT1, so attacks occur when energy demand exceeds supply. Episodic ataxias involve potassium (KCNA1) or calcium (CACNA1A) channels. Secondary forms come from lesions in the basal ganglia–thalamocortical circuit or metabolic disturbance.
det.clinical: Classification is by trigger and duration. PKD has very brief, frequent attacks from sudden movement, onset in childhood or adolescence and frequent association with infantile convulsions. PNKD has rarer but longer attacks precipitated by alcohol, caffeine, fatigue or emotion. PED appears after 10–15 minutes or more of exertion and lasts minutes. Hypnogenic forms are now largely recognised as frontal lobe epilepsy. ATP1A3 and ADCY5 disorders also produce paroxysmal features.
det.diagnosis: A careful history of triggers, duration, frequency and awareness, supported by video, usually identifies the category. Examination and EEG are normal between and often during attacks. Genetic testing confirms primary forms, while metabolic tests and MRI search for secondary causes, especially in adults with new attacks (MS, stroke, hyperglycaemia, hypoparathyroidism). Functional paroxysmal movement disorders are common and diagnosed on positive features.
det.treatment: Treatment depends on subtype: low-dose carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine for PKD; trigger avoidance plus clonazepam or other benzodiazepines for PNKD; ketogenic or modified Atkins diet for GLUT1-related PED; acetazolamide for episodic ataxia type 2 (and sometimes type 1). Treat secondary causes directly. Lifestyle measures such as avoiding sudden movement, sleep loss and alcohol help.
det.prognosis: Primary forms are usually benign and often lessen in adulthood; PKD in particular may remit.
pearls: Seconds-long attacks with sudden movement plus infantile seizures in the family: PRRT2 PKD.
Long attacks after coffee or alcohol: PNKD; exertional attacks: test for GLUT1 deficiency.
New paroxysmal dyskinesia in an adult: look for MS, stroke, hyperglycaemia or hypocalcaemia.

det.patho: Paroxysmal choreoathetosis is an older descriptive term covering the paroxysmal dyskinesias. Primary forms are mostly genetic: PRRT2 variants underlie most kinesigenic cases, PNKD (MR-1) variants the non-kinesigenic form, and SLC2A1 (GLUT1) the exercise-induced form. Secondary forms arise from multiple sclerosis plaques, basal ganglia infarcts, hypoparathyroidism, hyperglycaemia or thyroid disease.
det.clinical: Patients experience sudden, self-limited bouts of choreic, athetoid or dystonic movement, sometimes preceded by a tingling aura, with full awareness. Attacks may affect one side or both and may alternate sides. Frequency ranges from dozens per day to a few per year. Onset in adulthood, abnormal interictal examination or an atypical trigger profile should prompt a search for a secondary cause.
det.diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis relies on a careful account of triggers, duration and frequency, ideally with video. Interictal examination, EEG and MRI are normal in primary forms. Genetic testing confirms the subtype; in sporadic adult cases check calcium, glucose, thyroid function and look for demyelination.
det.treatment: Treatment depends on the subtype: kinesigenic forms respond dramatically to small doses of sodium-channel blockers such as carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine. Non-kinesigenic forms respond better to trigger avoidance and clonazepam. GLUT1-related exercise-induced attacks may improve with a ketogenic diet. Secondary forms improve with correction of the cause.
det.prognosis: Primary forms are benign and often lessen with age; secondary forms follow the underlying condition.
pearls: Ask three questions: what triggers it, how long it lasts, and how often.
Short, movement-triggered, carbamazepine-responsive attacks mean PRRT2-PKD until proven otherwise.
Adult-onset sporadic attacks: check glucose, calcium and MRI for MS.

det.patho: Paroxysmal dyskinesias are mostly channelopathy- or synaptopathy-like disorders in which basal ganglia circuits intermittently lose inhibitory control. PRRT2 regulates synaptic vesicle release and is linked to PKD and infantile seizures; PNKD encodes a protein involved in stress-related dopamine signalling; SLC2A1 defects reduce brain glucose supply during exertion. Secondary paroxysmal dyskinesias arise from lesions or metabolic disturbance affecting the same circuits.
det.clinical: PKD attacks last under a minute, occur many times a day and are triggered by sudden movement or startle. PNKD attacks last minutes to hours, occur a few times a week or less and follow alcohol, caffeine, fatigue or emotion. PED attacks follow 10–15 minutes or more of sustained exercise and usually affect the legs. Atypical onset age, abnormal examination or progressive course point to a secondary or complex genetic disorder.
det.diagnosis: History and video are central, since attacks are rarely witnessed by clinicians. Normal EEG and MRI support a primary disorder. Targeted gene panels or exome sequencing are increasingly used. In GLUT1 suspicion, a fasting lumbar puncture showing low CSF glucose relative to blood is informative.
det.treatment: PKD: low-dose carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine is first line. PNKD: avoid triggers; clonazepam or other benzodiazepines are most useful. PED: ketogenic diet for GLUT1 deficiency, and pacing of exercise. Secondary forms respond to correction of the underlying metabolic or structural problem.
det.prognosis: Generally benign; many primary forms improve or remit in adulthood.
pearls: Attack duration is the best single discriminator between PKD and PNKD.
Nocturnal 'paroxysmal dystonia' is usually frontal lobe epilepsy.
Interictal signs mean think secondary or a complex genetic syndrome.

det.patho: Paroxysmal dystonia arises when motor circuits generate brief bursts of sustained co-contraction. In primary forms, genetic changes in synaptic or channel proteins (PRRT2, PNKD, SLC2A1) are responsible. In demyelinating disease, ephaptic transmission between damaged axons in the cord or brainstem produces short, stereotyped, often painful tonic spasms.
det.clinical: Attacks are stereotyped for each patient and may be provoked by movement, hyperventilation, touch, emotion or alcohol depending on the cause. Secondary forms in MS or NMOSD usually appear in adults, cluster over weeks and may be accompanied by sensory symptoms. Primary forms begin in youth and run in families.
det.diagnosis: Establish the trigger profile and duration, and look for interictal signs. Normal EEG during attacks supports a non-epileptic origin. MRI of brain and spine is needed in adults; serology for AQP4 or MOG antibodies if demyelination is found. Check calcium and glucose in sporadic cases.
det.treatment: Low-dose carbamazepine, a sodium-channel blocker, works very well for tonic spasms and PKD. Clonazepam helps non-kinesigenic forms. Treat the underlying disease (immunotherapy in NMOSD or MS, calcium replacement in hypoparathyroidism).
det.prognosis: Tonic spasms of demyelination often resolve within months; primary forms tend to improve with age.

det.patho: Most PED arises from heterozygous loss-of-function variants in SLC2A1, encoding the GLUT1 glucose transporter at the blood-brain barrier. Low brain glucose during sustained activity makes the energy-demanding basal ganglia circuits fail, and ketones provide an alternative fuel. Other cases are due to PRRT2, GCH1 or PRKN variants, or are sporadic, and brain perfusion studies during attacks have shown reduced frontal and basal ganglia perfusion with cerebellar activation, consistent with a paroxysmal movement disorder.
det.clinical: The key feature is exertion as the only trigger: attacks come after 10–15 minutes of continued walking or running and are absent with short bursts of effort. The leg dystonia lasts 5–30 minutes and stops with rest, with preserved awareness. GLUT1 deficiency syndrome can present with a wider picture of infantile seizures, microcephaly, developmental delay and ataxia, but patients with milder variants have PED with or without epilepsy and migraine. Family history is common. A late presentation in adult life should prompt a look for Parkin disease or dopa-responsive dystonia.
det.diagnosis: Document the exercise trigger and attack duration with video or treadmill provocation. The classic confirmation is a fasting lumbar puncture showing hypoglycorrhachia with normal lactate, followed by SLC2A1 sequencing and deletion analysis; genetic testing is now often done first. Include PRRT2, GCH1 and PRKN in the genetic panel, and perform a levodopa trial in unexplained cases. EEG and MRI are usually normal; brain MRI is done to exclude structural disease.
det.treatment: A ketogenic diet, started early, is the cornerstone of GLUT1 deficiency treatment and usually abolishes the movement attacks and absence seizures; modified Atkins diet is an alternative for older children and adults who cannot adhere to a strict regimen. Drugs that inhibit GLUT1, such as phenobarbital, valproate and methylxanthines, should be avoided. When the cause is not GLUT1, levodopa, acetazolamide, anticonvulsants, clonazepam and trihexyphenidyl have been tried with variable results. Posteroventral pallidotomy has helped a rare patient with a drug-resistant sporadic form.
det.prognosis: The movement attacks are lifelong in many patients but are usually controlled with diet; early recognition of GLUT1 deficiency is important for protection of development and learning.
pearls: Foot dystonia after 15 minutes of walking points to PED; a fasting CSF glucose or SLC2A1 test is the key investigation.
A ketogenic diet is disease-specific therapy in GLUT1 deficiency.
Exercise-induced foot dystonia in a young adult may be early-onset Parkinson disease.

more: Brief attacks of dystonia or chorea lasting seconds, triggered by sudden movement, linked to PRRT2 variants, starting in childhood or adolescence, with a usually benign course. Dramatic response to low-dose carbamazepine or phenytoin; many remit in adulthood. Genetics reveal PRRT2 in most families. Idiopathic episodic dystonia or chorea triggered by sudden movement, PRRT2-related, responsive to low-dose carbamazepine.
ab: Primary paroxysmal dyskinesia/ primary paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia
merged: Primary paroxysmal dyskinesia/ primary paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia
th: อาการบิดเกร็งหรือกระตุกชั่วครู่ไม่กี่วินาที เกิดทันทีเมื่อเริ่มขยับตัวแบบกะทันหัน ไม่หมดสติ ตอบสนองดีมากต่อ carbamazepine ขนาดต่ำ
tempoNote: Brief attacks (<1 minute), often many per day; onset in childhood or adolescence, tends to lessen after age 20–30
feat: Attacks triggered by sudden movement after rest (standing up, starting to run, startle)
Dystonic, choreic or ballistic movements of one or both sides lasting seconds
Awareness preserved; often a brief sensory aura in the limb
Normal examination between attacks
Personal or family history of benign infantile seizures or migraine (PRRT2 spectrum)
inv: Video of attacks (phone recording is very helpful)
EEG normal interictally and usually during attacks
MRI normal; check calcium/PTH, glucose and thyroid to exclude secondary PKD
PRRT2 genetic testing (most familial cases)

case.who: 15-year-old boy, high-school student in Hat Yai
case.story: When the bell rings and he jumps up from his chair, his right arm and leg twist for about 10 seconds; he stays fully aware. It happens several times daily. As a baby he had brief seizures that stopped by age 2.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination; an attack is reproduced by asking him to stand quickly.
case.tests: EEG and MRI normal; calcium normal; PRRT2 c.649dupC detected.
case.q: Which drug and dose range typically controls these attacks?
case.a: Paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia (PRRT2): low-dose carbamazepine (e.g. 50–200 mg/day) or oxcarbazepine usually abolishes attacks.

det.patho: Most familial and many sporadic cases carry heterozygous loss-of-function PRRT2 variants; PRRT2 interacts with SNARE proteins and regulates neurotransmitter release and sodium-channel availability. The same gene is responsible for benign self-limited seizures in infancy and for the infantile convulsions and choreoathetosis syndrome (ICCA), and is linked to hemiplegic migraine and episodic ataxia. Secondary PKD occurs with MS, hypoparathyroidism, hyperglycaemia, head injury or basal ganglia lesions.
det.clinical: Onset is usually between 6 and 16 years, with male predominance in sporadic cases. Attacks are very brief, can occur up to dozens of times a day and may be preceded by tingling or tightness. Some patients learn to slow their movements to avoid them. Frequency often decreases in adulthood, and some remit.
det.diagnosis: Clinical criteria include identified kinesigenic trigger, short duration (<1 min), no loss of consciousness, normal examination, exclusion of other causes, onset age 1–20 years and response to phenytoin or carbamazepine. Home video and genetic testing support the diagnosis. Look for secondary causes, especially hypoparathyroidism and MS in adults.
det.treatment: Low-dose sodium-channel blockers — carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine or phenytoin, and lacosamide as an option — are highly effective, often at doses well below those used for epilepsy. Avoidance of sudden movements and of sleep deprivation also helps. Offer genetic counselling given autosomal dominant inheritance.
det.prognosis: Excellent — attacks are usually fully controlled with treatment and often wane with age.
pearls: Seconds-long dystonia on sudden standing, with full awareness: think PKD.
Dramatic response to a small dose of carbamazepine is almost diagnostic.
Ask about infantile seizures in the patient or family (PRRT2).
det.thd: PKD เป็นโรคที่มีอาการบิดเกร็งหรือกระตุกของแขนขาเพียงไม่กี่วินาที เกิดเมื่อเริ่มเคลื่อนไหวกะทันหัน เช่น ลุกจากเก้าอี้ ผู้ป่วยรู้สึกตัวตลอด ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจากยีน PRRT2 อาจมีประวัติชักในวัยทารก การตรวจระหว่างอาการปกติ EEG และ MRI ปกติ รักษาด้วย carbamazepine หรือ oxcarbazepine ขนาดต่ำซึ่งได้ผลดีมาก

qx.stem: A 15-year-old boy from Phitsanulok has dozens of brief attacks daily, each lasting under 30 seconds, of twisting of the left arm and grimacing when he suddenly stands up to answer the teacher or starts running. He stays fully conscious, and examination, EEG and MRI between attacks are normal. His mother had similar spells as a teenager that faded in her twenties; she also had infant convulsions.
qx.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Low-dose carbamazepine
Levodopa/carbidopa
Acetazolamide
Clonazepam with avoidance of coffee and alcohol
Botulinum toxin into the left biceps
qx.why: Very short, frequent attacks triggered by sudden movement with preserved awareness, onset in adolescence and a family history of benign infantile seizures fit PRRT2-related paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia. Low doses of sodium-channel blockers such as carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine usually stop the attacks. Avoiding caffeine and alcohol with clonazepam suits PNKD, acetazolamide suits episodic ataxia type 2, and levodopa suits dopa-responsive dystonia.

name: Paroxysmal nonkinesiogenic dyskinesia (PNKD)
formal: Attacks of dystonia or chorea lasting minutes to hours, triggered by alcohol, caffeine, fatigue or stress and not movement, from MR-1 variants, autosomal dominant.
simple: Longer episodes of abnormal movements triggered by alcohol, coffee or stress rather than movement.
more: Avoid triggers; clonazepam or benzodiazepines work better than carbamazepine. Prognosis is good and may improve with age. Attacks of dystonia and chorea lasting minutes to hours, triggered by alcohol, caffeine, stress or fatigue, caused by MR-1 (PNKD) mutations.
th: PNKD (Mount–Reback syndrome) คือโรคถ่ายทอดแบบ autosomal dominant จากยีน PNKD (MR-1) ทำให้เกิด dystonia หรือ chorea เป็นพัก ๆ นานราว 10 นาทีถึงหลายชั่วโมง กระตุ้นด้วยแอลกอฮอล์ กาแฟ ชา ความเหนื่อยและความเครียด โดยผู้ป่วยรู้สึกตัวดี ยาที่ใช้คือ clonazepam และการเลี่ยงตัวกระตุ้น
tempoNote: Attacks last 10 minutes to several hours, recur from several times a day to a few times a year, and start in infancy or childhood; they often become less frequent with age
feat: Attacks of dystonia, chorea or mixed movement lasting 10 minutes to hours, often with speech disturbance and sometimes severe enough to cause falls; consciousness is preserved
Triggered at rest by alcohol, coffee or tea, fatigue, hunger and emotional stress rather than sudden movement; sleep may end an attack
Sensory warnings (stiffness, tingling, a tense feeling) before the attack, and a normal examination between attacks
Autosomal dominant with high penetrance in the classic PNKD (MR-1) pedigrees; variants in KCNMA1 and CASR cause a similar syndrome in other families
Much longer and rarer attacks than in kinesigenic dyskinesia, and a poorer response to carbamazepine
inv: Home video of an attack, a trigger diary and family history; exam between attacks normal
EEG during or after attacks (normal), MRI brain (normal); CSF glucose or SLC2A1 testing when exertion is a trigger
Gene panel including PNKD (MR-1), KCNMA1, CASR, PRRT2, SLC2A1 and ADCY5 for those with a family history

case.story: Since the age of eight she has had attacks in which her arms and face twist and writhe for about an hour; they follow two beers or strong iced coffee. Her father and aunt describe the same pattern and she remains fully awake and speaks with difficulty.
case.exam: Normal between attacks; video shows facial grimacing and dystonic posturing of the arms with preserved awareness.
case.tests: MRI and EEG normal; heterozygous PNKD (MR-1) variant.
case.q: What advice and treatment are appropriate?
case.a: Avoid alcohol and caffeine and regulate sleep and stress; clonazepam (regular or at the start of an attack) is the best-studied drug, while carbamazepine is usually ineffective.

det.patho: Classical PNKD is caused by variants in the PNKD (MR-1) gene on chromosome 2, which encodes a protein that regulates synaptic neurotransmitter release; alcohol and caffeine are thought to destabilise this function. Variants in KCNMA1 (BK potassium channel) and CASR have been reported in related families, and secondary forms arise from stroke, multiple sclerosis or metabolic disease. Neurons of the basal ganglia are probably affected, and cerebral perfusion changes during attacks are consistent with a paroxysmal movement disorder and not epilepsy.
det.clinical: Attacks start in infancy or early childhood, consisting of a mix of dystonia, chorea and athetosis of the face, limbs and trunk that can last from 10 minutes to hours. The patient remains conscious, speech may be lost and attacks are sometimes aborted by sleep. Precipitants are alcohol, caffeine, fatigue and stress, never sudden voluntary movement. Between attacks the patient is neurologically normal and in the classic families the attacks become less frequent with age. Rarely there is fixed interictal dystonia in sporadic cases.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical and rests on the duration, the triggers, the lack of loss of consciousness and the family history. Video recording is invaluable. EEG, MRI and routine blood tests are normal, but they exclude epilepsy and secondary causes. Genetic testing confirms PNKD (MR-1) or reveals alternatives such as KCNMA1, CASR, SLC2A1 or ADCY5 disease. In children, remember to check CSF glucose when exercise triggers attacks.
det.treatment: Education about triggers is the first step, since avoidance of alcohol, coffee, tea and sleep deprivation can by itself cut attacks to a few per year. Clonazepam is the best-studied drug and can be taken regularly or as soon as an attack begins; other benzodiazepines, gabapentin and acetazolamide help some families. Carbamazepine and phenytoin, effective in kinesigenic forms, usually fail in PNKD. For rare severe, disabling cases, globus pallidus internus deep brain stimulation has controlled attacks.
det.prognosis: The condition is lifelong but benign, with attacks often becoming milder with age and no cognitive deterioration; quality of life depends on trigger control.
pearls: Duration decides the group: seconds for kinesigenic, minutes to hours for non-kinesigenic.
Alcohol and coffee trigger PNKD; low-dose carbamazepine does not cure it.
A video of the attack taken by relatives helps more than any test.
det.thd: PNKD คือโรคทางพันธุกรรมแบบ autosomal dominant ที่ทำให้เกิด dystonia หรือ chorea เป็นพัก ๆ นานหลายสิบนาทีถึงหลายชั่วโมง กระตุ้นด้วยแอลกอฮอล์ กาแฟ ชา และความเครียด โดยผู้ป่วยไม่หมดสติ ผลตรวจ EEG และ MRI ปกติ จึงต้องแยกจากโรคลมชักและ functional movement disorder การรักษาเน้นเลี่ยงตัวกระตุ้นและใช้ clonazepam ส่วน carbamazepine มักไม่ได้ผล ซึ่งต่างจากชนิด kinesigenic

Low-dose carbamazepine abolishes attacks in most patients
It is usually caused by variants in PNKD (MR-1) and avoiding triggers plus clonazepam is the mainstay
It is caused by GLUT1 deficiency and treated with a ketogenic diet

formal: Episodes of tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, sweating and dystonia after severe brain injury, from disconnection of autonomic control; treated with beta-blockers, gabapentin, bromocriptine.

det.patho: PSH is thought to follow disconnection of cortical and diencephalic inhibitory centres from brainstem and spinal sympathetic outflow. With inhibition lost, ordinary afferent input (pain, touch, visceral distension) is amplified into an excessive sympathetic and motor response, an excitatory-inhibitory ratio model. Diffuse axonal injury and deep lesions are particularly associated.
det.clinical: Episodes start days to weeks after injury, often as sedation is reduced, and recur several times a day, each lasting minutes to hours. Features include tachycardia, hypertension, tachypnoea, hyperthermia, diaphoresis and posturing. PSH increases energy use, causes weight loss, contractures and heterotopic ossification, and is linked to longer ICU stay and worse outcomes.
det.diagnosis: PSH is a clinical diagnosis after excluding sepsis, pulmonary embolism, hypoglycaemia, drug withdrawal, NMS, malignant hyperthermia and seizures. The PSH-AM combines a clinical feature scale and a diagnosis likelihood tool. Recognising the triggered, stereotyped and simultaneous nature of features is key.
det.treatment: Minimise triggers and give analgesia before cares. Propranolol (non-selective, lipophilic) controls heart rate and hyperthermia; gabapentin reduces afferent amplification; clonidine or dexmedetomidine reduce central sympathetic output; opioids such as morphine abort episodes. Bromocriptine and intrathecal baclofen are second-line options. Avoid antipyretics alone, as fever is central.
det.prognosis: Episodes usually fade over weeks to months; their presence marks more severe injury and slower recovery.
pearls: Think PSH when a TBI patient storms with every suction but cultures are negative.
Propranolol plus gabapentin is the practical backbone.
Always exclude sepsis first; PSH is a diagnosis of exclusion.
det.thd: Paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity พบในผู้ป่วยบาดเจ็บสมองรุนแรง โดยมีอาการพร้อมกันเป็นพัก ๆ คือหัวใจเต้นเร็ว ความดันสูง ไข้ เหงื่อออกมาก หายใจเร็ว และเกร็งแขนขา มักถูกกระตุ้นด้วยการดูดเสมหะหรือพลิกตัว ต้องแยกการติดเชื้อ ชัก NMS และ serotonin syndrome ก่อน รักษาด้วย propranolol, gabapentin, clonidine และให้ยาแก้ปวดก่อนทำหัตถการ

name: Parry–Romberg syndrome
formal: Progressive hemifacial atrophy affecting skin, fat, muscle and bone, with trigeminal neuralgia, migraine or epilepsy; related to linear scleroderma.

det.patho: The cause is unknown. Most authorities place it within the spectrum of localised scleroderma (morphoea), with inflammatory and fibrotic processes affecting subcutaneous tissue, muscle and bone in a segmental distribution. Neuroinflammatory or vascular changes may involve the ipsilateral brain. Infectious, sympathetic and trigeminal theories have been proposed without proof.
det.clinical: Onset is usually in the first two decades with gradual loss of facial volume on one side, sometimes with overlying skin hardening or pigment change. Neurological features occur in a substantial minority: focal epilepsy (sometimes drug-resistant), headache, trigeminal neuralgia-like pain, facial palsy and cognitive or behavioural change. Ocular and dental problems are common. Activity typically stabilises after several years, leaving fixed deformity.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, based on the pattern of progressive unilateral facial atrophy. MRI brain is advised in all, as ipsilateral white matter lesions, calcification or atrophy may be present even without symptoms; EEG for seizures. Autoimmune tests can be positive but do not confirm the diagnosis. Exclude other causes of facial asymmetry, lipodystrophy and post-traumatic atrophy.
det.treatment: During active disease, methotrexate with a period of systemic corticosteroids is commonly used, following localised scleroderma practice; mycophenolate is an alternative. Seizures are treated with standard anti-seizure drugs and, rarely, surgery. Once the process has burned out, reconstructive surgery (autologous fat grafting, flaps, implants) restores contour. Regular eye and dental review is needed.
det.prognosis: Self-limiting in most after several years, but cosmetic deformity persists without reconstruction; drug-resistant epilepsy affects a minority.
pearls: Hemifacial atrophy plus ipsilateral focal epilepsy: image the brain on the same side.
Parry–Romberg and en coup de sabre morphoea are overlapping conditions.
Delay reconstructive surgery until disease activity has stopped.
det.thd: Parry–Romberg syndrome คือภาวะใบหน้าซีกหนึ่งฝ่อลงช้า ๆ ทั้งผิวหนัง ไขมัน กล้ามเนื้อ และกระดูก มักเริ่มในเด็กหรือวัยรุ่น และสัมพันธ์กับ linear scleroderma แบบ en coup de sabre บางรายมีอาการทางระบบประสาท เช่น ชักเฉพาะที่ ปวดศีรษะ หรือปวดหน้า และ MRI พบรอยโรคในสมองข้างเดียวกับใบหน้าที่ฝ่อ รักษาช่วงที่โรคยังดำเนินอยู่ด้วย methotrexate ร่วมกับ steroid ให้ยากันชัก และผ่าตัดเสริมใบหน้าเมื่อโรคสงบ

name: Partial spinal cord syndrome
formal: Incomplete cord lesion patterns such as Brown-Séquard, anterior or central cord syndromes, with characteristic motor and sensory distributions below the lesion.
simple: Spinal cord damage that affects only part of the cord, so some movement or feeling is lost and some is kept.

feat: Brown-Séquard: ipsilateral weakness and loss of vibration/position, contralateral pain-temperature loss
Central cord: arms weaker than legs, cape-like or variable sensory loss, often after neck hyperextension
Anterior cord: paraplegia and loss of pain-temperature below the level with preserved dorsal column function
Posterior cord: sensory ataxia with positive Romberg, power largely preserved

det.patho: The spinal cord's tracts are arranged so that partial lesions produce recognisable patterns. Corticospinal and dorsal column fibres stay ipsilateral until the medulla, while spinothalamic fibres cross within one or two segments; central grey matter and medially placed arm fibres are vulnerable in central lesions, and the ventral cord, excluding the dorsal columns, receives its blood from the anterior spinal artery. Causes include trauma, disc and spondylotic compression, infarction, demyelination, tumour, infection and nutritional deficiency.
det.clinical: Central cord syndrome is the commonest incomplete traumatic pattern and typically affects older people with spondylosis after a minor fall. Anterior cord syndrome arises from infarction or retropulsed disc fragments and carries the worst motor outlook. Brown-Séquard syndrome is classically from penetrating trauma but in practice often incomplete, caused by disc herniation, tumour or MS. Posterior cord syndrome suggests B12 or copper deficiency, tabes dorsalis or extrinsic compression.
det.diagnosis: Map the motor, pinprick and joint-position level and test sacral sensation and anal tone; the ASIA (ISNCSCI) examination grades completeness. MRI is the key investigation and should be done urgently. Laboratory tests target the clinical pattern: B12, copper and syphilis for posterior column disease; antibody and CSF testing for inflammatory myelitis.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: urgent decompression for compressive or unstable lesions, antibiotics or drainage for abscess, high-dose steroids and plasma exchange for inflammatory myelitis, vitamin replacement for deficiency. Maintain mean arterial pressure in acute traumatic injury and prevent complications (pressure sores, DVT, bladder retention). Early rehabilitation is essential.
det.prognosis: Incomplete lesions recover far better than complete ones; central cord and Brown-Séquard syndromes often allow walking, while anterior cord syndrome has the poorest motor recovery.
pearls: Arms worse than legs after neck hyperextension in an older patient: central cord syndrome.
Preserved vibration with dense paraplegia: anterior spinal artery territory.
Sacral sparing defines an incomplete injury and better prognosis.
det.thd: Partial spinal cord syndrome คือรอยโรคไขสันหลังที่ไม่สมบูรณ์ ให้รูปแบบเฉพาะ เช่น Brown-Séquard (อ่อนแรงข้างเดียวกัน ชาเจ็บร้อนข้างตรงข้าม), central cord (แขนอ่อนแรงกว่าขา พบหลังคอแหงนในผู้สูงอายุ), anterior cord (อัมพาตและชาเจ็บแต่ยังรับรู้การสั่นได้) และ posterior cord (เดินเซจากสูญเสีย proprioception) ต้องทำ MRI ไขสันหลังโดยเร็วและรักษาตามสาเหตุ

name: Paucibacillary leprosy
formal: Tuberculoid or indeterminate leprosy with few skin patches and nerve thickening, causing sensory loss and mononeuropathy; strong cell-mediated response.
simple: A milder form of leprosy with few skin patches and numb areas.
th: โรคเรื้อนชนิดเชื้อน้อย มีวงด่างชาไม่กี่แห่ง เส้นประสาทใกล้รอยโรคโต อาจเป็น mononeuropathy ภูมิคุ้มกันต่อเชื้อดี
tempoNote: Slowly developing patches over months to years; reversal reactions can cause acute nerve loss
feat: One to five well-defined hypopigmented or reddish patches with loss of sensation and sweating
Thickened nerve near a patch or single nerve trunk (ulnar, peroneal, facial branches)
Mononeuropathy: claw fingers, foot drop or lagophthalmos
Type 1 (reversal) reaction: patches become swollen and tender with sudden nerve pain and weakness
inv: Sensation test of patches with cotton wisp and monofilament
Slit-skin smear usually negative
Skin or nerve biopsy: granulomas with few or no bacilli

case.story: A pale patch on his forearm has been numb for a year; recently his little finger feels weak.
case.exam: Single hypopigmented anaesthetic patch on the forearm, cord-like thick ulnar nerve at the elbow, weak finger abduction.
case.tests: Slit-skin smear negative; biopsy shows epithelioid granulomas around dermal nerves.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the WHO treatment duration?
case.a: Paucibacillary (tuberculoid) leprosy with ulnar neuropathy; rifampicin, dapsone and clofazimine for 6 months, with steroids if neuritis is active.

read.where: Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — Leprosy (Hansen’s Disease)

det.patho: Strong cell-mediated immunity contains M. leprae, producing well-formed granulomas with very few bacilli. The immune response itself damages dermal and nearby nerve trunks, so nerve involvement can be severe despite the low bacillary load.
det.clinical: The patches are sharply demarcated and anaesthetic, with loss of hair and sweating. Pure neuritic leprosy, without skin lesions, presents as a mononeuropathy with a thickened nerve and is easily missed. Reversal reactions can cause rapid paralysis and need urgent steroids.
det.diagnosis: WHO cardinal signs are an anaesthetic skin patch, a thickened nerve with sensory or motor loss, or acid-fast bacilli on smear; PB disease has up to five lesions and negative smears. Biopsy confirms when doubt exists, and nerve biopsy or ultrasound helps in pure neuritic forms.
det.treatment: WHO now recommends the same three drugs (rifampicin, dapsone, clofazimine) for PB leprosy for 6 months. Neuritis and reversal reactions are treated with prednisolone over several months. Protect anaesthetic areas, provide splints and physiotherapy, and screen contacts with single-dose rifampicin prophylaxis.
det.prognosis: Cure is expected with MDT; recovery of nerve function depends on prompt treatment of neuritis.
pearls: Test sensation inside any chronic pale patch in an endemic area.
Pure neuritic leprosy: a thick ulnar nerve may be the only clue.
Sudden weakness after starting MDT is a reaction, not drug failure.
det.thd: โรคเรื้อนชนิด paucibacillary เกิดในผู้ที่มีภูมิคุ้มกันต่อเชื้อดี มีวงด่างขาวหรือแดงชาไม่เกิน 5 แห่ง เส้นประสาทใกล้รอยโรคโต อาจเกิดนิ้วงอหรือเท้าตก ตรวจ smear มักไม่พบเชื้อ ชิ้นเนื้อพบ granuloma รักษาด้วยยาสามขนานนาน 6 เดือน และให้สเตียรอยด์เมื่อเส้นประสาทอักเสบ

name: Peak-dose dyskinesias
formal: Choreiform or dystonic movements during peak plasma levodopa levels in treated Parkinson disease, related to pulsatile dopaminergic stimulation; amantadine may help.
simple: Involuntary wriggling movements when medicine levels are highest in Parkinson disease.
th: การเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติแบบ chorea หรือ dystonia ที่เกิดขณะระดับ levodopa ในเลือดสูงสุด ในผู้ป่วยพาร์กินสันที่รักษามานาน
tempoNote: Recurs daily at the time of best medication effect, usually emerging after several years of levodopa
feat: Choreic, flowing movements of neck, trunk and limbs about 30–90 minutes after a levodopa dose
Coincide with the best 'on' motor state
Risk rises with younger onset age, longer disease, higher levodopa dose and female sex
Often less bothersome to the patient than to the family
Distinguish from diphasic dyskinesia, which occurs at the start and end of a dose
inv: Clinical: timing diary relating movements to doses
Video recording at home across a dosing cycle
No laboratory test required

case.who: 59-year-old shopkeeper from Ayutthaya with PD for 8 years
case.story: About an hour after each levodopa tablet his shoulders and head sway and twist; he says he feels at his best then, but customers stare.
case.exam: During the episode: generalized chorea with good mobility; before the next dose, mild bradykinesia returns.
case.tests: Motor diary confirms dyskinesia peaks 45–90 minutes post-dose.
case.q: How would you reduce these movements?
case.a: Peak-dose dyskinesia: lower each levodopa dose and give it more often, and add amantadine.

read.where: 10 Parkinson’s Disease: Advanced Disease, Motor Complications, and Management
9 - Atypical parkinsonism, parkinsonism-­plus syndromes and secondary parkinsonian disorders

det.patho: With progressive loss of nigral terminals the striatum loses its buffer for dopamine, so oral levodopa produces large swings in synaptic dopamine. Pulsatile stimulation leads to maladaptive plasticity in striatal medium spiny neurons, with altered D1 signalling and glutamatergic overactivity. When dopamine peaks, the indirect pathway is excessively suppressed and choreic movements emerge.
det.clinical: Dyskinesias are usually choreic but may include dystonic components, and often begin on the more affected side. They typically appear several years after levodopa initiation. Mild dyskinesia is often preferred by patients to being 'off'; severe forms cause falls, weight loss and social embarrassment.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is made by relating the timing of movements to doses with a diary or video. Classify into peak-dose, diphasic or off-period types, as management differs. Rule out other drugs that cause chorea.
det.treatment: Options include smaller, more frequent levodopa doses, adding a dopamine agonist or MAO-B inhibitor while trimming levodopa, and amantadine (immediate or extended-release). Continuous delivery strategies (levodopa–carbidopa intestinal gel, subcutaneous foslevodopa or apomorphine infusion) smooth fluctuations. Subthalamic or pallidal deep brain stimulation is highly effective for disabling dyskinesia. Clozapine is an option in selected patients.
det.prognosis: Dyskinesias persist as PD progresses but can usually be controlled; DBS or infusion therapy gives lasting benefit in suitable patients.
pearls: Ask when the movements occur relative to the tablet: peak, beginning-and-end, or off.
Amantadine is the main drug that directly reduces dyskinesia.
Fear of dyskinesia should not delay levodopa; disease duration matters more than early exposure.
det.thd: Peak-dose dyskinesia คืออาการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติแบบ chorea ที่เกิดขณะระดับ levodopa สูงสุด ประมาณ 30–90 นาทีหลังกินยา ในผู้ป่วยพาร์กินสันที่รักษามาหลายปี เกิดจากการกระตุ้นโดปามีนแบบเป็นพัก ๆ ทำให้ striatum เปลี่ยนแปลง การรักษาคือแบ่ง levodopa เป็นขนาดเล็กลงแต่บ่อยขึ้น เพิ่ม amantadine และพิจารณายาแบบต่อเนื่องหรือ DBS ในรายรุนแรง

name: Pelizaeus–Merzbacher disease (PMD)
formal: X-linked hypomyelinating leukodystrophy from PLP1 mutations, with nystagmus, hypotonia, spasticity and developmental delay in infancy.
simple: An inherited condition in boys where nerve insulation fails to form properly, causing abnormal eye movements and delayed development.
more: PLP1 duplication is the most common cause (also point mutations and null); MRI shows diffuse hypomyelination; sequencing or MLPA. Treatment is supportive with antispasticity and seizure management; milder spastic paraplegia SPG2 allelic.
th: โรคเนื้อสมองขาวสร้างไมอีลินไม่สมบูรณ์ถ่ายทอดทางโครโมโซม X จากยีน PLP1 เด็กชายมีตากระตุกตั้งแต่ขวบแรก ตัวอ่อน แล้วกลายเป็นเกร็งและพัฒนาการช้า
tempoNote: Nystagmus in the first weeks to months of life; motor milestones stall, then slow progression or plateau over years
feat: Boys with pendular or rotatory nystagmus and head titubation in early infancy
Early floppiness that evolves into spastic quadriparesis, ataxia and choreoathetosis
Delayed motor development with relatively better comprehension than speech or movement
Severe connatal form (stridor, seizures) at one end; mild SPG2 spastic paraplegia at the other
Carrier mothers are usually unaffected but may develop mild late spasticity
inv: MRI after about 1 year: diffuse T2-bright white matter with almost no myelination progress on serial scans
PLP1 copy-number testing (MLPA or microarray) first, since duplication is the commonest cause; then sequencing
Evoked potentials (BAER waves after I absent or delayed) support central hypomyelination

case.story: Eyes have jerked side to side since 6 weeks of age; he still cannot sit and his head wobbles. A maternal uncle used a wheelchair from childhood.
case.exam: Pendular nystagmus, head titubation, axial hypotonia with brisk reflexes and upgoing toes; smiles and follows voices.
case.tests: MRI shows uniformly unmyelinated white matter; BAER has only wave I; PLP1 duplication on MLPA.
case.q: What is the inheritance and why is this not a demyelinating leukodystrophy?
case.a: X-linked PMD: myelin never forms properly (hypomyelination) rather than being destroyed; mothers carry the duplication.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — leukodystrophies

det.patho: PLP1 encodes proteolipid protein, the main protein of central myelin. Extra copies or misfolding missense variants overload oligodendrocytes and trigger stress and cell death, so myelin is never laid down; complete loss of the protein paradoxically causes a milder disease with later axonal degeneration. Peripheral myelin is largely spared. The disorder is X-linked and affects about 1 in 200,000–500,000 boys.
det.clinical: The classic form shows nystagmus and hypotonia in infancy, head shaking, delayed sitting and later spasticity, ataxia and involuntary movements; many learn some speech but few walk independently. The connatal form starts at birth with stridor, feeding failure and seizures and shortens life markedly. Null alleles and some missense changes produce SPG2, a slowly progressive spastic paraplegia sometimes with mild neuropathy. Nystagmus may fade with age, which can mislead later examiners.
det.diagnosis: Suspect PMD in a boy with early nystagmus and an MRI showing persistent diffuse lack of myelin on two scans at least 6 months apart. Copy-number analysis of PLP1 detects the common duplication; sequencing finds point variants. If PLP1 is normal, test GJC2 and other hypomyelination genes through a leukodystrophy panel or exome. Very early MRI may be hard to interpret because myelination is normally incomplete.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy is approved; trials of oligodendrocyte cell therapy and antisense approaches against PLP1 are experimental. Management is supportive: physiotherapy, orthoses and antispasticity drugs, seizure control, feeding support and gastrostomy, orthopaedic surveillance for hips and spine, and communication aids. Genetic counselling for the mother and female relatives is essential.
det.prognosis: Classic PMD patients often live into middle adulthood with severe disability; connatal forms commonly die in childhood, while SPG2 has near-normal lifespan.
pearls: Infant boy + nystagmus + MRI that never myelinates: test PLP1 copy number first.
Hypomyelination (myelin never made) differs from demyelination (myelin lost) on MRI pattern and course.
Milder PLP1 variants may present to adult clinics as complicated spastic paraplegia.
det.thd: Pelizaeus–Merzbacher disease เกิดจากยีน PLP1 บนโครโมโซม X ซึ่งจำเป็นต่อการสร้างไมอีลินในสมอง เด็กชายมีตากระตุกตั้งแต่ไม่กี่เดือนแรก ศีรษะสั่น ตัวอ่อน ต่อมากลายเป็นเกร็งและเดินเซ MRI พบเนื้อสมองขาวไม่สร้างไมอีลินแม้ตรวจซ้ำ วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจจำนวนชุดยีน PLP1 การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคองและให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรมแก่ครอบครัว

ddx.pt: Same clinical-radiological picture in girls or boys with recessive GJC2 variants; PLP1 normal
Irritability, regression and thick nerves with low GALC activity; demyelination with neuropathy, not static hypomyelination
Mild PLP1 cases (SPG2) can mimic pure HSP; MRI white-matter change and nystagmus point back to PLP1

name: Pelizaeus–Merzbacher-like disease (PMLD)
formal: Hypomyelinating leukodystrophy clinically like PMD but without PLP1 mutation, often due to GJC2 (connexin 47) mutations, with nystagmus and developmental delay.
simple: A rare inherited disorder similar to Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease with poorly formed nerve insulation.
th: hypomyelinating leukodystrophy ที่อาการคล้าย PMD แต่ไม่มีการกลายพันธุ์ PLP1 ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจากยีน GJC2 (connexin 47) มีตากระตุกและพัฒนาการช้า
tempoNote: Nystagmus in the first months; slow motor development then gradual spasticity
feat: Nystagmus in early infancy, hypotonia, delayed motor milestones
Progressive spasticity, ataxia, dysarthria; some achieve limited walking
Autosomal recessive, so girls and boys affected (unlike X-linked PMD)
Cognition relatively preserved compared with motor deficit
Peripheral neuropathy may occur in some cases
inv: MRI: diffuse hypomyelination (T2 bright, T1 near-normal white matter), sometimes brainstem involvement
PLP1 testing negative; GJC2 sequencing (and other hypomyelination genes)
BAEP abnormal; NCS may show mild neuropathy

case.story: Eyes have wobbled since 2 months; she cannot sit without support. Parents are cousins.
case.exam: Pendular nystagmus, head titubation, axial hypotonia with brisk limb reflexes.
case.tests: MRI diffuse hypomyelination; PLP1 normal; GJC2 homozygous variant.
case.q: How does this differ genetically from classic Pelizaeus–Merzbacher disease?
case.a: PMLD is autosomal recessive (GJC2) and affects girls; classic PMD is X-linked (PLP1) and affects boys.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Pelizaeus–Merzbacher Disease and Pelizaeus–Merzbacher-Like Disease

det.patho: GJC2 encodes connexin 47, a gap junction protein in oligodendrocytes that couples them with astrocytes (via connexin 43). Loss of this coupling impairs myelin formation and maintenance, causing hypomyelination. Other genes produce similar 'PMD-like' pictures, so the term covers a heterogeneous group.
det.clinical: Infants develop nystagmus, hypotonia and delayed motor development, progressing to spasticity and ataxia over childhood. Many acquire some speech and cognitive function. The course is similar to classic PMD but tends to be milder in cognition. A milder spastic paraplegia phenotype (SPG44) also arises from GJC2 variants.
det.diagnosis: MRI showing diffuse hypomyelination in a child with early nystagmus suggests the group. PLP1 testing should be done first in boys; when negative, test GJC2 and broader hypomyelination panels or exome.
det.treatment: No disease-specific treatment. Supportive care includes physiotherapy, management of spasticity, seizures (if present), nutrition and communication aids. Genetic counselling for recessive inheritance.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; many survive into adulthood with significant motor disability.
pearls: Infantile nystagmus plus hypomyelination on MRI: PMD or PMLD.
A girl with a PMD picture points to GJC2 or other recessive genes.
Hypomyelination (never formed) differs from demyelination (lost).
det.thd: PMLD เป็น hypomyelinating leukodystrophy ที่อาการคล้าย Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease แต่ถ่ายทอดแบบ autosomal recessive จากยีน GJC2 (connexin 47) จึงพบได้ทั้งเด็กหญิงและชาย มีตากระตุกตั้งแต่ไม่กี่เดือนแรก พัฒนาการช้า ต่อมาขาเกร็งและเดินเซ MRI พบ hypomyelination ทั่วไป วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีน การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง
