name: Penicillamine dermatopathy
formal: Skin complications of penicillamine such as elastosis perforans serpiginosa, pemphigus and cutis laxa-like change, occurring during treatment of Wilson disease and other conditions.
simple: Skin damage, including wrinkling, blistering and fragile skin, caused by penicillamine treatment.
more: Diagnosed from drug history and skin biopsy. Switch to trientine or reduce dose; some lesions heal slowly or leave scars.
th: ผื่นและความผิดปกติของผิวหนังจากยา D-penicillamine เช่น elastosis perforans serpiginosa, pemphigus, ผิวหนังหย่อนยาน ซึ่งพบในผู้ป่วย Wilson ที่ใช้ยานี้นาน เป็นผลข้างเคียงทางผิวหนัง ไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาท
tempoNote: Appears months to years into penicillamine therapy (early rashes can occur within weeks)
feat: Not a neurological disease: a skin adverse effect of penicillamine used for Wilson disease, cystinuria or rheumatoid arthritis
Early hypersensitivity rashes (morbilliform, urticarial) in the first weeks
Long-term: elastosis perforans serpiginosa (serpiginous keratotic papules on the neck), cutis laxa-like wrinkling, pseudoxanthoma elasticum-like change
Autoimmune blistering (pemphigus foliaceus) and poor wound healing
inv: Skin biopsy: abnormal 'lumpy-bumpy' elastic fibres; direct immunofluorescence for pemphigus
Review penicillamine dose and duration; check copper status and other penicillamine toxicities (urine protein, blood count)

case.who: 28-year-old woman from Songkhla with Wilson disease on penicillamine for 9 years
case.story: Raised, ring-shaped crusted papules on her neck and wrinkled loose skin over the elbows.
case.exam: Serpiginous keratotic papules on the lateral neck; neurological exam stable apart from mild dysarthria.
case.tests: Skin biopsy shows transepidermal elimination of abnormal elastic fibres.
case.q: What is the cause and how is Wilson treatment adjusted?
case.a: Penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa; switch to trientine (or zinc for maintenance) and continue copper monitoring.

det.patho: Penicillamine chelates copper and interferes with cross-linking of collagen and elastin, partly by inhibiting copper-dependent lysyl oxidase. Abnormal elastic fibres are then extruded through the skin or leave it lax. The drug also contains a thiol group that can provoke autoimmunity, leading to pemphigus, lupus-like illness or myasthenia gravis.
det.clinical: Dermatopathy is cumulative and dose related, usually after years of high-dose therapy. Lesions are cosmetic but can be persistent. Clinicians should also watch for other penicillamine toxicities: nephrotic syndrome, cytopenias, lupus-like syndrome, drug-induced myasthenia, and early paradoxical neurological worsening in Wilson disease.
det.diagnosis: Based on drug history and characteristic skin appearance, confirmed by biopsy showing distorted elastic fibres or pemphigus immunofluorescence. Exclude primary connective tissue disorders.
det.treatment: Reduce dose or switch to trientine, or zinc for maintenance in stable Wilson disease. Pemphigus usually remits after withdrawal but may need steroids. Some elastic damage is permanent. Specialist dermatology input helps.
det.prognosis: Rashes and pemphigus usually improve after stopping; elastic tissue changes heal slowly and may scar.
pearls: Penicillamine skin changes are a reason to switch to trientine in Wilson disease.
Penicillamine can also cause myasthenia gravis and paradoxical neurological worsening.
This lexicon entry is a drug adverse effect, not a neurological disorder.
det.thd: Penicillamine dermatopathy คือผลข้างเคียงทางผิวหนังจากยา D-penicillamine ซึ่งใช้รักษาโรค Wilson ยารบกวนการสร้าง elastin และ collagen ทำให้เกิดผื่นตุ่มเป็นแนวโค้งที่คอ ผิวหย่อนยาน หรือ pemphigus ไม่ใช่โรคของระบบประสาท วินิจฉัยจากประวัติยาและชิ้นเนื้อผิวหนัง รักษาโดยลดยาหรือเปลี่ยนเป็น trientine หรือ zinc

ddx.pt: The underlying disease being treated; neurological worsening needs separate assessment
Inherited skin laxity and joint hypermobility from birth, not drug related
Another penicillamine immune complication (drug-induced MG) that may coexist

name: Penicillin cortical myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus and encephalopathy from high-dose penicillin, especially in renal failure, due to GABA-A antagonism by beta-lactams.
simple: Muscle jerks and confusion caused by very high levels of penicillin antibiotic.
th: อาการกระตุกแบบ myoclonus และสับสนจากยาเพนิซิลลินหรือ beta-lactam ขนาดสูง โดยเฉพาะในผู้ป่วยไตวาย เพราะยาไปยับยั้ง GABA-A receptor ในสมอง
tempoNote: Develops over hours to a few days after starting or increasing the antibiotic
feat: Multifocal, stimulus-sensitive cortical myoclonus with confusion or reduced consciousness
May progress to seizures or non-convulsive status epilepticus
Risk factors: renal impairment, high doses, older age, prior brain disease, intrathecal or intraventricular use
Similar toxicity with cefepime, ceftazidime and carbapenems (especially imipenem)
Resolves after dose reduction or stopping the drug
inv: Renal function and calculation of appropriate dosing
EEG: generalized slowing, triphasic-like or periodic discharges, or non-convulsive seizures
Exclude other causes: uraemia, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, CNS infection

case.who: 71-year-old man on haemodialysis in a Khon Kaen medical ward
case.story: Three days after starting high-dose intravenous penicillin G for streptococcal endocarditis he becomes drowsy and has frequent jerks of arms and face.
case.exam: Confused, multifocal arrhythmic myoclonus worsened by touch, asterixis absent, no meningism.
case.tests: EEG shows diffuse slowing with periodic sharp waves; urea unchanged from baseline.
case.q: What is the cause and what should be done?
case.a: Beta-lactam (penicillin) neurotoxicity due to accumulation in renal failure; reduce or switch the antibiotic, consider extra dialysis, and give a benzodiazepine for seizures.

det.patho: Penicillins and several other beta-lactams bind to and antagonise GABA-A receptors, lowering cortical inhibition. Renal failure, hypoalbuminaemia and a leaky blood-brain barrier raise CNS levels. The result is cortical hyperexcitability that ranges from myoclonus to seizures and encephalopathy.
det.clinical: Patients, usually older or with kidney disease, develop confusion, hallucinations, myoclonic jerks and sometimes seizures within days of high-dose therapy. Cefepime is now the most frequently reported culprit in many hospitals. Symptoms are frequently mistaken for septic or uraemic encephalopathy.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it when encephalopathy and myoclonus coincide with a beta-lactam in a patient with reduced clearance. EEG helps detect non-convulsive seizures and periodic patterns. Drug levels are rarely available, so diagnosis is clinical and confirmed by improvement after withdrawal.
det.treatment: Stop or reduce the beta-lactam, or switch to a less neurotoxic agent. Haemodialysis can speed removal of some drugs such as cefepime. Treat seizures or status with benzodiazepines and, if needed, levetiracetam. Dose antibiotics according to creatinine clearance to prevent recurrence.
det.prognosis: Usually fully reversible within days of stopping the drug; delayed recognition can lead to status epilepticus.
pearls: New myoclonus on a beta-lactam in a dialysis patient: think drug toxicity before blaming sepsis.
Always dose beta-lactams for renal function.
Request EEG to find hidden non-convulsive seizures.

name: Periodic paralysis
formal: Channelopathy causing episodic flaccid weakness, hypo- or hyperkalaemic, triggered by rest after exercise or carbohydrate meals, from CACNA1S or SCN4A mutations.
simple: Attacks of temporary muscle weakness, usually inherited and linked to potassium levels.
ab: อัมพาตเป็นพัก ๆ
th: อ่อนแรงแขนขาแบบปวกเปียกเป็นพัก ๆ จากช่องไอออนของกล้ามเนื้อผิดปกติ สัมพันธ์กับระดับโพแทสเซียม แต่ละครั้งหายเองในชั่วโมงถึงวัน ในไทยต้องคิดถึง thyrotoxic periodic paralysis และ hypokalaemia จากสาเหตุอื่นเสมอ
tempoNote: Attacks last minutes to hours (hyperPP) or hours to a day or more (hypoPP); often on waking or after rest following exercise; fixed weakness may appear in later life
feat: Episodes of flaccid limb weakness, proximal more than distal, with reduced reflexes during the attack and normal strength between
Consciousness, sensation, bulbar and respiratory muscles usually spared
Triggers: rest after exertion, carbohydrate-rich meals, alcohol, cold, stress, steroids or insulin
Hypokalaemic form: night or early-morning attacks lasting hours; hyperkalaemic form: shorter attacks, sometimes with myotonia
Thyrotoxic form: young Asian men, attacks may be the first sign of hyperthyroidism
inv: Serum potassium during the attack (may normalise quickly), plus magnesium, phosphate and acid–base status
TSH and free T4 in every first episode; urine potassium and urine/serum K ratio to exclude renal losses (e.g. distal RTA)
ECG: U waves and prolonged QT with low K, peaked T waves with high K; long QT and ventricular ectopy suggest Andersen–Tawil
Long exercise test on EMG between attacks; genetic testing (CACNA1S, SCN4A, KCNJ2)

case.who: 28-year-old man, construction worker from Nakhon Pathom
case.story: Woke at 4 a.m. after a night of beer and sticky rice unable to lift his legs or arms. He has lost 5 kg in two months and feels hot and jittery.
case.exam: Symmetric proximal weakness 2/5 in legs, 3/5 in arms, absent reflexes, normal sensation, pulse 118 regular, fine tremor, small diffuse goitre.
case.tests: K 1.9 mmol/L, normal bicarbonate, low urine potassium, TSH suppressed, free T4 high; ECG shows U waves.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what precaution applies to potassium replacement?
case.a: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis; give modest potassium doses and recheck often because rebound hyperkalaemia is common; a non-selective beta-blocker helps until euthyroid.

det.patho: Primary periodic paralyses are skeletal muscle channelopathies. Hypokalaemic periodic paralysis is usually caused by CACNA1S or SCN4A variants that create an abnormal 'gating pore' leak, so fibres depolarise and become inexcitable when potassium falls. Hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis arises from SCN4A gain-of-function variants, and Andersen–Tawil syndrome from KCNJ2 (Kir2.1) loss of function. Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis is an acquired form, seen mainly in Asian men, in which thyroid hormone boosts Na/K-ATPase activity on a background of susceptibility (including KCNJ18 variants).
det.clinical: Attacks of flaccid weakness may involve all four limbs or only the exercised muscles; breathing and swallowing are rarely affected, but severe hypokalaemia can cause arrhythmia. Primary hypoPP usually starts in the teens; hyperPP often in childhood with brief attacks provoked by fasting or potassium-rich food. Andersen–Tawil adds long QT/ventricular arrhythmias and dysmorphism (low-set ears, small jaw, clinodactyly). Over decades many patients develop a permanent proximal myopathy.
det.diagnosis: Document potassium during an attack and look for secondary causes: thyrotoxicosis, renal or gastrointestinal potassium loss, diuretics, liquorice, and distal renal tubular acidosis (relatively common in north-east Thailand). A low urine potassium excretion during the attack suggests a shift into cells (periodic paralysis) rather than loss. Between attacks the McManis long exercise test shows a delayed fall in CMAP amplitude. Genetic testing confirms primary forms and guides family counselling.
det.treatment: Acute hypokalaemic attacks: oral potassium chloride in small repeated doses (IV only if unable to swallow or arrhythmia), avoiding dextrose-containing fluids and monitoring for rebound. Hyperkalaemic attacks often abort with mild exercise or carbohydrate; inhaled salbutamol helps. Prevention: avoid triggers, consider acetazolamide or dichlorphenamide, and potassium-sparing diuretics for hypoPP. Thyrotoxic forms need propranolol acutely and definitive control of hyperthyroidism, after which attacks cease.
det.prognosis: Attack frequency often falls after middle age, but a late fixed myopathy is common in primary forms; TPP resolves once euthyroid.
pearls: A young Thai man paralysed on waking after a carbohydrate-rich night: check potassium and TSH.
Reflexes are depressed or absent during attacks, so GBS is the main bedside mimic.
Rebound hyperkalaemia is a real risk when treating TPP aggressively.
Long QT plus periodic paralysis plus dysmorphic features: Andersen–Tawil (KCNJ2).
det.thd: Periodic paralysis คืออาการอ่อนแรงแขนขาแบบปวกเปียกเป็นพัก ๆ จากช่องไอออนในกล้ามเนื้อผิดปกติ ระหว่างอาการ reflex ลดลง แต่ความรู้สึกปกติ มักเกิดตอนตื่นนอนหรือหลังพักจากการออกแรงหรือกินแป้งมาก ชนิดโพแทสเซียมต่ำพบบ่อยที่สุด ในไทยต้องตรวจ TSH เพราะ thyrotoxic periodic paralysis พบบ่อยในชายหนุ่ม และต้องแยก distal RTA รักษาด้วยการให้โพแทสเซียมอย่างระวังภาวะโพแทสเซียมสูงย้อนกลับ ป้องกันด้วยหลีกเลี่ยงสิ่งกระตุ้นและ acetazolamide

name: Perioperative plexopathies
formal: Brachial or lumbosacral plexus injury from surgical positioning, traction, tourniquets or retractors during an operation.
simple: Nerve network injury occurring during or after surgery, from stretch or pressure.
more: Most are neurapraxic and recover over weeks to months; EMG and imaging guide prognosis.
th: การบาดเจ็บของ brachial หรือ lumbosacral plexus ระหว่างผ่าตัด จากท่าจัด การดึง tourniquet หรือ retractor
tempoNote: Deficit noticed on waking from anaesthesia or in the first postoperative days
feat: Weakness and numbness in a plexus pattern noticed after surgery
Brachial: arm abduction, sternotomy retraction (lower trunk), shoulder surgery, beach-chair or prone positions
Lumbosacral: lithotomy position, retractor compression of psoas, pelvic haematoma
Pain out of proportion with delayed onset suggests post-surgical inflammatory neuropathy instead
Most are neurapraxic and recover
inv: Early baseline examination; EMG/NCS after about 3 weeks to gauge axonal loss
Imaging (CT/MRI) urgently if haematoma or retroperitoneal bleeding is possible
MRI neurography or ultrasound for traction injury or inflammatory changes

case.who: 63-year-old man after coronary bypass surgery at a heart centre in Bangkok
case.story: On day one after sternotomy he notices numb little and ring fingers and weak grip in the left hand.
case.exam: Weak finger abduction and thumb flexion, numbness of the medial hand and forearm.
case.tests: NCS at 3 weeks: low ulnar and medial antebrachial cutaneous sensory responses, denervation in C8–T1 muscles outside the ulnar territory.
case.q: Where is the lesion and why does the medial forearm matter?
case.a: Lower trunk brachial plexopathy from sternal retraction; medial antebrachial cutaneous involvement places it above the ulnar nerve.

det.patho: Most injuries arise from stretch or compression during prolonged positioning, traction or retraction, causing focal demyelination (neurapraxia) or axonal damage. Sternotomy retraction pushes the first rib into the lower trunk. Retroperitoneal haematoma or retractor blades compress the lumbar plexus. A separate immune-mediated postoperative neuropathy can occur remote from the surgical field.
det.clinical: Deficits appear on waking or within a day and follow a plexus distribution. Pain is variable; severe pain beginning days later, especially in an unusual distribution, suggests an inflammatory mechanism. Lumbosacral injuries cause hip flexion and knee extension weakness or foot drop.
det.diagnosis: Careful localisation separates plexus from peripheral nerve and root lesions. EMG at three weeks quantifies axonal loss and helps prognosis. Urgent imaging is needed when anticoagulation or vascular procedures raise the possibility of haematoma.
det.treatment: Most patients need only physiotherapy, splinting and pain management. Haematomas may require evacuation. Inflammatory postoperative neuropathy confirmed by biopsy or imaging may respond to corticosteroids. Surgical repair is considered for documented nerve transection or no recovery by several months.
det.prognosis: Neurapraxic injuries recover within weeks to months; axonal injuries recover slowly and may be incomplete.
pearls: Post-sternotomy hand weakness is often lower trunk, not ulnar nerve.
New lumbar plexopathy on anticoagulation: image for retroperitoneal haematoma.
Delayed severe pain after surgery suggests an inflammatory neuropathy.

name: Peripheral myoclonus
formal: Myoclonic jerks arising from peripheral nerve, plexus or root lesions, such as hemifacial spasm or spinal root disease.
simple: Muscle jerks that start from a damaged nerve outside the brain and spinal cord.
th: การกระตุกของกล้ามเนื้อที่มีต้นกำเนิดจากเส้นประสาทส่วนปลาย รากประสาท ข่ายประสาท หรือเซลล์ anterior horn แทนที่จะมาจากสมองหรือไขสันหลัง
tempoNote: Persistent, often for months to years after the nerve or root lesion
feat: Rhythmic or irregular jerks confined to muscles of one nerve, root or plexus
Often persist during sleep
Usually follows nerve, plexus or root injury, or anterior horn disease (e.g. post-polio)
Hemifacial spasm is the classic example
Rare; a central generator is far more common and must be excluded
inv: EMG/NCS: localise the peripheral lesion; jerk bursts confined to one nerve territory
MRI of the relevant root, plexus or spinal segment
MRI brain with posterior fossa views for hemifacial spasm

case.story: Six months after a deep cut to his right upper arm, his biceps and brachioradialis twitch rhythmically, even at night.
case.exam: Partial radial and musculocutaneous weakness; visible jerks in those muscles only.
case.tests: EMG shows chronic denervation and repetitive bursts restricted to the injured nerves; spinal MRI normal.
case.q: Where is the myoclonus generated?
case.a: Peripheral myoclonus from the injured nerves; botulinum toxin injections can help.

det.patho: Damage to a nerve, root, plexus or anterior horn cell can create ectopic impulse generation and ephaptic cross-talk between injured axons. Secondary changes in spinal circuits after peripheral injury may also contribute. The resulting discharges activate muscles of the affected territory independently of the brain.
det.clinical: Jerks are localised to the muscles of the damaged structure and may be rhythmic or irregular, spontaneous or provoked by movement. They often continue during sleep. Examples include hemifacial spasm, post-radiation or traumatic plexopathy, and the multifocal jerks of post-polio syndrome or motor neuron disease.
det.diagnosis: Neurophysiology confirms a peripheral lesion and shows that bursts are confined to its territory. Imaging excludes spinal cord or brainstem generators. The term is often over-applied, so central sources such as segmental spinal myoclonus should be considered carefully.
det.treatment: Injecting botulinum toxin into the jerking muscles usually helps most. Clonazepam, levetiracetam or carbamazepine help some patients. Treat any compressive or structural cause, such as microvascular decompression for hemifacial spasm.
det.prognosis: Often persistent but usually manageable with botulinum toxin.
pearls: Jerks restricted to one nerve territory that continue in sleep suggest a peripheral generator.
Hemifacial spasm is classed by some as peripheral myoclonus.
Botulinum toxin is the treatment of choice.

name: Peripheral neuropathy
formal: Dysfunction of peripheral nerves causing distal sensory loss, weakness and areflexia, from diabetes, alcohol, drugs, vitamin deficiency, immune or hereditary causes.
simple: Damage to nerves in the hands and feet, causing numbness, tingling, pain or weakness.
more: Disorders of peripheral nerves producing sensory loss, weakness and autonomic features; axonal or demyelinating, with causes such as diabetes, toxins, immune and inherited disease.

feat: Glove-and-stocking numbness, tingling or burning that starts in the toes
Distal weakness (foot drop, poor toe walking) and loss of ankle jerks

Patterns matter: length-dependent, multifocal (mononeuritis multiplex), proximal plus distal, or sensory ganglionopathy

Nerve conduction and EMG: axonal versus demyelinating, symmetric versus multifocal

case.who: 61-year-old woman from Ubon Ratchathani with type 2 diabetes
case.story: Burning feet at night for a year, now numb to the ankles; recently stepped on a nail without noticing.
case.exam: Absent ankle reflexes, reduced pinprick and vibration to mid-shin, normal strength, healed ulcer on right sole.
case.tests: HbA1c 9.2%; B12 low-normal with raised methylmalonic acid (on metformin for 10 years); NCS shows length-dependent axonal sensory neuropathy.
case.q: What two causes may be contributing, and what are the key management steps?
case.a: Diabetic neuropathy plus metformin-associated B12 deficiency; improve glycaemic control, replace B12, treat pain (duloxetine, pregabalin or amitriptyline) and arrange foot care.

det.patho: Neuropathy arises from damage to the axon, the myelin sheath, or the sensory cell bodies. Length-dependent axonal degeneration is most common, because the longest axons are most vulnerable to metabolic and toxic stress. Demyelinating neuropathies are often immune (GBS, CIDP) or inherited (CMT1). Vasculitis damages nerves in a patchy, asymmetric way.
det.clinical: Describe the neuropathy by fibre type (motor, sensory, autonomic, small or large), distribution, symmetry and tempo. Common causes include diabetes, alcohol, B12 deficiency, chemotherapy and other drugs, kidney failure, hypothyroidism, HIV, leprosy (important in Thailand), paraproteins and hereditary disease. Red flags are rapid progression, asymmetry, prominent weakness, early arm involvement, autonomic failure and a family history.
det.diagnosis: A focused history (drugs, alcohol, toxins, family) and examination define the pattern. Basic blood tests identify the cause in many cases, and electrodiagnosis separates axonal from demyelinating and multifocal disease. Further tests follow the pattern rather than a blanket panel. Up to a quarter of chronic axonal neuropathies in older adults remain idiopathic after full work-up.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: glucose control, stopping alcohol or neurotoxic drugs, vitamin replacement, immunotherapy for immune neuropathies. Neuropathic pain responds to duloxetine, pregabalin or gabapentin, or tricyclics, with topical options for focal pain. Foot care, orthoses, physiotherapy and fall prevention reduce complications. Acute progressive weakness needs admission and monitoring of respiratory function.
det.prognosis: Variable; slowly progressive axonal neuropathies rarely cause severe disability, whereas treatable immune neuropathies improve if recognised early.
pearls: Always check B12 in diabetic patients on long-term metformin.
Asymmetric painful neuropathy evolving over weeks: think vasculitis and act quickly.
Leprosy should be considered in Thailand when there are thickened nerves and skin patches.
det.thd: ปลายประสาทอักเสบหรือเสื่อม (peripheral neuropathy) ทำให้ชาแบบถุงมือถุงเท้า ปวดแสบร้อน อ่อนแรงปลายเท้า และ reflex ข้อเท้าหาย สาเหตุพบบ่อยคือเบาหวาน แอลกอฮอล์ ขาดวิตามิน B12 ยา และโรคภูมิคุ้มกัน วินิจฉัยจากรูปแบบอาการ เลือดพื้นฐาน และ NCS รักษาตามสาเหตุ ร่วมกับยาลดปวดประสาท และการดูแลเท้าเพื่อป้องกันแผล

name: Peripheral vertigo
formal: Vestibular spinning sensation from labyrinth or vestibular nerve disease such as BPPV, neuritis or Menière disease, with horizontal-torsional nystagmus suppressed by fixation.

case.who: 48-year-old woman presenting to an emergency department in Hat Yai
case.story: Woke with constant spinning and vomiting two days after a cold; worse with head movement but present at rest.
case.exam: Left-beating horizontal-torsional nystagmus suppressed by fixation, abnormal head impulse to the right, no skew, hearing normal, walks with help but no limb ataxia.
case.tests: Audiogram normal; not imaged as HINTS is peripheral.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what treatment speeds recovery?
case.a: Right vestibular neuritis; short-term antiemetics, early vestibular rehabilitation and possibly a brief corticosteroid course.

det.patho: Peripheral vertigo arises when signals from the semicircular canals or vestibular nerve become asymmetric. Causes include canalith debris (BPPV), viral or inflammatory nerve injury (neuritis), endolymphatic hydrops (Menière), labyrinthitis, perilymph fistula and ototoxicity. The brain interprets the imbalance as rotation and gradually compensates.
det.clinical: The timing pattern points to the cause: seconds with head position change in BPPV, minutes to hours with fluctuating hearing and aural fullness in Menière, and a single prolonged attack in neuritis. Peripheral nystagmus is unidirectional, mainly horizontal-torsional, and suppressed by fixation. Patients can usually walk with some veering.
det.diagnosis: In acute continuous vertigo, a peripheral HINTS pattern by a trained examiner is more sensitive than early MRI for excluding stroke. Positional testing identifies BPPV. Audiometry, vHIT, calorics and VEMPs refine the diagnosis; imaging is needed when central features or atypical findings exist.
det.treatment: BPPV responds to repositioning manoeuvres. Vestibular neuritis is treated with short-term vestibular suppressants, early rehabilitation and sometimes steroids. Menière disease is managed with salt moderation, betahistine (evidence limited), intratympanic steroids or gentamicin for refractory cases. Avoid prolonged vestibular suppressants which slow compensation.
det.prognosis: Generally good; most patients compensate within weeks, though recurrences occur in BPPV and Menière.
pearls: Abnormal head impulse is reassuring in acute vertigo; a normal one is worrying.
Direction-changing nystagmus or skew deviation means central until proven otherwise.
Stop vestibular sedatives after a few days to allow compensation.

name: Peritonitis
formal: Inflammation of the peritoneum, usually bacterial infection; neurologically relevant as shunt infection and abdominal complication of ventriculoperitoneal shunts.
simple: Infection or inflammation of the lining of the abdomen, causing severe belly pain and fever.
more: Diagnose from abdominal tenderness, fever and leucocytosis; ascitic neutrophils over 250 per mm3 define spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and coagulase-negative staphylococci typify shunt infection. Treat with antibiotics and shunt externalisation.
th: การอักเสบของเยื่อบุช่องท้อง ส่วนใหญ่จากการติดเชื้อแบคทีเรีย ไม่ใช่โรคทางระบบประสาท แต่เกี่ยวข้องเพราะเป็นภาวะแทรกซ้อนหรือสาเหตุของการติดเชื้อสาย VP shunt
tempoNote: Acute over hours to days; shunt-related infection may smoulder over weeks
feat: Not a neurological disease: abdominal pain, tenderness, guarding, fever
In VP shunt patients: abdominal pain, pseudocyst or ascites plus shunt malfunction (headache, vomiting, drowsiness)
Bowel perforation by the distal catheter can seed the shunt with gut organisms
Shunt infection organisms: skin flora (coagulase-negative staphylococci, Cutibacterium) or gram-negatives after perforation
inv: Ultrasound or CT abdomen for pseudocyst, collection or catheter perforation
Shunt tap or CSF sample for cell count, Gram stain and culture
CT or MRI brain for ventricular size; blood cultures

case.who: 6-year-old girl from Nakhon Phanom with a VP shunt for post-meningitic hydrocephalus
case.story: Four days of fever, abdominal pain and vomiting; today she is drowsy and complains of headache.
case.exam: Tender distended abdomen, GCS 13, no focal signs.
case.tests: Ultrasound shows an abdominal CSF pseudocyst; shunt tap grows Staphylococcus epidermidis; CT shows enlarged ventricles.
case.q: What is the management principle?
case.a: Shunt infection with peritonitis/pseudocyst: externalise or remove the shunt (EVD), give intravenous antibiotics, then reinsert once CSF is sterile.

det.patho: Peritonitis is inflammation of the peritoneal lining, usually from infection after perforation, spontaneous seeding of ascites in cirrhosis, or peritoneal dialysis. In neurosurgical patients the distal end of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt links the peritoneum to the CSF, so infection can spread in either direction. Bacteria colonising the catheter form biofilm that antibiotics alone rarely clear.
det.clinical: This is a general surgical and medical condition rather than a neurological disease. In shunted patients, abdominal pain, distension, pseudocyst formation or fever may accompany or precede signs of raised intracranial pressure from shunt failure. Gram-negative shunt infection should prompt a search for bowel perforation by the catheter.
det.diagnosis: Abdominal imaging identifies collections, pseudocysts and catheter position. CSF from the shunt reservoir or ventricles is essential for culture. In cirrhotic ascites, a neutrophil count above 250 cells/mm3 indicates spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Brain imaging assesses ventricular size.
det.treatment: Systemic peritonitis is managed with antibiotics and surgical source control. Shunt-related infection generally needs removal or externalisation of the shunt, external ventricular drainage, and intravenous (sometimes intraventricular) antibiotics, followed by a new shunt once cultures clear. Involve both neurosurgery and general surgery.
det.prognosis: Most shunt infections are cured with hardware removal and antibiotics, but repeated infections worsen neurodevelopmental outcome.
pearls: Abdominal pain plus headache in a shunted child: think shunt infection or pseudocyst.
Gram-negative organisms in shunt CSF suggest bowel perforation.
Infected shunt hardware nearly always has to come out.
det.thd: Peritonitis คือการอักเสบของเยื่อบุช่องท้อง ไม่ใช่โรคทางระบบประสาทโดยตรง แต่เกี่ยวข้องในผู้ป่วยที่ใส่ VP shunt เพราะการติดเชื้อสามารถลามระหว่างช่องท้องและน้ำไขสันหลังได้ ผู้ป่วยอาจปวดท้อง มีไข้ ร่วมกับปวดศีรษะ อาเจียน ซึมจาก shunt ทำงานผิดปกติ ต้องตรวจภาพช่องท้องและเพาะเชื้อน้ำไขสันหลัง การรักษาคือถอดหรือเปลี่ยน shunt เป็น EVD และให้ยาปฏิชีวนะทางหลอดเลือด

Shunt blockage without infection; afebrile, normal CSF cells

name: Peroneal neuropathies
formal: Common peroneal nerve injury at the fibular neck, causing foot drop and sensory loss over the dorsum of foot, from compression, trauma or weight loss.
simple: Damage to a nerve near the knee causing a dropped foot and numbness on the top of the foot.
th: เส้นประสาท peroneal ถูกกดที่หัวกระดูกน่อง — เท้าตก ชาหลังเท้า แต่การบิดเท้าเข้า (inversion) ยังดี
feat: Foot drop with weak dorsiflexion and eversion; inversion and plantar flexion preserved
Numbness of lateral shin and dorsum of foot
Triggers: crossing legs, weight loss, prolonged squatting, casts, bed rest, knee surgery
inv: NCS/EMG: conduction block or axon loss at the fibular head; short head of biceps femoris normal
Ultrasound/MRI if no compression history (ganglion cyst)

case.story: After losing 15 kg and sitting cross-legged for hours at a meditation retreat, her right foot slaps when she walks.
case.exam: Weak ankle dorsiflexion and eversion, normal inversion, numb dorsum of foot, normal ankle jerk.
case.tests: Peroneal motor conduction block across the fibular head; normal L5 paraspinals.
case.q: Which muscle test separates this from an L5 radiculopathy?
case.a: Ankle inversion (tibialis posterior, tibial nerve, L5) — preserved in peroneal neuropathy, weak in L5 radiculopathy.

read.where: 5. CASE PRESENTATIONS ILLUSTRATING THE DIAGNOSTIC METHOD

qx.stem: A 40-year-old man from Kanchanaburi has a left foot drop that began after months of squatting on rubber-plantation work. Dorsiflexion and eversion are weak, and he has numbness on the dorsum of the foot. You need to separate a fibular head lesion from an L5 radiculopathy.
qx.q: Which finding favours a lesion at the fibular head?
opts: Fibrillations in the L5 paraspinal muscles and gluteus medius
A normal superficial peroneal response with abnormal tibialis posterior EMG
Needle changes in tibialis posterior together with the biceps femoris short head
Local velocity drop or block at the fibular head, while tibialis posterior and paraspinal muscles are normal
Reduced sural and tibial responses with absent ankle jerks
qx.why: A fibular head neuropathy affects the common peroneal fibres below the knee, so tibialis posterior (tibial, L5) and gluteus medius are spared, the biceps femoris short head is spared when the lesion is below the branch, and nerve conduction shows focal slowing or block across the fibular head. Abnormalities in tibialis posterior, gluteal muscles or paraspinals indicate an L5 root or sciatic lesion, and sural or tibial involvement points to a polyneuropathy or more proximal lesion.

files.chapter: 5. CASE PRESENTATIONS ILLUSTRATING THE DIAGNOSTIC METHOD

ddx.pt: Back pain, weak inversion and hip abduction, abnormal paraspinal EMG
Recurrent palsies, family history, PMP22 deletion
Bilateral, symmetric, pes cavus, lifelong

aN: peroneal neuropathy | fibular neuropathy | common peroneal palsy | foot drop at fibular head | crossed leg palsy

det.patho: The common peroneal (fibular) nerve winds superficially around the fibular neck, where it is easily compressed or stretched. Weight loss removes the protective fat pad, and habitual leg crossing, squatting, kneeling, tight casts or prolonged immobility compress the nerve. The deep branch tends to be more affected than the superficial branch. Space-occupying lesions such as intraneural ganglion cysts arise from the superior tibiofibular joint.
det.clinical: Foot drop develops suddenly or over days, causing a steppage or slapping gait and tripping. Ankle dorsiflexion, toe extension and eversion are weak, whereas inversion, plantar flexion and the ankle jerk are spared. Sensory loss involves the outer shin and the top of the foot, and a Tinel sign may be present at the fibular neck. Pain is uncommon with compression; marked pain should raise concern for ganglion cyst, tumour or vasculitis.
det.diagnosis: Examine ankle inversion and hip abduction carefully: weakness of either points to L5 radiculopathy or sciatic or plexus lesions. NCS show conduction block or slowing across the fibular head, or reduced amplitudes with axon loss. EMG of short head of biceps femoris (sciatic innervated) is normal in peroneal neuropathy and abnormal in sciatic lesions, and paraspinals are normal. Imaging with ultrasound or MRI is indicated without a clear compressive cause, or when progressive.
det.treatment: Remove the cause: stop leg crossing and squatting, pad the knee, adjust casts, and address weight loss. An ankle-foot orthosis improves gait and prevents falls during recovery, with physiotherapy to avoid Achilles contracture. Surgery is reserved for ganglion cysts, masses, lacerations or lack of recovery after several months; tendon transfer may help in permanent foot drop.
det.prognosis: Compressive lesions with predominant conduction block usually recover well within weeks to months. Severe axonal injury recovers slowly and incompletely.
pearls: Preserved inversion separates peroneal palsy from L5 radiculopathy.
Short head of biceps femoris on EMG separates peroneal from sciatic lesions.
Recurrent or bilateral pressure palsies: test for HNPP.
det.thd: Peroneal neuropathy เกิดจากเส้นประสาทถูกกดที่หัวกระดูกน่อง มักหลังน้ำหนักลด นั่งไขว่ห้าง นั่งยอง ๆ หรือใส่เฝือก ทำให้เท้าตก กระดกเท้าและบิดเท้าออกไม่ได้ แต่บิดเท้าเข้า (inversion) ปกติ และ ankle jerk ปกติ ชาหลังเท้าและหน้าแข้งด้านนอก NCS พบ conduction block ที่หัวกระดูกน่อง รักษาด้วยเลี่ยงการกดทับ ใส่ AFO และส่วนใหญ่ฟื้นตัวดี ถ้าไม่มีสาเหตุกดทับชัดให้ทำ ultrasound/MRI หา ganglion cyst

name: Peroxisomal disorders
formal: Inherited metabolic diseases with impaired peroxisome function, such as X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy and Zellweger spectrum, with very-long-chain fatty acid elevation.
simple: Inherited diseases where small cell structures cannot break down certain fats, damaging the brain and nerves.
more: Diagnose by raised plasma very long chain fatty acids, phytanic and pristanic acids, plasmalogens and bile acid intermediates, with PEX or ABCD1 gene testing. Treatment is supportive; Refsum responds to diet and X-ALD to transplantation.
th: กลุ่มโรคเมตาบอลิกทางพันธุกรรมที่ peroxisome ทำงานผิดปกติ เช่น X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, Zellweger spectrum และ Refsum มีกรดไขมันสายยาวมาก (VLCFA) สูง
tempoNote: Neonatal onset in Zellweger spectrum, childhood or adult in X-ALD and Refsum disease; most progress over years
feat: Zellweger spectrum (PEX genes): neonatal hypotonia, seizures, dysmorphic face, liver disease, retinal dystrophy and deafness; milder patients survive to childhood or beyond
X-linked ALD: cerebral demyelination in boys aged 4–10, adrenomyeloneuropathy in men, and adrenal insufficiency; some female carriers develop myelopathy
Refsum disease: retinitis pigmentosa, anosmia, polyneuropathy, ataxia, deafness and ichthyosis from phytanic acid accumulation
Rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata: short proximal limbs, cataracts and severe developmental delay (PEX7)
Mostly autosomal recessive; ABCD1 (X-ALD) is X-linked
inv: Plasma very long-chain fatty acids (C26:0, C26:1 and ratios C24/C22, C26/C22); phytanic and pristanic acid; red cell plasmalogens
Gene panel (PEX genes, ABCD1, PHYH, PEX7); newborn screening for X-ALD in several countries
MRI brain with Loes score in X-ALD (parieto-occipital pattern with leading-edge enhancement); MRI spine; adrenal function (ACTH, cortisol)
Ophthalmology, audiology and liver function tests

case.story: Over three months his schoolwork deteriorated, he became inattentive, and his vision seemed worse. He started to fall while running. His maternal uncle died young with an undiagnosed brain illness. His skin looks darker than before.
case.exam: Poor visual attention, mild spastic gait, brisk reflexes, increased skin pigmentation.
case.tests: MRI shows symmetric parieto-occipital white-matter hyperintensity with peripheral contrast enhancement; plasma C26:0 raised; ACTH high and cortisol low; ABCD1 pathogenic variant.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what time-sensitive treatments exist?
case.a: Childhood cerebral X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy. Replace adrenal steroid and urgently assess for haematopoietic stem cell transplantation or gene therapy at an early MRI stage; screen at-risk male relatives.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Peroxisomal Disorders
Section II: Epidemiology, Etiology, and Diagnosis

det.patho: Peroxisomes are small organelles that carry out degradation of the longest fatty acid chains (VLCFA), synthesis of plasmalogens and bile acids, and alpha-oxidation of phytanic acid. Biogenesis disorders (the Zellweger spectrum, from PEX gene variants) lose the organelle itself, whereas single-enzyme or transporter defects such as ABCD1-related X-ALD or PHYH-related Refsum disease block only one pathway. Accumulating toxic lipids and loss of ether lipids damage myelin, adrenal cortex, retina and nerve.
det.clinical: Severe Zellweger spectrum babies are hypotonic, dysmorphic, seizure-prone and usually die in infancy, while intermediate phenotypes survive with developmental delay, deafness, retinopathy and liver disease. X-ALD has three common forms: childhood cerebral disease with rapid decline, adrenomyeloneuropathy with progressive spastic paraparesis in adult men, and Addison disease alone. Refsum disease appears in adolescence or adulthood with night blindness, anosmia, neuropathy and cerebellar signs.
det.diagnosis: Measure plasma VLCFA first for Zellweger spectrum and X-ALD, and phytanic acid for Refsum disease; plasmalogens identify rhizomelic disease. Genetic testing confirms and enables family screening and prenatal testing. MRI pattern and Loes score stage cerebral X-ALD. Check cortisol and ACTH in every male with elevated VLCFA, since adrenal failure can precede neurological symptoms.
det.treatment: No cure exists for most; treatment is targeted. In X-ALD: adrenal hormone replacement, regular MRI surveillance of asymptomatic boys, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation or autologous gene therapy for early cerebral disease (Loes score low, normal or mild function). In Refsum disease: phytanic acid-restricted diet and plasma exchange for acute crises. Zellweger spectrum care is symptomatic, with cholic acid for bile acid deficiency in some centres, seizure control, hearing aids and liver monitoring. Lorenzo's oil is not recommended for established disease.
det.prognosis: Severe Zellweger spectrum disease is fatal within the first year; cerebral X-ALD without early transplantation leads to rapid deterioration; Refsum disease responds to diet if started early.
pearls: A boy with school decline and adrenal insufficiency needs VLCFA; screen brothers and maternal relatives.
Check adrenal function in every male with raised VLCFA.
Transplantation works only if done at an early MRI stage, so surveillance of at-risk boys matters.
det.thd: Peroxisomal disorders คือกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่ peroxisome ทำงานผิดปกติ ทำให้กรดไขมันสายยาว (VLCFA) หรือ phytanic acid สะสมและทำลาย myelin ต่อมหมวกไต จอตา และเส้นประสาท ตัวอย่างได้แก่ Zellweger spectrum ในทารก X-ALD ที่พบในเด็กชายและชายผู้ใหญ่ และ Refsum disease วินิจฉัยด้วยการวัด VLCFA phytanic acid ตรวจ MRI และตรวจยีน ABCD1 หรือ PEX การรักษา X-ALD ต้องให้ฮอร์โมนต่อมหมวกไตและพิจารณาปลูกถ่ายเซลล์ต้นกำเนิดเมื่อพบโรคระยะแรก ส่วน Refsum ควบคุมอาหารและทำ plasma exchange

name: Perry syndrome
formal: Autosomal dominant DCTN1-related parkinsonism with depression, weight loss and central hypoventilation, with TDP-43 pathology.
simple: A rare inherited illness with Parkinson-like symptoms, depression, weight loss and breathing problems.
th: โรคพาร์กินโซนิซึมกรรมพันธุ์ชนิด autosomal dominant จากยีน DCTN1 มีอาการซึมเศร้า น้ำหนักลด และหายใจไม่พอจากสมองส่วนกลาง พยาธิสภาพเป็น TDP-43
tempoNote: Onset in the 40s–50s with progression over about 5 years
feat: Levodopa-responsive or partly responsive parkinsonism of early-middle adult onset
Depression, apathy, sometimes suicidality, often preceding motor signs
Unexplained weight loss
Central hypoventilation, worse in sleep, often the cause of death
Autosomal dominant family history; DCTN1 (dynactin) variants
inv: Polysomnography and arterial or transcutaneous CO2 for hypoventilation
DCTN1 genetic testing
DaT-SPECT shows presynaptic dopaminergic loss; MRI largely normal

case.story: Two years of depression and 10 kg weight loss, then slowness and stiffness; his mother died at 52 with 'Parkinson' and breathing failure.
case.exam: Bradykinesia, rigidity, hypomimia, shallow breathing at rest.
case.tests: Overnight study shows sleep hypoventilation with rising CO2; DCTN1 pathogenic variant.
case.q: Which complication must be addressed to prolong life?
case.a: Central hypoventilation of Perry syndrome; non-invasive ventilation (or tracheostomy with ventilation).

read.where: Etiology and pathogenesis of Parkinson disease

det.patho: Perry syndrome is caused by missense variants in DCTN1, which encodes the p150 subunit of dynactin, a motor-protein complex needed for retrograde axonal transport. Pathology shows severe nigral neuron loss and loss of serotonergic neurons in the medullary raphe and respiratory centres, with TDP-43 inclusions rather than Lewy bodies. Fewer than a few hundred cases are reported worldwide.
det.clinical: Psychiatric symptoms and weight loss typically come first, followed by parkinsonism around the fifth decade. Hypoventilation, initially nocturnal, appears later and causes sudden respiratory failure. Some patients also show supranuclear gaze palsy or frontotemporal features. Disease duration from onset to death is usually around five years.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in young-onset familial parkinsonism with depression, weight loss and hypoventilation. Confirm with DCTN1 testing. Sleep studies and blood gases are needed to detect respiratory involvement before crisis.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying treatment is available. Levodopa may help motor symptoms modestly. Non-invasive ventilation or ventilation via tracheostomy can prevent death from respiratory failure. Antidepressants, nutritional support and genetic counselling are important.
det.prognosis: Poor; median survival about five years from onset without ventilatory support.
pearls: Parkinsonism + depression + weight loss + hypoventilation = Perry syndrome.
Pathology is TDP-43, not synuclein.
Screen breathing at night; most patients die from hypoventilation.
det.thd: Perry syndrome เป็นโรคพาร์กินโซนิซึมทางพันธุกรรมชนิด autosomal dominant จากยีน DCTN1 พบน้อยมาก อาการเริ่มด้วยซึมเศร้าและน้ำหนักลด ต่อมามีพาร์กินโซนิซึม และหายใจไม่พอจากสมองส่วนกลางโดยเฉพาะขณะหลับ พยาธิสภาพเป็น TDP-43 ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง ให้ levodopa ยาต้านเศร้า และช่วยหายใจแบบ NIV

name: Persistent akathisia
formal: Chronic restlessness with inner urge to move persisting after dopamine blocker withdrawal; part of tardive syndromes.
simple: A lasting feeling of restlessness and need to move, remaining after stopping a medicine.
th: อาการกระสับกระส่ายนั่งไม่ติดที่เป็นนานเกิน 3–6 เดือนหรือยังคงอยู่หลังหยุดยาต้าน dopamine เป็นส่วนหนึ่งของ tardive syndromes
tempoNote: Lasts beyond several months of treatment or persists for months after the dopamine blocker is stopped
feat: Long-standing restlessness, often with less subjective distress than acute akathisia
Coexists with tardive dyskinesia or dystonia in many patients
May worsen after dose reduction or withdrawal (withdrawal-emergent form)
Repetitive movements such as leg crossing, marching, rocking or moaning
Usually after prolonged exposure to antipsychotics or metoclopramide
inv: Full drug history including antiemetics such as metoclopramide and prochlorperazine
Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale and Barnes scale
Iron studies, TSH and renal function to exclude restless legs mimics

case.who: 63-year-old female market vendor from Nakhon Ratchasima
case.story: Took metoclopramide daily for 'gastritis' for three years; stopped eight months ago. Still feels compelled to keep moving, rocks while sitting, and has lip smacking.
case.exam: Constant trunk rocking, orobuccolingual dyskinesia, no parkinsonism.
case.tests: Ferritin 120 ng/mL, TSH normal, creatinine normal.
case.q: What syndrome is this and which drug class can help?
case.a: Persistent (tardive) akathisia with tardive dyskinesia; a VMAT2 inhibitor may be tried alongside avoidance of further dopamine blockers.

read.where: Chapter 9 Movement Disorders — Movement Disorders Associated with Dopamine Receptor Blockade or Dopamine Depletion
17 - The tardive syndromes: Phenomenology, concepts on pathophysiology and treatment, and other neuroleptic-­induced syndromes

det.patho: Long-term dopamine receptor blockade is thought to cause maladaptive receptor supersensitivity and changes in striatal and cortical circuits, similar to tardive dyskinesia. Withdrawal unmasks or aggravates the problem. Risk factors include older age, female sex, longer exposure and mood disorders.
det.clinical: Terminology varies: chronic akathisia continues during treatment; tardive akathisia begins late or after stopping; withdrawal akathisia appears on discontinuation and may be transient. Patients may habituate to the inner feeling while the motor component persists. Frequent overlap with orofacial dyskinesia helps diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, relying on exposure history and phenomenology. Exclude restless legs, agitation from mood or anxiety disorders, and other hyperkinetic disorders. Imaging is not needed unless there are atypical focal signs.
det.treatment: Avoid further dopamine antagonists when possible. VMAT2 inhibitors (tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine, valbenazine) help tardive syndromes and may ease akathisia. Propranolol, mirtazapine, benzodiazepines, clonazepam or opioids have been tried with variable benefit. If an antipsychotic is essential, clozapine or quetiapine carry lower risk.
det.prognosis: Often long-lasting; slow improvement over years is possible after the offending drug is withdrawn.
pearls: Metoclopramide is a common, avoidable cause in general practice.
Withdrawal can transiently worsen tardive symptoms; do not restart the blocker reflexively.
Look for tardive dyskinesia in anyone with chronic akathisia.
det.thd: Persistent akathisia คืออาการกระสับกระส่ายที่เป็นเรื้อรังหลายเดือนหรือยังอยู่หลังหยุดยาต้าน dopamine เช่น antipsychotic หรือ metoclopramide จัดอยู่ใน tardive syndromes มักพบร่วมกับ tardive dyskinesia การวินิจฉัยใช้ประวัติยาและลักษณะอาการ การรักษาคือเลี่ยงยาที่เป็นสาเหตุ อาจใช้ VMAT2 inhibitor, propranolol, mirtazapine หรือ benzodiazepine

name: Personality disorder
formal: Enduring maladaptive pattern of inner experience and behaviour present from adolescence or early adulthood, causing distress or impairment; differentiate from frontal lobe personality change.
simple: A lifelong pattern of thinking and behaving that is very different from what is expected and causes difficulties in life and relationships.
th: รูปแบบความคิด อารมณ์ และพฤติกรรมที่ผิดปกติอย่างถาวรตั้งแต่วัยรุ่นหรือต้นวัยผู้ใหญ่ ต้องแยกจากการเปลี่ยนบุคลิกภาพจากโรคสมอง
tempoNote: Present since adolescence or early adulthood and stable over years; new personality change in later life suggests organic disease
feat: Psychiatric, not a primary neurological disease; matters to neurologists as a differential of personality change
Enduring pattern of problems in self-identity, emotion regulation and relationships causing distress or impairment
ICD-11 grades severity (mild, moderate, severe) with trait domains such as negative affectivity, dissociality and disinhibition
Onset in adolescence or early adulthood, consistent across settings
Late-onset personality change suggests frontal lesions, bvFTD, Huntington disease, epilepsy or brain injury
inv: Detailed collateral history about premorbid personality
Neurological examination and cognitive testing; MRI if change is recent or late in life
Psychiatric assessment for coexisting mood, substance use or trauma-related disorders

case.who: 47-year-old businessman from Bangkok referred by a psychiatrist
case.story: Over the past two years he has become rude, impulsive, overspends and eats sweets compulsively; his wife says he was previously polite and careful.
case.exam: Disinhibited, little insight, frontal release signs; MoCA 24 with poor verbal fluency.
case.tests: MRI shows bilateral frontal and anterior temporal atrophy; FDG-PET shows frontal hypometabolism.
case.q: Is this a personality disorder?
case.a: No — a new personality change in mid-life suggests behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia; personality disorders start early and remain stable.

read.where: Chapter 30 Neuropsychiatry — Personality Disorder and Personality Change

det.patho: Personality disorders arise from an interaction of heritable temperament, early adversity and attachment difficulties. Neuroimaging studies report altered fronto-limbic connectivity in some types, but there is no lesion-based mechanism. They are psychiatric diagnoses and are listed here chiefly to help separate them from organic personality change.
det.clinical: ICD-11 now describes a single personality disorder diagnosis graded by severity, with optional trait domains and a borderline pattern specifier. Patients show long-standing difficulties with sense of self, emotional control and relationships. In neurology clinics, personality disorder may coexist with functional neurological disorder, chronic pain or non-epileptic seizures. The key neurological task is to recognise when apparent personality problems are new and caused by brain disease.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is made by psychiatric assessment of long-term patterns, supported by informants. Red flags for organic personality change include onset after age 40, a clear change from previous character, cognitive decline, neurological signs, seizures or a family history of neurodegeneration. MRI, cognitive testing and sometimes FDG-PET or genetic testing are then appropriate.
det.treatment: Structured psychological therapies such as dialectical behaviour therapy and mentalisation-based therapy are the main treatments, particularly for the borderline pattern. Medication treats coexisting conditions rather than the disorder itself. In neurology settings, clear communication, consistent boundaries and coordinated care with psychiatry improve outcomes.
det.prognosis: Many patients improve over time, especially with therapy, although interpersonal difficulties may persist.
pearls: Personality disorders begin early; a new personality change in mid-life is organic until proved otherwise.
Collateral history about premorbid personality is the single most useful step.
Coexisting personality disorder does not exclude genuine neurological disease.
det.thd: Personality disorder เป็นโรคทางจิตเวช มีรูปแบบความคิด อารมณ์ และความสัมพันธ์ที่ผิดปกติอย่างต่อเนื่องตั้งแต่วัยรุ่น ไม่ใช่โรคทางระบบประสาทโดยตรง ประเด็นสำคัญสำหรับแพทย์ระบบประสาทคือการแยกจากการเปลี่ยนบุคลิกภาพที่เพิ่งเกิดในวัยกลางคน ซึ่งอาจเป็น bvFTD หรือรอยโรคสมองส่วนหน้า ควรซักประวัติจากญาติ ตรวจความจำ และส่ง MRI เมื่อมีข้อสงสัย การรักษาหลักคือจิตบำบัดร่วมกับจิตแพทย์

name: Phaeochromocytoma
formal: Catecholamine-secreting tumour of adrenal medulla causing episodic headache, sweating, palpitations and hypertension; associated with VHL, MEN2 and NF1.
simple: A rare tumour of the adrenal gland releasing adrenaline-like hormones, causing pounding headaches, sweating and high blood pressure.
th: เนื้องอกของต่อมหมวกไตชั้นในที่หลั่ง catecholamine ทำให้ปวดศีรษะเป็นพัก เหงื่อออก ใจสั่น และความดันสูง สัมพันธ์กับ VHL, MEN2 และ NF1
tempoNote: Paroxysms last minutes to an hour, occurring daily to monthly; may be triggered by drugs or pressure on the abdomen
feat: Classic triad: paroxysmal headache, sweating and palpitations
Sustained or paroxysmal hypertension; orthostatic drop between attacks
Pallor, tremor, anxiety and chest or abdominal pain during attacks
Hypertensive crisis can cause PRES, stroke, RCVS or seizures
Hereditary in about one third: VHL, MEN2, NF1, SDHx genes
inv: Plasma free or 24-hour urine fractionated metanephrines
CT or MRI of adrenals; functional imaging (Ga-68 DOTATATE PET) for multifocal disease
Germline genetic testing for all patients

case.story: Attacks of pounding headache, drenching sweat and racing heart lasting 20 minutes, several times a week; BP was 220/120 during one attack.
case.exam: Between attacks BP 150/95, otherwise normal; several café-au-lait macules noted.
case.tests: Plasma normetanephrine markedly elevated; CT shows a 4 cm left adrenal mass.
case.q: What must be given before surgery?
case.a: Alpha-blockade (e.g. doxazosin or phenoxybenzamine) for 1–2 weeks with volume expansion, adding beta-blockade only after alpha-blockade.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Adrenal Disorders
Chapter 53: Headache attributed to disorders of homeostasis

det.patho: Chromaffin cell tumours of the adrenal medulla (or extra-adrenal paragangliomas) release noradrenaline, adrenaline or dopamine episodically or continuously. Germline mutations in genes including VHL, RET, NF1, SDHB/D and others are found in roughly 30–40%. SDHB-related tumours have the highest malignant potential.
det.clinical: Episodic headache is present in most patients and is typically bilateral, pounding and short-lived. Paroxysms can be provoked by exertion, pressure, anaesthesia, dopamine antagonists (metoclopramide), beta-blockers given alone, glucocorticoids and tricyclics. Neurological complications include PRES, intracerebral haemorrhage, RCVS and catecholamine cardiomyopathy. This is an endocrine tumour with neurological consequences.
det.diagnosis: Biochemical testing with plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrines is the first step; results several times above the upper limit are highly specific. Then image to localise and perform genetic testing. Avoid provoking drugs before alpha-blockade.
det.treatment: Preoperative alpha-blockade with fluid and salt loading, then laparoscopic adrenalectomy. Hypertensive crises are treated with phentolamine, nicardipine or nitroprusside. Metastatic disease may receive radionuclide therapy (MIBG or PRRT), chemotherapy or targeted agents. Lifelong biochemical follow-up is needed.
det.prognosis: Excellent after complete removal of a benign tumour; recurrence risk persists, especially in hereditary forms.
pearls: Headache + sweating + palpitations — check metanephrines.
Never start a beta-blocker alone in suspected phaeochromocytoma.
Metoclopramide can provoke a crisis.
det.thd: Phaeochromocytoma เป็นเนื้องอกของต่อมหมวกไตชั้นในที่หลั่ง catecholamine เป็นพัก ทำให้ปวดศีรษะตุบ ๆ เหงื่อออก ใจสั่น และความดันสูงเฉียบพลัน อาจทำให้เกิด PRES หรือเลือดออกในสมอง ส่วนหนึ่งเป็นกรรมพันธุ์ร่วมกับ VHL, MEN2, NF1 วินิจฉัยด้วยระดับ metanephrines และภาพถ่ายต่อมหมวกไต รักษาด้วยการให้ alpha-blocker ก่อนแล้วจึงผ่าตัด

name: Phenobarbitone chorea
formal: Chorea caused by phenobarbitone and other antiepileptic drugs, reversible on drug withdrawal.
simple: Jerky involuntary movements caused by the seizure medicine phenobarbitone.
th: chorea ที่เกิดจากยา phenobarbital หรือยากันชักอื่น พบบ่อยในเด็กหรือผู้ที่มีรอยโรคสมองเดิม และหายได้เมื่อลดหรือหยุดยา
tempoNote: Appears days to weeks after starting or increasing the drug, often with toxic levels; fades over days to weeks after withdrawal
feat: New flowing, irregular movements of face, limbs or trunk in a patient on phenobarbital or another antiseizure drug
More likely in children, the elderly, those with prior brain injury, or with polytherapy (phenytoin, valproate, lamotrigine, carbamazepine)
Often accompanied by sedation, ataxia or nystagmus when levels are high
No family history or progressive cognitive change
Resolves after dose reduction or stopping the culprit drug
inv: Serum antiseizure drug levels (phenobarbital, phenytoin) and liver function
Exclude metabolic causes: glucose, sodium, calcium, thyroid function
MRI if focal or atypical features suggest a structural basal ganglia lesion

case.story: Has had cerebral palsy with seizures since infancy; phenobarbital was doubled 3 weeks ago after a cluster of fits. Parents now see restless writhing of his arms and grimacing.
case.exam: Drowsy, generalised random choreic movements of limbs and face superimposed on known spastic diplegia; no fever or new focal deficit.
case.tests: Phenobarbital level well above the therapeutic range; glucose, electrolytes and calcium normal.
case.q: What is the most likely cause and the first step?
case.a: Drug-induced chorea from phenobarbital toxicity on a vulnerable brain; reduce the dose (or switch drug) and the movements should settle.

det.patho: The mechanism is not fully clear; antiseizure drugs may alter dopaminergic and GABAergic balance in the striatum, and the effect is unmasked mainly where basal ganglia are already damaged. High serum levels and combinations of drugs raise the risk. It is an idiosyncratic and dose-related phenomenon rather than a lasting toxic injury.
det.clinical: Chorea may be generalised or focal and may be accompanied by dystonia, orofacial dyskinesia or signs of drug intoxication. It is reported mainly in children with static encephalopathy, and in adults on phenytoin or polytherapy. The movements are not progressive and there is no dementia. Phenytoin and lamotrigine are more frequently implicated than phenobarbital in modern series.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis rests on a clear temporal link to starting or increasing an antiseizure drug and resolution after withdrawal. Measure drug levels, and rule out metabolic, autoimmune, vascular and genetic causes when the history is incomplete. Imaging is needed only if there are focal signs or if chorea persists after the drug is stopped.
det.treatment: Lower or stop the offending drug and substitute another antiseizure medication if seizure control requires it, avoiding abrupt barbiturate withdrawal that can provoke seizures. Symptomatic treatment is rarely necessary; a short course of a dopamine-depleting drug may be used for disabling movements. Document the reaction to avoid re-challenge.
det.prognosis: Usually fully reversible within days to weeks; persistent chorea should prompt a search for another cause.
pearls: In a child with cerebral palsy and new chorea, look at the drug chart and levels before ordering genetic tests.
Taper barbiturates gradually; sudden withdrawal can provoke status epilepticus.
Phenytoin is the antiseizure drug most often linked with chorea and orofacial dyskinesia.
det.thd: Phenobarbitone chorea คือ chorea ที่เกิดจากยากันชัก โดยเฉพาะเมื่อระดับยาสูงหรือใช้ยาหลายตัว มักพบในเด็กที่มีรอยโรคสมองเดิม เช่น cerebral palsy ผู้ป่วยมีการเคลื่อนไหวกระตุกไหลไม่เป็นจังหวะ ร่วมกับง่วงหรือเดินเซ ตรวจระดับยาและแยกสาเหตุทางเมตาบอลิก รักษาโดยค่อย ๆ ลดหรือเปลี่ยนยา อาการมักหายภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์

ddx.pt: Umbrella group; check other agents such as levodopa, stimulants, oral contraceptives and dopamine blockers on withdrawal
Child with recent streptococcal infection, carditis or emotional lability; ASO/anti-DNase B raised, no drug change
Non-progressive chorea from early childhood with family history (NKX2-1), not linked to medication

name: Phonic tics
formal: Vocal tics such as throat clearing, sniffing, grunts or coprolalia, simple or complex, features of Tourette syndrome.
simple: Repeated sounds made involuntarily, like throat clearing or grunts.
th: อาการ tic ที่เป็นเสียง เช่น กระแอม สูดจมูก ครางฮึ่ม หรือพูดคำหรือประโยคซ้ำ ๆ รวมถึงคำหยาบ เป็นองค์ประกอบสำคัญของ Tourette syndrome
tempoNote: Waxing and waning over months to years; individual tics are brief and intermittent
feat: Simple: sniffing, throat clearing, coughing, grunting, squeaks
Complex: words, phrases, echolalia, palilalia, coprolalia (minority of Tourette patients)
Preceded by an urge, briefly suppressible, followed by relief
Fluctuate in type and severity; worse with stress, fatigue or excitement
Motor plus phonic tics for over a year, starting before 18, defines Tourette syndrome
inv: Clinical diagnosis; screen for ADHD, OCD, anxiety and learning difficulties
ENT or allergy review only if sniffing or coughing is suspected to be organic
MRI or EEG only if atypical (adult onset, abnormal examination)

case.story: For a year he has repeatedly cleared his throat and sniffed despite allergy treatment; he also blinks hard and jerks his shoulder. Teachers complain he cannot sit still.
case.exam: Frequent throat clearing and eye blinking that he can hold back briefly; normal neurological examination.
case.tests: None required; ADHD rating scale positive.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the first-line approach?
case.a: Tourette syndrome with phonic and motor tics plus ADHD; education and CBIT (behavioural therapy), treating ADHD, and alpha-2 agonist if needed.

det.patho: Tics arise from dysfunction of cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loops, with imbalance between excitation and inhibition in the striatum and a likely role of dopamine. Phonic tics involve circuits that control laryngeal, respiratory and orofacial musculature. Genetics is complex and polygenic, and environmental factors modulate expression.
det.clinical: Phonic tics usually appear a year or two after motor tics, typically in childhood, and peak in early adolescence. Simple phonic tics are often mistaken for allergy or habitual cough. Coprolalia is socially prominent but occurs only in a minority. Many children improve markedly by adulthood.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, based on history and observation; tics may be suppressed in clinic, so home video helps. DSM-5 separates provisional tic disorder, chronic motor or vocal tic disorder, and Tourette syndrome. Look for comorbid ADHD and OCD, which often cause more impairment than the tics.
det.treatment: Education and reassurance suffice for mild tics. Comprehensive Behavioural Intervention for Tics (CBIT) is first-line therapy when treatment is needed. Medications include alpha-2 agonists (clonidine, guanfacine), aripiprazole and other antipsychotics, and topiramate; botulinum toxin may help focal vocal tics. Treat comorbidities in parallel.
det.prognosis: Most improve substantially by late adolescence; a minority have persistent tics into adulthood.
pearls: Persistent throat clearing or sniffing unresponsive to allergy treatment may be a phonic tic.
Premonitory urge and brief suppressibility are hallmarks of tics.
Coprolalia is not required for Tourette syndrome.
det.thd: Phonic tic คืออาการ tic ที่เป็นเสียง ชนิดง่ายเช่น กระแอม สูดจมูก ครางฮึ่ม ชนิดซับซ้อนเช่น พูดคำซ้ำ พูดเลียนแบบ หรือพูดคำหยาบ มีความรู้สึกอยากทำก่อนและกลั้นได้ชั่วคราว ถ้ามีร่วมกับ motor tic นานเกิน 1 ปีก่อนอายุ 18 ปีคือ Tourette syndrome ควรค้นหา ADHD และ OCD ร่วม การรักษาเริ่มจากให้ความรู้และ CBIT แล้วจึงพิจารณายา เช่น clonidine หรือ aripiprazole

Abrupt onset, often in adolescence or adulthood, complex and less suppressible
Rhythmic, patterned, no premonitory urge, common in autism

name: Phosphate disorders
formal: Hypophosphataemia or hyperphosphataemia, with hypophosphataemia causing proximal myopathy, rhabdomyolysis and respiratory weakness, especially in refeeding.
simple: Too low or too high phosphate in the blood, which can lead to weakness and breathing problems.
more: Treat cause and replace phosphate carefully; watch for refeeding syndrome.
th: ภาวะฟอสเฟตในเลือดต่ำหรือสูง โดยฟอสเฟตต่ำทำให้กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง กล้ามเนื้อสลาย และหายใจล้มเหลว โดยเฉพาะในกลุ่มอาการ refeeding
tempoNote: Develops over hours to days, especially in the first days of refeeding or in the ICU
feat: Severe hypophosphataemia (below about 0.3 mmol/L): proximal and respiratory muscle weakness
Rhabdomyolysis, failure to wean from ventilation, cardiac dysfunction
Encephalopathy, seizures, paraesthesia; rarely a GBS-like ascending weakness
Risk: refeeding after starvation, alcoholism, diabetic ketoacidosis treatment, critical illness
Hyperphosphataemia mainly acts via hypocalcaemia (tetany, seizures)
inv: Serum phosphate, calcium, magnesium, potassium; CK
Renal function; urinary phosphate if renal wasting suspected
Blood gases and respiratory monitoring in severe cases

case.who: 45-year-old man with alcohol use disorder admitted to a hospital in Nakhon Ratchasima
case.story: Malnourished on admission; three days after starting full enteral feeding he became too weak to lift his arms and breathless.
case.exam: Diffuse weakness, reduced reflexes, shallow breathing, confused.
case.tests: Phosphate 0.18 mmol/L, magnesium low, CK 6,000 U/L.
case.q: What caused his weakness and how should it be prevented?
case.a: Refeeding hypophosphataemia; start feeding slowly with thiamine and prophylactic phosphate, monitoring electrolytes daily.

det.patho: Phosphate is essential for ATP and 2,3-DPG. When severely depleted, muscle cells cannot sustain energy production and membrane integrity, leading to weakness and rhabdomyolysis, while reduced oxygen delivery and neuronal energy failure affect the brain. In refeeding, insulin drives phosphate into cells and body stores collapse rapidly.
det.clinical: Mild hypophosphataemia is usually asymptomatic. Severe deficiency causes proximal and respiratory weakness, failure to wean, cardiac failure, haemolysis, confusion and seizures. It often coexists with low potassium, magnesium and thiamine, which add to neurological effects. Hyperphosphataemia, mostly in kidney failure, causes symptoms through secondary hypocalcaemia and calcification.
det.diagnosis: Measure phosphate in at-risk patients, especially during the first days of refeeding. Look for coexisting electrolyte disturbances and thiamine deficiency. CK identifies rhabdomyolysis. Consider other causes of acute weakness if correction does not lead to improvement.
det.treatment: Replace phosphate orally for mild deficiency and intravenously for severe or symptomatic deficiency, monitoring calcium and renal function. Prevent refeeding syndrome by introducing calories gradually, giving thiamine before feeding, and checking electrolytes daily. Treat hyperphosphataemia with dietary restriction, binders and dialysis.
det.prognosis: Weakness usually resolves with correction; untreated severe cases can be fatal from respiratory or cardiac failure.
pearls: Weakness a few days into refeeding: check phosphate first.
Give thiamine before glucose in malnourished patients.
Low phosphate is a reversible cause of failure to wean.
det.thd: Phosphate disorders ที่สำคัญทางประสาทวิทยาคือฟอสเฟตในเลือดต่ำรุนแรง ทำให้กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง กล้ามเนื้อสลาย หายใจล้มเหลว และสับสน มักเกิดใน refeeding syndrome ผู้ติดสุรา และผู้ป่วยวิกฤต ป้องกันโดยเริ่มให้อาหารช้า ๆ ให้ thiamine ก่อน และตรวจเกลือแร่ทุกวัน รักษาด้วยการให้ฟอสเฟตทางปากหรือหลอดเลือดดำ

name: Phosphatidate phosphatase 1 deficiency
formal: LPIN1 deficiency causing recurrent childhood rhabdomyolysis triggered by fasting or infection, with myoglobinuria and raised CK.
simple: An inherited muscle condition in which illness or fasting causes muscle breakdown and dark urine.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมยีนด้อยจากยีน LPIN1 ทำให้เด็กเล็กเกิดกล้ามเนื้อสลายรุนแรงซ้ำ ๆ เมื่อมีไข้หรืออดอาหาร CK สูงมาก ปัสสาวะสีโค้ก
tempoNote: Attacks begin in infancy or early childhood, usually under 6 years, triggered by febrile illness, fasting or anaesthesia
feat: Recurrent severe rhabdomyolysis with muscle pain, weakness and dark urine
Triggers: viral fever, fasting, anaesthesia, exercise
CK often above 10,000 and sometimes over 100,000 U/L during attacks
Normal or near-normal muscle strength and CK between episodes
Risk of acute kidney injury, hyperkalaemia and cardiac arrhythmia during crises
inv: CK, urine myoglobin, potassium, creatinine during attacks
Acylcarnitine profile and urine organic acids to exclude fatty-acid oxidation defects (usually normal)
Genetic testing: biallelic LPIN1 variants (a common intragenic deletion in Europeans)

case.story: Second episode of leg pain, refusal to walk and cola-coloured urine during a febrile cold.
case.exam: Tender calves and thighs, weak hip flexors, alert.
case.tests: CK 180,000 U/L; potassium 5.9 mmol/L; acylcarnitine profile normal.
case.q: Which gene should be tested and what is the acute management?
case.a: LPIN1; aggressive IV fluids with dextrose, correct hyperkalaemia, treat fever and monitor renal function.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Disorders of Phospholipid Synthesis

det.patho: LPIN1 encodes lipin-1, a phosphatidate phosphatase that converts phosphatidic acid to diacylglycerol and also regulates gene expression of lipid metabolism. Its loss disrupts membrane lipid balance and mitochondrial function in skeletal muscle; during metabolic stress muscle membranes break down. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
det.clinical: It is one of the leading genetic causes of severe recurrent rhabdomyolysis in early childhood. Episodes can be life-threatening through hyperkalaemia, arrhythmia and renal failure. Some children develop mild persistent myalgia or exercise intolerance; cardiac involvement has been reported.
det.diagnosis: Suspect in a young child with recurrent febrile rhabdomyolysis and normal metabolic screening. Molecular testing within a rhabdomyolysis or metabolic myopathy panel confirms it. Muscle biopsy may show lipid accumulation but is often nonspecific.
det.treatment: No disease-specific therapy exists. Management is prompt hospital care during illness with high-volume IV fluids containing glucose, avoidance of fasting, early antipyretics and caution with anaesthesia. An emergency letter for families helps. Trials of corticosteroids or other agents have been small and remain experimental.
det.prognosis: Attacks may become less frequent with age, but a minority of children die during episodes.
pearls: Toddler + fever + CK in the hundred-thousands: test LPIN1.
Normal acylcarnitines do not exclude a genetic rhabdomyolysis.
Give an emergency plan: early IV glucose and fluids with every febrile illness.
det.thd: Phosphatidate phosphatase 1 deficiency หรือ LPIN1 deficiency เป็นโรคยีนด้อยที่ทำให้เด็กเล็กเกิดกล้ามเนื้อสลายรุนแรงซ้ำ ๆ เมื่อมีไข้หรืออดอาหาร CK สูงมากและปัสสาวะสีเข้ม เสี่ยงไตวายและโพแทสเซียมสูง ตรวจ acylcarnitine มักปกติ ยืนยันด้วยยีน LPIN1 รักษาโดยให้สารน้ำและกลูโคสทางหลอดเลือดอย่างรวดเร็วเมื่อเจ็บป่วย และหลีกเลี่ยงการอดอาหาร

ddx.pt: Mostly later childhood or adult onset after prolonged exercise; abnormal acylcarnitines
Exercise-induced cramps with second wind; no fever trigger
Umbrella term; trauma, drugs and toxins are commoner causes

aN: lpin1 deficiency | lipin 1 deficiency | lpin1 related rhabdomyolysis | lipin 1 myopathy

name: Photosensitive myoclonic epilepsy
formal: Photoparoxysmal generalised epilepsy triggered by flickering light, with myoclonic jerks and generalised tonic-clonic seizures, often in adolescents.
simple: Seizures and jerks triggered by flashing or flickering lights.
th: โรคลมชักทั่วไปที่ถูกกระตุ้นด้วยแสงกะพริบหรือลวดลาย มีกระตุกแบบ myoclonic และชักเกร็งกระตุกทั้งตัว มักเริ่มในวัยรุ่น
tempoNote: Seizures provoked within seconds of flicker exposure; onset usually between 7 and 20 years
feat: Myoclonic jerks, absences or tonic-clonic seizures triggered by flashing lights, screens, sunlight through trees or striped patterns
Onset usually in late childhood or adolescence, girls more than boys
Often part of genetic generalised epilepsy, especially juvenile myoclonic epilepsy or eyelid myoclonia with absences
Normal development and neurological examination
Spontaneous seizures may also occur; pure reflex forms are less common
inv: EEG with standardised intermittent photic stimulation showing a generalised photoparoxysmal response
MRI usually normal; required if seizures are focal or examination is abnormal
If progressive decline or ataxia: consider progressive myoclonic epilepsy work-up

case.story: Had a convulsion while playing a fast-flashing mobile game late at night; she admits to brief arm jerks when sunlight flickers through roadside trees.
case.exam: Normal neurological and developmental examination.
case.tests: EEG shows generalised polyspike-wave discharges at 15–20 Hz photic stimulation; MRI normal.
case.q: Which drug and lifestyle advice suit her best?
case.a: Photosensitive generalised epilepsy: valproate is most effective but avoided in girls of childbearing potential, so levetiracetam is a good first choice; avoid sleep loss, cover one eye near flicker, reduce screen brightness and distance.

read.where: Chapter 10 Epilepsy and Related Disorders — reflex and photosensitive epilepsies

det.patho: The visual cortex in susceptible people synchronises excessively to flicker of about 10–25 Hz or high-contrast patterns, and the discharge rapidly generalises through thalamocortical circuits. Photosensitivity is strongly inherited and often clusters with genetic generalised epilepsies; specific genes such as CHD2 explain a minority. The trait peaks in adolescence and often lessens in adult life.
det.clinical: Most patients have myoclonic jerks of the arms or eyelids or a generalised tonic-clonic seizure provoked by television, video games, discotheques or flickering natural light. Some have only reflex seizures, while others also have unprovoked seizures as part of JME or eyelid myoclonia with absences (Jeavons syndrome). Self-induction by waving fingers before the eyes occurs in some children. Progressive cognitive or motor decline is not expected and should trigger a search for a progressive myoclonic epilepsy.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis combines a typical history with a photoparoxysmal response on EEG during standardised intermittent photic stimulation. Generalised responses carry more weight than responses confined to the occipital region. Normal MRI and examination fit the diagnosis. Look carefully for spontaneous seizures, absences or morning jerks that define the broader syndrome.
det.treatment: Broad-spectrum antiseizure drugs work best: valproate is the most effective but should be avoided in women who may become pregnant; levetiracetam, lamotrigine (may aggravate myoclonus) and clobazam are alternatives. Avoid carbamazepine and phenytoin, which can worsen myoclonus. Teach avoidance: watch screens from a distance in a lit room, cover one eye when exposed, and keep regular sleep. Patients with only rare reflex seizures may manage with avoidance alone.
det.prognosis: Good; seizures are usually well controlled, and photosensitivity often declines in the third decade, though JME-associated cases need long-term treatment.
pearls: Covering one eye abolishes most photic triggering because binocular stimulation drives the response.
Carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine and phenytoin can aggravate generalised myoclonic epilepsies.
Photosensitivity plus cognitive decline means a progressive myoclonic epilepsy until proved otherwise.
det.thd: Photosensitive myoclonic epilepsy คือโรคลมชักทั่วไปที่ถูกกระตุ้นด้วยแสงกะพริบ จอเกม หรือลวดลายตัดกันชัด มักเริ่มในวัยรุ่น มีกระตุกแขนหรือเปลือกตาและชักทั้งตัว ตรวจ EEG ระหว่างกระตุ้นแสงจะเห็น photoparoxysmal response รักษาด้วย levetiracetam หรือ valproate (หลีกเลี่ยงในหญิงวัยเจริญพันธุ์) และแนะนำให้นอนพอ ปิดตาข้างหนึ่งเมื่อเจอแสงกะพริบ

ddx.pt: Morning jerks after sleep deprivation; about a third are photosensitive, so the two overlap heavily
Marked photosensitivity plus progressive action myoclonus and ataxia; cognition slowly worsens
Teenager with visual seizures, myoclonus and rapid cognitive decline; occipital spikes and inclusions on skin biopsy

name: Phrenic nerve neuropathies
formal: Injury or dysfunction of the phrenic nerve, causing hemidiaphragm paralysis and dyspnoea, from surgery, trauma, neuralgic amyotrophy or tumour.
simple: Damage to the nerve controlling the diaphragm, causing breathlessness.
th: เส้นประสาท phrenic เสียหาย ทำให้กะบังลมอัมพาตข้างเดียวหรือสองข้าง หายใจเหนื่อยโดยเฉพาะเมื่อนอนราบ
tempoNote: Acute after surgery or neuralgic amyotrophy; gradual with tumour infiltration
feat: Unilateral palsy often asymptomatic or mild exertional dyspnoea; found as raised hemidiaphragm on X-ray
Bilateral palsy: orthopnoea, breathlessness when bending or in water, paradoxical abdominal movement
Causes: cardiac or neck surgery, interscalene block, trauma, neuralgic amyotrophy, tumour (lung, mediastinal), cervical root disease
Neuralgic amyotrophy: shoulder pain then dyspnoea
Sleep-disordered breathing with morning headache in bilateral cases
inv: Chest X-ray and ultrasound or fluoroscopic sniff test for diaphragm motion
Supine vs upright spirometry (large supine fall in vital capacity suggests bilateral weakness)
Phrenic NCS and diaphragm EMG
CT chest/neck to exclude tumour along the nerve's course

case.story: Two weeks after severe right shoulder pain, he becomes breathless lying flat and when bending to tie shoes.
case.exam: Paradoxical inward abdominal motion on inspiration when supine, mild weakness of right shoulder abduction.
case.tests: Upright FVC 68% falling to 45% supine; ultrasound shows absent movement of both hemidiaphragms; CT chest normal.
case.q: What is the likely cause and what supports breathing at night?
case.a: Bilateral phrenic neuropathy from neuralgic amyotrophy; nocturnal non-invasive ventilation while awaiting slow recovery.
