det.patho: The phrenic nerve arises from C3–C5 and descends over scalenus anterior, through the thorax beside the pericardium to the diaphragm. Injury may be traumatic, iatrogenic (cardiac surgery cold injury, central line placement, neck dissection, interscalene block), inflammatory (neuralgic amyotrophy), compressive (tumour) or part of a generalised neuropathy.
det.clinical: Unilateral lesions are usually well tolerated at rest but limit exercise, particularly in obesity or lung disease. Bilateral palsy causes severe orthopnoea and hypoventilation, especially during REM sleep. Neuralgic amyotrophy is a common unrecognised cause and may be isolated to the phrenic nerve.
det.diagnosis: A raised hemidiaphragm prompts ultrasound or a sniff test. Supine spirometry, phrenic nerve conduction studies and diaphragm EMG confirm and localise the lesion. Cross-sectional imaging excludes compressive lesions; ask about recent shoulder pain, surgery and procedures.
det.treatment: Treat the cause where possible. Non-invasive ventilation corrects nocturnal hypoventilation in bilateral palsy. Diaphragm plication helps selected patients with persistent unilateral paralysis; phrenic nerve repair or grafting is offered in specialist centres for some traumatic or chronic lesions.
det.prognosis: Neuralgic and surgical injuries often recover over 1–3 years, but recovery can be incomplete.
pearls: Orthopnoea with clear lungs: test diaphragm strength.
Supine drop in vital capacity over 25% suggests significant diaphragm weakness.
Ask about shoulder pain in the preceding weeks.
det.thd: Phrenic nerve neuropathy ทำให้กะบังลมอัมพาต หากเป็นข้างเดียวมักมีอาการน้อยและพบจากภาพเอกซเรย์กะบังลมยกสูง หากเป็นสองข้างจะหอบเหนื่อยเมื่อนอนราบและหายใจไม่พอตอนหลับ สาเหตุได้แก่ ผ่าตัดหัวใจหรือคอ neuralgic amyotrophy และเนื้องอก ตรวจด้วย ultrasound หรือ sniff test และ spirometry ท่านอนเทียบท่านั่ง รักษาตามสาเหตุและใช้ NIV ตอนกลางคืน

name: Phylloquinone (vitamin K) deficiency
formal: Impaired clotting factor synthesis causing bleeding, including intracranial haemorrhage in newborns, from malabsorption, antibiotics or warfarin.
simple: Low vitamin K, which causes poor blood clotting and bleeding, including in the brain of newborns.
th: ขาดวิตามินเคทำให้สร้างปัจจัยการแข็งตัวของเลือดไม่ได้ เกิดเลือดออกง่าย รวมถึงเลือดออกในสมองของทารก จากการดูดซึมผิดปกติ ยาปฏิชีวนะ หรือ warfarin
tempoNote: Late infant bleeding peaks at 2–12 weeks; adults develop it over days to weeks of poor intake, antibiotics or malabsorption
feat: A coagulation disorder, not a primary neurological disease; neurological harm comes from intracranial bleeding
Late infantile form: exclusively breastfed baby without vitamin K at birth, often with cholestasis, presenting with sudden intracranial haemorrhage
Bruising, mucosal, gut or umbilical bleeding; seizures, bulging fontanelle and drowsiness with brain bleeds
Adults: malabsorption, cholestatic liver disease, prolonged antibiotics with poor intake, warfarin excess or superwarfarin poisoning
Platelet count and fibrinogen are normal
inv: Prolonged PT/INR (and later APTT) with normal platelets and fibrinogen; corrects with vitamin K
PIVKA-II raised; serum vitamin K levels rarely needed
Cranial ultrasound or CT for suspected intracranial haemorrhage
Look for cause: liver function, bilirubin, coeliac screen; brodifacoum assay if superwarfarin suspected

case.who: 7-week-old exclusively breastfed baby boy from a rural district of Sakon Nakhon
case.story: Home birth without vitamin K injection; for two days poor feeding and vomiting, then a seizure.
case.exam: Pale, bulging fontanelle, drowsy; prolonged jaundice noted by the mother.
case.tests: Hb 7 g/dL, platelets normal, PT and APTT markedly prolonged, fibrinogen normal; CT shows a large subdural and parenchymal haemorrhage.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and how could it have been prevented?
case.a: Late vitamin K deficiency bleeding (likely with underlying cholestasis); give IV vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma or PCC urgently. A single intramuscular vitamin K dose at birth prevents it.

det.patho: Vitamin K is the cofactor needed to gamma-carboxylate prothrombin, factors VII, IX, X and proteins C and S. Without it the liver releases inactive factors (PIVKAs) and bleeding follows. Newborns have low stores and breast milk contains little vitamin K, so deficiency develops in the first weeks; cholestasis worsens absorption. In adults, poor diet plus antibiotics that reduce gut flora, fat malabsorption and vitamin K antagonists are the usual causes.
det.clinical: Neonatal deficiency bleeding is grouped into early (first 24 h, often maternal drugs such as anticonvulsants), classic (days 2–7, gut and skin bleeding) and late (2–12 weeks). The late form is the most dangerous for the brain: intracranial haemorrhage occurs in about half of cases, causing seizures, death or long-term disability. In adults, intracranial bleeding usually reflects warfarin over-anticoagulation or long-acting rodenticide poisoning.
det.diagnosis: An isolated prolonged PT (later both PT and APTT) with normal platelets and fibrinogen, corrected by vitamin K, is characteristic. PIVKA-II confirms functional deficiency. In infants, always look for underlying liver disease (biliary atresia) and consider non-accidental injury if coagulation is normal.
det.treatment: Give vitamin K intravenously (slow infusion) for active bleeding; it takes several hours to work, so add prothrombin complex concentrate or fresh frozen plasma for life-threatening haemorrhage, including all intracranial bleeds. Neurosurgical evacuation is considered for large haematomas. Prevention is a single 1 mg intramuscular dose of vitamin K at birth (lower in preterm infants), which is standard in Thailand. Superwarfarin poisoning needs high-dose oral vitamin K for months.
det.prognosis: Prognosis of late infant bleeding with intracranial haemorrhage is guarded, with notable mortality and neurodevelopmental sequelae; adults recover quickly once corrected unless a large bleed occurred.
pearls: Infant with intracranial bleed + prolonged PT + no vitamin K at birth = late VKDB.
Prolonged jaundice in a breastfed infant with bleeding: look for cholestasis.
Vitamin K alone is too slow for intracranial bleeding: add PCC or FFP.
det.thd: การขาดวิตามินเคทำให้ตับสร้างปัจจัยการแข็งตัวของเลือด II, VII, IX และ X ไม่ได้ จึงเลือดออกง่าย ในทารกที่กินนมแม่และไม่ได้ฉีดวิตามินเคตอนแรกเกิดอาจมีเลือดออกในสมองช่วงอายุ 2–12 สัปดาห์ ทำให้ชัก ซึม และเสียชีวิตได้ ส่วนผู้ใหญ่พบจากการดูดซึมผิดปกติ ยาปฏิชีวนะ หรือ warfarin ตรวจพบ PT ยาวแต่เกล็ดเลือดปกติ รักษาด้วยวิตามินเคทางหลอดเลือดร่วมกับ PCC หรือ FFP เมื่อเลือดออกรุนแรง และป้องกันได้ด้วยการฉีดวิตามินเคแก่ทารกแรกเกิดทุกราย

qx.stem: A 6-week-old exclusively breastfed Thai infant who was born at home and received no prophylaxis presents with vomiting, a bulging fontanelle and a seizure. CT shows a subdural and parenchymal haemorrhage. PT and aPTT are markedly prolonged with normal platelets and fibrinogen.
qx.q: What is the appropriate treatment and underlying lesson?
opts: Platelet transfusion alone
Intravenous vitamin K with clotting factor replacement as needed; late haemorrhagic disease is preventable by newborn vitamin K prophylaxis
Exchange transfusion for hyperbilirubinaemia
Factor VIII concentrate
Desmopressin
qx.why: Late vitamin K deficiency bleeding affects breastfed infants who missed prophylaxis and often presents with intracranial haemorrhage, with prolonged PT and aPTT but normal platelets. Treatment is parenteral vitamin K with prothrombin complex or plasma if bleeding is severe. Normal platelets and fibrinogen argue against thrombocytopenia or DIC.

name: Physiological myoclonus
formal: Normal myoclonic jerks such as hiccups, sleep starts and hypnic jerks, without disease.
simple: Harmless muscle jerks like hiccups or twitching as you fall asleep.
th: การกระตุกของกล้ามเนื้อที่เป็นเรื่องปกติในคนทั่วไป เช่น สะดุ้งตอนเคลิ้มหลับ สะอึก หรือสะดุ้งตกใจ ไม่ได้เป็นโรค
tempoNote: Brief, situational jerks occurring throughout life
feat: Hypnic jerks (sleep starts) at sleep onset, sometimes with a falling sensation
Hiccups: diaphragmatic myoclonus
Anxiety- or exercise-induced jerks and benign infantile feeding myoclonus
Normal neurological examination and no progression
Not a disease; recognising it avoids unnecessary tests
inv: None in typical cases
Video-polysomnography if jerks are frequent, injurious or atypical
Investigate persistent hiccups (over 48 hours) for medullary, thoracic or metabolic causes

case.who: 30-year-old nurse from Bangkok working night shifts
case.story: As she drifts off to sleep she often feels a sudden whole-body jolt, as if missing a step, which wakes her; it is worse after strong coffee and long shifts.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination.
case.tests: None needed.
case.q: What is this and how should she be advised?
case.a: Hypnic jerks (physiological myoclonus); reassure, improve sleep hygiene and reduce caffeine.

det.patho: Physiological myoclonus arises from normal circuits: hypnic jerks reflect brainstem reticular activation as wakefulness gives way to sleep, and hiccups are a reflex involving vagal and phrenic pathways with a brainstem centre. These jerks occur in healthy people and do not imply nervous-system disease.
det.clinical: Sleep starts are common, often single, and may be accompanied by a visual or falling sensation. They increase with caffeine, stress, sleep deprivation and exercise late in the day. Hiccups are usually brief but persistent hiccups can signal brainstem lesions (e.g. NMOSD area postrema), metabolic disturbance or diaphragmatic irritation.
det.diagnosis: History is usually sufficient. Investigation is reserved for frequent, distressing, progressive jerks or those with other neurological features, when polysomnography or EEG can distinguish epilepsy, propriospinal myoclonus or other sleep disorders.
det.treatment: Reassurance and sleep hygiene. Reduce stimulants. Persistent hiccups may need treatment of the cause, and drugs such as baclofen, metoclopramide or chlorpromazine for symptom relief.
det.prognosis: Benign.
pearls: Hypnic jerks are normal and need no tests.
Hiccups lasting more than two days deserve investigation, including MRI of the medulla.
Morning jerks on waking are not physiological; think JME.
det.thd: Physiological myoclonus คือการกระตุกที่เป็นปกติของร่างกาย เช่น สะดุ้งตอนเคลิ้มหลับ (hypnic jerk) และสะอึก ไม่ใช่โรค มักมากขึ้นเมื่อดื่มกาแฟ เครียด หรืออดนอน ตรวจร่างกายปกติ ไม่ต้องตรวจเพิ่ม แนะนำสุขอนามัยการนอนและลดคาเฟอีน แต่หากสะอึกนานเกิน 48 ชั่วโมงควรหาสาเหตุ เช่น รอยโรคที่ก้านสมองส่วน medulla

ddx.pt: Morning jerks after waking, with generalized seizures and EEG spike-wave
Repetitive axial flexion jerks lying down at sleep onset, persistent and troublesome
Small, persistent twitches throughout sleep stages on polysomnography

aN: normal myoclonus | hypnic jerks | sleep starts | hiccups singultus | benign physiological jerks

name: Physiological tremor
formal: Low-amplitude, high-frequency postural tremor of 8-12 Hz present in everyone, enhanced by anxiety, caffeine, drugs and thyrotoxicosis.
simple: A fine normal tremor that everyone has, which can become more noticeable with stress, caffeine or some medicines.
th: อาการสั่นละเอียดความถี่สูงประมาณ 8–12 Hz ที่มีในทุกคน มักมองไม่เห็น แต่จะชัดขึ้นเมื่อวิตกกังวล ดื่มกาแฟ ใช้ยาบางชนิด หรือมีไทรอยด์เป็นพิษ
tempoNote: Always present at low amplitude; becomes visible transiently or while a provoking factor persists
feat: Fine, fast, symmetric hand tremor seen with posture and movement
Normally invisible; enhanced by anxiety, fatigue, cold, caffeine, hypoglycaemia
Drugs: beta-agonists, theophylline, valproate, lithium, SSRIs, thyroxine, steroids
Thyrotoxicosis and alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal enhance it
No other neurological signs; resolves when the cause is removed
inv: Thyroid function tests and glucose
Medication and substance review (caffeine, alcohol, energy drinks)
Accelerometry: frequency drops with wrist loading, unlike central tremors

case.who: 26-year-old medical intern in a Bangkok hospital
case.story: During night calls his hands shake when holding a syringe; he drinks four cans of coffee and takes salbutamol for asthma.
case.exam: Fine symmetric postural tremor, no rest tremor, no other signs; pulse 104.
case.tests: TSH low, free T4 high.
case.q: What kind of tremor is this and what is the main cause?
case.a: Enhanced physiological tremor, mainly from hyperthyroidism with added caffeine and salbutamol.

det.patho: Physiological tremor results from mechanical resonance of the limb plus synchronised firing of motor units and stretch-reflex loops, with a small central oscillator component. Increased beta-adrenergic drive raises muscle spindle sensitivity and motor unit synchrony, enlarging the tremor. It is therefore enhanced by catecholamines, thyroid hormone and many drugs.
det.clinical: The enhanced form is a fine, high-frequency postural tremor seen when holding the arms out or doing precise tasks. It fluctuates with emotional state, time of day and stimulant intake. It does not spread to the head or voice and does not cause disability apart from fine work.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical with exclusion of reversible contributors: thyroid function, glucose, medication review and withdrawal states. Neurophysiology can show that the peak frequency falls with added weight, reflecting its mechanical-reflex origin. Asymmetry, rest tremor or neurological signs suggest another diagnosis.
det.treatment: Remove triggers: correct thyroid excess, reduce caffeine, adjust offending drugs. Propranolol taken as needed before performance situations is effective. Reassurance is often enough.
det.prognosis: Benign and reversible once the provoking cause is removed.
pearls: Always check thyroid function in new-onset fine postural tremor.
A frequency that falls when the hand is weighted points to a peripheral mechanical origin.
Asthma inhalers, valproate and lithium are common iatrogenic culprits.
det.thd: Physiological tremor คืออาการสั่นละเอียดความถี่สูง 8–12 Hz ที่มีในทุกคน โดยปกติมองไม่เห็น แต่จะชัดขึ้นเมื่อวิตกกังวล อดนอน ดื่มกาแฟ ใช้ยาบางชนิด (salbutamol, valproate, lithium) หรือไทรอยด์เป็นพิษ เรียก enhanced physiological tremor ควรตรวจไทรอยด์ น้ำตาล และทบทวนยา รักษาโดยแก้สาเหตุ และใช้ propranolol เมื่อจำเป็น

ddx.pt: Larger amplitude, often familial, alcohol-responsive, slower 4–10 Hz, progresses
Same phenomenology but clearly linked to a drug start or dose change
Variable frequency, entrains with tapping, distractible

name: Pick’s disease
formal: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia with 3R tau Pick bodies and ballooned neurons, with personality change, disinhibition and language impairment.
simple: A type of dementia that damages the front and side of the brain, causing personality and language changes.
more: MRI shows frontal and anterior temporal atrophy; FDG-PET shows frontotemporal hypometabolism. Pick bodies are tau-positive and argyrophilic, and there is no disease-modifying treatment; use SSRIs and non-drug measures for behaviour.
th: โรคสมองเสื่อมกลุ่ม frontotemporal ที่มีพยาธิสภาพ tau ชนิด 3R (Pick bodies) ทำให้บุคลิกภาพเปลี่ยน ขาดการยับยั้ง และภาษาเสื่อม
tempoNote: Insidious onset usually age 50–65, progressing over 5–10 years
feat: Early personality change, disinhibition, apathy and loss of empathy
Compulsive behaviours and dietary change (sweet craving, overeating)
Language decline (non-fluent or semantic features) in some
Memory and visuospatial skills relatively spared early
Marked 'knife-edge' frontal and anterior temporal atrophy, often asymmetric
inv: MRI: severe focal frontal and anterior temporal atrophy
FDG-PET: frontotemporal hypometabolism
Amyloid biomarkers negative (to exclude frontal Alzheimer disease)
Genetic testing if family history (MAPT, GRN, C9orf72); definite diagnosis needs neuropathology

case.story: Over two years he has spent the family savings on lottery tickets, tells crude jokes at funerals and eats only sweets.
case.exam: Disinhibited, little insight, perseverative; MMSE 26, fails FAB; no motor signs.
case.tests: MRI shows striking bilateral frontal and anterior temporal atrophy; CSF amyloid normal.
case.q: Which syndrome is this and what histology might be found at autopsy?
case.a: Behavioural variant FTD; Pick's disease (3R tau with Pick bodies) is one possible pathology.

det.patho: Pick's disease is a sporadic frontotemporal lobar degeneration defined by Pick bodies — round argyrophilic inclusions of 3-repeat tau — and ballooned neurons (Pick cells) in frontal and temporal cortex and hippocampal dentate gyrus. It accounts for a minority of FTLD cases. Historically the term was used for all frontotemporal dementia; it is now reserved for this specific pathology.
det.clinical: Most patients present with behavioural variant FTD; others show non-fluent or semantic language decline. Motor neuron disease is not typical. Disease progression causes mutism, dependence and death. Clinical features cannot reliably separate Pick pathology from other FTLD types in life.
det.diagnosis: In life, diagnose the clinical syndrome (bvFTD or PPA criteria) supported by frontotemporal atrophy or hypometabolism and negative Alzheimer biomarkers. Tau PET tracers are being studied but are not reliable for 3R tau. Definite Pick's disease requires autopsy.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying treatment. SSRIs or trazodone can reduce disinhibition and compulsions; antipsychotics only with caution. Cholinesterase inhibitors are not helpful and may worsen behaviour. Carer support, financial and legal protection, and supervision are vital.
det.prognosis: Median survival about 7–10 years from onset.
pearls: Pick's disease is a pathological, not a clinical, diagnosis.
Pick bodies are 3R tau; CBD and PSP are 4R.
Avoid cholinesterase inhibitors in FTD behaviour.
det.thd: Pick’s disease เป็นโรคสมองเสื่อมกลุ่ม frontotemporal ที่มีพยาธิสภาพ tau ชนิด 3R เรียกว่า Pick bodies ผู้ป่วยบุคลิกภาพเปลี่ยน ขาดการยับยั้ง ใช้เงินฟุ่มเฟือย ชอบกินหวาน หรือภาษาเสื่อม ความจำช่วงแรกค่อนข้างดี MRI พบสมองส่วนหน้าและขมับฝ่อชัดเจน การวินิจฉัยแน่นอนต้องอาศัยการตรวจสมองหลังเสียชีวิต การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคองและใช้ SSRI ควบคุมพฤติกรรม

name: Pill-rolling tremor
formal: Characteristic parkinsonian rest tremor of 4-6 Hz of thumb and fingers, resembling rolling a pill, which diminishes on action.
simple: A tremor in the thumb and finger that looks like rolling a pill, typical of Parkinson disease.
th: อาการสั่นขณะพักของนิ้วโป้งและนิ้วชี้คล้ายการปั้นเม็ดยา ความถี่ 4–6 Hz ลดลงเมื่อขยับมือ เป็นอาการเด่นของโรคพาร์กินสัน
tempoNote: Insidious onset, usually unilateral, slowly spreading over years
feat: Rhythmic flexion-extension of fingers against the thumb at rest, 4–6 Hz
Dampens with voluntary action and disappears in sleep
Increases with mental stress, counting backwards or walking
Often asymmetric; may involve leg, lip, jaw or chin but rarely head
A clinical sign, not a disease: strongly suggests Parkinson disease
inv: Examine for bradykinesia and rigidity to establish parkinsonism
DaT-SPECT if differentiation from dystonic or essential tremor is uncertain
Drug history for dopamine blockers

case.story: Holding his alms bowl, he noticed his right fingers moving rhythmically when his hand rested on his lap, and his handwriting is getting smaller.
case.exam: Right thumb-index rest tremor that stops on reaching and increases with mental arithmetic; right bradykinesia and cogwheeling.
case.tests: No dopamine-blocking drugs; MRI normal.
case.q: What does this sign point to?
case.a: Parkinsonian rest tremor, together with bradykinesia indicating Parkinson disease.

read.where: Chapter 3: Epidemiological Methods for Studying Movement Disorders

det.patho: Parkinsonian rest tremor is thought to arise from abnormal oscillations in the basal ganglia that entrain the cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuit (the 'dimmer-switch' model). Its severity correlates poorly with dopamine loss, and serotonergic and noradrenergic deficits may contribute. It explains why tremor responds less predictably to levodopa than bradykinesia.
det.clinical: Rest tremor is the presenting feature in about two-thirds of PD patients and is usually unilateral at onset. It may re-emerge after a delay when the arms are held out (re-emergent tremor). Pure tremor-dominant PD often progresses slowly. Rest tremor can also be seen in drug-induced parkinsonism, and occasionally in essential tremor of long duration.
det.diagnosis: Observe hands resting in the lap, during walking and while performing a mental task. Rest tremor alone is not parkinsonism; bradykinesia must also be shown. DaT imaging distinguishes degenerative causes from dystonic, essential or functional tremor.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying parkinsonism; levodopa and dopamine agonists improve tremor in many patients. Anticholinergics are occasionally used in young patients but avoided in the elderly. Refractory tremor responds well to deep brain stimulation or focused-ultrasound thalamotomy.
det.prognosis: Tracks the course of PD; tremor-dominant phenotypes generally progress more slowly.
pearls: Distraction with mental arithmetic brings out a hidden rest tremor.
Rest tremor that stops with action and returns after a pause is classic PD.
Head tremor argues against PD tremor.
det.thd: Pill-rolling tremor คืออาการสั่นขณะพักของนิ้วโป้งกับนิ้วชี้คล้ายการปั้นเม็ดยา ความถี่ 4–6 Hz ลดลงเมื่อขยับมือและหายตอนหลับ มักเริ่มข้างเดียว เป็นอาการเด่นของโรคพาร์กินสัน แต่ต้องมี bradykinesia ร่วมจึงจะวินิจฉัย parkinsonism ได้ รักษาด้วย levodopa หรือ dopamine agonist และพิจารณา DBS หรือ focused ultrasound ในรายดื้อยา

name: Pilocytic astrocytoma
formal: WHO grade 1 astrocytoma with biphasic pattern and Rosenthal fibres, often cerebellar in children, with BRAF alterations and cyst with mural nodule; good prognosis.
simple: A slow-growing brain tumour, mainly in children, often in the cerebellum and often curable with surgery.
th: เนื้องอก astrocyte เกรด 1 พบในเด็กและวัยหนุ่มสาว มักเป็นถุงน้ำร่วมกับก้อนเล็กที่ติดสีเข้มในซีรีเบลลัม หรือพบที่ optic pathway และ hypothalamus (ร่วมกับ NF1) ผ่าตัดเอาออกหมดแล้วมักหายขาด
tempoNote: Weeks to months of headache, vomiting and clumsiness in a child with cerebellar tumour; optic and hypothalamic forms can be silent for years
feat: Mainly a tumour of childhood and early adult life; cerebellum is the classic site, followed by optic nerve and chiasm, hypothalamus and brainstem
Cerebellar tumours present with raised pressure (morning headache, vomiting, papilloedema) from fourth-ventricle compression and with ataxia or head tilt
Optic pathway tumours in NF1 may be found on screening or cause proptosis, visual loss, nystagmus or precocious puberty
Classic imaging is a cyst with a strongly enhancing mural nodule, but about one in three is solid
Molecular signature is MAPK activation, usually KIAA1549::BRAF fusion, or BRAF V600E and NF1 loss in some
inv: MRI with contrast of brain and, for hypothalamic or midline tumours, the spine; cyst wall may not enhance
Histology: biphasic pattern with Rosenthal fibres and eosinophilic granular bodies, low mitotic rate; BRAF fusion testing
In suspected NF1 optic glioma, ophthalmology with acuity, fields and discs; biopsy is not needed with typical imaging in a known NF1 child
Postoperative MRI within 72 hours to confirm complete removal

case.story: Six weeks of morning headaches with vomiting, then clumsy walking and a persistent head tilt to the right.
case.exam: Bilateral papilloedema, right-sided limb dysmetria and a broad-based gait; no neurocutaneous signs.
case.tests: MRI shows a large right cerebellar cyst with a 2 cm enhancing mural nodule and mild hydrocephalus. After steroids, the nodule and cyst wall are resected; histology: pilocytic astrocytoma, KIAA1549::BRAF fusion, CNS WHO grade 1.
case.q: Is adjuvant therapy needed after complete removal, and what drug class helps if an unresectable lesion progresses?
case.a: No adjuvant therapy is needed after complete excision. For unresectable BRAF-altered tumours, MEK/BRAF inhibitors (dabrafenib plus trametinib, or tovorafenib) are used, avoiding radiotherapy in young children.

det.patho: Pilocytic astrocytoma is a circumscribed, slowly growing, biphasic tumour of piloid (hair-like) bipolar cells with Rosenthal fibres and eosinophilic granular bodies. It is driven by MAPK pathway activation: KIAA1549::BRAF fusion in cerebellar tumours, other BRAF or FGFR1 alterations elsewhere, and NF1 loss in neurofibromatosis. Rosenthal fibres are not specific; they also appear in gliosis and Alexander disease. Few tumours show anaplasia, and the lesion is CNS WHO grade 1.
det.clinical: Cerebellar tumours produce hydrocephalus with headache, vomiting and papilloedema, then ataxia and head tilt. Optic pathway tumours may be unilateral with proptosis or bilateral chiasmatic with visual field loss, nystagmus and diencephalic features such as precocious puberty. The course is indolent, and some optic pathway tumours stabilise or regress on their own in NF1.
det.diagnosis: MRI is characteristic: cyst plus enhancing mural nodule (the cyst wall enhances only when tumour-lined), or a solid enhancing mass. Hydrocephalus is common. Tissue confirms diagnosis and BRAF status. In NF1 children with typical optic pathway thickening, biopsy is often avoided, and visual assessment drives the decision to treat. Differential diagnosis includes haemangioblastoma (adult), medulloblastoma and ependymoma (solid, restricted diffusion).
det.treatment: Management of raised pressure with steroids is often enough before elective surgery; ventricular drainage is reserved for patients in extremis. Gross total resection of the nodule cures cerebellar tumours and needs no radiotherapy. Unresectable or progressive tumours in the optic pathway or brainstem receive chemotherapy such as carboplatin with vincristine, or targeted therapy: dabrafenib plus trametinib for BRAF V600E tumours, tovorafenib for BRAF-altered relapsed tumours, and selumetinib for NF1-associated disease. Radiotherapy is avoided in young children and in NF1 because of cognitive, vascular and second-tumour risks.
det.prognosis: Cure is expected after complete excision with ten-year survival above 90%; unresectable tumours often stabilise for years but may need repeated treatment and cause visual morbidity.
pearls: Cyst with enhancing mural nodule in a child's cerebellum: resect the nodule, not just drain the cyst.
Optic pathway glioma in NF1: screen eyes yearly, treat for visual decline, and avoid radiotherapy.
BRAF fusions, not V600E, are typical for cerebellar pilocytic tumours; V600E suggests other histologies such as ganglioglioma or pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma.
det.thd: Pilocytic astrocytoma เป็นเนื้องอกเกรด 1 ในเด็ก มักอยู่ที่ซีรีเบลลัมเป็นถุงน้ำร่วมกับก้อนเล็กที่ enhance ทำให้ปวดศีรษะ อาเจียน และเดินเซ จากภาวะน้ำคั่งสมอง เนื้องอกเกิดจากการกระตุ้น MAPK pathway โดยเฉพาะ KIAA1549::BRAF การผ่าตัดเอาก้อนออกหมดมักหายขาด ส่วนก้อนที่ผ่าไม่ได้ เช่น ที่ optic pathway ใช้ยาเคมีบำบัดหรือยากลุ่ม BRAF/MEK inhibitor และหลีกเลี่ยงการฉายรังสีในเด็กเล็กและผู้ป่วย NF1

qx.stem: An 8-year-old boy from Lampang has morning headaches and vomiting for a month. MRI shows a right cerebellar cyst with a strongly enhancing mural nodule and obstructive hydrocephalus. Complete resection of the nodule is achieved, and pathology shows biphasic piloid tissue with Rosenthal fibres.
qx.q: Which molecular alteration is most likely, and what is the usual next step?
opts: IDH1 mutation; adjuvant radiotherapy and temozolomide
KIAA1549::BRAF fusion; MRI surveillance without adjuvant therapy
H3 K27M mutation; focal radiotherapy
1p/19q codeletion; PCV chemotherapy
MYC amplification; craniospinal radiotherapy
qx.why: Cerebellar pilocytic astrocytoma is driven by MAPK activation, most often the KIAA1549::BRAF fusion, and a complete resection is usually curative, so follow-up imaging is enough. For unresectable or recurrent paediatric low-grade glioma, targeted drugs such as tovorafenib (BRAF fusions or V600) or dabrafenib with trametinib (V600E) are now used. The other alterations belong to diffuse gliomas, midline gliomas or medulloblastoma.

qx.stem: A 9-year-old girl in Chiang Rai has had intermittent headaches and a head tilt for several weeks. MRI shows a large cerebellar hemispheric cyst whose fluid is slightly brighter than CSF on FLAIR, with a small avidly enhancing nodule on its wall; the cyst wall itself does not enhance and there is little surrounding oedema.
qx.q: Which diagnosis fits, and how does this tumour usually behave?
opts: Haemangioblastoma; always associated with a VHL variant
Medulloblastoma; requires craniospinal radiotherapy
Pilocytic astrocytoma; circumscribed, often cured by complete resection of the nodule
Abscess; needs urgent drainage
Ependymoma; arises from the fourth ventricular floor
qx.why: A cerebellar cyst with an enhancing mural nodule and a non-enhancing wall in a child suggests pilocytic astrocytoma (CNS WHO grade 1, frequently with a BRAF alteration). Resecting the nodule is usually curative. Haemangioblastoma occurs in adults, and medulloblastoma is a solid, diffusion-restricting midline mass.

ddx.pt: Midline vermian, hyperdense solid tumour with restricted diffusion in a younger child, with leptomeningeal spread
Fills the fourth ventricle, extends through foramina, calcified and heterogeneous, with a cleavage plane from the vermis
Cystic cerebellar mass with a nodule in an adult, flow voids, and links to von Hippel-Lindau disease

name: Pineal region tumours
formal: Germ cell tumours, pineocytoma, pineoblastoma and others causing Parinaud syndrome and obstructive hydrocephalus; markers AFP and hCG in germ cell types.
simple: Tumours near the pineal gland deep in the brain that can cause hydrocephalus and trouble looking up.
ab: Papillary tumour of the pineal region
th: เนื้องอกบริเวณ pineal ประกอบด้วยกลุ่ม germ cell (germinoma เป็นชนิดที่พบบ่อยที่สุด), pineal parenchymal (pineocytoma, pineoblastoma) และเนื้องอกอื่น ทำให้น้ำคั่งสมอง Parinaud syndrome และอาจมีบิดเบือนการเจริญเติบโตทางเพศ การตรวจ AFP/beta-hCG และชิ้นเนื้อกำหนดการรักษา
tempoNote: Weeks to months of headache, vomiting and upgaze limitation; pineoblastoma can progress over weeks, pineocytoma over years
feat: Obstructive hydrocephalus from aqueduct compression: headache, vomiting, papilloedema, drowsiness
Parinaud dorsal midbrain syndrome: upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus, light-near dissociation, lid retraction (Collier sign)
Ataxia or hearing loss from tectal and cerebellar compression; precocious puberty in boys with hCG-secreting tumours
Germ cell tumours are the most common (especially in young males), pineal parenchymal tumours range from pineocytoma (grade 1) and intermediate tumours (grade 2-3) to pineoblastoma (grade 4)
Pineoblastoma can occur with RB1 mutation (trilateral retinoblastoma) or DICER1 syndrome and seeds the CSF early
inv: MRI brain and spine with contrast: homogeneously enhancing midline mass at the quadrigeminal plate; calcification displaced outward (exploded) in germ cell tumours and engulfed in pineal parenchymal tumours
Serum and CSF AFP, beta-hCG and PLAP; CSF cytology after spine imaging
Endoscopic third ventriculostomy with biopsy at the same sitting for hydrocephalus; stereotactic biopsy when markers are negative
Ophthalmology and RB1 or DICER1 genetics in pineoblastoma

case.story: Three months of headaches, nausea and difficulty looking up; family notes sleepiness in class.
case.exam: Papilloedema, upgaze palsy with convergence-retraction nystagmus on attempted upward saccades, pupils light-near dissociated.
case.tests: MRI shows an enhancing pineal mass 3 cm with obstructive hydrocephalus; serum and CSF AFP normal, beta-hCG mildly raised (15 IU/L). Endoscopic third ventriculostomy with biopsy: germinoma. Spinal MRI negative.
case.q: Why are tumour markers and the biopsy decisive in a pineal mass?
case.a: Germinoma, non-germinomatous germ cell tumour, pineoblastoma and pineocytoma need very different treatment: markers support germ cell tumours (AFP or high hCG suggests non-germinomatous disease), biopsy defines the rest. Germinoma is cured with chemotherapy plus radiotherapy, pineoblastoma needs craniospinal irradiation and intensive chemotherapy.

read.where: Chapter 13 Tumors of the Pineal Region
Chapter 39 Pineal Region Tumors in Children

det.patho: The pineal gland gives rise to germ cell tumours (about half of pineal region tumours in Asian populations), pineal parenchymal tumours, glial tumours, cysts, meningiomas and metastases. Pineal parenchymal tumours are graded: pineocytoma (grade 1), pineal parenchymal tumour of intermediate differentiation (grade 2 or 3) and pineoblastoma (grade 4), with CNS5 recognising molecular groups including DICER1 and miRNA processing mutations and MYC/FOXR2 activated forms. Germ cell tumours in Asian children are more frequent than in the West.
det.clinical: Hydrocephalus and Parinaud syndrome dominate. Endocrine presentation includes precocious puberty (hCG), diabetes insipidus if suprasellar disease coexists. Spread along the ventricles and CSF is common in pineoblastoma and non-germinomatous tumours. Haemorrhage into the tumour can cause apoplexy-like deterioration.
det.diagnosis: MRI plus tumour markers narrow the possibilities; confirmation by endoscopic or stereotactic biopsy is advised unless markers are clearly diagnostic. CSF should be taken from the ventricle at the time of endoscopy if not by lumbar puncture, which is unsafe with hydrocephalus. Spine MRI and CSF cytology stage the disease. Differential diagnosis includes pineal cyst, tectal glioma, meningioma, dermoid and metastasis.
det.treatment: Hydrocephalus is treated first, preferably by endoscopic third ventriculostomy which allows biopsy and CSF sampling. Pure germinoma receives chemotherapy and low-dose whole-ventricular radiotherapy with cure rates over 90 percent. Non-germinomatous tumours need intensive platinum chemotherapy with focal or craniospinal irradiation and second-look surgery. Pineocytoma is cured by gross total resection, and the book recommends radical surgery for it; pineoblastoma requires maximal resection, craniospinal irradiation and chemotherapy. Genetic counselling is advised for RB1 and DICER1 carriers.
det.prognosis: Germinoma is highly curable, pineocytoma has long survival after resection, whereas pineoblastoma has a five-year survival of about 50-60 percent in children and lower in infants.
pearls: Pineal mass plus hydrocephalus in a young male: check AFP and beta-hCG, and do ETV with biopsy.
Avoid lumbar puncture when hydrocephalus is present.
Pineocytoma is a surgical disease, germinoma is a radiochemotherapy disease.
det.thd: เนื้องอกบริเวณ pineal ได้แก่ germ cell tumour (เช่น germinoma), เนื้องอกจากเซลล์ pineal (pineocytoma, pineoblastoma) และอื่น ๆ ผู้ป่วยมีน้ำคั่งสมอง ปวดศีรษะ อาเจียน และ Parinaud syndrome คือมองขึ้นบนไม่ได้ ควรวัด AFP และ beta-hCG และทำ ETV ร่วมกับตัดชิ้นเนื้อ การรักษาต่างกันมาก germinoma ใช้เคมีบำบัดและฉายรังสี pineocytoma ใช้ผ่าตัด ส่วน pineoblastoma ต้องผ่าตัด ฉายรังสีทั่วระบบประสาทและเคมีบำบัด

name: Pituitary disorders
formal: Disorders of hormone excess or deficiency from the pituitary, including adenomas, apoplexy and hypopituitarism, with endocrine and visual field effects.
simple: Problems of the pituitary gland, which controls many hormones, sometimes causing vision changes.
more: Investigate with morning cortisol, prolactin, IGF-1, TSH, pituitary-protocol MRI and visual fields. Treat with transsphenoidal surgery, cabergoline for prolactinoma and hormone replacement; apoplexy needs urgent steroids and decompression.
th: กลุ่มโรคของต่อมใต้สมอง ทั้งฮอร์โมนเกินหรือขาด เช่น adenoma, apoplexy และ hypopituitarism มีผลต่อต่อมไร้ท่อและลานสายตา
tempoNote: Adenomas grow over months to years; apoplexy is abrupt
feat: Bitemporal hemianopia from chiasmal compression
Hormone excess: prolactinoma, acromegaly, Cushing disease, TSH-oma
Hormone deficiency: fatigue, hypogonadism, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, diabetes insipidus (rarer)
Apoplexy: thunderclap headache, ophthalmoplegia, visual loss, collapse
Headache common but nonspecific
inv: Morning cortisol, prolactin (with dilution), IGF-1, TSH/free T4, LH/FSH, sex steroids, sodium
Pituitary-protocol MRI with contrast
Formal visual fields (Humphrey or Goldmann) and OCT

case.story: Has bumped into people on both sides for a year; recently tired, low libido and needs bigger shoes.
case.exam: Coarse features, large hands, bitemporal hemianopia on confrontation, normal eye movements.
case.tests: IGF-1 three times normal, GH not suppressed on glucose; MRI 2.5 cm macroadenoma compressing the chiasm; testosterone low.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the usual first-line treatment?
case.a: Acromegaly from a GH-secreting macroadenoma; transsphenoidal surgery, with hormone replacement as required.

det.patho: Most pituitary disease arises from benign pituitary neuroendocrine tumours, which may secrete hormones or, when large, compress the chiasm, cavernous sinus and normal gland. Other causes include hypophysitis, infiltrative disease, trauma, radiotherapy and postpartum infarction (Sheehan syndrome). Apoplexy is sudden haemorrhage or infarction of an adenoma.
det.clinical: Presentations are endocrine (hormone excess or deficiency), visual (bitemporal or junctional field loss, optic atrophy) or both. Apoplexy is a neurosurgical and endocrine emergency with thunderclap headache, ophthalmoplegia (third nerve most common), visual loss and adrenal crisis. Incidental adenomas are common on imaging.
det.diagnosis: Combine dynamic and baseline hormone tests with pituitary MRI and formal fields. Measure prolactin with dilution in large tumours to avoid the hook effect. In suspected apoplexy, draw cortisol and give hydrocortisone without waiting for results.
det.treatment: Prolactinomas are treated with dopamine agonists (cabergoline) even when large. Other functioning and compressive tumours usually need transsphenoidal surgery, with medical therapy (somatostatin analogues, pegvisomant, steroidogenesis inhibitors) and radiotherapy as adjuncts. Replace deficient hormones, giving glucocorticoid before thyroxine. Apoplexy requires steroid cover and decompression when vision is threatened.
det.prognosis: Generally good; visual fields often improve after decompression, and hormone replacement is often lifelong.
pearls: Bitemporal hemianopia: image the pituitary.
Replace cortisol before thyroxine in hypopituitarism.
Prolactinomas shrink with cabergoline — surgery is rarely first-line.
det.thd: Pituitary disorders คือโรคของต่อมใต้สมอง ส่วนใหญ่เป็น adenoma ที่หลั่งฮอร์โมนเกิน (prolactin, GH, ACTH) หรือก้อนใหญ่กด optic chiasm ทำให้ลานสายตาด้านข้างขาดทั้งสองข้าง และทำให้ฮอร์โมนอื่นขาด Pituitary apoplexy เป็นภาวะฉุกเฉินที่ปวดศีรษะรุนแรงทันที ตามัว กลอกตาไม่ได้ ตรวจฮอร์โมน MRI และลานสายตา การรักษาได้แก่ cabergoline สำหรับ prolactinoma การผ่าตัดผ่านจมูก และให้ฮอร์โมนทดแทนโดยให้ cortisol ก่อน thyroxine

name: Pituitary tumours
formal: Mostly benign adenomas causing hormone excess or deficiency and bitemporal hemianopia from chiasm compression; prolactinoma most common.
simple: Usually non-cancerous growths of the pituitary gland that disturb hormones and may affect vision.
th: เนื้องอกต่อมใต้สมอง (pituitary neuroendocrine tumour) ส่วนใหญ่ไม่ร้ายแรง แบ่งเป็น functioning (prolactinoma, GH, ACTH, TSH) และ non-functioning ที่มักมาด้วยตามัวจาก optic chiasm ถูกกด (bitemporal hemianopia) ปวดศีรษะ และฮอร์โมนต่ำ ต้องตรวจฮอร์โมนทั้งแกน และแยก prolactinoma ซึ่งรักษาด้วยยาเป็นอันดับแรก ออกจากเนื้องอกชนิดอื่นที่ต้องผ่าตัดผ่านโพรงจมูก
tempoNote: Years of silent growth or endocrine change; sudden worsening only with apoplexy
feat: Macroadenoma is larger than 1 cm: upward growth compresses the chiasm to cause bitemporal hemianopia (often superior quadrants first), lateral growth invades the cavernous sinus to cause diplopia, headache is common

About 70% secrete a hormone: prolactin (amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea in women, sexual dysfunction and large tumours in men), growth hormone (acromegaly with carpal tunnel, sleep apnoea, hypertension, diabetes), ACTH (Cushing disease), rarely TSH (central hyperthyroidism)
Non-functioning adenomas present late with mass effect and loss of pituitary function; mild prolactin elevation can arise from stalk compression
Hypopituitarism develops in sequence (gonadotrophs, GH, thyrotrophs, then ACTH) and diabetes insipidus is uncommon before surgery
Pituitary apoplexy: sudden headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia and collapse from haemorrhage or infarction of the tumour
inv: Dedicated pituitary MRI with gadolinium; CT is only for bone anatomy or when MRI cannot be done

Endocrine panel: prolactin (with dilution if the tumour is large and the value modest, to avoid the hook effect), IGF-1, 8 a.m. cortisol or 24-hour urinary or late-night salivary cortisol with dexamethasone suppression when Cushing is suspected, free T4 with TSH, LH, FSH and sex steroids
Formal visual fields (perimetry), visual acuity and OCT of the retinal nerve fibre layer before and after treatment

case.who: 52-year-old man, a van driver from Chiang Rai
case.story: He has bumped his van against the kerb on the left side three times this month, has felt tired for a year and stopped having morning erections.
case.exam: Bitemporal hemianopia on confrontation, mild temporal pallor of both discs, normal eye movements, reduced body hair.
case.tests: MRI shows a 3.2 cm sellar and suprasellar mass lifting the chiasm; prolactin 62 ng/mL on direct assay but 3,100 ng/mL after 1:100 dilution; low testosterone and low free T4 with inappropriately normal TSH; morning cortisol low-normal.
case.q: What is the first-line treatment and what must be given first?
case.a: Giant prolactinoma with hook effect. Start a dopamine agonist (cabergoline) with close visual monitoring, and replace cortisol first if adrenal insufficiency is confirmed before thyroxine. Surgery is for failure, intolerance or visual deterioration.

det.patho: Pituitary tumours arise from anterior pituitary cells and are now termed pituitary neuroendocrine tumours; they are classified by hormone and transcription factor lineage (PIT1, TPIT, SF1). The old stain-based labels (chromophobe, acidophil, basophil) are obsolete because most apparently non-secretory tumours produce hormones detectable by immunostaining. Most are benign monoclonal adenomas, microadenomas are under 1 cm, and invasive or aggressive behaviour is uncommon. Posterior pituitary tumours are rare and metastases are the commonest lesion there.
det.clinical: Patients present with endocrine syndromes, with mass effect, or incidentally. Compression of the chiasm causes bitemporal field loss that patients often do not notice, and monocular loss from asymmetric compression or optic nerve involvement can occur. Acromegaly develops insidiously and carries two to three times the mortality because of cardiac, respiratory and metabolic complications. Cushing disease usually involves a microadenoma smaller than 5 mm, so imaging can be normal. TSH-secreting tumours are rare and are often large when found, sometimes after mistaken thyroid ablation.
det.diagnosis: Pair MRI with hormone testing in every sellar mass: a prolactin level, IGF-1 (a single random GH is unreliable), tests of the adrenal, thyroid and gonadal axes, and a water-deprivation or osmolality assessment only if diabetes insipidus is suspected. Prolactin above about 150–200 ng/mL with a macroadenoma points to a prolactinoma, while moderate elevations in a large mass suggest stalk compression or a hook effect. Cushing syndrome is confirmed biochemically before the source is pursued, and may need inferior petrosal sinus sampling because many corticotroph adenomas are not visible. Visual fields and OCT document damage and prognosis.
det.treatment: Prolactinomas are treated with dopamine agonists such as cabergoline, which normalise prolactin and shrink most tumours, even large ones with visual loss. Most other functioning and non-functioning tumours with mass effect are removed by an endoscopic transsphenoidal approach, followed by medication (somatostatin analogues, pegvisomant for acromegaly, steroidogenesis inhibitors for Cushing) or stereotactic radiosurgery for residual disease. Non-functioning microadenomas and incidentalomas without visual or endocrine effect are observed with periodic MRI and hormones. Hormone replacement is lifelong when needed, with glucocorticoid before thyroxine.
det.prognosis: Outcomes are good in expert hands: vision often improves if optic atrophy is not advanced, and prolactinomas often remain controlled on medication, but lifelong endocrine follow-up is needed.
pearls: Always check prolactin before operating on a sellar mass; dopamine agonists change the plan.
A 1:100 dilution rescues the hook effect: a huge mass with a modest prolactin should be re-assayed.
In hypopituitarism replace cortisol before thyroxine to avoid precipitating adrenal crisis.
det.thd: เนื้องอกต่อมใต้สมองส่วนใหญ่เป็น adenoma ชนิดไม่ร้ายแรง ประมาณ 70% หลั่งฮอร์โมน เช่น prolactin, GH, ACTH ถ้าโตเกิน 1 ซม. จะกด optic chiasm ทำให้ลานสายตาแคบด้านนอกทั้งสองข้าง (bitemporal hemianopia) ปวดศีรษะ และฮอร์โมนต่ำ การตรวจประกอบด้วย MRI ต่อมใต้สมอง ตรวจฮอร์โมนทุกแกน (ถ้าก้อนใหญ่แต่ prolactin ต่ำให้เจือจางตัวอย่างเพื่อกัน hook effect) และตรวจลานสายตา รักษา prolactinoma ด้วย cabergoline ส่วนชนิดอื่นผ่าตัดผ่านโพรงจมูก (transsphenoidal) ร่วมกับยาหรือรังสี และให้ฮอร์โมนทดแทนโดยให้ cortisol ก่อน thyroxine

qx.stem: A 58-year-old man from Udon Thani has a sudden severe headache with vomiting, double vision and blurred vision. He has a right third nerve palsy and a bitemporal field defect. Blood pressure is 88/50 mmHg and sodium is 128 mmol/L. CT shows a haemorrhagic sellar mass extending above the sella, and the angiogram is normal.
qx.q: Which is the most urgent first step?
opts: Start cabergoline and recheck the visual fields in a month
Begin intravenous mannitol for raised intracranial pressure
Give intravenous hydrocortisone after taking blood for cortisol and other pituitary hormones
Lumbar puncture to exclude aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage
Start levothyroxine to correct hypothyroidism
qx.why: Pituitary apoplexy can cause acute adrenal insufficiency, which explains the hypotension and hyponatraemia and can be fatal. Stress-dose hydrocortisone comes first, followed by early transsphenoidal decompression if vision is worsening or severely affected. Giving thyroxine before steroids can precipitate adrenal crisis, and cabergoline alone is not appropriate for acute apoplexy with visual loss.

name: Plasmocytoma
formal: Solitary plasma cell tumour of bone or soft tissue, affecting skull base or spine with cord or nerve root compression; may progress to myeloma.
simple: A single growth of abnormal plasma cells in bone that can press on nerves or the spinal cord.
th: เนื้องอก plasma cell ก้อนเดี่ยวในกระดูกหรือเนื้อเยื่ออ่อน มักที่กระดูกสันหลังหรือฐานกะโหลก กดไขสันหลังหรือรากประสาท อาจกลายเป็น multiple myeloma
tempoNote: Weeks to months of bone pain before deficit
feat: Older adults with localised bone pain, especially thoracic spine
Cord compression, radiculopathy or cranial neuropathies (skull base)
Lytic lesion on imaging without other myeloma features
Small paraprotein may be present
High risk of progression to multiple myeloma
inv: MRI spine; whole-body low-dose CT or PET-CT to exclude other lesions
SPEP, immunofixation, free light chains
Bone marrow biopsy (clonal plasma cells must be below 10%)
Biopsy of the lesion

case.story: Two months of mid-back pain, now leg weakness.
case.exam: Spastic paraparesis with T6 sensory level.
case.tests: MRI: lytic T5 lesion with epidural extension; PET no other lesions; marrow normal; biopsy: monoclonal plasma cells.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what is the definitive treatment?
case.a: Solitary plasmacytoma of bone with cord compression; decompression as needed, then local radiotherapy, with lifelong monitoring for myeloma.

det.patho: A plasmacytoma is a localised clonal plasma cell tumour. Solitary bone plasmacytoma arises in axial skeleton; extramedullary forms occur in the head and neck. Bone destruction and soft tissue extension compress neural structures.
det.clinical: Local pain is followed by neurological compression. Skull base lesions cause cranial neuropathies. Systemic myeloma features such as anaemia, hypercalcaemia and renal failure are absent by definition.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires biopsy-proven clonal plasma cells in one lesion, normal or minimally involved marrow and no other lesions on whole-body imaging. Paraprotein studies set a baseline for follow-up.
det.treatment: Radiotherapy to the lesion is the main treatment and often curative locally; surgery for instability or cord compression. Patients with marrow involvement may receive systemic therapy.
det.prognosis: Good local control, but most solitary bone plasmacytomas progress to myeloma within about 10 years.
pearls: Always image the whole skeleton before calling a plasmacytoma solitary.
Sclerotic plasmacytoma with neuropathy suggests POEMS.
Follow paraprotein levels for progression.
det.thd: Plasmacytoma คือเนื้องอก plasma cell ก้อนเดี่ยว มักเกิดที่กระดูกสันหลังหรือฐานกะโหลกในผู้สูงอายุ ทำให้ปวดหลังและกดไขสันหลัง รากประสาท หรือเส้นประสาทสมอง ต้องตรวจทั้งร่างกายและไขกระดูกเพื่อแยก multiple myeloma รักษาด้วยการฉายรังสีเฉพาะที่และผ่าตัดถ้ามีการกด และต้องติดตามเพราะอาจกลายเป็น myeloma

name: Plectin deficiency
formal: Autosomal recessive PLEC deficiency causing epidermolysis bullosa simplex with muscular dystrophy, and sometimes myasthenic features.
simple: An inherited condition with skin blistering and muscle weakness caused by a missing structural protein.
more: Diagnosis with skin and muscle immunostaining and PLEC genetics; supportive care, with some myasthenic cases improving on pyridostigmine.
ab: Epidermolysis bullosa simplex with muscular dystrophy
th: โรคพันธุกรรมยีนด้อยจากการขาด plectin ทำให้ผิวหนังพองง่ายร่วมกับกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงแบบ muscular dystrophy และบางรายมีอาการแบบ myasthenia
tempoNote: Skin blistering from birth or infancy; muscle weakness appears in childhood to adulthood and slowly worsens
feat: Fragile skin that blisters after minor friction from the newborn period, often with nail and tooth enamel changes
Slowly progressive proximal limb and sometimes facial or eye muscle weakness, starting from childhood to middle age
Ptosis, ophthalmoparesis and fatigable weakness in some patients, reflecting a coexisting neuromuscular junction defect
Possible laryngeal or airway narrowing and breathing difficulty; a limb-girdle form without skin disease also exists
inv: CK mildly to moderately raised; muscle biopsy shows dystrophic change and loss of plectin on immunostaining
Skin biopsy immunofluorescence: absent or reduced plectin at the basal keratinocyte layer
Repetitive nerve stimulation for decrement when fatigable features are present
PLEC gene sequencing confirms biallelic variants

case.story: Since infancy her hands and feet blister after rubbing. Over five years she has found climbing stairs and lifting her arms harder, and her eyelids droop by evening.
case.exam: Healed blister scars on feet, dystrophic toenails, bilateral ptosis worse after sustained upgaze, hip and shoulder girdle weakness.
case.tests: CK 1,100 U/L; 3-Hz stimulation shows 15% decrement; skin and muscle immunostaining lack plectin.
case.q: What single protein links her skin and muscle findings, and which drug may help the fatigable part?
case.a: Plectin (PLEC) — epidermolysis bullosa simplex with muscular dystrophy; pyridostigmine can help some patients with myasthenic features.

det.patho: Plectin is a large cytolinker protein that anchors intermediate filaments to hemidesmosomes in skin and to costameres, Z-discs, mitochondria and the postsynaptic membrane in muscle. Biallelic loss of function of PLEC weakens both basal keratinocytes and muscle fibres, so skin splits within the basal layer and muscle undergoes progressive dystrophic damage. Isoform-specific variants explain why some patients have only muscle disease. It is very rare, with fewer than a few hundred reported families.
det.clinical: The usual picture is lifelong skin fragility followed, sometimes decades later, by a slowly progressive myopathy affecting limb girdles and occasionally facial, bulbar and extraocular muscles. A subset has fatigable weakness and ptosis because the neuromuscular junction is also affected. Airway involvement and cardiomyopathy have been reported and can be life threatening. Other PLEC phenotypes include pyloric atresia in neonates and an isolated limb-girdle dystrophy.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it when blistering skin disease and a myopathy coexist. Skin and muscle immunostaining showing absent plectin are strong supportive evidence, and PLEC sequencing confirms the diagnosis. Repetitive stimulation helps show a transmission defect. Muscle MRI and biopsy show non-specific dystrophic features, so the skin history is the key clue.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying treatment exists. Wound and skin care, physiotherapy, respiratory monitoring with ventilatory support when needed, and cardiac review are the mainstays. Pyridostigmine has improved fatigable weakness in some reported patients and is reasonable to try when decrement is shown. Anaesthetists should be warned about airway fragility and skin injury.
det.prognosis: Progression is slow but variable; respiratory and airway complications determine survival in the more severe cases.
pearls: Blistering skin plus a dystrophy means think of plectin.
A positive decrement in a dystrophy patient may be treatable with pyridostigmine.
Not every PLEC patient has skin disease: one limb-girdle form spares the skin.
det.thd: plectin เป็นโปรตีนยึดโครงสร้างเซลล์ทั้งในผิวหนังและกล้ามเนื้อ เมื่อขาดจะเกิดผิวหนังพองง่ายตั้งแต่เด็กและกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงแบบ dystrophy ช้าๆ บางรายมีหนังตาตกและอ่อนล้าแบบ myasthenia การวินิจฉัยใช้ย้อม plectin ในผิวหนัง/กล้ามเนื้อและตรวจยีน PLEC การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง บางรายตอบสนองต่อ pyridostigmine

name: Pleomorphic xanthoastrocytomas (PXAs)
formal: Superficial temporal lobe astrocytoma in young people with seizures, BRAF V600E mutation and mostly good prognosis.
simple: A rare, usually slow-growing brain tumour near the surface, causing seizures in young people.
th: เนื้องอกกลีโอมาแบบตื้นที่ผิวสมอง มักอยู่กลีบขมับของเด็กโตและผู้ใหญ่ตอนต้น มาด้วยชัก มักมีการกลายพันธุ์ BRAF V600E และพยากรณ์โรคค่อนข้างดี
tempoNote: Seizures for months to years before diagnosis; grade 3 tumours can grow over weeks to months
feat: Children and young adults with long-standing focal seizures
Superficial, often temporal, cyst with an enhancing mural nodule abutting the meninges
Headache or focal deficit only when large or in the higher-grade form
BRAF V600E mutation and CDKN2A/B deletion in most
CNS WHO grade 2 or 3 depending on mitotic activity
inv: MRI with contrast: cortical cyst-plus-nodule, often with adjacent dural enhancement
Surgical histology with molecular testing (BRAF V600E, CDKN2A/B, methylation profile)
EEG and post-operative MRI surveillance

case.who: 19-year-old male university student from Chiang Mai
case.story: Five years of brief episodes of déjà vu with lip-smacking; recently had his first generalised seizure.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination.
case.tests: MRI: 3 cm right temporal cortical cyst with an enhancing nodule touching the dura; resection shows pleomorphic cells with lipid-laden cytoplasm, BRAF V600E positive.
case.q: Which molecular finding offers a targeted treatment option if it recurs?
case.a: BRAF V600E: recurrent or unresectable PXA may respond to BRAF plus MEK inhibitors (e.g. dabrafenib with trametinib).

det.patho: PXA is a rare astrocytic tumour (under 1% of gliomas) arising near the brain surface. Its large bizarre cells, lipid-laden xanthomatous cells and reticulin network give the name. Most harbour BRAF V600E with homozygous CDKN2A/B deletion, linking it to MAPK pathway activation; WHO 2021 grades tumours 2 or 3 by mitotic count.
det.clinical: The typical patient is a child or young adult with chronic drug-resistant focal seizures, most often from temporal lobe lesions. Larger tumours cause headache, raised intracranial pressure or focal deficits. Grade 3 tumours behave more aggressively and can disseminate along CSF pathways. Rarely PXA transforms or co-exists with ganglioglioma.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows a peripheral cystic mass with an enhancing nodule and frequent meningeal contact; calcification and oedema are variable. Definitive diagnosis needs tissue with immunohistochemistry and molecular testing; DNA methylation profiling helps separate PXA from epithelioid glioblastoma and ganglioglioma. Staging MRI of the spine is considered for grade 3 tumours.
det.treatment: Gross total resection is the main treatment and often controls seizures. Radiotherapy is used for grade 3 or incompletely resected recurrent tumours; chemotherapy has limited effect. BRAF and MEK inhibitors produce useful responses in BRAF V600E-positive recurrent tumours. Continue antiseizure medication and follow with serial MRI.
det.prognosis: Grade 2 PXA has 5-year survival around 80–90%, especially after complete resection; grade 3 has notably shorter survival.
pearls: Young person + temporal seizures + superficial cyst with a nodule touching dura: PXA or ganglioglioma.
Always test BRAF V600E; it opens targeted therapy for recurrence.
Extent of resection is the strongest modifiable prognostic factor.
det.thd: Pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma เป็นเนื้องอกกลีโอมาที่อยู่ตื้นใกล้เยื่อหุ้มสมอง มักพบที่กลีบขมับในเด็กโตและผู้ใหญ่ตอนต้น อาการเด่นคือชักเรื้อรัง MRI เป็นถุงน้ำมีก้อนเนื้อติดสี วินิจฉัยด้วยชิ้นเนื้อและตรวจ BRAF V600E รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัดออกให้มากที่สุด ถ้ากลับเป็นซ้ำอาจใช้ยามุ่งเป้า BRAF/MEK หรือฉายรังสี

name: Plexiform neurofibromas
formal: Diffuse nerve sheath tumours pathognomonic of NF1 involving multiple fascicles, with risk of malignant transformation; MEK inhibitors can shrink them.
simple: Large soft nerve tumours seen in neurofibromatosis that can grow along nerves and sometimes turn cancerous.
th: เนื้องอกปลอกประสาทแบบกระจายหลาย fascicle ที่จำเพาะต่อ NF1 อาจกลายเป็นมะเร็ง และยา MEK inhibitor ช่วยให้ยุบได้
tempoNote: Congenital, grow fastest in early childhood and adolescence
feat: Diffuse soft-tissue swelling, 'bag of worms' texture, overlying pigmentation or hypertrichosis
Disfigurement, pain, limb overgrowth, airway or spinal compression
Present in about a quarter to half of NF1 patients (many internal)
Lifetime MPNST risk roughly 8–15% in NF1
Atypical nodular lesions are precursors of MPNST
inv: MRI (including whole-body) with volumetric measurement
FDG-PET for suspicious growth or pain
Biopsy of distinct nodular lesions

case.story: Enlarging soft swelling on the right side of the neck since infancy, now causing pain and difficulty turning the head.
case.exam: Large soft mass with hyperpigmented overlying skin; multiple café-au-lait macules and freckles in both axillae.
case.tests: MRI: extensive plexiform neurofibroma involving cervical roots and brachial plexus; no FDG-avid nodules.
case.q: What medical therapy can shrink this tumour?
case.a: MEK inhibitor such as selumetinib (or mirdametinib), which reduces volume and pain in many children.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Neurocutaneous Syndromes

det.patho: Plexiform neurofibromas arise from Schwann cell precursors with NF1 loss, growing along many nerve fascicles or branches. Additional loss of CDKN2A/B produces atypical neurofibromas, and further hits (PRC2 loss) produce MPNST.
det.clinical: They may be superficial (disfiguring) or deep (compressing airway, spinal cord, bowel). Pain, functional loss and cosmetic concerns dominate. New pain or rapid growth raises concern for malignant change.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows multilobulated T2 bright masses with the 'target sign'. Whole-body MRI quantifies burden; PET and biopsy evaluate suspicious lesions.
det.treatment: MEK inhibitors (selumetinib, mirdametinib) shrink inoperable plexiform neurofibromas in most children and some adults. Surgery is used for accessible tumours but complete removal is rare. Pain management and physiotherapy support function.
det.prognosis: Chronic morbidity from growth and compression; MPNST is a major cause of reduced life expectancy in NF1.
pearls: Plexiform neurofibroma is pathognomonic for NF1.
New pain in a known plexiform tumour needs PET.
MEK inhibitors have changed management.
det.thd: Plexiform neurofibroma คือเนื้องอกปลอกประสาทที่โตตามหลาย fascicle เป็นลักษณะจำเพาะของ NF1 อาจทำให้ใบหน้าหรือแขนขาผิดรูป ปวด และกดอวัยวะสำคัญ เสี่ยงกลายเป็น MPNST ประมาณ 8–15% ตลอดชีวิต ยา MEK inhibitor เช่น selumetinib ช่วยให้ก้อนยุบและลดปวดในหลายราย

Encapsulated painful nodules on a nerve, NF2 or schwannomatosis
Rapid lymph node enlargement with systemic symptoms

name: Plexopathy
formal: Lesion of brachial or lumbosacral plexus from trauma, neoplasm, radiation or neuralgic amyotrophy, with multi-root deficits.
simple: Damage to a nerve network at the shoulder or hip causing arm or leg weakness and numbness.
more: Diagnose with EMG, nerve conduction and MRI plexus imaging, with CSF protein often raised in neuralgic amyotrophy or radiation injury. Treat the cause: analgesia, physiotherapy, immunotherapy for inflammatory forms and surgery for traumatic lesions. Disorders of brachial or lumbosacral plexus from trauma, tumour, radiation, inflammation or diabetes, with patchy weakness and sensory loss across several nerve roots. Diagnose with EMG and MRI of brachial or lumbosacral plexus, with neuralgic amyotrophy preceded by acute pain, and radiation plexopathy appearing years after treatment. Treatment depends on the cause and includes steroids, analgesia and rehabilitation.
th: รอยโรคที่ร่างแหประสาทแขนหรือขา ทำให้อ่อนแรงและชาเป็นหย่อมคร่อมหลายรากประสาทและหลายเส้นประสาท
tempoNote: Acute after trauma or in neuralgic amyotrophy; subacute to chronic with tumour infiltration, radiation or diabetes
feat: Weakness, wasting and sensory loss that do not fit a single root or a single peripheral nerve
Reflex loss in the affected limb with sparing of the paraspinal muscles on EMG
Pain is prominent in neuralgic amyotrophy, tumour infiltration and diabetic radiculoplexus neuropathy
Horner syndrome suggests lower trunk or T1 involvement near the lung apex
Radiation injury tends to be painless, upper-trunk predominant and may show myokymia
inv: Nerve conduction and EMG: reduced sensory potentials (lesion beyond the dorsal root ganglion) with normal paraspinal muscles
MRI of the brachial or lumbosacral plexus with contrast; CT or PET when tumour is suspected
Fasting glucose/HbA1c, and CSF or inflammatory markers when an immune cause is considered

case.who: 58-year-old woman from Khon Kaen, treated for left breast cancer 6 years ago
case.story: Over 4 months her left hand has become weak and numb along the inner forearm, with an aching shoulder at night.
case.exam: Wasting of the small hand muscles, weak finger flexors, reduced triceps jerk, sensory loss over medial forearm and ring and little fingers, left ptosis and small pupil.
case.tests: Absent ulnar and medial antebrachial cutaneous sensory responses; normal cervical paraspinals; MRI shows an enhancing mass at the lower trunk.
case.q: Why is this a plexus lesion rather than C8 radiculopathy, and which cause is likely?
case.a: Sensory responses are lost (post-ganglionic) and paraspinals are spared; painful lower-trunk lesion with Horner syndrome suggests tumour infiltration rather than radiation plexopathy.

read.where: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves — Plexopathies

det.patho: The brachial plexus (C5–T1) and lumbosacral plexus (L1–S4) mix fibres from several roots before they form named nerves, so damage produces deficits spanning several root and nerve territories. Causes include traction or penetrating trauma, compression by tumour or haematoma, direct neoplastic infiltration, delayed radiation fibrosis, immune-mediated inflammation (neuralgic amyotrophy) and microvasculitis in diabetic or non-diabetic radiculoplexus neuropathy. The lesion lies distal to the dorsal root ganglion, which is why sensory nerve action potentials fall.
det.clinical: Presentation depends on the part involved: upper-trunk lesions weaken shoulder abduction and elbow flexion, lower-trunk lesions affect hand muscles and the medial forearm, and lumbosacral lesions weaken hip and knee movement with patchy leg numbness. Sudden severe pain followed by weakness suggests neuralgic amyotrophy; asymmetric thigh pain, weight loss and weakness in a diabetic suggests radiculoplexus neuropathy. Tumour infiltration is usually painful and progressive, whereas radiation plexopathy is often painless and appears months to years after treatment.
det.diagnosis: Clinical localisation is confirmed electrodiagnostically: low sensory potentials, denervation in muscles of several nerves sharing a plexus element, and normal paraspinal EMG. Dedicated plexus MRI shows masses, swelling or enhancement; PET-CT helps separate recurrent tumour from radiation change. Glucose, inflammatory markers, and sometimes CSF are added. Bilateral or very proximal involvement should prompt consideration of a root or anterior horn process instead.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: oncological therapy for infiltration, surgical exploration, grafting or nerve transfer for selected traumatic lesions (ideally within 3–6 months), and corticosteroids are sometimes given early in neuralgic amyotrophy or immune radiculoplexus neuropathy though evidence is limited. Neuropathic pain agents, physiotherapy to prevent contractures and frozen shoulder, and orthoses support recovery. Radiation plexopathy has no proven reversal; protect the limb and manage pain.
det.prognosis: Inflammatory and diabetic forms usually improve over months to years; traumatic avulsions and radiation injury recover poorly.
pearls: Lost sensory potentials with spared paraspinals point to plexus rather than root.
Painful lower-trunk plexopathy plus Horner syndrome after cancer suggests tumour; painless upper-trunk weakness with myokymia suggests radiation.
Diabetic thigh pain and weakness with weight loss is lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy, not just a compressive lesion.

name: Pneumococcal meningitis
formal: Bacterial meningitis due to Streptococcus pneumoniae, most common in adults, with fever, neck stiffness and encephalopathy; treat with ceftriaxone, vancomycin and dexamethasone.
simple: A serious brain-lining infection caused by pneumococcus bacteria, needing urgent antibiotics.
th: เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบจาก Streptococcus pneumoniae พบบ่อยที่สุดในผู้ใหญ่และตายสูงที่สุดในกลุ่มแบคทีเรีย ต้องให้ ceftriaxone ร่วมกับ vancomycin และ dexamethasone ก่อนหรือพร้อมยาปฏิชีวนะโดสแรก
tempoNote: Fever, headache and drowsiness evolve over hours to 2 days; often follows or accompanies otitis, sinusitis or pneumonia
feat: Fever, headache and neck stiffness with early drowsiness or stupor; altered consciousness is the strongest clinical pointer in adults
Seizures and focal deficits (hemiparesis, aphasia, cranial nerve palsy) are more frequent than with meningococcal disease
Source of entry: otitis media, mastoiditis, sinusitis, pneumonia, or a CSF leak after skull base fracture or surgery; recurrent meningitis suggests a persistent leak
Risk groups: age over 60, alcohol use, diabetes, splenectomy or hyposplenism, cochlear implant, HIV and other immunosuppression
Complications: raised intracranial pressure, cerebral infarction or venous thrombosis, hydrocephalus, sensorineural deafness
inv: Blood cultures first, then lumbar puncture unless it must be delayed for imaging (new seizure, immunosuppression, papilloedema, focal signs, severely reduced consciousness); never delay antibiotics for the scan
CSF: neutrophils in the hundreds to thousands, protein high, glucose low (CSF to blood ratio under 0.4); Gram stain shows lancet-shaped Gram-positive diplococci in most untreated cases
Pneumococcal antigen or multiplex PCR when pre-treated; penicillin and ceftriaxone MIC from the isolate
CT or MRI of sinuses, mastoids and skull base to look for a parameningeal focus or CSF leak; MRI brain if deficits persist

case.who: 64-year-old retired teacher with diabetes, living in Nakhon Ratchasima
case.story: Three days of right ear pain and runny nose, then high fever, headache and increasing sleepiness since morning; one brief generalised seizure in the emergency department.
case.exam: Temperature 39.2 C, GCS 10, stiff neck, purulent discharge from the right ear, no rash, mild left-sided weakness.
case.tests: CSF opening pressure 32 cm, 2,800 cells (90% neutrophils), glucose 1.1 mmol/L with blood glucose 9.8, protein 3.4 g/L; Gram-positive diplococci; blood culture later grows penicillin-intermediate S. pneumoniae.
case.q: What empirical regimen and adjunct should have been started before the scan?
case.a: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours plus vancomycin (and ampicillin because he is over 50), with dexamethasone 10 mg IV 6-hourly for 4 days given with or just before the first antibiotic dose; stop dexamethasone if the cause turns out not to be pneumococcus or Hib.

det.patho: Pneumococci colonise the nasopharynx and reach the subarachnoid space through the bloodstream or by direct spread from the ear, sinus or a skull defect. The polysaccharide capsule and pneumolysin help the organism evade complement and injure ciliated and endothelial cells. Once bacteria multiply in CSF, which lacks effective defences, lysis by antibiotics releases cell-wall fragments that drive a violent cytokine response, cerebral oedema, vasculitis and cortical injury. This host inflammation explains why pneumococcal meningitis kills more patients and leaves more deficits than other common causes.
det.clinical: Adults usually have an upper respiratory, ear or lung infection and then a fast drop in alertness; many are stuporous on arrival, and neck stiffness may be absent in elderly or deeply obtunded patients. Seizures and focal signs occur early in a sizeable minority. Death often comes days later from cardiorespiratory failure, raised pressure or herniation rather than from the first insult. Survivors may have deafness, cognitive slowing, epilepsy or hydrocephalus, and cochlear implant recipients face an especially high risk.
det.diagnosis: Take blood cultures and treat at once; lumbar puncture follows if there is no contraindication, and CT before the tap is reserved for patients with seizure, immunosuppression, focal deficit, papilloedema or marked impairment of consciousness. A neutrophilic CSF with low glucose and a Gram stain showing diplococci is almost diagnostic; antigen or PCR helps once antibiotics have started. The isolate must have penicillin and third-generation cephalosporin MICs reported, because resistant strains change the regimen. Look for the source (ears, sinuses, lungs, endocarditis, CSF leak) and test HIV status.
det.treatment: Empirical therapy is a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone 2 g twice daily) plus vancomycin, and ampicillin when age exceeds 50 or immunity is impaired; narrow after susceptibility is known, with a full course of 10 to 14 days for pneumococcus. Dexamethasone 10 mg every 6 hours for 4 days, started before or with the first antibiotic dose, lowers mortality and hearing loss in adults in high-income settings; evidence of benefit is weak in advanced HIV and in very late presenters. Treat seizures, raised pressure and shock, repair any CSF leak and give pneumococcal conjugate and polysaccharide vaccination afterwards to high-risk patients. Audiology should be arranged early, because ossification of the cochlea after meningitis makes late implant surgery harder.
det.prognosis: Mortality is about 20 to 30 per cent in adults even with modern care and falls with early dexamethasone; a quarter or more of survivors have hearing loss or neurological sequelae.
pearls: Treat first, image second: delay in the first hours is the strongest modifiable risk factor for death.
Pneumococcal meningitis plus a persistent ear or nasal discharge after trauma should prompt a hunt for a CSF leak.
Vancomycin penetrates CSF less well when dexamethasone damps inflammation, so use adequate dosing with a loading dose and monitor levels.
det.thd: Pneumococcal meningitis เป็นเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบจากแบคทีเรียที่พบบ่อยในผู้ใหญ่และมีอัตราตายสูงที่สุด มักตามหลังหูชั้นกลางอักเสบ ไซนัสอักเสบ ปอดอักเสบ หรือมีน้ำไขสันหลังรั่ว ผู้ป่วยมีไข้ ปวดศีรษะ คอแข็ง ซึมเร็ว และอาจชัก ต้องเจาะเลือดเพาะเชื้อแล้วให้ ceftriaxone ร่วมกับ vancomycin (เพิ่ม ampicillin ถ้าอายุเกิน 50 ปี) พร้อม dexamethasone ก่อนหรือพร้อมยาแรก ไม่ต้องรอผลภาพถ่ายถ้ามีข้อบ่งชี้ว่าต้องทำก่อน และต้องติดตามการได้ยินหลังหาย

qx.stem: A 34-year-old woman from Khon Kaen with fever, stiff neck and drowsiness has Gram-positive diplococci in the CSF. Ceftriaxone has just been started, and she asks about adjunctive corticosteroids.
qx.q: Which use of corticosteroids is consistent with WHO advice?
opts: Start dexamethasone after 24 hours of antibiotics and continue for 10 days
Do not use corticosteroids in bacterial meningitis
Start dexamethasone with the first antibiotic dose and continue for a maximum of 4 days when pneumococcus is confirmed
Give oral glycerol routinely
Continue dexamethasone for 4 weeks
qx.why: Outside epidemics, where a lumbar puncture is feasible, WHO strongly recommends intravenous corticosteroids, preferably dexamethasone, starting with the first antibiotic dose in suspected bacterial meningitis, and continuing for up to four days if the CSF and pathogen (pneumococcus or Hib) support it. Benefit declines with delay. Glycerol is not recommended, and steroids are not routinely used in meningococcal epidemics or cerebral malaria.

name: POEMS syndrome
formal: Plasma cell dyscrasia with polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, M-protein and skin changes, driven by VEGF; treated with radiotherapy or myeloma-directed therapy.
simple: A rare condition linked to abnormal blood cells that causes nerve damage, enlarged organs, hormone problems and skin changes.
th: POEMS — เส้นประสาทเสื่อม อวัยวะโต ต่อมไร้ท่อผิดปกติ โปรตีนโมโนโคลนอล (lambda) ผิวหนังเปลี่ยน VEGF สูงมาก มักถูกวินิจฉัยผิดเป็น CIDP
feat: Progressive distal, then proximal, demyelinating-axonal neuropathy with prominent weakness
Organomegaly, endocrinopathy, lambda M-protein, skin changes (hyperpigmentation, haemangiomas, clubbing)
Sclerotic bone lesions, Castleman disease, papilloedema, oedema/ascites, thrombocytosis
Often initially treated as CIDP without benefit
inv: Immunofixation (lambda light chain almost always) — small bands are easy to miss
Plasma/serum VEGF (markedly raised)
CT/PET-CT for sclerotic lesions; endocrine panel

case.q: What is the first-line treatment if the sclerotic lesion is solitary?

qx.why: A treatment-refractory demyelinating neuropathy with a lambda monoclonal protein, thrombocytosis, skin changes, organomegaly and oedema suggests POEMS syndrome. Markedly raised serum VEGF and sclerotic bone lesions on CT or skeletal survey are the key confirmatory findings; treatment targets the plasma-cell clone (radiotherapy or lenalidomide-based therapy, autologous transplant), not IVIG. Anti-MAG neuropathy is IgM kappa and distal, and nodal antibodies are another cause of poor IVIG response but do not explain the systemic features.
