det.patho: POEMS is a paraneoplastic syndrome of a small plasma-cell clone that almost always produces a lambda light chain. The clone drives very high levels of VEGF and other cytokines, which increase vascular permeability and cause oedema, organomegaly, skin changes and endoneurial microangiopathy. The neuropathy combines demyelination with prominent axonal loss and tends to be motor-predominant.
det.clinical: Patients usually present with a progressive, symmetric, distal-to-proximal sensorimotor neuropathy that is often misdiagnosed as CIDP and fails IVIG. Systemic clues include hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, endocrine disturbance (hypogonadism, hypothyroidism, diabetes), hyperpigmentation, glomeruloid haemangiomas, white nails, clubbing, peripheral oedema, ascites, pleural effusion, papilloedema, thrombocytosis and polycythaemia. Neuropathic pain and weight loss are frequent. Untreated disease progresses to wheelchair dependence and cardiorespiratory complications.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires polyneuropathy and a monoclonal plasma-cell disorder (both mandatory), at least one major criterion (sclerotic bone lesions, Castleman disease, raised VEGF) and at least one minor criterion. NCS show uniform slowing and more severe axonal loss than typical CIDP, with less temporal dispersion. Use immunofixation (small bands are easily missed), serum or plasma VEGF, and CT or PET-CT for sclerotic lesions; bone marrow biopsy may show lambda-restricted clonal plasma cells.
det.treatment: One to a few sclerotic lesions without marrow disease are treated with targeted radiotherapy. Widespread disease or marrow involvement is treated with systemic therapy such as lenalidomide-dexamethasone or autologous stem cell transplantation after high-dose chemotherapy. Avoid neurotoxic drugs such as bortezomib and thalidomide where possible, given the neuropathy. Supportive care includes orthoses, physiotherapy and management of oedema and endocrine deficits; VEGF is used to monitor response.
det.prognosis: With effective therapy most patients stabilise and neurological recovery continues slowly over 1–3 years; long-term survival is good.
pearls: IVIG-refractory 'CIDP' with a lambda band: check VEGF and look for sclerotic bone lesions.
Thrombocytosis and polycythaemia are useful laboratory hints.
Neurological improvement lags behind the haematological response by months.
det.thd: POEMS เป็นกลุ่มอาการจากเซลล์พลาสมาผิดปกติที่สร้าง lambda light chain และกระตุ้นให้ VEGF สูงมาก ทำให้เส้นประสาทเสื่อมแบบอ่อนแรงเด่น ร่วมกับอวัยวะโต ต่อมไร้ท่อผิดปกติ ผิวคล้ำ บวม และมีรอยโรคกระดูกแบบ sclerotic มักถูกวินิจฉัยผิดเป็น CIDP ที่ไม่ตอบสนองต่อ IVIG การวินิจฉัยใช้ immunofixation ระดับ VEGF และ CT/PET หารอยโรคกระดูก การรักษาคือฉายรังสีหากรอยโรคมีจำนวนน้อย หรือให้ยาเคมีบำบัดร่วมกับปลูกถ่ายเซลล์ต้นกำเนิดหากโรคกระจาย

name: POLG disorders
formal: Disorders caused by variants in POLG, the catalytic subunit of mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma, ranging from infantile Alpers–Huttenlocher syndrome to the adolescent/adult ataxia–neuropathy spectrum (MIRAS, SANDO) and progressive external ophthalmoplegia; valproate can precipitate fatal liver failure.
simple: Inherited faults in the enzyme that copies mitochondrial DNA, causing unsteadiness, numbness, seizures, droopy eyelids and, with the drug valproate, dangerous liver failure.
more: Confirmed by POLG sequencing; avoid valproate. Treatment is supportive; severity varies from childhood fatal to adult-onset forms.
th: โรคไมโทคอนเดรียจากยีน POLG — วัยรุ่น/ผู้ใหญ่มาด้วยเดินเซจากเส้นประสาทรับความรู้สึก พูดไม่ชัด หนังตาตก กลอกตาได้น้อย กระตุก ชักดื้อยา ห้ามใช้ valproate
tempoNote: Ataxia-neuropathy usually begins in the teens to 40s and progresses slowly; sudden stepwise worsening with status epilepticus or stroke-like episodes
feat: Sensory ataxia from dorsal root ganglion loss, with areflexia and positive Romberg
Cerebellar dysarthria, nystagmus and limb ataxia
Ptosis and external ophthalmoplegia (SANDO), often late
Myoclonus and focal occipital seizures that may become continuous (EPC) or evolve to status
Liver dysfunction, migraine-like headaches, gut dysmotility
inv: POLG sequencing (common recessive variants include p.A467T and p.W748S)
MRI: T2 lesions in thalami, cerebellar white matter, inferior olives; cortical stroke-like changes during seizures
NCS: sensory neuronopathy (absent sensory potentials, motor relatively spared)
Liver tests before any antiseizure drug; lactate; muscle biopsy may show multiple mtDNA deletions

case.who: 33-year-old woman, rice farmer from Roi Et
case.story: Unsteady in the dark for six years, eyelids drooping. Admitted with continuous jerking of the right hand and blurred vision; started on IV valproate at another hospital.
case.exam: Bilateral ptosis, limited upgaze, absent reflexes, loss of vibration and position sense to the hips, ataxic speech, right arm epilepsia partialis continua.
case.tests: NCS: absent sensory potentials with normal motor; MRI: left occipital cortical swelling and bilateral thalamic T2 lesions; ALT rising to 400 U/L on day 3.
case.q: What must be changed immediately, and what is the likely genetic diagnosis?
case.a: Stop valproate at once (risk of fatal liver failure) and switch to another agent such as levetiracetam; POLG ataxia–neuropathy spectrum (SANDO/MIRAS).

det.patho: Polymerase gamma replicates and repairs mitochondrial DNA. Recessive POLG variants cause mtDNA depletion (in brain and liver) or multiple deletions (in muscle and neurons), impairing oxidative phosphorylation. POLG is one of the commonest single-gene causes of mitochondrial disease, and the p.A467T and p.W748S variants are frequent in Europeans.
det.clinical: The ataxia–neuropathy spectrum combines sensory neuronopathy, cerebellar ataxia and dysarthria, with ophthalmoparesis, myoclonus and epilepsy variably present. Seizures often arise from the occipital lobe and can escalate to refractory status or epilepsia partialis continua, sometimes as the first presentation. Liver failure, psychiatric symptoms, parkinsonism and premature ovarian failure occur. Alpers–Huttenlocher syndrome is the severe infantile end, with intractable seizures and hepatic failure.
det.diagnosis: Consider POLG in any adult with sensory neuronopathy plus ataxia, ophthalmoplegia or new-onset refractory occipital seizures. MRI thalamic and olivary T2 lesions are suggestive. Confirm by POLG sequencing; test before prescribing valproate when the phenotype fits. Muscle biopsy may show COX-deficient fibres and multiple deletions.
det.treatment: Valproate is contraindicated because it can trigger fulminant, often fatal, liver failure in POLG disease. Use levetiracetam, benzodiazepines, lacosamide and other non-hepatotoxic agents; status epilepticus may need anaesthetic agents with care (limit prolonged propofol). Supportive care includes physiotherapy, ptosis surgery, nutrition and liver monitoring. Liver transplantation is generally not advised because neurological disease progresses.
det.prognosis: Variable; adult ataxia–neuropathy can be slow, but status epilepticus and liver failure are major causes of early death.
pearls: Sensory ataxia + ptosis/ophthalmoplegia + dysarthria = SANDO; test POLG.
Never give valproate to a suspected POLG patient; check liver tests and genetics.
New refractory occipital seizures or EPC in a young adult: consider POLG.
det.thd: POLG เป็นยีนที่ทำหน้าที่คัดลอก DNA ของไมโทคอนเดรีย ผู้ป่วยวัยรุ่นหรือผู้ใหญ่มีเดินเซจากเส้นประสาทรับความรู้สึกเสื่อม พูดไม่ชัด หนังตาตกและกลอกตาได้น้อย (SANDO/MIRAS) อาจมีกระตุกและชักจากสมองส่วน occipital จนเป็น status epilepticus ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน POLG ห้ามใช้ valproate เพราะทำให้ตับวายรุนแรง ใช้ levetiracetam หรือยาอื่นแทน

name: Poliomyelitis
formal: Enteroviral infection of anterior horn motor neurons causing asymmetric flaccid paralysis; prevented by vaccination.
simple: A virus infection that damages nerves controlling muscles, causing paralysis; prevented by vaccine.
more: Diagnose from acute asymmetric flaccid paralysis with CSF pleocytosis and stool or throat viral isolation; EMG shows denervation. No specific treatment exists, so care is supportive. Eradication relies on oral or inactivated vaccine.
th: โปลิโอเกิดจากไวรัสโปลิโอทำลายเซลล์ประสาทสั่งการที่ปีกหน้าไขสันหลัง ทำให้แขนขาอ่อนแรงแบบปวกเปียกไม่สมมาตร ไม่มีความผิดปกติของการรับความรู้สึก ป้องกันได้ด้วยวัคซีน ต้องรายงานทุกราย AFP
tempoNote: Prodromal fever then weakness evolving over 1 to 3 days (rarely a week) and then stabilising; later decades bring post-polio syndrome
feat: Fever, headache and sore throat (minor illness), a pause, then fever, meningism and severe muscle pain preceding asymmetrical flaccid paralysis
Legs more than arms, proximal more than distal; reflexes lost in the weak limbs while sensation stays intact
Bulbar form (cranial nerves IX and X most often) causes dysphagia, nasal voice and respiratory failure; respiratory muscle paralysis is the main killer
More than 90 per cent of infections are silent; paralysis occurs in about 1 in 200 non-immune infections

Strenuous exercise, injections, tonsillectomy and pregnancy during the early illness increase the risk of paralysis in a limb; B-cell immunodeficiency permits prolonged infection with vaccine-derived virus
inv: Two stool specimens taken 24 to 48 hours apart within 14 days of onset for poliovirus isolation and intratypic differentiation, as part of AFP surveillance
CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis early with mildly raised protein; PCR may support but does not replace stool culture
MRI: T2 hyperintensity of anterior horns; EMG after 2 to 3 weeks shows denervation in a patchy distribution
Vaccination history and exposure to oral polio vaccine recipients or travellers from endemic areas

case.who: 3-year-old unvaccinated boy from a migrant worker family at a construction site in Samut Sakhon
case.story: Four days of fever and leg pain; today he refuses to stand and drags his left leg.
case.exam: Alert, febrile, neck stiffness, flaccid left leg with absent knee and ankle reflexes, normal sensation, normal right leg.
case.tests: CSF 62 cells/µL (lymphocytes), protein 0.5 g/L; MRI shows T2 hyperintensity in the lumbar anterior horns.
case.q: What must be done immediately, beyond treatment of the child?
case.a: Report as acute flaccid paralysis at once, collect two stool samples within 14 days for poliovirus testing, and organise outbreak response immunisation of contacts and the community.

det.patho: Poliovirus, an enterovirus with three serotypes, is ingested, replicates in the pharynx and Peyer patches, and spreads in the blood. It reaches the CNS through the bloodstream or along peripheral nerves from muscle, then destroys anterior horn motor neurons and brainstem motor nuclei. The severity of paralysis tracks the number of neurons lost, not their location. Immunity is type-specific and lifelong; vaccine-derived strains can circulate where coverage is low.
det.clinical: Most infections are asymptomatic. A minority develops fever and meningitis, and 1 per cent or fewer of infections progress to paralysis. Pain and cramps precede weakness, which is asymmetrical and patchy and may involve one limb or the full body; reflexes vanish early in affected limbs. Bulbar polio causes swallowing and breathing failure, and mortality reaches 5 to 10 per cent in paralytic disease and more with respiratory involvement. Years later, decades after recovery, some patients develop post-polio syndrome with fatigue, pain and new weakness.
det.diagnosis: Any acute flaccid paralysis in a child under 15 is treated as polio until proven otherwise, and two stool samples within 14 days confirm the virus and its origin (wild or vaccine-derived). CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, which separates polio from Guillain-Barré syndrome; MRI shows anterior horn change; EMG shows patchy denervation. Other causes include enterovirus A71 and D68, West Nile and Japanese encephalitis flaviviruses, transverse myelitis and GBS. Report suspected cases without waiting for results.
det.treatment: There is no antiviral treatment; care is supportive with bed rest, pain control, respiratory support and swallowing management, followed by physiotherapy and orthoses to prevent contractures. Avoid intramuscular injections and strenuous exercise during the acute illness. Prevention relies on the vaccine: inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) is the backbone in most national programmes, and oral vaccine (bivalent and novel monovalent type 2) is used for outbreak response, with vaccine-derived virus responsible for the rare vaccine-associated paralysis. Thailand has been certified polio-free for years, but importations and vaccine-derived outbreaks elsewhere keep surveillance and immunisation essential.
det.prognosis: Weakness stabilises within a few weeks and partly recovers over about 2 years; permanent limb paralysis and deformities are common, and respiratory involvement carries the main risk of death.
pearls: Asymmetric flaccid paralysis with fever, preserved sensation and lymphocytic CSF equals polio until stool tests say otherwise.
Every AFP case in a child under 15 needs two stool samples within 14 days; the surveillance system depends on it.
Avoid injections in the early illness: intramuscular injection can localise paralysis to the injected limb.
det.thd: โปลิโอเกิดจากไวรัสโปลิโอที่ทำลายเซลล์ประสาทสั่งการที่ปีกหน้าไขสันหลังและก้านสมอง เด็กไม่ได้รับวัคซีนมีไข้ ปวดกล้ามเนื้อ แล้วอ่อนแรงแบบปวกเปียกไม่สมมาตร รีเฟล็กซ์หาย แต่ความรู้สึกปกติ ส่วนใหญ่ติดเชื้อโดยไม่มีอาการ น้ำไขสันหลังมีเซลล์ลิมโฟไซต์ ยืนยันด้วยตัวอย่างอุจจาระ 2 ครั้งภายใน 14 วัน ไม่มียาต้านไวรัสเฉพาะ ต้องรายงานเป็นผู้ป่วย AFP ทันทีและป้องกันด้วยวัคซีน

Sensory level and bladder involvement with a longitudinal cord lesion

name: Poliomyeloradiculitis
formal: Viral infection involving anterior horn cells and nerve roots, causing flaccid paralysis and radicular pain, as in polio or enterovirus infections.
simple: A viral infection of spinal nerve cells and roots causing weakness and pain.
th: การติดเชื้อไวรัสที่ลุกลามทั้ง anterior horn และรากประสาท ทำให้อัมพาตอ่อนปวกเปียกร่วมกับปวดตามแนวรากประสาท
tempoNote: Days to a few weeks
feat: Flaccid, often asymmetric limb weakness with areflexia
Radicular pain and sometimes patchy sensory loss from root involvement
Urinary retention when sacral roots are affected
Causes: enteroviruses, West Nile and Japanese encephalitis viruses, CMV in advanced HIV, VZV, rabies (paralytic form)
inv: CSF: pleocytosis (neutrophilic in CMV polyradiculitis), raised protein; PCR for enteroviruses, CMV, VZV, flaviviruses
MRI spine with contrast: anterior horn signal and root enhancement
EMG/NCS: denervation with low motor amplitudes, sensory changes if roots/DRG involved; HIV test and CD4

case.who: 36-year-old man with untreated HIV from Chon Buri
case.story: Over two weeks he developed burning buttock pain, leg weakness and difficulty passing urine.
case.exam: Flaccid paraparesis with absent leg reflexes, saddle hypoaesthesia, distended bladder.
case.tests: CD4 18 cells/µL; CSF 600 cells/µL mostly neutrophils, protein 2.5 g/L, CMV PCR positive; MRI cauda equina enhancement.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and treatment?
case.a: CMV lumbosacral polyradiculitis; IV ganciclovir (with or without foscarnet) then antiretroviral therapy timed to limit IRIS.

det.patho: Neurotropic viruses infect lower motor neurons and, unlike classic polio, also inflame dorsal and ventral roots and sometimes the dorsal root ganglia. Damage is a mix of direct cytolysis and inflammatory infiltration. The term is descriptive rather than a single disease.
det.clinical: The picture combines lower motor neuron weakness with radicular pain, which helps separate it from pure anterior horn disease. Sacral involvement causes retention and saddle sensory loss. Associated encephalitis (flaviviruses) or retinitis (CMV) give clues to the cause.
det.diagnosis: Confirm a lower motor neuron pattern on exam and EMG, then define the agent with CSF PCR, serology (IgM) and immune status. MRI excludes compression and shows root enhancement or anterior horn signal. Exclude GBS, compressive cauda equina lesions and lymphomatous infiltration.
det.treatment: Treatment depends on cause: ganciclovir or foscarnet for CMV, acyclovir for VZV, and supportive care for enteroviral and flaviviral infections. Bladder care, pain control and early rehabilitation are important. Start or optimise ART in HIV.
det.prognosis: Variable; enteroviral disease often leaves some weakness, while untreated CMV polyradiculitis is rapidly disabling.
pearls: Flaccid weakness plus root pain points beyond pure polio.
Neutrophilic CSF in advanced HIV with cauda equina syndrome: think CMV.
Always check CD4 count and HIV status.
det.thd: Poliomyeloradiculitis คือการติดเชื้อไวรัสที่ลุกลามทั้งเซลล์ประสาทสั่งการและรากประสาท ทำให้อ่อนแรงแบบปวกเปียก รีเฟล็กซ์หาย ร่วมกับปวดตามรากประสาทและปัสสาวะลำบาก สาเหตุเช่น enterovirus, ไวรัสกลุ่ม flavivirus และ CMV ในผู้ป่วย HIV ระยะท้าย วินิจฉัยด้วยน้ำไขสันหลังและ MRI รักษาตามเชื้อ เช่น ganciclovir สำหรับ CMV

ddx.pt: Purely motor, anterior horn only, unvaccinated child; stool poliovirus
Symmetric, acellular CSF with high protein
The HIV/CMV form of this syndrome in advanced immunosuppression

aN: polioradiculitis | poliomyeloradiculopathy | anterior horn and root infection | lumbosacral polyradiculomyelitis

name: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN)
formal: Necrotising vasculitis of medium arteries causing mononeuritis multiplex, stroke, hypertension and renal infarcts; hepatitis B associated.
simple: Inflammation of medium-sized arteries that can damage nerves, kidneys and other organs.
more: Diagnose from nerve and muscle biopsy or angiography showing aneurysms, with raised inflammatory markers; ANCA is usually negative. Treat with steroids plus cyclophosphamide, with antivirals and plasma exchange for hepatitis B related disease. Necrotising medium-vessel vasculitis causing mononeuritis multiplex, stroke and renal involvement; associated with hepatitis B.
th: หลอดเลือดขนาดกลางอักเสบแบบเนื้อตาย ทำให้เกิด mononeuritis multiplex stroke ความดันสูง และไตขาดเลือด สัมพันธ์กับไวรัสตับอักเสบบี และ ANCA มักเป็นลบ
tempoNote: Systemic illness over weeks to months with stepwise nerve infarcts; stroke and encephalopathy usually later
feat: Fever, weight loss, myalgia and arthralgia with a painful asymmetric mononeuritis multiplex (the commonest neurological feature)
Skin: livedo racemosa, nodules, ulcers or digital ischaemia
New hypertension, renal infarcts, abdominal pain from mesenteric ischaemia, testicular pain
CNS involvement (stroke, haemorrhage, encephalopathy) in a minority, usually later
Spares lungs and glomeruli; ANCA negative (separates it from microscopic polyangiitis)
inv: ESR/CRP raised; hepatitis B surface antigen and DNA, hepatitis C, ANCA (negative), cryoglobulins
NCS: multifocal axonal neuropathy
Biopsy of affected nerve with muscle, or skin nodule: necrotising inflammation of medium arteries
Mesenteric/renal angiography (CT or catheter): microaneurysms and stenoses when biopsy is not feasible

case.story: Two months of fever, 8 kg weight loss and abdominal pain after meals; then sudden right wrist drop and left foot drop with burning pain.
case.exam: BP 170/105, livedo on the thighs, testicular tenderness, right radial and left peroneal neuropathies.
case.tests: CRP 120, HBsAg positive with high viral load, ANCA negative, urine without casts; CT angiography shows renal and mesenteric microaneurysms.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and how does the HBV status change treatment?
case.a: Hepatitis B-associated PAN; treat with antiviral therapy plus a short course of steroids and plasma exchange rather than prolonged heavy immunosuppression.

read.where: Cerebrovascular Disease — Vasculitis of the Central Nervous System: Noninfectious Cerebral Vasculitis

Section 6 Systemic Disorders That Also Involve the Cerebrovascular System

det.patho: PAN is a necrotising vasculitis of medium and small muscular arteries without glomerulonephritis or capillary involvement. Segmental inflammation produces fibrinoid necrosis, thrombosis and aneurysms, leading to infarction of nerves, gut, kidney, skin and testis. Hepatitis B immune complexes cause a distinct subgroup that has become less common with vaccination. A PAN-like illness in children and young adults with early strokes is caused by ADA2 deficiency (DADA2).
det.clinical: More than half of patients have peripheral nerve involvement, usually as a painful mononeuritis multiplex that may later look like an asymmetric polyneuropathy. Systemic clues include fever, weight loss, renovascular hypertension, abdominal angina, skin lesions and orchitis. CNS manifestations (lacunar or territorial stroke, haemorrhage, seizures) are less common and often occur in uncontrolled disease or with hypertension.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis combines the clinical picture with biopsy of an involved tissue or angiographic microaneurysms in renal and mesenteric arteries. ANCA must be negative and small-vessel features absent. Test for HBV, HCV and HIV. In young patients with PAN-like disease and lacunar strokes, measure ADA2 activity or sequence ADA2.
det.treatment: Non-viral PAN is treated with glucocorticoids; cyclophosphamide is added for severe disease (neuropathy with major deficit, renal, gut, cardiac or CNS involvement), followed by azathioprine or methotrexate maintenance. HBV-associated PAN is managed with antivirals (e.g. entecavir or tenofovir), a brief steroid course and plasma exchange. DADA2 responds to TNF inhibitors, which prevent strokes. Control blood pressure carefully.
det.prognosis: With treatment, five-year survival exceeds 80%; relapses are more frequent in non-viral PAN, and gut, cardiac or renal involvement worsens outlook.
pearls: Mononeuritis multiplex + fever + new hypertension + negative ANCA: think PAN.
Always test hepatitis B; it changes treatment completely.
Childhood PAN with lacunar strokes: check ADA2 deficiency.
det.thd: PAN เป็นหลอดเลือดขนาดกลางอักเสบแบบเนื้อตาย ทำให้เส้นประสาทขาดเลือดเป็นเส้น ๆ (mononeuritis multiplex) ร่วมกับไข้ น้ำหนักลด ความดันสูง ปวดท้อง และอัณฑะเจ็บ ANCA มักเป็นลบและไม่มีไตอักเสบแบบ glomerulonephritis วินิจฉัยด้วยการตัดชิ้นเนื้อเส้นประสาทหรือกล้ามเนื้อ หรือพบหลอดเลือดโป่งพองเล็ก ๆ ในไตและลำไส้ รักษาด้วย steroid และ cyclophosphamide ในรายรุนแรง ส่วนรายที่สัมพันธ์กับไวรัสตับอักเสบบีต้องให้ยาต้านไวรัสร่วมกับ plasma exchange

qx.stem: A 59-year-old man from Surat Thani has six weeks of bilateral foot drop, painful nodules and livedo racemosa, with fever and weight loss. Sural nerve biopsy shows necrotising vasculitis of small-to-medium arteries. ANCA and cryoglobulin tests are negative, his urinalysis is normal and chest imaging is clear.
qx.q: Which feature favours PAN over granulomatosis with polyangiitis?
opts: c-ANCA positivity with sinus disease
Mononeuritis multiplex with livedo and skin nodules, negative ANCA and absence of glomerulonephritis or pulmonary haemorrhage
Asthma and blood eosinophilia
Pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis
Cryoglobulinaemia with hepatitis C
qx.why: Polyarteritis nodosa is a necrotising vasculitis of medium arteries, ANCA-negative and typically sparing the lungs and glomeruli, with axonal multiple mononeuropathy and cutaneous disease; hepatitis B, minocycline and monogenic autoinflammatory disorders are associations. Hepatitis B-associated PAN has a good prognosis when immunosuppression follows antiviral therapy. GPA brings sinonasal disease and PR3-ANCA, and EGPA brings asthma and eosinophilia.

name: Polycystic ovarian syndrome
formal: Endocrine disorder with anovulation, hyperandrogenism and polycystic ovaries; relevance to neurology includes valproate exposure and idiopathic intracranial hypertension.
simple: A common hormone condition causing irregular periods, excess hair growth and cysts on the ovaries.
th: โรคต่อมไร้ท่อในสตรีที่มีการตกไข่ผิดปกติและฮอร์โมนแอนโดรเจนสูง ไม่ใช่โรคทางระบบประสาท แต่เกี่ยวข้องกับยา valproate และภาวะ IIH
tempoNote: Begins around puberty and persists through reproductive life
feat: Irregular or absent periods from anovulation
Hirsutism, acne or raised androgen levels
Polycystic-appearing ovaries on ultrasound; often obesity and insulin resistance
Neurological relevance: more common in women with epilepsy, especially on valproate, and shares obesity risk with IIH
inv: Testosterone, LH/FSH, prolactin, TSH and 17-hydroxyprogesterone to exclude mimics
Pelvic ultrasound; fasting glucose, HbA1c and lipids

case.who: 19-year-old woman from Nakhon Pathom with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
case.story: Seizure-free for 3 years on valproate, but her periods have become infrequent and she has gained 12 kg with new facial hair.
case.exam: BMI 31, hirsutism on the chin, acanthosis nigricans on the neck; neurological examination normal, fundi normal.
case.tests: Raised free testosterone; ultrasound shows multiple peripheral ovarian follicles.
case.q: What endocrine problem is likely and how should her epilepsy treatment be reviewed?
case.a: PCOS-like syndrome associated with valproate; discuss switching to an alternative such as levetiracetam or lamotrigine, especially because of pregnancy risks.

read.where: Section IV: General Principles of Therapy

det.patho: PCOS is a common endocrine disorder of reproductive-age women driven by ovarian androgen excess, altered gonadotropin pulsatility and insulin resistance. It is not a neurological disease. Its link to neurology comes from valproate, which can raise androgens and weight, from shared obesity risk with idiopathic intracranial hypertension, and from a probable higher background rate in women with epilepsy.
det.clinical: This is a gynaecological and endocrine condition included here for its neurological associations. Women present with oligomenorrhoea, hirsutism, acne, subfertility and weight gain, and carry higher risks of diabetes, dyslipidaemia and sleep apnoea. In a neurology clinic it surfaces when menstrual disturbance or weight gain appears on valproate, or when an obese young woman has headache that needs fundoscopy.
det.diagnosis: Most clinicians use the Rotterdam criteria requiring two of: ovulatory dysfunction, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology, after excluding thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia, congenital adrenal hyperplasia and Cushing syndrome. Anti-Mullerian hormone is increasingly accepted as an alternative to ultrasound in adults. Screen metabolic risk.
det.treatment: Lifestyle and weight management, combined oral contraceptives for cycle and androgen control, and metformin for metabolic features are standard; fertility care uses ovulation induction such as letrozole. In women with epilepsy on valproate, review the drug because of teratogenicity and endocrine effects, and remember enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs reduce contraceptive efficacy.
det.prognosis: Long-term course depends on metabolic risk; symptoms often improve with weight loss and drug review.
pearls: Valproate in a young woman: ask about periods, weight and pregnancy plans.
Obese young woman with headache: look at the fundi before blaming PCOS-related weight.
PCOS is a diagnosis of exclusion; check TSH, prolactin and 17-OHP.
det.thd: PCOS เป็นโรคต่อมไร้ท่อในสตรี มีประจำเดือนผิดปกติ ขนดก และรังไข่มีถุงน้ำหลายใบ ไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาท แต่พบเกี่ยวข้องกับการใช้ valproate ในผู้ป่วยลมชัก และมีปัจจัยเสี่ยงร่วม (ภาวะอ้วน) กับ IIH การวินิจฉัยใช้เกณฑ์ Rotterdam หลังตัดโรคอื่นออก ควรทบทวนยากันชักในหญิงวัยเจริญพันธุ์

ddx.pt: Also causes obesity and hirsutism but with striae, proximal myopathy and raised cortisol
Menstrual change and weight gain with high TSH; check before diagnosing PCOS
Shares obesity and young women; headache and papilloedema are the clues to look for

aN: pcos | polycystic ovary syndrome | stein leventhal syndrome

name: Polyglutamine tract disorders
formal: CAG repeat expansion diseases, including Huntington disease, SCAs, SBMA and DRPLA, with toxic gain of function and anticipation.
simple: Inherited brain diseases caused by a repeated stretch in a gene, including Huntington disease.
th: กลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมจาก CAG repeat ขยายตัวจนได้โปรตีนที่มี glutamine ยาวผิดปกติ เช่น Huntington, SCA1/2/3/6/7/17, SBMA และ DRPLA มี anticipation
tempoNote: Adult onset in most; longer repeats give earlier, more severe disease
feat: Members: HD, DRPLA, SBMA (Kennedy) and the SCAs numbered 1, 2, 3, 6, 7 and 17 — nine in all
Progressive neurodegeneration with ataxia, chorea, parkinsonism, dementia or motor neuron loss depending on gene
Anticipation: earlier onset in successive generations, especially via paternal transmission
Autosomal dominant except SBMA (X-linked)
Repeat length inversely correlates with age at onset
inv: Targeted repeat-size testing of the suspected gene, or ataxia repeat panel
MRI pattern: caudate atrophy (HD), pontocerebellar atrophy (SCA2/3), pure cerebellar (SCA6)
Pre-test genetic counselling, especially for predictive testing

case.story: Gradually unsteady for four years with double vision; his father and grandfather became wheelchair-bound, his father at a younger age.
case.exam: Gait ataxia, bulging eyes, facial fasciculations, spastic legs.
case.tests: ATXN3 CAG expansion confirmed.
case.q: What concept explains the younger onset in each generation?
case.a: Anticipation from CAG repeat instability and expansion — here in SCA3 (Machado–Joseph disease), part of the polyglutamine group.

read.where: Chapter 24 Cerebellar Ataxias and Related Conditions — The Ataxic Disorders

det.patho: Expanded CAG repeats in coding exons produce proteins with long polyglutamine stretches that misfold, aggregate and disturb transcription, proteostasis and mitochondrial function. Toxicity is largely gain-of-function, with some loss of normal protein role. Repeat instability during meiosis explains anticipation.
det.clinical: The phenotype depends on which protein is affected and in which neurons it is expressed: chorea and psychiatric change in HD, ataxia with variable extras in SCAs, myoclonic epilepsy and dementia in juvenile DRPLA, and lower motor neuron weakness with gynaecomastia in SBMA. SCA3 is among the most common dominant ataxias in Asia. Juvenile forms with large expansions differ markedly from adult forms.
det.diagnosis: Testing targets the specific repeat according to phenotype and ethnicity. Intermediate or reduced-penetrance alleles complicate interpretation. Predictive testing of asymptomatic relatives follows established counselling protocols.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy is approved for any polyglutamine disease; antisense oligonucleotides and gene-silencing strategies are in trials. Symptomatic treatment includes tetrabenazine or deutetrabenazine for chorea, physiotherapy, speech and swallowing therapy, and psychiatric support. Genetic counselling for families is essential.
det.prognosis: Relentlessly progressive over 10–30 years; survival varies by disease and repeat length.
pearls: Anticipation plus dominant inheritance = think repeat expansion.
SBMA is the X-linked member — look for gynaecomastia and perioral fasciculations.
Friedreich’s ataxia and FXTAS are repeat diseases but not polyglutamine ones.
det.thd: Polyglutamine tract disorders เป็นกลุ่มโรคจาก CAG repeat ขยายตัวในยีน ได้โปรตีนที่มี glutamine ยาวผิดปกติ จับตัวเป็นก้อนและเป็นพิษต่อเซลล์ประสาท ได้แก่ Huntington, SCA หลายชนิด DRPLA และ SBMA มีลักษณะ anticipation คือรุ่นหลังเป็นเร็วกว่า วินิจฉัยด้วยตรวจขนาด repeat ยังไม่มียารักษาให้หายขาด ใช้การรักษาตามอาการและให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

name: Polymyositis
formal: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy with subacute symmetric proximal weakness, raised CK, endomysial CD8 T-cell infiltrate and steroid response.
simple: A muscle inflammation causing weakness in the shoulders and hips, treated with immune-suppressing drugs.
more: Biopsy shows CD8 T cells invading non-necrotic fibres expressing MHC class I; EMG shows myopathic units with spontaneous activity. It is a diagnosis of exclusion needing rule-out of inclusion body myositis; add methotrexate or azathioprine.
th: กล้ามเนื้ออักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกัน ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อต้นแขนต้นขาอ่อนแรงทั้งสองข้างแบบกึ่งเฉียบพลัน CK สูง ปัจจุบันถือว่าเป็นการวินิจฉัยที่พบน้อยและต้องแยก IBM, IMNM และ overlap myositis ก่อน
tempoNote: Weakness builds over weeks to a few months; a course over years should prompt a rethink towards inclusion body myositis or dystrophy
feat: Symmetric weakness of hip and shoulder girdles and neck flexors: trouble rising from chairs, climbing steps, lifting arms
No rash (unlike dermatomyositis); muscle aches are mild or absent in most
Dysphagia from pharyngeal muscle involvement in some
Extramuscular clues to an overlap/antisynthetase picture: interstitial lung disease, arthritis, Raynaud's, mechanic's hands
Ocular and facial muscles spared; reflexes preserved until weakness is marked
inv: CK raised (often 5–50 times normal); ALT/AST and LDH also rise from muscle
EMG: fibrillations with short, small, polyphasic motor units; MRI thigh shows oedema to guide biopsy
Myositis-specific and associated antibodies (Jo-1 and other anti-synthetases, SRP, HMGCR, PM-Scl, Ku); HRCT chest and lung function
Muscle biopsy: endomysial CD8 T cells invading non-necrotic fibres with widespread MHC class I up-regulation; screen for malignancy

case.story: Over ten weeks she has struggled to climb the stairs to her flat and to hang laundry; she has a dry cough and her fingers turn white in the cold.
case.exam: Neck flexion 4/5, deltoids and hip flexors 4-/5, distal strength normal; cracked rough skin on the radial sides of her fingers; fine basal crackles.
case.tests: CK 4,800 U/L, anti-Jo-1 positive; HRCT shows basal non-specific interstitial pneumonia; MRI thighs shows symmetrical muscle oedema.
case.q: Which syndrome is this and what drives the long-term prognosis?
case.a: Antisynthetase syndrome (polymyositis-type myositis with ILD, Raynaud's and mechanic's hands); lung disease largely determines outcome.

det.patho: Polymyositis is a T-cell–mediated myopathy in which cytotoxic CD8 lymphocytes attack muscle fibres that abnormally express MHC class I. Modern antibody testing and biopsy reclassification have shown that many cases once labelled polymyositis are in fact inclusion body myositis, necrotising myopathy, antisynthetase syndrome or overlap myositis, so 'pure' polymyositis is now uncommon. It mainly affects adults and is more frequent in women.
det.clinical: Patients develop symmetrical proximal limb and neck-flexor weakness over weeks to months, sometimes with dysphagia or respiratory muscle weakness. Skin signs should be sought carefully, because subtle dermatomyositis changes alter the diagnosis. Interstitial lung disease, arthritis, fever and Raynaud's indicate an antisynthetase or overlap syndrome. Cardiac involvement (myocarditis, arrhythmia) is under-recognised.
det.diagnosis: Combine clinical pattern, raised CK, myopathic EMG, MRI oedema and a biopsy showing the characteristic inflammatory pattern. Send a myositis antibody panel, since the antibody predicts organ involvement and drug response. Exclude drugs (statins, alcohol, checkpoint inhibitors, colchicine), hypothyroidism, infection and muscular dystrophy with inflammatory change, and screen for cancer according to age and antibody. A steroid-unresponsive 'polymyositis' should be re-biopsied with IBM in mind.
det.treatment: First line is prednisolone about 1 mg/kg/day (or IV methylprednisolone for severe disease) plus an early second-line immunosuppressant: methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate. IVIG helps refractory disease and dysphagia; rituximab is used for antisynthetase or refractory cases, and ILD may need mycophenolate, tacrolimus or cyclophosphamide. Taper steroids slowly guided by strength rather than CK alone, protect bone, and add physiotherapy once inflammation is controlled.
det.prognosis: Most improve with treatment, but many need long-term immunosuppression; ILD, cardiac involvement, older age and cancer worsen outcome.
pearls: Before accepting polymyositis, exclude IBM, IMNM, dermatomyositis sine dermatitis and dystrophy.
Mechanic's hands + ILD + myositis = check anti-synthetase antibodies.
Rising weakness on steroids with falling CK: think steroid myopathy.

det.patho: Roots lack a strong perineurial barrier and lie bathed in CSF, so inflammatory, infectious and neoplastic processes in the subarachnoid space attack many roots together. Compression by stenosis or arachnoiditis and ischaemic or metabolic damage (diabetes) are other mechanisms.
det.clinical: Weakness affects both proximal and distal muscles with reflex loss in the involved segments. Pain is often prominent and sensory loss spans several dermatomes. Involvement of the cauda equina produces saddle anaesthesia and bladder failure. The tempo and setting (immunosuppression, cancer, diabetes) are the main clues to cause.
det.diagnosis: Contrast MRI of the spine and CSF analysis are the pivotal tests. Electrophysiology shows denervation in paraspinal and limb muscles of multiple myotomes, with abnormal F waves or H reflexes and preserved sensory responses when the lesion is preganglionic. Repeat CSF cytology may be needed for malignancy.
det.treatment: Treatment depends on cause: IVIG or plasma exchange for GBS, immunotherapy for CIDP, antivirals for CMV or HSV, antituberculous therapy, intrathecal or systemic chemotherapy for leptomeningeal disease and decompression for compressive causes. Supportive care includes bladder management and rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: Highly variable: good in GBS and treatable infections, poor in leptomeningeal malignancy.
pearls: Preserved sensory nerve action potentials with sensory loss means the lesion is proximal to the ganglion.
CMV polyradiculopathy has a neutrophilic CSF — unusual for a virus.
Enhancing roots on MRI need CSF cytology to exclude malignancy.

det.patho: Autosomal recessive deficiency of lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) leads to glycogen accumulation inside lysosomes and autophagic build-up in skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle. Residual enzyme activity determines the phenotype: near-absent activity causes the infantile cardiomyopathic form, while partial activity gives late-onset disease. The intronic c.-32-13T>G variant is common in Caucasian late-onset patients; different variants prevail in Asia.
det.clinical: Infantile-onset Pompe presents in the first months with hypotonia, feeding difficulty, macroglossia, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and early death if untreated. Late-onset disease can appear from childhood to late adulthood as a slowly progressive limb-girdle pattern with striking axial and abdominal weakness, scoliosis and early diaphragm involvement. Orthopnoea, morning headache, daytime sleepiness or unexplained respiratory failure may be the presenting complaint. Some patients have only raised CK, and basilar or other intracranial aneurysms are reported.
det.diagnosis: Screen by measuring GAA enzyme activity on a dried blood spot, confirmed in lymphocytes or fibroblasts and by biallelic GAA variants. CK is normal to moderately raised. EMG may show myopathic units with myotonic or complex repetitive discharges, particularly in paraspinal muscles. A fall in vital capacity of more than about 10–25% from sitting to supine indicates diaphragmatic weakness. Muscle MRI shows paraspinal and posterior thigh involvement; biopsy may show vacuoles but can be non-diagnostic, so enzyme testing should not be skipped.
det.treatment: Enzyme replacement therapy with recombinant GAA (alglucosidase alfa, or newer avalglucosidase alfa or cipaglucosidase alfa with miglustat) is given intravenously every two weeks. Respiratory surveillance with sitting/supine FVC and sleep studies guides nocturnal non-invasive ventilation. Physiotherapy, scoliosis management and nutrition matter. Infants need cardiology input, and CRIM-negative infants may require immune tolerance induction to prevent antibody neutralisation.
det.prognosis: ERT has transformed infantile survival and stabilises or slows decline in many late-onset patients, though response varies. Respiratory failure remains the main cause of death in adults.
pearls: Respiratory failure out of proportion to limb weakness: test GAA.
Always measure supine as well as sitting FVC in a suspected myopathy.
Dried blood spot GAA is cheap and should precede biopsy.
det.thd: Pompe เกิดจากขาดเอนไซม์ GAA ในไลโซโซม ทำให้ไกลโคเจนสะสมในกล้ามเนื้อ ชนิดทารกมีกล้ามเนื้อปวกเปียกและหัวใจโต ชนิดผู้ใหญ่มีต้นขา/ลำตัวอ่อนแรงช้า ๆ และกะบังลมอ่อนแรงตั้งแต่ต้น (หายใจลำบากเมื่อนอนราบ ปวดหัวตอนเช้า) วินิจฉัยด้วย dried blood spot GAA และยีน GAA ตรวจ FVC ท่านั่งเทียบท่านอน รักษาด้วยเอนไซม์ทดแทนทุก 2 สัปดาห์ร่วมกับเครื่องช่วยหายใจกลางคืนเมื่อจำเป็น

name: Porphyria
formal: Heme biosynthesis enzyme disorder; acute porphyrias cause abdominal pain, neuropathy, seizures and psychosis; triggered by drugs, fasting and hormones.
simple: An inherited metabolic problem causing attacks of belly pain, nerve problems and confusion.
more: Diagnose acute attacks by raised urine porphobilinogen and delta-aminolevulinic acid, then confirm with enzymology or gene testing. Treat with IV hemin and glucose and avoid precipitants; the neuropathy is mainly motor axonal and mimics GBS.
th: กลุ่มโรคเอนไซม์สร้าง heme บกพร่อง ชนิดเฉียบพลันมีปวดท้องรุนแรง ปัสสาวะสีเข้ม เส้นประสาทอักเสบแบบสั่งการ ชัก และอาการทางจิต กระตุ้นด้วยยา การอดอาหาร และฮอร์โมน
tempoNote: Attacks build over hours to days; neuropathy follows abdominal pain by days and can peak within 1–4 weeks
feat: Severe abdominal pain, vomiting and constipation with soft abdomen; tachycardia and hypertension
Acute motor axonal neuropathy, often proximal and arm-predominant, can progress to respiratory failure
Confusion, anxiety, psychosis, seizures and hyponatraemia (SIADH)
Triggers: enzyme-inducing drugs, alcohol, fasting, infection, menstrual cycle
Mostly women aged 15–45; cutaneous photosensitivity only in variegate porphyria and hereditary coproporphyria

Urine ALA and porphyrins, plasma fluorescence scan and faecal porphyrins to type the porphyria

case.story: Three days of severe colicky abdominal pain after starting a crash diet; a negative laparoscopy was done. Now her arms are weak and she is agitated.
case.exam: HR 128, BP 170/100; proximal arm weakness with reduced reflexes; abdomen soft; dark reddish urine in the bag.

case.q: Which treatment should be started and which common drugs must be avoided?
case.a: Acute hepatic porphyria attack: give IV hemin and carbohydrate, stop porphyrinogenic drugs (e.g. barbiturates, phenytoin, carbamazepine, sulfonamides); treat seizures with safe agents such as levetiracetam or gabapentin.

det.patho: Porphyrias are inherited defects of the eight-step heme pathway. In acute hepatic porphyrias (AIP, variegate, hereditary coproporphyria and ALAD deficiency) triggers that induce hepatic ALA synthase cause neurotoxic precursors, especially ALA, to build up. These damage autonomic, peripheral and central neurons. Most carriers of dominant variants never have attacks (low penetrance).
det.clinical: Attacks start with poorly localised abdominal pain, vomiting, constipation, tachycardia and hypertension, often leading to needless surgery. Neuropathy is mainly motor axonal, may begin in proximal arms, and can involve cranial and respiratory nerves; sensory loss may follow a 'bathing-trunk' pattern. CNS effects include delirium, psychosis, seizures, often driven by hyponatraemia, and PRES. Cutaneous porphyrias (e.g. porphyria cutanea tarda) cause skin blistering without neurological attacks.
det.diagnosis: A raised spot urine PBG in a symptomatic patient is the key test and should be sent urgently; a normal PBG during symptoms essentially rules out an acute attack from AIP, VP or HCP. Typing uses urine, plasma and faecal porphyrins, then genetic confirmation. Erythrocyte enzyme assays alone are unreliable. Check sodium, magnesium and renal function and monitor vital capacity.
det.treatment: Stop all unsafe drugs (check a porphyria drug database), treat pain with opioids and nausea with safe antiemetics, and give IV hemin (3–4 mg/kg/day, 4-day course) as early as possible; glucose infusion is a temporary measure. Correct hyponatraemia carefully and use safe antiseizure drugs. Recurrent attacks can be prevented with givosiran, an siRNA against ALAS1, or with GnRH analogues for cyclical attacks; liver transplantation is a last resort. Long-term surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma, hypertension and kidney disease is recommended.
det.prognosis: Most attacks resolve fully if treated early; severe neuropathy may take months to recover and can leave residual weakness.
pearls: Abdominal pain + hyponatraemia + motor neuropathy in a young woman: send urine PBG.
Many antiseizure drugs precipitate attacks; levetiracetam, gabapentin and benzodiazepines are generally safe.
GBS mimic: porphyric neuropathy is axonal, often proximal and arm-first, with normal CSF protein early.
det.thd: Porphyria ชนิดเฉียบพลันเกิดจากเอนไซม์สร้าง heme บกพร่อง เมื่อถูกกระตุ้นด้วยยา การอดอาหาร หรือฮอร์โมน จะมีสารตั้งต้นคั่งและเป็นพิษต่อเส้นประสาท ผู้ป่วยปวดท้องรุนแรง หัวใจเต้นเร็ว ความดันสูง โซเดียมต่ำ ชักหรือสับสน และอ่อนแรงจากเส้นประสาทแบบ axonal วินิจฉัยด้วยระดับ PBG ในปัสสาวะสูง รักษาด้วย hemin ทางหลอดเลือด หยุดยากระตุ้น และป้องกันซ้ำด้วย givosiran

det.patho: These tremors arise from abnormal sensorimotor network activity that is switched on by specific motor programmes or limb positions. Their position along the essential tremor–dystonia spectrum is debated; some cases behave like a focal dystonia, others like a restricted essential tremor. Structural lesions are rarely found.
det.clinical: Primary writing tremor is the best known: oscillation appears when the pen touches paper or when the hand adopts the writing posture. Other examples include tremor only when the arm is held in a wing-beating position or when holding a phone, and occupational tremors in musicians or athletes. Onset is in adulthood with gradual progression; spread to other tasks is uncommon but possible.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis rests on careful examination comparing many postures and actions. Look for dystonic features, mirror movements and a null point. Exclude drug, thyroid and parkinsonian causes when the history suggests them. Neurophysiology can document frequency and burst pattern but is not required.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin targeted to the muscles driving the tremor is often the most effective option. Propranolol, primidone or anticholinergic drugs help some patients. Adaptive tools (thick pens, writing with the other hand) and occupational therapy are useful, and deep brain stimulation is reserved for disabling refractory cases.
det.prognosis: Usually stays confined and non-disabling outside the provoking task.
pearls: Always test the exact task the patient complains about; routine postures may look normal.
Look for dystonic posturing: it changes how you label and treat the tremor.
Botulinum toxin tends to work better than oral drugs for task-specific tremor.
det.thd: อาการสั่นชนิดนี้เกิดเฉพาะเมื่ออยู่ในท่าหรือทำงานบางอย่าง เช่น เขียนหนังสือ ส่วนท่าอื่นๆ ปกติ เชื่อว่าอยู่ระหว่าง essential tremor กับ dystonia การวินิจฉัยต้องให้ผู้ป่วยทำงานที่กระตุ้นอาการจริง การรักษาได้ผลดีด้วย botulinum toxin ส่วนยา propranolol หรือ primidone ช่วยได้บางราย

18 - Myoclonus: Phenomenology, etiology, physiology, and treatment

det.patho: Positive myoclonus results from a sudden synchronous discharge reaching motor neurons, generating a short EMG burst (typically under 100 ms in cortical forms). Generators can be cortical, cortico-subcortical, brainstem reticular, spinal segmental or propriospinal. The term is used to separate active jerks from negative myoclonus, where an interruption of ongoing muscle activity causes the movement.
det.clinical: Jerks may be spontaneous, action-induced or stimulus-sensitive. Physiological examples include hypnic jerks and hiccups; pathological causes include epilepsy syndromes, post-hypoxic injury, renal or hepatic failure, drugs (opioids, gabapentinoids, cephalosporins), neurodegenerative disease and prion disease. Distribution and triggers help guess the generator.
det.diagnosis: First establish that the movement is myoclonus rather than tic, tremor or chorea, then classify by distribution, trigger and physiology. Bloods for metabolic causes and a medication review come first. Neurophysiology (EMG burst duration, back-averaging, giant SEPs, C-reflex) can locate the source and guide drug choice.
det.treatment: Correct the cause: metabolic correction, stopping offending drugs, treating seizures. For cortical myoclonus, levetiracetam, valproate, piracetam and clonazepam are used, often in combination. Avoid drugs that may worsen myoclonus in some settings, such as carbamazepine, phenytoin or gabapentinoids in progressive myoclonus epilepsy.
det.prognosis: Depends entirely on the cause; toxic-metabolic myoclonus usually resolves when the trigger is corrected.
pearls: Positive and negative myoclonus often appear together in metabolic encephalopathy.
Gabapentin and pregabalin accumulate in renal failure and are common causes of jerks.
Describe distribution, trigger and timing first; physiology then refines the source.

name: Post Lyme syndrome
formal: Persistent fatigue, pain and cognitive complaints after treated Lyme disease; not due to ongoing infection and no benefit from prolonged antibiotics.
simple: Lasting tiredness, aches and poor concentration that continue after Lyme disease has been treated.
th: อาการอ่อนเพลีย ปวด และความคิดช้าที่ยังคงอยู่หลังรักษาโรค Lyme ครบแล้ว ไม่ได้เกิดจากการติดเชื้อต่อเนื่อง และยาปฏิชีวนะต่อนานไม่ช่วย
tempoNote: Symptoms persist for 6 months or more after standard antibiotic treatment
feat: Fatigue, widespread musculoskeletal pain and subjective cognitive slowing after treated Lyme disease
Normal neurological examination and no objective new signs of infection
Symptoms are disabling for some but tend to improve slowly over time
Lyme disease is very rare in Thailand; history of travel to endemic areas (North America, Europe) is essential
inv: Review of the original diagnosis and treatment; serology stays positive for years and does not show active infection
Screen for other causes: thyroid, anaemia, depression, sleep disorders
MRI or CSF only if objective neurological signs appear

case.who: 40-year-old Thai engineer returned from 3 years working in the north-eastern United States
case.story: Treated with doxycycline for erythema migrans and facial palsy a year ago; the palsy recovered but he still feels exhausted, aches and forgets words.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination; no joint swelling.
case.tests: Lyme IgG remains positive; FBC, TSH, CRP normal; MRI brain normal.
case.q: Does the positive serology justify another long course of antibiotics?
case.a: No — this fits post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome; persistent antibodies are expected, and prolonged antibiotics show no benefit in trials; give symptom-based rehabilitation.

read.where: Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — Lyme Neuroborreliosis

det.patho: The cause is not established. Proposed contributors include persistent immune activation, residual tissue injury, central sensitisation and psychological factors; evidence for persisting viable Borrelia in humans after standard therapy is lacking. It resembles other post-infectious fatigue syndromes.
det.clinical: This is a symptom syndrome rather than a structural neurological disease. Patients report fatigue, pain, poor concentration and sleep disturbance beginning within 6 months of a properly diagnosed and treated Lyme infection and lasting more than 6 months. Objective neurological deficits are absent, and new deficits should prompt a different diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: Confirm that Lyme disease was genuinely diagnosed and adequately treated, then exclude alternative causes such as depression, sleep apnoea, thyroid disease and rheumatological disorders. Serology is not useful for monitoring because antibodies persist. Beware of commercial tests that are not validated.
det.treatment: Randomised trials found that prolonged oral or intravenous antibiotics do not improve outcomes and carry harm, so they are not recommended. Management is supportive: graded activity, sleep hygiene, pain management, treatment of mood disorders and reassurance.
det.prognosis: Most patients improve gradually over months to a few years.
pearls: Positive Lyme antibodies after treatment are expected and do not mean active infection.
Long-term antibiotics do not help and can cause serious complications.
New objective signs need a fresh diagnostic work-up.
det.thd: post Lyme syndrome คืออาการเหนื่อยล้า ปวดตามตัว และสมาธิไม่ดีที่คงอยู่หลังรักษาโรค Lyme ครบแล้ว ตรวจร่างกายปกติ ผลเลือดแอนติบอดีที่ยังบวกไม่ได้หมายถึงติดเชื้ออยู่ งานวิจัยพบว่าการให้ยาปฏิชีวนะต่อเนื่องนานไม่ช่วยและมีโทษ การดูแลเน้นฟื้นฟูและรักษาตามอาการ ในไทยพบน้อยมาก ควรถามประวัติเดินทาง

name: Post pump chorea
formal: Choreoathetosis after cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass in children, related to hypoxic-ischaemic injury of basal ganglia and cerebellum.
simple: Writhing movements in children after heart surgery using a bypass machine.
th: chorea และ athetosis ที่เกิดในเด็กหลังผ่าตัดหัวใจที่ใช้เครื่องปอดหัวใจเทียม สัมพันธ์กับสมองส่วน basal ganglia ขาดเลือดหรือออกซิเจน
tempoNote: Begins within about 2 weeks of surgery (often days 2–7 after a lucid interval); may resolve over weeks or persist
feat: Young child (often under 2 years, cyanotic heart disease) after open-heart surgery with deep hypothermia or circulatory arrest
Generalised choreoathetosis, orofacial dyskinesias and hypotonia appearing days after surgery
Irritability, feeding and swallowing difficulty; developmental regression in severe cases
Severity ranges from mild transient chorea to persistent severe movement disorder
inv: MRI brain: often normal or nonspecific; may show basal ganglia or diffuse hypoxic-ischaemic changes
EEG to exclude subclinical seizures if consciousness fluctuates
Rule out metabolic and drug causes (electrolytes, glucose, drug levels)

case.who: 14-month-old girl at a cardiac centre in Bangkok
case.story: Underwent repair of tetralogy of Fallot with deep hypothermic circulatory arrest. On day 5 after an initially normal recovery she began writhing and making jerky facial movements.
case.exam: Continuous generalised choreoathetoid movements, hypotonia, poor feeding, no focal weakness.
case.tests: MRI shows no clear structural lesion; EEG without seizures; electrolytes normal.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and how is it managed?
case.a: Post-pump chorea; supportive care with nutrition and sedation, and symptomatic drugs such as haloperidol, tetrabenazine or benzodiazepines; many children improve over weeks to months.

det.patho: The exact mechanism is unclear. Proposed factors include deep hypothermia, prolonged circulatory arrest, rapid cooling and rewarming, microemboli and hypocapnia, injuring the basal ganglia and their connections. Autopsy of fatal cases has shown pallidal neurons dropping out with reactive gliosis. The incidence has fallen from several percent to around 1% or less with improved bypass techniques.
det.clinical: Typically affects infants and young children with cyanotic congenital heart disease who undergo prolonged bypass. After surgery there is often a short period of normal recovery, followed by chorea, athetosis, orofacial dyskinesia and hypotonia. Mild cases resolve within weeks; severe cases, especially those with marked dyskinesia, may have lasting movement disorder and developmental delay.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical: onset of choreoathetosis within days to two weeks after cardiac surgery with bypass, after excluding seizures, metabolic derangement and drug effects. MRI is often unremarkable, which does not exclude the diagnosis.
det.treatment: Management is supportive and symptomatic: nutrition (often tube feeding), sedation for exhausting movements, and drugs such as haloperidol, tetrabenazine, benzodiazepines or chloral hydrate, with variable response. Physiotherapy and developmental follow-up are important. Prevention focuses on bypass technique: limiting circulatory arrest time and careful temperature and pH management.
det.prognosis: Mild cases often resolve completely; severe forms carry a risk of persistent movement disorder, cognitive impairment and occasionally death.
pearls: Chorea starting days after paediatric bypass surgery: think post-pump chorea.
A lucid interval before chorea is typical.
Normal MRI does not rule it out.
det.thd: Post pump chorea คืออาการกระตุกแบบ chorea และ athetosis ที่เกิดในเด็กเล็กหลังผ่าตัดหัวใจโดยใช้เครื่องปอดหัวใจเทียม โดยเฉพาะเมื่อใช้ภาวะอุณหภูมิต่ำมากและหยุดการไหลเวียน อาการมักเริ่มหลังผ่าตัดไม่กี่วันหลังช่วงที่ดูปกติ ร่วมกับกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนปวกเปียกและกลืนลำบาก MRI มักปกติ การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคองและใช้ยาเช่น haloperidol หรือ tetrabenazine รายไม่รุนแรงมักหายเอง

name: Post stroke movement disorders (PSMD)
formal: Hyperkinetic or hypokinetic movement disorders after stroke, including hemichorea-hemiballism, dystonia, tremor, myoclonus and parkinsonism, often from basal ganglia or thalamic infarcts or haemorrhage.
simple: Abnormal movements such as jerking, tremor or twisting that develop after a stroke.
more: MRI localises the lesion; treatment is tetrabenazine, antipsychotics, anticholinergics or botulinum toxin depending on type; many settle over months.
th: ความผิดปกติของการเคลื่อนไหวหลัง stroke ทั้งแบบเคลื่อนไหวมากและน้อย เช่น hemichorea-hemiballism dystonia tremor myoclonus และ parkinsonism มักเกิดจากรอยโรคที่ basal ganglia หรือ thalamus
tempoNote: Hemichorea-ballism appears within days; dystonia, tremor (Holmes) and parkinsonism may appear months to years later
feat: Hemichorea-hemiballism: commonest acute PSMD, contralateral to subthalamic, striatal or thalamic lesions
Delayed dystonia (often hand or arm) after putaminal or thalamic lesions, frequently in younger patients
Holmes (rubral) tremor: slow, rest-postural-action tremor weeks to months after thalamic or midbrain lesions
Asterixis, myoclonus, thalamic 'jerky dystonic unsteady hand' and vascular parkinsonism
Usually contralateral to the lesion; ipsilateral or bilateral forms are rare
inv: MRI with DWI/SWI to localise the infarct or haemorrhage
Glucose and HbA1c (non-ketotic hyperglycaemic hemichorea mimics stroke)
Vascular work-up as for any stroke; DaT-SPECT may help separate vascular from degenerative parkinsonism

case.story: Hypertensive and diabetic; woke with wild flinging movements affecting his left arm and leg, which cease only during sleep.
case.exam: Large-amplitude involuntary proximal movements of left limbs, mild left weakness.
case.tests: Glucose 140 mg/dL; MRI DWI shows a small acute infarct in the right subthalamic nucleus.
case.q: What is the movement disorder and how is it treated?
case.a: Hemiballism-hemichorea from a subthalamic infarct; treat with tetrabenazine or a neuroleptic such as haloperidol while giving secondary stroke prevention; most improve over weeks.

det.patho: Strokes disrupt basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical circuits. Loss of subthalamic or indirect-pathway output disinhibits the thalamus, producing chorea and ballism, while lesions in putamen or thalamus can lead to delayed dystonia, probably through maladaptive plasticity and secondary degeneration. Combined dentatorubrothalamic and nigrostriatal damage leads to Holmes tremor. Movement disorders occur in roughly 1–4% of stroke patients.
det.clinical: Hyperkinetic disorders predominate. Acute hemichorea-ballism usually appears in the first days and tends to settle over weeks to months. Dystonia and tremor are typically delayed, sometimes appearing as motor power recovers. Thalamic lesions can give a mixed picture with sensory ataxia, dystonic posturing and pseudoathetosis. Parkinsonism from vascular lesions often affects gait more than hands.
det.diagnosis: Match the phenomenology to an appropriately located lesion in time. MRI is the key test; small lesions may be missed on CT. Check glucose to exclude hyperglycaemic chorea, review medications, and consider other structural lesions (tumour, abscess, demyelination). The diagnosis is clinical-radiological.
det.treatment: Treat according to movement type: tetrabenazine, haloperidol or other antipsychotics for chorea-ballism; anticholinergics or botulinum toxin for focal dystonia; levodopa trial and drugs such as clonazepam for Holmes tremor; levodopa trial for parkinsonism. Severe, persistent cases may benefit from deep brain stimulation (e.g. GPi or Vim). Continue secondary stroke prevention and rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: Acute hemiballism often remits spontaneously; delayed dystonia and Holmes tremor tend to persist and need long-term treatment.
pearls: Acute hemiballism in an elderly vasculopath: check glucose before calling it a stroke.
Delayed onset (months) is typical for dystonia and Holmes tremor after stroke.
Holmes tremor may respond partly to levodopa because nigral pathways are often involved.

name: Post-anoxic myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus after cardiac arrest: acute status myoclonus carries a poor prognosis, whereas chronic action myoclonus (Lance-Adams) occurs in survivors.
simple: Muscle jerks after the brain loses oxygen, for example after a cardiac arrest.
th: อาการกระตุกหลังสมองขาดออกซิเจนจากหัวใจหยุดเต้น แบบเฉียบพลันในผู้ป่วยโคม่ามักพยากรณ์ไม่ดี ส่วนแบบเรื้อรัง (Lance-Adams) เกิดในผู้รอดชีวิตที่รู้ตัว
tempoNote: Acute form within 24–72 hours of arrest in comatose patients; chronic action myoclonus emerges days to weeks later as consciousness returns
feat: Acute: generalised, often continuous jerks of face, trunk and limbs in a comatose patient after resuscitation
Chronic (Lance-Adams): action and intention myoclonus in an awake survivor, disrupting walking and hand use
Negative myoclonus of the legs causes 'bouncy' gait and falls in the chronic form
Stimulus sensitivity to touch or noise is common
inv: EEG: burst-suppression or suppressed background with time-locked discharges suggests severe injury in the acute form
Multimodal prognostication: pupillary and corneal reflexes, SSEP N20, neuron-specific enolase, CT/MRI diffusion
EEG–EMG back-averaging and SEPs in chronic cases to confirm a cortical source

case.who: 52-year-old man from Bangkok, 10 days after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest from ventricular fibrillation
case.story: He has woken up and can talk, but whenever he tries to drink or stand his arms and legs jerk so violently that he spills and falls.
case.exam: Alert and oriented; jerks with reaching and when touched; none at rest; legs give way in brief lapses when standing.
case.tests: EEG background reactive with spikes linked to jerks; MRI unremarkable.
case.q: What syndrome is this, and how does its outlook differ from jerks seen in coma on day 1?
case.a: Lance-Adams syndrome (chronic post-hypoxic action myoclonus); unlike early status myoclonus in coma it carries a good survival outlook and responds to levetiracetam, valproate, clonazepam or piracetam.

det.patho: Global hypoxia injures vulnerable cortical layers, hippocampus, cerebellar Purkinje cells and brainstem. Acute myoclonus in coma reflects widespread cortical and subcortical injury, sometimes with brainstem reticular generators. Chronic Lance-Adams myoclonus is thought to arise from cortical hyperexcitability with loss of inhibitory, partly serotonergic, control and cerebellar damage.
det.clinical: Two forms must be separated. Early myoclonus in a comatose patient, especially when generalised and persistent with a malignant EEG, is associated with poor outcome, but it is not on its own sufficient to withdraw care because some patients with reactive EEGs recover. The chronic form appears as the patient wakes, with action myoclonus, negative myoclonus, dysarthria and ataxia; cognition may be relatively preserved.
det.diagnosis: In the acute phase follow current resuscitation guidance and use a multimodal approach (no earlier than 72 hours after normothermia), combining examination, EEG, SSEP, biomarkers and imaging. Video-EEG helps decide whether jerks are epileptic. In chronic cases, clinical features plus neurophysiology confirm cortical myoclonus.
det.treatment: Acute myoclonus with epileptiform EEG may be treated with levetiracetam, valproate or propofol and benzodiazepines. Chronic Lance-Adams myoclonus responds to levetiracetam, valproate, clonazepam and piracetam, often in combination; sodium oxybate has been used off-label. Rehabilitation focusing on gait safety and assistive devices is important.
det.prognosis: Acute generalised status myoclonus with malignant EEG has high mortality; Lance-Adams survivors often improve slowly over years.
pearls: Do not equate any early jerks with hopeless prognosis; use multimodal assessment.
Lance-Adams patients are awake and jerk with action, not at rest.
Lapses of leg tone (negative myoclonus) make survivors fall often.
det.thd: myoclonus หลังสมองขาดออกซิเจนมี 2 แบบ แบบแรกเกิดใน 1–3 วันหลังหัวใจหยุดเต้นขณะผู้ป่วยยังโคม่า มักพยากรณ์ไม่ดีแต่ต้องประเมินหลายวิธีร่วมกัน แบบที่สองคือ Lance-Adams syndrome เกิดในผู้รอดชีวิตที่รู้สึกตัว กระตุกเมื่อเคลื่อนไหว รักษาด้วย levetiracetam, valproate, clonazepam หรือ piracetam และพยากรณ์ดีกว่า

qx.stem: A 22-year-old asthmatic woman had a 9-minute respiratory arrest. She awakens on day 4 and becomes alert and conversant. Two weeks later, whenever she reaches for a cup or tries to walk, she has jerks of the limbs that make her fall; at rest she is still. EEG shows a normal background with occasional vertex-predominant spike-waves time-locked to some jerks.
qx.q: Which statement about her condition is correct?

Withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy should be discussed
This is chronic post-hypoxic action myoclonus (Lance–Adams); levetiracetam, clonazepam or valproate may help
It is a functional movement disorder and needs psychotherapy only
Phenytoin is the drug of choice
qx.why: Action-induced myoclonus emerging after the patient regains consciousness is Lance–Adams syndrome, which has a relatively good cognitive prognosis and responds to levetiracetam, piracetam, clonazepam or valproate. It must be separated from early generalised myoclonic status in comatose survivors with suppressed backgrounds, which carries a grim prognosis. Phenytoin is generally ineffective for cortical myoclonus.

name: Post-concussion syndrome
formal: Persistent headache, dizziness, fatigue, cognitive and mood symptoms after mild traumatic brain injury beyond weeks to months; multifactorial.
simple: Headache, dizziness and poor concentration lasting for weeks or months after a mild head injury.
th: อาการปวดศีรษะ เวียนศีรษะ เหนื่อยล้า สมาธิความจำไม่ดี และอารมณ์แปรปรวนที่คงอยู่นานเกินคาดหลังการบาดเจ็บศีรษะเล็กน้อย
tempoNote: Most concussion symptoms settle within 2–4 weeks; persistent symptoms last beyond a month and sometimes years
feat: Headache, often migraine-like or tension-type, after mild head injury
Dizziness, light and noise sensitivity, poor sleep and fatigue
Problems with concentration, slowed thinking and irritability or anxiety
Neurological examination and standard imaging usually normal
inv: CT/MRI when red flags (worsening headache, focal signs, anticoagulation, older age) to exclude haematoma
Screen for mood disorder, sleep disorder and analgesic overuse
Vestibular and cervical assessment for dizziness; neuropsychological testing if symptoms persist

case.story: Three months after a minor crash with brief loss of consciousness he has daily headaches, dizziness when turning, trouble remembering fares and feels short-tempered. He takes paracetamol almost every day.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination; tender neck muscles; positional testing negative.
case.tests: CT brain on the day of injury normal; MRI now normal; PHQ-9 suggests moderate depression.
case.q: What factors maintain his symptoms and what is the plan?
case.a: Persistent post-concussion symptoms with medication overuse, cervical and mood components; limit analgesics, graded return to activity, treat depression and give headache prophylaxis and vestibular/neck physiotherapy.

det.patho: Concussion causes transient metabolic and microstructural disturbance of neurons and axons. Persistent symptoms are multifactorial: subtle axonal injury in some, plus vestibular and cervical dysfunction, migraine biology, sleep disruption, mood disorders, expectation and litigation stress, and medication overuse. No single lesion explains the syndrome.
det.clinical: Symptoms cluster into somatic (headache, dizziness, fatigue), cognitive (attention, memory) and emotional (irritability, anxiety, low mood) domains. Predictors of slow recovery include prior migraine or psychiatric history, high early symptom burden and female sex. Examination is typically normal, and progressive or focal findings require a fresh look for structural causes.
det.diagnosis: This is a clinical diagnosis after a documented head injury, once structural complications have been excluded. Use imaging guided by red flags rather than routinely. Validated symptom scales and screening for depression, anxiety, PTSD and sleep problems guide treatment. Advanced imaging and blood biomarkers remain research tools for individual prognosis.
det.treatment: Early education and reassurance reduce chronicity. Encourage graded aerobic activity and staged return to work or study rather than prolonged rest. Treat headache phenotype (with avoidance of analgesic overuse), and offer vestibular rehabilitation, cervical physiotherapy, CBT and treatment of mood and sleep disorders. Multidisciplinary rehabilitation helps refractory cases.
det.prognosis: Most recover within 3 months; a minority have symptoms for a year or more, often linked to psychological and headache factors.
pearls: Prolonged rest after concussion delays recovery; graded activity is preferred.
Daily analgesic use can turn post-traumatic headache into medication-overuse headache.
Re-image if headache worsens or focal signs appear, especially in the elderly or anticoagulated.

case.story: On day 2 she develops a severe occipital headache within a minute of sitting up to breastfeed, settling completely when she lies down.
case.exam: Afebrile, neck slightly stiff on sitting, no focal deficit, normal fundi.
case.tests: None needed initially; BP normal and no proteinuria.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the definitive treatment if conservative care fails?
case.a: Post-dural puncture headache; an epidural blood patch is the most effective treatment if symptoms persist or are severe.

read.where: Chapter 50: Headache attributed to non-vascular intracranial disorder

det.patho: A hole in the dura allows CSF to leak faster than it is produced, lowering intracranial CSF volume. In the upright position the brain sags and pain-sensitive meninges and bridging veins are stretched, with compensatory venous dilatation adding to the pain. Cutting-bevel and larger-gauge needles create bigger defects.
det.clinical: The headache is typically frontal or occipital, severe and clearly postural, often with neck pain, nausea and auditory symptoms. It usually starts within 2 days and most cases settle within a week or two. Loss of postural character, focal signs, seizures or reduced consciousness suggest complications such as subdural haematoma or cerebral venous thrombosis.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical, based on a dural puncture within the past 5 days and an orthostatic headache. Exclude pre-eclampsia, meningitis, venous sinus thrombosis and intracranial haemorrhage in postpartum patients with atypical features. MRI findings of intracranial hypotension support the diagnosis but are not needed in typical cases.
det.treatment: Simple analgesia, hydration and caffeine give modest relief; bed rest does not prevent PDPH. An epidural blood patch is the most effective treatment for persistent or disabling headache and can be repeated. Sphenopalatine ganglion blocks and greater occipital nerve blocks are alternatives. Prevention relies on small atraumatic (pencil-point) needles and replacing the stylet before withdrawal.
det.prognosis: Usually self-limiting; most resolve within 1–2 weeks, and blood patch success exceeds 70% with the first attempt.
pearls: Use an atraumatic needle for diagnostic LP to cut the risk.
Routine bed rest after LP does not prevent the headache.
A headache that stops being postural may signal a subdural haematoma.
det.thd: PDPH คืออาการปวดศีรษะหลังเจาะหลัง เกิดจากน้ำไขสันหลังรั่ว ปวดมากเมื่อลุกนั่งหรือยืน และดีขึ้นเมื่อนอนราบ มักเริ่มใน 1–2 วันและหายเองใน 1–2 สัปดาห์ การรักษาเบื้องต้นคือยาแก้ปวด ดื่มน้ำ และคาเฟอีน ถ้าไม่ดีขึ้นให้ทำ epidural blood patch การป้องกันใช้เข็มปลายมนขนาดเล็ก

Not strongly positional; may follow delivery but with typical migraine features
