name: Post-herpetic neuralgia
formal: Neuropathic pain persisting more than 3 months after herpes zoster rash, with allodynia; treated with gabapentinoids, tricyclics or lidocaine patches.
simple: Long-lasting nerve pain in the area where shingles occurred.
th: อาการปวดแบบปวดเส้นประสาทที่คงอยู่เกิน 3 เดือนหลังเป็นงูสวัด บริเวณผิวหนังที่เคยมีผื่น มักมีปวดเมื่อสัมผัสเบาๆ
tempoNote: Pain persisting at least 3 months after the zoster rash heals
feat: Burning, aching or lancinating pain in the dermatome of a prior shingles rash
Allodynia: light touch or clothing provokes pain
Sensory loss or scarring and pigment change in the same dermatome
Commonest in thoracic dermatomes and the V1 (ophthalmic) territory; risk rises sharply with age
inv: Clinical diagnosis from history of zoster and dermatomal distribution
Check renal function before gabapentinoids and an ECG in older patients before tricyclics

case.story: She had shingles on the right chest 5 months ago. The rash healed but she still has burning pain there and cannot wear a bra or let the blanket touch her skin.
case.exam: Scarred, hypopigmented band over right T5; light brushing provokes severe pain; motor and reflexes normal.
case.tests: Creatinine clearance 45 mL/min.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and what first-line treatment would you choose given her renal function?
case.a: Post-herpetic neuralgia; a topical lidocaine 5% patch plus a renally adjusted low-dose gabapentinoid is reasonable first line; recommend recombinant zoster vaccine for prevention in others.

det.patho: Varicella-zoster virus reactivates in a dorsal root or cranial ganglion and causes inflammation and necrosis of the ganglion, root and peripheral nerve. Loss of large and small fibres, ectopic firing of damaged nociceptors and central sensitisation in the dorsal horn sustain pain after the rash heals. Age and immune decline are major risk factors.
det.clinical: Pain is continuous burning or aching with superimposed shocks and marked allodynia. Risk factors include age over 50, severe acute pain, extensive rash and ophthalmic involvement. Pain interferes with sleep and mood and can be very disabling in the elderly.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical: dermatomal neuropathic pain persisting 3 months or more after zoster. Examination shows sensory abnormalities in the affected dermatome. Investigations are needed only when the history is uncertain or another cause such as a spinal lesion is suspected.
det.treatment: First-line options are gabapentin or pregabalin (dose adjusted for renal function), tricyclic antidepressants at low dose (cautious in the elderly), and topical lidocaine 5% plasters; high-concentration capsaicin patches are second line. Opioids are a last resort. Prevention matters most: recombinant zoster vaccine for adults over 50 and early antivirals during acute zoster.
det.prognosis: Many patients improve over 1–2 years, but a minority have persistent pain.
pearls: Vaccination is the best way to reduce PHN.
Use topical lidocaine early in frail elderly to limit systemic side effects.
Dose gabapentinoids by renal function to avoid confusion and myoclonus.
det.thd: post-herpetic neuralgia คืออาการปวดแสบร้อนที่ผิวหนังบริเวณเคยเป็นงูสวัดนานเกิน 3 เดือน มักมีปวดแม้สัมผัสเบาๆ พบมากในผู้สูงอายุ เกิดจากเชื้อไวรัสทำลายปมประสาทและเส้นประสาท การรักษาใช้ gabapentin/pregabalin ปรับตามการทำงานของไต ยา tricyclic ขนาดต่ำ หรือแผ่นแปะ lidocaine และการป้องกันที่ดีที่สุดคือวัคซีนงูสวัด

ddx.pt: Brief electric shocks in a trigeminal division without preceding rash or sensory scarring
Acute zoster of the geniculate ganglion with facial palsy and ear vesicles
Regional limb pain with swelling, colour and sweating change, not dermatomal

aN: phn | postherpetic neuralgia | post zoster neuralgia | postherpetic pain

name: Post-infectious myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus following infection, sometimes due to immune-mediated encephalitis such as opsoclonus-myoclonus or brainstem encephalitis.
simple: Muscle jerks that appear after an infection.
th: อาการกระตุกที่เกิดตามหลังการติดเชื้อ มักเกิดจากภูมิคุ้มกันทำลายสมอง เช่น opsoclonus-myoclonus หรือก้านสมองอักเสบ
tempoNote: Develops days to a few weeks after a viral or bacterial infection, then usually improves over weeks to months
feat: Multifocal action myoclonus starting after an upper respiratory, gastrointestinal or other infection
Often with ataxia, tremor and sometimes chaotic multidirectional saccades (opsoclonus)
Irritability, sleep disturbance and encephalopathy in some, particularly children
In children, an underlying neuroblastoma must be excluded even when an infection preceded symptoms
inv: MRI brain (often normal), CSF for pleocytosis or oligoclonal bands, viral PCR
Neuronal antibody panels in serum and CSF
Tumour screen: urine catecholamines and chest/abdominal imaging in children; CT body in adults

case.story: Ten days after a febrile flu-like illness she develops jerky arms when reaching, unsteady gait and her eyes 'dancing'.
case.exam: Multifocal action myoclonus, truncal ataxia, opsoclonus; alert and oriented.
case.tests: MRI normal; CSF 12 lymphocytes, protein mildly raised; antibody panel negative; CT chest–abdomen–pelvis normal.
case.q: What is the likely syndrome and the first-line treatment?
case.a: Post-infectious opsoclonus–myoclonus syndrome; immunotherapy with corticosteroids or IVIG after tumour screening, with symptomatic clonazepam or levetiracetam.

det.patho: An immune response triggered by infection is thought to target brainstem, cerebellar or cortical structures, producing disinhibition of myoclonus generators. Specific antibodies are rarely found. Triggers reported include many respiratory viruses, enteroviruses, Mycoplasma, streptococcus and SARS-CoV-2.
det.clinical: Onset is subacute after a recognised infection, with myoclonus, ataxia and sometimes opsoclonus, tremor and behavioural change. Adults tend to recover better than paraneoplastic cases. Children with opsoclonus–myoclonus may have an occult neuroblastoma regardless of a preceding infection.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on timing after infection plus exclusion of direct CNS infection, toxic-metabolic causes, drug effects, prion disease and paraneoplastic syndromes. MRI and CSF are often unremarkable or only mildly inflammatory. Antibody testing and tumour screening are essential, and repeat screening is advisable if recovery is incomplete.
det.treatment: Immunotherapy (high-dose corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange) is commonly used, with rituximab in refractory paediatric opsoclonus–myoclonus. Symptomatic agents include clonazepam, levetiracetam and valproate. Treat any identified infection or tumour.
det.prognosis: Most adult post-infectious cases improve substantially over months; children may have lasting behavioural and learning problems.
pearls: A preceding infection does not exclude neuroblastoma in a child with opsoclonus–myoclonus.
Normal MRI is common; the diagnosis is clinical with exclusion.
Adults with post-infectious forms usually do better than paraneoplastic ones.
det.thd: post-infectious myoclonus คืออาการกระตุกที่เกิดหลังติดเชื้อไม่กี่วันถึงสัปดาห์ เชื่อว่าเกิดจากภูมิคุ้มกันทำลายก้านสมองหรือสมองน้อย มักมีเดินเซและตากระตุกแบบ opsoclonus ร่วม ต้องตัดการติดเชื้อโดยตรง ยา และมะเร็งออก โดยเฉพาะ neuroblastoma ในเด็ก การรักษาใช้ steroid หรือ IVIG ร่วมกับยาลดกระตุก ผู้ใหญ่ส่วนใหญ่ฟื้นตัวดี

ddx.pt: Broader syndrome that may be paraneoplastic; post-infectious cases form one subgroup
Late measles complication with periodic myoclonus, progressive dementia and very high CSF measles antibodies
Relentless dementia with myoclonus, no preceding infection, typical MRI and EEG

name: Post-intensive care syndrome
formal: New or worsened physical weakness, cognitive impairment and psychiatric problems after critical illness, including critical illness neuromyopathy.
simple: Weakness, memory problems and low mood that persist after a stay in intensive care.
th: ปัญหาที่เกิดใหม่หรือแย่ลงหลังป่วยหนักในไอซียู ทั้งกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง ความคิดความจำเสื่อม และปัญหาทางจิตใจ เช่น ซึมเศร้า วิตกกังวล PTSD
tempoNote: Apparent at ICU discharge and may persist months to years
feat: ICU-acquired weakness from critical illness myopathy and/or polyneuropathy
Cognitive impairment (attention, memory, executive) often after delirium
Anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress symptoms
Fatigue, sleep disturbance, joint contractures and reduced exercise capacity
Family members may develop psychological distress (PICS-F)
inv: Screening at follow-up: MRC sum score, grip strength, MoCA, HADS, IES-R
Nerve conduction and EMG (including direct muscle stimulation) for ICU-acquired weakness
Exclude new stroke, hypoxic injury, metabolic and medication causes

case.story: Spent 3 weeks ventilated for septic shock with delirium. Two months after discharge she cannot climb stairs, forgets appointments and wakes with nightmares of the ICU.
case.exam: Symmetric proximal weakness with reduced reflexes; MoCA 21/30; anxious and hypervigilant.
case.tests: NCS reduced CMAP amplitudes with preserved sensory responses; EMG myopathic units.
case.q: Which three domains of PICS are affected here?
case.a: Physical (critical illness myopathy), cognitive (post-delirium impairment) and psychological (PTSD symptoms); refer to rehabilitation and an ICU follow-up clinic.

det.patho: Critical illness causes muscle and nerve injury through inflammation, microvascular dysfunction, immobility, hyperglycaemia, corticosteroids and neuromuscular blockers. Brain dysfunction relates to delirium, hypoxia, hypotension and sedation. Psychological harm reflects frightening experiences, delusional memories and loss of control. Up to half of ICU survivors have at least one domain affected.
det.clinical: Patients describe weakness, fatigue, poor memory and concentration, low mood, anxiety and nightmares; many cannot return to work. Weakness is symmetric and proximal, with swallowing and respiratory muscle involvement possible. Cognitive deficits resemble mild traumatic brain injury and may persist for years. Family members often carry substantial psychological burden too.
det.diagnosis: PICS is a descriptive syndrome diagnosed by structured screening of physical, cognitive and mental health after ICU discharge. Electrodiagnostic studies distinguish myopathy from neuropathy. New neurological deficits should prompt imaging for complications such as stroke.
det.treatment: Prevention follows the ICU 'ABCDEF' bundle: pain control, spontaneous awakening and breathing trials, careful sedation choice, delirium monitoring, early mobility and family engagement; ICU diaries may reduce PTSD. After discharge, structured rehabilitation, cognitive training, psychological therapy and ICU follow-up clinics help. Avoid unnecessary steroids and neuromuscular blockers, and control glucose.
det.prognosis: Many improve over 6–12 months, but a substantial minority have lasting disability and reduced quality of life.
pearls: Ask every ICU survivor about weakness, memory and mood — all three.
Delirium duration predicts long-term cognitive impairment.
Normal sensory responses favour CIM; reduced ones suggest CIP.
det.thd: Post-intensive care syndrome คือกลุ่มปัญหาหลังผู้ป่วยรอดจากไอซียู ได้แก่ กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงจาก critical illness myopathy หรือ polyneuropathy ความคิดความจำแย่ลงโดยเฉพาะหลังเคยเพ้อ และปัญหาจิตใจ เช่น ซึมเศร้า วิตกกังวล PTSD ญาติก็อาจได้รับผลกระทบ การป้องกันใช้แนวทาง ABCDEF bundle ในไอซียู และหลังจำหน่ายควรมีการฟื้นฟูร่างกาย ฝึกความคิด และดูแลจิตใจ

ddx.pt: The muscle component itself, with low CMAPs and normal sensory responses
Axonal sensorimotor neuropathy with reduced sensory and motor amplitudes
Demyelinating features, CSF albuminocytological dissociation; onset not linked to ICU care

aN: pics | post icu syndrome | pics f family | post critical illness syndrome

name: Post-polio syndrome
formal: Late progressive weakness, fatigue and pain decades after poliomyelitis, from motor unit overuse and attrition of surviving motor neurons.
simple: New muscle weakness and tiredness appearing many years after recovery from polio.
more: Diagnosis needs a history of prior polio, new weakness after stable years and exclusion of other causes; EMG shows large reinnervated motor unit potentials. Management includes pacing, orthotics and ventilatory support; IVIG has not shown consistent benefit.
th: อ่อนแรงและล้าใหม่ในผู้ที่เคยเป็นโปลิโอเมื่อหลายสิบปีก่อน — เกิดหลังช่วงอาการคงที่ยาวนาน
tempoNote: Decades after acute polio (often 30+ years); slow, sometimes stepwise
feat: Childhood paralytic (or even non-paralytic) polio, then many years of stable function
New weakness and wasting — in old polio limbs and in limbs that seemed unaffected
Fatigue is the most disabling complaint; muscle and joint pain, cold intolerance
Sometimes new swallowing or breathing difficulty
Sensation and reflexes in unaffected limbs are normal
inv: EMG: chronic neurogenic change with large motor units, ± new denervation; normal sensory studies
Exclude mimics: radiculopathy, entrapment, ALS, myopathy, thyroid disease (MRI spine, bloods)
Respiratory function and sleep study if night-time symptoms

case.story: Had polio aged 3 with a weak right leg, worked normally for 50 years; over 2 years increasingly tired by afternoon, and now the left leg also gives way.
case.exam: Wasted right leg with absent knee jerk; mild new left quadriceps weakness, no fasciculation, normal sensation, no UMN signs.
case.tests: EMG: large-amplitude long-duration motor units in both legs with a few fibrillations; MRI lumbar spine shows only mild degeneration.
case.q: What must be excluded before calling this post-polio syndrome?
case.a: Other treatable causes of new weakness — compressive radiculopathy, entrapment, myopathy, thyroid disease — and ALS. PPS is a diagnosis of exclusion; management is paced rehabilitation and energy conservation.

ddx.pt: UMN signs and relentless spread; no remote polio with long stable interval
No history of polio; progression is faster and generalizes
Root pain, dermatomal sensory loss and imaging correlate

aN: pps | post poliomyelitis syndrome | late effects of polio

det.patho: After acute poliomyelitis, surviving motor neurons sprout extra terminal branches to adopt orphaned muscle fibres, creating giant motor units. Over decades these overstretched units cannot maintain all their terminals, so distal axonal branches drop out and new weakness appears. Normal ageing loss of motor neurons, overuse and possibly low-grade inflammation contribute. It affects a substantial proportion of polio survivors, mainly those who had paralytic disease.
det.clinical: After at least 15 years of neurological stability, patients notice new fatigue, slowly progressive weakness, muscle and joint pain, and reduced endurance. Weakness may also affect muscles that seemed spared, because subclinical denervation was widespread. Cold intolerance, sleep-disordered breathing, dysphagia and falls are common. Progression is slow, often with plateaus.
det.diagnosis: It is a diagnosis of exclusion based on a history of paralytic polio with partial recovery, a long stable period, and new weakness or fatigue lasting at least a year without another cause. EMG confirms chronic denervation with large motor units and normal sensory studies. Exclude radiculopathy, entrapment neuropathy, myopathy, thyroid disease, anaemia, depression, sleep apnoea and ALS. Respiratory function tests and polysomnography are needed if hypoventilation is suspected.
det.treatment: Management is rehabilitative: pacing activity, energy conservation, individually tailored non-fatiguing exercise, orthoses, mobility aids and weight control. Treat sleep-disordered breathing with nocturnal non-invasive ventilation and manage swallowing difficulties with speech therapy. IVIG has shown only modest effects and is not routine. Anaesthetists should be warned about respiratory weakness and sensitivity to sedatives.
det.prognosis: Decline is usually slow, and life expectancy is generally not shortened unless there is significant respiratory involvement.
pearls: PPS is not reactivation of the virus; it is late failure of oversized motor units.
Overwork worsens symptoms — pacing beats strengthening to exhaustion.
det.thd: Post-polio syndrome เกิดในผู้ที่เคยป่วยเป็นโปลิโอเมื่อหลายสิบปีก่อน เซลล์ประสาทสั่งการที่เหลือรอดต้องแตกแขนงไปเลี้ยงกล้ามเนื้อจำนวนมาก เมื่อเวลาผ่านไปจึงเสื่อมจนเกิดอ่อนแรงใหม่ อาการเด่นคืออ่อนล้า อ่อนแรงช้าๆ ปวดกล้ามเนื้อ และอาจหายใจหรือกลืนลำบาก การวินิจฉัยต้องตัดสาเหตุอื่นออกก่อน เช่น รากประสาทถูกกด หรือ ALS การรักษาเน้นฟื้นฟู ออกกำลังพอดี จัดสรรพลังงาน และใช้เครื่องช่วยหายใจตอนกลางคืนเมื่อจำเป็น

name: Post-synaptic CMS
formal: Congenital myasthenic syndromes with defects at the postsynaptic membrane, such as acetylcholine receptor or rapsyn mutations, causing fatigable weakness from infancy.
simple: Inherited muscle weakness that worsens with activity, caused by a fault in how nerve signals are received by muscles.
th: กลุ่มโรคกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงแต่กำเนิดจากความผิดปกติที่ฝั่งหลังรอยต่อประสาทกล้ามเนื้อ เช่น ตัวรับ acetylcholine หรือ rapsyn ทำให้อ่อนล้าตั้งแต่ทารก
tempoNote: Lifelong from infancy or childhood with fluctuations and crises during infections; slow-channel forms may start later
feat: Ptosis, ophthalmoparesis, weak cry and feeding difficulty from birth or early childhood
Fatigable limb weakness and delayed motor milestones
Episodes of respiratory failure during infections, especially with rapsyn defects
Slow-channel forms show neck and wrist/finger extensor weakness and a repetitive CMAP after one stimulus
AChR antibodies are negative
inv: Repetitive nerve stimulation (decrement) and single-fibre EMG (jitter)
Repetitive CMAP after a single stimulus suggests slow-channel syndrome or AChE deficiency
Negative AChR and MuSK antibodies; next-generation sequencing CMS gene panel (CHRNE, RAPSN, CHRNA1, others)

case.story: Droopy eyelids since birth that worsen in the evening; twice admitted to ICU with breathing failure during chest infections.
case.exam: Bilateral ptosis, mild ophthalmoparesis, fatigable arm abduction; reflexes normal.
case.tests: 3-Hz RNS shows 20% decrement; AChR and MuSK antibodies negative; CHRNE biallelic variants.
case.q: Which drug is first line and which drug class would harm a slow-channel case?
case.a: AChR deficiency CMS: pyridostigmine (often with 3,4-diaminopyridine); in slow-channel CMS pyridostigmine worsens weakness and fluoxetine or quinidine are used instead.

det.patho: Postsynaptic CMS are inherited defects of the endplate: reduced AChR number (commonly recessive CHRNE variants), abnormal channel kinetics (slow-channel, usually dominant, prolonging openings and causing endplate myopathy; fast-channel, recessive, shortening them), or defective AChR clustering (RAPSN, and related pathway genes). The common result is reduced safety margin of transmission.
det.clinical: Most present at birth or in infancy with ptosis, feeding and respiratory difficulty and fatigable weakness; some present later. Rapsyn deficiency is notable for crises with infections and arthrogryposis. Slow-channel syndrome often appears in childhood or adulthood with selective weakness of neck and finger extensors.
det.diagnosis: Suspect CMS in fatigable weakness from early life with negative antibodies and no response to immunotherapy. Neurophysiology confirms transmission failure, a repetitive CMAP points to slow-channel or AChE deficiency, and genetic panels or exome sequencing identify the subtype, which determines treatment.
det.treatment: AChR deficiency and fast-channel forms respond to pyridostigmine and 3,4-diaminopyridine; salbutamol or ephedrine can add benefit. Slow-channel syndrome is worsened by cholinesterase inhibitors and is treated with fluoxetine or quinidine, which block the open channel. Plan for respiratory crises with infections and avoid neuromuscular-blocking drugs where possible.
det.prognosis: Usually stable or slowly changing with correct treatment; respiratory crises in infancy are the main danger.
pearls: Antibody-negative fatigable weakness from infancy suggests CMS.
A repetitive CMAP is a red flag against pyridostigmine.
Genetic subtype guides treatment more than the clinical picture does.
det.thd: post-synaptic CMS เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมที่ตัวรับ acetylcholine หรือโปรตีนจัดกลุ่มตัวรับ (rapsyn) ผิดปกติ ทำให้หนังตาตก กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนล้าตั้งแต่ทารก และอาจหายใจล้มเหลวเมื่อติดเชื้อ ผลแอนติบอดี MG เป็นลบ วินิจฉัยด้วย RNS/SFEMG และตรวจยีน การรักษาขึ้นกับชนิด ส่วนใหญ่ใช้ pyridostigmine และ 3,4-DAP แต่ slow-channel ต้องใช้ fluoxetine หรือ quinidine

ddx.pt: Autoimmune, later onset with positive antibodies; responds to immunotherapy
Floppy infant with areflexia and tongue fasciculations; no decrement-type fatigability or ptosis
Raised CK and dystrophic biopsy; weakness not fatigable

aN: postsynaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome | achr deficiency cms | slow channel cms | fast channel cms | rapsyn cms

name: Post-traumatic cervical dystonia
formal: Neck dystonia developing days to months after neck or head trauma, often with pain and sometimes a peripheral origin, with abnormal sustained head postures.
simple: A twisting or tilting of the head and neck that starts after an injury.
more: Treat with botulinum toxin injections and physiotherapy; many have persistent pain, and spontaneous improvement is less likely.
th: คอบิดเกร็งผิดท่าที่เกิดหลังบาดเจ็บที่คอหรือศีรษะไม่กี่วันถึงเดือน มักปวดมากและท่าคอค่อนข้างคงที่
tempoNote: Appears days to months after injury and tends to persist
feat: Sustained abnormal head and neck posture developing after neck trauma, sometimes minor
Prominent neck and shoulder pain, often more than in idiopathic cervical dystonia
Fixed posture with limited range of movement and fewer sensory tricks
Some cases have features of functional dystonia; consider this carefully
inv: Cervical spine imaging (X-ray, CT, MRI) to exclude fracture, atlantoaxial subluxation or disc disease
Examination under distraction and for functional signs; EMG to map active muscles for botulinum toxin

case.story: Two months after a rear-end car accident her head has turned and tilted to the left; she has constant neck pain and cannot straighten her neck.
case.exam: Fixed left rotation and tilt, painful hypertrophied left sternocleidomastoid; no sensory trick; normal limbs.
case.tests: MRI cervical spine shows no fracture or subluxation.
case.q: What must be excluded first, and what is the main symptomatic treatment?
case.a: Exclude structural spine injury such as atlantoaxial rotatory subluxation; then botulinum toxin with physiotherapy, while considering a functional component.

det.patho: The mechanism is uncertain. Peripheral injury may alter sensory input and trigger maladaptive plasticity in predisposed individuals, but many fixed post-traumatic postures share features with functional dystonia. Structural spine causes must be excluded.
det.clinical: Compared with idiopathic cervical dystonia, post-traumatic forms start sooner after injury, are more painful, often fixed, show reduced range of movement and seldom respond to sensory tricks. Shoulder elevation and laterocollis are common. Medicolegal issues are frequent.
det.diagnosis: Rule out cervical fracture, rotatory subluxation, disc herniation and posterior fossa lesions by imaging. Assess for positive features of functional dystonia (variability, distractibility, sudden onset). EMG helps target treatment.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin injections and physiotherapy are mainstays, although response is often less than in idiopathic forms. Analgesia and treatment of mood and sleep disorders help. If functional features are present, explain the diagnosis and offer specialist physiotherapy and psychological therapy.
det.prognosis: Persistent symptoms are common; spontaneous remission is uncommon.
pearls: Always exclude atlantoaxial subluxation in post-traumatic torticollis, especially in children.
Fixed painful posture soon after minor trauma should raise the possibility of functional dystonia.
Response to botulinum toxin is usually more modest than in idiopathic cervical dystonia.
det.thd: post-traumatic cervical dystonia คือคอบิดเกร็งที่เกิดหลังอุบัติเหตุที่คอหรือศีรษะ มักปวดมาก ท่าคอแข็งไม่เปลี่ยน และไม่ค่อยมี sensory trick ต้องตรวจภาพกระดูกคอเพื่อตัดกระดูกหักหรือข้อเคลื่อนก่อน และพิจารณาภาวะ functional dystonia ร่วมด้วย การรักษาใช้ botulinum toxin และกายภาพบำบัด แต่มักตอบสนองน้อยกว่าชนิดไม่ทราบสาเหตุ

ddx.pt: Idiopathic cervical dystonia with mobile, often sensory-trick-responsive posture and no trauma link
Sudden onset, fixed posture, pain and inconsistency on examination
Neck pain with trigger points but no sustained involuntary posture

aN: post traumatic torticollis | peripherally induced cervical dystonia | trauma related cervical dystonia | post whiplash dystonia

name: Post-traumatic stress disorder(PTSD)
formal: Psychiatric disorder after trauma with intrusive re-experiencing, avoidance, hyperarousal and negative mood or cognition lasting beyond one month.
simple: A mental health condition after a frightening event with flashbacks, nightmares and feeling on edge.
th: โรคเครียดหลังเหตุการณ์สะเทือนขวัญ มีภาพผุดซ้ำ ฝันร้าย หลีกเลี่ยง อารมณ์ด้านลบ และตื่นตัวเกินเหตุนานเกิน 1 เดือน พบร่วมกับ TBI functional seizures อาการปวดเรื้อรัง และปัญหาการนอน
tempoNote: Symptoms begin soon after the trauma in most people but may reach full criteria months later (delayed expression); duration over 1 month is required, and many cases become chronic
feat: Intrusive memories, flashbacks and trauma-related nightmares, with distress or physiological reactions to reminders
Avoidance of reminders and persistent negative thoughts and mood such as blame, numbness and detachment
Hyperarousal: exaggerated startle, irritability, poor concentration, sleep disruption and reckless behaviour
A dissociative subtype has depersonalisation or derealisation; complex PTSD in ICD-11 adds problems with emotion regulation, self-image and relationships
Overlaps with mild TBI, functional seizures, chronic pain, headache, depression and substance use
inv: Clinical interview with validated tools (PCL-5 screen, CAPS-5 for diagnosis)
Screen for depression, suicidality, alcohol and drug use
Assess for coexisting brain injury when the trauma involved head impact or blast; neuroimaging only if there are neurological signs

case.story: Eight months after a fatal road crash he attended, he relives the scene when he hears sirens, avoids the highway, sleeps 3 hours with nightmares and has become irritable with his family; he drinks more to sleep.
case.exam: Hypervigilant and startles easily; normal neurological examination; no head injury at the scene.
case.tests: PCL-5 score is 52; PHQ-9 14; AUDIT suggests hazardous drinking; no investigation is needed.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the first-line treatment?
case.a: PTSD with comorbid depression and hazardous alcohol use; offer trauma-focused psychotherapy (CPT, prolonged exposure or EMDR), with sertraline, paroxetine or venlafaxine if therapy is unavailable or declined, and address alcohol use.

det.patho: PTSD reflects failure of fear memories to extinguish after trauma, with an overactive amygdala and insula and weaker regulation from medial prefrontal cortex and hippocampus. Noradrenergic overactivity drives hyperarousal and nightmares, and HPA axis changes are present but not specific. Smaller hippocampal volume may be partly a pre-existing risk factor. Genetic, developmental and social factors, and peritraumatic dissociation, shape who develops the disorder.
det.clinical: Most people have acute stress reactions after trauma that fade within weeks; PTSD is diagnosed when symptoms persist beyond a month and cause impairment. Neurologists meet PTSD in patients with mild TBI, headache, chronic pain, functional neurological symptoms, sleep disorders and dissociative attacks. Nightmares and disrupted sleep are very common and can be confused with parasomnias. Depression, alcohol misuse and suicidality often coexist.
det.diagnosis: DSM-5-TR requires that the person faced, witnessed or learned of a threat to life, serious injury or sexual violence, with symptoms in four clusters (intrusion, avoidance, negative mood and cognition, arousal) lasting over a month. Acute stress disorder covers the first month. The PCL-5 is a useful screen, and CAPS-5 is the reference interview. Overlap with post-concussion symptoms is large, so careful history separates head-injury effects from psychological ones, while recognising they often coexist.
det.treatment: Trauma-focused psychotherapies (cognitive processing therapy, prolonged exposure, EMDR) are first line in current guidelines. Sertraline, paroxetine and venlafaxine are the main drug options; benzodiazepines are discouraged because they do not help and may worsen outcomes. Prazosin may help trauma nightmares in some patients despite mixed trial results. Treat comorbid alcohol use, depression and sleep problems, and coordinate with rehabilitation when TBI coexists; MDMA-assisted therapy has not been approved.
det.prognosis: Many people recover with or without treatment within a year, but a substantial minority have chronic or relapsing symptoms, especially after interpersonal or repeated trauma.
pearls: Post-concussion symptoms and PTSD often coexist after a head injury, and both need treatment.
Avoid benzodiazepines for PTSD; trauma-focused therapy is first line.
ICD-11 complex PTSD adds problems of emotion regulation, self-concept and relationships.
det.thd: PTSD เกิดหลังเหตุการณ์ที่เสี่ยงต่อชีวิตหรือความรุนแรง มีภาพเหตุการณ์ผุดซ้ำ ฝันร้าย หลีกเลี่ยงสิ่งเตือนความจำ อารมณ์ด้านลบ และตื่นตัวมาก นานเกิน 1 เดือน มักพบร่วมกับการบาดเจ็บสมองเล็กน้อย functional seizures อาการปวดเรื้อรัง และการดื่มสุรา การรักษาหลักคือจิตบำบัดที่เน้นบาดแผลทางใจ เช่น CPT หรือ EMDR และยา sertraline paroxetine หรือ venlafaxine ไม่ควรใช้ benzodiazepine

ddx.pt: Headache, dizziness and cognitive complaints after a head injury; often coexists with PTSD after blast or road crashes
Dissociative attacks that may be triggered by trauma reminders; normal ictal video-EEG
Amnesia, depersonalisation or identity disturbance dominate rather than intrusions and hyperarousal

aN: ptsd | post traumatic stress disorder | posttraumatic stress disorder | complex ptsd

name: Post-traumatic tics
formal: Tics appearing after head injury or other trauma, sometimes functional, with abrupt onset.
simple: Repeated sudden movements or sounds that start after an injury.
th: อาการ tic ที่เกิดขึ้นใหม่หลังบาดเจ็บที่ศีรษะหรือร่างกาย มักเริ่มทันทีในผู้ใหญ่ และหลายรายเป็นชนิด functional
tempoNote: Usually begins within days to months after injury, often abruptly in adulthood
feat: New tics after head or peripheral trauma in someone without a childhood tic history
Motor tics more often than vocal; may be complex
Abrupt adult onset, lack of premonitory urge or suppressibility and inconsistency suggest functional tics
Coexisting anxiety, PTSD or post-concussion symptoms are common
inv: MRI brain to look for basal ganglia or frontal injury
Video recording; assess for functional features and psychiatric comorbidity

case.story: Two weeks after a moderate head injury in a road accident he develops repetitive facial grimaces, head jerks and throat clearing that he cannot hold back.
case.exam: Varied, complex movements that increase when attention is on them and fade with a distracting task; no premonitory urge described.
case.tests: MRI brain shows small frontal contusions, basal ganglia normal.
case.q: Which features favour a functional rather than organic tic disorder?
case.a: Abrupt adult onset after trauma, no premonitory urge or suppressibility, and distractibility suggest functional tics; explain the diagnosis and refer for behavioural therapy.

det.patho: Organic secondary tics are rare and attributed to injury of frontal–striatal circuits. Many reported post-traumatic tic cases have features of functional movement disorder, and genetic predisposition with unmasking of latent tic disorder is another possibility.
det.clinical: Tics usually begin soon after the injury, sometimes in adults with no childhood history. Typical organic tics are stereotyped, preceded by an urge and briefly suppressible. Functional tic-like behaviours are often complex, start abruptly, are variable and lack these features.
det.diagnosis: Take a careful childhood history for previous tics and a family history. MRI helps identify structural injury. Video assessment of urge, suppressibility and distractibility helps separate organic from functional phenotypes.
det.treatment: For organic tics, comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics (CBIT) and drugs such as aripiprazole or clonidine are used. Functional tics respond better to explanation and specialist behavioural therapy than to tic medication. Treat comorbid anxiety, PTSD or depression.
det.prognosis: Variable; functional forms can improve after diagnosis is accepted and therapy begins.
pearls: Ask about childhood tics: trauma may unmask a pre-existing disorder.
Adult-onset, abrupt and complex tics after injury suggest a functional cause.
Organic tics have a premonitory urge and brief suppressibility.
det.thd: post-traumatic tics คือ tic ที่เกิดขึ้นใหม่หลังบาดเจ็บศีรษะหรือร่างกาย พบน้อย ต้องถามประวัติ tic ตอนเด็กเพราะอาจเป็นการกำเริบของโรคเดิม หลายรายมีลักษณะ functional เช่น เริ่มทันทีในผู้ใหญ่ ไม่มีความรู้สึกอยากทำก่อน และหายเมื่อเบี่ยงความสนใจ การรักษาใช้พฤติกรรมบำบัด และยาในกรณี tic จากโรคทางกาย

ddx.pt: Childhood onset, waxing–waning motor and vocal tics with premonitory urges
Main alternative or overlapping diagnosis; positive functional features
Jerks without urge or suppressibility, often triggered by stimuli

aN: secondary tics after trauma | post traumatic tic disorder | acquired tics after head injury

name: Post-traumatic tremor
formal: Rest, postural or kinetic tremor after head trauma, commonly from midbrain or cerebellar injury, including rubral tremor of Holmes.
simple: Shaking that starts after a head injury.
th: อาการสั่นที่เริ่มหลังบาดเจ็บศีรษะ อาจสั่นขณะพัก ท่าทาง หรือเคลื่อนไหว มักมาจากความเสียหายของสมองส่วนกลาง (midbrain) หรือสมองน้อย รวมถึง Holmes tremor
tempoNote: Often begins weeks to months after the injury, sometimes after a symptom-free interval, then persists
feat: Tremor beginning after a head injury, often with a delay of weeks to months
Rest, postural and kinetic components; Holmes pattern is low frequency (2–5 Hz), coarse and proximal, worst on action
Usually unilateral or asymmetric, contralateral to a midbrain, thalamic or cerebellar injury
Accompanied by ataxia, weakness, diplopia or other brainstem signs
Markedly disabling for feeding and writing, with a poor response to medication
inv: MRI (including susceptibility sequences) for midbrain, thalamic or cerebellar contusion, haemorrhage or diffuse axonal injury
Dopamine transporter imaging when a rest tremor suggests nigrostriatal damage
Exclude drugs, thyroid disease, alcohol withdrawal and a functional component

case.who: 34-year-old motorcycle taxi rider from Chiang Rai
case.story: Six weeks after leaving hospital following severe head injury from a road traffic accident, his right arm began shaking, worse when reaching for a glass or holding a spoon.
case.exam: Coarse 3 Hz tremor of the right arm present at rest, increasing with posture and worse with reaching, mild right ataxia, left upward gaze impairment.
case.tests: MRI shows old haemorrhage and gliosis in the left midbrain tegmentum; dopamine transporter scan is mildly reduced on the left.
case.q: Which pathway is likely injured, and what treatments should be tried?
case.a: Cerebellothalamic outflow in the midbrain (Holmes tremor); trial of levodopa, then thalamic Vim stimulation or lesioning if disabling.

det.patho: Post-traumatic tremor reflects injury to the circuits that regulate movement, particularly cerebellothalamic fibres in the superior cerebellar peduncle at the midbrain level, the thalamus, the cerebellum or the nigrostriatal system. Interruption of cerebellar outflow produces the low-frequency, large-amplitude tremor of Holmes type. Diffuse axonal injury and haemorrhage give multiple small lesions in these pathways.
det.clinical: Tremor typically appears after a delay of weeks to months, when the initial coma, weakness or ataxia has improved. The classic Holmes pattern combines rest, postural and kinetic tremor, with kinetic dominating, a frequency of 2 to 5 Hz and prominent proximal involvement. Associated ataxia, weakness and oculomotor signs are common. Some cases are mainly cerebellar-type, some parkinsonian-type with rest tremor, and a fraction are functional or peripheral.
det.diagnosis: Characterise the tremor by activation condition, frequency and distribution, then look at the injury sites with MRI including susceptibility-weighted sequences. Dopamine transporter imaging may show reduced uptake if the nigrostriatal pathway is damaged, which predicts levodopa response. Remove aggravating factors such as stimulant drugs and exclude metabolic causes. A functional component is suggested by variability, distractibility and entrainment.
det.treatment: Medical therapy is disappointing. Options include levodopa when nigrostriatal damage is present, anticholinergics, propranolol, primidone, clonazepam and, in some reports, isoniazid with pyridoxine. Botulinum toxin may help focal tremor. For disabling, refractory tremor, thalamic deep brain stimulation (Vim, sometimes with adjacent targets) or focused ultrasound thalamotomy gives the best chance of benefit and should be considered after stabilisation. Rehabilitation and weighted utensils help daily function.
det.prognosis: May persist for years, although some improve spontaneously in the first year; severe Holmes-type tremor often remains disabling.
pearls: Delayed onset after head injury plus tremor at rest, posture and action points to midbrain outflow injury.
A trial of levodopa is worthwhile if dopamine transporter imaging shows deficit.
Surgery is an early option for severe, disabling tremor.
det.thd: Post-traumatic tremor คืออาการสั่นหลังบาดเจ็บที่ศีรษะ มักเริ่มหลังผ่านไปหลายสัปดาห์ถึงเดือน เกิดจากความเสียหายของเส้นทางสมองน้อย-ทาลามัสที่ midbrain ทำให้สั่นช้า แรง ทั้งขณะพัก ท่าทาง และเคลื่อนไหว (Holmes tremor) ตรวจ MRI และ DaT scan ตอบสนองต่อยาน้อย อาจลองยา levodopa และถ้าสั่นมากพิจารณา DBS หรือ focused ultrasound ที่ thalamus

name: Postencephalitic parkinsonism
formal: Parkinsonism following encephalitis lethargica, with oculogyric crises, behavioural changes and tau pathology without Lewy bodies.
simple: Parkinson-like illness appearing years after sleeping sickness encephalitis.
more: Historical complication of the 1918 influenza epidemic; MRI shows substantia nigra gliosis. Levodopa responses are often initially good with sensitivity to dyskinesias; now rare, with similar syndromes after other encephalitides. Parkinsonism following encephalitis lethargica of 1916-1930s, with oculogyric crises and sleep disturbance, without Lewy bodies.
th: พาร์กินสันที่เกิดหลังโรคสมองอักเสบ encephalitis lethargica ในอดีต มีอาการตาเหลือกค้าง (oculogyric crisis) และพฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน ปัจจุบันพบน้อยมาก
tempoNote: Developed months to years after acute encephalitis and progressed slowly; modern cases follow other encephalitides
feat: Parkinsonism (bradykinesia, rigidity) after an episode of encephalitis, often in young people
Oculogyric crises: episodes of forced upward eye deviation
Sleep–wake disturbance, behavioural and personality change, tics or compulsions
Marked levodopa sensitivity with early dyskinesia and psychiatric side effects
inv: MRI: may show substantia nigra or midbrain damage after the encephalitis
Review of history and investigation of any modern encephalitis (Japanese encephalitis, West Nile, autoimmune)

case.story: Two years after a severe Japanese encephalitis infection he moves slowly, has a mask-like face and episodes where his eyes lock upward for minutes.
case.exam: Hypomimia, bradykinesia, axial rigidity, no tremor; upward gaze crisis witnessed in clinic.
case.tests: MRI shows bilateral thalamic and substantia nigra T2 changes from the earlier infection.
case.q: Which historical syndrome does this resemble, and what caution applies to levodopa?
case.a: A modern postencephalitic parkinsonism resembling von Economo's; start levodopa at low dose because these patients develop dyskinesias and behavioural effects easily.

read.where: 9 - Atypical parkinsonism, parkinsonism-­plus syndromes and secondary parkinsonian disorders

det.patho: Classic PEP followed the encephalitis lethargica epidemic of about 1916–1930, whose cause is still unknown (influenza, an enterovirus and post-infectious autoimmunity have all been proposed). Pathology shows nigral neuron loss with neurofibrillary tangles (tau) and no Lewy bodies. Similar syndromes now follow Japanese encephalitis, West Nile virus and some autoimmune encephalitides.
det.clinical: Parkinsonism appeared after a latent period, often in younger adults, with oculogyric crises, respiratory irregularities, tics, obsessive behaviour, sleep inversion and personality change. The course was slowly progressive over decades. Today it is mainly of historical importance but post-viral parkinsonism is still seen in Asia after Japanese encephalitis.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical with a documented encephalitis history. MRI may show residual nigral, thalamic or basal ganglia damage. Exclude drug-induced parkinsonism, Wilson disease in the young and autoimmune encephalitis.
det.treatment: Levodopa often helps but patients are prone to early dyskinesia, fluctuations and psychiatric side effects, so titrate slowly. Anticholinergics have been used for oculogyric crises. Rehabilitation is important.
det.prognosis: Historical patients survived decades with slowly worsening disability.
pearls: Oculogyric crises plus parkinsonism outside drug exposure suggest a postencephalitic cause.
Pathology is tau-based without Lewy bodies.
In Thailand, consider Japanese encephalitis as a modern cause.
det.thd: postencephalitic parkinsonism คืออาการพาร์กินสันที่เกิดหลังสมองอักเสบ encephalitis lethargica ในช่วงปี 1916–1930 มีตาเหลือกค้าง ปัญหาการนอน และพฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน พยาธิสภาพเป็น tau ไม่มี Lewy body ปัจจุบันพบลักษณะคล้ายกันหลังติดเชื้อสมองอักเสบเจอี การรักษาใช้ levodopa ขนาดต่ำเพราะเกิด dyskinesia ได้ง่าย

name: Posterior circulation aneurysms
formal: Aneurysms of vertebral, basilar and posterior cerebral arteries, with subarachnoid haemorrhage or brainstem compression; higher rupture risk and technically difficult treatment.
simple: Bulges in blood vessels at the back of the brain that can bleed or press on the brainstem.
th: หลอดเลือดโป่งพองของ vertebral basilar และ posterior cerebral artery ทำให้เลือดออกใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมองหรือกดก้านสมอง มีความเสี่ยงแตกสูงกว่าและรักษาได้ยากกว่า
tempoNote: Rupture gives sudden thunderclap SAH; large or dolichoectatic aneurysms compress brainstem slowly over months
feat: About 10–15% of intracranial aneurysms; basilar tip is the commonest site, then PICA origin and vertebral artery
Rupture: thunderclap headache, vomiting, reduced consciousness, often more severe SAH with IVH and hydrocephalus
Mass effect: III palsy (basilar tip/PCA), lower cranial nerve palsies, brainstem compression from giant or fusiform aneurysms
Embolic posterior circulation strokes from thrombus in fusiform/dolichoectatic aneurysms
Vertebral dissecting aneurysms can present with neck pain and SAH
inv: CT brain then CTA; catheter DSA with 3D rotation for planning
MRI/MRA for unruptured aneurysms and mass effect; vessel wall imaging in research or selected cases
Risk scoring for unruptured aneurysms (e.g. PHASES), which assigns higher risk to posterior location

case.story: Smoker with hypertension; collapsed after the worst headache of her life while cooking.
case.exam: GCS 13, neck stiffness, right pupil slightly larger than left; no limb weakness.
case.tests: CT: diffuse SAH with blood in the fourth ventricle and early hydrocephalus; CTA shows a 7 mm basilar tip aneurysm.
case.q: Which treatment is usually preferred for this location, and what complication requires an immediate procedure?
case.a: Endovascular coiling is generally favoured for basilar tip aneurysms; acute hydrocephalus needs an external ventricular drain.

read.where: Section 7 Non-Inflammatory Disorders of the Arterial Wall

det.patho: Saccular aneurysms arise at branch points where haemodynamic stress and wall weakness meet, influenced by hypertension, smoking, female sex and familial factors. In the posterior circulation they occur at the basilar apex, superior cerebellar and PICA origins and the vertebrobasilar junction. Fusiform and dolichoectatic aneurysms reflect diffuse wall degeneration or dissection and can enlarge and thrombose.
det.clinical: Ruptured posterior circulation aneurysms tend to produce more severe haemorrhage, with intraventricular extension, hydrocephalus and early brainstem dysfunction. Unruptured aneurysms are often incidental but may present with cranial neuropathy or brainstem compression when large. Natural history studies show higher rupture risk than for similar-size anterior aneurysms, except the cavernous carotid.
det.diagnosis: Non-contrast CT is the first test for suspected SAH, followed by CTA; DSA remains the reference for small aneurysms and treatment planning. A negative CTA with a perimesencephalic bleeding pattern suggests non-aneurysmal SAH, but vertebrobasilar aneurysm must be excluded. Dissecting vertebral aneurysms may need repeat imaging.
det.treatment: Acute SAH care follows guideline principles: secure the aneurysm early, nimodipine for delayed ischaemia, manage hydrocephalus and avoid hypovolaemia. Endovascular coiling (with stent or balloon assistance) is preferred for most posterior aneurysms because surgery near the brainstem is hazardous; flow diverters are used for selected fusiform or large lesions. Unruptured aneurysms are treated or observed after weighing size, growth, symptoms, age and comorbidity; smoking cessation and BP control are advised.
det.prognosis: Outcome after rupture depends mainly on clinical grade; giant and fusiform basilar aneurysms carry a poor natural history.
pearls: Posterior location adds points to rupture-risk scores such as PHASES.
Coiling is generally first choice for basilar tip aneurysms.
Perimesencephalic SAH pattern still needs vascular imaging to exclude a basilar aneurysm.
det.thd: หลอดเลือดโป่งพองของระบบ posterior circulation เช่น ปลาย basilar หรือจุดแยก PICA พบราว 10–15% ของ aneurysm ทั้งหมด แต่เสี่ยงแตกสูงกว่า เมื่อแตกมักทำให้เลือดออกรุนแรง เข้าโพรงสมองและเกิด hydrocephalus ถ้าไม่แตกอาจกดเส้นประสาทสมองหรือก้านสมอง วินิจฉัยด้วย CT, CTA และ DSA การรักษาส่วนใหญ่ใช้การใส่ขดลวด (coiling) หรือ flow diverter เพราะการผ่าตัดบริเวณก้านสมองเสี่ยงสูง

name: Posterior communicating (PCOM) artery aneurysms
formal: Aneurysms at the internal carotid-posterior communicating junction, commonly causing painful third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil.
simple: A bulge in a brain artery that can press on a nerve to the eye, causing a droopy lid and large pupil.
more: Posterior communicating artery aneurysm, often causing painful third nerve palsy with pupil involvement, or subarachnoid haemorrhage when ruptured.
th: หลอดเลือดโป่งพองบริเวณรอยต่อ internal carotid กับ posterior communicating artery มักทำให้เส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 3 อ่อนแรงร่วมกับปวดและรูม่านตาขยาย หรือทำให้เลือดออกใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมองเมื่อแตก
tempoNote: Third nerve palsy develops over hours to days as the sac expands; rupture is sudden
feat: Painful third nerve palsy: ptosis, eye 'down and out', diplopia with a dilated poorly reactive pupil
Pupil involvement reflects compression of superficial pupillomotor fibres
Expanding palsy may precede rupture: a neurosurgical emergency
Rupture: thunderclap headache, SAH, sometimes temporal lobe haematoma
Among the commonest intracranial aneurysm sites, more common in women
inv: Urgent CTA (or MRA) for any acute painful or pupil-involving third nerve palsy
Catheter DSA if non-invasive imaging is negative but suspicion remains high

case.story: Three days of severe left frontal headache followed by a drooping left eyelid and double vision.
case.exam: Left complete ptosis, eye abducted and depressed, pupil 6 mm unreactive; other cranial nerves normal.
case.tests: CT no blood; CTA shows an 8 mm left ICA-PComA aneurysm.
case.q: Why is this an emergency even without SAH?
case.a: An acutely expanding aneurysm causing third nerve palsy has a high short-term risk of rupture; it should be secured within days by clipping or coiling.

det.patho: These saccular aneurysms arise from the ICA wall at the origin of the posterior communicating artery and usually point backward and downward toward the oculomotor nerve. Pulsatile expansion, thrombosis within the sac or small bleeds compress or irritate the nerve. Risk factors are those of intracranial aneurysms generally: hypertension, smoking, female sex, family history and connective tissue or polycystic kidney disease.
det.clinical: The classic unruptured presentation is an acute painful third nerve palsy with pupil involvement; partial palsies and initial pupil sparing occur and may later progress. Rupture causes SAH with or without temporal lobe haemorrhage. Some aneurysms are discovered incidentally. Third nerve recovery may be partial, with aberrant regeneration (lid elevation on downgaze or adduction).
det.diagnosis: Any acute third nerve palsy with pain or pupil involvement, and any partial or progressing palsy, requires urgent vascular imaging; CTA detects most aneurysms of this size. DSA is used when CTA is equivocal. Pupil-sparing complete palsy in an older vasculopath may be microvascular but still commonly gets imaging in current practice.
det.treatment: The aneurysm should be secured promptly, by microsurgical clipping or endovascular coiling depending on anatomy and local expertise; some studies suggest better third nerve recovery after clipping, though coiling is widely used. Ruptured aneurysms are managed with standard SAH care including nimodipine. Diplopia may be managed with occlusion, prisms or later strabismus surgery.
det.prognosis: Most third nerve palsies improve after treatment, with better recovery if treated early and if the palsy was partial.
pearls: Painful pupil-involving third nerve palsy = PCOM aneurysm until proved otherwise.
Pupil sparing does not exclude aneurysm when the palsy is partial.
Aberrant regeneration of the third nerve implies a compressive cause rather than microvascular ischaemia.
det.thd: หลอดเลือดโป่งพองที่ PCOM อยู่ใกล้เส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 3 จึงมักมาด้วยปวดศีรษะหรือปวดรอบตาร่วมกับหนังตาตก ตาเบนออกด้านล่าง และรูม่านตาขยาย ถือเป็นภาวะฉุกเฉินเพราะเสี่ยงแตกเร็ว ต้องทำ CTA หรือ MRA ทันที ถ้าแตกจะเกิดเลือดออกใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมอง รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัด clipping หรือใส่ขดลวด coiling ให้เร็วที่สุด

name: Posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (PION)
formal: Ischaemic optic neuropathy of the retrobulbar optic nerve with sudden visual loss and normal disc, after surgery, hypotension, anaemia or giant cell arteritis.
simple: Sudden vision loss from poor blood supply to the back part of the eye nerve, with a normal-looking eye exam.
th: เส้นประสาทตาส่วนหลังลูกตาขาดเลือด ทำให้ตามัวเฉียบพลันโดย optic disc ปกติในช่วงแรกและมี RAPD พบหลังผ่าตัดใหญ่ ความดันต่ำ ซีดมาก หรือ giant cell arteritis ผลลัพธ์แย่กว่า optic neuritis
tempoNote: Sudden onset, often noticed on waking after surgery; disc pallor appears 4–8 weeks later
feat: Abrupt, painless (or mildly painful) loss of sight affecting one eye or both
Normal-appearing optic disc at onset, with RAPD and visual field loss
Typical setting: prolonged spine or cardiac surgery, hypotension, severe anaemia, or giant cell arteritis
Older age and vascular risk factors; prone positioning increases risk
Optic atrophy develops weeks later; MRI may show diffusion restriction in the nerve
inv: Urgent ESR, CRP and platelets; temporal artery work-up when GCA is possible
MRI orbit and brain with diffusion-weighted imaging and contrast to exclude compression and demyelination
Haemoglobin, blood pressure and intraoperative record review
Visual fields, colour vision and OCT for follow-up

case.who: 63-year-old man after a spinal fusion in Bangkok
case.story: Woke up from a prolonged prone operation with blood loss and low blood pressure, unable to see from the left eye. No eye pain.
case.exam: Left eye no light perception, left RAPD, normal-looking discs and retina, right eye normal.
case.tests: Haemoglobin 7 g/dL post-operatively; ESR normal; MRI shows no compressive lesion; DWI is positive in the left orbital optic nerve.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and what can be done?
case.a: Perioperative posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy. Correct anaemia and hypotension, exclude GCA and compression, and counsel on the poor prognosis; there is no proven treatment, so prevention in high-risk surgery is key.

det.patho: Behind the globe the optic nerve receives its blood from pial branches arising from the ophthalmic and other arteries, a watershed area vulnerable to low perfusion. Systemic hypotension, severe anaemia, venous congestion from prone positioning, or arteritic occlusion cause infarction. Perioperative PION is classically linked with spine surgery and cardiac bypass.
det.clinical: Vision loss is abrupt, usually painless, unilateral or bilateral, and is detected on awakening after surgery. Examination shows RAPD without disc swelling, and optic pallor appears after several weeks. Patients are often elderly with vascular risk factors. GCA must be considered in non-surgical cases. Severe visual loss and bilateral involvement are common in perioperative cases.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical after excluding compressive, inflammatory and infiltrative causes. MRI with diffusion imaging may show nerve infarction. Red flags for alternative diagnosis are age under 50, pain, bilateral loss, progression beyond one week and systemic symptoms. Test for GCA and check anaemia and perfusion.
det.treatment: No treatment is proven. Management is to restore blood pressure and haemoglobin and treat GCA immediately with high-dose steroids if suspected. Prevention in high-risk surgery involves limiting blood loss and anaemia, keeping mean arterial pressure adequate, avoiding head-down positioning and shortening operations.
det.prognosis: Poor: recovery is limited in most patients, much worse than with optic neuritis.
pearls: Post-operative visual loss with normal discs is PION until proven otherwise.
Always exclude GCA in older patients.
Disc swelling points to anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy instead.
det.thd: PION คือการขาดเลือดของเส้นประสาทตาส่วนหลังลูกตา ทำให้ตามัวทันทีโดย optic disc ยังปกติ มักพบหลังผ่าตัดที่เสียเลือดมากหรือความดันต่ำ หรือจาก giant cell arteritis ตรวจพบ RAPD ต้องทำ MRI และเจาะเลือดหา ESR/CRP ยังไม่มีการรักษาที่พิสูจน์ได้ ให้แก้ภาวะซีดและความดันต่ำและให้สเตียรอยด์ทันทีถ้าสงสัย GCA การพยากรณ์ไม่ดี

Triggers: severe hypertension, eclampsia, renal failure, calcineurin inhibitors, chemotherapy
Usually reversible with control of the trigger
inv: MRI FLAIR: symmetric parieto-occipital subcortical vasogenic oedema
BP, renal function, magnesium, drug levels

qx.stem: A 31-year-old woman with severe pre-eclampsia (BP 195/115 mmHg) has headache, visual blurring and a generalised seizure. MRI FLAIR shows bilateral symmetric subcortical hyperintensities in the parieto-occipital regions with high ADC and no enhancement.
qx.q: Which therapy is the most urgent?
opts: Intravenous alteplase
High-dose methylprednisolone
Prompt control of blood pressure, magnesium sulfate and delivery planning
Cyclophosphamide pulse
Plasma exchange
qx.why: PRES with vasogenic oedema in the posterior watershed regions is reversible if the cause is removed; in eclampsia the treatment is BP reduction, magnesium sulfate for seizure prevention and obstetric delivery. Thrombolysis is contraindicated, and immunosuppression has no role unless an immune cause is identified. High ADC distinguishes vasogenic oedema from infarct.

qx.stem: A 62-year-old man with severe COPD exacerbation and hypercapnia develops headache, visual blurring and a seizure. BP is 190/110 mmHg. MRI shows bilateral parieto-occipital T2/FLAIR hyperintensities without restricted diffusion.
qx.q: What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Gradual blood pressure reduction, seizure control and removal of the precipitant, with correction of hypercapnia
Rapid normalisation of blood pressure to normal within minutes
Thrombolysis
Immediate craniotomy
High-dose steroids only
qx.why: PRES is a vasogenic oedema syndrome linked to loss of autoregulation and endothelial dysfunction, here with hypercapnia and hypertension as precipitants. Management is controlled BP reduction (about 25 percent in the first hours), antiseizure drugs and treating triggers; over-rapid lowering risks ischaemia.

det.patho: Failure of cerebral autoregulation and endothelial dysfunction allow fluid to leak into the brain, producing vasogenic oedema with a posterior predominance, where sympathetic vascular innervation is sparser. Two complementary models exist: hyperperfusion when pressure overwhelms the autoregulatory ceiling, and endothelial injury with vasoconstriction and relative hypoperfusion from circulating toxins, cytokines or drugs; overlap with RCVS is common. Triggers include abrupt severe hypertension, pre-eclampsia/eclampsia (also postpartum), renal failure, sepsis, autoimmune disease such as lupus, transplantation and drugs such as calcineurin inhibitors, chemotherapy and anti-VEGF agents. BP may be only modestly raised in drug-related or septic cases.
det.clinical: Patients develop headache, altered awareness ranging from confusion to coma, visual disturbances from blurring and hemianopia to cortical blindness, and seizures, which may become status epilepticus and are the presenting feature in most. Focal motor deficits are less common. Onset is over hours to days, often in a hospitalised patient after a BP surge or a new drug. Atypical forms involve the frontal lobes, brainstem, cerebellum, basal ganglia or even the spinal cord. Some cases bleed (about 1 in 7) or develop restricted diffusion, which predicts permanent damage.
det.diagnosis: MRI FLAIR shows largely symmetric subcortical and cortical oedema in parieto-occipital regions, often with superior frontal sulcus or watershed (holohemispheric) patterns, usually without restricted diffusion; CT is less sensitive. Look for the trigger: BP, renal function, magnesium, calcineurin inhibitor levels, pregnancy status, autoimmune serology and signs of sepsis. Exclude CVT with venography, and consider bilateral PCA infarction, encephalitis, PML, osmotic demyelination and toxic leukoencephalopathy when the course or imaging is unusual; vessel imaging may show reversible vasoconstriction. Repeat MRI after treatment helps confirm reversibility, and EEG is useful when awareness stays depressed.
det.treatment: Lower BP in a controlled way (roughly 20–25% in the first hours) with titratable IV agents such as nicardipine or labetalol, avoiding abrupt falls that could cause watershed infarction. Treat seizures and status epilepticus with standard antiseizure drugs, and treat in an ICU if awareness is impaired. In eclampsia give magnesium sulfate and arrange delivery. Stop or reduce the culprit immunosuppressant or chemotherapy where possible; some patients can later be rechallenged cautiously or switched to an alternative. Correct fluid, magnesium and electrolyte disturbances; antiseizure drugs can usually be withdrawn within weeks to a few months once clinical and MRI recovery is complete.
det.prognosis: Clinical and radiological recovery within days to weeks is the rule; haemorrhage, extensive oedema or infarction carry a risk of lasting deficit or epilepsy, and recurrence occurs in a minority if triggers persist.
pearls: Cortical blindness with brisk pupils = occipital pathology such as PRES.
Normotension does not exclude PRES in patients on tacrolimus or chemotherapy.
The name misleads: it is not always posterior and not always reversible.
Eclampsia can appear for the first time after delivery; think PRES in a postpartum woman with headache and seizures.
det.thd: PRES คือสมองบวมแบบ vasogenic จากการที่หลอดเลือดสมองคุมความดันตัวเองไม่ได้และเยื่อบุหลอดเลือดเสียหาย มักพบบริเวณสมองส่วนหลัง (parieto-occipital) สาเหตุคือความดันสูงเฉียบพลัน ครรภ์เป็นพิษ (รวมถึงหลังคลอด) ไตวาย sepsis หรือยา เช่น tacrolimus และยาเคมีบำบัด อาการคือปวดศีรษะ ตามัวจนถึงตาบอดจากสมอง ชัก และซึม วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI FLAIR และต้องแยก CVT รักษาโดยลดความดันประมาณ 20–25% ในชั่วโมงแรก ๆ คุมชัก หยุดยาที่เป็นสาเหตุ และให้ magnesium ในครรภ์เป็นพิษ ส่วนใหญ่หายได้ภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์

name: Posthemiplegic dystonia
formal: Delayed dystonia in the hemiplegic limbs after stroke or perinatal injury, from basal ganglia lesion.
simple: Twisting muscle posture in a weak arm or leg that develops months after a stroke or early brain injury.
th: dystonia ที่เกิดภายหลังในแขนขาข้างที่อ่อนแรงจาก stroke หรือสมองบาดเจ็บช่วงปริกำเนิด เนื่องจากรอยโรคที่ basal ganglia
tempoNote: Delayed onset months to years after the injury (even decades after perinatal insult), then may progress before stabilising
feat: Dystonic posturing of the previously weak arm and/or leg, often appearing as strength recovers
Lesion in the contralateral putamen, caudate or thalamus (infarct, haemorrhage, trauma or perinatal injury)
Younger age at injury is associated with longer latency before dystonia appears
May progress for some years; can coexist with tremor, chorea or athetosis
Differs from spasticity: twisting, action-induced postures rather than velocity-dependent tone
inv: MRI brain: contralateral basal ganglia or thalamic lesion
Exclude other causes of hemidystonia (tumour, Wilson disease in young patients, demyelination)

case.story: Had left hemiparesis after a right putaminal haemorrhage at age 15 from an AVM; over the last three years his left hand twists and curls whenever he tries to write.
case.exam: Mild left weakness, action-induced flexion-pronation posturing of the left hand and inverted left foot when walking.
case.tests: MRI shows an old cavity in the right putamen.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what treatments help?
case.a: Delayed posthemiplegic hemidystonia; botulinum toxin for focal problems, oral anticholinergics, physiotherapy and in refractory cases deep brain stimulation.

read.where: Chapter 11 — Dystonia: Phenomenology, classification, etiology, pathology, biochemistry, and genetics

det.patho: Damage to the putamen, caudate or thalamus disrupts basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical circuits. The latency suggests that maladaptive plasticity, sprouting and secondary degeneration drive the dystonia rather than the acute lesion itself. Lesions in the putamen tend to cause limb dystonia; thalamic lesions often cause distal hand dystonia with sensory features.
det.clinical: Dystonia emerges in the affected limbs after a latent period of months to years, sometimes many years after perinatal injury. It is usually hemidystonia, with the arm often more affected. Movement or posture worsens with action. Some patients develop progression over several years before plateauing.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical with a compatible lesion on MRI. Spasticity, contractures and dystonia often coexist, so careful examination for action-induced twisting postures is needed. In young patients with hemidystonia and an unclear lesion, other causes such as Wilson disease or tumours should be excluded.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin is useful for focal problems. Anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl), baclofen and benzodiazepines may help. Physiotherapy, splinting and occupational therapy prevent contractures. Deep brain stimulation of the GPi is less effective in secondary than in genetic dystonias but helps some patients; thalamic procedures have also been used.
det.prognosis: Usually persistent; treatment improves function modestly.
pearls: Delayed dystonia in a limb that was weak after a stroke: think posthemiplegic dystonia.
Latency is longer when the injury occurred in childhood.
Secondary dystonia responds less to DBS than primary genetic dystonia.
det.thd: Posthemiplegic dystonia คือ dystonia ที่เกิดภายหลังในแขนขาข้างที่เคยอ่อนแรงจาก stroke หรือสมองบาดเจ็บ โดยอาจเกิดหลังจากนั้นหลายเดือนถึงหลายปี เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ putamen caudate หรือ thalamus ด้านตรงข้าม ผู้ป่วยมีมือหรือเท้าบิดเกร็งเมื่อเคลื่อนไหว ต่างจาก spasticity วินิจฉัยด้วยอาการและ MRI รักษาด้วย botulinum toxin ยา anticholinergic กายภาพบำบัด และ DBS ในรายดื้อยา

name: Postpartum neuropathy
formal: Peripheral nerve injury after delivery, such as femoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, peroneal or obstetric palsy of lumbosacral trunk.
simple: Nerve damage in the leg or pelvis after childbirth, causing numbness or weakness.
th: การบาดเจ็บของเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายในมารดาหลังคลอด เช่น femoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, peroneal หรือ lumbosacral trunk
tempoNote: Noticed in the first hours to days after delivery; usually recovers over weeks to months
feat: The commonest complaint is numbness over the outer thigh (lateral femoral cutaneous nerve)
Femoral palsy: knee buckling and absent knee jerk after lithotomy with hip flexion
Foot drop from peroneal compression (stirrups, squatting) or lumbosacral trunk injury
Risk: prolonged second stage, large baby, nulliparity, prolonged lithotomy
Neuraxial anaesthesia is rarely the cause but is often blamed
inv: Clinical localisation to nerve, plexus or root
NCS/EMG after about 3 weeks if deficit persists
Urgent MRI spine if bilateral signs, back pain, fever or sphincter disturbance (epidural haematoma or abscess)

case.story: After a long labour with pushing in lithotomy for two hours, she finds her right knee gives way when standing.
case.exam: Weak right knee extension and hip flexion, absent knee jerk, numb anterior thigh and medial calf; back and sphincters normal.
case.tests: EMG at 3 weeks shows mild denervation in right quadriceps and iliopsoas, normal adductors.
case.q: Which nerve is affected and what is the outlook?
case.a: Right femoral neuropathy from compression or stretch at the inguinal ligament during lithotomy; good recovery expected over weeks to months with physiotherapy.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Neurological Aspects of Pregnancy
Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Complications of Obstetric Anaesthesia

det.patho: Most postpartum neuropathies result from compression or stretch during labour and delivery: hip flexion and abduction in lithotomy kink the femoral nerve under the inguinal ligament, stirrups or prolonged squatting compress the peroneal nerve, and the fetal head compresses the lumbosacral trunk. Neurapraxia predominates.
det.clinical: Deficits are usually unilateral and follow a single nerve territory. Sensory symptoms alone are common; weakness, especially femoral or foot drop, is less common but more disabling. Bilateral deficits, back pain or bladder dysfunction suggest a neuraxial complication.
det.diagnosis: Careful examination localises the lesion and distinguishes nerve from root and plexus. EMG at three weeks quantifies axonal loss. MRI is needed urgently when epidural haematoma or abscess is possible.
det.treatment: Supportive care with physiotherapy, ankle-foot orthoses for foot drop, knee bracing for femoral palsy and reassurance. Avoid prolonged lithotomy and extreme hip flexion as prevention in future deliveries.
det.prognosis: Most women recover fully within weeks to a few months.
pearls: Postpartum foot drop: check ankle inversion to separate lumbosacral trunk from peroneal nerve.
Epidural anaesthesia is rarely responsible but must be excluded when signs are bilateral.
Lateral thigh numbness is the most frequent postpartum nerve complaint.
det.thd: Postpartum neuropathy คือเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายของมารดาบาดเจ็บระหว่างการคลอด มักจากการกดหรือยืดในท่า lithotomy หรือศีรษะทารกกด lumbosacral trunk ที่พบบ่อยคือชาต้นขาด้านนอก รองลงมาคือ femoral palsy และเท้าตก ส่วนใหญ่ฟื้นตัวเองภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์ถึงเดือน หากมีอาการสองข้าง ปวดหลัง หรือปัสสาวะผิดปกติต้องทำ MRI ด่วนเพื่อแยก epidural hematoma

name: Postsynaptic disorders related to CMS
formal: Congenital myasthenic syndromes from defects in acetylcholine receptor subunits or rapsyn, DOK7, MUSK, with slow-channel or fast-channel kinetics.
simple: Inherited forms of myasthenia where the receptor on the muscle side of the junction is faulty.
more: Genetic testing; treatment depends on type, such as pyridostigmine, 3,4-DAP or salbutamol, and quinidine for slow channel.
th: กลุ่มโรค congenital myasthenic syndrome ที่ผิดปกติฝั่งหลังรอยต่อประสาทกล้ามเนื้อ เช่น ตัวรับ acetylcholine, rapsyn, DOK7, MUSK การรักษาต่างกันตามชนิดยีน
tempoNote: Onset from birth to adulthood; lifelong with fluctuations
feat: Fatigable ptosis and limb weakness from early life with negative AChR/MuSK antibodies
DOK7 forms: limb-girdle pattern, often little ophthalmoparesis, worsened by pyridostigmine
Slow-channel forms: selective neck and finger extensor weakness, repetitive CMAP
Respiratory crises during infection in rapsyn and some AChR defects
inv: RNS and single-fibre EMG; look for repetitive CMAP
Genetic panel/exome including CHRNA1, CHRNB1, CHRND, CHRNE, RAPSN, DOK7, MUSK, AGRN, LRP4
Muscle biopsy is rarely needed; may show tubular aggregates in some forms

case.story: Since starting school he has had difficulty running and climbing stairs, worse with exercise; pyridostigmine prescribed for presumed myasthenia made him weaker.
case.exam: Waddling gait, proximal weakness with fatigability, mild ptosis, normal eye movements.
case.tests: Decrement on RNS of trapezius; AChR and MuSK antibodies negative; DOK7 biallelic variants.
case.q: Why did pyridostigmine worsen him, and what treatment should replace it?
case.a: DOK7 CMS often deteriorates on cholinesterase inhibitors; salbutamol or ephedrine are effective alternatives.

det.patho: Postsynaptic CMS arise from defects in AChR subunits (deficiency or abnormal kinetics) or in the agrin–LRP4–MuSK–DOK7–rapsyn pathway that clusters and maintains AChRs. The result is reduced endplate response or structural endplate simplification. Inheritance is mostly recessive, except dominant slow-channel syndrome.
det.clinical: Phenotypes range from neonatal respiratory failure and arthrogryposis to mild limb-girdle weakness in adulthood. Ocular involvement is prominent in AChR deficiency but limited in DOK7 forms. Fatigability, fluctuations and crises with infection, fever or stress are typical.
det.diagnosis: Neurophysiology shows transmission failure; a repetitive CMAP suggests slow-channel or AChE deficiency. Antibody tests are negative. Genetic testing is required and defines therapy. Family history may be absent due to recessive inheritance.
det.treatment: Pyridostigmine and 3,4-diaminopyridine benefit AChR deficiency, rapsyn and fast-channel forms. Beta-2 agonists (salbutamol, ephedrine) are preferred for DOK7, MUSK, AGRN and LRP4 forms, and are useful adjuncts elsewhere. Slow-channel forms use fluoxetine or quinidine and avoid cholinesterase inhibitors.
det.prognosis: With accurate genetic diagnosis, many patients stabilise or improve; respiratory crises remain the main risk.
pearls: A 'myasthenia' that gets worse on pyridostigmine suggests DOK7 or slow-channel CMS.
Limb-girdle fatigable weakness with negative antibodies: think DOK7.
Salbutamol is a cheap and effective option for clustering-pathway CMS.
det.thd: postsynaptic CMS เป็นกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมของตัวรับ acetylcholine และโปรตีนที่ช่วยจัดกลุ่มตัวรับ (rapsyn, DOK7, MUSK) ทำให้กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนล้าตั้งแต่เด็ก การตรวจแอนติบอดีเป็นลบ ต้องอาศัย RNS และตรวจยีน การรักษาต่างกันตามชนิด เช่น pyridostigmine สำหรับ AChR deficiency ส่วน DOK7 ใช้ salbutamol และ slow-channel ใช้ fluoxetine

Autoimmune MuSK disease with bulbar weakness and anti-MuSK antibodies; not genetic
Synaptic CMS with repetitive CMAP and slow pupils; pyridostigmine harmful

name: Postural tachycardia syndrome (PoTS)
formal: Orthostatic intolerance with sustained heart rate rise of 30 bpm or more on standing without hypotension, causing palpitations, fatigue and presyncope.
simple: A condition where the heart races when standing up, causing dizziness and tiredness.
th: ชีพจรเร็วขึ้นมากเมื่อลุกยืน มีใจสั่น มึนงง เหนื่อยง่าย แต่ความดันไม่ตก — พบบ่อยในหญิงอายุน้อย
tempoNote: Symptoms recur daily on standing; often begins after a viral illness, surgery or pregnancy and lasts months to years
feat: Light-headedness, palpitations, tremulousness and fatigue within minutes of standing, relieved by lying
Heart rate rise of 30 bpm or more (40 in teens) within 10 minutes upright, without orthostatic hypotension
Worse in heat, after meals, after exertion and around menstruation
Brain fog, headache, exercise intolerance; acrocyanosis of legs when standing
Common associations: joint hypermobility, deconditioning, post-COVID, migraine
inv: Active stand test or tilt table: HR and BP every minute for 10 minutes
ECG, thyroid function, CBC/ferritin, cortisol if suspected, medication review
Selected cases: QSART/sweat test and skin biopsy for small fibre neuropathy, plasma catecholamines

case.story: Since dengue fever 6 months ago, she feels her heart racing and her vision greying when standing on the ward; she must sit after 5 minutes. Hot days are worst.
case.exam: Supine HR 72, BP 108/70; after 8 minutes standing HR 128, BP 112/74; feet purple-blue.
case.tests: ECG sinus tachycardia only; TSH, Hb and ferritin normal.
case.q: What first-line measures would you offer?
case.a: Education, 2–3 L fluid and extra salt daily, compression garments, avoiding triggers and a graded recumbent-to-upright exercise programme; drugs such as propranolol (low dose), ivabradine, fludrocortisone or midodrine are added if needed.

read.where: Chapter 32 Autonomic Aspects of Neurology (orthostatic intolerance with posturally induced tachycardia; management of PoTS)
27 Fits, faints, funny turns, and falls in the differential diagnosis of the dizzy patient
Chapter 8 Dysautonomia, Postural Hypotension, and Syncope

det.patho: PoTS is a final common pattern of several overlapping mechanisms rather than one disease: patchy sympathetic denervation of leg and splanchnic vessels (often with small-fibre neuropathy) that lets blood pool on standing, low plasma and red-cell volume with a blunted renin–aldosterone response, a hyperadrenergic state with standing noradrenaline commonly 600 pg/mL or more, and cardiovascular deconditioning that follows any period of inactivity. Autoimmunity is suspected in some (post-infectious onset, autoantibodies against adrenergic or muscarinic receptors) but is unproven, and mast-cell activation is a debated association. It usually begins between 15 and 50, about four to five times more often in women, frequently after a viral illness (including COVID-19 and dengue), surgery, trauma or pregnancy. Joint hypermobility (hypermobile Ehlers–Danlos), chronic fatigue syndrome, migraine and functional bowel disorders cluster with it.
det.clinical: Upright posture brings light-headedness, palpitations, tremulousness, breathlessness, chest discomfort, blurred or greying vision and fatigue within minutes, eased by sitting or lying; heat, meals, alcohol, exertion, mornings and the premenstrual phase make it worse. Many also report brain fog, headache, poor sleep, nausea, bloating, exercise intolerance and purple-red mottling of dependent legs (acrocyanosis). Near-fainting is far more common than true syncope, though some also have vasovagal faints; there is no generalised autonomic failure such as anhidrosis or fixed pupils. Anxiety usually follows the symptoms rather than causing them. Red flags for another diagnosis are syncope with injury or during exertion, weight loss, abnormal neurological signs, orthostatic hypotension, or a resting tachycardia that does not change with posture.
det.diagnosis: Diagnose with an active 10-minute stand (lie 5–10 minutes, then record HR and BP each minute standing) or a head-up tilt: a sustained rise of at least 30 bpm (40 bpm at age 12–19) without a fall of 20/10 mmHg or more, plus chronic orthostatic symptoms for at least 3 months. Exclude dehydration, blood loss or anaemia, iron deficiency, hyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma, adrenal insufficiency, drugs (diuretics, vasodilators, antidepressants, stimulants or beta-blocker withdrawal), prolonged bed rest and inappropriate sinus tachycardia. A resting ECG is mandatory, with echo or Holter only if indicated. In selected or atypical cases, autonomic tests (QSART or sweat testing, Valsalva, skin biopsy) look for small-fibre neuropathy, and supine and standing catecholamines define the hyperadrenergic phenotype.
det.treatment: Explanation and non-drug measures come first and help most patients: 2–3 L of fluid and extra salt daily (unless contraindicated), waist-high or abdominal compression, raising the head of the bed, smaller low-carbohydrate meals, avoiding heat and alcohol, counter-manoeuvres, and a graded exercise programme that starts horizontal (rowing, recumbent cycling, swimming) and moves upright over months. Medicines are matched to the dominant mechanism and used off-label: low-dose propranolol, a cardioselective beta-blocker such as bisoprolol, or ivabradine to blunt the tachycardia; fludrocortisone or short-term desmopressin to expand volume; midodrine (which does not speed the heart) for pooling; pyridostigmine; and clonidine or methyldopa for hyperadrenergic patients with labile hypertension. Treat iron deficiency, migraine, sleep and mood problems, and avoid ephedrine-type stimulants. Regular IV saline is a short-term rescue only, and immunotherapy is not recommended outside trials.
det.prognosis: Most improve over 1–5 years, especially adolescents and those with a post-infectious onset, but a minority stay significantly limited and symptoms can relapse with illness, pregnancy or inactivity.
pearls: The key number is the heart-rate rise, not the absolute rate — and the blood pressure must not fall.
A 10-minute stand test in clinic costs nothing and makes the diagnosis in most cases.
Reconditioning starts horizontal and moves upright over weeks; bed rest makes PoTS worse.
Tachycardia already present at rest, not changing with posture, suggests inappropriate sinus tachycardia or a systemic cause.
det.thd: PoTS คือภาวะที่ชีพจรเพิ่มขึ้นอย่างน้อย 30 ครั้ง/นาที (40 ในวัยรุ่น) ภายใน 10 นาทีหลังลุกยืน โดยความดันไม่ตก และมีอาการเรื้อรังเกิน 3 เดือน กลไกมีหลายแบบ เช่น เลือดคั่งที่ขาจากเส้นประสาทอัตโนมัติส่วนปลายเสีย ปริมาตรเลือดน้อย หรือระบบ sympathetic ทำงานมากเกิน มักพบในหญิงอายุน้อย หลังติดเชื้อไวรัส (เช่น ไข้เลือดออก COVID-19) และร่วมกับข้อหลวม ผู้ป่วยใจสั่น มึนงง ตาพร่า เหนื่อยง่าย สมองตื้อ ขาเป็นสีม่วงเมื่อยืน วินิจฉัยด้วย active stand test หรือ tilt table และต้องตัดภาวะขาดน้ำ โลหิตจาง ไทรอยด์เป็นพิษ และยา การรักษาหลักคือดื่มน้ำ 2–3 ลิตร เพิ่มเกลือ ใส่ชุดรัดหน้าท้องหรือถุงน่องสูง ฝึกออกกำลังกายเริ่มจากท่านอน แล้วเสริมยาตามกลไก เช่น propranolol ขนาดต่ำ ivabradine fludrocortisone หรือ midodrine
