name: Postural tremor
formal: Tremor appearing when a limb is held against gravity, seen in essential tremor, enhanced physiological tremor and drug-induced states.
simple: Shaking that occurs when holding the arms out.
th: อาการสั่นที่เกิดเมื่อยกแขนหรือขาค้างต้านแรงโน้มถ่วง พบใน essential tremor, physiological tremor ที่เพิ่มขึ้น และจากยา
tempoNote: Chronic in essential tremor; can appear subacutely with drugs, thyroid disease or anxiety
feat: Tremor emerges with the arms stretched out in front or in the wing-beating posture
Typical in essential tremor, enhanced physiological tremor and drug-induced tremor
Re-emergent tremor in Parkinson disease is postural but begins after a delay
This is a clinical sign, not a disease in itself, so look for the underlying cause
inv: Thyroid function, glucose, calcium, liver and renal function
Medication and caffeine/alcohol review; drug levels (lithium, valproate)
Spiral drawing and accelerometry; DaT scan only if parkinsonism is suspected

case.story: Over 2 months her hands shake when holding her phone or a cup; she has lost weight and feels hot and anxious.
case.exam: Fine fast tremor with arms outstretched, no rest tremor; tachycardia, warm moist skin, lid lag.
case.tests: TSH suppressed, free T4 raised.
case.q: What kind of tremor is this and how is it managed?
case.a: Enhanced physiological postural tremor from hyperthyroidism; treat the thyroid and use a beta-blocker for symptoms.

det.patho: Postural tremor results from oscillation in central networks (cerebello-thalamo-cortical loops in essential tremor) or from amplified peripheral mechanical-reflex oscillation in enhanced physiological tremor. Drugs and adrenergic states increase muscle spindle sensitivity and tremor amplitude.
det.clinical: This is a phenomenological sign. Fine fast tremor with recent onset suggests enhanced physiological tremor (thyrotoxicosis, drugs, anxiety, hypoglycaemia). A slowly progressive symmetric tremor with kinetic component suggests essential tremor. Asymmetric tremor with other signs suggests dystonic tremor, Parkinson disease or a structural lesion.
det.diagnosis: Examine in several postures and actions and at rest, look for dystonia, bradykinesia and ataxia. Review medications, caffeine and alcohol. Check thyroid function and basic metabolic tests. Neurophysiology and DaT scan are reserved for uncertain cases.
det.treatment: Treat the cause where possible (thyroid, stop or reduce drug). For essential tremor, propranolol or primidone are first line; topiramate is an alternative. Disabling refractory tremor may be treated with DBS or focused ultrasound thalamotomy.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause; enhanced physiological tremor resolves, essential tremor slowly progresses.
pearls: Always check thyroid function and medication list in a new postural tremor.
A delayed postural tremor may be re-emergent parkinsonian tremor.
Postural tremor alone does not mean essential tremor.
det.thd: postural tremor คืออาการสั่นเมื่อยกแขนค้างต้านแรงโน้มถ่วง เป็นอาการแสดงที่พบได้จากหลายสาเหตุ เช่น essential tremor, ไทรอยด์เป็นพิษ ความวิตกกังวล คาเฟอีน และยา (valproate, lithium) ควรตรวจไทรอยด์และทบทวนยา การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ ส่วน essential tremor ใช้ propranolol หรือ primidone

ddx.pt: Slowly progressive bilateral postural/kinetic tremor, often familial, without thyroid or drug cause
Fine fast postural tremor from anxiety, thyrotoxicosis, caffeine or drugs; resolves with the cause
Tremor that started with valproate, lithium, beta-agonists or similar

aN: postural action tremor | static tremor | sustention tremor

name: Postural tremor in Parkinson’s disease
formal: Re-emergent or postural tremor in Parkinson disease, often with latency after posture adoption, and less levodopa responsive than rest tremor.
simple: Shaking when holding the arms out in someone with Parkinson disease.
th: อาการสั่นท่ายกแขนในผู้ป่วยพาร์กินสัน มักเริ่มหลังยกแขนค้างไม่กี่วินาที (re-emergent tremor) และอาจตอบสนองต่อ levodopa น้อยกว่าการสั่นขณะพัก
tempoNote: Part of the progressive course of Parkinson disease
feat: Tremor that stops when the arms are first raised, then returns after a latency of several seconds (re-emergent)
Same frequency as the rest tremor, usually 4–6 Hz
A separate faster pure postural tremor without latency is also seen in some PD patients
Coexists with bradykinesia, rigidity and asymmetric rest tremor
inv: Clinical examination with timed posture holding
DaT SPECT if diagnosis is uncertain versus essential or dystonic tremor
Accelerometry can document latency

case.story: His right hand shakes at rest and spills his rice when he holds the spoon still for a while.
case.exam: Right rest tremor; when arms extended the tremor stops, then returns after 6 seconds; right bradykinesia and cogwheel rigidity.
case.tests: None required; DaT scan would show reduced right putamen-dominant uptake contralateral.
case.q: What is this postural tremor and does it point away from PD?
case.a: Re-emergent tremor, a continuation of PD rest tremor; it supports, not refutes, Parkinson disease.

det.patho: Re-emergent tremor is thought to be the rest tremor re-appearing once a new posture becomes stable, driven by basal ganglia–cerebello-thalamic network oscillation. Its frequency matches rest tremor and it is generally dopaminergic responsive to a similar extent, although some patients respond less well.
det.clinical: Up to half of PD patients show postural tremor. Re-emergent tremor is the commonest type and may be more disabling than rest tremor during activities like holding a cup. A smaller group has a faster postural tremor without latency, sometimes representing coexisting essential tremor.
det.diagnosis: Hold the arms out for at least 10–20 seconds to observe latency. Combine with other features of parkinsonism. DaT imaging helps when isolated tremor makes PD uncertain.
det.treatment: Optimise dopaminergic therapy first; levodopa usually helps re-emergent tremor. Propranolol, anticholinergics (in younger patients) or clozapine may help resistant tremor. DBS of the STN, GPi or Vim is effective for refractory tremor.
det.prognosis: Follows the course of PD; tremor-dominant PD tends to progress more slowly.
pearls: Wait several seconds with arms outstretched; the latency is the clue.
Re-emergent tremor favours PD over essential tremor.
A fast postural tremor without latency in PD may be a separate essential-like tremor.
det.thd: อาการสั่นท่ายกแขนในพาร์กินสันที่พบบ่อยคือ re-emergent tremor คือเมื่อยกแขนครั้งแรกจะหยุดสั่น แล้วกลับมาสั่นหลังผ่านไปหลายวินาที ความถี่เท่ากับการสั่นขณะพัก ลักษณะนี้สนับสนุนการวินิจฉัย PD มากกว่า essential tremor การรักษาเริ่มจากปรับยา levodopa และพิจารณา DBS ในรายดื้อยา

name: Potassium aggravated myotonias (PAM)
formal: Sodium channel myotonia (SCN4A) with myotonia triggered by potassium intake or worsened after exercise, with no weakness.
simple: An inherited muscle stiffness that is made worse by foods rich in potassium.
more: Subtypes are myotonia permanens and acetazolamide-responsive myotonia; treat with mexiletine and acetazolamide.
th: กลุ่ม sodium channel myotonia (SCN4A) ที่อาการกล้ามเนื้อเกร็งค้างถูกกระตุ้นด้วยโพแทสเซียมหรือหลังออกกำลังกาย โดยไม่มีอ่อนแรงเป็นพัก ๆ
tempoNote: Begins in childhood or adolescence; lifelong, fluctuating with diet and exercise
feat: Myotonia provoked by potassium-rich food and typically delayed some minutes after exercise
Little or no cold sensitivity and no true episodic paralysis
Spectrum from fluctuating mild myotonia to continuous severe myotonia and acetazolamide-responsive myotonia
Painful stiffness is common, with face, jaw and limb involvement
Autosomal dominant SCN4A variants; muscle hypertrophy may occur
inv: EMG: myotonic discharges without dystrophic features
Short and long exercise tests and cooling test help separate it from paramyotonia and chloride myotonia
SCN4A sequencing for confirmation
Serum potassium challenge is not advised outside specialist units

case.story: Painful stiffness of her legs and jaw that is worse a few minutes after exercise and after heavy eating of banana and durian; cold weather makes no difference.
case.exam: Lid lag and grip myotonia on percussion and release; strength normal.
case.tests: EMG shows myotonic discharges; short exercise test has no decrement; SCN4A variant found.
case.q: Which drug is first-line, and what dietary advice applies?
case.a: Mexiletine (sodium channel blocker); acetazolamide helps some subtypes, and potassium-rich foods are limited.

read.where: 36: Myotonic Muscle Disorders and Periodic Paralysis Syndromes
Infectious Diseases of the Nervous System

det.patho: Gain-of-function variants in SCN4A, encoding the Nav1.4 sodium channel alpha subunit, impair fast inactivation and leave a persistent inward current. A modest rise in extracellular potassium is enough to depolarise the fibre and trigger repetitive firing, but not enough to inactivate channels, so stiffness appears without paralysis. The sodium channel disorders are dominantly inherited and share a gene with paramyotonia and hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis, which is why phenotypes overlap.
det.clinical: Stiffness affects limbs, face and jaw, often with pain, and starts typically several minutes after exercise or potassium intake rather than immediately. There is no clear warm-up effect and cold plays little part. Severity ranges from mild fluctuating myotonia to near-continuous stiffness that limits daily life, and muscle bulk can be increased. Neuromuscular blockade with suxamethonium can provoke masseter or generalised spasm, so anaesthetists should be told.
det.diagnosis: A history of potassium and delayed post-exercise triggers with a clean examination apart from myotonia suggests a sodium channelopathy. EMG shows myotonic discharges, and exercise and cooling test patterns help to distinguish subtypes. SCN4A sequencing confirms the diagnosis. Myotonic dystrophy types 1 and 2 must be excluded in anyone with weakness, cataract, cardiac or systemic features.
det.treatment: Mexiletine is the most effective drug, started low and titrated, with ECG baseline and review of cardiac history; lamotrigine, carbamazepine or flecainide-type alternatives are used when it is not tolerated. Acetazolamide helps a subgroup and is especially useful in the acetazolamide-responsive form. Moderate dietary potassium, avoiding suxamethonium and counselling about strenuous activity complete management.
det.prognosis: Generally benign with normal lifespan and no progressive weakness, though pain and stiffness may impair work and quality of life.
pearls: Delayed stiffness after exercise, worse with potassium, unaffected by cold: sodium channel myotonia.
Myotonia without paralysis separates PAM from hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis.
Mexiletine is the drug to try, but check the ECG first.
det.thd: PAM เป็นโรคกลุ่ม sodium channel myotonia จากยีน SCN4A ถ่ายทอดแบบ autosomal dominant ผู้ป่วยมีกล้ามเนื้อเกร็งแข็งและปวด มักเกิดหลังออกกำลังกายสักพักหรือหลังกินอาหารโพแทสเซียมสูง เช่น กล้วยและทุเรียน โดยไม่ไวต่อความเย็นและไม่มีอัมพาตเป็นพัก ๆ ตรวจ EMG พบ myotonic discharge และยืนยันด้วยตรวจยีน การรักษาใช้ mexiletine เป็นหลัก บางรายตอบสนองต่อ acetazolamide และควรเลี่ยง suxamethonium

name: Pott’s disease
formal: Tuberculous spondylodiscitis with vertebral collapse, kyphosis (gibbus), cold abscess and cord compression.
simple: Tuberculosis of the spine that destroys vertebrae and can press on the spinal cord.
more: Pott disease: tuberculous infection of vertebrae, causing back pain, kyphosis, paraplegia and paravertebral abscess.
th: วัณโรคกระดูกสันหลัง ทำให้กระดูกยุบ หลังค่อมเป็นมุม (gibbus) ฝีเย็น และกดไขสันหลังจนขาอ่อนแรง
tempoNote: Back pain for months before deformity or paraplegia; neurological decline can accelerate over days
feat: Chronic thoracic or lumbar back pain with local tenderness and stiffness
Gibbus deformity from anterior vertebral collapse
Paravertebral or psoas cold abscess, sometimes pointing in the groin
Spastic paraparesis with sensory level and sphincter problems from cord compression
Constitutional symptoms: weight loss, night sweats, low-grade fever (may be absent)
inv: MRI spine with contrast: two or more contiguous vertebrae, relative disc sparing, large paraspinal abscess, subligamentous spread
CT-guided biopsy for AFB smear, Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra, culture and histology
Chest X-ray, HIV test, ESR/CRP

case.story: Mid-back pain for five months and, over the last two weeks, stiff, weak legs and difficulty urinating.
case.exam: Angular kyphosis at T9, spastic paraparesis, sensory level at T10.
case.tests: MRI: destruction of T8–T9 with a large paraspinal abscess compressing the cord; Xpert positive on biopsy.
case.q: What is the management?
case.a: Antituberculous therapy for 9–12 months plus surgical decompression and stabilisation because of progressive deficit and kyphosis.

read.where: Chapter 14 Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders

det.patho: Haematogenous spread of M. tuberculosis seeds the vascular anterior vertebral body; infection spreads beneath the anterior longitudinal ligament to adjacent levels, destroying bone with relatively late disc involvement. Collapse produces kyphosis, and abscess, granulation tissue or bony fragments compress the cord. Late-onset paraplegia can follow severe healed deformity.
det.clinical: The thoracic spine is commonest, then lumbar and cervical. Pain may be the only feature for months, and many patients lack pulmonary TB. Neurological deficit occurs in a substantial minority and can progress quickly. Craniovertebral junction TB causes neck pain and quadriparesis.
det.diagnosis: MRI is the imaging test of choice. Tissue diagnosis by image-guided or open biopsy confirms TB and drug susceptibility; histology shows caseating granulomas. Cultures take weeks, so molecular tests are valuable. Distinguish from pyogenic infection, brucellosis, melioidosis (important in Thailand) and tumours.
det.treatment: Standard first-line antituberculous drugs (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) for 2 months then isoniazid and rifampicin to a total of 9–12 months. Surgery is indicated for neurological deficit that is progressive or not improving, spinal instability, severe or progressive kyphosis, or diagnostic uncertainty. Steroids are not routine. Provide bracing, rehabilitation and HIV care where relevant.
det.prognosis: Most respond well to treatment; neurological recovery is good if decompression is timely.
pearls: Contiguous vertebrae with a big abscess and spared disc: think TB.
Absence of lung TB does not exclude spinal TB.
Consider melioidosis and brucellosis as mimics in Southeast Asia.

name: Preorgasmic sex headache
formal: Dull bilateral headache increasing with sexual excitement, sometimes a muscle contraction type; excluded secondary causes.
simple: A dull headache that builds up with sexual arousal.
ab: Primary headache associated with sexual activity (preorgasmic)
th: ปวดศีรษะตื้อทั้งสองข้างที่ค่อย ๆ เพิ่มขึ้นตามระดับความตื่นเต้นทางเพศ ก่อนถึงจุดสุดยอด หลังตัดสาเหตุ secondary แล้ว
tempoNote: Builds gradually over minutes during sexual activity; recurs in bouts over weeks to months
feat: Dull, pressing, bilateral or occipital ache that climbs as sexual arousal rises
Often accompanied by tightness of jaw and neck muscles
Can be cut short by stopping intercourse before orgasm
Men more often than women; clusters of attacks, then long remissions
Overlaps with the explosive orgasmic form, which ICHD-3 now lumps into one entity

Lumbar puncture if CT is negative but a thunderclap onset is described

case.story: For three weeks he has had a tightening ache at the back of the head that builds during intercourse; it fades within an hour if he stops. No sudden peak, no vomiting.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination and blood pressure 126/80 mmHg; neck muscles tender.
case.tests: CT brain and CT angiography normal; no vasoconstriction seen.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and which secondary causes had to be excluded first?
case.a: Primary headache associated with sexual activity (preorgasmic type); SAH, arterial dissection and RCVS were excluded by imaging.

det.patho: The mechanism is not well defined. A muscle-contraction component (jaw and neck clenching) is thought to drive the dull build-up, while sympathetic surges and transient rises in blood pressure may contribute. Many sufferers also have migraine or exertional headache, suggesting a shared low threshold for exertion-triggered pain.
det.clinical: The ache starts mild and rises in step with excitement, typically bilateral or occipital and pressing in quality. Stopping activity before climax usually prevents escalation. Attacks tend to come in bouts lasting weeks to months and may then disappear for years. Any abrupt explosive onset, neurological deficit, vomiting or altered consciousness makes it a secondary headache until proven otherwise.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical and only after exclusion of structural and vascular causes at the first presentation. CT and CT angiography (or MRI with MRA) look for subarachnoid blood, aneurysm, dissection and vasoconstriction; lumbar puncture is added when the onset was thunderclap and CT is unrevealing. ICHD-3 groups preorgasmic and orgasmic types as a single primary headache associated with sexual activity, with episodic and chronic forms.
det.treatment: Reassurance and explanation are central once imaging is clear. A more passive role and avoiding prolonged arousal can reduce attacks. Indomethacin or a triptan taken 30–60 minutes beforehand helps many patients; a short daily beta-blocker course is used during active bouts. Muscle relaxation of the neck and jaw may be useful for the pressing type.
det.prognosis: Benign; most bouts settle spontaneously within months, though recurrence after a long gap is common.
pearls: Gradual build-up with arousal suggests preorgasmic; sudden peak at climax suggests orgasmic — both need imaging the first time.
Several thunderclap sex-related headaches within days point to RCVS, not a primary headache.
Pre-emptive indomethacin is the classic preventive option.

simple: Inherited muscle weakness caused by faulty release of the chemical messenger from nerves.
th: congenital myasthenic syndrome ชนิดที่ความผิดปกติอยู่ที่ปลายประสาทก่อน synapse เช่น ขาด choline acetyltransferase ทำให้หยุดหายใจเป็นพัก ๆ และอ่อนแรงล้าง่าย

feat: Neonatal hypotonia, weak cry and feeding difficulty, sometimes with arthrogryposis

case.story: Third admission for sudden blue spells during a cold; each time he needed bag-mask ventilation, then recovered within hours. An older sibling died suddenly at 4 months.
case.exam: Between episodes he feeds slowly, has mild bilateral ptosis and a weak cry that tires after a few minutes.
case.tests: AChR and MuSK antibodies negative; 3 Hz RNS normal, but decrement emerges after 5 minutes of 10 Hz stimulation; exome finds biallelic CHAT variants.
case.q: Why was the first RNS normal and what is the key preventive measure?
case.a: Presynaptic CMS from ChAT deficiency only shows decrement after acetylcholine stores are depleted; give pyridostigmine, train parents in apnoea monitoring and resuscitation, and treat infections early.

read.where: Chapter 17 Disorders of the Neuromuscular Junction — Congenital Myasthenic Syndromes
Chapter 17 Disorders of the Neuromuscular Junction — Presynaptic Congenital Myasthenic Syndromes
Case 41: A weak infant with episodic apnea

det.patho: These disorders impair the nerve terminal's ability to make, package or release acetylcholine. In ChAT deficiency the enzyme that joins choline and acetyl-CoA is defective, so transmitter supply is just adequate at rest but runs out during sustained activity such as fever-driven breathing. Defects in the high-affinity choline transporter (SLC5A7), vesicular acetylcholine transporter (SLC18A3) or release machinery (SNAP25, SYT2, VAMP1, MUNC13-1) give overlapping pictures.
det.clinical: Typical presentation is a floppy neonate who has sudden life-threatening apnoea, often with intercurrent illness, and may be well between attacks. Ptosis and ophthalmoparesis are less prominent than in postsynaptic forms. Some children have developmental delay, possibly secondary to hypoxic episodes. Release-machinery defects can resemble Lambert–Eaton with low CMAP and facilitation.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in any infant with recurrent unexplained apnoea, especially with hypotonia or a sibling death. Standard RNS can be normal; prolonged high-frequency stimulation or testing after exercise unmasks decrement, and a slow recovery of CMAP is typical. Antibody tests are negative. Genetic testing confirms the gene and guides therapy and counselling.
det.treatment: Pyridostigmine is the main treatment and reduces crises; 3,4-diaminopyridine may help some, especially release-defect forms. Families need apnoea monitors, resuscitation training and an emergency plan for fevers. Avoid neuromuscular-blocking agents and drugs that impair transmission (aminoglycosides, magnesium) where possible. Respiratory support during infections may be needed.
det.prognosis: Apnoeic crises tend to lessen with age; long-term outlook is good if early hypoxic events are prevented, although sudden death in infancy is a real risk.
pearls: Normal RNS at rest does not exclude a presynaptic CMS; ask for prolonged 10 Hz stimulation.
Recurrent apnoea with fever in a floppy infant plus a sibling death should prompt CMS testing.
Pyridostigmine helps ChAT deficiency, unlike some postsynaptic forms where it worsens weakness.
det.thd: Presynaptic CMS เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมที่ปลายประสาทสร้างหรือปล่อย acetylcholine ได้ไม่พอ ที่พบบ่อยคือ CHAT deficiency เด็กมักตัวอ่อนและหยุดหายใจเฉียบพลันเวลาเป็นไข้หรือติดเชื้อ ระหว่างช่วงนั้นอาจดูปกติ RNS ปกติได้ถ้าไม่กระตุ้นนาน ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน รักษาด้วย pyridostigmine และสอนผู้ปกครองเฝ้าระวังการหยุดหายใจ

Episodic apnoea with infection or stress, sometimes the only sign
Variable ptosis and fatigable limb weakness

case.story: Born floppy and needed ventilation for 5 days; since then has had two sudden breathing arrests during diarrhoeal illnesses.
case.exam: Mild ptosis, weak neck flexion, normal reflexes, no fasciculations, development a little delayed.
case.tests: Antibodies negative; RNS at 3 Hz normal; decrement after 10 Hz conditioning; exome shows biallelic SLC5A7 variants.
case.q: Which part of the neuromuscular junction is faulty, and what drugs are tried?
case.a: The presynaptic choline uptake step (choline transporter); pyridostigmine first, sometimes adding 3,4-DAP, with apnoea precautions.

det.patho: Presynaptic CMS covers defects in choline uptake (SLC5A7), acetylcholine synthesis (CHAT), vesicle loading (SLC18A3) and exocytosis (SNAP25, SYT2, VAMP1, MUNC13-1/UNC13A, others). Each reduces the number of transmitter quanta available or released, so safety margin falls during repetitive firing. Some genes are also active in the brain, explaining cognitive or other CNS features in certain subtypes.
det.clinical: The common thread is infantile onset with crises of apnoea, often precipitated by fever, and a milder interictal weakness. SLC5A7 has a spectrum from severe neonatal disease to distal motor neuropathy. SYT2 dominant forms resemble LEMS with distal weakness and areflexia that improves after exercise. Severity varies widely, even within one family.
det.diagnosis: Clinical suspicion plus electrophysiology: decrement may need prolonged stimulation, while exocytosis defects can show increment. Antibodies are negative and CK is normal. Genetic confirmation is essential because treatment choices differ between subtypes.
det.treatment: Pyridostigmine is usually first line; 3,4-diaminopyridine helps release defects and some synthesis defects. Salbutamol or ephedrine are used mainly in postsynaptic forms and have limited roles here. Apnoea monitoring, early treatment of infections and caution with anaesthetic agents are central. Genetic counselling is offered.
det.prognosis: Many children improve with age and treatment, but untreated crises carry risk of hypoxic brain injury or death.
pearls: Think of presynaptic CMS when a negative-antibody infant has crises with fever.
Increment after brief exercise in a child can point to a release defect such as SYT2.
Exact gene diagnosis matters because therapies are subtype-specific.

det.patho: A clonal plasma-cell population secretes misfolded immunoglobulin light chains (lambda more often than kappa) that aggregate as amyloid fibrils in tissues. In nerves, deposits in the endoneurium, vessel walls and dorsal root ganglia cause axonal degeneration, with small myelinated and unmyelinated fibres affected first. Heart, kidney, liver, gut and soft tissue are frequently involved, and cardiac involvement largely determines survival.
det.clinical: A painful, length-dependent small-fibre neuropathy with burning feet, loss of pain and temperature sensation and early autonomic failure (orthostatic hypotension, erectile dysfunction, diarrhoea or constipation, early satiety) is typical. Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome may precede the diagnosis by years. Systemic features include fatigue, weight loss, heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, hepatomegaly, macroglossia and periorbital bruising. Progression is faster than in hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis.
det.diagnosis: Screen with serum and urine immunofixation and serum free light chains. Tissue confirmation by Congo red staining (fat pad aspirate, bone marrow, or affected organ) is required, and the amyloid type must be determined by mass spectrometry or immunohistochemistry to exclude transthyretin amyloid. Stage cardiac disease with NT-proBNP, troponin, echocardiography and cardiac MRI. Standard NCS may be normal early; skin biopsy and autonomic testing are more sensitive.
det.treatment: Haematological therapy aims at rapid, deep suppression of the light chain clone; daratumumab combined with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib and dexamethasone is the current first-line standard, with autologous stem cell transplantation for selected fit patients. Bortezomib can worsen neuropathy, so neurological status needs close monitoring. Supportive care includes neuropathic pain treatment, midodrine or droxidopa and compression for orthostatic hypotension, and careful fluid management.
det.prognosis: Prognosis is driven by cardiac stage and haematological response; neuropathy improves slowly, if at all, even after a good response.
pearls: Painful small-fibre neuropathy + autonomic failure + weight loss in an older adult: think AL amyloid.
Always type the amyloid — treating TTR amyloid with chemotherapy is a serious error.
Prior bilateral carpal tunnel release is an important historical clue.

case.story: Woke with left arm weakness and slurred speech. No smoking, normal blood pressure, no oestrogen use; a purple net-like skin pattern on both thighs for years.
case.exam: Left arm paresis, mild dysarthria, broken livedo racemosa on the thighs, no joint swelling or rash on the face.

det.patho: Antiphospholipid antibodies, chiefly against β2-glycoprotein I, activate endothelial cells, platelets, monocytes and complement and tip the balance towards thrombosis in arteries, veins and the microcirculation. The brain is the commonest arterial target. A second hit such as surgery, infection, pregnancy or oestrogen often precipitates an event on a background of persistent antibodies. 'Primary' denotes antibody disease occurring without lupus or another connective tissue disease.
det.clinical: Stroke and TIA are the dominant neurological events, often in people under 50 and often recurrent without treatment. Cerebral venous thrombosis, migraine-like headache, seizures, chorea, myelitis, cognitive decline with multifocal white matter lesions, and an MS-like picture all occur but fall outside the classification items. Livedo racemosa, mild thrombocytopenia and mitral or aortic valve thickening are useful clues, as are early pregnancy losses and severe pre-eclampsia. A rare catastrophic form causes thrombosis in several organs within days.
det.diagnosis: A clinical event plus persistent antibodies (two positive results at least 12 weeks apart) is the working diagnosis. The 2023 ACR/EULAR classification rules, designed for research, require the clinical event and a positive test within three years and then at least three clinical and three laboratory points, with unprovoked arterial thrombosis and high-titre IgG anticardiolipin plus anti-β2GPI weighted most heavily. Lupus anticoagulant is unreliable on heparin, warfarin or a DOAC, so ELISAs or expert review help, and transient low-titre positivity after infection should not be over-read. Echocardiography and an SLE screen complete the work-up.
det.treatment: After arterial thrombosis, long-term warfarin (INR 2–3) is the standard; specialists sometimes add low-dose aspirin or target a higher INR after recurrence. DOACs, particularly rivaroxaban, were inferior in trials of triple-positive patients and should not be used for arterial or high-risk disease. Hydroxychloroquine may reduce recurrence, and vascular risk factors are controlled strictly. Oestrogen-containing contraception is stopped, and pregnancy requires heparin plus aspirin under combined obstetric and rheumatology care.
det.prognosis: Recurrence is common without anticoagulation, but many patients do well on warfarin; cumulative small infarcts can lead to cognitive impairment.
pearls: Young stroke with miscarriages or livedo racemosa: send LA, aCL and anti-β2GPI, and repeat them after 12 weeks.
Avoid DOACs after arterial events or in triple-positive patients; warfarin with INR 2–3 is preferred.
A single positive test or a result taken during acute thrombosis or anticoagulation can mislead; confirm before labelling.
det.thd: Primary APS คือภาวะที่ antiphospholipid antibody ทำให้เลือดแข็งตัวง่ายโดยไม่มี SLE ผู้ป่วยอาจมี stroke ในคนอายุน้อย ลิ่มเลือดดำ ผื่น livedo racemosa เกล็ดเลือดต่ำ หรือแท้งซ้ำ ต้องตรวจ lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin และ anti-β2GPI ซ้ำหลังอย่างน้อย 12 สัปดาห์ เกณฑ์จำแนกปี 2023 ใช้ระบบคะแนนสำหรับงานวิจัย ส่วนการรักษาหลัง stroke ใช้ warfarin ที่ INR 2–3 และหลีกเลี่ยงยากลุ่ม DOAC โดยเฉพาะผู้ที่ผลบวกทั้งสามชนิด

qx.stem: A 36-year-old woman has a left MCA branch infarct. She does not smoke, has normal blood pressure and has no features of lupus. Lupus anticoagulant, IgG anticardiolipin (95 units) and IgG anti-β2GPI (110 units) are positive and remain positive on repeat testing 13 weeks later.
qx.q: Which long-term antithrombotic plan is most appropriate?
opts: Rivaroxaban 20 mg daily
Aspirin 100 mg daily alone
Apixaban 5 mg twice daily
Warfarin adjusted to an INR between 2 and 3
Clopidogrel alone after six months
qx.why: Arterial thrombosis with triple-positive, high-titre antibodies defines the highest-risk APS group, in which warfarin is the standard. Trials with rivaroxaban and apixaban found more arterial events, particularly strokes, than with warfarin, so DOACs are avoided. Aspirin or clopidogrel alone does not give enough protection in definite thrombotic APS.

name: Primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC)
formal: Autoimmune chronic cholestatic liver disease with anti-mitochondrial antibodies, associated with sensory neuropathy, Sjogren and fatigue.
simple: A long-term autoimmune disease destroying liver bile ducts, sometimes linked with nerve and dry eye problems.
more: Treated with ursodeoxycholic acid; liver transplantation in advanced disease.
th: โรคตับอักเสบเรื้อรังจากภูมิคุ้มกันชนิดน้ำดีคั่ง (anti-mitochondrial antibody บวก) ที่อาจพบร่วมกับ sensory neuropathy, Sjögren และอ่อนเพลีย
tempoNote: Slowly progressive over years to decades
feat: Mostly middle-aged women with itch, fatigue and raised alkaline phosphatase
Not primarily a neurological disease; neurological links are secondary or associated
Associated sensory neuropathy, small-fibre neuropathy or rare xanthomatous neuropathy from high lipids
Overlap with Sjögren syndrome, autoimmune thyroid disease and rarely myositis or myasthenia
Advanced disease brings fat-soluble vitamin deficiency (vitamin E) and hepatic encephalopathy
inv: ALP and GGT raised; anti-mitochondrial antibody (M2) positive; anti-sp100/gp210 in AMA-negative cases
Nerve conduction studies and skin biopsy if neuropathic symptoms
Vitamin E, B12 levels and lipid profile

case.story: Two years of itching and tiredness; now burning, tingling feet and dry eyes.
case.exam: Mild jaundice, excoriations, xanthelasma, reduced pin-prick in a stocking pattern, ankle reflexes present.
case.tests: ALP 620 U/L, AMA positive, NCS normal; skin biopsy shows reduced intraepidermal nerve fibre density.
case.q: What is the likely cause of her foot symptoms and what associated condition should be checked?
case.a: Small-fibre neuropathy associated with PBC; screen for Sjögren syndrome and vitamin deficiencies.

read.where: Chapter 50 Connective Tissue Diseases, Vasculitis, and the Nervous System

det.patho: PBC (now usually called primary biliary cholangitis) is autoimmune destruction of small intrahepatic bile ducts, with anti-mitochondrial antibodies against the pyruvate dehydrogenase E2 subunit. Chronic cholestasis leads to fibrosis and cirrhosis. Neurological involvement arises from associated autoimmunity, lipid deposits around nerves, malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins and end-stage liver failure.
det.clinical: This is a hepatology disease rather than a primary neurological one. Patients are mostly women over 40 with fatigue and pruritus, sometimes found by chance on liver tests. Neurological associations include painful small-fibre or sensory neuropathy, xanthomatous neuropathy with very high cholesterol, vitamin E deficiency ataxia, hepatic encephalopathy and acquired hepatocerebral degeneration. Fatigue can be profound and is not explained by liver severity.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on persistent cholestatic liver tests with positive AMA, or specific ANA patterns, and biopsy only in doubtful cases. In neuropathic symptoms do NCS, and skin biopsy if NCS is normal. Check vitamin E, B12, glucose and thyroid function, and look for Sjögren syndrome.
det.treatment: Ursodeoxycholic acid is first line; obeticholic acid, fibrates and newer PPAR agonists (seladelpar, elafibranor) are used for inadequate response. Liver transplantation is for end-stage disease. Neuropathic pain is managed with standard agents, and vitamin deficiencies are replaced.
det.prognosis: With early UDCA response, survival approaches that of the general population; neuropathy is usually mild.
pearls: Itchy middle-aged woman with high ALP plus neuropathy: check AMA.
Cholestasis can cause vitamin E deficiency with a spinocerebellar syndrome.
Xanthomatous neuropathy occurs only with extreme hypercholesterolaemia.
det.thd: PBC (primary biliary cholangitis) เป็นโรคตับจากภูมิคุ้มกันทำลายท่อน้ำดีเล็ก พบในผู้หญิงวัยกลางคน มีคันและอ่อนเพลีย ตรวจพบ ALP สูงและ AMA บวก ไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาทโดยตรง แต่อาจพบ small-fibre neuropathy, Sjögren, ขาดวิตามิน E หรือ hepatic encephalopathy รักษาด้วย ursodeoxycholic acid และเปลี่ยนตับในระยะท้าย

name: Primary bone tumours
formal: Tumours arising in bone such as osteosarcoma, chordoma and Ewing sarcoma, causing local pain and neural compression of cord or root.
simple: Cancers that begin in bone, which may press on nearby nerves or spinal cord.
th: เนื้องอกที่เกิดในกระดูกโดยตรง เช่น osteosarcoma, chordoma และ Ewing sarcoma ทำให้ปวดเฉพาะที่และกดไขสันหลังหรือรากประสาท
tempoNote: Variable: weeks for aggressive sarcomas, years for benign tumours and chordoma
feat: Benign: osteoid osteoma, osteoblastoma, haemangioma, aneurysmal bone cyst, giant cell tumour
Malignant: chordoma, chondrosarcoma, osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, plasmacytoma
Local pain, night pain, deformity
Neurological compression of cord, roots or skull-base nerves
Age and location strongly suggest the type
inv: CT for bone matrix and destruction
MRI for soft tissue and neural compression
Staging (chest CT, PET) and planned biopsy

case.story: One year of sacral pain and recent constipation and numbness in the saddle area.
case.exam: Saddle sensory loss, weak ankle plantar flexion, absent anal reflex.
case.tests: MRI: large midline sacral destructive mass with T2 bright lobules; biopsy: brachyury-positive tumour.
case.q: What tumour is this and how is it treated?
case.a: Sacral chordoma; en bloc resection where feasible, with high-dose (often proton) radiotherapy.

read.where: Chapter 14 Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders

det.patho: Primary bone tumours arise from bone-forming, cartilage, notochordal or marrow cells. Benign lesions predominate in the young; malignant primary tumours are rare compared with metastases. Their impact on the nervous system is by expansion and invasion of the canal or foramina.
det.clinical: Pain is the main symptom. Neurological deficits develop with compression. Age helps: osteoid osteoma and Ewing sarcoma in the young, chordoma and chondrosarcoma in middle age, myeloma and metastases in older adults.
det.diagnosis: CT and MRI suggest the type; histology confirms. Biopsy should be planned with the definitive surgeon to avoid tumour seeding.
det.treatment: Treatment ranges from ablation for osteoid osteoma to en bloc resection with chemotherapy or radiotherapy for sarcomas. Urgent decompression is needed for cord compression.
det.prognosis: Benign tumours do well; malignant spinal tumours have worse outcomes than limb tumours.
pearls: In adults, metastasis is far more common than primary bone tumour.
Midline sacral or clival destruction suggests chordoma.
Plan biopsy with the surgical team.
det.thd: Primary bone tumours คือเนื้องอกที่เกิดจากกระดูกโดยตรง มีทั้งชนิดไม่ร้าย เช่น osteoid osteoma และชนิดร้าย เช่น chordoma, chondrosarcoma, osteosarcoma และ Ewing sarcoma อาการหลักคือปวดเฉพาะที่ และกดไขสันหลังหรือรากประสาท อายุและตำแหน่งช่วยบอกชนิด การรักษาขึ้นกับชนิดของเนื้องอก ในผู้ใหญ่ต้องแยกจากมะเร็งแพร่กระจายซึ่งพบบ่อยกว่า

name: Primary CNS lymphoma (PCNSL)
formal: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma confined to CNS, with periventricular homogeneously enhancing lesions, steroid-sensitive; treated with high-dose methotrexate.
simple: A cancer of immune cells that starts in the brain, often shrinking dramatically with steroids.
ab: มะเร็งต่อมน้ำเหลืองในสมอง
th: มะเร็งต่อมน้ำเหลือง B-cell ชนิด DLBCL ที่จำกัดอยู่ในสมอง ไขสันหลัง ตา หรือน้ำไขสันหลัง พบในผู้สูงอายุหรือผู้ติดเชื้อ HIV ก้อนจับสีสม่ำเสมอรอบโพรงสมอง ยุบได้เร็วเมื่อได้สเตียรอยด์ จึงควรเลี่ยงสเตียรอยด์ก่อนตัดชิ้นเนื้อ
tempoNote: Weeks to a few months of progressive cognitive, behavioural or focal symptoms
feat: Usually over 60 and immunocompetent; also in HIV, transplant and other immunosuppression (EBV-driven)
Personality change, confusion and focal deficits evolving over weeks; seizures less common than with gliomas
Deep periventricular, basal ganglia or corpus callosum lesions; multiple in about a third
Blurred vision or floaters from vitreoretinal involvement in up to a quarter
Dramatic but temporary shrinkage after corticosteroids
inv: MRI: homogeneously enhancing, diffusion-restricting periventricular mass(es) with modest oedema; ring enhancement suggests immunosuppression
Stereotactic biopsy before steroids if possible; CSF cytology and flow cytometry, or vitreous biopsy, can sometimes replace it
Staging: slit-lamp/ophthalmology review, HIV test, CT chest–abdomen–pelvis or body PET, bone marrow, testicular ultrasound in older men
Baseline renal function and creatinine clearance before high-dose methotrexate

case.who: 67-year-old male rice farmer from Suphan Buri
case.story: Over 6 weeks he became apathetic, forgot family names and began veering to the left when walking. A local clinic gave dexamethasone, which helped for a week.
case.exam: Slowed, disoriented to date, mild left hemiparesis.
case.tests: MRI: two homogeneously enhancing lesions abutting the right lateral ventricle and splenium, bright on DWI. HIV negative. Steroid stopped; biopsy after 10 days showed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what is the backbone of treatment?
case.a: Primary CNS lymphoma; high-dose methotrexate-based induction (often with rituximab and other agents), then consolidation tailored to fitness.

det.patho: Almost all PCNSL are diffuse large B-cell lymphomas of activated B-cell type, frequently carrying MYD88 L265P and CD79B mutations that drive B-cell receptor and NF-κB signalling. Tumour cells cluster around blood vessels and infiltrate diffusely beyond the visible MRI lesion. In immunosuppressed patients, EBV infection drives the tumour.
det.clinical: Presentation is usually with frontal-type cognitive or behavioural change, focal deficits or raised intracranial pressure over weeks. Ocular involvement causes painless floaters or blurred vision and can precede brain disease (primary vitreoretinal lymphoma). Leptomeningeal and spinal cord involvement are less common. B symptoms are rare; systemic lymphoma must be excluded because secondary CNS lymphoma is managed differently.
det.diagnosis: Typical imaging raises suspicion, but tissue is mandatory. Corticosteroids can cause lymphoma cells to undergo apoptosis and make biopsy non-diagnostic, so delay them when safe; if already given, stop and re-image before biopsy or repeat biopsy later. CSF cytology and flow cytometry, MYD88 analysis or IL-10 levels in CSF or vitreous support the diagnosis. Complete staging includes eye examination and body imaging.
det.treatment: Induction uses high-dose methotrexate-based polychemotherapy, commonly with rituximab plus cytarabine and/or thiotepa or other agents depending on age and fitness. Fit patients usually consolidate with thiotepa-based high-dose chemotherapy and autologous stem cell transplantation; whole-brain radiotherapy is an alternative but causes delayed cognitive decline, especially in older adults. Older or frailer patients may receive maintenance therapy such as lenalidomide or temozolomide. Relapse options include ibrutinib, lenalidomide-based regimens and re-induction; HIV-associated PCNSL needs effective antiretroviral therapy.
det.prognosis: Long-term remission is possible in fit patients treated intensively; older patients have shorter median survival and higher neurotoxicity.
pearls: Do not give steroids before biopsy in a suspected lymphoma unless herniation is threatened.
Homogeneous periventricular enhancement with restricted diffusion is classic in immunocompetent patients.
Always look in the eyes — vitreoretinal lymphoma is part of PCNSL staging.
det.thd: PCNSL เป็นมะเร็งต่อมน้ำเหลือง B-cell ที่อยู่ในสมอง ตา หรือน้ำไขสันหลังเท่านั้น พบในผู้สูงอายุหรือผู้ภูมิคุ้มกันบกพร่อง อาการคือบุคลิกเปลี่ยน สับสน อ่อนแรงในเวลาหลายสัปดาห์ MRI พบก้อนรอบโพรงสมองจับสีสม่ำเสมอและ DWI สว่าง ก้อนยุบเร็วเมื่อให้สเตียรอยด์ทำให้ตัดชิ้นเนื้อไม่ได้ผล จึงควรเลี่ยงก่อนตัดชิ้นเนื้อ ต้องตรวจตาและตรวจหามะเร็งทั่วร่าง รักษาด้วย high-dose methotrexate ร่วมกับยาอื่นและ rituximab แล้วตามด้วย consolidation

qx.stem: A 64-year-old rice farmer from Roi Et has three weeks of forgetfulness and left leg clumsiness. MRI shows a homogeneously enhancing periventricular mass crossing the corpus callosum with restricted diffusion. HIV serology is negative. He was started on dexamethasone by a district hospital and the lesion has shrunk markedly on repeat imaging.
qx.q: What is the best next step toward a diagnosis?
opts: Stop steroids, wait for the lesion to regrow, then perform stereotactic biopsy
Treat empirically as toxoplasmosis with pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine
Give whole-brain radiotherapy without tissue because the response proves lymphoma
Proceed to biopsy now, ideally with steroids withheld from this point, as tissue is still required despite the response
Obtain a PET-CT and treat as metastasis if any extracranial uptake is seen
qx.why: Steroids can be lympholytic and may leave non-diagnostic tissue, but a response does not replace histology; biopsy should still proceed promptly, with further steroids avoided if the patient is stable. Waiting for regrowth wastes time, and empirical radiotherapy or toxoplasma therapy without tissue is not appropriate in an HIV-negative patient.

qx.stem: A 66-year-old HIV-negative man from Suphan Buri has four weeks of personality change, headache and slight left-sided weakness. MRI shows a homogeneously enhancing periventricular mass in the right basal ganglia and corpus callosum with marked diffusion restriction and little oedema. He is alert and not herniating. The admitting team wants to start dexamethasone before the neurosurgical review.
qx.q: What should be done next?
opts: Start dexamethasone 8 mg twice daily and reimage in two weeks
Arrange whole-brain radiotherapy without tissue diagnosis
Begin empirical anti-toxoplasma treatment
Plan gross total surgical resection of the mass
Withhold corticosteroids and obtain an urgent stereotactic biopsy, with slit-lamp examination and body staging
qx.why: Homogeneous enhancement with restricted diffusion near the ventricles or corpus callosum strongly suggests PCNSL. Steroids can shrink the tumour quickly and make biopsy non-diagnostic, so they are withheld if clinically safe until tissue is taken. Standard therapy is high-dose methotrexate-based induction (for example the MATRix regimen) followed by consolidation; resection gives no benefit and whole-brain radiotherapy alone is no longer first-line.

src.where: Case 37 Progressive ataxia with headache and focal signs

qx.stem: A 71-year-old woman from Nonthaburi has two weeks of slowing, apathy and falls. MRI shows a homogeneously enhancing lesion of the callosal splenium extending into the left periventricular white matter, with restricted diffusion and moderate oedema. She is HIV negative and is alert, with no signs of herniation. The ward team proposes dexamethasone 4 mg every 6 hours while waiting for the neurosurgical list.
qx.q: What is the best advice?
opts: Give dexamethasone now; it will not affect the biopsy result
Start empirical high-dose methotrexate without a tissue diagnosis
Give IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for presumed tumefactive demyelination
Treat empirically for toxoplasmosis for two weeks
Withhold corticosteroids if she is stable and obtain a stereotactic biopsy first, with ophthalmic and CSF evaluation
qx.why: A periventricular or callosal homogeneously enhancing lesion with restricted diffusion in an older adult suggests primary CNS lymphoma. Corticosteroids can make the lesion shrink and the biopsy non-diagnostic, so in a stable patient they are deferred until tissue is obtained; vitreous examination and CSF cytology with flow cytometry may also give the diagnosis. Treatment such as high-dose methotrexate follows histological confirmation, and toxoplasmosis is unlikely in an HIV-negative patient.

qx.stem: A 71-year-old retired teacher in Nakhon Ratchasima presents with three weeks of confusion and slowed speech; HIV testing is negative. Non-contrast CT shows a slightly hyperdense periventricular mass abutting the ependyma of the left frontal horn. On MRI the lesion enhances homogeneously and brightly, shows restricted diffusion with a low ADC, and has no central necrosis; a smaller similar nodule lies in the splenium.
qx.q: What should be done before any corticosteroid is given?
opts: Nothing; start dexamethasone immediately to shrink the lesion
Stereotactic biopsy (or CSF/vitreous cytology if safe), because steroids can make the tumour disappear and render pathology non-diagnostic
Whole-brain radiotherapy without tissue
Repeat MRI in a month and treat as demyelination
Lobectomy with wide margins
qx.why: Homogeneous avid enhancement, low ADC from dense cellularity and contact with the ventricular surface point to primary CNS lymphoma. Steroids are lympholytic and can cause a vanishing lesion, so they should be withheld unless herniation threatens until tissue is obtained. Treatment is high-dose methotrexate-based chemotherapy, not wide resection.

name: Primary dystonia
formal: Dystonia without other neurological abnormality or structural cause, often genetic such as DYT1, with sustained muscle contractions causing abnormal postures.
simple: Twisting and abnormal postures from overactive muscles, with no other cause found.
th: dystonia ที่ไม่มีอาการทางระบบประสาทอื่นร่วมและไม่มีสาเหตุทางโครงสร้าง มักเป็นพันธุกรรม เช่น DYT1 ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อเกร็งค้างเป็นท่าผิดปกติ
tempoNote: Gradual onset; childhood forms tend to generalise, adult forms usually stay focal
feat: Sustained or intermittent contractions causing twisting postures or repetitive movements
Dystonia is the only sign apart from tremor; no parkinsonism, weakness or cognitive change
Childhood onset often begins in a leg and spreads (TOR1A/DYT1, THAP1)
Adult onset is usually focal: cervical, blepharospasm, writer's cramp, laryngeal
Sensory trick (geste antagoniste) and task specificity are characteristic
inv: MRI brain normal; exclude Wilson disease (copper studies, slit-lamp) in under-50s
Levodopa trial to exclude dopa-responsive dystonia in young onset
Genetic testing (TOR1A, THAP1, GNAL, ANO3 and panels) especially in early onset

case.story: Started turning his right foot inward when walking a year ago; now his right arm twists when writing. Runs normally backwards.
case.exam: Action-induced dystonic inversion of right foot and arm posturing; normal strength, reflexes, eye movements and cognition.
case.tests: MRI brain normal, ceruloplasmin normal, no levodopa response; TOR1A GAG deletion detected.
case.q: Which diagnosis must be excluded before genetic dystonia, and which treatment helps most if generalised?
case.a: Dopa-responsive dystonia and Wilson disease; for disabling generalised DYT1 dystonia, globus pallidus internus DBS is very effective.

read.where: Review — diagnosis and pathogenesis of dystonia
11 - Dystonia: Phenomenology, classification, etiology, pathology, biochemistry, and genetics

det.patho: Isolated dystonia reflects abnormal network function across basal ganglia, cerebellum and sensorimotor cortex, with reduced inhibition and abnormal plasticity rather than visible degeneration. TOR1A (DYT1) is an autosomal dominant GAG deletion with about 30% penetrance; THAP1, GNAL, ANO3 and KMT2B are other genes. Most adult focal dystonias have no identified gene.
det.clinical: 'Primary dystonia' is the older term; current classification uses isolated dystonia. Early-onset cases often begin in a limb during action and can spread to become generalised, while adult-onset cases are usually focal or segmental. Tremor may accompany it. Additional neurological signs should prompt a search for a secondary or combined cause.
det.diagnosis: It is a clinical diagnosis based on phenomenology plus exclusion of structural, metabolic and drug causes. Young-onset patients need copper studies and a levodopa trial. MRI is expected to be normal. Genetic testing is guided by age and distribution.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin is first line for focal dystonia. Oral options include trihexyphenidyl (better tolerated in children), clonazepam and baclofen. GPi deep brain stimulation helps generalised and segmental dystonia, with best results in TOR1A. Physiotherapy and sensory retraining are supportive.
det.prognosis: Not life-shortening; childhood forms may become disabling without treatment, while focal adult forms usually stay localised.
pearls: Always do a levodopa trial in childhood-onset dystonia.
Leg onset in childhood predicts generalisation; adult onset usually stays focal.
DBS benefits in DYT1 can take months to appear.
det.thd: Primary (isolated) dystonia คือ dystonia ที่ไม่มีอาการทางระบบประสาทอื่นร่วม ไม่มีรอยโรคใน MRI มักเกิดจากยีน เช่น TOR1A (DYT1) เด็กมักเริ่มที่ขาแล้วลามทั่วตัว ผู้ใหญ่มักเป็นเฉพาะที่ เช่น คอบิด ต้องตัด Wilson disease และ dopa-responsive dystonia ก่อน รักษาด้วย botulinum toxin ยา anticholinergic และ DBS

name: Primary hypokalemic periodic paralysis type 1 (HypoKPP 1)
formal: Autosomal dominant periodic paralysis from CACNA1S mutations causing flaccid attacks with low potassium, triggered by carbohydrate or rest after exertion.
simple: An inherited condition with attacks of muscle weakness linked to low potassium, from a calcium channel gene change.
more: Treat with potassium and acetazolamide or dichlorphenamide; avoid high carbohydrate meals; late fixed myopathy can occur.
th: periodic paralysis ชนิดถ่ายทอดแบบ autosomal dominant จากยีน CACNA1S ทำให้อ่อนแรงทั้งตัวเป็นพัก ๆ ร่วมกับโพแทสเซียมต่ำ
tempoNote: Attacks last hours to a day, often on waking; onset in adolescence; later a fixed proximal myopathy may develop
feat: Attacks of flaccid limb weakness, often found on waking, sparing face and breathing in most cases
Triggers: carbohydrate-rich meal, alcohol, rest after heavy exercise, cold, stress, steroids
Serum potassium low during attacks; normal between them
Reflexes reduced or absent during the attack; no myotonia
Onset in teens; penetrance lower in women; late permanent proximal weakness common
inv: Serum K+ in attack (often < 3.0 mmol/L); exclude thyroid disease, renal and GI potassium loss
Long exercise test (McManis): late fall in CMAP amplitude between attacks
Genetic testing: CACNA1S (most), SCN4A variants define type 2
ECG during attack for hypokalaemic changes

case.story: After a football match and a large sticky-rice dinner he woke unable to lift his arms or stand. His father had similar morning attacks as a young man.
case.exam: Symmetric flaccid weakness of all four limbs, worse proximally; areflexia; normal speech and breathing.
case.tests: K+ 2.2 mmol/L, TSH normal; ECG shows U waves; CACNA1S variant found.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what preventive advice and drugs help?
case.a: Familial hypokalaemic periodic paralysis type 1; avoid big carbohydrate loads and rest after strenuous exercise, consider acetazolamide or dichlorphenamide and potassium-sparing diuretics.

read.where: Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Skeletal Muscle Channelopathies

det.patho: Missense changes in the voltage sensor of the muscle calcium channel (Cav1.1, CACNA1S) open an abnormal leak path, the gating-pore current. Under low potassium this leak keeps fibres partly depolarised, so sodium channels inactivate and the membrane becomes inexcitable. The trait is autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance in women; around a tenth of familial cases instead carry SCN4A variants (type 2).
det.clinical: First attacks usually arise in the second decade, typically in the early morning after a carbohydrate meal or rest following exertion. Weakness spreads over minutes to hours, involves limbs more than trunk and rarely the respiratory muscles, and resolves within hours to a day. Attack frequency often falls after the fourth decade, but a progressive vacuolar myopathy with fixed proximal weakness appears in many middle-aged patients.
det.diagnosis: Document low potassium during an attack and look for secondary causes: thyrotoxicosis, renal tubular acidosis, diuretics, diarrhoea and hyperaldosteronism. Between attacks the long exercise test shows a delayed CMAP decrement in most cases. Genetic testing for CACNA1S and SCN4A confirms the subtype and guides counselling; muscle biopsy is seldom needed.
det.treatment: Acute attacks respond to oral potassium chloride with ECG and level monitoring; intravenous potassium should be given in mannitol or saline, not dextrose, and cautiously to avoid rebound hyperkalaemia. Prevention includes low-carbohydrate, low-salt meals and avoiding sudden rest after heavy work. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide, dichlorphenamide) reduce attacks in many, while some SCN4A carriers worsen on them; potassium-sparing diuretics are alternatives.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is normal; the main long-term problem is a slowly progressive proximal myopathy.
pearls: Give IV potassium in saline or mannitol, never dextrose, which drives potassium further into cells.
Always check TSH: thyrotoxic periodic paralysis is far commoner in Thailand than familial disease.
Acetazolamide can worsen some SCN4A (type 2) patients — genotype matters.
det.thd: HypoKPP1 เกิดจากยีน CACNA1S ถ่ายทอดแบบ autosomal dominant ผู้ป่วยวัยรุ่นตื่นมาแขนขาอ่อนแรงปวกเปียกหลังกินแป้งมากหรือพักหลังออกกำลังหนัก โพแทสเซียมต่ำขณะมีอาการ ต้องตรวจ TSH แยก thyrotoxic periodic paralysis รักษาโดยให้ KCl ทางปากและป้องกันด้วยการคุมอาหารและ acetazolamide ในระยะยาวอาจมีกล้ามเนื้อต้นแขนขาอ่อนแรงถาวร

name: Primary lateral sclerosis (PLS)
formal: Pure upper motor neuron degeneration with progressive spasticity, pseudobulbar signs and no lower motor neuron findings for at least 3 years; slower than ALS.
simple: A slowly progressing disease causing stiffness and weakness through loss of upper motor neurons.
th: โรคเซลล์ประสาทสั่งการเสื่อมเฉพาะส่วนบน ทำให้ขาเกร็งค่อยๆ เป็นมากขึ้น พูดช้าแบบ pseudobulbar ไม่มีกล้ามเนื้อลีบ ดำเนินโรคช้ากว่า ALS
tempoNote: Slow progression over many years; diagnosis firm only after about 4 years without LMN signs
feat: Gradual spastic paraparesis, sometimes beginning in one leg and spreading
Spastic dysarthria, emotional lability and slow tongue movements
Hyperreflexia, extensor plantars, Hoffmann sign; no wasting or fasciculations
Urinary urgency can occur; sensation normal
Onset usually in the 50s; survival often exceeds 10 years
inv: MRI brain and spine to exclude compressive, demyelinating and structural causes
EMG repeated over time to detect evolving LMN involvement
B12, copper, HTLV-1, HIV, VLCFA in men, syphilis serology; HSP gene panel
Motor cortex atrophy or T2/SWI changes along corticospinal tracts may be seen

case.story: Five years of increasing leg stiffness, now walking with a cane; speech has become slow and strained.
case.exam: Spastic gait, brisk reflexes in all limbs, bilateral extensor plantars, brisk jaw jerk, no wasting or fasciculation, normal sensation.
case.tests: MRI spine and brain unremarkable apart from mild precentral atrophy; HTLV-1 negative; EMG no denervation; HSP panel negative.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and how does its outlook differ from ALS?
case.a: Primary lateral sclerosis; it progresses far more slowly, with survival commonly over a decade.

read.where: Chapter 15 Disorders of the Motor Cells: The Motor Neuron Diseases — Primary Lateral Sclerosis
27: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis and its Variants
Chapter 7: Motor Neuron Diseases: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis

det.patho: PLS is a degenerative disorder confined to upper motor neurons and corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts. Betz cell loss and TDP-43 pathology are reported, placing it at one end of the MND spectrum. Some patients labelled PLS later develop LMN signs and are then reclassified as UMN-predominant ALS.
det.clinical: Most present with slowly progressive leg spasticity; some start with bulbar dysfunction. Cramps, urgency and pseudobulbar affect are common. Weakness is mild compared with stiffness. Cognition is usually preserved but mild executive change can occur.
det.diagnosis: Consensus criteria require at least two years of progressive UMN dysfunction without LMN signs, with probable PLS at two to four years and definite PLS beyond four. Extensive testing excludes structural, demyelinating, infectious, metabolic and hereditary mimics. EMG should be repeated because early PLS can evolve to ALS. Transcranial magnetic stimulation and advanced MRI may support central motor involvement.
det.treatment: Treatment is symptomatic: baclofen, tizanidine, botulinum toxin and physiotherapy for spasticity; intrathecal baclofen for severe cases. Speech therapy and drugs such as dextromethorphan-quinidine or SSRIs help pseudobulbar affect. Riluzole has no proven benefit in pure PLS. Mobility aids and fall prevention are important.
det.prognosis: Slowly disabling, but life expectancy is usually much longer than in ALS.
pearls: No LMN signs after four years strongly favours PLS.
Always check HTLV-1 in Thai or other endemic-area patients with spastic paraparesis.
Repeat EMG; new denervation changes the label to ALS.
det.thd: PLS คือโรคเซลล์ประสาทสั่งการส่วนบนเสื่อมอย่างเดียว ทำให้ขาเกร็งและพูดช้าแบบ pseudobulbar โดยไม่มีกล้ามเนื้อลีบหรือเต้นระริก ดำเนินโรคช้ามาก ต้องตัดโรคอื่น เช่น การกดไขสันหลัง MS HTLV-1 และ HSP ออกก่อน และติดตาม EMG เป็นระยะ การรักษาเน้นลดเกร็งและกายภาพบำบัด พยากรณ์ดีกว่า ALS มาก

name: Primary mitochondrial diseases
formal: Disorders from mutations of mitochondrial or nuclear genes causing oxidative phosphorylation failure, such as MELAS, MERRF, Leigh and Kearns-Sayre syndromes.
simple: Inherited illnesses in which the cell's energy factories do not work, affecting the brain and muscles.
th: กลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมจากยีนใน mtDNA หรือยีนนิวเคลียสที่ทำให้การสร้างพลังงาน (OXPHOS) ล้มเหลว เช่น MELAS, MERRF, Leigh, Kearns-Sayre มีอาการหลายระบบ โดยเฉพาะสมอง กล้ามเนื้อ ตา หู หัวใจ
tempoNote: Slowly progressive with stepwise worsening during metabolic crises or stroke-like episodes
feat: Multisystem involvement in unrelated organs: brain, muscle, eye, ear, heart, kidney, gut, endocrine
Ptosis and external ophthalmoplegia, exercise intolerance, myopathy
Stroke-like episodes, seizures, myoclonus, ataxia, migraine-like headache
Sensorineural deafness, diabetes, short stature, cardiomyopathy or conduction block
Maternal inheritance (mtDNA) or autosomal patterns (nuclear genes)
inv: Blood and CSF lactate; GDF-15 and FGF-21 biomarkers
Genetic testing first: mtDNA sequencing (blood, urine, or muscle) and nuclear gene panels or exome/genome
MRI (stroke-like lesions, Leigh pattern), MR spectroscopy lactate peak, ECG and echo, audiology, ophthalmology
Muscle biopsy (ragged red and COX-negative fibres) when genetics is inconclusive

case.who: 24-year-old woman from Lamphun with diabetes and hearing aids
case.story: Sudden right-sided vision loss and confusion after a migraine-like headache; her mother is also deaf and diabetic.
case.exam: Right homonymous hemianopia, short stature, bilateral hearing loss.
case.tests: MRI: left occipital cortical lesion not following an arterial territory; lactate raised; m.3243A>G in urine epithelial cells.
case.q: Which mitochondrial syndrome is this and which supplement is used acutely?
case.a: MELAS; intravenous L-arginine during stroke-like episodes, avoid valproate.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Primary Mitochondrial Diseases
Progressive Encephalopathies With Onset Before Age 2

det.patho: Oxidative phosphorylation depends on proteins encoded by both mtDNA and nuclear genes. Pathogenic variants in either impair ATP production, hitting energy-hungry tissues hardest. With mtDNA variants, the proportion of mutant copies (heteroplasmy) differs between tissues and over time, explaining variable severity within families. Combined prevalence is about 1 in 5,000.
det.clinical: Syndromes include MELAS, MERRF, Leigh syndrome, Kearns-Sayre, CPEO, LHON, NARP, POLG disease and MNGIE, but many patients do not fit a named syndrome. Clues are involvement of two or more unrelated organ systems, maternal family history, and worsening during illness or with certain drugs. POLG disease may present with refractory epilepsy and liver failure.
det.diagnosis: Modern practice is genetics first: sequencing mtDNA (including deletions) and nuclear genes on blood, with urine or muscle when blood may miss heteroplasmic variants. Lactate and biomarkers support but are neither sensitive nor specific. Muscle biopsy and respiratory chain enzymology are reserved for unresolved cases.
det.treatment: No cure exists. Management includes surveillance for cardiac, endocrine, hearing and vision problems, exercise training, and treating seizures (avoid valproate, especially in POLG). L-arginine or citrulline are used for MELAS stroke-like episodes; idebenone is approved in some regions for LHON. Cofactor 'cocktails' (CoQ10, riboflavin, carnitine) have limited evidence, though specific deficiencies (primary CoQ10, riboflavin-responsive forms) respond well. Genetic counselling, including reproductive options such as preimplantation testing or mitochondrial donation, is important.
det.prognosis: Highly variable, from mild exercise intolerance to death in infancy (Leigh syndrome).
pearls: Two or more unrelated organ systems + maternal inheritance: think mitochondrial.
Avoid valproate in suspected mitochondrial disease, especially POLG.
Stroke-like lesions in MELAS are cortical and cross arterial boundaries.
det.thd: โรคไมโทคอนเดรียปฐมภูมิเกิดจากยีนใน mtDNA หรือนิวเคลียสที่ทำให้เซลล์สร้างพลังงานไม่ได้ อวัยวะที่ใช้พลังงานมากจึงได้รับผลกระทบ เช่น สมอง กล้ามเนื้อ ตา หู หัวใจ อาการหลากหลาย เช่น หนังตาตก กลอกตาไม่ได้ ชัก stroke-like episode หูหนวก เบาหวาน ปัจจุบันวินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีนเป็นหลัก ยังไม่มีการรักษาให้หายขาด เน้นดูแลอาการ หลีกเลี่ยง valproate และให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

name: Primary optic nerve sheath meningiomas
formal: Meningioma of the optic nerve sheath causing slowly progressive painless vision loss, optic atrophy and optociliary shunt vessels; imaging shows tram-track sign.
simple: A slow-growing tumour around the eye nerve causing gradual vision loss.
th: เนื้องอก meningioma ที่เกิดจากเยื่อหุ้มเส้นประสาทตา ทำให้ตามัวช้า ๆ ไม่เจ็บ optic atrophy และ optociliary shunt vessels; ภาพถ่ายพบ tram-track sign
tempoNote: Slow visual decline over months to years
feat: Painless, slowly progressive monocular visual loss, usually in middle-aged women
Relative afferent pupillary defect, colour vision loss and field defects
Disc swelling early, then pallor; optociliary shunt vessels are a classic clue
Mild proptosis and limited eye movements in some
Bilateral or childhood tumours suggest neurofibromatosis type 2
inv: MRI orbits with fat-suppressed gadolinium: tubular enhancing sheath around a non-enhancing nerve (tram-track)
CT may show calcification along the nerve sheath
Visual fields and OCT for baseline and monitoring

case.story: Over 18 months her left eye vision has dimmed with colours looking washed out; no pain on eye movement.
case.exam: VA 6/36 left, left RAPD, pale left disc with shunt vessels at its margin, mild left proptosis.
case.tests: MRI orbit shows circumferential enhancing tissue around the left optic nerve, tram-track on axial images.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what is the preferred treatment if vision keeps falling?
case.a: Primary optic nerve sheath meningioma; fractionated stereotactic radiotherapy, since surgery usually blinds the eye.

read.where: Chapter 22 Neuro-Ophthalmology — Primary Optic Nerve Sheath Meningiomas

det.patho: The tumour grows from arachnoid cap cells of the optic nerve sheath and encircles the nerve, compressing its pial blood supply and axons. Shunt vessels form as venous outflow through the central retinal vein is obstructed. Most are WHO grade 1; secondary sheath meningiomas spread into the orbit from sphenoid wing or planum tumours.
det.clinical: Slowly worsening vision in one eye is the rule, often discovered late because the other eye compensates. Transient obscurations with gaze may occur. The triad of visual loss, optic atrophy and optociliary shunts is suggestive but not universal. Children have more aggressive tumours and need NF2 assessment.
det.diagnosis: Contrast MRI of the orbits with fat suppression is the key test; the sheath enhances around a dark nerve. Calcification on CT supports it. Biopsy is avoided because of risk to vision. Differentials include glioma, sarcoid, lymphoma and perineuritis.
det.treatment: Observation is reasonable when vision is good and stable. Fractionated stereotactic radiotherapy or proton therapy preserves or improves vision in most patients with progressive loss. Surgery is reserved for blind, disfiguring eyes or intracranial spread.
det.prognosis: Untreated tumours usually lead to slow progressive visual loss; radiotherapy gives good long-term control.
pearls: Optociliary shunt vessels plus progressive optic atrophy: think sheath meningioma.
Tram-track on axial MRI and doughnut on coronal views.
Radiotherapy, not surgery, is the eye-sparing treatment.
det.thd: Optic nerve sheath meningioma เป็นเนื้องอกที่โตจากเยื่อหุ้มเส้นประสาทตา ทำให้ตามัวข้างเดียวช้า ๆ โดยไม่เจ็บ พบ RAPD ขั้วประสาทตาซีด และ optociliary shunt vessels MRI พบ tram-track sign รักษาด้วย fractionated stereotactic radiotherapy ส่วนการผ่าตัดมักทำให้ตาบอด

qx.stem: A 43-year-old female accountant from Chonburi has 18 months of slowly fading vision in the left eye. Acuity is 6/36 with a left relative afferent pupillary defect, and the left disc is pale with an optociliary shunt vessel. Contrast MRI of the orbits shows a thin, enhancing cuff of tissue around the left intraorbital optic nerve on axial images, with the non-enhancing nerve visible in the centre; CT shows fine linear calcification along the sheath.
qx.q: What is the best management option for this lesion if vision continues to decline?
opts: Fractionated stereotactic radiotherapy
Surgical excision of the tumour with preservation of the optic nerve
High-dose IV methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisolone
Optic nerve sheath fenestration
Systemic chemotherapy with carboplatin and vincristine
qx.why: The 'tram-track' enhancing sheath around a central nerve, calcification and an optociliary shunt are typical of primary optic nerve sheath meningioma. Because the tumour shares the nerve's blood supply, excision almost always blinds the eye, so fractionated stereotactic radiotherapy is the standard treatment for progressive visual loss. Steroids help optic neuritis or perineuritis, fenestration is for papilloedema, and carboplatin–vincristine is used for paediatric optic pathway glioma.

name: Primary paroxysmal exercise-induced dyskinesia
formal: Idiopathic dystonic attacks triggered by prolonged exercise lasting up to an hour, often due to GLUT1 deficiency.
simple: Attacks of muscle twisting brought on by long physical exercise.
th: ความผิดปกติของการเคลื่อนไหวเป็นพัก ๆ ที่เกิดหลังออกกำลังนาน มักเป็น dystonia ที่ขา นานไม่เกินชั่วโมง สาเหตุสำคัญคือ GLUT1 deficiency (SLC2A1)
tempoNote: Attacks of 5–30 minutes after 10–15 minutes or more of exertion
feat: Dystonia or chorea, usually in the legs, after prolonged walking or running
Attacks last minutes to under an hour and settle with rest
Fasting, stress or cold can also trigger
Associated features in GLUT1 cases: epilepsy, migraine, hemiplegic attacks, mild learning problems
Childhood onset; autosomal dominant inheritance often
inv: Paired fasting CSF and blood glucose: low CSF glucose and CSF/blood ratio <0.6 suggest GLUT1 deficiency
SLC2A1 sequencing; also consider PRRT2, ECHS1, PDH defects, GCH1
Video of attacks; interictal exam and MRI usually normal

case.story: After 20 minutes of football her right foot twists inward for 15 minutes; worse if she skips breakfast. Had absence seizures in early childhood.
case.exam: Normal between attacks; attack induced on treadmill shows foot inversion and leg chorea.
case.tests: Fasting CSF glucose 34 mg/dL with blood glucose 90 mg/dL (ratio 0.38); SLC2A1 variant found.
case.q: What treatment addresses the underlying mechanism?
case.a: Ketogenic diet (or modified Atkins), which supplies ketones as an alternative brain fuel in GLUT1 deficiency.

det.patho: Sustained exercise raises cerebral energy demand; if glucose transport into the brain is impaired (GLUT1, SLC2A1), basal ganglia circuits fail transiently. Other energy-pathway defects such as pyruvate dehydrogenase or ECHS1 deficiency produce similar attacks. Some cases remain without a known gene.
det.clinical: Attacks begin during or just after long exertion and affect the exercised limbs, typically the legs. Consciousness is preserved. A history of seizures, migraine, ataxia or haemolytic anaemia may point to GLUT1 deficiency. Attacks can be confused with cramps or functional episodes.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by provoking an attack with exercise and filming it. Lumbar puncture after fasting with matched blood glucose is the key screening test. Genetic testing then confirms the cause. Exclude dopa-responsive dystonia with a levodopa trial.
det.treatment: For GLUT1 deficiency, ketogenic or modified Atkins diet is effective and also helps seizures. Frequent carbohydrate snacks and avoiding fasting may reduce attacks. Antiseizure drugs work poorly, unlike in PKD. Levodopa or acetazolamide helps a few.
det.prognosis: Attacks often persist into adulthood but may lessen; outlook depends on the underlying cause.
pearls: Exercise-induced dystonia in a child: measure fasting CSF glucose.
Ketogenic diet treats the cause in GLUT1 deficiency.
Carbamazepine dramatically helps PKD but not PED.
det.thd: PED คือ dystonia หรือ chorea ที่ขาเป็นพัก ๆ หลังออกกำลังนาน อยู่หลายนาทีถึงไม่เกินชั่วโมง สาเหตุสำคัญคือ GLUT1 deficiency ที่ทำให้สมองได้กลูโคสไม่พอ ตรวจพบน้ำตาลใน CSF ต่ำเทียบกับเลือด ยืนยันด้วยยีน SLC2A1 รักษาด้วย ketogenic diet และหลีกเลี่ยงการอดอาหาร

Triggered by alcohol, coffee or stress at rest; longer attacks; PNKD gene
Exercise-worsening foot dystonia but daily, worse later in the day, levodopa responsive

name: Primary paroxysmal non-kinesigenic dystonic dyskinesia
formal: Idiopathic attacks of dystonia and chorea lasting minutes to hours, triggered by alcohol, caffeine or stress, from PNKD gene mutation.
simple: Longer episodes of twisting movements triggered by alcohol, caffeine or stress.
th: dystonia และ chorea เป็นพัก ๆ นานหลายนาทีถึงหลายชั่วโมง ไม่ได้เกิดจากการเคลื่อนไหว แต่กระตุ้นด้วยแอลกอฮอล์ กาแฟ ความเครียด สาเหตุจากยีน PNKD
tempoNote: Attacks of 10 minutes to several hours, a few per week or fewer
feat: Spontaneous attacks of dystonia, chorea or both, often with inability to speak but full awareness
Triggers: alcohol, coffee/tea, fatigue, emotional stress, hunger
Onset in childhood or adolescence; autosomal dominant family history common
Normal examination between attacks
Sleep can terminate an attack
inv: Interictal MRI and EEG normal; ictal EEG shows no epileptic activity
PNKD (MR-1) gene testing; panels include KCNMA1 and others
Home video of attacks

case.story: Since age 10 he has attacks where his neck twists and arms writhe for about an hour, often after iced coffee or at parties after a beer. His father has similar spells.
case.exam: Completely normal between episodes; filmed attack shows mixed dystonia and chorea with preserved awareness.
case.tests: MRI and EEG normal; heterozygous PNKD variant found.
case.q: Why would carbamazepine probably disappoint him, and what helps?
case.a: PNKD responds poorly to sodium-channel drugs; trigger avoidance plus clonazepam or other benzodiazepines are most useful.

det.patho: The PNKD (myofibrillogenesis regulator 1) protein interacts with synaptic release machinery; mutant forms reduce restraint on dopamine release in the striatum, especially under alcohol and caffeine. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with high penetrance. Phenocopies arise from KCNMA1, SLC2A1 and acquired causes such as MS or hypoparathyroidism.
det.clinical: Attacks are longer and rarer than in PKD and are not triggered by movement. Patients often describe a warning sensation before onset. Speech may be lost from oromandibular dystonia. Secondary cases from demyelination, stroke or metabolic disturbance tend to be later in onset and unilateral.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the history of triggers, duration and family pattern, plus video. Normal interictal neurology is expected. Genetic testing confirms classic cases. In sporadic or adult-onset cases, check calcium, glucose, thyroid and MRI to exclude secondary causes.
det.treatment: Avoid alcohol, caffeine and sleep deprivation. Clonazepam is the most consistently helpful; other benzodiazepines, gabapentin or acetazolamide can be tried. Sleeping through an attack may end it. Carbamazepine is usually ineffective.
det.prognosis: Attacks often become less frequent in mid-adulthood; disability between attacks is minimal.
pearls: Long attacks triggered by alcohol or coffee = non-kinesigenic.
Clonazepam is the drug of choice; carbamazepine rarely works.
New-onset PNKD in an adult: look for MS, stroke or metabolic causes.
det.thd: PNKD คือ dystonia ปนกับ chorea ที่เกิดเป็นพัก ๆ นานหลายนาทีถึงหลายชั่วโมง ถูกกระตุ้นด้วยแอลกอฮอล์ กาแฟ หรือความเครียด ไม่ได้เกิดจากการขยับตัว เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมยีน PNKD ระหว่างอาการตรวจปกติ รักษาด้วยการเลี่ยงสิ่งกระตุ้นและ clonazepam

ddx.pt: Seconds-long attacks triggered by sudden movement; carbamazepine responsive
Only after prolonged exercise; GLUT1 deficiency
Variable phenomenology, distractibility, onset later, other functional signs

name: Primary progressive aphasia (PPA)
formal: Neurodegenerative language disorder with isolated progressive aphasia for at least two years; non-fluent, semantic and logopenic variants (the last often Alzheimer pathology).
simple: A condition where language ability slowly worsens while other mental abilities are preserved at first.
more: Diagnosis by Gorno-Tempini criteria with MRI patterns: left frontal insula in nonfluent, anterior temporal in semantic, and left posterior temporal and parietal in logopenic. Check CSF amyloid or amyloid PET for logopenic type.
th: โรคสมองเสื่อมที่เริ่มด้วยความบกพร่องทางภาษาเด่นเพียงอย่างเดียวอย่างน้อย 2 ปี แบ่งเป็น nonfluent, semantic และ logopenic variants
tempoNote: Insidious, progressive over years; language isolated at least initially
feat: Language is the main and initially only domain affected; daily activities otherwise intact early
Nonfluent variant: effortful, agrammatic speech and apraxia of speech
Semantic variant: fluent but empty speech, loss of word meaning, poor naming and single-word comprehension
Logopenic variant: word-finding pauses, poor repetition of sentences, phonological errors
Onset usually 50s–60s; behaviour or memory change may follow
inv: Detailed language assessment by neuropsychologist or speech therapist
MRI: left inferior frontal/insular (nonfluent), anterior temporal (semantic), left temporoparietal (logopenic) atrophy
FDG-PET to show regional hypometabolism
CSF or plasma amyloid/tau biomarkers or amyloid PET, especially in logopenic variant

case.story: Over three years she has struggled to find words and often stops mid-sentence; she still manages money and drives. No memory complaint.
case.exam: Slow speech with long pauses, cannot repeat long sentences, single-word understanding and grammar preserved; MoCA reduced mainly by language items.
case.tests: MRI shows left posterior temporal and parietal atrophy; CSF shows low amyloid-beta 42 and raised p-tau.
case.q: Which PPA variant is this and what pathology is most likely?
case.a: Logopenic variant PPA with Alzheimer disease pathology.

Chapter 11 Cognitive Impairment and Dementia — Frontotemporal Dementia
