9 - Atypical parkinsonism, parkinsonism-­plus syndromes and secondary parkinsonian disorders

det.patho: PPA is a clinical syndrome from degeneration of the left-hemisphere language network. The nonfluent variant usually has tau pathology (CBD, PSP), the semantic variant mostly TDP-43 type C, and the logopenic variant Alzheimer pathology in most. Genetic forms (GRN, C9orf72, MAPT) occur in some families.
det.clinical: Diagnosis requires a progressive language disorder as the most prominent early feature, with relative sparing of memory, behaviour and visuospatial skills. Patients may be misdiagnosed with depression or stroke. Over time, nonfluent cases may develop parkinsonism or CBS/PSP, semantic cases behavioural change, and logopenic cases wider Alzheimer cognitive decline.
det.diagnosis: International consensus (Gorno-Tempini 2011) criteria define root PPA and the three variants by speech features, supported by imaging. Formal language testing is essential. Biomarkers help predict pathology and eligibility for anti-amyloid therapies. Exclude tumour, stroke and other structural causes with MRI.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying treatment exists for FTLD-related PPA. Speech and language therapy, communication aids and caregiver education are the mainstays. Cholinesterase inhibitors may be tried in logopenic (Alzheimer) PPA; anti-amyloid antibodies are considered in eligible biomarker-positive patients. Plan for future legal and care decisions early.
det.prognosis: Median survival is roughly 7–12 years from onset; progression varies by variant.
pearls: Agrammatism and apraxia of speech = nonfluent; loss of meaning = semantic; poor repetition = logopenic.
Logopenic PPA is usually Alzheimer disease.
Early language-only decline is not 'just stress'; image the brain.
det.thd: PPA เป็นสมองเสื่อมที่เริ่มจากปัญหาภาษาก่อนอย่างอื่น แบ่งเป็น 3 แบบ คือ nonfluent (พูดติดขัด ไวยากรณ์ผิด) semantic (พูดคล่องแต่ไม่รู้ความหมายคำ) และ logopenic (นึกคำไม่ออก ทวนประโยคยาวไม่ได้ มักเป็น Alzheimer) วินิจฉัยด้วยการประเมินภาษาและ MRI รักษาด้วยการฝึกพูดและการดูแลประคับประคอง

ddx.pt: Fluent speech with loss of word meaning and anterior temporal atrophy; TDP-43 pathology
Typical amnestic onset; logopenic PPA is an atypical language-led AD
Personality and behaviour change dominate rather than language

aN: ppa | primary progressive aphasia | mesulam aphasia | nfvppa svppa lvppa | progressive language disorder

name: Primary progressive multiple sclerosis
formal: MS with steadily worsening disability from onset without relapses, typically a progressive myelopathy in older adults; ocrelizumab is licensed.
simple: A type of multiple sclerosis that gets steadily worse from the start, without relapses.
th: MS ที่ความพิการเพิ่มขึ้นเรื่อย ๆ ตั้งแต่เริ่มโดยไม่มีช่วงกำเริบ ส่วนใหญ่เป็นไขสันหลังเสื่อมแบบค่อยเป็นค่อยไปในผู้ใหญ่อายุ 40 ขึ้นไป ยาที่ได้รับรองคือ ocrelizumab
tempoNote: Insidious worsening over at least one year, typically starting around age 40; occasional superimposed activity may occur
feat: Slowly worsening spastic paraparesis or asymmetric leg weakness, often one leg first
Bladder urgency, fatigue and sensory symptoms; vision usually spared
Less common: progressive cerebellar ataxia or cognitive decline
Equal sex ratio and older onset than relapsing MS
inv: MRI brain and spine: fewer brain lesions than relapsing MS, often prominent cord lesions and atrophy
CSF oligoclonal bands (supportive, and part of diagnostic criteria)
Exclude mimics: B12, copper, HTLV-1, syphilis, VLCFA in men, compressive cervical disease

case.story: Two years of a dragging right leg, then the left; walking distance has fallen from kilometres to 300 metres. No episodes of visual loss or sudden attacks.
case.exam: Spastic paraparesis worse on the right, bilateral extensor plantars, reduced vibration in feet, urinary urgency.
case.tests: MRI: three short cervical and thoracic cord lesions and several periventricular brain lesions; CSF oligoclonal bands positive; B12, HTLV-1 and VLCFA normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and which therapy has shown benefit?
case.a: Primary progressive MS; ocrelizumab slows disability progression, best in younger patients with MRI activity.

read.where: Chapter 19 Multiple Sclerosis and Demyelinating Diseases

det.patho: Progression reflects compartmentalised inflammation behind an intact blood-brain barrier (meningeal B-cell follicles, chronic active lesions with microglia) together with axonal loss and failure of remyelination. About 10–15% of MS starts this way. The same disease biology probably underlies secondary progression, with age being a major driver.
det.clinical: Patients describe gradual deterioration of walking over years without distinct attacks. The cord is the usual target, but progressive ataxia, hemiparesis or cognitive decline also occur. Disability measured by EDSS rises steadily, with many needing walking aids within 10 years.
det.diagnosis: The 2017 McDonald criteria require one year of progression plus two of: typical brain lesions, two or more cord lesions, and CSF oligoclonal bands. Because the presentation is a nonspecific progressive myelopathy, mimics must be actively excluded with spinal MRI, metabolic and infectious tests and, when suggested, genetic testing for hereditary spastic paraplegia or leukodystrophy.
det.treatment: Ocrelizumab is the licensed disease-modifying therapy and gives a modest reduction in disability progression; benefit is greatest in younger patients with enhancing lesions. Rehabilitation, spasticity treatment (baclofen, tizanidine, botulinum toxin), bladder management, fampridine for walking and fatigue strategies are central. BTK inhibitors and other agents targeting smouldering inflammation are under study.
det.prognosis: Disability accumulates faster than in relapsing MS, though the pace varies widely.
pearls: A progressive myelopathy after 40 is not MS until compressive, metabolic, infective and genetic causes are excluded.
Oligoclonal bands are especially valuable in this phenotype.
Age and MRI activity predict who benefits from immunotherapy.
det.thd: MS ชนิด primary progressive มีความพิการเพิ่มขึ้นเรื่อย ๆ ตั้งแต่ต้นโดยไม่มีช่วงกำเริบ พบในผู้ใหญ่อายุราว 40 ปี มักเริ่มด้วยขาเกร็งอ่อนแรงจากไขสันหลัง วินิจฉัยด้วยเกณฑ์ McDonald ร่วมกับ MRI และ oligoclonal band โดยต้องแยกโรคไขสันหลังอื่นออกก่อน ยาที่ได้รับรองคือ ocrelizumab ร่วมกับการฟื้นฟูและการรักษาอาการเกร็งและปัสสาวะ

qx.stem: A 46-year-old male rice-mill owner from Suphan Buri reports three years of slowly worsening stiffness and weakness of both legs without any distinct attack. He now walks 300 m before resting. MRI shows four cervical and thoracic cord lesions under two segments long and five periventricular brain lesions, one faintly enhancing. CSF shows restricted oligoclonal bands. Vitamin B12, copper, HIV and HTLV-1 serology are normal.
qx.q: Which disease-modifying treatment has the best evidence for slowing disability in his condition?
opts: Interferon beta-1a
Glatiramer acetate
Natalizumab
Monthly pulsed IV methylprednisolone
Ocrelizumab
qx.why: Progression from onset with cord and brain lesions and intrathecal bands fits primary progressive MS. Ocrelizumab is the agent shown in a phase 3 trial to reduce confirmed disability progression in PPMS, with more benefit in younger patients with enhancing lesions. Interferon, glatiramer and natalizumab failed in progressive MS trials, and repeated steroids have no proven disease-modifying effect.

name: Primary spinal cord tumours
formal: Intradural intramedullary tumours such as ependymoma and astrocytoma, or extramedullary tumours like meningioma and schwannoma, causing myelopathy and radicular pain.
simple: Tumours that start in or around the spinal cord and cause pain, weakness and numbness.
th: เนื้องอกปฐมภูมิของไขสันหลังและเยื่อหุ้ม เช่น ependymoma, astrocytoma, meningioma และ schwannoma ทำให้ไขสันหลังเสื่อมและปวดตามรากประสาท
tempoNote: Months to years of slowly progressive symptoms; occasional acute decline with haemorrhage
feat: Back or radicular pain, often worse lying down at night
Slowly progressive myelopathy: spasticity, sensory level, gait and sphincter disturbance
Intramedullary tumours: dissociated or suspended sensory loss, central cord pattern
Extramedullary tumours: Brown-Séquard-like pattern, early root pain
Associations: NF1 (astrocytoma), NF2 (ependymoma, schwannoma, meningioma), VHL (haemangioblastoma)
inv: MRI whole spine with contrast: intramedullary versus intradural extramedullary location; associated syrinx or cysts
MRI brain in NF2 or VHL; genetic testing where syndromic
Surgical biopsy or resection for histology and molecular grading

case.story: Two years of night-time neck pain and a year of numb hands that cannot feel hot water.
case.exam: Loss of pain and temperature in a cape distribution, wasting of hand muscles, mild spastic legs.
case.tests: MRI: well-defined enhancing central lesion C4–C6 with cap haemosiderin and a syrinx.
case.q: What is the likely tumour and treatment?
case.a: Intramedullary ependymoma; microsurgical gross total resection with neurophysiological monitoring.

read.where: Chapter 20 Neuro-Oncology — Primary Spinal Cord Tumours

det.patho: Intramedullary tumours in adults are mostly ependymomas, followed by astrocytomas and haemangioblastomas; in children astrocytomas predominate. Intradural extramedullary tumours are mainly schwannomas, meningiomas and neurofibromas. Spinal ependymomas are classified by molecular features (e.g. MYCN-amplified spinal ependymoma behaves aggressively) under WHO CNS5.
det.clinical: Pain is often the earliest symptom and may precede deficits by years. Intramedullary lesions produce central cord syndromes and sacral sparing; extramedullary lesions compress from one side with root pain then cord signs. Myxopapillary ependymoma of the filum causes low back pain and cauda equina features.
det.diagnosis: Contrast MRI localises the lesion; ependymomas are central and well circumscribed with haemosiderin caps, astrocytomas eccentric and infiltrative, haemangioblastomas with a nodule and large cyst. Meningiomas show dural attachment and schwannomas a dumbbell shape through the foramen. Histology and molecular testing guide grading.
det.treatment: Surgery with intraoperative monitoring is first-line; complete resection is often achievable for ependymoma, meningioma and schwannoma. Infiltrative astrocytomas are debulked or biopsied followed by radiotherapy and chemotherapy depending on grade and molecular profile. Belzutifan is used for VHL-associated tumours. Rehabilitation and bladder management are important.
det.prognosis: Benign, completely removed tumours have excellent control; high-grade astrocytomas carry poor survival.
pearls: Night-time back pain with progressive myelopathy needs MRI of the whole spine.
Haemosiderin cap at a tumour pole suggests ependymoma.
Multiple spinal tumours: think NF2 or VHL.
det.thd: Primary spinal cord tumours คือเนื้องอกที่เกิดในไขสันหลังหรือเยื่อหุ้ม เช่น ependymoma, astrocytoma, meningioma และ schwannoma ผู้ป่วยมักปวดหลังหรือปวดตามรากประสาทนำมาก่อนหลายเดือน แล้วเกิดอาการไขสันหลังเสื่อมช้า ๆ MRI ทั้งแนวไขสันหลังช่วยบอกชนิดและตำแหน่ง การรักษาหลักคือผ่าตัด บางชนิดต้องฉายรังสีหรือเคมีบำบัดเพิ่ม

name: Primary vasculitis
formal: Idiopathic inflammation of blood vessel walls, including giant cell arteritis, PAN and ANCA-associated vasculitis, with CNS or PNS involvement.
simple: Inflammation of blood vessels that starts without another disease, and can harm nerves and brain.
th: กลุ่มโรคหลอดเลือดอักเสบที่ไม่ทราบสาเหตุ เช่น GCA, PAN และ ANCA-associated vasculitis ซึ่งทำให้เกิด stroke หรือเส้นประสาทอักเสบหลายเส้นได้
tempoNote: Weeks to months typically; abrupt stroke or neuropathy may punctuate the course, and relapses are common
feat: Three broad groups: systemic primary vasculitis, brain-restricted vasculitis (PACNS), and secondary vasculitis due to infection, drugs, malignancy or connective tissue disease
Grouped by vessel size: large (GCA, Takayasu), medium (PAN, Kawasaki) and small (ANCA-associated and immune-complex vasculitides)
Peripheral nervous system: painful mononeuritis multiplex or asymmetric sensorimotor neuropathy, most often in microscopic polyangiitis, EGPA and PAN
CNS: multifocal infarcts, haemorrhage, encephalopathy, headache; ANCA disease can also cause hypertrophic pachymeningitis and hypophysitis
Systemic clues: fever, weight loss, raised ESR/CRP, rash, renal and pulmonary disease
inv: ESR, CRP, ANCA (MPO and PR3), ANA, complement, cryoglobulins, hepatitis B and C, urinalysis and renal function
Nerve conduction studies showing patchy axonal loss; combined nerve and muscle biopsy
MRI brain with vessel-wall imaging, CTA/MRA or catheter angiography; CSF and (when needed) brain biopsy for PACNS; temporal artery ultrasound or biopsy for GCA

case.who: 58-year-old farmer from Sakon Nakhon with asthma and sinusitis
case.story: Over 6 weeks, a painful foot drop on the right, then numbness of the left hand, with fever and weight loss.
case.exam: Right foot drop, left ulnar and median sensory loss, purpuric lesions on the shins.
case.tests: Eosinophilia, raised CRP and p-ANCA (MPO); nerve conduction shows asymmetric axonal changes; nerve and muscle biopsy shows necrotising vasculitis.
case.q: What kind of neuropathy pattern is this and what classification fits?
case.a: Mononeuritis multiplex from a primary systemic small-vessel vasculitis (EGPA); give steroid plus immunosuppression.

read.where: CNS vasculitis — Classification: primary systemic, primary non-systemic (PACNS) and secondary vasculitis
CNS vasculitis — Primary systemic vasculitis: ANCA-associated vasculitis

det.patho: Inflammation, often immune-complex or ANCA-mediated, damages the vessel wall, leading to stenosis, thrombosis or rupture. Small-vessel ANCA-associated disease (GPA with PR3 antibodies, MPA and EGPA with MPO) involves neutrophil activation, and granulomatous disease can also invade the CNS by contiguity from sinuses and orbit. Primary CNS angiitis is restricted to brain and spinal vessels, with generally normal systemic markers. The peripheral nerve is most often affected via vasa nervorum ischaemia.
det.clinical: Neurological involvement ranges from 55–79% in microscopic polyangiitis (mainly peripheral nerve, with CNS in 10–30%) to rare involvement in other forms. Mononeuritis multiplex, multifocal strokes, encephalopathy, cranial neuropathies, pachymeningitis and pituitary disease all occur. ANCA disease relapses in 40–50% of patients. GCA in patients over 50 presents with new headache, jaw claudication and risk of sudden blindness.
det.diagnosis: Start with the clinical syndrome and the pattern of vessel size, then screen: inflammatory markers, ANCA and other autoantibodies, infection and malignancy, kidney and lung assessment. ESR, CRP, ANA and ANCA are typically normal in PACNS, so imaging, CSF and often biopsy are required; MRI, angiography and CSF are abnormal in the large majority. Biopsy of an affected nerve with muscle gives the best yield for PNS disease. Always exclude infection, RCVS, atherosclerosis and malignancy before confirming a primary vasculitis.
det.treatment: Start high-dose glucocorticoids early for organ- or sight-threatening disease. Severe ANCA-associated vasculitis is induced with rituximab or cyclophosphamide plus steroids (avacopan can reduce steroid exposure), followed by maintenance with rituximab or azathioprine. PACNS is treated with steroids and cyclophosphamide, then azathioprine or mycophenolate; GCA receives prednisolone with tocilizumab as a steroid-sparing option. Monitor for infection, bone loss and relapse, and give prophylaxis against Pneumocystis.
det.prognosis: Treatment improves outcomes substantially, but relapse and treatment toxicity are frequent; untreated, neurological injury and mortality are high.
pearls: Painful asymmetric neuropathy accumulating nerve by nerve: think vasculitis and send ANCA and urine.
Any patient over 50 with new headache and high ESR gets steroids the same day to protect vision.
Biopsy a clinically affected sensory nerve together with muscle to raise yield.
det.thd: Primary vasculitis คือโรคหลอดเลือดอักเสบที่ไม่ได้เกิดจากโรคอื่น แบ่งตามขนาดหลอดเลือด เช่น GCA ในหลอดเลือดใหญ่ PAN ในหลอดเลือดขนาดกลาง และ ANCA-associated vasculitis ในหลอดเลือดเล็ก ระบบประสาทที่พบบ่อยคือ mononeuritis multiplex และสมองขาดเลือดหลายตำแหน่ง ตรวจ ESR, CRP, ANCA, ปัสสาวะ และชิ้นเนื้อเส้นประสาทหรือกล้ามเนื้อ บางรายต้องทำ angiography หรือตัดชิ้นเนื้อสมอง รักษาด้วยสเตียรอยด์ร่วมกับ rituximab หรือ cyclophosphamide

name: Primitive neuroepithelial tumours (PNET)
formal: Embryonal small blue cell tumours of CNS, now classified under embryonal tumours, occurring in supratentorial brain or pineal region; aggressive in children.
simple: Aggressive tumours of immature nerve cells, mainly in children.
th: เนื้องอกตัวอ่อน small blue cell ของระบบประสาทส่วนกลาง ปัจจุบันจัดอยู่ในกลุ่ม embryonal tumours ตาม molecular พบในเด็ก รุนแรง
tempoNote: Rapid progression over weeks
feat: Young children with raised intracranial pressure, seizures, focal deficits
Large heterogeneous supratentorial mass with haemorrhage and calcification
CSF dissemination common
The term 'CNS PNET' was removed in the 2016/2021 WHO classifications; tumours are reassigned by molecular profile (e.g. ETMR, CNS neuroblastoma FOXR2, high-grade glioma)
inv: MRI brain and spine with contrast
CSF cytology
Histology with molecular/methylation profiling

case.story: Three weeks of vomiting, irritability and a focal seizure.
case.exam: Papilloedema, left hemiparesis.
case.tests: MRI: large right frontal heterogeneous mass with cysts and haemorrhage; histology: small round blue cells; methylation profiling: CNS neuroblastoma FOXR2-activated.
case.q: Why is the old label 'PNET' no longer used?
case.a: Molecular profiling showed that 'PNETs' were several distinct tumours with different biology and outcomes; they are now named by molecular class.

read.where: Chapter 20 Neuro-Oncology — Primitive Neuroepithelial Tumours and Medulloblastomas

det.patho: PNETs were defined by small undifferentiated cells with neuronal differentiation. Molecular studies revealed distinct entities, including embryonal tumours with multilayered rosettes (C19MC alteration), CNS neuroblastoma (FOXR2), and tumours that actually belong to glioma or ependymoma groups.
det.clinical: Children present with raised pressure, seizures and focal deficits over weeks. Tumours are often large at diagnosis. CSF spread may produce spinal symptoms.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows a large heterogeneous mass; spinal MRI and CSF cytology stage the disease. Methylation profiling is now essential to assign the correct diagnosis.
det.treatment: Maximal resection, craniospinal radiotherapy (in older children) and intensive chemotherapy; very young children receive chemotherapy-based protocols to delay or avoid radiotherapy.
det.prognosis: Generally poor, varying markedly by molecular group.
pearls: 'PNET' is an outdated term; ask for molecular classification.
Stage the whole neuraxis.
Young age limits radiotherapy options.
det.thd: PNET คือเนื้องอกตัวอ่อนชนิด small round blue cell ของระบบประสาทส่วนกลาง พบในเด็กเล็ก ทำให้ความดันในกะโหลกสูง ชัก และอ่อนแรง ปัจจุบัน WHO ไม่ใช้คำว่า CNS PNET แล้ว แต่แบ่งตาม molecular เช่น ETMR และ CNS neuroblastoma FOXR2 การรักษาคือผ่าตัด รังสี และเคมีบำบัด พยากรณ์โรคขึ้นกับชนิดทาง molecular

Perivascular pseudorosettes; supratentorial ZFTA fusion types

name: Prion disease
formal: Fatal neurodegenerative disorder caused by misfolded prion protein, including sporadic CJD, familial, variant and kuru, with rapid dementia, myoclonus and spongiform change.
simple: A rare, fast, fatal brain illness caused by abnormally folded proteins, such as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
more: Group of transmissible neurodegenerative diseases from misfolded prion protein: sporadic, genetic, acquired or variant CJD, GSS and fatal familial insomnia, with rapid dementia and myoclonus.
th: โรคพรีออนคือโรคสมองเสื่อมที่ทำให้เสียชีวิตทุกราย เกิดจาก prion protein พับตัวผิดรูป ประมาณ 85% เกิดเอง 15% เป็นพันธุกรรม และน้อยกว่า 1% ได้รับจากภายนอก อาการหลักคือสมองเสื่อม เดินเซ และการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติ
tempoNote: Sporadic CJD runs weeks to months, vCJD and fatal familial insomnia about 1–1.5 years, GSS and some genetic forms several years; acquired forms are silent for years to decades before symptoms
feat: Three origins: spontaneous or sporadic (about 85%), inherited PRNP variants (about 15%) and acquired by exposure (under 1%)
Incidence is 1–2 per million per year, around 8000 cases worldwide annually; lifetime risk of dying of CJD is about 1 in 5000–6000

Core picture of dementia, ataxia and movement disorder, but the leading symptom differs: cognition (sCJD), psychiatric and painful sensory (vCJD), ataxia (GSS, growth-hormone iCJD, kuru), insomnia and dysautonomia (FFI)
Not contagious through contact or bodily fluids; transmission needs inoculation or eating infected tissue
Invariably fatal and no approved disease-modifying treatment
inv: MRI with DWI, ADC and FLAIR: cortical and striatal restriction in sCJD, pulvinar sign in vCJD, often normal diffusion in slow genetic forms
CSF RT-QuIC (very specific, about 85–95% sensitive in sCJD, often negative in slow forms) with total tau as a supportive marker
PRNP sequencing with codon 129 genotype in every patient, after genetic counselling, since 47% of genetic cases lack a family history
Mimic work-up (autoimmune, infectious, neoplastic, metabolic) and brain tissue only for definite diagnosis or when a treatable alternative is suspected

case.story: Five months of unsteady walking and slurred speech, then irritability and trouble with accounts. Her mother died at 60 of an unnamed 'dementia with clumsiness'.
case.exam: Cerebellar dysarthria, broad-based gait, limb ataxia, mild rigidity, mild cognitive impairment; no myoclonus yet.
case.tests: MRI shows mild cerebellar atrophy with no restricted diffusion; CSF RT-QuIC negative on two occasions, total tau mildly raised; EEG slow without periodic complexes.
case.q: Do the negative RT-QuIC and normal diffusion MRI make prion disease unlikely?
case.a: No. Slow genetic forms such as GSS are often RT-QuIC negative with normal diffusion; with a maternal history, give genetic counselling and send PRNP sequencing.

read.where: Chapter 95 Prion Diseases — Human Prion Diseases: Introduction, Epidemiology, What Are Prions
CJD board tutorial — definition and scope of prion disease
Chapter 11 Cognitive Impairment and Dementia — Prion Disease

det.patho: In every prion disease the normal cell-surface prion protein (PrPC) is converted into PrPSc, a stacked beta-sheet amyloid-like form that acts as a seed for further conversion. Mice lacking PrPC cannot be infected, showing that PrPC is necessary, and lowering PrPC prolongs survival, which makes it the prime treatment target. Different PrPSc strains explain why one protein sequence yields many clinical pictures. Origin is spontaneous in about 85%, dominantly inherited through PRNP in about 15%, and acquired (iatrogenic, dietary, laboratory) in fewer than 1%.
det.clinical: The shared syndrome is a quickly progressive dementia with ataxia and movement disorder, yet the presentation depends on type: confusion and visual or cerebellar signs in sCJD, months of depression and painful limb sensations in vCJD, ataxia in GSS and in growth-hormone iCJD, and insomnia with autonomic overactivity in FFI. Duration ranges from a few months (sCJD) through about 1–1.5 years (vCJD, FFI) to over a decade in some GSS families. The name CJD is used loosely, sometimes for all human prion disease and sometimes only for the sporadic form; the older label TSE is avoided because some inherited forms may not transmit and not all cases show vacuoles.
det.diagnosis: Start with MRI that includes DWI and ADC, CSF RT-QuIC, and a search for mimics; offer PRNP sequencing to every patient with a suspected prion disease, since a fast genetic form can look identical to sCJD. Test performance depends on type: fast forms behave like sCJD, whereas GSS, FFI, some octapeptide-repeat and stop-codon variants and variably protease-sensitive prionopathy often show normal diffusion MRI and negative RT-QuIC. Variant CJD has its own criteria built on early psychiatric features, painful sensory symptoms and the pulvinar sign. Definite diagnosis requires PrPSc in brain tissue at biopsy or autopsy, and older 14-3-3-based criteria are no longer the standard.
det.treatment: There is no cure and no drug approved for prion disease, so care is symptomatic (SSRI, quetiapine, levetiracetam or clonazepam for myoclonus) with early palliative involvement and family support. Genetic counselling should be offered to relatives, and preimplantation genetic diagnosis can prevent transmission to children of carriers. Research targets PrPC lowering (antisense oligonucleotides, siRNA, epigenetic silencing, anti-PrP antibodies), while doxycycline is being tested to delay onset in FFI carriers. Prions resist ordinary disinfection, so high-risk instruments are single-use, incinerated or processed with extended high-temperature steam sterilisation.
det.prognosis: Uniformly fatal; survival ranges from a few months in sCJD to many years in slow genetic types.
pearls: Prion disease is not contagious by touch or bedside care; the risk comes from contaminated neurosurgical instruments, tissue, hormones and blood products.
A negative RT-QuIC or normal diffusion MRI is common in slow genetic forms, so do not stop at the CSF.
Offer PRNP testing to everyone, because almost half of genetic cases have no family history.
det.thd: โรคพรีออนเกิดจากโปรตีน PrPC ปกติเปลี่ยนรูปเป็น PrPSc ซึ่งชักนำให้โปรตีนอื่นเปลี่ยนตามต่อเนื่อง ส่วนใหญ่เกิดขึ้นเอง บางส่วนมาจากยีน PRNP และส่วนน้อยติดมาจากหัตถการหรืออาหาร ผู้ป่วยมีสมองเสื่อมเร็ว เดินเซ และมีการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติ ตรวจด้วย MRI แบบ DWI และ ADC, RT-QuIC ในน้ำไขสันหลัง และควรตรวจยีน PRNP ในผู้ป่วยทุกราย ยังไม่มียารักษา จึงดูแลตามอาการ ให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม และป้องกันการแพร่ผ่านเครื่องมือผ่าตัด

name: Prodromal multiple sclerosis
formal: Early nonspecific symptoms such as pain, fatigue and mood or bladder disorders preceding clinical onset of MS, with increased healthcare use.
simple: Early vague symptoms that appear years before multiple sclerosis is diagnosed.
th: ช่วงก่อนเกิดอาการ MS ชัดเจนหลายปี ผู้ป่วยมีอาการไม่จำเพาะ เช่น ปวด อ่อนเพลีย อารมณ์ซึมเศร้า และปัสสาวะผิดปกติ และใช้บริการทางการแพทย์บ่อยขึ้น
tempoNote: Nonspecific symptoms and increased healthcare visits are detectable up to 5–10 years before the first recognised demyelinating event
feat: A research and epidemiological concept, not a diagnosis that can be made in an individual today
More visits for fatigue, headache, pain, sleep problems, dizziness and sensory complaints in the years before MS onset
More anxiety, depression, bladder and bowel symptoms in the same period
Raised serum neurofilament light chain may appear years before the first attack
inv: No validated test for prodromal MS; serum neurofilament light chain is a research biomarker
MRI only when clinically indicated; incidental typical lesions are classified as radiologically isolated syndrome

case.story: Over four years saw doctors repeatedly for fatigue, low mood, migratory pains and urinary frequency with normal tests. Then had numbness from the waist down for three weeks.
case.exam: Sensory level at T8, brisk knee jerks, positive Lhermitte sign.
case.tests: MRI: cord lesion at T7 and several periventricular ovoid lesions; CSF oligoclonal bands positive.
case.q: How should her earlier symptoms be interpreted?
case.a: They may represent the MS prodrome, recognised only in retrospect; they could not have established the diagnosis earlier.

read.where: Chapter 19 Multiple Sclerosis and Demyelinating Diseases — Multiple Sclerosis Variants

det.patho: Large population studies show that the disease process begins well before the first clinical attack. Subclinical inflammation and early neuroaxonal injury are thought to cause diffuse symptoms such as fatigue, pain and mood disturbance. Epstein-Barr virus infection precedes the rise in neurofilament light, supporting a causal sequence.
det.clinical: In the years before diagnosis, people later diagnosed with MS visit general practitioners, psychiatrists and urologists more often and take more medications than matched controls. Because such symptoms are widespread among healthy people, their predictive value for any individual is low. Children later diagnosed with MS show similar patterns.
det.diagnosis: There are no criteria for prodromal MS. It is recognised retrospectively. Clinicians should keep demyelinating disease in mind when nonspecific complaints are accompanied by any objective neurological sign, and should not order MRI simply for vague symptoms. Incidental MRI lesions without symptoms are classified as radiologically isolated syndrome.
det.treatment: No treatment is indicated on the basis of prodromal symptoms alone. Address each symptom (mood, sleep, pain, bladder) on its merits and encourage healthy habits such as not smoking and keeping vitamin D adequate. Research is exploring whether early detection could allow prevention trials.
det.prognosis: Not applicable as a standalone state; its importance is in understanding when MS biologically begins.
pearls: MS starts biologically years before the first attack.
Repeated healthcare use with unexplained symptoms is common before MS, but most such patients never develop MS.
Do not confuse prodromal MS with radiologically isolated syndrome, which requires MRI lesions.
det.thd: Prodromal MS คือช่วงหลายปีก่อนเกิดอาการ MS ชัดเจน ซึ่งผู้ป่วยมีอาการไม่จำเพาะ เช่น อ่อนเพลีย ปวด ซึมเศร้า นอนไม่หลับ และปัสสาวะผิดปกติ และพบแพทย์บ่อยขึ้น เป็นแนวคิดจากงานวิจัยระดับประชากร ยังไม่สามารถวินิจฉัยในรายบุคคลได้ และไม่มีการรักษาเฉพาะ สิ่งสำคัญคือการตรวจร่างกายอย่างละเอียดเมื่อมีอาการไม่ชัดเจน

name: Progressive ataxia palatal tremor (PAPT)
formal: Sporadic or genetic progressive cerebellar ataxia with palatal tremor, without olivary hypertrophy, sometimes in Alexander disease or POLG.
simple: A slowly worsening balance disorder together with rhythmic palate movements.
th: กลุ่มอาการเดินเซแบบ cerebellar ที่ค่อย ๆ แย่ลงร่วมกับ palatal tremor อาจเป็น sporadic หรือพันธุกรรม เช่น Alexander disease หรือ POLG
tempoNote: Gradual progression over years, usually adult onset
feat: Progressive gait and limb ataxia with dysarthria
Rhythmic palatal movements (about 1–3 Hz) without ear click, often unnoticed by the patient
May have pendular or oculopalatal nystagmus
Familial forms: adult Alexander disease (GFAP), POLG; sporadic forms often idiopathic
Pyramidal signs and bulbar dysfunction in some
inv: MRI: hypertrophic olivary degeneration (T2 bright, enlarged inferior olives) with cerebellar atrophy; medulla/cord atrophy in Alexander disease
GFAP and POLG testing; consider coeliac serology, SCA panel
Video and EMG of palatal movements

case.story: Four years of worsening unsteadiness and slurred speech; his wife noticed rhythmic movements at the back of his throat when he opens his mouth.
case.exam: Gait ataxia, scanning speech, 2 Hz soft palate elevation, pendular nystagmus, brisk reflexes.
case.tests: MRI shows bilateral olivary T2 hyperintensity and enlargement, cerebellar atrophy, and thinning of medulla and upper cord; GFAP variant found.
case.q: What is the syndrome and the underlying genetic disease?
case.a: Progressive ataxia with palatal tremor due to adult-onset Alexander disease.

det.patho: Damage to the Guillain–Mollaret triangle (dentate nucleus, red nucleus, inferior olive) causes olivary hypertrophy and rhythmic olivary firing, driving palatal and sometimes eye movements. In PAPT the damage is degenerative rather than a single lesion. Causes include adult Alexander disease, POLG mitochondrial disease, some SCAs and gluten-related ataxia; many sporadic cases have tau pathology.
det.clinical: Patients present with progressive ataxia; the palatal tremor is often asymptomatic and found only on inspection. Oculopalatal tremor with oscillopsia may occur. In Alexander disease there may be bulbar signs, dysautonomia and spasticity. Course is slow, over many years.
det.diagnosis: Look at the palate in every patient with ataxia. MRI shows bilateral olivary hyperintensity and enlargement plus cerebellar atrophy. Then pursue genetic testing (GFAP, POLG, SCA panel) and treatable causes such as coeliac disease.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy. Physiotherapy, speech therapy and fall prevention are central. Oscillopsia from pendular nystagmus may respond to gabapentin or memantine. Palatal tremor itself rarely needs treatment.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive disability over a decade or more; depends on cause.
pearls: Inspect the palate in progressive ataxia.
No ear click distinguishes symptomatic/PAPT from essential palatal tremor.
Medulla and cervical cord atrophy (tadpole sign) points to adult Alexander disease.
det.thd: PAPT คือภาวะเดินเซจาก cerebellum ที่ค่อย ๆ แย่ลง ร่วมกับเพดานอ่อนกระตุกเป็นจังหวะ ซึ่งผู้ป่วยมักไม่รู้ตัว MRI พบ inferior olive โตและสว่างใน T2 สาเหตุมี sporadic, adult Alexander disease (GFAP) และ POLG ยังไม่มีการรักษาเฉพาะ เน้นกายภาพและป้องกันการล้ม

ddx.pt: Ear click, no ataxia, normal MRI; often functional
Follows a single brainstem lesion (stroke, trauma) in the dentato-rubro-olivary pathway
Ataxia with prominent dysautonomia and parkinsonism; hot cross bun sign

name: Progressive ataxias
formal: Chronic cerebellar ataxias such as spinocerebellar ataxias, Friedreich ataxia, MSA-C and acquired causes with gradually worsening gait and coordination.
simple: Illnesses that cause increasing unsteadiness and clumsiness over time.
th: กลุ่มโรคที่ทรงตัวและประสานงานแย่ลงเรื่อย ๆ จากสมองน้อยหรือทางนำเข้าสมองน้อย ทั้งแบบพันธุกรรม (SCA, Friedreich, RFC1) แบบเสื่อมไม่ทราบสาเหตุ (MSA-C) และแบบที่หาสาเหตุได้ เช่น แอลกอฮอล์ ยา ภูมิคุ้มกัน
tempoNote: Months to years; subacute progression over weeks should prompt a search for paraneoplastic, immune, infective or nutritional causes
feat: Wide-based gait with veering, difficulty with tandem walking, and clumsy limbs with dysmetria
Scanning or slurred speech and gaze-evoked nystagmus or saccadic intrusions
Age of onset and tempo guide the cause: childhood onset favours recessive disorders, midlife onset dominant SCAs, and later onset MSA-C or acquired causes
Associated features give clues: neuropathy and areflexia (Friedreich, RFC1), dysautonomia and REM sleep behaviour disorder (MSA-C), retinal or cardiac signs
Recessive or sporadic forms often have no relatives affected, so an empty family tree cannot rule out a genetic cause
inv: MRI brain showing vermian or hemispheric atrophy, brainstem changes or the hot cross bun sign
Screen for treatable causes: vitamin B1, B12 and E, thyroid, coeliac and anti-GAD antibodies, paraneoplastic panel, drug levels and alcohol history
Genetic testing guided by pattern (repeat expansion panel for SCAs, FXN, RFC1) and autonomic testing when MSA-C is suspected

case.who: 58-year-old retired bus conductor from Udon Thani
case.story: Three years of unsteady walking, slurred speech and falls. Over the last year he has had dizziness on standing, difficulty passing urine and a habit of shouting and flailing his arms in his sleep, as his wife reports.
case.exam: Gait ataxia, mild limb dysmetria, gaze-evoked nystagmus, brisk reflexes and blood pressure dropping 40 mmHg systolic on standing.
case.tests: MRI shows pontine and cerebellar atrophy with a cross-shaped pontine signal; autonomic reflex testing is abnormal; paraneoplastic and genetic panels are negative.
case.q: Which acquired or degenerative disorder fits, and which findings make a hereditary ataxia less likely?
case.a: Cerebellar-type multiple system atrophy; onset after 30, autonomic failure and REM sleep behaviour disorder with negative family history and genetics point away from SCA.

read.where: Chapter 73: Cerebellar Disorders and Ataxias: Acquired Disorders
Chapter 24 Cerebellar Ataxias and Related Conditions

det.patho: Progressive ataxia results from dysfunction or loss of Purkinje cells and their connections in the cerebellum, spinocerebellar tracts, dorsal columns or peripheral sensory neurons. Genetic forms arise from repeat expansions such as the polyglutamine SCAs, GAA expansion in FXN or the biallelic RFC1 expansion, while acquired forms include toxic, nutritional, immune-mediated and structural causes. Tempo and age of onset are the best clues to category.
det.clinical: Patients first notice imbalance on uneven ground, a broad-based gait and slurred speech, later accompanied by limb incoordination, eye movement abnormalities and loss of independence. Subacute progression over weeks suggests paraneoplastic degeneration, gluten or anti-GAD ataxia, thiamine deficiency or infection rather than a genetic cause. Chronic sporadic forms in older adults raise cerebellar multiple system atrophy, alcohol-related degeneration or a craniovertebral lesion. Combination syndromes, such as cerebellar ataxia with vestibular areflexia and sensory neuronopathy (CANVAS), are now linked to RFC1.
det.diagnosis: Take a careful family, drug, alcohol and nutritional history, then do MRI to exclude structural causes and to see the pattern of atrophy. Order a screening panel for reversible causes and add genetic testing in patients with a family history, early onset or associated neuropathy. For late-onset sporadic ataxia with autonomic features, autonomic testing, polysomnography and the MRI hot cross bun sign support multiple system atrophy. Clinicians should ask about limb flailing or shouting in sleep to uncover REM sleep behaviour disorder.
det.treatment: Treat any identified cause: stop offending drugs such as phenytoin excess, replace thiamine or vitamin deficiencies, give immunotherapy for immune-mediated ataxias and treat the underlying tumour in paraneoplastic cases. For genetic and degenerative forms, care is mainly supportive with intensive physiotherapy, balance training, speech and swallowing therapy and fall prevention. Omaveloxolone is now approved for Friedreich ataxia, and management of orthostatic hypotension, bladder dysfunction and sleep-related stridor matters in MSA.
det.prognosis: Ranges from slow progression over decades in many SCAs to survival of roughly a decade from onset in MSA.
pearls: Subacute ataxia is a red flag for treatable paraneoplastic, immune, infective or nutritional causes.
Late-onset sporadic ataxia with dysautonomia or RBD is MSA-C until proved otherwise.
A normal-looking MRI does not exclude early genetic ataxia, and repeat-expansion tests are not part of ordinary exome sequencing.
det.thd: Progressive ataxia คือภาวะเดินเซและประสานงานแย่ลงเรื่อย ๆ จากสมองน้อยหรือทางนำเข้า ต้องดูอายุที่เริ่มเป็น ความเร็วของโรค ประวัติครอบครัว ยา แอลกอฮอล์ และอาการร่วม เช่น เส้นประสาทเสื่อมหรือความดันตกเมื่อลุกยืน ส่งตรวจ MRI หาสาเหตุที่รักษาได้ เช่น ขาดวิตามิน ภูมิคุ้มกัน หรือมะเร็ง แล้วจึงตรวจพันธุกรรม การรักษาหลักเป็นการแก้สาเหตุและกายภาพบำบัด ส่วนรูปแบบเสื่อมยังไม่มียาหยุดโรคยกเว้นบางชนิด เช่น Friedreich

name: Progressive bulbar palsy (PBP)
formal: Motor neuron disease variant with lower motor neuron bulbar onset causing dysarthria, dysphagia and tongue wasting with fasciculation.
simple: A form of motor neuron disease starting with speech and swallowing difficulty.
th: MND ชนิดเริ่มที่ก้านสมอง ทำให้พูดไม่ชัด กลืนลำบาก ลิ้นลีบและเต้นระริก ส่วนใหญ่ลุกลามไปแขนขาเป็น ALS
tempoNote: Progresses over months; most cases spread to the limbs within 1–2 years
feat: Nasal or slurred speech, choking on liquids, drooling
Wasted fasciculating tongue, weak palate and depressed gag
Mixed pseudobulbar signs (brisk jaw jerk, emotional lability) common
More frequent in older women
Aspiration, weight loss and early respiratory failure
inv: EMG of tongue, facial, cervical and thoracic paraspinal muscles
AChR and MuSK antibodies; repetitive nerve stimulation
MRI brain and skull base; videofluoroscopic swallow study

case.story: Four months of slurred speech and coughing when drinking water; lost 5 kg.
case.exam: Wasted tongue with fasciculations, weak palatal elevation, brisk jaw jerk, normal limb strength, no ptosis or fatigability.
case.tests: AChR and MuSK negative; EMG denervation in tongue and early changes in thoracic paraspinals; MRI brain normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what should be arranged early?
case.a: Progressive bulbar palsy (bulbar-onset MND); early speech/swallow assessment, gastrostomy and NIV planning.

det.patho: PBP reflects degeneration of motor nuclei in the medulla and pons (IX–XII and motor VII), usually as the presenting phase of ALS. The pathology is TDP-43 proteinopathy as in other sporadic ALS. Why some patients begin in bulbar regions is unknown.
det.clinical: Speech becomes slurred and nasal, swallowing of liquids is disrupted, and saliva pools. Tongue wasting and fasciculation reflect LMN loss, while a brisk jaw jerk and emotional lability indicate UMN involvement. Weight loss and aspiration pneumonia are frequent. Limb involvement usually appears within months to a couple of years.
det.diagnosis: EMG of bulbar and limb muscles shows denervation and may reveal spread before it is clinically obvious. Myasthenia must be excluded with antibodies and neurophysiology. MRI excludes brainstem or skull-base lesions. Kennedy disease testing is reasonable in men.
det.treatment: Management follows ALS care, including riluzole. Speech therapy, communication aids and voice banking should begin early. Gastrostomy is advisable before FVC falls below about 50% or when weight drops. Anticholinergics or botulinum toxin to salivary glands control drooling; NIV may be less tolerated with severe bulbar weakness.
det.prognosis: Worse than limb-onset ALS, with median survival around 2 years.
pearls: Wasted fasciculating tongue rules against myasthenia.
Bulbar ALS is commoner in older women.
Offer voice banking right after the diagnosis is made.
det.thd: Progressive bulbar palsy เป็น MND ที่เริ่มจากก้านสมอง ทำให้พูดไม่ชัด กลืนลำบาก น้ำลายไหล ลิ้นลีบและเต้นระริก ส่วนใหญ่จะลุกลามเป็น ALS เต็มรูปแบบ ต้องแยก myasthenia gravis และ Kennedy disease ด้วยการตรวจแอนติบอดีและ EMG การดูแลเน้นฝึกกลืน ใส่สายอาหาร PEG แต่เนิ่นๆ และวางแผนช่วยหายใจ พยากรณ์โรคแย่กว่า ALS ที่เริ่มจากแขนขา

name: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM)
formal: Brainstem and spinal inflammatory disease with stiffness, spasms, myoclonus and hyperekplexia, associated with glycine receptor antibodies; stiff-person spectrum.
simple: A rare immune illness causing muscle stiffness, spasms and brainstem problems.
more: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM), a stiff-person-spectrum disorder often linked to glycine receptor or GAD antibodies, causing spasms, brainstem signs and autonomic instability. Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus: brainstem and spinal inflammatory disease with stiffness, spasms, myoclonus and hyperekplexia, linked to glycine receptor antibodies. Check glycine receptor antibodies, and CSF pleocytosis; MRI often normal. Treat with high-dose steroids, IVIG or plasmapheresis, and symptomatic benzodiazepines or baclofen; screen for tumours, and outcome is variable, with some fatal.
th: PERM คือโรคอักเสบของก้านสมองและไขสันหลังแบบกึ่งเฉียบพลัน ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อแข็งเกร็ง ปวดเกร็งเมื่อถูกสัมผัสหรือตกใจ myoclonus สะดุ้งง่าย และอาการก้านสมองหรือระบบอัตโนมัติ ถือเป็นกลุ่ม stiff-person ชนิดรุนแรง มักพบแอนติบอดีต่อ glycine receptor และต้องรักษาด้วยยากดภูมิคุ้มกันโดยเร็ว
tempoNote: Builds across several weeks, sometimes months, with relapses; untreated, it can reach respiratory and autonomic failure
feat: Rigidity of trunk and proximal limbs, often beginning in one leg, with painful spasms provoked by touch, noise or emotion
Stimulus-sensitive myoclonus and exaggerated startle; the subacute, fluctuating course separates it from classic stiff-person syndrome
Brainstem features: eye movement disorders, nystagmus, ataxia, dysarthria, dysphagia and trismus; sensory symptoms, segmental wasting or areflexia in some
Autonomic crises with sweating, tachycardia, blood pressure swings, fever and sudden respiratory failure
Tumour association in a minority (thymoma, lymphoma, breast and lung cancer); a woman with stiff arms deserves a breast tumour search
inv: Serum and CSF antibodies to glycine receptor, GAD65, amphiphysin and DPPX; CSF often shows lymphocytes or oligoclonal bands
EMG with persistent firing of opposing muscle pairs at rest and exaggerated cutaneomuscular or startle reflexes
MRI brain and spine (usually normal or non-specific) to exclude structural myelopathy or brainstem disease
CT or PET of chest, abdomen and pelvis, with breast imaging, for an underlying tumour

case.story: Over six weeks his back and legs became stiff, with sudden painful jerks when touched or startled, then double vision and difficulty swallowing.
case.exam: Board-like abdominal wall and paraspinal muscles, stimulus-sensitive myoclonus, gaze-evoked nystagmus, sweating and a pulse of 118.
case.tests: CSF 18 lymphocytes/µL with oligoclonal bands; glycine receptor antibody is positive in serum and CSF; CT chest shows an anterior mediastinal mass.
case.q: How does this differ from classic stiff-person syndrome, and what is the treatment plan?
case.a: PERM adds brainstem, autonomic and myoclonic signs with an inflammatory CSF. Give high-dose methylprednisolone with IVIG or plasma exchange, benzodiazepines or baclofen for the spasms, monitor in a high-dependency unit, and resect the thymoma.

read.where: 13. Acute Spinal Rigidity — Progressive Encephalomyelitis With Rigidity and Myoclonus
18 - Myoclonus: Phenomenology, etiology, physiology, and treatment

det.patho: The condition is an inflammatory disease of grey matter in the brainstem and spinal cord, with perivascular infiltrates and loss of inhibitory interneurons. Antibodies to the glycine receptor alpha-1 subunit, identified after the book was written, are now found in many patients and impair glycinergic inhibition of motor neurons and brainstem reflexes. Other patients carry GAD65, amphiphysin or DPPX antibodies or a paraneoplastic tumour. The loss of interneuronal inhibition explains the continuous muscle activity, startle and spasms.
det.clinical: Rigidity may begin in one leg, as in the stiff-leg syndrome, and then spread to the trunk and the other limbs. Painful spasms, myoclonus and hyperekplexia accompany it. Brainstem dysfunction with diplopia, ataxia, bulbar weakness and trismus, together with sensory symptoms or segmental weakness, distinguishes it from stiff-person syndrome. The course over weeks, with relapses, is more aggressive. Autonomic crises and sudden central or obstructive respiratory failure account for most deaths.
det.diagnosis: Suspect PERM when stiff-person features come with brainstem signs or a subacute fluctuating course. Test serum and CSF for glycine receptor antibodies and for GAD65, amphiphysin and DPPX, perform EMG and image the brain and spine. CSF pleocytosis supports the inflammatory form. Because cancer is associated, a systematic tumour search is mandatory. Exclude tetanus, strychnine poisoning, structural cord disease, serotonin syndrome and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
det.treatment: Start immunotherapy early: intravenous methylprednisolone, then IVIG (total 2 g/kg, spread over several days) or plasma exchange, with rituximab or other agents for relapse or poor response. Benzodiazepines (clonazepam, diazepam) and baclofen relieve spasms, and intrathecal baclofen must never be stopped abruptly. Patients with bulbar or autonomic involvement need high-dependency monitoring because respiratory arrest can be sudden. Remove any thymoma or tumour.
det.prognosis: Mortality was high in older series, mainly from respiratory failure and autonomic crises, but early immunotherapy has improved outcomes, and many patients recover substantially. Relapses and residual stiffness are common.
pearls: Stiff-person signs plus brainstem signs or a subacute course equal PERM until proved otherwise.
Test glycine receptor antibodies, not only GAD65.
Never stop baclofen suddenly, and treat the spasms and autonomic crisis in a monitored bed.

Tetanus follows a wound and has normal CSF, and baclofen alone does not alter the immune disease.

18 - Myoclonus: Phenomenology, etiology, physiology, and treatment

det.patho: This umbrella covers neurodegenerative and metabolic disorders in which seizures are an important early feature. Many are inherited lysosomal, mitochondrial or protein-clearance disorders that damage cortical and cerebellar neurons; examples include Unverricht–Lundborg disease, Lafora disease, neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses, MERRF, sialidosis, neuronopathic Gaucher and DRPLA. Cortical hyperexcitability produces myoclonus, and neuronal loss produces dementia and ataxia.
det.clinical: Typical patients are previously normal children or adolescents whose seizures and myoclonus gradually worsen, followed by ataxia and cognitive decline. Visual failure, deafness, hearing loss, neuropathy, short stature or organ involvement provide diagnostic clues. The pace varies from rapid (Lafora, infantile NCL) to slow over decades (Unverricht–Lundborg). Early cases are easily mislabelled as juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.
det.diagnosis: Red flags are drug resistance, worsening myoclonus, new ataxia, cognitive decline or abnormal examination in what seemed a generalised epilepsy. EEG shows background slowing; MRI may show atrophy. Next-generation sequencing panels or exome now give most diagnoses, supplemented by enzymes, biopsy for inclusions, ophthalmology and lactate studies. Identify the cause because it guides prognosis, counselling and specific therapy (e.g. cerliponase alfa for CLN2).
det.treatment: Seizure and myoclonus control relies on valproate, levetiracetam, clonazepam, zonisamide, perampanel and brivaracetam; piracetam may help myoclonus. Avoid sodium-channel blockers and GABA-analogue drugs that aggravate myoclonus. Disease-specific options are limited: intraventricular cerliponase alfa for CLN2 disease, while other enzyme or gene therapies remain experimental. Multidisciplinary rehabilitation and palliative care are central.
det.prognosis: Generally poor and cause-dependent, ranging from death within a decade (Lafora) to survival into late adulthood with disability (Unverricht–Lundborg).
pearls: Generalised epilepsy that gets worse with myoclonus and falling grades: think PME, not refractory JME.
Phenytoin can accelerate deterioration in Unverricht–Lundborg disease.
Look in the eyes: visual loss or cherry-red spot narrows the differential quickly.
det.thd: Progressive epilepsies คือกลุ่มโรคลมชักที่มีการเสื่อมของสมองร่วมด้วย ส่วนใหญ่เป็นโรคพันธุกรรม เช่น Unverricht–Lundborg, Lafora, NCL และ MERRF เด็กหรือวัยรุ่นมีชักและกระตุก myoclonus ที่แย่ลงเรื่อย ๆ ร่วมกับเดินเซและความจำถดถอย วินิจฉัยด้วย EEG MRI ตรวจตาและตรวจยีน รักษาด้วย valproate levetiracetam clonazepam และหลีกเลี่ยง phenytoin หรือ carbamazepine

det.patho: CLN8 encodes an endoplasmic-reticulum membrane protein that helps traffic lysosomal enzymes; biallelic variants lead to lysosomal storage of autofluorescent lipopigment in neurons. In Finland a single founder variant causes the classic Northern epilepsy phenotype, while other CLN8 variants cause a more severe late-infantile NCL. The basis of the selective seizure-first phenotype is not well understood.
det.clinical: Children develop normally until seizures appear between ages 5 and 10; seizures are often frequent around puberty and then decline in adulthood. Cognitive decline becomes evident a few years after onset and continues gradually, leading to moderate to severe intellectual disability by adulthood. Behavioural disturbance, motor slowing and balance problems appear later. Visual failure is absent or minimal in the classic form.
det.diagnosis: Consider EPMR in a child with new epilepsy followed by cognitive decline, especially with Finnish ancestry or affected siblings. Confirm by CLN8 gene testing, which is usually included in NCL and epilepsy panels. EEG slowing and later brain atrophy are supportive. Exclude CLN3 and other NCLs by ophthalmic assessment and genetics.
det.treatment: There is no disease-specific therapy. Seizures are managed with broad-spectrum antiseizure drugs such as valproate, clonazepam and levetiracetam; avoid drugs that aggravate myoclonus. Provide special education, behavioural support and rehabilitation, and offer genetic counselling to the family.
det.prognosis: Survival into middle or later adulthood is usual, with progressive intellectual disability and motor decline.
pearls: Northern epilepsy: seizures first, sight preserved, intellect declines slowly.
Seizure frequency often falls after puberty even though cognition keeps declining.
Different CLN8 variants can give a much more severe late-infantile NCL picture.

det.patho: The cause is unknown; most evidence points to a localised autoimmune or inflammatory process overlapping with linear morphoea, with possible contributions from sympathetic dysfunction or trauma. Biopsies show inflammation and fibrosis of skin and fat, and brain lesions on the same side suggest an inflammatory or vasculopathic process extending intracranially.
det.clinical: It mostly begins in the first two decades with painless shrinking of one side of the face, typically in a trigeminal territory, progressing over years before stabilising. Eye problems (enophthalmos, uveitis), dental and jaw changes and hair loss may accompany it. Neurologically, focal epilepsy, headache, trigeminal neuralgia and occasionally focal deficits occur; brain MRI may be abnormal even without symptoms. This entry describes a systemic/dermatological disease with neurological involvement rather than a primary neurological disorder.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical, based on progressive unilateral facial atrophy, supported by dermatological evaluation. MRI brain is recommended in all patients to look for ipsilateral lesions; EEG if seizures. Exclude other causes of facial asymmetry such as lipodystrophy, trauma, facial nerve palsy and hemifacial microsomia.
det.treatment: During active disease methotrexate with or without corticosteroids is commonly used, with mycophenolate as an alternative. Seizures are treated with standard antiseizure drugs, and refractory epilepsy may need specialist evaluation. Once the disease is inactive, reconstructive procedures such as fat grafting or flaps restore contour.
det.prognosis: The disease usually burns out within a decade; cosmetic deficit remains, and epilepsy may persist in those with brain involvement.
pearls: Child with a slowly sinking cheek and new focal seizures: image the brain on the same side.
Parry–Romberg and linear scleroderma en coup de sabre lie on one spectrum.
Delay reconstruction until the atrophy is no longer active.

det.patho: Deterioration after ischaemic stroke has several mechanisms: extension of an occlusive thrombus, failure of collateral flow, recurrent embolism, or progressive occlusion of a deep perforator at its origin by parent-artery plaque. Branch atheromatous disease explains many small subcortical infarcts that enlarge over days. Secondary contributors such as hyperglycaemia, fever, dehydration and blood pressure dips push the penumbra into infarction.
det.clinical: Roughly a quarter of ischaemic strokes worsen early, and lacunar or pontine strokes are over-represented. The capsular warning syndrome describes repeated short bursts of pure motor or sensorimotor weakness that may end in a fixed capsular infarct. Patients with large-vessel occlusion may decline as collaterals fail, especially when sitting upright or after antihypertensives. Worsening must be documented with a structured scale so that true decline is not missed or overcalled.
det.diagnosis: Any measurable deterioration warrants immediate reassessment: repeat imaging for haemorrhage, oedema or infarct growth and vascular imaging for occlusion. Check glucose, sodium, temperature, oxygenation and blood pressure, and look for seizure or infection. MRI showing a comma-shaped deep infarct reaching the ventricle surface or a pontine infarct touching the basal surface suggests branch disease.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: thrombectomy for new or persisting large-vessel occlusion, dual antiplatelet therapy for minor stroke or branch disease, and careful permissive blood pressure with fluids and flat positioning when perfusion is marginal. Correct glucose, fever and dehydration. Tirofiban and argatroban have been tried for progressive lacunar stroke in Asian trials, but evidence remains limited and practice varies. Early mobilisation should be cautious while the deficit is unstable.
det.prognosis: Early worsening is linked to worse functional outcome and more disability at three months, although many branch-disease patients still regain walking.
pearls: Before calling it stroke progression, rule out bleeding, swelling, seizure and hypoglycaemia.
Stuttering pure motor episodes are a warning that a capsular or pontine infarct is coming.
Over-aggressive blood pressure lowering is a preventable cause of early deterioration.

det.patho: JC polyomavirus is acquired in childhood by most people and lies latent in the kidney and lymphoid tissue. With loss of T-cell control, rearranged neurotropic variants infect oligodendrocytes and astrocytes, causing lytic demyelination. Risk is highest with advanced HIV (CD4 usually under 200), natalizumab (higher with JCV antibody positivity, longer exposure and prior immunosuppressants), and with rituximab, transplant or haematological cancer.
det.clinical: Presentation is subacute and focal: weakness, visual field defects, language disturbance, behavioural change or ataxia, progressing steadily. Raised intracranial pressure, fever and headache are unusual, which helps distinguish it from abscess and lymphoma. When immunity recovers (ART or stopping natalizumab), inflammatory PML-IRIS may cause swelling, enhancement and abrupt worsening.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis combines a compatible clinical course, typical MRI and JCV DNA in CSF; brain biopsy is reserved for PCR-negative cases. MRI lesions are asymmetric, involve subcortical U-fibres, are dark on T1, bright on T2 and usually do not enhance; small punctate satellite lesions may be seen, especially with natalizumab. CSF cell count and protein are usually near normal.
det.treatment: There is no proven antiviral. The aim is immune reconstitution: start ART promptly in HIV, stop natalizumab (with plasma exchange to speed clearance in selected cases), and reduce immunosuppression where possible. Corticosteroids are used for IRIS with mass effect or rapid decline. Immune checkpoint inhibitors and virus-specific T cells are under study.
det.prognosis: One-year survival in HIV-related PML on ART is around 50–60%; natalizumab-PML has better survival but usually leaves disability.
pearls: Focal, non-enhancing white-matter disease without mass effect in an immunosuppressed patient = PML until proven otherwise.
U-fibre involvement helps separate PML from HIV leukoencephalopathy.
Worsening after ART may be IRIS rather than treatment failure.

det.patho: PMA is a motor neuron disease that clinically involves only lower motor neurons. Autopsy and imaging studies show that many patients have subclinical corticospinal tract involvement and TDP-43 pathology identical to ALS, so PMA is now viewed as part of the ALS spectrum. It accounts for a small minority of adult-onset MND and is more common in men.
det.clinical: Asymmetric distal or proximal limb weakness with wasting, fasciculations and cramps spreads over months to years to other regions. Reflexes are reduced or absent and there are no UMN signs, at least initially. A proportion develop UMN signs within a few years and are reclassified as ALS. Bulbar and respiratory involvement occurs later in the course.
det.diagnosis: EMG shows active and chronic denervation in multiple regions with normal sensory studies and no conduction block. A careful search for treatable or distinct mimics is essential: MMN, Kennedy disease, adult SMA, hexosaminidase A deficiency, paraproteinaemic and lead neuropathy, and inclusion body myositis. Under the Gold Coast criteria, progressive LMN dysfunction in two regions can qualify as ALS.
det.treatment: Management follows ALS principles, including riluzole, multidisciplinary care, nutritional support, physiotherapy and planning for respiratory support. Patients should be offered clinical trial participation where available.
det.prognosis: Survival is often longer than in classic ALS, though it varies widely; early respiratory involvement predicts a poor outcome.
pearls: Keep re-examining for UMN signs — PMA often evolves into ALS.
Exclude MMN and Kennedy disease before labelling a pure LMN syndrome.

det.patho: The syndrome reflects combined dysfunction of cerebellar outflow (dentate and its connections) and cortical motor excitability, producing cortical action myoclonus and ataxia. Causes span mitochondrial disorders, lysosomal storage, spinocerebellar degenerations, coeliac disease and autoimmune processes; the historical label 'Ramsay Hunt syndrome' (dyssynergia cerebellaris myoclonica) now describes this phenotype rather than a single disease.
det.clinical: Patients develop progressively disabling myoclonus on action and cerebellar ataxia, with only occasional seizures and little cognitive decline. The myoclonus worsens with stress and fine motor tasks and may cause sudden falls. Over time, the line between PMA and PME can blur as seizures or cognitive problems emerge. Associated features such as deafness, neuropathy or myopathy point to the cause.
det.diagnosis: Confirm cortical myoclonus neurophysiologically where available (giant SEPs, back-averaged EEG). Search for treatable causes first: coeliac serology, vitamin E, thyroid, autoimmune antibodies, then lactate and genetic testing including mitochondrial DNA and CSTB. MRI often shows cerebellar atrophy.
det.treatment: Antimyoclonic treatment includes levetiracetam, valproate, clonazepam and piracetam, often combined; zonisamide and perampanel are options. Avoid phenytoin, carbamazepine and pregabalin. Treat the underlying cause where possible (gluten-free diet, immunotherapy for autoimmune forms). Physiotherapy and walking aids reduce falls.
det.prognosis: Variable by cause; many patients become dependent on aids over years, while acquired forms may stabilise with treatment.
pearls: Myoclonus + ataxia with few seizures and good cognition: PMA rather than PME.
Always test for coeliac disease; it is one of the few treatable causes.
Action myoclonus mimics ataxia; jerks interrupt movement rather than producing smooth dysmetria.

det.patho: Gluten-triggered immunity, including antibodies to transglutaminase 6 expressed in the brain, is thought to injure cerebellar Purkinje cells and cortical circuits. det.clinical: The syndrome resembles other progressive myoclonic ataxias: disabling action myoclonus, ataxia and sometimes seizures, with relatively preserved cognition. Bowel symptoms may be minimal. It is much rarer than gluten ataxia without myoclonus. Clinicians must also watch for lymphoma.
det.diagnosis: Coeliac serology and duodenal biopsy confirm coeliac disease. Neurophysiology (giant SEPs, C-reflex, jerk-locked back-averaging) shows cortical myoclonus. Exclude other progressive myoclonic ataxia causes such as mitochondrial disease, EPM1 and sialidosis.
det.treatment: A strict gluten-free diet is the base but responses of myoclonus are often incomplete. Levetiracetam, piracetam, clonazepam and valproate help myoclonus. Immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG, mycophenolate) may be tried in refractory cases.
det.prognosis: Often progressive despite diet; disability can be severe.

more: Group of genetic disorders (Unverricht-Lundborg, Lafora, MERRF, NCLs, sialidosis) combining myoclonus, generalized seizures and progressive neurological decline, often with ataxia and dementia. det.patho: PMEs form an uncommon family of largely recessively inherited conditions in which neuronal degeneration produces cortical myoclonus, epilepsy and decline. Unverricht–Lundborg disease (EPM1) usually results from an expanded dodecamer repeat in the promoter of CSTB, reducing cystatin B, a protease inhibitor. Lafora disease results from EPM2A (laforin) or NHLRC1 (malin) variants, which lead to poorly branched glycogen accumulating as Lafora bodies in neurons, liver, muscle and sweat glands. Other causes include neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses, MERRF, sialidosis, action myoclonus–renal failure and some dentatorubral–pallidoluysian cases.
det.clinical: Unverricht–Lundborg begins at about 6–15 years with stimulus-sensitive myoclonus and morning convulsions; myoclonus becomes disabling over years, but intellect is relatively spared and survival often extends into later adulthood. Lafora disease begins in adolescence with visual occipital seizures, myoclonus and convulsions, then rapid cognitive and behavioural decline, leading to a vegetative state within about ten years. The early stage can look exactly like juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, so decline, ataxia or poor drug response are the clues.
det.diagnosis: Suspect PME when generalised epilepsy with myoclonus is accompanied by progressive neurological signs, a slowing EEG background or failure of standard drugs. Genetic testing is the main tool; note that the common CSTB repeat expansion is missed by standard exome sequencing and needs a specific assay. Skin biopsy for Lafora bodies, muscle biopsy for MERRF, fundoscopy for cherry-red spot or retinopathy, and enzyme or neuropathology studies help with other causes.
det.treatment: Treatment is symptomatic: valproate, levetiracetam, clonazepam, piracetam, brivaracetam, perampanel, topiramate and zonisamide may reduce myoclonus and seizures. Phenytoin worsens Unverricht–Lundborg disease and should be avoided, as should carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, gabapentin and pregabalin in myoclonic states. Supportive care includes physiotherapy, mobility aids, nutrition and genetic counselling; disease-modifying therapies for Lafora (e.g. glycogen-targeting approaches) are in research.
det.prognosis: Unverricht–Lundborg disease is slowly progressive with variable disability but often normal or near-normal lifespan; Lafora disease is relentlessly fatal, usually within about a decade.
pearls: JME that keeps worsening, with decline or ataxia, is a PME until proven otherwise.
Avoid phenytoin in Unverricht–Lundborg — it accelerates deterioration.
Exome can miss the CSTB repeat; order a specific test.
Visual seizures plus myoclonus and dementia in a teen: think Lafora and do an axillary skin biopsy.

det.patho: Progressive myoclonus arises when degeneration or metabolic disease disinhibits sensorimotor cortex or, less often, brainstem reticular circuits. Underlying processes include lysosomal storage, mitochondrial dysfunction, polyglucosan accumulation, protease inhibitor defects (cystatin B) and prion disease.
det.clinical: The entry describes a syndrome rather than a single disease. Clinically, separate progressive myoclonic epilepsy (myoclonus, seizures, cognitive decline) from progressive myoclonic ataxia (myoclonus and ataxia, few seizures, preserved cognition). Age at onset, ethnicity, visual and hearing involvement and family history narrow the list.
det.diagnosis: First confirm myoclonus and its generator with neurophysiology. Then search for the cause with MRI, metabolic tests, ophthalmic examination, genetic panels and sometimes biopsy. Exclude acquired treatable causes such as coeliac disease, drugs, uraemia and autoimmune disease.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying disease where possible. For cortical myoclonus use levetiracetam, valproate, clonazepam, piracetam or brivaracetam; avoid phenytoin, carbamazepine and gabapentin, which can worsen it. Perampanel helps some PMEs.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause, from slowly progressive (EPM1) to fatal within a decade (Lafora).
pearls: Sodium-channel antiseizure drugs can worsen progressive myoclonus.
Seizures and dementia suggest PME; ataxia with preserved cognition suggests PMA.
Look at the fundus: cherry-red spot or retinopathy narrows the cause.

det.patho: PME and PMA are phenotypes, not single diseases. They share cortical hyperexcitability with cerebellar degeneration, caused by genetic disorders of lysosomes, glycogen metabolism, mitochondria or protein turnover. PME implies enough cortical involvement to produce frequent seizures and cognitive decline, whereas PMA reflects predominantly cerebellar and sensorimotor involvement.
det.clinical: Patients show worsening myoclonus with action, sensory and visual stimuli, generalised seizures of variable frequency and progressive ataxia. In PME, cognition and behaviour decline; in PMA they remain largely intact. Individual diseases have signature clues: occipital seizures in Lafora disease, visual loss in NCL, cherry-red spot in sialidosis, hearing loss and myopathy in MERRF, and renal failure in AMRF.
det.diagnosis: Clinical and neurophysiological confirmation of cortical myoclonus is followed by a structured search for the cause with genetic testing first, supported by enzyme, lactate and biopsy studies. Note the phenotype may shift from PMA to PME as disease advances. Consider acquired causes such as coeliac disease in adults.
det.treatment: Combine broad-spectrum antiseizure medicines (valproate, levetiracetam, clonazepam, zonisamide, perampanel) with piracetam for myoclonus, and avoid myoclonus-aggravating drugs. Disease-specific approaches are limited (e.g. cerliponase alfa for CLN2). Rehabilitation, fall prevention, nutrition and psychosocial support are important.
det.prognosis: Depends on the cause, from slowly progressive with long survival to rapidly fatal.
pearls: PME vs PMA is a matter of seizures and cognition; the cause list overlaps.
Myoclonus often responds better to drug combinations than to monotherapy.
Avoid sodium-channel blockers and gabapentinoids.

det.patho: Neurodegeneration focuses on the left inferior frontal gyrus, insula and supplementary motor area. Pathology is usually 4-repeat tau (CBD, PSP), less often TDP-43 or Alzheimer disease. Mutations in GRN or MAPT occur in familial cases.
det.clinical: Speech is slow, effortful and error-prone, with apraxia of speech and grammatical simplification. Some patients have pure apraxia of speech first (primary progressive apraxia of speech). Over years, parkinsonism, limb apraxia, swallowing problems and executive dysfunction appear, often evolving into PSP or CBS.
det.diagnosis: Consensus criteria require agrammatism or apraxia of speech plus supportive features. Language testing and MRI pattern support the diagnosis; amyloid markers help rule out Alzheimer disease. Stroke and tumour must be excluded.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy. Speech therapy, augmentative communication devices and swallowing assessment are key. Cholinesterase inhibitors are not helpful in tau-related cases. Monitor for falls and dysphagia as motor signs emerge.
det.prognosis: Progressive decline over 8–10 years; mutism eventually develops in many.
pearls: Apraxia of speech plus agrammatism = nonfluent PPA.
Watch for evolution to PSP or CBS.
Single-word comprehension is preserved, unlike semantic dementia.

det.patho: Pathology, when available, shows a classic chronic demyelinating plaque, and the clinical course mirrors progressive MS. The lesion probably sits on a critical motor pathway where a single plaque is enough to drive progression. It is considered part of the MS spectrum rather than a separate disease, but evidence comes from small case series.
det.clinical: Patients are usually middle-aged and present with years of slowly worsening weakness on one side or in one limb. A minority later develop additional lesions and then fulfil MS criteria. Over time, disability progression resembles primary progressive MS.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires a single demyelinating lesion with progressive motor impairment for at least a year and exclusion of other causes. MS criteria for dissemination in space are not met. Exclusion of tumour (including glioma), sarcoidosis, vascular malformation, dural fistula, compression and infection is essential and may need repeated imaging or biopsy if the lesion grows or enhances atypically.
det.treatment: There is no specific trial evidence. Clinicians usually follow progressive MS management, sometimes using anti-CD20 therapy when there is evidence of activity, alongside spasticity treatment and rehabilitation. Patients should be monitored with serial MRI for new lesions.
det.prognosis: Usually slow progression of motor disability, similar to progressive MS; long-term data are limited.
pearls: A single lesion with relentless progression can still be demyelinating.
Lateral column cervical lesions and hemiparesis sparing the face are typical.
Re-image any atypical lesion that grows: tumour must be excluded.

det.patho: PSP is a four-repeat tauopathy in which tau aggregates as tufted astrocytes, neurofibrillary tangles and coiled bodies in the subthalamic nucleus, globus pallidus, midbrain and dentate nucleus. Loss of midbrain gaze centres (riMLF) explains the vertical saccade failure. It is mostly sporadic, with MAPT H1 haplotype as a risk factor, and onset is usually after 60.
det.clinical: The classic Richardson phenotype brings backward falls within the first year, slowed then restricted vertical saccades, axial rigidity with an extended neck, a staring wide-eyed face and frontal dysexecutive change with apathy. Speech becomes slurred and spastic, swallowing worsens and patients may rush to stand impulsively (rocket sign). Other phenotypes present predominantly with parkinsonism (PSP-P, can respond partly to levodopa early), progressive gait freezing, speech/language disorder or a corticobasal syndrome. Examiners like to ask about the applause sign, preserved doll's-eye responses and the square-wave jerks seen on fixation.
det.diagnosis: The 2017 MDS criteria combine four domains — ocular motor, postural instability, akinesia and cognitive dysfunction — at levels of certainty from suggestive to probable. Look carefully at the speed of vertical saccades before range becomes limited; slow downward saccades are an early and specific clue. MRI showing midbrain atrophy with relative pontine preservation (hummingbird or morning-glory appearance, low midbrain-to-pons ratio, raised MR parkinsonism index) supports the diagnosis. DAT SPECT is abnormal and does not separate PSP from PD. Exclude mimics such as Niemann–Pick type C, Whipple disease, vascular parkinsonism and normal pressure hydrocephalus.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying treatment exists; anti-tau antibodies have failed in trials. A levodopa trial (up to around 1 g/day) is reasonable, though benefit is small and brief. Management is multidisciplinary: physiotherapy and walking aids for falls, speech and swallow assessment with diet modification, prism glasses or reading aids, botulinum toxin for blepharospasm or apraxia of lid opening, and early advance care planning around feeding and aspiration.
det.prognosis: Median survival is roughly 6–8 years from onset, with aspiration pneumonia and fall-related injury the usual causes of death.
pearls: Ask 'Does he fall backwards?' — early backward falls in a new parkinsonian patient point to PSP, not PD.
Vertical saccades slow down before their range shrinks — test speed, not only range.
Preserved oculocephalic movements prove the gaze palsy is supranuclear.
det.thd: PSP เป็นโรคเสื่อมจากการสะสมโปรตีน tau ที่ midbrain และ basal ganglia ผู้ป่วยมักล้มไปข้างหลังตั้งแต่ปีแรก กลอกตาขึ้นลงช้าแล้วกลอกไม่ได้ คอและลำตัวแข็ง ร่วมกับปัญหาการคิดแบบ frontal การวินิจฉัยใช้เกณฑ์ MDS 2017 และ MRI ที่เห็น midbrain ฝ่อ (hummingbird sign) ยังไม่มียาชะลอโรค ลองให้ levodopa ได้แต่ผลน้อย เน้นป้องกันการล้ม ฝึกกลืน และวางแผนการดูแลระยะยาว

name: Progressive writer’s cramp
formal: Task-specific focal hand dystonia with gradually spreading cramping and posturing during writing, which may progress to involve other tasks or the other hand.
simple: Hand cramping and twisting when writing that slowly gets worse and may start to affect other tasks.
th: dystonia เฉพาะที่ของมือขณะเขียนหนังสือ ที่ค่อย ๆ ลามไปทำกิจกรรมอื่นหรือมืออีกข้าง
tempoNote: Begins task-specific and slowly worsens over years
feat: Cramping, flexion or extension of fingers and wrist only when writing at first
Gradual spread to other tasks (typing, eating, shaving) or to the other hand (mirror dystonia)
Tremor while writing; pen grip changes
No weakness or sensory loss; normal exam at rest
Adult onset, usually 30s–50s
inv: Clinical diagnosis; observe writing and other tasks
MRI and copper studies if young onset, rapid spread or other signs
EMG to map muscles for botulinum toxin

case.story: Five years ago his index finger lifted off the pen when writing; now his wrist flexes when using a mouse and spoon.
case.exam: Writing triggers wrist flexion and thumb extension; posturing appears in the left hand when the right writes; no other signs.
case.tests: MRI brain normal, ceruloplasmin normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the first-line treatment?
case.a: Progressive (complex) writer's cramp, a focal task-specific dystonia; EMG-guided botulinum toxin injections, plus writing aids and retraining.

det.patho: Task-specific dystonia reflects maladaptive plasticity and reduced inhibition in sensorimotor networks involving basal ganglia, cerebellum and cortex. Repetitive fine motor practice and genetic susceptibility both contribute. Progression means the abnormal motor programme becomes generalised to more tasks.
det.clinical: Simple writer's cramp affects writing alone; the progressive or 'complex' type spreads to other manual tasks and sometimes the opposite hand. Tremor may dominate. Cases with spread beyond the arm, early onset or other signs need investigation for secondary or combined dystonia.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical. Watch the patient write and perform other tasks; mirror movements help. Rule out parkinsonism, CBS, neuropathy and Wilson disease when indicated.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin targeted with EMG or ultrasound is most effective. Writing aids, larger pens, switching hands and sensorimotor retraining help. Oral trihexyphenidyl is modestly useful. Thalamic (Vo) lesioning or DBS is used in refractory cases in specialist centres.
det.prognosis: Usually remains confined to the upper limb; complete remission is uncommon.
pearls: Mirror dystonia in the other hand helps choose muscles to inject.
Spread beyond one arm should prompt a search for secondary causes.
Learning to write with the other hand can eventually trigger dystonia there too.
det.thd: Progressive writer's cramp คือ dystonia ของมือที่เกิดเฉพาะตอนเขียนหนังสือ แล้วค่อย ๆ ลามไปงานอื่น เช่น ใช้เมาส์ หรือมืออีกข้าง ตรวจร่างกายอื่นปกติ วินิจฉัยทางคลินิก รักษาด้วย botulinum toxin อุปกรณ์ช่วยเขียน และการฝึกใหม่

ddx.pt: Numbness and thenar weakness, not task-triggered posturing
Asymmetric limb dystonia with apraxia, rigidity and cortical sensory loss
Micrographia and slowness with rest tremor and rigidity; may begin with limb dystonia
