name: Prolactinoma
formal: Prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma causing amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, hypogonadism, and with macroadenomas headache and bitemporal hemianopia; treated first with dopamine agonists.
simple: A noncancerous pituitary gland tumour that makes too much prolactin hormone, causing hormone problems and sometimes headaches and vision loss.
th: Prolactinoma เป็นเนื้องอกต่อมใต้สมองที่หลั่ง prolactin พบบ่อยที่สุดในกลุ่มที่หลั่งฮอร์โมน ผู้หญิงมักมีประจำเดือนขาด น้ำนมไหล มีบุตรยาก ส่วนผู้ชายมักมาด้วยก้อนใหญ่ ตามัว ปวดศีรษะ และฮอร์โมนเพศต่ำ ต้องแยกสาเหตุอื่นของ prolactin สูง เช่น ยากลุ่ม dopamine antagonist การตั้งครรภ์ ไฮโปไทรอยด์ ไตวาย และ stalk effect รักษาด้วย cabergoline เป็นอันดับแรก
tempoNote: Months to years; macroprolactinomas in men often present late with visual or pituitary deficits
feat: Most common functioning pituitary tumour; microprolactinomas (under 1 cm) are common in women and macroprolactinomas more often in men
Women: oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, infertility; men: reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, gynaecomastia and often visual or headache complaints from a large tumour
Macroadenomas: headache, bitemporal hemianopia, cranial nerve palsies, hypopituitarism and occasionally CSF leak when the tumour shrinks
Prolactin level generally tracks tumour size: above about 150–200 ng/mL suggests a prolactinoma, while values below 100–150 in a large mass suggest stalk compression by a non-functioning tumour
Dramatic shrinkage with cabergoline in most patients, often with return of vision within days to weeks
inv: Serum prolactin; ask the laboratory to dilute the sample (1:100) if a large tumour has a surprisingly modest value (hook effect); consider macroprolactin if the patient is asymptomatic
Exclude pregnancy, hypothyroidism, renal failure, liver disease and drugs (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, domperidone, verapamil, SSRIs) before blaming the pituitary
Pituitary MRI with gadolinium, formal visual fields, and assessment of other pituitary axes

case.story: A year of headaches and reduced libido, and last month he clipped the side of his car while parking.
case.exam: Bitemporal hemianopia, no galactorrhoea, normal body hair.
case.tests: Prolactin 4,800 ng/mL; MRI shows a 3 cm sellar and suprasellar mass lifting the chiasm; low testosterone with low LH and FSH.
case.q: What is the first-line treatment?
case.a: Giant prolactinoma: cabergoline is first line even with visual loss, with close monitoring of fields and MRI; surgery is reserved for resistance, intolerance, apoplexy or CSF leak, and hormones are replaced if deficiency persists.

read.where: Chapter 44 Pituitary Adenomas – Evaluation and Nonsurgical Management — Prolactinomas; hyperprolactinaemia
Chapter 20 Sex Hormone, Pituitary, Parathyroid, and Adrenal Disorders and the Nervous System

det.patho: Lactotroph adenomas are clonal expansions of prolactin-secreting cells, usually sporadic, with MEN1 and AIP variants responsible in a minority. Prolactin suppresses hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility, producing hypogonadism, while dopamine from the hypothalamus tonically inhibits lactotrophs, which is why dopamine agonists work and why stalk compression raises prolactin. Larger tumours compress the chiasm, invade the cavernous sinuses or damage the rest of the pituitary.
det.clinical: Microprolactinomas typically declare themselves through reproductive symptoms in premenopausal women. In men and postmenopausal women the symptoms are subtle, and macroadenomas present with mass effect. Prolactin can also be raised by pregnancy and lactation, drugs, primary hypothyroidism, renal failure, cirrhosis, chest wall injury, stress, empty sella and macroprolactinaemia, usually below 200 ng/mL. Apoplexy can complicate large tumours.
det.diagnosis: Prolactin above about 150–200 ng/mL with a pituitary mass confirms a prolactinoma, but a hook effect or stalk effect must be considered when the value does not match the tumour size. Exclude secondary causes first. MRI defines size and invasion, visual fields and OCT measure function, and other pituitary axes are assessed because hypopituitarism is common in macroadenomas. A rule of thumb that the chance of prolactinoma rises with the prolactin value helps in the moderate range.
det.treatment: Cabergoline (starting 0.25–0.5 mg once or twice weekly, titrated to prolactin) is first line and normalises prolactin and shrinks most tumours; bromocriptine is an alternative and is preferred when pregnancy is wanted. Monitor fields and MRI, and watch for nausea, hypotension, impulse-control disorders and, at high doses, valvular heart disease. After at least two years of normal prolactin and a tumour that is no longer visible, a trial of withdrawal with surveillance is possible. Transsphenoidal surgery is for drug resistance or intolerance, apoplexy, CSF leak or when the patient prefers it; radiotherapy is for aggressive tumours. Dopamine agonist therapy is continued through macroprolactinoma pregnancy only when needed, with field monitoring.
det.prognosis: Excellent: most remain controlled with medication and some achieve long-term remission.
pearls: Even with vision loss, a dopamine agonist rather than surgery is first line.
A huge tumour with a modest prolactin: dilute the sample, think hook effect or non-functioning adenoma.
Always review drugs and thyroid function before a pituitary label.
det.thd: Prolactinoma เป็นเนื้องอกต่อมใต้สมองชนิดหลั่ง prolactin ที่พบบ่อยที่สุด ผู้หญิงมักมีประจำเดือนขาด น้ำนมไหล และมีบุตรยาก ส่วนผู้ชายมักมาตอนก้อนโต มีปวดศีรษะ ตามัวแบบลานสายตาแคบด้านนอกทั้งสองข้าง และฮอร์โมนเพศต่ำ ระดับ prolactin ที่สูงมากสัมพันธ์กับขนาดก้อน ถ้าก้อนใหญ่แต่ prolactin ต่ำให้เจือจางตัวอย่างเพื่อกัน hook effect และนึกถึง stalk effect ต้องแยกยา ไทรอยด์ ไต การตั้งครรภ์ รักษาเบื้องต้นด้วย cabergoline แม้มีปัญหาการมองเห็น

name: Prolonged disorder of consciousness (PDOC)
formal: Disorder of consciousness persisting beyond 28 days after brain injury, including vegetative state (unresponsive wakefulness) and minimally conscious state, assessed with serial behavioural scales and functional imaging.
simple: A long-lasting state after severe brain injury in which a person is awake or partly aware but cannot reliably communicate.
th: ภาวะความรู้สึกตัวผิดปกตินานเกิน 28 วันหลังสมองบาดเจ็บ ได้แก่ vegetative state/UWS และ minimally conscious state ต้องประเมินซ้ำด้วยแบบประเมินมาตรฐาน
tempoNote: Defined after 4 weeks; recovery can continue slowly for months, especially after traumatic injury
feat: Eyes open and sleep–wake cycles present after coma, but awareness absent (UWS) or inconsistent (MCS)
MCS: reproducible but variable signs such as visual pursuit, following a command or localising pain
Emergence from MCS: reliable functional communication or object use
Causes: traumatic brain injury, hypoxic-ischaemic injury, large stroke, encephalitis
High rates of misdiagnosis without structured repeated assessment
inv: Repeated Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R) assessments by trained staff
MRI for injury pattern; EEG to exclude non-convulsive seizures and assess background
Research or specialist tools: fMRI command paradigms, EEG-based covert awareness testing
Check correctable factors: hydrocephalus, sedating drugs, endocrine and metabolic disorders

case.story: Severe head injury two months ago; he opens his eyes, sleeps at night and grimaces, but family say he sometimes follows them with his eyes.
case.exam: Inconsistent visual pursuit of a mirror and once squeezes a hand on request; no verbal output.
case.tests: CT shows diffuse axonal injury and ventricular enlargement.
case.q: How would you classify his state and what treatable issue should be checked?
case.a: Minimally conscious state; assess for post-traumatic hydrocephalus and consider amantadine, which has trial support after TBI.

read.where: Chapter 25 Restorative Neurology, Rehabilitation and Brain Injury — Prolonged Disorders of Consciousness
Chapter 63 Care at the End of Life
Chapter 4: Coma And Other States Of Altered Awareness In The Intensive Care Unit
23 The Localization of Lesions Causing Coma

det.patho: Consciousness needs both arousal, from brainstem and thalamic activating systems, and awareness, from widespread cortico-thalamic networks. Diffuse axonal injury, hypoxic neuronal loss or bilateral thalamic damage can preserve arousal while disconnecting awareness. The degree of residual cortico-thalamic integration distinguishes UWS from MCS.
det.clinical: After coma, patients open their eyes and show sleep–wake cycles. In UWS, only reflexive behaviours occur; in MCS, there are inconsistent but genuine signs of awareness (MCS minus: pursuit, localisation; MCS plus: command following or intelligible words). Some patients show covert awareness on imaging despite no behavioural signs (cognitive-motor dissociation). Complications include spasticity, contractures, infection and paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity.
det.diagnosis: Use repeated CRS-R assessments, ideally five or more over a short period, with attention to arousal, positioning, sensory deficits and sedating drugs. EEG, evoked potentials and functional imaging help identify covert awareness. Labels should be revised over time; terms like permanent vegetative state are discouraged in favour of chronic with duration stated.
det.treatment: Provide specialist rehabilitation, nutrition, spasticity and posture management, and treatment of complications. Amantadine during the early months after traumatic injury has randomised evidence for faster recovery; zolpidem helps a small minority paradoxically. Ethical decisions about life-sustaining treatment follow local law and best-interest processes with families.
det.prognosis: Traumatic causes recover better than hypoxic ones; MCS carries a better outlook than UWS, and late improvement beyond a year is possible.
pearls: Always look for a mirror-tracking response — visual pursuit is often the first sign of MCS.
Rule out hydrocephalus, seizures and over-sedation before accepting a poor state.
Around a third of patients labelled vegetative show signs of awareness on careful testing.
det.thd: PDOC คือภาวะความรู้สึกตัวผิดปกตินานเกิน 28 วันหลังสมองบาดเจ็บรุนแรง แบ่งเป็น UWS ที่ลืมตาได้แต่ไม่มีสัญญาณรับรู้ และ MCS ที่มีสัญญาณรับรู้บ้างแต่ไม่สม่ำเสมอ ต้องประเมินซ้ำด้วย CRS-R หลายครั้งเพราะวินิจฉัยผิดบ่อย ควรหาสาเหตุที่แก้ไขได้ เช่น hydrocephalus ชัก หรือยากดประสาท และพิจารณา amantadine ในผู้บาดเจ็บศีรษะ การฟื้นตัวดีกว่าในกลุ่ม trauma เทียบกับสมองขาดออกซิเจน

name: Propionic acidaemia
formal: Autosomal recessive organic aciduria from propionyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency causing neonatal metabolic acidosis, hyperammonaemia, encephalopathy, basal ganglia injury and later dystonia or chorea.
simple: An inherited metabolic disease where the body cannot process certain proteins, causing acid and ammonia build-up that harms the brain.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมกรดอินทรีย์คั่งจากขาด propionyl-CoA carboxylase ทำให้เลือดเป็นกรด แอมโมเนียสูง สมองบวมในทารก และต่อมาเกิด dystonia หรือ chorea จาก basal ganglia เสียหาย
tempoNote: Neonatal crisis or later episodic decompensations on a chronic background
feat: Neonate well at birth then poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy and coma within days
Metabolic acidosis with high anion gap, ketosis and hyperammonaemia
Later-onset forms: episodic decompensation with infection, developmental delay
Basal ganglia stroke-like injury giving dystonia or chorea
Cardiomyopathy, long QT, pancreatitis and optic atrophy as complications
inv: Blood gas, ammonia, glucose, lactate during crisis
Plasma acylcarnitines (raised propionylcarnitine C3) and urine organic acids (3-hydroxypropionate, methylcitrate)
PCCA/PCCB genetic testing; newborn screening in some programmes
MRI: basal ganglia signal change; echocardiogram and ECG

case.who: 4-day-old boy born in Sakon Nakhon to consanguineous parents
case.story: Fed well for two days, then became sleepy, vomited and breathed rapidly.
case.exam: Lethargic, hypotonic, intermittent stiffening, tachypnoea, no sepsis focus.
case.tests: pH 7.12, anion gap 28, ammonia 420 µmol/L; acylcarnitines show high C3, urine shows methylcitrate.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what are the emergency steps?
case.a: Propionic acidaemia; stop protein, give high-calorie glucose with insulin as needed, start carglumic acid and ammonia scavengers, give carnitine, and arrange haemodialysis if ammonia stays high.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Propionic and Methylmalonic Acidaemias

det.patho: Propionyl-CoA carboxylase converts propionyl-CoA (from isoleucine, valine, methionine, threonine, odd-chain fats and gut bacteria) to methylmalonyl-CoA. Its deficiency causes propionyl-CoA build-up, secondary carnitine deficiency, urea cycle inhibition and mitochondrial energy failure. The striatum is vulnerable during crises, leading to metabolic stroke.
det.clinical: Classic neonatal onset brings encephalopathy and acidosis in the first week. Later-onset forms present with recurrent vomiting, ketoacidosis, failure to thrive, developmental delay or movement disorder. Long-term issues include intellectual disability, seizures, dystonia, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia and pancreatitis.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in any sick neonate with acidosis and hyperammonaemia. Acylcarnitine profile and urine organic acids give the biochemical diagnosis; genetic testing confirms. Echocardiography and ECG are part of baseline assessment.
det.treatment: Acute: stop protein briefly, give high-energy intravenous glucose and lipid, carnitine, carglumic acid and ammonia scavengers, and dialysis if needed. Long-term: protein-restricted diet with special formula, carnitine, intermittent metronidazole to reduce gut propionate, and sick-day plans. Liver transplantation reduces crises in severe cases. mRNA therapies are in trials.
det.prognosis: Neonatal forms carry significant mortality and neurological morbidity; outcomes improve with early diagnosis and specialist care.
pearls: Sick neonate with ketoacidosis and high ammonia: send acylcarnitines and urine organic acids.
Metabolic stroke of the basal ganglia leads to lasting dystonia.
Screen for cardiomyopathy and long QT throughout life.
det.thd: Propionic acidaemia เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมขาดเอนไซม์ propionyl-CoA carboxylase ทารกจะดูดนมไม่ดี อาเจียน ซึม หลังเกิดไม่กี่วัน มีเลือดเป็นกรดและแอมโมเนียสูง อาจทำให้ basal ganglia เสียหายเกิด dystonia ภายหลัง วินิจฉัยด้วย acylcarnitine (C3 สูง) และกรดอินทรีย์ในปัสสาวะ รักษาด้วยการงดโปรตีนช่วงวิกฤต ให้พลังงาน carnitine ยาลดแอมโมเนีย และอาหารจำกัดโปรตีนระยะยาว

Macrocephaly and acute striatal injury after illness, with glutaric acid in urine

name: Propranolol akathisia
formal: Drug-induced akathisia, an inner restlessness with inability to sit still, reported as a rare adverse effect of beta-blockers such as propranolol.
simple: A feeling of inner restlessness and urge to move that can be caused by the blood pressure drug propranolol.
th: อาการกระสับกระส่ายนั่งไม่ติดที่มีรายงานน้อยมากจาก propranolol ทั้งที่ propranolol เป็นยาหลักใช้รักษา akathisia
tempoNote: Isolated reports describe onset within days of starting; evidence is weak
feat: Rare and poorly substantiated; propranolol is a standard treatment for akathisia
Restlessness may instead reflect beta-blocker CNS effects: vivid dreams, insomnia, depression, fatigue
Check for a concurrent drug that truly causes akathisia (antipsychotic, SSRI, metoclopramide)
Abrupt beta-blocker withdrawal can cause tremor, palpitations and anxiety that resemble restlessness
inv: Drug timeline including recent beta-blocker withdrawal
Heart rate, blood pressure, TSH
Screen for depression and anxiety

case.story: Started propranolol for performance anxiety and escitalopram for low mood in the same week. Now restless and unable to sit through lessons.
case.exam: Fidgeting, shifting legs; HR 58/min; no rigidity or chorea.
case.tests: TSH normal; no further tests.
case.q: Which drug is the more likely cause of akathisia?
case.a: Escitalopram — SSRIs are a recognised cause; propranolol is more often used to treat akathisia.

det.patho: No convincing mechanism links propranolol to dopamine-related akathisia; its benefit in akathisia is thought to come from damping central noradrenergic activity. Lipophilic beta-blockers do enter the brain and can cause sleep disturbance and mood change, which patients may describe as restlessness.
det.clinical: Reports are rare and often confounded by other drugs. Symptoms are subjective restlessness or insomnia shortly after starting. Rebound after abrupt withdrawal produces tachycardia, tremor and anxiety rather than true akathisia.
det.diagnosis: Treat this label with caution: look hard for a more plausible culprit and for primary anxiety or thyroid disease. A dechallenge with symptom resolution supports a link.
det.treatment: Stop or switch the beta-blocker if the association seems genuine; taper rather than stop abruptly. Address other contributing medicines.
det.prognosis: Resolves after withdrawal of the responsible drug.
pearls: Propranolol treats akathisia far more often than it causes it.
Always search for a co-prescribed dopamine blocker or SSRI.
Taper beta-blockers to avoid rebound symptoms.
det.thd: Propranolol akathisia เป็นรายงานที่พบน้อยมากและหลักฐานไม่ชัดเจน เพราะ propranolol เป็นยาหลักใช้รักษา akathisia อาการกระสับกระส่ายที่เกิดขึ้นมักมาจากยาอื่นที่ใช้ร่วม เช่น SSRI หรือ antipsychotic หรือจากผลต่อการนอนและอารมณ์ ควรทบทวนยาทั้งหมดก่อน และถ้าต้องหยุด propranolol ให้ค่อย ๆ ลดยา

ddx.pt: Usually from dopamine blockers or serotonergic antidepressants
Leg discomfort worse at night, relieved by walking
Thyrotoxic tremor, weight loss and heat intolerance; beta-blockers may mask tachycardia

name: Propriospinal myoclonus
formal: Axial jerks arising from a spinal generator and spreading slowly up and down the cord via propriospinal pathways; often occurs on lying down and is frequently functional.
simple: Sudden jerks of the trunk and limbs, often when lying down trying to sleep, thought to start in the spinal cord.
th: Propriospinal myoclonus (PSM) คือการกระตุกของลำตัวเป็นแบบ flexion ที่เชื่อกันว่าเริ่มจากไขสันหลังและกระจายขึ้นลงช้า ๆ ตามทาง propriospinal มักเกิดเมื่อนอนหงายหรือเริ่มหลับ รบกวนการนอน พบสาเหตุโครงสร้างได้น้อย ส่วนใหญ่เป็น functional (psychogenic) ตรวจ polymyography และ Bereitschaftspotential ช่วยแยก ต้องทำ MRI ไขสันหลังเพื่อหาสาเหตุ
tempoNote: Repetitive jerks lasting months to years, usually appearing when relaxed, lying supine or during drowsiness at sleep onset; structural cases begin after a cord insult
feat: Sudden flexion jerks of the neck, trunk and hips (less often extension), sparing the face, sometimes spreading to the arms and legs
Typically triggered by lying supine, relaxation or drowsiness, may prevent sleep and often disappear with movement or concentration
Rare structural cases follow spinal trauma, tumour, myelitis, syrinx or disc herniation; most reported series have turned out to be functional
Features favouring a functional cause: variability, distractibility, premonitory urge, suggestibility and EMG bursts that can be voluntarily copied
Associated insomnia, daytime fatigue, anxiety and pain
inv: Polymyography: recruitment starting at a thoracic or abdominal segment (often rectus abdominis) with slow rostral and caudal spread over several tens of milliseconds
Back-averaged EEG for Bereitschaftspotential before jerks supports a functional origin; absent cortical correlate with no premotor potential supports a spinal origin
MRI of the whole spine (diffusion tensor imaging where available) to exclude a lesion; brain MRI and sleep study as indicated

case.story: For six months she has had sudden trunk jerks when she lies down to sleep, which began after a minor fall; the jerks disappear when she talks or concentrates, and they sometimes happen when she is told to expect them.
case.exam: Repetitive axial flexion jerks when supine, variable timing, stop with distraction and can be triggered by suggestion; neurological examination otherwise normal.
case.tests: MRI of spine normal; polymyography shows variable recruitment and a Bereitschaftspotential before the jerks.
case.q: What is the most likely mechanism and how should the patient be managed?
case.a: Functional (psychogenic) axial jerks mimicking propriospinal myoclonus; explain the diagnosis positively and refer for specialist physiotherapy and psychological therapy; clonazepam may help organic cases.

18 - Myoclonus: Phenomenology, etiology, physiology, and treatment

det.patho: Propriospinal myoclonus was described as arising from a spinal generator, usually thoracic, from which an impulse travels slowly along long propriospinal pathways to activate muscles up and down the axis at about 5–15 m/s. The pattern has also been shown to occur with a voluntary or functional generation, and many modern studies suggest that most cases are functional. Structural spinal cases are probably caused by disinhibition of spinal interneuron circuits after a lesion.
det.clinical: Patients describe sudden flexion jerks of the trunk and hips, which interfere with sleep because they occur in the relaxed supine state, ease with activity and increase when sleep begins. The facial muscles are spared in a spinal origin. Examination between jerks is normal. When 35 people sent for axial jerks were studied in one report, nearly all were judged functional, so a spinal diagnosis needs physiological proof. Anxiety, insomnia and chronic fatigue are common.
det.diagnosis: Observe the jerks supine and during a task, and look for variability, suggestibility and distractibility. Polymyography (EMG from several axial and limb muscles) documents the recruitment pattern; a stable spread at spinal conduction velocity suggests a spinal generator, while variable spread and a Bereitschaftspotential on back-averaged EEG suggest a functional origin. Whole-spine MRI is needed to exclude cord lesions. Sleep studies are useful to identify periodic limb movements or sleep-onset jerks and to document presence during wakefulness.
det.treatment: Where the cause is organic, treat the underlying lesion; clonazepam is the drug most often reported to help, followed by levetiracetam, valproate or botulinum toxin to the paraspinal and abdominal muscles. For the functional majority, give a clear explanation, then use specialised physiotherapy, behavioural relaxation techniques and cognitive behavioural therapy, with attention to sleep. Avoid repeated investigation and unnecessary anticonvulsants.
det.prognosis: Organic cases may improve if the lesion is treated; functional cases can recover with therapy, though chronic jerks with sleep disturbance are not uncommon.
pearls: Axial jerks at sleep onset that disappear with distraction are most often functional.
A Bereitschaftspotential before the jerk argues for a functional cause.
Image the whole spine before accepting a functional diagnosis.
det.thd: Propriospinal myoclonus (PSM) คือการกระตุกของลำตัวและสะโพกแบบงอ มักเกิดตอนนอนหงายหรือก่อนหลับ จนนอนไม่หลับ เชื่อว่าเริ่มจากไขสันหลังแล้วกระจายขึ้นลงช้า ๆ แต่รายงานจำนวนมากพบว่าเป็น functional (psychogenic) ต้องตรวจ MRI ไขสันหลังเพื่อหาสาเหตุ และใช้ polymyography กับ Bereitschaftspotential เพื่อแยก รักษาโดยอธิบายอย่างชัดเจนและกายภาพบำบัด ส่วนชนิดที่มีรอยโรคอาจใช้ clonazepam

name: Prosopagnosia
formal: Selective inability to recognize familiar faces despite intact vision, from lesions of the right fusiform or occipitotemporal cortex, or developmental.
simple: Not being able to recognize people by their faces, even close family, though vision is normal.
th: ไม่สามารถจดจำใบหน้าคนที่รู้จักได้ ทั้งที่การมองเห็นปกติ จากรอยโรคที่ fusiform หรือ occipitotemporal ด้านขวา หรือเป็นแต่กำเนิด
tempoNote: Acute after stroke or encephalitis; lifelong in developmental form; insidious in right temporal neurodegeneration
feat: Cannot recognise familiar people by their faces, sometimes including own reflection
Recognises people by voice, gait, clothing or hairstyle
Acquired form: right or bilateral fusiform/occipitotemporal lesions (PCA stroke, encephalitis, tumour)
Often accompanied by left upper quadrantanopia, achromatopsia or topographical disorientation
Developmental form affects about 2% of people without brain injury; right temporal FTD causes progressive form
inv: Bedside: recognising photographs of famous or family faces versus names
Formal tests: Cambridge Face Memory Test, Benton Facial Recognition Test
Visual fields and colour vision
MRI brain for stroke, lesion or right anterior temporal atrophy

case.story: After a sudden visual disturbance last month she could not recognise her regular customers until they spoke; she also finds colours look washed out.
case.exam: Acuity normal, left upper quadrantanopia, impaired colour naming; cannot identify family photos but names them by voice.
case.tests: MRI shows right posterior cerebral artery infarct involving the fusiform gyrus; Holter shows paroxysmal AF.
case.q: What is the deficit and its localisation?
case.a: Acquired prosopagnosia from right fusiform (occipitotemporal) infarction; start anticoagulation for AF and offer compensatory strategies.

det.patho: Face recognition relies on a ventral occipitotemporal network, especially the fusiform face area and occipital face area, which are right-dominant. Damage to these regions or their connections to anterior temporal person-knowledge stores disrupts face identity processing. Developmental prosopagnosia has no visible lesion and is thought to reflect altered network development, often familial.
det.clinical: Patients describe being unable to recognise friends, colleagues or relatives unless they hear their voice or see distinctive features. Some cannot recognise their own face in photographs. Acquired cases often have coexisting visual field defects, achromatopsia or topographical disorientation. In right temporal variant FTD, face recognition loss is accompanied by loss of knowledge about people and behavioural change.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis combines a typical history with failure on face recognition and memory tests despite adequate vision and preserved recognition through other cues. Distinguish apperceptive forms (cannot perceive faces) from associative forms (perceives but cannot link to identity). MRI identifies lesions or focal atrophy.
det.treatment: No drug treatment exists. Management focuses on the cause and on compensatory strategies such as relying on voice, context and distinctive features, name badges and informing colleagues. Training programmes have shown modest benefit in some developmental cases. Psychological support helps with social anxiety.
det.prognosis: Post-stroke prosopagnosia may partly improve; developmental prosopagnosia is lifelong; neurodegenerative forms progress.
pearls: Face blindness with a left upper quadrantanopia points to right fusiform damage.
Ask whether voice recognition is intact — it usually is.
Progressive face and person recognition loss suggests right temporal variant FTD.
det.thd: Prosopagnosia หรือภาวะจำหน้าคนไม่ได้ คือการที่ผู้ป่วยมองเห็นปกติแต่ไม่สามารถรู้ว่าใบหน้านั้นเป็นใคร ต้องอาศัยเสียงหรือการแต่งกาย เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ fusiform gyrus ด้านขวาหรือทั้งสองข้าง เช่น stroke ของ posterior cerebral artery หรือเป็นแต่กำเนิด หรือจากสมองกลีบขมับขวาเสื่อม ตรวจด้วยการให้ดูรูปคนรู้จักและ MRI การดูแลคือรักษาสาเหตุและสอนกลยุทธ์ชดเชย

name: Protozoan neurological infections
formal: Central nervous system infections by protozoa such as Toxoplasma, Plasmodium falciparum, trypanosomes, Naegleria and Acanthamoeba, causing encephalitis, abscesses or meningoencephalitis.
simple: Infections of the brain or nerves caused by single-celled parasites such as those causing malaria or toxoplasmosis.
th: การติดเชื้อโปรโตซัวในระบบประสาท เช่น Toxoplasma, มาลาเรียขึ้นสมอง, trypanosome, Naegleria และ Acanthamoeba ทำให้สมองอักเสบ ฝีในสมอง หรือเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ
tempoNote: Naegleria and cerebral malaria evolve over hours to days; toxoplasma and Acanthamoeba over days to weeks
feat: Cerebral malaria: fever, coma and seizures after travel or residence in forested border areas
Toxoplasmosis: multiple ring-enhancing lesions with focal deficits in advanced HIV
Naegleria: fulminant meningoencephalitis days after freshwater swimming or nasal irrigation
Acanthamoeba/Balamuthia: subacute granulomatous encephalitis in immunocompromised hosts; Acanthamoeba also causes keratitis
African trypanosomiasis: sleep disturbance and behaviour change; Chagas: reactivation masses in HIV
inv: Malaria thick and thin films and rapid antigen tests
Toxoplasma IgG, CD4, MRI; response to empirical therapy
CSF wet mount and PCR for free-living amoebae; brain biopsy when needed

case.story: A week of fever and chills, then confusion and a generalised seizure this morning.
case.exam: GCS 8, jaundice, no neck stiffness, retinal whitening on fundoscopy.
case.tests: Thick film: P. falciparum 6% parasitaemia; glucose 2.8 mmol/L; CT brain swelling only.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and first-line treatment?
case.a: Cerebral malaria (severe falciparum); IV artesunate plus correction of hypoglycaemia, seizure control and ICU support.

det.patho: Protozoa reach the CNS through blood (Plasmodium, Toxoplasma reactivation, trypanosomes) or via the olfactory nerve (Naegleria fowleri). Cerebral malaria results from sequestration of parasitised red cells in brain microvessels and inflammation rather than direct invasion. Toxoplasma reactivates from latent cysts when CD4 falls below about 100 cells/µL.
det.clinical: The clinical spectrum ranges from coma in cerebral malaria, focal masses in toxoplasmosis, fulminant meningoencephalitis in Naegleria, to subacute granulomatous encephalitis in Acanthamoeba and Balamuthia. Geography and exposure history are essential: Thai border forest areas for malaria, freshwater exposure for Naegleria, and HIV status for toxoplasmosis.
det.diagnosis: Blood films and antigen tests diagnose malaria; any febrile coma in an endemic setting needs a malaria test. Toxoplasmosis is diagnosed by typical imaging, positive serology and response to treatment within about two weeks. Free-living amoebae are found by CSF microscopy, PCR or brain biopsy, and trypanosomes in blood, lymph node or CSF.
det.treatment: Severe malaria: IV artesunate, supportive ICU care and no steroids. Toxoplasmosis: pyrimethamine with sulfadiazine and leucovorin (or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) then secondary prophylaxis until immune recovery. Naegleria: multidrug regimens including amphotericin B and miltefosine, with poor outcomes. Trypanosomiasis treatment depends on species and stage (fexinidazole, NECT, benznidazole).
det.prognosis: Cerebral malaria mortality is about 15–20% in adults; Naegleria is almost always fatal; toxoplasmosis responds well with ART.
pearls: Febrile coma after forest exposure in Thailand: test for malaria immediately.
Ring lesions in HIV that do not improve on toxo therapy in 2 weeks: biopsy for lymphoma.
Steroids are harmful in cerebral malaria.
det.thd: Protozoan neurological infections คือการติดเชื้อโปรโตซัวในระบบประสาท ที่สำคัญในไทยคือมาลาเรียขึ้นสมองในผู้ที่เข้าป่าตามแนวชายแดน และ toxoplasmosis ในผู้ป่วย HIV ระยะท้าย ส่วน Naegleria ทำให้สมองอักเสบรุนแรงหลังว่ายน้ำจืด การวินิจฉัยใช้ฟิล์มเลือด ภาพถ่ายสมอง และน้ำไขสันหลัง รักษาตามเชื้อ เช่น artesunate สำหรับมาลาเรีย และ pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine สำหรับ toxoplasma

name: Proximal hereditary motor neuropathy
formal: Hereditary motor neuropathy with predominantly proximal weakness and wasting, as in HMN-P due to TFG or related variants.
simple: An inherited nerve disease that weakens the muscles near the hips and shoulders.
more: Genetic testing and EMG exclude SMA; supportive management.
th: โรคเส้นประสาทสั่งการกรรมพันธุ์ที่อ่อนแรงและลีบบริเวณต้นแขนต้นขาเป็นหลัก เช่น HMSN-P จากยีน TFG
tempoNote: Adult onset, slowly progressive over decades
feat: Proximal limb weakness and wasting with fasciculations and muscle cramps
Mild distal sensory loss in HMSN-P despite the motor label
Autosomal dominant; TFG variant first described in Okinawa (Japan) and found in Korea, Brazil
Reflexes reduced or absent
Late dysphagia and respiratory weakness in some
inv: EMG: chronic neurogenic changes, fasciculations; sensory potentials reduced
CK mildly raised
SMN1 testing to exclude SMA, androgen receptor CAG repeat to exclude Kennedy disease
TFG and neuropathy gene panel

case.story: Ten years of difficulty getting up from a squat and lifting boxes, with frequent cramps; his mother had similar weakness.
case.exam: Proximal arm and leg wasting with fasciculations, areflexia, mild vibration loss at toes, no gynaecomastia.
case.tests: EMG chronic denervation, low sural SNAPs; SMN1 and AR repeat normal; TFG variant found.
case.q: Which two conditions must be excluded first?
case.a: Adult SMA (SMN1) and Kennedy disease (androgen receptor CAG repeat).

det.patho: TFG encodes a protein involved in ER-to-Golgi transport; the dominant mutation leads to TDP-43-positive inclusions and degeneration of motor neurons and sensory ganglia. Other genes are rarely implicated. Whether the disease is a neuronopathy or neuropathy remains debated.
det.clinical: Onset is in adulthood with proximal weakness, cramps and fasciculations, progressing slowly over decades. Distal sensory loss is mild. Late stages bring dysphagia and respiratory failure. Outside East Asian founder populations it is rare.
det.diagnosis: EMG shows chronic neurogenic change; sensory responses are mildly reduced. Genetic testing confirms. Exclude SMA, Kennedy disease, ALS and inflammatory neuropathies.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying treatment. Physiotherapy, orthoses, respiratory monitoring and swallowing assessment are the core of care.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; many remain ambulant for years, but respiratory involvement can occur late.
pearls: Proximal neurogenic weakness in adults: check SMN1 and AR first.
Mild sensory involvement is a clue to HMSN-P rather than SMA.
Family history with dominant pattern is important.
det.thd: Proximal hereditary motor neuropathy (เช่น HMSN-P จากยีน TFG) เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมที่ทำให้ต้นแขนต้นขาอ่อนแรงและลีบ มีตะคริวและกล้ามเนื้อเต้น เริ่มในวัยผู้ใหญ่และค่อย ๆ เป็นมากขึ้น ต้องแยกจาก SMA และ Kennedy disease ด้วยการตรวจยีน ยังไม่มีการรักษาเฉพาะ เน้นกายภาพและเฝ้าระวังการหายใจ

ddx.pt: X-linked; bulbar involvement, gynaecomastia, sensory neuronopathy
Proximal weakness without sensory involvement; SMN1 deletion
Rapid progression with upper motor neuron signs

name: Pseudo-orthostatic tremor
formal: Lower limb tremor resembling orthostatic tremor on standing but at lower frequency (below 13 Hz), with other tremor or parkinsonian features, unlike primary orthostatic tremor.
simple: A leg shaking while standing that looks like orthostatic tremor but has a slower rhythm and a different cause.
th: อาการสั่นที่ขาเวลายืนคล้าย orthostatic tremor แต่ความถี่ต่ำกว่า 13 Hz และมักมี tremor หรือ parkinsonism อื่นร่วม
tempoNote: Gradual, often in older adults with another movement disorder
feat: Leg tremor or unsteadiness on standing, relieved by walking or sitting
Frequency below 13 Hz (often 4–10 Hz), sometimes visible, unlike primary OT
Associated with Parkinson disease, essential tremor, ataxia or vascular disease
Other signs such as rigidity, bradykinesia or ataxia usually present
inv: Surface EMG of legs while standing: frequency under 13 Hz
DaT-SPECT if parkinsonism suspected
MRI brain

case.story: Feels his legs shake when queuing at the hospital, better once he walks; has had a slow right hand for a year.
case.exam: Visible 6 Hz leg tremor on standing, right-sided rigidity and bradykinesia, reduced arm swing.
case.tests: Leg EMG while standing shows 6 Hz bursts; DaT-SPECT reduced on the left.
case.q: How does this differ from primary orthostatic tremor?
case.a: Primary OT is 13–18 Hz, often not visible, without other signs; this lower-frequency tremor reflects Parkinson disease and may respond to levodopa.

det.patho: Pseudo-orthostatic tremor is a slower standing tremor generated by the same circuits that cause the patient's main tremor disorder, often a parkinsonian rest-postural tremor transferred to weight-bearing legs. It differs physiologically from the high-frequency central oscillator of primary OT.
det.clinical: Patients feel unsteady or shaky on standing, which eases with walking. Unlike primary OT, the tremor is often visible and accompanied by parkinsonism, ataxia or other tremors. Falls may occur.
det.diagnosis: Surface EMG is essential, showing frequency under 13 Hz. Examination looks for underlying parkinsonism or cerebellar signs; DaT-SPECT and MRI help.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying disorder: levodopa for Parkinson disease, propranolol or primidone for essential tremor. Walking aids and fall prevention help.
det.prognosis: Depends on the underlying disease.
pearls: Measure the frequency: under 13 Hz = pseudo-orthostatic.
Visible leg tremor on standing with parkinsonism suggests a levodopa-responsive cause.
det.thd: Pseudo-orthostatic tremor คืออาการขาสั่นเวลายืนคล้าย orthostatic tremor แต่ความถี่ต่ำกว่า 13 Hz มองเห็นได้ และมักมีโรคอื่นร่วม เช่น Parkinson disease หรือ essential tremor วินิจฉัยด้วย EMG ขาขณะยืน รักษาตามโรคต้นเหตุ เช่น levodopa

ddx.pt: 13–18 Hz high-frequency, felt more than seen, isolated; clonazepam/gabapentin
Main underlying cause; leg tremor improves with levodopa
Action tremor of arms; leg orthostatic tremor occasionally

aN: slow orthostatic tremor | orthostatic tremor plus | low frequency orthostatic tremor | secondary orthostatic tremor

name: Pseudo-parkinsonism
formal: Parkinsonian features such as rigidity, bradykinesia and tremor not caused by nigrostriatal degeneration, e.g. drug-induced, vascular or functional.
simple: Symptoms that look like Parkinson's disease but have another cause, such as medication.
th: กลุ่มอาการคล้ายพาร์กินสันที่ไม่ได้เกิดจากการเสื่อมของ nigrostriatal เช่น จากยา หลอดเลือด หรือ functional ซึ่งบางชนิดหายได้ถ้าแก้สาเหตุ
tempoNote: Weeks to months after a causative drug; stepwise in vascular disease; abrupt and inconsistent in functional cases
feat: Slowness and stiffness that tend to be symmetric, with or without postural or orofacial tremor
Drug causes: antipsychotics, antiemetics such as metoclopramide, calcium-channel blockers flunarizine and cinnarizine, valproate
Vascular cause: shuffling lower-body gait, pyramidal signs, extensive white-matter change, little levodopa effect
Functional cause: sudden onset, variable effort-dependent slowness, tremor that stops when distracted
Presynaptic dopamine imaging is usually normal, which separates most of these from degenerative disease
inv: Detailed medication list including antiemetics, vestibular suppressants and herbal or imported products
MRI brain for small-vessel disease, hydrocephalus or focal lesions
DaT-SPECT when the picture is uncertain or asymmetric
Reassess after drug withdrawal over several months

case.story: She took flunarizine daily for chronic dizziness for eight months. Over the last three months her family noticed she walks slowly with small steps and has stopped smiling. She has no sleep acting-out or loss of smell.
case.exam: Masked face, symmetric rigidity and bradykinesia, mild postural hand tremor, stooped shuffling gait with reduced arm swing on both sides; no gaze palsy.
case.tests: MRI brain shows mild periventricular small-vessel change only; DaT-SPECT shows symmetrical normal striatal uptake.
case.q: What is the likely cause and what is the first management step?
case.a: Drug-induced parkinsonism from flunarizine. Stop the drug and review over weeks to months; persistent or asymmetric signs would suggest an unmasked Parkinson disease.

read.where: 1 - Clinical overview and phenomenology of movement disorders

det.patho: Pseudo-parkinsonism covers any parkinsonian syndrome in which the nigrostriatal neurons are intact. The commonest mechanism is postsynaptic D2 receptor blockade or presynaptic dopamine depletion by drugs; vascular lesions that disrupt frontal-subcortical loops and structural problems such as hydrocephalus act differently. Older age, female sex and cognitive impairment raise the risk of drug effects, and some patients simply have subclinical Parkinson disease that the drug brought to light.
det.clinical: The picture is slowness, rigidity and often a flexed gait, but several features separate it from Parkinson disease: symmetry, early postural rather than rest tremor, oro-buccal movements and a lack of non-motor prodrome. Drug-related cases usually evolve within weeks to a few months of starting or increasing the agent. Vascular cases have a lower-body predominance with magnetic or wide-based steps, falls and pseudobulbar signs. Functional cases fluctuate with attention and show effortful rather than decrementing movement. Always ask about prochlorperazine, metoclopramide, flunarizine and cinnarizine, which are widely used in Thai primary care.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on a temporal link with the offending agent, exclusion of structural causes by MRI and, when doubt persists, normal DaT-SPECT. Improvement after drug withdrawal confirms the diagnosis but may take six months or longer. A scan that is abnormal despite a drug history means true presynaptic disease is present. Compare with early multiple system atrophy and PSP when levodopa response is poor and falls appear early.
det.treatment: Stop or replace the culprit, for example switching from a typical antipsychotic to quetiapine or clozapine when psychosis must still be treated and avoiding metoclopramide for nausea where possible. Anticholinergics are generally avoided in older patients because of cognitive harm. Levodopa is only worth a trial in vascular cases with documented benefit and in patients whose drug cannot be stopped. Treat hydrocephalus surgically when it is the cause. For functional cases, explanation and physiotherapy are the main approach.
det.prognosis: Most drug-induced cases improve within weeks to several months, but a minority persist and prove to be underlying Parkinson disease. Vascular forms respond poorly and progress with further infarcts.
pearls: Symmetric parkinsonism after a vertigo or nausea drug is drug-induced until proven otherwise.
Normal DaT-SPECT supports a non-degenerative cause; abnormal scans mean the drug unmasked disease.
Asking about all the tablets from every clinic visit often finds the culprit.
det.thd: Pseudo-parkinsonism คืออาการคล้ายพาร์กินสันที่ไม่ได้เกิดจากเซลล์ประสาทโดปามีนเสื่อม สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยคือยา เช่น flunarizine, cinnarizine, metoclopramide และยาคุมอาการทางจิต อาการมักเป็นสองข้างพอ ๆ กัน สั่นขณะทรงท่า และเกิดภายในหลายสัปดาห์ถึงหลายเดือนหลังเริ่มยา การวินิจฉัยใช้ประวัติยาและ MRI ร่วมกับ DaT-SPECT ที่ปกติ การรักษาหลักคือหยุดหรือเปลี่ยนยา ผู้ป่วยส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นภายในไม่กี่เดือน แต่บางรายที่ไม่ดีขึ้นอาจเป็นโรคพาร์กินสันอยู่ก่อน

Mainly gait and lower-body signs, stepwise course and heavy white-matter disease
Sudden onset, inconsistency and distractibility with normal dopamine imaging

aN: pseudoparkinsonism | secondary parkinsonism | non degenerative parkinsonism | drug induced pseudoparkinsonism

name: Pseudoakathisia
formal: Restless-looking movement or pacing from sensory disturbance, e.g. leg pain or paraesthesia, lacking the inner restlessness of true akathisia.
simple: Restless movement that looks like akathisia but comes from discomfort in the legs rather than inner restlessness.
th: การขยับตัวหรือเดินไปมาที่ดูเหมือน akathisia แต่ไม่มีความรู้สึกกระวนกระวายภายใน มักเกิดจากความผิดปกติของความรู้สึก หรือในผู้ป่วยที่สื่อสารไม่ได้
tempoNote: Usually persistent; may follow long-term antipsychotic exposure or accompany painful or sensory disorders
feat: Restless-appearing movements such as shifting, rocking, crossing legs or pacing
Patient denies the inner urge or tension that defines true akathisia
Can arise from leg pain or paraesthesia, or as a tardive phenomenon in long-term antipsychotic users
Also seen in patients with cognitive impairment who cannot report subjective restlessness
Term used in two senses; clarify which is meant in clinical notes
inv: Structured scale such as the Barnes Akathisia Rating Scale (objective and subjective items)
Medication history, including dopamine blockers and antidepressants
Neuropathy screen and iron studies if sensory symptoms

case.who: 55-year-old man with chronic schizophrenia living in a psychiatric rehabilitation home in Nonthaburi
case.story: Staff notice he shifts in his chair and walks up and down; he says he feels fine and has no urge to move.
case.exam: Frequent leg crossing and trunk rocking, mild orofacial dyskinesia, no parkinsonism.
case.tests: On haloperidol for 15 years; Barnes scale scores objective restlessness without subjective distress.
case.q: How does this differ from akathisia?
case.a: Pseudoakathisia — objective restlessness without inner urge, often a tardive feature; review the antipsychotic and treat like other tardive syndromes.

det.patho: In the movement-disorder literature, pseudoakathisia describes the motor features of akathisia without the subjective component, often as part of tardive syndromes after long dopamine-blocker exposure. It is thought to reflect maladaptive dopaminergic changes in the striatum. The term is also used loosely for restless movements driven by pain or abnormal sensation, where the mechanism is sensory rather than central.
det.clinical: Patients appear restless — shifting weight, rocking, pacing or moving the legs — yet deny distress or urge. It is commonly found in elderly, cognitively impaired or chronically medicated patients and may coexist with tardive dyskinesia. When pain or neuropathy is the driver, movements improve as the sensory problem is treated.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on careful questioning about inner restlessness and use of an akathisia rating scale. A medication review is essential. Examine for neuropathy, radiculopathy and other movement disorders, and check ferritin when restless legs are suspected.
det.treatment: If associated with antipsychotics, reduce the dose or switch to an agent with lower extrapyramidal liability, and consider VMAT2 inhibitors when part of a tardive syndrome. Propranolol, which helps acute akathisia, is less predictable here. Treat pain or neuropathy where present.
det.prognosis: Often persistent, particularly in tardive cases, but usually causes little distress.
pearls: Always ask the patient whether they feel restless inside.
Pseudoakathisia often travels with tardive dyskinesia.
In demented patients, objective restlessness may be the only sign of true akathisia.
det.thd: Pseudoakathisia คือการขยับตัวหรือเดินไปมาที่ดูเหมือน akathisia แต่ผู้ป่วยไม่มีความรู้สึกกระวนกระวายภายใน มักพบในผู้ที่ได้ยาต้านโรคจิตมานานซึ่งเป็นส่วนหนึ่งของ tardive syndrome หรือเกิดจากความปวดและชาที่ขา ต้องถามความรู้สึกภายในเสมอและทบทวนยา การรักษาคือปรับยาต้านโรคจิตและรักษาสาเหตุทางความรู้สึก

ddx.pt: Subjective inner restlessness is the defining feature
Evening urge to move the legs relieved by walking
Choreiform orofacial and limb movements without restlessness

aN: pseudo akathisia | objective akathisia without subjective restlessness | restless movements without inner restlessness

name: Pseudobulbar palsy
formal: Bilateral corticobulbar lesions causing dysarthria, dysphagia, brisk jaw jerk, spastic tongue and emotional lability; seen in motor neuron disease, PSP and bilateral strokes.
simple: A condition from damage to nerve pathways to the brainstem, causing slurred speech, trouble swallowing and sudden laughing or crying.
th: ภาวะที่ทางเดิน corticobulbar ทั้งสองข้างเสียหาย ทำให้พูดช้าแบบเกร็ง กลืนลำบาก ลิ้นแข็งโดยไม่ลีบ jaw jerk ไว และหัวเราะหรือร้องไห้ควบคุมไม่ได้ ต่างจาก bulbar palsy ที่เป็น LMN และต่างจาก opercular syndrome ที่เด่นเรื่องสั่งไม่ได้แต่ทำเองได้
tempoNote: Abrupt after a second hemispheric or capsular stroke; gradual in ALS, PSP, multiple sclerosis and diffuse small vessel disease
feat: Slow, strained, spastic dysarthria and dysphagia with choking on liquids
Small, stiff tongue with slow movements, no wasting or fasciculation
Brisk jaw jerk, exaggerated gag and snout or palmomental release signs
Pseudobulbar affect: sudden laughing or crying out of proportion to mood, ended abruptly
Bilateral corticobulbar damage, whether cortical, capsular or brainstem; the cortical opercular form lacks emotional release and shows the voluntary–automatic split most clearly
inv: MRI brain for bilateral infarcts, extensive small vessel disease, demyelination or midbrain atrophy
EMG of bulbar and limb muscles to look for lower motor neuron involvement suggesting ALS
Bedside swallow screen, then videofluoroscopy or FEES; aspiration risk decides diet and feeding route
Quantify pseudobulbar affect with a validated lability scale (CNS-LS) and screen for depression

case.who: 70-year-old woman from Phetchabun with hypertension and a stroke two years ago
case.story: After a new small left capsular infarct her speech became slow and strained, drinks make her cough, and she bursts into tears when the grandchildren arrive, then stops within seconds.
case.exam: Spastic dysarthria, small stiff tongue without fasciculation, brisk jaw jerk and gag, bilateral Babinski sign, emotional crying that is mismatched to mood and ends abruptly; she can still yawn and swallow saliva.
case.tests: MRI: old right corona radiata infarct, new left internal capsule infarct and widespread white matter lesions; Center for Neurologic Study–Lability Scale score is high.
case.q: Why is this pseudobulbar rather than bulbar palsy, and what would you offer for the crying episodes?
case.a: Upper motor neuron signs (brisk jaw jerk, stiff tongue) from bilateral corticobulbar lesions; keep her safe with a swallow assessment and treat the stroke risk, and offer an SSRI or low-dose tricyclic for the emotional lability.

read.where: Chapter 13 Cranial Nerve Disorders — Bulbar and Pseudobulbar Palsy
Chapter 13 Cranial Nerve Disorders — Pseudobulbar Palsy
17. Lower Brainstem and Cranial Nerve Dysfunction
20 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Cerebral Hemispheres

det.patho: The trigeminal motor, facial, glossopharyngeal, vagal and hypoglossal nuclei receive corticobulbar input from both hemispheres, so one-sided damage usually spares function. When both pathways are damaged at the cortex, subcortical white matter, internal capsule or upper brainstem, the nuclei lose voluntary and inhibitory supranuclear control but their lower motor neurons remain intact. Disinhibited brainstem reflex circuits explain the brisk jaw jerk, spasticity and emotional release. Opercular and subopercular lesions are a special pattern in which voluntary control is lost while automatic and emotional movements stay available.
det.clinical: Causes include bilateral strokes, diffuse small vessel disease, ALS, PSP, multiple sclerosis, traumatic injury and bilateral opercular lesions. Speech is slow, harsh and strained, and swallowing is uncoordinated, with aspiration a major risk. Pseudobulbar affect (episodes of laughing or crying without matching emotion) is often mistaken for depression. In the opercular syndrome the picture differs: onset is abrupt, muscles may be flaccid, emotional lability is rare, and voluntary use of face, tongue and pharynx is lost while yawning, smiling and reflex swallowing continue.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, based on upper motor neuron bulbar signs with evidence of bilateral pathway damage. Test voluntary against automatic movement; a striking dissociation suggests the opercular syndrome. MRI identifies vascular, demyelinating and degenerative causes, and EMG looks for mixed ALS. Swallow assessment defines safety, and a scale such as the CNS-LS helps quantify pseudobulbar affect.
det.treatment: Treat the cause, add speech and swallow therapy, adapt textures and use gastrostomy when oral intake fails. Pseudobulbar affect responds to SSRIs or low-dose tricyclics; dextromethorphan–quinidine is licensed in some countries but availability varies. Family education that the episodes are involuntary reduces distress. Antithrombotic therapy and risk-factor control prevent further bilateral damage.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause: stable or improving after stroke, relentless in ALS or PSP.
pearls: Spastic tongue, brisk jaw jerk and emotional lability point to supranuclear (pseudobulbar) disease, not bulbar palsy.
Lost voluntary movement with preserved yawning and smiling suggests the opercular or subopercular variant.
Pseudobulbar affect is treatable and often misread as depression.
det.thd: Pseudobulbar palsy เกิดจากรอยโรค corticobulbar ทั้งสองข้าง ทำให้พูดช้าแบบเกร็ง กลืนลำบาก ลิ้นแข็งไม่ลีบ jaw jerk ไว และหัวเราะหรือร้องไห้ควบคุมไม่ได้ ผู้ป่วยบางรายเป็น opercular syndrome ที่สั่งให้ขยับหน้าและลิ้นไม่ได้แต่ยังหาวหรือยิ้มได้เอง ตรวจ MRI ประเมินการกลืน และแยกจาก bulbar palsy ที่เป็น LMN รักษาตามสาเหตุ ฝึกพูดและกลืน และใช้ SSRI หรือ tricyclic ขนาดต่ำสำหรับ pseudobulbar affect

Acute, often limp muscles and little emotional release; voluntary movements are lost while yawning and laughing are spared

name: Pseudodementia
formal: Cognitive impairment caused by depression that mimics dementia, with variable effort, prominent complaints and good response to antidepressants.
simple: Memory and thinking problems caused by depression rather than true dementia, which often improve with treatment.
th: ภาวะบกพร่องทางการรู้คิดจากโรคซึมเศร้า (โดยเฉพาะวัยสูงอายุ) ที่ดูคล้ายสมองเสื่อม ดีขึ้นได้เมื่อรักษาซึมเศร้า แต่เป็นปัจจัยเสี่ยงและอาจเป็นสัญญาณแรกของสมองเสื่อมจริง
tempoNote: Cognitive complaints build over weeks to a few months alongside low mood; onset can often be dated
feat: Loud complaints of poor memory, often exceeding what relatives observe
Frequent 'don't know' answers, patchy and uneven results on tasks of similar difficulty
Recent and remote events lost to a similar degree; attention often fairly preserved
Psychomotor slowing with low mood, anhedonia, sleep and appetite change
No aphasia, apraxia or focal signs; recognition better than free recall
inv: Structured depression scale (GDS-15, PHQ-9) paired with MoCA or MMSE; a full dementia work-up is still advised
Reversible-cause screen: TSH, B12, glucose, electrolytes, calcium, drug and alcohol review, others as indicated
Neuropsychology (recognition vs recall, delayed-recall retention) and MRI brain; amyloid/tau biomarkers when the picture is uncertain
Re-test cognition after mood has recovered

case.who: 71-year-old retired civil servant from Chiang Mai
case.story: After a hospital admission and the loss of his sister he has felt hopeless for about three months, sleeps little and eats poorly. He insists his memory is 'finished', yet his son says he still manages the household bills and recalls family events.
case.exam: Slow, flat and tearful; answers 'I don't know' to many items but improves with encouragement. Fluent speech, normal naming, no apraxia, no focal signs.
case.tests: MoCA 21/30 with erratic errors; GDS-15 score 12; recognition clearly better than free recall; TSH, B12 and MRI brain unremarkable for age.
case.q: What is the most likely explanation, and what must be arranged after treatment starts?
case.a: Depression-related cognitive impairment (pseudodementia); treat the depression, then repeat cognitive testing once mood recovers and keep long-term follow-up because late-life depression can precede true dementia.

det.patho: Kiloh introduced the label in 1961 for cases that closely mimic dementia, and it is now used mainly for the cognitive profile of late-life depression. The name carries two parts: a real cognitive deficit (the dementia part) and the absence of a neurodegenerative cause (the pseudo part). Proposed mechanisms include poor effortful encoding, reduced motivation and arousal, frontal-subcortical dysfunction and, in some, temporal lobe change such as smaller hippocampi. Contemporary usage prefers depression-related cognitive impairment or late-life depression with cognitive symptoms.
det.clinical: Patients show slowed thinking, weak concentration and poor learning, with executive findings such as set-shifting difficulty and reduced fluency, and almost universal psychomotor slowing. Classic descriptions note that recent and remote events are lost alike, that gaps are patchy, and that 'don't know' replies are frequent, with performance swinging widely across tasks of comparable difficulty. Memory loss is generally milder than in Alzheimer disease, implicit memory is spared, and language and naming are mostly better than in dementia. The diagnosis is hard because normal ageing blurs the boundary, the two conditions may coexist, and early Alzheimer or Parkinson disease can itself bring low mood.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical and integrative: establish a depressive syndrome with a structured scale, characterise cognition with bedside and formal testing, and remove reversible contributors. Recognition performance, the rate of forgetting over delays and effort-dependent variability separate depression from Alzheimer disease better than total scores. Brief screens such as MMSE may show little difference, so neuropsychology adds value. Because false positive and false negative dementia diagnoses are both common, a full dementia evaluation is recommended whenever pseudodementia is suspected, and cognition must be reassessed after remission.
det.treatment: Treat the depression with an SSRI or similar agent, psychotherapy and behavioural activation, and use ECT for severe, psychotic or treatment-resistant illness. Avoid anticholinergic and sedative drugs that worsen cognition, and correct hearing, vision, sleep and isolation. Cognition often improves with mood, but some memory and executive deficits can persist after recovery, so monitor and consider rehabilitation. Schedule regular cognitive reviews rather than discharging the patient after one good response.
det.prognosis: In a long follow-up cohort, about 71 percent of patients with depressive pseudodementia later developed dementia versus about 18 percent of cognitively intact controls, whereas another series treated intensively saw cognition return to baseline with recurrences managed. Outcome therefore varies; lifelong surveillance is prudent.
pearls: Reversible cognitive impairment in moderate-to-severe late-life depression is a strong predictor of later dementia, not a reassurance.
Frequent 'don't know' answers, uneven effort and recognition better than recall favour depression; rapid forgetting and confident errors favour Alzheimer disease.
Mood recovery improves many but not all cognitive measures; retest after remission.
det.thd: Pseudodementia หรือภาวะบกพร่องทางการรู้คิดจากซึมเศร้า พบบ่อยในผู้สูงอายุ ผู้ป่วยมักบ่นเรื่องความจำมาก ตอบว่าไม่รู้บ่อย ทำแบบทดสอบได้ไม่สม่ำเสมอ ช้าลงทั้งความคิดและการเคลื่อนไหว แต่จำแบบมีตัวเลือกได้ดีกว่าการเล่าเอง การวินิจฉัยใช้แบบประเมินซึมเศร้าร่วมกับการทดสอบความจำ ตรวจหาสาเหตุที่แก้ไขได้ และประเมินสมองเสื่อมให้ครบถ้วน รักษาด้วยยาต้านซึมเศร้า จิตบำบัด หรือ ECT ในรายรุนแรง แล้วทดสอบความจำซ้ำเมื่อหายซึมเศร้า ควรติดตามระยะยาวเพราะผู้ป่วยส่วนหนึ่งกลายเป็นสมองเสื่อมจริงในภายหลัง

ddx.pt: Patient minimises deficits, tries hard, gives wrong answers, and forgets new material rapidly despite cues
Memory deficit persists and is stable or worsening after mood is treated, with no prominent depression
Stepwise or focal course with vascular risk factors, executive slowing and infarcts or white matter disease on MRI

aN: depressive pseudodementia | dementia syndrome of depression | reversible cognitive impairment of depression | depression related cognitive impairment

name: PSP-corticobasal syndrome (PSPCBS)
formal: Clinical presentation of corticobasal syndrome with underlying progressive supranuclear palsy pathology, showing asymmetric rigidity, apraxia and alien limb with eventual gaze palsy and falls.
simple: A condition that looks like corticobasal syndrome but is due to progressive supranuclear palsy, causing arm clumsiness and later eye movement problems.
more: MRI shows midbrain atrophy; diagnosis confirmed at autopsy. Symptomatic therapy only and survival is similar to PSP.
th: PSP ที่มาด้วยอาการแบบ corticobasal syndrome เช่น เกร็งข้างเดียว apraxia และ alien limb ต่อมาจึงมี gaze palsy และล้มบ่อย
tempoNote: Insidious, progressive over years
feat: Asymmetric limb rigidity, dystonia and bradykinesia unresponsive to levodopa
Limb apraxia, cortical sensory loss and alien limb phenomena
Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and early falls appear later
Frontal executive impairment and nonfluent speech in some
Pathology is 4-repeat tau of PSP type rather than CBD
inv: MRI: midbrain atrophy (hummingbird) with asymmetric frontoparietal atrophy
DaT-SPECT abnormal; FDG-PET asymmetric cortical and midbrain hypometabolism
Amyloid biomarkers to exclude Alzheimer-related CBS

case.story: Two years of a clumsy, stiff left hand that 'does its own thing'; now falling backwards.
case.exam: Left arm rigidity and dystonic posture, ideomotor apraxia, left agraphaesthesia, slow vertical saccades, positive retropulsion.
case.tests: MRI shows right parietal atrophy and midbrain atrophy; amyloid PET negative; no levodopa response.
case.q: Why is this called PSP-CBS rather than simply corticobasal degeneration?
case.a: CBS is the clinical syndrome; when vertical gaze palsy and early falls are added, PSP pathology is the more likely cause, though only autopsy settles it.

read.where: Chapter 9 Movement Disorders — Progressive Supranuclear Palsy
14 Progressive Supranuclear Palsy and Corticobasal Degeneration

det.patho: PSP is a 4-repeat tauopathy with tufted astrocytes and neurofibrillary tangles in the basal ganglia, subthalamic nucleus and brainstem. In PSP-CBS, tau burden extends more into frontoparietal cortex asymmetrically, producing cortical signs. Pathological overlap with CBD is considerable.
det.clinical: The 2017 MDS criteria recognise PSP-CBS as a variant: patients present with asymmetric limb rigidity, apraxia and cortical sensory signs, then develop the vertical gaze palsy, postural instability and frontal signs typical of PSP. It accounts for a small proportion of PSP. Clinical distinction from CBD is unreliable.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis uses MDS PSP criteria: CBS features plus at least one PSP core feature. MRI midbrain atrophy and an MR parkinsonism index support PSP. Amyloid biomarkers exclude Alzheimer CBS. Definitive diagnosis is neuropathological.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy; anti-tau trials have failed. Levodopa may be tried but rarely helps; botulinum toxin for painful dystonia. Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and swallowing therapy and early palliative planning are essential.
det.prognosis: Median survival about 6–8 years from onset, often ending in aspiration pneumonia.
pearls: CBS is a syndrome with several possible pathologies: CBD, PSP, Alzheimer disease, FTLD-TDP.
Vertical gaze palsy plus early falls in CBS point towards PSP pathology.
Check amyloid status before labelling CBS as tauopathy.
det.thd: PSP-CBS คือโรค PSP ที่แสดงอาการแบบ corticobasal syndrome เช่น แขนข้างหนึ่งเกร็ง ทำท่าทางไม่ได้ (apraxia) และ alien limb ต่อมาจึงมีกลอกตาขึ้นลงไม่ได้และล้มง่าย MRI พบ midbrain atrophy ร่วมกับสมองฝั่งตรงข้ามฝ่อ การยืนยันต้องตรวจพยาธิวิทยา รักษาแบบประคับประคอง

ddx.pt: Pathological entity; may produce CBS without prominent gaze palsy
Richardson phenotype with early falls and gaze palsy without marked asymmetry
Amyloid-positive CBS with memory or parietal predominance

aN: pspcbs | psp corticobasal syndrome | psp cbs | corticobasal presentation of psp | psp with predominant cbs

name: Psychogenic parkinsonism
formal: Functional parkinsonism with inconsistent, distractible slowness and tremor, sudden onset, lack of fatigue, entrainable tremor and normal dopamine imaging.
simple: Parkinson-like symptoms that arise from a functional brain problem rather than neurodegeneration, with signs that vary or improve when distracted.
more: Normal DaT scan helps. Explanation, physiotherapy and psychotherapy are the main treatments, and many improve.
th: parkinsonism แบบ functional ที่อาการช้าและสั่นไม่คงที่ เปลี่ยนเมื่อเบี่ยงความสนใจ เริ่มทันที และ DaT scan ปกติ
tempoNote: Often abrupt onset, sometimes after a trigger, then a fluctuating chronic course
feat: Sudden onset, often maximal early, sometimes after injury, illness or stress
Slowness without true decrement or fatigue of repetitive movements
Tremor that varies in frequency, entrains to tapping and stops with distraction
Effortful 'giving way' resistance rather than lead-pipe rigidity; no cogwheeling without tremor
Other functional signs (functional weakness, non-anatomical sensory loss) frequently coexist
inv: DaT-SPECT normal (important as true PD can coexist with functional features)
Accelerometry/EMG to document entrainment and frequency variability
MRI brain normal or non-specific

case.who: 45-year-old female market vendor from Nakhon Si Thammarat
case.story: After a motorcycle accident three months ago she suddenly became slow, stiff and tremulous in the right arm.
case.exam: Right arm tremor changes frequency and stops when she taps a rhythm with the left hand; finger taps slow but without progressive decrement; rigidity varies with conversation.
case.tests: DaT-SPECT normal; MRI brain normal.
case.q: What positive signs support the diagnosis and how should it be explained?
case.a: Functional parkinsonism (entrainment, distractibility, no decrement, normal DaT scan); explain it as a real, common, treatable problem of brain function and refer to specialist physiotherapy.

read.where: Chapter 9 Movement Disorders — Functional Movement Disorders
27 - Functional (psychogenic) movement disorders: Phenomenology, diagnosis, and treatment

det.patho: Functional movement disorders reflect abnormal brain control of movement, with altered attention, prediction and sense of agency, rather than structural damage. Precipitating events such as injury, panic or illness are common, and psychological factors may play a part, though they are not a prerequisite for making the diagnosis. Dopaminergic pathways are intact.
det.clinical: Functional parkinsonism is relatively rare among functional movement disorders. Patients show slowness that does not decrement, variable tremor and give-way resistance. Onset is often abrupt and early disability can be severe. Up to a small proportion of patients have a coexisting degenerative disorder, so caution is needed in older patients.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is made on positive clinical signs, not by exclusion alone. Entrainment, distractibility and variable resistance are key; neurophysiology adds objective support. A normal DaT-SPECT supports the diagnosis when clinical doubt exists.
det.treatment: Explain the diagnosis clearly and without stigma. Specialist physiotherapy using retraining and attention redirection is first line, often combined with CBT-based psychotherapy. Stop unhelpful dopaminergic drugs. Treat comorbid anxiety, depression or pain.
det.prognosis: Many improve with early diagnosis and therapy, but long duration and fixed beliefs predict persistence.
pearls: Diagnose functional disorders on positive signs, not just normal tests.
Lack of decrement on tapping is a strong clue.
A normal DaT-SPECT does not exclude drug-induced or vascular parkinsonism.
det.thd: Psychogenic (functional) parkinsonism คืออาการคล้ายพาร์กินสันจากการทำงานของสมองผิดปกติ ไม่ใช่เซลล์โดปามีนเสื่อม มักเริ่มทันที อาการสั่นเปลี่ยนตามจังหวะที่ให้เคาะและหายเมื่อเบี่ยงความสนใจ DaT-SPECT ปกติ รักษาด้วยการอธิบายและกายภาพบำบัดเฉพาะทางร่วมกับจิตบำบัด

ddx.pt: Gradual asymmetric onset, decrement on tapping, abnormal DaT-SPECT
Exposure to dopamine blockers; symmetric; normal DaT-SPECT but no functional signs
Umbrella category; parkinsonism is one of its less common forms

aN: functional parkinsonism | psychogenic parkinsonism | fnd parkinsonism | non organic parkinsonism

name: Psychogenic tremor
formal: Functional tremor with abrupt onset, variability, entrainment to external rhythm and distractibility, with coactivation sign and suggestibility.
simple: A shake that comes from a functional problem rather than disease damage, and often changes when attention is distracted.
more: Use accelerometry or surface EMG for entrainment and coherence; tremor frequency changes when tapping with the opposite hand. Treatment includes explanation, physiotherapy and CBT; prognosis is variable, with improvement in many. Functional tremor with variable frequency and amplitude, entrainment to voluntary rhythm, distractibility and co-contraction, often with a sudden onset and suggestibility.
th: Psychogenic (functional) tremor คือ functional tremor ที่พบบ่อยที่สุดในกลุ่ม functional movement disorder เริ่มเฉียบพลัน ความถี่และทิศทางเปลี่ยนได้ ถูกดึงความสนใจแล้วเปลี่ยนหรือหยุด และเกิด entrainment ตามจังหวะที่เคาะด้วยมืออีกข้าง ตรวจเสริมด้วย accelerometry และ coherence ได้ การรักษาคือการอธิบายอย่างชัดเจน กายภาพบำบัดเฉพาะทาง และการรักษาทางจิตใจเมื่อมีปัจจัยร่วม
tempoNote: Often begins suddenly, sometimes after an injury or emotional event, is maximal soon after onset and fluctuates; may persist for years without treatment
feat: Abrupt onset with an obvious precipitant in many patients, and a tremor that is present at rest, in posture and in action in the same patient
Entrainment: the tremor adopts the rhythm of voluntary tapping with the other hand, or the tremor stops or changes frequency during that task
Distractibility: amplitude drops when attention is drawn away (serial sevens, ballistic movements of the other hand) and increases when attention is on it
Coactivation sign: the limb stiffens and tremor increases when the examiner passively moves it, because opposing muscles co-contract; the tremor may spread or change body part over time
Often accompanied by give-way weakness, pain, fatigue or other functional signs; tremor is the commonest functional movement disorder
inv: Surface EMG with accelerometry: entrainment, variable frequency, coherence between limbs, increase of tremor with added weight (loading) in organic but not in functional tremor
Clinical examination for dystonic posturing, rigidity or other organic signs; MRI only if atypical
Thyroid tests and a drug review; DaT-SPECT if functional parkinsonism is suspected

case.story: Right-hand shaking began suddenly the day after a workplace dispute and injury to his shoulder; it changes from side-to-side to up-and-down, and he cannot hold a cup, yet he can sign his name with little shake.
case.exam: Tremor stops briefly when he throws a ball with the left hand and takes on the speed of left-hand tapping; no rigidity, normal reflexes, no other neurological signs.
case.tests: Accelerometry confirms entrainment and variable frequency.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the evidence-based treatment?
case.a: Functional tremor; positive explanation, specialist physiotherapy, and psychological therapy when relevant, avoiding unnecessary drugs.

27 - Functional (psychogenic) movement disorders: Phenomenology, diagnosis, and treatment
5 Electrophysiological Approaches to the Movement Disorder Patient

det.patho: Functional tremor reflects a disorder of motor control in which attention and expectation drive the movement. Tremor frequency often equals the rate that the patient can generate voluntarily (about 4–7 Hz), and entrainment suggests that the oscillation is under a form of attentional control. Functional imaging indicates altered connectivity in networks that process agency and self-attribution.
det.clinical: In large series from movement-disorder centres, tremor is the commonest functional movement disorder, and patients are more often women of working age. The tremor starts suddenly, is present in several postures, is variable in frequency and direction, and responds to distraction. Many patients have associated functional signs (weakness, sensory change, speech abnormalities) and psychological or pain comorbidity, but a trigger may be absent. Functional tremor can coexist with an organic tremor.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on positive signs: entrainment to a rhythm, distractibility, variability, coactivation and a rise in amplitude when attention is directed. Neurophysiology is very helpful: accelerometry shows variable frequency, and tests such as weight loading can separate it from essential tremor and parkinsonism, as the amplitude of the functional tremor tends to increase rather than fall with a heavier load in a different pattern. Investigations are targeted at the mimics, such as thyrotoxicosis, drug tremor and Wilson disease.
det.treatment: Give a confident positive diagnosis and explain that the tremor is genuine and potentially reversible. Specialist physiotherapy that retrains automatic movement by shifting attention away from the limb is the main treatment, and psychotherapy (cognitive behavioural therapy, trauma-focused therapy) helps when anxiety, depression or past trauma contribute. Avoid beta-blockers or anticholinergics in the hope of an effect, and avoid repeated tests. Education materials and patient groups support recovery.
det.prognosis: Many patients improve substantially with early diagnosis and therapy, but a sizeable group keep symptoms for years, and recovery is better with short duration and acceptance of the diagnosis.
pearls: Ask the patient to tap a rhythm with the other hand; the functional tremor follows or stops.
Tremor that is variable in frequency and direction is rarely organic.
Organic and functional tremor may coexist; do not stop looking after finding one.
det.thd: Psychogenic (functional) tremor คือ functional tremor ที่เกิดฉับพลัน ความถี่และทิศทางเปลี่ยนได้ ลดลงหรือหยุดเมื่อผู้ป่วยทำสิ่งที่ต้องใช้สมาธิ และเปลี่ยนตามจังหวะที่เคาะด้วยมืออีกข้าง (entrainment) ตรวจเพิ่มด้วย accelerometry/EMG ได้ ควรวินิจฉัยจาก positive signs และอธิบายผู้ป่วยอย่างชัดเจนว่าเป็นโรคจริงที่หายได้ การรักษาหลักคือกายภาพบำบัดเฉพาะทางและจิตบำบัดเมื่อมีปัจจัยร่วม

qx.stem: A 36-year-old nurse developed a right-hand tremor abruptly after a minor fall at work. The tremor varies in frequency and direction. When she is asked to tap a 3 Hz rhythm with her left hand, the right-hand tremor shifts to the same rhythm; when she performs serial sevens it pauses.
qx.q: How should these findings be interpreted?
opts: They suggest early Parkinson disease
They are positive signs supporting a functional tremor
They indicate essential tremor with anxiety
They are nonspecific and require DaT-SPECT before any diagnosis
They point to a cerebellar outflow tremor
qx.why: Entrainment to a contralateral rhythm and suppression with distraction are positive clinical signs of functional (psychogenic) tremor, and the diagnosis should be made on these signs rather than by exclusion. Organic tremors keep their own frequency. Management includes clear explanation and specialised physiotherapy or psychological therapy.

name: Pulmonary artery aneurysms (PAA)
formal: Focal pulmonary artery dilatation seen with Behcet disease, Hughes-Stovin syndrome and infection; may rupture causing haemoptysis and is relevant to neurology via cerebral venous thrombosis.
simple: A bulge in a lung artery that can burst, linked to inflammatory conditions such as Behcet disease.
th: หลอดเลือดแดงปอดโป่งพอง พบใน Behçet และ Hughes-Stovin syndrome อาจแตกทำให้ไอเป็นเลือด เกี่ยวข้องกับประสาทวิทยาผ่านภาวะหลอดเลือดดำในสมองอุดตัน
tempoNote: Develops over months; rupture with massive haemoptysis is sudden
feat: Not a primary neurological disease: a pulmonary vascular lesion with neurological associations
Main cause in young adults is Behçet disease, mostly in men
Haemoptysis, cough, chest pain; rupture can be fatal
Hughes-Stovin syndrome: PAA plus deep vein and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
Also from infection (mycotic), pulmonary hypertension or trauma
inv: CT pulmonary angiography to define aneurysms and in-situ thrombosis
MRI/MR venography of the brain when headache or papilloedema suggests CVT
Pathergy test, HLA-B51 and ophthalmology review for Behçet features

case.story: Recurrent oral and genital ulcers for years; now three weeks of headache, blurred vision and two episodes of coughing blood.
case.exam: Bilateral papilloedema, no focal weakness, oral aphthae, scrotal scars.
case.tests: CT pulmonary angiography: two right lower lobe artery aneurysms with mural thrombus; MRV: superior sagittal sinus thrombosis.
case.q: What unifying disease is present, and why is routine anticoagulation risky?
case.a: Vasculo-Behçet with pulmonary artery aneurysms and CVT; aneurysms may rupture, so immunosuppression is the backbone and anticoagulation is decided cautiously with specialist input.

det.patho: In Behçet disease, neutrophil and lymphocyte inflammation of the vasa vasorum weakens the pulmonary artery wall, leading to true or false aneurysms often lined by thrombus. The same vasculitic tendency produces venous thrombosis elsewhere, including dural sinuses. Hughes-Stovin syndrome is widely regarded as a Behçet variant without the mucocutaneous features.
det.clinical: Patients are usually young men with active Behçet disease who develop cough, fever, dyspnoea and haemoptysis, which may be massive. Neurological relevance is indirect: cerebral venous thrombosis, parenchymal neuro-Behçet lesions or embolic events may coexist. The entry is included in the lexicon as a systemic vascular lesion, not as a disease of the nervous system itself.
det.diagnosis: CT pulmonary angiography is the key test and also shows thrombus within aneurysms, which can mimic pulmonary embolism. Look for Behçet criteria (oral ulcers plus genital ulcers, eye, skin or pathergy findings). Image the brain venous sinuses when there are headache, visual blurring or seizures.
det.treatment: Treatment is high-dose glucocorticoids with cyclophosphamide or anti-TNF agents (infliximab) for Behçet-related aneurysms. Anticoagulation for venous thrombosis is controversial because of bleeding risk from aneurysms and is weighed case by case. Bleeding aneurysms need urgent embolisation or surgery.
det.prognosis: Mortality was high historically, but immunosuppression and endovascular therapy have improved survival; aneurysms can shrink with treatment.
pearls: Haemoptysis in a young man with orogenital ulcers: suspect Behçet pulmonary aneurysm.
Do not reflexively anticoagulate 'PE' in Behçet before excluding aneurysms.
Screen for CVT when such a patient has headache or papilloedema.
det.thd: Pulmonary artery aneurysm คือหลอดเลือดแดงปอดโป่งพอง ไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาทโดยตรง สาเหตุสำคัญคือ Behçet ในชายหนุ่ม อาจไอเป็นเลือดรุนแรง ความเกี่ยวข้องทางระบบประสาทคือมักพบร่วมกับ cerebral venous thrombosis ตรวจด้วย CT pulmonary angiography และ MRV สมอง รักษาด้วย steroid ร่วมกับ cyclophosphamide หรือ anti-TNF ส่วนการให้ยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือดต้องระวังเพราะเสี่ยงหลอดเลือดแตก

ddx.pt: The usual underlying cause; look for orogenital ulcers, uveitis and skin pathergy
The neurological complication to screen for; headache, papilloedema, seizures
