name: Pyogenic intracranial epidural abscess
formal: Collection of pus between dura and skull usually from sinusitis, otitis or neurosurgery, causing fever, headache and focal signs; needs drainage and antibiotics.
simple: A pocket of pus between the skull and the brain's outer covering, usually after a sinus or ear infection or surgery.
th: หนองสะสมระหว่างกะโหลกกับ dura มักตามหลังไซนัสอักเสบ หูหรือ mastoid อักเสบ หรือหลังผ่าตัดสมอง ทำให้ไข้ ปวดหัว และอาจมีอาการเฉพาะที่
tempoNote: Develops over days to weeks, more indolent than subdural empyema because the dura is bound to the skull
feat: Fever and headache, often localised, in an adolescent or young man with sinusitis, otitis or recent head surgery
Forehead swelling (Pott's puffy tumour) or ear discharge may point to the source
Focal deficits, seizures and raised intracranial pressure are less frequent than with subdural empyema
May extend into the subdural space, the meninges, brain tissue or a venous sinus
Subdural and epidural empyema in children arise from sinusitis, chronic mastoiditis, penetrating injury or meningitis
inv: Contrast MRI (or CT): a lens-shaped extra-axial collection that may cross the midline but not sutures; DWI shows restricted diffusion in pus
Blood cultures, CRP, white count; avoid lumbar puncture before imaging
Sinus or mastoid CT to find the source
Culture of pus at surgery for organism and sensitivity

case.story: After two weeks of nasal congestion he developed fever, frontal headache and a puffy forehead.
case.exam: Temperature 38.7 °C, tender boggy swelling over the forehead; no meningism or focal deficit.
case.tests: MRI: frontal sinusitis, frontal bone osteomyelitis and a lens-shaped enhancing extradural collection with restricted diffusion.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the treatment plan?
case.a: Frontal epidural abscess with Pott's puffy tumour; neurosurgical drainage with sinus surgery plus prolonged IV antibiotics covering streptococci, anaerobes and staphylococci.

read.where: Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — Intracranial Epidural Abscess

det.patho: Infection reaches the epidural space from paranasal sinuses, middle ear or mastoid by contiguity or emissary veins, or after craniotomy and trauma. The dura is firmly bound to the skull, so the collection grows slowly and stays localised, which explains the often indolent course. Common organisms are streptococci (especially the S. anginosus group), anaerobes and Staphylococcus aureus, often mixed.
det.clinical: Presentation is subacute fever and headache, sometimes with a swollen forehead or ear discharge, and many patients do not look unwell. Focal signs appear late or if the infection extends to the subdural space, where thrombosis of cortical veins and vasculitis lead to hemiparesis, seizures and decreasing consciousness. Meningitis that deteriorates after initial improvement, or persistent raised pressure of uncertain cause, should raise suspicion of an empyema.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is by neuroimaging: CT shows a lens-shaped hypodense collection under the skull and MRI with diffusion and contrast shows it more clearly, along with the sinus or bone infection. CSF is often unhelpful, showing mild lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose, and lumbar puncture risks herniation. Obtain cultures of blood and pus.
det.treatment: Management combines surgical drainage and source control (for example sinus washout or mastoidectomy) with prolonged intravenous antibiotics, commonly a third-generation cephalosporin and metronidazole with vancomycin when staphylococci are possible, narrowed to cultures and given for several weeks. Anticonvulsants treat seizures, and corticosteroids may be used to lower pressure in some children under specialist advice. Small, uncomplicated collections may be managed with antibiotics alone under close imaging follow-up.
det.prognosis: Good with early drainage and antibiotics; delays risk spread to subdural empyema, cerebral venous thrombosis and long-term deficits.
pearls: Teenager with sinusitis and forehead swelling: image for intracranial extension.
Epidural collections are lens-shaped; subdural empyema is crescentic and more dangerous.
Treat the source as well as the abscess.
det.thd: Epidural abscess ในกะโหลกคือหนองสะสมระหว่างกะโหลกกับเยื่อ dura มักเป็นภาวะแทรกซ้อนของไซนัสอักเสบ หูหรือ mastoid อักเสบ หรือหลังผ่าตัดสมอง ผู้ป่วยมีไข้ ปวดหัว บางรายหน้าผากบวม (Pott's puffy tumour) วินิจฉัยด้วย CT หรือ MRI เห็นก้อนรูปเลนส์ที่ผิวใต้กะโหลก หลีกเลี่ยงการเจาะหลังก่อนถ่ายภาพ รักษาด้วยการระบายหนอง กำจัดแหล่งติดเชื้อ และยาปฏิชีวนะทางหลอดเลือดดำนานหลายสัปดาห์

name: Pyomyositis
formal: Bacterial muscle abscess, usually Staphylococcus aureus, in tropical or immunocompromised patients, with fever, pain, swelling and raised CK.
simple: A pus-forming bacterial infection inside a muscle, causing fever and pain.
more: MRI or ultrasound is diagnostic; treat with drainage and antibiotics.
th: การติดเชื้อแบคทีเรียเป็นหนองในกล้ามเนื้อ มักเป็น Staphylococcus aureus พบในเขตร้อนหรือผู้ภูมิคุ้มกันต่ำ มีไข้ ปวด บวม
tempoNote: Evolves over 1–3 weeks from diffuse pain to abscess and sepsis
feat: Fever with localised deep muscle pain, often thigh, gluteal, iliopsoas or calf
Woody induration early, then fluctuant swelling
Risk factors: diabetes, HIV, malnutrition, trauma, injection drug use, chemotherapy
Iliopsoas abscess mimics hip disease or appendicitis
Can progress to septic shock if untreated
inv: MRI or ultrasound to locate and stage the collection
Blood cultures and aspirate culture; CK often normal or mildly raised
CRP and white cell count high; check glucose and HIV

case.who: 52-year-old male rubber tapper from Trang with diabetes
case.story: Ten days of fever and worsening pain in the left thigh after a fall; now cannot walk.
case.exam: Febrile, tender firm swollen left thigh without overlying redness; hip movement painful but possible.
case.tests: WBC 19,000, CRP 210 mg/L, HbA1c 11%; MRI thigh shows intramuscular abscess in vastus lateralis; pus grows MSSA.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the treatment?
case.a: Pyomyositis; drainage (percutaneous or surgical) plus antistaphylococcal antibiotics such as cloxacillin or cefazolin, and diabetes control.

det.patho: Healthy skeletal muscle resists infection, so pyomyositis usually requires an injured muscle plus transient bacteraemia, often in an immunocompromised or undernourished host. S. aureus causes most cases; streptococci, Gram-negatives, TB and fungi occur in some hosts. Melioidosis is an important cause in northeast Thailand.
det.clinical: Classically there are three stages: invasive (diffuse pain, low fever), suppurative (abscess, high fever) and late (sepsis, metastatic infection). It is a non-neurological infection but enters neurology differential diagnosis because of pain, limb weakness and raised muscle enzymes.
det.diagnosis: MRI is most sensitive; ultrasound guides aspiration. Cultures from blood and pus define the organism. CK is often surprisingly normal. In Thailand, send cultures for Burkholderia pseudomallei in diabetics.
det.treatment: Drain abscesses and give IV antibiotics targeted to culture; cover MRSA if prevalent and melioidosis in endemic areas. Duration is usually 2–6 weeks depending on extent. Control blood sugar and treat underlying immunosuppression.
det.prognosis: Good with early treatment; mortality rises with delayed diagnosis and sepsis.
pearls: Fever plus deep muscle pain in a diabetic: image for pyomyositis.
Normal CK does not exclude muscle infection.
Consider melioidosis in northeast Thai patients.
det.thd: Pyomyositis คือฝีหนองในกล้ามเนื้อจากแบคทีเรีย ส่วนใหญ่เป็น S. aureus พบบ่อยในผู้ป่วยเบาหวาน ภูมิคุ้มกันต่ำ หรือหลังบาดเจ็บ มีไข้และปวดบวมกล้ามเนื้อลึก ๆ เช่น ต้นขา วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI หรืออัลตราซาวนด์และเพาะเชื้อ รักษาด้วยการระบายหนองและยาปฏิชีวนะ ในภาคอีสานต้องนึกถึง melioidosis

name: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) deficiency
formal: Deficiency causing peripheral neuropathy, seizures in infants, dermatitis and anaemia; seen with isoniazid, alcohol or malnutrition, whereas excess also produces a sensory neuronopathy.
simple: Too little vitamin B6, which can cause nerve damage, seizures in babies and skin problems.
more: Check erythrocyte transaminase activity or plasma pyridoxal phosphate; infantile seizures respond to IV pyridoxine, and pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy involves ALDH7A1. Give prophylactic B6 with isoniazid; avoid chronic high-dose supplements.
th: ภาวะขาดวิตามินบี 6 ทำให้ปลายประสาทอักเสบ ชักในทารก ผื่นผิวหนังและโลหิตจาง พบในผู้ใช้ isoniazid ดื่มสุรา หรือขาดอาหาร ส่วนการได้รับเกินก็ทำให้ปลายประสาทเสียได้
tempoNote: Neuropathy develops over weeks to months of deficiency; infant seizures can be acute
feat: Distal sensory-predominant neuropathy with burning feet and paraesthesia
Seizures in neonates and infants, sometimes refractory status
Seborrhoeic dermatitis, angular cheilitis, glossitis, microcytic (sideroblastic) anaemia
Confusion, depression and irritability in adults
Risk: isoniazid, hydralazine, penicillamine, levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel, alcohol, dialysis, malnutrition
inv: Plasma pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP) level
Nerve conduction: length-dependent axonal sensorimotor neuropathy
In infants: EEG during IV pyridoxine trial and testing for ALDH7A1/PNPO dependency
Check other B vitamins, alcohol use and drug history

case.story: Started a 6-month TB regimen without B6 supplementation; after 2 months he has burning, numb feet. He also drinks daily.
case.exam: Stocking sensory loss to the ankles, absent ankle jerks, cracked lip corners.
case.tests: Low plasma PLP; NCS shows reduced sural amplitudes.
case.q: How could this have been prevented?
case.a: Isoniazid-related B6 deficiency neuropathy: routine pyridoxine 10–50 mg/day with isoniazid in at-risk patients prevents it; treat now with pyridoxine and stop alcohol.

read.where: Chapter 125: Neurologic Complications of Nutritional Disorders

det.patho: Pyridoxal 5'-phosphate is a cofactor for more than 100 enzymes, including those making GABA, serotonin and dopamine and those in haem synthesis. Deficiency lowers brain GABA, provoking seizures, and impairs peripheral nerve metabolism, causing axonal neuropathy. Isoniazid and similar drugs bind and inactivate pyridoxal; excessive supplementation is separately toxic to dorsal root ganglion neurons.
det.clinical: In adults the typical picture is a painful, distal, predominantly sensory neuropathy, sometimes with weakness, after months of deficiency, often alongside skin and mucosal signs and anaemia. Infants with dietary deficiency or genetic pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy develop seizures that resist standard drugs. Severe deficiency may cause confusion, depression and irritability. Deficiency often coexists with other nutritional problems.
det.diagnosis: Measure plasma PLP, recognising that inflammation and low albumin lower it. NCS shows axonal neuropathy. In infants with refractory seizures, give an IV or oral pyridoxine trial with EEG monitoring and send biomarkers and genes for pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (urinary alpha-AASA, ALDH7A1) and PNPO deficiency. Review drugs and alcohol.
det.treatment: Replace with oral pyridoxine at modest doses (for example 25–100 mg/day in adults) and correct the cause; prophylaxis is advised with isoniazid in people with diabetes, alcohol use, malnutrition, HIV, renal failure or pregnancy. Avoid long-term high doses, which can cause neuropathy. Infant seizures respond to pyridoxine 100 mg IV under monitoring; dependency syndromes need lifelong treatment, and PNPO deficiency may need pyridoxal phosphate.
det.prognosis: Neuropathy improves over months with replacement if caught early; delayed treatment of infantile forms can leave developmental impairment.
pearls: Isoniazid + no B6 + burning feet = preventable neuropathy.
Both too little and too much B6 damage nerves; check supplements in every neuropathy history.
Refractory neonatal seizures deserve a pyridoxine trial.
det.thd: ภาวะขาดวิตามินบี 6 พบในผู้ป่วยที่ได้ยา isoniazid โดยไม่ได้เสริม B6 ดื่มสุรา หรือขาดอาหาร ทำให้ปลายประสาทชาแสบร้อนที่เท้า ผื่นรอบปาก ซีด และในทารกทำให้ชักรักษายาก ตรวจระดับ PLP ในเลือดและ NCS รักษาด้วยการให้ B6 ขนาดพอเหมาะและป้องกันโดยให้ B6 คู่กับ isoniazid แต่การกิน B6 ขนาดสูงนาน ๆ ก็ทำให้เส้นประสาทเสียได้

name: Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) deficiency
formal: X-linked (PDHA1) or recessive disorder of pyruvate metabolism with lactic acidosis, hypotonia, ataxia, seizures, developmental delay and brain malformations such as Leigh-like lesions.
simple: An inherited energy metabolism disease causing weakness, seizures, and developmental delay due to lactic acid build-up.
more: Raised lactate and pyruvate; enzyme assay and genetics. A ketogenic diet and thiamine may help, but prognosis is guarded.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมการเผาผลาญ pyruvate (ส่วนใหญ่ X-linked จากยีน PDHA1) ทำให้กรดแล็กติกสูง ตัวอ่อน เดินเซเป็นพัก ๆ ชัก พัฒนาการช้า และมีความผิดปกติของสมองแบบ Leigh
tempoNote: Severe forms present with neonatal lactic acidosis; milder forms show episodic ataxia, dystonia or weakness triggered by illness or carbohydrate load
feat: Neonatal or infantile lactic acidosis with hypotonia, poor feeding and seizures
Developmental delay and microcephaly, sometimes brain malformations such as callosal agenesis or cysts
Leigh-type brain disease in infancy
Intermittent ataxia (median onset around 18 months), recurrent dystonia or episodic weakness in milder cases
Neuropathy mimicking Guillain-Barré syndrome in some patients
inv: Blood and CSF lactate and pyruvate: raised lactate with a normal lactate:pyruvate ratio
MRI and MR spectroscopy: lactate peak, basal ganglia or brainstem lesions, callosal agenesis
PDH enzyme activity in fibroblasts or lymphocytes; gene panel (PDHA1, PDHB, PDHX, DLAT, PDP1)

case.story: Since infancy he has had episodes of unsteady walking during fevers. After a festival with many sugary drinks he became floppy and drowsy.
case.exam: Truncal ataxia, mild hypotonia, intermittent abnormal eye movements, mildly delayed development.
case.tests: Plasma lactate 6 mmol/L with a lactate:pyruvate ratio of 12; MRI shows bilateral globus pallidus lesions; PDHA1 variant.
case.q: Which dietary strategy is the mainstay, and which vitamin should be trialled?
case.a: A ketogenic diet to bypass the block, plus a thiamine trial because some variants respond; avoid carbohydrate loading.

det.patho: The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, the rate-limiting link between glycolysis and the TCA cycle. When it fails, pyruvate is shunted to lactate and alanine, and the brain, which depends on glucose oxidation, becomes energy-starved. Most cases arise from the E1-alpha subunit gene PDHA1 on Xp22, with heterozygous females also affected because of skewed X-inactivation; other subunits and regulators cause autosomal recessive forms.
det.clinical: Presentations run from fatal neonatal lactic acidosis with brain malformations, through infantile Leigh syndrome, to milder disease with intermittent ataxia, recurrent dystonia, weakness or neuropathy provoked by fever or carbohydrate. Seizures, microcephaly and developmental delay are common. Facial dysmorphism resembling fetal alcohol syndrome is described in some. Episodic weakness can be mistaken for Guillain-Barré syndrome, so keep it in mind in children with relapsing courses.
det.diagnosis: Raised lactate and pyruvate with a normal lactate:pyruvate ratio (below about 20) favours PDH deficiency over a respiratory chain defect. CSF lactate is often more informative than blood. MRI and MRS show a lactate peak and basal ganglia, brainstem or callosal abnormalities. Enzyme assay and genetic testing confirm the diagnosis, and results guide family counselling.
det.treatment: A ketogenic diet supplies ketones as an alternative brain fuel and is the main therapy, ideally started early. High-dose thiamine is trialled because a few variants respond. Dichloroacetate, which activates residual PDH, can lower lactate but is not standard and carries neuropathy risk. During illness avoid high-dextrose infusions where possible, and treat seizures, acidosis and dehydration promptly.
det.prognosis: Variable. Severe neonatal forms are often fatal or leave profound disability, whereas milder forms treated early with ketogenic diet may achieve meaningful developmental gains.
pearls: High lactate with a normal lactate:pyruvate ratio points to PDH deficiency.
Worse after carbohydrate and better on ketogenic diet is the clinical signature.
Most PDHA1 cases are X-linked, so girls can be affected too.
det.thd: PDH deficiency เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมที่เอนไซม์ pyruvate dehydrogenase ทำงานไม่ได้ ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจากยีน PDHA1 บนโครโมโซม X ทำให้ pyruvate กลายเป็น lactate กรดแล็กติกในเลือดสูง สมองขาดพลังงาน เด็กอาจมีตัวอ่อน ชัก พัฒนาการช้า เดินเซเป็นพัก ๆ ตอนมีไข้หรือกินแป้งน้ำตาลมาก และ MRI พบรอยโรคแบบ Leigh วินิจฉัยจาก lactate สูงโดยอัตราส่วน lactate ต่อ pyruvate ปกติ ตรวจเอนไซม์และยีน การรักษาหลักคืออาหาร ketogenic ร่วมกับทดลองให้ thiamine และหลีกเลี่ยงน้ำตาลปริมาณมาก

name: Quetiapine akathisia
formal: Antipsychotic-induced akathisia presenting with subjective restlessness and motor urge, reported with quetiapine despite its low dopamine D2 affinity.
simple: Inner restlessness and an urge to keep moving caused by the medicine quetiapine.
th: akathisia จากยา quetiapine มีความรู้สึกกระวนกระวายภายในและอยากขยับตัว แม้ quetiapine จะจับ D2 receptor ได้น้อย
tempoNote: Days to weeks after starting or increasing the dose
feat: Inner restlessness, inability to sit still, need to pace
Rocking, shifting weight, crossing and uncrossing legs
Less common with quetiapine than high-potency antipsychotics but still reported
Can worsen anxiety, agitation and suicidal thoughts; may reduce adherence
Risk higher with rapid titration and combination with other dopamine blockers or SSRIs
inv: Clinical diagnosis; Barnes Akathisia Rating Scale
Review all drugs including antiemetics and SSRIs
Check ferritin; consider restless legs if symptoms are nocturnal and leg-focused

case.who: 28-year-old woman with bipolar disorder from Khon Kaen
case.story: Quetiapine was increased to 400 mg/day a week ago; she now feels unbearable restlessness and paces the ward at all hours.
case.exam: Constant shifting in the chair, marching on the spot when standing; no rigidity or tremor.
case.tests: Barnes scale global score 3; ferritin normal.
case.q: What is happening and what are the treatment options?
case.a: Quetiapine-induced akathisia; reduce the dose or switch, and consider propranolol, low-dose mirtazapine or a benzodiazepine.

read.where: Chapter 9 Movement Disorders — Movement Disorders Associated with Dopamine Receptor Blockade or Dopamine Depletion

det.patho: Akathisia is linked to mesocortical and mesolimbic dopamine blockade, with contributions from serotonergic and noradrenergic systems. Quetiapine dissociates rapidly from D2 receptors, giving lower risk, but akathisia still occurs, especially at higher doses or with other serotonergic or dopaminergic drugs.
det.clinical: Patients describe inner tension and urge to move, with visible restlessness. It is often mistaken for worsening psychosis or anxiety, leading to dose increases that make it worse. It may be associated with impulsivity and suicidality.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, based on temporal link to the drug and both subjective and objective restlessness. Rating scales help monitor response. Distinguish from agitation, RLS and anxiety.
det.treatment: Reduce dose, slow titration or switch to an agent with lower risk. Propranolol, mirtazapine (low dose), benzodiazepines and vitamin B6 have supportive evidence. Anticholinergics help mainly if parkinsonism coexists.
det.prognosis: Usually resolves within days to weeks after dose adjustment.
pearls: Restlessness after an antipsychotic increase is akathisia until proved otherwise.
Even low-D2 drugs like quetiapine can cause it.
Do not increase the antipsychotic for 'agitation' without excluding akathisia.
det.thd: Quetiapine akathisia คือภาวะกระวนกระวาย นั่งไม่ติด อยากขยับตัวตลอด หลังเริ่มหรือเพิ่มยา quetiapine แม้ยานี้จับ D2 ได้น้อย ต้องแยกจากอาการทางจิตกำเริบและ RLS รักษาโดยลดหรือเปลี่ยนยา และใช้ propranolol, mirtazapine ขนาดต่ำ หรือ benzodiazepine

Appears late or persists after stopping the drug

name: Rabbit syndrome
formal: Late antipsychotic-related perioral tremor producing rapid rhythmic lip movements about 5 Hz, distinct from tardive dyskinesia and responsive to anticholinergics.
simple: Fast regular lip movements, like a rabbit chewing, that can be a side effect of antipsychotic medicines.
th: อาการสั่นของริมฝีปากเป็นจังหวะเร็วประมาณ 5 Hz คล้ายกระต่ายเคี้ยว จากยาต้านโรคจิตใช้นาน ต่างจาก tardive dyskinesia และตอบสนองต่อยา anticholinergic
tempoNote: Appears months to years after antipsychotic exposure
feat: Fine, rapid, rhythmic vertical lip and jaw movements around 5 Hz
Tongue spared, unlike tardive dyskinesia
Persists during sleep less, worsens with stress
Often accompanied by other drug-induced parkinsonian signs
Typical with high-potency antipsychotics; reported with atypicals
inv: Clinical diagnosis with video; EMG can confirm rhythmic 4–6 Hz bursts
Medication review
MRI only if atypical or no drug exposure

case.who: 59-year-old man with schizophrenia from Suphan Buri
case.story: On haloperidol for 6 years; family notices quick chewing-like movements of his lips.
case.exam: Rhythmic 5 Hz vertical lip tremor, tongue still inside the mouth; mild symmetric bradykinesia.
case.tests: Video and EMG confirm 5 Hz rhythmic activity in orbicularis oris.
case.q: Why is this not tardive dyskinesia and what treatment helps?
case.a: It is rabbit syndrome: regular, rhythmic, tongue-sparing perioral tremor; it responds to anticholinergics and to reducing or switching the antipsychotic, whereas anticholinergics may worsen TD.

det.patho: Rabbit syndrome is a localised parkinsonian tremor from chronic D2 receptor blockade. Its rhythmicity and anticholinergic responsiveness align it with drug-induced parkinsonism rather than the hypersensitivity mechanism of tardive dyskinesia.
det.clinical: It appears after months or years of antipsychotic use, is rhythmic and restricted to lips and jaw. Patients may be unaware. It is rare and probably underrecognised.
det.diagnosis: Clinical observation; video and EMG help confirm rhythmic 4–6 Hz activity. Look at the tongue: sparing points to rabbit syndrome.
det.treatment: Anticholinergics (e.g., trihexyphenidyl, benztropine) are effective. Reduce the antipsychotic or switch to clozapine or quetiapine.
det.prognosis: Usually reversible with treatment, though some cases persist.
pearls: Rhythmic lip tremor sparing the tongue: rabbit syndrome.
Treat with anticholinergics, unlike TD.
det.thd: Rabbit syndrome คืออาการริมฝีปากสั่นเป็นจังหวะเร็วราว 5 Hz คล้ายกระต่ายเคี้ยว จากการใช้ยาต้านโรคจิตเป็นเวลานาน ลิ้นไม่ขยับ ซึ่งต่างจาก tardive dyskinesia ถือเป็น parkinsonism เฉพาะที่ รักษาด้วยยา anticholinergic และลดหรือเปลี่ยนยาต้านโรคจิต

name: Radiation-induced leucoencephalopathy
formal: Delayed diffuse white matter injury after cranial irradiation, often with methotrexate, causing cognitive decline, gait disorder and incontinence with periventricular T2 hyperintensity.
simple: White matter damage in the brain that appears months to years after radiation, causing memory, walking and bladder problems.
th: สมองส่วนเนื้อขาวเสียหายแบบกระจายหลังฉายรังสีที่ศีรษะหลายเดือนถึงหลายปี ทำให้ความคิดช้า เดินลำบาก และกลั้นปัสสาวะไม่ได้
tempoNote: Appears months to years after cranial radiotherapy and progresses slowly; may plateau
feat: History of whole-brain or large-field cranial irradiation, often combined with methotrexate
Slowed processing, poor attention and executive dysfunction more than pure amnesia
Short-stepped, unsteady gait and urinary urgency or incontinence
Confluent symmetric periventricular white matter T2/FLAIR change with ventricular enlargement
Microbleeds, calcification or atrophy may accompany later stages
inv: MRI brain with FLAIR and SWI to show diffuse white matter change, microbleeds and exclude tumour recurrence
Neuropsychological testing to document subcortical-frontal deficits
Consider high-volume CSF tap test if ventriculomegaly suggests hydrocephalus

case.story: Treated three years ago with whole-brain radiotherapy for lung cancer brain metastases. His wife notes he is slow, loses track of conversations and recently wets himself before reaching the toilet.
case.exam: Psychomotor slowing, poor verbal fluency, magnetic short-stepped gait, brisk reflexes; no new focal weakness.
case.tests: MRI: symmetric confluent periventricular FLAIR hyperintensity with enlarged ventricles and scattered microbleeds; no enhancing lesions.
case.q: What late complication explains this triad, and what treatable mimic should be considered?
case.a: Radiation-induced leukoencephalopathy; check for communicating hydrocephalus (tap test, possible shunt) and exclude recurrent metastasis.

det.patho: Radiation damages endothelium and oligodendrocyte precursors, leading to small-vessel hyalinisation, chronic hypoperfusion and progressive demyelination with axonal loss. Risk rises with total dose, large field size, fraction size, older age, vascular risk factors and concurrent or subsequent methotrexate. Neurogenesis in the hippocampus is also impaired, which adds to memory difficulty.
det.clinical: It typically emerges six months to several years after treatment as slowed thinking, inattention and executive dysfunction, then gait disturbance and urinary symptoms in more severe cases. Mild forms cause only subtle cognitive complaints, while severe forms produce a subcortical dementia with apathy and dependency. Children irradiated for medulloblastoma or leukaemia may show learning difficulty and falling IQ. Stroke-like episodes (SMART syndrome) and cavernomas are other late radiation effects to recognise.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis rests on a compatible time course after cranial radiotherapy and MRI showing diffuse, symmetric white matter change often with atrophy and microbleeds. Tumour recurrence, radiation necrosis (enhancing mass), PML, hydrocephalus and drug or metabolic encephalopathy must be excluded. Perfusion MRI or PET may help separate recurrence from treatment effect.
det.treatment: There is no proven reversal therapy. Memantine during and after whole-brain radiotherapy and hippocampal-avoidance techniques reduce cognitive decline and are now standard prevention where feasible. Treat vascular risk factors, consider shunting for coexisting hydrocephalus, and use stimulants or cholinesterase inhibitors on an individual basis. Rehabilitation, bladder management and caregiver support are central.
det.prognosis: Course is usually slowly progressive or stabilising; severe forms leave lasting disability.
pearls: Gait, cognition and bladder problems after brain irradiation: think radiation leukoencephalopathy but test for hydrocephalus.
Methotrexate given after radiotherapy markedly increases white matter injury.
Hippocampal sparing plus memantine is the modern way to prevent it.
det.thd: Radiation-induced leukoencephalopathy เป็นผลระยะยาวจากการฉายรังสีที่สมอง ทำให้เนื้อขาวเสียหายจากหลอดเลือดเล็กและเซลล์สร้างไมอีลิน ผู้ป่วยคิดช้า สมาธิลดลง เดินสั้น ๆ และกลั้นปัสสาวะไม่ได้ MRI พบ white matter hyperintensity กระจายสมมาตร ต้องแยกเนื้องอกกลับเป็นซ้ำและ NPH ป้องกันได้ด้วยการฉายรังสีเลี่ยง hippocampus และให้ memantine

qx.stem: A 66-year-old man treated two years ago for CNS lymphoma with high-dose methotrexate followed by whole-brain radiotherapy has developed slowed thinking, gait apraxia and urinary urgency. MRI shows confluent periventricular white matter hyperintensity and cortical atrophy without enhancing mass; PET shows no tumour.
qx.q: What best explains the lesson of this case for treatment planning?
opts: It is an acute reaction that resolves without sequelae
Delayed neurotoxicity is more frequent when whole-brain radiotherapy follows methotrexate in older patients, so it is often avoided or reduced in this group
It signifies relapse and requires repeat radiotherapy
It results from vitamin B12 deficiency alone
It is a feature of toxoplasmosis
qx.why: Combined chemoradiotherapy produces delayed leucoencephalopathy with dementia, gait disturbance and incontinence, especially after about 60 years of age, which is why upfront whole-brain radiotherapy is limited in older patients. Absence of enhancing tumour argues against relapse.

name: Radiation-induced neurological disease
formal: Spectrum of acute, early delayed and late injury to brain, spinal cord and nerves after radiotherapy, including necrosis, myelopathy, cognitive decline and neuropathies.
simple: Damage to the brain, spinal cord or nerves caused by radiation treatment, which can appear soon or many years later.
ab: radiation injury of the nervous system
th: กลุ่มความผิดปกติของสมอง ไขสันหลัง และเส้นประสาทที่เกิดจากการฉายรังสี แบ่งเป็นระยะเฉียบพลัน ระยะกลาง และระยะท้าย
tempoNote: Acute: days–weeks; early delayed: 1–6 months; late delayed: months to many years after treatment
feat: Acute: headache, nausea and worsened deficits from oedema during treatment
Early delayed: somnolence syndrome in children, transient worsening or Lhermitte sign
Late: focal radiation necrosis, leukoencephalopathy and cognitive decline, progressive myelopathy
Peripheral: painless brachial or lumbosacral plexopathy with myokymia, optic neuropathy, lower cranial neuropathies
Very late: vasculopathy with stroke, cavernomas and radiation-induced tumours such as meningioma
inv: MRI of the irradiated field, with perfusion or PET to separate necrosis from tumour
EMG/NCS for plexopathy (myokymic discharges support radiation over tumour)
Review radiation dose, field and timing with the oncology team

case.story: Had breast cancer treated with surgery and axillary radiotherapy eight years ago. Over a year her left hand has slowly become weak and numb without pain.
case.exam: Weakness of left shoulder and arm muscles in an upper-trunk pattern, patchy sensory loss, absent biceps jerk, woody induration of the supraclavicular skin.
case.tests: EMG shows myokymic discharges in left arm muscles; MRI brachial plexus has diffuse T2 change without a mass.
case.q: Which radiation complication is this and what feature argues against tumour infiltration?
case.a: Radiation-induced brachial plexopathy; painless slow progression with myokymia favours radiation injury over recurrent cancer, which is usually painful.

det.patho: Ionising radiation injures dividing glial progenitors and vascular endothelium, causing oedema early and small-vessel fibrosis, ischaemia and demyelination later. Damage depends on total dose, dose per fraction, volume irradiated, concurrent chemotherapy and host vascular health. Radiation can also induce DNA damage leading to secondary tumours many years later.
det.clinical: Acute reactions during treatment are oedema-related and steroid-responsive. Early delayed effects 1–6 months later include somnolence, transient worsening of tumour symptoms (pseudoprogression) and Lhermitte phenomenon from transient cord demyelination. Late effects are usually irreversible: radiation necrosis, leukoencephalopathy with dementia, progressive myelopathy, optic neuropathy, plexopathy, accelerated large-artery stenosis and moyamoya-like vasculopathy, cavernomas and new tumours. Endocrine failure from hypothalamic–pituitary irradiation may also impair cognition and energy.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis needs a compatible lesion inside the radiation field, appropriate latency, and exclusion of tumour progression, infection or paraneoplastic disease. Advanced MRI (perfusion, spectroscopy) and amino-acid or FDG-PET help separate necrosis from recurrence, though biopsy is sometimes needed. Neurophysiology is valuable for plexopathy.
det.treatment: Acute and early reactions respond to corticosteroids. Symptomatic radiation necrosis can be treated with steroids and bevacizumab, or surgical resection; hyperbaric oxygen has limited evidence. Late leukoencephalopathy and myelopathy have no proven reversal, so prevention through dose constraints, hippocampal sparing and memantine matters most. Pain, spasticity, bladder and rehabilitation care are supportive.
det.prognosis: Acute and early delayed effects usually resolve; late delayed injuries tend to be permanent or progressive.
pearls: Learn the three time windows: acute (oedema), early delayed (reversible demyelination), late delayed (necrosis/vasculopathy).
Painless plexopathy with myokymia years after radiotherapy suggests radiation injury; painful plexopathy suggests tumour.
Enhancing lesion after radiosurgery may be necrosis — perfusion imaging before calling it recurrence.
det.thd: Radiation-induced neurological disease คือความเสียหายต่อระบบประสาทจากการฉายรังสี แบ่งเป็นระยะเฉียบพลัน (สมองบวม) ระยะกลาง (ไมอีลินเสียชั่วคราว) และระยะท้าย (เนื้อสมองตาย เนื้อขาวเสื่อม ไขสันหลังเสื่อม และ plexopathy) การวินิจฉัยต้องอยู่ในบริเวณที่ฉายรังสีและแยกจากเนื้องอกกลับเป็นซ้ำ ระยะต้นตอบสนองต่อ steroid ส่วน radiation necrosis อาจใช้ bevacizumab แต่ภาวะระยะท้ายส่วนใหญ่ถาวร

name: Radiation-induced optic neuropathy
formal: Delayed painless visual loss 3 to 24 months after irradiation of the anterior visual pathway, with optic nerve or chiasm enhancement on MRI and poor recovery.
simple: Painless loss of vision months after radiation treatment near the eye or brain damages the optic nerve.
th: ตามัวโดยไม่เจ็บแบบล่าช้า 3–24 เดือนหลังฉายรังสีบริเวณทางเดินการมองเห็นส่วนหน้า MRI พบเส้นประสาทตาหรือ chiasm enhance และฟื้นตัวได้น้อย
tempoNote: Delayed onset months after radiotherapy, then progression over weeks
feat: Sudden or rapidly progressive painless visual loss, unilateral or bilateral
Typically 1–3 years (range months to years) after sellar, sinus, nasopharyngeal or orbital radiotherapy
Disc often normal initially (posterior involvement), pale later
Risk rises with dose above about 54 Gy, diabetes, older age, chemotherapy

case.story: Treated with chemoradiotherapy for nasopharyngeal carcinoma 18 months ago; over two weeks his left eye vision became dim.
case.exam: VA 6/60 left, left RAPD, discs look normal.
case.tests: MRI shows enhancement of the left intracranial optic nerve and chiasm without tumour recurrence.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what is the expected outcome?
case.a: Radiation-induced optic neuropathy; visual prognosis is poor, though bevacizumab, steroids or hyperbaric oxygen are sometimes tried early.

det.patho: Radiation causes delayed injury to the vascular endothelium and glial cells of the optic nerve, leading to an obliterative endarteritis, demyelination and necrosis. The latency reflects slow turnover of these cells. Dose per fraction and total dose are the main risk factors.
det.clinical: Patients develop painless, often abrupt visual loss months to years after radiotherapy near the visual pathway. Retrobulbar involvement means the disc is initially normal. Progression over weeks to severe loss is common, and the other eye may be affected.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the clinical setting plus MRI enhancement of the nerve or chiasm and exclusion of tumour recurrence. Visual fields document the pattern. Consider chiasmal compression, secondary tumours and ischaemic neuropathy.
det.treatment: There is no proven treatment. Hyperbaric oxygen, high-dose steroids and bevacizumab have been used with mixed results, ideally very early. Prevention by careful dose planning (keeping the optic pathway below tolerance) is most important.
det.prognosis: Most patients end with severe permanent visual loss in the affected eye.
pearls: Painless visual loss after head and neck radiotherapy: think RION, not only recurrence.
Normal disc at onset because injury is posterior.
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma survivors in Thailand are an at-risk group.
det.thd: Radiation-induced optic neuropathy เกิดจากเส้นประสาทตาเสียหายหลังฉายรังสีบริเวณศีรษะ เช่น มะเร็งโพรงหลังจมูก มักมีตามัวโดยไม่เจ็บหลังฉายรังสีหลายเดือนถึงหลายปี MRI พบเส้นประสาทตาหรือ chiasm enhance โดยไม่มีเนื้องอกกลับมา ยังไม่มีการรักษาที่ได้ผลแน่นอน และการมองเห็นมักไม่ฟื้น

name: Radiation-induced plexopathy
formal: Progressive brachial or lumbosacral plexus injury after radiotherapy, with painless weakness, sensory loss and myokymia on EMG; differentiated from tumour recurrence by pain absence.
simple: Nerve damage in the shoulder or pelvis area after radiation, causing slowly progressive weakness and numbness in the arm or leg.
th: brachial หรือ lumbosacral plexus เสียหายหลังฉายรังสีเป็นปีขึ้นไป ทำให้อ่อนแรงไม่เจ็บ ชา และ EMG พบ myokymia
tempoNote: Starts months to many years (often over a decade) after radiotherapy and progresses slowly
feat: History of radiotherapy to axilla, neck, supraclavicular region or pelvis (breast cancer, lymphoma, cervical cancer)
Painless or mildly painful progressive weakness and numbness, often upper trunk in brachial cases
Lymphoedema and indurated irradiated skin
Myokymic discharges on EMG are a strong clue
Tumour recurrence is the main alternative: more pain, lower trunk, Horner sign
inv: EMG/NCS: axonal loss with myokymia, sometimes conduction block
MRI plexus with contrast: diffuse T2 change without a mass
PET-CT if MRI equivocal to exclude recurrence; biopsy in difficult cases

case.who: 61-year-old woman in Bangkok treated for left breast cancer with surgery and axillary radiotherapy 14 years ago
case.story: Two years of slowly increasing weakness in the left shoulder and arm, mild tingling, little pain.
case.exam: Left deltoid, biceps and supraspinatus weakness, reduced biceps jerk, firm lymphoedematous arm, no Horner sign.
case.tests: EMG shows chronic denervation in C5–6 muscles with myokymic discharges; MRI shows diffuse plexus T2 signal and fibrosis without a mass; PET negative.
case.q: Is this cancer recurrence or radiation injury, and what can be offered?
case.a: Radiation-induced plexopathy (painless, upper trunk, myokymia, no mass); management is supportive — physiotherapy, pain control and lymphoedema care.

read.where: Chapter 20 Neuro-Oncology — Neurological Complications of Cancer Treatments

det.patho: Radiation damages small vessels and fibroblasts, causing progressive fibrosis that entraps and ischaemically injures plexus axons. The process continues long after treatment, explaining the late onset and progression. Risk rises with total dose, fraction size, concurrent chemotherapy and overlapping fields.
det.clinical: Onset is usually years after treatment, with slowly worsening painless weakness and sensory loss, often favouring the upper trunk in brachial cases. Fasciculations and myokymia may be seen. Some patients have an early transient form within months of treatment that recovers. Lumbosacral forms produce bilateral, asymmetric leg weakness.
det.diagnosis: Distinguishing radiation injury from tumour recurrence is the central question. Painless onset, myokymia on EMG and absence of a mass on MRI or PET favour radiation. Biopsy may be needed if imaging is equivocal.
det.treatment: No therapy reverses the damage; care focuses on physiotherapy, orthoses, lymphoedema management and neuropathic pain drugs. Neurolysis has a limited role. Pentoxifylline with vitamin E, hyperbaric oxygen and anticoagulation have been tried with weak evidence.
det.prognosis: Usually slowly progressive over years, leading to significant arm or leg disability in many patients.
pearls: Myokymia on EMG favours radiation injury over tumour.
Pain and Horner sign favour recurrence.
Onset can be decades after radiotherapy.
det.thd: Radiation-induced plexopathy คือ plexus เสียหายจากพังผืดและหลอดเลือดเล็กถูกทำลายหลังฉายรังสี มักเกิดหลังรักษามะเร็งเต้านมหรือมะเร็งในอุ้งเชิงกรานหลายปี อ่อนแรงค่อยเป็นค่อยไปและมักไม่ปวด EMG พบ myokymia ส่วน MRI ไม่พบก้อน ต้องแยกจากมะเร็งกลับเป็นซ้ำซึ่งมักปวดมากและมี Horner sign การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง

name: Radiation-induced tumours
formal: Secondary neoplasms such as meningiomas, gliomas and sarcomas arising years after radiotherapy in the irradiated field.
simple: Tumours that develop many years after radiation treatment, within the area that was treated.
th: เนื้องอกทุติยภูมิที่เกิดขึ้นในบริเวณที่เคยฉายรังสีหลายปีก่อน เช่น meningioma, glioma และ sarcoma
tempoNote: Latency of years to decades after radiotherapy (meningiomas often 20–35 years, gliomas around 10)
feat: New tumour inside a previously irradiated field, often after childhood cranial radiotherapy (leukaemia, medulloblastoma, tinea capitis in the past)
Meningiomas: frequently multiple, atypical histology, higher recurrence
Gliomas: usually high grade, poor prognosis
Sarcomas of bone or soft tissue in the skull or neck field
inv: Contrast MRI with comparison to old fields and imaging
Biopsy or resection for histology and molecular profile
Long-term MRI surveillance programmes for childhood cancer survivors

case.who: 33-year-old man from Bangkok, survivor of childhood leukaemia
case.story: He had cranial radiation at age 6; now he has headaches and a first focal seizure.
case.exam: Mild left arm weakness, otherwise normal.
case.tests: MRI: two dural-based enhancing masses in the right convexity and falx.
case.q: What is the likely cause of these tumours, and how do they differ from sporadic ones?
case.a: Radiation-induced meningiomas; they arise younger, are more often multiple and atypical, and recur more.

det.patho: Ionising radiation causes DNA double-strand breaks and chromosomal rearrangements; cells that survive with oncogenic changes can give rise to tumours many years later. Risk rises with dose, younger age at exposure and genetic predisposition (e.g. NF1, Li-Fraumeni). Radiation-induced meningiomas often carry NF2 rearrangements and complex karyotypes; gliomas frequently show PDGFRA amplification and differ molecularly from sporadic ones.
det.clinical: Presentation depends on the tumour type and site: headache, seizures, focal deficits or cranial neuropathies. Criteria for a radiation-induced tumour are that it arises in the radiation field, differs histologically from the original tumour, and appears after a latent period. Survivors also have higher rates of cavernous malformations and vasculopathy.
det.diagnosis: MRI identifies the lesion; distinguishing tumour from radiation necrosis may need perfusion MRI, spectroscopy or PET. Tissue confirms the diagnosis and grade. Review records of prior radiotherapy fields and doses.
det.treatment: Surgery is the main treatment for meningiomas; re-irradiation is used cautiously and selectively. Radiation-induced gliomas are treated similarly to sporadic high-grade gliomas but outcomes are worse, and prior radiation limits further dosing. Long-term survivorship clinics should provide MRI surveillance.
det.prognosis: Meningiomas are usually controllable but recur more often; induced gliomas and sarcomas have poor survival.
pearls: New brain tumour in a childhood cancer survivor: ask about cranial radiotherapy.
Multiple meningiomas in a young adult: think radiation or NF2.
Separate recurrent tumour from radiation necrosis with advanced imaging.
det.thd: Radiation-induced tumours คือเนื้องอกที่เกิดในบริเวณที่เคยฉายรังสี มักหลายปีถึงหลายสิบปีต่อมา ที่พบบ่อยคือ meningioma ซึ่งมักมีหลายก้อนและกลับเป็นซ้ำ และ glioma ชนิดรุนแรง ผู้ป่วยมีประวัติฉายรังสีศีรษะตั้งแต่เด็ก วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI และชิ้นเนื้อ รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัดเป็นหลัก และต้องตรวจติดตามผู้รอดชีวิตจากมะเร็งในเด็กระยะยาว

name: Radiculoneuropathy
formal: Combined disease of nerve roots and peripheral nerves, seen in diabetes, CIDP, Lyme, sarcoidosis and lymphomatous infiltration.
simple: Damage to both the nerve roots at the spine and the nerves beyond them, causing weakness, numbness and pain.
th: โรคที่เกิดพร้อมกันทั้งรากประสาทและเส้นประสาทส่วนปลาย พบในเบาหวาน CIDP โรคติดเชื้อ sarcoidosis และมะเร็งต่อมน้ำเหลืองแทรกซึมเส้นประสาท
tempoNote: Tempo depends on cause: weeks in diabetic or infectious forms, months to years in CIDP
feat: Weakness that is both proximal and distal, often asymmetric
Radicular pain, sometimes severe, in a root or plexus distribution
Early, widespread loss of reflexes
Sensory loss not confined to a stocking-glove pattern
Weight loss or systemic symptoms in diabetic, malignant or infectious forms
inv: NCS/EMG: prolonged F-waves and paraspinal denervation point to root involvement along with nerve changes
CSF: raised protein (cytoalbuminological dissociation); cells and cytology when infection or lymphoma is possible
MRI of spine and plexus with contrast: root enhancement or thickening
Glucose/HbA1c, serum electrophoresis, HIV, syphilis, Lyme where relevant; PET-CT if neurolymphomatosis suspected

case.who: 64-year-old man from Khon Kaen with type 2 diabetes
case.story: Severe burning pain in the right thigh began eight weeks ago, followed by wasting and weakness of that leg; he lost 8 kg.
case.exam: Right hip flexor and quadriceps weakness, absent right knee jerk, mild weakness of left ankle dorsiflexion; reduced sensation over the right thigh.
case.tests: HbA1c 7.2%; EMG shows denervation in right lumbar paraspinal and thigh muscles plus distal sensorimotor axonal changes; CSF protein 0.9 g/L, 2 cells.
case.q: What is the likely syndrome?
case.a: Diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy — a painful, asymmetric root, plexus and nerve disorder that usually improves slowly.

read.where: 13. Chronic Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyradiculoneuropathy, Multifocal Motor Neuropathy, and Related Disorders

det.patho: Radiculoneuropathy is a descriptive term for disease affecting spinal roots and peripheral nerves together. Mechanisms include immune-mediated demyelination (GBS, CIDP), microvasculitis (diabetic and non-diabetic radiculoplexus neuropathy), infection of roots (Lyme, CMV, HIV, syphilis, leprosy), granulomatous inflammation (sarcoidosis) and infiltration by lymphoma or carcinoma. The proximal root involvement explains early areflexia and proximal weakness.
det.clinical: Patients present with combined proximal and distal weakness, early widespread areflexia and sensory symptoms that do not follow a length-dependent pattern. Pain is prominent in vasculitic, diabetic, infectious and malignant forms. Systemic clues such as weight loss, rash, lymphadenopathy, fever or immunosuppression narrow the cause. Cauda equina involvement may add sphincter problems.
det.diagnosis: Electrodiagnosis shows nerve conduction abnormalities plus signs of root disease such as absent or delayed F-waves and paraspinal denervation. CSF protein is usually raised; pleocytosis suggests infection, malignancy or sarcoidosis. Gadolinium MRI may show enhancing or thickened roots. Targeted blood tests, PET-CT, and sometimes nerve or root biopsy identify the underlying cause.
det.treatment: Management is cause-directed: IVIG or plasma exchange for GBS; IVIG, steroids or plasma exchange for CIDP; antimicrobials for infection; chemotherapy for lymphomatous infiltration. Diabetic radiculoplexus neuropathy is mainly treated with pain control and rehabilitation; steroids may ease pain but evidence for altering outcome is limited. Neuropathic pain agents, physiotherapy and fall prevention apply to all.
det.prognosis: Outcome ranges from good recovery in GBS and diabetic radiculoplexus neuropathy to poor survival in neoplastic infiltration.
pearls: Proximal plus distal weakness with early global areflexia suggests roots are involved, not just nerves.
A lymphocytic CSF in a radiculoneuropathy should prompt a search for infection or lymphoma.
Painful asymmetric thigh weakness with weight loss in a diabetic is a radiculoplexus neuropathy, not simple diabetic polyneuropathy.
det.thd: Radiculoneuropathy หมายถึงโรคที่เกิดทั้งรากประสาทและเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายพร้อมกัน ผู้ป่วยอ่อนแรงทั้งต้นและปลายแขนขา reflex หายเร็ว และอาจปวดมาก สาเหตุได้แก่ GBS, CIDP, เบาหวาน โรคติดเชื้อ sarcoidosis และมะเร็งแทรกซึม ตรวจ EMG, น้ำไขสันหลัง และ MRI รากประสาทเพื่อหาสาเหตุ รักษาตามสาเหตุร่วมกับควบคุมอาการปวดและทำกายภาพ

name: Radiculopathy
formal: Dysfunction of a spinal nerve root, commonly from disc herniation or spondylosis, causing dermatomal pain, sensory loss, myotomal weakness and reduced reflexes.
simple: A pinched or irritated nerve at the spine causing pain, numbness or weakness that travels down an arm or leg.
more: Dysfunction of spinal nerve roots, most often compressive from disc or spondylosis, causing radicular pain, dermatomal sensory loss and myotomal weakness. MRI and EMG; mostly improve with conservative management; surgery for severe deficits.
th: รากประสาทไขสันหลังเสียหาย มักถูกกดจากหมอนรองกระดูกหรือกระดูกงอก ทำให้ปวดร้าวตาม dermatome ชา อ่อนแรงตาม myotome และ reflex ลด
tempoNote: Disc herniation often acute; spondylotic foraminal narrowing gradual and fluctuating
feat: Shooting pain radiating along a limb, aggravated by cough, sitting, Spurling or straight leg raise
Dermatomal sensory change and myotomal weakness (e.g. L5: great toe extension, hip abduction)
Reflex loss specific to the root: biceps C5–6, triceps C7, knee L3–4, ankle S1
Commonest roots: C6, C7, L5, S1
Red flags: cancer, fever, weight loss, saddle anaesthesia, sphincter change, progressive deficit
inv: MRI spine when deficit, red flags, or pain persists beyond about 6 weeks
EMG/NCS: paraspinal and myotomal denervation, normal sensory responses
Blood tests and infection or cancer screens if red flags

case.story: After lifting sacks, sudden low back pain then a week later pain radiating down the back of the left leg to the outer foot.
case.exam: Positive straight leg raise at 40°, weak left plantar flexion, absent left ankle jerk, numb lateral foot; sphincters normal.
case.tests: MRI shows left L5/S1 posterolateral disc herniation compressing the S1 root.
case.q: Which root is involved and what is the first-line management?
case.a: Left S1 radiculopathy; conservative care (analgesia, activity modification, physiotherapy) for 6–8 weeks, with surgery for progressive weakness, intractable pain or cauda equina features.

read.where: Chapter 14 Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders — Degenerative Disease of the Spine

det.patho: A root can be compressed by disc herniation or osteophytes in the lateral recess or foramen, and mechanical pressure plus local inflammatory mediators from disc material generate pain. Non-compressive causes include diabetes, zoster, infection, tumour and inflammatory disease. Damage lies proximal to the dorsal root ganglion, so sensory nerve action potentials are preserved.
det.clinical: Radicular pain with dermatomal paraesthesia is typical, with or without weakness and reflex loss. Cervical radiculopathy may cause pain in the scapula and arm; lumbar radiculopathy causes sciatica or femoral distribution pain. Bilateral or multiple-level involvement suggests stenosis or a non-compressive cause. Myelopathic signs indicate cord involvement.
det.diagnosis: The clinical picture often suffices; MRI confirms compression but disc abnormalities are common in asymptomatic people, so correlate carefully. EMG helps when imaging and symptoms disagree, or to separate root from plexus or nerve lesions.
det.treatment: Most acute radiculopathies improve with time, analgesia (NSAIDs, short-term neuropathic agents), activity modification and physiotherapy. Epidural steroid injection may give short-term relief. Surgery (discectomy, foraminotomy, cervical decompression) is indicated for progressive or severe motor deficit, cauda equina syndrome or persistent disabling pain.
det.prognosis: Most disc-related radiculopathies improve within 6–12 weeks; recurrence is common.
pearls: Normal sensory nerve action potentials in a numb territory point to a root lesion.
L5 radiculopathy weakens hip abduction and ankle inversion; peroneal palsy does not.
Imaging findings must match the clinical root.
det.thd: Radiculopathy คือรากประสาทไขสันหลังเสียหาย มักจากหมอนรองกระดูกเคลื่อนหรือกระดูกเสื่อมกด ทำให้ปวดร้าวลงแขนหรือขา ชาตาม dermatome อ่อนแรงตาม myotome และ reflex ของรากนั้นลดลง ส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นเองด้วยการรักษาแบบอนุรักษ์ภายใน 6–12 สัปดาห์ หากอ่อนแรงมากขึ้นหรือมี cauda equina syndrome ต้องผ่าตัด

name: Radiculoplexus neuropathy
formal: Immune-mediated, microvasculitic painful neuropathy affecting lumbosacral or cervical plexus with weight loss and monophasic course, sometimes diabetic.
simple: A painful condition from inflammation of nerve roots and plexus, usually leading to weakness in one limb.
more: Biopsy may show vasculitis; treatment with immunotherapy and pain management; gradual partial recovery.
th: เส้นประสาทรากและ plexus อักเสบจากหลอดเลือดเล็กอักเสบ ทำให้ปวดรุนแรงที่สะโพกหรือต้นขา ตามด้วยกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงและน้ำหนักลด พบบ่อยในเบาหวาน
tempoNote: Severe pain then weakness evolving over weeks to months, followed by slow partial recovery over 1–3 years
feat: Abrupt severe thigh, hip or buttock pain, often starting on one side and spreading to the other
Proximal more than distal leg weakness and wasting (quadriceps, hip flexors), absent knee jerk
Marked unintentional weight loss; often in older adults with well-controlled type 2 diabetes
Cervical (upper limb) and thoracic forms exist; a non-diabetic form looks the same
Monophasic course with gradual, often incomplete improvement
inv: EMG/NCS: multifocal axonal damage in roots, plexus and nerves with paraspinal denervation
MRI lumbar spine and plexus to exclude compression or tumour infiltration
HbA1c, ESR/CRP, CSF protein (often raised); nerve biopsy may show microvasculitis

case.who: 61-year-old man from Suphan Buri with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.0%)
case.story: Sudden burning pain in the right thigh two months ago; he has since lost 8 kg and now cannot climb onto a bus. The left thigh began to ache last week.
case.exam: Wasted right quadriceps, hip flexion 3/5, absent right knee jerk, mild left hip weakness, normal upper limbs.
case.tests: EMG: denervation in right L2–L4 myotomes and paraspinals with mild changes on the left; MRI spine shows no root compression.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what does the patient need to know about the course?
case.a: Diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy; pain control and rehabilitation, and recovery usually comes slowly over many months.

read.where: Chapter 36: Mononeuritis Multiplex: Vasculitis (Systemic, Nonsystemic) Neuropathies

det.patho: Nerve biopsies show inflammation of small epineurial vessels (microvasculitis) leading to ischaemic axonal injury across roots, plexus and peripheral nerves. The immune trigger is unknown; diabetes is a strong association but the same pathology occurs without it. Poor glycaemic control is not a prerequisite and the onset sometimes follows rapid weight loss or tightened glucose control.
det.clinical: The first symptom is usually intense deep pain in the hip or thigh, followed within days to weeks by proximal leg weakness and wasting. Spread to the other side is common and distal leg muscles may become involved. Weight loss can be striking and raises concern for cancer. Autonomic and sensory symptoms may be present, and cervical or thoracic radiculoplexus forms can occur alone or alongside the lumbosacral form.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the clinical pattern and electrodiagnostic evidence of multilevel axonal injury involving roots and plexus. MRI is needed to exclude compressive or neoplastic lesions and may show plexus enhancement. CSF protein is often raised with a normal cell count. Nerve biopsy is reserved for atypical or progressive cases.
det.treatment: Pain management with neuropathic agents and short-term opioids if needed is central, along with physiotherapy, falls prevention and glycaemic control. Immunotherapy (IV methylprednisolone or IVIG) may ease pain in the active phase, but trials have not shown clear acceleration of motor recovery. Explain the expected slow recovery to avoid unnecessary surgery.
det.prognosis: Most patients improve over one to three years, but residual weakness, especially distal, and pain are common; recurrence is uncommon.
pearls: Thigh pain plus weight loss plus proximal weakness in a diabetic is radiculoplexus neuropathy, not just diabetic polyneuropathy.
Paraspinal denervation on EMG shows that roots are involved.
Exclude malignant infiltration of the plexus with MRI before reassuring.
det.thd: Radiculoplexus neuropathy คือเส้นประสาทรากและ plexus เสียหายจากหลอดเลือดฝอยอักเสบ มักพบในผู้ป่วยเบาหวาน เริ่มด้วยปวดสะโพกหรือต้นขารุนแรง ตามด้วยต้นขาอ่อนแรง ลีบ และน้ำหนักลด อาจลามไปอีกข้าง ตรวจ EMG และ MRI เพื่อแยกการกดทับหรือมะเร็ง รักษาด้วยยาแก้ปวดเส้นประสาท กายภาพบำบัด อาจให้ steroid ระยะแรก โดยส่วนใหญ่ฟื้นตัวช้า ๆ ในหลายเดือน

name: Radiological contrast toxicity
formal: Neurotoxicity from iodinated or gadolinium contrast, causing encephalopathy, seizures, cortical blindness or transient deficits, especially with blood-brain barrier disruption or renal failure.
simple: Brain side effects such as confusion, seizures or temporary blindness after receiving imaging contrast dye.
th: พิษต่อระบบประสาทจากสารทึบรังสี iodinated หรือ gadolinium ทำให้สับสน ชัก ตาบอดจากสมองส่วนท้ายทอย หรืออ่อนแรงชั่วคราว พบบ่อยหลังฉีดเข้าหลอดเลือดสมองหรือเมื่อไตวาย
tempoNote: Begins minutes to hours after contrast exposure; usually resolves within 24–72 hours
feat: Encephalopathy, headache, seizures or transient focal deficits after angiography or intervention
Cortical blindness when posterior circulation was injected
Risk: large contrast volume, hypertension, renal failure, blood-brain barrier disruption
Accidental intrathecal gadolinium causes severe encephalopathy and seizures
Usually reversible, unlike stroke from the procedure
inv: Urgent non-contrast CT: cortical/subarachnoid hyperdensity or swelling in the territory injected
MRI with DWI to exclude procedural ischaemic stroke or haemorrhage
EEG if fluctuating consciousness (non-convulsive seizures)
Renal function; repeat CT shows contrast clearance within 1–2 days

case.story: Two hours after coiling of a basilar tip aneurysm he says he cannot see and becomes confused.
case.exam: Visual acuity hand movements only with normal pupils; disorientation without limb weakness.
case.tests: CT shows bilateral occipital cortical hyperdensity and sulcal effacement; MRI DWI normal.
case.q: Is this an ischaemic stroke, and what is the expected course?
case.a: Contrast-induced encephalopathy with cortical blindness; supportive care and hydration, and vision usually returns in 1–3 days.

det.patho: Hyperosmolar or chemotoxic contrast agents disrupt the blood-brain barrier, allowing contrast to leak into cortex and subarachnoid space and directly irritate neurons. This is more likely with high doses, selective intra-arterial injection, impaired renal clearance and pre-existing barrier damage. Gadolinium is neurotoxic in large amounts or when given intrathecally by error.
det.clinical: Symptoms follow within minutes to hours of an angiographic or interventional procedure: headache, confusion, seizures, cortical blindness, aphasia or hemiparesis matching the injected territory. Most resolve within 2–3 days without residue. Severe forms with cerebral oedema and coma are rare. This is a diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out procedural stroke and haemorrhage.
det.diagnosis: CT may show cortical enhancement or hyperdensity and sulcal effacement mimicking subarachnoid haemorrhage; dual-energy CT or rapid clearance on repeat imaging differentiates contrast from blood. MRI DWI helps exclude infarction. EEG detects non-convulsive seizures. Review contrast dose and renal function.
det.treatment: Management is supportive: hydration, blood-pressure control, seizure treatment and monitoring; corticosteroids and mannitol are sometimes used for oedema without strong evidence. Accidental intrathecal gadolinium requires intensive care, seizure control and sometimes CSF drainage. For future procedures, minimise contrast volume and prefer low-osmolar agents.
det.prognosis: Usually excellent with full recovery within days; rare fatal cases are reported.
pearls: Post-angiography cortical blindness with normal DWI: think contrast encephalopathy.
Contrast staining on CT can mimic subarachnoid blood; repeat imaging shows rapid clearance.
Check renal function and total contrast load in every case.
det.thd: Radiological contrast toxicity คือพิษของสารทึบรังสีต่อสมอง มักเกิดหลังฉีดสีเข้าหลอดเลือดสมองหรือทำหัตถการ โดยเฉพาะเมื่อใช้ปริมาณมากหรือไตทำงานไม่ดี ผู้ป่วยสับสน ชัก ตาบอดจากสมองส่วนท้ายทอย หรืออ่อนแรงชั่วคราว CT อาจเห็นสีติดผิวสมองคล้ายเลือดออก ต้องแยกจากสมองขาดเลือดด้วย MRI รักษาประคับประคองและส่วนใหญ่หายใน 1–3 วัน

Procedural emboli give restricted diffusion on MRI and lasting deficits

name: Raeder (paratrigeminal) syndrome
formal: Unilateral oculosympathetic palsy (miosis, ptosis, usually without anhidrosis) with trigeminal pain, from middle cranial fossa or carotid pathology.
simple: A drooping eyelid and small pupil with facial pain on one side, due to a problem near the base of the skull.
th: Horner syndrome ข้างเดียว (ม่านตาเล็ก หนังตาตก มักไม่มีเหงื่อออกผิดปกติ) ร่วมกับปวดบริเวณเส้นประสาท trigeminal จากพยาธิสภาพที่ middle cranial fossa หรือ carotid
tempoNote: Pain and Horner sign develop over hours to days
feat: Ipsilateral ptosis and miosis with preserved facial sweating (postganglionic Horner)
Pain in the forehead, eye or V1 territory; may resemble cluster headache
Type with additional cranial nerve palsies suggests parasellar or middle fossa mass
Painful Horner alone should prompt a search for carotid dissection
inv: Urgent MRI brain with MRA neck/CTA to exclude carotid dissection
MRI of cavernous sinus and middle cranial fossa
Apraclonidine or cocaine drops to confirm Horner

case.story: Three days of constant left forehead and eye pain after a vigorous badminton game; his wife noticed his left eyelid drooping.
case.exam: Left ptosis and miosis, normal facial sweating, no other cranial neuropathy, mild left V1 hypoaesthesia.
case.tests: CTA shows left internal carotid artery dissection with intramural haematoma below the skull base.
case.q: What is the key cause to exclude in painful Horner syndrome and how is it treated?
case.a: Internal carotid artery dissection; treat with antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy and monitor for stroke.

read.where: Chapter 22 Neuro-Ophthalmology — Disorders of the Sympathetic Nervous Supply to the Pupil

det.patho: Third-order sympathetic fibres travel with the internal carotid artery near the trigeminal ganglion. Lesions there, from dissection, tumour, inflammation or aneurysm, injure these fibres together with trigeminal branches. Fibres for facial sweating leave with the external carotid, so sweating is spared.
det.clinical: Historically divided into type I (with other cranial nerve palsies, often a mass lesion) and type II (no other cranial nerve signs, often benign or dissection-related). The label is now discouraged because many 'benign' cases are carotid dissections. Severe ipsilateral head pain with Horner syndrome is the hallmark.
det.diagnosis: Treat painful Horner syndrome as carotid dissection until imaging proves otherwise. MRI with fat-suppressed neck sequences and MRA or CTA is needed, plus imaging of the middle cranial fossa and cavernous sinus. Pharmacological testing confirms Horner when uncertain.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: antithrombotic therapy for dissection, surgery or radiotherapy for tumours, steroids for inflammation. Analgesia for pain.
det.prognosis: Depends on the cause; dissection-related pain usually settles, Horner may persist.
pearls: Painful Horner = carotid dissection until excluded.
Sweating is spared with postganglionic lesions.
Additional cranial nerve palsies suggest a parasellar mass.
det.thd: Raeder syndrome คือ Horner syndrome ข้างเดียวร่วมกับปวดหน้าผากหรือรอบตาในบริเวณเส้นประสาท trigeminal เหงื่อที่หน้ามักปกติ สาเหตุสำคัญที่ต้องตัดคือ internal carotid artery dissection รวมถึงเนื้องอกบริเวณ middle cranial fossa ต้องทำ MRI/MRA หรือ CTA และรักษาตามสาเหตุ

Short attacks with tearing and partial Horner, recurrent and stereotyped
Painful ophthalmoplegia from cavernous sinus inflammation; steroid responsive

name: Ramsay Hunt syndrome
formal: Varicella zoster reactivation in the geniculate ganglion causing facial palsy, ear pain and vesicles in the ear canal, sometimes with hearing loss and vertigo.
simple: Shingles near the ear that causes facial weakness, ear pain and blisters.
th: งูสวัดกำเริบที่ปมประสาท geniculate ทำให้หน้าเบี้ยว ปวดหู ตุ่มน้ำในช่องหู บางรายหูตึงและเวียนศีรษะ รักษาเร็วด้วยยาต้านไวรัสร่วมกับ steroid
tempoNote: Ear pain first, facial weakness peaking within days; the vesicles may follow or precede the palsy by several days
feat: Severe, deep ear pain in or behind the ear that exceeds the usual discomfort of Bell palsy
Lower motor neuron facial palsy involving the forehead, often more severe than Bell palsy
Vesicular rash in the concha, ear canal, tympanic membrane or auricle; sometimes in the mouth, palate or anterior tongue, and occasionally absent (zoster sine herpete)
Cochleovestibular involvement in a sizeable minority: tinnitus, sensorineural hearing loss, vertigo with nystagmus
Taste loss and reduced tearing; older adults and the immunosuppressed (HIV, steroids, malignancy) are at greater risk
inv: Clinical diagnosis from the ear examination; look carefully behind the ear and in the mouth
VZV PCR from vesicle swab, or serology, when the rash is subtle or absent
Audiometry and vestibular assessment; HIV testing in at-risk or unexplained cases
MRI with gadolinium (facial nerve enhancement) when atypical, bilateral, progressive or accompanied by other cranial nerve signs

case.who: 68-year-old retired teacher from Songkhla with diabetes
case.story: Four days of severe pain deep in the left ear, then his mouth began to droop and his left eye would not close. He noticed ringing in the left ear and a spinning feeling when he turned in bed.
case.exam: Complete left facial palsy including the forehead, small clustered vesicles on the concha and posterior auricular skin, left sensorineural hearing loss on tuning-fork testing, horizontal nystagmus beating to the right.
case.tests: VZV PCR from swab positive; audiogram shows mild-to-moderate left sensorineural loss; glucose 220 mg/dL.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what is the first treatment step?
case.a: Ramsay Hunt syndrome. Start valaciclovir (or aciclovir) with oral prednisolone as early as possible, eye protection for incomplete lid closure, and control of glucose.

read.where: 17. Lower Brainstem and Cranial Nerve Dysfunction

Chapter 96: Disorders of the Cranial Nerves and Brainstem

det.patho: Varicella zoster virus lies dormant in cranial ganglia after chickenpox and can reactivate in the geniculate ganglion when cell-mediated immunity wanes. Inflammation and oedema in the bony facial canal compress the nerve, and spread to adjacent nerves of the vestibulocochlear complex explains hearing loss and vertigo. Worse nerve damage than in Bell palsy arises because the virus invades the nerve directly as well as through oedema.
det.clinical: The earliest symptom is typically ear pain, followed within days by facial weakness that may be complete. Vesicles may precede the palsy, accompany it or trail it by days, and some patients never develop them. About a quarter or more of patients develop hearing loss, and vertigo and tinnitus are frequent. Eye closure may fail, so corneal injury is a real risk; the elderly and immunosuppressed show the widest involvement, sometimes with other cranial nerves.
det.diagnosis: Inspect the pinna, canal, tympanic membrane, palate and tongue in every patient with acute facial palsy and ear pain. PCR of vesicle fluid or a swab and serum antibodies confirm VZV when the picture is incomplete. Audiometry documents hearing loss, and MRI is reserved for atypical or progressive cases to look for nerve enhancement or other lesions. Distinguish from Bell palsy, otitis media with facial palsy, cholesteatoma, Lyme disease and skull base tumour.
det.treatment: Give an antiviral (valaciclovir 1 g three times daily for a week in adults, or aciclovir at an equivalent higher dose) together with prednisolone around 1 mg/kg daily for about 5 to 7 days followed by taper, starting within 3 days if possible. Use analgesia, eye lubrication with night taping for incomplete closure, and vestibular suppressants only briefly. Check blood glucose and consider HIV testing; the recombinant zoster vaccine lowers the risk of future shingles in older adults.
det.prognosis: Full recovery of facial function is considerably less likely than in Bell palsy and is better when treatment starts within the first 3 days; hearing loss may be permanent.
pearls: Always look in the ear (and mouth) in a facial palsy with ear pain.
Start antiviral plus steroid early; delay beyond a week lowers the chance of full recovery.
Protect the cornea in any patient who cannot close the eye.
det.thd: Ramsay Hunt syndrome คือโรคงูสวัดที่ปมประสาท geniculate ของเส้นประสาทใบหน้า ผู้ป่วยปวดหูมากแล้วหน้าเบี้ยวแบบ LMN รวมหน้าผาก มีตุ่มน้ำใสที่ใบหู ช่องหู หรือในปาก อาจมีหูอื้อ หูตึง และเวียนศีรษะ การวินิจฉัยอาศัยการตรวจหูอย่างละเอียดและ PCR ของตุ่มน้ำ ควรให้ยาต้านไวรัสร่วมกับ prednisolone โดยเร็วภายใน 3 วัน ดูแลกระจกตาด้วยน้ำตาเทียมและปิดตาตอนนอน การฟื้นตัวของใบหน้าและการได้ยินมักไม่ดีเท่า Bell palsy

name: Rapid progressive hemidystonia
formal: Hemidystonia developing over days to weeks, raising concerns about structural, vascular, inflammatory or neoplastic lesions of the contralateral basal ganglia, as well as drugs and metabolic causes.
simple: Twisting of one side of the body that gets worse quickly, which is a warning sign of an underlying brain problem.
more: Urgent MRI and blood tests, including glucose and autoimmune screen. Treatment is directed to the cause plus symptomatic therapy.
th: dystonia ครึ่งซีกที่เกิดภายในวันถึงสัปดาห์ ต้องหารอยโรคที่ basal ganglia ฝั่งตรงข้าม เช่น หลอดเลือด อักเสบ เนื้องอก ยา หรือเมตาบอลิก
tempoNote: Days to weeks
feat: Dystonic posturing of arm, leg and sometimes face on one side
Contralateral putamen, caudate or thalamus lesion in most cases
Causes: stroke, tumour, abscess, demyelination, nonketotic hyperglycaemia, autoimmune encephalitis, drugs
May follow delayed after a stroke or injury
Other signs (hemiparesis, sensory loss) may coexist
inv: Urgent MRI brain with contrast
Glucose, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid, copper studies
Autoimmune and infection screen (antibodies, HIV, toxoplasma) as indicated

case.who: 63-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes from Chachoengsao
case.story: Over a week, her left arm and leg twist into abnormal positions, with some flinging movements.
case.exam: Left hemidystonia with superimposed chorea, no weakness.
case.tests: Glucose 520 mg/dL, no ketones; CT shows right putaminal hyperdensity; MRI T1 bright putamen.
case.q: What is the cause and what is the treatment?
case.a: Nonketotic hyperglycaemic striatopathy; correct glucose, with temporary symptomatic treatment such as haloperidol or tetrabenazine if needed.

det.patho: Hemidystonia arises from contralateral basal ganglia or thalamic disruption interrupting pallidal-thalamocortical output. Rapid evolution suggests an active process: ischaemia, haemorrhage, mass, infection, inflammation or metabolic disturbance.
det.clinical: Rapid hemidystonia in adults is a red flag for a structural or metabolic cause. Delayed-onset hemidystonia can follow a static lesion months later. Associated features (fever, weight loss, cognitive change, seizures) help point to the cause.
det.diagnosis: Urgent contrast MRI is the cornerstone. Blood tests target glucose, calcium, thyroid, copper and inflammatory or infective causes. CSF analysis if encephalitis is suspected.
det.treatment: Treat the cause promptly. Symptomatic options include anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, baclofen and botulinum toxin. DBS is reserved for chronic refractory cases.
det.prognosis: Depends on the cause; metabolic causes often reverse, structural lesions may leave persistent dystonia.
pearls: New hemidystonia over days in an adult needs urgent imaging.
Check glucose: hyperglycaemic striatopathy is common in Asian older women.
det.thd: Rapid progressive hemidystonia คือ dystonia ครึ่งซีกที่เกิดในเวลาไม่กี่วันถึงสัปดาห์ ต้องหาสาเหตุที่ basal ganglia ฝั่งตรงข้าม เช่น stroke เนื้องอก ฝี การอักเสบ หรือน้ำตาลสูงแบบไม่มีคีโตน ต้องทำ MRI ด่วนและตรวจเลือด รักษาตามสาเหตุร่วมกับยาลดอาการ

Young patient, bilateral but may be asymmetric; KF rings

name: Rapid-onset dystonia parkinsonism
formal: ATP1A3-related disorder with abrupt dystonia and bradykinesia with bulbar involvement and rostrocaudal gradient, triggered by physical or emotional stress, with poor levodopa response.
simple: An inherited condition where stiffness, slowness and twisting spasms appear suddenly, often after stress.
more: ATP1A3 mutations cause autosomal dominant disease with variable penetrance; MRI is normal and DAT-SPECT may be normal. No effective treatment; alternating hemiplegia of childhood and CAPOS syndrome are allelic disorders, so avoid stress triggers. Autosomal dominant ATP1A3-related disorder with abrupt onset of dystonia and parkinsonism over hours to days, bulbar predominant, triggered by stress or fever (DYT12).
th: โรคจากยีน ATP1A3 ที่มี dystonia และ bradykinesia เกิดขึ้นเร็วภายในชั่วโมงถึงสัปดาห์ เด่นที่ใบหน้าและกล้ามเนื้อพูดกลืน ไล่จากบนลงล่าง กระตุ้นด้วยความเครียด ไม่ตอบสนองต่อ levodopa
tempoNote: Onset over hours to weeks, then stable with occasional later step-wise worsening
feat: Abrupt onset of dystonia and parkinsonism, usually in adolescence or young adulthood
Prominent bulbar symptoms: dysarthria, dysphagia, facial dystonia
Rostrocaudal gradient: face > arms > legs
Triggers: fever, alcohol binge, physical exertion, emotional stress, childbirth
Little or no response to levodopa; psychiatric symptoms common
inv: MRI brain normal
DaT-SPECT normal (postsynaptic/network disorder)
ATP1A3 sequencing; CSF HVA may be low

case.who: 20-year-old female university student from Chiang Mai
case.story: After a week of exams and heavy drinking at a festival, over 2 days her speech slurred, she struggled to swallow and her hands became stiff and slow.
case.exam: Oromandibular dystonia, severe dysarthria, arm dystonia and bradykinesia greater than legs; normal eye movements.
case.tests: MRI and DaT-SPECT normal; levodopa trial ineffective; heterozygous ATP1A3 variant.
case.q: Which features point to RDP rather than dopa-responsive dystonia?
case.a: Abrupt stress-triggered onset, bulbar predominance with rostrocaudal gradient, normal DaT-SPECT and no levodopa response.

det.patho: ATP1A3 encodes the alpha-3 subunit of the neuronal Na+/K+-ATPase. Loss of pump function impairs recovery after intense firing, particularly in cerebellum and basal ganglia, so stress-related bursts of activity can trigger lasting dysfunction. The same gene causes alternating hemiplegia of childhood and CAPOS syndrome.
det.clinical: Onset is typically abrupt in teenagers or young adults, sometimes after a clear trigger. Symptoms stabilise after the acute phase but rarely improve much; second episodes may cause further worsening. Depression, anxiety and psychosis are common. Penetrance is incomplete and family history may be absent.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it with abrupt onset, bulbar predominance and rostrocaudal gradient, plus normal MRI and DaT imaging. Genetic testing confirms. Exclude structural, metabolic and functional causes.
det.treatment: Levodopa and most medications are of limited benefit. Benzodiazepines, botulinum toxin and speech therapy help symptoms. DBS results are generally disappointing. Avoid known triggers such as alcohol binges.
det.prognosis: Disability usually persists after onset but life expectancy is normal.
pearls: Sudden bulbar dystonia-parkinsonism after stress in a young adult: test ATP1A3.
Normal DaT-SPECT distinguishes it from degenerative parkinsonism.
ATP1A3 spectrum also includes alternating hemiplegia of childhood.
det.thd: Rapid-onset dystonia parkinsonism เกิดจากยีน ATP1A3 ผู้ป่วยวัยรุ่นหรือผู้ใหญ่ตอนต้นมีอาการ dystonia และเคลื่อนไหวช้าเกิดขึ้นอย่างรวดเร็วหลังความเครียดหรือดื่มเหล้าหนัก พูดและกลืนลำบากเด่น อาการหนักที่หน้ามากกว่าแขนและขา MRI และ DaT-SPECT ปกติ levodopa ไม่ได้ผล รักษาตามอาการ
