name: Rapsyn deficiency
formal: Congenital myasthenic syndrome from RAPSN mutations (N88K common), with neonatal hypotonia, arthrogryposis and episodic crises.
simple: An inherited myasthenia where a protein that holds receptors in place at the muscle junction is faulty.
more: Autosomal recessive; responds to pyridostigmine and 3,4-diaminopyridine; crises triggered by infection.
th: กลุ่มอาการกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงแต่กำเนิดจากยีน RAPSN ทำให้ทารกตัวอ่อน ข้อติดแข็ง และหายใจล้มเหลวเป็นพัก ๆ เมื่อติดเชื้อ
tempoNote: Usually neonatal or infant onset; sudden crises with infection; a later-onset form appears in adolescence or adulthood
feat: Neonatal hypotonia, weak cry and suck, ptosis; eye movements often relatively spared
Arthrogryposis or mild joint contractures at birth
Episodic apnoea or respiratory crises with fever or infection
Fatigable weakness that improves with age in many children
Facial dysmorphism (long face, prognathism) in some
inv: Repetitive nerve stimulation: decrement (may need prolonged or 10 Hz stimulation); single-fibre EMG jitter
AChR and MuSK antibodies negative
Genetic testing: biallelic RAPSN variants, N88K founder variant common in Europe

case.story: Born with bent fingers and a weak cry; twice admitted to PICU with breathing pauses during colds.
case.exam: Mild bilateral ptosis, facial weakness, generalised hypotonia, full eye movements.
case.tests: RNS decrement 18% after 10 Hz stimulation; AChR antibody negative; RAPSN homozygous pathogenic variant.
case.q: Which drugs help, and what should parents be taught?
case.a: Pyridostigmine, often with 3,4-diaminopyridine; teach early hospital attendance with infections and consider home apnoea monitoring.

det.patho: Rapsyn anchors and clusters acetylcholine receptors at the postsynaptic membrane in response to agrin–LRP4–MuSK signalling. Biallelic RAPSN variants reduce receptor density at the endplate, lowering the safety margin for transmission. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
det.clinical: It ranks among the more common congenital myasthenic syndromes. The early-onset form shows hypotonia, feeding difficulty, contractures and life-threatening crises with infection; between crises children may be fairly well and often improve with age. A late-onset form causes mild limb weakness and can be mistaken for seronegative MG.
det.diagnosis: Suspect with fatigable weakness from birth, negative antibodies and a decrement on RNS. Genetic panels for CMS confirm the diagnosis. Absent or mild ophthalmoparesis helps separate it from AChR deficiency.
det.treatment: Pyridostigmine is first-line and 3,4-diaminopyridine adds benefit; salbutamol or ephedrine may help some. Prompt treatment of infections and respiratory support during crises are essential. Avoid drugs that impair neuromuscular transmission.
det.prognosis: Crises decline after early childhood in most; survival into adulthood with mild disability is typical when crises are managed.
pearls: Infant with arthrogryposis and infection-triggered apnoea: think rapsyn CMS.
Seronegative 'MG' since childhood may be a CMS.
Pyridostigmine helps rapsyn deficiency but worsens Dok-7 and slow-channel syndromes.
det.thd: Rapsyn deficiency เป็นกลุ่มอาการ congenital myasthenic syndrome ชนิดยีนด้อยจากยีน RAPSN ซึ่งทำให้ตัวรับ acetylcholine จับกลุ่มไม่ดี ทารกตัวอ่อน ดูดนมไม่ดี ข้อติดแข็ง และหยุดหายใจเป็นพักเมื่อติดเชื้อ ตรวจแอนติบอดีให้ผลลบ RNS มี decrement ยืนยันด้วยยีน รักษาด้วย pyridostigmine และ 3,4-diaminopyridine อาการมักดีขึ้นเมื่อโตขึ้น

qx.stem: A 3-year-old girl from Surat Thani was born with multiple joint contractures and has since had ptosis, a high-arched palate and normal eye movements. She has been hospitalised three times with respiratory failure during chest infections, and between crises walks with mild fatigue. Antibody tests are negative and the repetitive stimulation decrement is only about 8%.
qx.q: Which treatment is the best starting option?

Fluoxetine to close the acetylcholine receptor channel
Cyclophosphamide pulses to suppress autoimmunity
High-dose prednisolone for a presumed congenital myositis
Pyridostigmine, with amifampridine added if needed, plus an emergency plan for infections
qx.why: Arthrogryposis or contractures at birth, ptosis without ophthalmoplegia and crises triggered by infection, with a small decrement, suggest RAPSN-related CMS, in which rapsyn deficiency impairs receptor clustering. These patients generally respond to pyridostigmine, with amifampridine as an additional agent, and prognosis between crises is relatively good. Salbutamol is used for DOK7 and COLQ forms, and fluoxetine is for slow channel syndrome.

Autoimmune; antibodies positive, rarely in infancy apart from transient neonatal MG
Infant botulism: constipation, dilated pupils, descending paralysis

name: Rasmussen’s encephalitis
formal: Unilateral chronic inflammatory encephalitis in children with focal seizures, epilepsia partialis continua, progressive hemiparesis and hemisphere atrophy; T-cell mediated, treated with immunotherapy or hemispherectomy.
simple: A rare childhood brain inflammation on one side that causes difficult seizures, weakness and loss of brain tissue.
more: Rasmussen encephalitis is a unilateral chronic inflammatory brain disease of children with refractory focal seizures, epilepsia partialis continua, progressive hemiparesis and cognitive decline. MRI shows progressive hemispheric atrophy; immunotherapy slows it, but hemispherectomy is the definitive treatment for seizures.
th: สมองอักเสบเรื้อรังข้างเดียวในเด็ก ชักเฉพาะที่ดื้อยา มี epilepsia partialis continua อ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกมากขึ้นและสมองซีกนั้นฝ่อ เกิดจาก T cell รักษาด้วยภูมิคุ้มกันหรือผ่าตัดตัดการเชื่อมต่อสมองซีกนั้น
tempoNote: Prodrome of months, then an acute stage of escalating seizures and deficits over months, then a stable residual stage
feat: Child (median about 6 years) with focal seizures that become frequent and drug-resistant
Epilepsia partialis continua in about half
Progressive hemiparesis, hemianopia, cognitive decline and aphasia if dominant hemisphere
Unilateral, progressive cortical atrophy on serial MRI, starting around the insula
Adult-onset and bilateral forms exist but are rare
inv: Serial MRI: unilateral caudate head and insular-perisylvian atrophy with T2/FLAIR change
EEG: unilateral slowing and epileptiform discharges, often multifocal within one hemisphere
CSF may be normal or mildly inflammatory; antibody screen to exclude other autoimmune epilepsies
Brain biopsy (T-cell infiltrates, microglial nodules) when the diagnosis is uncertain

case.story: Left-hand twitching seizures started a year ago and now happen dozens of times daily despite three antiseizure drugs; her left hand has become weak.
case.exam: Continuous rhythmic jerking of left thumb and fingers, mild left hemiparesis.
case.tests: MRI: right insular and caudate atrophy, progressing compared with a scan 6 months ago; EEG right-hemisphere slowing and discharges.
case.q: What is the only treatment that reliably stops the seizures?
case.a: Rasmussen encephalitis: functional hemispherectomy (hemispherotomy); immunotherapy may slow progression when surgery is not yet acceptable.

det.patho: A cytotoxic CD8+ T-cell attack targets neurons and astrocytes of one hemisphere, with microglial activation and neuronal loss. The trigger is unknown; antibodies previously described are not thought to be causal. Why the process stays confined to one hemisphere remains unexplained.
det.clinical: After a variable prodrome of infrequent focal seizures, an acute phase brings frequent drug-resistant focal motor seizures, often epilepsia partialis continua, with progressive hemiparesis, visual field loss and cognitive decline. Eventually a residual stage with fixed deficits and continuing seizures follows. Adolescent and adult forms progress more slowly and may have a milder course.
det.diagnosis: The Bien criteria rely on focal seizures with or without EPC plus unilateral cortical deficits, unihemispheric EEG findings and unilateral focal cortical atrophy with signal change on MRI; biopsy or serial progression satisfies the remaining criteria. Exclude other causes of unilateral epilepsy such as cortical dysplasia, tumour, vasculitis, mitochondrial disease and autoimmune encephalitis.
det.treatment: Functional hemispherectomy (hemispherotomy) offers seizure freedom in most children but causes or confirms permanent hemiparesis and hemianopia; timing is a difficult decision, especially for dominant hemisphere disease. Immunotherapy (corticosteroids, IVIG, plasma exchange, tacrolimus, and newer agents such as natalizumab or adalimumab in reports) may slow progression. Antiseizure drugs rarely control seizures but reduce generalised attacks.
det.prognosis: Untreated disease leads to permanent hemiparesis and cognitive impairment; early surgery yields good seizure outcomes and young children often regain substantial function.
pearls: Refractory focal motor seizures + EPC + progressive unilateral atrophy: Rasmussen.
Serial MRI is key; atrophy starts around insula and caudate head.
Hemispherectomy earlier in childhood gives better language and motor reorganisation.
det.thd: Rasmussen encephalitis เป็นสมองอักเสบเรื้อรังข้างเดียวจาก T cell มักพบในเด็ก มีชักเฉพาะที่ดื้อยา บางรายกระตุกต่อเนื่อง (epilepsia partialis continua) อ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกและความคิดถดถอย MRI เห็นสมองซีกนั้นฝ่อมากขึ้นเรื่อย ๆ รักษาด้วยภูมิคุ้มกันบำบัดเพื่อชะลอโรค แต่การผ่าตัด hemispherotomy เป็นวิธีที่หยุดชักได้ดีที่สุด

ddx.pt: Port-wine stain and leptomeningeal angioma with calcification and hemiatrophy
Usually bilateral, subacute and antibody-positive with better immunotherapy response
Stroke-like lesions crossing vascular territories with lactate; may cause EPC but is often bilateral over time

name: Rathke’s pouch tumours
formal: Developmental sellar and suprasellar lesions, including Rathke cleft cysts and craniopharyngiomas, arising from pouch remnants, causing visual loss, headache and pituitary dysfunction.
simple: Growths near the pituitary gland that come from leftover tissue from early development and can affect vision and hormones.
th: รอยโรคในและเหนือ sella ที่เกิดจากเศษ Rathke’s pouch ได้แก่ Rathke cleft cyst และ craniopharyngioma ทำให้ตามัว ปวดศีรษะ และต่อมใต้สมองทำงานผิดปกติ
tempoNote: Slowly enlarging over years; craniopharyngioma peaks in childhood and in middle age
feat: Rathke cleft cyst: usually small, non-neoplastic, often incidental; may cause headache or hypopituitarism
Craniopharyngioma: true tumour, cystic and calcified, adamantinomatous (children) or papillary (adults)
Visual loss with bitemporal or asymmetric field defects
Growth failure, delayed puberty, diabetes insipidus in children
Hydrocephalus and hypothalamic obesity in larger tumours
inv: MRI pituitary with contrast; CT for calcification
Visual fields and acuity
Full pituitary hormone panel including sodium and urine osmolality

case.story: Short for his age, drinks large amounts of water at night, and recently complains of headache and blurred vision.
case.exam: Height below the 3rd percentile, bitemporal field loss, bilateral optic atrophy.
case.tests: MRI: mixed solid-cystic suprasellar mass; CT shows rim calcification; dilute urine with high sodium.
case.q: What is the most likely tumour?
case.a: Adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma arising from Rathke’s pouch remnants.

read.where: Chapter 20 Neuro-Oncology — Colloid Cysts, Rathke’s Pouch Tumours and Neurenteric Cysts
Chapter 11: Sella and Central Skull Base

det.patho: Rathke’s pouch is the embryological precursor of the anterior pituitary. Remnants can form an epithelial-lined, fluid-filled cleft cyst or give rise to craniopharyngioma. Adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma carries CTNNB1 (beta-catenin) mutations, while papillary craniopharyngioma carries BRAF V600E mutations.
det.clinical: Rathke cleft cysts are found on many autopsies and MRIs and usually cause nothing; a minority cause headache, visual loss or hormone deficiency. Craniopharyngiomas are benign histologically but adhere to the hypothalamus and optic apparatus, causing endocrine failure, visual loss, hydrocephalus and hypothalamic obesity and behaviour change.
det.diagnosis: MRI and CT distinguish a simple non-enhancing cyst (Rathke cleft) from a calcified, solid-cystic enhancing mass (craniopharyngioma). Endocrine and visual assessments are essential before treatment. Histology confirms and molecular testing identifies BRAF status in papillary type.
det.treatment: Symptomatic Rathke cleft cysts are drained and partly excised transsphenoidally. Craniopharyngiomas are treated with surgery, often limited resection plus radiotherapy (including proton therapy) to spare the hypothalamus. BRAF plus MEK inhibitors shrink papillary craniopharyngiomas. Lifelong hormone replacement is often needed.
det.prognosis: Rathke cleft cysts have an excellent prognosis; craniopharyngioma survival is good, but hypothalamic damage causes long-term morbidity.
pearls: Calcified suprasellar mass in a child = craniopharyngioma until proven otherwise.
Check sodium and urine osmolality — diabetes insipidus is common.
Papillary craniopharyngioma is BRAF V600E-driven and drug-responsive.
det.thd: Rathke’s pouch tumours คือรอยโรคจากเศษ Rathke’s pouch ได้แก่ Rathke cleft cyst ซึ่งเป็นถุงน้ำไม่ใช่เนื้องอกและมักพบโดยบังเอิญ กับ craniopharyngioma ซึ่งเป็นเนื้องอกที่มีหินปูนและถุงน้ำ พบมากในเด็กและวัยกลางคน ทำให้ตามัว ตัวเตี้ย เบาจืด และ hydrocephalus วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI CT และตรวจฮอร์โมน รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัดร่วมกับรังสี และใช้ยามุ่งเป้า BRAF ในชนิด papillary

name: Recessive intermediate CMT disease
formal: Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy with autosomal recessive inheritance and intermediate nerve conduction velocities (25 to 45 m/s), e.g. GDAP1 or KARS mutations.
simple: An inherited nerve disease causing weakness and numbness in the feet and hands, passed on when both parents carry the gene.
th: CMT ที่ถ่ายทอดแบบ autosomal recessive และความเร็วการนำประสาทอยู่ระหว่าง demyelinating กับ axonal (ประมาณ 25–45 m/s)
tempoNote: Onset in childhood, slowly progressive over decades
feat: Childhood onset of distal weakness and wasting with foot deformity (pes cavus)
Often more severe than dominant CMT; hand involvement and loss of walking possible
Parents unaffected; consanguinity raises suspicion
Genes include GDAP1, KARS1, PLEKHG5, COX6A1 and SBF2 variants depending on series
Some forms have vocal cord palsy (GDAP1) or developmental features (KARS1)
inv: NCS: upper limb motor velocities in the intermediate range (about 25–45 m/s)
Genetic panel or exome; PMP22 duplication testing alone will miss it
Family history and parental examination

case.who: 12-year-old boy from Pattani, parents are cousins
case.story: Clumsy running from age 5, frequent ankle sprains, now has trouble buttoning his school shirt.
case.exam: High arches, distal leg and hand wasting, bilateral foot drop, absent reflexes, mild hoarseness.
case.tests: Median motor velocity 34 m/s with low amplitudes; PMP22 duplication negative; panel shows homozygous GDAP1 variant.
case.q: How would you classify this neuropathy and what does it mean for his siblings?
case.a: Recessive intermediate CMT (GDAP1); each full sibling has a 25% risk of being affected and should be offered testing and counselling.

read.where: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves — Inherited Neuropathies

det.patho: Recessive intermediate CMT is genetically diverse. Many genes affect mitochondrial dynamics (GDAP1), protein translation (KARS1) or Schwann cell–axon interactions, producing combined axonal and myelin damage. The intermediate conduction velocity reflects this mixed pathology rather than a single mechanism.
det.clinical: Symptoms typically begin in early childhood with delayed or clumsy walking, followed by progressive distal weakness and wasting. Recessive forms are often more severe than dominant CMT, with hand involvement and sometimes loss of ambulation. Vocal cord paresis and diaphragmatic weakness can occur with GDAP1, and some KARS1 cases have hearing loss or developmental delay.
det.diagnosis: Nerve conduction studies show forearm motor velocities in the intermediate range with reduced amplitudes. Family history suggesting recessive inheritance and consanguinity point toward this group. A multigene panel or exome sequencing is needed; nerve biopsy is rarely required.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying therapy. Care is multidisciplinary with physiotherapy, orthoses, orthopaedic surgery for foot deformity and scoliosis, and occupational therapy for hand function. Monitoring of voice and breathing is important in GDAP1 cases. Genetic counselling is essential for families.
det.prognosis: Variable by gene; many recessive forms lead to significant disability by adulthood.
pearls: Intermediate velocities plus consanguinity suggest recessive intermediate CMT.
PMP22 testing alone misses most childhood-onset recessive forms.
Hoarse voice in a child with CMT: think GDAP1.
det.thd: Recessive intermediate CMT คือ Charcot–Marie–Tooth ที่ถ่ายทอดแบบ autosomal recessive และ NCS มีความเร็วกลาง ๆ ระหว่าง demyelinating กับ axonal ยีนที่พบเช่น GDAP1 และ KARS1 อาการเริ่มในวัยเด็ก มีเท้าโก่ง ปลายแขนขาลีบอ่อนแรง และมักรุนแรงกว่าชนิด dominant การวินิจฉัยใช้ NCS และตรวจยีน ไม่มีการรักษาเฉพาะ เน้นกายภาพ อุปกรณ์ช่วย และให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

Acquired, proximal as well as distal weakness, conduction block and raised CSF protein

name: Recurrent meningitis
formal: Repeated episodes of meningeal inflammation due to CSF leaks, immune defects, parameningeal foci, Mollaret syndrome (HSV-2) or autoinflammatory disorders.
simple: Meningitis that keeps coming back, often because of a leak of spinal fluid, weak immunity or a hidden infection.
th: เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบซ้ำหลายครั้ง สาเหตุจากรูรั่วน้ำไขสันหลัง ภูมิคุ้มกันบกพร่อง จุดติดเชื้อใกล้เยื่อหุ้มสมอง HSV-2 หรือโรคอักเสบในร่างกาย
tempoNote: Two or more separate episodes with symptom-free intervals
feat: Repeated bacterial episodes (often pneumococcal) suggest a CSF leak from skull base defect or trauma
Clear nasal or ear discharge, prior head injury or skull base surgery
Recurrent neisserial episodes suggest complement deficiency
Recurrent benign lymphocytic episodes: HSV-2 (Mollaret), drugs (NSAIDs, IVIG), Behçet, SLE, epidermoid cyst leakage
inv: CSF analysis each episode with HSV PCR; beta-2 transferrin or beta-trace protein on nasal fluid
High-resolution CT skull base and MRI/CT cisternography to locate leaks
Immunoglobulins, complement (CH50, AH50), HIV, splenic function

case.who: 29-year-old motorcycle taxi driver from Samut Prakan
case.story: Third episode of pneumococcal meningitis in four years; he had a bad head injury before the first.
case.exam: Clear fluid drips from the right nostril when he leans forward.
case.tests: Beta-2 transferrin positive in nasal fluid; CT shows a defect in the cribriform plate.
case.q: What prevents further episodes?
case.a: Surgical repair of the skull base CSF leak, plus pneumococcal vaccination.

read.where: Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — Chronic and Recurrent Meningitis
Chapter 50: Headache attributed to non-vascular intracranial disorder

det.patho: Recurrence reflects either a persistent route of entry (dural defect, dermal sinus, parameningeal infection), impaired host defence (complement, antibody or splenic deficiency, HIV), a recurring trigger (HSV-2 reactivation, drugs) or a non-infectious inflammatory process. Each mechanism points to a different preventive strategy.
det.clinical: Bacterial recurrences tend to be acute and severe, typically pneumococcal or H. influenzae with leaks, or meningococcal with complement deficiency. Mollaret-type episodes are shorter, self-limited lymphocytic meningitis lasting a few days. In children, look for a dermal sinus tract or inner ear malformation.
det.diagnosis: Document CSF findings in each episode. For bacterial recurrences, search for a leak (beta-2 transferrin, imaging) and test immunity. For aseptic recurrences, test HSV-2 PCR, review drugs, and look for autoimmune disease and cyst rupture on MRI.
det.treatment: Treat each episode according to its cause. Prevention means repairing leaks, vaccinating against pneumococcus, meningococcus and Hib, immunoglobulin replacement for antibody deficiency, and avoiding culprit drugs. Antiviral suppression for frequent HSV-2 episodes has limited trial support. Treat underlying systemic inflammatory disease.
det.prognosis: Excellent if a structural cause is repaired; untreated leaks carry ongoing risk with each episode.
pearls: Recurrent pneumococcal meningitis = CSF leak until proven otherwise.
Recurrent meningococcal disease = check complement.
Short benign lymphocytic episodes: send HSV-2 PCR.
det.thd: Recurrent meningitis คือเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบซ้ำหลายครั้ง ถ้าเป็นแบคทีเรียซ้ำ โดยเฉพาะ pneumococcus ให้นึกถึงรูรั่วน้ำไขสันหลังจากการบาดเจ็บหรือฐานกะโหลกผิดปกติ ถ้าเป็น meningococcus ซ้ำให้ตรวจระบบ complement ส่วนแบบ lymphocyte ที่หายเองมักเกิดจาก HSV-2 การป้องกันขึ้นกับสาเหตุ เช่น ผ่าตัดปิดรูรั่วและให้วัคซีน

name: Recurrent vertigo
formal: Repeated episodes of vertigo arising from vestibular migraine, Meniere disease, BPPV or posterior circulation ischaemia.
simple: Repeated attacks of spinning dizziness, which can be from inner ear problems, migraine or reduced blood flow to the brain.
th: อาการบ้านหมุนเป็นซ้ำหลายครั้ง สาเหตุสำคัญคือ vestibular migraine, Ménière, BPPV และการขาดเลือดของ posterior circulation
tempoNote: Attacks last seconds (BPPV), minutes (TIA), minutes to hours (Ménière, vestibular migraine) and recur over months
feat: A symptom pattern, not a single disease: classify by attack duration and trigger
Seconds with head position change: BPPV
Hours-long spells plus ear fullness, ringing and shifting hearing: Ménière disease
Minutes to hours with migraine history, light sensitivity or headache: vestibular migraine
Minutes with other brainstem symptoms in a vascular-risk patient: vertebrobasilar TIA
inv: Dix-Hallpike and supine roll tests during the visit
Audiometry for low-frequency sensorineural loss; video head impulse test
MRI with diffusion and vessel imaging when attacks are brief, new and accompanied by brainstem signs

case.story: Over a year she has had six spells of spinning lasting 2–6 hours with nausea and light intolerance; some come with a throbbing headache, and her mother had migraine.
case.exam: Normal between attacks, including hearing, Dix-Hallpike and head impulse test.
case.tests: Audiogram normal on two occasions; MRI brain normal.
case.q: Which diagnosis fits best, and what is the initial management?
case.a: Vestibular migraine; address triggers and sleep, consider prophylaxis such as propranolol or flunarizine, and treat attacks with antiemetics.

read.where: 20 Migraine and other episodic vestibular disorders

det.patho: Recurrent vertigo results from intermittent asymmetry of vestibular input. Mechanisms include free otoconia moving within a semicircular canal (BPPV), endolymphatic hydrops (Ménière), migraine-related changes in central vestibular processing, transient hypoperfusion of the labyrinth or brainstem, and rarely paroxysmal discharges from a compressed vestibular nerve or vestibular epilepsy.
det.clinical: The history is the main tool: ask how long attacks last, whether they are triggered by position, standing, sound or pressure, and which symptoms accompany them. BPPV causes brief positional spinning; Ménière gives hours-long attacks with ear symptoms; vestibular migraine has variable duration and migraine traits; TIA produces brief spells with other posterior circulation deficits. Panic and persistent postural-perceptual dizziness often coexist and modify the picture.
det.diagnosis: Use the Bárány Society criteria for BPPV, Ménière disease and vestibular migraine. Positional testing confirms and treats BPPV in the same visit. Audiometry is required for Ménière. Brain MRI with DWI and vascular imaging is indicated for new-onset short attacks in patients with vascular risk factors or any additional neurological symptom. Normal examination between attacks is expected and does not exclude disease.
det.treatment: Treatment follows the cause: repositioning manoeuvres for BPPV, salt moderation, betahistine or intratympanic therapy for Ménière, lifestyle measures and migraine prophylaxis for vestibular migraine, and urgent antithrombotic secondary prevention for TIA. Vestibular suppressants should be short-term only. Vestibular rehabilitation helps residual imbalance.
det.prognosis: BPPV and vestibular migraine usually respond well; Ménière disease may cause cumulative hearing loss; vertebrobasilar TIA carries a high early stroke risk.
pearls: Ask for attack duration first; it sorts most causes.
Isolated recurrent vertigo for more than six months is rarely vascular.
Positional testing should be part of every dizziness examination.
det.thd: Recurrent vertigo คืออาการบ้านหมุนเป็นซ้ำ ให้แยกสาเหตุตามระยะเวลาของแต่ละครั้ง: เป็นวินาทีตามท่าทางคือ BPPV, เป็นชั่วโมงร่วมกับหูอื้อเสียงในหูคือ Ménière, มีประวัติไมเกรนคือ vestibular migraine และเป็นไม่กี่นาทีร่วมกับอาการก้านสมองในผู้สูงอายุให้นึกถึง TIA ตรวจ Dix-Hallpike, audiogram และ MRI ตามข้อบ่งชี้ รักษาตามสาเหตุ

name: Reducing body myopathy
formal: Rare myopathy from FHL1 mutations with reducing bodies, which stain with menadione NBT, and variable weakness from infancy to adulthood.
simple: A rare inherited muscle disease where unusual clumps form inside muscle fibres.
more: X-linked; biopsy and FHL1 genetics; supportive care with cardiac and respiratory monitoring.
th: โรคกล้ามเนื้อหายากจากยีน FHL1 ที่ชิ้นเนื้อพบ reducing bodies ติดสี menadione-NBT อ่อนแรงได้ตั้งแต่ทารกถึงผู้ใหญ่
tempoNote: Infantile forms progress rapidly; adult forms slowly
feat: X-linked; males more severely affected, carrier females can be symptomatic
Proximal or scapuloperoneal weakness, sometimes asymmetric
Spinal rigidity, contractures and early respiratory weakness
Cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia in FHL1 spectrum
Overlaps with Emery–Dreifuss and scapuloperoneal myopathy
inv: CK mildly to moderately raised
Muscle biopsy: reducing bodies on menadione-NBT stain; electron-dense inclusions
FHL1 gene testing
Echocardiogram, ECG/Holter, spirometry

case.story: Gradually weakening shoulders and difficulty lifting his feet over three years; tires easily climbing stairs.
case.exam: Scapular winging, foot drop, rigid spine, elbow contractures; reduced FVC on spirometry.
case.tests: CK 650 U/L; biopsy shows inclusions staining with menadione-NBT; FHL1 variant; Holter shows atrial ectopy.
case.q: Which investigations must be repeated over time?
case.a: Cardiac (ECG, Holter, echo) and respiratory function, because FHL1 disease affects heart and breathing.

det.patho: FHL1 codes for a LIM-domain protein (FHL1) that helps build and maintain the sarcomere. Mutations cause misfolded aggregates (reducing bodies) that sequester other proteins and disrupt muscle integrity. Different FHL1 variants cause a spectrum including reducing body myopathy, scapuloperoneal myopathy and Emery–Dreifuss-like disease.
det.clinical: Severe infantile forms present with rapidly progressive weakness and respiratory failure. Later-onset forms show proximal or scapuloperoneal weakness, rigid spine and contractures. Cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia may occur. Female carriers may have mild weakness.
det.diagnosis: Muscle biopsy with menadione-NBT stain shows reducing bodies; genetic testing confirms FHL1 variants. Cardiac and respiratory assessment are essential.
det.treatment: No disease-specific therapy. Physiotherapy, contracture management, respiratory support including NIV, and cardiac care (pacemaker or ICD as indicated) are central. Genetic counselling for X-linked inheritance.
det.prognosis: Infantile forms may be fatal in childhood; later-onset forms progress slowly but may develop cardiac or respiratory complications.
pearls: Menadione-NBT stain is the clue for reducing bodies.
FHL1 variants can mimic Emery–Dreifuss dystrophy.
Screen heart and lungs regularly.
det.thd: Reducing body myopathy เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้อหายากจากยีน FHL1 ถ่ายทอดทาง X ชิ้นเนื้อพบ reducing bodies ติดสี menadione-NBT อ่อนแรงต้นแขนขาหรือแบบ scapuloperoneal กระดูกสันหลังแข็ง ข้อติด และอาจมีปัญหาหัวใจและการหายใจ ไม่มีการรักษาเฉพาะ ต้องติดตามหัวใจและการหายใจสม่ำเสมอ

name: Reflex sympathetic dystrophy (RSD)
formal: Older term for complex regional pain syndrome type 1, with disproportionate pain, allodynia, swelling, colour and temperature changes and trophic change after injury without nerve lesion.
simple: A long-lasting pain condition after an injury, with swelling, skin changes and extreme sensitivity in a limb.
more: Diagnosis by Budapest criteria; bone scintigraphy shows periarticular uptake, with type 2 CRPS following nerve injury. Treat with physiotherapy, desensitisation, bisphosphonates, steroids early, and neuropathic pain drugs. Complex regional pain syndrome with patchy bone demineralisation after trauma or immobilisation, causing pain, swelling, temperature and skin changes and stiffness in the affected limb. Older term for complex regional pain syndrome with burning pain, autonomic and trophic changes after trauma or stroke, e.g. shoulder-hand syndrome.
ab: Complex regional pain syndrome type I
th: ชื่อเดิมของ complex regional pain syndrome ชนิดที่ 1 ปวดมากเกินสัดส่วนหลังบาดเจ็บ มีบวม สีผิวและอุณหภูมิเปลี่ยน ผิวหนังและกระดูกบาง โดยไม่มีเส้นประสาทเสียหาย
tempoNote: Begins days to weeks after an injury, fracture, surgery or stroke and may become chronic
feat: Continuing pain out of proportion to the original injury, with allodynia and hyperalgesia
Swelling, sweating and colour or temperature asymmetry of the limb
Stiffness, reduced movement, tremor or dystonic posturing
Trophic changes in skin, hair and nails; patchy osteoporosis on X-ray
Type 2 (formerly causalgia) follows a definite nerve injury
inv: Clinical diagnosis using the Budapest criteria
X-ray for patchy demineralisation; three-phase bone scan may show periarticular uptake
NCS to look for a nerve lesion (type 2) and to exclude other causes

case.story: Six weeks after a wrist fracture treated with a cast, her hand is burning, swollen and cannot bear the touch of a sleeve.
case.exam: Red, shiny, sweaty right hand, 1.5 °C warmer than the left, finger stiffness, allodynia over the whole hand without a nerve distribution.
case.tests: X-ray: patchy osteopenia of the carpal bones; NCS normal.
case.q: Which condition is this and what is the most important treatment?
case.a: CRPS type 1 (reflex sympathetic dystrophy); early graded physiotherapy and desensitisation with pain control, plus a short steroid course or bisphosphonate in the early phase.

det.patho: The term reflex sympathetic dystrophy has been replaced by CRPS because sympathetic overactivity is not constant. Proposed mechanisms include exaggerated neurogenic inflammation, peripheral and central sensitisation, altered sympathetic-adrenergic coupling, autoimmunity and cortical reorganisation of the body map. Immobilisation seems to promote it.
det.clinical: It follows fracture, sprain, surgery, injection or stroke (shoulder-hand syndrome). The acute warm phase shows swelling, redness and warmth; later the limb can become cold, bluish and atrophic with contractures. Motor features include weakness, tremor and dystonia. Psychological distress is common but is a consequence rather than a proven cause.
det.diagnosis: Budapest criteria require continuing disproportionate pain plus symptoms and signs in sensory, vasomotor, sudomotor/oedema and motor/trophic categories, with no better explanation. Imaging supports but does not establish the diagnosis. Exclude infection, deep vein thrombosis, arthritis and compressive neuropathy.
det.treatment: Early active physiotherapy, graded motor imagery, mirror therapy and desensitisation are the mainstay. Drugs include neuropathic pain agents, short oral steroids in early inflammatory cases and bisphosphonates. Sympathetic blocks and spinal cord stimulation are options for resistant cases. Avoid prolonged immobilisation.
det.prognosis: Many acute cases improve within a year with early therapy, but a sizeable minority develop chronic pain and disability.
pearls: RSD = CRPS type 1; causalgia = CRPS type 2.
Measure skin temperature difference between limbs at the bedside.
Early mobilisation after fracture and stroke helps prevent it.

name: Refractory status epilepticus
formal: Status epilepticus persisting despite first and second line anticonvulsants, requiring anaesthetic agents and intensive care, with high morbidity.
simple: Seizures that continue even after the usual medicines have been tried, needing intensive care treatment.

tempoNote: Defined once seizures continue after adequate first-line and one second-line drug, typically 30–60 minutes from onset
feat: Convulsive or non-convulsive seizures continuing after benzodiazepine and an adequate second-line agent
Common causes: stroke, CNS infection, autoimmune encephalitis, tumour, drug withdrawal, metabolic or toxic insult
Convulsive activity may become subtle (twitching, eye deviation) while the EEG continues seizing
Systemic complications: hyperthermia, acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, aspiration, arrhythmia
Super-refractory if it persists or recurs 24 hours after starting anaesthetic
inv: Continuous EEG monitoring to guide anaesthetic titration and detect non-convulsive seizures
Glucose, electrolytes incl. Ca/Mg, drug levels, toxicology, liver and renal function, CK
CT then MRI; lumbar puncture for infection and autoimmune antibodies
If no cause: consider NORSE/FIRES work-up incl. autoimmune and paraneoplastic screening

case.story: Known epilepsy, stopped her drugs a week ago; generalised seizures have not stopped despite IV diazepam twice and a loading dose of phenytoin.
case.exam: Comatose, subtle rhythmic eye and mouth twitching, temperature 38.6 °C.
case.tests: Glucose normal; CK 3,500 U/L; CT unremarkable; EEG shows ongoing electrographic seizures.
case.q: What is the next treatment step?
case.a: Refractory status epilepticus: intubate and start a continuous anaesthetic infusion (midazolam or propofol), titrated to EEG seizure control for 24–48 hours, while reloading her usual drugs.

det.patho: Prolonged seizures cause internalisation of GABA-A receptors and upregulation of NMDA and AMPA receptors, so benzodiazepines lose potency and excitotoxic injury mounts. Neuronal death, cerebral oedema and systemic complications contribute to morbidity. About a quarter to a third of patients with status epilepticus become refractory.
det.clinical: RSE is defined as status that continues despite an appropriately dosed benzodiazepine and one second-line agent (levetiracetam, valproate, fosphenytoin or phenobarbital). Clinical signs may wane to subtle twitches while electrographic seizures continue, so coma without obvious convulsions does not mean seizures have stopped. Mortality ranges roughly 15–40%, depending on age and cause.
det.diagnosis: Determine the cause in parallel with treatment: metabolic panel, toxicology, antiseizure drug levels, neuroimaging, CSF analysis and autoimmune and infectious tests. Continuous EEG is essential to confirm control and detect relapse during anaesthetic weaning. In previously healthy patients without a clear cause, consider NORSE and autoimmune encephalitis early.
det.treatment: Secure airway and haemodynamics and start continuous midazolam, propofol or ketamine infusion (pentobarbital/thiopental where available), titrated to seizure suppression or burst suppression on EEG for about 24–48 hours before a slow wean. Continue and optimise maintenance antiseizure drugs. Treat the cause; consider immunotherapy early when autoimmune encephalitis or NORSE is suspected. Watch for propofol infusion syndrome, hypotension and infections.
det.prognosis: Prognosis depends mainly on cause, age and duration; anoxic and acute structural causes fare worst, drug withdrawal best.
pearls: Coma after convulsions stop is not proof of seizure control: get EEG.
Time matters: the longer seizures last, the less benzodiazepines work.
Unexplained RSE in a healthy adult: think NORSE and autoimmune encephalitis.
det.thd: Refractory status epilepticus คือภาวะชักต่อเนื่องที่ไม่หยุดแม้ให้ benzodiazepine และยากันชักขั้นที่สองในขนาดเพียงพอแล้ว ต้องใส่ท่อช่วยหายใจและให้ยาดมสลบต่อเนื่อง เช่น midazolam หรือ propofol ใน ICU ร่วมกับเฝ้า EEG ต่อเนื่อง ต้องหาสาเหตุไปพร้อมกัน เช่น หยุดยา ติดเชื้อ สมองอักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกัน หรือรอยโรคสมอง อัตราตายสูงและขึ้นกับสาเหตุ

qx.q: What is the best next management?

Add oral topiramate and observe for 2 hours
Give intravenous valproate at a high load given his liver disease
Request emergency epilepsy surgery assessment
Give intravenous thiamine only and wait for response
qx.why: Status persisting after a benzodiazepine and one adequate second-line drug is refractory and warrants airway protection and an anaesthetic infusion (midazolam, propofol or pentobarbital) guided by continuous EEG. Valproate is unwise in significant liver disease. Thiamine should be given in alcohol use but does not replace seizure control, and enteral drugs act too slowly.

name: Refsum disease
formal: Peroxisomal disorder from phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase deficiency causing retinitis pigmentosa, polyneuropathy, ataxia, ichthyosis and deafness; treated with dietary phytanic acid restriction.
simple: An inherited disorder where a fat from food builds up, causing vision loss, nerve damage, unsteadiness and dry skin.
more: Diagnose by raised plasma phytanic acid and PHYH or PEX7 testing; nerve conduction shows demyelinating neuropathy with raised CSF protein. Plasmapheresis or lipid apheresis lowers levels in acute attacks; avoid fasting; arrhythmia can occur.
th: โรค peroxisome ยีนด้อยที่สะสม phytanic acid — จอตาเสื่อม (ตาบอดกลางคืน) จมูกไม่ได้กลิ่น เส้นประสาทเสื่อมชนิด demyelinating ataxia หูตึง ผิวแห้งเป็นเกล็ด รักษาด้วยอาหาร
tempoNote: Onset late childhood to early adulthood with slow progression; acute worsenings follow fasting, weight loss, illness or surgery
feat: Night blindness and progressive retinitis pigmentosa, often the first symptom
Loss of smell in almost every patient
Demyelinating sensorimotor neuropathy with thickened nerves and high CSF protein
Cerebellar ataxia, sensorineural hearing loss and ichthyosis
Short fourth metatarsals or fingers; cardiac arrhythmia and cardiomyopathy

NCS: slow conduction; CSF protein high with normal cells

case.story: Cannot see at dusk for years; now numb feet and unsteady. He mentions he cannot smell fish sauce. Recent crash diet made him much weaker.

case.tests: NCS demyelinating range slowing; CSF protein 1.8 g/L; plasma phytanic acid 900 µmol/L (normal < 10).
case.q: Why did the diet make him worse, and what is the long-term treatment?
case.a: Weight loss mobilises phytanic acid from fat stores; treat with a phytanic-acid-restricted diet while avoiding fasting, and use plasmapheresis or lipid apheresis for acute crises.

det.patho: Phytanic acid is a branched-chain fatty acid obtained only from the diet (ruminant meat and dairy fat, some fish), needs peroxisomal alpha-oxidation. Variants in PHYH (phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase) or less often PEX7 block this step, so phytanic acid accumulates in nerve myelin, retina, skin and heart. Toxicity is roughly related to plasma levels, which explains rapid deterioration when fat stores are mobilised.
det.clinical: Retinitis pigmentosa and anosmia are the most constant features and often precede everything else. A demyelinating, sometimes relapsing neuropathy, ataxia, deafness and ichthyosis follow. Skeletal shortening of metatarsals is a helpful clue. Arrhythmia may cause sudden death, particularly during metabolic crises.
det.diagnosis: Measure plasma phytanic acid in any patient with retinopathy plus neuropathy or ataxia; it is grossly elevated. Confirm genetically. Infantile Refsum and other peroxisomal biogenesis disorders differ in age and have raised very-long-chain fatty acids and pristanic acid.
det.treatment: Restrict dietary phytanic acid (limit beef, lamb, dairy fat and certain fish) with dietitian support, maintaining adequate calories to prevent lipolysis. During acute deterioration, plasmapheresis or lipid apheresis rapidly lowers levels. Cardiac monitoring is essential; avoid prolonged fasting around surgery. Neuropathy, ataxia and ichthyosis improve with control; retinopathy, anosmia and deafness rarely recover.
det.prognosis: Long survival is possible with strict dietary control; untreated or poorly controlled patients risk sudden cardiac death.
pearls: Retinitis pigmentosa + anosmia + demyelinating neuropathy: send phytanic acid.
Never put a Refsum patient on a fasting or crash diet.
One of the few hereditary neuropathies with a dietary treatment.
det.thd: Refsum disease เป็นโรค peroxisome จากยีน PHYH ทำให้สะสม phytanic acid ที่ได้จากอาหาร ผู้ป่วยตาบอดกลางคืนจากจอตาเสื่อม จมูกไม่ได้กลิ่น เส้นประสาทเสื่อมแบบ demyelinating เดินเซ หูตึง และผิวเป็นเกล็ด ตรวจ phytanic acid ในเลือดสูงมาก รักษาด้วยการจำกัดอาหารที่มี phytanic acid ห้ามอดอาหาร และใช้ plasmapheresis เมื่ออาการกำเริบ

name: Relapsed glioblastoma
formal: Recurrent grade 4 IDH-wildtype glioma after standard temozolomide chemoradiotherapy, with dismal prognosis; options include re-resection, re-irradiation, lomustine or bevacizumab.
simple: An aggressive brain tumour that has come back after treatment.

tempoNote: Recurrence typically within 6–12 months of initial treatment
feat: New or worsening headache, seizures, focal deficits or cognitive decline
Enlarging enhancing lesion near the original resection cavity
Must be distinguished from pseudoprogression and radiation necrosis

case.story: Nine months after surgery and chemoradiation for IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, new word-finding difficulty and right hand weakness.
case.exam: Expressive aphasia, mild right hemiparesis; KPS 70.
case.tests: MRI: enlarging nodular enhancement with high perfusion at the cavity margin.
case.q: What options exist at this stage?
case.a: Re-resection if feasible, re-irradiation, lomustine or bevacizumab for symptom control, clinical trial and early palliative care discussion.

det.patho: Glioblastoma recurs because infiltrating cells beyond the resection margin survive therapy. Recurrent tumours may acquire hypermutation after temozolomide or new genetic changes that alter treatment sensitivity.
det.clinical: Most recurrences are local and present with progressive neurological deficits or seizures. Steroid dependence and fatigue are common. Quality of life considerations become central.
det.diagnosis: MRI with RANO criteria assesses progression; perfusion imaging and amino acid PET help separate tumour from treatment effect. Pseudoprogression is more likely within 12 weeks of radiotherapy.
det.treatment: No standard of care exists. Options include re-resection, re-irradiation, lomustine, bevacizumab (reduces oedema and steroid need, without proven overall survival gain), tumour-treating fields and trials. Best supportive care is appropriate for poor performance status.
det.prognosis: Median survival after recurrence is roughly 6–9 months.
pearls: Early enlargement after radiotherapy may be pseudoprogression.
Bevacizumab improves symptoms but not survival.
Discuss goals of care early.

name: Relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis
formal: Most common course of multiple sclerosis with episodes of neurological deficit followed by recovery, driven by inflammatory demyelination; treated with disease-modifying drugs.
simple: A form of multiple sclerosis with flare-ups of symptoms followed by periods of recovery.

Relapses: unilateral optic neuritis, partial myelitis with sensory symptoms, brainstem syndromes such as INO

det.patho: Autoreactive T and B cells cross the blood-brain barrier and attack myelin, causing focal inflammatory plaques with demyelination, axonal transection and gliosis. Risk factors include HLA-DRB1*15:01, prior Epstein-Barr virus infection, low vitamin D, smoking and adolescent obesity. Relapses correspond to new inflammatory lesions in clinically eloquent areas, while many lesions are silent.
det.clinical: About 85% of MS begins with a relapsing remitting course. Relapses last at least 24 hours and must be distinguished from pseudo-relapses due to infection or heat. Many patients, if untreated, enter secondary progression after 10–20 years. Fatigue, depression, cognitive slowing, bladder dysfunction and pain are common between relapses.
det.diagnosis: The 2017 McDonald criteria combine clinical attacks with MRI proof that lesions are spread across sites and over time, and allow oligoclonal bands to substitute for dissemination in time; a 2024 revision adds optic nerve involvement and imaging biomarkers such as the central vein sign. Exclude NMOSD, MOGAD, small vessel disease, vasculitis, infection and B12 deficiency. A typical clinical syndrome is essential; MRI lesions alone are not enough.
det.treatment: Relapses that cause disability are treated with methylprednisolone 500–1000 mg daily for 3–5 days, with plasma exchange for severe steroid-unresponsive attacks. Disease-modifying options range from moderate efficacy (interferon beta, glatiramer acetate, teriflunomide, dimethyl fumarate) to high efficacy (anti-CD20 therapies, natalizumab, S1P modulators, cladribine, alemtuzumab). Early high-efficacy therapy is increasingly preferred; selection must account for pregnancy plans, infection risk (JC virus, hepatitis B, TB) and access. Symptomatic care, vaccination and rehabilitation are integral.
det.prognosis: With modern therapy, many patients remain fully ambulant for decades; early effective treatment reduces long-term disability.
pearls: Always test AQP4-IgG before starting MS therapy in Asian patients; interferon, fingolimod and natalizumab can worsen NMOSD.
A new symptom with fever or urinary infection is often a pseudo-relapse; treat the infection first.
Bilateral INO in a young adult strongly suggests MS.

more: Diagnosis by video-polysomnography showing REM sleep without atonia; MRI is usually normal, and the majority convert to alpha-synucleinopathy within 10 to 15 years. Make the bedroom safe, avoid SSRIs and beta-blockers as precipitants. Parasomnia with loss of REM atonia leading to dream enactment, violent or injurious movements and vocalisation; is a strong prodromal marker of alpha-synucleinopathies. Polysomnography confirms REM sleep without atonia. Treat with bedroom safety, melatonin or clonazepam; many later develop Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia.

case.exam: No tremor or rigidity; mildly reduced arm swing on the right.

det.patho: Normally, pontine sublaterodorsal (subcoeruleus) neurons drive medullary circuits that inhibit spinal motor neurons during REM sleep. Synuclein pathology in these lower brainstem nuclei removes that atonia, so dream content is acted out. Because synuclein spreads from these areas upward, isolated RBD is the most specific known prodromal marker of the synucleinopathies — Parkinson's disease, MSA and dementia with Lewy bodies.
det.clinical: Most patients are men over 50, though women are probably under-recognised. Behaviours range from talking and twitching to violent punching and leaping from bed, typically in the later part of the night. Dreams involve confrontation or being chased, but daytime temperament is usually mild. Secondary RBD appears in narcolepsy, brainstem lesions, anti-IgLON5 disease and with antidepressants; drug-induced cases may still be a sign of underlying synucleinopathy.
det.diagnosis: ICSD-3 requires repeated sleep-related vocalisations or complex movements arising in REM (documented by PSG or presumed from dream enactment history) plus REM sleep without atonia on PSG. Video-PSG is important because OSA arousals, non-REM parasomnias and nocturnal frontal seizures can look similar. Screening questionnaires help in research but are not sufficient alone. After diagnosis, examine for subtle parkinsonism, cognition, smell and autonomic function.
det.treatment: Safety comes first: remove sharp objects, pad the floor, move the bed from windows or have the partner sleep separately. Melatonin (often 3–12 mg at bedtime) is first-line in older patients; clonazepam 0.25–1 mg at night is effective but can worsen falls, cognition and sleep apnoea. Review antidepressants and switch if possible. No treatment yet prevents conversion to neurodegenerative disease, but patients may join neuroprotection trials.
det.prognosis: Conversion to a defined synucleinopathy occurs at about 6% per year, exceeding 70% by 12 years.
pearls: Ask the bed partner — the patient rarely knows.
Isolated RBD in an older man is prodromal synucleinopathy until proven otherwise.
Treat OSA before diagnosing RBD; arousals from apnoea can mimic it.
det.thd: RBD คือการละเมอทำตามความฝันขณะหลับช่วง REM เพราะกลไกที่ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อหมดแรงในก้านสมองเสีย พบมากในชายอายุเกิน 50 ปี มักฝันว่าถูกทำร้ายแล้วต่อยเตะคู่นอน วินิจฉัยด้วย video-PSG ที่พบ REM sleep without atonia และต้องแยก OSA กับชักตอนกลางคืน รักษาโดยจัดห้องนอนให้ปลอดภัย ให้ melatonin หรือ clonazepam สิ่งสำคัญคือมากกว่าครึ่งจะกลายเป็น Parkinson, DLB หรือ MSA ภายใน 10–15 ปี จึงควรติดตามต่อเนื่อง

qx.stem: A 64-year-old retired soldier from Lopburi punches and kicks during dreams of being chased, and twice fell from bed. He has lost his sense of smell and has long-standing constipation. Neurological examination is normal. Video-polysomnography shows loss of muscle atonia with complex movements during REM sleep and no obstructive apnoea. He asks about the long-term outlook.
qx.q: Which counselling statement is most accurate?
opts: Most patients later convert to PD, DLB or MSA within 10–15 years, and he should be monitored
The disorder is benign and carries no added neurological risk
It is usually caused by obstructive sleep apnoea and resolves with CPAP
He is likely to develop Alzheimer disease rather than a synucleinopathy
Antidepressants are the treatment of choice for dream enactment
qx.why: Isolated RBD is the strongest prodromal marker of α-synucleinopathy: more than 70% phenoconvert to PD, DLB or MSA within about 12 years, and hyposmia and constipation add risk. Management is bedroom safety plus melatonin or clonazepam, and patients may be offered research studies (e.g. skin α-synuclein seeding assays). SSRIs, SNRIs and tricyclics can trigger or worsen RBD, and apnoea can mimic but does not cause it.

qx.stem: A 68-year-old farmer from Roi Et has punched the wall twice while apparently dreaming of fighting dogs, and his wife has a bruise on her arm. He has new constipation and loss of smell but no tremor or cognitive complaint. Polysomnography confirms REM sleep without atonia with dream-enactment behaviour. MRI brain is unremarkable.
qx.q: What is the most important counselling point beyond bedroom safety and clonazepam or melatonin?
opts: The disorder is benign and will not progress
Most patients with isolated RBD eventually develop a synucleinopathy such as Parkinson's disease, Lewy-body dementia or MSA, so periodic neurological follow-up is needed
It is a form of epilepsy and needs a sodium channel blocker
It results from sleep apnoea alone and resolves with CPAP
Symptoms prove he has Alzheimer disease
qx.why: Polysomnography-confirmed idiopathic RBD is a prodromal alpha-synucleinopathy in the large majority, with phenoconversion rates of roughly six to eight percent per year over long follow-up. Patients should be warned and monitored for motor, autonomic and cognitive change, and eligible individuals may be offered research participation. Sleep apnoea can cause pseudo-RBD, but polysomnography excludes it here.

qx.stem: A 66-year-old retired teacher from Khon Kaen has shouted and thrown punches in his sleep for two years, once striking his wife and recalling a dream of being attacked. He has reduced smell and chronic constipation, with a normal neurological examination. Video-polysomnography shows REM sleep with excess chin and limb muscle tone and dream-enacting behaviour; AHI is 4 per hour.
qx.q: How should he be counselled?
opts: The disorder is benign and unrelated to any later neurological disease
He has a psychiatric disorder related to trauma
He has a high likelihood of developing a synucleinopathy over the next one to two decades and needs follow-up and bedroom safety measures
He has nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy and needs carbamazepine
The condition will resolve once CPAP is started
qx.why: Idiopathic RBD confirmed by polysomnography is a prodromal synucleinopathy in most patients, evolving into Parkinson's disease, Lewy body dementia or MSA over about 10 to 15 years. Hyposmia and constipation support this. He needs safety measures, review of drugs that provoke RBD, treatment such as melatonin or clonazepam, and regular follow-up.

qx.stem: A 72-year-old retired civil servant from Nakhon Pathom has confirmed REM sleep behaviour disorder with frequent kicking and a recent fall from bed. He has mild memory complaints, previous falls and mild obstructive sleep apnoea. His family asks for the safest effective medicine.
qx.q: Which is the most appropriate initial drug?
opts: Melatonin at bedtime, with bedroom safety measures
Clonazepam 2 mg at bedtime
Zolpidem 10 mg
Quetiapine 100 mg
Amitriptyline 25 mg
qx.why: Melatonin, titrated up to several milligrams, has fewer adverse effects and is generally preferred in older patients with cognitive impairment, falls or sleep apnoea. Clonazepam is effective but can worsen apnoea, cognition and balance. Z-drugs, tricyclics and sedating antipsychotics can provoke or worsen RBD or increase fall risk.

name: Renal failure
formal: Kidney failure with neurological complications including uraemic encephalopathy, asterixis, neuropathy, restless legs, seizures and dialysis disequilibrium.
simple: Kidney failure, which can poison the brain and nerves, leading to confusion, shaking hands, numbness and seizures.
th: ภาวะไตวาย ซึ่งไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาทโดยตรงแต่มีภาวะแทรกซ้อนทางประสาท เช่น uraemic encephalopathy asterixis ปลายประสาทเสื่อม ขาอยู่ไม่สุข ชัก และ dialysis disequilibrium
tempoNote: Encephalopathy follows rapid or advanced loss of function; neuropathy and restless legs develop over months to years
feat: Systemic (kidney) disease, not a primary neurological disorder
Uraemic encephalopathy: fatigue, poor attention, asterixis, myoclonus, seizures, coma
Length-dependent sensorimotor neuropathy and restless legs syndrome; carpal tunnel from dialysis amyloid
Dialysis disequilibrium, PRES, subdural haematoma, stroke and drug toxicity (e.g. accumulation of renally cleared drugs)
Electrolyte effects: hyperkalaemic weakness, hypocalcaemic tetany
inv: Urea, creatinine, electrolytes incl. calcium, magnesium, phosphate; blood gas
CT/MRI to exclude subdural haematoma, stroke or PRES
EEG (triphasic waves or seizures) in encephalopathy; NCS for neuropathy
Review drug list for renally cleared agents (gabapentin, acyclovir, cefepime, metformin)

case.story: Diabetic CKD stage 5, has refused dialysis; over a week he became sleepy and confused with jerking of the hands.
case.exam: Drowsy, asterixis, multifocal myoclonus, stocking sensory loss with absent ankle jerks.
case.tests: Urea 220 mg/dL, creatinine 11 mg/dL; CT brain no acute lesion; EEG diffuse slowing with triphasic waves.
case.q: What is the neurological diagnosis and treatment?
case.a: Uraemic encephalopathy (plus uraemic neuropathy): start dialysis gently to avoid disequilibrium, stop renally accumulating drugs, treat seizures if they occur.

read.where: Chapter 28 Disorders of Consciousness and Intensive Care Neurology — Uraemic Encephalopathy
Chapter 57 Seizures and General Medical Disorders

det.patho: Retained uraemic toxins, disturbances of water, acid-base, calcium and phosphate, secondary hyperparathyroidism and drug accumulation impair neuronal excitability and peripheral nerve function. Dialysis itself causes complications: rapid solute shifts swell the brain (disequilibrium), anticoagulation predisposes to subdural haemorrhage, and beta-2 microglobulin amyloid compresses the median nerve.
det.clinical: Renal failure is a systemic disease that appears in this lexicon because of its many neurological complications. Uraemic encephalopathy produces fluctuating cognition, asterixis, myoclonus, seizures and coma. Chronic disease brings distal neuropathy, restless legs, cramps, autonomic dysfunction and cognitive impairment, plus a high stroke risk. Treatment-related complications include dialysis disequilibrium, PRES with immunosuppressants, and drug-induced encephalopathy.
det.diagnosis: Correlate neurological symptoms with renal function and exclude other causes, especially subdural haematoma, stroke, infection, non-convulsive seizures and drug toxicity. EEG helps in encephalopathy; NCS confirms neuropathy. Urea level alone correlates imperfectly with symptom severity.
det.treatment: Dialysis or transplantation is the definitive treatment for uraemic complications; begin dialysis gradually to prevent disequilibrium. Adjust or avoid renally cleared drugs, treat seizures with renally adjusted agents (levetiracetam needs dose adjustment after dialysis), and correct electrolytes. Restless legs respond to iron repletion, gabapentinoids at reduced doses, or dopamine agonists; neuropathy often improves after transplantation.
det.prognosis: Encephalopathy usually reverses with dialysis; neuropathy stabilises with dialysis and may improve markedly after transplant.
pearls: New confusion in a dialysis patient: check for subdural haematoma, drug accumulation and PRES before blaming uraemia.
Cefepime and acyclovir neurotoxicity are common, preventable causes in renal failure.
Kidney transplant is the most effective treatment for uraemic neuropathy.
det.thd: ไตวายไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาทโดยตรง แต่ทำให้เกิดภาวะแทรกซ้อนทางประสาทได้มาก เช่น uraemic encephalopathy ซึ่งมีสับสน asterixis กระตุก และชัก ปลายประสาทเสื่อม ขาอยู่ไม่สุข และภาวะจากการฟอกเลือด เช่น dialysis disequilibrium หรือเลือดออกใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมอง ต้องแยกสาเหตุอื่นด้วย CT EEG และทบทวนยาที่คั่งในไตวาย รักษาด้วยการฟอกเลือดอย่างค่อยเป็นค่อยไปหรือปลูกถ่ายไต

name: Repeat expansion diseases
formal: Inherited disorders from unstable nucleotide repeat expansions (e.g. Huntington, fragile X, SCAs, myotonic dystrophy) showing anticipation and variable penetrance.
simple: Inherited illnesses caused by a gene stretch repeated too many times, often getting worse or starting earlier in later generations.
th: กลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมจากลำดับเบสซ้ำที่ขยายตัวผิดปกติ เช่น Huntington, SCA, fragile X, myotonic dystrophy มักมี anticipation
tempoNote: Slowly progressive; age at onset falls with longer repeats and often in later generations
feat: Group of over 50 disorders caused by expansions of short DNA repeats (3–6 bases or longer)
Anticipation: earlier and more severe disease in successive generations
Parent-of-origin effect: paternal for Huntington and SCAs, maternal for congenital DM1 and fragile X
Phenotypes span chorea, ataxia, motor neuron disease, myopathy, neuropathy and dementia
Intermediate or premutation alleles can cause separate late-onset syndromes (e.g. FXTAS)
inv: Targeted PCR plus repeat-primed PCR or Southern blot for the specific locus
Standard exome sequencing misses most expansions; long-read sequencing or ExpansionHunter tools needed
Pre-test genetic counselling, especially for predictive testing in adults at risk

case.story: Two years of clumsiness and slurred speech. Her mother developed similar unsteadiness at 55, and her son, now 19, already stumbles.
case.exam: Gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria, slow saccades and brisk reflexes.
case.tests: Exome sequencing negative; targeted testing shows 58 CAG repeats in ATXN3.
case.q: Why was exome negative, and what explains the son's earlier onset?
case.a: Repeat expansions are poorly detected by short-read exome; longer repeats in the next generation (anticipation) give earlier onset — here SCA3/Machado–Joseph disease.

det.patho: Repeats become unstable above a threshold and tend to lengthen during transmission and in some tissues over life. Damage arises through several routes: toxic polyglutamine tracts (Huntington disease, DRPLA, SBMA and several dominant SCAs such as types 1, 2, 3 and 6), toxic RNA that traps splicing factors (DM1, DM2, FXTAS), repeat-associated non-AUG translation (C9orf72), and loss of gene expression when the expansion silences its gene (fragile X, Friedreich ataxia).
det.clinical: Coding CAG disorders give adult-onset neurodegeneration with ataxia, chorea or motor neuron features; non-coding expansions cause myotonic dystrophy, Friedreich ataxia, C9orf72 ALS–FTD, CANVAS (RFC1) and others. Anticipation and wide variability within one family are clues. Several newly recognised expansions, such as those in NOTCH2NLC (neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease) and FGF14 (SCA27B), are relatively common in Asian and late-onset ataxia populations.
det.diagnosis: The phenotype guides which locus to test. Repeat-primed PCR detects large expansions that standard PCR cannot amplify, and Southern blot sizes very large ones. Short-read exomes usually miss expansions, so a negative exome does not exclude them; long-read sequencing increasingly allows several loci to be screened at once. Predictive testing of healthy relatives follows structured counselling protocols.
det.treatment: Management is mostly symptomatic and multidisciplinary. Antisense oligonucleotide and gene-silencing approaches are in trials for Huntington disease, SCA3 and C9orf72, but none is yet a standard cure. Omaveloxolone is approved for Friedreich ataxia. Reproductive options include prenatal and preimplantation testing.
det.prognosis: Variable by disorder; larger repeats generally mean earlier onset and faster course.
pearls: Negative exome in a familial ataxia: ask specifically for repeat-expansion testing.
Paternal transmission drives big jumps in Huntington and SCA repeats; maternal in DM1 and fragile X.
Intermediate alleles can cause disease of their own (FXTAS, ALS risk with intermediate ATXN2).
det.thd: Repeat expansion diseases เป็นกลุ่มโรคที่เกิดจากลำดับเบสซ้ำยาวเกินเกณฑ์ เช่น Huntington, SCA, myotonic dystrophy, Friedreich ataxia และ fragile X ลักษณะเด่นคือ anticipation อาการเริ่มเร็วและรุนแรงขึ้นในรุ่นถัดไป การตรวจต้องใช้ PCR เฉพาะตำแหน่งหรือ repeat-primed PCR เพราะ exome มักตรวจไม่พบ การรักษาส่วนใหญ่ประคับประคอง ร่วมกับให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

name: Respiratory chain diseases
formal: Mitochondrial disorders from defects of oxidative phosphorylation complexes, causing multisystem disease with encephalopathy, myopathy, stroke-like episodes and lactic acidosis.
simple: Inherited problems with the cell's energy factories, affecting the brain, muscles and other organs.
th: โรคไมโทคอนเดรียจากความบกพร่องของ complex I–V ในการสร้างพลังงาน ทำให้เกิดโรคหลายระบบ เช่น encephalopathy, myopathy, stroke-like episodes และ lactic acidosis
tempoNote: Lifelong progression punctuated by acute crises triggered by illness, fasting or drugs
feat: Multisystem involvement in tissues with high energy demand: brain, muscle, heart, retina, ear
Ptosis and ophthalmoplegia, exercise intolerance and proximal weakness
Stroke-like episodes not respecting vascular territories, seizures, ataxia, hearing loss
Short stature, diabetes, cardiomyopathy, conduction block, GI dysmotility
Maternal (mtDNA) or Mendelian (nuclear gene, e.g. POLG) inheritance
inv: Lactate in blood and CSF; MR spectroscopy lactate peak
Genetic testing: mtDNA (blood, urine, muscle) and nuclear gene panels or exome
Muscle biopsy: ragged-red or COX-negative fibres, respiratory chain enzyme assays
ECG, echo, audiometry, glucose, ophthalmology

case.story: Short since childhood with hearing aids since age 15; now presents with headache, vomiting and right visual field loss over two days.
case.exam: Right homonymous hemianopia, bilateral sensorineural deafness, mild proximal weakness.
case.tests: Lactate 4.8 mmol/L; MRI: left occipital cortical swelling crossing PCA borders; mtDNA m.3243A>G heteroplasmy in urine.
case.q: Which respiratory chain syndrome is this and which antiseizure drug must be avoided?
case.a: MELAS; avoid valproate, and give IV arginine during the acute stroke-like episode.

read.where: Genetic Diseases of the Nervous System — Mitochondrial Diseases
Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Mitochondrial Respiratory Chain Diseases

det.patho: The respiratory chain comprises complexes I–IV plus ATP synthase in the inner mitochondrial membrane; subunits are encoded by both mtDNA and nuclear genes. Defects reduce ATP production and shift metabolism to anaerobic glycolysis, raising lactate. With mtDNA variants, the proportion of mutant copies (heteroplasmy) varies by tissue and explains variable severity within families.
det.clinical: Presentations span neonatal lactic acidosis, Leigh syndrome in infancy, MELAS, MERRF, Kearns-Sayre syndrome and CPEO in young adults, to isolated myopathy or neuropathy. Red flags are an unexplained combination of neurological and non-neurological features, maternal family clustering and worsening during infection. Valproate can precipitate liver failure in POLG disease.
det.diagnosis: Genetic testing is now first line: mtDNA sequencing (urine or muscle is better than blood for some variants) and nuclear gene panels or exome/genome sequencing. Muscle biopsy remains useful when genetics is unrevealing. Lactate, MRS, GDF-15 and FGF-21 are supportive markers but neither sensitive nor specific.
det.treatment: No cure exists. Management covers multisystem surveillance (cardiac, endocrine, hearing, vision), exercise training, avoiding mitochondrial toxins and treating crises promptly. IV and oral arginine or citrulline are used in MELAS. Coenzyme Q10 is given especially for primary CoQ10 deficiency; idebenone is licensed for LHON in some regions. Genetic counselling and reproductive options such as preimplantation diagnosis apply.
det.prognosis: Highly variable, from early childhood death to near-normal lifespan with a mild myopathy.
pearls: Stroke-like lesion crossing vascular territories plus deafness and short stature: think MELAS.
Avoid valproate until POLG disease is excluded.
Blood mtDNA can be falsely normal; test urine or muscle.
det.thd: Respiratory chain diseases คือโรคไมโทคอนเดรียที่ complex สร้างพลังงานบกพร่อง จากยีนใน mtDNA หรือ nuclear DNA ทำให้อวัยวะที่ใช้พลังงานมากเสีย เช่น สมอง กล้ามเนื้อ หัวใจ ตา และหู อาการเช่น หนังตาตก กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง ชัก stroke-like episode และหูหนวก ตรวจ lactate, MRS, ยีน และ muscle biopsy รักษาแบบประคับประคอง หลีกเลี่ยง valproate และให้ arginine ใน MELAS

name: Rest tremor
formal: Tremor appearing in a fully supported, relaxed limb, typically 4 to 6 Hz pill-rolling in Parkinson disease, and reducing with action.
simple: A shake that appears when a limb is relaxed and supported, typical of Parkinson's disease.
th: Rest tremor คือการสั่นขณะแขนขาวางพักเต็มที่ ความถี่ราว 4–6 Hz ลักษณะคล้ายปั้นยา (pill-rolling) พบเด่นใน Parkinson disease แต่ก็เกิดจาก drug-induced parkinsonism, Holmes tremor หรือ Wilson disease ได้ มักลดลงเมื่อเคลื่อนไหวและกลับมาใหม่เมื่อค้างท่า (re-emergent tremor)
tempoNote: Insidious over months to years in degenerative parkinsonism; subacute onset after a midbrain or thalamic lesion (Holmes tremor) or within weeks of starting a dopamine blocker
feat: Appears only when the limb is fully supported and relaxed, is usually asymmetric at onset and is typically 4–6 Hz, with thumb-on-finger pill-rolling, forearm pronation-supination or a foot or jaw tremor
Falls away when the limb starts to move, but commonly returns a few seconds after the arms are held out in front, a pattern called re-emergent tremor
Increased by walking, mental arithmetic and emotional stress and absent in deep sleep

Leg, lip and chin rest tremors are uncommon in essential tremor and favour Parkinson disease; a very slow (2–4 Hz) rest, postural and action tremor of the proximal arm after a midbrain lesion is Holmes tremor
A rest tremor may also occur in a minority of severe essential tremor, in dystonia and in drug-induced parkinsonism, so the cause depends on the neighbouring signs
inv: Examination for bradykinesia, rigidity and postural reflexes under distraction (counting, contralateral tapping) to bring out the rest tremor
DaT-SPECT or dopamine PET when a tremor-dominant syndrome cannot be separated from dystonic tremor or essential tremor with rest component

MRI brain for rapid, unilateral proximal or Holmes-type tremor; copper studies in patients under 50 years old; review of dopamine-blocking agents and of calcium-channel blocking drugs (e.g. flunarizine)

case.story: Eight months ago his right thumb began to rub against his forefinger while he watched television; his handwriting has become smaller and he walks with a shorter right arm swing. The tremor stops when he reaches for his tea.
case.exam: Right-hand 5 Hz pill-rolling at rest, appearing again about 10 seconds after both arms are held out; right-sided bradykinesia and cogwheel rigidity; reduced right arm swing.
case.tests: He takes no dopamine-blocking drugs; DaT-SPECT shows reduced uptake in the left putamen.
case.q: What does the rest tremor indicate and what is the treatment approach?
case.a: Parkinson disease with tremor-dominant onset; start levodopa or a dopamine agonist according to age and disability, knowing that tremor may respond less well than bradykinesia, and consider deep brain stimulation or focused ultrasound later if tremor remains disabling.

read.where: Chapter 9 Movement Disorders — ‘Typical’ Motor Presentation of Parkinson’s Disease

det.patho: The parkinsonian rest tremor is not simply caused by lack of dopamine in the striatum, because it correlates poorly with bradykinesia and responds less predictably to levodopa. Current work suggests that loss of dopaminergic neurons, especially in the retrorubral area, sets up abnormal basal ganglia activity which then drives an oscillation in the cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuit. This two-part model explains why surgical lesions or stimulation of the ventral intermediate thalamus abolish the tremor while leaving other signs.
det.clinical: Rest tremor is the presenting sign in roughly half of patients with Parkinson disease and is often noticed first by relatives. It begins in one hand, spreads to the leg on the same side, then to the opposite side over years, and may involve the jaw or lips but rarely the head or voice. Progression is usually slower in the tremor-dominant subtype than in the postural-instability and gait-difficulty subtype. A re-emergent postural tremor with the same frequency as the rest tremor is common and belongs to the same condition. Holmes tremor and rest tremor in dystonia, drug-induced parkinsonism, Wilson disease and rare spinocerebellar ataxias make up the differential.
det.diagnosis: Observe the limb fully supported and while the patient is distracted; ask the patient to count backward by sevens, since this increases a true rest tremor. The 2015 MDS criteria and the 2018 tremor consensus count rest tremor as a supportive feature of Parkinson disease, with bradykinesia required for the diagnosis. DaT-SPECT shows reduced uptake in Parkinson disease as well as in MSA and PSP, but is normal in drug-induced parkinsonism, dystonic tremor and essential tremor, which makes it useful when the clinical picture is unclear. Drug and toxin history, signs of a structural lesion and, in young patients, copper studies complete the work-up.
det.treatment: Levodopa and dopamine agonists are used first; the rest tremor responds in most patients but may need higher doses than bradykinesia, and an anticholinergic such as trihexyphenidyl can be added for young patients with severe tremor when cognition is intact. Beta-blockers have little effect on rest tremor, while clozapine in low dose is a rare rescue option. For disabling tremor despite adequate medication, subthalamic or ventral intermediate thalamic deep brain stimulation and MR-guided focused ultrasound (unilateral thalamotomy or pallidothalamic tractotomy) give lasting benefit. Drug-induced parkinsonism needs withdrawal or substitution of the offending drug with quetiapine or clozapine when antipsychotic treatment must continue.
det.prognosis: Rest tremor is often the most visible but least disabling feature; patients with tremor-dominant Parkinson disease generally keep their independence longer than those with gait-predominant disease.
pearls: Count backward by sevens to bring out a rest tremor.
A rest tremor that vanishes while the patient reaches for an object but returns after a few seconds of holding the arm out is parkinsonian.
Symmetric rest tremor soon after starting a drug points to drug-induced parkinsonism rather than Parkinson disease.
det.thd: Rest tremor คือการสั่นที่เห็นเมื่อแขนขาวางพักเต็มที่ ความถี่ประมาณ 4–6 Hz เหมือนปั้นยา มักเริ่มข้างเดียวและลดลงเมื่อเคลื่อนไหว แต่จะกลับมาเมื่อยกแขนค้างสักพัก (re-emergent tremor) สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยที่สุดคือ Parkinson disease แต่ต้องคิดถึงยาที่ปิดกั้น dopamine, flunarizine และ Holmes tremor ด้วย การรักษาเริ่มด้วย levodopa หรือ dopamine agonist ถ้าสั่นมากจนรบกวนชีวิต อาจใช้ DBS หรือ focused ultrasound

ddx.pt: Postural and kinetic tremor present from the moment the arms are held out and worse on the dot test, without bradykinesia
Slow, irregular rest, postural and action tremor after a midbrain or thalamic lesion, with a delay of weeks to months after the lesion
Usually symmetric tremor with bradykinesia that follows a dopamine-blocking drug or flunarizine and improves after withdrawal over weeks to months

name: Restless arm syndrome
formal: Variant of restless legs syndrome with urge to move the arms and unpleasant sensations worse at rest in the evening, relieved by movement.
simple: An uncomfortable urge to move the arms, worse when resting in the evening and relieved by moving.
th: รูปแบบหนึ่งของ restless legs syndrome ที่อยากขยับแขนพร้อมความรู้สึกไม่สบายขณะพัก โดยเฉพาะตอนเย็นและกลางคืน และดีขึ้นเมื่อขยับ
tempoNote: Nightly symptoms, persistent over months to years
feat: Urge to move the arms with unpleasant deep sensations
Worse at rest and in the evening or at night; relieved by movement
Often accompanies leg symptoms; isolated arm form is rare
May emerge with dopaminergic augmentation in RLS
Associated with iron deficiency, renal failure, pregnancy, neuropathy
inv: Ferritin and transferrin saturation
Renal function, glucose, B12
NCS if neuropathy suspected; exclude carpal tunnel or cervical radiculopathy

case.who: 58-year-old woman from Suphan Buri on haemodialysis
case.story: For months she cannot keep her arms still while watching TV at night; she has to wave or rub them to get relief, and her legs feel similar.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination.
case.tests: Ferritin 60 ng/mL, transferrin saturation 15%.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the first management step?
case.a: Restless legs/arm syndrome associated with uraemia and iron deficiency; replace iron and optimise dialysis, then consider alpha-2-delta ligands.

det.patho: Restless arm syndrome shares the mechanism of RLS: brain iron deficiency, dopaminergic dysfunction and circadian modulation. Augmentation from dopaminergic drugs can spread symptoms to the arms.
det.clinical: It is a variant of RLS with the same five diagnostic criteria applied to the arms. Isolated arm involvement is rare. Arm involvement in a patient on dopamine agonists suggests augmentation.
det.diagnosis: Clinical, using RLS criteria. Check iron studies and secondary causes. Exclude carpal tunnel syndrome, radiculopathy, akathisia and neuropathy.
det.treatment: Iron replacement if ferritin is under 75 ng/mL. Alpha-2-delta ligands (gabapentin, pregabalin) are first-line drugs; dopamine agonists are used cautiously because of augmentation. Low-dose opioids are reserved for refractory cases.
det.prognosis: Chronic but usually controllable; resolves after correcting reversible causes.
pearls: Arm spread on dopamine agonists suggests augmentation.
Check iron in every patient with RLS symptoms.
det.thd: Restless arm syndrome เป็นรูปแบบของ restless legs syndrome ที่มีความรู้สึกไม่สบายและอยากขยับแขนขณะพัก โดยเฉพาะตอนเย็นหรือกลางคืน ดีขึ้นเมื่อขยับ ควรตรวจเหล็ก ไต และแยกจาก carpal tunnel syndrome รักษาด้วยการให้เหล็กและยา gabapentin หรือ pregabalin ระวังภาวะ augmentation จากยา dopamine agonist

Whole-body restlessness after dopamine-blocking drugs, not circadian
