name: Restless legs syndrome (RLS)
formal: Sensorimotor disorder with urge to move the legs, worse at rest and evening, relieved by movement; linked to iron deficiency, renal failure and dopaminergic dysfunction.
simple: An urge to move the legs with uncomfortable feelings, mainly at night, relieved by moving.
more: Sensorimotor disorder with urge to move the legs at rest, worse at night and relieved by movement, associated with iron deficiency and dopaminergic dysfunction; treated with gabapentinoids or iron.
th: รู้สึกไม่สบายที่ขาและอยากขยับขาตอนพักหรือตอนกลางคืน ขยับแล้วดีขึ้น ทำให้นอนไม่หลับ สัมพันธ์กับภาวะขาดธาตุเหล็ก
tempoNote: Symptoms recur in the evening or at rest; course chronic with fluctuating frequency
feat: Urge to move the legs, usually with deep creeping or aching sensations
Starts or worsens at rest and in the evening or night
Relieved, at least partly, by walking or stretching
Periodic limb movements of sleep in most patients; insomnia and daytime fatigue
Triggers: iron deficiency, pregnancy, CKD/dialysis, antidepressants, antihistamines, antipsychotics
inv: Serum ferritin and transferrin saturation (treat if ferritin ≤75 µg/L or TSAT <20%)
CBC, renal function, glucose; consider B12 and neuropathy screen if sensory signs
Polysomnography only if diagnosis uncertain or other sleep disorder suspected (PLMS index)

case.story: For a year she cannot sit through a TV drama at night because her legs feel like ants crawling inside; she must get up and walk. Sleep is broken; her husband says she kicks in sleep.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination; pale conjunctivae.
case.tests: Hb 10.2 g/dL, ferritin 18 µg/L, TSAT 9%.
case.q: What is the first treatment step?
case.a: Restless legs syndrome with iron deficiency: replace iron (oral or IV) aiming for ferritin above 75 µg/L, look for the cause of iron loss, and review aggravating drugs before considering other agents.

read.where: Chapter 24: Restless legs syndrome / Willis–Ekbom disease

det.patho: RLS reflects brain iron deficiency in the substantia nigra and related circuits combined with altered dopaminergic and glutamatergic signalling, with strong genetic contribution (MEIS1, BTBD9 and others). Prevalence is several percent of adults, higher in women, pregnancy and kidney failure. Secondary forms arise with iron deficiency, uraemia and some drugs.
det.clinical: Patients describe an irresistible need to move with sensations that are hard to describe (crawling, pulling, electric) deep in the legs, sometimes the arms. Symptoms follow a circadian pattern and are triggered by immobility such as flights or meetings. Insomnia, mood disturbance and reduced quality of life are common. Augmentation — earlier, stronger, more widespread symptoms — can develop on dopamine agonists.
det.diagnosis: IRLSSG criteria need all five: urge to move, rest-induced, relieved by movement, evening/night predominance and not explained by another condition. Check iron status in all patients. Exclude mimics: leg cramps, positional discomfort, neuropathy, akathisia, venous disease and arthritis.
det.treatment: Correct iron (oral if ferritin ≤75 µg/L, IV ferric carboxymaltose if oral fails or TSAT very low) and remove aggravating drugs, alcohol and caffeine. Current guidance (AASM 2024) prefers alpha-2-delta ligands (gabapentin, gabapentin enacarbil, pregabalin) first-line and discourages routine dopamine agonists because of augmentation. Low-dose opioids help refractory or augmented cases. In pregnancy rely on iron and non-drug measures.
det.prognosis: Chronic but manageable; secondary forms often improve once iron is replaced or after pregnancy or kidney transplant.
pearls: Ferritin target in RLS (≥75 µg/L) is higher than the usual 'normal' cut-off.
Augmentation on dopamine agonists is the major long-term problem.
Ask about antihistamines, SSRIs/SNRIs, mirtazapine and antipsychotics.
det.thd: Restless legs syndrome คืออาการอยากขยับขาร่วมกับความรู้สึกไม่สบายลึก ๆ ในขา เป็นมากตอนพักและตอนกลางคืน ขยับหรือเดินแล้วดีขึ้น ทำให้นอนไม่หลับ สัมพันธ์กับธาตุเหล็กในสมองต่ำ ต้องตรวจ ferritin ทุกราย ให้ธาตุเหล็กถ้า ferritin ไม่เกิน 75 ปัจจุบันแนะนำยากลุ่ม gabapentin/pregabalin เป็นยาแรก และเลี่ยง dopamine agonist ระยะยาวเพราะเกิด augmentation

qx.stem: A 45-year-old woman from Ubon Ratchathani has had three months of an uncomfortable crawling urge to move her legs each evening when sitting, relieved by walking and worse at night. She has heavy menstrual periods. Neurological examination is normal. Ferritin is 28 ng/mL and transferrin saturation 12%.
qx.q: What is the most appropriate first treatment step?
opts: Start pramipexole at bedtime
Replace iron and investigate the cause of iron deficiency
Start long-term low-dose opioid
Start clonazepam
Prescribe a sedating antihistamine
qx.why: In RLS, ferritin up to about 75 ng/mL is treated with iron, by oral or, if intolerant or refractory, intravenous routes, and the cause of deficiency, here menorrhagia, should be addressed. Current guidance prefers iron and alpha-2-delta ligands over dopamine agonists because of augmentation. Antihistamines can aggravate RLS, and opioids are reserved for refractory cases.

src.where: Chapter 24 Restless legs syndrome / Willis–Ekbom disease

qx.stem: A 58-year-old man from Chonburi has taken pramipexole for RLS for three years, increasing the dose twice. Symptoms now begin at 2 p.m. instead of the evening, have spread to the arms and are worse after each dose increase. Ferritin is 60 ng/mL.
qx.q: What is the best management?
opts: Increase pramipexole again
Add a second dopamine agonist
Add levodopa at bedtime
Start tramadol
Correct iron, add an alpha-2-delta ligand, then taper the dopamine agonist
qx.why: Earlier onset during the day, spread to new body parts and worsening with higher doses define augmentation from dopaminergic therapy. Further dopaminergic increases worsen it. Management is to optimise iron, introduce gabapentin, pregabalin or gabapentin enacarbil, and gradually reduce the dopamine agonist; opioids are a later option.

qx.stem: A 52-year-old man from Rayong with restless legs syndrome and chronic kidney disease is taking several medicines and reports that symptoms became worse after changes to his prescription. His doctor wants to review the list for drugs that aggravate RLS.
qx.q: Which one of these would least probably worsen his symptoms?
opts: Sertraline
Diphenhydramine
Gabapentin
Metoclopramide
Haloperidol
qx.why: Antidopaminergic antiemetics and antipsychotics, sedating antihistamines, SSRIs and other antidepressants such as mirtazapine can all aggravate RLS. Gabapentin is a first-line treatment, though renal dosing is essential in kidney disease. Uraemia itself is also a recognised secondary cause.

name: Restrictive ophthalmopathy
formal: Limited eye movement from mechanical tethering of orbital muscles, as in thyroid eye disease, orbital myositis or entrapment, confirmed by positive forced duction test.
simple: Difficulty moving the eyes because the muscles around the eye are stiff or trapped, as in thyroid eye disease.
th: การกลอกตาจำกัดจากกล้ามเนื้อหรือเนื้อเยื่อเบ้าตาถูกตรึงทางกล เช่น thyroid eye disease, orbital myositis หรือกระดูกเบ้าตาหัก ยืนยันด้วย forced duction
tempoNote: Subacute in orbital inflammation or after trauma; chronic in thyroid eye disease
feat: Diplopia with limited movement away from the tethered muscle (e.g. poor elevation from a tight inferior rectus)
Positive forced duction test; saccades start briskly then stop abruptly
Rise in intraocular pressure when looking toward the limitation
Associated proptosis, lid retraction, chemosis or orbital pain depending on cause
Causes: thyroid eye disease, orbital myositis, blow-out fracture with entrapment, tumour, post-surgical scarring, IgG4 disease
inv: Forced duction test under topical anaesthesia
Orbital CT or MRI: muscle enlargement (tendon-sparing in thyroid, tendon-involving in myositis), fracture
Thyroid function and TSH-receptor antibodies

case.who: 52-year-old woman with treated Graves disease in Chiang Rai
case.story: Vertical double vision for four months, worse on looking up; eyes feel gritty.
case.exam: Lid retraction, mild proptosis, limited elevation of the right eye, positive forced duction on attempted elevation.
case.tests: CT orbits shows enlarged right inferior and medial recti with tendon sparing.
case.q: Why is elevation limited and how is this different from a third nerve palsy?
case.a: A fibrotic, enlarged inferior rectus tethers the eye; forced duction is positive and pupils and lids show no nerve-palsy pattern.

det.patho: Restriction results from muscle that cannot stretch (fibrosis, inflammation or infiltration) or from tissue trapped in a fracture or scar. Unlike neurogenic or myasthenic weakness, the muscles may contract normally but the globe cannot move against the mechanical tether.
det.clinical: Patients report diplopia, often vertical, in gaze away from the involved muscle. Saccades may be brisk until they abruptly stop. Associated features depend on the cause: eyelid retraction with proptosis in thyroid eye disease, painful onset in orbital myositis, trauma history in blow-out fractures.
det.diagnosis: A positive forced duction test confirms restriction. Orbital imaging defines the cause and pattern of muscle involvement. Thyroid function, TSH-receptor antibodies and, when relevant, IgG4 levels or biopsy complete the work-up.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: immunosuppression or teprotumumab for active thyroid eye disease, corticosteroids for orbital myositis, surgical release for entrapment. Prisms help small deviations; strabismus surgery is deferred until disease is inactive.
det.prognosis: Often good once inflammation settles, though residual diplopia may require surgery.
pearls: Positive forced duction = mechanical, not neurogenic.
Thyroid eye disease favours inferior and medial recti.
Orbital myositis enlarges the tendon too and is painful.
det.thd: Restrictive ophthalmopathy คือการกลอกตาจำกัดเพราะกล้ามเนื้อหรือเนื้อเยื่อในเบ้าตาถูกตรึงทางกล ไม่ใช่เส้นประสาทหรือ NMJ ผิดปกติ สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยที่สุดคือ thyroid eye disease รองลงมาคือ orbital myositis และกระดูกเบ้าตาหักที่มีกล้ามเนื้อติด ยืนยันด้วย forced duction test และภาพ CT/MRI เบ้าตา รักษาตามสาเหตุ

Fatigable variable weakness with ptosis; forced duction negative
Ptosis, pupil involvement and neurogenic pattern; forced duction negative

name: Retinal degeneration
formal: Progressive loss of photoreceptors or retinal pigment epithelium, genetic or acquired, causing nyctalopia, field loss and eventual blindness.
simple: A gradual loss of the light-sensing cells in the eye that leads to vision loss.
th: การเสื่อมของเซลล์รับแสงหรือ retinal pigment epithelium จากพันธุกรรมหรือสาเหตุภายหลัง ทำให้ตาบอดกลางคืน ลานสายตาแคบ และอาจตาบอดในที่สุด
tempoNote: Progressive over years; paraneoplastic forms subacute
feat: Night blindness and progressive peripheral field loss (rod-cone) or central loss (cone-rod)
Bone-spicule pigment, attenuated vessels, waxy disc pallor
Can be isolated (retinitis pigmentosa) or part of a neurological syndrome
Neurological associations: NCL, mitochondrial disease (NARP, Kearns–Sayre), Refsum, abetalipoproteinaemia, SCA7
Acquired: paraneoplastic (CAR/MAR), drug toxicity (hydroxychloroquine, vigabatrin)
inv: Fundoscopy, OCT, fundus autofluorescence
Electroretinography (ERG)
Genetic panel; phytanic acid, lipids, vitamin E as directed

case.story: Trouble seeing at night since his teens, now bumping into objects at his sides; recently unsteady walking.
case.exam: Bone-spicule pigment, narrowed fields, gait ataxia, absent ankle reflexes.
case.tests: ERG markedly reduced; vitamin E very low; MTTP variant.
case.q: Why look for a neurological association in a patient with retinal degeneration?
case.a: Some causes (abetalipoproteinaemia, Refsum, AVED) are treatable; here vitamin E supplementation can slow progression.

read.where: Chapter 22 Neuro-Ophthalmology — Ocular Involvement in Other Neurological Disease
Chapter 72: Hyperkinetic Movement Disorders: Chorea, Tic, and Dystonia

det.patho: Retinal degenerations result from genetic defects in phototransduction, photoreceptor structure, RPE metabolism or lipid handling, or from acquired toxic, immune or nutritional injury. Photoreceptor death follows a rod-first or cone-first pattern.
det.clinical: This is a broad ophthalmic category rather than a single neurological disease. Patients present with night blindness, field constriction or central vision loss. Neurologists encounter it in syndromic disorders such as NCL, mitochondrial diseases, Refsum disease, abetalipoproteinaemia and SCA7.
det.diagnosis: Ophthalmic examination, OCT, autofluorescence and ERG define the pattern. Genetic testing identifies the gene in most inherited cases. Metabolic tests target treatable syndromic causes. Subacute onset should prompt paraneoplastic antibody testing.
det.treatment: Gene therapy (voretigene for RPE65) is available for specific genotypes. Treat underlying causes: phytanic acid diet for Refsum, vitamin E and A for abetalipoproteinaemia. Low-vision rehabilitation is important.
det.prognosis: Usually progressive; rate depends on cause.
pearls: Retinopathy plus ataxia or neuropathy: think Refsum, abetalipoproteinaemia, NARP, SCA7.
ERG is the key test for photoreceptor dysfunction.
Rapid onset in an older adult: think paraneoplastic retinopathy.
det.thd: Retinal degeneration คือการเสื่อมของเซลล์รับแสงในจอตา ทำให้ตาบอดกลางคืนและลานสายตาแคบ อาจเป็นโรคตาเพียงอย่างเดียว เช่น retinitis pigmentosa หรือเป็นส่วนหนึ่งของโรคระบบประสาท เช่น Refsum, NARP, abetalipoproteinaemia ตรวจด้วย ERG, OCT และยีน บางสาเหตุรักษาได้

simple: Small non-cancerous growths in the retina often seen in tuberous sclerosis.

tempoNote: Usually stable and found incidentally
feat: Flat, translucent or calcified 'mulberry' lesions near the disc or posterior pole
Seen in about half of patients with tuberous sclerosis complex
Also in NF1 and occasionally isolated
Usually asymptomatic; rarely affect vision
Different from haemangioblastoma of von Hippel–Lindau

case.who: 7-year-old girl from Khon Kaen with seizures
case.story: Referred for routine eye check after starting vigabatrin for infantile spasms history.
case.exam: Several hypomelanotic macules and a facial angiofibroma; fundus shows a calcified mulberry lesion near the right disc.
case.tests: MRI shows cortical tubers and subependymal nodules; TSC2 variant.
case.q: What is the retinal finding and its significance?
case.a: Retinal astrocytic hamartoma, a major feature of tuberous sclerosis complex; usually benign and only needs monitoring.

det.patho: Retinal astrocytic hamartomas grow from astrocytes lying in the innermost retina near the nerve fibres. In TSC, loss of TSC1/TSC2 increases mTOR activity, driving hamartomatous growth. They may calcify over time.
det.clinical: Usually found on screening in TSC patients. Most are stable and asymptomatic. Rarely, they enlarge or cause exudation or vitreous haemorrhage. They can be confused with retinoblastoma in infants.
det.diagnosis: Fundoscopy and OCT; calcification seen on ultrasound. Finding one should prompt assessment for TSC or NF1.
det.treatment: Observation is usually enough. Laser or anti-VEGF for complicated lesions; mTOR inhibitors given for other TSC indications may shrink them.
det.prognosis: Excellent visually in most patients.
pearls: Retinal hamartoma is a major diagnostic criterion for tuberous sclerosis.
Distinguish from haemangioblastoma (VHL) and retinoblastoma.
det.thd: Retinal hamartoma เป็นเนื้องอกไม่ร้ายของเซลล์ glia ในจอตา พบบ่อยในผู้ป่วย tuberous sclerosis และบางครั้งใน NF1 มักไม่มีอาการและพบจากการตรวจคัดกรอง ลักษณะเป็นก้อนสีขาวคล้ายผลหม่อน เมื่อพบควรตรวจหา tuberous sclerosis ส่วนใหญ่ติดตามดูอย่างเดียว

name: Retinitis
formal: Inflammation of the retina from infection (CMV, toxoplasma, syphilis) or immune disease, with floaters, reduced vision and retinal whitening.
simple: Inflammation of the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye, causing blurred vision and floaters.
th: การอักเสบของจอประสาทตาจากเชื้อ (CMV, toxoplasma, syphilis, herpes) หรือโรคภูมิคุ้มกัน มีตาพร่า เห็นจุดลอย และจอตาขาวขุ่น
tempoNote: Viral necrotising forms progress over days; CMV in HIV over weeks
feat: Floaters, blurred vision, field loss; painless in CMV, painful red eye in acute retinal necrosis
Whitish retinal infiltrates or necrosis, with haemorrhages in CMV
Toxoplasma: focal retinochoroiditis next to an old scar with vitreous haze
Syphilis: placoid lesions or necrotising retinitis, may accompany neurosyphilis
This is primarily an ophthalmic condition; neurologists meet it with HIV, encephalitis and neurosyphilis

Aqueous or vitreous PCR (CMV, HSV, VZV, toxoplasma)
HIV and CD4, syphilis serology with CSF exam if positive

case.who: 35-year-old man with newly found HIV from Udon Thani
case.story: A month of floaters and a growing dark patch in his left eye's vision.
case.exam: Left eye: white granular retinal lesion with haemorrhages along the arcade; no pain.
case.tests: CD4 22 cells/µL; aqueous humour CMV PCR positive.
case.q: What is the treatment?
case.a: Induction with valganciclovir or IV ganciclovir (intravitreal injections if sight-threatening), then start ART.

det.patho: Pathogens reach the retina via the bloodstream or along neural routes (herpes viruses), causing necrosis of retinal layers. Immune status shapes the picture: CMV and progressive outer retinal necrosis in profound immunosuppression, acute retinal necrosis in immunocompetent people, and toxoplasma reactivation from congenital scars.
det.clinical: Retinitis is an eye disease rather than a neurological disease, but it is a clue to systemic and CNS infection. CMV retinitis signals CD4 below 50 and can coexist with CMV encephalitis or polyradiculitis. Ocular syphilis should be managed as neurosyphilis. Acute retinal necrosis may follow HSV encephalitis.
det.diagnosis: Ophthalmological exam is key, supported by ocular fluid PCR and serology. In HIV, CD4 count and plasma CMV PCR help. Syphilis serology is mandatory for all uveitis or retinitis presentations.
det.treatment: Treat the organism: ganciclovir or valganciclovir (foscarnet if resistant) for CMV; IV acyclovir or high-dose valacyclovir for acute retinal necrosis; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or pyrimethamine regimens for toxoplasma; IV penicillin for ocular syphilis. Intravitreal therapy is used for sight-threatening lesions. Restore immunity with ART.
det.prognosis: Depends on lesion location and timing; zone 1 CMV and retinal necrosis risk detachment and permanent loss.
pearls: Ocular syphilis = neurosyphilis for treatment purposes.
CMV retinitis means CD4 is very low; look for other CMV disease.
Screen the fundus in advanced HIV even without symptoms.
det.thd: Retinitis คือการอักเสบของจอประสาทตา ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจากเชื้อ เช่น CMV ในผู้ป่วย HIV ระยะท้าย, toxoplasma, ซิฟิลิส และไวรัสเริม ผู้ป่วยเห็นจุดลอยและตามัว ตรวจจอตาพบรอยขาวขุ่น เป็นโรคทางตาโดยตรง แต่เป็นเบาะแสของการติดเชื้อในระบบประสาท รักษาตามเชื้อ และตรวจ HIV กับซิฟิลิสทุกราย

name: Retinitis pigmentosa
formal: Inherited rod-cone dystrophy with night blindness, concentric field constriction and bone-spicule pigmentation; may occur in syndromes such as Refsum and Usher.
simple: An inherited eye disease with night blindness and gradually shrinking side vision.
th: โรคจอตาเสื่อมทางพันธุกรรมชนิด rod-cone ทำให้ตาบอดกลางคืน ลานสายตาแคบ และพบเม็ดสีรูปกระดูกที่จอตา บางครั้งเป็นส่วนหนึ่งของโรคทางระบบประสาท
tempoNote: Night blindness in childhood or youth, then slow constriction of fields over decades
feat: Night blindness first, then progressive 'tunnel' constriction of peripheral vision
Fundus: bone-spicule pigment, attenuated arterioles, waxy pale disc
Central acuity kept until late; cataract and macular oedema common
Isolated (non-syndromic) in most; syndromic with deafness (Usher), ataxia/neuropathy (Refsum, NARP, AVED, abetalipoproteinaemia), ophthalmoplegia (Kearns–Sayre)
Not primarily a neurological disease, but a key clue to neurogenetic syndromes
inv: Full-field ERG: reduced or absent rod then cone responses
Visual fields and OCT for macular oedema
In syndromic cases: phytanic acid, vitamin E, lipid profile, mtDNA testing, hearing test
Inherited retinal disease gene panel

case.story: Long-standing difficulty walking at night, now bumps into objects at his sides. Recently numb feet and unsteady gait; also poor sense of smell.
case.exam: Concentric field loss, bone-spicule pigment, distal sensory loss, absent ankle jerks, short fourth toes.
case.tests: ERG markedly reduced; plasma phytanic acid strongly elevated; nerve conduction shows demyelinating neuropathy.
case.q: Which neurological disease explains the retinopathy and why does it matter?
case.a: Refsum disease; it is treatable with a phytanic-acid-restricted diet and plasmapheresis in crises.

read.where: Chapter 22 Neuro-Ophthalmology — Ocular Involvement in Other Neurological Disease
Chapter 36: Hereditary Diseases of the Retina

det.patho: Variants in more than 80 genes (e.g. RHO, USH2A, RPGR) cause death of rod photoreceptors, followed by secondary cone loss. Inheritance can be dominant, recessive or X-linked. Pigment migrates from the retinal pigment epithelium into the inner retina, producing the bone-spicule appearance.
det.clinical: Symptoms begin with poor dark adaptation, followed by ring scotomas that coalesce into tunnel vision. Central vision is usually preserved until late adulthood. About a quarter of cases are syndromic; for neurologists the important associations are Usher syndrome (deafness), Refsum disease, abetalipoproteinaemia and vitamin E deficiency (ataxia, neuropathy), mitochondrial disease (NARP, Kearns–Sayre) and some neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses.
det.diagnosis: Ophthalmological diagnosis rests on fundus findings, field testing and ERG. Neurological red flags (ataxia, neuropathy, deafness, ophthalmoplegia, cardiomyopathy) should prompt metabolic tests such as phytanic acid, vitamin E and lipoproteins, and mitochondrial studies. Gene panels confirm the cause in most families and identify those eligible for gene therapy.
det.treatment: Voretigene neparvovec is a licensed gene therapy for biallelic RPE65 disease; other gene and cell therapies are in trials. Cataract surgery and treatment of macular oedema (carbonic anhydrase inhibitors) improve function. Treatable syndromic causes must not be missed: dietary phytanic acid restriction in Refsum disease and vitamin E supplementation in AVED and abetalipoproteinaemia. Low-vision rehabilitation is essential.
det.prognosis: Progressive over decades; many become legally blind by middle age, though timing depends strongly on the gene.
pearls: RP plus ataxia or neuropathy: check phytanic acid and vitamin E — both are treatable.
RP plus ptosis and ophthalmoplegia: think Kearns–Sayre and get an ECG.
Night blindness is the earliest symptom; ask about it directly.
det.thd: Retinitis pigmentosa เป็นโรคจอตาเสื่อมทางพันธุกรรม เริ่มจากตาบอดกลางคืนแล้วลานสายตาแคบลงเรื่อย ๆ จอตาพบเม็ดสีรูปกระดูก ส่วนใหญ่เป็นโรคตาอย่างเดียว แต่ถ้ามี ataxia, neuropathy, หูหนวก หรือหนังตาตกร่วม ต้องนึกถึง Refsum, AVED, NARP และ Kearns–Sayre ซึ่งบางโรครักษาได้ด้วยอาหารหรือวิตามิน

Pigmentary retinopathy plus PEO and heart block before age 20

aN: rp | rod cone dystrophy | pigmentary retinopathy | tapetoretinal degeneration

name: Retinitis, CMV
formal: Necrotising retinitis from cytomegalovirus in severely immunocompromised patients, especially AIDS, causing painless visual loss with haemorrhagic retinal lesions.
simple: A serious eye infection from cytomegalovirus in people with very weak immunity, causing vision loss.
th: จอประสาทตาอักเสบจาก cytomegalovirus พบในผู้ป่วยเอชไอวีที่ CD4 ต่ำมาก ตามัวไม่เจ็บ เห็นเงาลอย พบรอยขาวร่วมกับเลือดออกตามหลอดเลือดจอตา ต้องรักษาด้วยยาต้านไวรัสและเริ่ม ART
tempoNote: Painless visual loss progressing over days to weeks as retinal necrosis spreads at about 250 µm per week; sight-threatening within a month if untreated
feat: Floaters, flashes, blurred vision or a peripheral field defect, usually painless and without red eye; often begins in one eye, with the second eye involved later
Fundus: creamy-white granular necrotic retina with haemorrhages (pizza-pie or brush-fire pattern) tracking along the vascular arcades, with little vitritis
Occurs when CD4 is below 50 cells/µL in HIV, and in transplant recipients or patients on strong immunosuppression
Retinal detachment, optic nerve involvement and immune recovery uveitis after ART are the main complications
CMV disease elsewhere (colitis, polyradiculopathy, ventriculoencephalitis) may coexist, so neurological review is warranted
inv: Dilated fundus examination by an ophthalmologist (clinical diagnosis), with fundus photographs for monitoring
CD4 count, HIV viral load and blood CMV PCR; vitreous or aqueous PCR if the picture is atypical
Screen for other opportunistic infections; MRI and CSF PCR if headache, confusion or leg weakness appear
Check renal function and blood counts before valganciclovir, foscarnet or cidofovir

case.who: 36-year-old man from Chonburi, HIV diagnosed two weeks ago, CD4 21 cells/µL
case.story: Ten days of floaters and a grey spot in the upper field of the left eye; no pain or redness.
case.exam: Visual acuity 6/12 left; left fundus shows a wedge of white necrotic retina with haemorrhages along the inferotemporal arcade; right eye normal.
case.tests: CD4 21, HIV RNA 480,000 copies/mL; plasma CMV DNA detected; vitreous PCR positive for CMV.
case.q: What treatment and timing for antiretroviral therapy are appropriate?
case.a: Start valganciclovir 900 mg twice daily for 3 weeks then once daily (add intravitreal ganciclovir if lesions threaten the macula or optic disc), and start ART within about 2 weeks; monitor for immune recovery uveitis.

read.where: Chapter 11 Cytomegalovirus - patients with AIDS, congenital infection and retinitis, treatment
Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — Cytomegalovirus Infection
Chapter 36: Hereditary Diseases of the Retina

det.patho: CMV reactivates in the retina when CD4 cells fall below about 50 per microlitre, because cytotoxic T cell control of the latent virus fails. The virus infects retinal cells and the pigment epithelium directly and causes full-thickness necrosis that spreads outward, leaving atrophic scars. Congenital CMV also infects the retina in the fetus, producing chorioretinal scars that can reactivate later. In patients on ART, immune recovery uveitis arises when a restored immune response targets residual virus.
det.clinical: Patients notice floaters or an area of blur that expands, and the first eye is often followed by the second within months if untreated. Vision loss is painless. Examination shows peripheral or posterior zones of white retina with haemorrhage, with little overlying vitreous haze. Without therapy the lesion spreads and may cause retinal detachment, blindness and optic nerve damage. CMV retinitis is a marker of severe immunosuppression and often accompanies CMV in the brain, spinal roots or gut.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical in the right setting and is based on the characteristic fundus appearance in a patient with a low CD4 count. PCR of aqueous or vitreous fluid confirms atypical cases. Blood CMV PCR supports but does not prove retinitis. In patients with advanced HIV and CD4 below 100, regular ophthalmic screening is recommended because early lesions are asymptomatic. Positive neurological symptoms prompt MRI and CSF CMV PCR, since ventriculoencephalitis and polyradiculitis can coexist.
det.treatment: Oral valganciclovir (900 mg twice daily for 21 days, then 900 mg daily) is first-line for peripheral lesions, with intravitreal ganciclovir injections or implants added for lesions near the macula or optic nerve, or when absorption is uncertain. Foscarnet or cidofovir serve as alternatives for resistance or intolerance, with attention to renal toxicity and electrolytes. ART is started within about 2 weeks; maintenance therapy stops when CD4 stays above 100 for 3 to 6 months. Systemic ganciclovir reaches the CNS only partly, which matters when brain or root disease coexists. Retinal detachment needs vitreoretinal surgery.
det.prognosis: Good if treated early, with stabilisation of the retina in most; late presentation causes permanent loss, and recurrence occurs if CD4 stays low.
pearls: A painless, quiet eye with white necrotic retina in a patient with CD4 under 50 is CMV until proven otherwise.
Immune recovery uveitis can appear weeks after ART, causing floaters and macular oedema without active retinitis.
CMV retinitis in HIV is a clue to look for CMV elsewhere, including the nervous system.
det.thd: CMV retinitis เกิดจากไวรัส cytomegalovirus ทำลายจอประสาทตาในผู้ป่วยเอชไอวีที่ CD4 ต่ำกว่า 50 ผู้ป่วยมีตามัวหรือเห็นเงาลอยโดยไม่ปวด ตรวจจอตาพบรอยขาวเป็นแผลเน่าร่วมกับเลือดออกตามหลอดเลือด รักษาด้วย valganciclovir หรือฉีดยาเข้าวุ้นตา และเริ่ม ART ภายใน 2 สัปดาห์ ต้องติดตามภาวะ immune recovery uveitis และตรวจหา CMV ในระบบประสาทเมื่อมีอาการ

ddx.pt: Toxoplasma retinochoroiditis with dense vitritis and satellite scars, often with brain lesions
Painful eye movement, afferent pupillary defect and normal retina
Intraocular inflammation after ART start in a patient with prior CMV disease (immune recovery uveitis)

aN: retinitis | cmv | cmv retinitis | cytomegalovirus retinitis | cmvr | aids retinitis

name: Retinoblastoma (Rb)
formal: Childhood retinal malignancy from RB1 mutation presenting with leukocoria and strabismus; heritable form increases risk of pineoblastoma and second tumours.
simple: A cancer of the eye in young children caused by a gene change, often first noticed as a white pupil.
th: มะเร็งจอตาในเด็กจากยีน RB1 มาด้วยรูม่านตาสีขาว (leukocoria) และตาเข ชนิดถ่ายทอดทางพันธุกรรมเพิ่มความเสี่ยง pineoblastoma และมะเร็งชนิดที่สอง
tempoNote: Most diagnosed before age 5; heritable forms earlier and often bilateral
feat: Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex, often seen in photos)
Strabismus, red painful eye, poor vision
Bilateral or multifocal tumours indicate germline RB1 variant
Trilateral retinoblastoma: pineoblastoma with bilateral disease
Later risk of osteosarcoma and soft tissue sarcomas, especially after radiotherapy
inv: Urgent examination under anaesthesia by ocular oncologist
Ocular ultrasound (calcification) and MRI orbits and brain (optic nerve, pineal)
Avoid CT when possible because of radiation-induced second cancer risk
RB1 germline testing and screening of siblings

case.story: Her mother noticed a white glow in her left eye in a mobile phone photo; the eye has started to turn in.
case.exam: Left leukocoria, absent red reflex, esotropia.
case.tests: Ultrasound: calcified intraocular mass; MRI: no optic nerve or pineal involvement; RB1 testing pending.
case.q: What is the most urgent diagnosis and why does germline testing matter?
case.a: Retinoblastoma; germline RB1 variants mean risk of further tumours in either eye, pineoblastoma, later sarcomas and inheritance in offspring.

det.patho: Loss of both copies of the RB1 tumour suppressor in a developing retinal cell drives tumour formation. In heritable disease (about 40%), one variant is germline, so tumours are often bilateral and appear earlier; the remainder arise from two somatic hits. Rarely, MYCN amplification without RB1 loss causes aggressive unilateral tumours.
det.clinical: The commonest signs are leukocoria and strabismus. Advanced disease can spread through the optic nerve to the brain or metastasise to bone marrow. Trilateral disease with a pineal tumour is a neurological complication with poor prognosis. Survivors of heritable disease need lifelong surveillance for second cancers.
det.diagnosis: Ophthalmic examination under anaesthesia and ultrasound showing calcification establish the diagnosis; biopsy is avoided because of seeding risk. MRI evaluates optic nerve invasion and pineal disease. Germline genetic testing informs surveillance and family screening.
det.treatment: Treatment aims first at survival, then eye and vision salvage: intra-arterial or systemic chemotherapy, intravitreal chemotherapy, laser and cryotherapy for small tumours, and enucleation for advanced eyes. External beam radiotherapy is avoided where possible in heritable disease. Multidisciplinary care in a specialised centre improves outcomes.
det.prognosis: Cure rates exceed 95% in high-income settings; outcomes are worse in low-resource settings because of late presentation.
pearls: Leukocoria in a child is retinoblastoma until proven otherwise.
Bilateral tumours mean a germline RB1 variant.
Avoid unnecessary CT and radiotherapy in heritable cases.
det.thd: Retinoblastoma เป็นมะเร็งจอตาในเด็กเล็กจากการสูญเสียยีน RB1 ทั้งสองชุด มาด้วยรูม่านตาสีขาวเห็นได้ในรูปถ่ายและตาเข แบบถ่ายทอดทางพันธุกรรมมักเป็นสองข้างและเสี่ยง pineoblastoma กับมะเร็งกระดูกในภายหลัง วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจตาภายใต้ยาสลบ อัลตราซาวด์ และ MRI ไม่ควรตัดชิ้นเนื้อ การรักษาใช้เคมีบำบัด เลเซอร์ หรือควักลูกตา และตรวจยีนในครอบครัว

ddx.pt: Bilateral congenital retinal detachment in a boy without calcified mass
Astrocytic hamartomas in tuberous sclerosis, usually non-progressive
Visual loss and proptosis without leukocoria; NF1 association

aN: rb | retinoblastoma | rb1 related retinoblastoma | trilateral retinoblastoma

name: Retinopathy
formal: Disease of the retina from diabetes, hypertension or other vascular or toxic causes, with microaneurysms, haemorrhages and exudates and visual loss.
simple: Damage to the back of the eye, often from diabetes or high blood pressure, that can reduce vision.
th: โรคของจอประสาทตาจากเบาหวาน ความดันสูง หรือสาเหตุอื่น มีจุดเลือดออก microaneurysm และ exudate ทำให้ตามัว และสะท้อนภาวะหลอดเลือดเล็กทั่วร่างกายรวมถึงสมอง
tempoNote: Usually develops over years; malignant hypertension or toxic causes can act over days to weeks
feat: Ophthalmic, not neurological, disease but a window onto cerebral small vessels
Diabetic: microaneurysms, dot-blot haemorrhages, exudates, new vessels
Hypertensive: arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking, flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots; disc swelling in severe cases
Other causes: retinal vein or artery occlusion, drug toxicity (hydroxychloroquine), paraneoplastic and mitochondrial retinopathy
inv: Dilated fundoscopy, retinal photography, OCT
Blood pressure, HbA1c, lipids, renal function
Fluorescein angiography or electroretinogram as advised by ophthalmology

case.story: Two days of severe headache and blurred vision; he stopped his antihypertensives months ago.
case.exam: BP 230/140; bilateral flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and swollen optic discs; mild confusion.
case.tests: Creatinine raised; MRI: bilateral parieto-occipital vasogenic oedema.
case.q: What eye finding signals the emergency, and what is the brain complication?
case.a: Grade 4 hypertensive retinopathy with disc swelling (hypertensive emergency) and PRES/hypertensive encephalopathy; controlled IV blood pressure reduction.

read.where: Section 4 Vascular Conditions of the Eyes, Ears, and Brain

det.patho: Diabetic retinopathy arises from capillary pericyte loss, basement membrane thickening and leakage, progressing to ischaemia and neovascularisation driven by VEGF. Hypertensive retinopathy reflects arteriolar thickening and, in crises, failure of autoregulation with ischaemic nerve fibre infarcts and disc oedema. Both mirror changes in the cerebral microcirculation.
det.clinical: Early disease is silent; vision drops with macular oedema, haemorrhage or retinal detachment. Retinal microvascular signs predict stroke, cognitive decline and white matter disease. Neurologists meet retinopathy in hypertensive encephalopathy, diabetic patients with stroke, Susac syndrome (branch retinal artery occlusions) and mitochondrial disease.
det.diagnosis: Fundoscopy grades severity; OCT detects macular oedema. In a neurology context, combine fundus findings with blood pressure and brain imaging. Distinguish disc swelling from raised intracranial pressure by examining the rest of the retina and measuring blood pressure.
det.treatment: Systemic control of glucose, blood pressure and lipids is fundamental. Ophthalmic treatment includes anti-VEGF injections, laser photocoagulation and vitrectomy. In hypertensive emergency, lower pressure in a controlled way (about 25% in the first hours) to protect brain and retina.
det.prognosis: Screening and early therapy prevent most blindness; retinopathy is a marker of higher vascular and cognitive risk.
pearls: Always look at the fundi in a patient with stroke and uncontrolled hypertension or diabetes.
Swollen discs plus retinal haemorrhages and very high BP mean hypertensive emergency, not IIH.
Branch retinal artery occlusions with encephalopathy and hearing loss suggest Susac syndrome.
det.thd: Retinopathy คือโรคจอประสาทตาจากเบาหวาน ความดันสูง ยา หรือสาเหตุอื่น เป็นโรคทางตาแต่สะท้อนภาวะหลอดเลือดเล็กในสมอง ตรวจพบ microaneurysm เลือดออก exudate และ cotton-wool spot ถ้าความดันสูงมากร่วมกับขั้วประสาทตาบวมแสดงถึงภาวะฉุกเฉิน อาจมี PRES ร่วม รักษาโดยคุมน้ำตาลและความดัน และส่งจักษุแพทย์รักษาเฉพาะทาง

name: Rett syndrome
formal: X-linked MECP2 disorder in girls with normal early development then regression, loss of hand skills, stereotypic hand wringing, seizures and breathing irregularity.
simple: A genetic condition mainly in girls where early development is normal then speech and hand use are lost, with hand wringing and seizures.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมยีน MECP2 บนโครโมโซม X พบในเด็กหญิง พัฒนาการปกติช่วงแรกแล้วถดถอย สูญเสียการใช้มือ มีมือบิดซ้ำ ๆ ชัก และหายใจผิดปกติ
tempoNote: Apparently normal first 6–18 months, then regression over weeks to months, followed by a plateau and later motor decline
feat: Girl who loses purposeful hand use and spoken language after 6–18 months of near-normal development
Stereotyped hand-wringing, clapping or mouthing movements
Gait abnormalities (dyspraxia, toe-walking) and deceleration of head growth
Breathing irregularities while awake (hyperventilation, breath-holding), bruxism, sleep problems
Seizures in most, scoliosis, prolonged QTc, cold small feet
inv: MECP2 sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis (positive in ~95% of classic cases)
EEG for seizures (beware non-epileptic breathing and behavioural events)
ECG for QTc; spine X-ray for scoliosis; growth and bone health

case.story: Spoke a few words and fed herself at 12 months, but since 15 months she has stopped using her hands purposefully and no longer speaks.
case.exam: Constant midline hand-wringing and mouthing, poor eye contact, unsteady broad-based gait, head circumference dropped from 50th to 10th centile.
case.tests: De novo pathogenic MECP2 variant; ECG QTc 470 ms.
case.q: Which disease-specific drug is now approved, and what cardiac precaution applies?
case.a: Rett syndrome: trofinetide is approved (from age 2 in the US); avoid QT-prolonging drugs and monitor ECG.

read.where: Section II: Epidemiology, Etiology, and Diagnosis

det.patho: MECP2 encodes a chromatin-binding protein that regulates gene expression in mature neurons. Loss-of-function variants, usually de novo on the paternal X, disrupt synaptic maturation without major neuron loss, which is why the disorder is neurodevelopmental rather than neurodegenerative and is potentially reversible in animal models. Males with similar variants usually have severe neonatal encephalopathy; MECP2 duplication causes a separate male syndrome.
det.clinical: Classic Rett follows stages: early stagnation, rapid regression with loss of hand skills and speech, a plateau in which communication through eye gaze may improve, and late motor deterioration with rigidity and scoliosis. Hand stereotypies are the hallmark. Breathing dysrhythmia, autonomic and gastrointestinal problems, epilepsy and QT prolongation are frequent. Atypical forms include preserved-speech variants and early-seizure (CDKL5) or congenital (FOXG1) types now considered separate disorders.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical using consensus criteria (regression, loss of hand use and speech, gait abnormality, hand stereotypies) and confirmed with MECP2 testing. A negative test does not exclude a clinical diagnosis. EEG must be interpreted with video because many paroxysmal events are non-epileptic. Screen ECG, nutrition, scoliosis and bone density.
det.treatment: Trofinetide, an IGF-1 tripeptide analogue, was approved in 2023 in the United States and modestly improves core symptoms; diarrhoea is common. Supportive care includes antiseizure drugs, nutrition and gastrostomy, physiotherapy, augmentative communication, scoliosis management and avoidance of QT-prolonging medicines. Gene therapy trials are under way.
det.prognosis: Most girls live into adulthood, many into middle age; sudden death related to autonomic or cardiac dysfunction is a risk.
pearls: Girl with regression, loss of purposeful hand use and midline hand-wringing: test MECP2.
Many 'spells' are breathing or behavioural events; confirm seizures with video-EEG.
Check QTc and avoid QT-prolonging drugs.
det.thd: Rett syndrome เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมจากยีน MECP2 บนโครโมโซม X พบในเด็กหญิง พัฒนาการปกติจนอายุ 6–18 เดือนแล้วถดถอย สูญเสียการใช้มือและการพูด มีมือบิดหรือตบมือซ้ำ ๆ ศีรษะโตช้า หายใจผิดจังหวะ และชัก วินิจฉัยตามเกณฑ์ทางคลินิกและยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน รักษาแบบองค์รวม และปัจจุบันมียา trofinetide

qx.stem: A 2-year-old girl from Kanchanaburi walked and used a few words at 14 months, then over several months lost her words and purposeful hand use. She now wrings her hands continually, head growth has slowed and she has had two seizures. Her parents ask whether any treatment is aimed at the disease itself.
qx.q: Which statement about treatment of the likely disorder is correct?
opts: Carbamazepine is the drug of choice for her seizures and also restores hand function
MECP2 gene replacement therapy is approved for girls under five years
High-dose pyridoxine reverses the regression when started early
Trofinetide can ease several behavioural and motor symptoms but does not treat seizures, and diarrhoea is its commonest side effect
Levodopa corrects the hand stereotypies and is standard first-line therapy
qx.why: Girls with classic Rett syndrome (MECP2) develop normally for about a year, then lose language and hand skills and show stereotypies, slowing head growth and often seizures. Trofinetide is approved for symptoms of classic Rett syndrome; it does not control seizures, and its diarrhoea can be severe, so laxatives are stopped before it is started. No gene therapy is approved, and vitamins or dopaminergic drugs do not modify the disease.

ddx.pt: Happy demeanour, ataxia, absent speech and seizures, but no regression; UBE3A/15q11 defects
Early severe epilepsy (e.g. CDKL5, FOXG1 'atypical Rett') with delay from the start
Regression with visual loss and myoclonus, progressive without a plateau

name: Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS)
formal: Thunderclap headache with multifocal segmental arterial narrowing that resolves within 3 months; precipitated by vasoactive drugs and postpartum; complications include stroke and PRES.
simple: Sudden severe headaches caused by temporary narrowing of brain arteries, which can occasionally cause stroke.
th: หลอดเลือดสมองหดตัวเป็นปล้อง ๆ ชั่วคราว มาด้วยปวดหัวแบบฟ้าผ่าซ้ำหลายครั้งในไม่กี่วัน มักมีตัวกระตุ้น (หลังคลอด ยา serotonergic/vasoactive กัญชา ออกแรง) หายเองใน 3 เดือน
tempoNote: Clusters of explosive headaches over 1–3 weeks; artery narrowing peaks around the second to third week and clears by about 12 weeks
feat: Several thunderclap headaches over days, often set off by sex, straining, exertion, bathing or strong emotion
Trigger in the history: recent delivery, SSRIs/SNRIs, triptans, decongestants, cannabis, cocaine or amphetamines
Convexity (cortical sulcal) subarachnoid blood, lobar haemorrhage or watershed infarcts in a minority
PRES-like vasogenic oedema and seizures may coexist
CSF essentially normal (protein and cells not raised), unlike vasculitis
inv: CT/CTA then MRI with angiography; first imaging is normal in many patients, so repeat at about day 5–10 if suspicion stays
Catheter or CT angiography: multifocal 'string of beads' narrowing that reverses on follow-up imaging by 3 months
Lumbar puncture when aneurysmal SAH or vasculitis needs excluding
RCVS2 score (recurrent thunderclap, carotid intracranial involvement, vasoconstrictive trigger, sex, SAH) to separate from PACNS

case.who: 33-year-old woman, 9 days after caesarean section, Khon Kaen
case.story: Three sudden 'worst ever' headaches in four days, each peaking within a minute; the latest came while bending to lift her baby. She was given pseudoephedrine for a cold last week.
case.exam: BP 150/95; alert, no neck stiffness, no focal signs.
case.tests: CT: thin blood in one right frontal sulcus; CTA: no aneurysm but beaded narrowing of both MCAs and the basilar artery.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and which drug class should be avoided?
case.a: Postpartum RCVS triggered by a vasoactive decongestant; stop the trigger, control BP, avoid glucocorticoids (linked to worse outcome) and triptans; calcium-channel blockers such as nimodipine are often used for pain.

det.patho: A transient disorder of cerebral arterial tone in which sympathetic overdrive, endothelial dysfunction and oxidative stress cause segmental constriction and dilatation of medium and large intracranial arteries. Exposure to vasoactive substances or the postpartum state is found in roughly two-thirds. It mainly affects women aged 20–50 and overlaps biologically with PRES, cervical artery dissection and eclampsia.
det.clinical: The defining picture is a run of thunderclap headaches, sometimes with nausea, photophobia and agitation, separated by milder background pain. Complications follow a time pattern: convexity SAH and lobar bleeds tend to appear in the first week, while ischaemia in border zones typically comes later, as constriction spreads proximally. Seizures, cortical blindness and transient focal deficits occur. A severe fulminant course with diffuse infarction and oedema is rare but recognised, especially postpartum.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on acute severe headache plus documented multifocal segmental narrowing that normalises within about 12 weeks, with no aneurysmal SAH and normal or near-normal CSF. Early angiography may be falsely normal because spasm starts distally, so repeat imaging is reasonable. Transcranial Doppler can follow velocities. Treat a fixed, non-reversing narrowing with abnormal CSF or vessel-wall enhancement as possible vasculitis instead. Look for and remove triggers with a careful drug and recreational history.
det.treatment: Management is supportive: stop vasoactive and serotonergic drugs, rest, analgesia, laxatives, and avoid straining. Oral nimodipine or verapamil is widely used to ease headache, although it has not been proved to prevent strokes. Keep blood pressure moderate (avoid hypotension that may worsen ischaemia). Glucocorticoids are associated with worse outcome and should be avoided; intra-arterial vasodilators are reserved for rapid deterioration.
det.prognosis: Most recover fully within weeks to months; a few are left with deficits from infarction or haemorrhage, and recurrence is uncommon (about 5%).
pearls: Repeated thunderclaps over days, normal first CT/CTA: do not stop at one negative scan.
Cortical SAH over the convexity in someone under 60 points to RCVS; over 60, think of CAA.
Steroids help vasculitis but harm RCVS; get the diagnosis right before giving them.
det.thd: RCVS คือภาวะหลอดเลือดสมองหดตัวชั่วคราวแบบหลายตำแหน่ง ผู้ป่วยปวดศีรษะรุนแรงทันทีแบบฟ้าผ่าซ้ำหลายครั้ง มักสัมพันธ์กับหลังคลอดหรือยา/สารที่ทำให้หลอดเลือดหดตัว อาจมีเลือดออกใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมองบริเวณผิวสมองหรือสมองขาดเลือดตามมา ตรวจหลอดเลือดพบตีบเป็นปล้องและหายภายใน 3 เดือน การรักษาคือหยุดตัวกระตุ้น ให้ calcium channel blocker บรรเทาปวด และหลีกเลี่ยง steroid

qx.stem: A 38-year-old woman taking a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor has recurrent thunderclap headaches over 10 days, triggered by exertion and orgasm. CT and CSF are normal. MRA on day 4 shows multifocal beaded segmental narrowing of the MCA and PCA branches, and repeat MRA at 10 weeks is normal.
qx.q: Which statement about her condition is correct?
opts: Corticosteroids are first-line treatment
Vessel narrowing generally resolves within 3 months and triggers should be removed
Tissue confirmation by brain biopsy is mandatory
Cyclophosphamide is required to prevent relapse
Normal initial MRA excludes the diagnosis
qx.why: RCVS causes thunderclap headaches with reversible multifocal vasoconstriction, which may not be visible at the first angiogram and normalises in about 12 weeks. Triggers (serotonergic and sympathomimetic drugs, postpartum) are stopped and calcium channel blockers may be used, while steroids can worsen outcome. Vasculitis would show inflammatory CSF and persistent lesions and might need immunosuppression.

src.where: Chapter 5: Cerebral Vasculopathy: CNS Vasculitis, RCVS, and PRES — RCVS

qx.stem: A 38-year-old woman from Phuket, two weeks postpartum and taking a nasal decongestant, has repeated thunderclap headaches. CT angiography shows multifocal segmental narrowing ('string of beads'). CSF is normal, and a vessel wall MRI shows minimal enhancement.
qx.q: Which feature favours RCVS over PACNS?
opts: Insidious progressive course over months
Abnormal CSF with lymphocytic pleocytosis
Concentric vessel wall enhancement and thickening
Recurrent thunderclap headaches with normal CSF, a vasoactive trigger, and reversal of vessel narrowing within about 12 weeks
Biopsy-proven granulomatous vasculitis
qx.why: RCVS presents with recurrent thunderclap headache, often after pregnancy or vasoactive drugs, with normal or near-normal CSF, minimal wall enhancement and resolution of vessel changes within weeks. PACNS tends to have an insidious course, abnormal CSF in most, concentric wall enhancement on vessel wall MRI and biopsy evidence of vasculitis. Calcium channel blockers are commonly used in RCVS and glucocorticoids may worsen it.

qx.stem: Nine days after an uncomplicated delivery, a 30-year-old woman has four thunderclap headaches over five days, triggered by straining and bathing. BP is 150/90 mmHg and the examination is normal. CT and CSF are normal, and CTA shows multifocal segmental narrowing of several middle and posterior cerebral artery branches. She took a pseudoephedrine cold remedy last week.
qx.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Start high-dose IV methylprednisolone and plan brain biopsy
Stop vasoactive drugs, avoid triggers, give analgesia and consider a calcium-channel blocker, then repeat vessel imaging in about 3 months
Give sumatriptan for each headache
Perform intra-arterial angioplasty of all narrowed segments now
Start therapeutic anticoagulation for presumed venous thrombosis
qx.why: Recurrent thunderclap headaches after childbirth with segmental vasoconstriction and a sympathomimetic trigger are typical of RCVS. Management is supportive: remove vasoactive agents (including triptans), control BP, treat pain and often use nimodipine or verapamil, confirming reversal on follow-up imaging. Glucocorticoids are associated with worse outcomes in RCVS, which is why distinguishing it from primary CNS angiitis matters.

name: Rhabdomyolysis
formal: Breakdown of skeletal muscle releasing myoglobin and CK, from trauma, exertion, drugs, toxins or metabolic myopathy, causing myalgia, dark urine and AKI.
simple: Rapid muscle damage releasing contents into the blood, causing pain and dark urine and risk of kidney injury.
more: CK above 5 times the upper limit; treat with aggressive fluids and manage electrolytes; look for the cause.
th: กล้ามเนื้อสลายเฉียบพลัน — ปวด อ่อนแรง ปัสสาวะสีเข้ม CK สูงมาก เสี่ยงไตวาย
tempoNote: Hours to days after trigger; recurrent episodes suggest a metabolic myopathy
feat: Muscle pain, swelling and weakness, often in the exercised or compressed limbs
Tea- or cola-coloured urine; dipstick blood positive without red cells
Triggers: extreme exertion, heat, crush or prolonged immobilisation, alcohol, drugs, infection, seizures, hypokalaemia
Complications: acute kidney injury, hyperkalaemia, compartment syndrome, DIC
inv: CK (usually >5× upper limit, often far higher), serial until falling
Creatinine, potassium, calcium, phosphate, urinalysis
If recurrent or unexplained: metabolic work-up (acylcarnitines, forearm exercise test), genetic myopathy panel, biopsy after recovery

case.story: After a 10-km march in April heat followed by hundreds of squats, his thighs swelled and his urine turned dark brown.
case.exam: Tender, tense thighs, mild proximal weakness, normal reflexes, temperature 37.8 °C.
case.tests: CK 98,000 U/L, K 5.9 mmol/L, creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, urine dipstick 3+ blood with no RBC on microscopy.
case.q: What is the immediate management, and when would you look for an underlying myopathy?
case.a: Aggressive IV isotonic fluid to maintain high urine output, treat hyperkalaemia, monitor compartments. Investigate for a metabolic myopathy if episodes recur, follow mild exertion, or occur with fasting or fever.

read.where: Myopathies of Systemic Disease and Toxic Myopathies
Chapter 61 Disorders of Consciousness in Systemic Diseases

det.patho: Injury to the sarcolemma lets calcium flood the muscle cell, activating proteases and depleting ATP, so fibres necrose and release myoglobin, potassium, phosphate, urate and CK. Myoglobin causes kidney injury through tubular obstruction, direct haem toxicity and renal vasoconstriction, worsened by dehydration and acidic urine. Causes are physical (exertion, crush, heat), toxic (alcohol, cocaine, statins), infectious, electrolyte-related, or genetic disorders of muscle energy metabolism and membrane.
det.clinical: Presentation ranges from asymptomatic CK elevation to severe pain, swelling, weakness and dark urine. Muscle findings may be subtle in obtunded patients after a fall or overdose. Compartment syndrome should be suspected with a tense, very painful limb. In athletes and military trainees, unaccustomed eccentric exercise in heat is a common setting; an individual with several episodes or episodes after modest triggers likely has an underlying myopathy.
det.diagnosis: A CK of five or more times normal, together with a compatible picture, establishes the diagnosis; peak CK occurs at 1–3 days. Haem-positive dipstick without red cells supports myoglobinuria. Monitor potassium, calcium, phosphate, creatinine and coagulation. After recovery, recurrent or unexplained cases warrant metabolic testing (acylcarnitine profile, lactate/ammonia exercise testing), genetic panels (CPT2, PYGM, RYR1, LPIN1 and others) and sometimes biopsy, done weeks after the episode.
det.treatment: Give early, generous isotonic crystalloid to maintain urine output around 200–300 mL/h in adults, adjusting for cardiac function. Correct hyperkalaemia; avoid treating early hypocalcaemia unless symptomatic. Bicarbonate and mannitol lack clear benefit. Dialysis is used for refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis or fluid overload; fasciotomy for compartment syndrome. Remove triggers and counsel on graded return to exercise.
det.prognosis: Most patients recover fully; acute kidney injury usually reverses with prompt treatment. Mortality is mainly from hyperkalaemia, multiorgan failure or the underlying cause.
pearls: Dark urine with blood on dipstick but no red cells on microscopy suggests myoglobin.
Recurrent episodes or episodes after modest triggers = look for a metabolic or genetic myopathy.
Defer metabolic testing and biopsy until weeks after the attack.
det.thd: Rhabdomyolysis คือกล้ามเนื้อสลายเฉียบพลันจากการออกกำลังหนัก ความร้อน การถูกกดทับ ยา แอลกอฮอล์ หรือการติดเชื้อ ปล่อย myoglobin และโพแทสเซียมออกมา ผู้ป่วยปวดกล้ามเนื้อ ปัสสาวะสีโค้ก CK สูงมาก เสี่ยงไตวายและโพแทสเซียมสูง รักษาด้วยการให้สารน้ำทางหลอดเลือดจำนวนมากและแก้เกลือแร่ หากเป็นซ้ำหรือเกิดจากเหตุกระตุ้นเล็กน้อยควรตรวจหาโรคกล้ามเนื้อทางเมตาบอลิก

name: Rheumatic fever chorea gravidarum
formal: Sydenham chorea recurring in pregnancy (chorea gravidarum) after streptococcal rheumatic fever, with antibasal ganglia antibodies.
simple: Involuntary writhing movements in pregnancy in women who earlier had rheumatic fever.
th: Sydenham chorea ที่กลับเป็นซ้ำช่วงตั้งครรภ์ (chorea gravidarum) ในผู้ที่เคยเป็นไข้รูมาติก เกี่ยวข้องกับแอนติบอดีต่อ basal ganglia
tempoNote: Usually first trimester, resolves after delivery or earlier
feat: Generalised or hemichorea in early pregnancy
History of rheumatic fever or Sydenham chorea in childhood
Emotional lability and motor impersistence
May recur in later pregnancies or with oestrogen-containing contraceptives
Rheumatic heart disease may coexist
inv: ASO and anti-DNase B (may be negative in recurrences)
Echocardiogram for valvular disease
Exclude SLE/antiphospholipid syndrome, thyroid disease, Wilson disease
MRI brain usually normal

case.who: 24-year-old woman, 10 weeks pregnant, from Mae Hong Son
case.story: Two weeks of fidgety, dancing movements of arms and face; had rheumatic fever with chorea at age 9.
case.exam: Generalised chorea, milkmaid's grip, emotional lability; mitral regurgitation murmur.
case.tests: ASO normal, echo mild mitral regurgitation; ANA and antiphospholipid antibodies negative; TSH normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and how is it managed in pregnancy?
case.a: Chorea gravidarum due to reactivated Sydenham chorea; supportive care, and if severe low-dose haloperidol after the first trimester; monitor the heart.

det.patho: Molecular mimicry after group A streptococcal infection produces antibodies cross-reacting with basal ganglia neurons. Pregnancy hormones, particularly oestrogen, may sensitise dopamine receptors in previously affected striatum, unmasking chorea.
det.clinical: Chorea usually starts in the first trimester and settles in the third trimester or after delivery. Psychiatric symptoms, dysarthria and weakness may accompany it. Most patients have a prior history of rheumatic fever or Sydenham chorea.
det.diagnosis: Clinical, supported by history of rheumatic fever. Exclude SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome, hyperthyroidism, Wilson disease and drugs. Echocardiography assesses cardiac involvement.
det.treatment: Mild chorea needs only reassurance. For disabling chorea, low-dose haloperidol or benzodiazepines are used, ideally avoiding the first trimester. Penicillin prophylaxis continues per rheumatic fever guidance.
det.prognosis: Usually resolves after pregnancy; may recur in later pregnancies.
pearls: Chorea in early pregnancy: ask about childhood rheumatic fever.
Always screen for SLE and antiphospholipid syndrome.
Oestrogen pills can trigger similar recurrences.
det.thd: Chorea gravidarum จากไข้รูมาติกคืออาการ chorea ที่เกิดซ้ำช่วงตั้งครรภ์ในผู้หญิงที่เคยเป็น Sydenham chorea ตอนเด็ก มักเกิดไตรมาสแรกและหายหลังคลอด ต้องแยก SLE และ antiphospholipid syndrome ตรวจหัวใจด้วย echocardiogram รักษาตามอาการและให้ยาป้องกันไข้รูมาติกต่อ

name: Rheumatoid arthritis
formal: Chronic autoimmune synovitis with neurological complications including atlantoaxial subluxation, compressive neuropathies, vasculitic neuropathy and rare pachymeningitis.
simple: An autoimmune joint disease that can also squeeze or damage nerves and the spinal cord.
more: Seropositive disease with anti-CCP and rheumatoid factor; cervical MRI assesses atlantoaxial instability and myelopathy. Treat with DMARDs and surgical stabilisation if cord compression; vasculitic neuropathy needs steroids and cyclophosphamide.
th: โรคข้ออักเสบเรื้อรังจากภูมิคุ้มกัน มีภาวะแทรกซ้อนทางประสาท เช่น atlantoaxial subluxation, เส้นประสาทถูกกดทับ, vasculitic neuropathy และ pachymeningitis
tempoNote: Chronic disease; neurological complications evolve over months to years, cord compression may be acute
feat: Primarily a rheumatological disease with neurological complications
Atlantoaxial subluxation and basilar invagination causing myelopathy, neck pain, occipital pain
Entrapment neuropathies (carpal tunnel, ulnar, tarsal tunnel)
Rheumatoid vasculitis with mononeuritis multiplex
Rare rheumatoid pachymeningitis or nodules; drug-related complications (e.g., PML, infections)
inv: RF and anti-CCP; inflammatory markers
Flexion-extension cervical X-rays and MRI cervical spine for instability and cord compression
Nerve conduction studies; nerve biopsy if vasculitis suspected
MRI brain with contrast for pachymeningitis

case.who: 61-year-old woman from Samut Prakan with 20 years of RA
case.story: Three months of neck pain, tingling hands and clumsy walking; recent shock-like sensations on neck flexion.
case.exam: Hyperreflexia, Hoffmann sign, bilateral Babinski, wasted small hand muscles.
case.tests: Flexion views show 8 mm atlanto-dens interval; MRI shows cord compression at C1–C2 with pannus.
case.q: What is the complication and the treatment?
case.a: Atlantoaxial subluxation with myelopathy; surgical stabilisation (C1–C2 fusion) and careful airway management.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Rheumatoid Arthritis

det.patho: Synovial inflammation erodes the transverse ligament and odontoid, producing atlantoaxial instability and pannus. Synovitis compresses peripheral nerves at tunnels. Immune complex vasculitis of vasa nervorum causes ischaemic neuropathy. Rheumatoid nodules can form in meninges.
det.clinical: Neurological problems arise mostly in long-standing seropositive disease. Cervical myelopathy can be subtle, masked by joint deformity. Vasculitic neuropathy signals severe systemic disease. Immunosuppressive and biologic drugs add risks of infection, PML and demyelination (anti-TNF).
det.diagnosis: Cervical imaging with flexion-extension views and MRI; nerve conduction studies for neuropathies; nerve or muscle biopsy for vasculitis; MRI with contrast for pachymeningitis. Consider drug side effects.
det.treatment: Disease control with DMARDs and biologics; surgical stabilisation for cervical instability with myelopathy; decompression for entrapments; high-dose steroids and cyclophosphamide or rituximab for vasculitis. Anaesthetists must know about cervical instability before intubation.
det.prognosis: Myelopathy has a poor prognosis without surgery; vasculitis carries increased mortality.
pearls: Check cervical stability in RA before anaesthesia.
Mononeuritis multiplex in RA means rheumatoid vasculitis.
Anti-TNF drugs can trigger demyelination.
det.thd: Rheumatoid arthritis เป็นโรคข้ออักเสบเรื้อรังจากภูมิคุ้มกัน ไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาทโดยตรง แต่มีภาวะแทรกซ้อน เช่น กระดูกคอ C1–C2 เคลื่อนกดไขสันหลัง เส้นประสาทถูกกดทับ vasculitic neuropathy และ pachymeningitis ควรตรวจ MRI คอเมื่อมีอาการไขสันหลัง และระวังก่อนดมยาสลบ รักษาด้วย DMARDs และผ่าตัดยึดกระดูกคอเมื่อจำเป็น

name: Rhythmic movement disorder
formal: Sleep-related repetitive stereotyped movements such as head banging or body rocking, common in infants and usually benign, occurring at sleep onset.
simple: Repeated rocking or head banging around sleep time, common in young children and usually outgrown.
more: Differentiate from epilepsy or restless legs syndrome by video-polysomnography when needed; no investigation is required for typical childhood cases. Usually resolves by age 5; protect the head with padding, and consider clonazepam in persistent cases.
th: การเคลื่อนไหวซ้ำเป็นจังหวะช่วงง่วงหรือหลับ เช่น โขกศีรษะ หมุนศีรษะ หรือโยกตัว พบบ่อยในทารกและเด็กเล็ก ส่วนใหญ่ไม่อันตรายและหายเองเมื่อโต
tempoNote: Begins in infancy, peaks before age 2 and usually stops by about age 5; occasionally persists into adulthood
feat: Head banging, head rolling or body rocking at sleep onset or during light sleep, at roughly 0.5–2 beats per second
Each bout lasts minutes; the child is drowsy or asleep and often hums or makes noise
Very common in infants and toddlers; only a disorder when it disturbs sleep, causes injury or impairs daytime function
Persistence in older children or adults is linked with ADHD, developmental delay, autism, RLS and OSA
inv: Diagnosis by history and home video
Video-PSG only if seizures, OSA or another sleep disorder is suspected; bouts mostly arise from wake–sleep transition and light NREM
Developmental assessment if delay is suspected

case.story: Each night as he falls asleep he rocks on hands and knees and bangs his head against the cot for about 10 minutes; he is happy and developing well by day.
case.exam: Normal development and examination; small bruise on the forehead.
case.tests: None needed; video confirms rhythmic rocking at about once per second at sleep onset.
case.q: What is the management?
case.a: Sleep-related rhythmic movement disorder; reassure, pad the cot and secure loose bolts, keep a calm bedtime routine, and expect it to fade by school age.

read.where: Scoping Review on ADCY5-Related Movement Disorders

det.patho: Rhythmic movements are thought to be a self-soothing behaviour that uses vestibular stimulation to help the transition into sleep. Central pattern generators in the brainstem and spinal cord are probably involved. Persistence later in life may reflect developmental or attentional disorders, or arousals from another sleep problem.
det.clinical: Most infants show some rhythmic movement around sleep onset, and the habit declines steadily through early childhood. Forms include head banging (often face down), head rolling side to side, body rocking and, less often, leg rolling. Injury is uncommon but bruising and noise can be distressing to parents. Adult cases often have comorbid RLS, OSA or psychiatric disorders.
det.diagnosis: History and home video are usually enough. ICSD-3-TR requires repetitive, stereotyped rhythmic movements of large muscle groups that are sleep related and cause disturbance, injury or impairment. Video-PSG shows bouts at about 0.5–2 Hz mainly at sleep onset and in light NREM sleep, sometimes in REM sleep; it is used when epilepsy or another disorder is suspected.
det.treatment: Reassurance and safety measures such as padding and securing the bed are usually all that is needed. Ensure adequate sleep and treat any associated OSA or RLS. In older children or adults with injurious or disruptive movements, clonazepam at bedtime can help, and behavioural approaches such as controlled sleep restriction have been reported.
det.prognosis: Benign and usually self-limiting by early school age; a minority persist into adulthood.
pearls: Rhythmic rocking at sleep onset in a thriving toddler needs reassurance, not an EEG.
New or persistent rhythmic movements in an adult should prompt a search for OSA or RLS.
det.thd: Rhythmic movement disorder คือการโขกศีรษะ หมุนศีรษะ หรือโยกตัวเป็นจังหวะประมาณ 1 ครั้งต่อวินาทีช่วงกำลังจะหลับ พบบ่อยมากในทารกและเด็กเล็ก และมักหายก่อนอายุ 5 ปี วินิจฉัยจากประวัติและวิดีโอ ตรวจ video-PSG เฉพาะเมื่อสงสัยชักหรือ OSA การรักษาคือให้ความมั่นใจกับผู้ปกครอง จัดเตียงให้ปลอดภัย และใช้ clonazepam ในผู้ใหญ่ที่เป็นรุนแรง

name: Rhythmic myoclonus

det.patho: Rhythmic myoclonus arises from oscillating neuronal networks in the brainstem (inferior olive) or spinal cord segments, often released by a structural lesion. Loss of inhibitory interneurons allows rhythmic firing.
det.clinical: This entry describes a phenomenological category of myoclonus rather than a single disease. It is distinguished from tremor by its jerk morphology and from arrhythmic myoclonus by regularity. Persistence during sleep suggests a brainstem or spinal source.
det.diagnosis: EMG documents rhythm and duration of bursts; MRI looks for brainstem or cord lesions; EEG excludes cortical origin.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying lesion. Clonazepam, levetiracetam, valproate or carbamazepine may help; botulinum toxin for focal forms.
det.prognosis: Often persistent; depends on cause.
pearls: Rhythmic myoclonus that persists in sleep points to brainstem or spinal origin.
Look for a structural lesion with MRI.
det.thd: Rhythmic myoclonus คือการกระตุกของกล้ามเนื้อเป็นจังหวะสม่ำเสมอ 1–3 Hz มักเกิดจากรอยโรคที่ก้านสมอง เช่น palatal tremor หรือที่ไขสันหลัง เช่น spinal segmental myoclonus มักเป็นต่อเนื่องแม้ขณะหลับ ควรตรวจ MRI หาสาเหตุ รักษาด้วย clonazepam, levetiracetam หรือ botulinum toxin

name: Riboflavin deficiency
formal: Vitamin B2 deficiency causing angular stomatitis, glossitis, anaemia and rarely neuropathy; relevant to riboflavin-responsive Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere syndrome.
simple: Too little vitamin B2, causing mouth sores, anaemia and sometimes nerve problems.

Usually coexists with other B-vitamin deficiencies (alcohol, malabsorption, poor diet)

Infants may develop respiratory failure from diaphragm weakness
Transporter disorders improve or stabilise with high-dose oral riboflavin

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Vitamin and Mineral Deficiencies and Toxicity
Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Vitamin B2 (Riboflavin)

det.patho: Riboflavin is the precursor of FAD and FMN, cofactors for mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation and the respiratory chain. Dietary lack mainly affects rapidly renewing tissues such as skin and mucosa. Biallelic variants in riboflavin transporter genes SLC52A2 and SLC52A3 reduce cellular uptake and selectively damage cranial nerve nuclei, motor neurons, sensory ganglia and auditory pathways.
det.clinical: Nutritional deficiency produces mucocutaneous lesions and anaemia, usually with other vitamin deficits, and rarely a mild neuropathy. Transporter deficiency presents in infancy or childhood with progressive deafness, bulbar and facial weakness, neck and limb weakness, sensory ataxia, optic atrophy and respiratory insufficiency. Without treatment it is often fatal.
det.diagnosis: Nutritional cases are suspected clinically and confirmed with erythrocyte glutathione reductase activity. In transporter deficiency, acylcarnitines may be abnormal but are often normal, so genetic testing is decisive. Electrophysiology shows sensory and motor neuronopathy.
det.treatment: Dietary deficiency responds to riboflavin replacement and correction of other deficits. Transporter deficiency requires lifelong high-dose oral riboflavin, started as soon as suspected; many patients improve, sometimes dramatically. Supportive care includes hearing aids or cochlear implants, ventilatory support and nutrition.
det.prognosis: Good for nutritional deficiency; transporter disorders often stabilise or improve with early treatment but late-treated deficits may persist.
pearls: Childhood deafness plus bulbar palsy: start riboflavin before genetics return.
Dietary B2 deficiency rarely causes significant neurological disease on its own.
Riboflavin is also used for migraine prophylaxis.
det.thd: การขาดวิตามิน B2 จากอาหารมักทำให้ปากนกกระจอก ลิ้นอักเสบ และซีด ไม่ค่อยมีอาการทางประสาท ส่วนโรคพันธุกรรม riboflavin transporter deficiency (SLC52A2/A3) ทำให้เด็กหูหนวกแบบ sensorineural กลืนลำบาก หน้าและลิ้นอ่อนแรง และหายใจไม่พอ ซึ่งตรงกับ Brown–Vialetto–Van Laere syndrome โรคนี้รักษาได้ด้วย riboflavin ขนาดสูงตลอดชีวิต จึงควรเริ่มยาทันทีที่สงสัย

det.patho: Richardson syndrome is the classic phenotype of PSP, a 4-repeat tauopathy with neuronal and glial tau in the midbrain, subthalamic nucleus, globus pallidus and dentate nucleus. Midbrain atrophy explains gaze palsy and postural instability.
det.clinical: Onset is usually after 60 with falls and gait instability. Vertical gaze palsy may emerge later than falls. Frontal cognitive and behavioural changes and pseudobulbar features develop. It accounts for about half of PSP cases.
det.diagnosis: MDS 2017 criteria: probable PSP-RS requires vertical gaze palsy or slow vertical saccades plus early postural instability. MRI midbrain atrophy supports it. Exclude other causes such as vascular disease and NPC.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy. Levodopa trial is reasonable but usually unhelpful. Physiotherapy, falls prevention, speech and swallowing therapy, and early palliative care planning are important.
det.prognosis: Median survival about 6–7 years from onset, often death from aspiration pneumonia.
pearls: Early unprovoked backward falls are a PSP warning sign.
Slow vertical saccades precede gaze palsy.
Hummingbird sign on midsagittal MRI.

name: Rickettsial disease
formal: Vector-borne infections (Rocky Mountain spotted fever, scrub typhus) causing fever, rash, headache and meningoencephalitis via vasculitis, treated with doxycycline.
simple: Infections spread by ticks, mites or lice that cause fever, rash and sometimes brain inflammation.
th: การติดเชื้อ rickettsia ที่ติดต่อผ่านไรอ่อน เห็บ หมัด เช่น scrub typhus ทำให้ไข้ ผื่น ปวดศีรษะ และ meningoencephalitis รักษาได้ด้วย doxycycline
tempoNote: Fever and headache 6–21 days after the bite (scrub typhus 6–20 days); neurological signs in the second week, rapid response to antibiotic within 48 hours
feat: Scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi) is the main rickettsiosis in rural Thailand; murine typhus (Rickettsia typhi) in urban and port areas; spotted fever group elsewhere
Fever, severe headache, myalgia, conjunctival injection, lymphadenopathy and a truncal macular or maculopapular rash
Eschar at the chigger bite site, often in a skin fold (groin, axilla, waist), is a diagnostic clue but is missed in many patients
Meningitis or meningoencephalitis with confusion, seizures, cranial nerve palsy (including deafness) and rarely myelitis or Guillain–Barré syndrome

case.story: Seven days of fever, severe headache and body aches. On day 6 he became drowsy and had one seizure. He worked in a field near scrubland. He had been treated with paracetamol only.
case.exam: Febrile, drowsy, mild neck stiffness, generalised lymph node enlargement, a 1 cm black-crusted eschar in the left groin, macular rash on trunk.
case.tests: Platelets 82,000, ALT raised; CSF lymphocytes 120/mm3, protein 80 mg/dL, glucose normal; scrub typhus PCR positive; MRI brain normal.
case.q: What is the treatment and how fast should it work?
case.a: Doxycycline (or azithromycin) started on suspicion; fever typically falls within 24–48 hours. Neurological recovery follows in most patients.

read.where: Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — Rickettsial Disease
Chapter 38 Acute Bacterial Infections of the Central Nervous System

det.patho: Rickettsiae are obligate intracellular bacteria that enter endothelial cells and cause systemic vasculitis through direct cell injury and immune response. Scrub typhus is carried by larval trombiculid mites (chiggers) that bite rodents and humans, murine typhus by rat fleas, and spotted fevers (including Rocky Mountain spotted fever, caused by Rickettsia rickettsii) by ticks. Vascular leakage and perivascular inflammation in the meninges and brain give meningitis, encephalitis and focal deficits; microinfarcts explain focal signs.
det.clinical: Fever, headache and myalgia dominate; a rash and an eschar help but may be absent. In scrub typhus, headache is typically severe and some develop meningism, confusion or seizures. Complications include hearing loss, pneumonitis, hepatic dysfunction, shock and rare cranial neuropathy, acute flaccid paralysis or Guillain–Barré syndrome. Rocky Mountain spotted fever shows the rash beginning at wrists and ankles and is life-threatening when treatment is late.
det.diagnosis: Epidemiological clue (rural exposure, rainy season, field work) plus fever with eschar prompts treatment. Confirm with PCR of blood or eschar, or paired IgM/IFA serology, noting that serology may be negative early. CSF generally shows mild lymphocytic pleocytosis, which separates it from bacterial meningitis. The WHO meningitis guideline lists rickettsioses among non-pyogenic causes to consider in endemic settings.
det.treatment: Start doxycycline on clinical suspicion, 100 mg twice daily in adults (about 2.2 mg/kg twice daily in children, even under 8 years) for 5 to 7 days, continuing at least 3 days after the fever settles; azithromycin is an alternative, particularly in pregnancy and for doxycycline-tolerance concerns, and chloramphenicol is a fallback. Add supportive care for shock, seizures and organ dysfunction. Delay in treatment raises mortality, and a prompt response within 48 hours also supports the diagnosis.
det.prognosis: Excellent with early treatment; mortality rises with delayed therapy, severe organ failure or encephalopathy, and a few patients retain hearing loss.
pearls: Treat first, test later: a fever with eschar in an endemic area is scrub typhus until proven otherwise.
Beta-lactams and many other antibiotics do not cover rickettsiae; doxycycline does.
Rapid defervescence within 48 hours after doxycycline is itself diagnostic support.
det.thd: โรคริกเก็ตเซียพบได้ในไทย เช่น scrub typhus จากไรอ่อน (chigger) และ murine typhus จากหมัดหนู ผู้ป่วยมีไข้สูง ปวดศีรษะมาก ปวดเมื่อย ต่อมน้ำเหลืองโต ผื่น และอาจพบแผล eschar ตามซอกพับ บางรายมีเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ สมองอักเสบ ชัก หรือหูหนวก CSF มักเป็น lymphocytic วินิจฉัยด้วย PCR หรือ IgM serology แต่ควรให้ doxycycline ทันทีเมื่อสงสัย ไข้มักลดใน 24–48 ชั่วโมง ถ้ารักษาช้าจะมีอัตราตายสูงขึ้น

name: Riddoch syndrome
formal: Perception of motion in a blind visual field after occipital lesions, with preserved awareness of moving but not stationary stimuli (statokinetic dissociation).
simple: After brain damage a person cannot see still objects in a blind area but can notice things that move.
th: ภาวะที่ผู้ป่วยรับรู้การเคลื่อนไหวได้ในลานสายตาที่บอดจากรอยโรค occipital แต่มองไม่เห็นวัตถุที่อยู่นิ่ง (statokinetic dissociation)
tempoNote: Follows an occipital lesion; persists or improves with recovery
feat: A phenomenon/sign rather than a disease
Perception of moving objects in an otherwise blind hemifield
Stationary objects not seen; static perimetry shows a denser defect than kinetic perimetry
Usually after occipital stroke, tumour or trauma
Thought to reflect preserved motion pathways (V5/MT) bypassing V1

MRI brain to identify occipital lesion

case.story: Cannot see objects in his right visual field, but notices cars moving on his right.
case.exam: Right homonymous hemianopia on static testing; responds to moving targets in the defect.
case.tests: Kinetic perimetry shows a smaller field defect than static perimetry; MRI shows left occipital infarct.
case.q: What phenomenon is this?

read.where: Chapter 22 Neuro-Ophthalmology — Blindsight and Statokinetic Dissociation

det.patho: After damage to primary visual cortex, some visual information reaches extrastriate motion area V5/MT via the superior colliculus and pulvinar or spared V1 islands. This allows conscious detection of motion but not static form.
det.clinical: This entry describes a phenomenon rather than a disease. Patients with occipital lesions report seeing movement in an otherwise blind field. Statokinetic dissociation can also occur in optic nerve disease and is sometimes mistaken for functional visual loss.
det.diagnosis: Compare kinetic and static perimetry; MRI shows the underlying lesion. Recognise that it is a genuine organic phenomenon.
det.treatment: No specific treatment; visual rehabilitation and compensatory scanning training help hemianopia.
det.prognosis: Depends on the underlying lesion; may indicate better potential for recovery.
pearls: Kinetic fields may underestimate the defect in statokinetic dissociation.
Do not mislabel as functional visual loss.
