name: Westphal variant (rigid) Huntington’s disease
formal: Juvenile or Westphal variant of Huntington disease with parkinsonian rigidity, bradykinesia, dystonia, seizures and large CAG repeats rather than chorea.
simple: A form of Huntington's disease, often in young people, with stiffness and slowness instead of jerky movements.
more: Rigid variant of juvenile Huntington disease with CAG repeat expansion, bradykinesia and dystonia.
th: รูปแบบ rigid-akinetic ของ Huntington ที่เริ่มในวัยเด็กหรือวัยรุ่น มีแข็งเกร็ง เคลื่อนไหวช้า dystonia และชักมากกว่า chorea CAG repeat มักยาวมากและรับจากพ่อ ดำเนินโรคเร็ว
tempoNote: Onset in childhood or adolescence, typically before 20 years, progressing over a few years to a decade
feat: Rigidity, bradykinesia and dystonia dominate; chorea is slight or absent
Seizures in a large share, especially with very early onset
School decline, behavioural change and speech regression
CAG repeats often above 60, usually paternally transmitted with anticipation
Course is faster than adult-onset Huntington disease
inv: HTT CAG repeat sizing after genetic counselling
MRI: caudate and putaminal atrophy
EEG when seizures occur; copper studies and caeruloplasmin to exclude Wilson disease

case.story: Falling grades over a year, stiff walking, slurred speech and two nocturnal seizures; his father has chorea and cognitive decline.
case.exam: Generalised rigidity with slow movements, dystonic foot posturing, no chorea.
case.tests: MRI shows caudate atrophy; HTT repeat length 78 on one allele.
case.q: Why is chorea absent, and what does the father's history imply?
case.a: Large expansions in juveniles give the rigid Westphal phenotype; transmission from an affected father with anticipation explains the early age of onset.

det.patho: An expanded CAG repeat in HTT encodes a polyglutamine-rich huntingtin protein that aggregates and injures striatal medium spiny neurons. Repeat length correlates inversely with onset age, and large paternal expansions arise through instability during spermatogenesis. Juvenile cases show widespread cortical and striatal loss.
det.clinical: The juvenile form often starts with learning problems, behaviour change and gait stiffness. Rigid-akinetic parkinsonism, dystonia and seizures take the place of chorea, which can appear later if at all. Tremor, myoclonus and cerebellar signs can occur. Weight loss, swallowing difficulty and rapid cognitive decline follow.
det.diagnosis: Suspect in any child with progressive rigidity, seizures and a family history, though history can be absent through anticipation or non-paternity. Confirm by HTT repeat testing with pre- and post-test counselling, treating the child as part of a family-level decision. MRI atrophy supports but does not replace genetics. Exclude Wilson disease, mitochondrial and neurometabolic causes.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying treatment is available. Care is symptomatic: antiseizure drugs, baclofen or botulinum toxin for dystonia and rigidity, levodopa trial in selected rigid patients, nutrition and swallowing support, and psychosocial and educational help. Palliative planning and family genetic counselling are central.
det.prognosis: Median survival is much shorter than in adult-onset disease, often 10–15 years from onset, with severe disability earlier.
pearls: Childhood Huntington presents rigid, not choreic.
Large repeats come mainly via the father.
Seizures plus rigidity in a child with an affected parent should prompt HTT testing.
det.thd: Westphal variant เป็นชนิดเริ่มในเด็กของ Huntington ที่มี CAG repeat ยาวมาก มักรับจากพ่อ อาการหลักคือแข็งเกร็ง เคลื่อนไหวช้า dystonia ชัก และการเรียนถดถอย โดยไม่ค่อยมี chorea MRI พบ caudate ฝ่อ ยืนยันด้วยตรวจยีน HTT ยังไม่มีการรักษาที่ชะลอโรค ให้การรักษาตามอาการ ให้คำปรึกษาครอบครัว และวางแผนการดูแลระยะยาว

Nocturnal hypoventilation and restrictive respiratory failure while still walking
Phenotype overlaps with Emery–Dreifuss, LMNA, collagen VI and RYR1 disorders
inv: CK normal or slightly raised; EMG myopathic
Muscle MRI: selective pattern (e.g. sartorius and adductor involvement in SELENON disease)
Biopsy may show minicores or dystrophic change; gene panel (SELENON/SEPN1, LMNA, COL6, RYR1, FHL1)
Spirometry lying and sitting, overnight oximetry/capnography; ECG and echo for LMNA/FHL1 forms

case.story: Always thin and slow at sport; parents notice he cannot bend forward to touch his toes. Recently morning headaches and daytime sleepiness.
case.exam: Rigid cervical and thoracic spine, mild thoracic scoliosis, weak neck flexors, near-normal limb power, no calf hypertrophy.
case.tests: CK 180 U/L; FVC 52% predicted; overnight capnography shows hypercapnia; panel finds biallelic SELENON variants.
case.q: What syndrome is this and what is the urgent management priority?
case.a: SELENON-related rigid spine muscular dystrophy; start nocturnal non-invasive ventilation despite preserved walking.

det.patho: Rigid spine syndrome is a clinical pattern rather than one disease. The classic recessive form is caused by SELENON (formerly SEPN1) variants, which impair a selenoprotein of the endoplasmic reticulum involved in redox and calcium handling, leaving muscle vulnerable to oxidative stress. Similar pictures arise from LMNA, collagen VI, RYR1, FHL1 and other genes, so the label prompts a gene search rather than ending it.
det.clinical: Children are usually floppy or slightly delayed, then develop striking stiffness of the spine with loss of forward flexion and a progressive scoliosis. Limb weakness is mild and many walk into adult life, which lulls families and doctors. Diaphragmatic and intercostal weakness produce sleep hypoventilation that may appear in the first decade. Cardiac involvement is mainly secondary to lung disease in SELENON forms but primary in LMNA or FHL1 forms.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in a child with spinal rigidity and disproportionate respiratory impairment. Muscle MRI patterns help choose among candidate genes, and a neuromuscular gene panel or exome usually settles the cause. Biopsy can show multiminicores or nonspecific myopathic change. Lung function should be measured supine as well as upright to unmask diaphragm weakness.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying drug exists; antioxidant approaches such as N-acetylcysteine have been studied but are not standard. Care focuses on regular respiratory review with early non-invasive ventilation, cough assistance, vaccination, spinal monitoring and timely scoliosis surgery, and physiotherapy for contractures. Cardiac surveillance is essential where the underlying gene affects the heart.
det.prognosis: Limb function is often preserved for decades, but untreated respiratory failure can be fatal in adolescence; ventilation markedly improves survival.
pearls: A child who walks well yet has a vital capacity around half of predicted should prompt thought of SELENON myopathy.
Rigid spine is a phenotype: always look for cardiac genes such as LMNA before reassuring.
Morning headache and poor school performance may be the first signs of nocturnal hypercapnia.
det.thd: Rigid spine syndrome เป็นลักษณะทางคลินิกที่กระดูกสันหลังแข็งก้มไม่ได้และหลังคด สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยคือยีน SELENON แต่อาจเกิดจาก LMNA, collagen VI หรือ RYR1 ได้ ผู้ป่วยมักเดินได้ แต่กล้ามเนื้อหายใจอ่อนแรงจนเกิด hypoventilation ตอนกลางคืน การวินิจฉัยใช้ muscle MRI และตรวจยีน การดูแลเน้นตรวจสมรรถภาพปอด ใช้ NIV ตั้งแต่เนิ่น ๆ และติดตามหัวใจในบางยีน

ddx.pt: Early elbow and Achilles contractures with cardiac conduction block; EMD, LMNA or FHL1 genes
Finger-flexor and elbow contractures, keloids and follicular hyperkeratosis; collagen VI
Axial weakness with early respiratory failure but raised CK, vacuolar biopsy and low acid alpha-glucosidase

aN: rss | rigid spine muscular dystrophy | rsmd1 | sepn1 related myopathy | selenon myopathy

name: Riley–Day syndrome
formal: Familial dysautonomia, autosomal recessive HSAN III from IKBKAP mutation in Ashkenazi Jews, with absent tears, hypotension, labile blood pressure and insensitivity to pain.
simple: An inherited nerve disease causing poor pain sensation, no tears and unstable blood pressure.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมยีนด้อย HSAN ชนิดที่ 3 จากยีน ELP1 (IKBKAP) พบมากในชาว Ashkenazi Jew ไม่มีน้ำตา ความดันแกว่ง ไม่รู้สึกเจ็บ และมีวิกฤตอาเจียน
tempoNote: Congenital, with feeding difficulty from birth and slow progression through life
feat: Absent overflow tears when crying, corneal ulcers
Poor suck and aspiration in infancy; dysautonomic crises with vomiting, hypertension and sweating
Orthostatic hypotension alternating with supine hypertension
Reduced pain and temperature sensation, absent tendon reflexes, absent fungiform papillae on tongue
Proprioceptive ataxia and progressive optic neuropathy in adults
inv: Intradermal histamine test: no axon flare
Methacholine eye drops cause miosis (denervation supersensitivity)
ELP1 genetic testing (common splice variant in Ashkenazi founder population)

case.who: 3-year-old boy (international referral to a Bangkok hospital)
case.story: Feeding difficulty from birth, repeated pneumonias, and episodes of vomiting with blotchy skin; he never sheds tears when crying.
case.exam: Smooth tongue without fungiform papillae, absent reflexes, does not react to venepuncture.
case.tests: No flare after intradermal histamine; ELP1 founder variant homozygous.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the drug class used for crises?
case.a: Familial dysautonomia (Riley–Day); crises are treated with clonidine and benzodiazepines, orthostatic hypotension with droxidopa or midodrine.

read.where: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves — Hereditary Sensory Neuropathy

det.patho: A founder splice variant in ELP1 reduces functional protein in neurons, impairing development and survival of sensory and autonomic neurons. Small myelinated and unmyelinated fibres, dorsal root and sympathetic ganglia are depleted. Carrier frequency in Ashkenazi Jews is about 1 in 30; it is extremely rare in other populations.
det.clinical: Infants feed poorly and aspirate; tears are absent and corneas ulcerate. Dysautonomic crises bring vomiting, tachycardia, hypertension, sweating and skin blotching, often with stress. Blunted chemoreceptor responses make hypoxia dangerous. Afferent baroreflex failure produces wild blood pressure swings. Adults develop gait ataxia, chronic kidney disease and progressive visual loss.
det.diagnosis: Clinical picture plus absent histamine flare, absent fungiform papillae and alacrima; ELP1 testing confirms. In non-Ashkenazi children with similar features, test other HSAN genes. This disease is a key part of the hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy classification.
det.treatment: Supportive: gastrostomy and fundoplication, artificial tears, protection of the cornea and skin, careful management of anaesthesia and altitude. Crises are managed with clonidine, diazepam and antiemetics; carbidopa is used to blunt dopamine-mediated vomiting; droxidopa or midodrine for orthostatic hypotension. Splicing modulators are under investigation.
det.prognosis: Survival has improved with specialist care, with many patients now living into adulthood; sudden death, aspiration and renal failure remain major risks.
pearls: Crying without tears in an infant with feeding problems — think familial dysautonomia.
Absent fungiform papillae and no histamine flare are classic bedside clues.
Avoid hypoxia; these children do not sense it normally.
det.thd: Riley–Day syndrome หรือ familial dysautonomia เป็น HSAN ชนิดที่ 3 จากยีน ELP1 พบมากในชาว Ashkenazi Jew เซลล์ประสาทรับความรู้สึกและระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติพัฒนาไม่ปกติ ทำให้ร้องไห้ไม่มีน้ำตา ไม่รู้สึกเจ็บ ความดันแกว่ง และมีวิกฤตอาเจียน วินิจฉัยด้วยตรวจ histamine flare และตรวจยีน การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง

Alacrima with achalasia and adrenal insufficiency (AAAS gene)

name: Rire spasmodique
formal: Forced grinning facial spasm from sustained contraction of risorius, seen in tetanus (risus sardonicus) and some basal ganglia or brainstem disorders.
simple: A fixed, forced smile caused by muscle spasm, classically seen in tetanus.
th: อาการยิ้มแสยะที่เกิดจากกล้ามเนื้อใบหน้าหดเกร็งค้าง พบในบาดทะยักและโรคบางชนิดของ basal ganglia หรือก้านสมอง
tempoNote: Acute in tetanus or strychnine poisoning; chronic when due to dystonia or brainstem disease
feat: Fixed grin with raised eyebrows, drawn-back mouth corners and clenched jaw
In tetanus: trismus, neck and back rigidity, painful generalised spasms triggered by stimuli
Other causes: strychnine poisoning, Wilson disease ('vacuous smile'), oromandibular dystonia, pseudobulbar states
This is a clinical sign, not a disease on its own
inv: History of wound, vaccination status; tetanus is a clinical diagnosis
Toxicology for strychnine where suspected
Copper studies, slit-lamp exam and MRI in chronic cases

case.story: A week after stepping on a nail he finds it hard to open his mouth and his face feels pulled tight.
case.exam: Fixed grin, trismus, rigid abdominal wall; spasms provoked by noise; alert.
case.tests: CK mildly raised; no tetanus booster for over 20 years.
case.q: What does the facial sign indicate, and what is the treatment?
case.a: Risus sardonicus from generalised tetanus; human tetanus immunoglobulin, wound debridement, metronidazole, benzodiazepines or magnesium for spasms, and ICU airway care.

det.patho: Sustained contraction of facial muscles (risorius, zygomatic and frontalis) pulls the mouth into a grin. In tetanus, tetanospasmin blocks release of inhibitory transmitters (glycine, GABA) from spinal and brainstem interneurons, releasing motor neurons from inhibition; strychnine blocks glycine receptors directly. In dystonia the mechanism is abnormal basal ganglia output.
det.clinical: The sign is classically associated with tetanus, often alongside trismus, dysphagia and opisthotonus. In chronic conditions such as Wilson disease or dystonia it is less dramatic and varies with action. It must be distinguished from emotional laughter in pseudobulbar affect.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is of the underlying cause. Tetanus is diagnosed clinically from the context of a wound and incomplete vaccination; the spatula test (reflex bite on touching the pharynx) supports it. Other causes are sought by toxicology, copper studies and imaging.
det.treatment: Tetanus requires human tetanus immunoglobulin, wound care, metronidazole, spasm control with benzodiazepines, magnesium or neuromuscular blockade, airway protection and management of autonomic instability, followed by full vaccination. Dystonic causes respond to botulinum toxin and treatment of the cause (chelation in Wilson disease).
det.prognosis: Determined by the cause; tetanus mortality is substantial without ICU care.
pearls: Grin plus trismus after a wound: tetanus.
Tetanus does not confer immunity; vaccinate after recovery.
A fixed smile in a young person with tremor: check copper and look for KF rings.
det.thd: Rire spasmodique หรือ risus sardonicus เป็นอาการแสดง ไม่ใช่โรค คือใบหน้ายิ้มแสยะค้างจากกล้ามเนื้อใบหน้าหดเกร็ง สาเหตุสำคัญคือบาดทะยัก ซึ่งมักมีอ้าปากไม่ขึ้นและเกร็งทั้งตัว สาเหตุอื่นเช่นพิษ strychnine, Wilson disease และ dystonia การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ บาดทะยักต้องให้ immunoglobulin ทำแผล ยาคลายเกร็ง และดูแลใน ICU

name: Rosai–Dorfman disease (RDD)
formal: Non-Langerhans histiocytosis with S100-positive emperipolesis, causing lymphadenopathy and rarely dural-based CNS masses that mimic meningioma.
simple: A rare disease in which immune cells build up in lymph nodes and sometimes form growths in the brain coverings.
th: โรค histiocytosis ชนิด non-Langerhans มี emperipolesis ทำให้ต่อมน้ำเหลืองโตมาก บางรายมีก้อนติดเยื่อหุ้มสมองคล้าย meningioma
tempoNote: Slowly progressive masses over months; may wax and wane or regress spontaneously
feat: Painless bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy with fever and raised ESR in classic nodal disease
CNS disease often isolated: dural-based enhancing masses at convexity, skull base, cavernous sinus or spine
Headache, seizures, cranial neuropathies or myelopathy depending on site
Orbit, sinus, skin and bone involvement in some
inv: MRI: dural-based mass with dural tail, often T2 hypointense, mimicking meningioma
Biopsy: large S100-positive, CD68/CD163-positive, CD1a-negative histiocytes with emperipolesis
Molecular testing (KRAS, MAP2K1); IgG4 staining; PET-CT for staging

case.story: Headache and a first seizure; he had neck lumps that came and went for years.
case.exam: Rubbery cervical nodes, no focal deficit.
case.tests: MRI: two dural-based enhancing lesions resembling meningiomas; biopsy shows S100-positive histiocytes engulfing lymphocytes.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the usual first treatment for symptomatic CNS lesions?
case.a: Rosai–Dorfman disease with CNS involvement; surgical resection, with steroids or systemic therapy for residual or multifocal disease.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Rosai–Dorfman Disease
Chapter 5: Histiocytic tumours of the central nervous system

det.patho: RDD is a rare proliferation of activated histiocytes, now regarded as a clonal neoplasm in many cases because of MAPK pathway mutations (KRAS, NRAS, MAP2K1). Emperipolesis — intact lymphocytes within histiocyte cytoplasm — is characteristic. Some cases are associated with autoimmune disease, IgG4 overlap or familial syndromes.
det.clinical: Nodal disease affects young people with massive cervical nodes. CNS involvement is uncommon and often without nodal disease, affecting middle-aged adults. Spinal dural masses cause compressive myelopathy. The course is variable, with spontaneous regression possible.
det.diagnosis: Imaging cannot reliably separate RDD from meningioma, lymphoma or IgG4 disease, so biopsy is essential. Immunohistochemistry (S100+, CD1a−, langerin−) distinguishes it from Langerhans cell histiocytosis. Whole-body staging looks for other sites.
det.treatment: Surgical removal is used for accessible symptomatic CNS lesions. Corticosteroids reduce lesion size in some. Residual or multifocal disease may be treated with radiotherapy, cladribine, methotrexate, or MEK inhibitors such as cobimetinib when MAPK mutations are present. Observation suits asymptomatic stable disease.
det.prognosis: Generally favourable, though CNS disease can recur after incomplete resection.
pearls: A 'meningioma' with lymphadenopathy or atypical histology: consider RDD.
S100-positive, CD1a-negative histiocytes with emperipolesis are diagnostic.
MEK inhibitors are an option for refractory MAPK-mutant disease.
det.thd: Rosai–Dorfman disease เป็นโรค histiocytosis ชนิด non-Langerhans ที่พบน้อย มักทำให้ต่อมน้ำเหลืองที่คอโตมาก ในระบบประสาทพบเป็นก้อนติดเยื่อหุ้มสมองหรือไขสันหลังคล้าย meningioma ต้องตัดชิ้นเนื้อพบ histiocyte ที่ S100 บวกและมี emperipolesis การรักษาคือผ่าตัด สเตียรอยด์ หรือยามุ่งเป้า MEK ในรายที่ดื้อ

name: Ross syndrome
formal: Triad of tonic pupil, segmental anhidrosis and hyporeflexia from dysautonomic involvement of postganglionic sudomotor and dorsal root ganglion neurons.
simple: A rare condition with a large slow-reacting pupil, patchy lack of sweating and reduced reflexes.
ab: Tonic pupil, hyporeflexia and segmental anhidrosis
th: กลุ่มอาการ 3 อย่างคือ รูม่านตา tonic (คล้าย Adie) รีเฟล็กซ์ลดลง และเหงื่อไม่ออกเป็นบางส่วน มักมีเหงื่อออกมากชดเชยในบริเวณอื่น จากความผิดปกติของประสาทอัตโนมัติและ dorsal root ganglion
tempoNote: Slowly progressive over years; sweating deficit often spreads while pupil and reflex signs persist
feat: Tonic pupil: poor light reaction, slow near constriction and sectoral palsy of the iris sphincter
Segmental anhidrosis with compensatory hyperhidrosis in unaffected skin
Hyporeflexia or areflexia in the limbs
Heat intolerance, and sometimes orthostatic or cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction
Photophobia and blurred near vision from the tonic pupil
inv: Thermoregulatory sweat test to map anhidrosis and quantitate the affected body surface
Quantitative sudomotor axon reflex test and skin biopsy for small fibres
Pharmacological pupil testing with dilute pilocarpine to show cholinergic supersensitivity
Autonomic cardiovascular testing; exclude autoimmune, paraneoplastic and diabetic causes

case.story: For three years she noticed that the left half of her back and legs no longer sweat while her face and chest drip. The left pupil is large and she has trouble reading small print.
case.exam: Left pupil dilated, poor light reaction and slow near response, absent ankle and knee reflexes, normal strength.
case.tests: Thermoregulatory sweat test shows patchy anhidrosis over about 40 per cent of the body; dilute pilocarpine constricts the left pupil; routine blood tests, HbA1c and Sjogren antibodies negative.
case.q: What is the syndrome and what are its important mimics?
case.a: Ross syndrome (tonic pupil, hyporeflexia, segmental anhidrosis). Exclude diabetes, Sjogren syndrome, paraneoplastic and autoimmune ganglionopathy, and manage heat intolerance and hyperhidrosis symptomatically.

read.where: 8 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System

det.patho: The cause is probably degeneration of postganglionic parasympathetic neurons in the ciliary ganglion and of sympathetic sudomotor neurons, together with dorsal root ganglion neurons that give the areflexia. Most cases are idiopathic and may be autoimmune; it occasionally overlaps with Sjogren syndrome or follows infection. Sweat gland denervation shows a segmental distribution on thermoregulatory testing.
det.clinical: Patients, often young adults and more frequently women, present with a unilateral or bilateral tonic pupil, patchy loss of sweating that spreads over time, and generalised areflexia. Compensatory hyperhidrosis in preserved skin is often the main complaint, with heat intolerance. Some develop cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction, which is called progressive Ross syndrome.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical and the thermoregulatory sweat test best displays the sudomotor deficit. Pharmacological pupil testing confirms cholinergic supersensitivity. Other causes of sweating loss and pupil abnormality should be excluded: diabetes, amyloidosis, Sjogren syndrome, paraneoplastic neuropathy, toxic neuropathy and leprosy.
det.treatment: No cure is known. Treatment includes cooling strategies, avoidance of heat exposure, pilocarpine drops or reading glasses for the tonic pupil, sunglasses, and anticholinergics, topical aluminium agents or botulinum toxin for compensatory hyperhidrosis. Immunotherapy has been reported in autoimmune cases. Monitor for cardiovascular autonomic involvement.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive but non-life-threatening; heat intolerance and hyperhidrosis dominate quality of life.
pearls: Tonic pupil plus areflexia plus patchy sweating means Ross, not Adie alone.
Compensatory hyperhidrosis is often what brings the patient.
TST is the best test for restricted sudomotor failure.
det.thd: Ross syndrome ประกอบด้วย รูม่านตา tonic, รีเฟล็กซ์เอ็นลดลง และเหงื่อไม่ออกเป็นบางส่วนของร่างกาย ผู้ป่วยมักมีเหงื่อออกมากในบริเวณที่ยังปกติและทนความร้อนไม่ได้ การตรวจที่ดีคือ thermoregulatory sweat test และหยอด pilocarpine ความเข้มข้นต่ำ ต้องแยกโรคเบาหวาน Sjogren และ paraneoplastic การรักษาเป็นการบรรเทาอาการ

name: Roussy–Levy syndrome
formal: CMT type 1 phenotype with postural tremor and areflexia due to PMP22 duplication or MPZ mutations, with slowed nerve conduction.
simple: An inherited nerve disease with weak feet, absent reflexes and a hand tremor.
th: ภาวะ CMT ชนิด demyelinating ที่มีเท้าโก่ง รีเฟล็กซ์หาย ร่วมกับมือสั่นขณะยกแขนและเดินเซ
tempoNote: Onset in childhood or adolescence with very slow progression over decades
feat: Pes cavus, hammer toes and distal wasting typical of CMT1
Generalised areflexia
Hand tremor on posture and action that resembles essential tremor
Gait unsteadiness from large-fibre sensory loss, worse in the dark
Usually dominant family history; mild disability
inv: Nerve conduction: uniformly slowed motor velocities in the demyelinating range
Genetics: PMP22 duplication or MPZ variant (occasionally others)
MRI brain usually normal; no true cerebellar signs

case.story: Shaky handwriting and spilling coffee since her teens; trips easily on uneven ground. Her father has high-arched feet.
case.exam: Pes cavus, absent reflexes, distal leg wasting, reduced vibration at toes, positive Romberg, bilateral postural hand tremor, normal finger–nose accuracy.
case.tests: Median motor conduction velocity 22 m/s; testing shows PMP22 duplication.
case.q: How should this tremor be classified?
case.a: Roussy–Levy phenotype of CMT1A: neuropathic tremor with sensory ataxia, not a separate disease.

det.patho: The syndrome was described in a family with ataxia, areflexia and foot deformity, later found to carry CMT1 mutations, most often PMP22 duplication and sometimes MPZ variants. Tremor is thought to arise from distorted proprioceptive feedback and altered central processing of slowed, dispersed afferent input rather than from cerebellar degeneration.
det.clinical: Patients have the usual CMT1 picture of distal weakness, cavus feet and areflexia, plus a prominent postural and kinetic hand tremor and unsteadiness. The tremor may be the main complaint and leads to referral to movement clinics. Progression is very gradual and lifespan is not shortened.
det.diagnosis: Nerve conduction studies showing diffuse uniform slowing point to an inherited demyelinating neuropathy; genetic testing confirms the subtype. Look for features that would suggest Friedreich ataxia or a spinocerebellar ataxia instead, such as upgoing plantars, dysarthria or nystagmus. Modern usage treats Roussy–Levy as a descriptive variant of CMT rather than a distinct disease.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying therapy. Tremor may improve with propranolol or primidone as in essential tremor, and deep brain stimulation has been reported in severe cases. Orthoses, foot care, physiotherapy and genetic counselling follow standard CMT care.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive with mild to moderate disability; normal lifespan.
pearls: Tremor plus areflexia plus pes cavus: think CMT1 before essential tremor.
Romberg-positive unsteadiness here is sensory, not cerebellar.
Neuropathic tremor also occurs in IgM paraproteinaemic and CIDP neuropathies.
det.thd: Roussy–Levy syndrome คือ CMT1 (มักเป็น PMP22 duplication หรือ MPZ) ที่มีอาการมือสั่นเด่นร่วมกับเท้าโก่ง รีเฟล็กซ์หาย และเดินเซจากการรับรู้ตำแหน่งเสีย ตรวจ NCS พบการนำกระแสช้าทั่วไป ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน ไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ แต่ยาแบบ essential tremor อาจช่วยลดอาการสั่น ร่วมกับการฟื้นฟูและอุปกรณ์ช่วยเดิน

name: Rubella encephalitis, chronic
formal: Progressive rubella panencephalitis, rare late complication of congenital or childhood rubella causing dementia, ataxia and seizures, with high CSF antibodies.
simple: A very rare slowly worsening brain infection that appears years after rubella infection.
th: สมองอักเสบเรื้อรังที่ค่อย ๆ แย่ลงจากเชื้อหัดเยอรมันค้างในสมอง พบในวัยรุ่นหลังติดเชื้อตั้งแต่กำเนิด ทำให้สติปัญญาถดถอย เดินเซ ชัก และมีแอนติบอดีสูงใน CSF
tempoNote: Years after congenital or early rubella, a slow decline over several years, with death often 8–10 years after onset
feat: Dementia and behavioural change in adolescence, typically in a patient with stigmata of congenital rubella (deafness, cataract, heart defect)
Cerebellar ataxia is prominent and appears earlier than in subacute sclerosing panencephalitis
Seizures and myoclonus are present but less marked than in SSPE; later spasticity, dysarthria and loss of speech
Retinopathy or optic atrophy may accompany the brain disease
Relentless course to a bedbound, mute state over several years; no effective treatment
inv: CSF: raised protein and IgG with oligoclonal bands, sometimes 10–40 mononuclear cells; very high rubella antibody titre in serum and CSF with raised CSF-to-serum antibody index
EEG with diffuse slowing, only rarely periodic discharges
MRI: white matter change, ventricular enlargement and cerebellar atrophy; exclude SSPE with measles antibody

case.who: 15-year-old girl with hearing aids since infancy, Songkhla
case.story: Born in a rural area after her mother had a rash in early pregnancy. Over two years her school grades fell, she became clumsy, walking unsteady, and recently had her first generalised seizure.
case.exam: Cataract surgery scars, bilateral sensorineural deafness, slow responses, broad-based ataxic gait with limb dysmetria, a few myoclonic jerks.
case.tests: CSF protein elevated with oligoclonal bands and 18 lymphocytes; rubella IgG antibody in CSF markedly raised with high intrathecal index; measles antibody titre not raised; MRI shows cerebellar atrophy and white matter signal change.
case.q: Why not SSPE, and what can be offered?
case.a: Prominent cerebellar ataxia, history of congenital rubella and a rubella-specific antibody index point to progressive rubella panencephalitis, while measles titres are not elevated. There is no cure; give antiseizure drugs, supportive care and promote MMR vaccination.

read.where: Infectious Diseases of the Nervous System — Viral Infections — Slow or Chronic Viral Infections
5. Psychomotor Delay and Regression — Progressive Encephalopathies With Onset After Age 2

det.patho: Rubella virus persists in the brain after congenital infection or, rarely, after childhood rubella, and years later causes a chronic encephalitis with demyelination and gliosis. The persistent infection probably generates immune complexes that deposit in vessel walls, producing vasculitis and parenchymal damage. Congenital rubella involves the nervous system in most affected infants, so the substrate is a brain already injured earlier.
det.clinical: Progressive rubella panencephalitis was identified as a distinct disease in the 1970s. Illness begins in adolescence with dementia, then cerebellar ataxia that is more conspicuous than in SSPE, seizures, myoclonus, spasticity and visual loss. The course is protracted, often 8–10 years to death, and some patients stabilise for long periods. The condition is now very rare where rubella vaccination is established.
det.diagnosis: A characteristic course in an adolescent with stigmata of congenital rubella suggests the diagnosis. The CSF shows an inflammatory pattern with raised protein, intrathecal IgG synthesis and oligoclonal bands, and a markedly raised rubella antibody titre in serum and CSF is the confirmatory finding. EEG shows diffuse slowing, MRI shows atrophy and white matter signal. Measles antibody studies are needed to exclude SSPE, and genetic and metabolic causes of progressive myoclonic epilepsy, HIV and other chronic encephalitides should be excluded.
det.treatment: No antiviral or immunological treatment has proved effective. Care consists of antiseizure medication, spasticity and swallowing management, nutrition, rehabilitation, communication support and palliative planning. Prevention depends on high coverage with rubella-containing vaccine (MMR) and screening and vaccination of women before pregnancy, as rubella embryopathy is not treatable once established.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive and fatal over years, with severe disability in the later stages.
pearls: Cerebellar ataxia leading the picture, in a teenager with congenital rubella signs, favours rubella over SSPE.
CSF shows an inflammatory pattern with very high rubella-specific antibody; measles titres are not the answer.
Prevention by MMR vaccination and pre-pregnancy rubella immunity is the only effective measure.
det.thd: Chronic rubella encephalitis หรือ progressive rubella panencephalitis เกิดจากเชื้อหัดเยอรมันที่ยังอยู่ในสมองหลังติดเชื้อแต่กำเนิด ทำให้วัยรุ่นสติปัญญาถดถอย เดินเซเด่นกว่า SSPE ชักและกระตุก ตรวจพบ CSF โปรตีนสูง oligoclonal bands และ rubella antibody สูงมาก ส่วน EEG มักเห็นคลื่นช้า ปัจจุบันยังไม่มียารักษา จึงให้การรักษาตามอาการและเน้นป้องกันด้วยวัคซีน MMR และตรวจภูมิคุ้มกันหัดเยอรมันก่อนตั้งครรภ์

name: Rucksack palsy
formal: Brachial plexus injury from compression by heavy backpack straps, affecting upper trunk with shoulder and arm weakness, usually a neurapraxia.
simple: Temporary arm nerve injury from carrying a heavy backpack.
more: EMG confirms; resolves with rest and avoiding load over weeks to months. Traction injury to the upper trunk of the brachial plexus from heavy pack straps, causing painless shoulder and arm weakness with variable sensory loss. EMG localises the upper trunk lesion. Removing the load and rest typically lead to recovery over weeks to months.
th: การบาดเจ็บของ brachial plexus ส่วน upper trunk จากสายเป้หนักกดทับที่ไหล่ ทำให้ไหล่และต้นแขนอ่อนแรงโดยไม่ค่อยปวด
tempoNote: Begins during or right after carrying a heavy pack; recovery over weeks to months
feat: Painless weakness of shoulder abduction, external rotation and elbow flexion after carrying a heavy pack
Numbness over lateral arm and forearm (C5–C6 territory)
Sometimes long thoracic nerve involvement causing scapular winging
Seen in military recruits, hikers and students with heavy bags
Usually unilateral, on the side bearing more weight
inv: Nerve conduction and EMG at 2–4 weeks: upper trunk pattern, often conduction block (neurapraxia)
MRI of the brachial plexus if atypical, painful or not improving

case.who: 20-year-old male army conscript from Lop Buri
case.story: After a 25-km march with a 30-kg pack, he could not lift his right arm above shoulder level. No neck pain.
case.exam: Weak right deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus and biceps (MRC 3); reduced biceps reflex; sensory loss over lateral arm.
case.tests: EMG at 3 weeks: conduction block across Erb's point with few denervation potentials; cervical MRI normal.
case.q: Where is the lesion and what is the outlook?
case.a: Upper trunk brachial plexus (rucksack palsy); mainly neurapraxic, so strength usually returns within a few months with rest and physiotherapy.

read.where: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves — Plexopathies

det.patho: Straps compress and stretch the upper trunk and its branches where they cross the supraclavicular region near the coracoid. Pressure causes focal demyelination and conduction block; more severe or prolonged loading adds axonal loss. Frameless packs and absence of hip belts increase risk.
det.clinical: Weakness appears during or soon after load carrying and is often painless, sometimes with paraesthesia. Upper trunk muscles are most affected, occasionally with winging from long thoracic nerve compression. Bilateral or lower trunk involvement is uncommon.
det.diagnosis: History is usually diagnostic. Electrodiagnosis confirms a plexus localisation and indicates whether the injury is demyelinating (good prognosis) or axonal. Imaging excludes structural lesions when the story is atypical. Recurrent episodes warrant genetic testing for HNPP.
det.treatment: Remove the load, rest the limb and begin physiotherapy to maintain range and strengthen recovering muscles. Prevention includes lighter loads, frames with hip belts and padded straps. Surgery is rarely needed.
det.prognosis: Most recover fully within 2–3 months when the injury is mainly neurapraxic; axonal injuries take longer and may leave residual weakness.
pearls: Painless upper trunk weakness after load-bearing — think rucksack palsy, not brachial neuritis.
Conduction block on EMG predicts faster recovery.
Recurrent or bilateral episodes: test for HNPP.
det.thd: Rucksack palsy คือการบาดเจ็บของ upper trunk ของ brachial plexus จากการแบกเป้หนัก เช่น ทหารเดินทางไกล ผู้ป่วยยกไหล่และงอศอกไม่ขึ้น มีชาด้านนอกต้นแขน มักไม่ปวด EMG ช่วยยืนยันตำแหน่งและบอกพยากรณ์ การรักษาคือหยุดแบกน้ำหนัก ทำกายภาพ ส่วนใหญ่หายภายในไม่กี่เดือน

name: Sandhoff’s disease
formal: GM2 gangliosidosis from hexosaminidase A and B deficiency with infantile regression, startle, macular cherry-red spot and macrocephaly.
simple: An inherited fat storage disease in babies causing loss of skills, exaggerated startle and seizures.
th: โรคสะสม GM2 ganglioside จากเอนไซม์ hexosaminidase A และ B ต่ำ ทารกถดถอย ตกใจง่ายต่อเสียง ตามองไม่เห็น พบ cherry-red spot และตับม้ามโตเล็กน้อย
tempoNote: Infantile form regresses over months; later-onset forms progress over years
feat: Regression from 3 to 6 months with floppiness, exaggerated startle to noise and loss of vision
Macular cherry-red spot, later spasticity, macrocephaly and seizures
Mild liver and spleen enlargement and bony changes, unlike Tay–Sachs
Late-onset forms: ataxia, lower motor neuron weakness and psychiatric symptoms
Autosomal recessive HEXB disease with deficiency of both Hex A and Hex B
inv: Hexosaminidase A and total hexosaminidase activity in leucocytes or serum
HEXB gene testing
MRI with thalamic T2 hypointensity and white matter change; urine oligosaccharides
Fundoscopy

case.story: He smiled and rolled at 4 months, but now no longer reaches for toys and jumps violently at every door slam.
case.exam: Hypotonia with brisk reflexes, poor visual following, cherry-red macular spots, mild hepatomegaly and a growing head.
case.tests: Hexosaminidase A and B both markedly reduced; biallelic HEXB variants; CT shows bright thalami and MRI dark thalami on T2.
case.q: How does this differ from Tay–Sachs disease?
case.a: Sandhoff disease is a HEXB defect lowering both Hex A and Hex B, often with mild organomegaly; Tay–Sachs (HEXA) leaves Hex B normal and organs are unaffected.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Glycosphingolipidoses
Progressive Encephalopathies With Onset Before Age 2

det.patho: HEXB encodes the beta subunit shared by hexosaminidase A (alpha-beta) and hexosaminidase B (beta-beta). Absent activity of both enzymes prevents breakdown of GM2 ganglioside and related glycolipids and oligosaccharides, which pile up in neurons and, to a lesser degree, in visceral organs. Ballooned neurons then fail progressively. It is one of the sphingolipidoses alongside Tay–Sachs, Krabbe and Gaucher disease.
det.clinical: The infantile disease resembles Tay–Sachs: early development is normal, then from 3 to 6 months comes hypotonia, startle to sound, regression, blindness, seizures and later spasticity with a large head. A cherry-red spot is present. Liver and spleen enlargement, bone changes and cardiac involvement help separate it from Tay–Sachs. Juvenile and adult forms show cerebellar ataxia, SMA-like weakness, dysarthria and psychosis.
det.diagnosis: Enzyme assay is the key step: both Hex A and Hex B are low, whereas in Tay–Sachs only Hex A is deficient. HEXB sequencing confirms and allows carrier testing and prenatal diagnosis. Thalamic changes on imaging and a cherry-red spot on fundoscopy support the diagnosis. Exclude GM1 gangliosidosis and Niemann–Pick disease.
det.treatment: No approved disease-modifying therapy exists, although substrate reduction (miglustat) and gene therapy are being explored. Care is supportive: seizure control, feeding support (gastrostomy), secretion management, positioning and palliative care for families. Genetic counselling is offered to parents.
det.prognosis: The infantile form is fatal, usually in early childhood; later-onset forms progress more slowly.
pearls: Cherry-red spot plus organomegaly points to Sandhoff rather than Tay–Sachs.
Both Hex A and Hex B are low in Sandhoff disease.
Excess startle to noise is a classic early sign in GM2 disease.
det.thd: Sandhoff disease เกิดจากยีน HEXB กลายพันธุ์ ทำให้เอนไซม์ hexosaminidase A และ B ต่ำ GM2 ganglioside สะสมในเซลล์ประสาท ทารกพัฒนาการดีก่อนแล้วถดถอยช่วง 3-6 เดือน ตกใจง่ายต่อเสียง ตามองไม่เห็น ชัก พบ cherry-red spot และอาจตับม้ามโต ต่างจาก Tay-Sachs ตรวจวัดเอนไซม์และยีน HEXB เพื่อยืนยัน ยังไม่มียารักษาโรคโดยตรง ดูแลแบบประคับประคอง

name: Sandifer’s syndrome
formal: Gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants causing paroxysmal head and neck dystonic posturing mimicking seizures or torticollis.
simple: Infants with acid reflux who arch or twist the neck in a way that can look like seizures.
th: ภาวะกรดไหลย้อนในทารกที่ทำให้บิดคอเอียงศีรษะและแอ่นหลังเป็นพัก ๆ ดูคล้ายชักหรือคอเอียง แต่ไม่ใช่โรคลมชัก
tempoNote: Brief repeated episodes, typically linked to feeds, in infants and young children; resolves as reflux settles
feat: Paroxysmal neck extension, head tilt or rotation and back arching lasting seconds to a few minutes
Episodes cluster during or soon after feeding and stop during sleep
Reflux clues: regurgitation, feeding refusal, irritability, poor weight gain, sometimes anaemia
Normal neurological examination and development between episodes
Child is alert and responsive during the posture, without postictal drowsiness
inv: Clinical diagnosis supported by video of episodes related to feeds
Video-EEG during typical events when seizures are a real concern: no ictal change
Paediatric GI assessment: pH-impedance study or endoscopy if severe; look for hiatus hernia

case.story: Several times a day, usually 10–20 minutes after milk, she twists her head to one side and arches her back for about a minute while fussing. She often spits up feeds.
case.exam: Thriving but below her growth curve; normal tone, normal head control and normal neurological examination between events.
case.tests: Parent's phone video shows posturing with full alertness; video-EEG during an event normal.
case.q: What is the likely cause of these spells and how should they be managed?
case.a: Sandifer syndrome from gastro-oesophageal reflux; treat the reflux (feeding changes, thickened feeds, acid suppression if needed) rather than start antiseizure drugs.

read.where: 1 - Clinical overview and phenomenology of movement disorders

det.patho: Acid and non-acid reflux into the oesophagus causes discomfort, and the infant adopts abnormal neck and trunk postures that seem to ease the symptoms, perhaps by changing oesophageal position or clearance. The movements are a behavioural response rather than epileptic or primary dystonic activity. Hiatus hernia and neurological impairment increase the likelihood.
det.clinical: Onset is typically within the first months after birth, with stereotyped head tilt, neck extension or torticollis and opisthotonic arching, often accompanied by crying, gagging or apparent discomfort. Episodes are tied to meals and absent in sleep. Children with cerebral palsy or other neurological disability can show it at older ages, where it is easily mistaken for dystonia or seizures. Development is normal in otherwise healthy infants.
det.diagnosis: A careful history of timing relative to feeds and home video are often enough. When seizures cannot be excluded, video-EEG capturing an event without ictal change is reassuring. Reflux can be confirmed with pH-impedance monitoring or endoscopy when symptoms are severe or treatment fails. Consider other paroxysmal infant disorders, cervical spine or posterior fossa lesions if examination is abnormal.
det.treatment: Management targets reflux: smaller frequent feeds, upright positioning after feeds, thickened formula, a trial of cow's milk protein exclusion, and acid suppression in selected infants. Surgical fundoplication is reserved for refractory cases, especially in neurologically impaired children. Antiseizure medicines are not indicated.
det.prognosis: Excellent; posturing typically disappears once reflux is controlled or outgrown.
pearls: Head tilt and arching after feeds in an alert infant: think reflux before epilepsy.
Events never occur in sleep, unlike many seizures.
Home video plus a normal ictal EEG avoids needless antiseizure therapy.

name: Sanfilippo disease
formal: Mucopolysaccharidosis type III from heparan sulfate degradation defects with early behavioural change, hyperactivity, sleep disruption and rapid dementia.
simple: An inherited metabolic disease in children causing behaviour problems and loss of learned skills.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมสะสม heparan sulfate (MPS III) เด็กมีพฤติกรรมผิดปกติ ซนมาก นอนไม่หลับ แล้วพัฒนาการถดถอยจนสมองเสื่อม
tempoNote: Slowly progressive regression over years, beginning in the preschool period
feat: Early speech and motor delay, followed by marked hyperactivity, aggression, and autistic-like behaviour between ages 2 and 4
Severe sleep disturbance that resists treatment
Plateau, then loss of skills leading to dementia; seizures in roughly 40% and later motor decline
Mild somatic disease: coarse hair, mild facial change, hepatomegaly in about two-thirds, no dwarfism or corneal clouding
Autosomal recessive; four enzyme subtypes (IIIA SGSH, IIIB NAGLU, IIIC HGSNAT, IIID GNS), IIIA being most common

case.who: 5-year-old boy from Bangkok, second child of first-cousin parents
case.story: Late talking, then relentless running, climbing and aggression since age 3; sleeps only 4–5 hours a night and has begun to lose words. He was labelled as autism and ADHD.
case.exam: Thick, coarse hair, bushy eyebrows, mild hepatomegaly, hyperactive and not following commands; no corneal clouding, normal height.
case.tests: Urine GAG screen shows heparan sulfate excess; leukocyte N-sulfatase activity is deficient; MRI shows mild atrophy.
case.q: What diagnosis unites regression, sleeplessness and mild coarse features?
case.a: Sanfilippo disease (MPS IIIA); give supportive and behavioural care and genetic counselling.

read.where: 5 - Psychomotor Retardation and Regression — Mucopolysaccharidoses (MPS III, Sanfilippo disease)
Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Lysosomal Storage Disorders

det.patho: Four lysosomal enzymes needed to break down heparan sulfate are deficient, so the glycosaminoglycan accumulates in neurons and secondary storage of gangliosides drives neurodegeneration. Because only heparan sulfate is stored, the skeletal and corneal changes of Hurler and Hunter disease are largely absent. Inheritance is autosomal recessive and the gene for IIIA lies on chromosome 17q25.3. Brain involvement dominates, with severe cerebral disease in all four subtypes.
det.clinical: Development seems normal for about two years, followed by speech delay and a plateau, then a phase of intense hyperactivity and sleeplessness between about 2 and 4 years. Loss of acquired skills and dementia follow, then seizures, spasticity and swallowing difficulty. Most children have severe cognitive impairment by around 11 years, and death usually occurs in the second or third decade, although attenuated cases with later regression are recognised. Hepatomegaly, hirsutism and diarrhoea or recurrent ear infections are common.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in any preschool child with behaviour disorder that is followed by regression, especially with coarse hair. A positive urine glycosaminoglycan screen supports the diagnosis, but a normal screen does not exclude it, so measure the enzyme for the specific subtype and confirm with gene analysis. Cord blood and dried blood spot tests suit family testing. MRI helps exclude other causes but is non-specific.
det.treatment: Management is supportive: behavioural strategies, melatonin and sedative-hypnotics for sleep, antiseizure drugs for epilepsy (usually easy to control), swallowing and nutrition support, and palliative planning. Bone marrow transplant has been disappointing, and enzyme replacement cannot reach the brain when given intravenously. Gene therapy using AAV vectors and brain-directed enzyme delivery are in trials, and enrolment in these should be discussed. Genetic counselling covers carrier testing and prenatal options.
det.prognosis: Relentless; most patients die in adolescence or early adulthood, though attenuated forms live longer.
pearls: An autistic or hyperactive child who later loses skills and has coarse hair should prompt MPS III testing.
A normal urine GAG screen does not exclude Sanfilippo; measure the enzyme.
Severe insomnia and hyperactivity are hallmark behavioural features.

name: Sarcoglycanopathies
formal: Autosomal recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophies (LGMD R3-R6) from SGCA, SGCB, SGCG, and SGCD mutations, with early proximal weakness and often cardiomyopathy.
simple: A group of inherited muscle diseases, mainly weakening the hips and shoulders from childhood.
more: CK is very high; biopsy shows sarcoglycan deficiency; genetic confirmation; supportive care; cardiac screening.
ab: Severe childhood autosomal recessive muscular dystrophy
th: LGMD ชนิดยีนด้อยจากความผิดปกติของ sarcoglycan ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อต้นแขนขาอ่อนแรงตั้งแต่เด็ก CK สูงมาก และอาจมีหัวใจผิดปกติ

feat: Proximal leg then arm weakness with Gowers sign, toe walking and calf hypertrophy
Affects girls and boys equally (recessive), unlike Duchenne
Scapular winging and lumbar lordosis; loss of walking in teens in severe forms
Cardiomyopathy, especially with beta- and delta-sarcoglycan, and respiratory weakness
Intellect normal
inv: CK markedly raised (often 10–100 times normal)
Muscle biopsy: dystrophic changes with reduced sarcoglycan immunostaining, normal or mildly reduced dystrophin

case.who: 8-year-old girl from Pattani; parents are cousins
case.story: Falls often and walks on her toes; struggles to rise from the floor over two years.
case.exam: Gowers sign, waddling gait, enlarged calves, weak hip and shoulder girdle, mild winging; normal cognition.
case.tests: CK 14,000 U/L; biopsy shows absent alpha-sarcoglycan with preserved dystrophin; homozygous SGCA variant.
case.q: Why is this not Duchenne muscular dystrophy, and what screening is needed?
case.a: Recessive LGMD R3 (alpha-sarcoglycanopathy) in a girl with normal dystrophin; regular cardiac and respiratory surveillance.

read.where: Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Genetic Muscle Diseases

det.patho: The four sarcoglycans form a complex anchored to dystrophin that stabilises the sarcolemma during contraction. A defect in one subunit usually destabilises the whole complex, so immunostaining for all of them is reduced. Membrane fragility leads to repeated necrosis, regeneration failure and fibrofatty replacement. Founder variants are common in some populations and consanguinity increases risk.
det.clinical: Severe forms resemble Duchenne, beginning in early childhood with proximal weakness, calf hypertrophy and loss of ambulation in the second decade. Milder alpha-sarcoglycan variants can present in adolescence or adulthood, sometimes only with exercise intolerance or hyperCKaemia. Dilated cardiomyopathy and respiratory insufficiency are major late issues. Cognition is typically normal, which helps separate it from dystrophinopathy.
det.diagnosis: Very high CK with a dystrophic pattern in a girl, or in a boy with normal dystrophin, should prompt sarcoglycan testing. Biopsy immunostaining shows secondary reduction of all sarcoglycans, so the primary gene must be defined by genetic testing. A neuromuscular gene panel is now the first-line test in most centres. Muscle MRI and cardiac assessment add staging information.
det.treatment: Management is multidisciplinary: physiotherapy, stretching, orthoses, scoliosis monitoring, respiratory support and cardiac medication for cardiomyopathy. Corticosteroids lack strong evidence. AAV-based gene transfer for beta- and alpha-sarcoglycan disease is in clinical trials, so a confirmed genetic diagnosis matters for trial access.
det.prognosis: Variable; severe childhood forms lose walking in the teens and may die of cardiorespiratory failure in early adulthood, whereas milder variants have near-normal lifespan.
pearls: Duchenne-like girl with very high CK: think sarcoglycanopathy.
Loss of one sarcoglycan on staining reduces them all; the gene test tells you which is primary.
Screen the heart even when limb disease is mild.

det.patho: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem disease of non-caseating granulomas of unknown cause, thought to reflect an exaggerated T-cell response to an unidentified antigen. The nervous system is involved in around 5–10% of patients, and in a proportion the nervous system is the first or only site. Granulomas spread along the leptomeninges and perivascular spaces, preferring the skull base, hypothalamus and pituitary stalk, and can form parenchymal masses or cause a small-vessel vasculopathy.
det.clinical: Encephalopathic presentations range from subtle cognitive and mood change to delirium, depending on lesion burden, hydrocephalus and endocrine disturbance. Hypothalamic disease causes diabetes insipidus, hyperphagia, somnolence and thermoregulatory problems. Seizures arise from cortical or meningeal lesions and indicate more aggressive disease. Isolated neurological presentations without a known systemic diagnosis are common and make diagnosis difficult.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis follows consensus criteria graded possible, probable or definite: compatible clinical and MRI findings, exclusion of alternatives, and histology of granulomas from CNS tissue (definite) or from another organ (probable). Gadolinium MRI is the most useful neuro test. CSF is inflammatory but non-specific; CSF ACE has low accuracy. FDG-PET helps locate extra-neural biopsy sites. Rigorously exclude TB, fungal infection, lymphoma and other granulomatous disease, especially in Thailand where TB is common.
det.treatment: Corticosteroids are first line (often IV methylprednisolone then oral prednisolone with slow taper). Because relapse is common, a steroid-sparing drug (methotrexate, mycophenolate or azathioprine) is added early, and TNF-alpha inhibitors (infliximab) are now used early for severe parenchymal, hypothalamic or refractory disease. Treat seizures, hydrocephalus and endocrine deficits; screen for latent TB and hepatitis B before biologics.
det.prognosis: Many improve, but parenchymal and hypothalamic disease often relapses and leaves residual deficits; mortality is higher than in systemic-only disease.
pearls: Diabetes insipidus plus basal meningeal enhancement: think sarcoid, TB, lymphoma and histiocytosis.
Always look for a body site to biopsy before resorting to brain biopsy.
Exclude TB thoroughly before high-dose steroids and anti-TNF therapy.
det.thd: Sarcoid encephalopathy คือ neurosarcoidosis ที่เกิด granuloma ในเยื่อหุ้มสมองและเนื้อสมอง โดยเฉพาะบริเวณฐานสมองและ hypothalamus ทำให้ความจำและพฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน ชัก เบาจืด และหน้าเบี้ยว MRI พบเยื่อหุ้มสมองติดสีและก้อนในสมอง ยืนยันด้วยชิ้นเนื้อพบ granuloma ไม่มี caseation หลังแยกวัณโรคและมะเร็งต่อมน้ำเหลือง รักษาด้วยสเตียรอยด์ร่วมกับยากดภูมิหรือ infliximab

det.patho: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem disorder of non-caseating granulomas driven by an exaggerated T-helper cell response to an unknown antigen. Muscle granulomas are found on blind biopsy in a substantial minority of patients, but symptomatic myopathy is uncommon. Granulomas may destroy fibres directly or provoke surrounding inflammation.
det.clinical: Three patterns are described: a chronic progressive proximal myopathy, an acute or subacute myositis with pain and raised CK, and a nodular form with palpable masses. The chronic form tends to affect middle-aged or older women and may look like inclusion body myositis. Many patients have known sarcoidosis elsewhere, but muscle can be the first sign.
det.diagnosis: Muscle biopsy showing non-caseating granulomas is required, ideally guided by MRI or PET because involvement is patchy. Infections (TB, fungi), granulomatous myositis linked to myasthenia or thymoma, and foreign-body reactions must be excluded. Chest imaging, ACE, calcium and eye review support systemic sarcoidosis. CK may be normal in chronic disease.
det.treatment: Glucocorticoids are the first-line treatment, typically followed by methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate to reduce steroid exposure. TNF-alpha inhibitors such as infliximab are used in refractory disease. Physiotherapy is important. The chronic form responds less well than acute myositis.
det.prognosis: Acute and nodular forms often improve with treatment; chronic myopathy tends to stabilise rather than recover fully.
pearls: Granulomas on muscle biopsy are not always sarcoid — exclude TB and thymoma-associated granulomatous myositis.
Normal CK does not exclude chronic sarcoid myopathy.
Use MRI or PET to pick the biopsy site.

det.patho: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem disorder of non-caseating granulomas of unknown cause, thought to reflect an exaggerated Th1/Th17 response to an unidentified antigen. The optic nerve may be inflamed directly, infiltrated by granuloma, or compressed by meningeal or chiasmal disease. Optic involvement is among the commoner neuro-ophthalmic manifestations of neurosarcoidosis.
det.clinical: Visual loss develops over days to weeks and may be bilateral or sequential. Disc oedema, optic disc granulomas, uveitis and periphlebitis are clues on fundoscopy. Many patients have no known systemic sarcoidosis at presentation. Untreated or under-treated cases progress to optic atrophy, and relapse during steroid taper is characteristic.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on a compatible syndrome, enhancing nerve or meninges on MRI, and tissue proof of granulomas, usually from lung nodes, skin or lacrimal gland rather than the nerve. Serum ACE, lysozyme and soluble IL-2 receptor support but cannot confirm. Infection (especially tuberculosis in Thailand), lymphoma, NMOSD, MOGAD and syphilis must be excluded. Consensus criteria grade cases as definite, probable or possible.
det.treatment: High-dose corticosteroids (often IV methylprednisolone then oral prednisolone) are first-line. Because relapse is frequent, methotrexate, mycophenolate or azathioprine is added early as a sparing drug, and TNF-alpha inhibitors such as infliximab are used for severe or refractory disease. Screen for latent TB and hepatitis B before biologics.
det.prognosis: Prompt immunosuppression often stabilises or improves vision, but delayed treatment or relapses can leave permanent optic atrophy.
pearls: Optic neuritis that does not recover, or relapses when steroids stop, needs a sarcoid and lymphoma work-up.
Look for uveitis and hilar nodes; the nerve itself is rarely biopsied.
In Thailand, tuberculosis must be excluded before long-term immunosuppression.

det.patho: Sarcoidosis is an immune disorder in which activated macrophages and T cells form non-caseating granulomas in lung, lymph nodes, eye, skin and other organs. About 5–10% have clinical nervous system involvement, which can be the first or only manifestation. Granulomas spread along the leptomeninges and perivascular spaces, giving a predilection for the skull base, hypothalamus and cord surface. The disease is less common in Thai and other Asian populations than in northern Europeans and African Americans.
det.clinical: Facial nerve palsy is the classic presentation, sometimes with uveitis and parotid swelling (Heerfordt syndrome). Optic neuropathy, chronic meningitis, hydrocephalus, hypothalamic dysfunction, parenchymal masses, seizures and myelopathy occur, and small fibre neuropathy is frequent but often overlooked. Course may be monophasic (often facial palsy) or chronic and relapsing (parenchymal and cord disease).
det.diagnosis: The 2018 consensus grades neurosarcoidosis as definite (nervous system biopsy), probable (compatible neurological picture with granulomas elsewhere) or possible (no tissue). Body imaging (CT chest, FDG-PET) identifies an accessible biopsy target. CSF is inflammatory but not specific; CSF and serum ACE lack sensitivity. Infection (TB, fungi, syphilis), lymphoma and IgG4-related disease must be excluded, with mycobacterial and fungal stains and cultures on all tissue.
det.treatment: Corticosteroids are first line (often IV methylprednisolone then oral prednisolone tapered over months). Early steroid-sparing therapy with methotrexate, mycophenolate or azathioprine is usual for chronic disease. Anti-TNF therapy (infliximab) is increasingly used for parenchymal, cord or refractory disease. Manage hydrocephalus, seizures and endocrine deficits; screen for latent TB and hepatitis B before biologics.
det.prognosis: Isolated facial palsy usually recovers; parenchymal, cord and hypothalamic disease often leave deficits and relapse when treatment is reduced.
pearls: Bilateral facial palsy: think sarcoidosis, GBS variants, Lyme, HIV and leukaemic meningitis.
Dorsal subpial cord enhancement ('trident sign') suggests sarcoid myelitis.
In Thailand, exclude TB thoroughly before diagnosing neurosarcoidosis.
det.thd: Neurosarcoidosis คือ sarcoidosis ที่ลามมาที่ระบบประสาท เกิด granuloma แบบไม่มีเนื้อตายที่เยื่อหุ้มสมองบริเวณฐานกะโหลก ต่อมใต้สมอง และผิวไขสันหลัง อาการที่พบบ่อยคือใบหน้าอ่อนแรง เส้นประสาทตาอักเสบ เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบเรื้อรัง เบาจืด และไขสันหลังอักเสบ วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI, CSF และตัดชิ้นเนื้อจากต่อมน้ำเหลืองหรือปอดที่หาเจอด้วย CT หรือ PET ต้องแยกวัณโรคและ lymphoma ก่อนเสมอ รักษาด้วย steroid ร่วมยากดภูมิ เช่น methotrexate และอาจใช้ infliximab ในรายรุนแรง

det.patho: Sarcotubular myopathy was first described in a Hutterite family and later shown to be allelic with LGMD2H, both due to TRIM32 variants. TRIM32 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase involved in protein turnover and muscle regeneration; its loss leads to dilated sarcotubular elements and fibre degeneration. Other genes such as TRAPPC11 can produce vacuolar myopathies, but the exact mechanism in each is incompletely understood.
det.clinical: Weakness is proximal and slowly progressive, starting in childhood to adulthood. Many remain ambulant for decades. Some have facial weakness or exertional pain. Cardiac and respiratory involvement are uncommon but should be checked.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is made by gene testing in a patient with an LGMD phenotype. Light microscopy may show only small vacuoles; electron microscopy reveals the dilated sarcotubular system. Because the term is historical and morphological, most modern reports use LGMD R8 TRIM32-related.
det.treatment: No specific therapy exists. Physiotherapy, avoidance of excessive eccentric exercise, orthotic support and periodic cardiorespiratory screening form the basis of care, along with genetic counselling.
det.prognosis: Usually mild to moderate disability with normal or near-normal lifespan; data are limited by rarity.
pearls: Sarcotubular myopathy and LGMD R8 are the same TRIM32 disease.
Electron microscopy is what shows the dilated sarcotubules.
A rare entity: say what is unknown rather than extrapolating.

name: Satoyoshi’s syndrome
formal: Rare progressive disorder of painful muscle spasms, alopecia and diarrhoea with skeletal abnormalities, probably autoimmune.
simple: A rare illness with severe muscle cramps, hair loss and diarrhoea.
more: Rare syndrome of progressive painful muscle spasms with alopecia, diarrhoea and endocrine disturbance, often with autoimmune features, in young females. Reported responses to corticosteroids and immunotherapy; carbamazepine or dantrolene may reduce spasms; mostly reported from Japan.
ab: Progressive muscle spasm, alopecia and diarrhoea
th: โรคหายากที่มีตะคริวกล้ามเนื้อเจ็บปวดเป็นพัก ๆ ร่วมกับผมร่วงทั้งศีรษะ ท้องเสีย และกระดูกผิดรูป เชื่อว่าเกิดจากภูมิคุ้มกัน
tempoNote: Begins in childhood or adolescence; painful spasms come in attacks on a progressive background
feat: Intermittent, very painful muscle spasms starting in the legs and spreading to trunk and jaw, often several times a day
Hair loss progressing to alopecia universalis, usually early in the course
Chronic diarrhoea and malabsorption with growth failure
Endocrine problems such as amenorrhoea and short stature; skeletal deformities from repeated spasm stress
Mostly young girls, reported first and most often from Japan
inv: EMG during spasm shows high-frequency motor unit firing; nerve conduction and CK often near normal
Autoantibody screen (antinuclear and others reported; anti-GAD occasionally); look for associated autoimmune disease
Skeletal X-ray for epiphyseal lesions; endocrine and malabsorption work-up

case.story: For a year she has had attacks of excruciating cramps in the calves and thighs lasting minutes; her hair has fallen out almost completely and she has loose stools most days.
case.exam: Total scalp alopecia, thin build, tender contracted calf muscles during an attack, otherwise normal strength and reflexes.
case.tests: EMG shows involuntary bursts of motor units during spasm; ANA positive; X-ray irregular metaphyses of knees.
case.q: Which rare syndrome links painful spasms, alopecia and diarrhoea, and how is it usually treated?
case.a: Satoyoshi syndrome; corticosteroids, IVIG or other immunotherapy with symptomatic drugs such as dantrolene or carbamazepine for spasms.

det.patho: The cause is unknown, but associations with other autoimmune diseases, autoantibodies and responses to immunotherapy suggest an autoimmune mechanism. Spasms probably arise from hyperexcitable motor pathways; bone changes result from mechanical stress on growing epiphyses, and diarrhoea reflects gut malabsorption. Fewer than about 100 cases are recorded; no genetic basis has been found.
det.clinical: Symptoms typically begin between ages 6 and 15. Painful cramps start in the legs and spread, last up to minutes and leave muscles hard and sore; consciousness is preserved. Alopecia, diarrhoea with malabsorption, amenorrhoea and growth retardation develop over time. Untreated, it progresses with increasing disability, malnutrition and deformity.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical based on the characteristic triad, supported by EMG showing spasm-related motor unit discharges, skeletal X-ray changes and evidence of autoimmunity. Exclude stiff-person spectrum disorders, neuromyotonia, metabolic myopathies with cramps, and electrolyte disturbance such as hypocalcaemia.
det.treatment: Immunotherapy (corticosteroids, IVIG, and in reports tacrolimus or other agents) has led to improvement in many published cases. Muscle relaxants and membrane-stabilising drugs (dantrolene, carbamazepine, benzodiazepines) relieve spasms. Nutritional support, hormone replacement and orthopaedic care address the systemic features.
det.prognosis: Variable; early immunotherapy can bring marked improvement, while untreated cases may die from malnutrition or complications.
pearls: Painful spasms + alopecia + diarrhoea in a girl: Satoyoshi.
Responds to immunotherapy, supporting an autoimmune cause.
Check calcium and magnesium first to exclude tetany as a simple mimic.
det.thd: Satoyoshi syndrome เป็นโรคหายากที่พบในเด็กหญิง มีตะคริวกล้ามเนื้อรุนแรงเจ็บมากเป็นพัก ๆ ผมร่วงทั้งศีรษะ ท้องเสียเรื้อรัง โตช้า และกระดูกผิดรูป เชื่อว่าเกิดจากภูมิคุ้มกัน วินิจฉัยจากอาการร่วมกับ EMG และภาพรังสีกระดูก รักษาด้วยสเตียรอยด์หรือ IVIG ร่วมกับยาคลายกล้ามเนื้อ

Myokymia and continuous fibre activity with neuromyotonic discharges on EMG; CASPR2 antibodies
Acute onset after a wound with trismus and generalised spasms; no chronic course

name: SCAD deficiency
formal: Short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (ACADS) with raised ethylmalonic acid, often clinically benign but sometimes causing myopathy and developmental delay.
simple: A fat-processing enzyme deficiency that is often harmless, but can cause weakness or delay in some people.
more: Diagnosed by urine organic acids and gene testing; usually requires no treatment other than avoiding fasting.
th: ความผิดปกติของการเผาผลาญกรดไขมันสายสั้นจากยีน ACADS พบ ethylmalonic acid สูง ส่วนใหญ่ไม่มีอาการ บางรายมีกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงหรือพัฒนาการช้า
tempoNote: Usually detected by newborn screening; the majority remain well
feat: Most identified infants stay asymptomatic; now regarded as a biochemical phenotype of uncertain significance
Reported features: hypotonia, developmental delay, failure to thrive, seizures, myopathy
Raised C4 (butyrylcarnitine) on newborn screen and urinary ethylmalonic acid
Common ACADS susceptibility variants (c.625G>A, c.511C>T) in the general population
inv: Plasma acylcarnitines: raised C4; urine organic acids: ethylmalonic acid
ACADS sequencing; exclude other causes of high C4 (isobutyryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency) and of ethylmalonic aciduria (ETHE1, MADD)
Search for another explanation if the child is symptomatic

case.who: Newborn girl in Bangkok, followed in metabolic clinic
case.story: Newborn screening showed raised C4-carnitine. She feeds well and meets milestones at 9 months.
case.exam: Normal tone, growth and development.
case.tests: Urine ethylmalonic acid mildly raised; ACADS compound heterozygous variants.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and how should she be managed?
case.a: SCAD deficiency; reassure, avoid prolonged fasting during illness as a precaution, and look for other diagnoses if symptoms develop.

det.patho: SCAD performs the opening dehydrogenation step when four- and six-carbon acyl-CoAs are broken down inside mitochondria. Loss of activity raises butyryl-CoA, which is diverted to butyrylcarnitine and ethylmalonic acid. Two common polymorphisms reduce enzyme stability, and homozygosity for them is frequent in healthy people, which complicates interpretation.
det.clinical: Early reports described hypotonia, developmental delay, seizures and lipid-storage myopathy, but large newborn-screening cohorts show that nearly all biochemically affected children are well. Symptoms in an affected child are therefore often due to another condition. Adult cases with exercise intolerance or myopathy are rare and unproven.
det.diagnosis: Elevated C4-carnitine and urinary ethylmalonic acid with biallelic ACADS variants confirm the biochemical diagnosis. Isobutyryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (also high C4), MADD and ethylmalonic encephalopathy (ETHE1) must be distinguished. Clinicians should continue to investigate other causes in symptomatic patients rather than attributing everything to SCAD deficiency.
det.treatment: No specific treatment is usually required. Some centres advise avoiding prolonged fasting during intercurrent illness; carnitine or riboflavin have no proven benefit. Several screening programmes have removed SCAD deficiency from their panels because of its benign course.
det.prognosis: Excellent in the large majority.
pearls: High C4 on newborn screen: SCAD and IBD deficiency are both usually benign.
Symptomatic child with SCAD deficiency: keep looking for a second diagnosis.
Ethylmalonic acid also rises in MADD and ETHE1 disease, which are not benign.
det.thd: SCAD deficiency เป็นความผิดปกติของการสลายกรดไขมันสายสั้นจากยีน ACADS มักพบจากการคัดกรองทารกแรกเกิดที่ C4-carnitine สูงและ ethylmalonic acid ในปัสสาวะสูง ผู้ป่วยส่วนใหญ่ไม่มีอาการ จึงถือเป็นภาวะทางชีวเคมีที่ความสำคัญทางคลินิกไม่แน่ชัด หากเด็กมีอาการควรหาสาเหตุอื่นต่อ ไม่ต้องรักษาเฉพาะ

ddx.pt: Several acylcarnitine chain lengths raised; riboflavin-responsive myopathy possible
Raised C8; real risk of hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and sudden death with fasting
Lactic acidosis, ragged-red or COX-negative fibres and multisystem features

name: Scapuloperoneal muscular dystrophy
formal: Muscular dystrophy with weakness in shoulder girdle and peroneal muscles, from FHL1, LMNA or other mutations; includes dominant and X-linked forms.
simple: An inherited muscle disease affecting the shoulders and lower legs.
more: Genetic testing; evaluate for cardiomyopathy, as cardiac disease is common.
th: กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงเด่นที่สะบักไหล่และกล้ามเนื้อหน้าแข้ง (peroneal) ทำให้สะบักยื่นและเท้าตก มักต้องตรวจหัวใจ
tempoNote: Onset childhood to mid-adult life, slowly progressive
feat: Scapular winging and shoulder girdle weakness with sparing of the deltoid early
Ankle dorsiflexor weakness causing foot drop and steppage gait
Face usually spared, which helps separate it from FSHD
Contractures, rigid spine and cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia in FHL1 and LMNA forms
Inheritance may be dominant or X-linked (FHL1)
inv: CK normal to mildly raised; EMG myopathic (to separate neurogenic scapuloperoneal syndromes)
Muscle MRI and gene panel (FHL1, LMNA, MYH7, DES, TRPV4 for neurogenic forms); FSHD testing if face involved
ECG, Holter and echocardiography

case.who: 34-year-old man, motorcycle taxi driver from Bangkok
case.story: Shoulder blades stick out when he pushes; trips over kerbs for two years. His maternal uncle died suddenly in his forties.
case.exam: Bilateral scapular winging, weak serratus and periscapular muscles, bilateral foot drop, tight Achilles tendons, normal face.
case.tests: CK 520 U/L; EMG myopathic; ECG first-degree AV block; hemizygous FHL1 variant.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what is the most important additional management?
case.a: X-linked FHL1 scapuloperoneal myopathy; cardiology review with rhythm monitoring and possible device therapy.

det.patho: Scapuloperoneal weakness is a distribution, not a single disease. Myopathic forms arise from FHL1 (X-linked), LMNA, MYH7, desmin and others, while neurogenic forms are linked to TRPV4 and other motor neuron genes. Shared features include contractures and frequent cardiac involvement, reflecting proteins of the sarcomere, Z-disc or nuclear envelope.
det.clinical: Patients present with winging of the scapulae and foot drop, often in early adult life. Facial muscles are typically spared. Joint contractures, neck stiffness and respiratory weakness may appear. Cardiomyopathy, conduction block and arrhythmia can be the life-threatening feature and may precede obvious weakness.
det.diagnosis: First decide myopathic versus neurogenic with EMG and CK. Then use pattern on muscle MRI and a gene panel; test for FSHD if there is any facial or abdominal weakness. Cardiac evaluation is mandatory at diagnosis and on follow-up.
det.treatment: There is no curative therapy. Ankle-foot orthoses, physiotherapy, contracture management and respiratory monitoring are central. Cardiology input may lead to pacemaker or ICD placement and heart-failure medication. Genetic counselling for family members, including female carriers in X-linked forms.
det.prognosis: Limb disability progresses slowly; life expectancy depends largely on cardiac involvement.
pearls: Winging plus foot drop with a spared face: think FHL1 or LMNA and check the heart.
A neurogenic EMG points to a scapuloperoneal SMA such as TRPV4 instead.
Sudden death in a male maternal relative is a clue to X-linked FHL1.
det.thd: Scapuloperoneal muscular dystrophy คือกลุ่มโรคกล้ามเนื้อที่อ่อนแรงบริเวณสะบักและหน้าแข้ง ทำให้สะบักยื่นและเท้าตก หน้ามักปกติ สาเหตุมีหลายยีน เช่น FHL1, LMNA และ MYH7 มักมีข้อยึดและหัวใจผิดปกติ วินิจฉัยด้วย EMG, muscle MRI และตรวจยีน ต้องตรวจหัวใจเสมอ การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคองและอาจต้องใส่เครื่องกระตุ้นหัวใจ
