name: Schwannomas
formal: Benign nerve sheath tumours, including vestibular schwannoma, strongly associated with neurofibromatosis type 2 and schwannomatosis.
simple: Non-cancerous growths from nerve covering cells that can press on nerves.
th: เนื้องอกไม่ร้ายจาก Schwann cell ที่ขาดโปรตีน merlin (NF2) เป็นก้อนมีแคปซูลที่เส้นประสาทสมอง (พบบ่อยที่ vestibular), รากประสาทไขสันหลัง และเส้นประสาทส่วนปลาย ผ่าตัดหรือฉายรังสีเฉพาะจุดควบคุมได้ดี และอาจเกิดหลายก้อนใน NF2 หรือ schwannomatosis
tempoNote: Symptoms evolve slowly over years (hearing loss, facial numbness, radicular pain); acute worsening can follow haemorrhage into a cystic tumour
feat: Vestibular schwannoma: unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus, imbalance, later facial numbness and brainstem compression
Trigeminal schwannoma: facial numbness or neuralgia and masseter weakness, often as a dumbbell mass across the middle and posterior fossa
Lower cranial nerve (jugular foramen) schwannomas: hoarseness, dysphagia and tongue weakness; facial nerve schwannoma gives slowly progressive facial palsy
Spinal root schwannomas cause radicular pain and, when large, cord or cauda equina compression; spinal tumours may be multiple in NF2 and schwannomatosis
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas define NF2; schwannomatosis causes multiple painful schwannomas without vestibular tumours
inv: MRI with gadolinium and thin cuts through the internal auditory canal: avidly enhancing, well-circumscribed mass with an ice-cream-cone shape in the cerebellopontine angle; heterogeneity or cysts in large tumours
Pure tone audiometry and speech discrimination; ABR or vestibular testing where helpful; electromyography for nerve tumours
Histology: Antoni A and B areas with Verocay bodies, strong S100 and SOX10 positivity, hyalinised vessels
Genetic testing (NF2, SMARCB1, LZTR1) when tumours are multiple, bilateral or young-onset

case.story: Two years of decreased hearing and ringing in the left ear, now with mild unsteadiness and numbness of the left cheek.
case.exam: Left sensorineural hearing loss, reduced left corneal reflex, left gaze-evoked nystagmus, normal facial strength.
case.tests: Audiogram shows asymmetrical high-frequency loss with poor speech discrimination. MRI shows a 2.8 cm enhancing left cerebellopontine angle mass extending into the internal auditory canal and compressing the pons; right side normal. No family history.
case.q: What are the treatment options and how does bilateral disease change management?
case.a: Microsurgery (retrosigmoid or translabyrinthine), or stereotactic radiosurgery/fractionated radiotherapy for smaller or higher-risk patients; observation of small tumours with serial MRI. Bilateral tumours point to NF2, where hearing preservation is prioritised and bevacizumab can improve hearing and shrink tumours.

read.where: Chapter 14 Tumors of the Cranial Nerves

det.patho: Schwannomas arise from the Schwann cells of the nerve sheath and grow outside the fascicles, so the nerve is pushed aside and can be spared at surgery. Histology shows a cellular Antoni A pattern with palisading nuclei forming Verocay bodies and a looser Antoni B pattern. Loss of the NF2 gene product merlin (schwannomin) is the common genetic event in sporadic and NF2-related tumours. Schwannomatosis involves SMARCB1 or LZTR1 mutations. Cranial nerve tumours are almost always benign, WHO grade 1; malignant change is exceptional.
det.clinical: Vestibular schwannoma accounts for most intracranial tumours of nerve sheath origin and produces slowly progressive hearing loss, tinnitus and imbalance. Large tumours compress the brainstem and fourth ventricle. Trigeminal and jugular foramen tumours give cranial neuropathies; spinal tumours cause pain and cord compression. The book emphasises that growth is slow and treatment targets function, not survival, so decisions should consider the patient's age, hearing and tumour size.
det.diagnosis: MRI is diagnostic in most cases; the main differential diagnosis in the cerebellopontine angle is meningioma, epidermoid cyst and metastasis. Size classification (Koos, Samii) guides treatment. Audiological assessment is needed at baseline and follow-up. Genetic testing and family history are important when tumours are multiple or arise in the young, and the whole neuraxis may need to be imaged.
det.treatment: Small tumours with good hearing can be observed with serial MRI. Microsurgery cures many tumours with a risk to facial nerve and hearing that depends on size; stereotactic radiosurgery or fractionated radiotherapy controls growth in over 90 percent of small to medium tumours and spares facial function, with delayed hearing loss. Large symptomatic tumours need surgery, possibly followed by radiosurgery to residual. In NF2, bevacizumab can reduce tumour volume and improve hearing in some patients; auditory brainstem implants and cochlear implants support hearing. Spinal and peripheral schwannomas are resected with preservation of the parent nerve fascicles.
det.prognosis: Excellent control after complete excision or radiosurgery; hearing preservation and facial function are the quality-of-life concerns.
pearls: Unilateral sensorineural hearing loss plus tinnitus needs MRI of the internal auditory canal.
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas equal NF2; offer genetic counselling and screening of relatives.
Schwannomas grow extrafascicularly, so the parent nerve can often be preserved.
det.thd: Schwannoma เป็นเนื้องอกไม่ร้ายจาก Schwann cell ที่มีแคปซูลและเติบโตข้างเส้นประสาท พบบ่อยที่ vestibular nerve ทำให้หูตึงข้างเดียว หูอื้อ เสียการทรงตัว และอาจกดก้านสมองเมื่อก้อนใหญ่ MRI พบก้อน enhance ใน internal auditory canal ผู้ที่เป็นสองข้างต้องนึกถึง NF2 การรักษาคือเฝ้าติดตาม ผ่าตัด หรือฉายรังสีเฉพาะจุด และใช้ bevacizumab ใน NF2 ได้ผลดีทั้งด้านขนาดก้อนและการได้ยิน

ddx.pt: Broad dural base with dural tail, hyperostosis and calcification, and less involvement of the internal auditory canal
Intrafascicular, infiltrative nerve lesion, usually in NF1, without extrinsic encapsulation
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, ependymomas and juvenile cataracts

name: Schwartz–Jampel syndrome
formal: Autosomal recessive perlecan disorder causing myotonia, blepharophimosis, short stature and skeletal changes with continuous muscle fibre activity.
simple: An inherited condition with muscle stiffness, small eye openings and short stature.
more: HSPG2 mutations; EMG shows complex repetitive discharges and neuromyotonia-like activity, and CK may be mildly raised. Carbamazepine, phenytoin or mexiletine reduce stiffness; intellect is normal and life expectancy is generally preserved.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมแบบ autosomal recessive จากยีน HSPG2 (perlecan) ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อแข็งเกร็งต่อเนื่อง ตาหยีแคบ ตัวเตี้ย และกระดูกผิดรูป
tempoNote: Appears in infancy or early childhood; stiffness relatively stable, skeletal deformity progresses
feat: Fixed facial 'mask': narrow palpebral fissures (blepharophimosis), pursed lips, small mouth
Generalised muscle stiffness with hypertrophy and joint contractures
Short stature, bowed long bones, pectus carinatum, hip dysplasia
Continuous muscle-fibre activity rather than true myotonia; no percussion relaxation pattern
Intelligence usually normal; malignant-hyperthermia-like anaesthetic risk
inv: EMG: continuous complex repetitive or neuromyotonic-like discharges persisting under nerve block
Skeletal survey: platyspondyly, metaphyseal and epiphyseal dysplasia
CK normal or mildly raised; HSPG2 sequencing confirms

case.story: Parents noticed stiff walking, small eyes and a fixed facial expression since infancy; he is shorter than his peers.
case.exam: Blepharophimosis, puckered lips, firm hypertrophic thighs, hip and knee contractures, waddling gait, normal speech and play.
case.tests: EMG with continuous high-frequency discharges at rest; X-ray shows flattened vertebrae; biallelic HSPG2 variants.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and which practical risk must the family be told about?
case.a: Schwartz–Jampel syndrome type 1; anaesthetic complications including difficult airway and hyperthermia-like reactions.

read.where: 8 - Cramps, Muscle Stiffness, and Exercise Intolerance
36: Myotonic Muscle Disorders and Periodic Paralysis Syndromes

det.patho: Perlecan is a heparan sulfate proteoglycan of basement membranes and cartilage. Reduced perlecan at the neuromuscular junction is associated with loss of acetylcholinesterase anchoring and nerve terminal hyperexcitability, producing continuous muscle activity; in cartilage it disturbs growth plates. Complete loss of perlecan causes the lethal dyssegmental dysplasia instead.
det.clinical: Children present with stiffness, a characteristic tight facial expression, small eyes and short stature in the first years. Muscle bulk is often increased. Skeletal problems such as kyphoscoliosis, joint contractures and hip dysplasia worsen with growth. A severe neonatal type previously labelled SJS type 2 is now known to be Stüve–Wiedemann syndrome (LIFR).
det.diagnosis: The combination of dysmorphic face, stiffness and chondrodysplasia is suggestive. EMG reveals continuous spontaneous activity of uncertain origin, partly neural, partly muscular. Skeletal X-rays support the diagnosis and HSPG2 gene testing confirms it.
det.treatment: Sodium-channel blockers such as carbamazepine or mexiletine can reduce stiffness; botulinum toxin may help blepharospasm-like eye narrowing. Orthopaedic care, physiotherapy and stretching address contractures. Anaesthetic planning must cover difficult intubation and possible hyperthermia.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is near normal in SJS1; disability comes mainly from skeletal deformity.
pearls: Stiff child with small eyes and short stature: think Schwartz–Jampel.
Neonatal lethal 'type 2' is a different gene (LIFR, Stüve–Wiedemann).
Warn anaesthetists — airway and hyperthermia risk.
det.thd: Schwartz–Jampel syndrome เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมด้อยจากยีน HSPG2 ที่สร้าง perlecan ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อทำงานต่อเนื่องจนแข็งเกร็ง ใบหน้าตึง ตาหยีแคบ ตัวเตี้ย และกระดูกสันหลังแบน วินิจฉัยด้วย EMG และตรวจยีน รักษาด้วย carbamazepine หรือ mexiletine ร่วมกับดูแลกระดูกและต้องระวังการดมยาสลบ

Neonatal hypotonia and weakness rather than stiffness; maternal DM1

name: Sciatic neuropathy
formal: Injury to the sciatic nerve, from hip surgery, injection or compression, causing foot drop, posterior leg weakness and sensory loss with peroneal division predominance.
simple: Damage to the large nerve at the back of the leg, causing weakness and numbness in the leg and foot.
th: เส้นประสาท sciatic บาดเจ็บจากการผ่าตัดสะโพก การฉีดยาที่ก้น หรือถูกกดทับ ทำให้เท้าตกและชาขาส่วนล่าง เด่นที่แขนง peroneal
tempoNote: Usually abrupt after surgery, injection or compression; slower with tumour or endometriosis
feat: Foot drop with weakness of ankle eversion, and often plantarflexion and knee flexion
Sensory loss over lateral leg and foot, sometimes the sole
Peroneal division often affected more than tibial, mimicking peroneal palsy
Reduced or absent ankle jerk; hip abduction (gluteus medius) spared
Causes: hip arthroplasty, gluteal injection, prolonged sitting or coma, trauma, tumour
inv: EMG/NCS after 2–3 weeks: denervation in short head of biceps femoris distinguishes it from peroneal neuropathy; normal gluteal and paraspinal muscles exclude L5 root or plexus
MRI or ultrasound of pelvis and thigh to look for haematoma, tumour or entrapment
Check for compartment syndrome or rhabdomyolysis after prolonged immobility

case.story: Woke after left total hip replacement unable to lift her left foot, with burning over the top of the foot.
case.exam: Left foot drop, weak eversion and inversion, mild weakness of plantarflexion and knee flexion, reduced ankle jerk, normal hip abduction.
case.tests: EMG at 3 weeks: denervation in tibialis anterior, gastrocnemius and short head of biceps femoris; normal gluteus medius and paraspinals.
case.q: Where is the lesion?
case.a: Left sciatic nerve (peroneal-predominant) injured during hip arthroplasty, not a common peroneal or L5 lesion.

Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Complications of Obstetric Anaesthesia
3. Common Mononeuropathies of the Lower Extremities

det.patho: The sciatic nerve carries separate peroneal and tibial divisions from the pelvis to the popliteal fossa. The lateral peroneal division is more tethered at the sciatic notch and fibular head, has fewer protective connective-tissue layers and bigger fascicles, so it suffers more from stretch or pressure. Injury may be neurapraxic, axonotmetic or neurotmetic depending on mechanism.
det.clinical: Most cases follow hip surgery or fracture, misplaced gluteal injections, prolonged sitting or lying on hard surfaces (including intoxication), or penetrating trauma. Slowly progressive cases suggest a mass such as schwannoma, lymphoma or endometriosis, which may cause cyclical pain. Neuropathic pain can be severe. Because the peroneal fibres dominate, many patients look as though they have a fibular head palsy.
det.diagnosis: Careful examination of inversion, plantarflexion, knee flexion and hip abduction localises the lesion. EMG is decisive, especially sampling the short head of biceps femoris (sciatic peroneal division above the knee) and gluteal muscles. Imaging is needed when there is no clear cause or symptoms progress. Neuromuscular ultrasound can show nerve swelling, transection or compression.
det.treatment: Remove ongoing compression and evacuate any haematoma promptly. Provide an ankle-foot orthosis, physiotherapy to prevent contracture, and neuropathic pain medication. Surgical exploration is considered for transection or no recovery after several months. Tumours need specialist nerve surgery.
det.prognosis: Partial lesions often improve over months; recovery of the peroneal division is generally slower and less complete than the tibial division.
pearls: Foot drop with weak inversion and weak ankle jerk is not a simple peroneal palsy.
Short head of biceps femoris is the key EMG muscle.
Gluteal injections should be given in the upper outer quadrant to avoid the nerve.
det.thd: Sciatic neuropathy คือเส้นประสาท sciatic บาดเจ็บ มักเกิดหลังผ่าตัดสะโพก ฉีดยาเข้าก้นผิดตำแหน่ง หรือนอนกดทับนาน อาการคือเท้าตกและชา แขนง peroneal ได้รับผลมากกว่า จึงคล้าย peroneal palsy แต่จะมีอ่อนแรง inversion และ ankle jerk ลด EMG ที่ short head of biceps femoris ช่วยยืนยัน การรักษาคือแก้สาเหตุ ใส่ AFO และกายภาพ

name: Scombroid poisoning
formal: Histamine fish poisoning from spoiled fish, with flushing, headache, palpitations and abdominal pain.
simple: Food poisoning from spoiled fish causing flushing, headache and stomach upset.
th: อาหารเป็นพิษจาก histamine ในปลาที่เก็บไม่เย็นพอ เช่น ปลาทูน่า ปลาทู ทำให้หน้าแดง ปวดศีรษะ ใจสั่น และปวดท้องภายในไม่กี่นาทีถึงชั่วโมง ไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาท
tempoNote: Begins 10–60 minutes after eating and resolves within 12–24 hours
feat: Flushing of face and upper body, urticaria, warmth
Throbbing headache, palpitations, peppery or metallic taste
Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal cramps
Several people eating the same fish are often affected
Not an allergy, and not a neurotoxic fish poisoning
inv: Clinical diagnosis based on timing and the fish eaten
Histamine level in leftover fish for public health reporting
Serum tryptase normal (supports scombroid over anaphylaxis)

case.who: Three colleagues at a seafood restaurant in Hua Hin
case.story: Thirty minutes after sharing grilled tuna, all develop red faces, pounding headache and palpitations; one has diarrhoea.
case.exam: Facial flushing, mild tachycardia, BP normal, no wheeze or angio-oedema.
case.tests: None needed; leftover fish later found to contain high histamine.
case.q: What is the treatment?
case.a: Scombroid poisoning; antihistamines (H1 with or without H2 blockers), with adrenaline only if severe bronchospasm or hypotension.

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Scombroid

det.patho: Bacteria on improperly chilled fish decarboxylate histidine into histamine, which is heat-stable and not destroyed by cooking or freezing. Eating the fish delivers a large histamine load, producing vasodilatation and gastrointestinal symptoms. Tuna, mackerel, sardines and similar fish are typical sources.
det.clinical: Symptoms resemble an allergic reaction and are often misdiagnosed as fish allergy. Headache is throbbing and accompanied by flushing and palpitations. Severe reactions with bronchospasm or hypotension are rare but occur in people with asthma or those taking isoniazid, which blocks histamine metabolism. This is a toxic food illness, not a neurological disease.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical: rapid onset after eating fish, typical flushing and clusters of cases. Measuring histamine in the fish confirms. Distinguish from true fish allergy, which would recur with fresh fish, and from neurotoxic seafood poisonings such as ciguatera or tetrodotoxin.
det.treatment: Oral or intravenous H1 antihistamines, often with H2 blockers, give rapid relief. Fluids for vomiting and diarrhoea; adrenaline and bronchodilators for severe reactions. Report clusters to public health.
det.prognosis: Self-limiting within a day; no lasting effects.
pearls: Group of diners with flushing after tuna — scombroid, not allergy.
Cooking does not destroy histamine.
Isoniazid users get more severe reactions.
det.thd: Scombroid poisoning คืออาหารเป็นพิษจาก histamine ในปลาที่เก็บไม่เย็นพอ เช่น ปลาทูน่า ปลาทู แม้ปรุงสุกแล้ว histamine ก็ไม่ถูกทำลาย ผู้ป่วยมีอาการหน้าแดง ปวดศีรษะตุบ ๆ ใจสั่น และท้องเสียภายในไม่กี่นาทีถึงชั่วโมงหลังกิน มักเป็นพร้อมกันหลายคน ไม่ใช่การแพ้และไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาท รักษาด้วยยาต้าน histamine และหายเองภายในหนึ่งวัน

name: Secondary headache
formal: Headache attributed to underlying disease such as haemorrhage, tumour, infection or raised pressure, identified by red flag features.
simple: A headache caused by another medical problem rather than a primary headache disorder like migraine.
th: อาการปวดศีรษะที่เกิดจากโรคอื่น เช่น เลือดออกในสมอง เนื้องอก การติดเชื้อ หรือความดันในกะโหลกผิดปกติ ต้องคัดกรองด้วย red flags
tempoNote: Thunderclap in SAH, days to weeks in infection or venous thrombosis, weeks to months in tumour or IIH
feat: Headache caused by another disorder and closely linked in time to it
Red flags (SNOOP4 style): systemic illness, neurological signs, sudden onset, onset after 50, pattern change, positional, Valsalva or pregnancy-related
Causes: SAH, ICH, CVT, dissection, meningitis, tumour, IIH, intracranial hypotension, GCA, medication overuse
May mimic migraine or tension-type headache closely
inv: Urgent CT within hours for thunderclap onset; LP if CT negative and suspicion persists
MRI with contrast and MR venography for subacute progressive or positional headache
ESR/CRP in those over 50; fundoscopy for papilloedema

case.who: 29-year-old woman from Chon Buri, 10 days postpartum
case.story: Headache steadily worsening over five days, worse lying down, now with vomiting and one generalised seizure.
case.exam: Bilateral papilloedema, drowsy, mild left leg weakness.
case.tests: MRI/MRV: superior sagittal sinus thrombosis with right parasagittal haemorrhagic infarct.
case.q: Which red flags were present and what is the treatment?
case.a: Postpartum onset, progressive course, seizure, papilloedema and focal signs; anticoagulation with heparin despite the haemorrhagic infarct.

det.patho: Within the skull, the pain-sensitive tissues are the meninges, large vessels and venous sinuses, innervated mainly by trigeminal and upper cervical nerves. Secondary headache arises when these are stretched, inflamed, compressed or bathed in blood, or when intracranial pressure rises or falls. Systemic conditions such as hypertension, hypoxia and fever can also activate this system.
det.clinical: ICHD-3 defines secondary headache by a plausible cause and a temporal or causal link. Patterns include thunderclap (SAH, RCVS, dissection, pituitary apoplexy), progressive morning headache with vomiting (mass or raised pressure), positional headache (low CSF pressure), fever and neck stiffness (meningitis) and jaw claudication (GCA). A patient with known migraine can develop a new secondary headache, so a change in pattern matters.
det.diagnosis: History and examination with a red-flag screen decide who needs investigation. CT is first-line for sudden severe headache; MRI and MRV are more sensitive for venous thrombosis, tumours and low-pressure syndromes. LP measures pressure and looks for blood, infection or inflammation once mass lesions are excluded. Most patients without red flags have a primary headache and do not need imaging.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying cause (e.g. aneurysm securing, anticoagulation for CVT, antibiotics for meningitis, steroids for GCA, epidural blood patch for CSF leak) while giving appropriate analgesia. Withdraw overused analgesics in medication-overuse headache. Opioids should not mask a deteriorating condition.
det.prognosis: Depends on the cause; missed SAH or CVT carries high morbidity, whereas most causes are treatable when found early.
pearls: Worst, first or different headache needs investigation.
A normal CT after six hours does not exclude SAH; consider LP.
New headache after 50: check ESR/CRP and think GCA.
det.thd: Secondary headache คือปวดศีรษะจากโรคอื่น เช่น เลือดออกใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมอง หลอดเลือดดำในสมองอุดตัน เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ เนื้องอก หรือ GCA ต้องคัดกรองด้วย red flags เช่น ปวดทันที อายุเกิน 50 มีไข้ อาการทางระบบประสาท ปวดตามท่าทาง หรือหลังคลอด ตรวจด้วย CT, MRI/MRV หรือ LP ตามข้อบ่งชี้ และรักษาที่สาเหตุ

name: Secondary paroxysmal dyskinesia
formal: Paroxysmal movement attacks due to underlying lesions such as multiple sclerosis, stroke or trauma.
simple: Short attacks of involuntary movements caused by another brain disease.
th: การเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติเป็นพัก ๆ ที่เกิดจากรอยโรคในสมองหรือไขสันหลัง เช่น MS, stroke, บาดเจ็บ หรือความผิดปกติทางเมตาบอลิก
tempoNote: Brief stereotyped attacks lasting seconds to minutes, often many per day, starting weeks to months after the causal lesion
feat: Episodes of dystonia, chorea or ballism with preserved consciousness
Often hemibody, contralateral to a basal ganglia, thalamic or capsular lesion
Causes: MS (tonic spasms), stroke, head injury, hypoglycaemia, hyperthyroidism, hypoparathyroidism, encephalitis
Later age of onset and absent family history differ from primary forms
Often triggered by movement, hyperventilation or touch
inv: MRI brain and spinal cord with contrast
Glucose, calcium, parathyroid hormone, thyroid function
EEG during attacks if seizure is possible; video recording of events

case.who: 33-year-old woman from Chiang Mai with relapsing MS
case.story: For three weeks, many times a day, her right arm and leg twist and stiffen for about 30 seconds, sometimes provoked by standing up quickly.
case.exam: Between attacks mild right pyramidal signs; during an observed attack, painful dystonic posture of right limbs, fully alert.
case.tests: MRI: new enhancing lesion in the left cerebral peduncle; EEG during an attack normal.
case.q: What is this phenomenon and which drug usually stops it?
case.a: Paroxysmal tonic spasms (secondary paroxysmal dyskinesia from MS); low-dose carbamazepine, plus treatment of the MS relapse.

read.where: Movement Disorders — Peripheral and Miscellaneous Movement Disorders: Paroxysmal Dyskinesias

det.patho: Lesions in the basal ganglia-thalamocortical circuit or along the corticospinal pathway can produce episodic movements. In demyelination, ephaptic transmission between damaged axons generates brief discharges that spread along the tract. Metabolic causes alter neuronal excitability in the basal ganglia.
det.clinical: Attacks are stereotyped, brief and frequent, sometimes painful, and usually affect one side. In MS they can herald a relapse and typically settle within weeks to months. Post-stroke forms may appear months after the infarct. Hypoglycaemic and thyrotoxic forms resolve with metabolic correction.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by video and by imaging showing a relevant lesion. Metabolic screening is essential because it changes treatment. EEG helps when attacks resemble seizures. Consider functional movement disorder only after structural and metabolic causes are excluded and positive functional signs are present.
det.treatment: Sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine) often work at low doses, particularly in MS. Treat the underlying disease and correct metabolic disturbance. Benzodiazepines, acetazolamide or other antiseizure drugs are alternatives.
det.prognosis: Usually good in MS and metabolic causes; post-traumatic and post-stroke cases may persist but are often drug responsive.
pearls: New paroxysmal dystonia in a young adult may be the first sign of MS.
Low-dose carbamazepine is a useful first try.
Always check glucose, calcium and thyroid function.
det.thd: Secondary paroxysmal dyskinesia คือการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติเป็นพัก ๆ เช่น เกร็งบิดหรือกระตุก ที่เกิดจากรอยโรค เช่น MS, stroke, บาดเจ็บศีรษะ หรือเมตาบอลิก เช่น น้ำตาลต่ำ แคลเซียมต่ำ ต่างจากชนิดปฐมภูมิตรงที่เริ่มตอนโตและไม่มีประวัติครอบครัว ตรวจ MRI และเลือด รักษาด้วย carbamazepine ขนาดต่ำร่วมกับแก้สาเหตุ

EEG change, possible impaired awareness and post-ictal deficit
Limb-shaking TIA from severe carotid stenosis, provoked by standing and lasting minutes

name: Secondary progressive multiple sclerosis
formal: Phase of multiple sclerosis after relapsing disease with gradual worsening independent of relapses from neurodegeneration and chronic inflammation.
simple: A later stage of multiple sclerosis when disability slowly worsens even without clear relapses.
th: ระยะของ MS ที่ตามหลังช่วงกำเริบ-ฟื้นตัว โดยความพิการเพิ่มขึ้นเรื่อย ๆ โดยไม่ขึ้นกับการกำเริบ จากการเสื่อมของเซลล์ประสาทและการอักเสบเรื้อรัง
tempoNote: Gradual worsening over at least 6–12 months after years of relapsing disease, usually 10–20 years after onset if untreated
feat: Prior relapsing remitting history, then steady decline in walking without new attacks
Spastic paraparesis, ataxia, bladder and bowel dysfunction, and cognitive slowing
Active SPMS: occasional relapses or new MRI lesions still occur
Transition is recognised only retrospectively, often with delay
inv: Serial EDSS and timed walk to document progression independent of relapses
MRI: brain and cord atrophy; new or enhancing lesions define active SPMS
Exclude other causes of worsening: infection, B12, cervical compression, medication effects

case.who: 46-year-old woman from Chiang Rai with MS for 15 years
case.story: No relapses for six years, but her walking has gradually worsened from unlimited to needing a stick for 100 metres over two years; increasing urinary urgency.
case.exam: Bilateral spastic paraparesis, ataxia of the left arm, EDSS 6.0.
case.tests: MRI: marked brain atrophy, no new or enhancing lesions compared with two years ago; urine culture negative; B12 normal.
case.q: What phase is she in, and what are the therapeutic options?
case.a: Non-active secondary progressive MS; focus on rehabilitation and symptoms, while siponimod or anti-CD20 therapy benefit mainly those with ongoing activity.

read.where: Chapter 19 Multiple Sclerosis and Demyelinating Diseases
Chapter 62: Neuromuscular Disease in the Neuroscience Intensive Care Unit

det.patho: Progression is driven by smouldering inflammation behind the blood-brain barrier, expanding chronic active lesions, cortical demyelination, mitochondrial injury and loss of axonal reserve with age. New focal lesion formation declines, explaining why classical immunotherapies have less effect. Progression independent of relapse activity can start early in the disease.
det.clinical: Patients notice worsening gait, endurance and bladder control, often with cognitive decline and fatigue. The pace differs among patients. Superimposed relapses define active SPMS and suggest that immunotherapy may still help.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical: a history of relapsing disease followed by at least 6–12 months of steady worsening not explained by relapses. Pseudo-progression from infection, depression, pain, deconditioning or new comorbid disease such as cervical compression must be excluded. MRI helps classify activity but cannot by itself make the diagnosis.
det.treatment: Siponimod is approved for active SPMS; ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, cladribine and other relapsing therapies are used when relapses or new lesions continue. Older patients without activity may consider de-escalation because benefit falls and infection risk rises. Rehabilitation, spasticity drugs, fampridine, bladder management, cognitive and mental health support are core care.
det.prognosis: Disability usually continues to accumulate; the pace is slower in many treated cohorts than in historical series.
pearls: Worsening without relapses is the hallmark; check for infection and cervical compression first.
Activity (relapses or new lesions) is what predicts benefit from immunotherapy.
Progression independent of relapse activity can begin even in relapsing MS.
det.thd: MS ชนิด secondary progressive เป็นระยะต่อจาก relapsing remitting ที่ความพิการเพิ่มขึ้นเรื่อย ๆ โดยไม่มีการกำเริบ เกิดจากการเสื่อมของเซลล์ประสาทและการอักเสบเรื้อรังในสมอง ผู้ป่วยเดินแย่ลง ขาเกร็ง ปัสสาวะผิดปกติ ต้องตัดสาเหตุอื่นที่ทำให้แย่ลง เช่น ติดเชื้อ หรือกระดูกคอกดทับ ยาอย่าง siponimod หรือ anti-CD20 ได้ผลในรายที่ยังมี activity ร่วมกับการฟื้นฟู

name: Secondary tumours
formal: Metastatic cancers of brain, spine or nerves arising from lung, breast, melanoma or other primaries; commonly multiple with surrounding oedema.
simple: Cancers that spread to the brain or spine from elsewhere in the body.
th: มะเร็งแพร่กระจายมายังสมอง ไขสันหลัง เยื่อหุ้มสมอง หรือเส้นประสาท มักมาจากปอด เต้านม และ melanoma
tempoNote: Symptoms usually evolve over days to weeks; sudden onset with haemorrhage or seizure
feat: Headache, focal deficit, seizures or cognitive change in a patient with known or occult cancer
Often multiple lesions at grey–white junction with marked surrounding oedema
Haemorrhagic tendency with melanoma, renal, thyroid and choriocarcinoma
Spinal metastases: back pain then cord compression with weakness and sphincter loss
Leptomeningeal spread: multiple cranial neuropathies and radiculopathies
inv: MRI brain/spine with gadolinium
CT chest, abdomen and pelvis or PET-CT to find primary and stage
Biopsy when primary unknown or solitary lesion; CSF cytology for leptomeningeal disease

case.story: Two weeks of morning headache and clumsy left hand; one focal seizure yesterday. Weight loss 5 kg.
case.exam: Mild left hemiparesis, left pronator drift, no papilloedema.
case.tests: MRI: three ring-enhancing lesions with large oedema; CT chest: right upper lobe mass; biopsy: adenocarcinoma, EGFR mutation.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what modern factor guides treatment?
case.a: Brain metastases from lung adenocarcinoma; molecular profile (EGFR) allows CNS-penetrant targeted therapy alongside radiosurgery.

read.where: Chapter 26 Metastatic Disease and the Nervous System

det.patho: Metastases are the commonest intracranial tumours in adults. Tumour cells reach the brain via the arterial circulation and lodge at grey–white junctions and watershed zones; spine deposits usually arise in vertebral bodies and compress the cord from the epidural space. Lung, breast, melanoma, renal and gastrointestinal cancers are the main sources. Better systemic control of cancer has increased the proportion of patients living long enough to develop CNS spread.
det.clinical: Presentation includes headache, focal deficits, seizures, cognitive or behavioural change and raised pressure. Metastatic spinal cord compression starts with progressive, often nocturnal or recumbent back pain before weakness and sphincter disturbance. Leptomeningeal metastases cause multifocal cranial nerve, root and cerebral signs. Around a quarter of patients have no known primary at presentation.
det.diagnosis: Contrast MRI is the key test and is more sensitive than CT for small lesions. Systemic staging identifies the primary and biopsy targets. Tissue diagnosis is needed when the primary is unknown or the lesion is atypical; tumour molecular profiling (EGFR, ALK, HER2, BRAF) now guides treatment. Abscess, lymphoma, demyelination and primary glioma are the main mimics.
det.treatment: Dexamethasone reduces symptomatic oedema; antiseizure drugs are used only after a seizure. Options include surgical resection for large or symptomatic single lesions, stereotactic radiosurgery for limited numbers, and whole-brain radiotherapy with hippocampal avoidance and memantine for widespread disease. CNS-active targeted agents and immunotherapy are increasingly used. Spinal cord compression needs urgent steroids, MRI of the whole spine and surgery and/or radiotherapy.
det.prognosis: Survival ranges from weeks to years depending on performance status, number of lesions, systemic disease control and tumour biology.
pearls: New back pain in a cancer patient is cord compression until proven otherwise.
Melanoma, renal and thyroid metastases bleed.
Prophylactic antiseizure drugs are not recommended in seizure-free patients.
det.thd: Secondary tumours หรือมะเร็งแพร่กระจายเป็นเนื้องอกในสมองที่พบบ่อยที่สุดในผู้ใหญ่ มักมาจากปอด เต้านม melanoma และไต อาการคือปวดศีรษะ อ่อนแรงครึ่งซีก ชัก หรือปวดหลังและไขสันหลังถูกกด MRI มี contrast เป็นการตรวจหลัก ร่วมกับหามะเร็งต้นกำเนิดและตรวจ molecular profile การรักษาใช้ dexamethasone, ผ่าตัด, radiosurgery, ฉายรังสี และยามุ่งเป้าหรือ immunotherapy

name: Secondary vasculitis
formal: Vessel wall inflammation due to infection, drugs, malignancy or connective tissue disease, causing stroke, neuropathy or encephalopathy.
simple: Blood vessel inflammation caused by another illness or drug, which can damage the brain or nerves.
th: การอักเสบของหลอดเลือดที่มีสาเหตุชัดเจน เช่น การติดเชื้อ ยา โรคเนื้อเยื่อเกี่ยวพัน หรือมะเร็ง ต้องรักษาที่ต้นเหตุเป็นอันดับแรก
tempoNote: Evolves over days to months, depending on the trigger
feat: Infections: VZV vasculopathy, TB or syphilitic arteritis, hepatitis B (PAN-like), hepatitis C cryoglobulinaemia, HIV
Connective tissue disease: lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren syndrome
Drugs: antibiotics, NSAIDs, sulfonamides, antiepileptics, levamisole-laced cocaine, antithyroid agents (ANCA)
Cancer-related: lymphoma and paraneoplastic vasculitic neuropathy
Neurological pictures: stroke, mononeuritis multiplex, encephalopathy, aseptic meningitis
inv: Infection work-up: HIV, syphilis serology, hepatitis B/C, TB tests, CSF VZV PCR and intrathecal IgG
ANA, ENA, RF, complement, cryoglobulins, ANCA; drug and toxicology history
CSF analysis, vessel imaging, and nerve or brain biopsy when the diagnosis stays unclear

case.story: Zoster over the left forehead eight weeks ago; now abrupt right hand weakness and trouble speaking.
case.exam: Expressive aphasia, right arm weakness and healed vesicle scars in the left V1 dermatome.
case.tests: MRI shows a left MCA infarct; MRA a focal proximal left MCA narrowing; CSF has 12 lymphocytes and intrathecal anti-VZV IgG.
case.q: What caused the stroke and what is the treatment?
case.a: VZV vasculopathy, a secondary vasculitis; IV aciclovir with a short oral steroid course and antiplatelet therapy.

read.where: Chapter 18: Neurologic Complications Of Acute Vasculitis Syndromes
4. Approach to the Evaluation of Mononeuropathy Multiplex
Chapter 7: Unusual causes of ischemic stroke and transient ischemic attack

det.patho: Vessel walls may be inflamed through direct microbial invasion (VZV, TB, fungi, syphilis), immune complexes (hepatitis B, cryoglobulins in hepatitis C, lupus), drug-triggered autoimmunity (hypersensitivity reactions, ANCA with propylthiouracil or levamisole) or tumour-driven immunity. The injury and the ischaemia resemble primary vasculitis, yet the trigger decides treatment. Drug-related cases are often attributed on circumstantial evidence and can erupt about a week after exposure.
det.clinical: Vessel size and site shape the picture: large intracranial arteries cause stroke or encephalopathy, while disease of the vasa nervorum causes painful mononeuritis multiplex. The systemic setting supplies clues, such as recent zoster, TB contact, hepatitis risk, new drugs, rash, arthritis or nodes. In Thailand, TB meningitis and syphilis remain important infectious causes. Cranial neuropathies can arise from local granulomatous or vasculitic disease.
det.diagnosis: Pair vessel imaging and CSF studies with a targeted search for infection, autoantibodies and drug exposure. Biopsy of a clinically involved nerve or of brain tissue clarifies uncertain cases. Always consider an infectious cause before labelling any CNS vasculitis as primary, because the treatment differs.
det.treatment: Treat the cause first: antimicrobials (aciclovir for VZV, antivirals for hepatitis B or C), withdraw the offending drug, and treat the malignancy. Add immunosuppression for connective tissue disease or severe organ involvement, matched to the underlying condition. Steroids without anti-infective cover can worsen infectious vasculitis. Rituximab with IVIG has helped refractory vasculitic neuropathy in reports.
det.prognosis: Good when the trigger is removed or treated early; delay can leave permanent infarcts or nerve damage.
pearls: Stroke weeks after zoster: think VZV vasculopathy.
Look for infection and drugs before calling vasculitis primary.
Steroids alone are dangerous in infectious arteritis.
det.thd: Secondary vasculitis คือหลอดเลือดอักเสบที่มีสาเหตุรองรับ เช่น การติดเชื้อ (VZV, วัณโรค, ซิฟิลิส, ตับอักเสบบี/ซี) ยา โรคเนื้อเยื่อเกี่ยวพันอย่าง SLE และมะเร็ง ผู้ป่วยอาจมีอัมพฤกษ์ อัมพาต สมองอักเสบ หรือ mononeuritis multiplex ตรวจหาเชื้อ ภูมิคุ้มกัน น้ำไขสันหลังและภาพหลอดเลือด รักษาที่ต้นเหตุก่อน เช่น aciclovir สำหรับ VZV แล้วเพิ่มยากดภูมิเมื่อจำเป็น

name: Segmental myoclonus
formal: Rhythmic jerks restricted to muscles of adjacent spinal or brainstem segments, from focal lesions such as palatal tremor or cord damage.
simple: Repeated jerks in a small group of neighbouring muscles caused by a local nerve problem.
th: การกระตุกเป็นจังหวะของกล้ามเนื้อที่เลี้ยงด้วยไขสันหลังหรือก้านสมองเพียงไม่กี่ปล้อง จากรอยโรคเฉพาะที่ และมักไม่หยุดขณะหลับ
tempoNote: Persistent rhythmic jerks once established; tempo of onset follows the underlying lesion
feat: Rhythmic or semi-rhythmic jerks (about 0.5–3 Hz) confined to one or a few adjacent segments
Little change with stimulus, action or distraction; often persists during sleep
Brainstem form: palatal tremor with ear clicks and sometimes pendular nystagmus
Spinal form: jerks of abdomen, one limb or trunk muscles from a cord lesion
Underlying causes: myelitis, tumour, trauma, ischaemia, syrinx, post-procedural
inv: MRI of the relevant cord or brainstem segment (and hypertrophic olivary degeneration on MRI in palatal tremor)
Surface EMG: long-duration bursts, synchronous in muscles of the segment
Further work-up guided by lesion: CSF, infection and autoimmune screen

case.story: Six months after a thoracic myelitis, her left abdominal wall jerks rhythmically day and night, waking her at times.
case.exam: Rhythmic 1 Hz contractions of left lower abdominal muscles unaffected by distraction; mild residual T10 sensory level.
case.tests: MRI: T2 scar at T9–T10; EMG: synchronous bursts of 200 ms in segment-limited muscles, persisting in sleep.
case.q: What is the movement disorder and where is it generated?
case.a: Spinal segmental myoclonus from the thoracic cord lesion.

read.where: 18 - Myoclonus: Phenomenology, etiology, physiology, and treatment

det.patho: A focal lesion releases spinal or brainstem interneuron networks, which fire rhythmically and drive the anterior horn cells of a few segments. In the brainstem, lesions of the dentato-rubro-olivary pathway cause hypertrophic olivary degeneration and palatal tremor, now classified as a tremor rather than myoclonus. The precise generators are incompletely understood.
det.clinical: Jerks are usually rhythmic, regular and confined to muscles innervated by adjacent segments. They tend to be insensitive to stimuli and continue in sleep. Spinal forms follow myelitis, trauma, tumour, ischaemia, anaesthesia or surgery; brainstem forms follow pontine or medullary stroke and other lesions.
det.diagnosis: Clinical observation and polymyography establish the pattern. MRI looks for a lesion at the appropriate level. Distinguish from propriospinal myoclonus, which spreads along the axis, and from functional jerks, which show variability, entrainment and distractibility.
det.treatment: Treat the cause where possible. Clonazepam, levetiracetam and other antiseizure drugs are tried with variable benefit. Botulinum toxin is useful for localised jerks such as palatal clicking. Evidence is mainly from case series.
det.prognosis: Often persistent if due to a fixed lesion; may resolve when inflammatory or compressive causes are treated.
pearls: Rhythmic jerks that continue in sleep suggest a segmental spinal or brainstem generator.
Ear clicking may be the presenting complaint of palatal tremor.
Always image the cord at and above the affected segments.
det.thd: Segmental myoclonus คือการกระตุกเป็นจังหวะของกล้ามเนื้อที่มาจากไขสันหลังหรือก้านสมองเพียงไม่กี่ปล้อง เกิดจากรอยโรค เช่น myelitis เนื้องอก หรือการบาดเจ็บ อาการมักไม่หายขณะหลับและไม่ตอบสนองต่อสิ่งกระตุ้น การตรวจหลักคือ MRI ตรงระดับนั้นและ EMG การรักษาคือรักษาสาเหตุ ร่วมกับ clonazepam, levetiracetam หรือ botulinum toxin

name: Seizure
formal: Transient episode of abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity producing altered awareness, motor, sensory or autonomic phenomena.
simple: A short burst of abnormal electrical activity in the brain causing shaking, staring or loss of awareness.
th: เหตุการณ์ชั่วคราวที่เซลล์ประสาทปล่อยไฟฟ้ามากผิดปกติและพร้อมกัน ทำให้เกิดอาการด้านการรู้สึกตัว การเคลื่อนไหว การรับรู้ หรือระบบอัตโนมัติ
tempoNote: Sudden onset, usually lasting seconds to a few minutes, often followed by a postictal phase
feat: Abrupt, stereotyped event: focal (aware or impaired awareness) or generalised onset, motor or non-motor
Clues: lateral tongue bite, eyes open during the event, cyanosis, postictal confusion or Todd's paralysis
Provoked (acute symptomatic) seizures arise from metabolic, toxic, infectious or acute structural causes
Unprovoked seizures raise the question of epilepsy (recurrence risk of 60% or more, or a defined syndrome)
Must be separated from syncope, functional seizures, TIA, migraine aura and sleep disorders
inv: Glucose, sodium, calcium, magnesium, renal and liver function; toxicology when relevant; ECG in every first event
Brain MRI with epilepsy protocol (CT in the emergency setting)
EEG, ideally within 24–48 hours; video-EEG for uncertain events
Lumbar puncture if infection or autoimmune encephalitis is suspected

case.who: 24-year-old male factory worker from Samut Prakan
case.story: After a night shift he was seen to stiffen, fall and jerk all four limbs for about a minute; afterwards he was confused for 20 minutes and has a sore tongue.
case.exam: Bite on the lateral tongue, sore muscles, normal neurological examination now.
case.tests: Glucose, sodium and ECG normal; MRI normal; EEG shows generalised polyspike-wave discharges.
case.q: Is this a seizure, and does he have epilepsy?
case.a: A generalised tonic-clonic seizure, likely provoked by sleep deprivation in a person with genetic generalised epilepsy; the EEG raises recurrence risk enough to discuss treatment and driving.

read.where: Section II: Epidemiology, Etiology, and Diagnosis
26 Procedures and Outcomes in Epilepsy Surgery

det.patho: A seizure reflects a transient imbalance between cortical excitation and inhibition, so that a population of neurons fires excessively and synchronously. Focal seizures start within one hemisphere network; generalised seizures engage bilateral networks rapidly, often via thalamocortical circuits. Causes include genetic channel and synaptic disorders, structural lesions, metabolic disturbance, toxins, infection and immune processes.
det.clinical: The ILAE 2017 framework classifies seizures by onset (focal, generalised, unknown), awareness for focal seizures, and motor or non-motor features. About 1 in 10 people has a seizure in their lifetime, but far fewer develop epilepsy. Acute symptomatic seizures occur within about a week of a brain insult or with a defined systemic trigger and carry lower recurrence risk. Prolonged seizures (over 5 minutes for convulsive) should be treated as status epilepticus.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical, based on a detailed eyewitness account, ideally with video. Distinguish epileptic seizures from mimics such as syncope, functional seizures, TIA, migraine, parasomnias and movement disorders. Investigations seek a cause and estimate recurrence risk: metabolic screen, ECG, MRI and EEG. An unremarkable EEG between attacks never rules epilepsy out; repeated or sleep-deprived recordings increase yield.
det.treatment: Acute: protect the patient, time the event, recovery position; give a benzodiazepine if it lasts beyond 5 minutes. Correct provoking factors. After a first unprovoked seizure, treatment is individualised; it is usually advised when the risk of recurrence is high (epileptiform EEG, structural lesion, nocturnal seizure) or the patient prefers. Give counselling on driving, sleep, alcohol, water safety and work at heights.
det.prognosis: After a first unprovoked seizure, around 40–50% recur within two years; most recurrences happen early.
pearls: One seizure is not epilepsy; define provoked versus unprovoked first.
Do an ECG after every first collapse with jerking; cardiac syncope can mimic seizures.
Lateral tongue biting is fairly specific for an epileptic tonic-clonic seizure.
det.thd: Seizure คืออาการชั่วคราวจากเซลล์สมองปล่อยไฟฟ้ามากผิดปกติ อาจเป็นชักเฉพาะที่หรือทั่วไป อาจเกิดจากสาเหตุเฉียบพลันเช่นน้ำตาลหรือโซเดียมต่ำ หรือเป็นโรคลมชัก ต้องแยกจากหมดสติแบบ syncope และชักจากจิตใจ ตรวจน้ำตาล เกลือแร่ ECG MRI และ EEG การรักษาขึ้นกับความเสี่ยงชักซ้ำ ถ้าชักนานเกิน 5 นาทีให้ benzodiazepine

name: Selenium deficiency
formal: Trace element deficiency linked to cardiomyopathy and myopathy, seen in total parenteral nutrition and malabsorption.
simple: Too little selenium in the body, which can weaken muscles and the heart.
th: ภาวะขาดธาตุซีลีเนียม พบในผู้ได้ TPN นานหรือการดูดซึมผิดปกติ ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อหัวใจและกล้ามเนื้อลายเสื่อม
tempoNote: Develops over months of inadequate intake or long-term parenteral nutrition
feat: Mainly a systemic nutritional disorder; neurology sees it as a cause of myopathy
Proximal muscle pain, weakness and raised CK in patients on long-term TPN
Dilated cardiomyopathy (Keshan disease in low-selenium regions)
Whitened nail beds, macrocytosis, hypothyroid features from impaired deiodinase
Risk groups: home TPN, short-bowel syndrome, severe malabsorption, phenylketonuria diets
inv: Plasma selenium and glutathione peroxidase activity (interpret with CRP — falls in inflammation)
CK, echocardiogram, thyroid function
Exclude other causes of myopathy: vitamin E, carnitine, drugs

case.who: 45-year-old woman in Khon Kaen on home TPN for 2 years after bowel resection
case.story: Over three months she has developed aching thighs and difficulty rising from a squat; she is breathless on stairs.
case.exam: Mild proximal weakness, tender muscles, pale nail beds, displaced apex beat.
case.tests: CK 1,100 U/L, plasma selenium very low, echocardiogram shows reduced ejection fraction.
case.q: What has caused her myopathy and heart failure?
case.a: Selenium deficiency from inadequate trace-element supplementation in TPN; replace selenium and monitor levels.

det.patho: Selenium is built into selenoproteins such as glutathione peroxidases, thioredoxin reductases and iodothyronine deiodinases. Deficiency weakens antioxidant defence, so muscle and heart cells suffer oxidative injury. Soil selenium content determines dietary intake, which is why endemic cardiomyopathy occurred in low-selenium regions of China.
det.clinical: Isolated deficiency is uncommon. In clinical practice it appears in long-term parenteral or enteral nutrition without trace elements, after bariatric or extensive bowel surgery, and in restrictive diets. Muscle pain, proximal weakness and high CK are the neurological manifestations; cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia are the dangerous ones. It is not a recognised direct cause of central nervous system disease.
det.diagnosis: Measure plasma selenium together with an inflammatory marker, because acute illness lowers levels independently of stores. Glutathione peroxidase activity reflects function. A biopsy is seldom needed; when done it shows nonspecific myopathic or necrotic changes. Coexisting deficiencies of zinc, copper and vitamin E should be checked.
det.treatment: Replace selenium orally or within parenteral nutrition, following nutrition-team dosing and monitoring. Muscle symptoms usually improve over weeks to months. Cardiac function may recover partially; established cardiomyopathy may need standard heart-failure therapy.
det.prognosis: Myopathy is usually reversible; prognosis depends on cardiac involvement.
pearls: Long-term TPN patient with myalgia and high CK: check selenium.
Low selenium during acute inflammation may not mean true deficiency.
Check other trace elements, especially copper (myelopathy) at the same time.
det.thd: Selenium deficiency เป็นภาวะขาดธาตุซีลีเนียม พบในผู้ป่วยได้ TPN นานหรือการดูดซึมผิดปกติ ทำให้ปวดและอ่อนแรงกล้ามเนื้อต้นแขนขา CK สูง และอาจมีกล้ามเนื้อหัวใจเสื่อม ตรวจระดับ selenium ร่วมกับ CRP รักษาด้วยการเสริม selenium ซึ่งกล้ามเนื้อมักดีขึ้น ควรตรวจแร่ธาตุอื่นเช่นทองแดงร่วมด้วย

name: Semantic dementia
formal: Frontotemporal dementia variant with fluent speech and progressive loss of word meaning, from anterior temporal atrophy, usually TDP-43 pathology.
simple: A kind of dementia where people gradually lose the meaning of words and objects but speak fluently.
th: FTD ชนิดที่พูดคล่องแต่ค่อย ๆ ลืมความหมายของคำและสิ่งของ จากสมองกลีบขมับส่วนหน้าฝ่อ มักเป็น TDP-43 type C
tempoNote: Insidious onset, usually 50s–60s, progressive over years
feat: Fluent, grammatical speech that becomes empty, with severe anomia
Loss of single-word comprehension (What is a 'hammer'?) and object knowledge
Surface dyslexia: reading irregular words as they are spelled
Episodic memory for recent events relatively preserved early
Right-predominant cases: loss of recognition of faces and emotional coldness, rigid behaviour
inv: MRI: asymmetric atrophy of the anterior and inferior temporal lobe (left more often)
FDG-PET: anterior temporal hypometabolism
Neuropsychology with naming, word-picture matching and semantic association tests
Amyloid/tau biomarkers usually negative; genetics rarely positive

case.story: Over two years he stopped understanding words like 'giraffe' and 'umbrella', calls all animals 'thing'. Still drives and recalls yesterday's appointments.
case.exam: Fluent speech with few nouns; cannot name or define common objects; repetition intact; reads 'yacht' phonetically.
case.tests: MRI: knife-edge atrophy of left anterior temporal pole; CSF amyloid normal.
case.q: Which PPA variant is this and what pathology is most likely?
case.a: Semantic variant PPA (semantic dementia); most often TDP-43 type C.

read.where: Chapter 11 Cognitive Impairment and Dementia — Major Neurodegenerative Dementias
Chapter 11 Cognitive Impairment and Dementia — Frontotemporal Dementia
Case 12 Progressive difficulty with naming and object identification
Case 1: Forgets names but has a new appreciation for polka music

det.patho: Semantic dementia results from focal degeneration of the anterior temporal lobes, a hub that binds features of concepts across modalities. Most cases have TDP-43 proteinopathy type C, often linked to annexin A11 pathology; tau or Alzheimer pathology is uncommon. It is usually sporadic, with lower genetic contribution than other FTD variants.
det.clinical: Patients lose knowledge of word and object meaning while speech remains fluent and grammatical. They substitute general terms, misunderstand nouns and fail to recognise less familiar items, then everyday objects and people. Behavioural change, rigid routines, food fads and loss of empathy develop, especially in right-sided cases where face recognition fails early. Day-to-day memory and visuospatial skills are relatively spared at first.
det.diagnosis: Consensus criteria require deficits in both confrontation naming and comprehension of single words, supported by loss of object knowledge, surface dyslexia/dysgraphia, and spared repetition and speech production. Imaging confirms anterior temporal atrophy or hypometabolism. Amyloid and tau biomarkers help exclude Alzheimer disease. Language testing in Thai should use culturally familiar items.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy is available. Cholinesterase inhibitors are not helpful and may worsen behaviour. Speech and language therapy, using personal vocabulary and picture aids, can preserve function for a time. SSRIs or trazodone may help compulsive behaviours; caregiver education and planning are vital.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive, with median survival often around 10–12 years from onset, longer than many other FTD syndromes.
pearls: Asks what a common word means = loss of semantics, not word-finding.
Surface dyslexia is a hallmark: irregular words read phonetically.
Right temporal variant may present with prosopagnosia and personality change rather than language loss.
det.thd: Semantic dementia หรือ semantic variant PPA คือ FTD ที่ผู้ป่วยพูดคล่องแต่ลืมความหมายของคำและสิ่งของ จากกลีบขมับส่วนหน้าฝ่อ ส่วนใหญ่เป็น TDP-43 type C ความจำเหตุการณ์ประจำวันค่อนข้างดีในระยะแรก MRI พบกลีบขมับหน้าฝ่อมาก ไม่มียาที่ชะลอโรค การรักษาเน้นฝึกพูด ใช้ภาพช่วยสื่อสาร และดูแลพฤติกรรม

qx.stem: A 63-year-old temple caretaker from Lampang speaks fluently and grammatically but keeps asking 'what is a ladle?' when his wife asks him to bring one. He reads the English word 'yacht' as it is spelled, cannot name common fruits, and no longer recognises some neighbours' faces; recent day-to-day memory is good. Repetition is intact.
qx.q: Which MRI pattern is most likely?
opts: Bilateral medial temporal atrophy symmetrical with parietal involvement
Left posterior frontal and insular atrophy
Midbrain atrophy with a 'hummingbird' profile
Bilateral parieto-occipital atrophy
Asymmetric anterior temporal pole atrophy, more on the left
qx.why: Loss of word and object meaning with fluent speech, surface dyslexia and preserved repetition is semantic-variant primary progressive aphasia, caused by anterior temporal lobe degeneration that is usually left-predominant; right-sided spread produces prosopagnosia and behavioural change. Underlying pathology is most often TDP-43 type C. Left frontoinsular atrophy fits the non-fluent variant, and parieto-occipital atrophy fits posterior cortical atrophy.

qx.stem: A 63-year-old retired bank clerk from Nonthaburi has three years of fluent but empty speech. She asks what a 'spoon' is when handed one, reads 'yacht' and 'pint' as they are spelled, and no longer recognises the faces of distant relatives. Memory for recent events and route-finding are good. MRI shows marked left more than right anterior and inferior temporal lobe atrophy.
qx.q: Which underlying pathology is most likely?
opts: Alzheimer plaques and tangles in a limbic-predominant distribution
Tau-positive Pick bodies (3-repeat tauopathy)
Alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies in the neocortex

qx.why: This is semantic dementia (svPPA): loss of word and object meaning, surface dyslexia and associative prosopagnosia with asymmetric anterior temporal atrophy. About 80–90% of cases have FTLD-TDP type C pathology, so it is one of the most pathology-predictable FTD syndromes. Pick bodies are more typical of behavioural variant FTD, and Alzheimer pathology usually underlies the logopenic variant.

name: Senile chorea
formal: Late-onset chorea without family history or identifiable cause, often vascular, with benign course.
simple: Jerky involuntary movements starting late in life with no clear cause or family history.
th: chorea ที่เริ่มในผู้สูงอายุโดยไม่มีประวัติครอบครัวหรือสาเหตุชัดเจน เป็นการวินิจฉัยหลังแยกสาเหตุอื่นหมดแล้ว
tempoNote: Gradual onset after 60; abrupt onset suggests vascular or metabolic cause
feat: Generalised or orofacial–limb chorea beginning after about age 60
No dementia, psychiatric disturbance or family history
Slow or no progression
A diagnosis of exclusion: many historical cases later proved to be Huntington disease
inv: HTT CAG repeat testing even without family history
Glucose, HbA1c, calcium, thyroid, liver/renal function, polycythaemia screen, ANA/antiphospholipid
MRI brain for strokes, basal ganglia T1 hyperintensity (hyperglycaemia) or other lesions; drug review

case.story: Restless fidgety movements of hands and face for one year; no family history; on no regular drugs.
case.exam: Mild generalised chorea, normal cognition and saccades, no parkinsonism.
case.tests: Glucose, thyroid, calcium, blood count, autoimmune screen normal; MRI only mild small-vessel change; HTT 18/20 repeats.
case.q: Can this be labelled senile chorea?
case.a: Yes, provisionally, after Huntington disease and metabolic, drug, vascular and autoimmune causes are excluded; keep under review.

det.patho: Senile chorea is a descriptive label, not a defined pathology. Older reports implicated striatal neuronal loss or vascular change, but genetic testing has shown that a sizeable share were actually Huntington disease with intermediate or reduced-penetrance repeats. The true frequency of a distinct idiopathic disorder is uncertain.
det.clinical: Chorea begins in late life, is often mild and may involve face and limbs. Cognitive and psychiatric changes are absent by definition. Progression is slow. Subsequent onset of dementia or behavioural change should prompt reassessment.
det.diagnosis: Work-up aims to exclude treatable or genetic causes: Huntington disease, hyperglycaemia, hyperthyroidism, polycythaemia vera, autoimmune and paraneoplastic disease, drugs and vascular lesions. Only when these are negative is the label used. Genetic counselling must precede HD testing even in the elderly because results affect relatives.
det.treatment: Many patients need no treatment. If movements are bothersome, low-dose tetrabenazine or an atypical antipsychotic can be used, watching for parkinsonism, depression and falls. Address fall risk and reassurance.
det.prognosis: Generally benign with little disability, unless an alternative cause emerges.
pearls: No family history does not exclude Huntington disease in old age.
Always check glucose; hyperglycaemic chorea is common in elderly Asian women.
The term is best reserved for a thoroughly investigated patient.
det.thd: Senile chorea คือ chorea ที่เริ่มในผู้สูงอายุโดยไม่มีสาเหตุและไม่มีประวัติครอบครัว ไม่มีสมองเสื่อม เป็นการวินิจฉัยหลังตัดสาเหตุอื่นออกหมด เช่น Huntington's disease, น้ำตาลสูง, ไทรอยด์, ยา และหลอดเลือด ส่วนใหญ่อาการไม่รุนแรงและไม่ต้องรักษา ถ้ารบกวนอาจใช้ tetrabenazine ขนาดต่ำ

ddx.pt: Late-onset HD with reduced penetrance alleles may lack family history; confirm with CAG testing
Levodopa, antipsychotics, anticonvulsants, oestrogen and stimulants
Non-ketotic hyperglycaemia or small stroke in elderly, usually one-sided and abrupt

name: Sensorimotor polyneuropathy
formal: Generalised length-dependent mixed nerve disease causing distal weakness and sensory loss, from metabolic, toxic, hereditary or inflammatory causes.
simple: Widespread nerve damage causing weakness and numbness, usually starting in the feet.
more: Nerve conduction shows reduced sensory and motor amplitudes with mild slowing in axonal types; the sural response is lost first. Look for treatable causes: glucose, B12, thyroid function, SPEP and medication review, and treat the cause. Peripheral nerve disorder affecting both motor and sensory fibres, from diabetes, Charcot-Marie-Tooth, toxins or inflammation.
th: เส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเสียแบบสมมาตรและขึ้นกับความยาว ทำให้ชาและอ่อนแรงปลายเท้าก่อน จากเมตาบอลิก สารพิษ พันธุกรรม หรือการอักเสบ
tempoNote: Usually slow over years; a subacute course points to toxic, inflammatory, vasculitic or paraneoplastic causes
feat: Stocking-then-glove numbness, tingling or pain starting in the toes
Distal weakness (toe extensors, ankle dorsiflexion) and wasting of foot muscles
Ankle jerks lost early; reduced vibration at the toes
Commonest causes: diabetes, alcohol, B12 deficiency, drugs, CKD, hypothyroidism, paraprotein, inherited CMT
Asymmetry, proximal weakness or rapid progression suggest a different, often treatable, process
inv: First-line screen: HbA1c/OGTT, B12 (± MMA), TSH, renal and liver tests, SPEP with immunofixation
NCS: reduced sural and peroneal amplitudes (axonal) or slowed velocities (demyelinating)
Second line by clue: HIV, hepatitis, ANA/ENA, vasculitis screen, genetics, CSF, nerve biopsy

case.who: 63-year-old man in Nakhon Pathom, diabetic (type 2) for 15 years
case.story: Numb feet for three years and recently cannot feel his slippers come off; minor burns on the soles from a hot floor.

case.q: What are the two likely contributors and what is the most important preventive step?
case.a: Diabetic neuropathy compounded by metformin-related B12 deficiency; daily foot care and protective footwear to prevent ulcers, plus B12 replacement and glucose control.

det.patho: Most sensorimotor polyneuropathies are axonal: metabolic or toxic stress impairs axonal transport and energy supply, so the longest fibres degenerate first from their distal ends. Demyelinating forms reflect Schwann cell or myelin disease, inherited or immune. Microvascular disease adds to injury in diabetes.
det.clinical: Sensory symptoms usually precede weakness. As fibres shorter than leg length become involved, numbness reaches the fingertips, giving the glove-and-stocking pattern. Balance falls and painless foot injuries follow. Autonomic features may accompany diabetic, amyloid and toxic forms.
det.diagnosis: A focused history (diabetes, alcohol, drugs, family history, weight loss) and examination usually define the pattern. Basic blood tests identify the commonest treatable causes. NCS confirms neuropathy and separates axonal from demyelinating forms; atypical features prompt extended tests. Up to a quarter remain idiopathic after full evaluation, especially in older adults.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: glucose control, alcohol cessation, B12 replacement, drug withdrawal or immunotherapy where applicable. Neuropathic pain responds to duloxetine, gabapentinoids or tricyclics. Foot care, footwear, balance training and orthoses reduce disability.
det.prognosis: Idiopathic and metabolic forms usually progress slowly; treatable causes may stabilise or improve.
pearls: Check B12 in diabetics on metformin.
Proximal weakness or asymmetry is not 'just diabetic neuropathy'.
SPEP with immunofixation belongs in the first-line screen.

formal: Group of peripheral nerve disorders predominantly affecting sensation, such as small fibre neuropathy, ganglionopathy and hereditary sensory neuropathies.
simple: Nerve diseases mainly causing numbness, tingling or pain.

Small fibre type: burning pain and temperature loss; large fibre type: sensory ataxia, pseudoathetosis, areflexia

det.patho: Sensory neuropathies arise from damage to distal sensory axons (length-dependent) or to dorsal root ganglion cell bodies (ganglionopathy). Ganglion neurons lack a full blood–nerve barrier, so toxins, antibodies and T cells reach them easily. Small and large fibre involvement determines whether pain or ataxia dominates.
det.clinical: Length-dependent forms begin in the feet. Ganglionopathies start anywhere, often in the hands, face or trunk, are asymmetric, and cause disabling sensory ataxia. Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathies begin early and cause painless injuries. Weakness is minimal, which separates these from sensorimotor neuropathies.
det.diagnosis: NCS shows reduced sensory potentials with normal motor responses; diffuse absence including the arms suggests ganglionopathy. Skin biopsy assesses small fibres. Screening for diabetes, B6, chemotherapy, Sjögren, paraneoplastic antibodies, HIV and genetic causes follows the pattern and tempo.
det.treatment: Remove toxins such as excess B6 and adjust chemotherapy. Immune ganglionopathies may respond to IVIG, steroids or other immunotherapy, especially early; paraneoplastic cases need tumour treatment. Symptomatic pain treatment, balance rehabilitation and foot protection are central.
det.prognosis: Toxic forms may improve after removal of the cause; ganglionopathies often leave permanent ataxia because neurons do not regenerate.
pearls: Absent radial sensory response with normal sural suggests non-length-dependent ganglionopathy.
Pseudoathetosis signals severe proprioceptive loss.
Ask about vitamin B6 supplements.
det.thd: Sensory neuropathies คือกลุ่มโรคเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายที่เด่นด้านความรู้สึก กำลังกล้ามเนื้อมักปกติ แบ่งเป็นชนิดขึ้นกับความยาว (เริ่มที่เท้า) และ ganglionopathy (ไม่สมมาตร เริ่มที่มือหรือหน้า และเดินเซจากเสีย proprioception) สาเหตุได้แก่ เบาหวาน วิตามิน B6 เกิน ยาเคมีบำบัด Sjögren และ paraneoplastic anti-Hu การตรวจ NCS พบ sensory response ลดลงแต่ motor ปกติ รักษาตามสาเหตุ

name: Septic encephalopathy
formal: Diffuse brain dysfunction accompanying systemic infection without direct CNS infection, via inflammation and impaired perfusion, causing delirium and EEG slowing.
simple: Confusion or drowsiness caused by severe body-wide infection.
th: สมองทำงานผิดปกติทั่วไปจากภาวะติดเชื้อในกระแสเลือด โดยไม่มีการติดเชื้อในสมองโดยตรง ทำให้สับสน ซึม หรือ delirium
tempoNote: Develops over hours to days with sepsis; usually reversible as infection resolves
feat: Inattention, fluctuating confusion, agitation or reduced consciousness during sepsis
Often precedes other organ failure; may be the first sign of sepsis in elderly
No focal signs or meningism; multifocal myoclonus or asterixis possible
Associated critical illness neuropathy/myopathy in prolonged ICU stay
Long-term cognitive impairment in survivors
inv: Exclude direct CNS infection (LP if meningism or no clear source), hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hepatic or uraemic factors, drugs
EEG: diffuse slowing or triphasic waves; exclude non-convulsive status
CT/MRI if focal signs or not improving (septic emboli, PRES, infarcts)
Delirium screening tools such as CAM-ICU

case.q: What explains the confusion and what is the treatment?

det.patho: Systemic inflammation affects the brain via cytokine signalling across circumventricular organs and the vagus, endothelial activation and blood–brain barrier leak, microglial activation, impaired microcirculation and neurotransmitter imbalance. Hypotension, hypoxaemia, metabolic derangements and sedatives compound injury. Ischaemic and haemorrhagic microlesions may be found at autopsy.
det.clinical: It ranges from subtle inattention to delirium and coma, typically without focal signs. It is common in ICU sepsis and is linked to higher mortality. Many survivors have lasting deficits in memory, attention and executive function, sometimes described as post-intensive care syndrome.
det.diagnosis: It is a diagnosis of exclusion in a septic patient with altered mental state. Rule out meningitis or encephalitis, metabolic and drug causes, Wernicke encephalopathy and non-convulsive seizures. EEG grading correlates with severity. Imaging is reserved for focal signs, seizures or failure to improve.
det.treatment: Management is control of infection and haemodynamic support. Minimise benzodiazepines, prefer light sedation and use non-drug delirium measures (orientation, sleep hygiene, early mobilisation). Correct glucose, sodium and other abnormalities. There is no specific neuroprotective drug proven to help.
det.prognosis: Usually improves with sepsis resolution, but severity predicts mortality and long-term cognitive decline.
pearls: New confusion in an older patient can be the first sign of sepsis.
Always exclude non-convulsive status with EEG when consciousness fails to improve.
Benzodiazepines worsen delirium; reduce them where possible.
det.thd: Septic encephalopathy คือสมองทำงานผิดปกติจากภาวะติดเชื้อในกระแสเลือด โดยไม่มีเชื้อในสมอง เกิดจากการอักเสบทั่วร่างกาย เลือดไปเลี้ยงสมองลดลง และ blood–brain barrier เสีย อาการคือสับสน ซึม หรือ delirium ไม่มีอาการเฉพาะที่ ต้องแยก meningitis, ความผิดปกติเกลือแร่, ยา และ NCSE การรักษาคือคุมการติดเชื้อ แก้ระบบไหลเวียน และลดยานอนหลับ

det.patho: Spondyloarthropathies are immune-mediated diseases linked to HLA-B27 and the IL-23/IL-17 axis, inflaming entheses, sacroiliac joints and the spine. Repeated inflammation leads to new bone formation and ankylosis, creating a long rigid lever that fractures easily. Chronic arachnoiditis and dural ectasia underlie the late cauda equina syndrome.
det.clinical: This is primarily a rheumatological disease; neurology becomes involved through complications. Fractures of the ankylosed spine follow trivial trauma and are often unstable and missed, with risk of delayed cord injury from epidural haematoma. Atlantoaxial subluxation causes neck pain and myelopathy. Insidious cauda equina syndrome with sphincter problems and sacral sensory loss occurs in long-standing disease.
det.diagnosis: Inflammatory back pain with sacroiliitis on MRI and HLA-B27 supports the rheumatic diagnosis. Any neck or back pain after trauma in a patient with AS warrants CT of the entire spine because non-contiguous fractures are common. MRI identifies cord compression, haematoma and dural ectasia.
det.treatment: The arthropathy is treated with NSAIDs and biologics (TNF or IL-17 inhibitors). Fractures need careful immobilisation in the patient's usual posture (not forced straight) and usually surgical fixation. Atlantoaxial instability may require fusion. Treatment options for cauda equina syndrome from dural ectasia are limited; surgery is debated.
det.prognosis: Rheumatic disease is controlled well with biologics; spinal fractures carry high rates of neurological injury and mortality in older patients.
pearls: Treat the AS spine like a long bone: minor trauma can cause unstable fractures.
Do not straighten a kyphotic neck when immobilising.
Slow cauda equina syndrome in old AS suggests dural ectasia.

name: Serotonin syndrome
formal: Drug-induced hyperserotonergic toxicity with hyperthermia, clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor and agitation, typically after combining serotonergic drugs.
simple: A dangerous reaction to excess serotonin from medicines, causing fever, agitation, tremor and muscle jerks.
more: Excess serotonergic activity causing hyperthermia, clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor and agitation, usually after serotonergic drug combinations.
th: Serotonin syndrome คือภาวะพิษจาก serotonin มากเกินไปจากยาเพียงตัวเดียวหรือหลายตัวร่วมกัน ภายในไม่กี่ชั่วโมงหลังเริ่มหรือเพิ่มยา ผู้ป่วยกระสับกระส่าย เหงื่อออก มือสั่น รีเฟล็กซ์ไว clonus ที่ขามากกว่าแขน และในรายรุนแรงมีไข้สูงและกล้ามเนื้อแข็ง วินิจฉัยด้วยเกณฑ์ Hunter และรักษาโดยหยุดยา ให้ benzodiazepine และ cyproheptadine

feat: Triad of neuromuscular excitation (clonus, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, tremor, rigidity), autonomic hyperactivity (sweating, fever, tachycardia, diarrhoea, dilated pupils) and mental change (agitation, confusion)
Inducible, spontaneous or ocular clonus is the most useful sign; findings are usually worse in the legs than the arms
Triggered by a combination of serotonergic agents, such as SSRIs or SNRIs with tramadol, pethidine, linezolid, triptans, dextromethorphan, ondansetron, MAOIs or methylene blue
Also follows overdose of a single drug, recreational MDMA or amphetamines, and herbal products such as St John's wort
Severe cases reach temperature above 41 °C, truncal rigidity, rhabdomyolysis, seizures, acidosis and DIC
inv: Clinical diagnosis by Hunter criteria after a full drug history including over-the-counter, herbal and recreational agents; no confirmatory blood test
CK, renal function, electrolytes, blood gases, coagulation screen and ECG for moderate and severe cases
Cultures, CSF if meningitis is possible, and toxicology to exclude infection, anticholinergic toxicity, NMS, malignant hyperthermia, thyroid storm and withdrawal

case.tests: CK 600 U/L, white count normal, urine toxicology negative; ECG sinus tachycardia.
case.q: What are the diagnosis and immediate steps?

det.patho: Serotonin toxicity arises from excess stimulation of serotonin receptors in the brainstem, spinal cord and periphery, with the 5-HT2A and 5-HT1A receptors most implicated. Drugs may raise serotonin by increasing its synthesis or release, blocking its reuptake, or preventing its breakdown by monoamine oxidase. The commonest dangerous pairing is an MAO inhibitor, including linezolid, selegiline and methylene blue, with another serotonergic agent. Fluoxetine and its metabolite persist for days to weeks, so a washout of about 5 weeks is advised before starting an MAOI, and 2 weeks after stopping an irreversible MAOI.
det.clinical: Onset is rapid, typically within 6 hours of the culprit change, and mild cases show tremor, hyperreflexia and diarrhoea. Moderate cases add clonus, agitation and a temperature around 38–39 °C. In severe illness the temperature rises above 41 °C, truncal rigidity develops and the patient may need paralysis and ventilation. The book also described Parkinson patients on levodopa, selegiline and an antidepressant, and migraine patients on triptans together with an antidepressant. Children and patients with HIV on interacting protease inhibitors are particularly vulnerable.
det.diagnosis: Use the Hunter criteria, which require exposure to a serotonergic drug plus one of: spontaneous clonus; inducible clonus with agitation or sweating; ocular clonus with agitation or sweating; tremor with hyperreflexia; or hypertonia with fever above 38 °C and clonus. They are more accurate than the older Sternbach criteria that the book used. Because rigidity can hide clonus, examine the legs carefully. Tests exclude other causes rather than confirm the syndrome.
det.treatment: Stop every serotonergic drug, give oxygen, intravenous fluids, cardiac monitoring and benzodiazepines for agitation and muscle activity. Active external cooling is required for fever, but antipyretics are ineffective because the heat comes from muscle. If benzodiazepines are not enough, cyproheptadine is given orally or by nasogastric tube, commonly 12 mg first and then 2 mg every 2 hours while symptoms continue, with 8 mg every 6 hours for maintenance. For temperatures above about 41 °C, use sedation, a non-depolarising neuromuscular blocker and ventilation, and avoid suxamethonium. Chlorpromazine and methysergide, mentioned in the book, are no longer favoured, and dantrolene and bromocriptine are not recommended.
det.prognosis: Mild and moderate cases usually resolve within 24 hours after stopping the drugs, and deaths are uncommon with prompt care. Syndromes involving long-acting agents or MAOIs last longer.
pearls: Clonus, especially ocular or ankle clonus, is the sign to look for; hyperreflexia in the legs is typical.
Onset in hours with a serotonergic drug separates it from NMS, which evolves over days.
Do not treat the fever with paracetamol alone; cool the patient and relax the muscles.
det.thd: Serotonin syndrome เกิดจากยาที่เพิ่ม serotonin เช่น SSRI ร่วมกับ tramadol, pethidine, linezolid หรือ MAOI ภายในไม่กี่ชั่วโมง ผู้ป่วยกระสับกระส่าย เหงื่อออก ท้องเสีย มือสั่น รีเฟล็กซ์ไว และมี clonus โดยเฉพาะที่ขา ถ้ารุนแรงจะมีไข้สูง กล้ามเนื้อแข็งและ rhabdomyolysis วินิจฉัยตามเกณฑ์ Hunter ไม่มีการตรวจเลือดยืนยัน การรักษาคือหยุดยาที่เกี่ยวข้อง ให้น้ำ ให้ benzodiazepine ลดความร้อนจากภายนอก และให้ cyproheptadine ถ้าอาการไม่ดีขึ้น รายรุนแรงต้องใช้ยาหย่อนกล้ามเนื้อและเครื่องช่วยหายใจ

qx.stem: A 45-year-old man from Buriram taking sertraline for depression is given tramadol after a motorcycle injury. Six hours later he is agitated and sweaty with diarrhoea, temperature 38.9 °C and pulse 126. His pupils are dilated, both ankles show sustained clonus and there is inducible ocular clonus. Leg reflexes are brisker than arm reflexes and tone is mildly raised. CK is 450 U/L.
qx.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Give dantrolene and bromocriptine as for neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Stop tramadol and sertraline, give fluids, benzodiazepines and active cooling, and add cyproheptadine if signs persist
Give paracetamol alone and observe on the ward
Administer haloperidol for the agitation
Start intravenous methylprednisolone
qx.why: Serotonergic drug combination, onset within hours, clonus and hyperreflexia worse in the legs meet the Hunter criteria for serotonin syndrome. Treatment is withdrawal of all serotonergic drugs, supportive care, benzodiazepines and external cooling, with cyproheptadine as a serotonin antagonist if this is not enough. Dantrolene and bromocriptine are used for NMS and can worsen serotonin toxicity, antipyretics do not work because the heat comes from muscle, haloperidol blocks dopamine and may cause harm, and steroids have no role.
