name: Sex headache
formal: Primary headache related to sexual activity, either preorgasmic dull ache or explosive orgasmic headache; thunderclap onset requires exclusion of subarachnoid haemorrhage.
simple: A headache that comes on during sex, sometimes suddenly and severe.
ab: Primary headache associated with sexual activity
th: ปวดศีรษะชนิดปฐมภูมิที่สัมพันธ์กับกิจกรรมทางเพศ อาจปวดตื้อก่อนถึงจุดสุดยอดหรือปวดระเบิดทันทีขณะถึงจุดสุดยอด ต้องแยก SAH และ RCVS ก่อน
tempoNote: Attacks last minutes to hours; often occur in clusters over weeks to months, then remit
feat: Dull bilateral head and neck ache rising with sexual excitement (preorgasmic type)
Sudden explosive headache at or just before orgasm (orgasmic type)
More common in men; association with migraine and exertional headache
First explosive attack must be investigated for SAH, RCVS and dissection
inv: First attack or thunderclap: CT brain, then LP if CT normal
CTA or MRA to look for aneurysm, dissection or segmental vasoconstriction (repeat if early study normal)

case.story: Three times in two weeks a sudden intense occipital headache began at orgasm, peaked within seconds and eased over an hour.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination, BP 135/85.
case.tests: CT brain and CSF normal; CTA on day 3 shows no aneurysm; repeat MRA at two weeks normal without vasoconstriction.
case.q: What is the diagnosis after this work-up, and what preventive option exists?
case.a: Primary headache associated with sexual activity (orgasmic type); indomethacin taken before sexual activity or a short course of propranolol.

read.where: Chapter 40: Primary cough headache, primary exertional headache, and primary headache associated with sexual activity

det.patho: The mechanism is uncertain; proposed factors include excessive contraction of head and neck muscles in the preorgasmic type and sudden surges in blood pressure and sympathetic tone at orgasm. Overlap with RCVS suggests some cases involve transient dysregulation of cerebral vascular tone.
det.clinical: Attacks are typically bilateral or occipital, last from a minute to several hours, and recur with subsequent sexual activity during a bout that may last weeks. Many patients then remain free for months or years. Persistent headache, vomiting, focal signs or altered consciousness suggest a secondary cause.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 requires headache caused by and occurring only during sexual activity, with no better explanation. Any first sudden attack demands exclusion of SAH, RCVS, dissection and pituitary apoplexy. Recurrent identical attacks after a full normal work-up can be managed as the primary disorder, but repeated thunderclaps within days should prompt repeat vascular imaging for RCVS.
det.treatment: Reassure and suggest temporary abstinence or a less strenuous role during a bout. Indomethacin 25–50 mg taken an hour before sexual activity, or daily propranolol during bouts, is commonly used. Triptans are generally avoided if RCVS is a possibility. Treat associated migraine.
det.prognosis: Benign; most bouts remit within months, though recurrence is possible.
pearls: First explosive headache with sex is SAH until proven otherwise.
Clusters of thunderclap headaches with sex or effort raise suspicion of RCVS.
Indomethacin before sexual activity is a practical preventive.
det.thd: Sex headache คือปวดศีรษะชนิดปฐมภูมิที่เกิดขณะมีเพศสัมพันธ์ มีสองแบบคือปวดตื้อค่อย ๆ เพิ่มก่อนถึงจุดสุดยอด และปวดระเบิดทันทีขณะถึงจุดสุดยอด ครั้งแรกต้องแยก SAH, RCVS และ dissection ด้วย CT, LP และตรวจหลอดเลือด ถ้าผลปกติอาจป้องกันด้วย indomethacin ก่อนกิจกรรมหรือ propranolol ส่วนใหญ่หายเองในไม่กี่เดือน

name: Sheehan syndrome
formal: Postpartum pituitary necrosis after haemorrhage with hypopituitarism, causing failure of lactation, amenorrhoea and fatigue.
simple: Pituitary gland damage after heavy bleeding in childbirth, causing hormone shortages.
th: ต่อมใต้สมองตายจากขาดเลือดหลังตกเลือดมากขณะคลอด ทำให้ไม่มีน้ำนม ไม่มีประจำเดือน อ่อนเพลีย และอาจมีภาวะ adrenal insufficiency หรือโซเดียมต่ำ
tempoNote: Rarely acute collapse after delivery; usually recognised months to years later with progressive hormone deficiency
feat: Endocrine rather than primary neurological disorder
History of severe postpartum haemorrhage with hypotension or transfusion
Failure of lactation and absent return of menses; loss of axillary and pubic hair
Fatigue, cold intolerance, hypotension, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia
May present to neurology with confusion, seizures from hyponatraemia, or coma
inv: Morning cortisol and ACTH, free T4 and TSH (low or inappropriately normal TSH), prolactin, LH, FSH, estradiol, IGF-1
Electrolytes (sodium) and glucose
MRI pituitary: enlarged gland acutely, later partial or complete empty sella

case.story: Severe bleeding after a home delivery two years ago needed four units of blood; she never breastfed and has had no periods since. Now brought in confused after a week of vomiting.
case.exam: Drowsy, pale, BP 85/50, sparse axillary hair.
case.tests: Sodium 116 mmol/L, glucose 2.8 mmol/L, cortisol 40 nmol/L with low ACTH, low free T4 with normal TSH; MRI: empty sella.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and which hormone must be replaced first?
case.a: Sheehan syndrome with secondary adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism; give hydrocortisone before thyroxine to avoid adrenal crisis.

det.patho: The pituitary enlarges during pregnancy and depends on a low-pressure portal blood supply. Severe obstetric haemorrhage with hypotension and vasospasm causes ischaemic necrosis of the anterior lobe; small sella size and coagulopathy may add risk. Posterior pituitary function is usually spared, although partial diabetes insipidus occurs.
det.clinical: Acute cases present with lactation failure, hypotension and hypoglycaemia soon after delivery. More often, deficiency of growth hormone, gonadotrophins, TSH and ACTH accumulates silently and is found years later, sometimes when an illness provokes adrenal crisis. Neurological presentations include confusion, seizures from hyponatraemia or hypoglycaemia, and hypothyroid myopathy.
det.diagnosis: Combine obstetric history with low pituitary hormone levels; dynamic tests (ACTH stimulation, insulin tolerance or glucagon tests) confirm partial deficits. MRI shows an empty or small sella in chronic cases. Exclude other sellar lesions.
det.treatment: Replace glucocorticoid first, then thyroxine, then sex hormones and, if appropriate, growth hormone. Teach sick-day steroid rules and provide emergency hydrocortisone. Correct hyponatraemia cautiously to avoid osmotic demyelination. Prevention relies on good obstetric care for haemorrhage.
det.prognosis: With lifelong replacement, prognosis is good; undiagnosed cases risk fatal adrenal crisis.
pearls: Ask every woman with hyponatraemia or hypoglycaemia about past postpartum haemorrhage and lactation.
Low free T4 with normal TSH points to central hypothyroidism.
Steroid before thyroxine.
det.thd: Sheehan syndrome คือต่อมใต้สมองส่วนหน้าตายจากขาดเลือดหลังตกเลือดมากขณะคลอด ทำให้ไม่มีน้ำนม ไม่มีประจำเดือน อ่อนเพลีย ความดันต่ำ น้ำตาลต่ำ และโซเดียมต่ำ อาจมาด้วยสับสนหรือชัก ตรวจฮอร์โมนต่อมใต้สมองและ MRI พบ empty sella รักษาด้วยการให้ฮอร์โมนทดแทน โดยให้ hydrocortisone ก่อน thyroxine

name: Shellfish poisoning
formal: Marine toxin intoxications including paralytic (saxitoxin), neurotoxic and amnesic (domoic acid) syndromes with paraesthesia, weakness, respiratory failure or memory loss.
simple: Poisoning from eating contaminated shellfish, causing tingling, weakness or memory loss.
th: พิษจากหอยที่สะสมสารพิษจากสาหร่าย ทำให้ชารอบปาก อ่อนแรง หายใจล้มเหลว หรือความจำเสื่อม แล้วแต่ชนิดของพิษ
tempoNote: Onset minutes to hours after eating; paralysis peaks within 12 hours and recovers over days
feat: Paralytic (saxitoxin): perioral and limb tingling, floating feeling, ataxia, bulbar and respiratory paralysis within hours
Neurotoxic (brevetoxin): paraesthesia, temperature reversal, GI upset, no paralysis
Amnesic (domoic acid): vomiting then confusion, seizures and lasting anterograde amnesia
Several people sharing the same seafood meal; outbreaks with algal blooms (red tide)
Cooking does not destroy the toxins
inv: Clinical diagnosis with dietary history; notify public health
Toxin assay of leftover shellfish (and sometimes urine) in reference laboratories
Monitor vital capacity and blood gases; NCS may show reduced amplitudes in saxitoxin
MRI and EEG in amnesic form (hippocampal injury)

case.who: Three members of a family from Chonburi
case.story: After eating mussels from a roadside stall, within an hour they had numb lips and fingers; the father now has slurred speech and breathlessness.
case.exam: Father: dysarthria, bilateral facial and limb weakness, reduced reflexes, normal pupils, vital capacity falling.
case.tests: Glucose and electrolytes normal; leftover mussels test positive for saxitoxin.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the priority?
case.a: Paralytic shellfish poisoning; respiratory support (ventilation) until the toxin clears, usually within 24–72 hours.

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Shellfish

det.patho: Filter-feeding bivalves concentrate toxins produced by dinoflagellates or diatoms. Saxitoxin and its analogues block voltage-gated sodium channels in nerve and muscle, similar to tetrodotoxin from pufferfish. Brevetoxin opens sodium channels, while domoic acid is a glutamate analogue that excites kainate receptors and damages the hippocampus. The toxins are heat stable.
det.clinical: Paralytic poisoning starts with perioral tingling spreading to limbs, then ataxia, dysarthria, dysphagia and flaccid weakness, with respiratory failure in severe cases while consciousness is often preserved. Neurotoxic poisoning is milder with paraesthesia and gastrointestinal symptoms. Amnesic poisoning, recognised after a Canadian outbreak, causes gastrointestinal upset, confusion, seizures, coma and permanent memory loss in older adults.
det.diagnosis: History of recent shellfish ingestion and similar illness in co-diners is usually sufficient. Laboratory toxin assays confirm but take time. Differentials include pufferfish tetrodotoxin poisoning (common concern in Thailand from horseshoe crab eggs and pufferfish), botulism, ciguatera and GBS.
det.treatment: There is no antidote. Give supportive care, observe at least 24 hours, consider activated charcoal early if the airway is protected, and ventilate for respiratory failure. Seizures in amnesic poisoning are treated with benzodiazepines and antiseizure drugs. Report to public health to prevent further cases.
det.prognosis: With timely ventilatory support, paralytic poisoning recovers fully within days; amnesic poisoning may leave lasting memory deficits.
pearls: Clusters of perioral numbness after seafood: think marine sodium channel toxin.
Patients with saxitoxin paralysis may be fully conscious while unable to breathe or speak.
Cooking or freezing does not make toxic shellfish safe.
det.thd: Shellfish poisoning คือพิษจากหอยที่สะสมสารพิษจากสาหร่าย ชนิด paralytic (saxitoxin) ปิด sodium channel ทำให้ชารอบปาก อ่อนแรง และหายใจล้มเหลวภายในชั่วโมง ชนิด amnesic (domoic acid) ทำให้ชักและความจำเสื่อม วินิจฉัยจากประวัติกินหอยและมีผู้ป่วยหลายคน ไม่มียาต้านพิษ รักษาแบบประคับประคองและใส่เครื่องช่วยหายใจจนพิษหมด

name: Short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache
formal: Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia with brief severe stabbing orbital pain and prominent lacrimation and conjunctival injection (SUNCT/SUNA).
simple: Very short, severe attacks of pain around one eye with tearing and redness.
th: TAC ชนิดหนึ่งที่มีอาการปวดแปลบรุนแรงรอบตาข้างเดียวนานเป็นวินาทีถึงไม่กี่นาที เกิดถี่มากต่อวัน ร่วมกับน้ำตาไหลและตาแดง (SUNCT) หรืออาการ autonomic อื่น (SUNA)
tempoNote: Attacks last 1–600 seconds, dozens to hundreds per day; episodic or chronic course
feat: Severe stabbing or sawtooth unilateral orbital or temporal pain lasting seconds to minutes
Very frequent attacks, often triggered by touch, chewing or washing the face
Ipsilateral conjunctival injection and tearing (SUNCT) or other autonomic signs (SUNA)
Usually no refractory period between attacks, unlike trigeminal neuralgia
Middle-aged adults; slightly more common in men
inv: MRI brain with pituitary views and trigeminal nerve high-resolution sequences
Look for pituitary tumours and neurovascular contact of the trigeminal nerve
Pituitary hormone screen if a sellar lesion is present

case.story: Up to 80 attacks a day of stabbing pain around the left eye lasting about 30 seconds, with the eye going red and watery each time; touching his face can set them off.
case.exam: During an attack: left conjunctival injection and tearing; otherwise normal.
case.tests: MRI: left trigeminal nerve contact by the superior cerebellar artery; pituitary normal.
case.q: Which drug is first-line?
case.a: SUNCT; lamotrigine is first-line prevention, with intravenous lidocaine for severe bouts.

read.where: Chapter 35: Cluster headache and other trigeminal autonomic

det.patho: Like other trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias, SUNCT/SUNA involves activation of the trigeminal-autonomic reflex with hypothalamic involvement shown on functional imaging. Neurovascular compression of the trigeminal nerve is found in a proportion and may contribute. Secondary forms occur with pituitary and posterior fossa lesions.
det.clinical: Attacks are brief, severe and very frequent, occurring as single stabs, groups of stabs or a sawtooth pattern. Cutaneous triggers are common. Autonomic signs are prominent in SUNCT and present but fewer in SUNA. There may be overlap with trigeminal neuralgia in some patients.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 criteria require at least 20 attacks of moderate to severe unilateral pain lasting 1–600 seconds, with at least one ipsilateral autonomic feature, occurring at least once a day. MRI is mandatory to exclude pituitary and posterior fossa lesions and to assess neurovascular conflict.
det.treatment: Lamotrigine is the preferred preventive; topiramate, oxcarbazepine, carbamazepine and gabapentin are alternatives. Intravenous lidocaine provides short-term control of severe flares. Occipital nerve block may help. Microvascular decompression benefits selected patients with neurovascular contact; occipital nerve or hypothalamic stimulation are reserved for refractory cases.
det.prognosis: Often chronic, but many achieve good control with prevention; remissions occur.
pearls: Very brief, very frequent attacks with a red, watery eye = SUNCT.
No refractory period distinguishes it from trigeminal neuralgia.
Lamotrigine first; indomethacin does not work.
det.thd: SUNCT/SUNA เป็นปวดศีรษะในกลุ่ม TAC ปวดแปลบรุนแรงรอบตาข้างเดียวครั้งละไม่กี่วินาทีถึงไม่กี่นาที แต่เป็นถี่มากหลายสิบถึงหลายร้อยครั้งต่อวัน ร่วมกับตาแดงและน้ำตาไหล อาจกระตุ้นได้จากการสัมผัสใบหน้า ต่างจาก trigeminal neuralgia ตรงที่ไม่มีช่วงพักหลังปวด ควรทำ MRI ดูต่อมใต้สมองและเส้นประสาท trigeminal ยาตัวแรกคือ lamotrigine

name: Sickle cell disease
formal: Haemoglobinopathy causing ischaemic stroke, silent infarcts, moyamoya-like vasculopathy and transcranial Doppler velocity elevation in children.
simple: An inherited blood disease where abnormal red blood cells can block brain arteries and cause stroke.
th: โรคเม็ดเลือดแดงรูปเคียว (HbSS) — เด็กเสี่ยง stroke สูง จากหลอดเลือดใหญ่ตีบ (ICA ปลาย/MCA) และ silent infarct คัดกรองด้วย TCD และป้องกันด้วยการให้เลือดสม่ำเสมอ
tempoNote: Strokes are acute events on a lifelong background; silent infarcts accumulate silently through childhood
feat: Ischaemic stroke peaks in children 2–9 years old with HbSS; haemorrhagic stroke more often in young adults
Steno-occlusive disease of the distal ICA and proximal MCA/ACA, sometimes with moyamoya collaterals
Silent cerebral infarcts in deep white matter causing learning and attention problems
Triggers: acute chest syndrome, severe anaemia, dehydration, infection, recent transfusion
Other neurological issues: headache, seizures, cerebral venous thrombosis, aneurysms
inv: Transcranial Doppler yearly from age 2 to 16: time-averaged mean maximum velocity ≥200 cm/s in ICA/MCA = high stroke risk
Acute stroke: MRI/MRA, full blood count, reticulocytes and HbS percentage
Haemoglobin electrophoresis/HPLC if genotype unknown

case.who: 7-year-old boy with HbSS, attending a regional hospital in Ubon Ratchathani
case.story: Woke up unable to lift his right arm and with slurred words after two days of fever and cough.
case.exam: Right hemiparesis with facial weakness, expressive aphasia; SpO2 92%, crackles at the left base.
case.tests: Hb 6.4 g/dL, HbS 88%; MRI: left MCA territory infarct; MRA: narrowing of the left terminal ICA.
case.q: What is the urgent treatment and how is recurrence prevented?
case.a: Exchange transfusion to bring HbS below 30% (with total Hb about 10 g/dL); then long-term transfusion programme (and hydroxyurea, or haematopoietic stem cell transplant where feasible).

read.where: Chapter 14 Stroke in children and young adults
Chapter 7 Unusual causes of ischemic stroke and transient ischemic attack
Section 3 Hereditary and Genetic Conditions and Malformations
Chapter 11: Neurological complications of red blood cell disorders

det.patho: A single substitution in the beta-globin gene produces HbS, which polymerises when deoxygenated, making red cells rigid and sickle-shaped. Chronic haemolysis depletes nitric oxide, and adhesive cells injure endothelium, leading to intimal hyperplasia of large intracranial arteries and small-vessel ischaemia. Anaemia raises cerebral blood flow and lowers reserve, so border-zone regions are vulnerable. The disease is most frequent in people of African, Middle Eastern and Indian ancestry; in Thailand haemoglobin E and thalassaemia are far more common.
det.clinical: Without screening, about one in ten children with HbSS has an overt stroke by age 20, and over a third accumulate silent infarcts. Strokes present with hemiparesis, aphasia or seizures, sometimes triggered by acute chest syndrome or aplastic crisis. Adults have more haemorrhagic strokes from moyamoya collaterals or aneurysms. Cognitive impairment, headache and posterior reversible encephalopathy after transfusion or steroids are also seen.
det.diagnosis: Confirm the genotype with haemoglobin HPLC or electrophoresis. Children need annual TCD screening; abnormal or conditional velocities guide transfusion. Acute focal deficits require urgent MRI with diffusion and MRA, and a blood count with HbS percentage. Consider screening MRI for silent infarcts at least once in school-age children.
det.treatment: Acute ischaemic stroke: urgent exchange transfusion (simple transfusion if exchange is delayed), oxygen, hydration and treatment of infection; adults may follow standard reperfusion pathways alongside transfusion. Secondary prevention is chronic transfusion keeping HbS below about 30% with iron chelation; hydroxyurea can replace transfusion in selected children with abnormal TCD after vessel normalisation. Stem cell transplantation, and newer gene-based therapies, offer cure in suitable patients. Revascularisation surgery may be considered for progressive moyamoya.
det.prognosis: Without transfusion, recurrence after a first childhood stroke is very high (over half); TCD screening with transfusion has cut first-stroke rates by about 90%.
pearls: TCD velocity ≥200 cm/s = start regular transfusion (STOP trial logic).
Exchange transfusion, not thrombolysis alone, is the cornerstone in a child with SCD stroke.
Over-transfusing to high haematocrit raises viscosity and can itself cause stroke.
det.thd: โรคเม็ดเลือดแดงรูปเคียว (HbSS) ทำให้เม็ดเลือดแดงแข็งและทำลายผนังหลอดเลือด เด็กเสี่ยงเป็น stroke จากหลอดเลือดใหญ่ในสมองตีบ และมี silent infarct ที่ทำให้การเรียนรู้แย่ลง คัดกรองด้วย transcranial Doppler ทุกปี เมื่อเป็น stroke ต้องให้ exchange transfusion ลด HbS ต่ำกว่า 30% และให้เลือดต่อเนื่องเพื่อป้องกันการกลับเป็นซ้ำ ในประเทศไทยพบน้อยกว่าธาลัสซีเมีย

qx.stem: A 7-year-old Thai-Lao boy with haemoglobin S and beta-thalassaemia is being followed for a transfusion programme. Transcranial Doppler shows a time-averaged mean maximal velocity of 215 cm/s in the right middle cerebral artery, confirmed on a second occasion. He has had no clinical stroke.
qx.q: Which intervention best lowers his risk of first stroke?
opts: Aspirin 75 mg daily
Warfarin with INR 2 to 3
Intravenous alteplase at the first symptom
Observation with repeat Doppler in 5 years
Regular exchange or simple transfusion to keep HbS below a target level, or hydroxyurea where transfusion is not feasible
qx.why: Two TCD velocities above 200 cm/s denote high stroke risk, and chronic transfusion lowered the risk of first stroke substantially in trial evidence; hydroxyurea is an accepted alternative when transfusion is impractical. Antiplatelets and anticoagulants are not proven, and Doppler should be repeated far sooner than five years.

name: Silent intracerebral haemorrhage
formal: Asymptomatic microbleeds or small intracerebral haemorrhages found incidentally on MRI, marking small vessel disease or amyloid angiopathy.
simple: Small bleeds in the brain that cause no symptoms and are found on scans.
th: จุดเลือดออกเล็ก ๆ ในสมองที่ไม่มีอาการ ตรวจพบโดยบังเอิญใน MRI (SWI/GRE) บ่งบอกโรคหลอดเลือดสมองขนาดเล็กหรือ cerebral amyloid angiopathy
tempoNote: Accumulate silently over years; number tends to increase with age and blood pressure
feat: Small round dark dots (2–10 mm) on SWI or T2* GRE MRI without matching symptoms
Deep (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons) location suggests hypertensive arteriolosclerosis
Strictly lobar or cortical location suggests cerebral amyloid angiopathy
Often coexists with lacunes, white matter hyperintensities and cortical superficial siderosis
Marker of future ICH and ischaemic stroke risk and of cognitive decline
inv: MRI with SWI or GRE; count and map microbleeds (Boston criteria 2.0 for CAA)
Blood pressure monitoring; review antithrombotic and anticoagulant use
Before anti-amyloid therapy: microbleed and siderosis screening (ARIA risk)

case.story: MRI done for mild memory complaints; no history of stroke. She takes aspirin for primary prevention.
case.exam: MoCA 24/30, otherwise normal.
case.tests: SWI: 14 strictly lobar microbleeds and focal cortical superficial siderosis; moderate white matter changes.
case.q: What underlying disease is likely and what medication decision follows?
case.a: Probable cerebral amyloid angiopathy; stop aspirin since it was for primary prevention, control blood pressure, and avoid anticoagulation unless strongly indicated.

det.patho: Microbleeds are small collections of haemosiderin-laden macrophages around fragile small vessels. Deep bleeds arise from hypertensive lipohyalinosis of penetrating arterioles; lobar ones from amyloid-beta deposition in cortical and leptomeningeal vessels. Both reflect vessel wall weakness that can also cause larger haemorrhage.
det.clinical: By definition they are asymptomatic, but many patients have cognitive impairment, gait slowing or a history of lacunar stroke. Larger silent haemorrhages are sometimes discovered as old slit-like cavities. In CAA, cortical superficial siderosis may cause transient focal neurological episodes (amyloid spells).
det.diagnosis: SWI is more sensitive than GRE. Distinguish mimics: calcification, flow voids, cavernous malformations and haemorrhagic metastases. Distribution guides aetiology, and the Boston 2.0 criteria use lobar microbleeds, siderosis and white matter features to diagnose probable CAA. A high count, especially more than 10, signals higher bleeding risk.
det.treatment: There is no treatment for the microbleeds themselves. Control blood pressure firmly, avoid unnecessary antiplatelet or anticoagulant drugs, and reconsider anticoagulation case by case in atrial fibrillation; left atrial appendage occlusion is an option in high-risk cases. Microbleeds are not a contraindication to IV thrombolysis when few, but very high burden raises bleeding risk.
det.prognosis: They predict recurrent stroke (both haemorrhagic and ischaemic) and cognitive decline; risk rises with number and lobar distribution.
pearls: Lobar microbleeds in an older adult: think CAA; deep ones: think hypertension.
Screen for microbleeds before starting lecanemab or donanemab.
Microbleeds alone should not stop indicated secondary prevention for ischaemic stroke.
det.thd: Silent intracerebral haemorrhage หรือ cerebral microbleeds คือจุดเลือดออกเล็ก ๆ ที่ไม่มีอาการ พบใน MRI แบบ SWI/GRE ถ้าอยู่ลึกบ่งบอกความดันสูง ถ้าอยู่ที่ผิวสมองบ่งบอก CAA เป็นตัวบ่งชี้ความเสี่ยงเลือดออกในสมอง stroke และสมองเสื่อม การดูแลคือคุมความดัน ทบทวนความจำเป็นของยาต้านเกล็ดเลือดและยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือด และตรวจก่อนให้ยา anti-amyloid

name: Simple tics
formal: Brief sudden stereotyped movements or sounds such as blinking or sniffing, characteristic of Tourette syndrome and preceded by premonitory urge.
simple: Short, sudden movements or sounds like eye blinking or throat clearing.
th: ติกแบบง่าย เป็นการเคลื่อนไหวหรือเสียงสั้น ๆ ซ้ำ ๆ เช่น กะพริบตา ยักไหล่ กระแอม มักมีความรู้สึกอยากทำก่อนและกลั้นได้ชั่วคราว
tempoNote: Begin in childhood, wax and wane over weeks to months; many fade by adulthood
feat: Brief, sudden, repetitive movements of one muscle group (blinking, grimacing, head jerk, shoulder shrug)
Simple phonic tics: sniffing, throat clearing, grunting, coughing
Premonitory urge and temporary suppressibility with rebound
Fluctuate in type and severity; worse with stress, excitement or tiredness, better with focused activity
May occur alone (provisional tic disorder) or as part of Tourette syndrome
inv: Clinical diagnosis; video from home is helpful
Screen for ADHD, OCD, anxiety and learning problems
Investigations only if atypical (late onset, abrupt, neurological signs): consider EEG, MRI, drug review

case.story: For four months frequent eye blinking and sniffing; teacher worries about allergy. He says he feels an itch in his eyes before blinking and can stop for a while in class.
case.exam: Repeated forceful blinks and nose wrinkling during the interview, otherwise normal neurological examination.
case.tests: None required; ophthalmology and allergy review normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the first-line approach?
case.a: Simple motor and phonic tics (provisional tic disorder); education and reassurance, behavioural therapy (CBIT) if impairing.

read.where: 1 - Clinical overview and phenomenology of movement disorders

det.patho: Tics are thought to arise from abnormal activity in cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loops, with dopaminergic and other neurotransmitter involvement and a strong polygenic contribution. Simple tics are very common in school-age children, with a male predominance.
det.clinical: Tics typically begin at around 4 to 8 years of age, often with eye blinking or facial tics, spreading rostrocaudally. Tics wax and wane and change form over time. A premonitory sensation and the ability to suppress briefly distinguish them from most other hyperkinetic movements. Duration under one year is provisional tic disorder; longer duration with only one type is persistent motor or vocal tic disorder.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, based on history and observation. Ask specifically about urges, suppressibility and comorbidities. Atypical features such as adult onset, progressive course or other neurological signs warrant further evaluation for secondary causes.
det.treatment: Most children need only explanation to family and school. Comprehensive Behavioural Intervention for Tics (CBIT) or habit reversal is first-line for bothersome tics. Medication (alpha-2 agonists such as clonidine or guanfacine, then aripiprazole or other dopamine blockers) is reserved for impairing tics. Treat comorbid ADHD or OCD, which are often more disabling.
det.prognosis: Most simple childhood tics improve or disappear by late adolescence.
pearls: Premonitory urge plus brief suppressibility = tic.
Eye blinking and sniffing are often misattributed to eye or allergy disease.
Comorbid ADHD/OCD frequently determines quality of life more than the tics.
det.thd: Simple tics คือการเคลื่อนไหวหรือเสียงสั้น ๆ ซ้ำ ๆ เช่น กะพริบตา ยักไหล่ สูดจมูก มักเริ่มในเด็กวัยเรียน มีความรู้สึกอยากทำก่อนและกลั้นได้ชั่วคราว อาการขึ้นลงตามความเครียด วินิจฉัยจากการซักประวัติและสังเกต ส่วนใหญ่แค่ให้ความรู้ ถ้ารบกวนมากใช้ CBIT หรือยา เช่น clonidine และ aripiprazole และส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นเมื่อเข้าวัยรุ่น

name: Sjögren syndrome
formal: Autoimmune exocrinopathy with sicca symptoms; neurological involvement includes sensory ganglionopathy, small fibre neuropathy, trigeminal neuropathy and myelopathy.
simple: An autoimmune disease causing dry eyes and mouth that can also damage nerves.
more: Autoimmune exocrine disease with Ro and La antibodies, sicca symptoms, and neurological involvement including sensory ganglionopathy, small fibre neuropathy, trigeminal neuropathy, and myelopathy. Schirmer test, anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies, and lip biopsy; immunotherapy for neurological disease, such as steroids, IVIG, or rituximab.
th: โรคภูมิคุ้มกันทำลายต่อมน้ำลายและน้ำตา ทำให้ปากแห้งตาแห้ง และอาจทำให้เกิดโรคระบบประสาท เช่น sensory ganglionopathy, small fiber neuropathy, trigeminal neuropathy และไขสันหลังอักเสบ
tempoNote: Sicca symptoms are often present for years; neurological complications may evolve over weeks (myelitis) or months (neuropathies)
feat: Dry eyes and dry mouth, parotid swelling, dental decay
Sensory ganglionopathy: non-length-dependent numbness, sensory ataxia, pseudoathetosis
Painful small-fibre neuropathy with burning in feet, face or trunk
Trigeminal sensory neuropathy or other cranial neuropathies
Longitudinally extensive myelitis or optic neuritis (often with AQP4 antibodies)
inv: ANA, rheumatoid factor, anti-La/SSB and anti-Ro/SSA; serum electrophoresis and cryoglobulins
Schirmer test, salivary flow and minor salivary gland (lip) biopsy for focal lymphocytic sialadenitis
NCS: absent sensory potentials without length gradient in ganglionopathy; skin biopsy for small-fibre loss
MRI spine/brain; AQP4-IgG if myelitis or optic neuritis

case.story: Eight months of numbness that started in her right hand and face, then both legs; she now sways in the dark and her eyes feel gritty.
case.exam: Areflexia, severe loss of joint position sense in all limbs, pseudoathetoid fingers with eyes closed, Romberg positive; power normal.
case.tests: Sensory nerve action potentials absent in arms and legs, motor studies normal; anti-Ro positive; lip biopsy focal lymphocytic sialadenitis.
case.q: Where is the lesion and what is the systemic disease?
case.a: Dorsal root ganglia (sensory ganglionopathy) due to Sjögren syndrome.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Sjögren Syndrome
Chapter 50 Connective Tissue Diseases, Vasculitis, and the Nervous System

det.patho: Sjögren syndrome is a systemic autoimmune disease with lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands and B-cell hyperactivity. Neurological damage results from lymphocytic inflammation of dorsal root and trigeminal ganglia, small-vessel vasculitis (sometimes with cryoglobulins), and associated antibody-mediated CNS disease such as AQP4-positive NMOSD. It affects women far more than men and carries an increased risk of lymphoma.
det.clinical: Peripheral nerve disease is the most common neurological manifestation: sensory ganglionopathy, painful small-fibre neuropathy, axonal sensorimotor neuropathy, mononeuritis multiplex and trigeminal neuropathy. CNS involvement includes myelitis, optic neuritis, brain white matter lesions and aseptic meningitis. Neurological symptoms can precede recognised sicca symptoms, so ask directly about dryness.
det.diagnosis: The 2016 ACR/EULAR criteria use anti-Ro positivity, lip biopsy focus score, Schirmer test, ocular staining and salivary flow. Many patients with neuropathy are seronegative, so lip biopsy is valuable. Nerve conduction patterns and skin biopsy define the neuropathy type; MRI and AQP4 testing are needed for CNS disease. Check cryoglobulins and paraprotein, which increase the risk of vasculitis and lymphoma.
det.treatment: Sicca symptoms are treated with artificial tears, saliva substitutes and pilocarpine. Neurological disease is treated according to type: steroids, IVIG, rituximab or cyclophosphamide for vasculitic neuropathy, myelitis or active ganglionopathy (early treatment works best); NMOSD-directed therapy when AQP4 is positive. Small-fibre pain is managed with neuropathic pain agents, and IVIG has been tried in selected cases. Hydroxychloroquine is used for systemic features.
det.prognosis: Ganglionopathy often stabilises but rarely reverses; vasculitic neuropathy and myelitis respond better to early immunotherapy. Lymphoma risk requires long-term follow-up.
pearls: Non-length-dependent sensory loss with sensory ataxia and no weakness: think ganglionopathy and test for Sjögren.
Seronegative Sjögren is common in neuropathy — do the lip biopsy.
Myelitis in Sjögren: test AQP4-IgG, as many have coexisting NMOSD.
det.thd: Sjögren syndrome เป็นโรคภูมิคุ้มกันที่ทำให้ตาแห้งและปากแห้ง ระบบประสาทที่เกี่ยวข้องบ่อยคือเส้นประสาทส่วนปลาย เช่น sensory ganglionopathy ที่ทำให้เดินเซเพราะเสียการรับรู้ตำแหน่ง small fiber neuropathy ที่ปวดแสบร้อน และ trigeminal neuropathy นอกจากนี้อาจมีไขสันหลังอักเสบร่วมกับ AQP4 วินิจฉัยด้วย anti-Ro/La, lip biopsy และ NCS รักษาตามชนิดของความผิดปกติด้วย steroid, IVIG หรือ rituximab

qx.stem: A 52-year-old woman has dry eyes and mouth for years and now complains of gait unsteadiness, loss of joint position sense and numb hands without weakness. Reflexes are absent and nerve conduction studies show absent sensory potentials with normal motor conduction.
qx.q: Which neuropathy is most characteristic?
opts: Acute motor axonal neuropathy
Hereditary pressure palsy
Diabetic amyotrophy
Sensory neuronopathy (dorsal root ganglionopathy)
Multifocal motor neuropathy
qx.why: Ataxic sensory neuronopathy with non-length-dependent sensory loss is a signature neurological manifestation of Sjögren syndrome. Motor conduction is normal because the lesion is in the dorsal root ganglia. The other options are motor-predominant or have different distributions.

name: Skeletal muscle channelopathies
formal: Genetic ion channel disorders causing myotonia or periodic paralysis, e.g. CLCN1, SCN4A and CACNA1S mutations.
simple: Inherited problems with muscle electrical channels causing stiffness or episodes of weakness.
th: กลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมของช่องไอออนในกล้ามเนื้อ ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อเกร็งคลายช้า (myotonia) หรืออ่อนแรงเป็นพัก ๆ (periodic paralysis)
tempoNote: Episodic stiffness or weakness from childhood or adolescence; some develop fixed weakness later
feat: Myotonia: muscle stiffness after rest improving with repeated contraction (warm-up), or worsening with cold/exercise (paramyotonia)
Periodic paralysis: attacks of flaccid weakness with high, low or normal potassium, often after rest following exercise or carbohydrate load
Main genes: CLCN1 (myotonia congenita), SCN4A (paramyotonia, hyperPP, some hypoPP), CACNA1S (hypoPP), KCNJ2 (Andersen–Tawil)
Muscle hypertrophy in myotonia congenita; late permanent proximal weakness in periodic paralysis
No dystrophic multisystem features (unlike myotonic dystrophy)
inv: EMG for myotonic discharges; short and long exercise tests and cooling studies
Potassium during attacks; thyroid function to exclude thyrotoxic periodic paralysis
Genetic testing of CLCN1, SCN4A, CACNA1S, KCNJ2; ECG for Andersen–Tawil

case.who: 19-year-old man, university student from Sakon Nakhon
case.story: Since teens, legs are stiff when he first stands to walk after class but loosen after a few steps; hands stick when gripping.
case.exam: Muscular build, grip myotonia that eases with repetition, percussion myotonia, normal strength.
case.tests: EMG: abundant myotonic discharges; CLCN1 compound heterozygous variants.
case.q: Which channelopathy is this and which drug helps?
case.a: Recessive myotonia congenita (Becker type, CLCN1); mexiletine reduces myotonia.

read.where: Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Genetic Muscle Diseases
Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Skeletal Muscle Channelopathies

det.patho: Channel variants alter muscle membrane excitability. Loss of chloride conductance (CLCN1) or gain of sodium channel function (SCN4A) produces repetitive firing and myotonia. Sustained depolarisation from sodium leak or aberrant gating-pore currents (in hypoPP) renders fibres inexcitable and causes paralysis. Over years, vacuolar myopathy may cause permanent weakness.
det.clinical: Myotonic disorders present with stiffness, cramps and warm-up or paradoxical worsening. Periodic paralyses present with episodes of flaccid weakness lasting minutes (hyperPP) to hours or days (hypoPP), with triggers like rest after exercise, carbohydrate meals, cold or fasting. Andersen–Tawil adds arrhythmias and skeletal features. Anaesthesia can trigger rigidity or prolonged weakness.
det.diagnosis: History, EMG with exercise and cooling protocols, and serum potassium during attacks guide the gene choice. Genetic testing confirms. Secondary causes such as thyrotoxicosis, renal tubular acidosis and potassium-wasting drugs must be excluded, especially in Thai patients with hypokalaemic paralysis.
det.treatment: Mexiletine is first-line for disabling myotonia; lamotrigine is an alternative. Periodic paralysis is managed with trigger avoidance, potassium supplementation or restriction as appropriate, and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as acetazolamide or dichlorphenamide. Andersen–Tawil requires cardiology input. Warn anaesthetists.
det.prognosis: Normal lifespan in most; episodic forms can leave persistent weakness in later decades.
pearls: Warm-up phenomenon = chloride channel; paradoxical myotonia with cold = sodium channel.
In Thailand, the commonest cause of hypokalaemic paralysis in young men is thyrotoxicosis, not genetics.
Periodic paralysis plus arrhythmia: think Andersen–Tawil and get an ECG.
det.thd: Skeletal muscle channelopathies เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมของช่องไอออนในกล้ามเนื้อ ได้แก่ CLCN1, SCN4A, CACNA1S และ KCNJ2 ทำให้เกิด myotonia หรืออ่อนแรงเป็นพัก ๆ (periodic paralysis) ไม่มีอาการหลายระบบแบบ myotonic dystrophy การวินิจฉัยใช้ EMG, exercise test, ระดับโพแทสเซียมขณะมีอาการ และตรวจยีน ต้องแยก thyrotoxic periodic paralysis การรักษาใช้ mexiletine และ acetazolamide

name: Skull-base tumours
formal: Neoplasms such as meningioma, chordoma and schwannoma affecting cranial nerves and brainstem, causing multiple cranial neuropathies.
simple: Growths at the bottom of the skull that press on nerves, causing problems like double vision or hearing loss.
th: เนื้องอกที่ฐานกะโหลก เช่น meningioma, chordoma, schwannoma และมะเร็งโพรงหลังจมูก ทำให้เส้นประสาทสมองหลายเส้นเสียและกดก้านสมอง
tempoNote: Benign tumours over years; malignant ones such as nasopharyngeal carcinoma over weeks to months
feat: Progressive, often sequential cranial neuropathies (e.g. VI then V then III)
Headache, facial numbness or pain, diplopia, hearing loss, dysphagia or hoarseness depending on level
Brainstem compression: long-tract signs, ataxia
Nasal obstruction, epistaxis, serous otitis or neck node in nasopharyngeal carcinoma (common in Southeast Asia)
inv: MRI with contrast and fat suppression of skull base; CT for bone erosion or hyperostosis
Nasoendoscopy and EBV DNA for nasopharyngeal carcinoma
Biopsy for histology; audiology and swallow assessment

case.story: Two months of right facial numbness and now double vision looking right; his right ear feels blocked.
case.exam: Right VI palsy, reduced sensation in V2–V3, right middle-ear effusion, firm upper neck node.
case.tests: MRI: nasopharyngeal mass invading the clivus and right cavernous sinus; plasma EBV DNA high.
case.q: What is the most likely tumour, and what is the treatment?
case.a: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma with skull base invasion; chemoradiotherapy (intensity-modulated radiotherapy with platinum, often induction chemotherapy).

det.patho: This umbrella covers benign tumours (meningioma, schwannoma, pituitary adenoma, glomus tumours), locally aggressive tumours (chordoma, chondrosarcoma) and malignancies (nasopharyngeal carcinoma, metastases, lymphoma, plasmacytoma). They damage nerves as they exit foramina and compress the brainstem or vessels.
det.clinical: The level determines the syndrome: anterior (olfactory, optic), middle (cavernous sinus, V, VI, Meckel cave), posterior (jugular foramen IX–XI, hypoglossal canal XII). Pain and rapid progression suggest malignancy. Perineural spread of head and neck cancers can produce slowly progressive numbness.
det.diagnosis: Dedicated contrast MRI with thin slices through the skull base is essential; standard brain MRI may miss small lesions. CT shows bone pattern. Biopsy, endoscopic where possible, defines histology. Systemic staging and EBV DNA are used for nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
det.treatment: Depends on histology: endoscopic or open microsurgery, stereotactic radiosurgery or proton therapy for chordoma and chondrosarcoma, chemoradiotherapy for nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and systemic treatment for lymphoma or metastases. Multidisciplinary skull base teams balance tumour control and cranial nerve preservation.
det.prognosis: Highly variable by tumour type, from excellent for small benign lesions to guarded for chordoma and advanced carcinoma.
pearls: Multiple cranial neuropathies on one side: image the skull base with contrast and fat suppression.
Unilateral middle-ear effusion in an adult with a VI palsy: look in the nasopharynx.
Numb chin can signal skull base or mandibular metastasis.
det.thd: Skull-base tumours คือกลุ่มเนื้องอกที่ฐานกะโหลก ทั้งชนิดไม่ร้าย เช่น meningioma, schwannoma และชนิดร้าย เช่น chordoma และมะเร็งโพรงหลังจมูกที่พบบ่อยในไทย ผู้ป่วยมีเส้นประสาทสมองเสียหลายเส้นทีละเส้น ปวดศีรษะ หน้าชา มองเห็นภาพซ้อน MRI ฐานกะโหลกแบบเฉพาะและชิ้นเนื้อเป็นหลักในการวินิจฉัย การรักษาขึ้นกับชนิดเนื้องอก

name: Sleep paralysis
formal: Transient inability to move at sleep onset or offset with preserved awareness, from intrusion of REM atonia; common in narcolepsy.
simple: Briefly being unable to move or speak when falling asleep or waking up.
more: Temporary inability to move or speak while falling asleep or waking, with preserved awareness from REM atonia intrusion; common in narcolepsy and sleep deprivation.
th: การขยับตัวไม่ได้ชั่วคราวตอนเริ่มหลับหรือตอนตื่น แต่ยังรู้สึกตัว เพราะ REM atonia แทรกเข้ามาในช่วงตื่น อาจมีภาพหลอนน่ากลัวร่วม พบในคนทั่วไปเมื่ออดนอนและพบบ่อยใน narcolepsy
tempoNote: Each episode lasts seconds to a few minutes and ends spontaneously or with touch or sound; recurrence varies from rare to frequent
feat: Inability to move limbs, trunk or head at sleep onset or on waking, with full awareness and intact breathing and eye movements
Often with frightening hallucinations such as a presence in the room or pressure on the chest
Triggers: sleep deprivation, irregular schedules, shift work, jet lag, supine sleep and stress
Common at least once in life in the general population; recurrent episodes are a feature of narcolepsy
inv: Diagnosis by history; no testing if isolated and without sleepiness
PSG and MSLT if there is excessive daytime sleepiness or cataplexy
Screen for anxiety, PTSD and sleep deprivation

case.story: During exam weeks, sleeping 4–5 hours a night, he twice woke unable to move for about a minute, sensing someone sitting on his chest; he could move his eyes and breathe.
case.exam: Normal; no daytime sleep attacks and no weakness with laughter.
case.tests: None needed.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and advice?
case.a: Isolated sleep paralysis from sleep deprivation; reassure, explain the mechanism and keep regular, sufficient sleep. Test for narcolepsy only if sleepiness or cataplexy develops.

read.where: Chapter 29 Disorders of Sleep — Sleep Paralysis and Automatic Behaviours

det.patho: Sleep paralysis is a mixed state in which the muscle atonia and dream imagery of REM sleep persist while the cortex is awake. It is most likely when REM sleep comes early or is fragmented, as after sleep deprivation, shift work or in narcolepsy. Genetic factors and anxiety contribute.
det.clinical: The person is awake, aware of the room and unable to move or speak, while eye movements and breathing continue, although many feel short of breath. Hallucinations of an intruder, pressure on the chest or floating are frequent and frightening, and many cultures have folk names for the experience. Episodes stop on their own within minutes, often faster with touch. Recurrent isolated sleep paralysis is diagnosed when episodes are frequent and distressing without narcolepsy.
det.diagnosis: The history is diagnostic. Ask about daytime sleepiness and cataplexy, because if present, PSG and MSLT are needed to test for narcolepsy. Seizures, periodic paralysis and panic attacks are the main mimics. Isolated episodes do not predict later narcolepsy.
det.treatment: Explanation and reassurance are often enough. Regular, sufficient sleep, avoiding supine sleep and managing stress reduce episodes. CBT approaches, including focusing on small movements to end episodes, are helpful. For frequent distressing episodes, REM-suppressing antidepressants such as SSRIs or clomipramine can be used, but withdraw them gradually.
det.prognosis: Benign; episodes usually become infrequent when sleep habits improve.
pearls: Isolated sleep paralysis without sleepiness or cataplexy does not need an MSLT.
Eye movements and breathing are spared because they are not affected by REM atonia.
det.thd: Sleep paralysis คือขยับตัวไม่ได้ชั่วคราวตอนเริ่มหลับหรือตอนตื่นแต่ยังรู้สึกตัว เพราะภาวะ atonia ของ REM ยังค้างอยู่ อาจเห็นภาพหลอนหรือรู้สึกมีคนกดทับหน้าอก พบในคนทั่วไปเมื่ออดนอนหรือเครียด และพบบ่อยใน narcolepsy วินิจฉัยจากประวัติ ถ้ามีง่วงกลางวันหรือ cataplexy ให้ตรวจ MSLT การรักษาคือให้ความมั่นใจ นอนให้พอ และใช้ยากด REM ในรายที่เป็นบ่อย

name: Sleep-related eating disorder
formal: NREM parasomnia with recurrent involuntary eating and impaired awareness, often with zolpidem use or sleepwalking.
simple: Eating in the night while partly asleep, often with no memory of it.
th: parasomnia ช่วง NREM ที่ผู้ป่วยลุกขึ้นมากินหรือดื่มซ้ำ ๆ ระหว่างหลับโดยรู้ตัวน้อยหรือจำไม่ได้ อาจกินของแปลกหรือไม่ปลอดภัย มักสัมพันธ์กับ zolpidem การละเมอเดิน และ RLS
tempoNote: Episodes recur most nights, typically within a few hours of falling asleep, over months to years; onset often in young adult women
feat: Recurrent eating out of partial arousal from sleep, often high-calorie or odd food combinations, sometimes inedible or toxic items
Reduced awareness and patchy or absent memory, with morning evidence such as wrappers in the kitchen
Injury from cooking or knives, weight gain and poor diabetes control
Associations: zolpidem and other hypnotics, history of sleepwalking, RLS, PLMS, OSA and daytime eating disorders
inv: History from the household and home video
Video-PSG to show arousals from NREM sleep and to look for OSA and PLMS
Ferritin and RLS screening; medicine review for Z-drugs, antipsychotics and lithium

case.story: Her flatmate finds her in the kitchen at 1 am eating peanut butter with raw noodles; she remembers nothing and has gained 6 kg. She started zolpidem for insomnia 3 months ago and has evening leg restlessness.
case.exam: Normal; BMI 27.
case.tests: Ferritin 18 ng/mL; video-PSG shows arousals from N3 with chewing movements and frequent PLMS.
case.q: What are the key management steps?
case.a: Sleep-related eating disorder; stop zolpidem, treat RLS and iron deficiency, secure the kitchen, and consider topiramate if episodes continue.

read.where: Chapter 51 Neurologic Aspects of Sleep Medicine

det.patho: SRED is a variant of the NREM arousal disorders in which a partial arousal releases feeding behaviour. Sedative hypnotics, especially zolpidem, raise the arousal threshold and favour this state. Shared mechanisms with RLS and PLMS, including dopaminergic dysfunction, are suggested by the strong overlap and the response to dopaminergic and anti-RLS treatment.
det.clinical: Most patients are young or middle-aged women who eat almost nightly, often within a few hours of sleep onset. Food choices are often unusual, and burns, cuts and choking can occur. Unlike night eating syndrome, awareness is reduced and memory is incomplete. Daytime eating disorders, sleepwalking history and RLS are common companions.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on recurrent episodes of dysfunctional eating after arousal from the main sleep period, with reduced awareness and at least one adverse consequence. Video-PSG supports the diagnosis and detects treatable triggers such as OSA and PLMS. Separate it from night eating syndrome, where the patient is fully awake, and from hypoglycaemia or seizures.
det.treatment: Remove triggers first: stop zolpidem or other provoking hypnotics and treat RLS, PLMS and OSA. Secure the kitchen and dangerous items. Topiramate has the best evidence among medicines, and dopaminergic agents or clonazepam can help selected patients. Manage any daytime eating disorder and weight gain alongside.
det.prognosis: Often chronic but improves when hypnotics are withdrawn and associated sleep disorders are treated.
pearls: New night-time eating on zolpidem is a complex sleep behaviour and a reason to stop the drug.
Ask every SRED patient about restless legs.
Full awareness of night eating suggests night eating syndrome, not a parasomnia.
det.thd: Sleep-related eating disorder เป็น parasomnia ช่วง NREM ผู้ป่วยลุกมากินอาหารระหว่างหลับโดยรู้ตัวน้อยและจำไม่ได้ อาจกินของแปลกหรืออันตรายและน้ำหนักขึ้น สัมพันธ์กับ zolpidem การละเมอเดิน RLS และ OSA วินิจฉัยด้วยประวัติและ video-PSG การรักษาคือหยุดยา zolpidem รักษา RLS/OSA เก็บของอันตราย และใช้ topiramate ถ้ายังเป็นอยู่

qx.stem: A 37-year-old woman from Phuket has gained 9 kg in six months. She finds half-eaten food and kitchen mess in the morning and recalls nothing, though her husband sees her eating in a daze. The episodes began after she started zolpidem 10 mg. She has no daytime binge eating. Polysomnography shows arousals from slow-wave sleep with eating, without apnoea.
qx.q: What is the best first intervention?
opts: Stop zolpidem and treat other triggers; consider topiramate if episodes persist
Increase zolpidem to improve sleep consolidation
Start an appetite stimulant
Prescribe carbamazepine for nocturnal seizures
Refer for bariatric surgery
qx.why: Sleep-related eating disorder is a NREM parasomnia with recurrent involuntary eating and partial amnesia, and zolpidem and other hypnotics are well-known triggers. Withdrawing the trigger and treating coexisting sleep disorders is first; topiramate or dopaminergic agents have been used in persistent cases. Seizure treatment is unlikely to help.

name: Slow channel syndrome
formal: Autosomal dominant congenital myasthenic syndrome from acetylcholine receptor gain-of-function mutations with prolonged channel opening; repetitive CMAP and worsening with pyridostigmine.
simple: An inherited muscle weakness condition caused by nerve-muscle signals that last too long.
th: congenital myasthenic syndrome ถ่ายทอดแบบ dominant จาก acetylcholine receptor ที่เปิดค้างนาน ทำให้อ่อนแรงเลือกที่คอและนิ้วเหยียด ยา pyridostigmine ไม่ได้ผลและอาจทำให้แย่ลง ตอบสนองต่อ fluoxetine หรือ quinidine
tempoNote: Normal at birth; onset from childhood to adulthood, slowly progressive with fluctuation
feat: Selective weakness and wasting of neck, wrist and finger extensors, with fatigable limb weakness
No symptoms at birth; onset ranges from childhood to adulthood with mild to severe disability
Ptosis and ophthalmoparesis are milder than in other congenital myasthenic syndromes
A single nerve stimulus evokes a repetitive CMAP; antibodies negative
Progressive respiratory insufficiency in some, and worsening with cholinesterase inhibitors
inv: Nerve conduction: repetitive CMAP after a single stimulus, plus decrement on 2–3 Hz stimulation
AChR and MuSK antibodies negative
Genetic testing of CHRNA1, CHRNB1, CHRND, CHRNE (gain-of-function variants) by panel or exome
Single-fibre EMG: jitter and blocking; spirometry for respiratory involvement

case.story: Since her teens her neck tires and her fingers droop when typing. Her father had weak hands. Pyridostigmine made her worse.
case.exam: Weak neck and finger extensors with forearm wasting, mild ptosis and fatigable arm abduction.
case.tests: Repetitive CMAP after a single ulnar stimulus; 15 percent decrement at 3 Hz; AChR antibody negative; heterozygous CHRNE variant.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and which treatment should be used or avoided?
case.a: Slow-channel congenital myasthenic syndrome; stop cholinesterase inhibitors and use an open-channel blocker such as fluoxetine or quinidine.

read.where: Chapter 17 Disorders of the Neuromuscular Junction — Congenital Myasthenic Syndromes

det.patho: Gain-of-function variants in the genes for AChR subunits (CHRNA1, CHRNB1, CHRND, CHRNE) prolong channel opening and slow decay of the endplate current. Excess calcium entry produces an endplate myopathy with degeneration of junctional folds, explaining selective weakness. Inheritance is usually autosomal dominant, although recessive and de novo cases are reported, and it makes up about half of congenital myasthenic syndromes.
det.clinical: Children or adults develop slowly progressive weakness with prominent neck, wrist and finger extensor involvement, sometimes with wasting that mimics motor neuron disease. Ptosis and ophthalmoparesis are less severe than in other forms. Fatigability is present, and some patients develop respiratory failure needing assisted ventilation. A family history is often found, and deterioration on pyridostigmine is a clue.
det.diagnosis: Suspect the disease in an antibody-negative patient with distal extensor-predominant weakness and a dominant family history. A single supramaximal stimulus yields a repetitive CMAP, and low-frequency stimulation shows decrement. There is no response to injection or oral anticholinesterase, and genetic testing by multigene panel or exome confirms the variant.
det.treatment: Pyridostigmine, thymectomy and immune suppression give no benefit, and the first can harm. Quinidine sulfate improves strength, and fluoxetine, which blocks the open mutant channel, is equally helpful in those who cannot take quinidine, often at high doses; salbutamol (albuterol) benefits some. Monitor respiratory function, ECG QT interval with quinidine, and drug interactions.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive but usually compatible with long survival when treated; respiratory support is occasionally required.
pearls: Repetitive CMAP after one stimulus plus worsening on pyridostigmine: slow-channel syndrome.
Neck and finger extensor weakness can mimic ALS or a distal myopathy.
Treat with fluoxetine or quinidine, never with cholinesterase inhibitors.
det.thd: Slow channel syndrome เป็น congenital myasthenic syndrome ชนิดที่พบบ่อยที่สุด ถ่ายทอดแบบ autosomal dominant จากยีนซับยูนิตของ acetylcholine receptor ทำให้ช่องเปิดค้างนานเกินไปและเกิด endplate myopathy ผู้ป่วยอ่อนแรงเลือกที่คอ ข้อมือและนิ้วเหยียด เริ่มตั้งแต่เด็กถึงวัยผู้ใหญ่ ตรวจ NCS พบ repetitive CMAP แอนติบอดีลบ ยา pyridostigmine ไม่ช่วยและอาจทำให้แย่ลง รักษาด้วย fluoxetine หรือ quinidine และอาจใช้ albuterol

qx.stem: A 24-year-old man from Chiang Rai has had progressive weakness of the neck and finger extensors since childhood, with a mild wrist drop and slight ptosis. His father had a similar problem. Pyridostigmine was started elsewhere and he felt worse. A single supramaximal stimulation of the ulnar nerve produces a repetitive CMAP, and high-rate stimulation causes decrement.
qx.q: Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Fluoxetine, or quinidine where available, with pyridostigmine stopped
Higher-dose pyridostigmine with 3,4-diaminopyridine
Intravenous immunoglobulin every four weeks
Plasma exchange followed by azathioprine
Thymectomy through a sternotomy
qx.why: Dominant weakness of the cervical and finger extensors with a repetitive CMAP after a single stimulus is the signature of slow channel syndrome, a gain-of-function defect that keeps the receptor open and causes calcium overload and endplate myopathy. Long-lived channel blockers, fluoxetine and quinidine, shorten the open time, while cholinesterase inhibitors and 3,4-diaminopyridine increase acetylcholine and worsen the syndrome. Immunotherapy is irrelevant.

name: Spinal muscular atrophy type 1 (Werdnig–Hoffmann)
formal: Severe infantile SMN1-related spinal muscular atrophy (Werdnig-Hoffmann) with onset under 6 months, hypotonia and inability to sit.
simple: The most severe form of SMA, where babies are very floppy and cannot sit.
more: Autosomal recessive; treatments include nusinersen, risdiplam and onasemnogene; early treatment greatly alters survival. Infantile-onset spinal muscular atrophy type 1 (SMN1 deletion) with hypotonia and early respiratory failure. Diagnosis by homozygous SMN1 deletion with one or two SMN2 copies; EMG shows denervation and fasciculations. Untreated, death occurs by two years; nusinersen, onasemnogene and risdiplam have changed survival, and early treatment is vital.
th: SMA ชนิดรุนแรงในทารก จากยีน SMN1 เริ่มอาการก่อน 6 เดือน ตัวอ่อนปวกเปียก นั่งเองไม่ได้ หายใจล้มเหลว
tempoNote: Onset before 6 months, rapid motor loss over weeks to months; course transformed by early treatment
feat: Profound hypotonia ('frog-leg' posture) with symmetrical proximal weakness
Never sits independently; head lag; alert face and normal social interaction
Tongue fasciculation, absent reflexes, weak cry and poor feeding
Paradoxical (diaphragmatic) breathing with bell-shaped chest
Untreated, most die or need permanent ventilation before age 2
inv: SMN1 exon 7 homozygous deletion test (diagnostic in about 95%)
SMN2 copy number to predict severity and guide therapy
Newborn screening where available
EMG rarely needed; CK normal or slightly raised

case.story: Mother noticed she lies still with legs flopped out and has trouble feeding; breathing looks like see-saw.
case.exam: Alert with bright eyes, profound hypotonia, no antigravity leg movement, absent reflexes, tongue fasciculation, abdominal breathing.
case.tests: Homozygous deletion of SMN1 exon 7; SMN2 two copies.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and why is urgency important?
case.a: SMA type 1; disease-modifying therapy (nusinersen, risdiplam or onasemnogene) works best given as early as possible.

read.where: Chapter 15 Disorders of the Motor Cells: The Motor Neuron Diseases — Spinal Muscular Atrophy

det.patho: Homozygous loss of SMN1 leaves only the paralogous SMN2 gene, which mostly produces a truncated protein due to exon 7 skipping. Low SMN protein causes degeneration of anterior horn cells and brainstem motor neurons. Two SMN2 copies usually produce type 1; more copies give milder disease.
det.clinical: Infants appear normal at birth or show reduced movements, then within months develop severe weakness, poor feeding and respiratory difficulty. Intercostal weakness with spared diaphragm gives paradoxical breathing. Facial expression and cognition are preserved, a striking contrast to the body weakness. Without treatment, aspiration and respiratory failure dominate.
det.diagnosis: Genetic testing for SMN1 deletion confirms the diagnosis; point mutations explain a small minority. SMN2 copy number guides prognosis and treatment eligibility. Newborn screening allows presymptomatic diagnosis. Other causes of floppy infant must be excluded when SMN1 is intact.
det.treatment: Three therapies are available: intrathecal nusinersen, oral risdiplam and one-time intravenous onasemnogene abeparvovec gene therapy. Earliest treatment, ideally presymptomatic, gives the best motor outcomes. Standards of care cover respiratory support, airway clearance, nutrition, orthopaedics and physiotherapy. In Thailand access depends on funding schemes and should be discussed early with families.
det.prognosis: Untreated survival is usually under 2 years; treated infants may sit, and presymptomatically treated children may walk.
pearls: Bright-eyed floppy baby with tongue fasciculation: SMA.
SMN2 copy number predicts severity.
Time is motor neurons; treat as soon as confirmed.
det.thd: SMA type 1 หรือ Werdnig–Hoffmann เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมจากการขาดยีน SMN1 ทารกจะอ่อนปวกเปียกตั้งแต่ก่อน 6 เดือน ลิ้นเต้นระริก ไม่มีรีเฟล็กซ์ แต่หน้าตาสดใสและพัฒนาการด้านสังคมปกติ ตรวจยืนยันด้วยการหา SMN1 deletion และนับจำนวน SMN2 ปัจจุบันมียา nusinersen risdiplam และยีนบำบัด onasemnogene ซึ่งได้ผลดีที่สุดเมื่อให้เร็วที่สุด

qx.stem: A 10-week-old girl from Ubon Ratchathani is floppy and has not lifted her head. She is alert and smiles, with a weak cry, tongue fasciculations, absent reflexes and a bell-shaped chest with paradoxical breathing. CK is normal.
qx.q: What is the most appropriate first investigation, and why must it be done urgently?
opts: Muscle biopsy, to define the myopathy
Brain MRI, to look for a malformation
Nerve conduction velocity in the legs
SMN1 copy-number analysis, because disease-modifying treatment is time-critical
Serum acetylcholine receptor antibodies
qx.why: The picture of an alert infant with hypotonia, areflexia and tongue fasciculation points to SMA, which is confirmed by SMN1 testing (homozygous exon 7 deletion). Nusinersen, risdiplam and onasemnogene therapy are most effective when started before significant motor neuron loss, so rapid testing is vital. Biopsy and MRI delay care, and antibody testing is not relevant.

name: SMA II (Intermediate form)
formal: Intermediate SMN1-related SMA with onset 6-18 months; able to sit but not walk, with tongue fasciculation, tremor and scoliosis.
simple: An SMA type where children can sit but never walk unaided.
more: SMN1 deletion, SMN2 copy number; disease-modifying therapy and respiratory and orthopaedic care.
th: SMA ชนิดที่ 2 เริ่มอาการอายุ 6–18 เดือน นั่งได้แต่ยืนเดินเองไม่ได้ ลิ้นสั่นพลิ้ว มือสั่นละเอียด และหลังคด ปัจจุบันมียารักษาที่ปรับ SMN2
tempoNote: Delayed motor milestones from 6–18 months; weakness plateaus in childhood then slowly declines with scoliosis and respiratory restriction
feat: Normal early development, then delayed motor milestones; child sits independently but cannot stand or walk unaided
Symmetric proximal weakness (legs more than arms), hypotonia and reduced or absent reflexes
Fine postural tremor of the fingers (minipolymyoclonus) and tongue fasciculation; extraocular muscles and cognition are spared
Progressive scoliosis, hip and knee contractures, jaw problems, and restrictive lung disease with weak cough
Biallelic SMN1 deletion in about 95%; SMN2 copy number is usually 3 and modifies severity
inv: SMN1 deletion or mutation analysis with SMN2 copy number; this confirms the diagnosis without biopsy
CK normal or mildly raised (up to 2–4 times); EMG neurogenic if done, but not required once genetics are positive
Spirometry, cough peak flow, sleep study, swallow assessment, and spine and hip radiographs
Baseline motor scales (HFMSE, RULM) to monitor therapy

case.story: She was bright and active but still could not pull to stand. At 12 months she could sit when placed but not crawl. Her parents noticed her hands trembling when she reached for toys.
case.exam: Alert, normal eye movements, proximal leg-predominant weakness, hypotonia, absent knee jerks, tongue fasciculation, fine finger tremor, no contractures yet.
case.tests: SMN1 homozygous exon 7 deletion; SMN2 has 3 copies; CK 280 U/L.
case.q: What is her likely SMA type and what treatment options exist?
case.a: SMA type 2. Offer SMN-targeted therapy: nusinersen intrathecally, oral risdiplam, or one-time gene therapy where age and weight criteria permit, with multidisciplinary respiratory, orthopaedic and nutritional care.

read.where: Chapter 15 Disorders of the Motor Cells: The Motor Neuron Diseases — Spinal Muscular Atrophy

det.patho: SMA results from loss of the survival motor neuron protein in alpha motor neurons because both copies of SMN1 on chromosome 5q are absent or defective. The nearly identical SMN2 gene yields only a small amount of full-length protein as most transcripts skip exon 7, so more SMN2 copies mean a milder disease. Anterior horn cells and, to a degree, lower brainstem motor nuclei degenerate, giving denervation and secondary muscle atrophy.
det.clinical: The intermediate type begins between 6 and 18 months; fetal movements and the neonatal period are normal. Children gain sitting but not standing, may stand with support for a while, and have proximal leg predominant weakness with hypotonia and areflexia. A fine tremor in the hands and tongue fasciculation are helpful clues. Over time scoliosis, contractures and restrictive respiratory insufficiency dominate, with infections as the main threat; intelligence is normal.
det.diagnosis: SMN1 deletion testing confirms it in about 95%; if a single deletion is found, sequence the second allele. SMN2 copy number gives prognostic information and is needed for trial and treatment eligibility. Distinguish from SMA types 1 and 3 by age at onset and best motor milestone, and from congenital myopathy, Pompe disease, and congenital muscular dystrophy by the neurogenic features and normal or mild CK.
det.treatment: Disease-modifying options act on SMN2 splicing (nusinersen, intrathecal, scheduled loading and maintenance doses; risdiplam, daily oral solution) or on SMN1 replacement (onasemnogene abeparvovec, one-time IV for very young children, with limits on age and weight); these are lifelong or one-off and best started as early as possible. Supportive care is equally vital: non-invasive ventilation and airway clearance, scoliosis surgery or bracing, nutrition, physiotherapy and wheelchair seating. Vaccinate and treat respiratory infections promptly.
det.prognosis: Most survive into adulthood with proper respiratory care; new therapies stabilise or improve function, especially when started early.
pearls: Sits but never stands is SMA II; walking at some point suggests SMA III.
Hand tremor and tongue fasciculation with normal intellect and reflexes lost: think of SMA.
Treatment benefit is greatest early, so refer for SMN-targeted therapy as soon as genetics confirm the diagnosis.
det.thd: SMA ชนิดที่ 2 เกิดจากการขาด SMN1 ทั้งสองยีน ทำให้เซลล์ anterior horn ตาย เด็กอาการเริ่มช่วง 6–18 เดือน นั่งได้แต่ยืนหรือเดินเองไม่ได้ กล้ามเนื้อใกล้ลำตัวอ่อนแรง reflex หายไป มือสั่นละเอียดและลิ้นสั่นพลิ้ว สติปัญญาปกติ ภายหลังมีหลังคดและปอดจำกัดการขยาย วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจ SMN1 และนับ SMN2 copy ปัจจุบันมี nusinersen, risdiplam และ gene therapy ในบางเกณฑ์ ควรเริ่มรักษาเร็ว ร่วมกับดูแลการหายใจ กระดูกสันหลัง และโภชนาการ

name: Spinal muscular atrophy type 3 (Kugelberg–Welander)
formal: Mild SMN1-related SMA (Kugelberg-Welander) with onset after 18 months and ability to walk, with proximal weakness.
simple: A milder SMA where children walk but gradually become weak.
more: SMN testing; disease-modifying therapy and physiotherapy; life expectancy is near normal. Juvenile-onset spinal muscular atrophy (SMA type III) from SMN1 deficiency, with proximal weakness, a waddling gait and loss of ambulation in some patients. Diagnose with SMN1 deletion, with copy number of SMN2 predicting severity; EMG shows chronic denervation and CK may be mildly raised. Treat with nusinersen, risdiplam or onasemnogene gene therapy, with scoliosis and respiratory care.
th: SMA ชนิดไม่รุนแรง เริ่มอาการหลัง 18 เดือน เดินได้ แต่กล้ามเนื้อต้นขาและสะโพกอ่อนแรงช้าๆ
tempoNote: Onset after 18 months (often childhood or adolescence) with slow decline; some lose walking in adulthood
feat: Achieves independent walking, then proximal leg weakness, frequent falls and Gowers sign
Waddling gait; stairs and getting up off the floor are hard
Hand tremor (minipolymyoclonus) and tongue fasciculations
Reflexes reduced or absent; no sensory loss
Often misdiagnosed as a muscular dystrophy; CK may be moderately raised

EMG: chronic neurogenic changes with large motor units
Pulmonary function and scoliosis surveillance

case.story: Walked at 15 months; for two years he falls during football and needs the handrail on stairs.
case.exam: Waddling gait, Gowers sign, proximal leg weakness, absent knee jerks, fine tremor of outstretched fingers, tongue fasciculations.
case.tests: CK 650 U/L; EMG large polyphasic motor units; SMN1 homozygous deletion with 4 SMN2 copies.
case.q: Why might he have been mistaken for a muscular dystrophy, and what treatment options exist?
case.a: Proximal weakness and raised CK mimic dystrophy; SMA type 3 can be treated with nusinersen or risdiplam.

det.patho: As in other SMA types, homozygous SMN1 loss causes motor neuron degeneration, but a higher SMN2 copy number (usually three or four) provides enough protein for milder disease. Motor units undergo reinnervation and enlargement, explaining the neurogenic EMG and fine tremor. Muscle may show secondary myopathic changes, sometimes with raised CK.
det.clinical: Children walk independently and later develop proximal leg weakness with falls, stair difficulty and waddling gait. Upper limbs follow, and some lose ambulation in adolescence or adulthood. Scoliosis and joint contractures are less severe than in type 2. Life expectancy is normal.
det.diagnosis: SMN1 deletion testing is definitive. EMG shows chronic denervation; biopsy, if done for a presumed myopathy, shows grouped atrophy. Exclude dystrophies, limb-girdle syndromes, Pompe disease and Kennedy disease in adults. SMN2 copy number helps counselling but does not perfectly predict course.
det.treatment: Nusinersen and risdiplam are approved and can stabilise or improve motor function; gene therapy use in older, heavier patients is limited. Physiotherapy, stretching, orthoses and weight management maintain mobility. Monitor respiration and spine. Genetic counselling for siblings and future pregnancies is important.
det.prognosis: Normal lifespan; disability ranges from mild weakness to loss of walking.
pearls: Proximal weakness, tongue fasciculation and finger tremor: think SMA, not dystrophy.
CK can be several times normal in SMA type 3.
Treatment benefits are greatest before major loss of motor units.

det.patho: Type 4 represents the mildest end of SMN1-related SMA, where several SMN2 copies maintain enough protein for normal motor development. Late motor neuron attrition causes slowly progressive weakness. Some adult-onset LMN syndromes labelled SMA are caused by other genes and should not be confused with SMN1-related disease.
det.clinical: Patients notice difficulty climbing stairs or rising from chairs in early or mid-adult life. Weakness is proximal and symmetrical, with cramps and fasciculations. Bulbar and respiratory muscles are usually spared. Course is slow and ambulation usually maintained.
det.diagnosis: SMN1 testing confirms it. EMG shows chronic neurogenic change; nerve conduction excludes neuropathy and conduction block. Androgen receptor testing excludes Kennedy disease in men. Muscle biopsy is rarely needed.
det.treatment: Nusinersen and risdiplam are approved across SMA types, though evidence in type 4 is limited and decisions balance cost and benefit. Exercise, physiotherapy and weight control maintain function. Genetic counselling is offered. Annual review of strength and respiratory function is sensible.
det.prognosis: Normal life expectancy with mild to moderate disability.
pearls: Adult with proximal weakness and fasciculation: test SMN1 as well as androgen receptor.
SMA type 4 rarely affects breathing or swallowing.
Not every adult LMN syndrome is SMN1-related.

det.patho: SVD is a collection of disorders of small penetrating arteries, arterioles, capillaries and venules. The commonest form, age- and hypertension-related arteriolosclerosis, thickens and stiffens vessel walls, impairs autoregulation and breaks down the blood–brain barrier; the result is chronic hypoperfusion of white matter, focal occlusions (lacunes) and rupture (deep haemorrhage). Cerebral amyloid angiopathy is the second sporadic form; genetic forms include CADASIL, CARASIL, COL4A1/2 disease and Fabry disease. SVD causes about a quarter of ischaemic strokes, most deep haemorrhages, and is the leading vascular contributor to dementia.
det.clinical: Presentations include acute lacunar syndromes, insidious cognitive decline marked by slowed processing and executive dysfunction, gait apraxia-like disturbance with falls, mood disorder, apathy and urinary symptoms. Many people are asymptomatic despite striking imaging. Progression is usually gradual with stepwise elements; WMH burden predicts stroke, dementia and death.
det.diagnosis: Imaging is defined by consensus STRIVE criteria (updated 2023): recent small subcortical infarct, lacunes of presumed vascular origin, WMH, perivascular spaces, cerebral microbleeds, cortical superficial siderosis and brain atrophy. A 'total SVD score' summarises burden. Microbleed distribution separates hypertensive arteriolopathy (deep) from CAA (lobar). In patients under about 55 or with family history, think of monogenic causes; confluent WMH reaching the temporal poles suggests CADASIL. Exclude demyelination, leukodystrophy and NPH when the pattern is atypical.
det.treatment: There is no specific disease-modifying drug. Control blood pressure (intensive lowering slows WMH progression), treat diabetes and dyslipidaemia, stop smoking and encourage physical and cognitive activity. After a lacunar stroke, use a single antiplatelet (cilostazol is attractive in Asia because of lower bleeding); avoid antiplatelets in purely incidental disease without stroke. Manage cognitive and mood symptoms, gait training and continence. Cholinesterase inhibitors have only modest effect.
det.prognosis: Variable: many remain stable for years, but heavy WMH load roughly doubles to triples risk of stroke and dementia.
pearls: Executive slowing + small-step gait + urinary urgency + WMH = classic SVD triad of symptoms.
Deep microbleeds suggest hypertensive SVD; strictly lobar microbleeds and siderosis suggest CAA.
BP control is the single most evidence-based intervention for slowing SVD.

det.patho: ANCA bind neutrophil enzymes, activate primed neutrophils and cause necrotising inflammation of capillaries, venules and arterioles with little immune deposit (pauci-immune). Immune complex forms deposit antibodies and complement in vessel walls. In nerves, epineurial arteriole occlusion causes ischaemic axonal loss, often at watershed zones in mid-arm and mid-thigh.
det.clinical: Systemic symptoms, ENT disease, lung and kidney involvement accompany painful sudden-onset mononeuropathies (peroneal, ulnar, median, radial). Overlap of many mononeuropathies can resemble a distal symmetrical neuropathy. GPA can cause hypertrophic pachymeningitis, orbital masses and cranial neuropathies; EGPA patients often have years of asthma and nasal polyps beforehand.
det.diagnosis: ANCA testing by antigen-specific assay is the first step, but ANCA-negative disease occurs, especially in EGPA and nerve-limited forms. Tissue confirmation from nerve, kidney or skin is valuable. Electrodiagnosis shows asymmetric axonal loss. Exclude infection, drugs and malignancy as secondary triggers.
det.treatment: Severe or neurological disease is induced with glucocorticoids plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide; plasma exchange is reserved for selected severe renal or pulmonary disease. Avacopan helps lower steroid use. Maintenance usually uses rituximab. EGPA can be treated with anti-IL-5 drugs such as mepolizumab or benralizumab. Provide neuropathic pain treatment, rehabilitation and infection prophylaxis.
det.prognosis: Remission rates are high; nerve recovery is slow and incomplete, and relapse requires vigilance.
pearls: Asthma, eosinophilia and foot drop: EGPA.
Always check urine for blood in suspected vasculitic neuropathy.
ANCA negative does not rule out small vessel vasculitis.

det.patho: SFN damages thinly myelinated Aδ and unmyelinated C fibres that carry pain, temperature and autonomic signals. Common causes are diabetes and prediabetes, Sjögren and other immune disorders, alcohol, chemotherapy, celiac disease, infections, paraproteins, amyloidosis and genetic sodium-channel variants (SCN9A, SCN10A, SCN11A). In roughly half, no cause is found despite full testing.
det.clinical: Patients describe burning, tingling, cold or stabbing pain that starts in the feet and may rise to the knees and then hands. Examination is often near normal apart from reduced pin and temperature sense or allodynia; preserved reflexes and vibration are typical. Autonomic involvement can cause sweating changes, orthostatic intolerance, gastrointestinal or sexual dysfunction. Patchy, face- or trunk-predominant pain points towards a ganglionopathy-type immune or metabolic process.
det.diagnosis: A normal NCS combined with typical symptoms and small-fibre signs supports the diagnosis; confirmation comes from reduced intraepidermal nerve fibre density on distal-leg punch biopsy or abnormal sudomotor/autonomic testing. Corneal confocal microscopy and quantitative sensory testing are adjuncts. A structured search for treatable causes is the main work, including a 2-hour glucose tolerance test, since fasting glucose and HbA1c can miss prediabetes.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: glycaemic control and weight loss, stopping alcohol or neurotoxic drugs, managing Sjögren or celiac disease. Neuropathic pain is treated with gabapentinoids, duloxetine, or tricyclics, with topical lidocaine or high-concentration capsaicin for focal pain. Immunotherapy is considered only in well-characterised immune-mediated cases, ideally in trials. Foot care and sleep support matter.
det.prognosis: Most patients do not progress to large-fibre neuropathy; pain often persists but can be controlled. Outcomes are better when a treatable cause is identified.
pearls: Normal NCS does not exclude neuropathy — it excludes large-fibre neuropathy.
Order an oral glucose tolerance test; prediabetes is a common hidden cause.
Pain beginning in face or trunk suggests a non-length-dependent, often immune process.
