det.patho: Sneddon syndrome is a non-inflammatory occlusive arteriopathy of small and medium arteries in skin and brain, with early endothelial injury followed by intimal proliferation and thrombosis. Antiphospholipid antibodies contribute in a subset, while others are antibody-negative; deficiency of adenosine deaminase 2 (ADA2) explains some familial and childhood cases. The 2023 ACR/EULAR rules assign points to persistent broken livedo racemosa but not to uniform livedo reticularis that fades with warmth, which echoes the bedside distinction.
det.clinical: Livedo racemosa typically precedes neurological events by years and is easier to see in cool surroundings. Strokes are usually small, cortical or subcortical, and repeated events lead to cognitive decline, mood change and seizures. Headache, dizziness and hypertension are common prodromal complaints, and cardiac valve thickening may coexist. Pregnancy loss can occur in antibody-positive women.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis combines widespread livedo racemosa with cerebrovascular events after exclusion of other causes. Antiphospholipid antibodies must be tested twice at least 12 weeks apart to separate antibody-positive from antibody-negative forms, and a patient with persistent high-titre antibodies and thrombosis may be classified as APS under the 2023 criteria in addition. Skin biopsy needs deep and multiple samples including the livedo band. ADA2 deficiency should be sought in young or familial presentations because treatment differs.
det.treatment: Antibody-positive patients are generally anticoagulated with warfarin (DOACs are not preferred in high-risk APS), whereas antibody-negative patients are usually given antiplatelet therapy, although the evidence is limited. Blood pressure control, smoking cessation and avoidance of oestrogen-containing contraception are routine. Hydroxychloroquine is sometimes added in antibody-positive disease. ADA2 deficiency responds to anti-TNF therapy.
det.prognosis: Untreated, recurrent strokes lead to vascular cognitive impairment; with anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy and risk-factor control the course is variable but often slower.
pearls: Young stroke plus fixed, broken livedo racemosa: think Sneddon and test aPL twice.
Livedo that fades with warmth and is uniform (reticularis) is usually physiological and does not count.
Test ADA2 in childhood or familial cases because anti-TNF therapy changes the outcome.

name: Sodium channel myasthenia
formal: Myasthenic syndrome from SCN4A mutations with fatigable weakness and episodic apnoea, from enhanced inactivation of the sodium channel.
simple: A rare inherited myasthenia due to a sodium channel fault in muscle.
more: Autosomal recessive; responds to acetazolamide and pyridostigmine.
ab: CMS due to Nav1.4 loss of function

feat: Very rare recessive postsynaptic CMS from muscle sodium channel loss of function
Fatigable limb, bulbar and eye weakness from birth or infancy

case.story: Weak suck at birth and two episodes of stopping breathing during fever needing ventilation; between episodes she tires quickly when climbing.
case.exam: Bilateral ptosis, mild facial and proximal weakness worsening with repeated effort.
case.tests: Decrement at 20 Hz stimulation but little at 3 Hz; biallelic SCN4A variants.
case.q: Which rare CMS fits and what does the family need at home?
case.a: Sodium channel myasthenia; an emergency respiratory plan with monitoring during infections, and trial of pyridostigmine or acetazolamide under specialist care.

det.patho: Nav1.4 generates the muscle action potential at the endplate. Loss-of-function variants, particularly those that enhance fast inactivation, raise the threshold so endplate potentials fail to trigger muscle firing, especially at higher frequencies. The same gene causes gain-of-function myotonia and periodic paralysis and recessive congenital myopathy, forming a spectrum.
det.clinical: Only a handful of families are described. Children show hypotonia, ptosis, bulbar and limb fatigability and sudden respiratory crises, sometimes recurrent and triggered by infection or exertion. Developmental outcome varies, and some have permanent weakness from associated myopathy.
det.diagnosis: Frequency-dependent decrement at high rates of stimulation is suggestive. Antibodies are negative, and the diagnosis requires genetic confirmation, usually from a CMS or neuromuscular panel or exome. Functional studies of variants support pathogenicity in research settings.
det.treatment: Evidence is anecdotal. Pyridostigmine and acetazolamide have been reported to help some patients. Respiratory monitoring, home apnoea plans and prompt treatment of infections are the mainstays.
det.prognosis: Uncertain given rarity; episodic apnoea is the main danger.
pearls: SCN4A spans myotonia, periodic paralysis, congenital myopathy and CMS.
Decrement that appears only at high-frequency stimulation is a clue.
Apnoea with fever in a weak child: think CMS and secure the airway.
det.thd: Sodium channel myasthenia เป็น CMS ที่พบน้อยมากจากยีน SCN4A แบบสูญเสียการทำงาน ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อไม่ตอบสนองต่อสัญญาณประสาทเมื่อกระตุ้นถี่ เด็กอ่อนแรงล้า หนังตาตก และหยุดหายใจเป็นพัก ๆ โดยเฉพาะเวลามีไข้ วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีน การรักษายังมีข้อมูลน้อย เน้นแผนดูแลการหายใจ

det.patho: SCN4A encodes the alpha subunit of Nav1.4, the main sodium channel of skeletal muscle. Gain-of-function variants that impair inactivation cause myotonia or, with more depolarisation, inexcitability and paralysis. Gating-pore leak variants underlie hypoPP type 2, while loss-of-function variants cause congenital myasthenic syndromes and congenital myopathies.
det.clinical: The phenotypes overlap within families. Paramyotonia gives cold-sensitive stiffness, typically facial and hand, sometimes followed by weakness. HyperPP gives short, frequent attacks in childhood, often with myotonia between attacks. Neonatal forms can cause stridor and apnoea. Permanent proximal weakness may develop with age.
det.diagnosis: A careful trigger history, EMG with cooling and exercise tests and potassium levels during attacks narrow the diagnosis; SCN4A sequencing confirms it. Exclude secondary causes of periodic paralysis and dystrophic myotonias.
det.treatment: Mexiletine is effective for myotonia and paramyotonia. HyperPP attacks can be shortened by light exercise, inhaled salbutamol or carbohydrate intake, and prevented by thiazide diuretics or carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide, dichlorphenamide). Avoid cold, potassium-rich foods and depolarising muscle relaxants; anaesthesia needs planning.
det.prognosis: Normal lifespan; quality of life depends on attack frequency and later fixed weakness.
pearls: Myotonia that worsens with repeated effort (paradoxical) points to SCN4A.
Eyelid paramyotonia is a quick bedside test in cold weather.
Suxamethonium can cause severe rigidity in myotonic disorders.
det.thd: Sodium channelopathies เกิดจากยีน SCN4A ใน sodium channel Nav1.4 ของกล้ามเนื้อ ทำให้เกิด paramyotonia congenita (เกร็งมากขึ้นเมื่อเจอความเย็นและใช้ซ้ำ), hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis และ potassium-aggravated myotonia วินิจฉัยด้วย EMG, cooling/exercise test และตรวจยีน การรักษาใช้ mexiletine สำหรับ myotonia และ acetazolamide หรือ thiazide เพื่อป้องกันอ่อนแรง

name: Somatic symptom disorder
formal: Persistent distressing physical symptoms with disproportionate thoughts and behaviours, frequently presenting to neurology as functional neurological disorders.
simple: Having real physical symptoms along with excessive worry about them.
th: ภาวะที่มีอาการทางกายเรื้อรังร่วมกับความคิด ความกังวล และพฤติกรรมต่ออาการมากเกินควร วินิจฉัยจากลักษณะบวก ไม่ใช่เพียงหาสาเหตุไม่พบ อาจพบร่วมกับโรคทางกายจริง ดูแลแบบต่อเนื่องและลดการตรวจซ้ำซ้อน
tempoNote: Symptoms persist, usually for more than 6 months, with changing bodily complaints over time and fluctuations under stress
feat: One or more distressing bodily symptoms (pain, fatigue, dizziness, numbness, weakness) that disrupt daily life
Excessive thoughts, anxiety or time and energy devoted to the symptoms, such as repeated consultations and tests
Can coexist with a proven medical disease; the diagnosis rests on disproportionate response, not on symptoms being unexplained
Related DSM-5-TR conditions: illness anxiety disorder (worry with few symptoms), functional neurological symptom disorder and factitious disorder
Often accompanied by depression, anxiety and functional syndromes such as fibromyalgia and irritable bowel syndrome
inv: Investigate red flags appropriately once, then avoid repeated low-yield tests
Screen for depression and anxiety (PHQ-9, GAD-7) and for somatic symptom burden (PHQ-15)
Gather previous records to coordinate care and avoid duplicated investigations

case.story: For 3 years she has had headaches, tingling hands, dizziness and fatigue; she has seen eight doctors, had three brain MRIs and spends hours each day reading about brain tumours.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination; she becomes tearful when told the latest results are normal and asks for another scan.
case.tests: MRI brain and nerve conduction studies are normal; HbA1c and B12 normal; PHQ-15 18, GAD-7 13.
case.q: What is the best way to manage her?
case.a: Somatic symptom disorder with anxiety; one named doctor offers regular scheduled visits, explains the symptoms without dismissing them, limits further tests to new red flags, and refers for CBT with an SSRI or SNRI for comorbid anxiety and pain.

read.where: Chapter 18: The approach to the difficult patient

det.patho: Somatic symptom disorder results from heightened attention to bodily sensations, catastrophic interpretation and illness behaviour, shaped by temperament, childhood illness experience, trauma, health anxiety and cultural ways of expressing distress. Central sensitisation and predictive processing models explain how real symptoms persist without tissue damage. Medical systems that reward repeated investigation can reinforce the cycle.
det.clinical: Patients present with persistent pain, fatigue, dizziness, sensory symptoms or multiple complaints across body systems and spend excessive time and worry on them. Many have been extensively investigated and feel dismissed. Illness anxiety disorder differs because worry about having a serious disease dominates while symptoms are few or mild. In Thai and other Asian settings, distress is often expressed bodily, so mood and anxiety must be asked about directly.
det.diagnosis: DSM-5-TR requires distressing somatic symptoms plus excessive thoughts, feelings or behaviours related to them, persisting for usually more than 6 months. The older requirement that symptoms be medically unexplained was removed, so the diagnosis can coexist with disease. ICD-11 uses the closely related term bodily distress disorder. Organic causes must be considered fairly, but the diagnosis should be made positively rather than after endless exclusion.
det.treatment: Management builds a consistent relationship with one clinician, regular scheduled appointments rather than crisis visits, explanation that validates symptoms, and limits on unnecessary investigation. CBT and related therapies have the best evidence, alongside graded activity and physiotherapy. Antidepressants (SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics at low dose) help comorbid depression, anxiety and pain. Avoid opioids and repeated invasive procedures.
det.prognosis: Often chronic and fluctuating, but distress and health care use can fall substantially with collaborative care.
pearls: Since DSM-5, the diagnosis no longer requires symptoms to be medically unexplained.
Scheduled visits with one doctor work better than open-ended, symptom-driven appointments.
Treat the thoughts and behaviours around the symptom, not only the symptom itself.
det.thd: Somatic symptom disorder คือภาวะที่มีอาการทางกายเรื้อรัง เช่น ปวด ชา เวียนศีรษะ อ่อนเพลีย ร่วมกับความกังวลและพฤติกรรมต่ออาการมากเกินควร เช่น ตรวจซ้ำหลายครั้ง เปลี่ยนแพทย์บ่อย การวินิจฉัยอาศัยลักษณะบวกและอาจมีโรคทางกายร่วมได้ การดูแลที่ดีคือมีแพทย์ประจำ นัดตรวจสม่ำเสมอ อธิบายอาการอย่างเข้าใจ จำกัดการตรวจที่ไม่จำเป็น และใช้ CBT ร่วมกับยาต้านซึมเศร้าเมื่อมีซึมเศร้า วิตกกังวล หรือปวดร่วม

name: Spasmodic dysphonia
formal: Focal laryngeal dystonia causing strained or breathy voice breaks during speech, treated with botulinum toxin injection.
simple: A voice problem where the voice box muscles spasm during speaking, making speech strained or shaky.

tempoNote: Usually begins insidiously between 30 and 50 years, worsens over months to a few years and then stays stable
feat: Adductor type (most common): strained, strangled voice with abrupt voice breaks on vowels and speech effort that is worse on the telephone or under stress
Abductor type: breathy, whispered voice breaks on voiceless consonants; mixed forms exist
Task-specific: speech is affected, while whispering, laughing, singing, crying or shouting may be normal or only minimally affected
May coexist with voice tremor, cervical dystonia, blepharospasm or writer's cramp, and in some families with variants such as THAP1 or TUBB4A
Sensory tricks, alcohol and sometimes a different pitch temporarily improve the voice
inv: Joint assessment by a neurologist and a laryngologist or speech-language pathologist with connected-speech tasks and perceptual rating

case.story: For a year her voice has cracked and sounded squeezed, especially on the phone and under stress. She can sing at karaoke and laugh normally.
case.exam: Intermittent strained voice breaks when counting 'eighty-eight'; normal neurological examination otherwise.
case.tests: Nasoendoscopy: irregular hyperadduction of vocal folds during speech, normal at rest and during whistling; no nodules or paralysis.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the first-line treatment?
case.a: Adductor spasmodic dysphonia (laryngeal dystonia); botulinum toxin injection into the thyroarytenoid muscles, repeated every few months, plus voice therapy.

read.where: 13 Treatment of dystonia — Botulinum toxin (spasmodic dysphonia)

det.patho: Spasmodic dysphonia is a task-specific focal dystonia of intrinsic laryngeal muscles with abnormal sensorimotor integration of laryngeal control at cortical, basal ganglia and brainstem levels. Brain imaging shows altered activation in laryngeal motor cortex and basal ganglia, and some families have dystonia genes such as THAP1, while environmental triggers such as upper respiratory infection and voice strain are reported. The speech specificity indicates that cortical speech networks are particularly affected.
det.clinical: Most patients are women between 30 and 50 years. The voice is effortful and intermittently strained (adductor type) or breathy (abductor type), is worst in conversation and on the telephone and best in laughter, singing or whispering. It causes anxiety, avoidance of social and work situations and sometimes misdiagnosis as a psychological or muscle tension voice disorder. A voice tremor often coexists. The condition is usually stable and not associated with swallowing or breathing problems.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis rests on perceptual voice analysis and flexible laryngoscopy during connected speech by an experienced neurologist and laryngologist. Look for associated dystonia and tremor, and take a drug history. Differential diagnoses are muscle tension dysphonia, vocal fold paralysis, laryngeal tremor, functional dysphonia, and speech disorders caused by Parkinson disease or ALS. Video and audio recordings document baseline severity.
det.treatment: Injection of botulinum toxin into the thyroarytenoid (and lateral cricoarytenoid) muscles, either bilaterally with small doses or unilaterally with larger doses, improves voice by about 75–95% in adductor cases with benefit lasting about 3–4 months; the adverse effects are transient breathy voice and mild swallowing difficulty. The abductor form requires posterior cricoarytenoid injection, which is less effective. Voice therapy supports the effect. Surgery such as selective laryngeal adductor denervation-reinnervation or thyroplasty gives longer relief in selected patients, and deep brain stimulation is still experimental.
det.prognosis: The disorder is lifelong but does not shorten life; with regular toxin or surgery most patients regain communicable speech.
pearls: Normal singing, laughing and whispering with a strained speaking voice suggests spasmodic dysphonia.
Look for laryngeal tremor on sustained vowels; it is often mistaken for spasmodic dysphonia.
Botulinum toxin to the thyroarytenoid muscle is the standard treatment for the adductor type.

name: Spasmodic torticollis
formal: Cervical dystonia causing involuntary neck muscle contractions, abnormal head posture and tremor, treated with botulinum toxin.
simple: Neck muscles that involuntarily twist or tilt the head.

feat: Sustained or jerky turning, tilting, flexion or extension of the head, often with shoulder elevation
Neck pain and muscle hypertrophy (e.g. sternocleidomastoid on one side)
Sensory trick: touching the chin or back of the head eases the posture
Irregular, directional head tremor that worsens when the patient resists the pull
Worse with stress, walking or fatigue; may spread to arm or face (segmental)

case.story: For 8 months her head keeps turning to the right with an aching neck; it settles if she rests a finger on her chin. She has never taken antipsychotics or metoclopramide.
case.exam: Head rotated right and tilted slightly, left sternocleidomastoid enlarged, jerky no-no tremor that worsens on turning left; rest of exam normal.
case.tests: MRI brain and cervical spine normal.
case.q: Which muscles are the usual first targets for botulinum toxin here?
case.a: Idiopathic cervical dystonia (torticollis to the right): the left sternocleidomastoid and the right splenius capitis are the main rotators to treat.

det.patho: Cervical dystonia is a network disorder involving basal ganglia, cerebellum and sensorimotor cortex, with loss of surround inhibition and abnormal sensorimotor integration. Most adult cases are idiopathic, though a few genes (e.g. GNAL, ANO3, THAP1) and trauma or drugs can cause it. Women are affected more often, and onset peaks in mid-life.
det.clinical: Posture is described by its components: rotation (torticollis), tilt (laterocollis), flexion (anterocollis), extension (retrocollis) and lateral or sagittal shift. Pain is common and often drives disability more than the posture. Up to a third have head tremor, and some later develop dystonia in the arm, jaw or eyelids. Spontaneous remission occurs in a minority, often relapsing later.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on recognising patterned, directional muscle overactivity, a sensory trick and the null point. Imaging is needed if onset is in childhood, if there is fixed posture, pain from bone or other neurological signs. Exclude drugs, Wilson disease in younger patients, atlantoaxial subluxation, posterior fossa or cervical lesions and ocular torticollis from trochlear palsy.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin injections every three months are first-line and help most patients; doses and muscles depend on the posture pattern, and EMG or ultrasound guidance improves targeting of deep muscles. Oral anticholinergics, clonazepam or baclofen give modest help. Physiotherapy supports injections. Pallidal (GPi) deep brain stimulation is an option for refractory cases.
det.prognosis: It is a long-term condition, but most patients achieve worthwhile relief with repeated toxin injections; a small proportion remit spontaneously.
pearls: A sensory trick strongly supports dystonia over other causes of abnormal neck posture.
Rotation to one side is driven by the opposite SCM and the same-side splenius.
Always ask about metoclopramide, antipsychotics and antiemetics.

name: Spasmus nutans
formal: Infantile triad of asymmetric pendular nystagmus, head nodding and torticollis, usually benign but chiasmal gliomas must be excluded.

case.who: 10-month-old boy at an eye hospital in Bangkok
case.story: Parents noticed his left eye shimmering and his head bobbing for two months; he tilts his head to look at toys.
case.exam: Fine high-frequency pendular nystagmus mainly in the left eye, head nodding, head tilt; normal fundi and development.
case.tests: MRI brain and orbits normal; ERG normal.

det.patho: The cause of idiopathic spasmus nutans is unknown; immaturity of the developing ocular motor and visual systems is suspected. Head nodding appears to be a compensatory strategy that reduces nystagmus through vestibulo-ocular interaction. Identical signs can arise from lesions of the anterior visual pathway, which is why imaging is required.
det.clinical: The triad usually emerges during infancy and fades within a few years. The nystagmus is characteristically fine, rapid, shimmering and dissociated between the eyes. Not all three features are always present. Some children retain subtle nystagmus or have mild amblyopia or strabismus.
det.diagnosis: Spasmus nutans is diagnosed only after excluding other causes; brain MRI including orbits is recommended for all, to exclude optic pathway glioma and other suprasellar lesions. Retinal dystrophies (e.g. congenital stationary night blindness) can mimic it and may need ERG.
det.treatment: No treatment is needed for idiopathic cases beyond monitoring and correcting refractive error, amblyopia or strabismus. Treat any underlying lesion found.
det.prognosis: Excellent; symptoms usually resolve by early childhood.
pearls: Shimmering, monocular nystagmus in an infant: image the chiasm.
Head nodding may be compensatory — it can reduce the nystagmus.
Normal MRI plus normal fundi: reassure and follow.

name: Spastic ataxia

simple: An inherited condition causing stiff legs and poor balance.

feat: Combination of lower-limb spasticity, extensor plantars and cerebellar ataxia
Distal amyotrophy and sensorimotor neuropathy (axonal and demyelinating) in ARSACS
Thickened retinal nerve fibre layer on OCT; yellow streaks around the disc
Pes cavus and dysarthria; nystagmus and saccadic pursuit
Other causes: SPG7, dominant SPAX genes, some SCAs and leukodystrophies
inv: MRI: superior vermis atrophy, linear pontine T2 hypointensities, thick middle cerebellar peduncles (ARSACS)
Nerve conduction: mixed axonal–demyelinating neuropathy

case.who: 16-year-old boy from Lopburi; parents are related

case.exam: Spastic ataxic gait, brisk knees but absent ankle jerks, extensor plantars, distal wasting, dysarthria, gaze-evoked nystagmus.
case.tests: MRI: superior vermis atrophy and pontine linear hypointense stripes; OCT: thick RNFL; biallelic SACS variants.

Chapter 24 Cerebellar Ataxias and Related Conditions — Inherited Ataxia Syndromes

det.patho: Spastic ataxias are inherited disorders affecting both corticospinal tracts and cerebellar pathways. ARSACS, the prototype, is caused by biallelic SACS variants; sacsin is a large chaperone-like protein involved in neurofilament organisation and mitochondrial dynamics, and its loss produces neurofilament bundling in neurons. Founder mutations explain the high prevalence in Quebec, but cases are found worldwide, including Asia.
det.clinical: ARSACS begins with gait unsteadiness in early childhood, followed by spasticity, dysarthria, distal wasting and neuropathy, with loss of walking often in mid-adulthood. Cognitive problems and urinary symptoms may occur. Other spastic ataxias present later and may be dominant (SPAX genes) or recessive (SPG7, which can look like an adult-onset cerebellar ataxia with mild spasticity).
det.diagnosis: The combination of pyramidal and cerebellar signs with neuropathy and the characteristic MRI and OCT features strongly suggests ARSACS. Next-generation sequencing panels or exome confirm the gene. Exclude acquired causes such as vitamin B12, copper or vitamin E deficiency, MS, cervical myelopathy and HTLV-1.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy exists. Physiotherapy, antispasticity drugs (baclofen, tizanidine) or botulinum toxin, orthoses, speech therapy and management of bladder symptoms improve function. Genetic counselling is important in consanguineous families.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; many need a wheelchair by the fourth or fifth decade, with reduced but often near-normal lifespan.
pearls: Spasticity + ataxia + neuropathy in a child: think ARSACS.
Linear pontine T2 hypointensities and thick RNFL on OCT are distinctive clues.
SPG7 is a common cause of adult-onset spastic ataxia.
det.thd: Spastic ataxia คือกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่มีทั้งขาเกร็งและเดินเซจาก cerebellum ตัวอย่างสำคัญคือ ARSACS จากยีน SACS ซึ่งเริ่มตั้งแต่เด็ก มี neuropathy ร่วม MRI พบ vermis ฝ่อและเส้นดำใน pons และ OCT พบ RNFL หนา วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีนและแยกภาวะขาดวิตามิน ไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ ใช้กายภาพบำบัดและยาลดเกร็ง

case.story: Two years of tingling and burning in both hands, then stiffness of the legs over six months.
case.exam: Reduced pain sensation over both arms, mild hand weakness, brisk reflexes and Babinski signs bilaterally.
case.tests: MRI shows a well-circumscribed enhancing intramedullary mass at C3–C5 with a haemosiderin cap and syrinx above and below.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and best treatment?
case.a: Spinal cord ependymoma; gross total microsurgical resection under neuromonitoring, often curative.

det.patho: Spinal ependymomas arise from ependymal cells of the central canal. Classic spinal ependymomas frequently show NF2 alterations and have a relatively indolent course. A distinct MYCN-amplified spinal ependymoma behaves aggressively with early dissemination. Myxopapillary ependymomas arise from the filum terminale and are now graded as CNS WHO grade 2.
det.clinical: Patients present with long-standing neck or back pain, sensory disturbance in the arms, and later weakness, spasticity and sphincter symptoms. Central location produces dissociated sensory loss. Haemorrhage into the tumour may cause sudden worsening. NF2 patients can have multiple spinal tumours.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows a central, well-demarcated enhancing mass with cord expansion, cysts and a haemosiderin cap. Whole-spine and brain imaging assess multiplicity and dissemination. Histology and molecular profiling confirm the diagnosis and identify aggressive subtypes.
det.treatment: Gross total resection through a midline myelotomy with neurophysiological monitoring is the treatment of choice and often curative because a cleavage plane usually exists. Radiotherapy is reserved for subtotal resection, recurrence or aggressive variants. Long-term MRI follow-up is needed.
det.prognosis: Excellent local control after complete resection; neurological outcome mirrors preoperative function.
pearls: Haemosiderin cap and central location favour ependymoma over astrocytoma.
Operate early — postoperative function rarely exceeds preoperative status.
Check for NF2 in young patients or multiple tumours.

case.who: 58-year-old taxi driver from Bangkok with hypertension and diabetes
case.story: While lifting a suitcase he felt a sudden stabbing pain between his shoulder blades; within 30 minutes both legs gave way and he could not pass urine.
case.exam: Flaccid paraplegia, areflexia, loss of pinprick and temperature below T6, but vibration and joint position normal at the toes; distended bladder.
case.tests: MRI at 8 h: longitudinal T2 hyperintensity of the anterior thoracic cord with restricted diffusion; CTA aorta: no dissection; CSF 2 cells, protein normal.
case.q: Which arterial syndrome explains this sensory pattern?
case.a: Anterior spinal artery infarction — the dorsal columns, supplied by the posterior spinal arteries, are spared.

read.where: Chapter 22: Neurologic Complications Of Cardiac Surgery
Section 6 Systemic Disorders That Also Involve the Cerebrovascular System

det.patho: The cord is supplied by one anterior spinal artery (anterior two-thirds) and paired posterior spinal arteries (dorsal columns), reinforced by segmental radicular arteries, most importantly the artery of Adamkiewicz (usually T9–L2 on the left). The upper thoracic cord is a relative watershed. Causes include aortic disease and surgery (open or endovascular repair), systemic hypotension, atherosclerosis or dissection of segmental arteries, fibrocartilaginous embolism of disc material, vasculitis and hypercoagulable states; a substantial proportion remain cryptogenic. Spinal cord infarction makes up about 1% of all strokes.
det.clinical: The anterior spinal artery syndrome — bilateral weakness, spinothalamic sensory loss and sphincter failure with preserved posterior column sensation — is the commonest form. Posterior spinal artery infarcts produce loss of proprioception and vibration with milder weakness. Sulcal artery infarcts give a hemicord (Brown-Séquard-like) picture, and central watershed infarcts after hypotension can cause pure motor loss. Pain at onset is common; peak deficit is usually reached within hours, which helps separate it from inflammatory myelitis.
det.diagnosis: Use clinical tempo plus MRI. Early MRI may be normal; repeat within 24–72 h with axial T2 and DWI. Supportive features include paired bright dots in both anterior horns on axial T2 ('owl-eye' sign), adjacent vertebral body infarction, and absence of enhancement initially. CSF is typically non-inflammatory. Image the aorta and look for embolic or haematological causes. Published diagnostic criteria (2019) rely on hyperacute onset, typical MRI and exclusion of alternatives.
det.treatment: There is no proven acute reperfusion therapy, though thrombolysis has been used in selected cases. Raise mean arterial pressure, avoid hypotension, and after aortic surgery use lumbar CSF drainage to improve cord perfusion pressure. Treat the cause (aortic repair, antiplatelet and statin for atherosclerotic disease). Supportive care includes bladder catheterisation, bowel regimen, pressure-area care, VTE prophylaxis and early rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: Outcome is variable: severe initial deficit and absent early improvement predict poor recovery, but many patients regain some walking ability; mortality is related to the underlying aortic or systemic disease.
pearls: Sudden back pain + paraplegia + spared vibration/position sense = anterior spinal artery infarct.
Peak deficit within hours favours infarction; days favours myelitis.
A normal MRI at 3 hours does not exclude it — repeat with DWI.
det.thd: Spinal cord infarction คือไขสันหลังขาดเลือดเฉียบพลัน มักเป็นเขต anterior spinal artery ผู้ป่วยมีปวดหลังเฉียบพลันแล้วขาอ่อนแรงภายในไม่กี่ชั่วโมง สูญเสียความรู้สึกเจ็บและร้อนเย็นใต้ระดับรอยโรค ปัสสาวะไม่ออก แต่การรับรู้ตำแหน่งข้อและการสั่นยังปกติ สาเหตุที่สำคัญคือโรคเอออร์ตา การผ่าตัดเอออร์ตา และความดันต่ำ วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI รวม DWI ซึ่งอาจต้องทำซ้ำ รักษาโดยเพิ่มความดัน ระบาย CSF ในรายหลังผ่าตัดเอออร์ตา แก้สาเหตุ และฟื้นฟู

det.patho: Bacteria reach the cord by haematogenous spread from distant infection, by contiguous spread from a dermal sinus or adjacent infection, or after trauma or surgery. Staphylococci and streptococci predominate, with Gram-negative, anaerobic, tuberculous, fungal and Listeria causes in some settings. Focal myelitis evolves into a capsulated collection that compresses and destroys cord tissue.
det.clinical: Acute cases resemble transverse myelitis with fever and pain; chronic cases mimic an intramedullary tumour over weeks. Children with a congenital dermal sinus may have recurrent meningitis before the abscess. Deficits can progress rapidly to complete paraplegia.
det.diagnosis: MRI with contrast and diffusion-weighted imaging is essential; restricted diffusion favours abscess over tumour. Search for the source (echo, chest imaging, skin and spine inspection). Definitive microbiology comes from surgical aspirate. TB must be considered in Thailand, especially with subacute course.
det.treatment: Combine urgent neurosurgical drainage (myelotomy and aspiration) with prolonged IV antibiotics, typically 6–8 weeks or longer, tailored to culture. Empirical therapy should cover staphylococci including MRSA where relevant, streptococci and Gram-negatives. Repair the dermal sinus and treat the primary source. Steroids are controversial.
det.prognosis: Outcome depends on deficit before treatment; mortality has fallen with MRI and antibiotics but residual paraparesis is common.
pearls: Fever plus myelopathy plus spinal dimple in a child: look for a dermal sinus abscess.
Diffusion restriction helps separate abscess from tumour.
Chronic intramedullary abscess may be afebrile.
det.thd: Spinal cord intramedullary abscess คือหนองภายในไขสันหลังซึ่งพบน้อยมาก เชื้อมาจากกระแสเลือดหรือรูต่อแต่กำเนิดที่ผิวหนังหลัง ผู้ป่วยมีไข้ ปวดหลัง ขาอ่อนแรงเร็ว และปัสสาวะผิดปกติ MRI พบก้อน ring-enhancing และ restricted diffusion การรักษาต้องผ่าตัดระบายหนองร่วมกับให้ยาปฏิชีวนะทางหลอดเลือดหลายสัปดาห์

feat: Classified by compartment: extradural (mostly metastases), intradural extramedullary (meningioma, schwannoma), intramedullary (ependymoma, astrocytoma, haemangioblastoma)
Pain (local or radicular, often nocturnal) is usually the first symptom
Progressive myelopathy with spasticity, sensory level and later sphincter dysfunction
Extramedullary lesions often give Brown–Séquard patterns; intramedullary lesions give suspended sensory loss
Associations: NF1, NF2, VHL
inv: MRI whole spine with contrast
CT for bony involvement; staging CT for suspected metastases
Histology; spinal angiography for vascular tumours

case.story: Eighteen months of right-sided chest wall band pain at night, now numb legs and unsteady walking.
case.exam: Spastic paraparesis, right leg weaker, left-sided pain loss below T7, right-sided proprioceptive loss.
case.tests: MRI shows a dural-based, homogeneously enhancing intradural extramedullary mass at T5 with dural tail, compressing the cord from the right.
case.q: What is the likely tumour and outcome after treatment?
case.a: Spinal meningioma; surgical resection usually leads to good neurological recovery.

det.patho: Spinal tumours injure the cord by compression, vascular compromise and, for intramedullary tumours, direct infiltration. Extradural metastases from breast, lung, prostate, kidney and myeloma are commonest overall. Intradural extramedullary tumours, mainly meningiomas and nerve sheath tumours, grow slowly and displace the cord. Intramedullary tumours are less frequent and expand the cord from within.
det.clinical: Pain, often worse lying down or at night, typically precedes neurological deficits by months in benign tumours. Radicular pain may mimic cardiac, abdominal or disc disease. Progressive myelopathy follows, and sphincter disturbance usually appears late. Metastatic compression can progress to paraplegia within days.
det.diagnosis: Contrast-enhanced MRI localises the compartment and suggests tumour type: dural tail for meningioma, dumbbell foraminal extension for schwannoma, central expansion for ependymoma. Whole-spine imaging excludes multiple lesions. Biopsy or resection gives the histological diagnosis, and systemic staging is performed for suspected metastases.
det.treatment: Benign intradural extramedullary tumours are treated by surgical excision with excellent results. Intramedullary tumours need specialised microsurgery with neuromonitoring. Metastatic compression requires dexamethasone, surgery for selected patients and radiotherapy. Stereotactic radiosurgery is an option for some lesions.
det.prognosis: Benign extramedullary tumours have excellent outcomes after resection; outcome in metastatic disease depends on ambulatory status and primary tumour.
pearls: Night-time band-like pain that is not cardiac or abdominal: image the thoracic spine.
Compartment on MRI predicts the tumour type.
Meningiomas are typically thoracic and in women.
det.thd: Spinal cord tumours คือเนื้องอกในช่องกระดูกสันหลัง แบ่งเป็นนอกเยื่อหุ้ม (มักเป็นมะเร็งแพร่กระจาย) ในเยื่อหุ้มแต่อยู่นอกไขสันหลัง (meningioma, schwannoma) และภายในเนื้อไขสันหลัง (ependymoma, astrocytoma) อาการแรกมักเป็นปวดหลังหรือปวดร้าวตอนกลางคืน แล้วตามด้วยขาอ่อนแรง เกร็ง ชา และปัสสาวะผิดปกติ การวินิจฉัยใช้ MRI ฉีดสี การรักษาคือผ่าตัด ฉายรังสี และยา steroid ในรายที่ถูกกดเฉียบพลัน

name: Spinal epidural abscess
formal: Infection in the epidural space (Staphylococcus aureus) causing back pain, fever and rapidly progressive neurological deficit, an emergency.
simple: A pocket of infection near the spinal cord causing back pain, fever and weakness.
ab: ฝีในช่องไขสันหลัง
th: ฝีหนองในช่อง epidural ของกระดูกสันหลัง มักจากเชื้อ Staphylococcus aureus ปวดหลังรุนแรง ไข้ แล้วอ่อนแรงขา ต้อง MRI และผ่าตัดด่วน
tempoNote: Back pain over days, then radicular pain, then weakness that can progress to paralysis within hours
feat: Severe localised back or neck pain with spinal tenderness
Fever (absent in a third or more), then radicular pain
Rapidly evolving weakness, sensory level and sphincter disturbance
Risk factors: diabetes, injecting drug use, recent spinal procedure or epidural, bacteraemia, haemodialysis
inv: Urgent gadolinium MRI of the whole spine (skip lesions occur)
Blood cultures (positive in about 60%), CRP and ESR (usually high), white count
CT-guided or operative aspirate for culture if blood cultures negative; avoid LP through the abscess

case.who: 61-year-old woman from Nakhon Si Thammarat with diabetes on haemodialysis
case.story: Five days of thoracic back pain, fever since yesterday, and this morning her legs feel heavy and she cannot pass urine.
case.exam: Temperature 38.9 °C, tenderness over T8, leg power 3/5, brisk knees, sensory level at T10, palpable bladder.
case.tests: CRP 210 mg/L, blood cultures grow MRSA; MRI T7–T9 dorsal epidural collection with rim enhancement compressing the cord.
case.q: What must happen now?
case.a: Spinal epidural abscess with cord compression: emergency surgical decompression and IV vancomycin, with spine surgeons involved immediately.

det.patho: Bacteria reach the epidural space by haematogenous spread (skin, urinary, dialysis access), by extension from spondylodiscitis or psoas abscess, or directly via procedures. Staphylococcus aureus causes about two thirds of cases, with MRSA increasingly common; Gram-negatives, streptococci and TB occur too. Cord damage results from direct compression plus septic thrombophlebitis and ischaemia, so deficits can worsen abruptly.
det.clinical: Classic progression is back pain, then nerve-root pain, then weakness and sensory and sphincter loss, and finally paralysis. The full triad of pain, fever and deficit is seen in only a minority at first contact, which leads to frequent misdiagnosis as musculoskeletal pain. Thoracic and lumbar regions are most often affected. Keep a high index of suspicion in at-risk patients with new back pain and raised CRP.
det.diagnosis: Gadolinium MRI of the whole spine is the test of choice, showing an enhancing epidural collection and often associated discitis or osteomyelitis. CRP and ESR are almost always raised and help trigger imaging. Blood cultures before antibiotics; if negative, obtain tissue by CT-guided or surgical aspiration. In Thailand, tuberculous and melioidosis spinal infection are important differentials, so request mycobacterial culture and Burkholderia-friendly media.
det.treatment: Emergency decompression with drainage plus antibiotics is standard for patients with neurological deficit; selected patients without deficit can be treated medically with very close neurological and imaging follow-up, but failure is common in diabetics, MRSA infection and high CRP. Empirical IV vancomycin plus an anti-Gram-negative agent (e.g. ceftriaxone or cefepime) is tailored to cultures. Treat for 6 weeks or longer if vertebral osteomyelitis is present.
det.prognosis: Outcome mirrors the deficit at surgery: those operated before paralysis or within about 24–36 hours of its onset recover best; mortality is around 5–15%.
pearls: Back pain + fever + high CRP in a diabetic or dialysis patient: image the whole spine urgently.
Do not wait for the triad; deficits can become irreversible within hours.
Never perform LP through a suspected epidural abscess.
det.thd: Spinal epidural abscess คือหนองในช่อง epidural ของกระดูกสันหลัง ส่วนใหญ่จาก Staphylococcus aureus ผู้ป่วยมีปวดหลังเฉพาะที่ ไข้ ปวดร้าวตามรากประสาท แล้วอ่อนแรงและปัสสาวะไม่ออกอย่างรวดเร็ว ปัจจัยเสี่ยงคือเบาหวาน ฟอกไต หรือเพิ่งทำหัตถการที่หลัง วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI ทั้งแนวกระดูกสันหลังพร้อมฉีดสี CRP มักสูงมาก รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัดระบายหนองด่วนร่วมกับยาปฏิชีวนะ ผลการรักษาขึ้นกับความรุนแรงของอาการก่อนผ่าตัด

name: Spinal epidural haematoma
formal: Collection of blood in the epidural space, spontaneous or anticoagulant related, with sudden back pain and cord compression.
simple: Bleeding around the spinal cord that causes sudden severe back pain and weakness.
th: Spinal epidural haematoma คือเลือดคั่งนอกเยื่อดูราในช่องไขสันหลัง มักเกิดในผู้ที่กินยากันเลือดหรือหลังเจาะหลัง/ฉีดยาชา epidural ผู้ป่วยปวดหลังหรือคอรุนแรงทันที ตามด้วยขาอ่อนแรง ชา และปัสสาวะไม่ออกภายในชั่วโมงถึงวัน ต้องทำ MRI ทั้งแนวกระดูกสันหลังทันที กลับฤทธิ์ยากันเลือด และผ่าตัด laminectomy ระบายก้อนเลือดโดยเร็ว ผลลัพธ์ดีกว่าถ้าผ่าตัดภายในไม่กี่ชั่วโมง
tempoNote: Severe pain at onset, then weakness evolving over minutes to hours, occasionally days
feat: Abrupt severe neck or back pain, often radicular or encircling the trunk, sometimes after minor strain, coughing or a procedure
Rapid paraparesis or tetraparesis, sensory level and sphincter failure; motor weakness may go unnoticed when bedridden with pain

A third of recent cases are associated with anticoagulants, and antiplatelets, thrombolytics, bleeding disorders, neuraxial puncture or catheter removal, spinal surgery, trauma and chiropractic manipulation raise risk
Spontaneous cases are rare and often thoracic or cervicothoracic; a haematoma from a vascular malformation, haemangioma or tumour is possible; a cervical haematoma can mimic a stroke with hemiparesis
The clot usually lies posterior to the cord, which allows removal by laminectomy
inv: Emergency MRI of the whole spine (T1, T2, gradient-echo); CT myelography if MRI cannot be done
INR, aPTT, platelets, fibrinogen, anti-Xa or drug-specific tests, and renal function
Spinal angiography later if a vascular malformation is suspected

case.who: 73-year-old man from Phichit on rivaroxaban for atrial fibrillation
case.story: He felt a tearing pain between the shoulder blades as he lifted a sack of rice; four hours later both legs were weak and numb and he could not urinate.
case.exam: Paraparesis 2/5, sensory level at T6, urinary retention, normal arms and cranial nerves.
case.tests: Creatinine clearance 40 mL/min; MRI shows a dorsal epidural collection from T3 to T6 compressing the cord.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what are the first steps?
case.a: Spontaneous spinal epidural haematoma on a direct oral anticoagulant. Stop the drug and reverse anticoagulation (prothrombin complex concentrate or andexanet alfa), then perform urgent decompressive laminectomy and haematoma evacuation; do not give thrombolysis.

det.patho: The valveless epidural venous plexus can bleed after sudden pressure rises or trauma, and less often arterial or malformation sources bleed. Anticoagulants, antiplatelet agents, thrombolytics and coagulopathy greatly increase the risk, as do neuraxial anaesthesia, lumbar puncture and spinal surgery. The expanding clot compresses the cord or cauda equina and impairs its blood supply, so damage depends on speed and duration of compression. Over 200 cases of varied cause have been reported, so it is rare but remains important.
det.clinical: Severe local pain with radicular component is the first sign, followed by neurological deficit that usually evolves over hours but sometimes over days. The level is most often thoracic in spontaneous cases. Cervical haematomas can produce hemiparesis and be mistaken for stroke, a dangerous error if thrombolysis is considered. After a neuraxial procedure or catheter removal, new back pain, leg numbness or weakness, or bowel and bladder dysfunction should be treated as a haematoma until proven otherwise.
det.diagnosis: Whole-spine MRI is the test of choice and shows an extradural collection whose signal changes with the age of blood. Check clotting studies, platelet count and anticoagulant activity at the same time. Differentiate from abscess (fever, inflammatory markers, rim enhancement), infarct (intramedullary signal) and myelitis by position and time course. Angiography is reserved for suspected vascular malformation or tumour.
det.treatment: Reverse anticoagulation and correct coagulopathy at once (vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate for warfarin, protamine for heparin, specific reversal agents or concentrates for DOACs), and arrange immediate surgical laminectomy with evacuation for significant or worsening deficits; results are better the sooner decompression is achieved, with good outcomes reported after surgery within about 6 to 12 hours and most recoveries within 72 hours. Spontaneous recovery without surgery is rare but described in patients with mild or quickly improving deficits, who may be observed closely. High surgical risk patients may need percutaneous drainage or conservative care. High-dose methylprednisolone is no longer recommended. Plan the timing of anticoagulant resumption with the cause.
det.prognosis: Outcome depends mainly on the pre-operative deficit and the delay to decompression; incomplete lesions operated early often recover well.
pearls: Sudden spinal pain plus leg weakness in an anticoagulated patient is a haematoma until proven otherwise.
A cervical epidural bleed can mimic stroke: ask about neck pain before thrombolysis.
Reverse anticoagulation first, then decompress without delay.
det.thd: Spinal epidural haematoma คือเลือดคั่งนอกเยื่อดูราที่กดไขสันหลัง พบมากในผู้ที่กินยากันเลือดหรือหลังหัตถการเจาะหลัง/epidural ผู้ป่วยปวดหลังหรือคอรุนแรงทันที ตามด้วยอ่อนแรงของขา ชา และปัสสาวะไม่ออกภายในไม่กี่ชั่วโมง การตรวจที่ดีที่สุดคือ MRI ทั้งแนวกระดูกสันหลัง และต้องตรวจการแข็งตัวของเลือดทันที รักษาโดยกลับฤทธิ์ยากันเลือดและผ่าตัด laminectomy นำก้อนเลือดออกโดยเร็ว ซึ่งช่วยให้ฟื้นตัวดีขึ้น

qx.stem: A 71-year-old retired teacher on apixaban for atrial fibrillation had a lumbar epidural steroid injection the previous afternoon. Overnight he developed severe back pain and over 6 hours both legs became weak, with numbness below the groin and urinary retention. MRI shows a dorsal epidural collection from T11 to L2 compressing the conus.
qx.q: What should be done next?
opts: High-dose methylprednisolone and repeat MRI in 24 hours
Reverse the anticoagulant and perform urgent decompressive laminectomy and evacuation
Lumbar puncture to exclude meningitis
Continue apixaban and arrange physiotherapy
Interventional radiology drain under CT guidance in a week
qx.why: A spinal epidural haematoma causing progressive deficit is a surgical emergency, and outcome is best when decompression happens within hours of onset. Anticoagulation should be reversed (andexanet alfa or prothrombin complex concentrate for a factor Xa inhibitor) before urgent laminectomy. Steroids do not relieve compression, and delay or lumbar puncture risks permanent paraplegia.

name: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA)
formal: Autosomal recessive SMN1-related motor neuron disease causing hypotonia, proximal weakness and areflexia; treated with nusinersen and gene therapy.
simple: An inherited disease where nerve cells to muscles are lost, causing weakness, mainly in children.
more: Diagnosis by SMN1 homozygous deletion testing; SMN2 copy number predicts severity. Risdiplam is an oral splice modifier; early presymptomatic treatment from newborn screening greatly improves outcome.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมเซลล์ประสาทสั่งการไขสันหลังเสื่อม (SMN1) — อ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขาสมมาตร ตั้งแต่ทารกถึงผู้ใหญ่ มียารักษา
feat: Symmetric proximal weakness, legs more than arms; hypotonia and areflexia
Severity by type: type 1 never sits, type 2 sits but never walks, type 3 walks, type 4 adult onset
Tongue fasciculation and fine hand tremor (minipolymyoclonus); face relatively spared
Respiratory weakness with relatively spared diaphragm (bell-shaped chest in infants)
inv: SMN1 exon 7 homozygous deletion; SMN2 copy number predicts severity
CK normal or mildly raised; EMG neurogenic

case.exam: Symmetric proximal leg weakness, absent knee jerks, tongue fasciculation, normal eye movements and alert face.
case.tests: SMN1 exon 7 homozygous deletion; 3 copies of SMN2.
case.q: Which treatments target the underlying defect?

qx.stem: A 5-month-old infant from Nakhon Ratchasima has no functioning SMN1 copies and is being counselled. The parents ask which genetic factor mainly determines whether the disease will be severe or mild.

aN: sma | spinal muscular atrophy | 5q sma | werdnig hoffmann | kugelberg welander | smn1

det.patho: 5q SMA is autosomal recessive and caused by loss of the SMN1 gene, usually by homozygous exon 7 deletion. The nearby SMN2 gene produces mostly truncated protein because of exon 7 skipping, so the number of SMN2 copies determines how much functional SMN protein remains and therefore the severity. Low SMN levels cause degeneration of anterior horn cells and lower brainstem motor nuclei. Before modern therapy it was a leading genetic cause of death in infancy.
det.clinical: Weakness is symmetric, proximal and greater in the legs than the arms, with hypotonia, areflexia, tongue fasciculations and preserved alertness. Type 0 presents before birth; type 1 infants never sit and have paradoxical breathing; type 2 sit but never walk; type 3 walk but may later lose ambulation; type 4 begins in adulthood. Intercostal weakness with a relatively spared diaphragm causes a bell-shaped chest. Scoliosis, contractures and feeding difficulty are major complications.
det.diagnosis: SMN1 deletion testing (MLPA or qPCR) confirms most cases, and SMN2 copy number is reported for prognosis and treatment planning. About 5% are compound heterozygous for a deletion and a point mutation, requiring sequencing. Newborn screening allows treatment before symptoms. CK is normal or mildly raised and EMG is neurogenic; biopsy is no longer needed.
det.treatment: Disease-modifying options include intrathecal nusinersen (antisense oligonucleotide increasing full-length SMN2 transcript), oral daily risdiplam (SMN2 splicing modifier) and onasemnogene abeparvovec (one-time AAV9 SMN1 gene therapy). Earliest possible treatment, ideally presymptomatic, gives the best results. Standard care covers respiratory support, nutrition, scoliosis management and physiotherapy.
det.prognosis: Treatment has transformed the outlook: many presymptomatically treated infants reach motor milestones close to normal, while untreated type 1 is usually fatal within two years.
pearls: Alert, floppy infant with tongue fasciculations and absent reflexes: test SMN1.
SMN2 copy number is the main modifier of severity.
Time is motor neurons — treat as early as possible.
det.thd: SMA เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมแบบยีนด้อย เกิดจากการขาดยีน SMN1 ทำให้เซลล์ประสาทสั่งการในไขสันหลังเสื่อม ความรุนแรงขึ้นกับจำนวนสำเนาของยีน SMN2 อาการคืออ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขาสมมาตร กล้ามเนื้อปวกเปียก รีเฟล็กซ์หาย ลิ้นเต้น แต่เด็กยังตื่นตัวดี การวินิจฉัยใช้การตรวจยีน SMN1 ปัจจุบันมียารักษา ได้แก่ nusinersen, risdiplam และ onasemnogene ซึ่งได้ผลดีที่สุดเมื่อเริ่มก่อนมีอาการ

name: Spinal myoclonus
formal: Jerks from spinal cord lesions or irritation, rhythmic or arrhythmic and persisting during sleep, caused by tumour, myelitis or trauma.
simple: Muscle jerks that begin in the spinal cord.
th: การกระตุกของกล้ามเนื้อที่มีต้นกำเนิดจากไขสันหลัง แบ่งเป็นแบบ segmental และ propriospinal อาจเกิดจากเนื้องอก myelitis หรือการบาดเจ็บ และมักไม่หายขณะหลับ
tempoNote: Onset follows the underlying lesion; jerks often persistent once established
feat: Segmental form: rhythmic jerks of a limb or trunk segment, continuing in sleep
Propriospinal form: axial flexion jerks of trunk, hips and neck, worse lying supine or when drowsy
Little influence of voluntary action, unlike cortical myoclonus
Causes: myelitis, tumour, trauma, ischaemia, syrinx, spinal anaesthesia, drugs
Many propriospinal cases turn out to be functional
inv: MRI whole spine with contrast
Multichannel surface EMG: long bursts (>100 ms); in propriospinal form, slow spread from one segment up and down
Back-averaging for Bereitschaftspotential to identify functional jerks; CSF if inflammation suspected

case.story: Two months of sudden jerks of trunk and hips when lying down to sleep, flinging him forward; no daytime weakness.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination; observed axial flexion jerks when lying supine.
case.tests: MRI spine normal; polymyography: jerks start in thoracic paraspinal muscles and spread slowly rostrally and caudally; no Bereitschaftspotential.
case.q: What type of myoclonus is this?
case.a: Propriospinal myoclonus, a form of spinal myoclonus; functional aetiology still to be considered carefully.

18 - Myoclonus: Phenomenology, etiology, physiology, and treatment

det.patho: Spinal myoclonus arises when spinal interneuron circuits escape supraspinal control or become hyperexcitable. In segmental myoclonus the generator is confined to a few segments; in propriospinal myoclonus, activity spreads slowly through long propriospinal pathways. Inflammation, compression, ischaemia, trauma and drugs can trigger these generators.
det.clinical: Segmental jerks are rhythmic and stereotyped, involve limb or trunk muscles of contiguous segments and persist in sleep. Propriospinal jerks are axial flexion movements, often in the relaxation period before sleep. Patients may complain of insomnia or embarrassment more than weakness. The neurological examination is either normal or reveals a myelopathy.
det.diagnosis: Neurophysiology defines the pattern and helps distinguish organic from functional jerks, which is crucial because many apparent propriospinal cases are functional. MRI looks for a cord lesion, and CSF, infection and autoimmune tests follow imaging findings.
det.treatment: Treat the cause. Clonazepam is commonly used, and levetiracetam, other antiseizure drugs or botulinum toxin for focal jerks have reported benefit. Functional forms respond best to explanation and physiotherapy-based rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: Variable; lesion-related jerks may persist, whereas inflammatory or drug-induced jerks often resolve.
pearls: Jerks that continue during sleep suggest a spinal generator.
Propriospinal myoclonus is often functional; check for Bereitschaftspotential.
Always image the entire spine.
det.thd: Spinal myoclonus คือการกระตุกที่เกิดจากไขสันหลัง แบ่งเป็น segmental (กระตุกเป็นจังหวะเฉพาะไม่กี่ปล้อง ไม่หายขณะหลับ) และ propriospinal (ลำตัวงอเกร็งกระตุกตอนนอนราบ) สาเหตุคือ myelitis เนื้องอก การบาดเจ็บ หรือยา แต่ propriospinal หลายรายเป็น functional การตรวจหลักคือ MRI ไขสันหลังและ EMG การรักษาคือแก้สาเหตุร่วมกับ clonazepam หรือ levetiracetam

ddx.pt: Variable latency, distractibility, Bereitschaftspotential before jerks
Brief distal action-induced jerks with giant SEPs and EEG correlate

name: Spinal neuronitis
formal: Inflammatory disorder of anterior horn or dorsal root ganglia, often post-infectious, with segmental weakness or sensory loss.
simple: Inflammation of nerve cells in the spinal cord causing weakness or numbness.
th: คำเรียกเชิงบรรยายสำหรับการอักเสบของ anterior horn หรือปมประสาทรากหลัง มักตามหลังติดเชื้อ ทำให้อ่อนแรงหรือชาเป็นปล้อง ไม่ใช่โรคที่มีเกณฑ์ชัดเจน
tempoNote: Days to weeks, often following a viral illness
feat: Segmental lower motor neuron weakness with wasting and areflexia in one or two limbs
Or segmental sensory loss and ataxia from dorsal root ganglion involvement
Preceding viral infection or vaccination in some
Not a well-defined disease; usually reclassified once a cause (enterovirus, VZV, flavivirus, autoimmune ganglionopathy) is found
inv: MRI spine: anterior horn or dorsal column signal; exclude compression
CSF: cells, protein, viral PCR and IgM
EMG/NCS: segmental denervation or non-length-dependent sensory loss

case.story: A week after a febrile illness with mouth ulcers, his left arm became weak and thin over five days.
case.exam: Flaccid weakness of left deltoid and biceps, absent biceps jerk, normal sensation.
case.tests: MRI: T2 signal in left anterior horn C5–C6; CSF 40 lymphocytes/µL; enterovirus PCR positive in throat swab.
case.q: How would you label this, and what is the outlook?
case.a: Enterovirus-associated anterior horn involvement (acute flaccid myelitis/spinal neuronitis); supportive rehabilitation with variable recovery.

det.patho: The term describes inflammation confined to spinal neurons, either anterior horn cells or dorsal root ganglion neurons, rather than white matter tracts. Proposed mechanisms include direct viral infection (enteroviruses such as EV-A71 and EV-D68, flaviviruses) and post-infectious immune attack. Evidence is limited because the label is used inconsistently.
det.clinical: Motor forms resemble polio with asymmetric segmental weakness; sensory forms resemble a sensory neuronopathy. Modern literature prefers more specific labels such as acute flaccid myelitis or sensory ganglionopathy. Clinicians should treat it as a syndrome needing a cause.
det.diagnosis: Localise with exam, MRI and neurophysiology; identify the agent with CSF and respiratory or stool viral testing. Exclude compression, GBS, brachial neuritis and autoimmune ganglionopathy (anti-Hu, Sjögren).
det.treatment: Supportive care and rehabilitation; antivirals for VZV or HSV; immunotherapy for confirmed autoimmune ganglionopathy. IVIG and steroids are sometimes used for acute flaccid myelitis but without proven benefit.
det.prognosis: Variable; motor neuron loss often leaves permanent segmental weakness.
pearls: Treat 'spinal neuronitis' as a description, then search for the cause.
Segmental flaccid weakness after a febrile illness: report as AFP and test for enteroviruses.
Non-length-dependent sensory loss: think ganglionopathy.
det.thd: Spinal neuronitis เป็นคำบรรยาย ไม่ใช่โรคที่มีเกณฑ์ชัดเจน หมายถึงการอักเสบที่ anterior horn หรือปมประสาทรากหลัง มักตามหลังติดเชื้อไวรัส ทำให้แขนหรือขาอ่อนแรงลีบเป็นปล้องหรือชาไม่เป็นแบบปลายมือปลายเท้า ต้องหาสาเหตุด้วย MRI น้ำไขสันหลัง และการตรวจไฟฟ้า รักษาแบบประคับประคองหรือตามสาเหตุที่พบ

ddx.pt: Prototype anterior horn infection; stool poliovirus testing required
Generalised symmetric weakness with acellular CSF
Full-width cord involvement with sensory level and sphincter disturbance

aN: spinal ganglionitis | anterior horn neuronitis | segmental myelitis neuronal | post infectious spinal neuronitis

name: Spinal osteomyelitis
formal: Vertebral bone infection, usually bacterial or tuberculous, with back pain, fever and risk of epidural abscess.
simple: An infection of the spine bones causing back pain and fever.
th: การติดเชื้อที่ตัวกระดูกสันหลัง (vertebral body) เน้นที่กระดูกและการลุกลามไปรอบ ๆ ผู้ป่วยปวดหลังเฉพาะที่ ไข้ไม่แน่นอน เสี่ยงฝีเหนือเยื่อดูราและกระดูกยุบ
tempoNote: Pyogenic infection evolves over days to weeks; tuberculous or brucellar disease takes months
feat: Focal spinal pain, worse at night or on percussion, often present for weeks before diagnosis
Fever in only a minority to half; weight loss in chronic forms
Host and exposure factors: diabetes, injection drug use, haemodialysis, endocarditis, recent spinal procedures or distant infection
Bone destruction, kyphosis or paraspinal and psoas collections
Radicular pain, weakness or myelopathy signal epidural extension
inv: CRP and ESR (raised in most), blood cultures before antibiotics
Contrast MRI of the whole spine, with CT for bone destruction
Image-guided bone biopsy for culture and histology (include TB and Burkholderia pseudomallei) if blood cultures are negative
Echocardiogram when bacteraemia involves S. aureus or streptococci

case.who: 58-year-old rubber-plantation worker with poorly controlled diabetes, Songkhla
case.story: Four weeks of mid-thoracic back pain, waking him at night, with 5 kg weight loss and low fevers; he has just developed a band-like discomfort around the chest.
case.exam: Percussion tenderness at T8, mild gait unsteadiness, brisk knee jerks, no clear sensory level.
case.tests: CRP 95 mg/L, HbA1c 11%; MRI shows T7–T8 vertebral marrow oedema with epidural enhancement and a paravertebral collection; biopsy culture grows S. aureus.
case.q: What is the main urgent concern, and what determines surgery?
case.a: Epidural extension threatening the cord; pathogen-directed IV antibiotics, with decompression and stabilisation if there is a deficit, abscess or instability.

read.where: Neurologic Disorders Associated with Bone and Joint Disease: Vertebral Osteomyelitis

Chapter 14 Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders

det.patho: Haematogenous seeding of the richly vascularised vertebral end-plate is the commonest route, followed by contiguous spread or direct inoculation after surgery or injection. Staphylococcus aureus leads worldwide, while Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Brucella and Burkholderia pseudomallei matter in Southeast Asia. Bone necrosis, collapse and extension into the epidural space produce the neurological complications.
det.clinical: Persistent focal back pain is nearly universal and is often attributed to degenerative disease for weeks. Elderly, diabetic and immunosuppressed patients are most at risk, and fever may be missing. Weakness, sphincter change or a sensory level means epidural spread and calls for same-day imaging. Concomitant infective endocarditis is found in a meaningful minority.
det.diagnosis: Combine persistent pain, raised inflammatory markers and MRI showing marrow oedema and enhancement, which is sensitive within days to two weeks. Obtain blood cultures first and then an image-guided bone biopsy when the organism is unknown, ideally before empirical therapy in stable patients. Ask about TB, brucellosis and melioidosis exposure, and exclude metastasis, compression fracture and inflammatory spondyloarthropathy.
det.treatment: Give organism-specific antibiotics for about 6 weeks in pyogenic infection, with an early switch to well-absorbed oral agents when appropriate; TB and melioidosis need much longer courses. Empirical therapy is reserved for sepsis or neurological compromise after cultures are drawn. Surgery is advised for progressive deficit, abscess, instability, deformity or failure of medical therapy. Bracing and glycaemic control support healing.
det.prognosis: Most patients are cured, but delayed diagnosis leaves persistent pain, deformity or neurological deficit, and mortality is higher in the elderly and in endocarditis.
pearls: Back pain that wakes the patient with raised CRP calls for MRI, not just analgesia.
Get cultures before antibiotics whenever the patient is neurologically stable.
In Thailand, keep TB and melioidosis on the list, especially in diabetics.
det.thd: Spinal osteomyelitis คือการติดเชื้อของตัวกระดูกสันหลัง ส่วนใหญ่มาจากเชื้อในกระแสเลือด พบ S. aureus บ่อย แต่ในไทยต้องนึกถึงวัณโรคและเมลิออยโดสิสด้วย ผู้ป่วยปวดหลังเฉพาะที่นานหลายสัปดาห์ ปวดตอนกลางคืน อาจมีหรือไม่มีไข้ ถ้าเริ่มอ่อนแรงแสดงว่ามีฝีกดทับไขสันหลัง ต้องทำ MRI ทันที เจาะเลือดเพาะเชื้อและเจาะชิ้นเนื้อก่อนให้ยาปฏิชีวนะเมื่อผู้ป่วยคงที่ ให้ยาตามเชื้อประมาณ 6 สัปดาห์ และผ่าตัดเมื่อมีอาการทางระบบประสาท กระดูกไม่มั่นคง หรือรักษาด้วยยาไม่ได้ผล

name: Spinal segmental myoclonus
formal: Rhythmic jerks of muscles supplied by one or a few cord segments, from focal spinal lesions.
simple: Repeated jerks in muscles linked to one area of the spinal cord.
th: การกระตุกเป็นจังหวะของกล้ามเนื้อที่เลี้ยงด้วยไขสันหลังหนึ่งหรือไม่กี่ปล้อง เกิดจากรอยโรคเฉพาะที่ในไขสันหลัง
tempoNote: Persistent once established; onset tied to the causative lesion
feat: Rhythmic 1–2 Hz jerks of one limb, abdominal wall or trunk segment
Unaffected by voluntary movement or stimuli in most cases; persists in sleep
Unilateral or bilateral depending on lesion
Associated myelopathic signs may be present or absent
inv: MRI of the corresponding cord level with contrast
Surface EMG: synchronous rhythmic bursts restricted to the segment
Search for myelitis, tumour, vascular malformation, trauma or post-surgical change

case.story: Since a cervical spine operation, her left upper arm twitches rhythmically all day and at night, disturbing her sleep.
case.exam: Regular 1.5 Hz contractions of left biceps and deltoid; mild left C5 sensory loss; no change with distraction.
case.tests: MRI: post-operative T2 change in left C5 cord; EMG: synchronous bursts in C5–C6 muscles continuing during sleep.
case.q: Where is the generator?
case.a: Spinal segmental myoclonus generated at the left C5–C6 cord.

read.where: Chapter 9 Movement Disorders — Spinal Segmental Myoclonus

det.patho: A focal spinal lesion leads to rhythmic discharge of a local population of anterior horn cells, possibly through loss of inhibitory interneurons or abnormal pacemaker activity. The precise mechanism is uncertain and probably varies with the underlying cause.
det.clinical: Jerks are regular and confined to muscles supplied by one or a few adjacent segments. They usually persist in sleep and are not suppressed by voluntary effort. Causes include myelitis, tumours, syrinx, spondylosis, trauma, ischaemia, spinal anaesthesia and infections such as HIV or herpes zoster.
det.diagnosis: Observation, EMG mapping of involved muscles and MRI of the relevant level establish the diagnosis. Absence of EEG correlate and continuation in sleep separate it from cortical and functional myoclonus. Focal fasciculations and continuous motor unit activity are other mimics.
det.treatment: Address the cause where possible. Symptomatic options include clonazepam, levetiracetam, carbamazepine and botulinum toxin injections into the affected muscles. Responses vary and evidence comes from case reports.
det.prognosis: Often persists with structural lesions; may resolve after treatment of inflammatory or compressive causes.
pearls: Rhythmic jerks in a single root distribution that continue in sleep suggest a spinal segmental generator.
Botulinum toxin is helpful for disabling focal segmental jerks.
Ask about prior spinal surgery, injections or zoster in that dermatome.
det.thd: Spinal segmental myoclonus คือการกระตุกเป็นจังหวะของกล้ามเนื้อที่มาจากไขสันหลังเพียงปล้องเดียวหรือไม่กี่ปล้อง จากรอยโรคเฉพาะที่ เช่น myelitis เนื้องอก หรือหลังผ่าตัด กระตุกต่อเนื่องแม้ขณะหลับ วินิจฉัยด้วย EMG และ MRI ตรงระดับนั้น รักษาสาเหตุและใช้ clonazepam, levetiracetam หรือ botulinum toxin

Limited to facial nerve territory; compression at root exit zone

name: Spinal subdural abscess
formal: Rare infection between dura and arachnoid, with back pain, fever and cord compression, requiring surgery and antibiotics.
simple: A rare spinal infection that can press on the spinal cord.
th: หนองที่อยู่ระหว่าง dura และ arachnoid ของไขสันหลัง พบน้อยมาก ทำให้ไข้ ปวดหลัง และไขสันหลังถูกกด ต้องผ่าตัดและให้ยาปฏิชีวนะ
tempoNote: Progresses over days; may deteriorate within hours
feat: Fever, severe back pain and radicular pain
Rapidly progressive myelopathy or cauda equina syndrome
Meningism common because of proximity to the subarachnoid space
Risk factors: diabetes, bacteraemia, spinal procedures or injections, IV drug use
Less spinal tenderness than epidural abscess and no vertebral destruction
inv: MRI with contrast: crescentic or lobulated collection with enhancing rim deep to dura, no epidural fat displacement
Blood cultures; CRP/ESR; WBC
Surgical specimen for culture; LP generally avoided

case.story: One week after a lumbar epidural steroid injection at a private clinic, developed fever, severe low back pain and now weakness of both legs.
case.exam: Fever 38.8 °C, neck stiffness, weak legs, reduced ankle jerks, saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention.
case.tests: MRI: rim-enhancing collection in subdural space from L2–S1 compressing cauda equina; blood culture grows Staphylococcus aureus.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and treatment?
case.a: Spinal subdural abscess; emergency decompression and drainage plus IV anti-staphylococcal antibiotics.

Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — Spinal Subdural Abscess

det.patho: Infection reaches the subdural space by haematogenous spread or direct inoculation during spinal procedures, surgery or trauma. Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest organism. Pus spreads along the potential space, causing compression, venous thrombosis and ischaemia of the cord or roots.
det.clinical: Symptoms resemble epidural abscess: fever, back and root pain, then weakness and sphincter disturbance. Meningism and CSF-like irritation are more frequent. Neurological decline may be abrupt from vascular involvement.
det.diagnosis: Contrast MRI distinguishes subdural from epidural collections by the position relative to dura and epidural fat, though separation can be difficult. Blood cultures may identify the organism; definitive cultures come from surgery. Lumbar puncture risks spreading infection and is usually avoided.
det.treatment: Urgent surgical decompression and drainage combined with prolonged IV antibiotics (usually 4–8 weeks) tailored to culture. Empirical regimens cover S. aureus including MRSA where prevalent, plus Gram-negatives. Control diabetes and remove infected hardware.
det.prognosis: Outcome depends on pre-operative deficit and speed of treatment; delays carry high rates of permanent paralysis and mortality.
pearls: Fever + back pain + new neurological deficit = spinal infection emergency.
Recent spinal injection or surgery is a key risk factor.
Subdural abscesses often show meningism, unlike most epidural abscesses.
det.thd: Spinal subdural abscess คือหนองระหว่างชั้น dura และ arachnoid ของไขสันหลัง พบน้อยมาก มักเกิดจาก Staphylococcus aureus หลังการติดเชื้อในกระแสเลือดหรือการฉีดยาที่หลัง อาการคือไข้ ปวดหลังรุนแรง อ่อนแรงขาและปัสสาวะผิดปกติ MRI ฉีดสีช่วยวินิจฉัย การรักษาเป็นภาวะฉุกเฉินคือผ่าตัดระบายหนองร่วมกับยาปฏิชีวนะ

name: Spinal tuberculosis
formal: Pott disease with vertebral destruction, kyphosis, paraspinal abscess and myelopathy.
simple: Tuberculosis of the spine causing back pain, spinal curvature and sometimes weakness.
th: วัณโรคที่กระดูกสันหลัง (Pott's disease) ทำให้กระดูกยุบ หลังค่อม ฝีข้างกระดูกสันหลัง และกดไขสันหลัง
tempoNote: Insidious over months; neurological deficits may progress over days to weeks
feat: Chronic back pain, stiffness and local tenderness, thoracic most often
Gibbus deformity and paraspinal or psoas cold abscess
Spastic paraparesis, sensory level, bladder dysfunction from compression
Weight loss and night sweats; pulmonary TB absent in many
Also includes non-osseous forms: tuberculous radiculomyelitis and intramedullary tuberculoma

Image-guided biopsy: AFB, Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra, culture, histology
Chest imaging, HIV test

case.story: Lower back pain for four months and lumps in her groin; now numb legs and weak hips.
case.exam: Tender L1, fluctuant swelling in the right groin, mild bilateral hip weakness, reduced reflexes.
case.tests: MRI: T12–L1 destruction with bilateral psoas abscesses; aspirate Xpert positive, rifampicin sensitive.
case.q: What is the treatment and when is surgery needed?
case.a: Antituberculous therapy for 9–12 months; surgery for progressive deficit, instability, large abscesses or deformity.

det.patho: M. tuberculosis spreads by blood to vertebral bodies, causing caseous destruction and abscess that tracks along ligaments and psoas sheaths. Cord compression results from abscess, granulation tissue, sequestered bone or kyphotic deformity. Tuberculous arachnoiditis and intramedullary tuberculoma can occur without bone disease.
det.clinical: It is the commonest form of skeletal TB and frequent in Thailand. Symptoms are slow and constitutional features may be mild. Children are prone to progressive kyphosis even after cure. Late-onset paraplegia can occur years later from deformity.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows the typical pattern; tissue confirmation with molecular tests and culture provides drug susceptibility. Histology shows caseating granulomas. Interferon-gamma release assays and tuberculin tests are supportive but cannot confirm active disease.
det.treatment: Standard four-drug intensive phase for 2 months followed by isoniazid and rifampicin to 9–12 months total. Surgery for neurological deficit not improving, instability, severe kyphosis or non-diagnostic biopsy. Drug-resistant TB needs specialist regimens. Rehabilitation, nutrition and HIV care are integral.
det.prognosis: Cure rates are high; neurological recovery is good when compression is relieved early.
pearls: Same entity as Pott's disease; consider both names when searching.
Psoas abscess with back pain in an endemic area: think TB.
Watch for paradoxical worsening after starting treatment, especially in HIV.
det.thd: Spinal tuberculosis หรือ Pott's disease คือวัณโรคกระดูกสันหลัง พบบ่อยในไทย ปวดหลังเรื้อรัง หลังค่อม มีฝีที่ psoas หรือข้างกระดูก และอาจกดไขสันหลังจนขาอ่อนแรง MRI เห็นกระดูกหลายข้อติดกันถูกทำลายและฝีขนาดใหญ่ ควรเจาะตรวจเชื้อและความไวต่อยา รักษาด้วยยาวัณโรค 9–12 เดือน และผ่าตัดในรายที่มีอาการทางประสาทหรือกระดูกไม่มั่นคง

qx.stem: A 34-year-old male construction worker from Myanmar working in Samut Sakhon has four months of thoracic back pain, night sweats and weight loss, and now has a spastic paraparesis. MRI shows destruction of the T7 and T8 vertebral bodies with relative preservation of the intervening disc, a large paravertebral collection with a thin smooth enhancing wall extending under the anterior longitudinal ligament over four levels, and an epidural component compressing the cord.
qx.q: Which imaging feature most favours tuberculous over pyogenic spondylitis?
opts: Relative disc sparing with subligamentous spread over several levels and a large thin-walled paraspinal abscess
Disc T2 hyperintensity with endplate erosion centred on the disc
Single-level involvement with a poorly defined phlegmon
Rapid onset over a few days with high fever
Enhancement of the facet joints
qx.why: Spinal TB characteristically spreads beneath the longitudinal ligaments to several contiguous levels, spares the disc relatively until late, and forms large thin, smooth-walled paravertebral abscesses, often with gibbus deformity. Pyogenic infection centres on the disc with early destruction and thick irregular phlegmon, and evolves faster. Management combines biopsy (Xpert MTB/RIF and culture), anti-tuberculous therapy and decompression for progressive deficit or instability.

name: Spinal tumours
formal: Primary or metastatic lesions of vertebrae, meninges or cord causing pain, radiculopathy and myelopathy.
simple: Growths in the spine or around the spinal cord that cause pain and weakness.
th: เนื้องอกของกระดูกสันหลัง เยื่อหุ้ม หรือไขสันหลัง ทั้งชนิดปฐมภูมิและแพร่กระจาย ทำให้ปวดหลัง ปวดร้าวตามรากประสาท และไขสันหลังถูกกด

feat: Extradural (commonest): metastases, myeloma, lymphoma — back pain then cord compression
Intradural extramedullary: meningioma, schwannoma, neurofibroma — radicular pain and Brown-Séquard picture
Intramedullary: ependymoma, astrocytoma, haemangioblastoma — central cord syndrome, dissociated sensory loss
Night pain or pain lying flat; sphincter disturbance later

case.who: 47-year-old woman, seamstress from Nakhon Si Thammarat
case.story: Eighteen months of band-like right chest-wall pain, now dragging left leg and unsteady in the dark.
case.exam: Right T6 radicular hyperalgesia, left leg weakness with brisk reflexes and up-going plantar, reduced pinprick and thermal sense on the right below T8, impaired vibration in the left leg.
case.tests: MRI: well-defined intradural extramedullary enhancing mass at T6 with dural tail, displacing the cord.
case.q: What is the likely tumour and syndrome?
case.a: Thoracic spinal meningioma causing a Brown-Séquard syndrome; surgical resection usually curative.

det.patho: Spinal tumours are grouped by compartment. Extradural lesions are mostly metastases from lung, breast, prostate, kidney, myeloma and lymphoma that erode vertebrae. Intradural extramedullary tumours, chiefly meningiomas and nerve sheath tumours, are usually benign. Intramedullary tumours are rarer: ependymomas in adults, astrocytomas in children, and haemangioblastomas in VHL.
det.clinical: Pain is the commonest early symptom: localised, radicular or nocturnal. Compression produces progressive weakness, sensory level, gait ataxia and sphincter problems. Intramedullary lesions give dissociated sensory loss and sacral sparing; extramedullary lesions often cause Brown-Séquard features and early radicular pain.
det.diagnosis: Gadolinium MRI of the whole spine localises the compartment and narrows the differential. Systemic staging and tissue diagnosis guide therapy. In patients with known cancer, a new back pain warrants urgent MRI even with a normal examination.
det.treatment: Metastatic spinal cord compression requires immediate dexamethasone, then surgery and/or radiotherapy depending on stability, tumour type and prognosis; stereotactic body radiotherapy is increasingly used. Benign intradural tumours are resected microsurgically. Intramedullary tumours are managed by maximal safe resection with adjuvant radiotherapy or chemotherapy for higher grades. Rehabilitation and bladder, bowel and pain care are essential.
det.prognosis: Benign extramedullary tumours have excellent outcomes; neurological recovery from metastatic compression depends mainly on ambulatory status at diagnosis.
pearls: Whether the patient can still walk when treatment starts predicts walking afterwards in metastatic compression.
Nocturnal or recumbent back pain is a red flag.
Radicular pain plus Brown-Séquard picture suggests intradural extramedullary tumour.
det.thd: Spinal tumours แบ่งตามตำแหน่งเป็น extradural (ส่วนใหญ่เป็นมะเร็งแพร่กระจาย), intradural extramedullary (meningioma, schwannoma) และ intramedullary (ependymoma, astrocytoma) อาการเริ่มด้วยปวดหลังหรือปวดร้าวตามรากประสาท แล้วจึงอ่อนแรงและปัสสาวะผิดปกติ MRI ทั้งแนวกระดูกสันหลังเป็นการตรวจหลัก การรักษาขึ้นกับชนิด เช่น dexamethasone ผ่าตัด และฉายรังสี
