name: Spinocerebellar ataxias (SCAs)
formal: Dominantly inherited cerebellar degenerations, many from CAG repeat expansions, with progressive gait ataxia, dysarthria and oculomotor signs.
simple: Inherited conditions that slowly cause poor balance and clumsy movement.
more: Test for common expansions (SCA1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 17) and use MRI to look for cerebellar and brainstem atrophy; SCA3 is most common worldwide. There is no disease-modifying treatment; riluzole or varenicline may give symptomatic benefit, and rehabilitation is key. Genetically diverse group (SCA types) with dominant inheritance, progressive ataxia, dysarthria and oculomotor abnormalities, frequently from CAG repeat expansions. Genetically heterogeneous group (spinocerebellar ataxias) with adult-onset progressive cerebellar syndrome, often from CAG repeat expansions and variable extracerebellar features.
th: กลุ่มโรคเดินเซทางพันธุกรรมแบบเด่น — SCA3 พบบ่อยในเอเชีย มักมีอาการเริ่มอายุ 30–50 ปี
tempoNote: Insidious adult onset with slow progression over 10–20+ years; anticipation in repeat-expansion types
feat: Progressive gait ataxia, dysarthria and limb incoordination with a parent similarly affected
Type-specific extras: slow saccades (SCA2), bulging eyes, dystonia and amyotrophy (SCA3), pure late ataxia with downbeat nystagmus (SCA6), retinal degeneration (SCA7)
Pyramidal signs, neuropathy, parkinsonism or cognitive change in several subtypes
Earlier and more severe onset in successive generations (anticipation) for CAG expansions
inv: MRI brain: cerebellar ± pontine atrophy
Gene panel for common repeat expansions (the common polyglutamine SCAs and DRPLA) then wider panels/genome testing
Exclude acquired causes: alcohol, drugs, thyroid, vitamin E/B12, anti-GAD and paraneoplastic antibodies

case.story: Five years of unsteady walking and slurred speech; her father had a similar problem and used a wheelchair by 55.
case.exam: Gait ataxia, dysarthria, gaze-evoked nystagmus, staring look with eyelid retraction, brisk knee jerks, faint fasciculation of the tongue.
case.tests: MRI: atrophy of cerebellum and pons; CAG expansion in ATXN3.
case.q: Which SCA is this, and what counselling is needed for her children?
case.a: SCA3 (Machado–Joseph disease). Each child has a 50% risk; predictive testing is offered only with genetic counselling.

Chapter 24 Cerebellar Ataxias and Related Conditions

det.patho: SCAs are dominantly inherited degenerations of the cerebellum and its connections. The most frequent types are caused by expanded CAG repeats encoding polyglutamine tracts in different proteins (ataxins, CACNA1A, TBP), which misfold and disrupt neuronal function; others arise from non-coding repeats or conventional mutations in ion channels and signalling genes. Longer repeats produce earlier onset, explaining anticipation, particularly with paternal transmission in some types. SCA3 is the commonest type worldwide and in many Asian populations.
det.clinical: The core is a slowly worsening cerebellar syndrome of gait ataxia, dysarthria, limb incoordination and abnormal eye movements. Accompanying features depend on subtype and help guide testing: very slow saccades in SCA2, a mix of dystonia, spasticity, parkinsonism and neuropathy in SCA3, a fairly pure late-onset ataxia in SCA6, visual loss in SCA7, and psychiatric or chorea features in SCA17 and DRPLA. Dysphagia and falls drive late disability.
det.diagnosis: A detailed family history across generations is the most useful starting point, though a parent may have died early or been misdiagnosed. MRI shows cerebellar atrophy with pontine involvement in several types. Targeted repeat-expansion testing of common SCAs is first line; repeat-primed PCR or long-read sequencing is needed for some, and exome/genome panels cover the conventional variants. Treatable acquired ataxias should be excluded even when a family history exists.
det.treatment: No therapy alters progression yet; antisense oligonucleotide trials are under way for SCA3 and others. Intensive physiotherapy and coordination training improve function. Symptomatic options include riluzole (modest evidence), levodopa for parkinsonism, botulinum toxin for dystonia, and 4-aminopyridine for episodic or downbeat features. Speech and swallowing therapy, fall prevention and genetic counselling are integral.
det.prognosis: Most types progress over 10–30 years to wheelchair dependence; SCA6 is slower and has near-normal lifespan. Aspiration pneumonia is a common terminal event.
pearls: Slow saccades point to SCA2; bulging eyes with fasciculation and dystonia point to SCA3.
A 'sporadic' late ataxia can still be an SCA — ask about parents who died young.
Predictive testing in at-risk relatives requires pre- and post-test counselling.
Harding's bedside grouping still helps: ADCA I = ataxia plus other neurological signs, ADCA II = ataxia with retinal degeneration (SCA7), ADCA III = near-pure cerebellar ataxia.
Attacks of ataxia beginning before age 20 and lasting hours to days call for testing of episodic-ataxia genes (KCNA1, CACNA1A); some carriers later progress to a fixed ataxia.
When repeat testing is negative, exome or genome sequencing finds a cause in roughly one third, far more than small targeted panels.
det.thd: SCA เป็นกลุ่มโรคเดินเซที่ถ่ายทอดแบบเด่น ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจาก CAG repeat expansion ทำให้สมองน้อยและก้านสมองฝ่อช้า ๆ อาการเริ่มวัยผู้ใหญ่ ได้แก่ เดินเซ พูดไม่ชัด ตากระตุก และมีอาการเฉพาะชนิด เช่น SCA2 saccade ช้า SCA3 ตาโปน dystonia กล้ามเนื้อลีบ ซึ่ง SCA3 พบบ่อยในเอเชีย วินิจฉัยด้วยประวัติครอบครัว MRI และตรวจยีน การรักษาเน้นกายภาพบำบัดและให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

formal: Group of hereditary or sporadic degenerations of cerebellum and spinal tracts with progressive ataxia.

case.exam: Gait ataxia, absent sensory action potentials suspected clinically, impaired head impulse test bilaterally.
case.tests: NCS: sensory neuronopathy; MRI: vermian atrophy; RFC1 biallelic expansion.
case.q: Which sporadic-looking degeneration is this?

8 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System

det.patho: This historical umbrella term covers degenerations of the cerebellum and its spinal connections (spinocerebellar tracts, posterior columns, corticospinal tracts). Causes include dominant repeat expansions and point mutations (SCAs), recessive disorders (Friedreich ataxia, AOA, ARSACS), X-linked and mitochondrial disorders, and sporadic neurodegenerations such as MSA-C. Modern practice classifies them by gene or mechanism rather than by the old pathological groupings.
det.clinical: The common thread is slowly progressive ataxia. Additional features help localise the cause: neuropathy and cardiomyopathy in Friedreich ataxia, ophthalmoplegia or slow saccades in SCA2/3, retinopathy in SCA7, autonomic failure in MSA. Recently identified FGF14 (SCA27B) and RFC1 expansions explain many late-onset 'sporadic' cases.
det.diagnosis: Take a careful family history and exclude acquired causes first. MRI shows pattern (cerebellar only versus pontocerebellar versus spinal atrophy). Genetic testing proceeds from repeat-expansion panels to exome or genome sequencing. Some cases remain unexplained.
det.treatment: Omaveloxolone is approved for Friedreich ataxia from age 16; vitamin E for AVED and other specific therapies exist for treatable metabolic ataxias. Otherwise care is rehabilitative: physiotherapy, speech and swallowing therapy, walking aids and fall prevention. Riluzole and acetazolamide have limited or subtype-specific evidence.
det.prognosis: Variable: years to decades to disability depending on cause.
pearls: Always rule out the treatable ataxias (vitamin E, B12, coeliac, hypothyroid, alcohol, immune).
Chronic cough plus late-onset ataxia — test RFC1.
Old term; today think in genes and patterns.
det.thd: Spinocerebellar degenerations เป็นคำรวมแบบเก่าของโรคเสื่อมของสมองน้อยและทางเดินประสาทในไขสันหลัง ทั้งชนิดพันธุกรรม เช่น SCA และ Friedreich ataxia และชนิดไม่ทราบสาเหตุ เช่น MSA-C ผู้ป่วยเดินเซมากขึ้นเรื่อย ๆ ต้องตัดสาเหตุที่รักษาได้ก่อน เช่น ขาดวิตามินอี B12 หรือภูมิคุ้มกัน แล้วตรวจ MRI และตรวจยีน การรักษาส่วนใหญ่เป็นกายภาพบำบัด ยกเว้นบางโรคที่มียาเฉพาะ

name: Spirochete infection
formal: Neurological infection by spirochetes such as Treponema pallidum or Borrelia burgdorferi, causing meningitis, cranial neuropathy and neurosyphilis or neuroborreliosis.
simple: Infection with spiral-shaped bacteria such as those causing syphilis or Lyme disease, which can harm the nervous system.
th: การติดเชื้อกลุ่ม spirochete ในระบบประสาท เช่น ซิฟิลิส Lyme และเลปโตสไปโรซิส ทำให้เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ เส้นประสาทสมองเสีย และสมองเสื่อม
tempoNote: Leptospirosis acute; early neurosyphilis and Lyme meningitis subacute; parenchymal neurosyphilis chronic over years
feat: Syphilis: meningitis, cranial neuropathies, ocular and otic syphilis, stroke (meningovascular), dementia (general paresis), tabes dorsalis
Lyme: lymphocytic meningitis, facial palsy, painful radiculitis (Bannwarth); mainly temperate regions
Leptospirosis: fever, myalgia, conjunctival suffusion and aseptic meningitis after flood or rice-field exposure (common in Thailand)
Borrelia relapsing fever causes meningitis in some regions
inv: Syphilis: treponemal and non-treponemal serology; CSF cells, protein, VDRL
Leptospirosis: PCR early, MAT or IgM serology later
Lyme: two-tier serology and CSF antibody index

case.story: Three months of personality change, poor memory and slurred speech; HIV positive, not on treatment.
case.exam: Disinhibited, impaired recall, small irregular pupils that accommodate but react poorly to light.
case.tests: Serum RPR 1:64, TPHA positive; CSF 30 lymphocytes/µL, protein 0.8 g/L, VDRL reactive.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and treatment?
case.a: General paresis (parenchymal neurosyphilis); IV aqueous penicillin G for 10–14 days and start ART.

det.patho: Spirochetes are motile spiral bacteria that disseminate early through the blood and cross into the CNS. Treponema pallidum causes meningitis, endarteritis of small and medium vessels, and later parenchymal invasion. Borrelia burgdorferi causes meningoradiculitis via inflammation of roots and cranial nerves. Leptospira causes systemic vasculitis with aseptic meningitis.
det.clinical: This is a group label rather than a single disease. Neurosyphilis has made a comeback alongside HIV, notably in MSM; ocular and otic syphilis are common modern presentations. Leptospirosis is endemic in Thailand and causes meningitis, encephalitis and rarely myelitis or GBS-like illness.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on specific serology and CSF analysis. CSF VDRL is specific but insensitive for neurosyphilis; a negative CSF FTA-ABS makes it unlikely. Leptospira PCR is best early, serology after the first week. Lyme diagnosis requires exposure history and intrathecal antibody production.
det.treatment: Neurosyphilis: IV aqueous penicillin G 18–24 million units/day for 10–14 days (ceftriaxone is an alternative); repeat serology to confirm response. Lyme neuroborreliosis: oral doxycycline or IV ceftriaxone for 14–21 days. Leptospirosis: penicillin, ceftriaxone or doxycycline with supportive care.
det.prognosis: Early syphilitic meningitis and Lyme respond well; parenchymal neurosyphilis improves only partially.
pearls: Test syphilis serology in any unexplained dementia, stroke in the young, uveitis or hearing loss.
Argyll Robertson pupils: light-near dissociation with small irregular pupils.
Fever, myalgia and calf pain after floods: think leptospirosis.
det.thd: Spirochete infection เป็นกลุ่มโรคติดเชื้อแบคทีเรียรูปเกลียว ที่สำคัญในระบบประสาทคือซิฟิลิส ซึ่งทำให้เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ หลอดเลือดสมองอุดตัน สมองเสื่อม และ tabes dorsalis ส่วนเลปโตสไปโรซิสพบบ่อยในไทยหลังน้ำท่วม และ Lyme พบในเขตอบอุ่น วินิจฉัยด้วยเซรุ่มและน้ำไขสันหลัง รักษาด้วย penicillin หรือ ceftriaxone ตามชนิดเชื้อ

name: Split hand syndrome
formal: Selective wasting of abductor pollicis brevis and first dorsal interosseous with preserved hypothenar muscles, typical for ALS.
simple: Wasting of the thumb-side hand muscles but not the little-finger side, typical in motor neuron disease.
th: ลักษณะกล้ามเนื้อมือฝ่อแบบแยก คือ APB และ FDI ฝ่อมากแต่ hypothenar ยังดี พบบ่อยใน ALS
tempoNote: Develops over months as an early sign of motor neuron disease
feat: A clinical sign rather than a disease: thenar and first dorsal interosseous wasting with relative hypothenar sparing
Highly suggestive of ALS when combined with fasciculations and UMN signs
Thought to reflect cortical (corticomotoneuronal) as well as spinal mechanisms
Also reported in some other conditions (Hirayama disease, SMA, CMT) but less pronounced
inv: EMG: active and chronic denervation in several regions; normal sensory responses
Split-hand index from CMAP amplitudes (APB × FDI / ADM) reduced
Exclude median/ulnar neuropathies and cervical radiculopathy

case.story: Six months of difficulty picking up coins and buttoning shirts with the right hand; occasional muscle twitching.
case.exam: Marked wasting of the thenar eminence and first web space with relatively full hypothenar bulk, fasciculations in both arms, brisk reflexes and Hoffmann sign.
case.tests: EMG shows widespread denervation in cervical and lumbosacral segments; sensory studies normal.
case.q: What does this hand pattern suggest?
case.a: Split hand syndrome typical of ALS; with UMN signs and widespread denervation, ALS is likely.

det.patho: APB and FDI receive strong corticomotoneuronal input for fine pinch, while ADM is less dependent on it. Preferential loss of these muscles is attributed to cortical hyperexcitability spreading down this pathway, plus differences in spinal motor neuron vulnerability and axonal excitability. Both cortical and peripheral factors seem to contribute.
det.clinical: Patients notice weak pinch, trouble with fine tasks and wasting of the thumb web. Inspection shows flattening of the thenar eminence and first dorsal space with a relatively full ulnar border. It often appears early in limb-onset ALS and may precede a firm diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: Recognition is clinical, supported by CMAP amplitudes: a low split-hand index favours ALS over mimics. The finding should prompt a full examination for fasciculations and upper motor neuron signs, EMG in multiple regions and exclusion of structural cervical disease and focal neuropathies.
det.treatment: The sign itself is not treated; management is that of the underlying disease. In ALS this includes riluzole, consideration of edaravone where available, multidisciplinary care, nutrition and respiratory support, and hand therapy with splints.
det.prognosis: Reflects the underlying disease.
pearls: Thenar and FDI wasted, hypothenar full = split hand: examine for ALS.
Carpal tunnel wastes thenar but spares FDI; ulnar neuropathy wastes FDI and hypothenar together.
The split-hand index can be calculated from routine motor conduction studies.
det.thd: Split hand syndrome คือลักษณะกล้ามเนื้อ APB และ FDI ฝ่อมากแต่กล้ามเนื้อ hypothenar ยังดี เป็นอาการแสดงไม่ใช่โรค พบบ่อยและพบเร็วใน ALS เชื่อว่าเกิดจากการกระตุ้นผ่าน corticomotoneuronal pathway ร่วมกับปัจจัยที่ไขสันหลัง เมื่อเห็นควรตรวจหา fasciculation และ UMN signs และส่ง EMG หลายตำแหน่ง

case.who: 72-year-old woman with a urinary catheter, in a provincial hospital in Nakhon Sawan
case.story: Ten days after treatment for a urinary tract infection she has severe low back pain that prevents her turning in bed and shoots into the right thigh.
case.exam: Temperature 38.2 °C, marked L4–L5 tenderness and paraspinal spasm, straight-leg raise limited by pain, normal power and reflexes.
case.tests: CRP 190 mg/L; blood culture grows Escherichia coli; MRI shows L4–L5 disc hyperintensity with end-plate erosion and a small anterior epidural collection.
case.q: How do you proceed, and how long is treatment?
case.a: Spondylodiscitis from urinary source; targeted antibiotics (IV then oral step-down) for about 6 weeks, close neurological monitoring and surgery only if deficit, instability or failure.

det.patho: In adults the disc is avascular, so bacteria lodge in the end-plate arterial loops and then break into the disc space; in young children disc vessels persist and the disc itself can be the primary site. Staphylococcus aureus is leading, followed by streptococci and Gram-negative rods of urinary origin. Disc destruction collapses the disc height and can seed epidural, paravertebral or psoas abscesses.
det.clinical: Pain dominates and neurology is typically intact initially, which tempts delay of weeks. Older age, diabetes, indwelling devices and recent bacteraemia raise risk. Neurological deficits appear in a minority and reflect epidural abscess or bone collapse. Hospital teams should ask about systemic sources because spondylodiscitis often marks a bacteraemic event.
det.diagnosis: MRI with gadolinium is the investigation of choice and may be subtle in the first days, so repeat it if suspicion persists. Positive blood cultures can avoid biopsy; otherwise image-guided sampling gives the organism and its susceptibilities. A diagnostic search for endocarditis or another primary source follows. Discriminate from degenerative Modic change, inflammatory arthritis, TB, brucellosis, melioidosis and malignancy.
det.treatment: In a stable patient, take cultures first and then give prolonged targeted antibiotics, with randomised data supporting about 6 weeks rather than 12 in most pyogenic cases. Oral step-down with high-bioavailability drugs is acceptable once improving. Spinal surgery is for neurological deficit, instability, large or undrainable abscess, or failure of therapy. Follow clinical course and CRP; repeat MRI only if worsening.
det.prognosis: Cure is expected with timely therapy, though chronic pain is common and older age or endocarditis raise mortality.
pearls: New severe focal back pain after a bacteraemic illness equals spondylodiscitis until proven otherwise.
Early MRI can be falsely reassuring; repeat if suspicion persists.
Staphylococcal or streptococcal cases deserve an echocardiogram.

name: Spontaneous oro-facial chorea
formal: Chorea of mouth and face in the elderly without drug exposure, similar to edentulous dyskinesia.
simple: Involuntary mouth and face movements in older people without a clear cause.
th: การเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติแบบ chorea ของปากและใบหน้าในผู้สูงอายุ โดยไม่เคยได้รับยาต้านโดปามีน มักสัมพันธ์กับการไม่มีฟันหรือฟันปลอมไม่พอดี
tempoNote: Insidious onset in old age; usually stable
feat: Repetitive chewing, lip-smacking, tongue movements and jaw deviation in an older adult
No exposure to dopamine-blocking drugs
Often edentulous or ill-fitting dentures; improves when chewing or with well-fitting dentures
Patients may be unaware; family notices
No other neurological signs in pure cases
inv: Detailed drug history including antiemetics (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine) and antipsychotics
Dental assessment

case.story: Constant chewing and lip movements for one year; has no teeth and does not wear dentures. Never took psychiatric or antiemetic drugs.
case.exam: Rhythmic chewing, lip pursing and tongue movements; no limb chorea or parkinsonism; edentulous.
case.tests: Glucose and thyroid normal; MRI mild atrophy only.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and simple first step?
case.a: Spontaneous (edentulous) orofacial dyskinesia; dental referral for well-fitting dentures and reassurance.

det.patho: The cause is uncertain. Proposed contributors include age-related changes in basal ganglia dopaminergic signalling and abnormal proprioceptive input from the mouth when teeth are lost, leading to habitual seeking of occlusion. Pathology is not well defined.
det.clinical: Older adults develop continuous oral and lingual movements that resemble tardive dyskinesia. Many are edentulous. Movements may lessen while eating, talking or with dentures in place. Patients are often untroubled, but tongue biting, ulcers or denture problems can occur.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires excluding prior dopamine-blocking exposure (including antiemetics and some calcium channel blockers such as flunarizine), Huntington disease, metabolic chorea and focal dystonia. Examine the whole body for limb chorea or parkinsonism.
det.treatment: Dental rehabilitation with proper dentures often helps. Reassurance is sufficient for many. If troublesome, VMAT2 inhibitors (tetrabenazine, or deutetrabenazine/valbenazine where available) or clonazepam may be tried, weighing side effects in the elderly.
det.prognosis: Usually benign and stable; it rarely causes disability.
pearls: Ask specifically about metoclopramide and flunarizine, common in Thailand, before calling it spontaneous.
Look in the mouth: lack of teeth is a key clue.
Limb involvement points away from a purely oral dyskinesia.
det.thd: Spontaneous oro-facial chorea คือการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติของปาก ลิ้น และขากรรไกรในผู้สูงอายุ โดยไม่เคยได้ยาต้านโดปามีน มักพบในคนที่ไม่มีฟันหรือฟันปลอมไม่พอดี ต้องแยก tardive dyskinesia โดยถามประวัติยา เช่น metoclopramide และ flunarizine การรักษาเริ่มที่ทำฟันปลอมให้พอดีและให้ความมั่นใจ ถ้ารบกวนอาจใช้ยา VMAT2 inhibitor

name: Sporadic Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (sCJD)
formal: Rapidly progressive prion disease with dementia, myoclonus, ataxia, cortical ribboning on DWI, periodic sharp waves and positive RT-QuIC.
simple: A rapidly progressing brain disease from abnormal proteins, causing quick loss of memory and movement control.
th: sCJD เป็นโรคพรีออนแบบเกิดขึ้นเองที่พบบ่อยที่สุด (ประมาณ 85% ของโรคพรีออนทั้งหมด) อายุเฉลี่ยราว 67 ปี สมองเสื่อมเร็วภายในสัปดาห์ถึงไม่กี่เดือน มี myoclonus และเดินเซ MRI DWI เห็น cortical ribboning และ CSF RT-QuIC ให้ผลบวก
tempoNote: Weeks to a few months from first symptom to akinetic mutism; median survival about 4.5–6 months and roughly 85% die within a year, while rarer subtypes (MM2-cortical, MV2K, VV1) last 1–2 years
feat: Rapid cognitive and behavioural decline with median onset near 67 years; early vague complaints (fatigue, headache, dizziness, irritability, sleep change) often delay recognition
Cortical visual symptoms (blurred or double vision, field loss, cortical blindness), aphasia, apraxia or neglect may be the opening feature, because the fault lies in the brain and not the eye
Cerebellar ataxia plus extrapyramidal or pyramidal signs; startle-sensitive myoclonus usually appears later, and akinetic mutism is the typical end state
Clinical tempo follows PRNP codon 129 and prion type: MM1/MV1 (about 70%) is the fast classic form, VV2 (about 16%) starts with ataxia, MM2-thalamic with insomnia, VV1 in the 40s
Not contagious by contact; most patients die of aspiration pneumonia
inv: MRI with DWI and ADC (never DWI alone): cortical ribbon and/or caudate–putamen restriction that spares the perirolandic cortex, abnormal in more than 90%; confirm restriction on ADC and in a second plane to avoid T2 shine-through and CSF-interface artefact
CSF RT-QuIC (second generation): specificity about 98% or higher, sensitivity roughly 85–95%; a negative result never excludes disease and blood-stained CSF may give false negatives

CSF total tau is the best single surrogate marker; 14-3-3 is supportive only; EEG periodic sharp-wave complexes appear in about two-thirds, mostly late; routine CSF cells and protein are usually near normal
Exclude mimics (autoimmune encephalitis antibodies in serum and CSF, lymphoma, vasculitis, metabolic and toxic causes) and offer PRNP sequencing

case.story: Six weeks of getting lost on her usual route to the market and blurred vision that an optometrist could not explain; then trouble with buttons and speech, and her daughter notices sudden body jerks when a door slams.
case.exam: Disoriented, left homonymous field defect, limb ataxia, rigidity and startle myoclonus; afebrile, no rash, no neck stiffness.
case.tests: MRI DWI bright ribbon along temporal and parieto-occipital cortex and both caudate nuclei with matching dark ADC, central sulcus spared; CSF 2 cells/µL, protein 55 mg/dL, RT-QuIC positive; autoimmune antibody panel negative; EEG slow with no periodic complexes.
case.q: Is the diagnosis established, and does the EEG without periodic complexes weaken it?
case.a: She meets RT-QuIC-based criteria for probable sporadic CJD. Periodic complexes occur in only about two-thirds and mostly late, so their absence changes nothing; support the family, report to surveillance and apply prion handling rules.

read.where: Chapter 95 Prion Diseases — Sporadic Prion Disease: Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease and Diagnosis

Chapter 11 Cognitive Impairment and Dementia — Sporadic Prion Disease
Part II: Viral Pathogens: Pathogenesis, Pathology, Diagnosis and Treatment

det.patho: The normal membrane-anchored prion protein (PrPC, encoded by PRNP on chromosome 20) refolds into a beta-sheet-rich, partly protease-resistant isoform (PrPSc) that templates the conversion of more PrPC. What triggers the first misfolding event is unknown; the similar annual incidence (around one to two cases per million) across surveyed countries points to a chance molecular event rather than an environmental cause. Strain differences of PrPSc, codon 129 genotype (MM, MV, VV) and the size of the protease-resistant fragment (type 1 or 2) give about six molecular subtypes. Tissue shows neuronal loss, astrocytosis and vacuolation (fluid-filled swellings of distal dendrites); only PrPSc deposition is specific.
det.clinical: Onset is usually in the late 60s and disease before 40 or after 80 is uncommon. Early symptoms are often vague (fatigue, headache, dizziness, mood or personality change, insomnia) so weeks pass before dementia becomes obvious. Visual-cortex problems, aphasia, apraxia, ataxia, rigidity and tremor may lead, with myoclonus following; akinetic mutism closes the illness. Younger patients tend to live longer and to present with mood, behaviour or sleep complaints. Examiners ask which findings are early (cognitive, cerebellar, visual) and which are late (myoclonus, periodic EEG complexes, mutism).
det.diagnosis: Current criteria (UK 2017, CDC 2018, European 2021) are RT-QuIC-based: a progressive neurological syndrome with a positive CSF RT-QuIC gives probable sCJD even without the classic signs; otherwise rapidly progressive cognitive impairment with two of four clinical groups (myoclonus, visual or cerebellar, pyramidal or extrapyramidal, akinetic mutism) plus a typical MRI, EEG or surrogate marker, after other causes are excluded. The older WHO 1998 criteria leaned on 14-3-3 and periodic complexes and were designed for surveillance, so they are now superseded for bedside use. A good MRI needs DWI with ADC confirmation, because T2 shine-through can make DWI look falsely bright. Because RT-QuIC misses roughly one case in ten, MRI, total tau and a thorough mimic work-up still matter. Definite diagnosis rests on neuropathology.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying drug is approved; randomised trials of flupirtine, quinacrine and doxycycline did not lengthen survival. Symptomatic options used in practice are an SSRI for depression and anxiety, quetiapine for agitation or psychosis (least parkinsonian effect), and levetiracetam, clonazepam or valproate for myoclonus. Bring in palliative care early because decline is fast, and direct families to CJD support groups. PrPC-lowering strategies (antisense oligonucleotide, anti-PrP antibody) are in early trials. Standard bedside precautions suffice, but neurosurgical instruments and high-risk tissue need prion protocols, with single-use or incineration preferred.
det.prognosis: Median survival is 4.5–6 months for MM1/MV1; MM2-cortical, MV2K and VV1 last 1–2 years. All cases are fatal.
pearls: Order MRI with DWI and ADC early in every rapidly progressive dementia; many CJD scans are misread unless the radiologist is asked to look for it.
A positive RT-QuIC in the right setting is close to diagnostic, but a negative one never rules CJD out.
Send antibody tests for autoimmune encephalitis before settling on CJD, as LGI1 and Hashimoto encephalopathy can mimic the MRI or EEG.
det.thd: sCJD เกิดจาก prion protein ปกติ (PrPC) เปลี่ยนรูปเองเป็น PrPSc แล้วชักนำโปรตีนอื่นให้เปลี่ยนตามจนเซลล์ประสาทตาย พบอายุราว 67 ปี มีสมองเสื่อมเร็ว เดินเซ ตาพร่ามัวจากสมองส่วนการเห็น และ myoclonus ตอนท้ายจะนอนนิ่งไม่พูด การวินิจฉัยปัจจุบันใช้ CSF RT-QuIC ร่วมกับ MRI แบบ DWI และ ADC ส่วน 14-3-3 และ EEG มีบทบาทน้อยลง ยังไม่มียารักษาให้หาย การดูแลคือรักษาตามอาการ ดูแลแบบประคับประคอง และระวังการแพร่ผ่านเครื่องมือผ่าตัดสมอง

qx.stem: A 69-year-old retired nurse in Nakhon Si Thammarat develops distorted vision and coloured shapes in her right visual field, then within eight weeks becomes confused, ataxic and has startle-induced jerks. Eye examination is normal. DWI MRI shows cortical ribbon restriction in the left occipital and parietal lobes with mild caudate involvement; EEG shows slowing without periodic complexes yet.
qx.q: Which CSF test provides the most specific support for the likely diagnosis?
opts: 14-3-3 protein
CSF RT-QuIC assay for prion seeding activity
Total tau alone
Oligoclonal bands
Aβ42/40 ratio
qx.why: A rapidly progressive dementia with visual onset (Heidenhain presentation), myoclonus, ataxia and cortical/striatal DWI restriction points to sporadic CJD. CSF RT-QuIC is about 90% sensitive and close to 100% specific and is part of current diagnostic criteria, whereas 14-3-3 and total tau are markers of rapid neuronal injury that can be raised in stroke, encephalitis or seizures. Oligoclonal bands and amyloid ratios do not address prion disease.

qx.stem: A 64-year-old retired teacher from Khon Kaen has progressive memory loss, unsteady gait and visual distortion over 3 months. She startles with sudden jerks to noise. EEG shows generalised biphasic and triphasic sharp complexes recurring roughly once per second on a slowed background.
qx.q: Which investigation combination best supports the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Serum ammonia and liver function tests
Brain MRI diffusion sequences showing cortical ribboning or striatal restriction, plus CSF RT-QuIC
Muscle biopsy for ragged red fibres
Nerve conduction studies
Serum measles antibody titre
qx.why: Rapid dementia, ataxia, visual symptoms, startle myoclonus and periodic sharp wave complexes near 1 Hz suggest sporadic CJD. Diffusion-weighted MRI with cortical or basal ganglia restriction and positive CSF RT-QuIC give high diagnostic accuracy. Triphasic waves from metabolic causes are slower and fluctuate; measles serology is for SSPE, whose complexes recur every several seconds.

qx.stem: A 62-year-old rubber-plantation owner from Trang has deteriorated over 10 weeks with unsteady gait, then visual distortions, startle-sensitive jerks and confusion. He now needs help to walk and cannot follow conversation. Routine blood tests, thyroid antibodies and a paraneoplastic panel are normal.
qx.q: Which investigation pair is most useful for an early diagnosis?

Nerve conduction studies and muscle biopsy
DaT-SPECT and cardiac MIBG
Amyloid PET and plasma p-tau217
MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging and CSF RT-QuIC for prion seeding activity
qx.why: Rapidly progressive ataxia, cortical visual symptoms, myoclonus and dementia suggest sporadic CJD. Cortical ribboning or striatal restricted diffusion on DWI and a positive CSF RT-QuIC (very high specificity) allow a probable diagnosis in life; periodic sharp-wave complexes on EEG may appear later. Treatable mimics such as autoimmune encephalitis or Hashimoto encephalopathy still need to be excluded.

qx.stem: A 69-year-old man from Phitsanulok has had three weeks of rapidly worsening apathy, disorientation and loss of speech. He has no myoclonus, visual symptoms or cerebellar signs. CSF RT-QuIC is positive, the MRI is equivocal, and a thorough work-up (including autoimmune antibodies and metabolic studies) finds no alternative cause.
qx.q: According to current RT-QuIC-based criteria, what is the diagnostic category?
opts: Probable sporadic CJD, because a progressive neurological syndrome with positive RT-QuIC and no alternative cause is enough
Only possible sporadic CJD, because he lacks two of the classic clinical features
No category can be assigned without a positive 14-3-3 result
Definite sporadic CJD, because RT-QuIC is equivalent to neuropathology
Excluded, because the MRI is not typical
qx.why: The UK 2017, CDC 2018 and European 2021 criteria let a progressive neurological syndrome plus positive RT-QuIC define probable sCJD without requiring the classic clinical signs, provided other causes are excluded. Definite diagnosis still needs brain pathology, and 14-3-3 is no longer required. An equivocal MRI does not exclude the diagnosis.

qx.stem: A 64-year-old woman has had eight weeks of rapidly progressive memory loss, then jerks of the arms and unsteady walking. EEG shows periodic sharp wave complexes. DWI shows cortical ribbon hyperintensity over the parietal, temporal and cingulate regions plus restricted diffusion in the caudate heads and putamina, with matching low ADC; T2 changes are subtle and there is no enhancement.

Susceptibility-weighted imaging; CSF cytology

The tempo and myoclonus separate it from Alzheimer disease, and autoimmune encephalitis should be excluded in parallel.

name: Sporadic hyperekplexia
formal: Exaggerated startle with stiffness and falls without GLRA1 mutation, may be symptomatic of brainstem lesions.
simple: An excessive startle reaction with stiffness and falls but no known gene cause.
th: ภาวะสะดุ้งตกใจมากผิดปกติร่วมกับตัวแข็งและล้ม โดยไม่มีการกลายพันธุ์ของยีน GLRA1 อาจเกิดจากรอยโรคที่ก้านสมอง
tempoNote: Onset at any age, often after a brainstem insult; course follows the cause
feat: Exaggerated startle to sudden noise, touch or surprise, not habituating
Brief generalised stiffness after startle causing falls without loss of consciousness
Nose-tap (glabellar tap) provokes a marked startle
Causes: brainstem stroke, encephalitis, MS, hypoxic injury, tumours, autoimmune (glycine receptor antibodies, PERM)
No neonatal history of stiffness or family history
inv: MRI brain with attention to brainstem
Polymyography: startle response beginning in brainstem-innervated muscles with short latency and poor habituation
Glycine receptor and GAD antibodies; genetic testing if family history or onset in infancy

case.story: Since a pontine infarct six months ago, any sudden sound makes him jump, stiffen and sometimes fall backwards.
case.exam: Mild left ataxic hemiparesis; repeated nose taps produce large startle responses that do not lessen.
case.tests: MRI: old right paramedian pontine infarct; glycine receptor antibodies negative.
case.q: What is the diagnosis?
case.a: Symptomatic (sporadic) hyperekplexia from a brainstem lesion.

det.patho: The startle reflex is generated in the caudal brainstem reticular formation and modulated by glycinergic inhibition. Lesions or inflammation of the brainstem, or antibodies against inhibitory synapses, disinhibit this circuit and produce an exaggerated response. In many sporadic cases without a lesion the cause remains unknown.
det.clinical: Patients have excessive, non-habituating startle with stiffening and falls, often with injuries. Startle may be accompanied by brainstem reticular myoclonus. Associated features depend on the cause, such as ataxia or cranial nerve signs after stroke, or rigidity and dysautonomia in PERM.
det.diagnosis: Distinguish pathological startle from normal anxiety-related startle and functional startle (which shows variable latency and pattern). Neurophysiology supports organic hyperekplexia. MRI and antibody testing find the cause; consider genetic testing if childhood onset.
det.treatment: Clonazepam is the most effective symptomatic drug. Treat underlying disease, e.g. immunotherapy for glycine receptor antibody disease. Fall prevention measures are important.
det.prognosis: Depends on underlying cause; symptoms often persist with fixed lesions but improve with treated autoimmune disease.
pearls: Non-habituating startle to nose tapping is a bedside sign.
Adult-onset hyperekplexia warrants brainstem imaging and glycine receptor antibodies.
Functional startle is common; check latency and pattern on EMG.
det.thd: Sporadic hyperekplexia คืออาการสะดุ้งตกใจมากผิดปกติ ตัวแข็งและล้ม โดยไม่มีสาเหตุทางพันธุกรรม มักเกิดจากรอยโรคที่ก้านสมอง เช่น stroke การอักเสบ หรือภูมิคุ้มกัน (glycine receptor antibody) ตรวจด้วย nose tap ที่ทำให้สะดุ้งซ้ำไม่ลดลง ต้องทำ MRI ก้านสมองและตรวจแอนติบอดี การรักษาใช้ clonazepam และรักษาสาเหตุ

ddx.pt: Neonatal stiffness, family history and GLRA1/SLC6A5/GLRB variants
Rigidity, myoclonus and brainstem signs with glycine receptor antibodies

name: Sporadic myopathy
formal: Muscle disease occurring without family history, such as sporadic inclusion body myositis or acquired inflammatory, toxic or endocrine myopathies, with proximal or distal weakness.
simple: Muscle weakness that appears without a family history and has an acquired cause.
more: Evaluate with CK, EMG, MRI and muscle biopsy. Treat the underlying cause; inclusion body myositis responds poorly to immunotherapy.
th: กลุ่มโรคกล้ามเนื้อที่ไม่มีประวัติครอบครัว เช่น inclusion body myositis, myositis จากภูมิคุ้มกัน จากยา หรือจากต่อมไร้ท่อ
tempoNote: Depends on cause: weeks for inflammatory or toxic, years for IBM
feat: Umbrella term, not a single disease: myopathy without a family history
Main groups: inflammatory (IIM, IBM), toxic/drug (statins, steroids, alcohol), endocrine (thyroid, Cushing), infective, critical illness
Some genetic myopathies appear sporadic (de novo, recessive, reduced penetrance)
Pattern of weakness and CK level narrow the cause
inv: CK, TSH, electrolytes, drug history
Myositis antibodies (HMGCR, SRP, Jo-1, cN1A), EMG and muscle MRI
Muscle biopsy; genetic testing when acquired causes are excluded

case.story: Four months of difficulty climbing onto buses and rising from chairs, starting after a statin was begun; no affected relatives.
case.exam: Symmetric hip and shoulder girdle weakness, no rash, normal sensation.
case.tests: CK 7,800 U/L, anti-HMGCR positive, biopsy shows necrotic fibres with little inflammation.
case.q: Which sporadic myopathy is this and why does stopping the statin not suffice?
case.a: Anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy; it is autoimmune and needs immunotherapy, not just statin withdrawal.

det.patho: Mechanisms depend on the cause: immune attack in inflammatory myopathies, mitochondrial or membrane toxicity from drugs, altered protein turnover from endocrine disease, and degeneration with inflammation in inclusion body myositis. The label simply indicates the absence of a recognised inherited basis.
det.clinical: Proximal symmetric weakness is the usual pattern. Asymmetric finger-flexor and quadriceps weakness after 50 suggests IBM; rapid severe weakness with very high CK suggests necrotizing myopathy; rash suggests dermatomyositis. Systemic clues such as interstitial lung disease, thyroid symptoms or new drugs are important.
det.diagnosis: A structured work-up starts with history, CK, thyroid and electrolytes, followed by EMG, MRI to choose a biopsy site and myositis antibody panels. Biopsy defines inflammatory and necrotizing patterns. If no acquired cause is found, gene panels are reasonable because recessive and de novo genetic myopathies can masquerade as sporadic disease.
det.treatment: Treatment is directed at the cause: remove toxic drugs, correct endocrine disturbance, and use immunotherapy (corticosteroids, steroid-sparing agents, IVIG) for inflammatory and necrotizing myopathies. IBM has no proven drug therapy; exercise and fall prevention are emphasised.
det.prognosis: Varies widely from full recovery (toxic, endocrine) to slow progression (IBM).
pearls: 'Sporadic' does not mean acquired — recessive and de novo genetic myopathies look sporadic.
Statin user with persistent weakness after stopping: test anti-HMGCR.
Finger flexor weakness in an older patient: think IBM.
det.thd: Sporadic myopathy เป็นคำรวมของโรคกล้ามเนื้อที่ไม่มีประวัติครอบครัว เช่น myositis, IBM, myopathy จากยาและต่อมไร้ท่อ การตรวจเริ่มจาก CK, TSH, ประวัติยา แล้วตามด้วย EMG, MRI, antibody และชิ้นเนื้อ ถ้าหาสาเหตุไม่ได้ควรตรวจยีนเพราะโรคพันธุกรรมบางชนิดดูเหมือนไม่มีประวัติครอบครัว การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ

ddx.pt: Over 50, finger flexor and quadriceps weakness, slow course, resistant to steroids

name: Sporadic prion disease
formal: Prion protein misfolding disease arising without mutation or exposure, mainly sporadic CJD.
simple: A brain disease from abnormal proteins that arises spontaneously, causing rapid dementia.
th: โรคพรีออนแบบเกิดเองมีหลายชนิดย่อยตามพันธุกรรมที่ codon 129 ของ PRNP และชนิดของ PrPSc: MM1/MV1 พบบ่อยที่สุดและดำเนินเร็ว VV2 เริ่มด้วยเดินเซ MM2-thalamic เริ่มด้วยนอนไม่หลับ และมี VPSPr ที่พบน้อยมากและดำเนินช้ากว่า
tempoNote: Weeks to months in the common MM1/MV1 type; roughly 1–2.5 years in MV2K, MM2-cortical, MM2-thalamic, VV1 and variably protease-sensitive prionopathy
feat: Subtype set by codon 129 (MM, MV, VV) and protease-resistant fragment (type 1 or 2): MM1/MV1 about 70%, VV2 16%, MV2 9%, MM2-thalamic 2%, MM2-cortical 2%, VV1 1%
MM1/MV1: fast dementia, myoclonus, periodic EEG complexes in about 70%; median survival a few months
VV2 and MV2K: ataxia at onset with dementia later; MV2K has cerebellar kuru plaques and lasts about 1.5 years
MM2-thalamic (sporadic fatal insomnia) starts with insomnia; MM2-cortical is a slower dementia of 12–16 months; VV1 starts in the 40s with cortical and striatal damage
About a third of cases carry mixed subtypes; variably protease-sensitive prionopathy is a separate, slow and often RT-QuIC-negative sporadic form
inv: PRNP sequencing gives codon 129 genotype and excludes a mutation; prion type is confirmed at autopsy by Western blot
MRI pattern and EEG help to subtype in life: periodic complexes are common in MM1 (about 73%) and MV1 (about 53%) but seen in just 12–18% of the VV1, VV2 and MV2 subtypes
CSF RT-QuIC (second generation, sensitivity varies by subtype) with total tau as a supportive marker

case.story: Four months of unsteady gait, slurred speech and falls; her family sees little change in memory until the last month, when she becomes slow and vague.
case.exam: Cerebellar dysarthria, gait and limb ataxia, mild cognitive slowing, no myoclonus.
case.tests: MRI DWI restriction in striatum, thalamus and scattered cortex with matching ADC; CSF RT-QuIC positive; EEG slow without periodic complexes; PRNP shows no mutation and codon 129 VV.
case.q: Which subtype fits, and why do the lack of early dementia and periodic complexes not argue against sCJD?
case.a: The VV2 subtype: it begins with ataxia, develops dementia later, and shows periodic complexes in only a minority, so a positive RT-QuIC with typical MRI still supports sporadic CJD.

Chapter 11 Cognitive Impairment and Dementia — Sporadic Prion Disease
Part II: Viral Pathogens: Pathogenesis, Pathology, Diagnosis and Treatment

det.patho: All sporadic prion disease results from a spontaneous conversion of PrPC to PrPSc, but the resulting strain differs by host codon 129 genotype and the protease-resistant core of PrPSc (type 1, about 21 kD, or type 2, about 19 kD). Together they define six subtypes (MM1/MV1, VV2, MV2, MM2-thalamic, MM2-cortical, VV1) that differ in site of damage and speed, and about one third of brains contain a mixture. Homozygosity at codon 129 is associated with faster decline than heterozygosity independent of prion type.
det.clinical: MM1/MV1 (about 70%, nearly all MM1) gives the textbook rapidly progressive dementia of a few months. VV2 (16%) starts with ataxia and adds dementia later, while MV2 (9%) is usually the kuru-plaque type (MV2K) with ataxia and a median survival near 1.5 years. MM2-thalamic (2%) begins with insomnia followed by ataxia and dementia, with pathology in thalamus and inferior olives and little vacuolation; MM2-cortical (2%) is a progressive dementia of 12–16 months with large confluent vacuoles; VV1 (1%) strikes in the 40s. Variably protease-sensitive prionopathy lies outside this scheme.
det.diagnosis: Subtype is only certain after Western blot and neuropathology, but in life the picture is approximated from codon 129 genotype, clinical onset, MRI pattern (cortical versus deep nuclei predominance), EEG periodic complexes and CSF markers. RT-QuIC diagnostic sensitivity varies with subtype, so a negative test in a slow case does not argue against a sporadic prion disease. Apply the same RT-QuIC-based criteria as for sCJD and exclude autoimmune, neoplastic and metabolic mimics. Knowing the subtype helps prognosis and clinical-trial selection.
det.treatment: Management is the same as for sCJD: symptomatic drug treatment, palliative care and prion-appropriate infection control, because no disease-modifying treatment exists. Subtype-specific information is mainly used for counselling the family about expected speed of decline. Trials of PrPC-lowering agents will likely enrol across subtypes.
det.prognosis: From a few months in MM1/MV1 to 1–2.5 years in slower subtypes; all die of the disease.
pearls: Ataxia first with dementia later suggests VV2 or MV2K rather than another cerebellar disease.
Insomnia as the leading symptom can be a sporadic prion disease, not only the inherited FFI.
Always send PRNP sequencing, because it gives codon 129 genotype and separates sporadic from a genetic look-alike.
det.thd: โรคพรีออนแบบเกิดเองแบ่งเป็นชนิดย่อยตามพันธุกรรมที่ตำแหน่ง codon 129 (MM, MV, VV) ร่วมกับชนิดของ PrPSc ชนิด MM1/MV1 พบบ่อยที่สุดและทำให้สมองเสื่อมเร็วภายในไม่กี่เดือน VV2 เริ่มด้วยอาการเดินเซ MM2-thalamic เริ่มด้วยนอนไม่หลับ ส่วน VPSPr พบน้อยมากและดำเนินช้ากว่า การตรวจยีน PRNP MRI และ RT-QuIC ช่วยประเมินชนิดและพยากรณ์ แต่ยังไม่มียารักษาให้หาย

qx.stem: A 59-year-old woman has a five-month illness that began with gait ataxia and slurred speech; dementia and slowness appeared only in the last month. EEG shows no periodic complexes. PRNP shows no mutation and codon 129 is VV, with type 2 prion protein at later autopsy.
qx.q: Which sporadic subtype fits best?
opts: MM1, the classic rapid dementia with myoclonus
MM2-thalamic, which begins with insomnia
VV2, which begins with ataxia and adds dementia later
MM2-cortical, a slow pure dementia of one to two years
VV1, a young-onset cortical and striatal dementia
qx.why: VV2 (about 16% of sporadic cases) typically starts with ataxia, develops dementia later, runs a short course and shows periodic complexes in only a minority. MM1 gives early rapid dementia and myoclonus, MM2-thalamic begins with insomnia and is MM, MM2-cortical is MM with a longer pure dementia, and VV1 begins in the 40s.

name: Sports concussion
formal: Mild traumatic brain injury in sport causing transient headache, confusion, amnesia and imbalance; repeated injury linked to chronic traumatic encephalopathy.
simple: A brain injury from a knock during sport that causes headache, confusion and memory problems.
ab: Mild traumatic brain injury in sport
th: Sport-related concussion คือการบาดเจ็บสมองเล็กน้อยจากแรงกระแทกในกีฬา ผู้เล่นมึนงง ปวดศีรษะ เสียการทรงตัวและความจำ โดยภาพ CT ปกติ ต้องหยุดเล่นทันทีและห้ามกลับลงแข่งวันเดียวกัน ใช้ SCAT6 ประเมิน พักสั้น ๆ แล้วเพิ่มกิจกรรมแบบขั้นบันได การกระทบซ้ำอาจทำให้อาการยืดเยื้อ และการกระทบศีรษะซ้ำเรื้อรังสัมพันธ์กับ CTE
tempoNote: Onset during or soon after play; most adults settle in 2–4 weeks, children and adolescents may take longer
feat: Dazed or vacant look, headache, nausea, dizziness, balance error, blurred vision or light sensitivity after a head or body impact, with or without loss of consciousness (present in a minority)
Cognitive slowing, amnesia for the event or the aftermath, irritability, sleep change and emotional lability appear immediately or hours later
Concussion can follow a blow to the body that whips the head, and many athletes are unaware that they have been concussed or fail to report it
Risk is highest in contact and collision sports; in matched sports female athletes report more concussions than males
A second impact before recovery can prolong symptoms; rare diffuse brain swelling in adolescents is the feared second-impact syndrome
inv: Sideline assessment: remove from play, check red flags, cervical spine, then SCAT6 (age 13 and older) or Child SCAT6; office assessment with SCOAT6 after the first day
Baseline testing is optional and no single computerised test has enough validity to decide return to play alone
CT only for red flags (deterioration, focal signs, seizure, repeated vomiting, suspected fracture); MRI for prolonged or atypical symptoms
Neuropsychological testing is reserved for prolonged cognitive symptoms; blood biomarkers are not validated for diagnosing concussion

case.who: 20-year-old female futsal player from Khon Kaen
case.story: She collided with a goalpost, stayed down for a minute, then said she felt 'in a fog'. She cannot recall the next five minutes and has a headache with nausea.
case.exam: Alert but slow, oriented to person and place only, poor tandem stance, no neck pain, no focal deficit.
case.tests: SCAT6 shows a high symptom score and poor delayed recall. CT is not needed as no red flags are present.
case.q: What are the immediate management and return-to-play steps?
case.a: Sport-related concussion: end the match, observe with a responsible adult, 24–48 hours of relative rest, then stepwise return to school and aerobic activity, and a graded return to sport only when symptom-free at rest and on exertion and cleared by a clinician.

27 Fits, faints, funny turns, and falls in the differential diagnosis of the dizzy patient

det.patho: Linear and rotational forces stretch axons and cause a cascade of ion flux, glutamate release, a spike in energy demand and a transient fall in cerebral blood flow, producing a reversible functional disturbance without changes on routine imaging. During this window of metabolic vulnerability a second impact may cause greater injury. Cumulative exposure to repetitive head impacts, rather than diagnosed concussions alone, is associated with chronic traumatic encephalopathy, which is a neuropathological diagnosis made after death.
det.clinical: Presentations range from a brief daze to prolonged confusion. Symptoms are physical (headache, dizziness), cognitive (fog, slowed reactions), emotional and sleep related, and may be delayed. Most adults recover within two weeks and young people within four; persistent symptoms often reflect migraine, vestibular or cervical injury, anxiety, depression or sleep problems rather than ongoing brain damage. Boxing and martial arts, football and rugby have high rates, but any sport with falls and collisions carries risk, and female athletes tend to report more concussions than males in comparable sports.
det.diagnosis: A clinician trained in concussion makes the diagnosis from the mechanism and the athlete's symptoms, signs and performance on cognition, balance and oculomotor tasks. The sport concussion assessment tools (SCAT6, Child SCAT6, and the office version SCOAT6 in the 2023 Amsterdam consensus) structure the evaluation but a normal result does not rule out concussion, and athletes can underperform at baseline. Any athlete with a suspected concussion is removed from play and is not left alone, and spinal injury is excluded first. Imaging is used only for red flags.
det.treatment: Remove from play on the same day and do not return to the match. After 24 to 48 hours of relative rest, light aerobic activity below the symptom threshold is encouraged, together with graded return to school or work, then to non-contact training and finally contact practice, with at least a day at each stage and a step back if symptoms recur. Treat post-traumatic headache, vestibular and cervical dysfunction with targeted therapy and screen for mood and sleep disorders. Return to full contact needs medical clearance; players with repeated concussions or prolonged recovery should have an individual discussion about continued participation.
det.prognosis: Full recovery is the rule; persistent symptoms are more common with previous concussions, migraine, mental health history or a high acute symptom burden.
pearls: When in doubt, sit them out: a suspected concussion ends play for the day.
Loss of consciousness is not needed for the diagnosis, and a normal CT does not exclude concussion.
Early gentle exercise helps recovery more than prolonged rest.
det.thd: Sport-related concussion เกิดจากการกระแทกศีรษะหรือลำตัวในกีฬา ทำให้มึนงง ปวดศีรษะ เสียสมดุล หรือความจำช่วงเหตุการณ์หาย โดยภาพ CT ปกติ ต้องหยุดเล่นทันทีและไม่ปล่อยให้อยู่คนเดียว ประเมินด้วย SCAT6 (อายุ 13 ปีขึ้นไป) หรือ Child SCAT6 ถ้าซึมลง อาเจียนซ้ำ หรือมีอาการทางระบบประสาทให้ส่ง CT การรักษาคือพักสั้น ๆ 24–48 ชั่วโมงแล้วกลับสู่การเรียนและกีฬาทีละขั้น และต้องได้รับอนุญาตจากแพทย์ก่อนกลับไปเล่นเต็มที่

qx.stem: A 16-year-old high-school footballer in Chiang Mai clashed heads with an opponent during a match. He did not lose consciousness but was dazed, asked the same questions repeatedly and complained of headache and nausea. On the sideline his balance was poor, and 20 minutes later he still has a headache. He is GCS 15 with no focal signs and no neck pain.
qx.q: Which is the most appropriate decision?
opts: Remove him from play for the day and start a graded, symptom-limited return-to-learn and return-to-sport plan
Let him return in the second half if a sideline check after 15 minutes is normal
Strict dark-room rest for two weeks before any activity
Return to full contact the next day if CT is normal
Admit for 48 hours of observation and repeat CT
qx.why: Any suspected concussion means no return to play on the same day. Current consensus advises a short period of relative rest followed by early light activity, a staged return-to-learn and return-to-sport, and medical clearance before full contact. Prolonged strict rest slows recovery, and a normal CT does not exclude concussion.

name: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)
formal: Malignancy of squamous epithelium whose head and neck forms spread perineurally to cranial nerves or metastasise to brain.
simple: A skin or mouth cancer that can spread along nerves to the brain.
th: มะเร็งเยื่อบุชนิด squamous ซึ่งชนิดที่ศีรษะและลำคอสามารถลามตามเส้นประสาทสมอง (perineural spread) หรือแพร่กระจายไปสมอง
tempoNote: Perineural spread causes slowly progressive cranial neuropathies over months
feat: Non-neurological malignancy with important neurological complications
Perineural spread of facial skin SCC along trigeminal (V2, V3) and facial nerves
Progressive facial numbness, formication, facial weakness months after skin lesion removal
Head and neck SCC can invade the skull base or cavernous sinus
Brain and leptomeningeal metastases from lung or oesophageal SCC
inv: MRI with thin-section contrast of cranial nerve pathways
Review history of previous skin cancer excision
Biopsy of nerve or tumour where feasible

case.story: Squamous cell carcinoma removed from the left cheek two years ago; now progressive numbness and crawling sensation over the left cheek.
case.exam: Reduced sensation in left V2, mild left facial weakness.
case.tests: MRI: enhancement and thickening of left maxillary nerve extending through foramen rotundum to the cavernous sinus.
case.q: What is the mechanism of these symptoms?
case.a: Perineural spread of cutaneous SCC along the trigeminal nerve; treated with surgery and/or radiotherapy, with immunotherapy (cemiplimab) for advanced disease.

det.patho: Squamous cell carcinoma arises from squamous epithelium of skin, head and neck mucosa, lung and oesophagus. Perineural invasion lets tumour cells travel along nerve sheaths toward the skull base, sometimes long after the primary is removed.
det.clinical: Perineural spread causes slowly progressive sensory symptoms followed by motor cranial nerve palsies. Facial skin SCC typically spreads along V2, V3 and VII. Head and neck SCC may cause lower cranial neuropathies; lung SCC can metastasise to brain.
det.diagnosis: High-resolution contrast MRI is the key test; nerve enlargement and enhancement along the pathway suggest spread. History of prior skin cancer is crucial. Biopsy confirms when possible.
det.treatment: Surgery and radiotherapy along the nerve pathway; immune checkpoint inhibitors (cemiplimab, pembrolizumab) for advanced cutaneous SCC.
det.prognosis: Perineural spread to the skull base carries a guarded prognosis.
pearls: Progressive facial numbness after skin cancer excision: think perineural spread.
Imaging must follow the whole nerve to the brainstem.
Formication may be the first symptom.
det.thd: Squamous cell carcinoma ไม่ใช่โรคทางระบบประสาทโดยตรง แต่มีภาวะแทรกซ้อนทางประสาทสำคัญ คือ perineural spread ของมะเร็งผิวหนังบริเวณใบหน้าตามเส้นประสาท trigeminal และ facial ทำให้หน้าชาและอ่อนแรงค่อยเป็นค่อยไป รวมถึงการลามฐานกะโหลกและแพร่กระจายไปสมอง วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI รักษาด้วยผ่าตัด รังสี และยาภูมิคุ้มกัน

name: St Louis encephalitis
formal: Mosquito-borne flavivirus in the Americas causing fever, headache, confusion and SIADH, especially in the elderly.
simple: A mosquito-spread viral brain infection, most serious in older people.
th: สมองอักเสบจากเชื้อไวรัสกลุ่ม flavivirus ที่ยุงรำคาญ (Culex) เป็นพาหะ พบในทวีปอเมริกา ส่วนใหญ่ไม่มีอาการ แต่ผู้สูงอายุอาจมีไข้ ปวดศีรษะ สับสน และโซเดียมต่ำจาก SIADH
tempoNote: Flu-like prodrome of a few days, then encephalopathy over days; illness lasts one to two weeks in most survivors
feat: Most infections are silent; symptomatic illness ranges from aseptic meningitis to encephalitis
Headache, vomiting and falling level of consciousness are typical, with fever
Slow evolution of symptoms, generalised weakness and tremor, with few focal signs or seizures, favour this over herpes simplex encephalitis
Severity and mortality rise with age; hyponatraemia from SIADH and urinary symptoms are well described in older adults
Summer and autumn cases after exposure to the Americas; the clinical picture overlaps with other flaviviruses
inv: CSF: moderate lymphocytic pleocytosis with mildly raised protein and normal glucose
Serum and CSF IgM for St Louis encephalitis virus, with confirmation by neutralisation because flaviviruses cross-react
MRI may show T2 signal in the thalamus, basal ganglia and substantia nigra; check sodium

case.story: Returned two weeks ago from visiting his daughter in Texas. Five days of fever and headache, then confusion, hand tremor and generalised weakness; no seizure.
case.exam: Febrile, disoriented, mild neck stiffness, coarse postural tremor, no focal weakness.
case.tests: Sodium 126 mmol/L; CSF with 180 cells, mostly lymphocytes, protein 0.8 g/L, normal glucose; HSV PCR negative; serum and CSF flavivirus IgM positive with neutralising confirmation for St Louis encephalitis virus; MRI bilateral thalamic T2 hyperintensity.
case.q: Why was a Thai-based flavivirus serology not enough here, and what is the treatment?
case.a: Flaviviruses such as Japanese encephalitis and dengue cross-react in serology, so confirmation by neutralisation and travel history is needed; treatment is supportive, with acyclovir given only until HSV is excluded.

Chapter 38 Acute Bacterial Infections of the Central Nervous System
Part I: Introduction: An Insight into Central Nervous System (CNS) Infections

det.patho: The virus is a mosquito-borne flavivirus that cycles between Culex mosquitoes and wild birds, with humans as incidental hosts. After peripheral replication it reaches the brain and produces neuronal injury concentrated in the thalamus, basal ganglia and brainstem. Older age raises the risk of symptomatic and fatal disease.
det.clinical: Infection is usually silent or limited to a flu-like illness lasting a few days. Symptomatic patients, particularly older adults, develop headache, vomiting and progressive drowsiness or confusion, sometimes with tremor and generalised weakness. Focal deficits and seizures are less common than in herpes simplex encephalitis. SIADH and urinary symptoms accompany the illness in a number of cases. Most patients recover over one to two weeks, but older patients may take months to improve and can have lasting cognitive or motor sequelae.
det.diagnosis: Consider the diagnosis in patients with encephalitis who have recent exposure in an endemic region, especially in late summer. CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with mildly raised protein and normal glucose. Diagnosis rests on IgM antibodies in serum or CSF, confirmed by neutralisation testing because of cross-reactivity with West Nile, Japanese encephalitis and dengue viruses, or a rise in titre between acute and convalescent samples. MRI can show deep grey matter involvement. HSV PCR should always be negative before settling on this diagnosis.
det.treatment: No specific antiviral is available, so care is supportive: airway protection, control of fever and seizures, treatment of raised intracranial pressure and correction of hyponatraemia. Empirical acyclovir is usual until herpes simplex encephalitis is excluded. Prevention relies on mosquito control and repellents; there is no human vaccine.
det.prognosis: Mortality is low in the young but rises sharply in the elderly, with reported figures in the range of several percent to more than ten percent in outbreaks.
pearls: Always start acyclovir first and withdraw it only when HSV is excluded.
Flavivirus IgM cross-reacts, so interpret in light of travel and local epidemiology.
Hyponatraemia is common in older patients and may worsen cerebral oedema.
det.thd: St Louis encephalitis เป็นสมองอักเสบจากไวรัสกลุ่ม flavivirus ที่ยุงรำคาญแพร่จากนกมาสู่คน พบในอเมริกา ผู้ติดเชื้อส่วนใหญ่ไม่มีอาการ แต่ผู้สูงอายุอาจมีไข้ ปวดศีรษะ สับสน มือสั่น และโซเดียมต่ำ วินิจฉัยจาก IgM ในเลือดหรือน้ำไขสันหลังและยืนยันด้วยวิธี neutralisation เพราะข้ามปฏิกิริยากับ JE และไข้เลือดออก การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง ให้ acyclovir ไว้ก่อนจนแยก HSV ได้ ไม่มีวัคซีนสำหรับคน

name: Stabbing headache
formal: Primary stabbing headache with brief ice-pick pain in the head, lasting seconds, often in migraineurs.
simple: Very brief, sharp jabs of head pain like an ice pick.
th: ปวดศีรษะปฐมภูมิแบบแปลบเหมือนเข็มแทง นานไม่กี่วินาที เกิดได้หลายตำแหน่ง มักพบในผู้ที่เป็นไมเกรน ไม่อันตราย
tempoNote: Each stab lasts up to a few seconds; stabs recur irregularly from once to many times a day
feat: Single or repeated jabs lasting 1–3 seconds
Location may move between different areas of the head
No cranial autonomic signs
More common in people with migraine or cluster headache, often in the same region
Children and adults affected
inv: Usually no tests needed with typical features and normal examination
MRI if stabs are always in one fixed location or new in an older patient
Check for coexisting migraine

case.story: Sudden sharp jabs like an ice pick, mostly around the right eye or temple but sometimes at the back, each lasting a second, several times a day.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination.
case.tests: None.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and is treatment needed?
case.a: Primary stabbing headache; reassurance is usually enough, indomethacin if frequent and troublesome.

det.patho: The cause is uncertain; transient dysfunction of central pain control or brief activation of trigeminal and occipital nociceptors is suspected. Its frequent coexistence with migraine suggests shared mechanisms.
det.clinical: Stabs are short and unpredictable, can cluster over days, and often occur where the person's migraine usually hurts. Some occur only in one area, which merits imaging. There are no accompanying autonomic features.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 criteria: head pain occurring spontaneously as single or series of stabs, each lasting up to a few seconds, recurring irregularly, without autonomic features. Exclude structural lesions when the stab is always in the same spot, and exclude trigeminal or occipital neuralgia.
det.treatment: Most need only explanation. Indomethacin is effective for frequent stabs; melatonin, gabapentin or COX-2 inhibitors are alternatives. Treat coexisting migraine.
det.prognosis: Benign, with spontaneous fluctuation over time.
pearls: Jabs that move around the head are reassuring.
Common in migraineurs — ask about it.
Indomethacin helps many patients.
det.thd: Stabbing headache หรือ ice-pick headache คือปวดศีรษะปฐมภูมิแบบแปลบเหมือนเข็มแทงนานไม่กี่วินาที อาจย้ายตำแหน่งไปมา ไม่มีน้ำตาไหลหรือตาแดง พบบ่อยในผู้ที่เป็นไมเกรน ถ้าเป็นตำแหน่งเดียวซ้ำ ๆ ควรตรวจภาพสมอง โดยทั่วไปไม่ต้องรักษา ถ้าเป็นบ่อยใช้ indomethacin ได้ผล

ddx.pt: Fixed V2/V3 territory, triggered by touch or chewing, with refractory periods
Fixed coin-shaped area with continuous background pain
Strictly unilateral orbital attacks with tearing and redness

name: Stargardt disease
formal: Autosomal recessive ABCA4 macular dystrophy with central visual loss in youth and yellow flecks.
simple: An inherited eye disease that causes loss of central vision in young people.
th: โรคจอตาส่วนกลางเสื่อมทางพันธุกรรม autosomal recessive จากยีน ABCA4 เริ่มในวัยเด็กหรือวัยรุ่น ทำให้ตามัวตรงกลางโดยปรับแว่นไม่ดีขึ้น จอประสาทตามีจุดเหลืองและฝ่อ
tempoNote: Onset in the first two decades, central acuity declining over years toward about 20/200
feat: Onset in childhood or adolescence with bilateral, symmetric central visual loss not corrected by glasses
Early fundus may look normal despite poor acuity; later macular atrophy with beaten-bronze change
Yellow-white pisciform flecks around the macula (fundus flavimaculatus pattern)
Colour vision loss, central scotoma and slow dark adaptation in some
Dark choroid on fluorescein angiography (silent choroid) in many cases
inv: Fundus autofluorescence and OCT showing flecks and photoreceptor loss
Full-field and multifocal ERG to separate macular-only from cone-rod involvement
ABCA4 gene testing with segregation in the family
Fluorescein angiography where available

case.story: Over two years she cannot read the blackboard even with new glasses. Peripheral vision and night vision feel fine. A cousin also has poor central vision.
case.exam: Acuity 20/100 in both eyes, normal pupils, central scotomas, yellowish flecks and mild macular pigment mottling on fundoscopy.
case.tests: Autofluorescence shows hypoautofluorescent macular atrophy with flecks; OCT shows outer-retinal loss; ERG shows normal cone and rod responses apart from macular loss; ABCA4 biallelic variants.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the key counselling points?
case.a: Stargardt macular dystrophy (ABCA4). Counsel about autosomal recessive inheritance, avoid vitamin A supplements and excess bright light, supply low-vision aids; clinical trials of gene and cell therapy are emerging.

read.where: Chapter 36: Hereditary Diseases of the Retina

det.patho: Loss of ABCA4 function prevents clearance of retinaldehyde from photoreceptor discs, so toxic bisretinoid compounds such as A2E accumulate as lipofuscin in the retinal pigment epithelium. The RPE then degenerates, followed by photoreceptors, with the macula the most vulnerable. Severity tracks the residual activity of the transporter, so there is a spectrum from Stargardt to cone-rod dystrophy.
det.clinical: Children notice reduced central vision, often attributed to refractive error or functional causes because the fundus can appear normal at first. Acuity usually falls within the first two decades toward the 20/200 range, while peripheral vision and mobility are mostly retained. Later onset forms with flecks and relative foveal sparing have better acuity. Colour vision may be impaired and prolonged dark adaptation occurs in some.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical with imaging and genetic confirmation. Autofluorescence, OCT and multifocal ERG detect macular dysfunction and show whether the generalised cone and rod function is preserved. Biallelic ABCA4 variants confirm the diagnosis. Mimics are cone dystrophy, Best disease, drug toxicity, optic neuropathy and non-organic visual loss.
det.treatment: No approved cure exists. Care involves low-vision rehabilitation, UV and bright-light protection, avoiding vitamin A overdosing, and genetic counselling. Research is active in gene replacement, visual cycle modulators and stem-cell approaches.
det.prognosis: Progressive central loss that usually stabilises at a legal-blindness level; peripheral function and independence are often preserved.
pearls: Normal-looking fundus does not exclude an early macular dystrophy; get autofluorescence and ERG.
Avoid vitamin A supplements in ABCA4 disease.
Variable ABCA4 alleles explain the overlap with cone-rod dystrophy.
det.thd: Stargardt เป็นโรคจอตาส่วนกลางเสื่อมที่พบบ่อยที่สุดในเด็กและวัยรุ่น เกิดจากยีน ABCA4 ผิดปกติ ทำให้เกิดสารพิษสะสมใน retinal pigment epithelium ผู้ป่วยตามัวตรงกลางทั้งสองข้างและแก้ด้วยแว่นไม่ได้ การตรวจใช้ autofluorescence, OCT, ERG และตรวจยีน ยังไม่มียารักษาให้หาย ให้คำแนะนำพันธุกรรม ป้องกันแสงจ้า หลีกเลี่ยงวิตามินเอเสริม และใช้อุปกรณ์ช่วยการมองเห็น

Subacute painless central loss in a young adult with maternal inheritance and normal retinal layers

name: Startle epilepsy
formal: Epilepsy with seizures precipitated by sudden unexpected stimuli, typically in children with hemiplegia or brain damage.
simple: Seizures set off by a sudden noise or touch.
th: โรคลมชักชนิด reflex ที่ชักเมื่อถูกกระตุ้นด้วยเสียงหรือสัมผัสที่ไม่คาดคิด มักเป็นชักเกร็งแบบ tonic ข้างเดียวในเด็กที่มีรอยโรคสมองหรืออัมพาตครึ่งซีก
tempoNote: Brief attacks provoked within a second or two of an unexpected stimulus; spontaneous seizures of other types often coexist
feat: Seizures triggered by sudden unexpected noise, touch or loss of balance, not by anticipated stimuli
Typically a brief, lateralised or asymmetric tonic seizure that may cause a fall; the paretic side is often involved
Most patients have early brain injury, hemiplegia or learning disability, and a lesion in the mesial frontal or perirolandic cortex
Other spontaneous focal or generalised seizures are usual; the condition is frequently drug resistant
Ictal discharge often arises from the supplementary motor area and mesial frontal cortex
inv: Video-EEG with a controlled, unexpected stimulus (clap, sudden touch) to document the reflex attack and its onset
MRI epilepsy protocol for mesial frontal or perirolandic lesions, malformation of cortical development or old infarct
Genetic and metabolic studies in children without a lesion; presurgical work-up if drug resistant

case.who: 9-year-old boy with right hemiparesis since a neonatal stroke, Chiang Mai
case.story: His mother saw him stiffen and fall to the ground whenever a door slammed or someone dropped a plate. The episodes last a few seconds. He has additional nocturnal seizures.
case.exam: Mild right spastic hemiparesis, mild learning difficulties, normal cranial nerves. A sudden handclap behind him during the examination provokes a brief tonic stiffening in his right arm and leg and he falls.
case.tests: Video-EEG shows a central and mesial frontal discharge preceding the stiffening. MRI shows an old left perirolandic infarct with cortical gliosis.
case.q: How is it separated from hyperekplexia, and what treatment strategies are available?
case.a: Hyperekplexia causes an exaggerated startle with generalised stiffness, normal EEG and a nose-tap response, with a neonatal onset and responds to clonazepam. Startle epilepsy has an ictal EEG correlate and needs antiseizure drugs for focal seizures, and surgery should be considered when the lesion is resectable and drugs fail.

read.where: Chapter 22: Epilepsy with Reflex Seizures — Proprioceptive-Induced Seizures and Startle Epilepsy

det.patho: Startle epilepsy is a symptomatic focal reflex epilepsy in which a sudden sensory stimulus engages a hyperexcitable network in the supplementary motor area and mesial frontal cortex, the same territory that mediates normal startle responses. Most patients have a structural substrate such as perinatal infarct, cortical dysplasia or other early injury. The network conducts the discharge to the contralateral side, which explains the tonic asymmetric semiology.
det.clinical: Attacks follow within seconds of an unexpected sound, touch or sudden movement, produce a brief tonic stiffening with or without a fall, and may repeat in clusters. Patients usually have hemiplegia, intellectual disability and additional spontaneous seizures, and the epilepsy is often medically intractable. Habituation after repeated stimuli can create a short refractory interval. Families describe anxiety about everyday noises, and injuries from falls are a real risk.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical with video-EEG confirmation that the attack is a seizure, ideally including provocation with a sudden stimulus. MRI looks for the underlying lesion, since subtle dysplasia may only be visible on high-resolution studies. Exclude hyperekplexia, which has a normal EEG and often a GLRA1 variant, cataplexy, myoclonic epilepsies, paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia and functional events. Evaluate for surgery when drug-resistant.
det.treatment: Antiseizure drugs for focal seizures are first-line; choice follows the child’s age and comorbidity. Counsel on avoiding sudden startling where possible, protect against falls with a helmet if drop attacks occur, and treat coexisting seizure types. When the seizure onset zone is concordant with a lesion and attacks are drug resistant, resection or disconnection of the mesial frontal focus can be considered. Other options include vagus nerve stimulation, ketogenic diet and, in selected centres, neuromodulation.
det.prognosis: Usually long-standing and difficult to control, reflecting the underlying brain injury; surgery gives the best chance of freedom in carefully chosen patients.
pearls: Tonic attacks provoked by an unexpected stimulus in a hemiplegic child: think startle epilepsy and get video-EEG.
Normal EEG and clonazepam response with neonatal stiffness suggest hyperekplexia, not epilepsy.
Look for the mesial frontal lesion: it is the target if surgery is possible.
det.thd: Startle epilepsy คือโรคลมชักที่ถูกกระตุ้นด้วยเสียงดังหรือสัมผัสที่ไม่ทันตั้งตัว ผู้ป่วยมักเกร็งแบบ tonic ชั่วครู่แล้วล้ม พบมากในเด็กที่เคยมีสมองเสียหาย เช่น อัมพาตครึ่งซีกหรือรอยโรคที่ mesial frontal ควรทำ video-EEG เพื่อพิสูจน์ว่าเป็นชัก และแยกจาก hyperekplexia ซึ่ง EEG ปกติและตอบสนองต่อ clonazepam การรักษาใช้ยากันชักสำหรับ focal seizure และพิจารณาผ่าตัดเมื่อยาไม่ได้ผล

Brief dystonic or choreic attacks triggered by sudden voluntary movement, preserved awareness, normal EEG
Variable, suggestible attacks without a consistent trigger or ictal EEG change

name: Statin myopathy
formal: Muscle toxicity from statins ranging from myalgia to necrotising immune-mediated myopathy with HMGCR antibodies and raised CK.
simple: Muscle pain or weakness caused by cholesterol-lowering statin medicines.
th: ปวดหรืออ่อนแรงกล้ามเนื้อจากยาลดไขมันกลุ่ม statin — ส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นเมื่อหยุดยา ถ้าไม่ดีขึ้นให้นึกถึง anti-HMGCR myopathy
tempoNote: Weeks to months after starting or raising the dose; toxic form settles within weeks of stopping
feat: Aching, cramps or heaviness in thighs and calves, often symmetric
Spectrum: myalgia with normal CK → mild CK rise → true weakness → rarely rhabdomyolysis
Risk rises with high-intensity statin, CYP3A4 inhibitors (macrolides, azoles), fibrates, hypothyroidism, renal impairment, older age
Toxic form improves after withdrawal; persisting or worsening weakness with very high CK suggests immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy
inv: CK at baseline and when symptomatic; TSH, renal and liver function
Anti-HMGCR antibody if weakness or high CK persists beyond 6–12 weeks off the drug
EMG/MRI thigh and muscle biopsy for persistent or atypical cases

case.who: 66-year-old man with diabetes and coronary stents
case.story: Atorvastatin was raised to 80 mg; a month later clarithromycin was added for pneumonia. He now has aching thighs and struggles to climb onto a songthaew.
case.exam: Mild symmetric hip flexor weakness, tender thighs, normal reflexes and sensation.
case.tests: CK 4,800 U/L, TSH normal, creatinine slightly raised; urine dipstick heme negative.
case.q: What is the next step, and when would you test for anti-HMGCR?
case.a: Stop the statin and the interacting antibiotic, hydrate and follow CK. If weakness or CK fails to settle after about 2–3 months off the statin, check anti-HMGCR for immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy.

read.where: Myopathies of Systemic Disease and Toxic Myopathies

det.patho: Statins block HMG-CoA reductase, lowering not only cholesterol but also downstream products such as ubiquinone and prenylated proteins that muscle needs for energy and membrane repair. Toxicity is dose-related and amplified by high blood levels from drug interactions or a SLCO1B1 transporter variant. A separate, much rarer entity is an autoimmune necrotizing myopathy in which antibodies target HMG-CoA reductase itself and the disease continues after the drug is gone.
det.clinical: Most patients describe muscle aches without weakness and with normal or near-normal CK; true myopathy with proximal weakness is less common, and rhabdomyolysis is rare. Symptoms usually begin within the first months or after a dose increase or new interacting drug. Nocebo effects are frequent, so symptoms that vanish on rechallenge with placebo are well documented. Red flags are objective weakness, dark urine, CK above ten times normal, and progression after stopping.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on timing, CK and response to withdrawal. Check thyroid, renal and liver function, vitamin D and interacting drugs. If symptoms and CK resolve within weeks, the toxic form is likely. Persisting proximal weakness with high CK after withdrawal calls for anti-HMGCR serology, EMG (irritable myopathic pattern), MRI for oedema and a biopsy showing scattered necrotic fibres with little inflammation.
det.treatment: Stop or reduce the statin and correct contributing factors. After recovery, options include a lower dose, a hydrophilic statin such as rosuvastatin or pravastatin, alternate-day dosing, or non-statin agents (ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitors, bempedoic acid). Coenzyme Q10 has weak evidence. Anti-HMGCR myopathy needs immunotherapy—typically IVIG with steroids and a steroid-sparing agent—and permanent statin avoidance.
det.prognosis: Toxic myopathy recovers fully in nearly all patients within weeks to a few months. Anti-HMGCR myopathy is chronic and often needs long-term immunotherapy.
pearls: Normal CK with aches is usually not dangerous myopathy; weakness plus high CK is.
Getting worse after the statin is stopped is the clue to anti-HMGCR necrotizing myopathy.
Look for the interacting drug: macrolides, azole antifungals, gemfibrozil, ciclosporin, amiodarone.
det.thd: Statin ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อปวดหรืออ่อนแรงได้ โดยเฉพาะขนาดสูงหรือใช้ร่วมกับยาที่ยับยั้ง CYP3A4 ส่วนใหญ่ CK ปกติหรือสูงเล็กน้อยและหายภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์หลังหยุดยา หากอ่อนแรงต่อเนื่องและ CK สูงมากแม้หยุดยาแล้ว ต้องตรวจ anti-HMGCR เพราะอาจเป็น immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy ซึ่งต้องรักษาด้วยยากดภูมิ

Slow relaxation of reflexes, cold intolerance; raised TSH (also a statin risk factor)
No drug link; inflammatory infiltrates on biopsy and often other autoimmune features
