name: Statokinetic dissociation
formal: Preservation of moving-object perception with failure to see static objects in a blind field, as in Riddoch phenomenon.
simple: Being able to see moving objects but not still ones in a blind part of vision.
th: ภาวะที่ในบริเวณลานสายตาบอด ผู้ป่วยยังเห็นวัตถุที่เคลื่อนไหวได้ แต่ไม่เห็นวัตถุที่อยู่นิ่ง ไม่ใช่โรค แต่เป็นปรากฏการณ์ทางคลินิก
tempoNote: Present as long as the underlying visual field defect persists; may signal recovery
feat: Moving targets perceived in a field area where static targets are not seen
Classically after occipital (V1) lesions, preserving motion processing via V5/MT pathways
Also found in optic nerve disease and glaucoma on perimetry
Kinetic perimetry shows larger field than static automated perimetry
Not a disease itself: a sign of residual visual function
inv: Compare kinetic (Goldmann) and static (Humphrey) perimetry
MRI brain to define the underlying occipital or optic pathway lesion

case.story: After a left occipital infarct she cannot see objects on her right side but notices cars moving there.
case.exam: Right homonymous hemianopia to static targets; detects moving hand in right field.
case.tests: Goldmann perimetry larger than Humphrey field in the right hemifield; MRI: left occipital infarct.
case.q: What phenomenon is this?
case.a: Statokinetic dissociation (Riddoch phenomenon) in an occipital hemianopia.

read.where: Chapter 22 Neuro-Ophthalmology — Disorders of Higher Visual Function
Chapter 22 Neuro-Ophthalmology — Blindsight and Statokinetic Dissociation

det.patho: Motion signals can reach extrastriate areas (V5/MT) via pathways that bypass the damaged primary visual cortex, including the superior colliculus–pulvinar route and direct LGN projections. Moving stimuli also produce stronger and more spatially summed signals than static ones, so they are detected in partially damaged fields.
det.clinical: Patients may say they see movement but not the object itself. The phenomenon is mostly found incidentally on perimetry comparison. It can occur in post-chiasmal and pre-chiasmal disease and is not specific to one site. Its presence may indicate potential for recovery.
det.diagnosis: Testing with moving and static targets in the same area shows the dissociation. Formal kinetic and static perimetry document it. The underlying lesion must be identified with imaging. It should not be mistaken for inconsistency suggesting functional loss.
det.treatment: There is no treatment for the phenomenon itself. Management targets the causative lesion and visual rehabilitation, such as scanning training for hemianopia.
det.prognosis: Depends on the underlying condition; preserved motion perception may be associated with better field recovery.
pearls: Kinetic fields larger than static fields do not automatically mean non-organic loss.
Riddoch first described this in soldiers with occipital injuries.
Related to but distinct from blindsight, where patients deny seeing yet respond above chance.
det.thd: Statokinetic dissociation หรือ Riddoch phenomenon คือการที่ผู้ป่วยมองเห็นวัตถุเคลื่อนไหวได้ในบริเวณลานสายตาที่มองไม่เห็นวัตถุนิ่ง พบบ่อยหลังรอยโรค occipital เพราะสัญญาณการเคลื่อนไหวไปถึง V5/MT ได้ทางอ้อม ไม่ใช่โรคแต่เป็นปรากฏการณ์ ตรวจพบเมื่อเทียบ kinetic กับ static perimetry ไม่ควรตีความว่าเป็น functional

ddx.pt: Cortical blindness with denial of blindness
Spiral or tubular fields inconsistent with optics; not a selective motion preservation
Complex formed visual hallucinations in a blind field, with insight; not genuine motion perception

aN: riddoch phenomenon | riddoch syndrome | skd | static kinetic dissociation

name: Status cataplecticus
formal: Prolonged continuous cataplexy episodes in narcolepsy, usually after sudden stopping of antidepressants.
simple: Long periods of sudden muscle weakness triggered by emotions in narcolepsy.
th: ภาวะ cataplexy ต่อเนื่องหรือเกิดซ้ำติดๆ กันนานเป็นชั่วโมงในผู้ป่วย narcolepsy มักเกิดหลังหยุดยาต้านซึมเศร้าที่ใช้ควบคุม cataplexy ทันที
tempoNote: Develops within days of abrupt antidepressant withdrawal and may last hours to days
feat: Repeated or continuous cataplexy with near-total loss of muscle tone for hours or days
Consciousness preserved; patient may appear paralysed or collapsed
Usually precipitated by sudden stopping of SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics or sodium oxybate
Rarely spontaneous or in Niemann–Pick type C and other secondary narcolepsy
Responds to restarting the withdrawn drug
inv: Medication history: recent stopping of antidepressants or oxybate
Reflexes absent during attacks; EEG shows wakefulness
Exclude stroke, seizures, functional disorder and periodic paralysis as clinically indicated

case.who: 31-year-old woman with narcolepsy type 1 attending a Bangkok sleep clinic
case.story: Stopped venlafaxine abruptly five days ago because she wanted to get pregnant; now collapses many times an hour whenever anyone talks to her and has spent the day on the sofa unable to stand.
case.exam: Awake and aware, flaccid with absent tendon reflexes during episodes, facial sagging and jaw dropping, normal between episodes.
case.tests: Electrolytes normal; EEG shows wakefulness during attacks.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the immediate treatment?
case.a: Status cataplecticus from abrupt antidepressant withdrawal; restart venlafaxine, then plan a slow taper and alternative pregnancy-compatible strategy.

det.patho: Cataplexy results from emotion-triggered activation of REM atonia circuits in a brain lacking hypocretin. Antidepressants suppress cataplexy by blocking monoamine reuptake and REM sleep; when stopped abruptly, rebound activation of atonia pathways causes a flood of attacks. Sodium oxybate withdrawal can produce a similar rebound.
det.clinical: Patients have frequent or near-continuous cataplexy, sometimes triggered by minimal emotion or even spontaneous, leaving them unable to stand or walk for hours to days. Consciousness and breathing are preserved. Distress, falls and injuries are common, and the picture may be misread as stroke, seizure or a functional disorder.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical in a patient with known narcolepsy and recent drug withdrawal. During attacks, tendon reflexes are absent and EEG shows wakefulness. In patients without known narcolepsy, consider secondary causes and investigate with PSG, MSLT and hypocretin when stable.
det.treatment: Restart the withdrawn medication promptly; this usually controls the episodes within hours to days. Future discontinuation should be gradual. Sodium oxybate, pitolisant or clomipramine can be used for refractory cataplexy. Ensure safety during attacks and avoid mislabelling as functional illness.
det.prognosis: Usually resolves fully once treatment is reinstated.
pearls: Never stop anticataplectic antidepressants abruptly.
Absent reflexes during an attack support cataplexy over functional weakness.
Ask about recent medication changes in any narcolepsy patient with sudden worsening.
det.thd: Status cataplecticus คือภาวะที่ผู้ป่วย narcolepsy มี cataplexy ซ้ำๆ ต่อเนื่องนานเป็นชั่วโมงหรือหลายวัน จนลุกยืนไม่ได้ แต่ยังรู้สึกตัวดี มักเกิดหลังหยุดยาต้านซึมเศร้าหรือ sodium oxybate ทันที ระหว่างเป็นจะไม่มี reflex และ EEG แสดงว่าตื่นอยู่ การรักษาคือกลับมาให้ยาเดิม แล้วค่อยๆ ลดยาอย่างช้าๆ ในอนาคต

Prolonged unresponsiveness with variable tone and preserved reflexes

name: Status dysmyelinisatus
formal: Historic term for severe pallidal or striatal myelination abnormality with marbled appearance leading to athetosis.
simple: An old term for abnormal brain wiring in the basal ganglia, causing writhing movements.
th: ศัพท์ทางพยาธิวิทยาแบบเก่า หมายถึง myelin ใน globus pallidus หรือ striatum ลดลงอย่างมากจนผิดปกติ สัมพันธ์กับ athetosis ปัจจุบันไม่ใช้เป็นชื่อโรคแล้ว
tempoNote: Historical neuropathological description of early-life injury or degeneration; static or progressive depending on cause
feat: Historic term (Vogt) for loss of myelin and gliosis in pallidum and striatum
Clinically associated with athetosis, dystonia and rigidity in childhood
Causes then lumped together; now recognised as kernicterus, hypoxic injury and neurodegenerative disorders
Distinguished from status marmoratus, which shows excess, marbled myelination
inv: MRI: pallidal T2 signal change (e.g. kernicterus), eye-of-the-tiger sign in PKAN
History of neonatal jaundice or hypoxia; genetic and metabolic testing for NBIA, Wilson and others

case.story: Severe neonatal jaundice requiring exchange transfusion; now writhing movements of limbs and hearing loss.
case.exam: Choreoathetosis, upward gaze limitation, sensorineural deafness, normal intellect.
case.tests: MRI: bilateral globus pallidus T2 hyperintensity; auditory brainstem responses absent.
case.q: How would an old pathologist have labelled this, and what is the modern diagnosis?
case.a: Historic label status dysmyelinisatus; modern diagnosis is kernicterus (bilirubin encephalopathy) causing athetoid cerebral palsy.

det.patho: The term described a pathological appearance of pale, myelin-deficient and shrunken pallidum and striatum, seen in several conditions, including kernicterus and some progressive degenerations. It does not indicate a single mechanism and has been replaced by specific diagnoses defined by aetiology, imaging and genetics.
det.clinical: Historically linked to childhood choreoathetosis and dystonia with rigidity. Today, patients previously given this label would be diagnosed with dyskinetic cerebral palsy from bilirubin or hypoxic injury, or with neurodegenerative disorders such as NBIA.
det.diagnosis: Use the term only in historical or pathological contexts. Clinical diagnosis now relies on perinatal history, MRI patterns and genetic or metabolic testing.
det.treatment: Treatment follows the modern diagnosis: management of dyskinetic cerebral palsy (anticholinergics, baclofen, botulinum toxin, deep brain stimulation in selected cases) or disease-specific care.
det.prognosis: Depends on the underlying condition.
pearls: Status dysmyelinisatus is a historic pathology label, not a current diagnosis.
Do not confuse with status marmoratus, which has excess myelin.
Kernicterus classically targets the globus pallidus and subthalamic nucleus.
det.thd: Status dysmyelinisatus เป็นศัพท์พยาธิวิทยาแบบเก่าของ Vogt หมายถึง globus pallidus และ striatum มี myelin น้อยและฝ่อ สัมพันธ์กับ athetosis ในเด็ก ปัจจุบันไม่ใช้เป็นชื่อโรคแล้ว แต่แยกเป็นสาเหตุเฉพาะ เช่น kernicterus, hypoxic injury และ NBIA การรักษาจึงขึ้นกับโรคที่แท้จริง

name: Status dystonicus
formal: Life-threatening severe generalised dystonia with rhabdomyolysis and respiratory risk, needing ICU management.
simple: A severe, long-lasting episode of twisting spasms that can be life-threatening.
th: Status dystonicus คือภาวะ dystonia รุนแรงทั่วร่างกายต่อเนื่องที่ต้องรับไว้ในโรงพยาบาลเร่งด่วน พบบ่อยในเด็กที่มี dystonia จากโรคทางพันธุกรรมหรือ cerebral palsy หลังติดเชื้อหรือเปลี่ยนยา อาการสำคัญคือปวด ไข้ กล้ามเนื้อสลาย และหายใจลำบาก การรักษาเน้นไอซียู ให้น้ำ ยากล่อมประสาท และยารักษา dystonia
tempoNote: Spasms intensify over hours to days in a child or adult with established dystonia; moderate and severe stages need urgent admission
feat: Increasingly frequent or continuous severe generalised dystonic spasms that defeat the usual treatment and need urgent admission
Pain, distress, sleep loss, fever, dehydration and high pulse; bulbar and respiratory compromise in severe stages
Rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria and acute kidney injury is the main systemic danger
Typical background is dyskinetic cerebral palsy, a genetic dystonia (GNAO1, ATP1A3, TOR1A, PANK2, KMT2B) or an acute brain injury
Triggers: infection, pain, surgery, missed or withdrawn drugs, intrathecal baclofen failure, DBS battery depletion or lead problem, dopamine blockers
inv: CK, creatinine, potassium, urine myoglobin, blood gas and lactate at admission and repeated every few hours in severe cases
Infection screen (blood, urine, chest, CSF if indicated) and a check of drug adherence and recent changes
Interrogation of a DBS device or inspection and refill check of an intrathecal baclofen pump
A staging record of severity (such as the consensus staging of the Lumsden group) to guide intensive care use

case.who: 9-year-old boy with dyskinetic cerebral palsy from Chiang Mai
case.story: After a chest infection and two days of missed baclofen he has constant severe twisting spasms and cries in pain.
case.exam: Temperature 38.9 °C, tachycardia, continuous opisthotonic and limb spasms, dark urine, difficulty handling secretions.
case.tests: CK 48,000 U/L, raised creatinine, chest X-ray with right lower lobe pneumonia.
case.q: Name the emergency and the key steps.
case.a: Status dystonicus. Admit to intensive care, give intravenous fluids, analgesia and antibiotics, restart baclofen, sedate with midazolam (intubate if secretions or airway are unsafe), then optimise anti-dystonic drugs and consider DBS if refractory.

det.patho: The condition represents decompensation of a chronic dystonia, in which pain, distress and fever feed a cycle of ever more intense muscle contraction. Loss of inhibitory control in basal ganglia and cerebellar-thalamic circuits is presumed, and infection or an abrupt drug or device change tips the balance. Muscle breakdown, hyperthermia, dehydration and metabolic acidosis follow.
det.clinical: Children are affected more often than adults, and the first sign may be a change in the character of habitual dystonia, with spasms that no longer respond to usual measures. Sleep disappears, the child screams in pain, feeding stops, and signs of exhaustion and organ strain follow. The worst complications are airway failure, rhabdomyolysis with kidney injury, and cardiac and hepatic strain. Severity staging helps decide how quickly to move to intensive care and to anaesthesia.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on recognition of rising dystonic activity with systemic effects. Check for triggers (infection, pain, constipation, drug stop, device failure) and look for complications through CK, urea and creatinine, potassium and blood gases. Differentiate NMS, serotonin syndrome, malignant hyperthermia, seizures, meningitis and baclofen withdrawal, each of which can also coexist.
det.treatment: Admit early to a high-dependency or intensive care unit and treat triggers: fluids, analgesia, antipyretics, antibiotics and nutrition. Sedation with midazolam, clonidine or dexmedetomidine is often first, with intubation, propofol and muscle relaxation for refractory cases; avoid suxamethonium in rhabdomyolysis. Add or optimise anti-dystonic drugs (baclofen, trihexyphenidyl, benzodiazepines, gabapentin, tetrabenazine, clonidine). Pallidal DBS or intrathecal baclofen can be life-saving in refractory cases, and several centres now operate in the acute phase. Plan afterwards how to prevent recurrence, including a rescue protocol for the family.
det.prognosis: Most children survive with intensive care, but recurrence is frequent and some are left with new deficits; death is reported in a minority.
pearls: Rising spasms in a child with dystonia plus fever is a medical emergency, not a drug-seeking pattern.
Check the baclofen pump and the DBS device in every case.
Rhabdomyolysis, not spasm itself, kills; follow the CK and urine output.
det.thd: Status dystonicus คือภาวะที่ dystonia รุนแรงขึ้นจนต้องเข้ารับการรักษาเร่งด่วน พบบ่อยในเด็กที่เป็น cerebral palsy ชนิด dyskinetic หรือ dystonia ทางพันธุกรรม หลังติดเชื้อ ปวด หรือหยุด baclofen ผู้ป่วยมีไข้ ปวดมาก นอนไม่หลับ กล้ามเนื้อสลายและไตวายได้ ต้องดูแลในไอซียู ให้น้ำ แก้ปวด รักษาการติดเชื้อ ใช้ midazolam หรือยาระงับประสาทอื่น เพิ่มยา dystonia และถ้าไม่ตอบสนองพิจารณา DBS หรือ intrathecal baclofen

qx.stem: An 11-year-old boy from Chiang Mai with dyskinetic cerebral palsy has had constant, painful twisting spasms for two days after a respiratory infection and a missed dose of baclofen. His temperature is 39 °C and pulse 150. Urine is dark; CK is 52,000 U/L and creatinine is rising. He cannot swallow his saliva.
qx.q: Which is the best plan?
opts: Admit to intensive care, give fluids, analgesia and antibiotics, restart baclofen and use midazolam sedation, with airway protection as needed
Send home on increased oral baclofen
Give haloperidol and observe on the general ward
Give suxamethonium to relax the muscles before intubation
Arrange outpatient botulinum toxin injection next week
qx.why: Escalating generalised dystonia with fever, rhabdomyolysis and bulbar compromise is status dystonicus. It requires intensive care: hydration to protect the kidneys, treatment of infection, restoration of baclofen, sedation with benzodiazepine infusion and airway protection, with DBS or intrathecal baclofen if refractory. Suxamethonium is dangerous in rhabdomyolysis because of hyperkalaemia, and outpatient management or dopamine blockers are inappropriate.

name: Status epilepticus
formal: Seizure lasting over 5 minutes or recurrent seizures without recovery, a neurological emergency needing benzodiazepines and antiepileptics.
simple: A seizure that will not stop, or repeated seizures without waking, needing emergency treatment.
th: ชักต่อเนื่องเกิน 5 นาทีหรือชักซ้ำโดยไม่ฟื้น — ภาวะฉุกเฉิน ต้องให้ยาตามลำดับเวลา
tempoNote: Treat at 5 minutes; neuronal injury risk after ~30 minutes
feat: Continuous seizure ≥5 min or repeated seizures without recovery
Non-convulsive status may present as unexplained coma or confusion
Causes: antiseizure drug withdrawal, stroke, infection, metabolic, autoimmune encephalitis
inv: Glucose immediately; electrolytes, Ca/Mg, drug levels, toxicology
Continuous EEG if not waking up

case.exam: Generalised tonic-clonic activity, SpO2 88%.
case.tests: Glucose 5.2 mmol/L.

det.patho: Status occurs when seizure-terminating mechanisms fail or seizure-sustaining mechanisms take over: GABA-A receptors are internalised while NMDA and AMPA receptors move to the synapse, so benzodiazepines lose potency the longer the seizure lasts. Prolonged seizures lead to excitotoxic neuronal injury, systemic hyperthermia, acidosis, rhabdomyolysis and cardiorespiratory compromise. Time point t1 (5 minutes) marks when to treat and t2 (around 30 minutes) when lasting damage becomes likely.
det.clinical: Convulsive status is obvious, but subtle motor signs (eyelid or facial twitching) may be all that remain later. Non-convulsive status presents as confusion, behavioural change, aphasia or coma and is common in ICU and elderly patients. Common triggers include low antiseizure drug levels, alcohol withdrawal, stroke, CNS infection, metabolic derangement, toxins and autoimmune encephalitis. Refractory status persists despite benzodiazepine and a second-line drug; super-refractory status continues 24 hours after anaesthesia. NORSE describes new-onset refractory status in a previously healthy person.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis of convulsive status is clinical; check capillary glucose at once. Send electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, renal and liver function, CK, blood gas, drug levels, toxicology and pregnancy test where relevant. Arrange urgent CT and, as indicated, MRI and lumbar puncture. Start continuous EEG if the patient does not wake within the expected time after convulsions stop, to detect non-convulsive status. Dissociative seizures, rigors and posturing in coma are key mimics.
det.treatment: Secure airway, breathing and circulation, give oxygen, and correct hypoglycaemia; give IV thiamine before glucose if alcohol misuse or malnutrition is possible. At 5 minutes give a benzodiazepine (IV lorazepam or diazepam, or IM midazolam/buccal midazolam pre-hospital), repeating once if needed. If seizures continue, load a second-line IV drug — levetiracetam, valproate or fosphenytoin/phenytoin are similarly effective. Refractory status requires intubation and anaesthetic infusion (midazolam, propofol or thiopental) titrated to EEG; treat the underlying cause in parallel, including immunotherapy for suspected autoimmune aetiology.
det.prognosis: Mortality is around 10–20% overall and higher in older patients, with acute symptomatic causes and refractory status; drug withdrawal-related status in known epilepsy has a better outlook.
pearls: Under-dosing benzodiazepines is the commonest treatment error — give a full dose early.
A patient who is not waking after convulsions stop may still be seizing: get an EEG.
Check glucose first and give thiamine where malnutrition or alcohol is possible.

name: Status marmoratus
formal: Perinatal hypoxic-ischaemic basal ganglia injury with marbled gliosis, leading to dyskinetic cerebral palsy.
simple: Brain injury around birth causing marbled scarring in deep brain areas and later movement problems.
ab: status marmoratus of the basal ganglia
dyskinetic CP from basal ganglia injury
th: รอยโรคของ basal ganglia และ thalamus จากภาวะขาดออกซิเจนรอบคลอด เนื้อสมองเป็นลายหินอ่อนจาก myelin ผิดที่ ทำให้เกิด cerebral palsy ชนิด dyskinetic
tempoNote: Injury occurs around birth; abnormal movements emerge over the first 1–2 years and the lesion itself does not progress
feat: History of acute profound perinatal asphyxia (e.g. cord prolapse, uterine rupture), often in a term baby
Early hypotonia, then dystonia and choreoathetosis appearing in late infancy
Feeding and speech difficulty from orofacial dyskinesia; cognition often better than motor function
Static course — new deficits or loss of skills argue against it
inv: MRI: symmetric T2 signal change and later volume loss in putamen, thalamus (ventrolateral) and sometimes perirolandic cortex
Review perinatal records (Apgar, cord pH, neonatal encephalopathy, seizures)
If history is weak or course progressive: metabolic and genetic work-up (e.g. glutaric aciduria type 1, mitochondrial disease)

case.story: Born at term after an emergency caesarean for cord prolapse, needed cooling for neonatal encephalopathy. He was floppy as a baby and now has twisting arm movements whenever he tries to reach.
case.exam: Truncal hypotonia, dystonic posturing of the arms on action, writhing tongue movements and drooling; good eye contact and understands simple commands.
case.tests: MRI shows bilateral posterior putaminal and lateral thalamic T2 hyperintensity with mild atrophy.
case.q: What is the pathological correlate and the clinical label?
case.a: Status marmoratus from deep grey matter hypoxic-ischaemic injury, producing dyskinetic cerebral palsy.

det.patho: A severe, abrupt drop in oxygen and blood flow near term injures the metabolically busy deep grey nuclei first, especially the putamen and ventrolateral thalamus. Neuronal loss is followed by gliosis and aberrant hypermyelination of fibres, which on cut section gives the striatum a white, marbled look — the origin of the name. The term is mostly pathological; in the MRI era clinicians usually describe the same injury as a basal ganglia–thalamus pattern of hypoxic-ischaemic injury.
det.clinical: Infants are typically hypotonic in the first year; dystonia, choreoathetosis and orofacial dyskinesia then emerge between about 9 months and 2 years as myelination matures. Speech and swallowing are often more disabled than intellect, so many children understand far more than they can express. Some movements worsen with emotion or effort and may even increase in adolescence, which can be mistaken for progression. Any true regression should prompt a search for another diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on a compatible perinatal history plus MRI showing the deep grey matter pattern; late scans show volume loss and gliosis. A clear sentinel event (abruption, cord prolapse, rupture) strengthens the link. Without such a history, consider metabolic causes (glutaric aciduria type 1, mitochondrial disease, kernicterus) and genetic dyskinesias, since some are treatable.
det.treatment: There is no treatment for the lesion; management targets the movement disorder and function. Options include anticholinergics such as trihexyphenidyl, baclofen (oral or intrathecal), botulinum toxin for focal problems and, in selected children, pallidal deep brain stimulation with modest gains. Augmentative communication, feeding support, physiotherapy and orthopaedic surveillance for hip and spine problems are central. Therapeutic hypothermia in the neonatal period reduces the chance of this outcome.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy depends on feeding, respiratory and mobility status; the brain lesion is static but disability is lifelong.
pearls: Marbled striatum = hypermyelinated gliotic scar after near-term hypoxic-ischaemic injury.
Putamen/thalamus involvement suggests asphyxia; globus pallidus involvement suggests kernicterus.
Regression is not part of status marmoratus — investigate for metabolic or genetic disease.
det.thd: Status marmoratus คือรอยโรคของ putamen และ thalamus จากการขาดออกซิเจนเฉียบพลันรุนแรงช่วงคลอด เนื้อสมองมี gliosis และ myelin เกินผิดที่จนดูเป็นลายหินอ่อน เด็กจะตัวอ่อนในขวบปีแรกแล้วเกิด dystonia และ choreoathetosis ตามมา เป็น dyskinetic cerebral palsy ที่ไม่แย่ลง วินิจฉัยจากประวัติคลอดร่วมกับ MRI รักษาตามอาการด้วยยา botulinum toxin กายภาพ และอุปกรณ์ช่วยสื่อสาร

The neonatal encephalopathy that precedes it; basal ganglia–thalamus pattern predicts later dyskinesia

name: Steal syndromes
formal: Haemodynamic diversion of blood from a vascular bed, e.g. subclavian steal causing vertebrobasilar insufficiency.
simple: Conditions where blood is diverted away from the brain or arm because of a narrowed artery.
th: กลุ่มภาวะที่เลือดถูกเบี่ยงออกจากบริเวณหนึ่งไปเลี้ยงอีกบริเวณจากการตีบหรือทางลัดของหลอดเลือด เช่น subclavian steal ทำให้มีอาการ vertebrobasilar
tempoNote: Symptoms are episodic, often provoked by exercising the affected arm or by haemodynamic changes, on a background of chronic stenosis
feat: Reversal of flow in a vessel to supply a territory distal to a proximal stenosis or shunt
Subclavian steal: retrograde vertebral flow; dizziness, vertigo, visual blurring or syncope with arm exercise
Arm claudication and a blood pressure difference of >15–20 mmHg between arms
Other forms: AVM-related steal, coronary-subclavian steal after internal mammary graft, dialysis access steal
Most radiological subclavian steal is asymptomatic
inv: Bilateral arm blood pressures and pulses
Duplex ultrasound showing reversed or alternating vertebral flow, sometimes with cuff provocation
CT or MR angiography of the aortic arch and great vessels
Vasculitis work-up (ESR, CRP) in young patients

case.story: When he chops wood with his left arm he becomes dizzy, sees double and his arm aches; symptoms ease when he stops.
case.exam: Left radial pulse weak and delayed; BP right arm 158/84, left arm 120/76; left supraclavicular bruit.
case.tests: Duplex shows reversed flow in the left vertebral artery; CTA shows tight proximal left subclavian stenosis.
case.q: Explain the mechanism and the treatment options.
case.a: Subclavian steal — blood flows down the left vertebral to feed the arm; risk-factor control and antiplatelet, with angioplasty and stenting for persistent symptoms.

det.patho: A steal occurs when a pressure gradient created by proximal stenosis, occlusion or a low-resistance shunt draws blood away from a territory that would normally receive it. In subclavian steal, stenosis proximal to the vertebral origin lowers pressure in the arm, so blood runs backward down the vertebral artery from the basilar circulation. In AVMs and fistulas, the low-resistance shunt diverts blood from surrounding brain.
det.clinical: Many patients with angiographic steal have no symptoms because the circle of Willis compensates. Symptomatic patients describe vertebrobasilar symptoms provoked by arm use, along with arm fatigue or pain. Coronary-subclavian steal causes angina in patients with internal mammary grafts. Atherosclerosis is the usual cause in older adults; Takayasu arteritis, radiation and congenital arch anomalies occur in younger patients.
det.diagnosis: A blood pressure difference between arms is the bedside clue. Duplex ultrasound demonstrates reversed or alternating vertebral flow, and reactive hyperaemia testing can unmask latent steal. CT or MR angiography shows the stenosis and other arch disease. Symptoms should be clearly linked to the steal before intervention, since incidental findings are common.
det.treatment: Asymptomatic steal needs only vascular risk-factor management with antiplatelets and statins. Symptomatic subclavian disease is treated with angioplasty and stenting, or surgical bypass such as carotid-subclavian bypass when endovascular treatment fails. Takayasu arteritis needs immunosuppression. AVM steal is managed according to the malformation.
det.prognosis: Subclavian steal itself rarely causes stroke; outcomes are mainly determined by coexisting atherosclerosis.
pearls: Measure blood pressure in both arms in any patient with posterior circulation symptoms.
Reversed vertebral flow on ultrasound is common and often silent.
Use the arm with the higher reading to guide blood pressure management.
det.thd: Steal syndromes คือภาวะที่เลือดถูกเบี่ยงจากบริเวณหนึ่งไปเลี้ยงอีกบริเวณ ตัวอย่างสำคัญคือ subclavian steal ที่ subclavian artery ตีบทำให้เลือดไหลย้อนลงทาง vertebral artery เมื่อใช้แขนจะเวียนศีรษะ ตาพร่า และปวดแขน ความดันโลหิตสองแขนต่างกัน ตรวจยืนยันด้วย duplex ultrasound และ CTA รักษาด้วยการควบคุมปัจจัยเสี่ยงและทำ stent เมื่อมีอาการ

name: Stereotypy
formal: Repetitive purposeless coordinated movements that are patterned, seen in autism, tardive syndromes and neurodegeneration.
simple: Repeated, patterned movements such as rocking or hand flapping.
th: Stereotypy คือการเคลื่อนไหวหรือเสียงซ้ำ ๆ เป็นจังหวะและแบบแผนเดียวกัน ไม่มีจุดประสงค์ชัดเจน เช่น ปรบมือ โยกตัว พยักหน้า พบทั้งในเด็กปกติ (primary stereotypy) ออทิสติก ภาวะพัฒนาการล่าช้า tardive syndrome catatonia และโรคสมองเสื่อม ต่างจาก tic ตรงที่เริ่มเร็ว รูปแบบคงที่ และไม่มี premonitory urge
tempoNote: Primary stereotypies begin before about 3 years of age, occur in bouts for years and often fade by adolescence; secondary forms persist with the underlying condition
feat: Repetitive, rhythmic, patterned movements with a fixed repertoire for each person: hand flapping, finger flicking, body rocking, head nodding, hand-wringing, or vocal sounds
Provoked by excitement, boredom, absorption or stress and stopped easily by distraction or by calling the child's name

Primary stereotypies occur in otherwise typical children; secondary ones accompany autism, intellectual disability, Rett syndrome, sensory deprivation, schizophrenia, catatonia, frontotemporal degeneration and tardive syndromes
Unlike tics: earlier onset, longer more predictable bouts, no premonitory urge or rebound, and a fixed form that does not change from week to week
May be simple (rocking, foot tapping) or complex (ritualised sequences); self-injurious forms such as head banging or biting occur in severe developmental disorders and Lesch–Nyhan syndrome
inv: Clinical observation and a home video; ask about onset, the setting and whether it can be interrupted
Developmental, language and autism assessment in children; drug history (stimulants, dopamine agonists or blockers) and substance use in adults
MRI, genetic or metabolic tests only for regression, dysmorphism, seizures or adult-onset stereotypy

case.who: 5-year-old girl from Chanthaburi with normal development
case.story: Since toddlerhood she flaps her hands and stands on her toes whenever she watches cartoons or is excited. She stops when her name is called and resumes a few minutes later.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination, speech and social interaction; flapping bouts lasting 10–20 seconds on excitement, no tics, no premonitory urge.
case.tests: Autism screening is negative; school performance is good.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and does she need medication?
case.a: Primary complex motor stereotypy; reassure the family, offer behavioural therapy such as habit reversal or awareness training if the movements cause distress, and avoid medication.

det.patho: Stereotypies are thought to result from dysfunction in cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loops, with altered dopaminergic signalling; animal models show that repeated stereotyped behaviour is driven by D2 receptor stimulation and enhanced by D1 activation. Physiological stereotypies are normal in infants, and primary stereotypies are probably a variant of the developmental repertoire that persists. In secondary forms, the movements reflect the underlying disease of the striatum and frontal circuits.
det.clinical: A stereotypy is a movement pattern, not a diagnosis. Primary (physiological or idiopathic) stereotypies start in early childhood in otherwise normal children, as hand or arm flapping, finger wiggling, head nodding or body rocking, usually with excitement or concentration; they continue for years and many diminish by adolescence. Secondary stereotypies occur in autism, intellectual disability, blindness or deafness, Rett syndrome, schizophrenia, catatonia, frontotemporal dementia, Tourette syndrome and as tardive stereotypies after dopamine blockers. Self-injury is a separate feature of some severe disorders.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis depends on observing the movement and its context. Establish onset age, form, fixed repertoire, triggers, ability to interrupt, impact on learning and comorbid conditions such as ADHD, anxiety and autism. Distinguish tics, which are variable and have a premonitory urge, compulsions, mannerisms, dystonia, epileptic automatisms and paroxysmal events. Ancillary tests are not needed for typical primary stereotypies; in adults consider drugs, tardive syndrome, structural or degenerative disease.
det.treatment: Education and reassurance are enough for most primary stereotypies. If the movements cause stigma or interfere with function, behavioural treatments such as awareness training and habit reversal have the best evidence. Medication is not recommended for primary stereotypies. For secondary stereotypies, treat the underlying condition; in autism, low-dose risperidone or aripiprazole help severe self-injury, and adults with tardive stereotypies need a dopamine-blocker review and a VMAT2 inhibitor if movements persist. Protective equipment and environmental safety are needed in self-injury.
det.prognosis: Primary stereotypies are benign and tend to lessen by late childhood or adolescence, while secondary forms follow the course of the underlying disorder.
pearls: A child who stops flapping when called by name probably has primary stereotypy, not a tic disorder.
Fixed repertoire, early onset and no urge point to stereotypy rather than tics.
New stereotyped movements in an adult should prompt a drug and frontal-lobe assessment.
det.thd: Stereotypy คือการเคลื่อนไหวซ้ำ ๆ เป็นจังหวะและแบบเดียวกันทุกครั้ง เช่น ปรบมือ โยกตัว พยักหน้า มักเกิดเมื่อตื่นเต้นหรือเบื่อ และหยุดได้เมื่อมีสิ่งดึงความสนใจ ต่างจาก tic ที่รูปแบบเปลี่ยนไปมาและมี premonitory urge เด็กปกติที่มี primary stereotypy ส่วนใหญ่ไม่ต้องใช้ยา ให้ความรู้ครอบครัวและใช้พฤติกรรมบำบัดถ้ารบกวน ส่วนรายที่มีโรคพื้นฐาน เช่น ออทิสติก หรือจากยา ต้องรักษาสาเหตุ

name: Steroid myopathy
formal: Proximal weakness from chronic glucocorticoid excess with normal CK and type 2 fibre atrophy.
simple: Muscle weakness in the thighs and shoulders caused by long-term steroid use.
more: CK is normal and EMG is usually normal, with biopsy showing type 2 fibre atrophy without inflammation; MRI is unremarkable. Treat by reducing or switching steroids, using a fluorinated-steroid-free regimen and exercise, with improvement over weeks to months.
th: กล้ามเนื้อต้นแขนต้นขาอ่อนแรงจากการใช้ steroid นาน ๆ — CK ปกติ
tempoNote: Chronic form develops over weeks to months of treatment; an acute form occurs with high-dose IV steroids in ICU
feat: Painless proximal weakness, legs before arms: trouble rising from chairs and climbing stairs
Cushingoid features: moon face, central obesity, skin thinning
Normal CK, normal sensation and reflexes
Higher risk with fluorinated steroids (dexamethasone) and doses above about 30 mg/day prednisolone
Acute ICU form (critical illness myopathy) with high-dose steroids ± neuromuscular blockers

EMG often normal or mildly myopathic without spontaneous activity

case.story: CK fell from 6,000 to normal on prednisolone 60 mg daily for 3 months, but she now struggles more to stand from a squat.
case.exam: Cushingoid face, symmetric hip flexor weakness, no muscle tenderness, normal reflexes.
case.tests: CK 90 U/L; EMG without fibrillations; MRI thigh shows no oedema, only fatty atrophy.
case.q: Is her myositis relapsing, or is this steroid myopathy, and what should be done?

det.patho: Glucocorticoids increase muscle protein breakdown through the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway and reduce protein synthesis by inhibiting IGF-1 and mTOR signalling. Fast-twitch type 2 fibres are most affected, so atrophy rather than necrosis is the result. Fluorinated compounds carry the highest risk.
det.clinical: The chronic form develops gradually with proximal leg weakness, often accompanied by other steroid side effects. It is easy to confuse with a relapse of the condition being treated, especially myositis or myasthenia. The acute form arises within days of very high doses, often in ICU with sepsis, and can include rhabdomyolysis.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by normal CK and a quiet EMG. In treated myositis, the absence of fibrillations and of MRI muscle oedema helps distinguish steroid myopathy from active inflammation; a trial of dose reduction is often decisive. Exclude hypokalaemia, thyroid dysfunction and vitamin D deficiency.
det.treatment: Reduce the steroid dose to the lowest effective level, switch to non-fluorinated agents, or use alternate-day dosing and steroid-sparing drugs. Resistance and aerobic exercise counteract atrophy. Ensure adequate protein intake and treat coexisting metabolic issues.
det.prognosis: Strength usually recovers over weeks to months after dose reduction.
pearls: Treated myositis getting weaker with normal CK: think steroids before escalating immunotherapy.
Dexamethasone is more myotoxic than equivalent prednisolone.
Exercise prevents and treats steroid myopathy.
det.thd: Steroid myopathy เกิดจากการใช้ corticosteroid ขนาดสูงหรือนาน ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อต้นขาต้นแขนอ่อนแรงโดยไม่ปวด CK ปกติ EMG มักปกติ ต้องแยกจากโรคเดิมกำเริบ เช่น myositis ซึ่งมี CK สูงและ EMG พบ fibrillation การรักษาคือลดขนาด steroid ใช้ยาลด steroid และออกกำลังกาย ส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นในหลายสัปดาห์ถึงเดือน

name: Stiff baby syndrome
formal: Hyperekplexia in infants with generalised hypertonia, exaggerated startle and apnoea, often GLRA1-related, relieved by clonazepam.
simple: A condition in newborns with very stiff muscles and an exaggerated startle.
more: Treat with clonazepam, and the Vigevano manoeuvre can abort attacks; consider shared pathogenic variants in GLRA1 and genetic testing. Attacks of apnoea can be fatal, and symptoms usually improve with age, although startle persists.
th: ภาวะ hyperekplexia ในทารก กล้ามเนื้อแข็งเกร็งทั้งตัวเมื่อตื่น ตกใจง่ายและรุนแรงเมื่อถูกสัมผัสหรือเสียงดัง อาจหยุดหายใจ มักเกี่ยวกับยีน GLRA1 ตอบสนองดีต่อ clonazepam
tempoNote: Present from birth with persistent stiffness while awake and startle-triggered spasms; hypertonia improves in the first year but startle persists
feat: Generalised hypertonia from birth that relaxes in sleep and is absent when the infant is calm and asleep
Exaggerated startle to unexpected touch, sound or handling, sometimes with a prolonged tonic spasm
Apnoea and cyanosis during sustained spasms, which can cause sudden death
Tapping the nose or forehead triggers a head-retraction jerk (positive nose-tap test)
Awareness is preserved and the EEG is normal during spasms

Exclude hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, infection, hypoxic injury and structural brainstem disease

case.story: Since birth she has been stiff when awake and jerks violently when touched or when a door bangs. Twice during a spasm she turned blue until her mother bent her head and knees to her chest.
case.exam: Generalised hypertonia that eases when asleep, brisk startle with head retraction on tapping the nose, normal tendon reflexes and alertness.
case.tests: Glucose, calcium and cranial ultrasound normal; video-EEG during spasm shows no epileptiform activity; GLRA1 variant on gene panel.
case.q: What manoeuvre and drug are used for the spasms, and which investigation excludes epilepsy?
case.a: Forced flexion of head and legs towards the trunk (Vigevano manoeuvre) to abort apnoea, and clonazepam long term; a video-EEG normal during the stiffening excludes epilepsy.

read.where: 18 - Myoclonus: Phenomenology, etiology, physiology, and treatment
Section II: Epidemiology, Etiology, and Diagnosis

det.patho: Hyperekplexia arises from impaired inhibitory glycinergic neurotransmission in the brainstem and spinal cord, most often from variants in GLRA1 for the glycine receptor alpha-1 chain. Other genes include SLC6A5 (glycine transporter), GLRB and GPHN. Failure of inhibition lowers the threshold of the brainstem startle circuit and causes tonic spasms.
det.clinical: Infants are rigid and hyperalert after birth and startle excessively to touch, noise or handling. Prolonged tonic spasms can obstruct breathing and cause cyanosis, apnoea or sudden death. Hypertonia lessens with age, but pathological startle, falls and sometimes injuries persist into childhood and adulthood. Awareness is retained, and the nose-tap response helps to separate it from epilepsy. Cognitive development is often normal, although some genetic forms carry developmental delay.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by normal EEG during the stiffening and by exclusion of metabolic derangement, infection and brainstem lesions. Genetic testing for GLRA1 and other glycinergic genes confirms the diagnosis and permits counselling. Continuous video-EEG distinguishes startle epilepsy, in which an EEG correlate accompanies the startle.
det.treatment: Teach parents to flex the infant's head and legs towards the trunk to terminate apnoeic spasms, and use cardiorespiratory monitoring in early life. Clonazepam is the standard drug and often markedly reduces startle; other options include valproate, levetiracetam and phenobarbital. Avoid sudden stimuli and aim for safe handling at home. Counsel families about recurrence risk.
det.prognosis: Hypertonia fades during the first years, and many people achieve good function with treatment, although startle persists.
pearls: Stiff when awake, relaxed in sleep, normal EEG, and a positive nose-tap test suggest hyperekplexia.
Head-and-leg flexion can be lifesaving for apnoeic spasms.
Do not mistake the startle for epilepsy and escalate antiseizure drugs without video-EEG.
det.thd: Stiff baby syndrome หรือ hyperekplexia ในทารกเกิดจากการยับยั้งผ่านตัวรับ glycine บกพร่อง มักจากยีน GLRA1 ทารกจะเกร็งตัวเมื่อตื่นและสะดุ้งแรงเมื่อถูกสัมผัสหรือได้ยินเสียงดัง อาจหยุดหายใจจนเขียว ใช้การงอศีรษะและขาเข้าหาลำตัวเพื่อหยุดอาการ EEG ปกติระหว่างเกร็ง การรักษาคือ clonazepam และให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม อาการเกร็งลดลงเมื่อโต แต่ยังสะดุ้งง่ายได้

name: Stiff leg/stiff limb syndrome
formal: Autoimmune disorder with progressive limb or trunk stiffness and painful spasms, often asymmetric and confined to one limb; linked to anti-GAD or glycine receptor antibodies and spinal interneuron dysfunction.
simple: A condition where one leg or arm becomes stiff and goes into painful spasms because the immune system disturbs nerve signals in the spinal cord.
th: กลุ่มอาการ stiff-person แบบเฉพาะที่ ขาหรือแขนข้างเดียวแข็งเกร็งและเกิดตะคริวเจ็บปวดจากแรงกระตุ้น พบแอนติบอดี GAD65 ได้บ่อย

feat: Fixed stiffness and painful spasms of one leg (sometimes an arm) with an abnormal foot posture
Spasms provoked by touch, movement, noise or emotion, and absent during sleep
Gait disturbance and falls; foot often held plantar-flexed and inverted
Some have sphincter or brainstem signs hinting at inflammation in cord or brainstem
May progress to classic stiff-person syndrome or its encephalomyelitis form

EMG showing continuous firing of agonist and antagonist muscles at rest, abolished by diazepam
MRI of spine and brain to exclude structural causes; cancer screen if amphiphysin or atypical features

case.who: 52-year-old woman from Chon Buri with type 1 diabetes
case.story: Over eight months her left leg became rigid with the foot turned inward; a sudden noise brings a painful spasm and she falls.
case.exam: Board-like left thigh and calf, fixed equinovarus foot, brisk reflexes in that leg; trunk and right side largely spared.
case.tests: Serum anti-GAD65 markedly elevated; needle EMG of the left thigh and shin muscles records nonstop motor unit firing, which ceases once IV diazepam is given.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and how is it treated?
case.a: Stiff limb syndrome within the stiff-person spectrum; GABA-enhancing drugs (diazepam, baclofen) plus immunotherapy such as IVIG.

read.where: Chapter 14 - Autoimmunity Against the Inhibitory Synapsis

det.patho: Antibodies to GAD65 or the glycine receptor mark autoimmunity against inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord and brainstem. Reduced GABA and glycine inhibition frees motor neurons, causing steady co-contraction and exaggerated reflex spasms. In the limb form, the process appears concentrated in certain spinal segments, and cord inflammation has been documented.
det.clinical: Onset is typically in middle age with gradual stiffness and spasms of one limb, most often a leg, producing an abnormal posture and pain. Stimuli and emotion trigger spasms. Some patients have bladder symptoms or brainstem signs, or later evolve into classic SPS or PERM. Associated conditions include type 1 diabetes, thyroid disease, vitiligo and, less often, cancer. Textbooks place it within the broader stiff-person spectrum.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on focal rigidity with spasms, supportive EMG showing continuous motor unit activity that diazepam suppresses, and antibody testing. Negative GAD65 does not exclude it, so test for glycine receptor and amphiphysin antibodies. Image the spine and brain to exclude structural lesions and consider a tumour search when atypical. Functional dystonia and orthopaedic contracture are the main mimics.
det.treatment: Symptomatic care uses benzodiazepines, baclofen (oral or intrathecal), gabapentin and botulinum toxin for focal spasm. Immunotherapy, with IVIG having the best evidence in the spectrum, is used for disabling disease; steroids, plasma exchange and rituximab are alternatives. Physiotherapy and falls prevention matter throughout.
det.prognosis: Usually chronic with partial response to therapy; early immunotherapy may limit spread.
pearls: A stiff foot with startle-induced spasms and high anti-GAD65 suggests stiff limb syndrome.
EMG that normalises with diazepam supports the diagnosis.
Look for other autoimmune disease, especially type 1 diabetes.

name: Stiff-person spectrum disorders (SPSD)
formal: Umbrella term covering classic stiff-person syndrome, stiff-limb variants, progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus, and paraneoplastic forms, united by autoantibodies and CNS hyperexcitability.
simple: A group of related rare immune conditions in which the nervous system causes muscle stiffness and spasms.

case.story: Over a year her back became stiff and she fears crossing roads; loud horns cause painful spasms that throw her to the ground.
case.exam: Rigid paraspinal and abdominal muscles, exaggerated lumbar lordosis, slow stiff gait, normal power and reflexes.

det.patho: SPSD results from reduced GABAergic and glycinergic inhibition in the spinal cord and brainstem. GAD65 antibodies are the best-known marker, though their direct pathogenicity is uncertain; glycine receptor, amphiphysin and DPPX antibodies are directed at surface or synaptic proteins and are more likely pathogenic. Paraneoplastic forms occur with breast cancer, small-cell lung cancer and thymoma.
det.clinical: Classic SPS starts insidiously in mid-adult life with axial stiffness, hyperlordosis and spasms. Anxiety and fear of falls are prominent. Variants include focal stiff-limb syndrome and PERM with brainstem dysfunction, autonomic instability and encephalopathy. Overlap with cerebellar ataxia or epilepsy occurs in GAD65 disease.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on clinical features, EMG demonstrating continuous motor unit activity and antibody testing. Paired serum and CSF GAD65 testing helps when titres are low. Search for malignancy in seronegative or atypical cases. Mimics include functional disorders, dystonia and spinal pathologies.
det.treatment: Symptomatic therapy includes benzodiazepines (diazepam) and baclofen, with gabapentin or levetiracetam as adjuncts. IVIG is first-line immunotherapy with trial evidence; plasma exchange, rituximab and other agents are used in refractory cases. Paraneoplastic forms need tumour treatment. Physiotherapy and psychological support help.
det.prognosis: Chronic, with variable response; many have persistent disability, but early immunotherapy can improve function.
pearls: Hyperlordosis plus spasms triggered by noise: think SPS.
Low-titre GAD65 is common in diabetes; SPS needs high titres.
Amphiphysin antibodies point to breast cancer.
det.thd: Stiff-person spectrum disorders คือกลุ่มโรคภูมิคุ้มกันที่ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อแกนกลางลำตัวแข็งเกร็ง มีอาการกระตุกเจ็บเมื่อได้ยินเสียงหรือถูกสัมผัส สัมพันธ์กับแอนติบอดี GAD65, glycine receptor หรือ amphiphysin EMG พบ continuous motor unit activity การรักษาใช้ diazepam, baclofen และ IVIG หรือ rituximab ในรายดื้อยา และต้องหามะเร็งในชนิด paraneoplastic

det.patho: SPS is an autoimmune disorder of central inhibitory circuits: antibodies against GAD65 (the enzyme producing GABA), amphiphysin or the glycine receptor are associated with reduced GABAergic and glycinergic inhibition of spinal and brainstem motor neurons. The result is continuous simultaneous firing of opposing muscle groups plus heightened startle-triggered spasms. It is rare, more common in women, and frequently coexists with other autoimmune conditions.
det.clinical: Onset is insidious in mid-adult life with aching stiffness of the lower back and abdomen, a fixed lumbar hyperlordosis and a slow, wide-based, stiff gait. Superimposed painful spasms are triggered by sudden noise, touch, cold or emotion and can cause falls 'like a statue'. Anxiety and fear of open spaces are common and secondary, often leading to a functional label. Variants include stiff-limb syndrome, and PERM with brainstem signs, myoclonus and encephalopathy. GAD antibodies may also accompany cerebellar ataxia, epilepsy or limbic encephalitis.
det.diagnosis: Very high serum anti-GAD65 titres (far above those seen in type 1 diabetes) support the diagnosis; CSF GAD antibodies with intrathecal synthesis add weight. Surface EMG shows continuous normal motor unit firing in paraspinal and abdominal muscles with simultaneous agonist–antagonist activity that disappears in sleep or after IV diazepam. Amphiphysin antibodies demand a search for breast or small-cell lung cancer. Exclude tetanus, myelopathy, dystonia and neuromyotonia.
det.treatment: Symptomatic treatment centres on GABA-enhancing drugs: benzodiazepines (diazepam often in high divided doses) and baclofen, with gabapentin, pregabalin or levetiracetam as add-ons; intrathecal baclofen is used in refractory cases. Immunotherapy with IVIG has the best evidence; rituximab, plasma exchange and steroids are alternatives. Paraneoplastic cases need tumour treatment. Avoid abrupt benzodiazepine withdrawal, which can precipitate dangerous spasms.
det.prognosis: Course is variable and often progressive, with falls and disability; many patients improve partly with treatment. Paraneoplastic and PERM forms carry a worse outlook.
pearls: Board-like abdomen and hyperlordosis that melt under anaesthesia or sleep: think SPS.
Low-titre GAD is common in diabetes; SPS titres are usually very high.
Amphiphysin antibodies point to breast cancer.
det.thd: Stiff-person syndrome เป็นโรคภูมิคุ้มกันต่อระบบยับยั้งในไขสันหลังและก้านสมอง (anti-GAD65, amphiphysin, glycine receptor) ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อหลังและท้องแข็งตลอด หลังแอ่น และกระตุกปวดเมื่อตกใจหรือถูกสัมผัส มักถูกวินิจฉัยผิดเป็นโรควิตกกังวล วินิจฉัยด้วย anti-GAD ระดับสูงมาก และ EMG ที่เห็นกล้ามเนื้อหดตัวพร้อมกันต่อเนื่องซึ่งหายเมื่อหลับหรือให้ diazepam รักษาด้วย diazepam, baclofen และ IVIG

name: Strachan syndrome
formal: Syndrome of painful sensory neuropathy, optic neuropathy and sometimes spastic paraparesis, described in nutritionally deprived populations, probably related to deficiency of B vitamins and other nutrients.
simple: A condition from poor nutrition causing burning pain and numb feet, vision loss and sometimes stiff legs.
th: กลุ่มอาการ painful sensory neuropathy, optic neuropathy และบางครั้ง spastic paraparesis ในผู้ขาดอาหาร โดยเฉพาะวิตามินบี
tempoNote: Develops over weeks to months during nutritional deprivation; may improve with repletion
feat: Painful burning feet and distal sensory loss
Bilateral central visual loss with caecocentral scotomas and temporal disc pallor
Sensorineural hearing loss, orogenital dermatitis in some
Spastic paraparesis or sensory ataxia in myelopathic forms
Occurs in famine, prison or war settings and with cassava or alcohol-related malnutrition
inv: Vitamin B1, B12, folate, copper, B6 levels
Nerve conduction: axonal sensory neuropathy
Visual fields, OCT and VEP; MRI spine if myelopathy

case.who: 48-year-old man from Bangkok living rough, heavy drinker and smoker
case.story: Three months of burning feet and gradually blurred vision in both eyes.
case.exam: VA 6/60 both eyes, central scotomas, pale temporal discs, reduced pinprick and vibration in feet, absent ankle jerks.
case.tests: Low thiamine and folate, borderline B12; NCS axonal sensory neuropathy.
case.q: What syndrome is this and what is the treatment?
case.a: Nutritional (Strachan-type) optic neuropathy with sensory neuropathy; B-complex replacement, nutrition, stop alcohol and tobacco.

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Tropical Ataxic Myeloneuropathy (Strachan Syndrome)

det.patho: Strachan described the syndrome in Jamaican sugar-plantation workers in the 1880s. Similar epidemics occurred in prisoners of war and in Cuba in the 1990s. Deficiency of multiple B vitamins, sulfur amino acids and antioxidants, sometimes with cyanide exposure from cassava or tobacco, is thought to impair mitochondrial function in long axons and the papillomacular bundle.
det.clinical: Patients develop painful distal sensory neuropathy, bilateral optic neuropathy with central scotomas, and sometimes deafness, dermatitis and spastic paraparesis. Onset is subacute over weeks to months. Coexisting malnutrition, alcohol use and smoking are frequent.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical in an appropriate nutritional context, supported by low vitamin levels, axonal neuropathy on NCS and visual field defects. Exclude LHON, toxic optic neuropathies, B12 deficiency, HIV, HTLV-1 and syphilis.
det.treatment: Give B-complex vitamins, including thiamine and B12, folate and adequate protein-calorie nutrition; stop alcohol and tobacco. Early treatment improves vision more than neuropathy. Community measures matter in epidemics.
det.prognosis: Vision often improves with early repletion; neuropathy and myelopathy may persist.
pearls: Bilateral central scotoma plus burning feet in malnutrition: think Strachan.
Cuban epidemic neuropathy in the 1990s is a modern example.
Treat deficiencies empirically while waiting for results.
det.thd: Strachan syndrome คือกลุ่มอาการชาเจ็บปลายเท้า เส้นประสาทตาเสื่อมทั้งสองข้าง และบางครั้งขาเกร็ง ในผู้ขาดอาหารโดยเฉพาะวิตามินบี เคยระบาดในจาเมกาและคิวบา การวินิจฉัยอาศัยประวัติขาดอาหาร ระดับวิตามินต่ำ และแยกโรคอื่น เช่น LHON และขาด B12 การรักษาคือให้วิตามินบีรวม อาหารเพียงพอ และหยุดเหล้าบุหรี่

name: Striatocapsular infarction
formal: Infarct of the striatum and anterior internal capsule from occlusion of lenticulostriate branches or the MCA stem, causing contralateral hemiparesis with or without aphasia or neglect.
simple: A stroke in deep brain structures that causes weakness on one side of the body and sometimes trouble with speech.
th: สมองขาดเลือดบริเวณ striatum และ internal capsule ส่วนหน้า ขนาดใหญ่กว่า lacune มักเกิดจาก MCA ต้นทางอุดตันหรือ emboli มีอ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกร่วมกับ aphasia หรือ neglect ได้
tempoNote: Sudden onset like any ischaemic stroke; cortical-type signs often improve faster than the motor deficit
feat: Abrupt contralateral hemiparesis, usually face and arm more than leg
Cortical-type signs despite a subcortical lesion: aphasia (left) or neglect (right) from cortical hypoperfusion
Comma-shaped infarct > 1.5–2 cm involving caudate, putamen and anterior limb of internal capsule
Often embolic (heart or carotid) or MCA stem occlusion with good leptomeningeal collaterals
inv: MRI DWI to show the comma-shaped lesion; CT may look normal early
CTA/MRA of MCA and ICA; look for proximal occlusion amenable to thrombectomy
Cardiac work-up: ECG monitoring for AF, echocardiography

case.story: Woke with right arm weakness and could only say a few words; she has palpitations and is on no treatment.
case.exam: Right face and arm weakness more than leg, non-fluent speech with good comprehension, no visual field cut.
case.tests: DWI shows a 3.5 cm comma-shaped infarct of the left caudate head, putamen and anterior capsule; ECG: atrial fibrillation; CTA: recanalised left MCA.
case.q: Why does a deep infarct cause aphasia, and what is the likely mechanism?
case.a: Striatocapsular infarction from transient embolic MCA stem occlusion; aphasia reflects cortical hypoperfusion or diaschisis — anticoagulate for AF.

det.patho: Several lenticulostriate branches are blocked together, usually because an embolus or thrombus occludes the MCA stem at their origins while cortical branches are rescued by pial collaterals. Less often, atheroma in the proximal MCA covers multiple branch ostia. The result is a large comma-shaped deep infarct, distinct from a single-perforator lacune. Because the mechanism is large-artery or embolic, recurrence risk follows the embolic source rather than small-vessel disease.
det.clinical: Hemiparesis dominated by face and arm is the core sign. Left-sided lesions commonly produce aphasia and right-sided lesions neglect or anosognosia, which reflect reduced cortical perfusion or disconnection rather than cortical infarction. Dysarthria and mild sensory loss may accompany it. The cortical signs often fade over days to weeks, whereas the motor deficit tends to persist.
det.diagnosis: DWI defines size and shape; a deep infarct larger than about 1.5–2 cm crossing caudate, putamen and capsule fits the label. Vessel imaging (CTA or MRA) checks the MCA and ICA, and perfusion imaging may show wider cortical hypoperfusion. Cardiac rhythm monitoring and echocardiography are essential because embolism is frequent. Avoid labelling it 'lacunar' since that steers away from the embolic work-up.
det.treatment: Acute care follows standard ischaemic stroke pathways: IV thrombolysis within the window and mechanical thrombectomy if a proximal occlusion persists. Secondary prevention depends on mechanism — anticoagulation for AF, carotid revascularisation for symptomatic stenosis, and antiplatelet plus intensive risk-factor control for intracranial atheroma. Early speech and physiotherapy matter as cortical signs usually recover.
det.prognosis: Aphasia and neglect tend to improve well; residual arm weakness is common. Outcome is better than for an equivalent cortical MCA infarct.
pearls: Deep infarct + cortical signs = think striatocapsular, not lacune.
Work it up as embolic or large-artery disease.
Good collaterals spare the cortex; that is why the lesion is deep and comma-shaped.
det.thd: Striatocapsular infarction คือสมองขาดเลือดบริเวณ caudate putamen และ internal capsule ส่วนหน้า ขนาดใหญ่เป็นรูปจุลภาค เกิดจาก lenticulostriate หลายแขนงถูกปิดพร้อมกันเพราะ MCA ต้นทางอุดตันชั่วคราวหรือ emboli ผู้ป่วยอ่อนแรงแขนและหน้ามากกว่าขา อาจมี aphasia หรือ neglect แม้รอยโรคอยู่ลึก ต้องหาแหล่ง emboli เช่น AF และรักษาตามสาเหตุ

name: Striatopallido-dentate calcification
formal: Bilateral calcification of basal ganglia, dentate nuclei and other regions, producing parkinsonism, chorea, ataxia, dementia or psychiatric signs; idiopathic (Fahr) or secondary to hypoparathyroidism and genetic causes.
simple: Calcium deposits in deep brain areas that can cause movement problems, memory loss and mood changes.
th: ภาวะหินปูนในสมองสองข้างที่ globus pallidus, striatum, dentate และ thalamus อาจเป็นพันธุกรรม (PFBC) หรือเกิดจากสาเหตุรอง เช่น hypoparathyroidism ทำให้มี parkinsonism, dystonia, ataxia สมองเสื่อม และชัก
tempoNote: Often silent for decades; symptoms usually emerge in adulthood and slowly progress
feat: Symmetric calcification of pallidum, striatum, dentate nuclei, thalamus and subcortical white matter on CT
Parkinsonism, dystonia, chorea, ataxia and dysarthria
Cognitive decline and psychiatric symptoms such as depression or psychosis
Seizures and migraine-like headache
Secondary causes include hypoparathyroidism, pseudohypoparathyroidism, infection and mitochondrial disease
inv: Non-contrast CT is the most sensitive way to see calcification; MRI is less reliable
Calcium, phosphate, PTH, magnesium and vitamin D
Gene panel for primary familial brain calcification: SLC20A2, PDGFRB, PDGFB, XPR1, MYORG, JAM2

case.story: Three years of slowed movement, clumsy speech, mood change and a first seizure; thyroid surgery was done 10 years ago.
case.exam: Mild rigidity, dysarthria, gait ataxia, positive Chvostek sign.
case.tests: CT shows dense symmetric calcification in basal ganglia and cerebellum; calcium low, phosphate high, PTH low.
case.q: Is this primary or secondary calcification, and what is the treatment?
case.a: Secondary to post-surgical hypoparathyroidism. Correct calcium with calcitriol and calcium supplements; calcification itself does not regress but symptoms may improve.

det.patho: Calcium-phosphate deposits form around small vessels in the basal ganglia, dentate and white matter, probably from disturbed phosphate transport or blood-brain barrier integrity. Primary familial brain calcification arises from variants in phosphate homeostasis and neurovascular genes, with autosomal dominant or recessive inheritance. Mild basal ganglia calcification is also an age-related incidental finding.
det.clinical: Many carriers are asymptomatic. When present, movement disorders, cognitive and psychiatric change, seizures and headache develop in varying combinations, and severity does not track the amount of calcification. In secondary disease, tetany, cataracts and hypocalcaemic seizures accompany the neurological signs. Family history should be sought.
det.diagnosis: Start with CT to confirm bilateral calcification, then test calcium, phosphate, PTH, magnesium and vitamin D to find a metabolic cause. Exclude infection, radiation, toxins and mitochondrial disease. If metabolic tests are normal and a pattern fits, genetic testing defines primary familial brain calcification. Distinguish from physiological calcification by extent, age and symptoms.
det.treatment: Correct any metabolic cause: calcium and active vitamin D for hypoparathyroidism with monitoring to avoid hypercalciuria. There is no therapy that removes calcification. Treat parkinsonism, dystonia, epilepsy and psychiatric features symptomatically, with levodopa response often modest, and offer genetic counselling.
det.prognosis: Highly variable, from lifelong silence to progressive disability; secondary forms may stabilise after metabolic correction.
pearls: Always check calcium and PTH when CT shows basal ganglia calcification with symptoms.
CT beats MRI for detecting calcium.
Calcification load does not predict symptom severity.
det.thd: ภาวะหินปูนในสมองสองข้างที่ basal ganglia, dentate nucleus และ thalamus พบได้ทั้งแบบพันธุกรรม (PFBC) และแบบรองจาก hypoparathyroidism หรือการติดเชื้อ อาการมี parkinsonism, dystonia, ataxia สมองเสื่อม จิตเวช และชัก CT เห็นหินปูนได้ดีที่สุด ต้องตรวจแคลเซียม ฟอสเฟต PTH และยีน รักษาสาเหตุทางเมตาบอลิกและรักษาตามอาการ แต่ยังไม่มียากำจัดหินปูน

name: Stroke
formal: Acute focal neurological deficit from cerebral ischaemia or haemorrhage; ischaemic subtypes include large-artery, cardioembolic, small-vessel and cryptogenic, managed by reperfusion and secondary prevention.
simple: Sudden loss of brain function when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked or a vessel bleeds, causing weakness, speech or vision problems.
ab: โรคหลอดเลือดสมอง
th: ภาวะสมองบาดเจ็บเฉียบพลันจากหลอดเลือดอุดตันหรือแตก ทำให้มีอาการทางระบบประสาทเฉพาะที่ทันที รักษาด้วยการเปิดหลอดเลือดให้เร็วที่สุดและป้องกันการเป็นซ้ำ
tempoNote: Deficit maximal within seconds to minutes; time-critical treatment windows (thrombolysis up to 4.5 h, thrombectomy up to 24 h in selected patients)
feat: Sudden focal deficit: face droop, arm/leg weakness, speech disturbance, visual loss, vertigo with ataxia (BE-FAST)
About 80–85% ischaemic, the rest intracerebral or subarachnoid haemorrhage
Ischaemic subtypes (TOAST): large-artery, cardioembolic, small-vessel, other determined, undetermined
Major risk factors: hypertension, diabetes, AF, smoking, dyslipidaemia, age
inv: Non-contrast CT immediately to exclude haemorrhage; capillary glucose
CTA (± perfusion) for large-vessel occlusion; MRI DWI for confirmation and small lesions
ECG and prolonged rhythm monitoring, echocardiography, lipids, HbA1c
Young or unexplained: dissection, thrombophilia, vasculitis, PFO assessment

case.story: His wife found him unable to speak with a weak right side 50 minutes after he was last seen well; known hypertension, stopped his pills.
case.exam: NIHSS 16: global aphasia, right hemiplegia, left gaze deviation, right hemianopia.
case.tests: CT no bleed (ASPECTS 9); CTA shows left M1 occlusion; glucose 132 mg/dL.
case.q: What is the acute plan?
case.a: Acute ischaemic stroke with LVO: IV thrombolysis (alteplase or tenecteplase) and immediate transfer for mechanical thrombectomy.

read.where: Cerebrovascular Disease — Acute Stroke Evaluation and Management

det.patho: Ischaemic stroke follows arterial occlusion by thrombus, embolus or small-vessel lipohyalinosis; a core of irreversible damage is surrounded by a salvageable penumbra whose survival depends on time and collateral flow. Haemorrhagic stroke results from rupture of small penetrating arteries (hypertension), amyloid-laden cortical vessels, aneurysms or malformations. Worldwide, stroke ranks among the top killers and the main source of acquired adult disability, with rising incidence in low- and middle-income countries including Thailand.
det.clinical: Presentation depends on the territory: anterior circulation strokes give hemiparesis, aphasia or neglect and field defects; posterior circulation strokes give vertigo, diplopia, ataxia, crossed signs or reduced consciousness. Headache, vomiting and depressed consciousness favour haemorrhage but cannot replace imaging. Early neurological deterioration may reflect infarct growth, haemorrhagic transformation, oedema or seizures. Common mimics include hypoglycaemia, seizures, migraine and functional disorders.
det.diagnosis: Immediate CT separates haemorrhage from ischaemia; CTA identifies large-vessel occlusion and perfusion or MRI mismatch can select late-window patients. MRI DWI confirms small or posterior fossa infarcts. Aetiological work-up covers vessels (carotid and intracranial), heart (ECG, monitoring, echo) and blood tests; in the young add dissection, thrombophilia, vasculitis and PFO evaluation. Classify by TOAST or similar to guide prevention.
det.treatment: For ischaemic stroke, IV thrombolysis within 4.5 hours (alteplase 0.9 mg/kg or tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg) and thrombectomy for proximal occlusion up to 24 hours in selected patients, increasingly including large-core cases. Stroke-unit care, swallow screening, early mobilisation and avoidance of complications improve outcomes. Secondary prevention: antiplatelets (short dual therapy after minor stroke/TIA), anticoagulation for AF, statin, blood pressure control, carotid revascularisation when indicated, and lifestyle change. Haemorrhagic stroke needs BP lowering, reversal of anticoagulation and neurosurgical review.
det.prognosis: About a third recover well, a third remain disabled and up to a fifth die within a year; early reperfusion clearly shifts outcomes toward independence.
pearls: Time is brain: document last known well, check glucose, scan first.
No imaging rule-out by symptoms alone — haemorrhage and ischaemia look alike clinically.
Find the mechanism; secondary prevention depends on it.
det.thd: Stroke คือภาวะสมองขาดเลือดหรือเลือดออกเฉียบพลัน ทำให้มีอาการทางระบบประสาทเฉพาะที่ทันที เช่น หน้าเบี้ยว แขนขาอ่อนแรง พูดไม่ชัด ต้องทำ CT ทันทีเพื่อแยกเลือดออก ถ้าเป็นชนิดขาดเลือดและอยู่ในเวลาให้ยาละลายลิ่มเลือดและพิจารณาลากลิ่มเลือดถ้ามีหลอดเลือดใหญ่อุดตัน จากนั้นค้นหาสาเหตุและป้องกันการเป็นซ้ำด้วยยาต้านเกล็ดเลือดหรือยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือด statin และคุมความดัน

qx.stem: A provincial hospital in northeast Thailand is planning a community programme to lower the number of first strokes. The team compares smoking, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, dyslipidaemia and hypertension, using data from large international case-control studies of stroke risk across regions.
qx.q: Which risk factor carries the largest population-attributable risk for stroke worldwide and should be the main target?
opts: Atrial fibrillation
Diabetes mellitus
Current smoking
Raised apolipoprotein B to A1 ratio
Hypertension
qx.why: Across regions, including Southeast Asia, hypertension accounts for the largest share of stroke burden, roughly half of population-attributable risk, and is the strongest single target for both ischaemic stroke and intracerebral haemorrhage. Atrial fibrillation carries a high individual risk but is less prevalent, while smoking, diabetes and lipids each contribute a smaller fraction. Screening and treating raised blood pressure therefore gives the greatest population effect.

qx.stem: A 55-year-old bus driver has moderate left hemiparesis 10 days after a right MCA infarct. He is motivated, eating well and has no depressive symptoms on screening. His son has read online that a daily antidepressant can 'rewire the brain' and asks the team to prescribe fluoxetine to speed up motor recovery.
qx.q: What is the most appropriate response?
opts: Prescribe fluoxetine 20 mg daily for 6 months for motor recovery
Explain that large trials found no improvement in functional outcome with routine fluoxetine and more fractures, and focus on intensive task-specific therapy
Prescribe amphetamine before each physiotherapy session
Delay rehabilitation until 3 months so that spontaneous recovery is complete
Start a tricyclic antidepressant instead, as it is cheaper
qx.why: Early small studies suggested a motor benefit, but FOCUS, AFFINITY and EFFECTS showed no improvement in functional outcome with fluoxetine 20 mg for 6 months, with more bone fractures and hyponatraemia. Antidepressants remain indicated for post-stroke depression, which should be screened for regularly. Early, repetitive task-oriented rehabilitation is the evidence-based approach, and very early high-dose mobilisation within 24 hours should be avoided.

det.patho: The term covers migraine-related prolonged focal deficits that mimic infarction. In SMART, delayed radiation injury to small vessels and neurons is thought to lower the threshold for cortical spreading depolarisation, causing transient cortical dysfunction, swelling and blood–brain barrier leak in the irradiated cortex. In hemiplegic migraine, channelopathies (CACNA1A, ATP1A2, SCN1A) produce neuronal hyperexcitability; in MELAS, mitochondrial energy failure underlies stroke-like episodes.
det.clinical: SMART typically appears many years after cranial irradiation, with migraine-type headache, unilateral cortical deficits and often seizures, lasting days to weeks. Hemiplegic migraine usually starts in adolescence with motor aura plus other aura types, sometimes with confusion, fever or coma in severe attacks. Any first-ever deficit with headache must be treated as possible stroke until imaging says otherwise. Recurrent episodes and residual deficits can occur.
det.diagnosis: First exclude infarction, haemorrhage, tumour recurrence, infection and radiation necrosis with MRI and gadolinium; DWI is typically negative or shows only patchy cortical change. SMART is suggested by a remote radiation history and transient gyral enhancement confined to the field. EEG helps detect non-convulsive seizures. Genetic or mitochondrial tests are guided by age, family history and systemic features.
det.treatment: Management is supportive: analgesia, antiseizure medication when seizures occur, and avoiding triptans or ergots when the deficit is unexplained or hemiplegic migraine is suspected. Some clinicians use short steroid courses in SMART, though evidence is anecdotal. Prevention options for hemiplegic migraine include verapamil, acetazolamide, flunarizine or lamotrigine. Treat MELAS with arginine and mitochondrial supportive care.
det.prognosis: Most attacks recover completely, but SMART and hemiplegic migraine can leave permanent deficits after repeated or prolonged episodes.
pearls: Remote cranial radiation + headache + cortical deficit + gyral enhancement = SMART.
Never label a first focal deficit 'migraine' without imaging.
Check EEG — seizures often drive or prolong the deficit.
det.thd: Stroke-like migraine attacks คืออาการไมเกรนร่วมกับอ่อนแรงหรือพูดไม่ได้นานคล้าย stroke พบใน hemiplegic migraine, MELAS และ SMART ที่เกิดหลังฉายรังสีสมองหลายปี MRI ของ SMART พบ cortical gyral enhancement หนาในบริเวณที่ฉายรังสีโดยไม่มี infarct ต้องแยก stroke เนื้องอกกลับเป็นซ้ำ และชักก่อนเสมอ รักษาประคับประคองและคุมชัก ส่วนใหญ่หายเองภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์

name: Strychnine poisoning
formal: Convulsant poisoning from glycine receptor antagonism in the spinal cord, causing generalised muscle spasms, opisthotonos and risus sardonicus while consciousness is preserved; treated with benzodiazepines and supportive care.
simple: A poisoning that blocks calming signals in the spinal cord, causing violent painful muscle spasms while the person stays awake.
th: พิษจากสาร strychnine ที่ต้านตัวรับ glycine ในไขสันหลัง ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อเกร็งกระตุกทั้งตัว หลังแอ่น หน้ายิ้มแสยะ โดยยังรู้สึกตัวดี
tempoNote: Symptoms start 15–60 minutes after ingestion; deaths usually occur within hours
feat: Generalised, intensely painful muscle spasms triggered by light touch, noise or light
Opisthotonos, risus sardonicus and trismus, with full awareness between and during spasms
Hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, lactic acidosis and hyperkalaemia from muscle activity
Death from respiratory muscle spasm and hypoxia
Source: rodenticide, adulterated street drugs or traditional remedies containing nux vomica
inv: Clinical diagnosis; serum or urine strychnine levels confirm later
CK, potassium, creatinine, blood gas and lactate, temperature monitoring
EEG is normal between spasms, helping to distinguish from seizures

case.story: Thirty minutes after drinking a herbal tonic, he developed repeated violent spasms of the whole body set off by any noise, yet he could describe the pain clearly.
case.exam: Arched back, clenched jaw with a fixed grin, temperature 39.5 °C, fully alert between spasms.
case.tests: CK 18,000 U/L, pH 7.15, lactate 9 mmol/L; toxicology later shows strychnine.
case.q: What is the mechanism and the immediate management?
case.a: Strychnine blocks spinal glycine receptors; give high-dose benzodiazepines, cool, protect the airway and, if spasms persist, sedate, paralyse and ventilate.

det.patho: Strychnine is a competitive antagonist at the postsynaptic glycine receptor, chiefly in the spinal cord and brainstem. Loss of glycinergic inhibition lets motor neurons fire in response to any input, producing simultaneous contraction of agonists and antagonists. Because the cortex is largely unaffected, consciousness is preserved.
det.clinical: Early symptoms include restlessness, twitching and heightened sensitivity to stimuli, quickly followed by generalised spasms lasting up to a minute. Extensors dominate, giving opisthotonos and extended limbs. Complications are hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, renal failure, acidosis and respiratory failure. Survivors improve within 24 hours, though muscle pain persists.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in sudden generalised spasms with retained awareness after ingestion of a pesticide, herbal remedy or street drug. Laboratory confirmation takes time and should not delay treatment. Distinguish from tetanus, seizures, dystonic reactions, NMS, serotonin syndrome and hypocalcaemic tetany.
det.treatment: Treatment is supportive and urgent: quiet dark room, high-dose IV benzodiazepines, and early intubation with neuromuscular blockade if spasms persist. Activated charcoal once the airway is secure. Treat hyperthermia aggressively, give fluids for rhabdomyolysis and correct acidosis and hyperkalaemia. There is no antidote.
det.prognosis: Good if the patient survives the first several hours with adequate supportive care.
pearls: Awake patient with generalised painful spasms: think strychnine or tetanus.
Avoid stimulating the patient; even examination can trigger spasms.
Early paralysis and ventilation prevent death from hypoxia and hyperthermia.
det.thd: พิษ strychnine ทำให้ตัวรับ glycine ในไขสันหลังถูกปิดกั้น กล้ามเนื้อทั้งตัวเกร็งกระตุกเมื่อถูกกระตุ้นเพียงเล็กน้อย หลังแอ่น หน้าแสยะ แต่ผู้ป่วยยังรู้สึกตัว อาจมีไข้สูง กล้ามเนื้อสลายและไตวาย ไม่มียาต้านพิษ รักษาด้วย benzodiazepine ขนาดสูง ลดสิ่งกระตุ้น และใส่ท่อช่วยหายใจพร้อมยาหย่อนกล้ามเนื้อหากยังเกร็ง
