name: Sturge–Weber syndrome
formal: Neurocutaneous disorder from somatic GNAQ mutation with facial port-wine stain, leptomeningeal angioma, seizures, glaucoma, hemiparesis and cognitive impairment; tram-track calcification on imaging.
simple: A birth condition with a facial birthmark and blood-vessel malformation on the brain surface, often causing seizures and eye pressure problems.
th: โรคที่มีปานแดงบริเวณหน้าตามแขนงประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 5 ร่วมกับหลอดเลือดผิดปกติที่เยื่อหุ้มสมอง ทำให้ชักตั้งแต่ขวบปีแรก อ่อนแรงครึ่งซีก พัฒนาการช้า และต้อหิน
tempoNote: Port-wine stain at birth; seizures usually begin in the first year; stroke-like episodes and hemiparesis may accumulate in early childhood, stabilising later
feat: Facial capillary malformation (port-wine stain) involving the forehead/upper eyelid (V1 territory)
Focal seizures starting in infancy, often in clusters with post-ictal hemiparesis
Stroke-like episodes, progressive hemiparesis, hemianopia and intellectual disability
Glaucoma (congenital or later) and choroidal haemangioma on the same side
Migraine-like headaches in older children and adults
inv: MRI brain with gadolinium: leptomeningeal enhancement, enlarged choroid plexus, cerebral atrophy; SWI for venous changes
CT (if done) shows gyriform tram-track cortical calcification in older children
EEG; regular intraocular pressure checks
Somatic GNAQ testing of affected skin is possible but not needed for diagnosis

case.story: Born with a red birthmark over the left forehead and eyelid; this week he had three seizures with right arm jerking and weakness that lasted a day.
case.exam: Left V1/V2 port-wine stain, mild right hemiparesis, enlarged left cornea.
case.tests: MRI: left parieto-occipital leptomeningeal enhancement with atrophy; intraocular pressure raised on the left.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what treatment reduces seizure-related injury?
case.a: Sturge–Weber syndrome; prompt seizure control (often with low-dose aspirin to reduce stroke-like episodes) and glaucoma treatment, with epilepsy surgery for refractory cases.

det.patho: Sturge–Weber syndrome results from a somatic activating mosaic variant in GNAQ (occasionally GNA11) arising early in development, affecting the vascular endothelium of skin, eye and leptomeninges. The leptomeningeal capillary–venous malformation causes poor venous drainage, venous stasis and chronic cortical ischaemia, leading to calcification and atrophy. It is not inherited.
det.clinical: A port-wine stain involving the upper face (forehead or upper eyelid) carries the highest risk of brain involvement. Seizures begin in most within the first two years, and clusters can trigger stroke-like episodes with lasting hemiparesis. Cognitive outcome correlates with early-onset and poorly controlled seizures and the extent of brain involvement. Glaucoma may be present at birth or appear later, so lifelong eye surveillance is required.
det.diagnosis: Infants with a high-risk port-wine stain should have contrast-enhanced MRI, ideally after a few months of age when sensitivity is better, or sooner if seizures occur. Leptomeningeal enhancement confirms brain involvement. Ophthalmic assessment with intraocular pressure measurements is essential. Bilateral or extensive disease predicts a more severe course.
det.treatment: Seizures are treated promptly with antiseizure medication; low-dose aspirin is widely used to reduce stroke-like events and seizures. Hemispherectomy or focal resection is considered for unilateral drug-resistant epilepsy. Glaucoma needs medical or surgical treatment; pulsed-dye laser lightens the port-wine stain. Sirolimus is under study. Headache and behavioural difficulties also need attention.
det.prognosis: Highly variable; good seizure control is associated with better neurodevelopmental outcome, while bilateral disease carries the worst prognosis.
pearls: Port-wine stain on the forehead/upper eyelid → screen for brain and eye involvement.
Tram-track cortical calcification on CT is a late sign.
Lifelong glaucoma surveillance is needed even if early eye checks are normal.
det.thd: Sturge–Weber syndrome เกิดจากการกลายพันธุ์เฉพาะที่ของยีน GNAQ ทำให้มีปานแดงบริเวณหน้าผากและเปลือกตาบน ร่วมกับหลอดเลือดผิดปกติที่เยื่อหุ้มสมองข้างเดียวกัน เด็กมักชักตั้งแต่ขวบปีแรก มีอ่อนแรงครึ่งซีก พัฒนาการช้า และต้อหิน MRI พบ leptomeningeal enhancement และสมองฝ่อ รักษาชักอย่างรวดเร็ว ใช้ aspirin ขนาดต่ำ ตรวจความดันตาสม่ำเสมอ และพิจารณาผ่าตัดในรายชักดื้อยา

name: Stuve–Wiedemann syndrome
formal: Rare autosomal recessive disorder (LIFR mutation) with neonatal bowel, respiratory and feeding difficulties, bone dysplasia with bowing, autonomic dysfunction and sweating or temperature instability.
simple: A rare inherited condition in babies with bent bones, feeding and breathing trouble and unstable body temperature control.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมหายากแบบยีนด้อยจากยีน LIFR มีปัญหาการหายใจ การกลืนในทารก กระดูกยาวโค้ง ข้อติด และระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติผิดปกติ เช่น ไข้สูงเป็นพักๆ
tempoNote: Neonatal onset with life-threatening episodes of hyperthermia and respiratory distress; survivors have progressive bone deformity
feat: Neonatal respiratory distress, feeding and swallowing difficulties
Episodes of unexplained hyperthermia, profuse sweating and temperature instability
Bowing of long bones with wide metaphyses, camptodactyly and joint contractures
Reduced corneal reflexes, absent tendon reflexes, reduced pain sensitivity; tongue fasciculation reported
Autosomal recessive LIFR variants; formerly confused with Schwartz–Jampel type 2
inv: Skeletal survey: bowed long bones and metaphyseal changes
LIFR gene testing
Autonomic and swallow assessment; ophthalmic exam for corneal anaesthesia

case.who: 2-week-old girl in a NICU in Hat Yai; parents are cousins
case.story: Repeated episodes of fever to 40°C with no infection found, choking on feeds and apnoeas.
case.exam: Bowed legs, flexed fingers, contractures, weak suck, reduced corneal reflexes, absent reflexes.
case.tests: Cultures negative; X-rays show bowing of femora and tibiae with wide metaphyses; LIFR homozygous variant.
case.q: What syndrome explains fever, swallowing problems and bent bones?
case.a: Stuve–Wiedemann syndrome; supportive care with temperature control, feeding and airway protection.

det.patho: LIFR encodes the leukaemia inhibitory factor receptor, which signals through gp130 and the JAK–STAT3 pathway. Loss of this signalling disturbs bone development and growth plate function and impairs the development or maintenance of autonomic and small sensory neurons. The resulting picture combines skeletal dysplasia with dysautonomia.
det.clinical: Newborns present with feeding difficulty, respiratory distress and life-threatening hyperthermic episodes. Survivors develop progressive bowing of the limbs, scoliosis, joint contractures and dental problems. Reduced pain and corneal sensation lead to injuries and corneal ulcers. Smooth tongue, absent reflexes and temperature dysregulation persist into childhood.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is suggested by the combination of neonatal dysautonomia and bowed long bones and confirmed by LIFR sequencing. It is more common in consanguineous families. Distinguish from Schwartz–Jampel syndrome, familial dysautonomia and congenital insensitivity to pain.
det.treatment: No specific therapy exists. Care includes active temperature management, feeding support (often gastrostomy), airway protection, eye care for corneal anaesthesia, and orthopaedic management of deformities. Families should receive genetic counselling.
det.prognosis: Infant mortality is high from hyperthermia and respiratory complications; survivors may live into adolescence or adulthood with skeletal disability.
pearls: Neonatal unexplained fevers plus bowed long bones: think Stuve–Wiedemann.
Protect anaesthetic corneas early.
It is not the same disease as Schwartz–Jampel despite older naming.
det.thd: Stuve–Wiedemann syndrome เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมหายากแบบยีนด้อยจากยีน LIFR ทารกมีปัญหาการกลืน การหายใจ และไข้สูงเป็นพักๆ โดยไม่มีการติดเชื้อ ร่วมกับกระดูกยาวโค้ง ข้อติด และระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติผิดปกติ รับรู้ความเจ็บและ corneal reflex ลดลง การวินิจฉัยจากภาพรังสีกระดูกและการตรวจยีน การรักษาเป็นการดูแลประคับประคอง คุมอุณหภูมิ ให้อาหาร และดูแลตา

name: Subacute combined degeneration
formal: Vitamin B12 deficiency myelopathy affecting dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts, with paraesthesias, sensory ataxia, spasticity and often neuropathy and megaloblastic anaemia.
simple: Spinal cord damage from low vitamin B12 causing tingling, poor balance and weak stiff legs.
ab: subacute combined degeneration of the cord
th: ขาดวิตามินบี 12 ทำให้ไขสันหลังส่วนหลังและข้างเสื่อม — ชาเท้า ทรงตัวไม่ได้ในที่มืด ขาเกร็ง

Spastic weakness with extensor plantars yet absent ankle jerks (cord + nerve)

case.exam: Absent vibration to the iliac crests, Romberg positive, brisk knees, absent ankle jerks, extensor plantars.
case.tests: B12 borderline, MMA high; MRI: dorsal column hyperintensity C2–C6.
case.q: Explain absent ankle jerks with extensor plantars.

qx.stem: A 21-year-old male student from Bangkok has six weeks of tingling hands and feet and unsteadiness in the dark. He admits inhaling nitrous oxide from cream chargers most weekends. He has lost vibration and joint position sense in the feet, a positive Romberg test, brisk knee jerks and absent ankle jerks. Serum B12 is 310 pmol/L (normal). MRI shows dorsal column T2 signal from C2 to C6.
qx.q: Which test best supports the suspected mechanism?
opts: Serum copper and zinc only
Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies
CSF oligoclonal bands
Nerve biopsy
Serum methylmalonic acid and homocysteine
qx.why: Nitrous oxide oxidises the cobalt in B12, inactivating it functionally, so serum B12 may be normal while methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are raised. Treatment is stopping nitrous oxide and giving intramuscular hydroxocobalamin, often with methionine. Copper deficiency is a mimic worth checking but is not the mechanism here, and intrinsic factor antibodies point to pernicious anaemia rather than recreational exposure.

qx.stem: A 60-year-old strict vegan from Chiang Rai has had six months of tingling in the feet, then a stiff, unsteady gait. Examination shows impaired vibration and proprioception in the legs, brisk knee jerks, absent ankle jerks and extensor plantar responses. MCV is 114 fL. MRI of the cervical cord shows T2 hyperintensity in the dorsal columns.
qx.q: What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Parenteral vitamin B12 (hydroxocobalamin or cyanocobalamin) replacement
Oral folic acid 5 mg daily alone
High-dose methylprednisolone
Intrathecal baclofen
Surgical decompression of the cervical canal
qx.why: Dorsal column and corticospinal involvement with macrocytosis in a strict vegan indicates subacute combined degeneration from B12 deficiency, which needs prompt parenteral B12 to prevent permanent deficits. Folic acid alone may improve the anaemia while allowing neurological worsening, and nitrous oxide exposure should also be excluded. Steroids and decompression do not address the cause.

qx.stem: A 24-year-old male university student from Bangkok who uses recreational nitrous oxide balloons at parties most weekends has six weeks of tingling feet, an unsteady gait in the dark and electric sensations down his back on neck flexion. Romberg is positive and vibration is lost at the ankles. Axial T2 MRI of the cervical cord shows symmetric hyperintensity confined to the dorsal columns from C2 to C6, forming an 'inverted V' shape. Serum B12 is low-normal.
qx.q: Which test best confirms the functional deficiency, and what treatment is required?
opts: Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies; oral folic acid alone
Serum copper; oral copper supplementation
AQP4-IgG; IV methylprednisolone
Serum methylmalonic acid and homocysteine; stop nitrous oxide and give intramuscular hydroxocobalamin
CSF oligoclonal bands; disease-modifying therapy
qx.why: Nitrous oxide inactivates cobalamin, so serum B12 can be normal while methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are raised; the inverted-V dorsal column T2 signal is typical of subacute combined degeneration. Treatment is abstinence and prompt parenteral B12. Folate alone may worsen the neurological injury, copper deficiency gives a similar picture but is not the best fit here, and NMOSD or MS lesions are not symmetrically confined to the dorsal columns.

det.patho: Vitamin B12 is needed for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; deficiency disrupts myelin synthesis, particularly in the large myelinated fibres of the posterior columns and the lateral pyramidal (corticospinal) pathways, beginning in the cervical and upper thoracic cord. Peripheral nerves, optic nerves and the brain may also be affected. Common causes are pernicious anaemia, gastric surgery, malabsorption, strict vegan diet, metformin or proton pump inhibitor use, and nitrous oxide, which inactivates B12.
det.clinical: Symmetric tingling in the feet (sometimes the hands first) is followed by impaired vibration and proprioception, sensory ataxia and Romberg positivity. Corticospinal involvement gives spastic leg weakness and extensor plantars, while a coexisting neuropathy may abolish ankle jerks. Cognitive change, depression, visual loss from optic neuropathy, and Lhermitte phenomenon can occur. Neurological damage may develop without anaemia or macrocytosis, especially if folate intake is high.
det.diagnosis: Measure serum B12 together with methylmalonic acid and homocysteine, because B12 levels in the low-normal range may hide true deficiency; both metabolites rise in B12 deficiency, only homocysteine in folate deficiency. Look for the cause: intrinsic factor and parietal cell antibodies, gastrin, coeliac serology, diet and drug history, and nitrous oxide use. MRI may show T2 hyperintensity of the dorsal columns (inverted V on axial images). Check copper, which can produce an identical myelopathy, and consider nerve conduction studies.
det.treatment: Start parenteral hydroxocobalamin or cyanocobalamin promptly, with frequent intramuscular injections in the first weeks for neurological involvement, then lifelong maintenance if the cause persists; high-dose oral B12 can be used for maintenance in many patients. Do not give folate alone, which can worsen the neurological picture. In nitrous oxide users, stop exposure and treat even if the B12 level looks normal. Physiotherapy helps recovery of gait.
det.prognosis: Improvement occurs over 6–12 months; the extent of recovery depends on severity and duration before treatment, and long-standing deficits may be permanent.
pearls: Normal haemoglobin does not exclude neurological B12 deficiency.
Recreational nitrous oxide is now a leading cause in young adults — ask directly.
Extensor plantars with absent ankle jerks: B12, copper, Friedreich ataxia, or combined cord and nerve disease.

det.patho: Clioquinol, a halogenated hydroxyquinoline antimicrobial used for diarrhoea, chelates metals and may interfere with copper, zinc and B12-dependent pathways, causing a distal axonopathy affecting long spinal tracts, peripheral nerves and optic nerves. The exact mechanism is still debated.
det.clinical: Gastrointestinal symptoms preceded progressive sensory neuropathy and myelopathy, with optic involvement in a minority. Thousands were affected in Japan before clioquinol was withdrawn in 1970, after which the epidemic disappeared.
det.diagnosis: Historical exposure to clioquinol with typical syndrome. Today, similar pictures prompt investigation of B12, copper, nitrous oxide, HIV, HTLV-1 and NMOSD.
det.treatment: Stop exposure. Supportive care with rehabilitation and symptomatic pain treatment. There is no specific antidote.
det.prognosis: Partial recovery is common, but many had permanent sensory loss, spasticity or visual impairment.
pearls: SMON is a classic lesson in drug-induced epidemic neurotoxicity.
Green tongue is a historic clue.
Modern mimics: copper deficiency and nitrous oxide myeloneuropathy.
det.thd: Subacute myelo-optic neuropathy (SMON) คือพิษจากยา clioquinol ที่ใช้รักษาท้องเสีย ระบาดในญี่ปุ่นช่วงทศวรรษ 1960 ทำให้ปวดท้องนำ ตามด้วยชาขาขึ้นมาจนถึงเอว ขาเกร็ง และตามัวจากเส้นประสาทตาเสื่อม ลิ้นอาจเป็นสีเขียว หยุดยาแล้วอาการดีขึ้นบางส่วน ปัจจุบันต้องแยกภาวะคล้ายกัน เช่น ขาด B12, ขาดทองแดง และ nitrous oxide

name: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE)
formal: Fatal progressive encephalitis from persistent defective measles virus after early childhood infection, with myoclonic jerks, cognitive decline, periodic EEG complexes and raised CSF measles antibodies.
simple: A rare, fatal brain infection years after measles, causing jerks, memory decline and loss of function.
th: SSPE เป็นโรคสมองอักเสบเรื้อรังจากไวรัสหัดที่หลบซ่อนอยู่ในสมองหลายปีหลังเป็นหัด เด็กมีพฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน การเรียนตก กล้ามเนื้อกระตุกเป็นจังหวะ และเสียชีวิตภายใน 1 ถึง 3 ปี ป้องกันได้ด้วยวัคซีนหัด
tempoNote: Appears 4 to 10 years (range 1 to 20+) after measles; evolves over months, then 1 to 3 years to death, though occasional long remissions occur
feat: Stage I: falling school performance, personality or behaviour change, forgetfulness, sometimes visual symptoms from macular disease
Stage II: stereotyped myoclonic jerks every few seconds with head drops and falls, seizures, dementia, ataxia, dystonia
Stage III: rigidity, decerebrate posturing, autonomic instability; stage IV: akinetic mutism and coma
History of measles under 2 years of age, measles before vaccination, or incomplete vaccination; boys, rural children and those without measles vaccine are most at risk
Retinal lesions (chorioretinitis, macular pigmentary change), optic atrophy or cortical blindness in some
inv: EEG: periodic high-voltage generalised slow complexes every 4 to 10 seconds, time-locked with the jerks (Radermecker complexes), often clearest in sleep
CSF: normal cells and glucose, high gamma globulin, oligoclonal bands and raised measles IgG antibody index; measles RNA in brain or CSF in some
MRI: periventricular and subcortical white matter T2 hyperintensities, later atrophy; basal ganglia may be involved
Fundoscopy for macular disease; exclude other causes with metabolic screening and prion tests in adults

case.who: 10-year-old boy from Mae Hong Son who had measles at 8 months and received no measles vaccine
case.story: Over four months his grades fell and handwriting worsened; for three weeks he has had brief head nods and falls every few seconds.
case.exam: Cognitive slowing, repetitive jerks of the trunk and neck about every 8 seconds, mild rigidity and pigmentary macular changes.
case.tests: EEG shows periodic complexes every 6 to 8 seconds; CSF measles IgG index markedly raised, oligoclonal bands present; MRI shows periventricular white matter hyperintensities.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and what can be offered?
case.a: SSPE; no cure exists. Offer sodium valproate or clonazepam for myoclonus, supportive care, and consider isoprinosine (inosine pranobex) with intrathecal or intraventricular interferon, which may slow progression in a subset; prevention is two doses of measles vaccine.

det.patho: SSPE is a persistent infection with measles virus whose genes have accumulated mutations, particularly in the matrix, fusion and haemagglutinin proteins, so that virions are not released and spread occurs cell to cell along synapses. Neurons and oligodendroglia contain intranuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions, and an intense lymphoplasmacytic reaction produces high local antibody levels. The virus enters the brain around the time of the original measles, remains quiet for years, and then causes progressive gray and white matter destruction. Early infection, before the immune system matures or while maternal antibody is present, is the main risk factor.
det.clinical: The onset is insidious and often misread as a behavioural or learning problem. Myoclonic jerks, seizures and cognitive decline develop over weeks to months, followed by rigidity, visual loss and autonomic failure. Adults and teenagers can present with visual impairment or fulminant forms. The course is typically one to three years, although rare patients stabilise for years. Because measles has re-emerged in under-vaccinated communities, SSPE is again a concern.
det.diagnosis: Typical clinical findings plus high measles antibody in CSF establish the diagnosis; EEG periodic complexes support it. Routine CSF cell count and glucose are normal, but immunoglobulin level and oligoclonal bands are raised. MRI is variable and often normal early. Brain biopsy is rarely needed. Rarely, adult-onset cases lack classic EEG, and alternative diagnoses (prion disease, autoimmune encephalitis, Whipple disease, leukodystrophies) must be excluded.
det.treatment: No therapy cures SSPE. Antiepileptic and antimyoclonic drugs (valproate, clonazepam, levetiracetam) improve comfort. Oral inosine pranobex with intraventricular interferon-alpha has shown stabilisation or slower progression in non-randomised studies and is used by specialist centres; ribavirin and other antivirals have limited evidence. Supportive care, nutrition, and palliation are central. Prevention is the focus: two doses of MMR vaccine, high community coverage and catch-up immunisation, and vaccination of infants during outbreaks.
det.prognosis: Median survival is 1 to 3 years in classic disease, and a minority show long plateaus; fulminant forms can kill within months.
pearls: School decline plus myoclonic head drops in a child with early measles: ask for EEG and CSF measles antibodies.
The risk after measles under 12 months is much higher than older estimates suggest; recent registries report about 1 in a few hundred to 1 in 2,000 for infants.
The vaccine does not cause SSPE; it prevents it.

name: Subarachnoid haemorrhage
formal: Bleeding into the subarachnoid space, usually from ruptured saccular aneurysm, causing thunderclap headache, meningism and often reduced consciousness; complications include rebleeding, vasospasm and hydrocephalus.
simple: Bleeding around the brain surface, usually from a burst aneurysm, causing a sudden severe headache and neck stiffness.

case.q: Why is the left pupil dilated?
case.a: The aneurysm compresses the left third nerve; pupillary fibres run superficially, so a compressive lesion dilates the pupil.

qx.stem: A 52-year-old male factory supervisor from Rayong develops a severe headache peaking over about a minute while straining on the toilet. He is alert, GCS 15, with mild neck stiffness and no focal signs. CT at 5 hours shows blood confined to the cisterns in front of the midbrain and pons without intraventricular extension. High-quality CT angiography and catheter angiography show no aneurysm.
qx.q: Which statement about this condition is correct?
opts: He needs repeat catheter angiography every three months for a year
This perimesencephalic non-aneurysmal pattern carries a low risk of rebleeding and vasospasm and an excellent prognosis
Lifelong anticoagulation is required to prevent venous recurrence
He should undergo prophylactic clipping of the basilar tip
The pattern indicates a ruptured posterior communicating aneurysm missed on angiography
qx.why: Blood confined anterior to the brainstem with negative angiography in an alert patient fits perimesencephalic non-aneurysmal SAH, probably of venous origin. Rebleeding, delayed ischaemia and hydrocephalus are uncommon and most patients return to normal life. With a classic pattern and good-quality negative angiography, repeat angiography is generally not needed, although a diffuse angiogram-negative pattern does require repeat imaging.

det.patho: About 85% of non-traumatic SAH comes from rupture of a saccular aneurysm at the circle of Willis, typically at the anterior communicating, posterior communicating or MCA bifurcation; about 10% is perimesencephalic non-aneurysmal SAH, a benign venous variant, and the rest stems from dissection, AVM, RCVS or other rare causes. Risk factors are smoking, hypertension, heavy alcohol use, family history and inherited conditions such as polycystic kidney disease; aneurysm size, site and irregular shape raise rupture risk. Blood in the subarachnoid space causes a sudden pressure surge with global ischaemia, meningeal irritation and impaired CSF absorption. Delayed cerebral ischaemia is now understood as multifactorial — large-artery vasospasm plus microvascular dysfunction, microthrombosis and spreading depolarisations.
det.clinical: The hallmark is a headache that peaks within a minute, often with vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia, brief loss of consciousness or seizure; a minor warning (sentinel) bleed may precede it by days. Neck stiffness may take hours to appear and is absent in deep coma. Focal signs suggest the aneurysm site or a haematoma: painful pupil-involving third nerve palsy with PComm aneurysm, bilateral leg weakness or abulia with AComm, and subhyaloid (Terson) haemorrhages imply a large rise in pressure. Complications follow a timeline: rebleeding (highest in the first 6–24 hours), acute hydrocephalus, delayed cerebral ischaemia (days 3–14), hyponatraemia, neurogenic pulmonary oedema and stress cardiomyopathy. Severity is graded with the WFNS or Hunt–Hess scales and blood load with the modified Fisher scale, which predicts vasospasm.
det.diagnosis: In an alert patient with thunderclap headache, non-contrast CT within 6 hours of onset on a modern scanner read by an expert is close to fully sensitive; sensitivity falls with time. If CT is negative and more than 6 hours have passed, perform LP no sooner than 12 hours after onset to look for xanthochromia (spectrophotometry where available). The Ottawa SAH rule helps decide who needs the work-up in neurologically intact patients. CTA identifies most aneurysms; DSA with 3D rotation remains the reference standard, and a negative first DSA with a diffuse bleed should be repeated. Consider RCVS, CVT, pituitary apoplexy, arterial dissection, intracranial hypotension and meningitis as alternative explanations.
det.treatment: Secure the aneurysm early, ideally within 24 hours, by endovascular coiling (preferred when both options suit) or surgical clipping. Until then control systolic BP (commonly below about 160), give analgesia and antiemetics, reverse anticoagulation and treat acute hydrocephalus with ventricular drainage; routine antifibrinolytics did not improve outcome. Give oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days, reducing the dose or splitting it if it causes hypotension. Maintain euvolaemia (prophylactic hypervolaemia and triple-H are abandoned), avoid hypotension and hyponatraemia, and monitor for DCI with frequent examination, transcranial Doppler or CT perfusion; lumbar drainage of blood-laden CSF reduced DCI-related infarction in a recent trial. Symptomatic DCI is treated with induced hypertension and, if refractory, intra-arterial vasodilators or angioplasty; statins and magnesium add nothing, and seizure prophylaxis, if used, should be brief.
det.prognosis: Overall case fatality approaches one third, with many survivors left with cognitive, mood or fatigue problems; grade on admission is the strongest predictor.
pearls: Thunderclap headache = SAH until proven otherwise; CT then LP if needed.
Nimodipine improves outcome but does not reliably prevent angiographic spasm.
Hyponatraemia after SAH is often cerebral salt wasting — do not fluid-restrict.
New deficit or drowsiness between days 3 and 14 = DCI until excluded; check sodium, hydrocephalus and perfusion.

name: Subchoreic Huntington’s disease (status subchoreacticus)
formal: Late phase of Huntington disease with reduced chorea turning to rigidity, bradykinesia and dystonia in advanced or juvenile-onset cases; the title wording is nonstandard for an akinetic-rigid stage.
simple: A late stage of Huntington disease in which the jerky movements fade and the body becomes stiff and slow.
th: ระยะท้ายของ Huntington disease ที่ chorea ลดลงแต่มี rigidity, bradykinesia และ dystonia เด่นขึ้น
tempoNote: Develops over years as HD advances; also the dominant picture from the start in many juvenile cases
feat: Known or suspected HD in whom chorea fades while stiffness, slowness and dystonic postures increase
Marked dysarthria, dysphagia, weight loss and falls
Advanced dementia and apathy usually accompany the motor change
Term is old and nonstandard; modern texts describe this as the late hypokinetic phase of HD
Juvenile-onset HD (Westphal) can show this rigid phenotype from early on
inv: HTT CAG repeat testing if the diagnosis was never genetically confirmed
MRI: caudate and diffuse cortical atrophy
Swallow assessment and nutritional review
Review of medication list: tetrabenazine or antipsychotics may be worsening parkinsonism

case.who: 52-year-old woman from Phitsanulok with genetically confirmed HD for 12 years
case.story: Family notes her jerky movements have nearly gone over 2 years, but she is now stiff, slow, chokes on rice and has fallen several times.
case.exam: Mild residual facial chorea, axial rigidity, bradykinesia, dystonic hand postures, slow saccades, severe dysarthria.
case.tests: Still on tetrabenazine 75 mg/day and haloperidol; MRI shows marked caudate atrophy.
case.q: Why has her chorea faded, and what should be adjusted?
case.a: Late hypokinetic (subchoreic) phase of HD plus drug-induced parkinsonism; taper anti-chorea drugs and focus on swallowing and falls.

det.patho: Huntington disease is caused by an expanded CAG repeat in HTT. Early loss affects striatal projection neurons of the indirect pathway, favouring chorea; as the disease progresses, direct-pathway neurons and cortex are also lost, shifting the picture toward a hypokinetic-rigid state. The label status subchoreacticus is historical and is not used in current classifications.
det.clinical: Chorea typically peaks in mid-stage disease and then declines while bradykinesia, rigidity, dystonia and gait failure dominate. Dysphagia, weight loss, incontinence and severe cognitive decline accompany this phase. Behavioural symptoms such as apathy become more prominent than irritability. Patients with large repeats or juvenile onset may be rigid from the start.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis rests on confirmed HD with a change in motor phenotype; genetic testing is needed if not already done. It is important to separate natural disease evolution from parkinsonism caused by anti-chorea medication. Intercurrent infection, dehydration or subdural haematoma after falls should be excluded when the decline is abrupt.
det.treatment: Reduce or stop VMAT2 inhibitors and dopamine blockers once chorea is no longer troublesome. Levodopa or amantadine can be tried cautiously for rigidity, watching for psychosis. Care is mainly multidisciplinary: swallow therapy, texture-modified diet or gastrostomy discussion, physiotherapy, seating, pressure care and advance care planning.
det.prognosis: This phase usually reflects advanced disease; death typically follows within several years, most often from aspiration pneumonia or complications of immobility.
pearls: Declining chorea in HD is not improvement; check for parkinsonism and dysphagia.
Always review anti-chorea drugs when an HD patient becomes stiff and slow.
Juvenile HD is often rigid rather than choreic (Westphal variant).
det.thd: Subchoreic HD เป็นคำเก่าที่หมายถึงระยะท้ายของ Huntington disease ซึ่ง chorea ลดลงแต่มีอาการแข็งเกร็ง เคลื่อนไหวช้า และ dystonia มากขึ้น ร่วมกับกลืนลำบาก น้ำหนักลด และสมองเสื่อม ต้องแยกจาก parkinsonism จากยา tetrabenazine หรือยาต้านโรคจิต การดูแลเน้นลดยาที่ไม่จำเป็น ฝึกกลืน ป้องกันการหกล้ม และวางแผนการดูแลระยะท้าย

det.patho: A narrowing or blockage in the subclavian artery before the point where the vertebral artery arises (left side in about three-quarters, because of its origin from the arch) reduces pressure beyond the lesion. The vertebral artery then fills retrogradely from the basilar junction to supply the arm. The brain is usually protected by the circle of Willis, which is why most patients have no neurological symptoms. Atherosclerosis is the main cause; Takayasu arteritis, radiation, thoracic outlet compression and congenital arch anomalies are others.
det.clinical: The steal phenomenon (reversed vertebral flow on ultrasound) is common and benign; the syndrome (symptoms) is rare. When present, posterior-circulation symptoms are brief and exercise-related; persistent stroke from steal alone is unusual, and a stroke should prompt a search for another mechanism. Arm claudication and finger ischaemia from emboli may occur. Coronary steal causes angina in patients whose bypass uses the left internal mammary artery.
det.diagnosis: The arm BP gradient is the bedside clue. Duplex documents vertebral flow direction (partial, alternating or complete reversal). CTA or MRA shows the culprit lesion and other arch disease. Coexisting carotid or vertebrobasilar stenosis increases symptom likelihood and should be sought.
det.treatment: Asymptomatic steal needs only vascular risk management (antiplatelet, statin, BP control using the higher arm reading, smoking cessation). Symptomatic patients, or those needing a patent left internal mammary graft, are treated by endovascular angioplasty and stenting or by surgical carotid-subclavian bypass/transposition. Takayasu disease requires immunosuppression before revascularisation.
det.prognosis: Benign neurologically in most cases; overall prognosis is governed by the associated coronary and cerebrovascular atherosclerosis.
pearls: Always measure BP in both arms; use the higher one for management decisions.
Steal on Doppler is common, but steal symptoms are rare — look for another cause of a stroke.
Vertigo or dizziness provoked by arm exercise is the classic history.

det.patho: Loss-of-function of HTRA1, a serine protease that modulates TGF-beta signalling, causes degeneration of arterial smooth muscle, intimal thickening and splitting of the elastic lamina within small penetrating arteries, without the granular osmiophilic material seen in CADASIL. Altered TGF-beta signalling in other tissues probably explains hair loss and disc degeneration. Biallelic variants cause CARASIL; some heterozygous variants cause a later-onset dominant small vessel disease that is now recognised as more common than the recessive form.
det.clinical: Onset is typically in the teens to 30s with alopecia and back pain preceding neurological disease. Lacunar strokes or a progressive gait disorder appear in young adulthood, followed by cognitive decline with apathy, irritability and pseudobulbar signs. Patients are usually normotensive. Heterozygous carriers present later (40s–60s) with stroke and leukoencephalopathy, often without alopecia.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in a young normotensive patient with diffuse leukoencephalopathy and lacunes, particularly with consanguinity, early baldness or premature spondylosis. MRI resembles CADASIL, including temporal pole involvement, and a pontine arc lesion is suggestive. Confirm by HTRA1 sequencing after excluding NOTCH3, COL4A1/2, Fabry disease and acquired causes.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying treatment exists. Manage with antiplatelet therapy after ischaemic events (weighing bleeding risk), physiotherapy for spasticity and gait, treatment of mood disorders, orthopaedic care for spinal disease and support for cognitive decline. Offer genetic counselling to the family, including carriers, given the dominant risk of some heterozygous variants.
det.prognosis: The disease advances to severe dementia and dependence over roughly 10 years from neurological onset.
pearls: Young bald man + back pain + leukoencephalopathy = check HTRA1.
Unlike CADASIL, migraine with aura is not a typical feature.
Heterozygous HTRA1 variants are a cause of adult-onset familial small vessel disease.

simple: A stroke deep in the brain from blockage of a tiny vessel, often causing weakness or numbness on one side.

det.patho: Chronic hypertension and diabetes damage the small penetrating arteries (lenticulostriate, thalamoperforating, pontine paramedian) through arteriolosclerosis and lipohyalinosis, leading to occlusion of a single perforator. Branch atheromatous disease at the origin of a perforator causes larger, more proximal deep infarcts that tend to worsen early. The process belongs to cerebral small vessel disease, which also causes white matter hyperintensities, microbleeds and vascular cognitive impairment.
det.clinical: The five classic syndromes cover most cases, with pure motor stroke the commonest. Absence of cortical features is the key clue. Deficits may stutter over the first 24–72 hours, sometimes with repeated stereotyped episodes. Recurrent small strokes accumulate into gait problems, pseudobulbar signs and dementia.
det.diagnosis: MRI DWI confirms an acute small deep infarct and shows background small-vessel disease. CTA or MRA checks for parent-artery disease and alternative mechanisms. Cardiac and carotid evaluation remain worthwhile because emboli occasionally produce lacunar syndromes. In young patients without risk factors consider monogenic small-vessel diseases (CADASIL, CARASIL) and vasculitis.
det.treatment: Thrombolysis is indicated within the time window just as for other ischaemic strokes. Secondary prevention centres on blood pressure targets (often < 130/80), statin, antiplatelet therapy (short-term dual therapy in the early high-risk period, then single agent), diabetes control and smoking cessation. Cilostazol is used in Asian practice for small-vessel disease with fewer bleeds.
det.prognosis: Early survival and functional outcome are better than for cortical stroke, but cumulative small-vessel disease raises long-term risks of recurrence and cognitive decline.
pearls: No cortical signs + one of the five syndromes = think lacune.
Fluctuating hemiparesis in the first day = capsular warning syndrome; watch closely.
Blood pressure control is the single most important prevention.
det.thd: Subcortical ischaemic stroke หรือ lacunar stroke เกิดจากหลอดเลือดเล็กในสมองส่วนลึกอุดตันจากความดันสูงและเบาหวาน แสดงเป็น pure motor, pure sensory หรือ ataxic hemiparesis โดยไม่มีอาการของเปลือกสมอง เช่น aphasia หรือ neglect MRI พบ infarct ขนาดเล็กในส่วนลึกพร้อม white matter change รักษาเหมือน ischaemic stroke ทั่วไปและเน้นคุมความดันอย่างเข้มงวด

det.patho: Generators lie in the brainstem reticular formation or other deep structures, so jerks spread up the brainstem and down the cord rather than following a cortical map. Hypoxia, metabolic derangement, drugs and structural brainstem lesions can increase reticular excitability. Genetic forms include SGCE-related myoclonus-dystonia and glycine receptor disorders.
det.clinical: Jerks are typically generalized and axial, involving neck, shoulder and trunk flexors, sometimes with blinking. Stimulus sensitivity is common, especially to sound or touch around the face. Some patients have predominantly proximal arm jerks with dystonia, as in myoclonus-dystonia. The pattern helps localise but not identify the cause.
det.diagnosis: Clinical observation is supplemented by multichannel EMG to see recruitment order and burst duration. Jerk-locked EEG averaging shows no cortical precursor, separating it from cortical forms. Imaging and metabolic, toxic and genetic testing are then chosen according to context. Functional jerks with variable latency and a Bereitschaftspotential should be considered.
det.treatment: Treat the cause where possible (correct metabolic disturbance, withdraw drugs). Clonazepam is the most useful symptomatic agent; levetiracetam and valproate have more effect on cortical forms but can be tried. Myoclonus-dystonia may respond to alcohol, benzodiazepines or pallidal (GPi) DBS.
det.prognosis: Outcome follows the underlying cause; metabolic or drug causes usually resolve, while genetic forms are lifelong but often non-progressive.
pearls: Classifying myoclonus physiologically guides drug choice.
Brainstem myoclonus spreads up and down from the lower brainstem; look at the recruitment order.
No cortical spike on back-averaging points away from cortical myoclonus.

det.patho: Abnormal excitability involves reciprocal circuits between cortex and thalamus, so jerks are linked to generalized epileptiform discharges. The same physiology underlies myoclonic seizures in idiopathic generalized epilepsies and many progressive myoclonus epilepsies. It is a neurophysiological class rather than a specific disease.
det.clinical: Patients have brief bilateral jerks, mainly of the arms and shoulders, often clustered after awakening. Generalized tonic-clonic seizures and absences may coexist. In progressive forms, action myoclonus, ataxia and cognitive decline accumulate over years. Triggers include sleep deprivation, alcohol and flashing lights.
det.diagnosis: EEG is key, showing generalized spike or polyspike-wave discharges time-locked to jerks. Back-averaging and SEPs help separate cortical subtypes. Progressive cases warrant genetic testing, skin or muscle biopsy for storage disorders where indicated, and MRI. Syncope-related jerks and functional jerks are common mimics.
det.treatment: Valproate remains the most effective broad agent in men and women not of childbearing potential; levetiracetam is preferred for women who may become pregnant. Clonazepam, perampanel, zonisamide and brivaracetam are additional options. Carbamazepine, phenytoin, oxcarbazepine and gabapentin can aggravate myoclonus and should be avoided.
det.prognosis: In JME seizures are usually well controlled but often recur if medication stops; PME prognosis depends on the genetic cause and may be poor.
pearls: Ask about morning jerks in any adolescent with a first tonic-clonic seizure.
Sodium-channel blockers can worsen myoclonic epilepsy.
Progressive myoclonus with ataxia and cognitive decline suggests a PME, not JME.

det.patho: Neurofibromas arise when Schwann cells lose the remaining NF1 allele, then recruit fibroblasts, mast cells and perineurial cells. det.clinical: They present as firm nodules palpable along nerves, sometimes causing local tenderness or paraesthesia. Unlike cutaneous lesions they carry modest malignant risk and indicate a heavier internal tumour load. They are not a disease in themselves but a feature of NF1.
det.diagnosis: Usually clinical in a patient with NF1; ultrasound helps distinguish them from lipomas. Imaging is needed if pain, rapid growth, hardness or neurological deficit develops. Atypical neurofibromas (ANNUBP) are premalignant and may be surgically removed.
det.treatment: Symptomatic or cosmetically troubling lesions are excised; MEK inhibitors may shrink some tumours. Teach patients the warning signs of malignant change. Follow up regularly in an NF clinic.
det.prognosis: Most remain benign; malignant transformation is uncommon but serious.
pearls: Firm and tender = subcutaneous; soft and painless = cutaneous.

det.patho: Extradural haematoma forms when a fracture tears the middle meningeal artery (or a dural sinus, especially in the posterior fossa) and arterial blood strips the dura from the skull; the clot expands quickly and is usually confined by the sutures. Acute subdural haematoma arises from cortical lacerations or torn bridging veins and is often accompanied by diffuse injury and swelling. Chronic subdural haematoma develops when a small bleed becomes encased in neomembranes with fragile vessels, local inflammation and fibrinolysis that keep it enlarging for weeks; cerebral atrophy and antithrombotic drugs predispose.
det.clinical: The classic EDH sequence is a brief loss of consciousness, a lucid interval and then deterioration, but many patients never show the full pattern and a full lucid interval is seen in only a minority. The sudden death mechanism is uncal herniation with midbrain compression, so bilateral Babinski signs or decerebration before surgery predict poor outcome. Acute SDH often presents in coma. Chronic SDH is a great mimic: slowing, headache, falls, aphasia, transient focal episodes or seizures, and bilateral lesions may produce few lateralising signs. Anticoagulation raises the risk of subdural bleeding even after minor trauma.
det.diagnosis: CT is the test of choice and is rapid. Classic EDH is biconvex and uniformly dense, in a minority crescentic or isodense in anaemia. Acute SDH is a hyperdense crescent that crosses sutures, while chronic SDH may be hypodense or isodense, with a fluid level or mixed density when bleeding recurs. Midline shift of more than 5 mm, effaced basal cisterns and thickness of 10 mm or more mark surgical lesions in head-injured patients, as does an EDH volume above 30 mL. Repeat imaging detects delayed haematoma. Check coagulation and platelet function.
det.treatment: Emergency evacuation by craniotomy is indicated for an EDH over 30 mL regardless of GCS, for any EDH with GCS below 9 and anisocoria, and for acute SDH over 10 mm thick or with shift over 5 mm, together with ICP control, airway protection and reversal of coagulopathy. Small EDHs (under 30 mL, under 15 mm, shift under 5 mm, GCS above 8 and no deficit) may be observed with serial CT in a neurosurgical centre. Chronic SDH is drained through one or two burr holes with a subdural drain; recurrence occurs in roughly 10–20%, and trials of middle meningeal artery embolisation (alone or after surgery) show lower recurrence and fewer reoperations. Oral steroids and tranexamic acid have not become standard after mixed trial results (the Dex-CSDH trial showed more complications with dexamethasone). Antithrombotics are held where the thrombotic risk allows.
det.prognosis: EDH has an excellent outcome if evacuated before deep coma (mortality about 5–10% in modern series); acute SDH mortality is high; chronic SDH usually improves after drainage.
pearls: Lens shape bounded by sutures = extradural; crescent across sutures = subdural.
Chronic SDH is a treatable cause of confusion, gait decline and 'stroke' in the elderly: CT early.
Check the CT again if the patient is deteriorating, since a delayed EDH can follow a normal first scan.
det.thd: EDH เกิดจากเส้นเลือดแดง middle meningeal ฉีกขาดจากกะโหลกแตก CT เป็นรูปเลนส์ไม่ข้ามรอยต่อกะโหลก ผู้ป่วยอาจมีช่วงรู้ตัวดีแล้วทรุดลงเร็ว ต้องผ่าตัดด่วนถ้าก้อนใหญ่กว่า 30 มล. หรือ GCS ต่ำและรูม่านตาไม่เท่ากัน ส่วน SDH เกิดจาก bridging vein ฉีก CT เป็นรูปจันทร์เสี้ยวข้ามรอยต่อ ชนิดเรื้อรังพบบ่อยในผู้สูงอายุและผู้กินยากันเลือดหรือกันเกล็ดเลือด มีสับสนปวดศีรษะเดินเซอ่อนแรงครึ่งซีก รักษาด้วยการเจาะระบายผ่านรู burr hole และปัจจุบันอาจใช้การอุด MMA เพื่อลดการเป็นซ้ำ

qx.stem: A 19-year-old motorcyclist without a helmet is brought in after a collision; he was briefly unconscious, then lucid, and now becomes drowsy with a dilated left pupil. CT shows a biconvex, lentiform hyperdense collection over the left temporal region that does not cross the coronal suture, with a linear fracture of the overlying squamous temporal bone and a swirl of lower-density material within it.
qx.q: What is the most likely source and best management?
opts: Bridging vein tear; burr-hole drainage next week
Middle meningeal artery bleed; emergency craniotomy and evacuation
Diffuse axonal injury; hyperosmolar therapy only
Venous sinus thrombosis; heparin
Contusion; repeat CT after 24 hours
qx.why: A lentiform extra-axial collection limited by sutures, overlying a temporal fracture, with a lucid interval, indicates an epidural haematoma from the middle meningeal artery. A swirl sign means active bleeding. With mass effect and a blown pupil this needs emergency surgical evacuation. Subdural bleeds are crescentic and cross sutures.

name: Chronic subdural haematoma
formal: Collection of blood between dura and arachnoid from torn bridging veins, acute or chronic, particularly in elderly or anticoagulated patients, presenting with headache, confusion or hemiparesis.
simple: A slow or sudden bleed under the brain's outer covering, often after a minor head knock in older people.
ab: เลือดคั่งใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมองเรื้อรัง
th: เลือดคั่งเรื้อรังใต้เยื่อดูราในผู้สูงอายุ มักเกิดหลังล้มเล็กน้อยหรือจำไม่ได้ พบมากในผู้ที่ใช้ยาต้านเกล็ดเลือดหรือยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือด หรือดื่มสุรา อาการค่อย ๆ สับสน ปวดศีรษะ อ่อนแรงครึ่งซีก เดินลำบาก รักษาด้วยเจาะรูระบาย
tempoNote: Builds over weeks (typically 3 weeks to a few months) after trivial or forgotten head trauma; symptoms fluctuate
feat: Older adult, often male, on antiplatelet or anticoagulant drugs, with brain atrophy, alcohol use or frequent falls
Gradual headache, confusion, drowsiness, gait decline or mild hemiparesis over weeks
Fluctuating symptoms and transient focal episodes that can mimic TIA or seizures
Bilateral in about a fifth — may cause cognitive decline without lateralising signs
Also seen with CSF shunts, coagulopathy and spontaneous intracranial hypotension
inv: Non-contrast CT: crescentic collection over the convexity, hypodense or mixed; isodense phase can be missed, especially if bilateral
MRI if CT is equivocal; it also shows membranes and septations
Platelets, coagulation, renal and liver function; record antithrombotic drugs and timing

case.who: 76-year-old retired male policeman from Sukhothai on aspirin and clopidogrel
case.story: Slipped in the bathroom 5 weeks ago without hitting hard. For 10 days he has been sleepy, repeating himself and dragging his right foot; symptoms vary through the day.
case.exam: Drowsy but rousable, mild right hemiparesis, extensor right plantar.
case.tests: CT: 20-mm left fronto-parietal crescentic mixed-density collection with 7-mm midline shift.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the usual definitive treatment?
case.a: Symptomatic chronic subdural haematoma; hold antiplatelets, correct platelet function if needed, and perform burr-hole drainage with a subdural drain (MMA embolisation can be added to reduce recurrence).

Chapter 28 Disorders of Consciousness and Intensive Care Neurology — Subdural Haematoma
5: Preparation of Muscle and Nerve Biopsy

det.patho: Minor trauma tears bridging veins in an atrophied brain where the subdural space is wide. The initial clot triggers inflammation and the growth of a neomembrane full of fragile, leaky capillaries supplied by middle meningeal artery branches; repeated microbleeding and local fibrinolysis enlarge the collection. Antithrombotic drugs, alcohol, coagulopathy, shunting and low CSF pressure all favour formation.
det.clinical: It is one of the commonest neurosurgical conditions in older adults and its incidence is rising with ageing and antithrombotic use. Presentation is insidious: headache, cognitive decline, drowsiness, falls, gait disturbance and hemiparesis, often fluctuating. Transient, stereotyped speech or motor episodes can occur from cortical irritation. A third or more of patients recall no injury.
det.diagnosis: CT shows a crescent following the skull contour that can cross sutures but not the midline; density changes with age (acute hyperdense, subacute isodense, chronic hypodense), and mixed densities indicate rebleeding. Isodense or bilateral collections may be overlooked when midline shift is absent — look for effaced sulci and medially displaced grey–white junction. In younger patients without trauma, consider intracranial hypotension, coagulopathy, or dural metastases.
det.treatment: Small, asymptomatic collections can be watched with repeat imaging while reviewing antithrombotic need. Symptomatic or large haematomas are drained, usually by burr-hole craniostomy with a subdural drain for about 48 hours, which halves recurrence. Middle meningeal artery embolisation, added to surgery or used alone in selected patients, lowers recurrence in recent randomised trials. Dexamethasone worsens outcomes and is not recommended. Reverse anticoagulation before surgery; decisions on restarting antithrombotics weigh thrombotic risk against rebleeding and are usually made within weeks.
det.prognosis: Most recover well after drainage, but recurrence needing re-operation occurs in roughly 10–20%, and frail older patients have increased mortality and loss of independence.
pearls: Fluctuating confusion in an older person on antiplatelets — CT for subdural.
Bilateral isodense SDH may show no midline shift; check the sulci.
Steroids are not a treatment for chronic SDH (Dex-CSDH trial).
Unexplained bilateral SDH in a younger adult — think spontaneous intracranial hypotension.
det.thd: Chronic subdural haematoma คือเลือดคั่งเรื้อรังระหว่างเยื่อดูรากับ arachnoid พบในผู้สูงอายุที่สมองฝ่อ ใช้ยาต้านเกล็ดเลือดหรือยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือด หรือดื่มสุรา มักหลังล้มเล็กน้อยหรือจำไม่ได้ อาการค่อย ๆ ปวดศีรษะ สับสน ซึม เดินลำบาก หรืออ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกแบบขึ้น ๆ ลง ๆ CT เห็นเลือดรูปพระจันทร์เสี้ยว ถ้ามีอาการรักษาด้วยเจาะรูระบายและใส่สายระบาย อาจเสริมด้วย MMA embolisation เพื่อลดการกลับเป็นซ้ำ ไม่ควรใช้ dexamethasone

name: Subhyaloid haemorrhage
formal: Retinal bleeding between the internal limiting membrane or hyaloid face and retina, often with subarachnoid haemorrhage (Terson syndrome) or raised pressure, causing sudden visual loss.
simple: A pool of blood in front of the retina that can suddenly blur vision, sometimes after a brain bleed.
th: เลือดออกใต้ชั้น internal limiting membrane หรือ posterior hyaloid ของจอตา เห็นเป็นรูปเรือมีระดับน้ำ มักพบร่วมกับ SAH หรือความดันในกะโหลกสูงเฉียบพลัน
tempoNote: Sudden at the time of the bleed or pressure surge; blood clears over weeks to months
feat: Dark red, boat-shaped preretinal blood with a flat upper fluid level, near the disc or macula
Sudden blurring or a central dark patch when the macula is covered; may be bilateral
Fundus clue to aneurysmal SAH (Terson syndrome), most often from an anterior communicating artery aneurysm; also seen with subdural haematoma or other abrupt intracranial pressure rises
Blood may break through into the vitreous, causing a vitreous haemorrhage
Other causes: Valsalva retinopathy, retinal artery macroaneurysm, abusive head trauma, severe anaemia, leukaemia, proliferative diabetic retinopathy
inv: Dilated fundoscopy; ocular B-scan ultrasound if the view is blocked
OCT to confirm a sub-ILM or subhyaloid location and check the macula
Urgent CT and CTA for SAH if there is thunderclap headache or reduced consciousness
FBC, coagulation screen and glucose/HbA1c; consider fluorescein angiography for macroaneurysm

case.story: Sudden worst headache and collapse yesterday; now drowsy in the ward and her family says her vision seems poor.
case.exam: GCS 13, neck stiffness; fundoscopy shows bilateral boat-shaped preretinal haemorrhages over the maculae.
case.tests: CT shows diffuse subarachnoid blood; CTA reveals an anterior communicating artery aneurysm.
case.q: What does the eye finding indicate and does it change the neurosurgical plan?
case.a: Terson syndrome, a marker of severe SAH; the aneurysm is secured first and ophthalmology follows up, with vitrectomy if vitreous blood persists.

det.patho: The blood collects between the retina and the posterior hyaloid or inner limiting membrane, and settles with gravity to form a fluid level. In Terson syndrome, acute intracranial pressure rise is thought to impede venous return from the retina through the cavernous sinus, rupturing retinal and peripapillary vessels. Other mechanisms include sudden venous pressure surges (Valsalva), rupture of a macroaneurysm, or bleeding from fragile new vessels.
det.clinical: Symptoms range from none to sudden vision loss with a central scotoma. Intraocular haemorrhage can be bilateral and is often missed in drowsy SAH patients, and it correlates with a more severe bleed and worse outcome. In infants, extensive multilayer retinal haemorrhages should prompt a child-protection assessment. Valsalva retinopathy typically follows coughing, vomiting or heavy lifting in an otherwise healthy person.
det.diagnosis: The appearance on dilated fundoscopy is typical. If there is any neurological context (headache, altered consciousness), image the brain and vessels for SAH. Ultrasonography detects blood when the view is hazy and distinguishes it from retinal detachment. Systemic work-up for blood dyscrasia, hypertension and diabetes is added when SAH is not found.
det.treatment: Treat the cause first, usually aneurysm repair. Vision often recovers spontaneously over a few months, so small or peripheral bleeds are observed. Persistent macular or vitreous blood may be cleared by vitrectomy or Nd:YAG laser hyaloidotomy, which gives early drainage in selected macular cases.
det.prognosis: Usually good for vision as the blood clears; overall outcome depends on the underlying cause.
pearls: Fundoscopy in every comatose patient: subhyaloid blood points to SAH.
Boat shape with a fluid level is the hallmark.
In infants, consider non-accidental injury.
det.thd: Subhyaloid haemorrhage คือเลือดที่คั่งอยู่ใต้ชั้น hyaloid ของจอตา มีลักษณะคล้ายเรือและมีระดับน้ำด้านบน ทำให้ตามัวเฉียบพลันถ้าเลือดอยู่ที่ macula ใน neurology ควรนึกถึง Terson syndrome จาก subarachnoid haemorrhage ที่หลอดเลือดโป่งพองแตก ควรตรวจจอตาผู้ป่วยซึม ตรวจสืบหาสาเหตุอื่น เช่น Valsalva macroaneurysm เลือดจาง และเบาหวาน เลือดมักดูดซึมเองใน 2-3 เดือน ถ้าไม่ดูดซึมอาจต้องผ่าตัดวุ้นตา

name: Sudden adult cardiac death syndrome (SADS)
formal: Sudden death in adults with no structural cause on autopsy, often attributed to inherited arrhythmia such as channelopathy, sometimes with overlap with epilepsy-related deaths.
simple: An unexpected death in a young or healthy adult with no clear cause found, often due to a heart rhythm disorder.
th: การเสียชีวิตเฉียบพลันในผู้ใหญ่ที่ผ่าศพแล้วไม่พบความผิดปกติโครงสร้างหัวใจ มักเชื่อว่าเกิดจากโรคหัวใจเต้นผิดจังหวะทางพันธุกรรม ไม่ใช่โรคทางระบบประสาท
tempoNote: Death within minutes; warning episodes (syncope, nocturnal seizures-like events) may precede it
feat: Not a neurological disease: sudden cardiac death with normal heart structure and negative toxicology
Often young adults, frequently during sleep or rest; Brugada syndrome is a key cause in Southeast Asia (historically 'lai tai')
Warning signs: exertional or startle-triggered syncope, nocturnal agonal breathing, family history of sudden death
Arrhythmic syncope can be misdiagnosed as epilepsy because of brief anoxic jerks
Relatives need cardiac and genetic screening
inv: In survivors or relatives: 12-lead ECG (including high precordial leads for Brugada), Holter, exercise test, echocardiogram, cardiac MRI
Drug challenge (ajmaline/flecainide) for suspected Brugada in specialist centres
Molecular autopsy (genetic testing of the deceased) and family cascade screening

case.story: His family wants advice after his elder brother died in his sleep with gasping noises; he himself had two night-time 'fits' last year labelled as epilepsy.
case.exam: Normal neurological and cardiac examination.
case.tests: ECG shows coved ST elevation in V1–V2 when leads are placed one interspace higher; EEG normal.
case.q: What should be done before continuing antiseizure drugs?
case.a: Refer urgently to cardiology: likely Brugada syndrome with arrhythmic 'seizures'; an ICD may be needed, and family members should be screened.

det.patho: Most autopsy-negative sudden deaths in young adults are due to inherited primary arrhythmia syndromes: Brugada syndrome, long QT syndrome, catecholaminergic polymorphic VT and others, many caused by cardiac ion channel variants. Some channel genes (e.g. SCN5A, KCNH2) are also expressed in the brain, so cardiac and epileptic phenotypes can overlap. In Thailand and the region, sudden nocturnal death in young men is strongly linked to Brugada syndrome.
det.clinical: Sudden death is often the first event, typically at rest, in sleep, or with triggers like fever, large meals, alcohol, exercise or loud noise depending on the syndrome. Survivors and relatives may report prior syncope, palpitations or night-time gasping. Neurologists meet the condition when arrhythmic syncope with convulsive jerks is mislabelled as epilepsy.
det.diagnosis: In the deceased, a full autopsy with toxicology and cardiac pathology plus molecular autopsy is recommended. In living relatives or survivors, ECG (with high leads), ambulatory monitoring, exercise testing, imaging and provocation tests identify the syndrome. In anyone with episodes of loss of consciousness, an ECG is mandatory before diagnosing epilepsy.
det.treatment: Management is cardiological: implantable cardioverter-defibrillator for high-risk patients, beta-blockers for long QT and CPVT, quinidine for selected Brugada cases, fever control, and avoidance of triggering drugs. Family screening identifies those at risk. Neurologists should review epilepsy diagnoses that rest on atypical events.
det.prognosis: Relatives identified early and treated have a much lower risk of sudden death.
pearls: Not neurological, but a vital mimic of epilepsy; get an ECG after every first convulsive collapse.
Nocturnal death with gasping in a young Thai man: think Brugada syndrome.
Some antiseizure and psychotropic drugs (sodium-channel blockers) can unmask Brugada patterns.
det.thd: SADS คือการเสียชีวิตเฉียบพลันในผู้ใหญ่ที่ผ่าศพแล้วหัวใจปกติ ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจากโรคหัวใจเต้นผิดจังหวะทางพันธุกรรม เช่น Brugada ซึ่งพบบ่อยในชายไทยที่เสียชีวิตขณะหลับ (ไหลตาย) ไม่ใช่โรคทางระบบประสาท แต่อาการหมดสติและกระตุกอาจถูกวินิจฉัยผิดเป็นโรคลมชัก จึงต้องตรวจ ECG ทุกครั้ง รักษาโดยแพทย์โรคหัวใจ เช่นใส่ ICD และตรวจคัดกรองญาติ

name: Sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP)
formal: Unexpected, non-traumatic death in a person with epilepsy, with or without a witnessed seizure, excluding status epilepticus; risk rises with frequent generalised tonic-clonic seizures, especially nocturnal.
simple: A sudden unexplained death in someone with epilepsy, mostly linked to poorly controlled seizures.
th: การเสียชีวิตอย่างไม่คาดคิดในผู้ป่วยโรคลมชัก ที่ไม่ได้เกิดจากอุบัติเหตุ จมน้ำ หรือ status epilepticus มักเกิดหลังชักเกร็งกระตุกขณะหลับ
tempoNote: Usually occurs at night, minutes after an unwitnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure
feat: Leading cause of epilepsy-related death in young adults with uncontrolled seizures; around 1 per 1000 adults with epilepsy per year
Victim typically found dead in bed, often prone, with evidence of a recent seizure
Strongest risk factor: frequent generalised tonic-clonic seizures, especially nocturnal and unsupervised
Other risks: drug-resistant epilepsy, poor adherence, early onset, intellectual disability, Dravet syndrome, living alone
Autopsy excludes other causes (definite SUDEP)
inv: Post-mortem examination with toxicology to classify as definite or probable SUDEP
In living patients: review seizure frequency, nocturnal events and adherence; consider ECG for arrhythmia overlap
Genetic testing where a channelopathy is suspected (e.g. SCN1A, SCN5A, KCNH2)

case.who: 22-year-old university student from Phitsanulok with epilepsy since age 10
case.story: He takes his levetiracetam irregularly and has about two tonic-clonic seizures a month, mostly in sleep; he lives alone in a dormitory and asks why his doctor talks about 'night supervision'.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination.
case.tests: EEG shows left temporal spikes; MRI left hippocampal sclerosis.
case.q: What is his main mortality risk and how can it be reduced?
case.a: SUDEP; improve adherence and seizure control (including surgical referral for drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy), and arrange nocturnal supervision or monitoring.

det.patho: Most witnessed or monitored cases show a terminal cascade after a generalised tonic-clonic seizure: postictal suppression of brain activity, failure of breathing (central apnoea), bradycardia and asystole. Brainstem dysfunction of arousal and respiratory control, possibly involving serotonin and adenosine, and the prone position worsen hypoxia. Shared cardiac and neuronal ion channel variants contribute in some patients.
det.clinical: Those most often affected are young and middle-aged people whose generalised tonic-clonic seizures continue, though children die of it too. Most deaths are unwitnessed and nocturnal. Patients and families are often unaware of the risk, so guidelines recommend discussing SUDEP with all people with epilepsy. Seizure-free patients have very low risk.
det.diagnosis: Definite SUDEP requires a sudden, unexpected, non-traumatic, non-drowning death in a person with epilepsy, with or without a seizure, excluding documented status epilepticus, and an autopsy showing no other cause. Probable SUDEP lacks an autopsy; 'SUDEP plus' denotes a contributing comorbidity.
det.treatment: Prevention is the key: achieve seizure control, especially of nocturnal tonic-clonic seizures, optimise medicines and adherence, and refer drug-resistant patients early for epilepsy surgery or neuromodulation. Nocturnal supervision, listening devices or wearable seizure detectors may reduce risk. Avoid sleep deprivation and alcohol excess. Discuss risk openly and sensitively.
det.prognosis: Risk falls substantially when generalised tonic-clonic seizures are controlled.
pearls: Generalised tonic-clonic seizure frequency is the strongest modifiable risk factor.
Discuss SUDEP with every patient with epilepsy, not just the drug-resistant.
Death in documented status epilepticus is not SUDEP.
det.thd: SUDEP คือการเสียชีวิตเฉียบพลันโดยไม่ทราบสาเหตุในผู้ป่วยโรคลมชัก มักพบเสียชีวิตบนเตียงหลังชักเกร็งกระตุกตอนกลางคืน ปัจจัยเสี่ยงสำคัญคือชักแบบ tonic-clonic บ่อย กินยาไม่สม่ำเสมอ และอยู่คนเดียว การป้องกันคือควบคุมชักให้ได้ กินยาสม่ำเสมอ ส่งผ่าตัดถ้าดื้อยา และมีคนดูแลตอนกลางคืน ควรอธิบายความเสี่ยงนี้ให้ผู้ป่วยทุกราย

name: Sulphite oxidase deficiency
formal: Autosomal recessive inborn error of sulphite metabolism with neonatal intractable seizures, lens dislocation and severe encephalopathy; sulphite accumulates, with raised urinary S-sulphocysteine.
simple: A rare inherited disorder where a toxic substance builds up and causes severe seizures and brain damage in babies.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมยีนด้อยที่ขาดเอนไซม์กำจัดซัลไฟต์ ทารกแรกเกิดชักรุนแรงที่ยากต่อยา สมองเสียหายรุนแรง และเลนส์ตาเคลื่อน คล้ายภาวะขาดออกซิเจนแรกเกิด
tempoNote: Seizures and feeding failure within the first days of life; lens dislocation over months; mild late-onset forms show delay, dystonia or episodic worsening
feat: Refractory seizures (focal, myoclonic or apparently generalised) from the first days of life, with irritability, poor feeding and opisthotonic posturing
Severe encephalopathy, axial hypotonia with limb hypertonia, and profound developmental failure
Ectopia lentis develops over months; dysmorphic features and hepatomegaly are described
MRI evolves from swelling to cystic white matter change and atrophy, mimicking hypoxic-ischaemic injury
Autosomal recessive SUOX variants; milder late-onset variants cause developmental delay, dystonia or episodic basal ganglia injury
inv: Fresh urine sulphite dipstick (false negatives are common), urine S-sulphocysteine and thiosulphate, low plasma total homocysteine
Uric acid normal in isolated deficiency but low in molybdenum cofactor deficiency, where urine xanthine and hypoxanthine rise
SUOX gene sequencing, with MOCS1 and MOCS2 to exclude cofactor deficiency; EEG may show burst suppression or multifocal discharges
MRI brain: poor grey–white differentiation, diffuse oedema, then cystic white matter and cerebellar atrophy

case.who: 6-day-old term boy, first child of consanguineous parents, Pattani
case.story: Normal delivery with good Apgar scores. From day 2 he fed poorly and became irritable, and on day 4 had repeated tonic and myoclonic seizures that did not stop with phenobarbital or levetiracetam.
case.exam: Opisthotonic posturing, poor eye contact, hypotonia of the trunk with stiff limbs, no dysmorphism obvious, no hepatomegaly.
case.tests: Glucose, ammonia, lactate and gases normal. EEG shows burst suppression. MRI shows diffuse oedema and early cystic change. Urine sulphite dipstick positive on a fresh sample; uric acid normal; SUOX homozygous variant.
case.q: What distinguishes this from molybdenum cofactor deficiency and from birth asphyxia?
case.a: Normal uric acid with raised sulphocysteine and no xanthine accumulation separates it from cofactor deficiency, and normal birth history with these metabolic markers separates it from hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy. Treatment is supportive; counsel the family about prognosis and offer genetic testing for future pregnancies.

read.where: Chapter 31: Epilepsy in the Setting of Inherited Metabolic and Mitochondrial Disorders — Molybdenum Cofactor Deficiency and Sulfite Oxidase Deficiency

det.patho: Sulphite oxidase, a mitochondrial enzyme that requires the molybdenum cofactor, converts sulphite to sulphate in the final step of cysteine and methionine catabolism. When it fails, sulphite accumulates and is toxic to neurons, possibly through reaction with disulphide bonds, and S-sulphocysteine builds up and acts as an excitotoxic agonist at glutamate receptors. Isolated deficiency results from SUOX variants; molybdenum cofactor deficiency (MOCS1, MOCS2) shares the same phenotype because it also removes sulphite oxidase activity.
det.clinical: The severe form begins in the neonatal period with feeding difficulty, irritability and intractable seizures that look like hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, but without a perinatal cause. Axial hypotonia, spasticity and failure to develop follow, and lens dislocation appears during infancy. Rarer late-onset cases have milder delay, movement disorder or acute neurological deterioration with illness. Severe cases die in early life or survive with profound disability.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in a newborn with refractory seizures, ectopia lentis or MRI cystic change not explained by birth events. A urine sulphite dipstick on freshly collected urine is simple but frequently falsely negative, so confirm by measuring S-sulphocysteine and thiosulphate, with low plasma total homocysteine as supporting clue. Uric acid and urinary purines separate isolated deficiency from cofactor deficiency. Confirmation is by SUOX sequencing, enzyme studies in fibroblasts, and prenatal testing is possible for subsequent pregnancies.
det.treatment: There is no proven disease-modifying therapy for isolated sulphite oxidase deficiency. Seizures are managed with standard antiseizure drugs, though they are often refractory, and nutrition support is needed. Restricting sulphur-containing amino acids (methionine and cysteine) has been tried, mainly in milder cases. Fosdenopterin, replacing the missing cofactor precursor, is approved for molybdenum cofactor deficiency type A and helps only that disease. Palliative care, family counselling and genetic advice are central.
det.prognosis: The neonatal severe form has a very poor prognosis, often death in infancy or early childhood; late-onset forms have variable but progressive disability.
pearls: Neonatal seizures with cystic MRI change but a normal birth history should prompt a metabolic search including sulphite.
Low uric acid points to molybdenum cofactor deficiency, which may be treatable in the type A form.
A negative urine dipstick does not exclude the disease: use fresh urine and measure S-sulphocysteine.
det.thd: Sulphite oxidase deficiency เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมยีนด้อย ทำให้ซัลไฟต์คั่งและเป็นพิษต่อสมอง ทารกมีอาการชักรุนแรงตั้งแต่ไม่กี่วันแรกที่ไม่ตอบสนองต่อยา กินนมไม่ดี ตัวเกร็งแอ่น และเลนส์ตาเคลื่อนในภายหลัง MRI คล้ายสมองขาดออกซิเจน ตรวจปัสสาวะสดด้วยแถบ sulphite และวัด S-sulphocysteine ส่วนกรดยูริกปกติแยกจากภาวะขาด molybdenum cofactor ปัจจุบันยังไม่มียารักษาที่ได้ผล เน้นการดูแลประคับประคองและให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

name: Super-refractory status epilepticus
formal: Status epilepticus persisting or recurring for 24 hours or more despite anaesthetic therapy, requiring continuous intravenous anaesthetics; causes include autoimmune encephalitis and cryptogenic FIRES.
simple: A seizure emergency that continues despite strong anaesthetic drugs for a day or more.
th: status epilepticus ที่ยังชักต่อเนื่องหรือกลับมาชักซ้ำนานตั้งแต่ 24 ชั่วโมงขึ้นไปแม้ให้ยาสลบทางหลอดเลือดแล้ว หรือชักซ้ำเมื่อลดยาสลบ
tempoNote: Defined after 24 hours of anaesthetic therapy; may last days to weeks
feat: Seizures continue or return on weaning anaesthetic infusions despite at least 24 hours of treatment
Often non-convulsive on EEG once the patient is sedated
Common causes: autoimmune encephalitis, CNS infection, stroke, anoxia, drug or alcohol withdrawal; many are NORSE or FIRES
High risk of systemic complications: infection, ileus, hypotension, propofol infusion syndrome
Significant mortality and long-term cognitive and epileptic sequelae
inv: Continuous EEG to guide anaesthetic depth (burst suppression or seizure suppression) and detect relapse
MRI, CSF analysis including viral PCR, cell count, and autoimmune encephalitis antibody panel in serum and CSF
Cancer screening (CT chest-abdomen, pelvic ultrasound or MRI for teratoma), toxicology, metabolic and genetic tests as indicated

case.who: 28-year-old woman from Nakhon Ratchasima, previously healthy
case.story: After a week of fever and headache she developed behavioural change and then continuous seizures; she has been on midazolam and propofol for 3 days in ICU and seizures recur each time infusions are reduced.
case.exam: Intubated, sedated, intermittent orofacial twitching.
case.tests: Continuous EEG shows recurrent right temporal seizures on weaning; CSF 30 lymphocytes with negative HSV PCR; MRI bilateral mesial temporal T2 signal; pelvic MRI ovarian teratoma.
case.q: What is the likely cause and what treatments should be added?
case.a: Super-refractory SE from probable anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis; continue anaesthetic control and start immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG or plasma exchange, then rituximab) and remove the teratoma.

read.where: Chapter 39 Status Epilepticus and Acute Seizures

det.patho: Prolonged seizures change receptor trafficking: GABA-A receptors are internalised and NMDA receptors increase, so benzodiazepines lose effect and excitotoxic injury grows. Neuroinflammation, especially interleukin-1 and interleukin-6 signalling, sustains seizures in cryptogenic cases. The longer SE persists, the harder it is to stop and the greater the neuronal damage.
det.clinical: Most patients have no prior epilepsy and an acute cause such as encephalitis, stroke, trauma or anoxia. A large share of cryptogenic cases are later attributed to autoimmune or post-infectious inflammation. Clinical signs become subtle under sedation, so EEG is essential. Complications of prolonged ICU care often determine outcome.
det.diagnosis: SRSE is defined by duration and response, not cause, so the work-up aims to find a treatable cause quickly: MRI, CSF studies, neuronal antibodies, infection screen, toxicology, metabolic and mitochondrial testing and tumour search. In children and young adults consider genetic causes and FIRES. Continuous EEG confirms ongoing seizures and guides therapy.
det.treatment: Options include continued or rotated anaesthetic infusions (midazolam, propofol, thiopental/pentobarbital) and ketamine, plus multiple antiseizure medicines. Early immunotherapy is recommended in NORSE without another cause: corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange, then second-line rituximab, and anakinra or tocilizumab for cryptogenic NORSE/FIRES. Ketogenic diet, hypothermia, VNS and epilepsy surgery are used in selected cases. Treat the underlying cause and prevent ICU complications.
det.prognosis: Mortality is around 30–50% in adults, and many survivors have epilepsy and cognitive impairment, although meaningful recovery can occur even after weeks.
pearls: In SRSE without a clear cause, start immunotherapy early rather than waiting for antibody results.
Continuous EEG is mandatory; clinical seizures disappear under sedation.
Ketamine and anakinra are increasingly used options in refractory cases.
det.thd: Super-refractory status epilepticus คือภาวะชักต่อเนื่องที่ยังชักหรือกลับมาชักซ้ำหลังให้ยาสลบทางหลอดเลือดนานกว่า 24 ชั่วโมง สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยคือสมองอักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกันหรือติดเชื้อ ต้องเฝ้าดูด้วย continuous EEG ค้นหาสาเหตุอย่างรวดเร็ว ให้ยาสลบ ketamine และยากันชักหลายตัว ร่วมกับให้ภูมิคุ้มกันบำบัดตั้งแต่เนิ่น ๆ อัตราตายสูงและมักมีผลแทรกซ้อนระยะยาว
