name: Superior orbital fissure syndrome
formal: Lesion at the superior orbital fissure involving cranial nerves III, IV, V1 and VI, causing ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, proptosis and forehead numbness, from tumour, trauma, inflammation or infection.
simple: Damage at the gap behind the eye that causes eye movement paralysis, drooping eyelid and forehead numbness.
th: รอยโรคที่ superior orbital fissure ทำให้เส้นประสาทสมอง III, IV, V1 และ VI เสีย กลอกตาไม่ได้ หนังตาตก ตาโปน และหน้าผากชา
tempoNote: Acute after trauma or infection; subacute with tumour or inflammation
feat: Ophthalmoplegia from combined III, IV and VI involvement
Ptosis and a dilated fixed pupil if parasympathetic fibres in III are affected
Numbness of forehead and upper lid (V1), loss of corneal reflex
Proptosis from venous congestion
Vision spared (optic canal not involved) — if vision is lost it is orbital apex syndrome
inv: CT orbit/skull base for fractures; MRI with contrast for tumour or inflammation
CBC, CRP, glucose, HbA1c (mucormycosis risk), ANCA, IgG4
Biopsy if mass or atypical inflammation

case.story: After a crash with facial injury he cannot open his left eye and sees double when the lid is lifted.
case.exam: Left complete ptosis, fixed dilated pupil, total ophthalmoplegia, numb forehead, mild proptosis; visual acuity 6/6.
case.tests: CT: fracture through the left greater wing of sphenoid involving the superior orbital fissure.
case.q: Why is this superior orbital fissure syndrome rather than orbital apex syndrome?
case.a: Vision and the optic nerve are spared; orbital apex syndrome adds optic neuropathy.

read.where: Chapter 13 Cranial Nerve Disorders — Peripheral Vth Nerve Lesions

det.patho: The superior orbital fissure transmits cranial nerves III, IV, V1 branches and VI, plus the superior ophthalmic vein and sympathetic fibres. Any lesion here — fracture, tumour (meningioma, metastasis, lymphoma), infection (fungal sinusitis, herpes zoster), inflammation or carotid-cavernous fistula — affects these structures together.
det.clinical: The syndrome is anatomical rather than a single disease. Total ophthalmoplegia with ptosis and forehead numbness, with preserved vision, localises it. Pain suggests inflammation or tumour; fever and sinusitis in a diabetic suggests mucormycosis, which is a surgical emergency.
det.diagnosis: Imaging with CT and contrast MRI identifies the cause. Laboratory tests target infection, inflammation and neoplasm. A biopsy may be required, especially when steroids are being considered, to avoid treating lymphoma or fungal infection with steroids alone.
det.treatment: Depends on cause: surgical decompression for compressive fractures in some, antifungal therapy and debridement for mucormycosis, steroids for idiopathic inflammation, oncological treatment for tumours, and endovascular therapy for fistulas.
det.prognosis: Traumatic and inflammatory cases often recover partly over months; outcome depends on the cause.
pearls: SOF + optic nerve = orbital apex syndrome; + V2 and Horner = cavernous sinus.
Diabetic with ophthalmoplegia and sinus disease: think mucormycosis.
Do not give steroids blindly before excluding infection and lymphoma.
det.thd: Superior orbital fissure syndrome เกิดจากรอยโรคที่รอยแยกเหนือเบ้าตา ทำให้เส้นประสาทสมอง III, IV, V1 และ VI เสียพร้อมกัน ผู้ป่วยหนังตาตก กลอกตาไม่ได้ หน้าผากชา และตาโปน แต่การมองเห็นปกติ ถ้าตามัวด้วยเรียก orbital apex syndrome สาเหตุเช่นกระดูกหัก เนื้องอก การติดเชื้อรา และการอักเสบ รักษาตามสาเหตุ

qx.stem: A 72-year-old woman with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes presents with severe pain around the left eye and a vesicular rash over the left upper eyelid and forehead. The eye is fixed in a down-and-out position with complete ptosis and a dilated pupil. Visual acuity is 6/6 with no relative afferent pupillary defect, and CT of the brain and orbits shows no mass.
qx.q: Which new finding would indicate that the process has extended from the superior orbital fissure to the orbital apex?
opts: Reduced visual acuity with a relative afferent pupillary defect
Loss of sensation over the left forehead
Paralysis of the left lateral rectus muscle
Reduced tear production on the left side
Pain on eye movement, worse on looking upward
qx.why: The superior orbital fissure transmits the third, fourth and sixth nerves and V1 but not the optic nerve; once vision falls and an afferent defect appears, the optic canal region is involved and the picture becomes orbital apex syndrome. Forehead numbness, abduction failure and reduced lacrimation are all expected within the fissure itself, and eye-movement pain does not localise further. Here herpes zoster ophthalmicus is the likely cause, but vision must be monitored closely.

ddx.pt: Adds V2 involvement and Horner; may be bilateral via intercavernous connections
Painful idiopathic granulomatous inflammation responding to steroids
Orbital inflammation with pain, chemosis and possible apex involvement

name: Supranuclear gaze palsy (SGP)
formal: Gaze paralysis from lesions above the oculomotor nuclei, as in progressive supranuclear palsy, with preserved reflex movements on oculocephalic testing and impaired voluntary vertical gaze.
simple: Difficulty voluntarily moving the eyes, especially looking up or down, caused by problems in the brain rather than the eye muscles.
more: Loss of voluntary eye movements with preserved reflex movements due to supranuclear lesions, typical of progressive supranuclear palsy and midbrain disease, often affecting vertical gaze first.
th: การกลอกตาตามสั่งบกพร่องจากรอยโรคเหนือ nucleus ของเส้นประสาทกลอกตา แต่ reflex (doll's eye) ยังปกติ พบบ่อยใน progressive supranuclear palsy
tempoNote: Chronic in degenerative disease; acute in stroke or Wernicke
feat: Voluntary saccades and pursuit limited, but oculocephalic (doll's head) movements full
Vertical (especially downward) involvement in PSP; slow saccades precede range limitation
Bell's phenomenon preserved
Causes: PSP, Niemann–Pick type C, Whipple disease, midbrain stroke, Wernicke, Huntington disease
Square-wave jerks and impaired convergence often coexist
inv: Bedside saccade velocity, pursuit and doll's head testing
MRI: midbrain atrophy ('hummingbird' sign) in PSP; lesions in stroke
Targeted tests: filipin/oxysterols or NPC genes, Whipple PCR, thiamine

case.story: Two years of backward falls and difficulty looking down at his food and the stairs.
case.exam: Slow vertical saccades, restricted downgaze that becomes full with doll's head manoeuvre, axial rigidity, astonished facial expression, retropulsion.
case.tests: MRI: midbrain atrophy with preserved pons (hummingbird sign).
case.q: How do you prove the gaze palsy is supranuclear?
case.a: Doll's head (oculocephalic) testing drives the eyes beyond the voluntary range; the diagnosis is progressive supranuclear palsy.

read.where: Chapter 22 Neuro-Ophthalmology — Central Disorders of Eye Movements
14 Progressive Supranuclear Palsy and Corticobasal Degeneration
8 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System

det.patho: Supranuclear pathways from cortex, basal ganglia and superior colliculus to brainstem gaze centres (riMLF for vertical, PPRF for horizontal) generate voluntary eye movements. Lesions here leave the ocular motor nuclei intact, so vestibular reflexes, which reach the nuclei directly, still move the eyes. In PSP tau pathology in the midbrain affects the riMLF and interstitial nucleus of Cajal.
det.clinical: Patients report difficulty looking down, reading or walking downstairs, or eye strain. Examination shows slow saccades early, then restricted range. In PSP vertical involvement precedes horizontal; in Niemann–Pick C, vertical saccade palsy appears in childhood or young adulthood. Acute supranuclear palsies follow midbrain or thalamic stroke.
det.diagnosis: Demonstrate that reflex movements exceed voluntary range. Assess saccade velocity carefully; slowing may be the earliest sign. MRI and disease-specific tests identify the cause.
det.treatment: Treat the cause where possible (thiamine, antibiotics for Whipple, miglustat for NPC). For PSP, management is supportive: prisms, reading aids, fall prevention and speech and swallowing therapy.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause; degenerative forms progress.
pearls: Slow vertical saccades are an early clue to PSP.
Reflex movements overcoming voluntary limits = supranuclear.
Vertical supranuclear palsy in a young adult: test for Niemann–Pick C.
det.thd: Supranuclear gaze palsy คือการกลอกตาตามสั่งบกพร่องจากรอยโรคเหนือ nucleus ของเส้นประสาทกลอกตา แต่ doll's eye ยังกลอกได้เต็ม พบบ่อยใน PSP ที่มองลงไม่ได้และหกล้มไปด้านหลัง สาเหตุอื่นได้แก่ Niemann-Pick C, Whipple, stroke ที่ midbrain และ Wernicke ตรวจด้วยการทดสอบ saccade และ doll's head ร่วมกับ MRI รักษาตามสาเหตุ

name: Supratentorial gliomas
formal: Primary brain tumours of the cerebral hemispheres, including astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma and glioblastoma in adults, presenting with seizures, headache or focal deficits.
simple: Tumours that grow from supporting brain cells in the upper brain, often causing seizures, headaches or weakness.
th: เนื้องอกสมองปฐมภูมิของซีกสมองใหญ่ เช่น astrocytoma oligodendroglioma และ glioblastoma ในผู้ใหญ่ มาด้วยชัก ปวดศีรษะ หรืออ่อนแรงเฉพาะที่
tempoNote: Low-grade tumours evolve over years; glioblastoma over weeks to months
feat: Seizures, often the first sign, especially in IDH-mutant low-grade tumours and oligodendroglioma
Progressive focal deficits (weakness, language or visual field loss) and personality change in frontal tumours
Raised intracranial pressure symptoms: morning headache, vomiting, papilloedema
WHO CNS5 (2021) classification uses molecular markers: IDH, 1p/19q codeletion, CDKN2A/B, TERT, EGFR
Glioblastoma: older adults, ring-enhancing necrotic mass; low-grade: younger adults, non-enhancing T2/FLAIR lesion
inv: MRI with contrast, perfusion and spectroscopy where available
Biopsy or maximal safe resection for histology and molecular profiling (IDH, 1p/19q, MGMT promoter methylation)
EEG if seizure type unclear; neurocognitive baseline

case.story: Three episodes of a rising feeling then speech arrest lasting a minute over the past two months; no headache.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination.
case.tests: MRI: non-enhancing T2/FLAIR-bright left frontal mass with calcification; resection shows IDH-mutant 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendroglioma, CNS WHO grade 2.
case.q: What molecular result most influences prognosis here, and what therapy follows surgery?
case.a: IDH mutation with 1p/19q codeletion confers a better prognosis; depending on residual tumour and risk, observation, vorasidenib, or radiotherapy with PCV chemotherapy are considered.

read.where: Chapter 20 Neuro-Oncology — High-Grade and Low-Grade Gliomas

det.patho: Diffuse gliomas arise from glial progenitor cells. The 2021 WHO classification separates IDH-mutant astrocytoma, IDH-mutant 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendroglioma and IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, the most common and aggressive. IDH mutation leads to the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate and is associated with better outcomes. Gliomas infiltrate along white matter, so complete removal is impossible.
det.clinical: Presentation depends on location and growth rate. Seizures dominate in slow-growing cortical tumours; rapidly growing glioblastoma causes progressive deficits, cognitive change and raised pressure over weeks. Elderly patients may present with confusion mistaken for dementia or stroke. Tumour-related epilepsy can be drug resistant.
det.diagnosis: MRI suggests the diagnosis; definitive classification requires tissue with integrated histology and molecular testing. Enhancement, necrosis and high perfusion suggest high grade, but some low-grade tumours enhance and some high-grade do not. Consider mimics such as tumefactive demyelination, abscess, lymphoma and metastasis before surgery.
det.treatment: Maximal safe resection is the foundation. Glioblastoma: radiotherapy with concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide (benefit greatest with MGMT promoter methylation), with tumour-treating fields as an option. IDH-mutant grade 2 gliomas: vorasidenib (an IDH inhibitor) for residual non-enhancing disease after surgery, or radiotherapy plus PCV/temozolomide for higher-risk cases. Supportive care includes dexamethasone for oedema, non-enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs such as levetiracetam, and thromboprophylaxis.
det.prognosis: Median survival is about 15–20 months for glioblastoma; IDH-mutant oligodendroglioma may be measured in decades.
pearls: New-onset focal seizure in an adult deserves an MRI to look for a tumour.
Molecular markers (IDH, 1p/19q) now define the tumour type more than histology alone.
Avoid enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs because of chemotherapy interactions.
det.thd: Supratentorial glioma เป็นเนื้องอกสมองปฐมภูมิในซีกสมองใหญ่ ผู้ใหญ่ที่พบได้แก่ astrocytoma oligodendroglioma และ glioblastoma มักมาด้วยชัก ปวดศีรษะ หรืออ่อนแรงเฉพาะที่ MRI ช่วยวินิจฉัย ต้องยืนยันด้วยชิ้นเนื้อและตรวจ IDH 1p/19q MGMT รักษาด้วยผ่าตัดให้ได้มากที่สุดอย่างปลอดภัย ตามด้วยฉายแสงและเคมีบำบัด หรือยา vorasidenib ในเนื้องอก IDH-mutant ระยะต้น

name: Surgical brachial plexopathies
formal: Iatrogenic injury to the brachial plexus from positioning, traction, retraction, sternotomy or regional anaesthesia, producing a patchy arm weakness and sensory deficit in the perioperative period.
simple: Damage to the nerve bundle supplying the arm that happens during or after an operation, causing arm weakness or numbness.
more: EMG and MRI or ultrasound localise the lesion. Most are neurapraxic and recover within weeks to months with physiotherapy; severe lesions may need nerve repair or transfer.
th: การบาดเจ็บของ brachial plexus จากการผ่าตัด เช่น ท่าจัด การดึง retractor การผ่าตัดเปิดกระดูกอก หรือการฉีดยาชาบริเวณ plexus
tempoNote: Deficit present on waking or within the first few days after surgery
feat: Patchy arm weakness and numbness in a plexus distribution after an operation
Lower trunk after sternotomy; upper trunk after shoulder surgery, head rotation or arm abduction beyond 90°
Interscalene block may add phrenic palsy or rarely direct nerve injury
Delayed severe pain suggests inflammatory post-surgical neuritis
Most injuries are neurapraxic
inv: Detailed motor and sensory mapping including medial antebrachial cutaneous territory
EMG/NCS after about 3 weeks

case.who: 38-year-old woman after arthroscopic shoulder surgery in the beach-chair position in Pattaya
case.story: After an interscalene block and surgery she cannot lift the right arm or bend the elbow; numb lateral arm.
case.exam: Weak deltoid, supra- and infraspinatus, biceps; reduced biceps jerk; numb lateral arm and forearm; mild hoarseness absent.
case.tests: EMG at 4 weeks: reduced recruitment in C5–6 muscles, mild denervation, normal paraspinals; MRI plexus no haematoma.
case.q: Where is the lesion and what is the expected course?
case.a: Upper trunk brachial plexopathy (neurapraxia from positioning or block); usually recovers over weeks to months with physiotherapy.

det.patho: Stretch from arm abduction, head turning or sternal retraction, direct compression and needle or local anaesthetic injury during regional block can damage the brachial plexus. Most injuries cause focal demyelination; severe stretch causes axonal loss. Inflammatory neuritis triggered by surgery is a distinct immune process.
det.clinical: The pattern depends on mechanism: upper trunk after shoulder procedures and head tilt, lower trunk after median sternotomy, and variable patterns after regional blocks. Pain may be minimal in pure neurapraxia.
det.diagnosis: Localise clinically, then confirm with EMG and NCS at three weeks; sensory nerve action potentials help separate plexus from root lesions. Imaging excludes haematoma or pseudoaneurysm after vascular access and identifies inflammatory change.
det.treatment: Physiotherapy, range-of-motion exercises and splinting to prevent contractures; analgesia for neuropathic pain. Steroids may help inflammatory forms. Surgical exploration is considered for no recovery at 3–6 months or known transection.
det.prognosis: Most recover within months; axonal injuries take longer and may be incomplete.
pearls: Medial antebrachial cutaneous loss separates lower trunk from ulnar nerve.
Sensory nerve action potentials fall in plexus but not root lesions.
Post-surgical pain followed by weakness suggests inflammatory neuritis rather than mechanical injury.

name: Susac’s syndrome
formal: Immune-mediated microangiopathy of brain, retina and cochlea causing encephalopathy, branch retinal artery occlusions and low-frequency hearing loss; callosal snowball lesions on MRI.
simple: A rare immune disease harming tiny vessels in the brain, eyes and ears, causing confusion, vision loss and deafness.
th: endotheliopathy จากภูมิคุ้มกันของหลอดเลือดเล็ก ทำให้ triad สมอง (encephalopathy, รอยโรคกลาง corpus callosum แบบ snowball) + branch retinal artery occlusion + หูดับความถี่ต่ำ พบในหญิงอายุ 20–40
tempoNote: Encephalopathy evolves over weeks; may run a monocyclic, polycyclic or chronic-continuous course over 1–5 years
feat: Headache, confusion, memory loss and behavioural change; sometimes ataxia or dysarthria
Branch retinal artery occlusions causing scotomas, often unnoticed by the patient
Sensorineural hearing loss at low-to-mid frequencies, tinnitus and vertigo
The full triad is present at onset in only a minority
inv: MRI: central corpus callosum 'snowball' lesions and later 'holes', plus internal capsule 'string of pearls' and leptomeningeal enhancement
Fluorescein angiography: branch occlusions and arterial wall hyperfluorescence (Gass plaques)
Pure-tone audiometry: low-frequency loss
CSF: high protein, few cells; oligoclonal bands usually absent

case.story: Four weeks of severe headache and increasing forgetfulness; she now repeats questions and her colleagues report strange behaviour. She mentions ringing in the left ear and a grey patch in her vision.
case.exam: Disoriented, mild gait ataxia; fundoscopy shows a whitish arteriolar segment in the right eye.
case.tests: MRI: multiple round lesions at the centre of the corpus callosum; audiogram: left low-frequency hearing loss; CSF protein 140 mg/dL, 3 cells, no OCB.
case.q: Name the syndrome and the eye test that best supports it.
case.a: Susac’s syndrome; fluorescein angiography showing branch retinal artery occlusion and segmental wall leakage.

det.patho: An immune-mediated (likely CD8 T-cell driven) injury to the endothelium of precapillary arterioles in the brain, retina and cochlea causes microinfarcts. Anti-endothelial antibodies are found in some patients but are not specific. Women aged 20–40 are mainly affected.
det.clinical: Brain involvement produces a subacute encephalopathy with headache, cognitive and psychiatric change, and sometimes long-tract or cerebellar signs. Retinal occlusions cause patchy field defects and may be silent; hearing loss is often bilateral and permanent. Because the triad seldom appears together at first, many patients are initially labelled as MS, ADEM or a primary psychiatric illness.
det.diagnosis: The 2016 diagnostic criteria require evidence of involvement of brain (typical MRI), retina (BRAO or arterial wall hyperfluorescence on fluorescein angiography) and inner ear (audiometry); incomplete forms are labelled probable or possible. Central callosal lesions and spokes are highly characteristic. Every patient with suspected Susac’s needs fluorescein angiography and audiometry even without symptoms. CSF often shows raised protein without oligoclonal bands.
det.treatment: Early and sustained immunosuppression prevents irreversible deficits: intravenous methylprednisolone followed by oral steroids, combined with IVIG, and add mycophenolate, rituximab or cyclophosphamide in severe or relapsing disease. Treatment usually continues for at least 2 years with slow tapering guided by MRI, fluorescein angiography and audiometry. Aspirin is often added. MS disease-modifying drugs are ineffective.
det.prognosis: The disease is often self-limiting after a few years, but hearing loss, visual field defects and cognitive deficits can persist if treatment is delayed.
pearls: Corpus callosum lesions in the middle (not the underside) + hearing loss = look at the retina.
Order fluorescein angiography even when vision seems normal.
Interferons and natalizumab are not for Susac’s.
det.thd: Susac’s syndrome เป็นโรคภูมิคุ้มกันทำลายผนังหลอดเลือดแดงขนาดเล็กในสมอง จอตา และหูชั้นใน พบในหญิงวัยหนุ่มสาว ผู้ป่วยมีอาการสับสน ความจำเสีย ปวดศีรษะ ตามัวเป็นบางส่วนจาก branch retinal artery occlusion และหูดับความถี่ต่ำ MRI พบรอยโรคกลม ๆ ตรงกลาง corpus callosum วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI, fluorescein angiography และ audiogram รักษาด้วย steroid ร่วมกับ IVIG และยากดภูมิ

qx.stem: A 30-year-old woman from Udon Thani, referred as possible ADEM, has six weeks of headache, forgetfulness and odd behaviour, plus ringing and muffled hearing in the left ear and a grey patch in her right visual field. Audiometry shows low-frequency sensorineural loss. MRI shows many small round T2 lesions in the centre of the corpus callosum and a few in the internal capsule, some enhancing.
qx.q: Which investigation is most useful next?
opts: CSF oligoclonal bands
Retinal fluorescein angiography
Serum MOG-IgG
Spinal MRI for silent cord lesions
Brain biopsy of an enhancing lesion
qx.why: Encephalopathy, low-frequency hearing loss and branch retinal artery occlusion form the Susac triad; central callosal 'snowball' lesions are characteristic. Fluorescein angiography shows branch retinal artery occlusions and segmental arterial wall hyperfluorescence, even when the patient does not notice visual loss, and confirms the diagnosis. MS and ADEM are the usual misdiagnoses; bands, MOG-IgG and cord imaging do not establish Susac, and biopsy is rarely needed.

name: Sydenham’s chorea
formal: Post-streptococcal autoimmune chorea in childhood, with rapid irregular movements, hypotonia, emotional lability and association with rheumatic fever; usually self-limiting over months.
simple: Jerky involuntary movements in children after a strep throat infection, linked to rheumatic fever.
more: Sydenham chorea, post-streptococcal autoimmune basal ganglia disease in children with chorea, hypotonia, emotional lability; features of rheumatic fever.
th: chorea ในเด็กหลังติดเชื้อ streptococcus กลุ่ม A เป็นส่วนหนึ่งของไข้รูมาติก มักมีอารมณ์แปรปรวน ต้องให้ penicillin ป้องกันระยะยาว
tempoNote: Begins weeks to months after a streptococcal throat infection, builds over days to weeks, usually remits within 6 months but can recur
feat: Chorea in a child aged 5–15, often worse on one side (hemichorea in some)
Motor impersistence: milkmaid grip and darting tongue
Hypotonia; clumsiness and dysarthria; occasionally severe weakness (chorea paralytica)
Emotional lability, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, anxiety or attention problems
May accompany or follow carditis, arthritis or other rheumatic fever signs
inv: ASO and anti-DNase B titres (may already be falling); throat culture
Echocardiography for rheumatic carditis — essential
ESR/CRP; exclude SLE/antiphospholipid, thyroid disease, drugs, pregnancy in teenagers
MRI usually normal; needed only if atypical

case.story: Two months after a sore throat she drops things, cannot sit still and her handwriting is untidy; she cries easily. Mother thought she was being naughty.
case.exam: Continuous flowing movements of the face and limbs, worse on the right; milkmaid grip, darting tongue, mild hypotonia; soft apical pansystolic murmur.
case.tests: ASO 640 IU/mL, anti-DNase B high; echo: mild mitral regurgitation; ANA negative.
case.q: Besides treating the chorea, what long-term step is mandatory?
case.a: Sydenham chorea with rheumatic carditis — secondary prophylaxis with benzathine penicillin every 3–4 weeks for many years (into adulthood given carditis).

read.where: Chapter 21 - Abnormal Movements in Neurological Autoimmune Disorders

det.patho: Antibodies raised against group A streptococcal antigens cross-react with basal ganglia neurons (molecular mimicry), altering dopaminergic signalling. It is a major criterion of acute rheumatic fever and remains common in low- and middle-income settings. Girls are affected more than boys, especially after puberty.
det.clinical: Chorea appears after a latent period of 1–6 months, often when other rheumatic signs have faded. Neuropsychiatric symptoms (emotional lability, OCD features, ADHD-like behaviour) can precede or outlast the movements. Most episodes last weeks to months; recurrences occur in a sizeable minority, sometimes triggered by pregnancy (chorea gravidarum) or oral contraceptives.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical within the Jones criteria; chorea alone is enough for rheumatic fever once other causes are excluded, and streptococcal serology is not mandatory because of the long latency. Always perform echocardiography because subclinical carditis is common. Exclude SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome, hyperthyroidism, drugs, Wilson disease and Huntington disease in atypical cases.
det.treatment: Give a course of penicillin to eradicate streptococci and start long-term secondary prophylaxis with benzathine penicillin. Mild chorea may need no symptomatic drugs; for disabling chorea use valproate, carbamazepine or a low-dose dopamine blocker (risperidone or haloperidol). Steroids (prednisolone) or IVIG are used for severe or refractory chorea. Address school and psychological needs.
det.prognosis: Usually resolves within 6–12 months, but recurrence and persistent neuropsychiatric symptoms are common; prognosis is mostly determined by heart involvement.
pearls: Chorea in a child: look for the heart — always order an echocardiogram.
Milkmaid grip and darting tongue show motor impersistence.
Secondary penicillin prophylaxis is as important as treating the movements.
det.thd: Sydenham chorea เป็น chorea ในเด็กหลังติดเชื้อ streptococcus กลุ่ม A ราว 1–6 เดือน เกิดจากภูมิคุ้มกันที่ทำปฏิกิริยาข้ามกับ basal ganglia เป็นส่วนหนึ่งของไข้รูมาติก ผู้ป่วยมีการเคลื่อนไหวกระตุกไหลไปมา milkmaid grip อารมณ์แปรปรวน ต้องทำ echo ทุกราย ให้ penicillin ฆ่าเชื้อและป้องกันระยะยาว รักษาอาการด้วย valproate หรือยาต้านโดปามีน รายรุนแรงให้ steroid

name: Symptomatic carotid stenosis
formal: Carotid stenosis causing ipsilateral transient ischaemic attack, amaurosis fugax or stroke within recent months, for which endarterectomy or stenting is considered depending on degree of stenosis.
simple: Narrowing of the neck artery that has already caused a stroke or warning episode, so surgery or stenting may be needed.
th: หลอดเลือดแดง internal carotid ตีบจาก atherosclerosis ซึ่งทำให้เกิด TIA, amaurosis fugax หรือ stroke ในฝั่งเดียวกันภายใน 6 เดือน ความเสี่ยงเกิดซ้ำสูงมากในช่วง 2 สัปดาห์แรก ควรทำ endarterectomy/stenting เร็ว
tempoNote: TIAs or minor stroke in the carotid territory within the past 6 months; recurrence risk is front-loaded into the first days to weeks
feat: Transient monocular blindness (amaurosis fugax) on the side of the stenosis
Contralateral face/arm/leg weakness or numbness, aphasia (dominant side) or neglect
Repeated stereotyped hemispheric TIAs, sometimes limb-shaking TIAs from low flow
Cervical bruit (unreliable — absent with near-occlusion, present with trivial disease)
Retinal cholesterol emboli (Hollenhorst plaques) on fundoscopy
inv: Carotid duplex as first screen; confirm severity with CTA or contrast MRA (NASCET method)
MRI DWI: cortical or border-zone infarcts in the ipsilateral territory
ECG and rhythm monitoring to exclude coexisting AF
Assess surgical fitness: cardiac status, renal function, neck anatomy

case.who: 68-year-old retired policeman from Nakhon Ratchasima, smoker
case.story: Twice in four days a 'grey curtain' came down over his right eye for two minutes; yesterday his left hand went weak and clumsy for 20 minutes.
case.exam: Neurologically normal now; soft bruit over the right carotid bifurcation; BP 158/90.
case.tests: MRI: two tiny DWI-bright cortical dots in the right MCA territory. CTA: 80% right ICA origin stenosis (NASCET) with ulcerated plaque; ECG sinus rhythm.
case.q: What is the definitive treatment and how quickly should it be done?
case.a: Right carotid endarterectomy (or stenting if surgery is unsuitable) ideally within 2 weeks, plus antiplatelet therapy, high-intensity statin and BP control.

det.patho: Atheroma forms at the carotid bifurcation and proximal ICA where flow separation and low shear stress occur. Strokes usually result from artery-to-artery embolism of thrombus or plaque debris from an unstable, ulcerated or haemorrhagic plaque, and less often from low flow beyond a tight stenosis with poor collaterals. Risk factors are age, male sex, smoking, hypertension, diabetes and dyslipidaemia; extracranial carotid disease is less frequent in East and South-East Asians than intracranial atherosclerosis, but still important.
det.clinical: A stenosis is called symptomatic when ipsilateral retinal or hemispheric TIA or non-disabling stroke occurred within the preceding 6 months. Clinical features include amaurosis fugax, cortical hand weakness, aphasia or neglect. Limb-shaking TIAs — brief jerky movements of a contralateral limb on standing — signal haemodynamic compromise. Recurrence risk is highest in the first 48 h to 2 weeks (perhaps 10–20% without treatment), so these patients need fast-track assessment.
det.diagnosis: Duplex ultrasound is the usual first test; a second modality (CTA or contrast-enhanced MRA) should confirm the degree before intervention. Measure stenosis by NASCET (narrowest lumen compared with normal distal ICA). Near-occlusion with distal collapse behaves differently and gains little from surgery. Plaque features such as intraplaque haemorrhage on MRI or microembolic signals on transcranial Doppler identify higher risk. Always look for alternative sources (AF, small vessel disease) because a coexisting stenosis may be incidental.
det.treatment: For 70–99% symptomatic stenosis, carotid endarterectomy markedly reduces stroke risk and should be performed within 2 weeks of the event if the surgical complication rate is low; for 50–69% the benefit is smaller and greatest in men, older patients and hemispheric events. Below 50%, intervention is harmful. Carotid stenting is an alternative, with outcomes closer to surgery in patients under about 70, those with hostile necks (radiation, restenosis) or high surgical risk. All patients need antiplatelet therapy (short dual therapy around the event), high-intensity statin with LDL target < 70 mg/dL (or lower), BP control and smoking cessation.
det.prognosis: With timely revascularisation and medical therapy, the subsequent annual stroke risk falls to roughly that of asymptomatic disease; delay forfeits much of the benefit.
pearls: The benefit of endarterectomy decays fast — aim for surgery within 14 days of the index event.
Use NASCET measurement; 70–99% gains most, near-occlusion and < 50% do not benefit.
Limb-shaking TIA is a haemodynamic warning of a critical carotid stenosis, not a seizure.

name: Symptomatic choreic syndromes
formal: Chorea due to an underlying cause such as drugs, stroke, autoimmune disease or metabolic disorders rather than a primary hereditary chorea.
simple: Jerky involuntary movements caused by another illness, drug or brain injury rather than inherited disease.
th: chorea ที่มีสาเหตุชัดเจน เช่น stroke น้ำตาลในเลือดสูงแบบ non-ketotic ยา autoimmune ไทรอยด์เป็นพิษ หรือการตั้งครรภ์ แทนที่จะเป็นโรคพันธุกรรม
tempoNote: Acute or subacute onset over days to weeks; often improves when the cause is corrected
feat: Brief, irregular, flowing involuntary movements, often unilateral (hemichorea) with a structural or metabolic cause
Commonest adult causes: stroke, non-ketotic hyperglycaemia (older Asian women), drugs (levodopa, stimulants, oral contraceptives)
Autoimmune: Sydenham's chorea, SLE/antiphospholipid syndrome, anti-IgLON5 and other autoimmune encephalitis
Others: thyrotoxicosis, pregnancy (chorea gravidarum), polycythaemia vera, HIV/toxoplasmosis
inv: Glucose and HbA1c, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function, FBC (polycythaemia)
MRI: striatal infarct or haemorrhage; T1 putaminal hyperintensity in hyperglycaemic chorea
ANA, antiphospholipid antibodies, ASO/anti-DNase B, pregnancy test, drug review; HIV
If no cause: HTT and other genetic chorea testing

case.story: One week of continuous flinging movements of her left arm and leg; recently stopped her diabetes tablets.
case.exam: Left hemichorea–hemiballism, otherwise alert with no weakness.
case.tests: Glucose 480 mg/dL, no ketones, HbA1c 13%; CT: right putaminal hyperdensity without mass effect; MRI T1 bright putamen.
case.q: What is the cause and treatment?
case.a: Non-ketotic hyperglycaemic hemichorea; correct glucose and use a dopamine-blocking drug (e.g. haloperidol) or tetrabenazine short-term if movements persist.

det.patho: Chorea arises when the indirect basal ganglia pathway is disrupted, releasing thalamocortical motor drive — most often by lesions of the striatum or subthalamic nucleus, excess dopaminergic activity, or antibodies and metabolic disturbances affecting striatal neurons. In hyperglycaemic chorea, vascular and metabolic injury to the putamen (possibly via GABA depletion and petechial change) underlies the characteristic T1 hyperintensity. Autoimmune forms involve antibodies cross-reacting with basal ganglia antigens.
det.clinical: Acute or subacute onset, asymmetry and older age favour a symptomatic cause, whereas slow generalised chorea with a family history suggests a hereditary disease. Hemiballism is the high-amplitude, proximal end of the same spectrum and usually reflects contralateral subthalamic or striatal lesions. Associated features (diabetes, fever, rash, pregnancy, drug exposure, thyroid signs) guide the search. Movements disappear in sleep and may cause exhaustion and injury.
det.diagnosis: Start with glucose, electrolytes, thyroid, calcium, blood count and a medication review, then neuroimaging. Autoimmune serology (ANA, antiphospholipid antibodies, streptococcal titres, neuronal antibodies) suits younger or subacute cases. CSF and HIV testing are indicated when infection is possible. Genetic testing is reserved for progressive or familial cases or when no acquired cause is found.
det.treatment: Correct the underlying cause first: control glucose, stop the culprit drug, treat thyrotoxicosis or autoimmune disease. Symptomatic options include VMAT2 inhibitors (tetrabenazine, deutetrabenazine), antipsychotics (haloperidol, risperidone, olanzapine) and, for Sydenham's, valproate or immunotherapy in severe cases. Many vascular and metabolic cases settle within weeks to months. Refractory post-stroke hemiballism rarely requires surgery.
det.prognosis: Generally good once the trigger is corrected; post-stroke and hyperglycaemic chorea usually fade, although some patients are left with mild persistent movements.
pearls: Older Asian woman, uncontrolled diabetes, hemichorea, bright putamen on T1 = hyperglycaemic chorea.
Acute unilateral chorea is vascular until proven otherwise.
Check pregnancy, contraceptives and thyroid in a young woman with new chorea.

name: Symptomatic generalized myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus affecting the body widely, resulting from diffuse brain disorder such as metabolic, toxic, post-hypoxic or neurodegenerative encephalopathy.
simple: Widespread sudden muscle jerks caused by a brain problem such as poisoning, low oxygen or metabolic disease.
th: myoclonus ทั่วตัวที่เป็นผลจากภาวะสมองทำงานผิดปกติแบบกระจาย เช่น ไตวาย ตับวาย ยา ขาดออกซิเจน หรือโรคสมองเสื่อม
tempoNote: Usually appears with the underlying encephalopathy and resolves with correction; chronic in degenerative causes
feat: Multifocal or generalized jerks at rest and with action, often with asterixis
Accompanied by confusion, drowsiness or delirium
Common triggers: uraemia, liver failure, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, sepsis
Drug causes: opioids, gabapentinoids, cefepime, lithium, SSRIs, tramadol
Post-hypoxic and prion disease are important non-metabolic causes

Drug levels and medication review, including renal dose adjustment

case.who: 74-year-old man from Chachoengsao with CKD stage 5 not yet on dialysis
case.story: Admitted with pneumonia, started on cefepime; by day 3 is confused with jerks of arms, face and legs.
case.exam: Drowsy, multifocal myoclonus at rest and with posture, bilateral asterixis, no focal weakness.
case.tests: Urea 180 mg/dL, creatinine 9.2 mg/dL; EEG shows triphasic-like waves without electrographic seizures.
case.q: What is causing the jerks and what is the plan?
case.a: Symptomatic generalized myoclonus from cefepime neurotoxicity on uraemia; stop or switch cefepime and arrange dialysis.

det.patho: Diffuse disturbance of neuronal excitability, from toxins, electrolyte imbalance or energy failure, lowers the threshold for cortical and brainstem discharges. Reduced drug clearance in renal or hepatic failure is a frequent contributor. Several generators may be active at once, giving multifocal jerks.
det.clinical: The jerks are usually irregular and multifocal, affecting face, trunk and limbs, and often coexist with negative myoclonus (asterixis). Altered consciousness is the rule. Severity tracks the metabolic state. In prion disease, myoclonus is accompanied by rapidly progressive dementia and is often startle-sensitive.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by laboratory tests showing the cause. A careful medication review, with attention to renally cleared drugs, frequently reveals the culprit. EEG excludes non-convulsive status and may show diffuse slowing or triphasic waves. Imaging is needed when there are focal signs or no metabolic explanation.
det.treatment: Correct the underlying disorder and remove offending drugs; dialysis can clear some agents. Symptomatic treatment with clonazepam or levetiracetam (renally adjusted) may help when jerks are distressing. Avoid escalating sedatives that may worsen encephalopathy.
det.prognosis: Usually reversible when the metabolic or drug cause is corrected; outcome is poor when due to prion disease or severe hypoxic injury.
pearls: New myoclonus in a renal patient: check the drug chart first (cefepime, gabapentin, opioids).
Asterixis plus multifocal myoclonus suggests a metabolic encephalopathy.
Get an EEG if consciousness is impaired to exclude non-convulsive status.

name: Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage (sICH)
formal: Haemorrhagic transformation of ischaemic infarct or thrombolysis-related bleed with neurological worsening, defined by haematoma and clinical deterioration within about 24-36 hours of treatment.
simple: A bleed in the brain after a stroke or clot-busting treatment that makes symptoms worse.
th: เลือดออกในสมองหลังให้ยาละลายลิ่มเลือดหรือหลังลากลิ่มเลือดที่ทำให้อาการแย่ลงอย่างชัดเจน เป็นภาวะแทรกซ้อนสำคัญที่สุดของการรักษา reperfusion
tempoNote: Usually within 24–36 hours of thrombolysis or thrombectomy; most occur in the first 12 hours
feat: Neurological worsening (e.g. NIHSS rise ≥ 4) with new blood on imaging after reperfusion therapy
Warning signs during or after infusion: headache, vomiting, sudden BP surge, falling consciousness
Rate about 2–7% after IV thrombolysis depending on definition (SITS-MOST, ECASS, NINDS)
Risk factors: large infarct core, high glucose, high BP, older age, delayed reperfusion, antithrombotics
inv: Stop the infusion and do urgent non-contrast CT
Fibrinogen, PT/INR, aPTT, platelets, cross-match
Classify by Heidelberg bleeding classification (HI1–2, PH1–2) and clinical worsening

case.story: Given alteplase for a right MCA stroke; 4 hours later he complains of severe headache, vomits and becomes drowsy.
case.exam: GCS falls from 15 to 10, NIHSS from 12 to 20, BP 205/110 mmHg.
case.tests: CT: parenchymal haematoma occupying more than 30% of the infarct with mass effect (PH2); fibrinogen 120 mg/dL.
case.q: What are the immediate steps?
case.a: Symptomatic ICH after thrombolysis: stop any infusion, give cryoprecipitate (and consider tranexamic acid), lower BP, involve neurosurgery and neurocritical care.

read.where: Ch. 13 Specific treatment of acute ischemic stroke
Chapter 8 Stroke and Cerebrovascular Diseases — Management of Acute Intracerebral Haemorrhage

det.patho: Ischaemia damages the blood–brain barrier and microvessels; reperfusion and fibrinolytic drugs then allow blood to leak into the infarct. Larger cores, prolonged ischaemia, hyperglycaemia and hypertension increase endothelial injury and haemorrhage risk. Alteplase also lowers fibrinogen, which promotes ongoing bleeding. Microbleed burden and amyloid angiopathy contribute in older patients.
det.clinical: Most cases present within the first day with headache, vomiting, BP spike or a sudden fall in consciousness or new focal deficit. Petechial haemorrhagic infarction (HI) is common and usually harmless; dense parenchymal haematoma (PH2) carries most of the excess mortality. Definitions vary between trials, so quoted rates differ. Asymptomatic haemorrhage on routine 24-hour imaging does not count as sICH.
det.diagnosis: Any deterioration after reperfusion therapy requires stopping the infusion and urgent CT. Correlate imaging type (HI1, HI2, PH1, PH2, remote PH) with clinical worsening using SITS-MOST, ECASS III or Heidelberg definitions. Check fibrinogen and coagulation to guide reversal.
det.treatment: Stop alteplase or tenecteplase, give cryoprecipitate to restore fibrinogen (target above about 150–200 mg/dL), and consider tranexamic acid; platelet transfusion has a role only in specific circumstances. Control BP (systolic below about 140–160 mmHg), manage ICP, and consult neurosurgery for evacuation in selected cases. Prevention relies on careful patient selection, strict BP control before and after treatment (< 180/105 mmHg) and glucose management.
det.prognosis: Mortality is about 50% for PH2-type sICH; survivors often have greater disability.
pearls: Headache or vomiting during alteplase = stop infusion, scan.
Cryoprecipitate first — alteplase depletes fibrinogen.
Keep BP < 180/105 for 24 hours after thrombolysis.
det.thd: sICH คือเลือดออกในสมองหลังให้ยาละลายลิ่มเลือดหรือลากลิ่มเลือดที่ทำให้อาการแย่ลง พบประมาณร้อยละ 2–7 มักเกิดใน 24–36 ชั่วโมงแรก มีอาการปวดศีรษะ อาเจียน ความดันพุ่ง หรือซึมลง ต้องหยุดยาทันที ทำ CT ตรวจ fibrinogen ให้ cryoprecipitate และพิจารณา tranexamic acid ควบคุมความดัน และปรึกษาศัลยแพทย์ระบบประสาท

name: Symptomatic myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus caused by an identifiable underlying disorder such as metabolic, post-anoxic, toxic or structural disease rather than essential or epileptic.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks caused by another illness such as organ failure, brain injury or medication.
th: อาการกระตุกสั้น ๆ แบบ myoclonus ที่เกิดจากโรคหรือภาวะที่ระบุได้ เช่น ภาวะเมตาบอลิก ยา สมองขาดออกซิเจน หรือรอยโรคในสมอง
tempoNote: Tempo follows the cause: acute with toxins or metabolic failure, chronic in degenerative disease
feat: Most common category of myoclonus seen in hospital practice
Often multifocal, action-provoked and stimulus-sensitive, together with encephalopathy in metabolic cases
Causes: renal or liver failure, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, drugs (opioids, gabapentinoids, cefepime, lithium, SSRIs), post-hypoxic injury, CJD, neurodegeneration
Negative myoclonus (asterixis) commonly accompanies metabolic forms
Improves when the cause is reversed in metabolic and drug-related cases
inv: Electrolytes, glucose, renal and liver function, ammonia, calcium, magnesium, drug levels and medication review
EEG to look for epileptic or periodic patterns; EMG/EEG back-averaging to localise cortical versus subcortical origin
MRI brain or spine, and CSF/RT-QuIC if CJD suspected

case.story: Admitted with cellulitis and given cefepime; two days later she is confused with frequent jerks of the arms and face.
case.exam: Drowsy, multifocal myoclonus worse with action, bilateral asterixis.
case.tests: EEG shows generalised periodic discharges with triphasic morphology; electrolytes stable.
case.q: What is the likely cause and management?
case.a: Symptomatic myoclonus from cefepime neurotoxicity in renal failure; stop or switch the antibiotic and arrange extra dialysis, with a benzodiazepine if needed.

det.patho: Myoclonus results from sudden bursts of neuronal discharge in cortex, brainstem or spinal cord. Metabolic and toxic derangements increase cortical excitability and disrupt inhibitory circuits; hypoxic injury damages cortical and cerebellar inhibitory neurons; degenerative diseases destroy them progressively. The level of origin can be inferred from neurophysiology.
det.clinical: Symptomatic myoclonus may be focal, segmental, multifocal or generalised. In metabolic and drug-induced states it usually accompanies confusion and asterixis. Post-hypoxic myoclonus appears acutely in coma (often grave prognosis) or later as Lance-Adams action myoclonus. In neurodegenerative disease (CJD, Alzheimer's, Lewy body dementia, corticobasal syndrome) it accompanies cognitive or motor decline.
det.diagnosis: First confirm it is myoclonus, then search for the cause with metabolic screen, drug review, imaging and EEG. Neurophysiology (EEG-EMG polygraphy, back-averaging) helps classify cortical, subcortical and spinal forms, guiding treatment. Persistent unexplained myoclonus with rapid cognitive decline should prompt CJD testing.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: correct metabolic disturbance, withdraw the offending drug, dialysis where relevant. Symptomatic drugs are chosen by origin: cortical myoclonus responds to levetiracetam, valproate, piracetam and clonazepam; subcortical and spinal forms to clonazepam. Avoid drugs that worsen myoclonus such as carbamazepine and phenytoin in some forms.
det.prognosis: Metabolic and drug-related myoclonus usually resolves; outcome in other forms depends on the underlying disease.
pearls: Always review the drug chart: opioids, gabapentinoids, cefepime and lithium are frequent culprits.
Asterixis plus myoclonus in a confused patient points to metabolic encephalopathy.
Early generalised myoclonus after cardiac arrest differs from later Lance-Adams syndrome in prognosis.
det.thd: Symptomatic myoclonus คืออาการกระตุกสั้น ๆ จากสาเหตุที่ระบุได้ เช่น ไตหรือตับวาย เกลือแร่ผิดปกติ ยาบางชนิด สมองขาดออกซิเจน หรือโรคสมองเสื่อม มักมาพร้อมความสับสนและ asterixis ต้องทบทวนยาและตรวจเลือด EEG และ MRI รักษาที่สาเหตุเป็นหลัก หากจำเป็นใช้ levetiracetam valproate หรือ clonazepam

name: Symptomatic palatal tremor
formal: Rhythmic palatal movements due to a lesion in the Guillain-Mollaret triangle, often with inferior olive hypertrophy after brainstem stroke, with ear clicking and sometimes ocular oscillation.
simple: Rhythmic movements of the soft palate at the back of the mouth after brainstem damage, sometimes causing ear clicking.
th: การเคลื่อนไหวเป็นจังหวะของเพดานอ่อนหลังรอยโรคใน Guillain–Mollaret triangle เช่น stroke ที่ก้านสมอง มี inferior olive โตจากการเสื่อมแบบ hypertrophic
tempoNote: Appears weeks to months (often 3–12 months) after a brainstem or cerebellar lesion and usually persists
feat: Rhythmic 1–3 Hz contraction of levator veli palatini, persisting in sleep
Usually no ear click (unlike essential palatal tremor, which involves tensor veli palatini)
Often pendular vertical or torsional nystagmus (oculopalatal tremor) causing oscillopsia
Accompanied by signs of the original lesion: ataxia, cranial nerve palsies, hemiparesis
inv: MRI: T2-bright, enlarged inferior olivary nucleus (hypertrophic olivary degeneration) plus the causative lesion
Look for causes: pontine haemorrhage, infarct, demyelination, trauma, tumour
If no lesion and progressive ataxia: consider Alexander disease (GFAP) or PAPT

case.story: Eight months after a right pontine haemorrhage he notices the world bouncing up and down, worse when reading.
case.exam: Rhythmic 2 Hz palatal elevation that continues when he is distracted, synchronous vertical pendular nystagmus, residual left hemiparesis and right limb ataxia.
case.tests: MRI: old right dorsal pontine haemosiderin and an enlarged T2-bright right inferior olive.
case.q: Explain the anatomy.
case.a: Symptomatic (oculo)palatal tremor from interruption of the dentato-rubro-olivary pathway (central tegmental tract) causing hypertrophic olivary degeneration.

read.where: 18 - Myoclonus: Phenomenology, etiology, physiology, and treatment

det.patho: The Guillain–Mollaret triangle links the dentate nucleus, the contralateral red nucleus and the inferior olive via the superior cerebellar peduncle, central tegmental tract and inferior cerebellar peduncle. A lesion interrupting input to the olive (usually the central tegmental tract or dentate) causes trans-synaptic degeneration in which olivary neurons enlarge, vacuolate and become electrically coupled, generating rhythmic output. The olive is hypertrophic before later atrophy.
det.clinical: The palate moves rhythmically and continuously, including during sleep; many patients are unaware of it. The disabling feature is often the associated pendular nystagmus, giving oscillopsia. Ear clicks are uncommon because the tensor muscle is usually spared. Rhythmic movements can spread to face, larynx, diaphragm or limbs.
det.diagnosis: Examine the palate with the mouth open at rest and look for synchronous eye oscillations. MRI shows olivary T2 hyperintensity and enlargement from a few weeks to months after the injury, along with the causal lesion. Distinguish from essential palatal tremor, which lacks a lesion and often has ear clicks, and from functional palatal movements.
det.treatment: Treatment is symptomatic and often unsatisfying. For oscillopsia, gabapentin or memantine can reduce nystagmus. For troublesome ear clicks, botulinum toxin into the tensor veli palatini can help. Clonazepam, valproate or anticholinergics have been tried with limited benefit.
det.prognosis: Usually lifelong; the palatal movement rarely causes disability but the nystagmus may.
pearls: Palatal tremor that persists in sleep with an olive bright on T2 = symptomatic.
Look at the eyes — oculopalatal tremor causes oscillopsia.
Dentate, red nucleus, olive: the Guillain–Mollaret triangle.
det.thd: Symptomatic palatal tremor เกิดหลังรอยโรคใน Guillain–Mollaret triangle เช่น pontine haemorrhage ทำให้ inferior olive โตจาก hypertrophic olivary degeneration เพดานอ่อนกระตุกเป็นจังหวะต่อเนื่องแม้ขณะหลับ มักมี pendular nystagmus ร่วมทำให้ภาพสั่น MRI พบ olive โตและสว่างใน T2 รักษาตามอาการด้วย gabapentin หรือ memantine สำหรับตาสั่น

qx.stem: A 55-year-old man recovered from a right pontine-midbrain haemorrhage 14 months ago. He now notices oscillopsia, and his wife sees his throat 'pulsing' even during sleep. Examination shows rhythmic 2 Hz elevation of the soft palate, pendular vertical nystagmus and right limb ataxia. MRI shows T2 hyperintensity and enlargement of the left inferior olive.
qx.q: Disruption of which pathway best explains this syndrome?
opts: Corticospinal tract in the cerebral peduncle
Medial longitudinal fasciculus between the abducens and oculomotor nuclei
The dentato-rubro-olivary circuit (Guillain–Mollaret triangle)
Nigrostriatal dopaminergic projection
Spinothalamic tract in the lateral medulla
qx.why: Symptomatic palatal tremor appears months after a lesion of the dentate–red nucleus–central tegmental tract–inferior olive loop, followed by hypertrophic olivary degeneration on MRI. It persists in sleep, often accompanies oculopalatal nystagmus and, unlike essential palatal tremor, rarely causes ear clicks because levator rather than tensor veli palatini is involved. The other pathways would give weakness, internuclear ophthalmoplegia, parkinsonism or sensory loss instead.

name: Symptomatic startle syndromes
formal: Exaggerated startle responses secondary to brainstem or diffuse brain lesions or metabolic disease, distinct from hereditary hyperekplexia.
simple: Excessive jumping or stiffening when startled, caused by brain injury or illness.
th: การสะดุ้งตกใจมากผิดปกติที่เกิดจากรอยโรคก้านสมอง โรคสมองแบบกระจาย หรือ metabolic ต่างจาก hyperekplexia ทางพันธุกรรม
tempoNote: Appears after the causative lesion or illness; persists while the cause remains
feat: Excessive, poorly habituating startle to sudden noise or touch
Causes: brainstem stroke, inflammation or tumour; post-hypoxic injury; CJD; stiff-person spectrum; metabolic encephalopathy
Other signs of the causative disease are usually present
May lead to falls when startle is followed by stiffening
Lacks the neonatal stiffness and family history of hereditary forms
inv: MRI brain with focus on the brainstem
Anti-GAD65 and anti-glycine receptor antibodies
EEG and EMG startle studies; metabolic screen

case.story: Over 4 months she jumps violently and sometimes falls at sudden sounds, with stiff back muscles and episodes of painful spasms.
case.exam: Lumbar hyperlordosis, rigid paraspinal muscles, exaggerated startle to a hand clap without habituation.
case.tests: Anti-GAD65 very high titre; paraspinal EMG records ongoing involuntary motor unit firing at rest; MRI normal.
case.q: What is the cause of her excessive startle?
case.a: Symptomatic startle due to stiff-person syndrome (anti-GAD65).

det.patho: The startle reflex is generated in the caudal brainstem reticular formation and is normally inhibited by higher centres and glycinergic interneurons. Lesions or disorders that remove this inhibition, or antibodies against inhibitory synapses, lead to an amplified response. Causes include brainstem vascular or inflammatory lesions, hypoxic injury and autoimmune encephalomyelitis.
det.clinical: The startle response is larger, spreads more widely and fails to habituate with repetition. It may be followed by brief stiffness and falls. The accompanying picture depends on the cause, such as brainstem signs, rigidity with spasms in stiff-person spectrum disorders, or rapid dementia in prion disease.
det.diagnosis: Clinical observation plus EMG startle testing can confirm an exaggerated response. MRI and antibody testing (GAD65, glycine receptor, amphiphysin) look for a structural or autoimmune cause. Psychogenic excessive startle shows variable latency and more elaborate movements.
det.treatment: Treat the cause, for example immunotherapy for autoimmune disease. Clonazepam is the most useful symptomatic drug; other benzodiazepines, levetiracetam or valproate may be added. Fall-prevention measures are important.
det.prognosis: Variable; it often improves with treatment of the cause, while structural brainstem lesions can leave persistent startle.
pearls: Startle that does not habituate is pathological.
Check anti-GAD and anti-glycine receptor antibodies in adult-onset excessive startle.
Clonazepam helps most forms of excessive startle.
det.thd: Symptomatic startle syndromes คือการสะดุ้งมากผิดปกติที่เกิดภายหลังจากโรคอื่น เช่น รอยโรคที่ก้านสมอง ภาวะขาดออกซิเจน หรือโรคภูมิคุ้มกัน เช่น stiff-person syndrome การสะดุ้งจะไม่ลดลงเมื่อกระตุ้นซ้ำและอาจทำให้ล้ม ตรวจ MRI และ antibody เช่น anti-GAD65 รักษาสาเหตุร่วมกับ clonazepam

name: Symptomatic tremors
formal: Tremors resulting from identifiable disease such as stroke, multiple sclerosis, drugs or metabolic causes, as opposed to essential tremor.
simple: Shaking caused by another disease, injury or drug rather than inherited or essential tremor.
th: อาการสั่นที่เกิดจากสาเหตุที่ระบุได้ เช่น stroke, multiple sclerosis, ยา หรือภาวะเมตาบอลิก ต่างจาก essential tremor ที่ไม่มีสาเหตุ
tempoNote: Drug or metabolic tremor appears with exposure; lesional (Holmes) tremor appears weeks to months after the injury
feat: Enhanced physiological tremor from drugs (valproate, lithium, beta-agonists, amiodarone) or thyrotoxicosis, hypoglycaemia
Cerebellar intention tremor after cerebellar stroke or MS
Holmes tremor: slow rest + postural + kinetic tremor after midbrain or thalamic lesion
Asymmetric onset, sudden appearance or associated signs suggest a symptomatic cause
inv: Drug review; TSH, glucose, calcium, liver and renal function, caeruloplasmin if under 50
MRI brain if focal signs, asymmetry or acute onset
DaT scan when parkinsonian tremor is uncertain

case.story: Six months after an episode of brainstem demyelination, her right hand shakes coarsely when she reaches for a glass and even slightly at rest.
case.exam: Slow 3 Hz right arm tremor at rest, worse on posture and much worse on target approach; right internuclear ophthalmoplegia.
case.tests: MRI: demyelinating plaque in the left superior cerebellar peduncle–midbrain region.
case.q: What tremor is this?
case.a: Holmes (rubral) tremor, a symptomatic tremor from a midbrain lesion disrupting cerebellar outflow and nigrostriatal fibres.

read.where: Chapter 48: Ischemic Stroke: Common Causes and Diagnosis

det.patho: Tremor generators involve oscillating loops between cerebellum, thalamus, cortex and basal ganglia. Drugs and metabolic states amplify physiological tremor by increasing peripheral and central excitability. Structural lesions of the cerebellum or its outflow (dentate, superior cerebellar peduncle, red nucleus, thalamus) produce intention tremor; combined damage to cerebellar outflow and nigrostriatal fibres gives Holmes tremor with a delayed onset reflecting maladaptive plasticity.
det.clinical: The history of drugs, alcohol withdrawal, thyroid symptoms, prior stroke, trauma or demyelination is central. Drug and metabolic tremors are usually bilateral, fine and postural. Lesional tremors are often unilateral, coarse and low-frequency, with accompanying ataxia, ocular signs or hemiparesis. Functional tremor shows variability, entrainment and distractibility.
det.diagnosis: Classify tremor by activation (rest, postural, kinetic, intention), frequency and distribution, then look for a cause. Blood tests cover thyroid, glucose, calcium, liver and kidney, plus copper studies in young patients. MRI is indicated for asymmetric, acute or atypical tremor. Electrophysiology can help separate functional from organic tremor.
det.treatment: Remove or reduce offending drugs and correct metabolic causes. Cerebellar and Holmes tremor respond poorly to drugs; levodopa helps some Holmes tremor, and propranolol, primidone, clonazepam or topiramate are tried. Weighted utensils and occupational therapy support function. Thalamic (VIM) DBS or focused ultrasound may help disabling lesional tremor, sometimes combined with targeting the posterior subthalamic area.
det.prognosis: Drug and metabolic tremors resolve with correction; lesional tremors usually persist but may partially improve.
pearls: Always review medications first — valproate, lithium and beta-agonists are classic.
Rest + postural + intention tremor weeks after a midbrain lesion = Holmes tremor.
Young tremor: check copper and caeruloplasmin for Wilson's disease.
det.thd: Symptomatic tremor คืออาการสั่นที่มีสาเหตุชัดเจน เช่น ยา valproate lithium ไทรอยด์เป็นพิษ น้ำตาลต่ำ หรือรอยโรคที่ cerebellum ก้านสมองและ thalamus จาก stroke หรือ MS ชนิด Holmes tremor สั่นช้า ๆ ทั้งขณะพัก ยกแขนและเอื้อมหยิบ เกิดหลังรอยโรคหลายสัปดาห์ ควรทบทวนยา ตรวจเลือด และ MRI เมื่อมีอาการข้างเดียวหรือเริ่มทันที รักษาตามสาเหตุ

name: Synaptic CMS
formal: Group of congenital myasthenic syndromes due to defects in synaptic proteins such as acetylcholinesterase, rapsyn or agrin pathway, causing fatigable weakness from infancy.
simple: Inherited conditions of the nerve-muscle junction causing weakness that worsens with activity, starting in early life.
th: กลุ่ม congenital myasthenic syndrome ที่ความผิดปกติอยู่ใน synaptic cleft/basal lamina เช่น COLQ (ขาด acetylcholinesterase) ทำให้อ่อนแรงล้าตั้งแต่เด็ก
tempoNote: Onset at birth or in childhood; fluctuating, sometimes slowly progressive
feat: Fatigable ptosis, limb and axial weakness from infancy or childhood; respiratory crises possible
Strictly classified: COLQ (endplate AChE deficiency), LAMB2 and some collagen-anchor defects
COLQ: repetitive CMAP after single stimulus, slow pupillary light response, worsening with pyridostigmine
Antibodies against AChR and MuSK are negative
Some sources group agrin/LRP4/MuSK/DOK7 here, though these are usually counted as postsynaptic
inv: Repetitive nerve stimulation: decrement; look for repetitive CMAP after a single shock
Single-fibre EMG: increased jitter
AChR and MuSK antibodies negative; CMS gene panel (COLQ, LAMB2 and others)

case.story: Weak since infancy with poor head control; walks with frequent falls and gets breathless when running. Pyridostigmine prescribed elsewhere made him weaker.
case.exam: Bilateral ptosis, mild ophthalmoparesis, axial and proximal weakness, lumbar lordosis, sluggish pupil reactions.
case.tests: Repetitive stimulation shows decrement and a double CMAP after single stimuli; antibodies negative; COLQ biallelic variants.
case.q: Why did pyridostigmine worsen him and what is better?
case.a: Endplate acetylcholinesterase deficiency (COLQ synaptic CMS); cholinesterase inhibitors worsen it — ephedrine or salbutamol is used.

det.patho: In COLQ deficiency, acetylcholinesterase cannot anchor to the basal lamina, so acetylcholine persists in the cleft, producing prolonged endplate currents, depolarisation block and an endplate myopathy. LAMB2 defects alter the synaptic architecture and also cause nephrotic syndrome and eye abnormalities (Pierson syndrome). These are autosomal recessive.
det.clinical: Onset ranges from neonatal hypotonia with respiratory crises to childhood-onset fatigable weakness. Axial and proximal weakness with scoliosis or lordosis is common; ophthalmoparesis is often mild. Slow pupillary light reflexes are a clue to AChE deficiency. Symptoms fluctuate and may worsen with infection.
det.diagnosis: Neurophysiology shows decrement on repetitive stimulation and abnormal jitter; a repetitive CMAP after a single stimulus suggests COLQ deficiency or slow-channel syndrome. Negative AChR and MuSK antibodies plus early onset prompt a CMS gene panel or exome. Muscle biopsy is rarely needed now.
det.treatment: Avoid cholinesterase inhibitors in COLQ deficiency. Beta-adrenergic agonists such as ephedrine or salbutamol (albuterol) are effective over weeks to months. Respiratory monitoring, physiotherapy and scoliosis care are important; drugs that impair neuromuscular transmission should be avoided.
det.prognosis: Severe neonatal forms may be life-threatening; with beta-agonist therapy many patients improve and remain ambulant.
pearls: Worsening on pyridostigmine in a child with myasthenia: think COLQ or slow-channel CMS.
A double CMAP after a single stimulus is the electrophysiological clue.
Salbutamol or ephedrine is the main treatment for COLQ CMS.

det.patho: More than 30 genes are known. Defects can reduce acetylcholine synthesis or release (presynaptic), disturb the enzyme or basal lamina in the cleft (synaptic), or alter receptor number, kinetics or clustering on the muscle membrane (postsynaptic). Most are recessive; slow-channel syndrome is dominant.
det.clinical: Presentation varies from neonatal hypotonia and apnoea to childhood or adult limb-girdle fatigable weakness. Ptosis is common; ophthalmoplegia is more frequent with AChR deficiency. DOK7 and GFPT1 forms often show limb-girdle weakness with little eye involvement. Sudden apnoeic episodes with fever are typical of CHAT deficiency.
det.diagnosis: Fatigable weakness with negative antibodies and early onset suggests CMS. Neurophysiology confirms an NMJ defect, and genetic testing identifies the subtype, which matters for treatment. Muscle biopsy may show tubular aggregates in GFPT1 or DPAGT1 forms.
det.treatment: Treatment depends on genotype: pyridostigmine and 3,4-diaminopyridine for AChR deficiency and fast-channel forms; salbutamol or ephedrine for DOK7, COLQ and AGRN forms; fluoxetine or quinidine for slow-channel syndrome, where pyridostigmine worsens weakness. Respiratory monitoring and an emergency plan for apnoeic crises are essential.
det.prognosis: Most patients remain stable or improve with the correct therapy; some forms carry risk of sudden respiratory failure in childhood.
pearls: Antibody-negative myasthenia in a young person: consider CMS before thymectomy or immunotherapy.
Wrong drug for the genotype can make things worse.
Limb-girdle weakness without ophthalmoplegia suggests DOK7 or GFPT1.

more: Hyponatraemia with concentrated urine from excess ADH release, seen with CNS disease, lung cancer or drugs; causes confusion, seizures and coma if severe, treated by fluid restriction.

case.who: 68-year-old man from Samut Songkhram with trigeminal neuralgia
case.story: Since his oxcarbazepine dose was increased he has been increasingly confused and unsteady; today he had a brief generalised seizure.
case.exam: Euvolaemic, drowsy, no focal signs.
case.tests: Sodium 116 mmol/L, serum osmolality 245, urine osmolality 480, urine sodium 55; TSH and cortisol normal.
case.q: What is the cause and how should the sodium be corrected?
case.a: Drug-induced SIADH from oxcarbazepine; for symptomatic severe hyponatraemia give 3% saline boluses, aim for a rise of 4–6 mmol/L initially but no more than about 8–10 mmol/L in 24 hours, then fluid restriction and stop the drug.

read.where: Chapter 28 Disorders of Consciousness and Intensive Care Neurology — Hyponatraemia
Chapter 21 The Skin and Neurologic Disease

det.patho: Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) is released despite low plasma osmolality, either from the posterior pituitary under abnormal stimulation (CNS disease, pain, nausea, drugs) or ectopically from tumours. Water is retained through renal V2 receptors, diluting sodium; a natriuresis keeps volume near normal. Brain cells swell as water enters; over 48 hours they adapt by losing osmolytes, which makes rapid correction dangerous.
det.clinical: Symptoms depend on the level and speed of the fall in sodium. Mild chronic hyponatraemia causes subtle attention deficits, gait unsteadiness and falls; acute severe hyponatraemia causes vomiting, seizures, coma and brain herniation. Neurological patients are at particular risk after SAH, neurosurgery and with carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine.
det.diagnosis: Criteria: low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine (>100 mOsm/kg), urine sodium usually >30 mmol/L on normal salt intake, clinical euvolaemia, and normal thyroid and adrenal function without recent diuretics. In SAH, distinguishing SIADH from cerebral salt wasting (hypovolaemic) is crucial because fluid restriction can worsen vasospasm.
det.treatment: Severe symptoms: 3% hypertonic saline boluses (e.g. 100–150 mL) repeated as needed to raise sodium by about 5 mmol/L, limiting correction to roughly 8–10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours (less in high-risk patients) to avoid osmotic demyelination. Chronic: fluid restriction, treat cause, stop offending drugs; oral urea or tolvaptan for refractory cases with careful monitoring. In SAH avoid fluid restriction; use salt or fludrocortisone instead.
det.prognosis: Resolves when the cause is removed; outcome is mostly determined by the underlying disease and by avoiding correction-related injury.
pearls: Carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine are classic neurological causes.
Do not fluid-restrict after SAH; differentiate from cerebral salt wasting.
Too-fast correction risks osmotic demyelination days later.

Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Cannabis and Synthetic Cannabinoids

det.patho: These compounds are full, high-potency agonists of CB1 and CB2 receptors, unlike THC which is a partial agonist; many also lack cannabidiol and have active metabolites. Constantly changing chemical structures make toxicity unpredictable. Excess CB1 activation reduces GABA release, which may explain seizures, while vasospasm, platelet activation and cardiac arrhythmia contribute to stroke and myocardial infarction.
det.clinical: Users present with severe agitation, psychosis, catatonia, delirium or reduced consciousness, often with tachycardia and hypertension. Seizures, rhabdomyolysis, hyperthermia and kidney injury occur. Ischaemic strokes, including large-vessel occlusions, have been reported in young users. Outbreaks have also involved contamination with anticoagulant rodenticides (brodifacoum) causing severe bleeding.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on history and the clinical toxidrome because routine immunoassays detect THC, not synthetic cannabinoids. Specialist mass spectrometry can confirm specific compounds but is slow. Work-up should exclude other intoxicants, hypoglycaemia, infection and structural brain disease, and check kidneys, CK, ECG and troponin. Check coagulation if bleeding is present.
det.treatment: Treatment is supportive: a calm environment, benzodiazepines as first-line for agitation and seizures, antipsychotics only cautiously, IV fluids, cooling and cardiac monitoring. Treat stroke according to standard pathways, mindful of possible vasospasm. Offer substance use counselling and follow-up for persistent psychosis.
det.prognosis: Most recover within a day, but deaths from seizures, cardiac events and stroke are reported; recurrent use may cause persistent psychosis.
pearls: Cannabis-like history + seizures + negative THC screen = think synthetic cannabinoids.
Benzodiazepines are the mainstay.
Young stroke: ask specifically about synthetic drugs.

read.where: Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System (Spirochaete CNS infections: syphilis)
Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — Syphilis
Chapter 11 Stroke as a Complication of General Medical Disorders

det.patho: Treponema pallidum invades the CSF early in infection in many patients; most clear it, but persistence leads to inflammatory meningitis and endarteritis of small and medium arteries (meningovascular disease) within months to years. Over decades, chronic infection of the brain parenchyma causes general paresis, and inflammation of dorsal roots and columns causes tabes dorsalis. HIV infection and MSM (men who have sex with men) carry the highest risk, and syphilis rates have risen in Thailand among young adults.
det.clinical: Early neurosyphilis includes asymptomatic CSF abnormality, symptomatic meningitis with cranial nerve palsies, meningovascular strokes in young adults, and ocular or otic syphilis, which may present without other neurological signs. Late disease includes general paresis (personality change, grandiosity, mood disorder, dementia, seizures) and tabes dorsalis (lightning pains, sensory ataxia, Argyll Robertson pupils, Charcot joints). Mixed pictures are common, and the illness is a classic mimic of psychiatric disease.
det.diagnosis: Start with serum treponemal and non-treponemal tests. A reactive serum treponemal test with neurological, eye or ear features warrants LP. A reactive CSF VDRL confirms neurosyphilis but misses many cases; a negative CSF treponemal test (TPHA/FTA-ABS) makes it unlikely. Supportive features are CSF lymphocytes above 5 per µL (above 20 in untreated HIV) and raised protein. Ocular and otic syphilis are treated as neurosyphilis even if CSF is normal.
det.treatment: Standard therapy is IV aqueous penicillin G totalling 18–24 million units a day, split into doses given 4-hourly or run as an infusion, for a course of 10–14 days; procaine penicillin IM with oral probenecid, or ceftriaxone 2 g daily, are alternatives. Penicillin allergy in pregnancy requires desensitisation. Warn about the Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction (fever, worsening symptoms within 24 hours). Test and treat sexual partners, screen for HIV and other STIs, and repeat serum RPR (and CSF if abnormal or not improving) at intervals.
det.prognosis: Early forms usually respond well; general paresis may stabilise or partly improve, but established deficits from strokes or tabes often persist.
pearls: Young stroke + headache prodrome: check syphilis serology.
New psychiatric illness with Argyll Robertson pupils in a young man: think general paresis.
Ocular and otic syphilis are treated as neurosyphilis.
CSF VDRL negative does not exclude neurosyphilis.

qx.stem: A 41-year-old marketing manager in Pattaya has become boastful, spends money wildly and makes silly jokes at meetings; he has lost 5 points on MoCA over a year. His pupils are small, irregular and constrict poorly to light but well to a near target. Serum TPHA is positive and RPR is 1:64; CSF shows 28 lymphocytes/mm³, protein 0.8 g/L and a reactive VDRL. HIV serology is negative.
qx.q: Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Penicillin G (aqueous crystalline) IV, 18–24 million units daily for 10–14 days
A single dose of benzathine penicillin 2.4 million units IM
Oral doxycycline for 7 days
Ceftriaxone 1 g IM once
Donepezil and an antipsychotic, as damage is irreversible
qx.why: General paresis with Argyll Robertson pupils, a reactive CSF VDRL and CSF pleocytosis confirms neurosyphilis, which needs IV aqueous penicillin G for 10–14 days (procaine penicillin with probenecid is an alternative). Benzathine penicillin does not reach treponemicidal CSF levels, and short oral or single-dose regimens are for early non-neurological syphilis. Cognitive and behavioural changes can partly improve with treatment, and CSF and serum titres are followed up.

qx.stem: A 54-year-old man from Chiang Mai has 8 months of personality change, grandiose statements, poor memory and slurred speech. Pupils are small, irregular, and constrict on accommodation but not to light. Serum RPR is positive at 1:64 with positive treponemal tests; HIV is negative. CSF has 42 white cells/uL, protein 0.85 g/L and a reactive VDRL.
qx.q: Which treatment is recommended?
opts: A single intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin 2.4 million units
Oral doxycycline for 2 weeks alone
Ceftriaxone 1 g once
Azithromycin single dose
Intravenous aqueous penicillin G 18-24 million units daily for 10-14 days (or procaine penicillin with probenecid)
qx.why: Dementia, Argyll Robertson pupils and CSF pleocytosis with reactive VDRL indicate general paresis, a late form of neurosyphilis. Treatment requires penicillin at CNS-penetrating doses, usually intravenous aqueous penicillin G for 10-14 days. A single benzathine dose does not reach adequate CSF levels, and alternatives such as ceftriaxone are used only when penicillin cannot be given.

qx.stem: A 38-year-old man with HIV on antiretroviral therapy (CD4 410) completes 14 days of intravenous penicillin G for syphilitic meningitis with headache and cranial nerve VIII involvement. CSF before treatment had 120 white cells/uL and a reactive VDRL. He asks how treatment success will be judged.
qx.q: What is the best way to follow response?
opts: Repeat the CSF at about 6 months, expecting the cell count to fall (and then normalise), and follow serum non-treponemal titres
Treat as cured because he completed the course
Repeat the treponemal serology, which should become negative
Obtain MRI alone
Check only the CD4 count
qx.why: CSF pleocytosis is the most sensitive marker of activity and should fall within six months of treatment; failure or relapse suggests retreatment. Serum RPR or VDRL titres should also fall at least fourfold. Treponemal tests usually stay positive for life, so they are not useful for follow-up, and HIV coinfection raises the chance of incomplete response.

det.patho: Treponema pallidum infects the vasa vasorum of the aortic wall, producing obliterative endarteritis, ischaemia of the media and loss of elastic fibres. The weakened ascending aorta and arch dilate, the aortic valve ring stretches and the coronary ostia may narrow. The process is a late manifestation of untreated infection, now uncommon where penicillin is widely used.
det.clinical: It is an aortic, not a neurological, disease, but neurologists meet it in patients with neurosyphilis or stroke. Presentations include aortic regurgitation, angina from ostial narrowing, an aneurysm compressing surrounding structures (hoarseness, cough, dysphagia) or rupture. Thrombus in a dilated aorta can embolise, and severe regurgitation or rupture can cause cerebral hypoperfusion.
det.diagnosis: Positive treponemal serology plus imaging of an ascending aortic aneurysm with wall thickening or calcification makes the diagnosis; histology after surgery is confirmatory. Every patient needs CSF analysis to exclude neurosyphilis and an HIV test. Distinguish from large-vessel vasculitis and degenerative aneurysm.
det.treatment: Treat late syphilis with penicillin (IV penicillin G if neurosyphilis is present; otherwise weekly benzathine penicillin for three weeks). Antibiotics do not reverse established aneurysm or valve disease, so cardiothoracic surgery is needed for large aneurysms or significant regurgitation. Follow serology and imaging and screen sexual partners.
det.prognosis: Untreated large aneurysms carry high rupture risk; surgical repair outcomes are similar to other aortic aneurysm surgery.
pearls: Ascending aortic aneurysm + positive syphilis serology: always do a lumbar puncture.
Tabes dorsalis and syphilitic aortitis are both tertiary syphilis.
This is a cardiac/aortic disease with neurological links, not a primary CNS disorder.

det.patho: Treponema pallidum invades the CNS early, and persistent infection causes meningitis, endarteritis and parenchymal inflammation. The periaqueductal and pretectal midbrain region is a classic site, explaining Argyll Robertson pupils. Midbrain gummas or vasculitic infarcts can also occur.
det.clinical: Patients present with eye movement disorders, ptosis and pupillary abnormalities, sometimes with cognitive or psychiatric change. Other neurosyphilis features may coexist. In people with HIV, presentations can be earlier and more aggressive. The term appears in older literature and is not a distinct modern diagnostic category.
det.diagnosis: Positive serum serology plus CSF abnormalities (pleocytosis, high protein, reactive CSF-VDRL, which is specific but insensitive) support neurosyphilis. MRI may show midbrain lesions, meningeal enhancement or infarcts. Tumour, demyelination, tuberculosis and Wernicke encephalopathy should be considered.
det.treatment: Aqueous crystalline penicillin G IV 18–24 million units per day for 10–14 days is standard; procaine penicillin with probenecid is an alternative. Ceftriaxone may be used in penicillin allergy where desensitisation is not feasible. Watch for Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction, treat partners and test for HIV. Repeat CSF and serology to confirm response.
det.prognosis: Inflammation usually settles with treatment, but established pupil and ocular motor deficits may persist.
pearls: Argyll Robertson pupils are small with an irregular outline; large pupils with light-near dissociation suggest Parinaud or Adie.
Test every neurosyphilis patient for HIV.
Syphilis remains common in Thailand; serology belongs in many neuro work-ups.
