det.patho: Loss of tolerance to nuclear antigens produces autoantibodies and immune complexes that inflame many organs. In the nervous system, mechanisms include thrombosis from antiphospholipid antibodies, small-vessel vasculopathy (true vasculitis is rare), antibodies crossing a damaged blood–brain barrier (e.g. anti-NMDA receptor/anti-ribosomal P), and cytokine-driven dysfunction. Accelerated atherosclerosis and cardiac emboli add to stroke risk.
det.clinical: The ACR defines 19 neuropsychiatric syndromes, ranging from headache and mood disorders to stroke, seizures, psychosis, chorea, myelitis and neuropathies. Many events occur early in the disease or during flares, but secondary causes (infection, hypertension, uraemia, drugs) are common. Longitudinally extensive myelitis should prompt testing for aquaporin-4 antibodies, as NMOSD may coexist. Cognitive dysfunction is frequent but often mild.
det.diagnosis: First confirm SLE (EULAR/ACR 2019 criteria) and assess activity. For each neurological event, judge attribution to lupus versus other causes, aided by MRI, CSF, EEG, antiphospholipid testing and echocardiography. No single test proves neuropsychiatric lupus; it is a diagnosis of exclusion supported by serological activity.
det.treatment: Inflammatory manifestations (psychosis, myelitis, acute confusional state, mononeuritis) are treated with high-dose glucocorticoids plus cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate or rituximab; plasma exchange or IVIG may help refractory cases. Thrombotic events with antiphospholipid antibodies need long-term warfarin (DOACs are less effective in high-risk APS). Hydroxychloroquine is recommended for nearly all patients. Treat seizures, psychosis and mood symptoms with standard agents.
det.prognosis: Most neuropsychiatric events improve with treatment, but stroke and cognitive impairment contribute substantially to long-term disability.
pearls: Neurological symptoms in lupus: rule out infection and drugs before escalating immunosuppression.
Stroke in lupus → test antiphospholipid antibodies and echo for Libman-Sacks.
Chorea in a young woman: think lupus/APS, pregnancy and contraceptives.

4. Approach to the Evaluation of Mononeuropathy Multiplex

det.patho: Immune-mediated inflammation of vessel walls narrows or occludes vessels, causing tissue ischaemia, or weakens them, causing aneurysm or rupture. Mechanisms vary: granulomatous T-cell disease in large-vessel vasculitis, immune-complex deposition in PAN and cryoglobulinaemia, and ANCA-driven neutrophil activation in small-vessel disease. Peripheral nerves are vulnerable because the vasa nervorum form a watershed supply.
det.clinical: Mononeuritis multiplex is the classic neurological picture, sometimes overlapping into an asymmetric polyneuropathy. CNS involvement is less common but includes ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke, encephalopathy, seizures, pachymeningitis and cranial neuropathies. Systemic clues include fever, weight loss, rash, renal or lung involvement, sinus disease and arthralgia. Secondary vasculitis may accompany infection (HBV, HCV, HIV, syphilis), connective tissue disease, drugs or malignancy.
det.diagnosis: Combine clinical features with inflammatory markers, ANCA and other serology, infection screen and organ evaluation. Electrodiagnostics document neuropathy pattern, and combined nerve–muscle biopsy is the gold standard for vasculitic neuropathy. Vessel imaging (CTA, MRA, PET, angiography) shows stenoses or microaneurysms. Always exclude infection and endocarditis before starting immunosuppression.
det.treatment: Induction usually combines high-dose glucocorticoids with rituximab or cyclophosphamide for organ-threatening disease, followed by maintenance (rituximab, azathioprine, methotrexate). Avacopan can reduce steroid use in ANCA vasculitis. Tocilizumab is used in GCA. Treat secondary vasculitis by addressing the cause (e.g. antivirals for HBV-PAN). Provide neuropathic pain management and rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: Modern treatment achieves remission in most, but relapses are common and nerve recovery is slow and often incomplete.
pearls: Painful sequential nerve palsies = mononeuritis multiplex = think vasculitis.
Exclude infection (endocarditis, HBV, HCV, HIV) before immunosuppression.
Nerve plus muscle biopsy raises diagnostic yield.

det.patho: A granulomatous panarteritis infiltrates the adventitia and media of the aorta and its main branches, causing wall thickening, fibrosis and stenosis, and sometimes aneurysm when the media is destroyed. The cause is unknown; HLA-B52 associations are well described in Asian populations. Inflammation can be silent while structural damage progresses.
det.clinical: An early systemic phase with fever, weight loss and arthralgia is often missed. The occlusive phase brings limb claudication, absent pulses, bruits and asymmetric BP. Neurological features arise from hypoperfusion (orthostatic dizziness, visual disturbance, syncope) and from emboli or thrombosis (TIA, stroke); hypertension from renal artery stenosis increases haemorrhagic stroke risk.
det.diagnosis: The 2022 ACR/EULAR criteria require age at diagnosis 60 or under plus imaging evidence of large-vessel vasculitis, scored with clinical and imaging features. CTA or MRA maps stenoses; FDG-PET and wall enhancement help judge activity, since ESR and CRP are unreliable. Always measure BP in both arms (and legs) and listen for bruits.
det.treatment: Glucocorticoids induce remission; a steroid-sparing agent is used from the start (methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate) or a biologic (tocilizumab, TNF inhibitors) in refractory or relapsing disease. Antiplatelet therapy reduces ischaemic events. Angioplasty or bypass is reserved for critical stenosis and ideally performed in remission because restenosis is common when inflammation is active. Treat hypertension, measuring BP in an unaffected limb.
det.prognosis: Survival exceeds 90% at 10 years with treatment, but relapses and vascular complications are common.
pearls: Young woman + stroke + absent arm pulse = Takayasu until proved otherwise.
Check BP in both arms in every young stroke.
Normal ESR does not exclude active disease.

case.story: For 5 years has had weakness and wasting of both hands, painless burns on his forearms and a weak face. He had tonsillectomy as a child for large yellowish tonsils.
case.exam: Bilateral facial weakness, intrinsic hand wasting, loss of pain and temperature over face, arms and upper trunk with preserved vibration.
case.tests: HDL 3 mg/dL, total cholesterol 90 mg/dL; MRI cervical spine normal; ABCA1 biallelic variants.

det.patho: Loss-of-function variants in ABCA1 impair cholesterol efflux from cells to apolipoprotein A-I, so HDL particles are not formed and cholesterol esters accumulate in macrophages and Schwann cells. Inheritance is autosomal recessive; heterozygotes have reduced HDL. How lipid storage damages nerves is not fully understood.
det.clinical: About half of affected people develop neuropathy. One pattern is relapsing multifocal mononeuropathies; the other is a slowly progressive syringomyelia-like neuropathy with facial diplegia, upper-limb wasting and loss of pain and temperature in the face and arms. Tonsillar enlargement with orange colour is a classic but easily missed clue.
det.diagnosis: A near-absent HDL in a patient with unusual neuropathy is the key screening finding. Genetic testing for ABCA1 confirms the diagnosis. Imaging excludes syringomyelia, and leprosy and other multifocal neuropathies need exclusion.
det.treatment: No specific therapy exists. Management is supportive: protection of insensate skin, physiotherapy, eye care for facial weakness, and cardiovascular risk management. Genetic counselling is offered to families.
det.prognosis: Neuropathy is slowly progressive or relapsing; life expectancy may be reduced by premature vascular disease in some.
pearls: Ask about tonsillectomy and check HDL in a puzzling neuropathy with facial involvement.
Pseudosyringomyelic pattern plus normal cord MRI: think Tangier.
Very low HDL is a cheap, decisive clue.
det.thd: Tangier disease เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมยีน ABCA1 ทำให้ HDL ต่ำมากจนเกือบเป็นศูนย์ มีทอนซิลโตสีส้มเหลือง และ neuropathy ได้ 2 แบบ คือ mononeuropathy หลายเส้นเป็นๆ หายๆ หรือแบบคล้าย syringomyelia ที่ชาความร้อนเย็นบริเวณหน้าและแขนร่วมกับกล้ามเนื้อมือลีบ ตรวจ lipid profile และยีนเพื่อยืนยัน ไม่มีการรักษาเฉพาะ ใช้การดูแลประคับประคอง

name: Tardive akathisia
formal: Persistent inner restlessness with an urge to move after long-term dopamine blocker exposure, often with dyskinesia; difficult to treat.
simple: A distressing feeling of needing to keep moving that develops after prolonged use of certain psychiatric medicines.
th: อาการกระสับกระส่ายต้องขยับตลอดเวลาที่เกิดหลังใช้ยาต้าน dopamine เป็นเวลานาน และคงอยู่แม้หยุดยา
tempoNote: Appears after months to years of exposure; may persist for years after withdrawal
feat: Inner restlessness with an urge to move; rocking, crossing legs, pacing
Onset late in treatment or after dose reduction/withdrawal
Frequently coexists with tardive dyskinesia
Worsens rather than improves soon after stopping the drug
Distress, insomnia and risk of suicidality
inv: Clinical diagnosis; detailed drug history including metoclopramide and prochlorperazine
Barnes Akathisia Rating Scale for severity
Iron studies and renal function to exclude restless legs and other causes

case.who: 39-year-old woman from Nonthaburi with schizophrenia, on haloperidol for 6 years
case.story: Haloperidol was switched to aripiprazole 3 months ago; since then she cannot sit through meals, rocks constantly and sleeps poorly.
case.exam: Shifts weight while standing, repeatedly crosses and uncrosses legs; mild orobuccal dyskinesia.
case.tests: Ferritin 120 ng/mL; renal and thyroid function normal.
case.q: What is the likely cause of her restlessness?
case.a: Tardive akathisia (with mild tardive dyskinesia), unmasked by the switch and persisting on a less potent blocker.

det.patho: Prolonged dopamine receptor blockade is thought to produce maladaptive changes in mesocortical and striatal circuits, possibly with receptor supersensitivity and altered noradrenergic and serotonergic modulation. Exact mechanisms are uncertain. Risk rises with potent D2 blockers, high doses and long exposure.
det.clinical: Patients describe an unpleasant inner need to move, with leg crossing, shifting, rocking and pacing. Symptoms can begin during long-term use or after dose reduction and may be mistaken for psychotic agitation or anxiety. Coexisting tardive dyskinesia or dystonia is common.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical and depends on timing relative to drug exposure and persistence. Acute akathisia, restless legs, anxiety, agitation and drug withdrawal states must be considered. Rating scales help track response.
det.treatment: Review the need for the dopamine blocker and consider clozapine or quetiapine if antipsychotic treatment is still needed. Options with variable evidence include propranolol, mirtazapine, benzodiazepines and VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine), which are licensed mainly for tardive dyskinesia. Avoid increasing the antipsychotic to mask symptoms.
det.prognosis: Often persistent for years; some patients improve slowly after the offending drug is removed.
pearls: Agitation in a patient on antipsychotics may be akathisia; raising the dose worsens it.
Tardive forms persist or emerge after withdrawal, unlike acute akathisia.
Ask about antiemetics such as metoclopramide.
det.thd: Tardive akathisia คืออาการกระสับกระส่ายนั่งไม่ติดที่เกิดหลังใช้ยาต้าน dopamine นานหลายเดือนถึงหลายปี และอาจคงอยู่หรือแย่ลงหลังหยุดยา มักพบร่วมกับ tardive dyskinesia ต้องแยกจาก acute akathisia และ restless legs การรักษาคือทบทวนยา เปลี่ยนเป็น clozapine หรือ quetiapine และพิจารณา propranolol, mirtazapine หรือ VMAT2 inhibitor

name: Tardive dyskinesia (TD)
formal: Late-onset involuntary orofacial and limb movements after prolonged dopamine receptor blocker exposure, treated with VMAT2 inhibitors or drug withdrawal.
simple: Involuntary mouth and body movements that develop after long use of certain antipsychotic drugs.
more: Diagnosis by exposure history; risk factors include age, female sex and duration; switch to clozapine or quetiapine when needed. Valbenazine and deutetrabenazine are FDA-approved; prevent with the lowest dose of antipsychotic, and monitor with AIMS.
th: การเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติของปาก ลิ้น ขากรรไกรแบบซ้ำ ๆ หลังใช้ยาต้านโดปามีนนาน ๆ อาจเป็นถาวร
tempoNote: Appears after months to years of dopamine-receptor blocker use, or on stopping/lowering the dose; may persist
feat: Repetitive chewing, lip smacking, pouting and tongue protrusion or writhing
Patterned, stereotyped movements; patients are often unaware of them
Trunk rocking, pelvic thrusting, finger piano-playing or respiratory dyskinesia
Often unmasked or worsened when the causative drug is reduced or stopped
May coexist with tardive dystonia, akathisia or drug-induced parkinsonism
inv: Detailed drug history: antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, flunarizine/cinnarizine, amoxapine
AIMS scale to grade severity and follow treatment
Exclude look-alikes if exposure is unclear: thyroid, glucose, copper, HD gene test, MRI

case.who: 58-year-old woman from Nakhon Si Thammarat with schizophrenia
case.story: On haloperidol for 6 years; her daughter notices she keeps chewing and pushing out her tongue, worse since the dose was reduced last month.
case.exam: Continuous orobuccolingual movements, finger piano-playing, mild bradykinesia; she can stop the tongue movements briefly when asked.
case.tests: Glucose, TSH normal; AIMS score 18.
case.q: What medication change is preferred, and what specific drug class can treat the dyskinesia?
case.a: Tardive dyskinesia: switch to clozapine or quetiapine if antipsychotic is still needed, avoid anticholinergics, and consider a VMAT2 inhibitor (valbenazine/deutetrabenazine, or tetrabenazine).

read.where: Chapter 17 The tardive syndromes: Phenomenology, concepts on pathophysiology and treatment, and other neuroleptic-induced syndromes

det.patho: Chronic D2-receptor blockade is thought to cause postsynaptic dopamine receptor supersensitivity, maladaptive striatal plasticity and possibly oxidative injury. Risk rises with older age, female sex, diabetes, mood disorders, cumulative dose and first-generation agents, though second-generation antipsychotics also cause it. Metoclopramide is an important non-psychiatric culprit.
det.clinical: Classic TD is a rhythmic, stereotyped orobuccolingual dyskinesia, but the tardive spectrum also includes dystonia (often retrocollis), akathisia, myoclonus, tics and tremor. Symptoms commonly emerge on dose reduction (withdrawal-emergent) and may be masked by increasing the dose. Severe cases impair eating, speech, breathing and social life.
det.diagnosis: Requires at least a few months of dopamine-blocker exposure (shorter in the elderly) with onset during or within weeks of stopping. Use AIMS at baseline and regularly. Exclude Huntington disease, Wilson disease, chorea from systemic causes and edentulous dyskinesia. Tardive dystonia and akathisia should be recognised because their treatment differs.
det.treatment: Prevent by using the lowest effective dose, avoiding long metoclopramide courses and monitoring. Once present, reassess the need for the drug; switching to clozapine or quetiapine may help. VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine, tetrabenazine) have the best evidence. Clonazepam and ginkgo biloba have weaker support; anticholinergics may worsen TD. Botulinum toxin for focal tardive dystonia, and GPi DBS for severe refractory cases.
det.prognosis: Many cases persist for years even after the drug is stopped; remission is more likely in young patients and when detected early.
pearls: Ask about metoclopramide and flunarizine — not only antipsychotics.
Anticholinergics help acute dystonia and parkinsonism but can worsen TD.
VMAT2 inhibitors are the specific evidence-based treatment.
det.thd: Tardive dyskinesia เป็นการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติซ้ำ ๆ ที่ปาก ลิ้น ขากรรไกร หลังได้ยาต้านโดปามีนเป็นเวลานาน เช่น haloperidol หรือ metoclopramide มักแย่ลงเมื่อลดยา ควรใช้ยาขนาดต่ำสุดและประเมินด้วย AIMS เป็นระยะ การรักษาคือทบทวนความจำเป็นของยา เปลี่ยนเป็น clozapine หรือ quetiapine และใช้ VMAT2 inhibitor เลี่ยงยา anticholinergic

qx.stem: A 47-year-old woman with schizophrenia from Chiang Mai has taken haloperidol for twelve years. She now has constant lip smacking, tongue rolling and writhing finger movements that embarrass her at work. Her psychosis is stable and she wishes to keep working. The psychiatrist is considering increasing the haloperidol to suppress the movements.
qx.q: Which approach is most appropriate?
opts: Increase haloperidol, since higher doses temporarily mask the movements
Add benztropine to treat the dyskinesia
Start a VMAT2 inhibitor such as valbenazine or deutetrabenazine and review whether the antipsychotic can be switched to a lower-risk agent
Stop all antipsychotics abruptly and observe
Begin botulinum toxin injections to the tongue as first-line treatment
qx.why: Current guidance treats bothersome tardive dyskinesia with a VMAT2 inhibitor while optimising the antipsychotic, for example by switching to clozapine or another lower-risk drug when psychiatric stability allows. Raising the dose only masks symptoms and prolongs exposure, anticholinergics often worsen tardive dyskinesia, and abrupt withdrawal can cause a withdrawal-emergent dyskinesia and relapse.

name: Tardive dystonia
formal: Sustained abnormal postures and twisting after chronic dopamine antagonist exposure, often involving neck, trunk or face, and persistent after withdrawal.
simple: Painful twisting postures of the neck, face or trunk that develop after long use of certain psychiatric drugs.
more: Treat by switching to clozapine or quetiapine, botulinum toxin and VMAT2 inhibitors, and DBS of GPi for severe refractory cases. Young males and early onset are risk factors; anticholinergics may worsen the problem.
th: Tardive dystonia คือท่าบิดเกร็งที่คงอยู่ เช่น คอแหงนไปด้านหลัง (retrocollis) หลังแอ่น หรือกระพริบตาแรง เกิดหลังใช้ยาปิดกั้น dopamine นานเป็นเดือนถึงปี พบในชายอายุน้อยมากกว่า tardive dyskinesia และมักไม่หายแม้หยุดยา รักษาด้วย botulinum toxin, VMAT2 inhibitor และ DBS ที่ GPi ในรายรุนแรง
tempoNote: Starts months to years after beginning the drug (sometimes within the first year), often progresses for several months and then plateaus; remission occurs in a minority, and persistence beyond a year is common
feat: Retrocollis, torticollis, trunk arching (opisthotonic or lateral flexion), blepharospasm and jaw or tongue dystonia; the limbs are involved with hyperpronation, wrist flexion and plantar flexion
Onset is earlier and the patients are younger and more often male than in tardive dyskinesia; a childhood-onset form is seen with early exposure
Can be painful and disabling and may cause fixed deformity or respiratory and swallowing difficulty when severe
Often coexists with orobuccolingual dyskinesia or akathisia; sensory tricks may help less consistently than in idiopathic dystonia
Persists after withdrawal in most patients; anticholinergics, unlike in acute dystonia, are often ineffective and may worsen coexisting dyskinesia
inv: Detailed exposure history (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, amoxapine); note onset relative to the last dose
Serum ceruloplasmin, a 24-hour collection for urinary copper, and slit-lamp examination in patients under 50 years to exclude Wilson disease
MRI brain when asymmetric, rapidly worsening or with other neurological signs; genetic dystonia panel when family history or no drug link

case.who: 28-year-old man from Samut Sakhon with schizoaffective disorder
case.story: Treated with haloperidol decanoate and later aripiprazole for four years. Over six months his neck has bent backward and his trunk arches when he walks; lying flat relieves it.
case.exam: Fixed retrocollis with trunk extension, grimacing and repeated tongue protrusion; no rigidity, normal reflexes; the posture eases when he touches his chin.
case.tests: Ceruloplasmin and urinary copper normal; no Kayser–Fleischer rings; MRI normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what are the treatment options?
case.a: Tardive dystonia; coordinate a change to a lower-risk antipsychotic such as clozapine, give botulinum toxin to the neck muscles and consider a VMAT2 inhibitor, with globus pallidus deep brain stimulation for severe drug-resistant cases.

read.where: Chapter 9 Movement Disorders — Movement Disorders Associated with Dopamine Receptor Blockade or Dopamine Depletion

det.patho: Tardive dystonia is thought to share the receptor-supersensitivity mechanism proposed for other tardive syndromes, but the age and sex distribution and the response to treatment differ, suggesting a distinct vulnerability of the dystonia-related circuits, which involve the basal ganglia, thalamus and sensorimotor cortex. Some patients carry a genetic predisposition to dystonia that is unmasked by the drug, which is why a family history matters.
det.clinical: The commonest pattern is cervical and axial: retrocollis and trunk extension are almost typical of the tardive form, in contrast to the torticollis of idiopathic cervical dystonia. Cranial involvement (blepharospasm, jaw opening, tongue dystonia) and limb postures follow. Many patients have mixed tardive syndromes, with dyskinesia or akathisia. The onset averages a few years after starting the drug, sooner than for classic tardive dyskinesia, and young men are overrepresented. Pain, sleep disturbance and fixed deformity are the major reasons to treat early.
det.diagnosis: A temporal link to a dopamine receptor blocker, a compatible dystonic phenotype and exclusion of Wilson disease and genetic dystonia establish the diagnosis. The definition used in practice requires the movement to begin during or soon after exposure and to persist for at least a month after the drug has been stopped. Video documentation helps follow response to treatment, and a validated scale such as the Burke–Fahn–Marsden or the Toronto Western Spasmodic Torticollis scale gives an objective baseline.
det.treatment: Withdraw or change the culprit drug if the psychiatric state permits, preferring clozapine or quetiapine because of their low risk. Botulinum toxin injected into the dystonic neck and trunk muscles is the most dependable treatment for focal postures. VMAT2 inhibitors (deutetrabenazine, valbenazine, older tetrabenazine) reduce dystonia in many patients, and trials with trihexyphenidyl, baclofen, clonazepam or levodopa are options when pain or spasm is prominent. In severe refractory cases bilateral pallidal deep brain stimulation can give substantial and durable relief.
det.prognosis: Spontaneous remission occurs in a minority, mostly after early withdrawal; many patients stay chronically affected, but treatment with toxin, VMAT2 inhibitors or stimulation can restore good function.
pearls: Retrocollis and trunk arching in a young man on antipsychotics should suggest tardive dystonia.
Unlike acute dystonia, tardive dystonia rarely responds to an injection of an anticholinergic.
Check ceruloplasmin in everyone under 50 with new dystonia, even when a drug history is present.
det.thd: Tardive dystonia คืออาการเกร็งบิดผิดท่าอย่างต่อเนื่อง เช่น คอแหงนไปด้านหลัง หลังแอ่น กระพริบตาแรง ที่เกิดหลังใช้ยาปิดกั้น dopamine มานาน มักพบในชายอายุน้อย ต้องแยก Wilson disease และ dystonia ทางพันธุกรรมก่อนเสมอ การรักษาคือปรับหรือเปลี่ยนยาจิตเวชร่วมกับจิตแพทย์ ฉีด botulinum toxin ที่กล้ามเนื้อคอ ใช้ VMAT2 inhibitor และพิจารณา DBS ที่ GPi ถ้าไม่ตอบสนอง

name: Tardive myoclonus
formal: Brief, shock-like involuntary jerks arising after prolonged exposure to dopamine blockers, forming part of tardive syndromes.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks that appear after long use of certain antipsychotic medicines.
th: การกระตุกสั้นๆ แบบไฟช็อตที่เกิดหลังใช้ยาต้าน dopamine เป็นเวลานาน เป็นส่วนหนึ่งของ tardive syndromes

det.patho: The mechanism is unknown; it is assumed to share the long-term striatal changes of other tardive syndromes, possibly with altered cortical excitability. Evidence comes from small case series.
det.clinical: Jerks are usually postural and action-related in the upper limbs and are often mild. They may coexist with tardive dyskinesia or tremor. Many patients are older and have had many years of exposure.
det.diagnosis: This is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring prolonged dopamine blocker exposure and absence of metabolic, toxic or epileptic causes. Neurophysiology can confirm that the movements are myoclonic.
det.treatment: Review the antipsychotic and reduce or switch if possible. Clonazepam or levetiracetam may reduce jerks; VMAT2 inhibitors may help coexisting dyskinesia. Evidence is limited.
det.prognosis: Usually mild but persistent; disability is uncommon.
pearls: Before labelling myoclonus tardive, check lithium, renal function and antidepressants.
Tardive syndromes often overlap; look for orofacial dyskinesia.
det.thd: Tardive myoclonus คือการกระตุกสั้นๆ ของแขนขณะยกหรือใช้งานที่เกิดหลังใช้ยาต้าน dopamine เป็นเวลานาน พบไม่บ่อยและมักพบร่วมกับ tardive dyskinesia ต้องตัดสาเหตุอื่น เช่น lithium ไตวาย หรือยาอื่นก่อน การรักษาคือทบทวนยาและใช้ clonazepam หรือ levetiracetam

name: Tardive parkinsonism
formal: Parkinsonism persisting or emerging late after prolonged neuroleptic exposure, sometimes persisting after withdrawal and needing differentiation from Parkinson disease.
simple: Slowness and stiffness like Parkinson disease that persist after long-term use of certain psychiatric drugs.

case.story: Took flunarizine for dizziness for 2 years and was found to be slow and stiff; it was stopped 1 year ago but she remains slow.
case.exam: Symmetric bradykinesia and rigidity, no rest tremor, normal eye movements, no postural hypotension.
case.tests: DaT-SPECT shows normal striatal uptake.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis?
case.a: Persistent (tardive) drug-induced parkinsonism; the normal DaT scan argues against Parkinson disease.

read.where: Chapter 9 Movement Disorders — Movement Disorders Associated with Dopamine Receptor Blockade or Dopamine Depletion

det.patho: Dopamine blockade can cause parkinsonism that usually reverses after withdrawal. When it persists, two explanations exist: subclinical Parkinson disease unmasked by the drug, or a genuine long-lasting drug effect on striatal function. Whether a true tardive parkinsonism exists is still debated.
det.clinical: Patients have bradykinesia, rigidity and gait slowing that continue after the drug is stopped. Symmetry and absence of progression favour a drug effect. Coexisting orofacial dyskinesia may be seen.
det.diagnosis: DaT imaging is useful: a normal scan supports a drug-related cause and an abnormal scan suggests neurodegeneration. Reassessment over time is needed. Other secondary causes such as vascular parkinsonism or normal pressure hydrocephalus should be excluded.
det.treatment: Ensure the offending drug is stopped and avoid future dopamine blockers. Levodopa or amantadine may give partial benefit. Physiotherapy and fall prevention help. Where an antipsychotic is needed, quetiapine or clozapine are preferred.
det.prognosis: Some improve slowly over 1–2 years; persistence with abnormal DaT imaging usually means evolving Parkinson disease.
pearls: Flunarizine and cinnarizine are common hidden causes of parkinsonism in Thai practice.
Use DaT-SPECT when parkinsonism persists after drug withdrawal.
Allow up to 6–12 months for recovery before calling it persistent.
det.thd: Tardive parkinsonism คือ parkinsonism ที่ยังคงอยู่แม้หยุดยาต้าน dopamine นานแล้ว แนวคิดนี้ยังมีข้อถกเถียง เพราะผู้ป่วยหลายรายมี Parkinson disease แฝงอยู่ DaT-SPECT ที่ปกติช่วยสนับสนุนว่าเกิดจากยา ควรหยุดยา เช่น flunarizine หรือยาต้านโรคจิต และพิจารณา levodopa หรือ amantadine

name: Tardive stereotypies
formal: Repetitive, purposeless, stereotyped movements such as rocking or lip smacking emerging after chronic dopamine blocker exposure.
simple: Repetitive purposeless movements, such as lip smacking or rocking, after long-term use of some psychiatric drugs.
th: การเคลื่อนไหวซ้ำๆ เป็นแบบแผนโดยไม่มีจุดประสงค์ เช่น โยกตัว เคี้ยวปาก หลังได้รับยาต้าน dopamine เป็นเวลานาน
tempoNote: Appears after months to years of dopamine-blocker exposure and often persists after the drug is stopped
feat: Repetitive, patterned, rhythmic movements: chewing, lip smacking, tongue rolling, trunk rocking, foot tapping
The classic orobuccolingual form of tardive dyskinesia is stereotypic rather than choreic
Follows chronic exposure to antipsychotics or metoclopramide
Often worsens transiently when the offending drug is reduced or stopped
May coexist with tardive dystonia, akathisia or parkinsonism
inv: Detailed drug history including antiemetics such as metoclopramide
AIMS (Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale) for baseline and follow-up
Exclude Huntington disease, Wilson disease and edentulous dyskinesia when history is unclear

case.story: Took metoclopramide for 'gastritis' from a local clinic for two years; family notices continuous chewing and lip-smacking.
case.exam: Rhythmic chewing and tongue rolling that she can suppress for a few seconds; no chorea of limbs; good dentition.
case.tests: Normal MRI and copper studies; no family history of chorea.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what treatment is effective?
case.a: Tardive stereotypy (classic oral tardive dyskinesia) from metoclopramide; stop the drug and use a VMAT2 inhibitor such as tetrabenazine or valbenazine if disabling.

read.where: Chapter 9 Movement Disorders — Movement Disorders Associated with Dopamine Receptor Blockade or Dopamine Depletion
1 - Clinical overview and phenomenology of movement disorders

det.patho: Chronic blockade of striatal D2 receptors is thought to cause receptor upregulation and maladaptive plasticity in basal ganglia circuits, together with loss of GABAergic striatal function. These changes generate repetitive, patterned motor programmes. Older age, female sex, diabetes and high cumulative dose increase risk.
det.clinical: The commonest presentation is a rhythmic oral-buccal-lingual pattern, but trunk rocking, pelvic thrusting, rubbing or marching in place are also seen. Movements are suppressible briefly and decrease with distraction or sleep. They can emerge or intensify after a dose reduction, sometimes called withdrawal-emergent dyskinesia. Many patients are unaware, but some develop chewing injuries, dysphagia or social distress.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis needs at least several months of dopamine-blocker exposure, onset during or within weeks of stopping treatment, and exclusion of other causes. Video and AIMS scoring document severity. Spontaneous dyskinesias in elderly edentulous people and Huntington disease are the key mimics.
det.treatment: Reduce or stop the causative drug when psychiatrically safe, or switch to clozapine or quetiapine. VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine, tetrabenazine) have the best evidence. Anticholinergics should be avoided because they may worsen tardive dyskinesia. Botulinum toxin helps focal oromandibular forms.
det.prognosis: Movements may improve slowly after drug withdrawal but persist in many patients; VMAT2 inhibitors provide symptomatic control.
pearls: Classic oral tardive dyskinesia is stereotypic: the same movement repeated in a pattern.
Metoclopramide is a common but overlooked cause in Thai practice.
Do not treat tardive stereotypy with anticholinergic drugs.
det.thd: Tardive stereotypies คือการเคลื่อนไหวซ้ำๆ เป็นแบบแผน เช่น เคี้ยวปาก ดูดริมฝีปาก หรือโยกตัว หลังได้รับยาต้าน dopamine เช่นยาต้านโรคจิตหรือ metoclopramide เป็นเวลานาน อาการอาจเพิ่มขึ้นชั่วคราวเมื่อหยุดยา การรักษาคือหยุดหรือเปลี่ยนยา และใช้ยากลุ่ม VMAT2 inhibitor เช่น tetrabenazine หลีกเลี่ยงยา anticholinergic

name: Tardive syndromes
formal: Group of delayed-onset movement disorders from dopamine receptor blockers, including dyskinesia, dystonia, akathisia, tremor, myoclonus and stereotypies.
simple: A set of movement problems that appear after long-term use of certain psychiatric or stomach medicines.
th: Tardive syndromes คือกลุ่มความผิดปกติของการเคลื่อนไหวที่เกิดช้าหลังได้รับยาที่ปิดกั้นตัวรับ dopamine เช่น antipsychotic, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine และมักอยู่นานแม้หยุดยา มีหลายแบบ ได้แก่ dyskinesia รอบปาก, dystonia, akathisia, tic, myoclonus และ tremor ปัจจุบันรักษาด้วยยากลุ่ม VMAT2 inhibitor (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine)
tempoNote: Appears after months to years of exposure (the textbook definition accepts onset as late as 6 months following the final dose and persistence for at least a month after stopping); may emerge when the dose is cut or the drug is changed
feat: Classic tardive dyskinesia: repetitive, nearly rhythmic movements of lips, tongue and jaw (chewing, lip smacking, tongue protrusion), often with finger and toe movements or trunk rocking
Other forms are named by their movement: tardive dystonia, akathisia, stereotypy, tics, myoclonus, tremor and a withdrawal-emergent syndrome in children; a tardive parkinsonism is doubtful

Causes are all dopamine-receptor-blocking drugs: first- and second-generation antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine and similar antiemetics, and sometimes amoxapine; the risk is lower, but not zero, with second-generation agents
Risk rises with age, female sex, longer exposure, affective illness, diabetes and a history of acute extrapyramidal reactions
Often unmasked or worsened when the dose is reduced and temporarily suppressed when the dose is increased, and usually less bothersome to patients than to their families
inv: Drug history with dose, duration and indication; formal rating with the Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale (AIMS) at baseline and every 6–12 months
Exclude other causes of orofacial and limb dyskinesia: Huntington disease, Wilson disease, neuroacanthocytosis, thyroid disease, mouth or denture problems and ageing-related (spontaneous) dyskinesia
Basic blood tests, copper and ceruloplasmin if under 50 years; neuroimaging only when the picture is atypical

case.who: 64-year-old woman with schizophrenia from Khon Kaen
case.story: She has taken haloperidol for 20 years, changed to risperidone five years ago. Her family notices constant chewing and tongue rolling that is worse when she is anxious, and she cannot tolerate her dentures.
case.exam: Repetitive tongue protrusion and lip smacking, finger movements, no rigidity or tremor; mental state stable; AIMS 14.
case.tests: Glucose and thyroid tests normal; MRI is not needed.
case.q: What are the management options?
case.a: Do not simply stop the antipsychotic; if possible change to the lowest effective dose or to clozapine or quetiapine with the psychiatrist, and start a VMAT2 inhibitor (valbenazine or deutetrabenazine) when the movements are troublesome.

Chapter 32 Drug-Induced Disorders of the Nervous System

det.patho: The prevailing idea is that long-term blockade of striatal D2 receptors causes receptor supersensitivity and changes the balance of striatal output pathways, but neurotoxic stress, changes in striatal interneurons and GABAergic dysfunction are also proposed. The mechanism does not explain why only some patients are affected or why the movements may persist for years after withdrawal. Drug-induced movements that appear early, such as acute dystonia and akathisia, are separate entities with different mechanisms.
det.clinical: The textbook recognises several tardive phenotypes. Classic orobuccolingual dyskinesia is the commonest, and many patients are unaware of it. Tardive dystonia, often retrocollis or trunk arching, and tardive akathisia are more disabling, and tardive tics, myoclonus and tremor are rarer. The prevalence in long-term first-generation antipsychotic users was 20–30% in older studies; it is lower with newer drugs, but metoclopramide and prochlorperazine in gastroenterology or general practice are common causes that doctors forget. Symptoms may fluctuate with emotion and disappear in sleep.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis rests on dopamine-blocker exposure, a compatible movement phenotype and exclusion of other causes. Document the baseline with the AIMS and a video, and repeat it regularly. Spontaneous orofacial dyskinesia of elderly people, Huntington disease, Wilson disease and other choreas are the main mimics, together with ill-fitting dentures and functional movements. Investigations are guided by age and context; imaging is usually normal.
det.treatment: Review the necessity of the offending drug, avoid metoclopramide and similar agents where alternatives exist, and replace a first-generation antipsychotic with a lower-risk agent such as quetiapine or clozapine when psychiatric status allows. Valbenazine (once daily) and deutetrabenazine (twice daily) are the VMAT2 inhibitors approved for tardive dyskinesia and are recommended first-line by current psychiatric guidelines, with tetrabenazine as an older, less well tolerated alternative; they can cause somnolence, depression and, with tetrabenazine and deutetrabenazine, parkinsonism, so mood needs monitoring. Botulinum toxin helps focal dystonia, and pallidal (GPi) deep brain stimulation is a proven option for severe refractory tardive syndromes.
det.prognosis: Remission occurs in a minority after withdrawal, mainly in younger patients and when the drug is stopped early; in most patients the movements persist but can be well controlled with treatment.
pearls: Count anti-nausea drugs as dopamine blockers: metoclopramide and prochlorperazine cause many tardive syndromes.
Tardive dyskinesia may appear when the antipsychotic is reduced and improve when it is increased, which should not tempt a doctor to raise the dose.
Use AIMS at baseline and every 6–12 months in anyone on long-term dopamine blockers.
det.thd: Tardive syndromes คือกลุ่มอาการผิดปกติของการเคลื่อนไหวที่เกิดหลังใช้ยาปิดกั้น dopamine นาน เช่น antipsychotic, metoclopramide และ prochlorperazine ที่พบบ่อยคือการเคี้ยวปาก แลบลิ้น และอาจมี dystonia, akathisia, tic หรือ myoclonus ได้ ควรประเมินด้วย AIMS ตั้งแต่ก่อนเริ่มยา แล้วปรึกษาจิตแพทย์เพื่อลดหรือเปลี่ยนยา การรักษาปัจจุบันใช้ valbenazine หรือ deutetrabenazine และ botulinum toxin สำหรับ dystonia เฉพาะที่

qx.stem: A 58-year-old woman with schizophrenia has taken haloperidol for 12 years. For eight months she has had continuous chewing, lip pursing and tongue darting that embarrass her. Her psychiatrist has already switched her to clozapine, but the movements persist and are moderately disabling.
qx.q: Which is the best evidence-based next treatment for the movements?
opts: Add benztropine
Restart haloperidol at a higher dose
Add valbenazine or deutetrabenazine
Add levodopa
Add propranolol
qx.why: VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine; tetrabenazine where these are unavailable) are first-line for persistent tardive dyskinesia. Anticholinergics may worsen classic oral-buccal-lingual dyskinesia, and increasing the dopamine blocker only masks the movements temporarily. Levodopa and propranolol have no role here.

name: Tardive tremor
formal: Postural or action tremor appearing late after prolonged dopamine receptor antagonist therapy.
simple: Shaking that develops after long use of certain psychiatric drugs.
more: Distinguish from Parkinson tremor by history of neuroleptic exposure and by DAT-SPECT being normal. Management is to reduce or stop the offending drug and consider propranolol or VMAT2 inhibitors.
th: อาการสั่นขณะยกแขนหรือใช้งานที่เกิดหลังใช้ยาต้าน dopamine เป็นเวลานาน และคงอยู่หลังหยุดยา
tempoNote: Appears after prolonged exposure; persists or worsens after withdrawal
feat: Postural and action tremor (about 3–5 Hz), sometimes also at rest
Persists after dopamine blocker withdrawal, unlike acute drug-induced tremor
Often accompanied by tardive dyskinesia
Rare; may respond to tetrabenazine
inv: Medication and exposure history (lithium, valproate, SSRIs as alternative causes)
Thyroid function
DaT-SPECT if parkinsonian tremor suspected

case.who: 63-year-old man from Ayutthaya with schizoaffective disorder
case.story: Antipsychotic stopped 8 months ago after 10 years of use; since then his hands shake when holding a glass and writing.
case.exam: Coarse postural and kinetic tremor of both hands, mild orofacial dyskinesia, no bradykinesia or rigidity.
case.tests: TSH normal, not on lithium or valproate; DaT-SPECT normal.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and treatment option?
case.a: Tardive tremor; tetrabenazine or another VMAT2 inhibitor can be tried.

det.patho: Proposed to arise from long-term dopamine receptor supersensitivity similar to tardive dyskinesia, rather than receptor blockade. The response to dopamine-depleting agents supports this, but data are limited to small case series.
det.clinical: The tremor is prominent with posture and action, may involve the head or legs, and coexists with other tardive movements. Bradykinesia is absent, which helps separate it from drug-induced parkinsonism.
det.diagnosis: Requires chronic exposure, persistence after stopping and absence of other causes such as essential tremor, thyroid disease or other tremorogenic drugs. DaT imaging is normal.
det.treatment: VMAT2 inhibitors such as tetrabenazine may reduce tremor. Anticholinergics are usually ineffective. Avoid reintroducing dopamine blockers if possible; clozapine is the safer antipsychotic choice.
det.prognosis: Often persistent; improvement may occur with VMAT2 inhibitors.
pearls: A tremor that worsens after stopping an antipsychotic suggests a tardive mechanism.
Tardive tremor responds to dopamine depletion, not anticholinergics.
det.thd: Tardive tremor คืออาการมือสั่นขณะยกหรือใช้งานที่เกิดหลังใช้ยาต้าน dopamine นาน และยังคงอยู่หลังหยุดยา มักพบร่วมกับ tardive dyskinesia แต่ไม่มีอาการเคลื่อนไหวช้าหรือแข็ง DaT-SPECT ปกติ อาจตอบสนองต่อ tetrabenazine หรือ VMAT2 inhibitor

name: Tarui disease
formal: Glycogen storage disease type VII, phosphofructokinase deficiency (PFKM), with exercise intolerance, cramps, myoglobinuria and compensated haemolysis; avoidance of high-carbohydrate load before exercise.
simple: An inherited muscle energy disorder causing cramps, weakness and dark urine after intense exercise.
more: Diagnosis by muscle biopsy enzyme studies and genetic testing. Avoid strenuous exercise and high carbohydrate meals before activity; a ketogenic diet may help. Tarui disease, phosphofructokinase deficiency (PFKM), with exertional cramps, myoglobinuria, and haemolysis, and carbohydrate-triggered worsening. Diagnosed by enzyme assay and gene testing; avoid strenuous exercise and high-carbohydrate meals before activity.
th: โรคสะสมไกลโคเจนชนิดที่ 7 จากขาดเอนไซม์ phosphofructokinase ในกล้ามเนื้อ ทำให้ปวดเกร็งเมื่อออกกำลัง ปัสสาวะสีเข้ม และเม็ดเลือดแดงแตก
tempoNote: Exercise-induced attacks from childhood; a late-onset form gives fixed proximal weakness
feat: Exercise intolerance with cramps, early fatigue and myoglobinuria after intense effort
Compensated haemolysis: raised reticulocytes, bilirubin, gallstones, hyperuricaemia
Out-of-wind phenomenon: symptoms worse after carbohydrate-rich meal (glucose not usable)
No second wind, unlike McArdle disease
Late-onset form with progressive proximal weakness
inv: CK raised between attacks; forearm exercise test: flat lactate rise with normal ammonia
Reticulocytes, bilirubin, uric acid
Muscle biopsy: glycogen excess, absent PFK activity; PFKM gene testing

case.story: Since childhood has had cramps with sprinting; after a training run following a large rice breakfast he developed severe muscle pain and cola-coloured urine.
case.exam: Tender thighs, mild jaundice, otherwise normal strength between episodes.
case.tests: CK 25,000 U/L, reticulocytes 6%, uric acid high; forearm test shows no lactate rise; PFKM pathogenic variants.
case.q: Which glycogen disorder and why did breakfast matter?
case.a: Tarui disease (GSD VII); glucose intake lowers free fatty acids that the muscle depends on, worsening exercise tolerance.

det.patho: Autosomal recessive variants in PFKM abolish muscle phosphofructokinase, a rate-limiting glycolytic enzyme. Muscle cannot metabolise glucose or glycogen anaerobically, and red cells lose part of their PFK activity, causing mild haemolysis. Glycogen and an abnormal polysaccharide may accumulate.
det.clinical: The classic form begins in childhood with exercise-induced cramps, fatigue and pigmenturia after intense or isometric exercise. Nausea and vomiting can occur. Carbohydrate meals before exercise worsen tolerance. Hyperuricaemia and gout can develop. A rare late-onset form causes fixed weakness, and a severe infantile form exists.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it when a McArdle-like picture coexists with haemolysis or hyperuricaemia, and when there is no second wind. Non-ischaemic forearm testing shows a blunted lactate response. Genetic testing is the preferred confirmation; biopsy enzyme assay is an alternative.
det.treatment: No specific therapy. Avoid intense or isometric exercise and high-carbohydrate meals before activity; regular moderate aerobic exercise is encouraged. A ketogenic diet has been tried in individual cases. Treat rhabdomyolysis promptly with fluids to protect the kidneys.
det.prognosis: Generally compatible with normal lifespan; risks include renal failure from rhabdomyolysis and gradual weakness in later life.
pearls: McArdle-like symptoms with haemolysis suggest PFK deficiency.
Sugar before exercise helps McArdle but harms Tarui patients.
Dark urine after exertion needs CK and renal checks.
det.thd: Tarui disease หรือ GSD VII เกิดจากขาดเอนไซม์ phosphofructokinase ในกล้ามเนื้อ ทำให้ปวดเกร็งเมื่อออกกำลังหนัก ปัสสาวะสีโคล่า และมีเม็ดเลือดแดงแตกเล็กน้อย ต่างจาก McArdle ตรงที่ไม่มี second wind และการกินน้ำตาลก่อนออกกำลังทำให้อาการแย่ลง ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน PFKM รักษาโดยหลีกเลี่ยงการออกกำลังหนักและดูแลภาวะ rhabdomyolysis

name: Task-specific tremor
formal: Tremor appearing only during a specific skilled task such as writing, a form of action tremor often with dystonic features.
simple: Shaking of the hand that only occurs when doing a particular task such as writing.
th: อาการสั่นที่เกิดเฉพาะเวลาทำงานบางอย่าง เช่น เขียนหนังสือหรือเล่นดนตรี โดยงานอื่นไม่สั่น
tempoNote: Gradual onset, slowly progressive or stable
feat: Tremor only (or mainly) during a particular skilled task: writing, playing an instrument, using tools
Primary writing tremor is the best-known form
Often overlaps with writer's cramp (dystonic features) and may respond to alcohol
Other actions with the same hand are largely normal
No parkinsonism or cerebellar signs
inv: Clinical; observe the task and a range of other actions
Spiral drawing and handwriting samples
Accelerometry/EMG to distinguish tremor from dystonic jerks if unclear

case.story: For 3 years her hand shakes only when writing on the board or marking papers; pouring water and buttoning are normal.
case.exam: Coarse 5–6 Hz pronation-supination tremor on writing; no tremor holding arms out; no dystonic posture; normal tone.
case.tests: Thyroid normal; handwriting sample shows jagged strokes.
case.q: What type of tremor is this, and what treatments help?
case.a: Task-specific (primary writing) tremor; propranolol, primidone or botulinum toxin, plus writing aids.

read.where: 9 - Atypical parkinsonism, parkinsonism-­plus syndromes and secondary parkinsonian disorders

det.patho: Task-specific tremor is thought to reflect abnormal sensorimotor integration for highly practised motor programmes, sharing mechanisms with focal dystonia. Some cases appear related to essential tremor. Whether it is a variant of dystonia, essential tremor or a separate entity remains debated.
det.clinical: Tremor appears only during a particular task or posture (for example holding a pen), causing disability in that job while daily life is otherwise unaffected. Primary writing tremor often starts in mid-life and is usually unilateral. Musicians and craft workers may develop similar tremors.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is based on careful observation of the triggering task and comparison with other actions. Look for dystonic posturing, mirror movements and other tremor types. Imaging is generally unnecessary unless there are additional signs.
det.treatment: Propranolol, primidone or anticholinergics help some patients. Botulinum toxin injected into forearm muscles guided by EMG can be effective. Writing aids, thicker pens and keyboard use reduce disability. Thalamic DBS is an option for severe cases.
det.prognosis: Usually remains confined to the task with slow or no progression.
pearls: Watch the patient write and also pour, point and hold a posture.
Look for dystonic posture; writing tremor and writer's cramp often overlap.
det.thd: Task-specific tremor คืออาการสั่นที่เกิดเฉพาะเวลาทำงานบางอย่าง ที่พบบ่อยคือสั่นขณะเขียนหนังสือ (primary writing tremor) ขณะที่การใช้มือแบบอื่นปกติ อาจซ้อนทับกับ writer's cramp วินิจฉัยจากการสังเกตขณะทำงานนั้น รักษาด้วย propranolol, primidone, botulinum toxin และอุปกรณ์ช่วยเขียน

Bilateral postural and kinetic tremor across many tasks

name: Tauopathies
formal: Neurodegenerative disorders characterised by tau protein accumulation, including Alzheimer disease, progressive supranuclear palsy, corticobasal degeneration and frontotemporal dementias.
simple: Brain diseases in which an abnormal protein called tau builds up, causing memory, movement or behaviour problems.
more: Diagnosis uses MRI patterns, FDG-PET, CSF tau and amyloid, and tau-PET research; pathology confirms tau isoforms (3R, 4R, or both). Currently no disease-modifying therapy exists, though anti-tau trials are in progress; the genes MAPT and GRN are relevant.
th: กลุ่มโรคสมองเสื่อมที่มีโปรตีน tau สะสมผิดปกติ เช่น Alzheimer, PSP, CBD และ Pick’s disease
tempoNote: Insidious onset, steadily progressive over years
feat: Umbrella term: secondary tauopathy with amyloid (Alzheimer disease) and primary tauopathies (PSP, CBD, Pick disease, AGD, CTE)
Classified by isoform: 4R (PSP, CBD, AGD), 3R (Pick disease), 3R+4R (Alzheimer, CTE)
Clinical syndromes overlap: amnestic dementia, bvFTD, PPA, PSP syndrome, corticobasal syndrome
Atypical parkinsonism that responds poorly to levodopa suggests a 4R tauopathy
Familial forms from MAPT mutations cause FTD with parkinsonism
inv: MRI pattern: midbrain atrophy (PSP), asymmetric frontoparietal atrophy (CBD), knife-edge frontotemporal atrophy (Pick)
CSF or plasma p-tau and amyloid markers separate Alzheimer pathology from primary tauopathy
FDG-PET hypometabolism pattern; tau-PET (approved for AD, investigational for 4R tau)
MAPT gene testing when family history is positive

case.story: Over two years he has fallen backwards repeatedly, become slow and apathetic, and has trouble looking down at his plate.
case.exam: Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy for downgaze, axial rigidity, square-wave jerks, frontal release signs; no tremor.
case.tests: MRI midbrain atrophy with 'hummingbird' sign; plasma p-tau217 normal; no response to levodopa.

det.patho: Tau stabilises axonal microtubules; in tauopathies it becomes hyperphosphorylated, misfolds and aggregates into filaments that spread between connected neurons in a prion-like way. Alternative splicing of MAPT exon 10 yields 3R or 4R isoforms, and each disease shows a characteristic isoform ratio, filament fold (resolved by cryo-EM) and cell distribution — neurons, astrocytes (tufted in PSP, plaques in CBD) or oligodendrocytes. Alzheimer disease is the commonest tauopathy, driven by amyloid; primary tauopathies lack significant amyloid.
det.clinical: Clinical syndromes map imperfectly onto pathology: PSP pathology may present as Richardson syndrome, parkinsonism, gait freezing or speech apraxia; CBD may present as corticobasal syndrome, bvFTD or non-fluent aphasia; Pick disease usually as bvFTD or semantic or non-fluent PPA. Chronic traumatic encephalopathy follows repetitive head impact. Argyrophilic grain disease and primary age-related tauopathy cause milder late-life amnestic syndromes. MAPT mutation carriers develop FTD with parkinsonism in mid-life.
det.diagnosis: Definite diagnosis is pathological. In life, clinical criteria (e.g. MDS-PSP criteria) plus imaging patterns guide classification, and fluid biomarkers (p-tau181, p-tau217, amyloid ratios) identify Alzheimer pathology. Currently available tau-PET tracers bind Alzheimer tau well but 4R tau less reliably; 4R-selective tracers are in development. Exclude treatable mimics such as NPH, structural lesions and autoimmune encephalitis.
det.treatment: Anti-amyloid antibodies apply only to Alzheimer disease; there is no approved disease-modifying treatment for primary tauopathies, and anti-tau antibodies and antisense trials have so far been disappointing or are ongoing. Care is symptomatic: trial of levodopa, botulinum toxin for dystonia, SSRIs for behaviour, speech and swallow therapy, falls prevention and advance care planning.
det.prognosis: Primary tauopathies such as PSP and CBD typically lead to death within 6–10 years of onset.
pearls: 4R: PSP, CBD, AGD; 3R: Pick disease; 3R+4R: Alzheimer disease and CTE.
Clinical syndrome is not pathology — corticobasal syndrome can be caused by AD, CBD or PSP.
Normal plasma p-tau217 in a dementia patient makes Alzheimer pathology unlikely and points toward other proteinopathies.
det.thd: Tauopathies คือกลุ่มโรคสมองเสื่อมที่โปรตีน tau พับผิดรูปและสะสมในเซลล์ประสาทหรือเซลล์เกลีย แบ่งตาม isoform เป็น 4R (PSP, CBD), 3R (Pick’s disease) และ 3R+4R (Alzheimer) อาการมีได้หลายแบบ เช่น ความจำเสื่อม พฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน พูดลำบาก หรือ parkinsonism ที่ไม่ตอบสนองต่อ levodopa การวินิจฉัยอาศัยอาการ ภาพ MRI และ biomarker ปัจจุบันยังไม่มียาชะลอโรคสำหรับ primary tauopathy

name: Tay–Sachs disease
formal: Autosomal recessive HEXA deficiency causing GM2 ganglioside storage; the infantile form brings regression, startle and a cherry-red spot, whereas late-onset (juvenile or adult) disease presents with cerebellar ataxia, lower motor neuron weakness and psychiatric illness.
simple: An inherited fat-storage disease that in babies causes loss of skills, but in teenagers or adults causes unsteadiness, leg weakness and mental health problems.
more: Deficiency of beta-hexosaminidase A causing GM2 gangliosidosis, with infantile Tay-Sachs or later-onset forms with ataxia, dystonia and motor neuron disease features.
th: GM2 gangliosidosis จาก hexosaminidase A ต่ำ — ชนิดผู้ใหญ่ (LOTS) มาด้วยเดินเซ สมองน้อยฝ่อ ต้นขาลีบอ่อนแรงแบบ LMN พูดติด และอาการทางจิต
tempoNote: The late-onset form starts in the teens or early adult life and progresses slowly over decades; infantile form regresses within the first year
feat: Proximal leg weakness with quadriceps wasting, cramps and fasciculations
Cerebellar ataxia and halting, stuttering dysarthria
Psychosis, mood disorder or cognitive decline in a third or more
Tremor or dystonia; reflexes may be brisk or reduced
Infantile form: exaggerated startle, macular cherry-red spot, macrocephaly and regression
inv: Hexosaminidase A activity in serum or leucocytes (low; with HEXB disease both A and B low)
HEXA (or HEXB) gene testing
MRI: marked cerebellar atrophy with relatively spared cerebrum
EMG: chronic denervation; NCS often mildly axonal

case.story: Since his late teens he struggles to climb stairs; for two years his speech has become hesitant and he walks unsteadily. Treated for depression last year.
case.exam: Bilateral quadriceps wasting with fasciculations, mild finger–nose ataxia, broad gait, stammering dysarthria, preserved sensation.
case.tests: CK mildly raised; EMG chronic denervation; MRI striking cerebellar atrophy; leucocyte hexosaminidase A 4% of normal.
case.q: Which lysosomal disorder unites the motor neuron, cerebellar and psychiatric features?
case.a: Late-onset GM2 gangliosidosis (adult Tay–Sachs, HEXA).

det.patho: Hexosaminidase A, made of an alpha subunit (HEXA) and a beta subunit (HEXB), degrades GM2 ganglioside within lysosomes. Null variants cause the infantile disease; variants leaving a few percent of activity cause juvenile or adult forms in which cerebellar Purkinje cells and spinal motor neurons are most affected. Founder variants occur in Ashkenazi Jewish and other groups, but cases are seen worldwide.
det.clinical: Late-onset Tay–Sachs usually begins in the teens or twenties with proximal leg weakness and wasting that mimics a motor neuron disease, then cerebellar ataxia and a characteristic hesitant, stuttering speech. Psychiatric presentations (psychosis, bipolar disorder, depression) are common and may come first. Infantile disease, by contrast, causes loss of milestones from about 6 months, startle to sound, seizures, blindness and death in early childhood.
det.diagnosis: Measure hexosaminidase A (and total hexosaminidase to detect Sandhoff disease) in any young adult with LMN weakness plus cerebellar atrophy or psychiatric illness. Confirm with gene testing. EMG shows chronic denervation, and MRI shows disproportionate cerebellar atrophy.
det.treatment: Treatment is supportive; substrate reduction with miglustat has not shown clear benefit, and gene therapy is in trials. Some antipsychotics (notably haloperidol and other phenothiazine-type drugs) and tricyclics have been reported to worsen neurology; mood stabilisers such as lithium are often preferred. Provide physiotherapy, speech therapy and genetic counselling, including carrier testing.
det.prognosis: Late-onset disease is slowly progressive with many decades of survival; infantile disease is usually fatal by 3–5 years.
pearls: Young adult with quadriceps wasting, stuttering speech and cerebellar atrophy: check hexosaminidase A.
Psychosis may precede motor signs; choose psychiatric drugs carefully.
Sandhoff disease (HEXB) gives a similar adult picture with low total hexosaminidase.
det.thd: Tay–Sachs เกิดจากเอนไซม์ hexosaminidase A ต่ำ ทำให้ GM2 ganglioside สะสม ชนิดทารกมีพัฒนาการถดถอย สะดุ้งง่าย และ cherry-red spot ส่วนชนิดเริ่มช้าในวัยรุ่นหรือผู้ใหญ่มาด้วยต้นขาลีบอ่อนแรงคล้ายโรค motor neuron เดินเซ สมองน้อยฝ่อชัด พูดติด และอาการทางจิต ตรวจระดับเอนไซม์และยีน HEXA รักษาแบบประคับประคองและเลือกยาจิตเวชอย่างระมัดระวัง

name: Temporal lobe epilepsy
formal: Focal epilepsy from mesial or lateral temporal onset, commonly hippocampal sclerosis, with epigastric aura, déjà vu, automatisms and impaired awareness; may need surgery.
simple: Seizures starting in the temple area of the brain, often with odd feelings, staring and repetitive movements.
th: ลมชักจากสมองกลีบขมับ — มีลางบอกเหตุแบบรู้สึกคุ้นเคยหรือจุกท้อง แล้วเหม่อ ทำปากขมุบขมิบ

Behavioural arrest, oral and manual automatisms, dystonic contralateral hand
Post-ictal confusion; dysphasia if dominant hemisphere
Hippocampal sclerosis often after childhood febrile seizures
inv: MRI epilepsy protocol (hippocampal sclerosis)
EEG/video-EEG; surgical work-up if drug resistant

case.story: Episodes beginning with a rising feeling in his stomach and intense familiarity, then he stares and smacks his lips for a minute and cannot recall it.
case.exam: Normal.
case.tests: MRI: right hippocampal atrophy with T2 hyperintensity.
case.q: If two appropriate drugs fail, what should be offered?
case.a: Referral for epilepsy surgery evaluation — drug-resistant mesial TLE has good surgical outcomes.

qx.stem: A 30-year-old teacher with right mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, seizure-free on lamotrigine 200 mg/day, is now 8 weeks pregnant with a planned pregnancy. She has taken folic acid since before conception. Her pre-pregnancy lamotrigine trough level was documented. At 20 weeks she reports two episodes of her typical rising epigastric aura.
qx.q: Which management is most appropriate?
opts: Switch to valproate, which is not affected by pregnancy
Check the lamotrigine level and raise the dose to bring it back to her pre-pregnancy level, then plan a reduction after delivery
Reassure her, because auras do not progress in pregnancy
Stop folic acid because it lowers lamotrigine levels
Add phenobarbital to protect the fetus from convulsions
qx.why: Lamotrigine clearance rises sharply during pregnancy, often by more than half, mostly through increased glucuronidation. The recommended approach is regular level monitoring against the individual pre-pregnancy baseline, raising the dose when levels or seizure control fall, and lowering it over the first few weeks after delivery to avoid toxicity. Valproate is the most teratogenic option, and folic acid should continue.

qx.stem: A 37-year-old woman has drug-resistant focal impaired awareness seizures with an early rising sensation, oral automatisms and postictal word-finding difficulty. Her 3 T epilepsy-protocol MRI is normal. Video-EEG shows left anterior temporal seizure onset and interictal spikes.
qx.q: Which additional result would most support moving toward left temporal surgery?
opts: Diffuse bilateral hypometabolism on FDG-PET
Interictal FDG-PET showing hypometabolism limited to the left temporal lobe
Hypermetabolism in the right frontal lobe on interictal PET
A normal neuropsychology profile with strong verbal memory
Bilateral independent temporal spikes on prolonged EEG
qx.why: In MRI-negative temporal lobe epilepsy, interictal FDG-PET hypometabolism in the same temporal lobe as the EEG onset is the most useful supporting test, and concordant cases have surgical outcomes close to those of lesional cases. Diffuse or contralateral abnormalities and bilateral independent spikes argue against a single focus. Strong preoperative verbal memory raises the risk of memory loss after left-sided surgery rather than supporting it.

qx.stem: Four candidates are being considered for left anterior temporal lobectomy at a Bangkok epilepsy center. fMRI shows left-hemisphere language dominance in all four.
qx.q: Which candidate faces the greatest risk of a meaningful decline in verbal memory after surgery?
opts: A 22-year-old with seizures since age 3, marked left hippocampal sclerosis and poor baseline verbal memory
A 45-year-old with seizure onset at 40, a normal-appearing left hippocampus and above-average baseline verbal memory
A 30-year-old whose intracarotid amobarbital test showed failed memory after left-side injection
A 28-year-old with a left temporal pole cavernoma and right-hemisphere memory support on testing
A 35-year-old with left hippocampal sclerosis and severe preoperative naming deficits
qx.why: Verbal memory decline after dominant temporal resection is predicted by a functionally healthy structure: late onset, an MRI-normal hippocampus and good preoperative verbal memory. Early onset with severe sclerosis and poor baseline memory suggests function has already shifted elsewhere. Failure of memory on the same side during an amobarbital or etomidate test, or fMRI showing the other side supporting memory, also predicts a lower risk.

qx.stem: A 34-year-old man with drug-resistant focal impaired awareness seizures had bilateral stereo-EEG. Over two weeks it recorded nine seizures, five starting independently in the right hippocampus and four in the left hippocampus. MRI is normal, and his verbal and visual memory are both average.
qx.q: Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Right anterior temporal lobectomy
Bilateral mesial temporal resection
Corpus callosotomy
Responsive neurostimulation with depth leads in both hippocampi
No further treatment, because neuromodulation does not help temporal lobe epilepsy
qx.why: Removing both mesial temporal lobes would cause severe amnesia, and a one-sided resection leaves the other independent focus untouched. Responsive neurostimulation detects activity at each hippocampal lead and delivers stimulation there. Seizure reduction increases over the years, and its chronic recordings can later show whether one side dominates, which would make a resection possible. Callosotomy is mainly for drop attacks.

det.patho: Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy most often stems from hippocampal sclerosis — neuronal loss and gliosis in CA1 and CA3 — frequently following prolonged febrile seizures or other early insults. Other causes include low-grade tumours, cavernomas, focal cortical dysplasia, post-encephalitic damage and autoimmune encephalitis. It is the commonest drug-resistant focal epilepsy in adults.
det.clinical: Seizures often start with an aura that is in fact a focal aware seizure: rising epigastric sensation, déjà vu or jamais vu, fear, or an unpleasant smell or taste. These may evolve into impaired awareness with motionless staring, lip-smacking, chewing and fumbling hand automatisms, and contralateral dystonic arm posturing that helps lateralise. Seizures last 1–2 minutes and are followed by confusion; dominant-side onset may leave temporary language difficulty. Some seizures spread to bilateral tonic-clonic attacks. Memory complaints and mood disorders are common comorbidities.
det.diagnosis: A detailed witness account is central. MRI with an epilepsy protocol (thin coronal T2/FLAIR perpendicular to the hippocampus) detects hippocampal sclerosis and other lesions. Routine EEG may show anterior temporal spikes, but a normal EEG between seizures never rules it out; video-EEG telemetry captures typical events. In drug-resistant cases, pre-surgical evaluation adds neuropsychology, PET, functional MRI and sometimes intracranial EEG. New-onset adult TLE warrants consideration of autoimmune (e.g. LGI1) or neoplastic causes.
det.treatment: Focal-onset seizures respond to drugs such as lamotrigine, levetiracetam, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, lacosamide or zonisamide; choice depends on age, sex, comorbidity and interactions. Drug resistance is defined as failure of two tolerated, appropriately chosen drugs; at that point refer for surgical evaluation. Anterior temporal lobectomy or selective amygdalohippocampectomy offers seizure freedom to about two-thirds of suitable patients; laser ablation, vagus nerve stimulation, responsive neurostimulation or deep brain stimulation are alternatives.
det.prognosis: About a third of patients remain drug-resistant; surgery in well-selected hippocampal sclerosis yields high seizure freedom and better quality of life.
pearls: Dystonic posturing of one hand usually points to seizure onset in the opposite temporal lobe.
Two failed drugs means refer for surgery — do not keep adding a third and fourth for years.
Late-onset TLE with memory loss and hyponatraemia: check LGI1 antibodies.

name: Tension-type headache (TTH)
formal: Most common primary headache with bilateral pressing, non-pulsatile mild to moderate pain lasting hours, without nausea or aura, and not worsened by activity.
simple: A common headache feeling like a tight band around the head, usually mild and without nausea.
ab: ปวดหัวจากความเครียด
th: ปวดศีรษะชนิดปฐมภูมิที่พบบ่อยที่สุด ปวดตื้อ ๆ บีบรัดรอบศีรษะทั้งสองข้าง ไม่รุนแรงมาก ไม่คลื่นไส้ ไม่แย่ลงเมื่อเดิน ถ้าเป็นถี่ต้องระวังการใช้ยาแก้ปวดเกินจน MOH
tempoNote: Attacks last 30 minutes to several days; infrequent (< 1 day/month), frequent (1–14 days/month) or chronic (≥ 15 days/month for more than 3 months)
feat: Bilateral pressing or band-like ache, mild to moderate, not throbbing
Not made worse by routine activity such as climbing stairs
No nausea; at most one of light or noise sensitivity
Pericranial muscle tenderness on palpation is common, especially in frequent forms
Normal neurological examination; frequent forms linked to stress, poor sleep, anxiety and depression

case.story: For a year she has had a dull tightness across her forehead and the back of her head most afternoons, rated 4/10, while working long hours on screens; she still exercises during the pain. No nausea or visual symptoms.
case.exam: Tender trapezius and temporalis muscles; normal fundi and neurological examination.
case.tests: Diary: headache 12 days/month; paracetam on 6 days. No imaging needed.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what preventive option is reasonable if lifestyle measures fail?
case.a: Frequent episodic tension-type headache; add relaxation/physical therapy and, if needed, low-dose amitriptyline at night, while keeping analgesic days under the overuse threshold.

det.patho: Worldwide, tension-type headache is the commonest of all headache disorders. Infrequent episodes probably reflect peripheral nociception from tender pericranial myofascial tissues, while chronic forms involve central sensitisation of trigeminal and spinal dorsal horn neurons and weakened descending pain control. Stress, sleep loss and mood disorder lower the threshold; genetics contribute modestly.
det.clinical: Pain is bilateral, pressing and of mild to moderate intensity, and people usually carry on with their activities. Photophobia or phonophobia may occur alone but not together, and there is no vomiting. The chronic form, present on at least half the days of each month, often coexists with anxiety, depression, insomnia and medication overuse. Many patients actually have migraine with mild attacks, so look for migrainous features before settling on the label.
det.diagnosis: Apply ICHD-3: at least two of bilateral location, pressing quality, mild–moderate intensity and no aggravation by routine activity, plus no nausea and not both photo- and phonophobia. The examination should be normal. A new or changing daily headache in someone over 50, or one with focal signs, papilloedema, fever, weight loss or positional character needs investigation for secondary causes. Always count analgesic days.
det.treatment: Acute attacks respond to paracetamol, aspirin or an NSAID such as ibuprofen; avoid opioids and combination products and limit simple analgesics to under 15 days a month. For frequent or chronic forms, amitriptyline started at 10 mg at night and titrated slowly is first-line prophylaxis; mirtazapine or venlafaxine are alternatives. Non-drug therapies — physiotherapy, posture correction, relaxation, biofeedback, CBT, regular sleep and exercise — have good evidence. Treat coexisting depression or sleep apnoea.
det.prognosis: Episodic forms often remit or fluctuate; the chronic form is harder to treat and roughly half improve over a few years with combined measures.
pearls: If light and sound sensitivity occur together, or nausea is present, think migraine.
Count analgesic days at every visit — overuse converts episodic into chronic daily headache.
Amitriptyline doses for headache are low; warn about dry mouth and morning drowsiness.

formal: Tremor that increases in amplitude as the limb approaches a target, typical of cerebellar outflow lesions.
simple: Shaking that gets worse as the hand reaches for a target, caused by cerebellar damage.

tempoNote: Course follows the cause: stroke acute, MS relapsing, degeneration chronic
feat: Low-frequency (<5 Hz) tremor increasing in amplitude near the target on finger-nose or heel-shin testing
Accompanied by dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia and ataxia

case.story: Two weeks of clumsy right hand; her spoon shakes more as it reaches her mouth. One episode of blurred vision a year ago.
case.exam: Right finger-nose test shows tremor increasing near the target with past-pointing; right dysdiadochokinesia; brisk reflexes.
case.tests: MRI shows multiple periventricular and right cerebellar peduncle lesions, one enhancing; CSF oligoclonal bands positive.
case.q: What does the tremor localise to, and what is the likely disease?
case.a: Right cerebellar outflow (superior peduncle); multiple sclerosis relapse.

read.where: 1 - Clinical overview and phenomenology of movement disorders

det.patho: Damage to the cerebellum or its outflow (dentate nucleus, superior cerebellar peduncle, red nucleus, thalamus) disrupts feedforward control and error correction during goal-directed movement. As the limb nears the target, repeated corrections overshoot, producing oscillation.
det.clinical: Tremor is absent at rest, minimal with posture and worst near the end of a reach. Dysmetria, decomposition of movement and other cerebellar signs accompany it. Severe outflow lesions can cause wide-amplitude proximal tremor that is very disabling.
det.diagnosis: Bring it out with the standard limb coordination manoeuvres (finger-nose and heel-shin). Imaging identifies structural or demyelinating lesions; drug levels and alcohol history address toxic causes. Distinguish from functional tremor, which varies and is distractible.
det.treatment: Treat the cause where possible. Drugs are of limited benefit; options include primidone, propranolol, topiramate, clonazepam or isoniazid in MS with modest effect. Weighted utensils, occupational therapy and limb weighting help function. Thalamic DBS or focused ultrasound may be considered in selected refractory cases.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause; tremor from stroke or MS may partly improve, whereas degenerative causes progress.
pearls: Tremor that grows near the target localises to the cerebellum or its outflow.
In a young adult, think MS first.
Drug treatment is disappointing; rehabilitation matters.
det.thd: Terminal tremor หรือ intention tremor คืออาการสั่นที่แรงขึ้นเมื่อมือเข้าใกล้เป้าหมาย เช่น ตรวจ finger-nose พบในรอยโรคของ cerebellum หรือทางออกของ cerebellum เช่น MS, stroke หรือพิษจากยา ตรวจ MRI สมองส่วนหลัง รักษาตามสาเหตุ ยาช่วยได้น้อย ควรใช้กายภาพและอุปกรณ์ช่วย

name: Terson’s syndrome
formal: Vitreous haemorrhage associated with subarachnoid haemorrhage or raised intracranial pressure, causing visual loss.
simple: Bleeding in the eye jelly that occurs with brain bleeds, causing blurred vision.
th: ภาวะเลือดออกในวุ้นตาร่วมกับเลือดออกใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมอง (SAH) หรือความดันในกะโหลกสูงขึ้นอย่างรวดเร็ว ทำให้ตามัวหรือเห็นเงาลอย ควรตรวจก้นตาในผู้ป่วย SAH ทุกราย
tempoNote: Appears at the time of or within days of haemorrhage; vitreous blood may clear over months or persist
feat: Visual blurring, floaters or marked visual loss after subarachnoid haemorrhage or severe head injury
Intraocular haemorrhage at subretinal, intraretinal, subhyaloid or vitreous levels; vitreous bleeding defines Terson syndrome
Often bilateral, but may go unnoticed in comatose or sedated patients
Associated with higher grade SAH and with worse outcome
Retinal subhyaloid and peripapillary haemorrhages are visible on fundoscopy
inv: Dilated fundoscopy in all patients with aneurysmal SAH
B-scan ocular ultrasound when the vitreous hides the retina
Ophthalmology review with OCT, and vision testing once conscious

case.story: Thunderclap headache and brief loss of consciousness; CT shows diffuse subarachnoid haemorrhage and a posterior communicating artery aneurysm, which is coiled. On day 5 she says everything looks dark and she sees floating spots.
case.exam: Drowsy but follows commands, Hunt and Hess grade III; visual acuity is counting fingers on the left; fundoscopy shows subhyaloid haemorrhage with vitreous haze.
case.tests: B-scan shows dense vitreous haemorrhage in the left eye; CT angiography confirms successful aneurysm treatment.
case.q: What is the mechanism and how is persistent visual loss managed?
case.a: A sudden rise in intracranial pressure causes retinal venous rupture and bleeding into the vitreous; many clear spontaneously, and vitrectomy is considered if there is no clearing after about three months or in bilateral dense haemorrhage.

det.patho: Terson syndrome is intraocular, particularly vitreous, haemorrhage accompanying a sudden rise in intracranial pressure. A proposed mechanism is abrupt transmission of pressure to the optic nerve sheath with venous obstruction and rupture of retinal and peripapillary vessels, with blood tracking into the vitreous. It is most often associated with aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage but also occurs after traumatic brain injury and other causes of severe intracranial hypertension.
det.clinical: About a quarter of patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage have retinal haemorrhage, and some of them have vitreous haemorrhage with severe visual loss or floaters. It can be bilateral. Patients in coma or under sedation cannot report symptoms, so it is easily missed. It occurs more often in higher-grade haemorrhage, and its presence is a marker of severe injury and worse outcome.
det.diagnosis: Perform dilated fundoscopy in all patients with SAH when the clinical state allows; haemorrhages seen at the disc or macula are the visible sign. When the vitreous is opaque, B-scan ultrasound identifies the haemorrhage and excludes retinal detachment. Ophthalmology review should be requested when visual loss is reported.
det.treatment: Many vitreous haemorrhages clear spontaneously over weeks to months with observation. Pars plana vitrectomy is considered when blood persists for several months, in bilateral dense haemorrhage, with retinal detachment or membrane formation, and sooner in children at risk of amblyopia. Neuro-ophthalmic treatment of the underlying SAH takes priority, and patients should be advised about visual recovery.
det.prognosis: Visual outcome is generally good after spontaneous clearing or vitrectomy, although macular scarring or detachment can leave permanent loss.
pearls: Look at the fundi in every SAH patient, especially when consciousness is impaired.
Visual loss after SAH is not always optic or occipital; check the vitreous.
Terson syndrome signals severe haemorrhage and predicts worse neurological outcome.
det.thd: Terson syndrome คือเลือดออกในวุ้นตาร่วมกับ SAH หรือความดันในกะโหลกพุ่งสูงทันที พบประมาณหนึ่งในสี่ของผู้ป่วย SAH มีเลือดออกที่จอตา ทำให้ตามัวหรือเห็นเงาลอย ผู้ป่วยซึมจะบอกอาการไม่ได้ จึงควรตรวจก้นตาทุกราย ใช้ B-scan ถ้าวุ้นตาขุ่น ส่วนใหญ่เลือดจะค่อย ๆ ดูดซึมเอง ถ้าไม่ดีขึ้นใน 3-6 เดือนหรือเป็นสองข้าง พิจารณาผ่าตัด vitrectomy
