name: Thalamocortical seizures
formal: Generalised epileptic seizures arising from abnormal thalamocortical oscillation, as in absence epilepsy with spike-wave discharges.
simple: Seizures caused by abnormal electrical loops between the thalamus and cortex, such as brief staring spells.
th: แนวคิดของการชักแบบทั่วไปที่เกิดจากวงจรไฟฟ้าระหว่าง thalamus และเปลือกสมองแกว่งผิดปกติ เช่น absence seizure ที่มี spike-wave
tempoNote: Brief seizures lasting seconds, often many per day
feat: A pathophysiological term rather than a separate disease: describes seizures generated in thalamocortical loops
Typical example: absence seizures with sudden arrest of activity and 3 Hz spike-wave
Also underlies some generalised myoclonic and tonic-clonic seizures in genetic generalised epilepsies
Provoked by hyperventilation, sleep deprivation and sometimes photic stimulation
Worsened by sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine, phenytoin) and some GABAergic drugs (vigabatrin, tiagabine)
inv: EEG with hyperventilation: generalised spike-wave discharges
MRI usually normal in genetic generalised epilepsy

case.story: Teachers report she 'blanks out' many times a day for a few seconds and loses her place in reading.
case.exam: Normal; asking her to hyperventilate for 2 minutes triggers a 10-second stare with eyelid flutter.
case.tests: EEG shows 3 Hz generalised spike-wave discharges during the event.
case.q: Which brain circuit generates these seizures and which drug class can worsen them?
case.a: A thalamocortical circuit generating typical absence seizures; sodium-channel blockers like carbamazepine can aggravate them, whereas ethosuximide or valproate treat them.

det.patho: The thalamus and cortex are linked in a reciprocal loop. Thalamic reticular nucleus neurons, through GABA-B receptors and T-type calcium channels, generate rhythmic burst firing that normally produces sleep spindles. In absence epilepsy, a hyperexcitable cortical region drives this circuit into synchronous 3 Hz spike-wave oscillation. Ethosuximide blocks T-type calcium channels, explaining its specific efficacy.
det.clinical: The prototypical clinical expression is the typical absence seizure in childhood or juvenile absence epilepsy, but thalamocortical mechanisms also contribute to myoclonic and generalised tonic-clonic seizures in genetic generalised epilepsies. Seizures are brief, frequent and provoked by hyperventilation.
det.diagnosis: This is a mechanistic description; in practice diagnose the seizure type and epilepsy syndrome by clinical description and EEG. Generalised spike-wave with a normal background and normal MRI supports a genetic generalised epilepsy.
det.treatment: For absence seizures, ethosuximide is first choice when they occur alone; valproate when generalised tonic-clonic seizures coexist (avoiding it in girls and women of childbearing potential where possible), and lamotrigine or levetiracetam as alternatives. Avoid carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, gabapentin, vigabatrin and tiagabine, which can worsen these seizures.
det.prognosis: Depends on syndrome; childhood absence epilepsy often remits by adolescence.
pearls: T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons explain why ethosuximide works on absences.
Hyperventilation in clinic is a simple test for absence seizures.
Sodium-channel blockers can aggravate thalamocortical seizures.
det.thd: Thalamocortical seizures เป็นคำอธิบายกลไกการชักแบบทั่วไปที่เกิดจากวงจรระหว่าง thalamus กับเปลือกสมองแกว่งพร้อมกันผิดปกติ ตัวอย่างคือ absence seizure ที่เด็กเหม่อนิ่งไม่กี่วินาที และ EEG มี spike-wave 3 Hz ยา ethosuximide ได้ผลเพราะยับยั้ง T-type calcium channel ส่วนยากลุ่ม sodium channel blocker อาจทำให้ชักมากขึ้น

feat: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, later constipation
Severe burning pain of the feet with ascending sensory and motor loss
Alopecia, nail Mees lines, dry scaly skin
Encephalopathy, seizures, ophthalmoplegia, optic neuropathy, tachycardia in heavy exposure

case.story: Vomiting and abdominal pain after a meal, then severe burning feet; two weeks later his hair comes out in handfuls; his wife has similar pains.
case.exam: Allodynia, distal weakness, absent ankle jerks, scalp alopecia, resting tachycardia, mild confusion.
case.tests: Urine thallium markedly raised; NCS: axonal sensorimotor neuropathy.
case.q: Which antidote is used and why does it work?
case.a: Oral Prussian blue binds thallium secreted into the gut, interrupting enterohepatic recirculation; haemodialysis may be added.

det.patho: Thallium substitutes for potassium in cell transport and binds to mitochondrial and sulfhydryl-containing enzymes, impairing energy metabolism. Long axons, hair follicles, heart and brain are particularly affected. Enterohepatic recycling prolongs its half-life.
det.clinical: A gastrointestinal phase is followed by a painful ascending neuropathy, then alopecia. High doses cause encephalopathy, seizures, coma, cranial neuropathies, cardiac arrhythmias and death. Survivors may have residual neuropathy and cognitive or psychiatric problems.
det.diagnosis: Urine thallium confirms exposure. NCS documents axonal damage. Clustered cases or a suspicious history should lead to early testing, as delays worsen outcomes.
det.treatment: Prussian blue orally, gastric decontamination where appropriate, enhanced elimination with haemodialysis, and supportive care including analgesia and cardiac monitoring. Report suspected criminal or environmental poisoning to authorities.
det.prognosis: Depends on dose and treatment speed; mortality is significant with large ingestions and residual neuropathy is common.
pearls: Painful neuropathy plus later alopecia is the classic pair.
Prussian blue is the specific antidote.
Think poisoning when several household members are affected.
det.thd: พิษ thallium เกิดจากการกินโดยตั้งใจหรือถูกวางยา ระยะแรกมีอาการทางเดินอาหาร ตามด้วยปวดแสบเท้ารุนแรงและอ่อนแรงลามขึ้น ประมาณ 2 สัปดาห์ผมร่วง ในรายรุนแรงมีซึม ชัก และหัวใจเต้นผิดจังหวะ วินิจฉัยจากระดับ thallium ในปัสสาวะ รักษาด้วย Prussian blue และ hemodialysis

name: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency
formal: Thiamine deficiency causing Wernicke encephalopathy, Korsakoff syndrome and beriberi, typically in alcohol misuse or malnutrition.
simple: Low vitamin B1 that can cause confusion, eye movement problems, poor balance and nerve damage.
more: Treat suspected Wernicke encephalopathy immediately with IV thiamine before glucose; diagnosis is clinical with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and confusion; MRI shows mammillary body and periaqueductal change. Measure red cell transketolase or whole-blood thiamine.

tempoNote: Wernicke is acute; dry beriberi neuropathy subacute; Korsakoff amnesia chronic
feat: Wernicke: confusion, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus, gait ataxia (full triad in a minority)
Korsakoff: severe anterograde amnesia with confabulation
Dry beriberi: painful sensorimotor axonal neuropathy, can mimic GBS

case.q: What must be given immediately, and in what order relative to glucose?

det.patho: Thiamine pyrophosphate is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase. Deficiency impairs glucose metabolism, causing lactate accumulation, energy failure and focal neuronal injury in regions with high thiamine turnover (medial thalamus, mammillary bodies, periaqueductal grey, cerebellar vermis). Body stores are small and can be exhausted in weeks.
det.clinical: Wernicke encephalopathy is often missed because the classic triad is present in a minority; any malnourished or vomiting patient with confusion deserves treatment. Untreated, it progresses to coma or permanent Korsakoff amnesia. Dry beriberi causes a painful, sometimes rapidly progressive axonal neuropathy. In Thailand and Southeast Asia, infantile beriberi and thiamine deficiency with high-carbohydrate polished rice diets remain relevant.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical and treatment should not await tests. MRI findings are supportive but may be normal. Blood thiamine taken before replacement confirms deficiency. Look for and correct magnesium deficiency, which impairs thiamine utilisation.
det.treatment: Give high-dose parenteral thiamine promptly (regimens of around 500 mg IV three times daily for several days are widely recommended for suspected Wernicke), then oral maintenance. Give thiamine before glucose in at-risk patients. Prophylactic thiamine for alcohol misuse, hyperemesis and refeeding. Correct magnesium and address underlying cause.
det.prognosis: Eye signs respond within hours to days; ataxia and memory improve less, and many develop lasting Korsakoff syndrome if treatment is delayed.
pearls: Don't wait for the full triad — treat on suspicion.
Thiamine before glucose in malnourished or alcoholic patients.
Bariatric surgery and hyperemesis are now common non-alcohol causes.
det.thd: Thiamine deficiency (ขาดวิตามินบี 1) ทำให้เกิด Wernicke encephalopathy (สับสน กลอกตาผิดปกติ เดินเซ) Korsakoff syndrome (ความจำใหม่เสีย) และ beriberi (ปลายประสาทอักเสบ หรือหัวใจล้มเหลว) พบในผู้ติดสุรา อาเจียนมาก หลังผ่าตัดกระเพาะ และขาดอาหาร ต้องให้ thiamine ทางหลอดเลือดดำขนาดสูงทันทีโดยไม่ต้องรอผลตรวจ และให้ก่อนกลูโคส MRI อาจพบรอยโรคที่ thalamus และรอบ aqueduct

formal: Akathisia caused by the antipsychotic thioridazine, with inner restlessness and inability to stay still.
simple: A feeling of restlessness and need to move caused by a particular antipsychotic medicine.

det.patho: Thioridazine blocks D2 receptors, and akathisia is thought to involve mesocortical dopaminergic blockade with secondary noradrenergic and serotonergic effects. Its strong anticholinergic activity partly offsets extrapyramidal effects, so akathisia is less common than with high-potency agents.
det.clinical: Patients feel restless and anxious, with an urge to move that is relieved by pacing. It may be mistaken for worsening psychosis or anxiety, leading to inappropriate dose increases.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the temporal link to starting or increasing thioridazine and typical motor restlessness. Other causes of agitation, withdrawal states and restless legs should be considered. ECG is essential because of QT risk.
det.treatment: Reduce or stop thioridazine; because of cardiac risk, a safer antipsychotic is usually chosen. Propranolol, mirtazapine (low dose) or a short benzodiazepine course can relieve akathisia. Avoid combining with other QT-prolonging drugs or CYP2D6 inhibitors.
det.prognosis: Acute akathisia usually resolves within days to weeks of stopping or reducing the drug.
pearls: Restlessness after a dose increase is akathisia until proven otherwise.
Thioridazine needs ECG monitoring because of QTc prolongation.
det.thd: Thioridazine akathisia คืออาการกระสับกระส่ายนั่งไม่ติดที่เกิดจากยา thioridazine มักเกิดหลังเริ่มยาหรือเพิ่มขนาดยา อาจถูกเข้าใจผิดว่าโรคจิตกำเริบ ยานี้ยังทำให้ QTc ยาวได้จึงต้องตรวจ ECG การรักษาคือลดหรือหยุดยา เปลี่ยนเป็นยาที่ปลอดภัยกว่า และใช้ propranolol หรือ mirtazapine

formal: Autosomal dominant myotonia congenita from CLCN1 mutations with muscle stiffness after rest that eases with exercise, with muscle hypertrophy.
simple: An inherited condition where muscles stay stiff after rest but loosen with repeated movement.
th: myotonia congenita ชนิดยีนเด่นจาก CLCN1 กล้ามเนื้อแข็งหลังพักแล้วดีขึ้นเมื่อขยับซ้ำ (warm-up) และกล้ามเนื้อโต

case.story: Since childhood his legs 'lock' when he starts running after sitting; after a few strides he moves freely. His mother and brother have the same.
case.exam: Muscular build, slow hand opening after a firm grip improving with repetition, percussion myotonia of thenar muscles, normal strength.

det.patho: CLCN1 encodes the muscle chloride channel ClC-1, which stabilises the resting membrane. Dominant-negative variants reduce chloride conductance, so potassium accumulating in the T-tubules after activity depolarises the membrane and triggers runs of after-discharges perceived as stiffness. Repeated activity reduces myotonia through sodium channel slow inactivation and other adaptations.
det.clinical: Stiffness after rest affects legs, hands, jaw and eyelids, often first noticed as difficulty starting to run or releasing grip. Muscle hypertrophy gives a muscular appearance. Unlike myotonic dystrophy there are no systemic features. Symptoms may worsen in pregnancy and with hypothyroidism. The phenotype is generally milder than the recessive Becker form.
det.diagnosis: Clinical warm-up myotonia with a dominant family history is suggestive. EMG demonstrates myotonic discharges; the short exercise test with cooling helps separate chloride from sodium channel myotonia. CLCN1 testing confirms, though some variants act dominantly in one family and recessively in another.
det.treatment: Many need no drug. Mexiletine is the first-line agent for disabling stiffness, after ECG screening; alternatives include lamotrigine, carbamazepine, phenytoin or acetazolamide. Patients should avoid depolarising muscle relaxants such as suxamethonium, which can cause severe masseter spasm, and inform anaesthetists.
det.prognosis: Normal life expectancy with non-progressive symptoms.
pearls: Warm-up = chloride channel (myotonia congenita); paradoxical worsening with exercise and cold = paramyotonia.
No weakness, cataract or cardiac disease distinguishes it from DM1.
Avoid suxamethonium; mexiletine is first-line therapy.
det.thd: Thomsen’s disease เป็น myotonia congenita ชนิดยีนเด่นจาก CLCN1 ช่องคลอไรด์ทำงานลดลงทำให้กล้ามเนื้อหดตัวค้าง ผู้ป่วยแข็งเกร็งเมื่อเริ่มขยับหลังพักแล้วดีขึ้นเมื่อขยับซ้ำ กล้ามเนื้อโตแต่ไม่อ่อนแรง EMG พบ myotonic discharges รักษาด้วย mexiletine เมื่อจำเป็น และต้องหลีกเลี่ยง suxamethonium

formal: Spinal vascular malformations in the thoracic region causing progressive myelopathy, venous congestion or haemorrhage.
simple: Abnormal tangles of blood vessels in the mid spine that can cause leg weakness and numbness.
th: Spinal dural AV fistula ระดับทรวงอกส่วนล่างและ conus เป็นรอยโรคที่พบบ่อยที่สุดในกลุ่มนี้ ทำให้ขาอ่อนแรงชาและกลั้นปัสสาวะไม่ได้ช้า ๆ ในชายอายุมาก สัญญาณอันตรายคือเลวลงหลังออกกำลังหรือหลังให้สเตียรอยด์ ต้องส่งตรวจ spinal angiography เพื่อหาจุดรั่วแล้วรักษาด้วยการอุดหรือผ่าตัดตัดหลอดเลือดดำ
tempoNote: Dural fistulas: months to years, often stepwise and aggravated by exertion; intramedullary lesions in this region may bleed abruptly
feat: Mean age of dural fistula patients is around 60, mostly men; the fistula usually sits in the lower thoracic or upper lumbar canal at a root sleeve, yet it causes oedema of the conus several segments away
Back pain in about a third, then leg weakness, numbness, urinary retention or urgency, constipation and erectile dysfunction; gait fatigue after walking or standing is typical
Mixed picture: spastic legs with brisk knee jerks and extensor plantars together with absent ankle jerks from conus involvement
Deterioration after steroid injection, lumbar epidural procedures, a hot bath or spinal surgery for presumed stenosis is a recognised warning
Acute collapse (Foix-Alajouanine-type) happens when venous thrombosis or congestion overwhelms the cord; true intradural thoracic AVMs present more with bleeding
inv: MRI thoracolumbar spine: central T2 hyperintensity over several segments with a peripheral hypointense rim, dilated perimedullary veins and mild enhancement
Dynamic contrast MR angiography (or CT angiography) to estimate the fistula level before catheter angiography
Selective spinal digital subtraction angiography with study of all thoracic, lumbar, sacral and sometimes intracranial feeders is the gold standard and is done by an experienced operator

case.story: Eighteen months of heavy, numb legs after walking 300 metres, then urinary urgency; spinal stenosis was diagnosed on lumbar MRI and he had a caudal steroid injection, after which he could hardly stand for a week.
case.exam: Spastic paraparesis 4/5 with brisk knee jerks, absent ankle jerks, sensory loss below T10, reduced anal tone, wide-based gait.
case.tests: MRI T8 to conus shows long T2 hyperintensity with dorsal flow voids; spinal angiography locates a fistula at the left T10 radicular artery draining into a single dilated vein.
case.q: What should have raised suspicion and how is it treated?
case.a: Long cord signal reaching the conus with serpentine voids in an older man, and deterioration after steroid. A spinal dural AV fistula is closed by surgical interruption of the draining vein or by embolisation with liquid agent.

det.patho: In a spinal dural fistula, one radicular artery feeds directly into a radicular vein in the dural root sleeve. Arterial pressure travels backwards into the valveless coronal venous plexus, which reduces the arterial-to-venous pressure difference in the cord and causes chronic venous hypertension, oedema and ischaemia. Most fistulae are acquired and thoracolumbar, and the fistula is often several levels above the conus signal. Intramedullary and perimedullary lesions in the thoracic cord are true high-flow shunts that behave differently and bleed.
det.clinical: The typical course is a slow, stuttering decline in walking with sensory symptoms and sphincter disturbance, and it frequently takes more than a year to reach the right diagnosis. Signs of upper and lower motor neuron involvement can coexist because the conus and lower cord are swollen. Exercise, standing and Valsalva transiently worsen symptoms. Without treatment most patients progress to paraplegia, and a minority collapse acutely in a necrotic myelopathy. Spinal bruit and cutaneous angiomas are uncommon.
det.diagnosis: Consider the diagnosis in anyone with progressive myelopathy and a long central cord signal and no inflammatory or compressive cause. MRI findings are supportive in most but can be subtle, so careful review of the dorsal subarachnoid space is needed. Catheter angiography should look for all feeders, including the artery of Adamkiewicz and iliac and intracranial sources, because the true fistula level cannot be inferred from the cord signal.
det.treatment: The aim is to obliterate the shunt and divide the proximal draining vein. Microsurgical interruption through a small laminectomy has a high lasting success rate, while endovascular embolisation with a penetrating liquid agent can be curative but has a higher recurrence if the vein is not reached. Intramedullary AVMs need a multidisciplinary team using embolisation and/or surgery while preserving the supply of normal cord. Avoid corticosteroids, correct hypotension, and begin physiotherapy and bladder training after closure.
det.prognosis: Gait and strength often stabilise or improve after closure, while bladder and sexual function recover less well; results are best when treatment follows within a year of onset.
pearls: Lumbar stenosis does not cause cord oedema; look for a thoracic fistula when MRI shows long T2 signal in the conus.
Back pain after a steroid injection followed by paraparesis should prompt a vascular cause.
A negative MRI does not exclude the lesion if the story is typical: consider angiography.
det.thd: ในช่วงทรวงอกส่วนล่าง ความผิดปกติที่พบบ่อยคือ dural AV fistula ซึ่งทำให้ความดันหลอดเลือดดำที่ไขสันหลังสูง เกิดบวมและขาดเลือดที่ conus ผู้ป่วยมักเป็นชายอายุมาก มีอาการขาอ่อนแรง ชา และปัสสาวะผิดปกติค่อยเป็นค่อยไป มักถูกวินิจฉัยผิดเป็นโรคกระดูกสันหลังตีบ MRI แสดงสัญญาณ T2 สูงยาวพร้อม flow void และยืนยันด้วย spinal angiography รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัดหรืออุดหลอดเลือดดำที่รั่ว ควรหลีกเลี่ยงสเตียรอยด์เพราะอาจทำให้อาการแย่ลง

name: Thoracic radiculopathies
formal: Dysfunction of thoracic nerve roots, causing band-like trunk pain and sensory loss in a dermatomal pattern; causes include disc or spondylotic compression, herpes zoster, diabetes and tumour.
simple: A pinched or irritated nerve at chest level that causes belt-like pain or numbness around the ribs or abdomen.
more: MRI of the thoracic spine and sometimes EMG guide diagnosis. Treat the cause (decompression, antivirals, glycaemic control) plus neuropathic pain drugs; diabetic forms often improve over months.
th: ความผิดปกติของรากประสาทระดับอก ทำให้ปวดแสบรัดเป็นแถบรอบลำตัวและชาตาม dermatome พบน้อยกว่าคอและเอว สาเหตุ เช่น งูสวัด เบาหวาน หมอนรองกระดูก หรือเนื้องอก
tempoNote: Zoster and diabetic forms evolve over days to weeks; compressive causes over weeks to months
feat: Band-like or girdle pain around the chest or abdomen, often unilateral and sharp or burning
Dermatomal sensory loss or allodynia that follows a thoracic level
Abdominal wall bulging or Beevor sign when lower thoracic roots are involved
Pain aggravated by cough, Valsalva or movement in compressive causes
Vesicular rash in zoster; weight loss and diffuse pain in diabetic truncal neuropathy
inv: MRI of thoracic spine with contrast to exclude cord compression, tumour, abscess and disc herniation
Needle EMG of thoracic paraspinal and abdominal wall muscles when diagnosis is unclear
HbA1c and glucose; zoster serology or PCR when there is no rash but suspicion remains
Chest and abdominal imaging for visceral pain mimics such as cardiac, pulmonary or pancreatic disease

case.who: 62-year-old man from Nakhon Si Thammarat who has had diabetes for 15 years
case.story: For two months he has had a burning, belt-like pain on the left lower chest wall and flank that wakes him at night, with 6 kg weight loss. Heart and abdomen were evaluated without cause.
case.exam: Hypoaesthesia and allodynia over the left T8–T10 dermatomes, mild abdominal wall asymmetry, normal limb strength and reflexes.
case.tests: HbA1c 10.2%; MRI thoracic spine shows no compression; EMG shows denervation in left thoracic paraspinals and lower abdominal wall.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and how is it managed?
case.a: Diabetic truncal radiculopathy (thoracic radiculopathy). Improve glycaemic control gradually, treat pain with gabapentinoids, duloxetine or tricyclics, and reassure that symptoms usually recover over months.

read.where: Chapter 14 Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders — Degenerative Disease of the Spine

det.patho: Thoracic roots are damaged by compression from disc or spondylotic spurs, by herpes zoster in the dorsal root ganglion, by microvasculitis and ischaemia in diabetes, or by tumour and infection of the spine. Roots lie proximal to the dorsal root ganglion so sensory action potentials stay normal. The thoracic spine is rigid, so symptomatic disc disease is uncommon.
det.clinical: The patient has girdle pain and sensory change confined to one or a few dermatomes, with variable motor involvement that shows as abdominal bulging. Diabetic truncal neuropathy produces burning pain, weight loss and often self-limited recovery. Zoster produces vesicles after pain begins. Red flags include myelopathy, bilateral symptoms, fever, cancer history and night pain. Visceral causes such as angina, pleurisy and pancreatitis can mimic.
det.diagnosis: Imaging of the thoracic spine excludes structural lesions, particularly cord compression, and electrodiagnosis shows denervation in thoracic paraspinals and rectus abdominis muscles with normal sensory nerve potentials. Routine nerve studies of the limbs are normal. Diagnosis rests on dermatomal localisation, diabetes status, rash and imaging; remember intrathoracic and abdominal visceral causes.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: antivirals for early zoster, glycaemic control for diabetic radiculopathy, surgery, radiotherapy or antibiotics for compressive, tumour or infectious causes. Neuropathic pain responds to gabapentin, pregabalin, duloxetine or tricyclics, and topical lidocaine; intercostal blocks may be used in refractory cases.
det.prognosis: Diabetic and zoster-related forms commonly improve over months, although postherpetic neuralgia can persist; compressive causes depend on timely treatment.
pearls: Normal limb examination does not exclude thoracic root disease.
Abdominal wall bulging with truncal pain suggests diabetic truncal neuropathy.
Always exclude cord compression with MRI before attributing to a benign cause.
det.thd: Thoracic radiculopathy ทำให้ปวดแสบรัดเป็นแถบรอบอกหรือท้อง ชาตาม dermatome และอาจมีผนังหน้าท้องโป่งข้างเดียว สาเหตุที่พบได้แก่ งูสวัด เบาหวาน หมอนรองกระดูก เนื้องอก หรือการติดเชื้อ ต้องทำ MRI กระดูกสันหลังส่วนอกเพื่อแยกการกดทับไขสันหลัง และอาจตรวจ EMG รักษาตามสาเหตุและใช้ยาลดปวดประสาท เช่น gabapentin, pregabalin, duloxetine

name: Thoracic spine degenerative disease
formal: Wear-related degeneration of thoracic discs and joints, rarely causing myelopathy or radiculopathy with band-like pain.
simple: Age-related wear in the mid back that can sometimes press on the spinal cord or nerves.
th: ความเสื่อมของหมอนรองกระดูกและข้อต่อในกระดูกสันหลังส่วนอก ซึ่งไม่ค่อยทำให้ไขสันหลังหรือรากประสาทถูกกด แต่ถ้าเกิดจะปวดรัดรอบอกหรือขาเกร็งอ่อนแรง
tempoNote: Usually slowly progressive; occasional acute deterioration with disc extrusion
feat: Mid-back pain and band-like chest or abdominal pain (thoracic radiculopathy)
Myelopathy: spastic paraparesis, sensory level on the trunk, bladder disturbance
Thoracic discs are often calcified; ossified ligamentum flavum is common in East Asian patients
Symptoms can mimic cardiac, gallbladder or renal disease
Much rarer than cervical or lumbar degenerative disease
inv: MRI whole spine (to define level and exclude tandem lesions)
CT to show calcified discs or ossified ligaments for surgical planning
Exclude cardiac and abdominal causes of band-like pain

case.story: One year of stiff legs and frequent trips, recent urinary urgency; mild mid-back ache.
case.exam: Spastic paraparesis, brisk knee and ankle jerks, upgoing toes, sensory level at T10, normal arms.
case.tests: MRI: T10–11 cord compression with T2 cord signal; CT shows ossified ligamentum flavum posteriorly.
case.q: Why is the arm examination normal and what is the treatment?
case.a: The lesion is thoracic, below the arm segments; decompressive laminectomy by a spinal surgeon.

read.where: Chapter 14 Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders — Degenerative Disease of the Spine

det.patho: The thoracic spine is stabilised by the rib cage, so degenerative change is less frequent, but the canal is narrow and the cord has a limited blood supply. Disc herniation (often calcified), facet hypertrophy and ossification of the ligamentum flavum or posterior longitudinal ligament can compress the cord. OLF is relatively common in Japanese, Chinese and other Asian populations.
det.clinical: Presentations include axial pain, radicular band pain at the level and slowly progressive myelopathy with spastic gait and sphincter changes. Upper limbs are spared. Disc herniation can produce surprisingly variable symptoms and is often misdiagnosed initially.
det.diagnosis: MRI confirms the level and cord signal change; many incidental thoracic disc protrusions exist, so correlate with the clinical level. CT characterises calcification or ossification that affects surgical approach. Rule out intrinsic cord disease and vascular malformations.
det.treatment: Pain without myelopathy is managed conservatively. Progressive or significant myelopathy requires surgical decompression; calcified central discs may need anterior or lateral approaches, and OLF is treated by posterior laminectomy. Surgery carries higher neurological risk than in cervical or lumbar regions.
det.prognosis: Early surgery for myelopathy gives the best results; long-standing deficits improve less.
pearls: Sensory level on the trunk with normal arms: image the thoracic spine.
Band-like pain can masquerade as visceral disease.
Ossified ligamentum flavum is a common cause in Asian patients.
det.thd: โรคกระดูกสันหลังส่วนอกเสื่อมพบน้อยกว่าคอและเอว แต่ช่องไขสันหลังแคบ จึงอาจกดไขสันหลังจนขาเกร็งอ่อนแรง มีระดับความรู้สึกที่ลำตัว และปัสสาวะผิดปกติ หรือกดรากประสาททำให้ปวดรัดรอบอก สาเหตุได้แก่ หมอนรองกระดูกที่มีหินปูน และ ossified ligamentum flavum ซึ่งพบบ่อยในชาวเอเชีย MRI และ CT ช่วยวินิจฉัย หากมี myelopathy ต้องผ่าตัดลดการกด

name: Thoracic spine disease
formal: Disorders of the thoracic spine such as degenerative disease, tumour or infection causing myelopathy and radicular pain.
simple: Problems in the middle of the spine that can compress the spinal cord or nerve roots.
th: กลุ่มโรคของกระดูกสันหลังส่วนอก เช่น หมอนรองกระดูกเสื่อม เนื้องอก หรือการติดเชื้อ ทำให้ไขสันหลังเสื่อมและปวดตามรากประสาทรอบลำตัว
tempoNote: Degenerative disease over months to years; tumour and infection over weeks
feat: Band-like chest or abdominal pain in a dermatomal pattern (thoracic radiculopathy)
Spastic paraparesis, sensory level on the trunk, bladder disturbance
Arms normal — distinguishes from cervical myelopathy
Causes: calcified thoracic disc, ossified ligamentum flavum or posterior longitudinal ligament, metastases, TB, infection
Umbrella term rather than a single disease
inv: MRI whole spine (thoracic disease is easily missed on lumbar-only imaging)
CT for calcification and ossified ligaments
Bone scan or PET and biopsy when malignancy or infection is suspected

case.story: Eight months of stiff legs, tripping and band-like numbness around his lower chest.
case.exam: Spastic paraparesis, brisk knee and ankle reflexes, upgoing plantars, sensory level T8, normal arms.
case.tests: MRI: ossified ligamentum flavum compressing the cord at T9–T10; CT confirms ossification.
case.q: Why was lumbar MRI earlier normal, and what is the treatment?
case.a: The lesion was above the lumbar field; decompressive laminectomy is indicated for progressive myelopathy.

read.where: Chapter 14 Spinal Column and Spinal Cord Disorders — Degenerative Disease of the Spine

det.patho: The thoracic canal is narrow and the cord's blood supply relatively tenuous, so small compressive lesions cause myelopathy. Degenerative thoracic discs are often calcified and central. Ossification of ligaments is particularly common in East Asian populations, including Thailand. Metastases favour the thoracic spine because of its size and venous drainage.
det.clinical: Thoracic myelopathy presents with leg spasticity, gait disturbance and sensory level; pain may be thoracic or radicular. Herpes zoster, intercostal neuralgia and visceral disease can mimic radicular pain. A sensory level must be examined on the back as well as the front.
det.diagnosis: MRI of the entire spine identifies the level and nature of compression or intrinsic lesion; CT helps surgical planning for ossification. Investigate red flags (weight loss, fever, cancer history) with targeted tests. Neurophysiology rarely adds much.
det.treatment: Depends on cause: decompression for compressive degenerative lesions with progressive myelopathy; radiotherapy and surgery for metastases; antimicrobials for infection. Conservative care for radicular pain without myelopathy. Thoracic surgery carries a higher neurological risk than cervical or lumbar surgery.
det.prognosis: Outcome depends on cause and on the duration and severity of myelopathy before treatment.
pearls: Spastic legs with normal arms: image the thoracic spine.
Sensory level can be several segments below the actual lesion.
Ossified ligamentum flavum and OPLL are common in Asian patients.
det.thd: Thoracic spine disease เป็นคำรวมของโรคกระดูกสันหลังส่วนอก เช่น หมอนรองกระดูกเสื่อม เอ็นกลายเป็นกระดูก เนื้องอกแพร่กระจาย และการติดเชื้อ ผู้ป่วยขาเกร็งอ่อนแรง เดินลำบาก มีระดับความรู้สึกที่ลำตัวและปวดรอบอก แต่แขนปกติ ต้องทำ MRI ส่วนอก เพราะ MRI เอวอย่างเดียวจะพลาด การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ เช่น ผ่าตัดลดการกด

Arms and hands involved, cervical compression on MRI

name: Thought disorder
formal: Disorganised thinking evident as derailed, tangential or incoherent speech, a core feature of schizophrenia and some organic brain states.
simple: Muddled, jumbled thinking that makes speech hard to follow.
th: ความผิดปกติของรูปแบบความคิดที่สะท้อนออกมาเป็นการพูดวกวน ออกนอกเรื่อง หรือไม่ต่อเนื่อง พบในโรคจิตเภทและภาวะสมองผิดปกติบางอย่าง เป็นอาการไม่ใช่โรค
tempoNote: Depends on cause: hours in delirium, weeks in acute psychosis, years in schizophrenia or dementia
feat: A sign, not a disease: abnormal organisation of thought shown through speech
Tangential answers, derailment between topics, neologisms or incoherent word salad
Poverty of speech content or thought blocking in negative forms
Seen in schizophrenia, mania, delirium, frontal and temporal lesions, and some dementias
Must be separated from aphasia, where the language system itself is damaged
inv: Mental status exam with formal language testing (naming, repetition, comprehension)
Screen for delirium causes: infection, metabolic tests, drugs
MRI and EEG if acute, late onset or with focal neurological signs

case.story: Admitted with a urinary infection; overnight his speech becomes rambling and drifts from topic to topic with odd made-up words.
case.exam: Inattentive, cannot name months backwards; repetition and naming are intact; no hemiparesis.
case.tests: Sodium 122 mmol/L; urine culture growing E. coli.
case.q: Is this a psychotic thought disorder or something else?
case.a: Disorganised thinking from delirium due to sepsis and hyponatraemia; attention deficit and acute fluctuation are the clues.

det.patho: Formal thought disorder reflects a failure to organise and monitor the flow of ideas, linked to dysfunction of frontal-temporal language and executive networks and semantic processing. In schizophrenia it correlates with superior temporal and prefrontal abnormalities. Organic causes disrupt the same networks through diffuse metabolic insult or focal lesions.
det.clinical: Positive forms include tangentiality, derailment, pressure, neologisms and incoherence; negative forms include poverty of speech, poverty of content and blocking. In mania, ideas race with recognisable links (flight of ideas). In delirium, disorganised thinking accompanies inattention and fluctuation. The entry describes a sign rather than a neurological disease.
det.diagnosis: Assess through conversation and record verbatim samples. The key bedside step is separating thought disorder from aphasia: aphasic patients have naming, repetition or comprehension errors, whereas thought-disordered patients usually have intact language mechanics. Acute onset, older age or focal signs require a medical and neurological work-up.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: antipsychotics for primary psychosis, mood stabilisers for mania, correction of the medical trigger in delirium, and management of structural lesions. Avoid sedating a delirious patient without searching for the underlying problem.
det.prognosis: Depends entirely on the cause; delirium-related disorganisation usually resolves with the trigger.
pearls: Check naming and repetition — if they fail, think aphasia rather than psychosis.
New disorganised speech in an older inpatient is delirium until proved otherwise.
Flight of ideas in mania keeps logical links; derailment in schizophrenia loses them.
det.thd: Thought disorder คือความผิดปกติของรูปแบบความคิดที่เห็นได้จากการพูด เช่น ออกนอกเรื่อง วกวน หรือใช้คำแปลก ๆ เป็นอาการไม่ใช่โรค พบในโรคจิตเภท mania delirium และรอยโรคสมองบางตำแหน่ง ต้องแยกจาก aphasia โดยตรวจการเรียกชื่อ การพูดตาม และความเข้าใจภาษา ถ้าเริ่มเป็นเฉียบพลันหรือในผู้สูงอายุควรหาสาเหตุทางกายก่อนเสมอ

name: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
formal: Thrombotic microangiopathy from ADAMTS13 deficiency causing haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, fever, renal dysfunction and fluctuating neurological deficits.
simple: A blood clotting disorder causing low platelets and tiny clots that can cause confusion, stroke-like symptoms and kidney problems.
th: thrombotic microangiopathy จากการขาด ADAMTS13 ทำให้เกล็ดเลือดต่ำ เม็ดเลือดแดงแตก และมีอาการทางระบบประสาทที่เปลี่ยนแปลงไปมา
tempoNote: Develops over days; a medical emergency; relapses can occur months to years later
feat: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with schistocytes and severe thrombocytopenia
Fluctuating neurological signs: confusion, headache, transient focal deficits, seizures, stroke
Fever, abdominal pain and mild renal impairment; full classic pentad is uncommon
Usually acquired autoimmune (anti-ADAMTS13 antibodies); rarely congenital
Triggers: pregnancy, HIV, drugs, autoimmune disease
inv: Blood smear for schistocytes, LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin, reticulocytes, DAT negative
ADAMTS13 activity (<10% confirms) and inhibitor; PLASMIC score while awaiting results
Troponin, renal function, HIV, pregnancy test; MRI brain for neurological symptoms

case.story: Three days of headache and episodes of right hand numbness and word-finding difficulty that come and go; bruises on her legs.
case.exam: Mild fever, petechiae, intermittent expressive aphasia, no fixed weakness.
case.tests: Hb 7.2 g/dL, platelets 12,000/µL, many schistocytes, LDH 1,450 U/L, creatinine 1.3 mg/dL; ADAMTS13 activity <5% with inhibitor.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the urgent treatment?
case.a: Immune TTP; urgent plasma exchange with corticosteroids, plus caplacizumab and rituximab.

det.patho: ADAMTS13 cleaves ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers. When its activity is severely reduced, usually by autoantibodies, these multimers cause platelet-rich microthrombi in small vessels of brain, heart and kidneys. Red cells are sheared, causing haemolysis. Congenital TTP results from biallelic ADAMTS13 variants and often presents in childhood or pregnancy.
det.clinical: Neurological involvement occurs in most patients and fluctuates: headache, confusion, transient aphasia or weakness, seizures and coma. Ischaemic strokes may appear on MRI even in milder cases. Cardiac involvement can cause sudden death. Renal impairment is usually mild, unlike haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
det.diagnosis: Suspect TTP when thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic haemolysis appear together; the PLASMIC score estimates likelihood. ADAMTS13 activity below 10% confirms the diagnosis. Exclude DIC (normal coagulation in TTP), HUS, malignant hypertension, HELLP syndrome and drug-induced microangiopathy.
det.treatment: Begin daily plasma exchange as soon as TTP is suspected, together with corticosteroids. Caplacizumab, an anti-vWF nanobody, reduces thrombotic events and time to platelet recovery; rituximab lowers the risk of relapse. Platelet transfusion is avoided unless there is life-threatening bleeding. Congenital TTP is treated with plasma infusion or recombinant ADAMTS13.
det.prognosis: Untreated mortality is very high; with prompt plasma exchange most survive, but relapses and long-term cognitive and mood problems are common.
pearls: Low platelets plus anaemia plus fluctuating neuro signs: look at the blood smear now.
Do not give platelets routinely in TTP.
Survivors need long-term monitoring of ADAMTS13 for relapse.
det.thd: TTP เป็นภาวะฉุกเฉินจากการขาดเอนไซม์ ADAMTS13 มักเกิดจาก autoantibody ทำให้เกิดลิ่มเลือดเล็กในหลอดเลือดสมองและอวัยวะอื่น ผู้ป่วยมีเกล็ดเลือดต่ำ เม็ดเลือดแดงแตกพบ schistocyte และมีอาการทางสมองที่เปลี่ยนแปลงไปมา เช่น สับสน พูดไม่ได้ชั่วคราว หรือชัก รักษาด่วนด้วย plasma exchange ร่วมกับ steroid, caplacizumab และ rituximab

qx.stem: A 34-year-old nurse in Songkhla presents with fluctuating confusion and a transient right hemiparesis. Platelets are 11 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 7.4 g/dL with schistocytes, LDH is raised, creatinine is near normal and PT and aPTT are normal. The PLASMIC score is high.
qx.q: What should be done before the ADAMTS13 result returns?
opts: Platelet transfusion to correct thrombocytopenia
Intravenous alteplase for the focal deficit
Start plasma exchange with corticosteroids, and add caplacizumab when available, without waiting
Heparin infusion for suspected microvascular thrombosis

qx.why: Microangiopathic haemolysis with severe thrombocytopenia and neurological signs and a high PLASMIC score warrants immediate plasma exchange and steroids, as mortality is high without treatment. Platelet transfusion can fuel thrombosis and is avoided unless life-threatening bleeding occurs, and thrombolysis or heparin are not effective in a primary ADAMTS13 deficiency.

name: Thunderclap headache
formal: Abrupt severe headache reaching maximum intensity within a minute, requiring exclusion of subarachnoid haemorrhage, RCVS, dissection and venous thrombosis.
simple: A sudden extremely severe headache that peaks within a minute and needs urgent investigation.
th: ปวดศีรษะรุนแรงทันทีถึงจุดสูงสุดภายใน 1 นาที ต้องตรวจหา SAH, RCVS, หลอดเลือดฉีกขาด และหลอดเลือดดำอุดตันทุกครั้ง
tempoNote: Peak within 60 seconds, lasting at least 5 minutes; RCVS causes recurrent thunderclaps over 1–3 weeks
feat: Severe headache reaching maximal intensity in under a minute
Causes: SAH, RCVS, cervical artery dissection, CVT, pituitary apoplexy, ICH, SIH, colloid cyst, PRES
Triggers: exertion, sex, Valsalva, postpartum, vasoactive drugs
Primary thunderclap headache is a diagnosis of exclusion
inv: Non-contrast CT within 6 hours (very sensitive for SAH)
LP for xanthochromia if CT negative beyond 6 hours

case.story: Third explosive headache in a week, each during exertion, 10 days after delivery; using a nasal decongestant.
case.exam: BP 158/96 mmHg, no meningism or focal signs.
case.tests: CT and LP normal; CTA shows multifocal segmental narrowing of MCA and PCA branches.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what should be avoided?
case.a: Postpartum RCVS presenting as recurrent thunderclap headache; stop vasoactive drugs, use calcium channel blocker (nimodipine) and avoid triptans, ergots and glucocorticoids.

det.patho: Thunderclap headache is a syndrome, not a disease: sudden pain arises when pain-sensitive structures (meninges, large arteries, dural sinuses) are abruptly stretched, irritated by blood, or exposed to rapid pressure changes. Aneurysmal SAH accounts for about 10% of cases presenting to emergency departments; RCVS is the commonest cause in recurrent thunderclap. Some cases have no identifiable cause (primary thunderclap headache).
det.clinical: The defining feature is the speed of onset rather than severity alone. Associated syncope, vomiting, neck stiffness, seizures or focal deficits raise the likelihood of a structural cause. Recurrent attacks over days, especially postpartum or with serotonergic or sympathomimetic drugs, favour RCVS. Orthostatic features suggest SIH; visual loss and ophthalmoplegia suggest pituitary apoplexy.
det.diagnosis: Non-contrast CT is first-line; within 6 hours of onset a modern CT read by an experienced radiologist virtually excludes SAH. Beyond that, LP with spectrophotometry for xanthochromia (after 12 hours) is needed if CT is negative. Vascular imaging (CTA/MRA) and venous imaging follow when SAH is excluded but suspicion persists. RCVS vasoconstriction may appear only on repeat imaging after several days.
det.treatment: Management depends on the cause: aneurysm securing and nimodipine for SAH, withdrawal of triggers and calcium channel blockers for RCVS, antithrombotic therapy for dissection, anticoagulation for CVT. Analgesia should avoid vasoconstrictors until RCVS and vascular causes are excluded. Primary thunderclap headache needs reassurance and observation.
det.prognosis: Prognosis follows the cause; primary thunderclap headache is benign, while SAH carries substantial mortality.
pearls: Peak in under a minute = thunderclap: always investigate.
CT within 6 hours; otherwise LP for xanthochromia.
Recurrent thunderclaps over days = RCVS until proven otherwise.
det.thd: Thunderclap headache คือปวดศีรษะรุนแรงทันทีถึงจุดสูงสุดภายใน 1 นาที เป็นกลุ่มอาการที่ต้องหาสาเหตุทุกครั้ง โดยเฉพาะ SAH, RCVS, หลอดเลือดคอฉีกขาด, CVT และ pituitary apoplexy ทำ CT ทันที ถ้าเกิน 6 ชั่วโมงและ CT ปกติให้เจาะน้ำไขสันหลังดู xanthochromia ตามด้วย CTA หรือ MRA รักษาตามสาเหตุและหลีกเลี่ยงยาหดหลอดเลือดจนกว่าจะแยก RCVS ได้

det.patho: Thymomas arise from thymic epithelial cells, which present self-antigens to developing T cells. Neoplastic epithelium often lacks AIRE expression and fails to delete autoreactive T cells, which escape and drive autoimmunity against AChR, titin, ryanodine receptor, CASPR2 and other targets. This explains the strong association with multiple paraneoplastic syndromes.
det.clinical: Many tumours are found incidentally or during MG evaluation. Thymoma-associated MG tends to be generalised and moderate to severe and peaks in middle age. Other presentations include neuromyotonia, Morvan syndrome, autoimmune encephalitis, myocarditis with myositis (also seen with checkpoint inhibitors) and haematological or immunodeficiency syndromes. Autoimmune disease may appear even years after resection and can signal recurrence.
det.diagnosis: Contrast CT of the chest is the first test; MRI or PET can clarify invasion. Biopsy is often avoided for resectable lesions because of seeding concerns. Staging by Masaoka–Koga or TNM and WHO histological typing guide adjuvant treatment.
det.treatment: Complete surgical resection with thymectomy is standard, performed once MG is controlled (pre-operative IVIG or plasma exchange if bulbar or respiratory weakness). Radiotherapy and chemotherapy are used for invasive, incompletely resected or recurrent tumours. MG usually still needs immunotherapy after surgery; follow-up imaging continues for many years.
det.prognosis: Encapsulated tumours have excellent survival after resection; invasive types and thymic carcinoma do worse.
pearls: Image the chest in every new AChR-positive MG.
Anti-titin or anti-RyR positivity in a young MG patient suggests thymoma.
New autoimmune syndrome years after thymoma surgery: look for recurrence.
det.thd: Thymoma เป็นเนื้องอกของต่อมไทมัสในช่องอกส่วนหน้า เกี่ยวข้องกับ MG ราว 10–15% และโรคภูมิต้านตนเองอื่น เช่น neuromyotonia, Morvan syndrome และ red cell aplasia ผู้ป่วย MG ใหม่ทุกรายควรทำ CT ช่องอก การรักษาหลักคือผ่าตัด thymectomy หลังคุม MG ให้คงที่ และอาจต้องฉายแสงในชนิดลุกลาม

case.exam: Bilateral fatigable ptosis, nasal voice after counting to 30, neck flexor weakness, proximal limb fatigability.

case.q: What is the definitive management after stabilising MG?

det.patho: About 10–15% of MG patients have a thymoma, and around a third of thymoma patients develop MG. The tumour's epithelial cells express muscle-like antigens and allow escape of autoreactive T cells because of defective AIRE expression and immature T-cell selection. The resulting antibodies target AChR and often titin and ryanodine receptors, which mark more severe disease.
det.clinical: Weakness is generalised in most, with bulbar and respiratory involvement more common than in other MG subgroups. Other thymoma-related autoimmune conditions include neuromyotonia, autoimmune encephalitis, myositis with myocarditis, pure red cell aplasia and hypogammaglobulinaemia (Good syndrome). MG may first appear after thymectomy or with tumour recurrence. Immune checkpoint inhibitors given for thymic tumours can trigger severe MG-myositis-myocarditis overlap.
det.diagnosis: Every newly diagnosed MG patient should have chest CT or MRI. Strongly positive AChR antibodies plus titin or RyR antibodies in a patient under 60 raise suspicion of thymoma. Electrophysiology confirms the junction defect. Staging (Masaoka-Koga) and WHO histology guide oncological management.
det.treatment: Stabilise myasthenia first, using IVIG or plasma exchange before surgery if there is bulbar or respiratory weakness. Complete surgical resection of the thymoma is the key step; radiotherapy or chemotherapy is added for invasive tumours. Most patients still need long-term immunotherapy: steroids, azathioprine or mycophenolate, and newer agents such as complement inhibitors (eculizumab, ravulizumab, zilucoplan) or FcRn blockers (efgartigimod, rozanolixizumab) for refractory AChR-positive disease. Monitor for tumour recurrence with periodic chest imaging.
det.prognosis: MG after thymoma surgery often improves less than in thymic hyperplasia, and long-term immunotherapy is common; survival depends mainly on tumour stage.
pearls: Image the chest in every new MG patient.
Anti-titin or anti-RyR antibodies in a young or middle-aged patient point towards thymoma.
Optimise MG before thymectomy to avoid post-operative crisis.
det.thd: MG ที่มี thymoma พบประมาณ 10–15% ของผู้ป่วย MG มักอายุกลางคน AChR antibody ผลบวกสูง และมักรุนแรง มีอาการกลืนลำบากหรือหายใจล้มเหลวได้ ต้องทำ CT หรือ MRI ทรวงอกในผู้ป่วย MG ทุกราย การรักษาคือควบคุม MG ให้คงที่ก่อน แล้วผ่าตัดเอา thymoma ออกทั้งหมด ร่วมกับยากดภูมิระยะยาวและติดตามการกลับเป็นซ้ำของเนื้องอก

qx.q: What is the most appropriate management of the mediastinal mass?

Surgical resection (thymectomy) once myasthenia is optimised before surgery

Thymoma is an indication for complete surgical resection regardless of MG severity, after optimising neuromuscular function (sometimes with IVIG or plasma exchange) to avoid postoperative crisis. Percutaneous biopsy of a resectable encapsulated mass risks seeding, and observation or primary radiotherapy is not standard.

det.patho: Thyroid hormone controls muscle metabolism, ion channels and nerve function. Excess increases catabolism and Na/K-ATPase activity, which, with channel variants such as KCNJ18, can trigger potassium shifts into cells and paralysis. Deficiency slows muscle contraction and relaxation, causes glycosaminoglycan deposition (carpal tunnel) and raises CK. Autoimmune thyroid disease associates with myasthenia and SREAT.
det.clinical: Hyperthyroid patients present with proximal weakness, tremor, sometimes bulbar weakness, and in Asian men with periodic paralysis after carbohydrate loads or rest after exercise. Hypothyroid patients have fatigue, cramps, myalgia, pseudohypertrophy, slow reflexes, carpal tunnel syndrome, ataxia and sometimes coma. Neuromuscular features may dominate the presentation.
det.diagnosis: Thyroid function tests should be part of the evaluation of any myopathy, periodic paralysis, unexplained neuropathy or encephalopathy. CK, potassium during attacks and EMG help characterise the problem.
det.treatment: Correct the thyroid state; most neuromuscular effects reverse over weeks to months. Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis requires careful potassium replacement and propranolol until euthyroid. Treat associated myasthenia or SREAT according to their own protocols.
det.prognosis: Generally excellent once euthyroid; attacks of periodic paralysis stop with control of thyrotoxicosis.
pearls: Check TSH in any myopathy with raised CK.
Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis is common in young Asian men and may be the first sign of hyperthyroidism.
Delayed relaxation of the ankle jerk suggests hypothyroidism.
det.thd: โรคไทรอยด์ทั้งเกินและขาดมีผลต่อเส้นประสาทและกล้ามเนื้อ ไทรอยด์เกินทำให้ต้นแขนขาอ่อนแรง มือสั่น และ thyrotoxic periodic paralysis ที่พบบ่อยในชายเอเชียอายุน้อย ไทรอยด์ขาดทำให้ปวดกล้ามเนื้อ CK สูง reflex คลายตัวช้า และ carpal tunnel ควรตรวจ TSH ในผู้ป่วยกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงทุกราย การแก้ไขระดับฮอร์โมนมักทำให้อาการดีขึ้น

det.patho: Excess thyroid hormone accelerates protein breakdown and mitochondrial energy turnover, reducing contractile efficiency and muscle mass. Type I fibres shift towards faster isoforms. The result is a non-inflammatory, non-necrotic myopathy, which explains the normal CK.
det.clinical: Weakness is common in thyrotoxicosis if sought, often noticed when lifting arms or climbing. Wasting of shoulder muscles can be striking. Older patients with apathetic hyperthyroidism may present mainly with weakness and weight loss. Concomitant MG (in a few percent of Graves patients) and periodic paralysis should be considered when weakness fluctuates.
det.diagnosis: In a compatible clinical setting, thyroid function tests make the diagnosis. CK is typically normal. EMG and biopsy are not routinely needed but may show mild myopathic features. Any fatigability, ptosis or diplopia warrants AChR antibody testing; eye movement limits may also reflect thyroid eye disease.
det.treatment: Restoring euthyroidism with antithyroid drugs, radioiodine or surgery is curative. Beta-blockers relieve adrenergic symptoms and tremor. Physiotherapy helps recovery of strength over the following months.
det.prognosis: Strength recovers fully in most within months of control.
pearls: Proximal weakness with brisk reflexes and normal CK: check TSH.
Hypothyroid myopathy raises CK; thyrotoxic myopathy usually does not.
Graves disease plus diplopia: separate thyroid eye disease from coexisting MG.
det.thd: Thyrotoxic myopathy คือกล้ามเนื้อต้นแขนขาอ่อนแรงและลีบในผู้ป่วยไทรอยด์เป็นพิษ reflex มักไว และ CK ปกติ วินิจฉัยด้วยผลไทรอยด์ ต้องแยก thyrotoxic periodic paralysis และ MG ที่พบร่วมได้ รักษาไทรอยด์ให้ปกติแล้วกำลังกล้ามเนื้อจะฟื้นภายในไม่กี่เดือน

aN: hyperthyroid myopathy | thyrotoxic proximal myopathy | chronic thyrotoxic myopathy | graves myopathy

name: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis
formal: Hypokalaemic periodic paralysis triggered by hyperthyroidism, with episodic proximal weakness, mainly in Asian men.
simple: Episodes of sudden muscle weakness in people with an overactive thyroid, due to low potassium shifts.
more: Check low potassium during attacks with low urinary potassium excretion; thyroid function is abnormal and CACNA1S is usually normal. Treat attacks with cautious oral potassium, avoid rebound hyperkalaemia, give propranolol, and cure the hyperthyroidism.
th: อัมพาตอ่อนแรงทั้งตัวเป็นพัก ๆ ร่วมกับโพแทสเซียมต่ำ ในผู้ป่วยไทรอยด์เป็นพิษ พบมากในชายเอเชีย
tempoNote: Attacks over hours, often at night or morning after carbohydrate or rest post-exercise; stop when euthyroid
feat: Young Asian man with sudden flaccid weakness of legs then arms, often on waking
Triggers: high-carbohydrate meal, alcohol, rest after exercise
Hypokalaemia from intracellular shift, not total body loss
Thyrotoxic signs may be subtle; attack can be the first presentation of Graves disease
Risk of arrhythmia from hypokalaemia
inv: Serum K+ low; TSH suppressed with high free T4/T3
Low urinary potassium excretion (spot K/Cr ratio) supports a shift
ECG: U waves, sinus tachycardia, sometimes high-grade AV block or VT
Phosphate and magnesium often low as well

case.who: 29-year-old male construction worker from Samut Prakan
case.story: After drinking beer and eating a large meal he woke at 4 a.m. unable to move his legs; by morning his arms were weak too. Recent weight loss and sweating.
case.exam: Flaccid quadriparesis with areflexia, normal sensation and cranial nerves, pulse 118/min, fine tremor.
case.tests: K+ 1.9 mmol/L, TSH < 0.01, free T4 high, low urinary K/Cr ratio.
case.q: How should potassium be replaced and what prevents recurrence?
case.a: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis; give small cautious doses of KCl and a non-selective beta-blocker (propranolol) because rebound hyperkalaemia is common; cure hyperthyroidism to stop attacks.

read.where: Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Skeletal Muscle Channelopathies
Chapter 18 Thyroid Disease and the Nervous System

det.patho: Thyroid hormone and catecholamines upregulate Na+/K+-ATPase, while insulin after a carbohydrate meal pushes potassium into cells. In susceptible people, often with variants in the inward-rectifier potassium channel gene KCNJ18 or other loci, reduced potassium efflux allows the membrane to depolarise paradoxically and become inexcitable. Asian men are affected far more often than women despite Graves disease being more common in women.
det.clinical: Attacks start with leg weakness and spread to arms within hours; respiration and bulbar muscles are usually spared. Many patients have only mild thyrotoxic symptoms. Untreated, attacks recur until euthyroidism is achieved. It may be triggered by thyroid hormone excess from any cause, including thyroiditis or exogenous thyroxine.
det.diagnosis: Hypokalaemia with low urinary potassium excretion during a paralytic attack in a thyrotoxic patient is diagnostic. Measure thyroid function in every patient with hypokalaemic paralysis. Distinguish from renal or gastrointestinal potassium loss and from familial periodic paralysis.
det.treatment: Give potassium in small doses with frequent monitoring; aggressive replacement risks rebound hyperkalaemia as potassium returns from cells. Non-selective beta-blockers (propranolol) rapidly abort attacks and prevent recurrence until antithyroid treatment works. Definitive therapy of hyperthyroidism (antithyroid drugs, radioiodine or surgery) eliminates attacks; carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are not useful.
det.prognosis: Excellent once euthyroid; attacks can recur if hyperthyroidism relapses.
pearls: Hypokalaemic paralysis in a Thai man: check TSH first.
Watch for rebound hyperkalaemia — potassium shifts back as the attack ends.
Propranolol both treats and prevents attacks; acetazolamide does not help.
det.thd: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis พบบ่อยในชายเอเชียที่มีไทรอยด์เป็นพิษ ตื่นมาแขนขาอ่อนแรงปวกเปียกหลังกินแป้งหรือดื่มเหล้า โพแทสเซียมต่ำเพราะเคลื่อนเข้าเซลล์ ต้องให้ KCl อย่างระมัดระวังเพราะเสี่ยงโพแทสเซียมสูงตามมา ให้ propranolol และรักษาไทรอยด์ให้หายจึงจะไม่กลับเป็นซ้ำ

qx.stem: A 28-year-old Thai man wakes with inability to stand after a carbohydrate-rich dinner. Examination shows flaccid proximal limb weakness with hyporeflexia, a pulse of 118 and a small goitre. Serum potassium is 1.9 mmol/L and TSH is suppressed.
qx.q: What is the right initial management?
opts: Large infusions of potassium in 5% dextrose without monitoring
Cautious oral or intravenous potassium replacement in non-glucose fluids, with a non-selective beta-blocker and treatment of hyperthyroidism
Insulin and glucose infusion to drive potassium into cells
Acetazolamide as definitive therapy
Plasma exchange
qx.why: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis involves an intracellular potassium shift, and while total body potassium is normal, careful potassium replacement avoids rebound hyperkalaemia. Propranolol attenuates the adrenergic drive and the definitive treatment is control of thyrotoxicosis. Glucose or insulin worsens the shift, and acetazolamide can worsen the attack in this variant.

ddx.pt: Familial, onset in teens, thyroid function normal
Progresses over days, sensory symptoms, normal potassium

aN: tpp | thyrotoxic hypokalemic periodic paralysis | hyperthyroid periodic paralysis | secondary hypokalemic periodic paralysis

name: Thyrotoxicosis chorea
formal: Chorea resulting from hyperthyroidism, typically resolving when thyroid function is normalised.
simple: Jerky involuntary movements caused by an overactive thyroid.
th: chorea ที่เกิดจากภาวะต่อมไทรอยด์ทำงานเกิน และมักหายเมื่อควบคุมไทรอยด์ได้
tempoNote: Develops over weeks with the thyrotoxic state; resolves over weeks after euthyroidism
feat: Generalized or hemichorea in a patient with thyrotoxicosis, more often in women
Accompanied by tremor, weight loss, tachycardia, heat intolerance
MRI of basal ganglia usually normal
Improves with antithyroid therapy; beta-blockers help early
Rare; other causes of chorea should still be excluded
inv: TSH, free T4/T3; TSH receptor antibodies
MRI brain to exclude structural, vascular or hyperglycaemic causes
Glucose, calcium, autoimmune screen (ANA, antiphospholipid), pregnancy test

case.story: Six weeks of restless, fidgety movements of arms and face, palpitations and 6 kg weight loss.
case.exam: Generalized chorea, fine postural tremor, goitre with bruit, lid lag, pulse 128.
case.tests: TSH <0.01 mIU/L, free T4 4.5 ng/dL, TRAb positive; MRI brain normal; ANA and antiphospholipid negative.
case.q: What is the cause of the chorea and how is it treated?
case.a: Thyrotoxicosis (Graves) chorea; propranolol and methimazole, with chorea expected to settle as thyroid function normalises.

det.patho: Excess thyroid hormone is thought to increase dopamine receptor sensitivity in the striatum or alter dopamine turnover, lowering the threshold for chorea. Patients with prior basal ganglia vulnerability (e.g. past Sydenham chorea) may be more susceptible. The mechanism is not fully proven.
det.clinical: Chorea is usually generalized, sometimes unilateral, and appears alongside typical thyrotoxic features. It can be the presenting complaint. Severity often parallels thyroid hormone levels.
det.diagnosis: Thyroid function tests confirm thyrotoxicosis; other causes of chorea, including autoimmune, structural, metabolic and drug causes, are excluded with imaging and blood tests. Improvement with treatment of thyroid disease supports the diagnosis.
det.treatment: Treat thyrotoxicosis with antithyroid drugs, radioiodine or surgery as appropriate. Propranolol often reduces chorea quickly. Dopamine blockers or tetrabenazine can be used briefly for severe chorea.
det.prognosis: Excellent; chorea typically resolves once euthyroidism is achieved.
pearls: Check TSH in every adult with new chorea.
Propranolol helps both tremor and chorea in thyrotoxicosis.
det.thd: Thyrotoxicosis chorea คือ chorea ที่เกิดจากไทรอยด์เป็นพิษ พบบ่อยในผู้หญิงอายุน้อย ร่วมกับใจสั่น น้ำหนักลด และมือสั่น ควรตรวจ TSH ในผู้ป่วย chorea ทุกราย และตัดสาเหตุอื่น เช่น SLE หรือการตั้งครรภ์ รักษาด้วยยาต้านไทรอยด์และ propranolol ซึ่งอาการมักหายเมื่อไทรอยด์กลับมาปกติ

ddx.pt: Child or teenager after streptococcal infection, often with carditis; thyroid normal
Chorea with antiphospholipid antibodies, rash, arthritis, cytopenias
Chorea arising in pregnancy; check pregnancy test in young women

aN: hyperthyroid chorea | thyrotoxic chorea | graves disease chorea | chorea of hyperthyroidism

name: Tic convulsif
formal: Hemifacial spasm sometimes combined with trigeminal neuralgia, producing painful facial spasms.
simple: Painful twitching of one side of the face combined with facial nerve pain.
th: ภาวะที่มีกล้ามเนื้อใบหน้ากระตุกครึ่งซีก (hemifacial spasm) ร่วมกับปวดเส้นประสาท trigeminal ข้างเดียวกัน มักเกิดจากหลอดเลือดกดเบียดเส้นประสาท 5 และ 7
tempoNote: Chronic condition with paroxysms of facial pain and spasm
feat: Coexistent ipsilateral hemifacial spasm and trigeminal neuralgia
Brief electric-shock facial pain triggered by touch, chewing or talking
Involuntary clonic and tonic twitching starting around the eye and spreading to the lower face
Often caused by a tortuous or ectatic vertebrobasilar artery compressing cranial nerves V and VII
Rare; more common in older adults
inv: MRI with high-resolution CISS/FIESTA and MR angiography to show neurovascular compression
Exclude cerebellopontine angle tumour, aneurysm or demyelination

case.who: 63-year-old woman from Lop Buri with hypertension
case.story: For two years her right eyelid has twitched and the twitching now pulls her mouth; in the past six months she has had stabbing right cheek pain when brushing her teeth.
case.exam: Intermittent right hemifacial spasm with eye closure and mouth retraction; trigger zone over right upper lip; no sensory loss.
case.tests: MRI/MRA: elongated right vertebral and basilar artery contacting the right trigeminal root and facial nerve root exit zone.
case.q: What is the combined syndrome and which treatment can address both?
case.a: Tic convulsif from vascular compression of cranial nerves V and VII; microvascular decompression can treat both, with carbamazepine for pain and botulinum toxin for spasm meanwhile.

read.where: Chapter 10 Cranial Nerve VII (The Facial Nerve) — hemifacial spasm

det.patho: Pulsatile vascular contact where the trigeminal and facial roots join the brainstem leads to focal demyelination and ephaptic transmission, producing paroxysmal pain and spasm. A dolichoectatic vertebrobasilar artery is often responsible when both nerves are affected; tumours and other lesions are occasional causes.
det.clinical: Patients have the typical features of both disorders on the same side: involuntary unilateral facial muscle contractions and lancinating pain in trigeminal territory. Either can appear first. Bilateral or progressive deficits suggest a structural lesion.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by MRI showing neurovascular compression and excluding mass lesions or multiple sclerosis. EMG can show lateral spread in hemifacial spasm.
det.treatment: Medical therapy: carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine for trigeminal pain; botulinum toxin injections for hemifacial spasm. Microvascular decompression addressing both nerves offers potential cure in suitable patients. Treat any structural cause.
det.prognosis: Good relief is achieved in most patients after decompression; medical therapy controls symptoms in many.
pearls: Hemifacial spasm + trigeminal neuralgia on the same side = tic convulsif.
Look for a dolichoectatic vertebrobasilar artery on MRA.
Microvascular decompression can treat both problems in one operation.
det.thd: Tic convulsif คือภาวะที่มี hemifacial spasm ร่วมกับ trigeminal neuralgia ข้างเดียวกัน มักเกิดจากหลอดเลือดที่ยาวคดเคี้ยวกดเส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 5 และ 7 ตรวจ MRI และ MRA เพื่อดูการกดทับและแยกเนื้องอก รักษาด้วย carbamazepine สำหรับอาการปวด botulinum toxin สำหรับอาการกระตุก หรือผ่าตัด microvascular decompression

ddx.pt: Spasm alone without trigeminal pain
Paroxysmal pain without facial muscle spasm
Bilateral eyelid closure, no lower face spread and no pain

aN: painful tic convulsif | hemifacial spasm with trigeminal neuralgia | cushing tic convulsif

name: Tic disorders
formal: Group of neurodevelopmental conditions with sudden repetitive movements or vocalisations, including Tourette syndrome and persistent motor or vocal tic disorders.
simple: Conditions causing sudden repeated movements or sounds that are hard to control.
more: Diagnosis is clinical (DSM-5): onset before 18 years, with motor and vocal tics for more than a year in Tourette. Treat with behavioural therapy (CBIT), alpha-2 agonists or antipsychotics, and botulinum toxin; many improve in adolescence.
ab: Persistent (chronic) motor or vocal tic disorder
th: กลุ่มโรคพัฒนาการทางระบบประสาทที่มีอาการกระตุกหรือส่งเสียงซ้ำๆ ทันที ได้แก่ Tourette syndrome และ persistent motor/vocal tic disorder
tempoNote: Onset in childhood (4–8 years); waxing-waning; often peaks around 10–12 years and improves by adulthood
feat: Tourette: multiple motor plus at least one vocal tic for over 1 year, onset before 18
Persistent motor or vocal tic disorder: only one type for over 1 year
Provisional tic disorder: tics present less than 1 year
Common comorbidities: ADHD, OCD, anxiety, learning problems
Tics wax and wane, worsen with stress or excitement, and can be briefly suppressed
inv: Clinical diagnosis; video from home helps
Screen for ADHD, OCD, anxiety and sleep problems
EEG or MRI only if atypical (late onset, regression, focal signs)

case.story: For 18 months he has had eye blinking, neck jerks and shoulder shrugs, plus repeated sniffing and throat clearing; teachers complain he is distracted.
case.exam: Several brief stereotyped tics during consultation, which he can hold back briefly; neurological exam otherwise normal.
case.tests: None needed; ADHD rating scale suggests inattention.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the first-line treatment?
case.a: Tourette syndrome with ADHD; education and behavioural therapy (CBIT), medication only if tics are impairing.

det.patho: Tic disorders reflect abnormal function in cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits with altered dopaminergic signalling and reduced inhibitory control. They are highly heritable with polygenic risk; rare variants in genes such as SLITRK1 and HDC have been reported. Environmental factors (perinatal stress) may contribute.
det.clinical: Tics begin with simple motor tics of the face and head, followed by vocal tics such as sniffing. Complex tics, echolalia or coprolalia occur in a minority. A premonitory urge relieved by the tic is typical in older children. Severity fluctuates over weeks and is often greatest around early adolescence.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is based on DSM-5 criteria and observation; tests are rarely needed. Distinguish from stereotypies, myoclonus, chorea, functional tics and seizures. Assess impairment and comorbidities, which often matter more than the tics.
det.treatment: Education and reassurance are enough for many. Comprehensive Behavioral Intervention for Tics (CBIT) or exposure and response prevention is first-line when tics are troublesome. Medications include alpha-2 agonists (clonidine, guanfacine), aripiprazole and other antipsychotics; topiramate and botulinum toxin for focal tics are options. DBS is reserved for severe refractory adults.
det.prognosis: Most children improve markedly by early adulthood; a minority continue with significant tics.
pearls: Premonitory urge and brief suppressibility distinguish tics from most other movements.
Treat the comorbidity causing most impairment (often ADHD or OCD).
Sudden-onset complex tics in teenagers may be functional.
det.thd: Tic disorders เป็นกลุ่มโรคที่เริ่มในเด็ก มีการกระตุกหรือส่งเสียงซ้ำๆ ที่กลั้นได้ชั่วคราวและมีความรู้สึกอยากทำก่อน ได้แก่ Tourette syndrome ที่มีทั้ง motor และ vocal tics นานกว่า 1 ปี มักพบร่วมกับ ADHD และ OCD วินิจฉัยทางคลินิก รักษาด้วยการให้ความรู้และ behavioural therapy (CBIT) และใช้ยา เช่น clonidine หรือ aripiprazole เมื่อจำเป็น

ddx.pt: Non-suppressible, random chorea after streptococcal infection, without premonitory urge
Abrupt onset in adolescence or adulthood with complex tics, often after social media exposure
Rhythmic, patterned movements (hand flapping) starting earlier, often with autism; no premonitory urge

aN: tourette syndrome spectrum | persistent chronic motor or vocal tic disorder | provisional tic disorder | gilles de la tourette syndrome | ts

name: Tick paralysis
formal: Acute ascending flaccid paralysis caused by a neurotoxin from feeding engorged ticks, producing areflexia and ataxia through blocked neuromuscular or axonal conduction.
simple: Weakness spreading up the body from a tick bite, which usually goes away once the tick is found and removed.
more: Diagnosis is clinical, by finding the tick, often on the scalp. Nerve studies may show low motor amplitudes. Prompt tick removal leads to recovery within hours to days; untreated cases can cause respiratory failure.
th: อัมพาตจากพิษของเห็บที่ฝังตัวอยู่ ทำให้เดินเซ แล้วอ่อนแรงแบบ flaccid ไล่ขึ้นจากขา reflex หาย ไม่มีไข้และ CSF ปกติ พบในเด็กหญิงผมยาว หาตัวเห็บแล้วดึงออกอาการจะดีขึ้นเร็ว
tempoNote: Develops over 1–2 days after a tick has fed for about 4–6 days; improves within hours to a day of removal
feat: Unsteady gait, then ascending symmetrical flaccid weakness with absent reflexes
Mainly young children, particularly girls with long hair; also outdoor workers
Ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, bulbar weakness and respiratory failure if the tick is left
Little sensory loss, no fever, normal CSF
An engorged tick on scalp, ear canal, neck or groin
inv: Meticulous skin and scalp search, including behind the ears and the ear canal
Nerve conduction: low motor amplitudes with near-normal velocities
CSF normal (separates from GBS); monitor forced vital capacity

case.story: Two days of clumsy walking, then unable to stand; no fever. Family had camped near forest and she has thick long hair.
case.exam: Alert, ataxic, symmetric leg weakness, absent knee and ankle jerks, normal sensation.
case.tests: CSF protein normal; careful scalp search finds an engorged tick behind the left ear.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and what is the essential action?
case.a: Tick paralysis. Remove the whole tick promptly with fine forceps; weakness typically resolves within a day, with respiratory monitoring meanwhile.

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Ticks

det.patho: A neurotoxin in the saliva of an engorged female tick (Dermacentor, Ixodes and others) interferes with acetylcholine release at the motor endplate and slows conduction in distal motor axons. Because secretion rises as the tick feeds, weakness appears only after several days of attachment, and it fades soon once the tick is gone.
det.clinical: The syndrome begins with restlessness, paraesthesia or unsteadiness, then ascending flaccid paralysis with areflexia over hours. Bulbar and ocular involvement and respiratory failure follow if the tick remains. Hair conceals the tick, so scalp examination is essential in every child with acute weakness. Sensation is largely spared and there is no fever.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical: acute ataxia or ascending paralysis, plus finding the tick. Normal CSF protein and quick recovery after removal separate it from Guillain-Barré syndrome. Nerve conduction, if done, shows reduced compound muscle action potentials. Other mimics are botulism, myasthenia, polio, spinal cord compression and periodic paralysis.
det.treatment: Remove the tick intact by grasping close to the skin with fine forceps and pulling steadily, without squeezing the body. Provide supportive care, including respiratory monitoring and ventilatory support if needed. Some tick species, notably Ixodes holocyclus in Australia, can cause progression after removal and need observation and antiserum where available. Check the child for further ticks.
det.prognosis: Excellent with prompt removal; delayed recognition risks death from respiratory failure.
pearls: Look in the hair and ear canals of every child with acute ataxia or weakness.
Rapid recovery after removal and normal CSF argue against GBS.
Ptosis and bulbar signs warn of impending respiratory failure.
det.thd: Tick paralysis เกิดจากพิษของเห็บที่กัดฝังตัว ทำให้เดินเซแล้วอ่อนแรงแบบ flaccid ไล่ขึ้นจากขา reflex หาย ไม่มีไข้ และน้ำไขสันหลังปกติ มักพบในเด็กหญิงผมยาว การวินิจฉัยอาศัยการค้นหาเห็บทั่วศีรษะ หูและผิวหนัง การรักษาคือดึงเห็บออกทั้งตัวอย่างระมัดระวัง ซึ่งอาการจะดีขึ้นใน 1 วัน และเฝ้าระวังการหายใจ

Descending paralysis with early pupillary and cranial nerve involvement

aN: tick toxicosis | tick borne paralysis | ixodid tick paralysis

name: Tickborne disease
formal: Infections transmitted by ticks with neurological involvement, such as Lyme neuroborreliosis, tick-borne encephalitis and Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
simple: Infections spread by tick bites that can sometimes affect the brain and nerves.
th: กลุ่มโรคติดเชื้อจากเห็บ เช่น Lyme, tick-borne encephalitis, rickettsia และ tick paralysis ที่พบในไทยส่วนใหญ่เป็นนักเดินทางหรือโรค rickettsia
tempoNote: Days to weeks after bite; Lyme neurological stage weeks to months later
feat: Lyme: erythema migrans, facial palsy (may be bilateral), painful radiculitis and lymphocytic meningitis
Tick-borne encephalitis: biphasic fever, then meningitis, encephalitis or flaccid limb paralysis in Europe and Asia
Rickettsial spotted fevers: fever, rash, headache and encephalopathy
Tick paralysis: ascending flaccid weakness that reverses after tick removal
Umbrella term; in Thailand the main relevance is travellers and mite-borne scrub typhus
inv: Exposure history and a full skin and scalp search for ticks
Serology and PCR: Lyme two-tier testing, TBE IgM, rickettsial serology or PCR
CSF analysis for pleocytosis and intrathecal antibodies
MRI brain or spine for encephalitis and myelitis

case.who: 45-year-old Thai traveller returning from hiking in Austria
case.story: Ten days after a tick bite she had a flu-like illness, felt well for a week, then developed fever, headache and confusion.
case.exam: Drowsy with neck stiffness, flaccid weakness of the right arm, absent biceps reflex.
case.tests: CSF 120 lymphocytes/µL; TBE IgM positive in serum and CSF; MRI shows anterior horn signal in the cervical cord.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and treatment?
case.a: Tick-borne encephalitis with myelitic involvement. There is no specific antiviral, so give supportive care, and advise vaccination before future travel.

read.where: Chapter 12: Neurologic Manifestations Of Viral Outbreaks
Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — Tickborne Disease
Chapter 52: Headache attributed to infections: nosography

det.patho: Ticks transmit spirochaetes (Borrelia), flaviviruses (TBE virus), rickettsiae, Anaplasma and neurotoxin-bearing salivary products. Each causes a different pattern: immune-mediated radiculitis and meningitis in Lyme disease, parenchymal viral injury in TBE, vasculitis in rickettsial infection, and presynaptic block in tick paralysis. Co-infection from a single tick is possible.
det.clinical: Clinical features depend on geography. Lyme disease evolves from rash to neuroborreliosis, producing the triad of painful radiculitis, meningitis and cranial neuropathy. TBE begins with a flu-like phase, then in about a third causes CNS disease, with anterior horn damage giving flaccid arm weakness. Rickettsial infections cause headache, rash and encephalopathy. In tropical Thailand, true tick-borne illness is rare, and scrub typhus and murine typhus predominate among rickettsial infections.
det.diagnosis: Take a travel and outdoor exposure history and examine the skin. Lyme requires two-tier serology with CSF antibody index in neurological disease; TBE is diagnosed by IgM and IgG in serum and CSF; rickettsial disease by PCR or paired serology. Treatment often has to start before confirmation when rickettsial infection is likely.
det.treatment: Lyme neuroborreliosis responds to doxycycline or IV ceftriaxone for about two to four weeks. Rickettsial infections need prompt doxycycline without waiting for results. TBE has no antiviral and care is supportive, with vaccine prevention. Tick paralysis resolves quickly after careful removal of the tick, which should be sought in the hair. Prevent by protective clothing and prompt tick removal.
det.prognosis: Lyme neurological disease responds well to antibiotics, while TBE can leave residual weakness or cognitive problems in a proportion of cases. Tick paralysis recovers fully when diagnosed.
pearls: Look under the hair for a tick in any acute ascending flaccid paralysis.
Start doxycycline early whenever rickettsial infection is possible.
Biphasic fever with CNS signs after European hiking suggests TBE.
det.thd: Tickborne disease เป็นชื่อกลุ่มโรคที่ติดต่อโดยเห็บ ได้แก่ Lyme disease ที่ทำให้หน้าเบี้ยว ปวดรากประสาท เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ, tick-borne encephalitis ที่มีไข้สองช่วงแล้วสมองอักเสบหรืออ่อนแรงแบบ flaccid, rickettsia ที่มีไข้ ผื่น ปวดศีรษะ และ tick paralysis ที่อ่อนแรงขึ้นจากเท้าและหายเมื่อเอาเห็บออก ในประเทศไทยพบน้อย ส่วนใหญ่เป็นนักเดินทางหรือโรค scrub typhus การวินิจฉัยใช้ประวัติสัมผัส ซีรัม PCR และน้ำไขสันหลัง รักษา Lyme และ rickettsia ด้วย doxycycline ส่วน TBE รักษาแบบประคับประคอง
