name: Tics
formal: Brief, stereotyped, suppressible movements or vocalisations preceded by premonitory urge, characteristic of Tourette syndrome.
simple: Sudden repeated movements or sounds that a person feels a build-up urge to make.
th: Tic คือการเคลื่อนไหวหรือเปล่งเสียงที่เกิดขึ้นเร็ว ซ้ำ ไม่เป็นจังหวะ กลั้นได้ชั่วคราว และมักมีความรู้สึกอยากทำก่อน (premonitory urge) แบ่งเป็นแบบ motor/phonic และ simple/complex พบมากใน Tourette syndrome แต่อาจเกิดจากยา สมองอักเสบหรือสมองบาดเจ็บ การรักษาเริ่มด้วย CBIT (habit reversal) แล้วใช้ยา alpha-2 agonist หรือ aripiprazole/risperidone ตามความรุนแรง
tempoNote: Tics wax and wane over weeks, appear in bouts and typically begin at 5–7 years, peak at 10–12 years and lessen in adolescence in many patients
feat: Simple motor (eye blink, grimace, head jerk, shoulder shrug) and simple vocal (sniff, throat clear, grunt) tics; complex tics include touching, jumping, repeating words or gestures (echophenomena) and, rarely, coprolalia
Premonitory urge or discomfort before the tic, brief voluntary suppression, then relief or rebound; tics are worse with stress and excitement and better with absorbed concentration
Variable repertoire that changes over weeks, and tics persist in light sleep
Primary tics belong to the Tourette spectrum; secondary tics follow drugs (stimulants, levodopa, antiepileptics), encephalitis, head injury, stroke, neuroacanthocytosis or Huntington disease
Commonly accompanied by ADHD, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, anxiety and learning difficulties, which often cause more disability than the tics
inv: Clinical diagnosis with history of onset, family history and comorbid conditions; severity scored with the Yale Global Tic Severity Scale
Drug review and a search for secondary causes only when onset is late, abrupt, rapidly progressive or accompanied by other neurological signs
MRI, genetic or antibody testing for atypical cases; ASO titres or PANDAS testing are not routinely helpful

case.story: Three months of new repetitive grunting and neck jerks after a motorcycle accident with head injury; he had no childhood tics, and takes no stimulant or dopaminergic drugs.
case.exam: Simple motor and vocal tics that he can briefly hold back; mild cognitive slowing; no parkinsonism.
case.tests: MRI shows old frontal contusions.
case.q: How should these tics be classified?
case.a: Secondary (post-traumatic) tics rather than the primary Tourette spectrum, which starts in childhood; manage with education, behavioural therapy and, if needed, a low-dose alpha-2 agonist or aripiprazole.

read.where: 1 - Clinical overview and phenomenology of movement disorders
Chapter 34: Functional (Psychogenic) Movement Disorders: Phenomenology, Diagnosis and Treatment

det.patho: Tics arise from dysfunction in cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits, with disinhibition of striatal motor and limbic regions, abnormal dopaminergic signalling and altered cortical excitability. Twin and family studies show strong heritability with many small genetic contributions, and rare variants in genes such as SLITRK1, HDC and CNTNAP2 have been found in selected families. Premonitory urges relate to insular and cingulate activity, which explains why tics can be suppressed but not eliminated.
det.clinical: Tics typically start at around age 4-8 years, often as eye blinking or throat clearing, spreading in a rostrocaudal direction. The repertoire and severity change over time, they are worse with stress, excitement or tiredness, and many people suppress them in public and release them at home. Tourette syndrome needs both motor and vocal tics for at least a year, but many children with tics have a transient or chronic motor tic disorder. Most patients also have ADHD, OCD or anxiety, and the comorbidity often determines treatment. Sudden severe tics in adolescents or adults, particularly of complex type, may be functional.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical and relies on onset age, semiology, premonitory urge, suppressibility and variability over time. Investigations are rarely needed. Consider secondary causes if the onset is late, the movements are atypical (dystonic, myoclonic, or with parkinsonism), there are neurological signs, or the patient takes stimulants, antiepileptics, levodopa or dopamine blockers. The Yale Global Tic Severity Scale or a video rating guides follow-up, and screening for ADHD, OCD, depression and anxiety is part of the assessment.
det.treatment: Education about the natural course is the first step and many children need nothing more. Comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics (CBIT), which uses awareness training and competing responses, is the first-line treatment when tics are troublesome. Medication is for functional impairment: alpha-2 agonists (clonidine, guanfacine) are preferred for mild to moderate tics with ADHD, and aripiprazole or risperidone are the best-evidenced options for severe tics, with VMAT2 inhibitors, topiramate or botulinum toxin to specific muscle groups as alternatives. Deep brain stimulation of the thalamus or globus pallidus is reserved for rare, severe, treatment-resistant adult cases. Treat comorbid ADHD or OCD in parallel.
det.prognosis: In most children tics improve by late adolescence, with about half having little or no tics as adults; severe adult persistence is uncommon.
pearls: Ask 'Do you feel an urge before the movement?'; a yes strongly favours a tic.
Disability often comes from ADHD, OCD or anxiety rather than the tics themselves.
First-line treatment for bothersome tics is behavioural (CBIT), not a dopamine blocker.
det.thd: Tic คือการเคลื่อนไหวหรือเปล่งเสียงสั้น ๆ ซ้ำ ๆ ที่กลั้นได้ชั่วคราว มักมีความรู้สึกอยากทำก่อน และเปลี่ยนรูปแบบได้ตามช่วงเวลา มักเริ่มช่วงอายุ 5–7 ปี และดีขึ้นเมื่อโตเป็นวัยรุ่น ผู้ป่วยจำนวนมากมี ADHD หรือ OCD ร่วมด้วย การรักษาเริ่มด้วยการให้ความรู้และ CBIT ถ้ามีผลต่อชีวิตจึงใช้ยา เช่น clonidine/guanfacine หรือ aripiprazole/risperidone ถ้าเริ่มมี tic ในผู้ใหญ่ ให้ตรวจหาสาเหตุทุติยภูมิและภาวะ functional tics

name: Tilted optic disc
formal: Congenital anomaly where the optic disc appears oblique, causing a bitemporal visual field defect that mimics chiasmal disease.
simple: A harmless birth variation in the shape of the optic nerve head that can mimic a visual field loss.
ab: Situs inversus of the optic disc
th: ความผิดปกติแต่กำเนิดที่ขั้วประสาทตาเอียง อาจทำให้ลานสายตาบกพร่องด้าน temporal ทั้งสองข้างคล้ายรอยโรคที่ chiasm
tempoNote: Congenital and non-progressive
feat: Oval, obliquely oriented disc with inferonasal crescent and situs inversus of vessels
Often bilateral, associated with myopia and astigmatism
Superotemporal field defects that do not respect the vertical meridian
Normal visual acuity once refraction is corrected
Congenital anomaly, not a disease; mainly important as a chiasmal mimic
inv: Refraction-corrected visual fields: defects cross the vertical midline and improve with myopic correction
OCT of the optic nerve and macula
MRI of chiasm only if defects respect the vertical meridian or progress

case.who: 19-year-old female university student from Nakhon Pathom
case.story: Referred because a screening visual field test showed bitemporal defects; she has no visual complaints apart from high myopia.
case.exam: Visual acuity 6/6 with glasses; both discs oval and tilted with inferonasal crescents; pupils normal.
case.tests: Repeat fields with appropriate lens correction show superotemporal defects crossing the vertical meridian; normal endocrine tests.
case.q: Does she need urgent pituitary imaging?
case.a: Tilted optic discs mimicking bitemporal hemianopia; defects that cross the midline and change with refraction are reassuring, so imaging is only needed if doubt remains.

det.patho: The anomaly is thought to result from incomplete closure of the inferonasal part of the embryonic fissure, leaving a tilted disc with ectasia of the inferonasal fundus. The underlying retinal area is myopic and thinner, producing refractive scotomas.
det.clinical: Usually found incidentally on fundoscopy or visual field testing. Patients may have myopic astigmatism. Visual field loss is commonly superotemporal and may appear bitemporal, leading to unnecessary concern about chiasmal compression. Complications such as choroidal neovascularisation are uncommon.
det.diagnosis: Fundoscopy shows the characteristic disc appearance. Field defects that cross the vertical meridian and lessen with additional refractive correction support a refractive cause. MRI is reserved for defects that respect the midline, progress or are accompanied by other signs.
det.treatment: No treatment is needed apart from correcting refraction. Follow-up with fields and OCT confirms stability.
det.prognosis: Benign and stable.
pearls: Bitemporal defects that cross the midline suggest tilted discs, not chiasmal compression.
Repeat the field test with a stronger myopic lens.
det.thd: Tilted optic disc เป็นความผิดปกติแต่กำเนิดที่ขั้วประสาทตาเอียง มักพบร่วมกับสายตาสั้นและสายตาเอียง อาจทำให้ลานสายตาด้าน temporal บกพร่องทั้งสองข้างจนดูคล้ายเนื้องอกต่อมใต้สมอง แต่ความผิดปกติมักข้ามเส้นแบ่งกลางและดีขึ้นเมื่อแก้ไขค่าสายตา ไม่ต้องรักษา และส่ง MRI เฉพาะเมื่อลักษณะไม่ชัดเจน

name: Tin neurotoxicity
formal: Neurotoxicity of organotin compounds causing headache, cerebral oedema, seizures and cognitive changes.
simple: Brain damage from poisoning with tin-containing chemicals.
th: พิษต่อระบบประสาทจากสารประกอบดีบุกอินทรีย์ ทำให้ปวดศีรษะ สมองบวม ชัก และความจำหรือพฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน
tempoNote: Symptoms appear hours to days after exposure; recovery can take months, with lasting deficits
feat: Triethyltin: cerebral white matter oedema with headache, vomiting, papilloedema and reduced consciousness
Trimethyltin: limbic system damage with memory loss, aggression, confusion, hearing loss and seizures
Exposure from industrial use (PVC stabilisers, biocides, antifouling paint) or contaminated products
Inorganic tin is far less neurotoxic
Hypokalaemia has been reported with trimethyltin
inv: Blood and urine tin levels (specialist laboratory)
MRI: white matter oedema (triethyltin) or limbic changes
EEG for seizures; electrolytes including potassium

case.who: 40-year-old male chemical plant worker from Rayong
case.story: After cleaning a reactor vessel without protection, he developed headache, tinnitus and mood swings, then became forgetful and had two seizures within a week.
case.exam: Disoriented, poor recall, irritable, no focal weakness.
case.tests: Urine tin markedly raised; MRI subtle mesial temporal signal change; potassium 3.0 mmol/L.
case.q: What exposure caused this picture and what is the management?
case.a: Trimethyltin poisoning; remove from exposure, supportive care, seizure control and correction of potassium; occupational investigation of co-workers.

det.patho: Organotin compounds are lipid-soluble and cross the blood-brain barrier. Triethyltin causes vacuolation and intramyelinic oedema of white matter, producing cerebral swelling. Trimethyltin selectively kills neurons in the hippocampus, limbic system and other areas, causing memory and behavioural syndromes. Human data come largely from industrial accidents and a historical French contaminated medicine disaster.
det.clinical: Acute triethyltin intoxication presents with headache, vomiting, visual disturbance and decreased consciousness from raised intracranial pressure. Trimethyltin exposure causes fatigue, headache, tinnitus and hearing loss, then confusion, amnesia, aggression and seizures. Some patients recover, but persisting cognitive deficits are common in severe cases.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis relies on a history of exposure plus a compatible syndrome, supported by raised tin levels in blood or urine. Imaging and EEG show the extent of injury. Exclude infections, autoimmune encephalitis and other toxicants.
det.treatment: There is no proven antidote; chelators have not been shown to help. Management is removal from exposure, decontamination, supportive care, treatment of raised intracranial pressure, seizures and electrolyte abnormalities, and rehabilitation. Report as an occupational exposure.
det.prognosis: Variable; mild cases recover, while severe exposures may cause death or permanent memory impairment.
pearls: Triethyltin swells white matter; trimethyltin damages the limbic system.
Ask about industrial chemicals in any unexplained encephalopathy with seizures.
Inorganic tin is much less toxic than organotins.
det.thd: พิษจากสารประกอบดีบุกอินทรีย์พบในงานอุตสาหกรรม triethyltin ทำให้เนื้อสมองสีขาวบวม ปวดศีรษะ อาเจียน และซึม ส่วน trimethyltin ทำลายระบบ limbic ทำให้ความจำเสื่อม ก้าวร้าว สับสน และชัก วินิจฉัยจากประวัติสัมผัสและระดับดีบุกในเลือดหรือปัสสาวะ ไม่มียาต้านพิษ รักษาแบบประคับประคองและหยุดการสัมผัส

name: Tocopherol (vitamin E) deficiency
formal: Vitamin E deficiency causing spinocerebellar ataxia, neuropathy and retinopathy, from malabsorption or ataxia with vitamin E deficiency (TTPA gene).
simple: Low vitamin E causing poor balance, nerve damage and sometimes vision problems.
more: Deficiency of vitamin E causing spinocerebellar ataxia, neuropathy and retinopathy. Check serum alpha-tocopherol with the lipid ratio; abetalipoproteinaemia and cholestatic malabsorption must be excluded, while AVED has TTPA mutations. Treat with high-dose oral vitamin E, which can halt progression.
th: การขาดวิตามินอี ทำให้เดินเซแบบ spinocerebellar, neuropathy และจอประสาทตาเสื่อม จากการดูดซึมไขมันผิดปกติหรือยีน TTPA
tempoNote: Develops over years of deficiency; progression halts or partly reverses with replacement
feat: Progressive ataxia with proprioceptive loss, areflexia and extensor plantars (Friedreich-like)
Ophthalmoplegia, retinopathy and head titubation in some
Causes: fat malabsorption (cholestasis, cystic fibrosis, short bowel, bariatric surgery), abetalipoproteinaemia, AVED
Develops slowly; children with cholestasis are especially vulnerable
Treatable; early replacement prevents progression
inv: Serum alpha-tocopherol; ratio to total lipids in hyperlipidaemia
Lipid profile, liver function, coeliac and malabsorption tests
Nerve conduction (sensory axonal), TTPA gene testing if no malabsorption

case.story: Three years of worsening unsteady gait in the dark and clumsy hands; no diarrhoea; her parents are first cousins.
case.exam: Head titubation, loss of vibration and joint position in the feet, absent reflexes, bilateral extensor plantars, positive Romberg.
case.tests: Serum vitamin E very low with normal lipids and no malabsorption; echocardiogram normal; homozygous TTPA variant.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and why is it important not to miss?
case.a: Ataxia with vitamin E deficiency (TTPA); lifelong high-dose vitamin E supplementation halts progression.

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Vitamin E
8 Vitamin E deficiency and its neurological effects
Chapter 15 Neurologic Manifestations of Nutritional Disorders
11. NEUROPATHIES ASSOCIATED WITH VITAMIN AND ESSENTIAL MINERAL DEFICIENCIES AND MALABSORPTION

det.patho: Vitamin E is a lipid-soluble antioxidant protecting neuronal membranes. Deficiency causes degeneration of large sensory axons, dorsal columns, spinocerebellar tracts and retina. In AVED, TTPA variants impair hepatic loading of tocopherol into lipoproteins despite normal absorption. In malabsorption, lack of bile or lipoprotein transport limits uptake.
det.clinical: The picture resembles Friedreich ataxia: gait ataxia, proprioceptive loss, areflexia and pyramidal signs. Head tremor, dystonia and retinopathy can occur. In children with cholestatic liver disease, signs may appear within a few years. Cardiomyopathy is less common than in Friedreich ataxia.
det.diagnosis: Measure serum vitamin E in every patient with unexplained ataxia or sensory neuronopathy, interpreting it in relation to lipids. Look for causes of fat malabsorption; if none, test for TTPA variants. Neurophysiology shows sensory axonal neuropathy.
det.treatment: Oral vitamin E replacement, often in high doses, is the treatment; water-miscible forms help malabsorption. In AVED, lifelong supplementation is needed with periodic levels. Treat the underlying gastrointestinal or liver disease.
det.prognosis: Progression stops with replacement, and early treatment may lead to partial recovery; established deficits often persist.
pearls: Check vitamin E in any Friedreich-like ataxia; it is treatable.
Bariatric surgery and chronic cholestasis are modern causes.
AVED is a recessive disease seen in consanguineous families.
det.thd: การขาดวิตามินอีทำให้เกิดอาการคล้าย Friedreich ataxia คือเดินเซ เสียความรู้สึกตำแหน่ง ไม่มี reflex และอาจมีจอประสาทตาเสื่อม สาเหตุมาจากการดูดซึมไขมันผิดปกติ เช่น โรคตับหรือ cystic fibrosis หรือจากยีน TTPA (AVED) ควรตรวจระดับวิตามินอีในผู้ป่วยเดินเซทุกราย เพราะรักษาได้ด้วยการให้วิตามินอีขนาดสูง

name: Todd’s paralysis
formal: Transient focal weakness after a seizure, lasting minutes to hours, and resolving spontaneously.
simple: Temporary weakness of a limb after a seizure that usually clears within hours.
th: อาการอ่อนแรงเฉพาะที่ชั่วคราวหลังชัก นานเป็นนาทีถึงชั่วโมง และหายได้เอง
tempoNote: Follows a seizure; usually resolves within 36 hours, most within a few hours
feat: Focal weakness of a limb or one side after a focal or secondarily generalised seizure
Can also cause postictal aphasia, hemianopia or sensory loss
Resolves spontaneously, typically within hours and almost always by 48 hours
Lateralises the seizure onset to the opposite hemisphere
Can mimic stroke, especially when the seizure was unwitnessed
inv: Glucose immediately; CT/CT angiography or MRI to exclude stroke when the history is unclear
MRI may show transient cortical diffusion restriction or swelling after prolonged seizures
EEG may show postictal focal slowing

case.who: 58-year-old man from Bangkok with a previous left frontal contusion
case.story: Found on the floor confused; wife heard a thud and saw jerking of the right arm. He now cannot move his right arm well.
case.exam: Right arm power 3/5, right facial droop, slowly improving over 2 hours, tongue bitten.
case.tests: Glucose normal; CT/CTA no acute infarct or occlusion; old left frontal encephalomalacia; EEG left frontal slowing.
case.q: What explains the weakness, and what pitfall in stroke pathways must be avoided?
case.a: Todd's paralysis after a focal-to-bilateral seizure; avoid misdiagnosing as stroke and giving thrombolysis unnecessarily, while still imaging to exclude a vascular cause.

read.where: Chapter 3: Is it a vascular event and where is the lesion?

det.patho: The mechanism is not fully understood. Possible explanations include exhaustion of neurons after intense firing, active inhibition, transient hypoperfusion after seizures, and receptor desensitisation. The deficit reflects the cortical region involved in the seizure.
det.clinical: Todd's paralysis follows around 5–13% of seizures, often after prolonged or focal motor seizures. It ranges from mild weakness to complete hemiplegia and may include speech or visual deficits. Duration correlates with seizure length. It can be mistaken for stroke when seizures are unwitnessed.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical: a focal deficit following a seizure that resolves completely. Imaging is still required to exclude stroke, haemorrhage or tumour, especially in older patients or when the history is unclear. Persisting deficit beyond 48 hours should prompt reconsideration.
det.treatment: No specific treatment is needed for the paralysis. Treat the underlying seizure disorder and any cause, and consider antiseizure therapy. In acute stroke pathways, a witnessed seizure at onset is a relative caution for thrombolysis unless imaging confirms an acute arterial occlusion or infarct.
det.prognosis: Full recovery is the rule.
pearls: Postictal weakness lateralises the seizure focus to the contralateral hemisphere.
Seizure-mimic of stroke: always check glucose and image.
Deficits lasting more than 48 hours suggest a structural lesion.
det.thd: Todd's paralysis คืออาการอ่อนแรงเฉพาะที่ชั่วคราวหลังชัก อาจมีพูดไม่ได้หรือมองไม่เห็นครึ่งซีกร่วม มักหายภายในไม่กี่ชั่วโมงและแทบทั้งหมดภายใน 48 ชั่วโมง ช่วยบอกตำแหน่งจุดกำเนิดชักที่สมองซีกตรงข้าม ต้องแยกจากโรคหลอดเลือดสมองด้วยการตรวจน้ำตาลและภาพถ่ายสมอง ไม่ต้องรักษาเฉพาะ รักษาที่สาเหตุการชัก

name: Tolosa–Hunt syndrome
formal: Painful ophthalmoplegia from idiopathic granulomatous inflammation of the cavernous sinus or orbital apex, responsive to steroids.
simple: Painful inflammation behind the eye causing eye movement problems that responds quickly to steroids.
th: ปวดรอบเบ้าตาข้างเดียวร่วมกับอัมพาตเส้นประสาทสมองคู่ III IV หรือ VI จากการอักเสบแบบ granuloma ใน cavernous sinus, superior orbital fissure หรือเบ้าตา ตอบสนองต่อ steroid ดี แต่ต้องแยกโรคอื่นก่อน
tempoNote: Pain leads or accompanies ocular palsy over days; may remit untreated and relapse after months or years
feat: Steady unilateral orbital or periorbital pain, often described as gnawing
Ipsilateral ocular motor palsy (III most often, then VI, IV), sometimes with V1 sensory loss or pupil sympathetic involvement
Optic nerve or VII, VIII involvement occasionally reported
Pain usually settles within days of starting corticosteroids
A diagnosis reached only after tumour, infection, vascular and other inflammatory causes are excluded
inv: Contrast MRI of orbit and cavernous sinus: enhancing soft tissue in the sinus, fissure or orbital apex
ESR, CRP, glucose or HbA1c, ANCA, IgG4, ACE and infection screens (syphilis, TB, fungal where relevant)
MRA or CTA (or catheter angiography) to exclude aneurysm or carotid-cavernous fistula
CSF or tissue biopsy for atypical course or inadequate steroid response; repeat MRI after treatment

case.who: 52-year-old male rubber-plantation worker from Surat Thani
case.story: Five days of dull right eye-socket pain, then drooping of the eyelid and double vision on looking sideways.
case.exam: Right partial ptosis with limited adduction and abduction, normal pupil size, reduced sensation over the right forehead, visual acuity 6/6.
case.tests: MRI: enhancing tissue in right cavernous sinus extending to the superior orbital fissure; MRA normal; HbA1c, ESR, ANCA and syphilis serology negative; nasopharynx clear on endoscopy.
case.q: What is the working diagnosis, and what must be done after pain relief with steroids?
case.a: Tolosa–Hunt syndrome; repeat imaging and observe for relapse, because lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma and IgG4 disease can mimic it and also respond to steroids.

det.patho: Non-specific granuloma-forming inflammation fills the cavernous sinus or extends through the orbital fissure toward the orbit, squeezing or invading the cranial nerves that pass there. The trigger is unknown, and overlap with idiopathic orbital inflammation and IgG4-related disease is recognised. The condition is rare, with an annual incidence usually quoted at about one per million.
det.clinical: Typical patients report steady, boring pain behind or around one eye, followed within days by diplopia from third, fourth or sixth nerve palsy. The first trigeminal division can be involved, and the pupil may be spared or affected. In ICHD-3 (section 13.8) the pain lies on the lesion side, begins around the time the inflammation develops, and is either confined to the V1 area (with or without V2 spread) or provoked by moving the eye. Untreated episodes can settle by themselves and then recur, and spontaneous remission does not prove benignity.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 asks for one-sided orbital or periorbital pain, MRI or biopsy proof of granulomatous inflammation, and palsy of at least one same-side nerve from III, IV or VI, with no better alternative diagnosis. Treat the label as one of exclusion: tumour (lymphoma, meningioma, metastasis, nasopharyngeal carcinoma), infection (fungal, TB, zoster), aneurysm, carotid-cavernous fistula, vasculitis, sarcoidosis, IgG4 disease and diabetic ocular neuropathy all need to be considered. Biopsy is warranted when imaging is atypical, the course is progressive, or steroids fail. Follow-up imaging after treatment should show shrinkage of the lesion.
det.treatment: A standard approach is high-dose corticosteroid, for example prednisolone around 1 mg/kg daily for one to two weeks, then tapered over several weeks, with pain generally easing within 72 hours. Slow tapering and repeat review lower relapse risk. Steroid-sparing agents such as methotrexate or azathioprine are used for repeated relapses, and radiotherapy or biologics are rarely needed. A quick steroid response must not stop the search for lymphoma or other masses.
det.prognosis: Most patients recover cranial nerve function well, but relapses are common and may affect either side. Long-term follow-up is advised.
pearls: Steroid responsiveness is not diagnostic; lymphoma, sarcoid and IgG4 disease also improve.
In Southeast Asia, check the nasopharynx in any painful ophthalmoplegia.
A pupil-involving third nerve palsy with pain needs vascular imaging first.
det.thd: Tolosa–Hunt syndrome คืออาการปวดรอบเบ้าตาข้างเดียวร่วมกับอัมพาตของเส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 3, 4 หรือ 6 จากการอักเสบแบบ granuloma ใน cavernous sinus หรือ superior orbital fissure ผู้ป่วยมักปวดตื้อ ๆ หลังตา แล้วมีหนังตาตกหรือเห็นภาพซ้อน MRI พบเนื้อเยื่อที่ติดสี contrast ใน cavernous sinus ต้องแยกเนื้องอก มะเร็งหลังโพรงจมูก lymphoma การติดเชื้อรา aneurysm และ carotid-cavernous fistula ก่อน การรักษาคือ steroid ขนาดสูงแล้วค่อย ๆ ลด ปวดมักทุเลาภายในไม่กี่วัน แต่ต้องตรวจภาพซ้ำและติดตามเพราะอาจกลับเป็นซ้ำ

name: Tongue protrusion dystonia
formal: Focal oromandibular dystonia where the tongue pushes involuntarily out of the mouth, often task-specific or tardive.
simple: Involuntary pushing of the tongue out of the mouth.
th: oromandibular dystonia ชนิดที่ลิ้นดันออกนอกปากโดยไม่ตั้งใจ มักเกิดขณะกินหรือพูด หรือเป็น tardive
tempoNote: Gradual onset; persistent; may be task-specific to eating or speaking
feat: Involuntary tongue thrusting that pushes food out of the mouth and interferes with speech
Often triggered by eating (feeding dystonia) or talking
Causes: tardive dystonia, neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation, chorea-acanthocytosis, Lesch–Nyhan, idiopathic
May coexist with jaw-opening dystonia and blepharospasm
Weight loss and tongue/lip biting in severe cases
inv: Drug history (antipsychotics, metoclopramide)
MRI brain with iron-sensitive sequences; blood smear for acanthocytes; CK
Wilson screen and genetic testing guided by age and associated features

case.story: Two years of tongue pushing out when he eats so food falls from his mouth; he also bites his lips and tongue. Recently had a seizure.
case.exam: Feeding dystonia with tongue protrusion, mild chorea, absent ankle jerks, lip scarring.
case.tests: CK 1,800 U/L; blood smear shows acanthocytes; MRI shows caudate atrophy.
case.q: Which disorder causes this classic eating dystonia?
case.a: Chorea-acanthocytosis (VPS13A) presenting with tongue protrusion (feeding) dystonia.

det.patho: This is a form of focal dystonia from dysfunction of basal ganglia–sensorimotor networks controlling oral movements. Many cases are secondary to tardive exposure, neuroacanthocytosis, PKAN and other neurodegenerations, while some are idiopathic.
det.clinical: The tongue pushes forward involuntarily, especially when food is placed in the mouth, which leads to feeding difficulties, dysarthria and weight loss. In chorea-acanthocytosis, eating dystonia with self-biting is a hallmark. Combined jaw and lip dystonia is common.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical; the search for a cause is guided by drug history, age and associated signs. Blood smear, CK, liver function, Wilson screen, MRI and genetic panels help identify secondary causes.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin injected into genioglossus can help but carries a risk of dysphagia; careful dosing is essential. Oral agents (anticholinergics, clonazepam, tetrabenazine) give limited benefit. Sensory tricks, dental devices and speech therapy can help; DBS has been used in refractory cases.
det.prognosis: Usually chronic; outcome depends heavily on the underlying cause.
pearls: Food pushed out of the mouth by the tongue is a classic clue to chorea-acanthocytosis.
Genioglossus botulinum toxin requires low doses to avoid dysphagia.
det.thd: Tongue protrusion dystonia คือ dystonia ที่ลิ้นดันออกนอกปาก โดยเฉพาะขณะกินทำให้อาหารหลุดออกจากปาก พบในโรค chorea-acanthocytosis, tardive dystonia, PKAN หรือไม่ทราบสาเหตุ ตรวจหาสาเหตุด้วยประวัติยา MRI และ blood smear หา acanthocyte รักษาด้วย botulinum toxin ขนาดต่ำที่ลิ้นร่วมกับการฝึกพูดและกลืน

name: Tongue tremor
formal: Rhythmic tongue movement from essential tremor, parkinsonism or palatal tremor.
simple: Shaking of the tongue.
th: อาการสั่นเป็นจังหวะของลิ้น พบใน essential tremor, Parkinson disease, palatal tremor หรือภาวะ enhanced physiological tremor
tempoNote: Course follows the underlying tremor disorder
feat: Rhythmic oscillation of the tongue at rest or on protrusion
Rest tongue and jaw tremor suggest Parkinson disease
Postural tongue tremor accompanies voice and head tremor in essential tremor
Enhanced physiological tremor from thyrotoxicosis, alcohol withdrawal or drugs
A sign rather than a disease; fasciculation must be distinguished
inv: Examine tongue at rest in the mouth and protruded
Thyroid function, drug history, alcohol history
EMG of tongue if fasciculations (MND) are a concern; DaT-SPECT if parkinsonism uncertain

case.story: Wife notes his chin and tongue shake when he sits watching TV; he has become slower dressing over a year.
case.exam: Rest tremor of jaw and tongue, right hand rest tremor, bradykinesia and rigidity on the right.
case.tests: Thyroid normal; no drug exposure.
case.q: What does the tongue tremor indicate here?
case.a: Rest tongue and jaw tremor as part of Parkinson disease.

det.patho: Tremor of the tongue arises from the same central oscillators that produce limb tremor: basal ganglia circuits in parkinsonism, cerebello-thalamo-cortical networks in essential tremor, and the dentato-olivary pathway in palatal tremor. Enhanced physiological tremor reflects increased peripheral sensitivity.
det.clinical: Tongue tremor can be seen at rest within the mouth or on protrusion. It may cause dysarthria or difficulty with wind instruments. Accompanying signs identify the cause.
det.diagnosis: Careful examination distinguishes tremor from fasciculation, myoclonus and chorea. Tests depend on suspected cause: thyroid function, drug review, imaging, DaT-SPECT.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying disorder: levodopa for parkinsonian tremor, propranolol or primidone for essential tremor, removal of drugs or correction of thyroid status for enhanced physiological tremor. Botulinum toxin is occasionally used.
det.prognosis: Depends on the underlying cause.
pearls: Look at the tongue resting in the floor of the mouth to see fasciculations; protrusion causes normal tremulousness.
Jaw and tongue rest tremor favour Parkinson disease.
det.thd: Tongue tremor คืออาการสั่นของลิ้นเป็นจังหวะ พบได้ใน Parkinson disease (สั่นขณะพัก), essential tremor (สั่นเมื่อแลบลิ้น) และ enhanced physiological tremor ต้องแยกจาก fasciculation ใน MND โดยดูลิ้นขณะอยู่ในปาก การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ

name: Tonic limb and axial seizures
formal: Seizures with simultaneous tonic stiffening of axial and limb muscles, as in Lennox-Gastaut syndrome.
simple: Seizures where the trunk and limbs stiffen suddenly.
th: การชักแบบเกร็งที่กล้ามเนื้อลำตัวและแขนขาเกร็งพร้อมกัน พบบ่อยใน Lennox–Gastaut syndrome โดยเฉพาะขณะหลับ
tempoNote: Brief seizures of seconds, frequently in clusters and during non-REM sleep
feat: Sudden stiffening of neck, trunk and limbs, with arms raised and flexed, lasting seconds
Most frequent in non-REM sleep; daytime attacks cause falls and injuries
Hallmark seizure type of Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, along with atypical absences and atonic seizures
Associated with intellectual disability and other developmental and epileptic encephalopathies
May be subtle in sleep: eye opening, brief apnoea, slight trunk flexion
inv: Video-EEG including sleep: generalised paroxysmal fast activity (10–20 Hz) or electrodecrement during the seizure
Interictal slow spike-wave below 2.5 Hz in LGS
MRI and genetic testing to find the underlying cause

case.who: 10-year-old boy from Udon Thani with developmental delay
case.story: Parents describe several brief episodes nightly where he stiffens with arms up; during the day he occasionally drops and hits his head.
case.exam: Intellectual disability, no focal weakness, helmet worn.
case.tests: Sleep EEG: bursts of generalised fast activity with tonic stiffening; slow spike-wave interictally.
case.q: What seizure type is this and which syndrome is suggested?
case.a: Tonic seizures in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome; treatments include valproate, clobazam, rufinamide, lamotrigine, cannabidiol or fenfluramine, with ketogenic diet, VNS or callosotomy for drop attacks.

det.patho: Tonic seizures arise from widespread bilateral cortical and subcortical networks, with involvement of brainstem motor pathways. They are characteristic of epileptic encephalopathies with diffuse brain dysfunction from structural, genetic or metabolic causes.
det.clinical: Seizures last a few seconds to a minute, consisting of sustained contraction of axial and proximal limb muscles. They often occur in clusters, mostly during sleep. In wakefulness they cause sudden falls. Autonomic signs such as apnoea, flushing and tachycardia are common.
det.diagnosis: Video-EEG is essential: ictal EEG shows generalised low-voltage fast activity or electrodecrement. Recording sleep improves detection. Identify the syndrome and underlying cause with MRI and genetic testing.
det.treatment: Tonic seizures are often drug resistant. Options include valproate, clobazam, lamotrigine, rufinamide, topiramate, cannabidiol (Epidiolex) and fenfluramine for LGS. Ketogenic diet, VNS and corpus callosotomy can reduce drop attacks. Some drugs (e.g. benzodiazepines intravenously) can occasionally provoke tonic status in LGS.
det.prognosis: Usually persistent, reflecting the underlying epileptic encephalopathy.
pearls: Nocturnal tonic seizures are the most common seizure type in Lennox–Gastaut syndrome.
Ictal EEG shows fast activity or flattening, not spike-wave.
Callosotomy targets drop attacks when medications fail.
det.thd: Tonic limb and axial seizures คือการชักเกร็งพร้อมกันทั้งลำตัวและแขนขา แขนยกงอ นานไม่กี่วินาที มักเกิดขณะหลับเป็นชุด ๆ และทำให้ล้มเมื่อเกิดตอนตื่น เป็นลักษณะสำคัญของ Lennox–Gastaut syndrome EEG ขณะชักพบคลื่นเร็วทั่วไป รักษายากต้องใช้ยาหลายตัว เช่น valproate clobazam rufinamide cannabidiol อาหาร ketogenic VNS หรือผ่าตัด callosotomy

name: Tonic seizures
formal: Seizures with sustained muscle contraction and stiffening, often in children with diffuse brain disease.
simple: Seizures in which muscles stiffen and the body becomes rigid.
th: การชักที่กล้ามเนื้อเกร็งค้างนานไม่กี่วินาทีถึงนาที โดยไม่มีระยะกระตุกตาม มักพบในเด็กที่มีโรคสมองกระจาย เช่น Lennox–Gastaut
tempoNote: Attacks last seconds to about a minute, often clustered in sleep
feat: Sustained stiffening of muscles without a clonic phase; may be generalised or focal (e.g. supplementary motor area)
Typical of epileptic encephalopathies, especially Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, often during non-REM sleep
Falls and facial or head injury when they occur while standing
Accompanied by apnoea, flushing, tachycardia or pupil dilation
Focal tonic seizures arising in the supplementary motor area cause asymmetric 'fencing' postures with preserved awareness
inv: Video-EEG with sleep recording: generalised fast activity or electrodecrement during generalised tonic seizures
MRI brain for structural cause; genetic and metabolic testing in children

case.who: 6-year-old girl from Surat Thani with a history of infantile spasms
case.story: Mother notices that at night she suddenly stiffens with arms raised and eyes open for about 10 seconds, several times each night.
case.exam: Moderate developmental delay, no focal signs.
case.tests: Video-EEG captures tonic stiffening with generalised fast rhythmic activity; interictal slow spike-wave at 2 Hz.
case.q: What seizure type is shown, and what does the evolution from infantile spasms suggest?
case.a: Generalised tonic seizures; evolution of West syndrome to Lennox–Gastaut syndrome.

read.where: Chapter 9 - Seizures and Antibodies Against Surface Antigens
6 EEG and Semiology in Generalized Epilepsies

det.patho: Generalised tonic seizures reflect bilateral activation of cortical and subcortical motor systems, with involvement of brainstem pathways. Focal tonic seizures usually arise from the supplementary sensorimotor area of the mesial frontal lobe. They are most frequent in individuals with widespread brain dysfunction.
det.clinical: Generalised tonic seizures cause symmetrical stiffening of trunk and limbs, often with upward eye deviation and apnoea, lasting under a minute. They cluster in sleep and can cause falls when awake. Focal tonic seizures produce asymmetric postures, sometimes with retained awareness, and may be mistaken for functional events. Tonic status epilepticus can occur in LGS.
det.diagnosis: Characterise the events by video-EEG, recording sleep whenever possible because most attacks are nocturnal. Generalised tonic seizures show diffuse fast activity or a sudden flattening of the trace, whereas supplementary motor area seizures may produce little scalp change and are easily mislabelled as functional. Then define the syndrome and its cause with MRI, genetic panels and metabolic tests. Separate them from epileptic spasms, non-epileptic tonic spasms and paroxysmal dyskinesias.
det.treatment: Treatment depends on the syndrome. In LGS, valproate, clobazam, lamotrigine, rufinamide, topiramate, cannabidiol and fenfluramine are used, often in combination; ketogenic diet, VNS and callosotomy are options. Focal tonic seizures may respond to focal epilepsy drugs and surgery if a lesion is identified.
det.prognosis: Often drug resistant when part of an epileptic encephalopathy.
pearls: Tonic seizures in sleep are a hallmark of Lennox–Gastaut syndrome.
Supplementary motor area seizures cause bizarre asymmetric postures with awareness, mimicking functional events.
Record sleep to capture tonic seizures on EEG.
det.thd: Tonic seizure คือการชักเกร็งค้างไม่กี่วินาทีโดยไม่มีระยะกระตุก พบบ่อยในเด็กที่มีโรคสมองกระจายเช่น Lennox–Gastaut มักเกิดขณะหลับเป็นชุด ๆ ถ้าเกิดตอนยืนจะล้ม ชนิดเฉพาะที่จากบริเวณ supplementary motor area ทำให้ท่าทางบิดไม่สมมาตรขณะยังรู้สึกตัว วินิจฉัยด้วย video-EEG รักษาตามกลุ่มอาการโรคลมชัก

name: Tonic spasms
formal: Brief painful contractions of muscle, as in multiple sclerosis (paroxysmal tonic spasms) or stiff-person syndrome.
simple: Short, painful muscle tightening episodes, often seen in multiple sclerosis.
th: อาการกล้ามเนื้อเกร็งเจ็บเป็นพัก ๆ สั้น ๆ ที่แขนขาข้างหนึ่ง พบในโรค MS NMOSD หรือ stiff-person ไม่ใช่การชักจากสมอง
tempoNote: Each spasm lasts seconds to 2 minutes; attacks recur many times a day over weeks and then remit
feat: Brief painful stereotyped tonic posturing of one or more limbs, often unilateral
Triggered by movement, touch, hyperventilation or emotion; awareness preserved
Particularly common in NMOSD with longitudinally extensive myelitis, also MS
Can also be seen in stiff-person spectrum disorders and tetany
Respond very well to low-dose carbamazepine or other sodium channel blockers
inv: MRI spinal cord and brain for demyelinating lesions; AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG
EEG normal during spasms, excluding seizures
Calcium and magnesium to exclude tetany

case.who: 36-year-old woman from Nakhon Pathom with recent transverse myelitis
case.story: Since recovering from myelitis she has many daily episodes of painful stiffening of the right arm and leg lasting 30 seconds, especially when she stands up.
case.exam: Mild spastic paraparesis, sensory level at T6; an episode shows tonic flexion of the right arm with extension of the leg, fully aware.
case.tests: MRI longitudinally extensive cervicothoracic lesion; AQP4-IgG positive; EEG normal.
case.q: What are these episodes and which simple treatment works?
case.a: Paroxysmal tonic spasms of NMOSD; low-dose carbamazepine usually abolishes them, alongside long-term NMOSD immunotherapy.

read.where: 6 - Medical treatment of the motor features of Parkinson disease

det.patho: Demyelinated axons in the spinal cord or brainstem become hyperexcitable and generate ectopic impulses that spread to adjacent fibres by ephaptic transmission. The resulting discharges activate motor pathways, producing brief tonic contractions. Sodium channel blockers stabilise these membranes.
det.clinical: Spasms appear during or after a demyelinating attack, often weeks into recovery, and may be the first sign of relapse. They are intensely painful, stereotyped and frequent, lasting under two minutes. Awareness is preserved. They usually remit over weeks to months.
det.diagnosis: The clinical description is usually diagnostic. Imaging identifies the responsible lesion, and antibody testing distinguishes NMOSD, MOGAD and MS. Normal EEG during an episode separates them from epileptic seizures.
det.treatment: Low-dose carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine usually stops the spasms within days; lacosamide, gabapentin, acetazolamide and baclofen are alternatives if these are not tolerated. Treatment can often be withdrawn after a few months of freedom from attacks. The underlying demyelinating disease needs its own immunotherapy, both for the acute attack and for relapse prevention. Check sodium if carbamazepine is used in older or polymedicated patients.
det.prognosis: Spasms typically resolve within months with or without treatment.
pearls: Painful tonic spasms after myelitis suggest NMOSD.
Carbamazepine in low doses is dramatically effective.
Awareness preserved and EEG normal: not seizures.

name: Tonic–clonic seizure
formal: Generalised seizure with tonic stiffening followed by rhythmic clonic jerking and postictal state.
simple: A seizure with stiffening followed by shaking and then drowsiness.
th: การชักแบบทั่วไปที่เริ่มด้วยเกร็งทั้งตัวแล้วกระตุกเป็นจังหวะ ตามด้วยระยะหลังชักที่สับสนหรือหลับ
tempoNote: Usually 1–3 minutes; over 5 minutes counts as status epilepticus
feat: Loss of awareness, tonic stiffening often with a cry, then rhythmic clonic jerking slowing toward the end
Lateral tongue bite, urinary incontinence, cyanosis and frothing may occur
Postictal confusion, headache, drowsiness and muscle aches
Generalised onset (genetic generalised epilepsy) or focal to bilateral (focal epilepsy) onset
Strongest risk factor for SUDEP and injury
inv: Glucose, electrolytes, ECG, and toxicology if relevant
MRI brain; EEG to classify generalised versus focal epilepsy
Prolactin rise within 20 minutes supports an epileptic event but is rarely needed

case.story: At a party after staying up all night, he fell, stiffened then jerked for 90 seconds. He has had morning arm jerks for a year.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination; bitten lateral tongue.
case.tests: EEG with photic stimulation shows generalised polyspike-wave; MRI normal.
case.q: What epilepsy syndrome is likely and which drug should be avoided?
case.a: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy; carbamazepine may worsen myoclonus and absences. Levetiracetam or lamotrigine are often used (valproate effective but avoided in women of childbearing potential).

det.patho: The seizure begins either simultaneously in bilateral networks (generalised onset) or in a focal region spreading to both hemispheres. Tonic stiffening reflects sustained high-frequency firing; clonic jerking reflects intermittent inhibition interrupting this firing. Postictal suppression results from active inhibitory mechanisms and metabolic exhaustion.
det.clinical: A tonic phase of 10–20 seconds is followed by a clonic phase of up to a minute or two. Breathing is impaired, then deep stertorous respiration follows. Patients are confused or asleep afterwards. A focal aura or asymmetrical features suggest focal onset. Complications include injuries, aspiration, shoulder dislocation and vertebral fractures.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical with eyewitness or video. Features favouring epileptic seizure: eyes open, lateral tongue bite, postictal confusion. Investigations seek the cause and classify the epilepsy. Exclude convulsive syncope, functional seizures and hypoglycaemia.
det.treatment: First aid: protect head, time the event, recovery position, no objects in mouth. Give benzodiazepine (buccal midazolam, rectal or IV diazepam, IV lorazepam) if lasting beyond 5 minutes. Long-term choices: levetiracetam, lamotrigine, valproate (avoid in women of childbearing potential where possible) for generalised; lamotrigine, levetiracetam, carbamazepine and others for focal epilepsy.
det.prognosis: Most patients achieve control with medication; persistent tonic-clonic seizures carry injury and SUDEP risk.
pearls: Eyes are usually open during an epileptic tonic-clonic seizure.
Lateral tongue bite favours epileptic seizure over syncope or functional events.
Seizures lasting more than 5 minutes require emergency treatment.
det.thd: Tonic-clonic seizure คือการชักที่เริ่มด้วยเกร็งทั้งตัวแล้วกระตุกเป็นจังหวะ ตามด้วยสับสนหรือหลับหลังชัก อาจกัดลิ้นด้านข้างหรือปัสสาวะราด เกิดได้จากโรคลมชักทั่วไปหรือเฉพาะที่ที่ลามสองซีก ต้องแยกจาก syncope และชักจากจิตใจ ปฐมพยาบาลโดยจัดท่าตะแคง ถ้านานเกิน 5 นาทีให้ benzodiazepine และเลือกยากันชักระยะยาวตามชนิดโรคลมชัก

Can cause convulsions; check glucose immediately

name: Torsion dystonia
formal: Generalised dystonia, typically early onset (DYT1), with sustained twisting postures and torsion of the limbs and trunk.
simple: Twisting, sustained abnormal body postures from muscle contractions, often starting in childhood.
th: dystonia แบบทั่วตัวที่เริ่มในเด็ก มักจากยีน TOR1A (DYT1) ทำให้แขนขาและลำตัวบิดเกร็งเป็นท่าผิดปกติ
tempoNote: Begins in childhood or adolescence, spreads over years, then stabilises
feat: Onset usually in a leg or arm in childhood, spreading to become generalized
Twisting postures of limbs and trunk, worse with action
Cognition and other neurological systems normal
TOR1A GAG deletion is autosomal dominant with low penetrance (about 30%)
Excellent response to GPi deep brain stimulation
inv: TOR1A testing; dystonia gene panel if negative
Levodopa trial to exclude dopa-responsive dystonia
MRI brain, copper studies to exclude secondary causes

case.story: Right foot began turning inward when walking 2 years ago; now his trunk twists and his right arm postures when writing. His father has mild writer's cramp.
case.exam: Inversion of right foot on walking, truncal torsion, dystonic posture of right arm on action, normal cognition and reflexes.
case.tests: MRI and copper studies normal; no response to 3-month levodopa trial; TOR1A GAG deletion detected.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the most effective treatment if disabling?
case.a: DYT1 (TOR1A) early-onset generalized torsion dystonia; GPi deep brain stimulation.

read.where: 11 - Dystonia: Phenomenology, classification, etiology, pathology, biochemistry, and genetics

det.patho: TOR1A encodes torsinA, an AAA+ ATPase in the nuclear envelope and ER. A 3-bp GAG deletion disrupts its function, altering neuronal development and synaptic plasticity in motor circuits without obvious neurodegeneration. Other genes (THAP1, GNAL) and unknown causes account for further cases.
det.clinical: Onset is typically before age 26, often in a limb during a specific action, such as walking. The dystonia spreads to other limbs and the trunk, while cranial muscles are relatively spared in TOR1A cases. Progression usually slows after several years.
det.diagnosis: Clinical recognition of isolated generalized dystonia is followed by genetic testing. A levodopa trial is essential in all early-onset dystonia to avoid missing dopa-responsive dystonia. Secondary causes are excluded with MRI and metabolic tests.
det.treatment: Anticholinergics such as trihexyphenidyl in high doses help children. Baclofen and benzodiazepines are additional options; botulinum toxin is useful for focal targets. GPi DBS gives substantial long-lasting improvement in TOR1A dystonia. Physiotherapy and orthoses support function.
det.prognosis: Cognition and lifespan are normal; disability can be severe without treatment but DBS often restores function.
pearls: Always trial levodopa in childhood-onset dystonia.
Limb-onset dystonia in a child tends to generalize; adult-onset focal dystonia rarely does.
DYT1 has low penetrance, so family history may be mild or absent.
det.thd: Torsion dystonia คือ dystonia ทั่วตัวที่เริ่มในเด็ก มักเริ่มที่ขาหรือแขนแล้วกระจายไปทั้งตัว สาเหตุสำคัญคือยีน TOR1A (DYT1) ถ่ายทอดแบบ autosomal dominant แต่แสดงออกเพียงบางคน สติปัญญาปกติ ต้องลองให้ levodopa เพื่อแยก dopa-responsive dystonia รักษาด้วย trihexyphenidyl, botulinum toxin และ DBS ที่ GPi ซึ่งได้ผลดีมาก

name: Touch epilepsy
formal: Reflex epilepsy in which seizures are provoked by tactile stimuli.
simple: Seizures triggered by being touched.
th: โรคลมชักชนิด reflex ที่ชักเมื่อถูกสัมผัส ถูหรือแตะบริเวณร่างกายจุดใดจุดหนึ่ง
tempoNote: Seizures follow within seconds of touching a specific body area
feat: Seizures triggered by touching, rubbing or tapping a particular skin area
Typically focal seizures starting with sensations in the touched region, possibly spreading to motor or generalised seizures
Commonly associated with lesions of the parietal or perirolandic cortex
Some patients learn to abort seizures with counter-stimulation
Can coexist with spontaneous seizures
inv: Video-EEG with stimulation of the trigger zone to provoke and record an ictal change over the contralateral parietal region
MRI for structural lesions near the sensorimotor cortex

case.who: 26-year-old man from Phuket with prior head injury
case.story: Whenever someone rubs his left forearm, he feels tingling spreading up the arm followed by jerking of the left hand.
case.exam: Mild left-sided sensory loss.
case.tests: Video-EEG: rubbing the left forearm triggers a right centroparietal seizure; MRI right parietal gliosis.
case.q: What type of epilepsy is this and how is it managed?
case.a: Touch (somatosensory reflex) epilepsy from a right parietal lesion; focal antiseizure medications and evaluation for surgery if drug resistant.

det.patho: Somatosensory input reaches a hyperexcitable cortical region in the primary sensory or adjacent cortex, which then initiates a seizure. Lesions such as scars, dysplasia or tumours near the sensorimotor cortex are often found. It is one of the rarer reflex epilepsies.
det.clinical: The trigger zone is typically on the contralateral limb or face. Seizures begin with focal sensory phenomena, followed by focal motor activity and sometimes bilateral convulsions. Patients often avoid touching the area. Spontaneous seizures may also occur.
det.diagnosis: Video-EEG with stimulation confirms the reflex nature and localises the onset. MRI identifies the lesion. Distinguish from non-epileptic paroxysmal movement disorders and functional events.
det.treatment: Focal antiseizure medications (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, carbamazepine, lacosamide) are usual first-line therapy. Avoiding the trigger reduces seizures. Drug-resistant cases may be candidates for resective surgery.
det.prognosis: Variable; depends on the underlying lesion and drug response.
pearls: Ask about specific triggers in every patient with focal seizures.
Video-EEG with deliberate stimulation can confirm the diagnosis.
A parietal lesion is often responsible.
det.thd: Touch epilepsy เป็นโรคลมชักชนิด reflex ที่ชักเมื่อถูกสัมผัสหรือถูบริเวณใดบริเวณหนึ่ง มักเริ่มด้วยอาการชาหรือแปลบที่จุดนั้นแล้วกระตุกตาม พบร่วมกับรอยโรคที่สมองส่วน parietal วินิจฉัยด้วย video-EEG โดยกระตุ้นจุดนั้น และ MRI หารอยโรค รักษาด้วยยากันชักชนิดเฉพาะที่ และพิจารณาผ่าตัดหากดื้อยา

Triggered by sudden movement, no ictal EEG change

name: Tourette’s syndrome
formal: Chronic tic disorder with multiple motor and one or more vocal tics for over a year, onset in childhood, often with ADHD or OCD.
simple: A condition with repeated movement and sound tics, starting in childhood.
more: Neurodevelopmental tic disorder with multiple motor and at least one vocal tic for over a year, onset in childhood, often with OCD and ADHD, involving cortico-striato-thalamic circuits.
th: tic ทั้งการเคลื่อนไหวและเสียงหลายแบบ เริ่มก่อนอายุ 18 ปี เป็นนานกว่า 1 ปี มักมี ADHD หรือ OCD ร่วม และดีขึ้นเมื่อโตเป็นผู้ใหญ่
tempoNote: Onset around 5–7 years, peak severity about 10–12, waxing and waning; often lessens by adulthood
feat: Multiple motor tics (blinking, grimacing, shoulder shrug) and at least one vocal tic (sniffing, throat clearing, words)
Premonitory urge relieved by the tic; tics can be briefly suppressed with rebound later
Waxing and waning course with changing tic repertoire; worse with stress, excitement or fatigue
Frequent comorbid ADHD, OCD, anxiety and learning or behaviour difficulties
Coprolalia is uncommon (minority of patients)
inv: Clinical diagnosis — no test confirms it
Screen for ADHD, OCD, anxiety, depression and school problems
EEG only if episodes could be seizures; MRI or labs only if atypical (late onset, regression, other neurological signs)

case.story: Two years of eye blinking, then head jerks and repeated throat clearing; he says he feels an itch in the throat that he has to release. Teachers note poor attention.
case.exam: Several brief eye-blinking and neck-jerk tics during the visit, suppressible when asked; neurological examination otherwise normal.
case.tests: None needed; Conners rating scale suggests ADHD.
case.q: What is the first-line approach for tics that bother him at school?
case.a: Tourette syndrome: education plus behavioural therapy (CBIT/habit reversal); if medication is needed, an alpha-2 agonist such as clonidine or guanfacine also helps the ADHD.

det.patho: Tourette syndrome is a polygenic neurodevelopmental disorder with strong heritability, involving cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits and dopaminergic hyperactivity. Interneuron loss in the striatum has been described. It is about three to four times more common in boys and affects up to roughly 1% of school-aged children.
det.clinical: Simple motor tics in the face usually appear first, followed by vocal tics a year or two later. Complex tics include touching, echolalia and copropraxia. Comorbidities such as ADHD and OCD frequently cause more impairment than the tics themselves. Severity peaks in early adolescence and declines in most by adulthood, though a minority have persistent or severe tics, including self-injurious ones.
det.diagnosis: DSM-5 requires two or more motor tics plus a minimum of one vocal tic (not necessarily at the same time) for over a year, onset before 18, and no other cause. Distinguish tics from chorea, myoclonus, dystonia, stereotypies and functional tics. Investigations are reserved for atypical features such as onset in adulthood, rapid change or neurological deficit.
det.treatment: Education and reassurance suffice for many. Comprehensive Behavioural Intervention for Tics is first-line when treatment is needed. Medications include alpha-2 agonists, then aripiprazole or other dopamine blockers and VMAT2 inhibitors for severe tics; topiramate is an option. Botulinum toxin helps focal troublesome tics and DBS is reserved for severe refractory adults. Treat ADHD and OCD in their own right.
det.prognosis: Most children improve markedly by early adulthood; the comorbidities often determine long-term outcome.
pearls: Premonitory urge plus brief suppressibility identifies a tic.
Coprolalia is not required; most patients never have it.
Ask about ADHD and OCD — they often drive the disability.
det.thd: Tourette syndrome เป็นโรคพัฒนาการทางระบบประสาท มี tic ทั้งการเคลื่อนไหวและเสียงหลายแบบนานเกิน 1 ปี เริ่มก่อนอายุ 18 ปี ผู้ป่วยรู้สึกอยากทำก่อน (premonitory urge) และกลั้นได้ชั่วคราว มักมี ADHD หรือ OCD ร่วม วินิจฉัยทางคลินิก รักษาด้วยการให้ความรู้ พฤติกรรมบำบัด (CBIT) และยาเช่น clonidine หรือ aripiprazole เมื่อจำเป็น ส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นเมื่อโต

name: Toxic and metabolic encephalopathy
formal: Diffuse brain dysfunction from systemic metabolic derangement or toxins, causing confusion, asterixis, tremor, myoclonus and seizures.
simple: Confusion and brain dysfunction caused by poisons or body chemistry problems.
ab: Acute confusional state of metabolic origin
th: สมองทำงานผิดปกติแบบกระจายจากความผิดปกติทางเมตาบอลิกหรือสารพิษ ทำให้สับสน ซึม asterixis มือสั่น กระตุก และชัก
tempoNote: Develops over hours to days with the underlying disturbance; usually reversible when corrected
feat: Fluctuating attention and arousal (delirium) progressing to stupor or coma
Asterixis, multifocal myoclonus and tremor; seizures in some causes
Pupillary reflexes usually preserved even in deep coma (except some drug overdoses)
Causes: hypo/hyperglycaemia, hypo/hypernatraemia, hypercalcaemia, uraemia, liver failure, sepsis, hypercapnia, drugs and toxins, Wernicke's
Absence of focal signs in most cases
inv: Glucose, electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, renal and liver function, ammonia, blood gas, thyroid, toxicology, drug levels
EEG: diffuse slowing, triphasic waves; excludes non-convulsive status
Brain imaging to exclude structural causes; CSF if infection suspected

case.who: 65-year-old man from Chachoengsao with diabetes and cirrhosis
case.story: Increasingly confused and sleepy over two days after a urinary tract infection.
case.exam: Drowsy, disoriented, bilateral asterixis, multifocal twitching, no focal weakness.
case.tests: Ammonia raised, sodium 128, glucose normal, urine culture E. coli; CT head normal; EEG diffuse slowing with triphasic waves.
case.q: What is the likely encephalopathy and its management?
case.a: Toxic-metabolic encephalopathy from hepatic encephalopathy precipitated by infection and hyponatraemia; treat infection, lactulose, rifaximin and careful sodium correction.

det.patho: Diffuse cerebral dysfunction results when systemic disturbances alter neuronal energy supply, neurotransmission or membrane excitability. Examples include ammonia-driven astrocyte swelling in liver failure, uraemic toxins, cytokine and microcirculatory effects in sepsis, and direct drug toxicity. Ascending arousal pathways and cortical networks are both affected.
det.clinical: Delirium with inattention and fluctuating arousal is the core feature. Asterixis, multifocal myoclonus, tremor and seizures suggest a metabolic cause. Focal signs are uncommon but may occur with hypoglycaemia or hyperglycaemia. Older and cognitively impaired patients are more vulnerable.
det.diagnosis: The approach is to exclude structural, infectious and epileptic causes and to identify metabolic and toxic disturbances with targeted laboratory testing. EEG is helpful to exclude non-convulsive status and to grade severity. Imaging is needed if focal signs or no clear cause.
det.treatment: Correct the cause quickly: glucose, sodium at safe rates, calcium and oxygenation or ventilation for hypercapnia. Give thiamine before glucose to anyone at nutritional risk. Treat sepsis, use dialysis for uraemia, lactulose and rifaximin for hepatic encephalopathy, and specific antidotes for poisonings. Minimise sedatives, use non-drug delirium measures, and treat seizures if they occur.
det.prognosis: Usually reversible if treated early; prolonged or severe episodes may leave cognitive deficits, and mortality reflects the underlying illness.
pearls: Preserved pupils in deep coma suggest a metabolic cause.
Asterixis and multifocal myoclonus are clues to metabolic encephalopathy.
Give thiamine before glucose in malnourished or alcoholic patients.
det.thd: Toxic and metabolic encephalopathy คือสมองทำงานผิดปกติทั่วไปจากความผิดปกติทางเมตาบอลิกหรือสารพิษ เช่น น้ำตาล โซเดียม ไตวาย ตับวาย ติดเชื้อในกระแสเลือด หรือยา ผู้ป่วยสับสน ซึม มี asterixis และกระตุก อาจชัก ตรวจเลือดหาสาเหตุ EEG และภาพถ่ายสมองเพื่อแยกโรคอื่น รักษาที่สาเหตุ แล้วมักฟื้นตัวได้

name: Toxic and nutritional neuropathies
formal: Neuropathies caused by toxins such as alcohol, solvents, metals or drugs and nutritional deficits such as B vitamins, causing distal sensory-motor loss.
simple: Nerve damage from poisons or poor nutrition.
th: neuropathy จากสารพิษ (สุรา ตัวทำละลาย โลหะ ยา) หรือขาดสารอาหาร (วิตามินบี ทองแดง) ทำให้ชาและอ่อนแรงปลายแขนขา
tempoNote: Usually develops over weeks to months of exposure or deficiency
feat: Length-dependent sensory or sensorimotor neuropathy, often painful
Nutritional causes: B1, B6 (deficiency or excess), B12, folate, copper, vitamin E
Toxic causes: alcohol, chemotherapy, metronidazole, isoniazid, nitrofurantoin, arsenic, lead, thallium, n-hexane

Settings: alcohol use, bariatric surgery, malabsorption, poor diet, occupational exposure

case.who: 47-year-old man drinking heavily for 20 years in Roi Et
case.story: Painful burning feet and unsteadiness; eats little and has lost weight.
case.exam: Distal pinprick and vibration loss, absent ankle jerks, mild distal weakness, calf tenderness.
case.tests: Low thiamine, low folate; NCS: axonal sensorimotor neuropathy.
case.q: What are the main factors and what to give first?
case.a: Combined alcohol toxicity and nutritional (thiamine, folate) deficiency; give thiamine first, correct other vitamins and support abstinence.

det.patho: Toxins disrupt axonal transport, mitochondrial function or microtubules, while deficiency of vitamins and trace elements impairs energy metabolism and myelin maintenance. Long axons are most vulnerable, producing a dying-back neuropathy. Combined toxic and nutritional mechanisms are common, notably in chronic alcohol use.
det.clinical: Most patients develop distal sensory symptoms, often painful, with later weakness. Some deficiencies cause myelopathy (B12, copper), optic neuropathy (B12, B1, toxins) or encephalopathy (thiamine). Systemic signs such as skin changes, anaemia or GI symptoms provide clues.
det.diagnosis: A detailed dietary, alcohol, drug, occupational and surgical history drives targeted testing. NCS documents an axonal neuropathy. Vitamin and trace element levels and heavy metal screens confirm the cause.
det.treatment: Remove the toxin, replace deficient nutrients (thiamine before glucose in at-risk patients), and treat pain. Address the underlying problem: alcohol services, nutrition support after bariatric surgery, occupational safety.
det.prognosis: Improvement is usual if the cause is corrected early; long-standing axonal loss recovers slowly or incompletely.
pearls: Bariatric surgery patients need lifelong copper and vitamin monitoring.
Too much vitamin B6 is neurotoxic, as is too little.
Give thiamine before glucose in malnourished patients.

name: Toxic and nutritional optic neuropathies
formal: Optic nerve damage caused by toxins, such as methanol or ethambutol, and deficiencies, leading to central visual loss and colour impairment.
simple: Vision loss from poisoning or poor nutrition that damages the optic nerves.
th: เส้นประสาทตาเสียทั้งสองข้างจากสารพิษหรือยา (ethambutol, methanol, linezolid, amiodarone) หรือจากขาดวิตามิน ทำให้ตามัวไม่ปวดและมี centrocaecal scotoma
tempoNote: Weeks to months of symmetric dimming for most causes (ethambutol typically 3–6 months after starting); methanol blinds within hours to a day or two
feat: Painless, nearly symmetric blurring of central vision in both eyes with dull colour, especially reds, out of proportion to the drop in acuity
Bilateral centrocaecal or central scotomas that are easier to map with a red target
Discs normal at first, sometimes with subtle hyperaemia or splinter haemorrhages, then temporal pallor as papillomacular fibres degenerate
Pupils may react normally or sluggishly; a marked relative afferent defect is unusual when both nerves are equally affected
Triggers include ethambutol, linezolid, amiodarone, methotrexate, methanol, heavy metals, deficiency of B12, thiamine, folate or copper, and tobacco and alcohol misuse
inv: Acuity, Ishihara or colour plates, central field testing with a red target, and OCT measuring nerve fibre and ganglion cell layer thickness in the retina
B12 with methylmalonic acid, folate, thiamine, copper and zinc; drug and exposure history including TB regimen; blood methanol, osmolar gap and acid–base status if acute
MRI of orbits and brain with contrast to exclude compression or demyelination; mitochondrial DNA testing for LHON when the cause is unclear or the patient is a smoker with no deficiency

case.who: 58-year-old man on treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis, Phitsanulok
case.story: Four months into a four-drug regimen he noticed that reading became difficult and colours looked washed out in both eyes. There was no eye pain. He lost weight and drinks rice spirit most evenings.
case.exam: Acuity 6/24 right and 6/30 left, Ishihara 2/15 in both eyes, normal pupillary light reflexes, mild temporal pallor of the discs, bilateral central scotomas on red-target testing.
case.tests: OCT shows early thinning of the papillomacular bundle. MRI orbits normal. Serum B12 low-normal, folate low, renal function reduced.
case.q: Which drug is the suspect, and what should be done now?
case.a: Ethambutol, possibly aggravated by renal impairment and nutritional deficiency. Stop it at once with the TB team (substitute an alternative drug), treat the deficiencies with B vitamins and counselling on alcohol, and follow acuity and fields.

read.where: Chapter 20: Ocular side effects of systemic medication — Ethambutol

det.patho: The papillomacular bundle has high energy demand and thin or unmyelinated fibres, so it is sensitive to impaired mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, the shared mechanism proposed for nutritional, toxic and hereditary optic neuropathies. Cyanide from tobacco, formate from methanol, and drugs that disturb mitochondria (linezolid, ethambutol through copper chelation and other mechanisms) injure the same fibres. Deficits of B12, folate, thiamine and copper add to the vulnerability, which is why several factors often combine.
det.clinical: Vision fades over weeks in both eyes with similar severity, colour perception drops disproportionately, and there is no pain. The disc is typically normal at presentation; pallor emerges later. Ethambutol injury is dose and duration related and more likely in renal impairment. Methanol produces headache, nausea, abdominal pain and visual blurring within a day, with an anion-gap acidosis and optic disc hyperaemia; permanent blindness is common without rapid treatment. Look for peripheral neuropathy, glossitis, anaemia and cognitive change as clues to deficiency.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on history, symmetric painless central visual loss with dyschromatopsia and centrocaecal scotomas, supportive OCT, and a search for cause. Always check B12, folate and copper and inspect the drug list. Because compression, demyelination and LHON can look the same, obtain MRI and, if there is no explanation, mitochondrial testing. Screening visual function before and during ethambutol or linezolid therapy allows early detection.
det.treatment: Remove the offending agent immediately and arrange an alternative with the prescribing team. Correct nutrition: balanced diet, a multivitamin, thiamine and folate, and B12 replacement, given first when both B12 and folate are low so that cord degeneration is not provoked. Stop smoking and alcohol. For methanol poisoning treat as an emergency with an alcohol dehydrogenase blocker such as fomepizole, bicarbonate, folinic or folic acid, and haemodialysis. Visual recovery after stopping ethambutol is usual but incomplete in some.
det.prognosis: Outcome is good if the cause is removed early, especially for nutritional and ethambutol-related cases, but late pallor with a persistent central scotoma follows delay. Methanol often leaves permanent loss.
pearls: Symmetric painless central visual loss with poor colour vision means toxic or nutritional until proven otherwise.
Check B12, folate and copper in every case; replace B12 first when B12 and folate are both low.
Test colour vision and fields before and during ethambutol or linezolid, and stop at the first visual symptom.

Acute pneumonitis, eosinophilia and rash, followed by myalgia, neuropathy, contractures and scleroderma-like skin

case.who: Teaching vignette: 35-year-old woman in a hypothetical outbreak, presenting to a provincial hospital in northeast Thailand
case.story: Several family members fell ill after buying cheap unlabelled cooking oil; weeks later she develops muscle pain, stiff skin and brief jerks of her limbs.

case.tests: Marked eosinophilia; NCS shows axonal sensorimotor neuropathy; EMG myopathic changes.
case.q: Which historical syndrome does this resemble and who should be notified?

det.patho: In the Spanish toxic oil syndrome, rapeseed oil denatured with aniline was refined and sold as edible oil; fatty acid anilides and related esters are suspected toxins, but the exact agent was never proven. An immune-mediated vasculopathy with eosinophilic infiltration is thought to underlie the multisystem disease. Mechanisms of myoclonus in this setting are unknown.
det.clinical: The outbreak affected about 20,000 people, with an acute phase of pneumonitis, rash and eosinophilia, an intermediate phase of myalgia and thrombosis, and a chronic phase with neuropathy, muscle wasting, contractures and sclerodermiform skin. Neuromuscular cramps and involuntary movements including myoclonus were described in some cases. The entity label is historical and poorly characterised.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis depends on exposure history in an outbreak context and exclusion of other causes of myoclonus and neuropathy. Eosinophilia and the multisystem picture support it. Public health investigation is essential.
det.treatment: There is no specific antidote. Management is supportive with removal of the source, corticosteroids in acute inflammatory phases (with limited evidence), physiotherapy and symptomatic treatment of myoclonus with clonazepam or levetiracetam.
det.prognosis: Long-term studies of the Spanish outbreak showed persistent disability and increased mortality in many survivors.
pearls: Clusters of unexplained neuromuscular illness should trigger a food or toxin investigation.
Eosinophilia plus myalgia and neuropathy recalls toxic oil syndrome and eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome.

formal: Acute or subacute brain dysfunction due to poisoning, causing confusion and reduced consciousness; often reversible when the toxin is removed.
simple: Confusion or drowsiness caused by a poison affecting the brain.

feat: Confusion, agitation or reduced consciousness after exposure to drugs, alcohol or environmental toxins
Toxidromes guide diagnosis: anticholinergic, cholinergic, sympathomimetic, sedative-hypnotic, opioid, serotonergic
May include seizures, myoclonus, tremor, ataxia or hyperthermia
Common culprits: sedatives, antidepressants, anticonvulsants (valproate hyperammonaemia), antibiotics (cefepime, metronidazole), chemotherapy, carbon monoxide, organophosphates, heavy metals

case.who: 45-year-old woman from Songkhla with a liver abscess
case.story: After four weeks of metronidazole she has slurred speech, unsteady gait and confusion.
case.exam: Dysarthria, bilateral limb ataxia, nystagmus, mild confusion.
case.tests: MRI: symmetrical T2 hyperintensity of the dentate nuclei and splenium of the corpus callosum.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and treatment?
case.a: Metronidazole-induced encephalopathy; stop the drug, after which symptoms and MRI changes usually resolve.

det.patho: Toxins interfere with brain function in several ways: by acting on neurotransmitter receptors (anticholinergic, GABAergic or glutamatergic effects), by blocking energy production (carbon monoxide, cyanide), by creating metabolic disturbance (hyperammonaemia from valproate), or by injuring tissue directly (metronidazole, heavy metals, solvents). Older age, kidney or liver failure, and polypharmacy raise vulnerability. Some agents cause delayed white matter injury after apparent recovery.
det.clinical: The picture depends on the agent: delirium, agitation, sedation, hallucinations, seizures, myoclonus, ataxia and autonomic disturbance are all possible. Recognising a toxidrome narrows the list quickly. Some exposures cause delayed syndromes, such as leukoencephalopathy weeks after carbon monoxide poisoning. In hospital, drug toxicity in renal failure is a frequent and overlooked cause.
det.diagnosis: History of exposure is critical, supported by toxidrome recognition, toxicology testing and specific investigations. MRI may show characteristic patterns. Exclude metabolic, infective and structural causes.
det.treatment: Stop the offending agent and provide supportive care. Use antidotes when available: naloxone for opioids, flumazenil cautiously, physostigmine for anticholinergic toxicity, atropine and pralidoxime for organophosphates, hyperbaric or high-flow oxygen for carbon monoxide, and dialysis for dialysable toxins. Treat seizures with benzodiazepines.
det.prognosis: Generally good with timely management, but some toxins cause permanent damage.
pearls: Always review the medication chart in any encephalopathic patient.
Cefepime and metronidazole are frequent hospital causes of toxic encephalopathy, particularly in renal failure.
Check ammonia in valproate-treated patients with confusion.

name: Toxic leukoencephalopathy
formal: White matter injury from toxins such as toluene, heroin vapour or chemotherapy, causing subacute dementia, ataxia and spasticity.
simple: Damage to the brain's wiring from poisons or certain drugs.
th: เนื้อขาวของสมองเสียหายจากสารพิษ เช่น ทินเนอร์ heroin ที่สูดควัน หรือยาเคมีบำบัด ทำให้สับสน เดินเซ และเกร็ง

Ataxia, dysarthria and spasticity; solvent abusers may have tremor and hearing loss

Often improves partly when the toxin stops

case.exam: Slow responses, scanning dysarthria, broad-based ataxic gait, bilateral Babinski signs, mild sensorineural hearing loss.
case.tests: MRI: diffuse cerebral white matter T2 hyperintensity with loss of grey–white contrast and cerebellar atrophy.
case.q: Which toxin is responsible and what is the most important intervention?
case.a: Chronic toluene leukoencephalopathy; stopping exposure through addiction treatment is key, with partial recovery possible.

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Toxic Leukoencephalopathy

det.patho: Lipophilic toxins concentrate in myelin-rich white matter and injure oligodendrocytes and myelin sheaths, sometimes with intramyelinic oedema seen as restricted diffusion. Mechanisms vary: methotrexate disturbs folate and adenosine pathways, heroin pyrolysate causes spongiform vacuolation, toluene causes diffuse demyelination with atrophy, and carbon monoxide causes delayed demyelination. Severity correlates with dose and duration.
det.clinical: Mild cases show inattention, slowed processing and personality change; moderate cases add ataxia and gait problems; severe cases progress to akinetic mutism, spastic quadriparesis or death. Heroin vapour inhalation ('chasing the dragon') causes cerebellar ataxia evolving over weeks. Chemotherapy-associated forms can appear acutely with stroke-like deficits after intrathecal or high-dose methotrexate, or later as chronic leukoencephalopathy. Chronic solvent abusers often also have optic atrophy, sensorineural deafness and tremor.
det.diagnosis: A detailed exposure history and MRI are central. Acute forms often show symmetric diffusion restriction in deep white matter or corpus callosum; chronic forms show confluent T2 change and atrophy. Exclude infection, demyelinating disease, leukodystrophies and metabolic encephalopathy with CSF, bloods and genetic testing where indicated.
det.treatment: Remove the toxin first. Supportive care and rehabilitation form the basis; coenzyme Q10 and antioxidants have been tried in heroin leukoencephalopathy with low-level evidence. Methotrexate-related acute toxicity may improve with dextromethorphan or aminophylline in reports, and leucovorin rescue is standard practice. Hyperbaric oxygen may reduce delayed sequelae after carbon monoxide poisoning.
det.prognosis: Variable — mild cases recover substantially after exposure ends, whereas severe spongiform disease can be fatal or leave permanent disability.
pearls: Always ask about solvent sniffing and inhaled drugs in a young person with unexplained leukoencephalopathy.
Acute methotrexate leukoencephalopathy can mimic stroke on DWI and often resolves within days.
Symmetric posterior limb internal capsule and cerebellar white matter involvement suggests heroin vapour.

case.who: 80-year-old woman from Nan with CKD stage 4
case.story: Started on pregabalin 150 mg twice daily for zoster pain; after 5 days she is drowsy with jerks of both arms and falls.

det.patho: Drugs and toxins cause myoclonus through serotonergic excess, GABAergic changes, glutamatergic or opioid effects, or direct cortical irritation. Accumulation in renal or hepatic impairment is a common precipitant. Bismuth and other heavy metals cause a myoclonic encephalopathy with ataxia.
det.clinical: Myoclonus is usually multifocal, worse with action, and may coexist with confusion, ataxia or tremor. Serotonin syndrome adds hyperthermia, autonomic instability and lower-limb clonus. Lithium toxicity causes tremor, myoclonus, ataxia and confusion.
det.diagnosis: A temporal link to a new drug, a dose change or impaired clearance is key. Drug levels and renal function are checked. EEG excludes non-convulsive status. Myoclonus persisting after withdrawal requires further evaluation.
det.treatment: Withdraw or reduce the offending agent; haemodialysis for lithium or some antibiotics. Clonazepam or levetiracetam (renally adjusted) can be used briefly. For serotonin syndrome, stop serotonergic drugs, give supportive care and consider cyproheptadine.
det.prognosis: Usually fully reversible after removal of the cause.
pearls: Pregabalin, gabapentin and cefepime must be renally dosed.
Look for toxic causes before ordering complex tests in an older patient with new myoclonus.

det.patho: Neurotoxins act on neuronal cell bodies, axonal transport, microtubules, mitochondria or myelin. Most produce a distal axonopathy affecting long fibres; some (platinum, B6 excess) damage dorsal root ganglia, and a few produce demyelination or giant axonal swellings (n-hexane). Dose and duration govern severity.
det.clinical: Symptoms start in the feet with numbness and paraesthesias, sometimes pain, followed by weakness. Systemic features often reveal the toxin. Group outbreaks suggest occupational or food exposure. Symptoms may worsen for weeks after removal before improving.
det.diagnosis: History is the key; NCS confirms and characterises the neuropathy. Blood, urine, hair or nail measurements confirm metals. Exclusion of common causes such as diabetes and B12 deficiency is still required.
det.treatment: Stop the exposure, adjust or replace neurotoxic drugs, and use chelation for some metals. Treat neuropathic pain and provide rehabilitation. Notify occupational health or public health agencies when relevant.
det.prognosis: Many improve after removal, but severe axonal loss or ganglion damage may be permanent.
pearls: Ask about work, hobbies, supplements and chemotherapy.
Clusters of cases point to occupational or food sources.
Coasting after withdrawal does not mean ongoing exposure.
