case.story: Several weeks after buying cheap unlabelled cooking oil from a street vendor, she developed fever, cough and rash; months later severe muscle pain, thickened skin and weakness.
case.exam: Indurated skin, distal weakness and sensory loss, contractures, absent reflexes.
case.tests: Marked eosinophilia early; NCS axonal neuropathy; biopsy shows perineural and perivascular inflammation.

det.patho: Industrial rapeseed oil denatured with aniline was illegally refined and sold as cooking oil. Fatty acid anilides and related esters (such as PAP derivatives) are suspected toxins, though the exact agent and immune mechanism remain uncertain. An immune-mediated vasculopathy with eosinophilic inflammation affected many organs.
det.clinical: The illness evolved through an acute pulmonary phase, an intermediate phase of myalgia, eosinophilia and thrombosis, and a chronic phase with scleroderma-like skin, neuropathy, myopathy, contractures and pulmonary hypertension. Neuromuscular involvement caused much of the long-term disability.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis was epidemiological and clinical: exposure to the oil plus the characteristic phases and eosinophilia. Today the entity is mainly of historical and teaching value; new cases would prompt a search for a toxic exposure.
det.treatment: Treatment was supportive with corticosteroids for acute lung disease and immunosuppression of uncertain benefit for later phases. Rehabilitation addressed contractures and weakness.
det.prognosis: Several hundred died in the early years; many survivors had chronic disability and increased cardiovascular mortality.
pearls: A model of toxic, immune-mediated multisystem disease.
Compare with eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome.
Eosinophilia plus neuropathy plus skin thickening suggests a toxic or eosinophilic syndrome.

name: Transient global amnesia (TGA)
formal: Sudden temporary anterograde amnesia lasting hours, with preserved alertness and personal identity, typically in middle-aged or older people and without lasting deficits.
simple: Sudden temporary memory loss lasting some hours, after which memory returns.
th: อาการความจำเสื่อมเฉียบพลันชั่วคราว จำเรื่องใหม่ไม่ได้และถามซ้ำ ๆ นานไม่เกิน 24 ชั่วโมง แล้วหายเป็นปกติ
tempoNote: Sudden onset, lasts usually 2–12 hours (by definition < 24 h); recurrence uncommon
feat: Sudden inability to lay down new memories with repetitive questioning ('Where are we? What day is it?')
Alert, knows own identity, can perform complex tasks; no focal neurological signs
Often triggered by exertion, cold water, sexual intercourse, Valsalva or emotional stress
Typically age 50–70; resolves within 24 hours leaving a gap for the episode
Witness is needed for diagnosis
inv: MRI DWI 24–72 hours after onset may show tiny dot-like CA1 hippocampal lesions
EEG if episodes are brief (< 1 h) or recurrent, to look for transient epileptic amnesia
Glucose and basic bloods; vascular work-up only if atypical features

case.story: After swimming in cold sea water she kept asking her husband where they were and why, repeating the same questions every few minutes for five hours.
case.exam: Alert, knows her name, follows commands, no weakness or ataxia; cannot recall three words after five minutes.
case.tests: Normal CT on arrival; MRI DWI on day 2 shows a 3 mm dot in the left hippocampus; EEG normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what should you tell her about the future?
case.a: Transient global amnesia; benign, recurrence is uncommon and it does not increase stroke risk, so no antiplatelet therapy is needed.

read.where: Cognitive functions — Transient Global Amnesia, p. 351

det.patho: The mechanism remains uncertain. The leading idea is transient dysfunction of hippocampal CA1 neurons, which are vulnerable to metabolic stress, possibly provoked by venous congestion from Valsalva-like manoeuvres with jugular valve incompetence, or by spreading depression as in migraine. Migraine history is a recognised risk factor; atherosclerotic stroke risk is not raised.
det.clinical: Patients abruptly cannot form new memories and also lose some recent past memories, so they ask the same questions repeatedly while remaining alert and socially appropriate. Personal identity, language and skills are preserved and there are no other neurological signs. The episode usually lasts a few hours and recovery is gradual, leaving a permanent gap for the attack. Mild anxiety, headache or nausea may accompany it.
det.diagnosis: Clinical criteria require a witnessed episode of anterograde amnesia, no clouding of consciousness or loss of identity, no focal deficits or seizure features, absence of recent head trauma or active epilepsy, and resolution within 24 hours. Delayed DWI MRI with thin slices shows punctate hippocampal lesions in a high proportion, supporting the diagnosis. Atypical, short or recurrent episodes need EEG to exclude transient epileptic amnesia.
det.treatment: No treatment is required beyond reassurance and observation until recovery. Avoid unnecessary antithrombotic therapy. Address triggers if obvious and explain that the risk of recurrence is low.
det.prognosis: Excellent — no lasting cognitive deficit in most and recurrence in under one in ten per few years.
pearls: Repetitive questioning with preserved identity in a 60-year-old after exertion or cold water = TGA until proved otherwise.
Episodes under an hour, on waking, or recurring point to transient epileptic amnesia.
DWI hippocampal dots appear 1–3 days later; a normal early scan does not exclude TGA.
det.thd: Transient global amnesia คืออาการที่จำเรื่องใหม่ไม่ได้ทันทีและถามคำถามเดิมซ้ำ ๆ แต่ยังรู้สึกตัวดีและรู้ว่าตัวเองเป็นใคร มักเกิดในวัย 50–70 ปีหลังออกแรง ลงน้ำเย็น หรือเครียด อาการหายเองภายใน 24 ชั่วโมง MRI DWI หลัง 1–3 วันอาจเห็นจุดเล็กใน hippocampus ไม่ต้องให้ยาต้านเกล็ดเลือด และมักไม่เป็นซ้ำ

qx.stem: A 63-year-old Thai woman was bathing in cold water when her husband noticed she repeatedly asked what day it was. She was alert, recognised family and had a normal examination. Memory for new events returned fully after about eight hours.
qx.q: Which feature is required for the diagnosis?
opts: Loss of personal identity
Abrupt anterograde amnesia witnessed by an observer, without focal deficits or impaired consciousness
Concurrent generalised seizure
Persistent retrograde amnesia for years
Fluctuating attention with visual hallucinations
qx.why: TGA is defined by transient, witnessed anterograde amnesia lasting less than about 24 hours, with preserved alertness and identity and no other deficits. Loss of identity suggests a psychogenic fugue, and seizures or hallucinations point elsewhere.

qx.stem: A 58-year-old man has a typical episode of TGA after strenuous exertion. MRI performed 36 hours later with diffusion sequences shows a punctate hyperintensity in the lateral hippocampus.
qx.q: What is the best interpretation?
opts: Evidence of embolic stroke requiring anticoagulation
Proof of herpes encephalitis
Indicates recurrence is very likely
A characteristic delayed hippocampal finding, not a marker of high stroke risk
Autoimmune encephalitis
qx.why: Small CA1 diffusion lesions often appear 24 to 72 hours after TGA and are thought to reflect metabolic stress rather than embolism. Prognosis for stroke or dementia is generally benign, so no anticoagulation is needed.

qx.stem: A 66-year-old man is brought in after 5 hours of repeatedly asking where he is. The history is being taken to decide whether this is transient global amnesia or another cause.
qx.q: Which finding argues against transient global amnesia?
opts: Prior migraine
Recent emotional stress
Accompanying focal limb weakness or abnormal movements with automatisms
Repetitive questioning
Normal CT
qx.why: Focal neurological deficits, stereotyped automatisms with brief repeated spells, or impaired attention suggest posterior cerebral ischaemia or temporal lobe seizures. Migraine, stress triggers and repetitive questions are all typical of TGA.

name: Transmissible encephalopathies
formal: Prion diseases transmitted between individuals, including kuru, iatrogenic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and variant CJD.
simple: Brain diseases caused by abnormal proteins that can be passed from one person to another.
th: โรคพรีออนที่ติดต่อระหว่างบุคคลหรือจากสัตว์ เช่น kuru, iatrogenic CJD และ variant CJD ทำให้สมองเสื่อมเร็วและเสียชีวิต
tempoNote: Rapid decline over months once symptoms start, but the incubation after exposure can last years to decades
feat: Rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus, ataxia, visual or pyramidal and extrapyramidal signs; akinetic mutism at the end

Acquired routes: cadaveric growth hormone, dura or corneal grafts, contaminated neurosurgical instruments and depth electrodes (iatrogenic), beef from BSE-affected cattle (variant), ritual cannibalism (kuru)
Direct brain inoculation gives a shorter incubation and a course like sporadic CJD; peripheral exposure gives a much longer lag
Variant CJD hits young adults (mean onset in the late twenties) with psychiatric symptoms and painful limb dysaesthesia first, then ataxia and dementia over about a year
Codon 129 of PRNP matters: methionine homozygosity is universal in variant CJD, and valine homozygosity is over-represented in growth-hormone cases
inv: MRI with DWI and FLAIR: cortical ribbon and basal ganglia restriction in iatrogenic disease; bilateral pulvinar high signal in most variant CJD
CSF RT-QuIC (excellent specificity in sporadic and iatrogenic CJD, lower sensitivity in variant), 14-3-3 and total tau as supportive
EEG: periodic sharp-wave complexes may appear in iatrogenic but not in variant CJD
Exposure history (surgery, grafts, hormones, transfusion, residence in BSE-affected countries); tonsil or brain biopsy only when non-invasive tests fail, with prion-safe handling

case.who: 54-year-old civil servant from Songkhla who had meningioma surgery with a cadaveric dural patch about 20 years earlier
case.story: Eight weeks of forgetfulness, then unsteady walking and a startle-triggered jerk of the arms; a month later he stopped speaking much.
case.exam: Disoriented, cerebellar gait ataxia, stimulus-sensitive myoclonus, brisk reflexes.
case.tests: MRI DWI shows restricted diffusion in the cortex and striatum; CSF RT-QuIC is positive; EEG has periodic discharges.
case.q: Which question in the history points to the cause, and what must happen to the instruments used for any procedure on him?
case.a: Past neurosurgery with a dural graft suggests iatrogenic CJD; instruments need prion-specific decontamination or single use and the case is reported to infection control.

read.where: Chapter 116: Prion Disorders: Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease and Related Disorders

det.patho: A misfolded, protease-resistant form of the prion protein (PrPSc) recruits normal cellular PrP (PrPC) into the same abnormal fold, so the pathology spreads like an infection without nucleic acid. The acquired forms are the smallest group: roughly a few hundred iatrogenic cases and a little over two hundred variant cases have been described worldwide, most of the latter in the United Kingdom. Variant CJD is linked to dietary exposure to bovine spongiform encephalopathy, while kuru spread through funerary handling of brain tissue in Papua New Guinea. Susceptibility and incubation depend on the codon 129 genotype.
det.clinical: Iatrogenic CJD looks like sporadic disease when prions are placed in the brain, while peripheral exposure such as pituitary hormone gives a slower onset that often begins with cerebellar signs. Variant CJD starts with depression, anxiety or withdrawal, together with persistent painful sensory symptoms in a limb more than the face, and neurological signs follow after months. Myoclonus, chorea, dementia and finally akinetic mutism appear as disease advances. Kuru presents as progressive cerebellar ataxia with tremor, and is now historical.
det.diagnosis: Use the clinical syndrome plus a combination of MRI, CSF RT-QuIC and EEG, graded as possible, probable or definite (definite requires neuropathology). Pulvinar signal on a T2 or FLAIR image supports variant CJD, and periodic EEG complexes are absent in that variant. The exposure history is as informative as any test. Rule out treatable mimics first: autoimmune and infectious encephalitis, Hashimoto encephalopathy, toxic and metabolic causes, and lymphoma.
det.treatment: No treatment alters the course, so care is symptomatic and palliative: clonazepam or valproate for myoclonus, management of agitation and swallowing, and early advance-care planning. Prion experimental trials exist but none is established. Prevention rests on sterilisation procedures that destroy prions (strong alkali or hypochlorite combined with prolonged high-temperature autoclaving, or incineration), single-use instruments for high-risk procedures and donor deferral policies. Report to the national surveillance programme.
det.prognosis: Fatal; iatrogenic cases with direct inoculation die within months, and variant CJD has a mean illness of about 14 months.
pearls: Always ask about dural grafts, pituitary hormone, corneal transplants and past neurosurgery.
Psychiatric onset plus limb pain in a young adult with pulvinar signal is variant CJD until shown otherwise.
Routine autoclaving does not inactivate prions.
det.thd: Transmissible encephalopathies คือโรคพรีออนที่ได้รับจากภายนอก ได้แก่ iatrogenic CJD จากการปลูกถ่ายเยื่อหุ้มสมอง ฮอร์โมนการเจริญเติบโตจากศพ หรือเครื่องมือผ่าตัดปนเปื้อน, variant CJD ที่สัมพันธ์กับวัวบ้า และ kuru ผู้ป่วยมีสมองเสื่อมเร็ว กล้ามเนื้อกระตุก เดินเซ ใน variant CJD มักเริ่มด้วยอาการทางจิตเวชและปวดแปลบที่แขนขา MRI อาจเห็นสัญญาณ pulvinar ตรวจน้ำไขสันหลังด้วย RT-QuIC ยังไม่มียารักษาให้หาย ดูแลแบบประคับประคองและต้องทำความสะอาดเครื่องมือด้วยวิธีเฉพาะสำหรับพรีออน

name: Transverse myelitis
formal: Inflammation of a spinal cord segment, causing weakness, sensory level and sphincter dysfunction, from MS, NMOSD, MOGAD, infection or post-infectious causes.
simple: Inflammation across the spinal cord causing leg weakness, numbness and bladder trouble.
th: ไขสันหลังอักเสบเฉียบพลัน — ขาอ่อนแรงสองข้าง ชาถึงระดับหนึ่ง ปัสสาวะไม่ออก ภายในวัน–สัปดาห์
tempoNote: Nadir between 4 hours and 21 days
feat: Bilateral weakness, a sensory level and early bladder dysfunction
Band-like pain at the level
Causes: post-infectious, MS, NMOSD, MOGAD, sarcoid, SLE
inv: Urgent MRI whole spine to exclude compression, then MRI brain
CSF cells, oligoclonal bands; AQP4/MOG antibodies

case.exam: Legs 3/5, T8 sensory level, brisk reflexes, extensor plantars, palpable bladder.

det.patho: Transverse myelitis is immune-mediated inflammation across one or more spinal cord segments, damaging ascending and descending tracts and the grey matter. It may follow infection or vaccination, or be the first event of MS, NMOSD or MOGAD; systemic diseases (SLE, Sjögren syndrome, sarcoidosis) and direct infections (HSV, VZV, HIV, syphilis, TB, schistosomiasis) are other causes. When no cause is found it is labelled idiopathic.
det.clinical: Symptoms develop over hours to days and peak within 4 hours to 3 weeks: bilateral but often asymmetric weakness, a sensory level, band-like truncal pain and early bladder and bowel dysfunction. Reflexes may be reduced during spinal shock before becoming brisk. A partial myelitis with asymmetric sensory symptoms and a short lesion is typical of MS, whereas a complete, severe myelitis with a longitudinally extensive lesion (three or more segments) points to NMOSD or MOGAD. Hyperacute onset within minutes suggests infarction rather than inflammation.
det.diagnosis: Image the whole spine urgently to exclude compression, then confirm intrinsic cord inflammation (T2 lesion, often enhancing). CSF usually shows pleocytosis and/or raised IgG index; check oligoclonal bands. Test serum AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG with cell-based assays, and screen for systemic autoimmunity, infections, B12, copper and HIV/syphilis. Brain MRI estimates future MS risk. Mimics include cord infarction, dural arteriovenous fistula (venous congestion), compressive myelopathy, radiation myelopathy and nutritional myelopathy.
det.treatment: First-line treatment is high-dose IV methylprednisolone (commonly 1 g per day, given for 3–5 days); plasma exchange is added for severe or steroid-unresponsive cases, especially when motor function is poor. Antimicrobials are given if an infectious cause is suspected. Supportive care covers bladder catheterisation, bowel care, DVT prophylaxis, pressure care, pain and spasticity management and early rehabilitation. Long-term immunotherapy depends on the cause — MS disease-modifying therapy or NMOSD relapse prevention.
det.prognosis: Roughly a third of patients recover well, a third have moderate and a third severe residual disability; rapid onset, complete paraplegia and spinal shock predict poorer recovery.
pearls: Every acute myelopathy is compressive until the MRI says otherwise.
Longitudinally extensive myelitis: check AQP4 and MOG antibodies.
Onset in minutes with back pain and a spared dorsal column suggests cord infarction.
det.thd: Transverse myelitis คือไขสันหลังอักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกัน อาจตามหลังการติดเชื้อ หรือเป็นอาการแรกของ MS, NMOSD, MOGAD หรือโรค autoimmune ทั้งตัว อาการเกิดในชั่วโมงถึงไม่กี่สัปดาห์ ด้วยขาอ่อนแรงสองข้าง ชาถึงระดับหนึ่ง ปวดรัดรอบลำตัว และปัสสาวะผิดปกติ ต้องทำ MRI ไขสันหลังทันทีเพื่อแยกการกดทับ แล้วตรวจน้ำไขสันหลังและแอนติบอดี AQP4/MOG รักษาด้วย methylprednisolone ขนาดสูง ถ้าไม่ดีขึ้นให้ plasma exchange ร่วมกับการฟื้นฟู

name: Trauma cervical dystonia
formal: Cervical dystonia that follows neck or head injury.
simple: Neck twisting or abnormal head postures that begin after an injury.
th: cervical dystonia ที่เกิดหลังการบาดเจ็บที่คอหรือศีรษะ มักมีปวดคอมากและการเคลื่อนไหวคอจำกัด
tempoNote: Appears days to months after injury; frequently persists
feat: Onset within days to a year after neck or head injury
Fixed head posture with marked pain and limited range of movement
Fewer sensory tricks and less improvement in sleep than idiopathic cervical dystonia
Overlap with functional dystonia is common and should be considered
Medicolegal context often present
inv: MRI cervical spine to exclude structural injury, atlantoaxial subluxation
MRI brain if central injury suspected
Neurophysiology rarely needed; assess for functional features

case.story: Two months after a crash with neck sprain, his head is pulled to the right with severe neck pain; no tremor.
case.exam: Fixed rotation of head to the right, painful restricted neck movement, no sensory trick, no fluctuation with distraction.
case.tests: MRI cervical spine shows no fracture or subluxation; brain MRI normal.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and treatment?
case.a: Post-traumatic (peripherally induced) cervical dystonia; botulinum toxin and physiotherapy, while assessing for functional overlap.

det.patho: Peripheral injury may alter sensory input and promote maladaptive plasticity in sensorimotor circuits in susceptible people. Central injury to the basal ganglia can also cause dystonia, typically with a delay. The relative contribution of functional mechanisms is debated.
det.clinical: Patients usually have a fixed posture with prominent pain and restricted range, often with shoulder elevation. Sensory tricks and remission are less common than in idiopathic cervical dystonia. Some show features suggesting functional dystonia, such as variability and distractibility.
det.diagnosis: History of injury followed by dystonia, exclusion of orthopaedic causes (fracture, subluxation) and careful assessment for functional signs. Imaging is used to exclude structural lesions.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin injections, physiotherapy and pain management are main treatments. Oral anticholinergics or benzodiazepines may help. Multidisciplinary rehabilitation is useful where functional features coexist.
det.prognosis: Often chronic and less responsive than idiopathic cervical dystonia.
pearls: Exclude atlantoaxial rotatory subluxation in post-traumatic torticollis.
Fixed painful dystonia after minor injury: consider functional dystonia.
det.thd: Trauma cervical dystonia คือ cervical dystonia ที่เกิดหลังการบาดเจ็บที่คอหรือศีรษะ ผู้ป่วยมักมีคอบิดค้างท่าเดียว ปวดมาก และไม่ค่อยมี sensory trick ต้องตัดภาวะกระดูกคอเคลื่อนด้วย MRI และประเมินว่ามีลักษณะ functional ร่วมหรือไม่ รักษาด้วย botulinum toxin กายภาพบำบัด และการจัดการความปวด

name: Traumatic axonal injury (TAI)
formal: Diffuse shearing injury to white matter axons after rotational head trauma, producing coma or persistent disability with microbleeds on MRI.
simple: Widespread stretching damage to brain wiring from a severe head injury.
th: การบาดเจ็บของแกนประสาทแบบกระจายจากแรงเฉือนเมื่อศีรษะหมุนเร็วในอุบัติเหตุ ทำให้หมดสติหรือพิการถาวร MRI พบ microbleeds
tempoNote: Injury occurs instantly; consequences evolve over hours to months with long-term disability
feat: Coma from the moment of injury, often with a relatively normal CT
Lesions at grey-white junction, corpus callosum and dorsolateral brainstem
Common after high-speed road traffic accidents, especially motorcycles
Long-term cognitive slowing, attention, memory and behavioural problems
Autonomic storms (paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity) may occur
inv: CT brain (often minor findings: small petechial haemorrhages)
MRI with SWI/GRE and DWI: microbleeds and diffusion restriction; DTI in research
Monitoring of ICP when indicated

case.who: 19-year-old motorcyclist from Chiang Mai without a helmet
case.story: High-speed crash; unconscious at scene, GCS 6 on arrival.
case.exam: GCS 6, no focal lateralising signs, episodes of fever, tachycardia and posturing.
case.tests: CT shows a few small haemorrhages at the grey-white junction and corpus callosum; MRI SWI shows numerous microbleeds including dorsal midbrain.
case.q: What is the injury type and what explains the episodes?
case.a: Diffuse traumatic axonal injury (grade 3 with brainstem involvement); paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity.

read.where: Chapter 28 Disorders of Consciousness and Intensive Care Neurology — Diffuse Axonal Injury

det.patho: Rotational acceleration and deceleration stretch axons, disrupting the cytoskeleton and axonal transport, leading to swelling and secondary disconnection over hours. Small vessels shear, producing petechial haemorrhages. The corpus callosum and brainstem are especially vulnerable. Pathological grading ranges from hemispheric lesions to callosal and brainstem involvement.
det.clinical: Patients are often comatose from impact without a large mass lesion. Recovery may be slow, passing through disorders of consciousness and post-traumatic amnesia. Long-term outcomes include cognitive slowing, executive dysfunction, mood and behavioural change, and spasticity. Autonomic storms can follow severe cases.
det.diagnosis: CT may underestimate injury; MRI with SWI is most sensitive for haemorrhagic lesions, and DWI detects acute non-haemorrhagic damage. Brainstem lesions predict worse outcome. Blood biomarkers such as GFAP and UCH-L1 are emerging for triage.
det.treatment: There is no specific therapy. Management follows brain injury guidelines: airway, ventilation, avoid hypoxia and hypotension, control ICP, prevent secondary injury. Paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity is treated with beta-blockers, gabapentin, opioids or clonidine. Early rehabilitation and long-term cognitive and psychological support are essential.
det.prognosis: Highly variable; extensive brainstem and callosal involvement predicts poor outcome, though younger patients can make substantial late gains.
pearls: Coma with an unimpressive CT after high-speed trauma: think diffuse axonal injury and get an MRI.
SWI is the best sequence for microbleeds.
Helmets and road safety are the main prevention.
det.thd: Traumatic axonal injury คือการบาดเจ็บของแกนประสาทแบบกระจายจากแรงหมุนของศีรษะ มักเกิดในอุบัติเหตุรถจักรยานยนต์ความเร็วสูง ผู้ป่วยหมดสติตั้งแต่เกิดเหตุแต่ CT อาจพบแค่จุดเลือดออกเล็กๆ MRI SWI พบ microbleeds ที่ corpus callosum และก้านสมอง ไม่มีการรักษาเฉพาะ เน้นป้องกันการบาดเจ็บซ้ำเติมและฟื้นฟูระยะยาว

name: Traumatic brachial plexus lesions
formal: Injury to the brachial plexus from trauma, such as traction or avulsion, causing arm weakness and sensory loss, depending on roots involved.
simple: Nerve damage at the shoulder from injury, causing arm weakness and numbness.
th: การบาดเจ็บของ brachial plexus จากอุบัติเหตุ เช่น ถูกดึงหรือรากประสาทถูกกระชากขาด ทำให้แขนอ่อนแรงและชาตามรากประสาทที่เสีย
tempoNote: Instant deficit; recovery or chronic deficit and pain over months to years
feat: Motorcycle accidents are the main cause in young Thai men
Upper (C5–6) lesions: shoulder abduction and elbow flexion weak; lower (C8–T1): hand weakness, possible Horner
Root avulsion (preganglionic): Horner, serratus/rhomboid weakness, preserved SNAPs in an anaesthetic area
Severe deafferentation pain is common after avulsion
Associated injuries: clavicle fracture, subclavian artery, spinal cord
inv: MRI or CT myelography for pseudomeningoceles (avulsion)
NCS/EMG after 3 weeks: SNAPs preserved in preganglionic lesions; paraspinal denervation
Vascular imaging if pulse deficit

case.story: Fell with his left shoulder forced downward; since then the left arm is flail and numb, with severe burning pain.
case.exam: Complete flaccid left arm, left Horner syndrome, sensory loss from C5 to T1, winging of scapula.
case.tests: CT myelography shows pseudomeningoceles at C6–T1; at 4 weeks, sensory nerve action potentials remain present despite anaesthesia.
case.q: Is this pre- or post-ganglionic and what is the plan?
case.a: Preganglionic root avulsion of the whole plexus; early referral for nerve transfer surgery and treatment of deafferentation pain.

det.patho: Traction from violent separation of the head and shoulder, or arm hyperabduction, stretches or ruptures the plexus. Injury can be preganglionic (roots torn from the cord, no spontaneous recovery) or postganglionic (rupture or stretch, potentially repairable). Lesions range from neurapraxia to complete rupture.
det.clinical: The pattern of weakness and sensory loss reflects the involved roots or trunks. Horner syndrome and serratus anterior or rhomboid weakness point to proximal root avulsion. Neuropathic deafferentation pain can be severe. Associated vascular and bony injuries are common.
det.diagnosis: Clinical examination maps the lesion. Electrodiagnostic studies after about three weeks distinguish preganglionic from postganglionic injury. MRI or CT myelography shows pseudomeningoceles and root avulsion. Ultrasound and MRI neurography may show postganglionic lesions.
det.treatment: Early referral to a peripheral nerve surgeon is key; nerve grafts and transfers are most successful within 3–6 months. Avulsions are managed by nerve transfers (e.g. intercostal, spinal accessory, contralateral C7). Physiotherapy prevents contractures. Pain is treated with neuropathic agents; DREZ lesioning can relieve refractory avulsion pain.
det.prognosis: Postganglionic stretch injuries often recover; complete avulsions need surgery and outcomes for hand function are limited.
pearls: Preserved SNAPs in a numb arm mean a preganglionic avulsion.
Horner syndrome after a fall suggests T1 avulsion.
Do not wait too long; nerve surgery has a time window.
det.thd: การบาดเจ็บ brachial plexus จากอุบัติเหตุพบบ่อยในชายหนุ่มที่ขี่รถจักรยานยนต์ แขนอ่อนแรงและชาตามรากประสาทที่เสีย ถ้ารากประสาทถูกกระชากขาดจะพบ Horner syndrome และปวดแสบรุนแรง ตรวจ EMG หลัง 3 สัปดาห์และ CT myelography เพื่อแยกตำแหน่ง ควรส่งผ่าตัดย้ายเส้นประสาทภายใน 3–6 เดือนและควบคุมอาการปวด

name: Traumatic brain injury (TBI)
formal: Brain injury from external mechanical force, causing a spectrum from concussion to coma, with focal contusions, haematomas and diffuse axonal injury.
simple: Brain damage caused by a blow or violent movement of the head.
ab: การบาดเจ็บที่ศีรษะ
th: สมองบาดเจ็บจากแรงภายนอก ตั้งแต่ concussion จนถึงโคม่า จัดความรุนแรงด้วย GCS มีทั้งรอยช้ำ เลือดออก และ diffuse axonal injury เป้าหมายสำคัญคือป้องกันการบาดเจ็บซ้ำเติมจากขาดออกซิเจน ความดันต่ำ และความดันในกะโหลกสูง
tempoNote: Injury is instantaneous, secondary damage evolves over hours to days (swelling, expanding haematoma); sequelae can persist for months to years
feat: Severity by post-resuscitation GCS: mild 13–15, moderate 9–12, severe 3–8; also by duration of amnesia and loss of consciousness
Focal injuries (contusions at frontal and temporal poles, extradural/subdural haematoma) and diffuse axonal injury
Red flags after mild injury: anticoagulation, age > 65, vomiting, seizure, worsening headache, falling GCS, skull fracture signs
Secondary insults — hypoxia, hypotension, fever, hypo/hyperglycaemia, raised ICP — worsen outcome
Long-term: post-traumatic epilepsy, cognitive and mood change, headache, pituitary dysfunction, increased dementia risk
inv: Non-contrast CT head per validated rules (e.g. Canadian CT Head Rule / national guidance); add CT cervical spine as indicated
MRI (SWI, DWI) for unexplained deficits or suspected diffuse axonal injury
Coagulation screen and reversal planning in anticoagulated patients; glucose, sodium
ICP monitoring in severe TBI with abnormal CT; serum GFAP/UCH-L1 can help decide on CT in mild injury

case.who: 22-year-old male delivery rider from Pathum Thani
case.story: Unhelmeted motorcycle crash; brief loss of consciousness, then confused. On arrival 40 minutes later he is increasingly drowsy.
case.exam: GCS 8 (E2 V2 M4), right pupil 5 mm sluggish, left hemiparesis, scalp laceration over the right temple.
case.tests: CT: 15-mm right convex subdural collection with 8-mm midline shift and frontal contusions; cervical CT normal.
case.q: What are the immediate priorities?
case.a: Severe TBI with acute subdural haematoma and herniation signs: secure airway, avoid hypoxia and hypotension, head-up 30°, osmotherapy as a bridge, and emergency craniotomy for evacuation, followed by ICU management with ICP and CPP targets.

det.patho: Primary injury occurs at impact: contusions where the brain strikes bony ridges, lacerations, haematomas, and shearing of axons from rotational acceleration (diffuse axonal injury in corpus callosum, grey–white junctions and dorsolateral brainstem). Secondary injury follows from excitotoxicity, inflammation, oedema, ischaemia, raised ICP and systemic insults. Road traffic crashes, especially motorcycles, dominate in Thailand; falls dominate in older adults.
det.clinical: Mild TBI (concussion) causes transient confusion, amnesia, headache, dizziness and slowed thinking that usually settle within weeks. Moderate and severe injuries produce reduced consciousness, focal deficits, seizures and signs of raised pressure or herniation (pupil dilatation, Cushing response). Older and anticoagulated patients can deteriorate hours after an apparently trivial fall. Later complications include hydrocephalus, CSF leak, meningitis, post-traumatic epilepsy, endocrine failure, spasticity, and neuropsychiatric change.
det.diagnosis: CT is the initial test and validated decision rules decide who needs it after mild injury. Classify by GCS, pupils and CT findings (Marshall/Rotterdam scores) to guide prognosis. MRI detects microbleeds and axonal injury that CT misses. Repeat CT for any clinical deterioration. Always consider coexisting cervical spine injury, intoxication and the medical event (seizure, syncope, stroke) that may have caused the fall.
det.treatment: Follow ATLS: airway protection with cervical spine control, oxygenation and blood pressure targets (avoid SpO2 below 90% and systolic pressure below about 100–110 mmHg). Evacuate significant haematomas urgently; in ICU, keep the head elevated, ensure sedation and analgesia, normocapnia, normothermia and normal sodium and glucose, and treat ICP above about 22 mmHg with osmotherapy (mannitol or hypertonic saline), CSF drainage, and decompressive craniectomy in refractory cases. Tranexamic acid within 3 hours benefits mild-to-moderate TBI; corticosteroids increase mortality and must not be used. Short-term antiseizure prophylaxis reduces early seizures only. Rehabilitation and follow-up for cognitive, mood and endocrine sequelae are essential.
det.prognosis: Most mild injuries recover, though a minority have persistent symptoms; severe TBI carries roughly 30–40% mortality, and survivors often have lasting disability.
pearls: Hypoxia and hypotension each roughly double mortality in severe TBI — prevent them.
Steroids are harmful in TBI (CRASH trial).
Older anticoagulated patients need a low threshold for CT and a repeat if they worsen.
det.thd: TBI คือสมองบาดเจ็บจากแรงกระแทก จัดความรุนแรงด้วย GCS (เล็กน้อย 13–15, ปานกลาง 9–12, รุนแรง 3–8) มีทั้งสมองช้ำ เลือดออกใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมอง และ diffuse axonal injury ในไทยสาเหตุหลักคืออุบัติเหตุจักรยานยนต์ การรักษาเน้นป้องกันการบาดเจ็บซ้ำเติม ได้แก่ ภาวะขาดออกซิเจน ความดันต่ำ และ ICP สูง ผ่าตัดเอาก้อนเลือดออกเมื่อจำเป็น ห้ามใช้สเตียรอยด์ tranexamic acid ภายใน 3 ชั่วโมงช่วยในรายเล็กน้อยถึงปานกลาง และต้องฟื้นฟูระยะยาว

name: Traumatic optic neuropathy
formal: Optic nerve injury following head trauma, causing sudden visual loss, relative afferent pupillary defect, and variable optic atrophy.
simple: Vision loss from damage to the optic nerve after an injury.
th: การบาดเจ็บของเส้นประสาทตาจากแรงกระแทกบริเวณหน้าผากหรือเบ้าตา ทำให้ตามัวทันทีหรือตามัวเร็ว มี RAPD และขั้วประสาทตาซีดตามมาภายหลัง
tempoNote: Visual loss at the moment of injury (most cases) or hours to days later when swelling or haematoma compresses the nerve; disc pallor after 3–6 weeks
feat: Monocular visual loss soon after a blow to the forehead, brow or midface, from road traffic crashes, falls or assault
Relative afferent pupillary defect is the key sign and may be the only one when the patient is drowsy; the optic disc looks normal at first
Indirect injury (force transmitted through the skull to the canal) is far more common than direct injury (bone fragment, avulsion, canal haematoma)
Colour desaturation and a central or altitudinal field defect; the globe may look otherwise unharmed
Pallor of the disc appears weeks later and marks the permanent axonal loss
inv: Bedside acuity, colour plates and swinging-light test in every head-injured patient who can be examined; document before any treatment
Thin-slice CT of orbits and optic canals for canal fracture, orbital haematoma or foreign body
MRI orbits if CT is unrevealing or the loss is out of proportion; urgent ophthalmology review to exclude globe, retinal or vitreous injury

case.who: 26-year-old motorcycle taxi rider from Chiang Mai
case.story: He fell from his bike without a full-face helmet and struck his right brow on the road. After a brief loss of consciousness he woke up in the emergency room saying the right eye could only see hand movement. There was no eye pain.
case.exam: GCS 15, brow laceration, right eye acuity hand movements with a clear RAPD and absent red colour recognition; the disc and retina look normal; extraocular movements are full.
case.tests: CT shows a small fracture of the right orbital roof extending near the optic canal with no haematoma or bony fragment touching the nerve.
case.q: Which mechanism is likely, and is high-dose corticosteroid justified?
case.a: Indirect optic nerve injury within the canal. High-dose steroids are not recommended: no proven visual benefit and, after head injury, a possible harm. Observe, serial acuity, and consider surgery only for a compressing fragment or haematoma.

det.patho: Most injuries are indirect: a frontal or brow impact sends force through the skull that concentrates at the intracanalicular segment, where the nerve is tightly bound to dura and has little room for swelling. Contusion, shearing of the nerve's small vessels and ischaemic oedema inside the canal produce secondary axonal loss. Direct injury is rarer and results from a bone spicule, avulsion from the globe, or a haematoma within the nerve sheath or orbit.
det.clinical: Vision drops at once in most patients, but it can also deteriorate over hours when swelling or bleeding builds, and that delayed group is the one in whom decompression is argued. The patient may be intubated or drowsy, so the swinging-light test is often the only reliable examination and must be done early and recorded. Associated injuries are common: skull base or orbital fracture, carotid-cavernous fistula, frontal contusion, and globe rupture. Pallor of the disc becomes obvious from the third to sixth week.
det.diagnosis: It is a clinical diagnosis resting on reduced acuity or colour, a field defect and an RAPD in a patient with plausible trauma and an initially normal disc. CT with thin cuts through the canal looks for fracture, bone fragments and a haematoma that might be removed. MRI helps when CT is negative or the nerve itself needs inspection. Rule out ocular causes (hyphaema, vitreous haemorrhage, retinal detachment, commotio) and chiasmal or posterior pathway injury.
det.treatment: Remove any remediable cause of compression, for example drain an orbital haematoma, decompress the canal when a fragment or sheath haematoma threatens the nerve, and treat a carotid-cavernous fistula. For the common indirect form, neither high-dose methylprednisolone nor routine canal decompression has been shown to improve vision, and steroids after head injury were linked to higher mortality, so observation after discussion with ophthalmology and neurosurgery is reasonable. Treat associated raised intracranial pressure and protect the eye.
det.prognosis: Variable: a proportion improve partly without treatment, but a presenting acuity of no light perception predicts a poor outcome. Pallor with a permanent field defect is the usual end result.
pearls: A relative afferent pupillary defect in an unconscious head-injured patient is the optic nerve talking: check it early and write it down.
A normal disc does not exclude it; pallor shows only after several weeks.
Avoid routine high-dose steroids after head injury; evidence does not show visual benefit.
det.thd: ภาวะนี้เกิดเมื่อแรงกระแทกบริเวณหน้าผากหรือเบ้าตาส่งไปทำลายเส้นประสาทตาในช่อง optic canal ผู้ป่วยมักตามัวทันทีโดยจอตาและขั้วประสาทตาดูปกติในตอนแรก แต่ตรวจพบ RAPD และมองสีผิดปกติ ควรตรวจ pupil และบันทึกให้เร็ว แล้วทำ CT ช่อง optic canal เพื่อหาการหักหรือก้อนเลือดที่กดเส้นประสาท การให้ steroid ขนาดสูงไม่ได้ช่วยให้การมองเห็นดีขึ้นและอาจเป็นอันตรายหลังบาดเจ็บศีรษะ จึงรักษาตามสาเหตุและผ่าตัดเฉพาะรายที่มีการกดทับชัดเจน ขั้วประสาทตาจะซีดภายใน 3–6 สัปดาห์

Spontaneous painless loss in an older vascular patient with a swollen disc, without a blow to the head

name: Traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage
formal: Bleeding into the subarachnoid space following head trauma, often over convexities.
simple: Bleeding around the brain after a head injury.
more: Subarachnoid haemorrhage resulting from head injury, commonly overlying cortex, associated with contusion.
th: เลือดออกในช่อง subarachnoid หลังศีรษะได้รับบาดเจ็บ มักอยู่ที่ร่องสมองบริเวณ convexity ใกล้ contusion พบบ่อยที่สุดในบรรดา SAH ทั้งหมด
tempoNote: Present on initial CT after injury; blood clears over days
feat: Head injury followed by headache, vomiting, confusion; severity reflects associated brain injury
Thin blood in cortical sulci over the convexities or along the tentorium, often near contusions
Commonest cause of SAH overall, more frequent than aneurysmal SAH
Vasospasm and hydrocephalus are less common than in aneurysmal SAH
inv: Non-contrast CT: sulcal blood at the impact or contrecoup site, with contusions, SDH or fractures
CTA if blood is in basal cisterns, history unclear (did a bleed cause the fall?) or pattern atypical
Repeat CT if neurological worsening; coagulation screen

case.story: Thrown off his bike without a helmet; briefly unconscious, now headache and vomiting.
case.exam: GCS 14, scalp laceration over the right parietal region, no focal signs.
case.tests: CT: blood in right parietal and frontal sulci, small left frontal contrecoup contusion, no basal cistern blood.
case.q: Traumatic or aneurysmal SAH, and what further imaging is needed?
case.a: Traumatic SAH (convexity distribution with contusion and clear trauma); CTA is not routinely needed but repeat CT if he worsens.

read.where: Ch. 9 What caused this subarachnoid hemorrhage?

det.patho: Acceleration–deceleration and impact forces tear small cortical vessels and bridging veins in the subarachnoid space, so blood layers in sulci near contusions and fractures. The amount of subarachnoid blood is a marker of injury severity rather than the main injury itself. Inflammatory products of haemolysis can still provoke vasospasm and impaired CSF absorption, though less than in aneurysmal SAH.
det.clinical: Most patients present with features of the head injury — concussion, headache, vomiting, confusion — and outcome is driven by coexisting contusions, haematomas and diffuse axonal injury. Isolated small tSAH in a patient with GCS 15 generally has an excellent course. Delayed deterioration may reflect expanding contusions, hydrocephalus or, rarely, vasospasm.
det.diagnosis: CT typically shows thin sulcal blood over the convexities, often at the impact or contrecoup site. A pattern dominated by basal cisterns or Sylvian fissures, or a story suggesting the bleed came before the fall (sudden headache, collapse), should prompt CTA for an aneurysm. Correct coagulopathy and review antithrombotics.
det.treatment: Treatment follows head injury protocols: observation, analgesia, BP control, correction of coagulopathy, and repeat CT if the clinical state changes. Isolated mild tSAH with normal neurology may be managed with brief observation according to local pathways. Nimodipine is not routinely recommended because trials have not shown consistent benefit. Treat associated injuries and seizures as needed.
det.prognosis: Isolated mild tSAH has a good prognosis; worse outcomes relate to associated brain injury, older age and larger blood volume.
pearls: Trauma is the commonest cause of SAH.
Convexity sulcal blood after injury = traumatic; cisternal blood = consider aneurysm.
Ask whether the headache came before the fall.
det.thd: Traumatic SAH คือเลือดออกในช่อง subarachnoid หลังศีรษะได้รับบาดเจ็บ เป็นสาเหตุ SAH ที่พบบ่อยที่สุด CT มักพบเลือดบาง ๆ ในร่องสมองบริเวณ convexity ใกล้ contusion ถ้าเลือดอยู่ใน basal cistern เป็นหลักหรือปวดศีรษะก่อนล้ม ควรทำ CTA หา aneurysm รักษาตามแนวทางบาดเจ็บศีรษะ ถ้าเป็นเล็กน้อยและรู้ตัวดีมักหายดี

name: Tremor
formal: Involuntary rhythmic oscillation of a body part, classified into rest, postural, kinetic and intention tremors; includes essential tremor and parkinsonian tremor.
simple: Involuntary rhythmic shaking of a body part.
th: Tremor คือการสั่นเป็นจังหวะของส่วนใดส่วนหนึ่งของร่างกาย แบ่งตามลักษณะเป็น rest tremor และ action tremor (postural, kinetic, intention, task-specific, isometric) ปัจจุบันใช้เกณฑ์ฉันทามติ MDS 2018 ที่ดูทั้งลักษณะทางคลินิกและสาเหตุ สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยคือ essential tremor, Parkinson disease, enhanced physiological tremor และยา
tempoNote: Most tremors are slowly progressive over years; a tremor that appears over days to weeks points to a drug, a metabolic state such as thyrotoxicosis, a structural lesion or a functional disorder
feat: First establish if the tremor occurs with the limb fully supported and relaxed or appears only with action (posture, movement toward a target, a particular task or a sustained muscle contraction)
Describe the distribution and frequency: hands, head, voice, jaw, legs; slow (under 4 Hz), parkinsonian (about 4–6 Hz) or faster (6–12 Hz) rhythms suggest different oscillators

Look for the company it keeps: bradykinesia and rigidity, dystonic postures, cerebellar signs, neuropathy, thyroid signs or a family history; the 2018 MDS scheme calls a tremor isolated, or combined with other signs, and then asks for the cause

Re-emergent tremor (a rest tremor that returns a few seconds after the arms are held out), task- and position-specific tremors (writing, wing-beating posture) and isometric tremor (orthostatic tremor) are named patterns worth recognising
Many drugs and states enhance a physiological tremor: beta-agonists, valproate, lithium, steroids, caffeine, withdrawal from alcohol, anxiety and thyrotoxicosis
inv: Thyroid function, glucose, electrolytes and a careful drug and caffeine history; add copper studies and ceruloplasmin under about 50 years old
MRI brain when tremor is unilateral, rapidly progressive, cerebellar or accompanied by other neurological signs; DaT-SPECT when parkinsonism cannot be settled clinically
Surface EMG or accelerometry to measure frequency and entrainment when a functional or orthostatic tremor is suspected

case.who: 58-year-old woman, primary-school teacher in Chiang Rai
case.story: For about eight years her hands shake when she writes on the board or lifts a glass of water; her mother had the same. A small glass of wine seems to calm it. Recently her head has begun to nod slightly.
case.exam: Bilateral postural and kinetic hand tremor of about 8 Hz that worsens on the dot-approximation test, mild head titubation, no rest tremor, normal tone, normal arm swing and a normal tandem walk.
case.tests: TSH, glucose and electrolytes normal; she takes no tremorogenic drugs; MRI is not needed.
case.q: How is this tremor classified and what is the first medication?
case.a: An isolated bilateral action tremor of long duration, that is essential tremor (with head involvement); propranolol is the usual first choice, primidone the alternative, and focused ultrasound or thalamic (VIM nucleus) deep brain stimulation is reserved for drug-resistant disabling cases.

read.where: 4 - Parkinsonism: Clinical features and differential diagnosis

det.patho: Tremor is produced by oscillating neural circuits. The parkinsonian rest tremor arises from basal ganglia output that entrains the cerebello-thalamo-cortical loop, whereas essential tremor, dystonic tremor and cerebellar tremors seem to depend mainly on the cerebellar-thalamic pathway; mechanical and reflex oscillation of the limb explains enhanced physiological tremor. Because different oscillators are involved, no single drug works for all tremors.
det.clinical: Phenomenology comes first: rest tremor needs a fully supported, relaxed limb, while action tremor is divided into postural (arms held against gravity), kinetic (during movement, including terminal or intention tremor in cerebellar disease), task- or position-specific (for example primary writing tremor) and isometric tremor. Distribution adds information, since voice, head, jaw and leg tremors each have a short list of causes. The older textbook habit of calling essential tremor purely monosymptomatic is now questioned, and the 2018 MDS scheme introduced essential tremor plus when soft extra signs such as impaired tandem gait or questionable dystonia are present. Parkinsonian patients may show a re-emergent postural tremor that has the same frequency and the same levodopa response as their rest tremor, and this feature is a common cause of confusion with essential tremor.
det.diagnosis: Take the history of onset, family history, alcohol response, drugs and thyroid symptoms, then observe the tremor at rest, in posture, in finger-to-nose movement, during writing and spiral drawing, and while walking. Look for slowing of repetitive movements, which converts the diagnosis to parkinsonism, and for dystonic posturing or cerebellar signs. Laboratory work is limited to thyroid function, glucose and drug review, with copper studies in younger patients; MRI is for atypical or lateralised tremor. DaT-SPECT separates degenerative parkinsonism from tremor syndromes, but a normal scan in a patient with a tremor-dominant syndrome (the so-called scans without evidence of dopaminergic deficit group) should lead to a re-look at dystonic tremor or essential tremor with rest component.
det.treatment: Treat the cause where one exists: stop or reduce the offending drug, correct thyroid disease and limit caffeine. For essential tremor propranolol (up to about 240 mg daily if tolerated) or primidone (start at 12.5–25 mg at night and increase slowly) are first-line, with topiramate, gabapentin or a benzodiazepine as alternatives; botulinum toxin helps selected head, voice and hand tremors but may weaken the grip. Parkinsonian rest tremor is treated with levodopa or a dopamine agonist, using a short trial of an anticholinergic only in young patients without cognitive risk. Disabling tremor that resists drugs is an indication for deep brain stimulation (ventral intermediate thalamus, or subthalamic nucleus in Parkinson disease) or for MR-guided focused ultrasound thalamotomy, which can treat one side without an incision.
det.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the cause: essential tremor tends to progress slowly over decades and mostly causes functional and social disability, while tremor from drugs or thyroid disease resolves after correction.
pearls: Name the tremor by what the limb is doing when it shakes, then look for other signs; the label of a disease comes second.
A rest tremor that returns a few seconds after posture is held is still a parkinsonian tremor, not essential tremor.
Check drugs first: valproate, lithium, salbutamol and thyroid hormone are classic causes of a new postural tremor.
det.thd: Tremor คือการสั่นเป็นจังหวะ ควรแยกก่อนว่าสั่นขณะอยู่นิ่ง (rest tremor) หรือสั่นเมื่อใช้งานแขนขา (action tremor) แล้วจึงหาอาการร่วม เช่น เคลื่อนไหวช้า แข็งเกร็ง ท่าทางบิดผิดปกติ หรือสัญญาณ cerebellar เกณฑ์ MDS 2018 ใช้ทั้งลักษณะอาการและสาเหตุ การตรวจพื้นฐานคือไทรอยด์ น้ำตาล และทบทวนยา ส่วนการรักษา essential tremor ใช้ propranolol หรือ primidone ถ้าดื้อยาและรบกวนชีวิตมาก พิจารณา DBS หรือ focused ultrasound ที่ thalamus

files.chapter: 4 - Parkinsonism: Clinical features and differential diagnosis

ddx.pt: Bilateral postural and kinetic arm tremor of years, often familial and alcohol-responsive, without bradykinesia
Asymmetric rest tremor with bradykinesia and rigidity, and a tremor that is re-emergent rather than present on holding posture at once
Fine, fast postural tremor that follows a trigger such as thyrotoxicosis, caffeine, a beta-agonist or anxiety and fades when it is removed

aN: rest tremor | action tremor | postural tremor | kinetic tremor | intention tremor

name: Tremor akinetic–rigid syndromes
formal: Syndromes combining tremor with akinesia and rigidity, such as Parkinson disease and atypical parkinsonism.
simple: Conditions with shaking along with slowness and stiffness.
th: กลุ่มอาการที่มีทั้งสั่น เคลื่อนไหวช้า และแข็งเกร็ง เช่น Parkinson disease และ atypical parkinsonism
tempoNote: Gradually progressive over years
feat: Bradykinesia plus rigidity and/or rest tremor
Parkinson disease is the commonest cause; tremor-dominant subtype progresses more slowly
Atypical parkinsonism (MSA, PSP, CBD) usually less tremor, poor levodopa response
Secondary causes: drugs, vascular, Wilson disease, NPH
Descriptive syndrome term
inv: Clinical; levodopa trial
DaT-SPECT if diagnosis uncertain; MRI to exclude secondary causes
Copper studies under 50; drug review

case.story: Left hand rest tremor for 2 years and slowness with buttons; no falls or urinary problems.
case.exam: Left rest tremor, left bradykinesia and cogwheel rigidity, reduced arm swing, normal eye movements.
case.tests: MRI normal; excellent response to levodopa.
case.q: Which syndrome and most likely cause?
case.a: Tremor-dominant akinetic-rigid syndrome due to Parkinson disease.

read.where: Chapter 9 Movement Disorders — Tremor Combined with Parkinsonism

det.patho: Loss of nigrostriatal dopaminergic input (Parkinson disease, atypical parkinsonism) or functional dopamine blockade disrupts basal ganglia motor circuits, causing akinesia and rigidity. Tremor involves interactions between basal ganglia and cerebello-thalamic circuits.
det.clinical: Patients have slowness, rigidity, reduced facial expression and gait changes, often with rest tremor. Red flags for atypical parkinsonism include early falls, rapid progression, early dysautonomia, gaze palsy and poor levodopa response.
det.diagnosis: MDS clinical criteria for Parkinson disease guide diagnosis; a levodopa trial supports it. DaT-SPECT helps when drug-induced or essential tremor is possible. MRI looks for atypical features (hot cross bun, midbrain atrophy) or secondary causes.
det.treatment: Levodopa is the most effective drug; dopamine agonists and MAO-B inhibitors are alternatives. Tremor may also respond to anticholinergics in younger patients. Exercise and physiotherapy are important. DBS or focused ultrasound can help refractory tremor.
det.prognosis: Tremor-dominant Parkinson disease tends to progress more slowly; atypical syndromes progress faster.
pearls: Tremor-dominant parkinsonism usually means Parkinson disease.
Absence of tremor and early falls point to atypical parkinsonism.
det.thd: Tremor akinetic–rigid syndromes คือกลุ่มอาการที่มีทั้งสั่น เคลื่อนไหวช้า และแข็งเกร็ง สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยที่สุดคือ Parkinson disease ส่วน MSA, PSP และ CBD มักสั่นน้อยกว่าและตอบสนองต่อ levodopa ไม่ดี ต้องแยกจากยาเช่น flunarizine การรักษาคือ levodopa กายภาพบำบัด และ DBS ในรายที่เหมาะสม

files.chapter: Chapter 71: Hyperkinetic Movement Disorders: Tremor and Myoclonus

ddx.pt: Asymmetric, levodopa-responsive with rest tremor
Early autonomic failure, poor levodopa response, irregular jerky tremor
Symmetric, on dopamine blockers or flunarizine, normal DaT-SPECT

aN: tremulous parkinsonism | tremor dominant parkinsonism | parkinsonian syndromes with tremor | akinetic rigid syndromes with tremor

name: Tricyclic antidepressants akathisia
formal: Akathisia caused by tricyclic antidepressants, with restlessness and inner urge to move.
simple: Restlessness and need to keep moving caused by a type of antidepressant.
th: akathisia จากยาต้านเศร้ากลุ่ม tricyclic เช่น amitriptyline, nortriptyline, imipramine ทำให้กระสับกระส่ายอยากขยับตัว ดีขึ้นเมื่อลดหรือหยุดยา
tempoNote: Days to a few weeks after starting or increasing a tricyclic
feat: Inner urge to move with restless legs, pacing or rocking after a tricyclic is started
Amitriptyline and nortriptyline are commonly used in Thai neurology clinics for pain and headache
Usually dose-related and reversible
Can coexist with tricyclic anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation) and tremor
Distinct from tricyclic-worsened restless legs syndrome, which follows a nightly pattern
inv: Drug and dose history including interacting drugs (SSRIs, metoclopramide, antipsychotics)
ECG if high dose or overdose suspected
Ferritin and renal function when restless legs is in the differential

case.story: Given amitriptyline 25 mg for chronic migraine prevention; after it is raised to 50 mg she feels she must keep walking and cannot sit through films.
case.exam: Restless shifting while seated, normal tone and reflexes, no myoclonus.
case.tests: Ferritin 90 ng/mL, TSH normal.
case.q: How would you manage her migraine prevention now?
case.a: This is TCA-induced akathisia; lower the dose or switch to another preventive such as propranolol, topiramate or a CGRP-targeted drug.

det.patho: Tricyclics raise synaptic serotonin and noradrenaline; serotonergic inhibition of dopaminergic neurons and noradrenergic excess are thought to produce akathisia. Individual sensitivity, high doses and co-prescribed dopamine antagonists increase risk. The exact mechanism remains uncertain.
det.clinical: Restlessness emerges early in treatment or after dose increases. Patients may describe anxiety, irritability or insomnia rather than using the word restlessness. Objective movements include shifting, crossing legs and pacing. It is less frequent than with antipsychotics but under-recognised.
det.diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis based on timing and phenomenology. Separate from anxiety, restless legs syndrome, hyperthyroidism, serotonin toxicity and drug withdrawal. A rating scale such as Barnes helps follow change.
det.treatment: Reduce or stop the tricyclic, or switch to another drug class. Propranolol in low doses is commonly used; short benzodiazepine courses can help. Review interacting drugs that worsen akathisia.
det.prognosis: Typically resolves within days to weeks of stopping or reducing the drug.
pearls: Low-dose tricyclics for pain or headache can still cause akathisia.
Patients often call it anxiety — ask whether they feel driven to move.
Combinations with metoclopramide or antipsychotics raise the risk.
det.thd: Akathisia จากยา tricyclic เช่น amitriptyline ที่ใช้รักษาปวดหัวหรือปวดเส้นประสาท ทำให้ผู้ป่วยรู้สึกกระวนกระวายและต้องขยับตัวตลอด มักเกิดหลังเริ่มยาหรือเพิ่มขนาด ผู้ป่วยมักเล่าว่าวิตกกังวลมากกว่าจะบอกว่าอยากขยับ การรักษาคือลดหรือเปลี่ยนยา และใช้ propranolol ขนาดต่ำช่วยได้

ddx.pt: Usually caused by antipsychotics or antiemetic dopamine blockers rather than antidepressants
Evening and rest-related leg urge relieved by movement
Restlessness with clonus, sweating, hyperthermia when serotonergic drugs are combined

aN: tca induced akathisia | tricyclic akathisia | amitriptyline akathisia | antidepressant akathisia

name: Trigeminal neuralgia
formal: Episodic severe unilateral lancinating facial pain in trigeminal territory, usually from vascular root compression; treated with carbamazepine or surgery.
simple: Sudden severe stabbing facial pain, often triggered by touch or chewing.
more: Paroxysmal severe stabbing pain in the trigeminal distribution, usually vascular compression of the nerve root, treated with carbamazepine.
th: ปวดใบหน้าแบบไฟช็อตเป็นวินาที — กระตุ้นโดยแปรงฟัน เคี้ยว ลมพัด ตอบสนองดีต่อ carbamazepine
feat: Paroxysms of electric-shock pain lasting seconds in V2/V3
Triggered by light touch, chewing, talking, cold wind
Normal sensation between attacks in the classical form
Bilateral or sensory loss suggests MS or a mass
inv: MRI with high-resolution brainstem sequences: neurovascular compression, MS plaque, tumour

case.story: Stabbing jolts in the right cheek and jaw lasting 2 seconds, dozens per day; she has stopped brushing her teeth on that side.
case.exam: Normal facial sensation and corneal reflex.
case.tests: MRI: superior cerebellar artery contacting the right trigeminal root.
case.q: First-line drug?
case.a: Carbamazepine (or oxcarbazepine); microvascular decompression if refractory.

read.where: Chapter 57 Surgical treatment of cranial neuralgias
Chapter 9 Cranial Nerve V (The Trigeminal Nerve)

files.chapter: Chapter 57: Surgical treatment of cranial neuralgias

ddx.pt: Minutes–hours, orbital, autonomic features
Younger, bilateral TN or other relapses, demyelinating lesions
Constant burning after zoster, usually V1

aN: tic douloureux | tn | trigeminal neuralgia

det.patho: Classical TN results from a blood vessel, most often the superior cerebellar artery, pressing on the trigeminal root at or near its entry into the pons and distorting it; focal demyelination lowers the firing threshold so that light touch sets off bursts of ectopic discharge that spread between neighbouring fibres (ephaptic transmission). Secondary TN is due to an identifiable disease — a multiple sclerosis plaque in the pontine root entry zone or a cerebellopontine angle tumour such as an epidermoid cyst, meningioma or schwannoma — and idiopathic TN shows neither on MRI. Annual incidence is roughly 4–13 per 100,000, rising with age, with a modest excess in women. People with MS have a much higher lifetime risk, and their TN is more often bilateral.
det.clinical: Pain arrives as abrupt electric-shock or stabbing paroxysms that last under a second to at most two minutes, confined to one or more trigeminal divisions — V2 and V3 most often, V1 alone rarely. Harmless stimuli over trigger zones around the nose, lips or gums — touch, talking, chewing, brushing teeth, shaving or a cold breeze — set off attacks, and a short refractory period may follow a volley; patients often freeze their face mid-attack. Some have a concomitant continuous ache between paroxysms, which responds less well to drugs and to surgery. Remissions of weeks to years are typical early on, but bouts tend to lengthen over time and patients may stop eating or drinking for fear of triggering pain. Red flags for a secondary cause are onset before 40, bilateral pain, objective sensory loss or a reduced corneal reflex, hearing loss, other cranial nerve signs or poor response to carbamazepine.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 defines TN by recurrent one-sided facial paroxysms in a trigeminal distribution, lasting up to two minutes, of severe electric, shooting or stabbing quality and provoked by innocuous stimuli. Every patient should have MRI including high-resolution 3D T2 (CISS/FIESTA) and MR angiography sequences through the cerebellopontine angle, to show neurovascular contact with root displacement or atrophy (supporting classical TN) and to exclude MS plaques or tumours; simple contact without deformity is common in healthy people and is not diagnostic on its own. The examination should check trigeminal sensation and corneal reflex symmetry specifically. Trigeminal reflex studies can help where MRI is not possible. Main mimics are dental pain, temporomandibular disorder, post-herpetic neuralgia, painful post-traumatic trigeminal neuropathy, giant cell arteritis in older patients and SUNCT/SUNA (autonomic signs, longer bursts).
det.treatment: Carbamazepine (started low, e.g. 100–200 mg twice daily, and titrated to effect) or oxcarbazepine is first-line and helps most patients; monitor sodium, blood count and liver tests, and test for HLA-B*15:02 before carbamazepine in Thai, Han Chinese and other Southeast Asian patients because of the Stevens–Johnson/TEN risk, which extends to oxcarbazepine. Lamotrigine, baclofen, gabapentin, pregabalin or botulinum toxin injections can be added or substituted when control is incomplete. Severe exacerbations that stop the patient eating or drinking may need admission for IV fluids and IV fosphenytoin or lidocaine, or a local anaesthetic nerve block as a bridge. Refer early for surgery when drugs fail or are poorly tolerated: microvascular decompression is the most durable option for classical TN in fit patients, while percutaneous balloon compression, glycerol rhizolysis, radiofrequency thermocoagulation or stereotactic radiosurgery suit older or frail patients and MS-related TN, at the price of some facial numbness. Concomitant continuous pain may need added amitriptyline or a gabapentinoid.
det.prognosis: Most patients respond to drugs at first, but benefit often fades or side effects accumulate; after microvascular decompression roughly 70–80% are pain-free at ten years, whereas ablative procedures and radiosurgery give shorter relief with more sensory loss.
pearls: Ask Thai and other Southeast Asian patients' HLA-B*15:02 status before starting carbamazepine.
Facial numbness between attacks is not classical TN — image for a lesion.
Patients may avoid eating and lose weight; check nutrition and hydration.
Constant burning pain lasting hours is not classical TN — rethink dental, TMJ or neuropathic causes.
det.thd: Trigeminal neuralgia คือปวดใบหน้าแบบไฟช็อตหรือแทงแปลบ ครั้งละไม่ถึงวินาทีจนถึง 2 นาที ตามแขนงเส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 5 (มักเป็น V2/V3) กระตุ้นได้จากการสัมผัส พูด เคี้ยว แปรงฟัน หรือลมพัด สาเหตุคลาสสิกคือหลอดเลือด (มักเป็น superior cerebellar artery) กดและทำให้รากประสาทผิดรูป ส่วนสาเหตุทุติยภูมิได้แก่ MS หรือเนื้องอกที่ cerebellopontine angle จึงควรทำ MRI แบบ high-resolution ทุกราย และระวังสัญญาณเตือน เช่น อายุน้อยกว่า 40 ชาหน้า หรือปวดสองข้าง ยาหลักคือ carbamazepine หรือ oxcarbazepine โดยคนไทยต้องตรวจ HLA-B*15:02 ก่อนให้ carbamazepine เพราะเสี่ยง SJS/TEN ถ้ายาไม่ได้ผลหรือทนยาไม่ได้ให้พิจารณา microvascular decompression หรือหัตถการผ่านผิวหนัง/radiosurgery ในผู้สูงอายุ

name: Trigeminal schwannomas
formal: Benign tumours of the trigeminal nerve root or ganglion, causing facial numbness, pain or weakness of chewing muscles.
simple: Non-cancerous tumours of the facial sensation nerve, causing numbness or pain in the face.
th: เนื้องอกชนิดไม่ร้ายของ Schwann cell ที่รากหรือปมประสาท trigeminal ทำให้ชาหน้า ปวดหน้า หรือกล้ามเนื้อเคี้ยวอ่อนแรง
tempoNote: Slowly progressive over years
feat: Second commonest intracranial schwannoma after vestibular, but still rare
Facial numbness or paraesthesia is the commonest symptom; pain resembling trigeminal neuralgia in some
Wasting of temporalis/masseter and jaw deviation to the affected side
Can extend into middle and posterior fossae (dumbbell) affecting CN VI, VII, VIII and brainstem
Bilateral or multiple schwannomas suggest NF2-related schwannomatosis
inv: MRI with gadolinium through Meckel's cave and skull base: enhancing dumbbell lesion
CT for bony foramen enlargement or erosion
Blink reflex and masseter EMG can document V involvement

case.story: Two years of tingling on the left cheek, now numb, with brief stabbing pains and difficulty chewing on the left.
case.exam: Reduced pinprick in V2–V3, absent left corneal reflex, wasted left temporalis, jaw deviating left on opening.
case.tests: MRI shows an enhancing dumbbell mass from Meckel's cave into the posterior fossa.
case.q: Which finding argues against classical trigeminal neuralgia?
case.a: Fixed sensory loss and motor V weakness; this is a trigeminal schwannoma.

det.patho: These benign nerve sheath tumours arise from Schwann cells of the trigeminal root, ganglion or peripheral divisions. They grow slowly, compressing the nerve and adjacent structures. Most are sporadic; some occur in NF2-related schwannomatosis through loss of merlin.
det.clinical: Numbness in one or more divisions is the leading symptom, often preceded by paraesthesia. Facial pain is less typical than in neuralgia and usually accompanied by sensory loss. Large tumours cause diplopia from abducens involvement, hearing loss, facial weakness, ataxia or hydrocephalus. Corneal reflex loss raises the risk of neurotrophic keratopathy.
det.diagnosis: MRI with contrast shows a well-defined enhancing mass, sometimes cystic, in Meckel's cave, the cavernous sinus or cerebellopontine angle, often with a dumbbell shape across the petrous apex. Differential diagnosis includes meningioma, epidermoid and metastasis. Facial pain with abnormal sensation always merits imaging.
det.treatment: Small asymptomatic tumours may be observed with serial MRI. Microsurgical resection via skull-base approaches is used for large or compressive lesions; stereotactic radiosurgery suits small to medium tumours or residual disease and offers good control. Eye protection is needed when corneal sensation is lost.
det.prognosis: Good tumour control in most; sensory deficits often persist after treatment.
pearls: Facial pain plus fixed numbness or chewing weakness = image for a lesion, not 'just' neuralgia.
Dumbbell lesion over the petrous apex is a classic trigeminal schwannoma shape.
Lost corneal reflex: protect the eye.
det.thd: Trigeminal schwannoma เป็นเนื้องอกไม่ร้ายของเส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 5 พบน้อย ผู้ป่วยชาหน้าเรื้อรัง อาจปวดคล้าย trigeminal neuralgia แต่ตรวจพบชาถาวรหรือกล้ามเนื้อเคี้ยวลีบ MRI พบก้อนรูปดัมเบลบริเวณ Meckel's cave รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัดหรือ radiosurgery และต้องดูแลกระจกตาถ้า corneal reflex หาย

ddx.pt: Paroxysmal pain with normal examination; MRI may show only vascular contact
Dural-based with dural tail, may involve cavernous sinus
General entry; consider NF2-related schwannomatosis if multiple

aN: trigeminal neuroma | trigeminal neurinoma | fifth nerve schwannoma | gasserian ganglion schwannoma

name: Trigeminal sensory neuropathy
formal: Disease of the trigeminal nerve causing facial numbness, often with connective tissue disease or idiopathic, sparing motor function.
simple: Numbness of part of the face due to disease of the trigeminal nerve.
th: เส้นประสาท trigeminal ด้านความรู้สึกเสีย ทำให้หน้าชา มักสัมพันธ์กับโรค connective tissue หรือไม่ทราบสาเหตุ กล้ามเนื้อเคี้ยวมักปกติ
tempoNote: Gradual onset over weeks to months
feat: Facial numbness, sometimes paraesthesia or pain, in one or more trigeminal divisions
Often bilateral in connective tissue disease (systemic sclerosis, MCTD, Sjögren)
Motor V (masseter) usually spared
Red flags: progressive, motor V involvement, other cranial nerves, numb chin (malignancy)
Lesion usually at trigeminal ganglion
inv: MRI brain and skull base with contrast and fat suppression
Blink reflex studies
ANA, ENA (anti-RNP, Ro/La), Scl-70, ESR; consider CSF

case.who: 44-year-old woman with Raynaud phenomenon from Lampang
case.story: Six months of numbness spreading over both cheeks and chin, with tingling while eating.
case.exam: Reduced light touch and pinprick in V2 and V3 bilaterally, corneal reflexes reduced, masseter strength normal, puffy fingers.
case.tests: MRI normal; anti-U1-RNP strongly positive; blink reflex R1 delayed bilaterally.
case.q: What is the underlying disease and what should be excluded on imaging?
case.a: Trigeminal sensory neuropathy from mixed connective tissue disease; MRI must exclude perineural tumour or skull base lesions.

read.where: Chapter 13 Cranial Nerve Disorders — Trigeminal Nerve (V)

det.patho: Trigeminal sensory neuropathy usually reflects inflammatory injury of the trigeminal ganglion or its branches, often in connective tissue diseases. Similar sensory involvement can follow tumour infiltration, perineural spread of skin cancer, amyloid, sarcoid or toxins such as trichloroethylene.
det.clinical: Numbness starts in one division and may spread; it can be bilateral. Pain and taste disturbance sometimes occur. Motor function is spared, which helps separate it from tumours. Systemic clues such as Raynaud, sicca or skin tightening point to the underlying disease.
det.diagnosis: Contrast MRI of the skull base and trigeminal pathway is mandatory to exclude structural causes. Blink reflex testing confirms trigeminal involvement. Serology for connective tissue disease and, in selected cases, CSF and biopsy complete the work-up.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying disease; idiopathic or connective tissue cases may stabilise with time, and immunotherapy helps in some. Corneal protection is important when V1 is affected. Neuropathic pain drugs relieve dysaesthesia.
det.prognosis: Usually persistent but non-disabling; progression or new signs warrant repeat imaging.
pearls: Bilateral facial numbness with Raynaud: think connective tissue disease.
Numb chin in an adult may be the first sign of cancer.
Motor V involvement argues for a structural lesion.
det.thd: Trigeminal sensory neuropathy คือเส้นประสาท trigeminal ด้านความรู้สึกผิดปกติ ทำให้หน้าชาข้างเดียวหรือสองข้าง กล้ามเนื้อเคี้ยวปกติ มักสัมพันธ์กับโรค connective tissue เช่น MCTD, systemic sclerosis และ Sjögren ต้องทำ MRI ฐานกะโหลกเพื่อแยกเนื้องอกหรือการลามตามเส้นประสาท และตรวจ autoantibody รักษาตามโรคพื้นฐาน

ddx.pt: Mental nerve involvement as a sign of metastatic cancer or lymphoma
Progressive numbness with motor V weakness; mass on MRI
Paroxysmal electric pain with normal sensation between attacks

aN: tsn | trigeminal neuropathy | idiopathic trigeminal sensory neuropathy | facial numbness syndrome

name: Trilaminar myopathy
formal: Rare congenital myopathy with trilaminar fibres on oxidative staining, with variable weakness.
simple: A very rare muscle disease named from the three-layered appearance of fibres on biopsy.
more: Biopsy is diagnostic; supportive care.
th: congenital myopathy ที่พบน้อยมาก ชิ้นเนื้อกล้ามเนื้อพบ fibre ที่มี 3 ชั้นเมื่อย้อม oxidative ความรุนแรงแตกต่างกัน
tempoNote: Neonatal or early-childhood onset; course poorly defined because few cases are reported
feat: Described in very few patients; mainly neonatal hypotonia or rigidity with raised CK
Biopsy: fibres with three concentric zones on oxidative and other stains
Genetic basis not established; some trilaminar fibres seen in other myopathies
Weakness, feeding and breathing difficulties variable
inv: CK, EMG (myopathic)
Muscle biopsy with oxidative stains and electron microscopy
Exome or congenital myopathy gene panel to look for a known cause

case.who: 3-month-old boy at a university hospital in Bangkok
case.story: Stiff and weak since birth with poor feeding; needed brief respiratory support.
case.exam: Generalized hypotonia with stiff limbs, weak cry, reduced movements, no facial dysmorphism.
case.tests: CK 2,500 U/L; biopsy shows many trilaminar fibres; exome does not identify a definite pathogenic variant.
case.q: What is the provisional biopsy-based label and what should parents be told?
case.a: Trilaminar myopathy; it is a rare morphological diagnosis with uncertain cause and prognosis, so supportive care and follow-up genetic reanalysis are advised.

det.patho: Trilaminar fibres show a central zone, an intermediate zone and a peripheral zone with different staining properties, likely reflecting disorganised myofibrils. The genetic cause is unknown, and it is unclear whether it is a distinct disease or a non-specific pattern.
det.clinical: Reported cases presented in the neonatal period with hypotonia or rigidity, weakness, raised CK and sometimes respiratory problems. Long-term course is not well described.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is based on muscle biopsy morphology. Genetic testing should be done to find a defined congenital myopathy or dystrophy; reanalysis over time may identify a cause.
det.treatment: Supportive care: respiratory monitoring, nutrition, physiotherapy and orthopaedic care. No specific therapy.
det.prognosis: Unknown; limited case reports suggest variable outcomes.
pearls: Treat rare morphological labels as provisional until genetics clarifies.
High CK in a floppy infant broadens the differential to dystrophies.
det.thd: Trilaminar myopathy เป็น congenital myopathy ที่พบน้อยมาก วินิจฉัยจากชิ้นเนื้อกล้ามเนื้อที่พบ fibre มี 3 ชั้น ผู้ป่วยที่รายงานมีอาการตั้งแต่แรกเกิด กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงหรือแข็ง CK สูง ยังไม่ทราบยีนสาเหตุ การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคองและควรตรวจพันธุกรรมซ้ำเป็นระยะ

ddx.pt: Cores lacking oxidative activity, RYR1 variants, malignant hyperthermia risk
Rods on Gomori trichrome, facial weakness, normal or mildly raised CK
Central nuclei and ptosis/ophthalmoplegia; MTM1, DNM2 or BIN1

aN: trilaminar fibre myopathy | congenital trilaminar myopathy | ringel trilaminar myopathy

name: Triosephosphate isomerase deficiency
formal: Autosomal recessive glycolytic enzyme defect causing haemolytic anaemia, progressive neuromuscular disease and early death.
simple: A rare inherited metabolic disorder causing anaemia and progressive nervous system damage.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมที่ขาดเอนไซม์ triosephosphate isomerase ทำให้เม็ดเลือดแดงแตกเรื้อรัง มีโรคประสาทและกล้ามเนื้อที่แย่ลงเรื่อยๆ และเสียชีวิตเร็ว
tempoNote: Haemolysis from infancy; progressive neurological decline in early childhood
feat: Congenital haemolytic anaemia with jaundice
Progressive neuromuscular weakness (motor neuronopathy/neuropathy), hypotonia and dystonia
Recurrent infections and cardiomyopathy; respiratory failure common
Autosomal recessive TPI1 variants (common Glu104Asp)
Most die in childhood; milder forms reported
inv: Red cell enzyme assay: low TPI activity; elevated dihydroxyacetone phosphate
TPI1 genetic testing
NCS/EMG, MRI brain, echocardiogram

case.story: Jaundiced and anaemic since birth requiring transfusions; now losing ability to sit and has abnormal arm postures.
case.exam: Pallor, splenomegaly, hypotonia, weak limbs, absent reflexes, dystonic hand posture.
case.tests: Hb 7 g/dL, reticulocytes 15%, DAT negative; red cell TPI activity very low; homozygous TPI1 variant.
case.q: What is the diagnosis?
case.a: Triosephosphate isomerase deficiency.

det.patho: TPI converts dihydroxyacetone phosphate to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate in glycolysis. Deficiency causes accumulation of DHAP and toxic methylglyoxal, impairing energy production in red cells and neurons. The common Glu104Asp variant destabilises the enzyme rather than abolishing activity.
det.clinical: Presents in infancy with haemolytic anaemia, followed by progressive neurological disease: hypotonia, weakness, areflexia, dystonia and spasticity. Cardiomyopathy, infections and respiratory failure contribute to early death. Milder adult cases are rare.
det.diagnosis: Red cell enzyme assays showing reduced TPI activity with raised DHAP support the diagnosis; genetic testing confirms. Exclude other enzymopathies and SMA with neurophysiology and genetic tests.
det.treatment: No specific treatment is available. Care is supportive: transfusions, folate, splenectomy in selected cases (limited benefit), respiratory and nutritional support. Gene or enzyme therapy remains experimental.
det.prognosis: Poor; most affected children die before age 6, though milder variants exist.
pearls: Haemolytic anaemia plus progressive neuromuscular disease in a child suggests TPI deficiency.
Ask for red cell glycolytic enzyme assays in non-immune haemolysis with neurological signs.
det.thd: Triosephosphate isomerase deficiency เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมด้อยที่ขาดเอนไซม์ในวิถี glycolysis ทำให้เม็ดเลือดแดงแตกตั้งแต่แรกเกิดและมีโรคประสาทกล้ามเนื้อที่แย่ลงเรื่อยๆ เช่น อ่อนแรง ไม่มี reflex และ dystonia วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจเอนไซม์ในเม็ดเลือดแดงและยีน TPI1 ไม่มีการรักษาเฉพาะ ส่วนใหญ่เสียชีวิตในวัยเด็ก

Episodic regression with lactic acidosis and basal ganglia lesions; no haemolysis
Aldolase A deficiency with haemolysis and myopathy, very rare
