name: Trochlear (IVth) nerve palsy
formal: Palsy of the fourth cranial nerve causing vertical diplopia, head tilt away from the lesion and difficulty looking down and in; causes include trauma and microvascular disease.
simple: Weakness of an eye muscle causing double vision, often with the head tilted.
th: อัมพาตเส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 4 ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อ superior oblique อ่อนแรง เห็นภาพซ้อนแนวตั้งหรือเอียงชัดเวลามองลง เช่น ลงบันไดหรืออ่านหนังสือ มักเอียงศีรษะไปด้านตรงข้าม สาเหตุบ่อยคืออุบัติเหตุศีรษะและเป็นมาแต่กำเนิด
tempoNote: Acute after head injury or microvascular ischaemia; congenital palsies decompensate gradually in adulthood
feat: Vertical or oblique diplopia, worse looking down and away from the affected eye (reading, stairs)
Hypertropia of the affected eye, increasing on contralateral gaze and ipsilateral head tilt
Compensatory head tilt to the opposite shoulder; old photographs may show a long-standing tilt
Torsional diplopia (images tilted) especially in bilateral traumatic palsies
Large vertical fusional range suggests a congenital, decompensated palsy
inv: Parks–Bielschowsky three-step test, ideally with Maddox rod or prism cover measurements
Fundus torsion (excyclotorsion) and double Maddox rod for bilateral cases
MRI if no trauma, no congenital features and no vascular risk, or if other signs appear
Ice/rest test or AChR antibodies, thyroid tests when the pattern does not fit

case.story: After a crash with a brief loss of consciousness two weeks ago he sees two images, one above the other and tilted, mainly when walking down stairs.
case.exam: Right hypertropia worse on left gaze and on right head tilt; he tilts his head to the left; other eye movements full; pupils normal.
case.tests: CT shows small frontal contusion only; MRI no brainstem lesion.
case.q: Which nerve, and why is it vulnerable in head injury?
case.a: Right trochlear nerve; it is long and thin, exits the dorsal midbrain and runs around the brainstem where it is stretched or bruised against the tentorial edge.

read.where: Chapter 8 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System

det.patho: The trochlear nerve is the only cranial nerve to exit the dorsal brainstem; its fibres decussate before leaving, so a nuclear lesion affects the opposite superior oblique. It has the longest intracranial course and is the thinnest cranial nerve, making it vulnerable to closed head injury. The superior oblique mainly intorts and depresses the eye in adduction, which explains the down-gaze and torsional symptoms. Common causes are trauma, congenital palsy, microvascular ischaemia and, rarely, tumour or aneurysm.
det.clinical: Patients complain of vertical or tilted double images, typically worse when reading or descending stairs. They adopt a head tilt to the opposite side to minimise diplopia. Congenital palsies may present in adult life when fusion breaks down, often after illness or fatigue; old photographs showing a head tilt are useful. Bilateral palsies after severe head trauma cause marked torsion and a V-pattern esotropia.
det.diagnosis: The three-step test identifies the weak muscle: hypertropia on primary gaze, worse on contralateral gaze and on ipsilateral head tilt. Distinguish skew deviation (a brainstem/cerebellar sign), which typically decreases when the patient lies supine and shows the higher eye incyclotorted rather than excyclotorted. Image patients without a clear traumatic, congenital or microvascular explanation. Consider myasthenia and thyroid eye disease if findings vary or are restrictive.
det.treatment: Most acquired microvascular palsies recover spontaneously; vertical prisms help during recovery. Persistent or congenital decompensated palsies may need strabismus surgery (e.g. inferior oblique weakening or superior oblique tuck), usually after 6–12 months of stability. Occlusion can be used temporarily.
det.prognosis: Microvascular palsies recover within months; traumatic palsies recover in roughly half, bilateral ones less often.
pearls: Head tilt to the opposite shoulder + vertical diplopia on reading = think IV palsy.
Skew deviation mimics IV palsy; the upright–supine test helps separate them.
Check old photographs for long-standing head tilt (congenital decompensation).
det.thd: อัมพาตเส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 4 ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อ superior oblique อ่อนแรง ตาข้างที่เป็นลอยสูงขึ้น เห็นภาพซ้อนแนวตั้งหรือภาพเอียง ชัดเวลามองลงต่ำ เช่น อ่านหนังสือหรือลงบันได ผู้ป่วยมักเอียงศีรษะไปข้างตรงข้าม ใช้ three-step test ช่วยวินิจฉัย สาเหตุบ่อยคืออุบัติเหตุศีรษะ เป็นมาแต่กำเนิด หรือหลอดเลือดเล็กขาดเลือด ส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นเอง ใช้ปริซึมช่วยระหว่างรอ และผ่าตัดกล้ามเนื้อตาในรายที่ไม่หาย

name: Tropical ataxic myeloneuropathy
formal: Myeloneuropathy in tropical regions linked to cassava cyanide toxicity and nutritional deficiency, with ataxia, spastic paraparesis and optic atrophy.
simple: A disease in tropical areas causing leg weakness, unsteady walking and nerve damage, linked to diet.
th: โรคไขสันหลังและเส้นประสาทเสื่อมในเขตร้อน สัมพันธ์กับการกินมันสำปะหลังที่มีไซยาไนด์ร่วมกับภาวะขาดสารอาหาร ทำให้เดินเซ ขาเกร็ง และตามัว
tempoNote: Insidious onset over months to years in adults with a long monotonous cassava-based diet
feat: Sensory ataxia with numb, burning feet and loss of joint position and vibration sense
Mild spastic paraparesis with brisk knees but often depressed ankle jerks
Bilateral optic atrophy with reduced acuity; sensorineural hearing loss in some
Background of poverty, protein-poor diet and poorly processed cassava as a staple
Endemic mainly in parts of West Africa; sporadic elsewhere with similar diets
inv: Blood thiocyanate and urinary thiocyanate raised in many; B12, folate, copper and vitamin E to exclude mimics
Nerve conduction: length-dependent sensory-predominant axonal neuropathy
MRI spine usually normal or shows mild cord atrophy; HTLV-1 and HIV serology
Visual evoked potentials and audiometry when vision or hearing is affected

case.who: 48-year-old Myanmar migrant farm worker seen at a district hospital in Tak
case.story: For two years he has had burning soles, unsteady walking in the dark and slowly blurring vision. For years his main food was home-processed cassava with little meat.
case.exam: Pale optic discs, absent ankle jerks, brisk knee jerks, extensor plantars, Romberg positive, stocking sensory loss.
case.tests: B12, copper and HTLV-1 normal; serum thiocyanate high; NCS shows axonal sensory neuropathy; MRI spine unremarkable.
case.q: Which diet-linked syndrome fits the triad of myelopathy, neuropathy and optic atrophy here?
case.a: Tropical ataxic myeloneuropathy linked to chronic cyanogen exposure from cassava plus poor protein intake.

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System
Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Tropical Ataxic Myeloneuropathy (Strachan Syndrome)

det.patho: Cassava roots contain linamarin, which releases cyanide when the plant is poorly soaked or dried. The body detoxifies cyanide to thiocyanate using sulphur from methionine and cysteine, so a diet low in sulphur-rich protein leaves the nervous system exposed. Long-term exposure is thought to injure dorsal root ganglia, long spinal tracts and optic nerves, although co-existing B-vitamin deficiencies probably contribute and the exact toxic mechanism is not settled.
det.clinical: Adults, often older and poor, develop a slowly worsening mixture of sensory ataxia, distal sensory loss and mild leg spasticity. Optic atrophy and hearing loss complete the picture in a proportion. It differs from konzo, the other cassava-linked disorder, which strikes abruptly and produces a non-progressive pure spastic paraparesis in children and young women. Outside endemic regions it is rare, so any case should prompt a careful search for treatable deficiencies.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical and epidemiological: compatible signs, a long history of cassava-heavy diet and exclusion of other myeloneuropathies. Raised thiocyanate supports exposure but is not specific. Always measure B12, folate, copper and zinc, and test for HTLV-1, HIV and syphilis, since these mimic the picture closely. Nerve conduction shows an axonal sensory neuropathy; spinal MRI mainly serves to exclude compression.
det.treatment: There is no specific antidote for the chronic disease. Management is dietary: proper cassava processing (prolonged soaking, fermentation, sun-drying), more protein and a broad vitamin supplement, alongside correction of any measured deficiency. Physiotherapy, walking aids and low-vision support help function. Public health measures on food processing are the most effective prevention.
det.prognosis: Deficits tend to stabilise once diet improves, but established optic atrophy and sensory ataxia usually recover little.
pearls: Myelopathy plus neuropathy plus optic atrophy: check B12, copper and diet before calling it idiopathic.
Konzo is acute and purely spastic; TAN is slow and mainly ataxic.
Thiocyanate marks cyanide exposure but does not prove causation.
det.thd: Tropical ataxic myeloneuropathy พบในผู้ที่กินมันสำปะหลังที่แปรรูปไม่ดีเป็นอาหารหลักร่วมกับขาดโปรตีน ไซยาไนด์และการขาดวิตามินทำลายไขสันหลัง เส้นประสาทส่วนปลาย และเส้นประสาทตา ผู้ป่วยเดินเซ ชาปลายเท้า ขาเกร็งเล็กน้อย และตามัวจาก optic atrophy การวินิจฉัยอาศัยประวัติอาหารและการแยกโรคที่รักษาได้ เช่น ขาด B12 ขาดทองแดง หรือ HTLV-1 การรักษาคือปรับอาหาร เสริมโปรตีนและวิตามิน และกายภาพบำบัด

Spastic paraparesis with bladder symptoms dominates; positive HTLV-1 serology in blood and CSF
Nutritional neuropathy with orogenital dermatitis and amblyopia; overlapping nutritional picture

name: True primary myoclonic epilepsies
formal: Generalised epilepsies with myoclonic seizures as the main feature, including juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.
simple: Epilepsies in which the main seizure type is sudden muscle jerks.
th: กลุ่มโรคลมชักชนิดทั่วไปทางพันธุกรรมที่มีการชักแบบกระตุก myoclonic เป็นลักษณะเด่น เช่น juvenile myoclonic epilepsy โดยสมองไม่เสื่อม
tempoNote: Lifelong tendency; myoclonic jerks typically cluster shortly after waking
feat: Myoclonic jerks, especially of the arms in the morning, without loss of awareness
Often accompanied by generalised tonic-clonic seizures and sometimes absences
Examples: juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, the benign infantile myoclonic form and Doose (myoclonic-atonic) epilepsy
Normal neurological examination and cognition (in contrast to progressive myoclonic epilepsies)
Provoked by sleep deprivation, alcohol and flashing lights
inv: EEG: generalised polyspike-wave discharges, often photosensitive
MRI usually normal

case.story: She spills her coffee every morning due to arm jerks and had one tonic-clonic seizure after exam-night sleep loss.
case.exam: Normal examination.
case.tests: EEG: generalised 4–6 Hz polyspike-wave, triggered by photic stimulation.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and which medication is preferred in a teenage girl?
case.a: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy; levetiracetam or lamotrigine are preferred over valproate in females of childbearing potential.

read.where: Chapter 21 Genetic Generalized Epilepsies with Adolescent Onset — Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy

det.patho: These epilepsies are polygenic with contributions from ion channel and other genes, causing hyperexcitable thalamocortical and cortical networks. No structural brain abnormality is detected. Myoclonic jerks arise from generalised discharges.
det.clinical: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy is the most common: adolescent onset of morning myoclonic jerks, tonic-clonic seizures and sometimes absences. Infant and early childhood forms have different features. Development and cognition are normal, though subtle frontal executive differences may be found in JME.
det.diagnosis: Clinical history (often must be asked directly about morning jerks) plus EEG showing generalised polyspike-wave. Normal MRI and normal neurological examination. Exclude progressive myoclonic epilepsies if decline or ataxia appears.
det.treatment: Valproate is highly effective but avoided in females of childbearing potential where possible; levetiracetam and lamotrigine (which may worsen myoclonus in some) are alternatives; topiramate and zonisamide are options. Avoid carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine and phenytoin, which can aggravate myoclonus. Lifestyle advice on sleep and alcohol is important.
det.prognosis: Seizures are usually well controlled, but JME often requires lifelong treatment.
pearls: Ask specifically about morning jerks; patients may not report them.
Avoid carbamazepine; it may worsen myoclonus.
Normal cognition and examination separate primary myoclonic epilepsies from progressive ones.
det.thd: True primary myoclonic epilepsies คือกลุ่มโรคลมชักทั่วไปทางพันธุกรรมที่มีอาการกระตุก myoclonic เป็นหลัก ตัวอย่างสำคัญคือ juvenile myoclonic epilepsy วัยรุ่นมีแขนกระตุกตอนเช้าและชักเกร็งกระตุกเมื่ออดนอน EEG พบ polyspike-wave ทั่วไป MRI ปกติ สติปัญญาปกติ รักษาด้วย levetiracetam lamotrigine หรือ valproate และหลีกเลี่ยง carbamazepine

ddx.pt: Progressive cognitive decline, ataxia and worsening myoclonus over years
Early childhood with myoclonic-atonic drop attacks
Non-epileptic myoclonus with normal EEG

name: Trunk tremor
formal: Tremor of the trunk, as in essential tremor or orthostatic tremor.
simple: Shaking of the body trunk.
th: อาการสั่นของลำตัว เป็นลักษณะทางคลินิก (ไม่ใช่โรคเฉพาะ) พบได้ใน essential tremor, orthostatic tremor และโรคสมองน้อย
tempoNote: Usually gradual, following the course of the underlying tremor disorder
feat: Rhythmic to-and-fro movement of the trunk, often with head titubation
Mostly appears when sitting or standing unsupported and settles on lying down
Accompanies limb, head or voice tremor in essential tremor or cerebellar disease
In orthostatic tremor the legs and trunk shake at very high frequency only on standing
May worsen gait and balance and cause falls
inv: Careful examination in sitting, standing and lying positions; look for cerebellar and parkinsonian signs
Surface EMG to measure frequency (about 13–18 Hz in orthostatic tremor)
MRI brain when cerebellar or brainstem signs, or rapid evolution, are present

case.story: Has had shaky hands for 20 years; recently his whole upper body sways rhythmically when he sits on a stool, and he feels less steady walking.
case.exam: Bilateral postural and kinetic hand tremor, 'no-no' head tremor, trunk oscillation when seated unsupported, mild tandem gait difficulty, no bradykinesia.
case.tests: Thyroid function normal; MRI brain shows only age-related changes.
case.q: Is trunk tremor a diagnosis, and what underlying disorder is most likely?
case.a: No — it is a sign; here it is part of long-standing essential tremor with axial spread.

det.patho: Trunk tremor reflects oscillation in the same networks that drive limb tremor: the cerebello-thalamo-cortical loop in essential and cerebellar tremor, and a presumed brainstem or cerebellar generator in orthostatic tremor. Midline cerebellar (vermis) disease particularly affects axial muscles. Because it is a sign, its cause is that of the parent disorder.
det.clinical: This is a phenomenological description rather than a disease. In essential tremor it appears later, together with head and voice tremor. Cerebellar disease gives slower, irregular axial oscillation, often with titubation and gait ataxia. Orthostatic tremor produces a feeling of unsteadiness on standing still that is relieved by walking or sitting, and the tremor may be felt more than seen. Functional tremor of the trunk varies with distraction.
det.diagnosis: Define posture-dependence (sitting, standing, lying), frequency and accompanying signs. Palpating the thigh or auscultating the leg muscles while standing can reveal the rapid beat of orthostatic tremor; surface EMG confirms it. Brain imaging is needed when cerebellar signs, asymmetry or recent onset suggest a structural cause. Check thyroid function and drugs that enhance tremor.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying disorder: propranolol or primidone for essential tremor, clonazepam or gabapentin for orthostatic tremor, and lesion-directed therapy for structural cerebellar disease. Axial tremor responds less well to drugs and thalamic stimulation than limb tremor. Physiotherapy, walking aids and fall prevention are important.
det.prognosis: Determined by the parent condition; truncal involvement usually signals a more advanced or more disabling phase.
pearls: Ask the patient to stand still: unsteadiness that eases with walking suggests orthostatic tremor.
Trunk tremor is a sign — always name the underlying disorder.
Titubation with gait ataxia points to the cerebellar vermis.
det.thd: Trunk tremor คืออาการสั่นของลำตัว เป็นอาการแสดงไม่ใช่โรค พบใน essential tremor ระยะหลัง orthostatic tremor ที่สั่นเร็วเฉพาะตอนยืน และโรคของสมองน้อยโดยเฉพาะ vermis ควรตรวจในท่านั่ง ยืน นอน และใช้ EMG วัดความถี่ถ้าสงสัย orthostatic tremor การรักษาขึ้นกับโรคต้นเหตุ ร่วมกับการป้องกันการหกล้ม

ddx.pt: Fast leg and trunk tremor only on standing, relieved by sitting or walking; 13–18 Hz on EMG
Bilateral action tremor of hands with head or voice involvement; axial tremor appears with longer duration
Intention tremor, dysmetria and truncal ataxia with titubation; look for a cerebellar lesion

aN: truncal tremor | axial tremor | truncal titubation | trunk oscillation

name: TTR-related amyloidosis
formal: Hereditary or wild-type transthyretin amyloidosis with progressive sensorimotor and autonomic neuropathy, carpal tunnel syndrome, and cardiomyopathy.
simple: A condition where an abnormal transport protein forms deposits in nerves and heart.
more: Diagnosed by TTR gene testing and biopsy; treat with patisiran, vutrisiran, inotersen, eplontersen, tafamidis, or liver transplantation.
th: amyloidosis จาก transthyretin ทั้งแบบพันธุกรรมและแบบ wild-type ทำให้ sensorimotor และ autonomic neuropathy, carpal tunnel และกล้ามเนื้อหัวใจหนา
tempoNote: Progressive over years; untreated hereditary neuropathy advances through stages within about a decade
feat: Length-dependent painful small-fibre neuropathy evolving to sensorimotor loss
Autonomic: orthostatic hypotension, diarrhoea or constipation, erectile dysfunction, weight loss
Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar canal stenosis, biceps tendon rupture
Cardiomyopathy with heart failure and conduction block (prominent in wild-type)
Vitreous opacities and renal involvement in some variants
inv: TTR gene sequencing (Val30Met, Ala97Ser common in some Asian populations)
Tissue biopsy with Congo red and mass spectrometry typing
Cardiac: echo, MRI, troponin/NT-proBNP; technetium pyrophosphate scintigraphy (after excluding AL)
Serum free light chains and immunofixation to exclude AL amyloidosis

case.story: Two years of burning feet, diarrhoea, weight loss and dizziness on standing; carpal tunnel release in both hands a few years earlier.
case.exam: Distal pain and temperature loss, mild distal weakness, postural hypotension without compensatory tachycardia.
case.tests: NCS: axonal sensorimotor neuropathy; echo: thick ventricular walls; TTR sequencing shows a pathogenic variant; light chains normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what disease-modifying options exist?
case.a: Hereditary ATTR amyloidosis with polyneuropathy and cardiomyopathy; TTR silencers (patisiran, vutrisiran, eplontersen) or stabilisers (tafamidis), plus cardiac care.

read.where: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves — Familial Amyloid Polyneuropathy
Companion to Peripheral Neuropathy: chapters (see text)

det.patho: Transthyretin is a tetramer made by the liver that carries thyroxine and retinol. Pathogenic variants (or ageing, in wild-type disease) destabilise the tetramer; monomers misfold and deposit as amyloid fibrils in nerves, ganglia, heart and other tissues. Disease-modifying therapy either stabilises the tetramer or reduces hepatic TTR production.
det.clinical: Hereditary forms present in adulthood with small-fibre and autonomic neuropathy that spreads to large fibres and motor loss. Carpal tunnel syndrome, often bilateral, precedes neuropathy by years. Cardiomyopathy causes heart failure and arrhythmias; wild-type ATTR mainly affects older men with heart failure and carpal tunnel.
det.diagnosis: Suspect ATTR in progressive neuropathy with autonomic failure, weight loss, cardiac disease or carpal tunnel history. Genetic testing establishes hereditary disease; tissue biopsy with typing confirms amyloid. Exclude AL with light chains and immunofixation before relying on cardiac scintigraphy.
det.treatment: Gene silencers (patisiran, vutrisiran, inotersen, eplontersen) reduce TTR production and slow or stabilise neuropathy; tafamidis and acoramidis stabilise the tetramer. Liver transplantation is now rarely used. Supportive care for autonomic symptoms, pain and cardiac complications is essential, and family members should be offered testing and counselling.
det.prognosis: Untreated hereditary disease is fatal within about 10 years of onset; modern therapies substantially alter the course.
pearls: Bilateral carpal tunnel plus neuropathy plus heart failure: think ATTR.
Unexplained weight loss and diarrhoea with neuropathy suggests amyloid.
ATTR neuropathy is often misdiagnosed as CIDP.

det.patho: Haematogenous spread during primary infection or reactivation forms small subpial or subependymal foci (Rich foci) that rupture into the subarachnoid space, producing thick basal exudate. Exudate entraps cranial nerves, blocks CSF flow and inflames penetrating arteries, causing infarcts. Parenchymal foci enlarge into tuberculomas or abscesses.
det.clinical: Tuberculous meningitis is the most severe form of TB and common in Thailand. Prodromal malaise is followed by meningism, cranial neuropathies and declining consciousness. MRC grade at presentation predicts outcome. Paradoxical worsening during treatment or with ART initiation is common.
det.diagnosis: CSF findings and molecular tests are central; Xpert Ultra improves sensitivity, but a negative result does not exclude TB, so large CSF volumes and repeat testing help. Imaging shows basal enhancement, hydrocephalus and infarcts. Scoring systems help when microbiology is negative; empirical treatment should not be delayed in suspected cases.
det.treatment: Isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for 2 months then isoniazid and rifampicin for a total of 9–12 months; adjunctive dexamethasone in HIV-negative patients (evidence in HIV-positive patients did not show benefit in a recent trial). Higher-dose rifampicin is being studied. Manage hydrocephalus with shunting or drainage, and hyponatraemia carefully. Delay ART for some weeks in HIV-associated TB meningitis.
det.prognosis: Mortality remains around 20–30% overall and higher in HIV; many survivors have neurological sequelae.
pearls: Lymphocytic CSF with low glucose and a VI palsy: TB meningitis until proven otherwise.

det.patho: A tuberculous abscess forms when the caseous core of a tuberculoma liquefies and bacilli multiply freely in the semifluid pus. It is surrounded by vascular granulation tissue but often lacks the well-formed granulomatous wall of a tuberculoma. Impaired cell-mediated immunity, especially HIV, favours this form. The abscess behaves as an expanding mass and responds poorly to antimicrobials alone.
det.clinical: Presentation resembles a pyogenic abscess but evolves over weeks: headache, fever, focal signs and seizures, with rapid worsening when oedema increases. Lesions are usually supratentorial and frequently solitary. Concurrent pulmonary or meningeal TB is common, and patients may already be on therapy when the lesion is found. Rupture into the ventricles causes ventriculitis and sudden decline.
det.diagnosis: Imaging cannot reliably separate tuberculous from pyogenic abscess, though multiloculation and a lipid-lactate spectrum without amino-acid peaks lean to TB. Aspiration is both diagnostic and therapeutic; AFB smear is usually positive and Xpert Ultra gives a result and rifampicin resistance within hours. Always send the pus for bacterial, fungal and Nocardia studies as well. HIV testing is mandatory, and the CD4 count shapes the differential.
det.treatment: Surgical drainage (repeated stereotactic aspiration or excision of the capsule for multiloculated or recurrent lesions) is combined with the standard CNS TB regimen of 2 months HRZE and HR to complete about 12 months, guided by susceptibility. Corticosteroids are used for mass effect. In HIV, ART follows after several weeks of TB therapy, with readiness to manage IRIS. Seizure prophylaxis is chosen with rifampicin interactions in mind.
det.prognosis: Outcome is good when the abscess is drained early and the strain is susceptible; mortality is higher in advanced HIV, ventricular rupture and drug resistance.
pearls: Tuberculoma: few bacilli, solid core, drugs alone. Tuberculous abscess: pus full of bacilli, needs drainage.
Xpert Ultra on aspirated pus gives the answer and rifampicin resistance the same day.
Treat an HIV patient with a ring lesion and negative Toxoplasma IgG as possible TB or lymphoma, and aspirate early.

det.patho: A tuberculoma is a conglomerate of granulomas with a caseous necrotic centre surrounded by epithelioid cells, giant cells and a fibrous capsule. It arises from blood-borne bacilli seeded during primary or reactivated infection. Bacilli are sparse in a solid caseating lesion, which explains low culture yield, whereas liquefaction allows multiplication and abscess formation. Drug penetration into the relatively anaerobic core may be limited, one reason why long courses are used.
det.clinical: Seizures dominate in supratentorial lesions, while infratentorial tuberculomas, more common in children, present with ataxia, cranial nerve palsies or hydrocephalus. Large or multiple lesions raise intracranial pressure. Systemic illness is often absent, so the lesion may first be called a tumour. Lesions can emerge or enlarge during therapy for TB elsewhere, typically within the first few months.
det.diagnosis: MRI is the key test: the T2-hypointense core and lipid-lactate peak point to caseation, and the absence of a scolex helps separate it from a degenerating cysticercus. Evidence of active TB elsewhere supports a trial of therapy without biopsy. CSF can be normal in an isolated tuberculoma, so a normal tap does not exclude it. Biopsy is reasonable when the lesion is solitary, atypical or progressive and TB has not been proven, because glioma, lymphoma and fungal granulomas look similar.
det.treatment: Treat with the WHO drug-susceptible regimen for CNS TB: 2 months of HRZE then HR, generally for a total of 12 months, extended when lesions remain active on MRI. Short corticosteroid courses help symptomatic oedema and paradoxical enlargement. Seizures are treated with a non-enzyme-inducing antiseizure medicine where possible, because rifampicin lowers levels of carbamazepine, phenytoin, valproate and lamotrigine. Surgery is rarely needed except for diagnosis, mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus.
det.prognosis: Most lesions regress on treatment; seizure freedom is usual once the lesion resolves, although calcified scars can remain epileptogenic.
pearls: Rifampicin is a strong enzyme inducer: choose levetiracetam or adjust doses of older antiseizure medicines.
A solid caseating tuberculoma is T2 dark; a cysticercus is T2 bright with a dot (scolex).
Resolution on MRI lags behind clinical cure, and small residual enhancement is not proof of failure.

qx.q: What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Switch to a second-line regimen for presumed drug resistance
Stop rifampicin because it is causing the lesions
Continue the same regimen, give corticosteroids and an antiseizure medicine
Start albendazole for coexisting neurocysticercosis

qx.why: New tuberculomas in an adherent patient with a susceptible isolate, appearing after initial improvement, are a paradoxical reaction, not treatment failure. The regimen is kept, steroids reduce the inflammatory response and seizures are treated. Changing drugs without evidence of resistance is wrong, and surgery is reserved for diagnostic doubt, abscess or mass effect.
