det.patho: During the bacteraemia of primary or reactivated infection, Mycobacterium tuberculosis lodges in small caseous foci beneath the pia or ependyma (Rich foci); when one discharges into the subarachnoid space meningitis follows, whereas a focus that enlarges instead becomes a tuberculoma. A thick, sticky exudate settles in the basal cisterns, where it traps cranial nerves, blocks CSF flow at the aqueduct, fourth-ventricle outlets and arachnoid villi, and inflames the walls of the supraclinoid carotid, proximal MCA and their perforators. The result is the typical triad of hydrocephalus, basal ganglia–capsular infarcts and cranial neuropathies. HIV is the strongest risk factor; diabetes, alcohol, malnutrition, corticosteroids and TNF blockers also raise risk, and Thailand remains a high-burden country.
det.clinical: A prodrome of malaise, poor appetite, low-grade fever and headache usually lasts one to several weeks before vomiting, meningism (only about half have a stiff neck), confusion and falling consciousness appear. Cranial nerve palsies are common—VI most often, then III, IV and VII—and hearing loss or bulbar palsy can follow; vision may fail from papilloedema, optochiasmatic arachnoiditis, a compressive tuberculoma or later ethambutol toxicity. Hemiparesis from perforator infarcts, seizures, movement disorders (tremor, chorea, myoclonus, dystonia), choroidal tubercles and hyponatraemia are other clues, and spinal arachnoiditis can add radicular pain, paraparesis and bladder failure. Severity is graded by the modified British MRC scale (I: GCS 15 without focal signs; II: GCS 11–14 or focal signs; III: GCS 10 or less), which strongly predicts outcome.
det.diagnosis: CSF is usually clear with raised pressure, a few to several hundred cells (lymphocytic, though neutrophils can predominate early or in HIV), protein typically 1–5 g/L (higher with spinal block) and glucose below half the blood level. No single test is sensitive: smear for acid-fast bacilli is positive in only 10–50% and needs a large volume (ideally 6–10 mL) read carefully; culture remains the reference and gives susceptibilities but takes up to six weeks; Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra detects roughly half to three-quarters of cases and reports rifampicin resistance, so a negative result never excludes TBM. Contrast MRI may show basal enhancement, hydrocephalus, infarcts in the caudate–capsule–thalamus region and tuberculomas. Search for disease elsewhere (chest X-ray abnormal in about half, sputum Xpert, abdominal ultrasound, node or marrow biopsy) and test for HIV; TST and IGRA cannot separate latent from active infection. Start treatment on clinical grounds when suspicion is reasonable — waiting for confirmation costs lives.
det.treatment: Begin isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide plus a fourth drug for 2 months, then isoniazid and rifampicin to complete 9–12 months, always with pyridoxine; because ethambutol enters the CSF poorly, many experts choose moxifloxacin or levofloxacin as the fourth agent. Dexamethasone (starting near 0.4 mg/kg per day in severe disease, tapered off over 6–8 weeks) reduces death in HIV-negative adults, but a 2023 trial in adults with HIV found no survival benefit, so practice there varies. In HIV, start ART after a delay of several weeks rather than immediately to limit severe immune reconstitution. Obstructive or symptomatic hydrocephalus needs external drainage, VP shunt or endoscopic third ventriculostomy; check sodium, liver tests and vision regularly, and seek expert input when drug resistance is suspected. Intensified regimens (higher-dose rifampicin, linezolid) and adjunctive aspirin are still being evaluated in trials.
det.prognosis: Mortality remains above 20% (much higher with HIV, MRC grade III or drug resistance) and around a third of survivors have serious sequelae; treatment started before consciousness falls gives the best chance of a good recovery.
pearls: Subacute meningitis with a sixth nerve palsy and low sodium in Thailand: start anti-TB treatment early rather than waiting for cultures.
Lymphocytic CSF with low glucose: TB, cryptococcus, partially treated or Listeria meningitis, malignant meningitis — and GFAP astrocytopathy as a mimic.
New tuberculomas or worsening after starting treatment is usually a paradoxical reaction, not drug failure — but check adherence and resistance.
Send big CSF volumes repeatedly; one negative smear or Xpert means little.
det.thd: TBM คือเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบจากวัณโรค ยังพบบ่อยในไทย โดยเฉพาะผู้ติดเชื้อ HIV เบาหวาน หรือติดสุรา เชื้อทำให้เกิดหนองข้นที่ฐานสมอง กดเส้นประสาทสมอง อุดทางเดินน้ำไขสันหลังจนโพรงสมองโต และทำให้หลอดเลือดเล็กอักเสบจนเกิด infarct ที่ basal ganglia อาการค่อยเป็นหลายสัปดาห์ด้วยไข้ต่ำ ปวดศีรษะ อาเจียน แล้วซึมลง มักมีตาเหล่จาก CN VI และโซเดียมต่ำ น้ำไขสันหลังมี lymphocyte โปรตีนสูงมาก น้ำตาลต่ำ ควรส่งปริมาณมาก ตรวจ AFB, Xpert Ultra และเพาะเชื้อ แต่ผลลบไม่ตัดโรค จึงต้องเริ่มยาวัณโรค 4 ตัวเร็ว รวม 9–12 เดือน ร่วมกับ dexamethasone (ในผู้ไม่ติด HIV) และระบายน้ำในโพรงสมองเมื่อจำเป็น

name: Tuberous sclerosis
formal: Neurocutaneous disorder from TSC1 or TSC2 mutation with cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, seizures, angiofibromas and cognitive impairment.
simple: An inherited disorder causing benign growths in the brain, skin and organs, with seizures and learning problems.
more: Tuberous sclerosis complex, an autosomal dominant TSC1 or TSC2 disorder with cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, seizures including infantile spasms, intellectual disability and angiofibromas.
th: โรคทางพันธุกรรมจากยีน TSC1 หรือ TSC2 ทำให้เกิดก้อนเนื้อไม่ร้ายในหลายอวัยวะ ชักตั้งแต่ทารก (infantile spasms) ปัญหาพัฒนาการ ผื่นหน้าแบบ angiofibroma และวงด่างขาวบนผิวหนัง
tempoNote: Cardiac rhabdomyomas may be seen before birth; seizures start in infancy; skin, kidney and lung lesions appear progressively through childhood and adult life
feat: Epilepsy in most, often starting as infantile spasms or focal seizures in the first year
Hypomelanotic macules (ash-leaf), facial angiofibromas, shagreen patch, periungual fibromas
Intellectual disability, autism and TSC-associated neuropsychiatric disorders (TAND)
Cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, and SEGA that may block the foramen of Monro
Renal angiomyolipomas, cardiac rhabdomyomas, lung lymphangioleiomyomatosis in women, retinal hamartomas
inv: MRI brain: cortical/subcortical tubers, calcified subependymal nodules, SEGA surveillance
EEG (including in infants before seizures are obvious); echocardiogram, renal imaging, ophthalmology, skin examination with Wood's lamp
Genetic testing of TSC1/TSC2 (about 10–15% have no mutation identified)
Chest CT in adult women for lymphangioleiomyomatosis; BP and renal function

case.story: For two weeks she has had clusters of sudden flexion jerks on waking; she no longer smiles as she did. A heart 'lump' was seen on antenatal scan.
case.exam: Three white leaf-shaped macules on her trunk, more obvious under Wood's lamp; developmental regression; otherwise normal.
case.tests: EEG hypsarrhythmia; MRI multiple cortical tubers and calcified subependymal nodules; echo two rhabdomyomas.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the preferred first-line treatment for her spasms?
case.a: Tuberous sclerosis complex with infantile spasms; vigabatrin is first line in TSC.

det.patho: TSC is autosomal dominant, though two-thirds of cases are de novo. TSC1 (hamartin) and TSC2 (tuberin) form a complex that restrains mTORC1; loss of function leads to unchecked cell growth and hamartomas in many organs. TSC2 variants generally cause more severe disease. The birth incidence is about 1 in 6,000.
det.clinical: Presentation varies widely, from severe infantile epilepsy and intellectual disability to adults with minor skin signs found when a relative is diagnosed. Epilepsy affects around 85%, and early, drug-resistant seizures predict worse cognition. TAND includes autism, ADHD, anxiety and learning disability. SEGAs grow mainly in childhood and adolescence and can cause hydrocephalus. In adults, renal angiomyolipomas (bleeding risk) and lung LAM dominate morbidity.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis uses the 2021 International TSC Consensus criteria: either a pathogenic TSC1/TSC2 variant, or a combination of major and minor clinical features (definite TSC needs two major features or one major plus two minor). Surveillance includes regular brain MRI until age 25, renal imaging every 1–3 years, EEG in infancy, neuropsychiatric screening and lung assessment in adult women.
det.treatment: Vigabatrin is first line for infantile spasms and is also used preventively in infants with epileptiform EEG before seizures in some centres. Drug-resistant epilepsy may respond to everolimus (an mTOR inhibitor), cannabidiol, epilepsy surgery or the ketogenic diet. Everolimus also shrinks SEGAs and angiomyolipomas, and sirolimus treats LAM; topical sirolimus reduces facial angiofibromas. Coordinate care through a multidisciplinary TSC clinic.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is near normal for many, but outcomes depend on epilepsy severity, intellectual disability, renal and lung disease.
pearls: Infant with spasms + hypopigmented macules + cardiac rhabdomyoma: tuberous sclerosis.
Vigabatrin is the drug of choice for spasms in TSC.
mTOR inhibitors treat several TSC manifestations at once.
det.thd: Tuberous sclerosis complex เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมจากยีน TSC1 หรือ TSC2 ซึ่งควบคุม mTOR ทำให้เกิดก้อนเนื้อไม่ร้ายในสมอง ไต หัวใจ ปอด และผิวหนัง อาการเด่นคือชักตั้งแต่ทารกโดยเฉพาะ infantile spasms พัฒนาการช้า ออทิสติก ผื่นวงด่างขาวรูปใบไม้ และ angiofibroma ที่หน้า MRI พบ cortical tubers และ subependymal nodules รักษาชักด้วย vigabatrin และใช้ everolimus ในรายดื้อยาหรือมี SEGA หรือก้อนที่ไต ต้องติดตามหลายอวัยวะตลอดชีวิต

qx.stem: A 6-month-old boy with cardiac rhabdomyomas found on fetal ultrasound and several hypomelanotic macules develops clusters of brief flexor spasms on waking. EEG shows hypsarrhythmia, and MRI shows multiple cortical tubers and subependymal nodules.
qx.q: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
opts: Prednisolone with no other drug
Carbamazepine
Vigabatrin, with a plan for visual monitoring
Ketogenic diet before any drug
Everolimus alone
qx.why: In infantile epileptic spasms syndrome caused by tuberous sclerosis complex, vigabatrin works better than hormonal therapy and is first line. The family must be told about irreversible peripheral visual field loss with long-term use, which is hard to assess in infants. Everolimus is an adjunct for drug-resistant TSC seizures, and carbamazepine can make spasms worse.

ddx.pt: Café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling and neurofibromas; seizures less common; no tubers
Facial port-wine stain with leptomeningeal angioma and tram-track calcification; not hamartomas
Infantile spasms of other cause — look for skin, cardiac and MRI clues of TSC in every case

aN: bourneville disease | tsc | tuberous sclerosis complex | tsc1 | tsc2 | hamartin | tuberin | cortical tubers | sega | subependymal giant cell astrocytoma | angiofibroma | ash leaf macule | everolimus

name: Tubular aggregate myopathy
formal: Myopathy with proximal weakness, myalgia or cramps where biopsy shows tubular aggregates of sarcoplasmic reticulum; caused by STIM1 or ORAI1 calcium-handling gene variants or sporadic forms.
simple: A muscle disease causing weakness and cramps in which muscle samples show abnormal tube-like clumps.
more: CK may be mildly raised; diagnosis by biopsy and genetics, often dominant inheritance. Treatment is supportive; progression is usually slow.
ab: Tubular aggregate myopathy with Stormorken overlap
th: โรคกล้ามเนื้อทางพันธุกรรมที่ชิ้นเนื้อพบ tubular aggregates จากความผิดปกติของการควบคุมแคลเซียม (STIM1, ORAI1) ทำให้ปวด ตะคริว และอ่อนแรงต้นแขนขา
tempoNote: Childhood to adult onset; slowly progressive over decades
feat: Exercise-related myalgia, cramps and stiffness, sometimes before any weakness
Slowly progressive proximal leg-predominant weakness
Ankle and other joint contractures; mild CK elevation
Stormorken overlap: constricted pupils, low platelets, small spleen, ichthyosis, short stature
Usually autosomal dominant gain-of-function variants
inv: CK normal to moderately raised (often a few times normal)
Muscle biopsy: tubular aggregates in type 2 fibres, red on Gomori trichrome, dark on NADH
Gene panel: STIM1, ORAI1 (also CASQ1 rarely)
Platelet count, pupils and spleen imaging when Stormorken features suspected

case.who: 26-year-old man, office worker from Khon Kaen
case.story: Since his teens he has had painful cramps after football, and now struggles to rise from the floor. His mother has small pupils and easy bruising.
case.exam: Mild hip girdle weakness, tight Achilles tendons, bilateral miosis, no fatigability.
case.tests: CK 650 U/L; platelets 90,000; biopsy shows tubular aggregates in type 2 fibres; STIM1 pathogenic variant.
case.q: What unifies his cramps, weakness, miosis and his mother's bleeding?
case.a: STIM1-related tubular aggregate myopathy on the Stormorken syndrome spectrum.

det.patho: STIM1 senses calcium in the sarcoplasmic reticulum and opens ORAI1 channels in the plasma membrane to refill stores (store-operated calcium entry). Dominant gain-of-function variants keep this pathway switched on, causing excess calcium entry, muscle dysfunction and secondary accumulation of tightly packed sarcoplasmic reticulum tubules. The same pathway in platelets, spleen, skin and iris explains the Stormorken features; loss-of-function variants instead cause immunodeficiency.
det.clinical: Presentations range from isolated myalgia and cramps with high CK to progressive proximal weakness with contractures. Onset may be in childhood or adulthood. Some carry the full multisystem Stormorken phenotype or a milder York platelet picture. Tubular aggregates themselves are a nonspecific finding and can appear in periodic paralysis, toxic exposure and other conditions.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in a patient with exertional pain or cramps, mild CK rise and characteristic biopsy aggregates, especially with dominant family history or low platelets and miosis. Biopsy is suggestive but not specific; genetic confirmation in STIM1 or ORAI1 is required. Exclude metabolic myopathies with exercise testing and acylcarnitine profile where appropriate.
det.treatment: No disease-specific treatment is approved; calcium-entry inhibitors are under study. Care focuses on physiotherapy, contracture management and pain control. Bleeding risk from thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction should be considered before surgery. Genetic counselling for dominant inheritance.
det.prognosis: Usually slowly progressive with preserved walking for many years; life expectancy is generally not shortened.
pearls: Small pupils plus low platelets plus myopathy: think STIM1 (Stormorken).
Tubular aggregates are a biopsy clue, not a diagnosis on their own.
Gain-of-function STIM1/ORAI1 gives myopathy; loss of function gives immunodeficiency.
det.thd: Tubular aggregate myopathy เกิดจากยีน STIM1 หรือ ORAI1 ที่ทำงานมากเกินไป ทำให้แคลเซียมเข้าเซลล์กล้ามเนื้อมากผิดปกติ ผู้ป่วยมีตะคริว ปวดกล้ามเนื้อเวลาออกแรง และอ่อนแรงต้นขาช้า ๆ บางรายมีรูม่านตาเล็ก เกล็ดเลือดต่ำ ม้ามเล็ก (Stormorken syndrome) ชิ้นเนื้อพบ tubular aggregates และยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง

ddx.pt: Cramps and second-wind phenomenon; flat lactate on forearm test; absent myophosphorylase
Distal plus proximal weakness, cardiomyopathy; desmin-positive protein aggregates rather than tubules
Subacute weakness with inflammatory biopsy and response to immunotherapy; no family history

aN: tam | stim1 myopathy | orai1 myopathy | tubular aggregate myopathy with stormorken overlap

name: Tumour-related epilepsy
formal: Seizures caused by brain tumour, particularly low-grade glioma.
simple: Seizures caused by a growth in the brain.
th: โรคลมชักที่เกิดจากเนื้องอกสมอง โดยเฉพาะเนื้องอกที่โตช้า เช่น low-grade glioma และ ganglioglioma
tempoNote: Seizures may precede tumour diagnosis by years in slow-growing tumours
feat: Focal seizures with or without bilateral spread, reflecting the tumour location
Highest frequency with glioneuronal tumours (ganglioglioma, DNET) and IDH-mutant low-grade gliomas
Temporal and frontal cortical tumours are most epileptogenic
Often drug resistant
Change in seizure pattern may signal tumour progression
inv: MRI with contrast; repeat imaging when seizures worsen
EEG to characterise seizures
Histology and molecular profiling (IDH, BRAF) after surgery

case.story: Since age 12 he has had brief episodes of déjà vu and lip smacking several times a month despite two medications.
case.exam: Normal examination.
case.tests: MRI: cortically based right mesial temporal cystic lesion with a nodule; resection shows ganglioglioma.
case.q: What treatment approach offers the best chance of seizure freedom?
case.a: Early complete resection of the tumour (including surrounding epileptogenic cortex); many become seizure free.

det.patho: Tumours cause seizures through mechanical and chemical effects on surrounding cortex: altered glutamate and GABA signalling, peritumoral inflammation, blood-brain barrier disruption and changes in ion concentrations. IDH-mutant tumours produce 2-hydroxyglutarate, which resembles glutamate and may promote epileptogenesis. Glioneuronal tumours themselves contain abnormal neurons.
det.clinical: Seizures occur in most patients with low-grade gliomas and glioneuronal tumours and in a lower proportion with glioblastoma or metastases. They may be the only symptom for years. Focal impaired awareness seizures are common in temporal tumours. New or worsening seizures can indicate tumour growth.
det.diagnosis: MRI is essential in any new focal seizure. Combine EEG with imaging to establish that the tumour is the cause. Histology and molecular diagnosis are obtained surgically.
det.treatment: Levetiracetam is commonly used; lacosamide, lamotrigine and others are alternatives. Avoid enzyme-inducing drugs because of interactions with chemotherapy and steroids. Primary prophylaxis is not recommended in patients without seizures. Surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy all can reduce seizures; extended resection of epileptogenic cortex improves outcomes.
det.prognosis: Gross total resection achieves seizure freedom in many patients; seizure control often parallels tumour control.
pearls: Every adult with new focal seizures needs an MRI.
Avoid enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs in patients receiving chemotherapy.
Recurrence of seizures may be the first sign of tumour progression.
det.thd: Tumour-related epilepsy คือการชักที่เกิดจากเนื้องอกสมอง พบมากในเนื้องอกที่โตช้า เช่น ganglioglioma และ low-grade glioma มักเป็นชักเฉพาะที่และดื้อยา ต้องตรวจ MRI ในทุกรายที่ชักเฉพาะที่ครั้งแรก รักษาด้วยยากันชักชนิดที่ไม่กระตุ้นเอนไซม์ เช่น levetiracetam และผ่าตัดเนื้องอก ซึ่งมักทำให้หายชักได้

ddx.pt: Hippocampal sclerosis without a mass lesion
Small cysts or calcifications causing seizures in endemic areas
Older patients with known malignancy and multiple lesions

aN: brain tumour related epilepsy | btre | tumour associated epilepsy | epilepsy due to brain tumour

name: Type III glycogenosis
formal: Cori-Forbes disease from AGL debranching enzyme deficiency causing hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly, myopathy, and cardiomyopathy.
simple: An inherited problem storing sugar in liver and muscle, causing low blood sugar and weakness.
more: Diagnosed by AGL testing and enzyme assays; frequent high-protein feeds and cornstarch.
th: โรคสะสมไกลโคเจนจากยีน AGL ขาดเอนไซม์ debrancher ทำให้น้ำตาลต่ำ ตับโตในเด็ก และกล้ามเนื้อและหัวใจผิดปกติในผู้ใหญ่
tempoNote: Liver features in infancy; myopathy emerges or progresses in adult life
feat: Childhood: hepatomegaly, fasting hypoglycaemia, short stature, hyperlipidaemia
Liver problems often improve after puberty; myopathy then progresses (type IIIa)
Proximal and distal weakness, often marked in calves and hand muscles; exercise intolerance
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in many type IIIa patients
Mild axonal neuropathy may coexist; type IIIb affects liver only
inv: Raised CK, transaminases and lipids; fasting hypoglycaemia with ketosis
EMG myopathic with irritable features; muscle biopsy shows vacuoles filled with glycogen
AGL gene testing; echocardiography and liver ultrasound

case.story: As a child he had a big abdomen and low sugars needing frequent feeds. Now he struggles with stairs and his hands are getting weak.
case.exam: Distal and proximal weakness with wasting of calves and intrinsic hand muscles, mild hepatomegaly.
case.tests: CK 1,200 U/L, ALT mildly raised, echocardiogram shows septal hypertrophy, biopsy with subsarcolemmal glycogen, biallelic AGL variants.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and which organs need regular surveillance?
case.a: GSD IIIa (Cori–Forbes disease); monitor heart (cardiomyopathy), liver (fibrosis, adenoma, HCC) and muscle.

read.where: Chapter 18 Disorders of Muscle — Glycogenoses and Lipid Storage Disorders

det.patho: Recessive AGL variants disable glycogen debranching enzyme, so glycogen breakdown stops at branch points and abnormal short-branched glycogen (limit dextrin) accumulates in liver and muscle. Type IIIa affects liver and muscle; IIIb, about 15%, affects liver only. Gluconeogenesis is intact, which makes hypoglycaemia milder than in GSD I.
det.clinical: Infants and children show hepatomegaly, fasting hypoglycaemia, growth delay and high lipids. Many improve in adolescence, but adults with IIIa develop slowly progressive myopathy with combined proximal and distal weakness, sometimes resembling motor neuron disease because of distal wasting. Cardiomyopathy may be asymptomatic or severe. Liver fibrosis, adenomas and hepatocellular carcinoma can occur in adulthood.
det.diagnosis: Hypoglycaemia with ketosis, high transaminases and CK suggests the diagnosis. Muscle biopsy reveals vacuolar glycogen storage. Genetic testing for AGL is now the preferred confirmation over enzyme assay. Baseline and serial echocardiography and liver imaging are part of the work-up.
det.treatment: Children need frequent meals, uncooked cornstarch and a high-protein diet to prevent hypoglycaemia; high protein may also benefit muscle and heart. Ketogenic or modified diets have been explored for cardiomyopathy. Management is multidisciplinary, including cardiology, hepatology and physiotherapy; liver transplantation is reserved for cirrhosis or tumour.
det.prognosis: Survival into adulthood is usual; morbidity comes from progressive myopathy, cardiomyopathy and liver complications.
pearls: Childhood liver disease that 'got better', then adult distal and proximal weakness: think GSD III.
Distal wasting with high CK may mimic motor neuron disease — check EMG and biopsy.
Ketotic hypoglycaemia (unlike GSD I) and raised CK are clues.
det.thd: GSD III หรือ Cori–Forbes disease เกิดจากขาดเอนไซม์ debrancher (ยีน AGL) ไกลโคเจนผิดรูปสะสมในตับและกล้ามเนื้อ เด็กมีตับโตและน้ำตาลต่ำเวลาอดอาหาร พอโตอาการตับมักดีขึ้นแต่กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงทั้งต้นและปลายแขนขา และอาจมีกล้ามเนื้อหัวใจหนา รักษาด้วยอาหารโปรตีนสูงและ cornstarch ร่วมกับติดตามหัวใจและตับ

ddx.pt: Lysosomal glycogenosis; respiratory and axial weakness, no hypoglycaemia; enzyme therapy available
Phosphorylase kinase deficiency with milder liver and occasional muscle disease
Genetic distal weakness without liver involvement or hypoglycaemia

aN: gsd iii | cori disease | forbes disease | cori forbes disease | debranching enzyme deficiency | agl deficiency

name: Type IV glycogenosis
formal: Andersen disease from GBE1 mutation producing abnormal polyglucosan, with liver cirrhosis, myopathy, or adult polyglucosan body disease.
simple: An inherited glycogen-storage condition forming abnormal sugar chains, damaging liver, muscle, or nerves.
more: Biopsy shows polyglucosan bodies; GBE1 testing; liver transplantation is considered in progressive liver disease.
th: โรคสะสมไกลโคเจนจากยีน GBE1 ขาดเอนไซม์แตกกิ่ง ทำให้เกิด polyglucosan สะสม มีได้ตั้งแต่ตับแข็งในเด็ก กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง ถึง APBD ในผู้ใหญ่
tempoNote: Ranges from fetal/neonatal lethal forms to adult-onset neurodegeneration
feat: Classic hepatic form: failure to thrive and cirrhosis in early childhood
Neuromuscular forms: fetal akinesia, neonatal hypotonia, childhood or adult myopathy, cardiomyopathy
Adult polyglucosan body disease (APBD): neurogenic bladder, spastic paraparesis, neuropathy, cognitive decline
Polyglucosan bodies in liver, muscle, nerve and brain
inv: Liver or muscle biopsy: PAS-positive, diastase-resistant polyglucosan bodies
Branching enzyme activity in leucocytes or fibroblasts
GBE1 genetic testing; MRI brain/spine in adults (white matter and cord atrophy)

case.story: Three years of urinary urgency, then stiff legs and numb feet; family notes mild forgetfulness.
case.exam: Spastic paraparesis, distal sensory loss, absent ankle jerks, mildly reduced recall.
case.tests: MRI: diffuse periventricular white matter change and thin cervical cord; nerve conduction axonal neuropathy; leucocyte branching enzyme activity low; GBE1 variants.
case.q: Which disorder links bladder, spasticity, neuropathy and white matter disease here?
case.a: Adult polyglucosan body disease, the adult neurological form of GSD IV.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Glycogen Storage Diseases

det.patho: Glycogen branching enzyme introduces branch points during synthesis. Deficiency yields long, poorly branched glucose chains resembling amylopectin that are insoluble and form polyglucosan bodies. These deposits damage hepatocytes, myocytes, cardiomyocytes, axons and astrocytes; residual enzyme activity largely determines which phenotype appears.
det.clinical: Most childhood cases have progressive cirrhosis in the first years of life. Neuromuscular variants range from fetal akinesia with arthrogryposis and fatal neonatal hypotonia to childhood myopathy with cardiomyopathy. In adults, APBD appears after 40 with bladder dysfunction, spastic gait, sensory-motor neuropathy and later cognitive impairment, and is especially frequent in Ashkenazi Jewish carriers of the p.Y329S variant.
det.diagnosis: Biopsy of affected tissue demonstrates diastase-resistant polyglucosan inclusions; sural nerve or skin biopsy helps in APBD. Enzyme activity confirms the defect, and GBE1 sequencing defines variants. MRI in APBD shows white matter changes and atrophy of medulla and cord.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy is established. Liver transplantation can be life-saving in the hepatic form, though extrahepatic disease may progress. Triheptanoin has been studied in APBD with limited benefit; care focuses on bladder management, spasticity, physiotherapy and cardiac monitoring.
det.prognosis: Hepatic and neonatal forms are often fatal in childhood without transplant; APBD progresses slowly over years.
pearls: Neurogenic bladder first, then spastic paraparesis and neuropathy in a middle-aged adult: think APBD.
Polyglucosan bodies are diastase-resistant, unlike normal glycogen.
One enzyme, many phenotypes — from cirrhosis in infants to leukodystrophy-like disease in adults.
det.thd: GSD IV หรือ Andersen disease เกิดจากยีน GBE1 ทำให้ไกลโคเจนไม่แตกกิ่งและกลายเป็น polyglucosan สะสม เด็กมักมีตับแข็ง บางรายมีกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงหรือหัวใจผิดปกติ ผู้ใหญ่เกิด APBD มีปัสสาวะผิดปกติ ขาเกร็ง ปลายประสาทเสื่อม และความจำลดลง ยังไม่มีการรักษาเฉพาะ เด็กชนิดตับอาจต้องปลูกถ่ายตับ

ddx.pt: The adult neurological expression of the same enzyme defect
Adrenomyeloneuropathy also gives spastic paraparesis and neuropathy; high VLCFA
Liver and muscle disease with hypoglycaemia; debranching rather than branching defect

aN: gsd iv | andersen disease | glycogen branching enzyme deficiency | gbe1 deficiency | amylopectinosis

name: Type IX glycogenosis
formal: Phosphorylase kinase deficiency with X-linked or autosomal recessive forms (PHKA1, PHKA2, PHKB, PHKG2), causing hepatomegaly, hypoglycaemia, or exercise intolerance.
simple: An inherited glycogen-processing problem causing an enlarged liver or muscle cramps.
more: Diagnosed by gene testing; dietary management with cornstarch and protein.
th: โรคสะสมไกลโคเจนจากขาดเอนไซม์ phosphorylase kinase ส่วนใหญ่เป็นชนิดตับ (ตับโต น้ำตาลต่ำ) ซึ่งมักดีขึ้นตามอายุ ชนิดกล้ามเนื้อพบน้อย ทำให้ออกกำลังไม่ทนและเป็นตะคริว
tempoNote: Liver form from infancy, improving after puberty; muscle form with exercise-induced episodes
feat: Liver forms (PHKA2 X-linked, PHKB, PHKG2): hepatomegaly, fasting ketotic hypoglycaemia, growth delay
PHKG2 form can progress to liver fibrosis or cirrhosis
Muscle form (PHKA1, X-linked): exercise intolerance, cramps, rarely myoglobinuria, mild weakness
Many children improve markedly after puberty
inv: Fasting glucose and ketones, liver enzymes, lipids, CK
Phosphorylase kinase activity in red cells or liver (normal red-cell activity does not exclude some forms)
Gene panel for PHKA1, PHKA2, PHKB, PHKG2; forearm exercise test may be blunted in muscle form

case.story: Protuberant abdomen, short for age, and sweaty and drowsy when meals are delayed.
case.exam: Liver 6 cm below costal margin, no splenomegaly, normal muscle strength.
case.tests: Fasting glucose 2.8 mmol/L with high ketones; ALT 210; lactate and uric acid normal; PHKA2 hemizygous variant.
case.q: What feature separates this from GSD type I, and what is the treatment?
case.a: Lactate and uric acid stay normal and ketosis is prominent; frequent meals, uncooked cornstarch at night and a high-protein diet.

det.patho: Phosphorylase kinase activates glycogen phosphorylase, the enzyme that releases glucose from glycogen. It has four subunits encoded by different genes, so deficiency can affect the liver, muscle or both depending on the subunit. Glycogen accumulates in liver cells, and fasting glucose release is impaired, though gluconeogenesis is intact. It is one of the commonest glycogen storage diseases.
det.clinical: The X-linked liver form (PHKA2) is most frequent and usually mild, with hepatomegaly and hypoglycaemia that improve with age. PHKG2 and PHKB forms can be more severe, with fibrosis. The rare muscle-only form (PHKA1) presents in adolescents or adults with exercise intolerance and cramps, overlapping with McArdle disease but milder. It is a metabolic disease with a minor neuromuscular face.
det.diagnosis: Gene panel testing is the usual first step. Enzyme activity in erythrocytes or tissue supports it but can mislead. Liver biopsy (glycogen accumulation, fibrosis) is reserved for uncertain cases. In the muscle form, CK may be mildly raised and biopsy shows subsarcolemmal glycogen.
det.treatment: Prevent hypoglycaemia with frequent high-protein meals and cornstarch, adjusted with growth. Monitor liver function and imaging, especially in PHKG2. The muscle form needs graded aerobic exercise and avoidance of intense bursts; no specific drug therapy exists.
det.prognosis: Usually favourable; most liver forms improve, though PHKG2 carries a cirrhosis risk.
pearls: Ketotic hypoglycaemia + hepatomegaly with normal lactate and urate: think GSD IX or VI rather than GSD I.
Muscle-only PhK deficiency is a rare, mild McArdle look-alike.
Normal red-cell PhK activity does not exclude the disease; use genetics.
det.thd: Type IX glycogenosis เกิดจากขาด phosphorylase kinase ทำให้ปล่อยกลูโคสจากไกลโคเจนไม่ได้ ชนิดที่พบบ่อยเป็นชนิดตับ เด็กมีตับโต น้ำตาลต่ำเมื่ออดอาหาร และตัวเตี้ย ซึ่งมักดีขึ้นหลังวัยรุ่น ชนิดกล้ามเนื้อพบน้อย ทำให้ออกกำลังไม่ทนและเป็นตะคริว วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีน รักษาด้วยการกินอาหารบ่อย โปรตีนสูง และแป้งข้าวโพดดิบก่อนนอน

ddx.pt: Hepatomegaly and hypoglycaemia plus progressive myopathy and cardiomyopathy with high CK
Pure muscle disease with second-wind phenomenon and flat lactate on forearm test
Rhabdomyolysis after prolonged exercise or fasting, no cramps during short effort

aN: gsd ix | gsd type ix | phosphorylase kinase deficiency | phk deficiency | gsd ixa

name: Type VIII glycogenosis
formal: Older designation for phosphorylase b kinase deficiency, now classed with type IX, with exercise intolerance or hepatic glycogenosis.
simple: An old name for a rare inherited sugar-storage disease affecting muscle or liver.
more: Diagnosed by genetic testing of PHKA/PHKB genes; treatment is supportive with dietary management.
th: ชื่อเดิมของภาวะพร่องเอนไซม์ phosphorylase b kinase ซึ่งปัจจุบันจัดรวมเป็น glycogen storage disease type IX ทำให้ตับโตหรือทนการออกกำลังไม่ได้
tempoNote: Liver forms present in infancy or childhood; muscle form gives episodic exercise symptoms from adolescence or adulthood
feat: Historical label; most modern texts file all phosphorylase kinase defects under GSD IX
Liver forms: hepatomegaly, growth delay, fasting hypoglycaemia and raised transaminases in childhood
Muscle form (PHKA1, X-linked): mild exercise intolerance, cramps, occasional myoglobinuria
Some early reports described a neurodegenerative brain form, now poorly substantiated
Liver disease often improves with age
inv: Fasting glucose, lipids, liver enzymes; liver ultrasound for hepatomegaly
CK at rest and after exercise; forearm exercise test may be normal or mildly blunted
Enzyme activity in red cells, liver or muscle (normal red cell activity does not exclude it)
Gene panel: PHKA1, PHKA2, PHKB, PHKG2

case.who: 3-year-old boy brought to a Bangkok children's hospital
case.story: Parents noticed a large abdomen and he becomes sweaty and irritable if breakfast is late.
case.exam: Liver edge 6 cm below costal margin, no splenomegaly, normal tone and reflexes, height on 5th centile.
case.tests: Fasting glucose 2.8 mmol/L with ketones; ALT 180 U/L; PHKA2 hemizygous variant.
case.q: What older eponymous number might appear for this disorder in old notes, and what is the current label?
case.a: Phosphorylase kinase deficiency — once called type VIII, now classified as GSD type IX (X-linked liver form).

det.patho: Phosphorylase b kinase is a multi-subunit enzyme that activates glycogen phosphorylase. Deficiency slows glycogen breakdown in liver, muscle or both depending on which subunit gene is affected (PHKA2, PHKB, PHKG2 for liver; PHKA1 for muscle). The numbering of glycogenoses has varied between authors, so type VIII is now regarded as an outdated label and the condition is grouped with GSD IX.
det.clinical: Liver forms are the commonest and resemble a mild hepatic glycogenosis with hepatomegaly, short stature and ketotic fasting hypoglycaemia; PHKG2 forms can progress to fibrosis. The muscle form is rare and mild, causing exercise intolerance, cramps or no symptoms. Older literature linked 'type VIII' to a progressive brain disorder, but this association is not well supported today.
det.diagnosis: Clinical suspicion from hepatomegaly with fasting ketotic hypoglycaemia, or from exertional muscle symptoms, is confirmed by gene panel testing. Enzyme assays in blood cells can be misleading because some subtypes spare red cells. Liver biopsy is rarely needed now.
det.treatment: Frequent meals, uncooked cornstarch at night and a higher-protein diet prevent hypoglycaemia in liver forms. Monitor growth, liver enzymes and, for PHKG2, fibrosis. Muscle forms need sensible exercise advice only. No enzyme-specific therapy exists.
det.prognosis: Most liver forms improve after childhood; PHKG2 variants carry a risk of cirrhosis.
pearls: Glycogenosis numbering is inconsistent; check the enzyme, not just the type number.
Normal red cell PhK activity does not exclude liver PhK deficiency.
Ketotic hypoglycaemia with hepatomegaly suggests GSD III, VI or IX rather than GSD I.
det.thd: Type VIII glycogenosis เป็นชื่อเก่าของภาวะพร่อง phosphorylase b kinase ซึ่งปัจจุบันจัดเป็น GSD type IX แบบตับพบบ่อยกว่า ทำให้ตับโต ตัวเตี้ย น้ำตาลต่ำเมื่ออดอาหาร แบบกล้ามเนื้อพบน้อยและอาการเบา เช่น เหนื่อยง่ายหรือตะคริวเวลาออกกำลัง วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีน PHKA1/PHKA2/PHKB/PHKG2 รักษาด้วยการกินอาหารบ่อยและแป้งดิบก่อนนอน

ddx.pt: Current umbrella term for the same phosphorylase kinase defects
Debrancher deficiency: hepatomegaly plus later distal myopathy and cardiomyopathy, higher CK
Pure muscle disease with second-wind phenomenon and absent myophosphorylase

aN: gsd viii | phosphorylase b kinase deficiency | phk deficiency | glycogenosis type viii obsolete term

name: Type X glycogenosis
formal: Phosphoglycerate mutase deficiency (PGAM2) with exercise-induced cramps and myoglobinuria.
simple: A rare inherited condition where muscles lack an enzyme needed for energy, causing cramps and dark urine after exercise.
more: Enzyme assay and gene testing; avoid strenuous exertion; no specific therapy.
th: โรคสะสมไกลโคเจนชนิดกล้ามเนื้อจากขาดเอนไซม์ phosphoglycerate mutase ทำให้ปวดเกร็งกล้ามเนื้อเมื่อออกแรงหนักและปัสสาวะสีโคล่าจาก myoglobin
tempoNote: Exercise-provoked attacks from adolescence; normal strength between
feat: Cramps and pain during brief intense exercise (sprinting, lifting)
Episodes of myoglobinuria after heavy exertion
Strength usually normal between attacks; CK mildly raised at rest
No second-wind phenomenon (unlike McArdle disease)
Tubular aggregates may be seen on biopsy
inv: CK at rest and after episodes; renal function and potassium during attacks
Forearm exercise test: lactate rise blunted but not absent
PGAM2 gene testing; muscle enzyme assay if needed

case.story: Severe forearm and thigh cramps during push-up drills, followed twice by dark urine.
case.exam: Normal strength and bulk at rest.
case.tests: CK 900 at rest, 45,000 after drills; forearm test shows a reduced lactate rise; PGAM2 biallelic variants.
case.q: Why was McArdle disease considered less likely?
case.a: No second wind and lactate still rose partly; distal glycolysis defect (PGAM) rather than phosphorylase deficiency.

det.patho: Muscle PGAM converts 3-phosphoglycerate to 2-phosphoglycerate in glycolysis. Deficiency limits ATP from anaerobic glycolysis during short bursts of high-intensity work, when muscle relies on glycogen. Glycogen content is usually only mildly raised. It is autosomal recessive and very rare, first described in African-American patients but now reported widely.
det.clinical: Symptoms start from early childhood into adolescence, with exercise-induced cramps and pigmenturia. Between attacks patients are normal, though some develop mild fixed weakness later. Heterozygotes may have mild symptoms.
det.diagnosis: Suspect in exercise intolerance with rhabdomyolysis and a blunted lactate response. Gene testing confirms; muscle biopsy may show tubular aggregates and mild glycogen excess. Exclude other glycolytic and lipid metabolism disorders with a metabolic myopathy panel.
det.treatment: No specific treatment. Avoid intense anaerobic exertion, encourage moderate aerobic training, and maintain hydration. Treat rhabdomyolysis with IV fluids and monitor kidneys and potassium.
det.prognosis: Benign apart from rhabdomyolysis risk; life expectancy normal.
pearls: Distal glycolytic defects give a blunted, not flat, lactate rise.
Brief intense exercise provokes symptoms; long endurance work is better tolerated.
Tubular aggregates on biopsy are a clue to PGAM deficiency.
det.thd: Type X glycogenosis เกิดจากขาดเอนไซม์ phosphoglycerate mutase ในกล้ามเนื้อ ทำให้สร้างพลังงานแบบไม่ใช้ออกซิเจนได้น้อย ผู้ป่วยเป็นตะคริวและปวดกล้ามเนื้อเมื่อออกแรงหนักในช่วงสั้น ๆ และอาจมีปัสสาวะสีเข้มจาก myoglobin ระหว่างครั้งแข็งแรงปกติ ยืนยันด้วยยีน PGAM2 ไม่มียาเฉพาะ ควรเลี่ยงการออกแรงหนักแบบฉับพลันและดื่มน้ำให้พอ

files.chapter: 8. Cramps, Muscle Stiffness, and Exercise Intolerance
8 - Cramps, Muscle Stiffness, and Exercise Intolerance

ddx.pt: Second-wind phenomenon and flat lactate with high ammonia on forearm test
Another distal glycolytic defect (beta-enolase) with very similar exercise intolerance
Rhabdomyolysis after prolonged rather than brief intense exercise, or with fasting and fever

aN: gsd x | phosphoglycerate mutase deficiency | pgam deficiency | pgam2 deficiency | muscle pgam deficiency

name: Type XI glycogenosis
formal: Lactate dehydrogenase A deficiency (LDHA) with exertional myalgia, rhabdomyolysis, and skin lesions.
simple: A rare condition with muscle breakdown and pain after exercise from lacking a muscle enzyme.
more: Low lactate production on forearm test; gene testing; avoid heavy exercise.
th: โรคเมแทบอลิซึมกล้ามเนื้อที่พบน้อยจากยีน LDHA ทำให้ปวดกล้ามเนื้อเมื่อออกแรง rhabdomyolysis และผื่นผิวหนัง
tempoNote: Exercise-induced episodes from childhood or adolescence; normal between attacks
feat: Exertional myalgia, stiffness and cramps during intense anaerobic effort
Episodes of rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria; risk of acute kidney injury
Erythematous scaly skin rash (annular or psoriasis-like) in some patients
Rare: reported mainly from Japan
Serum LDH strikingly low relative to raised CK — a laboratory clue
inv: Serum LDH low with high CK during episodes; LDH isoenzymes show absent M subunit
Forearm exercise test: lactate fails to rise while pyruvate rises excessively
LDHA gene testing

case.story: After a university fitness test he had painful stiff thighs and dark urine. A similar episode followed a basketball tournament; he also has a recurrent scaly rash on his arms.
case.exam: Tender swollen thighs, normal strength at rest, annular scaly patches on forearms.
case.tests: CK 45,000 U/L but serum LDH unexpectedly low; forearm test shows no lactate rise with high pyruvate; LDHA variants found.
case.q: Which lab clue points to the diagnosis?
case.a: Low serum LDH despite massive CK rise — muscle lactate dehydrogenase deficiency (GSD XI).

det.patho: LDH converts pyruvate to lactate, regenerating NAD+ so glycolysis can continue during anaerobic work. In muscle the M (LDHA) subunit predominates; its absence blocks this step, glycolytic flux stalls and ATP supply fails during intense exercise, leading to fibre breakdown. Skin keratinocytes also depend on LDHA, which may explain the rash.
det.clinical: Patients are usually well at rest and develop pain, cramps and rhabdomyolysis after short bursts of vigorous effort. Myoglobinuria can cause renal failure. Some women report uterine stiffness during labour requiring caesarean section. Skin lesions may precede muscle symptoms.
det.diagnosis: A disproportionately low serum LDH in the face of high CK is the hallmark. The ischaemic or non-ischaemic forearm test shows a flat lactate curve with exaggerated pyruvate rise, which separates it from other glycolytic defects. LDH isoenzyme analysis and LDHA sequencing confirm the diagnosis.
det.treatment: No specific therapy; patients should avoid sudden intense anaerobic exertion, build fitness with moderate aerobic activity and hydrate well. Rhabdomyolysis is managed with fluids and renal monitoring. Obstetric teams should be aware of possible uterine involvement.
det.prognosis: Normal life expectancy with lifestyle adjustment; renal injury during severe episodes is the main risk.
pearls: Very high CK with low LDH: think LDHA deficiency.
Flat lactate with high pyruvate on forearm testing is characteristic.
Rash plus exercise-induced rhabdomyolysis is a rare but memorable combination.
det.thd: GSD XI เกิดจากขาดเอนไซม์ lactate dehydrogenase ชนิด A ในกล้ามเนื้อ ทำให้ระบบ glycolysis หยุดชะงักเมื่อออกแรงหนัก ผู้ป่วยปวดตึงกล้ามเนื้อและมี rhabdomyolysis หลังออกกำลังแบบหนักช่วงสั้น บางรายมีผื่นผิวหนัง จุดสังเกตคือ CK สูงมากแต่ LDH ในเลือดต่ำ ไม่มีการรักษาเฉพาะ ให้หลีกเลี่ยงการออกแรงหนักทันทีและดื่มน้ำมาก ๆ

ddx.pt: Second-wind phenomenon; lactate and ammonia patterns differ and LDH is raised in attacks
Rhabdomyolysis with prolonged exercise, fasting or fever rather than brief intense effort
Glycolytic defect with haemolysis and gout; no lactate rise either

aN: gsd xi | lactate dehydrogenase a deficiency | ldha deficiency | muscle ldh deficiency | ldh m deficiency

name: Type XII glycogenosis
formal: Aldolase A deficiency (ALDOA), with exercise intolerance, rhabdomyolysis, and haemolytic anaemia.
simple: A rare inherited enzyme deficiency causing muscle pain and breakdown with exercise, and anaemia.
more: Enzyme assay and gene testing; supportive care and exercise avoidance.
th: โรคพร่องเอนไซม์ aldolase A (ALDOA) ที่หายากมาก ทำให้โลหิตจางจากเม็ดเลือดแดงแตกและกล้ามเนื้อสลายเป็นพัก ๆ โดยเฉพาะเวลามีไข้
tempoNote: Lifelong haemolysis with episodic rhabdomyolysis triggered by fever or exertion
feat: Very rare autosomal recessive glycolytic defect; few families reported
Chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia with jaundice
Recurrent rhabdomyolysis and dark urine, often during febrile illness
Exercise intolerance and weakness; some with short stature or intellectual disability
inv: Blood count, reticulocytes, bilirubin, LDH for haemolysis
CK during attacks (can be very high) and urine myoglobin; renal function
Red cell aldolase activity; ALDOA gene sequencing

case.who: 9-year-old boy admitted to a provincial hospital in Nakhon Ratchasima
case.story: During a febrile influenza illness he developed leg pain and cola-coloured urine; he has been mildly jaundiced and anaemic since infancy.
case.exam: Icteric, pale, tender calves, mild proximal weakness, mild splenomegaly.
case.tests: CK 48,000 U/L, Hb 8.5 g/dL, reticulocytes 12%, Coombs negative; red cell aldolase markedly reduced; ALDOA biallelic variants.
case.q: Which glycolytic enzyme defect links lifelong haemolysis with fever-induced rhabdomyolysis?
case.a: Aldolase A deficiency (GSD XII).

det.patho: Aldolase A splits fructose-1,6-bisphosphate in glycolysis in red cells and skeletal muscle. Biallelic ALDOA variants reduce activity and protein stability, especially at higher temperature, which explains why fever triggers attacks. Red cells depend on glycolysis and therefore haemolyse chronically, while muscle fails under high energy demand.
det.clinical: Only a handful of cases are described, so the spectrum is uncertain. Reported features include congenital haemolytic anaemia, episodes of rhabdomyolysis with fever, exercise intolerance and, in some, developmental delay or dysmorphic features. Despite the GSD label, glycogen accumulation in muscle is not a prominent finding.
det.diagnosis: Consider it when non-immune haemolysis coexists with recurrent myoglobinuria. Measure red cell glycolytic enzymes and confirm with ALDOA sequencing; exclude G6PD deficiency, PFK deficiency and fatty acid oxidation defects.
det.treatment: Treatment is supportive: early antipyretics and fluids during febrile illness, vigorous hydration and renal protection during rhabdomyolysis, transfusion when anaemia is severe, and folate. Avoid strenuous exercise and prolonged fasting. Splenectomy has been tried in some haemolytic enzymopathies but evidence here is minimal.
det.prognosis: Variable; recurrent rhabdomyolysis risks kidney injury, and outcomes are poorly characterised given the few reported cases.
pearls: Haemolysis plus rhabdomyolysis: think of glycolytic enzymopathies (PFK, aldolase A, PGK).
Fever, not just exercise, can precipitate attacks in aldolase A deficiency.
GSD XII is a glycolysis defect; glycogen stores are not markedly increased.
det.thd: Type XII glycogenosis คือภาวะพร่องเอนไซม์ aldolase A ในวิถี glycolysis พบน้อยมาก ผู้ป่วยมีโลหิตจางจากเม็ดเลือดแดงแตกเรื้อรังตั้งแต่เด็ก และมีกล้ามเนื้อสลายปัสสาวะสีโคล่าเป็นพัก ๆ เมื่อมีไข้หรือออกแรง วินิจฉัยด้วยการวัดเอนไซม์ในเม็ดเลือดแดงและตรวจยีน ALDOA การรักษาเน้นลดไข้ ให้สารน้ำป้องกันไตวาย และให้เลือดเมื่อจำเป็น

ddx.pt: PFK deficiency: exertional cramps with mild compensated haemolysis and hyperuricaemia
Fever- or fasting-induced rhabdomyolysis without haemolytic anaemia
Glycolytic haemolysis with progressive neurological disease and early death

aN: gsd xii | aldolase a deficiency | aldoa deficiency | glycogenosis xii

name: Type XIII glycogenosis
formal: Beta-enolase deficiency (ENO3) causing exercise intolerance and myalgia with raised CK.
simple: A very rare inherited muscle enzyme deficiency causing exercise-related pain and fatigue.
more: Gene testing; supportive management.
th: โรคสะสมไกลโคเจนชนิดกล้ามเนื้อที่หายากมาก จากขาดเอนไซม์ beta-enolase (ยีน ENO3) ทำให้ออกกำลังไม่ทน ปวดกล้ามเนื้อ และ CK สูง
tempoNote: Exercise-related myalgia from adolescence or adulthood
feat: Exercise intolerance and myalgia, sometimes with rhabdomyolysis
Persistently raised CK at rest
Strength mostly normal; mild weakness reported in some
Very few patients described worldwide
inv: CK; forearm exercise test with blunted lactate rise
ENO3 gene testing; muscle biopsy with enzyme assay

case.story: Since his teens, thigh pain after running uphill and two hospital visits for dark urine after football.
case.exam: Normal strength and reflexes.
case.tests: CK 1,200 at rest; blunted lactate rise; ENO3 biallelic variants.
case.q: What advice is the main treatment?
case.a: Avoid intense anaerobic bursts, keep moderate aerobic activity and hydration; there is no specific drug.

det.patho: Beta-enolase is the muscle-specific isoform of enolase, which converts 2-phosphoglycerate to phosphoenolpyruvate in glycolysis. Deficiency reduces ATP generation during anaerobic exercise. Only a handful of patients have been reported, so the full spectrum is not known.
det.clinical: Reported patients had exercise intolerance, myalgia and episodes of rhabdomyolysis with chronically raised CK. Onset has ranged from adolescence to adulthood. No CNS involvement is described.
det.diagnosis: Requires a metabolic myopathy gene panel or exome; enzyme assay on muscle is confirmatory. Biopsy may show mild subsarcolemmal glycogen accumulation.
det.treatment: Supportive: activity modification, aerobic conditioning and prompt treatment of rhabdomyolysis. No disease-specific therapy has been studied.
det.prognosis: Appears benign but data are very limited.
pearls: Extremely rare; consider only after common metabolic myopathies are excluded.
Distal glycolytic defects share a blunted lactate rise and no second wind.
Genetic panels now diagnose most of these ultra-rare enzymopathies.
det.thd: Type XIII glycogenosis เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้อเมตาบอลิกที่หายากมากจากขาด beta-enolase (ยีน ENO3) ทำให้ปวดกล้ามเนื้อเมื่อออกแรงหนักและบางครั้งเกิด rhabdomyolysis ค่า CK สูงแม้ตอนพัก วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีน ไม่มียาเฉพาะ ดูแลด้วยการปรับกิจกรรมและดื่มน้ำเพียงพอ

ddx.pt: More common; second wind present and lactate flat on testing
PGAM deficiency, clinically almost identical; separated by gene testing
Myalgia with raised CK linked to statin start, improving after withdrawal

aN: gsd xiii | beta enolase deficiency | eno3 deficiency | muscle enolase deficiency

name: Type XIV glycogenosis
formal: Phosphoglucomutase 1 deficiency (PGM1), a congenital disorder of glycosylation with hepatopathy, myopathy, cleft palate, and hypoglycaemia.
simple: A rare inherited condition affecting sugar processing, with muscle, liver, and other problems.
more: Galactose supplementation is effective; diagnosis by transferrin glycosylation and gene testing.
th: ความผิดปกติจากยีน PGM1 ที่เป็นทั้งโรคสะสมไกลโคเจนและ congenital disorder of glycosylation มีกล้ามเนื้อผิดปกติ ตับผิดปกติ เพดานโหว่ และน้ำตาลต่ำ
tempoNote: Multisystem from infancy; exercise-induced muscle episodes in older children and adults
feat: Exercise intolerance, cramps and rhabdomyolysis; raised CK
Hepatopathy with raised transaminases; episodic hypoglycaemia
Cleft palate or bifid uvula and Pierre Robin sequence
Dilated cardiomyopathy (can be fatal), growth delay, endocrine and clotting abnormalities
Intelligence usually normal
inv: Transferrin isoelectric focusing: mixed type 1 and type 2 pattern
CK, liver enzymes, glucose, clotting factors, echocardiogram
PGM1 enzyme activity in fibroblasts or muscle; PGM1 sequencing

case.story: Had cleft palate repaired as an infant and recurrent low sugars when ill. Now gets painful legs and dark urine after long football games.
case.exam: Short stature, repaired cleft, normal strength at rest, mild hepatomegaly.
case.tests: CK 9,000 U/L after exercise, ALT 140 U/L, abnormal transferrin glycosylation pattern, biallelic PGM1 variants.
case.q: Which diagnosis unites cleft palate, liver disease and exercise-induced rhabdomyolysis, and is there a specific treatment?
case.a: PGM1-CDG (GSD XIV); oral D-galactose supplementation can improve glycosylation, liver function and hypoglycaemia.

det.patho: Phosphoglucomutase 1 interconverts glucose-1-phosphate and glucose-6-phosphate, linking glycogen metabolism to glycolysis and to synthesis of UDP-sugars needed for glycosylation. Deficiency therefore impairs glycogen use in muscle during exercise and reduces nucleotide sugars, causing defective N-glycosylation of many proteins.
det.clinical: Presentation is broad. Infants may show cleft palate, hypoglycaemia, liver dysfunction and failure to thrive; older patients have exercise intolerance and rhabdomyolysis. Dilated cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia are the main causes of death. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, coagulopathy and short stature may occur.
det.diagnosis: An abnormal transferrin glycoform pattern combining features of type 1 and type 2 CDG points to the diagnosis. Enzyme assay and PGM1 genetic testing confirm it. Muscle biopsy may show glycogen accumulation but is not required.
det.treatment: Oral D-galactose supplementation improves glycosylation, hypoglycaemia and liver enzymes in many patients and is the main targeted therapy; its effect on muscle and heart is less clear. Frequent meals or cornstarch prevent hypoglycaemia. Cardiac surveillance and caution with strenuous exertion are advised.
det.prognosis: Variable; cardiomyopathy determines survival, otherwise many live into adulthood.
pearls: Cleft palate + hypoglycaemia + rhabdomyolysis = think PGM1-CDG.
Transferrin isoelectric focusing is the screening test for CDG.
One of the few CDGs with a dietary therapy (galactose).

name: Typical absence seizure
formal: Brief generalised nonconvulsive seizure with abrupt impaired awareness and 3 Hz spike-wave on EEG, typical of childhood absence epilepsy.
simple: A brief staring spell with sudden loss of awareness, mainly in children.
th: การชักทั่วไปแบบไม่เกร็งกระตุก เหม่อนิ่งเป็นวินาทีโดยเริ่มและหยุดทันที EEG มี spike-wave 3 Hz พบใน childhood absence epilepsy
tempoNote: Seizures last 4–20 seconds and may occur dozens to hundreds of times daily
feat: Abrupt arrest of activity and blank stare lasting seconds, then immediate resumption
Mild automatisms, eyelid flutter or head drop may occur
No postictal confusion
Provoked by hyperventilation; frequent through the day
Typical of childhood absence epilepsy and juvenile absence epilepsy
inv: EEG with hyperventilation: generalised 3 Hz spike-wave discharges, normal background
MRI not usually needed in typical cases
GLUT1 deficiency testing (CSF glucose, SLC2A1) if onset before 4 years or drug resistant

case.story: Teachers notice brief staring spells during class many times a day; he does not remember them.
case.exam: Hyperventilation for 2 minutes provokes a 10-second stare with eyelid fluttering.
case.tests: EEG: generalised 3 Hz spike-wave discharges with normal background.
case.q: What is the first-line treatment?
case.a: Ethosuximide is preferred for childhood absence epilepsy without tonic-clonic seizures.

read.where: 10 Electro-Clinical Syndromes by Age of Onset—Childhood, Adolescence, and Adult

det.patho: Absences arise when thalamocortical circuits fall into synchronous rhythmic firing at about 3 Hz. Thalamic T-type calcium channels and GABA-B mediated inhibition are central to this rhythm, which explains why ethosuximide helps and some GABAergic drugs worsen it. Inheritance is usually polygenic. GLUT1 deficiency is an important treatable cause in early-onset or drug-resistant cases.
det.clinical: Childhood absence epilepsy starts around 4–10 years with many daily absences in otherwise normal children. Juvenile absence epilepsy begins around puberty with less frequent absences and more tonic-clonic seizures. Learning may suffer from frequent absences.
det.diagnosis: EEG with hyperventilation confirms the diagnosis, showing generalised 3 Hz spike-wave. Neurological examination is normal. Test for GLUT1 deficiency if onset is early or drugs fail.
det.treatment: Ethosuximide is first choice for childhood absence epilepsy with absences alone, as shown in a large randomised trial. Valproate is equally effective and covers tonic-clonic seizures, but its teratogenic risk limits its use in girls. Lamotrigine is better tolerated but less effective. Avoid carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, gabapentin, vigabatrin and tiagabine; a ketogenic diet is used for GLUT1 deficiency.
det.prognosis: Childhood absence epilepsy remits in most by adolescence; juvenile absence epilepsy is more often lifelong.
pearls: Hyperventilation in clinic triggers absences in most untreated children.
No postictal confusion distinguishes typical absences from focal impaired awareness seizures.
Ethosuximide is the first choice for childhood absence epilepsy.
det.thd: Typical absence seizure คือการชักแบบเหม่อนิ่งสั้น ๆ ไม่กี่วินาที เริ่มและหยุดทันที ไม่มีอาการสับสนหลังชัก พบบ่อยในเด็กวัยเรียน กระตุ้นได้ด้วยการหายใจเร็ว EEG พบ spike-wave 3 Hz ทั่วไป ยา ethosuximide เป็นยาตัวแรก หลีกเลี่ยงยากลุ่ม carbamazepine ส่วนใหญ่หายเองเมื่อโต

name: UDD distal myopathy
formal: Late-onset autosomal dominant distal myopathy (tibial muscular dystrophy) from titin gene variants, causing anterior compartment weakness with foot drop after age 35 to 45.
simple: An inherited muscle disease starting in middle age, causing weakness in the front of the lower legs and difficulty lifting the foot.
more: MRI shows tibialis anterior involvement; confirmed by TTN testing, with severe disease in homozygotes (limb-girdle phenotype). Progression is slow and most remain walking; orthoses help.
th: distal myopathy ชนิดยีนเด่นจากยีน titin เริ่มหลังอายุ 35 ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อ tibialis anterior อ่อนแรงและเท้าตก
tempoNote: Onset after 35, very slow progression over decades
feat: Ankle dorsiflexor weakness causing foot drop and tripping, often asymmetric
Begins after age 35; remains mild, most stay ambulant
Hands and proximal muscles usually spared; heart typically normal
Most reported in Finland (FINmaj variant) but recognised elsewhere
Biallelic variants cause a severer limb-girdle phenotype (LGMD R10)
inv: CK normal or mildly raised; EMG myopathic in tibialis anterior
Muscle MRI: fatty change in anterior tibial muscles, later hamstrings
Biopsy: rimmed vacuoles; TTN sequencing (C-terminal variants)

case.story: Over five years he has started catching his right toes on tree roots; now both feet slap when walking.
case.exam: Bilateral foot drop with wasted anterior tibial compartments, normal sensation and reflexes, strong hands.
case.tests: CK 260 U/L, myopathic EMG in tibialis anterior, MRI fatty replacement of anterior compartments, heterozygous C-terminal TTN variant.
case.q: Why is this not a peroneal neuropathy?
case.a: Bilateral, painless, no sensory loss, myopathic EMG and MRI pattern — Udd tibial muscular dystrophy.

det.patho: Titin is the giant elastic protein spanning half a sarcomere. Heterozygous truncating or missense variants in its final exons disrupt the M-band region and binding to calpain-3, leading to secondary calpain-3 loss and degeneration of selected muscles. Homozygous variants produce more widespread weakness.
det.clinical: Typically the patient notices tripping or a slapping gait in middle age. Weakness is confined to the anterior leg compartment for years, and later may spread mildly to hamstrings or glutei. Cardiomyopathy is not a usual feature, distinguishing it from other titinopathies.
det.diagnosis: Distal anterior weakness with normal sensation, myopathic EMG and characteristic MRI pattern suggest the diagnosis. Biopsy may show rimmed vacuoles and dystrophic changes. Interpretation of TTN variants is difficult because of the gene's size and frequent benign variants; segregation and specialist review help.
det.treatment: No disease-specific therapy. Ankle-foot orthoses, physiotherapy and fall prevention maintain mobility. Cardiac screening is reasonable once because other TTN variants cause cardiomyopathy.
det.prognosis: Benign course; most remain ambulant for life.
pearls: Late-onset bilateral foot drop with normal sensation: think distal myopathy.
Udd affects the anterior leg; Miyoshi the posterior calf.
TTN variants are common — interpret with care.
det.thd: UDD distal myopathy หรือ tibial muscular dystrophy เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้อยีนเด่นจากยีน titin เริ่มหลังอายุ 35 กล้ามเนื้อหน้าแข้งอ่อนแรงทำให้เท้าตกทั้งสองข้าง โดยไม่มีอาการชา โรคดำเนินช้ามากและผู้ป่วยส่วนใหญ่ยังเดินได้ ตรวจ MRI กล้ามเนื้อและยีน TTN ช่วยวินิจฉัย การรักษาเป็นอุปกรณ์พยุงข้อเท้าและกายภาพบำบัด

name: Ulcerative colitis
formal: Chronic inflammatory bowel disease associated with neurological complications such as venous thrombosis, neuropathy and myelopathy.
simple: A bowel inflammation disease that can sometimes affect nerves and brain vessels.
th: โรคลำไส้ใหญ่อักเสบเรื้อรังชนิดหนึ่งของ IBD ไม่ใช่โรคทางประสาทโดยตรง แต่ทำให้เกิดภาวะแทรกซ้อน เช่น หลอดเลือดดำสมองอุดตัน เส้นประสาทอักเสบ และผลข้างเคียงทางประสาทจากยาที่ใช้รักษา
tempoNote: Bowel disease relapses and remits over years; neurological complications tend to cluster around active flares or follow drug exposure
feat: Bloody diarrhoea, urgency and tenesmus from continuous mucosal inflammation starting at the rectum
Clotting tendency during flares: cerebral venous thrombosis and, less often, arterial stroke
Peripheral nerve problems: axonal sensory neuropathy, demyelinating neuropathy, or mononeuropathies
Treatment-linked events: PML on some biologics, demyelination with anti-TNF agents, metronidazole neuropathy, PRES on calcineurin inhibitors
Rarer links: myelopathy from B12 or copper deficiency after colectomy/malabsorption, and an excess of demyelinating CNS disease
inv: Colonoscopy with biopsy (gastroenterology) to confirm and grade disease activity
MRI brain with MR or CT venography for headache, seizures or focal signs during a flare
Nerve conduction studies; B12, folate, copper, thiamine and vitamin E levels
Review the drug list (anti-TNF, natalizumab/vedolizumab, metronidazole, ciclosporin) against the neurological picture

case.who: 29-year-old woman from Khon Kaen with known ulcerative colitis
case.story: In the middle of a severe flare with bloody stools and dehydration she develops a worsening headache over three days, then a focal seizure of the left hand.
case.exam: Drowsy but oriented, mild left arm weakness, bilateral papilloedema; no neck stiffness or fever.
case.tests: Hb 9 g/dL, platelets 520,000; CT venography shows filling defects in the superior sagittal and right transverse sinuses with a small right parietal haemorrhagic infarct.
case.q: Which neurological complication of active colitis is this, and is anticoagulation contraindicated by the rectal bleeding?
case.a: Cerebral venous thrombosis provoked by the inflammatory, dehydrated state; anticoagulation is still standard, with close gastroenterology input on bleeding and urgent control of the flare.

Chapter 13 Other Neurologic Disorders Associated with Gastrointestinal Disease

det.patho: Ulcerative colitis is an immune-mediated mucosal inflammation of the colon; it is a gastrointestinal disease, and the nervous system is affected secondarily. Active inflammation raises fibrinogen, factor VIII and platelet counts, which, together with dehydration, steroids and immobility, makes venous and arterial thrombosis more likely. Malabsorption after surgery, immune cross-reactivity and the side effects of immunosuppressive and biologic drugs account for most other neurological links.
det.clinical: This is not a primary neurological disorder; neurologists meet it through its complications. Cerebral venous thrombosis classically appears during a flare as headache, seizures or focal deficits. Neuropathies include length-dependent axonal sensory forms and occasional inflammatory demyelinating neuropathy. Patients on anti-TNF therapy may develop new demyelinating lesions or Guillain-Barré-like illness, and those on integrin blockers are monitored for PML. Prolonged metronidazole can give a painful neuropathy or cerebellar toxicity.
det.diagnosis: Confirm the bowel diagnosis with gastroenterology and establish disease activity at the time neurological symptoms began. Image the brain with venous sequences when headache or seizures occur in a flare. Investigate neuropathy with nerve studies plus vitamin and trace-element levels, and check drug exposures carefully. Consider the more common causes of each syndrome first rather than attributing everything to IBD.
det.treatment: Treat the complication on its own merits: venous thrombosis is anticoagulated despite colonic bleeding unless haemorrhage is life-threatening, and VTE prophylaxis in hospitalised flares is recommended. Replace deficient vitamins and copper. Stop or switch a suspected culprit drug (for example anti-TNF in new demyelination, metronidazole in neuropathy). Controlling bowel inflammation lowers the thrombotic risk.
det.prognosis: Outcome depends on the specific complication; venous thrombosis usually recovers well with prompt anticoagulation, whereas drug-related PML carries significant disability.
pearls: Headache plus seizure during an IBD flare: image the venous sinuses.
New MS-like lesions on anti-TNF therapy should prompt drug withdrawal and review.
Rectal bleeding is not an absolute contraindication to anticoagulating venous sinus thrombosis.
det.thd: Ulcerative colitis เป็นโรคลำไส้ใหญ่อักเสบเรื้อรัง ไม่ใช่โรคระบบประสาทโดยตรง แต่ช่วงที่โรคกำเริบเลือดจะแข็งตัวง่าย จึงเกิด cerebral venous thrombosis ได้ นอกจากนี้อาจมีเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเสื่อม ขาดวิตามิน B12 หรือทองแดง และผลข้างเคียงจากยา เช่น anti-TNF, metronidazole หรือ PML จากยาชีวภาพ การรักษาคือแก้ภาวะแทรกซ้อนตามสาเหตุร่วมกับคุมโรคลำไส้

name: Ullrich congenital muscular dystrophy (UCMD)
formal: Collagen VI-related congenital muscular dystrophy with proximal weakness, distal joint hyperlaxity, proximal contractures, follicular hyperkeratosis and respiratory failure, from COL6A1-3 variants.
simple: An inherited muscle disease present from birth with weakness, very loose finger joints, tight hips and knees, and breathing problems.
more: Diagnosis by collagen VI immunostaining and gene testing; inheritance may be recessive or de novo dominant. Management is respiratory support, orthopaedic care and nocturnal ventilation.
th: congenital muscular dystrophy จากยีน collagen VI มีกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง ข้อนิ้วหลวมมาก แต่ข้อใหญ่ติดแข็ง และปัญหาการหายใจ
tempoNote: Present at birth or infancy; progressive, with walking lost in childhood or early teens in most
feat: Neonatal hypotonia with striking distal joint hyperlaxity (fingers, wrists, ankles)
Proximal contractures of elbows, knees, hips; early spinal rigidity and scoliosis
Soft velvety palms, keloid scars, follicular hyperkeratosis on extensor skin
Normal intelligence; heart usually unaffected
Early restrictive respiratory failure, often while still walking
inv: CK normal or mildly raised
Muscle MRI: outside-in pattern in vastus lateralis, central 'shadow' in rectus femoris
Collagen VI staining on biopsy or fibroblasts; COL6A1/A2/A3 sequencing
Regular spirometry and overnight studies

case.story: Floppy at birth; walked late at 2.5 years and now falls often. Parents note her fingers bend back far and her elbows will not straighten.
case.exam: Hyperextensible fingers, fixed elbow and knee contractures, proximal weakness, rough skin on arms, keloid on a vaccination scar.
case.tests: CK 380 U/L, MRI shows rim-like fatty change of vastus lateralis, de novo dominant COL6A1 variant; FVC 65% predicted.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and which complication needs proactive monitoring?
case.a: Ullrich congenital muscular dystrophy; respiratory failure (nocturnal hypoventilation) — start NIV when needed.

det.patho: Collagen VI is a microfibrillar protein of the extracellular matrix around muscle fibres, secreted by fibroblasts. Recessive or dominant-negative COL6 variants abolish or distort the matrix, disturbing the mechanical link between muscle and its surroundings, impairing autophagy and causing mitochondrial dysfunction and fibre loss.
det.clinical: Infants show hypotonia, congenital hip dislocation or torticollis, and lax distal joints contrasting with proximal contractures. Many walk briefly but lose ambulation by early adolescence. Scoliosis and spinal rigidity progress, and respiratory failure appears before about age 10, often requiring NIV. The skin findings are a useful bedside clue.
det.diagnosis: Clinical pattern plus muscle MRI is highly suggestive. Immunostaining of collagen VI in muscle or cultured fibroblasts shows absent or reduced protein. Genetic testing of the three COL6 genes confirms the diagnosis; many severe cases arise from de novo dominant variants.
det.treatment: Care is supportive: stretching and splinting, scoliosis surgery, nutritional support and early non-invasive ventilation. Cyclosporin was trialled to correct mitochondrial dysfunction, but no disease-modifying drug is approved. Genetic counselling differs for recessive versus dominant cases.
det.prognosis: Survival into adulthood is common with ventilatory support; respiratory failure is the main threat.
pearls: Lax fingers with stiff elbows = collagen VI disease.
Respiratory failure may come before loss of walking — test FVC and sleep.
Keloids and follicular hyperkeratosis are skin clues.
det.thd: Ullrich congenital muscular dystrophy เกิดจากยีน collagen VI เด็กตัวอ่อนตั้งแต่เกิด ข้อนิ้วหลวมมากแต่ข้อศอกข้อเข่าติดแข็ง ผิวมีตุ่มขนคุดและแผลเป็นนูน กล้ามเนื้อต้นแขนขาอ่อนแรงและมักเสียความสามารถในการเดินในวัยรุ่น ปัญหาสำคัญคือการหายใจล้มเหลวซึ่งต้องติดตามสม่ำเสมอ รักษาแบบประคับประคองและใช้เครื่องช่วยหายใจแบบไม่รุกล้ำ

case.exam: Reduced sensation little finger and dorsal ulnar hand, wasting of first dorsal interosseous, Froment sign positive, Tinel at the medial elbow.
case.tests: Ulnar motor conduction block across the elbow segment; normal C8 paraspinal EMG.

det.patho: The ulnar nerve is vulnerable where it runs superficially behind the medial epicondyle and through the cubital tunnel beneath the fibrous arch joining the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris. Elbow flexion narrows the tunnel and stretches the nerve, while external pressure from leaning adds compression. Less common sites are Guyon's canal at the wrist (ganglion, cycling, fracture) and the axilla. Leprosy, diabetes and HNPP increase susceptibility.
det.clinical: Elbow lesions cause numbness of the little finger, the ulnar half of the ring finger and the ulnar border of the hand both dorsally and on the palm. Motor involvement causes weak pinch and finger spreading, wasting of the first web space, and clawing of the fourth and fifth digits in advanced cases. Froment's sign reflects adductor pollicis weakness, and Wartenberg's sign is a persistently abducted little finger. Symptoms are worse at night or when the elbow is held flexed. Wrist lesions vary by branch involved and may be purely motor.
det.diagnosis: Nerve conduction studies localise the lesion by showing focal conduction block or slowing at the elbow segment; short-segment inching improves precision. EMG documents axon loss and, by sparing flexor carpi ulnaris or not, can help. Check the dorsal ulnar cutaneous sensory response to separate elbow from wrist lesions. Ultrasound shows nerve swelling and can reveal subluxation or a mass. Exclude C8/T1 radiculopathy, lower trunk plexopathy and motor neuron disease, which affect median-innervated hand muscles too.
det.treatment: Mild cases are managed conservatively: avoid leaning on the elbow and prolonged flexion, use a padded elbow or a night splint holding the elbow in extension, and review after several months. Persistent sensory symptoms, progressive weakness or axon loss justify surgical decompression (in situ release or transposition), which have broadly similar outcomes. Space-occupying lesions at Guyon's canal need excision.
det.prognosis: Sensory symptoms usually improve; established wasting recovers incompletely, particularly in older patients with long-standing denervation.
pearls: Dorsal ulnar hand numbness places the lesion proximal to the wrist.
Medial forearm numbness suggests C8/T1 root or lower trunk, not ulnar nerve.
Thenar weakness with ulnar signs: look beyond the ulnar nerve.

formal: Acute unilateral vestibular loss from vestibular neuritis or labyrinthitis, causing vertigo, nystagmus and imbalance.
simple: Inner ear balance nerve damage on one side, causing a spinning sensation.
th: การสูญเสียการทำงานของ vestibular ข้างเดียวเฉียบพลัน จาก vestibular neuritis หรือ labyrinthitis ทำให้บ้านหมุน nystagmus และเดินเซ

feat: Sudden, continuous rotational vertigo with nausea and vomiting
Horizontal-torsional nystagmus beating away from the affected ear, suppressed by fixation
Positive head impulse to the affected side; no skew
Veering toward the lesion but able to stand

case.exam: Right-beating horizontal-torsional nystagmus, abnormal head impulse to the left, no skew, normal hearing, can stand with assistance.

case.q: What is the diagnosis and why should vestibular suppressants be brief?

det.patho: Vestibular neuritis is thought to result from reactivation of latent herpes simplex virus or inflammation of the vestibular nerve, usually affecting the superior division. Labyrinthitis involves the inner ear itself, with hearing loss. The sudden asymmetry of vestibular input causes vertigo until the brain compensates.
det.clinical: Vertigo is sudden, severe and continuous for days, with vomiting and imbalance, and improves gradually over weeks. Some patients later develop BPPV or persistent dizziness. The nystagmus and head impulse findings support a peripheral cause.
det.diagnosis: A peripheral HINTS pattern, no other neurological signs and normal hearing support vestibular neuritis. Video head impulse testing and calorics confirm the deficit. MRI is required when central signs or a normal head impulse are found.
det.treatment: Short-term antiemetics and vestibular suppressants, early mobilisation and vestibular rehabilitation. A short course of corticosteroids started early may improve recovery of caloric function, though the effect on long-term symptoms is debated.
det.prognosis: Most recover over weeks to months; some have persistent imbalance or develop PPPD.
pearls: A normal head impulse in acute vertigo is a warning sign for stroke.
Hearing loss with acute vertigo can mean AICA infarction.
Early exercise speeds compensation.

det.patho: Monocular visual failure places the lesion in front of the chiasm: ocular media, retina or optic nerve. The cause may be vascular (retinal arterial or venous occlusion, ischaemic optic neuropathy), inflammatory or demyelinating (optic neuritis, NMOSD, MOGAD), compressive, toxic-nutritional or hereditary (Leber optic neuropathy). Anatomical thinking by speed of onset, pain and age sorts most cases.
det.clinical: In typical optic neuritis in the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial, about 92% had eye pain, most had dyschromatopsia, and nearly 90% regained 20/25 or better vision. NMO-related optic neuritis causes worse loss at onset and less recovery. Vascular events are painless and abrupt, with retinal artery occlusion producing a cherry-red spot and non-arteritic ischaemic neuropathy producing a swollen disc and altitudinal field loss. Leber hereditary optic neuropathy presents as painless subacute loss in young men with sequential involvement of the other eye. Foster Kennedy syndrome signals a frontal mass.
det.diagnosis: Document acuity, colour vision, pupils, fundus and fields, then match them to a causal pattern. In patients over 50, check ESR and CRP immediately and consider temporal artery assessment. Imaging of the orbit and brain with contrast is needed for atypical optic neuritis and compressive suspicion; vascular imaging and cardiac work-up for embolic patterns. Antibody testing (AQP4, MOG) is required in severe, bilateral, recurrent or poorly recovering optic neuritis.
det.treatment: Treat time-critical causes first: GCA with high-dose corticosteroid before biopsy, and retinal artery occlusion with an immediate stroke pathway. Typical optic neuritis is treated with intravenous methylprednisolone, which speeds recovery without changing the final outcome, and with MS risk assessment; NMOSD and MOGAD require steroid and early plasma exchange if poor response, followed by preventive immunotherapy. Compressive lesions need decompression, nutritional and toxic causes need removal and replacement, and vascular risk factors need control.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause: excellent for typical optic neuritis, poor for central retinal artery occlusion and untreated GCA.
pearls: An RAPD with a normal fundus still means optic nerve disease until proven otherwise.
Older patient with monocular loss: ESR, CRP and steroids before anything else if GCA is possible.
Transient monocular loss is a TIA equivalent: investigate the carotid.

name: Unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (UWS)

simple: A condition where a person appears awake, eyes open, but shows no signs of awareness.

Brainstem reflexes, breathing and autonomic function usually intact

det.patho: Widespread cortical or thalamic damage, or disconnection of thalamocortical pathways, abolishes awareness while the brainstem arousal systems continue to generate wakefulness. Hypoxic injury preferentially damages cortex, hippocampus, basal ganglia and thalamus; traumatic injury causes diffuse axonal damage. The term UWS was introduced to avoid the pejorative word 'vegetative'.
det.clinical: After a period of coma, patients open their eyes and resume sleep–wake cycles but show only reflex behaviours. Visual fixation or pursuit, command following or consistent localisation indicate a minimally conscious state instead. Recovery is more likely after trauma than after hypoxia. Complications include spasticity, contractures, infections and paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis needs repeated standardised bedside examination over time, ideally with the CRS-R, in an environment free of sedatives and with attention to sensory deficits. Up to around a third of patients labelled UWS show signs of awareness on careful testing. Functional imaging or EEG-based command paradigms may reveal covert consciousness (cognitive-motor dissociation).
det.treatment: Care focuses on nutrition, tracheostomy, skin and bladder care, spasticity management and treating complications. Amantadine has evidence for speeding recovery after traumatic injury. Discussions about goals of care should involve family and follow local legal frameworks.
det.prognosis: Prospects of recovering awareness fall with time, more steeply after hypoxic than traumatic injury; late improvements are reported, so avoid early labels of permanence.
pearls: Eye opening is not awareness; visual pursuit is a key sign of MCS.
Repeat assessments — single-examination misdiagnosis is common.
Exclude locked-in syndrome by asking for vertical eye movements.
