name: Unverricht–Lundborg disease (EPM1)
formal: Progressive myoclonic epilepsy from CSTB mutation (Baltic myoclonus), with stimulus-sensitive myoclonus, seizures and ataxia.
simple: An inherited condition causing muscle jerks, seizures and unsteadiness beginning in adolescence.
more: Diagnosis by CSTB dodecamer repeat expansion testing; autosomal recessive, with generalised spike-wave on EEG. Valproate, levetiracetam, zonisamide and piracetam help; avoid phenytoin, which may worsen the disease; prognosis is better than in Lafora disease. Unverricht-Lundborg disease, an autosomal recessive progressive myoclonic epilepsy from CSTB mutation, with stimulus-sensitive myoclonus, tonic-clonic seizures and mild ataxia. Historical term for Unverricht-Lundborg disease, an autosomal recessive progressive myoclonic epilepsy from CSTB mutations with stimulus-sensitive myoclonus, seizures and mild decline.
th: โรคลมชักแบบ progressive myoclonic epilepsy จากยีน CSTB ที่มีอาการกระตุกไวต่อสิ่งกระตุ้น ชัก และเดินเซ เริ่มในวัยเด็กตอนปลายถึงวัยรุ่น
tempoNote: Onset at 6–16 years; progression over years, often stabilising in adulthood
feat: Stimulus-sensitive action myoclonus, worse in the morning, progressively disabling
Generalised tonic-clonic seizures, usually controllable
Ataxia, dysarthria and incoordination develop later
Cognition relatively preserved compared with other progressive myoclonic epilepsies
Autosomal recessive, most commonly from a dodecamer repeat expansion in CSTB
inv: EEG: generalised spike-wave discharges and photosensitivity with slowed background
CSTB genetic testing (repeat expansion analysis)
MRI usually normal or mild atrophy

det.patho: Cystatin B normally restrains lysosomal cathepsins; when it is missing, protease activity rises and vulnerable neurons, particularly inhibitory cortical and cerebellar cells, are lost. Most patients carry an expanded dodecamer repeat in the CSTB promoter region on at least one allele, which reduces gene expression. Inheritance is autosomal recessive. It is the most common progressive myoclonic epilepsy in several populations.
det.clinical: Onset is in late childhood or adolescence with myoclonus and tonic-clonic seizures. Myoclonus becomes the main disability, provoked by movement and stimuli. Ataxia and mild cognitive decline may follow. Disease often stabilises after early adulthood, and many have near-normal lifespan with good care.
det.diagnosis: Clinical features of progressive myoclonic epilepsy with relatively preserved cognition and photosensitive EEG suggest ULD. Confirm with CSTB testing. Exclude other PMEs with targeted genetic tests, skin biopsy or enzyme assays.
det.treatment: Valproate is first line; clonazepam, levetiracetam, piracetam, topiramate, zonisamide and perampanel are used. Avoid sodium channel blockers (phenytoin, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine) and gabapentinoids, which worsen symptoms. Supportive therapies include physiotherapy and occupational therapy.
det.prognosis: Most survive into later adulthood with variable disability; earlier phenytoin use was associated with worse outcomes.
pearls: Least severe of the progressive myoclonic epilepsies; cognition relatively spared.
Phenytoin worsens ULD and should be avoided.
Common in Finland and Mediterranean populations, but occurs worldwide.

1 - Clinical overview and phenomenology of movement disorders

det.patho: UMN lesions interrupt corticospinal and associated cortico-reticulospinal pathways anywhere from motor cortex to spinal cord. Loss of descending inhibition increases stretch reflex excitability, giving spasticity and hyperreflexia, while loss of fine voluntary control causes weakness and slowness. This is a clinical syndrome, not a disease, and the cause must always be sought.
det.clinical: Patients report stiffness, clumsiness, tripping and fatigue. Weakness follows a pyramidal pattern with slowed rapid movements. Early after an acute lesion, tone and reflexes can be reduced before spasticity appears. The distribution and associated findings tell where the lesion lies.
det.diagnosis: Examination confirms the UMN pattern, and localisation determines imaging. Brain MRI for hemiparesis with cortical or cranial signs; spinal MRI for paraparesis or a sensory level. Laboratory tests address metabolic, infectious and inflammatory causes. If LMN signs coexist, consider MND, cervical radiculomyelopathy or B12/copper deficiency.
det.treatment: Treat the cause (decompression, stroke care, immunotherapy). Spasticity management uses stretching, physiotherapy, baclofen, tizanidine, botulinum toxin and intrathecal baclofen. Orthoses and gait training support mobility. Bladder management is often needed in spinal causes.
det.prognosis: Depends entirely on the underlying cause.
pearls: Acute UMN lesions can be flaccid and areflexic at first.
Brisk jaw jerk places the lesion above the foramen magnum.
UMN signs plus wasting and fasciculation should raise MND.

det.patho: Retained uraemic toxins such as guanidino compounds and middle molecules, disturbed neurotransmitter balance, parathyroid hormone excess and electrolyte and acid-base abnormalities together impair neuronal function. Inhibitory GABAergic transmission is reduced and excitatory activity increased, explaining myoclonus and seizures. Severity correlates more with how fast kidney function falls than with absolute urea values.
det.clinical: Early symptoms are cognitive dulling and fatigue, progressing to confusion, hallucinations, myoclonus, asterixis and seizures. Severe cases lead to coma. Additional neurological complications of renal failure include neuropathy, restless legs and drug toxicity.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis rests on encephalopathy with advanced renal failure after other causes are excluded. Look carefully for drug accumulation, PRES, infection, subdural haematoma, hypertensive encephalopathy and electrolyte disorders. EEG shows non-specific slowing and sometimes triphasic waves, and helps exclude non-convulsive status. Improvement after dialysis supports the diagnosis.
det.treatment: Dialysis is definitive and usually leads to improvement within days. Manage seizures with benzodiazepines and renally adjusted antiseizure drugs (levetiracetam with dose adjustment). Correct electrolytes and review medications.
det.prognosis: Good if dialysis is timely; prolonged uraemia may cause lasting cognitive deficits.
pearls: Asterixis and multifocal myoclonus with high urea suggest uraemic encephalopathy.
Always check for drug accumulation in renal failure.
Gradual dialysis reduces risk of disequilibrium syndrome.

det.patho: Retained solutes in kidney failure, together with chronic hyperkalaemia that depolarises axons, are thought to disrupt axonal membrane function and transport, producing a length-dependent axonopathy with secondary demyelination. No single uraemic toxin has been proven responsible. Coexisting diabetes, vascular disease and nutritional deficits add to nerve injury.
det.clinical: Patients describe distal paraesthesia, burning or cramps, followed by sensory loss and distal weakness. Severity tracks with kidney function and dialysis adequacy. Restless legs, autonomic symptoms (postural hypotension, impotence) and mononeuropathies are common companions. A rapidly progressive weakness should raise other causes, including CIDP or vasculitis.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on a compatible clinical picture, nerve conduction showing a symmetric axonal neuropathy, and exclusion of other causes, particularly diabetes, which often coexists. Look for drug toxicity (dose adjustment for renal function), B12 deficiency, paraproteins and amyloidosis. Focal problems, for example carpal tunnel compression or ischaemic monomelic neuropathy after fistula surgery need separate recognition.
det.treatment: The most effective measures are adequate dialysis and kidney transplantation, which often produces clear improvement within months. Neuropathic pain can be treated with gabapentinoids or tricyclics at renally adjusted doses. Control potassium, correct nutritional deficiencies and provide foot care.
det.prognosis: Usually stabilises with adequate dialysis and frequently improves after successful transplantation.
pearls: Transplantation, not more drugs, is the most effective treatment.
Reduce gabapentin and pregabalin doses in kidney failure to avoid toxicity.
Sudden hand pain and weakness after fistula creation: think ischaemic monomelic neuropathy.
det.thd: Uraemic neuropathy เป็นปลายประสาทเสื่อมแบบ axonal ในผู้ป่วยไตวายเรื้อรังระยะท้าย มีอาการชาแสบร้อนปลายเท้า ตะคริว ขาอยู่ไม่สุข และอ่อนแรงปลายเท้า ต้องแยกจากเบาหวาน ขาด B12 และยา การรักษาที่ได้ผลที่สุดคือฟอกไตให้เพียงพอและปลูกถ่ายไต ยาแก้ปวดประสาทต้องปรับขนาดตามการทำงานของไต

name: Uraemic restless legs syndrome
formal: Restless legs syndrome occurring in patients with renal failure, often improved with transplantation.
simple: Restless legs with an urge to move that occurs in kidney failure.
th: กลุ่มอาการขาอยู่ไม่สุขในผู้ป่วยไตวายเรื้อรัง พบบ่อยในผู้ฟอกไต และมักดีขึ้นหลังปลูกถ่ายไต
tempoNote: Nightly symptoms that persist while on dialysis; often resolve within weeks of transplantation
feat: Urge to move the legs with unpleasant deep sensations, worse at rest and in the evening
Relieved by walking or stretching; may disturb sitting through dialysis sessions
Periodic limb movements in sleep and insomnia
Iron deficiency and anaemia common; may coexist with uraemic neuropathy
inv: Clinical diagnosis using standard RLS criteria
Ferritin, transferrin saturation, haemoglobin, calcium, phosphate, PTH
Nerve conduction if neuropathy suspected

case.who: 62-year-old woman on haemodialysis in Udon Thani
case.story: Every evening she feels a crawling ache deep in both calves and must get up and walk; she cannot sit still during dialysis.
case.exam: Normal strength and reflexes, mild distal vibration loss.
case.tests: Ferritin 60 ng/mL, transferrin saturation 14%, Hb 9.2 g/dL.
case.q: Which reversible factor should be addressed first?
case.a: Iron deficiency — replete iron (IV during dialysis) and optimise anaemia management before dopaminergic drugs.

det.patho: The mechanism is incompletely understood. Brain iron deficiency affecting dopaminergic transmission, anaemia, uraemic toxins and coexisting neuropathy are all thought to contribute. The rapid improvement after transplantation suggests a reversible metabolic driver.
det.clinical: Symptoms meet standard RLS criteria and are often more severe than in primary RLS, interfering with sleep and dialysis sessions. Poor sleep contributes to fatigue, depression and lower quality of life. Augmentation with dopamine agonists is a particular concern because treatment is often long-term.
det.diagnosis: Use the standard clinical criteria: urge to move, rest-induced, relieved by movement, evening worsening, and not explained by another condition. Exclude leg cramps, positional discomfort, neuropathy and akathisia from drugs. Check iron indices with a higher ferritin target than in the general population.
det.treatment: Correct iron deficiency (IV iron is convenient on dialysis) and anaemia, and optimise dialysis. Non-drug measures include exercise during dialysis and avoiding caffeine, alcohol and sedating antihistamines. Gabapentin at low renally adjusted doses, or low-dose dopamine agonists, can be used with attention to accumulation and augmentation. Transplantation usually resolves symptoms.
det.prognosis: Tends to persist while on dialysis but often disappears after a successful kidney transplant.
pearls: Check ferritin and transferrin saturation in every dialysis patient with RLS.
Avoid metoclopramide and sedating antihistamines, which worsen RLS.
Gabapentinoids accumulate in kidney failure — start very low.
det.thd: Uraemic RLS คือกลุ่มอาการขาอยู่ไม่สุขในผู้ป่วยไตวายเรื้อรังโดยเฉพาะผู้ฟอกไต มีความรู้สึกไม่สบายลึก ๆ ที่ขาและอยากขยับ เป็นมากตอนพักและตอนเย็น ดีขึ้นเมื่อเดิน ควรตรวจและแก้ภาวะขาดธาตุเหล็กและโลหิตจาง ปรับการฟอกไต และใช้ยา gabapentin หรือ dopamine agonist ขนาดต่ำ อาการมักหายหลังปลูกถ่ายไต

name: Urea cycle disorders
formal: Inborn errors of ammonia detoxification causing hyperammonaemic encephalopathy, vomiting, seizures and coma.
simple: Inherited disorders where ammonia builds up in the blood and harms the brain.
th: กลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่ร่างกายกำจัดแอมโมเนียไม่ได้ ทำให้แอมโมเนียในเลือดสูง อาเจียน ชัก และโคม่า
tempoNote: Neonatal crises in severe forms; later-onset forms have episodic decompensation triggered by illness or protein load
feat: Neonatal: normal at birth, then poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, seizures and coma within days
Late-onset: episodic confusion, vomiting, ataxia, psychiatric symptoms, often triggered by infection, fasting, protein meals or valproate
Respiratory alkalosis early in hyperammonaemia
OTC deficiency is X-linked; female carriers may present in adulthood
Arginase deficiency presents with progressive spastic diplegia rather than crises
inv: Plasma ammonia (free-flowing sample, on ice, analysed promptly)
Plasma amino acids (citrulline, arginine), urine orotic acid
Genetic testing for specific enzyme defects

case.story: Becomes confused and agitated, then drowsy; she has always avoided meat.
case.exam: Encephalopathic, no focal signs.
case.tests: Ammonia 280 µmol/L, normal liver function, raised urinary orotic acid, low citrulline; OTC variant found.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the emergency treatment?
case.a: Late-onset OTC deficiency triggered by postpartum catabolism; stop protein, give IV glucose (with insulin if needed), nitrogen scavengers (sodium benzoate/phenylacetate), arginine and urgent haemodialysis if ammonia remains high.

read.where: Chapter 36 Seizures Due to Inborn Errors of Metabolism
14 Specific dietary management of certain neurological disorders

det.patho: The urea cycle in the liver converts ammonia to urea. Deficiency of any enzyme (CPS1, OTC, ASS1, ASL, ARG1) or NAGS leads to accumulation of ammonia and glutamine, causing astrocyte swelling, cerebral oedema and neurotoxicity. OTC deficiency is X-linked; the others are autosomal recessive.
det.clinical: Severe forms present in neonates with rapid encephalopathy after protein feeding begins. Later-onset forms can present at any age with episodic hyperammonaemia triggered by catabolic stress, high protein intake, steroids, or valproate. Chronic symptoms include developmental delay, learning disability, protein aversion and psychiatric features.
det.diagnosis: Measure ammonia in any unexplained encephalopathy. Plasma amino acids and urine orotic acid differentiate specific defects. Confirm with genetic testing. Newborn screening detects some disorders.
det.treatment: Emergency: stop protein, give high-calorie IV glucose and lipid, nitrogen scavengers (sodium benzoate, sodium phenylacetate), arginine or citrulline, and haemodialysis for severe hyperammonaemia. Long-term: protein-restricted diet, essential amino acid supplements, oral nitrogen scavengers (sodium or glycerol phenylbutyrate), and liver transplantation for severe forms. Avoid valproate.
det.prognosis: Outcome depends on peak and duration of hyperammonaemia; early treatment and transplantation improve survival.
pearls: Measure ammonia in any unexplained encephalopathy, including adults.
Valproate can precipitate crises in undiagnosed urea cycle disorders.
Postpartum encephalopathy may reveal OTC deficiency in women.
det.thd: Urea cycle disorders เป็นกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่ตับกำจัดแอมโมเนียไม่ได้ ทารกแรกเกิดซึม อาเจียน ชัก และโคม่าหลังเริ่มกินนม ผู้ใหญ่อาจมีอาการเป็นพัก ๆ เมื่อป่วยหรือกินโปรตีนมาก ตรวจแอมโมเนีย กรดอะมิโน และ orotic acid ในปัสสาวะ รักษาฉุกเฉินด้วยหยุดโปรตีน ให้กลูโคส ยาขับไนโตรเจน และฟอกไตเมื่อแอมโมเนียสูงมาก

name: Uveomeningeal syndromes
formal: Group of inflammatory conditions, including uveitis with meningitis such as Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease, Behcet disease or sarcoidosis.
simple: Conditions involving inflammation of both the eye and the brain's coverings.
th: กลุ่มโรคที่มีการอักเสบของ uvea ร่วมกับเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ สาเหตุ เช่น VKH, Behçet, sarcoidosis, วัณโรค ซิฟิลิส และมะเร็งต่อมน้ำเหลือง
tempoNote: Eye and meningeal symptoms usually appear within days to weeks of each other; some causes relapse
feat: Red painful eye, photophobia or blurred vision from anterior, posterior or panuveitis
Headache, neck stiffness and fever from meningitis
Cranial neuropathies, encephalopathy or hearing loss in some causes
Skin, mucosal or systemic clues: oral ulcers, vitiligo, poliosis, erythema nodosum, lymphadenopathy
inv: Ophthalmology review: slit lamp, fundoscopy, OCT and fluorescein angiography
CSF: cell count, protein, glucose, cultures, PCR, cytology and flow cytometry
Serology: syphilis, HIV, TB tests, ACE; HLA-B51 not diagnostic but supportive
MRI brain with contrast; chest imaging for sarcoidosis or TB

case.story: Recurrent painful mouth ulcers for two years, now a red painful left eye and a week of headache with fever.
case.exam: Neck stiffness, left hypopyon uveitis, genital ulcer scar, pustular lesions at venepuncture site.
case.tests: CSF 120 cells (mixed), protein 0.8 g/L, glucose normal, cultures negative; MRI enhancing lesion in the midbrain.
case.q: Which cause of uveomeningitis is most likely?
case.a: Neuro-Behçet disease — recurrent oral and genital ulcers, hypopyon uveitis, pathergy and brainstem involvement.

read.where: Section III Other Inflammatory CNS Disorders and Neuroimmunologic Mimics
Chapter 21 The Skin and Neurologic Disease

det.patho: These are conditions in which the same inflammatory or infectious process affects the uveal tract and the meninges, reflecting shared antigens (melanocytes in VKH), vasculitis (Behçet), granulomas (sarcoidosis) or infiltration (lymphoma, infection). Causes differ by region; in Asia VKH, Behçet and tuberculosis are prominent. The common thread is that eye findings can point to the meningitis diagnosis.
det.clinical: Patients present with headache, meningism and eye symptoms in either order. Clues by cause: VKH with bilateral exudative retinal detachments, tinnitus and later depigmentation; Behçet with oral and genital ulcers and pathergy; sarcoidosis with cranial neuropathies and lung disease; syphilis with rash or HIV; lymphoma with vitreous cells in older adults. Infectious causes must be ruled out before steroids.
det.diagnosis: Careful ophthalmological phenotyping (granulomatous vs non-granulomatous, anterior vs posterior, unilateral vs bilateral) narrows the list greatly. CSF analysis, including cytology and flow cytometry, plus infectious studies, MRI and chest imaging complete the work-up. Biopsy of accessible tissue (lymph node, skin, vitreous) may be needed.
det.treatment: Treat infection when present (penicillin for syphilis, antituberculous therapy, antivirals). Inflammatory causes receive systemic corticosteroids, often high-dose initially, followed by immunomodulators such as azathioprine, mycophenolate, TNF inhibitors (Behçet, sarcoidosis) or cyclosporine. Ophthalmology co-management is essential to protect vision.
det.prognosis: Outcome depends on cause and speed of treatment; visual loss is the major long-term disability.
pearls: A slit-lamp examination can solve a meningitis puzzle.
Exclude TB and syphilis before high-dose steroids in uveomeningitis.
Older patient with 'steroid-responsive' uveitis and brain lesions: consider lymphoma.
det.thd: Uveomeningeal syndromes คือกลุ่มโรคที่ตาอักเสบชนิด uveitis ร่วมกับเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ สาเหตุที่พบในไทย เช่น VKH, Behçet, sarcoidosis วัณโรค ซิฟิลิส และ lymphoma ลักษณะตาช่วยบอกสาเหตุได้มาก ต้องตรวจตาอย่างละเอียด เจาะน้ำไขสันหลัง และหาโรคติดเชื้อก่อน รักษาตามสาเหตุ ถ้าเป็นการอักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกันใช้ steroid และยากดภูมิ

name: Vacuolar myelopathy
formal: Spinal cord degeneration with vacuolation of white matter, such as HIV vacuolar myelopathy or B12 deficiency.
simple: Spinal cord damage that causes leg weakness and loss of position sense.
th: ไขสันหลังเสื่อมแบบมีช่องว่างในเนื้อขาว พบบ่อยใน HIV ระยะท้าย ให้อาการขาเกร็งอ่อนแรงและเสียการรับรู้ตำแหน่งข้อคล้ายขาด B12
tempoNote: Gradual spastic leg weakness over months
feat: Slowly progressive spastic paraparesis with brisk reflexes and extensor plantars
Impaired vibration and proprioception in the feet, giving a sensory ataxia
Early bladder urgency and erectile dysfunction; no clear sensory level
Usually advanced HIV with low CD4; may coexist with HIV dementia or neuropathy
inv: MRI spine often normal or shows thoracic cord atrophy or faint dorsal T2 signal
B12, methylmalonic acid, homocysteine, copper, HTLV-1 serology, syphilis serology
HIV viral load and CD4; CSF to exclude infections such as CMV or VZV myelitis

case.who: 45-year-old woman from Chiang Rai with long-standing poorly treated HIV
case.story: Eight months of stiff legs, tripping on stairs and urinary urgency, no back pain.
case.exam: Spastic paraparesis, brisk knee jerks, extensor plantars, absent toe vibration and position sense, no sensory level.
case.tests: CD4 90; B12, copper and HTLV-1 normal; MRI shows mild thoracic cord thinning only.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and why exclude B12 and copper deficiency?
case.a: HIV vacuolar myelopathy, a diagnosis of exclusion; B12 and copper deficiency give the same dorsal-lateral column picture and are treatable.

read.where: Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — HIV-Related Vacuolar Myelopathy
Chapter 17: Nondegenerative Diseases of the Spine
Chapter 112: Retroviral Infections of the Nervous System

det.patho: Myelin sheaths in the lateral and dorsal columns swell into vacuoles, most marked in the thoracic cord, with lipid-laden macrophages and little direct viral infection of neurons. Disturbed methylation (a transmethylation defect resembling B12 deficiency) driven by immune activation is the leading hypothesis. Similar vacuolar change is seen in B12 and copper deficiency.
det.clinical: It was found in a large share of AIDS autopsies before modern ART, though many cases were silent. Symptomatic patients develop slowly increasing leg stiffness, gait unsteadiness and bladder symptoms over months. Arms are spared until late and pain is not prominent. It often accompanies HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder or distal sensory neuropathy.
det.diagnosis: This is a diagnosis of exclusion in a person with HIV and a progressive myelopathy. Check B12 with metabolites, copper, HTLV-1, syphilis, and image the spine to exclude compression. CSF studies rule out opportunistic viral myelitis and lymphoma. MRI may be normal or show cord atrophy.
det.treatment: Effective antiretroviral therapy is the cornerstone and may stabilise or partly improve symptoms. Correct any coexisting vitamin or copper deficiency. Supplementation with methionine has been tried without proven benefit. Antispasticity drugs, bladder care and physiotherapy improve function.
det.prognosis: Often stabilises with viral suppression, but established deficits usually persist.
pearls: HIV + spastic paraparesis + posterior column loss + no sensory level: think vacuolar myelopathy, then exclude B12, copper and HTLV-1.
It looks pathologically like subacute combined degeneration but B12 is normal.
Back pain or a sensory level suggests another cause such as compression or lymphoma.
det.thd: Vacuolar myelopathy คือไขสันหลังเสื่อมที่เนื้อขาวด้านข้างและด้านหลังเกิดช่องว่าง พบใน HIV ระยะท้าย ผู้ป่วยขาเกร็งอ่อนแรงทีละน้อย เสียการรับรู้ตำแหน่งข้อ และกลั้นปัสสาวะไม่ดี ต้องแยกจากขาด B12 ขาดทองแดง และ HTLV-1 เพราะภาพคล้ายกัน การรักษาหลักคือยาต้านไวรัส HIV ร่วมกับกายภาพบำบัด

name: Valproic acid catatonia
formal: Catatonia occurring with valproate-associated hyperammonaemic encephalopathy.
simple: A state of reduced movement and response linked to a seizure medicine.
th: catatonia ที่เกิดร่วมกับภาวะสมองผิดปกติจากแอมโมเนียสูงจากยา valproate แม้ระดับยาและการทำงานของตับปกติ ดีขึ้นเมื่อหยุดยา
tempoNote: Days to weeks after starting valproate or a dose rise, sometimes after adding interacting drugs
feat: Mutism, staring, posturing, negativism or waxy flexibility in a patient taking valproate
Associated drowsiness, confusion, asterixis or increased seizures
Serum ammonia raised, often with normal liver enzymes and therapeutic valproate levels
Risk factors: topiramate co-therapy, carnitine deficiency, urea cycle defects
Improves after valproate withdrawal, with or without lorazepam
inv: Venous ammonia (on ice, processed promptly), liver function, valproate level
EEG to exclude non-convulsive status epilepticus; triphasic or slow background supports encephalopathy
Carnitine level; plasma amino acids and urine orotic acid if a urea cycle defect is suspected

case.story: Started valproate for bipolar disorder three weeks ago; topiramate was added for weight. She now sits motionless and silent for hours.
case.exam: Holds limbs in imposed positions, resists passive movement, intermittent asterixis.
case.tests: Ammonia 145 µmol/L, valproate level therapeutic, ALT normal; EEG diffuse slowing, no seizures.
case.q: What is the cause and treatment?
case.a: Valproate-induced hyperammonaemic encephalopathy with catatonia; stop valproate (and topiramate), give lorazepam and consider L-carnitine.

det.patho: Valproate metabolites inhibit carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I and deplete carnitine, impairing urea synthesis and raising ammonia without liver damage. Ammonia increases brain glutamine, causing astrocyte swelling and disturbed GABA and glutamate transmission. Catatonia probably reflects dysfunction of fronto-basal ganglia circuits under this metabolic stress.
det.clinical: Patients become slowed, mute and immobile, sometimes with posturing, echophenomena and refusal to eat. Fluctuating confusion, vomiting, asterixis and seizure worsening are common. It may occur early or after years of stable use, particularly when interacting drugs are added. Catatonia carries risks of dehydration, pressure injury and venous thromboembolism.
det.diagnosis: Measure ammonia in any valproate-treated patient with new behavioural change or encephalopathy, even if levels and liver tests are normal. Use a catatonia rating scale (Bush–Francis). EEG excludes non-convulsive status, which can also present as catatonia. Consider an underlying urea cycle disorder in severe or recurrent cases.
det.treatment: Stop valproate and replace with another antiseizure or mood-stabilising drug. Lorazepam is first-line for catatonia; L-carnitine is commonly given to aid ammonia clearance; lactulose may help. Avoid antipsychotics while catatonic because of the risk of NMS-like deterioration. Severe cases may need haemodialysis.
det.prognosis: Usually reversible within days of stopping valproate when recognised early.
pearls: Normal valproate level and liver tests do not exclude valproate hyperammonaemia.
Topiramate plus valproate is a classic risky pair.
Before calling catatonia psychiatric, check ammonia and EEG.
det.thd: Valproic acid catatonia เกิดจากยา valproate ทำให้แอมโมเนียในเลือดสูงแม้ตับปกติและระดับยาปกติ ผู้ป่วยนิ่ง ไม่พูด คงท่าทางแปลก ๆ ร่วมกับซึมสับสนหรือ asterixis ควรตรวจ ammonia และ EEG เพื่อแยกชักแบบไม่กระตุก การรักษาคือหยุด valproate ให้ lorazepam และพิจารณา L-carnitine โดยมากหายเป็นปกติ

ddx.pt: Rigidity, fever, autonomic instability and high CK after dopamine blockers
Raised ammonia with liver failure, jaundice and abnormal liver tests
Inborn defects unmasked by valproate; very high ammonia with abnormal amino acid profile

aN: valproate induced catatonia | valproate hyperammonemic encephalopathy | vhe catatonia | valproate encephalopathy

name: Vanishing white matter disease
formal: Leukodystrophy from EIF2B mutations with episodic deterioration after fever or trauma, ataxia and spasticity.
simple: An inherited disease of brain white matter with sudden worsening after fever or head injury.
more: Autosomal recessive leucodystrophy from EIF2B mutations, with cerebellar ataxia, spasticity and episodic worsening after fever or head trauma, with vanishing white matter on MRI.
th: leukodystrophy จากยีน EIF2B1–5 มีอาการแย่ลงเป็นช่วง ๆ หลังมีไข้หรือบาดเจ็บศีรษะเล็กน้อย ร่วมกับ ataxia และขาเกร็ง และ white matter สลายเป็นน้ำบน MRI
tempoNote: Chronic progression punctuated by abrupt deteriorations after fever, minor head trauma or fright
feat: Cerebellar ataxia and spasticity with relatively preserved cognition early
Sudden severe decline, sometimes coma, after febrile illness or mild head injury
Onset from antenatal to adult; earlier onset = faster course
Ovarian failure in affected women (ovarioleukodystrophy)
Adult forms may present with cognitive or psychiatric decline
inv: MRI: diffuse symmetric white matter signal change that progressively becomes CSF-like (rarefaction) on FLAIR
CSF glycine raised in some, asialotransferrin low
Genetic testing of EIF2B1–EIF2B5

case.story: Walked normally, but after a minor fall onto his head he became unable to walk for weeks and never fully recovered. A dengue fever later caused further decline and drowsiness.
case.exam: Truncal and limb ataxia, spastic legs with extensor plantars, alert and interactive.
case.tests: MRI shows diffuse white matter with FLAIR signal close to CSF; biallelic EIF2B5 variants.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what preventive advice matters most?
case.a: Vanishing white matter disease; prevent and promptly treat fever (antipyretics, vaccinations) and avoid head trauma.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Vanishing White Matter Disease
Progressive Encephalopathies With Onset After Age 2

det.patho: The five EIF2B genes encode subunits of eukaryotic initiation factor 2B, which controls protein synthesis and the integrated stress response. Recessive variants reduce its activity, so astrocytes and oligodendrocytes respond abnormally to stress; astrocytes are dysmorphic and myelin is poorly maintained, leading to cystic white matter breakdown.
det.clinical: Classic childhood onset is between 2 and 6 years with ataxia and spasticity, followed by stepwise worsening with infections or trauma, sometimes causing coma or death. Infantile forms are rapidly fatal; adult-onset forms progress slowly and can present with cognitive decline, psychiatric symptoms, seizures or ovarian failure.
det.diagnosis: MRI is often diagnostic, showing symmetric diffuse white matter abnormality that over time takes on CSF signal with residual radiating strands. Genetic confirmation of biallelic EIF2B variants establishes the diagnosis. CSF glycine and asialotransferrin are supportive but not routinely needed.
det.treatment: No approved disease-modifying therapy, although drugs that modulate the integrated stress response (such as guanabenz and eIF2B activators) are being trialled. Management prevents stressors: early antipyretics, vaccinations, avoidance of contact sports and careful anaesthesia. Corticosteroids have been used in acute crises without proven benefit.
det.prognosis: Variable; childhood forms often lead to death within a decade, adult forms survive much longer.
pearls: Child with ataxia who collapses after fever or minor head trauma: think VWM.
MRI white matter that looks like CSF on FLAIR is the hallmark.
Ovarian failure plus leukodystrophy in a woman: consider VWM.

name: Variant Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (vCJD)
formal: Prion disease from bovine spongiform encephalopathy exposure, with young onset, psychiatric symptoms, pulvinar sign on MRI and fatal course.

det.patho: Classical bovine spongiform encephalopathy prions, spread when cattle ate scrapie-contaminated animal protein, crossed the species barrier into humans. Unlike sporadic CJD, the agent first multiplies in lymphoid tissue (tonsil, spleen, appendix) and reaches the brain later; the brain shows florid plaques, a dense core ringed by vacuoles, and a type 2B protease-resistant fragment on Western blot. Nearly all clinical cases are MM at codon 129, but two patients who died from other causes carried the agent in lymphoid tissue while being MV, so heterozygotes may be silent carriers or have very long incubation. An estimated 1–2 per 4000 people in the UK carry vCJD prions in lymphoid tissue.
det.clinical: Patients are young, and the first months look psychiatric (depression, anxiety, withdrawal, delusions) so many are first seen by a psychiatrist. Persistent painful sensory symptoms, probably from thalamic involvement, are a relatively unique early feature. Ataxia, chorea, dystonia or myoclonus and then dementia follow, with mean survival of about 14 months. The epidemic peaked around 2000, with 178 cases in the UK and 28 in France among 232 worldwide; North American cases were exposed elsewhere. Transfusion transmission has been documented in five recipients (four received non-leukodepleted red cells before 1999), with incubation of 6–8.5 years in those who became ill, and one laboratory-acquired case was reported in 2019.
det.diagnosis: Diagnostic criteria require a progressive neuropsychiatric course longer than 6 months, no alternative explanation, no iatrogenic exposure and no familial form, plus at least four of five clinical features (early psychiatric change, dementia, ataxia, painful sensory complaints, and myoclonus, chorea or dystonia). A non-sporadic EEG and bilateral pulvinar high signal make a probable case; a positive tonsil biopsy can substitute for the MRI sign. The pulvinar sign is well validated on T2/FLAIR but the benefit on DWI is less certain, and the sign is rarely seen in some sporadic subtypes such as MV2K. Definite diagnosis requires brain pathology; one 2016 UK patient looked like sCJD clinically and was found to have vCJD only at autopsy.
det.treatment: No treatment alters the course; manage depression, pain, myoclonus and agitation symptomatically and involve palliative care. Public-health measures include notification, tracing of blood and tissue exposure, and restrictions on blood donation by people with a history of UK residence in the BSE era, as set by national blood services. Surgical instruments from a suspected case follow prion decontamination rules or are destroyed. Because infected asymptomatic donors can transmit before symptoms, long-term lymphoid carriers remain a concern for transfusion and invasive procedures.
det.prognosis: Mean duration about 14 months from onset; always fatal.
pearls: Months of psychiatric symptoms plus burning limb pain in a young adult, then ataxia and a pulvinar sign, should raise vCJD.
The pulvinar sign requires the posterior thalamus to be more intense than the front of the putamen; a bright thalamus alone is not enough.
Ask about residence anywhere with BSE-era beef, not only the UK: some North American patients were exposed in Saudi Arabia and other countries.
det.thd: vCJD เกิดจาก prion ของโรควัวบ้า (BSE) ที่ข้ามสายพันธุ์มาสู่คนผ่านการกินเนื้อวัวปนเปื้อน และพบน้อยมากที่ติดผ่านการให้เลือด พบในคนหนุ่มสาว เริ่มด้วยซึมเศร้า วิตกกังวล และปวดแสบปวดร้อนที่แขนขานานหลายเดือน ตามด้วยเดินเซ การเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติ และสมองเสื่อม ใช้เวลาเฉลี่ยราว 14 เดือน MRI พบ pulvinar sign และ EEG มักไม่มี periodic complex การยืนยันใช้ชิ้นเนื้อต่อมทอนซิลหรือสมอง ไม่มียารักษาและต้องแจ้งหน่วยงานสาธารณสุข

qx.stem: A 66-year-old Bangkok taxi driver had a left frontal and caudate infarct eight months ago. His wife says he now sits for hours without starting anything, takes far longer to finish simple chores and cannot plan a shopping trip, although he still recalls recent family news. High-dose vitamin E

qx.why: In vascular cognitive impairment the main modifiable driver is ongoing small-vessel and recurrent stroke injury, and intensive BP lowering reduced incident MCI in SPRINT MIND; standard secondary prevention completes the package. det.patho: Cerebrovascular disease damages cognition through several routes: multiple cortical infarcts, single strategic infarcts (thalamus, angular gyrus, caudate, genu of the internal capsule), haemorrhages, and — most commonly — small vessel disease with white matter rarefaction, lacunes and microinfarcts that disconnect frontal–subcortical circuits. Hypertension, diabetes, smoking and ageing drive arteriolosclerosis, with chronic hypoperfusion, blood–brain barrier leakage and impaired perivascular clearance contributing; CAA and genetic arteriopathies such as CADASIL (NOTCH3) are other causes. Mixed vascular and Alzheimer pathology is the norm in older people, and each lowers the threshold at which the other produces dementia. VCI is the second commonest cause of dementia and is especially prevalent in Asian populations with high hypertension and stroke rates.
det.clinical: The cognitive profile is dominated by slowed thinking, poor attention, executive dysfunction, apathy and depression, with memory retrieval worse than storage, so cueing helps recall. Course may be stepwise after strokes or gradually progressive with small vessel disease, and the two often combine. Associated features include short-stepped gait with falls, urinary urgency, pseudobulbar affect, parkinsonism of the lower body and focal signs. Post-stroke cognitive impairment affects a large proportion of survivors in the first year; dementia after a first stroke is around one in ten and much higher after recurrent or severe strokes. Examiners often ask how to separate it from Alzheimer disease and NPH.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires cognitive impairment plus imaging evidence of cerebrovascular disease judged sufficient to explain it, using frameworks such as VICCCS or VasCog that grade severity (mild VCI vs major VCD) and subtype (post-stroke, subcortical ischaemic, multi-infarct, mixed). MRI shows white matter hyperintensities (graded by Fazekas), lacunes, microbleeds, enlarged perivascular spaces and infarcts, described with STRIVE terminology. Neuropsychological testing should include processing speed and executive tasks; MoCA (with Thai versions) is more sensitive than MMSE. Screen for depression, B12 deficiency, thyroid disease, syphilis and NPH, and consider amyloid or tau biomarkers when mixed disease is suspected. Young onset, family history, migraine with aura or anterior temporal and external capsule lesions prompt NOTCH3 testing.
det.treatment: Aggressive vascular risk control is the core: BP lowering (intensive targets reduced incident MCI in trial data), diabetes and lipid control, stopping smoking, physical activity and treating hearing loss and sleep apnoea. Secondary stroke prevention follows usual rules, but antiplatelets are given for prior stroke, not for white matter disease alone; cilostazol is being studied for small vessel disease. Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine give modest cognitive benefit and are mainly used in mixed or post-stroke dementia. Treat depression, address apathy, and support function with rehabilitation, occupational therapy, caregiver education and planning for capacity and safety. Avoid anticholinergic and sedative drugs that worsen cognition and gait.
det.prognosis: Progression is variable and often steeper than in Alzheimer disease, with higher rates of further stroke, falls and death.
pearls: Slowness and dysexecutive features outweigh amnesia in subcortical VCI.
Most late-life dementia is mixed — vascular plus Alzheimer pathology.
Young onset with migraine aura and anterior temporal white matter lesions = test for CADASIL (NOTCH3).
Good BP control in midlife is the best-evidenced way to protect the brain from VCI.

det.patho: Vascular dementia is cognitive decline caused mainly by cerebrovascular injury. Mechanisms include multiple cortical infarcts, single strategically placed infarcts (thalamus, caudate, angular gyrus), and most often diffuse small vessel disease with lacunes and white matter rarefaction that disconnect frontal–subcortical circuits. Hypertension, diabetes and age drive arteriolosclerosis, while amyloid angiopathy and coexisting Alzheimer pathology frequently add to the burden.
det.clinical: Classic multi-infarct cases decline in steps after clinical strokes, but the more frequent subcortical form progresses gradually and can be mistaken for a neurodegenerative dementia. The cognitive profile features slowing, inattention and executive failure, with relatively better recognition memory. Gait disorder, urinary symptoms, emotional lability and depression are typical. Post-stroke dementia may appear soon after a large stroke or emerge over the following year.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires cognitive impairment that interferes with daily function plus imaging evidence of cerebrovascular disease sufficient to explain it, and a plausible temporal or clinical link (criteria such as VASCOG or VICCCS formalise this). MRI is central. Look for coexisting Alzheimer disease, as mixed dementia is the commonest pattern in older adults; CSF or PET amyloid markers can help when the picture is unclear. Rule out depression, medication effects and metabolic causes.
det.treatment: No drug reverses vascular brain injury; the priority is preventing further damage through blood pressure control, antithrombotic therapy when indicated, statins, glucose control, smoking cessation and exercise. Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine give modest benefit and are reasonable in mixed or uncertain cases. Treat depression, address falls and continence, and support carers. Avoid excessive BP lowering in frail patients with orthostatic symptoms.
det.prognosis: Survival is generally shorter than in Alzheimer disease because of recurrent stroke and cardiovascular events; good risk-factor control can slow decline.
pearls: Executive slowing with cue-responsive recall suggests a subcortical vascular process.
Pure vascular dementia is uncommon in the elderly; assume mixed pathology until shown otherwise.
Use MoCA rather than MMSE alone — MMSE under-detects executive deficits.

The sudden onset argues against slow small-vessel or degenerative disease, CAA spares the thalamus, and prion disease progresses rather than stabilises.

det.patho: Vascular malformations are structural abnormalities in which vessels are formed or connected abnormally. AVMs are direct artery-to-vein shunts through a tangle (nidus) without capillaries; cavernous malformations are clusters of thin-walled sinusoids prone to repeated small bleeds; developmental venous anomalies are variant drainage veins; capillary telangiectasias are dilated capillaries; dural AV fistulas are acquired shunts in the dura, often after sinus thrombosis or trauma. Genetic forms include familial cavernomas (KRIT1, CCM2, PDCD10) and AVMs in hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia.
det.clinical: This term is an umbrella; each subtype behaves differently. AVMs most often present in young adults with haemorrhage or seizures; cavernomas cause seizures, focal deficits from small bleeds, or nothing at all, with brainstem lesions particularly symptomatic. Dural fistulas with cortical venous reflux may cause haemorrhage, dementia-like decline or pulsatile tinnitus. DVAs and telangiectasias rarely cause symptoms, though a DVA may coexist with a cavernoma.
det.diagnosis: MRI with susceptibility sequences characterises most lesions; cavernomas show a mixed-signal core with a haemosiderin rim and are angiographically occult. Catheter angiography is essential for AVMs and fistulas to map feeders, drainage and associated aneurysms, and to grade risk. In acute haemorrhage, repeat imaging after the clot resolves can reveal a hidden malformation.
det.treatment: Management balances lifetime bleeding risk against treatment risk. Ruptured AVMs are usually treated by microsurgery, stereotactic radiosurgery or embolisation alone or combined; for unruptured AVMs, conservative care is often preferred after the ARUBA trial. Symptomatic accessible cavernomas may be resected, especially with recurrent bleeding or drug-resistant epilepsy. Dural fistulas with cortical venous drainage are closed endovascularly or surgically. Seizures are treated with standard antiseizure medication.
det.prognosis: Untreated AVMs bleed at roughly 2–4% per year, higher after a first rupture; incidental DVAs and telangiectasias have an excellent outlook.
pearls: Lobar haemorrhage in a young normotensive patient: look for a vascular malformation.
Cavernomas do not show on angiography — they are an MRI (SWI) diagnosis.
Never resect a DVA; it drains normal brain.
det.thd: Vascular malformations คือหลอดเลือดสมองหรือไขสันหลังที่มีโครงสร้างผิดปกติ ได้แก่ AVM, cavernoma, DVA, capillary telangiectasia และ dural AV fistula ผู้ป่วยอายุน้อยอาจมาด้วยเลือดออกในสมองหรือชัก ตรวจด้วย MRI (SWI) และยืนยันด้วย angiography การรักษาขึ้นกับชนิดและความเสี่ยง เช่น ผ่าตัด radiosurgery หรือ embolization ส่วน DVA มักไม่ต้องรักษา

name: Vascular malformations, spinal
formal: Abnormal spinal vessels such as dural arteriovenous fistula or cavernoma, causing progressive myelopathy or haemorrhage.
simple: Abnormal blood vessels in the spine that can cause leg weakness or bleeding.
th: ความผิดปกติของหลอดเลือดไขสันหลังแบ่งเป็นสี่ชนิดหลัก ที่พบบ่อยที่สุดคือ dural AV fistula (ชนิดที่ I) ในชายวัยกลางคน ทำให้ขาอ่อนแรงและกลั้นปัสสาวะไม่ได้ค่อย ๆ แย่ลงจากความดันหลอดเลือดดำสูง ส่วน glomus AVM และ perimedullary fistula มักเลือดออกเฉียบพลันในคนอายุน้อย MRI เห็น flow void ที่ผิวไขสันหลัง และยืนยันด้วย spinal angiography
tempoNote: Dural fistulas worsen over months to years, sometimes stepwise and with effort; intramedullary AVMs and perimedullary fistulas present with sudden pain and deficit from bleeding, often before age 30
feat: Type I (dural arteriovenous fistula) makes up most adult lesions: a middle-aged or older man with progressive leg weakness, numbness, back pain and sphincter and sexual dysfunction from venous congestion of the lower cord

Type II (intramedullary glomus AVM) and type IV (perimedullary fistula on the cord surface) are high-flow and usually bleed, giving sudden severe back pain (coup de poignard), subarachnoid blood or haematomyelia in a younger patient
Type III (juvenile or metameric AVM) fills the whole cord cross-section, may involve bone and skin, and can produce scoliosis or a cutaneous angioma
Foix-Alajouanine syndrome describes a subacute necrotic myelopathy with ascending level and flaccid paraplegia; it is now understood as venous hypertension, not always irreversible
Cavernous malformations, vertebral haemangiomas and spinal haemangioblastomas are separate vascular lesions that can mimic these; a spinal bruit or back angioma is a rare but useful sign
inv: MRI of the whole spine: long T2 hyperintensity of the lower cord with a hypointense rim and serpiginous flow voids on the cord surface in most cases, with variable enhancement; a normal MRI does not exclude the lesion
Spinal catheter angiography is required for planning: it must cover every radicular feeder along the neuraxis, including the artery of Adamkiewicz and sacral and occasionally intracranial sources
Contrast MR or CT angiography can suggest the level and reduce the area to be studied but cannot replace catheter angiography
Myelography is mostly obsolete and carries a risk of puncturing a dilated vessel

case.story: Two years of low back ache and legs that tire and go numb after standing for the morning tap; recent erectile failure and a weak urinary stream. A lumbar epidural steroid injection for suspected stenosis was followed by a week of worse weakness.
case.exam: Spastic-flaccid paraparesis (3+/5) with absent ankle jerks, extensor plantars, patchy sensory loss below T10 and reduced anal tone.
case.tests: MRI shows T2 hyperintensity from T8 to the conus tip with dorsal flow voids; spinal angiography finds a fistula at a right T9 radicular artery with a single draining vein.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and how is it treated?
case.a: Spinal dural arteriovenous fistula (type I) causing congestive myelopathy. Occlude the draining vein at the fistula point by surgical disconnection or by endovascular embolisation with liquid agents; incomplete closure recurs. Avoid steroids.

det.patho: Spinal vascular malformations are rare and make up a small percentage of intraspinal masses, mostly presenting between age 20 and 60. In the classic Anglo-French scheme type I is a dural fistula, an acquired shunt between a radicular artery and a vein in the nerve-root sleeve that arterialises the coronal venous plexus; type II is a compact glomus nidus inside the cord; type III is a large juvenile malformation occupying the cord and surrounding tissues; type IV is a direct arterial-to-vein fistula on the cord surface, subdivided by size. Venous hypertension lowers perfusion pressure and causes chronic ischaemia in dural lesions, while the high-flow intradural lesions bleed or steal flow.
det.clinical: Around four out of five cases present with a slowly progressive deficit, usually back pain with leg weakness and sensory loss that evolves over months to years, so the lesion is mistaken for degenerative disease, myelitis or a tumour. The dural type often mixes pyramidal signs with wasting and areflexia, and has a stuttering course that may be worsened by exercise, hot bath or steroids. About one in five present suddenly, usually under age 30, from bleeding into the subarachnoid space, cord or epidural space. A bruit over the spine is found in only a few percent, and a cutaneous angioma in a minority.
det.diagnosis: Suspect the fistula in any patient with unexplained long-segment cord signal at the conus, especially an older man, and look for flow voids on T2 images. MRI shows the voids in most and also rules out compressive causes, but only catheter angiography defines feeders and drainage; it should be performed in a centre with experience and must survey all possible feeders. Intradural malformations need detailed classification because the treatment differs. Myelography is rarely needed today.
det.treatment: Type I fistulae almost always need treatment, either by occluding the origin of the draining vein surgically or by embolising the fistula point with liquid adhesive that reaches the proximal vein; a fistula not fully eliminated will recur. Type II glomus lesions are treated by embolisation, microsurgery or both, in a specialist team, preserving arteries of passage to avoid new deficits. The juvenile type III often has a natural history better than the risks of attempted cure, so treatment is conservative or palliative. Type IV fistulae are managed by size and anatomy, with embolisation for large ones and surgery for small ones on the filum or conus. Avoid corticosteroids in suspected dural fistula and give rehabilitation and bladder care afterwards.
det.prognosis: Early closure of a dural fistula usually stabilises or improves gait; long-standing deficits and sphincter loss recover less. Outcome after intramedullary haemorrhage depends on the size of the bleed and the malformation type.
pearls: Older man + progressive myelopathy + long T2 cord signal to the conus + dorsal flow voids = dural AV fistula until proven otherwise.
Worsening after steroids in a presumed myelitis is a clue to venous congestion.
The fistula can be many levels from the cord oedema, so the whole neuraxis must be studied at angiography.
det.thd: ความผิดปกติของหลอดเลือดไขสันหลังที่พบบ่อยที่สุดคือ dural arteriovenous fistula (ชนิด I) เป็นทางลัดระหว่างหลอดเลือดแดงกับหลอดเลือดดำที่ปลอกหุ้มรากประสาท ทำให้ความดันหลอดเลือดดำที่ไขสันหลังสูง ผู้ป่วยมักเป็นชายวัยกลางคนขึ้นไป ขาอ่อนแรงชาและกลั้นปัสสาวะไม่ได้ค่อยเป็นค่อยไป ส่วน AVM ชนิดอื่นมักเลือดออกเฉียบพลันในคนอายุน้อย MRI พบสัญญาณ T2 สูงยาวและ flow void ที่ผิวไขสันหลัง ยืนยันด้วยการฉีดสีหลอดเลือดไขสันหลัง รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัดตัดหลอดเลือดดำหรืออุดด้วยกาว และควรหลีกเลี่ยงสเตียรอยด์

qx.stem: A 66-year-old retired tuk-tuk driver in Bangkok has 14 months of stepwise leg weakness that gets worse after walking a few hundred metres, numb feet, urinary urgency and constipation. Both legs show a mix of brisk knee jerks, absent ankle jerks and distal wasting. Thoracolumbar MRI shows central T2 hyperintensity from T7 to the conus with a T2-hypointense rim and serpiginous flow voids on the dorsal cord surface. A previous doctor gave prednisolone and he deteriorated.
qx.q: What is the most appropriate next investigation?
opts: Lumbar puncture for oligoclonal bands
Serum aquaporin-4 IgG and repeat steroids
Selective spinal digital subtraction angiography
Electromyography and nerve conduction studies only
MRI brain to look for demyelination
qx.why: Progressive venous congestive myelopathy with dorsal flow voids in an older man is a spinal dural arteriovenous fistula until proved otherwise; corticosteroids may worsen it by raising venous pressure. Contrast MR angiography can localise the feeding level, but catheter spinal DSA is the gold standard and guides endovascular or surgical disconnection of the draining vein. Early treatment gives the best functional outcome, so inflammatory work-ups should not delay angiography.

qx.stem: A 63-year-old male construction foreman from Rayong has 10 months of stepwise leg weakness and numbness that worsen after walking, with recent urinary hesitancy. After he was given IV dexamethasone for presumed transverse myelitis, his legs became markedly weaker. MRI shows a long central T2 hyperintensity from T8 to the conus with cord swelling, and serpiginous flow voids running over the posterior cord surface.
qx.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder
Spinal dural arteriovenous fistula
Spinal cord infarction from aortic atheroma
Intramedullary ependymoma
Subacute combined degeneration
qx.why: Progressive, exercise-aggravated myelopathy in an older man, a long conus-reaching T2 lesion from venous hypertension and dorsal perimedullary flow voids are typical of a spinal dural AV fistula; steroids often worsen it by raising venous pressure. Spinal angiography localises the fistula for embolisation or surgical disconnection. NMOSD and ependymoma lack flow voids, infarction is abrupt, and B12 deficiency affects the dorsal columns symmetrically without cord swelling.

case.who: 67-year-old man from Samut Prakan, 2 days after open repair of a thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm
case.story: On waking from sedation he cannot move his legs and has not passed urine.
case.exam: Flaccid paraplegia, absent leg reflexes, loss of pinprick below T8 with preserved vibration and joint position at the toes.
case.tests: MRI shows T2 hyperintensity of the anterior cord from T7 to the conus with diffusion restriction; CSF protein mildly raised, no cells.
case.q: Which syndrome is this, and which measure can still be tried?
case.a: Anterior spinal artery territory infarction after aortic surgery; raise mean arterial pressure and drain CSF via a lumbar drain to improve cord perfusion, then rehabilitate.

det.patho: The spinal cord receives one anterior and two posterior spinal arteries fed by segmental radicular arteries, notably the artery of Adamkiewicz for the lower thoracic cord. Arterial ischaemia follows aortic disease or surgery, systemic hypotension, atherosclerosis, dissection, vasculitis, embolism (including fibrocartilaginous material from a disc) or hypercoagulable states. Venous ischaemia occurs when cord drainage is impaired, mainly by dural AV fistulas, and haemorrhage arises from malformations or anticoagulation.
det.clinical: The arterial form presents abruptly, often with pain at the level, followed by bilateral weakness, spinothalamic loss and sphincter failure, sparing dorsal column sensation in anterior syndromes. Posterior spinal artery infarcts selectively affect proprioception. Fibrocartilaginous embolism often follows a minor strain in a young person. The venous form is insidious and fluctuating. Hyperacute peak (under about 12 hours) favours a vascular rather than inflammatory cause.
det.diagnosis: Emergency MRI excludes compression. Early scans may be normal; diffusion imaging and repeat imaging at 24–72 hours improve sensitivity. Characteristic findings are grey-matter predominant T2 signal and adjacent vertebral body infarction. CSF is usually non-inflammatory. Work-up targets the cause: aortic imaging, vascular risk factors, thrombophilia in the young and spinal angiography for suspected fistula.
det.treatment: Acute arterial infarction is managed with blood pressure augmentation, CSF drainage in the post-aortic-surgery setting, antiplatelet therapy for atherothrombotic causes, and prevention of complications (bladder care, DVT prophylaxis, pressure care). Thrombolysis is not established. Venous congestive myelopathy requires closure of the fistula. Early intensive rehabilitation is key.
det.prognosis: Outcome depends on initial severity; many patients regain some walking ability, but those with complete paraplegia at onset often remain dependent.
pearls: Maximum deficit within minutes plus sparing of vibration and position sense = anterior spinal artery syndrome.
A normal first MRI does not exclude cord infarction; repeat with DWI.
Fibrocartilaginous embolism: young person, minor exertion, sudden myelopathy.
det.thd: Vascular myelopathy คือโรคไขสันหลังจากความผิดปกติของหลอดเลือด แบบที่พบบ่อยคือ anterior spinal artery infarct ซึ่งมาด้วยปวดหลังแล้วขาอ่อนแรงทันที เสียความรู้สึกเจ็บปวดและอุณหภูมิ แต่ vibration ยังอยู่ มักเกิดหลังผ่าตัดเส้นเลือดแดงใหญ่หรือความดันต่ำ ส่วนอีกแบบคือเลือดดำคั่งจาก dural AV fistula ที่ค่อย ๆ แย่ลง การรักษาคือเพิ่ม perfusion ระบาย CSF ในกรณีหลังผ่าตัดเอออร์ตา และฟื้นฟู

name: Vascular parkinsonism
formal: Parkinsonism from small vessel disease affecting the basal ganglia and white matter, with lower-body parkinsonism and poor levodopa response.
simple: Slowness, stiffness and shuffling walking caused by multiple small strokes.
more: MRI shows extensive white matter hyperintensities with lacunes and basal ganglia infarcts; DAT-SPECT is usually normal, unlike Parkinson disease. Treat vascular risk factors, antiplatelets and physiotherapy; levodopa response is modest.
th: parkinsonism จาก small vessel disease — เดินซอยเท้าสั้น ฐานกว้าง เด่นที่ขา (lower-body) แขนปกติ มักไม่สั่น ตอบ levodopa น้อย MRI มี white matter disease หรือ lacune ที่ basal ganglia
tempoNote: Most often insidious and slowly progressive; less commonly appears abruptly after a strategic basal ganglia infarct
feat: Symmetrical, legs-predominant slowness with short shuffling steps on a widened base and freezing
Upper limbs relatively spared; arm swing often preserved; rest tremor rare
Early falls, postural instability and pyramidal signs (brisk reflexes, extensor plantars)
Pseudobulbar features, urinary urgency and executive cognitive impairment
Vascular risk factors: hypertension, diabetes, smoking
inv: MRI: confluent white matter hyperintensities and/or lacunes in basal ganglia, thalamus or frontal white matter
DaT-SPECT usually normal or patchy (helps separate from Parkinson’s disease)
Levodopa trial (up to about 1 g/day for 3 months) to identify the minority who respond

case.who: 74-year-old man, long-standing hypertension and diabetes, Suphan Buri
case.story: Two years of worsening walking: tiny steps, feet seem 'stuck to the floor' at doorways, several falls. No tremor; handwriting unchanged.
case.exam: Wide-based shuffling gait with freezing, retropulsion on pull test; arms swing normally; brisk reflexes and bilateral Babinski; mild frontal executive slowing.
case.tests: MRI: extensive periventricular and deep white matter hyperintensities with lacunes in both lentiform nuclei; no response to levodopa 600 mg/day.
case.q: What features favour a vascular rather than idiopathic cause?
case.a: Symmetrical lower-body predominance with preserved arm swing, no rest tremor, pyramidal signs, heavy small vessel disease on MRI and poor levodopa response.

det.patho: Cerebral small vessel disease disrupts the frontal–basal ganglia–thalamic loops and long periventricular fibres that control gait initiation and posture, rather than destroying nigral dopaminergic neurons. Less often a single lacune in the putamen, globus pallidus or substantia nigra produces acute contralateral parkinsonism. Hypertension and diabetes are the main risk factors; it accounts for a few percent of all parkinsonism.
det.clinical: The typical patient is elderly with a gait disorder dominated by short steps, start hesitation and freezing, a broad base and poor balance, while hand movements and facial expression are relatively normal. Falls come early. Cognitive slowing, pseudobulbar affect, urinary urgency and pyramidal signs reflect the underlying white matter disease. Progression is steady or stepwise rather than fluctuating.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by neuroimaging showing substantial small vessel disease or strategically placed infarcts, and by a temporal link to strokes when present. White matter changes are common in the elderly, so imaging alone does not prove the diagnosis; a normal DaT scan helps exclude coexisting Parkinson’s disease. Consider NPH, PSP and drug-induced parkinsonism, and recognise that mixed pathology is frequent.
det.treatment: Give an adequate levodopa trial because a minority, especially those with nigrostriatal lacunes, benefit. Physiotherapy focusing on gait, balance, cueing strategies and fall prevention is the mainstay. Control vascular risk factors (blood pressure, diabetes, lipids, smoking) and treat depression and urinary symptoms. Deep brain stimulation is not effective.
det.prognosis: Disability progresses over years, with falls and cognitive decline driving loss of independence; survival is shorter than in Parkinson’s disease.
pearls: 'Lower-body parkinsonism': legs stuck, arms normal.
Brisk reflexes and Babinski in a shuffling elderly patient argue against idiopathic PD.
Always try levodopa before calling it non-responsive.
det.thd: Vascular parkinsonism เกิดจากโรคหลอดเลือดสมองขนาดเล็กทำลายวงจรควบคุมการเดินในเนื้อขาวและ basal ganglia ผู้ป่วยสูงอายุเดินก้าวสั้น ซอยเท้า ฐานกว้าง เท้าติดพื้น หกล้มง่าย แต่แขนแกว่งปกติและมักไม่สั่น อาจมี reflex ไวและความคิดช้าลง MRI พบ white matter disease หรือ lacune ตอบสนองต่อ levodopa ไม่ดี การรักษาหลักคือกายภาพบำบัดและควบคุมปัจจัยเสี่ยงหลอดเลือด

qx.stem: A 76-year-old woman from Phetchaburi with long-standing hypertension has progressive short-stepped walking with freezing, mild leg rigidity and preserved arm swing. Levodopa had little effect.
qx.q: Which description best fits vascular parkinsonism?
opts: Asymmetric rest tremor with excellent sustained levodopa response and abnormal DaT
Early severe dysautonomia with the hot-cross-bun sign
Visual hallucinations and REM sleep behaviour disorder
Lower-body predominant parkinsonism with poor levodopa response, bilateral deep white matter or basal ganglia lesions, and usually a normal DaT scan
Vertical gaze palsy and square-wave jerks with the hummingbird sign
qx.why: Vascular parkinsonism is a lower-body presentation with gait impairment, poor levodopa response and abnormal white matter on MRI. Most patients have bilateral deep white matter or basal ganglia lesions and a normal DaT scan, though the consensus keeps the diagnosis informal because criteria are not established and MRI hyperintensities correlate only modestly. Vascular risk factors should be managed. The alternatives describe PD, MSA, DLB and PSP.

case.who: 74-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension and diabetes from Nakhon Sawan

case.q: Why is this unlikely to be classic PSP, and what treatment matters most?

det.patho: Multiple small vessel infarcts and diffuse white matter disease disrupt frontal-subcortical circuits and midbrain pathways involved in vertical gaze and postural control. A single strategic midbrain or thalamic infarct can also produce vertical gaze palsy. It is a clinical-radiological mimic rather than a separate disease.
det.clinical: Patients show PSP-like features: vertical gaze limitation, early falls, axial rigidity and pseudobulbar signs. Clues to a vascular cause are stepwise progression, asymmetry, prominent pyramidal signs, urinary symptoms and heavy vascular risk burden. Response to levodopa is usually poor in both conditions.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the clinical picture plus MRI evidence of substantial cerebrovascular disease and absence of marked midbrain atrophy. Some patients have both PSP pathology and vascular lesions, so certainty is limited in life. Measure midbrain to pons ratio and consider DaT-SPECT.
det.treatment: Manage vascular risk factors (BP, glucose, lipids, antiplatelet therapy as indicated). A levodopa trial is reasonable. Physiotherapy, gait training, fall prevention, speech and swallow therapy are central.
det.prognosis: Variable; further vascular events can cause stepwise decline.
pearls: Stepwise course with heavy small vessel disease: think vascular mimic before PSP.
Hummingbird sign favours true PSP.
Both pathologies can coexist in older patients.

det.patho: Inflammation and necrosis of the walls of epineurial arteries cause ischaemic infarction of nerve fascicles. Because nerve blood supply is patchy, infarcts produce discrete axonal lesions in individual nerves, often in watershed regions of the mid-arm and mid-thigh. Systemic causes include ANCA-associated vasculitis (especially EGPA and MPA), polyarteritis nodosa, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren syndrome, cryoglobulinaemia from hepatitis C, and drugs or infections. Nonsystemic vasculitic neuropathy is confined to the peripheral nerves.
det.clinical: Classic presentation is acute or subacute painful mononeuritis multiplex, with new deficits appearing in different nerves over days to weeks, often peroneal, tibial, ulnar or median. As lesions accumulate, the picture may resemble an asymmetric or even symmetric distal polyneuropathy, so the history of stepwise onset is key. Burning or deep aching pain is prominent. Systemic vasculitis adds constitutional symptoms, skin lesions, arthritis, renal or pulmonary involvement, and eosinophilia with asthma in EGPA.
det.diagnosis: NCS show asymmetric axonal loss, sometimes with pseudo-conduction block in the first days after infarction. Investigations include inflammatory markers, ANCA, ANA, ENA, rheumatoid factor, cryoglobulins, complement, hepatitis B and C, HIV, eosinophil count, urinalysis and renal function. A combined nerve and muscle biopsy (e.g. superficial peroneal nerve with peroneus brevis, or sural nerve), chosen from an affected but not absent nerve, gives the highest yield. Definite diagnosis requires vessel wall inflammation with damage; supportive features are probable. Diabetic and infectious mimics must be considered.
det.treatment: Treat promptly to prevent further nerve infarcts. Induction uses high-dose corticosteroids, combined with cyclophosphamide or rituximab for systemic vasculitis or severe/progressive nonsystemic disease; maintenance uses azathioprine, methotrexate or rituximab. Hepatitis-related vasculitis also needs antiviral treatment. Neuropathic pain, physiotherapy and orthoses are essential, and steroid-related bone and infection prophylaxis should be considered.
det.prognosis: Most patients stabilise with treatment and many improve slowly over months to years, though residual pain and weakness are common. Systemic vasculitis outcome depends on organ involvement; relapses occur.
pearls: Painful stepwise mononeuropathies in different limbs: rule out vasculitis.
Biopsy a nerve that is affected but still conducting.
Nonsystemic vasculitic neuropathy has normal markers — biopsy is the only route to diagnosis.
det.thd: Vasculitic neuropathy เกิดจากหลอดเลือดที่เลี้ยงเส้นประสาทอักเสบจนเส้นประสาทขาดเลือดเป็นจุด ๆ ทำให้ปวดและอ่อนแรง/ชาทีละเส้นแบบ mononeuritis multiplex อาจมีโรคทั้งระบบ เช่น ANCA vasculitis, PAN, rheumatoid, cryoglobulin หรือจำกัดอยู่เฉพาะเส้นประสาท ส่งตรวจ ANCA, cryoglobulin, ไวรัสตับ และทำ nerve/muscle biopsy เพื่อยืนยัน รักษาเร็วด้วย steroid ขนาดสูงร่วมกับ cyclophosphamide หรือ rituximab

det.patho: Nerve biopsies in these conditions show inflammation and microvasculitis of epineurial vessels with ischaemic axonal injury, multifocal fibre loss and evidence of prior bleeding. The lumbosacral region is affected most, typically involving roots, plexus and peripheral nerves together, which is why 'radiculoplexus neuropathy' is preferred. Diabetes is the main association, but an identical non-diabetic form exists; the trigger for the immune attack is unknown.
det.clinical: Onset is usually unilateral with severe pain, followed by proximal then distal weakness that commonly spreads to the opposite leg. Autonomic symptoms and weight loss are frequent. Thoracic radiculopathy causing abdominal wall pain and bulging, and cervical forms resembling neuralgic amyotrophy, may coexist. The process is monophasic in most, with slow improvement once the active phase ends.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical and electrophysiological: multifocal axonal loss across roots, plexus and nerves in the appropriate setting. MRI excludes structural causes and may show plexus enhancement or muscle denervation oedema. Screen for systemic vasculitis, malignancy and infection; nerve biopsy is reserved for atypical or progressive cases. Differential includes lumbar stenosis, CIDP, malignant infiltration and amyloidosis.
det.treatment: Pain management with neuropathic agents and sometimes opioids in the acute phase is the main need, together with physiotherapy, gait aids and fall prevention. Corticosteroids or IVIG have been used to relieve pain and are sometimes given early in severe cases, but trial evidence that they change motor outcome is limited. Optimise glucose control without very rapid tightening.
det.prognosis: Most patients improve over 1–3 years and regain walking, though residual weakness and pain are common; recurrence is uncommon.
pearls: Thigh pain then quadriceps weakness plus weight loss in a diabetic: radiculoplexus neuropathy, not 'just' disc disease.
Paraspinal denervation on EMG shows root involvement — the lesion is not confined to the plexus.
It can occur in well-controlled or newly diagnosed diabetes.

det.patho: Vasculitis is immune-mediated inflammation that damages blood vessel walls, causing narrowing, occlusion, aneurysm or rupture and ischaemia of the tissues supplied. Mechanisms include immune complex deposition, ANCA-driven neutrophil activation, T-cell granulomatous inflammation and direct infection of the vessel wall. The Chapel Hill nomenclature groups disorders by the size of vessel affected; nerves are vulnerable because vasa nervorum are small arteries in the epineurium.
det.clinical: Peripheral nerve involvement, usually mononeuritis multiplex or an asymmetric polyneuropathy, is the commonest neurological feature of systemic vasculitis. Central involvement causes multifocal strokes, encephalopathy, seizures or headache and occurs in primary angiitis of the CNS or as part of systemic disease. Large-vessel disease causes visual loss and TIAs (giant cell arteritis) or limb claudication and absent pulses (Takayasu). Non-systemic vasculitic neuropathy is confined to nerve.
det.diagnosis: Combine clinical pattern with serology and tissue confirmation whenever possible. Nerve plus muscle biopsy gives the best yield for peripheral disease. For CNS vasculitis, MRI usually shows multiple infarcts of different ages, CSF is often inflammatory and angiography can show beading, but angiographic appearances are not specific and biopsy may be needed. Always exclude infection, malignancy (especially lymphoma) and RCVS before immunosuppression.
det.treatment: Severe systemic or CNS vasculitis is induced with high-dose corticosteroids plus cyclophosphamide or rituximab, followed by maintenance with azathioprine, methotrexate, mycophenolate or rituximab; avacopan is an option to reduce steroid exposure in ANCA-associated disease. Giant cell arteritis is treated with prompt steroids and often tocilizumab. Infection-related vasculitis needs antimicrobial therapy (e.g. antivirals for VZV, antivirals and plasma exchange for HBV-PAN). Prophylaxis against Pneumocystis and bone protection are standard.
det.prognosis: Most forms respond to treatment, but nerve recovery is slow and incomplete; relapses are common in ANCA-associated disease.
pearls: Painful asymmetric neuropathy evolving in steps = think vasculitis and biopsy early.
Exclude infection and RCVS before giving strong immunosuppression for 'CNS vasculitis'.
Angiographic beading is not proof of vasculitis.

det.patho: In connective tissue diseases, immune complexes, complement activation and autoantibodies inflame small and medium arteries, including the vasa nervorum, leading to ischaemic nerve infarcts. Rheumatoid vasculitis develops mainly in long-standing, seropositive, nodular disease and has become less common with modern disease control. In SLE, true vasculitis is less frequent than thrombosis from antiphospholipid antibodies, and in Sjögren syndrome vasculitis often links with cryoglobulins.
det.clinical: The usual neurological form is mononeuritis multiplex or an asymmetric sensorimotor neuropathy with pain, sometimes becoming confluent and resembling a symmetric neuropathy. Skin vasculitis, ulcers, digital gangrene and scleritis are frequent companions. CNS vasculitis is uncommon; strokes in SLE more often reflect antiphospholipid syndrome, emboli from Libman-Sacks endocarditis or accelerated atherosclerosis. Systemic sclerosis more often causes trigeminal neuropathy and myopathy than vasculitic neuropathy.
det.diagnosis: Electrodiagnosis documents the multifocal axonal pattern; combined nerve and muscle biopsy provides definite evidence and excludes amyloid or other infiltration. Serology confirms the underlying CTD and activity (complement, dsDNA, cryoglobulins). Exclude drug toxicity (for example leflunomide, anti-TNF), compression neuropathies and diabetic mononeuropathies. In CNS presentations, check antiphospholipid antibodies and echocardiography.
det.treatment: Initiate high-dose glucocorticoids (often IV methylprednisolone pulses followed by oral prednisolone) with cyclophosphamide or rituximab for nerve or organ-threatening disease, then maintain with azathioprine, methotrexate or mycophenolate. Plasma exchange may be added for severe cryoglobulinaemic disease. Treat neuropathic pain, protect bones, provide infection prophylaxis, and add anticoagulation where antiphospholipid thrombosis is the mechanism.
det.prognosis: Early treatment halts new nerve infarcts, but recovery of established deficits is slow and partial; rheumatoid vasculitis carries notable mortality from systemic involvement.
pearls: New foot drop in long-standing seropositive RA: consider rheumatoid vasculitis, not just compression.
In lupus with stroke, think antiphospholipid thrombosis before vasculitis.
Biopsy a nerve with a muscle — the combination raises the diagnostic yield.
det.thd: Vasculitis ที่สัมพันธ์กับโรค connective tissue เช่น RA, SLE, Sjögren เกิดจาก immune complex ทำให้หลอดเลือดเล็กและกลางอักเสบ เส้นประสาทขาดเลือดเป็นจุด ๆ จึงเกิด mononeuritis multiplex ร่วมกับแผลผิวหนังหรือนิ้วขาดเลือด ยืนยันด้วย NCS และชิ้นเนื้อเส้นประสาทร่วมกล้ามเนื้อ รักษาด้วย steroid ขนาดสูงร่วมกับ rituximab หรือ cyclophosphamide ยิ่งรักษาเร็วยิ่งลดการเสียเส้นประสาทถาวร

name: Versive seizures
formal: Seizures with forced head and eye turning to one side, from frontal eye field or other frontal onset.
simple: Seizures in which the head and eyes turn forcibly to one side.
ab: Forced head and eye deviation seizure
th: การชักที่ศีรษะและตาถูกดึงหันไปด้านเดียวอย่างแรงและค้าง มักมาจากสมองส่วนหน้าฝั่งตรงข้าม และเป็นสัญญาณช่วยบอกข้างของจุดกำเนิดชัก
tempoNote: Seconds to a minute or two per event; frequently the last focal sign before a bilateral tonic-clonic seizure
feat: Forced, sustained conjugate turning of eyes and head to one side, the chin pulled far round
A forced turn, especially the one seen just ahead of generalisation, points to the hemisphere opposite the turn
Arises from frontal eye field or supplementary motor area, or from temporal, parietal or occipital cortex after spread
Often accompanied by tonic arm posturing or a fencing posture, and may be followed by a bilateral convulsion
Gentle, early head turning is a poor guide and may go to the same side as the focus
inv: Video-EEG to capture the sequence and the direction of the first and the last turn
MRI epilepsy protocol for a structural cause (scar, tumour, malformation of cortical development)

case.story: Three years after a motorbike head injury he has attacks of about one minute: his head and eyes swing hard to the right, the right arm stiffens, then he falls and convulses. His wife says he cannot resist the turn.
case.exam: Neurological examination is normal between attacks.
case.tests: Video-EEG shows left frontal onset and a forced rightward head turn about ten seconds before generalisation; MRI shows left frontal gliosis.
case.q: What does the direction of the forced turn tell you, and what should happen if two drugs fail?
case.a: A forced late turn to the right localises the focus to the left hemisphere; drug-resistant cases should go for presurgical evaluation.

read.where: 8 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System

det.patho: Cortical discharge in the frontal eye field or neighbouring premotor cortex drives the eyes and neck to the side away from the active hemisphere. Seizures starting in temporal, parietal or occipital cortex can produce the same turn once they spread forward. For this reason versive movement is often seen near the transition to bilateral involvement.
det.clinical: A true versive event is forceful, maintained and involuntary, with eyes deviated as far as they will go. It tends to last from several seconds to a minute and may be followed by tonic posturing and then a bilateral tonic-clonic seizure. Awareness is often preserved at the start and lost as the seizure spreads. Many people have no aura and a normal examination, so a witness account is the key piece of history. Children's books describe the same phenomenon under the term adversive seizure.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis rests on a clear description or, better, video recording of the event, backed by EEG. Long-term video-EEG lets observers decide whether the turn was forced and which direction it took first and last. MRI looks for a causative lesion. In epilepsy surgery programmes the late forced turn is treated as a reliable contralateral lateralising sign, whereas an early non-forced turn is given little weight.
det.treatment: Treat as focal epilepsy with a sodium-channel blocker or levetiracetam, choosing the drug to suit age, sex and comorbidity. A structural lesion is treated on its own merits. If seizures continue after two appropriate drugs, refer for presurgical assessment, since resection can cure a good proportion of lesional frontal epilepsy. Patients should receive advice on driving, heights and bathing.
det.prognosis: Outcome follows the cause: seizure freedom is common in post-traumatic or non-lesional cases on drugs, while frontal lesions with nocturnal clusters are often drug-resistant.
pearls: A forced turn just before the convulsion points away from the side of the turn, that is to the opposite hemisphere.
Do not use early, gentle head turning to lateralise.
Frontal seizures can be brief, bizarre and nocturnal; consider functional seizures only after video-EEG.
