name: Vertical gaze palsy
formal: Loss of voluntary upward and/or downward gaze from midbrain lesions, as in Parinaud syndrome or PSP.
simple: Inability to look up or down because of damage in the upper brainstem.
th: การกลอกตาขึ้นและ/หรือลงทำไม่ได้จากรอยโรคที่ midbrain เช่น Parinaud syndrome หรือ PSP
tempoNote: Acute in stroke or hydrocephalus, subacute in tumour, chronic in degenerative disease
feat: Upgaze palsy (dorsal midbrain/Parinaud): light-near dissociation, convergence-retraction nystagmus, lid retraction (Collier sign)
Downgaze palsy: bilateral riMLF lesions, typical in PSP and thalamo-mesencephalic infarcts
Combined up and down palsy from larger midbrain lesions
Bell's phenomenon preserved in supranuclear forms
Causes: pineal tumours, hydrocephalus/shunt failure, midbrain stroke, MS, Wernicke, PSP, NPC, Whipple
inv: MRI brain (pineal region, aqueduct, midbrain, thalami)
Doll's head test to confirm supranuclear nature
Shunt assessment in shunted patients; tumour markers (AFP, beta-hCG) for pineal germ cell tumours

case.story: Two months of headache, vomiting in the morning and difficulty looking up at the classroom board.
case.exam: Upgaze palsy, light-near dissociated pupils, convergence-retraction nystagmus on attempted upgaze, bilateral papilloedema.
case.tests: MRI: pineal mass compressing the tectum with obstructive hydrocephalus; serum beta-hCG raised.
case.q: What syndrome and what likely tumour type?
case.a: Parinaud (dorsal midbrain) syndrome from a pineal germ cell tumour (germinoma), with hydrocephalus.

read.where: Chapter 22 Neuro-Ophthalmology — Central Disorders of Eye Movements

det.patho: Vertical gaze is generated in the rostral midbrain: the riMLF generates vertical saccades, the interstitial nucleus of Cajal holds gaze, and the posterior commissure carries upgaze signals. Lesions of the posterior commissure produce upgaze palsy; bilateral riMLF lesions produce downgaze or combined palsy.
det.clinical: Upgaze palsy is the commonest form and typically arises from pineal tumours, hydrocephalus or dorsal midbrain stroke. Downgaze palsy is more specific for PSP or bilateral thalamomesencephalic infarction (artery of Percheron). Patients complain of difficulty reading or walking downstairs (downgaze) or looking up. Mild upgaze limitation is normal in older people.
det.diagnosis: Determine direction, whether reflexes overcome the deficit, associated pupillary and lid signs, and tempo. MRI is the key investigation. Exclude restrictive (thyroid, orbital) and myopathic or neuromuscular causes.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: CSF diversion for hydrocephalus, tumour-specific therapy, stroke management, thiamine for Wernicke. Prisms and reading aids help symptomatically.
det.prognosis: Variable; hydrocephalus-related palsy often recovers after CSF diversion, degenerative causes progress.
pearls: Upgaze palsy plus light-near dissociation: dorsal midbrain.
Downgaze palsy in an older patient with falls: PSP.
Shunted child with new upgaze palsy: shunt failure until proven otherwise.
det.thd: Vertical gaze palsy คือการกลอกตาขึ้นหรือลงไม่ได้จากรอยโรคที่ midbrain มองขึ้นไม่ได้มักเป็น Parinaud syndrome จากเนื้องอก pineal หรือ hydrocephalus มีรูม่านตาตอบสนองต่อแสงน้อยกว่ามองใกล้และ convergence-retraction nystagmus มองลงไม่ได้พบใน PSP และ stroke บริเวณ thalamus-midbrain ตรวจ MRI และรักษาตามสาเหตุ เช่น ระบายน้ำไขสันหลังหรือรักษาเนื้องอก

name: Vestibular migraine
formal: Episodic vertigo with or without headache, migraine features and photophobia, without other cause.
simple: Dizziness attacks linked to migraine.
ab: ไมเกรนเวียนหัว
th: ไมเกรนที่แสดงอาการเป็นเวียนศีรษะซ้ำ ๆ นานตั้งแต่ไม่กี่นาทีถึง 3 วัน อาจมีหรือไม่มีปวดศีรษะร่วม เป็นสาเหตุเวียนศีรษะซ้ำที่พบบ่อยที่สุดอย่างหนึ่งในวัยทำงาน
tempoNote: Episodes last 5 minutes to 72 hours and recur over years; patterns often change around menopause
feat: Recurrent spontaneous, positional or visually induced vertigo or head-motion dizziness of moderate–severe intensity
Migraine features in at least half of episodes: headache, photophobia/phonophobia, or visual aura
Past or current migraine history, motion sickness from childhood, and family history common
Mild bilateral tinnitus or aural pressure possible, but no progressive hearing loss
Examination normal between attacks; central positional or spontaneous nystagmus may be seen during them
inv: Mainly clinical; audiogram to exclude Ménière's when ear symptoms occur
Video head impulse and calorics usually normal or mildly abnormal

Headache/vertigo diary to identify triggers and response to prevention

case.who: 35-year-old female bank officer from Chiang Mai
case.story: For two years she has had episodes of spinning or rocking lasting 2–8 hours, about twice a month, often around her period or after poor sleep; light bothers her during attacks, and she has had migraines since her teens.
case.exam: Normal neurological and neuro-otological examination between attacks, including head impulse and Dix–Hallpike.
case.tests: Audiogram normal; MRI brain normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what is your treatment plan?
case.a: Vestibular migraine; address sleep and triggers, use a vestibular sedative or triptan for attacks, and start migraine prophylaxis (e.g. propranolol, flunarizine, amitriptyline or venlafaxine).

read.where: Chapter 20 Migraine and other episodic vestibular disorders

det.patho: The mechanism likely mirrors migraine itself: altered processing in brainstem and thalamocortical vestibular networks, with trigeminovascular activation and neuropeptides such as CGRP sensitising vestibular nuclei. Vestibular and nociceptive pathways share relay nuclei, explaining motion sensitivity. It affects around 1% of the population, with a strong female predominance.
det.clinical: Attacks vary widely: spontaneous spinning, positional vertigo, head-motion intolerance or visually induced dizziness, lasting minutes to days. Headache may be absent in many attacks or come before, during or after the vertigo. Motion sickness, visual vertigo and anxiety are common companions, and some develop persistent dizziness (PPPD) between attacks. In children it may present as benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood.
det.diagnosis: Bárány/ICHD-3 criteria require at least five vestibular episodes of 5 minutes to 72 hours, a history of migraine, and migraine features in at least half of the episodes, with no better alternative explanation; 'probable' VM applies when only one of the last two criteria is met. Exclude Ménière's with audiometry, BPPV with positional testing and posterior circulation ischaemia when risk factors or new neurological signs exist.
det.treatment: Lifestyle measures (regular sleep and meals, hydration, trigger management) and vestibular rehabilitation help many. Acute attacks may respond to triptans, antiemetics or short-acting vestibular sedatives. Prophylaxis uses standard migraine drugs — beta-blockers, flunarizine, amitriptyline, venlafaxine, topiramate — and CGRP-pathway antibodies are an emerging option. Treat comorbid anxiety.
det.prognosis: Symptoms usually improve with prophylaxis and lifestyle change, though the condition tends to persist for years with fluctuations.
pearls: Vertigo spells + migraine history + no hearing loss = vestibular migraine until proved otherwise.
Headache does not have to occur with every attack.
A new 'vestibular migraine' in an older vascular patient needs evaluation for TIA.
det.thd: Vestibular migraine คือไมเกรนที่แสดงออกเป็นเวียนศีรษะซ้ำ ๆ นาน 5 นาทีถึง 3 วัน อาจปวดศีรษะหรือไม่ก็ได้ มักมีแพ้แสงแพ้เสียง ประวัติไมเกรนและเมารถตั้งแต่เด็ก การตรวจระหว่างอาการมักปกติและการได้ยินปกติ ต้องแยก Ménière’s BPPV และ TIA รักษาโดยปรับพฤติกรรม นอนให้พอ หลีกเลี่ยงสิ่งกระตุ้น ใช้ยาป้องกันไมเกรน เช่น propranolol flunarizine amitriptyline และฝึกกายภาพการทรงตัว

name: Vestibular neuritis
formal: Acute vestibular syndrome from inflammation of the vestibular nerve, with prolonged vertigo, nystagmus and unsteadiness without hearing loss.
simple: Sudden severe spinning dizziness caused by inflammation of the balance nerve in the ear.
th: เส้นประสาทการทรงตัวอักเสบ — เวียนหัวบ้านหมุนต่อเนื่องหลายวัน คลื่นไส้ ได้ยินปกติ
tempoNote: Continuous vertigo over days
feat: Acute continuous vertigo, nausea, unsteadiness; hearing preserved
Unidirectional horizontal-torsional nystagmus beating away from the lesion
Positive head impulse test toward the affected side
inv: HINTS examination (head impulse, nystagmus, test of skew)

case.exam: Left-beating horizontal nystagmus increasing on left gaze, corrective saccade on right head impulse, no skew, can walk with help.
case.tests: Hearing normal.
case.q: Which side is affected and why is this reassuring?

ddx.pt: Normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus or skew (HINTS central)
Brief positional episodes only
Hearing loss and recurrent attacks

aN: vestibular neuronitis | acute vestibular syndrome | labyrinthitis

det.patho: Vestibular neuritis (acute unilateral vestibulopathy) is believed to be an inflammatory, probably viral, neuropathy of the vestibular nerve; reactivation of latent herpes simplex virus type 1 in the vestibular (Scarpa) ganglion is the favoured explanation, though direct proof is lacking. The superior division, which serves the horizontal and anterior canals and the utricle, is affected far more often than the inferior division, possibly because its bony channel is longer and tighter. Abrupt loss of resting input from one labyrinth unbalances the two vestibular nuclei, producing spontaneous nystagmus, vertigo and postural imbalance until the brain recalibrates through central compensation. It is among the commonest causes of acute peripheral vertigo, usually in adults aged 30–60; when hearing is also lost the term labyrinthitis is used.
det.clinical: Severe rotatory vertigo builds over minutes to hours and persists for days, with nausea, vomiting and unsteadiness; patients prefer to lie still with the affected ear up, and any head movement makes it worse. Spontaneous horizontal-torsional nystagmus beats toward the healthy side, increases when looking in that direction, and is dampened by visual fixation; the patient leans or falls toward the affected side but can usually stand. A viral upper respiratory illness sometimes precedes it, hearing is preserved and there are no other neurological symptoms. The rarer inferior-division form spares the horizontal canal, so the bedside head impulse may look normal and the picture can be confused with a central lesion. Symptoms settle over days to weeks, though dizziness with quick head turns can linger, and some patients go on to persistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD) or secondary BPPV.
det.diagnosis: This is a diagnosis of the acute vestibular syndrome made at the bedside. The HINTS examination in a patient with ongoing vertigo and nystagmus favours a peripheral cause when the head impulse is abnormal toward the affected side, nystagmus is unidirectional (beating away, increased with gaze in that direction and suppressed by fixation) and there is no skew deviation. Any central sign — a normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, skew, severe truncal ataxia (unable to stand unaided) or new hearing loss — requires MRI with DWI, remembering that DWI in the first 48 hours can miss small posterior circulation strokes and should be repeated if suspicion persists. HINTS-plus adds a bedside hearing check, because sudden one-sided hearing loss with vertigo may signal AICA territory ischaemia. Video head impulse testing (reduced gain, typically below about 0.7, with corrective saccades) and caloric testing (canal paresis above about 25%) confirm the deficit, and vestibular evoked myogenic potentials help show which nerve division is involved.
det.treatment: Antiemetics and vestibular suppressants (such as dimenhydrinate, ondansetron or a brief benzodiazepine) are for the first three days at most, because sedation slows compensation. Corticosteroids begun within about 72 hours of onset, given as a tapering course over roughly 2–3 weeks, improve recovery of measured vestibular function, although the long-term gain in symptoms is less certain; antivirals add nothing. Early mobilisation and a structured vestibular rehabilitation programme of gaze-stabilisation, balance and habituation exercises are the cornerstone and should start within days. At follow-up, check for secondary BPPV and for PPPD, which is managed with rehabilitation, explanation and sometimes an SSRI.
det.prognosis: Most patients return to normal activity within weeks; caloric or head-impulse function recovers fully in about half, but central compensation makes any residual deficit unnoticeable except during rapid head movements. Recurrence is rare, while a minority later develop BPPV in the same ear or PPPD.
pearls: HINTS is only valid in a patient with continuous vertigo and spontaneous nystagmus at the time of examination.
A normal head impulse in acute vertigo is a dangerous finding — it suggests stroke.
Get patients moving early; bed rest and prolonged vestibular sedatives slow recovery.
Always test hearing: new one-sided deafness with acute vertigo can be an AICA stroke, not labyrinthitis.
det.thd: Vestibular neuritis คือการอักเสบของเส้นประสาทการทรงตัว (มักเป็น superior division) น่าจะเกิดจากไวรัสเริมที่แฝงอยู่ใน vestibular ganglion ทำให้บ้านหมุนรุนแรงต่อเนื่องหลายวัน คลื่นไส้อาเจียน เดินเซไปด้านที่เป็น แต่การได้ยินปกติ และเห็น nystagmus ทิศทางเดียวตีไปด้านปกติ การตรวจ HINTS ที่บ่งว่าเป็นส่วนปลาย คือ head impulse ผิดปกติ nystagmus ทิศทางเดียว และไม่มี skew ถ้ามีลักษณะของ central หรือการได้ยินลดลงเฉียบพลันต้องทำ MRI เพื่อหาสโตรก (DWI ช่วงแรกอาจปกติ) ยืนยันได้ด้วย video head impulse test หรือ caloric test รักษาด้วยยาแก้เวียนและแก้อาเจียนไม่เกิน 3 วัน ให้ steroid ภายใน 72 ชั่วโมงแรกเพื่อช่วยการฟื้นตัวของเส้นประสาท และสำคัญที่สุดคือรีบลุกเดินและทำกายภาพฟื้นฟูการทรงตัว

name: Vestibular schwannoma
formal: Benign tumour of the vestibulocochlear nerve sheath, causing unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus and imbalance; bilateral in NF2.
simple: A non-cancerous growth on the hearing and balance nerve causing hearing loss and unsteadiness.
th: เนื้องอกไม่ร้ายจากเยื่อหุ้มเส้นประสาท vestibular ทำให้หูดับข้างเดียว เสียงในหู และเสียการทรงตัว ถ้าเป็นสองข้างพบใน NF2
tempoNote: Slow growth, on average 1–2 mm per year; sudden hearing loss can occur
feat: Progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss with poor speech discrimination
Unilateral tinnitus; mild imbalance rather than vertigo
Sudden sensorineural hearing loss can be the first presentation
Larger tumours: facial numbness, absent corneal reflex, ataxia, hydrocephalus
Facial palsy is uncommon before surgery
inv: Gadolinium MRI of internal auditory canals (or high-resolution T2 screening)
Pure tone and speech audiometry; ABR as a secondary test
NF2 genetic testing if bilateral or young with other tumours

case.story: Noticed she cannot hear the phone with her left ear and has constant left-sided ringing for a year.
case.exam: Weber lateralises right, Rinne positive both sides, mild left gait drift, cranial nerves otherwise normal.
case.tests: Audiogram shows left high-frequency sensorineural loss with poor word recognition; MRI shows a 1.2 cm enhancing left intracanalicular mass.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what are the management choices?
case.a: Left vestibular schwannoma; options include MRI surveillance, stereotactic radiosurgery or microsurgery.

det.patho: These tumours usually arise from the vestibular divisions of the eighth nerve near the porus of the internal auditory canal. Sporadic tumours result from somatic biallelic NF2 inactivation; bilateral tumours define NF2-related schwannomatosis. Hearing loss reflects cochlear nerve compression and also biochemical effects on the cochlea.
det.clinical: Typical patients are middle-aged with gradual one-sided hearing loss and tinnitus. Vestibular compensation means vertigo is uncommon, but imbalance is frequent. Larger tumours reach the brainstem and trigeminal nerve and can cause hydrocephalus. In NF2 tumours appear in young adults and hearing preservation is a major concern.
det.diagnosis: Contrast MRI is the gold standard and detects small intracanalicular lesions. Audiometry characterises hearing class for treatment planning. Asymmetry of more than about 15 dB at two frequencies or unexplained unilateral tinnitus should prompt imaging. Bilateral tumours or associated meningiomas require genetic assessment.
det.treatment: Small, slow tumours are often observed with repeat MRI. Stereotactic radiosurgery controls most small to medium tumours with low facial nerve risk. Microsurgery is preferred for large tumours with brainstem compression. In NF2, bevacizumab and hearing rehabilitation such as auditory brainstem implants are used.
det.prognosis: Benign with excellent survival; long-term issues are hearing loss, tinnitus, imbalance and facial nerve function.
pearls: Unilateral tinnitus or asymmetric hearing loss warrants MRI.
Early facial palsy is unusual and suggests another diagnosis.
Corneal reflex loss signals a larger tumour.
det.thd: Vestibular schwannoma หรือ acoustic neuroma เป็นเนื้องอกไม่ร้ายของเส้นประสาท vestibular อาการเด่นคือหูดับข้างเดียวช้าๆ เสียงในหู และเซเล็กน้อย ก้อนใหญ่จะกดเส้นประสาท V และก้านสมอง วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI internal auditory canal การรักษาเลือกได้ทั้งเฝ้าติดตาม radiosurgery และผ่าตัด ถ้าพบสองข้างให้นึกถึง NF2

qx.stem: A 49-year-old man in Phitsanulok has had four years of left hearing loss and tinnitus, and now mild imbalance. Thin-section post-contrast MRI shows an avidly enhancing mass centred in the left internal auditory canal that widens the porus and extends into the cerebellopontine angle, forming an acute angle with the petrous bone. The canal is flared; the dural tail is absent.
qx.q: Which description best fits the imaging pattern and its significance?
opts: Ice-cream-cone configuration; typical of vestibular schwannoma, and bilateral lesions would suggest NF2
Obtuse bone angle with dural tail; typical of meningioma
Fluid-signal cyst with restricted diffusion; epidermoid
Fusiform basilar ectasia; vascular loop
Ring-enhancing lesion; metastasis
qx.why: A mass arising in the internal auditory canal with an expanded canal and a cerebellopontine-angle component forms the classic ice cream cone of vestibular schwannoma. Bilateral tumours should prompt evaluation for neurofibromatosis type 2. Meningiomas meet the petrous bone at an obtuse angle with a dural tail and rarely widen the canal.

qx.stem: A 55-year-old male school director from Phetchabun has two years of progressive left hearing loss and tinnitus with mild unsteadiness. MRI shows a 2.2 cm enhancing cerebellopontine angle mass on the left that extends into and widens the internal auditory canal, forming an acute angle with the petrous bone, with small intratumoral cysts and no dural tail.
qx.q: Which feature most reliably distinguishes this lesion from a cerebellopontine angle meningioma?
opts: Homogeneous contrast enhancement
Location in the cerebellopontine angle
T2 hyperintensity relative to brain
Adjacent oedema in the middle cerebellar peduncle
Extension into and widening of the internal auditory canal with an acute angle to the petrous ridge
qx.why: Vestibular schwannomas grow from within the internal auditory canal, so they widen the porus and form an 'ice cream on a cone' with an acute angle to the bone; cystic change is common. Meningiomas are broad-based on the petrous dura with an obtuse angle, a dural tail and sometimes hyperostosis or calcification, and rarely expand the canal. Enhancement, CPA location and T2 signal are shared by both.

case.who: 63-year-old man from Ayutthaya with hypertension and diabetes
case.story: Sudden right-sided deafness and severe vertigo with vomiting this morning; cannot walk.
case.exam: Right deafness, direction-fixed left-beating nystagmus, right head impulse normal, right limb ataxia.

det.patho: The eighth nerve carries cochlear and vestibular fibres through the internal auditory canal to the brainstem. It can be damaged by compression (schwannoma, meningioma, vascular loops), inflammation or infection (viral neuritis, zoster, bacterial or carcinomatous meningitis, sarcoid), ischaemia in AICA territory, trauma, and iron deposition in superficial siderosis. Retrocochlear lesions impair neural synchrony, explaining poor speech understanding.
det.clinical: Presentations combine hearing loss, tinnitus and vestibular symptoms in varying proportions. Acute cases include vestibular neuritis, sudden hearing loss and stroke; chronic progressive loss suggests a tumour. Look for neighbouring cranial nerve signs, cerebellar signs and meningeal features. Bilateral disease narrows the differential considerably.
det.diagnosis: Audiological tests separate cochlear from retrocochlear loss; ABR shows prolonged latencies in nerve lesions. Vestibular testing assesses the superior and inferior divisions. MRI with contrast is mandatory for unexplained retrocochlear findings. CSF studies are needed when meningitis or infiltration is suspected.
det.treatment: Treatment follows the cause: tumour management, antivirals and steroids for zoster, steroids for idiopathic sudden hearing loss, stroke care for AICA infarction, and vestibular rehabilitation for residual imbalance. Hearing aids, CROS devices or cochlear implants restore some hearing where the nerve is intact. Microvascular decompression is reserved for selected vestibular paroxysmia cases resistant to carbamazepine.
det.prognosis: Highly variable: viral neuritis usually compensates, whereas nerve-destroying lesions leave permanent deafness.

det.patho: Enteroviruses enter through the gut or throat, replicate in lymphoid tissue and, in a minority, reach the CNS by viraemia or retrograde axonal transport. They selectively destroy anterior horn cells and the motor nuclei of the brainstem. Wild poliovirus persists only in a few countries; vaccine-derived poliovirus outbreaks and non-polio enteroviruses (EV-A71 in Asia, EV-D68 worldwide) now cause most such paralysis.
det.clinical: Most infections are silent or cause a minor febrile illness. Paralytic disease begins with fever and myalgia, then rapid flaccid weakness, often asymmetric and proximal, without sensory loss. Bulbar involvement endangers swallowing and breathing. EV-A71 outbreaks in Southeast Asia have produced brainstem encephalitis with cardiopulmonary collapse in young children.
det.diagnosis: Any child under 15 with acute flaccid paralysis must be reported and have stool tested for poliovirus as part of WHO surveillance. Enterovirus testing should include respiratory and stool specimens because CSF yield is low. MRI showing anterior horn grey matter signal supports the diagnosis, and electrodiagnosis confirms a motor neuronopathy.
det.treatment: There is no proven antiviral. Management is supportive: ventilatory monitoring, swallowing protection, pain control and early rehabilitation. IVIG is sometimes used in severe EV-A71 disease, with limited evidence. Prevention relies on polio vaccination (OPV/IPV) and, in some Asian countries, EV-A71 vaccines.
det.prognosis: Partial recovery occurs over months, but many keep focal weakness and atrophy; post-polio syndrome can appear decades later.
pearls: Asymmetric flaccid weakness + fever + normal sensation = anterior horn until proved otherwise.
Stool, not CSF, is the best specimen for enterovirus detection.
Every acute flaccid paralysis in a child is a notifiable event for polio surveillance.
det.thd: ไวรัสกลุ่มนี้ได้แก่ poliovirus และ enterovirus 71, D68 เข้าทางปากและลำไส้ แล้วทำลายเซลล์ประสาทสั่งการที่ anterior horn ของไขสันหลัง เด็กมีไข้ก่อนแล้วแขนหรือขาอ่อนแรงปวกเปียกไม่สมมาตร รีเฟล็กซ์หาย แต่ความรู้สึกปกติ ต้องเก็บอุจจาระส่งตรวจและรายงานเป็นกรณี AFP ไม่มียาต้านไวรัสเฉพาะ การป้องกันด้วยวัคซีนสำคัญที่สุด

name: Viral and post-infectious myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus following viral infection or post-infectious inflammation, such as opsoclonus-myoclonus.
simple: Muscle jerks that develop after a viral illness.

tempoNote: Days to weeks after or during an infection; usually monophasic
feat: Sudden shock-like jerks of limbs or trunk, often action-induced
Frequently with ataxia, tremor or chaotic eye movements (opsoclonus)
Preceding fever, respiratory or gastrointestinal illness
Reported after enterovirus, EBV, mycoplasma, dengue, influenza and SARS-CoV-2
Children and adults; usually improves over weeks to months

case.story: Ten days after a febrile flu-like illness she developed jerking of her arms when reaching, unsteady walking and shimmering vision.
case.exam: Multidirectional chaotic saccades, action myoclonus of arms and trunk, wide-based gait.
case.tests: MRI normal; CSF 12 lymphocytes, protein 0.5 g/L; antibody panel and CT chest-abdomen-pelvis negative.
case.q: What syndrome is this, and what treatment is commonly used?
case.a: Post-infectious opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia; treat with corticosteroids or IVIG with symptomatic clonazepam.

det.patho: Two mechanisms are recognised. Some viruses directly infect the brainstem, cerebellum or cortex (encephalitic myoclonus). More often the illness triggers an immune response against brainstem and cerebellar circuits, producing a post-infectious syndrome after a short latent period. Specific antibodies are rarely found, and the target is uncertain.
det.clinical: Presentations include generalised or multifocal action myoclonus, myoclonus-ataxia with opsoclonus, and myoclonus within an encephalitis. The post-infectious form typically follows a minor illness by one to three weeks and is monophasic. Encephalitic forms come with fever, reduced consciousness or seizures. In children, opsoclonus-myoclonus calls for a careful search for neuroblastoma before labelling it post-infectious.
det.diagnosis: Establish the myoclonus type clinically and with neurophysiology, then look for the cause: MRI, CSF analysis with viral PCR and serology, autoimmune and paraneoplastic antibodies, and tumour screening. Exclude drug-induced, metabolic (renal, hepatic) and hypoxic myoclonus. The diagnosis of a post-infectious mechanism is one of exclusion supported by timing.
det.treatment: Symptomatic drugs such as clonazepam, levetiracetam or valproate reduce jerks. Immunotherapy with corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange is commonly used for post-infectious opsoclonus-myoclonus and appears to speed recovery, though trial evidence is limited. Treat the infection when a specific antiviral or antibiotic exists.
det.prognosis: Adults with post-infectious myoclonus-ataxia usually recover well over weeks to months; paediatric opsoclonus-myoclonus may leave cognitive and behavioural sequelae.
pearls: Opsoclonus in a toddler: look hard for neuroblastoma.
A short gap after a mild infection favours an immune mechanism over direct infection.
Always check renal and liver function and drug list before blaming the virus.

det.patho: Viruses invade the brain via blood or nerves, infecting neurons and glia and causing inflammation and necrosis. Some infections trigger brain dysfunction without direct invasion via cytokines or immune responses. Post-infectious autoimmunity, including anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis after HSV, can follow.
det.clinical: Presentation includes fever, headache, encephalopathy, seizures and focal deficits. Specific patterns: HSV with temporal lobe features, JE with parkinsonism and thalamic involvement, rabies with hydrophobia, dengue with encephalopathy and haemorrhage. Children with influenza may develop acute necrotising encephalopathy.
det.diagnosis: CSF analysis, PCR and serology identify the pathogen. MRI patterns support the diagnosis. Exclude bacterial meningitis, autoimmune encephalitis, metabolic causes and non-convulsive status.
det.treatment: Start IV aciclovir empirically in suspected encephalitis until HSV is excluded. Supportive care includes seizure control, management of raised ICP and fluid balance. Specific antivirals exist for HSV, VZV and CMV; immunotherapy for post-infectious and autoimmune conditions. Prevention through vaccination (JE, measles, rabies).
det.prognosis: Variable; HSV and JE carry significant mortality and long-term sequelae.
pearls: Start aciclovir early in any suspected encephalitis.
Thalamic lesions in a febrile child from rural Thailand suggest Japanese encephalitis.
Relapse after HSV encephalitis may be autoimmune (NMDA receptor), not viral.

det.patho: Enteroviruses are spread by the faecal-oral and respiratory routes, replicate in the gut and lymphoid tissue, and reach the meninges through viraemia. The choroid plexus and meningeal vessels are the likely entry points. Local release of cytokines causes the headache and CSF lymphocytosis without much parenchymal injury. Other viruses reach the meninges by reactivation from sensory ganglia (HSV-2, VZV) or by arthropod bite (arboviruses).
det.clinical: Symptoms start abruptly with fever and a severe, often frontal headache; photophobia, nausea and a stiff neck follow, while consciousness remains clear. The illness is milder in adults than in infants and is self-limited in a week or so, although fatigue and headache can linger. Young infants may have only fever and irritability, and parechovirus in neonates can cause sepsis-like illness with a normal CSF count. A relapsing pattern suggests HSV-2.
det.diagnosis: The aim is to prove a viral cause and exclude treatable mimics. CSF PCR for enterovirus is the best test; HSV and VZV PCR should be sent in women with recurrent episodes, genital lesions or severe disease. Multiplex meningitis/encephalitis panels speed diagnosis but occasionally give false positives, so results are read with the clinical picture. A low CSF glucose, very high protein, long prodrome, or immunosuppression should widen the work-up to tuberculosis, cryptococcus and syphilis.
det.treatment: Treatment is supportive: analgesia, antipyretics, antiemetics and fluids. Antibiotics can be stopped once bacterial cultures are negative and a viral cause is confirmed or the picture is typical and the patient improves. Aciclovir is considered for HSV-2 meningitis with severe symptoms or neurological features; the benefit of suppressive valaciclovir for recurrent episodes is unproven. No specific antiviral is licensed for enteroviruses, and pleconaril was not approved. Hand hygiene reduces spread, and vaccination prevents mumps and varicella-related meningitis.
det.prognosis: Excellent in children and adults; neonates and immunocompromised patients may have prolonged illness or sequelae.
pearls: A positive viral PCR in a well-looking patient with lymphocytic CSF allows early discharge and antibiotic stop.
Early in the illness the CSF can still be neutrophilic, so repeating the tap at 6 to 12 hours can show the switch to lymphocytes.
Always ask about NSAIDs, trimethoprim and IVIG when meningitis is sterile.

case.q: What is the diagnosis and treatment?

det.patho: Viruses injure the spinal cord by direct infection of neurons or glia (enteroviruses, flaviviruses, herpesviruses), by vasculopathy (VZV), or by triggering a post-infectious immune reaction. The pattern depends on the virus: anterior horn cells for enteroviruses and West Nile or Japanese encephalitis virus, white matter and roots for herpesviruses, chronic cord inflammation for HIV and HTLV-1.
det.clinical: Presentations range from an acute flaccid paralysis to a transverse myelitis with sensory level, to lumbosacral radiculitis with urinary retention (Elsberg syndrome, often HSV-2). CMV polyradiculomyelitis occurs with very low CD4 counts. VZV myelitis may follow shingles by days to weeks or occur without rash in immunosuppressed patients.
det.diagnosis: MRI first excludes compression and characterises the lesion. CSF PCR should be broad, and VZV antibody index adds sensitivity when PCR is negative. Check immune status and test serum for AQP4 and MOG antibodies because immune myelitis is more common than infective. Electrodiagnosis helps when anterior horn or root disease is suspected.
det.treatment: Aciclovir for HSV and VZV, ganciclovir or foscarnet for CMV, and antiretroviral therapy for HIV. Corticosteroids are sometimes added for VZV myelitis once antiviral cover is in place. Enteroviral and flaviviral myelitis have no specific antiviral and need supportive care. Early bladder management, thromboprophylaxis and rehabilitation matter for all.
det.prognosis: Variable; herpesvirus myelitis treated early can recover well, while anterior horn destruction often leaves permanent weakness.
pearls: Recent shingles + myelopathy = VZV myelitis; treat with IV aciclovir.
Urinary retention + sacral radicular pain in a young adult: think HSV-2 (Elsberg syndrome).
Low CD4 + cauda equina syndrome with neutrophilic CSF: CMV polyradiculitis.

det.patho: After primary chickenpox, VZV stays latent in cranial and dorsal root ganglia. On reactivation it can spread along trigeminal and other afferent fibres into the adventitia of cerebral arteries, producing transmural inflammation, intimal thickening, and loss of smooth muscle that leads to stenosis, occlusion, aneurysm or dissection. Immunosuppression and older age increase risk. Other viruses cause vasculitis mainly through immune complexes (HBV with PAN, HCV with cryoglobulins) or direct infection in HIV and CMV.
det.clinical: VZV vasculopathy presents with TIAs, ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke, headache, cognitive change or spinal cord infarction, usually weeks to months after zoster, though a third or more may have had no rash. Disease affects large proximal vessels in immunocompetent people and small distal vessels more in the immunocompromised. Childhood stroke after chickenpox is a recognised form with a unilateral focal arteriopathy. HIV-associated vasculopathy can cause fusiform aneurysms in children and young adults.
det.diagnosis: Look for recent zoster or varicella, then image the arteries; vessel-wall MRI shows concentric enhancement. CSF pleocytosis is common but not universal. The anti-VZV IgG antibody index in CSF is the most sensitive marker; VZV PCR is often negative by the time strokes occur. Screen for HIV and hepatitis, and exclude RCVS, atherosclerosis and primary angiitis.
det.treatment: VZV vasculopathy is treated with intravenous aciclovir (usually 10–15 mg/kg 8-hourly, adjusted for renal function, for about 14 days) plus a short oral steroid course to reduce inflammation, and standard antiplatelet secondary prevention. Immunosuppressed patients may need longer antivirals. Hepatitis B–related PAN is treated with antivirals with or without plasma exchange; HIV vasculopathy with antiretroviral therapy. Recombinant zoster vaccination reduces zoster and possibly subsequent stroke.
det.prognosis: Prompt antiviral therapy usually stops further events; deficits from completed infarcts often persist, and untreated disease can recur.
pearls: Stroke weeks after V1 zoster on the same side as the infarct: VZV vasculopathy.
Check the CSF anti-VZV IgG index — PCR alone misses most cases.
Absence of a rash does not exclude VZV vasculopathy.

det.patho: The neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses share lysosomal accumulation of autofluorescent lipopigments in neurons and retina and cause neurodegeneration. Fourteen genes are now recognised, and inheritance is autosomal recessive except for one adult form. When visual failure is the first symptom in a school-age child, CLN3 is the usual cause.
det.clinical: Vision declines between four and seven years, followed by seizures and dementia in the next several years, with myoclonus, ataxia, behavioural problems and later parkinsonism. Earlier forms differ: CLN1 begins before two years with regression and microcephaly, and CLN2 at two to four years with seizures and ataxia before sight is lost. Children are often seen by ophthalmology several times before the neurological disease declares itself.
det.diagnosis: Test ERG and fundi, examine a blood film, and send gene or enzyme studies appropriate to the age at onset (PPT1 and TPP1 enzymes in the young, CLN3 sequencing in juvenile cases). Diagnosis now relies on molecular genetics rather than the older eponyms and age bands. Electron microscopy of skin or conjunctiva can show characteristic inclusions.
det.treatment: Treatment of CLN3 is supportive: vision aids, seizure control, management of psychiatric features and parkinsonism, nutrition, physiotherapy and palliative care. Cerliponase alfa, given into the ventricles, slows motor decline in CLN2 and is the only NCL-specific therapy. Genetic counselling and family testing are essential.
det.prognosis: Progressive in all types, with survival varying from childhood in infantile forms to the third decade in CLN3.
pearls: Progressive visual failure plus seizures in a child: NCL until proven otherwise.
Order the gene by age at onset, because CLN2 is treatable.
Vacuolated lymphocytes point to CLN3.
det.thd: กลุ่ม NCL หรือ Batten disease เป็นโรคสะสมไลโซโซมที่พบหลายชนิดตามยีน CLN1 ถึง CLN14 ชนิดที่เริ่มด้วยตามัวในเด็กวัยเรียนคือ CLN3 ต่อมามีชัก myoclonus สมองเสื่อม และ parkinsonism ตรวจ ERG จอตา blood film และตรวจยีนตามอายุที่เริ่ม ยังไม่มียาจำเพาะสำหรับ CLN3 ให้การดูแลแบบประคับประคอง ส่วน CLN2 มี cerliponase alfa ดังนั้นการหาชนิดทางพันธุกรรมสำคัญมาก

name: Visual agnosia
formal: Inability to recognise objects visually despite intact vision, due to lesions in occipitotemporal cortex.
simple: Seeing but not being able to recognise objects, caused by damage in the visual part of the brain.
th: ภาวะที่ตามองเห็นได้ปกติแต่สมองแปลความหมายวัตถุที่เห็นไม่ได้ จากรอยโรคที่ occipitotemporal cortex
tempoNote: Sudden after posterior cerebral artery stroke or hypoxia; insidious in posterior cortical atrophy and other degenerations
feat: Cannot name or show the use of a seen object, yet identifies it at once by touch, sound or verbal description
Acuity, fields (often apart from a superior quadrant or hemifield) and basic visual perception are adequate for the task
Apperceptive type: cannot copy or match shapes; associative type: copies well but still does not know what the drawing is
Often travels with prosopagnosia, alexia, colour loss or topographical disorientation
Lesions usually bilateral ventral occipitotemporal (fusiform, lateral occipital) or left-dominant for associative forms

Neuropsychology (e.g. VOSP-type batteries) to classify the level of breakdown

case.tests: MRI shows acute bilateral inferior occipitotemporal infarcts in posterior cerebral artery territory.
case.q: What is the cognitive deficit and why does touch rescue naming?

det.patho: Object recognition depends on the ventral visual stream running from occipital cortex into the fusiform and inferior temporal regions. Damage early in this pathway prevents a coherent shape percept (apperceptive form), whereas damage later, or disconnection from language and semantic stores, leaves the percept intact but stripped of meaning (associative form). Bilateral posterior cerebral artery infarction, carbon monoxide or other hypoxic injury, and posterior cortical atrophy are the usual causes.
det.clinical: Patients bump into the problem in daily life: they cannot find items in a cupboard, mistake objects, or rely on touch and context. Insight is often reasonable, which distinguishes it from confusional states. Accompanying defects such as alexia without agraphia, achromatopsia, face blindness and route-finding difficulty help localise the lesion. In neurodegenerative cases the onset is gradual, and patients may first visit an optometrist repeatedly with normal eye tests.
det.diagnosis: The core requirement is a recognition failure confined to vision with adequate elementary vision and preserved naming through other senses. Testing copying, matching and categorising separates apperceptive from associative types. Anomia and general dementia must be excluded, since an aphasic patient also fails to name by touch. MRI identifies infarcts or posterior atrophy; amyloid or tau biomarkers help when posterior cortical atrophy from Alzheimer pathology is suspected.
det.treatment: Treat the cause, for example secondary stroke prevention or Alzheimer-directed care. Rehabilitation teaches compensatory strategies: using touch and sound, labelling the home, keeping objects in fixed places and verbalising features. Occupational therapy assessment for driving and safety is important. Some recovery occurs after stroke over months, but there is no specific drug treatment.
det.prognosis: Stroke-related agnosia may improve partially; degenerative forms progress with the underlying disease.
pearls: If touch rescues naming, the problem is visual recognition, not language.
Can the patient copy the drawing? Yes suggests associative, no suggests apperceptive agnosia.
Repeated normal eye examinations in someone 'who cannot see properly' should prompt thinking of posterior cortical atrophy.

name: Visual simultanagnosia
formal: Component of Balint syndrome: inability to perceive more than one object at a time, from bilateral parieto-occipital lesions.
simple: Being able to see only one object at a time, unable to take in a whole scene.

Loses objects that are in plain view; reading text and following lines is very difficult

det.patho: The dorsal attention network in both parieto-occipital regions lets us hold several objects in awareness and shift between them. When it is damaged bilaterally, attention collapses onto one object or fragment at a time. Typical causes are watershed infarction between middle and posterior cerebral artery territories after hypotension, hypoxic brain injury and posterior cortical atrophy, most often from Alzheimer disease.
det.clinical: Patients appear to have poor eyesight yet can identify a tiny object if it is the only thing they look at. They struggle with reading, finding items on a cluttered table, recognising a scene and navigating. A ventral form, seen with left occipitotemporal lesions, allows scene understanding but slows reading letter by letter. Insight varies; in posterior cortical atrophy memory is relatively spared early, so the visual complaint dominates.
det.diagnosis: Ask the patient to describe a complex picture and note fragmentary report of details without the theme. Navon figures and counting scattered dots are simple confirmatory tests. Look for optic ataxia and gaze apraxia to complete Balint syndrome. MRI and, when appropriate, amyloid or tau biomarkers define the cause; ophthalmological examination should be essentially normal.
det.treatment: Address the cause: vascular risk control after border-zone infarction, Alzheimer-directed therapy including cholinesterase inhibitors where indicated. Occupational therapy uses decluttering, high contrast, verbal cueing and one-item-at-a-time strategies. Driving must stop. Low-vision services can help even though the eye itself is healthy.
det.prognosis: Partial improvement can follow stroke or hypoxia; in posterior cortical atrophy the deficit slowly worsens.
pearls: Seeing the trees but not the forest: details are reported, the scene is missed.
Simultanagnosia plus optic ataxia plus ocular apraxia equals Balint syndrome.
A middle-aged person with 'eye problems' and normal eye tests may have posterior cortical atrophy.

det.patho: Spatial perception is processed in the dorsal visual stream, running from occipital cortex to the posterior parietal lobe (the where pathway). The right hemisphere is dominant for spatial attention and location judgements, so right parietal damage produces the most pronounced deficits. Bilateral lesions, as in posterior cortical atrophy, give the most disabling picture.
det.clinical: Patients misjudge distances, bump into objects, struggle with stairs, reading maps and dressing, and become lost in familiar surroundings. They can usually name objects, which separates this from object agnosia. Left hemispatial neglect, anosognosia and constructional difficulties often coexist after right hemisphere stroke. In posterior cortical atrophy, patients often first consult optometrists repeatedly before the cortical cause is recognised.
det.diagnosis: Bedside screening uses dot counting, line orientation and figure copying, followed by formal neuropsychology. Ophthalmic assessment confirms that acuity and fields do not explain the symptoms. MRI shows the lesion or posterior atrophy; FDG-PET and amyloid or tau biomarkers help define the underlying neurodegeneration.
det.treatment: Treatment follows the cause, with stroke rehabilitation or cholinesterase inhibitors in Alzheimer-related posterior cortical atrophy. Occupational therapy teaches compensatory strategies such as verbal cueing, consistent home layout, high-contrast markings and safe mobility. Driving should usually stop.
det.prognosis: Post-stroke deficits often partly recover; in neurodegenerative disease they progress.
pearls: A patient who sees well but cannot find things, dress or park may have a dorsal stream problem, not an eye problem.
Visuospatial complaints with relatively preserved memory point to posterior cortical atrophy.
Dot counting is a quick and sensitive bedside test.

name: Vitamin A deficiency

feat: Night blindness is the earliest symptom, from impaired rhodopsin regeneration in rods

At risk: malnutrition, fat malabsorption, bariatric surgery, cystic fibrosis, chronic liver or biliary disease, alcohol misuse

det.patho: Retinol is converted to 11-cis retinal, the chromophore of rhodopsin, and to retinoic acid, which controls epithelial differentiation. When stores are depleted, rods fail first, and mucus-secreting goblet cells are lost, leaving dry, keratinised conjunctiva and cornea that melt by liquefactive necrosis. Immunity is also impaired, so infection and deficiency worsen each other. Low intake plus infection (measles, diarrhoea) is the usual cause in children, while malabsorption and bariatric surgery are common in adults.
det.clinical: Nyctalopia comes first, followed by dry eyes, Bitot spots and corneal changes. Children may present with severe illness, poor growth and corneal clouding. Peripheral neuropathy or cerebellar signs may reflect associated deficiencies (vitamin E, B12, copper) in malabsorption, so look for those. In infants, deficiency can produce a bulging fontanelle with raised pressure.
det.diagnosis: Diagnose from risk factors, night blindness and slit-lamp signs, supported by a low serum retinol interpreted in the context of CRP. Response to supplementation is itself confirmatory. Differentiate from inherited rod dystrophies, glaucoma and medication effects.
det.treatment: Give high-dose vitamin A early: the WHO schedule uses oral retinol on two consecutive days and again about two weeks later, with doses scaled to age, and corneal disease is treated as an emergency in hospital alongside intense lubrication and topical antibiotics. Correct protein-energy malnutrition, zinc and other deficiencies, and treat the infection. In malabsorption or after bariatric surgery, lifelong monitoring and water-miscible supplements are needed. Avoid excess dosing, especially in pregnancy.
det.prognosis: Night blindness and xerosis reverse with treatment; corneal scarring from ulceration is permanent, and severe deficiency in children is associated with high mortality.
pearls: Night blindness after bariatric surgery: check vitamin A (and zinc).
Too much vitamin A, not too little, is the classic drug-and-diet trigger of intracranial hypertension.
Low retinol during acute infection may be artefactual; recheck when CRP settles.
det.thd: ภาวะขาดวิตามินเอทำให้ตาบอดกลางคืนเป็นอาการแรก ต่อมาตาแห้ง เกิด Bitot spot กระจกตาแห้ง เป็นแผล และเปื่อยยุ่ย (keratomalacia) ซึ่งเป็นภาวะฉุกเฉิน พบในเด็กขาดสารอาหาร ผู้ป่วยหลังผ่าตัดกระเพาะ และโรคดูดซึมไขมัน ตรวจระดับ retinol ในเลือดร่วมกับ CRP รักษาด้วยวิตามินเอขนาดสูงตามแนวทางองค์การอนามัยโลก ดูแลตา แก้ไขภาวะขาดสารอาหารอื่น และระวังไม่ให้ได้รับมากเกินไป

name: VLCAD deficiency
formal: Very-long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (ACADVL) with cardiomyopathy in infants, or rhabdomyolysis with exertional myalgia in adolescents.
simple: An inherited fat-burning defect causing muscle pain or heart weakness, especially during fasting or exercise.
more: Acylcarnitine and gene testing; avoid fasting, a low-fat diet with medium-chain triglycerides, and triheptanoin.
th: ความผิดปกติของการสลายกรดไขมันสายยาวมากจากยีน ACADVL ทารกมีหัวใจผิดปกติ ส่วนวัยรุ่นและผู้ใหญ่มี rhabdomyolysis หลังออกกำลังหรืออดอาหาร
tempoNote: Infant forms are acute and life-threatening; later forms give recurrent attacks
feat: Severe neonatal form: hypertrophic or dilated cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, hypoketotic hypoglycaemia
Hepatic childhood form: hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with fasting or illness
Later-onset myopathic form: exercise- or fasting-induced myalgia and rhabdomyolysis
Normal strength and CK between attacks in adult forms
Detected by newborn screening (raised C14:1 carnitine)
inv: Plasma acylcarnitines: raised C14:1 (best during stress)
CK during attacks, glucose, ketones, ECG and echocardiogram
ACADVL sequencing; enzyme or flux studies in fibroblasts if variants unclear

case.who: 20-year-old female nursing student from Chiang Mai
case.story: After a night of fasting during a religious retreat and a long hike, she developed severe thigh pain and cola-coloured urine; two milder episodes occurred in her teens.
case.exam: Tender proximal muscles, normal strength between attacks.
case.tests: CK 62,000 U/L, creatinine raised, acylcarnitine profile with high C14:1, biallelic ACADVL variants.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what dietary approach reduces attacks?
case.a: Myopathic VLCAD deficiency; avoid fasting, take carbohydrate before exercise, and use a low long-chain fat diet with MCT or triheptanoin.

read.where: Chapter 27 Inherited Disorders of Metabolism — Fatty Acid Oxidation Defects

det.patho: VLCAD sits on the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it initiates the beta-oxidation of 14- to 20-carbon fatty acids. Its deficiency deprives heart, liver and muscle of energy during prolonged exercise, fasting, cold or infection, when fat is the main fuel, and toxic long-chain acylcarnitines accumulate.
det.clinical: Three phenotypes are described. The neonatal cardiac form is the most severe, with cardiomyopathy and sudden death. The childhood hepatic form produces hypoketotic hypoglycaemia during illness. Adolescents and adults with residual enzyme activity have episodes of exertional myalgia, rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria and are otherwise well.
det.diagnosis: Acylcarnitine analysis, ideally during an attack, shows elevated C14:1 and related species. Between attacks profiles can be near normal. ACADVL sequencing confirms; functional fibroblast studies resolve uncertain variants. Newborn screening identifies many asymptomatic infants, some of whom never develop symptoms.
det.treatment: Avoid fasting and provide carbohydrate during illness. Limit long-chain fats and supplement medium-chain triglycerides; in some countries triheptanoin is approved to treat disorders of long-chain fatty acid oxidation. Rhabdomyolysis needs IV glucose and fluids. Carnitine supplementation is generally not recommended.
det.prognosis: Adult myopathic forms do well with precautions; infant cardiac forms carry significant mortality.
pearls: Rhabdomyolysis after fasting, prolonged exercise or fever: think fatty acid oxidation defects.
Acylcarnitines are most informative during an attack.
IV dextrose, not just fluids, during an acute episode.
det.thd: VLCAD deficiency เป็นความผิดปกติของการสลายกรดไขมันสายยาวมากจากยีน ACADVL ทารกอาจมีกล้ามเนื้อหัวใจผิดปกติและน้ำตาลต่ำ ส่วนวัยรุ่นและผู้ใหญ่มีปวดกล้ามเนื้อและ rhabdomyolysis หลังอดอาหารหรือออกกำลังนาน ตรวจ acylcarnitine พบ C14:1 สูง รักษาโดยไม่อดอาหาร ลดไขมันสายยาว เสริม MCT และให้กลูโคสทางหลอดเลือดเมื่อมีอาการ

name: Vocal tics
formal: Involuntary vocalisations as part of Tourette syndrome, ranging from simple sounds to words.
simple: Repeated sounds or words made involuntarily.
th: เสียงหรือคำพูดที่เปล่งออกมาโดยไม่ตั้งใจเป็นส่วนหนึ่งของโรคติก เช่น Tourette syndrome ตั้งแต่เสียงกระแอมจนถึงคำพูด
tempoNote: Usually begin in childhood after motor tics; wax and wane over months
feat: Simple: throat clearing, sniffing, grunting, coughing, squeaks
Complex: syllables, words, phrases, echolalia, palilalia, rarely coprolalia
Preceded by an urge and briefly suppressible, with rebound afterwards
Fluctuate with stress, fatigue and excitement; less during focused activity
Often misdiagnosed as allergy, asthma or habit cough
inv: Clinical diagnosis; video from home helps
Screen for ADHD, OCD, anxiety and learning difficulties
Investigations only for atypical features (late onset, progression, other neurological signs)

case.who: 10-year-old boy brought to a paediatric neurology clinic in Bangkok
case.story: For a year he sniffs and clears his throat many times a day despite two courses of allergy medicine; he also blinks and shrugs.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination; during the consultation he suppresses sounds, which burst out in the waiting room.
case.tests: None required; ENT review normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis if motor and vocal tics have both been present for over a year?
case.a: Tourette syndrome — the sniffing and throat clearing are simple vocal tics.

read.where: Chapter 34: Functional (Psychogenic) Movement Disorders: Phenomenology, Diagnosis and Treatment

det.patho: Tics arise from dysfunction of cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits that normally suppress unwanted motor programmes. Dopaminergic overactivity in the striatum and reduced inhibitory interneuron activity are implicated. Vocal tics reflect the same mechanism acting on laryngeal, respiratory and articulatory muscles.
det.clinical: Vocal tics usually follow motor tics by a year or two and range from simple noises to words and phrases. Coprolalia is uncommon (a minority of Tourette patients) despite its fame. The tics wax and wane and often peak around early adolescence. Comorbid ADHD, OCD and anxiety frequently cause more disability than the tics themselves.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical. Classify as provisional tic disorder (under a year), chronic vocal tic disorder (vocal only, over a year) or Tourette syndrome (motor plus vocal over a year). Atypical onset, progression or other neurological signs should prompt investigation for secondary causes such as Sydenham chorea, drug effects or neurodegenerative disease.
det.treatment: Education and reassurance are often enough. Behavioural therapy (comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics, habit reversal) is first-line when treatment is needed. Medications include alpha-2 agonists (clonidine, guanfacine) and, for more severe cases, aripiprazole or other dopamine-blocking drugs. Botulinum toxin into the vocal cords is occasionally used for disabling loud tics, and DBS is reserved for refractory adults.
det.prognosis: Most improve substantially by late adolescence or early adulthood.
pearls: Chronic sniffing or throat clearing unresponsive to allergy treatment may be a tic.
Coprolalia is not required for Tourette syndrome.
Treat the comorbid ADHD or OCD — it often matters more.
det.thd: Vocal tics คือเสียงที่เปล่งออกมาโดยไม่ตั้งใจ เช่น กระแอม สูดจมูก หรือพูดคำซ้ำ เป็นอาการของโรคติกและ Tourette syndrome มีความรู้สึกอยากทำก่อนและกลั้นได้ชั่วคราว อาการขึ้นลงตามความเครียด วินิจฉัยทางคลินิก ควรคัดกรอง ADHD และ OCD ร่วม การรักษาเริ่มจากการให้ความรู้และ behavioural therapy ยาที่ใช้ได้แก่ clonidine หรือ aripiprazole ส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นเมื่อโตเป็นผู้ใหญ่

name: Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada disease
formal: Autoimmune panuveitis with meningoencephalitis, poliosis, vitiligo and hearing loss, in pigmented populations.
simple: An immune disease causing eye inflammation, headache, hearing loss and patchy loss of skin or hair colour.
th: โรคภูมิคุ้มกันทำลายเซลล์สร้างเม็ดสี ทำให้ตาอักเสบทั้งสองข้าง เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ หูอื้อ และต่อมาผิวหนังด่างขาว ผมขาว พบในคนผิวสีเข้มรวมทั้งคนเอเชีย
tempoNote: Prodrome of headache and meningism for days, then acute bilateral uveitis; untreated cases become chronic and recurrent
feat: Flu-like prodrome with headache, neck stiffness and scalp tenderness
Sudden bilateral blurred vision from granulomatous panuveitis with serous retinal detachments
Tinnitus, hearing loss and vertigo
Weeks to months later: vitiligo, whitened eyelashes or hair (poliosis), alopecia, 'sunset glow' fundus
No history of penetrating eye injury (distinguishes it from sympathetic ophthalmia)
inv: Fluorescein angiography and OCT: multiple pinpoint leaks and subretinal fluid
CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis, especially in the first weeks
Audiometry for sensorineural loss
Exclude syphilis, TB and sarcoidosis

case.story: A week of headache and neck pain followed by sudden blurred vision in both eyes and ringing in her ears.
case.exam: Bilateral anterior chamber cells, swollen optic discs and bullous serous retinal detachments; mild neck stiffness.
case.tests: OCT subretinal fluid in both eyes; CSF 60 lymphocytes, protein mildly raised; VDRL and TB tests negative.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the urgent treatment?
case.a: Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada disease; high-dose systemic corticosteroids started promptly, with early steroid-sparing immunosuppression.

det.patho: VKH is a T-cell-mediated autoimmune attack on melanocyte antigens such as tyrosinase, affecting the choroid, meninges, inner ear and skin. It is associated with HLA-DR4 and HLA-DRB1*04:05 and is more common in Asian, Hispanic, Middle Eastern and Native American populations. Women are affected somewhat more often, usually in the third to fifth decades.
det.clinical: The course runs through prodromal (meningeal), acute uveitic, convalescent (depigmentation) and chronic recurrent stages. Neurological features include headache, meningism, rarely focal signs or encephalopathy, plus auditory and vestibular symptoms. Complete forms include ocular, neurological/auditory and skin features; incomplete or probable forms are common at presentation before depigmentation appears.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the revised international criteria: bilateral uveitis without trauma or surgery history, supported by neurological, auditory and skin findings. Fluorescein angiography, OCT and indocyanine green angiography show characteristic choroidal involvement. CSF pleocytosis is supportive early. Infectious mimics, especially syphilis and tuberculosis, must be excluded.
det.treatment: Early high-dose corticosteroids (often IV methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisolone tapered over at least 6 months) are essential to prevent chronic disease. Early addition of immunomodulators such as cyclosporine, azathioprine, mycophenolate or adalimumab reduces recurrence and steroid toxicity. Cataract, glaucoma and choroidal neovascularisation need ophthalmological management.
det.prognosis: With prompt and adequate treatment most patients keep good vision; delayed or brief therapy risks a chronic recurrent course with visual loss.
pearls: Bilateral uveitis plus meningism plus tinnitus in an Asian adult: think VKH.
Steroids must be prolonged — short courses invite chronic disease.
Sympathetic ophthalmia looks similar but follows eye trauma or surgery.
det.thd: VKH เป็นโรคภูมิคุ้มกันที่ทำลายเซลล์เม็ดสีในตา เยื่อหุ้มสมอง หูชั้นใน และผิวหนัง พบบ่อยในคนเอเชีย เริ่มด้วยปวดศีรษะคอแข็ง ตามด้วยตามัวทั้งสองข้างจาก panuveitis และจอประสาทตาหลุดลอกแบบมีน้ำ อาจมีหูอื้อ ต่อมาเกิดด่างขาวและผมขาว รักษาด้วย steroid ขนาดสูงเป็นเวลานานร่วมกับยากดภูมิ เพื่อป้องกันการกลับเป็นซ้ำ

name: Von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) disease
formal: Autosomal dominant VHL mutation with retinal and CNS haemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma and phaeochromocytoma.
simple: An inherited condition causing tumours in the brain, eyes, kidneys and adrenal glands.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมแบบ autosomal dominant จากยีน VHL ทำให้เกิด haemangioblastoma ที่จอตา สมองน้อย ไขสันหลัง ร่วมกับมะเร็งไตและ phaeochromocytoma
tempoNote: Lifelong tumour predisposition; CNS lesions grow in spurts with quiet periods, symptoms usually from the second decade on
feat: Cerebellar haemangioblastoma: headache, vomiting, ataxia; cyst with enhancing mural nodule
Spinal and brainstem haemangioblastomas often with syrinx; retinal haemangioblastomas threaten vision
Clear-cell renal carcinoma and renal or pancreatic cysts; phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma
Endolymphatic sac tumours causing hearing loss, tinnitus and vertigo
Family history of early tumours; around one fifth are de novo
inv: MRI brain and whole spine with contrast; internal auditory canal imaging
Germline VHL gene testing and cascade testing of relatives
Plasma or urine metanephrines (before any surgery) and abdominal MRI for kidney and pancreas
Dilated retinal examination; audiology

case.who: 26-year-old man from Phitsanulok whose father died of kidney cancer at 44
case.story: Three months of morning headache, unsteadiness and recent vomiting.
case.exam: Bilateral papilloedema, right limb ataxia, wide-based gait; retinal examination shows a red vascular nodule in the left eye.
case.tests: MRI shows a right cerebellar cyst with an enhancing nodule; Hb 18.5 g/dL; plasma normetanephrine elevated.
case.q: What unifying diagnosis fits, and what must be done before the posterior fossa operation?
case.a: VHL disease; exclude and treat phaeochromocytoma (alpha-blockade) before anaesthesia to avoid a hypertensive crisis.

read.where: Chapter 34 Systemic Conditions and Neurology — Neurocutaneous Syndromes

det.patho: The VHL protein targets hypoxia-inducible factors for degradation. When both copies are lost in a cell, HIF-2alpha accumulates and drives VEGF, erythropoietin and other growth signals, producing highly vascular tumours. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with high penetrance; genotype influences risk, with missense variants carrying more phaeochromocytoma risk.
det.clinical: CNS haemangioblastomas affect cerebellum, spinal cord and brainstem and cause symptoms mainly through associated cysts or syrinx rather than the nodule itself. Retinal lesions may be the first finding and can cause detachment. Renal cell carcinoma is the main cause of death, while phaeochromocytoma may present with paroxysmal hypertension or a crisis during surgery. Some patients have polycythaemia from tumour erythropoietin.
det.diagnosis: Clinical criteria rely on haemangioblastoma plus a characteristic visceral tumour, or a single lesion with a positive family history; germline VHL testing confirms most cases. Anyone with multiple or young-onset haemangioblastoma should be tested. Surveillance protocols include yearly eye examination and metanephrines from childhood, and periodic brain, spine and abdominal MRI. Screen for catecholamine excess before every operation.
det.treatment: Symptomatic CNS lesions are resected, often with cyst drainage; stereotactic radiosurgery is an option for small inaccessible tumours. Belzutifan, an oral HIF-2alpha inhibitor, is approved for VHL-associated renal carcinoma, CNS haemangioblastoma and pancreatic tumours not needing immediate surgery and has changed management. Retinal lesions are treated with laser or cryotherapy. Lifelong multidisciplinary surveillance is essential.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy has improved with surveillance; renal cancer and CNS tumour burden remain the main threats.
pearls: Cyst plus enhancing mural nodule in the cerebellum of a young adult: think haemangioblastoma, then think VHL.
Always check metanephrines before surgery in VHL.
Polycythaemia with a posterior fossa mass is a classic haemangioblastoma clue.
det.thd: VHL เป็นโรคพันธุกรรม autosomal dominant ที่ยีนควบคุม HIF เสียไป ทำให้เกิดเนื้องอกหลอดเลือด haemangioblastoma ที่สมองน้อย ไขสันหลัง และจอตา ร่วมกับมะเร็งไตชนิด clear cell และ phaeochromocytoma วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI และตรวจยีน VHL ต้องตรวจ metanephrine ก่อนผ่าตัดเสมอ การรักษามีทั้งผ่าตัด radiosurgery และยา belzutifan ร่วมกับการตรวจคัดกรองตลอดชีวิต

name: Walker-Warburg syndrome
formal: Severe congenital muscular dystrophy with cobblestone lissencephaly, hydrocephalus, cerebellar malformation and eye anomalies, due to defective alpha-dystroglycan glycosylation (POMT1, POMT2, FKTN and others).
simple: The most severe inherited muscle and brain malformation syndrome of newborns, with floppiness, brain and eye abnormalities.
more: Very high CK; autosomal recessive with prenatal diagnosis possible. Treatment is supportive and most affected infants die in the first years of life.
th: congenital muscular dystrophy ชนิดรุนแรงที่สุดในกลุ่ม dystroglycanopathy มีสมองผิดรูปแบบ cobblestone lissencephaly น้ำในโพรงสมองคั่ง และตาผิดปกติ

feat: Severe neonatal hypotonia and weakness, very high CK
Cobblestone (type II) lissencephaly, hydrocephalus, brainstem and cerebellar hypoplasia
Eye anomalies: microphthalmia, cataract, retinal dysplasia, anterior chamber defects
Seizures and profound developmental impairment
Autosomal recessive; genes include POMT1, POMT2, FKTN, FKRP, ISPD (CRPPA)
inv: CK markedly raised
Brain MRI: cobblestone cortex, kinked brainstem, cerebellar cysts, hydrocephalus
Biopsy: reduced glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan; gene panel
Antenatal ultrasound/MRI can detect hydrocephalus and malformation

case.who: Newborn boy at a regional hospital in Ubon Ratchathani
case.story: Antenatal scan showed enlarged ventricles. At birth he is floppy with poor suck and cloudy eyes.
case.exam: Severe hypotonia, weak cry, macrocephaly, bilateral cataracts and microphthalmia.
case.tests: CK 8,500 U/L; MRI shows cobblestone cortex, hydrocephalus and hypoplastic pons; biallelic POMT1 variants.
case.q: What is the syndrome and what counselling is needed?
case.a: Walker–Warburg syndrome; poor prognosis, palliative-focused care, and recessive recurrence risk of 25% with prenatal testing available.

read.where: 18. Disorders of Cranial Volume and Shape

det.patho: Alpha-dystroglycan must be extensively O-mannosylated to bind laminin and other matrix proteins in muscle, brain and eye. Defects in any of the enzymes building this glycan disrupt the link to the basement membrane, causing muscle degeneration and over-migration of neurons through gaps in the pial surface, giving a cobblestone cortex.
det.clinical: Babies present with profound hypotonia, eye malformations, seizures and hydrocephalus. Development is severely limited and most die within the first years of life. It sits at the severe extreme of a spectrum that includes MEB disease, Fukuyama congenital dystrophy and milder limb-girdle dystroglycanopathies.
det.diagnosis: The combination of very high CK, characteristic brain MRI and eye anomalies is diagnostic clinically. Muscle immunostaining with glycosylation-dependent antibodies shows loss of alpha-dystroglycan. Genetic panels confirm the gene, enabling prenatal diagnosis in future pregnancies.
det.treatment: Treatment is supportive: shunting for hydrocephalus, antiseizure medications, feeding support and respiratory care, with early involvement of palliative services. Genetic counselling is essential.
det.prognosis: Very poor; survival beyond early childhood is unusual.
pearls: Floppy baby + very high CK + brain malformation + eye anomalies = dystroglycanopathy.
WWS is the most severe; MEB and Fukuyama are milder relatives.
Same genes (e.g. FKRP) can cause adult limb-girdle dystrophy.
det.thd: Walker–Warburg syndrome เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้อแต่กำเนิดชนิดรุนแรงที่สุดในกลุ่ม dystroglycanopathy ทารกตัวอ่อนมาก CK สูง สมองผิดรูปแบบ cobblestone lissencephaly มีน้ำคั่งในโพรงสมอง และตาผิดปกติ เช่น ต้อกระจก ตาเล็ก ส่วนใหญ่เสียชีวิตในวัยทารก การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคองและให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

case.story: Woke with double vision and his wife noticed both eyes looking outward.
case.exam: Exotropia both eyes, neither eye adducts past midline, abducting nystagmus bilaterally, convergence absent, pupils normal.
case.tests: MRI diffusion shows a small paramedian midbrain infarct.
case.q: Name the syndrome and localise it.
case.a: WEBINO from bilateral medial longitudinal fasciculus damage in the paramedian midbrain.

read.where: 8 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System

det.patho: The medial longitudinal fasciculus carries signals from the abducens nucleus to the contralateral medial rectus subnucleus. Damage to both bundles prevents adduction on lateral gaze; when the lesion also involves the medial rectus subnuclei or convergence pathways in the midbrain, both eyes drift outwards at rest. Pontine variants exist, so exotropia does not prove a midbrain lesion.
det.clinical: Patients present with horizontal diplopia and the eyes visibly turned outward. On lateral gaze the adducting eye lags while the abducting eye beats outward. Associated findings such as vertical gaze palsy, ptosis or hemiparesis indicate a wider brainstem lesion. Ischaemic stroke and multiple sclerosis account for most cases, with trauma, tumour, Wernicke encephalopathy and infection less often.
det.diagnosis: The clinical pattern is distinctive; MRI confirms the lesion, though small infarcts may be missed on early scans. Choose the work-up by age and risk factors. Myasthenia gravis can mimic INO and should be tested when imaging is normal. Thiamine should be given if nutrition is in doubt before testing.
det.treatment: Manage the cause: acute stroke pathways, secondary prevention, or MS relapse treatment and disease-modifying therapy. Diplopia can be relieved with occlusion or prisms; strabismus surgery is considered only after six months of stable deviation. Many vascular cases improve over weeks to months.
det.prognosis: Partial or complete recovery is common, more so in demyelination than in large brainstem infarcts.
pearls: Both eyes out, neither eye adducts: WEBINO.
Preserved convergence hints at a pontine lesion; lost convergence favours midbrain.
Pseudo-INO from myasthenia must be excluded when MRI is clean.
det.thd: WEBINO คือ INO ทั้งสองข้างร่วมกับตาเขออกทั้งสองข้างตั้งแต่ท่ามองตรง เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ MLF ทั้งสองข้าง มักอยู่ที่ midbrain สาเหตุพบบ่อยคือ stroke ในผู้สูงอายุและ multiple sclerosis ในคนอายุน้อย ตรวจ MRI ก้านสมองเพื่อยืนยัน ถ้า MRI ปกติให้นึกถึง myasthenia gravis การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ และแก้ภาพซ้อนด้วยการปิดตาหรือ prism

name: Welander distal myopathy
formal: Late-onset autosomal dominant distal myopathy beginning in the hands, especially finger and wrist extensors, linked to a TIA1 variant; mainly reported in Sweden and Finland.
simple: An inherited muscle disease in older adults that starts with weak hands and fingers and slowly spreads.
more: CK is normal or mildly raised and biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles. There is no specific treatment; progression is slow and lifespan is normal.
th: distal myopathy ชนิดยีนเด่นเริ่มหลังอายุ 40 อ่อนแรงที่กล้ามเนื้อเหยียดนิ้วและข้อมือก่อน เกี่ยวกับยีน TIA1 พบมากในสวีเดนและฟินแลนด์
tempoNote: Onset usually after 40, slowly progressive over decades
feat: Weakness of finger and wrist extensors first, often starting in the index finger
Later spread to toe and ankle extensors
Proximal muscles largely spared; life expectancy normal
Mild distal sensory changes reported in some
Founder variant TIA1 E384K, especially Scandinavian families; rare in Asia
inv: CK normal or mildly raised; EMG myopathic
Biopsy: rimmed vacuoles and myopathic changes

case.story: Over three years she has struggled to straighten her index fingers when typing; recently her toes catch on steps.
case.exam: Weak finger and wrist extensors, mild ankle dorsiflexor weakness, normal grip and proximal strength, reflexes preserved.
case.tests: CK 320 U/L, myopathic EMG, biopsy with rimmed vacuoles, heterozygous TIA1 E384K.
case.q: Which distal myopathy starts in the hands of older adults?
case.a: Welander distal myopathy.

det.patho: TIA1 is an RNA-binding protein involved in stress granule formation. The founder variant increases its tendency to phase-separate, promoting stable stress granules and protein aggregation in muscle; co-inheritance of SQSTM1 variants may modify severity. The result is a rimmed-vacuolar myopathy.
det.clinical: Onset is usually in the fifth decade or later with weakness of finger extension, clumsiness of fine movements and later foot drop. Progression is slow and disability modest. Homozygous patients have earlier and more widespread disease.
det.diagnosis: Distal hand-extensor weakness in a late-onset myopathy with rimmed vacuoles suggests the diagnosis, confirmed by TIA1 genotyping. Neurogenic causes such as radial or posterior interosseous neuropathy, MMN and motor neuron disease should be excluded by EMG.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy exists. Hand therapy, splints, adaptive devices and orthoses for foot drop help function.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; normal lifespan.
pearls: Late-onset finger extensor weakness: Welander; late-onset foot drop: Udd.
Rimmed vacuoles are shared with IBM, but the pattern differs.
Exclude posterior interosseous neuropathy with EMG first.
det.thd: Welander distal myopathy เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้อยีนเด่นจาก TIA1 เริ่มหลังอายุ 40 อ่อนแรงที่กล้ามเนื้อเหยียดนิ้วและข้อมือก่อน แล้วค่อยลามมาที่ข้อเท้า ชิ้นเนื้อพบ rimmed vacuoles ต้องแยกจาก IBM และโรคเส้นประสาท โรคดำเนินช้า รักษาด้วยกายภาพและอุปกรณ์ช่วย

name: Wernicke’s aphasia
formal: Fluent aphasia from left posterior superior temporal lesion, with impaired comprehension and paraphasic speech.
simple: Speech that sounds fluent but makes little sense, with poor understanding.
th: ภาวะพูดคล่องแต่ไร้ความหมายและไม่เข้าใจคำพูดของผู้อื่น จากรอยโรคสมองซีกซ้ายบริเวณ superior temporal gyrus ส่วนหลัง
tempoNote: Usually sudden with stroke; gradual if due to tumour or degeneration
feat: Fluent, effortless speech with normal prosody but empty content, paraphasias and neologisms
Severely impaired comprehension of spoken and written language
Poor repetition and naming; patient often unaware of errors (anosognosia)
Usually no hemiparesis; may have right superior quadrantanopia
Frequently misread as confusion or psychosis
inv: Urgent CT/CT angiography or MRI: inferior division left MCA territory infarct is the commonest cause
Bedside language assessment: fluency, comprehension, repetition, naming, reading, writing
Cardioembolic work-up (ECG, Holter, echocardiogram) since embolic occlusion is typical

case.who: 72-year-old man from Nakhon Ratchasima with atrial fibrillation
case.story: Family brought him because he suddenly started 'talking nonsense' at breakfast and does not follow instructions; he seems unbothered.
case.exam: Fluent speech full of wrong and invented words, cannot point to objects on command or repeat a phrase; no limb weakness; right upper visual field defect.
case.tests: CT angiography: blocked left MCA inferior (lower) division branch; NIHSS 7.
case.q: Where is the lesion and why is he at risk of being mislabelled?
case.a: Left posterior superior temporal gyrus (inferior MCA division); fluent jargon with no weakness can be mistaken for delirium or psychiatric illness, delaying stroke treatment.

read.where: Chapter 11 Cognitive Impairment and Dementia — Speech and Language
20 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Cerebral Hemispheres

det.patho: Damage to the posterior part of the left superior temporal gyrus and adjacent auditory association cortex disrupts mapping between speech sounds and meaning. Embolism to the lower division branch of the left MCA is the commonest cause; haemorrhage, tumour, abscess, herpes encephalitis and neurodegeneration are others. Because motor cortex is spared, there is usually no hemiparesis.
det.clinical: Speech is fluent and grammatically framed but lacks meaning, filled with phonemic and semantic paraphasias and neologisms (jargon). Comprehension, repetition, naming, reading and writing are all impaired, and patients often lack awareness, which may make them agitated or appear psychotic. A visual field defect may be the only other sign. Recovery tends to evolve towards a milder fluent aphasia such as anomic or conduction aphasia.
det.diagnosis: Identify the aphasia profile at the bedside: fluent output, poor comprehension, poor repetition. Treat as a stroke code if acute — imaging and vessel imaging should not be delayed by uncertainty about psychiatric illness. Formal speech and language assessment documents severity and guides therapy.
det.treatment: Acute ischaemic cases are eligible for thrombolysis and thrombectomy by standard criteria, including medium-vessel occlusion in selected patients. Long term, intensive speech and language therapy improves outcomes; communication partners should use short sentences, gestures and checking. Secondary stroke prevention is guided by the cause, usually anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation.
det.prognosis: Partial improvement is common over months, though comprehension deficits often persist in large lesions.
pearls: New 'confusion' with fluent nonsense speech and no weakness: check language properly and call a stroke code.
Fluent + poor comprehension + poor repetition = Wernicke; if repetition is spared, think transcortical sensory aphasia.
Right superior quadrantanopia supports a posterior temporal lesion.
det.thd: Wernicke’s aphasia เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ superior temporal gyrus ส่วนหลังของสมองซีกซ้าย มักจาก stroke ของแขนงล่างของ MCA ผู้ป่วยพูดคล่องแต่ไม่มีความหมาย มีคำผิดและคำที่แต่งขึ้น ไม่เข้าใจคำพูด พูดตามไม่ได้ และมักไม่รู้ตัว มักไม่มีแขนขาอ่อนแรงจึงถูกเข้าใจผิดว่าสับสนหรือป่วยทางจิต ต้องรีบส่งตรวจภาพสมองแบบ stroke fast track และฟื้นฟูด้วยการฝึกพูด

name: Wernicke’s encephalopathy
formal: Thiamine deficiency causing the triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia, often in alcohol misuse, treated with parenteral thiamine.
simple: A brain emergency from low vitamin B1 causing confusion, abnormal eye movements and unsteady walking.
more: MRI may show mammillary body and periaqueductal T2 hyperintensity; diagnose clinically, and thiamine should be given before glucose. Treat with high-dose IV thiamine, 500 mg three times daily; untreated, it progresses to Korsakoff syndrome and death. Acute thiamine deficiency encephalopathy with the triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia, associated with alcoholism, malnutrition and hyperemesis; MRI shows periventricular lesions and mammillary body change. Treat immediately with high-dose intravenous thiamine before glucose to prevent Korsakoff syndrome. Early treatment can fully reverse features.

Risk: alcohol, hyperemesis, bariatric surgery, malnutrition, refeeding

inv: Clinical — treat on suspicion

case.q: Why give thiamine before glucose?
