qx.stem: A 34-year-old woman from Songkhla has had relentless vomiting for six weeks after sleeve gastrectomy. She is now apathetic and disoriented, walks with a wide-based unsteady gait, and has horizontal nystagmus with bilateral abducens weakness. Capillary glucose is 3.2 mmol/L and a nurse is about to give 50% dextrose.
qx.q: What should be done first?
opts: Give the dextrose and recheck glucose before any other treatment
Order MRI brain to confirm mammillary body change before treating
Give oral thiamine 100 mg daily and observe
Send a whole-blood thiamine level and wait for the result
Give IV thiamine (e.g. 500 mg) before or with the glucose and continue high-dose IV thiamine
qx.why: This is Wernicke encephalopathy from post-bariatric vomiting; glucose loading without thiamine can precipitate or worsen it. Give high-dose parenteral thiamine (commonly 500 mg IV three times daily for several days) immediately, with glucose given alongside rather than delayed. MRI and thiamine levels support the diagnosis but must not delay treatment, and oral low-dose thiamine is inadequate.

qx.stem: A 27-year-old woman from Nonthaburi had a sleeve gastrectomy three months ago and has vomited most meals for six weeks. She is now drowsy and disoriented, cannot walk without support and has horizontal nystagmus with bilateral abducens weakness. Capillary glucose is 3.4 mmol/L and the night nurse is preparing 50% dextrose; MRI is booked for the morning.
qx.q: What is the most appropriate immediate step?
opts: Give dextrose now and thiamine after the MRI confirms the diagnosis
Send a whole-blood thiamine level and wait for the result
Start oral multivitamins at discharge
Give high-dose IV thiamine (e.g. 500 mg three times daily) before or with the glucose, then continue IV dosing
Perform a lumbar puncture to exclude encephalitis first
qx.why: Confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia after bariatric surgery with protracted vomiting is Wernicke's encephalopathy until proven otherwise; treatment is clinical and must not wait for MRI or thiamine levels. Glucose without thiamine can precipitate or worsen the encephalopathy, so thiamine is given first or together. Delay risks permanent Korsakoff amnesia; MRI may show symmetric medial thalamic, mammillary and periaqueductal signal that can mimic variant CJD.

qx.stem: A 48-year-old man from Chiang Rai with chronic alcohol use is brought to the emergency room confused, with nystagmus, bilateral abducens weakness and a wide-based gait. Capillary glucose is low at 52 mg/dL. The team prepares an intravenous glucose bolus.
qx.q: What is the correct sequence of treatment?
opts: Give glucose first, then thiamine after the glucose is stable
Give oral thiamine 100 mg daily and observe
Give intravenous thiamine at high dose before or together with glucose, then continue thiamine for several days
Give magnesium alone and delay thiamine until the MRI
Give folate only
qx.why: The triad of confusion, ocular signs and ataxia indicates Wernicke encephalopathy; glucose given before thiamine can precipitate or worsen the encephalopathy by consuming the remaining thiamine. High-dose intravenous thiamine (for example 500 mg three times daily for two to three days, then lower doses) should be given before or with glucose, with magnesium replacement as a cofactor. Oral thiamine is poorly absorbed in alcohol use disorder, and delay for imaging is inappropriate.

det.patho: Thiamine (vitamin B1) is a cofactor for enzymes of glucose metabolism; body stores last only a few weeks. When thiamine is depleted, energy failure and oxidative injury hit regions of high metabolic demand around the third ventricle, aqueduct and fourth ventricle — the medial thalami, mammillary bodies, periaqueductal grey, oculomotor and vestibular nuclei and cerebellar vermis. Alcohol use disorder is the classic setting, but hyperemesis, bariatric surgery, cancer, dialysis, starvation and refeeding are increasingly recognised.
det.clinical: The full triad of confusion, eye movement abnormalities and gait ataxia is present in only a minority; many patients show just one or two elements or only altered mental state. Eye findings include nystagmus, lateral rectus palsy, conjugate gaze palsy and, rarely, pupillary change. Hypothermia, hypotension and coma occur in severe cases. If untreated, patients develop Korsakoff syndrome, with profound anterograde and retrograde amnesia and confabulation, which may be permanent.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical; the Caine criteria (two of dietary deficiency, eye signs, cerebellar dysfunction, and altered mental state or memory impairment) improve sensitivity in people with alcohol use disorder. MRI showing symmetric T2/FLAIR or DWI change in the medial thalami, mammillary bodies and periaqueductal region supports it but a normal scan does not exclude it. Blood thiamine (or transketolase) levels can be drawn but treatment must not wait for the result. Exclude hypoglycaemia, hepatic encephalopathy, intoxication, posterior circulation stroke and Miller Fisher syndrome.
det.treatment: Give high-dose parenteral thiamine immediately — commonly 500 mg IV three times daily for several days, then lower doses — before or together with glucose. Correct magnesium, which is needed for thiamine-dependent enzymes. Give prophylactic parenteral thiamine to at-risk patients (alcohol withdrawal, hyperemesis, refeeding). After the acute phase, continue oral thiamine, nutritional support and alcohol treatment.
det.prognosis: Eye signs often improve within hours to days and ataxia over weeks, but memory deficits frequently persist; untreated, mortality is substantial.
pearls: Treat on suspicion: thiamine is cheap and safe, missed WE is devastating.
Low magnesium can make thiamine therapy ineffective.
Think of WE after bariatric surgery or hyperemesis, not only in alcohol use.

name: West syndrome
formal: Epileptic encephalopathy in infancy with infantile spasms, developmental regression and hypsarrhythmia on EEG.
simple: A serious infant epilepsy with clusters of spasms and developmental regression.
more: EEG shows hypsarrhythmia; MRI and metabolic and genetic work-up should be done urgently (tuberous sclerosis, ARX, CDKL5). First-line treatment is ACTH, prednisolone or vigabatrin, especially in tuberous sclerosis. Epileptic spasms in infancy, typically with hypsarrhythmia on EEG and developmental regression (West syndrome); causes include tuberous sclerosis and hypoxic injury; treated with ACTH or vigabatrin.
th: ทารกอายุราว 3–12 เดือนผงกตัวเกร็งเป็นชุด ๆ ตอนตื่นนอน พัฒนาการถดถอย EEG เป็น hypsarrhythmia — ต้องรักษาด่วนด้วย steroid/ACTH หรือ vigabatrin
tempoNote: Spasms come in clusters, especially on waking; onset usually 3–12 months, with developmental plateau or regression over weeks
feat: Brief symmetric flexion or extension spasms of neck, trunk and limbs lasting about a second, repeated in clusters
Clusters typically appear just after waking and may be mistaken for colic or startle
Loss of social smile, visual attention or motor milestones once spasms begin
Underlying cause often evident: tuberous sclerosis, hypoxic–ischaemic injury, malformation, Down syndrome or a genetic variant
inv: Prolonged video-EEG including sleep and a waking cluster: hypsarrhythmia (chaotic high-voltage slowing with multifocal spikes) and ictal electrodecrement with spasms
MRI brain and Wood's-lamp skin examination for tuberous sclerosis

case.who: 6-month-old boy brought to a provincial hospital in Surin
case.story: For two weeks he has 'startles' in runs of 10–20 each morning after waking, crying between jerks. He has stopped smiling and no longer follows faces.
case.exam: Poor visual fixation, reduced axial tone; three hypopigmented oval patches on the back under ultraviolet light.
case.tests: Sleep EEG: hypsarrhythmia; a recorded cluster shows each spasm with diffuse voltage attenuation. MRI: cortical tubers and subependymal nodules.
case.q: What is the syndrome and which first-line drug is particularly favoured given the cause?
case.a: Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome (West syndrome) due to tuberous sclerosis complex; vigabatrin is the preferred first treatment in TSC.

det.patho: Epileptic spasms are an age-dependent response of the immature brain to many different insults, structural, genetic, metabolic or unknown. Abnormal interaction between cortex and brainstem with a stress-hormone (CRH) component is proposed, which may explain why corticosteroids and ACTH help. Incidence is roughly 1 in 2,000–4,000 live births.
det.clinical: The 2022 ILAE term is infantile epileptic spasms syndrome (IESS), which covers spasms starting between 1 and 24 months with or without full hypsarrhythmia; West syndrome is the classic triad of spasms, hypsarrhythmia and regression. Spasms are often misread as colic, reflux or Moro responses, delaying care. Asymmetric spasms or associated focal seizures suggest a focal structural lesion. Some infants have no prior delay and a normal MRI, which carries a better outlook.
det.diagnosis: Video-EEG that captures a cluster is the key test; a normal awake EEG does not exclude it, so record sleep and the waking period. Search for a cause with MRI, skin examination, ophthalmology, genetic testing and metabolic studies (including a trial of pyridoxine in selected infants). Recognising IESS is a paediatric neurology emergency because the time to effective treatment influences development.
det.treatment: First-line options are high-dose oral prednisolone or ACTH, or vigabatrin; vigabatrin is preferred in tuberous sclerosis, and combined hormone plus vigabatrin gives faster cessation in some trials. Response is judged within about two weeks by stopping of spasms and resolution of hypsarrhythmia. Hormonal therapy needs blood pressure, glucose and infection monitoring; vigabatrin carries a risk of peripheral visual field loss and reversible MRI signal change. Second-line choices include ketogenic diet, topiramate or other agents, and epilepsy surgery for a resectable lesion.
det.prognosis: Most children have lasting developmental impairment and many go on to other seizure types, including Lennox–Gastaut syndrome; outlook is best with no identified cause and rapid response.
pearls: Clusters on waking plus loss of smile in an infant = IESS until proven otherwise.
Ask parents to film events — video often makes the diagnosis.
Tuberous sclerosis with spasms: vigabatrin first.
det.thd: West syndrome หรือ IESS เป็นโรคลมชักในทารกอายุ 1–24 เดือน (มากสุด 3–12 เดือน) ทารกจะผงกตัวหรือเหยียดเกร็งเป็นชุด ๆ มักหลังตื่นนอน ร่วมกับพัฒนาการถดถอย EEG พบ hypsarrhythmia สาเหตุพบบ่อยคือ tuberous sclerosis สมองขาดออกซิเจน หรือความผิดปกติทางพันธุกรรม ต้องรักษาเร่งด่วนด้วย prednisolone ขนาดสูง ACTH หรือ vigabatrin (เลือก vigabatrin ใน TSC) ยิ่งรักษาเร็วพัฒนาการยิ่งดี

name: Whipple’s disease
formal: Tropheryma whipplei infection with arthralgia, diarrhoea and CNS involvement including oculomasticatory myorhythmia.
simple: A rare bacterial infection of the gut that can affect the brain, causing memory loss and eye movement problems.
more: Diagnosis by PAS-positive macrophages on small bowel biopsy and PCR for the organism in blood, CSF or tissue. Treat with ceftriaxone for 2 weeks then long-term co-trimoxazole for a year; relapse in the CNS is possible.

det.patho: Tropheryma whipplei is a ubiquitous environmental bacterium that causes disease only in people with a particular, poorly defined defect in macrophage and Th1 immune handling. Infected macrophages filled with the organism accumulate in the small bowel, joints, heart and brain and give the characteristic PAS-positive foamy appearance. In the brain, macrophages and microglia carry the bacilli, with neurons rarely involved. Tetracycline-based treatment, which crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly, was historically followed by high rates of CNS relapse.
det.clinical: Classical disease starts with years of arthralgia, followed by weight loss, diarrhoea and fever; neurological disease can appear in three scenarios: with systemic disease, as a relapse after treated gut disease, or as isolated CNS disease. Cognitive decline, ophthalmoplegia and myoclonus form a characteristic triad but only about 15 per cent show all three. Oculomasticatory myorhythmia appears in perhaps one fifth. Hypothalamic dysfunction and psychiatric disturbance are common, and the dementia is sometimes mistaken for Alzheimer disease.
det.diagnosis: Evaluate any unexplained subacute encephalopathy with supranuclear gaze palsy, myoclonus or hypothalamic signs, particularly with weight loss or arthropathy. PCR on CSF and duodenal biopsy, with PAS histology and electron microscopy where available, establishes the diagnosis. PAS positivity is not specific, and PCR positivity in saliva or stool can indicate carriage, so results need clinical correlation. CSF PCR is also used to monitor response.
det.treatment: Treatment must reach the CNS and be prolonged. Current practice begins with intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily (or meropenem, or penicillin with streptomycin) for about 2 weeks, followed by oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for at least 1 year, since sulfamethoxazole alone appears to carry the activity; the combination of doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine is an alternative. The organism is inherently resistant to trimethoprim, and relapse on TMP-SMX alone has been reported, so some experts add or switch to sulfadiazine, doxycycline or cefixime. A paradoxical inflammatory worsening weeks to months into therapy resembles IRIS and often responds to corticosteroids. Follow CSF PCR until negative and clinical review for years.
det.prognosis: Without treatment the disease is fatal; with modern regimens most patients stabilise, although neurological deficits may persist and CNS relapse remains the main threat.
pearls: Eye oscillation in time with jaw contraction almost always means Whipple disease.
Normal gut biopsy does not exclude CNS Whipple disease; send CSF PCR.
Use antibiotics with good CNS penetration and continue treatment for a year or longer.

det.patho: White matter consists of myelinated axons and glia; damage may come from loss of myelin (demyelination), failure to form it (hypomyelination), ischaemia of penetrating arterioles, toxic injury, infection of oligodendrocytes or genetic metabolic defects. Disconnection of frontal-subcortical circuits underlies much of the cognitive profile.
det.clinical: Presentation depends on cause and age. Children with leukodystrophies show developmental regression, spasticity and ataxia; young adults with MS relapse; older adults with small vessel disease develop gradual cognitive slowing, gait apraxia and urinary urgency. Toxic and infectious forms often evolve over weeks.
det.diagnosis: MRI pattern recognition is the core skill: distribution, symmetry, involvement of U-fibres, enhancement and diffusion restriction narrow the differential. Clinical context, CSF, metabolic studies and targeted or broad genetic testing follow. Repeat imaging can show evolution typical of specific diseases.
det.treatment: Treatment is that of the cause: vascular risk control in SVD, disease-modifying therapy in MS, withdrawing toxins, immune reconstitution in PML, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation or gene therapy in selected leukodystrophies when done early.
det.prognosis: Highly variable from reversible (PRES) to relentlessly progressive (some leukodystrophies).
pearls: Read the MRI pattern before ordering a broad panel.
Temporal pole and external capsule involvement: think CADASIL.
Posterior symmetric white matter in a boy with behaviour change: check VLCFA (X-ALD).

Chelation should be introduced gradually because paradoxical neurological deterioration occurs, more often with penicillamine.

qx.stem: A 20-year-old man from Surat Thani has six months of slurred speech, a coarse proximal arm tremor when the arms are held outstretched, and personality change. opts: Lifelong low-copper diet alone
Immediate liver transplantation for all neurological presentations

qx.why: Wilson disease needs lifelong decoppering. Chelators (trientine or D-penicillamine) mobilise copper first, but neurological worsening can occur with rapid copper mobilisation, so doses are increased gradually; zinc blocks intestinal absorption and is used for maintenance. Diet helps only slightly, transplantation is reserved for acute liver failure or decompensated cirrhosis, and iron chelators are irrelevant.

det.patho: Biallelic mutations in ATP7B impair copper incorporation into caeruloplasmin and its excretion into bile, so copper builds up in the liver and spills into the blood, brain, cornea and kidneys. Free copper drives oxidative injury, especially in the putamen, thalamus and brainstem. It is autosomal recessive with a prevalence near 1 in 30,000.
det.clinical: Hepatic presentations (asymptomatic transaminase rise, chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis or acute liver failure with haemolysis) dominate in childhood, whereas neurological or psychiatric presentations usually start in the teens to 30s. Neurological forms include a coarse proximal 'wing-beating' tremor, dystonia with a fixed open-mouth smile, parkinsonism, ataxia, dysarthria and drooling. Psychiatric changes — mood disorder, impulsivity, falling school performance or psychosis — may precede motor signs. Kayser–Fleischer rings are present in about 95% of neurological cases but are often absent in purely hepatic disease.
det.diagnosis: Combine clinical signs with copper studies: low caeruloplasmin (below about 0.1 g/L is strongly suggestive), raised 24-hour urinary copper, and slit-lamp examination for KF rings. The Leipzig score integrates these with liver copper content and ATP7B genotyping. MRI often shows symmetric T2 change in the putamen, thalamus and brainstem. Pitfalls: caeruloplasmin can be falsely normal during inflammation and low in heterozygotes, protein loss or malnutrition. Screen all first-degree relatives.
det.treatment: Lifelong decoppering therapy is required: chelators (D-penicillamine or trientine) for symptomatic disease, and zinc salts (which block intestinal copper absorption) for maintenance or presymptomatic cases. Introduce chelators gradually, because neurological worsening can occur early in treatment, especially with penicillamine. Avoid copper-rich foods such as shellfish, nuts, chocolate and liver early on. Monitor urinary copper, blood count and renal function; liver transplantation is curative for fulminant failure or decompensated cirrhosis.
det.prognosis: With early, adherent treatment survival approaches normal and many neurological signs improve over 1–3 years; stopping therapy can be fatal.
pearls: Any unexplained movement disorder or liver disease before age 40 deserves copper studies.
Neurological Wilson disease without KF rings is unusual — look with a slit lamp, not just a penlight.
Early paradoxical worsening on chelation is a known hazard; start low and titrate.

det.patho: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in DCAF17, a nucleolar protein of unclear function linked to the ubiquitin ligase system, cause the syndrome. det.clinical: Endocrine and dermatological features usually precede neurological ones. Dystonia, dysarthria and dysphagia appear later and progress. Intellectual disability and hearing loss vary in severity, and some patients have seizures or ECG abnormalities. Knowledge comes from a few hundred reported cases, so the natural history is incompletely defined.
det.diagnosis: Suspect with the combination of alopecia, hypogonadism, diabetes and dystonia, especially with consanguinity. Genetic testing confirms. MRI white matter disease is common and supportive.
det.treatment: There is no disease-specific therapy. Hormone replacement for hypogonadism, diabetes management, hearing aids and educational support are needed. Dystonia may partly respond to anticholinergics, botulinum toxin or, in selected cases, deep brain stimulation.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; long-term outcome data are limited.
pearls: Alopecia plus hypogonadism plus dystonia — think DCAF17.
Endocrine features usually appear before the movement disorder.
Counsel families about recessive inheritance in consanguineous unions.

det.patho: Repetitive, highly skilled movements combined with predisposing factors lead to maladaptive plasticity in sensorimotor cortex and basal ganglia. Studies show reduced inhibition at several levels and blurred cortical hand maps. Genetic susceptibility is suspected but no single gene explains most cases.
det.clinical: This is an umbrella for task-specific focal dystonias. Writer's cramp is the commonest; musicians' dystonia often ends professional careers; similar syndromes occur in typists, tailors, hair stylists and sports players. Symptoms start as reduced precision and progress to visible posturing, cramping discomfort or tremor. Some progress to involve other tasks (dystonic writer's cramp).
det.diagnosis: Observation of the triggering task is the key. Sensory tricks may help transiently. Neurophysiology is not routinely needed. Exclude orthopaedic and nerve problems, and consider secondary causes when the onset is young, progression is fast, or there are additional neurological signs.
det.treatment: EMG- or ultrasound-guided botulinum toxin into the overactive muscles is the most effective option. Retraining strategies, ergonomic adaptation (thicker pens, instrument modification) and occupational therapy help. Oral anticholinergics benefit a minority. Thalamic (Vo) lesions or DBS are performed in specialised centres for refractory cases.
det.prognosis: Usually chronic; spontaneous remission is uncommon, but many maintain function with toxin and adaptation.
pearls: Watch the patient do the task — examination at rest is often normal.
Mirror dystonia helps confirm the diagnosis and target injections.
Pain is usually mild; prominent pain suggests another cause.

name: Writer’s cramp
formal: Task-specific focal hand dystonia with cramping during writing.
simple: Hand cramping that occurs only while writing.
more: Task-specific focal hand dystonia triggered by writing, causing abnormal finger and wrist postures, often with tremor, and reflecting abnormal sensorimotor cortical plasticity.
th: Writer’s cramp คือ task-specific focal hand dystonia ที่เกิดเฉพาะเวลาเขียนหนังสือ นิ้วหรือข้อมือเกร็งผิดท่า เขียนช้าและอ่านไม่ออก พบได้ในวัย 30–50 ปี รักษาด้วยการฉีด botulinum toxin ใต้การนำของ EMG ฝึกประสาทรับความรู้สึกใหม่ และพิจารณายา trihexyphenidyl หรือผ่าตัดสมองในรายรุนแรง
tempoNote: Starts gradually in adulthood over months, often worsens for a year or two and then stabilises; spread to other manual tasks happens in a minority
feat: Abnormal grip and postures only while writing: excessive pen pressure, finger flexion or extension, wrist flexion, elbow lifting or shoulder elevation
Simple writer's cramp affects only writing, while dystonic (progressive) forms spread to other fine tasks such as using a spoon or shaving
Handwriting is slow, cramped and tiring, with forearm aching; strength, tone, sensation and reflexes are normal
Mirror dystonia (posturing of the dystonic hand when the other hand writes) and sensory tricks may be seen; the underlying tremor appears in about a quarter as dystonic tremor
Related task-specific forms include musician's cramp, typist's cramp and golfer's or tennis yips; a neighbouring dystonic tremor is the commonest accompaniment
inv: Observation of writing and drawing a spiral, and examination of other tasks to look for spread
NCS/EMG to exclude ulnar or median neuropathy, cervical radiculopathy or motor neuron disease when there is pain, numbness or wasting
MRI brain or cervical spine only for young onset, rapid progression, asymmetric signs or a poor response to initial treatment; copper studies under 50 years

case.story: Over two years writing reports by hand has become tiring: his index finger extends and his wrist bends after a few lines, and he now grips the pen so hard that it digs into his fingers. Typing and eating are fine.
case.exam: Normal at rest; during writing the pen is squeezed, the wrist flexes and the elbow lifts; mirror posturing of the right hand appears when the left hand writes; no weakness or sensory loss.
case.tests: Nerve conduction studies and cervical spine MRI are normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the most useful treatment?
case.a: Simple writer's cramp (task-specific focal hand dystonia); botulinum toxin injected under EMG guidance into the overactive forearm muscles, combined with pen adaptations and hand retraining.

det.patho: Writer's cramp is a task-specific focal dystonia with loss of inhibitory control in the sensorimotor cortex and basal ganglia. Studies show reduced intracortical inhibition, lowered GABA levels in the sensorimotor cortex and basal ganglia, and blurred finger representations in the somatosensory cortex, so that overlapping motor and sensory patterns make agonist and antagonist muscles contract at the same time. Repetitive stereotyped practice combined with genetic susceptibility is thought to drive the plastic changes.
det.clinical: Most patients are between 30 and 50 years old and have no other neurological disease. The patient describes tight, tired fingers and an illegible script that needs more and more effort; a very forceful pen grip is typical. The abnormality appears only for the specific task at first and may later occur in other fine movements. Anxiety is common but is a result, not the cause. A positive family history of dystonia is found in a few patients. Musicians, typists and craftspeople develop similar cramps with their own tools.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical and needs a careful look at the writing posture, with an unfilled complaint of pain or weakness prompting a neuropathic or myopathic search. Nerve conduction studies exclude entrapment neuropathies, and EMG during writing can identify which muscles contribute to the posture before treatment. Brain MRI is for atypical cases only. The differential includes primary writing tremor, early Parkinson disease with micrographia and functional dystonia.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin injected under EMG or ultrasound guidance into selected flexor and extensor forearm muscles is the standard treatment and is better for the simple form; weakness of the fingers is the main side effect. Behavioural and sensory retraining, adaptive pens with thick barrels, grip aids and splinting, or switching to typing or voice-recognition tools, help function. Trihexyphenidyl and other oral drugs bring only limited benefit. In disabling drug-resistant cases thalamic lesioning or deep brain stimulation, and in some centres focused ultrasound, have been used with partial success.
det.prognosis: Symptoms usually stay confined to the hand and often stabilise, and with toxin and adaptive measures most patients keep working; spontaneous remission is uncommon.
pearls: Writing difficulty without weakness, numbness or tremor in a middle-aged adult is dystonia until proved otherwise.
Look for mirror dystonia in the other hand when the patient writes with the left.
Warn patients before botulinum toxin that grip weakness is the price of improvement.
det.thd: Writer's cramp คือ focal dystonia ของมือที่เกิดเฉพาะขณะเขียนหนังสือ นิ้วหรือข้อมือเกร็งผิดท่า ปากกาถูกบีบแรง ลายมือช้าและอ่านยาก โดยกำลังและความรู้สึกปกติ ควรตรวจ NCS ถ้ามีอาการชาหรือกล้ามเนื้อลีบ และแยกจาก primary writing tremor และ Parkinson disease การรักษาที่ได้ผลดีคือฉีด botulinum toxin ใต้ EMG ร่วมกับฝึกการเขียนและใช้ปากกาปรับรูป

qx.stem: A 42-year-old accountant has five years of cramping of the right hand that appears only when he writes, with the wrist flexing and the index finger lifting off the pen. Typing and using chopsticks are normal. Neurological examination is otherwise normal and MRI brain is unremarkable.
qx.q: Which treatment has the best evidence for improving his writing?
opts: Oral clonazepam
EMG-guided botulinum toxin injections into the involved forearm muscles
Carpal tunnel release
Levodopa
Bilateral GPi deep brain stimulation
qx.why: Writing-only hand cramping like this is a task-related focal dystonia, and targeted botulinum toxin injection guided by EMG or ultrasound is the most effective treatment, often combined with writing aids and retraining. Oral drugs give modest benefit, carpal tunnel release does not treat dystonia, and DBS is not used for isolated focal hand dystonia except in rare research settings.

name: Writing tremor
formal: Task-specific tremor occurring during writing, a variant of essential tremor.
simple: Hand shaking that occurs when writing.
th: อาการสั่นเฉพาะเวลาเขียน (task-specific tremor) อยู่ระหว่าง essential tremor และ dystonia
tempoNote: Gradual onset in middle age; slow progression
feat: Rhythmic pronation-supination tremor (about 5–7 Hz) when writing
Type A appears only when writing; type B also when holding the hand in the writing position
Little tremor during other tasks such as drinking
No sustained dystonic posture, though subtle dystonia may coexist
Often improves with alcohol or propranolol in some patients
inv: Clinical diagnosis by observing writing and Archimedes spirals
Surface EMG to measure frequency and look for co-contraction
Thyroid function; MRI only for atypical features

case.story: For three years his hand shakes as soon as he starts writing his signature, but he drinks soup without spilling.
case.exam: No rest or postural tremor; on writing, rhythmic pronation-supination tremor; no posturing.
case.tests: Thyroid normal; EMG tremor 6 Hz during writing only.
case.q: What task-specific disorder is this, and which treatments may help?
case.a: Primary writing tremor (type A); options are propranolol, primidone, botulinum toxin or, if severe, thalamic DBS.

det.patho: Primary writing tremor is a task-specific tremor whose classification is debated: some regard it as a variant of essential tremor, others as a form of dystonic tremor, given overlapping physiology. Cerebellar and sensorimotor cortex involvement has been shown in imaging studies. Its cause is unknown.
det.clinical: Patients have tremor that starts on writing and stops when writing ends, usually involving forearm rotation. A position-sensitive form also appears when the hand adopts the writing posture without a pen. Other tasks are spared or minimally affected. It is less common than writer's cramp.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, observing writing and spirals; EMG can document the tremor frequency and pattern. Exclude essential tremor (tremor in many tasks), writer's cramp (posturing) and parkinsonism. Imaging is not needed unless there are other signs.
det.treatment: Responses vary between patients. Propranolol, primidone or anticholinergic drugs help some. Botulinum toxin into pronators or forearm muscles can reduce tremor. Writing aids and changing grip help, and thalamic DBS has been effective in severe cases.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive or stable; does not lead to other neurological disease.
pearls: Tremor confined to writing, without posturing: primary writing tremor.
Check whether it occurs in the writing posture without a pen (type B).
Overlap with writer's cramp is common — look carefully for subtle dystonia.
det.thd: Writing tremor คืออาการสั่นที่เกิดเฉพาะเวลาเขียน มักเป็นการบิดข้อมือเข้า-ออกเป็นจังหวะ ไม่มีท่าทางเกร็งแบบ dystonia และงานอื่นไม่ค่อยสั่น ยังถกเถียงว่าเป็นกลุ่ม essential tremor หรือ dystonic tremor วินิจฉัยจากการดูขณะเขียน รักษาด้วย propranolol, primidone, botulinum toxin หรือ DBS ในรายที่รุนแรง

ddx.pt: Abnormal sustained posture during writing rather than rhythmic tremor
Postural and kinetic tremor in many tasks, not just writing

aN: primary writing tremor | pwt | task specific writing tremor | type a b writing tremor

name: X-linked ataxia syndromes
formal: Group of hereditary ataxias with X-linked inheritance, including fragile X tremor ataxia syndrome.
simple: Inherited balance disorders passed through the X chromosome.
th: กลุ่มโรคสมองน้อยเสื่อมทางพันธุกรรมที่ถ่ายทอดทางโครโมโซม X เช่น FXTAS ซึ่งพบในชายสูงอายุที่เป็นพาหะ premutation ของ FMR1
tempoNote: Childhood onset in congenital forms; adult onset (over 50) in FXTAS
feat: Affected males through unaffected or mildly affected mothers; no male-to-male transmission
FXTAS: late-onset intention tremor, gait ataxia, cognitive decline, neuropathy, autonomic failure
Other members: X-linked sideroblastic anaemia with ataxia (ABCB7), ATP2B3 congenital ataxia, PRPS1 disorders, OPHN1
Adrenomyeloneuropathy can present with ataxia and spastic paraparesis in men
Female carriers may have milder symptoms, premature ovarian insufficiency (FMR1)
inv: FMR1 CGG repeat sizing (premutation 55–200)
MRI: middle cerebellar peduncle T2 hyperintensity in FXTAS; cerebellar atrophy in others
Very long chain fatty acids for adrenomyeloneuropathy; blood film for sideroblastic anaemia
Gene panel or exome for childhood X-linked ataxias

case.story: Three years of worsening hand tremor and unsteady walking, recent forgetfulness. His grandson has autism and intellectual disability.
case.exam: Kinetic tremor, gait ataxia, mild distal sensory loss, impaired executive function.
case.tests: MRI shows bilateral middle cerebellar peduncle T2 hyperintensity; FMR1 CGG repeat 95.
case.q: Which X-linked ataxia links him to his grandson's condition?
case.a: Fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome — he carries an FMR1 premutation; the grandson has full fragile X syndrome.

read.where: Chapter 24 Cerebellar Ataxias and Related Conditions

det.patho: Mechanisms differ by gene. In FXTAS, a premutation-length CGG repeat in FMR1 causes toxic RNA gain of function with intranuclear inclusions in neurons and astrocytes. ABCB7 variants disturb mitochondrial iron-sulphur cluster export, causing sideroblastic anaemia and cerebellar hypoplasia. ATP2B3 encodes a cerebellar calcium pump, and adrenomyeloneuropathy arises from ABCD1 loss with very long chain fatty acid accumulation.
det.clinical: FXTAS is the most common X-linked ataxia in adults: men over 50 with tremor, ataxia, parkinsonism, neuropathy and cognitive decline; women carriers are less often and less severely affected. Childhood-onset X-linked ataxias are rare and often congenital or non-progressive, with developmental delay. A family history of fragile X syndrome, autism or premature ovarian failure is a powerful clue.
det.diagnosis: Take a three-generation family history. Test FMR1 repeat size in any older adult with unexplained ataxia or tremor plus cognitive change. Look for middle cerebellar peduncle sign on MRI, though it is not universal. Use VLCFA testing, blood film and gene panels for other members.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy exists for most. Symptomatic options include beta-blockers or primidone for tremor, physiotherapy for gait, and management of cognitive and mood symptoms. Adrenomyeloneuropathy needs adrenal function monitoring and replacement. Genetic counselling is essential because daughters of affected men are obligate carriers.
det.prognosis: FXTAS progresses over years to loss of independent walking and cognitive decline; outlook of other forms depends on the gene.
pearls: Grandfather with ataxia-tremor and grandchild with intellectual disability: test FMR1.
Middle cerebellar peduncle hyperintensity is a classic FXTAS clue.
Adult men with spastic-ataxic gait: check VLCFA for adrenomyeloneuropathy.
det.thd: X-linked ataxia syndromes คือกลุ่มโรคเดินเซทางพันธุกรรมที่ถ่ายทอดทางโครโมโซม X ส่วนใหญ่เกิดในผู้ชาย ที่สำคัญที่สุดคือ FXTAS ในชายอายุเกิน 50 ปีที่เป็นพาหะ premutation ของยีน FMR1 มีมือสั่น เดินเซ ความจำแย่ลง MRI พบสัญญาณผิดปกติที่ middle cerebellar peduncle ประวัติครอบครัวที่มีหลานเป็น fragile X หรือออทิสติกเป็นเบาะแสสำคัญ การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคองและให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

Autosomal dominant with affected individuals in each generation, including women

name: X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (Lubag)
formal: Lubag: X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism in Filipino men, TAF1 haplotype, with focal dystonia progressing to parkinsonism.
simple: An inherited movement disorder in men of Filipino descent causing dystonia then parkinsonism.
more: X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (DYT3), from Filipino Panay island ancestry, with adult-onset focal dystonia progressing to parkinsonism; associated with a TAF1 mutation. X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (Lubag) is a Filipino X-linked disorder from a SVA retrotransposon insertion in TAF1, with adult onset focal dystonia becoming generalised, followed by parkinsonism. Diagnosis by genetic testing of the TAF1 haplotype; no cure. Treat with anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, botulinum toxin and deep brain stimulation.
th: dystonia ร่วมกับ parkinsonism ที่ถ่ายทอดทางโครโมโซม X พบในชายเชื้อสายฟิลิปปินส์จากเกาะปาไน เกิดจากการแทรกของ SVA ในยีน TAF1
tempoNote: Adult onset (mean about 40 years); dystonia generalises over a few years, then parkinsonism dominates
feat: Men of Filipino (mainly Panay island) ancestry; female carriers rarely symptomatic
Starts as focal dystonia (jaw, neck, blepharospasm, limb) that generalises
Parkinsonism emerges later and may become the main problem
Striatal atrophy, especially caudate and putamen
Poor and short-lived response to levodopa
inv: Genetic test for the SVA retrotransposon insertion in TAF1 (or associated haplotype)
MRI: caudate and putaminal atrophy; may show putaminal rim hyperintensity
Exclude Wilson disease (ceruloplasmin, slit-lamp) in any young dystonia

case.who: 41-year-old Filipino English teacher working in Bangkok
case.story: Eighteen months of forced jaw opening and neck twisting, now spreading to his trunk; recently slower and stooped. His maternal uncle had a similar illness.
case.exam: Oromandibular and cervical dystonia, truncal dystonia, bradykinesia and rigidity, no tremor at rest.
case.tests: Ceruloplasmin normal; MRI shows striatal atrophy; TAF1 SVA insertion detected.
case.q: Which X-linked movement disorder fits, and which treatment has the best evidence for the dystonia?
case.a: X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (Lubag); pallidal DBS for disabling dystonia, plus botulinum toxin for focal targets.

det.patho: A SINE-VNTR-Alu retrotransposon inserted in an intron of TAF1 reduces expression of normal TAF1 transcripts, disturbing transcription in striatal neurons. The length of a hexanucleotide repeat within the insertion modifies age of onset. Medium spiny neurons of the striosomal compartment degenerate first, followed by broader striatal loss.
det.clinical: Most patients develop focal dystonia in their thirties or forties that generalises within about five years. Parkinsonism then becomes prominent, and dystonia may lessen as the disease advances. Bulbar involvement causes dysphagia and aspiration. Depression and anxiety are common. The condition is highly prevalent among men from Capiz on Panay and in the Filipino diaspora.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in any man of Filipino ancestry with adult-onset dystonia or dystonia-parkinsonism, especially with a maternal family history. Confirm with targeted genetic testing. MRI shows striatal atrophy. Exclude Wilson disease and drug-induced syndromes.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin helps focal components. Oral drugs (anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, zolpidem in some) offer modest benefit. Bilateral GPi DBS can markedly improve dystonia, though parkinsonism may continue to progress. Levodopa may help parkinsonism briefly. Swallowing assessment, nutrition and psychosocial support are essential.
det.prognosis: Progressive over 10–20 years; aspiration pneumonia and malnutrition are common causes of death.
pearls: Filipino man with adult-onset dystonia: think Lubag.
Dystonia first, parkinsonism later — the reverse of many degenerative disorders.
GPi DBS helps the dystonia more than the parkinsonism.
det.thd: X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (Lubag) พบในชายเชื้อสายฟิลิปปินส์โดยเฉพาะจากเกาะปาไน เกิดจากการแทรกของ SVA ในยีน TAF1 เริ่มด้วย focal dystonia ในวัยผู้ใหญ่แล้วลามทั่วตัว ต่อมามี parkinsonism เด่น MRI พบ striatum ฝ่อ วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีน การรักษาใช้ botulinum toxin ยารับประทาน และ GPi DBS ซึ่งช่วย dystonia ได้ดี

name: X-linked myopathy with excessive autophagy (XMEA)
formal: X-linked vacuolar myopathy from VMA21 variants causing slowly progressive proximal weakness in boys, with autophagic vacuoles and sparing of cardiac muscle.
simple: An inherited muscle disease in boys causing slowly worsening weakness in the hips and thighs.
more: CK is mild to moderately raised; biopsy shows autophagic vacuoles with sarcolemmal features. Treatment is supportive, and many remain ambulant into adulthood.
th: โรคกล้ามเนื้อถ่ายทอดทางโครโมโซม X จากยีน VMA21 ทำให้เด็กชายมีกล้ามเนื้อต้นขาอ่อนแรงช้า ๆ โดยหัวใจไม่เกี่ยวข้อง และชิ้นเนื้อพบ autophagic vacuoles
tempoNote: Onset in childhood, very slow progression; most walk into later adulthood
feat: Boys with slowly progressive proximal leg weakness, quadriceps prominent
Heart and brain spared (contrast with Danon disease)
CK moderately raised
Carrier women usually unaffected
Very rare; families described in Europe, North America and Asia
inv: Biopsy: autophagic vacuoles with sarcolemmal features, complement (C5b-9) deposition on fibre surface
VMA21 sequencing (often non-coding or splice variants)
ECG and echo to exclude Danon disease

case.story: Slow runner since primary school; now has difficulty climbing stairs. A maternal uncle had similar weakness but walked into old age.
case.exam: Proximal leg weakness with thin thighs, mild shoulder involvement, normal cognition and heart sounds.
case.tests: CK 1,400 U/L, normal echocardiogram, biopsy shows autophagic vacuoles with MAC deposition, VMA21 variant.
case.q: Why is Danon disease less likely?
case.a: No cardiomyopathy or intellectual disability; this is XMEA, a pure, slowly progressive myopathy.

det.patho: VMA21 is an assembly chaperone for the vacuolar ATPase that acidifies lysosomes. Reduced function raises lysosomal pH, impairs degradation and triggers compensatory overactivation of autophagy. Autophagic vacuoles with sarcolemmal features accumulate, and complement deposits on the fibre surface, though the disease is not inflammatory.
det.clinical: Affected boys develop slowly progressive proximal weakness, mostly of the legs, during childhood. Many remain ambulant until late adult life. Cardiac, respiratory and central nervous system involvement is absent or minimal, which distinguishes it from other autophagic vacuolar myopathies.
det.diagnosis: Muscle biopsy is characteristic, showing vacuoles lined by sarcolemmal proteins and membrane attack complex deposition. Genetic testing of VMA21 confirms; variants are often in non-coding regions and may be missed by standard exome analysis. Cardiac assessment helps exclude Danon disease.
det.treatment: No specific therapy; supportive physiotherapy, orthotics and genetic counselling for carrier females. Immunosuppression is not indicated despite complement deposition.
det.prognosis: Slow progression with long-preserved walking and normal life expectancy in most.
pearls: Autophagic vacuolar myopathy in a boy: check the heart — Danon vs XMEA.
Complement on the fibre surface does not mean myositis here.
VMA21 variants can hide in non-coding regions.
det.thd: XMEA เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้อถ่ายทอดทางโครโมโซม X จากยีน VMA21 ทำให้ lysosome ไม่เป็นกรดเพียงพอ เกิด autophagic vacuoles สะสม เด็กชายมีต้นขาอ่อนแรงช้า ๆ แต่หัวใจและสมองปกติ ต่างจาก Danon disease ชิ้นเนื้อพบ vacuoles และ complement ที่ผิวเซลล์ ไม่มีการรักษาเฉพาะ

name: Yellow star thistle poisoning in horses
formal: Equine nigropallidal encephalomalacia from ingestion of Centaurea solstitialis, causing necrosis of globus pallidus and substantia nigra with dystonia, dysphagia and abnormal chewing; a veterinary toxic parkinsonism model.
simple: A poisoning of horses from eating a weed that damages deep brain areas, causing stiff face muscles and trouble eating.
th: โรคในม้า (ไม่ใช่โรคของมนุษย์) จากการกินพืช yellow star thistle เป็นเวลานาน ทำให้ globus pallidus และ substantia nigra ตาย เกิดการเคี้ยวผิดปกติและกินอาหารไม่ได้
tempoNote: Abrupt onset after weeks to months of grazing the plant; deficits are permanent
feat: Veterinary disorder of horses; quoted in neurology as a model of toxic pallidonigral necrosis
Sudden inability to prehend and chew food; lips and tongue held in abnormal postures (dystonia of the mouth)
Continuous chewing movements, yawning, head pressing
Symmetric necrotic lesions in both pallidal nuclei and the nigral pars reticulata
Animals starve or dehydrate without support
inv: History of grazing infested pasture in dry seasons
MRI or necropsy shows symmetric pallidonigral lesions
No human diagnostic tests apply

case.who: Imported 10-year-old horse at a riding club near Hua Hin
case.story: Fed for several months on hay bought from a region where the plant grows; suddenly cannot pick up feed and keeps its mouth half open.
case.exam: Lips retracted, tongue protruding and rolling, constant chewing, otherwise alert with normal gait.
case.tests: Veterinary necropsy after euthanasia shows bilateral softening of globus pallidus and substantia nigra.
case.q: Why do neurologists mention this horse disease?
case.a: It is a natural model of selective toxic damage to the pallidum and nigra, comparable to human toxic dystonia-parkinsonism (e.g. CO or manganese).

det.patho: Yellow star thistle (Centaurea solstitialis) contains sesquiterpene lactones such as repin that are toxic to dopaminergic and pallidal neurons, possibly through glutathione depletion and oxidative stress. Horses must eat large amounts over weeks before lesions appear. Other species are rarely affected.
det.clinical: This is a veterinary condition, not a human disease. Affected horses suddenly lose the ability to grasp and chew food, with dystonic posturing of the lips and tongue and repetitive chewing. Gait is usually preserved. The deficit is permanent, and most animals are euthanised.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis in horses relies on exposure history and characteristic oral signs, confirmed by imaging or necropsy showing bilateral pallidonigral necrosis. Rabies and other equine encephalitides are considered in the veterinary differential.
det.treatment: There is no effective treatment; management is preventive (pasture control and avoiding contaminated hay). For human neurology the value is conceptual, illustrating how selective toxins can damage basal ganglia output nuclei.
det.prognosis: Poor in horses; lesions do not recover.
pearls: Not a human disease — a veterinary model of toxic basal ganglia injury.
Lesions mirror the human pallidonigral damage from CO, cyanide or manganese.
Oromandibular dystonia in horses parallels feeding dystonia in human pallidal disorders.
det.thd: Yellow star thistle poisoning เป็นโรคของม้า ไม่ใช่โรคของคน เกิดจากการกินพืช Centaurea solstitialis เป็นเวลานาน ทำให้ globus pallidus และ substantia nigra ตายทั้งสองข้าง ม้าจะเคี้ยวและหยิบอาหารไม่ได้ ปากและลิ้นเกร็งผิดท่า ไม่มีทางรักษา ในทางประสาทวิทยาใช้เป็นตัวอย่างของสารพิษที่ทำลาย basal ganglia แบบจำเพาะ คล้ายพิษ CO หรือแมงกานีสในคน

name: Zebra body myopathy
formal: Rare congenital or early-onset myopathy with distinctive zebra-striped subsarcolemmal inclusions on electron microscopy, with proximal weakness and hypotonia; genetics heterogeneous, ACTA1 linked in some.
simple: A rare muscle disease in which muscle samples under the electron microscope show zebra-like stripes, causing weakness.
more: Diagnosis relies on biopsy ultrastructure and gene testing. Care is supportive including respiratory monitoring; course varies from mild to severe.
th: congenital myopathy ที่พบน้อยมาก ชิ้นเนื้อด้วยกล้องจุลทรรศน์อิเล็กตรอนพบ zebra bodies ลายแถบ อ่อนแรงต้นแขนขาและกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนปวกเปียก
tempoNote: Congenital or early childhood onset; mostly static or slowly progressive
feat: Very few reported cases; nature as a distinct entity is uncertain
Neonatal or infantile hypotonia, delayed motor milestones
Mild proximal and facial weakness, reduced reflexes
Zebra bodies are also seen normally near myotendinous junctions and in other myopathies, so they are nonspecific
Some cases linked to ACTA1 variants, overlapping with other actin myopathies
inv: CK normal or mildly raised
Muscle biopsy with electron microscopy (striated zebra bodies, away from tendon insertion)
Congenital myopathy gene panel (ACTA1 and others)
Respiratory function and sleep study

case.who: 2-year-old boy referred to a university hospital in Songkhla
case.story: Floppy since birth, sat at 12 months and is not yet walking; feeds slowly.
case.exam: Generalised hypotonia, mild facial weakness, proximal weakness, depressed reflexes, no tongue fasciculation.
case.tests: CK 150 U/L; SMN1 testing normal; biopsy EM shows many zebra bodies; ACTA1 heterozygous variant.
case.q: Why must the biopsy result be interpreted with caution?
case.a: Zebra bodies are nonspecific (also at myotendinous junctions); genetic results define the disorder, here an ACTA1-related congenital myopathy.

det.patho: Zebra bodies are electron-dense striated structures made of actin and Z-disc material. They occur normally at myotendinous junctions and in various myopathies, so their specificity is limited. A small number of patients with a congenital myopathy dominated by zebra bodies have been described, at least one with an ACTA1 variant, suggesting it may belong to the actin-related myopathy spectrum rather than being a separate disease.
det.clinical: Reported patients had congenital hypotonia, delayed milestones and mild non-progressive proximal weakness. Because so few cases exist, the full phenotype, inheritance and natural history are unknown. In practice, such a child is managed like other congenital myopathies.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires EM showing numerous zebra bodies in muscle away from tendon insertion, in a child with a congenital myopathy phenotype. Genetic testing with a congenital myopathy panel or exome is essential and frequently reclassifies the disorder. Exclude SMA and congenital myotonic dystrophy.
det.treatment: Supportive: physiotherapy, orthoses, monitoring for scoliosis, nutritional support and surveillance of respiratory function including nocturnal hypoventilation. Inform anaesthetists about the myopathy. Genetic counselling depends on the variant.
det.prognosis: Limited data; reported cases have been mild and stable.
pearls: Zebra bodies alone are not diagnostic — they occur at normal myotendinous junctions.
Treat a 'zebra body myopathy' label as provisional until genetics are done.
Monitor breathing at night in all congenital myopathies.
det.thd: Zebra body myopathy เป็น congenital myopathy ที่พบน้อยมาก ชิ้นเนื้อด้วยกล้องอิเล็กตรอนพบ zebra bodies แต่สิ่งนี้ไม่จำเพาะ พบได้ในกล้ามเนื้อปกติใกล้รอยต่อเอ็น เด็กมีภาวะตัวอ่อนแต่กำเนิด พัฒนาการช้า อ่อนแรงต้นแขนขาเล็กน้อย บางรายสัมพันธ์กับยีน ACTA1 จึงควรตรวจยีนเสมอ การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคองและเฝ้าระวังการหายใจ

name: Zinc deficiency
formal: Deficiency that can cause neuropathy, myelopathy or, via copper deficiency, ataxia; excess zinc causes copper deficiency myeloneuropathy.
simple: Low zinc can contribute to nerve and taste problems.
th: ขาดสังกะสีทำให้ผื่น ท้องเสีย และรับรสผิดปกติ ส่วนสังกะสีเกินทำให้ขาดทองแดงจนเกิด myeloneuropathy
tempoNote: Weeks to months of deficiency; months to years of excess zinc before copper deficiency myelopathy
feat: Zinc deficiency: dermatitis around mouth and extremities, alopecia, diarrhoea, taste and smell loss, poor wound healing
Settings: malabsorption, alcohol, parenteral nutrition, chronic diarrhoea, acrodermatitis enteropathica
Excess zinc (denture cream, supplements) causes copper deficiency myeloneuropathy with sensory ataxia and spasticity
Anaemia and neutropenia accompany copper deficiency
Neurological effects of pure zinc deficiency are less well defined
inv: Serum zinc and copper, ceruloplasmin
Full blood count for anaemia and neutropenia
MRI spine for dorsal column T2 signal in myeloneuropathy

case.story: Uses large amounts of denture adhesive daily for years; progressive unsteady gait and numb feet for a year.
case.exam: Sensory ataxia, positive Romberg, brisk knee jerks, absent ankle jerks, upgoing toes.
case.tests: Serum copper very low, zinc high; anaemia and neutropenia; MRI shows dorsal column T2 signal.
case.q: What is the mechanism and how is it treated?
case.a: Zinc excess induces intestinal metallothionein that traps copper, causing copper deficiency myeloneuropathy; stop the zinc source and replace copper.

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System — Vitamin and Mineral Deficiencies and Toxicity
11 Neurological consequences of copper and zinc deficiency

det.patho: Zinc is a cofactor for many enzymes and transcription factors. Deficiency mainly affects skin, gut, immunity, taste and growth. Excess zinc upregulates enterocyte metallothionein, which binds copper and prevents its absorption, leading to copper deficiency that damages the dorsal columns, corticospinal tracts and peripheral nerves.
det.clinical: Deficiency presents with periorificial dermatitis, diarrhoea, alopecia and altered taste; neurological symptoms such as mood change may occur but are nonspecific. Zinc excess presents months to years later with a B12-like myeloneuropathy and cytopenias.
det.diagnosis: Measure serum zinc (interpreting with albumin and inflammation) and copper with ceruloplasmin. In myeloneuropathy, low copper with high zinc points to zinc excess; search for denture cream, supplements or occupational sources.
det.treatment: Replace zinc in deficiency. For zinc-induced copper deficiency, stop the zinc source and give copper supplements; haematological recovery is faster than neurological recovery.
det.prognosis: Skin and gut features of deficiency respond quickly; neurological deficits from copper deficiency often improve only partially.
pearls: Ask about denture cream in unexplained myeloneuropathy.
Low copper with high zinc indicates zinc excess.
Cytopenias plus myelopathy suggests copper deficiency.
det.thd: การขาดสังกะสีทำให้ผื่นรอบปากและมือเท้า ผมร่วง ท้องเสีย และรับรสผิดปกติ ส่วนการได้รับสังกะสีมากเกินไป เช่น ใช้ครีมติดฟันปลอมปริมาณมาก ทำให้ร่างกายดูดซึมทองแดงไม่ได้ เกิด copper deficiency myeloneuropathy คล้าย subacute combined degeneration ร่วมกับซีดและเม็ดเลือดขาวต่ำ การรักษาคือหยุดแหล่งสังกะสีและให้ทองแดงทดแทน

name: Zoster-associated encephalitis
formal: Encephalitis complicating VZV reactivation, with headache, fever, confusion and vasculopathy, mostly in immunosuppressed patients.
simple: Brain infection after shingles virus reactivates, causing confusion and fever.
th: สมองอักเสบจากการกลับมาของเชื้อ varicella zoster มีไข้ ปวดศีรษะ สับสน และอาจมีหลอดเลือดสมองอักเสบร่วม พบมากในผู้ป่วยภูมิคุ้มกันต่ำและผู้สูงอายุ
tempoNote: Develops over days, often within 1–3 weeks of a zoster rash, but may occur without any rash
feat: Fever, headache, confusion, behaviour change and seizures in an elderly or immunosuppressed person
Recent dermatomal rash (especially trigeminal or cervical), sometimes disseminated, sometimes absent
Vasculopathic component: focal deficits from infarcts or small-vessel ischaemia
May coexist with cranial neuropathies (Ramsay Hunt), myelitis or meningitis
Second most common identified cause of viral encephalitis after HSV in many series
inv: CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein; PCR for VZV DNA plus the anti-VZV IgG antibody index
MRI brain: multifocal white-grey junction lesions, infarcts, or normal early
EEG for subclinical seizures; HIV test and review of immunosuppressive drugs

case.who: 74-year-old man from Nakhon Si Thammarat receiving chemotherapy for lymphoma
case.story: Ten days after a painful vesicular rash over the right side of the neck he becomes feverish, sleepy and muddled, then has a generalised seizure.
case.exam: Temperature 38.5 °C, disoriented, mild neck stiffness, left pronator drift; crusting lesions in the right C3 dermatome.
case.tests: CSF 120 cells (lymphocytes), protein 1.1 g/L, glucose normal, VZV PCR positive; MRI shows small bilateral subcortical infarcts and patchy white matter signal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the drug of choice?
case.a: VZV encephalitis with vasculopathy in an immunocompromised patient; intravenous aciclovir 10–15 mg/kg every 8 hours with dose adjusted to renal function, often with a short steroid course for vasculopathy.

read.where: Infectious Diseases of the Nervous System — Viral Infections: Herpes Zoster

det.patho: VZV reactivates from sensory ganglia when cell-mediated immunity wanes with age, malignancy, transplantation, HIV or immunosuppressive drugs. The virus reaches the brain through neural spread or viraemia, and much of the brain injury reflects infection of cerebral vessels (a small- and large-vessel vasculopathy) rather than purely parenchymal infection. Ischaemic and demyelinating lesions at grey–white junctions are typical.
det.clinical: Patients develop fever, headache, altered consciousness, delirium, focal deficits and seizures over days. Rash usually precedes symptoms by one to three weeks but may be absent, especially in immunocompromised patients. Associated cranial neuropathies, meningitis, myelitis or cerebellitis can occur. In children, cerebellitis after chickenpox is a separate, usually benign entity.
det.diagnosis: CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis and raised protein; VZV PCR is often positive early, while anti-VZV IgG intrathecal synthesis supports later or vasculopathic disease. Multiplex PCR panels help but should not replace specific testing when suspicion is high. MRI may show infarcts, multifocal lesions or be normal; MRA or vessel-wall imaging assesses arterial involvement. Exclude HSV, other opportunistic infections and lymphoma.
det.treatment: Start empirical intravenous aciclovir in suspected encephalitis without waiting for results, and continue for 10–14 days or longer in immunosuppressed patients when VZV is confirmed; maintain hydration and adjust for renal function to avoid crystal nephropathy. A short corticosteroid course is often added when vasculopathy is prominent, though evidence is limited. Treat seizures, reduce immunosuppression where possible, and offer recombinant zoster vaccine later for prevention.
det.prognosis: Mortality is notable in immunocompromised and elderly patients, and survivors frequently have cognitive or focal deficits; early aciclovir improves outcome.
pearls: Encephalitis plus a recent dermatomal rash: send VZV PCR and antibody index.
Zoster encephalitis is largely a vasculopathy — look for infarcts on MRI.
Hydrate well on high-dose aciclovir to prevent acute kidney injury.
det.thd: Zoster-associated encephalitis คือสมองอักเสบจากเชื้องูสวัดที่กลับมาเป็นซ้ำ พบในผู้สูงอายุและผู้มีภูมิคุ้มกันต่ำ มาด้วยไข้ ปวดศีรษะ สับสน ชัก และอาการเฉพาะที่ มักเกิดภายใน 1–3 สัปดาห์หลังผื่นงูสวัด แต่บางรายไม่มีผื่น กลไกส่วนใหญ่คือหลอดเลือดสมองอักเสบทำให้มี infarct หลายจุด ตรวจ CSF หา VZV PCR และ antibody index รักษาด้วย acyclovir ทางหลอดเลือดดำโดยเร็ว

name: Α-synucleinopathy
formal: Group of neurodegenerative diseases with pathological aggregates of alpha-synuclein, including Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies and multiple system atrophy.
simple: A group of brain diseases caused by build-up of an abnormal protein called alpha-synuclein.
more: Diagnosis is clinical with biomarkers such as DaT scan and skin or CSF seed assays. Treatment is symptomatic and disease-modifying therapy remains under study.
th: กลุ่มโรคสมองเสื่อมที่มีการสะสมของโปรตีน alpha-synuclein ได้แก่ Parkinson disease, DLB, MSA และ pure autonomic failure
tempoNote: Slowly progressive over years, often with a prodrome (RBD, anosmia, constipation) years before motor signs
feat: Lewy body diseases: Parkinson disease, PD dementia, pure autonomic failure, dementia with Lewy bodies
Glial inclusion disease: multiple system atrophy (oligodendroglial cytoplasmic inclusions)
Shared prodrome: REM sleep behaviour disorder, hyposmia, constipation, orthostatic hypotension
Clinical mix of parkinsonism, cognitive fluctuation, hallucinations and autonomic failure
Contrasts with tauopathies (PSP, CBD) which lack RBD and early autonomic failure
inv: Clinical criteria for each disorder; DaT-SPECT shows presynaptic dopaminergic loss
Seed amplification assays (CSF, skin) detect misfolded alpha-synuclein
Skin biopsy for phosphorylated alpha-synuclein in nerve fibres
Polysomnography for RBD; MIBG cardiac scintigraphy and autonomic testing

case.story: For eight years his wife says he shouts and punches in his sleep; he has lost his sense of smell and has had constipation. Now his right hand is slow.
case.exam: Right-sided bradykinesia and rigidity, rest tremor, reduced arm swing, orthostatic BP drop of 20 mmHg.
case.tests: Polysomnography: REM sleep without atonia; DaT-SPECT reduced left putaminal uptake; CSF alpha-synuclein seed assay positive.
case.q: To which protein family does his disease belong, and what was his earliest clue?
case.a: Alpha-synucleinopathy (Parkinson disease); the dream enactment (RBD) years earlier.

read.where: 9 - Atypical parkinsonism, parkinsonism-­plus syndromes and secondary parkinsonian disorders
9 Parkinson’s Disease: Premotor Features, Diagnosis, and Early Management

det.patho: Alpha-synuclein is a presynaptic protein that can misfold into aggregates that spread between connected neurons in a prion-like fashion. In Lewy body diseases aggregates form neuronal Lewy bodies and neurites, often starting in the enteric nervous system, olfactory bulb or lower brainstem. In MSA they accumulate in oligodendrocytes as glial cytoplasmic inclusions. SNCA mutations or multiplications and GBA variants increase risk.
det.clinical: The synucleinopathies share prodromal features such as RBD, hyposmia, constipation and depression, sometimes decades before diagnosis. Parkinson disease presents with asymmetric parkinsonism; DLB with early dementia, fluctuations, visual hallucinations and parkinsonism; MSA with severe autonomic failure plus parkinsonism or cerebellar ataxia; pure autonomic failure with isolated autonomic failure, which may later convert to PD, DLB or MSA. Idiopathic RBD carries a high long-term risk of conversion.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis uses clinical criteria for each disorder, supported by DaT-SPECT, cardiac MIBG and polysomnography. Seed amplification assays in CSF or skin can now detect alpha-synuclein pathology with high sensitivity for Lewy body disease, and biological staging frameworks (e.g. SynNeurGe, NSD-ISS) have been proposed for research. These tests do not by themselves distinguish PD from DLB.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy is approved; antibody and other trials are ongoing. Symptomatic treatment includes dopaminergic drugs for parkinsonism, cholinesterase inhibitors for DLB/PDD, careful antipsychotic choice (quetiapine, clozapine, pimavanserin), melatonin or clonazepam for RBD and management of orthostatic hypotension. Avoid typical antipsychotics in DLB because of severe sensitivity.
det.prognosis: Progressive; MSA has the most rapid course (median survival under a decade), PD the slowest.
pearls: RBD strongly predicts a future synucleinopathy, not a tauopathy.
Seed amplification assays detect synuclein biology, not a specific clinical syndrome.
Severe neuroleptic sensitivity is a hallmark of DLB.
det.thd: Alpha-synucleinopathy คือกลุ่มโรคที่มีการสะสมโปรตีน alpha-synuclein ผิดปกติ ได้แก่ Parkinson disease, DLB, MSA และ pure autonomic failure มีอาการนำร่วมกันเช่น RBD (ละเมอทำตามฝัน) จมูกไม่ได้กลิ่น ท้องผูก ก่อนมีอาการทางการเคลื่อนไหวหลายปี การวินิจฉัยใช้เกณฑ์ทางคลินิกร่วมกับ DaT-SPECT และ seed amplification assay จากน้ำไขสันหลังหรือผิวหนัง ยังไม่มียาชะลอโรค การรักษาเป็นการรักษาตามอาการ

name: Anti-Mi-2 antibody
formal: A myositis-specific autoantibody against the Mi-2 nuclear helicase (CHD3/CHD4) of the nucleosome-remodelling deacetylase complex; it marks classic dermatomyositis with florid skin disease, high CK and a generally good response to immunotherapy, with relatively low rates of interstitial lung disease and cancer.
simple: A blood antibody test that points to the 'classic' type of dermatomyositis: obvious skin rash, clearly weak muscles and very high muscle enzymes, but usually a good response to treatment and fewer lung and cancer problems.
th: Anti-Mi-2 เป็นแอนติบอดีจำเพาะต่อโรคกล้ามเนื้ออักเสบ พบใน dermatomyositis ชนิดคลาสสิก ผื่นชัด กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงและ CK สูงมาก แต่ตอบสนองต่อการรักษาดี และพบโรคปอดกับมะเร็งน้อยกว่ากลุ่มอื่น
tempoNote: Weakness and rash usually build over weeks to a few months; after treatment the titre tends to fall in parallel with CK
feat: Phenotype: classic dermatomyositis with heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, V-sign and shawl sign, often extensive and photo-distributed
Muscle: symmetric proximal weakness that is usually more marked than in other DM subtypes, with very high CK
Joints and vessels: arthralgia, arthritis and Raynaud phenomenon are common companions
Lungs and cancer: interstitial lung disease and malignancy are less frequent than with MDA5, TIF1-gamma or NXP2 antibodies
Course: brisk recovery of strength and CK with standard immunotherapy; mortality lower than in Mi-2-negative DM
inv: Myositis antibody panel (line immunoblot); treat an isolated weak band with caution and confirm that the clinical picture fits
CK, aldolase and transaminases — usually markedly raised; repeat to follow treatment
Muscle MRI (STIR oedema) and, when needed, biopsy: perifascicular atrophy and MxA expression, with more fibre necrosis than in other DM subsets
Baseline lung function and chest HRCT, ECG, and age-appropriate cancer screening (risk is lower, not absent)

case.who: 42-year-old woman, rubber-farm worker from Surat Thani
case.story: Two months of a violet rash around the eyes and a red patch over the upper back and shoulders after working outdoors, followed by trouble climbing into the pickup truck and lifting latex buckets.
case.exam: Heliotrope rash, shawl sign, Gottron papules on the knuckles; neck flexor and hip flexor weakness MRC 3/5; reflexes and sensation normal.
case.tests: CK 9,800 U/L; myositis line blot strongly positive for Mi-2 only; HRCT chest normal; muscle MRI shows symmetric thigh oedema.
case.q: What does this antibody imply for prognosis and the work-up that still matters?
case.a: Mi-2-positive classic dermatomyositis: expect a good response to steroids plus a steroid-sparing agent and lower lung and cancer risk, but still do age-appropriate cancer screening and protect her skin from sunlight.

det.patho: Mi-2 is a nuclear helicase within the NuRD chromatin-remodelling complex that helps switch genes off. It is expressed more strongly in regenerating dermatomyositis muscle and in sun-exposed skin, which may be why these patients show prominent photodistributed rash and active muscle disease. The antibody is a marker of a type I interferon-driven dermatomyositis rather than the direct cause of fibre injury.
det.clinical: Most patients have textbook dermatomyositis: heliotrope and V-neck rash, shawl sign, Gottron papules and nailfold changes, with proximal weakness that develops over weeks. CK is typically far higher than in other DM subtypes and biopsy shows more necrotic fibres. Arthralgia and Raynaud phenomenon are frequent, while clinically amyopathic disease and rapidly progressive lung involvement are uncommon. Reported prevalence varies widely between cohorts, from about one in ten to over half of adult DM, and is lower in juvenile DM.
det.diagnosis: Commercial line immunoblots detect the antibody but give false positives, especially weak isolated bands, so the result must match the phenotype. Supportive tests are a high CK, muscle MRI oedema and a biopsy with perifascicular pathology and MxA staining. Because a positive Mi-2 result predicts lower but not zero risk of ILD and cancer, baseline lung assessment and age-appropriate cancer screening are still recommended.
det.treatment: Initial therapy is glucocorticoids, usually combined early with methotrexate, mycophenolate or azathioprine to limit steroid exposure. Intravenous immunoglobulin is effective for refractory skin and muscle disease and has trial evidence in dermatomyositis. Sun protection and topical therapy help the skin, and physiotherapy supports recovery.
det.prognosis: Strength and CK usually improve well and relapse is manageable; survival is better than in Mi-2-negative dermatomyositis. Antibody titres tend to fall with CK, so they may help track activity.
pearls: Mi-2 = classic DM: bad rash, high CK, good outcome.
A strong Mi-2 band with no rash or weakness should make you doubt the blot before doubting the patient.
Lower cancer risk is not no cancer risk — adults with DM still need screening.

Older patients, slow asymmetric finger-flexor and quadriceps weakness, no rash, steroid-unresponsive, cN1A antibodies

name: Anti-Jo-1 antibody
formal: The commonest anti-aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase autoantibody, directed against histidyl-tRNA synthetase; it defines the anti-synthetase syndrome, a combination of myositis, interstitial lung disease, non-erosive arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, mechanic's hands and fever, in which lung disease largely determines outcome.
simple: A blood antibody that points to 'anti-synthetase syndrome': weak muscles plus scarring of the lungs, sore joints, cold fingers that change colour and rough cracked skin on the fingers. The lungs decide how well the patient does.
th: Anti-Jo-1 เป็นแอนติบอดีต่อเอนไซม์ histidyl-tRNA synthetase พบบ่อยที่สุดในกลุ่ม anti-synthetase ทำให้เกิดกลุ่มอาการกล้ามเนื้ออักเสบร่วมกับโรคปอดอักเสบชนิด ILD ข้ออักเสบ Raynaud และผิวหนังนิ้วมือหนาแตกแบบมือช่าง
tempoNote: Weakness, cough or joint pain usually evolve over weeks to months; lung disease may appear first, together with the muscle, or later, and can flare years after onset
feat: Classic triad: myositis, interstitial lung disease and arthritis; any one may be missing at presentation
Mechanic's hands (hyperkeratotic fissured radial fingers) and 'hiker's feet'; Raynaud phenomenon can come long before weakness
Lung: ILD in most patients during follow-up, often an NSIP or organising-pneumonia pattern; it may be the only finding at first
Muscle: proximal weakness with clearly raised CK is common with Jo-1, more so than with PL-7 or PL-12
Survival is better than with non-Jo-1 synthetase antibodies; co-positivity for Ro52 signals more severe lung disease
inv: Myositis line blot or ELISA for Jo-1 (ELISA can quantify titre), plus Ro52 and the other synthetases
CK and aldolase; Jo-1 titre roughly follows CK and muscle or joint activity
HRCT chest, full lung function with DLCO and 6-minute walk; echocardiogram if pulmonary hypertension is suspected
Muscle MRI and biopsy if needed: perifascicular necrosis and perimysial fragmentation are typical of anti-synthetase myopathy

case.who: 51-year-old man, rice farmer from Roi Et
case.story: Three months of dry cough and breathlessness walking up the field bund, aching swollen finger joints, and fingers that turn white in cold water; for six weeks he has struggled to rise from a squat.
case.exam: Thick, cracked skin along the sides of both index fingers; fine 'velcro' crackles at both lung bases; hip flexor weakness MRC 4-/5; no rash on face or knuckles.
case.tests: CK 3,400 U/L; Jo-1 and Ro52 strongly positive; HRCT shows lower-lobe ground glass with reticulation; FVC 64 % predicted, DLCO reduced.
case.q: Which organ will drive treatment decisions, and what does the Ro52 band add?
case.a: Anti-synthetase syndrome with Jo-1: the ILD sets the intensity of therapy (steroid plus mycophenolate or tacrolimus, rituximab if refractory), and Ro52 co-positivity warns of a more severe lung course.

det.patho: Histidyl-tRNA synthetase is a cytoplasmic enzyme that charges tRNA with histidine during protein synthesis. Immune tolerance to it may break first in the lung, where the antigen is abundant and can be modified by smoking or irritants, which could explain why lung and muscle are linked targets. Muscle biopsy shows perifascicular fibre necrosis and perimysial connective tissue damage, distinct from the perifascicular atrophy of dermatomyositis.
det.clinical: Jo-1 accounts for roughly one in ten to one in four adult myositis patients and is the most frequently detected synthetase antibody. The full picture combines proximal weakness, ILD, non-erosive polyarthritis that can mimic rheumatoid arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, mechanic's hands and fever, but patients often present to a chest physician or rheumatologist with only one or two parts. ILD develops in the large majority; in about a third it is the first problem, and in most others it starts at about the same time as the myopathy. Its pace ranges from an incidental CT finding to a subacute or even fulminant course.
det.diagnosis: A positive Jo-1 result together with any of the core features is enough to label anti-synthetase syndrome; proposed 2024-2025 classification criteria place the antibody at the centre. Every positive patient needs HRCT and lung function even without respiratory symptoms, and lung testing is repeated during follow-up. ANA by immunofluorescence may show only cytoplasmic staining or be negative, so a negative ANA does not exclude the syndrome.
det.treatment: Glucocorticoids are combined from the start with a steroid-sparing agent chosen for the lung: mycophenolate, azathioprine or tacrolimus. Rituximab is effective for refractory muscle or lung disease, and Jo-1 positivity predicted a good response in the RIM trial. IVIG or cyclophosphamide is used for severe flares, and an antifibrotic such as nintedanib is added when fibrosis keeps progressing despite immunosuppression.
det.prognosis: Muscle disease usually responds; the long-term threat is fibrotic lung disease and secondary pulmonary hypertension. Synthetase-positive ILD is more steroid-responsive than antibody-negative ILD, and Jo-1 patients live longer on average than those with other synthetase antibodies.
pearls: Cracked fingers plus cough plus weak hips = check Jo-1 and order an HRCT.
Jo-1 can present as 'seronegative rheumatoid arthritis' or 'idiopathic NSIP' for years.
Jo-1 with Ro52 is a red flag for worse lung disease.
det.thd: Anti-Jo-1 เป็นแอนติบอดีที่พบบ่อยที่สุดในกลุ่ม anti-synthetase syndrome ผู้ป่วยมีกล้ามเนื้อต้นขาอ่อนแรง CK สูง ร่วมกับปอดอักเสบชนิด ILD ข้ออักเสบ Raynaud และมือช่าง โดยปอดเป็นตัวกำหนดความรุนแรงและการพยากรณ์โรค ผู้ป่วยทุกรายควรตรวจ HRCT และสมรรถภาพปอดแม้ไม่มีอาการ การรักษาใช้สเตียรอยด์ร่วมกับ mycophenolate หรือ tacrolimus และใช้ rituximab เมื่อดื้อต่อการรักษา หากพบ Ro52 ร่วมด้วยให้ระวังโรคปอดรุนแรง

Also ILD with hand and skin changes, but synthetase blot is negative, CK is low and the lung can fail within weeks
ILD, arthritis and mechanic's hands too, but with scleroderma features and no synthetase antibody

name: Anti-PL-7 antibody
formal: An anti-synthetase autoantibody against threonyl-tRNA synthetase; it produces the anti-synthetase syndrome with a tendency toward more severe interstitial lung disease, milder or later myositis, frequent skin changes and a worse long-term outcome than anti-Jo-1.
simple: One of the 'anti-synthetase' antibodies, like Jo-1. Patients often have bigger lung problems and smaller muscle problems, so it is easily taken for a lung-only illness.
th: Anti-PL-7 เป็นแอนติบอดีต่อ threonyl-tRNA synthetase ในกลุ่ม anti-synthetase ผู้ป่วยมักมีโรคปอด ILD เด่นและรุนแรงกว่า Jo-1 ขณะที่อาการกล้ามเนื้ออาจน้อยหรือมาทีหลัง
tempoNote: Cough and exertional breathlessness often precede any weakness by months; some patients never develop clinically obvious myositis
feat: Lung-predominant anti-synthetase syndrome: ILD is frequent, can be the sole finding at onset, and tends to be more severe than with Jo-1
Muscle: myopathy is present in many but CK is often only mildly raised; a minority stay clinically amyopathic
Skin: mechanic's hands, Gottron-like papules or a DM-type rash are relatively common
Raynaud phenomenon, arthralgia and fever as in other synthetase syndromes; pericardial effusion is described
inv: Extended myositis line blot (Jo-1 negative does not exclude the syndrome); check Ro52 alongside
HRCT chest, spirometry with DLCO, oxygen saturation on exertion
CK, aldolase and muscle MRI to look for subclinical myositis
Echocardiogram for pericardial effusion or pulmonary hypertension

case.who: 46-year-old woman, school teacher from Chiang Rai
case.story: Treated twice for 'pneumonia' over five months without improvement; now breathless climbing to her second-floor classroom, with sore wrists and fingers that blanch in the morning.
case.exam: Bibasal fine crackles; scaly fissured skin on the radial index fingers; faint violet papules over the knuckles; strength near normal except neck flexion 4/5.
case.tests: CK 420 U/L; Jo-1 negative, PL-7 strongly positive, Ro52 positive; HRCT shows NSIP pattern with consolidation; FVC 58 %.
case.q: Why was this missed for five months, and what should change now?
case.a: PL-7 anti-synthetase syndrome presents mainly through the lung with little muscle disease and a negative Jo-1. Treat as myositis-associated ILD with steroids plus mycophenolate or tacrolimus and consider early rituximab.

det.patho: Threonyl-tRNA synthetase charges tRNA with threonine. As with other synthetase antibodies, the immune response appears to involve lung tissue early, and the clinical expression leans further toward the lung than with Jo-1. Muscle pathology, when sampled, resembles other anti-synthetase myopathy with perifascicular necrosis.
det.clinical: PL-7 is among the more frequent non-Jo-1 synthetase antibodies, each of which is found in only a few percent of myositis patients, with higher reported rates in Japanese cohorts. Patients often reach a chest clinic first. Myopathic features are still common in some series, but CK tends to be lower than in Jo-1 disease, and skin lesions resembling dermatomyositis are seen more often. ILD is frequent and may be severe.
det.diagnosis: Because many laboratories historically tested only Jo-1, PL-7 disease is under-recognised; an extended line blot is needed whenever ILD comes with Raynaud, arthritis, mechanic's hands or mild CK elevation. Weak isolated bands should be confirmed by another method. Baseline and serial HRCT and lung function are essential.
det.treatment: Management follows myositis-associated ILD: glucocorticoids with mycophenolate, azathioprine or a calcineurin inhibitor, escalating to rituximab or cyclophosphamide for progressive disease. Antifibrotic therapy is added for progressive pulmonary fibrosis. Pneumocystis prophylaxis is given during combined immunosuppression.
det.prognosis: Survival is worse than with Jo-1, mainly because of delayed diagnosis and more extensive lung fibrosis. Early recognition and combined immunosuppression improve outcome.
pearls: Jo-1 negative is not 'synthetase negative' — ask for the extended panel.
PL-7 and PL-12 patients usually meet the pulmonologist before the neurologist.
A near-normal CK does not exclude myositis in PL-7 disease; image the thighs.
det.thd: Anti-PL-7 เป็นแอนติบอดีกลุ่ม anti-synthetase ที่อาการทางปอดเด่นกว่า Jo-1 ผู้ป่วยมักไปพบแพทย์ด้วยไอและเหนื่อยจาก ILD ก่อนจะมีอาการกล้ามเนื้อ CK มักสูงไม่มาก จึงถูกวินิจฉัยช้า การส่งตรวจเฉพาะ Jo-1 ไม่เพียงพอ ต้องส่ง myositis panel แบบครบ การรักษาเหมือน ILD จากโรคกล้ามเนื้ออักเสบ และการพยากรณ์โรคแย่กว่ากลุ่ม Jo-1

Even more lung-dominant, with little or no myositis and scleroderma-like features
Idiopathic ILD lacks mechanic's hands, Raynaud and synthetase antibodies — always send a myositis panel in unexplained NSIP
