det.patho: CASPR2 forms a complex with contactin-2 (TAG-1) that holds Kv1 channels at the juxtaparanode of myelinated fibres and at CNS synapses. IgG4 antibodies interfere with this complex, increasing motor and sensory nerve excitability and also altering pain pathways in dorsal root ganglia. The HLA-DRB1*11:01 link in central disease suggests a T-cell-driven break in tolerance, while thymoma supplies the trigger in paraneoplastic cases.
det.clinical: Presentations range from purely peripheral (cramps, stiffness, myokymia, hyperhidrosis and neuropathic pain) to purely central (limbic encephalitis with focal seizures, ataxia) and the combined Morvan syndrome, in which severe insomnia, hallucinations, autonomic overactivity and weight loss accompany neuromyotonia. Gait unsteadiness from episodic or persistent ataxia helps separate CASPR2 from LGI1 disease. Pain is often under-recognised and may be the main complaint. Patients are almost always older men.
det.diagnosis: Cell-based assay is the standard; tissue-based staining of brain or nerve adds specificity. Low-titre serum positivity occurs in people without a compatible illness, so isolated weak results need confirmation in CSF or by a second method. EMG documents peripheral hyperexcitability. Search for thymoma at diagnosis and if symptoms recur. In Graus 2021 terms CASPR2 is a lower-risk antibody overall, but the cancer probability rises sharply in Morvan syndrome.
det.treatment: Symptomatic relief from sodium-channel blockers (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine) for cramps and neuromyotonia and neuropathic-pain drugs for pain. Immunotherapy includes steroids, IVIG or plasma exchange, with rituximab for relapsing or refractory disease — IgG4-driven disorders often respond well to B-cell depletion. Thymoma resection and oncological treatment are essential when a tumour is present.
det.prognosis: About half have a good or complete response to immunotherapy and/or tumour treatment and a further large group improve partially. Relapse occurs in about a quarter. Pain frequently persists despite immunological improvement. Thymoma-related cases depend heavily on tumour control.
pearls: Older man + muscle rippling + burning pain + insomnia: send CASPR2 and image the mediastinum.
A weak serum CASPR2 band without a matching syndrome is more likely noise than disease.
Ataxia and pain favour CASPR2; faciobrachial seizures and low sodium favour LGI1.
det.thd: Anti-CASPR2 พบเกือบทั้งหมดในชายสูงอายุ อาการมีตั้งแต่กล้ามเนื้อกระตุกเป็นคลื่น ตะคริว ปวดแสบร้อน เดินเซ ไปจนถึงสมองอักเสบและ Morvan syndrome ที่นอนไม่หลับ เหงื่อออกมาก และประสาทหลอน ผลบวกระดับต่ำในเลือดเพียงอย่างเดียวอาจเป็นผลบวกปลอม ควรยืนยันด้วยน้ำไขสันหลังหรือวิธีตรวจอื่น ต้องตรวจหา thymoma ทุกราย การรักษาใช้ยาปรับภูมิคุ้มกันร่วมกับ rituximab ในรายที่กลับเป็นซ้ำ และยากันชักกลุ่ม sodium channel ช่วยลดตะคริว

name: Anti-GABA-A receptor antibody
formal: An IgG1 autoantibody against the alpha1, beta3 or gamma2 subunits of the GABA-A receptor that reduces synaptic receptor density; it marks an encephalitis of any age with refractory seizures or status epilepticus and multifocal cortical-subcortical FLAIR lesions, associated with thymoma in about a third of adults.
simple: A blood and spinal-fluid test for a brain inflammation that causes non-stop seizures and many patchy white-and-grey-matter spots on MRI. It can affect children or adults; adults should be checked for a thymus tumour.
th: Anti-GABA-A receptor เป็นแอนติบอดีต่อตัวรับ GABA-A ทำให้เกิดสมองอักเสบที่ชักรุนแรงหรือชักต่อเนื่อง MRI มีรอยโรคหลายตำแหน่งทั้งเปลือกสมองและเนื้อขาว พบได้ทุกวัย และในผู้ใหญ่ราวหนึ่งในสามมี thymoma
tempoNote: Seizures escalate over days to a few weeks, often into refractory status epilepticus; children may follow a viral illness
feat: Target and class: alpha1/beta3/gamma2 subunits of the GABA-A receptor; IgG1 antibodies that reduce receptor clusters at inhibitory synapses
Who: any age from infancy to old age (median around 40), equal sex ratio
Phenotype: encephalopathy with drug-resistant seizures, often escalating to status epilepticus or epilepsia partialis continua; catatonia and behavioural change also occur
MRI signature: multiple 'fluffy' cortical and subcortical T2/FLAIR lesions in two or more regions in over 80%
Tumour: thymoma in roughly 30% (mostly adults); may coexist with post-herpes autoimmunity or other neural antibodies
inv: Serum and CSF GABAAR-IgG by cell-based assay; high serum titres are more specific, and CSF positivity strengthens low-titre results
MRI brain: multifocal asymmetric cortical-subcortical FLAIR lesions without diffusion restriction or much enhancement
Continuous EEG: frequent electrographic seizures or periodic discharges on a slow background
CT chest for thymoma; CSF cell count (pleocytosis in a quarter to half) and oligoclonal bands

case.who: 8-year-old boy from Chiang Rai, referred to a provincial paediatric ICU
case.story: Two weeks after a febrile cold he developed right-hand jerking that spread to clusters of focal seizures, then generalised status epilepticus needing intubation despite three antiseizure drugs.
case.exam: Intubated, continuous right-sided facial and arm clonic jerks off sedation; no meningism.
case.tests: MRI: numerous patchy cortical and subcortical FLAIR hyperintensities in both hemispheres without restricted diffusion; CSF 18 lymphocytes/µL; HSV PCR negative; serum and CSF GABAAR-IgG positive on cell-based assay.
case.q: How does the antibody change management of this refractory status epilepticus?
case.a: It identifies anti-GABA-A receptor encephalitis: add immunotherapy (methylprednisolone with IVIG or plasma exchange, then rituximab or cyclophosphamide if seizures persist) alongside anaesthetic seizure control; thymoma screening matters mainly in adults.

read.where: Chapter 9 - Seizures and Antibodies Against Surface Antigens

det.patho: Antibodies bind extracellular epitopes of the alpha1, beta3 or gamma2 subunits and lower the number of GABA-A receptors at synapses, weakening fast inhibitory transmission and producing a highly epileptogenic cortex. Complement-mediated injury is not the main mechanism. In some children the disease follows a viral illness or herpes encephalitis, and thymoma provides the trigger in adults.
det.clinical: Seizures are the dominant feature — often frequent, refractory and evolving to status epilepticus or epilepsia partialis continua — together with confusion, behavioural change, catatonia or a movement disorder. Children may present with refractory seizures and developmental regression. Low-titre serum antibodies without CSF positivity are associated with milder, less specific pictures (such as opsoclonus or stiff-person features).
det.diagnosis: High-titre serum and CSF antibodies on cell-based assay, combined with the characteristic multifocal cortical and subcortical MRI pattern, are strongly suggestive. CSF may show pleocytosis, raised protein or oligoclonal bands. Evaluate for thymoma and test for co-existing neural antibodies (for example GAD65 or NMDAR). Exclude infection, mitochondrial disease and post-ictal change, which can also produce multifocal signal.
det.treatment: Treat the seizures aggressively and start immunotherapy early: IV methylprednisolone with IVIG or plasma exchange, followed by rituximab or cyclophosphamide when status persists. Remove a thymoma if found. Anaesthetic infusions and ketogenic diet may be needed in super-refractory status.
det.prognosis: The disease is immunotherapy-responsive and MRI lesions frequently regress, but death occurs in roughly 10-20%, usually from refractory status epilepticus or its ICU complications. Survivors may have residual epilepsy or cognitive deficits; children often recover substantially.
pearls: Refractory status plus many fluffy cortical-subcortical FLAIR lesions: send GABA-A receptor antibodies.
A post-viral child with NORSE deserves antibody testing and early immunotherapy, not just more antiseizure drugs.
In adults, image the mediastinum — thymoma is the usual partner.
det.thd: Anti-GABA-A receptor พบได้ทั้งเด็กและผู้ใหญ่ ทำให้ชักถี่และชักต่อเนื่องที่ดื้อต่อยากันชัก ภาพ MRI มีรอยโรคเป็นหย่อมๆ หลายตำแหน่งทั้งเปลือกสมองและเนื้อขาวซึ่งเป็นลักษณะเฉพาะ ควรส่งตรวจทั้งเลือดและน้ำไขสันหลัง และในผู้ใหญ่ต้องหา thymoma การรักษาต้องให้ยาปรับภูมิคุ้มกันร่วมกับการคุมชักอย่างเข้มข้นตั้งแต่ต้น แม้ตอบสนองดี แต่ยังมีอัตราตายจากภาวะชักต่อเนื่องราวร้อยละ 10-20

files.chapter: Chapter 9 - Seizures and Antibodies Against Surface Antigens
Considerations about the diagnosis of antibody-negative autoimmune encephalitis

ddx.pt: The syndrome label; GABAAR antibodies are one identifiable cause, alongside NMDAR and other surface antibodies or cryptogenic disease
Post-infectious multifocal lesions too, but with less seizure burden, more white-matter and deep grey involvement and often MOG antibodies
Also seizure-predominant, but older smokers with a medial temporal limbic picture and frequent SCLC

aN: gaba a receptor antibody | gabaar antibody | gaba a r antibody | gabaa receptor igg | anti gabaar | gabaar igg | gamma aminobutyric acid a receptor antibody

name: Anti-GABA-B receptor antibody
formal: An IgG1 autoantibody against the B1 subunit of the metabotropic GABA-B receptor that blocks receptor function; it marks a limbic encephalitis of older adults with early, severe seizures and is paraneoplastic in about half, nearly always small cell lung cancer.
simple: A blood and spinal-fluid test for a memory-and-seizure brain inflammation in older people, often smokers. Half have small cell lung cancer, so a positive result means a careful cancer search.
th: Anti-GABA-B receptor เป็นแอนติบอดีต่อตัวรับ GABA-B ทำให้สมองอักเสบส่วน limbic ร่วมกับชักรุนแรงในผู้สูงอายุ ราวครึ่งหนึ่งพบมะเร็งปอดชนิด small cell
tempoNote: Seizures and confusion usually build over days to weeks; an occasional patient has a slower, rapidly progressive dementia-like course
feat: Target and class: B1 subunit of the GABA-B receptor; IgG1 antibodies that block receptor signalling without internalisation
Who: median age around 60, slight male excess; smokers are over-represented
Phenotype: limbic encephalitis dominated by early frequent or refractory seizures and status epilepticus, with confusion and memory loss; ataxia or opsoclonus-myoclonus occasionally
Tumour: about 50% overall, mainly small cell lung cancer; antibodies to KCTD16 or SOX1 alongside GABABR point strongly to SCLC
Graus 2021: an intermediate-risk paraneoplastic antibody
inv: Serum and CSF GABABR-IgG by cell-based assay; add KCTD16 and onconeural (Hu, SOX1) antibodies where available
CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis in most
MRI: medial temporal T2/FLAIR change in under half; EEG with temporal seizures or status
CT chest and, if negative, FDG-PET/CT; repeat screening every 6 months for about 2 years when the first search is clear

case.who: 63-year-old man, former long-distance truck driver from Nakhon Ratchasima, 45 pack-years of smoking
case.story: Ten days of confusion and repeated questions, then three focal-to-bilateral seizures in one night despite phenytoin.
case.exam: Disoriented, cannot form new memories, no focal weakness; ongoing subtle right-face twitching.
case.tests: MRI: bilateral medial temporal FLAIR hyperintensity; CSF 45 lymphocytes/µL; serum and CSF GABABR-IgG positive; CT chest shows a left hilar mass, biopsy small cell carcinoma.
case.q: What does the antibody predict about long-term outlook?
case.a: Seizures often settle with immunotherapy, but the outlook is governed by the small cell lung cancer — treat the tumour promptly, as tumour-associated cases have more neurological relapses and higher mortality.

det.patho: The GABA-B receptor is a metabotropic receptor that produces slow, prolonged inhibition. Antibodies to the B1 subunit block its activation, removing this brake and favouring seizures and memory dysfunction, with little receptor loss. In SCLC the tumour expresses the receptor and initiates the response; companion antibodies to KCTD16 (an auxiliary subunit) are almost confined to tumour cases.
det.clinical: Older patients present with confusion, amnesia and behavioural change accompanied by early, prominent and often refractory seizures. Some have ataxia, opsoclonus-myoclonus or a slow dementia-like course. Seizures may lead to status epilepticus requiring ICU care. Neurological features may precede cancer diagnosis by months.
det.diagnosis: Cell-based assay of serum and CSF; CSF pleocytosis is common and MRI is abnormal in around two thirds, half with medial temporal change. A positive result, especially with KCTD16 or SOX1 antibodies, demands a thorough search for SCLC by CT and FDG-PET, repeated if initially negative. Under the 2021 PNS-Care criteria a positive test with a compatible syndrome and cancer supports definite paraneoplastic disease.
det.treatment: Steroids plus IVIG or plasma exchange at the outset, together with prompt oncological treatment of the tumour; second-line agents for non-paraneoplastic refractory disease. Antiseizure drugs are needed but often insufficient until immunotherapy takes effect.
det.prognosis: Around nine in ten patients show some response to immunotherapy. Non-paraneoplastic cases do well; tumour-associated cases have more recurrent neurological symptoms and higher mortality, mainly from cancer progression.
pearls: Seizure-dominant limbic encephalitis in an older smoker: send GABA-B receptor antibodies and scan the chest.
KCTD16 antibodies beside GABABR mean SCLC until proven otherwise.
The brain often responds; the cancer decides survival.
det.thd: Anti-GABA-B receptor พบในผู้สูงอายุ โดยเฉพาะผู้สูบบุหรี่ อาการเด่นคือชักถี่หรือชักต่อเนื่องร่วมกับสับสนและความจำเสื่อม ราวครึ่งหนึ่งมีมะเร็งปอดชนิด small cell จึงต้องตรวจ CT และ PET-CT และตรวจซ้ำเป็นระยะหากครั้งแรกไม่พบ อาการทางสมองมักตอบสนองต่อยาปรับภูมิคุ้มกัน แต่การพยากรณ์โรคขึ้นกับการควบคุมมะเร็งเป็นหลัก

ddx.pt: The disease page for this antibody — clinical course and management
Hu- or SOX1-related limbic encephalitis with SCLC targets intracellular antigens and responds poorly to immunotherapy
Limbic encephalitis with prominent amnesia and psychiatric features; tumours include thymoma, breast and lung

aN: gaba b receptor antibody | gababr antibody | gaba b r antibody | gabab receptor igg | anti gababr | gababr igg | gamma aminobutyric acid b receptor antibody

name: Anti-AMPAR antibody
formal: An autoantibody binding GluA1/GluA2 subunits of AMPA-type glutamate receptors that causes receptor internalisation; it marks a limbic encephalitis with prominent amnesia, confusion, seizures and psychiatric change in middle-aged to older adults, with an underlying tumour (thymoma, lung, breast or ovary) in about two thirds.
simple: A blood and spinal-fluid test for a brain inflammation that wipes out short-term memory and causes confusion, fits or odd behaviour. Most patients have a hidden tumour, so a full cancer search is needed.
th: Anti-AMPAR เป็นแอนติบอดีต่อหน่วยย่อย GluA1/GluA2 ของตัวรับ AMPA ทำให้สมองอักเสบส่วน limbic ความจำเสื่อม สับสน ชัก และพฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน ราวสองในสามพบเนื้องอก เช่น thymoma มะเร็งปอด เต้านม หรือรังไข่
tempoNote: Develops over days to weeks; relapses are common, particularly when no tumour is found or treated
feat: Target: extracellular domains of GluA1/GluA2; antibodies cross-link and remove AMPA receptors from synapses

Who: middle-aged to elderly adults (mean early 50s, wide range); predominantly women (Dalmau & Graus 2022, ch. 5.2.2, p. 403). Uy 2021 Table 1 prints a sex ratio of '2:1' in an M:F column, which conflicts with this — ratio unresolved, check the primary series
Phenotype: subacute amnesia and confusion with seizures and psychiatric or behavioural change; occasionally a pure psychosis or rapidly progressive dementia
MRI: abnormal in most, typically bilateral medial temporal FLAIR hyperintensity
Tumour: in about 70% — thymoma, small cell lung cancer, breast and ovarian cancers; Graus 2021 intermediate-risk antibody
inv: Serum and CSF AMPAR-IgG (GluA1/GluA2) by cell-based assay, with an onconeural panel because coexisting antibodies are frequent
MRI brain (bilateral medial temporal change), EEG, CSF (abnormal in about 70%)
CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, mammography or breast MRI, pelvic imaging, then FDG-PET/CT if negative
Repeat tumour screening during follow-up and at any relapse

case.story: Three weeks of asking the same questions repeatedly, misplacing money, irritability and two episodes of staring with lip-smacking.
case.exam: Disoriented to time; cannot recall any of five words; no focal deficits.
case.tests: MRI: symmetric bilateral hippocampal FLAIR hyperintensity; CSF 15 cells/µL, protein 62 mg/dL; serum and CSF AMPAR-IgG positive; CT chest shows an anterior mediastinal mass, later confirmed as thymoma.
case.q: What should the antibody result trigger beyond immunotherapy?
case.a: An aggressive tumour search and treatment — here thymectomy — plus first-line immunotherapy; tumour control lowers relapse risk, and patients should stay under long-term tumour surveillance.

read.where: 5.2.2 AMPA Receptor (AMPAR) Antibodies, p. 403 — source of the female-predominant sex ratio and median age ~60

det.patho: Antibodies to GluA1/GluA2 subunits cross-link AMPA receptors and cause their internalisation, reducing fast excitatory transmission in the hippocampus and triggering compensatory changes in inhibitory circuits. The effect is reversible after antibody removal. Tumours expressing AMPA receptors (notably thymoma, lung and breast cancers) initiate many cases.
det.clinical: The textbook account describes a female predominance, with a median age around 60 (one review table gives a different male-to-female figure, so treat the ratio as approximate). The core picture is subacute limbic encephalitis: profound loss of recent memory, confusion, seizures, agitation and sometimes psychosis. Atypical forms include isolated psychiatric illness and a rapidly progressive dementia. Additional antibodies (onconeural or other surface antibodies) are not rare and can add other features.
det.diagnosis: Cell-based assay of serum and CSF confirms the antibody; MRI typically shows bilateral medial temporal changes and the CSF is inflammatory in most. Because the tumour rate is high, a full-body cancer search (including breast and thymus) is mandatory and should be repeated if negative.
det.treatment: First-line immunotherapy plus treatment of any tumour; second-line agents (rituximab, cyclophosphamide) for refractory or relapsing disease, and maintenance immunosuppression is often considered because relapses are frequent.
det.prognosis: Most patients improve from the nadir and survivors frequently reach mild disability, but residual memory problems are common and relapses occur. Roughly one in seven dies, usually from the associated cancer rather than the encephalitis.
pearls: Limbic encephalitis + tumour hunt: AMPAR is one of the antibodies where cancer is more likely than not.
Look in the mediastinum and the breasts, not only the lungs.
Plan for relapse — follow these patients long term.
det.thd: Anti-AMPAR ทำให้เกิดสมองอักเสบส่วน limbic ในผู้ใหญ่วัยกลางคนถึงสูงอายุ มีความจำระยะสั้นเสื่อมรุนแรง สับสน ชัก และอาการทางจิต ราวสองในสามมีเนื้องอก จึงต้องตรวจหาอย่างละเอียดทั้ง thymus ปอด เต้านม และรังไข่ การรักษาคือยาปรับภูมิคุ้มกันร่วมกับรักษาเนื้องอก ผู้ป่วยส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นแต่กลับเป็นซ้ำได้บ่อย และการเสียชีวิตมักเกิดจากมะเร็ง

ddx.pt: The syndrome; AMPAR is one of several causes (LGI1, GABABR, Hu, GAD65, HSV)
Seizure-led limbic encephalitis in older smokers with small cell lung cancer
Fever, asymmetric temporal necrosis with haemorrhage and positive HSV PCR

aN: ampa receptor antibody | ampar antibody | ampar igg | anti ampar | glua1 antibody | glua2 antibody | anti glur1 2 | ampar1 2 antibody

name: Anti-DPPX antibody
formal: An autoantibody against dipeptidyl-peptidase-like protein 6, a regulatory partner of neuronal Kv4.2 potassium channels, also present and the myenteric plexus; it marks a multifocal encephalitis with CNS hyperexcitability (myoclonus, tremor, hyperekplexia, PERM-like features), cognitive decline and a gastrointestinal prodrome of diarrhoea and weight loss, sometimes with B-cell lymphoma.
simple: A blood and spinal-fluid test for a rare immune illness that often starts with months of diarrhoea and weight loss, then causes jumpiness, jerks, tremor, exaggerated startle and memory trouble.
th: Anti-DPPX เป็นแอนติบอดีต่อโปรตีน DPPX ซึ่งเป็นหน่วยย่อยของช่องโพแทสเซียม Kv4.2 ทำให้เกิดท้องเสียและน้ำหนักลดนำมาก่อน แล้วตามด้วยอาการสะดุ้งง่าย กระตุก สั่น ความจำเสื่อม และอาจสัมพันธ์กับมะเร็งต่อมน้ำเหลืองชนิด B-cell
tempoNote: Gastrointestinal symptoms and weight loss can precede neurological signs by months; the neurological illness progresses over months and tends to relapse when immunotherapy is reduced
feat: Target: DPPX on neurons (hippocampus, cerebellum, striatum) and the myenteric plexus; antibodies reduce DPPX and Kv4.2 at the cell surface
Prodrome: chronic diarrhoea, bloating and marked weight loss, often investigated by gastroenterologists first
CNS hyperexcitability: myoclonus, tremor, hyperekplexia, agitation, sleep disturbance; PERM-like rigidity in some
Cognitive and psychiatric change, brainstem signs and dysautonomia complete the multifocal picture
Tumour: B-cell neoplasm (e.g. gastrointestinal follicular lymphoma, CLL) in about one in ten
inv: Serum and CSF DPPX-IgG by cell-based assay (tissue-based staining shows a characteristic neuropil pattern)
MRI brain usually normal; CSF mild pleocytosis or raised protein in about a third; EEG slowing common
Gastrointestinal work-up for alternative causes of diarrhoea and weight loss
Haematological screen: blood count, protein electrophoresis, CT or PET for lymphoma

case.story: Five months of watery diarrhoea and 12 kg weight loss with normal colonoscopy, followed by jumpy startles, shaking hands, poor sleep and forgetfulness.
case.exam: Exaggerated startle to light tap on the nose, multifocal action myoclonus, postural tremor, mild truncal rigidity; MoCA 21/30.
case.tests: MRI brain normal; CSF 8 cells/µL, protein 58 mg/dL; serum and CSF DPPX-IgG positive; CT abdomen and serum electrophoresis unremarkable.
case.q: Why did the gut symptoms come first, and what does the antibody imply for treatment length?
case.a: DPPX is expressed in the myenteric plexus, so enteric hyperexcitability causes diarrhoea and weight loss; the disease responds to immunotherapy in most but relapses when treatment is withdrawn, so long-term maintenance (e.g. rituximab or mycophenolate) and lymphoma surveillance are usually needed.

read.where: Chapter 3 - Pathogenesis and Disease Mechanisms in Neuronal Antibody-Mediated Encephalitis

det.patho: DPPX regulates Kv4.2 potassium channels that control dendritic excitability and pacing in neurons and myenteric plexus cells. Antibodies decrease surface DPPX and Kv4.2, causing neuronal hyperexcitability in the CNS and in the enteric nervous system, which explains the combination of startle, myoclonus and diarrhoea.
det.clinical: A typical course begins with diarrhoea, other gastrointestinal complaints and marked weight loss, followed by a multifocal CNS disorder: cognitive impairment, confusion, psychiatric symptoms, CNS hyperexcitability (myoclonus, tremor, hyperekplexia, seizures), brainstem features (ocular movement disorders, dysphagia), ataxia and dysautonomia. Some patients resemble PERM.
det.diagnosis: Cell-based assay of serum and CSF, ideally with tissue-based confirmation. MRI is normal or non-specific and CSF findings are modest, so the antibody is the key test. Exclude prion disease, Whipple disease and other causes of malabsorption, and search for B-cell lymphoma.
det.treatment: Steroids, IVIG and plasma exchange often help, and many patients need long-term immunosuppression (rituximab, mycophenolate, azathioprine) because symptoms return when treatment is tapered. Treat any associated lymphoma. Benzodiazepines can ease startle and myoclonus.
det.prognosis: About 60-70% improve with immunotherapy, sometimes substantially, but relapses during tapering are frequent and some are left with cognitive or motor deficits. Early diagnosis improves results.
pearls: Diarrhoea and weight loss followed by startle and myoclonus: think DPPX.
Normal MRI and near-normal CSF do not argue against it.
Taper slowly — DPPX disease is relapse-prone.
det.thd: Anti-DPPX เป็นโรคพบน้อยแต่มีลักษณะเฉพาะ มักเริ่มด้วยท้องเสียเรื้อรังและน้ำหนักลดนำมาก่อนหลายเดือน แล้วตามด้วยสะดุ้งง่าย กระตุก มือสั่น ตัวแข็ง และความจำเสื่อม MRI และน้ำไขสันหลังมักปกติหรือผิดปกติเล็กน้อย จึงต้องอาศัยการตรวจแอนติบอดี ควรตรวจหามะเร็งต่อมน้ำเหลือง ผู้ป่วยส่วนใหญ่ตอบสนองต่อยาปรับภูมิคุ้มกันแต่กลับเป็นซ้ำได้เมื่อลดยา จึงมักต้องใช้ยากดภูมิระยะยาว

Considerations about the diagnosis of antibody-negative autoimmune encephalitis

ddx.pt: The PERM phenotype is usually GlyR-associated; DPPX causes a PERM-like picture with prominent gut symptoms and weight loss
Rapid dementia with myoclonus, DWI cortical ribboning and RT-QuIC positivity; no diarrhoea prodrome
Diarrhoea, weight loss and CNS signs too, but oculomasticatory myorhythmia, arthralgia and Tropheryma whipplei PCR

aN: dppx antibody | dppx igg | anti dppx | dipeptidyl peptidase like protein 6 antibody | dpp6 antibody | anti dpp6

name: Anti-glycine receptor antibody
formal: An IgG1/IgG3 autoantibody against the alpha1 subunit of the inhibitory glycine receptor of brainstem and spinal cord; it marks PERM and other stiff-person spectrum disorders, and occasionally limbic encephalitis or focal epilepsy, with thymoma in a minority.
simple: A blood and spinal-fluid test for a brainstem and spinal-cord immune disorder that causes stiffness, painful spasms, jumpiness to noise or touch, jerks and eye-movement problems. It often responds to immune treatment.
th: Anti-glycine receptor เป็นแอนติบอดีต่อตัวรับไกลซีนในก้านสมองและไขสันหลัง ทำให้เกิด PERM และกลุ่มอาการ stiff-person ที่มีกล้ามเนื้อแข็ง เกร็งกระตุก สะดุ้งง่าย และการกลอกตาผิดปกติ บางรายมี thymoma
tempoNote: PERM develops over weeks and can become life-threatening; milder stiff-person spectrum courses evolve over months to years with relapses
feat: Target and class: alpha1 subunit of the GlyR; IgG1 and IgG3 antibodies that reduce receptor surface expression and can fix complement
Who: any age (median around 50), equal sex ratio
Phenotype: PERM (rigidity, stimulus-sensitive spasms and myoclonus, hyperekplexia, brainstem signs, dysautonomia) and classic or partial stiff-person syndrome
Sensory clues: allodynia, dysaesthesia and prominent itch are frequent
Tumour: thymoma in about 15%; lymphoma and other cancers occasionally; co-existing GAD65 antibodies in some
inv: Serum GlyR-IgG by live cell-based assay, plus CSF to confirm intrathecal antibody; low-titre serum results also occur in MS, epilepsy and other conditions
EMG: continuous motor unit activity in agonists and antagonists, exaggerated exteroceptive reflexes and stimulus-induced spasms
MRI brain and spine (usually normal or non-specific; small cord lesions in some); CSF pleocytosis in about 40%
CT chest for thymoma; check GAD65 and DPPX antibodies as companions or alternatives

case.story: Six weeks of progressive back and leg stiffness, spasms triggered by noise or touch, double vision and intense itching of the arms; admitted after a spasm caused a fall.
case.exam: Board-like paraspinal and abdominal rigidity, stimulus-induced spasms with myoclonic jerks, exaggerated startle, gaze-evoked nystagmus with slow saccades, sweating and tachycardia.
case.tests: EMG: continuous motor unit firing in trunk muscles; serum and CSF GlyR-IgG positive; GAD65 negative; MRI brain and spine normal; CT chest shows a small thymoma.
case.q: What is the syndrome and why is the outlook not hopeless?
case.a: PERM with GlyR antibodies and thymoma: it is life-threatening acutely (autonomic and respiratory crises), but responds to immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG or plasma exchange, then rituximab), thymectomy and symptomatic GABAergic drugs; survivors usually do well.

det.patho: Glycine receptors mediate fast inhibition of motor neurons and interneurons in the brainstem and spinal cord. Antibodies against the alpha1 subunit cause receptor internalisation and complement-mediated loss, releasing motor neurons from inhibition and producing rigidity, spasms and an excessive startle. Intrathecal antibody production is common.
det.clinical: The spectrum runs from classic stiff-person syndrome and stiff-limb syndrome to PERM, which adds brainstem signs (eye-movement disorders, dysphagia, dysarthria), myoclonus, encephalopathy and dysautonomia that can cause sudden death. Sensory symptoms such as allodynia and itch are characteristic. A smaller group has limbic encephalitis or focal epilepsy with GlyR antibodies.
det.diagnosis: A live cell-based assay is the reference; CSF positivity confirms relevance, because low-titre serum GlyR antibodies are found in unrelated disorders. EMG shows continuous motor unit activity and stimulus-induced reflex spasms. MRI and CSF are often unremarkable but can show mild inflammation. Screen for thymoma and test companion antibodies.
det.treatment: Symptomatic: benzodiazepines and baclofen (oral or intrathecal) for stiffness and spasms. Immunotherapy: steroids, IVIG and plasma exchange, with rituximab or cyclophosphamide for severe or relapsing disease. Thymectomy when a thymoma is present. Monitor closely for autonomic and respiratory crises in PERM.
det.prognosis: In early series about one in ten died during the acute illness, but most survivors had a good outcome with little residual disability after long-term follow-up. Relapses occur and may need maintenance immunosuppression.
pearls: Stiffness plus startle plus abnormal eye movements: think PERM and send GlyR antibodies.
Itch and allodynia are unexpected but real GlyR clues.
Interpret low-titre serum GlyR only alongside a fitting syndrome and ideally CSF.
det.thd: Anti-glycine receptor ทำให้เกิด PERM และกลุ่มอาการ stiff-person ผู้ป่วยมีกล้ามเนื้อลำตัวและขาแข็ง เกร็งกระตุกเมื่อโดนเสียงหรือสัมผัส สะดุ้งง่าย กลอกตาผิดปกติ และอาจคันหรือปวดผิวหนังร่วมด้วย ช่วงเฉียบพลันอาจรุนแรงจากระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติและการหายใจ แต่ตอบสนองดีต่อยาปรับภูมิคุ้มกัน ร่วมกับ benzodiazepine และ baclofen ควรตรวจหา thymoma และยืนยันผลด้วยน้ำไขสันหลังเพราะผลบวกต่ำๆ ในเลือดอาจไม่เกี่ยวข้อง

ddx.pt: The main syndrome marked by GlyR antibodies
Classic SPS is usually GAD65-associated; GlyR adds more brainstem signs, myoclonus and better immunotherapy response
Trismus, generalised spasms and a wound source; no antibodies and a monophasic course

name: Anti-MOG antibody
formal: An IgG1 autoantibody against conformational epitopes of myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein on the outer myelin surface, detected by live or fixed cell-based assay with full-length human MOG; it defines MOG antibody-associated disease (MOGAD) — optic neuritis, myelitis, ADEM, brainstem or cortical encephalitis — distinct from multiple sclerosis and AQP4-positive NMOSD.
simple: A blood test that identifies a type of inflammatory 'demyelinating' disease different from MS: swollen optic nerves with severe visual loss, spinal cord inflammation or brain inflammation, often in children and young adults. It usually responds well to steroids but can come back.
th: Anti-MOG เป็นแอนติบอดีต่อโปรตีน MOG บนผิวปลอกประสาท ใช้วินิจฉัย MOGAD ซึ่งทำให้ประสาทตาอักเสบ ไขสันหลังอักเสบ ADEM หรือสมองอักเสบ แยกจาก MS และ NMOSD ชนิด AQP4 มักตอบสนองดีต่อสเตียรอยด์แต่กลับเป็นซ้ำได้
tempoNote: Attacks develop over days; the disease is monophasic in many (especially children) but relapses in about half, often when steroids are tapered quickly
feat: Target and class: MOG, a minor surface component of CNS myelin; IgG1 antibodies, complement activation is modest
Who: any age, median late 30s in adults; ADEM-type onset typical of children; equal sex ratio
Optic neuritis: often bilateral, severe, with disc swelling and long anterior optic-nerve lesions with perineural enhancement
Myelitis: long or short lesions with conus involvement, grey-matter 'H sign', and bladder, bowel and erectile dysfunction
Brain: ADEM, fluffy poorly marginated lesions, brainstem or cerebellar peduncle lesions, and unilateral cortical encephalitis with seizures (FLAMES)
inv: Serum MOG-IgG by cell-based assay (full-length human MOG, IgG1- or Fc-specific secondary); titre matters — low positives need supporting clinical/MRI features (2023 international MOGAD criteria)
CSF MOG-IgG when serum is negative but suspicion is high; CSF pleocytosis is common, unpaired oligoclonal bands uncommon
MRI brain, orbits and whole spine with contrast; OCT and visual evoked potentials
AQP4-IgG in parallel to separate NMOSD; avoid screening typical MS presentations (false positives)

case.story: Painful loss of vision in both eyes over five days, two weeks after a febrile respiratory illness.
case.exam: Visual acuity counting fingers right, 6/60 left; marked bilateral optic disc swelling; small right relative afferent pupillary defect; no other deficits.
case.tests: MRI orbits: long-segment enhancement of both anterior optic nerves with perineural (optic sheath) enhancement; brain MRI normal; serum MOG-IgG positive at high titre on live cell-based assay; AQP4-IgG negative; CSF 12 cells/µL, OCB negative.
case.q: How does the antibody change acute and long-term management?
case.a: It defines MOGAD optic neuritis: give high-dose IV methylprednisolone (plasma exchange if poor response) with a slow oral taper over months, expect good visual recovery, and recheck the titre — persistent high titres and early relapse favour maintenance therapy such as IVIG, azathioprine or mycophenolate.

det.patho: MOG sits on the outermost myelin lamella, making it accessible to circulating antibodies. MOG-IgG1 is mainly produced in the periphery; CNS injury involves CD4 T cells and inflammatory demyelination with relative axonal preservation, unlike the astrocytopathy of AQP4 NMOSD. Antibody titres may fall to negative in monophasic disease and persist in relapsing disease.
det.clinical: Attacks include optic neuritis (frequently bilateral with marked disc swelling), transverse myelitis (often with conus and grey-matter involvement), ADEM in children, brainstem and cerebellar syndromes, and cortical encephalitis presenting with seizures and headache. Seizures and encephalopathy are recognised features. Recovery is usually good, but sphincter dysfunction after myelitis and visual loss after repeated optic neuritis may remain.
det.diagnosis: The 2023 international MOGAD criteria require a core demyelinating event, a positive MOG-IgG cell-based assay and exclusion of better explanations including MS. Clear high-titre positivity suffices; low titres, or fixed-assay positivity without a titre, require supportive features (for example bilateral optic neuritis, perineural enhancement, conus lesion or fluffy brain lesions). Serum is the preferred sample, but CSF-only positivity occurs. Testing is not recommended for typical MS presentations because the positive predictive value is low.
det.treatment: Acute attacks: high-dose IV methylprednisolone, plasma exchange for severe or steroid-refractory attacks, and a gradual steroid taper because early relapses follow abrupt withdrawal. Maintenance after relapse (or a severe first attack): IVIG has the best observational data, with azathioprine and mycophenolate as alternatives; rituximab works less consistently than in NMOSD; tocilizumab is used for refractory cases. Several anti-FcRn and anti-IL-6 receptor trials were underway in 2024-2026.
det.prognosis: Most patients recover well from individual attacks, with good long-term vision and walking in the majority. About half relapse, especially those with persisting high titres. Long-term disability accrues from attack severity rather than progressive disease.
pearls: Bilateral, swollen-disc optic neuritis with long anterior nerve lesions: send MOG-IgG and AQP4-IgG together.
A low MOG titre in a classic MS picture is more likely a false positive than MOGAD.
Taper steroids slowly — relapse after a quick stop is typical.
det.thd: Anti-MOG ใช้วินิจฉัย MOGAD ซึ่งพบได้ทุกวัยรวมทั้งเด็ก ผู้ป่วยมีประสาทตาอักเสบสองข้างร่วมกับขั้วประสาทตาบวม ไขสันหลังอักเสบโดยเฉพาะส่วน conus หรือ ADEM ควรตรวจด้วย cell-based assay ในเลือด และแปลผลตามระดับ titre ร่วมกับลักษณะทางคลินิกและ MRI ตามเกณฑ์ปี 2023 ผลบวกต่ำในผู้ป่วยที่เหมือน MS อาจเป็นผลบวกปลอม การรักษาเฉียบพลันคือสเตียรอยด์ขนาดสูงและลดยาช้าๆ ส่วนรายที่กลับเป็นซ้ำใช้ IVIG azathioprine หรือ mycophenolate

name: Anti-IgLON5 antibody
formal: A predominantly IgG4 (with IgG1) autoantibody against the neuronal cell-adhesion molecule IgLON5, strongly linked to the HLA-DQB1*05:01 / DRB1*10:01 haplotype; it marks anti-IgLON5 disease, a chronic disorder of older adults that sits between autoimmunity and neurodegeneration, combining NREM/REM parasomnia with sleep-disordered breathing, bulbar dysfunction, a PSP-like gait disorder, cognitive decline and chorea, with an underlying tauopathy.
simple: A blood and spinal-fluid test for a slowly progressive illness of older people that disturbs sleep (acting out dreams, loud breathing or choking at night), swallowing and speech, balance and memory. It can look like Parkinson-type diseases but sometimes improves with immune treatment.
th: Anti-IgLON5 เป็นแอนติบอดีชนิด IgG4 เป็นหลักต่อโปรตีนยึดเซลล์ประสาท IgLON5 สัมพันธ์กับ HLA-DRB1*10:01 ทำให้เกิดโรคเรื้อรังในผู้สูงอายุ มีความผิดปกติขณะหลับ กลืนลำบาก เดินลำบากคล้าย PSP และความจำเสื่อม ร่วมกับพยาธิสภาพ tau
tempoNote: Typically insidious over months to years (median several years before diagnosis); a minority present subacutely over weeks
feat: Target and class: IgLON5 adhesion protein; IgG4 antibodies block its binding to partners, while IgG1 antibodies internalise it
Who: median age early 60s, equal sex ratio; most carry HLA-DQB1*05:01 or DRB1*10:01; cancer and other autoimmunity rare
Sleep: NREM and REM parasomnia with purposeful movements, stridor, obstructive apnoea — video-polysomnography is diagnostic support
Other syndromes: bulbar (dysphagia, dysarthria, vocal cord palsy, central hypoventilation), PSP-like gait instability with gaze palsy, cognitive decline with or without chorea
Pathology: neuronal 3R/4R tau deposits predominating in hypothalamus and brainstem tegmentum
inv: Serum and CSF IgLON5-IgG by cell-based assay (tissue-based neuropil pattern supportive)
Video-polysomnography for parasomnia, stridor and abnormal sleep architecture
MRI usually normal or showing brainstem atrophy; CSF protein raised in about half, pleocytosis in about a third
HLA typing as supportive evidence; serum neurofilament light as an activity marker

case.who: 68-year-old man, retired postal clerk from Phitsanulok
case.story: Three years of shouting and grabbing in sleep with loud nocturnal stridor, then 8 months of choking on rice, slurred speech and two backward falls. Earlier labelled as REM sleep behaviour disorder and then possible PSP.
case.exam: Mild dysarthria, limited vertical saccades, postural instability, slight generalised chorea; MoCA 24/30.
case.tests: Video-PSG: undifferentiated NREM sleep with vocalisations and purposeful movements, stridor and obstructive apnoeas; serum and CSF IgLON5-IgG positive; HLA-DRB1*10:01 carrier; MRI mild brainstem atrophy.
case.q: Why test for this antibody in an apparent neurodegenerative syndrome?
case.a: Anti-IgLON5 disease can mimic RBD, PSP or MSA but may respond to immunotherapy (best with combinations including second-line agents such as rituximab), especially when treated before severe tau-related damage; CPAP or tracheostomy may be needed for stridor.

read.where: Considerations about the diagnosis of antibody-negative autoimmune encephalitis

det.patho: IgLON5 is a neuronal adhesion molecule. Patient antibodies cause irreversible internalisation of IgLON5 clusters and disturb neuronal cytoskeleton, and autopsies show neuronal tau deposition in the hypothalamus and brainstem tegmentum. The strong HLA association and antibody effects support a primary autoimmune process that leads to secondary neurodegeneration, explaining why early treatment matters most.
det.clinical: Four overlapping presentations are recognised: a sleep presentation (abnormal behaviours during REM as well as non-REM sleep, stridor, obstructive apnoea, excessive daytime sleepiness), a bulbar syndrome, a PSP-like syndrome with gait instability and gaze palsy, and cognitive decline with or without chorea. Dysautonomia, fasciculations and sudden death during sleep from central hypoventilation or laryngospasm are reported.
det.diagnosis: Cell-based assay of serum and CSF; video-polysomnography is highly informative. MRI is often normal and CSF may show raised protein. HLA typing supports but does not make the diagnosis. Consider testing in atypical PSP, MSA or RBD presentations with stridor, bulbar features or chorea.
det.treatment: Respond to immunotherapy in up to half initially, but sustained benefit is less common. Combination therapy and second-line agents (rituximab, cyclophosphamide) give better results than single first-line agents. CPAP or tracheostomy for stridor and sleep apnoea, feeding support for dysphagia.
det.prognosis: Untreated disease progresses, with mortality from aspiration, sleep-related respiratory events or sudden death. Earlier diagnosis, lower neurofilament levels and absence of advanced tau pathology predict better response.
pearls: Parasomnia with stridor in an older adult: request video-PSG and IgLON5 antibodies.
An apparent PSP or MSA with prominent sleep and bulbar features deserves IgLON5 testing.
Treat early and in combination — late disease is largely tau-driven.
det.thd: Anti-IgLON5 เป็นโรคที่อยู่กึ่งกลางระหว่างภูมิคุ้มกันกับสมองเสื่อม พบในผู้สูงอายุ อาการเด่นคือละเมอทำท่าทางขณะหลับ หายใจเสียงดังหรือหยุดหายใจขณะหลับ กลืนลำบาก พูดไม่ชัด ล้มบ่อย และความจำเสื่อม คล้าย PSP หรือ MSA การตรวจ video-polysomnography ช่วยมาก ผู้ป่วยบางรายตอบสนองต่อยาปรับภูมิคุ้มกัน โดยเฉพาะเมื่อให้ร่วมกันหลายชนิดและให้ตั้งแต่ระยะแรก

name: Anti-neurexin-3-alpha antibody
formal: A rare autoantibody against neurexin-3-alpha, a presynaptic adhesion protein that organises synapse development and function; it marks a severe encephalitis of young to middle-aged adults with a prodrome of fever, headache or gastrointestinal upset, followed by confusion, seizures, reduced consciousness and sometimes orofacial dyskinesia and hypoventilation, with substantial mortality in the first reported series.
simple: A rare antibody test for a severe brain inflammation in younger adults that starts like a flu or stomach bug and then causes confusion, fits and drowsiness. Testing is mostly done in research laboratories.
th: Anti-neurexin-3-alpha เป็นแอนติบอดีพบน้อยต่อโปรตีนยึดไซแนปส์ด้านก่อนไซแนปส์ ทำให้สมองอักเสบรุนแรงในผู้ใหญ่อายุน้อยถึงวัยกลางคน เริ่มด้วยไข้ ปวดศีรษะ หรืออาการทางเดินอาหาร แล้วตามด้วยสับสน ชัก และซึมลง
tempoNote: A febrile or gastrointestinal prodrome is followed within days to weeks by rapidly deepening encephalopathy
feat: Target: neurexin-3-alpha on presynaptic terminals; antibodies lower neurexin-3-alpha levels and the number of synapses in cultured neurons
Who: young to middle-aged adults (median mid-40s), more women
Phenotype: prodrome of fever, headache or diarrhoea, then confusion, seizures, decreased level of consciousness, sometimes orofacial dyskinesia and central hypoventilation needing ventilation
Investigations: CSF abnormal in all reported patients; MRI medial temporal signal in a minority
No consistent tumour association; some patients had other autoimmune conditions
inv: Serum and CSF testing by cell-based assay in a reference or research laboratory (not in routine commercial panels)
Tissue-based immunohistochemistry screen showing neuropil reactivity when commercial panels are negative
CSF analysis (pleocytosis, raised IgG index), MRI brain, EEG
Exclude infective encephalitis thoroughly, given the febrile prodrome

case.story: Four days of fever, headache and diarrhoea, then increasing confusion over a week and two generalised seizures; she became drowsy and needed intubation for poor breathing effort.
case.exam: GCS 8 off sedation, intermittent orofacial dyskinesia, no meningism, no focal limb weakness.
case.tests: CSF 40 lymphocytes/µL with raised IgG index; HSV and other viral PCRs negative; commercial autoimmune encephalitis panel negative; tissue-based assay showed neuropil staining, and a research laboratory confirmed neurexin-3-alpha antibodies; MRI normal.
case.q: What does a negative commercial panel mean when the clinical picture strongly suggests autoimmune encephalitis?
case.a: It does not exclude antibody-mediated disease: start immunotherapy on clinical grounds (Graus 2016 possible autoimmune encephalitis) and send samples for tissue-based screening and research-level assays, which can reveal rare targets such as neurexin-3-alpha.

det.patho: Neurexins are presynaptic adhesion molecules that pair with postsynaptic partners to build and tune synapses. Patient antibodies reduce neurexin-3-alpha clustering and decrease synapse number in neuronal cultures, consistent with a direct pathogenic effect.
det.clinical: In the small initial series, patients had a prodrome of fever, headache, nausea or diarrhoea, then developed confusion, seizures and falling consciousness; several had orofacial dyskinesia and some needed ventilatory support for central hypoventilation. The picture overlaps strongly with NMDAR encephalitis.
det.diagnosis: Specific testing is limited to reference and research laboratories, so suspicion usually arises when tissue-based assays show neuropil reactivity but standard cell-based panels are negative. CSF was abnormal in every reported case and MRI was usually normal.
det.treatment: Treated as other surface-antibody encephalitides: early first-line immunotherapy with escalation to rituximab or cyclophosphamide, plus intensive supportive care.
det.prognosis: Of the first reported patients, a substantial proportion (around two in five) died despite immunotherapy and the others recovered partially, although numbers were very small and outcomes in later reports may differ.
pearls: Commercial panel negative + strongly suspected autoimmune encephalitis: send tissue-based screening and research assays.
Neurexin-3-alpha encephalitis looks like NMDAR encephalitis after a febrile or gut prodrome.
Treat on clinical grounds — waiting for a rare antibody wastes time.
det.thd: Anti-neurexin-3-alpha เป็นแอนติบอดีที่พบน้อยมาก ทำให้สมองอักเสบรุนแรงในผู้ใหญ่อายุน้อยถึงวัยกลางคน มักเริ่มด้วยไข้ ปวดศีรษะ หรือท้องเสีย แล้วตามด้วยสับสน ชัก และซึมจนต้องใช้เครื่องช่วยหายใจ คล้ายกับ NMDAR encephalitis การตรวจทำได้เฉพาะห้องปฏิบัติการอ้างอิงหรือห้องวิจัย จึงควรเริ่มยาปรับภูมิคุ้มกันตามอาการทางคลินิกโดยไม่ต้องรอผล

name: Anti-GAD65 antibody
formal: An autoantibody against GAD65, the smaller isoform of glutamic acid decarboxylase — an intracellular enzyme that synthesises GABA in inhibitory nerve terminals and pancreatic islets; at low titre it is common in type 1 diabetes and the general population, whereas high serum titres with intrathecal synthesis mark neurological GAD65 autoimmunity — stiff-person spectrum disorder, cerebellar ataxia, temporal lobe epilepsy/limbic encephalitis and overlaps — usually without cancer.
simple: A blood test that is positive at low levels in many people with type 1 diabetes, but at very high levels (and in spinal fluid) points to an immune nerve disease: stiff muscles with spasms, unsteady walking, or hard-to-control seizures from the temporal lobe.
th: Anti-GAD65 เป็นแอนติบอดีต่อเอนไซม์สร้าง GABA ภายในเซลล์ ระดับต่ำพบบ่อยในเบาหวานชนิดที่ 1 แต่ถ้าระดับสูงมากในเลือดร่วมกับพบในน้ำไขสันหลัง บ่งชี้โรคระบบประสาทจากภูมิคุ้มกัน เช่น stiff-person syndrome ataxia ของสมองน้อย และโรคลมชักกลีบขมับ ส่วนใหญ่ไม่สัมพันธ์กับมะเร็ง
tempoNote: Stiff-person and epilepsy phenotypes progress over months to years; cerebellar ataxia may be subacute (weeks) or slowly progressive
feat: Target: intracellular GAD65; the antibody is a marker of a T-cell-mediated process rather than a proven direct cause of neuronal dysfunction
Titre matters: high serum titres (well above the diabetes range) and CSF positivity with intrathecal synthesis indicate neurological relevance
Syndromes: stiff-person spectrum (axial rigidity, spasms, startle), cerebellar ataxia, drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy or limbic encephalitis, and overlaps including PERM
Companions: type 1 diabetes, thyroid disease, pernicious anaemia and vitiligo; GlyR or GABAAR antibodies may coexist
Tumour: uncommon (thymoma, lung or neuroendocrine cancer occasionally); consider in older patients, atypical features or other neural antibodies — Graus 2021 low-risk antibody
inv: Serum GAD65 titre by quantitative immunoassay (ELISA or RIA) — report the titre, not just positive/negative; confirm low-intermediate results with CSF
CSF GAD65 with antibody index for intrathecal synthesis, cells and oligoclonal bands
EMG for continuous motor unit activity (stiff-person); MRI brain (medial temporal change in epilepsy, cerebellar atrophy late)
HbA1c, thyroid function and B12; chest CT if risk factors or atypical features

case.who: 44-year-old woman, primary-school teacher from Nakhon Si Thammarat, with type 1 diabetes since age 30
case.story: One year of a stiff lower back and legs, a hunched posture, and sudden spasms when a motorbike horn sounded behind her; she now walks slowly holding the wall and fears crossing open spaces.
case.exam: Lumbar hyperlordosis with board-like paraspinal and abdominal muscles, stimulus-induced spasms, exaggerated startle; strength, reflexes and eye movements normal.
case.tests: Serum GAD65 >2,000 IU/mL (far above the diabetes range); CSF GAD65 positive with raised antibody index; EMG continuous motor unit activity in paraspinal and abdominal muscles relieved by IV diazepam; GlyR negative; CT chest normal.
case.q: Her endocrinologist says GAD antibodies are expected with type 1 diabetes — is this result meaningful?
case.a: Yes: the very high serum titre plus CSF intrathecal synthesis and a typical syndrome establish GAD65 stiff-person syndrome; treat with diazepam and baclofen and add IVIG, which has randomised evidence in SPS.

read.where: 8 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System

det.patho: GAD65 is a cytoplasmic enzyme bound to synaptic vesicles in GABAergic terminals. Because the antigen is intracellular, the antibody is probably a marker of a cytotoxic T-cell process rather than the direct cause of disease, although some patient antibodies can reduce GABA release experimentally. Loss of GABAergic inhibition in spinal cord, brainstem, cerebellum and hippocampus explains the stiffness, ataxia and seizures.
det.clinical: Stiff-person spectrum disorder causes fluctuating axial and proximal limb rigidity, painful spasms triggered by noise, touch or emotion, hyperlordosis and task-specific phobia. Cerebellar ataxia affects gait and eye movements, sometimes after a period of stiff-person features. GAD65-associated epilepsy is usually focal temporal, chronic and drug-resistant; a limbic encephalitis picture occurs in some. Overlaps between these syndromes are common, and other organ-specific autoimmunity is frequent.
det.diagnosis: The key question is titre: low titres are found in type 1 diabetes and in a few percent of healthy people, while neurological disease usually has very high serum titres and CSF antibodies with intrathecal synthesis. Laboratories use different units, so compare with the reporting laboratory's high-titre threshold. EMG supports stiff-person syndrome. A tumour search is advised when the patient is older, a smoker, has rapid progression or has coexisting onconeural antibodies.
det.treatment: Symptomatic: benzodiazepines (diazepam, clonazepam) and baclofen, including intrathecal baclofen for severe stiffness; antiseizure drugs for epilepsy. Immunotherapy: IVIG has randomised evidence in SPS; steroids, plasma exchange, rituximab or mycophenolate are used for refractory cases, though a randomised rituximab trial in SPS was negative. Epilepsy and long-standing ataxia respond less well than stiff-person syndrome.
det.prognosis: Course is chronic and fluctuating. Stiff-person syndrome often improves with GABAergic drugs and IVIG but rarely remits; epilepsy frequently remains drug-resistant; ataxia may stabilise with early immunotherapy. Mortality relates mainly to falls, autonomic crises and sedation.
pearls: A positive GAD result is meaningless without the titre — always ask for the number.
Type 1 diabetes explains low titres, not stiff-person syndrome; very high titres plus CSF positivity are the neurological signature.
GAD65 epilepsy is the hard-to-treat end of autoimmune epilepsy; do not expect a dramatic immunotherapy response.
det.thd: Anti-GAD65 ต้องแปลผลตามระดับ titre เสมอ ระดับต่ำพบได้บ่อยในเบาหวานชนิดที่ 1 และคนทั่วไป ส่วนระดับสูงมากในเลือดร่วมกับพบในน้ำไขสันหลังบ่งชี้โรคระบบประสาท ได้แก่ stiff-person syndrome ataxia ของสมองน้อย และโรคลมชักกลีบขมับที่ดื้อยา ส่วนใหญ่ไม่เกี่ยวกับมะเร็ง การรักษาใช้ diazepam baclofen และ IVIG ซึ่งได้ผลดีในกลุ่ม stiff-person มากกว่ากลุ่มโรคลมชัก

name: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis
formal: Autoimmune encephalitis driven by IgG that binds the GluN1 portion of the NMDA receptor, producing psychiatric symptoms, seizures, orofacial dyskinesia, decreased consciousness and autonomic instability; associated with ovarian teratoma in young women.
simple: An immune attack on brain receptors, often in young women, that starts with strange behaviour or psychosis and progresses to seizures, abnormal movements and reduced consciousness; it is treatable.
th: สมองอักเสบจากภูมิต้านทานต่อตัวรับ NMDA — เริ่มด้วยพฤติกรรมแปลก ประสาทหลอน แล้วชัก ปากขยับเอง ซึมลง พบร่วมกับเนื้องอกรังไข่

aN: anti nmdar encephalitis | nmda encephalitis | nmdar | autoimmune encephalitis nmda

det.patho: IgG antibodies to the GluN1 subunit cross-link NMDA receptors and cause their internalisation, reducing glutamatergic signalling without much neuronal death, which explains the potential for full recovery. Triggers include ovarian teratomas containing neural tissue and prior HSV encephalitis; many cases have no identifiable trigger. Among autoimmune encephalitides it ranks among the commonest, mainly in children and young women.
det.clinical: A viral-like prodrome is followed by psychiatric symptoms — anxiety, insomnia, agitation, bizarre behaviour, psychosis or catatonia — and then by memory loss, speech reduction, seizures and abnormal movements, especially orofacial and limb dyskinesias. Later stages bring decreased consciousness, autonomic instability (tachy- or bradycardia, labile BP, hyperthermia) and central hypoventilation needing ventilation. Children more often present with seizures or movement disorders; men less often have a tumour. Many patients are first admitted to psychiatry.
det.diagnosis: Test for GluN1 IgG in CSF, which is more sensitive and specific than serum testing (serum can be falsely positive or negative). CSF often shows mild lymphocytosis and oligoclonal bands; MRI is normal in most or shows non-specific FLAIR change. EEG commonly shows diffuse slowing, and the extreme delta brush pattern is characteristic in severe cases. Search for a teratoma with pelvic ultrasound and MRI in women, and consider testicular imaging in men. The Graus criteria allow probable diagnosis and early treatment before antibody results.
det.treatment: First-line immunotherapy is high-dose IV methylprednisolone with IVIG (total 2 g/kg, split across 2–5 days) and/or plasma exchange, combined with prompt removal of any tumour. If there is no clear improvement in about two weeks, escalate to rituximab and/or cyclophosphamide; refractory cases may receive other agents within specialist care. Supportive ICU care for dysautonomia, hypoventilation and seizures is often prolonged. Antipsychotics can worsen dyskinesia and mimic neuroleptic malignant syndrome — use them cautiously.
det.prognosis: About 80% of patients achieve good functional recovery, though it may take 1–2 years; relapses occur in around 10–15%, less often after tumour removal and second-line therapy.
pearls: A young woman with new psychosis plus seizures, dyskinesia or dysautonomia needs an LP and NMDAR antibodies.
Test CSF, not only serum.
Recovery is slow; long ICU stays are not a reason to stop aggressive treatment.

aN: cord compression | mscc | metastatic spinal cord compression | compressive myelopathy | epidural abscess | cervical spondylotic myelopathy

det.patho: Extrinsic pressure compromises cord tissue directly and through venous congestion and ischaemia, producing oedema and eventually infarction if not relieved. Malignant compression arises mostly from vertebral body metastases (breast, lung, prostate, kidney, myeloma, lymphoma) and occurs mostly at thoracic levels. Other causes include degenerative cervical myelopathy, disc herniation, epidural abscess (diabetes, IV drug use, bacteraemia, spinal procedures), epidural haematoma (anticoagulation) and trauma.
det.clinical: Back or neck pain usually comes first, often worse at night, lying flat or with coughing, and may radiate in a band (radicular pain). Weakness, numbness below a level, gait ataxia and later urinary retention and constipation follow; once a patient is non-ambulant, recovery is much less likely. Cervical spondylotic myelopathy evolves slowly with clumsy hands, Hoffmann sign and spastic gait. Fever and raised inflammatory markers suggest abscess; sudden onset on anticoagulation suggests haematoma.
det.diagnosis: Obtain MRI of the whole spine as an emergency (within 24 hours, sooner if neurological deficit), because multiple levels are often involved. Use CT myelography if MRI is contraindicated. Investigate the cause: blood cultures and inflammatory markers for abscess, coagulation studies for haematoma, and staging or biopsy when malignancy is new. Examine sensory level and perineal sensation, and measure post-void residual volume.
det.treatment: For malignant compression give dexamethasone (commonly 16 mg/day in divided doses with gastric protection) and arrange urgent oncology and spine surgery review; decompressive surgery followed by radiotherapy benefits selected patients with good prognosis, while radiotherapy alone suits others. Epidural abscess needs IV antibiotics and usually surgical drainage; haematoma needs reversal of anticoagulation and evacuation. Degenerative myelopathy with progressive deficit is treated by surgical decompression. Pain control, bladder care, VTE prophylaxis and rehabilitation are integral.
det.prognosis: Functional outcome mirrors the neurological state at treatment: most patients walking at diagnosis remain ambulant, whereas few paraplegic patients regain walking.
pearls: New back pain in a patient with cancer deserves early MRI before weakness develops.
Image the whole spine — skip lesions are common in metastatic disease.
Fever plus back pain plus neurological signs = epidural abscess until proven otherwise.

aN: classic migraine | migraine aura | visual aura | scintillating scotoma | fortification spectra

det.patho: Aura is caused by cortical spreading depolarisation, a slowly propagating wave of neuronal and glial depolarisation (about 3 mm per minute) followed by suppressed activity; this explains the gradual march of symptoms across the visual field or body. The wave can activate meningeal trigeminal afferents, and release of CGRP and other neuropeptides in the trigeminovascular system generates the headache, sensitising central pathways. Familial hemiplegic migraine shows the same process driven by ion-channel or pump mutations (CACNA1A, ATP1A2, SCN1A). Migraine with aura roughly doubles ischaemic stroke risk, an effect amplified by smoking and oestrogen-containing contraceptives and linked in part to PFO and endothelial factors.
det.clinical: Visual aura is most common — a scintillating zigzag or scotoma expanding across the visual field over minutes — followed by sensory aura (tingling spreading up the hand to the face and tongue) and less often speech disturbance. Each symptom lasts 5–60 minutes and symptoms occur in succession rather than all at once. Headache usually follows within an hour but aura may occur alone, especially in older people (late-life migraine accompaniments). Hemiplegic migraine (motor aura, sometimes with confusion or coma) and migraine with brainstem aura (vertigo, dysarthria, diplopia, ataxia) are distinct subtypes. Complications include persistent aura without infarction lasting over a week and migrainous infarction, where an attack's usual aura persists and imaging shows an infarct in the matching area.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical using ICHD-3: at least two attacks with fully reversible visual, sensory or speech aura, plus at least three of six features — gradual spread over 5 minutes or more, two or more symptoms in succession, each lasting 5–60 minutes, at least one unilateral, at least one positive, and headache accompanying or following within an hour. Red flags requiring imaging and vascular work-up include first aura after 50, sudden onset, motor or prolonged aura, aura always on the same side, or a changing pattern. Distinguish from TIA (sudden, negative, simultaneous symptoms), focal seizures (faster spread, brief, often with automatisms), amyloid spells in the elderly, and RCVS or dissection when headache is severe. EEG is not routinely needed; genetic testing is reserved for familial hemiplegic forms.
det.treatment: Acute treatment uses NSAIDs or paracetamol with an antiemetic, with triptans taken at headache onset rather than during aura; gepants and lasmiditan are alternatives when vascular disease makes triptans unsuitable, and triptans are traditionally avoided in hemiplegic and brainstem aura. Preventive options include propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate, flunarizine (widely used in Thailand), candesartan, valproate (not in women who may conceive), CGRP monoclonal antibodies, gepants for prevention and, for chronic migraine, botulinum toxin. Combined hormonal contraception should be avoided in women with aura; progestogen-only methods are acceptable. Address smoking, BP and lipids, and avoid medication overuse (simple analgesics on 15 or more days, triptans on 10 or more days a month). PFO closure for migraine alone is not recommended outside trials.
det.prognosis: Attacks often lessen with age, and isolated aura without headache becomes more frequent later in life; absolute stroke risk remains low in young women without other risk factors.
pearls: Positive phenomena that spread slowly = aura; sudden negative deficits = TIA.
Combined oral contraceptives are contraindicated in migraine with aura.
Persistent aura beyond an hour needs imaging for migrainous infarction.
A first aura after age 50 is a diagnosis of exclusion — image the brain and vessels first.

aN: hypoglycemia | low blood sugar | neuroglycopenia

det.patho: The brain depends almost entirely on glucose; when blood glucose falls (usually below about 3.0 mmol/L or 54 mg/dL) adrenergic counter-regulation produces warning symptoms, and further falls cause neuroglycopenia. Most cases occur in people with diabetes on insulin or sulfonylureas; other causes are alcohol, liver or renal failure, sepsis, adrenal insufficiency and insulinoma. Repeated episodes blunt the warning response (impaired awareness).
det.clinical: Autonomic symptoms — sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger, anxiety — precede confusion, odd behaviour, slurred speech, seizures and coma. Focal deficits, including hemiparesis that resolves with glucose, can closely mimic stroke. Elderly patients and those on beta-blockers may have no warning. Prolonged severe hypoglycaemia can cause permanent damage to the hippocampus, basal ganglia and cortex.
det.diagnosis: Check capillary glucose immediately in any acute neurological presentation and confirm with a laboratory sample. Whipple's triad — symptoms, low glucose, relief with glucose — supports the diagnosis in non-diabetic patients. In unexplained cases, draw insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, beta-hydroxybutyrate and a sulfonylurea screen during the episode. MRI after severe events may show DWI changes in cortex, hippocampi or internal capsule, sometimes reversible.
det.treatment: Give oral glucose if the patient is alert and can swallow; otherwise IV dextrose (for example 10% dextrose 150–200 mL or 50% dextrose 50 mL) or IM glucagon. Give thiamine first in malnourished or alcohol-dependent patients. Sulfonylurea-related hypoglycaemia can recur for many hours, so observe and consider octreotide. Review diabetes medications and educate on prevention.
det.prognosis: Rapid correction usually leads to full recovery; prolonged coma carries a risk of lasting cognitive impairment.
pearls: No stroke code should proceed without a glucose result.
Sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia is prolonged — admit and monitor.
Thiamine before or with glucose in at-risk patients prevents Wernicke encephalopathy.

qx.stem: A 61-year-old man from Phrae on new treatment for hypertension develops a sudden severe frontal headache with vomiting, followed by double vision and a drooping right eyelid. BP is 92/58 mmHg, sodium 128 mmol/L. He has a complete right third nerve palsy and bitemporal field loss. CT shows an enlarged pituitary fossa with a haemorrhagic sellar mass.

opts: Lumbar puncture to exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage
Start cabergoline before any other measure
Fluid restriction to correct hyponatraemia
Urgent CT angiography and coiling of a posterior communicating aneurysm
Give IV hydrocortisone (e.g. 100 mg) after drawing cortisol, then urgent neurosurgical and endocrine review

Lumbar puncture to exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage
Give IV hydrocortisone immediately, check electrolytes and pituitary hormones, and involve neurosurgery about decompression
Start cabergoline and repeat MRI in two weeks
Give IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for presumed hypophysitis

The haemorrhagic sellar mass explains the third nerve palsy, so aneurysm imaging or LP is not the priority; cabergoline is for prolactinoma and hypophysitis does not bleed.

aN: apoplexy | pituitary hemorrhage

det.patho: Sudden haemorrhage or infarction within a pituitary adenoma — often previously undiagnosed — causes rapid expansion of the sellar contents. Pressure spreads upward to the chiasm and laterally into the cavernous sinuses, while destruction of normal gland causes acute hypopituitarism. Precipitants include anticoagulation, surgery, pituitary stimulation tests, pregnancy, dopamine agonists and hypertension.
det.clinical: Abrupt severe headache, often thunderclap, with nausea and vomiting is typical. Visual loss (bitemporal field defects or reduced acuity) and ophthalmoplegia from III, IV or VI palsies follow; the third nerve is most often affected. Meningism and reduced consciousness may occur from blood in the subarachnoid space. Acute ACTH deficiency causes hypotension, hyponatraemia and collapse, which can be fatal if missed.
det.diagnosis: MRI of the pituitary is the investigation of choice, showing a sellar mass with haemorrhage; CT may miss it. Take blood for cortisol, thyroid function, prolactin, gonadotrophins, electrolytes and glucose, but do not delay steroid treatment for results. Formal visual acuity and fields guide management. SAH, CVT, meningitis and basilar artery thrombosis are the main mimics.
det.treatment: Give IV hydrocortisone (100 mg bolus then ongoing replacement) promptly to all suspected cases, along with fluid resuscitation. Management is shared between neurosurgery, endocrinology and ophthalmology. Patients with severe or deteriorating visual loss or reduced consciousness usually undergo early transsphenoidal decompression; milder cases may be managed conservatively with close monitoring. Long-term hormone replacement is frequently needed.
det.prognosis: Ophthalmoplegia usually recovers; visual field outcome depends on severity and duration of compression, and many patients need lifelong hormone therapy.
pearls: Thunderclap headache + ophthalmoplegia + visual loss = image the sella.
Give hydrocortisone before any test results return.
CT can look normal; MRI is needed.

aN: chronic paroxysmal hemicrania | cph | episodic paroxysmal hemicrania

det.patho: Paroxysmal hemicrania (PH) is one of the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias: nociceptive traffic in the trigeminal system reflexly switches on cranial parasympathetic outflow, so one-sided pain arrives together with eye and nose autonomic signs. Functional imaging shows activity in the posterior hypothalamic region, much as in cluster headache, yet why indomethacin abolishes PH so completely remains unexplained. Older pooled series suggested a female excess (around 2–3 to 1), but more recent prospective cohorts find the sexes roughly equally affected, unlike the clear male excess of cluster headache; most patients first develop attacks in their thirties or forties, although cases from childhood to the ninth decade are described. During attacks CGRP and VIP rise in the cranial venous blood and normalise with indomethacin, and the hypothalamic activation seen in the untreated state is absent once indomethacin has made the patient pain-free. The chronic form, with no remission or remissions shorter than three months, is seen more often than the episodic form. Secondary PH has been linked to pituitary and other parasellar tumours, vascular malformations and posterior fossa lesions.
det.clinical: Attacks are severe and strictly one-sided, usually always on the same side (although up to about 15% have attacks on either side), centred on the orbit, temple or forehead, last roughly 2–30 minutes and come more than five times a day for over half of the active period, including at night. Ipsilateral tearing, conjunctival redness, nasal blockage or discharge, lid swelling, forehead sweating, ptosis or miosis accompany the pain, and many patients become agitated during the attack. A minority of attacks are set off mechanically by bending, turning the head or pressing over the upper neck. Between attacks there is usually no pain or only a mild ache; a continuous one-sided background headache points instead to hemicrania continua. Photophobia or nausea can appear and do not exclude the diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 asks for at least 20 attacks of typical duration and frequency with at least one ipsilateral autonomic feature or restlessness, and for complete prevention by therapeutic doses of indomethacin. A practical oral trial begins at 25 mg three times daily and is stepped up every few days to 50 mg and then 75 mg three times daily, judging the effect over about 1–2 weeks; where an injectable indomethacin test is available it gives a quicker answer. A partial response usually means the dose was too low or the diagnosis is different. Every patient needs MRI brain with pituitary views, with pituitary hormone tests when imaging or history raises concern. The key mimics are cluster headache (longer and fewer attacks, male excess, no indomethacin effect), SUNCT/SUNA (stabs of seconds with cutaneous triggers), hemicrania continua and trigeminal neuralgia.
det.treatment: Indomethacin is the drug of choice; once attacks are abolished, step down to the smallest dose that keeps the patient free (often 25–100 mg/day) and co-prescribe a proton pump inhibitor. Review renal function, blood pressure and gastrointestinal symptoms at intervals, particularly in older people. For indomethacin intolerance, partly effective options include COX-2 inhibitors such as celecoxib or etoricoxib (mindful of cardiovascular risk), piroxicam, topiramate (helping roughly two in five in pooled reports) and verapamil (less often), with isolated reports of hypothalamic or occipital nerve stimulation in refractory cases; sumatriptan, oxygen and occipital or supraorbital nerve blocks rarely help, in contrast to cluster headache. In episodic PH the drug can be withdrawn when a bout is expected to finish and restarted at relapse. Any secondary cause found on imaging should be treated directly.
det.prognosis: PH is benign and usually fully controlled by indomethacin; the long-term concerns are drug toxicity and the need for maintenance therapy in the chronic form, although some patients enter lasting remission.
pearls: Many short, one-sided attacks a day with autonomic signs, especially in a woman, should make you think PH before cluster.
The indomethacin response is part of the definition; a failed full-dose trial calls for rethinking the diagnosis.
Image every patient — pituitary and parasellar lesions can produce an indomethacin-responsive PH picture.
Always cover indomethacin with gastric protection and check renal function.
Absent autonomic signs (about one patient in ten) should not stop an indomethacin trial when the attack pattern fits.
Oxygen and triptans that rescue cluster attacks do little in PH — failure of both is another hint to try indomethacin.

aN: faint | vasovagal syncope | reflex syncope | convulsive syncope | cardiac syncope

det.patho: Transient global cerebral hypoperfusion — systolic pressure falling to roughly 50–60 mmHg for several seconds — causes loss of consciousness and tone. Reflex (vasovagal, situational, carotid sinus) syncope arises from inappropriate vasodilatation and/or bradycardia; orthostatic syncope reflects autonomic failure, hypovolaemia or drugs; cardiac syncope results from arrhythmia or structural heart disease and carries the worst prognosis.
det.clinical: Reflex syncope typically follows prolonged standing, pain, emotion, micturition or coughing, with a prodrome of warmth, nausea, sweating and fading vision. Loss of consciousness lasts seconds to under a minute, with pallor and rapid reorientation. Brief irregular jerks occur in many fainters and are often mistaken for seizure. Syncope during exertion, while supine, with palpitations or a family history of sudden death suggests a cardiac cause.
det.diagnosis: A detailed eyewitness history plus examination, lying and standing BP and a 12-lead ECG resolve most cases. High-risk ECG features include conduction block, long or short QT, Brugada pattern, pre-excitation and ischaemia. Further tests are chosen by suspicion: echocardiography, ambulatory or implantable loop monitoring, tilt-table testing and carotid sinus massage. EEG and brain imaging are not routinely helpful. Features against syncope include prolonged post-ictal confusion, lateral tongue biting and head turning.
det.treatment: Reflex syncope is managed with explanation, trigger avoidance, hydration, counter-pressure manoeuvres and, rarely, medication or pacing for cardioinhibitory forms. Orthostatic hypotension responds to stopping offending drugs, fluids and salt, compression garments, and midodrine or fludrocortisone. Cardiac syncope requires treating the underlying arrhythmia or structural disease, including pacemakers or ICDs.
det.prognosis: Reflex syncope is benign apart from injury; cardiac syncope carries a substantially increased mortality.
pearls: Jerks during a faint do not mean epilepsy — ask about prodrome and recovery speed.
Exertional syncope is cardiac until proven otherwise.
Every patient with transient loss of consciousness needs an ECG.

Chapter 50: Headache attributed to non-vascular intracranial disorder

aN: carcinomatous meningitis | leptomeningeal carcinomatosis | neoplastic meningitis

det.patho: Cancer cells reach the leptomeninges mostly through the blood (via choroid plexus or meningeal vessels), but also by direct spread from dural, subdural or parenchymal deposits, by creeping along nerve sheaths, or by spillage during resection of posterior fossa metastases; once in the CSF they drift and settle over the brain surface, cranial nerves, cord and roots. It complicates roughly 3–8% of cancers, with breast cancer the commonest solid primary, followed by lung cancer (small cell, and EGFR- or ALK-driven adenocarcinoma) and melanoma; leukaemias and lymphomas seed the meninges readily, and in a small minority the meningeal disease is the first sign of cancer. Tumour coating the arachnoid villi or basal cisterns impairs CSF absorption, giving communicating hydrocephalus in about one in ten.
det.clinical: Early complaints are often vague — nausea, vomiting, fatigue, intermittent confusion or an odd new headache — before signs appear at several separate levels of the neuraxis: multiple cranial nerve palsies (diplopia, facial weakness, sensorineural deafness, numb chin), patchy radicular pain and numbness, asymmetric lower motor neuron leg weakness and sphincter disturbance from cauda equina involvement. Raised pressure can cause papilloedema, seizures and plateau waves with transient loss of awareness, while frank meningism is unusual. The tempo is weeks, typically in someone with advanced, often progressing systemic cancer. Any cancer patient with unexplained, progressive multifocal neurology and an unremarkable brain scan deserves a deliberate search for this diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: Obtain gadolinium MRI of the whole brain and spine before LP, because puncture itself can produce meningeal enhancement; look for linear or nodular enhancement of sulci, cerebellar folia, brainstem surface ('sugar coating'), cranial nerves and cauda equina roots, which is seen in roughly 70% (CT is far less sensitive). CSF is nearly always abnormal — raised pressure and protein, low glucose ratio, lymphocytes — and malignant cells on cytology confirm the diagnosis; send at least 10 mL to the lab promptly, since one sample detects around two-thirds and three samples about 90%. Flow cytometry helps in haematological cancers, and CSF circulating tumour cell counts or tumour DNA sequencing increase sensitivity and can reveal targetable mutations. EANO–ESMO criteria separate cytology-proven from probable or possible disease using clinical and MRI findings; infection (TB, fungi), sarcoidosis, ICI meningitis and post-procedural enhancement are the main mimics.
det.treatment: Care is palliative and tailored to performance status, systemic disease control and tumour biology. Focal radiotherapy to bulky or symptomatic sites (posterior fossa, cauda equina) is the mainstay; proton craniospinal irradiation improved survival in a phase II trial for selected breast and lung cancer patients, whereas photon craniospinal treatment is limited by marrow toxicity. CNS-penetrant systemic agents are increasingly preferred — for example osimertinib for EGFR-mutant lung cancer, newer ALK inhibitors, HER2-directed drugs and immunotherapy in melanoma — while intrathecal methotrexate, cytarabine or thiotepa (or intrathecal trastuzumab in HER2-positive breast cancer) via an Ommaya reservoir or LP has a debated survival benefit and is useless with blocked CSF flow. Treat hydrocephalus with shunting, give steroids, analgesia and seizure control as needed, and involve palliative care early.
det.prognosis: Median survival is typically 2–6 months; breast cancer, haematological malignancy and tumours with an effective targeted drug fare better, whereas poor performance status, encephalopathy and melanoma or lung primaries without a target do worst.
pearls: Several cranial nerve and root deficits at different levels in a cancer patient = leptomeningeal disease until shown otherwise.
Scan the whole neuraxis before the LP, then send large-volume CSF for cytology and repeat up to three times.
A numb chin or new unilateral deafness in someone with known cancer is a red flag.
Ask oncology about actionable mutations — targeted drugs now change survival for some patients.
