case.who: 58-year-old female teacher from Nonthaburi, never smoked
case.story: Two weeks of right-hand clumsiness and morning headaches; she had a dry cough for three months.
case.exam: Right pronator drift and right-hand dysmetria.
case.tests: MRI: three ring-enhancing lesions (left frontal, left parietal, right cerebellar) with marked oedema. CT chest: left upper lobe mass. Biopsy: lung adenocarcinoma with EGFR exon 19 deletion.
case.q: What treatment approach fits this molecular finding?
case.a: Brain metastases from EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma; dexamethasone for oedema, an intracranially active EGFR inhibitor such as osimertinib, with stereotactic radiosurgery for lesions that are symptomatic or do not respond.

read.where: Chapter 26 Metastatic Disease and the Nervous System

det.patho: Tumour cells reach the brain through arterial blood and lodge where vessels narrow at the grey–white junction and border zones; about 80% occur in the cerebral hemispheres, 15% in the cerebellum and 5% in the brainstem. Successful colonisation requires crossing the blood–brain barrier and adapting to the brain microenvironment. Better systemic control and longer survival have made brain metastases more common, partly because many drugs penetrate the brain poorly.
det.clinical: Presentation is with headache, focal weakness, speech or visual change, cognitive decline, gait ataxia or seizures, often over a few weeks. Haemorrhage produces stroke-like onset. Some patients are asymptomatic and found on staging MRI, which is routine in small-cell and advanced non-small-cell lung cancer, HER2-positive or triple-negative breast cancer and melanoma. Coexisting leptomeningeal disease should be suspected with cranial nerve palsies, hydrocephalus or radicular pain.
det.diagnosis: MRI with contrast shows round enhancing lesions, often multiple, with vasogenic oedema; a solitary lesion in a patient without known cancer needs tissue to exclude primary tumour, lymphoma or abscess. Perfusion, spectroscopy and diffusion imaging help with mimics, and with treatment-related radiation necrosis later. Molecular testing of the primary or brain lesion (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, HER2, BRAF) directly shapes management.
det.treatment: Dexamethasone (lowest effective dose, tapered) for symptomatic oedema; antiseizure medicine only if seizures have occurred. Surgical resection suits a large, symptomatic or diagnostically uncertain accessible lesion, usually followed by radiosurgery to the cavity. Stereotactic radiosurgery is preferred for limited numbers of lesions to spare cognition; whole-brain radiotherapy, with hippocampal avoidance and memantine where feasible, is reserved for widespread disease. Brain-penetrant systemic drugs — osimertinib for EGFR, alectinib or lorlatinib for ALK, tucatinib or trastuzumab deruxtecan for HER2, combined immune checkpoint inhibitors for melanoma — can control intracranial disease and may defer radiotherapy. Patients with poor performance status and no systemic options may benefit most from best supportive care.
det.prognosis: Highly variable: from a few months with poor performance status to several years in targetable lung cancer, HER2-positive breast cancer or melanoma responsive to therapy.
pearls: A new seizure or headache in a cancer patient is metastasis until imaging says otherwise.
Oedema out of proportion to lesion size at the grey–white junction suggests metastasis.
Ask for EGFR/ALK results — targeted drugs reach the brain and change the plan.
In Thailand, consider tuberculoma and neurocysticercosis when ring lesions appear without known cancer.
det.thd: Brain metastases คือมะเร็งจากอวัยวะอื่นแพร่มาที่สมอง พบบ่อยที่สุดในบรรดาเนื้องอกสมองผู้ใหญ่ ต้นตอที่พบบ่อยคือปอด เต้านม melanoma ไต ลำไส้ใหญ่ อาการปวดศีรษะ อ่อนแรง ชัก หรือเดินเซ MRI มักพบหลายก้อนที่รอยต่อเนื้อเทาเนื้อขาวและบวมรอบมาก การรักษาขึ้นกับจำนวนก้อนและสภาพผู้ป่วย ได้แก่ dexamethasone ลดบวม ผ่าตัด radiosurgery ฉายรังสีทั้งสมอง และยามุ่งเป้าที่เข้าสมองได้ เช่น osimertinib ในมะเร็งปอด EGFR

qx.stem: A 60-year-old woman who has smoked for decades presents with headache and unsteady gait. Contrast MRI shows seven enhancing nodules, several ring-like, located at the grey-white junction in both hemispheres and the cerebellum, each with disproportionately large vasogenic oedema for its size. Management involves stereotactic radiosurgery or systemic therapy guided by molecular profiling, rather than whole-brain radiotherapy by default.

formal: Reactivation of latent Toxoplasma gondii infection in the brain of severely immunosuppressed patients (usually advanced HIV with CD4 below 100 cells/µL), causing multiple ring-enhancing lesions, typically in basal ganglia and at the grey–white junction with focal deficits, seizures and encephalopathy.

case.q: What is the next step?

det.patho: Toxoplasma gondii is acquired by eating undercooked meat or ingesting oocysts shed by cats, after which bradyzoite cysts persist lifelong in brain and muscle. When CD4 T-cell immunity collapses, cysts rupture and tachyzoites cause necrotising abscesses, especially in the basal ganglia and corticomedullary junction. In Thailand, seroprevalence is lower than in Europe, but toxoplasmosis remains a leading cause of focal brain lesions in AIDS.
det.clinical: Patients present over days to weeks with headache, fever, confusion, focal deficits and seizures. Basal ganglia lesions can produce hemichorea-hemiballism, which strongly suggests toxoplasmosis in HIV. Chorioretinitis may coexist. Severe disease can cause diffuse encephalitis without discrete lesions.
det.diagnosis: In a patient with CD4 below 100, positive Toxoplasma IgG and typical multiple enhancing lesions, empirical therapy is reasonable and the response confirms the diagnosis. A negative IgG, a single lesion, or failure to improve in 10–14 days should prompt biopsy or other testing for lymphoma (CSF EBV PCR, thallium SPECT or FDG-PET). Avoid steroids unless mass effect is life-threatening, as they can blur the response in lymphoma.
det.treatment: Standard therapy is pyrimethamine (loading then daily) with sulfadiazine and folinic acid for at least 6 weeks; where pyrimethamine is hard to obtain, as in many Thai hospitals, high-dose trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole is an effective alternative. Clindamycin replaces sulfadiazine for sulfa allergy. Follow with secondary prophylaxis until CD4 is above 200 for 6 months on ART; start ART within about 2 weeks. Primary prophylaxis with co-trimoxazole is given to seropositive patients with CD4 below 100.
det.prognosis: Most patients improve within 2 weeks of treatment; residual deficits and epilepsy are common, and relapse occurs without prophylaxis or immune recovery.
pearls: Multiple ring lesions + CD4 < 100 + positive IgG: treat for toxoplasmosis and re-image in 2 weeks.
No improvement after 2 weeks: think lymphoma and biopsy.
Hemiballism in AIDS is toxoplasmosis until proven otherwise.

name: Neurocysticercosis
formal: Infection of the central nervous system by the larval cysts of the pork tapeworm Taenia solium, acquired by ingesting eggs from a human carrier; the commonest cause of acquired epilepsy in endemic regions, with parenchymal cysts causing seizures and extraparenchymal cysts causing hydrocephalus.

case.who: 24-year-old woman from Mae Sot, Tak, who worked in a pig farm near the border
case.story: Two focal seizures with jerking of the left hand spreading to the arm, then a generalised seizure last night; otherwise healthy.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination, normal fundi.
case.tests: CT: two small calcified dots and one right frontal cyst; MRI: the cyst contains an eccentric bright nodule and there is a second ring-enhancing lesion with oedema; EITB positive.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and treatment?
case.a: Parenchymal neurocysticercosis with viable and degenerating cysts; antiseizure medication, albendazole with corticosteroids (add praziquantel if more than two viable cysts), and screen the household for a tapeworm carrier.

read.where: Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System (Parasitic diseases: neurocysticercosis)
Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — Neurocysticercosis

det.patho: Humans are the definitive host of Taenia solium; eating undercooked infected pork leads to intestinal tapeworm (taeniasis), whereas swallowing eggs shed by a carrier (faecal–oral, often via food handlers) leads to cysticercosis. Larvae lodge in brain, muscle and eye. Living cysts evade immunity; seizures and oedema usually come when the cyst degenerates and provokes inflammation, passing through vesicular, colloidal, granular nodular and calcified stages. Calcified lesions can still trigger seizures with periodic perilesional oedema.
det.clinical: Parenchymal disease presents mainly with seizures and headache. Extraparenchymal cysts in the ventricles (often the fourth) or basal cisterns cause hydrocephalus, chronic meningitis and vasculitic strokes, and carry a worse prognosis. Massive infection can cause cysticercal encephalitis with diffuse oedema, especially in children. Spinal and ocular forms are uncommon. In Thailand, the disease clusters in the north and northeast and among migrants from neighbouring countries.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis uses revised Del Brutto criteria combining imaging, serology, clinical and epidemiological data. A cyst with a visible scolex on MRI is pathognomonic. CT is best for calcifications, MRI for cysts in ventricles and cisterns (FLAIR, 3D sequences). EITB serology helps when there are multiple lesions; antigen tests suggest live cysts. Tuberculoma and other granulomas are the key alternatives for a single enhancing lesion.
det.treatment: Treat seizures with standard antiseizure drugs. For viable parenchymal cysts, albendazole 15 mg/kg/day for 10–14 days with corticosteroids is recommended, adding praziquantel when there are more than two cysts; check fundi first and avoid antiparasitic drugs in cysticercal encephalitis. Calcified lesions need only seizure control. Hydrocephalus needs CSF diversion; ventricular cysts are best removed endoscopically. Prevent reinfection: treat tapeworm carriers, improve sanitation and pig husbandry.
det.prognosis: Seizures usually become controllable, and many patients can stop medication after cysts resolve; extraparenchymal disease has higher morbidity.
pearls: Hole-with-dot on MRI = cyst with scolex.
Eating pork gives tapeworm; ingesting eggs from a carrier gives cysticercosis — vegetarians can be infected.
Look at the fundi before antiparasitic drugs; do not treat cysticercal encephalitis with them.
det.thd: Neurocysticercosis เกิดจากตัวอ่อนพยาธิตืดหมูเข้าไปฝังในสมองหลังกินไข่พยาธิที่ปนเปื้อนจากคนที่มีพยาธิตัวแก่ ไม่ใช่จากการกินหมูดิบโดยตรง อาการเด่นคือชัก บางรายมีน้ำคั่งในโพรงสมอง MRI เห็นถุงน้ำที่มีจุดหัวพยาธิ (scolex) และ CT เห็นจุดหินปูน รักษาด้วยยากันชัก albendazole ร่วมกับ steroid (เพิ่ม praziquantel ถ้ามีหลายถุง) ตรวจจอตาก่อนให้ยา และตรวจหาคนในบ้านที่มีพยาธิตืด พบมากในภาคเหนือ อีสาน และแรงงานข้ามชาติ

qx.stem: A 30-year-old woman from northern Thailand has focal seizures. CT shows a 1 cm cystic lesion with a small eccentric dot inside, mild surrounding oedema and a ring of enhancement; two older calcified nodules lie in the right parietal lobe. MRI shows the cystic lesion with an internal scolex bright on T1 and T2.
qx.q: What is the correct interpretation?
opts: Vesicular-colloidal stage cysticercus with scolex; treat with antiseizure drug plus albendazole (with corticosteroid cover)
Healed nodular calcified stage; no treatment needed for any lesion
Tuberculoma with caseation; start antituberculous therapy
Glioma; plan resection
Toxoplasmic abscess; start pyrimethamine
qx.why: A cyst with an eccentric scolex (the dot-in-a-hole sign) is pathognomonic for neurocysticercosis, and coexisting calcified lesions show disease at several stages. name: Rabies
formal: Almost invariably fatal acute encephalomyelitis caused by a lyssavirus transmitted mainly through dog bites, presenting as furious rabies with hydrophobia and aerophobia or as paralytic rabies with ascending flaccid weakness; prevented by prompt wound care, vaccine and rabies immunoglobulin.
simple: A virus caught from the bite of an infected animal, usually a dog, which attacks the brain and is nearly always fatal once symptoms start, but can be prevented by vaccination right after the bite.
ab: โรคพิษสุนัขบ้า
โรคกลัวน้ำ
th: โรคพิษสุนัขบ้า ไวรัสจากน้ำลายสัตว์ (สุนัขเป็นส่วนใหญ่ในไทย) เข้าสู่ระบบประสาท เมื่อมีอาการแล้วเสียชีวิตเกือบทุกราย มีแบบคลุ้มคลั่ง กลัวน้ำ กลัวลม และแบบอัมพาต ป้องกันได้ด้วยการล้างแผล วัคซีน และ RIG
tempoNote: Incubation usually 1–3 months (days to over a year); once symptoms start, death typically follows within 1–2 weeks (furious) or somewhat longer (paralytic)
feat: Prodrome of fever and pain, itching or tingling at the healed bite site
Furious form: agitation, fluctuating consciousness, hydrophobic and aerophobic spasms, hypersalivation, autonomic instability
Paralytic form: flaccid weakness starting in the bitten limb and ascending, with preserved alertness early — mimics GBS
History of dog (or cat, bat) exposure weeks to months earlier, often without adequate PEP
inv: Ante-mortem: saliva RT-PCR (repeat samples), nuchal skin biopsy for viral antigen/RNA, CSF and serum antibodies in the unvaccinated
MRI: ill-defined T2 change in brainstem, hypothalamus, hippocampi, deep grey matter and cord, enhancing late
CSF: mild lymphocytic pleocytosis or normal

case.who: 47-year-old man from Surin who was bitten on the hand by a stray puppy 2 months ago and only washed the wound
case.story: Three days of fever and burning pain up the bitten arm, then anxiety and inability to drink water because his throat goes into spasm.
case.exam: Agitated but intermittently lucid, drooling, violent pharyngeal and neck spasms when offered a cup of water or when a fan blows on his face.
case.tests: Saliva RT-PCR positive for rabies virus; MRI subtle T2 hyperintensity in the brainstem and hypothalamus.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, what can be offered, and who else needs attention?
case.a: Furious rabies; give palliative care with sedation and analgesia in isolation, and assess family and staff with saliva exposure for post-exposure prophylaxis.

det.patho: Rabies virus in saliva enters muscle and peripheral nerve at the wound, then travels by retrograde axonal transport to the spinal cord and brain, where it spreads widely with little inflammation and spares the immune response until late. From the brain it moves outward to salivary glands and skin. Most human deaths in Asia, including Thailand, follow dog bites; bats are a minor source. Neuronal dysfunction rather than gross destruction explains the dramatic symptoms.
det.clinical: After a non-specific prodrome with local neuropathic symptoms, about two thirds develop furious rabies: episodic agitation, hydrophobic spasms on attempting to drink, aerophobia, hypersalivation, hallucinations and autonomic storms, progressing to coma. The paralytic form causes flaccid weakness from the bitten limb, sphincter involvement and percussion myoedema, with longer survival; it is often misdiagnosed as GBS. Coma, multiorgan failure and death are almost universal.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical in a patient with an animal exposure; laboratory confirmation uses RT-PCR on several saliva samples, nuchal skin biopsy, CSF and, in the unvaccinated, rabies antibodies in serum or CSF. A single negative test does not exclude rabies. In Thailand, reference laboratories (e.g. the Queen Saovabha Memorial Institute of the Thai Red Cross) support testing. Staff should use barrier precautions.
det.treatment: There is no effective treatment once symptoms appear; experimental coma-induction protocols are not recommended. Provide palliative care with sedation, analgesia and family support. Prevention after exposure is highly effective: wash the wound thoroughly with soap and water for about 15 minutes; give rabies vaccine for WHO category II exposures and vaccine plus rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into the wound for category III, using the national (Thai MOPH/Thai Red Cross) intradermal or intramuscular schedule. Start PEP immediately regardless of the delay since the bite; previously vaccinated people need only booster doses without RIG.
det.prognosis: Clinical rabies is almost always fatal; very few survivors are recorded. PEP given promptly and correctly is nearly 100% protective.
pearls: Pain or tingling at an old bite site with fever: suspect rabies prodrome.
Paralytic rabies is a GBS mimic — always ask about animal bites.
Never delay PEP to observe the animal; start now and stop only if the animal remains healthy for 10 days (dogs/cats).
Do not suture deep bites tightly before RIG infiltration.
det.thd: โรคพิษสุนัขบ้าเกิดจากไวรัสในน้ำลายสัตว์ ส่วนใหญ่ในไทยมาจากสุนัข ไวรัสเดินทางตามเส้นประสาทเข้าสู่ไขสันหลังและสมอง ระยะฟักตัวมักเป็นเดือน อาการเริ่มด้วยไข้และปวดชาที่แผลเดิม แล้วกลัวน้ำ กลัวลม น้ำลายมาก กระวนกระวาย หรือเป็นแบบอัมพาตคล้าย GBS เมื่อมีอาการแล้วเสียชีวิตเกือบทั้งหมด จึงต้องป้องกันหลังสัมผัส ได้แก่ ล้างแผลด้วยสบู่และน้ำนาน 15 นาที ฉีดวัคซีนตามตารางของกระทรวงสาธารณสุขหรือสภากาชาดไทย และให้ RIG ฉีดรอบแผลในการสัมผัสระดับ 3 โดยเริ่มทันทีไม่ต้องรอดูอาการสัตว์

name: Syringomyelia
formal: A fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) within the spinal cord, most often associated with Chiari I malformation or arachnoiditis, causing a cape-like sensory pattern in which pain and temperature are lost but other modalities are spared, segmental arm wasting with areflexia, and long-tract signs below the lesion.

ab: ไซริงโกไมอีเลีย
th: โพรงน้ำในไขสันหลัง มักสัมพันธ์กับ Chiari I ทำให้สูญเสียความรู้สึกเจ็บและร้อนเย็นแบบ cape แต่สัมผัสและ vibration ปกติ แขนลีบ reflex แขนหาย ขาเกร็ง แผลไหม้ที่ไม่รู้สึกเจ็บ

feat: Dissociated sensory loss: pain and temperature lost over shoulders and arms ('cape'), touch and vibration spared
Painless burns or cuts on hands; neuropathic burning pain in the affected segments
Wasting of hand muscles with lost arm reflexes; spastic legs and extensor plantars
Scoliosis (especially in children) and Charcot joints of the shoulder or elbow
With Chiari I: cough-provoked occipital headache; syringobulbia gives facial sensory loss, bulbar palsy and nystagmus
inv: MRI whole spine and brain: intramedullary CSF-signal cavity, tonsillar descent, cause of obstruction
Gadolinium to exclude tumour-associated syrinx (enhancing nodule) and arachnoiditis
Phase-contrast (CSF flow) MRI at the foramen magnum in selected cases

case.who: 28-year-old female garment factory worker from Samut Prakan
case.story: Burned her right hand on a hot iron without feeling it; she has a year of occipital headaches when she coughs or laughs.
case.exam: Loss of pinprick and temperature over both shoulders and arms (right more than left) with preserved touch and joint position, wasting of right first dorsal interosseous, absent biceps and supinator jerks, brisk knee jerks, mild thoracic scoliosis.
case.tests: MRI: cerebellar tonsils 9 mm below the foramen magnum and a syrinx from C3 to T4.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and treatment?
case.a: Chiari I malformation with cervicothoracic syringomyelia; posterior fossa (foramen magnum) decompression to restore CSF flow.

det.patho: A syrinx forms when CSF flow across the foramen magnum or along the spinal subarachnoid space is obstructed, so pulsatile pressure drives fluid into the cord. The commonest association is Chiari I malformation; others are post-infective or post-haemorrhagic arachnoiditis (including after TB meningitis), spinal trauma, intramedullary tumours and tethered cord. The cavity expands centrally, first interrupting crossing spinothalamic fibres in the anterior commissure, then anterior horn cells and finally the long tracts.
det.clinical: Typical findings are segmental pain and temperature loss while dorsal column sensation is spared, painless injuries, burning pain, hand wasting with arm areflexia, and spastic legs. Scoliosis may be the only sign in children. Extension into the medulla (syringobulbia) causes facial sensory loss in an onion-skin pattern, dysphagia, tongue wasting and nystagmus. Symptoms may worsen with coughing, straining or minor trauma.
det.diagnosis: MRI of the whole neuraxis with gadolinium defines the cavity, identifies Chiari malformation or arachnoiditis, and excludes tumour (enhancing nodule, asymmetric cyst). A small, stable central canal dilatation without symptoms is a common incidental finding and should not be overtreated. Neurophysiology may show denervation in affected myotomes.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: foramen magnum decompression for Chiari-associated syrinx, tumour resection, untethering, or arachnoid adhesiolysis. Direct shunting of the syrinx is reserved for selected cases as results are less durable. Manage neuropathic pain, protect insensate skin (hand care to prevent burns), and monitor scoliosis. Asymptomatic small cavities are followed with clinical review and MRI.
det.prognosis: Surgery halts progression in most and improves pain and some deficits, but established wasting and sensory loss usually persist.
pearls: Cape-like pain and temperature loss sparing touch = central cord lesion.
Painless burns on the hands in a young adult: examine for syringomyelia.
Always give gadolinium to exclude a tumour-associated syrinx.
det.thd: Syringomyelia คือโพรงน้ำในไขสันหลัง เกิดจากการไหลเวียนของน้ำไขสันหลังบริเวณ foramen magnum ถูกขัดขวาง ส่วนมากจาก Chiari I หรือพังผืดหลังติดเชื้อหรือบาดเจ็บ ทำให้สูญเสียความรู้สึกเจ็บและร้อนเย็นที่ไหล่และแขนเป็นรูปผ้าคลุมไหล่ แต่สัมผัสและการรับรู้ตำแหน่งยังดี มือลีบ reflex แขนหาย ขาเกร็ง มักมีแผลไหม้ที่ไม่เจ็บ และกระดูกสันหลังคด วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI ทั้งสมองและไขสันหลังพร้อมฉีดสี รักษาที่สาเหตุ เช่น ผ่าตัดขยาย foramen magnum ใน Chiari

name: Persistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD)
formal: A chronic functional vestibular disorder in which non-spinning dizziness, unsteadiness or rocking are present on the majority of days for three months or longer, aggravated by upright posture, movement and complex visual surroundings, usually triggered by an earlier vestibular, medical or psychological event.
simple: A long-lasting feeling of dizziness or unsteadiness that continues after an earlier dizzy illness has healed, because the brain's balance system stays on high alert.
th: เวียนศีรษะหรือโคลงเคลงเรื้อรังแทบทุกวันนานเกิน 3 เดือน แย่ลงเวลายืน เดิน หรืออยู่ในที่มีภาพเคลื่อนไหวมาก มักเกิดตามหลังโรคเวียนศีรษะอื่นที่หายแล้ว เป็นความผิดปกติเชิงหน้าที่ของระบบทรงตัว รักษาได้
tempoNote: Begins soon after a triggering event (BPPV, vestibular neuritis, vestibular migraine, panic, concussion) and persists for months to years; symptoms wax and wane through the day
feat: Non-spinning dizziness, rocking or unsteadiness present on the majority of days for three months or longer
Worse when upright, with own or passive motion, and in busy visual environments (supermarkets, screens, traffic)
Often follows an acute vestibular event, migraine, panic attack or head injury
Normal or near-normal examination; stiff, cautious gait that may improve with distraction
Common comorbid anxiety, depression and hypervigilance about balance; avoidance behaviour
inv: Clinical diagnosis by Bárány Society criteria; examine for active BPPV, nystagmus and gait signs
Vestibular tests (vHIT, calorics) to identify any residual peripheral deficit from the trigger
Audiogram if ear symptoms; MRI only if focal signs or red flags
Screen for anxiety and depression (e.g. GAD-7, PHQ-9)

case.story: Eight months ago she had vestibular neuritis that settled within weeks, but since then she has felt rocking 'like on a boat' every day, worse in shopping malls and when scrolling her phone; she now avoids going out alone.
case.exam: No spontaneous or positional nystagmus, normal head impulse test, Romberg normal; walks slowly with wide base and arms stiff, but gait normalises while counting backwards.
case.tests: vHIT normal both sides; MRI brain normal; GAD-7 score 12.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the main treatment approach?
case.a: PPPD triggered by vestibular neuritis; explain the diagnosis positively, start vestibular rehabilitation with habituation, add CBT and an SSRI/SNRI if needed.

det.patho: PPPD is thought to arise when the postural control system fails to readapt after a destabilising event. High-threat postural strategies (stiffening, short steps), increased reliance on vision and hypervigilant attention to balance persist after the trigger resolves. Functional imaging shows altered activity and connectivity between vestibular, visual and anxiety-related cortical networks. It is one of the commonest causes of chronic dizziness in neuro-otology clinics.
det.clinical: Patients describe constant swaying, rocking or light-headedness, rarely true spinning, fluctuating through the day and worsened by standing, walking and visual motion. Many have a history of BPPV, vestibular neuritis, vestibular migraine, panic attacks or concussion. Anxiety, fatigue and avoidance can lead to marked disability. Examination is normal or shows only the residue of the trigger plus a cautious, stiff gait.
det.diagnosis: The Bárány Society criteria (2017) require: dizziness or unsteadiness on the majority of days for three months or longer, persistent symptoms without specific provocation but worse with upright posture, motion and complex visual stimuli, a precipitating event, significant distress or functional impairment, and no better explanation. PPPD is a positive diagnosis, not just exclusion, but active coexisting disorders such as BPPV or vestibular migraine must be identified and treated.
det.treatment: Explain that the symptoms are real and result from a balance system that has become over-protective. Vestibular rehabilitation with gradual habituation to motion and visual stimuli is central. SSRIs or SNRIs help many even without major anxiety, and cognitive behavioural therapy addresses hypervigilance and avoidance. Avoid long-term vestibular suppressants such as betahistine or prochlorperazine, which delay compensation.
det.prognosis: Most improve substantially with combined rehabilitation, medication and CBT, though symptoms may recur during stress or illness.
pearls: Daily rocking dizziness for months after a resolved vertigo illness, worse in supermarkets: PPPD.
It is a positive diagnosis with specific criteria — not 'nothing found'.
Stop chronic vestibular sedatives; they block recovery.
Look for and treat coexisting BPPV or vestibular migraine.
det.thd: PPPD คือภาวะเวียนศีรษะหรือโคลงเคลงเรื้อรังแทบทุกวันนานเกิน 3 เดือน แย่ลงเวลายืน เดิน หรืออยู่ในที่ที่มีภาพเคลื่อนไหวมาก เช่น ห้างสรรพสินค้า มักเริ่มหลังโรคเวียนศีรษะอื่นที่หายแล้ว เช่น BPPV หรือ vestibular neuritis เกิดจากระบบทรงตัวของสมองยังอยู่ในภาวะระวังภัยมากเกินไป การตรวจร่างกายมักปกติ รักษาด้วยการอธิบายให้เข้าใจ ฝึกกายภาพการทรงตัว ยากลุ่ม SSRI/SNRI และ CBT และควรหยุดยาแก้เวียนที่ใช้ระยะยาว

name: Meralgia paraesthetica

Purely sensory: normal strength and knee jerk
Worse with standing, walking or hip extension; eased by sitting

Risk factors: obesity, pregnancy, diabetes, tight belts or work equipment belts, hip/spine surgery positioning

case.who: 38-year-old male security guard from Pathum Thani

case.tests: Ultrasound: swollen right LFCN at the inguinal ligament; diagnostic local anaesthetic injection abolishes the pain.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the first-line management?

det.patho: Derived from the L2 and L3 roots, the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is purely sensory; it crosses the pelvis and exits under or through the lateral inguinal ligament near the anterior superior iliac spine, where it angulates sharply. Compression at this point by abdominal girth, tight clothing, belts, pregnancy, or traction during surgery (prone spinal surgery, hip replacement, iliac crest graft harvest) produces focal demyelination or axonal injury. Diabetes increases susceptibility.
det.clinical: Patients describe burning, tingling or numbness over the outer front of the thigh, sometimes with hypersensitivity to clothing. Symptoms often worsen after long standing or walking and can be bilateral. There is never weakness or reflex loss, which is the key distinction from L2–L3 radiculopathy and plexopathy. A few cases result from proximal pathology such as retroperitoneal tumour, appendicitis or psoas haematoma.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is mostly clinical, based on a sensory deficit confined to the LFCN territory with normal motor examination. NCS can show reduced or absent sensory responses compared with the other side but may be technically unreliable, especially in obesity. High-resolution ultrasound demonstrates nerve swelling and allows a guided anaesthetic block that confirms the diagnosis. Investigate further if the deficit spreads or weakness appears.
det.treatment: Most cases improve with conservative measures: removing compressive belts or clothing, weight reduction, and neuropathic pain treatment (topical lidocaine, gabapentinoids, amitriptyline). Ultrasound-guided corticosteroid and local anaesthetic injection helps persistent symptoms. Refractory cases may undergo surgical decompression or neurectomy, or pulsed radiofrequency treatment.
det.prognosis: Usually benign; most patients improve within months, though numbness may persist.
pearls: Outer thigh burning with no weakness and a normal knee jerk: meralgia paraesthetica.
Any motor or reflex change points to L2–L3 root, plexus or femoral nerve instead.
Ask about belts, tool belts, pregnancy, weight gain and recent prone surgery.
det.thd: Meralgia paraesthetica เกิดจากเส้นประสาทผิวหนังด้านข้างต้นขาถูกกดใต้เอ็นขาหนีบใกล้ปุ่มกระดูกเชิงกรานด้านหน้า ทำให้ชาหรือแสบร้อนที่ต้นขาด้านนอก โดยไม่มีอ่อนแรงและ reflex เข่าปกติ พบบ่อยในคนอ้วน ตั้งครรภ์ เบาหวาน หรือใส่เข็มขัดรัด วินิจฉัยจากอาการและตรวจร่างกาย อาจใช้ ultrasound ช่วย รักษาโดยคลายเข็มขัด ลดน้ำหนัก ใช้ยาบรรเทาปวดปลายประสาท และฉีดยาในรายที่ไม่ดีขึ้น

name: Radial neuropathy
formal: Mononeuropathy of the radial nerve or its branches, most often compressed at the spiral groove of the humerus, causing wrist and finger drop with sensory loss over the dorsal first web space; lesions of the posterior interosseous branch spare sensation and wrist extension.
simple: Damage to the radial nerve in the arm, often from pressure while sleeping, so that the wrist and fingers hang down and cannot lift.

Spiral groove lesion: brachioradialis weak, triceps spared; axillary lesion: triceps weak too
Numbness on the back of the hand around the first web space (absent in posterior interosseous lesions)
Posterior interosseous lesion: finger drop with radial deviation on wrist extension, no sensory loss
Apparent weakness of finger abduction and grip because the wrist is flexed — test with the wrist supported
inv: NCS/EMG after about 1–2 weeks: localise level (conduction block across the spiral groove vs axonal loss), check triceps and brachioradialis
Ultrasound or MRI of the nerve if no clear compression history, after fracture, or progressive
Glucose and screen for HNPP or mononeuritis multiplex if recurrent or multiple
X-ray humerus in trauma (mid-shaft fracture)

case.story: After a party he fell asleep drunk in a chair with his right arm hooked over the backrest. He woke unable to lift his right hand.
case.exam: Right wrist and finger extensors 1/5, brachioradialis weak, triceps normal; finger abduction appears weak but is normal with the wrist supported; numb patch over the dorsal first web space; reflexes otherwise normal.
case.tests: NCS at day 10: conduction block of the radial nerve across the spiral groove with preserved distal amplitude.
case.q: Where is the lesion and what is the outlook?
case.a: Radial nerve injury in the spiral groove ('Saturday night palsy'); mostly demyelinating, so he should recover within weeks to a couple of months, using a wrist splint and physiotherapy.

18. FOCAL NEUROPATHIES: NERVE INJURIES, ENTRAPMENTS, AND OTHER MONONEUROPATHIES

det.patho: The radial nerve (C5–T1, mainly C6–C8) arises from the posterior cord, winds around the humerus in the spiral groove, then divides at the elbow into the motor posterior interosseous nerve and the sensory superficial radial nerve. Compression in the spiral groove during deep sleep or intoxication, humeral shaft fracture, injections, tourniquets and crutches are common causes. The posterior interosseous nerve can be compressed at the arcade of Frohse or by masses such as lipomas or ganglia, and the superficial radial nerve by tight watches, handcuffs or casts.
det.clinical: Spiral groove lesions produce wrist and finger drop with weak brachioradialis and supinator but preserved triceps, plus dorsal hand numbness. Axillary lesions also weaken triceps. Posterior interosseous neuropathy causes finger drop with radial wrist deviation and no sensory loss, and superficial radial neuropathy (Wartenberg syndrome) causes pain and numbness only. A central lesion of the hand knob in the motor cortex can mimic radial palsy, but finger flexors are also weak and reflexes may change.
det.diagnosis: Careful examination of triceps, brachioradialis, supinator and sensory distribution localises the level. Electrodiagnosis distinguishes conduction block (good prognosis) from axonal loss and excludes C7 radiculopathy, plexopathy and multifocal neuropathies. Ultrasound or MRI helps when there is no clear compressive history, or after fracture to judge whether the nerve is entrapped or transected.
det.treatment: Most compressive palsies are managed with a wrist–finger extension (cock-up or dynamic) splint, physiotherapy to prevent contractures and avoidance of further pressure. Nerve injury with humeral fracture usually recovers spontaneously; exploration is considered if no clinical or EMG recovery by 3–6 months, or earlier for open injuries. Tendon transfers are used when recovery fails. Masses compressing the posterior interosseous nerve are removed surgically.
det.prognosis: Pure demyelinating compression typically recovers within 6–8 weeks; axonal injuries take several months and may be incomplete.
pearls: Support the wrist before testing finger abduction — otherwise radial palsy looks like an ulnar or C8 lesion.
Triceps spared + brachioradialis weak = spiral groove.
Finger drop without sensory loss and with radial wrist deviation = posterior interosseous nerve.
Bilateral wrist drop: think lead poisoning or multifocal neuropathy.

name: Myelomeningocele (open spina bifida)
formal: An open neural tube defect in which the unclosed caudal neural placode and its meninges protrude through a dorsal vertebral defect without skin cover, almost always accompanied by a Chiari II hindbrain malformation and frequently by hydrocephalus.
simple: A birth defect where part of the baby's spinal cord sits open on the back, causing leg weakness, bladder and bowel problems and often fluid build-up in the brain.

tempoNote: Present from birth (defect forms by about the fourth week after conception); lifelong, with later deterioration from shunt failure, Chiari II brainstem symptoms, syrinx or retethering

Later problems: shunt blockage, syringomyelia, retethering, scoliosis, latex allergy, pressure sores, learning difficulty
Linked to low maternal folate, valproate or carbamazepine exposure, pregestational diabetes and obesity
inv: Antenatal: second-trimester anomaly ultrasound (lemon-shaped skull, banana-shaped cerebellum, spinal defect); raised maternal serum AFP

case.who: Newborn girl in a provincial hospital in Nakhon Phanom; mother 22, took no vitamins before pregnancy
case.story: Born at term after no antenatal scan; a raw, red, fluid-leaking sac sits over her lower back.
case.exam: Lumbosacral open lesion; legs move only at the hips; patulous anus; head circumference at the 90th centile with a full fontanelle.
case.tests: Cranial ultrasound shows enlarged lateral ventricles; MRI shows a small posterior fossa with the cerebellum herniated through the foramen magnum.
case.q: What is the urgent plan for the back, the head and the next pregnancy?
case.a: Cover the lesion with moist sterile dressing, nurse prone, give antibiotics and close it surgically within about 48 hours; watch for and treat hydrocephalus (shunt or ETV with choroid plexus cauterisation); advise high-dose folic acid before any future pregnancy.

det.patho: The caudal neural tube fails to fold and fuse during primary neurulation, so the cord remains a flat plate that is later injured by exposure to amniotic fluid and trauma (the 'two-hit' idea that underpins fetal repair). Leakage of CSF through the open defect during fetal life lets the hindbrain sink into a small posterior fossa, producing the Chiari II malformation and blocking CSF outflow. Risk factors include folate deficiency, variants in folate-pathway genes, antiseizure drugs (especially valproate), maternal diabetes, obesity and early-pregnancy hyperthermia. Birth prevalence is roughly 0.5–1 per 1000 where folate fortification is absent.
det.clinical: The level of the defect sets the motor picture: thoracic and high lumbar lesions leave paraplegia, whereas low lumbar and sacral ones allow walking with orthoses. Nearly all children have neurogenic bladder and bowel, and many have club feet, hip dislocation or scoliosis. Hydrocephalus usually appears in the first weeks of life; Chiari II brainstem dysfunction shows as inspiratory stridor from vocal cord palsy, central apnoea, weak cry and poor feeding. In older children, new weakness, worsening gait, bladder change or scoliosis should prompt a search for shunt malfunction first, then tethering or syrinx. Executive and visuospatial learning problems are common even with normal IQ.
det.diagnosis: Most cases are now identified antenatally by the mid-trimester ultrasound, with maternal serum AFP as a supporting screen. Fetal MRI defines lesion level and hindbrain herniation for counselling. After birth the diagnosis is visual; MRI of the neuraxis looks for Chiari II, hydrocephalus, syrinx and split cord. Baseline renal ultrasound, bladder pressure studies and orthopaedic assessment guide long-term care.
det.treatment: Postnatally, keep the placode moist and covered, position prone, avoid latex and close the defect within about 48–72 hours. Prenatal open repair before 26 weeks, as in the MOMS trial, halves the need for shunting and improves motor outcome but raises risks of preterm birth and uterine dehiscence; fetoscopic techniques are expanding in specialist centres. Hydrocephalus is treated with a VP shunt or endoscopic third ventriculostomy with choroid plexus cauterisation. Lifelong multidisciplinary care covers clean intermittent catheterisation and anticholinergics, bowel programmes, orthopaedics, mobility aids, skin care and transition to adult services. Prevention is folic acid 0.4 mg daily from at least a month before conception to 12 weeks, rising to 4–5 mg daily after a previous affected pregnancy or with valproate exposure.
det.prognosis: Most children now reach adulthood; outcome depends on lesion level, shunt complications and symptomatic Chiari II, which remains the leading cause of early death.
pearls: Any deterioration in a child with spina bifida is shunt malfunction until proven otherwise.
Stridor or apnoea in an infant with MMC signals Chiari II brainstem compromise — an emergency.
Folic acid must start before conception; neural tube closure is finished before many women know they are pregnant.
det.thd: Myelomeningocele คือภาวะที่ไขสันหลังส่วนท้ายเปิดออกนอกร่างกายตั้งแต่กำเนิด ทำให้ขาอ่อนแรง ชาใต้ระดับรอยโรค และควบคุมปัสสาวะอุจจาระไม่ได้ เกือบทุกรายมี Chiari II และส่วนใหญ่มี hydrocephalus ที่ต้องผ่าตัดระบายน้ำ วินิจฉัยได้ตั้งแต่ในครรภ์ด้วยอัลตราซาวนด์และ AFP การรักษาคือปิดแผลภายใน 48–72 ชั่วโมงหลังคลอด หรือผ่าตัดในครรภ์ในศูนย์เฉพาะทาง ป้องกันโดยให้กรดโฟลิก 0.4 mg ต่อวันก่อนตั้งครรภ์ และ 4–5 mg ในหญิงที่มีความเสี่ยงสูง

name: Anencephaly
formal: A lethal open neural tube defect from failure of the rostral neuropore to close, leaving the forebrain without skull vault or scalp so that it degenerates into a vascular stromal remnant (area cerebrovasculosa).
simple: A severe birth defect in which most of the brain and the top of the skull do not form, so the baby cannot survive.
th: ความผิดปกติของท่อประสาทส่วนหัวที่ปิดไม่สนิท ทารกไม่มีกะโหลกด้านบนและสมองส่วนหน้า เสียชีวิตก่อนหรือไม่นานหลังคลอด ตรวจพบได้ตั้งแต่อัลตราซาวนด์ไตรมาสแรก ป้องกันได้บางส่วนด้วยกรดโฟลิก

Bulging eyes ('frog-like' face) because the orbits are shallow
Brainstem may function briefly, allowing reflex movements and breathing after birth
Polyhydramnios from impaired fetal swallowing; frequently combined with spinal rachischisis
Shares risk factors and prevention with spina bifida (folate, valproate, diabetes)

case.who: 28-year-old second-pregnancy mother attending antenatal clinic in Udon Thani at 12 weeks
case.story: First-trimester screening scan; she has not started folic acid and her first child had no problems.
case.exam: Uterine size matches dates; no maternal symptoms.
case.tests: Ultrasound: normal heartbeat and limbs but no bony skull above the orbits, with disorganised tissue floating free in amniotic fluid.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what counselling is needed for the future?
case.a: Acrania–anencephaly sequence, a lethal defect; offer counselling on pregnancy options and advise 4–5 mg folic acid daily from before the next conception, as recurrence risk is a few per cent.

det.patho: The rostral neuropore normally seals at about day 25–26 of embryonic life; when it does not, the forebrain develops uncovered by mesenchyme, so no skull vault or scalp forms. Exposed neural tissue is damaged by amniotic fluid and mechanical trauma, passing through a stage called exencephaly before collapsing into a haemorrhagic stromal mass. The brainstem, cerebellum and spinal cord may be partly preserved. Causes are multifactorial: folate insufficiency, MTHFR and other folate-pathway variants, maternal diabetes, obesity, valproate, hyperthermia and some chromosomal disorders. It is roughly as common as spina bifida in unfortified populations and more frequent in female fetuses.
det.clinical: Most are now detected and many pregnancies end before term; ongoing pregnancies often develop polyhydramnios and may deliver early. Liveborn infants lack the cranial vault, have protruding eyes and may show sucking, grasping and breathing driven by the brainstem. Consciousness in any meaningful sense is absent. Survival beyond the first week is very rare. Coexisting spinal defects, cleft palate and other anomalies occur.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is made on ultrasound, reliably from the first-trimester scan once the vault should be ossified (about 11 weeks onward). Maternal serum AFP is very high but imaging has largely replaced it as the primary test. Look for spinal involvement (craniorachischisis) and additional anomalies that might indicate a chromosomal or syndromic cause, which changes recurrence counselling. Post-mortem examination helps family counselling when the cause is uncertain.
det.treatment: There is no treatment for the defect itself. Care centres on sensitive, non-directive counselling about continuing or ending the pregnancy, and on comfort-focused care for any liveborn infant. Parents should be offered bereavement support. For future pregnancies, folic acid 4–5 mg daily starting at least a month before conception and continuing through the first trimester greatly lowers recurrence, together with good glycaemic control and review of teratogenic medicines.
det.prognosis: Uniformly fatal; recurrence after one affected pregnancy is about 2–4%, reduced substantially by high-dose folate.
pearls: Anencephaly and spina bifida are two ends of the same neural tube defect family — the same folate advice prevents both.
It is detectable at the 11–14 week scan; do not wait for the anomaly scan.
A prior neural tube defect in either parent or a sibling qualifies for high-dose folic acid.
det.thd: Anencephaly คือภาวะที่ท่อประสาทส่วนหัวปิดไม่สนิท ทารกไม่มีกะโหลกด้านบนและสมองส่วนหน้าเสื่อมสลายไป ตรวจพบได้ตั้งแต่อัลตราซาวนด์อายุครรภ์ 11–14 สัปดาห์ ไม่มีการรักษาและทารกเสียชีวิตเกือบทั้งหมด การดูแลเน้นการให้คำปรึกษาครอบครัวและการดูแลแบบประคับประคอง ครรภ์ถัดไปควรได้กรดโฟลิก 4–5 mg ต่อวันก่อนตั้งครรภ์เพื่อลดโอกาสเกิดซ้ำ

det.patho: Cephaloceles probably arise after neural tube closure from a failure of the overlying mesenchyme to separate cleanly from neuroectoderm, leaving a bony gap through which dura and brain herniate. The sac may hold only meninges and CSF (meningocele) or dysplastic, often non-functional brain and parts of the ventricles. Occipital forms predominate in Europe and North America, while frontoethmoidal forms are notably frequent in South-East Asia, including Thailand, Cambodia and Myanmar, for reasons not fully explained. Genetic syndromes (ciliopathies such as Meckel–Gruber), amniotic band disruption and teratogens are recognised causes.
det.clinical: Occipital lesions range from small skin-covered nodules to giant sacs larger than the head, often with microcephaly, hydrocephalus, cortical malformations, visual impairment and seizures. Frontoethmoidal lesions cause a visible facial mass with hypertelorism and nasal distortion but usually less brain dysfunction. Basal (transsphenoidal, transethmoidal) lesions are hidden and may present late with nasal obstruction, CSF rhinorrhoea, recurrent meningitis or pituitary and visual problems. Atretic (rudimentary) parietal cephaloceles look like small scalp nodules but may mark underlying venous anomalies.
det.diagnosis: Antenatal ultrasound and fetal MRI identify most large lesions. After birth, MRI determines sac contents, ventricular involvement and coexisting malformations, while MR venography shows whether dural venous sinuses run into the sac — vital before surgery. CT clarifies the bone defect. Any midline nasal mass in a child must be imaged before biopsy because nasal gliomas, dermoids and encephaloceles look similar. Genetic evaluation is recommended when other anomalies are found.
det.treatment: Surgical repair aims to excise non-viable herniated tissue, close the dura watertight and reconstruct the skull; timing ranges from urgent (open or leaking sacs) to elective in infancy for skin-covered lesions. Frontoethmoidal repair is a combined neurosurgical and craniofacial operation that also corrects hypertelorism. Associated hydrocephalus may need shunting or endoscopic treatment. Seizures, vision and development are followed long term. Folate supplementation is advised for future pregnancies, although evidence is weaker than for spina bifida.
det.prognosis: Pure meningoceles and frontoethmoidal lesions generally do well after repair; large occipital lesions containing brain, with microcephaly or hydrocephalus, carry high mortality and disability.
pearls: Never biopsy a midline nasal mass in a child without imaging — it may connect to the brain.
In Thailand the frontoethmoidal type is relatively common, unlike Western series where occipital dominates.
Recurrent bacterial meningitis plus clear nasal drip: look for a basal encephalocele or skull-base defect.
det.thd: Encephalocele คือการโป่งของเยื่อหุ้มสมองและเนื้อสมองผ่านรูโหว่ของกะโหลกศีรษะแต่กำเนิด ชนิดท้ายทอยมักรุนแรงเพราะมีเนื้อสมองมากและมี hydrocephalus ร่วม ส่วนชนิด frontoethmoidal ที่จมูกและหน้าผากพบบ่อยในไทยและมักมีพัฒนาการดีกว่า ต้องทำ MRI/MRV และ CT ก่อนผ่าตัด ห้ามตัดชิ้นเนื้อก้อนที่สันจมูกในเด็กโดยไม่ตรวจภาพก่อน การรักษาคือผ่าตัดปิดเยื่อหุ้มสมองและซ่อมกะโหลก

simple: A birth defect where the lower spine and tailbone do not form properly, causing weak legs and bladder and bowel problems; it is more common in babies of mothers with diabetes.
th: ความผิดปกติแต่กำเนิดที่กระดูกก้นกบและกระดูกสันหลังส่วนเอวบางส่วนไม่เจริญ ขาอ่อนแรงและผิดรูป กระเพาะปัสสาวะทำงานผิดปกติ สัมพันธ์กับมารดาที่เป็นเบาหวานก่อนตั้งครรภ์
tempoNote: Present from birth and largely static; deterioration suggests secondary tethering or a coexisting lesion
feat: Flat buttocks, short intergluteal cleft, narrow hips and palpable absence of the sacrum
Leg weakness and deformities (club feet, hip contractures, popliteal webs) with sensation relatively spared compared with motor function
Neurogenic bladder and bowel in nearly all, with risk of upper-tract renal damage
Truncated, wedge-shaped high conus or, alternatively, a low tethered cord on MRI
Associated anorectal malformation, renal agenesis, VACTERL-type anomalies; Currarino triad with a presacral mass
inv: MRI of the whole spine: level of vertebral loss, conus shape and position, tethering, syrinx, presacral mass
Plain spine and pelvic radiographs to grade sacral deficiency
Renal ultrasound and urodynamic studies
MNX1 gene testing when the Currarino triad (sacral defect, presacral mass, anorectal malformation) is suspected

case.who: 2-year-old boy from Chonburi; his mother has had type 1 diabetes since age 12 with poor control in pregnancy
case.story: He cannot stand, has thin legs and wets constantly; he was treated twice for urinary infection.
case.exam: Flattened buttocks, short gluteal cleft, wasted lower legs with bilateral club feet; hip and knee flexion contractures; light touch preserved down to the feet; no ankle jerks.
case.tests: MRI: sacrum absent below S1, conus ends abruptly at T12 with a blunt, wedge-shaped tip. Ultrasound: bilateral hydronephrosis.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what is the most pressing organ to protect?
case.a: Caudal regression syndrome linked to maternal diabetes; the kidneys — start clean intermittent catheterisation and urology care to prevent renal damage.

det.patho: Disturbed development of the caudal cell mass and secondary neurulation, together with notochord and somite defects, leaves the lowest spine and cord missing or malformed. Maternal pregestational diabetes is the best known risk factor, raising the risk many-fold, although most mothers of affected children are not diabetic. Familial forms include Currarino syndrome from MNX1 variants (dominant). The spectrum ranges from minor coccygeal absence to complete lumbosacral agenesis; sirenomelia, with fused legs, is now considered a separate entity.
det.clinical: Two neurological patterns are recognised: a high, abruptly ending wedge-shaped conus with a more severe, stable deficit, or a low-lying, tethered conus with milder bony loss whose function can worsen over time. Motor loss usually exceeds sensory loss because ventral motor columns are more affected than neural-crest-derived sensory ganglia. Most patients have neurogenic bladder, constipation or incontinence, and many have orthopaedic deformities. Mild forms may only show up later with incontinence or as an incidental finding.
det.diagnosis: Suspicion arises antenatally (short spine, abnormal lower limbs in a diabetic pregnancy) or at birth from the typical buttock appearance. Spinal radiographs and MRI define bony level, conus morphology and any tethering, lipoma, syrinx or presacral mass. Assess kidneys, bladder function, anorectal anatomy and the heart. In familial cases or with a presacral mass, test for MNX1 and examine relatives.
det.treatment: Management is multidisciplinary: urology for bladder protection (catheterisation, antimuscarinics, later reconstructive surgery), bowel programmes, orthopaedics for contractures and foot deformities, and rehabilitation with orthoses or wheelchairs. Neurosurgical untethering is offered when a low tethered cord produces progressive signs. Presacral masses in Currarino syndrome are removed because of infection and rare malignancy risk. Optimal glucose control before and during pregnancy reduces risk in diabetic mothers.
det.prognosis: Intelligence is usually normal and life expectancy good in milder forms; severity depends on the bony level, renal function and associated malformations.
pearls: Flat buttocks and a short gluteal cleft in an infant of a diabetic mother should prompt a spinal MRI.
A high blunt conus means a fixed deficit; a low tethered conus means possible deterioration and a surgical target.
Sacral defect + presacral mass + anorectal malformation = Currarino triad (MNX1).
det.thd: Caudal regression syndrome คือความผิดปกติแต่กำเนิดที่กระดูกก้นกบและกระดูกสันหลังส่วนล่างไม่เจริญ พบบ่อยขึ้นในทารกของมารดาที่เป็นเบาหวาน มีอาการขาอ่อนแรงผิดรูป กล้ามเนื้อเสียมากกว่าการรับความรู้สึก และกระเพาะปัสสาวะทำงานผิดปกติ ตรวจด้วย MRI ทั้งกระดูกสันหลัง ร่วมกับประเมินไตและการขับถ่าย รักษาแบบสหสาขาเพื่อปกป้องไตและช่วยการเคลื่อนไหว และผ่าตัดคลายไขสันหลังเมื่อมีภาวะไขสันหลังถูกดึงรั้ง

name: Split cord malformation (diastematomyelia)
formal: A form of closed spinal dysraphism in which a segment of the spinal cord is divided longitudinally into two hemicords, either in separate dural sacs divided by a bony or cartilaginous spur (type I) or within one dural sac separated by a fibrous band (type II), commonly with tethering and vertebral anomalies.
simple: A birth defect where part of the spinal cord is split into two halves, often held by a bony spike, which can slowly damage nerves to the legs and bladder.
th: ไขสันหลังแยกเป็นสองซีกตามยาวแต่กำเนิด อาจมีแกนกระดูกหรือพังผืดคั่นกลาง มักพบขนดกกลางหลัง กระดูกสันหลังคดผิดรูป และอาการขาอ่อนแรงหรือปัสสาวะผิดปกติที่ค่อย ๆ เป็นมากขึ้นจากการดึงรั้งไขสันหลัง
tempoNote: Congenital; often silent at birth, then slowly progressive deficits during growth spurts, with occasional abrupt worsening after forced flexion or trauma
feat: Midline back marker, classically a hairy patch ('faun tail'), dimple or haemangioma, most often lumbar
Asymmetric leg weakness and wasting, unequal leg or foot size, cavus foot or club foot
Bladder dysfunction, back or leg pain; signs progress with growth
Congenital scoliosis and vertebral segmentation anomalies; split cord found on pre-scoliosis-surgery MRI
Coexists with myelomeningocele, dermal sinus or tight filum terminale
inv: MRI of the whole spine: two hemicords, septum, conus level, filum, syrinx
Thin-slice CT to show a bony or cartilaginous spur that MRI may under-call
Urodynamics and baseline neurophysiology (EMG/SSEP) before surgery

case.who: 9-year-old girl from Phitsanulok referred by an orthopaedic surgeon for scoliosis
case.story: A tuft of long dark hair on her lower back has been there since birth; for a year she trips on her right foot and has started wetting at night again.
case.exam: Hairy patch at L2; right calf thinner and right foot smaller with a high arch; right ankle jerk absent; thoracolumbar scoliosis.
case.tests: MRI: two hemicords from L1 to L3 in separate dural sacs with a low-lying conus at L4. CT: bony spur crossing the canal at L2.
case.q: Which type is this, and why must it be treated before the scoliosis is corrected?
case.a: Type I split cord malformation with tethering; the spur and filum must be released first, because straightening the spine against a fixed cord can cause paraplegia.

det.patho: Split cord malformation is thought to arise around the third week of gestation, when an abnormal adhesion between ectoderm and endoderm forces the notochord to split, inducing two hemineural plates; mesenchyme trapped between them forms either a bony spur with two dural tubes (type I) or a thin fibrous septum with one dural tube (type II). Vertebral body anomalies, hemivertebrae and fusion defects are frequent. The same embryological error is invoked for neurenteric cysts. Females are more often affected, and lumbar levels are favoured.
det.clinical: Many children appear normal at birth; symptoms appear as the spine grows and the spur or a tight filum tethers the cord. Typical features are asymmetric leg weakness, leg-length or foot-size discrepancy, orthopaedic foot deformity, back or leg pain, and bladder or bowel dysfunction. A hairy patch is the commonest cutaneous clue. Adults can present for the first time after trauma or heavy lifting, with pain and new neurological deficit. Type II lesions are more often asymptomatic.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows the two hemicords and associated tethering, syrinx, lipoma or dermal sinus; CT best demonstrates the spur and vertebral anomalies. Screen any child with a hairy patch, congenital scoliosis or unexplained asymmetric foot deformity. Urodynamic studies document subclinical bladder involvement. Neurophysiology helps establish a baseline before surgery.
det.treatment: Symptomatic lesions are treated by removing the spur or septum, reconstructing a single dural sac and sectioning a tight filum, under intraoperative neuromonitoring. Prophylactic surgery for asymptomatic type I lesions is commonly recommended, especially before corrective scoliosis surgery, while asymptomatic type II lesions may be observed. Physiotherapy, orthoses and bladder management follow. Long-term review watches for retethering and curve progression.
det.prognosis: Surgery reliably stops progression and pain often improves; established weakness and bladder dysfunction recover only partly.
pearls: Hairy patch on the lower back = image the spine.
Always exclude a split cord or tethered cord before corrective scoliosis surgery.
CT shows the bony spur better than MRI.
det.thd: Split cord malformation หรือ diastematomyelia คือไขสันหลังแยกเป็นสองซีกตั้งแต่กำเนิด ชนิดที่ 1 มีแกนกระดูกคั่นและแยกถุงเยื่อหุ้ม ชนิดที่ 2 มีพังผืดคั่นในถุงเดียว มักมีขนดกกลางหลังและกระดูกสันหลังคด อาการขาอ่อนแรงข้างเดียว เท้าผิดรูป และปัสสาวะผิดปกติค่อย ๆ เป็นมากขึ้นตามการเติบโต วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI ร่วมกับ CT รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัดเอาแกนกระดูกออกและคลายไขสันหลัง ควรทำก่อนผ่าตัดแก้กระดูกสันหลังคด

name: Neurenteric cyst
formal: A congenital, non-neoplastic cyst lined by endoderm-derived mucin-secreting epithelium resembling gut or respiratory mucosa, usually intradural extramedullary and ventral to the cervicothoracic cord, less often intracranial in the prepontine or cerebellopontine region.
simple: A rare fluid-filled sac present from birth, lined by gut-like tissue, that usually sits in front of the spinal cord and can slowly press on it.
th: ถุงน้ำแต่กำเนิดที่ผนังบุด้วยเยื่อบุคล้ายลำไส้หรือทางเดินหายใจ มักอยู่ด้านหน้าไขสันหลังส่วนคอและอก ทำให้ปวดและไขสันหลังถูกกดช้า ๆ รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัดเอาออกให้หมด
tempoNote: Slowly progressive or fluctuating compressive symptoms, usually presenting in children or young adults; occasional sudden worsening or chemical meningitis when the cyst leaks
feat: Neck or back pain with radicular symptoms, then progressive myelopathy
Symptoms may wax and wane as the cyst fills and drains
Ventral intradural extramedullary location at cervical or upper thoracic levels
Associated vertebral anomalies (butterfly vertebra, fusion, anterior spina bifida) or mediastinal/abdominal cysts in children
Intracranial forms in front of the brainstem cause cranial nerve palsies, headache or hydrocephalus
inv: MRI spine/brain: smooth, non-enhancing cyst, often slightly brighter than CSF on T1 and FLAIR due to protein; usually little or no diffusion restriction
CT for vertebral body defects
Chest and abdominal imaging in children for linked foregut cysts
Histology confirms the endodermal lining after excision

case.who: 24-year-old female garment worker from Samut Prakan
case.story: Eight months of neck pain radiating to both shoulders, then six weeks of stiff legs and clumsy hands; symptoms improved for a while before returning worse.
case.exam: Brisk reflexes in all limbs, bilateral Hoffmann sign, spastic gait, no sensory level.
case.tests: MRI: well-defined, non-enhancing 2 cm cyst ventral to the cord at C4–C5, slightly brighter than CSF on T1; C5 vertebral body partially fused.
case.q: What is the likely lesion and what determines recurrence after surgery?
case.a: Intradural neurenteric cyst; recurrence depends mainly on whether the entire cyst wall is removed.

det.patho: During the third week the notochord must separate cleanly from the endoderm; persistence of an endodermal remnant within the developing spinal canal is thought to yield a cyst lined by cuboidal or columnar, often ciliated or mucin-producing cells. The same disturbance explains associated vertebral defects and, in severe forms, a fistula linking gut and spinal canal (split notochord syndrome). They are not tumours, although malignant change has been reported very rarely. Most lie ventral to the cord at cervical or upper thoracic levels; intracranial cases favour the prepontine cistern and posterior fossa.
det.clinical: Patients usually present in childhood or early adulthood with local pain, radicular symptoms and gradually worsening myelopathy; fluctuation reflects changing cyst volume. Children may have additional mediastinal or abdominal enteric cysts and vertebral anomalies, and some present with meningitis from a fistulous tract. Rupture of cyst contents can cause aseptic (chemical) meningitis. Intracranial lesions cause headache, cranial nerve deficits or hydrocephalus.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows a well-circumscribed, non-enhancing cyst that is isointense to slightly hyperintense to CSF on T1 and does not suppress fully on FLAIR because of protein content; diffusion restriction is usually absent, which helps separate it from an epidermoid. CT reveals coexisting vertebral defects. Differential diagnosis includes arachnoid cyst, epidermoid and dermoid cysts, and cystic schwannoma. Definitive diagnosis requires histology showing endodermal epithelium.
det.treatment: Complete surgical excision of the cyst wall, under neuromonitoring, is the treatment of choice and offers the best chance of cure. Ventral cervical lesions may need anterior corpectomy or extended posterior approaches; when the wall is densely adherent to the cord, partial removal with drainage is accepted, but recurrence is common and follow-up MRI is required. Steroids may help chemical meningitis after spillage.
det.prognosis: Good after complete excision; subtotal resection carries a substantial recurrence risk over years.
pearls: Ventral intradural cyst with a vertebral body anomaly = think neurenteric cyst.
Unlike epidermoid, it usually does not restrict diffusion.
Fluctuating symptoms do not exclude a compressive cyst.
det.thd: Neurenteric cyst คือถุงน้ำแต่กำเนิดที่บุด้วยเยื่อบุคล้ายลำไส้ มักอยู่ด้านหน้าของไขสันหลังส่วนคอหรืออกในชั้นใต้เยื่อดูรา ผู้ป่วยเด็กหรือผู้ใหญ่อายุน้อยมีอาการปวดคอ ปวดร้าว และไขสันหลังถูกกดช้า ๆ อาการอาจดีขึ้นแล้วแย่ลงสลับกัน MRI พบถุงน้ำไม่จับสารทึบรังสี มักมีความผิดปกติของกระดูกสันหลังร่วม รักษาโดยผ่าตัดเอาผนังถุงออกทั้งหมดเพื่อลดการกลับเป็นซ้ำ

name: Congenital dermal sinus tract (with spinal dermoid/epidermoid cyst)
formal: An epithelium-lined tract from a midline skin opening that may pass through the dura to the spinal cord, filum or cauda equina, often ending in an intraspinal dermoid or epidermoid cyst, and predisposing to meningitis, abscess and cord tethering.
simple: A tiny hole in the skin over the spine, present from birth, that can tunnel down to the spinal cord and let infection in or end in a cyst.
th: รูหรือรอยบุ๋มเล็ก ๆ กลางหลังที่มีทางเชื่อมลงไปถึงเยื่อหุ้มหรือไขสันหลังตั้งแต่กำเนิด อาจมีถุง dermoid หรือ epidermoid อยู่ปลายทาง ทำให้เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบซ้ำ ฝีในไขสันหลัง หรือไขสันหลังถูกดึงรั้ง
tempoNote: Present from birth; may stay silent, then present acutely with meningitis or abscess, or gradually with cyst compression and tethering
feat: Pinpoint midline opening above the gluteal cleft, often with hair, a skin tag, capillary stain or hypertrichosis; may ooze
Recurrent or unusual bacterial meningitis (staphylococci, Gram-negatives, anaerobes, mixed flora)
Intraspinal abscess or infected dermoid causing back pain, fever and rapidly progressive weakness
Chemical meningitis when cyst contents leak
Signs of tethered cord: gait change, foot deformity, bladder dysfunction
inv: MRI lumbosacral spine with contrast (and DWI): tract course, intradural cyst, conus level, abscess
Spinal ultrasound in young infants as an initial screen
CSF and blood cultures when meningitis is present (with imaging first if a mass is suspected)

case.who: 3-year-old boy from Lampang admitted for a second bout of meningitis in a year
case.story: Fever, neck stiffness and vomiting; the first episode six months ago grew E. coli, which puzzled the team for a toddler.
case.exam: Meningism; a small pit with a few hairs at L4 above the gluteal cleft, with slight surrounding redness; mild weakness of ankle dorsiflexion on the left.
case.tests: CSF: neutrophilic pleocytosis, low glucose, mixed Gram-negative and Gram-positive organisms. MRI: tract from the skin pit to an intradural rim-enhancing cyst at L3 with a low-lying conus.
case.q: What explains recurrent meningitis, and what definitive treatment is needed?
case.a: Infected dermal sinus tract with an intraspinal dermoid; after antibiotics, complete excision of the tract and cyst with intradural exploration and untethering.

det.patho: When the neural tube separates from the surface ectoderm (disjunction) in the fourth week, a focal failure leaves a strand of ectoderm connecting skin to the neural tissue. As the spine grows, the tract is drawn upward, so it often enters the canal several levels above its skin opening. Because the lining is skin, desquamated keratin and appendages accumulate to form epidermoid or dermoid cysts. About half of tracts penetrate the dura, and many attach to the conus or filum, tethering the cord.
det.clinical: Presentation includes an incidental cutaneous finding, recurrent or atypical meningitis, intraspinal abscess with rapidly evolving weakness, aseptic meningitis from cyst rupture, and slowly progressive tethered cord or compressive signs. Lumbosacral is the most frequent site, followed by occipital (where tracts may reach the posterior fossa). Simple coccygeal pits located within the gluteal cleft and close to the anus, with a visible base, are usually blind and benign; openings above the cleft, those with stigmata, or those draining fluid are suspicious.
det.diagnosis: MRI is the definitive investigation and should include the whole tract and the conus; DWI helps identify epidermoid content and contrast shows abscess. Ultrasound can screen infants before posterior element ossification. Never probe the tract or inject contrast into it, because this introduces infection. In meningitis with organisms suggesting skin or bowel flora, or a second episode, examine the entire midline from occiput to coccyx.
det.treatment: Suspicious tracts are excised early, before infection, by following the tract to its termination and opening the dura when it continues intradurally, removing any cyst and releasing tethering. Infected cases need antibiotics and urgent drainage, followed by complete excision; prior infection makes surgery harder and increases deficits. Dermoid capsules adherent to neural tissue may be left partly to protect function, accepting a recurrence risk. Long-term follow-up checks for recurrence and retethering.
det.prognosis: Excellent when removed before infection; prior meningitis, abscess or established deficits worsen outcome.
pearls: Midline dimple above the gluteal cleft with hair or stain = image, do not probe.
A second meningitis episode, or one with enteric or skin flora, needs a search for a dermal sinus or skull-base leak.
The tract climbs: the intraspinal lesion often lies several segments above the skin opening.
det.thd: Dermal sinus tract คือทางเชื่อมที่บุด้วยผิวหนังจากรูเล็ก ๆ กลางหลังลงไปถึงเยื่อหุ้มหรือไขสันหลัง มักมีขน ปาน หรือติ่งเนื้อร่วม ปลายทางอาจเป็นถุง dermoid หรือ epidermoid ทำให้เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบซ้ำจากเชื้อแปลก ๆ ฝีในไขสันหลัง หรือไขสันหลังถูกดึงรั้ง ตรวจด้วย MRI และห้ามใช้เครื่องมือแหย่รู การรักษาคือผ่าตัดเลาะทางเชื่อมจนสุดปลาย รวมถึงเปิดเยื่อดูราเอาถุงออก ควรทำก่อนเกิดการติดเชื้อ

name: Tethered cord syndrome (TCS)
formal: A stretch-induced dysfunction of the conus medullaris and lower cord caused by abnormal fixation of the caudal cord (tight or fatty filum terminale, lipomyelomeningocele, split cord, dermal sinus or scar after spina bifida repair), producing progressive lower-limb, bladder, bowel and pain symptoms.
simple: A condition where the bottom of the spinal cord is stuck in place, so it is stretched as the child grows or the back bends, slowly damaging nerves to the legs and bladder.
th: ภาวะที่ปลายไขสันหลังถูกยึดติดไว้กับโครงสร้างด้านล่าง ทำให้ถูกดึงยืดเมื่อเด็กโตหรือก้มหลัง เกิดปวดหลังปวดขา ขาอ่อนแรง เท้าผิดรูป และปัสสาวะผิดปกติที่ค่อย ๆ แย่ลง รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัดคลายไขสันหลัง

feat: Back and leg pain worse with bending or sitting cross-legged; perineal pain in adults
Progressive gait change, toe walking, leg asymmetry, cavus or club foot

Urodynamic studies — a sensitive marker of early dysfunction and of response to surgery

case.who: 12-year-old girl from Nakhon Ratchasima, a school volleyball player
case.story: Over a year, low back and leg pain that worsens when she bends forward; she now wets herself during games and her left foot has developed a high arch.
case.exam: Small fatty lump over the sacrum; left ankle plantarflexion weak, left ankle jerk absent; reduced perianal sensation; mild lumbar scoliosis.
case.tests: MRI: conus at L4 attached to a thickened fatty filum. Urodynamics: detrusor overactivity with poor compliance.
case.q: What is the syndrome, and why act now rather than wait?
case.a: Tethered cord syndrome from a fatty filum and lipoma; surgical untethering halts progression, and bladder and motor deficits that become established often do not recover.

det.patho: Normally the conus ascends to about L1–L2 by early infancy and moves freely within the canal. When the caudal cord is anchored, longitudinal traction during growth and flexion stretches neurons and small vessels, reducing blood flow and oxidative metabolism; experimental and intraoperative studies show reversible metabolic failure that becomes permanent with continued stretch. Causes include a tight or fat-infiltrated filum, lipomyelomeningocele and other spinal lipomas, split cord malformation, dermal sinus tract, caudal regression and scar after myelomeningocele closure. Radiological tethering is almost universal after spina bifida repair, but only a minority become symptomatic.
det.clinical: In children, the common pattern is gradual worsening of gait, asymmetric foot deformity, leg length difference, back or leg pain and bladder dysfunction, often during a growth spurt. Scoliosis may progress quickly. Adults usually present with diffuse back, perineal and leg pain, sensory change, weakness and sphincter disturbance, sometimes after a strain or childbirth. In repaired myelomeningocele, retethering presents as new pain, spasticity, worsening gait or bladder change once shunt malfunction and syrinx have been excluded.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis combines a compatible progressive clinical picture with MRI evidence of a fixed caudal cord (low conus, thick or fatty filum, or a tethering lesion). A low conus alone is not the syndrome; the term 'occult tethered cord' for symptoms with a normally positioned conus is controversial. Urodynamics document objective bladder dysfunction. Exclude HSP, peripheral neuropathy, lumbar disc disease and, in spina bifida, shunt failure and syrinx.
det.treatment: Symptomatic patients should undergo untethering: sectioning of the filum, or complex lipoma resection and dural reconstruction, with intraoperative monitoring of motor and sphincter pathways. Spinal column shortening osteotomy is an option for recurrent tethering. Asymptomatic fatty filum is often observed, though some centres operate prophylactically; asymptomatic complex lipomas remain debated. After surgery, continue bladder management, physiotherapy and surveillance for retethering.
det.prognosis: Pain responds best to surgery; motor function often stabilises or improves, while long-standing bladder dysfunction improves less predictably.
pearls: Toe walking, a new cavus foot or recurrent wetting in a school-age child with a sacral fatty lump suggests tethered cord.
In a child with repaired spina bifida, check the shunt before blaming retethering.
Treat the syndrome, not the MRI: a low conus without symptoms is not an automatic operation.
det.thd: Tethered cord syndrome คือภาวะที่ปลายไขสันหลังถูกตรึงไว้จาก filum ที่หนาหรือมีไขมัน ก้อนไขมัน ไขสันหลังแยก หรือพังผืดหลังผ่าตัด spina bifida ทำให้ไขสันหลังถูกยืดและขาดเลือดเมื่อเด็กโตหรือก้มหลัง มีอาการปวดหลังปวดขา เดินผิดปกติ เท้าโก่ง และปัสสาวะผิดปกติที่แย่ลงเรื่อย ๆ วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI ที่พบ conus อยู่ต่ำร่วมกับ urodynamics รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัดคลายไขสันหลังก่อนที่ความเสียหายจะถาวร

name: Holoprosencephaly (HPE)
formal: A malformation spectrum caused by incomplete midline cleavage of the embryonic forebrain into two hemispheres, graded as alobar, semilobar, lobar and middle interhemispheric variant, usually with midline facial anomalies and hypothalamic–pituitary dysfunction.
simple: A birth defect in which the front of the brain does not split properly into left and right halves, often with an unusual face and serious developmental problems.
th: ความผิดปกติแต่กำเนิดที่สมองส่วนหน้าไม่แบ่งเป็นสองซีกอย่างสมบูรณ์ มักมีใบหน้าผิดปกติแนวกลาง เช่น ตาชิดกัน ปากแหว่งกลาง ฟันหน้ากลางซี่เดียว ร่วมกับพัฒนาการช้า ชัก และเบาจืดจากต่อมใต้สมอง
tempoNote: Congenital, formed in the third to fourth week after conception; static malformation with lifelong neurodevelopmental and endocrine consequences
feat: Midline facial anomalies that broadly reflect severity: cyclopia or proboscis, hypotelorism, median cleft lip, single central maxillary incisor
Developmental delay, microcephaly (or macrocephaly with a dorsal cyst and hydrocephalus), spasticity and dystonia
Hypothalamic dysfunction: central diabetes insipidus, temperature instability, feeding and sleep problems
Seizures in a substantial minority
Causes: trisomy 13, SHH, ZIC2, SIX3 and other gene variants, maternal diabetes, Smith–Lemli–Opitz syndrome
inv: MRI brain: degree of hemispheric fusion, absent or partial falx, fused thalami/basal ganglia, single ventricle, dorsal cyst
Karyotype/chromosomal microarray, then HPE gene panel or exome
Serum sodium and osmolality, pituitary hormones; 7-dehydrocholesterol if Smith–Lemli–Opitz is suspected
Antenatal ultrasound and fetal MRI

case.who: Newborn boy in Khon Kaen born to a 33-year-old mother with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes
case.story: Hard to feed, sleepy, and over the second day passes large volumes of dilute urine.
case.exam: Eyes set close together, flat nasal bridge, median cleft of the upper lip, small head.
case.tests: Serum sodium 156 mmol/L with dilute urine. MRI: frontal lobes fused across the midline with a single frontal ventricle, absent anterior falx, partially fused thalami. Karyotype normal; SHH variant found.
case.q: What is the malformation, and which endocrine problem explains the high sodium?
case.a: Semilobar holoprosencephaly; central diabetes insipidus from hypothalamic involvement, treated with desmopressin and careful fluid balance.

det.patho: Signalling from the prechordal plate and ventral midline — principally the Sonic hedgehog pathway — normally induces the forebrain to divide into two hemispheres and shapes the midface. Disruption in the third to fourth week leaves the prosencephalon partly or wholly undivided, together with defects of the facial midline. About half of liveborn cases are chromosomal (trisomy 13 above all, also trisomy 18 and triploidy), and among the rest variants in SHH, ZIC2, SIX3, TGIF1 and others, often with variable expressivity, are found. Maternal diabetes, alcohol, retinoic acid and cholesterol synthesis defects such as Smith–Lemli–Opitz contribute. It is common in early embryos but most are lost before birth; birth prevalence is roughly 1 in 10,000.
det.clinical: Alobar forms, with a single ventricle and no interhemispheric fissure, usually have severe facial anomalies and profound disability. Semilobar and lobar forms show progressively better separation and milder features, and the middle interhemispheric variant fuses the posterior frontal and parietal lobes instead. Most children have developmental delay, motor impairment with hypotonia then spasticity or dystonia, and feeding difficulties. Endocrine problems — especially central diabetes insipidus, but also other pituitary deficits — are frequent and can be life-threatening. Mildly affected relatives may only have a single central incisor or hypotelorism.
det.diagnosis: MRI classifies the subtype by the extent of the interhemispheric fissure, falx, ventricles, thalamic and basal ganglia fusion and associated dorsal cyst. Chromosomal analysis comes first, followed by a gene panel or exome, with parental testing because autosomal dominant variants show reduced penetrance. Check electrolytes and pituitary function, and measure 7-dehydrocholesterol when there are genital anomalies or syndactyly. Prenatal diagnosis by ultrasound and fetal MRI allows counselling.
det.treatment: Care is supportive and multidisciplinary: desmopressin and fluid management for diabetes insipidus, hormone replacement for other pituitary deficits, gastrostomy for unsafe swallowing, antiseizure medicines, management of spasticity and dystonia, and shunting for hydrocephalus or an enlarging dorsal cyst. Craniofacial surgery may repair clefts. Genetic counselling guides future pregnancies, and good glycaemic control and folate are advised for diabetic mothers. Palliative care input is appropriate for severe alobar forms.
det.prognosis: Most infants with alobar HPE die early, though some live for years; lobar and milder forms often survive into adulthood with variable disability.
pearls: 'The face predicts the brain' — usually, but not always; a single central incisor can be the only clue in a carrier parent.
Check sodium in any infant with HPE: central diabetes insipidus is common.
Trisomy 13 is the leading chromosomal cause; SHH is the leading single-gene cause.
det.thd: Holoprosencephaly คือภาวะที่สมองส่วนหน้าไม่แยกเป็นซีกซ้ายขวาอย่างสมบูรณ์ แบ่งเป็นชนิด alobar, semilobar, lobar และ middle interhemispheric variant มักมีความผิดปกติของใบหน้าแนวกลาง เช่น ตาชิดกัน ปากแหว่งกลาง หรือฟันหน้ากลางซี่เดียว เด็กมีพัฒนาการช้า เกร็ง ชัก และมักมีเบาจืดจากความผิดปกติของ hypothalamus สาเหตุสำคัญคือ trisomy 13 ยีน SHH และมารดาเป็นเบาหวาน วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI และตรวจพันธุกรรม การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคองและแก้ไขต่อมไร้ท่อ
