name: Hydranencephaly
formal: An encephaloclastic disorder in which most of both cerebral hemispheres, chiefly in carotid territories, are destroyed in utero and replaced by a CSF-filled membranous sac, with relative preservation of the thalami, brainstem, cerebellum and often posterior cerebral artery territory.
simple: A rare condition where most of the baby's brain hemispheres are destroyed before birth and replaced by fluid, while the brainstem still works.
th: ภาวะที่สมองใหญ่ทั้งสองซีกถูกทำลายตั้งแต่อยู่ในครรภ์และถูกแทนที่ด้วยน้ำไขสันหลัง เหลือเพียงก้านสมอง ทาลามัส และสมองน้อย ทารกแรกเกิดอาจดูปกติแต่ไม่มีพัฒนาการ ส่องไฟผ่านศีรษะได้
tempoNote: Brain destruction occurs in the second trimester; infants may seem normal for days to weeks, then show failure to develop, irritability, hypertonia and progressive head enlargement
feat: Newborn may look and feed normally because brainstem reflexes are intact
Head transilluminates brightly; head size normal at birth but often enlarges later
No developmental progress, poor visual attention, irritability, hypertonia, seizures
Falx usually present, thalami separate; small posterior or inferior temporal cortical remnants may remain
Causes: bilateral ICA occlusion, congenital CMV or toxoplasmosis, monochorionic twin demise, maternal toxins, Fowler syndrome
inv: Cranial ultrasound, CT or MRI: supratentorial space filled with fluid, absent cortical mantle, preserved thalami and posterior fossa structures
MRA/CTA may show absent or attenuated supraclinoid carotid flow
Congenital infection screen (CMV PCR, toxoplasma serology) and twin-pregnancy history
EEG: markedly suppressed or near-isoelectric cortical activity

case.who: 6-week-old girl brought from Mae Hong Son, survivor of a twin pregnancy in which the co-twin died at 22 weeks
case.story: She feeds by mouth and cries, but does not fix or follow and has become very irritable with stiff limbs; her head is growing quickly.
case.exam: Bulging fontanelle, head circumference above the 97th centile, bright glow on transillumination, brisk reflexes, intact sucking and pupillary reflexes.
case.tests: CT: supratentorial space filled with CSF, no cortical mantle except small occipital remnants, falx present, thalami and cerebellum preserved.
case.q: How does this differ from severe hydrocephalus, and what is the aim of care?
case.a: Hydranencephaly from in-utero destruction (twin demise), with no recoverable cortex, unlike hydrocephalus where a thin mantle persists; care is palliative, with CSF diversion only to control head size and comfort.

det.patho: Hydranencephaly is an end-stage destructive lesion: after the hemispheres have formed, a severe insult in the second trimester liquefies brain in the internal carotid territories, and the necrotic tissue is resorbed to leave a fluid sac covered by leptomeninges. Proposed causes include bilateral supraclinoid carotid occlusion, intrauterine infection (CMV, toxoplasmosis, others), death of a monochorionic co-twin, maternal carbon monoxide or drug exposure, and the autosomal recessive proliferative vasculopathy of Fowler syndrome (FLVCR2). Vertebrobasilar structures are spared, explaining preserved thalami, brainstem and cerebellum. Prevalence is roughly 1–2 per 10,000 births.
det.clinical: At birth the infant may seem normal, feeding and crying through brainstem function, so diagnosis can be delayed until failure to reach milestones, irritability, abnormal tone or rapid head growth appears. Visual responsiveness is poor, seizures and temperature or feeding problems are common, and some develop hydrocephalus because CSF production continues without adequate absorption. Remarkably, a few children show limited responsiveness to familiar voices and touch.
det.diagnosis: Transillumination is a bedside clue, and imaging confirms the absence of cerebral mantle with intact falx, separate thalami and posterior fossa structures. The key distinctions are maximal hydrocephalus, where a thin cortical rim persists and treatment can restore development, and alobar holoprosencephaly, where the falx is absent and thalami are fused. Investigate for congenital infection, twin history and family history suggesting Fowler syndrome, which recurs. EEG typically shows severely depressed cortical activity.
det.treatment: There is no restorative treatment. Care is palliative and family-centred, addressing feeding, seizures, comfort and spasticity. CSF diversion (shunt or endoscopic choroid plexus coagulation) is used to limit progressive macrocephaly and ease nursing. Genetic counselling is indicated when Fowler syndrome or another inherited cause is identified.
det.prognosis: Most infants die within the first year, although some survive several years with intensive supportive care.
pearls: A normal-looking newborn can still have hydranencephaly — brainstem reflexes are preserved.
Falx present, thalami separate: hydranencephaly; falx absent, thalami fused: alobar holoprosencephaly.
Always look for a cortical rim: if present, it is hydrocephalus and potentially treatable.
det.thd: Hydranencephaly คือภาวะที่สมองใหญ่ทั้งสองซีกในเขตหลอดเลือด carotid ถูกทำลายตั้งแต่อยู่ในครรภ์ไตรมาสสองและกลายเป็นถุงน้ำ เหลือเพียงทาลามัส ก้านสมอง และสมองน้อย สาเหตุได้แก่หลอดเลือด carotid อุดตัน การติดเชื้อในครรภ์ แฝดเสียชีวิตในครรภ์ หรือ Fowler syndrome ทารกอาจดูปกติหลังคลอดแต่ไม่มีพัฒนาการ ส่องไฟผ่านศีรษะได้ ต้องแยกจาก hydrocephalus ที่ยังมีเนื้อสมองบาง ๆ และรักษาได้ การดูแลเป็นแบบประคับประคอง และอาจทำ shunt เพื่อลดขนาดศีรษะ

name: Dandy–Walker malformation (DWM)
formal: A posterior fossa malformation defined by hypoplasia and upward rotation of the cerebellar vermis, a cystically dilated fourth ventricle filling an enlarged posterior fossa, and elevation of the tentorium and torcular, often with hydrocephalus and other brain or systemic anomalies.
simple: A brain malformation at the back of the head where the middle part of the cerebellum is underdeveloped and a large fluid cyst forms, often causing a big head and fluid build-up.
th: ความผิดปกติแต่กำเนิดของโพรงสมองด้านหลัง สมองน้อยส่วน vermis เจริญไม่เต็มที่และหมุนขึ้น โพรงสมองที่สี่ขยายเป็นถุงน้ำ โพรงสมองด้านหลังใหญ่ มักมี hydrocephalus ทำให้ศีรษะโต
tempoNote: Congenital; most diagnosed antenatally or in the first year with macrocephaly and hydrocephalus; milder forms may surface later with ataxia or delay
feat: Enlarging head with prominent occiput and bulging fontanelle from hydrocephalus
Hypotonia, delayed motor milestones, truncal ataxia and nystagmus
Variable cognition, strongly influenced by associated brain anomalies such as corpus callosum agenesis or cortical malformations
Systemic associations: cardiac, facial, eye, renal and limb anomalies; PHACE syndrome with segmental facial haemangioma
Causes include chromosomal anomalies (trisomies 18, 13, 9), ZIC1/ZIC4 deletions, FOXC1 variants and many syndromes
inv: MRI brain (sagittal midline): small, rotated vermis; fourth ventricle cyst; high torcular; ventricular size; associated malformations
Fetal MRI after about 20 weeks, when the vermis should be fully formed
Echocardiography, eye examination and chromosomal microarray or exome
Cranial ultrasound for serial monitoring of ventricles in infancy

case.story: His head has grown faster than expected, he cannot yet hold it up, and he vomits often.
case.exam: Head circumference well above the 97th centile, prominent occiput, tense fontanelle, setting-sun eyes, marked hypotonia; red plaque-like haemangioma over the right forehead and cheek.
case.tests: MRI: hypoplastic, upwardly rotated vermis; large fourth ventricular cyst filling an enlarged posterior fossa; raised torcular; enlarged lateral and third ventricles. MRA: abnormal right internal carotid artery.
case.q: What is the malformation, which syndrome links it to the skin lesion, and how is the hydrocephalus treated?
case.a: Dandy–Walker malformation within PHACE syndrome; CSF diversion (ventriculoperitoneal or cystoperitoneal shunt, or both, or endoscopic options), plus cardiac and eye screening.

det.patho: DWM reflects disordered development of the rhombencephalic roof and cerebellar primordium early in gestation: the vermis fails to grow normally and the membranous fourth ventricle roof balloons into a cyst, expanding the posterior fossa and pushing the tentorium and torcular upward. Outflow of CSF is often impaired, so hydrocephalus develops in most cases, frequently after birth. It is genetically heterogeneous: chromosomal aneuploidies and copy-number changes (including 3q24 deletions with ZIC1/ZIC4 and 6p25 with FOXC1), single-gene syndromes and environmental factors have all been implicated. Birth prevalence is roughly 1 in 25,000–35,000.
det.clinical: Most infants present with macrocephaly and signs of raised pressure, hypotonia and motor delay; ataxia and nystagmus become evident later. Associated CNS malformations (callosal agenesis, heterotopia, polymicrogyria, occipital encephalocele) and systemic anomalies largely determine cognitive outcome. Children with isolated DWM can develop normally once hydrocephalus is controlled. A large segmental facial haemangioma raises the possibility of PHACE syndrome.
det.diagnosis: MRI is decisive: assess vermis size and rotation, fourth ventricle, posterior fossa volume, torcular position and the supratentorial brain. Older umbrella terms such as 'Dandy–Walker variant' have been abandoned in favour of precise descriptions — isolated vermian hypoplasia, Blake pouch cyst (normal vermis rotated by a cyst, usually benign) and mega cisterna magna. Prenatal diagnosis before about 18–20 weeks is unreliable because the vermis is still forming. Genetic testing and screening of heart, eyes and kidneys complete the work-up.
det.treatment: Symptomatic hydrocephalus requires CSF diversion: ventriculoperitoneal shunt, cystoperitoneal shunt, or a combined system, chosen according to whether the aqueduct is patent; endoscopic third ventriculostomy with or without choroid plexus cauterisation and aqueductal stenting are alternatives in selected children. Simple cyst membrane excision is seldom used now because it often fails. Long-term care involves developmental therapy, epilepsy management, and screening for associated anomalies, with genetic counselling for families.
det.prognosis: Highly variable; isolated forms with treated hydrocephalus may have normal intelligence, whereas associated malformations or syndromes predict significant disability.
pearls: Triad: small upturned vermis, fourth ventricle cyst, raised torcular.
Do not call it DWM on a scan before about 20 weeks — the vermis is not yet complete.
Facial segmental haemangioma plus posterior fossa malformation = PHACE; check arteries, heart and eyes.
det.thd: Dandy–Walker malformation คือความผิดปกติของโพรงสมองด้านหลังที่ vermis เล็กและหมุนขึ้น โพรงสมองที่สี่ขยายเป็นถุงน้ำ และ torcular อยู่สูง ส่วนใหญ่มี hydrocephalus ทำให้ศีรษะโต กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนปวกเปียก พัฒนาการช้า และเดินเซ พยากรณ์โรคขึ้นกับความผิดปกติอื่นของสมองและอวัยวะที่พบร่วม วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI ร่วมกับตรวจหัวใจ ตา และพันธุกรรม รักษา hydrocephalus ด้วย shunt หรือการผ่าตัดส่องกล้อง

name: Arachnoid cyst
formal: A benign, usually congenital collection of CSF-like fluid enclosed within a split or duplicated arachnoid membrane, most often in the middle cranial fossa, and also suprasellar, posterior fossa, quadrigeminal, convexity or spinal; the large majority are incidental and stable.
simple: A fluid-filled pocket in the thin membrane around the brain or spinal cord, usually harmless and found by chance on a scan.
th: ถุงน้ำที่อยู่ระหว่างชั้นเยื่อ arachnoid มีน้ำคล้ายน้ำไขสันหลัง ส่วนใหญ่อยู่บริเวณ middle cranial fossa และพบโดยบังเอิญ ไม่ต้องรักษา ยกเว้นรายที่กดเนื้อสมอง ทำให้เกิด hydrocephalus หรือมีเลือดออกร่วม
tempoNote: Usually silent for life; symptomatic cysts give slowly evolving headache, macrocephaly or hydrocephalus, while bleeding into or around the cyst after minor head injury causes acute deterioration
feat: Most are discovered incidentally on CT or MRI done for unrelated reasons, especially headache
Middle cranial fossa location in about half, more often left-sided and in males; skull may bulge over large cysts
Suprasellar cysts can cause hydrocephalus, visual loss, endocrine disturbance and bobble-head doll movements
Posterior fossa cysts may block CSF flow and cause hydrocephalus or ataxia
Rupture or bleeding after minor trauma, producing subdural hygroma or chronic subdural haematoma in young people
inv: MRI: smooth extra-axial cyst matching CSF on all sequences, complete suppression on FLAIR, no diffusion restriction, no enhancement
CT shows scalloping or remodelling of adjacent bone
Visual fields and endocrine tests for suprasellar cysts
Neuropsychological or developmental assessment before considering surgery for non-specific complaints

case.who: 17-year-old male football player from Chiang Rai
case.story: Two weeks after heading the ball hard, he has worsening headache, vomiting and drowsiness; a previous MRI for headache at 14 showed 'a fluid cyst' and he was told it was harmless.
case.exam: Drowsy but rousable, mild right pronator drift, papilloedema.
case.tests: CT: large left middle fossa arachnoid cyst with an adjacent left chronic subdural haematoma causing midline shift.
case.q: What complication has occurred, and how should young people with such cysts be counselled?
case.a: Chronic subdural haematoma related to a middle fossa arachnoid cyst after minor trauma; needs neurosurgical drainage, and patients should know to seek care promptly for headache after head knocks, though contact sport restrictions remain individual.

det.patho: Most arachnoid cysts arise during development when the arachnoid membrane splits and fluid accumulates between its layers; mechanisms for enlargement include active secretion by the cyst wall, slit-valve flow from the subarachnoid space and osmotic gradients. Secondary (acquired) cysts can follow infection, haemorrhage or surgery. On MRI they are found in roughly 1–2% of the population, more often in children and males. Middle fossa cysts are graded by Galassi type I–III according to size and mass effect.
det.clinical: The usual scenario is an incidental cyst in someone scanned for headache, which is usually unrelated. Genuine symptoms arise from mass effect or CSF obstruction: macrocephaly and skull asymmetry in infants, raised pressure symptoms, focal signs or seizures with large convexity cysts, hydrocephalus with suprasellar or posterior fossa cysts, and visual or endocrine problems from suprasellar ones. Middle fossa cysts predispose to subdural haematoma or hygroma and intracystic bleeding after relatively minor trauma. Spinal arachnoid cysts may cause myelopathy or radicular pain and may change size with posture.
det.diagnosis: MRI is diagnostic, showing an extra-axial cyst identical to CSF on T1, T2 and FLAIR, without restricted diffusion or enhancement; this separates it from epidermoid, neurenteric, neoplastic and parasitic cysts. CT shows chronic bone remodelling. Decide carefully whether symptoms are truly attributable: headache alone, without hydrocephalus or raised pressure, seldom justifies treatment. Serial imaging is rarely needed in adults with typical incidental cysts but is reasonable in young children with large cysts.
det.treatment: Asymptomatic cysts are observed. Symptomatic ones are treated by fenestration into the basal cisterns or ventricles, preferably endoscopically (endoscopic ventriculocystocisternostomy is the standard for suprasellar cysts), by microsurgical fenestration, or by cystoperitoneal shunting, which works well but introduces shunt dependence. Associated subdural haematoma is drained, with or without addressing the cyst. Spinal cysts causing compression are fenestrated or excised, and the dural defect is closed.
det.prognosis: Excellent for incidental cysts, which rarely change; surgery for clearly symptomatic cysts usually relieves hydrocephalus and pressure symptoms, while non-specific headache often persists.
pearls: CSF on every sequence, including FLAIR and DWI = arachnoid cyst; restriction on DWI = epidermoid.
Headache plus an incidental arachnoid cyst rarely means the cyst caused the headache.
Young person with a middle fossa cyst and new headache after a minor knock: scan for subdural haematoma.
det.thd: Arachnoid cyst คือถุงน้ำแต่กำเนิดในชั้นเยื่อ arachnoid มีน้ำเหมือนน้ำไขสันหลัง พบบ่อยที่ middle cranial fossa และส่วนใหญ่พบโดยบังเอิญ ไม่ต้องรักษา MRI เห็นสัญญาณเหมือนน้ำไขสันหลังทุก sequence และไม่จำกัดการแพร่บน DWI ซึ่งต่างจาก epidermoid ผ่าตัดเฉพาะรายที่มี hydrocephalus กดสมอง หรือมีอาการชัดเจน เช่น ส่องกล้องเจาะผนังถุงหรือทำ shunt ผู้ป่วยอายุน้อยที่มีถุงน้ำบริเวณขมับควรระวังเลือดออกใต้เยื่อดูราหลังศีรษะกระแทก

name: Lissencephaly (agyria–pachygyria spectrum)
formal: A malformation of neuronal migration in which the cerebral surface is smooth or has too few, overly broad gyri over a thickened, poorly layered cortex, most often caused by variants in PAFAH1B1 (LIS1), DCX or tubulin genes such as TUBA1A, or by the 17p13.3 deletion of Miller–Dieker syndrome.
simple: A brain that forms without its normal folds because nerve cells failed to travel to the right place before birth, causing severe developmental delay and seizures.
th: ความผิดปกติจากการเคลื่อนที่ของเซลล์ประสาทในครรภ์ ทำให้ผิวสมองเรียบหรือมีรอยหยักน้อยและกว้างเกินไป เด็กมีพัฒนาการช้ารุนแรง กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนปวกเปียกแล้วเกร็ง และชักแบบ infantile spasms สาเหตุหลักคือยีน LIS1, DCX, TUBA1A หรือ Miller–Dieker
tempoNote: Present from birth; poor feeding and floppiness in early infancy, epileptic spasms usually begin within the first year, and spasticity emerges over childhood
feat: Profound global developmental delay with axial hypotonia that later turns into limb spasticity
Epileptic spasms in infancy, often evolving into drug-resistant mixed seizures
Feeding and swallowing failure with recurrent aspiration pneumonia
MRI gradient points to the gene: posterior-predominant in LIS1, anterior-predominant in DCX (males)
Distinctive facial features (prominent forehead, bitemporal narrowing, small nose) in Miller–Dieker syndrome
inv: MRI brain: smooth or broad-gyral surface, thick cortex (often 10–20 mm), cell-sparse layer, figure-of-eight shape on axial images
Chromosomal microarray or FISH for 17p13.3 deletion, then a malformation gene panel or exome
EEG: high-amplitude fast rhythms or hypsarrhythmia; video-EEG to characterise spasms
Swallow assessment and nutritional review

case.who: 5-month-old boy from Khon Kaen referred by a community hospital paediatrician
case.story: He has fed slowly since birth, never held his head up, and over the past two weeks has had clusters of sudden flexion jerks on waking.
case.exam: Marked head lag, poor visual fixation, mildly small head circumference; no skin lesions.
case.tests: MRI: almost featureless parieto-occipital surface with thick cortex and somewhat broader gyri frontally; EEG hypsarrhythmia; microarray normal, gene panel shows a PAFAH1B1 variant.
case.q: What is the malformation, and how should the spasms be treated?
case.a: LIS1-related classic lissencephaly (posterior > anterior); treat the epileptic spasms promptly with ACTH/prednisolone or vigabatrin and plan supportive care, including feeding support and family genetic counselling.

det.patho: Neurons born in the ventricular zone must climb radial glia to the cortical plate; LIS1 and DCX regulate the microtubule motors and stability that drive this journey, so loss of either leaves a thick, four-layered cortex with few or no gyri. Heterozygous PAFAH1B1 loss and the larger 17p13.3 deletion (which also removes YWHAE) give posterior-predominant disease, whereas DCX on the X chromosome gives anterior-predominant agyria in hemizygous males. Tubulin genes (TUBA1A, TUBB2B, TUBB3) add abnormal basal ganglia, callosal and cerebellar defects, while RELN and VLDLR forms pair the malformation with cerebellar hypoplasia and ARX causes X-linked lissencephaly with ambiguous genitalia.
det.clinical: Babies may look normal at birth apart from feeding trouble, then fail to reach motor and social milestones. Epileptic spasms appear in most during the first year and are followed by tonic, atonic and focal seizures that rarely respond fully to medicines. Over time, children develop spastic quadriparesis, microcephaly and severe intellectual disability; most never walk or speak. Miller–Dieker syndrome adds characteristic facial dysmorphism and sometimes cardiac or genital anomalies. Milder pachygyria, particularly in DCX or mosaic LIS1 cases, can allow some speech and walking.
det.diagnosis: MRI is diagnostic: the cortex is abnormally thick and smooth, and the front-versus-back gradient guides genetic testing. Start with microarray or targeted FISH for 17p13.3 because deletions are common, then a multigene malformations panel or exome; parental testing clarifies recurrence risk. In DCX-related cases, check the mother for a subcortical band, which may be clinically silent. Distinguish classic lissencephaly from cobblestone malformation, which has an irregular surface, white-matter signal change, eye abnormalities and raised CK.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying therapy. Treat epileptic spasms early with hormonal therapy or vigabatrin and then use broad-spectrum antiseizure medicines; ketogenic diet and VNS help some children with drug-resistant epilepsy. Gastrostomy reduces aspiration and improves nutrition, and physiotherapy, orthoses and spasticity treatment maintain comfort. Palliative care and family genetic counselling, including prenatal options in future pregnancies, are part of standard care.
det.prognosis: Severe classic forms carry high childhood mortality, mainly from aspiration and status epilepticus, though many survive into adolescence with good supportive care; milder pachygyria has a better outlook.
pearls: Posterior-worse smooth brain suggests LIS1; anterior-worse in a boy suggests DCX — and check his mother's MRI.
Always order a microarray: Miller–Dieker is a contiguous gene deletion missed by single-gene tests.
Dysmorphic basal ganglia plus cerebellar hypoplasia with a simplified gyral pattern points to a tubulinopathy.
det.thd: Lissencephaly คือภาวะผิวสมองเรียบหรือมีรอยหยักน้อยและกว้าง จากเซลล์ประสาทเคลื่อนที่ไปยังเปลือกสมองไม่สำเร็จในครรภ์ ยีนที่พบบ่อยคือ LIS1 (เด่นด้านหลัง), DCX (เด่นด้านหน้าในเด็กชาย) และ TUBA1A ส่วน Miller–Dieker เป็นการขาดหายของโครโมโซม 17p13.3 ร่วมกับหน้าตาผิดรูป เด็กมีพัฒนาการช้ารุนแรง ชักแบบ infantile spasms กลืนลำบากและสำลักบ่อย วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI แล้วตรวจ microarray และยีน การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง ควบคุมชัก ดูแลโภชนาการ และให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

name: Subcortical band heterotopia (double cortex syndrome)
formal: A neuronal migration disorder in which a symmetric ribbon of grey matter lies within the white matter beneath an apparently normal cortex, usually in females heterozygous for a DCX variant and less often from mosaic DCX or PAFAH1B1 variants.
simple: A condition, mostly in girls and women, where a second strip of brain cells sits under the normal brain surface, which often causes epilepsy and sometimes learning difficulties.
th: ความผิดปกติจากการเคลื่อนที่ของเซลล์ประสาท ทำให้มีแถบเนื้อเทาซ้อนอยู่ใต้เปลือกสมองที่ดูปกติ คล้ายมีเปลือกสมองสองชั้น พบเกือบทั้งหมดในผู้หญิงที่มียีน DCX ผิดปกติ ทำให้เป็นโรคลมชักและอาจมีสติปัญญาบกพร่องตามความหนาของแถบ
tempoNote: Lifelong structural abnormality; seizures usually start in childhood or adolescence, occasionally in adulthood
feat: Mostly female; intellect ranges from normal to moderately impaired
Epilepsy is present in most and is frequently drug-resistant, including focal and generalised seizure types
Thicker bands and more pachygyria of the overlying cortex predict worse cognition and seizures
Some patients evolve to a Lennox–Gastaut-like picture with drop attacks
Affected mothers can have sons with frank lissencephaly
inv: MRI with thin volumetric T1 and FLAIR: smooth band of grey-matter signal separated from cortex by a thin white-matter layer, often front-predominant
DCX sequencing and deletion analysis (consider low-level mosaic testing in males); PAFAH1B1 if posterior-predominant
EEG and video-EEG to define seizure types

case.who: 19-year-old female university student from Chiang Mai
case.story: She has had monthly convulsions and frequent brief staring spells since age 12 despite trials of three medicines; she studied in a normal school with some extra help.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination; mildly slow processing on bedside cognitive testing.
case.tests: MRI (initially reported normal on 1.5 T): bilateral symmetric bands of grey matter beneath the frontal cortex. Gene testing: heterozygous DCX variant.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and what genetic counselling point matters for her future children?
case.a: Subcortical band heterotopia from DCX; as an X-linked condition, each son has a 50% risk of severe lissencephaly and each daughter a 50% risk of band heterotopia.

det.patho: Doublecortin, encoded on Xq22.3, stabilises microtubules in migrating neurons. In heterozygous females, random X-inactivation means some neurons express only the faulty allele; these neurons stall in the white matter and form the band, while the rest reach the cortex normally. Males with the same germline variant develop anterior-predominant lissencephaly; males with band heterotopia usually carry somatic mosaic DCX or LIS1 variants.
det.clinical: Seizures are the usual reason for presentation, with onset typically in childhood; focal seizures, atypical absences, tonic and atonic attacks can coexist, and drug resistance is common. Cognitive ability is variable and tracks the thickness of the band and any coexisting pachygyria. Mildly affected women may first come to attention when they give birth to a son with lissencephaly. The examination is often normal.
det.diagnosis: High-resolution MRI shows a symmetric, smooth subcortical stripe of grey-matter signal, usually thickest frontally in DCX disease; thin bands are easily overlooked on routine scans. Genetic testing of DCX, including copy number analysis, is positive in most familial and many sporadic female cases, while mosaic testing on deep sequencing of blood or tissue may be needed in males. Differentiate from periventricular nodules, transmantle dysplasia and diffuse pachygyria.
det.treatment: Antiseizure medicines are chosen by seizure type, but many patients remain uncontrolled. Resective surgery generally fails because the epileptic network involves both the band and the overlying cortex; corpus callosotomy can reduce drop attacks, and VNS or dietary therapy are alternatives. Provide X-linked genetic counselling, cognitive assessment and educational support.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is usually normal; the burden is determined by seizure control and cognitive level, which vary widely.
pearls: A woman with drug-resistant epilepsy and a 'normal' MRI deserves a careful look for a thin subcortical band.
Same DCX variant: band in daughters, lissencephaly in sons.
Focal resection rarely works; think palliative surgery or neuromodulation.
det.thd: Subcortical band heterotopia หรือ double cortex คือมีแถบเนื้อเทาอยู่ใต้เปลือกสมองซึ่งดูปกติ พบเกือบทั้งหมดในผู้หญิงที่มียีน DCX ผิดปกติบนโครโมโซม X อาการเด่นคือโรคลมชักซึ่งมักดื้อยา และสติปัญญาแตกต่างกันตามความหนาของแถบ MRI ความละเอียดสูงช่วยวินิจฉัยเพราะแถบบางอาจมองข้ามได้ การรักษาใช้ยากันชัก ส่วนการผ่าตัดตัดจุดชักมักไม่ได้ผล อาจใช้ callosotomy หรือ VNS และต้องให้คำปรึกษาว่าลูกชายเสี่ยง lissencephaly

name: Periventricular nodular heterotopia (PVNH)
formal: A malformation in which nodules of neurons that never left the ventricular zone line the walls of the lateral ventricles, most commonly as bilateral contiguous nodules due to X-linked dominant FLNA variants in females, and otherwise as unilateral or sporadic forms.
simple: Small clumps of brain cells stuck along the walls of the brain's fluid spaces, which commonly cause seizures starting in the teenage years while intelligence is often normal.
th: ก้อนเซลล์ประสาทที่ไม่เคลื่อนออกจากผนังโพรงสมอง เกาะอยู่ตามผนัง lateral ventricle ชนิดสองข้างมักเกิดจากยีน FLNA ในผู้หญิง ทำให้ชักเริ่มในวัยรุ่น สติปัญญามักปกติ และอาจมีโรคหัวใจหลอดเลือดหรือข้อหลวมร่วม
tempoNote: Congenital lesion; seizures typically start in the second decade but may begin at any age, some carriers never have seizures
feat: Focal seizures, often beginning in adolescence, in a person with normal or near-normal intelligence
Bilateral rows of smooth nodules matching grey matter on every MRI sequence, without enhancement or calcification
FLNA cases: female predominance, aortic dilatation or valve disease, patent ductus, joint hypermobility, lung or gut problems
Reading difficulty and subtle processing deficits despite normal IQ
Seizures may arise from nodules, overlying cortex or both together
inv: MRI: nodules isointense to grey matter in all sequences lining the ventricular walls
FLNA testing in bilateral cases; broader gene panel or microarray in atypical or syndromic patterns
Echocardiography (and aortic imaging) in FLNA-related disease
Video-EEG and stereo-EEG if surgery is considered

case.story: Since age 15 she has had episodes of a strange taste and unreality followed by confusion; a recent tonic–clonic seizure led to referral. She was born with a heart murmur.
case.exam: Normal neurology; hypermobile fingers and elbows.
case.tests: MRI: bilateral smooth nodules along the lateral ventricular walls with grey-matter signal. Echo: mildly dilated aortic root. Genetics: heterozygous FLNA truncating variant.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and what non-neurological follow-up is needed?
case.a: FLNA-related periventricular nodular heterotopia; she needs periodic cardiac and aortic surveillance plus genetic counselling, because affected male pregnancies are often lost.

det.patho: Filamin A is an actin-binding protein needed for neurons to detach from the ventricular lining and begin migrating, and for the integrity of the ependymal surface. Loss of function on the X chromosome produces bilateral heterotopia in heterozygous females and is frequently lethal in males in utero. Rarer causes include recessive ARFGEF2 (with microcephaly and severe delay), 5q14.3 and other copy number changes, and nongenetic injuries; unilateral nodules are often sporadic and may coexist with other malformations.
det.clinical: Epilepsy is the main problem and usually begins in the teens with focal seizures that can be temporal or posterior in semiology. Cognition is usually normal, although dyslexia and slow processing are common. FLNA disease is multisystem: patent ductus arteriosus, valvular dysplasia, progressive aortic dilatation, Ehlers–Danlos-like joint laxity, constipation and lung disease can occur. Extensive nodules, unilateral disease with additional cortical malformation, or recessive forms carry greater developmental impairment.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows rounded nodules that match grey matter on every sequence, smoothly lining the ventricles, without the calcification, enhancement or growth that would suggest tuberous sclerosis or tumour. Bilateral contiguous nodules in a woman should prompt FLNA testing; males and atypical patterns warrant broader testing. Evaluate the heart and aorta in confirmed FLNA cases. For drug-resistant epilepsy, stereo-EEG is often needed because the nodule and cortex form a joint network.
det.treatment: Antiseizure medicines control seizures in many patients. For drug-resistant cases, stereo-EEG-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy, radiofrequency thermocoagulation of nodules, or resection that includes connected cortex can be effective in selected patients. Cardiology follows aortic size, and genetic counselling addresses X-linked inheritance and pregnancy loss.
det.prognosis: Many have controllable epilepsy and normal lives; outcome worsens with drug resistance, extensive malformation or major cardiovascular involvement.
pearls: Grey-matter signal nodules lining the ventricles, no calcium, no enhancement: heterotopia, not tuberous sclerosis.
Bilateral PVNH in a woman: think FLNA and image the heart and aorta.
Seizure onset can be in the nodule, the cortex, or both — map before ablating.
det.thd: PVNH คือก้อนเซลล์ประสาทที่ค้างอยู่ตามผนังโพรงสมองเพราะไม่ได้เคลื่อนที่ออกไป ชนิดสองข้างมักเกิดจากยีน FLNA บนโครโมโซม X ในผู้หญิง ทำให้ชักแบบ focal เริ่มในวัยรุ่น สติปัญญามักปกติ อาจมีปัญหาหัวใจ หลอดเลือดแดงใหญ่โป่ง และข้อหลวมร่วม MRI เห็นก้อนสัญญาณเท่าเนื้อเทาโดยไม่มีหินปูนหรือการ enhance ซึ่งต่างจาก tuberous sclerosis รักษาด้วยยากันชัก รายดื้อยาพิจารณา SEEG และ laser ablation

name: Polymicrogyria (PMG)
formal: A malformation of late cortical organisation in which the cortex forms many abnormally small, fused folds, arising from genetic causes or prenatal injury such as congenital cytomegalovirus infection or vascular disruption, with bilateral perisylvian polymicrogyria as the commonest pattern.
simple: A brain surface with too many tiny, crowded folds, which can cause seizures, speech and swallowing problems or weakness depending on where it is.
th: เปลือกสมองที่มีรอยหยักเล็กและถี่ผิดปกติ เกิดจากพันธุกรรมหรือการบาดเจ็บของสมองในครรภ์ เช่น ติดเชื้อ CMV แต่กำเนิด หรือขาดเลือด ชนิดที่พบบ่อยคือบริเวณ perisylvian สองข้าง ทำให้พูดไม่ชัด กลืนลำบาก น้ำลายไหล และชัก

feat: Bilateral perisylvian form: oromotor weakness with drooling, dysarthria, poor tongue movement and feeding difficulty (an opercular syndrome)
Epilepsy in most, sometimes with electrical status epilepticus in sleep
Unilateral PMG: congenital hemiparesis and focal seizures; extensive bilateral PMG: quadriparesis and intellectual disability
Congenital CMV clues: microcephaly, periventricular calcifications, white-matter changes and sensorineural hearing loss
Associated with 22q11.2 deletion and with megalencephaly syndromes (PIK3R2, PIK3CA)
inv: High-resolution MRI (thin T1/T2): irregular, bumpy cortex with stippled grey–white junction; may look falsely thick on low resolution
CT or SWI for calcifications; newborn urine/saliva CMV PCR or dried blood spot PCR when infection is suspected
Microarray and malformation gene panel or exome
EEG including sleep; hearing assessment and speech–swallow evaluation

case.who: 6-year-old girl from Suphan Buri brought by her grandmother
case.story: She drools constantly, speaks only a few unclear words though she understands well, chokes on rice, and recently started having night-time focal seizures.
case.exam: Cannot protrude or move the tongue side to side voluntarily, but yawns and laughs normally; brisk jaw jerk; limbs nearly normal.
case.tests: MRI: bilateral irregular small gyri around both Sylvian fissures. EEG: near-continuous spike-wave in sleep. CMV PCR on stored newborn blood spot: negative; microarray normal.
case.q: What is the syndrome and what does the dissociation between voluntary and emotional facial movement indicate?
case.a: Bilateral perisylvian polymicrogyria; automatic–voluntary dissociation reflects bilateral opercular (cortical) involvement, an anterior opercular (Foix–Chavany–Marie-type) syndrome.

det.patho: Polymicrogyria develops late in neuronal migration and during cortical organisation; the outer cortical layers fuse across sulci, creating many small gyri and an irregular inner border. It can result from germline or mosaic variants (for example GPR56/ADGRG1 in frontoparietal PMG, tubulin genes, PIK3R2 or PIK3CA in megalencephaly syndromes, 22q11.2 deletion), or from destructive insults in the second trimester such as congenital cytomegalovirus, Zika virus, twin–twin transfusion and in-utero arterial ischaemia. The same pathology lines the clefts of schizencephaly.
det.clinical: Presentation depends on extent and location. The bilateral perisylvian syndrome gives pseudobulbar oromotor dysfunction, delayed and unclear speech, swallowing problems and drooling, with automatic–voluntary dissociation of face and tongue movements. Epilepsy affects most patients and may include atypical absences, drop attacks and sleep-activated spike-wave. Unilateral disease resembles hemiplegic cerebral palsy, whereas generalised PMG causes severe intellectual and motor disability. Congenital CMV adds hearing loss, chorioretinitis and microcephaly.
det.diagnosis: Use thin-slice volumetric MRI; on poorer images PMG can be mistaken for pachygyria because fused gyri look thick. Look for calcification and white-matter signal change, which point to CMV, and assess hearing. Genetic testing (microarray, panels, exome; tissue testing for mosaic megalencephaly variants) has rising yield. Congenital CMV is confirmed by PCR on urine or saliva in the first three weeks after birth, or on the newborn dried blood spot afterwards.
det.treatment: Management is supportive: antiseizure medicines (with prompt treatment of sleep-activated status epilepticus), speech and swallowing therapy, augmentative communication, physiotherapy and educational support. Selected patients with unilateral or focal PMG and drug-resistant epilepsy benefit from resection or hemispherotomy. Newborns with symptomatic congenital CMV are treated with oral valganciclovir for 6 months when started within the first month, which modestly improves hearing and developmental outcomes.
det.prognosis: Highly variable, from near-normal function with focal unilateral PMG to severe disability with diffuse involvement; epilepsy control is a major determinant.
pearls: Drooling, dysarthria and inability to move the tongue on command but normal laughter: think bilateral perisylvian PMG.
PMG with periventricular calcification and deafness: congenital CMV until proven otherwise.
Thick-looking cortex on a low-resolution scan may actually be PMG — re-image with thin slices.

name: Schizencephaly
formal: A congenital cleft extending through the full thickness of a cerebral hemisphere from the pial surface to the lateral ventricle, lined by polymicrogyric grey matter, and classified as closed-lip (walls apposed) or open-lip (separated by CSF), unilateral or bilateral.
simple: A split in the brain that runs from the surface to the fluid space inside, present from birth, causing weakness on one or both sides, seizures and developmental problems.
th: รอยแยกแต่กำเนิดในซีกสมองที่ทะลุจากผิวสมองถึงโพรงสมอง โดยขอบรอยแยกบุด้วยเนื้อเทาแบบ polymicrogyria แบ่งเป็นแบบปากปิดและปากเปิด ทำให้อ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกหรือทั้งตัว ชัก และพัฒนาการช้า
tempoNote: Present from birth; severe bilateral forms are recognised in infancy, mild unilateral closed-lip forms may present later with seizures or mild hemiparesis
feat: Unilateral closed-lip cleft: mild contralateral hemiparesis and focal seizures, often near-normal cognition
Bilateral or open-lip clefts: spastic quadriparesis, microcephaly, severe intellectual disability and blindness in some
Absent septum pellucidum and optic nerve hypoplasia in a subset (septo-optic dysplasia spectrum)
Cleft edges lined with irregular grey matter (polymicrogyria), often with a dimple on the ventricular wall
Linked to in-utero vascular disruption, congenital CMV, twin pregnancy and young maternal age
inv: MRI: grey-matter-lined cleft connecting the brain surface to the ventricle; assess septum, optic nerves and contralateral hemisphere
Ophthalmology and endocrine testing if septo-optic dysplasia features are present
CMV testing and COL4A1/COL4A2 or broader genetic testing where suggested
EEG for seizures

case.story: He walks with a limp and uses his left hand less; last month he had a focal seizure with right gaze deviation and left arm jerking.
case.exam: Mild left hemiparesis with brisk reflexes and an upgoing left plantar; head circumference normal; normal vision.
case.tests: MRI: narrow cleft in the right frontal region with grey-matter-lined walls touching each other, extending to the lateral ventricle; septum pellucidum absent.
case.q: Name the lesion and its subtype, and explain why it differs from porencephaly.
case.a: Unilateral closed-lip schizencephaly; the cleft is lined by malformed grey matter, whereas a porencephalic cavity is lined by white matter or gliosis after destruction of formed brain.

read.where: Chapter 9: Congenital Disorders of the Brain and Spine

det.patho: Most schizencephaly is thought to follow a disruptive event during the second trimester, such as focal ischaemia or infection, that destroys part of the germinal matrix and developing hemisphere; the surviving cortex at the edges then organises abnormally into polymicrogyria. Recognised associations include congenital CMV, monochorionic twinning, maternal trauma or substance exposure, young maternal age and COL4A1/COL4A2 variants. Earlier reports of EMX2 mutations have not been consistently confirmed.
det.clinical: The phenotype parallels cleft size and number. Small unilateral closed-lip clefts may cause only mild hemiparesis or late-onset seizures, while large or bilateral open-lip clefts cause severe motor disability, intellectual impairment and microcephaly. Epilepsy is common, especially with unilateral clefts, and may be focal or drug-resistant. Visual and endocrine problems point to associated septo-optic dysplasia.
det.diagnosis: MRI is decisive: identify grey matter lining the cleft walls and continuing to the ventricle, and note whether lips are apposed or separated. A small closed-lip cleft can be missed unless a ventricular dimple is noticed. Look for polymicrogyria elsewhere, absent septum pellucidum and optic hypoplasia. Investigate causes with congenital infection testing in infancy and genetic testing in familial or syndromic cases.
det.treatment: Care is multidisciplinary: physiotherapy, orthoses and spasticity management, antiseizure medicines, developmental and educational support, and vision and hormone assessment when septo-optic dysplasia is present. Drug-resistant unilateral cases may be candidates for resection or hemispherotomy after presurgical evaluation. Shunting is reserved for hydrocephalus or an expanding open-lip cavity.
det.prognosis: Unilateral closed-lip clefts often allow independent walking and near-normal cognition; bilateral open-lip clefts carry severe lifelong disability.
pearls: Cleft lined by grey matter = schizencephaly; cavity lined by white matter = porencephaly.
Always look for an absent septum pellucidum and optic nerve hypoplasia.
Closed-lip clefts can be subtle — a dimple in the ventricular wall is the clue.
det.thd: Schizencephaly คือรอยแยกแต่กำเนิดในซีกสมองที่ทะลุจากผิวสมองถึงโพรงสมอง ขอบบุด้วยเนื้อเทาผิดปกติแบบ polymicrogyria แบ่งเป็นปากปิดและปากเปิด และข้างเดียวหรือสองข้าง เชื่อว่าเกิดจากการขาดเลือดหรือติดเชื้อ เช่น CMV ในไตรมาสที่สอง อาการตั้งแต่อ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกเล็กน้อยและชัก ไปจนถึงเกร็งทั้งตัวและสติปัญญาบกพร่องรุนแรง อาจพบร่วมกับ septo-optic dysplasia วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI รักษาแบบประคับประคอง กายภาพ ยากันชัก และพิจารณาผ่าตัดในรายดื้อยา

name: Porencephaly
formal: A fluid-filled cavity within a cerebral hemisphere that usually communicates with the lateral ventricle and is lined by white matter or gliotic tissue, resulting from destruction of brain tissue by fetal or perinatal haemorrhage or infarction, with familial forms linked to COL4A1 and COL4A2 variants.
simple: A hole filled with fluid inside the brain, usually left by a stroke or bleed before or around birth, which may cause weakness on one side and seizures.
th: โพรงน้ำในเนื้อสมองที่มักต่อกับโพรงสมอง บุด้วยเนื้อขาวหรือแผลเป็น เกิดจากสมองถูกทำลายจากเลือดออกหรือขาดเลือดตั้งแต่ในครรภ์หรือแรกเกิด ทำให้อ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกและชัก ชนิดในครอบครัวสัมพันธ์กับยีน COL4A1/COL4A2
tempoNote: Static lesion formed in late fetal or perinatal life; signs usually evident in the first year, with seizures appearing at any age
feat: Congenital hemiparesis (hemiplegic cerebral palsy) with or without seizures
Cavity lined by white matter or gliosis, without the grey-matter lining of schizencephaly
COL4A1/2 clues: family history, cerebral small vessel disease, intracerebral haemorrhage, cataracts, retinal arterial tortuosity
Systemic COL4A1 features: kidney cysts or haematuria, muscle cramps with raised CK, intracranial aneurysms (HANAC)
Large cysts may expand and cause raised pressure
inv: MRI: smooth-walled CSF cavity lined by gliotic white matter; SWI for haemosiderin and microbleeds; look for leukoencephalopathy
COL4A1/COL4A2 testing in familial, bilateral or haemorrhagic cases or with eye/kidney findings
Thrombophilia and maternal history (e.g. trauma, alloimmune thrombocytopenia) when relevant
Ophthalmology, urinalysis and renal function, and CK in suspected COL4A1 disease

case.story: He has had mild right-sided weakness since infancy and occasional focal seizures. His mother had a lobar haemorrhage at 50 and his younger sister has cataracts.
case.exam: Mild right spastic hemiparesis with a shorter right arm; reduced visual acuity from bilateral lens opacities.
case.tests: MRI: large left fronto-parietal CSF cavity opening into the lateral ventricle, diffuse periventricular white-matter hyperintensities and several microbleeds. Retina: arterial tortuosity. Genetics: COL4A1 missense variant.
case.q: What unifying diagnosis explains the brain, eye and family findings, and what practical advice follows?
case.a: COL4A1-related porencephaly with small vessel disease; avoid anticoagulants and contact sports or head trauma where possible, control blood pressure, and offer family testing; caesarean delivery is often recommended for an affected fetus.

det.patho: When previously normal brain is destroyed in the third trimester or around birth, the developing brain cannot mount a full astrocytic scar, so a smooth cavity forms and often joins the ventricle. Common causes are germinal matrix–intraventricular haemorrhage with periventricular venous infarction in preterm infants and perinatal arterial ischaemic stroke at term. COL4A1 and COL4A2 encode the type IV collagen chains of vascular basement membranes; dominant variants make small vessels fragile, giving familial porencephaly, adult small vessel disease and haemorrhage, eye malformations and kidney or muscle involvement.
det.clinical: Most patients present with hemiparesis noticed in infancy, sometimes with early hand preference, and many develop focal epilepsy. Cognitive effects vary with lesion size and side. In COL4A1/2 disease, the spectrum extends to adult stroke, haemorrhage after minor trauma, migraine, cataract, retinal haemorrhages, aneurysms, haematuria and muscle cramps. Some cysts enlarge and require drainage.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows a CSF-signal cavity with smooth walls of gliotic white matter and no grey-matter lining, distinguishing it from schizencephaly and from arachnoid or parasitic cysts. Haemosiderin suggests a haemorrhagic origin. Genetic testing for COL4A1/COL4A2 is indicated in familial, bilateral or unexplained cases and when white-matter disease, microbleeds or eye and kidney signs coexist. Evaluate other causes of perinatal stroke as clinically appropriate.
det.treatment: Treatment targets the consequences: rehabilitation, spasticity management and antiseizure medicines, with epilepsy surgery or hemispherotomy for selected drug-resistant patients. Expanding cysts or hydrocephalus may need fenestration or shunting. In COL4A1/2 carriers, avoid anticoagulants and antithrombotics when possible, control blood pressure, minimise head trauma and plan delivery with obstetric input.
det.prognosis: The lesion itself is static; outcome depends on motor deficit and seizure control, while COL4A1/2 carriers face lifelong haemorrhagic and ischaemic stroke risk.
pearls: Cavity lined by white matter after brain destruction = porencephaly; grey-matter-lined cleft = schizencephaly.
Porencephaly plus cataracts, retinal vessel tortuosity or family stroke: test COL4A1/COL4A2.
COL4A1 carriers bleed easily — think twice before anticoagulation.
det.thd: Porencephaly คือโพรงน้ำในเนื้อสมองที่เกิดจากสมองถูกทำลายจากเลือดออกหรือขาดเลือดตั้งแต่ปลายการตั้งครรภ์หรือแรกเกิด ผนังบุด้วยเนื้อขาวหรือแผลเป็น ต่างจาก schizencephaly ที่บุด้วยเนื้อเทา อาการมักเป็นอ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกตั้งแต่ทารกและชัก ถ้ามีประวัติครอบครัว ต้อกระจก หลอดเลือดจอตาคดเคี้ยว หรือเลือดออกในสมอง ให้นึกถึงยีน COL4A1/COL4A2 การรักษาเป็นการฟื้นฟู ยากันชัก และในผู้มียีนนี้ควรเลี่ยงยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือดและการกระแทกศีรษะ

name: Focal cortical dysplasia (FCD)
formal: A localised malformation of cortical development with disordered cortical lamination that may also contain dysmorphic neurons and balloon cells, classified by the ILAE into types I, II and III, frequently caused by somatic or germline variants in the mTOR pathway, and among the commonest causes of drug-resistant focal epilepsy amenable to surgery.
simple: A small patch of brain that formed in a disorganised way before birth and is a common cause of seizures that do not respond to medicine but can often be cured by surgery.
th: บริเวณเปลือกสมองที่เจริญผิดรูปแต่กำเนิดเป็นหย่อม ๆ แบ่งตาม ILAE เป็น type I, II, III มักเกิดจากยีนในวิถี mTOR เป็นสาเหตุสำคัญของโรคลมชักชนิด focal ที่ดื้อยาและรักษาหายได้ด้วยการผ่าตัด
tempoNote: Seizures usually start in childhood (often before age 5), sometimes in adolescence or adulthood; frequently frequent, clustered and nocturnal
feat: Drug-resistant focal seizures, often frequent, stereotyped and sleep-related, especially frontal
Can present with epilepsia partialis continua or focal status epilepticus
Type II MRI: cortical thickening, blurred grey–white junction, FLAIR hyperintensity tapering to the ventricle (transmantle sign, typical of IIb)
Type I and small bottom-of-sulcus type II lesions are often MRI-negative or subtle
Interictal EEG may show near-continuous rhythmic focal spiking over the lesion
inv: 3 T epilepsy-protocol MRI (3D T1, 3D FLAIR, thin coronal T2) read by an experienced neuroradiologist; post-processing (morphometric analysis) for subtle lesions
Video-EEG telemetry; FDG-PET, ictal SPECT and MEG to localise MRI-negative cases
Stereo-EEG when non-invasive data are discordant
Genetic testing (germline DEPDC5/NPRL2/NPRL3, TSC) and somatic testing of resected tissue

case.story: Since age 3 she has had up to ten brief nightly seizures in which she abruptly sits up, grimaces and raises her left arm; three antiseizure medicines have failed.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination; mild attention difficulties at school.
case.tests: Video-EEG: right frontal-onset seizures from sleep. Re-read 3 T MRI: small right superior frontal region of cortical thickening with a FLAIR tail to the ventricle.
case.q: What is the likely lesion, and what is the best management now?
case.a: Focal cortical dysplasia type IIb at the bottom of a sulcus; she should undergo presurgical evaluation for complete resection or laser ablation, which offers a high chance of seizure freedom.

read.where: The Epilepsies — Causes of Epilepsy: Cortical Dysplasia

det.patho: FCD arises when progenitor cells in one area of the developing cortex acquire a defect in growth signalling or migration. Type II lesions are mTORopathies: brain-somatic variants in MTOR, PIK3CA, AKT3, RHEB and others, or germline loss in GATOR1 genes (DEPDC5, NPRL2, NPRL3) or TSC1/2 with a second somatic hit, drive overactive mTORC1, giving dysmorphic neurons (IIa) and balloon cells (IIb). Type I shows abnormal radial or tangential layering without dysmorphic neurons, and type III is dysplasia adjacent to another principal lesion (hippocampal sclerosis, tumour, vascular malformation, or early acquired injury). The 2022 ILAE update integrates genetics into an integrated diagnosis and recognises related entities such as mild malformation of cortical development with oligodendroglial hyperplasia (MOGHE).
det.clinical: Seizures often start in early childhood and are frequent, abrupt and stereotyped; frontal lesions cause brief hypermotor or tonic seizures from sleep, and central lesions can cause epilepsia partialis continua. Large or multilobar lesions may present in infancy with epileptic spasms and developmental slowing. Cognitive and behavioural problems often reflect seizure burden and improve after successful surgery. FCD is the most frequent pathology in paediatric epilepsy surgery series and the third most frequent in adults.
det.diagnosis: High-quality 3 T MRI with dedicated sequences is essential, and many 'non-lesional' scans become positive when reviewed by an epilepsy neuroradiologist or with post-processing. Typical type II signs are focal cortical thickening, blurring, T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and a transmantle tail; type I is often invisible or shows only lobar volume loss. Electroclinical data, PET hypometabolism and SPECT help, and stereo-EEG defines the zone when imaging is negative. Histology after resection confirms the type, and somatic genetic testing of tissue is increasingly routine.
det.treatment: Antiseizure medicines rarely achieve lasting control, so patients failing two appropriate drugs should be referred early for surgery. Complete resection of the lesion and associated epileptogenic zone is the strongest predictor of seizure freedom; laser interstitial thermal therapy suits deep or bottom-of-sulcus lesions, and neuromodulation (RNS, DBS, VNS) is used when resection would harm eloquent cortex. mTOR inhibitors are effective in TSC-associated epilepsy and are being studied in other mTORopathies; germline GATOR1 findings change family counselling.
det.prognosis: After complete removal, roughly 60–75% become seizure-free, with best results in MRI-visible type IIb; outcomes are poorer with type I, MRI-negative or incompletely resected lesions.
pearls: A FLAIR tail from cortex to ventricle (transmantle sign) is the signature of FCD type IIb.
Frequent stereotyped nocturnal frontal seizures with a 'normal' MRI: request an expert re-read and post-processing.
FCD IIb and tubers share balloon cells — both are mTOR pathway disorders.
det.thd: Focal cortical dysplasia คือหย่อมเปลือกสมองที่เจริญผิดรูปแต่กำเนิด ILAE แบ่งเป็น type I (เรียงชั้นผิดปกติ), type II (มี dysmorphic neurons และ balloon cells ใน IIb) และ type III (อยู่ข้างรอยโรคอื่น) type II มักเกิดจากยีนในวิถี mTOR ผู้ป่วยมักชักแบบ focal ถี่ ๆ ตอนนอนตั้งแต่เด็กและดื้อยา MRI 3 T ที่อ่านโดยผู้เชี่ยวชาญอาจเห็นเปลือกสมองหนา ขอบเทา-ขาวไม่ชัด และ transmantle sign การผ่าตัดเอารอยโรคออกทั้งหมดหรือ laser ablation ให้โอกาสหายชักสูง ควรส่งประเมินผ่าตัดเร็วเมื่อยาสองตัวไม่ได้ผล

qx.stem: A 14-year-old boy has many brief hypermotor seizures from sleep every night despite three medications. MRI shows a right superior frontal sulcus with a blurred grey–white boundary and a funnel-shaped FLAIR hyperintensity running from the cortex down to the lateral ventricle. Scalp EEG shows near-continuous right frontal rhythmic spikes.
qx.q: Which histology is most likely, and what is the outlook with complete resection?
opts: FCD type IIb with balloon cells; complete resection carries a high chance of seizure freedom
FCD type I; resection rarely helps
Low-grade glioma; radiotherapy is preferred
Cavernous malformation; observation is best
Hippocampal sclerosis; temporal lobectomy is required
qx.why: A transmantle FLAIR sign that tapers toward the ventricle is characteristic of FCD type IIb, which has dysmorphic neurons and balloon cells and is often an mTOR pathway (somatic variant) disorder. Complete resection of a type II lesion visible on MRI gives some of the best seizure outcomes in extratemporal surgery. Type I dysplasia is often invisible on MRI and has worse outcomes.

qx.stem: A 19-year-old woman has drug-resistant seizures with right arm tingling and then jerking. Repeated 3 T MRIs were read as normal, and scalp EEG shows only poorly localized left centroparietal sharp waves. MEG finds a tight cluster of interictal spike dipoles at the depth of the left postcentral sulcus. Re-review of the MRI at that spot shows a subtle bottom-of-sulcus dysplasia.
qx.q: Why was MEG particularly helpful here?
opts: MEG mainly records radially oriented currents on gyral crowns
MEG is mostly sensitive to tangential currents in sulcal walls, and magnetic fields are barely distorted by the skull and scalp
MEG records deep hippocampal activity better than depth electrodes
MEG measures glucose metabolism
MEG works best when recorded during a generalized convulsion
qx.why: MEG detects magnetic fields from currents that run tangentially, such as those in the walls and depths of sulci. Unlike EEG, those fields are not smeared by the skull, so source models can localize them tightly. A focused dipole cluster can guide a second look at the MRI and the placement of SEEG electrodes. MEG is weaker for deep or purely radial sources, and its clinical role is interictal spike localization and functional mapping.

qx.stem: A 19-year-old university student in Khon Kaen has had brief nocturnal seizures with bicycling leg movements and shouting since age 9, up to five a night. Adequate trials of levetiracetam, lacosamide and oxcarbazepine at tolerated doses have failed. A 3-T epilepsy-protocol MRI shows blurring of the grey–white junction at the bottom of a right superior frontal sulcus with a funnel-shaped T2/FLAIR signal tapering towards the ventricle.
qx.q: What should be done next?
opts: Add a fourth and fifth antiseizure medication before further work-up
Refer to a comprehensive epilepsy centre for presurgical evaluation
Diagnose psychogenic non-epileptic seizures because consciousness seems preserved
Start a ketogenic diet as the definitive long-term treatment
Offer vagus nerve stimulation as first choice
qx.why: Failure of two appropriately chosen and tolerated drugs defines drug-resistant epilepsy (ILAE), and the 'transmantle sign' points to FCD type IIb, an mTOR-pathway lesion with high seizure-freedom rates after complete resection. Presurgical evaluation (video-EEG, PET, MEG or SEEG as needed) should not be delayed. Further drug trials rarely give seizure freedom, hypermotor frontal seizures are often misdiagnosed as psychogenic, and VNS is palliative rather than curative.

name: Hypothalamic hamartoma with gelastic seizures
formal: A congenital, non-neoplastic mass of disorganised neurons and glia attached to the hypothalamus near the tuber cinereum and mammillary bodies, which, when intrahypothalamic, is intrinsically epileptogenic and causes gelastic seizures, and, when pedunculated, more often causes central precocious puberty.
simple: A harmless-growing lump of brain tissue at the base of the brain that causes spells of unnatural laughing from infancy and sometimes very early puberty.
th: ก้อนเนื้อสมองที่ไม่ใช่มะเร็งติดกับ hypothalamus มาแต่กำเนิด ถ้าฝังอยู่ใน hypothalamus จะเป็นจุดกำเนิดชักแบบหัวเราะ (gelastic seizures) ตั้งแต่ทารก ถ้าเป็นก้อนห้อยมักทำให้เข้าสู่วัยรุ่นก่อนวัย

case.story: Since he was a few months old he has had several daily episodes of sudden, forced giggling lasting 10–20 seconds with a frightened look; now he also has drop attacks and aggressive outbursts.
case.exam: Pubic hair and enlarged penis for age; otherwise non-focal.
case.tests: Scalp EEG during an episode: nonspecific; MRI: 1 cm sessile, non-enhancing mass arising from the third ventricular floor, isointense to grey matter. LH elevated.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and what treatment offers the best chance of seizure control?
case.a: Hypothalamic hamartoma with gelastic epilepsy and central precocious puberty; minimally invasive ablation (MRI-guided laser therapy or stereotactic thermocoagulation) or disconnection by a specialist team, plus GnRH agonist for puberty.

det.patho: Hypothalamic hamartomas are developmental malformations made of small clusters of GABAergic interneurons and larger pyramidal-like neurons that fire spontaneously, making the lesion itself the seizure generator. Seizures then propagate via the mammillothalamic tract and cingulate networks, producing other seizure types and secondary epileptogenesis. Most cases are sporadic; somatic GLI3 and other Sonic hedgehog pathway variants are common, and germline GLI3 variants cause Pallister–Hall syndrome. Lesions contain GnRH-secreting neurons, which explains precocious puberty.
det.clinical: Gelastic seizures are short laughing attacks without true merriment, sometimes with a pressure-to-laugh aura, recurring many times daily from infancy and frequently mistaken for normal infant laughter or colic. Over childhood many develop focal impaired-awareness, tonic, atonic and generalised seizures, resembling Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, alongside cognitive decline, aggression and psychiatric comorbidity — a picture of epileptic encephalopathy. Larger sessile lesions carry the worst epilepsy, whereas small pedunculated lesions may cause only precocious puberty.
det.diagnosis: Suspect the diagnosis in any child with stereotyped laughing or crying spells. Scalp EEG is often normal or falsely localising, and depth recordings from the hamartoma show the true onset. MRI shows a non-enhancing lesion of grey-matter signal that does not grow, unlike glioma or craniopharyngioma; thin-slice imaging is needed to detect small lesions. Classify attachment (intrahypothalamic versus pedunculated) to guide treatment and check pubertal hormones.
det.treatment: Antiseizure medicines seldom control gelastic seizures. Current practice favours minimally invasive approaches: MRI-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy or stereotactic radiofrequency thermocoagulation achieve freedom from gelastic seizures in a large majority with fewer complications than open resection; endoscopic disconnection and stereotactic radiosurgery (with delayed effect) are alternatives. Risks include transient hyperphagia, weight gain, sodium disturbance and memory impairment. GnRH agonists treat precocious puberty, and early epilepsy treatment can halt or reverse behavioural decline.
det.prognosis: Untreated, severe forms progress to an epileptic encephalopathy; successful early ablation often improves seizures, behaviour and cognition.
pearls: Laughing spells since infancy plus early puberty: MRI the hypothalamus.
Scalp EEG lies in HH — the hamartoma itself generates the seizures.
Laser ablation has largely replaced open surgery for intrahypothalamic hamartomas.

name: Microcephaly (primary and secondary)
formal: A head circumference lying over 2 SD under the mean for age, sex and gestation (severe if below −3 SD), divided into primary (congenital, present at birth, from reduced neuron production) and secondary (postnatal, from later loss or failed growth), with congenital infections such as cytomegalovirus and Zika virus among important acquired causes.
simple: A head that is much smaller than expected because the brain has not grown properly, either from before birth or after, often with developmental delay.
th: ศีรษะเล็กกว่าค่าเฉลี่ยมากกว่า 2 SD แบ่งเป็นชนิดปฐมภูมิ (เป็นตั้งแต่เกิด จากการสร้างเซลล์ประสาทน้อย) และทุติยภูมิ (ศีรษะโตช้าลงหลังเกิด) สาเหตุมีทั้งพันธุกรรม การติดเชื้อในครรภ์ เช่น CMV และ Zika แอลกอฮอล์ และการขาดออกซิเจน
tempoNote: Primary: small head already at birth and growing in parallel below the curve; secondary: normal birth OFC with falling centiles over months to years
feat: Head circumference below −2 SD, with sloping forehead in severe congenital forms
Developmental delay or intellectual disability (more likely with severe microcephaly), seizures and spasticity in many
Congenital Zika: severe microcephaly with collapsed skull and redundant scalp, subcortical calcifications, arthrogryposis and eye lesions
Congenital CMV: periventricular calcifications, polymicrogyria, sensorineural hearing loss, petechiae and hepatosplenomegaly
Falling head centiles after birth suggest Rett, Angelman, hypoxic–ischaemic injury, metabolic disease or malnutrition
inv: Accurate serial OFC plotted on appropriate charts (WHO/INTERGROWTH-21st), with parental head sizes
MRI brain (CT for calcification if needed): simplified gyri, malformations, injury pattern
Congenital infection testing: CMV PCR on urine/saliva (first 3 weeks) or newborn blood spot; Zika serology/PCR with travel or regional exposure; toxoplasma and rubella as indicated
Microarray and exome; metabolic screen (e.g. maternal PKU, serine, glucose transporter) and hearing and eye tests

case.who: Newborn girl at a provincial hospital in Ratchaburi
case.story: Antenatal ultrasound at 32 weeks showed a small head; the mother recalls a fever with rash and red eyes in the first trimester during a local mosquito-borne outbreak.
case.exam: OFC −4 SD with overlapping sutures and excess scalp folds; hypertonia, clenched fists and stiff knees.
case.tests: CT: scattered subcortical calcifications, ventriculomegaly and simplified gyri. Zika IgM positive in infant and mother; CMV PCR negative.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis, and what follow-up does the infant need?
case.a: Congenital Zika syndrome with severe primary microcephaly; she needs long-term neurodevelopmental, seizure, swallowing, eye and hearing follow-up and family support.

read.where: Chapter 21 The Skin and Neurologic Disease

det.patho: Brain size is set mainly by the number of neural progenitor divisions in early gestation. Primary (congenital) microcephaly results from too few neurons produced: autosomal recessive MCPH genes such as ASPM, WDR62 and CDK5RAP2 affect the mitotic spindle and centrosome, while Zika virus and CMV kill or disrupt progenitor cells; fetal alcohol, maternal PKU and severe placental insufficiency also act early. Secondary (postnatal) microcephaly reflects later failure of growth or loss of tissue, from hypoxic–ischaemic injury, postnatal infection, genetic encephalopathies (Rett, Angelman), metabolic disorders or malnutrition. Usage varies: some authors use primary for intrinsic genetic causes regardless of timing.
det.clinical: Genetic primary microcephaly (MCPH) often gives a small but structurally simple brain with mild-to-moderate intellectual disability and few motor signs. Infectious and destructive causes produce more severe disability, epilepsy, spasticity, swallowing problems, visual and hearing loss. Congenital Zika syndrome shows severe microcephaly with skull collapse, calcifications at the grey–white junction, contractures and macular scarring; congenital CMV is the leading infectious cause of sensorineural hearing loss and can coexist with polymicrogyria. Measuring parents' heads helps recognise benign familial microcephaly.
det.diagnosis: Measure OFC accurately and repeatedly, correct for gestation, and interpret it with length, weight and parental heads. MRI distinguishes malformations, simplified gyral pattern and injury. Diagnose congenital CMV by PCR of urine or saliva within the first three weeks (after that, the newborn dried blood spot is needed to prove congenital timing), and test for Zika where exposure is plausible, as transmission has occurred in Thailand. Genetic testing (microarray, exome or genome) has high yield in unexplained cases; add metabolic tests when development regresses or other organs are involved.
det.treatment: There is no treatment that restores brain growth; care focuses on seizures, feeding and nutrition, spasticity, vision, hearing and early intervention therapies. Symptomatic congenital CMV detected in the first month is treated with valganciclovir for 6 months. Prevention includes mosquito avoidance and condoms for pregnant women in Zika-affected areas, hygiene measures to reduce CMV acquisition in pregnancy, rubella vaccination and avoidance of alcohol. Provide genetic counselling for recessive causes, where recurrence risk is 25%.
det.prognosis: Outcome ranges from near-normal in familial or mild genetic forms to profound disability and shortened life in severe infectious or destructive microcephaly.
pearls: Always measure the parents' heads before labelling a child microcephalic.
A head that was normal at birth and then falls behind points to an acquired or progressive postnatal process.
Periventricular calcification suggests CMV; subcortical calcification with skull collapse suggests Zika.
det.thd: Microcephaly คือศีรษะเล็กกว่าค่าเฉลี่ยมากกว่า 2 SD ชนิดปฐมภูมิเป็นตั้งแต่เกิดจากเซลล์ประสาทถูกสร้างน้อย เช่น ยีน MCPH หรือติดเชื้อ Zika และ CMV ในครรภ์ ส่วนชนิดทุติยภูมิศีรษะปกติตอนเกิดแล้วโตช้าลง เช่น HIE, Rett, Angelman หรือโรคเมตาบอลิก ควรวัดรอบศีรษะซ้ำและวัดของพ่อแม่ ตรวจ MRI ตรวจ CMV PCR ในปัสสาวะหรือน้ำลายภายใน 3 สัปดาห์แรก และตรวจพันธุกรรม การรักษาเป็นการดูแลชัก การกิน การได้ยิน การมองเห็น และกระตุ้นพัฒนาการ ทารก CMV มีอาการให้ valganciclovir

name: Williams syndrome (Williams–Beuren syndrome)
formal: A multisystem disorder caused by a heterozygous 1.5–1.8 Mb microdeletion at 7q11.23 that includes the elastin gene, producing elastin arteriopathy (supravalvular aortic stenosis and other arterial stenoses, including cerebral arteries), characteristic facies, mild-to-moderate intellectual disability with a highly sociable personality and visuospatial weakness, and infantile hypercalcaemia.
simple: A genetic condition from a small missing piece of chromosome 7 that causes narrowed arteries, a friendly chatty personality, learning difficulty and a typical facial appearance.
th: กลุ่มอาการทางพันธุกรรมจากการขาดหายของโครโมโซม 7q11.23 ซึ่งรวมยีน elastin ทำให้หลอดเลือดแดงตีบหลายตำแหน่ง รวมถึงหลอดเลือดสมองซึ่งเสี่ยง stroke ในเด็ก มีใบหน้าลักษณะเฉพาะ สติปัญญาบกพร่องเล็กน้อยถึงปานกลาง เป็นมิตรช่างพูดมาก และแคลเซียมในเลือดสูงในวัยทารก
tempoNote: Features evolve from infancy (feeding difficulty, hypercalcaemia, murmur) through childhood (learning profile) to adulthood (hypertension, diabetes); strokes can occur at any age
feat: Broad forehead, periorbital fullness, stellate iris, short upturned nose, long philtrum and wide mouth with full lips
Supravalvular aortic stenosis, peripheral pulmonary stenosis, renal artery stenosis and early hypertension
Intracranial arteriopathy (ICA/MCA stenosis, moyamoya pattern) causing childhood ischaemic stroke
Overfriendly, socially disinhibited personality with anxiety, ADHD, hyperacusis and strong expressive language but poor visuospatial skills
Infantile hypercalcaemia, hypothyroidism, early diabetes and joint contractures
inv: Chromosomal microarray (or FISH for ELN) to confirm the 7q11.23 deletion
Echocardiography, blood pressure monitoring and renal artery imaging
Serum and urine calcium, thyroid function, glucose tolerance in adults
MRI/MRA of brain and neck vessels for any focal deficit or TIA-like episode

case.who: 8-year-old girl from Bangkok with a heart murmur since infancy
case.story: She is talkative and friendly with strangers but struggles with drawing and puzzles. This morning she suddenly developed right arm weakness and difficulty finding words.
case.exam: BP 135/90; systolic ejection murmur at the upper right sternal border; right arm weakness and expressive dysphasia; typical facial features.
case.tests: MRI: acute left MCA cortical infarct; MRA: tight left supraclinoid ICA stenosis. Echo: supravalvular aortic stenosis. Microarray: 7q11.23 deletion.
case.q: What links her stroke, murmur and personality, and what anaesthetic precaution is crucial?
case.a: Williams syndrome with elastin arteriopathy affecting the aorta and cerebral arteries; general anaesthesia and sedation carry a risk of sudden cardiac arrest from coronary and outflow involvement, so they require cardiac assessment and an experienced team.

det.patho: The recurrent deletion arises from unequal crossing-over between low-copy repeats flanking 7q11.23 and removes about 25–27 genes. Elastin haploinsufficiency causes smooth-muscle overgrowth and thickened walls in large and medium arteries, leading to fixed stenoses of the aorta, pulmonary, renal, coronary and cerebral arteries. Loss of genes such as GTF2I and LIMK1 is linked to the distinctive social and visuospatial profile. Most cases are de novo, and an affected person has a 50% chance of passing it on.
det.clinical: Infants often have feeding difficulty, irritability, constipation, colic and sometimes hypercalcaemia. The cognitive profile combines mild-to-moderate intellectual disability with good expressive language and very weak visuospatial construction, alongside excessive friendliness, anxiety, phobias and attention problems. Cardiovascular disease dominates morbidity: supravalvular aortic stenosis, pulmonary stenoses, hypertension and mid-aortic narrowing. Cerebral arteriopathy can cause ischaemic stroke, TIA or moyamoya-like collaterals, and sudden death may occur during anaesthesia or sedation. Adults develop diabetes, obesity, hearing loss and early ageing changes.
det.diagnosis: The facial and behavioural gestalt with supravalvular aortic stenosis suggests the diagnosis, confirmed by chromosomal microarray, which also defines deletion size. Baseline evaluation includes echocardiography, four-limb blood pressure, renal ultrasound, calcium, thyroid and hearing tests. Neurovascular imaging with MRA or CTA is indicated for any neurological event, and some centres screen asymptomatic children. Isolated SVAS from a point mutation in ELN lacks the cognitive and facial features.
det.treatment: Management follows published health-supervision guidelines: cardiology follow-up with surgical repair or catheter treatment of significant stenoses, antihypertensive therapy, avoidance of extra calcium and vitamin D in hypercalcaemia, and endocrine screening. Children with cerebral arteriopathy and stroke receive acute stroke care, antiplatelet therapy and revascularisation for moyamoya-type disease in selected cases. Plan any sedation or anaesthesia in a centre familiar with the risks. Behavioural therapy, anxiety treatment and educational support tailored to verbal strengths are important.
det.prognosis: Many live into adulthood with support; cardiovascular complications and sudden death related to arterial stenosis or anaesthesia account for most early mortality.
pearls: Murmur plus friendly, chatty child plus poor drawing: think Williams and check for SVAS.
Stroke in a child with Williams syndrome reflects elastin arteriopathy of intracranial vessels.
Sedation and general anaesthesia are high-risk events in Williams syndrome.
det.thd: Williams syndrome เกิดจากการขาดหายของโครโมโซม 7q11.23 ซึ่งรวมยีน elastin ทำให้ผนังหลอดเลือดแดงหนาและตีบ เช่น supravalvular aortic stenosis หลอดเลือดไต และหลอดเลือดสมองซึ่งทำให้เกิด stroke หรือภาพแบบ moyamoya ได้ในเด็ก เด็กมีใบหน้าเฉพาะ เป็นมิตรช่างพูดมาก แต่ทักษะมิติสัมพันธ์ไม่ดี สติปัญญาบกพร่องเล็กน้อยถึงปานกลาง และอาจมีแคลเซียมสูงในวัยทารก วินิจฉัยด้วย microarray ดูแลโดยติดตามหัวใจ ความดัน แคลเซียม และระวังมากเมื่อดมยาสลบ
