name: Prader–Willi syndrome (PWS)
formal: An imprinting disorder caused by loss of expression of paternally inherited genes in the 15q11.2–q13 region (paternal deletion, maternal uniparental disomy or an imprinting defect), characterised by severe neonatal hypotonia and poor feeding followed by hyperphagia and obesity, hypothalamic endocrine dysfunction, mild intellectual disability and a distinctive behavioural profile.
simple: A genetic condition in which babies are very floppy and feed poorly, but as children develop an extreme, constant hunger, along with short height, delayed puberty and learning and behaviour problems.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมจากการขาดการแสดงออกของยีนจากพ่อบนโครโมโซม 15q11–q13 ทารกปวกเปียกมากและดูดนมไม่ดี ต่อมาอยากอาหารตลอดเวลาจนอ้วน ตัวเตี้ย ฮอร์โมนเพศต่ำ สติปัญญาบกพร่องเล็กน้อย และมีปัญหาพฤติกรรม
tempoNote: Hypotonia and failure to thrive in infancy; hyperphagia emerges around 2–8 years and persists for life; psychiatric problems may appear in adolescence and adulthood
feat: Severe neonatal hypotonia with weak suck needing tube feeding, then catch-up and insatiable hunger with food seeking
Short stature, small hands and feet, almond-shaped eyes, hypopigmentation and hypogonadism (undescended testes)
Mild-to-moderate intellectual disability, temper outbursts, skin picking, rigidity and obsessive traits
Sleep-disordered breathing, excessive daytime sleepiness, high pain threshold and temperature instability
Scoliosis, growth hormone deficiency, and psychosis particularly in the uniparental disomy subtype
inv: DNA methylation analysis of 15q11.2 (SNRPN region): detects more than 99% of cases
Microarray/FISH and UPD studies to define the subtype for counselling
Polysomnography before and during growth hormone treatment; endocrine tests (GH, thyroid, sex hormones, glucose)
Spine radiographs for scoliosis

case.who: 6-week-old boy in the neonatal ward of a regional hospital in Nakhon Ratchasima
case.story: Born after reduced fetal movements, he has been floppy and too weak to breastfeed, requiring nasogastric feeding; he rarely cries.
case.exam: Profound axial and limb hypotonia with preserved reflexes, alert face, almond-shaped eyes, small genitalia with undescended testes, no fasciculations.
case.tests: CK normal; SMN1 testing negative; 15q11.2 methylation shows only the maternal pattern; microarray: paternal 15q11–q13 deletion.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and what problem must the family prepare for in the coming years?
case.a: Prader–Willi syndrome (paternal deletion); hyperphagia with life-threatening obesity will emerge in early childhood, so strict food security, early growth hormone therapy and multidisciplinary follow-up are needed.

read.where: Section II: Epidemiology, Etiology, and Diagnosis

det.patho: Genes in 15q11.2–q13 are imprinted: several, including SNORD116 and SNRPN/MAGEL2/NDN, are normally expressed only from the paternal chromosome. PWS results from a paternal deletion (about 65–75%), maternal uniparental disomy (about 20–30%) or an imprinting centre defect (1–3%). Loss of these genes disrupts hypothalamic function, causing defective satiety, growth hormone and gonadotropin deficiency, autonomic and thermoregulatory problems and abnormal sleep regulation. Angelman syndrome is the reciprocal disorder of maternal loss in the same region.
det.clinical: Infants are profoundly hypotonic with a poor suck and little crying, and often need tube feeding; reflexes and alertness are preserved. Through early childhood appetite increases until hyperphagia dominates, with food foraging and rapid obesity unless the environment is controlled. Children have short stature, delayed puberty, mild intellectual disability, speech articulation problems, temper outbursts, skin picking and compulsive behaviours. Adults risk obesity-related diabetes, sleep apnoea, heart failure, choking and gastric rupture after binges, and psychosis, especially with maternal UPD.
det.diagnosis: Methylation-specific testing of the 15q11.2 imprinting region is the first and most sensitive test and should be considered in any markedly hypotonic newborn without another explanation. Further studies determine whether the cause is deletion, UPD or imprinting defect, which matters for recurrence risk. Distinguish from neuromuscular causes of neonatal hypotonia (SMA, congenital myotonic dystrophy, congenital myopathies) and from other obesity syndromes.
det.treatment: Early diagnosis allows feeding support in infancy and anticipatory control of food access later, with family education and locked food storage. Recombinant growth hormone, started in infancy, improves muscle tone, body composition, height and development; screen for obstructive sleep apnoea before and during therapy. Sex hormone replacement, thyroid and adrenal assessment, scoliosis care and behavioural or psychiatric treatment (often SSRIs for compulsions) are standard. In 2025 the FDA approved extended-release diazoxide choline to reduce hyperphagia in people aged 4 years and older with PWS.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy has improved with early diagnosis and growth hormone, but obesity complications, respiratory problems, choking and gastric events still cause premature death.
pearls: Floppy alert newborn with preserved reflexes and a weak suck: send a 15q11.2 methylation test.
Same region, different parent: paternal loss = Prader–Willi, maternal loss = Angelman.
Never assume a person with PWS will stop eating when full — the satiety signal is missing.

name: Achondroplasia — neurological complications
formal: Neurological complications of achondroplasia, the commonest skeletal dysplasia caused by gain-of-function FGFR3 variants, including foramen magnum stenosis with cervicomedullary compression and central apnoea in infancy, ventriculomegaly or hydrocephalus from venous outflow obstruction, and lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication in later life.

case.story: She has not yet sat unsupported, and her mother notices pauses in breathing during sleep and that she uses her right hand far less than her left.
case.exam: Macrocephaly; generalised hypotonia but brisk reflexes with sustained ankle clonus; mild right-sided weakness.
case.tests: MRI: severe foramen magnum narrowing compressing the cervicomedullary junction with T2 cord signal change; moderate ventriculomegaly. Polysomnography: central apnoeas.
case.q: What is the cause of her findings, and what is the treatment?
case.a: Foramen magnum stenosis with cervicomedullary compression; she needs urgent neurosurgical foramen magnum decompression to prevent sudden death and further cord injury.

read.where: Chapter 9: Congenital Disorders of the Brain and Spine
18. Disorders of Cranial Volume and Shape

det.patho: About 80% of achondroplasia arises de novo, usually from the recurrent FGFR3 c.1138G>A (p.Gly380Arg) variant, which constitutively activates a negative regulator of endochondral bone growth; transmission is autosomal dominant, and new variants become more likely as the father's age rises. Bones formed by endochondral ossification grow short, including the skull base: the foramen magnum is small and the jugular foramina narrowed. This causes cervicomedullary compression in infancy, venous outflow obstruction that enlarges ventricles, and a narrow spinal canal with short pedicles that predisposes to stenosis at all levels.
det.clinical: Infants have rhizomelic limb shortening, macrocephaly with frontal bossing and midface hypoplasia, and delayed motor milestones are expected. Red flags for cervicomedullary compression are central apnoea, feeding or swallowing problems, persistent hypotonia beyond what is typical, asymmetric weakness, hyperreflexia and clonus; it is a recognised cause of sudden infant death. Ventriculomegaly is common but usually non-progressive. In adulthood, lumbar stenosis causes walking-limited leg pain, numbness and weakness, sometimes acute cord or cauda equina syndromes; a thoracolumbar gibbus may worsen compression.
det.diagnosis: Current international consensus recommends routine MRI of the craniocervical junction and sleep studies in infancy, with neurological examination at every visit, and urgent imaging for red flags. Grading systems for foramen magnum stenosis use cord compression and signal change to guide surgery. Track head growth on condition-specific charts and image ventricles if growth accelerates or raised pressure features appear. For adult claudication, MRI defines the level and extent of stenosis, which is often multilevel.
det.treatment: Symptomatic or severe foramen magnum stenosis is treated by suboccipital decompression, which reduces morbidity and death; mild asymptomatic narrowing is followed closely. Progressive hydrocephalus needs a shunt or endoscopic procedure, though most ventriculomegaly needs only observation. Symptomatic lumbar stenosis is treated with wide multilevel decompression, often with fusion when kyphosis is present. Vosoritide, a daily subcutaneous C-type natriuretic peptide analogue, increases growth velocity in children with open growth plates; its effect on foramen magnum size and neurological outcomes is under study, and other FGFR3-targeted drugs such as infigratinib are in late-phase trials.
det.prognosis: Intelligence is normal and life expectancy is near normal after infancy, but craniocervical compression contributes to excess infant mortality and spinal stenosis is the leading source of disability in adult life.
pearls: Every baby with achondroplasia needs a craniocervical MRI and sleep study, even without symptoms.
Clonus, asymmetric weakness or central apnoea in an achondroplastic infant means cervicomedullary compression until shown otherwise.
Big head and big ventricles are common and usually benign — act on progression or raised pressure signs.

name: Epilepsy of infancy with migrating focal seizures (EIMFS)
formal: A developmental and epileptic encephalopathy starting in the first months of life in which near-continuous focal seizures wander from one hemisphere or region to another, most often caused by a de novo gain-of-function KCNT1 variant.
simple: A severe epilepsy of young babies where seizures keep jumping from one side of the brain to the other and development stalls.
ab: Epilepsy of infancy with migrating focal seizures

tempoNote: Starts between the first week and about 6 months of life in a previously normal baby; within weeks the seizures cluster into near-continuous runs, then partly ease in survivors after infancy
feat: Focal motor seizures (head or eye turning, limb clonus) with autonomic features such as flushing, apnoea or drooling
Successive seizures arise in different areas and may hop to the opposite hemisphere while one is still going on
Rapid clustering into daily runs that resist ordinary antiseizure drugs
Loss of skills, axial hypotonia, acquired microcephaly and later movement disorder
De novo KCNT1 variant in about half; SCN2A, SCN1A, SLC12A5 and others in the rest

case.who: 2-month-old girl born at term in Khon Kaen
case.story: She was feeding and smiling normally until six weeks, then began having episodes of eye deviation with one arm jerking and her face going red; now there are dozens a day and she no longer tracks faces.
case.exam: Floppy trunk, poor visual fixation, head circumference has dropped from the 50th to the 10th centile.
case.tests: Video-EEG captures seizures arising from the left temporal region, then the right frontal region, some overlapping; MRI normal; trio exome finds a de novo KCNT1 missense variant.
case.q: What is the syndrome, and why does the gene result matter?
case.a: EIMFS, the migrating focal seizure syndrome of infancy; a KCNT1 gain-of-function variant prompts trials of precision options such as quinidine (variable benefit) alongside potassium bromide, the ketogenic diet or other agents.

read.where: Seizures and Epilepsy in Early Life — Migrating Partial Seizures of Infancy
Chapter 26 Infantile Epileptic Encephalopathies and De Novo Mutations — Epilepsy of Infancy With Migrating Focal Seizures

det.patho: Most cases come from de novo heterozygous KCNT1 variants that raise the activity of a sodium-activated potassium channel; excess potassium current is thought to silence inhibitory interneurons more than excitatory cells, leaving cortex hyperexcitable. Other implicated genes include SCN2A, SCN1A, SCN8A, SLC12A5, TBC1D24, PLCB1 and QARS, reflecting a phenotype rather than a single disease. Brain structure is usually normal at onset, and later atrophy reflects ongoing seizures and the genetic disorder itself. It is rare, but probably under-recognised where long EEG monitoring is scarce.
det.clinical: A baby who has been developing well starts having brief focal motor seizures, often with eye or head version, limb jerking and autonomic change such as flushing, apnoea or pallor. Over days to weeks the seizures multiply into clusters or near-continuous activity, with each seizure starting in a different place. Development stops and regresses, tone becomes poor, head growth slows, and a hyperkinetic or dystonic movement disorder may appear later. Many infants need intensive care for apnoea or status, and early deaths occur from respiratory complications.
det.diagnosis: The ILAE 2022 criteria require onset under 12 months (usually in the first six), focal seizures that migrate between hemispheres or regions on EEG, and developmental slowing. Capturing several seizures on prolonged video-EEG is essential, because a short routine record may just look multifocal. Genetic testing should be sent early; metabolic causes and a pyridoxine or pyridoxal-phosphate trial are addressed in parallel. Distinguish it from EIDEE (suppression-burst background), infantile epileptic spasms syndrome, Dravet syndrome and structural lesions.
det.treatment: Seizures are usually resistant to standard agents. Potassium bromide, stiripentol, clonazepam or other benzodiazepines, levetiracetam, phenobarbital, cannabidiol and the ketogenic diet have each helped some children. Quinidine, which blocks the KCNT1 channel, gives inconsistent results, needs ECG monitoring for QT prolongation, and is limited by poor brain penetration; newer KCNT1-targeted treatments and antisense approaches are in trials. Supportive care covers feeding, airway protection, physiotherapy and family counselling, including discussion of goals of care.
det.prognosis: Developmental outcome is usually severe; seizures may become less frequent after infancy, but early mortality is substantial.
pearls: Seizures that wander from one hemisphere to the other in a young infant: think EIMFS and send KCNT1.
A single short EEG can miss migration; record long enough to catch several events.
Quinidine for KCNT1 is a cautious trial with ECG monitoring, not a reliable cure.

name: Myoclonic epilepsy in infancy (MEI)
formal: A self-limited generalised epilepsy of infants and toddlers with otherwise normal development, characterised by brief myoclonic jerks of the head and arms that coincide with generalised spike- or polyspike-wave discharges, sometimes triggered by touch or sudden noise.
simple: A mild epilepsy of babies and toddlers who make quick head-nodding or arm-jerking movements, which usually goes away with treatment and time.

Awareness kept; jerks are more frequent on drowsiness and early sleep
Reflex form triggered by unexpected noise or touch, occasionally by light
Development normal before onset; no other seizure types apart from occasional febrile seizures
Responds well to valproate or levetiracetam

Sleep recording (jerks and discharges increase in drowsiness and light sleep); test touch and sound in the reflex type

case.story: His mother films him nodding his head sharply and flinging both arms out several times a day, mainly when he is sleepy in the stroller; loud claps sometimes provoke the same movement.
case.exam: Sits, crawls and babbles normally; no neurological deficit.
case.tests: Video-EEG: each nod corresponds to a 1-second burst of generalised polyspike-wave; background and sleep architecture normal; MRI not needed after normal development is confirmed.
case.q: How does this differ from infantile spasms and from benign myoclonus of infancy?
case.a: This is myoclonic epilepsy in infancy: unlike West syndrome there are no clustered spasms, no hypsarrhythmia and no regression; unlike benign myoclonus of infancy the EEG shows discharges with each jerk. Valproate or levetiracetam is used.

read.where: Seizures and Epilepsy in Early Life — Myoclonic Epilepsy in Infancy (MEI)

det.patho: MEI is regarded as an early-life genetic generalised epilepsy, probably with polygenic inheritance; relatives with epilepsy or febrile seizures are frequent, and rare monogenic cases are reported. It is uncommon, accounting for a small fraction of epilepsy starting before age three. Neuroimaging is normal, and discharges arise from thalamocortical networks as in other generalised epilepsies.
det.clinical: An infant or toddler with normal development develops very short jerks that mainly involve the head and upper limbs, so parents describe a nod, a blink with upward gaze or a startle-like fling of the arms. Jerks may come singly or in brief runs, often around falling asleep, and do not cause loss of awareness. In the reflex subtype, sudden sounds or touch provoke them, and these children tend to do especially well. Developmental regression or additional seizure types should prompt a search for another syndrome.
det.diagnosis: Video-EEG with surface EMG is the key test: each jerk corresponds to a generalised spike- or polyspike-wave discharge lasting a second or so, while the background stays normal. Interictal records may be normal while awake, so sleep should be included. The main differentials are infantile epileptic spasms syndrome, non-epileptic benign myoclonus of infancy, Dravet syndrome (fever sensitivity and long seizures), and early Doose syndrome; atypical features warrant MRI and genetic testing. ILAE 2022 groups MEI with the self-limited syndromes of infancy.
det.treatment: Valproate is the traditional first choice and usually controls the jerks; levetiracetam is a reasonable alternative, particularly in girls where long-term valproate is undesirable. Clonazepam can be added if needed. Sodium channel blockers such as carbamazepine may worsen myoclonus and are avoided. Treatment is generally continued for one to two years of freedom from jerks and then withdrawn.
det.prognosis: Seizures remit in most children; a minority later have mild learning or attention difficulties, and occasional generalised tonic-clonic seizures can appear in later childhood.
pearls: Head nods in a normally developing toddler with a polyspike on each nod = MEI, not West syndrome.
Benign myoclonus of infancy looks similar but has a normal EEG during the events.
Ask whether noises or touch trigger the jerks — the reflex subtype has an excellent outlook.

name: Self-limited infantile epilepsy (SeLIE)
formal: A self-limited focal epilepsy that starts before age two in developmentally normal infants, with clusters of brief focal seizures, a normal interictal EEG and remission within months; familial cases are usually caused by heterozygous PRRT2 variants.
simple: A harmless-in-the-long-run epilepsy of babies who have short bunches of seizures over a day or two and then grow out of it.

Her father had similar seizures as a baby and now has brief twisting spells of his legs when he jumps up suddenly.
case.exam: Normal tone, alert, developmentally normal; afebrile.
case.tests: Glucose, electrolytes and calcium normal; interictal EEG normal; MRI normal; PRRT2 heterozygous frameshift variant in the child and father.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and what explains the father's movement episodes?
case.a: Self-limited (familial) infantile epilepsy due to PRRT2; the father's attacks are paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia, the same gene producing the ICCA pattern across a lifetime.

read.where: Seizures and Epilepsy in Early Life — Benign Infantile Seizures

det.patho: In families, autosomal dominant PRRT2 variants (often the recurrent c.649dupC) account for most cases; PRRT2 encodes a synaptic protein that dampens neurotransmitter release, and its loss makes young cortex transiently excitable. SCN2A and KCNQ2 variants cause the related neonatal-infantile form, which starts within the first few months. Non-familial cases are often of unknown cause. The age-limited window probably reflects maturation of ion channels and synaptic proteins.
det.clinical: An infant with normal development has a sudden run of focal seizures over one to three days, typically with motion arrest, staring, head and eye deviation, cyanosis and then clonic jerking that may become bilateral. Seizures are short and the infant recovers fully between them. A few clusters can occur over subsequent weeks. Family members may have had infant seizures, and PRRT2 carriers may later develop paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia, hemiplegic migraine or episodic ataxia.
det.diagnosis: ILAE 2022 renamed benign (familial) infantile seizures as SeLIE, with or without a family history. The diagnosis rests on age of onset, normal development and examination, normal interictal EEG, and exclusion of acute symptomatic causes such as hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, infection, gastroenteritis-associated seizures and trauma. MRI is not required in a classic familial case but is wise if any feature is atypical or the family history is absent. PRRT2 testing confirms familial cases and informs counselling.
det.treatment: Short clusters may need nothing beyond acute benzodiazepine; when maintenance is chosen, carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine at low dose is very effective in PRRT2 cases, and levetiracetam or phenobarbital are alternatives. Treatment is usually withdrawn after several months without seizures, typically before age two. Parents should be reassured and taught seizure first aid, and adult carriers told about the risk of kinesigenic dyskinesia, which also responds to low-dose carbamazepine.
det.prognosis: Excellent: seizures stop in infancy and development remains normal; some PRRT2 carriers have paroxysmal movement disorders later.
pearls: Clusters of focal seizures in a normal 6-month-old with a normal EEG and a family history: think SeLIE and PRRT2.
Ask relatives about brief movement attacks on sudden standing — PRRT2 links SeLIE with PKD.
Low-dose carbamazepine works well in PRRT2 disorders, for both the seizures and the dyskinesia.

Chapter 18 Generalized Epilepsy Febrile Seizure Plus (GEFs+)

det.patho: GEFS+ is a family-level diagnosis: the same variant produces different phenotypes, shaped by modifier genes and environment. Missense SCN1A variants reduce function of Nav1.1 sodium channels in inhibitory interneurons; SCN1B (channel beta subunit), GABRG2 (GABA-A receptor gamma subunit) and STX1B are other known genes, and PCDH19 causes a related female-predominant clustering epilepsy. Only a minority of families have an identified variant, and many are probably polygenic. Fever-sensitive seizures reflect temperature-dependent channel behaviour in the immature brain.
det.clinical: Within one pedigree, some members have simple febrile seizures, others have febrile seizures plus (persisting after age 6 or mixed with afebrile generalised tonic-clonic seizures), and a few have absences, myoclonic, atonic or focal seizures. Most affected people develop normally and stop having seizures by adolescence. The severe end of the spectrum includes epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures and, uncommonly, Dravet syndrome. Some families include adults with temporal lobe epilepsy.
det.diagnosis: Suspect GEFS+ when a child's febrile seizures persist beyond six years or are joined by afebrile seizures, and when the family history shows several relatives with febrile or afebrile seizures. EEG is often normal or shows generalised spike-wave; MRI is usually normal. Genetic testing helps counselling and points away from sodium channel blockers if an SCN1A loss-of-function variant is found, but a negative test does not exclude the diagnosis. Recognise Dravet syndrome early if seizures are prolonged and development slows.
det.treatment: Many members need no daily medicine; rescue benzodiazepine for long seizures and fever advice are enough. When treatment is needed, valproate, levetiracetam, clobazam or topiramate are suitable; avoid carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin and lamotrigine when an SCN1A loss-of-function variant is present, as they can aggravate seizures. Antipyretics ease discomfort but do not prevent febrile seizures. Genetic counselling should explain variable expressivity to parents planning further children.
det.prognosis: Generally favourable, with remission in late childhood for most; outcome depends on where the individual sits within the spectrum.
pearls: GEFS+ describes a family, not a single patient's syndrome.
Febrile seizures after age 6, or alongside afebrile tonic-clonic seizures, is 'febrile seizures plus'.
Inherited missense SCN1A = usually GEFS+; de novo truncating SCN1A = usually Dravet.

qx.q: Which is the best explanation for this family's pattern?
opts: A familial epilepsy spectrum with autosomal dominant inheritance, variable phenotypes and incomplete penetrance, often involving SCN1A or SCN1B
Mitochondrial inheritance through the maternal line only
Autosomal recessive inheritance requiring consanguinity

Most affected members have a benign course, unlike progressive myoclonus epilepsies.

name: Acute symptomatic neonatal seizures
formal: Seizures occurring within the first 28 days after birth (or up to 44 weeks' postmenstrual age in preterm infants) provoked by an acute brain insult — chiefly hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, arterial ischaemic stroke, intracranial haemorrhage, CNS infection or a metabolic disturbance — as opposed to neonatal-onset epilepsy.
simple: Seizures in a newborn baby caused by a sudden problem such as lack of oxygen at birth, a stroke, bleeding, infection or low sugar or calcium.
th: อาการชักในทารกแรกเกิดอายุไม่เกิน 28 วันที่เกิดจากสาเหตุเฉียบพลัน เช่น สมองขาดออกซิเจนจากการคลอด สมองขาดเลือด เลือดออกในสมอง ติดเชื้อ น้ำตาลหรือแคลเซียมต่ำ หลายครั้งชักแต่คลื่นสมองเท่านั้นโดยไม่มีอาการให้เห็น
tempoNote: Usually within the first 72 hours after the insult (HIE typically within 12–24 h of birth); seizures are often frequent for 1–3 days and then subside as the acute injury evolves
feat: Seizures are frequently subtle or purely electrographic, especially after hypothermia or sedation
Clinical types (ILAE 2021): motor (clonic, tonic, myoclonic, automatisms, spasms), non-motor (autonomic, behavioural arrest) or sequential; usually focal
Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy is the leading cause at term, followed by stroke and haemorrhage
Focal clonic seizures in a well-appearing term baby suggest perinatal arterial stroke
Hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, hyponatraemia, meningitis and drug withdrawal are treatable causes not to miss
inv: Immediate bedside glucose, then calcium, magnesium, sodium, blood gas and lactate
Continuous video-EEG (or amplitude-integrated EEG if unavailable) to confirm and quantify seizures and monitor treatment
Septic work-up including lumbar puncture; HSV PCR when indicated
Cranial ultrasound early; MRI with DWI (days 2–5 after HIE) for stroke, haemorrhage and injury pattern

case.who: Term baby boy, 10 hours old, at a provincial hospital in Surin
case.story: Born after prolonged labour with thick meconium and Apgar scores of 2 and 5; he was transferred for therapeutic hypothermia. Nurses see repetitive lip-smacking and cycling leg movements, and desaturations without obvious cause.
case.exam: Lethargic, hypotonic, weak suck, exaggerated Moro absent; on cooling at 33.5°C.
case.tests: Glucose 3.8 mmol/L, calcium normal; aEEG shows repetitive rises in the lower margin; conventional EEG confirms rhythmic left central discharges, several without visible movement; MRI on day 4 shows basal ganglia and thalamic restricted diffusion.
case.q: What is the cause of the seizures, and how should they be treated?
case.a: Acute symptomatic seizures from moderate–severe HIE; continue hypothermia, treat EEG-confirmed seizures with phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV first-line (levetiracetam, phenytoin or midazolam next), and stop the antiseizure drug before discharge once seizures have resolved.

read.where: 4 Neonatal EEG and Neonatal Seizures — Neonatal Seizures; Neonatal Seizures Management

det.patho: Neonatal seizures are more common than at any other age in childhood, at roughly 1–3 per 1000 term births and much higher in preterm infants. The immature brain has excitatory GABA signalling (high intracellular chloride from NKCC1 dominance), which favours seizures and blunts the effect of GABAergic drugs. About 80% are acute symptomatic: hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy causes the largest share at term, followed by arterial ischaemic stroke, intraventricular and other intracranial haemorrhage, sinovenous thrombosis, meningitis or encephalitis, and transient metabolic upsets such as hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia and dysnatraemia. The remainder are neonatal-onset epilepsies (genetic, structural or metabolic).
det.clinical: The ILAE 2021 neonatal framework recognises that many seizures have no clinical sign, so it starts with EEG and then describes the predominant feature: motor (automatisms, clonic, epileptic spasms, myoclonic, tonic), non-motor (autonomic, behavioural arrest) or sequential. Neonatal seizures are almost always focal; generalised tonic-clonic seizures essentially do not occur. HIE seizures start within the first day and are often multifocal and numerous, whereas perinatal arterial stroke typically presents at 12–72 hours with focal clonic seizures in a baby who is otherwise relatively well. Jitteriness (stimulus-sensitive, stops with gentle restraint) and benign sleep myoclonus are common non-epileptic mimics.
det.diagnosis: Confirmation needs EEG, because clinical observation both misses electrographic seizures and over-calls non-epileptic movements; continuous video-EEG is the standard in high-risk infants, with aEEG as a practical screening tool where full EEG is lacking. Check glucose and electrolytes at once, then look for infection and imaging evidence of injury, with MRI including diffusion weighting as the most informative study. If no acute cause emerges or seizures are refractory, consider neonatal-onset epilepsies, pyridoxine- or PLP-dependent epilepsy, and other inborn errors, and send genetic testing early.
det.treatment: Correct hypoglycaemia (10% dextrose bolus) and hypocalcaemia (IV calcium gluconate) immediately and treat infection; therapeutic hypothermia within 6 hours is standard for moderate–severe HIE in term infants and reduces seizure burden. Phenobarbital (20 mg/kg IV, with further boluses) remains first-line in ILAE 2023 guidance, having outperformed levetiracetam in the NEOLEV2 trial; phenytoin/fosphenytoin, levetiracetam, midazolam or lidocaine are second-line options. Treat electrographic seizures as well as clinical ones, aiming to reduce total seizure burden. Once acute symptomatic seizures have stopped, discontinue antiseizure medication before discharge rather than continuing for months.
det.prognosis: Outcome depends on the underlying injury; roughly a fifth to a third develop later epilepsy or neurodevelopmental impairment, with the worst outcomes after severe HIE, large haemorrhage or high seizure burden.
pearls: Most neonatal seizures are subtle or electrographic only — rely on EEG, not observation alone.
Check glucose before anything else in a seizing newborn.
Focal clonic seizures in a well term baby on day 1–3: image for perinatal arterial stroke.

qx.stem: A term boy born after a prolonged second stage with thick meconium needs bag-mask ventilation and has cord pH 6.95. At 10 hours he has lip smacking and bicycling of the legs; a loading dose of phenobarbital is given and the movements stop. Bedside nurses now report he is quiet, but the aEEG trace shows repeated rises of the lower margin lasting 2–4 minutes.
qx.q: What is the most appropriate interpretation and next step?
opts: Movements have resolved, so no further monitoring is required
Ongoing electrographic-only seizures; confirm with conventional video EEG and escalate treatment
Normal sleep–wake cycling; continue routine care
Artefact from the cooling mattress; reposition the electrodes and ignore
Drug effect of phenobarbital; reduce the maintenance dose
qx.why: After a first antiseizure dose, many neonates show electroclinical uncoupling: clinical signs disappear while electrographic seizures continue. Repeated rises of the aEEG lower border suggest seizures, which should be confirmed with conventional video EEG and treated. Sleep–wake cycling produces gradual sinusoidal changes, not abrupt brief elevations, and phenobarbital tends to suppress rather than create such events.

name: Epilepsy with myoclonic absences (EMA)
formal: A rare childhood-onset generalised epilepsy whose defining seizure is an absence accompanied by rhythmic ~3 Hz myoclonic jerks of the shoulders and arms with progressive tonic arm elevation, time-locked to generalised 3 Hz spike-wave; it is frequently drug-resistant and often associated with intellectual disability.
simple: A childhood epilepsy in which brief staring spells come with rhythmic jerking and slow lifting of both arms.

Male predominance; intellectual disability present before onset or emerging in about half

Developmental and cognitive assessment
MRI brain, chromosomal microarray and epilepsy gene panel (associations include Angelman syndrome and chromosomal anomalies)

case.story: His teacher reports many daily episodes in which he stops writing, stares, and both shoulders jerk rhythmically while his arms slowly rise; each lasts about half a minute. He was already slower to learn than classmates.
case.exam: Mild intellectual disability, otherwise normal; hyperventilation in clinic provokes a typical event.
case.tests: Video-EEG: 3 Hz generalised spike-wave lasting 25 seconds with deltoid EMG bursts matching each spike; MRI normal; microarray normal.
case.q: Why is this not childhood absence epilepsy, and what treatment is usual?
case.a: Prominent rhythmic myoclonus with tonic arm elevation defines epilepsy with myoclonic absences, which carries a less favourable outlook than CAE; valproate combined with ethosuximide is the standard approach, with lamotrigine or levetiracetam added if needed.

det.patho: EMA is a generalised epilepsy driven by thalamocortical spike-wave circuits, like other absence epilepsies, but with strong motor cortex involvement producing rhythmic myoclonus. Causes are heterogeneous: relatives with epilepsy are frequent, and genetic or chromosomal disorders (Angelman syndrome, trisomy 12p, other copy-number variants, SYNGAP1 and other genes) are found in a minority; many cases have no identified cause. It accounts for well under 1% of childhood epilepsies, with boys affected more often.
det.clinical: Seizures are absences of variable depth accompanied by rhythmic jerks, mainly of the shoulders, arms and sometimes legs, synchronous with 3 Hz spike-wave; superimposed tonic contraction lifts the arms progressively, which is the visual hallmark. Episodes last 10–60 seconds and recur many times a day, and hyperventilation provokes them reliably. Around half of children have intellectual disability, either pre-existing or developing over the course, particularly when seizures continue. Generalised tonic-clonic, atonic or atypical absence seizures may appear, and some children evolve toward a Lennox–Gastaut-like picture. ILAE 2022 places EMA among the generalised epilepsy syndromes of childhood.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis depends on capturing an event with video-EEG and polygraphic EMG, showing generalised 3 Hz spike-wave in which each spike is followed by a myoclonic jerk, with tonic contraction building through the seizure. The interictal background is usually normal or mildly slow. Investigate for an underlying cause with MRI and genetic testing (microarray, gene panel), especially if development was already delayed. Distinguish from childhood absence epilepsy with mild myoclonic components, epilepsy with eyelid myoclonia, myoclonic-atonic epilepsy and Lennox–Gastaut syndrome.
det.treatment: Valproate is the usual first drug, and adding ethosuximide is the classic combination for persisting absences; lamotrigine (often synergistic with valproate), levetiracetam, clobazam, topiramate or zonisamide are further options. Carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin and vigabatrin can aggravate absences and myoclonus and are avoided. Ketogenic dietary therapy may help drug-resistant cases. Support for learning and schooling is part of management.
det.prognosis: Roughly half achieve seizure freedom; persistence of seizures and later onset of cognitive decline are linked, and some children develop additional seizure types.
pearls: Absences plus rhythmic shoulder jerks and rising arms = myoclonic absences, not CAE.
Hyperventilation in clinic, with phone video, often captures the diagnostic event.
Valproate plus ethosuximide is the classic regimen; avoid sodium channel blockers.

name: Childhood occipital visual epilepsy (COVE)
formal: A self-limited focal epilepsy of school-age children (ILAE 2022) in which brief, frequent occipital seizures produce elementary visual hallucinations or transient blindness, often followed by headache, with occipital spikes that appear when the eyes are closed; it replaces the older label idiopathic childhood occipital epilepsy of Gastaut.
simple: A childhood epilepsy where short fits start in the back of the brain, so the child sees coloured spots or briefly goes blind, and it usually fades away within a few years.
ab: Gastaut type idiopathic childhood occipital epilepsy
idiopathic childhood occipital epilepsy of Gastaut
th: โรคลมชักเฉพาะที่ในเด็กวัยเรียนที่จุดกำเนิดอยู่สมองส่วนท้ายทอย ชักสั้น ๆ เห็นวงกลมสีหรือตามืดไปชั่วครู่ แล้วมักปวดศีรษะตาม คล้ายไมเกรน ส่วนใหญ่หายเองภายในไม่กี่ปี
tempoNote: Onset usually 6–12 years (range about 3–16); seizures last seconds to a few minutes and may occur several times a day; most remit within 2–7 years
feat: Sudden coloured circles or blobs, often in one half of the visual field, lasting seconds to a few minutes
Ictal blindness, eye or head deviation, or forced blinking may follow; awareness is often kept early on
Post-ictal headache, sometimes throbbing with vomiting, in up to half — easily mislabelled as migraine
Normal development and examination; seizures mostly while awake and can be frequent
Occipital spike-wave that appears with eye closure or darkness (fixation-off sensitivity)
inv: EEG: occipital or posterior spikes, blocked by eye opening; some children also show centrotemporal spikes
MRI brain is mandatory to rule out occipital lesions (dysplasia, tumour, calcification, ischaemic scar)
Consider metabolic or genetic tests (e.g. coeliac antibodies, mitochondrial or Lafora testing) if atypical, regressing or with myoclonus

case.story: Several times a week he reports bright multicoloured balls floating in his right visual field for under a minute; twice his vision went dark and he then had a pounding headache and vomited.
case.exam: Normal neurological and fundoscopic examination; normal school progress.
case.tests: EEG: left occipital spikes that vanish when he opens his eyes. MRI brain normal.
case.q: Why is this not simply migraine with aura, and what is the expected course?
case.a: The visual phenomena are brief, coloured and circular rather than slowly spreading monochrome zigzags, with occipital spikes; this is childhood occipital visual epilepsy, which usually responds to carbamazepine or similar and remits within a few years.

det.patho: COVE is thought to be an age-related, genetically influenced hyperexcitability of the occipital cortex in a structurally normal brain; no single causative gene is known. It is far less common than self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes and makes up only a small fraction of childhood epilepsies. The ILAE 2022 classification groups it with the other self-limited childhood focal syndromes and retires the Gastaut eponym.
det.clinical: Children describe brief elementary visual hallucinations, typically small bright coloured shapes that may drift or multiply, sometimes followed by loss of vision, eye deviation, head turning or spread to a hemiclonic or bilateral convulsion. Seizures are short but can be numerous, sometimes daily. A post-ictal headache that throbs and brings nausea leads many families and clinicians to diagnose migraine. Intellect and examination stay normal; regression, myoclonus or worsening vision should prompt a search for a progressive cause.
det.diagnosis: History of brief stereotyped coloured visual phenomena plus occipital spikes enhanced by eye closure supports the diagnosis. Neuroimaging is required, because occipital seizures in children are frequently symptomatic. Atypical cases call for checks for coeliac disease with occipital calcification, mitochondrial disease, Lafora disease and other progressive myoclonic epilepsies. Note that occipital spikes alone are non-specific and also appear in children who never have seizures.
det.treatment: Because seizures are often frequent, most children are treated; carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine are classically effective, and levetiracetam or lamotrigine are reasonable alternatives. Treat the post-ictal headache with simple analgesics. Medication can usually be withdrawn after a two-year seizure-free period. Explain the benign course to families while keeping review for atypical features.
det.prognosis: Remission occurs in most children within a few years of onset, although a minority continue to have seizures into adolescence.
pearls: Coloured circles lasting seconds = occipital seizure; monochrome zigzags lasting minutes = migraine aura.
Occipital spikes that disappear on eye opening (fixation-off sensitivity) are a hallmark.
Always image: symptomatic occipital epilepsy is common in children.
det.thd: COVE (ชื่อเดิม Gastaut type) เป็นโรคลมชักเฉพาะที่ในเด็กวัยเรียน เด็กจะเห็นวงกลมหรือจุดสีสว่างเพียงไม่กี่วินาทีถึงนาที อาจตามืดชั่วคราว แล้วปวดศีรษะคล้ายไมเกรน EEG พบ occipital spikes ที่หายไปเมื่อเปิดตา ต้องทำ MRI เพื่อแยกรอยโรคที่ท้ายทอยเสมอ รักษาด้วย carbamazepine หรือยากันชักอื่น และส่วนใหญ่หายภายในไม่กี่ปี

Two episodes ended with head turning and a convulsion. MRI is normal. EEG shows right occipital spike-wave that appears when he closes his eyes and disappears with eye opening.
qx.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Childhood occipital visual epilepsy
Migraine with aura
Panayiotopoulos syndrome
Occipital lobe infarction
Charles Bonnet syndrome
qx.why: Brief, frequent, coloured circular visual hallucinations that may spread to motor seizures, with occipital spikes showing fixation-off sensitivity, define childhood occipital visual epilepsy. Migraine aura is typically black-and-white zigzag, builds over minutes and lasts longer. Panayiotopoulos syndrome has younger onset and autonomic rather than visual seizures.

tempoNote: Onset about 8–20 years (peak 10–16); absences last 5–30 seconds and occur daily or less; the tendency usually lasts into adult life
feat: Typical absences with sudden arrest and staring, often with less complete loss of awareness than in childhood absence epilepsy
Absences are not dozens per day; many patients only notice them when asked
Generalised tonic–clonic seizures in about 80%, often after waking or sleep loss; myoclonic jerks in a minority
Normal development, examination and MRI; family history of epilepsy is common
Absence status epilepticus (prolonged confusion) can occur
inv: EEG: generalised spike- or polyspike-and-wave at 3–5.5 Hz on a normal background, provoked by hyperventilation
Hyperventilation in clinic may reproduce an absence; video helps
MRI only if focal features, abnormal examination or atypical course

case.who: 14-year-old girl in Mathayom 2 from Chiang Mai
case.story: Her teacher notices she sometimes stops writing and stares for about ten seconds, a few times a week; last month she had a convulsion the morning after staying up late watching series.
case.exam: Normal examination; three minutes of hyperventilation reproduce a brief stare with eyelid flutter.
case.tests: EEG: generalised 3.5–4 Hz spike-and-wave during hyperventilation; background normal.
case.q: Which ILAE syndrome fits better than childhood absence epilepsy, and why does the drug choice differ?
case.a: Juvenile absence epilepsy — later onset, sparse absences and tonic–clonic seizures; ethosuximide alone would not cover the convulsions, so a broad-spectrum drug (lamotrigine or levetiracetam; valproate only with careful counselling in girls) is needed.

read.where: 10 Electro-Clinical Syndromes by Age of Onset — Juvenile Absence Epilepsy (JAE)

det.patho: JAE shares the thalamocortical spike-wave mechanism of other idiopathic generalised epilepsies, driven by complex polygenic inheritance with occasional rare variants. It represents a modest proportion of IGE and overlaps genetically and clinically with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. The ILAE 2022 proposal lists it as one of four IGE syndromes.
det.clinical: Absences start around puberty, are shorter and fewer than in childhood absence epilepsy, and may leave partial responsiveness. Most patients also develop generalised tonic–clonic seizures, typically in early morning or after sleep deprivation and alcohol. Some have occasional myoclonic jerks, and absence status may present as hours of confusion. Learning and behaviour are usually normal, though attention problems are reported.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis combines age of onset, absence frequency and EEG; it should not be applied when absences began before about 8 years or occur many times daily. Hyperventilation is the best bedside provocation. Exclude structural or focal epilepsy if there are lateralised features, and consider GLUT1 deficiency if absences began very early or with paroxysmal exertional symptoms. Classifying correctly matters because sodium-channel drugs can worsen absences.
det.treatment: Choose a broad-spectrum antiseizure medicine; valproate is the most effective but should be avoided in females of childbearing potential unless other options fail, so lamotrigine or levetiracetam are frequent choices. Ethosuximide controls absences but not tonic–clonic seizures and is used only as add-on. Avoid carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, gabapentin, pregabalin and vigabatrin. Counsel on regular sleep, moderation of alcohol and driving rules.
det.prognosis: Seizures are controlled in most people, but relapse after withdrawal is common, so long-term treatment is usually advised.
pearls: Teenager with rare absences plus convulsions = JAE, not late CAE.
Ethosuximide monotherapy leaves tonic–clonic seizures untreated.
Carbamazepine or phenytoin can aggravate absences and trigger absence status.
det.thd: JAE เป็นโรคลมชักทั้งสมองที่เริ่มช่วงวัยรุ่น มีอาการเหม่อสั้น ๆ ไม่บ่อย และเกือบทุกรายมีชักเกร็งกระตุกทั้งตัว มักเกิดตอนเช้าหรือหลังอดนอน EEG พบ spike-wave ทั่วสมองความถี่ 3–5 Hz ที่กระตุ้นได้ด้วยการหายใจเร็ว รักษาด้วยยากว้างขวาง เช่น lamotrigine หรือ levetiracetam (valproate ต้องระวังในผู้หญิง) และหลีกเลี่ยง carbamazepine หรือ phenytoin มักต้องกินยาระยะยาว

qx.stem: A 12-year-old boy has a convulsion soon after waking on the morning of a football tournament. On questioning he has had brief blank spells a few times per week for a year, not daily. EEG shows bursts of generalised spike-and-wave and polyspike-wave at 3.5–4 Hz, provoked by hyperventilation; background is normal.
qx.q: Which statement best fits the most likely syndrome?
opts: Absences are typically many per day and remit by age 10
Ethosuximide alone is sufficient because it controls convulsions
Generalised tonic–clonic seizures are common and treatment is often lifelong; valproate is effective
The prognosis resembles self-limited focal epilepsy of childhood
Epilepsy surgery is usually curative
qx.why: Onset around puberty, less frequent absences, slightly faster spike-wave and accompanying tonic–clonic seizures point to juvenile absence epilepsy. Most patients need long-term therapy; valproate covers both seizure types (lamotrigine or levetiracetam are alternatives in females). Ethosuximide does not prevent tonic–clonic seizures.

ddx.pt: Starts at 4–10 years with many absences per day; convulsions uncommon and usually remits in adolescence
Morning myoclonic jerks are the dominant and defining seizure type; absences are minor if present
Staring spells from temporal lobe seizures last longer, have aura, automatisms and post-ictal confusion

name: Epilepsy with generalised tonic–clonic seizures alone (GTCA)
formal: An idiopathic generalised epilepsy syndrome (ILAE 2022) of adolescence or early adulthood in which generalised tonic–clonic seizures are the only seizure type, frequently but not necessarily soon after waking, with generalised spike-wave on EEG; the older label was awakening grand mal epilepsy.
simple: A type of inherited generalised epilepsy where the only seizures are big whole-body convulsions, often in the morning, in an otherwise healthy young person.
ab: Epilepsy with generalised tonic–clonic seizures alone
epilepsy with grand mal on awakening
th: โรคลมชักทั้งสมองกลุ่ม IGE ที่มีแต่ชักเกร็งกระตุกทั้งตัวอย่างเดียว ไม่มีอาการเหม่อหรือกระตุกสั้น ๆ มักเกิดหลังตื่นนอนหรืออดนอน พบในวัยรุ่นถึงผู้ใหญ่ตอนต้น
tempoNote: Onset mostly 10–25 years (can be later); seizures are infrequent, often within two hours of waking; predisposition is usually lifelong
feat: Generalised tonic–clonic seizures with no aura and no other seizure type on careful questioning
Clustering after waking or during evening relaxation; triggered by sleep deprivation, alcohol and stress
Normal development, cognition, examination and MRI
Family history of IGE in some
Photosensitivity in a minority
inv: EEG: generalised spike- or polyspike-wave at 3–5.5 Hz, best captured on sleep-deprived or awakening recordings
MRI if any focal feature or late onset, to exclude focal epilepsy with rapid spread
Ask specifically about morning jerks and absences to exclude JME and JAE

case.story: He has had three convulsions in two years, each on a weekend morning after night shifts and drinking with friends; he denies any jerks, blank spells or warning.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination.
case.tests: Sleep-deprived EEG: brief bursts of generalised 4 Hz polyspike-wave. MRI brain normal.
case.q: Which ILAE generalised syndrome is this, and what lifestyle points matter?
case.a: GTCA (an IGE syndrome with convulsions only); start a broad-spectrum drug such as lamotrigine or levetiracetam and counsel about sleep regularity, alcohol and shift-work triggers.

read.where: 10 Electro-Clinical Syndromes by Age of Onset — Epilepsy with GTC Seizures Only

det.patho: Like other IGE syndromes, GTCA arises from genetically determined thalamocortical hyperexcitability with mostly polygenic inheritance. The ILAE 2022 classification renamed it to make clear that a waking pattern is typical but not required. It accounts for a sizeable minority of IGE and is probably underdiagnosed in adults.
det.clinical: The patient has generalised convulsions only, often in the first hours after waking or when relaxing in the evening. Sleep loss, alcohol, fatigue and, in some, flickering light are typical triggers. Seizures are usually infrequent. Careful questioning frequently uncovers subtle morning jerks or absences, which reclassifies the patient as JME or JAE.
det.diagnosis: Confirm the events are epileptic and that no other seizure type exists. Generalised spike-wave on EEG supports the syndrome, but a normal routine EEG is common, so sleep-deprived recording helps. A focal onset, focal EEG or abnormal imaging points to focal epilepsy with fast spread. Provoked seizures from alcohol withdrawal, hypoglycaemia or drugs must be excluded.
det.treatment: Lamotrigine, levetiracetam and valproate are effective; valproate should be avoided in women who could become pregnant unless other options fail. Avoid drugs that can aggravate generalised epilepsies if the syndrome is uncertain. Lifestyle counselling about sleep, alcohol and shift work is a core part of care. Driving regulations and safety advice should be discussed at diagnosis.
det.prognosis: Control is good for most patients, but relapse after drug withdrawal is frequent, so long-term therapy is typical.
pearls: Ask about morning jerks before labelling GTCA — many turn out to be JME.
Weekend morning convulsions after sleep loss and alcohol are a classic story.
A normal routine EEG does not exclude it; repeat with sleep deprivation.
det.thd: GTCA คือโรคลมชักทั้งสมองในกลุ่ม IGE ที่มีเฉพาะชักเกร็งกระตุกทั้งตัว ไม่มีเหม่อหรือกระตุก มักเกิดหลังตื่นนอน หลังอดนอนหรือดื่มเหล้า EEG อาจพบ spike-wave ทั่วสมองโดยเฉพาะเมื่อตรวจหลังอดนอน รักษาด้วย lamotrigine, levetiracetam หรือ valproate (ระวังในผู้หญิง) ร่วมกับปรับการนอนและเลี่ยงแอลกอฮอล์

ddx.pt: Morning myoclonic jerks precede convulsions; must be asked about directly
Aura or lateralised onset, focal EEG discharges or a lesion on MRI; may look generalised because of rapid spread
Postural or emotional trigger, pallor, a few jerks and rapid reorientation without tongue-biting on the side

name: Familial mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (FMTLE)
formal: An autosomal dominant focal epilepsy with incomplete penetrance in which several relatives have seizures of mesial temporal origin, often mild with déjà vu or epigastric auras, a normal or near-normal MRI in many, and generally good drug response.
simple: A family-inherited form of temporal lobe epilepsy where several relatives have mild spells such as déjà vu or a rising stomach feeling.
ab: autosomal dominant mesial temporal lobe epilepsy
benign familial mesial temporal lobe epilepsy
th: โรคลมชักกลีบขมับด้านในที่ถ่ายทอดในครอบครัวแบบยีนเด่น ญาติหลายคนมีอาการเดจาวูหรือจุกลิ้นปี่ขึ้นมาสั้น ๆ ส่วนใหญ่อาการไม่รุนแรงและตอบสนองต่อยาดี
tempoNote: Onset usually in adolescence or adulthood (median around the second to third decade); brief focal seizures recurring over years, often infrequent
feat: Two or more relatives with focal seizures of mesial temporal type
Prominent déjà vu, fear or epigastric rising sensation; some only have auras and never seek care
Focal impaired-awareness or bilateral tonic–clonic seizures are infrequent in most families
MRI is often normal; hippocampal sclerosis is seen in some families and in some members
Prior febrile seizures are uncommon in most families
inv: Detailed three-generation family history, interviewing relatives about déjà vu spells
EEG: anterior or mid-temporal epileptiform discharges in some; often normal
Epilepsy-protocol MRI to look for hippocampal sclerosis or other lesion
Genetic testing has low yield; panels may be considered to exclude other familial focal epilepsies

case.story: For years she has had short spells of intense familiarity with a rising stomach feeling; after one recent spell she lost awareness and her colleagues saw lip-smacking. Her mother and a brother describe similar 'déjà vu attacks' they never reported.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination.
case.tests: EEG: right mid-temporal sharp waves. MRI: no hippocampal sclerosis.
case.q: What familial syndrome should be considered, and what is the usual treatment response?
case.a: Familial mesial temporal lobe epilepsy; most patients respond well to a single focal antiseizure medicine such as lamotrigine or levetiracetam.

read.where: 10 Electro-Clinical Syndromes by Age of Onset — Familial Temporal Lobe Epilepsy

det.patho: Inheritance is autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance, and some families likely carry oligogenic or polygenic susceptibility; no single major gene explains most families. Hippocampal sclerosis may be present in some members even without drug resistance, showing that it can be a consequence of genetic as well as acquired factors. The condition differs from autosomal dominant epilepsy with auditory features (lateral temporal, LGI1 or RELN).
det.clinical: Most affected people have mild auras such as déjà vu, a dreamy state, fear, or epigastric discomfort, sometimes progressing to impaired awareness with oral automatisms. Bilateral convulsions are uncommon. Because spells are mild, many relatives never seek medical care, so the family history only emerges when asked directly. A minority of families show a more severe course with hippocampal sclerosis and drug resistance.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires a typical mesial temporal semiology in the patient and confirmation of similar events in at least one other relative. EEG and MRI may be normal. Search for acquired causes such as hippocampal sclerosis, tumour or encephalitis, and distinguish from familial lateral temporal epilepsy with auditory auras. Genetic testing seldom yields a diagnosis but can identify other familial focal epilepsy genes.
det.treatment: Standard focal antiseizure medicines are used, and many patients become seizure-free on monotherapy; some with auras only may choose no treatment after discussion. Drug-resistant cases with concordant hippocampal sclerosis can be considered for epilepsy surgery. Genetic counselling should address incomplete penetrance and the generally mild phenotype.
det.prognosis: Most patients have a benign course, though a minority develop drug-resistant epilepsy.
pearls: Ask relatives specifically about déjà vu spells — they are often unreported.
Hippocampal sclerosis can occur in familial cases without febrile seizures.
Auditory auras in a family suggest the lateral temporal (LGI1/RELN) syndrome instead.
det.thd: FMTLE เป็นโรคลมชักกลีบขมับด้านในที่ถ่ายทอดแบบยีนเด่นแต่ไม่ทุกคนที่มียีนจะมีอาการ ญาติหลายคนมีอาการเดจาวู กลัว หรือจุกลิ้นปี่ขึ้นมาสั้น ๆ ซึ่งมักไม่เคยมาพบแพทย์ MRI มักปกติแต่บางครอบครัวพบ hippocampal sclerosis ส่วนใหญ่ตอบสนองดีต่อยากันชักชนิดเดียว

name: Familial focal epilepsy with variable foci (FFEVF)
formal: An autosomal dominant focal epilepsy with incomplete penetrance in which different family members have focal seizures arising from different cortical regions, each individual keeping a single consistent focus, most often due to inactivating germline changes in DEPDC5, NPRL2 or NPRL3, the genes of the GATOR1 complex.
simple: A family epilepsy where each relative has fits that start from a different part of the brain, often due to changes in genes that act as a brake on brain-cell growth signals.
ab: Familial focal epilepsy with variable foci
familial partial epilepsy with variable foci
th: โรคลมชักเฉพาะที่ที่ถ่ายทอดในครอบครัว แต่ละคนชักจากสมองคนละตำแหน่ง มักเกิดจากยีนกลุ่ม GATOR1 (DEPDC5, NPRL2, NPRL3) บางรายมี focal cortical dysplasia และดื้อยา
tempoNote: Onset from infancy to adulthood (mean around the second decade), even within one family; seizures recur over years
feat: Family members with focal epilepsy from different lobes — frontal (often nocturnal hypermotor), temporal, parietal or occipital
Each person keeps one stable focus over time
Penetrance incomplete (roughly 60%), so unaffected carriers and skipped generations are common
Some carriers have focal cortical dysplasia (often type II) and drug-resistant seizures
Raised SUDEP risk reported in GATOR1 families
inv: Detailed family history of seizure types across relatives
Epilepsy-protocol MRI with attention to subtle focal cortical dysplasia (bottom-of-sulcus)
Gene panel or exome testing for DEPDC5, NPRL2 and NPRL3
Video-EEG and presurgical work-up if drug-resistant

case.story: He has brief nocturnal attacks with thrashing of the limbs from sleep since age 11, despite two drugs. His father had temporal lobe seizures in his twenties, and a paternal aunt has seizures starting with tingling in one arm.
case.exam: Normal examination.
case.tests: MRI: subtle left superior frontal sulcus dysplasia. Gene panel: pathogenic DEPDC5 truncating variant.
case.q: What is the familial syndrome, and what treatment option should be considered?
case.a: FFEVF due to DEPDC5 (GATOR1) variant with focal cortical dysplasia; refer for presurgical evaluation, as resection of the dysplasia can stop seizures.

read.where: 10 Electro-Clinical Syndromes by Age of Onset — Familial Focal Epilepsy with Variable Foci

det.patho: DEPDC5, NPRL2 and NPRL3 form the GATOR1 complex, which inhibits mTORC1 signalling; heterozygous loss of function leads to mTOR overactivity and neuronal hyperexcitability. A second somatic hit in brain tissue can produce focal cortical dysplasia type II, which explains why some carriers have lesional, drug-resistant epilepsy. GATOR1 variants are among the commonest genetic causes of familial focal epilepsy.
det.clinical: The defining feature is variability between relatives: one may have nocturnal frontal hypermotor seizures, another temporal seizures, another parietal sensory seizures. Within a person, the focus stays fixed. Severity ranges from mild epilepsy to infantile spasms or developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. Cognition is usually normal, but psychiatric and learning difficulties occur in some, and sudden unexpected death in epilepsy has been reported in several families.
det.diagnosis: Suspect FFEVF when a family includes several people with focal epilepsies of different localisation. Genetic testing for GATOR1 genes confirms the diagnosis; variants of uncertain significance need segregation analysis. High-resolution MRI and expert review should look for subtle dysplasia, and an apparently non-lesional case may still have a small bottom-of-sulcus lesion. Negative results do not exclude a polygenic or undiscovered cause.
det.treatment: Treat with standard focal antiseizure medicines. Drug-resistant patients, especially those with visible dysplasia, should be referred early for presurgical evaluation, since resection often gives good results. mTOR inhibitors are under study but not established for GATOR1 epilepsy. Genetic counselling should cover dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance and SUDEP risk.
det.prognosis: Course varies widely; many respond to medication, while lesional cases may need surgery to become seizure-free.
pearls: Different lobes in different relatives = think GATOR1 (DEPDC5, NPRL2, NPRL3).
Germline plus somatic second hit can cause focal cortical dysplasia type II.
Look hard for bottom-of-sulcus dysplasia; surgery can be curative.
det.thd: FFEVF เป็นโรคลมชักเฉพาะที่ถ่ายทอดแบบยีนเด่น ญาติแต่ละคนชักจากสมองคนละกลีบ แต่ในคนเดียวกันตำแหน่งคงที่ สาเหตุหลักคือยีน DEPDC5, NPRL2, NPRL3 ซึ่งยับยั้ง mTOR บางรายมี focal cortical dysplasia ทำให้ดื้อยา ควรตรวจพันธุกรรม ทำ MRI ละเอียด และส่งประเมินผ่าตัดเมื่อดื้อยา

name: Post-traumatic epilepsy (PTE)
formal: Epilepsy characterised by recurrent unprovoked seizures that begin more than one week after a traumatic brain injury and are attributed to it, as distinct from early post-traumatic seizures within the first seven days, which are acute symptomatic events.
simple: Epilepsy that develops weeks to years after a head injury because the scarred brain becomes prone to fits.
ab: ลมชักหลังอุบัติเหตุศีรษะ
th: โรคลมชักที่เกิดหลังได้รับบาดเจ็บที่ศีรษะเกิน 7 วัน (อาจหลายปีต่อมา) เนื่องจากแผลเป็นในสมอง ต่างจากชักภายใน 7 วันแรกซึ่งเป็นชักจากสาเหตุเฉียบพลัน
tempoNote: Late seizures begin more than 7 days after injury; most within 2 years, but risk persists for a decade or more
feat: Focal seizures, frequently frontal or temporal, often evolving to bilateral convulsions
Risk rises with severity: penetrating injury, depressed skull fracture, cortical contusion, subdural haematoma, prolonged coma or amnesia
Early post-traumatic seizures (first week) increase the chance of later epilepsy
About one-third or more after penetrating war injuries; a few percent after mild TBI
Drug resistance is relatively common
inv: MRI with susceptibility-weighted imaging to show contusion, gliosis and haemosiderin
EEG: focal slowing and epileptiform discharges; video-EEG for unclear events
Rule out other causes of new seizures (late subdural haematoma, alcohol, metabolic)

case.who: 38-year-old male motorcycle rider from Udon Thani
case.story: A year after a crash with a left frontal contusion and a seizure on day 3, he now has episodes of head turning to the right followed by a convulsion, once every month.
case.exam: Mild word-finding difficulty; otherwise normal.
case.tests: MRI: left frontal encephalomalacia with haemosiderin rim on SWI. EEG: left frontal sharp waves.
case.q: Why do these seizures count as epilepsy, unlike the seizure on day 3, and does early prophylaxis prevent this?
case.a: Unprovoked seizures beyond the first week after TBI define post-traumatic epilepsy; prophylactic drugs given in the first week reduce early seizures only and do not prevent later epilepsy.

read.where: 14 Epilepsy Secondary to Specific Mechanisms — Post-traumatic Epilepsy

det.patho: Traumatic injury causes blood breakdown with iron deposition and free radical damage, blood–brain barrier disruption, inflammation, neuronal loss and gliosis, which together reorganise cortical networks over months (epileptogenesis). Traumatic brain injury causes a noticeable share of acquired epilepsy in young adults, and road traffic accidents make this especially relevant in Thailand. Risk correlates with the depth and extent of cortical damage.
det.clinical: Seizures usually start within the first two years but can appear much later. They are typically focal with or without impaired awareness, reflecting frontal and temporal contusions, and often generalise. Coexisting cognitive deficits, mood disorders, headache and functional seizures complicate assessment. People with PTE have higher rates of status epilepticus and drug resistance than those with many other acquired epilepsies.
det.diagnosis: Separate early seizures in the first week (acute symptomatic, not epilepsy) from late unprovoked seizures; a single late seizure carries a high recurrence risk, so many clinicians diagnose epilepsy after one. MRI with blood-sensitive sequences identifies the scar, and EEG helps confirm a focal epilepsy. Exclude new structural problems such as subdural haematoma, alcohol withdrawal and metabolic triggers. Video-EEG is helpful when events are atypical.
det.treatment: Short courses of levetiracetam or phenytoin for seven days after severe TBI reduce early seizures but do not prevent epilepsy, so prophylaxis should not be continued beyond the first week without seizures. Established PTE is treated like other focal epilepsy, with levetiracetam, lamotrigine, lacosamide or carbamazepine chosen by tolerability and interactions. Drug-resistant cases may benefit from surgery when a single focus is identified, or from neuromodulation. Rehabilitation, driving advice and treatment of mood and cognitive problems are important.
det.prognosis: A sizeable proportion achieve control, but drug resistance is more frequent than in many epilepsies and seizures may persist lifelong.
pearls: Day 1–7 seizure after TBI = acute symptomatic; after day 7 = consider post-traumatic epilepsy.
Prophylactic ASMs beyond a week do not prevent PTE.
Penetrating injury and depressed fracture carry the highest risk.
det.thd: PTE คือโรคลมชักที่เกิดหลังบาดเจ็บศีรษะเกิน 7 วัน ส่วนการชักในสัปดาห์แรกถือเป็นชักจากสาเหตุเฉียบพลัน ความเสี่ยงสูงในแผลทะลุ กะโหลกยุบ contusion และเลือดออกใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมอง การให้ยากันชัก 7 วันแรกลดการชักระยะแรกแต่ไม่ป้องกัน PTE รักษาเหมือน focal epilepsy และพิจารณาผ่าตัดถ้าดื้อยา

name: Autoimmune-associated epilepsy
formal: Under ILAE 2020 terminology, seizures with an immune cause are split into acute symptomatic seizures caused by an autoimmune encephalitis, which usually stop once the encephalitis is treated, and autoimmune-associated epilepsy, an enduring seizure tendency linked to a chronic immune process, typically with antibodies to intracellular antigens such as GAD65.
simple: Epilepsy caused by the body's own immune system attacking the brain; some forms go away with immune treatment, others become lasting epilepsy.
ab: acute symptomatic seizures secondary to autoimmune encephalitis
th: ลมชักที่เกิดจากภูมิคุ้มกันทำลายสมอง แบ่งเป็นชักเฉียบพลันจาก autoimmune encephalitis ที่หายได้เมื่อรักษาภูมิคุ้มกัน กับ autoimmune-associated epilepsy ที่เป็นเรื้อรัง เช่น anti-GAD65
tempoNote: Acute symptomatic seizures develop over days to weeks with encephalitis; autoimmune-associated epilepsy persists over months to years
feat: New-onset seizures, often frequent and drug-resistant, with cognitive, psychiatric or sleep changes
Clues: faciobrachial dystonic seizures (LGI1), orofacial dyskinesia (NMDAR), autonomic instability, viral prodrome, recent cancer
Temporal lobe seizures with déjà vu or piloerection in an adult without prior epilepsy
Intracellular antibody group (GAD65, Hu, Ma2) often evolves into chronic drug-resistant epilepsy
Antibody Prevalence in Epilepsy (APE2) score of 4 or more makes antibody positivity likely
inv: Paired serum and CSF neural antibody panels (cell-surface and intracellular)
CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein, oligoclonal bands or raised IgG index
MRI: mesial temporal T2/FLAIR hyperintensity or swelling; EEG for subclinical seizures
Cancer screening (CT chest-abdomen-pelvis, testicular or pelvic ultrasound, PET as needed)

case.story: Over six weeks he has had dozens of brief jerks of the right arm and face each day, plus memory lapses; his wife says he gets goose bumps before some spells. Two antiseizure drugs did not help.
case.exam: Disoriented to date; brief right face–arm dystonic spasms observed.
case.tests: Sodium 128 mmol/L. MRI: left mesial temporal FLAIR hyperintensity. Serum LGI1 antibody positive.
case.q: Is this autoimmune-associated epilepsy or acute symptomatic seizures from encephalitis, and what is the key treatment?
case.a: Acute symptomatic seizures secondary to anti-LGI1 encephalitis; early immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG or plasma exchange) usually stops the faciobrachial seizures and limits cognitive damage.

read.where: 14 Epilepsy Secondary to Specific Mechanisms — Autoimmune Epilepsy
Immune-related encephalitis after immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy

det.patho: Antibodies against cell-surface receptors or channels (NMDAR, LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, AMPA, GABA-A) alter synaptic function directly and are often reversible. Antibodies to intracellular antigens (GAD65, Hu, Ma2) mark T-cell–mediated neuronal damage, which tends to cause permanent hippocampal injury and enduring epilepsy. The ILAE 2020 position paper formalised this split to guide prognosis and treatment.
det.clinical: Patients usually present with new seizures that rapidly become frequent and resistant to standard medicines, together with memory loss, behavioural or psychiatric change, sleep disturbance or autonomic features. Syndrome-specific clues help: faciobrachial dystonic seizures in LGI1, dyskinesia and catatonia in NMDAR, stiff-person features or diabetes in GAD65, and severe status epilepticus in GABA-A or GABA-B. Some adults present with isolated late-onset temporal lobe epilepsy and subtle inflammatory signs.
det.diagnosis: Apply clinical criteria for autoimmune encephalitis and use the APE2 score (new rapidly progressive mental change, neuropsychiatric or autonomic features, viral prodrome, faciobrachial seizures or dyskinesia, drug resistance, cancer, inflammatory CSF and limbic MRI change) to select patients for antibody testing; a score of 4 or more strongly predicts a positive result. Test serum and CSF together, since some antibodies are found mainly in CSF. Infections, particularly HSV, must be excluded early, and seronegative cases may still be autoimmune. RITE2 helps estimate the chance of response to immunotherapy.
det.treatment: Acute symptomatic seizures from cell-surface antibody encephalitis are treated with prompt first-line immunotherapy (high-dose methylprednisolone, IVIG 2 g/kg, or plasma exchange), escalating to rituximab or cyclophosphamide if response is incomplete, plus tumour removal where relevant. Antiseizure medicines control seizures meanwhile and can often be weaned after recovery. Autoimmune-associated epilepsy with GAD65 or onconeural antibodies responds poorly to immunotherapy and is managed like chronic drug-resistant focal epilepsy, sometimes including surgery. Sodium-channel blockers may be particularly useful in LGI1, with care regarding rash.
det.prognosis: Most cell-surface antibody syndromes become seizure-free with early immunotherapy, while intracellular antibody syndromes usually leave persisting epilepsy.
pearls: Cell-surface antibody = acute symptomatic seizures, usually reversible; intracellular antibody (GAD65) = lasting epilepsy.
APE2 ≥ 4 justifies antibody testing in new-onset drug-resistant epilepsy.
Faciobrachial dystonic seizures barely respond to ASMs but respond to immunotherapy.
det.thd: ลมชักจากภูมิคุ้มกันแบ่งตาม ILAE 2020 เป็นชักเฉียบพลันจาก autoimmune encephalitis (แอนติบอดีที่ผิวเซลล์ เช่น LGI1, NMDAR ซึ่งหายได้ด้วยการรักษาภูมิคุ้มกัน) และ autoimmune-associated epilepsy ที่เป็นถาวร (เช่น GAD65) ควรสงสัยเมื่อชักใหม่ ดื้อยาเร็ว ร่วมกับความจำเสียหรืออาการทางจิต ใช้ APE2 score ≥4 ช่วยตัดสินส่งตรวจแอนติบอดีในเลือดและน้ำไขสันหลัง รักษาด้วย steroid, IVIG หรือ plasma exchange และหามะเร็งร่วม

name: Familial hemiplegic migraine (FHM)
formal: A monogenic, autosomal dominant subtype of migraine with aura in which the aura includes fully reversible motor weakness together with visual, sensory or speech symptoms, and a parent, sibling, child or other close (first/second-degree) relative has the same kind of attack; known genes are CACNA1A (FHM1), ATP1A2 (FHM2), SCN1A (FHM3) and, less often, PRRT2.
simple: An inherited migraine where the warning symptoms include temporary weakness of one side of the body, and other family members have the same attacks.
ab: ไมเกรนอัมพาตครึ่งซีกทางพันธุกรรม
th: ไมเกรนชนิดมีออร่าที่ถ่ายทอดทางพันธุกรรมแบบยีนเด่น ออร่ามีแขนขาอ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกชั่วคราวร่วมกับตามัว ชา หรือพูดผิดปกติ และมีญาติใกล้ชิดเป็นแบบเดียวกัน
tempoNote: Onset usually in childhood or adolescence (often about 12–17 years); motor aura typically lasts 5 minutes to 72 hours but can persist for days to weeks
feat: Aura with motor weakness that spreads gradually (hand, then arm, then face) together with visual, sensory or language symptoms
Aura often longer than 60 minutes; headache may be mild or absent
Severe attacks: confusion, fever, coma, seizures, CSF pleocytosis and cortical oedema, sometimes after minor head trauma or angiography
FHM1 may add progressive cerebellar ataxia and nystagmus; FHM2 epilepsy and learning difficulty; FHM3 repetitive daily blindness
Familial attacks tend to be more frequent and severe than sporadic ones
inv: Urgent MRI with DWI and vascular imaging at a first attack to exclude stroke; may show cortical swelling or hypoperfusion
EEG during attacks shows contralateral slowing, which helps separate from Todd paralysis after seizures
Genetic testing of CACNA1A, ATP1A2, SCN1A and PRRT2
CSF only if fever or encephalopathy (may show pleocytosis); exclude infection

case.story: During school she saw flashing lights, then tingling spread from her right hand along the arm and into the face, followed by right arm weakness and difficulty speaking for three hours, then a throbbing headache. Her mother and uncle have had similar 'paralysis migraines'.
case.exam: Right arm power 3/5 at onset, normal by next day; mild gaze-evoked nystagmus.
case.tests: MRI with DWI and MRA normal. Genetic testing: pathogenic CACNA1A missense variant.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and which preventive medicines are reasonable?
case.a: Familial hemiplegic migraine type 1; prevention with verapamil, flunarizine, acetazolamide or lamotrigine (topiramate is of debated benefit), and counselling to avoid triggers such as minor head trauma.

read.where: Chapter 5: Biological science of headache channels

det.patho: All FHM genes increase neuronal or synaptic excitability: CACNA1A gain-of-function raises glutamate release, ATP1A2 loss impairs astrocytic clearance of potassium and glutamate, and SCN1A gain-of-function increases inhibitory interneuron firing that paradoxically promotes depolarisation. The result is a lowered threshold for strong cortical spreading depression, which explains the prolonged motor aura. Hemiplegic migraine is rare (around 0.01%), and familial and sporadic forms appear equally common.
det.clinical: Attacks typically begin in childhood or adolescence with a progressive aura of visual, sensory and motor symptoms, often lasting longer than typical aura. Weakness spreads gradually and can last hours to weeks; basilar features (vertigo, diplopia, dysarthria) are common. Severe attacks may produce encephalopathy, fever, seizures, coma, CSF lymphocytosis and swelling of one hemisphere, occasionally with permanent deficits. Episodic or progressive ataxia, epilepsy and intellectual disability occur in some genotypes, and families often report earlier and more severe attacks in younger members.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 requires migraine with aura including fully reversible motor weakness plus visual, sensory or speech symptoms, and a close (first- or second-degree) family member who has the same attacks. A first attack needs emergency stroke imaging; after diagnosis, repeated attacks with a known pattern need not be re-imaged each time unless atypical. Differential diagnosis includes TIA and stroke, seizures with post-ictal paresis, SMART after radiotherapy, HaNDL, MELAS, CADASIL, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, RVCL-S and moyamoya. A normal gene panel cannot rule out FHM.
det.treatment: Acute attacks are treated with NSAIDs, antiemetics and, in some patients, intranasal ketamine; triptans and ergots have traditionally been avoided due to vasoconstriction concerns, though small series suggest triptans may be tolerated, so decisions are individualised. Preventive options include verapamil, flunarizine, acetazolamide and lamotrigine; topiramate efficacy is debated. Patients should avoid known triggers, including minor head trauma, and should carry information about their diagnosis to prevent unnecessary thrombolysis. Data on CGRP-targeted therapies in hemiplegic migraine are limited.
det.prognosis: Attacks often lessen with age, but some patients develop persistent ataxia, cognitive impairment or, rarely, residual deficits after severe attacks.
pearls: Motor aura plus a relative with the same = FHM; test CACNA1A, ATP1A2, SCN1A, PRRT2.
Minor head trauma or cerebral angiography can trigger a severe, prolonged attack.
Prevention: verapamil, flunarizine, acetazolamide, lamotrigine — topiramate debated.
det.thd: FHM เป็นไมเกรนมีออร่าที่ถ่ายทอดแบบยีนเด่น ออร่ามีอ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกค่อย ๆ ลามจากมือขึ้นแขนและหน้า ร่วมกับตามัว ชา หรือพูดลำบาก อาจนานเกิน 60 นาทีถึงหลายวัน เกิดจากยีน CACNA1A, ATP1A2, SCN1A หรือ PRRT2 ที่ทำให้เกิด cortical spreading depression รุนแรง ครั้งแรกต้องทำ MRI แยก stroke และป้องกันด้วย verapamil, flunarizine, acetazolamide หรือ lamotrigine
