name: Sporadic hemiplegic migraine (SHM)
formal: Migraine with aura that includes fully reversible motor weakness plus visual, sensory or speech symptoms, in a person with no first- or second-degree relative affected; some cases harbour de novo variants in the same genes as familial hemiplegic migraine.
simple: Migraine with temporary one-sided weakness in someone whose family does not have the same problem.
th: ไมเกรนที่มีออร่าเป็นอ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกชั่วคราว แต่ไม่มีญาติเป็นแบบเดียวกัน อาการแยกจาก FHM ไม่ได้ บางรายเป็นยีนกลายพันธุ์ใหม่
tempoNote: First attacks usually in adolescence (similar age to FHM); motor aura from about 5 minutes to 72 hours, rarely longer
feat: Motor aura with gradual spread, accompanied by visual, sensory or speech aura, followed by headache in most
No affected first- or second-degree relatives
Clinically indistinguishable from familial forms, though usually less frequent and less severe
Frequently mistaken for stroke or TIA at first presentation
inv: First attack: emergency MRI with DWI plus vessel imaging, and stroke pathway review
EEG to exclude seizures with post-ictal weakness
Genetic panel (CACNA1A, ATP1A2, SCN1A, PRRT2), particularly with early onset or additional neurological features

case.story: She developed zigzag lights, then numbness and weakness spreading from the left hand to the face over 30 minutes, lasting four hours, then a severe headache. No relatives have migraine with weakness.
case.exam: Mild left pronator drift on arrival, resolved by the next morning.
case.tests: MRI with DWI and MRA normal; EEG showed right hemisphere slowing during the attack.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and when should the stroke team still be involved?
case.a: Sporadic hemiplegic migraine; every first or atypical episode must be managed as possible stroke until imaging excludes it.

det.patho: SHM shares the cortical spreading depression mechanism of FHM. A minority carry de novo or incompletely penetrant variants in CACNA1A, ATP1A2, SCN1A or PRRT2, while most have no identified variant and probably polygenic susceptibility. Prevalence is similar to familial forms.
det.clinical: Attacks resemble FHM, with progressive visual and sensory aura followed by motor weakness, often over 60 minutes, and headache. Age of onset is comparable, usually around adolescence. Attacks are generally less frequent and severe than in FHM, but prolonged attacks with confusion or seizures occur. Early-onset cases with epilepsy or ataxia are more likely to have a pathogenic variant.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 criteria match those for FHM except for the absence of an affected relative. Because a first attack is indistinguishable from stroke, imaging is mandatory, and atypical features (sudden onset, no positive aura, older age) should prompt full stroke and seizure work-up. Exclude secondary mimics such as HaNDL, MELAS, CADASIL, moyamoya and SMART. Genetic testing may reclassify some cases as de novo FHM.
det.treatment: Management mirrors FHM: NSAIDs and antiemetics acutely, with individualised decisions on triptans. Preventive options include verapamil, flunarizine, acetazolamide and lamotrigine, with debated benefit from topiramate. Patients should carry a note or card describing their diagnosis to avoid unnecessary thrombolysis, while recognising that a new pattern still requires evaluation.
det.prognosis: Most patients have intermittent attacks with full recovery, and frequency often lessens with age.
pearls: SHM and FHM look identical; the family history is the only difference.
Treat the first attack as stroke until proven otherwise.
Gene testing can convert apparently sporadic cases to de novo FHM.
det.thd: SHM คือไมเกรนที่มีอ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกเป็นออร่าแต่ไม่มีญาติเป็น อาการเหมือน FHM อายุเริ่มใกล้กันแต่มักรุนแรงและถี่น้อยกว่า การเป็นครั้งแรกต้องคิดถึง stroke และทำ MRI เสมอ การป้องกันใช้ verapamil, flunarizine, acetazolamide หรือ lamotrigine เช่นเดียวกับ FHM

name: Syndrome of transient headache and neurological deficits with CSF lymphocytosis (HaNDL)
formal: A self-limited syndrome of one to several episodes of migraine-like headache with transient neurological deficits (most often hemisensory, hemiparesis or aphasia) lasting hours, accompanied by CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis with negative infectious work-up and normal structural imaging, resolving within about three months.
simple: A rare condition in which a young adult has a few bouts of headache with stroke-like symptoms and inflamed spinal fluid, and then recovers completely.
ab: Syndrome of transient headache and neurological deficits with CSF lymphocytosis
transient headache and neurological deficits with CSF lymphocytosis
th: กลุ่มอาการที่มีปวดศีรษะคล้ายไมเกรนร่วมกับอาการทางระบบประสาทชั่วคราว เช่น ชาหรืออ่อนแรงครึ่งซีก พูดไม่ได้ และพบเม็ดเลือดขาว lymphocyte สูงในน้ำไขสันหลัง หายได้เองภายในราว 3 เดือน
tempoNote: One to about twelve episodes, each lasting hours (rarely over a day), clustered within up to 3 months; does not usually recur afterwards
feat: Young adults (about 15–50 years), slight male predominance, often no prior migraine
Moderate to severe headache with hemisensory symptoms, hemiparesis or aphasia; visual aura is less common
Viral-like prodrome in about a quarter to a third
CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis (often tens to hundreds of cells), raised protein and sometimes raised opening pressure
Complete recovery between episodes; normal structural MRI
inv: MRI with DWI and angiography: no infarct or vasculopathy; perfusion may show reversible hemispheric hypoperfusion
Lumbar puncture: lymphocytic pleocytosis with negative cultures, PCR and serology
EEG may show focal slowing during attacks

case.story: A week after a cold, he had three episodes in ten days of right-hand and face numbness with difficulty finding words for two to four hours, followed by severe bifrontal headache.
case.exam: Between episodes the examination is normal; no fever or neck stiffness.
case.tests: MRI with DWI and CTA normal. CSF: 85 lymphocytes/µL, protein 0.85 g/L, glucose normal; HSV PCR and cultures negative.
case.q: What syndrome is this, and what treatment mistake should be avoided?
case.a: HaNDL; recognising it prevents repeated thrombolysis or unnecessary long-term antimicrobial therapy — management is supportive once infection is excluded.

det.patho: The cause is unknown; a post-viral immune response triggering aseptic leptomeningeal inflammation and cortical spreading depression is suspected. Antibodies to the T-type calcium channel subunit CACNA1H have been reported in some patients, supporting an autoimmune mechanism. The syndrome is rare and probably underrecognised.
det.clinical: Patients develop recurrent episodes of headache, often throbbing and severe, with focal deficits that may evolve over minutes like an aura. Hemisensory symptoms are most common, followed by aphasia and hemiparesis, and some patients have confusion. Episodes last hours and recur across days to weeks. Between episodes and after the syndrome ends, patients are well.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 criteria include episodes of migraine-like headache with transient deficits, CSF lymphocytosis above 15 cells/µL with negative aetiological studies, and resolution within three months. Infective meningoencephalitis (particularly HSV, VZV, HIV, syphilis, Lyme), neurosarcoidosis, CNS vasculitis, leptomeningeal malignancy and stroke must be excluded. MRI should be normal apart from possible perfusion changes. Note that hemiplegic migraine may also show CSF pleocytosis during severe attacks, so family and long-term history matter.
det.treatment: Management is supportive with analgesics and antiemetics; antivirals may be started empirically until HSV is excluded. Thrombolysis is not indicated once the diagnosis is secure, but at first presentation acute stroke protocols may proceed because the diagnosis cannot be made immediately. There is no proven role for steroids or long-term prophylaxis. Reassure the patient that the syndrome is self-limited.
det.prognosis: Excellent; episodes stop within three months and recurrence later is uncommon.
pearls: FHM-like attacks plus lymphocytic CSF in a young adult = HaNDL.
A well patient between attacks with normal MRI and DWI argues against encephalitis.
Self-limited within 3 months — recurrence beyond that should prompt reassessment.
det.thd: HaNDL พบในผู้ใหญ่อายุน้อย มีปวดศีรษะคล้ายไมเกรนร่วมกับชา อ่อนแรงครึ่งซีก หรือพูดไม่ได้ครั้งละหลายชั่วโมง เป็นซ้ำได้หลายครั้งภายใน 3 เดือน น้ำไขสันหลังพบ lymphocyte สูงโปรตีนสูงแต่ไม่พบเชื้อ และ MRI ปกติ สาเหตุน่าจะเป็นภูมิคุ้มกันหลังติดเชื้อไวรัส รักษาตามอาการ หายเองได้ดี แต่ต้องแยกการติดเชื้อและ stroke ก่อนเสมอ

name: Late-life migraine accompaniments
formal: Recurrent transient neurological episodes resembling migraine aura — visual scintillations, spreading paraesthesia, speech disturbance — occurring in middle-aged or older adults, often without headache, described by C. Miller Fisher; it is a diagnosis made only after imaging and work-up exclude TIA, cerebral amyloid angiopathy and seizures.
simple: Migraine-type warning symptoms, such as flashing lights or tingling, that start in older people without a headache and turn out to be harmless once other causes are checked.
ab: migraine aura without headache in the elderly
th: อาการออร่าแบบไมเกรนที่เกิดในผู้สูงอายุ เช่น เห็นแสงระยิบ ชาลามไปตามแขน หรือพูดติดขัด มักไม่มีปวดศีรษะ ต้องแยกจาก TIA และ CAA ด้วยภาพถ่ายสมองก่อนวินิจฉัย
tempoNote: First appears after about 40–50 years; each episode builds over minutes and lasts about 15–60 minutes; may recur in clusters over months
feat: Positive symptoms (scintillations, tingling) that march or spread over several minutes
Successive symptoms (visual then sensory then speech) in sequence, not all at once
Headache absent or mild in most; prior migraine history in some but not all
Repeated identical episodes over months with no lasting deficit
Imaging normal for age; no convexity subarachnoid blood or siderosis
inv: MRI including DWI and susceptibility-weighted (SWI/T2*) sequences to exclude infarct, convexity SAH, cortical superficial siderosis and microbleeds
Vascular imaging (CTA/MRA or carotid ultrasound), ECG and cardiac rhythm monitoring as for TIA
EEG if symptoms are brief, stereotyped or include altered awareness

case.who: 68-year-old retired male civil servant from Lampang
case.story: Over four months he has had five episodes of shimmering zigzag lights in the right visual field, followed by tingling that spreads from the right fingers to the lips over ten minutes, each fully clearing within 40 minutes; no headache.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination; blood pressure 138/82.
case.tests: MRI with DWI and SWI: no infarct, microbleeds or cortical siderosis. Carotid duplex and 7-day Holter normal.
case.q: Why is imaging essential before calling these migraine accompaniments, and what treatment error must be avoided if the MRI had shown cortical siderosis?
case.a: Spreading positive symptoms favour migraine aura, but CAA-related transient focal neurological episodes look identical and can only be separated by blood-sensitive MRI; in CAA, starting antiplatelet or anticoagulant drugs raises the risk of lobar haemorrhage.

read.where: Chapter 11: Implementing the International Classification of Headache

det.patho: These episodes are thought to represent cortical spreading depression occurring without trigeminovascular activation, so the aura appears without headache. Ageing reduces headache expression in migraine, while aura may persist or appear for the first time. The concept was introduced by C. Miller Fisher, who collected cases mistakenly treated as cerebrovascular events.
det.clinical: Typical features include visual scintillations, spreading paraesthesias, speech disturbance and, less often, weakness, appearing gradually and moving from one modality to the next. Episodes usually last 15–60 minutes and may cluster. Headache is absent or minor, and many patients have no migraine history. The examination is normal between attacks.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is by exclusion: in an older adult, TIA and CAA-related transient focal neurological episodes (amyloid spells) can look the same, and only imaging distinguishes them. MRI must include DWI and blood-sensitive sequences to look for infarcts, convexity subarachnoid haemorrhage, cortical superficial siderosis and lobar microbleeds. Vascular and cardiac assessment proceeds as for TIA. Features that favour migraine aura include gradual spread, sequential symptoms, positive phenomena and identical repeated episodes.
det.treatment: Once alternative causes are excluded, reassurance is the main treatment, along with management of vascular risk factors. Frequent episodes may be reduced by preventive agents such as verapamil, lamotrigine or low-dose tricyclics, chosen with age-related side effects in mind. Avoid starting antithrombotic therapy reflexively, because in undetected CAA it increases haemorrhage risk. Re-evaluate if the pattern changes.
det.prognosis: Generally benign, though some studies suggest slightly higher vascular risk, so ongoing risk factor control is sensible.
pearls: Older person with aura and no headache: image with SWI before calling it migraine.
March and sequential symptoms favour aura; sudden maximal deficits favour TIA.
Amyloid spells mimic aura — antiplatelets can be harmful in CAA.
det.thd: Late-life migraine accompaniments คือออร่าแบบไมเกรนในผู้สูงอายุ เช่น เห็นแสงระยิบ ชาลามจากนิ้วขึ้นปาก หรือพูดติดขัดครั้งละ 15–60 นาที มักไม่ปวดศีรษะ ต้องแยกจาก TIA และ transient focal neurological episodes จาก CAA ซึ่งแยกได้ด้วย MRI ที่มี DWI และ SWI เท่านั้น ถ้าตรวจไม่พบสาเหตุอื่นให้ความมั่นใจผู้ป่วย และไม่ควรเริ่มยาต้านเกล็ดเลือดโดยอัตโนมัติ

name: Hypomelanosis of Ito (pigmentary mosaicism)
formal: A neurocutaneous phenotype in which streaks and whorls of hypopigmented skin follow the lines of Blaschko, reflecting a mosaic genetic change confined to some cell lines; brain involvement (developmental delay, epilepsy, asymmetric brain overgrowth) occurs in a large minority.
simple: A skin pattern of pale swirls caused by a gene change present in only some of the body's cells, sometimes with learning problems and seizures.
th: ภาวะผิวหนังเป็นแถบหรือวงขาวซีดตามแนว Blaschko จาก mosaicism ของยีนหรือโครโมโซม บางรายมีพัฒนาการช้า ลมชัก และสมองซีกหนึ่งโตผิดปกติ
tempoNote: Skin pattern present at birth or noticed in infancy; neurological features (delay, seizures) appear in the first years and are static rather than progressive
feat: Pale whorls, swirls and stripes tracking Blaschko lines on trunk and limbs, without a preceding blister or warty stage
Developmental delay or intellectual disability and autism features in a substantial subset
Seizures, sometimes infantile spasms, often drug-resistant when a cortical malformation is present
Asymmetry: hemimegalencephaly, limb or facial hemihypertrophy
Extra-cutaneous findings: eye, dental, hair and skeletal anomalies
inv: Wood lamp examination to make faint pale streaks visible in fair skin
Karyotype or microarray on skin fibroblasts or buccal cells; blood may be normal because the variant is mosaic
MRI brain for hemimegalencephaly, polymicrogyria, heterotopia or white matter change
EEG when spells or regression occur

case.who: 18-month-old girl from Khon Kaen brought by her grandmother
case.story: Clusters of brief flexion jerks on waking for three weeks; she is not yet walking and says no words.
case.exam: Swirled, marble-cake pale streaks over the trunk and left leg, sharpest under Wood lamp; head circumference 75th centile with a larger left skull; mild right-sided hypotonia.
case.tests: EEG hypsarrhythmia; MRI shows an enlarged left hemisphere with thick cortex; blood karyotype normal, skin fibroblasts show mosaic trisomy.
case.q: What links the skin, the seizures and the asymmetric brain?
case.a: Hypomelanosis of Ito from chromosomal mosaicism with hemimegalencephaly causing infantile spasms; she needs urgent spasm treatment and epilepsy surgery assessment.

read.where: Section II: Epidemiology, Etiology, and Diagnosis

det.patho: The term is now treated as a descriptive phenotype rather than a single disease: a post-zygotic genetic change creates two populations of skin cells that differ in pigment output, and their migration during embryogenesis paints the Blaschko pattern. Causes include mosaic aneuploidy or structural chromosome changes and mosaic single-gene variants, notably in mTOR-pathway and chromatin genes. The same mosaic clone may sit in brain tissue, explaining cortical malformations and unilateral overgrowth.
det.clinical: Skin findings are usually the first clue, ranging from obvious stripes to marks that only show under ultraviolet light. Neurological involvement is variable: many children are cognitively typical, whereas those with brain malformations show delay, autism, epilepsy (including infantile spasms) and focal motor signs. Body asymmetry, strabismus, dental anomalies and scalp hair changes may accompany the skin pattern. Course is static; worsening suggests uncontrolled seizures rather than progression of the condition.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on recognising the linear-whorled hypopigmentation and excluding a prior inflammatory or vesicular phase (which would point to incontinentia pigmenti). Because the variant is mosaic, blood studies are often normal; testing a skin biopsy, fibroblasts or buccal cells with microarray or deep sequencing raises yield. MRI and EEG define brain involvement. Examine the eyes, teeth and limbs for associated anomalies.
det.treatment: No therapy alters the pigment pattern, and it needs none. Management is developmental: early intervention, education support and autism services. Seizures are treated by type, with ACTH, prednisolone or vigabatrin for infantile spasms; refractory epilepsy with hemimegalencephaly should be referred early for hemispherotomy assessment. Genetic counselling is generally reassuring because most mosaic changes are not inherited.
det.prognosis: Outcome depends almost entirely on brain involvement; children without cortical malformation or epilepsy often develop normally.
pearls: Blaschko lines form V shapes on the back and S-shaped whorls on the flank — a sign of mosaicism, not of a single disease.
Normal blood karyotype does not exclude mosaicism; test skin or buccal cells.
Hemimegalencephaly with drug-resistant spasms: think early hemispherotomy.
det.thd: Hypomelanosis of Ito ปัจจุบันถือเป็นลักษณะของ pigmentary mosaicism คือมียีนหรือโครโมโซมผิดปกติในเซลล์เพียงบางส่วน ทำให้ผิวเป็นริ้วหรือวงขาวซีดตามแนว Blaschko เด็กบางรายมีสมองผิดรูปร่วม เช่น hemimegalencephaly จึงพัฒนาการช้าและชักยาก การตรวจเลือดอาจปกติ ควรตรวจจากผิวหนังหรือกระพุ้งแก้ม การรักษาเน้นควบคุมชักและส่งเสริมพัฒนาการ รายชักดื้อยาควรประเมินผ่าตัด

ddx.pt: Pale lesions are discrete ash-leaf or confetti macules, not Blaschko streaks; tubers, SEN and cardiac rhabdomyoma
Hyperpigmented café-au-lait spots and freckling, neurofibromas and optic glioma
Port-wine facial stain with leptomeningeal angioma and cortical calcification, not hypopigmented whorls

name: Incontinentia pigmenti (IP)
formal: An X-linked dominant ectodermal disorder due to inactivating IKBKG (NEMO) variants, usually lethal in male fetuses, in which girls show staged skin lesions along Blaschko lines with variable involvement of teeth, hair, nails, retina and brain.
simple: A gene disorder in girls that causes blisters, then warty patches, then brown swirls on the skin, and can damage the eyes and brain.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมถ่ายทอดแบบ X-linked dominant จากยีน IKBKG (NEMO) พบเกือบทั้งหมดในเพศหญิง มีผื่นผิวหนังเปลี่ยนเป็นระยะตามแนว Blaschko ร่วมกับความผิดปกติของฟัน จอประสาทตา และสมอง
tempoNote: Skin passes through stages from birth to adulthood; brain injury (neonatal seizures, infarcts) usually happens in the first weeks and is then static
feat: Neonatal red papules and blisters in lines, followed by warty plaques, then grey-brown swirls, finally pale atrophic hairless streaks
Neonatal seizures, encephalopathy and focal infarcts or haemorrhage from small vessel occlusion
Retinal vasculopathy with avascular periphery, neovascularisation and risk of detachment
Peg-shaped or missing teeth, patchy scalp alopecia and nail dystrophy
Mother or sisters with subtle skin or dental signs; history of miscarried male pregnancies
inv: Blood count: marked eosinophilia during the blistering stage
Skin biopsy in the vesicular stage: eosinophilic spongiosis
IKBKG testing (the common exon 4–10 deletion needs a targeted assay) and X-inactivation study
Early MRI brain and dilated retinal examination with repeat screening

case.who: 7-day-old girl in a provincial hospital nursery in Nakhon Si Thammarat
case.story: Developed lines of red, crusting blisters on both legs at day 3 and then repeated right arm twitching.
case.exam: Linear vesicles following whorled bands on legs and trunk; right arm clonic jerks; afebrile; mother has a few conical teeth and a patch of thin scalp hair.
case.tests: Eosinophils 18%; CSF and HSV PCR negative; MRI DWI shows scattered left frontal cortical and white matter restriction; EEG left frontal seizures.
case.q: What unifies the blisters, the family clues and the seizures?
case.a: Incontinentia pigmenti (IKBKG): neonatal inflammatory small vessel injury to the brain; she needs seizure control, urgent retinal screening and genetic testing of mother and baby.

read.where: Section II: Epidemiology, Etiology, and Diagnosis

det.patho: NEMO is the regulatory subunit of the IKK complex needed to activate NF-kB, which protects cells against TNF-driven apoptosis. In females random X-inactivation leaves a mosaic of normal and NEMO-deficient cells; deficient cells die early and provoke inflammation, eventually leaving skewed X-inactivation. Hemizygous males usually die in utero, except those with mosaicism or Klinefelter karyotype; hypomorphic variants in boys cause a different immunodeficiency with ectodermal dysplasia. Brain and retinal damage arise from inflammatory occlusive small vessel disease in the newborn period.
det.clinical: Skin stages overlap and may be missed: blistering in the first weeks, warty lesions in months, then hyperpigmented whorls through childhood, finally pale atrophic streaks in adults, sometimes the only clue in mothers. About a third have neurological involvement, mostly neonatal seizures, encephalopathy and focal infarcts leading to hemiparesis, epilepsy or intellectual disability; later-onset problems are uncommon. Retinal ischaemia can cause detachment and blindness, so eye screening is time-critical. Teeth, hair and nails are affected in most.
det.diagnosis: Clinical criteria combine typical skin stages along Blaschko lines with minor features (dental, hair, nail, retinal) and family history; molecular confirmation of IKBKG is standard, using an assay that detects the recurrent large deletion. Eosinophilia and skin histology support the diagnosis early. Neonates with seizures need MRI with DWI and susceptibility imaging, and infection must be excluded before attributing blisters to IP.
det.treatment: There is no disease-specific therapy. Treat seizures conventionally; some centres use short courses of corticosteroids in neonates with active brain inflammation, but evidence is limited. Arrange retinal examination soon after diagnosis and repeatedly in early childhood, with laser or cryotherapy for neovascularisation. Gentle skin care prevents infection of blisters; dental rehabilitation and genetic counselling for the family (50% risk to each daughter, male pregnancy loss) complete care.
det.prognosis: Children without neonatal brain involvement usually have normal intelligence; neurological and retinal complications determine long-term disability.
pearls: Linear blisters plus eosinophilia in a newborn girl: think IP, but exclude HSV first.
Ask the mother about conical teeth, miscarriages and pale streaks on her legs.
Retinal screening is urgent because ischaemic retinopathy is treatable before detachment.
det.thd: Incontinentia pigmenti เกิดจากยีน IKBKG (NEMO) บนโครโมโซม X จึงพบในเด็กหญิง ส่วนทารกชายมักเสียชีวิตในครรภ์ ผื่นเริ่มเป็นตุ่มน้ำเรียงเป็นเส้น ต่อมาเป็นปื้นหนา แล้วเป็นสีน้ำตาลเป็นวง และสุดท้ายเป็นแถบซีด ทารกบางรายชักและมีสมองขาดเลือดจุดเล็ก ๆ ในช่วงแรกเกิด และมีหลอดเลือดจอตาผิดปกติ จึงต้องตรวจตาเร็ว การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคองร่วมกับให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรมแก่ครอบครัว

Pale macules, tubers and cardiac rhabdomyoma; no blistering-to-pigment stage sequence

name: Wyburn-Mason syndrome (Bonnet–Dechaume–Blanc syndrome)
formal: A rare, non-inherited congenital disorder in which arteriovenous malformations of the retina are linked with ipsilateral AVMs along the visual pathway (optic nerve, chiasm, thalamus, midbrain) and sometimes the face and jaw; it is now grouped with the craniofacial arteriovenous metameric syndromes.
simple: A birth defect where tangled abnormal vessels in one eye are joined by similar tangles in the brain on the same side.
th: กลุ่มอาการแต่กำเนิดที่ไม่ถ่ายทอดทางพันธุกรรม มี AVM ที่จอประสาทตาร่วมกับ AVM ในสมองข้างเดียวกันตามแนวทางเดินการมองเห็น อาจทำให้ตามัว เลือดออกในสมอง หรือชัก
tempoNote: Congenital lesion with slowly progressive visual loss; acute events from haemorrhage (brain, retina, gums or nose) at any age
feat: Unilateral, dilated and tortuous retinal vessels (racemose AVM) with reduced acuity or field loss in that eye
Ipsilateral intracranial AVM along the optic nerve, chiasm, thalamus or midbrain
Proptosis, headache, hemianopia or brainstem signs from mass effect or steal
Facial or maxillo-mandibular vascular lesions with risk of severe bleeding at dental extraction
Intracranial or subarachnoid haemorrhage, seizures
inv: Dilated fundoscopy and fluorescein angiography of the retinal AVM
MRI with MRA of brain and orbits along the whole visual pathway
Catheter angiography to map feeders before any intervention
Dental and facial vascular assessment before extractions or facial surgery

case.who: 22-year-old female university student from Chiang Mai
case.story: Gradual blurring of the right eye since secondary school; this morning she had a sudden severe headache with vomiting.
case.exam: Right visual acuity counting fingers, relative afferent pupillary defect; right fundus shows large, worm-like dilated vessels without a capillary bed; left homonymous visual field defect; neck stiffness.
case.tests: CT shows right thalamic haemorrhage with intraventricular extension; angiography reveals an AVM running from the right optic tract into the thalamus and midbrain.
case.q: What single diagnosis explains the eye and the bleed?
case.a: Wyburn-Mason syndrome: retinal AVM with an ipsilateral retino-cerebral AVM that has bled.

read.where: Section 3 Hereditary and Genetic Conditions and Malformations

det.patho: The malformations are thought to arise from a segmental developmental error in the neural crest and mesoderm that will form the optic vesicle, diencephalon, midbrain and face, so lesions line up in one metamere on one side. Direct artery-to-vein shunts without capillaries enlarge slowly and can bleed, compress neighbouring tissue or steal flow. There is no recognised inheritance pattern, and only several hundred cases are reported.
det.clinical: Most cases come to attention in childhood or early adulthood through visual loss in one eye, often found incidentally on fundoscopy. The retinal lesion may cause vein occlusion, neovascular glaucoma or vitreous haemorrhage. Brain lesions present with headache, hemianopia, hemiparesis, cranial neuropathies, seizures or haemorrhage; large orbital lesions give proptosis. Facial and jaw lesions can bleed catastrophically after tooth extraction.
det.diagnosis: Fundoscopy showing a unilateral high-flow retinal AVM should prompt brain and orbit MRI/MRA. Catheter angiography defines the extent and the arterial supply. Exclude other syndromic vascular conditions: HHT (multiple, inherited, mucocutaneous telangiectasia), VHL (haemangioblastomas) and Sturge–Weber (capillary-venous lesions). Ophthalmology, neurosurgery and neuro-interventional teams should review together.
det.treatment: Retinal AVMs are generally observed; laser, anti-VEGF or vitrectomy treat complications. Intracranial AVMs are often deep and extensive along eloquent visual and brainstem structures, so surgery is rarely feasible; embolisation and radiosurgery are considered case by case, and many are managed conservatively with blood pressure control and seizure treatment. Warn dentists and surgeons about facial lesions.
det.prognosis: Vision in the affected eye is often poor; life-threatening risk comes from haemorrhage of the deep intracranial malformation.
pearls: One eye with a tangle of large retinal vessels: image the whole visual pathway on the same side.
Non-inherited and one-sided, unlike HHT and VHL.
Dental extraction near a jaw lesion can cause torrential bleeding.
det.thd: Wyburn-Mason syndrome เป็นความผิดปกติแต่กำเนิดที่ไม่ถ่ายทอดทางพันธุกรรม มี AVM ที่จอตาข้างหนึ่งร่วมกับ AVM ในสมองข้างเดียวกันตามแนว optic nerve, chiasm, thalamus และ midbrain ผู้ป่วยมักตามัวข้างเดียว บางรายมีเลือดออกในสมอง ชัก หรือลานสายตาผิดปกติ วินิจฉัยด้วยการส่องจอตา MRI/MRA และ angiography การรักษาส่วนใหญ่เป็นแบบติดตามเพราะรอยโรคอยู่ลึก และต้องระวังเลือดออกรุนแรงหากถอนฟันบริเวณที่มีรอยโรค

name: Sjögren–Larsson syndrome (SLS)
formal: An autosomal recessive neurocutaneous disorder of fatty aldehyde metabolism caused by biallelic ALDH3A2 variants, characterised by congenital ichthyosis, spastic diplegia or tetraplegia and intellectual disability, with a distinctive white matter disease and crystalline macular dots.
simple: An inherited disorder causing scaly itchy skin from birth, stiff legs and slow learning, because the body cannot break down certain fats.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมถ่ายทอดแบบยีนด้อยจากยีน ALDH3A2 ทำให้สลายไขมันกลุ่ม fatty aldehyde ไม่ได้ มีผิวหนังเป็นเกล็ดตั้งแต่แรกเกิด ขาเกร็ง (spastic diplegia) และสติปัญญาบกพร่อง
tempoNote: Ichthyosis at or soon after birth; spasticity emerges in the first 1–3 years and then changes little, with slow decline in some adults
feat: Generalised, itchy, dark, lamellar scaling, heaviest on neck, flexures and lower abdomen; face often spared
Spastic diplegia more than arms, toe walking, contractures — many never walk independently
Intellectual disability, speech delay and sometimes seizures
Glistening yellow-white crystalline dots around the fovea; photophobia
Preterm birth is common; parents may be consanguineous
inv: MRI brain: periventricular and deep white matter T2 hyperintensity, mostly frontal–parietal
MR spectroscopy: abnormal lipid peak near 1.3 ppm in white matter — a characteristic clue
ALDH3A2 sequencing; FALDH enzyme activity in fibroblasts; raised urinary leukotriene B4
Fundoscopy for macular crystalline dots

case.who: 3-year-old boy from Yala, son of first-cousin parents
case.story: Born at 35 weeks with dry, peeling skin that never improved; walks only on tiptoes holding furniture and uses few words.
case.exam: Thick, brownish scaling on neck and trunk with constant scratching; brisk reflexes, scissoring and ankle clonus in both legs; arms mildly affected.
case.tests: MRI: bilateral periventricular white matter signal change; MRS shows a lipid peak in white matter; fundus has shiny perifoveal dots; ALDH3A2 biallelic variant.
case.q: Why do ichthyosis and spastic diplegia occur together here?
case.a: Sjögren–Larsson syndrome: FALDH deficiency affects both skin barrier lipids and myelin, giving ichthyosis plus spastic diplegia.

read.where: Genetic Diseases of the Nervous System — Neurocutaneous Disorders: Sjögren-Larsson Syndrome

det.patho: Fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase converts long-chain aliphatic aldehydes to fatty acids; its loss causes aldehydes and related lipids to accumulate and to form adducts with proteins and lipids. In skin this disturbs the lamellar lipid barrier, producing ichthyosis; in brain it disrupts myelin, giving white matter disease; leukotriene B4 is not degraded, which may drive itch. Inheritance is autosomal recessive, and the condition is more frequent in founder populations.
det.clinical: Infants are often born preterm with redness and scaling that evolves into persistent itchy ichthyosis. Motor delay with spasticity of legs more than arms appears in the first years, together with intellectual disability that is usually moderate. About a third to half develop seizures. Photophobia and reduced acuity with perifoveal glistening dots are typical. The neurological picture is largely stable after early childhood, though some adults lose mobility.
det.diagnosis: The triad of congenital ichthyosis, spastic diplegia and intellectual disability is highly suggestive. MRI shows bilateral white matter hyperintensity with relative sparing of U fibres, and MRS adds a lipid peak that is unusual for other leukoencephalopathies. Confirm with ALDH3A2 sequencing or fibroblast enzyme assay. Distinguish from other ichthyosis syndromes with neurological involvement, such as multiple sulfatase deficiency and Refsum disease.
det.treatment: Care is supportive and multidisciplinary: emollients and keratolytics for skin, physiotherapy, orthoses, botulinum toxin and orthopaedic surgery for spasticity and contractures, education support and seizure treatment. Zileuton, a leukotriene synthesis inhibitor, has been used for itch with variable benefit. Aldehyde-trapping agents have been studied for skin disease but are not established practice. Offer genetic counselling to families.
det.prognosis: Most survive into adulthood; disability is dominated by spasticity and intellectual impairment.
pearls: Ichthyosis + spastic diplegia + intellectual disability = think SLS.
A white matter lipid peak on MRS is a strong imaging clue.
Unrelated to Sjögren syndrome (sicca) — a common name trap.
det.thd: Sjögren–Larsson syndrome เกิดจากยีน ALDH3A2 ผิดปกติแบบยีนด้อย ทำให้ร่างกายสลาย fatty aldehyde ไม่ได้ ไขมันสะสมที่ผิวหนังและ myelin เด็กจึงมีผิวหนังเป็นเกล็ดคันตั้งแต่เกิด ขาเกร็งแบบ spastic diplegia และพัฒนาการช้า MRI พบรอยโรคที่ white matter และ MRS มี lipid peak ส่วนจอตามีจุดขาวแวววาว การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง ดูแลผิว ลดเกร็ง และกายภาพบำบัด

name: Classical homocystinuria (cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency)
formal: An autosomal recessive disorder of methionine metabolism caused by CBS deficiency, producing very high plasma total homocysteine with lens dislocation, marfanoid habitus, intellectual disability, osteoporosis and arterial and venous thromboembolism including stroke and cerebral venous thrombosis.
simple: An inherited enzyme problem that lets homocysteine build up in the blood, causing clots and strokes in young people, dislocated eye lenses and learning problems.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมแบบยีนด้อยที่ขาดเอนไซม์ cystathionine beta-synthase ทำให้ homocysteine ในเลือดสูงมาก เกิดเลนส์ตาเคลื่อน รูปร่างคล้าย Marfan สติปัญญาบกพร่อง และลิ่มเลือดอุดตันทั้งหลอดเลือดแดงและดำ รวมถึง stroke และ CVT ในคนอายุน้อย
tempoNote: Lifelong metabolic disease; strokes, venous thrombosis and seizures occur as acute events, often triggered by surgery, dehydration or immobility
feat: Ectopia lentis (typically displaced downward), severe myopia
Tall, thin build with long limbs, scoliosis and osteoporosis — mimics Marfan but with stiff rather than lax joints
Arterial ischaemic stroke, cerebral venous thrombosis, DVT/PE at a young age
Intellectual disability, psychiatric symptoms and seizures in B6-non-responsive forms
Thrombosis risk rises around surgery, anaesthesia and pregnancy
inv: Plasma total homocysteine (often > 100 µmol/L untreated) with high methionine and low cystathionine
Check B12, folate and renal function to exclude acquired causes; CBS gene testing
Pyridoxine responsiveness trial with repeat homocysteine
MRI/MRV and arterial imaging after neurological events; slit-lamp examination

case.who: 19-year-old male vocational student from Nakhon Ratchasima
case.story: Sudden right-sided weakness and inability to speak; as a child he had surgery for dislocated lenses and needed extra help at school.
case.exam: Tall and slim, high-arched palate, thick glasses; right hemiparesis and non-fluent aphasia; joints are not hypermobile.
case.tests: MRI left MCA infarct; echocardiogram and aorta normal; plasma total homocysteine 210 µmol/L, methionine raised; B12 normal.
case.q: Which metabolic disorder caused a stroke in this young man with 'Marfan-like' features?
case.a: Classical homocystinuria (CBS deficiency); start pyridoxine, folate, B12, betaine and a low-methionine diet, and screen siblings.

det.patho: CBS uses pyridoxal phosphate to join homocysteine and serine into cystathionine. When it fails, homocysteine and methionine accumulate; homocysteine damages endothelium, promotes platelet activation and coagulation, and interferes with collagen and fibrillin cross-linking, explaining lens zonule failure and skeletal changes. Roughly half of patients have residual enzyme activity that improves with high-dose pyridoxine. Other inherited causes of severe homocystinuria — remethylation defects such as MTHFR deficiency and cobalamin C disease — present differently and have low methionine.
det.clinical: Presentation is usually in childhood with lens dislocation and myopia, developmental delay, or a marfanoid build, but milder B6-responsive patients may first appear as adults with thrombosis. Thromboembolism affects veins and arteries of any size, causing stroke, sinus thrombosis, pulmonary embolism and peripheral arterial events; it is the main cause of death. Psychiatric illness, seizures and extrapyramidal signs can occur. Without treatment about half have a vascular event by around 30 years of age.
det.diagnosis: Measure fasting plasma total homocysteine in any young patient with unexplained stroke or venous thrombosis plus lens, skeletal or developmental clues. Classical CBS deficiency shows very high homocysteine with high methionine; remethylation defects have low or normal methionine. Exclude B12 and folate deficiency, renal failure and drugs. Confirm with CBS sequencing, and test pyridoxine response. Newborn screening by methionine misses many B6-responsive cases.
det.treatment: Give pyridoxine at escalating doses and assess response; add folate and B12. Non-responders and partial responders need a methionine-restricted diet with methionine-free amino acid supplements and betaine, which remethylates homocysteine to methionine. Targets are commonly a total homocysteine below about 100 µmol/L, and lower (around 50) in B6-responsive patients. Stroke and thrombosis are treated conventionally; extra precautions are needed around surgery and pregnancy (hydration, thromboprophylaxis), and nitrous oxide should be avoided because it impairs remethylation.
det.prognosis: Early detection and good metabolic control greatly reduce vascular events and preserve intellect; poorly controlled adults remain at high thrombotic risk.
pearls: Young stroke + lens dislocation + 'Marfan' body: check homocysteine.
Lens displacement: downward in homocystinuria, upward in Marfan (classic exam point, not absolute).
Avoid nitrous oxide anaesthesia and plan thromboprophylaxis for any surgery.
det.thd: Classical homocystinuria เกิดจากขาดเอนไซม์ CBS ทำให้ homocysteine และ methionine ในเลือดสูงมาก ผู้ป่วยมีเลนส์ตาเคลื่อน รูปร่างสูงผอมคล้าย Marfan แต่ข้อไม่หลวม สติปัญญาบกพร่อง และเกิดลิ่มเลือดอุดตันได้ทั้ง stroke, CVT และ DVT ตั้งแต่อายุน้อย ควรตรวจ total homocysteine ในผู้ป่วย stroke อายุน้อยที่มีลักษณะชวนสงสัย การรักษาใช้ pyridoxine (B6), folate, B12, betaine และอาหารจำกัด methionine และต้องระวังลิ่มเลือดช่วงผ่าตัดหรือตั้งครรภ์

name: Pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE)
formal: An autosomal recessive disorder of ectopic calcification caused by ABCC6 variants, in which elastic fibres of skin, Bruch membrane and medium-sized arteries become mineralised, giving characteristic skin papules, angioid streaks with choroidal neovascularisation, premature peripheral arterial disease and an increased risk of small vessel ischaemic stroke.
simple: An inherited disease where calcium builds up in elastic tissue, causing yellow bumpy skin on the neck, eye bleeding and narrowed arteries that can lead to strokes.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมแบบยีนด้อยจากยีน ABCC6 ทำให้มีแคลเซียมเกาะเส้นใย elastic ในผิวหนัง จอประสาทตา และผนังหลอดเลือด มีตุ่มเหลืองที่ข้างคอ angioid streaks และเสี่ยงหลอดเลือดแดงตีบและ stroke จากหลอดเลือดเล็ก
tempoNote: Skin changes in childhood or adolescence, visual loss from mid-adulthood; strokes and TIAs occur as acute events on a slowly progressive arteriopathy
feat: Small yellowish papules coalescing into soft, lax plaques on the sides of the neck, axillae, groin and antecubital fossae
Angioid streaks on fundoscopy; central visual loss from choroidal neovascularisation and bleeding
Early intermittent claudication with calcified, narrowed limb arteries; GI bleeding occasionally
Lacunar infarcts, white matter disease and TIAs at a young age; intracranial arterial stenosis
Hypertension is common and adds to stroke risk
inv: Skin biopsy from a lesion with calcium (von Kossa) stain showing fragmented, mineralised elastic fibres
ABCC6 genetic testing
Dilated fundoscopy and OCT angiography by ophthalmology
MRI brain for lacunes and white matter change; vascular imaging; ankle–brachial index

case.story: Two brief episodes of left hand and face numbness this month; for years she has had calf pain walking uphill and her central vision in the right eye became distorted last year.
case.exam: Yellow, cobblestone papules on both sides of the neck and in the axillae; weak foot pulses; neurological examination now normal.
case.tests: Fundus: grey-brown angioid streaks radiating from both discs with a right macular scar; MRI: several small deep infarcts and periventricular white matter change; skin biopsy shows calcified elastic fibres.
case.q: What systemic disease links her skin, eyes, legs and brain?
case.a: Pseudoxanthoma elasticum (ABCC6) with small vessel cerebral ischaemia and peripheral arterial disease.

det.patho: ABCC6 is a transporter mainly expressed in liver; its loss lowers circulating inorganic pyrophosphate, the main natural brake on soft tissue calcification. Elastic fibres in dermis, Bruch membrane and the internal elastic lamina of medium arteries therefore mineralise and fragment. Arterial disease involves narrowing and stiffening rather than aneurysm in most cases; cerebral involvement is predominantly small vessel disease, with occasional large intracranial stenosis.
det.clinical: Skin lesions on the neck and flexures usually appear in childhood or adolescence and are often ignored as cosmetic. Angioid streaks are almost universal by adulthood, and choroidal neovascularisation can cause sudden central visual loss, sometimes after minor eye trauma. Peripheral arterial disease begins unusually early. Neurologically, patients show lacunar infarcts, TIAs, white matter changes and vascular cognitive decline; reports of intracranial aneurysms exist but the association is uncertain.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis combines typical skin lesions, angioid streaks and either a skin biopsy with calcified elastic fibres or biallelic ABCC6 variants. Young adults with lacunar stroke or early claudication should be examined for neck papules and fundal streaks. Brain MRI and vascular imaging characterise cerebral involvement. Look for PXE-like phenotypes (e.g. GGCX-related disease) and haemoglobinopathies, which can also cause angioid streaks.
det.treatment: No therapy reverses calcification. Stroke prevention follows standard practice: antiplatelet therapy after ischaemic events, strict blood pressure, lipid and glucose control, and smoking cessation; aspirin is used thoughtfully because of retinal and GI bleeding risk. Intravitreal anti-VEGF injections have transformed outcomes of choroidal neovascularisation. Avoid contact sports that risk eye injury. Pyrophosphate-based and other anti-calcification therapies are in trials.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is near normal, but central vision loss and cerebral small vessel disease drive disability.
pearls: 'Plucked chicken skin' on the neck in a young lacunar stroke patient — look at the fundus for angioid streaks.
Angioid streaks: PXE, Paget disease of bone, sickle cell disease and Ehlers–Danlos are classic causes.
Anti-VEGF has made sight-saving treatment available for the eye complication.
det.thd: Pseudoxanthoma elasticum เกิดจากยีน ABCC6 ทำให้ pyrophosphate ในเลือดต่ำ แคลเซียมจึงเกาะเส้นใย elastic ที่ผิวหนัง จอตา และหลอดเลือดแดง ผู้ป่วยมีตุ่มสีเหลืองข้างคอและข้อพับ angioid streaks ที่จอตาและอาจเกิดเส้นเลือดงอกใหม่จนตามัว มีหลอดเลือดแดงขาตีบเร็ว และ lacunar stroke หรือ white matter disease ตั้งแต่อายุน้อย ยังไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ การดูแลคือควบคุมปัจจัยเสี่ยงหลอดเลือด ใช้ยาต้านเกล็ดเลือดอย่างระวัง และฉีด anti-VEGF เข้าตาเมื่อมีภาวะแทรกซ้อนที่จอตา

name: Marfan syndrome — neurological and neurovascular aspects
formal: An autosomal dominant fibrillin-1 (FBN1) disorder of connective tissue with aortic root dilatation, ectopia lentis and skeletal overgrowth, whose neurological complications include dural ectasia with spontaneous intracranial hypotension, stroke from aortic dissection or valve-related embolism, cervical artery dissection and spinal cord ischaemia.
simple: An inherited weakness of connective tissue that makes people tall with loose joints and weak blood vessels, which can cause leaking spinal fluid, torn arteries and strokes.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมแบบยีนเด่นจากยีน FBN1 มีเส้นเลือดใหญ่ aortic root โป่ง เลนส์ตาเคลื่อน และรูปร่างสูงแขนขายาว ทางระบบประสาทพบ dural ectasia ทำให้ CSF รั่ว (SIH) stroke จาก aortic dissection หรือลิ่มเลือดจากลิ้นหัวใจ และหลอดเลือดคอฉีกขาด
tempoNote: Lifelong condition; neurological events are acute (stroke, dissection, paraplegia) or subacute (orthostatic headache from CSF leak)
feat: Tall stature, arm span greater than height, arachnodactyly, chest wall deformity, scoliosis, lax joints; upward lens dislocation
Lumbosacral dural ectasia in most adults: low back pain, radicular symptoms, and spontaneous CSF leak with orthostatic headache
Stroke from aortic dissection extending into neck vessels, from mitral/aortic valve disease and AF, or after aortic surgery
Acute paraplegia from spinal cord ischaemia when aortic dissection or repair compromises segmental arteries
Cervical artery dissection and intracranial aneurysm are reported, though the link is weaker than in vascular EDS or Loeys–Dietz
inv: Echocardiography for aortic root Z-score and valves; CT/MR angiography of the whole aorta when symptoms arise
FBN1 genetic testing; apply the revised Ghent criteria
Spine MRI for dural ectasia and extradural CSF; brain MRI for features of intracranial hypotension
CTA/MRA head and neck in stroke or neck pain

case.who: 28-year-old male basketball coach from Bangkok, previously told he has 'loose lenses'
case.story: Ten days of headache that appears within minutes of standing and goes away when lying flat, with neck ache and muffled hearing.
case.exam: Very tall with long fingers, positive wrist and thumb signs, pectus excavatum; diastolic murmur; neurological examination normal.
case.tests: Echo: aortic root Z-score 3.2; MRI brain: diffuse pachymeningeal enhancement, sagging brainstem; spine MRI: wide lumbosacral dural sac with extradural fluid.
case.q: What causes the headache, and what else must be monitored?
case.a: Spontaneous intracranial hypotension from a CSF leak through Marfan dural ectasia; he also needs regular aortic root surveillance and blood pressure control.

read.where: Section 3 Hereditary and Genetic Conditions and Malformations

det.patho: Fibrillin-1 forms the microfibril scaffold of elastic fibres and regulates TGF-beta availability. Defective fibrillin weakens the aortic media, lens zonules and dura, while excess TGF-beta signalling promotes progressive aortic dilatation. Dural weakness lets the thecal sac balloon under CSF pressure, scalloping vertebrae and creating meningeal diverticula that may rupture. Most cases are inherited dominantly, with about a quarter arising de novo.
det.clinical: Neurologists meet Marfan patients through orthostatic headache from CSF leaks, back pain and radiculopathy from dural ectasia, or stroke. Strokes may be embolic (valve prolapse, AF, prosthetic valves), result from dissection extending into the carotids, or occur peri-operatively; abrupt paraplegia accompanies thoracoabdominal dissection. Sudden chest or back pain with a neurological deficit should prompt urgent aortic imaging before any thrombolysis. Headache, low back pain and scoliosis-related symptoms are common contributors to reduced quality of life.
det.diagnosis: Use the revised Ghent nosology: aortic root dilatation with ectopia lentis or an FBN1 variant, or a systemic score in a person with family history. Brain and spine MRI with heavily T2-weighted imaging detect dural ectasia and extradural CSF; myelography helps localise leaks. In a young stroke with marfanoid features, check the aorta, heart and cervical arteries, and measure homocysteine to exclude homocystinuria.
det.treatment: Long-term care follows cardiology protocols: beta-blocker or angiotensin receptor blocker to slow aortic growth, regular imaging, and prophylactic root replacement at threshold diameters. Spontaneous intracranial hypotension is treated with epidural blood patching or targeted repair, recognising that ectatic dura may complicate procedures. Acute ischaemic stroke treatment requires excluding aortic dissection first because thrombolysis is contraindicated in dissection. Anticoagulation is needed after mechanical valve replacement.
det.prognosis: With modern aortic surveillance and surgery, life expectancy approaches normal; aortic dissection remains the leading cause of death and of severe neurological complications.
pearls: Stroke with chest or back pain in a tall young adult: image the aorta before thrombolysis.
Dural ectasia is a major Ghent systemic feature and a cause of spontaneous CSF leak.
Marfan habitus + lens dislocation + young thrombosis: rule out homocystinuria.
det.thd: Marfan syndrome เกิดจากยีน FBN1 ผิดปกติแบบยีนเด่น ทำให้ผนัง aorta เยื่อหุ้มไขสันหลัง (dura) และเอ็นยึดเลนส์ตาอ่อนแอ ทางระบบประสาทพบ dural ectasia ทำให้ปวดหลังและ CSF รั่วจนเกิด orthostatic headache (SIH) อาจเกิด stroke จาก aortic dissection หรือลิ่มเลือดจากลิ้นหัวใจ และอัมพาตครึ่งล่างจากไขสันหลังขาดเลือด ผู้ป่วย stroke ที่มีเจ็บหน้าอกหรือหลังร่วมด้วยต้องตรวจ aorta ก่อนให้ยาละลายลิ่มเลือด

name: COL4A1/COL4A2-related cerebral small vessel disease
formal: An autosomal dominant disorder of the vascular basement membrane caused by variants in COL4A1 or COL4A2 (type IV collagen), producing a spectrum from fetal or perinatal haemorrhage with porencephaly and schizencephaly to adult small vessel disease with deep intracerebral haemorrhage, lacunes, leukoencephalopathy and intracranial aneurysms, often with eye, kidney and muscle involvement (HANAC).
simple: An inherited weakness of the walls of tiny brain vessels that can cause bleeding in the brain before birth or in adults, leaving holes or scars in the brain.
ab: hereditary angiopathy with nephropathy, aneurysms and muscle cramps
brain small vessel disease with haemorrhage
th: โรคหลอดเลือดสมองขนาดเล็กทางพันธุกรรมแบบยีนเด่นจากยีน COL4A1/COL4A2 (collagen type IV) ทำให้เลือดออกในสมองตั้งแต่ในครรภ์จนเกิด porencephaly หรือในผู้ใหญ่เกิด ICH, lacune, white matter disease และ aneurysm ร่วมกับความผิดปกติของตา ไต และกล้ามเนื้อ
tempoNote: Static deficits from prenatal or perinatal injury; acute haemorrhagic or ischaemic strokes at any age, often after trauma, birth or anticoagulation
feat: Infantile hemiparesis ('cerebral palsy') with porencephalic cyst or schizencephaly, epilepsy and learning difficulty
Adult deep or lobar ICH, sometimes after head injury, exertion or antithrombotic drugs
MRI small vessel picture: white matter hyperintensity, lacunes, microbleeds, enlarged perivascular spaces
Eye signs: retinal arteriolar tortuosity, cataract, anterior segment dysgenesis
HANAC features: haematuria, renal cysts, muscle cramps with raised CK, intracranial carotid siphon aneurysms
inv: MRI with SWI and FLAIR: porencephaly, white matter disease, microbleeds
MRA/CTA for intracranial aneurysms (especially carotid siphon)
Genetic testing for COL4A1 and COL4A2 (small vessel disease or cerebral palsy panel)
Urinalysis, renal ultrasound, CK and eye examination

case.who: 34-year-old female office worker from Nonthaburi with mild right hemiparesis since infancy, labelled cerebral palsy
case.story: Collapsed with sudden headache and worsening right-side weakness after a minor fall from a motorbike; her son had a brain bleed at birth.
case.exam: Dense right hemiparesis, dysarthria; both retinas show tortuous small arterioles; trace haematuria on dipstick.
case.tests: CT: left basal ganglia haemorrhage beside an old porencephalic cavity; MRI: diffuse white matter hyperintensity and microbleeds; COL4A1 pathogenic variant.
case.q: What genetic disorder links her childhood 'cerebral palsy', her son's neonatal bleed and today's ICH?
case.a: COL4A1-related small vessel disease; avoid anticoagulants and contact sports, and plan caesarean delivery for future pregnancies with an at-risk fetus.

det.patho: COL4A1 and COL4A2 encode the alpha-1 and alpha-2 chains of type IV collagen, which assemble into a triple helix in basement membranes of vessels, eye, kidney and muscle. Most pathogenic variants replace a glycine in the helical domain, causing misfolding, intracellular retention and stress, and a fragile basement membrane. Vessels become prone to rupture with minor physical stress, such as vaginal birth or trauma. Penetrance and severity vary widely, even within a family.
det.clinical: Fetal or perinatal haemorrhage leads to porencephaly, schizencephaly, hydranencephaly or congenital hemiparesis, often with epilepsy and intellectual disability. Adults present with deep ICH, lacunar strokes, migraine, cognitive decline or incidental white matter disease. Extra-neurological clues include retinal arteriolar tortuosity, congenital cataract, Axenfeld–Rieger anomaly, haematuria and renal cysts, cramps with elevated CK, and Raynaud phenomenon. The HANAC subtype combines angiopathy, nephropathy, aneurysms and cramps.
det.diagnosis: Suspect the disorder in porencephaly, unexplained young or familial ICH, or small vessel disease without vascular risk factors, especially when eye or renal signs are present. Genetic testing of COL4A1/COL4A2 confirms it; variants of uncertain significance are common, so segregation and phenotype correlation matter. Image the intracranial arteries for aneurysms. Fetal ultrasound or MRI may show prenatal haemorrhage in affected pregnancies.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying treatment. Prevention focuses on avoiding triggers of haemorrhage: contact sports, heavy straining and, where possible, anticoagulants and antiplatelets; control blood pressure well. Caesarean section is usually recommended when the fetus may be affected, to reduce birth-related cerebral bleeding. Manage epilepsy, spasticity and cognitive problems in the usual way; consider aneurysm management case by case. Offer cascade testing and genetic counselling.
det.prognosis: Highly variable, ranging from asymptomatic carriers to severe early disability or fatal haemorrhage.
pearls: Porencephaly in a child + ICH in a young relative: test COL4A1/COL4A2.
Retinal arteriolar tortuosity is a bedside clue to an otherwise hidden brain arteriopathy.
Avoid anticoagulation and plan caesarean delivery when the fetus is at risk.
det.thd: COL4A1/COL4A2-related small vessel disease เป็นโรคทางพันธุกรรมแบบยีนเด่นของ collagen type IV ในผนังหลอดเลือดเล็ก ทำให้หลอดเลือดเปราะ อาจเลือดออกในสมองตั้งแต่ในครรภ์จนเกิด porencephaly และอาการคล้าย cerebral palsy หรือในผู้ใหญ่เกิด ICH, lacune และ white matter disease มักมีหลอดเลือดจอตาคดเคี้ยว ต้อกระจก ปัสสาวะมีเลือด และตะคริวกล้ามเนื้อ (HANAC) ยังไม่มีการรักษาเฉพาะ ควรหลีกเลี่ยงยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือด กีฬาที่กระแทก และพิจารณาผ่าคลอดเมื่อทารกเสี่ยง

name: Retinal vasculopathy with cerebral leukoencephalopathy and systemic manifestations (RVCL-S)
formal: An autosomal dominant small vessel disease due to TREX1 frameshift variants at the C-terminal end, typically beginning in mid-adult life with retinal capillary vasculopathy, subcortical infarcts and contrast-enhancing pseudotumoural brain lesions, migraine, and systemic involvement of kidney, liver and gut.
simple: An inherited disease of tiny blood vessels that damages the retina, brain, kidneys and liver in middle age, often starting with migraine and failing vision.
ab: Retinal vasculopathy with cerebral leukoencephalopathy and systemic manifestations
hereditary endotheliopathy with retinopathy, nephropathy and stroke (HERNS)
th: โรคหลอดเลือดเล็กทางพันธุกรรมแบบยีนเด่นจากยีน TREX1 อาการเริ่มวัยกลางคน มีหลอดเลือดจอตาผิดปกติ สมองขาดเลือดใต้เปลือกสมองหรือก้อนรอยโรคคล้ายเนื้องอก ปวดศีรษะไมเกรน และหลอดเลือดผิดปกติที่ไต ตับ และทางเดินอาหาร
tempoNote: Onset usually 35–55 years; migraine may precede by years, then progressive visual loss and stepwise or subacute neurological decline over 5–10 years
feat: Retinal vasculopathy: capillary drop-out, microaneurysms, telangiectasia and cotton-wool spots causing progressive visual loss
Migraine (often without aura in the curator's notes series) frequently precedes other features
Subcortical infarcts and focal white matter lesions; tumour-like enhancing lesions with oedema and necrosis that mimic glioma, lymphoma or abscess
Systemic vasculopathy: proteinuria and renal failure, liver nodular regenerative hyperplasia, GI bleeding, anaemia, Raynaud phenomenon
Dominant family history of early death, blindness or 'brain tumours'; occasional sporadic de novo cases
inv: Retinal examination with fluorescein angiography
MRI with contrast: punctate enhancing lesions and larger pseudotumours with surrounding oedema; follow-up imaging
TREX1 gene testing (C-terminal frameshift)
Renal function and urine protein, liver enzymes and imaging, blood count

case.who: 46-year-old male civil servant from Lampang with long-standing migraine
case.story: Over a year his vision has become patchy in both eyes; now three weeks of right hand clumsiness and slowed thinking. His mother died at 52 of a 'brain tumour' and kidney failure.
case.exam: Bilateral reduced acuity; fundi show cotton-wool spots, microaneurysms and areas of capillary closure; mild right pronator drift and dysmetria.
case.tests: MRI: ring-enhancing left frontal white matter lesion with oedema and several small enhancing subcortical lesions; creatinine raised with proteinuria; TREX1 frameshift variant.
case.q: What disorder links his migraine, retinopathy, renal disease and tumour-like brain lesion?
case.a: RVCL-S (TREX1): a dominantly inherited small vessel disease whose brain lesions mimic tumour; biopsy shows vasculopathy, not neoplasm.

det.patho: TREX1 is a 3'–5' DNA exonuclease anchored to the endoplasmic reticulum by its C-terminus. RVCL-S variants truncate this tail, so the enzyme keeps its nuclease activity but loses normal localisation, which disturbs ER-related processes such as glycan handling and leads to an obliterative small vessel endotheliopathy. This is distinct from loss-of-function TREX1 variants that cause interferon-driven Aicardi–Goutières syndrome or familial chilblain lupus. Affected vessels show thickened, multilaminated basement membranes and fibrinoid necrosis.
det.clinical: Visual loss from retinal capillary closure is the most consistent early feature. Migraine, Raynaud phenomenon and mild liver or kidney abnormalities may precede neurological signs. Brain involvement brings focal deficits, cognitive and psychiatric change, seizures and headache from small infarcts and enlarging contrast-enhancing lesions that are often biopsied as suspected tumour. Systemic involvement includes renal failure, hypertension, anaemia, GI bleeding and nodular regenerative hyperplasia of the liver; hypothyroidism and bone lesions are reported.
det.diagnosis: Suspect RVCL-S in a middle-aged patient with retinal vasculopathy plus brain white matter or mass-like enhancing lesions, especially with renal or liver disease or a family history of early death. MRI characteristically shows punctate enhancing lesions and larger lesions with necrosis and oedema; calcification may be present. Genetic testing for TREX1 C-terminal variants confirms the diagnosis and can avoid repeated brain biopsy. Exclude vasculitis, lymphoma, MS, Susac and CADASIL.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy is established. Corticosteroids may reduce oedema around enhancing lesions temporarily; anti-VEGF agents have been used for retinal and brain oedema in small series. Laser photocoagulation treats retinal neovascularisation. Manage blood pressure, renal failure, anaemia, migraine and seizures conventionally, and provide genetic counselling for at-risk relatives; clinical trials of targeted approaches are ongoing.
det.prognosis: Progressive course, with death commonly 5–10 years after neurological onset, mainly from cerebral or systemic complications.
pearls: Migraine + retinal vasculopathy + kidney or liver disease + enhancing 'tumours' in a family: think RVCL-S (TREX1).
Same gene, different disease: Aicardi–Goutières is an infantile interferonopathy, RVCL-S an adult vasculopathy.
Genetic testing can spare patients repeated brain biopsies for suspected tumour.
det.thd: RVCL-S เป็นโรคหลอดเลือดเล็กทางพันธุกรรมแบบยีนเด่นจาก TREX1 ส่วนปลาย C-terminal มักเริ่มอายุ 35–55 ปี ผู้ป่วยมีไมเกรนนำมาก่อน ตามัวจากหลอดเลือดฝอยจอตาตีบตัน สมองขาดเลือดใต้เปลือกสมอง และรอยโรคที่จับสารทึบรังสีคล้ายเนื้องอก ร่วมกับหลอดเลือดผิดปกติที่ไต ตับ และทางเดินอาหาร การตรวจยีนช่วยยืนยันและเลี่ยงการตัดชิ้นเนื้อซ้ำ ยังไม่มีการรักษาเฉพาะ ใช้ steroid ลดบวมชั่วคราวและดูแลประคับประคอง

name: Acromegaly — neurological aspects
formal: Chronic growth hormone and IGF-1 excess, almost always from a somatotroph pituitary neuroendocrine tumour (PitNET, formerly adenoma), whose neurological manifestations include headache, chiasmal visual field loss, cavernous sinus cranial neuropathies, carpal tunnel and other entrapment neuropathies, myopathy, spinal stenosis and obstructive sleep apnoea.
simple: Too much growth hormone from a pituitary tumour, which enlarges hands, face and soft tissues and causes headaches, numb hands, weak muscles and poor sleep.
th: ภาวะ growth hormone และ IGF-1 เกินเรื้อรังจากเนื้องอกต่อมใต้สมอง (somatotroph PitNET) ทางระบบประสาทพบปวดศีรษะ ลานสายตาผิดปกติ carpal tunnel syndrome กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง กระดูกสันหลังตีบ และนอนกรนหยุดหายใจ
tempoNote: Insidious over 5–10 years before diagnosis; occasional acute events from pituitary apoplexy
feat: Coarsened face, enlarged jaw with tooth gaps, spade-like hands and feet, increasing ring and shoe size; sweating
Headache, often more severe than tumour size suggests; bitemporal field loss or cranial nerve III/IV/VI palsy with large tumours
Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome and other entrapment or generalised neuropathy
Proximal myopathy with fatigue; arthropathy and spinal canal stenosis
Obstructive (and sometimes central) sleep apnoea, hypertension, diabetes and cardiomyopathy
inv: Serum IGF-1 against age- and sex-specific range (best screening test)
Oral glucose tolerance test: failure of GH to suppress confirms
Pituitary MRI with contrast; formal visual field testing
Other pituitary hormones, prolactin; nerve conduction studies and sleep study as indicated

case.who: 47-year-old male long-haul truck driver from Chonburi
case.story: Two years of numb, tingling hands that wake him at night, daily headaches, loud snoring with daytime sleepiness, and his wedding ring no longer fits.
case.exam: Prominent jaw and brow, large fleshy hands, positive Phalen test bilaterally, thenar wasting on the right; temporal field cuts to confrontation; mild hip flexor weakness.
case.tests: NCS: bilateral median neuropathy at the wrist; IGF-1 three times the upper limit, GH not suppressed after glucose; MRI: 2.4 cm pituitary macroadenoma touching the chiasm; AHI 38.
case.q: What single diagnosis ties together his hands, headache, vision and sleep?
case.a: Acromegaly from a GH-secreting pituitary macroadenoma; refer for transsphenoidal surgery and treat the sleep apnoea before anaesthesia.

det.patho: Somatotroph tumours secrete GH, which drives hepatic IGF-1; together they cause growth of bone, cartilage and soft tissue, fluid retention and insulin resistance. Entrapment neuropathies come from oedema and soft tissue swelling within fixed tunnels, and a diffuse neuropathy from nerve enlargement and diabetes. Large tumours compress the chiasm or invade the cavernous sinus. Rare causes include ectopic GHRH secretion and genetic syndromes such as MEN1, AIP variants and McCune–Albright; WHO 2022 classifies the lesion as a pituitary neuroendocrine tumour (PitNET).
det.clinical: The average delay to diagnosis is several years because changes are gradual; old photographs help. Neurological presentations include headache (sometimes persisting after cure), bitemporal hemianopia, diplopia, bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, proximal myopathy, lumbar or cervical stenosis and sleep apnoea with fatigue and cognitive complaints. Systemic features — hypertension, diabetes, cardiomyopathy, colon polyps and arthropathy — determine mortality. Sudden headache with ophthalmoplegia suggests apoplexy.
det.diagnosis: Measure IGF-1 in anyone with typical features or unexplained bilateral carpal tunnel, sleep apnoea and diabetes. A raised IGF-1 is confirmed by lack of GH suppression after an oral glucose load (nadir above about 1 µg/L, or lower cut-offs with sensitive assays). Pituitary MRI localises the tumour; assess other axes, prolactin and visual fields. Exclude physiological IGF-1 elevation in pregnancy and adolescence.
det.treatment: Transsphenoidal surgery by an experienced pituitary surgeon is first line and is curative in most microadenomas. Persistent disease is treated with somatostatin receptor ligands (octreotide, lanreotide, pasireotide), the GH receptor antagonist pegvisomant, or cabergoline, with radiotherapy for resistant cases. Somatostatin analogues often relieve headache quickly. Carpal tunnel symptoms and myopathy frequently improve with biochemical control, so decompression surgery can sometimes wait; sleep apnoea needs CPAP and airway assessment before anaesthesia.
det.prognosis: Normalising IGF-1 restores near-normal life expectancy; skeletal and joint changes are largely permanent.
pearls: Bilateral carpal tunnel + snoring + headache in a man with big hands: check IGF-1.
Headache in acromegaly can be disproportionate to tumour size and responds to somatostatin analogues.
Treat sleep apnoea and secure the difficult airway before pituitary surgery.
det.thd: Acromegaly เกิดจาก growth hormone และ IGF-1 เกินจากเนื้องอกต่อมใต้สมอง (ปัจจุบันเรียก PitNET ตาม WHO 2022) ทำให้มือเท้าใหญ่ หน้าเปลี่ยน ทางระบบประสาทพบปวดศีรษะ ลานสายตาด้านข้างหายจากกด chiasm, carpal tunnel syndrome ทั้งสองข้าง กล้ามเนื้อต้นแขนขาอ่อนแรง กระดูกสันหลังตีบ และ sleep apnoea คัดกรองด้วย IGF-1 ยืนยันด้วย OGTT และ MRI ต่อมใต้สมอง รักษาหลักด้วยผ่าตัด transsphenoidal และยากลุ่ม somatostatin analogue หรือ pegvisomant

name: Central diabetes insipidus (arginine vasopressin deficiency, AVP-D)
formal: Hypotonic polyuria caused by deficient secretion of arginine vasopressin from the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary — renamed arginine vasopressin deficiency (AVP-D) by international endocrine societies in 2022 — resulting from surgery, trauma, tumours, infiltrative or inflammatory disease, genetic defects or idiopathic causes.
simple: The brain does not make enough of the water-saving hormone, so the person passes large amounts of dilute urine and feels very thirsty.
th: ภาวะขาดฮอร์โมน arginine vasopressin จาก hypothalamus หรือต่อมใต้สมองส่วนหลัง ทำให้ปัสสาวะออกมากและเจือจาง กระหายน้ำมาก ในปี 2022 เปลี่ยนชื่อเป็น arginine vasopressin deficiency (AVP-D) สาเหตุพบบ่อยคือหลังผ่าตัดต่อมใต้สมอง อุบัติเหตุ เนื้องอก และโรคอักเสบแทรกซึม
tempoNote: Abrupt after neurosurgery or head injury (sometimes triphasic over 1–2 weeks); gradual over weeks to months with tumours or infiltration
feat: Polyuria (> 3 L/day in adults or > 50 mL/kg/day) with very dilute urine and nocturia
Thirst and a preference for cold water; hypernatraemia when water access or thirst is impaired
After pituitary surgery: polyuria, then a SIADH-like phase with hyponatraemia, then permanent DI (triphasic)
Clues to cause: headache, field loss, anterior pituitary failure, growth failure or precocious puberty in children
Adipsic form after hypothalamic injury is dangerous: severe hypernatraemia without thirst
inv: Paired serum sodium/osmolality and urine osmolality; 24-hour urine volume
Hypertonic saline- or arginine-stimulated copeptin (preferred over the classic water deprivation test in many centres)
MRI pituitary–hypothalamus: absent posterior bright spot, stalk thickening or mass
Anterior pituitary hormones; tumour markers (AFP, beta-hCG) and work-up for LCH, sarcoid, hypophysitis when the stalk is thick

case.who: 15-year-old girl from Udon Thani in grade 9
case.story: Six months of drinking up to 6 litres a day and waking 4 times a night to pass urine; her periods have stopped and she has had headaches.
case.exam: Height below her expected centile; bitemporal reduction to confrontation; otherwise normal neurological examination.
case.tests: Serum sodium 146 mmol/L, urine osmolality 120 mOsm/kg; glucose normal; MRI: thickened pituitary stalk and a suprasellar mass, no posterior bright spot; CSF beta-hCG raised.
case.q: What causes her polyuria, and why does the stalk matter?
case.a: Central DI (AVP-D) from a suprasellar germinoma; stalk thickening with DI in a teenager demands tumour markers and often biopsy.

det.patho: Vasopressin is made in supraoptic and paraventricular neurons and transported down the stalk to the posterior pituitary. Symptoms appear when roughly 80–90% of these neurons are lost; damage to the stalk alone may be transient because hormone can be released higher up. Common causes are transsphenoidal surgery, head injury, craniopharyngioma, germinoma, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, metastases, hypophysitis, sarcoidosis and post-ischaemic or hypoxic injury; familial dominant AVP variants and Wolfram syndrome are inherited forms. The 2022 renaming to AVP deficiency (and AVP resistance for the nephrogenic form) aims to avoid confusion with diabetes mellitus.
det.clinical: Patients with intact thirst usually keep sodium normal by drinking, so polyuria and nocturia dominate. Hypernatraemia develops when thirst is absent, the patient is sedated or unconscious, or water is restricted, causing confusion, seizures and coma. Post-operative DI may follow a triphasic pattern: early polyuria, a phase of hyponatraemia as stored hormone leaks out, and then permanent deficiency. Anterior pituitary hormone deficits and visual symptoms point to a structural lesion; masking of DI by coexisting cortisol deficiency can reveal itself after steroid replacement.
det.diagnosis: First confirm hypotonic polyuria and exclude hyperglycaemia, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia and diuretics. A high-normal or high sodium with dilute urine favours DI; a low-normal sodium suggests primary polydipsia. Hypertonic saline-stimulated copeptin (low value indicates AVP-D) is more accurate than water deprivation, and arginine stimulation is a simpler alternative. MRI of the hypothalamic–pituitary region is mandatory once central DI is found, and a thick stalk needs serial imaging, tumour markers and systemic work-up.
det.treatment: Desmopressin (oral, sublingual, intranasal or parenteral) is the mainstay, titrated to control nocturia and sodium; warn about hyponatraemia, allow occasional breakthrough polyuria and check sodium early after starting. Hospital patients who cannot drink need careful IV fluids and frequent sodium monitoring. Treat the underlying cause (surgery, chemoradiotherapy for germinoma, steroids for hypophysitis). Patients should carry an alert card, as missed doses during illness or surgery can cause dangerous hypernatraemia.
det.prognosis: Post-operative DI often resolves within weeks; DI from tumours, infiltration or genetic causes is usually permanent but well controlled with desmopressin.
pearls: 2022 nomenclature: central DI = AVP deficiency (AVP-D); nephrogenic DI = AVP resistance (AVP-R).
DI with a thick pituitary stalk in a child or young adult: germinoma or LCH until proven otherwise.
Watch for the hyponatraemic middle phase after pituitary surgery — do not keep giving desmopressin blindly.
det.thd: Central diabetes insipidus ปัจจุบันเรียก arginine vasopressin deficiency (AVP-D) เกิดจาก hypothalamus หรือต่อมใต้สมองส่วนหลังสร้างหรือหลั่ง vasopressin ไม่พอ ผู้ป่วยปัสสาวะมากและเจือจาง กระหายน้ำ ถ้าดื่มน้ำไม่ได้จะเกิด hypernatraemia สาเหตุพบบ่อยคือหลังผ่าตัดต่อมใต้สมอง อุบัติเหตุศีรษะ เนื้องอก เช่น germinoma และ craniopharyngioma และโรคอักเสบแทรกซึม วินิจฉัยด้วยค่า osmolality คู่กัน copeptin และ MRI รักษาด้วย desmopressin และระวังโซเดียมต่ำ

name: Primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM)
formal: A fulminant, almost always fatal meningoencephalitis caused by the thermophilic free-living amoeba Naegleria fowleri, which enters through the nasal mucosa during exposure to warm fresh water and tracks along olfactory nerve fibres through the cribriform plate.
simple: A very rare but deadly brain infection from a tiny amoeba living in warm ponds, rivers or poorly chlorinated water that gets into the brain through the nose.

Early change in smell or taste, then severe frontal headache, fever and vomiting
Rapid slide into meningism, confusion, seizures and coma from raised intracranial pressure

case.who: 11-year-old boy from Suphan Buri, previously healthy
case.story: Six days after spending a hot April afternoon diving in a shallow irrigation pond, he complained that food tasted strange, then developed a pounding headache, high fever and repeated vomiting. Ceftriaxone was started at the district hospital but he became drowsy overnight.
case.exam: Temperature 39.8 °C, marked neck stiffness, GCS 9, bilateral papilloedema; no rash.
case.tests: CSF turbid with 3,800 cells/µL (90% neutrophils), glucose 12 mg/dL, protein 420 mg/dL; Gram stain negative. A wet preparation of warm CSF shows actively moving organisms.
case.q: What organism is responsible and which drug combination should be started immediately?
case.a: Naegleria fowleri (PAM); start the multidrug regimen centred on amphotericin B and miltefosine, with azithromycin, fluconazole, rifampicin and dexamethasone, plus aggressive ICP control, and alert the public health office.

det.patho: Naegleria fowleri thrives in warm fresh water, hot springs and inadequately chlorinated pools, and multiplies best above about 30 °C, so cases cluster in hot months. Infection follows forceful entry of water into the nose; trophozoites attach to olfactory mucosa, migrate along olfactory nerve bundles through the cribriform plate and reach the olfactory bulbs and frontal base. There they cause haemorrhagic necrosis and intense neutrophilic inflammation with rapidly rising intracranial pressure. Swallowing contaminated water does not cause disease, and it is not spread person to person. Sporadic cases have been reported from Thailand and other tropical countries.
det.clinical: The illness is indistinguishable at first from acute bacterial meningitis: fever, severe headache, nausea, vomiting and neck stiffness, sometimes preceded by altered smell or taste reflecting olfactory involvement. Within one to three days patients become confused, have seizures and lapse into coma. Cranial nerve palsies, papilloedema and signs of herniation are common by the time of admission. The single most useful clue is the exposure history, which must be asked for actively in any child or young adult with culture-negative purulent meningitis.
det.diagnosis: CSF is purulent with low glucose, high protein and often red cells, and the Gram stain is negative. A direct wet mount of fresh, unrefrigerated CSF may show motile amoebae with lobopodia; Giemsa or Wright stains can identify trophozoites that might otherwise be mistaken for macrophages. Confirmation is by PCR, culture on bacteria-seeded agar or metagenomic next-generation sequencing through a reference laboratory. Neuroimaging is non-specific and mainly serves to exclude abscess or other causes before LP.
det.treatment: Treatment must be started on suspicion. Current regimens combine amphotericin B (conventional deoxycholate preferred for its in-vitro activity, IV and sometimes intrathecal), miltefosine, fluconazole, azithromycin, rifampicin and dexamethasone. Intensive care focuses on aggressive control of raised ICP with osmotherapy, sedation, hyperventilation only as rescue and, in survivors, therapeutic normothermia or mild hypothermia. Miltefosine supply should be arranged early through infectious disease or public health channels. Prevention advice includes holding the nose or using nose clips in warm fresh water and using boiled, filtered or sterile water for nasal irrigation or ritual nasal rinsing.
det.prognosis: Mortality exceeds 95%; the very few survivors were diagnosed and treated early with multidrug regimens and aggressive ICP management.
pearls: Culture-negative purulent meningitis plus recent freshwater swimming: examine a warm CSF wet mount for amoebae.
Disturbed smell or taste early in meningitis hints at olfactory entry.
Never refrigerate CSF when amoebae are suspected; the trophozoites lose motility.
det.thd: PAM เกิดจากอะมีบา Naegleria fowleri ที่อยู่ในน้ำจืดอุ่น เช่น บ่อ คลอง สระที่คลอรีนไม่พอ เชื้อเข้าทางจมูกแล้วไชผ่านเส้นประสาทรับกลิ่นเข้าสมองส่วนหน้า ผู้ป่วยมีไข้ ปวดศีรษะ คอแข็ง ซึมลงจนโคม่าภายในไม่กี่วัน น้ำไขสันหลังเหมือนแบคทีเรียแต่ย้อม Gram ไม่พบเชื้อ ให้ส่ง CSF สดไม่แช่เย็นดู wet mount และ PCR รักษาด้วยยาหลายตัว เช่น amphotericin B, miltefosine, fluconazole, azithromycin, rifampicin ร่วมกับลดความดันในสมอง แต่ส่วนใหญ่ยังเสียชีวิต

name: Granulomatous amoebic encephalitis (GAE)
formal: A subacute to chronic, usually fatal, granulomatous and haemorrhagic-necrotising encephalitis caused by the free-living amoebae Acanthamoeba spp. (mainly in immunocompromised hosts) or Balamuthia mandrillaris (also in immunocompetent children and adults), reaching the brain haematogenously from skin or lung.

feat: Weeks of headache, low-grade fever, personality change and focal deficits or seizures
Host: HIV/AIDS, transplant, chemotherapy, diabetes, alcohol use; Balamuthia also in healthy people exposed to soil

Failure to respond to antibacterial, antituberculous or toxoplasma treatment
