Metagenomic next-generation sequencing of CSF or tissue; skin lesion biopsy if present
CSF: mild lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein; organisms seldom seen

case.who: 52-year-old kidney transplant recipient from Nakhon Ratchasima on tacrolimus and prednisolone
case.story: Over five weeks he became forgetful and irritable, then had two focal seizures of the right arm. He grows vegetables and often works in wet soil barehanded. Empirical toxoplasma treatment for two weeks did not help.
case.exam: Low-grade fever, mild right hemiparesis, ataxia on finger–nose testing on the left; a firm, painless, violaceous plaque on his left forearm.
case.tests: MRI: five ring-enhancing lesions in the left frontal lobe, left cerebellum and pons, some with haemorrhage. Toxoplasma IgG negative. Biopsy of the frontal lesion: necrotising granulomas with amoebic cysts and trophozoites around vessels; PCR positive for Balamuthia mandrillaris.
case.q: Which pathogen and what management approach is used?
case.a: Balamuthia granulomatous amoebic encephalitis; multidrug therapy including miltefosine, flucytosine, pentamidine, a macrolide, fluconazole and sulfadiazine (newer regimens add nitroxoline), reduction of immunosuppression and resection of accessible lesions.

det.patho: Acanthamoeba and Balamuthia live in soil, dust and water worldwide. They enter through skin wounds or the lower respiratory tract and spread by blood to the brain, where they cause angiitis, haemorrhagic necrosis and granulomatous inflammation; granulomas are poorly formed in profoundly immunosuppressed hosts. Acanthamoeba mainly affects people with HIV, transplants, chemotherapy, diabetes, liver disease or alcohol misuse, and also causes contact-lens keratitis. Balamuthia also affects immunocompetent children and adults, has caused transmission through organ donation, and often produces a facial or limb skin plaque months before neurological disease.
det.clinical: The course runs over weeks to months. Patients present with headache, behavioural change, focal seizures, hemiparesis, cranial nerve palsies, ataxia and eventually raised intracranial pressure and coma. Fever is often low grade or absent. Because the lesions are multifocal and mass-like, patients are frequently treated first for tumour, tuberculomas or toxoplasmosis. A chronic, painless, indurated skin plaque or non-healing ulcers should raise the possibility.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows multiple ring or nodular enhancing lesions, often with haemorrhage and surrounding oedema, sometimes resembling infarcts because of the vasculitic component. CSF is non-specific, with lymphocytes and high protein, and amoebae are rarely seen. Diagnosis usually requires brain or skin biopsy showing trophozoites and double-walled cysts around blood vessels, confirmed by immunofluorescence or PCR at a reference centre. Metagenomic sequencing of CSF or tissue has increasingly made the diagnosis in life. Many cases are still diagnosed only at autopsy.
det.treatment: No single drug is reliably effective, so multidrug regimens are given for months. Combinations for Acanthamoeba include miltefosine, pentamidine, a sulfonamide, flucytosine, fluconazole or voriconazole, and a macrolide; for Balamuthia similar drugs are used, and nitroxoline (an old urinary antiseptic) has been added successfully in recent case reports. Immunosuppression should be reduced where possible, and accessible lesions or skin plaques can be surgically removed. Drug toxicity, especially renal and haematological, requires close monitoring. Specialist infectious disease and public health input is needed early.
det.prognosis: Mortality is above 90%, but survivors are increasingly reported with early diagnosis, prolonged multidrug therapy and surgery.
pearls: Multiple ring lesions that fail toxoplasma or TB therapy in an immunocompromised patient: think of amoebae and biopsy.
A chronic facial skin plaque before encephalitis points to Balamuthia.
Acanthamoeba also causes keratitis in contact-lens wearers, but keratitis rarely leads to encephalitis.

name: Angiostrongylus cantonensis eosinophilic meningitis (neuroangiostrongyliasis)
formal: Eosinophilic meningitis or meningoencephalitis caused by larvae of the rat lungworm Angiostrongylus cantonensis acquired by eating raw or undercooked snails, slugs or paratenic hosts, and the commonest cause of eosinophilic meningitis in Thailand and Southeast Asia.
simple: A worm infection of the brain lining caught from eating raw snails, causing a very bad headache and odd skin sensations that usually gets better over a few weeks.
ab: เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบจากพยาธิหอยโข่ง

tempoNote: Symptoms begin about 1–3 weeks after eating the infected host; headache usually settles over 2–8 weeks
feat: Severe, persistent headache with neck stiffness, nausea and vomiting, often with little or no fever
Migratory paraesthesia, burning or hyperaesthesia of the trunk and limbs
Transient sixth or seventh nerve palsy and blurred vision; consciousness usually preserved in adults
History of eating raw or undercooked apple snails, giant African land snails, frogs, monitor lizards or contaminated vegetables
Larvae may reach the eye (ocular angiostrongyliasis) and cause sudden visual loss
inv: LP: high opening pressure; CSF eosinophils ≥10% of white cells (or >10 cells/µL), modestly raised protein, normal or slightly low glucose
Full blood count: peripheral eosinophilia is usual but not universal

MRI: often normal or shows leptomeningeal enhancement, small T2 lesions; fundoscopy for papilloedema or an intraocular worm

case.story: Two weeks after a family party where he ate koi hoi (spicy raw apple snail salad), he developed a severe constant headache with vomiting and a crawling, burning feeling over his back. He had only mild fever and no seizures.
case.exam: Alert and oriented; mild neck stiffness, left lateral rectus palsy, patchy hyperaesthesia over the trunk; fundi show early papilloedema.
case.tests: Blood eosinophils 18%. LP opening pressure 32 cmH2O; CSF 640 cells/µL with 35% eosinophils, protein 92 mg/dL, glucose 48 mg/dL (plasma 98). CT brain normal.
case.q: What is the most likely cause and what is the recommended treatment?
case.a: Angiostrongylus cantonensis eosinophilic meningitis; oral prednisolone (about 60 mg/day for two weeks) shortens headache, with repeat LP to relieve raised pressure and analgesia; albendazole may be added with steroids, and the eye should be checked for larvae first.

det.patho: The adult worm lives in the pulmonary arteries of rats; larvae shed in rat faeces infect snails and slugs, which humans eat raw or undercooked (Pila apple snails, Achatina giant African snails), or swallow via paratenic hosts such as freshwater prawns, frogs, monitor lizards or vegetables contaminated with snail slime. Swallowed third-stage larvae migrate to the brain and meninges, where they die without completing their cycle. Dying larvae provoke an eosinophil-rich inflammatory reaction along their tracks and in the subarachnoid space, causing raised pressure and focal injury. North-eastern Thailand reports the largest share of cases, linked to traditional raw snail dishes eaten with alcohol.
det.clinical: The dominant symptom is intense headache, often occipital or bifrontal, with nausea, vomiting and neck stiffness; fever is mild or absent. Paraesthesia, burning pain and hyperaesthesia of the skin are characteristic. Abducens or facial palsy and blurred vision from papilloedema occur, and larvae in the eye cause uveitis or retinal damage. Most adults have a benign, self-limited course over several weeks. Heavy infections, especially in young children, can produce encephalitis, radiculomyelitis, coma and death.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical in endemic areas: eosinophilic meningitis plus a compatible food history. Eosinophilic meningitis is defined by at least 10 eosinophils/µL or eosinophils forming at least 10% of CSF white cells; eosinophils may be missed without proper staining (Wright or Giemsa). Serology and CSF PCR help confirm the diagnosis in reference laboratories. Larvae are rarely seen in CSF. Imaging is mostly to exclude haemorrhage or focal lesions, which favour gnathostomiasis.
det.treatment: Symptomatic care with analgesia and repeated therapeutic LP for raised pressure is the basis. A Thai randomised trial showed that a two-week course of oral prednisolone shortens the duration of headache and reduces repeated LPs. Albendazole combined with a corticosteroid is widely used; anthelmintics alone are avoided because dying larvae may intensify inflammation. Before starting therapy, examine the eye; an intraocular worm should be removed surgically or by laser. Public education about cooking snails and washing vegetables is the main prevention.
det.prognosis: Most adults recover fully within weeks; a minority have prolonged headache or paraesthesia, and deaths occur mainly with heavy infections or encephalitis.
pearls: Eosinophilic meningitis in Thailand: ask about raw snails (Angiostrongylus) and raw fish (Gnathostoma).
Severe headache with normal consciousness and burning skin paraesthesia is typical of angiostrongyliasis.
Steroids help; always check the eye for a live worm before treatment.
det.thd: โรคนี้เกิดจากพยาธิปอดหนู Angiostrongylus cantonensis ติดต่อจากการกินหอยโข่ง หอยเชอรี่ หอยทาก กุ้ง กบหรือตะกวดดิบ ตัวอ่อนไชไปที่สมองแล้วตาย ทำให้เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบชนิดอีโอซิโนฟิล อาการเด่นคือปวดศีรษะรุนแรงมาก คลื่นไส้อาเจียน คอแข็งเล็กน้อย ชาแสบตามผิวหนัง อาจมีเส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 6 อ่อนแรง แต่ผู้ป่วยมักรู้สึกตัวดี น้ำไขสันหลังมีอีโอซิโนฟิลอย่างน้อย 10% ความดันสูง รักษาด้วย prednisolone ประมาณ 2 สัปดาห์ เจาะหลังลดความดัน อาจให้ albendazole ร่วมกับสเตียรอยด์ ส่วนใหญ่หายดี และต้องตรวจตาหาตัวพยาธิก่อนให้ยา

det.patho: Adult Gnathostoma worms live in the stomach wall of cats and dogs; eggs hatch in water, pass through copepods and then fish, frogs, snakes or birds, which harbour third-stage larvae. Humans are accidental hosts after eating raw, fermented or lime-marinated flesh; the larva cannot mature and wanders through tissues for years. It enters the nervous system along nerve roots, producing tracks of haemorrhagic necrosis with eosinophilic inflammation in roots, cord and brain. Thailand is the major endemic focus, with cases also across Southeast Asia, Japan, Mexico and in travellers.
det.clinical: Most infections cause recurrent migratory subcutaneous swellings. Neurological disease classically starts with sudden, severe radicular pain followed by rapidly evolving paraplegia or quadriplegia, sensory level and sphincter failure (radiculomyelitis). Others present with encephalitis, cranial nerve palsies, or a thunderclap headache from subarachnoid or intracerebral haemorrhage, sometimes with several bleeds over days. Ocular invasion may cause uveitis or a visible worm. Compared with angiostrongyliasis, the disease is focal, destructive and more often fatal.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in eosinophilic meningitis or myelitis with haemorrhage, radicular pain or migratory swellings and a raw-fish history. CSF shows eosinophils and frequently blood or xanthochromia. MRI demonstrates cord swelling and haemorrhagic tracks or multiple small lobar haemorrhages. Specific immunoblot serology supports the diagnosis; recovering the worm from skin or eye is definitive but uncommon. Exclude aneurysm, AVM and other causes of eosinophilic CSF.
det.treatment: Albendazole for three weeks or ivermectin (about 0.2 mg/kg for two days) are the anthelmintics used; evidence for benefit in CNS disease is limited, and corticosteroids are commonly given to reduce inflammation and cord oedema. Supportive care covers analgesia for neuropathic pain, bladder and bowel management, prevention of pressure sores and thrombosis, and early rehabilitation. Haemorrhage is managed as for other ICH, and hydrocephalus may need drainage. Prevention relies on thorough cooking of fish, frogs and poultry; marinating or fermenting does not kill larvae.
det.prognosis: Mortality has been reported at around 8–25%, and many survivors with myelitis keep long-term weakness or sphincter problems.
pearls: Sudden radicular pain followed by paraplegia in a raw-fish eater: think Gnathostoma.
Bloody or xanthochromic CSF with eosinophils separates it from angiostrongyliasis.
Lime juice, salt and fermentation do not make raw fish safe.
det.thd: พยาธิตัวจี๊ดติดจากการกินปลาน้ำจืดดิบ ส้มปลา ปลาส้ม กบหรือไก่ไม่สุก ตัวอ่อนเดินทางในร่างกายได้นานหลายปี ส่วนใหญ่ทำให้ผิวหนังบวมเคลื่อนที่ได้ แต่ถ้าไชเข้าระบบประสาทจะปวดร้าวตามรากประสาทอย่างรุนแรงทันที แล้วขาอ่อนแรง ปัสสาวะไม่ออก หรือมีเลือดออกใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมองและในเนื้อสมอง น้ำไขสันหลังมีอีโอซิโนฟิลและมักมีเลือดปน MRI เห็นไขสันหลังบวมและรอยเลือดตามทางที่พยาธิไช รักษาด้วย albendazole 21 วันหรือ ivermectin ร่วมกับสเตียรอยด์และฟื้นฟู อัตราตายและความพิการสูงกว่าพยาธิหอยโข่ง

qx.stem: A 35-year-old rice farmer from Khon Kaen, who ate raw fermented fish last month, develops sudden radicular arm pain and, within five days, flaccid paraparesis with a sensory level and urinary retention. CSF is xanthochromic with 400 white cells/uL, 25 percent eosinophils. MRI of the cervicothoracic cord shows swelling with long-segment T2 hyperintensity.
qx.q: Which test best confirms the parasite responsible?
opts: Serum and CSF immunoblot for Gnathostoma spinigerum (the 24-kDa band), alongside the Angiostrongylus immunoblot to exclude it
Stool examination for ova alone
Blood film for malarial parasites
Brain biopsy
India ink stain of CSF
qx.why: Eosinophilic xanthochromic CSF with radiculomyelitis after eating raw intermediate hosts in northeast Thailand suggests gnathostomiasis. Immunoblotting for the 24-kDa antigen is the accepted serological confirmation, and the 31-kDa band marks Angiostrongylus cantonensis, the main alternative. Stool examination is unhelpful as the worm does not shed eggs in humans in this setting, and India ink detects cryptococcus.

name: Rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis
formal: An angioinvasive mould infection by fungi of the order Mucorales (Rhizopus, Mucor, Lichtheimia and others) that starts in the nose and paranasal sinuses and spreads to the orbit, cavernous sinus, internal carotid artery and brain, mainly in diabetic ketoacidosis, steroid use and neutropenia.
simple: A fast, aggressive fungus infection that spreads from the nose and sinuses into the eye and brain, mostly in people with badly controlled diabetes or on steroids.

case.who: 58-year-old man from Phetchabun with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes
case.story: Admitted with DKA after a week of left cheek pain and swelling; two days later the left eye swelled shut and went blind.
case.exam: Left proptosis, complete left ophthalmoplegia, no light perception, absent corneal reflex and numbness over V1-V2; black necrotic patch on the left middle turbinate.
case.tests: Glucose 520 mg/dL, pH 7.12; MRI shows left maxillary and ethmoid sinus disease with non-enhancing turbinate, orbital apex infiltration and cavernous sinus thrombosis; biopsy shows broad aseptate hyphae invading vessels.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what three actions are immediate?
case.a: Rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis: start high-dose liposomal amphotericin B, arrange urgent surgical debridement (ENT with or without orbital exenteration), and correct DKA while stopping or reducing steroids.

det.patho: Mucorales spores are inhaled from soil and rotting plant matter. Acidosis, high glucose and free iron blunt neutrophil function and favour the fungus, which then invades arterial walls, causing thrombosis and tissue death; it travels through bone and along vessels and nerves into the orbit, cavernous sinus and frontal lobe. DKA is the classic setting; steroids, neutropenia, transplant and deferoxamine also predispose. See Mucorales (pathogen) for the organism.
det.clinical: Early symptoms mimic sinusitis: facial pain, swelling, nasal blockage, dark discharge, tooth pain or numbness. Black eschar appears late. Orbital invasion produces periorbital oedema, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia and visual loss, and cavernous sinus or carotid involvement leads to bilateral signs and infarcts. The 2026 review notes that fever may be absent and that medial rectus involvement can limit eye movement.
det.diagnosis: Endoscopic biopsy is the key step, with direct microscopy of tissue for aseptate hyphae and culture or PCR. MRI and CT define the extent and look for carotid and cavernous sinus involvement. Because beta-D-glucan and galactomannan are negative, a negative result should never delay treatment. Ocular examination excludes retinal involvement.
det.treatment: A medical-surgical emergency: liposomal amphotericin B at high dose started before confirmation, repeated surgical debridement, and reversal of predisposing factors (correct DKA, stop or minimise steroids, stop deferoxamine). Isavuconazole or posaconazole are used as adjuncts or oral step-down for at least 6 months, guided by interval imaging. Voriconazole does not cover Mucorales. A trial of the iron chelator deferasirox added to amphotericin did not help.
det.prognosis: Mortality remains high and rises further with cerebral or carotid involvement or continued steroids; survivors often lose an eye or have facial disfigurement.
pearls: Painful ophthalmoplegia in DKA is mucormycosis until proven otherwise; look in the nose.
Black eschar is late; its absence does not exclude disease, and fungal biomarkers are negative.
Voriconazole covers Aspergillus but not Mucorales; use amphotericin B (see Mucorales (pathogen)).
det.thd: Mucormycosis หรือเชื้อราดำ เกิดจากเชื้อราในกลุ่ม Mucorales ที่หายใจเข้าทางจมูก ในภาวะ DKA น้ำตาลสูง หรือได้สเตียรอยด์ เชื้อบุกรุกผนังหลอดเลือดทำให้เนื้อตายสีดำและลามจากไซนัสเข้าเบ้าตา cavernous sinus และสมองภายในไม่กี่วัน อาการคือปวดบวมใบหน้า ชา ตาโปน กลอกตาไม่ได้ ตาบอด หรืออัมพาตจากหลอดเลือด carotid อุดตัน ควรส่องกล้องจมูกและตัดชิ้นเนื้อทันที ผลตรวจ beta-D-glucan และ galactomannan มักเป็นลบ รักษาด้วย liposomal amphotericin B ขนาดสูง ผ่าตัดเนื้อตายออก แก้ DKA และลดสเตียรอยด์ แล้วต่อด้วย isavuconazole หรือ posaconazole อัตราตายสูง

name: Central nervous system aspergillosis
formal: Invasive infection of the brain by Aspergillus species, usually A. fumigatus, spreading by blood from the lungs in immunocompromised hosts or directly from the paranasal sinuses, and causing angioinvasive haemorrhagic infarcts, abscesses, mycotic aneurysms and sometimes chronic granulomatous lesions.
simple: A mould infection that reaches the brain from the lungs or sinuses in people with weak immunity, blocking blood vessels and forming abscesses.
th: การติดเชื้อรา Aspergillus ในสมอง มักแพร่จากปอดทางกระแสเลือดในผู้ภูมิคุ้มกันต่ำ หรือลามจากไซนัส ทำให้หลอดเลือดอุดตัน เกิด infarct มีเลือดออกและฝีหลายตำแหน่ง ยาหลักคือ voriconazole
tempoNote: Days to a few weeks in profound immunosuppression; sino-orbital granulomatous forms evolve over months
feat: Haematological malignancy, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, transplant, prolonged steroids, genetic neutrophil disorders; about a third have no known risk factor
Headache, focal deficit or seizure over days to weeks, often with lung nodules or a cough
Multiple abscesses (about 70%), usually single in immunocompetent hosts; haemorrhagic infarcts, mycotic aneurysms, cavernous sinus thrombosis
Sino-orbital or skull-base disease with cranial neuropathies in diabetes or apparently healthy hosts (A. flavus in hot climates)
Meningitis is uncommon; organism page: Aspergillus species (pathogen)
inv: MRI with contrast and SWI: ring lesions with haemorrhage, restricted diffusion, wedge infarcts; CT chest for nodules with halo sign
CSF Aspergillus PCR (highly specific); serum and CSF galactomannan and beta-D-glucan; lumbar puncture only if safe
Biopsy or aspiration: narrow septate hyphae branching at acute angles; culture for species and susceptibility
Voriconazole trough monitoring once treatment begins

case.who: 52-year-old woman with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia on a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, from a Bangkok tertiary centre
case.story: Ten days of headache and progressive right arm weakness, with a few weeks of dry cough.
case.exam: Afebrile, right arm weakness 3/5, no meningism.
case.tests: Chest CT: nodule with halo; MRI brain: ring-enhancing lesion in left frontal lobe with restricted diffusion and haemorrhage; serum galactomannan index 2.1; CSF Aspergillus PCR positive.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the first-line drug?
case.a: Invasive CNS aspergillosis; voriconazole (with trough level monitoring) is first line, liposomal amphotericin B or isavuconazole alternatives, plus neurosurgical drainage of the accessible lesion and reduction of immunosuppression.

det.patho: Aspergillus conidia are inhaled everywhere. In neutropenia, transplant, tyrosine kinase inhibitor use and high-dose steroid use they germinate in the lung and invade blood vessels, seeding the brain where hyphae block small and medium arteries. Haemorrhagic infarction evolves into abscess, often in perforator territories, and arterial wall invasion can form fragile mycotic aneurysms. Direct spread from sinusitis occurs in diabetes and sometimes in healthy people. See Aspergillus species (pathogen).
det.clinical: Patients present with headache and focal deficits over days to weeks, often with a preceding cough or lung disease. Abscesses account for most cases, solitary lesions are more typical in immunocompetent patients, and meningitis, infarction, haemorrhage and cavernous sinus syndromes are less frequent. Steroids can mask fever. Skull-base and sino-orbital forms mimic tumour or Tolosa-Hunt syndrome.
det.diagnosis: CSF Aspergillus PCR is highly specific and may avoid biopsy. Galactomannan is positive in a minority of CNS cases in serum (sensitivity is low, around 20% in the review) but is more useful in CSF; it can cross-react with Histoplasma and Talaromyces and give false positives from beta-lactam antibiotics or certain foods. Tissue showing thin septate hyphae with culture confirms the diagnosis and permits susceptibility testing.
det.treatment: Voriconazole is first-line for several months, with trough level monitoring for efficacy and toxicity (visual change, hepatitis, hallucinations); liposomal amphotericin B is second-line and isavuconazole an alternative. Drain or resect accessible lesions, reduce immunosuppression and restore neutrophils where possible. Duration is individualised and guided by clinical, radiological and mycological resolution. Prolonged neutropenia calls for posaconazole or voriconazole prophylaxis.
det.prognosis: Prognosis is poor, particularly with immunocompromise or reduced consciousness at presentation; survival improved with voriconazole and surgery but remains well below that of most CNS infections.
pearls: Haemorrhagic infarcts with fever in a neutropenic patient: suspect angioinvasive mould.
CSF PCR is the most specific test; a negative serum galactomannan does not rule it out.
Voriconazole treats Aspergillus but not Mucorales; see Aspergillus species (pathogen) and Mucorales (pathogen).
det.thd: Aspergillosis ในสมองเกิดจากเชื้อรา Aspergillus ที่หายใจเข้าไปแล้วแพร่จากปอดทางกระแสเลือดในผู้ป่วยภูมิคุ้มกันต่ำ เช่น neutropenia ปลูกถ่ายอวัยวะ ได้ยากลุ่ม tyrosine kinase inhibitor หรือสเตียรอยด์ขนาดสูง เชื้อรุกล้ำหลอดเลือดทำให้สมองขาดเลือด มีเลือดออก และกลายเป็นฝีหลายตำแหน่ง บางรายลามจากไซนัส ผู้ป่วยปวดศีรษะ ชัก หรืออ่อนแรงเฉียบพลัน ตรวจ MRI, CSF PCR และ galactomannan รักษาด้วย voriconazole ร่วมกับผ่าตัดระบายฝีและลดยากดภูมิ โดยติดตามระดับยา

name: Coccidioidal meningitis
formal: Chronic basilar granulomatous meningitis caused by the dimorphic fungi Coccidioides immitis or C. posadasii, endemic in the dry south-western USA, in northern Mexico, and in scattered areas of Central and South America, and complicated by hydrocephalus and vasculitic infarcts.
simple: A slow fungus infection of the brain lining caught by breathing desert dust in the American Southwest or Latin America, causing months of headache and needing lifelong treatment.
th: เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบเรื้อรังจากเชื้อรา Coccidioides ที่พบในเขตทะเลทรายของอเมริกาตะวันตกเฉียงใต้ เม็กซิโก และอเมริกาใต้ ในคนไทยพบในผู้ที่เคยไปทำงานหรือเที่ยวที่นั่น มักเกิดโพรงสมองโตและต้องกิน fluconazole ตลอดชีวิต
tempoNote: Weeks to months of headache, usually within about 6 months of exposure; relapses if suppressive therapy is stopped
feat: Travel or residence in Arizona, the Central Valley of California, northern Mexico or other arid endemic areas, even years earlier
Persistent headache, low-grade fever and weight loss, later confusion and gait disturbance
Communicating hydrocephalus, the commonest complication, sometimes the presenting problem
Vasculitic strokes of basal perforating arteries and cranial neuropathies
Higher risk of dissemination with HIV, steroids, biologics, pregnancy and diabetes; organism page: Coccidioides species (pathogen)
inv: CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis (eosinophils suggest the diagnosis), raised protein, low glucose
CSF Coccidioides antigen and complement-fixing antibody are the most useful tests; PCR is less sensitive; culture yield is poor and the mould is a laboratory hazard
MRI: basal meningeal enhancement, communicating hydrocephalus, infarcts
Chest imaging for prior pneumonia

case.who: 39-year-old Thai chef who worked for four years in a restaurant in Phoenix, Arizona
case.story: Eight months before returning to Thailand he had a flu-like illness with cough and painful red shin lesions. Three months of worsening headache, evening fevers and now unsteady walking and urinary urgency.
case.exam: Mild neck stiffness, slow cognition, magnetic gait, bilateral papilloedema.
case.tests: MRI: enlarged ventricles with basal cistern enhancement. CSF 220 cells/µL (lymphocytes 80%, eosinophils 8%), glucose 28 mg/dL, protein 180 mg/dL; Gram, AFB and India ink negative; CrAg negative; CSF Coccidioides antibody positive.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and how long is antifungal therapy continued?
case.a: Coccidioidal meningitis with hydrocephalus; high-dose fluconazole, usually lifelong because relapse is the rule on stopping, with a ventricular shunt for hydrocephalus; steroids for vasculitic infarcts are sometimes added.

det.patho: Coccidioides lives in alkaline desert soil and its arthroconidia are inhaled when dust is stirred by wind, construction or farming. Most infections are a self-limited pneumonia (valley fever), but in a minority the fungus spreads by blood to the meninges. Thick basal exudate causes hydrocephalus and arteritis of penetrating vessels with deep infarcts. Cases outside the endemic zone arise from travel, migration or reactivation under immunosuppression, as detailed in Coccidioides species (pathogen).
det.clinical: Headache is almost universal and may be the only symptom for weeks. Fever, vomiting, confusion and personality change follow, while meningism is often mild. Communicating hydrocephalus is the most common complication, causing gait disturbance, incontinence and papilloedema. Basal vasculitis causes lacunar-type strokes and spinal arachnoiditis can occur. Untreated, the disease is usually fatal.
det.diagnosis: CSF eosinophilia is a helpful hint. CSF Coccidioides antigen assays are highly sensitive and specific according to the 2026 review, serology is less accurate, PCR is less sensitive and culture or direct microscopy is rarely positive. MRI shows basilar enhancement and hydrocephalus. A careful travel history is essential, because clinicians outside endemic regions rarely consider the diagnosis.
det.treatment: Fluconazole at moderately high dose is first-line, and because recurrence is common after stopping (around 80% in the review), suppression is lifelong. Itraconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole or isavuconazole are used for intolerance or failure, and intrathecal amphotericin B is reserved for refractory disease. Hydrocephalus usually needs a shunt, with obstruction a frequent problem. Dexamethasone is used for vasculitic complications.
det.prognosis: Most patients survive on lifelong azole therapy, but hydrocephalus, strokes and relapse on stopping treatment are the main threats.
pearls: Always take a travel history in chronic meningitis; desert dust exposure points to Coccidioides.
CSF eosinophils plus basal meningitis and hydrocephalus; antigen and antibody tests beat culture.
Treatment is lifelong; stopping fluconazole leads to relapse (see Coccidioides species (pathogen)).
det.thd: Coccidioidal meningitis เกิดจากเชื้อรา Coccidioides ที่อยู่ในดินทะเลทรายทางตะวันตกเฉียงใต้ของสหรัฐฯ เม็กซิโก และละตินอเมริกา ผู้ป่วยหายใจเอาสปอร์เข้าไป ส่วนใหญ่เป็นปอดอักเสบเล็กน้อย แต่บางรายเชื้อแพร่ไปเยื่อหุ้มสมองที่ฐานสมอง ทำให้ปวดศีรษะนานหลายเดือน โพรงสมองโต และสมองขาดเลือดจากหลอดเลือดอักเสบ น้ำไขสันหลังมีลิมโฟไซต์และบางครั้งมี eosinophil ตรวจ antigen หรือแอนติบอดีใน CSF รักษาด้วย fluconazole ตลอดชีวิตและใส่ shunt ถ้าโพรงสมองโต ในคนไทยต้องถามประวัติเดินทางไปพื้นที่ระบาด

name: Cytomegalovirus encephalitis (CMV ventriculoencephalitis)
formal: Reactivated cytomegalovirus infection of the brain in severely immunocompromised patients (advanced HIV with CD4 <50 cells/µL, transplant recipients), presenting as subacute encephalitis or ventriculoencephalitis and often accompanied by CMV retinitis or lumbosacral polyradiculitis.
simple: A brain infection by a common herpes-type virus that only becomes dangerous in people with very weak immunity, causing confusion and eye or nerve root problems.
th: สมองอักเสบจากไวรัส CMV ที่กลับมากำเริบในผู้ภูมิคุ้มกันต่ำมาก เช่น HIV ที่มี CD4 ต่ำกว่า 50 หรือผู้ปลูกถ่ายอวัยวะ ทำให้สับสน เส้นประสาทสมองผิดปกติ และอาจมีจอประสาทตาอักเสบหรือรากประสาทส่วนล่างอักเสบร่วม รักษาด้วย ganciclovir ร่วมกับ foscarnet
tempoNote: Evolves over days to a few weeks; ventriculoencephalitis is often more rapid than HIV-associated dementia
feat: Advanced HIV (CD4 usually <50 cells/µL) not on effective ART, or recent transplant
Subacute confusion, apathy and disorientation evolving over days to weeks
Brainstem signs: nystagmus, cranial nerve palsies, ataxia; hyponatraemia from adrenal or hypothalamic involvement
Concurrent CMV retinitis (floaters, field loss) in a substantial proportion
Ascending flaccid leg weakness, sacral numbness and urinary retention when roots of the cauda equina are involved
inv: MRI with contrast: periventricular ependymal enhancement and ventricular enlargement; nodular brain lesions less often
CSF CMV PCR (high sensitivity and specificity); CSF often shows neutrophils with low glucose in polyradiculitis
Dilated fundoscopy by ophthalmology for retinitis; CD4 count and HIV viral load
Serum sodium and morning cortisol; blood CMV viral load (supportive only)

case.who: 33-year-old man from Chiang Rai with newly diagnosed HIV, CD4 18 cells/µL, not yet on ART
case.story: Over ten days his family noticed he was slow, muddled and kept asking the same questions. For three days he has had numb buttocks, weak legs and difficulty passing urine.
case.exam: Disoriented to time, horizontal nystagmus, flaccid paraparesis with absent knee and ankle reflexes, saddle hypoaesthesia; fundi show fluffy yellow-white retinal lesions with haemorrhage.
case.tests: Na 126 mmol/L. MRI: smooth enhancement lining the lateral ventricles and enhancement of cauda equina roots. CSF 480 cells/µL, 70% neutrophils, glucose 30 mg/dL; Gram stain and cryptococcal antigen negative; CMV PCR strongly positive.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what is the initial treatment?
case.a: CMV ventriculoencephalitis with lumbosacral polyradiculitis and retinitis; induction with IV ganciclovir plus foscarnet until clear improvement, then maintenance valganciclovir, and start ART after about two weeks while watching for IRIS.

det.patho: CMV establishes lifelong latency after primary infection; nearly all Thai adults are seropositive. With profound loss of cell-mediated immunity it reactivates and infects ependymal, endothelial and glial cells, producing necrotising ventriculitis, microglial nodules with owl-eye inclusions, and necrosis of nerve roots. Since effective ART became widely available CNS disease is uncommon in HIV, but it still occurs in people diagnosed late and in transplant recipients. Congenital CMV is a separate entity causing microcephaly, periventricular calcification and hearing loss.
det.clinical: Two main brain syndromes are seen: a diffuse micronodular encephalitis resembling HIV dementia but faster, and ventriculoencephalitis with confusion, cranial nerve palsies, nystagmus and ataxia evolving over a few weeks. Hyponatraemia, adrenalitis and retinitis provide useful clues. Lumbosacral polyradiculitis produces subacute flaccid paraparesis, areflexia, perineal sensory loss and urinary retention, often progressing over days to weeks. CMV can also cause myelitis and a mononeuritis multiplex in advanced HIV.
det.diagnosis: CSF CMV PCR is the cornerstone; a positive result in the right clinical context is diagnostic, and quantitative levels help monitor response. Polyradiculitis typically gives a neutrophilic pleocytosis with low glucose and high protein, while encephalitis may produce milder changes. MRI shows ependymal enhancement and ventricular enlargement or root enhancement of the cauda equina. Blood CMV viral load is not specific for CNS disease. Exclude cryptococcal, tuberculous and syphilitic infection and lymphoma, which can coexist.
det.treatment: For CNS disease, most guidelines advise induction with combined IV ganciclovir (5 mg/kg twice daily) and foscarnet (90 mg/kg twice daily), adjusted for renal function, until symptoms clearly improve. Maintenance with oral valganciclovir continues until immune recovery on ART (for example CD4 above 100 cells/µL for several months). In HIV, ART is usually started within about two weeks of CMV therapy, watching for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome. Monitor blood counts (ganciclovir), renal function, calcium and magnesium (foscarnet); suspect resistance (UL97/UL54 mutations) if disease progresses. Reduce immunosuppression in transplant patients.
det.prognosis: Ventriculoencephalitis carries a high mortality, and survivors often keep cognitive deficits; polyradiculitis treated early can recover partially or fully.
pearls: Confusion plus hyponatraemia plus ependymal enhancement in AIDS: think CMV ventriculitis.
Neutrophilic CSF with low glucose in a patient with HIV and cauda equina syndrome suggests CMV polyradiculitis.
Always ask ophthalmology to examine the retina; retinitis often accompanies CNS CMV.
det.thd: CMV encephalitis เกิดจากไวรัส CMV ที่แฝงอยู่ในร่างกายกลับมากำเริบเมื่อภูมิคุ้มกันต่ำมาก เช่น ผู้ป่วย HIV ที่ CD4 ต่ำกว่า 50 หรือผู้ปลูกถ่ายอวัยวะ ไวรัสทำลายผนังโพรงสมอง ทำให้สับสนภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์ มีตากระตุก เส้นประสาทสมองอ่อนแรง โซเดียมต่ำ และบ่อยครั้งมีจอประสาทตาอักเสบ หากเชื้อลงรากประสาทส่วนล่างจะมีขาอ่อนแรงแบบอ่อนปวกเปียก ชาบริเวณก้น และปัสสาวะไม่ออก วินิจฉัยด้วย CMV PCR ในน้ำไขสันหลังและ MRI ที่เห็นผนังโพรงสมองติดสี รักษาด้วย ganciclovir ร่วมกับ foscarnet ตามด้วย valganciclovir และเริ่ม ART ภายในราว 2 สัปดาห์

name: West Nile neuroinvasive disease (WNND)
formal: Neurological disease caused by West Nile virus, a mosquito-borne flavivirus maintained in birds and transmitted by Culex mosquitoes, presenting as meningitis, encephalitis with movement disorders, or an acute flaccid paralysis from anterior horn cell infection.

case.who: 67-year-old retired teacher from Bangkok who returned from a two-month August visit to his daughter in Texas
case.story: Five days after returning he had fever, headache and a faint rash, then became confused, his hands began shaking, and his left arm became floppy and weak over one day.
case.exam: Disoriented, coarse postural and rest tremor of both hands, cogwheel rigidity; flaccid weakness of the left arm (MRC 1/5) with absent biceps reflex and normal sensation.
case.tests: CSF 160 cells/µL (lymphocytes 70%), protein 95 mg/dL, normal glucose; HSV and VZV PCR negative. MRI: bilateral thalamic T2 hyperintensity. CSF West Nile IgM positive; dengue and JE neutralisation titres much lower than West Nile.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and why must flavivirus serology be interpreted carefully in a Thai patient?
case.a: West Nile neuroinvasive disease (encephalitis with acute flaccid paralysis); management is supportive. Thai patients often have antibodies from dengue, Japanese encephalitis or JE vaccination, which cross-react, so neutralisation testing is needed to confirm the specific virus.

det.patho: West Nile virus is a flavivirus related to Japanese encephalitis, dengue and Zika. Culex mosquitoes transmit it between birds; humans and horses are dead-end hosts. Rarely it spreads through blood transfusion or organ transplant. About 80% of infections are silent, roughly 20% cause West Nile fever, and fewer than 1% invade the nervous system, especially in older adults, transplant recipients and those on immunosuppressants. The virus targets neurons of the thalamus, basal ganglia, brainstem, cerebellum and anterior horn cells.
det.clinical: Neuroinvasive disease presents as meningitis, encephalitis or acute flaccid paralysis, alone or in combination. Encephalitis often shows prominent tremor, myoclonus or parkinsonian features, and altered consciousness. The flaccid paralysis is a poliomyelitis-like syndrome: abrupt, asymmetric, painless or mildly painful weakness with reduced reflexes and preserved sensation; involvement of phrenic or bulbar motor neurons can require ventilation. Less often radiculopathy, brachial plexopathy or GBS follows. Recovery is slow, and fatigue and weakness can persist for months.
det.diagnosis: Detection of West Nile IgM in CSF is the preferred test; IgM persists for months, so timing and clinical fit matter. Serum antibodies cross-react with other flaviviruses, which is especially relevant in Thailand where dengue and JE exposure or vaccination are common, so plaque reduction neutralisation testing at a reference laboratory is used for confirmation. RT-PCR is useful in immunocompromised patients with weak antibody responses. MRI may be normal or show deep grey matter or anterior horn lesions, and EMG confirms a motor neuronopathy pattern.
det.treatment: Treatment is supportive: monitoring for respiratory failure, airway protection, seizure control, prevention of complications and early rehabilitation. No antiviral or immunotherapy has proven benefit; IVIG, interferon and monoclonal antibodies have been tried in case series without convincing results. Reducing immunosuppression in transplant patients is sensible. Prevention relies on mosquito avoidance and screening of blood and organ donors in affected regions; no human vaccine is licensed.
det.prognosis: Mortality of neuroinvasive disease is about 10% and higher in the elderly with encephalitis; many survivors of paralysis or encephalitis have lasting weakness, fatigue or cognitive problems.
pearls: Encephalitis with tremor or parkinsonism plus asymmetric flaccid limb weakness suggests a flavivirus such as West Nile or JE.
In Thai patients flavivirus IgM cross-reacts; confirm with neutralisation tests.
Normal sensation and an anterior horn EMG pattern separate West Nile paralysis from GBS.

name: Intracranial subdural empyema
formal: A pus collection lying between dura and arachnoid, usually over the cerebral convexity or along the falx, most often arising from frontal sinusitis or otomastoiditis, and behaving as a rapidly progressive neurosurgical emergency.
simple: Pus collecting under the tough outer covering of the brain, usually spreading from an infected sinus or ear, which needs urgent surgery.
ab: หนองใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมองชั้นดูรา
th: หนองที่สะสมใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมองชั้นดูรา มักลามมาจากไซนัสอักเสบส่วนหน้าหรือหูชั้นกลางอักเสบ พบบ่อยในวัยรุ่นชาย ผู้ป่วยแย่ลงเร็ว มีไข้ ชัก อ่อนแรงครึ่งซีก ต้องผ่าตัดระบายหนองด่วนและให้ยาปฏิชีวนะทางหลอดเลือดนานหลายสัปดาห์
tempoNote: Hours to a few days from sinus symptoms to seizures and coma; post-operative cases can be more indolent
feat: Adolescent or young adult male with recent frontal sinusitis or chronic ear discharge
Fever, severe headache and vomiting progressing quickly to drowsiness
Focal motor seizures and contralateral hemiparesis or aphasia; leg-predominant weakness with parafalcine collections
Forehead swelling over the frontal sinus (Pott's puffy tumour) or periorbital oedema
Meningism with signs of rising intracranial pressure; LP is unsafe
inv: MRI with contrast and DWI: crescentic or lentiform convexity/interhemispheric collection with marked diffusion restriction and rim enhancement
Contrast CT if MRI unavailable (may underestimate small collections); CT sinuses and temporal bones for the source
Blood cultures, inflammatory markers; Gram stain and culture of surgical pus including anaerobes
Avoid lumbar puncture (herniation risk, low yield)

case.story: He had a week of blocked nose and frontal headache treated with oral amoxicillin. Over the next two days he developed high fever, a soft swelling on his forehead, vomiting, and then jerking of his right arm and face.
case.exam: Temperature 39.5 °C, GCS 12, tender boggy swelling over the forehead, neck stiffness, right hemiparesis (MRC 3/5) and expressive aphasia.
case.tests: WBC 21,000/µL, CRP 210 mg/L. MRI: left frontal sinusitis with osteomyelitis, a thin crescentic left convexity collection extending along the falx with bright DWI signal and rim enhancement, and mild mass effect.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what are the key management steps?
case.a: Subdural empyema from frontal sinusitis with Pott's puffy tumour; urgent craniotomy to evacuate pus plus ENT drainage of the sinus, IV ceftriaxone plus metronidazole (with vancomycin if staphylococci are possible) for several weeks, and antiseizure medication.

det.patho: Infection reaches the subdural space mainly through valveless emissary veins draining infected frontal or ethmoid sinuses, the middle ear and mastoid, or by direct bony erosion; other sources include penetrating trauma, neurosurgery, infected subdural haematoma and, in infants, bacterial meningitis. Because the subdural space has no barriers, pus spreads widely over the convexity and along the falx. Thrombophlebitis of cortical veins and venous sinuses leads to venous infarction, cerebral oedema and seizures. Typical organisms are Streptococcus anginosus group, anaerobes and Staphylococcus aureus, with Gram-negative bacteria after surgery or otitis.
det.clinical: Most patients are adolescent and young adult males, reflecting the growth of the frontal sinuses. Fever and headache from sinusitis are followed within days by vomiting, altered consciousness, focal or generalised seizures and hemiparesis, aphasia or gaze deviation. Parafalcine collections can produce leg-predominant weakness. Pott's puffy tumour, periorbital swelling or ear discharge point to the source. Deterioration can be rapid, with herniation and death if the collection is not drained.
det.diagnosis: Contrast MRI with diffusion imaging is the investigation of choice: subdural pus shows strong diffusion restriction and an enhancing membrane, separating it from sterile effusion or chronic haematoma. CT may miss thin or parafalcine collections, especially early. Sinus and temporal bone imaging identifies the source, and blood cultures plus surgical pus Gram stain and culture (aerobic and anaerobic) guide antibiotics. Lumbar puncture is contraindicated because of mass effect.
det.treatment: Subdural empyema is a neurosurgical emergency. Drainage by craniotomy is generally preferred for convexity collections because it allows wider evacuation and lower re-operation rates than burr holes; small parafalcine or infant collections may be managed differently. The infected sinus or mastoid should be drained in the same or an early session. Start empirical IV ceftriaxone or cefotaxime plus metronidazole, adding vancomycin for post-operative or trauma cases, then tailor to cultures and continue for about 3–6 weeks. Treat seizures promptly, manage raised intracranial pressure, and consider venous sinus thrombosis.
det.prognosis: With early drainage mortality is now around 10% or less, but late epilepsy and residual focal deficits are common.
pearls: Teenager with sinusitis, fever and focal seizures: get an MRI with DWI for subdural empyema.
Forehead swelling over a sinus (Pott's puffy tumour) signals frontal bone osteomyelitis and intracranial risk.
Never do an LP first; a normal-looking CT does not exclude a thin empyema.
det.thd: Subdural empyema คือหนองที่อยู่ระหว่างเยื่อดูราและอะแร็กนอยด์ มักลามมาจากไซนัสหน้าผากอักเสบหรือหูชั้นกลางอักเสบผ่านหลอดเลือดดำ จึงพบบ่อยในวัยรุ่นชาย ผู้ป่วยมีไข้ ปวดศีรษะ อาเจียน แล้วซึมลง ชักเฉพาะที่ และอ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกภายในไม่กี่วัน อาจมีหน้าผากบวม (Pott's puffy tumour) ตรวจ MRI DWI เห็นหนองรูปพระจันทร์เสี้ยวตามผิวสมองหรือแนว falx ห้ามเจาะหลัง ต้องผ่าตัดระบายหนอง (มักใช้ craniotomy) ร่วมกับระบายไซนัส ให้ ceftriaxone ร่วมกับ metronidazole ทางหลอดเลือด 3–6 สัปดาห์ และควบคุมอาการชัก

name: Human African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness)
formal: A tsetse fly-transmitted protozoal infection of sub-Saharan Africa by Trypanosoma brucei gambiense (chronic, West and Central Africa) or T. b. rhodesiense (acute, East and Southern Africa) that progresses from a haemolymphatic first stage to a meningoencephalitic second stage with disruption of the sleep–wake cycle, psychiatric change and death if untreated.
simple: A parasite infection from tsetse fly bites in Africa that first causes fevers and swollen glands and later enters the brain, making people sleep in the day, stay awake at night and become confused.
ab: โรคเหงาหลับ
th: โรคเหงาหลับจากเชื้อโปรโตซัว Trypanosoma brucei ที่แมลงวันเซตซีในแอฟริกาเป็นพาหะ ระยะแรกมีไข้และต่อมน้ำเหลืองโต ระยะที่สองเชื้อเข้าสมอง ทำให้ง่วงกลางวัน นอนไม่หลับกลางคืน บุคลิกเปลี่ยน และเสียชีวิตถ้าไม่รักษา ปัจจุบันมียากินอย่าง fexinidazole
tempoNote: Gambiense: months to years before stage 2; rhodesiense: stage 2 within weeks
feat: Residence, work or travel in sub-Saharan Africa with tsetse fly exposure (rural, forest or safari areas)
Painful chancre at the bite site (more with rhodesiense), intermittent fevers, headache, pruritus
Posterior cervical lymphadenopathy (Winterbottom sign), hepatosplenomegaly
Stage 2: daytime somnolence with night-time insomnia, apathy, psychosis, tremor, abnormal movements and ataxia
Delayed deep hyperaesthesia after pressure (Kérandel sign); final coma and cachexia
inv: Microscopy of blood (thick film, concentration methods), lymph node aspirate or chancre fluid for trypanosomes
Serological screening for gambiense (card agglutination test or rapid diagnostic test), followed by parasitological confirmation
LP for staging: CSF white cells >5/µL or trypanosomes defines stage 2; raised IgM
MRI may show white matter and basal ganglia T2 changes; exclude malaria, HIV and TB

case.who: 41-year-old Thai army officer who served 14 months with a UN peacekeeping mission in South Sudan
case.story: Since returning home six months ago his wife says he dozes off during meals and meetings but wanders the house at night. He has become irritable and suspicious, with intermittent fevers and headaches.
case.exam: Apathetic, slowed speech, fine tremor of the hands, enlarged rubbery posterior cervical lymph nodes, mild splenomegaly.
case.tests: Anaemia, high ESR and polyclonal IgM; malaria tests negative; HIV negative. Lymph node aspirate shows trypanosomes. CSF 42 white cells/µL with raised protein; trypanosomes seen after centrifugation.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, the stage, and the current first-line oral therapy?
case.a: Gambiense human African trypanosomiasis, stage 2 (meningoencephalitic); oral fexinidazole for 10 days is suitable when CSF white cells are below 100/µL, whereas severe stage 2 is treated with nifurtimox–eflornithine combination therapy (NECT); notify and seek advice from WHO-linked centres.

read.where: Infectious Diseases of the Nervous System — Trypanosomiasis
Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System — Protozoa — African Trypanosomiasis (Sleeping Sickness)

det.patho: Tsetse flies (Glossina) inoculate metacyclic trypanosomes, which multiply locally (chancre) and then spread via lymph and blood, evading immunity by repeatedly switching their variant surface glycoprotein coat. This antigenic variation produces waves of parasitaemia and fever and a large polyclonal IgM response. Once parasites cross the blood–brain and choroid plexus barriers, parasites cause a meningoencephalitis with perivascular cuffing by lymphocytes, plasma cells and morular (Mott) cells, particularly affecting the hypothalamus and deep white matter. T. b. gambiense causes over 90% of reported cases; T. b. rhodesiense is a zoonosis from game and cattle and progresses much faster.
det.clinical: Stage 1 features fevers, headache, malaise, itching, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and sometimes facial oedema or rash. In gambiense disease this may last months to years with mild symptoms; in rhodesiense disease it is acute and stage 2 can follow within weeks. Stage 2 brings disruption of circadian sleep (fragmented sleep with daytime somnolence), mood and behavioural change, psychosis, tremor, choreoathetosis, ataxia, and deep hyperaesthesia, ending in stupor, seizures and death. Travellers returning from East African safaris usually present with acute rhodesiense infection and a visible chancre.
det.diagnosis: Gambiense infection is screened serologically and confirmed by finding parasites in blood, lymph node aspirate or CSF; rhodesiense parasitaemia is high enough for blood film diagnosis. Staging by LP is required for treatment decisions: CSF white cell count above 5/µL or the presence of trypanosomes indicates stage 2, and counts above 100/µL indicate severe disease. Molecular methods are available in reference laboratories. Exclude co-existing malaria, HIV and tuberculosis.
det.treatment: For gambiense disease, oral fexinidazole for 10 days is now recommended for stage 1 and non-severe stage 2 in patients aged 6 years and over; severe stage 2 receives nifurtimox–eflornithine combination therapy (NECT), and pentamidine remains an option for early stage 1. Acoziborole, a single-dose oral drug, is being introduced in endemic programmes. For rhodesiense disease, WHO guidance now includes fexinidazole for most patients, with suramin for stage 1 and melarsoprol for stage 2 as older alternatives; melarsoprol carries a significant risk of fatal post-treatment reactive encephalopathy. Drugs are supplied through WHO, so specialist tropical medicine advice should be sought immediately. Follow-up includes clinical review for relapse.
det.prognosis: Untreated stage 2 is almost always fatal; with modern treatment cure rates exceed 90%, although some patients retain neuropsychiatric sequelae.
pearls: Day-night sleep reversal and personality change in someone who lived in rural Africa: think sleeping sickness.
Staging LP decides treatment: >5 white cells/µL or parasites in CSF means stage 2.
Do not confuse with Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis), which rarely affects the CNS except in immunosuppression.
det.thd: โรคเหงาหลับเกิดจากเชื้อ Trypanosoma brucei ที่มีแมลงวันเซตซีเป็นพาหะในแอฟริกาใต้ซาฮารา ชนิด gambiense ดำเนินโรคช้าเป็นเดือนถึงปี ส่วนชนิด rhodesiense ดำเนินโรคเร็วภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์ ระยะแรกมีไข้เป็นพัก ๆ ต่อมน้ำเหลืองหลังคอโต ม้ามโต ระยะที่สองเชื้อเข้าสมอง ทำให้ง่วงกลางวันแต่ไม่หลับกลางคืน บุคลิกภาพเปลี่ยน มือสั่น เดินเซ จนซึมและเสียชีวิต ในคนไทยพบได้ในผู้ที่ไปทำงานหรือเป็นทหารรักษาสันติภาพในแอฟริกา ต้องเจาะหลังเพื่อแบ่งระยะ รักษาด้วย fexinidazole แบบกินหรือ NECT ในรายรุนแรง โดยประสานผ่านองค์การอนามัยโลก

name: Chronic migraine (CM)
formal: A migraine disorder in which headache occurs on at least 15 days monthly over more than three months, with at least eight of those days showing migraine features or responding to migraine-specific drugs (ICHD-3 1.3).
simple: Migraine that has become so frequent that the person has a headache on at least half the days of every month.
ab: ไมเกรนเรื้อรัง
th: ไมเกรนชนิดเรื้อรัง ปวดศีรษะตั้งแต่ 15 วันต่อเดือนนานเกิน 3 เดือน และอย่างน้อย 8 วันมีลักษณะไมเกรน มักพัฒนามาจากไมเกรนเป็นครั้งคราวร่วมกับการใช้ยาแก้ปวดมากเกิน
tempoNote: Usually evolves gradually over months to years from episodic migraine ('chronification'); can revert to episodic with treatment
feat: Headache on most days of the month, mixing full migraine days with milder featureless days
Long history of episodic migraine whose attack frequency has crept upward
Frequent overuse of acute medicines (paracetamol, NSAIDs, combination analgesics, triptans)
Common companions: poor sleep, depression, anxiety, obesity, high caffeine intake
Marked disability with lost work or school days; a headache diary reveals the true day count
inv: Headache diary for at least 1 month to count headache days, migraine days and acute-drug days
Neurological and fundus examination; MRI brain only if red flags, atypical features or abnormal exam
Screen for medication overuse, sleep apnoea, mood disorder; check BP and BMI

case.story: She has had migraine since university, but over two years her headaches have become near-daily. She takes a paracetamol–caffeine tablet or an ergotamine pill on about 20 days each month.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination and fundi; BP 124/80; BMI 29.
case.tests: Diary: headache on 22 days a month, 10 with throbbing pain, nausea and light sensitivity; no MRI needed.
case.q: What two diagnoses apply, and how should she be managed?
case.a: Chronic migraine plus medication overuse headache; withdraw the overused drugs with education and a bridge, and start prevention such as topiramate, onabotulinumtoxinA or a CGRP monoclonal antibody.

read.where: Chapter 4 Diagnosis of Primary Chronic Daily Headaches

det.patho: Chronic migraine affects roughly 1–2% of adults and around 3% of people with episodic migraine move into the chronic range each year. Risk factors for this shift include high baseline attack frequency, acute-medication overuse, obesity, depression, sleep disorders, stressful life events and caffeine excess. Repeated attacks are thought to sensitise trigeminovascular and central pain pathways, with reduced descending inhibition from the brainstem, so the threshold for further attacks keeps falling. Allodynia during attacks is a marker of central sensitisation.
det.clinical: Patients describe a near-constant background headache with superimposed days of throbbing, disabling migraine. Many have lost track of individual attacks, which is why a prospective diary is essential. Associated features include neck pain, fatigue, cognitive complaints and allodynia. Psychiatric and pain comorbidity is common and worsens outcomes. The ICHD-3 (2018) definition is unchanged in substance from the beta version; medication overuse no longer blocks the diagnosis and is coded alongside it.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, based on the diary count of total headache days, migraine-like days and treatment days over at least three months. Secondary causes deserve a fresh look whenever the pattern changes: idiopathic intracranial hypertension, sleep apnoea, CVT, low-pressure headache and space-occupying lesions can all present as daily headache. Imaging is reserved for red flags or abnormal findings. Always screen for medication overuse (simple analgesics on 15 or more days, triptans, ergots, opioids or combination drugs on 10 or more days a month).
det.treatment: Address medication overuse through education and withdrawal, limiting acute drugs to two or three days a week. Evidence-based preventives include topiramate, onabotulinumtoxinA (155 units across 31 head and neck sites every 12 weeks), the CGRP-pathway monoclonal antibodies (erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab, eptinezumab) and the oral gepant atogepant; amitriptyline, propranolol, candesartan and flunarizine are widely used though less studied in chronic migraine. Current guidance from headache societies allows CGRP antibodies as first-line prevention where access permits. Judge response after about three months, aiming for at least a 30–50% drop in monthly migraine days. Treat sleep, mood and weight in parallel and add behavioural therapy.
det.prognosis: With prevention and removal of overuse, a large share revert to episodic migraine within one to two years, but relapse is common, especially if overuse returns.
pearls: Count days, not attacks — 15 or more headache days a month for three months, eight of them migrainous.
Medication overuse is the most fixable driver; diagnose and treat both together.
Botulinum toxin is proven for chronic, not episodic, migraine.
det.thd: ไมเกรนเรื้อรังคือการปวดศีรษะตั้งแต่ 15 วันต่อเดือนติดต่อกันเกิน 3 เดือน โดยอย่างน้อย 8 วันเป็นปวดแบบไมเกรน มักค่อย ๆ เพิ่มจากไมเกรนเป็นพัก ๆ เมื่อใช้ยาแก้ปวดถี่ นอนไม่ดี หรือมีภาวะซึมเศร้า การวินิจฉัยอาศัยสมุดบันทึกอาการ และต้องคัดกรองการใช้ยาแก้ปวดเกินขนาดทุกราย การรักษาคือหยุดยาที่ใช้มากเกิน ร่วมกับยาป้องกัน เช่น topiramate, onabotulinumtoxinA หรือยากลุ่ม anti-CGRP

name: Hemicrania continua (HC)
formal: A primary headache with continuous, strictly one-sided pain lasting over three months, punctuated by flares with ipsilateral cranial autonomic features or restlessness, and an absolute response to indomethacin (ICHD-3 3.4).
simple: A never-ending headache on one side of the head that flares up with a red, watering eye and goes away completely with the drug indomethacin.
th: ปวดศีรษะข้างเดียวต่อเนื่องไม่หายเกิน 3 เดือน มีช่วงปวดมากขึ้นพร้อมน้ำตาไหล ตาแดง คัดจมูกข้างเดียวกัน และหายสนิทเมื่อให้ indomethacin
tempoNote: Continuous daily background pain for months to years with superimposed exacerbations lasting hours to days; a minority have pain-free remissions (remitting subtype)
feat: Side-locked, continuous mild-to-moderate pain that never switches sides
Flares of severe pain with ipsilateral tearing, conjunctival injection, nasal congestion, ptosis or eyelid oedema
Restlessness or agitation during flares; migrainous features (nausea, photophobia) can appear
Foreign-body ('sand in the eye') sensation and brief stabbing jabs on the same side
Complete relief with adequate-dose indomethacin — the defining feature
inv: Indomethacin trial: oral dose escalated (e.g. 25 mg three times daily up to 75 mg three times daily over 2–3 weeks) or an intramuscular 'indotest'
MRI brain with pituitary views (and vascular imaging if indicated) to exclude secondary mimics
Review for medication overuse, which can blunt the indomethacin response

case.story: For 18 months she has had a constant ache behind the right eye that never fully leaves. Several times a week it intensifies for hours with a watering right eye and blocked right nostril, and she paces the room.
case.exam: Mild right ptosis and conjunctival redness during a flare; otherwise normal.
case.tests: MRI brain and pituitary normal; carbamazepine and triptans failed; pain vanished within two days on indomethacin 50 mg three times daily.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what precautions does long-term treatment need?
case.a: Hemicrania continua; continue the lowest effective indomethacin dose with a proton-pump inhibitor and monitor renal function, BP and GI symptoms.

det.patho: Hemicrania continua is grouped with the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias in ICHD-3 (2018), as it was in the beta. Functional imaging during pain shows activation of the posterior hypothalamus and dorsal pons, overlapping both TAC and migraine networks. It is more common in women, usually starts in adulthood and is likely under-recognised. Why indomethacin, but not most other NSAIDs, works remains unexplained; effects on nitric oxide signalling and CSF pressure have been proposed.
det.clinical: The background pain is usually moderate and centred around the eye, temple or forehead. Exacerbations bring severe pain with one or more ipsilateral autonomic features, though these are often milder than in cluster headache, and many patients feel restless. Migrainous symptoms during flares lead to frequent misdiagnosis as chronic migraine. The ICHD-3 recognises a remitting subtype (pain-free spells of at least 24 hours) and an unremitting subtype (continuous for at least a year).
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis requires the clinical pattern plus an unequivocal response to therapeutic doses of indomethacin. Every patient with side-locked continuous headache deserves an indomethacin trial. Secondary mimics include pituitary tumours, internal carotid dissection, posterior fossa lesions, cervicogenic headache and sinus disease, so MRI is advised. Medication overuse should be stopped because it can obscure the response.
det.treatment: Indomethacin is first line, commonly 75–225 mg a day, then tapered to the lowest dose that keeps pain away; give a proton-pump inhibitor and monitor kidney function and BP. If indomethacin is not tolerated, options with weaker evidence include COX-2 inhibitors such as celecoxib, melatonin, gabapentin, topiramate, greater occipital nerve block and onabotulinumtoxinA. Neuromodulation (occipital or vagus nerve stimulation) is reserved for refractory cases. Some patients can periodically try reducing the dose to test for remission.
det.prognosis: Most patients need long-term treatment; the unremitting form is more common than the remitting one. Indomethacin adverse effects, mainly gastrointestinal, are the main long-term problem.
pearls: Any side-locked, continuous unilateral headache deserves an indomethacin trial.
Autonomic features can be subtle — ask about a gritty or watering eye during flares.
Migrainous symptoms in flares do not rule it out; the indomethacin response decides.
det.thd: Hemicrania continua คือปวดศีรษะข้างเดียวต่อเนื่องตลอดเวลาเกิน 3 เดือน มีช่วงปวดรุนแรงขึ้นพร้อมน้ำตาไหล ตาแดง คัดจมูก หรือกระสับกระส่าย มักถูกวินิจฉัยผิดว่าเป็นไมเกรนเรื้อรัง การวินิจฉัยต้องดีขึ้นอย่างสมบูรณ์ด้วย indomethacin และควรทำ MRI เพื่อแยกสาเหตุอื่น เช่น เนื้องอกต่อมใต้สมอง การรักษาหลักคือ indomethacin ขนาดต่ำสุดที่คุมได้ ร่วมกับยาป้องกันกระเพาะ และติดตามการทำงานของไตและความดัน

name: Retinal migraine
formal: A rare migraine subtype with repeated, fully reversible visual disturbance confined to one eye (scintillations, scotoma or blindness) accompanying migraine headache, after other causes of transient monocular visual loss are excluded (ICHD-3 1.2.4).
simple: A rare type of migraine in which the vision in one eye flickers or goes dark for a short time, together with a migraine headache.

Migraine headache during or after the visual episode
Usually young adults who already have migraine themselves or in close relatives
Normal eye and neurological examination between attacks

Carotid imaging and cardiac evaluation (ECG, echocardiography) to exclude embolic amaurosis
ESR/CRP in older patients (giant-cell arteritis); antiphospholipid antibodies and thrombophilia screen when suggested

case.who: 26-year-old female nurse from Khon Kaen with migraine since adolescence
case.story: Three times this year her left eye has gradually gone dark from the edges over 10 minutes, clearing within half an hour, followed by a throbbing left temporal headache with nausea. Covering the right eye during one episode confirmed only the left eye was affected.
case.exam: Normal visual acuity, fields, pupils and fundi between attacks; normal neurological examination.
case.tests: Carotid Doppler, echocardiogram, ESR, antiphospholipid antibodies and MRI brain all normal.
case.q: How do you confirm that the aura is truly monocular, and what drugs might you avoid?
case.a: Ask her to cover each eye during an attack or draw the field defect; consider avoiding triptans and ergots and use NSAIDs plus a preventive such as a beta-blocker, verapamil or topiramate.

det.patho: The mechanism is uncertain; vasospasm of the retinal or ciliary circulation has been observed during some attacks, and spreading depression within the retina has also been proposed. The condition is genuinely rare, and many reported cases turn out to be homonymous cortical aura that the patient attributes to one eye. Retinal migraine is distinct from the loose lay term 'ocular migraine', which is often used for ordinary visual aura.
det.clinical: Episodes can be positive (sparkles, flashes) or negative (greying, blackout) and are confined to one eye. Headache usually follows within an hour and has migraine features. Permanent monocular loss from retinal or optic nerve infarction has been described, which would then be classed as migrainous infarction. Persistent or progressive visual loss, onset after 50, or vascular risk factors should prompt an aggressive search for other causes.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 (2018), like the beta, requires the monocular nature to be confirmed by examination during an attack or by a field drawing made after clear instruction, and other causes must be excluded. Work-up targets embolic, haemodynamic and inflammatory causes: fundoscopy, carotid ultrasound or CTA, cardiac evaluation, ESR/CRP, and in young patients antiphospholipid antibodies, thrombophilia and vasculitis markers. Optical coherence tomography and fluorescein angiography may help if ischaemia is suspected.
det.treatment: Acute attacks are usually treated with NSAIDs or simple analgesics. Many clinicians avoid triptans and ergots because of theoretical vasoconstrictive risk to the retina, although evidence is limited. Preventives with calcium-channel or anti-aura rationale — verapamil, beta-blockers, topiramate, lamotrigine or flunarizine — are reasonable when attacks are frequent; low-dose aspirin is sometimes added. Stop smoking and avoid oestrogen-containing contraceptives.
det.prognosis: Most patients keep normal vision, but a small minority develop permanent visual defects, so follow-up with ophthalmology is wise.
pearls: Ask the patient to cover each eye during an attack — most 'one-eye' auras are actually homonymous.
Retinal migraine is a diagnosis of exclusion; amaurosis fugax and giant-cell arteritis come first.
Permanent monocular loss reclassifies the event as migrainous infarction.

name: Status migrainosus
formal: A complication of migraine in which a typical but debilitating migraine attack continues for more than 72 hours, with only brief relief from treatment or sleep (ICHD-3 1.4.1).
simple: A migraine attack that is very bad and will not stop for more than three days.
th: ภาวะแทรกซ้อนของไมเกรน ปวดไมเกรนรุนแรงต่อเนื่องเกิน 72 ชั่วโมง มักต้องรักษาในห้องฉุกเฉินด้วยยาฉีดและแยกสาเหตุอันตรายอื่นก่อน

Disabling pain over three days with nausea, vomiting, photophobia and phonophobia
Dehydration and inability to keep oral medication down
Frequently linked to medication overuse, stress, sleep loss or hormonal triggers
No new neurological signs — their presence demands a search for a secondary cause

case.who: 31-year-old female garment-factory worker from Samut Prakan
case.story: Her usual left-sided migraine began four days ago and has not settled despite repeated ibuprofen and two doses of a triptan. She has been vomiting and unable to work.
case.exam: Dry mucosa, BP 118/76, afebrile; no neck stiffness, normal fundi and neurological examination.
case.tests: Normal electrolytes; urine pregnancy test negative; no imaging needed given a typical attack and normal exam.
case.q: What emergency treatment is appropriate, and what reduces early recurrence?
case.a: IV fluids, an IV dopamine antagonist (metoclopramide or prochlorperazine) with ketorolac, then dexamethasone to cut recurrence; avoid opioids and consider DHE or an occipital nerve block if still refractory.

det.patho: Status migrainosus reflects failure of the normal termination of a migraine attack, with persistent trigeminovascular activation and central sensitisation. It occurs in a small proportion of people with migraine at some point, more often in those with frequent attacks, medication overuse, psychiatric comorbidity or hormonal shifts. Gastroparesis and vomiting reduce absorption of oral drugs and help perpetuate the attack.
det.clinical: Patients present after three or more days of their typical migraine, exhausted, dehydrated and often anxious. Aura can occur but is not required. Attack features should match previous attacks; a new pattern, older age at first presentation, focal deficits, altered consciousness or systemic symptoms should prompt investigation. ICHD-3 (2018) keeps this under complications of migraine, as did the beta, and advises coding medication overuse headache separately if present.
det.diagnosis: This is a clinical diagnosis in a person with established migraine. Neuroimaging is not routine but is needed when red flags are present; CT venography or MR venography looks for CVT, and CT/LP or CTA for SAH, RCVS and dissection. Pituitary apoplexy, IIH and hypertensive emergencies are other causes of prolonged severe headache.
det.treatment: Give IV fluids and an IV dopamine antagonist (metoclopramide 10 mg or prochlorperazine 10 mg, with diphenhydramine to prevent akathisia), plus an IV NSAID such as ketorolac. Dihydroergotamine IV is effective when there is no vascular disease and no triptan within 24 hours. Dexamethasone (about 10 mg IV) reduces early recurrence, and greater occipital nerve block is a useful adjunct. IV valproate and magnesium are second-line options; opioids and barbiturates should be avoided because they worsen recurrence and overuse. Admission is needed for refractory cases, with a plan for prevention and for stopping any overused drugs.
det.prognosis: Most attacks break with parenteral therapy within one to two days, but recurrence within days is common without corticosteroid cover and preventive treatment.
pearls: Typical migraine lasting over 72 hours plus a normal examination is status migrainosus; any new sign changes the diagnosis.
Dopamine antagonist plus NSAID plus fluids is first-line; dexamethasone lowers recurrence.
Avoid opioids in the ED — they increase return visits and medication overuse.

name: Migrainous infarction
formal: Ischaemic stroke occurring during a typical attack of migraine with aura, in which one or more aura symptoms last beyond an hour and imaging shows an infarct in the corresponding territory, with other stroke causes excluded (ICHD-3 1.4.3).
simple: A rare stroke that happens during a usual migraine aura, when the aura does not go away and a scan shows brain damage in the matching area.
th: สมองขาดเลือดที่เกิดระหว่างการกำเริบของไมเกรนชนิดมี aura โดยอาการ aura ไม่หายเกิน 1 ชั่วโมงและภาพสมองพบ infarct ตรงกับอาการ ต้องแยกสาเหตุอื่นของ stroke ออกก่อน
tempoNote: Begins like the patient's usual aura, but one or more aura symptoms fail to resolve after 60 minutes; deficit then follows a stroke-recovery course
feat: Patient with known migraine with aura whose present attack matches previous ones
Aura symptom (most often visual field loss) persisting beyond an hour
Infarct mainly in the posterior circulation, especially occipital cortex
Young adults, particularly women; smoking and oestrogen-containing contraceptives add risk
Diagnosis of exclusion after a full young-stroke work-up
inv: MRI with DWI to show an acute infarct matching the aura symptoms
Vascular imaging (CTA/MRA) for dissection, vasculopathy or RCVS
Cardiac work-up including echocardiography with bubble study for PFO; rhythm monitoring

case.who: 29-year-old woman from Phitsanulok who smokes and takes a combined oral contraceptive
case.story: She has had visual zig-zag auras before migraine for ten years. Today the usual right-sided zig-zags were followed by a headache, but the right visual field stayed dark more than six hours later.
case.exam: Right homonymous hemianopia; otherwise normal neurological examination; BP 122/78.
case.tests: MRI DWI acute left occipital infarct; CTA normal; ECG and echocardiogram normal with no PFO; antiphospholipid antibodies negative.
case.q: Is this migrainous infarction, and what long-term changes are needed?
case.a: Yes, once other causes are excluded; stop smoking and the combined pill, give antiplatelet therapy and migraine prevention without vasoconstrictors, and avoid triptans and ergots.

det.patho: Migraine with aura roughly doubles the risk of ischaemic stroke, but true migrainous infarction — a stroke arising during an aura — is rare, accounting for a small fraction of strokes in young people. Proposed mechanisms include profound oligaemia from cortical spreading depression, vasospasm, endothelial dysfunction, platelet activation and hypercoagulability. Smoking and oestrogen-containing contraceptives multiply risk, and a PFO is found more often in people with aura.
det.clinical: The attack starts like the patient's usual aura, but the deficit does not fade. The posterior circulation is most often affected, giving homonymous field defects or brainstem and cerebellar signs. Headache often accompanies the event. A stroke in a migraineur that does not occur during a typical aura is classed as ischaemic stroke coexisting with migraine, not migrainous infarction; ICHD-3 (2018) keeps this distinction from the beta.
det.diagnosis: Confirm the infarct with MRI DWI and ensure it matches the persistent aura symptom. Then exclude other causes as for any young stroke: cervical artery dissection, cardioembolism and PFO, antiphospholipid syndrome, vasculitis, RCVS, CADASIL, MELAS and drug-induced vasospasm (triptan, ergot, sympathomimetics). The label should only be used after this work-up is negative.
det.treatment: Acute management is that of ischaemic stroke, including thrombolysis or thrombectomy if eligible. For secondary prevention, give antiplatelet therapy, stop smoking and stop oestrogen-containing contraceptives. Avoid triptans and ergots after an infarct; use NSAIDs and antiemetics for attacks. Preventives such as topiramate, valproate, lamotrigine, flunarizine or candesartan are reasonable; data on CGRP antibodies and gepants after stroke are limited, so they are used cautiously. PFO closure is not routinely indicated for migraine alone.
det.prognosis: Deficits are often mild and recovery is usually good, though small risks of recurrence persist, especially if risk factors continue.
pearls: Aura lasting more than an hour in a migraineur needs urgent MRI — do not wait for it to pass.
Migrainous infarction is diagnosed only after a full young-stroke work-up is negative.
After a migrainous infarct, avoid triptans, ergots, smoking and oestrogen-containing pills.

det.patho: The cause is unknown; persistent cortical hyperexcitability or repetitive waves of spreading depression in visual cortex are proposed. Perfusion imaging in some cases shows regional hypoperfusion without infarction. It is rare, usually bilateral and visual, and arises in people with established migraine with aura.
det.clinical: Patients describe a continuous or fluctuating version of their aura with positive visual phenomena that interfere with reading, driving and screen work. Headache may or may not continue. ICHD-3 (2018) keeps this as a migraine complication, and stresses that it differs from visual snow syndrome, which is a continuous static-like disturbance with palinopsia and other visual symptoms often in people without aura. Persisting symptoms beyond 60 minutes need urgent exclusion of stroke.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires symptoms typical of the person's previous auras, lasting at least a week, with MRI showing no infarct. EEG helps exclude occipital status epilepticus, and ophthalmology examination excludes retinal disease. Posterior reversible encephalopathy, RCVS and posterior cortical atrophy are occasional mimics.
det.treatment: No treatment is proven; small series and case reports describe benefit from lamotrigine, acetazolamide, topiramate, valproate and, acutely, IV magnesium or intranasal ketamine. Reassurance and coping strategies for visual disability are important. Avoid triptans and ergots while the aura persists, given the uncertain vascular state. Treat any coexisting medication overuse.
det.prognosis: Symptoms can resolve within weeks but may last for months or years; most patients have no structural damage.
pearls: Aura beyond an hour → MRI first; persistence beyond a week with a normal scan defines this entity.
EEG is needed to exclude occipital non-convulsive status.
Lamotrigine and acetazolamide are the most commonly tried treatments, with limited evidence.

case.story: She has had migraine with visual zig-zag aura since age 14. Twice this year a typical 20-minute aura was followed within 30 minutes by a generalised convulsion witnessed by roommates.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination.
case.tests: MRI brain normal; interictal EEG shows mild left occipital sharp waves; no photosensitivity.

det.patho: Migraine and epilepsy share comorbidity and some genetic substrates, such as mutations in CACNA1A, ATP1A2 and SCN1A that cause familial hemiplegic migraine. Cortical spreading depression is thought to lower the seizure threshold in susceptible cortex, so an aura can occasionally trigger a seizure. Genuine cases are rare, and the term migralepsy has been criticised because many reported cases were probably occipital seizures.
det.clinical: The patient has typical migraine with aura and, during or shortly after the aura, develops a focal or generalised seizure. The opposite sequence — headache occurring during or after a seizure — is a separate entity in ICHD-3 (2018), classified as headache attributed to epileptic seizure, and ictal epileptic headache is a rare form in which headache is the seizure itself. ICHD-3 retains this aura-triggered entity from the beta version.
det.diagnosis: A careful account of the visual phenomena is crucial: migraine aura is slowly spreading, often black-and-white or zig-zag and lasts 5–60 minutes, while occipital seizure images are brief, coloured and circular. EEG (ideally ictal or prolonged) and epilepsy-protocol MRI are needed. Consider genetic testing when hemiplegic aura or a strong family history is present.
det.treatment: Choose an antiseizure medication with migraine-preventive effect, such as valproate (avoid in women of childbearing potential where possible) or topiramate; lamotrigine may reduce aura. Treat migraine attacks early and address triggers like sleep deprivation. Driving and safety advice follow standard epilepsy rules.
det.prognosis: Good if both conditions are controlled; recurrence depends on control of the underlying migraine with aura.
pearls: Order matters: aura then seizure within an hour = aura-triggered seizure; seizure then headache = post-ictal headache.
Brief coloured circles suggest occipital epilepsy, not migraine aura.
Topiramate or valproate can treat both migraine and seizures.
