name: Epicrania fugax
formal: A primary headache with brief (seconds) paroxysms of stabbing pain that travel in a line or zigzag across one side of the scalp from one point to a distant point, sometimes ending with ipsilateral autonomic signs (ICHD-3 appendix A4.11).
simple: Very short electric-like jabs of pain that shoot across one side of the head from back to front or front to back.
th: ปวดศีรษะแบบแปลบสั้นไม่กี่วินาที ที่วิ่งเป็นเส้นหรือซิกแซกข้ามหนังศีรษะข้างหนึ่ง จากจุดหนึ่งไปอีกจุดหนึ่ง บางรายมีน้ำตาไหลหรือตาแดงข้างเดียวกันตอนท้าย
tempoNote: Each paroxysm lasts about 1–10 seconds; attacks occur spontaneously or are triggered, recurring over weeks to years
feat: Brief stabbing or electric pain that moves rapidly across the scalp in a line or zigzag
Travels between fixed start and end points, usually back of head to forehead/eye (forward) or the reverse
Strictly one-sided, involving different nerve territories along its path
May end with ipsilateral tearing, red eye or rhinorrhoea
Interictal tenderness at the starting point is common
inv: MRI brain and clinical examination of the scalp to exclude structural lesions
Careful history to separate movement of pain from fixed jabs (stabbing headache) or fixed coin-sized pain (nummular)

case.who: 52-year-old female market vendor from Udon Thani
case.story: For eight months she has had sudden 3-second jabs that shoot from behind her left ear across the top of her head to the left eyebrow, several times daily. Some end with left eye tearing.
case.exam: Tender spot behind the left ear; otherwise normal neurological exam.
case.tests: MRI brain normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and does it need treatment?
case.a: Epicrania fugax; reassurance may suffice, and gabapentin, lamotrigine, carbamazepine or onabotulinumtoxinA can be tried if attacks are frequent.

det.patho: Epicrania fugax was described in 2008; in both the ICHD-3 beta and the final ICHD-3 (2018) it is listed only in the appendix (A4.11), meaning it still needs more validation before full acceptance. The mechanism is unknown; a peripheral origin in scalp nerves with central spread is proposed, given the fixed starting point and tenderness. It is rare, affects middle-aged adults and is slightly more common in women.
det.clinical: Each paroxysm lasts seconds and travels along a linear or zigzag path between two points; forward epicrania fugax (occipital to front) is most common, with backward variants also reported. Attacks can be spontaneous or triggered by touch or movement. Ipsilateral autonomic features may occur near the end. Some patients have background tenderness at the start point.
det.diagnosis: Recognition rests on history: the brief pain visibly travels across the scalp. Exclude secondary causes with MRI, especially when there are neurological signs or atypical features. Distinguish it from stabbing headache, nummular headache, occipital neuralgia and SUNCT/SUNA.
det.treatment: Many patients need only reassurance. For frequent attacks, gabapentin, lamotrigine, carbamazepine, pregabalin or onabotulinumtoxinA have been reported to help; local anaesthetic nerve block at the starting point is another option. Evidence comes from small case series.
det.prognosis: Course is variable; some remit spontaneously, others persist for years at low disability.
pearls: Key feature: the pain moves across the scalp within a single few-second attack.
Still an appendix diagnosis in ICHD-3 2018 (A4.11) — not yet in the main classification.
Most need reassurance only; gabapentin or lamotrigine for frequent attacks.

name: Cyclic vomiting syndrome (CVS)
formal: A recurrent, stereotyped disorder in which discrete, intense bouts of nausea and vomiting last from about an hour to several days and are separated by symptom-free intervals; once other causes are excluded, ICHD-3 groups it with the migraine-related episodic syndromes of childhood.
simple: A condition, mostly in children, where bouts of non-stop vomiting come and go in a repeating pattern, with the child completely well in between.
th: โรคอาเจียนเป็นรอบ ๆ อย่างรุนแรงซ้ำแบบเดิมทุกครั้ง ช่วงระหว่างรอบเป็นปกติ พบบ่อยในเด็กและสัมพันธ์กับไมเกรน ต้องแยกโรคทางศัลยกรรม เมแทบอลิก และสมองก่อน
tempoNote: Bouts of 1 hour to 10 days recur every few weeks to months, often at a predictable interval; normal health between bouts
feat: Stereotyped bouts: same time of onset (often early morning), same length, same symptoms each time
Vomiting is intense, at least four times an hour at the peak, with pallor and lethargy
Complete return to baseline between bouts
Triggers include infection, excitement or stress (birthdays, holidays), sleep loss and fasting
Migraine in the patient or relatives is frequent; many children go on to develop migraine
inv: During a bout: glucose, electrolytes, renal function, venous gas, lactate, ammonia; urine ketones
Metabolic screen during a bout when onset is before age 2 or bouts follow fasting/protein load (plasma amino acids, acylcarnitines, urine organic acids, urine PBG/ALA)

MRI brain if any neurological sign, headache that wakes the child, or progressive course

case.who: 7-year-old girl from Nakhon Sawan, brought to the paediatric ward for the fifth time this year
case.story: Each time she wakes about 5 a.m. feeling sick, then vomits every 10–15 minutes for a day and a half, lying pale and listless in a dark room. Between episodes she attends school normally; her mother has migraine.
case.exam: Moderately dehydrated, pale and drowsy but rousable; soft non-tender abdomen; normal fundi, gait and reflexes.
case.tests: Mild ketosis and low bicarbonate, normal glucose and ammonia; abdominal ultrasound and a previous upper GI study normal; she is well again 36 h after IV fluids.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis, and how should future bouts be prevented and treated?
case.a: Cyclic vomiting syndrome; rescue with dextrose-containing IV fluids, an antiemetic such as ondansetron and a quiet dark room, and prophylaxis (amitriptyline over age 5, or cyproheptadine/propranolol) because bouts are frequent and disruptive.

det.patho: The mechanism is not settled; current models invoke a hypersensitive brain–gut axis with hypothalamic–pituitary stress activation, autonomic imbalance and shared susceptibility with migraine. Mitochondrial DNA variants (e.g. 16519T and 3010A) are over-represented in maternally inherited cases, which supports an energy-metabolism component. The syndrome is most often recognised between ages 3 and 7, but an adult form is increasingly reported, frequently linked with chronic cannabis use, anxiety and migraine.
det.clinical: A typical bout passes through a prodrome of nausea and pallor, an emetic phase of relentless vomiting with retching, abdominal pain, drooling and lethargy, and then a rapid recovery phase in which appetite returns. Children may appear almost stuporous, which can be mistaken for encephalopathy. Headache, photophobia and fever may accompany the bout. Red flags pointing elsewhere include bilious vomiting, haematemesis, abdominal distension, onset in infancy, bouts provoked by fasting or protein intake, abnormal neurological signs and a progressively worsening rather than episodic course.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical and rests on a stereotyped, recurrent pattern with full recovery between bouts; ICHD-3 code 1.6.1.1 (the beta used the spelling 'cyclical') requires a minimum number of typical bouts, and gastroenterologists use the closely similar Rome IV definition. Investigations are aimed at mimics: surgical causes such as intestinal malrotation with intermittent volvulus, renal tract obstruction, inborn errors of metabolism, porphyria, adrenal insufficiency and raised intracranial pressure. In adolescents and adults, ask about daily cannabis use and relief from hot showers, which suggest cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome. Blood and urine samples are most informative when taken during a bout, before fluids are given.
det.treatment: Acute care aims to shorten the bout: early IV fluids containing 10% dextrose, correction of electrolytes, ondansetron, and sedation with a quiet dark environment; intranasal or subcutaneous sumatriptan can help older children and adults at bout onset. Prophylaxis is offered when bouts are frequent, prolonged or need admission: cyproheptadine is used below about 5 years, amitriptyline in older children and adults, with propranolol as an alternative; topiramate, coenzyme Q10 and L-carnitine are adjuncts, and aprepitant has been used for refractory cases. Identify and modify triggers such as sleep loss, fasting and emotional stress, and give the family a written emergency plan. Adults should stop cannabis and be screened for anxiety and depression.
det.prognosis: Most children outgrow the bouts by adolescence, but a large proportion go on to develop migraine headache.
pearls: Stereotyped bouts with complete wellness in between is the core of the diagnosis.
Bilious vomiting is never CVS until malrotation is excluded.
Take metabolic samples during the bout, before dextrose is running.

name: Abdominal migraine
formal: A primarily childhood episodic disorder of recurrent moderate-to-severe midline or periumbilical abdominal pain lasting hours to about three days, accompanied by vasomotor and gastrointestinal symptoms such as pallor, anorexia and nausea, with normal health between attacks and no structural or metabolic cause.
simple: Repeated attacks of strong tummy pain around the belly button in a child, linked to migraine, with no headache needed and the child fine between attacks.
ab: recurrent abdominal pain of migraine type

case.who: 9-year-old boy from Chiang Rai, seen in the paediatric clinic with his mother
case.story: For a year he has had episodes of aching pain around the navel lasting most of a day, about once a month, when he lies still, refuses food and looks very pale. His mother and older sister have migraine; he gets car-sick on mountain roads.
case.exam: Thriving, on the 50th centile for weight; abdomen soft and non-tender between attacks; neurological examination normal.
case.tests: FBC, ESR, urinalysis and abdominal ultrasound normal; coeliac serology negative.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and what can be offered?
case.a: Abdominal migraine; explain the diagnosis, use rest, ibuprofen and an antiemetic for attacks, consider nasal sumatriptan, and offer prophylaxis such as propranolol, cyproheptadine or flunarizine if attacks are frequent.

det.patho: Abdominal migraine is thought to share the central mechanisms of migraine — altered hypothalamic and brainstem processing with enhanced visceral sensitivity along the gut–brain axis — rather than a primary gut disease. Prevalence estimates in school-age children range from about 1% to 4%, with a peak between ages 7 and 10 and a slight female predominance. The strong family history and later transition to migraine headache support a common genetic susceptibility.
det.clinical: Attacks begin suddenly or after a short prodrome of irritability, fatigue or yawning, and the child usually wants to lie quietly. Pain is felt in the midline and described as dull or simply sore rather than colicky. Pallor, flushing, anorexia, nausea and occasional vomiting accompany the pain, and photophobia may be present even without headache. Red flags for organic disease include pain away from the midline, pain waking the child, weight loss or growth failure, bloody stools, persistent vomiting, fever, urinary symptoms or abnormal examination.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 (1.6.1.2) and Rome IV both define the disorder clinically by repeated typical attacks with normal function in between and the absence of another explanation; a modest number of tests is enough when there are no red flags. Distinguish it from functional abdominal pain (more continuous, less autonomic), cyclic vomiting syndrome (vomiting dominates), inflammatory bowel disease, coeliac disease, peptic disease, intermittent intussusception or volvulus, renal tract obstruction and porphyria. A diary of attacks helps both diagnosis and the decision about prophylaxis.
det.treatment: Treatment starts with explanation and reassurance, regular meals, adequate sleep and management of stress. Attacks can be treated with rest in a quiet room, paracetamol or ibuprofen, an antiemetic, and in older children intranasal sumatriptan, although evidence is limited. When attacks are frequent or cause missed school, prophylaxis with propranolol, cyproheptadine, flunarizine, amitriptyline or pizotifen (where available) is reasonable for several months, then tapered. Behavioural approaches such as relaxation and cognitive behavioural therapy are useful additions.
det.prognosis: Attacks usually fade by the early teenage years, but many children go on to develop migraine headache in adolescence or adulthood.
pearls: Midline pain with pallor and anorexia in a child with a migraine family, and normal between attacks, suggests abdominal migraine.
No headache is required for the diagnosis.
Pain off the midline, weight loss or night waking are red flags for organic disease.

name: Benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood (BPV)
formal: A migraine-related episodic disorder of young children with recurrent, abrupt attacks of vertigo that last minutes to hours while the child stays fully conscious, often with nystagmus, unsteadiness, vomiting, pallor or fear, and normal neurological, hearing and vestibular findings between attacks; the 2021 Bárány Society–IHS consensus now classifies such children as vestibular migraine of childhood or recurrent vertigo of childhood.
simple: Short, sudden spells of spinning dizziness in a toddler or young child, who becomes scared and unsteady, then quickly returns to normal; it is an early form of migraine.
th: อาการบ้านหมุนเป็นพัก ๆ ในเด็กเล็ก เกิดทันที นานไม่กี่นาทีถึงไม่กี่ชั่วโมง เด็กกลัว เดินเซ ไม่หมดสติ ระหว่างครั้งตรวจปกติ เป็นกลุ่มอาการที่สัมพันธ์กับไมเกรน และหายเองเมื่อโตขึ้น

Rapid, complete recovery; the child resumes play within minutes
Normal hearing, neurological and vestibular examination between attacks
Family history of migraine; motion sickness common; may later develop migraine or vestibular migraine

MRI brain if any persistent neurological sign, headache red flags or progressive course

case.who: 3-year-old girl from Ubon Ratchathani, brought by her grandmother
case.story: Several times over six months she has suddenly cried out, sat down and gripped the furniture, refusing to walk, with her eyes 'jumping' for about two minutes. She stays alert and talks throughout, then gets up and plays as if nothing happened; her father has migraine.
case.exam: Normal growth; normal gait, tandem stance for age, eye movements and cranial nerves between attacks; ear drums normal.
case.tests: Hearing screen and tympanometry normal; a home video shows horizontal nystagmus with the child alert and frightened.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what does the family need to know?
case.a: Benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood (recurrent vertigo of childhood in the 2021 consensus); reassure that it is migraine-related and self-limiting, keep a diary, review for new signs, and reserve preventive drugs for unusually frequent attacks.

det.patho: BPV is regarded as an age-dependent expression of migraine, probably reflecting transient dysfunction of central vestibular pathways or the labyrinth's blood supply in a migraine-prone brain. Among children younger than 5 with repeated spells of vertigo it is the leading diagnosis, with population prevalence estimates around 2–3%. Children with BPV have higher rates of family migraine and of later migraine than controls.
det.clinical: Most children first present as toddlers, at roughly 2–4 years. Young children cannot describe spinning, so parents report sudden fear, unsteadiness, refusal to stand, clinging, head tilt, nystagmus, vomiting or pallor; consciousness and speech are preserved. Attacks are brief, typically minutes, and the child recovers fully at once. Persistent imbalance, hearing loss, ear discharge, headache on waking, altered consciousness or any abnormal sign between attacks argues against the diagnosis and calls for further work-up, including posterior fossa imaging.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 (1.6.2) defines BPV clinically by repeated abrupt, self-resolving vertigo with typical associated signs and a normal interictal examination, hearing and vestibular function. A 2021 joint consensus from the Bárány Society with the IHS introduced criteria for children under 18 that split the condition into vestibular migraine of childhood (definite or probable, when migraine features are present) and recurrent vertigo of childhood (at least three moderate-to-severe episodes lasting a minute to 72 hours without migraine features); ICHD-3 still lists BPV, so both terms are encountered. Exclude otitis media with effusion, vestibular neuritis, BPPV (rare at this age), seizures with vertiginous aura, episodic ataxia, and posterior fossa tumours or malformations.
det.treatment: Most children need only explanation, reassurance and a symptom diary, because attacks are short and the condition remits. During an attack, keep the child safe and lying down; antiemetics are rarely needed. For frequent or distressing attacks, migraine prophylaxis such as cyproheptadine or flunarizine can be tried for a few months. Review periodically for new signs and for the emergence of migraine headache.
det.prognosis: Attacks generally stop by early school age; a substantial minority later develop migraine or vestibular migraine.
pearls: Toddler with sudden frightened unsteadiness and nystagmus, fully conscious and normal minutes later: think BPV.
Newer 2021 terms: 'vestibular migraine of childhood' (migraine features present) or 'recurrent vertigo of childhood' (none).
Any interictal abnormality or persistent ataxia needs MRI of the posterior fossa.
det.thd: Benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood คืออาการบ้านหมุนเป็นพัก ๆ ในเด็กอายุราว 2–4 ปี เกิดขึ้นกะทันหันและนานไม่กี่นาที ระหว่างนั้นเด็กกลัว เดินไม่ได้ อาจเห็นตากระตุก แต่รู้ตัวดีตลอด และกลับมาเล่นได้ทันทีหลังหาย ถือเป็นอาการแสดงของไมเกรนตามวัย ในปี 2021 Bárány Society กับ IHS แบ่งเป็น vestibular migraine of childhood กับ recurrent vertigo of childhood ถ้าตรวจระหว่างครั้งไม่ปกติต้องทำ MRI ส่วนการรักษาส่วนใหญ่คืออธิบายให้ครอบครัวสบายใจ

name: Cold-stimulus headache
formal: A primary headache provoked by cold applied to the head or by cold food, drink or air passing over the palate and pharynx, typically brief and resolving within minutes once the cold is removed; ICHD-3 divides it into external-application and ingestion/inhalation subtypes.
simple: A short, sharp headache that comes on when something very cold touches the head or goes into the mouth, like the 'brain freeze' from ice cream.
th: ปวดหัวจากความเย็น เช่น กินไอศกรีมหรือน้ำแข็งเร็ว ๆ หรือศีรษะสัมผัสลมหรือน้ำเย็นจัด ปวดแปลบที่หน้าผากหรือขมับ และหายภายในไม่กี่นาทีเมื่อเลิกสัมผัสความเย็น
tempoNote: Begins within seconds of the cold stimulus and resolves within about 10–30 minutes of removing it
feat: Ingested type: sharp frontal or temporal pain seconds after cold food or drink touches the palate
External type: diffuse head pain after exposure of an unprotected head to very cold air or water
Pain peaks quickly and settles within minutes after the stimulus stops
More frequent and more intense in people with migraine; may be felt on the usual migraine side
Neurological examination normal
inv: Clinical diagnosis; no tests needed for the typical picture
Imaging only if pain is prolonged, thunderclap-like without a clear trigger, or neurological signs appear

case.story: Whenever she gulps a shaved-ice dessert on a hot afternoon, a stabbing pain shoots into both temples within seconds, makes her stop eating and fades after about half a minute. She has had migraine without aura since secondary school.
case.exam: Normal general and neurological examination; no sinus or dental tenderness.
case.tests: None required.
case.q: What is this headache, and what advice helps?
case.a: Cold-stimulus headache from ingestion of cold; eat cold food slowly, keep it on the front of the tongue and press the tongue to the palate to warm it — no investigations or drugs are needed.

read.where: Chapter 3 Diagnosis of Other Primary Headaches

det.patho: Rapid cooling of the palate and posterior pharynx activates trigeminal and possibly glossopharyngeal afferents and is accompanied by a brief surge of flow in the anterior cerebral circulation, with pain referred to the forehead and temples. External cold may act through scalp vasoconstriction and stimulation of cutaneous trigeminal and upper cervical endings. Brain freeze is extremely common, experienced by roughly a third or more of the general population, and more so in those with migraine.
det.clinical: The ingested form causes a sudden, intense, stabbing or pressing pain in the midfrontal or temporal region, sometimes on one side, peaking within seconds and usually lasting less than a minute. The external form, seen with diving into cold water, cold winds on an uncovered head or cryotherapy, produces a more diffuse ache. People with migraine may report that cold sometimes sets off a full migraine attack, which should be classified separately. Pain that lasts longer, recurs without a cold trigger or is accompanied by other symptoms warrants a different explanation.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 code 4.5 (4.5.1 external application, 4.5.2 ingestion or inhalation) is a clinical diagnosis based on a clear cold trigger, rapid onset and quick resolution after the stimulus stops. In ICHD-3 this entity sits among the other primary headaches (chapter 4), having been moved there from the secondary-headache chapter of ICHD-II. Exclude trigeminal neuralgia when cold on the face or teeth provokes paroxysms, dental sensitivity, and any secondary cause when the pattern is atypical.
det.treatment: Reassurance and avoidance are sufficient: consume cold foods and drinks slowly, warm the palate by pressing the tongue against it, and cover the head in cold weather or when swimming in cold water. Preventive medication is not used. If cold reliably triggers migraine attacks, manage the migraine itself with acute and, when indicated, preventive treatment.
det.prognosis: Benign and self-limiting; it does not signal structural disease.
pearls: Brain freeze is a recognised primary headache, coded under ICHD-3 4.5.
Cold triggering facial electric shocks suggests trigeminal neuralgia instead.
Pressing the tongue on the palate shortens an attack.
det.thd: Cold-stimulus headache คืออาการปวดหัวที่เกิดขึ้นทันทีเมื่อกินหรือดื่มของเย็นจัดจนเย็นถึงเพดานปาก หรือเมื่อศีรษะโดนลมหรือน้ำเย็นจัด ส่วนใหญ่ปวดแปลบที่หน้าผากหรือขมับไม่กี่วินาทีถึงไม่กี่นาทีแล้วหายเอง และพบบ่อยกว่าในคนที่เป็นไมเกรน วินิจฉัยได้จากประวัติโดยไม่ต้องตรวจเพิ่ม การดูแลคือกินของเย็นช้า ๆ เอาลิ้นแตะเพดานปากให้อุ่น และใส่หมวกเมื่ออากาศหนาว

Sudden severe headache without a brief cold trigger must be imaged to exclude SAH or RCVS
Brief jabs occur spontaneously, not tied to a cold stimulus

name: External-pressure headache
formal: A primary headache caused by sustained compression of, or traction on, the pericranial soft tissues — by tight headwear, goggles or helmets (external-compression headache) or by pulled-back hair or headgear straps (external-traction headache) — maximal at the site of the stimulus and resolving within an hour of its removal.
simple: A headache caused by something squeezing or pulling on the head, such as a tight helmet, swimming goggles or a tight ponytail, which goes away soon after it is taken off.
th: ปวดหัวจากแรงกดหรือแรงดึงที่หนังศีรษะ เช่น หมวกกันน็อก แว่นว่ายน้ำ หรือมัดผมตึง ปวดตรงจุดที่ถูกกดหรือดึง และหายภายใน 1 ชั่วโมงหลังถอดออก
tempoNote: Begins within about an hour of sustained compression or traction and resolves within an hour after it is removed
feat: Pressing or pulling pain maximal under the band, strap, goggles or tied hair
Appears only while the pressure or traction is sustained
Clears within an hour of removing the cause, without other symptoms
May set off a migraine attack in susceptible people
Normal examination apart from local scalp tenderness
inv: Clinical diagnosis; trial removal or loosening of the headwear or hairstyle
Imaging only if pain persists after removal or other features suggest a secondary cause

case.story: Since switching to a smaller full-face helmet, he gets a tight, pressing ache across the forehead and over both temples after about 40 minutes of riding. The pain clears within half an hour of taking the helmet off and never occurs on his days off.
case.exam: Red pressure marks across the forehead; mild tenderness at the same site; neurological examination normal.
case.tests: None needed.
case.q: What type of headache is this and what is the fix?
case.a: External-compression headache; change to a properly fitted helmet with adequate padding — no drugs or scans are required.

read.where: Chapter 3 Diagnosis of Other Primary Headaches

det.patho: Continuous pressure or pulling stimulates mechanosensitive afferents in the scalp and pericranial tissues supplied by branches of the trigeminal nerve (supraorbital, supratrochlear, auriculotemporal) and the occipital nerves. Sustained stimulation can cause local sensitisation, and in people prone to migraine it may trigger central activation. External-compression headache is common among wearers of helmets, swim goggles, tight hats and head-mounted devices; external-traction headache is classically seen with tight ponytails or braids.
det.clinical: Pain begins while the pressure or traction persists, is felt most at the site of the stimulus and is usually pressing or pulling in quality. It typically eases quickly once the cause is removed. Patients with migraine may notice that prolonged pressure turns into a full attack, which is then coded as migraine. Persistent headache after removal, local lumps, scalp lesions or neurological symptoms should prompt a search for other causes, such as supraorbital or occipital neuralgia or a skull lesion.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 code 4.6, with subtypes 4.6.1 (compression) and 4.6.2 (traction), is diagnosed clinically when the headache occurs during sustained mechanical stimulation, is maximal at that site and settles within an hour of removing it. External-traction headache was newly added in ICHD-3, and both subtypes now sit with the other primary headaches rather than among secondary headaches. A simple removal trial confirms the diagnosis.
det.treatment: Remove or adjust the cause: choose properly fitted and padded helmets or goggles, loosen headbands and change tight hairstyles. Simple analgesics are rarely needed because pain stops once the stimulus is gone. If the trigger cannot be avoided (for example occupational helmets), take regular breaks to relieve pressure. Treat coexisting migraine on its own merits.
det.prognosis: Excellent; symptoms disappear once the mechanical cause is corrected.
pearls: Pain maximal under the strap, band or goggles and gone within an hour of removal is diagnostic.
Ponytail headache is external-traction headache (ICHD-3 4.6.2).
If headache persists after removal, look for another cause.
det.thd: External-pressure headache คืออาการปวดหัวที่เกิดจากมีสิ่งกดหรือดึงหนังศีรษะเป็นเวลานาน ถ้าเป็นแรงกด เช่น หมวกกันน็อก แว่นว่ายน้ำ หรือหมวกคับ เรียกว่า external-compression ส่วนแรงดึงจากการมัดผมตึงเรียกว่า external-traction อาการปวดมักมากที่สุดตรงจุดที่ถูกกดหรือดึง และหายภายในหนึ่งชั่วโมงหลังถอดออก วิธีแก้คือเลือกอุปกรณ์ที่ขนาดพอดี คลายสายรัด และเลิกมัดผมแน่น ส่วนใหญ่ไม่ต้องใช้ยา

name: Red ear syndrome (RES)
formal: A rare episodic syndrome of unilateral or bilateral burning pain in and around the ear with simultaneous reddening and warmth of the pinna, occurring as an idiopathic (often childhood, migraine-associated) form or secondary to upper cervical, temporomandibular, thalamic or cranial-nerve pathology, and frequently coexisting with migraine or trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias.
simple: Attacks of burning pain in the ear with the ear turning bright red and hot for minutes to hours, often in people who also have migraine.
th: อาการปวดแสบร้อนที่หูร่วมกับใบหูแดงและร้อนเป็นพัก ๆ นานเป็นนาทีถึงชั่วโมง มักพบร่วมกับไมเกรนหรือ cluster headache หรือเกิดจากความผิดปกติของกระดูกคอส่วนบน ข้อต่อขากรรไกร หรือ thalamus
tempoNote: Attacks last from seconds to several hours and recur from several times daily to a few times a month
feat: Burning or aching ear pain with visible redness and warmth of the pinna, usually one side
Attacks may be triggered by touching the ear, heat, chewing, neck movement, exercise or hair brushing
Frequently occurs during or alongside migraine or cluster/TAC attacks
Children and adolescents usually have the primary, migraine-linked form
Adults more often have a secondary cause (C2–C3 disease, TMJ, thalamic lesion, glossopharyngeal neuralgia)
inv: Clinical diagnosis supported by photographs of an attack
MRI of the cervical spine and brain (craniocervical junction, thalamus, posterior fossa) when onset is in adulthood or examination is abnormal
ENT and dental/TMJ assessment to exclude local ear or jaw pathology

case.who: 14-year-old girl from Khon Kaen with migraine without aura
case.story: For a year her left ear suddenly turns bright red and burns for 20–60 minutes, sometimes at the start of a migraine and sometimes alone, especially after brushing her hair or on hot days. Ice packs give some relief.
case.exam: Between attacks the ear, cervical spine, jaw and neurological examination are normal; a phone photo shows a flushed left pinna.
case.tests: Otoscopy normal; MRI brain and cervical spine normal.
case.q: What is the condition, and how is it managed?
case.a: Primary red ear syndrome associated with migraine; explain it, use local cooling for attacks, and if frequent try a migraine preventive such as propranolol, amitriptyline or flunarizine.

read.where: Chapter 2 Diagnosis of Trigeminal Autonomic Cephalalgias

det.patho: The pinna is supplied by the auriculotemporal branch of the trigeminal nerve and by the great auricular and lesser occipital nerves from C2–C3, so the syndrome is thought to arise from antidromic release of vasodilator peptides (such as CGRP) along these afferents, from trigeminal autonomic reflex activation, or from both. This explains its coexistence with migraine and TACs and its association with upper cervical root irritation. Primary cases appear mainly in children and young people, while secondary cases are linked with C3 root compression, cervical spondylosis, TMJ dysfunction, thalamic lesions, herpes zoster and glossopharyngeal neuralgia.
det.clinical: Attacks consist of a burning or aching sensation of the ear with redness that may involve the lobe or the whole pinna and sometimes spread to the cheek. Episodes may be spontaneous or provoked by touch, heat, exercise, chewing, neck movement or hair grooming, and can be unilateral or switch sides. In migraine-associated cases the ear may flush during the headache phase or independently. Coexisting tearing, ptosis or restlessness suggests a link with a TAC. Onset in older adults or with fixed neurological signs points to a secondary cause.
det.diagnosis: There are no formal ICHD-3 criteria; red ear syndrome is a descriptive syndrome, and the patient's other headache disorder (migraine, cluster headache, paroxysmal hemicrania or SUNCT/SUNA) is classified in its own right. Diagnosis relies on history and, ideally, a photograph or observation of an attack. Exclude local ear infection, relapsing polychondritis (persistent inflammation sparing the lobe), erythromelalgia, Frey-type auricular flushing, and in adults image the craniocervical junction, upper cervical spine and thalamus.
det.treatment: Treat the associated headache disorder: migraine preventives (propranolol, amitriptyline, flunarizine, topiramate or a CGRP-pathway drug in adults) often reduce ear attacks, and indomethacin is tried when a paroxysmal hemicrania–like pattern is present. Gabapentin or pregabalin can help neuropathic burning. Local cold packs relieve individual attacks. Secondary forms may respond to treating the cause, greater occipital or C2–C3 nerve blocks, or botulinum toxin; evidence comes from case series only.
det.prognosis: Primary childhood cases often lessen with age; secondary cases depend on the underlying lesion.
pearls: Burning red pinna plus migraine in a teenager is usually primary red ear syndrome.
Ear innervation by C2–C3 explains links with upper cervical disease — image the neck in adults.
Relapsing polychondritis spares the earlobe; red ear syndrome does not.
det.thd: Red ear syndrome คือกลุ่มอาการที่มีปวดแสบร้อนที่หูร่วมกับใบหูแดงและร้อนเป็นพัก ๆ ในเด็กและวัยรุ่นมักเป็นชนิดปฐมภูมิซึ่งสัมพันธ์กับไมเกรน แต่ในผู้ใหญ่ควรหาสาเหตุ เช่น โรคกระดูกคอระดับ C2–C3, ข้อต่อขากรรไกร, รอยโรคที่ thalamus หรือ glossopharyngeal neuralgia กลไกเกี่ยวกับเส้นประสาท trigeminal และรากประสาทคอส่วนบนซึ่งหลั่งสารขยายหลอดเลือด เช่น CGRP การรักษาคือรักษาโรคปวดศีรษะที่เป็นร่วม ใช้ยาป้องกันไมเกรน และประคบเย็นตอนมีอาการ

name: High-altitude headache
formal: A secondary headache attributed to hypobaric hypoxia that develops within about 24 hours of ascending above roughly 2,500 m and resolves within 24 hours of descent, often as the earliest symptom of acute mountain sickness.
simple: A headache that starts after travelling up to a high mountain place because there is less oxygen in the air, and gets better after going back down.
th: ปวดหัวเมื่อขึ้นที่สูงเกิน 2,500 เมตรภายใน 24 ชั่วโมง เกิดจากออกซิเจนต่ำ มักเป็นอาการแรกของ acute mountain sickness หายเมื่อลงที่ต่ำ ป้องกันด้วยการขึ้นช้า ๆ และ acetazolamide
tempoNote: Onset 6–24 hours after ascent above about 2,500 m; resolves within a day of descent or acclimatisation
feat: Bilateral frontal or diffuse dull or throbbing ache, worse with exertion, straining, coughing or lying flat
Often accompanied by nausea, anorexia, fatigue, dizziness and poor sleep (acute mountain sickness)
Risk rises with fast ascent, sleeping altitude, prior altitude illness and history of migraine
Ataxia, confusion or drowsiness signal high-altitude cerebral oedema (HACE) — an emergency
Improves with simple analgesics, oxygen or descent
inv: Clinical diagnosis; pulse oximetry supports hypoxaemia
Lake Louise AMS score to grade severity
Check gait (tandem walk) and conscious level for HACE; MRI after evacuation if HACE is suspected
Exclude CO poisoning (heaters in closed tents/huts), dehydration and hypoglycaemia

case.who: 45-year-old Thai teacher on a trekking tour in Nepal
case.story: Eight hours after flying into a town at 3,500 m and walking up to a lodge, she developed a throbbing frontal headache worse on bending, with nausea, no appetite and broken sleep. She has a history of migraine.
case.exam: SpO2 86% on room air; alert; normal tandem gait; no focal signs.
case.tests: Lake Louise score 5 (mild-to-moderate AMS); no heater in the room.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, how should it be treated, and how could it have been prevented?
case.a: High-altitude headache as part of acute mountain sickness; rest without further ascent, ibuprofen or paracetamol, antiemetic, oxygen or descent if not improving, and acetazolamide; prevention is slower ascent with rest days and prophylactic acetazolamide.

read.where: Chapter 1 Breathing and the Nervous System
Chapter 53: Headache attributed to disorders of homeostasis

det.patho: Hypobaric hypoxia causes cerebral vasodilatation, increased cerebral blood flow and mild vasogenic and cytotoxic swelling; in people with tight intracranial reserve this raises pressure and activates the trigeminovascular system, with nitric oxide, free radicals and inflammatory mediators contributing. Above 2,500 m, a large proportion of unacclimatised visitors develop headache, and the risk increases with altitude, speed of ascent, exertion, dehydration and a history of migraine. Thai travellers commonly encounter it on treks in the Himalaya, Tibet, Yunnan and the Andes.
det.clinical: The headache is usually bilateral, frontal or generalised, dull or throbbing, and worse with exertion, lying down, coughing or straining. When it is accompanied by gastrointestinal upset, fatigue or dizziness, acute mountain sickness is present, graded with the 2018 Lake Louise score. Progression to ataxia, confusion, drowsiness or severe vomiting suggests high-altitude cerebral oedema, and breathlessness at rest or cough suggests high-altitude pulmonary oedema; both can be fatal without descent. Altitude can also trigger a typical migraine attack in migraineurs.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 10.1.1 attributes the headache to altitude when it develops after ascending above about 2,500 m, worsens with continued ascent and settles within a day of descent; the IHS files it within the group of headaches caused by low oxygen or CO2 retention. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by oximetry and serial gait checks. Consider carbon monoxide exposure from heaters and stoves, dehydration, hypoglycaemia, alcohol, sinusitis and, if signs are focal, intracranial haemorrhage or venous sinus thrombosis (polycythaemia and dehydration raise this risk).
det.treatment: Prevention is most effective: above 3,000 m increase sleeping altitude by no more than about 500 m per day with a rest day every 3–4 days, maintain hydration and avoid alcohol; acetazolamide 125 mg twice daily started a day before ascent is first-line pharmacological prophylaxis for moderate- to high-risk ascents, and dexamethasone is an alternative when acetazolamide cannot be used. Mild headache responds to ibuprofen or paracetamol with a halt to further ascent. Moderate to severe AMS is treated with acetazolamide, oxygen, a portable hyperbaric bag or descent; HACE requires immediate descent, oxygen and dexamethasone (8 mg then 4 mg six-hourly).
det.prognosis: Usually resolves within one to three days with acclimatisation or descent; untreated progression to HACE can be fatal.
pearls: Headache plus ataxia at altitude is HACE until proven otherwise — descend.
Never ascend further with symptoms of acute mountain sickness.
Acetazolamide 125 mg twice daily is the standard prophylaxis.
det.thd: High-altitude headache เป็นอาการปวดหัวจากภาวะออกซิเจนต่ำที่เริ่มภายใน 24 ชั่วโมงหลังขึ้นไปบนที่สูงเกินราว 2,500 เมตร และมักเป็นอาการแรกของ acute mountain sickness ถ้าเดินเซหรือสับสนต้องคิดถึง HACE ซึ่งต้องพาลงที่ต่ำทันที ให้ออกซิเจนและ dexamethasone การป้องกันคือขึ้นทีละน้อยไม่เกิน 500 เมตรต่อวัน ดื่มน้ำให้พอ และกิน acetazolamide 125 mg วันละ 2 ครั้ง ส่วนกรณีที่ปวดไม่มากให้ ibuprofen หรือ paracetamol และหยุดไต่ระดับขึ้นไปอีก

name: Sleep apnoea headache
formal: A secondary headache present on awakening in people with obstructive sleep apnoea (apnoea–hypopnoea index of 5 or more), typically bilateral and pressing without migraine features, usually settling within four hours of waking and improving or resolving with effective treatment of the apnoea.
simple: A morning headache caused by repeated stops in breathing during sleep, which goes away when the sleep apnoea is treated.
th: ปวดหัวตอนตื่นนอนในผู้ที่มีภาวะหยุดหายใจขณะหลับ ปวดตื้อทั้งสองข้าง ไม่มีอาการแบบไมเกรน หายภายใน 4 ชั่วโมง และดีขึ้นเมื่อรักษาด้วย CPAP
tempoNote: Recurrent morning headaches on most days for months, each lasting under 4 hours after waking
feat: Bilateral, pressing headache present on waking, gone within about 4 hours
Usually no nausea, photophobia or phonophobia
Loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas, unrefreshing sleep and daytime sleepiness
Obesity, large neck, retrognathia, hypertension; partner reports gasping
Improves or disappears with effective CPAP
inv: Polysomnography or home sleep apnoea testing (AHI ≥5/h)
Screening questionnaires: STOP-Bang, Epworth sleepiness scale
Morning arterial or venous CO2 if hypoventilation (obesity hypoventilation, neuromuscular disease) is suspected
Headache diary to document response to treatment

case.who: 52-year-old taxi driver from Bangkok with obesity (BMI 33) and hypertension
case.story: For eight months he has woken almost daily with a dull, tight ache across his whole head that clears by mid-morning after coffee. His wife says he snores loudly and stops breathing at night, and he nods off at red lights.
case.exam: Neck circumference 44 cm, crowded oropharynx, BP 156/96; neurological examination and fundi normal.
case.tests: Polysomnography AHI 38/h with oxygen nadir 78%; Epworth score 15.
case.q: What is the cause of his headache and what treatment will relieve it?
case.a: Sleep apnoea headache from severe obstructive sleep apnoea; CPAP with weight loss and reduced evening alcohol should resolve the morning headache — and he should not drive while sleepy until treated.

read.where: Chapter 51 Neurologic Aspects of Sleep Medicine

det.patho: Repeated upper-airway collapse during sleep causes intermittent hypoxaemia, hypercapnia with cerebral vasodilatation, surges in intrathoracic pressure and blood pressure, and fragmented sleep; nocturnal CO2 retention and transient rises in intracranial pressure are the leading explanations for morning headache. Morning headache is reported by roughly a fifth to a third of people with obstructive sleep apnoea, more often in severe disease. Many patients have overlapping migraine or tension-type headache that sleep fragmentation makes worse.
det.clinical: The headache is present on waking, usually bilateral, pressing and of mild-to-moderate intensity, without migraine features, and fades within a few hours. It occurs on many mornings and parallels the severity of the sleep-disordered breathing. Patients often describe loud snoring, witnessed pauses, choking awakenings, nocturia, poor concentration and daytime sleepiness. Morning headache is non-specific, so raised intracranial pressure, hypercapnic respiratory failure, depression, bruxism, caffeine withdrawal and medication overuse also need to be considered.
det.diagnosis: In ICHD-3 (code 10.1.4, within the hypoxia/hypercapnia group) the headache is attributed to apnoea when sleep studies confirm obstructive sleep apnoea, the headache appeared or worsened with it, and it improves when the apnoea is treated; typical features are frequent morning occurrence, bilateral pressing quality and resolution within hours. Confirm the sleep disorder with polysomnography or home testing. Check morning CO2 when obesity hypoventilation or neuromuscular weakness is possible, and consider fundoscopy and imaging if headache is progressive, focal signs appear or papilloedema is seen.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying apnoea: CPAP is first-line for moderate to severe disease and typically relieves the headache within weeks when used for most of the night. Alternatives include mandibular advancement devices, positional therapy, upper-airway surgery or hypoglossal nerve stimulation in selected cases; weight reduction (including the dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist tirzepatide, approved since 2024 for OSA with obesity) reduces severity. Advise avoiding alcohol and sedatives at night. Avoid escalating daily analgesics, which risks medication overuse headache.
det.prognosis: The headache usually resolves or improves markedly with effective CPAP use.
pearls: Bilateral pressing headache on waking that clears within 4 hours plus snoring: order a sleep study.
Response to CPAP confirms the link.

name: Cardiac cephalalgia
formal: A secondary headache caused by myocardial ischaemia, usually brought on by exertion and relieved by rest or nitroglycerin, which may occur with or without chest pain and can mimic migraine; recognising it matters because vasoconstrictor migraine drugs are contraindicated.
simple: A headache that is really a sign of the heart not getting enough blood, coming on with exercise and easing with rest or heart medicine.
th: ปวดหัวที่เป็นอาการของกล้ามเนื้อหัวใจขาดเลือด มักเกิดตอนออกแรงและหายเมื่อพักหรืออมยา nitroglycerin อาจไม่มีเจ็บหน้าอก ห้ามให้ triptan หรือ ergot
tempoNote: Attacks with exertion lasting minutes, settling with rest; can present acutely during myocardial infarction
feat: New headache in a person over 50 with vascular risk factors, provoked by exertion
Relieved within minutes by rest or sublingual nitroglycerin
May be severe and accompanied by nausea, sweating or breathlessness; chest pain can be absent
Pain may be bilateral, occipital, frontal or diffuse
ECG changes or troponin rise during an episode
inv: 12-lead ECG during symptoms and serial high-sensitivity troponin
Exercise stress test or stress imaging reproducing headache with ischaemic changes
Coronary CT angiography or invasive coronary angiography
Brain imaging (CT/MRI with angiography) to exclude SAH, RCVS or other exertional causes

case.who: 63-year-old retired farmer from Suphan Buri with diabetes, hypertension and heavy smoking
case.story: For three weeks he has had a pressing occipital and frontal headache with sweating whenever he climbs the stairs to his house or carries rice sacks; it settles within 5–10 minutes of sitting down. He denies chest pain, and a clinic gave him an ergotamine tablet for presumed migraine.
case.exam: BP 150/90, pulse 88 regular; neurological examination and fundi normal.
case.tests: Resting ECG normal; treadmill test at 5 minutes reproduced the headache with 2 mm ST depression in V4–V6, relieved by sublingual nitroglycerin; coronary angiography showed severe left anterior descending stenosis.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what medication must be stopped?
case.a: Cardiac cephalalgia (headache as an angina equivalent); stop ergotamine (and avoid triptans), start antianginal and secondary prevention therapy, and refer for revascularisation, which usually abolishes the headache.

read.where: Chapter 59 Headache in General Medical Conditions
Chapter 53: Headache attributed to disorders of homeostasis

det.patho: The mechanism is uncertain; proposed explanations include convergence of cardiac vagal and sympathetic afferents with trigeminal and upper cervical pain pathways in the brainstem and spinal cord, release of ischaemia-related mediators (bradykinin, serotonin, histamine) that sensitise intracranial vessels, and reduced venous return with transiently raised intracranial pressure during ischaemia. It is uncommon but probably under-recognised, especially in older patients with diabetes in whom chest pain may be absent.
det.clinical: The typical patient is over 50 with coronary risk factors and has a new headache that comes on with physical effort and fades with rest, sometimes accompanied by nausea, sweating, breathlessness or arm discomfort. Pain may be moderate to severe and of variable site, and headache is the sole manifestation of ischaemia in a substantial share of reported cases. Headache can also accompany acute myocardial infarction at rest. A history of migraine-like attacks starting late in life, provoked by exertion, should always raise this possibility.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 code 10.6 attributes the headache to cardiac ischaemia when it develops alongside proven acute myocardial ischaemia, worsens with exercise and is relieved by nitroglycerin or by treating the ischaemia. Evidence comes from an ECG and troponin during an episode, stress testing that reproduces the headache together with ischaemic changes, and coronary imaging. Brain imaging with vascular study is still needed to exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage, RCVS, arterial dissection and primary exercise headache, which share the exertional trigger.
det.treatment: Manage as acute coronary syndrome or stable angina according to the presentation: antiplatelet therapy, high-intensity statin, beta-blocker, nitrates and risk-factor control, with coronary revascularisation (PCI or CABG) when indicated, which typically abolishes the headache. Stop and avoid triptans, ergotamine and other vasoconstrictors, which can precipitate infarction; NSAIDs are also best avoided. Ditans (lasmiditan) lack vasoconstrictor action but are not appropriate while the cause is untreated ischaemia.
det.prognosis: Excellent for the headache once ischaemia is treated; the overall outlook is that of the underlying coronary disease.
pearls: New exertional headache after 50 with vascular risk: think heart, not migraine.
Relief with nitroglycerin is a key clue — nitrates usually worsen migraine.
Never give a triptan or ergot to someone with suspected cardiac cephalalgia.
det.thd: Cardiac cephalalgia คืออาการปวดหัวที่เป็นตัวแทนอาการของกล้ามเนื้อหัวใจขาดเลือด มักพบในคนอายุมากกว่า 50 ปีที่มีปัจจัยเสี่ยงหลอดเลือด ปวดเวลาออกแรงแล้วหายเมื่อพักหรืออมยา nitroglycerin และบางรายไม่มีเจ็บหน้าอกเลย การวินิจฉัยใช้ ECG, troponin, การทดสอบออกกำลังกาย และการตรวจหลอดเลือดหัวใจ โดยต้องตรวจสมองเพื่อแยก SAH และ RCVS ร่วมด้วย การรักษาคือรักษาโรคหลอดเลือดหัวใจหรือทำ revascularisation ซึ่งช่วยให้อาการปวดหัวหายไป และห้ามให้ triptan หรือ ergot เด็ดขาด

name: Post-traumatic headache (PTH)
formal: Secondary headache that first appears, or clearly worsens, within about a week of a head injury or whiplash (or of regaining consciousness or the ability to report pain); it is called acute while it lasts under 3 months and persistent once it goes beyond 3 months.
simple: A headache that starts soon after a knock to the head or a neck jolt, and sometimes keeps going for months.
th: ปวดศีรษะที่เริ่มภายในราว 7 วันหลังศีรษะกระแทกหรือคอสะบัด (whiplash) ถ้าเกิน 3 เดือนเรียกว่า persistent มักมีลักษณะคล้ายไมเกรนหรือ tension-type และพบบ่อยกว่าในผู้บาดเจ็บเล็กน้อย
tempoNote: Begins within 7 days of the injury; acute form settles within 3 months, persistent form lasts longer and often becomes daily
feat: Onset tied in time to head trauma or whiplash; often more frequent after mild than after severe injury
Usually a migraine-like or tension-type-like phenotype, sometimes with neck pain or occipital features
Accompanied by dizziness, poor concentration, sleep disturbance, irritability and low mood
Daily analgesic use frequently adds medication-overuse headache
Neurological examination is normal; new deficits or worsening must prompt imaging
inv: CT brain at presentation by head-injury decision rules (e.g. Canadian CT Head Rule); anticoagulated or elderly patients image early
Repeat imaging (CT/MRI) if headache escalates, deficits appear or drowsiness develops — think chronic subdural haematoma
CTA neck when neck pain, Horner syndrome or ischaemic symptoms raise dissection
Headache diary with analgesic days; mood and sleep screening (PHQ-9, GAD-7)

case.who: 24-year-old female nursing student from Khon Kaen
case.story: She fell off a motorbike two months ago, hitting the left side of her head with a brief blackout. Since then she has throbbing headaches four days a week with light sensitivity, and she takes ibuprofen most days.
case.exam: Neurological examination is normal; neck movements are full but the left upper trapezius is tender.
case.tests: CT on the day of injury and a recent MRI are normal; her diary shows analgesic use on 16 days a month.
case.q: How is this classified and what should be done first?
case.a: Acute post-traumatic headache with a migraine phenotype, now at risk of medication overuse; cap analgesics to under 10 days a month, start a preventive (e.g. amitriptyline or propranolol), encourage graded aerobic activity and sleep hygiene.

read.where: ICHD-3 5.1–5.4 Headache attributed to trauma or injury to the head and/or neck
Headaches, Traumatic Brain Injury, and Concussion
Chapter 46: Headache attributed to head or neck trauma

det.patho: Mechanisms are thought to combine trigeminovascular activation, altered pain modulation after diffuse axonal strain, release of neuropeptides such as CGRP, and injury to neck muscles, joints and occipital nerves. Psychological stress, poor sleep and pre-existing migraine increase vulnerability. Paradoxically the risk is higher after mild injury than after severe brain injury. Litigation does not fully explain persistence, as symptoms often continue after settlement.
det.clinical: ICHD-3 separates headache after head injury (5.1 acute, 5.2 persistent, each with mild or moderate-to-severe subtypes) from headache after whiplash (5.3 and 5.4). There is no unique phenotype: about half resemble migraine and many resemble tension-type headache, with some cervicogenic or occipital-neuralgia-like pain. Associated problems include dizziness, fatigue, impaired attention, insomnia, anxiety and depression. Red flags are worsening headache, vomiting, confusion, focal signs or seizures in the days to weeks after the injury.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis rests on the close timing between injury and onset (within 7 days) and exclusion of structural complications. Imaging is used according to injury-severity rules acutely and repeated when the course is atypical. Classify the headache phenotype (migraine-like, tension-like, occipital or cervical) because it guides therapy. Record analgesic days to catch medication overuse, and screen for mood disorder, sleep disturbance and post-traumatic stress.
det.treatment: Management follows the primary headache the phenotype resembles: acute NSAIDs or triptans for migraine-like attacks with strict limits on use, and preventives such as amitriptyline, propranolol or topiramate. Data for CGRP-targeted drugs in PTH remain limited, so they are reserved for refractory migraine-like cases. After 24–48 h of relative rest, a graded return to aerobic activity, school and work helps recovery; prolonged rest does not. Occipital nerve blocks, neck physiotherapy, vestibular rehabilitation, CBT and treatment of insomnia and depression are useful adjuncts.
det.prognosis: Most acute PTH resolves within 3 months, but a sizeable minority develops persistent headache, particularly with prior migraine, female sex, high early symptom load or medication overuse.
pearls: Headache that keeps getting worse after a head knock is subdural haematoma until imaging says otherwise.
Treat the phenotype: migraine-like PTH responds to migraine therapy.
Check analgesic days at every visit — overuse silently converts PTH into a daily headache.
det.thd: PTH คือปวดศีรษะที่เริ่มภายใน 7 วันหลังบาดเจ็บศีรษะหรือ whiplash ถ้าหายภายใน 3 เดือนเรียก acute ถ้านานกว่านั้นเรียก persistent ลักษณะมักเหมือนไมเกรนหรือ tension-type จึงรักษาตามแบบที่คล้าย ต้องระวังยาแก้ปวดเกินขนาด (MOH) และถ้าปวดมากขึ้นเรื่อย ๆ หรือมีอาการทางระบบประสาทต้องทำภาพสมองซ้ำเพื่อหา chronic subdural haematoma ส่งเสริมให้กลับไปทำกิจกรรมแบบค่อยเป็นค่อยไป

name: Cervicogenic headache
formal: Secondary headache referred from a disorder of the upper cervical spine or its soft tissues (joints, discs, muscles, C1–C3 nerves), usually unilateral and side-locked, provoked by neck movement or pressure and relieved by blocking the painful cervical structure.
simple: A one-sided headache that actually comes from a problem in the upper neck.
th: ปวดศีรษะที่ต้นเหตุอยู่ที่กระดูกคอส่วนบน (C1–C3) ข้อต่อ หรือกล้ามเนื้อคอ ปวดข้างเดียวไม่สลับข้าง เริ่มจากท้ายทอยลามไปหน้าผากหรือรอบตา และแย่ลงเมื่อขยับคอ
tempoNote: Fluctuating or continuous pain over months to years, with flares provoked by neck posture or movement
feat: Strictly one-sided pain starting in the neck or occiput and spreading forward to the temple, forehead or eye
Pain triggered or worsened by neck movement, sustained awkward posture or pressure over the upper neck
Reduced cervical range of motion; positive flexion–rotation test (restricted C1–C2 rotation)
Ipsilateral shoulder or arm discomfort may coexist; migrainous features are mild if present
Diagnostic block of the culprit joint or nerve temporarily abolishes the pain
inv: Clinical diagnosis; cervical X-ray or MRI only shows structure — degenerative findings are common in painless people
MRI cervical spine (with craniocervical junction) when red flags, radicular signs or myelopathy are present
Image-guided diagnostic blocks (third occipital nerve / C2–3 medial branch, C1–2 joint) in specialist centres
CTA or MRA neck if acute neck pain with headache suggests vertebral artery dissection

case.story: For a year she has had right-sided pain that begins at the back of her neck and spreads to the right eye after long hours at the computer. It never switches sides and eases with neck massage.
case.exam: Right C2–3 paraspinal tenderness reproduces the headache; right rotation is limited in the flexion–rotation test; neurological examination is normal.
case.tests: MRI shows mild C2–3 facet arthropathy; an image-guided right third occipital nerve block abolishes the pain for several hours.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and which treatment fits?
case.a: Cervicogenic headache from the right C2–3 facet joint; start a structured physiotherapy programme of manual therapy and deep neck flexor exercise, with radiofrequency neurotomy of the third occipital nerve if pain persists.

read.where: Chapter 54: Headache or facial pain attributed to disorders of cranium,

det.patho: Afferents from C1–C3 converge with trigeminal afferents on the trigeminocervical nucleus in the upper cervical dorsal horn, so pain from neck structures is felt in the head and face. Common sources are the C2–3 zygapophyseal joint (supplied by the third occipital nerve), the atlanto-axial joint and upper cervical muscles. Whiplash, spondylosis and prolonged poor posture are frequent backgrounds. Lower cervical disease can contribute but less consistently.
det.clinical: Pain is moderate, non-throbbing and side-locked, beginning in the neck and spreading to the oculo-fronto-temporal region. Neck movement, sustained postures or pressure over the upper neck provoke flares. Neck stiffness and reduced rotation are typical, and ipsilateral shoulder or arm pain may occur. Mild nausea or photophobia can appear but are less prominent than in migraine. Hemicrania continua and migraine without aura are the major look-alikes.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 (11.2.1) asks for clinical, laboratory or imaging evidence of a cervical source, a plausible temporal or physical link (onset with the lesion, worsening with neck provocation) and abolition of headache after blockade of the cervical structure or its nerve. Imaging abnormalities alone are not enough because spondylosis is near-universal with age. Exclude dissection, posterior fossa lesions, Chiari malformation and craniocervical junction disease. Response to indomethacin argues for hemicrania continua instead.
det.treatment: First-line care is active physiotherapy combining manual mobilisation with craniocervical flexor and scapular exercises, plus posture and ergonomic advice. Greater occipital nerve block with local anaesthetic (± steroid) can relieve flares. For block-confirmed C2–3 facet pain, radiofrequency neurotomy of the third occipital nerve gives months of relief. Tricyclics, gabapentinoids or SNRIs help some patients; surgery is reserved for structural lesions with neurological compromise.
det.prognosis: Many improve with a sustained exercise programme; recurrence is common and radiofrequency procedures often need repeating after about a year.
pearls: Side-locked, neck-triggered pain with restricted upper-neck rotation is the classic triad.
Abnormal cervical imaging does not prove the diagnosis — a positive diagnostic block does.
A brand-new neck pain plus headache is dissection until shown otherwise.
det.thd: Cervicogenic headache เกิดจากกระแสประสาทจากคอส่วนบน C1–C3 มาบรรจบกับ trigeminal nucleus ทำให้รู้สึกปวดที่ศีรษะและรอบตา ปวดข้างเดียวไม่สลับข้าง ขยับคอแล้วปวด ภาพ MRI ที่เสื่อมไม่ได้ยืนยันโรคเพราะพบบ่อยในคนปกติ การฉีดยาชาบล็อกเส้นประสาทหรือข้อต่อแล้วหายปวดช่วยยืนยัน รักษาหลักคือกายภาพบำบัดแบบออกกำลังกล้ามเนื้อคอ ร่วมกับบล็อกเส้นประสาทหรือ radiofrequency

name: Retropharyngeal calcific tendinitis (acute longus colli tendinitis)
formal: Acute aseptic inflammation of the upper longus colli tendon caused by calcium hydroxyapatite deposition anterior to C1–C2, producing severe neck pain, painful neck movement, odynophagia and occipital headache that settle spontaneously within one to two weeks.
simple: Calcium crystals inflame a deep neck muscle tendon, causing sudden, very painful neck stiffness and painful swallowing that goes away by itself.
ab: hydroxyapatite deposition disease of the neck
th: การอักเสบเฉียบพลันของเอ็นกล้ามเนื้อ longus colli หน้ากระดูกคอ C1–C2 จากผลึกแคลเซียม ทำให้ปวดคอรุนแรง ก้มเงยหันคอลำบาก กลืนเจ็บ และปวดท้ายทอย หายเองได้ใน 1–2 สัปดาห์ แต่ต้องแยกจากหนองหลังคอหอยและเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ
tempoNote: Onset over hours to a few days; resolves within about 1–2 weeks with anti-inflammatory treatment
feat: Abrupt severe posterior neck and occipital pain; head held still, often slightly flexed
Neck extension and rotation are markedly painful (often more than flexion)
Odynophagia or dysphagia; low-grade fever and mildly raised CRP/ESR or white count
Mimics meningism but consciousness, CSF and neurological examination are normal
Typical age 30–60 years; often missed and over-investigated
inv: CT neck: amorphous calcification in front of C1–C2 with prevertebral soft-tissue swelling — the key finding
MRI: prevertebral oedema or smooth effusion without rim-enhancing abscess wall or lymphadenopathy
Lateral cervical X-ray may show widened prevertebral space and calcification
Blood count, CRP; lumbar puncture only if meningitis remains a real concern

case.who: 41-year-old male rice farmer from Suphan Buri
case.story: He woke with severe pain at the back of his head and neck that worsened over a day; he cannot look up and swallowing hurts. He is not confused.
case.exam: Temperature 37.8 °C; neck movement in every direction is painful, worst on extension; no rash; neurological examination is normal.
case.tests: CRP 28 mg/L, WBC 11,000; CT neck shows a crescent of calcification anterior to C2 with prevertebral swelling but no rim-enhancing collection.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and does he need surgery or antibiotics?
case.a: Acute calcific tendinitis of longus colli; neither — NSAIDs (± a short steroid course) and reassurance, with symptoms expected to settle in 1–2 weeks.

read.where: ICHD-3 11.2.2 Headache attributed to retropharyngeal tendonitis

det.patho: Hydroxyapatite crystals deposit in the superior oblique fibres of the longus colli tendon near its insertion on the atlas. Rupture of the deposit releases crystals into surrounding tissue and provokes an acute foreign-body-type inflammation with prevertebral oedema. The process is sterile and self-limiting, comparable to calcific tendinitis of the shoulder.
det.clinical: Patients present with sudden or rapidly worsening neck pain, stiffness and occipital headache, often with painful swallowing and mild fever. Extension and rotation are particularly restricted. The picture is frequently mistaken for meningitis, retropharyngeal abscess or dissection, leading to unnecessary lumbar punctures, antibiotics or surgery. Neurological signs are absent.
det.diagnosis: CT shows the defining amorphous calcification anterior to C1–C2 together with prevertebral soft-tissue swelling; MRI shows oedema or a smooth fluid collection without the rim enhancement, gas or nodes of an abscess. Inflammatory markers are only mildly elevated. The ICHD-3 entry (11.2.2) requires imaging evidence of the tendon inflammation plus headache that tracks its course.
det.treatment: Treatment is conservative: NSAIDs, sometimes a brief course of oral corticosteroid, soft diet and analgesia. Antibiotics, drainage and immobilisation are unnecessary once an abscess has been excluded. Symptoms that fail to improve within about two weeks, rising markers or neurological signs should prompt re-imaging for infection or another diagnosis.
det.prognosis: Excellent; symptoms resolve within one to two weeks and the calcification is reabsorbed. Recurrence is uncommon.
pearls: Painful neck extension plus odynophagia plus calcification in front of C2 equals longus colli tendinitis.
Ask the radiologist to look specifically at the prevertebral space at C1–C2 on CT.
Correct recognition avoids needless antibiotics and surgery.
det.thd: โรคนี้เกิดจากผลึกแคลเซียมสะสมที่เอ็นกล้ามเนื้อ longus colli หน้า C1–C2 แล้วแตกออกทำให้อักเสบเฉียบพลัน ผู้ป่วยปวดคอและท้ายทอยมาก เงยคอไม่ได้ กลืนเจ็บ อาจมีไข้ต่ำ ๆ CT คอเห็นหินปูนหน้าต่อ C2 และเนื้อเยื่อบวมโดยไม่มีหนอง รักษาด้วย NSAIDs หรือ steroid ระยะสั้นแล้วหายเองใน 1–2 สัปดาห์ ไม่ต้องผ่าตัดหรือให้ยาปฏิชีวนะ

name: Trochleitis and primary trochlear headache
formal: Periorbital and frontal pain arising from the trochlea–superior oblique tendon region at the superomedial orbit, either from inflammation (trochleitis) or without inflammatory signs (primary trochlear headache), characteristically aggravated by eye movements and relieved by peritrochlear steroid injection.
simple: Pain at the inner upper corner of the eye socket from the small pulley of an eye muscle, made worse by looking up and in.
th: ปวดบริเวณมุมบนด้านในของเบ้าตาจากรอก trochlea ของกล้ามเนื้อ superior oblique อาจเป็นจากการอักเสบ (trochleitis) หรือไม่มีการอักเสบ (primary trochlear headache) ปวดมากขึ้นเมื่อกลอกตาขึ้นบน กดเจ็บที่ trochlea ตอบสนองดีต่อการฉีด steroid รอบ trochlea
tempoNote: Continuous or fluctuating periorbital pain over weeks to months, sometimes recurring
feat: Unilateral (occasionally bilateral) pain at the superomedial orbit radiating to forehead or temple
Pain worsens with vertical eye movements, especially looking up with the eye adducted
Exquisite tenderness on pressing the trochlea; diplopia is uncommon
Can trigger or worsen migraine attacks in people with migraine
Linked with inflammatory arthritis, lupus, psoriasis and enteropathic disease in some cases
inv: Clinical diagnosis: palpation of the trochlea reproducing the pain
MRI orbits with contrast: enhancement or swelling around the trochlea in trochleitis; normal in primary trochlear headache
ESR/CRP, ANA, rheumatoid factor when systemic inflammatory disease is suspected
Diagnostic–therapeutic peritrochlear injection of local anaesthetic with corticosteroid

case.who: 38-year-old female teacher from Chiang Mai with migraine
case.story: For six weeks she has had a constant ache at the inner corner of her left eyebrow that worsens when reading and looking at the board; her migraine attacks have become more frequent.
case.exam: Pressing the left trochlea reproduces the pain exactly; looking up and inward hurts; eye movements are full without diplopia; fundi normal.
case.tests: MRI orbit shows mild enhancement around the left trochlea; ESR and ANA are normal.
case.q: What is the cause and what is the most effective treatment?
case.a: Left trochleitis aggravating her migraine; a peritrochlear injection of corticosteroid with local anaesthetic usually gives rapid and lasting relief, with NSAIDs as an alternative.

det.patho: The trochlea is a cartilaginous pulley at the superomedial orbital rim through which the superior oblique tendon glides. Inflammation of the tendon sheath and pulley (trochleitis) produces local pain, which can sensitise trigeminal pathways and provoke migraine. In primary trochlear headache the same pain and tenderness occur without inflammatory change, suggesting a dysfunction of trochlear pain afferents. Secondary trochleitis accompanies rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, spondyloarthritis and enteropathic arthritis.
det.clinical: Patients report a continuous ache over the inner upper orbit that may spread across the forehead, aggravated by reading or looking upward. Pressure on the trochlea reproduces the pain precisely. Diplopia is rare but acquired Brown syndrome can occur when swelling restricts tendon movement. Coexisting migraine is common, and treating the trochlear source often reduces migraine frequency.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, confirmed by trochlear tenderness and response to peritrochlear injection. ICHD-3 (2018) codes it as 11.3.4 Trochlear headache (11.3.5 in the beta), a heading that covers both trochleitis and primary trochlear headache. MRI may show peritrochlear enhancement; screen for systemic inflammatory disease when other features suggest it. Exclude frontal sinusitis, orbital inflammation and orbital masses.
det.treatment: A single peritrochlear injection of corticosteroid (often mixed with local anaesthetic) relieves most patients within days, and can be repeated. Oral NSAIDs are an alternative or bridge. Treat any associated rheumatological disease and continue appropriate migraine prevention in patients with migraine.
det.prognosis: Usually excellent after injection, although recurrences occur and may need repeat treatment.
pearls: Always press on the trochlea in anyone with inner-orbit pain or worsening migraine.
Pain on looking up and in points to the superior oblique pulley.
Peritrochlear steroid is both the test and the treatment.
det.thd: Trochlea เป็นรอกที่มุมบนด้านในของเบ้าตาซึ่งเอ็น superior oblique ลอดผ่าน เมื่ออักเสบจะปวดรอบตาและหน้าผากข้างนั้น ปวดเพิ่มเมื่อกลอกตาขึ้นและกดเจ็บที่ trochlea ชัดเจน อาจกระตุ้นให้ไมเกรนกำเริบบ่อยขึ้น รักษาด้วยการฉีด steroid รอบ trochlea ซึ่งมักได้ผลดีมาก หรือใช้ NSAIDs

ddx.pt: Proptosis, chemosis, ophthalmoplegia and diffuse orbital enhancement beyond the trochlea
Episodic attacks with nausea and photophobia and no fixed trochlear tenderness between attacks
Short severe orbital attacks with tearing and rhinorrhoea, often at night, without trochlear tenderness

name: Nervus intermedius neuralgia
formal: Rare cranial neuralgia of the nervus intermedius (sensory–parasympathetic part of the facial nerve) causing brief paroxysms of stabbing pain deep in the ear canal, often set off by touching the posterior canal wall, sometimes with taste, salivary or lacrimal disturbance.
simple: Sudden electric stabs of pain deep inside one ear coming from a small branch of the facial nerve.
th: โรคปวดเส้นประสาทที่พบน้อยของ nervus intermedius (แขนงรับความรู้สึกของเส้นประสาทเส้นที่ 7) ปวดแปลบเหมือนไฟช็อตลึกในรูหูเป็นพัก ๆ กระตุ้นได้จากการแตะผนังด้านหลังของรูหู ต้องแยกจาก glossopharyngeal neuralgia และงูสวัดที่หู (Ramsay Hunt)
tempoNote: Paroxysms lasting seconds to minutes, occurring in bouts over weeks to months with remissions
feat: Unilateral lancinating pain felt deep in the external auditory canal, sometimes radiating to the parieto-occipital area
Trigger zone on the posterior wall of the ear canal or near the auricle
Occasional disturbance of lacrimation, salivation or taste during attacks
Normal facial strength and hearing in the classical form
Herpes zoster of the geniculate ganglion causes a painful neuropathic variant
inv: Otoscopy and ENT examination to exclude ear and temporomandibular disease
MRI with high-resolution CISS/FIESTA sequences of the CP angle for neurovascular contact (often AICA) or tumour
Examine for vesicles in the ear canal and facial weakness (zoster)

case.who: 47-year-old female market vendor from Nakhon Pathom
case.story: For three months she has had sudden stabbing pains deep inside her right ear lasting a few seconds, many times a day, set off when she cleans the ear with a cotton bud.
case.exam: Touching the posterior wall of the right ear canal triggers a paroxysm; facial movement, taste and hearing are normal; no vesicles; throat and swallowing do not trigger pain.
case.tests: Otoscopy, audiogram and ENT review normal; MRI CISS shows a loop of AICA contacting the right VII–VIII complex.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the first treatment?
case.a: Classical nervus intermedius neuralgia; start carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine, with microvascular decompression or intermedius sectioning considered if drug therapy fails.

det.patho: The nervus intermedius carries taste from the anterior tongue, parasympathetic fibres to the lacrimal and salivary glands, and sensation from part of the ear canal and auricle via the geniculate ganglion. As in trigeminal neuralgia, focal demyelination at the root entry zone, often from vascular contact (AICA or PICA loops), is thought to produce ephaptic, high-frequency firing. Herpes zoster of the geniculate ganglion is the main cause of secondary painful neuropathy. Overlap with glossopharyngeal and vagal sensory territories makes the anatomy hard to separate.
det.clinical: Patients describe brief, unilateral, electric pain deep in the ear, sometimes spreading behind the ear or to the parietal scalp, triggered by touching the ear canal or by cold air. Between paroxysms there may be a dull ache. Disturbed tearing, salivation or taste can accompany attacks. Painful variants with ongoing burning pain follow zoster.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 (13.3.1) defines the neuralgia by recurrent short paroxysms in the ear canal distribution with a trigger zone, without another cause. Otological, dental and temporomandibular causes must be ruled out, as must CP-angle tumours, multiple sclerosis and zoster. High-resolution MRI identifies neurovascular contact but such contact can be seen in asymptomatic people. Overlap with glossopharyngeal neuralgia is frequent, and intraoperative nerve stimulation is sometimes needed to clarify the culprit nerve.
det.treatment: Sodium-channel blockers (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine) are first line, with gabapentin, pregabalin or baclofen as alternatives or add-ons. For refractory pain, surgery through a retrosigmoid approach combines microvascular decompression with sectioning of the nervus intermedius, often with decompression or rhizotomy of the upper glossopharyngeal–vagal rootlets. Zoster-related pain is managed with antivirals early and neuropathic agents later.
det.prognosis: Spontaneous remissions occur; refractory cases often achieve good long-term relief after surgery in experienced hands.
pearls: Deep ear stabs triggered from the ear canal, with normal otoscopy, suggests intermedius neuralgia.
If swallowing triggers the ear pain, think glossopharyngeal neuralgia instead.
Always look for vesicles in the ear canal and palate.
det.thd: Nervus intermedius เป็นแขนงรับความรู้สึกและ parasympathetic ของเส้นประสาทเส้นที่ 7 เมื่อผิดปกติจะปวดแปลบลึกในหูข้างเดียวเป็นวินาที กระตุ้นจากการแตะรูหู อาจมีน้ำตา น้ำลาย หรือรับรสผิดปกติร่วม ต้องตรวจหูให้ปกติและแยกงูสวัด เนื้องอก หรือ glossopharyngeal neuralgia รักษาแรกด้วย carbamazepine หรือ oxcarbazepine ถ้าไม่ได้ผลอาจผ่าตัด MVD ร่วมตัดเส้นประสาท

ddx.pt: Pain in the throat, tonsil and ear triggered by swallowing or talking, sometimes with syncope
Ear pain with vesicles, facial palsy and hearing or balance disturbance from geniculate zoster
Paroxysms in V2/V3 facial territory triggered by chewing, talking or touching the face

name: Occipital neuralgia
formal: Brief shooting or stabbing pain in the occipital region, along the course of an occipital nerve (greater, lesser or third), often with scalp dysaesthesia and tenderness over the nerve, temporarily abolished by local anaesthetic block of the affected nerve.
simple: Sharp electric jabs of pain running up the back of the head along one of the scalp nerves.
th: ปวดแปลบเหมือนไฟช็อตจากท้ายทอยแล่นขึ้นไปหนังศีรษะตามแนวเส้นประสาท greater, lesser หรือ third occipital มักมีหนังศีรษะเจ็บเวลาแตะหรือหวีผม กดเจ็บที่จุดเส้นประสาทออกมา และหายชั่วคราวเมื่อฉีดยาชาบล็อกเส้นประสาท
tempoNote: Paroxysms of seconds to minutes, recurring daily for weeks to months, often with a background ache
feat: Unilateral or bilateral shooting pain from the suboccipital region up over the vertex
Allodynia or dysaesthesia of the scalp — brushing hair or lying on a pillow hurts
Tenderness and a Tinel-like trigger at the nerve's exit point (about one-third of the way from occiput to mastoid)
Pain may refer to the eye or forehead through trigeminocervical convergence
Local anaesthetic block of the nerve abolishes pain temporarily
inv: Clinical diagnosis supported by response to greater/lesser occipital nerve block
MRI brain and cervical spine with craniocervical junction when atypical, progressive or with neurological signs
Consider vessel imaging if acute onset with neck pain (vertebral dissection)
Inspect the scalp for zoster vesicles or masses

case.story: For a month he has had jolts of pain shooting from the left base of his skull to the top of his head many times a day; combing his hair and resting his head on the pillow hurt.
case.exam: Pressing over the left greater occipital nerve reproduces the pain; patchy reduced sensation over the left occiput; neck movement mildly painful; rest of examination normal.
case.tests: MRI brain and cervical spine show only mild spondylosis; a left greater occipital nerve block with lidocaine abolishes the pain within minutes.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and how should it be managed?
case.a: Left greater occipital neuralgia; repeat occipital nerve blocks (± steroid) with neck physiotherapy, and add carbamazepine, gabapentin or pregabalin if attacks continue.

det.patho: The greater occipital nerve (from the C2 dorsal ramus) pierces the semispinalis and trapezius aponeuroses before supplying the posterior scalp; the lesser occipital nerve (C2–C3) and third occipital nerve (C3) supply adjacent territories. Irritation by muscle tension, trauma, entrapment, upper cervical arthrosis, nearby vessels or tumours can generate ectopic discharges. Many cases have no identifiable cause. Convergence with trigeminal afferents in the upper cervical cord explains pain spreading to the eye.
det.clinical: Patients describe brief, lancinating pains travelling from the suboccipital area over the posterior scalp, often against a background ache. Scalp sensitivity on light touch is typical, and pressure over the nerve exit reproduces the pain. Sensation in the territory may be reduced. The term is often misused for any occipital headache; most occipital pain is migraine, tension-type or cervicogenic.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 (13.4) requires paroxysmal pain in an occipital nerve distribution, signs of dysaesthesia or nerve tenderness, and temporary relief with local anaesthetic block of the nerve. Imaging is needed if the picture is atypical, progressive or associated with neurological signs, to exclude posterior fossa or craniocervical lesions, C2 schwannoma, spinal cord disease and vertebral dissection. Zoster in the C2 dermatome is a frequent secondary cause.
det.treatment: Occipital nerve block with local anaesthetic, with or without corticosteroid, gives both diagnosis and relief and can be repeated. Physiotherapy, posture correction, heat and massage help when muscle tension contributes. Neuropathic drugs (carbamazepine, gabapentin, pregabalin, tricyclics) are used for frequent attacks. For refractory cases, pulsed radiofrequency of the occipital nerve or occipital nerve stimulation are options; destructive neurectomy is rarely used because of dysaesthesia and recurrence.
det.prognosis: Many respond to blocks and medication; chronic cases may need repeated procedures.
pearls: True occipital neuralgia is paroxysmal and shooting — a steady occipital ache is usually something else.
A positive block is part of the definition, not just treatment.
New occipital neuralgia in an older person: check for zoster and upper cervical or posterior fossa pathology.
det.thd: Occipital neuralgia คือปวดแปลบแล่นจากท้ายทอยขึ้นหนังศีรษะตามแนวเส้นประสาท occipital ร่วมกับหนังศีรษะเจ็บเวลาแตะ และกดที่จุดเส้นประสาทออกแล้วปวด การฉีดยาชาบล็อกเส้นประสาทแล้วหายเป็นส่วนหนึ่งของการวินิจฉัย ต้องแยกจากไมเกรนและ cervicogenic headache ถ้าอาการไม่ทั่วไปควร MRI รักษาด้วยบล็อกเส้นประสาท กายภาพบำบัด และยากลุ่ม neuropathic

Occipital headache brought on by coughing or straining; tonsillar descent on MRI
Neck and arm pain with radicular signs; C2 root disease is rare and usually from upper cervical pathology
