name: Painful post-traumatic trigeminal neuropathy (PPTTN)
formal: Unilateral facial or oral neuropathic pain confined to the territory of an injured trigeminal branch (or branches) that develops within months of an identifiable injury to that nerve (dental, surgical or facial trauma), with positive and/or negative sensory signs in the affected territory.
simple: Long-lasting burning or electric facial pain after a trigeminal nerve branch is damaged, often by dental work.
th: ปวดใบหน้าหรือในช่องปากแบบ neuropathic ข้างเดียวตามแขนงเส้นประสาท trigeminal หลังเส้นประสาทได้รับบาดเจ็บ เช่น ถอนฟันคุด รากฟันเทียม รักษารากฟัน หรือกระดูกใบหน้าหัก มีทั้งชาและปวดแสบปวดร้อน มักเป็นต่อเนื่อง
tempoNote: Starts within about 6 months of the injury (often within days) and commonly becomes continuous for years
feat: Pain confined to the injured branch territory (commonly inferior alveolar, lingual or infraorbital nerve)
Continuous burning, aching or tingling pain, sometimes with superimposed brief paroxysms
Numbness plus allodynia or hyperalgesia in the same area
Clear history of dental extraction, implant, root canal, orthognathic surgery or facial fracture
Repeated dental or surgical interventions tend to worsen rather than cure the pain
inv: Quantitative sensory mapping of the territory (light touch, pinprick, temperature, two-point)
Dental panoramic X-ray or cone-beam CT to see implant or root filling encroaching on the canal
MRI with neurography sequences or trigeminal reflex studies in selected cases
Exclude tumour along the nerve when trauma history is weak or deficits progress

case.story: Two weeks after a lower right wisdom tooth was removed she noticed numbness of the right lower lip and chin, which has turned into a constant burning pain over four months; brushing her lip makes it worse.
case.exam: Reduced pinprick and touch over the right lower lip and chin with allodynia; motor trigeminal function and other cranial nerves are normal.
case.tests: Cone-beam CT shows the extraction socket adjacent to the right inferior alveolar canal; MRI brain normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what should be avoided?
case.a: Painful post-traumatic trigeminal neuropathy of the right inferior alveolar nerve; treat with neuropathic agents (e.g. amitriptyline, pregabalin) and topical options, and avoid further extractions or exploratory surgery that may worsen it.

det.patho: Injury to a peripheral trigeminal branch — by crush, stretch, transection, chemical damage from root-canal materials or compression by an implant — triggers ectopic firing in damaged axons, peripheral and central sensitisation, and loss of inhibitory control in the trigeminal nucleus. Only a minority of nerve injuries become painful, suggesting genetic and psychological susceptibility. The inferior alveolar and lingual nerves are most often involved because of their relation to lower molar surgery. Deliberate ablation (rhizotomy) can produce a related syndrome, anaesthesia dolorosa.
det.clinical: Pain begins soon after the injury and is usually continuous, burning or squeezing, with intermittent sharp jabs. Patients have numbness, pins-and-needles, allodynia and sometimes altered taste in the affected area. Eating, speaking, shaving or applying makeup may provoke pain. Distress, sleep loss and depression are common, and many patients undergo repeated dental procedures before diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 (13.1.2.3) requires facial or oral pain in the territory of an injured trigeminal branch, onset within 6 months of the traumatic event, and clinically evident sensory signs (positive or negative). Map sensory change carefully and document the procedure history. Imaging checks for implants or root fillings encroaching on the canal. Exclude ongoing dental infection, tumour and trigeminal neuralgia.
det.treatment: For acute iatrogenic injury, early recognition matters: removing an implant or root filling within 24–36 h and referring lingual or inferior alveolar transections for microsurgical repair within weeks give the best chance of recovery. Established pain is treated with neuropathic agents (tricyclics, gabapentin or pregabalin, SNRIs), topical lidocaine or capsaicin, and sometimes botulinum toxin. Psychological therapy and patient education are part of care. Avoid further irreversible dental or surgical procedures aimed at the pain.
det.prognosis: Often chronic; partial improvement with medication is typical and full resolution is uncommon once pain is established.
pearls: Numbness plus burning pain after dental work equals nerve injury, not a dental infection.
Implant or root-filling encroachment is a surgical emergency — remove it within about 36 h.
Trigeminal neuralgia usually has no sensory deficit; PPTTN almost always does.
det.thd: PPTTN เกิดจากเส้นประสาท trigeminal แขนงปลายบาดเจ็บ เช่น จากถอนฟันคุดหรือใส่รากฟันเทียม ทำให้ชาร่วมกับปวดแสบปวดร้อนต่อเนื่องในบริเวณนั้น ต่างจาก trigeminal neuralgia ที่ปวดแปลบเป็นพักและมักไม่ชา การรักษาใช้ยา neuropathic เช่น amitriptyline หรือ pregabalin และยาทาเฉพาะที่ ถ้าบาดเจ็บใหม่ ๆ จากรากฟันเทียมควรถอดออกเร็ว ควรหลีกเลี่ยงการทำหัตถการฟันซ้ำเพราะมักทำให้แย่ลง

name: Recurrent painful ophthalmoplegic neuropathy (RPON)
formal: Repeated episodes in which an ocular motor nerve (usually the oculomotor) becomes weak together with headache on the same side, the pain sometimes starting days before the palsy, once compressive, infiltrative and inflammatory causes are excluded; formerly called ophthalmoplegic migraine.
simple: Repeated bouts of one-sided headache followed by weakness of an eye-moving nerve, usually in children.
ab: recurrent third nerve palsy with headache
th: โรคที่มีอาการซ้ำ ๆ ของปวดศีรษะข้างเดียวร่วมกับอัมพาตเส้นประสาทกลอกตา ส่วนใหญ่เป็นเส้นที่ 3 พบบ่อยในเด็ก เดิมเรียก ophthalmoplegic migraine แต่ปัจจุบันเชื่อว่าเป็นโรคเส้นประสาทอักเสบแบบ demyelinating ต้องแยกโป่งพอง เนื้องอก และ Tolosa–Hunt ก่อน
tempoNote: Attacks of headache followed within up to 2 weeks by ocular palsy lasting days to weeks, recurring months or years apart
feat: Usually begins in childhood; the third nerve is involved far more often than the sixth or fourth
Unilateral headache (often migraine-like) precedes or accompanies the palsy, sometimes by several days
Ptosis, diplopia and often pupil involvement on the same side
Recovery over weeks, but repeated attacks can leave a lasting deficit
MRI may show focal thickening and enhancement of the cisternal oculomotor nerve
inv: MRI brain with contrast and thin cuts through the cavernous sinus and orbit: nerve enhancement, exclude tumour and inflammation
CTA or MRA (or catheter angiography) to exclude a posterior communicating aneurysm in any painful third nerve palsy
Blood glucose/HbA1c, ESR/CRP; LP when infection or inflammation is possible

case.story: He had three days of severe right-sided headache with vomiting, then his right eyelid drooped and he saw double. His mother says a similar episode two years ago recovered completely.
case.exam: Complete right ptosis, eye down and out, right pupil 6 mm and poorly reactive; other cranial nerves and fundi normal.
case.tests: MRA normal; MRI shows thickening and enhancement of the right oculomotor nerve at its exit from the midbrain; CSF normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and how is it managed?
case.a: Recurrent painful ophthalmoplegic neuropathy; after excluding aneurysm and other lesions, a short course of corticosteroids is often given and migraine-type prophylaxis considered if attacks recur.

det.patho: Once considered a migraine variant, the disorder is now regarded as a recurrent demyelinating (possibly inflammatory) neuropathy of the ocular motor nerve, supported by nerve thickening and enhancement on MRI. The headache may arise from local inflammation of the nerve sheath and trigeminal innervation. The mechanism of recurrence remains unknown.
det.clinical: Most patients are children or young adults. A unilateral, sometimes migraine-like headache is followed within up to 14 days by an ipsilateral palsy, typically of the third nerve with ptosis and mydriasis, less often of the sixth or fourth. The palsy resolves over weeks, but recurrent attacks may leave residual ptosis, aberrant regeneration or pupillary abnormality.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 2018 lists it as 13.10 (13.9 in the beta) and moved it out of the migraine chapter. Diagnosis requires at least two attacks with the characteristic association and exclusion of orbital, parasellar and posterior fossa lesions. Every first painful third nerve palsy needs vascular imaging for aneurysm and contrast MRI for tumour (e.g. schwannoma) and inflammation. Nerve enhancement supports but is not specific for RPON.
det.treatment: Corticosteroids are commonly given during attacks and may speed recovery, though trial evidence is lacking. Analgesia treats the headache. When attacks are frequent, preventive agents used for migraine are sometimes tried. Follow-up imaging is advisable if the course changes, since a slowly growing schwannoma can mimic recurrent attacks.
det.prognosis: Individual attacks usually recover, but cumulative permanent ocular motor deficits develop in a substantial minority with repeated episodes.
pearls: Ophthalmoplegic migraine was renamed because it behaves as a cranial neuropathy, not migraine.
Painful third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil is an aneurysm until vessel imaging is clear — even in a child.
Thick enhancing cisternal III nerve on MRI is the radiological clue.
det.thd: RPON เดิมเรียก ophthalmoplegic migraine มักพบในเด็ก มีปวดศีรษะข้างเดียวนำมาก่อนแล้วตามด้วยอัมพาตเส้นประสาทกลอกตา ส่วนใหญ่เส้นที่ 3 และเป็นซ้ำได้ MRI อาจเห็นเส้นประสาทเส้นที่ 3 หนาและ enhance ปัจจุบันจัดเป็นโรคของเส้นประสาทสมอง ไม่ใช่ไมเกรน ต้องแยกโป่งพองของหลอดเลือด เนื้องอก และ Tolosa–Hunt ก่อนเสมอ มักให้ steroid ช่วงที่เป็น

name: Persistent idiopathic facial pain (PIFP)
formal: Chronic daily facial and/or oral pain of varying character, poorly localised and not following a peripheral nerve distribution, lasting more than 2 hours a day for over 3 months, with normal neurological examination and no identifiable cause; formerly called atypical facial pain.
simple: Long-term daily facial pain without any cause that tests or examination can find.

tempoNote: Daily, mostly continuous pain for months to years, often starting after a minor dental or facial procedure
feat: Deep, dull, aching or nagging pain, sometimes with brief sharp exacerbations, usually unilateral
Commonly felt in the nasolabial fold, cheek or jaw; may spread to a wider area over time
No trigger zones and no consistent sensory deficit
Often follows dental treatment; repeated dental procedures fail to help
Frequent comorbid depression, anxiety and other chronic pain conditions
inv: Thorough dental, ENT and TMJ assessment, with dental X-rays
MRI brain and skull base (including nasopharynx and pterygopalatine fossa) to exclude tumour
Nasopharyngoscopy where nasopharyngeal carcinoma is common or ear fullness, nosebleeds or nodes are present
Screen mood and sleep; blood tests only if systemic disease is suspected

case.story: Since a root canal 18 months ago she has had an all-day aching pain in her left cheek and upper teeth; two further teeth were extracted without benefit. She sleeps poorly and feels low.
case.exam: No trigger points; facial sensation, cranial nerves, jaw function and oral examination normal; no neck nodes.
case.tests: Dental radiographs normal; MRI brain and skull base with contrast normal; nasopharyngoscopy normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what is the treatment approach?
case.a: Persistent idiopathic facial pain; stop further dental procedures, explain the condition, and use amitriptyline or an SNRI (venlafaxine, duloxetine) with CBT, treating sleep and mood.

read.where: Chapter 54: Headache or facial pain attributed to disorders of cranium,

det.patho: The cause is uncertain. Neurophysiological and quantitative sensory studies in some patients show subtle trigeminal dysfunction, suggesting that minor nerve injury and central sensitisation contribute, so the boundary with post-traumatic trigeminal neuropathy is blurred. Psychological factors, particularly depression and anxiety, modify the experience but are not the sole explanation. Middle-aged women are most affected.
det.clinical: Pain is chronic, daily and present for most of the day, usually unilateral, ill-defined and deep, often centred on the cheek, nasolabial fold, jaw or teeth. It may extend beyond anatomical territories over time. Patients frequently have undergone multiple dental or sinus procedures. Atypical odontalgia (persistent tooth pain after dental work) is considered a subform.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 2018 lists it as 13.12 (13.11 in the beta): pain recurring daily for over 2 hours a day across more than 3 months, poorly localised, not in a nerve distribution, with normal examination and no explanatory lesion. It is a diagnosis of exclusion that requires careful dental assessment and imaging of the skull base. In Thailand nasopharyngeal carcinoma must be actively excluded, and sinus, salivary and temporomandibular disease considered.
det.treatment: Education and a clear explanation that the pain is real but not dental are central, along with stopping further invasive procedures. Tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline, nortriptyline) are first line; SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine) and gabapentinoids are alternatives. CBT and treatment of depression, anxiety and insomnia improve outcome. Interventional procedures have little role.
det.prognosis: Often chronic with partial response; a minority remit, and prognosis is better with early diagnosis and avoidance of repeated surgery.
pearls: Each further tooth extracted for unexplained facial pain usually makes PIFP worse.
Always image the skull base and scope the nasopharynx before labelling facial pain idiopathic.
Continuous pain without triggers or deficits separates PIFP from trigeminal neuralgia and neuropathy.
det.thd: PIFP หรือ atypical facial pain คือปวดใบหน้าลึก ๆ ทุกวันนานกว่า 3 เดือน ตำแหน่งไม่ชัดและไม่ตามแนวเส้นประสาท ตรวจร่างกายและภาพถ่ายปกติ มักเริ่มหลังทำฟันแล้วยิ่งทำฟันซ้ำยิ่งแย่ ในคนไทยต้องตรวจหามะเร็งโพรงหลังจมูกก่อน รักษาด้วย amitriptyline หรือยา SNRI ร่วมกับ CBT และดูแลภาวะซึมเศร้า นอนไม่หลับ

name: Headache attributed to temporomandibular disorder (TMD)
formal: Headache or facial pain in the temporal and preauricular region caused by a temporomandibular disorder — disease of the jaw joint, disc or masticatory muscles — provoked by jaw movement, function or parafunction and reproduced by examination of the joint or muscles.
simple: Headache at the temples and in front of the ear coming from problems with the jaw joint or chewing muscles.
th: ปวดศีรษะบริเวณขมับและหน้าหูจากความผิดปกติของข้อต่อขากรรไกรหรือกล้ามเนื้อบดเคี้ยว ปวดมากขึ้นเมื่อเคี้ยว อ้าปาก หรือกัดฟัน มักมีเสียงคลิกที่ขากรรไกรและอ้าปากได้น้อย รักษาแบบอนุรักษ์เป็นหลัก
tempoNote: Recurrent or persistent pain over months, with flares after chewing, stress or nocturnal clenching
feat: Unilateral or bilateral temporal, preauricular or jaw pain, often worse on waking or after chewing
Pain on jaw opening, chewing, yawning or clenching; tenderness of masseter, temporalis or the TMJ
Joint clicking, crepitus, deviation or limited mouth opening (<35–40 mm)
Bruxism, clenching and stress are common contributors; often coexists with migraine or TTH
Examining the jaw reproduces the patient's familiar headache
inv: Clinical examination using DC/TMD principles (palpation, mouth-opening range, joint sounds)
Dental review for occlusal wear, bruxism and dental pathology
Panoramic X-ray, CBCT or TMJ MRI only for suspected structural joint disease, trauma or arthritis
ESR/CRP in anyone over 50 with new jaw pain to exclude giant-cell arteritis

case.who: 27-year-old female call-centre worker from Pathum Thani
case.story: For eight months she has had aching pain at both temples and in front of her right ear, worse in the morning and when chewing sticky rice; her partner hears her grinding her teeth at night.
case.exam: Mouth opening 34 mm with deviation to the right and a right TMJ click; palpation of the right masseter and temporalis reproduces her headache; neurological examination normal.
case.tests: Dental examination shows flattened worn molars; ESR normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the first-line treatment?
case.a: Headache attributed to TMD (myofascial pain with disc displacement and bruxism); start education, soft diet, jaw rest and heat, jaw exercises, a night-time occlusal splint and stress management, with short-term NSAIDs or low-dose amitriptyline.

read.where: ICHD-3 11.7 Headache attributed to temporomandibular disorder (TMD)

det.patho: TMD is a group of conditions involving the masticatory muscles (myalgia, myofascial pain), the articular disc (displacement with or without reduction) and the joint itself (arthralgia, osteoarthritis). Parafunction such as clenching and bruxism, trauma, joint hypermobility, stress and central sensitisation contribute. Trigeminal input from the jaw converges with headache pathways, so TMD both causes headache and aggravates migraine.
det.clinical: Pain is felt in the temples, cheeks, preauricular area and jaw, often worse on waking or after prolonged chewing or talking. Clicking, crepitus, catching or locking of the jaw and reduced opening may be present. Ear fullness, tinnitus and neck pain are frequent associated complaints. TMD is common in young and middle-aged women and often coexists with migraine, tension-type headache and other chronic pain.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 (11.7) requires a TMD diagnosis plus headache that is worsened by jaw movement or function and reproduced by provocation of the TMJ or masticatory muscles. The Diagnostic Criteria for TMD (DC/TMD) provide a validated examination protocol. Imaging is reserved for suspected structural joint disease. In patients over 50, new jaw or temple pain mandates exclusion of giant-cell arteritis; dental pain, parotid disease and ear disease are other mimics.
det.treatment: Most patients improve with conservative measures: explanation, jaw rest, soft diet, heat, avoiding gum and wide yawning, jaw stretching exercises and posture work. A stabilisation (occlusal) splint at night helps bruxism, and short courses of NSAIDs or low-dose tricyclics relieve pain. CBT and stress management are effective for chronic cases, and botulinum toxin to masticatory muscles is sometimes used. Irreversible occlusal adjustment or joint surgery is rarely justified.
det.prognosis: Usually favourable with conservative care, though symptoms often fluctuate and recur with stress.
pearls: Ask about jaw clicking, morning jaw ache and teeth grinding in every temporal headache.
If palpating the masseter or temporalis reproduces the headache, think TMD.
New jaw pain on chewing after age 50 is giant-cell arteritis until ESR/CRP say otherwise.
det.thd: TMD คือความผิดปกติของข้อต่อขากรรไกร หมอนรองข้อ หรือกล้ามเนื้อบดเคี้ยว ทำให้ปวดขมับและหน้าหู ปวดมากขึ้นเมื่อเคี้ยวหรือกัดฟัน มีเสียงคลิกหรืออ้าปากได้น้อย กดกล้ามเนื้อแล้วเกิดอาการปวดแบบเดิม รักษาด้วยการให้ความรู้ พักขากรรไกร อาหารอ่อน ประคบอุ่น บริหารขากรรไกร ใส่ splint ตอนกลางคืน และยาแก้ปวดระยะสั้น ในผู้สูงอายุต้องแยก giant-cell arteritis

name: Headache attributed to rhinosinusitis (sinus headache)

simple: Facial or head pain from a genuine sinus infection, which is much rarer than people think — most 'sinus headaches' are migraine.
ab: ไซนัสอักเสบ
th: ปวดศีรษะหรือปวดใบหน้าจากโพรงไซนัสอักเสบจริงซึ่งมีน้ำมูกข้นเขียวเหลือง คัดจมูก และพบการอักเสบจากการส่องกล้องหรือ CT ปวดดีขึ้นเมื่อการอักเสบหาย ส่วนคนที่คิดว่าตนเองปวดหัวจากไซนัสซ้ำ ๆ ส่วนใหญ่เป็นไมเกรน

feat: Facial pressure or pain over the cheeks, forehead or behind the eyes, worse bending forward
Purulent nasal discharge, nasal obstruction, reduced smell, often fever
Headache course parallels the sinus inflammation

Recurrent 'sinus headache' with nasal symptoms but no pus is usually migraine with cranial autonomic features
inv: Clinical diagnosis for uncomplicated acute rhinosinusitis; nasal endoscopy to see purulence
CT sinuses when chronic, recurrent or complicated disease or sphenoid involvement is suspected
Contrast CT/MRI brain and orbit urgently for periorbital swelling, diplopia, visual loss, meningism or altered consciousness

case.story: He has been given antibiotics five times in two years for 'sinus headaches': throbbing pain over both eyes and cheeks once or twice a month, with a blocked runny nose, lasting a day and worse with light; he takes paracetamol often.
case.exam: Nasal endoscopy between attacks shows no pus; neurological examination normal.
case.tests: CT sinuses normal; headache diary shows attacks linked to sleep loss with photophobia and nausea.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and what should change?
case.a: Migraine without aura with cranial autonomic symptoms, not rhinosinusitis; stop antibiotics, treat attacks with NSAIDs or a triptan, limit analgesic days and consider prevention.

det.patho: Inflammation and obstruction of the sinus ostia cause mucosal swelling, retained secretions and pressure changes that stimulate trigeminal nociceptors in the sinus mucosa. Viral upper respiratory infection is the usual trigger, with secondary bacterial infection in a minority. Chronic rhinosinusitis is generally painless except during acute exacerbations. Conversely, trigeminal activation during migraine produces nasal congestion and rhinorrhoea, which explains why migraine is so often mislabelled as sinus disease.
det.clinical: True rhinosinusitis headache accompanies purulent discharge, nasal blockage, reduced smell, fever and facial tenderness, typically after a cold. Pain worsens on bending or lying down and improves as the infection clears. Isolated sphenoid sinusitis presents with severe deep headache and may involve cranial nerves or cause meningitis. Warning signs — periorbital swelling, proptosis, diplopia, reduced vision, severe frontal swelling, meningism or confusion — indicate orbital or intracranial spread.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 gives separate codes for the acute form (11.5.1) and the chronic or recurring form (11.5.2); both require clinical, endoscopic and/or imaging evidence of sinus inflammation and a headache that follows its time course. Acute bacterial sinusitis is suggested by symptoms persisting beyond 10 days, worsening after initial improvement, or severe onset with fever and purulence. Repeated 'sinus headaches' without pus, with photophobia, nausea and a normal CT should be re-diagnosed as migraine; this misdiagnosis is very common.
det.treatment: Uncomplicated acute rhinosinusitis is treated with saline irrigation, intranasal corticosteroids and analgesics; antibiotics (e.g. amoxicillin–clavulanate) are reserved for probable bacterial disease. Chronic rhinosinusitis is managed by ENT with long-term intranasal steroids, irrigation and sometimes endoscopic surgery or biologics for nasal polyps. Complicated disease needs admission, IV antibiotics, imaging and surgical drainage; suspected mucormycosis needs urgent debridement and amphotericin. When migraine is the true diagnosis, treat it as migraine and stop repeated antibiotics.
det.prognosis: Headache from acute rhinosinusitis resolves with the infection; persistent recurrent 'sinus headache' usually reflects migraine and improves once treated as such.
pearls: Most people who believe they have recurrent sinus headache meet criteria for migraine.
No pus, no sinusitis headache — ask for discharge, fever and smell change.
Severe headache with sinusitis plus eye signs or drowsiness signals orbital or intracranial spread; image urgently.
det.thd: ปวดศีรษะจากไซนัสอักเสบจริงต้องมีน้ำมูกข้น คัดจมูก อาจมีไข้ และเห็นการอักเสบจากการส่องกล้องหรือ CT ปวดจะหายตามการอักเสบ ผู้ที่ปวดหัวเป็นพัก ๆ ซ้ำ ๆ แล้วคิดว่าเป็นไซนัสส่วนใหญ่เป็นไมเกรนซึ่งมีคัดจมูกน้ำมูกใสได้ จึงไม่ควรให้ยาปฏิชีวนะซ้ำ ถ้ามีตาบวม เห็นภาพซ้อน ซึม หรือในผู้ป่วยเบาหวานที่มีสะเก็ดดำในจมูก ต้องรีบตรวจหาภาวะแทรกซ้อนในเบ้าตาและสมอง

name: Neurological complications of dengue (neurodengue)
formal: Nervous system and muscle disorders occurring during or after infection with any of the four dengue virus serotypes (an Aedes-borne flavivirus), including metabolic or shock-related encephalopathy, true dengue encephalitis, intracranial haemorrhage or infarction, post-infectious immune syndromes such as GBS, ADEM and myelitis, myositis and acute hypokalaemic paralysis.
simple: Dengue fever can sometimes affect the brain, nerves or muscles, causing confusion, fits, bleeding in the brain, sudden weakness or paralysis.
ab: ไข้เลือดออกขึ้นสมอง
th: ภาวะแทรกซ้อนทางระบบประสาทและกล้ามเนื้อจากไข้เลือดออกเดงกี เช่น สมองทำงานผิดปกติจากช็อกหรือตับวาย สมองอักเสบ เลือดออกในสมอง กล้ามเนื้ออักเสบ อ่อนแรงจากโพแทสเซียมต่ำ และ GBS หลังติดเชื้อ

True encephalitis is uncommon: fever with seizures and reduced consciousness, sometimes with thalamic, basal ganglia or brainstem MRI changes

CBC with platelets and haematocrit trend, liver enzymes, sodium, potassium, glucose, CK and clotting profile
CT for suspected bleeding; MRI brain or spine for encephalitis, ADEM or myelitis

case.who: 23-year-old female university student from Chonburi, previously well
case.story: On the third day of high fever, headache and body aches she woke unable to lift her arms or stand, although she could speak and swallow normally.
case.exam: Alert, BP 104/66; symmetric flaccid weakness grade 2/5 proximally, absent reflexes, normal sensation; petechiae on the forearms after tourniquet test.
case.tests: Dengue NS1 positive; platelets 62,000/µL, haematocrit 44%; serum potassium 2.1 mmol/L, CK mildly raised; ECG shows U waves; TSH normal.
case.q: What explains the paralysis, and how should it be managed?
case.a: Dengue-associated acute hypokalaemic paralysis; give potassium replacement with cardiac monitoring and repeat levels, expect recovery within a day or two, and continue close fluid and platelet monitoring for the critical phase.

Part II: Viral Pathogens: Pathogenesis, Pathology, Diagnosis and Treatment

det.patho: Dengue is the most common arboviral infection in Thailand, with yearly epidemics peaking in the rainy season. Most neurological illness is indirect: plasma leakage, shock, hepatic dysfunction, hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia disturb brain function, while thrombocytopenia and consumptive coagulopathy predispose to haemorrhage. The virus can also enter the CNS, since viral RNA, NS1 antigen and specific IgM have been found in CSF and brain tissue, giving a genuine encephalitis in a minority. Immune cross-reaction after infection underlies GBS, ADEM and myelitis, and hypokalaemia reflects potassium shift into cells together with renal and gut losses.
det.clinical: Neurological involvement is reported in a few percent of hospitalised patients and is part of what WHO calls expanded dengue syndrome. Encephalopathy usually appears around defervescence in patients with warning signs, severe leakage or liver failure, whereas encephalitis brings seizures, focal signs or coma and may occur without shock. Bleeding presents as abrupt headache, focal deficits or falling GCS when platelets are very low. Hypokalaemic paralysis and myositis tend to occur early in the febrile phase; GBS, ADEM, optic neuritis, brachial neuritis and myelitis follow after one to four weeks. Dengue maculopathy may cause blurred vision during recovery.
det.diagnosis: Confirm dengue with NS1 or RT-PCR early and IgM/IgG serology later; a rising haematocrit with falling platelets supports the clinical picture. Separate metabolic encephalopathy from encephalitis by checking sodium, glucose, ammonia, liver function and perfusion; CSF dengue IgM, NS1 or PCR and MRI changes favour CNS infection. Lumbar puncture is often deferred until platelets and clotting are safe. Serology cross-reacts with JE and Zika, so interpret results with vaccination history and paired samples, and always exclude HSV, bacterial meningitis, scrub typhus, leptospirosis and malaria.
det.treatment: There is no licensed antiviral, so care rests on careful phase-guided fluid management, correction of electrolytes and glucose, seizure control and protection of the airway. Paracetamol is preferred for fever; aspirin, NSAIDs and intramuscular injections are avoided. Intracranial bleeding needs platelet and coagulation support and neurosurgical review, though surgery is limited by bleeding risk. Hypokalaemic paralysis responds quickly to potassium replacement; GBS is treated with IVIG or plasma exchange in the usual way, and ADEM or myelitis with high-dose corticosteroids once infection is controlled. Prevention relies on vector control and vaccination: TAK-003 is now licensed in Thailand for people aged 4 years and older.
det.prognosis: Most encephalopathy and hypokalaemic weakness resolve completely; encephalitis and especially intracranial haemorrhage carry substantial mortality and residual deficits.
pearls: A confused dengue patient needs sodium, glucose, liver function and perfusion checked before assuming encephalitis.
Acute flaccid quadriparesis on day 2–4 of dengue: measure potassium straight away.
Check platelets and clotting before any lumbar puncture in suspected dengue.
det.thd: ไข้เลือดออกเดงกีทำให้เกิดอาการทางระบบประสาทได้หลายแบบ ที่พบบ่อยคือสมองทำงานผิดปกติจากช็อก ตับวาย โซเดียมหรือน้ำตาลต่ำในช่วงวิกฤต ส่วนสมองอักเสบจากเชื้อโดยตรงพบน้อยกว่า เลือดออกในสมองสัมพันธ์กับเกล็ดเลือดต่ำมาก ในระยะไข้อาจอ่อนแรงทั้งตัวจากโพแทสเซียมต่ำ ซึ่งแก้ได้เร็วด้วยการให้โพแทสเซียม และหลังหายไข้ 1–4 สัปดาห์อาจเกิด GBS, ADEM หรือไขสันหลังอักเสบ การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคองตามระยะของโรค หลีกเลี่ยง NSAIDs และตรวจเกล็ดเลือดก่อนเจาะหลังเสมอ

case.who: 69-year-old male rubber tapper from Songkhla with diabetes
case.story: During a local outbreak he developed fever, a blotchy rash and such painful wrists and ankles that he could not grip a knife. On day 5 he became confused and had two generalised seizures.
case.exam: Drowsy, GCS 12, swollen tender wrists, no meningism, no focal limb weakness.

case.q: What is the likely diagnosis, and what does treatment involve?
case.a: Chikungunya meningoencephalitis in an older adult; supportive care with seizure control, fluids and analgesia, keep aciclovir only until HSV is excluded, and avoid NSAIDs until dengue is ruled out.

det.patho: Chikungunya virus is an alphavirus spread by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, the same vectors as dengue, and has caused large outbreaks in Thailand, particularly in the southern provinces. The virus replicates in fibroblasts, joint tissue and muscle, and can infect the choroid plexus, meningeal and ependymal cells, with oligodendrocyte and astrocyte involvement in severe cases. Neonates acquire infection from viraemic mothers at delivery and are vulnerable to severe encephalopathy. Later immune-mediated syndromes reflect cross-reactive antibody and T-cell responses after the virus has cleared.
det.clinical: The acute illness begins suddenly with fever, rash and severe symmetric arthralgia; neurological problems appear in a small proportion, more often in atypical or severe cases. Encephalitis brings confusion, seizures and sometimes focal deficits, and older adults may simply present with delirium. Infants exposed at birth develop fever, poor feeding, seizures and white-matter injury. Weeks later patients may develop GBS (including axonal forms), ADEM, myelitis or optic neuritis, often when the arthritis is still active. Chronic arthralgia lasting months is common and helps distinguish chikungunya from dengue.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis combines the clinical pattern with RT-PCR in the viraemic first week and IgM antibodies thereafter, ideally including CSF for encephalitis. Because dengue circulates in the same places and seasons, both should be tested together. CSF is usually mildly inflammatory; MRI may be normal or show white-matter and callosal lesions. HSV, bacterial meningitis, JE, scrub typhus and metabolic causes need to be excluded.
det.treatment: There is no specific antiviral; management is supportive, with seizure control, airway protection and paracetamol for pain until dengue is excluded, after which NSAIDs can be used for arthritis. GBS is treated with IVIG or plasma exchange, and ADEM, myelitis or optic neuritis with high-dose corticosteroids. Mosquito control, repellents and bed nets remain the main prevention. A live-attenuated and a virus-like-particle vaccine were licensed in some countries in 2023–2025, but the live vaccine has safety restrictions in older adults and neither is routinely available in Thailand.
det.prognosis: Most adults recover, but encephalitis in neonates and the elderly carries notable mortality and neurodevelopmental or cognitive sequelae.
pearls: Fever with severe hand and wrist arthralgia plus confusion in an outbreak area: think chikungunya encephalitis.
Test for dengue and chikungunya together; they share vectors and seasons.
Neonates born to mothers febrile around delivery are at highest risk of severe CHIKV encephalopathy.
det.thd: ชิคุนกุนยาหรือไข้ปวดข้อยุงลายเกิดจาก alphavirus ที่ยุงลายเป็นพาหะเหมือนไข้เลือดออก อาการเด่นคือไข้สูง ผื่น และปวดข้อมือข้อเท้ารุนแรง ส่วนน้อยมีสมองอักเสบ ซึม ชัก โดยเฉพาะทารกที่ติดจากแม่ช่วงคลอดและผู้สูงอายุ หลังไข้ลงอาจเกิด GBS, ADEM หรือไขสันหลังอักเสบ วินิจฉัยด้วย RT-PCR ในสัปดาห์แรกและ IgM หลังจากนั้น ควรตรวจเดงกีควบคู่ การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง

Multifocal demyelination after any infection or vaccine, usually in children, without active viraemia
Generic acute ascending areflexic weakness; look for preceding fever with arthritis to link it to CHIKV

name: Neuroleptospirosis
formal: Nervous system involvement in leptospirosis, a zoonotic spirochaetal infection acquired through skin or mucosal contact with water or soil contaminated by animal urine, most commonly aseptic lymphocytic meningitis in the immune phase and less often encephalitis, intracranial haemorrhage, myelitis, cranial or peripheral neuropathy and GBS.
simple: Leptospirosis is a germ caught from rat urine in flood water or rice fields, and besides fever, red eyes and kidney or liver failure it can inflame the brain coverings or cause bleeding in the brain.
th: โรคฉี่หนูที่มีอาการทางระบบประสาท ส่วนใหญ่เป็นเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบแบบ aseptic ในระยะภูมิคุ้มกัน บางรายมีสมองอักเสบ เลือดออกในสมอง ไขสันหลังอักเสบ หรือเส้นประสาทอักเสบ พบบ่อยในชาวนาภาคอีสานหลังน้ำท่วม
tempoNote: Incubation 2–30 days (usually 1–2 weeks) after water exposure; the septicaemic phase lasts about a week, then meningitis and other immune-phase complications appear over the next 1–2 weeks
feat: Farmer, flood victim or sewer worker with abrupt fever, intense calf myalgia and conjunctival suffusion
Severe headache and neck stiffness in the second week with lymphocytic CSF and normal glucose
Jaundice, acute kidney injury, thrombocytopenia or pulmonary haemorrhage in severe (Weil) disease
Intracerebral or subarachnoid haemorrhage, confusion or seizures in severe cases
Occasional myelitis, cerebellar ataxia, facial or other cranial palsies and GBS
inv: Leptospira PCR in blood (first week) and urine (after the first week); rapid IgM tests for early screening
Microscopic agglutination test (MAT) on paired sera for confirmation — a fourfold rise or a high single titre
Creatinine, bilirubin, liver enzymes, CK, platelets and chest imaging
CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis, mildly raised protein, normal glucose; CT/MRI for focal signs or falling GCS

case.story: Ten days after wading barefoot through flooded paddies to rescue his buffalo, he developed fever, chills and painful calves. A week later the fever returned with a splitting headache and vomiting.
case.exam: Temperature 38.6 °C, red eyes without discharge, mild jaundice, tender calves, neck stiffness; no focal deficit.
case.tests: Creatinine 3.4 mg/dL, bilirubin 5.8 mg/dL, platelets 70,000/µL, CK 1,900 U/L; CSF 190 cells/µL (85% lymphocytes), protein 74 mg/dL, glucose normal, Gram stain negative; leptospira rapid IgM positive.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and which antibiotic would you start?
case.a: Leptospirosis with aseptic meningitis in the immune phase and features of Weil disease; start IV penicillin G or ceftriaxone, support renal function, and confirm with MAT on paired sera.

read.where: Chapter 39 Spirochetal Infections of the Nervous System

det.patho: Pathogenic Leptospira species are shed in the urine of rats, cattle, pigs and dogs and survive in warm wet soil and water; humans are infected through cuts, softened skin or mucosa. Thailand reports thousands of cases yearly, concentrated in the northeast among rice farmers during the rainy season and after floods. Spirochaetes spread through the blood and reach the CSF early, but most neurological illness occurs when antibody appears and organisms are cleared, implicating immune complex and inflammatory injury. Vasculitis, endothelial damage and thrombocytopenia explain haemorrhage, while immune mechanisms underlie myelitis and GBS.
det.clinical: The septicaemic phase brings sudden fever, rigors, headache, prominent calf and lumbar myalgia and conjunctival suffusion. After a short improvement some patients develop the immune phase with meningitis, uveitis and recurrent fever; many more have CSF pleocytosis without symptoms. Severe disease combines jaundice, acute kidney injury, myocarditis and pulmonary haemorrhage, and these patients may become confused or have intracranial bleeding. Less common presentations include encephalitis, transverse myelitis, cerebellar syndrome, cranial nerve palsies, mononeuritis and GBS, sometimes weeks after the fever.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in any febrile patient with relevant exposure, myalgia and red eyes, especially if renal or liver dysfunction coexists. PCR detects leptospiral DNA in blood early and in urine later; rapid IgM tests and ELISA help at the bedside, while MAT on paired sera remains the reference standard. CSF shows a lymphocytic or mixed pleocytosis with normal glucose, and organisms are rarely cultured. In Thailand, scrub typhus, dengue, malaria and melioidosis are the main febrile mimics and may coexist.
det.treatment: Antibiotics should start without waiting for confirmation: oral doxycycline for mild disease and IV penicillin G or ceftriaxone for severe or neurological disease, usually for 7 days. A Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction may follow the first doses. Supportive care with fluids, early dialysis for oliguric renal failure, ventilatory support for pulmonary haemorrhage and correction of thrombocytopenia matters most for survival. Corticosteroids and plasma exchange have uncertain benefit; GBS is treated with IVIG in the usual way. Doxycycline prophylaxis may be considered for high-risk short exposures such as flood clean-up.
det.prognosis: Leptospiral meningitis usually resolves without sequelae; mortality is driven by pulmonary haemorrhage, renal failure and intracranial bleeding in severe disease.
pearls: Fever, calf pain and red eyes after flood or rice-field work: leptospirosis until proved otherwise.
Aseptic meningitis plus raised creatinine, bilirubin and CK is a classic leptospirosis combination.
Doxycycline treats both leptospirosis and scrub typhus — useful when the two cannot be separated.
det.thd: โรคฉี่หนูเกิดจากเชื้อ Leptospira ที่ปนอยู่ในปัสสาวะสัตว์ ติดผ่านบาดแผลหรือผิวหนังที่แช่น้ำนาน พบมากในชาวนาภาคอีสานช่วงฤดูฝนและหลังน้ำท่วม อาการระบบประสาทที่พบบ่อยที่สุดคือเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบแบบ aseptic ในสัปดาห์ที่สอง ร่วมกับไข้ ปวดน่อง ตาแดง ตัวเหลือง ไตวาย ในรายรุนแรงอาจมีเลือดออกในสมอง ไขสันหลังอักเสบ หรือ GBS วินิจฉัยด้วย PCR, rapid IgM และ MAT รักษาด้วย doxycycline หรือ penicillin G/ceftriaxone ร่วมกับการประคับประคองไตและปอด

name: Neuromelioidosis (Burkholderia pseudomallei CNS infection)
formal: Central nervous system infection by Burkholderia pseudomallei, a soil and water saprophyte endemic in northeast Thailand and northern Australia, typically presenting as a brainstem or cerebellar encephalitis with cranial nerve palsies plus weakness or ataxia from long-tract involvement, or as brain abscesses, extra-axial collections, meningitis or myelitis.
simple: Melioidosis is a serious infection caught from wet soil and muddy water, and when it reaches the brain it usually attacks the brainstem, causing facial weakness, double vision and limb weakness, or forms pus pockets.
ab: เมลิออยด์ขึ้นสมอง
th: เมลิออยโดสิสขึ้นสมองจากเชื้อ Burkholderia pseudomallei ในดินและน้ำ พบมากในอีสาน ผู้ป่วยเบาหวานเสี่ยงสูง มักเป็นก้านสมองอักเสบที่มีเส้นประสาทสมองอัมพาตและแขนขาอ่อนแรง หรือเป็นฝีในสมองหลายตำแหน่ง
tempoNote: Fever and headache for several days to a few weeks before cranial nerve and limb signs accumulate; may follow skin, scalp or lung infection
feat: Rice farmer or outdoor worker with diabetes, heavy alcohol use, chronic kidney disease or thalassaemia, often in the rainy season
Fever and headache followed by unilateral facial weakness, sixth nerve palsy, bulbar signs and contralateral or ipsilateral limb weakness
MRI: T2 lesions in the brainstem and cerebellar peduncles with small ring-enhancing microabscesses that track along white-matter pathways
Alternatively single or multiple brain abscesses, subdural or epidural collections, often with skull or scalp infection
Coexisting pneumonia, liver or splenic abscesses or prostatic abscess may point to the organism
inv: Blood, urine, throat swab, pus and CSF cultures; warn the laboratory, as the organism may be mislabelled as Pseudomonas or a contaminant
MRI brain and spine with contrast
CSF: moderate pleocytosis (neutrophil or lymphocyte predominant), high protein, normal or mildly low glucose; culture often negative
Ultrasound or CT of abdomen for liver, spleen and prostate abscesses; chest imaging

case.who: 53-year-old male rice farmer from Ubon Ratchathani with poorly controlled diabetes
case.story: Two weeks of fever and frontal headache were followed by drooping of the right side of his face, double vision and clumsiness of the left hand.
case.exam: Temperature 38.4 °C; right lower motor neuron facial palsy, right sixth nerve palsy, left hemiparesis 4/5 with extensor plantar, right limb ataxia.
case.tests: MRI: T2 hyperintensity of the right pons and middle cerebellar peduncle with several tiny rim-enhancing foci; CSF 140 cells/µL, protein 130 mg/dL, glucose 60% of blood; blood culture grows an oxidase-positive Gram-negative rod with wrinkled colonies on day 3.
case.q: What organism should be suspected, and what antibiotic plan applies?
case.a: Burkholderia pseudomallei brainstem encephalitis (neuromelioidosis); give high-dose IV meropenem for at least 8 weeks with added co-trimoxazole, then prolonged oral co-trimoxazole eradication therapy, and tightly control glucose.

read.where: Chapter 38 Acute Bacterial Infections of the Central Nervous System

det.patho: Burkholderia pseudomallei lives in wet soil and surface water and infects through skin inoculation, inhalation or ingestion; northeast Thailand has one of the highest burdens worldwide. Neurological disease occurs in a few percent of melioidosis cases. Experimental and clinical evidence suggest that the bacterium can climb along cranial nerves, especially the trigeminal and olfactory routes, into the brainstem, which would explain the striking brainstem predilection and the way lesions spread along fibre tracts. Diabetes, alcohol excess, renal disease and thalassaemia impair neutrophil function and raise risk.
det.clinical: The classic presentation is subacute fever and headache, then progressive unilateral cranial nerve palsies (VII and VI most often, bulbar nerves later) with limb weakness or ataxia — a picture that can mimic Listeria or Bickerstaff encephalitis. Others present with one or several brain abscesses, subdural or epidural empyema, meningitis, or myelitis and spinal abscess. Scalp or skull osteomyelitis with adjacent extra-axial collection is another recognised pattern. Pneumonia, deep organ abscesses and septic shock may coexist, but neurological disease can also occur with little systemic illness.
det.diagnosis: Culture is the diagnostic standard; send multiple specimens because CSF cultures are frequently negative. Laboratories outside endemic areas may misidentify the organism, so clinicians should state the suspicion and handle isolates with appropriate biosafety. Serology (indirect haemagglutination) is of limited value in endemic regions where background positivity is high. MRI showing brainstem T2 change with small enhancing abscesses that extend along tracts is highly suggestive in the right context.
det.treatment: Treatment has an intensive and an eradication phase. For neurological disease, high-dose IV meropenem (2 g every 8 hours) for at least 8 weeks is preferred, often with co-trimoxazole added for its CNS penetration; ceftazidime is an alternative where meropenem is unavailable. Eradication therapy with oral co-trimoxazole follows for at least 3–6 months, longer for CNS disease, to prevent relapse. Abscesses and empyema may require surgical drainage, and blood glucose control is essential.
det.prognosis: Mortality remains high (around a quarter or more), and survivors often keep cranial nerve or motor deficits; relapse occurs when eradication therapy is short or incomplete.
pearls: Diabetic Isan farmer with fever and evolving brainstem signs: think melioidosis and start meropenem.
MRI lesions spreading along brainstem and cerebellar tracts with microabscesses are characteristic.
A Gram-negative rod reported as 'Pseudomonas' from an endemic patient may be B. pseudomallei — ask the lab to check.
det.thd: เมลิออยโดสิสขึ้นสมองเกิดจากเชื้อ Burkholderia pseudomallei ที่อยู่ในดินและน้ำ พบมากในชาวนาอีสาน โดยเฉพาะผู้ป่วยเบาหวาน เชื้อน่าจะไต่ไปตามเส้นประสาทสมองเข้าสู่ก้านสมอง ผู้ป่วยมักมีไข้ ปวดศีรษะ แล้วตามด้วยหน้าเบี้ยว ตาเหล่ เห็นภาพซ้อน และแขนขาอ่อนแรง MRI พบรอยโรคที่ก้านสมองพร้อมฝีเล็ก ๆ วินิจฉัยด้วยการเพาะเชื้อจากเลือดหรือหนอง รักษาด้วย meropenem ขนาดสูงอย่างน้อย 8 สัปดาห์ ตามด้วย co-trimoxazole หลายเดือนเพื่อป้องกันการกลับเป็นซ้ำ

Listeria rhombencephalitis looks similar; distinguish by culture and exposure history

name: Neurobrucellosis
formal: Nervous system involvement in brucellosis, a zoonosis caused by Brucella species acquired from unpasteurised dairy products or contact with infected goats, sheep or cattle, presenting mainly as subacute to chronic meningitis or meningoencephalitis with cranial neuropathies (especially hearing loss), radiculopathy, myelopathy, white-matter lesions or stroke.
simple: Brucellosis is an infection from raw goat or cow milk or farm animals, and when it spreads to the nervous system it causes a slow meningitis, deafness or weakness that can look like tuberculosis.
ab: โรคแท้งติดต่อในคน
th: บรูเซลโลสิสขึ้นระบบประสาท ติดจากนมแพะหรือนมวัวที่ไม่ผ่านการฆ่าเชื้อหรือสัมผัสสัตว์ป่วย มักเป็นเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบเรื้อรังคล้ายวัณโรค ร่วมกับหูตึง เส้นประสาทหรือไขสันหลังผิดปกติ
tempoNote: Systemic undulant fever for weeks to months; neurological features develop over weeks and may appear long after the initial febrile illness
feat: Goat or sheep farmer, abattoir or laboratory worker, or someone drinking raw goat milk, with relapsing fever, sweats and joint or back pain
Chronic headache with meningism and lymphocytic CSF, high protein and low glucose — easily mistaken for TB meningitis
Sensorineural hearing loss and other cranial nerve palsies
Spondylitis (often lumbar) with radiculopathy, epidural abscess or myelopathy
Diffuse white-matter lesions, small-vessel stroke or psychiatric change in some patients
inv: Blood and CSF cultures with prolonged incubation; alert the laboratory because Brucella is a common cause of lab-acquired infection
Serology: standard tube agglutination, Coombs anti-Brucella test or ELISA in serum and CSF; PCR where available
CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, low glucose; exclude TB with Xpert MTB/RIF and culture
MRI brain and spine, audiometry

case.story: For four months he has had evening fevers, drenching sweats and low back pain, and over the last month his hearing has faded in both ears and he has a constant headache. He drinks fresh goat milk daily.
case.exam: Mild neck stiffness, bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, lumbar spine tenderness, no limb weakness; hepatosplenomegaly.
case.tests: CSF 120 cells/µL (lymphocytes), protein 190 mg/dL, glucose 30 mg/dL (blood 110); Xpert MTB/RIF negative; serum Brucella agglutination 1:640; blood culture grows small Gram-negative coccobacilli after 7 days; MRI L3–L4 spondylodiscitis.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and what treatment is needed?
case.a: Neurobrucellosis with spondylitis; combine ceftriaxone with doxycycline and rifampicin (ceftriaxone for the first weeks, oral drugs for several months), and advise against raw milk consumption.

det.patho: Brucella melitensis, abortus and suis are small intracellular Gram-negative coccobacilli that survive inside macrophages and spread to the reticuloendothelial system, bones, joints and nervous system. Humans are infected by eating unpasteurised milk or cheese, inhaling aerosols or handling placentas and carcasses. Human cases are uncommon in Thailand but have been linked to goat farming and raw goat milk, particularly in the south. CNS disease reflects direct infection of the meninges, an immune-mediated vasculitis and demyelination, and spread from vertebral foci.
det.clinical: Neurological involvement occurs in a small percentage of brucellosis and may be the main presentation. The commonest picture is a smouldering meningitis or meningoencephalitis with headache, fever, confusion and cranial nerve palsies, among which eighth nerve deafness is characteristic. Other forms include polyradiculoneuropathy, myelitis, spinal epidural abscess from spondylitis, white-matter disease resembling demyelination, small-vessel infarcts or haemorrhage, intracranial hypertension and depression or psychosis. Systemic clues include undulant fever, sweats with a peculiar odour, arthralgia, sacroiliitis, hepatosplenomegaly and orchitis.
det.diagnosis: Consider it in any chronic lymphocytic meningitis with low glucose when TB tests are negative and there is animal or raw dairy exposure. Confirm with positive cultures, which need prolonged incubation, or with anti-Brucella antibodies or PCR in CSF; supportive serum titres strengthen the case. MRI may show meningeal enhancement, white-matter lesions, infarcts or spinal involvement. Laboratory staff should be warned because aerosolised cultures can infect them.
det.treatment: No single standard exists, but most regimens combine an agent with good CNS penetration, usually IV ceftriaxone for the first 4–6 weeks, with oral doxycycline and rifampicin continued for at least 3–6 months, guided by clinical and CSF response. Co-trimoxazole is an alternative third drug. Corticosteroids are sometimes added for severe inflammation or cranial neuropathy, and abscesses may need drainage. Preventive messages focus on boiling or pasteurising milk and using protection when handling birthing animals.
det.prognosis: Most patients improve with prolonged combination therapy, but hearing loss and other deficits can persist and relapses follow short courses.
pearls: TB-like meningitis with deafness in a goat farmer or raw goat milk drinker: send Brucella serology.
Warn the microbiology lab when brucellosis is suspected — it is a classic laboratory-acquired infection.
Treatment lasts months, not weeks, and needs at least two or three drugs.
det.thd: บรูเซลโลสิสเกิดจากเชื้อ Brucella ที่ติดจากนมแพะ นมวัวดิบ หรือการสัมผัสสัตว์ป่วย ในไทยพบน้อยแต่มีรายงานในผู้เลี้ยงแพะ อาการทางระบบประสาทมักเป็นเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบเรื้อรัง น้ำไขสันหลังคล้ายวัณโรค ร่วมกับหูตึงทั้งสองข้าง ปวดหลังจากกระดูกสันหลังอักเสบ หรือรอยโรคเนื้อขาวในสมอง วินิจฉัยด้วยการเพาะเชื้อที่ต้องรอนานและการตรวจแอนติบอดีในเลือดและน้ำไขสันหลัง รักษาด้วยยาหลายตัว เช่น ceftriaxone ร่วมกับ doxycycline และ rifampicin นานหลายเดือน

name: Nipah virus encephalitis
formal: An acute, often fatal encephalitis caused by Nipah virus, a henipavirus carried by Pteropus fruit bats and transmitted to humans through infected pigs, food such as raw date-palm sap contaminated by bat secretions, or close contact with patients, with a recognised relapsing and late-onset form months to years after recovery.
simple: Nipah is a rare but very dangerous virus from fruit bats that causes brain swelling, fits and coma, and can spread from person to person.
ab: ไวรัสนิปาห์
th: สมองอักเสบเฉียบพลันรุนแรงจากไวรัสนิปาห์ที่มีค้างคาวแม่ไก่เป็นแหล่งรังโรค ติดผ่านหมู อาหารที่ปนเปื้อนสารคัดหลั่งค้างคาว หรือติดจากคนสู่คน อัตราตายสูง
tempoNote: Incubation usually 4–14 days (occasionally weeks); fever to coma in a few days; relapsing or late-onset encephalitis may appear months to years later
feat: Recent exposure to pigs, raw date-palm sap or a Nipah patient in an outbreak area (Bangladesh, India, earlier Malaysia)
Fever and headache progressing rapidly to confusion, seizures and coma
Brainstem and autonomic signs: segmental myoclonus, areflexia, abnormal pupils, tachycardia and hypertension
Cough and breathlessness or ARDS, especially with the Bangladesh strain, favouring person-to-person spread
MRI: many small discrete T2 lesions in subcortical and deep white matter
inv: RT-PCR on throat swab, CSF, urine and blood through the national reference laboratory under high-level biosafety
Nipah IgM and IgG ELISA in serum and CSF
MRI brain; CSF usually shows mild lymphocytic pleocytosis and raised protein
Immediate notification and infection control with contact tracing

case.who: 31-year-old Thai male construction worker who returned to Bangkok from a district in Bangladesh
case.story: Nine days after drinking fresh date-palm sap with villagers during the winter harvest, he developed fever, headache and a cough. On day 4 he became confused and then unrousable after a seizure.
case.exam: GCS 7, tachycardia 136/min, BP 182/104, unequal sluggish pupils, myoclonic jerks of the trunk, absent reflexes; crackles at both lung bases.
case.tests: CSF 45 lymphocytes/µL, protein 95 mg/dL; MRI multiple small bilateral subcortical white-matter hyperintensities; chest X-ray bilateral infiltrates; Nipah RT-PCR positive in throat swab and CSF.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and what must the hospital do immediately besides supportive care?
case.a: Nipah virus encephalitis; give intensive supportive care and notify the Department of Disease Control at once, with airborne-contact isolation, protection of staff and tracing of contacts — there is no proven antiviral.

read.where: Chapter 42 Nervous System Complications of Systemic Viral Infections

det.patho: Nipah virus is a paramyxovirus whose natural hosts are Pteropus fruit bats across South and South-East Asia, including Thailand, where bats carry the virus although no human cases have been reported. The first large outbreak in Malaysia and Singapore (1998–99) spread through pigs, whereas recurrent outbreaks in Bangladesh and India arise from raw date-palm sap or fruit contaminated by bats and then spread between people, and Kerala has seen repeated clusters. The virus targets endothelium, causing a systemic vasculitis with thrombosis and small infarcts, and also infects neurons directly. Persistence of virus in the CNS explains relapsing and late-onset encephalitis.
det.clinical: After a febrile prodrome with headache, dizziness and vomiting, patients rapidly become confused, drowsy and comatose, often with seizures. Brainstem involvement is prominent: segmental myoclonus, areflexia, hypotonia, abnormal pupils and doll's eye responses, along with autonomic storms of tachycardia and hypertension. Respiratory involvement ranges from cough to ARDS and is commoner with Bangladesh/India strains. Survivors may have persisting deficits, and a minority develop relapse or delayed encephalitis, sometimes years later, with focal seizures and cortical lesions.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis relies on epidemiological suspicion — travel to or residence in an outbreak area with bat, pig, sap or patient exposure — and laboratory confirmation by RT-PCR from throat swab, CSF, urine or blood, plus IgM/IgG serology. Samples must be handled under high-level biosafety by reference laboratories. MRI typically shows numerous small hyperintense lesions in white matter, distinct from the larger confluent changes of ADEM. Other treatable encephalitides such as HSV must still be excluded.
det.treatment: No antiviral is proven; ribavirin has been used without clear benefit, and investigational monoclonal antibodies (such as m102.4) and remdesivir have been given under emergency or trial protocols. Management is intensive supportive care with seizure control, ventilation and management of raised ICP and autonomic instability. Strict infection control, including isolation and personal protective equipment for staff, prevents nosocomial spread. Prevention depends on avoiding raw date-palm sap and fruit bitten by bats, protecting pig farms and rapid public health response; vaccines remain in clinical trials.
det.prognosis: Case fatality ranges from about 40% to over 70% depending on the outbreak; around a fifth of survivors have lasting neurological deficits or later relapse.
pearls: Encephalitis with segmental myoclonus, areflexia and hypertension after travel to Bangladesh or Kerala: think Nipah and isolate.
Raw date-palm sap is the classic exposure in South Asian outbreaks.
Survivors need long-term follow-up because relapse can occur years later.
det.thd: ไวรัสนิปาห์มีค้างคาวแม่ไก่เป็นรังโรค ติดสู่คนผ่านหมู น้ำหวานจากต้นอินทผลัมหรือผลไม้ที่ค้างคาวกิน และติดจากคนสู่คนได้ มีการระบาดในมาเลเซีย บังกลาเทศ และอินเดีย ผู้ป่วยมีไข้ ปวดศีรษะ แล้วซึม ชัก โคม่าอย่างรวดเร็ว ร่วมกับกระตุกเป็นปล้อง ๆ ม่านตาผิดปกติ ความดันสูงชีพจรเร็ว และอาการปอด วินิจฉัยด้วย RT-PCR จากคอ CSF และปัสสาวะ ต้องแยกผู้ป่วยและแจ้งกรมควบคุมโรคทันที ยังไม่มียาต้านไวรัสที่ได้ผลชัดเจน อัตราตายสูง

name: Neurological manifestations of COVID-19 (including post-COVID condition)
formal: Neurological disorders occurring during or after SARS-CoV-2 infection, including headache, smell and taste loss, encephalopathy and delirium, ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke, cerebral venous thrombosis, seizures, rare encephalitis, ADEM or acute necrotising encephalopathy, Guillain–Barré syndrome, myopathy, and persisting post-COVID symptoms such as cognitive difficulty, fatigue and dysautonomia.
simple: COVID-19 can affect the brain and nerves, from losing smell and having headaches to strokes, confusion and nerve damage, and some people have brain fog and tiredness for months afterwards.
ab: โควิดลงสมอง
th: อาการทางระบบประสาทจากโควิด-19 ทั้งระยะเฉียบพลัน เช่น ปวดศีรษะ ไม่ได้กลิ่น สับสน หลอดเลือดสมองตีบหรือแตก GBS และระยะหลัง (long COVID) เช่น สมองตื้อ อ่อนเพลีย ใจสั่นเวลายืน
tempoNote: Smell loss, headache, encephalopathy and stroke occur in the first days to weeks; GBS and ADEM follow within about 2–6 weeks; post-COVID condition is defined by symptoms persisting beyond 3 months from infection
feat: Sudden loss of smell or taste and headache, often in mild infection
Delirium or encephalopathy in older or critically ill patients, mostly from hypoxia, sepsis, inflammation and drugs
Ischaemic stroke (including large-vessel occlusion with high D-dimer), intracerebral haemorrhage on anticoagulation or ECMO, and venous sinus thrombosis
Post-infectious GBS, ADEM, acute necrotising encephalopathy and myelitis; critical illness neuromyopathy in ICU survivors
Long COVID: fatigue, cognitive slowing, headache, post-exertional symptoms, orthostatic intolerance and sleep disturbance
inv: SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR or antigen test; inflammatory markers, D-dimer, glucose, sodium and oxygenation
CT/CTA or MRI for focal deficits; MR venography for suspected venous thrombosis
CSF and EEG for encephalopathy or seizures (CSF is usually normal and viral RNA is rarely detected); NCS for GBS
Long COVID: targeted tests to exclude other causes (thyroid, anaemia, B12, sleep disorders, depression) and an active stand test for orthostatic tachycardia

case.who: 62-year-old male taxi driver in Bangkok with diabetes and hypertension
case.story: On day 6 of COVID-19 pneumonia, while on high-flow oxygen in the ward, he was suddenly unable to move his left arm and leg and his speech became slurred.
case.exam: Right gaze preference, left hemiplegia, left facial weakness, left-sided neglect; NIHSS 16; SpO2 94% on high-flow oxygen.
case.tests: CT no haemorrhage; CTA right M1 occlusion; D-dimer 6,200 ng/mL, CRP 120 mg/L; ECG sinus rhythm; SARS-CoV-2 PCR positive.
case.q: What acute treatment is appropriate, and how should secondary prevention be decided?
case.a: COVID-19-associated acute ischaemic stroke; offer standard reperfusion (IV thrombolysis if eligible and mechanical thrombectomy) with infection-control precautions, then investigate the usual stroke mechanisms and give anticoagulation only for standard indications.

det.patho: SARS-CoV-2 rarely infects brain tissue directly; most neurological injury is secondary to hypoxia, systemic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, coagulopathy, cardiac embolism, metabolic derangement and drugs used in severe disease. Smell loss arises from infection of supporting cells in the olfactory epithelium rather than the olfactory neurons themselves. Post-infectious immune responses explain GBS, ADEM and myelitis, while post-COVID condition likely involves several overlapping mechanisms, including persistent inflammation, viral antigen persistence, autonomic dysfunction, microvascular injury and deconditioning. Risk of severe neurological complications has fallen considerably with population immunity, vaccination and newer variants.
det.clinical: In the acute phase, headache, myalgia and anosmia or ageusia are common, whereas encephalopathy affects mainly older or severely ill patients and is associated with worse outcomes. Stroke risk rises during and shortly after infection, and early in the pandemic large-vessel strokes occurred in younger patients with few risk factors; haemorrhage is linked to anticoagulation and ECMO. Children may develop acute necrotising encephalopathy or neurological features of MIS-C. Weeks later GBS, ADEM, myelitis or optic neuritis may emerge, and ICU survivors often have critical illness weakness. Long COVID most often brings fatigue, cognitive complaints, headache, dysautonomia and sleep problems that fluctuate and worsen after exertion.
det.diagnosis: Acute neurological syndromes are diagnosed with the same tools as without COVID, keeping in mind that infection may be coincidental. CSF is usually bland and SARS-CoV-2 RNA is rarely found, so a positive nasal test does not prove CNS infection. Imaging may show infarcts, microbleeds, posterior reversible encephalopathy, leukoencephalopathy or necrotising lesions. WHO defines post-COVID condition as symptoms starting within 3 months of infection, lasting at least 2 months and not explained by another diagnosis, so alternative causes must be sought before applying the label.
det.treatment: Acute stroke is managed with standard thrombolysis and thrombectomy pathways while protecting staff; antithrombotic choice follows the usual stroke mechanism. Delirium is managed by treating hypoxia and sepsis, minimising sedatives and supporting sleep and orientation. GBS receives IVIG or plasma exchange, ADEM high-dose steroids, and seizures standard antiseizure drugs. Antivirals such as nirmatrelvir–ritonavir or remdesivir reduce severe illness in high-risk patients but have no proven role in treating established neurological complications. For long COVID, care is symptom-based and multidisciplinary — pacing for post-exertional malaise, management of orthostatic tachycardia, cognitive rehabilitation, sleep and mood support — and vaccination lowers the risk of developing it.
det.prognosis: Most smell loss and mild symptoms recover over weeks to months; encephalopathy and stroke during COVID carry higher mortality, and a minority of post-COVID patients have symptoms lasting a year or more.
pearls: In COVID-19 encephalopathy, look first for hypoxia, sepsis, metabolic upset and drugs — direct viral encephalitis is rare.
COVID-related stroke still gets standard reperfusion therapy; do not delay it for infection concerns.
Post-COVID condition is a diagnosis of exclusion with a time-based definition; screen for orthostatic tachycardia and sleep or mood disorders.
det.thd: โควิด-19 ทำให้เกิดอาการทางระบบประสาทได้หลายแบบ ในระยะเฉียบพลันพบปวดศีรษะ ไม่ได้กลิ่นไม่รู้รส สับสนในผู้สูงอายุหรือผู้ป่วยหนัก และหลอดเลือดสมองตีบหรือแตก ซึ่งส่วนใหญ่เกิดจากภาวะขาดออกซิเจน การอักเสบ และเลือดแข็งตัวง่าย มากกว่าเชื้อเข้าสมองโดยตรง หลังติดเชื้อหลายสัปดาห์อาจเกิด GBS หรือ ADEM ส่วน long COVID คืออาการที่ยังคงอยู่หลัง 3 เดือน เช่น สมองตื้อ อ่อนเพลีย ใจสั่นเวลายืน การรักษาใช้แนวทางมาตรฐานของแต่ละภาวะ และฟื้นฟูแบบสหสาขา

name: Hepatic myelopathy
formal: A progressive, predominantly motor spastic paraparesis arising in chronic liver disease with marked portosystemic shunting (spontaneous, surgical or TIPS), attributed to pyramidal-tract damage in the spinal cord from gut-derived toxins that bypass hepatic clearance.
simple: Slowly worsening stiff, weak legs in someone with long-standing liver disease, because blood skips the liver and its toxins hurt the spinal cord.
th: ภาวะไขสันหลังเสื่อมในผู้ป่วยโรคตับเรื้อรังที่มีทางลัดเลือด portosystemic shunt ทำให้ขาสองข้างเกร็งอ่อนแรงค่อย ๆ มากขึ้น การรับความรู้สึกมักปกติ การปลูกถ่ายตับเร็วเป็นการรักษาเดียวที่ช่วยได้จริง
tempoNote: Insidious over months to years, usually after repeated episodes of hepatic encephalopathy or after a shunt procedure; rarely reverses once established
feat: Symmetric spastic paraparesis with brisk reflexes and extensor plantars; arms largely spared
Sensation and sphincters typically normal or only mildly affected
Background of cirrhosis or non-cirrhotic portal hypertension with a large shunt or TIPS
Prior or coexisting episodes of hepatic encephalopathy and high ammonia
Lactulose and rifaximin help the encephalopathy but seldom the gait
inv: MRI spine to exclude compression or other causes; cord usually looks normal; brain MRI may show pallidal T1 hyperintensity
Serum ammonia, liver tests; abdominal imaging to define the shunt
Exclude mimics: B12, copper, HTLV-1, HIV, syphilis serology
Central motor conduction time on TMS may be prolonged before clinical change

case.who: 52-year-old former rice-whisky drinker from Khon Kaen with hepatitis B cirrhosis and a TIPS placed two years ago
case.story: Over eight months his walking has become stiff and scissoring; he now needs a stick. He had three admissions for confusion that settled with lactulose.
case.exam: Spastic legs, power 4/5 proximally, crossed adductors, bilateral Babinski; normal joint position and vibration; no sensory level; mild asterixis.
case.tests: Ammonia raised; MRI whole spine normal; B12, copper, HTLV-1 and HIV negative; CT abdomen shows a patent TIPS and large splenorenal collateral.
case.q: What is the likely cause of his gait disorder, and what treatment has the best chance of helping?
case.a: Hepatic (portosystemic shunt) myelopathy; refer early for liver transplantation, with shunt reduction or occlusion considered while waiting.

det.patho: The disorder appears when portal blood reaches the systemic circulation without passing through the liver, so ammonia, manganese and other nitrogenous compounds reach the nervous system in high concentration. Pathology shows symmetrical loss of myelin and axons in the lateral corticospinal tracts, most marked in the thoracic and lumbar cord, with relative sparing of posterior columns. Risk rises with the size of the shunt rather than with the severity of hepatocellular failure, and it can occur in non-cirrhotic portal hypertension and congenital shunts. It is uncommon and probably under-recognised in cirrhosis clinics.
det.clinical: Patients develop slowly progressive leg stiffness and weakness, often after one or more bouts of overt hepatic encephalopathy. The picture is a pure or nearly pure upper motor neuron paraparesis: spasticity, hyperreflexia and Babinski signs, while upper limbs, sensation and bladder are relatively spared. Many become wheelchair-bound within a few years if the shunt persists. Coexisting parkinsonism or cognitive slowing suggests overlap with acquired hepatocerebral degeneration.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the clinical setting and exclusion of other myelopathies. MRI of the spine is usually unremarkable but is essential to rule out compression, demyelination and inflammatory lesions; brain MRI may show globus pallidus T1 brightness from manganese. Check B12, copper, HTLV-1, HIV, syphilis and consider hereditary spastic paraplegia when there is family history. Motor evoked potentials can reveal corticospinal dysfunction even before symptoms appear. Document the shunt anatomy with Doppler, CT or MR angiography.
det.treatment: Ammonia-lowering measures (lactulose, rifaximin, protein-adequate diet, zinc correction) are used but rarely reverse the deficit. Liver transplantation is the only intervention with consistent reports of improvement or arrest, and the chance of recovery falls with disease duration, so referral should be early. Reducing or occluding a TIPS or embolising a large spontaneous shunt may stabilise selected patients when hepatic reserve allows. Spasticity is managed with physiotherapy, baclofen or tizanidine (cautiously in liver failure) and botulinum toxin.
det.prognosis: Without transplantation the paraparesis usually progresses or plateaus at a disabling level; early transplantation can bring partial or substantial recovery.
pearls: Cirrhosis plus a pure spastic paraparesis with normal sensation and normal spine MRI: think shunt myelopathy.
Shunt size matters more than liver failure severity — ask about TIPS.
Transplant early; lactulose alone does not fix the legs.

name: Pancreatic encephalopathy
formal: An acute encephalopathy complicating severe acute pancreatitis, usually within the first one to two weeks, attributed to systemic inflammation, released pancreatic enzymes and microcirculatory injury of brain white matter, and diagnosed after excluding metabolic, toxic, septic and nutritional causes.
simple: Sudden confusion or agitation in a person with bad pancreatitis, after other causes like low sugar, alcohol withdrawal and vitamin B1 lack have been ruled out.
th: ภาวะสมองทำงานผิดปกติเฉียบพลันในผู้ป่วยตับอ่อนอักเสบรุนแรง มีสับสน กระสับกระส่าย ประสาทหลอน ชัก หรือซึม เป็นการวินิจฉัยโดยแยกโรค ต้องคิดถึง Wernicke encephalopathy และให้ thiamine เสมอ
tempoNote: Appears within days of the onset of severe pancreatitis (typically days 2–14); may fluctuate and usually parallels the course of systemic illness
feat: Agitation, disorientation, hallucinations or reduced consciousness during severe pancreatitis
Sometimes seizures, dysarthria, focal signs or meningism
Accompanies organ failure: ARDS, shock, renal failure, high inflammatory markers
Late-onset cases (after about two weeks) are often Wernicke encephalopathy from fasting and vomiting
Diagnosis of exclusion; associated with higher mortality
inv: Glucose, sodium, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, ammonia, blood gases, cultures; alcohol and drug history
MRI brain: patchy or confluent white-matter T2/FLAIR change; check for Wernicke pattern and PRES
EEG for diffuse slowing or non-convulsive seizures
LP when infection is possible and safe

case.who: 45-year-old male construction foreman from Chonburi admitted to ICU with alcohol-related necrotising pancreatitis
case.story: On day 5 he became agitated, pulled out lines and described insects on the wall; he was on nil by mouth with ongoing vomiting.
case.exam: GCS 13, disoriented, no nystagmus or ophthalmoplegia at first, tremulous, febrile 38.4 °C; no focal weakness.
case.tests: Glucose, sodium and calcium corrected; ammonia normal; CT abdomen extensive necrosis; MRI brain scattered periventricular FLAIR hyperintensities; EEG diffuse slowing.
case.q: Beyond treating the pancreatitis, which two diagnoses must be actively covered while labelling this pancreatic encephalopathy?
case.a: Alcohol withdrawal delirium and Wernicke encephalopathy — give high-dose IV thiamine before glucose and treat withdrawal; also search for sepsis from infected necrosis.

det.patho: Severe pancreatitis releases phospholipase A2, trypsin and lipase into the circulation together with a cytokine surge; these are thought to injure capillary endothelium and myelin, producing blood–brain barrier leakage, oedema and demyelination. Hypoxaemia, shock, electrolyte swings and microthrombosis add to the damage. Thiamine depletion from alcohol use, vomiting and prolonged fasting explains many late cases, so the term overlaps with nutritional encephalopathy.
det.clinical: Encephalopathy usually emerges in the first fortnight of a severe attack with psychomotor agitation, confusion, hallucinations or delusions, progressing in some patients to stupor or coma. Seizures, aphasia, hemiparesis, dysarthria and meningeal signs are described. It clusters with multiorgan failure, so most affected patients are in intensive care. Symptoms appearing after the second week, with eye movement abnormalities or ataxia, should be treated as Wernicke until proven otherwise.
det.diagnosis: No specific test exists; the label is applied after excluding hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia, uraemia, hepatic encephalopathy, hypoxaemia, sepsis, drug toxicity and alcohol withdrawal. MRI may show multifocal or confluent white-matter lesions; posterior PRES-like oedema and Wernicke changes should be specifically sought. EEG shows nonspecific slowing and helps detect non-convulsive seizures. Serum myelin basic protein and phospholipase A2 have been studied but are not used routinely.
det.treatment: Management is supportive and directed at the pancreatitis: fluids, oxygenation, organ support, enteral nutrition, and drainage or necrosectomy when indicated. Give parenteral thiamine generously to any patient at nutritional risk, ideally before glucose. Correct electrolytes, treat seizures, manage withdrawal with benzodiazepines, and use antipsychotics sparingly for dangerous agitation. Avoid sedatives that mask evolving neurological change.
det.prognosis: Its presence marks a severe attack with notably higher mortality; survivors usually recover cognition, though some retain deficits from white-matter or Wernicke injury.
pearls: Pancreatic encephalopathy is a diagnosis of exclusion — rule out glucose, sodium, calcium, sepsis and withdrawal first.
Late or eye-movement-rich confusion after pancreatitis is Wernicke until shown otherwise.
Thiamine is cheap and safe; give it before glucose.

name: Neurological manifestations of hypercalcaemia
formal: Central and neuromuscular dysfunction caused by raised serum ionised calcium — most often from primary hyperparathyroidism or malignancy — ranging from fatigue, low mood and cognitive slowing to delirium and coma, with proximal weakness and occasionally PRES or vasoconstriction.
simple: Too much calcium in the blood makes people tired, weak, low in mood and, when severe, confused or drowsy.
ab: stones, bones, groans and psychic moans
th: แคลเซียมในเลือดสูงทำให้อ่อนเพลีย ซึมเศร้า ความคิดช้า กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง และถ้ารุนแรงจะสับสน ซึมจนโคม่า สาเหตุบ่อยคือ hyperparathyroidism และมะเร็ง รักษาด้วยการให้น้ำเกลือ ยากลุ่ม bisphosphonate หรือ denosumab และแก้สาเหตุ

PTH first: high/inappropriately normal suggests parathyroid; suppressed PTH points to PTHrP, vitamin D or bone disease

case.who: 68-year-old retired teacher from Nakhon Si Thammarat with a recent cough and weight loss
case.story: Over two weeks she became withdrawn, constipated and drowsy; her family thought she had depression until she stopped recognising them.
case.exam: Drowsy, disoriented, dry mucosae; mild symmetric proximal weakness; reflexes preserved; no focal signs.
case.tests: Corrected calcium 3.9 mmol/L, creatinine raised, PTH suppressed, PTHrP high; chest CT shows a hilar mass consistent with squamous cell carcinoma; CT brain normal.
case.q: What explains her encephalopathy, and what are the first treatment steps?
case.a: Humoral hypercalcaemia of malignancy; IV saline rehydration, an IV bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid) or denosumab, with calcitonin for rapid early lowering, then cancer-directed care.

det.patho: Extracellular calcium stabilises membranes by raising the threshold for sodium-channel opening, so excess calcium reduces neuronal and muscle excitability, producing slowed cognition, lethargy and weakness. Hypercalcaemia also causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and volume depletion, which worsens renal clearance of calcium and deepens encephalopathy. Severe levels can induce cerebral vasoconstriction, PRES and seizures. Primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy (PTHrP, osteolytic metastases, myeloma, lymphoma with calcitriol excess) account for about 90% of cases; vitamin D toxicity, granulomatous disease, thiazides and lithium are other causes.
det.clinical: Mild hypercalcaemia (below about 3.0 mmol/L) is often asymptomatic or causes vague tiredness, low mood and memory complaints. Moderate to severe levels bring confusion, psychosis, somnolence and eventually coma, together with polyuria, vomiting, constipation, abdominal pain and dehydration. Neuromuscular involvement gives proximal weakness and fatigue; hyperparathyroidism can mimic motor neuron disease with brisk reflexes and wasting, which reverses after surgery. Headache, seizures and transient focal deficits suggest PRES or vasoconstriction.
det.diagnosis: Confirm with ionised or albumin-corrected calcium and repeat if borderline. PTH divides causes: elevated or normal PTH indicates parathyroid-mediated disease (or familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia, separated by urinary calcium excretion), while a suppressed PTH should prompt PTHrP, vitamin D metabolites, myeloma screen and cancer imaging. Look for ECG changes such as shortened QT. Brain imaging is reserved for focal features, seizures or atypical course.
det.treatment: Symptomatic or severe hypercalcaemia (above about 3.5 mmol/L) is an emergency: restore volume with isotonic saline, then give an IV bisphosphonate such as zoledronic acid; denosumab is used in renal impairment or bisphosphonate-refractory disease. Calcitonin lowers calcium within hours but its effect wanes in two days. Glucocorticoids help in calcitriol-driven states (lymphoma, granulomas, vitamin D toxicity), and haemodialysis is reserved for refractory cases with renal failure. Stop thiazides, lithium, calcium and vitamin D supplements, then treat the cause — parathyroidectomy for primary hyperparathyroidism.
det.prognosis: Neurological symptoms usually resolve as calcium normalises; in malignancy, hypercalcaemia often signals advanced disease with limited survival.
pearls: Check calcium in any unexplained delirium, new depression in older adults, or proximal weakness.
PTH is the first branching test: high means parathyroid, suppressed means look for cancer or vitamin D.
Rehydrate first — saline, then bisphosphonate; loop diuretics only after volume is restored.
det.thd: แคลเซียมในเลือดสูงลดความตื่นตัวของเซลล์ประสาทและกล้ามเนื้อ ทำให้อ่อนเพลีย ซึมเศร้า ความคิดช้า กล้ามเนื้อต้นแขนต้นขาอ่อนแรง ถ้าสูงมากจะสับสนจนโคม่า ร่วมกับปัสสาวะมาก ท้องผูก และขาดน้ำ สาเหตุหลักคือ primary hyperparathyroidism และมะเร็ง ตรวจ PTH เป็นขั้นแรกเพื่อแยกสาเหตุ รักษาเร่งด่วนด้วยน้ำเกลือ zoledronic acid หรือ denosumab และแก้ที่ต้นเหตุ
