name: Neurological manifestations of hyponatraemia
formal: Brain dysfunction caused by low serum sodium (below 135 mmol/L) through water entry into brain cells and cerebral oedema, ranging from subtle gait and attention problems in chronic mild cases to seizures, coma and herniation in acute severe cases; overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia risks osmotic demyelination.
simple: Low blood salt makes the brain swell, causing anything from unsteadiness and confusion to fits and coma, and fixing it too fast can damage the brain too.
th: โซเดียมในเลือดต่ำทำให้น้ำเข้าเซลล์สมองจนสมองบวม อาการตั้งแต่เดินเซ สมาธิไม่ดี ไปจนถึงชักและโคม่า ถ้าเป็นเฉียบพลันรุนแรงให้ 3% saline แต่ถ้าเป็นเรื้อรังต้องแก้ช้า ไม่เกิน 8–10 mmol/L ใน 24 ชั่วโมง เพื่อป้องกัน osmotic demyelination
tempoNote: Acute (under 48 h) hyponatraemia causes cerebral oedema and seizures at higher sodium levels; chronic (over 48 h or unknown) is better tolerated but brittle to fast correction
feat: Chronic mild: inattention, slowed thinking, unsteady gait and falls, fractures
Moderate: nausea, headache, confusion, lethargy
Severe/acute: vomiting, seizures, reduced consciousness, respiratory arrest from herniation
Common settings: thiazides, SSRIs, carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine, SIADH after SAH or meningitis, marathon running, ecstasy, low-solute intake
Overcorrection can trigger delayed dysarthria, dysphagia, quadriparesis (osmotic demyelination)
inv: Serum sodium, glucose (pseudohyponatraemia), serum osmolality
Urine osmolality and urine sodium; volume status assessment
TSH and morning cortisol before diagnosing SIADH
Sodium every 2–4 h during correction; CT brain if trauma, focal signs or uncertain cause

case.who: 74-year-old woman from Lampang started on hydrochlorothiazide and sertraline a month ago
case.story: She has had two falls this week, was vomiting this morning and had a generalised seizure in the emergency department.
case.exam: Drowsy after the seizure, GCS 12, euvolaemic, no focal deficit.
case.tests: Sodium 112 mmol/L, glucose normal, serum osmolality low, urine osmolality 450 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 60 mmol/L; TSH and cortisol normal; CT brain normal.
case.q: How should her sodium be raised, and what limit applies over the first 24 hours?
case.a: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia: give a 100–150 mL bolus of 3% saline (repeat up to two to three times) aiming for a 4–6 mmol/L rise to stop seizures, then correct slowly — no more than 8 mmol/L in 24 h given chronicity and high ODS risk; stop the thiazide and SSRI.

det.patho: A fall in plasma tonicity draws water into cells; because the skull limits expansion, brain swelling raises intracranial pressure. Within about 48 hours astrocytes export potassium, chloride and organic osmolytes (glutamate, taurine, myo-inositol) to restore volume, which is why chronic hyponatraemia causes fewer symptoms. That adaptation is slow to reverse, so a rapid rise in sodium dehydrates adapted cells and injures oligodendrocytes, producing osmotic demyelination. Premenopausal women, children and patients with hypoxia have less reserve and suffer brain injury at milder levels.
det.clinical: Symptoms depend on the speed of fall more than the nadir. Acute drops (postoperative hypotonic fluids, exercise, ecstasy, psychogenic polydipsia) can cause seizures and herniation even at 120–125 mmol/L. Chronic mild hyponatraemia, once thought harmless, impairs attention and gait and increases falls, fractures and hospital mortality. In neurological patients, SIADH and cerebral salt wasting after subarachnoid haemorrhage, meningitis or brain injury are common, and antiseizure drugs such as carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine are frequent culprits.
det.diagnosis: Confirm hypotonic hyponatraemia (exclude hyperglycaemia and lab artefact), then use urine osmolality to separate maximal dilution (below 100 mOsm/kg, as in polydipsia or low solute intake) from ADH-driven states. Urine sodium and clinical volume status distinguish hypovolaemic losses, SIADH and oedematous states, though bedside volume assessment is unreliable. Exclude hypothyroidism and glucocorticoid deficiency before calling it SIADH. Classify severity by symptoms, not just by number.
det.treatment: For severe symptoms (seizures, coma, vomiting with confusion), give 3% saline as 100–150 mL boluses or a calculated infusion aiming for a 4–6 mmol/L rise, which is usually enough to reverse herniation risk. Thereafter, limit correction in chronic cases to 8–10 mmol/L per 24 h (8 mmol/L if high ODS risk: sodium ≤ 120, alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalaemia, liver disease). If the rise overshoots, re-lower with desmopressin plus 5% dextrose or use a desmopressin clamp strategy. Treat the cause: fluid restriction, urea or SGLT2 inhibitors for SIADH, isotonic saline for hypovolaemia, stopping offending drugs; vaptans need close monitoring and are avoided in liver disease.
det.prognosis: Most recover fully with careful correction; poor outcomes come from untreated acute cerebral oedema or from osmotic demyelination after overcorrection.
pearls: Acute and symptomatic: treat with hypertonic saline promptly — fear of ODS should not delay it.
Chronic: the first 4–6 mmol/L buys safety; then stay under 8–10 mmol/L per day.
Watch for brisk water diuresis when the cause (thiazide, hypovolaemia, cortisol) is removed — that is how overcorrection happens.
det.thd: Hyponatraemia ทำให้น้ำเข้าเซลล์สมองและสมองบวม ความรุนแรงขึ้นกับความเร็วที่โซเดียมลดลงมากกว่าตัวเลข อาการมีตั้งแต่เดินเซ หกล้มบ่อย สับสน จนถึงชักและโคม่า ถ้ามีอาการรุนแรงให้ 3% saline 100–150 mL เพื่อยกโซเดียมขึ้น 4–6 mmol/L แล้วจำกัดการแก้ไม่เกิน 8–10 mmol/L ใน 24 ชั่วโมง เพราะการแก้เร็วเกินไปทำให้เกิด osmotic demyelination ต้องหาสาเหตุ เช่น SIADH ยา thiazide ยาจิตเวช และขาด cortisol

name: Accidental hypothermia — neurological aspects
formal: Unintentional fall of core body temperature below 35 °C, producing progressive central nervous system depression — from confusion and ataxia to coma with fixed pupils — together with cardiac instability, in which the cold brain tolerates hypoxia unusually well and neurological prognosis cannot be judged until rewarming.
simple: When the body gets too cold, the brain slows down step by step until the person is unconscious, but a cold brain can survive a long time, so doctors rewarm before deciding anything.
ab: not dead until warm and dead
th: ภาวะอุณหภูมิกายต่ำกว่า 35 °C โดยไม่ตั้งใจ ทำให้สมองทำงานช้าลงเป็นลำดับ ตั้งแต่สับสน เดินเซ จนโคม่ารูม่านตาขยายไม่ตอบสนอง แต่สมองที่เย็นทนการขาดออกซิเจนได้นาน ห้ามประเมินว่าเสียชีวิตจนกว่าจะอุ่นร่างกายแล้ว
tempoNote: Develops over hours with cold exposure or immersion; faster in the elderly, intoxicated, hypothyroid or immobile patient
feat: Mild (32–35 °C): shivering, clumsiness, dysarthria, poor judgement, ataxia
Moderate (28–32 °C): shivering stops, drowsiness, paradoxical undressing, hyporeflexia, dilating pupils
Severe (below 28 °C): coma, fixed dilated pupils, absent reflexes, risk of VF/asystole
Look-alike of brain death; must be excluded before brainstem death testing
Triggers: alcohol, sedatives, hypoglycaemia, hypothyroidism, stroke, spinal cord injury, elderly living alone
inv: Core temperature with a low-reading oesophageal, bladder or rectal probe
ECG (Osborn J waves, bradycardia, arrhythmia); potassium, glucose, blood gases
TSH, cortisol, toxicology, CK; CT head if trauma or focal signs
Serum potassium in arrest helps decide whether to continue ECMO rewarming

case.who: 70-year-old man found at dawn in a rice field in Chiang Rai during the cool season after a night of drinking
case.story: Neighbours found him unresponsive and wet; time down is unknown.
case.exam: Rectal temperature 27 °C, GCS 4, pupils 6 mm sluggish, areflexic, slow weak carotid pulse.
case.tests: ECG: sinus bradycardia 34/min with prominent J waves; glucose 3.1 mmol/L; potassium 4.2 mmol/L; ethanol raised; CT head normal.
case.q: Can coma and dilated pupils here be used to predict a poor outcome, and how should he be rewarmed?
case.a: No — severe hypothermia alone can cause this picture; treat glucose, handle gently, and rewarm actively (warm IV fluids, forced-air and, if arrest or instability occurs, ECMO/cardiopulmonary bypass), reassessing neurology only once normothermic.

det.patho: Cooling slows enzymatic reactions and cerebral metabolism by roughly 6–7% per degree, so consciousness fades progressively and electrical activity becomes isoelectric near 20 °C. The same fall in demand protects neurons from ischaemia, explaining intact survival after prolonged cold arrest. Cold depresses myocardial conduction and raises the threshold for ventricular fibrillation risk below about 28 °C. Hypothalamic thermoregulation fails in elderly, intoxicated, septic and endocrine-deficient patients and with lesions of the hypothalamus or high spinal cord.
det.clinical: The Swiss staging grades severity by consciousness and shivering when no thermometer is available: conscious and shivering, impaired without shivering, unconscious, and no vital signs. Early neurological signs include slurred speech, ataxia and confusion, followed by apathy, paradoxical undressing, hyporeflexia, rigidity and pupillary dilatation. Below 28 °C coma with fixed pupils and absent brainstem reflexes can occur in a fully recoverable patient. Rewarming may unmask injuries, intoxication or a primary neurological event such as stroke or haemorrhage.
det.diagnosis: Measure core temperature with a low-reading probe; standard thermometers stop around 34 °C. Search for precipitants: glucose, ethanol and drugs, thyroid and adrenal function, sepsis and trauma. The ECG shows bradycardia, prolonged intervals and Osborn waves. Clinical and EEG criteria for brain death are invalid until core temperature is above 35–36 °C.
det.treatment: Move the patient gently and horizontally to limit arrhythmias, remove wet clothing and insulate. Mild cases rewarm passively; moderate cases need active external rewarming with forced warm air and warmed IV fluids. Hypothermic cardiac arrest or instability warrants transfer for extracorporeal life support (ECMO or bypass), with prolonged CPR; defibrillation and adrenaline are limited below 30 °C. Give thiamine and glucose as indicated, and hydrocortisone or thyroid replacement when deficiency is suspected.
det.prognosis: Outcome depends on the cause and associated asphyxia rather than the depth of cooling; witnessed cold arrest without asphyxia treated with ECMO can yield good neurological survival, whereas avalanche or drowning with prior hypoxia does worse.
pearls: Nobody is dead until warm and dead — no prognostication or brain death testing while hypothermic.
Hypothermia with no shivering means the patient is at least moderately cold.
Always ask why the patient got cold: alcohol, hypoglycaemia, stroke, sepsis, hypothyroidism.
det.thd: Accidental hypothermia คืออุณหภูมิแกนกลางต่ำกว่า 35 °C สมองทำงานช้าลงตามอุณหภูมิ ตั้งแต่พูดไม่ชัด เดินเซ สับสน จนโคม่ารูม่านตาขยาย แต่การเผาผลาญที่ลดลงทำให้สมองทนการขาดเลือดได้ดี จึงห้ามประเมินพยากรณ์หรือวินิจฉัยสมองตายขณะตัวยังเย็น การรักษาคือเคลื่อนย้ายอย่างนุ่มนวล อุ่นร่างกาย และใช้ ECMO ในรายที่หัวใจหยุดเต้น ต้องค้นหาสาเหตุร่วม เช่น สุรา น้ำตาลต่ำ ไทรอยด์ต่ำ หรือติดเชื้อ

name: Calcineurin inhibitor neurotoxicity
formal: Neurological adverse effects of tacrolimus or ciclosporin, ranging from common tremor, headache, paraesthesia and insomnia to serious encephalopathy, seizures, cortical blindness and PRES, and less often akinetic mutism, peripheral neuropathy or painful leg syndrome, typically early after organ or stem-cell transplantation.
simple: Anti-rejection drugs tacrolimus and ciclosporin can cause shaking, headaches and sometimes fits, confusion or brain swelling at the back of the head.
th: ผลข้างเคียงทางระบบประสาทจากยากดภูมิ tacrolimus และ ciclosporin พบบ่อยคือมือสั่น ปวดศีรษะ ชาปลายมือเท้า รายรุนแรงมีชัก สับสน ตามองไม่เห็น และ PRES มักเกิดช่วงแรกหลังปลูกถ่ายอวัยวะ แก้โดยลดหรือเปลี่ยนยาและคุมความดัน
tempoNote: Most serious events occur in the first weeks to months after transplantation or after dose increases and interacting drugs; tremor can persist chronically
feat: Postural/action tremor (very common), headache, insomnia, paraesthesia
Seizures, confusion, visual loss or cortical blindness — often with PRES on MRI
Can occur with drug levels in the target range
Aggravated by hypertension, hypomagnesaemia, hypocholesterolaemia, high-dose steroids, azole antifungals
Rare: akinetic mutism, ataxia, demyelinating neuropathy, calcineurin inhibitor-induced bone/leg pain
inv: Trough tacrolimus or ciclosporin level, magnesium, cholesterol, renal function, blood pressure
MRI brain with FLAIR/DWI: parieto-occipital vasogenic oedema (PRES), exclude infarct or haemorrhage
EEG for non-convulsive seizures if confused
Exclude infection (CSF, PCR for HSV, CMV, JC virus), drug interactions and graft-related metabolic causes

case.who: 29-year-old woman from Udon Thani, three weeks after a living-donor kidney transplant from her brother
case.story: She developed a pounding headache and blurred vision, then had a generalised seizure; her clinic had added fluconazole for oral thrush a week earlier.
case.exam: BP 182/104, post-ictal confusion, reduced visual acuity with normal pupils and fundi, fine postural tremor.
case.tests: Tacrolimus trough markedly above target, magnesium 0.5 mmol/L; MRI bilateral parieto-occipital subcortical FLAIR hyperintensity without diffusion restriction.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and what precipitated it?
case.a: Tacrolimus-associated PRES, precipitated by azole inhibition of CYP3A4 raising levels plus hypertension and hypomagnesaemia; hold or reduce tacrolimus (or switch to belatacept/mTOR inhibitor with the transplant team), control BP, replace magnesium and treat seizures.

det.patho: Tacrolimus and ciclosporin bind immunophilins and block calcineurin, which is also abundant in neurons and vascular endothelium. Toxicity is thought to involve endothelial dysfunction with blood–brain barrier breakdown and vasogenic oedema, sympathetic activation, raised blood pressure and direct neuronal excitability; P-glycoprotein dysfunction allows more drug into the brain. Low cholesterol increases free ciclosporin entry, and hypomagnesaemia (caused by the drugs' renal effect) lowers the seizure threshold. Both drugs are CYP3A4 substrates, so azoles, macrolides, diltiazem and grapefruit raise levels, whereas rifampicin and several enzyme-inducing antiseizure drugs lower them.
det.clinical: Minor toxicity — tremor, headache, paraesthesia, insomnia and anxiety — affects a large share of recipients and is dose-related. Major toxicity occurs in a minority, most often in the first month: seizures, delirium, visual disturbance or cortical blindness, and focal deficits, usually as PRES. Less typical presentations include akinetic mutism, cerebellar syndrome, posterior leukoencephalopathy extending to brainstem or cerebellum, and a demyelinating polyneuropathy resembling CIDP. Allogeneic stem-cell transplant patients with graft-versus-host disease prophylaxis are particularly susceptible.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in any transplant recipient with new neurological symptoms on a CNI, but remember that levels may be normal. MRI is the key test: vasogenic oedema in parieto-occipital regions, sometimes frontal, cerebellar or with haemorrhage, without restricted diffusion in typical cases. Infection is the main alternative in immunosuppressed patients — opportunistic organisms such as Listeria, Cryptococcus, Toxoplasma, CMV, HHV-6 and JC virus — so CSF studies are usually required. Also check magnesium, glucose, sodium, renal and hepatic function, and look for graft rejection or thrombotic microangiopathy.
det.treatment: Reduce or withhold the calcineurin inhibitor in liaison with the transplant team and correct the factors that potentiate it: blood pressure, magnesium, interacting medicines. Switching to another agent — for example from ciclosporin to tacrolimus or vice versa, or to an mTOR inhibitor (sirolimus, everolimus) or belatacept — usually allows recovery while protecting the graft. Seizures are treated with levetiracetam, which has minimal interactions; enzyme-inducing drugs such as phenytoin and carbamazepine lower CNI levels. Tremor can be managed by dose reduction or a once-daily extended-release tacrolimus formulation.
det.prognosis: Most cases, including PRES, recover over days to weeks after adjustment; delays in recognition can leave infarction, haemorrhage or epilepsy.
pearls: Transplant patient with seizure and headache: check BP, magnesium and CNI level, then MRI for PRES.
Normal drug levels do not rule out CNI toxicity.
Use levetiracetam rather than enzyme inducers, and beware azoles and macrolides raising tacrolimus.
det.thd: Calcineurin inhibitor (tacrolimus, ciclosporin) ยับยั้ง calcineurin ทั้งในเม็ดเลือดขาว เซลล์ประสาท และเยื่อบุหลอดเลือด ทำให้เกิดอาการตั้งแต่มือสั่น ปวดศีรษะ ชา จนถึงชัก สับสน ตาบอดจากเปลือกสมอง และ PRES มักเกิดช่วงแรกหลังปลูกถ่าย ระดับยาอาจปกติได้ ปัจจัยเสริม ได้แก่ ความดันสูง magnesium ต่ำ และยาที่ยับยั้ง CYP3A4 เช่น azole การรักษาคือลดหรือเปลี่ยนยาร่วมกับทีมปลูกถ่าย คุมความดัน แก้ magnesium และใช้ levetiracetam ถ้าชัก ต้องแยกการติดเชื้อฉวยโอกาสเสมอ

qx.stem: Three weeks after allogeneic stem cell transplantation, a 38-year-old woman on tacrolimus develops headache, visual blurring and a generalised seizure. BP is 178/102 mmHg and magnesium is low. MRI shows bilateral parieto-occipital vasogenic oedema with no restricted diffusion.
qx.q: Which is the best immediate approach?
opts: Control blood pressure, correct magnesium, treat seizures and reduce or switch the calcineurin inhibitor
Escalate tacrolimus to treat graft-versus-host disease
Lumbar puncture for CNS infection before any other action
Thrombolysis for posterior circulation stroke
Start high-dose methotrexate
qx.why: The picture is posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome due to calcineurin inhibitor toxicity, so triggers are corrected, seizures are treated and the drug is reduced or replaced with an alternative immunosuppressant. Raising the dose would worsen it, and thrombolysis is inappropriate with vasogenic oedema.

name: Methotrexate neurotoxicity
formal: Nervous system injury from methotrexate, especially when given intrathecally or in high intravenous doses, appearing as acute chemical meningitis, a subacute stroke-like encephalopathy with fluctuating focal deficits and restricted diffusion in white matter, or a delayed progressive leukoencephalopathy — the last enhanced by cranial irradiation.
simple: The cancer drug methotrexate, especially when given into the spine or in big doses, can irritate the brain coverings, cause sudden stroke-like weakness or speech loss, or slowly damage the brain's white matter.
th: พิษต่อระบบประสาทจาก methotrexate โดยเฉพาะการฉีดเข้าช่องไขสันหลังหรือให้ขนาดสูง มี 3 แบบ คือ เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบจากสารเคมีเฉียบพลัน อาการคล้ายสโตรกภายในไม่กี่วันถึงสัปดาห์ และ white matter เสื่อมช้า ๆ ระยะยาวโดยเฉพาะเมื่อฉายแสงร่วม
tempoNote: Chemical arachnoiditis within hours of intrathecal dosing; stroke-like encephalopathy typically 2–14 days after high-dose or intrathecal therapy; leukoencephalopathy months to years later
feat: Acute: headache, neck stiffness, fever, vomiting after intrathecal dose (aseptic chemical meningitis)
Subacute stroke-like: alternating or fluctuating hemiparesis, aphasia, dysarthria, seizures; DWI restriction in centrum semiovale not matching an arterial territory
Chronic: progressive cognitive decline, gait disorder, incontinence with confluent white-matter change and calcification
Rare transverse myelopathy after intrathecal therapy
Common in children with ALL; risk higher with cranial radiotherapy, high cumulative dose and impaired clearance
inv: MRI with DWI/ADC: bilateral periventricular/centrum semiovale restricted diffusion in subacute form; FLAIR leukoencephalopathy chronically
Methotrexate level and renal function after high-dose therapy
Plasma homocysteine (raised) and folate

case.who: 12-year-old boy from Surat Thani with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia in consolidation
case.story: Nine days after high-dose IV and intrathecal methotrexate he suddenly could not speak and his right arm went weak; next day the weakness shifted to the left side.
case.exam: Expressive dysphasia, fluctuating right then left hemiparesis, normal consciousness, no meningism.
case.tests: MRI: bilateral centrum semiovale diffusion restriction not respecting vascular territories; MRA and MRV normal; CSF no blasts; homocysteine raised.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and what is the outlook?
case.a: Subacute methotrexate-induced stroke-like syndrome; it usually resolves within days, and dextromethorphan has been used off-label; methotrexate can often be resumed after discussion with the oncology team.

read.where: Chapter 28 Neurologic Complications of Chemotherapy and Radiation Therapy

det.patho: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, depleting reduced folates and S-adenosylmethionine needed for myelin methylation, and raises homocysteine and its excitatory metabolites, which act on NMDA receptors. Adenosine release and direct toxicity to oligodendrocytes and endothelium also contribute. The acute stroke-like syndrome reflects cytotoxic oedema in deep white matter; the chronic form shows demyelination, axonal swelling, necrosis and calcification, particularly where radiotherapy has damaged the blood–brain barrier and increased drug penetration. Delayed clearance from renal impairment or third-space fluid (effusions, ascites) raises exposure.
det.clinical: Intrathecal dosing can produce headache, neck stiffness, fever and vomiting within hours, usually self-limited. The subacute encephalopathy presents about a week or two after treatment with abrupt focal deficits — hemiparesis, aphasia, dysarthria, dysphagia — that may switch sides, plus seizures or altered awareness; it is a recognised acute event during ALL treatment. The delayed leukoencephalopathy evolves over months to years with learning and memory problems, behaviour change, spasticity, ataxia and, at worst, dementia. A rare intrathecal-related myelopathy causes paraparesis and sphincter dysfunction.
det.diagnosis: Relate symptoms to the timing of high-dose or intrathecal therapy. Diffusion-weighted MRI showing bilateral or shifting restricted diffusion in the centrum semiovale outside arterial boundaries supports the subacute syndrome; FLAIR may be initially normal. Exclude arterial stroke, venous sinus thrombosis (especially with asparaginase), CNS leukaemia relapse, infection, PRES and posterior fossa syndromes. Chronic leukoencephalopathy shows confluent periventricular FLAIR change, atrophy and calcification on CT.
det.treatment: Acute chemical meningitis responds to supportive care and analgesia; steroids may be co-administered prophylactically. For high-dose regimens, ensure hydration, urinary alkalinisation, leucovorin rescue and drug-level monitoring, with glucarpidase for toxic levels from delayed clearance. The subacute syndrome usually resolves spontaneously; dextromethorphan (an NMDA antagonist) and aminophylline (adenosine antagonist) have been used with case-series support. Rechallenge is generally possible and is decided with oncology. Chronic leukoencephalopathy has no specific therapy; neurocognitive rehabilitation and educational support are central, and avoiding unnecessary cranial irradiation is the main preventive strategy.
det.prognosis: The acute and subacute forms usually resolve within days with little residual deficit; chronic leukoencephalopathy is generally permanent and may progress.
pearls: Child with ALL plus sudden shifting hemiparesis a week after methotrexate: think stroke-like methotrexate toxicity, get DWI.
Restricted diffusion that ignores vascular territories and reverses quickly is the imaging clue.
Radiation plus methotrexate is the worst combination for late white-matter damage.
det.thd: Methotrexate ยับยั้งเมแทบอลิซึมของ folate ทำให้ homocysteine สูงและทำลาย white matter อาการมี 3 แบบ แบบเฉียบพลันหลังฉีดเข้าช่องไขสันหลังคือปวดศีรษะ คอแข็ง ไข้ แบบกึ่งเฉียบพลันประมาณ 1–2 สัปดาห์หลังให้ยาคือมีอาการคล้ายสโตรก อ่อนแรงสลับข้าง พูดไม่ได้ MRI พบ DWI restriction ใน centrum semiovale และมักหายเองในไม่กี่วัน แบบเรื้อรังคือ leukoencephalopathy ทำให้ความจำและการเรียนรู้แย่ลงถาวร โดยเฉพาะเมื่อฉายแสงที่สมองร่วมด้วย

name: Eclampsia
formal: New-onset generalised seizures (or unexplained coma) in a woman with pre-eclampsia, occurring from the second half of pregnancy to the postpartum weeks, reflecting endothelial dysfunction and failed cerebral autoregulation, usually with PRES on imaging and sometimes with haemorrhage, infarction or reversible vasoconstriction.
simple: Fits in a pregnant or recently delivered woman with high blood pressure from pre-eclampsia; treated with magnesium, blood pressure control and delivery.

feat: Generalised tonic-clonic seizures in pre-eclampsia; hypertension may be modest
Warning symptoms: severe headache, blurred vision, scotomata, cortical blindness, epigastric pain

Foetal monitoring

case.who: 24-year-old primigravida from Nakhon Ratchasima, 8 days after a normal vaginal delivery
case.story: She developed a severe headache over two days with flashing lights, then had a generalised seizure at home. Antenatal BP readings had been borderline.
case.exam: BP 168/110, drowsy, bilateral visual field constriction, brisk reflexes, no papilloedema; urine protein 2+.
case.tests: Platelets 98 × 10⁹/L, ALT mildly raised; MRI bilateral occipital and posterior parietal vasogenic oedema; MRV normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and what is first-line seizure treatment?
case.a: Late postpartum eclampsia with PRES; magnesium sulfate (4–6 g IV loading, then 1–2 g/h for 24 h) plus antihypertensive treatment (labetalol, hydralazine or nifedipine).

det.patho: Abnormal placentation releases anti-angiogenic factors (soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1, soluble endoglin) that cause widespread endothelial dysfunction. In the brain, endothelial injury and abrupt blood-pressure surges exceed autoregulation, especially in the posterior circulation with sparse sympathetic innervation, leading to vasogenic oedema (PRES), and sometimes vasospasm, ischaemia or haemorrhage. Pregnancy also lowers the seizure threshold and raises blood–brain barrier permeability. Eclampsia remains a significant cause of maternal death, particularly where antenatal care is limited.
det.clinical: Seizures are typically generalised and self-limited, though recurrent episodes and status occur. Most women have premonitory headache, visual disturbance, altered mental state or upper abdominal pain; hypertension and proteinuria may be absent at the time of the first fit. A third or more of cases arise intrapartum or postpartum, and late postpartum eclampsia (beyond 48 h) is easily misdiagnosed. Complications include intracerebral haemorrhage — the leading neurological cause of death — cortical blindness, aspiration, pulmonary oedema, HELLP and placental abruption.
det.diagnosis: Seizures in pregnancy after 20 weeks or postpartum with hypertension should be treated as eclampsia until shown otherwise. Neuroimaging is not needed for every typical case but is advised for focal deficits, prolonged coma, seizures despite magnesium, late postpartum onset or atypical features; MRI usually shows PRES. Exclude CVT, RCVS, subarachnoid or intracerebral haemorrhage, TTP, hypoglycaemia, epilepsy, and infection. Laboratory tests define HELLP and organ involvement.
det.treatment: Protect the airway, position on the left side and give magnesium sulfate, which is superior to diazepam or phenytoin for preventing recurrence; monitor reflexes, respiration and urine output, and reverse toxicity with calcium gluconate. Lower severe blood pressure (≥160/110) promptly with IV labetalol, IV hydralazine or oral nifedipine, aiming for gradual control. Stabilise and deliver the baby; delivery is the definitive treatment. Low-dose aspirin from early pregnancy in high-risk women reduces pre-eclampsia, and long-term cardiovascular risk follow-up is recommended.
det.prognosis: Most women recover fully once PRES resolves; mortality and lasting deficits relate mainly to intracranial haemorrhage, and future cardiovascular and stroke risk is increased.
pearls: Magnesium sulfate, not benzodiazepines or phenytoin, is the drug of choice for eclamptic seizures.
Postpartum headache with seizures up to 6 weeks after delivery: think eclampsia, CVT and RCVS.
Hypertension may be mild and proteinuria absent at the first seizure.

name: Neurogenic stunned myocardium
formal: Acute, usually reversible left ventricular dysfunction triggered by a catecholamine surge after sudden brain injury — classically aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, also stroke, seizures, trauma or encephalitis — with ECG changes, modest troponin rise and regional wall-motion abnormality not matching a coronary territory, including the Takotsubo pattern.
simple: A sudden brain injury can flood the heart with stress hormones and temporarily weaken it, mimicking a heart attack even though the coronary arteries are open.
th: ภาวะกล้ามเนื้อหัวใจห้องล่างซ้ายทำงานลดลงชั่วคราวหลังสมองบาดเจ็บเฉียบพลัน เช่น SAH จากหลอดเลือดโป่งพองแตก เพราะมี catecholamine หลั่งมาก พบ ECG ผิดปกติ troponin สูงเล็กน้อย และผนังหัวใจบีบตัวผิดปกติไม่ตรงกับเส้นเลือดหัวใจ มักกลับเป็นปกติในไม่กี่สัปดาห์
tempoNote: Appears within hours to the first two days after the brain insult; wall motion typically recovers over days to weeks
feat: Most typical after high-grade aneurysmal SAH; also ischaemic stroke (insular), ICH, status epilepticus, TBI
ECG: deep T-wave inversion, QT prolongation, ST changes, arrhythmias
Troponin raised but often less than expected for the extent of dysfunction
Echo: hypokinesis not in one coronary territory — basal/mid (reverse Takotsubo) or apical ballooning
Can cause hypotension, pulmonary oedema and worsen cerebral perfusion
inv: 12-lead ECG and continuous monitoring
Serial troponin and BNP/NT-proBNP
Transthoracic echocardiography; repeat to document recovery
Coronary angiography or CT coronary angiography when ischaemic heart disease cannot be excluded and it will change management

case.who: 48-year-old female market vendor from Phitsanulok with sudden worst-ever headache and collapse
case.story: CT shows diffuse thick subarachnoid blood (WFNS grade IV); six hours later she becomes hypotensive and hypoxic.
case.exam: GCS 9, BP 85/50 on noradrenaline, crackles at both lung bases, no murmur.
case.tests: ECG: widespread deep T inversion and QTc 540 ms; troponin moderately raised; echo LVEF 30% with basal and mid hypokinesis and apical sparing; CTA anterior communicating aneurysm.
case.q: What explains the cardiac findings, and does she need emergency coronary angiography before the aneurysm is secured?
case.a: Neurogenic stunned myocardium (reverse Takotsubo pattern) from catecholamine surge; treat supportively and secure the aneurysm — coronary angiography is not routinely needed unless the picture strongly suggests coronary occlusion.

read.where: Chapter 10 Cardiac Manifestations of Acute Neurologic Lesions

det.patho: Sudden brain injury, particularly involving the insula, hypothalamus or raised intracranial pressure, triggers a massive sympathetic discharge with release of noradrenaline from cardiac nerve endings. The local catecholamine excess causes calcium overload, contraction-band necrosis and stunning of myocytes, in a distribution that follows sympathetic nerve density rather than coronary anatomy. The process overlaps with Takotsubo syndrome; the basal (inverted) pattern is relatively more common in SAH. Female sex, poor clinical grade and larger haemorrhages increase risk.
det.clinical: ECG abnormalities appear in most patients with SAH, while echocardiographic dysfunction occurs in a minority — more often in poor-grade cases. Patients may develop hypotension, cardiogenic shock, arrhythmias including torsades de pointes, and pulmonary oedema, which together compromise cerebral perfusion and increase delayed cerebral ischaemia. Chest pain is rarely reported because consciousness is impaired. Dysfunction generally resolves within days to a few weeks.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is made by recognising an acute brain injury followed by ECG change, moderate troponin elevation and regional wall-motion abnormality extending beyond a single coronary distribution, and then demonstrating recovery. Echocardiography should be performed in poor-grade SAH or whenever haemodynamic instability, arrhythmia or raised troponin occurs. Coronary angiography is reserved for those who have risk factors and a pattern compatible with coronary occlusion, and must be weighed against antiplatelet/anticoagulant requirements before aneurysm securing.
det.treatment: Management is supportive: treat hypotension with inotropes such as dobutamine or milrinone where appropriate (vasopressors increase afterload), diuretics for pulmonary oedema, and correction of potassium and magnesium to protect against QT-related arrhythmias. Avoid QT-prolonging drugs. Secure the aneurysm promptly, and maintain euvolaemia and cerebral perfusion during the vasospasm window. Beta-blockade is considered once haemodynamically stable, and repeat echocardiography documents recovery.
det.prognosis: Cardiac function usually normalises within weeks; however, its presence predicts higher rates of delayed cerebral ischaemia, poor neurological outcome and death after SAH.
pearls: Deep T-wave inversion and troponin rise after SAH is usually the brain talking, not the coronaries.
Wall-motion loss that crosses coronary territories and recovers in weeks suggests neurogenic stunning.
Keep potassium and magnesium normal and watch QTc — torsades is the dangerous rhythm.
det.thd: Neurogenic stunned myocardium เกิดหลังสมองบาดเจ็บเฉียบพลัน โดยเฉพาะ SAH จากหลอดเลือดโป่งพองแตก ระบบซิมพาเทติกหลั่ง catecholamine จำนวนมากทำให้กล้ามเนื้อหัวใจบีบตัวลดลงชั่วคราว พบ T wave กลับหัวลึก QT ยาว troponin สูงปานกลาง และ echo พบผนังหัวใจบีบตัวผิดปกติที่ไม่ตรงกับเส้นเลือดหัวใจเส้นเดียว ทำให้ความดันต่ำและปอดบวมน้ำ ซึ่งทำให้สมองขาดเลือดเพิ่ม รักษาแบบประคับประคองด้วย inotrope แก้เกลือแร่ และรีบปิดหลอดเลือดโป่งพอง หัวใจมักกลับเป็นปกติในไม่กี่สัปดาห์

name: Neurogenic pulmonary oedema
formal: Acute protein-rich pulmonary oedema developing within minutes to hours of a severe central nervous system insult — such as subarachnoid haemorrhage, traumatic brain injury, intracerebral haemorrhage or prolonged seizures — produced by a sympathetic surge that raises pulmonary vascular pressure and damages the capillary barrier, in the absence of primary heart or lung disease.
simple: Fluid suddenly floods the lungs after a major brain injury because the brain's stress signals overload the lung blood vessels.
th: ภาวะน้ำท่วมปอดเฉียบพลันที่เกิดภายในนาทีถึงชั่วโมงหลังสมองบาดเจ็บรุนแรง เช่น SAH บาดเจ็บศีรษะ หรือชักต่อเนื่อง เกิดจากระบบซิมพาเทติกกระตุ้นจนความดันในหลอดเลือดปอดสูงและผนังหลอดเลือดรั่ว มักหายใน 2–3 วันถ้าดูแลแบบประคับประคองได้ดี

Bilateral infiltrates on chest imaging without evidence of primary cardiac failure or aspiration
Triggers: SAH, severe TBI, ICH, status epilepticus, raised ICP, brainstem lesions
Can coexist with neurogenic stunned myocardium, blurring the cardiogenic/non-cardiogenic distinction
Hypoxaemia worsens secondary brain injury

Arterial blood gas; PaO2/FiO2 ratio

Exclude aspiration and pneumonia (sputum, clinical course)

case.who: 19-year-old male university student from Bangkok with known epilepsy, missed medications
case.story: Brought in after three generalised seizures without recovery between them; after the third he became breathless and coughed frothy pink sputum.
case.exam: SpO2 82% on room air, RR 34, bilateral crackles, BP 150/90, no cardiac murmur; post-ictal GCS 10.
case.tests: Chest X-ray: bilateral perihilar alveolar shadowing; echo normal LV function; BNP mildly raised; ABG PaO2/FiO2 160.
case.q: What caused the pulmonary infiltrates, and how should this be managed?
case.a: Neurogenic (post-ictal) pulmonary oedema; stop the seizures, give oxygen with CPAP or ventilation with PEEP as needed, avoid fluid overload, and expect resolution within 2–3 days.

det.patho: Sudden rises in intracranial pressure or injury to hypothalamic and medullary vasomotor centres (including the area postrema and nucleus tractus solitarius) unleash a massive alpha-adrenergic discharge. Systemic and pulmonary vasoconstriction displace blood into the low-resistance pulmonary circulation and abruptly raise capillary pressure, while catecholamines and inflammatory mediators make the endothelium leaky — the 'blast' hypothesis combining hydrostatic and permeability components. The result is a protein-rich oedema that can persist after pressures normalise. Concurrent myocardial stunning adds a cardiogenic element.
det.clinical: Breathlessness, tachypnoea, hypoxaemia and pink frothy secretions arise soon after the cerebral event, often in an unconscious patient where it is first noticed as falling saturation or rising ventilator pressures. It is seen in a meaningful minority of poor-grade SAH, severe TBI and status epilepticus, and is reported in sudden unexpected death in epilepsy. Most cases resolve in a few days, but severe hypoxaemia contributes to secondary brain injury and mortality.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires a recent CNS insult, bilateral infiltrates and hypoxaemia, with exclusion of aspiration pneumonia, ventilator-associated pneumonia, transfusion-related lung injury, fluid overload and primary cardiac failure. Echocardiography separates cardiogenic contribution from stunned myocardium; normal LV function supports a predominantly neurogenic mechanism. Rapid onset and rapid resolution favour NPE over aspiration, which is often unilateral and slower to clear.
det.treatment: Treat the brain insult first: control seizures, reduce intracranial pressure, secure aneurysms. Provide oxygen, non-invasive ventilation or intubation with lung-protective ventilation and PEEP, titrating PEEP to avoid compromising cerebral venous return and intracranial pressure. Aim for euvolaemia, using cautious diuresis rather than fluid restriction where SAH vasospasm is a concern. Alpha-blockade, dobutamine or other agents are used case by case; there is no specific evidence-based drug.
det.prognosis: NPE is usually self-limited over 48–72 hours, but its presence is associated with more severe brain injury and higher mortality.
pearls: Frothy pink sputum soon after a seizure or SAH with a normal heart is neurogenic pulmonary oedema until proven otherwise.
Rapid onset and rapid clearance distinguish NPE from aspiration.
Ventilate with PEEP but watch ICP; avoid dehydrating a patient at risk of vasospasm.

name: CLIPPERS (chronic lymphocytic inflammation with pontine perivascular enhancement responsive to steroids)
formal: A rare, steroid-dependent inflammatory disorder of the hindbrain defined by subacute brainstem and cerebellar signs with punctate and curvilinear gadolinium-enhancing lesions centred on the pons, perivascular T-cell-predominant infiltrates, and a diagnosis reached only after mimics such as lymphoma, sarcoidosis and antibody-mediated diseases are excluded.
simple: An uncommon inflammation of the brainstem that shows tiny bright 'pepper' spots on MRI, causes unsteadiness and double vision, and gets better with steroids but tends to return when they are stopped.

th: โรคอักเสบเรื้อรังของก้านสมองบริเวณ pons ที่ MRI เห็นจุดและเส้นเล็ก ๆ ติด gadolinium กระจายเหมือนโรยพริกไทย ตอบสนองดีต่อ steroid แต่มักกลับเป็นซ้ำเมื่อลดยา ต้องแยกจาก lymphoma, sarcoidosis, GFAP และ MOG ก่อนเสมอ

CSF cell count, protein, oligoclonal bands, cytology and flow cytometry; serum and CSF AQP4-IgG, MOG-IgG and GFAP-IgG
Systemic screen for sarcoidosis and lymphoma: chest CT, serum ACE/soluble IL-2 receptor, whole-body FDG-PET, LDH
Brain biopsy (ideally before steroids) when features are atypical: large or ring lesions, mass effect, poor or incomplete steroid response

case.story: Over five weeks she developed a lurching walk, slurred speech and double vision when looking to either side. She had no fever, weight loss or visual blurring.
case.exam: Gaze-evoked nystagmus, bilateral limb and gait ataxia, scanning dysarthria, brisk reflexes; no papilloedema.
case.tests: MRI: dozens of tiny dot-like and linear enhancing lesions scattered through the pons and middle cerebellar peduncles without mass effect. CSF: 8 cells, mildly raised protein; cytology, flow cytometry, AQP4, MOG and GFAP antibodies negative; chest CT and FDG-PET unremarkable.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis, and what must be planned when steroids are tapered?
case.a: CLIPPERS after a careful exclusion work-up; she needs a slow taper with a steroid-sparing agent and close MRI follow-up, with biopsy if the response is incomplete or new atypical lesions appear.

read.where: Section III Other Inflammatory CNS Disorders and Neuroimmunologic Mimics

det.patho: First described in 2010, CLIPPERS is thought to be a T-cell-driven perivascular inflammation of the hindbrain; biopsies show CD3-positive (mainly CD4) T cells with some B cells and macrophages clustered around small vessels, spilling into the parenchyma, without vasculitis, granulomas or demyelination as the dominant change. No antibody target has been found, and many authors now regard it as a syndrome — a radiological and clinical pattern shared by several processes — rather than a single disease. Its predilection for the pons is unexplained.
det.clinical: Adults of any age, typically middle-aged, present with subacute ataxia, dysarthria, diplopia, facial paraesthesia or vertigo; spinal cord or cognitive involvement occurs in some. Symptoms resolve quickly with steroids, which supports the diagnosis but does not prove it, because lymphoma, sarcoidosis and other inflammatory disorders also improve. Relapses typically follow steroid reduction below a threshold dose. Red flags that argue for an alternative diagnosis include fever, B symptoms, lesions larger than a few millimetres, mass effect, ring enhancement, marked restricted diffusion, and steroid resistance.
det.diagnosis: Proposed criteria (Tobin et al., 2017) require a characteristic hindbrain clinical syndrome, homogeneous punctate or curvilinear enhancement predominantly in the pons, prompt steroid responsiveness, and the absence of a better explanation; supportive histology is perivascular T-cell infiltration without lymphoma, granuloma or vasculitis. Current practice emphasises a broad exclusion work-up: CSF studies including cytology and flow cytometry, AQP4-, MOG- and GFAP-IgG, sarcoidosis and lymphoma screening with chest CT and FDG-PET, and testing for infection (tuberculosis, syphilis, Whipple disease) and histiocytosis. CLIPPERS-like imaging has been reported in lymphoma (including after years of apparent CLIPPERS), GFAP astrocytopathy, MOGAD, neurosarcoidosis, neuro-Behçet and Erdheim–Chester disease. Biopsy is recommended whenever any atypical feature is present, ideally before steroids are given.
det.treatment: Acute treatment is high-dose IV methylprednisolone, commonly 1 g per day over 3–5 days, then a slow oral prednisolone taper lasting months. Because relapse is common once daily prednisolone falls below roughly 20–30 mg, methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate is usually added early to spare steroids; rituximab or other agents are used for refractory disease. Continue bone protection, glucose and infection monitoring during long steroid courses. Any relapse while on adequate immunotherapy, or atypical new lesions, should prompt re-evaluation for lymphoma rather than simple escalation.
det.prognosis: With sustained immunotherapy most patients remain stable or improve, but repeated relapses can leave permanent ataxia and brainstem atrophy; a minority are later reclassified, most importantly as CNS lymphoma.
pearls: Peppered pons + dramatic steroid response = think CLIPPERS, but treat the label as provisional.
Steroids can make lymphoma vanish on MRI and in biopsy — sample first when the picture is atypical.
Plan a steroid-sparing drug from the start; tapering steroids alone usually ends in relapse.
det.thd: CLIPPERS เป็นภาวะอักเสบเรื้อรังรอบหลอดเลือดเล็กใน pons และสมองน้อยจาก T cell ผู้ป่วยมีเดินเซ พูดไม่ชัด เห็นภาพซ้อนแบบค่อยเป็นค่อยไป MRI เห็นจุดและเส้นเล็ก ๆ ติดสีกระจายทั่ว pons ไม่มี mass effect ไม่มี biomarker จำเพาะ จึงต้องตัด lymphoma, neurosarcoidosis, GFAP astrocytopathy, MOGAD และการติดเชื้อออกก่อน ถ้าลักษณะไม่ตรงแบบควรตัดชิ้นเนื้อก่อนให้ steroid รักษาด้วย methylprednisolone ขนาดสูงแล้วลดช้า ๆ ร่วมกับยากดภูมิที่ช่วยลด steroid เช่น methotrexate หรือ azathioprine

name: Colloid cyst of the third ventricle
formal: A benign, mucin-filled, epithelium-lined cyst arising at the roof of the anterior third ventricle near the foramina of Monro, which can intermittently or suddenly block CSF outflow from both lateral ventricles and cause positional headache, acute obstructive hydrocephalus and sudden death.
simple: A small, harmless-looking jelly-filled bubble in the middle of the brain that can suddenly plug the fluid drain, causing severe headache, collapse or even death.
ab: headache attributed to colloid cyst of the third ventricle
neuroepithelial cyst of the third ventricle
th: ถุงน้ำเมือกชนิดไม่ร้ายที่หลังคาของ third ventricle ใกล้ foramen of Monro อาจอุดทางเดินน้ำไขสันหลังเป็นพัก ๆ หรือทันที ทำให้ปวดศีรษะรุนแรงฉับพลัน หมดสติ หรือเสียชีวิตเฉียบพลันได้
tempoNote: Often silent for years; symptomatic patients have brief attacks of sudden headache lasting minutes to hours, and a single obstruction can progress to coma within hours
feat: Abrupt, severe, often thunderclap-like headache, sometimes brought on or relieved by changing head position
Attacks with nausea, vomiting, blurred vision, drop attacks, leg weakness or brief loss of consciousness
Between attacks the examination may be normal; papilloedema and short-term memory problems with chronic obstruction
Imaging: round lesion at the foramen of Monro, often hyperdense on CT, with dilated lateral ventricles and a normal-sized fourth ventricle
Small risk of sudden deterioration and death, even in previously stable patients
inv: Urgent non-contrast CT in an acute attack: hyperdense anterior third ventricle mass and lateral ventriculomegaly
MRI with FLAIR and contrast to define size, signal (variable T1/T2 by viscosity) and hydrocephalus; avoid lumbar puncture
Neurosurgical assessment of size, symptoms and ventricle size to decide on surveillance versus resection

case.who: 29-year-old male construction foreman from Udon Thani
case.story: For months he has had sudden pounding headaches when bending to lift cement bags, easing when he lies back. Today, after one such headache, his legs gave way and he collapsed for a minute.
case.exam: Drowsy but rousable, bilateral early papilloedema, no focal limb signs.
case.tests: CT: 12 mm hyperdense round lesion at the foramen of Monro with dilated lateral ventricles; third ventricle posterior part and fourth ventricle normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and what should not be done next?
case.a: Colloid cyst of the third ventricle with acute obstructive hydrocephalus; avoid lumbar puncture and arrange emergency neurosurgery (external ventricular drain and/or cyst removal).

read.where: ICHD-3 7.4.1.1 Headache attributed to colloid cyst of the third ventricle

det.patho: Colloid cysts are developmental, probably endodermal, lesions with a single layer of ciliated or mucin-secreting cells and a thick gelatinous content. Sitting on the anterior roof of the third ventricle, they can act like a ball valve over both foramina of Monro, so CSF backs up into the lateral ventricles while the rest of the ventricular system stays small. Sudden complete obstruction raises intracranial pressure abruptly and can compress the hypothalamus, which may explain rapid collapse and cardiac arrhythmia. They make up around 1% of intracranial tumours and present mostly between 20 and 50 years.
det.clinical: Many are incidental findings on scans done for other reasons. Symptomatic patients describe short, intense headaches that start suddenly, are sometimes triggered or relieved by posture, and may be accompanied by vomiting, dimming of vision, leg weakness or fainting; chronic obstruction gives a raised-pressure headache with papilloedema and memory impairment from fornix stretching. Warning signs of high risk are cyst size above about 1 cm, hydrocephalus, FLAIR hyperintensity, symptoms and young age. ICHD-3 (2018), as in the beta, keeps a dedicated category (7.4.1.1) for headache in which the cyst is shown, the headache relates in time to it, and it settles after treatment; it describes recurrent thunderclap-type attacks, often with impaired consciousness.
det.diagnosis: CT is usually sufficient in the emergency department: a well-defined hyperdense round lesion at the foramen of Monro with asymmetric or symmetric lateral ventricle dilatation. MRI characterises the cyst, whose signal varies with protein content, and excludes look-alikes such as subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, central neurocytoma, cysticercus cyst, choroid plexus papilloma or a basilar tip aneurysm. Lumbar puncture is contraindicated when obstructive hydrocephalus is present. Because sudden death can occur, a positional or thunderclap headache with ventriculomegaly should never be labelled primary headache without imaging review.
det.treatment: Acute deterioration with hydrocephalus needs emergency neurosurgical decompression, usually an external ventricular drain followed by definitive cyst resection. Symptomatic cysts, or those with hydrocephalus, are removed electively, either endoscopically (less invasive, slightly higher recurrence) or microsurgically via a transcallosal or transcortical approach (more complete removal); shunting alone is a secondary option. Small asymptomatic cysts without ventricular enlargement can be followed with serial MRI, and patients should be taught to seek urgent care for sudden severe headache. Headache attributed to the cyst usually stops after successful treatment.
det.prognosis: Outcome after timely resection is generally excellent; the main dangers are delayed recognition, with a small but real risk of sudden death, and postoperative memory problems from fornix injury.
pearls: Positional thunderclap headache + big lateral ventricles + small fourth ventricle = look at the foramen of Monro.
Hyperdense dot at the top of the third ventricle on CT is easy to miss — always check it in a headache CT.
Do not perform lumbar puncture in obstructive hydrocephalus.
det.thd: Colloid cyst เป็นถุงน้ำเมือกชนิดไม่ร้ายที่อยู่ด้านหน้าของ third ventricle ตรงตำแหน่ง foramen of Monro เมื่อถุงน้ำไปอุดทางเดิน CSF จะทำให้ lateral ventricle ทั้งสองข้างโตเฉียบพลัน ผู้ป่วยปวดศีรษะรุนแรงทันทีที่อาจสัมพันธ์กับท่าทาง อาเจียน ขาอ่อนแรงทรุดลง หรือหมดสติ และอาจเสียชีวิตเฉียบพลัน CT มักเห็นก้อนกลมเนื้อทึบสูงร่วมกับโพรงสมองโต ห้ามเจาะหลัง รักษาโดยการใส่ท่อระบายและผ่าตัดเอาถุงน้ำออก ถุงน้ำขนาดเล็กที่ไม่มีอาการติดตามด้วย MRI ได้ (ICHD-3 7.4.1.1)

qx.stem: A 34-year-old man was woken by a sudden severe headache that eased when he lay down, and he recalls a brief episode of leg weakness without losing consciousness. Non-contrast CT shows a 1.4 cm round hyperdense nodule at the anterosuperior third ventricle at the foramen of Monro, with mild enlargement of both lateral ventricles.
qx.q: What is the most important consideration?
opts: It is a calcified granuloma and needs no follow-up
It is a cavernous malformation; start anticoagulation
It can obstruct both foramina of Monro suddenly, so urgent neurosurgical review for endoscopic removal is warranted
Treat with lumbar puncture for presumed idiopathic intracranial hypertension
Order PET-CT to find the primary tumour
qx.why: A round hyperdense lesion at the foramen of Monro with hydrocephalus is a colloid cyst, which can act as a ball valve and cause positional headaches, drop attacks and sudden death. Symptomatic lesions with ventriculomegaly merit endoscopic resection. Lumbar puncture is hazardous with obstructive hydrocephalus.

name: Headache attributed to epileptic seizure (ictal epileptic headache and post-ictal headache)
formal: Headache caused by an epileptic seizure, either during it — ictal epileptic headache, formerly hemicrania epileptica, where headache is the seizure manifestation and coincides with EEG ictal activity — or, far more commonly, after it — post-ictal headache, starting within hours of the seizure and resolving within about 72 hours.
simple: A headache that comes from a seizure — rarely the headache is the seizure itself, but much more often it is the pounding headache people get in the hours after a fit.
th: ปวดศีรษะที่เกิดจากการชัก แบ่งเป็นชนิดที่ปวดระหว่างชัก (ictal epileptic headache หรือ hemicrania epileptica) ซึ่งพบน้อยมากและ EEG มีคลื่นชักขณะปวด กับชนิดหลังชัก (post-ictal headache) ซึ่งพบบ่อยมาก เริ่มภายในไม่กี่ชั่วโมงหลังชักและหายภายใน 3 วัน
tempoNote: Ictal: lasts as long as the seizure discharge (minutes, sometimes longer in non-convulsive status) and stops when it ends; post-ictal: begins within 3 hours of the seizure and resolves within 72 hours
feat: Post-ictal headache follows up to half of tonic–clonic and many focal seizures; often bilateral, throbbing, migraine-like, with nausea and photophobia
Ictal epileptic headache: headache that starts with the electrographic seizure, frequently on the side of the discharge, and ends abruptly when it is stopped
Pain can be the sole ictal feature or can precede motor, sensory or dyscognitive signs; rapid response to IV antiseizure medication supports it
More common in occipital and temporal lobe epilepsy and in people who also have migraine
Migraine aura triggering a seizure (migralepsy) is debated and is no longer a formal ICHD-3 diagnosis
inv: EEG during the headache is essential for ictal epileptic headache — ideally video-EEG capturing ictal discharge that coincides with pain
MRI brain to exclude structural epilepsy or a secondary headache cause (haemorrhage, tumour, venous thrombosis)
In new seizure plus severe headache, CT/CTA or MR venography first to rule out SAH, CVT or RCVS before attributing pain to the seizure

case.who: 21-year-old female university student from Chiang Mai with known right occipital lobe epilepsy
case.story: She came with a three-hour right-sided throbbing headache unlike her usual migraine, with flickering coloured circles in the left visual field that would not settle. Earlier she had been missing doses during exams.
case.exam: Alert, oriented; intermittent left homonymous visual disturbance; no papilloedema or meningism.
case.tests: MRI normal apart from known small right occipital cortical dysplasia; urgent EEG showed continuous right occipital rhythmic spike activity. After IV levetiracetam the discharge stopped and the headache vanished within minutes.
case.q: What headache type is this, and what is the key diagnostic evidence?
case.a: Ictal epileptic headache (focal non-convulsive seizure); headache tied in time to an EEG ictal discharge and stopping as soon as the seizure is aborted.

read.where: ICHD-3 7.6 Headache attributed to epileptic seizure
Chapter 50: Headache attributed to non-vascular intracranial disorder

det.patho: Post-ictal headache probably reflects trigeminovascular activation and cortical spreading depolarisation after a seizure, together with post-ictal hypoperfusion and neurotransmitter release, which explains its migraine-like features. Ictal epileptic headache implies that the seizure discharge itself activates pain pathways, perhaps via cortical areas linked to trigeminal nociception or meningeal vessels. Shared genetics and cortical hyperexcitability underlie the two-way link between migraine and epilepsy, each roughly doubling the risk of the other.
det.clinical: Post-ictal headache is common, under-reported and can be more disabling than the seizure; it is usually generalised, moderate to severe, and lasts hours, and is particularly frequent in occipital lobe epilepsy and after convulsions. Ictal epileptic headache is rare and is suspected when pain, commonly ipsilateral to the epileptic focus, coincides with or announces a seizure, especially with focal visual phenomena or altered responsiveness. ICHD-3 (2018) renamed the beta's 'hemicrania epileptica' to ictal epileptic headache, accepting that it need not be strictly one-sided, and kept post-ictal headache under 7.6. The proposed condition of migraine aura-triggered seizure is retained only in the appendix because evidence is limited.
det.diagnosis: In ICHD-3 terms, ictal epileptic headache requires headache that develops at the same time as the seizure, typically ipsilateral to an ictal discharge, and stops promptly once the seizure ends spontaneously or with treatment; proof needs EEG recorded during the pain. Post-ictal headache is diagnosed when headache begins within three hours of a partial or generalised seizure and remits within three days. Exclude secondary causes, especially when a first seizure and headache occur together: SAH, CVT, RCVS, PRES, infection and tumour. Visual aura with coloured circular images lasting a few minutes and stereotyped repeated events points to occipital seizures rather than migraine.
det.treatment: Ictal epileptic headache is treated as a seizure: acute IV benzodiazepine or levetiracetam/valproate for prolonged events, then optimised maintenance antiseizure therapy; analgesics are ineffective while the discharge continues. Post-ictal headache responds to simple analgesics or NSAIDs taken early, and patients with migraine-like post-ictal pain may benefit from a triptan if there is no contraindication. Improving seizure control is the most effective prevention. For people with both epilepsy and migraine, valproate (outside women of childbearing potential) and topiramate cover both conditions.
det.prognosis: Both forms are benign in themselves and fall away as seizure control improves; misdiagnosis of ictal headache as migraine delays seizure treatment.
pearls: A headache that stops the moment IV antiseizure medication is given is a seizure until proven otherwise.
Ask epilepsy patients about post-ictal headache — it is common and treatable.
Hemicrania epileptica is now called ictal epileptic headache (ICHD-3 7.6.1); post-ictal headache is 7.6.2.
det.thd: ปวดศีรษะที่เกิดจากการชักมี 2 แบบ แบบระหว่างชัก (ictal epileptic headache เดิมเรียก hemicrania epileptica) พบน้อย ปวดพร้อมกับคลื่นชักใน EEG มักอยู่ข้างเดียวกับจุดชัก และหายทันทีเมื่อหยุดชัก ต้องใช้ EEG ขณะปวดเพื่อยืนยัน ส่วนแบบหลังชัก (post-ictal headache) พบบ่อย เริ่มภายใน 3 ชั่วโมงหลังชัก ลักษณะคล้ายไมเกรนและหายภายใน 72 ชั่วโมง รักษาด้วยยาแก้ปวดหรือ NSAID และควบคุมการชักให้ดี ก่อนสรุปต้องตัดเลือดออกใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมองหรือหลอดเลือดดำสมองอุดตันออกเสมอ

name: Acute angle-closure glaucoma (headache mimic)
formal: An ophthalmic emergency in which the peripheral iris suddenly blocks the drainage angle of the anterior chamber, causing a rapid rise in intraocular pressure with severe periocular or hemicranial headache, nausea and vomiting, a red eye, corneal oedema with haloes, a fixed mid-dilated pupil and risk of permanent visual loss within hours.
simple: A sudden blockage of the eye's drainage system that makes eye pressure shoot up, causing a severe one-sided headache with vomiting, a red painful eye and blurred vision — it can blind the eye if it is not treated quickly.
ab: headache attributed to acute angle-closure glaucoma
th: ภาวะฉุกเฉินทางตาที่มุมระบายน้ำในช่องหน้าม่านตาปิดทันที ความดันลูกตาสูงมาก ปวดตาและปวดศีรษะข้างเดียวรุนแรง คลื่นไส้อาเจียน ตาแดง เห็นแสงเป็นวงรุ้ง รูม่านตาขยายครึ่งหนึ่งและไม่ตอบสนองต่อแสง มักถูกวินิจฉัยผิดเป็นไมเกรนหรือเลือดออกในสมอง
tempoNote: Attack develops over minutes to hours, often in dim light or after dilating or anticholinergic drugs; brief self-resolving (intermittent/subacute) attacks may precede it
feat: Severe unilateral pain around the eye, brow or forehead, often spreading to the hemicranium, with nausea and vomiting
Red eye with ciliary flush, steamy (hazy) cornea, haloes around lights and blurred vision
Fixed mid-dilated oval pupil and a stony-hard globe to palpation; shallow anterior chamber
Triggers: darkness, pharmacological mydriasis, anticholinergics, antihistamines, tricyclics, topiramate (bilateral drug-induced angle closure)
Risk: older age, female sex, hyperopia, East and South-East Asian ancestry, previous episodes
inv: Measure intraocular pressure immediately (often above 40–50 mmHg)
Slit-lamp examination and gonioscopy (both eyes; the fellow eye is usually narrow) by ophthalmology
Neuroimaging only if eye findings are absent or atypical — CT does not exclude angle closure

case.who: 63-year-old woman from Nakhon Si Thammarat who wears reading glasses for long-sightedness
case.story: Two hours after watching a soap opera in a dark room she developed a crushing right forehead headache, vomited repeatedly and saw coloured rings around the lamp. The emergency team suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage.
case.exam: Right eye red with hazy cornea, pupil 5 mm oval and unreactive, acuity counting fingers; eye feels hard compared with the left. GCS 15, no meningism or limb signs.
case.tests: Non-contrast CT brain normal. Intraocular pressure right 58 mmHg, left 16 mmHg; shallow anterior chambers both eyes.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and what is the immediate management?
case.a: Acute primary angle-closure glaucoma mimicking a neurological headache; urgent pressure lowering with topical beta-blocker, alpha-agonist and pilocarpine plus systemic acetazolamide (and mannitol if needed), then laser iridotomy to both eyes.

read.where: ICHD-3 11.3.1 Headache attributed to acute angle-closure glaucoma
Chapter 13: Acute headache in the emergency department
Case 38: "When I watch television, I lose my sight"

det.patho: Primary angle closure occurs in eyes with a crowded anterior segment — short axial length, a large or forward-placed lens and a narrow angle. Relative pupillary block, worst when the pupil is mid-dilated, pushes the peripheral iris forward so that aqueous outflow through the trabecular meshwork is suddenly cut off and pressure climbs steeply. The pain arises from ocular and trigeminal (ophthalmic division) nociceptors, so it is felt across the brow and head. Secondary angle closure follows drugs (topiramate and sulfonamides causing ciliary body swelling, anticholinergics, adrenergic agents), lens swelling or retinal vein occlusion; angle-closure glaucoma is notably common in Asian populations including Thailand.
det.clinical: The classic attack is abrupt, painful and unilateral, with nausea and vomiting that can dominate the picture and send patients to medical or neurological services. Eye redness, haloes, blurred vision and a mid-dilated unreactive pupil are the giveaways, yet they may be overlooked if the eye is not examined. Intermittent attacks, sometimes at night or in dim settings and relieved by sleep or bright light, may present as recurrent headache with transient blurring before a full crisis. ICHD-3 code 11.3.1 covers headache caused by this condition, which develops alongside the rise in pressure and settles as the glaucoma is treated; the 2018 version kept this category from the beta.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical and confirmed by an elevated intraocular pressure with a closed angle on gonioscopy; check the fellow eye, which is usually predisposed. Any patient with acute headache plus a red eye, reduced vision or an abnormal pupil should have the pressure measured before a neurological label is applied. Distinguish it from a compressive third nerve palsy (ptosis and eye-movement deficit, white eye), carotid–cavernous fistula, uveitis and cluster headache. Neuroimaging is normal and should not delay ophthalmic assessment.
det.treatment: This is an emergency requiring same-day ophthalmology: lower pressure with topical timolol, apraclonidine or brimonidine and, once pressure begins to fall, pilocarpine; give systemic acetazolamide and, for very high pressure, IV mannitol or oral glycerol (with care in diabetes and renal impairment), and treat pain and vomiting. Definitive treatment is laser peripheral iridotomy in the affected eye and prophylactically in the fellow eye, or lens extraction in many cases. Drug-induced bilateral angle closure from topiramate is managed by stopping the drug and using cycloplegics and aqueous suppressants, and miotics are avoided because the mechanism differs. Avoid anticholinergic and mydriatic drugs in known narrow-angle eyes until treated.
det.prognosis: Prompt pressure reduction and iridotomy usually preserve vision; delayed treatment beyond several hours to days risks permanent optic nerve damage and chronic glaucoma.
pearls: Headache + vomiting + red eye + mid-dilated fixed pupil: measure the eye pressure, do not stop at a normal CT.
Topiramate can cause bilateral angle closure within the first weeks — relevant when it is prescribed for migraine.
Treat both eyes: the fellow eye has a high risk of a future attack.
det.thd: ต้อหินมุมปิดเฉียบพลันเกิดเมื่อม่านตาส่วนรอบนอกอุดมุมระบายน้ำในตา ความดันลูกตาสูงขึ้นมากอย่างรวดเร็ว ผู้ป่วยปวดตาและปวดศีรษะข้างเดียวรุนแรง คลื่นไส้อาเจียน ตาแดง กระจกตาขุ่น เห็นวงรุ้งรอบแสงไฟ รูม่านตาขยายครึ่งหนึ่งไม่ตอบสนองต่อแสง จึงมักถูกคิดว่าเป็นไมเกรนหรือเลือดออกในสมอง ตัวกระตุ้นได้แก่ที่มืด ยาขยายม่านตา ยา anticholinergic และ topiramate การวินิจฉัยคือวัดความดันลูกตา รักษาฉุกเฉินด้วยยาหยอดลดความดันตา acetazolamide และ mannitol แล้วทำ laser iridotomy ทั้งสองตา

name: Second impact syndrome (SIS)
formal: A rare, often fatal or devastating complication in which a second, sometimes minor, head impact sustained before recovery from a first concussion is followed within minutes by loss of cerebral vascular autoregulation and rapid, diffuse brain swelling, typically in adolescents and young adults in contact sport.
simple: When a young athlete who still has symptoms from one concussion takes another knock to the head, the brain can swell very quickly and dangerously — sometimes causing death — which is why no one should return to play until fully recovered.
ab: malignant brain oedema after repeat concussion
diffuse cerebral swelling after minor head injury
th: ภาวะสมองบวมอย่างรวดเร็วและรุนแรงที่เกิดเมื่อได้รับการกระแทกศีรษะครั้งที่สองก่อนหายจากการกระทบกระเทือนสมองครั้งแรก พบในวัยรุ่นและคนหนุ่มสาวที่เล่นกีฬาปะทะ อาจเสียชีวิตหรือพิการรุนแรง ป้องกันได้ด้วยการห้ามกลับไปเล่นจนกว่าอาการหายสนิท
tempoNote: Collapse within seconds to a few minutes of the second impact, which may occur days to weeks after an initial concussion that was still symptomatic
feat: Adolescent or young adult athlete (football, rugby, boxing, Muay Thai, combat sports) still symptomatic from a recent concussion
Second blow may look trivial; the player is briefly dazed, then collapses with rapidly declining consciousness
Fixed dilated pupils, loss of eye movements and respiratory failure from brain herniation within minutes
CT: diffuse or hemispheric brain swelling, effaced cisterns, often with only a thin subdural haematoma
Very high mortality and severe disability in survivors
inv: Emergency CT brain: diffuse swelling disproportionate to any haematoma, midline shift and basal cistern effacement
ICP monitoring in neurocritical care; MRI later for diffuse axonal injury and infarcts
Careful history of the first concussion and symptom status at the time of the second impact

case.who: 16-year-old male school football player from Khon Kaen
case.story: Four days after a head clash in a match he still had headache and poor concentration but did not tell his coach. In training he headed a hard ball, stood for a few seconds looking stunned, then fell to the ground unresponsive.
case.exam: GCS 5 within minutes, bilateral dilated poorly reactive pupils, irregular breathing.
case.tests: CT: marked swelling of the left hemisphere with a thin left subdural haematoma, 9 mm midline shift and effaced basal cisterns.
case.q: What syndrome is suspected, and how could it have been prevented?
case.a: Second impact syndrome; prevention depends on removing any concussed player from play and allowing return only through a graded protocol after full symptom resolution and medical clearance.

det.patho: The proposed mechanism is that the brain, still in the metabolic and vascular vulnerability that follows concussion, loses autoregulation after a second blow, producing sudden vascular engorgement, a steep rise in intracranial pressure and herniation. Many reported cases have a thin acute subdural haematoma with hemispheric swelling far out of proportion to it, suggesting a dysregulated hyperaemic response rather than mass effect from blood. Young age seems to increase susceptibility; some researchers argue that diffuse cerebral swelling can follow even a single impact, so whether a prior concussion is required remains debated.
det.clinical: Typically an adolescent player who has not recovered from a recent concussion — often unreported — takes another hit, which may be small or to the body with head acceleration. The player may stay on their feet for a moment, appear dazed, then collapses within a few minutes with rapid coma, dilated pupils and respiratory failure. The interval between the two impacts ranges from hours to a few weeks. Survivors often have severe cognitive, motor and behavioural sequelae.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical and radiological: documented recent concussion with ongoing symptoms, a second head impact, then catastrophic deterioration with CT showing diffuse or unilateral swelling, frequently with a small subdural collection. Exclude a large extradural or subdural haematoma requiring evacuation, cervical artery dissection and cardiac causes of collapse on the field. The rarity of confirmed cases and incomplete histories make true incidence uncertain.
det.treatment: Management is emergency neurotrauma care: airway and ventilation, avoidance of hypoxia and hypotension, rapid CT, osmotic therapy, ICP-directed neurocritical care and early neurosurgical review for decompressive craniectomy or evacuation of any haematoma. Because treatment often fails, prevention is the cornerstone: any athlete with suspected concussion is removed from play the same day and returns only through a stepwise return-to-learn and return-to-sport protocol (current international consensus, Amsterdam 2022/2023) after symptoms resolve and medical clearance is given. Coaches, parents and players should be educated, and youth athletes need a more conservative timeline.
det.prognosis: Mortality is reported in roughly half of cases and nearly all survivors have lasting disability, though published numbers come from small case series.
pearls: 'If in doubt, sit them out' — the only reliable treatment for second impact syndrome is prevention.
A thin subdural with massive hemispheric swelling in a young athlete should prompt questions about a recent concussion.
Never allow same-day return to play after a suspected concussion, especially in children and adolescents.
det.thd: Second impact syndrome คือภาวะสมองบวมฉับพลันรุนแรงเมื่อสมองที่ยังไม่หายจากการกระทบกระเทือน (concussion) ครั้งแรกถูกกระแทกซ้ำ เชื่อว่าเกิดจากการเสียการควบคุมการไหลเวียนเลือดในสมอง ทำให้ความดันในกะโหลกสูงและสมองเคลื่อนภายในไม่กี่นาที พบในวัยรุ่นที่เล่นฟุตบอล รักบี้ มวยไทย หรือกีฬาปะทะ ผู้ป่วยอาจยืนงงชั่วครู่แล้วล้มหมดสติ CT เห็นสมองบวมมากเกินสัดส่วนกับเลือดใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมองที่บาง อัตราตายและพิการสูงมาก การรักษาเป็นแบบ neurocritical care แต่หัวใจสำคัญคือป้องกัน โดยให้นักกีฬาที่สงสัย concussion หยุดเล่นทันที และกลับมาเล่นตามขั้นตอนเมื่ออาการหายสนิทแล้วเท่านั้น

ddx.pt: Transient symptoms without deterioration of consciousness; CT normal or only minor findings
Lucid interval of minutes to hours with a large biconvex haematoma causing the mass effect, not diffuse swelling
Persistent headache, dizziness and cognitive or mood complaints for weeks to months after concussion without acute collapse

name: Hyperviscosity syndrome (HVS)
formal: A clinical syndrome in which markedly thickened blood, usually from a monoclonal IgM (or less often IgA/IgG) paraprotein or extreme leucocytosis or erythrocytosis, slows microcirculatory flow and produces mucosal bleeding, visual loss and diffuse or multifocal brain dysfunction.
simple: The blood becomes so thick, usually from too much abnormal antibody protein, that it flows sluggishly through tiny vessels and starves the eyes and brain of oxygen.
th: ภาวะเลือดหนืดมากจาก paraprotein (มักเป็น IgM ใน Waldenström) หรือเม็ดเลือดขาว/แดงสูงมาก ทำให้เลือดไหลช้าในหลอดเลือดฝอย เกิดเลือดออกตามเยื่อบุ ตามัว ปวดศีรษะ เวียนศีรษะ สับสนจนถึงโคม่า รักษาเร่งด่วนด้วย plasmapheresis
tempoNote: Builds over days to weeks as paraprotein rises; may tip into acute confusion, stroke or coma after transfusion or dehydration
feat: Classic triad: oozing from gums or nose, blurred vision, and neurological complaints
Headache, dizziness, vertigo, hearing loss, unsteady gait, drowsiness progressing to stupor
Fundi: dilated sausage-link retinal veins, flame haemorrhages, sometimes papilloedema
Usually serum viscosity above about 4–5 cP; strokes and venous thrombosis can occur
Leukostasis variant in acute leukaemia with very high blast counts: hypoxia plus confusion
inv: Serum viscosity, serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and quantitative IgM/IgA/IgG
Full blood count with film (rouleaux, blast count, haematocrit), creatinine, calcium
Dilated fundoscopy; MRI brain with DWI and venography if focal signs or headache
Bone marrow examination (MYD88 L265P for Waldenström) once stabilised

case.who: 68-year-old retired rice farmer from Suphan Buri
case.story: Three weeks of tiredness, nosebleeds and blurred vision, then two days of slurred speech and sleepiness; a clinic had given him a red-cell transfusion for anaemia the day before.
case.exam: Drowsy but rousable, mild ataxia, no lateralising weakness; fundi with dilated tortuous veins and scattered retinal haemorrhages.
case.tests: Hb 8 g/dL with marked rouleaux; total protein very high; IgM paraprotein 5.8 g/dL; serum viscosity 6 cP; MRI no infarct.
case.q: What is the emergency treatment, and why was the transfusion harmful?
case.a: Urgent plasmapheresis to lower IgM, followed by Waldenström-directed therapy; transfusion raised whole-blood viscosity further and should be deferred until after plasma exchange.

read.where: Chapter 25 Neurologic Manifestations of Hematologic Disorders — hyperviscosity and plasma cell dyscrasias
Chapter 13: Neurological complications of white blood cell disorders
Section 6 Systemic Disorders That Also Involve the Cerebrovascular System

det.patho: Viscosity rises steeply once a large pentameric IgM, or polymerising IgA or IgG3, accumulates in plasma; cellular causes include acute leukaemia with high blast counts, polycythaemia and sickle crises. Sluggish flow in capillaries and venules causes tissue hypoxia, venous engorgement and fragile vessels that bleed. Paraproteins also coat platelets and impair their function, which adds to bleeding. Waldenström macroglobulinaemia accounts for most paraprotein cases; myeloma causes it less often.
det.clinical: Symptoms usually emerge when viscosity passes about four times that of water, though the threshold varies between patients. Neurological features range from headache, vertigo, tinnitus and diplopia to confusion, seizures, stroke and coma; the old term coma paraproteinaemicum refers to the extreme end. Visual blurring with venous engorgement on fundoscopy is the best bedside clue. Heart failure can follow plasma volume expansion. In leukostasis, pulmonary infiltrates and hypoxia accompany the cerebral picture.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it whenever a patient with known or possible paraproteinaemia, or a very high white or red count, presents with bleeding, visual change and encephalopathy. Measure serum viscosity directly and look in the fundi; total protein much higher than albumin is a hint on routine chemistry. Immunofixation identifies the paraprotein class. Image the brain to exclude haemorrhage, infarction, venous thrombosis and leptomeningeal infiltration (Bing-Neel syndrome). Remember that pseudohyponatraemia may appear when protein is very high.
det.treatment: Symptomatic hyperviscosity is a haematological emergency: plasmapheresis quickly lowers IgM and relieves symptoms, and one or two exchanges are often enough to start. Avoid red-cell transfusion and diuretics until viscosity has been reduced, and correct dehydration. Definitive control in Waldenström usually uses rituximab-based regimens (with bendamustine) or BTK inhibitors such as zanubrutinib; plasma exchange should precede rituximab because of the IgM flare. Leukostasis is managed with cytoreduction (hydroxyurea, induction chemotherapy) and leukapheresis in selected cases; polycythaemia with venesection.
det.prognosis: Neurological and visual symptoms usually reverse promptly after plasma exchange if retinal or cerebral infarction has not occurred; long-term outlook depends on the underlying cancer.
pearls: Bleeding, blurred vision and confusion in an elderly person with very high total protein should prompt fundoscopy and a serum viscosity.
Do not transfuse red cells before plasmapheresis in hyperviscosity; it can precipitate coma.
Check for IgM flare when rituximab is started in Waldenström; exchange plasma first if IgM is high.
det.thd: Hyperviscosity syndrome เกิดเมื่อเลือดหนืดมาก ส่วนใหญ่จาก IgM paraprotein ใน Waldenström macroglobulinaemia หรือเม็ดเลือดขาวสูงมากใน acute leukaemia อาการเด่นคือเลือดกำเดา/เหงือกออก ตามัว และอาการทางสมอง เช่น ปวดศีรษะ เวียนศีรษะ ซึม จนถึงโคม่า ตรวจตาพบหลอดเลือดดำในจอตาโป่งพองคล้ายไส้กรอก ยืนยันด้วย serum viscosity และ immunofixation รักษาเร่งด่วนด้วย plasmapheresis และหลีกเลี่ยงการให้เลือดก่อนลดความหนืด
