name: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with cerebral thrombosis (HIT)
formal: An immune prothrombotic reaction in which IgG antibodies against platelet factor 4–heparin complexes activate platelets, causing platelet count to fall 5–10 days following heparin exposure together with venous or arterial thrombosis, including cerebral venous sinus thrombosis and ischaemic stroke; vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia (VITT) is a related anti-PF4 disorder triggered by adenoviral-vector vaccines without heparin.
simple: A dangerous reaction to the blood thinner heparin in which the platelets drop but, paradoxically, clots form, sometimes in the veins or arteries of the brain.
th: ภาวะภูมิคุ้มกันต่อ PF4-heparin ทำให้เกล็ดเลือดต่ำแต่กลับเกิดลิ่มเลือดทั้งหลอดเลือดดำและแดง รวมถึง cerebral venous thrombosis และ stroke มักเกิดวันที่ 5–10 หลังได้ heparin ต้องหยุด heparin ทุกชนิดทันทีและเปลี่ยนเป็นยาต้านการแข็งตัวที่ไม่ใช่ heparin ส่วน VITT เป็นกลไกคล้ายกันหลังวัคซีนชนิด adenoviral vector
tempoNote: Platelet fall typically 5–10 days after starting heparin (within 24 h if heparin was given in the past 100 days); thrombosis can appear abruptly, even after heparin is stopped
feat: Platelet count falls by more than half from baseline, usually to a moderate nadir (20–100 × 10^9/L), rather than to very low levels
New thrombosis despite or because of heparin: DVT/PE, limb arterial occlusion, CVT, ischaemic stroke
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis with haemorrhagic venous infarcts and headache, seizures or focal deficits
Skin necrosis at heparin injection sites or acute systemic reaction after an IV heparin bolus
Bleeding is uncommon despite thrombocytopenia
inv: 4Ts score to estimate pre-test probability before ordering antibody tests
Anti-PF4/heparin immunoassay (ELISA or rapid assay), confirmed with a functional assay (serotonin release or heparin-induced platelet activation)
CT/MR venography and CTA/MRA when headache, seizure or focal signs arise; Doppler ultrasound for limbs
D-dimer and fibrinogen; for VITT, anti-PF4 ELISA (rapid tests are often falsely negative)

case.who: 58-year-old woman from Nonthaburi, day 7 after knee replacement
case.story: She was on prophylactic enoxaparin; on day 7 she developed a severe headache, then a focal seizure of the left arm. Platelets had fallen from 260 to 85 × 10^9/L.
case.exam: Drowsy, mild left hemiparesis, bilateral papilloedema; right calf swollen.
case.tests: CT small right parietal haemorrhagic infarct; CT venography thrombosis of the superior sagittal sinus and a cortical vein; Doppler calf DVT; 4Ts score 7; anti-PF4/heparin ELISA strongly positive.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and how should anticoagulation be changed?
case.a: HIT with cerebral venous sinus thrombosis; stop all heparin (including flushes) and start a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban or fondaparinux, or a DOAC once stable, despite the small haemorrhage; avoid platelet transfusion and do not start warfarin until platelets recover.

Chapter 11 Stroke as a Complication of General Medical Disorders
Chapter 12: Neurological complications of platelet disorders and disorders of coagulation
Chapter 21: Cerebral Venous Thrombosis Due to Vaccine-Induced Thrombotic Thrombocytopenia

det.patho: Heparin binds platelet factor 4 and forms large complexes that expose new epitopes; some patients make IgG against them. The immune complexes engage platelet FcγIIa receptors, triggering platelet activation, thrombin generation and consumption of platelets. Unfractionated heparin, surgical (especially cardiac and orthopaedic) settings and female sex carry higher risk; low-molecular-weight heparin causes it less often. In VITT and spontaneous HIT, anti-PF4 antibodies arise without heparin, and VITT has a striking predilection for cerebral and splanchnic veins.
det.clinical: The key is timing: a platelet fall between days 5 and 10 of heparin, or a rapid fall if heparin was used recently. Thrombosis develops in about half of patients if untreated, venous more often than arterial. Neurological events include CVT with venous haemorrhage, arterial stroke, and occasionally transient global amnesia-like or encephalopathic episodes after IV bolus. VITT presented 4–30 days after ChAdOx1 or Ad26 vaccines with CVT, very low fibrinogen, high D-dimer and thrombocytopenia, often with intracerebral haemorrhage.
det.diagnosis: Calculate the 4Ts score; a low score effectively excludes HIT and avoids unnecessary testing. With intermediate or high probability, stop heparin while sending an anti-PF4/heparin immunoassay; strong positivity plus a positive functional assay confirms it. Image the brain and venous sinuses when neurological symptoms appear, and screen limbs for silent DVT. Exclude sepsis, DIC, drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia and TTP.
det.treatment: Stop every source of heparin and begin a therapeutic non-heparin anticoagulant: argatroban or bivalirudin when renal function is poor or a procedure is likely, fondaparinux, or a DOAC (rivaroxaban, apixaban) in stable patients; this applies even to CVT with small haemorrhagic infarcts. Avoid prophylactic platelet transfusion. Start warfarin only after platelets have recovered, overlapping with a parenteral agent, and reverse warfarin with vitamin K if it was already given. High-dose IVIG (1 g/kg daily for 2 days) blocks antibody-mediated platelet activation and is used in severe or refractory cases and in VITT. Anticoagulate for at least 3 months after thrombosis and record heparin allergy prominently.
det.prognosis: Untreated HIT with thrombosis carries substantial limb loss and mortality; prompt switch to a non-heparin agent has greatly improved outcomes, though cerebral events remain the most dangerous.
pearls: A platelet fall on day 5–10 of heparin with any new clot is HIT until proved otherwise.
Thrombocytopenia in HIT is a reason to anticoagulate, not to transfuse platelets.
In CVT always check the platelet count; low platelets suggest HIT, VITT, APS or a myeloproliferative cause.
det.thd: HIT เกิดจากแอนติบอดีต่อ PF4-heparin กระตุ้นเกล็ดเลือด ทำให้เกล็ดเลือดลดลงมากกว่าครึ่งในวันที่ 5–10 หลังได้ heparin พร้อมกับเกิดลิ่มเลือด เช่น DVT, CVT หรือ stroke ประเมินด้วย 4Ts score และยืนยันด้วย anti-PF4 ELISA ร่วมกับ functional assay การรักษาคือหยุด heparin ทุกชนิดทันทีและให้ argatroban, fondaparinux หรือ DOAC ห้ามให้เกล็ดเลือดป้องกัน VITT หลังวัคซีน adenoviral vector มีกลไกคล้ายกันและมักเกิด CVT

qx.stem: Seven days after coronary bypass surgery, a 66-year-old man on unfractionated heparin develops a headache and seizure. Platelets have fallen from 240 to 70 x10^9/L, and MR venography shows superior sagittal sinus thrombosis. The 4T score is high.
qx.q: Which anticoagulant strategy is most appropriate?
opts: Continue heparin and add warfarin
Stop all heparin including flushes and use a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban, bivalirudin or fondaparinux
Switch to low-molecular-weight heparin
Stop anticoagulation entirely because platelets are low
Start warfarin alone at once
qx.why: HIT is a prothrombotic state caused by anti-PF4 antibodies, so all heparin must stop and an alternative anticoagulant given while the thrombosis is treated. LMWH cross-reacts, warfarin alone can precipitate venous limb gangrene before platelet recovery, and withholding anticoagulation leaves the thrombosis untreated.

name: Cardiac myxoma and stroke
formal: Embolic ischaemic stroke, and less often cerebral aneurysm formation, caused by fragments of tumour or overlying thrombus from a cardiac myxoma, a benign primary heart tumour that most often arises from the interatrial septum in the left atrium.
simple: A non-cancerous jelly-like tumour inside the heart sheds pieces that travel to the brain and block arteries, causing strokes.
th: เนื้องอกหัวใจชนิดไม่ร้ายที่พบบ่อยที่สุด มักอยู่ใน left atrium ชิ้นเนื้องอกหรือลิ่มเลือดหลุดไปอุดหลอดเลือดสมองทำให้ stroke ในคนอายุน้อย อาจมีไข้ น้ำหนักลด ESR สูง วินิจฉัยด้วย echocardiography และรักษาด้วยการผ่าตัดเอาออก
tempoNote: Sudden embolic events, often recurrent before the tumour is found; constitutional symptoms may smoulder for months; aneurysms can form months to years after embolisation
feat: Stroke or TIA in a young or middle-aged adult without vascular risk factors, often in several territories
Positional breathlessness, syncope or a diastolic tumour plop from mitral orifice obstruction
Fever, weight loss, arthralgia, anaemia and high ESR/CRP from tumour IL-6 production
Peripheral or retinal emboli; late fusiform or saccular distal aneurysms from tumour invasion of the vessel wall
Familial or recurrent myxomas with spotty pigmentation and endocrine tumours suggest Carney complex
inv: Transthoracic echocardiography, followed by TOE to define attachment and exclude other masses
Cardiac MRI or CT to characterise the mass when echo is equivocal
MRI DWI for multi-territory infarcts; CTA or catheter angiography for distal aneurysms
Histology of the excised tumour (and embolectomy material, if retrieved) confirms myxoma

case.who: 39-year-old female office worker from Khon Kaen
case.story: Sudden right-hand clumsiness and word-finding trouble; she had had low-grade fevers, joint aches and episodes of breathlessness when lying on her left side for four months.
case.exam: Mild expressive aphasia and right hand weakness; sinus rhythm; soft early diastolic sound at the apex.
case.tests: MRI: small acute infarcts in left MCA and right PCA territories; ESR 78; TTE: a 4 cm mobile mass attached to the interatrial septum prolapsing into the mitral valve.
case.q: What is the cause of her strokes and what is the definitive treatment?
case.a: Left atrial myxoma with tumour embolism; urgent surgical excision with a margin of septum, since anticoagulation does not prevent tumour emboli.

det.patho: Myxomas are benign neoplasms of multipotent mesenchymal cells, about three-quarters in the left atrium on a stalk near the fossa ovalis. Their friable, gelatinous surface sheds tumour fragments and acquires thrombus, both of which embolise. Tumour cells that lodge in distal arteries can invade the wall, producing late aneurysms and occasionally metastatic growth. Most are sporadic in middle-aged women; Carney complex (PRKAR1A) causes multiple, recurrent tumours at younger ages.
det.clinical: Presentation follows three themes: obstruction of the mitral orifice, embolism and constitutional inflammation. Embolism occurs in roughly a third of patients and favours the brain, often producing multiple cortical infarcts, retinal artery occlusion or limb ischaemia. Systemic features can mimic vasculitis or endocarditis. Neurological red flags in a young patient are repeated strokes in different territories, an inflammatory blood picture and positional cardiac symptoms.
det.diagnosis: Echocardiography is diagnostic in most patients; TOE improves detail of attachment and excludes a second mass. Differentiate from thrombus (usually in the appendage, associated with AF or mitral stenosis), papillary fibroelastoma (small valvular frond) and malignant tumours using MRI tissue characteristics. Brain imaging should look for infarcts of different ages and for aneurysms, which may enlarge after surgery. Pathology from resected tissue or retrieved embolus confirms the diagnosis.
det.treatment: Acute stroke is managed with standard pathways; mechanical thrombectomy can retrieve myxomatous emboli, whereas IV thrombolysis has uncertain benefit and is used case by case. Surgical resection should be done promptly because further embolism is common while waiting; timing after a large infarct balances haemorrhagic risk during bypass. Anticoagulation does not prevent tumour embolism and is not a substitute. Follow-up echocardiography detects recurrence, and patients with Carney complex need family screening and lifelong surveillance. Myxomatous aneurysms are monitored with imaging; few require treatment.
det.prognosis: After complete excision recurrence is low in sporadic cases; neurological outcome depends on the burden of prior emboli.
pearls: A young adult with multi-territory strokes, fever and high ESR needs echocardiography for endocarditis and myxoma.
Myxoma emboli are tumour, so anticoagulation will not stop them; surgery does.
Late intracranial aneurysms after myxoma embolism warrant vascular imaging even years after resection.
det.thd: Cardiac myxoma เป็นเนื้องอกหัวใจชนิดไม่ร้ายที่พบบ่อยที่สุด มักติดที่ผนังกั้นห้องบนซ้าย ชิ้นเนื้องอกหรือลิ่มเลือดหลุดไปอุดหลอดเลือดสมองได้หลายตำแหน่ง ผู้ป่วยมักอายุน้อย มีไข้ ปวดข้อ น้ำหนักลด ESR สูง และหอบเหนื่อยตามท่า วินิจฉัยด้วย TTE/TOE รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัดเอาเนื้องอกออกโดยเร็ว เพราะยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือดป้องกันชิ้นเนื้องอกหลุดไม่ได้

name: Cancer-associated ischaemic stroke
formal: Ischaemic stroke in a patient with active malignancy that is caused by cancer-related mechanisms—most often a hypercoagulable state with embolism (Trousseau syndrome, frequently via NBTE), and also tumour compression or invasion of vessels, treatment toxicity or infection—typically producing multiple small infarcts across several arterial territories.
simple: Strokes that happen because a cancer makes the blood clot too easily, so many small clots travel to different parts of the brain.
th: Stroke ในผู้ป่วยมะเร็งที่เกิดจากกลไกของมะเร็งเอง ที่พบบ่อยคือภาวะเลือดแข็งตัวง่าย (Trousseau) ทำให้ลิ่มเลือดเล็ก ๆ หลุดไปหลายเขตหลอดเลือด MRI พบ infarct กระจายสามเขตขึ้นไป D-dimer สูงมาก มักเป็นมะเร็งชนิด adenocarcinoma เช่น ปอด ตับอ่อน กระเพาะ
tempoNote: Sudden deficits, often recurrent within weeks; may be the first sign of an undiagnosed cancer or appear during chemotherapy or progression
feat: Multiple small acute infarcts in three or more arterial territories, often bilateral and in both circulations
Very high D-dimer (often several times the upper limit) with or without low fibrinogen or platelets
Adenocarcinoma (lung, pancreas, gastric, ovarian, cholangiocarcinoma) most often; may be stage IV or occult
Concurrent DVT/PE, migratory superficial thrombophlebitis or other arterial emboli
Few conventional vascular risk factors and no large-artery or AF explanation
inv: MRI DWI pattern; D-dimer, fibrinogen, platelets and peripheral film for DIC
TOE for NBTE vegetations (TTE often misses them); cardiac rhythm monitoring
Cancer search when unknown: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, tumour markers (CA 19-9, CA-125, CEA), consider PET-CT
Lower-limb Doppler and bubble study if paradoxical embolism is possible

case.story: Two weeks after a minor left-hand weakness that recovered, she developed sudden difficulty naming objects and right visual field loss. She had lost 6 kg over three months.
case.exam: Anomic aphasia, right homonymous hemianopia, mild left hand weakness; sinus rhythm; swollen left calf.
case.tests: MRI multiple small acute infarcts in both MCA territories and the left PCA territory; D-dimer 18 µg/mL FEU; TOE small mitral vegetations, cultures negative; CT chest shows a lung mass with liver lesions (adenocarcinoma, EGFR-mutant).
case.q: What is the stroke mechanism and how should secondary prevention be chosen?
case.a: Cancer-associated hypercoagulability with NBTE (Trousseau syndrome); anticoagulation (low-molecular-weight heparin preferred, DOAC an option in selected cases) plus prompt oncological treatment, since antiplatelets alone do not control the process.

det.patho: Tumours release tissue factor, cancer procoagulant, mucins and extracellular vesicles, and they activate neutrophils to form extracellular traps; together these generate thrombin and platelet activation. Sterile fibrin–platelet vegetations on heart valves (NBTE) and in-situ microthrombi embolise to the brain. Other mechanisms in cancer include conventional atherosclerosis or AF, tumour embolism, compression or invasion of arteries (head and neck tumours, meningeal disease), radiation vasculopathy, chemotherapy-related thrombosis (cisplatin, VEGF inhibitors, L-asparaginase) and septic emboli.
det.clinical: Up to about one in ten stroke patients have cancer, and in some the stroke uncovers it. Cryptogenic embolic strokes in active cancer tend to be multiple, small, bilateral and to recur early despite antiplatelet therapy. Encephalopathy may dominate when lesions are numerous. Systemic clues include weight loss, venous thromboembolism, migratory thrombophlebitis and abnormal coagulation tests. Stroke recurrence and death rates are high, closely tracking cancer activity.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it with the three-territory DWI pattern, very high D-dimer and no conventional cause. TOE is the key cardiac test; TTE is insensitive for small vegetations. When no cancer is known, a focused search (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, markers, then PET-CT) is reasonable in patients with this pattern and raised D-dimer. Exclude infective endocarditis with repeated blood cultures, and consider APS, TTP and DIC. Falling D-dimer on treatment supports the mechanism.
det.treatment: Acute reperfusion therapy follows usual eligibility; thrombolysis and thrombectomy are not contraindicated by cancer itself, but brain metastases, recent surgery or coagulopathy may change the decision. For hypercoagulable or NBTE-related strokes, parenteral anticoagulation with low-molecular-weight heparin is preferred; DOACs (apixaban, edoxaban) are used in selected patients by extrapolation from cancer-associated VTE, with attention to gastrointestinal and genitourinary bleeding risk. When a conventional mechanism such as atherosclerosis is responsible, standard antiplatelet and statin therapy apply. Effective oncological treatment is part of secondary prevention, and goals of care should be discussed early.
det.prognosis: Median survival after a hypercoagulable cancer stroke is often only months, reflecting advanced disease; outcome is better when the cancer is treatable.
pearls: Small infarcts in three territories plus a very high D-dimer suggest occult cancer; ask about weight loss and check the chest and abdomen.
TOE, not TTE, is the test to find NBTE vegetations.
Antiplatelet therapy alone rarely stops Trousseau-type recurrences; anticoagulation and cancer control are needed.
det.thd: Stroke ที่สัมพันธ์กับมะเร็งเกิดได้หลายกลไก ที่สำคัญคือภาวะเลือดแข็งตัวง่ายจากมะเร็ง (Trousseau syndrome) ซึ่งมักทำให้เกิด NBTE และลิ่มเลือดหลุดไปหลายเขตหลอดเลือด ลักษณะเด่นคือ MRI พบ infarct เล็ก ๆ หลายเขต ร่วมกับ D-dimer สูงมาก ควรทำ TOE และค้นหามะเร็งที่ซ่อนอยู่ การป้องกันซ้ำใช้ LMWH หรือ DOAC ในรายที่เหมาะสม ร่วมกับรักษามะเร็ง

Stroke-like multifocal lesions from tumour cells filling small vessels; skin biopsy, high LDH, no D-dimer surge

name: Relapsing polychondritis (neurological involvement)
formal: A rare immune-mediated disease with recurrent inflammation of cartilage (ears, nose, larynx–trachea, joints) and of proteoglycan-rich tissues, whose nervous system involvement includes cranial neuropathies, audiovestibular loss, aseptic meningitis or meningoencephalitis, CNS vasculitis and stroke.
simple: An autoimmune disease that repeatedly inflames the cartilage of the ears and nose and can also inflame the nerves, inner ear, brain coverings or brain itself.
th: โรคภูมิคุ้มกันที่ทำให้กระดูกอ่อนอักเสบซ้ำ ๆ เช่น ใบหูแดงบวมแต่ติ่งหูไม่เป็น จมูกยุบ หลอดลมตีบ อาการทางระบบประสาทได้แก่เส้นประสาทสมองอักเสบ หูหนวก เวียนศีรษะ เยื่อหุ้มสมองหรือสมองอักเสบ และหลอดเลือดสมองอักเสบ รักษาด้วย steroid และยากดภูมิ
tempoNote: Relapsing flares over weeks with cumulative damage; neurological complications may appear at any point, sometimes before the cartilage signs are recognised
feat: Painful red swollen ear that spares the lobule; later floppy ear, saddle nose, hoarseness or stridor
Sudden sensorineural hearing loss and vertigo, which may mimic posterior circulation stroke
Cranial neuropathies (facial, optic, abducens, trigeminal) and ocular inflammation (episcleritis, scleritis, uveitis)
Aseptic meningitis or limbic/diffuse meningoencephalitis with confusion, seizures and CSF lymphocytosis
Stroke or encephalopathy from CNS vasculitis; overlap with ANCA vasculitis or myelodysplasia
inv: ESR/CRP, ANCA, full blood count (macrocytosis and cytopenias in men raise VEXAS: UBA1 testing)
MRI brain with contrast: meningeal or dural enhancement, patchy cortical-subcortical T2/FLAIR lesions
CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein, sometimes oligoclonal bands; exclude infection
Audiometry; CT airway or PET-CT showing cartilage uptake; ear cartilage biopsy if needed

case.story: Two episodes of a hot, painful red left ear treated as cellulitis, then a week of fever, headache and increasing confusion; he also noticed hearing loss in the right ear.
case.exam: Disoriented; both ears thickened with sparing of the lobules; saddle-nose deformity; red eye with scleritis; right sensorineural deafness.
case.tests: ESR 102; CSF 60 lymphocytes, protein 1.1 g/L, normal glucose, cultures and PCR negative; MRI patchy bilateral temporal FLAIR hyperintensities with leptomeningeal enhancement; MCV 108 with thrombocytopenia.
case.q: Which systemic diagnosis unifies these findings, and which genetic test is worth sending?
case.a: Relapsing polychondritis with meningoencephalitis; treat with high-dose steroids plus an immunosuppressant, and test UBA1 because macrocytosis and cytopenia in a middle-aged man suggest VEXAS syndrome.

det.patho: Autoimmunity targets matrix components of cartilage (type II, IX and XI collagen, matrilin-1) and similar proteoglycan-rich structures in the eye, inner ear, heart valves and vessels. Neurological damage arises mainly from small- and medium-vessel vasculitis affecting cranial nerves, the labyrinthine artery and brain vessels, plus direct meningeal inflammation. About a third of patients have an associated autoimmune, vasculitic or haematological disorder. Somatic UBA1 mutations in blood stem cells (VEXAS syndrome) explain a substantial share of severe cases in older men.
det.clinical: Auricular chondritis is the hallmark and eventually occurs in most patients; nasal, laryngotracheal, articular and ocular involvement follow. Neurological complications occur in a minority but carry high morbidity: sudden deafness and vertigo, facial or optic neuropathy, aseptic meningitis, limbic-type or diffuse meningoencephalitis, pachymeningitis, stroke and rarely myelitis. Encephalitis can relapse and lead to cortical atrophy and dementia. Airway collapse is the most dangerous non-neurological complication.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, based on characteristic cartilage inflammation in at least two sites or one site with histology and treatment response; ear swelling sparing the lobule is the bedside clue. In meningoencephalitis, CSF and MRI are inflammatory but nonspecific, so infection (including tuberculosis and herpes), autoimmune encephalitis antibodies and lymphoma must be excluded. PET-CT can show cartilage uptake and guide biopsy. Screen for associated vasculitis and myelodysplasia, and send UBA1 testing in older men with macrocytosis.
det.treatment: Mild cartilage disease responds to NSAIDs, colchicine or low-dose steroid. Neurological, ocular or airway involvement needs high-dose glucocorticoids (often IV methylprednisolone pulses), adding methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate to spare steroid; cyclophosphamide or rituximab is used for vasculitis or severe encephalitis. TNF inhibitors and tocilizumab are reported options in refractory disease, and VEXAS may respond to JAK inhibitors or azacitidine. Hearing loss benefits from early steroids; airway disease may require stenting.
det.prognosis: Course is relapsing with gradual damage; neurological and airway complications and VEXAS association predict worse survival.
pearls: Red, painful ear that spares the lobule is chondritis, not cellulitis.
Unexplained aseptic meningoencephalitis plus deafness or red eyes: examine the ears and nose.
Older man with polychondritis, macrocytosis and fevers: think VEXAS (UBA1).
det.thd: Relapsing polychondritis เป็นโรคภูมิคุ้มกันที่โจมตีกระดูกอ่อนและเนื้อเยื่อที่มี proteoglycan มาก อาการเด่นคือใบหูอักเสบแต่ติ่งหูปกติ จมูกยุบ และหลอดลมตีบ อาการทางระบบประสาทเกิดจากหลอดเลือดอักเสบและเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ เช่น หูหนวกเฉียบพลัน เวียนศีรษะ เส้นประสาทสมองอักเสบ และ meningoencephalitis รักษาด้วย steroid ขนาดสูงร่วมกับยากดภูมิ และในชายสูงอายุที่มีเม็ดเลือดแดงใหญ่ควรตรวจหา VEXAS

name: Erythromelalgia
formal: A syndrome of episodic burning pain, redness and warmth of the extremities provoked by heat or exertion and relieved by cooling, occurring as a primary inherited sodium channelopathy (SCN9A gain-of-function in Nav1.7) or secondary to myeloproliferative neoplasms, small-fibre neuropathy, drugs or autoimmune disease.
simple: Attacks of red, hot, burning hands or feet set off by warmth and eased by cold, caused by overactive pain nerves or by a blood disorder.
th: กลุ่มอาการปวดแสบร้อน แดง และร้อนที่มือเท้าเป็นพัก ๆ กระตุ้นด้วยความร้อนหรือการออกกำลัง และดีขึ้นเมื่อแช่น้ำเย็น ชนิดปฐมภูมิเกิดจากยีน SCN9A ส่วนชนิดทุติยภูมิพบกับ essential thrombocythaemia/polycythaemia vera และ small-fibre neuropathy
tempoNote: Attacks last minutes to days, triggered by warmth, standing or exercise; primary form starts in childhood and persists lifelong, secondary form may begin in adulthood with the underlying disease
feat: Burning pain, redness and heat of feet (and sometimes hands, face or ears) during attacks
Triggered by warm environments, bedding, exercise or dependency; patients plunge limbs into ice water
Skin may be normal between attacks; cold-water soaking leads to maceration, ulcers and infection
Secondary form with high platelets (essential thrombocythaemia, polycythaemia vera) responds dramatically to aspirin
Primary form: childhood onset, autosomal dominant family history, poor response to aspirin
inv: Full blood count and film; JAK2, CALR and MPL testing if platelets or haematocrit are high
Small-fibre assessment: skin biopsy intraepidermal nerve fibre density, QSART or sudomotor testing
SCN9A genetic testing for early-onset or familial cases
Screen secondary causes: glucose/HbA1c, autoimmune serology, drug review (calcium channel blockers, bromocriptine)

case.story: Since age 6 his feet become red, hot and intensely burning on warm afternoons and after football; he sleeps with his feet in a bucket of iced water. His mother had similar symptoms.
case.exam: Between attacks the feet look normal except for macerated skin and a healing ulcer; during an induced attack the feet are bright red and hot; sensation normal.
case.tests: Normal blood count; nerve conduction normal; heterozygous SCN9A gain-of-function variant.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and which treatments have targeted rationale?
case.a: Primary (inherited) erythromelalgia due to Nav1.7 gain of function; cool without immersion, and try sodium channel blockers such as mexiletine, lidocaine infusion or carbamazepine (some variants respond well) alongside topical agents.

det.patho: In primary erythromelalgia, dominant gain-of-function variants in SCN9A lower the activation threshold of Nav1.7 channels in nociceptors and sympathetic neurons, so warmth triggers bursts of pain and vasodilation. Secondary erythromelalgia in myeloproliferative neoplasms reflects platelet-mediated arteriolar inflammation and microthrombi, which explains its aspirin sensitivity. Other secondary forms accompany small-fibre neuropathy, diabetes, lupus, and drugs such as nifedipine, verapamil and ergot-derived dopamine agonists.
det.clinical: Attacks begin in the feet and spread proximally, with redness, heat, swelling and burning that can be disabling. Patients avoid warmth, use fans and soak limbs in cold water, which causes immersion injury, ulceration and infection. Primary cases start in childhood and run in families; adult-onset cases should prompt a search for a blood disorder or neuropathy. Erythromelalgia may precede the haematological diagnosis by years.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical, based on the triad of burning pain, redness and warmth with heat provocation and relief by cooling; photographs of attacks are valuable. Check blood counts and, where indicated, JAK2/CALR/MPL to find a myeloproliferative cause. Investigate small fibres with skin biopsy and autonomic tests, and review medications. Genetic testing for SCN9A is reserved for early-onset or familial disease.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: low-dose aspirin (and cytoreduction when needed) is very effective in thrombocythaemia-related disease. Advise gentle cooling with fans or elevation instead of ice-water immersion, and protect damaged skin. Topical lidocaine, capsaicin or compounded amitriptyline–ketamine may help; systemic options include gabapentinoids, SNRIs and tricyclics. Sodium channel blockers (mexiletine, carbamazepine, IV lidocaine) are useful in primary disease, sometimes guided by the specific variant, and selective Nav1.7 blockers remain investigational. Severe refractory pain needs multidisciplinary pain care.
det.prognosis: Primary erythromelalgia is lifelong but variable; aspirin-responsive secondary forms carry the prognosis of the underlying neoplasm.
pearls: Heat-provoked red, burning feet relieved by ice in an adult: check the platelet count.
Ice-water soaking relieves attacks but causes ulcers; teach safer cooling.
Nav1.7 gain of function causes erythromelalgia; loss of function causes congenital insensitivity to pain.
det.thd: Erythromelalgia คืออาการปวดแสบร้อน ผิวแดงและร้อนที่เท้าหรือมือเป็นพัก ๆ กระตุ้นด้วยความร้อนหรือการออกแรง และดีขึ้นเมื่อทำให้เย็น ชนิดปฐมภูมิเกิดจากยีน SCN9A ที่ทำให้ช่องโซเดียม Nav1.7 ทำงานมากเกิน เริ่มในวัยเด็กและมีประวัติครอบครัว ชนิดทุติยภูมิพบกับเกล็ดเลือดสูงจาก myeloproliferative neoplasm ซึ่งตอบสนองดีต่อ aspirin และพบกับ small-fibre neuropathy ควรแนะนำให้ทำให้เย็นด้วยพัดลมแทนการแช่น้ำแข็ง

name: Perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PND)
formal: An umbrella term for cognitive impairment linked to anaesthesia and surgery, comprising postoperative delirium (acute fluctuating inattention within about a week), delayed neurocognitive recovery (up to 30 days) and postoperative neurocognitive disorder (measurable decline persisting from 30 days to 12 months, formerly postoperative cognitive dysfunction, POCD).
simple: Problems with attention, memory or thinking that start after an operation, from short-lived confusion in the first days to slower thinking that can last months.
th: กลุ่มความผิดปกติด้านความคิดความจำที่สัมพันธ์กับการผ่าตัดและการดมยา ได้แก่ postoperative delirium (สับสนเฉียบพลันใน 1–7 วันแรก), delayed neurocognitive recovery และ postoperative neurocognitive disorder ที่คงอยู่ 1–12 เดือน พบมากในผู้สูงอายุที่มีภาวะสมองเสื่อมหรือเปราะบางเดิม
tempoNote: Delirium usually starts on postoperative days 1–3 and fluctuates; persistent cognitive decline is defined at 30 days to 12 months after surgery
feat: Fluctuating inattention and disorganised thinking after surgery; hypoactive form is common and easily missed
Risk rises with older age, pre-existing cognitive impairment, frailty, sensory loss, alcohol use and major surgery (cardiac, hip fracture, vascular)
Precipitants: pain, opioids, benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, hypoxia, infection, electrolyte shifts, urinary retention, sleep loss
Persistent decline in memory, attention or executive speed on testing weeks to months later, despite resolution of delirium
Associated with longer stay, falls, institutionalisation, later dementia and higher mortality
inv: Daily screening with 4AT or CAM/CAM-ICU; preoperative cognitive baseline (Mini-Cog or MoCA) in older patients
Search for precipitants: electrolytes, glucose, blood gas, infection screen, drug chart review, bladder scan
CT or MRI brain if focal signs, fall, anticoagulation or unexplained persistence (perioperative stroke)
Formal neuropsychological testing at follow-up to document postoperative neurocognitive disorder

case.who: 81-year-old grandmother from Ayutthaya, 2 days after hip fracture fixation
case.story: She had mild forgetfulness at home. After surgery under spinal anaesthesia she became drowsy by day and agitated at night, pulling at her catheter; she was receiving tramadol and chlorpheniramine for itching.
case.exam: Inattentive (cannot list months backwards), fluctuating alertness, no focal signs; bladder distended; hearing aids and glasses left at home.
case.tests: 4AT score 9; sodium 129 mmol/L; urine retention 900 mL on bladder scan; CT brain shows only chronic small vessel change.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what should be done first?
case.a: Postoperative delirium (part of perioperative neurocognitive disorders) on a background of probable mild cognitive impairment; relieve retention, correct sodium, stop anticholinergic drugs and limit tramadol, return glasses and hearing aids, reorient and restore sleep, reserving low-dose antipsychotic only for dangerous agitation.

det.patho: Surgical trauma triggers systemic inflammation, with cytokines and damage-associated signals crossing a weakened blood–brain barrier and activating microglia. Neurotransmitter imbalance (cholinergic deficiency, dopaminergic excess), disrupted sleep and circadian rhythm, hypoperfusion, microemboli in cardiac surgery and drug effects add to the injury. Vulnerability lies mainly with the patient: reduced cognitive reserve, neurodegeneration and frailty predict who will decompensate. Choice of general versus regional anaesthesia makes little difference to the risk in recent trials.
det.clinical: Postoperative delirium affects roughly 15–50% of older surgical patients depending on surgery and frailty, most often in the first three days, and the hypoactive form predominates. Delayed neurocognitive recovery describes deficits that remain at discharge but resolve within a month. Postoperative neurocognitive disorder is a decline from baseline on objective testing lasting up to 12 months; it may unmask or accelerate an underlying neurodegenerative process. Patients and families often report slower thinking, poorer memory and reduced independence.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis of delirium is bedside and clinical, using DSM-5 features and validated tools (4AT, CAM); it requires an acute change in attention and awareness. For later stages, the nomenclature introduced in 2018 links perioperative cognitive change to DSM-5 neurocognitive disorder criteria, which require a preoperative baseline. Exclude perioperative stroke, non-convulsive seizures, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, Wernicke encephalopathy, alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal and fat embolism after long-bone fracture.
det.treatment: Prevention is the most effective strategy: preoperative cognitive and frailty screening, avoiding benzodiazepines and anticholinergics, multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia, early mobilisation, hydration, nutrition, sensory aids, sleep protection and family involvement (multicomponent programmes such as HELP). Processed EEG to avoid excessive anaesthetic depth and intraoperative dexmedetomidine have some supporting evidence, though trial results are mixed. Once delirium occurs, treat precipitants and use nonpharmacological care; short courses of low-dose haloperidol or an atypical antipsychotic are reserved for distress or danger, and benzodiazepines are used only for alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal. Arrange cognitive follow-up after discharge.
det.prognosis: Most delirium resolves within days, but it predicts persistent cognitive decline, functional loss, dementia and higher one-year mortality, especially in frail older adults.
pearls: Document a preoperative cognitive baseline; without it postoperative decline cannot be measured.
Hypoactive delirium looks like a quiet, sleepy patient; screen every older surgical patient daily with 4AT.
Check the bladder, the drug chart and the sodium before reaching for an antipsychotic.
det.thd: Perioperative neurocognitive disorders เป็นคำรวมของความผิดปกติด้านความคิดหลังผ่าตัด ตั้งแต่ postoperative delirium ที่สับสนขึ้นลงใน 1–3 วันแรก ไปจนถึงความคิดความจำถดถอยที่คงอยู่นานถึง 12 เดือน (เดิมเรียก POCD) ปัจจัยเสี่ยงหลักคือผู้สูงอายุที่มีสมองเสื่อมหรือเปราะบางเดิม ตัวกระตุ้นได้แก่ ปวด ยากล่อมประสาท ยา anticholinergic ปัสสาวะคั่ง เกลือแร่ผิดปกติ และติดเชื้อ การป้องกันด้วยมาตรการหลายด้านสำคัญที่สุด และควรตรวจติดตามความจำหลังจำหน่าย

name: Skeletal fluorosis with myeloradiculopathy
formal: Chronic fluoride poisoning, usually from drinking high-fluoride groundwater for many years, in which fluoride builds up in bone and ligaments, causing osteosclerosis and ligament ossification that narrow the spinal canal and foramina and produce a compressive myelopathy and radiculopathy.
simple: Too much fluoride in well water over many years makes the bones and spinal ligaments thick and hard, which slowly squeezes the spinal cord and nerve roots.
ab: ฟลูออไรด์เกิน
th: พิษฟลูออไรด์เรื้อรังจากการดื่มน้ำบาดาลที่มีฟลูออไรด์สูงเป็นเวลานาน ทำให้กระดูกหนาแข็งและเอ็นยึดกระดูกสันหลังกลายเป็นกระดูก จนกดไขสันหลังและรากประสาท พบในบางพื้นที่ของอินเดีย จีน และภาคเหนือของไทย
tempoNote: Exposure over many years (often from childhood); spinal symptoms creep in over years, with stepwise worsening after minor neck trauma
feat: Mottled, brown-stained or pitted teeth in someone raised in a high-fluoride area (dental fluorosis is the clue)
Years of back and neck stiffness, painful joints and reduced spinal mobility, sometimes with fixed flexion deformities
Slowly progressive spastic quadriparesis or paraparesis with sensory level, often cervical, plus radicular pain or wasting
Radiographs: diffusely dense, chalky bones, ossified interosseous membranes of forearm or leg, and calcified spinal ligaments
Several family members or neighbours sharing one water source may be affected
inv: Fluoride level of the drinking-water source (WHO guideline upper limit 1.5 mg/L) and urine or serum fluoride
Plain films of spine, pelvis and forearm: osteosclerosis, osteophytes, interosseous membrane calcification
MRI and CT of spine: ossified posterior longitudinal ligament and ligamentum flavum, canal and foraminal stenosis, cord signal change
Exclude mimics: B12, HTLV-1 serology, renal function (renal failure increases fluoride retention)

case.who: 52-year-old rice farmer from rural Lamphun who has drunk water from the same deep tube well all his life
case.story: Over four years his neck became stiff and painful and now his legs feel heavy and his hands clumsy; his wife and brother also complain of stiff backs.
case.exam: Brownish mottled teeth; neck and lumbar spine nearly immobile; spastic quadriparesis with brisk reflexes, bilateral Babinski and Hoffmann signs, impaired vibration in the feet.
case.tests: Forearm X-ray shows a calcified interosseous membrane and dense bones; MRI shows multilevel cervical canal narrowing from ossified ligaments with cord T2 change; well-water fluoride is several times the WHO limit.
case.q: What unifying diagnosis explains the teeth, bones and myelopathy, and what are the two management priorities?
case.a: Skeletal fluorosis with compressive cervical myelopathy; stop exposure by switching to a safe, defluoridated water source for the household, and refer for decompressive spinal surgery while deficits are still modest.

det.patho: Fluoride is readily absorbed from water and binds avidly to bone mineral, replacing hydroxyl groups in hydroxyapatite and stimulating osteoblasts. Years of high intake produce thickened, brittle, sclerotic bone, bony outgrowths and ossification of ligaments and tendon insertions, including the posterior longitudinal ligament and ligamentum flavum. The neurological damage is mostly mechanical, from canal and foraminal narrowing, although a direct neurotoxic effect has been proposed. Endemic belts follow geology: parts of India, China, East Africa and the Middle East, and in Thailand some northern provinces with fluoride-rich groundwater and hot springs; poor nutrition, low calcium intake, heavy labour and renal impairment increase susceptibility.
det.clinical: Dental fluorosis appears when exposure occurs during tooth formation and is a useful marker of lifelong exposure. Early skeletal disease gives vague aches, stiffness and joint pains that are easily labelled as arthritis; later the spine becomes rigid with kyphosis and contractures. Neurological involvement develops in a minority, usually as a slowly progressive cervical or thoracic compressive myelopathy, with or without radicular pain, wasting and reflex loss from root compression. Minor falls can precipitate sudden deterioration because the cord has little reserve in a narrow, rigid canal. Non-skeletal effects such as gastrointestinal upset and possible cognitive effects in children have been described.
det.diagnosis: Suspect the diagnosis in anyone from an endemic area with dental mottling, a stiff spine and myelopathy. Plain radiographs showing generalised osteosclerosis with calcification of the forearm or leg interosseous membranes are highly suggestive. CT best demonstrates ligament ossification, and MRI shows the levels and degree of cord compression and signal change. Raised water, urine or serum fluoride confirms exposure, though levels vary and should be read with the clinical and radiological picture. Exclude degenerative spondylosis, OPLL of other causes, renal osteodystrophy, osteoblastic metastases, myelofibrosis and Paget disease.
det.treatment: There is no proven drug to remove fluoride already fixed in bone, so the core intervention is ending exposure through defluoridation, rainwater harvesting or an alternative low-fluoride supply for the whole household and community. Improving calcium, vitamin D, vitamin C and overall nutrition is advised and may slow progression. Symptomatic cord compression needs surgical decompression (laminectomy or laminoplasty, sometimes anterior procedures), ideally before severe deficits; the bone is hard and vascular, making surgery technically demanding. Physiotherapy and management of spasticity and pain complete care.
det.prognosis: Bone changes are largely irreversible, but stopping exposure halts progression; outcome after decompression is best when surgery is done early, before long-standing myelopathy.
pearls: Mottled teeth plus a calcified forearm interosseous membrane in a patient with myelopathy should prompt a question about the household water source.
Several affected relatives sharing one tube well points to an environmental, not genetic, cause.
Fluorosis is a cause of OPLL-like canal stenosis; always ask about lifelong residence when OPLL appears in a farmer from an endemic area.
det.thd: ฟลูออไรด์จากน้ำบาดาลจับกับกระดูกทำให้กระดูกหนาแข็งและเอ็นกระดูกสันหลังกลายเป็นกระดูก จนช่องไขสันหลังแคบ ผู้ป่วยมีฟันลาย กระดูกสันหลังแข็ง และอ่อนแรงแบบเกร็งจากไขสันหลังถูกกด ภาพรังสีพบกระดูกทึบขาวและพังผืดระหว่างกระดูกแขนมีหินปูน ยืนยันด้วยระดับฟลูออไรด์ในน้ำและปัสสาวะ การรักษาหลักคือเปลี่ยนแหล่งน้ำดื่มให้ปลอดภัย ปรับโภชนาการ และผ่าตัดลดการกดไขสันหลังก่อนอาการรุนแรง

Younger onset inflammatory back pain, sacroiliitis, HLA-B27 and syndesmophytes rather than dense bones
Spastic paraparesis with bladder involvement, positive HTLV-1 serology and no canal compromise on MRI

name: Iodine deficiency disorders (IDD) — neurological cretinism
formal: The spectrum of effects of inadequate iodine intake, in which lack of thyroid hormone during fetal and early postnatal brain development causes outcomes ranging from mild loss of IQ to endemic cretinism, either neurological (intellectual disability, deaf-mutism, proximal spastic diplegia, strabismus) or myxoedematous (hypothyroid dwarfism).
simple: When a mother and baby do not get enough iodine, the baby's brain cannot develop normally, which can cause low intelligence, deafness and stiff legs, and is fully preventable with iodised salt.
ab: ขาดไอโอดีน
th: ภาวะขาดไอโอดีนในแม่และทารก ทำให้ขาดฮอร์โมนไทรอยด์ช่วงสมองกำลังพัฒนา ผลมีตั้งแต่ IQ ลดลงเล็กน้อยจนถึงเครติน (cretinism) ที่มีปัญญาอ่อน หูหนวก และขาเกร็ง ป้องกันได้ด้วยเกลือเสริมไอโอดีน
tempoNote: Damage is fixed during pregnancy and early infancy; deficits are static and lifelong, while goitre and hypothyroid features may evolve
feat: Intellectual disability from mild cognitive lowering to severe impairment, often with poor school performance across a whole community
Neurological type: sensorineural deafness or deaf-mutism, squint, and spastic rigidity mostly of the proximal legs with a characteristic shuffling gait
Myxoedematous type: short stature, coarse skin, delayed bone age and overt hypothyroidism, with milder neurological signs
Goitre in mothers or siblings; hypothyroxinaemia in early pregnancy is the critical window
Milder IDD: reduced IQ, impaired motor skills and hearing in otherwise normal-appearing children
inv: Neonatal heel-prick TSH screening (raised TSH; national programme in Thailand)
TSH, free T4 and thyroid ultrasound in the child; maternal thyroid function
Urinary iodine concentration (population marker; median below 100 µg/L in schoolchildren or below 150 µg/L in pregnancy suggests deficiency)
Audiometry and developmental/IQ assessment; brain MRI to exclude other causes of spastic diplegia

case.who: 9-year-old boy from a remote hill village in Nan province, brought to a provincial clinic
case.story: He has never learnt to speak, walks with stiff legs since late infancy and lags far behind his classmates; his mother has a large neck swelling and the family uses non-iodised rock salt.
case.exam: Deaf with no speech, convergent squint, spasticity and brisk reflexes most marked at the hips and knees, short stature not prominent; no goitre.
case.tests: Free T4 and TSH near normal; audiometry shows profound bilateral sensorineural loss; MRI shows no structural lesion; village survey finds low urinary iodine and many goitres.
case.q: Which form of iodine deficiency disorder is this, and which intervention would have prevented it?
case.a: Neurological endemic cretinism, from maternal iodine deficiency during early pregnancy; prevention is adequate iodine before and during pregnancy through iodised salt and iodine supplements for pregnant and lactating women.

read.where: Chapter 10 Iodine deficiency disorders and their neurological consequences
Chapter 18 Thyroid Disease and the Nervous System — Neurologic Features of Congenital Hypothyroidism

det.patho: Iodine is needed to make thyroxine, and thyroid hormone drives neuronal migration, myelination, synapse formation and cochlear development. Before the fetal thyroid works (around mid-gestation), the fetus depends entirely on maternal T4, so maternal hypothyroxinaemia in the first half of pregnancy causes the neurological form of cretinism with deafness and motor signs. Ongoing postnatal hypothyroidism adds the myxoedematous form, and coexisting selenium deficiency or thiocyanate from cassava may shift the balance between types. Iodine deficiency remains the leading preventable cause of intellectual disability worldwide; Thailand has reduced it through salt iodisation and supplementation in pregnancy, but pockets persist in remote upland areas.
det.clinical: Severe endemic deficiency produces cretins, while much larger numbers of children show modest cognitive and motor deficits that only become obvious at population level. Neurological cretins have intellectual disability, deaf-mutism, squint, proximal spastic rigidity of the legs and sometimes extrapyramidal signs, but are often clinically euthyroid. Myxoedematous cretins have growth failure, delayed puberty, coarse features and hypothyroidism, with less deafness. Goitre is common in the community and in mothers. Deficits established in utero do not reverse, whereas hypothyroid features respond to treatment.
det.diagnosis: In an individual child the diagnosis rests on the clinical pattern in the setting of known community deficiency, together with thyroid function and audiometry. Neonatal TSH screening identifies congenital hypothyroidism of any cause and, when many raised values cluster in an area, also signals population deficiency. Iodine status of a community is judged by median urinary iodine, goitre prevalence and neonatal TSH distribution rather than single measurements. Imaging and genetic testing help exclude cerebral palsy, inherited thyroid dyshormonogenesis and other causes of deafness with spasticity.
det.treatment: Prevention is the treatment: universal salt iodisation, iodine supplementation (about 250 µg/day) for pregnant and breastfeeding women, and iodised oil in severely deficient settings without salt access. Infants with raised TSH on screening need prompt levothyroxine started in the first weeks of life, which protects cognition in those whose brains were not already injured in utero. Established neurological cretinism needs supportive care: hearing aids, special education, physiotherapy and spasticity management. Excess iodine can trigger thyroid dysfunction, so programmes should be monitored.
det.prognosis: Neurological deficits acquired during pregnancy are permanent; correcting iodine status prevents new cases and allows normal development in the next generation.
pearls: The fetus relies on maternal T4 until mid-gestation, so iodine sufficiency before conception and in the first trimester matters most.
Neurological cretins may have normal thyroid function at the time they are examined; a normal TSH does not exclude the diagnosis.
Deaf-mutism plus proximal leg spasticity and squint in a child from a goitrous area is the classic triad.
det.thd: การขาดไอโอดีนทำให้แม่และทารกมีฮอร์โมนไทรอยด์ไม่พอในช่วงที่สมองพัฒนา โดยเฉพาะครึ่งแรกของการตั้งครรภ์ที่ทารกยังต้องพึ่ง T4 จากแม่ เครตินชนิดระบบประสาทมีปัญญาอ่อน หูหนวกเป็นใบ้ ตาเข และขาเกร็ง ส่วนชนิด myxoedematous ตัวเตี้ยและมีภาวะไทรอยด์ต่ำ การป้องกันคือเกลือเสริมไอโอดีน ยาเม็ดไอโอดีนในหญิงตั้งครรภ์ และคัดกรอง TSH ทารกแรกเกิดเพื่อให้ levothyroxine เร็ว

name: Protein–energy malnutrition (PEM) — neurological consequences
formal: Undernutrition from inadequate intake of energy and protein, presenting as marasmus (severe wasting), kwashiorkor (oedematous malnutrition) or a mixed form, which in early childhood impairs brain growth and development and, at any age, predisposes to neuropathy, encephalopathy and refeeding-related neurological complications.
simple: Not getting enough food and protein, especially in young children, slows brain growth and learning, and feeding too fast afterwards can cause dangerous salt and vitamin problems.
th: ภาวะขาดพลังงานและโปรตีน ได้แก่ marasmus (ผอมแห้ง) และ kwashiorkor (บวม) ในเด็กเล็กทำให้สมองเติบโตช้า พัฒนาการล่าช้า ในทุกวัยเสี่ยงต่อปลายประสาทเสื่อมและภาวะ refeeding ที่ทำให้ฟอสเฟต โพแทสเซียม แมกนีเซียมต่ำ และ Wernicke
tempoNote: Weeks to months of deprivation; refeeding complications appear within the first 2–5 days of renewed feeding
feat: Child: apathy, irritability, hypotonia, reduced head growth and delayed motor, language and social milestones
Marasmus: extreme wasting and loss of subcutaneous fat; kwashiorkor: pitting oedema, flaky dermatosis, sparse pale hair and fatty liver
Reversible brain 'shrinkage' on imaging with enlarged ventricles and sulci
Transient coarse tremor, myoclonus or rigidity during nutritional recovery (kwashiorkor shaking syndrome)
Refeeding: weakness, paraesthesia, confusion, seizures, arrhythmia and heart failure from low phosphate, potassium, magnesium and thiamine
inv: Anthropometry: weight-for-height Z-score, MUAC (below 115 mm in children 6–59 months indicates severe acute malnutrition), oedema; adults BMI and GLIM criteria
Glucose, electrolytes including phosphate, magnesium and potassium daily during early refeeding
Albumin, blood count, infection screen (sepsis, TB, HIV) and micronutrient levels as indicated
Developmental assessment; brain imaging only when focal signs or atypical course

case.who: 20-month-old girl from a migrant labourers' camp at the Thai–Myanmar border
case.story: Weaned early onto rice water and sweetened condensed milk, she has become listless and stopped walking; her feet and face have swollen over three weeks.
case.exam: Apathetic, cries weakly; pitting oedema of feet and face, peeling skin patches on the legs, thin reddish hair, hypotonia; cannot sit unsupported though she walked at 13 months.
case.tests: Albumin 1.8 g/dL, glucose 52 mg/dL, Hb 8.2 g/dL; phosphate low-normal. On day 3 of therapeutic feeding she develops irritability and weakness with phosphate falling to 0.5 mmol/L.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and what explains her day-3 deterioration?
case.a: Kwashiorkor (oedematous severe acute malnutrition) with developmental regression; the deterioration is refeeding syndrome with hypophosphataemia, managed by slowing feeds, replacing phosphate, potassium and magnesium, and giving thiamine.

read.where: Chapter 1 Role of nutrition in the growth and development of nervous system

det.patho: Energy and protein lack slows brain growth, myelination and dendritic and synaptic development, most damagingly from late pregnancy to about two years of age. Kwashiorkor involves oedema, hypoalbuminaemia and oxidative stress in addition to deficiency, while marasmus is an adaptive starvation state with fat and muscle loss. Coexisting deficiencies of iron, iodine, zinc and B vitamins, together with infection, poverty and lack of stimulation, add to the neurological harm. In refeeding, a sudden insulin surge drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells and consumes thiamine, which can cause cardiac, muscle and neurological failure.
det.clinical: Children show apathy, withdrawn behaviour, hypotonia, microcephaly and delayed milestones, and survivors of early malnutrition often have lasting deficits in attention, memory and school performance. Kwashiorkor shaking syndrome describes tremor, myoclonus and rigidity that appear during recovery and usually settle over weeks. Adults with severe undernutrition, as in anorexia nervosa, chronic alcohol use, cancer, prolonged fasting or after bariatric surgery, may develop polyneuropathy, proximal weakness, cognitive slowing and Wernicke encephalopathy. Refeeding syndrome typically emerges within the first few days of feeding with weakness, paraesthesia, delirium, seizures, arrhythmia and fluid overload; osmotic demyelination has been reported.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical and anthropometric: in children, WHO severe acute malnutrition is defined by very low weight-for-height, low MUAC or bilateral pitting oedema; in adults, the GLIM framework combines weight loss, low BMI or muscle mass with reduced intake or disease burden. Laboratory tests look for hypoglycaemia, electrolyte disturbance, anaemia, infection and specific micronutrient deficits. Brain imaging may show apparent atrophy that improves with recovery and should not be over-interpreted. Identify refeeding risk before starting feeds: very low BMI, little or no intake for over 5–10 days, recent weight loss, low baseline electrolytes, or alcohol misuse.
det.treatment: Children with severe acute malnutrition follow WHO staged care: treat hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration and infection, start with low-volume F-75 formula, then advance to F-100 or ready-to-use therapeutic food, with micronutrients and later catch-up growth and play stimulation. For adults at high refeeding risk, give thiamine before feeds, start cautiously (around 10 kcal/kg/day in the highest-risk group) and increase over several days, monitoring and replacing phosphate, potassium and magnesium daily. Avoid rapid fluid loading in oedematous children. Long-term developmental follow-up, early stimulation programmes and community prevention (breastfeeding, complementary feeding, food security) matter as much as acute care.
det.prognosis: Mortality of complicated severe malnutrition falls sharply with structured protocols; cognitive deficits after prolonged early-life malnutrition may persist but improve with stimulation and adequate nutrition.
pearls: Give thiamine before the first glucose-containing feed or drip in a malnourished patient to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy.
Falling phosphate on days 2–4 of feeding is the warning sign of refeeding syndrome — check it daily.
New tremor or myoclonus while a kwashiorkor child is recovering is usually the benign shaking syndrome, not a new disease.
det.thd: ภาวะขาดพลังงานและโปรตีนในเด็กเล็กทำให้สมองเติบโตและสร้าง myelin ไม่เต็มที่ เด็กเฉื่อยชา ตัวอ่อน และพัฒนาการช้า kwashiorkor มีบวมและผิวหนังลอก ส่วน marasmus ผอมแห้ง ในผู้ใหญ่พบปลายประสาทเสื่อมและ Wernicke ได้ ระวัง refeeding syndrome ในวันที่ 2–5 ของการให้อาหาร ซึ่งฟอสเฟต โพแทสเซียม แมกนีเซียมต่ำ ให้ thiamine ก่อน เริ่มอาหารช้า ๆ และตรวจเกลือแร่ทุกวัน

Severe hypophosphataemia with weakness, respiratory failure or rhabdomyolysis is the hallmark of refeeding syndrome

name: Neurological manifestations of hypernatraemia
formal: Neurological dysfunction caused by serum sodium above 145 mmol/L with plasma hypertonicity, in which water leaves brain cells, producing lethargy, confusion, weakness, seizures and coma and, when rapid, brain shrinkage with tearing of bridging veins, haemorrhage or venous sinus thrombosis.
simple: When the blood is too salty, usually because the person cannot drink enough water, the brain dries out and shrinks, causing confusion, drowsiness and sometimes bleeding or seizures.
th: โซเดียมในเลือดสูงกว่า 145 mmol/L ทำให้น้ำออกจากเซลล์สมอง สมองหดตัว เกิดซึม สับสน ชัก จนโคม่า หากเกิดเร็วอาจมีเลือดออกในสมองจากเส้นเลือดดำฉีกขาด พบบ่อยในผู้สูงอายุติดเตียงที่ดื่มน้ำเองไม่ได้ และในภาวะ diabetes insipidus
tempoNote: Acute if developed within 48 h (higher risk of haemorrhage, can be corrected quickly); chronic if longer, when brain adaptation makes rapid correction risky
feat: Lethargy, irritability, confusion and reduced consciousness, often with intense thirst in those able to sense it
Muscle weakness, twitching, hyperreflexia, rigidity or myoclonus; seizures mainly with rapid change or over-rapid correction
Occurs in people who cannot reach or ask for water: frail elderly, infants, intubated or post-neurosurgical patients
Acute severe cases: intracerebral, subarachnoid or subdural bleeding and cerebral venous thrombosis
Rhabdomyolysis and osmotic demyelination are rare complications
inv: Serum sodium, plasma and urine osmolality, urine sodium, glucose and urea
Urine osmolality interpretation: very dilute urine suggests diabetes insipidus; concentrated urine suggests extrarenal water loss or poor intake
Desmopressin response test if diabetes insipidus is suspected; copeptin where available
CT or MRI brain when consciousness is impaired, there are focal signs or seizures (haemorrhage, venous thrombosis, demyelination)

case.who: 84-year-old bedbound woman with advanced dementia from a nursing home in Nonthaburi
case.story: After four days of fever from a urinary infection, staff noticed she was drowsier and was barely taking fluids; she was brought in after a brief generalised seizure.
case.exam: Dry mucosa, GCS 9, temperature 38.4 °C, diffuse hyperreflexia and multifocal myoclonic jerks, no focal weakness.
case.tests: Sodium 168 mmol/L, urea raised, glucose normal; urine osmolality 720 mOsm/kg; CT brain shows atrophy without haemorrhage.
case.q: What is the cause of her encephalopathy, and how should sodium be corrected?
case.a: Hypernatraemia from insensible losses and poor water intake (concentrated urine argues against diabetes insipidus); treat the infection and replace free water, lowering sodium gradually, roughly 10 mmol/L per day for this chronic case, with frequent sodium checks.

det.patho: Sodium is the main determinant of plasma tonicity, so hypernatraemia means relative water deficit, from lack of intake, renal water loss (central or nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, osmotic diuresis), extrarenal losses (fever, sweating, diarrhoea) or sodium loading (hypertonic saline, sodium bicarbonate, mis-mixed infant formula). Water moves out of neurons and glia and the brain shrinks; a sudden fall in brain volume can stretch and tear bridging veins and small vessels. Within one to two days the brain gains electrolytes and organic osmolytes such as myoinositol and glutamine to restore volume, which protects it but makes rapid lowering of sodium dangerous because water then rushes back in. Thirst normally prevents hypernatraemia, so it mostly affects those with impaired thirst or no access to water.
det.clinical: Symptoms track the speed and size of the rise more than the absolute value. Early features are thirst, restlessness, irritability and lethargy, progressing to confusion, stupor and coma; infants may show a high-pitched cry and hyperpnoea. Neuromuscular irritability with twitching, hyperreflexia and rigidity is common, and weakness can arise from associated hypokalaemia, hypophosphataemia or rhabdomyolysis. Seizures are uncommon with the rise itself and more often occur during too-fast correction, when cerebral oedema develops. Acute severe hypernatraemia, as in salt poisoning or neonates, may cause intracranial haemorrhage or venous sinus thrombosis with focal deficits.
det.diagnosis: Confirm hypertonicity and assess volume status, then use urine osmolality to separate causes: maximally concentrated urine points to water loss outside the kidney or inadequate intake, whereas inappropriately dilute urine suggests diabetes insipidus, which is confirmed by response to desmopressin and, increasingly, by copeptin testing. Calculate the free water deficit to plan replacement and check for hyperglycaemia, renal failure and drug causes such as lithium or mannitol. Imaging is warranted for impaired consciousness, focal signs or seizures, looking for haemorrhage, venous thrombosis or osmotic demyelination. Remember that hypernatraemia in a hospitalised patient is often iatrogenic from inadequate free water.
det.treatment: Treat the cause and replace water, enterally where possible or with hypotonic fluid such as 5% dextrose or 0.45% saline, also replacing ongoing losses. For chronic hypernatraemia (over 48 h or unknown duration) a conservative target of about 10 mmol/L reduction in 24 hours is widely used, although recent adult data suggest faster correction is less harmful than once thought; in children the slower approach is still emphasised. Acute hypernatraemia of a few hours, such as salt ingestion, can be corrected rapidly, sometimes with dialysis. Give desmopressin for central diabetes insipidus, monitor sodium every few hours during treatment, and assess swallowing, thirst access and feeding plans before discharge.
det.prognosis: Mortality is high in hospitalised patients with severe hypernatraemia, largely reflecting the underlying illness; survivors of acute haemorrhagic or thrombotic complications may have permanent deficits.
pearls: Hypernatraemia almost always implies that the patient could not drink: look for frailty, dementia, intubation or impaired thirst.
Seizures during treatment suggest cerebral oedema from too-rapid correction — stop hypotonic fluid and recheck sodium.
Very dilute urine despite high sodium points to diabetes insipidus; concentrated urine points to water loss or poor intake.
det.thd: โซเดียมสูงเกิดจากขาดน้ำเทียบกับเกลือ เช่น ผู้สูงอายุที่ดื่มน้ำเองไม่ได้ ไข้ ท้องเสีย หรือ diabetes insipidus น้ำออกจากเซลล์ทำให้สมองหดตัว ผู้ป่วยซึม สับสน กล้ามเนื้อกระตุก จนโคม่า และอาจมีเลือดออกในสมองถ้าเกิดเร็ว ภายใน 48 ชั่วโมงสมองจะปรับตัวด้วย osmolyte ดังนั้นภาวะเรื้อรังต้องลดโซเดียมช้า ๆ ประมาณ 10 mmol/L ต่อวัน ใช้ osmolality ปัสสาวะช่วยแยกสาเหตุ

name: Cerebral and spinal echinococcosis (hydatid disease)
formal: Infection of the brain or spine by the larval stage of Echinococcus tapeworms: cystic echinococcosis (E. granulosus) forms large, usually solitary, fluid-filled cysts that compress tissue, whereas alveolar echinococcosis (E. multilocularis) produces infiltrative, enhancing, tumour-like metastatic lesions; spinal disease mainly involves vertebrae and epidural space.
simple: A dog tapeworm larva grows into a slowly enlarging water-filled bag inside the head or spine and presses on the nerves around it.
ab: ถุงน้ำพยาธิตืดสุนัขในสมอง
th: การติดเชื้อตัวอ่อนพยาธิตืดสุนัข Echinococcus ที่เข้าไปเป็นถุงน้ำขนาดใหญ่ในสมองหรือกระดูกสันหลัง ทำให้มีอาการจากการกดเบียด ในไทยพบน้อยมาก มักเป็นผู้ที่เคยอยู่ในพื้นที่เลี้ยงแกะ/แพะร่วมกับสุนัข การผ่าตัดต้องเอาถุงออกทั้งใบโดยไม่ให้แตก
tempoNote: Cysts enlarge by roughly 1–5 cm per year, so symptoms build over months to years; sudden worsening suggests rupture, haemorrhage or acute hydrocephalus
feat: Most cerebral cases are children or young adults with headache, vomiting and papilloedema from a big space-occupying cyst
Focal deficits or seizures depend on site; the parietal region in the middle cerebral artery territory is typical
Spinal form: back pain, radiculopathy and slowly progressive paraparesis from vertebral and epidural cysts
Liver or lung cysts coexist in many, and contact with sheep-herding dogs is the usual exposure
Cyst rupture can trigger anaphylaxis and seed daughter cysts along the operative field or CSF
inv: CT/MRI brain or spine: large round thin-walled cyst with CSF-like content, little or no enhancement or oedema (CE); multilobulated enhancing lesions in alveolar disease
Abdominal ultrasound and chest imaging to look for liver and lung cysts (WHO-IWGE ultrasound staging)
Serology (ELISA, immunoblot) supports the diagnosis but may be negative with isolated brain cysts
Histology of the excised cyst wall (laminated layer, germinal layer, protoscolices) is confirmatory; avoid diagnostic needle puncture

case.who: 29-year-old man from Nakhon Phanom who spent four years as a farm hand on a sheep and goat farm in the Middle East
case.story: Since returning he has had worsening morning headaches for six months, then two weeks of vomiting and clumsiness of the left hand; he recalls feeding the farm dogs scraps of offal.
case.exam: Bilateral papilloedema, mild left hemiparesis and left-sided sensory inattention.
case.tests: MRI: 7 cm smooth spherical cyst in the right parietal lobe, signal identical to CSF, no rim enhancement and almost no surrounding oedema; liver ultrasound shows a 4 cm cyst with a double wall.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis, and what surgical principle matters most?
case.a: Cerebral cystic echinococcosis; the cyst should be delivered intact (hydrostatic or gentle dissection technique) under albendazole cover, because spillage can cause anaphylaxis and recurrence.

det.patho: Dogs and other canids carry the adult worm and pass eggs in faeces; humans become accidental intermediate hosts by swallowing eggs from soil, hands or contaminated food. The released embryo crosses the gut wall and lodges mostly in liver and lung, with the brain affected in roughly 1–2% of cases and the spine and other bones in a small fraction. A CE cyst has an outer host fibrous layer, a laminated acellular layer and an inner germinal layer that buds brood capsules and protoscolices; alveolar disease from E. multilocularis grows by budding outward like a malignancy.
det.clinical: Primary brain cysts are mostly solitary and supratentorial and are seen most often in children, who present with raised intracranial pressure and an enlarging head or focal signs that seem mild relative to cyst size. Secondary (metastatic) multiple cysts follow rupture of a cardiac or other cyst into the circulation. Spinal hydatidosis usually starts in the vertebral body, spreads to the epidural space and compresses the cord or cauda equina; neurological recovery is often incomplete. Alveolar echinococcosis of the brain nearly always comes with liver disease and behaves like metastatic tumour.
det.diagnosis: Imaging is the backbone of diagnosis: a cerebral CE cyst is typically round, sharply defined, contains CSF-like fluid, lacks a scolex and shows little or no enhancement or oedema, while daughter cysts give a multivesicular look. Serology is helpful when positive but has limited sensitivity for brain-only disease, so a negative result leaves the diagnosis open. Look for the primary focus with abdominal ultrasound and chest imaging. Percutaneous aspiration of an intracranial cyst is avoided because of the risks of leak, anaphylaxis and seeding.
det.treatment: Complete removal of the intact cyst is the treatment of choice for cerebral CE, using careful dissection with saline irrigation (hydrostatic delivery) and pads soaked in scolicidal solution around the field. Albendazole (about 10–15 mg/kg/day, typically 400 mg twice daily with a fatty meal) is given before and for months after surgery, and is the main option for inoperable, multiple or recurrent cysts; some centres add praziquantel peri-operatively. Monitor liver enzymes and blood counts on albendazole. Spinal disease needs decompression and stabilisation plus prolonged albendazole, and alveolar disease needs long-term or lifelong albendazole with surgery where feasible.
det.prognosis: Intact removal of a solitary cerebral CE cyst usually gives a good outcome; rupture, multiple cysts, spinal involvement and alveolar disease carry high recurrence and disability.
pearls: Huge cyst, little oedema, no enhancement, no scolex: think hydatid rather than tumour or cysticercus.
Never needle the cyst — leakage risks anaphylaxis and secondary seeding.
Always scan the liver and lungs when a brain hydatid cyst is suspected.
det.thd: Echinococcosis เกิดจากกลืนไข่พยาธิตืดสุนัขที่ปนเปื้อนดินหรืออาหาร ตัวอ่อนกลายเป็นถุงน้ำ มักอยู่ที่ตับและปอด ส่วนน้อยไปที่สมองหรือกระดูกสันหลัง ภาพ MRI เป็นถุงกลมใหญ่ น้ำเหมือน CSF ไม่ค่อยมี enhancement หรือบวมรอบ ๆ การรักษาหลักคือผ่าตัดเอาถุงออกทั้งใบอย่างระวังไม่ให้แตก ร่วมกับ albendazole ก่อนและหลังผ่าตัด ห้ามเจาะดูดถุงเพราะอาจเกิด anaphylaxis และแพร่กระจาย

name: Cerebral sparganosis (Spirometra)
formal: Brain or spinal cord infection by the migrating plerocercoid larva (sparganum) of Spirometra tapeworms, acquired from raw frog, snake or poultry flesh, frog or snake poultices applied to wounds or eyes, or drinking water containing infected copepods, and producing slowly shifting granulomatous lesions.
simple: A thin worm larva from raw frog or snake meat (or a frog-skin poultice) crawls slowly through the brain, leaving a trail of inflamed tissue that moves over time.
ab: พยาธิตืดกบ
พยาธิตืดงูขึ้นสมอง
th: การติดเชื้อตัวอ่อนพยาธิตืด Spirometra (sparganum) ในสมองหรือไขสันหลัง จากการกินกบ งู หรือไก่ดิบ การพอกแผลด้วยเนื้อกบ หรือดื่มน้ำที่มีโคพีพอด ตัวอ่อนเคลื่อนที่ช้า ๆ ทำให้รอยโรคใน MRI ย้ายตำแหน่ง การรักษาหลักคือผ่าตัดเอาตัวพยาธิออกทั้งตัว
tempoNote: Symptoms accumulate over months to years; serial scans show lesions shifting a few millimetres to centimetres as the larva migrates
feat: Adult with focal seizures, slowly progressive hemiparesis or headache, often for months before diagnosis
Exposure history: raw frog or snake meat, raw snake blood or bile, frog-flesh poultice on a wound or eye, or untreated stream water
Larva may also be felt as a migrating subcutaneous lump or cause ocular sparganosis
Blood eosinophilia is present in only a minority, so a normal count does not exclude it
Lesions move between scans — the single most useful clue
inv: MRI with contrast: clustered or beaded ring enhancement with a 'tunnel' or tract sign, white-matter oedema and ex vacuo atrophy
Repeat MRI over weeks to months to show migration of the enhancing focus
Anti-sparganum IgG ELISA in serum and CSF (available in Thai reference laboratories) supports the diagnosis
Surgical removal with identification of the ribbon-like larva confirms it; CT may show small calcifications

case.who: 51-year-old woman rice farmer from Sakon Nakhon
case.story: Over a year she had brief episodes of right-hand twitching, then gradual weakness of the right arm. She often cooked frog in a lightly heated larb and years ago treated an eye ulcer with a frog-flesh poultice.
case.exam: Mild right upper-limb weakness with brisk reflexes; no fever.
case.tests: MRI: conglomerate beaded ring-enhancing lesions in left frontal white matter with a tubular track; a scan three months later shows the enhancing focus has moved 2 cm posteriorly. Serum anti-sparganum ELISA positive; eosinophils normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the definitive treatment?
case.a: Cerebral sparganosis; surgical (often stereotactic- or navigation-guided) removal of the entire live larva, because antiparasitic drugs are unreliable.

det.patho: Spirometra adults live in dogs and cats; eggs hatch in water, copepods carry the first larval stage, and frogs, snakes and other vertebrates harbour the plerocercoid. Humans become paratenic hosts by eating raw flesh, applying it to wounds or eyes, or swallowing infected copepods; the larva cannot mature but survives for years and wanders. In tissue it provokes granulomatous inflammation with eosinophils and leaves necrotic tracks, and in the brain it prefers the cerebral hemispheres, especially frontal and parietal white matter. Thailand, China, Korea and Vietnam account for most reported cases.
det.clinical: The typical patient is an adult with a long history of seizures, headache or a creeping focal deficit such as hemiparesis or hemisensory loss; spinal sparganosis gives a slowly progressive myelopathy. Symptoms may wax and wane as the larva moves and the inflammation shifts. A migrating subcutaneous swelling, a periorbital mass or a past wound poultice is a valuable clue. Because the course is slow and eosinophilia often absent, many patients are first labelled with tumour, tuberculoma or vasculitis.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows irregular or beaded clustered ring enhancement, sometimes a tunnel-shaped tract, with adjacent white-matter oedema and later atrophy; change in position on serial imaging is highly suggestive. Specific ELISA for anti-sparganum IgG in serum or CSF has good sensitivity and specificity, though it can cross-react with other cestodes. Histology of the excised worm (a solid, unsegmented, ribbon-like larva) is definitive. Exclude tuberculoma, abscess, glioma and gnathostomiasis.
det.treatment: Complete surgical removal of the living larva is the definitive treatment and should be timed to the latest imaging, since the worm may have moved; leaving the head (scolex) behind risks recurrence. Praziquantel is commonly tried, sometimes at high doses (e.g. 50–75 mg/kg/day for several days or repeated courses), for inoperable or deep lesions, but evidence of cure is limited. Antiseizure medicines control seizures, and corticosteroids may help oedema. Follow with MRI and serology.
det.prognosis: Seizures and deficits often improve after the larva is removed; residual epilepsy and fixed deficits are common when diagnosis is delayed for years.
pearls: A lesion that moves between scans is sparganum until proved otherwise.
Ask specifically about frog or snake poultices and raw snake bile or blood, not only about eating raw meat.
Surgery, not drugs, is the cure — and use the newest MRI to plan it.
det.thd: Sparganosis เกิดจากตัวอ่อนพยาธิตืด Spirometra ที่ได้จากการกินกบ งู ไก่ดิบ ดื่มน้ำดีหรือเลือดงู พอกแผลหรือตาด้วยเนื้อกบ หรือดื่มน้ำที่ไม่สะอาด ตัวอ่อนชอนไชในสมองช้า ๆ ทำให้ชักเฉพาะที่หรืออ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกค่อยเป็นค่อยไป MRI เห็นรอยโรค ring enhancement เป็นกลุ่มหรือเป็นช่องอุโมงค์ และย้ายตำแหน่งเมื่อตรวจซ้ำ ตรวจ ELISA ช่วยยืนยัน การรักษาที่ได้ผลคือผ่าตัดเอาตัวพยาธิออกทั้งตัว ส่วน praziquantel ได้ผลไม่แน่นอน

name: Coenurosis
formal: A rare zoonotic infection in which the larval cyst (coenurus) of the dog tapeworm Taenia multiceps (or related species) develops in the brain parenchyma, ventricles, basal subarachnoid space, eye or subcutaneous tissue, causing mass effect, arachnoiditis and obstructive hydrocephalus.
simple: A dog tapeworm egg swallowed by mistake grows into a cyst packed with many worm heads inside the brain, which can block the fluid pathways.
ab: โคเอนูโรซิส
th: โรคหายากจากตัวอ่อนพยาธิตืดสุนัข Taenia multiceps ที่เป็นถุงน้ำมีหัวพยาธิหลายหัวภายใน อยู่ในเนื้อสมอง โพรงสมอง หรือช่องน้ำใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมองฐานกะโหลก ทำให้น้ำคั่งในสมองและอาการเหมือนก้อนในสมอง รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัดเอาถุงออกและใส่สายระบายน้ำสมองเมื่อจำเป็น
tempoNote: Cysts grow over months; basal and ventricular disease may decompensate within days when CSF flow suddenly blocks
feat: Raised intracranial pressure: headache, vomiting, papilloedema and gait disturbance from obstructive hydrocephalus
Focal seizures or hemiparesis with parenchymal cysts; cranial nerve palsies with basal arachnoiditis
Exposure to dogs living alongside sheep or goats (dogs eat infected brains of livestock)
Ocular and subcutaneous cysts may coexist
Mimics racemose neurocysticercosis; tissue examination usually makes the diagnosis
inv: MRI: thin-walled, sometimes multilocular cysts with multiple mural nodules (scolices), basal cistern or ventricular cysts and hydrocephalus
CSF: lymphocytic or eosinophilic pleocytosis with raised protein in basal disease
Histology of the excised cyst: many invaginated scolices on one membrane (unlike a single scolex of cysticercus)
Serology is unreliable and cross-reacts with cysticercosis

case.who: 38-year-old goat farmer from Narathiwat whose dogs roam among the herd
case.story: Four months of increasing headache, then a week of unsteady gait, urinary urgency and slowed thinking.
case.exam: Bilateral papilloedema, left sixth-nerve palsy and a broad-based gait.
case.tests: MRI: grape-like multilocular cysts in the suprasellar and prepontine cisterns with tiny mural nodules, enhancing basal meninges and hydrocephalus. Excised cyst wall shows numerous scolices on a single membrane.
case.q: Which parasite fits, and what is the immediate management?
case.a: Coenurosis from Taenia multiceps; relieve hydrocephalus (shunt or endoscopic surgery), excise accessible cysts, and give albendazole or praziquantel with steroid cover.
