det.patho: Taenia multiceps lives in the intestine of dogs and wild canids; sheep and goats are the usual intermediate hosts, where the larva in the brain causes the staggering disease known as gid. Humans are accidental hosts after swallowing eggs from dog faeces. The coenurus is a fluid-filled bladder bearing many scolices budding from its inner wall, and it may grow larger than a cysticercus and form grape-like clusters in the basal cisterns. Most human cases come from Africa, with sporadic reports elsewhere; T. serialis tends to cause subcutaneous or ocular cysts.
det.clinical: Parenchymal cysts behave like a slowly growing mass, with seizures, focal weakness or personality change. Cysts in the ventricles or basal subarachnoid space cause obstructive or communicating hydrocephalus and chronic basal arachnoiditis with cranial neuropathies and sometimes vasculitic infarcts. Ocular coenurosis presents with visual loss or a painful eye. Presentation may be sudden when a cyst blocks the fourth ventricle.
det.diagnosis: Imaging shows cysts that look like cysticerci or hydatid cysts, but multiple mural nodules within one cyst and clustering in the cisterns hint at coenurosis. Because serology cross-reacts and is not standardised, the diagnosis usually comes from the surgical specimen, where many scolices attached to a single bladder wall separate it from both cysticercus and hydatid. CSF may show eosinophils and high protein. Rule out neurocysticercosis, hydatid disease, tuberculous meningitis and cystic tumours.
det.treatment: Surgical excision of accessible cysts and CSF diversion for hydrocephalus are the mainstays. Albendazole (15 mg/kg/day) or praziquantel are used as adjuncts or for inoperable cysts, given with corticosteroids to blunt the inflammatory response to dying larvae; evidence comes from case reports. Shunts may block with inflammatory debris and need revision. Prevention relies on deworming dogs and stopping them from eating livestock brains.
det.prognosis: Parenchymal cysts removed whole carry a fair outlook, whereas basal and ventricular disease has a high rate of recurrence, shunt failure and death.
pearls: Many scolices on one cyst membrane = coenurus; one scolex = cysticercus; brood capsules and daughter cysts = hydatid.
Think of it in racemose-looking basal cysts in someone close to dogs and sheep or goats but with no pork link.
Steroid cover is needed when cysticidal drugs are used, as with cysticercosis.

name: Neuroschistosomiasis (cerebral and spinal cord schistosomiasis)
formal: Central nervous system involvement by Schistosoma eggs and the granulomatous reaction around them, usually presenting as a lumbosacral myeloradiculopathy (conus medullaris and cauda equina) with S. mansoni or S. haematobium, or as encephalopathy, seizures and tumour-like cerebral granulomas with S. japonicum and S. mekongi.
simple: Eggs from blood flukes caught by wading or swimming in infected fresh water lodge in the lower spinal cord or the brain and set off inflammation that can paralyse the legs or cause seizures.
ab: พยาธิใบไม้เลือดขึ้นไขสันหลัง
th: ภาวะที่ไข่พยาธิใบไม้เลือด Schistosoma ไปติดอยู่ในไขสันหลังส่วนล่าง (conus, cauda equina) หรือสมอง ทำให้เกิด granuloma อักเสบ อาการคือขาอ่อนแรง ปวดหลัง ปัสสาวะผิดปกติ หรือชัก ได้จากการลงแช่น้ำจืด เช่น แม่น้ำโขงตอนใต้หรือแอฟริกา รักษาด้วย corticosteroid ร่วมกับ praziquantel
tempoNote: Spinal disease evolves over days to a few weeks, months after water exposure; cerebral disease may appear in the acute (Katayama) phase or years later as a granulomatous mass
feat: Lumbar or leg pain followed by flaccid or mixed paraparesis, saddle sensory loss and urinary retention
Exposure months earlier: swimming or wading in endemic fresh water (Africa, Middle East, Brazil; Mekong in Laos and Cambodia for S. mekongi)
Cerebral form: headache, seizures, encephalopathy or focal signs from egg granulomas, mostly with S. japonicum
Blood eosinophilia is common but not universal; gut or bladder symptoms may be absent
Outcome depends on speed of steroid treatment
inv: MRI spine: expanded conus with T2 hyperintensity and patchy, arborised or micronodular ('ramified') enhancement, with nerve-root thickening
CSF: mild lymphocytic or eosinophilic pleocytosis and raised protein; Schistosoma antibodies in CSF if available
Serum schistosome serology, stool and urine microscopy for eggs, and rectal or bladder biopsy to find eggs
MRI brain in cerebral form: clustered nodular enhancing lesions with central linear enhancement and oedema

case.who: 33-year-old Thai construction worker back from a two-year contract in East Africa
case.story: He swam in a lake on weekends there. Three months after return he developed severe low back and buttock pain, then over ten days leg weakness and urinary retention.
case.exam: Asymmetric flaccid weakness of both legs, absent ankle reflexes, saddle hypoaesthesia and a palpable bladder.
case.tests: MRI: swollen conus with long T2 signal and beaded, branching enhancement; CSF 30 cells (eosinophils present), protein 1.1 g/L; serum Schistosoma serology positive; eggs of S. mansoni on rectal biopsy.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the treatment priority?
case.a: Schistosomal myeloradiculopathy (spinal neuroschistosomiasis); start high-dose corticosteroids promptly together with praziquantel, without waiting for surgery.

read.where: Chapter 46 Parasitic Infections of the Central Nervous System — Schistosomiasis
Chapter 8: What caused this intracerebral hemorrhage?

det.patho: Cercariae penetrate skin in fresh water, mature in the portal or vesical veins and lay eggs; eggs reach the CNS by retrograde flow through valveless venous plexuses (Batson plexus to the lower cord, or via portal–systemic shunts) or by worms straying into ectopic veins. Damage comes mainly from the host's granulomatous response to egg antigens rather than from the worm itself. S. mansoni and S. haematobium eggs favour the conus and cauda equina, while the small, abundant eggs of S. japonicum (and S. mekongi along the Lao–Cambodian Mekong) more often reach the brain.
det.clinical: Spinal schistosomiasis typically starts with lumbar or radicular pain, followed within days or weeks by leg weakness, sensory loss and sphincter failure, a pattern that combines conus and cauda equina signs; a granulomatous mass type and a more myelitic type are described. Cerebral disease can appear early as an acute encephalitis-like illness during Katayama fever, or later as single or multiple tumour-like granulomas causing seizures and focal deficits. Many patients never had a recognised systemic or urinary illness, so the travel and swimming history is key.
det.diagnosis: A presumptive diagnosis rests on a compatible lower-cord syndrome, typical MRI, evidence of exposure or infection (eggs in stool, urine or rectal biopsy, or positive serology) and exclusion of other causes; serum serology alone cannot separate past from active infection, and CSF antibodies add specificity. Spinal MRI shows conus enlargement with heterogeneous, often arborised enhancement. Biopsy is reserved for uncertain cases, especially mass lesions. Exclude other causes of myelitis, cord tumour and tuberculosis.
det.treatment: Corticosteroids are the most important treatment and should start early — for example IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days followed by oral prednisolone around 1 mg/kg/day, tapered over a few months. Praziquantel kills adult worms (commonly 40 mg/kg/day for S. mansoni/haematobium and 60 mg/kg/day in divided doses for S. japonicum/mekongi; many clinicians repeat or extend courses in neurological disease) and should be given under steroid cover. Surgery is limited to decompression for rapidly worsening compression or diagnostic doubt. Bladder care, thromboprophylaxis and rehabilitation complete management.
det.prognosis: Early steroid and praziquantel treatment brings good recovery in most; delayed treatment leaves permanent paraparesis and bladder dysfunction in a substantial proportion.
pearls: Conus plus cauda equina syndrome in a young adult with freshwater exposure: think schistosomiasis.
Steroids first and fast — the granuloma, not the worm, does the damage.
Thai travellers to southern Laos and Cambodia (Khong Island) can acquire S. mekongi.
det.thd: Neuroschistosomiasis เกิดจากไข่พยาธิใบไม้เลือดไปค้างในไขสันหลังส่วนปลายหรือสมอง ทำให้เกิด granuloma อักเสบ ผู้ป่วยมีประวัติลงเล่นน้ำจืดในพื้นที่ระบาด เช่น แอฟริกา หรือแม่น้ำโขงตอนใต้ อาการเด่นคือปวดหลังร้าวลงขา ขาอ่อนแรง ชารอบก้น ปัสสาวะไม่ออก MRI พบ conus บวมและมี enhancement แตกแขนง ต้องรีบให้ corticosteroid ขนาดสูงร่วมกับ praziquantel ยิ่งรักษาเร็วยิ่งฟื้นตัวดี

name: Cerebral paragonimiasis
formal: Brain (and occasionally spinal) infection by migrating lung flukes of the genus Paragonimus, acquired from raw or undercooked freshwater crabs or crayfish, producing haemorrhagic tracks, eosinophilic meningitis, granulomas and later calcified multilobulated masses, usually alongside or after pulmonary disease.
simple: A lung worm caught from eating raw freshwater crab wanders up into the brain, causing seizures, headache and bleeding spots that later turn into calcified clusters.
ab: พยาธิใบไม้ปอดขึ้นสมอง
th: การติดพยาธิใบไม้ปอด Paragonimus ที่ชอนไชจากปอดขึ้นไปในสมอง จากการกินปูน้ำตก ปูนา หรือกุ้งน้ำจืดดิบหรือสุกไม่ทั่ว ทำให้ชัก ปวดศีรษะ เลือดออกในสมอง หรือเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบชนิด eosinophil ภาพเรื้อรังเป็นหินปูนเป็นกลุ่มคล้ายฟองสบู่ รักษาด้วย praziquantel
tempoNote: Early migratory phase brings acute meningitis or haemorrhage within months of infection; chronic granulomatous and calcified stages cause seizures and deficits for years
feat: Chronic cough with rusty or bloody sputum and pleural effusion, often misdiagnosed as tuberculosis, precedes or accompanies brain disease
Seizures, headache, hemiparesis or visual field loss; children and young adults most affected
Diet history: raw or lightly cooked mountain or paddy crabs (som tam poo dong, crab paste) or crayfish
Peripheral eosinophilia and eosinophilic CSF in the active phase
Late stage: 'soap-bubble' or grape-cluster calcifications in one temporal–occipital region
inv: CT/MRI: early conglomerate ring-enhancing lesions with haemorrhage and oedema (grape-cluster sign); late multilobulated calcified masses with atrophy
Chest radiograph/CT: nodules, cavities, ring shadows or pleural effusion; sputum or pleural fluid for eggs
Serum and CSF Paragonimus serology (ELISA or immunoblot), available in Thai reference laboratories
CSF: eosinophilic pleocytosis, raised protein, sometimes xanthochromia

case.story: He has had a cough with streaks of blood for eight months, treated as tuberculosis without improvement. He recently had his first convulsion, preceded by flashing lights in the left visual field. He often eats raw mountain crab caught from waterfalls near his village.
case.exam: Left homonymous hemianopia; chest has dull right base.
case.tests: Eosinophils 18%; chest CT shows cavitating nodules and a right pleural effusion; brain MRI shows clustered ring-enhancing lesions with blood products in the right occipital lobe; Paragonimus immunoblot positive; Paragonimus eggs in sputum.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and treatment?
case.a: Cerebral paragonimiasis (likely P. heterotremus); praziquantel 25 mg/kg three times daily for 2–3 days with corticosteroid cover and an antiseizure medicine.

read.where: Chapter 46 Parasitic Infections of the Central Nervous System — Paragonimiasis

det.patho: Metacercariae in crab or crayfish muscle excyst in the gut, cross the bowel wall and diaphragm, and mature in the lungs, where they encapsulate in cystic cavities. Worms can stray upward through soft tissue around the jugular foramen and carotid canal to reach the brain, especially the temporal and occipital lobes. Their wandering leaves haemorrhagic, necrotic tracks with intense eosinophilic inflammation, followed by granulomas and dense calcification. In Thailand P. heterotremus is the main species, with foci in northern, north-eastern and central provinces.
det.clinical: The early invasive stage looks like meningitis, meningoencephalitis or a sudden intracerebral haemorrhage, while the later stage produces epilepsy, progressive hemiparesis, visual field defects and cognitive decline. About half have current or past lung symptoms, and pleural disease is common. Spinal involvement causes an extradural mass with cord compression. Ectopic subcutaneous migrating nodules may be another clue.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it when someone from an endemic district who eats raw freshwater crab and has lung lesions plus a brain lesion or eosinophilic meningitis. MRI in the active phase shows multiple conglomerated ring-enhancing nodules with haemorrhage and a tract-like pattern; CT later shows characteristic round or oval calcifications grouped in a cluster. Serology (ELISA, immunoblot) is the main confirmatory test because eggs are rarely found in CSF, though sputum, stool or pleural fluid may contain them. Tuberculosis is the most frequent misdiagnosis.
det.treatment: Praziquantel 25 mg/kg three times daily for 2–3 days is the standard drug; triclabendazole (10 mg/kg, one or two doses) is the main alternative. Corticosteroids are given before and during treatment in cerebral disease to limit oedema and reaction to dying worms, and courses may be repeated if serology or imaging remains active. Seizures need antiseizure medicine, and surgery is reserved for large haematoma, abscess-like mass, spinal compression or diagnostic doubt. Late calcified disease responds poorly to drugs and is managed as structural epilepsy.
det.prognosis: Early-stage disease usually responds well to praziquantel; once lesions have calcified, seizures and deficits often persist.
pearls: 'Tuberculosis' not improving on treatment plus eosinophilia and raw-crab eating: check Paragonimus.
Grape-cluster ring enhancement with blood products in a young patient from Loei, Saraburi or Nakhon Nayok — think lung fluke.
Soap-bubble calcifications in one posterior region are the chronic signature.
det.thd: Cerebral paragonimiasis เกิดจากพยาธิใบไม้ปอดที่ได้จากการกินปูน้ำจืดหรือปูภูเขาดิบ เช่น ส้มตำปูดิบ พยาธิไปอยู่ที่ปอดก่อน (ไอเป็นเลือด มักถูกคิดว่าเป็นวัณโรค) แล้วชอนไชขึ้นสมอง ทำให้ชัก ปวดศีรษะ เลือดออกในสมอง MRI เห็นก้อนเป็นกลุ่มคล้ายพวงองุ่นมีเลือดออก ระยะเรื้อรังเป็นหินปูนคล้ายฟองสบู่ วินิจฉัยด้วย serology และหาไข่ในเสมหะ รักษาด้วย praziquantel 25 mg/kg วันละ 3 ครั้ง 2–3 วัน ร่วมกับ steroid

name: Cerebral malaria (Plasmodium falciparum)
formal: A form of severe falciparum malaria defined by impaired consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale below 11 in adults, Blantyre Coma Scale below 3 in children) or repeated seizures in a patient with asexual P. falciparum parasitaemia after other causes of encephalopathy, such as hypoglycaemia, have been excluded or corrected.
simple: A dangerous type of malaria in which infected red blood cells clog the small vessels of the brain, causing fits and coma within days of fever.
ab: มาลาเรียขึ้นสมอง
th: มาลาเรียชนิดรุนแรงจากเชื้อ Plasmodium falciparum ที่ทำให้ซึมจนถึงโคม่าหรือชักซ้ำ เพราะเม็ดเลือดแดงที่ติดเชื้ออุดหลอดเลือดเล็กในสมอง พบในผู้เดินทางหรือคนที่อยู่ตามแนวชายแดน เช่น ตาก เป็นภาวะฉุกเฉิน ต้องให้ artesunate ทางหลอดเลือดดำทันทีและแก้ภาวะน้ำตาลต่ำ
tempoNote: Coma develops over hours to a few days after fever begins (often within 1–2 days in children); onset of illness usually 1–4 weeks after exposure
feat: Fever and travel or residence in a malarious area (Thai–Myanmar and Thai–Cambodian borders, forest work) followed by drowsiness, delirium or coma
Seizures (very frequent in children, less so in adults); symmetrical upper motor neuron signs, abnormal posturing or dysconjugate gaze; focal signs uncommon
Malarial retinopathy (retinal whitening, vessel changes, haemorrhages) supports the diagnosis
Other severe malaria features: hypoglycaemia, severe anaemia, jaundice, acute kidney injury, acidosis, pulmonary oedema, shock
Neck stiffness and photophobia are not typical — their presence should prompt lumbar puncture for meningitis
inv: Thick and thin blood films (repeat every 6–12 h if negative) and rapid diagnostic test; quantify parasitaemia
Capillary glucose immediately and repeatedly; lactate, renal and liver function, blood count, coagulation, blood cultures
Lumbar puncture when safe to exclude bacterial meningitis; CSF is normal or near-normal in cerebral malaria
Fundoscopy for malarial retinopathy; CT/MRI if focal signs, prolonged coma or doubt (brain swelling is common in children)

case.who: 24-year-old Karen migrant labourer from a maize farm near Mae Sot, Tak
case.story: Three days of fever with chills and headache, then he became confused and could not be woken this morning; he had a generalised seizure in the ambulance.
case.exam: Temperature 39.6 °C, GCS 8, mild jaundice, extensor plantar responses bilaterally, no neck stiffness; fundi show patchy retinal whitening.
case.tests: Thin film: P. falciparum 6% parasitaemia; glucose 2.8 mmol/L; creatinine 2.4 mg/dL; lactate 5 mmol/L; CSF normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the first-line antimalarial?
case.a: Cerebral (severe) falciparum malaria; give IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 hours then daily until oral intake is possible (at least 24 h), then complete a full course of an artemisinin combination therapy, while correcting glucose and treating seizures.

read.where: Chapter 46 Parasitic Infections of the Central Nervous System — Cerebral Malaria
Infectious Diseases of the Nervous System — Parasitic Infections: Cerebral Malaria

det.patho: Erythrocytes infected with mature P. falciparum express the PfEMP1 adhesin and stick to endothelium of cerebral microvessels (via receptors such as EPCR and ICAM-1), forming rosettes with uninfected cells. The resulting sequestration and microvascular obstruction, plus endothelial activation, inflammation and blood–brain barrier leakage, cause brain swelling, especially in children; metabolic factors such as hypoglycaemia, acidosis and seizures add to coma. Most cases arise in sub-Saharan African children, while in South-East Asia adults are affected more often and multi-organ failure is common. Severe malaria in Thailand is now uncommon and concentrated along forested border areas.
det.clinical: After a febrile prodrome, consciousness declines over hours to a couple of days; children often present with seizures, sometimes subtle or non-convulsive, and may show brainstem signs from swelling. Adults usually have a diffuse symmetrical encephalopathy with frequent kidney injury, jaundice, acidosis and acute lung injury. Retinopathy distinguishes true cerebral malaria from incidental parasitaemia in endemic children. After recovery, a minority develop a delayed post-malaria neurological syndrome of confusion, tremor or ataxia, and children may be left with epilepsy, cognitive and behavioural problems.
det.diagnosis: Confirm P. falciparum on blood film or rapid test in any febrile person with altered consciousness and possible exposure; a single negative film does not exclude it. Correct hypoglycaemia first and reassess, then apply the WHO severe malaria criteria. Exclude bacterial meningitis, viral encephalitis, sepsis, hypoglycaemia and post-ictal states — lumbar puncture once safe, or empirical antibiotics if delayed. Imaging is reserved for focal signs, persistent coma or suspected alternatives.
det.treatment: Per WHO guidance, IV (or IM) artesunate is first-line for all severe malaria: 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 hours and then once daily (3 mg/kg for children under 20 kg) until oral treatment can be taken after at least 24 hours, followed by a full 3-day artemisinin-based combination; parenteral quinine is only a fallback, and pre-referral rectal artesunate is used where IV treatment is not available. Supportive care includes glucose monitoring, benzodiazepines for seizures (avoid routine prophylactic phenobarbital), cautious fluids, transfusion for severe anaemia, dialysis for kidney failure and empirical antibiotics when sepsis cannot be excluded. Corticosteroids, mannitol and other adjunctive agents do not help and some cause harm. Check haemoglobin in the weeks after artesunate for delayed haemolysis.
det.prognosis: Even with artesunate, mortality is roughly 10–20%; around 10–20% of surviving children have lasting neurological or cognitive deficits, whereas most adult survivors recover fully.
pearls: Fever plus coma after forest or border exposure: do a blood film and check glucose before anything else.
Artesunate beats quinine for mortality in both adults and children — start it without waiting for full investigations.
Steroids are harmful in cerebral malaria; do not give them for brain swelling.
det.thd: มาลาเรียขึ้นสมองเกิดจากเม็ดเลือดแดงที่ติดเชื้อ P. falciparum เกาะติดผนังหลอดเลือดเล็กในสมอง ทำให้สมองบวมและขาดเลือด ผู้ป่วยมีไข้แล้วซึมลงจนโคม่าหรือชักซ้ำ มักร่วมกับไตวาย ตัวเหลือง น้ำตาลต่ำ เลือดเป็นกรด วินิจฉัยด้วย blood film หรือ rapid test และต้องแยกเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ การรักษาคือ IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg ที่ 0, 12, 24 ชั่วโมงแล้ววันละครั้ง ตามด้วยยา ACT จนครบ ร่วมกับดูแลประคับประคอง ห้ามให้ steroid

name: Lemierre syndrome
formal: Septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein following an oropharyngeal infection, usually caused by the anaerobe Fusobacterium necrophorum, with bacteraemia and metastatic septic emboli; intracranial spread can produce septic dural sinus thrombosis, meningitis, subdural empyema or carotid involvement.
simple: A throat infection that spreads into a large neck vein, forms an infected clot and sends germs to the lungs and sometimes to the brain.
th: การติดเชื้อในคอหอยหรือต่อมทอนซิลที่ลุกลามเข้าหลอดเลือดดำ internal jugular เกิดลิ่มเลือดติดเชื้อ มักเป็นเชื้อ Fusobacterium necrophorum ทำให้มีหนองกระจายไปปอด และอาจลามเข้าโพรงกะโหลกจนเกิดลิ่มเลือดในไซนัสดำหรือเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ
tempoNote: Sore throat or dental infection, then within days to about one week high fevers, rigors, neck pain and swelling; neurological complications follow over days
feat: Recent pharyngitis, tonsillitis, peritonsillar abscess or dental infection in an otherwise healthy adolescent or young adult
Swinging fever with unilateral neck pain, tenderness or swelling along the sternocleidomastoid
Septic pulmonary emboli: cough, pleuritic pain, multiple cavitating nodules
Intracranial extension: headache, papilloedema, meningism, lower cranial nerve palsies, Horner syndrome or seizures
Sepsis with raised inflammatory markers, often thrombocytopenia and abnormal liver tests
inv: Blood cultures held for anaerobes (Fusobacterium grows slowly)
Contrast CT neck or Doppler ultrasound for internal jugular thrombosis; CT chest for septic emboli
MRI brain with MR venography (or CT venography) for sigmoid/transverse sinus thrombosis, empyema or abscess
Lumbar puncture only after imaging excludes mass effect when meningitis is suspected

case.story: A week after a painful sore throat treated at a pharmacy, he develops rigors, a swollen tender left neck and a pounding headache with vomiting.
case.exam: Temperature 39.6 °C, tender cord-like swelling along the left jugular vein, bilateral papilloedema, mild neck stiffness, no focal weakness.
case.tests: CT neck shows left internal jugular thrombus; MRV shows thrombosis of the left sigmoid and transverse sinuses; CT chest has several cavitating nodules; anaerobic blood culture grows Fusobacterium necrophorum on day 4.
case.q: What is the syndrome and what are the cornerstones of treatment?
case.a: Lemierre syndrome with septic venous sinus thrombosis; prolonged IV beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor or carbapenem (often with metronidazole), drainage of any collection, and anticoagulation considered for the intracranial venous thrombosis.

det.patho: Fusobacterium necrophorum, a commensal anaerobe of the oropharynx, invades through tonsillar or peritonsillar tissue into the parapharyngeal space and the adjacent internal jugular vein. The resulting infected thrombus seeds the blood, and emboli lodge mainly in the lungs but also in joints, liver and other organs. Retrograde propagation through the jugular bulb carries infection into the sigmoid and transverse sinuses, and from there into the meninges, subdural space or brain. Inflammation of the carotid sheath can affect the carotid artery and the IX–XII cranial nerves and sympathetic chain.
det.clinical: The usual patient is a previously healthy teenager or young adult in whom a sore throat seems to settle and is followed several days later by high fever, rigors and lateral neck pain. Lung involvement with breathlessness and pleuritic pain is common. Neurological complications include headache and papilloedema from septic venous sinus thrombosis, meningism, hemiparesis or seizures from venous infarction or empyema, lower cranial nerve palsies and Horner syndrome. The condition was called the forgotten disease because antibiotic use made it rare, but cases have increased in recent decades.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in any young person with sepsis after pharyngitis plus neck pain or multiple lung nodules. Contrast CT of the neck or ultrasound shows jugular thrombosis; CT chest shows peripheral cavitating nodules. MRI with venography defines intracranial venous thrombosis and empyema. Blood cultures must be incubated anaerobically and may take several days; tell the laboratory, and use 16S PCR on pus when cultures are negative after antibiotics.
det.treatment: Give prolonged intravenous antibiotics active against anaerobes and beta-lactamase producers, such as piperacillin–tazobactam, ampicillin–sulbactam or a carbapenem, often with metronidazole, typically for 3–6 weeks guided by response. Drain abscesses and empyemas surgically. Anticoagulation is not routine for isolated neck vein thrombosis but is usually given when thrombus extends into the cerebral sinuses or progresses despite antibiotics, as in other CVT. Jugular ligation is now reserved for uncontrolled septic embolisation.
det.prognosis: With early recognition and appropriate antibiotics mortality is a few percent, but delayed diagnosis and intracranial extension raise the risk of death and lasting deficits.
pearls: Sore throat, then rigors and a painful neck: image the jugular vein.
Ask the laboratory to hold blood cultures for anaerobes.
Headache or papilloedema in Lemierre means MR venography for septic sinus thrombosis.
det.thd: Lemierre syndrome เกิดจากการติดเชื้อในคอหอยหรือทอนซิลลุกลามเข้าหลอดเลือดดำ internal jugular จนเกิดลิ่มเลือดติดเชื้อ เชื้อที่พบบ่อยคือ Fusobacterium necrophorum ผู้ป่วยมักเป็นวัยรุ่นที่เจ็บคอแล้วต่อมามีไข้หนาวสั่น ปวดบวมข้างคอ และมีก้อนหนองในปอด ถ้าลามเข้ากะโหลกทำให้เกิดลิ่มเลือดใน sigmoid/transverse sinus หรือเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ รักษาด้วยยาปฏิชีวนะครอบคลุม anaerobe นานหลายสัปดาห์ ระบายหนอง และพิจารณายาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือดเมื่อมี CVT

ddx.pt: Bland CVT lacks the preceding throat infection, septic picture and cavitating lung emboli
Murmur and valvular vegetations on echocardiography; emboli are arterial rather than via the jugular vein
Meningitis may complicate Lemierre, but primary meningitis has no neck vein thrombus or septic lung nodules

name: Perimesencephalic non-aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage
formal: A benign form of spontaneous subarachnoid haemorrhage in which blood is centred anterior to the midbrain or pons in the interpeduncular and prepontine cisterns, with negative vascular imaging; it is thought to be venous in origin and carries a low risk of rebleeding or vasospasm.
simple: A small bleed around the brainstem that causes a sudden severe headache but is not from an aneurysm and usually heals without lasting harm.
th: เลือดออกใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมองชนิดไม่ได้เกิดจากหลอดเลือดโป่งพอง เลือดอยู่หน้าก้านสมองส่วน midbrain หรือ pons ตรวจหลอดเลือดไม่พบความผิดปกติ เชื่อว่าเกิดจากหลอดเลือดดำ พยากรณ์โรคดีมาก เลือดออกซ้ำน้อย
tempoNote: Thunderclap or rapidly building headache, often a little slower than aneurysmal rupture; patient usually stays alert; recovery over days to weeks
feat: Sudden severe headache with neck stiffness but preserved consciousness (WFNS grade I–II)
Focal deficits and seizures are rare
CT: blood confined to cisterns in front of the midbrain/pons, at most minimal extension into the proximal Sylvian or interhemispheric fissures, no frank intraventricular blood
CT angiography and catheter angiography show no aneurysm
Low rates of rebleeding, delayed cerebral ischaemia and hydrocephalus
inv: Non-contrast CT early (pattern recognition is most reliable within about 3 days)
CT angiography; many centres also perform DSA, particularly if the blood pattern is atypical or CTA quality is limited
MRI brain/spine when angiography is negative but the pattern is not typical (e.g. spinal vascular malformation, dissection)

case.story: While lifting luggage into his car he notices a headache building to its worst over about a minute, with vomiting; he drives home and comes to hospital the next morning.
case.exam: Alert, GCS 15, mild neck stiffness, no focal signs; BP 158/92 mmHg.
case.tests: CT shows a small amount of blood in the interpeduncular and prepontine cisterns only; CTA and subsequent DSA show no aneurysm or dissection.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and is a repeat catheter angiogram routinely needed?
case.a: Perimesencephalic non-aneurysmal SAH; with a classic pattern and a good-quality negative angiogram, routine repeat angiography is generally not required and the outlook is excellent.

det.patho: Perimesencephalic haemorrhage accounts for roughly a tenth of spontaneous subarachnoid haemorrhages and about two-thirds of angiogram-negative cases. The source is unknown, but the limited volume, slow onset and anatomy point to rupture of a vein or venous plexus near the brainstem, and some patients have primitive deep venous drainage patterns such as direct drainage of the basal vein of Rosenthal into dural sinuses. Exertion and straining often precede the bleed. A vertebrobasilar aneurysm can rarely mimic the pattern, which is why vascular imaging is mandatory.
det.clinical: Patients present with abrupt headache, sometimes reaching its peak over a minute or more, with nausea, photophobia and neck stiffness. Consciousness is typically preserved and there are no focal signs. Complications such as hydrocephalus or delayed ischaemia are uncommon, and most patients are discharged quickly. Some experience temporary headaches, fatigue or mood symptoms in the following months.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis depends on an early CT with a strict blood distribution (centred anterior to the brainstem, no frank intraventricular extension, no complete filling of the Sylvian fissures) plus negative angiography. Most guidelines accept a high-quality negative CTA, while others still advise DSA; when the pattern is classic and the first DSA is negative, repeat angiography adds little. A non-perimesencephalic angiogram-negative pattern needs repeat imaging at 1–2 weeks and MRI to search for a hidden cause.
det.treatment: Management is supportive: analgesia, antiemetics, blood pressure control and early mobilisation. Nimodipine is often started until the diagnosis is confirmed and many stop it once angiography is negative and the pattern is classic. Intensive monitoring for vasospasm is usually unnecessary. Patients can be reassured that rebleeding is very rare and that life expectancy is normal.
det.prognosis: Excellent: nearly all patients return to independence, and recurrence or rebleeding is exceptional.
pearls: Alert patient, blood in front of the brainstem, negative angiogram: think perimesencephalic, not missed aneurysm.
The pattern can only be read reliably on an early CT.
A vertebrobasilar aneurysm can look similar, so vascular imaging is never skipped.
det.thd: Perimesencephalic non-aneurysmal SAH เป็นเลือดออกใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมองที่อยู่เฉพาะหน้าก้านสมอง (interpeduncular และ prepontine cistern) ผู้ป่วยปวดศีรษะเฉียบพลันแต่รู้สึกตัวดี ไม่มีอาการเฉพาะที่ CTA หรือ DSA ไม่พบหลอดเลือดโป่งพอง เชื่อว่าเลือดมาจากหลอดเลือดดำ ภาวะแทรกซ้อนเช่นหลอดเลือดหดเกร็งหรือเลือดออกซ้ำพบน้อยมาก รักษาแบบประคับประคองและพยากรณ์โรคดี แต่ต้องตรวจหลอดเลือดทุกรายเพื่อไม่พลาด aneurysm ในระบบ vertebrobasilar

name: Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder of the CNS (PTLD)
formal: A lymphoid proliferation, usually EBV-driven diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, arising in solid-organ or haematopoietic stem-cell transplant recipients because of iatrogenic T-cell immunosuppression; CNS involvement may be isolated (primary CNS PTLD) or part of systemic disease.
simple: A type of lymphoma that grows in the brain of people taking anti-rejection drugs after a transplant, often linked to the Epstein–Barr virus.
ab: Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder of the CNS
th: มะเร็งต่อมน้ำเหลืองที่เกิดในผู้ป่วยหลังปลูกถ่ายอวัยวะซึ่งได้ยากดภูมิคุ้มกัน ส่วนมากสัมพันธ์กับไวรัส EBV อาจเกิดเฉพาะในสมองหรือร่วมกับอวัยวะอื่น ต้องแยกจากการติดเชื้อฉวยโอกาส เช่น toxoplasma, nocardia, เชื้อรา และ PML
tempoNote: Weeks of progressive headache, confusion or focal deficit, usually months to years after transplantation (CNS disease tends to occur later than early nodal PTLD)
feat: Kidney (most common in Thailand), liver, heart, lung or stem-cell transplant recipient on calcineurin inhibitor, mycophenolate or belatacept
Subacute confusion, personality change, headache, seizures or focal weakness
Often afebrile; systemic B symptoms only if extracerebral disease
Single or multiple periventricular or deep enhancing lesions, frequently ring-enhancing with necrosis (unlike the solid enhancement of PCNSL in immunocompetent patients)
Higher risk with EBV-seronegative recipient of EBV-positive graft and with intensive T-cell-depleting induction
inv: MRI brain with contrast, diffusion and perfusion; whole-body PET-CT for systemic disease
Plasma EBV DNA load; CSF cytology, flow cytometry and EBV PCR when safe
Stereotactic biopsy for histology and EBER in situ hybridisation (avoid steroids before biopsy if possible)
Exclude opportunistic infection: toxoplasma serology/PCR, cryptococcal antigen, fungal markers, JC virus PCR, nocardia cultures

case.who: 56-year-old woman from Ubon Ratchathani, 4 years after a deceased-donor kidney transplant
case.story: Three weeks of slowed thinking, word-finding problems and new left-sided headaches; her family says she forgets her tacrolimus doses.
case.exam: Afebrile, disoriented to date, mild right pronator drift, no meningism.
case.tests: MRI: two ring-enhancing periventricular lesions in the left hemisphere with restricted diffusion of the solid rim; plasma EBV DNA high; toxoplasma IgG negative; biopsy shows a large B-cell lymphoma that is positive for EBV.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what are the first therapeutic steps?
case.a: Primary CNS PTLD; reduce immunosuppression with the transplant team (often switching to an mTOR inhibitor), then high-dose methotrexate-based chemotherapy with rituximab, with whole-brain radiotherapy or other consolidation as needed.

read.where: Chapter 2: Immunodeficiency-associated primary CNS diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

det.patho: Suppressing T-cell immunity to prevent rejection removes control of latent EBV-infected B cells, allowing polyclonal then monoclonal B-cell proliferation. Most CNS PTLD is monomorphic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma positive for EBV, though EBV-negative cases occur late after transplantation. The brain may be the only site, perhaps because it is shielded from immune surveillance and from systemic reduction of immunosuppression. Risk depends on the type and intensity of immunosuppression, EBV mismatch, the organ transplanted and time since transplant.
det.clinical: Primary CNS PTLD usually appears years after kidney transplantation, presenting over weeks with cognitive or behavioural change, headache, seizures or focal signs. Fever and night sweats are often absent unless disease is systemic. Imaging shows one or more enhancing lesions, often periventricular or in deep grey matter, frequently with central necrosis and ring enhancement that mimics abscess or toxoplasmosis. Leptomeningeal or ocular involvement may occur.
det.diagnosis: Biopsy is the key step, because the radiological differential includes toxoplasma, nocardia, fungal abscess, tuberculoma, PML and glioma. Plasma EBV DNA supports but does not prove the diagnosis, and CSF studies may be diagnostic when lumbar puncture is safe. Steroids before biopsy can make lymphoma vanish and should be avoided where possible. Staging includes PET-CT, ophthalmological assessment and bone marrow when indicated.
det.treatment: Reduction of immunosuppression is the first step and is coordinated with the transplant team to balance tumour control against graft loss; switching from a calcineurin inhibitor to an mTOR inhibitor such as sirolimus is common. Rituximab alone penetrates the brain poorly, so most patients receive high-dose methotrexate-based chemotherapy with rituximab, sometimes with cytarabine, with whole-brain radiotherapy for consolidation or for those unfit for chemotherapy. EBV-specific cytotoxic T cells (for example tabelecleucel, approved in Europe in 2022) are an option for relapsed or refractory EBV-positive disease. Seizures are treated with agents that do not interact with transplant drugs, such as levetiracetam.
det.prognosis: Historically poor, but contemporary methotrexate-based regimens achieve durable remission in a substantial proportion; outcome is worse with poor performance status and late EBV-negative disease.
pearls: New ring-enhancing lesion in a transplant recipient: think of PTLD as well as abscess and toxoplasma.
Check plasma EBV load and avoid steroids before the biopsy.
Treatment starts with cutting back immunosuppression in partnership with the transplant team.
det.thd: PTLD ในระบบประสาทส่วนกลางเป็นมะเร็งต่อมน้ำเหลืองชนิด B-cell ที่เกิดในผู้ป่วยหลังปลูกถ่ายอวัยวะซึ่งได้ยากดภูมิคุ้มกัน ส่วนใหญ่สัมพันธ์กับไวรัส EBV อาการค่อย ๆ เป็นภายในหลายสัปดาห์ เช่น สับสน ปวดศีรษะ ชัก หรืออ่อนแรงครึ่งซีก MRI มักพบรอยโรคขอบจับสีแบบวงแหวน ต้องแยกจาก toxoplasmosis, ฝีจากเชื้อรา/nocardia และ PML การวินิจฉัยต้องตัดชิ้นเนื้อ รักษาโดยลดยากดภูมิคุ้มกันร่วมกับทีมปลูกถ่าย และให้ high-dose methotrexate ร่วมกับ rituximab

name: Acute HIV infection — neurological syndromes
formal: Neurological disorders arising during primary HIV infection (seroconversion), including aseptic meningitis, meningoencephalitis, Bell palsy and other cranial neuropathies, Guillain–Barré syndrome, brachial neuritis, sensory ganglionopathy and myelopathy, often accompanying a mononucleosis-like illness before HIV antibodies are detectable.
simple: Nerve or brain problems that can happen in the first weeks after catching HIV, sometimes before the usual HIV antibody test turns positive.
th: อาการทางระบบประสาทที่เกิดในช่วงติดเชื้อ HIV ระยะแรก (seroconversion) เช่น เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบชนิดไม่มีหนอง ใบหน้าอัมพาต GBS หรือเส้นประสาทรับความรู้สึกอักเสบ มักมีไข้ ผื่น เจ็บคอร่วมด้วย และผลแอนติบอดีอาจยังเป็นลบ ต้องตรวจ HIV RNA หรือ p24 antigen
tempoNote: Begins 2–6 weeks after exposure, often with fever, rash and sore throat; neurological features evolve over days to weeks and many improve as viraemia falls
feat: Mononucleosis-like prodrome: fever, maculopapular rash, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, mouth ulcers
Headache with lymphocytic aseptic meningitis or, less often, encephalitis or seizures
Facial palsy or other cranial neuropathy
Acute demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (GBS) with CSF pleocytosis rather than pure albuminocytological dissociation
Painful sensory ganglionopathy/neuropathy or brachial plexitis in some
inv: Fourth-generation HIV antigen/antibody assay plus HIV-1 RNA viral load (antibody tests can be negative in the window period)
CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein; CSF HIV RNA
Nerve conduction studies for weakness or sensory loss; MRI brain/spine as indicated
Screen for co-transmitted infections: syphilis, hepatitis B and C

case.who: 24-year-old male university student from Chiang Rai
case.story: Two weeks of fever, sore throat and a faint rash on the trunk, followed by five days of ascending leg weakness and tingling in the hands; reports a new sexual partner six weeks earlier.
case.exam: Symmetric distal-predominant weakness, absent reflexes, mild bilateral facial weakness, cervical lymphadenopathy.
case.tests: Nerve conduction shows a demyelinating pattern; CSF protein 1.1 g/L with 22 lymphocytes/µL; HIV antigen/antibody assay reactive with antibody confirmation indeterminate, HIV-1 RNA 3.8 million copies/mL.
case.q: Why is the CSF cell count a clue here, and what treatment should accompany IVIG?
case.a: Pleocytosis in an otherwise typical GBS suggests an infective trigger such as acute HIV; start antiretroviral therapy promptly (rapid ART initiation) alongside standard GBS care.

read.where: Case 44 HIV seroconversion and dorsal root ganglioneuronopathy

det.patho: HIV reaches the nervous system within days of infection, carried by infected monocytes and lymphocytes, and is detectable in CSF early. Neurological features in the acute phase reflect a combination of direct viral invasion of the meninges, high-level immune activation with cytokine release, and immune-mediated attack on peripheral nerve and dorsal root ganglia. CD8 lymphocytosis and transient CD4 depletion during this phase may unmask other infections. The extent of early CNS seeding may influence later reservoirs, which is one argument for rapid treatment.
det.clinical: Most acute infections cause a flu-like illness, and neurological involvement occurs in a minority, most often headache and aseptic meningitis. Other presentations include facial palsy, GBS, brachial neuritis, painful sensory neuropathy or ganglionopathy, myelopathy and, rarely, encephalitis with seizures or rhabdomyolysis. Symptoms often appear while antibody tests are still negative or indeterminate. Any young adult with an unexplained acute neurological syndrome plus fever, rash or recent risk exposure should be tested.
det.diagnosis: Use a fourth-generation antigen/antibody immunoassay and an HIV-1 RNA test; a very high viral load with negative or indeterminate antibody differentiation confirms acute infection, and repeat testing documents seroconversion. CSF typically shows a mild lymphocytic pleocytosis and raised protein. In GBS, more than about 50 cells/µL argues against idiopathic GBS and points to HIV, Lyme disease, CMV or lymphoma. Neurophysiology and MRI define the syndrome.
det.treatment: Start antiretroviral therapy rapidly, ideally within days of diagnosis, using a regimen such as bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide or dolutegravir-based therapy (Thai national guidelines favour dolutegravir-based first line); obtain resistance testing and baseline labs without delaying treatment. Manage GBS with IVIG or plasma exchange and standard supportive care; Bell palsy with prednisolone. Unlike cryptococcal or TB meningitis, acute HIV meningitis is not a reason to delay ART. Offer partner notification, PrEP counselling for partners and screening for other sexually transmitted infections.
det.prognosis: Most acute neurological syndromes resolve fully or largely with ART and standard treatment; long-term outlook is that of treated HIV, close to normal life expectancy.
pearls: Window-period HIV: a negative antibody test does not exclude it — ask for HIV RNA.
GBS with CSF pleocytosis is a clue to HIV seroconversion.
Start ART promptly; acute HIV meningitis does not need the delay used for cryptococcal or TB meningitis.
det.thd: การติดเชื้อ HIV ระยะเฉียบพลัน (seroconversion) อาจมีอาการทางระบบประสาท เช่น เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบชนิดไม่มีหนอง ใบหน้าอัมพาต GBS เส้นประสาทแขนอักเสบ หรือ ganglionopathy มักมีไข้ ผื่น เจ็บคอ ต่อมน้ำเหลืองโตนำมาก่อน ผลตรวจแอนติบอดีอาจยังเป็นลบ จึงต้องตรวจ antigen/antibody รุ่นที่ 4 ร่วมกับ HIV RNA ถ้าพบ GBS ที่น้ำไขสันหลังมีเซลล์สูงให้นึกถึง HIV รักษาด้วยการเริ่มยาต้านไวรัสโดยเร็วร่วมกับการรักษาตามกลุ่มอาการ

name: Subjective cognitive decline (SCD)
formal: A self-perceived, persistent worsening of cognition compared with a person's previous level, not related to an acute event, in someone whose performance on standardised cognitive testing remains within the normal range for age and education.
simple: Feeling that your memory or thinking has got worse even though proper memory tests still come out normal.
ab: ความจำแย่ลงตามความรู้สึก
th: ผู้ป่วยรู้สึกว่าความจำหรือความคิดแย่ลงเรื้อรัง แต่ผลตรวจทางประสาทจิตวิทยายังปกติ สาเหตุพบบ่อยคือซึมเศร้า วิตกกังวล นอนไม่พอ และยา บางรายเป็นระยะแรกสุดของ Alzheimer จึงควรติดตามเป็นระยะ ไม่แนะนำตรวจ biomarker ในคนที่ไม่มีอาการผิดปกติจริงนอกงานวิจัย
tempoNote: Complaints persist for months to years; most people stay stable, but roughly a quarter progress to MCI over several years, more often when SCD-plus features are present
feat: Self-reported decline in memory or word finding with normal scores on validated tests and full independence
Frequent links to low mood, anxiety, poor sleep, chronic pain, sedative or anticholinergic drugs
Higher risk of later Alzheimer's disease when onset is after 60, memory-focused, within the last 5 years, worrying to the person and confirmed by an informant (SCD-plus)
Ability to give a detailed, self-critical account of lapses — often the patient attends alone
inv: Informant history and validated cognitive tests (MoCA, a delayed-recall test such as FCSRT); repeat in 12–24 months
Screen mood, anxiety, sleep (including sleep apnoea), hearing and medication burden
Basic blood tests (B12, thyroid, glucose, renal and liver function) and MRI if red flags or an unusual course
Amyloid or plasma p-tau217 testing is not recommended routinely in cognitively unimpaired people outside research

case.who: 58-year-old female hospital pharmacist from Nakhon Ratchasima, recently promoted
case.story: For a year she has felt she forgets colleagues' names and loses her train of thought in meetings; she sleeps 5 hours a night and feels constantly tense. Her husband notices nothing unusual.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination. MoCA 29/30; delayed recall 5/5. PHQ-9 suggests moderate depression and GAD-7 high anxiety.
case.tests: B12, TSH, glucose normal. Detailed neuropsychology within normal limits for age and education.
case.q: How should her complaint be classified and managed?
case.a: Subjective cognitive decline with prominent mood and sleep contributors; treat the depression, anxiety and sleep problem, address risk factors and reassess cognition in 1–2 years rather than ordering amyloid tests.

read.where: Case 2 Man with subjective complaints but abnormal CSF

Series 1 — New landscape of the diagnosis of Alzheimer disease

det.patho: SCD is a symptom state rather than one disease. In many people it reflects anxiety, depression, poor sleep or medication effects, while in a minority it is the first perception of early Alzheimer pathology before tests can detect change. Population studies show amyloid positivity rises with age and with SCD-plus features, and SCD roughly doubles the risk of later dementia compared with people without complaints.
det.clinical: Patients describe word-finding pauses, forgotten names, misplaced items and difficulty concentrating, yet keep working and managing finances. Informants usually notice little; when the informant is more worried than the patient, true impairment is more likely. Red flags for an underlying neurodegenerative process include onset after 60, a memory-dominant pattern, progression on serial tests and family concern. Functional cognitive disorder overlaps strongly and is suggested by vivid self-monitoring and mismatch between reported lapses and daily performance.
det.diagnosis: SCD is diagnosed when the person reports persistent decline, standardised testing is normal for age and education, and no other disorder fully explains the complaint. The 2024 Alzheimer's Association revised criteria allow a biological AD diagnosis in an unimpaired person with abnormal core biomarkers, but they advise against testing asymptomatic people in routine care; a positive result neither predicts timing nor opens access to anti-amyloid therapy. Serial testing over 1–2 years is the most useful clinical tool.
det.treatment: Treat contributors first: depression and anxiety (CBT, SSRIs), insomnia or sleep apnoea, hearing loss and anticholinergic or sedative drugs. Advise on modifiable dementia risk factors — blood pressure, diabetes, exercise, smoking, alcohol, social engagement and education (Lancet Commission 2024). Cholinesterase inhibitors and anti-amyloid antibodies have no role. Offer follow-up and, where available, referral to prevention research.
det.prognosis: Most people remain stable or improve; a minority, mainly older people with SCD-plus features or positive biomarkers, progress to MCI and dementia over 5–10 years.
pearls: Normal tests plus a worried patient who comes alone usually means SCD; a worried family and an unconcerned patient suggests real decline.
Look for depression, anxiety, poor sleep and anticholinergic drugs before thinking of neurodegeneration.
Biomarker testing in cognitively unimpaired people is a research tool, not routine care.
det.thd: SCD คือภาวะที่ผู้ป่วยรู้สึกว่าความจำแย่ลงเอง แต่การทดสอบมาตรฐานยังปกติและยังทำงานได้ตามปกติ สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยคือซึมเศร้า วิตกกังวล นอนไม่พอ และยาที่มีฤทธิ์ anticholinergic ส่วนน้อยเป็นระยะแรกของ Alzheimer โดยเฉพาะผู้สูงอายุที่มีญาติสังเกตเห็นด้วย การดูแลคือรักษาสาเหตุร่วม ปรับปัจจัยเสี่ยง และนัดตรวจซ้ำทุก 1–2 ปี ไม่แนะนำตรวจ amyloid ในคนที่ผลทดสอบปกติ

name: Posterior cortical atrophy (PCA)
formal: A neurodegenerative syndrome with progressive, early and predominant impairment of visuospatial and visuoperceptual function, often with elements of Balint and Gerstmann syndromes, due to parieto-occipital cortical degeneration and caused by Alzheimer's disease pathology in most cases.
simple: A form of dementia, usually Alzheimer's disease, that first damages the back of the brain so that people have trouble seeing and judging space while their eyes are healthy.
ab: สมองส่วนหลังฝ่อ
th: กลุ่มอาการสมองเสื่อมที่เริ่มด้วยปัญหาการมองเห็นเชิงพื้นที่และการรับรู้ภาพ ทั้งที่ตาปกติ จากสมองส่วน parieto-occipital ฝ่อ ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจากพยาธิสภาพ Alzheimer ความจำมักดีในระยะแรก ผู้ป่วยมักไปพบจักษุแพทย์หลายครั้งก่อนได้รับการวินิจฉัย
tempoNote: Insidious onset usually between 50 and 65 years; slow progression over years with later spread to memory, language and executive function
feat: Trouble reading lines of text, judging distance, finding objects in clutter, parking or pouring, with normal acuity and eye examination
Simultanagnosia, optic ataxia and oculomotor apraxia (Balint), and dyscalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia and left–right confusion (Gerstmann)
Dressing apraxia, environmental disorientation and sometimes object or face recognition difficulty
Relatively preserved episodic memory, insight and language early; frequent depression and anxiety
Younger onset than typical Alzheimer's disease; repeated optometry or ophthalmology visits before diagnosis
inv: Neuro-ophthalmic and cognitive testing targeting visuospatial and visuoperceptual function; visual fields (homonymous defects can occur)
MRI: bilateral parieto-occipital atrophy, often right > left, with relative hippocampal sparing; FDG-PET occipitoparietal hypometabolism
Amyloid and tau biomarkers (amyloid PET, CSF Aβ42/40 and p-tau, plasma p-tau217) to confirm AD pathology
If AD biomarkers are negative, consider DLB (DaT-SPECT), CBD, and rapidly progressive causes such as CJD (DWI MRI, RT-QuIC)

case.story: For two years he has misjudged steps, spills water beside the glass and cannot find the gold chain he is looking at on his bench. Three eye clinics found no cause and his glasses were changed twice.
case.exam: Acuity 6/6 both eyes, normal fundi and fields. He describes one item of a busy picture at a time, misreaches for objects in either field, cannot copy a cube, and miscalculates simple change; recalls 4/5 words after delay.
case.tests: MRI bilateral parieto-occipital atrophy with mild right predominance; hippocampi nearly normal. Plasma p-tau217 raised and amyloid PET positive.
case.q: What is the syndrome and the likely pathology?
case.a: Posterior cortical atrophy due to Alzheimer's disease; offer a cholinesterase inhibitor, low-vision rehabilitation and safety advice (stop driving), and discuss anti-amyloid therapy eligibility if he meets MCI or mild dementia criteria and MRI is suitable.

read.where: 22 Vascular Syndromes of the Forebrain, Brainstem, and Cerebellum

det.patho: Over 80% of cases are caused by Alzheimer pathology with plaques and especially tangles concentrated in occipital, parietal and posterior temporal association cortex; minority causes are corticobasal degeneration, Lewy body disease and prion disease. The dorsal visual stream (where and how) is usually hit hardest, giving spatial and reaching problems, while ventral stream involvement causes object, face and colour recognition difficulty. APOE ε4 is less over-represented than in typical AD, and onset is earlier.
det.clinical: The earliest complaints are usually about reading, driving, stairs, finding things and judging distances, so patients often see optometrists for years. Examination shows elements of Balint syndrome, Gerstmann syndrome, constructional and dressing apraxia and alexia, with memory, language and insight relatively spared until later. Anxiety and depression are common because insight is preserved. Some patients develop myoclonus or parkinsonism, which should prompt thought of non-AD pathology.
det.diagnosis: Consensus criteria (2017) require an insidious, progressive syndrome dominated by visual and parietal deficits with relative sparing of memory, language and behaviour, and no other cause such as tumour, stroke or primary eye disease. MRI or FDG-PET shows posterior predominant change. Because most cases are AD, amyloid PET, CSF or plasma p-tau217 testing confirms the cause and allows inclusion under the 2024 biological AD framework; negative AD biomarkers should trigger a search for Lewy, CBD or prion disease.
det.treatment: Cholinesterase inhibitors are used as for AD. Anti-amyloid antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab) may be considered for biomarker-confirmed AD at the MCI or mild dementia stage if MRI and APOE criteria are met, although PCA was not specifically studied. Practical support is crucial: low-vision and occupational therapy, audio books, talking devices, uncluttered home layout, stopping driving and treating anxiety or depression.
det.prognosis: Progression is gradual over about 8–12 years, with later memory and language decline resembling AD; insight usually remains longer than in amnestic AD.
pearls: Normal eye examination plus inability to read or reach accurately in a person in their fifties should suggest PCA.
Test for simultanagnosia with a busy picture and for optic ataxia by reaching in peripheral vision.
Most PCA is Alzheimer's disease, so biomarkers confirm it and open access to AD treatments and trials.
det.thd: PCA คือสมองเสื่อมที่เริ่มจากสมองส่วนหลัง (parieto-occipital) ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจาก Alzheimer อาการเด่นคืออ่านหนังสือลำบาก กะระยะไม่ได้ หยิบของพลาด มองเห็นทีละส่วน (simultanagnosia) ทั้งที่ตาปกติ ความจำมักดีในช่วงแรก ยืนยันด้วย MRI และ biomarker ของ Alzheimer เช่น amyloid PET หรือ plasma p-tau217 รักษาด้วย cholinesterase inhibitor ร่วมกับการฟื้นฟูการมองเห็นและงดขับรถ

name: Mixed dementia (Alzheimer's disease with cerebrovascular disease)
formal: Dementia in which Alzheimer's disease pathology and clinically meaningful cerebrovascular disease (infarcts, small vessel disease or haemorrhage) coexist and both are judged to contribute to the cognitive decline; it is the commonest pathology found in very old people with dementia.
simple: Dementia caused by a combination of Alzheimer's disease and damage from strokes or narrowed small blood vessels in the brain.
ab: สมองเสื่อมชนิดผสม
th: สมองเสื่อมที่เกิดจาก Alzheimer ร่วมกับโรคหลอดเลือดสมอง (infarct, small vessel disease หรือเลือดออก) ทั้งสองส่วนทำให้ความจำเสื่อม พบบ่อยมากในผู้สูงอายุมาก การรักษาคือ cholinesterase inhibitor ร่วมกับควบคุมปัจจัยเสี่ยงหลอดเลือดอย่างเข้มงวด และมักไม่เหมาะกับยา anti-amyloid
tempoNote: Gradual decline typical of AD, sometimes with abrupt steps after strokes; more common after age 80
feat: Episodic memory loss of Alzheimer type combined with slowed processing and executive dysfunction
Gradual progression interrupted by stepwise worsening or new focal signs after strokes
Vascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, atrial fibrillation) and gait slowing or urinary urgency
MRI showing both hippocampal or temporoparietal atrophy and infarcts or extensive white matter disease
inv: MRI with FLAIR and SWI: infarcts, lacunes, white matter hyperintensities, microbleeds plus medial temporal atrophy
AD biomarkers (CSF, amyloid PET or plasma p-tau217) to prove the Alzheimer component when it alters management
Vascular work-up: BP, HbA1c, lipids, ECG/rhythm monitoring, carotid imaging when relevant
Neuropsychology covering memory and executive/processing speed domains

case.who: 81-year-old retired female schoolteacher from Sukhothai with hypertension and diabetes
case.story: Three years of gradually forgetting appointments and repeating stories; a year ago she suddenly became slower and needed help with cooking after a brief episode of right-hand weakness.
case.exam: MoCA 16/30 with poor recall and executive errors; mild right pronator drift, short-stepped gait.
case.tests: MRI: bilateral hippocampal atrophy, an old left corona radiata lacune, several other lacunes and confluent white matter hyperintensities; plasma p-tau217 elevated.
case.q: What type of dementia is this and how should it be treated?
case.a: Mixed dementia (AD plus cerebrovascular disease); start a cholinesterase inhibitor, control BP, diabetes and lipids, continue antiplatelet secondary prevention, and avoid anti-amyloid antibodies because of the vascular burden.

det.patho: Autopsy series show that most people dying with dementia after 80 have more than one pathology, with AD changes and vascular lesions being the commonest pairing. Vascular injury lowers the threshold at which amyloid and tau produce symptoms, so smaller amounts of each pathology can add up to dementia. Shared risk factors, for example hypertension, diabetes and APOE ε4, link the two, and cerebral amyloid angiopathy sits at their crossroads.
det.clinical: The picture combines AD-type amnesia with the slowing, apathy, executive dysfunction and gait change typical of small vessel disease. A gradually progressive course with superimposed steps, or a stroke that unmasks a pre-existing memory problem, is common. Depression, urinary symptoms and falls occur more often than in pure AD. Clinicians often under-recognise one component, especially vascular change in AD clinics and AD pathology in stroke clinics.
det.diagnosis: There are no robust clinical criteria; the diagnosis rests on a syndrome compatible with AD plus imaging evidence of cerebrovascular disease thought to contribute (VASCOG and NIA-AA frameworks). Biomarkers can confirm the Alzheimer component, and the 2024 AA revised criteria emphasise reporting copathologies. MRI with SWI quantifies infarcts, white matter disease and microbleeds, which also matters for anti-amyloid eligibility.
det.treatment: Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine give modest benefit as in AD. Aggressive vascular risk control — BP (SPRINT MIND supports intensive control), diabetes, lipids, smoking, exercise and anticoagulation for AF — prevents further vascular injury. Anti-amyloid antibodies are generally unsuitable when MRI shows more than minimal vascular disease, multiple microbleeds or prior haemorrhage, or when anticoagulation is needed. Treat depression and support carers.
det.prognosis: Decline is often faster than in either pure AD or pure vascular dementia, and mortality is higher, partly due to recurrent stroke.
pearls: In the very old, mixed pathology is usual rather than exceptional.
A stroke can unmask previously silent AD — ask about memory before the event.
Vascular burden on MRI often rules out anti-amyloid antibodies but makes risk-factor control even more valuable.
det.thd: Mixed dementia คือสมองเสื่อมที่มีทั้ง Alzheimer และโรคหลอดเลือดสมองร่วมกัน พบบ่อยที่สุดในผู้ที่อายุมากกว่า 80 ปี อาการมีทั้งความจำเสื่อมแบบ Alzheimer และความคิดช้า การวางแผนบกพร่อง เดินช้า บางรายแย่ลงเป็นขั้นหลัง stroke MRI พบทั้งสมองส่วน hippocampus ฝ่อและรอยโรคหลอดเลือด รักษาด้วย cholinesterase inhibitor ร่วมกับคุมความดัน เบาหวาน ไขมัน และมักไม่เหมาะกับยา anti-amyloid

name: Occipital condyle syndrome
formal: Skull-base syndrome of unilateral occipital headache and neck pain with an ipsilateral hypoglossal (XII) nerve palsy, caused by a lesion of the occipital condyle and hypoglossal canal, most often metastatic cancer.
simple: A one-sided ache at the back of the head with a tongue that drifts to the same side, usually because cancer has spread to the skull-base bone.
ab: skull base metastasis with XII palsy
isolated hypoglossal palsy with occipital pain
th: กลุ่มอาการปวดท้ายทอยข้างเดียวร่วมกับเส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 12 อ่อนแรงข้างเดียวกัน (ลิ้นเบี้ยวไปข้างที่ปวด) มักเกิดจากมะเร็งแพร่กระจายมาที่ occipital condyle เป็นสัญญาณแรกของมะเร็งได้
tempoNote: Steadily worsening pain over weeks; tongue weakness may follow the pain by days to weeks
feat: Constant unilateral occipital pain, worse with neck flexion or turning the head toward the opposite side
Ipsilateral XII palsy: tongue deviates toward the lesion on protrusion, with later wasting and fasciculation of that half
Tenderness over the upper neck behind the mastoid; dysarthria for lingual sounds
Often the first sign of cancer (breast, prostate, lung, kidney, lymphoma or myeloma)
Other lower cranial nerves (IX–XI) may join as the lesion grows toward the jugular foramen
inv: MRI of the skull base with gadolinium and fat suppression, plus thin-slice CT for cortical bone erosion of the condyle
Staging: CT chest–abdomen–pelvis or FDG-PET/CT, bone scan, PSA, mammography, serum free light chains
Biopsy of the most accessible lesion; CSF cytology if leptomeningeal spread is suspected

case.who: A 64-year-old retired teacher from Lampang treated for breast cancer seven years earlier.
case.story: For five weeks she has had a nagging right-sided pain behind the ear spreading to the crown, now waking her at night; her family notices she slurs words with 't' and 'l' sounds.
case.exam: Protruded tongue points to the right with wasting of the right half; neck rotation to the left reproduces the pain; other cranial nerves are normal.
case.tests: Head CT reported normal; skull-base MRI shows an enhancing lesion replacing the right occipital condyle and extending into the hypoglossal canal; bone scan shows two vertebral hot spots.
case.q: What is the syndrome and the likely cause?
case.a: Occipital condyle syndrome from metastatic breast cancer; plain head CT often misses skull-base lesions. Treatment is focal radiotherapy plus systemic oncological therapy, with steroids and analgesia for pain.

read.where: Case 3 Occipital pain with tongue deviation

det.patho: The occipital condyle contains the hypoglossal canal, so destruction of the condyle stretches dura and periosteum (pain) and compresses the XII nerve as it exits. Haematogenous bone metastasis is the dominant cause; myeloma, lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, chordoma, osteomyelitis and skull-base infection are less common. The syndrome is uncommon but frequently overlooked, partly because routine brain imaging does not cover the condyles well.
det.clinical: Patients describe a constant, unilateral occipital or upper cervical ache that is aggravated by moving the head, sometimes with neck stiffness. Tongue deviation and dysarthria appear at the same time or later; patients may not notice the tongue weakness themselves. In about half of patients the syndrome is the presenting feature of an unknown or long-dormant cancer. As the tumour grows, lower cranial nerves at the jugular foramen and the upper cervical roots can become involved.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in any older patient or cancer survivor with new persistent occipital pain, and always look at the tongue. The key study is contrast MRI focused on the craniocervical junction and skull base, with fat-saturated sequences, complemented by CT bone windows. Routine head CT and standard brain MRI can be falsely reassuring. Once a lesion is found, stage the whole body and obtain tissue unless a known cancer makes biopsy unnecessary.
det.treatment: Management is oncological: external-beam radiotherapy or stereotactic radiosurgery to the condyle usually relieves pain within weeks, combined with systemic therapy matched to the primary tumour. Corticosteroids, neuropathic agents and opioids control pain meanwhile. Assess craniocervical stability if the condyle is extensively destroyed, as fixation may be needed. Speech and swallowing therapy help when XII and other bulbar nerves are affected.
det.prognosis: Pain often responds to radiotherapy, but tongue weakness recovers less reliably; survival depends on the primary cancer and is often limited because of disseminated disease.
pearls: New occipital pain plus a tongue that points to the painful side is skull-base metastasis until proven otherwise.
Ask the radiologist to image the craniocervical junction; a normal head CT does not exclude the lesion.
Cancer history may be remote, so ask about treatment from many years ago.
det.thd: Occipital condyle syndrome คืออาการปวดท้ายทอยข้างเดียวต่อเนื่อง ร่วมกับลิ้นอ่อนแรงข้างเดียวกันจากเส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 12 ถูกกดใน hypoglossal canal สาเหตุส่วนใหญ่คือมะเร็งแพร่กระจายมาที่กระดูกฐานกะโหลก และอาจเป็นอาการแรกของมะเร็ง การตรวจที่สำคัญคือ MRI ฐานกะโหลกพร้อมฉีดสารทึบรังสีและ CT bone window เพราะ CT สมองทั่วไปมักมองไม่เห็น รักษาด้วยการฉายรังสีเฉพาะที่ร่วมกับการรักษามะเร็งต้นเหตุ

name: Intracranial dural arteriovenous fistula (dAVF)
formal: Acquired abnormal shunt between meningeal arteries and a dural venous sinus or cortical vein within the dura, whose risk depends on venous drainage pattern; retrograde cortical venous drainage causes venous hypertension, haemorrhage and non-haemorrhagic neurological deficits.
simple: A short-circuit between arteries and veins inside the tough covering of the brain, which can cause a whooshing noise in the ear, headaches, seizures, dementia or bleeding.
th: ทางเชื่อมผิดปกติระหว่างหลอดเลือดแดงของเยื่อหุ้มสมองกับ venous sinus มักเกิดภายหลัง เช่น หลังลิ่มเลือดอุดตันในหลอดเลือดดำสมอง อาการมีตั้งแต่เสียงวูบในหูตามจังหวะชีพจร ไปจนถึงเลือดออกในสมอง ความเสี่ยงขึ้นกับว่ามีการไหลย้อนเข้าหลอดเลือดดำผิวสมองหรือไม่
tempoNote: Often indolent over months; may present acutely with haemorrhage or subacutely with venous-congestive encephalopathy or myelopathy
feat: Pulsatile tinnitus and an audible retro-mastoid or orbital bruit (benign sinus-draining fistulas)
Red eye with chemosis, proptosis and diplopia when draining via the cavernous sinus/ophthalmic veins
Headache, seizures, progressive cognitive decline or parkinsonism from venous hypertension when cortical veins fill retrogradely
Intracerebral or subarachnoid haemorrhage; posterior fossa fistulas may drain down to the cervical cord and cause myelopathy
Association with prior cerebral venous thrombosis, head trauma, surgery or prothrombotic states
inv: MRI/MRA: dilated cortical veins, flow voids, venous congestion oedema, sinus occlusion; 4D/time-resolved MRA or CTA can suggest the fistula
Catheter digital subtraction angiography with selective external carotid injections — gold standard to grade drainage (Borden/Cognard)
Thrombophilia screen when linked to venous sinus thrombosis

case.who: A 52-year-old rubber-plantation owner from Surat Thani who had left transverse sinus thrombosis treated two years ago.
case.story: Over four months he developed a swishing sound in his left ear in time with his pulse, then morning headaches, and last week a focal seizure starting in the right hand.
case.exam: Loud bruit behind the left mastoid; mild right pronator drift; fundi show early disc swelling.
case.tests: MRI shows serpiginous enhancing veins over the left temporal-parietal cortex with surrounding T2 hyperintensity; DSA shows a fistula fed by occipital and middle meningeal branches draining into the occluded sinus segment and backward into cortical veins (Cognard IIa+b).
case.q: What is the diagnosis and why is treatment urgent?
case.a: Dural AVF after venous sinus thrombosis; retrograde cortical venous drainage carries a high annual risk of haemorrhage and venous infarction, so the fistula should be disconnected, usually by transarterial or transvenous embolisation.

det.patho: Most intracranial dAVFs are acquired in adults, typically after venous sinus thrombosis, trauma or surgery, when venous hypertension and angiogenic signalling open dural arteriovenous channels. They cluster at the transverse–sigmoid sinus, cavernous sinus, tentorium and anterior cranial fossa. Clinical risk is governed by drainage: fistulas that drain only antegrade into a sinus are usually benign, whereas those that reflux into cortical veins (Borden II–III, Cognard IIb–V) produce venous congestion, infarction and haemorrhage. Tentorial and anterior cranial fossa fistulas almost always drain cortically.
det.clinical: Benign fistulas cause pulsatile tinnitus, bruit and orbital signs. Aggressive fistulas may present with intracranial haemorrhage or with non-haemorrhagic deficits: seizures, focal weakness, subacute dementia, parkinsonism or raised intracranial pressure with papilloedema. Fistulas at the foramen magnum or tentorium can drain into perimedullary veins and cause a progressive brainstem–cervical myelopathy that is easily mistaken for demyelination or tumour. Symptoms can change over time as drainage patterns evolve.
det.diagnosis: Listen over the orbit and mastoid in every patient with unexplained pulsatile tinnitus, intracranial hypertension, venous congestion or atypical white-matter oedema. MRI may show flow voids, enhancing dilated veins and oedema; time-resolved MRA increases sensitivity. Normal non-invasive imaging does not exclude a small fistula. Six-vessel catheter angiography including both external carotids is required to confirm the diagnosis, identify feeders and classify venous drainage.
det.treatment: Fistulas with cortical venous reflux should be treated promptly. Endovascular embolisation (transarterial embolisation with liquid agents (Onyx or n-BCA), or transvenous coil occlusion of a non-functioning sinus segment) is first-line; open surgical disconnection of the draining vein is used for anterior cranial fossa or tentorial lesions and failed embolisation, and radiosurgery is an option for residual low-risk lesions. Benign fistulas can be observed or treated for intolerable tinnitus, with repeat imaging if symptoms change. Treat underlying venous thrombosis and prothrombotic conditions.
det.prognosis: Untreated fistulas with cortical venous drainage carry an annual risk of haemorrhage or new deficit of several percent up to more than 10%; complete obliteration is usually curative, and venous-congestive deficits often improve.
pearls: Pulsatile tinnitus with a bruit after sinus thrombosis: think dAVF.
Risk lies in the venous drainage, not the size of the fistula.
A slowly progressive brainstem or cervical myelopathy can come from a craniocervical dAVF — angiography must include the external carotids and vertebrals.
det.thd: Dural AVF ในกะโหลกคือทางลัดระหว่างหลอดเลือดแดงของ dura กับ venous sinus มักเกิดภายหลังลิ่มเลือดอุดตันหลอดเลือดดำสมอง การบาดเจ็บ หรือการผ่าตัด ถ้าระบายเลือดเข้าสู่ sinus อย่างเดียวมักมีแค่เสียงวูบในหู แต่ถ้าไหลย้อนเข้าหลอดเลือดดำผิวสมองจะเสี่ยงชัก สมองเสื่อม และเลือดออก การวินิจฉัยต้องใช้ DSA และรักษาด้วยการอุดหลอดเลือดผ่านสายสวนหรือผ่าตัดตัดหลอดเลือดดำที่ระบายออก

qx.stem: A 64-year-old man who had earlier thrombosis of the transverse sinus has pulsatile tinnitus. He then develops an intracerebral haemorrhage in the right temporal lobe. DSA shows an arteriovenous fistula in the wall of the transverse sinus with retrograde cortical venous reflux, which is dilated and tortuous.
qx.q: Why is this fistula considered high risk?
opts: Because tinnitus is present
Because the transverse sinus is involved
Because there is cortical venous drainage, which predicts haemorrhage and venous hypertension
Because the patient is male
Because the patient is over 60

name: Opercular syndrome (Foix–Chavany–Marie syndrome)
formal: Cortical form of pseudobulbar palsy from bilateral (or occasionally unilateral dominant) lesions of the anterior frontal–parietal operculum, producing loss of voluntary control of facial, lingual, pharyngeal and masticatory muscles with preserved automatic and emotional movements of the same muscles.
simple: Damage to the speech-and-mouth control areas of the brain so that a person cannot move their face, tongue or throat on command, yet can still smile, yawn or blink by reflex.
th: กลุ่มอาการ opercular หรือ Foix–Chavany–Marie เกิดจากรอยโรคทั้งสองข้างของ operculum หรือเส้นใย corticobulbar ที่อยู่ใต้เปลือกสมอง (subopercular) ผู้ป่วยอ้าปาก แลบลิ้น เคี้ยว กลืนตามคำสั่งไม่ได้ แต่ยังหาว ยิ้ม หัวเราะได้เอง เรียกว่า automatic–voluntary dissociation สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยคือ stroke ซ้ำสองข้าง และอย่าสับสนกับ GBS หรือ myasthenia gravis
tempoNote: Usually abrupt or stepwise over a few days when a new infarct joins an older contralateral lesion, then partial recovery over weeks; chronic or fluctuating in encephalitis, epilepsy or neurodegeneration
feat: Anarthria or severe dysarthria with drooling and inability to chew or swallow to command, while comprehension and writing are preserved
Cannot close the eyes tightly, open the mouth or protrude the tongue on request, yet yawns, laughs, cries or swallows reflexively (automatic-voluntary dissociation)
The lesion may be in the opercular cortex or in the subcortical corticobulbar fibres (corona radiata, internal capsule, brainstem); a fresh lesion commonly joins an old one on the opposite side
Jaw jerk and gag are often preserved, the tongue is small and stiff without wasting or fasciculation, and pathological laughing or crying is usually absent, unlike classic pseudobulbar palsy
Symptoms may worsen over days before recovering; unfamiliarity with the syndrome leads to needless investigation for GBS, myasthenia, encephalitis or motor neuron disease
inv: MRI with DWI: bilateral opercular infarcts, or one acute subcortical infarct (corona radiata, internal capsule) with an older infarct on the other side; look for a hidden second lesion when only one is seen
Stroke work-up: CT/MR angiography, ECG with prolonged rhythm monitoring, echocardiography
Bedside demonstration of dissociation, then videofluoroscopy or FEES to define aspiration risk before any oral feeding
Only if the picture is atypical: EEG, CSF, autoimmune and infective tests, EMG with repetitive stimulation, and AChR/MuSK antibodies when ptosis or fatigability is present

case.who: 66-year-old woman from Khon Kaen with diabetes and hypertension
case.story: Three years ago a left lentiform lacunar stroke left her with a slightly clumsy right hand. Over two days she lost speech, began to drool and could not swallow her rice porridge; her husband says she still giggles at the television.
case.exam: Mute but nods and writes accurate answers; on command she cannot open her mouth, protrude the tongue or close her eyes firmly, yet she yawns widely and laughs spontaneously. Gag and jaw jerk are present, tongue is small without fasciculation, mild left arm weakness with bilateral extensor plantars; no ptosis or fatigability.
case.tests: MRI: acute right corona radiata infarct near the internal capsule and an old left lentiform lacune with moderate small vessel disease; sinus rhythm on 24-hour Holter. Anti-AChR antibody negative and pyridostigmine gives no benefit.
case.q: What explains the combination of voluntary paralysis and preserved yawning and laughing, and what is the main early risk?
case.a: Sub-opercular (Foix–Chavany–Marie) syndrome: interruption of bilateral corticobulbar pathways, here a new right subcortical lesion on top of an old left one, leaves reflex and emotional pathways intact. Aspiration is the danger, so keep her nil by mouth, arrange tube feeding and swallow rehabilitation, and treat the stroke.

9 - Atypical parkinsonism, parkinsonism-­plus syndromes and secondary parkinsonian disorders

det.patho: Voluntary movement of the face, tongue, jaw and pharynx is generated in motor cortex and travels in corticobulbar fibres, while yawning, laughing, crying and reflex swallowing run through extrapyramidal, limbic and brainstem pathways that remain intact. Interrupting the voluntary route on both sides, either at the opercular cortex around the insula or in the subcortical fibres below it, produces automatic-voluntary dissociation. Most patients have had an earlier stroke on the other side, and the new lesion removes the compensating capacity of the hemisphere that had been coping. Strictly one-sided lesions probably also depend on subtle opposite-sided damage or remote functional effects.
det.clinical: Onset is acute or stepwise, with severe dysarthria progressing to anarthria, drooling, facial diplegia and inability to chew or swallow on command. The patient understands everything and can write. Compared with typical pseudobulbar palsy, emotional outbursts are rare and the affected muscles may be limp, although in the subcortical form the tongue can be stiff and the jaw jerk preserved. Limb weakness is mild and often asymmetric from the old infarct. Deterioration over a few days can raise fears of a progressive neuromuscular disease.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis rests on demonstrating the dissociation at the bedside: ask the patient to open the mouth and protrude the tongue, then watch for a spontaneous yawn, smile or reflex swallow. MRI usually shows either bilateral opercular lesions or one acute subcortical lesion plus an old contralateral one. Check for gag, jaw jerk, tongue wasting and fasciculation to exclude lower motor neuron bulbar palsy, and for fatigability, ptosis and antibodies to exclude myasthenia. Unremarkable CSF and viral, autoimmune and EMG studies support a vascular cause when the picture is typical.
det.treatment: Treatment is that of the underlying stroke: antithrombotic therapy, rhythm and vascular work-up, blood pressure and glucose control. In the acute phase protect the airway with nasogastric feeding, suctioning, cough assistance and an anticholinergic patch for drooling if secretions pool. Speech and swallow therapy begin early and decide when oral feeding is safe, with gastrostomy for prolonged failure. Steroids and pyridostigmine do not help and should not be continued when the diagnosis is clear.
det.prognosis: After vascular opercular or subopercular syndrome, recovery is often substantial over weeks to months, although persistent dysarthria or dysphagia remains in some.
pearls: Cannot open the mouth to command but yawns widely: think opercular or subopercular syndrome.
The lesion need not be cortical: an internal capsule or corona radiata infarct plus an old contralateral lesion can do it.
Recognising the syndrome early prevents needless GBS, myasthenia and encephalitis treatments.
