name: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI)
formal: Objective decline in one or more cognitive domains, beyond that expected for age and education and reported by the patient or an informant, with essentially preserved independence in everyday activities; it is a syndrome that may reflect early neurodegenerative, vascular or reversible causes.
simple: Memory or thinking problems that are clearly worse than before and show up on testing, but not bad enough to stop a person from managing daily life.
th: ภาวะความจำหรือการคิดลดลงกว่าเดิมชัดเจนและตรวจพบได้จากแบบทดสอบ แต่ยังช่วยเหลือตัวเองในชีวิตประจำวันได้ อาจเป็นระยะแรกของ Alzheimer หรือเกิดจากสาเหตุที่แก้ไขได้ ต้องหาสาเหตุและติดตามต่อเนื่อง
tempoNote: Insidious decline over months to years; abrupt or stepwise change suggests vascular, metabolic or other causes
feat: Subjective concern from patient or family plus objective impairment on testing (e.g. MoCA below norms for education)
Amnestic type: poor delayed recall not helped by cues; non-amnestic types affect executive, language or visuospatial function
Complex activities (finances, medications) may be slightly less efficient, but independence is preserved
Annual progression to dementia roughly 10–15% in clinic cohorts; some revert to normal
inv: Cognitive screening (MoCA, Thai MoCA or TMSE) and, when unclear, formal neuropsychological testing
Reversible-cause screen: B12, thyroid function, glucose, calcium, renal/liver function, syphilis/HIV when indicated, medication review, depression and sleep apnoea screen
MRI brain for hippocampal atrophy, vascular burden and other lesions
Biomarkers in selected patients: CSF Aβ42/40 and p-tau, amyloid PET, or validated plasma p-tau217

case.who: A 68-year-old retired accountant from Bangkok who still runs his household and drives.
case.story: His wife reports that over two years he repeats questions, forgets appointments unless written down, and recently missed paying an electricity bill; he admits he relies on notes far more than before.
case.exam: Thai MoCA 22/30, losing points on delayed recall that cues do not help; neurological examination normal; no depression on screening.
case.tests: B12, thyroid and glucose normal; MRI shows mild bilateral hippocampal atrophy; plasma p-tau217 is elevated and CSF shows low Aβ42/40.
case.q: How would you classify his condition and what can be offered?
case.a: Amnestic MCI with biomarker evidence of Alzheimer pathology (MCI due to AD); options include risk-factor management, exercise and cognitive engagement, and, where available and eligible after MRI and APOE counselling, an anti-amyloid antibody (lecanemab or donanemab) with ARIA monitoring.

det.patho: MCI is a clinical stage, not a single disease. Most amnestic MCI in older adults reflects Alzheimer pathology, but cerebrovascular disease, Lewy body disease, LATE (limbic TDP-43), hippocampal sclerosis, argyrophilic grain disease and mixed pathology are common, and depression, sleep apnoea, medications or metabolic problems can produce a similar picture. Prevalence rises from about 6–8% in the 60s to over 25% by the 80s.
det.clinical: Petersen-style subtypes separate amnestic from non-amnestic and single- from multiple-domain MCI, which helps predict the underlying cause: amnestic multidomain MCI often progresses to AD dementia, while executive or visuospatial predominance raises vascular or Lewy body possibilities. Informant history is critical. Clues to non-AD causes include hallucinations, RBD, parkinsonism, gait disorder, early behavioural change or a stepwise course.
det.diagnosis: Confirm decline with history from an informant and objective testing adjusted for age and education; establish that daily function is essentially preserved. Screen for reversible contributors and depression, and image with MRI. Biomarkers (CSF, amyloid PET or validated blood tests such as plasma p-tau217) define MCI due to AD and are required before anti-amyloid therapy; they should be interpreted alongside the clinical picture, not alone. No rating scale or single cut-off makes the diagnosis.
det.treatment: Address vascular risk factors, hearing loss, sleep apnoea, depression and harmful medications (especially anticholinergics and sedatives); encourage aerobic exercise, social and cognitive activity, and a Mediterranean-style diet. Cholinesterase inhibitors have not shown durable benefit in MCI and are not routinely recommended. For biomarker-confirmed MCI or mild dementia due to AD, lecanemab and donanemab modestly slow decline; they require baseline MRI, APOE genotyping for risk counselling, scheduled MRI monitoring for ARIA, and exclusion of patients on anticoagulants or with extensive microbleeds. Plan for finances, driving and advance care while capacity is intact, and reassess every 6–12 months.
det.prognosis: Clinic cohorts progress to dementia at about 10–15% per year, higher with positive AD biomarkers; a minority revert to normal, especially when a reversible factor is treated.
pearls: MCI is a syndrome — always ask what is causing it.
Preserved independence separates MCI from dementia; the informant tells you this.
Anti-amyloid antibodies need biomarker confirmation and MRI safety monitoring for ARIA.

name: Segmental zoster paresis
formal: Focal lower motor neuron weakness in a myotome corresponding to, or adjacent to, the dermatome of a herpes zoster eruption, due to spread of varicella-zoster virus inflammation from the dorsal root ganglion to the ventral root, plexus or anterior horn.
simple: Shingles that not only causes a painful rash but also weakens the muscles supplied by the same nerve root, such as an arm, shoulder or belly wall.
th: งูสวัดที่นอกจากทำให้ผื่นและปวดตามแนวเส้นประสาทแล้ว ยังทำให้กล้ามเนื้อในระดับรากประสาทเดียวกันอ่อนแรงแบบ lower motor neuron เช่น แขนยกไม่ขึ้นหรือผนังหน้าท้องโป่ง ส่วนใหญ่ค่อย ๆ ฟื้นตัว
tempoNote: Weakness appears days to a few weeks after the rash (occasionally before it) and recovers over months
feat: Painful vesicular dermatomal rash (current or recent), then weakness in the matching segment
Upper limb (C5–C6: deltoid, biceps, scapular muscles) most common; thoracic segments give an abdominal wall bulge (pseudohernia); lumbosacral gives leg weakness or bladder dysfunction
Reduced reflexes in the segment and wasting later; sensory loss and pain follow the rash dermatome
Commoner in older or immunosuppressed patients
inv: EMG/NCS: denervation in the affected myotome and paraspinal muscles; localises root versus plexus
MRI of the relevant spine/plexus: enhancement of root or plexus, and to exclude compressive lesions
CSF VZV PCR/antibody if myelitis, meningitis or atypical features; HIV test and immune status review

case.who: A 74-year-old woman from Chiang Rai with type 2 diabetes.
case.story: Three weeks after a painful band of blisters over her right shoulder and outer arm, she can no longer lift the arm to comb her hair; the scabs are healing but the burning pain persists.
case.exam: Healing crusts in the right C5 dermatome; deltoid and biceps 2/5 with scapular winging on abduction; right biceps reflex absent; legs normal.
case.tests: EMG shows fibrillations in deltoid, biceps, infraspinatus and C5 paraspinals with normal sensory nerve action potentials; cervical MRI shows enhancement of the right C5 root without disc compression.
case.q: What explains her weakness and how will she do?
case.a: Segmental zoster paresis of the C5 segment; give antiviral therapy if still within the active phase, treat neuropathic pain and start physiotherapy; most patients recover useful strength over 6–18 months.

det.patho: VZV reactivates in a dorsal root or cranial ganglion and normally causes sensory ganglionitis. In a few percent of cases inflammation, haemorrhagic necrosis or demyelination spreads to the adjacent ventral root, spinal nerve, plexus or anterior horn, producing motor deficits. Cranial nerve equivalents include facial palsy in Ramsay Hunt syndrome and ophthalmoplegia with zoster ophthalmicus. Older age, malignancy, HIV and immunosuppressive drugs increase risk.
det.clinical: Weakness usually follows the rash by about two weeks and lies in the same segment, although it can involve neighbouring levels. Cervical involvement gives shoulder and proximal arm weakness; thoracic involvement causes a unilateral abdominal bulge that can be mistaken for a hernia; lumbosacral zoster may cause foot drop, quadriceps weakness or urinary retention. Zoster sine herpete (no rash) makes diagnosis difficult. Look also for myelitis, vasculopathy or meningitis, which are other VZV complications.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical when dermatomal rash and matching LMN weakness coexist; EMG confirms segmental denervation and helps distinguish root from plexus involvement. MRI excludes compressive lesions and may show root or plexus enhancement. When there is no rash, VZV DNA in CSF or rising VZV IgG/IgM in serum and CSF support the diagnosis. Check HIV and immune status in younger patients.
det.treatment: Treat acute zoster with valacyclovir, famciclovir or aciclovir (IV aciclovir if immunocompromised or with CNS involvement); evidence that antivirals prevent paresis is limited but treatment is reasonable while the rash is active. Short corticosteroid courses are sometimes used but lack strong evidence. Manage neuropathic pain with gabapentinoids, tricyclics or topical agents, and begin physiotherapy early to prevent contractures such as frozen shoulder. Recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV) for adults aged 50 and over and for immunocompromised adults reduces zoster and its complications.
det.prognosis: Between two-thirds and three-quarters of patients regain good strength, usually within a year; recovery is slower or incomplete with severe denervation.
pearls: Always look for a rash or scabs in a patient with acute segmental arm weakness.
A unilateral abdominal bulge after thoracic shingles is a pseudohernia from paresis, not a surgical hernia.
Recombinant zoster vaccine is the best prevention in older and immunocompromised adults.

name: Anterior communicating artery (ACoA) aneurysm
formal: Saccular aneurysm at the junction of the anterior cerebral arteries and the anterior communicating artery, the commonest site of ruptured intracranial aneurysms, whose rupture or treatment may cause bilateral medial frontal damage with abulia, amnesia and leg-predominant weakness.
simple: A bulge on the small artery joining the two front brain arteries; if it bursts, it can cause bleeding and later damage to the parts of the brain that control the legs, memory and motivation.
th: หลอดเลือดโป่งพองที่ anterior communicating artery เป็นตำแหน่งที่แตกบ่อยที่สุด เมื่อแตกอาจเกิด vasospasm ของ anterior cerebral artery ทั้งสองข้าง ทำให้ขาอ่อนแรงทั้งสองข้าง (paraparesis) เฉยเมย และความจำเสื่อม
tempoNote: Thunderclap headache at rupture; delayed deficits from vasospasm peak around days 4–14
feat: Thunderclap headache, neck stiffness and reduced consciousness at rupture; blood in the interhemispheric fissure and gyrus rectus haematoma
Bilateral ACA territory infarction from vasospasm: leg-predominant weakness of both legs (cerebral paraparesis), urinary incontinence
Abulia, akinetic mutism, disinhibition and confabulating amnesia (basal forebrain/ACoA syndrome)
Unruptured lesions are usually asymptomatic; large ones may compress the optic chiasm
inv: Non-contrast CT within 6 h of onset; LP for xanthochromia if CT is negative later
CTA, then catheter DSA with 3D rotation to define neck, dome and A1 dominance
Transcranial Doppler and clinical monitoring for delayed cerebral ischaemia; CT perfusion when deterioration occurs

case.who: A 46-year-old female market vendor from Udon Thani who smokes and has untreated hypertension.
case.story: She collapsed with a sudden worst-ever headache while lifting a crate; coiling of an aneurysm was done the next day. On day 7 nurses note she lies quietly, does not ask for food and cannot move her legs well.
case.exam: Abulic, answers with single words after long delay; both legs 2/5 distally and proximally with arms near normal; bilateral Babinski signs; incontinent.
case.tests: Initial CT showed blood concentrated in the interhemispheric fissure; DSA confirmed an ACoA aneurysm; day-7 CT perfusion shows delayed perfusion in both medial frontal lobes and TCD shows high ACA velocities.
case.q: What is causing the new deficits and what is the management?
case.a: Delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm of both ACAs after ACoA aneurysm rupture; maintain euvolaemia, continue nimodipine, consider induced hypertension now the aneurysm is secured, and endovascular intra-arterial vasodilator or angioplasty if refractory.

det.patho: ACoA aneurysms account for roughly a third of ruptured intracranial aneurysms. Asymmetric A1 segments with a dominant side increase haemodynamic stress at the junction. Rupture deposits blood in the interhemispheric fissure and lamina terminalis region, which predisposes to bilateral ACA vasospasm, while damage to perforators supplying the basal forebrain, septum and fornix causes amnesia and personality change. Smoking, hypertension, female sex, family history and polycystic kidney disease raise risk.
det.clinical: Rupture presents as a sudden severe headache with or without loss of consciousness, vomiting and meningism. Delayed cerebral ischaemia between days 3 and 14 may produce bilateral medial frontal infarction: weakness that is worse in the legs than the arms (a cerebral cause of paraparesis that can mimic a spinal lesion), urinary incontinence, abulia or akinetic mutism. Survivors may have the ACoA syndrome of anterograde amnesia, confabulation and executive and emotional change.
det.diagnosis: CT is highly sensitive early; CTA identifies most aneurysms, and DSA with 3D reconstruction guides treatment. Recognise vasospasm by new deficits or reduced consciousness, supported by rising TCD velocities, CT perfusion and angiography. In a patient with paraparesis after SAH, check the brain before imaging the spine.
det.treatment: Secure the aneurysm early, usually within 24–72 h, by endovascular coiling (with or without stent or flow-diverting adjuncts) or microsurgical clipping, chosen by a neurovascular team. Give oral nimodipine for 21 days at 60 mg every 4 h, maintain euvolaemia, control blood pressure before securing, and manage hydrocephalus with external ventricular drainage. Prophylactic hypervolaemia and triple-H therapy are no longer advised; induced hypertension and endovascular rescue (intra-arterial vasodilators, balloon angioplasty) treat symptomatic vasospasm. Unruptured ACoA aneurysms are assessed with tools such as PHASES and UIATS; treatment is favoured for larger, growing or irregular lesions in younger patients.
det.prognosis: About a third of patients with aneurysmal SAH die or remain dependent; ACoA rupture survivors frequently have lasting memory and behavioural deficits even with good motor recovery.
pearls: Paraparesis after SAH may be cerebral: bilateral ACA infarction from vasospasm.
Abulia and confabulation after ACoA rupture reflect basal forebrain damage.
Nimodipine for 21 days; avoid prophylactic hypervolaemia.

name: Radiologically isolated syndrome (RIS)
formal: Incidental brain or spinal MRI lesions with the shape, size and distribution typical of CNS demyelination in a person who has never had a clinical episode suggestive of multiple sclerosis, and in whom no other condition accounts better for the findings.
simple: MRI scans done for another reason show spots that look like multiple sclerosis, but the person has never had any MS symptoms.
ab: ภาพ MRI คล้าย MS โดยไม่มีอาการ
th: พบรอยโรคลักษณะ demyelination แบบ MS จาก MRI ที่ทำด้วยเหตุผลอื่น (เช่น ปวดศีรษะ อุบัติเหตุ) โดยผู้ป่วยไม่เคยมีอาการทางระบบประสาทแบบ MS มาก่อน ราวครึ่งหนึ่งจะมีอาการทางคลินิกภายใน 10 ปี
tempoNote: Asymptomatic at discovery; roughly a third have a first clinical event within 5 years and about half within 10 years, highest risk with spinal cord or infratentorial lesions, CSF bands and youth
feat: MRI performed for headache, trauma or imaging research shows ovoid periventricular, juxtacortical or infratentorial T2 lesions
No history of optic neuritis, myelitis, brainstem or other episodes typical of demyelination, and a normal or nonspecific neurological examination
Lesions often show a central vein sign and may enhance or increase in number over time
Risk of conversion higher with spinal cord lesions, gadolinium-enhancing lesions, CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands, age under 37 and male sex
Usually young adults, more often women; headache is the commonest reason the scan was done
inv: Full brain and whole-spine MRI with contrast using an MS protocol; susceptibility imaging for central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions
CSF oligoclonal bands or kappa free light chain index
Exclude mimics: AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG (cell-based), vascular risk screen, B12, connective tissue and infection serology as indicated
Repeat MRI at about 6–12 months to look for dissemination in time

case.who: 29-year-old female accountant from Khon Kaen who had brain MRI for long-standing episodic migraine
case.story: She has never had visual loss, numbness, weakness, double vision or bladder problems; her headaches are typical migraine without aura.
case.exam: Completely normal neurological examination, including fundi and visual acuity.
case.tests: MRI: five ovoid periventricular lesions perpendicular to the ventricles and two juxtacortical lesions, one with a central vein; cervical cord MRI shows a small lesion at C3; CSF has unique oligoclonal bands; AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG negative.
case.q: What is this situation called, and how does the 2024 McDonald revision treat it?
case.a: Radiologically isolated syndrome; because she has dissemination in space with positive CSF (and a cord lesion), the 2024 revision allows a diagnosis of MS even without a clinical attack, and treatment discussion is appropriate.

det.patho: RIS is thought to represent the earliest detectable, subclinical stage of CNS demyelinating disease in many people, with the same inflammatory plaques found in MS but in clinically silent regions. Lesions accumulate before any attack, and some patients already show cortical lesions, brain atrophy or retinal nerve fibre layer thinning. Not every case is MS: migraine, small vessel disease and other disorders can create look-alike white matter spots, which is why strict morphology rules matter.
det.clinical: By definition there is no history of a clinical event typical of demyelination. People are usually discovered because of a scan for headache, head injury, dizziness or another unrelated complaint. Careful questioning sometimes uncovers a forgotten earlier episode, which reclassifies the patient. Subtle signs such as mild cognitive slowing or fatigue are reported but do not change the label. About half develop a first attack or primary progressive course within a decade; spinal cord lesions are the strongest single predictor.
det.diagnosis: The original 2009 Okuda criteria required lesions meeting Barkhof-type dissemination in space; the 2023 revised RIS criteria accept one lesion in at least two of the four classic locations when supported by two of three risk markers (spinal cord lesion, CSF oligoclonal bands, new T2 or enhancing lesion on follow-up). The 2024 McDonald revision goes further: a person with RIS who fulfils dissemination in space plus dissemination in time, or positive CSF (oligoclonal bands or kappa free light chain index), or a sufficient number of central vein sign lesions can be diagnosed with MS. Mimics must be excluded, including AQP4- and MOG-antibody disease in Asian patients.
det.treatment: Not every patient needs medication. Two randomised trials (teriflunomide in TERIS and dimethyl fumarate in ARISE) showed that treatment roughly halves the chance of a first clinical event, so treatment is discussed for higher-risk patients and for those who now meet the 2024 MS definition. Others are followed with MRI every 6–12 months for the first years and taught to report new symptoms promptly. Treat vascular risk factors, stop smoking and maintain vitamin D sufficiency.
det.prognosis: Variable: many remain asymptomatic for years, but cord lesions, CSF bands and enhancing lesions predict earlier conversion to clinical MS.
pearls: Ask again about past episodes — a forgotten numb leg or blurred eye years ago changes RIS into MS.
Spinal cord lesions are the strongest predictor that RIS will become clinical MS.
Under the 2024 McDonald revision some RIS patients (DIS plus DIT, positive CSF or central vein sign) already qualify as MS.
det.thd: RIS คือการพบรอยโรคคล้าย MS จาก MRI โดยบังเอิญในคนที่ไม่เคยมีอาการ MS ต้องแยกจากรอยโรค white matter ของไมเกรนหรือ small vessel disease ประเมินด้วย MRI ทั้งสมองและไขสันหลัง ตรวจ CSF OCB/kappa FLC และ AQP4/MOG ตามเกณฑ์ McDonald 2024 ผู้ป่วยบางรายที่มี DIS ร่วมกับ DIT หรือ CSF บวก หรือ central vein sign วินิจฉัยเป็น MS ได้เลย ยา teriflunomide และ dimethyl fumarate ลดโอกาสเกิดอาการครั้งแรกได้

name: Tumefactive demyelinating lesion (tumefactive MS)
formal: A large (usually over 2 cm) inflammatory demyelinating lesion of the brain that mimics a tumour or abscess through size, oedema, mass effect or ring enhancement, occurring as a first event, within MS, MOGAD or NMOSD, or after withdrawal of some MS drugs.
simple: A big patch of MS-type inflammation in the brain that looks like a tumour on the scan.
ab: รอยโรค demyelination คล้ายเนื้องอก
th: รอยโรค demyelination ขนาดใหญ่ (> 2 ซม.) ที่มีบวมหรือกดเบียดคล้ายเนื้องอกสมองหรือฝี ลักษณะเด่นคือ open-ring enhancement ด้านที่หันเข้าหา cortex เปิด การวินิจฉัยต้องแยกจาก glioma, lymphoma และ abscess และระวังให้ steroid ก่อนตัดชิ้นเนื้อหากสงสัย lymphoma
tempoNote: Develops over days to a few weeks; may be the first event or appear years into MS, or 2–6 months after stopping natalizumab or fingolimod
feat: Subacute hemiparesis, aphasia, hemianopia, headache, confusion or seizures — cortical features are more frequent than in ordinary MS lesions
Lesion > 2 cm with relatively little mass effect for its size and an incomplete ring of enhancement open toward the grey matter
Peripheral T2-hypointense rim, dilated veins running through the lesion and peripheral diffusion restriction
Other smaller ovoid lesions elsewhere in brain or cord support demyelination
Usually responds quickly to high-dose corticosteroids or plasma exchange
inv: MRI with contrast, DWI, perfusion and MR spectroscopy (low rCBV favours demyelination; very high choline and low rCBV may not separate it from lymphoma)
CSF oligoclonal bands, cytology and flow cytometry; serum AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG by cell-based assay
Spine MRI and CT chest/abdomen when the picture is atypical
Stereotactic biopsy when imaging and CSF cannot exclude glioma, lymphoma or infection — ideally before steroids

case.who: 34-year-old female teacher from Phitsanulok, previously well
case.story: Over 10 days she developed right hand clumsiness, then word-finding problems and a dull headache; no fever or weight loss.
case.exam: Mild non-fluent aphasia, right pronator drift and brisk right reflexes; fundi normal.
case.tests: MRI: 3.5 cm left frontal white matter lesion with modest oedema and a C-shaped rim of enhancement open toward the cortex; two small ovoid periventricular lesions on the other side; perfusion shows low blood volume; CSF has unique oligoclonal bands; AQP4- and MOG-IgG negative.
case.q: What is the most likely lesion type, and what is the first treatment?
case.a: Tumefactive demyelinating lesion; with typical open-ring imaging, low perfusion and CSF bands, give IV methylprednisolone (plasma exchange if poor response) and plan MS disease-modifying therapy, keeping biopsy for atypical evolution.

det.patho: The lesion is an intense focus of inflammatory demyelination with macrophages, reactive astrocytes (sometimes atypical Creutzfeldt cells) and relative axonal preservation, which is why it can be mistaken for glioma on biopsy. Tumefactive lesions occur in MS, in MOGAD, in NMOSD and after rebound following natalizumab or fingolimod withdrawal; Balo concentric sclerosis is a related pattern with alternating rings. The large size probably reflects a burst of inflammation that overwhelms the usual perivenular limits of a plaque.
det.clinical: Most patients are young or middle-aged adults, more often women. Compared with ordinary MS relapses, tumefactive lesions more often produce cortical features such as aphasia, neglect, hemianopia, seizures and encephalopathy, and may cause headache from raised pressure. Many have a solitary lesion at onset; others show it later in the course of established MS. Recurrence of a second tumefactive lesion is uncommon but possible.
det.diagnosis: MRI clues include an incomplete (open) ring of enhancement whose open side faces the cortex or basal ganglia, a T2-hypointense rim, venules crossing the lesion, peripheral rather than central diffusion restriction, low relative cerebral blood volume and modest mass effect for its size. Additional typical lesions, CSF oligoclonal bands and a prompt steroid response support demyelination. Test AQP4- and MOG-IgG because the treatment differs. Biopsy is required when imaging is atypical or the lesion keeps growing; steroids should be held before biopsy when lymphoma is in the differential.
det.treatment: Acute: IV methylprednisolone for 3–5 days at 1 g daily; plasma exchange for steroid-refractory or life-threatening lesions; treat raised pressure and seizures. Long term, patients with MS should start a high-efficacy therapy such as an anti-CD20 antibody; caution with fingolimod, which has been linked to tumefactive relapses. Treat MOGAD or NMOSD according to their own pathways. Repeat MRI at about 4–8 weeks to confirm shrinkage.
det.prognosis: Usually good with substantial recovery; long-term course often resembles typical relapsing MS, and some patients have only one event.
pearls: An open ring of enhancement facing the cortex is the single most useful clue to demyelination.
Do not give steroids before biopsy if lymphoma is a real possibility.
Think of rebound or tumefactive relapse a few months after stopping natalizumab or fingolimod.
det.thd: Tumefactive demyelinating lesion คือรอยโรค demyelination ใหญ่กว่า 2 ซม. ที่คล้ายเนื้องอก อาการเด่นเป็นแบบ cortical เช่น aphasia ชัก หรือสับสน MRI มักเห็น open-ring enhancement, perfusion ต่ำ และกดเบียดไม่มากเมื่อเทียบกับขนาด ส่งตรวจ CSF OCB และ AQP4/MOG ถ้าสงสัย lymphoma ให้งด steroid จนกว่าจะได้ชิ้นเนื้อ รักษาด้วย IV methylprednisolone หรือ plasma exchange และเริ่มยา MS ประสิทธิภาพสูง

name: Anti-KLHL11 paraneoplastic encephalitis
formal: A paraneoplastic rhombencephalitis associated with Kelch-like protein 11 IgG, occurring mainly in men with testicular germ cell tumours (especially seminoma), presenting with progressive ataxia, diplopia, vertigo and sensorineural hearing loss or tinnitus; KLHL11 is classed as a high-risk antibody in the 2021 paraneoplastic criteria.
simple: An immune attack on the brainstem and cerebellum triggered by a testicular cancer, causing unsteadiness, double vision, dizziness and hearing loss.
ab: สมองอักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกันสัมพันธ์มะเร็งอัณฑะ
th: สมองส่วน brainstem และ cerebellum อักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกัน (anti-KLHL11) ในชายวัยหนุ่มถึงกลางคนที่มีมะเร็งอัณฑะชนิด germ cell โดยเฉพาะ seminoma อาการคือเดินเซ เห็นภาพซ้อน เวียนศีรษะ หูอื้อหรือได้ยินลดลง ต้องตรวจ ultrasound อัณฑะทุกราย

MRI brain: may be normal or show temporal, brainstem or cerebellar T2 change, later cerebellar atrophy
CSF: mild pleocytosis, raised protein and oligoclonal bands

case.who: 41-year-old male truck driver from Nakhon Sawan
case.story: Three months of ringing and reduced hearing in the left ear, followed by six weeks of worsening imbalance and double vision when looking to the side.
case.exam: Gaze-evoked nystagmus, bilateral limb dysmetria, wide-based gait and left sensorineural hearing loss on tuning-fork testing.
case.tests: MRI brain normal; CSF 12 cells/µL with oligoclonal bands; serum and CSF KLHL11-IgG positive; testicular ultrasound shows a 9 mm hypoechoic right testicular mass.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the key next management step?
case.a: Anti-KLHL11 paraneoplastic rhombencephalitis from a testicular seminoma; urgent orchiectomy with oncological treatment plus immunotherapy (IV steroids, IVIG or plasma exchange).

det.patho: KLHL11 is an intracellular protein; the antibody is a marker of a cytotoxic T-cell attack on neurons in the brainstem, cerebellum and sometimes the temporal lobes, triggered by antigen expressed in the germ cell tumour. A strong HLA association (DQB1*02:01 and DRB1*15:01 region) has been described. Because the target is intracellular, damage is largely irreversible once neurons are lost.
det.clinical: Most patients are men in their 30s to 50s. Hearing loss, tinnitus or vertigo commonly precede a progressive ataxic syndrome with nystagmus, diplopia, dysarthria and gait failure; some add seizures, memory loss, myoclonus or a jaw-opening dystonia. Coexisting Ma2 antibodies occur. The cancer is often small and may be found only on ultrasound or even after orchiectomy of a burnt-out tumour.
det.diagnosis: Detection of KLHL11-IgG in serum or CSF in a compatible syndrome, with a germ cell tumour found, fulfils a definite paraneoplastic neurological syndrome under the 2021 PNS-Care criteria (high-risk antibody, high PNS-Care score). Every positive man needs testicular ultrasound and tumour markers, then body CT or FDG-PET; repeat screening every 6 months for about 2 years if the first search is negative. MRI is often normal early and CSF inflammatory changes support the diagnosis.
det.treatment: Remove and treat the tumour as fast as possible — this is the most important step. Give immunotherapy (IV methylprednisolone, IVIG or plasma exchange, then possibly rituximab or cyclophosphamide) to try to stop progression, accepting that recovery of lost function is limited. Provide vestibular and gait rehabilitation and hearing aids.
det.prognosis: Most patients stabilise rather than improve; earlier tumour treatment gives the best chance of halting progression.
pearls: Ataxia plus hearing loss or tinnitus in a young or middle-aged man: test for KLHL11 and scan the testes.
The testicular tumour may be tiny or burnt-out; a normal examination does not exclude it.
Like other intracellular-antigen syndromes, the response to immunotherapy is modest — speed matters.
det.thd: Anti-KLHL11 encephalitis เป็นกลุ่มอาการ paraneoplastic ที่พบในผู้ชายที่มีมะเร็งอัณฑะ (seminoma) อาการเด่นคือได้ยินลดลงหรือหูอื้อ ตามด้วยเดินเซ เห็นภาพซ้อน และตากระตุก แอนติบอดีนี้จัดเป็น high-risk ตามเกณฑ์ PNS 2021 ต้องตรวจ ultrasound อัณฑะและ tumor marker ทุกราย การรักษาหลักคือผ่าตัดเอามะเร็งออกเร็วร่วมกับยากดภูมิ แต่อาการมักแค่คงที่

name: Paraneoplastic myelopathy
formal: An immune-mediated spinal cord disorder occurring in association with cancer, typically producing an insidious or subacute progressive myelopathy with symmetric, longitudinally extensive, tract-specific T2 lesions (lateral or dorsal columns) and paraneoplastic antibodies such as amphiphysin, CRMP5 or ANNA-1 (Hu).
simple: Damage to the spinal cord caused by the immune system reacting to a hidden cancer.
ab: โรคไขสันหลังจากภูมิคุ้มกันสัมพันธ์มะเร็ง

feat: Progressive spastic paraparesis or quadriparesis, often asymmetric at first

case.story: Over four months, stiff heavy legs, falls and urinary urgency, with tingling feet; 6 kg weight loss.
case.exam: Spastic paraparesis MRC 4/5, brisk reflexes and bilateral Babinski, reduced vibration to the iliac crests, no clear sensory level.
case.tests: MRI: symmetric, longitudinally extensive T2 signal of both lateral columns from T2 to T9 with faint enhancement; CSF protein 82 mg/dL, 9 cells, oligoclonal bands; CRMP5-IgG positive; FDG-PET shows an avid hilar node with small cell carcinoma on EBUS biopsy.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and why is the MRI pattern helpful?

det.patho: The cancer expresses neural proteins that trigger an immune response, largely T-cell mediated when the antigen is intracellular (CRMP5, ANNA-1) and partly antibody mediated with amphiphysin. The inflammation tends to select specific long tracts — corticospinal, dorsal column — producing symmetric, longitudinally extensive lesions. The most frequent associated tumours are breast adenocarcinoma and small cell lung carcinoma; checkpoint inhibitor therapy can unmask or trigger the syndrome.
det.clinical: Patients are usually in their 60s and present with a steadily progressive myelopathy over weeks to months, often before the cancer is known. Motor (spastic) and sensory involvement, sphincter problems and pain are common, and many also have peripheral neuropathy, optic neuropathy, ataxia or encephalopathy, reflecting multifocal paraneoplastic disease. About half need a wheelchair within a year.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it when progressive myelopathy has symmetric tract-specific or longitudinally extensive lesions with enhancement and no compression, deficiency or infection. Send serum and CSF antibody panels; CRMP5, amphiphysin and ANNA-1 are high-risk antibodies under the 2021 PNS-Care criteria. CSF is often inflammatory. Search for cancer with CT, mammography and FDG-PET, repeating screening if negative. Exclude B12 and copper deficiency, HTLV-1, dural fistula, NMOSD, MOGAD and sarcoidosis.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying cancer as soon as possible. Give early immunotherapy — IV methylprednisolone, IVIG or plasma exchange, followed by steroid-sparing agents (cyclophosphamide, rituximab) as appropriate to the oncological plan. Rehabilitation, spasticity and bladder management are essential.
det.prognosis: Generally poor: many patients become wheelchair dependent, though some stabilise with early tumour treatment and immunotherapy.
pearls: Symmetric tract-specific T2 lesions in a progressive myelopathy should prompt a paraneoplastic antibody panel.
Amphiphysin with myelopathy or stiffness points to breast cancer; CRMP5 or ANNA-1 to small cell lung cancer.
Look for associated optic neuropathy, neuropathy or ataxia — paraneoplastic disease is often multifocal.
det.thd: Paraneoplastic myelopathy คือไขสันหลังอักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกันที่เกิดร่วมกับมะเร็ง มักพบในผู้สูงอายุที่สูบบุหรี่หรือมีมะเร็งเต้านม อาการขาอ่อนแรงเกร็งค่อย ๆ แย่ลง MRI เห็นรอยโรคยาวและสมมาตรตาม tract ให้ตรวจแอนติบอดี CRMP5, amphiphysin, ANNA-1 ใน serum และ CSF และหามะเร็งด้วย PET-CT รักษามะเร็งและให้ยากดภูมิโดยเร็ว แต่การพยากรณ์โรคมักไม่ดี

name: Orbital apex syndrome (Jacod syndrome)
formal: A lesion at the apex of the orbit that damages the optic nerve together with the oculomotor, trochlear and abducens nerves and the first (sometimes second) division of the trigeminal nerve, producing visual loss, ophthalmoplegia and periorbital pain or numbness.
simple: A problem at the very back of the eye socket that squeezes the nerve for vision and the nerves that move the eye, so the eye is painful, droopy, stuck and may go blind.
ab: ปลายเบ้าตาอักเสบหรือถูกกดทับ
th: รอยโรคที่ปลายเบ้าตา (orbital apex) ทำให้เส้นประสาทตา (CN II) และเส้นประสาท CN III, IV, VI ร่วมกับ V1 (บางรายถึง V2) เสียพร้อมกัน ผู้ป่วยปวดรอบและหลังเบ้าตา ตามัว กลอกตาไม่ได้ หนังตาตก ภาวะนี้ต้องรีบหาสาเหตุเพราะอาจเป็นเชื้อรา มะเร็ง หรือการอักเสบ
tempoNote: Days in invasive fungal infection, zoster, trauma or inflammation; weeks to months with tumour
feat: Visual loss with a relative afferent pupillary defect and reduced colour vision — the optic nerve is involved, which separates this from a lesion confined to the superior orbital fissure
Ophthalmoplegia from combined oculomotor, trochlear and abducens palsies; ptosis is often complete and the pupil may be fixed and dilated
Peri- or retro-orbital pain, with numbness over the forehead and sometimes the cheek (V1, occasionally V2)
Proptosis, chemosis and a swollen lid when the lesion extends forwards into the orbit; the eye may look normal when the process is very posterior
A painful, rapidly progressive course with diabetes or immunosuppression should raise urgent concern for invasive fungal disease
inv: MRI orbits and brain with fat-suppressed contrast sequences, plus CT of the orbits and skull base to look at bone erosion, sinus disease and the superior orbital fissure
Urgent ENT nasal endoscopy and tissue sampling in a diabetic or immunocompromised patient (mucormycosis, aspergillosis)
Bloods: glucose and HbA1c, ESR/CRP, FBC; ANCA, ACE, IgG4, EBV DNA and cultures as directed by the suspected cause
Biopsy when imaging does not give the answer; lumbar puncture only after imaging if lymphoma or leptomeningeal disease is considered

case.who: 58-year-old woman from Nakhon Ratchasima with long-standing poorly controlled type 2 diabetes
case.story: Four days of worsening pain behind the right eye, then the lid drooped and vision fell to 'shadows'; she had a blocked nose and dark crusting inside the right nostril.
case.exam: Complete right ptosis, eye fixed in the midline, dilated unreactive pupil with RAPD, reduced forehead sensation, mild proptosis; HbA1c 12%.
case.tests: MRI: inflammatory soft-tissue change filling the right orbital apex, extending from the ethmoid and sphenoid sinuses with loss of enhancement of the nasal turbinate; nasal biopsy shows broad non-septate hyphae.
case.q: What is the syndrome, what is the most urgent diagnosis, and what should happen within hours?
case.a: Orbital apex syndrome from rhino-orbital mucormycosis; start liposomal amphotericin B, correct glucose and acidosis, and arrange urgent surgical debridement with ENT and ophthalmology.

det.patho: The orbital apex is a crowded space where the optic canal and the superior orbital fissure meet, and the common tendinous ring anchors the extraocular muscles. A mass or inflammation here compresses or infiltrates every structure passing through at once. The causes fall into infection, inflammation, tumour and trauma, and the pattern of speed and pain points to which.
det.clinical: Patients present with deep orbital ache, double vision, ptosis and falling vision, the last being the clue that the process has reached beyond the fissure. The pupil depends on the balance of parasympathetic loss from the third nerve and sympathetic fibres, so it may be dilated, mid-sized or normal. Numbness of the forehead and cornea predisposes to exposure keratopathy. In immunosuppressed or diabetic patients the course can be explosive over a few days, and black nasal crusting or a necrotic palate is a late sign. In Southeast Asia nasopharyngeal carcinoma and skull base extension of sinus disease also feature in the differential.
det.diagnosis: Treat it as a time-critical localisation exercise: map the combination of second, third, fourth, sixth and V1 deficits, then image. MRI with contrast and fat suppression is the best modality for the soft tissue and the optic nerve sheath, while CT shows bony destruction and sinus opacification. Infection requires tissue; a negative culture does not exclude mucormycosis. If imaging is clean, think of orbital myositis, IgG4-related disease, sarcoidosis, vasculitis such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and herpes zoster ophthalmicus.
det.treatment: Treatment is directed at the cause and should start before the final diagnosis when fungal disease is likely. Invasive mucormycosis needs liposomal amphotericin B, glycaemic and acid-base control and early surgical debridement; aspergillosis is treated with voriconazole or isavuconazole. Inflammatory causes respond to high-dose corticosteroids but only after infection and lymphoma are reasonably excluded. Tumours need oncology and radiotherapy planning, and zoster is treated with intravenous aciclovir in the severe form.
det.prognosis: Depends on the cause and the speed of treatment; vision loss is often permanent when the optic nerve is damaged for more than a few days.
pearls: Visual loss is what separates orbital apex from superior orbital fissure syndrome.
Painful ophthalmoplegia with vision loss in a diabetic means invasive fungal disease until proven otherwise.
Image the cavernous sinus and skull base as well; the lesion rarely respects the orbital boundary.

qx.stem: A 58-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes (HbA1c 12%) has four days of worsening right retro-orbital pain, complete ptosis, a fixed dilated pupil, forehead numbness and vision down to hand movements with a relative afferent pupillary defect. There is black crusting in the right nostril. MRI shows inflammatory soft tissue at the orbital apex extending from the sphenoid and ethmoid sinuses.
qx.q: Which management should happen within hours?
opts: Start oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg and review after a week
Give intravenous aciclovir and wait for the viral PCR
Begin radiotherapy to the orbit after oncology review
Start liposomal amphotericin B, control glucose, and arrange urgent surgical debridement with ENT and ophthalmology
Perform a lumbar puncture to exclude fungal meningitis before treatment
qx.why: Optic nerve involvement plus ophthalmoplegia and V1 loss defines orbital apex syndrome, and in a diabetic with nasal necrosis the leading diagnosis is invasive rhino-orbital mucormycosis, which kills within days without antifungal therapy, glycaemic control and debridement. Steroids alone worsen fungal infection, and aciclovir, radiotherapy or lumbar puncture do not address it. The treatment cannot wait for culture or biopsy results.

ddx.pt: Same ocular motor and V1 deficits but the optic nerve is spared and vision is normal
Posterior to the apex; V2 is often involved, proptosis is less marked and vision is usually preserved unless the optic nerve is reached
Steroid-responsive granulomatous inflammation; a diagnosis of exclusion after tumour, infection and vasculitis are ruled out

name: Numb cheek syndrome (infraorbital and maxillary nerve neuropathy)
formal: Isolated numbness of the cheek, upper lip and side of the nose from damage to the infraorbital or maxillary (V2) nerve, sometimes with weakness of the lower facial branches, and classically a warning sign of perineural spread of a facial malignancy.
simple: A numb patch on the cheek and upper lip that can be the first sign of a tumour travelling along the facial nerves.
th: ชาที่แก้ม ปีกจมูกและริมฝีปากบนจากเส้นประสาท infraorbital หรือ V2 เสีย บางรายมีริมฝีปากล่างตกจากแขนงของ CN VII ร่วมด้วย ต้องนึกถึงมะเร็งผิวหนังหน้า (SCC) หรือเนื้องอกที่ลามตามเส้นประสาท (perineural spread) เป็นอันดับแรก
tempoNote: Usually progressive over weeks to months; sudden onset after trauma, dental work or zoster
feat: Numbness or tingling of the cheek, lateral nose, lower eyelid and upper lip in the distribution of the infraorbital nerve
Spread proximally gives V2 loss at the foramen rotundum, then V3 or V1 and finally cavernous sinus signs with diplopia
'Numb cheek–limp lower lip' variant: marginal mandibular branch weakness of the facial nerve is added when the tumour reaches the facial branches
History of a treated facial skin cancer, a non-healing facial lesion or a maxillary sinus tumour is the commonest background
Pain is usually absent; the examination of the corneal reflex and other cranial nerves defines how far the lesion has spread
inv: MRI of the face and skull base with thin-section fat-suppressed contrast sequences following V2 from the infraorbital foramen to the cavernous sinus
CT of the facial bones for infraorbital canal widening, foramen rotundum enlargement or maxillary sinus tumour
Tissue diagnosis of the primary lesion (skin, nasal cavity, sinus) and head and neck oncology assessment
Exclude benign causes: dental history, zygomatic trauma, herpes zoster, diabetes, syphilis

case.who: 71-year-old male rice farmer from Surin who had a squamous cell carcinoma excised from the left cheek two years earlier
case.story: Three months of numbness over the left cheek and upper lip, followed by a drooping lower lip when he smiles and recent double vision on looking left.
case.exam: Reduced pinprick over the left V2 territory, weak left marginal mandibular branch, mild left abducens palsy; no skin recurrence is visible.
case.tests: MRI: perineural enhancement and thickening of the left infraorbital nerve extending through foramen rotundum into the cavernous sinus.
case.q: What is the explanation, and why is the scar not reassuring?
case.a: Perineural spread of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma along V2; the nerve can carry tumour well beyond a healed scar, and treatment is surgery and radiotherapy by a head and neck oncology team.

read.where: Numb chin and numb cheek syndromes

det.patho: Malignant cells, most often cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, travel along the perineurium of the trigeminal and facial nerves in the space between nerve fascicles and their sheath. Spread can be centripetal and occur without a visible mass along the nerve. The infraorbital nerve is a terminal branch of V2, and its connections with the facial nerve branches explain why the cheek and lower lip can both be affected.
det.clinical: The patient first notices numbness or a pins-and-needles sensation of the cheek, which is easily mistaken for a dental problem. Later the area becomes unreliable for sensing hot or cold and some people bite their lip. Spread to the cavernous sinus brings diplopia and pain; spread to the facial nerve produces a lower lip droop or an incomplete smile. A new infraorbital numbness in someone with a history of facial skin cancer must be treated as recurrence until imaging says otherwise.
det.diagnosis: Careful mapping of the sensory territory, corneal reflexes and every cranial nerve is the first step. MRI with thin sections and fat suppression is the best test, showing nerve thickening, asymmetric enhancement and effacement of fat in the pterygopalatine fossa, but a normal scan does not exclude disease early on. Biopsy of the nerve or primary lesion confirms the cause. Other causes include maxillary sinus carcinoma, lymphoma, adenoid cystic carcinoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
det.treatment: Treatment is that of the underlying cancer: wide surgical excision with clear margins and adjuvant radiotherapy covering the course of the nerve toward the skull base, and sometimes systemic therapy. Immunotherapy with PD-1 inhibitors such as cemiplimab is an option in advanced cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. Neuropathic pain, if present, is treated symptomatically. Benign causes are managed on their own terms.
det.prognosis: Perineural spread worsens prognosis and is a risk factor for recurrence and regional failure, but early detection while the nerve is still partly functional improves local control.
pearls: A numb cheek in a patient with a treated facial skin cancer is perineural spread until proven otherwise.
The nerve can carry tumour past a healed scar, so a normal skin examination is not reassuring.
Order MRI with fat-suppressed contrast that follows V2 all the way to the cavernous sinus.

qx.stem: A 71-year-old farmer from Surin had a squamous cell carcinoma removed from the left cheek two years ago. He now has three months of numbness over the left cheek and upper lip, followed by a drooping left lower lip when he smiles and mild diplopia on looking to the left. The skin scar looks healed with no nodule.
qx.q: What is the most appropriate investigation?

Skin patch testing for contact allergy near the scar
Nerve conduction study of the infraorbital nerve
Observation, since the healed scar excludes recurrence

Thin-section contrast MRI is the best test. The added lower lip droop and sixth nerve palsy show progression, and early treatment with surgery and radiotherapy improves control.

name: Collet–Sicard syndrome
formal: Unilateral paralysis of the glossopharyngeal, vagus, accessory and hypoglossal nerves (cranial nerves IX–XII) from a lesion at or immediately below the jugular foramen and hypoglossal canal, without brainstem long tract signs.
simple: One side of the throat, voice box, shoulder and tongue stops working because a lesion at the skull base presses on the four lower cranial nerves.
ab: ชาและอัมพาตเส้นประสาทสมองคู่ล่าง
th: เส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 9, 10, 11 และ 12 ข้างเดียวกันเสียพร้อมกัน ทำให้กลืนลำบาก เสียงแหบ ไหล่ตกและลิ้นเบี่ยง จากรอยโรคที่ jugular foramen ร่วมกับ hypoglossal canal เช่น glomus tumour, metastasis, nasopharyngeal carcinoma หรือ carotid dissection โดยไม่มีสัญญาณ brainstem
tempoNote: Weeks to months with tumour or infection; acute with trauma, dissection or thrombosis
feat: Dysphagia with nasal regurgitation, aspiration, absent gag on one side and reduced taste at the back of the tongue and a lost gag reflex on one side (IX, X)
Hoarse, breathy voice from vocal cord paralysis and palate drooping with a curtain movement of the pharynx (X)
Weakness of the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid causing shoulder droop and difficulty turning the head to the opposite side (XI)
Tongue deviation to the side of the lesion with atrophy and fasciculations over time (XII)
No Horner syndrome — the sympathetic chain is spared, which separates it from Villaret syndrome
inv: MRI of skull base and neck with contrast, MR angiography or CT angiography of the carotid and vertebral arteries
CT skull base bone window for erosion of the jugular foramen or hypoglossal canal
Flexible laryngoscopy for vocal cord mobility, speech and swallow assessment with a modified barium swallow or FEES
Work up for tumour (nasopharyngoscopy, biopsy, PET-CT) and infection as indicated

case.story: Two months of choking on liquids, a weak voice and an ache in the right neck; his shoulder 'feels heavy' and food falls out of the right side of the mouth.
case.exam: Right palate lower with uvula pulled left, right vocal cord immobile, weak right trapezius and sternocleidomastoid, tongue deviates to the right with atrophy; no Horner syndrome, limbs normal.
case.tests: MRI: enhancing mass in the right nasopharynx and parapharyngeal space eroding the jugular foramen and hypoglossal canal; biopsy shows non-keratinising nasopharyngeal carcinoma, EBV DNA elevated.
case.q: Which cranial nerves are involved, what is the eponym, and which cancer is the commonest cause locally?
case.a: Right IX–XII palsy, Collet–Sicard syndrome; nasopharyngeal carcinoma is the leading malignant cause in Thailand, and treatment is chemoradiotherapy.

read.where: 13 Cranial Nerve XI (The Spinal Accessory Nerve)

det.patho: The glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory nerves leave through the jugular foramen while the hypoglossal nerve exits through its own canal in the occipital bone a short distance behind. A single process at the jugular tubercle, occipital condyle or the carotid space below can hit all four. Compression, perineural invasion, bone destruction, thrombosis of the jugular bulb and arterial dissection are the common mechanisms.
det.clinical: Presentation is a cluster of bulbar-type symptoms on one side without the crossed motor and sensory signs of a medullary stroke. Aspiration pneumonia, weight loss and a nasal voice are common reasons for presentation. Because the sympathetic fibres run just outside, a coexisting Horner syndrome turns the label into Villaret syndrome. Neck pain, ear pain or occipital pain is typical with tumour or carotid dissection. Cervical carotid dissection causes an abrupt pain-and-palsy presentation in younger patients.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical, and the work is to find the cause. MRI with contrast shows the mass or infiltrating process and MR/CT angiography shows dissection, aneurysm or jugular vein thrombosis; CT bone windows document skull base erosion. Metastasis, glomus tumours, schwannomas, chordoma, lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma head the neoplastic list. Skull base osteomyelitis, tuberculosis and fungal infection must be excluded in diabetic or immunosuppressed patients. A swallow assessment guides safety.
det.treatment: Management is cause-specific: radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy for nasopharyngeal carcinoma and metastasis, surgery or radiosurgery for glomus tumours and schwannomas, antithrombotic therapy for dissection or thrombosis, and prolonged antimicrobials for osteomyelitis. Supportive measures include speech and swallow therapy, nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding when aspiration is unsafe, and medialisation of the vocal cord for persistent dysphonia. Dexamethasone may reduce oedema around tumour while the plan is made.
det.prognosis: Governed by the cause; some palsies recover when the lesion is treated early, while those from invasive tumours often persist.
pearls: IX to XII on one side with no Horner syndrome is Collet–Sicard; add Horner and it becomes Villaret.
Brainstem signs are absent; if they are present, think of a medullary lesion instead.
In Thai patients, check the nasopharynx first.

name: Villaret syndrome
formal: Combined one-sided palsy of the glossopharyngeal, vagus, accessory and hypoglossal nerves with an ipsilateral Horner syndrome from cervical sympathetic injury, arising from disease in the retroparotid and retrostyloid parapharyngeal compartment.
simple: The four lower cranial nerves on one side fail and the pupil and eyelid on that side show Horner syndrome, because something is growing in the space behind the jaw below the skull base.
ab: ชาและอัมพาต IX–XII ร่วมกับ Horner
th: เส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 9, 10, 11, 12 ข้างเดียวเสีย ร่วมกับ Horner syndrome ข้างเดียวกัน จากรอยโรคในช่อง retroparotid หรือ parapharyngeal ใต้ฐานกะโหลก เช่น ต่อมน้ำเหลืองโต เนื้องอก ฝี หรือ carotid dissection
tempoNote: Weeks to months with tumour or nodal disease; days with abscess or dissection
feat: Dysphagia, hoarseness, shoulder droop and tongue deviation on the same side from IX–XII palsy
Ipsilateral Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, facial anhidrosis) from the cervical sympathetic fibres alongside the internal carotid artery
Facial pain, neck swelling or a palpable upper cervical mass is common because the lesion lies outside the skull
Normal limbs, consciousness and eye movements — the brainstem is spared
The facial nerve may also be affected when the lesion extends into the parotid region, and trismus suggests masticator or pterygoid involvement
inv: Contrast MRI of the neck and skull base covering the retrostyloid parapharyngeal space, with CT angiography or MRA of the carotid
Nasopharyngoscopy and ENT biopsy; PET-CT for staging when malignancy is suspected
FNA or core biopsy of neck nodes; serum EBV DNA in endemic regions
Pharmacological pupil testing (apraclonidine) and ice-pack or bedside sweat check if the Horner syndrome is subtle

case.who: 48-year-old female teacher from Nakhon Si Thammarat
case.story: Right-sided neck swelling for six weeks, then a hoarse voice, choking on liquids and a drooping right eyelid.
case.exam: Right palatal weakness, immobile right vocal cord, weak trapezius, tongue deviates to the right, right ptosis with miosis and reduced sweating; a firm 3 cm right level II neck node.
case.tests: MRI neck: heterogeneous mass in the right retrostyloid space displacing the internal carotid artery; node biopsy shows metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma.
case.q: Which syndrome is this, and what makes it different from Collet–Sicard syndrome?
case.a: Villaret syndrome; the extra Horner syndrome shows that the cervical sympathetic chain is involved, placing the lesion in the retroparotid space, not simply at the skull base.

read.where: 12 Cranial Nerves IX and X (The Glossopharyngeal and Vagus Nerves)

det.patho: Below the jugular foramen the lower cranial nerves and the cervical sympathetic chain run together with the internal carotid artery and jugular vein in the retrostyloid compartment of the parapharyngeal space. A mass, an inflamed node, an abscess or a dissecting artery in this narrow corridor can injure the nerves one after another. The combination of lower cranial palsies with Horner syndrome is therefore a good localising sign for an extracranial, retroparotid lesion.
det.clinical: Features resemble Collet–Sicard syndrome with the addition of ptosis, a small pupil and reduced sweating on the same side. Many patients present with dysphagia or a hoarse voice before they notice the eye. A mass in the upper neck, ear pain and trismus are clues pointing outside the skull. Carotid dissection in a younger patient with neck pain and Horner syndrome should be considered at once. Eponymous names in this field overlap, so always list the nerves involved.
det.diagnosis: Neck and skull base MRI with contrast, plus CT or MR angiography, is the key investigation. The work-up of malignant causes includes nasopharyngoscopy, nodal biopsy and PET-CT; nasopharyngeal carcinoma, thyroid and lung cancer, lymphoma, paraganglioma and schwannoma are the usual culprits. Infection and abscess are suggested by fever and raised inflammatory markers. Confirm the sympathetic lesion with apraclonidine testing when the pupils are subtle.
det.treatment: Therapy depends on the cause: radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy for nasopharyngeal carcinoma, surgery for resectable tumours and nodal disease, drainage plus antibiotics for abscess, and antithrombotic treatment for dissection. Swallowing therapy and nutritional support are vital and a vocal cord injection or medialisation can improve the voice. Pain control and airway observation are needed if the neck mass is large.
det.prognosis: Varies with the underlying cause; nerve palsies from benign or inflammatory causes can improve, but those from malignancy usually require oncological control.
pearls: Horner syndrome added to IX–XII points to the retroparotid space, not the skull base.
Feel the neck and look in the nasopharynx; the answer is often extracranial.
A painful neck with Horner syndrome and a lower cranial palsy suggests carotid dissection.

qx.stem: A 48-year-old woman presents with a six-week history of a lump in the right upper neck, hoarseness and dysphagia. Examination shows weak palatal elevation, an immobile right vocal cord, weak right trapezius, tongue deviation to the right, and right ptosis with miosis and reduced facial sweating. There are no long tract signs.
qx.q: What does the additional ptosis and miosis tell you about the site of the lesion?
opts: A medullary infarct has damaged the nucleus ambiguus and descending sympathetic fibres
The lesion lies in the cavernous sinus, where sympathetic fibres run with V1
The jugular foramen alone is involved, because Horner syndrome is part of that syndrome
The cervical sympathetic chain is involved, placing the lesion in the retroparotid parapharyngeal space below the skull base
A lesion of the oculomotor nucleus in the midbrain explains both findings
qx.why: Cranial nerves IX to XII together with Horner syndrome is Villaret syndrome; below the skull base the sympathetic chain runs next to the carotid sheath and the lower cranial nerves, so a mass or node in the retroparotid space can injure all of them. A medullary stroke would produce crossed signs and ataxia, and the cavernous sinus does not contain the lower cranial nerves. The jugular foramen lesion alone spares the tongue and the sympathetic fibres.

name: Tapia syndrome
formal: Ipsilateral paralysis of the vagus (recurrent laryngeal) and hypoglossal nerves, producing vocal cord palsy and tongue weakness with sparing of the palate and, usually, the shoulder muscles, most often caused by an extracranial injury after intubation or neck and cardiac procedures.
simple: A hoarse voice and a tongue that pushes to one side after a breathing tube or neck operation, because the voice-box nerve and the tongue nerve on that side were stretched or pressed.
ab: recurrent laryngeal and hypoglossal nerve palsy
ภาวะเส้นประสาท X และ XII เสียหลังใส่ท่อช่วยหายใจ
th: เส้นประสาท vagus (recurrent laryngeal) และ hypoglossal ข้างเดียวกันเสีย ทำให้เสียงแหบจากสายเสียงเป็นอัมพาตและลิ้นเบี่ยงไปข้างที่เป็น พบบ่อยหลังใส่ท่อช่วยหายใจ การผ่าตัดคอ กระดูกสันหลังส่วนคอ หรือผ่าตัดหัวใจ
tempoNote: Appears immediately or within days of the airway or neck procedure; most improve over weeks to months
feat: Hoarse, breathy voice with an immobile vocal cord on laryngoscopy (X, recurrent laryngeal branch)
Tongue deviates to the weak side with ipsilateral wasting if the palsy persists (XII)
Palatal movement and gag are usually preserved, and trapezius and sternocleidomastoid strength is often normal
Context is the key: recent endotracheal intubation, prone or neck-flexed positioning, cervical spine surgery, shoulder arthroscopy, or cardiac and thoracic surgery
A central form with the same pattern is described in medullary lesions affecting the nucleus ambiguus and hypoglossal nucleus
inv: Flexible laryngoscopy to confirm vocal cord immobility and rule out an arytenoid dislocation from the tube
MRI of the neck and posterior fossa to exclude a compressing mass, dissection or a medullary stroke
Review of anaesthetic records: tube size and cuff pressure, duration of intubation and head position
Swallow assessment for aspiration risk; EMG of the laryngeal muscles if recovery is delayed

case.story: He underwent anterior cervical discectomy under general anaesthesia and woke with a weak, breathy voice and difficulty pushing food around the mouth on the right.
case.exam: Right vocal cord immobile, tongue deviates to the right with no atrophy, palate elevates symmetrically, shoulder strength is normal, no Horner syndrome.
case.tests: MRI neck shows post-operative change without a collection or mass; brain MRI is normal; swallow study shows silent aspiration of thin liquids.
case.q: Which two nerves are involved, and what is the likely mechanism and prognosis?
case.a: Tapia syndrome with right vagus (recurrent laryngeal) and hypoglossal palsy from compression or stretch around the airway device and neck positioning; many recover over weeks to months with swallowing therapy.

read.where: Skull base syndromes: anatomy, step approach, foramen syndromes

det.patho: The vagus and hypoglossal nerves lie close together at the level of the first and second cervical vertebrae, near the carotid sheath, where the hypoglossal nerve crosses over the vagus. Pressure from the tube cuff or laryngeal mask, extreme neck flexion or rotation, and traction during operations compress both nerves at the same level. The superior laryngeal branch and the palatal branches leave higher up, which explains why the palate is spared while the vocal cord is paralysed.
det.clinical: Patients wake from anaesthesia or return from a procedure with hoarseness, a weak cough and a tongue that does not move to the opposite side. Swallowing difficulty and aspiration are the major risks. The hallmark is the asymmetric tongue and vocal cord weakness without other cranial nerve involvement. It is under-recognised because hoarseness after intubation is common and attributed to local trauma. Bilateral involvement is rare but can compromise the airway.
det.diagnosis: Direct laryngoscopy confirms vocal cord immobility, and tongue examination shows deviation. Imaging is needed to exclude structural causes when the history is not clearly iatrogenic: MRI of the neck and skull base, and CT or MRA for carotid dissection. Arytenoid dislocation can mimic a cord palsy and is judged by laryngeal EMG and stroboscopy. An isolated hypoglossal and vagal pattern without a procedure should prompt a search for a mass at the skull base.
det.treatment: Most patients improve with watchful waiting, voice and swallow therapy and nutritional support. Nasogastric feeding or a short course of enteral feeding may be needed in the early period of aspiration. Injection laryngoplasty or medialisation thyroplasty is offered if the voice does not recover by three to six months. Underlying structural causes are managed in the usual way, and careful positioning and cuff pressure monitoring prevent recurrence.
det.prognosis: Usually good for post-intubation cases, with recovery over weeks to a year; persistent hoarseness occurs in a minority.
pearls: Voice-box palsy plus tongue deviation after anaesthesia is Tapia syndrome; check the position and tube record.
Palate and shoulder strength are spared, which separates it from skull base syndromes.
Always look at the larynx directly; a dislocated arytenoid mimics a palsy.
det.thd: Tapia syndrome คือเส้นประสาท vagus (recurrent laryngeal) และ hypoglossal ข้างเดียวกันเสียพร้อมกัน ทำให้เสียงแหบและลิ้นเบี่ยง แต่เพดานปากและไหล่ปกติ พบบ่อยหลังใส่ท่อช่วยหายใจ ผ่าตัดคอหรือหัวใจ ต้องส่องกล่องเสียงและทำ MRI ถ้าไม่มีประวัติหัตถการชัดเจน ส่วนใหญ่ฟื้นได้ด้วย speech/swallow therapy และให้ฉีดสายเสียงถ้าเสียงไม่ดีขึ้น

qx.stem: A 63-year-old retired bus driver from Songkhla undergoes a six-hour anterior cervical discectomy under general anaesthesia and wakes with a breathy voice and difficulty moving food in the mouth. The soft palate rises symmetrically, the gag is present, shoulder shrug is normal, the tongue deviates to the right, and laryngoscopy shows an immobile right vocal cord. Brain and neck MRI show only post-operative change.
qx.q: Which explanation best fits this picture?
opts: A right lateral medullary infarct with Wallenberg syndrome
Right jugular foramen syndrome from a skull base metastasis
Combined right vagus (recurrent laryngeal) and hypoglossal nerve injury at the upper cervical level from airway device pressure or neck positioning
Bulbar-onset myasthenia gravis unmasked by anaesthesia
Right glossopharyngeal neuralgia triggered by intubation
qx.why: Hoarseness from a vocal cord palsy plus ipsilateral tongue weakness with a spared palate and spared accessory nerve is Tapia syndrome, usually extracranial and associated with intubation, extreme neck positioning or neck and cardiac surgery. A medullary infarct would produce crossed sensory loss, ataxia and Horner syndrome, and a jugular foramen lesion would involve IX and XI and not the hypoglossal nerve. Most patients recover with swallowing therapy over weeks to months.

name: Garcin syndrome (half-base syndrome)
formal: Progressive unilateral paralysis of most or all cranial nerves, typically caused by a destructive skull base lesion, with no brainstem long tract signs and no intracranial hypertension.
simple: One side of the skull base is slowly destroyed, so almost all the nerves of the face, eye, ear and throat on that side stop working one after another while the brain itself still works.
ab: กลุ่มอาการเส้นประสาทสมองข้างเดียวเสียหมด
th: เส้นประสาทสมองเกือบทุกคู่ข้างเดียวกันเสียแบบค่อยเป็นค่อยไป จากรอยโรคที่ทำลายฐานกะโหลกครึ่งซีก โดยไม่มีอาการ brainstem หรือ ICP สูง สาเหตุสำคัญคือ nasopharyngeal carcinoma, chordoma, metastasis และการติดเชื้อฐานกะโหลก
tempoNote: Cranial nerves fail one by one over weeks to months
feat: Sequential involvement of many cranial nerves on one side, usually five or more, often beginning with abducens, trigeminal or lower cranial nerves
Severe, persistent headache or facial pain on the same side, often the reason for presentation
No pyramidal signs, no sensory level or ataxia, normal consciousness and no papilloedema, so the brainstem and cortex are spared
Skull base destruction on CT and sometimes a mass in the nasopharynx or neck nodes
Rapid neurological disability from cranial neuropathies despite a normal brain parenchyma on MRI
inv: Contrast MRI with fat suppression and CT of the skull base showing bone destruction and the extent of nerve involvement
Nasopharyngoscopy with biopsy; serum EBV DNA and VCA-IgA in endemic regions
Chest and abdomen imaging, PET-CT and bone survey for metastasis, myeloma and lymphoma
If infection is suspected: ESR/CRP, cultures, fungal markers and tissue; lumbar puncture only after imaging

case.story: Right headache and double vision for four months, then right facial numbness, hearing loss, hoarse voice and difficulty swallowing; he has lost 8 kg.
case.exam: Right abducens palsy, V1–V3 hypoesthesia with weak masticatory muscles, facial weakness, sensorineural deafness, right palatal and vocal cord palsy, shoulder droop and tongue deviation; limbs and gait normal.
case.tests: CT: destruction of the right clivus and petrous apex; MRI: nasopharyngeal mass invading the skull base and cavernous sinus with normal brain parenchyma; biopsy shows nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
case.q: Name the syndrome, the commonest cause here, and why there are no long tract signs.
case.a: Garcin syndrome (half-base syndrome) due to nasopharyngeal carcinoma; the tumour spreads along the base of skull outside the brain, so cranial nerves fail while the brainstem is untouched.

read.where: Skull base syndromes: anatomy, step approach, foramen syndromes

det.patho: The cranial nerves exit the skull through foramina along the base of the skull. A malignant, infectious or inflammatory process that spreads along one half of the skull base can compress or invade each nerve in turn, while the brain stays free. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma extends from the fossa of Rosenmüller through the foramen lacerum and cavernous sinus, producing the typical sequence. Primary skull base tumours and metastases are the other leading causes.
det.clinical: The course is slowly progressive over weeks to months, and the first nerves affected depend on the location. Pain is usually severe. The syndrome is called incomplete when only some nerves are involved and bilateral if the lesion crosses the midline. Absence of pyramidal signs and papilloedema reflects the extra-axial spread. Patients often arrive after being treated for sinusitis, migraine or dental pain for months, so ask early about neck lumps, epistaxis and hearing loss.
det.diagnosis: Garcin syndrome is a descriptive diagnosis and the aim is to find the cause. High-resolution contrast MRI and CT define the destruction and the route of spread, and endoscopic biopsy of the nasopharynx or the skull base lesion confirms tissue. Causes include nasopharyngeal carcinoma, chordoma, chondrosarcoma, plasmacytoma and myeloma, lymphoma, metastases, leptomeningeal disease, skull base osteomyelitis, tuberculosis and fungal infection, Paget disease and rarely granulomatous inflammation.
det.treatment: Treatment is that of the underlying disease. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is treated with concurrent chemoradiotherapy and, in advanced disease, immunotherapy-containing regimens; chordoma needs surgery and proton or carbon-ion radiotherapy; infection requires prolonged targeted antimicrobials; metastases need radiotherapy and systemic therapy. Symptomatic care includes eye protection, nutritional support, speech and swallow therapy, and analgesia for neuropathic pain.
det.prognosis: Determined by the cause; nasopharyngeal carcinoma has a reasonable response to chemoradiotherapy whereas metastasis and recurrent disease carry a worse outlook.
pearls: Many cranial nerves on one side with a normal brain on MRI is a skull base lesion.
No long tract signs or papilloedema is part of the definition.
Biopsy the nasopharynx in endemic areas before accepting a benign explanation.
det.thd: Garcin syndrome หรือ half-base syndrome คือเส้นประสาทสมองเกือบทุกคู่ข้างเดียวกันเสียตามลำดับ ปวดศีรษะหรือใบหน้ารุนแรง โดยไม่มีอาการ brainstem และไม่มี ICP สูง บ่งชี้รอยโรคที่ฐานกะโหลกด้านนอกสมอง สาเหตุสำคัญคือ nasopharyngeal carcinoma, chordoma, metastasis และการติดเชื้อฐานกะโหลก ตรวจ MRI/CT ฐานกะโหลก ส่องจมูกและตัดชิ้นเนื้อ แล้วรักษาตามสาเหตุ

qx.stem: A 50-year-old fruit vendor from Chanthaburi has had four months of right headache, then diplopia, facial numbness, hearing loss, hoarseness and swallowing difficulty. He has lost 7 kg. The limbs, gait, consciousness and fundi are normal, and MRI of the brain parenchyma is normal but shows an enhancing soft tissue mass at the right skull base.
qx.q: What is the best next step to establish the diagnosis?
opts: Nasopharyngoscopy with biopsy, supported by contrast MRI and CT of the skull base and plasma EBV DNA
Lumbar puncture with cytology, because the brain MRI is normal
Empirical high-dose methylprednisolone for presumed Tolosa–Hunt syndrome
Electromyography of the tongue and larynx to confirm the cranial neuropathies
Repeat MRI in three months to assess progression before biopsy
qx.why: Progressive unilateral involvement of most cranial nerves without long tract signs or raised pressure is Garcin (half-base) syndrome and points to an extra-axial destructive skull base process; nasopharyngeal carcinoma is the leading malignant cause in Thailand. Direct endoscopic biopsy gives tissue quickly. Empirical steroids could mask lymphoma and delay diagnosis, and Tolosa–Hunt syndrome does not destroy bone. Waiting wastes time and lumbar puncture does not address the mass.

name: Laminin β2 deficiency (Pierson syndrome)
formal: An autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic LAMB2 variants, in which absence of laminin β2 in the glomerular, retinal, lens and neuromuscular basement membranes produces congenital nephrotic syndrome, microcoria and visual impairment, with a congenital myasthenic syndrome and developmental delay.
simple: A rare inherited disorder in which one structural protein is missing from the kidney, eye and nerve-muscle junction, causing early kidney failure, tiny fixed pupils, poor vision and weak floppy muscles.
ab: ภาวะขาด laminin β2
th: เกิดจากยีน LAMB2 กลายพันธุ์แบบถ่ายทอดยีนด้อย ทำให้เกิดโรคไตเนฟโฟรติกตั้งแต่กำเนิด รูม่านตาเล็ก (microcoria) ตามองไม่เห็น กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงจาก neuromuscular junction ผิดปกติ และพัฒนาการล่าช้า ยา pyridostigmine อาจทำให้แย่ลง
tempoNote: Present from birth; severe forms die in infancy from renal failure or respiratory failure, milder forms survive longer
feat: Congenital nephrotic syndrome with heavy proteinuria and hypoalbuminaemia in the first weeks of life, progressing to end-stage kidney disease
Microcoria (fixed, tiny pupils) and visual impairment from retinal and lens abnormalities
Neonatal hypotonia, feeding difficulty and breathing weakness from the neuromuscular junction defect
Developmental delay and, in some, a milder or atypical phenotype with isolated nephrotic syndrome or eye disease
Fatigable weakness is not easy to see in a newborn; the clue is the combination of kidney, pupils and hypotonia
inv: LAMB2 gene sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis; the gene panel for congenital nephrotic syndrome often includes it
Urine protein/creatinine ratio, serum albumin and creatinine; renal ultrasound often shows enlarged echogenic kidneys; kidney biopsy shows diffuse mesangial sclerosis
Slit-lamp and fundus examination for microcoria, cataract, retinal changes
Repetitive nerve stimulation (decrement at low and high rates) and low CMAP amplitude; no AChR or MuSK antibodies

case.who: 7-week-old girl from Udon Thani, born at term to unrelated parents
case.story: Generalised oedema from week 3, poor suck and limp posture; her mother noticed the pupils always looked 'pin-point' and never reacted to light.
case.exam: Hypotonic infant with ascites, weak cry, tiny fixed pupils, poor visual following and reduced limb movements.
case.tests: Urine protein 4+; albumin 1.7 g/dL; creatinine raised; renal ultrasound shows enlarged kidneys; biallelic truncating LAMB2 variants; RNS shows decrement.
case.q: What is the unifying diagnosis, and which usual myasthenia drug should be used with caution?
case.a: Pierson syndrome (laminin β2 deficiency); pyridostigmine can worsen the neuromuscular junction weakness, whereas ephedrine or salbutamol have been used with some benefit, alongside renal support and genetic counselling.

det.patho: Laminin β2 is a component of the heterotrimeric laminin 221 and laminin 521 in the basement membranes of the glomerulus, ciliary body, lens and the synaptic cleft of the motor endplate. Loss of the β2 chain disrupts the filtration barrier, ocular muscle function and the organisation of the synaptic basal lamina. At the neuromuscular junction the presynaptic terminal shrinks, active zones are lost, the cleft widens and Schwann cell processes enter it, which reduces transmitter release.
det.clinical: The severe classical form presents in the neonatal period with nephrotic syndrome, microcoria and neonatal hypotonia, and children usually die in infancy from kidney failure or infection unless dialysis and transplantation are possible. Neuromuscular features are often masked by systemic illness and may be recognised only on electrodiagnostic testing. Less severe variants show nephrotic syndrome of later onset, ocular problems or only a milder neuromuscular phenotype. It is rare but is the best example of a syndromic synaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome.
det.diagnosis: A newborn with congenital nephrotic syndrome should have LAMB2 sequencing early, together with an ophthalmology review for the pupils. Nerve conduction shows small compound action potentials, and repetitive stimulation shows a decremental response at low and high frequency. Antibody tests exclude autoimmune myasthenia. Mutation type predicts severity: truncating biallelic variants give the full syndrome while missense variants may give milder forms.
det.treatment: Management is supportive and multidisciplinary. Renal care includes albumin infusions, diuretics, nephrectomy and dialysis in some cases and later transplantation, and ventilatory and feeding support are given as needed. Pyridostigmine should be avoided or used with great caution because it can worsen the junction, while ephedrine and salbutamol have been tried with reported benefit through mechanisms that are not fully understood. Genetic counselling and prenatal testing are offered to the family.
det.prognosis: Poor in the classical form, with death in infancy; survival is longer in milder variants or when renal replacement is available.
pearls: Tiny fixed pupils plus congenital nephrotic syndrome plus hypotonia is Pierson syndrome.
Pyridostigmine can worsen synaptic CMS such as laminin β2 deficiency; try ephedrine or salbutamol.
Look for the syndromic clue: no other CMS has kidney or pupil involvement.
det.thd: Laminin β2 deficiency หรือ Pierson syndrome เกิดจากยีน LAMB2 กลายพันธุ์แบบยีนด้อย ทำให้เกิดโรคไตเนฟโฟรติกตั้งแต่กำเนิด รูม่านตาเล็กตายึดติดและมองไม่เห็น ร่วมกับกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงจากความผิดปกติของ neuromuscular junction ตรวจพบ decrement ใน RNS ยา pyridostigmine อาจทำให้แย่ลง ใช้ ephedrine หรือ salbutamol ได้ ร่วมกับดูแลไตและให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม
