name: SNAP25-related congenital myasthenic syndrome (SNAP25B deficiency)
formal: A presynaptic form of congenital myasthenia due to variants in SNAP25, a SNARE protein needed for calcium-triggered release of acetylcholine, usually presenting in the newborn with hypotonia, joint contractures and respiratory failure and accompanied by epilepsy, intellectual disability and cerebellar ataxia.
simple: A rare genetic fault in a protein that lets nerve endings release their chemical messenger, causing weak muscles from birth together with seizures, learning problems and clumsiness.
ab: CMS with ataxia and intellectual disability
th: ความผิดปกติของยีน SNAP25 ซึ่งเป็นโปรตีนในกลุ่ม SNARE ที่ช่วยปล่อย acetylcholine จากปลายประสาท ทำให้ทารกกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง ข้อติด หายใจล้มเหลว ร่วมกับชัก พัฒนาการล่าช้าและเดินเซ ยา amifampridine อาจช่วยกำลังกล้ามเนื้อแต่ไม่ช่วย ataxia ขณะที่ pyridostigmine มักไม่ได้ผล
tempoNote: From birth, with persistent weakness and a central nervous system phenotype that evolves through childhood
feat: Reduced fetal movements, neonatal hypotonia, cyanosis or respiratory failure and multiple joint contractures at birth
Fatigable weakness with decrement on low-rate repetitive stimulation
Epilepsy with generalised spike-wave discharges, intellectual disability and sometimes behavioural disorders, as SNAP25 also works in central synapses
Cerebellar ataxia that develops in childhood and does not respond to treatment aimed at the junction
Weakness improves little with pyridostigmine, which is a pointer to a presynaptic exocytosis defect
inv: Targeted CMS panel or exome including SNAP25; compare with SYT2, VAMP1, UNC13A and other presynaptic genes
RNS: low baseline CMAP amplitude with decrement at low rates; single fibre EMG shows increased jitter and blocking
EEG for spike-wave activity; MRI brain; developmental assessment
Exclude AChR and MuSK antibodies, spinal muscular atrophy and other causes of neonatal hypotonia

case.who: 3-year-old boy from Phayao, the first child of healthy parents
case.story: Born with multiple contractures and needed ventilation for the first weeks; fed through a tube for months; later seizures with staring spells and unsteady walking.
case.exam: Mildly hypotonic with fatigable proximal weakness and ptosis late in the day, intention tremor and wide-based gait; developmental quotient about 60.
case.tests: RNS shows low baseline CMAP and a 20% decrement at 3 Hz; EEG shows generalised spike-wave; exome shows a de novo pathogenic SNAP25 variant; AChR and MuSK antibodies negative.
case.q: Which treatment is more likely to help muscle strength than pyridostigmine, and what will it not fix?
case.a: Amifampridine, which prolongs presynaptic depolarisation and increases calcium-dependent release; it may improve strength but does not reverse the ataxia or cognitive problems.

det.patho: SNAP25 is a presynaptic SNARE protein that forms the complex with syntaxin and VAMP2, allowing synaptic vesicles to fuse with the membrane when calcium enters. The brain and motor nerve terminal both depend on it, which accounts for the combination of junction failure and central nervous system disease. Variants can impair vesicle priming and fusion, reducing the number of acetylcholine quanta released with each impulse.
det.clinical: Newborns show hypomotility, contractures and respiratory difficulty at birth. Later childhood brings intellectual disability, epilepsy, ataxia and sometimes behavioural disturbance. The weakness fluctuates and gets worse with fever or fatigue but is less prominent than the central features in older children. Because neuromuscular and CNS features coincide, the condition is an example of a syndromic presynaptic CMS.
det.diagnosis: Suspect a presynaptic exocytosis defect in a hypotonic infant with a decrement and no antibodies, with epilepsy or developmental delay as the clue. Electrodiagnosis shows small CMAPs and a decrementing response at slow rates, with jitter on single fibre EMG. Genetic confirmation is by exome or panel testing, with parental samples for de novo variants. The yield of testing is highest when clinical features include both myasthenic and CNS manifestations.
det.treatment: There is no established protocol, but amifampridine has improved motor performance in reported patients without altering the ataxia. Pyridostigmine is usually ineffective and may worsen presynaptic forms; salbutamol or ephedrine is another option. Epilepsy is treated with an antiseizure medicine such as levetiracetam, and supportive care involves ventilatory and feeding assistance, physiotherapy and educational support. Genetic counselling is advised.
det.prognosis: Variable; the neuromuscular weakness can improve with age while cognitive and cerebellar problems often persist.
pearls: Myasthenic weakness plus epilepsy, ataxia and intellectual disability points to SNAP25.
Pyridostigmine is usually ineffective; amifampridine is the drug to try.
Think of it as a presynaptic CMS with brain involvement.
det.thd: SNAP25-related CMS เกิดจากความผิดปกติของโปรตีน SNAP25 ในกลุ่ม SNARE ที่ช่วยปล่อย acetylcholine ทารกอ่อนแรง ข้อติดและหายใจลำบากตั้งแต่เกิด ร่วมกับชัก พัฒนาการช้าและเดินเซ RNS พบ decrement ตรวจยืนยันด้วยยีน SNAP25 ยา pyridostigmine มักไม่ได้ผล ใช้ amifampridine เพื่อเพิ่มกำลัง แต่ไม่ช่วย ataxia และให้ยากันชักตามความเหมาะสม

name: Synaptotagmin-2 (SYT2) congenital myasthenic syndrome
formal: A presynaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome, usually autosomal dominant, due to variants in the calcium-binding domain of synaptotagmin-2, which presents in childhood with foot deformity and distal weakness resembling a motor neuropathy, and shows low CMAP amplitudes with marked facilitation after exercise on repetitive stimulation.
simple: A genetic fault in the calcium sensor of the nerve ending causes weakness of the feet and hands from childhood that looks like a nerve disease but is actually at the nerve-muscle junction.
th: ความผิดปกติของยีน SYT2 ซึ่งเป็นตัวรับแคลเซียมที่ปลายประสาททำให้การปล่อย acetylcholine บกพร่อง เด็กมักมีเท้าผิดรูป อ่อนแรงที่ปลายแขนขาและ reflex ลดลงคล้ายโรคเส้นประสาทยนต์ RNS พบ CMAP ต่ำ มี decrement ที่ความถี่ต่ำและ facilitation หลังออกกำลังชัดเจน รักษาด้วย amifampridine
tempoNote: Childhood onset with slow or non-progressive course; may be mistaken for a hereditary motor neuropathy
feat: Onset in infancy or childhood with pes cavus or other foot deformity, delayed motor milestones and walking difficulty
Distal limb weakness and wasting with reduced or absent reflexes, mimicking distal hereditary motor neuropathy
Sometimes mild bulbar or ocular weakness is present, and weakness may be fatigable
Dominant family history in many cases; the variant sits in the calcium-binding domain of the protein
Exercise or high-rate stimulation transiently improves strength and the compound action potential
inv: Nerve conduction: reduced CMAP amplitude with normal sensory studies and normal velocities, favouring a junction disorder over axonal neuropathy
RNS: decrement at low rate and a pronounced increment (several hundred per cent) after brief exercise or high-frequency stimulation
Single-fibre EMG shows jitter and blocking; antibodies (AChR, MuSK, VGCC) negative
SYT2 gene sequencing within a neuromuscular or CMS panel

case.who: 10-year-old girl from Roi Et with a similarly affected father
case.story: Since toddlerhood she has had high-arched feet, tires on walking and cannot run; her father walked on his toes as a child and has weak hands.
case.exam: Pes cavus, weak ankle dorsiflexion and finger abduction, reduced ankle jerks; no sensory loss; mild fatigable ptosis.
case.tests: Sensory NCS normal, motor CMAP low; RNS shows 15% decrement at 3 Hz and 300% increment after 10 seconds of exercise; heterozygous SYT2 variant in the calcium-binding domain, also present in her father.
case.q: Why is this not a hereditary motor neuropathy, and what drug is most likely to help?
case.a: Normal sensory studies, fatigable weakness and a large post-exercise increment point to a presynaptic junction disorder (SYT2 CMS); amifampridine can improve motor function and jitter.

det.patho: Synaptotagmin-2 is the main calcium sensor on synaptic vesicles at the motor nerve terminal, coupling the calcium influx from an action potential to vesicle fusion. Dominant variants in the calcium-binding domain make release less sensitive to calcium, so at rest fewer quanta are released and the end-plate potential is small. A burst of activity raises residual calcium, which can overcome the defect, explaining the facilitation after exercise.
det.clinical: The picture is a long-standing distal weakness with foot deformity in a child, often misdiagnosed as hereditary motor neuropathy or axonal CMT. Clues are a fluctuating or fatigable component, mild ocular or bulbar signs and a family history. Reflexes are reduced but can improve after exercise as in LEMS. Severity varies even within a family, and some patients are only mildly affected.
det.diagnosis: The electrodiagnostic pattern is the key. Low CMAPs with normal sensory potentials and a pronounced increment after exercise point to a presynaptic disorder. Differentiate from acquired LEMS by age, family history and absence of VGCC antibodies and malignancy. Confirm with SYT2 sequencing; negative sequencing should prompt testing of related genes such as VAMP1 and SNAP25.
det.treatment: Amifampridine, which blocks presynaptic potassium channels and so lengthens the nerve terminal action potential, improves motor function and jitter in reported patients, although it does not change the nerve conduction results. Pyridostigmine may add a small effect. Seizure risk with amifampridine requires dose caution, and orthotic support, physiotherapy and orthopaedic management of foot deformity are standard.
det.prognosis: Usually slowly progressive or stable; many patients are ambulant into adulthood with treatment.
pearls: Distal weakness with normal sensory studies and a big post-exercise increment is a presynaptic CMS, not CMT.
Consider LEMS-like physiology in a child: think SYT2.
Amifampridine is the drug to try; check seizure history first.

name: Primary acetylcholine receptor (AChR) deficiency congenital myasthenic syndrome
formal: A postsynaptic congenital myasthenic syndrome in which recessive loss-of-function variants, most often in the epsilon subunit gene CHRNE, reduce the number of acetylcholine receptors at the endplate, causing early-onset fatigable ptosis, ophthalmoparesis and limb weakness that usually respond to cholinesterase inhibitors and amifampridine.
simple: Too few acetylcholine receptors are built on the muscle, so the muscles tire easily and the eyelids droop from early childhood, but treatment usually works well.
ab: Primary acetylcholine receptor  deficiency congenital myasthenic syndrome
th: กลุ่ม CMS ที่ตัวรับ acetylcholine บนกล้ามเนื้อมีจำนวนลดลง ส่วนใหญ่จากยีน CHRNE (epsilon subunit) ถ่ายทอดแบบยีนด้อย ผู้ป่วยมีหนังตาตก กลอกตาลำบาก อ่อนแรงและล้าง่ายตั้งแต่เด็ก ตอบสนองต่อ pyridostigmine และ amifampridine ได้ดีในส่วนใหญ่
tempoNote: Present from infancy or early childhood, fluctuating, with exacerbations during infections; usually stable or slowly improving with treatment
feat: Congenital or early-onset ptosis with ophthalmoparesis and limited eye movements, often with facial and bulbar weakness
Fatigable limb weakness of mild to moderate degree, with delayed motor milestones and sometimes respiratory crises during infections
Autosomal recessive; epsilon-subunit null variants are the commonest because the fetal gamma subunit partly substitutes
Variants in the alpha, beta or delta subunits are usually more severe, causing fetal akinesia or early death
AChR, MuSK and LRP4 antibodies are negative and the response to IVIG or thymectomy is absent
inv: RNS at 2–3 Hz shows a decrement; single-fibre EMG shows increased jitter and blocking
CMS gene panel or exome including CHRNE, CHRNA1, CHRNB1, CHRND and RAPSN; compare with the kinetic-defect forms
Antibody screen (AChR, MuSK, LRP4) negative; consider CK, which is normal or mildly elevated
Muscle biopsy is rarely required but may show reduced end-plate AChR staining with bungarotoxin

case.who: 17-year-old boy from Nan who had droopy eyelids from toddlerhood
case.story: Drooping eyelids since infancy, a squint corrected at age 5, and episodes of weakness and breathlessness with each respiratory infection; he stopped sports because of fatigue.
case.exam: Bilateral ptosis, ophthalmoparesis with limited elevation and abduction, mild facial weakness, fatigable proximal weakness; no skeletal malformation.
case.tests: AChR and MuSK antibodies negative; RNS at 3 Hz shows 25% decrement; panel shows biallelic CHRNE loss-of-function variants; CT chest normal.
case.q: Why do the symptoms usually improve with pyridostigmine, and why is thymectomy not useful?
case.a: Cholinesterase inhibition prolongs acetylcholine in the cleft to compensate for fewer receptors, and 3,4-diaminopyridine adds further release; the disease is genetic, not autoimmune, so immunotherapy and thymectomy do not help.

det.patho: Acetylcholine receptors at the endplate are pentamers composed of alpha, beta, delta and epsilon subunits in adults, with the fetal gamma subunit replacing epsilon in the fetus. Recessive null variants in the epsilon gene reduce the number of adult-type receptors, though gamma-containing receptors persist and partly compensate. Mutations of the other subunits, with no substitute, often lead to fetal akinesia deformation sequence or early death.
det.clinical: Most children are recognised in infancy because of ptosis and limited eye movement, and weakness is mild to moderate with a fluctuating course. Respiratory crises triggered by infection can occur, especially in the first years, and some patients have a transient worsening around puberty or pregnancy. Facial and bulbar involvement is typical, and the face may look long with a high-arched palate. In older patients with mild phenotypes the diagnosis can be made late and misattributed to seronegative myasthenia gravis.
det.diagnosis: A seronegative patient with early-onset ocular and generalised myasthenia and a decrementing response should be tested for CMS. Gene panel testing detects variants in the main subunit genes and, importantly, helps distinguish AChR deficiency from kinetic defects and RAPSN, DOK7 and COLQ forms, because treatment differs. Electrodiagnostic findings support the diagnosis but cannot subtype. Functional receptor studies are research tools.
det.treatment: Pyridostigmine is the first-line treatment, usually started at around 0.5–1 mg/kg per dose and titrated to response, and amifampridine can be added when there is residual weakness. Salbutamol or ephedrine has been used as an add-on in some CMS types. Anaesthetic care must avoid or reduce neuromuscular blockers and prevent respiratory infection triggers. Genetic counselling is provided.
det.prognosis: Generally favourable with treatment, though ocular signs may persist and respiratory events need vigilance in early childhood.
pearls: Seronegative ptosis and ophthalmoparesis from childhood is CMS until proven otherwise.
CHRNE variants are the commonest; the fetal gamma subunit buffers the loss.
Pyridostigmine usually helps AChR deficiency but worsens slow channel syndrome and DOK7 and COLQ forms.
det.thd: Primary AChR deficiency CMS คือการมีตัวรับ acetylcholine บนกล้ามเนื้อน้อยลง ส่วนใหญ่จากยีน CHRNE แบบยีนด้อย ผู้ป่วยมีหนังตาตก ตาขยับจำกัด อ่อนแรงและล้าง่ายตั้งแต่เด็ก ตรวจ RNS พบ decrement และไม่พบแอนติบอดี ตอบสนองดีต่อ pyridostigmine และ amifampridine ไม่ต้องใช้ immunotherapy หรือ thymectomy ควรระวังการหายใจล้มเหลวเมื่อติดเชื้อ

name: GFPT1-related congenital myasthenic syndrome
formal: A limb-girdle form of congenital myasthenic syndrome with tubular aggregates on muscle biopsy, caused by recessive variants in GFPT1, the rate-limiting enzyme of the hexosamine pathway, which impairs glycosylation of proteins at the neuromuscular junction; most patients respond to pyridostigmine and amifampridine.
simple: A genetic problem in how sugar chains are attached to proteins at the nerve-muscle junction, producing tiring weakness of the hips and shoulders that usually responds to treatment.
th: CMS จากยีน GFPT1 ซึ่งเป็นเอนไซม์ในวิถี hexosamine ที่จำเป็นต่อ glycosylation ของโปรตีนที่ neuromuscular junction ผู้ป่วยมีกล้ามเนื้อต้นแขนต้นขา (limb-girdle) อ่อนแรงและล้าง่ายเริ่มในวัยเด็ก มักไม่มีตาขยับจำกัด ตัดชิ้นเนื้อพบ tubular aggregates ตอบสนองต่อ pyridostigmine และ amifampridine ได้ดี
tempoNote: Childhood onset with fluctuating, usually non-progressive weakness; worsens during illness
feat: Proximal limb-girdle weakness with fatigability, usually noticed in the first decade, with difficulty climbing stairs or rising from the floor
Ocular muscles and the face are relatively spared, in contrast to AChR deficiency or slow channel syndrome
Normal or mildly raised CK (up to about ten times normal) and a myopathic-looking biopsy
Tubular aggregates, rimmed vacuoles and type 1 fibre predominance on biopsy, with small, simplified endplates
Recessive inheritance; some patients are asymptomatic until adolescence
inv: RNS: decrement at 2–3 Hz, which may require testing of proximal muscles; single-fibre EMG shows jitter and blocking
CK (normal to ten-fold elevation); AChR and MuSK antibodies negative
Muscle biopsy with NADH and ATPase stains for tubular aggregates and fibre type changes; electron microscopy of endplates is research-only
GFPT1 gene sequencing, ideally within a limb-girdle weakness or CMS panel that also covers DPAGT1, ALG2, ALG14, GMPPB

case.story: He has always been slow at sports and now cannot climb stairs or stand from a squat after a few repetitions; weakness is worse in the afternoon and after a viral illness.
case.exam: Mild proximal weakness with lordosis, normal eye movements, no ptosis, fatigable shoulder abduction; reflexes present.
case.tests: CK 600 U/L; RNS of the deltoid shows a 20% decrement; biopsy shows tubular aggregates; compound heterozygous GFPT1 variants; AChR and MuSK antibodies negative.
case.q: What treatment is likely to help, and what is the useful clue that points away from LGMD?
case.a: Pyridostigmine, with amifampridine if needed; fatigable weakness, decrement on RNS and tubular aggregates indicate a junction disorder rather than a dystrophy.

det.patho: GFPT1 catalyses the first and rate-limiting step in the hexosamine pathway, which supplies UDP-N-acetylglucosamine for N- and O-linked glycosylation. Reduced activity probably impairs glycosylation of AChR subunits and other junction and muscle proteins, leading to fewer receptors and abnormal endplate structure. The tissue specificity to the neuromuscular junction is not fully understood, since the enzyme is widely expressed.
det.clinical: The usual story is a child or adolescent with limb-girdle weakness that fluctuates, with relatively normal eye movements. Weakness may be mild and be mistaken for a muscular dystrophy or an inflammatory myopathy. Respiratory crises are uncommon, and intellect is normal, which differentiates it from DPAGT1-related disease where intellectual disability may be associated. Exacerbations occur with infection and, in some, after prolonged physical activity.
det.diagnosis: Consider GFPT1 CMS in any patient with limb-girdle weakness plus fatigable features, a decrementing response and tubular aggregates on biopsy. Repetitive stimulation of proximal muscles can reveal a decrement missed in distal muscles. Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis and distinguishes it from DOK7 and other CMS types, in which treatment differs. The antibody tests and thymus imaging exclude autoimmune myasthenia.
det.treatment: Cholinesterase inhibitors are the foundation: pyridostigmine in divided doses is the usual first step and, if the effect is partial, 3,4-diaminopyridine is added. Salbutamol has been used in refractory cases. The response is usually better than in DPAGT1 disease. Anaesthetic management requires caution with neuromuscular blockers, and infections need early treatment.
det.prognosis: Usually good with treatment, with stable or slowly progressive weakness; some patients develop fixed proximal weakness over years.
pearls: Limb-girdle CMS with sparing of the eye muscles suggests a glycosylation gene.
Tubular aggregates on biopsy plus a decrement should prompt GFPT1 testing.
Respond to pyridostigmine and amifampridine; this is different from DOK7 where pyridostigmine can worsen.

name: DPAGT1-related congenital myasthenic syndrome
formal: A limb-girdle congenital myasthenic syndrome with tubular aggregates caused by recessive variants in DPAGT1, which encodes the enzyme that begins N-linked glycosylation, and which may include intellectual disability and a poorer response to cholinesterase inhibitors than GFPT1 disease.
simple: A genetic fault in the first step of attaching sugar chains to proteins that causes tiring weakness of the hips and shoulders, sometimes with learning problems.
th: CMS จากยีน DPAGT1 ซึ่งเป็นเอนไซม์ขั้นแรกของ N-glycosylation ทำให้ผู้ป่วยกล้ามเนื้อต้นแขนต้นขาอ่อนแรงและล้าง่าย พบ tubular aggregates ในชิ้นเนื้อ บางรายมีความบกพร่องทางสติปัญญา ตอบสนองต่อ pyridostigmine น้อยกว่า GFPT1 แต่ยังลองใช้ร่วมกับ amifampridine ได้
tempoNote: Childhood to adolescent onset; fluctuating, mildly progressive weakness
feat: Limb-girdle pattern of weakness with fatigability, beginning in infancy or childhood
Facial and ocular involvement are variable and generally mild; some have scoliosis or lordosis
Intellectual disability or learning difficulty in a subset, reflecting the broader glycosylation role
Tubular aggregates, vacuoles and fibre type disproportion on muscle biopsy
Partial and variable response to pyridostigmine; amifampridine is often more helpful
inv: RNS: decrement at low-rate stimulation; single-fibre EMG shows jitter or blocking
CK normal or mildly raised; antibody tests for AChR, MuSK and VGCC negative
Muscle biopsy: tubular aggregates (NADH), autophagic vacuoles, fibre type abnormalities
DPAGT1 gene sequencing; consider transferrin isoform analysis for a congenital disorder of glycosylation if multisystem features are present

case.who: 12-year-old girl from Kanchanaburi with mild learning difficulty
case.story: She tires quickly walking to school and has a waddling gait with an increased back curve; she is slower in class than her peers.
case.exam: Proximal weakness in hip and shoulder girdle, lumbar lordosis, valgus feet, normal eye movements; mild cognitive delay.
case.tests: CK 380 U/L; RNS decrement of 18% at 3 Hz; biopsy shows tubular aggregates and fibre type disproportion; DPAGT1 compound heterozygous missense variants.
case.q: What treatment strategy is appropriate, and how does the expected response compare with GFPT1 disease?
case.a: Try pyridostigmine and add amifampridine, monitoring the benefit; response is typically more modest than in GFPT1 disease, so physiotherapy and supportive care are also important.

det.patho: DPAGT1 encodes the enzyme that starts the dolichol pathway for N-linked glycosylation in the endoplasmic reticulum by transferring N-acetylglucosamine to dolichol phosphate. Partial loss of function reduces N-glycosylation of junctional proteins such as the AChR subunits, producing fewer and less stable receptors and small, simplified endplates. The disease is thus a restricted form on the spectrum of congenital disorders of glycosylation.
det.clinical: The picture overlaps with GFPT1 disease: childhood-onset proximal weakness that fluctuates, with mild or no ocular involvement. Some patients have joint contractures, scoliosis and intellectual disability, and complete loss of function causes a severe multisystem disorder with early death. Patients seen in neuromuscular clinics usually have a hypomorphic genotype confined to muscle. A family history of siblings with similar problems suggests recessive inheritance.
det.diagnosis: Test for DPAGT1 when a seronegative limb-girdle CMS has tubular aggregates, particularly with learning difficulty. Electrodiagnostic study confirms a junction defect, and a CMS gene panel gives a definitive answer. Transferrin glycoform analysis may be abnormal in more severe genotypes. Exclude limb-girdle muscular dystrophy and inflammatory myopathy.
det.treatment: A trial of pyridostigmine is reasonable but may give only partial benefit; amifampridine often adds to the effect. Salbutamol or ephedrine has been tried as adjuncts. Because evidence is limited, treatment is individualised with objective measures such as timed stairs or the six-minute walk and repeated assessment. Supportive therapy includes physiotherapy, bracing for scoliosis, and attention to educational needs.
det.prognosis: Variable; mild forms remain functional, while more severe genotypes progress and may need respiratory support.
pearls: Limb-girdle CMS with tubular aggregates is either GFPT1 or DPAGT1; consider glycosylation genes.
Response to pyridostigmine is usually weaker than in GFPT1; add amifampridine.
Intellectual disability and other organ involvement suggest a broader glycosylation disorder.

name: Langerhans cell histiocytosis of the CNS (LCH)
formal: A clonal myeloid neoplasm of CD1a- and langerin-positive histiocytes, driven by MAPK pathway mutations (most often BRAF V600E), that affects the nervous system through craniofacial bone lesions, hypothalamic–pituitary infiltration with central diabetes insipidus, mass lesions, or a delayed neurodegenerative syndrome of the cerebellum and brainstem.
simple: A rare blood-cell tumour, mostly in children, that can damage the skull bones and the pituitary stalk (causing extreme thirst and urination) and years later can slowly harm balance and thinking.
ab: Langerhans cell histiocytosis of the CNS
th: LCH เป็นมะเร็งกลุ่ม myeloid ของเซลล์ Langerhans ที่มักพบในเด็ก ทำให้เกิดรอยโรคกระดูกกะโหลก ก้านต่อมใต้สมองหนาจนเกิดเบาจืดชนิด central และบางรายเกิดภาวะเสื่อมของสมองน้อยและก้านสมองตามมาหลายปีหลังรักษา
tempoNote: Diabetes insipidus and bone lesions develop over weeks to months; the neurodegenerative form appears years after the first diagnosis and progresses slowly
feat: Polyuria and polydipsia from central diabetes insipidus, often the first or the only neurological clue

case.who: 6-year-old boy from Lampang brought to a provincial paediatric clinic
case.story: For three months he has been drinking water from the bathroom tap at night and wetting the bed again; his mother also felt a soft painless lump above his left ear.
case.exam: Alert and growing slightly below his centile; a tender scalp swelling over the left parietal bone; neurological examination otherwise normal.
case.tests: Serum sodium 148 mmol/L with dilute urine; MRI shows a 4 mm thickened enhancing pituitary stalk, absent posterior bright spot and a lytic parietal bone lesion; biopsy shows CD1a- and langerin-positive cells carrying BRAF V600E.
case.q: What unifies the skull lump and the thirst, and which late complication must be watched for?
case.a: Langerhans cell histiocytosis with hypothalamic–pituitary involvement causing central diabetes insipidus; he needs desmopressin, systemic therapy and long-term surveillance for neurodegenerative LCH.

det.patho: LCH is now classed as an inflammatory myeloid neoplasm: a myeloid precursor acquires an activating MAPK mutation, most often BRAF V600E and otherwise MAP2K1, ARAF or kinase fusions, and its progeny form lesions with a dense inflammatory background. Where in the haematopoietic hierarchy the mutation arises predicts how widespread the disease will be. Neurodegenerative LCH reflects slow infiltration of mutant microglia-like cells with secondary neuronal loss rather than an antibody or paraneoplastic process.
det.clinical: Children are affected most, with a smaller adult peak. Skull and facial bone lesions may extend into the epidural space or orbit, and lesions of the sphenoid, orbit, temporal or mastoid bones raise the later risk of diabetes insipidus and neurodegeneration. Central diabetes insipidus is the most frequent permanent sequela and may come before, with or after the bone disease, sometimes with anterior pituitary failure. Parenchymal or dural mass lesions are uncommon. The neurodegenerative form surfaces years later as clumsy gait, slurred speech, tremor, mood or school problems and may advance to severe disability.
det.diagnosis: Tissue confirmation is required: lesional cells express CD1a and langerin (CD207) with S100, and mutation testing guides targeted therapy. MRI of the stalk, hypothalamus and posterior fossa is mandatory, and a stalk over about 3 mm with loss of the bright spot is suspicious. Isolated stalk thickening without a biopsy target is followed closely with whole-body imaging, tumour markers and repeated MRI, because germinoma and hypophysitis look identical early. In ND-LCH, radiological change in dentate nuclei and pons often precedes symptoms, so survivors with high-risk bone sites are scanned and tested periodically.
det.treatment: Single bony lesions may need only curettage or observation, whereas multisystem or CNS-risk disease is treated with vinblastine and prednisolone, with cytarabine or cladribine as alternatives in relapse or in adults. BRAF inhibitors (dabrafenib, vemurafenib) and MEK inhibitors (cobimetinib, trametinib) produce high response rates, including in mass lesions and neurodegenerative LCH, though disease often returns when they stop. Diabetes insipidus rarely recovers and is managed with desmopressin and careful sodium monitoring. Survivors need endocrine, hearing, cognitive and neurological follow-up for many years.
det.prognosis: Survival is excellent for single-system disease; diabetes insipidus is usually permanent, and established neurodegenerative LCH responds only partially to therapy.
pearls: A child with diabetes insipidus and a thick pituitary stalk needs a search for skull, skin and lung lesions before any stalk biopsy.
BRAF V600E status matters: targeted kinase inhibitors can control refractory and neurodegenerative disease.
Survivors with orbital, temporal or mastoid lesions deserve periodic MRI of the dentate nuclei and pons.
det.thd: LCH เกิดจากเซลล์ myeloid ที่มีการกลายพันธุ์ในสาย MAPK โดยเฉพาะ BRAF V600E อาการทางระบบประสาทที่พบบ่อยคือเบาจืดจากก้านต่อมใต้สมองหนา และรอยโรคกระดูกกะโหลก วินิจฉัยจากชิ้นเนื้อที่ย้อม CD1a และ langerin รักษาด้วย vinblastine ร่วม prednisolone หรือ cytarabine และใช้ยายับยั้ง BRAF/MEK ในรายดื้อยา ต้องติดตามผู้รอดชีวิตระยะยาวเพราะอาจเกิด neurodegenerative LCH ทำให้เดินเซ พูดไม่ชัด และการเรียนถดถอย

name: Primary dural marginal zone lymphoma (dural MALT lymphoma)
formal: An indolent extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue type that arises in the dura, forming plaque-like or nodular dural masses that closely mimic meningioma, and that has a much more favourable outlook than the aggressive CNS lymphoma of diffuse large B-cell type.
simple: A slow-growing lymphoma that grows on the brain's outer covering and looks like a meningioma on scans, but is usually curable with surgery or light radiotherapy.
ab: extranodal marginal zone lymphoma of the dura
th: มะเร็งต่อมน้ำเหลืองชนิด marginal zone (MALT) ที่เกิดที่เยื่อดูรา โตช้า ภาพ MRI คล้าย meningioma มาก พบบ่อยในผู้หญิงวัยกลางคน พยากรณ์โรคดีกว่า PCNSL ชนิด DLBCL มาก
tempoNote: Headache, seizures or focal deficits evolve over months; systemic B symptoms are typically absent
feat: Middle-aged adult, more often a woman, with headache, a first seizure or a slowly progressive focal deficit
One or several homogeneously enhancing dural masses or en-plaque dural thickening, often with a dural tail and mild oedema
No fever, night sweats or weight loss; systemic staging is usually negative
Lesions may sit over the convexity, falx, tentorium or along the spinal dura
inv: MRI brain or spine with contrast and diffusion (diffusion restriction is variable, often less than in DLBCL)
Biopsy or resection: small CD20-positive B cells, CD5 and CD10 negative, often plasmacytic differentiation with light chain restriction
Staging with whole-body PET-CT, bone marrow and serum protein electrophoresis; screen for IgG4 and autoimmune disease if suggested

case.who: 52-year-old female school teacher from Nakhon Pathom seen in a neurosurgical clinic
case.story: She has had right-sided headaches for six months and two brief episodes of left-hand tingling that spread up the arm; she has no weight loss or fever.
case.exam: Normal apart from mild left pronator drift.
case.tests: MRI shows a 3 cm enhancing plaque along the right frontoparietal convexity dura with a dural tail; the neurosurgeon resects a presumed meningioma, but pathology shows small CD20-positive, CD5- and CD10-negative B cells with kappa restriction; PET-CT and marrow are negative.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and how does it change her management?
case.a: Primary dural marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma; after staging, focal low-dose radiotherapy or observation after complete resection is enough, and whole-brain radiotherapy or high-dose methotrexate is not needed.

det.patho: Marginal zone lymphomas usually arise where chronic antigen stimulation creates organised lymphoid tissue, and the dura may acquire such tissue through meningothelial interactions or local inflammation. The tumour consists of small centrocyte-like and monocytoid B cells, often with plasma-cell differentiation and colonised follicles. Some cases coexist with autoimmune disease or IgG4-rich infiltrates, suggesting an inflammatory drive. Spread outside the CNS is unusual and transformation to large-cell lymphoma is rare.
det.clinical: Symptoms reflect a slowly enlarging extra-axial mass: headache, focal seizures, mild hemiparesis, visual or cranial nerve symptoms with skull base lesions, or radicular and cord symptoms with spinal dural disease. Patients usually look well, without B symptoms, and the clinical course spans months. Most are operated on as presumed meningiomas, so the diagnosis is frequently a surprise from pathology. Multifocal dural disease is possible.
det.diagnosis: Imaging shows an enhancing dural-based lesion indistinguishable from meningioma, sometimes with marked dural thickening along the falx or tentorium and adjacent vasogenic oedema. Histology with an immunohistochemistry panel and clonality studies establishes a low-grade B-cell lymphoma and excludes reactive pachymeningitis and lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. Full staging with PET-CT, bone marrow, CSF cytology when leptomeningeal spread is suspected and serum paraprotein studies confirms the disease is localised.
det.treatment: Localised disease does very well with gross resection, focal radiotherapy (low doses around 24 Gy are effective), or both. Rituximab alone or with chemotherapy such as bendamustine is used for multifocal, unresectable or relapsed disease. The intensive high-dose methotrexate and whole-brain approaches used for CNS DLBCL are avoided because of neurotoxicity in patients expected to survive for decades. Follow-up MRI tracks local recurrence.
det.prognosis: Excellent: most patients achieve durable control, and lymphoma-related death is uncommon.
pearls: A meningioma that turns out to be lymphoma is often a dural MALT lymphoma — think of it when histology shows small B cells.
Staging is negative in most cases; this is a localised, curable disease.
Do not treat it like PCNSL: focal radiotherapy, not whole-brain irradiation or high-dose methotrexate.
det.thd: dural MALT lymphoma เป็นมะเร็งต่อมน้ำเหลืองชนิดเกรดต่ำที่ขึ้นบนเยื่อดูรา ภาพ MRI เหมือน meningioma จึงมักวินิจฉัยได้หลังผ่าตัดจากผลชิ้นเนื้อ ต้องตรวจ staging ทั่วร่างกายซึ่งมักปกติ รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัดและ/หรือฉายรังสีเฉพาะที่ขนาดต่ำ หรือ rituximab ในรายหลายตำแหน่ง ไม่ต้องใช้ high-dose methotrexate แบบ PCNSL พยากรณ์โรคดีมาก

name: Myeloid sarcoma of the CNS (chloroma)
formal: An extramedullary tumour mass of myeloid blasts that involves the dura, epidural space, orbit, cranial or spinal nerves or, rarely, the brain parenchyma; it may accompany, precede or herald relapse of acute myeloid leukaemia, myelodysplastic syndrome or blast crisis of a myeloproliferative neoplasm, and is treated as acute myeloid leukaemia.
simple: A solid lump made of leukaemia cells that grows outside the bone marrow, for example on the brain covering or around the spinal cord, and can be the first sign of leukaemia.
th: myeloid sarcoma (chloroma) คือก้อนเนื้องอกของเซลล์ blast ชนิด myeloid ที่อยู่นอกไขกระดูก เช่น เยื่อดูรา ช่อง epidural เบ้าตา หรือเส้นประสาท อาจพบก่อน ร่วมกับ หรือเป็นสัญญาณกลับเป็นซ้ำของ AML รักษาเหมือน AML
tempoNote: Symptoms progress over days to weeks; epidural masses can cause rapid cord compression
feat: Back pain followed by leg weakness and sphincter disturbance from an epidural mass compressing the cord or cauda equina
Dural-based or orbital mass with headache, proptosis or cranial nerve palsy
Lesions are hyperdense on CT, enhance homogeneously and restrict diffusion, mimicking lymphoma, meningioma or haematoma
Blood count may be normal (isolated myeloid sarcoma) or show circulating blasts
Associated with monocytic AML, t(8;21), inv(16), KMT2A rearrangements and relapse after stem cell transplant
inv: MRI brain or whole spine with contrast urgently if cord compression is suspected
Biopsy with myeloperoxidase, CD33, CD34, CD117, CD68 and lysozyme staining; cytogenetics and NGS on the tissue
Full blood count, smear, bone marrow aspirate and biopsy; CSF cytology and flow cytometry when meninges are involved

case.who: 34-year-old male motorcycle taxi driver from Bangkok in remission from AML with t(8;21) for ten months
case.story: Over two weeks he developed mid-back pain, then tingling in both legs and difficulty starting urination.
case.exam: Mild spastic paraparesis, sensory level at T8 and brisk knee reflexes.
case.tests: Blood count normal; MRI shows a homogeneously enhancing posterior epidural mass from T6 to T8 compressing the cord; CT-guided biopsy shows myeloperoxidase-positive myeloid blasts with the same RUNX1::RUNX1T1 fusion.
case.q: What is this lesion and what does it mean for his leukaemia?
case.a: An epidural myeloid sarcoma representing extramedullary AML relapse; he needs urgent dexamethasone and radiotherapy or decompression, then systemic re-induction and consideration of allogeneic transplant.

det.patho: Myeloid sarcoma is the tissue form of AML: blasts with myeloid or monocytic differentiation infiltrate extramedullary sites and form a mass. The green colour that gave the name chloroma comes from myeloperoxidase. Adhesion molecule expression in certain genetic subgroups and immune escape after transplantation favour extramedullary growth. The CNS is reached through bone, dura and nerve sheaths more than through the parenchyma.
det.clinical: The commonest neurological picture is spinal epidural compression with back pain, radicular pain and evolving paraparesis, followed by skull base, orbital and dural masses causing headache, proptosis or cranial nerve palsies. Nerve and plexus deposits cause painful neuropathies. It may appear before marrow disease is evident, at diagnosis, or as the first sign of relapse, including after allogeneic transplantation.
det.diagnosis: Biopsy is required; without immunohistochemistry the lesion is easily mistaken for lymphoma, Ewing sarcoma or a small round blue cell tumour. Myeloperoxidase, CD33, CD117, CD34 and monocytic markers (CD68, CD163, lysozyme) confirm lineage, and genetic testing on the tissue guides therapy. A bone marrow examination and CSF study are mandatory even when blood counts are normal, and PET-CT maps other deposits.
det.treatment: Spinal cord compression is an emergency: dexamethasone plus urgent radiotherapy or surgical decompression. Definitive treatment is systemic AML induction tailored to genetics, including targeted drugs such as FLT3 or IDH inhibitors, with venetoclax-based regimens in unfit patients, and allogeneic stem cell transplantation for relapse or high-risk disease. Focal radiotherapy consolidates bulky or residual lesions.
det.prognosis: Outcome follows the underlying AML genetics and response; isolated myeloid sarcoma treated as AML has outcomes similar to marrow AML.
pearls: In a patient with AML in remission, a new epidural or dural mass is relapse until proven otherwise.
Ask the pathologist for myeloperoxidase and CD117 when a dural tumour looks like lymphoma.
Normal blood counts do not exclude it — isolated myeloid sarcoma can precede marrow leukaemia.
det.thd: myeloid sarcoma เป็นก้อนของเซลล์ AML นอกไขกระดูก ทางระบบประสาทมักพบเป็นก้อนใน epidural กดไขสันหลัง หรือก้อนที่ดูรา เบ้าตา และเส้นประสาทสมอง ภาพคล้าย lymphoma หรือ meningioma ต้องตัดชิ้นเนื้อย้อม myeloperoxidase และ CD117 และตรวจไขกระดูก การกดไขสันหลังต้องให้ dexamethasone และฉายรังสีหรือผ่าตัดด่วน จากนั้นรักษาแบบ AML ทั้งระบบ

name: Neuroleukaemiosis (leukaemic infiltration of peripheral nerves)
formal: Direct infiltration of cranial nerves, spinal roots, plexuses or peripheral nerves by leukaemic cells, producing painful mononeuropathies, multiple mononeuropathy, plexopathy or a polyradiculoneuropathy; it frequently signals systemic or extramedullary relapse even when the marrow appears in remission.
simple: Leukaemia cells creep into the nerves, causing pain, numbness or weakness in a limb, and often warn that the leukaemia is coming back.
th: neuroleukaemiosis คือการที่เซลล์มะเร็งเม็ดเลือดขาวแทรกเข้าไปในเส้นประสาทส่วนปลาย รากประสาท หรือ plexus ทำให้ปวด ชา อ่อนแรงเฉพาะเส้น มักเป็นสัญญาณว่าโรคกลับเป็นซ้ำแม้ไขกระดูกยังดูปกติ
tempoNote: Pain and deficits evolve over weeks; several nerves may be added sequentially
feat: Severe, often nocturnal neuropathic pain in the territory of one nerve, root or plexus, followed by weakness
Asymmetric multiple mononeuropathy or cranial neuropathies (facial, trigeminal, oculomotor)
Sometimes a symmetric polyradiculoneuropathy that mimics Guillain–Barré syndrome
Fusiform nerve enlargement or a nerve mass on MRI neurography, strongly FDG-avid on PET
Occurs in AML (especially monocytic), ALL and CLL, often during apparent remission or after transplant
inv: MRI of the affected plexus or nerve with contrast (neurography) and whole-body FDG-PET
Nerve conduction studies and EMG to map the pattern (usually axonal, multifocal)
CSF cytology and flow cytometry, bone marrow examination, and fascicular nerve biopsy when imaging is not diagnostic

case.who: 41-year-old female rice farmer from Suphan Buri, eight months after allogeneic stem cell transplant for monocytic AML
case.story: She has three weeks of burning pain down the back of the right thigh that wakes her at night, then a right foot drop; a week later her left face starts to droop.
case.exam: Weak right ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion with absent ankle reflex, sensory loss in the sciatic territory, and a left lower motor neuron facial palsy.
case.tests: Nerve conduction shows a right sciatic axonopathy; MRI shows a thickened, enhancing right sciatic nerve and lumbosacral plexus; PET is intensely avid along the nerve; marrow shows 1% blasts with donor chimerism falling; nerve fascicle biopsy shows myeloid blast infiltration.
case.q: What explains her multifocal neuropathy and what is the treatment strategy?
case.a: Neuroleukaemiosis heralding AML relapse; focal radiotherapy relieves pain and protects function, and systemic therapy using agents that cross the blood–nerve barrier (for example high-dose cytarabine) or cellular therapy is needed.

read.where: Chapter 6: Neurological complications of myeloid malignancies

det.patho: Leukaemic cells reach nerves either by blood-borne spread across the blood–nerve barrier or by tracking from the leptomeninges along roots. The endoneurium shields cells from chemotherapy that does not cross this barrier, so the nerve behaves like a sanctuary site similar to the CNS and testes. Infiltration compresses and destroys axons, causing axonal loss, while also inflaming the nerve sheath, which explains the intense pain. Monocytic AML and T-cell leukaemias appear over-represented.
det.clinical: The usual story is relentless, burning or aching pain in a limb followed within days to weeks by weakness and sensory loss, often in the sciatic, brachial plexus or facial territory. Several nerves may be affected in sequence, and cranial neuropathies may coexist with meningeal disease. A symmetric polyradiculoneuropathy is a less common pattern that can be misread as GBS or CIDP. The process can occur when blood counts and marrow look normal, and in post-transplant patients may precede overt relapse by weeks.
det.diagnosis: MRI neurography shows nerve thickening, T2 hyperintensity and enhancement, and PET demonstrates high FDG uptake along nerve segments; both help choose a biopsy site. Electrodiagnosis typically shows multifocal axonal loss. CSF cytology and flow cytometry are often negative when infiltration is purely peripheral, so a negative CSF does not exclude it. Fascicular biopsy with immunohistochemistry gives the definitive answer and excludes vasculitis, infection (for example herpes zoster or CMV) and drug neuropathy.
det.treatment: Focal fractionated radiotherapy to the involved nerve or plexus quickly reduces pain and can recover function. Because neuroleukaemiosis predicts systemic relapse, systemic treatment is required: re-induction with agents that penetrate nerve such as high-dose cytarabine, methotrexate or fludarabine, targeted drugs according to genetics, and allogeneic transplant or donor lymphocyte infusion where feasible. Neuropathic pain needs aggressive multimodal management.
det.prognosis: Generally poor, because it marks refractory or relapsing leukaemia; nerve recovery depends on how early treatment begins.
pearls: A painful focal neuropathy in a leukaemia survivor deserves PET or MRI neurography, not just an EMG.
Negative CSF and marrow do not rule it out — the nerve can be the only site of relapse.
Treat both the nerve (radiotherapy) and the patient (systemic therapy), because systemic relapse usually follows.
det.thd: neuroleukaemiosis คือเซลล์ leukaemia แทรกเข้าเส้นประสาทส่วนปลาย ทำให้ปวดแสบรุนแรงตามเส้นประสาทแล้วตามด้วยอ่อนแรง อาจเป็นหลายเส้นหรือคล้าย GBS ตรวจด้วย MRI neurography และ PET ซึ่งพบเส้นประสาทบวมและดูดกลูโคสสูง ยืนยันด้วยการตัดชิ้นเนื้อเส้นประสาท รักษาด้วยการฉายรังสีเฉพาะที่ร่วมกับเคมีบำบัดที่ผ่าน blood–nerve barrier ได้ และมักต้องพิจารณาปลูกถ่ายไขกระดูก

name: Intracranial haemorrhage in acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL)
formal: Spontaneous intraparenchymal, subdural or subarachnoid bleeding caused by the consumptive and hyperfibrinolytic coagulopathy of acute promyelocytic leukaemia (PML::RARA), a leading cause of early death that is prevented mainly by starting all-trans retinoic acid at the first suspicion and aggressively correcting platelets and fibrinogen.
simple: A dangerous brain bleed that happens early in a special type of leukaemia because the blood loses its clotting ability; immediate vitamin-A-derived treatment and blood products save lives.
ab: Intracranial haemorrhage in acute promyelocytic leukaemia
th: เลือดออกในสมองในผู้ป่วย acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL) เกิดจากภาวะ DIC ร่วมกับ hyperfibrinolysis เป็นสาเหตุการเสียชีวิตระยะแรกที่สำคัญ ต้องเริ่ม ATRA ทันทีที่สงสัยและให้เกล็ดเลือดกับ fibrinogen ให้เพียงพอ
tempoNote: Bleeding typically occurs at presentation or in the first two weeks of induction, often within hours
feat: Sudden headache, vomiting, seizures or reduced consciousness in a patient with bruising, gum or nose bleeding and pancytopenia
Multifocal lobar haematomas with fluid levels, often with subdural or subarachnoid blood
Low fibrinogen, prolonged PT, high D-dimer and severe thrombocytopenia out of proportion to the blast count
Higher risk with high white cell count, very low fibrinogen, raised creatinine and poor performance status
Smear shows abnormal hypergranular promyelocytes, often with Auer rod bundles (faggot cells)
inv: Non-contrast CT brain immediately in any neurological change
FBC, smear, PT, aPTT, fibrinogen and D-dimer repeated at least twice daily during induction
Bone marrow with PML::RARA by PCR or FISH (do not wait for the result to start ATRA)

case.who: 27-year-old female garment factory worker from Samut Prakan brought to an emergency department
case.story: For one week she has had gum bleeding and bruises; this morning she developed a severe headache, vomited and then had a generalised seizure.
case.exam: Drowsy, GCS 12, left hemiparesis, scattered ecchymoses and petechiae.
case.tests: WBC 18 × 10⁹/L with hypergranular promyelocytes, platelets 9 × 10⁹/L, fibrinogen 0.6 g/L, PT prolonged, D-dimer very high; CT shows a right frontal lobar haematoma and a thin left subdural collection.
case.q: What must be done in the next hour?
case.a: Treat as APL: start ATRA immediately before genetic confirmation, give cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate to keep fibrinogen above 1.5 g/L and platelets above 50 × 10⁹/L, avoid lumbar puncture and invasive procedures, and add arsenic trioxide and cytoreduction for this high-risk count.

read.where: Chapter 6: Neurological complications of myeloid malignancies

det.patho: The PML::RARA fusion blocks differentiation at the promyelocyte stage. Leukaemic promyelocytes express tissue factor and cancer procoagulant that drive disseminated intravascular coagulation, while abundant annexin A2 on their surface accelerates plasmin generation, adding primary hyperfibrinolysis. The result is profound hypofibrinogenaemia and platelet consumption, so that small vessels in the brain and meninges bleed spontaneously. Differentiation therapy dismantles this process within days.
det.clinical: Haemorrhage is the main cause of death in the first weeks, and the brain is the most lethal site. Patients present with headache, vomiting, seizures, focal deficits or sudden coma, often at the very first presentation, while the blood film is still being reviewed. Bleeds may be multiple and of different ages. ATRA also brings its own neurological issues: idiopathic intracranial hypertension–like headache and papilloedema, and differentiation syndrome with hypoxia and encephalopathy.
det.diagnosis: Suspicion arises from the smear and the coagulation profile; CT brain is done immediately when any neurological symptom appears. Genetic confirmation of PML::RARA by PCR or FISH follows, but treatment must not wait for it. Coagulation tests are repeated frequently because fibrinogen and platelets can drop quickly in the first days of therapy. Lumbar puncture is avoided during the coagulopathic phase.
det.treatment: Start ATRA at first suspicion. Low- and intermediate-risk APL is treated with ATRA plus arsenic trioxide; high-risk disease (WBC above 10 × 10⁹/L) adds anthracycline or gemtuzumab ozogamicin to bring the count down. Supportive targets are platelets at least 30–50 × 10⁹/L and fibrinogen above 1.5 g/L, using cryoprecipitate, fibrinogen concentrate and fresh frozen plasma; heparin and routine tranexamic acid are not recommended. Neurosurgical evacuation is rarely possible until the coagulopathy is corrected, so management is mostly medical with seizure control and ICP measures.
det.prognosis: Once induction is survived, APL is among the most curable leukaemias (above 90% long-term survival), but ICH at onset carries high mortality and residual disability.
pearls: Hypergranular promyelocytes plus low fibrinogen: start ATRA tonight, do not wait for PML::RARA.
Keep fibrinogen above 1.5 g/L and platelets above 30–50 × 10⁹/L during induction to prevent brain bleeding.
Headache on ATRA may be drug-induced intracranial hypertension, but scan first to exclude haemorrhage.
det.thd: APL ทำให้เกิด DIC ร่วมกับ hyperfibrinolysis จนเกล็ดเลือดและ fibrinogen ต่ำมาก เลือดออกในสมองเป็นสาเหตุเสียชีวิตสำคัญในช่วงแรก เมื่อเห็น promyelocyte ผิดปกติร่วมกับ fibrinogen ต่ำ ให้เริ่ม ATRA ทันทีโดยไม่ต้องรอผลยีน PML::RARA ให้ cryoprecipitate และเกล็ดเลือดตามเป้า และหลีกเลี่ยงการเจาะหลัง ถ้าผ่านช่วงแรกไปได้โรคนี้มีโอกาสหายขาดสูงมาก

qx.stem: A 27-year-old man presents with bruising and gum bleeding. Smear shows abnormal promyelocytes, platelets are 18 x10^9/L, fibrinogen is 0.8 g/L and D-dimer is very high. Within hours of arrival he develops a severe headache and drowsiness, and CT shows a lobar haemorrhage.
qx.q: What should be started immediately?
opts: Await cytogenetics before any leukaemia therapy
Tranexamic acid and cytarabine only after confirmation
All-trans retinoic acid on suspicion, with aggressive platelet and fibrinogen support
Heparin to treat the coagulopathy
Hydroxyurea alone
qx.why: APL is a medical emergency with hyperfibrinolysis and DIC, and intracranial haemorrhage is a leading early cause of death. ATRA is started at clinical suspicion without waiting for the PML-RARA result, alongside platelets above about 30 to 50 and fibrinogen above 1.5 g/L, then arsenic trioxide is added.

name: Myeloproliferative neoplasms, neurological complications (MPN)
formal: Neurological consequences of the Philadelphia-negative myeloproliferative neoplasms — polycythaemia vera, essential thrombocythaemia and primary myelofibrosis — chiefly arterial ischaemic stroke and TIA, cerebral venous thrombosis, microvascular symptoms such as migraine-like headache and transient visual disturbance, bleeding with extreme thrombocytosis, and spinal cord compression from extramedullary haematopoiesis.
simple: Bone marrow disorders that make too many red cells or platelets thicken the blood and cause strokes, clots in brain veins and headaches.
th: กลุ่มโรค myeloproliferative neoplasm (PV, ET, myelofibrosis) ทำให้เลือดข้นและเกล็ดเลือดทำงานผิดปกติ เกิดหลอดเลือดสมองตีบ หลอดเลือดดำในสมองอุดตัน ปวดศีรษะ ตามัวชั่วขณะ และบางรายเลือดออกเมื่อเกล็ดเลือดสูงมาก ควรตรวจ JAK2 ในผู้ป่วย CVT ที่หาสาเหตุไม่ได้
tempoNote: Stroke and CVT are acute events; microvascular symptoms (headache, visual blurring, erythromelalgia) recur episodically
feat: Ischaemic stroke or TIA in a younger patient with high haemoglobin, haematocrit or platelet count
Cerebral venous or splanchnic (portal, hepatic) vein thrombosis, sometimes with normal blood counts (masked MPN)
Episodic migraine-like headache, scintillations, transient monocular blurring, dizziness and erythromelalgia that respond to aspirin
Facial plethora, aquagenic pruritus and splenomegaly
Bleeding with platelets above about 1000–1500 × 10⁹/L from acquired von Willebrand syndrome
inv: FBC, film and iron studies (iron deficiency can mask polycythaemia)
JAK2 V617F; if negative, JAK2 exon 12, CALR and MPL mutations
Bone marrow biopsy and serum erythropoietin as per WHO/ICC criteria; brain MRI with MRV or CTV after an event

case.who: 46-year-old male rubber plantation owner from Surat Thani admitted with a severe headache
case.story: Four days of worsening headache followed by a focal seizure of the right arm; he has had itching after warm showers for a year and his face always looks red.
case.exam: Plethoric face, palpable spleen tip, mild right-hand weakness and bilateral papilloedema.
case.tests: Hb 19.2 g/dL, haematocrit 58%, platelets 620 × 10⁹/L; CT venography shows superior sagittal and left transverse sinus thrombosis with a small left frontal haemorrhagic infarct; JAK2 V617F positive.
case.q: What is the underlying disorder and what are the two pillars of treatment?
case.a: Polycythaemia vera causing cerebral venous thrombosis; anticoagulate (LMWH then long-term anticoagulation), and control the MPN with phlebotomy to haematocrit below 45% plus cytoreduction such as hydroxyurea or ropeginterferon, as he is high risk after thrombosis.

read.where: Chapter 6: Neurological complications of myeloid malignancies
Chapter 12: Neurological complications of platelet disorders and disorders of coagulation
Section 3 Hereditary and Genetic Conditions and Malformations

det.patho: Acquired driver mutations in JAK2, CALR or MPL activate JAK–STAT signalling in haematopoietic stem cells, increasing red cells, platelets and activated neutrophils. Thrombosis results from raised blood viscosity, activated platelets and leucocytes, neutrophil extracellular traps and an endothelium that also carries the JAK2 mutation in some patients. Very high platelet counts adsorb large von Willebrand multimers, paradoxically causing bleeding. Myelofibrosis drives extramedullary haematopoiesis that can compress the cord or roots.
det.clinical: Thrombosis is often the event that reveals the disease, and cerebrovascular events are among the most frequent. Strokes may be large-artery, cardioembolic-like or small-vessel, and recurrence is common if the MPN is untreated. CVT and splanchnic vein thrombosis are typical of JAK2-positive disease in young adults, especially women. Microvascular symptoms — headache, visual flickering, transient paraesthesia, dizziness and burning red extremities — are common and improve with aspirin. Rare complications include chorea in polycythaemia vera and spinal cord compression in myelofibrosis.
det.diagnosis: WHO 2022 and International Consensus Classification criteria combine blood counts (haemoglobin or haematocrit thresholds for polycythaemia vera, sustained platelets above 450 × 10⁹/L for essential thrombocythaemia), a driver mutation and marrow morphology. JAK2 V617F testing is recommended in unexplained CVT or splanchnic thrombosis even with normal counts, because hypersplenism, bleeding or iron deficiency may hide the disease. Secondary causes of erythrocytosis (hypoxia, smoking, high altitude, renal tumours, testosterone) and of thrombocytosis (iron deficiency, inflammation, splenectomy) must be excluded.
det.treatment: Acute stroke management follows usual protocols; thrombolysis and thrombectomy are not contraindicated by the MPN itself. Long term, all patients with polycythaemia vera receive low-dose aspirin and phlebotomy to keep haematocrit below 45%, and patients aged 60 or older or with prior thrombosis also get cytoreduction (hydroxyurea, ropeginterferon alfa-2b, or ruxolitinib if resistant). Essential thrombocythaemia is treated according to thrombotic risk, with aspirin and hydroxyurea or anagrelide or interferon. Venous thrombosis requires anticoagulation, generally long-term while the MPN is active, and vascular risk factors are controlled strictly.
det.prognosis: With phlebotomy and cytoreduction the recurrence risk falls substantially; life expectancy is near normal in many with ET and PV, but recurrent thrombosis and transformation to myelofibrosis or AML remain risks.
pearls: Test JAK2 V617F in every unexplained cerebral or splanchnic vein thrombosis, even with a normal blood count.
Haematocrit target in polycythaemia vera is below 45% — phlebotomy plus aspirin.
Extreme thrombocytosis can cause bleeding rather than clotting because of acquired von Willebrand syndrome.
det.thd: MPN เช่น polycythaemia vera และ essential thrombocythaemia เกิดจากการกลายพันธุ์ JAK2, CALR หรือ MPL ทำให้เลือดข้นและเกล็ดเลือดไวต่อการจับตัว เสี่ยงต่อ stroke และ CVT รวมทั้งอาการปวดศีรษะหรือตามัวชั่วคราวที่ดีขึ้นด้วย aspirin ควรตรวจ JAK2 ใน CVT ที่ไม่ทราบสาเหตุ การรักษาคือ aspirin เจาะเลือดออกให้ haematocrit ต่ำกว่า 45% และให้ยาลดเม็ดเลือดเช่น hydroxyurea หรือ interferon ในรายเสี่ยงสูง

name: Multiple myeloma, neurological complications
formal: Myeloma can affect the nervous system in many ways: spinal cord and cauda equina compression from vertebral disease or plasmacytoma, radiculopathy from collapse, skull base and cranial nerve lesions, rare leptomeningeal myelomatosis, metabolic encephalopathy from hypercalcaemia, renal failure or hyperviscosity, amyloid and treatment-related neuropathies, and neurotoxicity of BCMA-directed cellular and bispecific therapies.
simple: Myeloma, a cancer of plasma cells in bone, can crush the spine and press on nerves, upset blood calcium and kidneys to cause confusion, and its treatments can damage nerves.
th: multiple myeloma มีภาวะแทรกซ้อนทางระบบประสาทหลายแบบ ที่สำคัญคือไขสันหลังถูกกดจากกระดูกสันหลังยุบหรือ plasmacytoma, สับสนจากแคลเซียมสูงหรือไตวาย, ปลายประสาทอักเสบจาก amyloid หรือยา bortezomib/thalidomide และพิษต่อระบบประสาทจาก CAR-T ที่จับ BCMA
tempoNote: Cord compression evolves over days to weeks after back pain; metabolic encephalopathy may develop over days
feat: Older adult with back pain, anaemia, renal impairment or hypercalcaemia (CRAB features)
Thoracic back pain progressing to paraparesis and sensory level from vertebral collapse or epidural plasmacytoma
Confusion, drowsiness and constipation from hypercalcaemia; headache and visual blurring from IgA or IgG3 hyperviscosity
Painful length-dependent sensory neuropathy after bortezomib or thalidomide, or with AL amyloidosis (carpal tunnel, autonomic failure)
Cranial neuropathies from skull base plasmacytoma or leptomeningeal myeloma; delayed parkinsonism or cranial nerve palsy after BCMA CAR-T
inv: Whole-spine MRI urgently with any back pain plus neurological symptoms
Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation, serum free light chains, calcium, creatinine, FBC
Bone marrow plasma cell percentage and cytogenetics; whole-body low-dose CT or PET-CT
Nerve conduction studies; CSF cytology and flow cytometry when leptomeningeal disease is suspected

case.who: 67-year-old retired male mechanic from Nakhon Ratchasima
case.story: Two months of mid-back pain treated as muscle strain, then over five days his legs became stiff and he could not climb steps; his family says he has been unusually sleepy and constipated.
case.exam: Spastic paraparesis grade 3/5, sensory level at T10, brisk reflexes and extensor plantars; mildly confused.
case.tests: Corrected calcium 3.3 mmol/L, creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, Hb 8.9 g/dL; IgG kappa paraprotein 46 g/L; MRI shows T9 vertebral collapse with an epidural soft-tissue mass compressing the cord.
case.q: What is the cause of both the paraparesis and the confusion, and what are the immediate steps?
case.a: Multiple myeloma with epidural plasmacytoma causing cord compression plus hypercalcaemic encephalopathy; give dexamethasone, urgent radiotherapy or surgical decompression, IV fluids and a bisphosphonate or denosumab for calcium, then begin anti-myeloma therapy.

15. Paraproteinemic Neuropathy: Distinguishing the Ominous From the Ordinary

det.patho: Clonal plasma cells expand in bone marrow, activate osteoclasts and suppress osteoblasts, producing lytic lesions and vertebral fractures; tumour may break through cortex into the epidural space. The monoclonal protein and light chains damage kidneys and can raise viscosity or deposit as amyloid in nerves. Hypercalcaemia arises from bone resorption. CNS invasion is uncommon but signals aggressive biology. Newer immune therapies targeting BCMA, GPRC5D and other antigens bring cytokine-mediated and on-target neurotoxicities.
det.clinical: Spinal cord compression is the key emergency: back pain precedes weakness, and outcome depends on function at the start of treatment. Radiculopathy follows foraminal narrowing from collapse. Skull base and orbital plasmacytomas involve cranial nerves. Metabolic encephalopathy (calcium, uraemia, hyperviscosity, infection) is common and reversible. Neuropathy may be due to AL amyloid, to drugs (bortezomib, thalidomide), or to POEMS when lambda light chains and sclerotic lesions are present. After BCMA CAR-T, ICANS appears early, while a delayed movement and neurocognitive syndrome with parkinsonism, or isolated cranial nerve palsies, may follow weeks later.
det.diagnosis: International Myeloma Working Group criteria require clonal marrow plasma cells at least 10% or a biopsy-proven plasmacytoma plus a myeloma-defining event: CRAB features or a SLiM biomarker (marrow plasma cells 60% or more, involved to uninvolved free light chain ratio 100 or more, or more than one focal MRI lesion). Whole-spine MRI is mandatory with neurological symptoms because compression can occur at multiple levels. Leptomeningeal myeloma is confirmed by CSF plasma cells on cytology or flow cytometry.
det.treatment: Cord compression needs high-dose dexamethasone and urgent radiotherapy, with surgery for spinal instability or bony fragments; kyphoplasty treats painful fractures without compression. Systemic treatment uses quadruplet induction (anti-CD38 antibody with bortezomib, lenalidomide and dexamethasone) followed by autologous transplant where eligible, with CAR-T or bispecific antibodies in relapse. Hypercalcaemia is managed with fluids, zoledronic acid or denosumab; hyperviscosity with plasmapheresis. Bortezomib neuropathy is reduced by subcutaneous weekly dosing and dose adjustment.
det.prognosis: Myeloma remains largely incurable but median survival now exceeds a decade for many standard-risk patients; neurological recovery after compression depends on early treatment.
pearls: Back pain plus anaemia and high creatinine in an older adult: think myeloma and image the whole spine.
Confusion in myeloma is hypercalcaemia, uraemia, hyperviscosity or infection until proven otherwise.
Parkinsonism weeks after BCMA CAR-T is a recognised delayed neurotoxicity, distinct from early ICANS.
det.thd: multiple myeloma ทำให้กระดูกสันหลังยุบหรือมีก้อน plasmacytoma กดไขสันหลัง ต้องให้ dexamethasone และฉายรังสีหรือผ่าตัดเร่งด่วน อาการสับสนมักมาจากแคลเซียมสูง ไตวาย เลือดหนืด หรือการติดเชื้อ ปลายประสาทอักเสบอาจเกิดจาก amyloid หรือยา bortezomib และ thalidomide วินิจฉัยตามเกณฑ์ IMWG จาก plasma cell ในไขกระดูกร่วมกับ CRAB หรือ SLiM

qx.stem: A 68-year-old woman with known myeloma develops two days of severe back pain, weakness of both legs and inability to pass urine. MRI shows a T8 vertebral plasmacytoma with epidural extension compressing the cord. Neurological deficit is incomplete.
qx.q: What is the best immediate management?
opts: High-dose dexamethasone with urgent radiotherapy or decompressive surgery in discussion with oncology
Outpatient analgesia and bisphosphonate
Intrathecal chemotherapy
Plasma exchange
Lumbar puncture to look for light chains
qx.why: Compressive myelopathy from a plasmacytoma is an emergency, and steroids with prompt radiotherapy, or surgery when there is instability, offer the best chance of keeping function; myeloma-directed systemic therapy follows. Myeloma is usually very radiosensitive, and lumbar puncture below a compressive lesion can worsen the deficit.

name: High-dose cytarabine cerebellar toxicity
formal: An acute pancerebellar syndrome, sometimes with encephalopathy or seizures, that develops within days of high-dose cytarabine (Ara-C, typically 1–3 g/m² per dose), due to Purkinje cell injury; risk rises with age, renal impairment, cumulative dose and prior toxicity, and the drug must be stopped at the first cerebellar sign.
simple: A strong leukaemia drug, cytarabine, can poison the balance centre of the brain, causing slurred speech and unsteady walking a few days after treatment begins.
th: cytarabine ขนาดสูง (HiDAC) ทำให้เกิดพิษต่อสมองน้อยภายในไม่กี่วันหลังเริ่มยา มีพูดไม่ชัด ตากระตุก เดินเซ เสี่ยงมากในผู้สูงอายุและผู้ที่ไตเสื่อม ต้องตรวจอาการสมองน้อยก่อนให้ยาทุกครั้งและหยุดยาทันทีเมื่อพบความผิดปกติ
tempoNote: Begins 3–8 days after starting high-dose cytarabine; most improve over 1–2 weeks after stopping, some are left with permanent ataxia
feat: Nystagmus, scanning dysarthria, limb dysmetria and gait ataxia appearing a few days into a high-dose cycle
Drowsiness, confusion or seizures may accompany severe cases
Risk factors: age over about 50–60, creatinine clearance below 60 mL/min, liver dysfunction, high cumulative dose, previous cytarabine toxicity
MRI is often normal at first; cerebellar atrophy may appear later
inv: Bedside cerebellar check (speech, nystagmus, finger–nose, handwriting) before every dose
Creatinine and liver tests; MRI brain to exclude haemorrhage, infection or leukaemic infiltration
CSF only if infection or CNS relapse is a realistic alternative and platelets allow

case.who: 63-year-old female market vendor from Udon Thani receiving consolidation for AML
case.story: On day 4 of high-dose cytarabine (3 g/m² twice daily) the nurse notices that her signature has become shaky and her speech sounds slurred; she has felt unsteady going to the bathroom.
case.exam: Gaze-evoked nystagmus, dysarthria, bilateral finger–nose dysmetria and wide-based gait; alert and oriented.
case.tests: Creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 1.6 mg/dL since day 1; MRI brain normal; platelets 22 × 10⁹/L.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what should be done with the remaining doses?
case.a: High-dose cytarabine cerebellar toxicity aggravated by worsening renal function; stop cytarabine immediately and do not rechallenge with high doses, provide supportive care and falls precautions.

det.patho: Cytarabine is a pyrimidine analogue that, at high doses, crosses the blood–brain barrier in large amounts. Purkinje cells, especially those deep in the folial sulci, are selectively lost, with Bergmann gliosis, though the precise toxic mechanism is unknown and may be distinct from inhibition of DNA synthesis. Reduced renal clearance of the inactive metabolite uracil arabinoside and genetic variants in activating enzymes are linked to higher brain exposure.
det.clinical: Symptoms start a few days after high-dose courses with nystagmus, slurred speech and clumsiness and may progress to inability to sit or stand. Encephalopathy, somnolence and seizures occur in more severe cases. Intrathecal cytarabine can cause a separate transverse myelopathy or chemical arachnoiditis, and peripheral neuropathy is reported with high doses. Most patients improve within one to two weeks after stopping, but a minority, particularly older people with renal failure, remain ataxic.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical, based on timing and exclusion. MRI is needed to exclude cerebellar haemorrhage, infection such as PML or fungal abscess, and leukaemic infiltration; it is commonly normal early, with atrophy in permanent cases. Metabolic and drug causes of encephalopathy are checked. Many centres document a standardised cerebellar examination before each dose so that early signs are not missed.
det.treatment: Stop cytarabine at the first convincing cerebellar sign; there is no antidote. Doses are reduced in renal impairment and in older patients, and high-dose rechallenge after toxicity is avoided. Supportive care includes falls prevention, physiotherapy and seizure treatment if needed; corticosteroids have no proven benefit.
det.prognosis: Most recover fully or partially within weeks; persistent disabling ataxia occurs in a minority, mainly when the drug was continued after symptoms began.
pearls: Check handwriting and finger–nose before every high-dose cytarabine dose.
Rising creatinine during HiDAC is a warning sign for cerebellar toxicity.
Stopping promptly is the only effective treatment — continuing the course risks permanent ataxia.
det.thd: พิษต่อสมองน้อยจาก cytarabine ขนาดสูงเกิดจาก Purkinje cell ถูกทำลาย อาการคือตากระตุก พูดไม่ชัด มือสั่นเมื่อจับสิ่งของ และเดินเซภายใน 3–8 วันหลังเริ่มยา ผู้สูงอายุและผู้ที่ไตเสื่อมเสี่ยงสูง ตรวจ MRI เพื่อแยกเลือดออกหรือการติดเชื้อ รักษาด้วยการหยุดยาทันทีและไม่ให้ขนาดสูงซ้ำ ส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นในไม่กี่สัปดาห์

name: Ifosfamide-induced encephalopathy
formal: An acute, usually reversible toxic encephalopathy occurring hours to a few days after ifosfamide infusion, attributed to the metabolite chloroacetaldehyde, ranging from somnolence and hallucinations to asterixis, myoclonus, non-convulsive seizures and coma; management is stopping the infusion with supportive care, and methylene blue or thiamine are often given.
simple: A chemotherapy drug, ifosfamide, can make patients confused, sleepy or hallucinating within a day of the infusion; it usually clears within a few days after the drug is stopped.
th: ifosfamide ทำให้เกิดสมองทำงานผิดปกติเฉียบพลันภายในไม่กี่ชั่วโมงถึงไม่กี่วันหลังให้ยา มีง่วงซึม สับสน เห็นภาพหลอน มือสั่นแบบ asterixis จนถึงชักแบบไม่มีอาการเกร็งหรือโคม่า ส่วนใหญ่หายภายใน 2–3 วันหลังหยุดยา
tempoNote: Onset from a few hours to about 2–4 days after infusion begins; resolves over 48–72 hours in most once the drug is stopped
feat: Somnolence, confusion, agitation and visual hallucinations during or soon after an ifosfamide course
Asterixis, multifocal myoclonus, extrapyramidal signs, urinary incontinence; severe cases progress to coma
EEG shows diffuse slowing, triphasic waves or non-convulsive status epilepticus
Risk factors: low serum albumin, renal impairment, bulky pelvic tumour, prior cisplatin, previous episode, high dose or oral route
inv: EEG promptly in any reduced consciousness to look for non-convulsive status
Electrolytes, glucose, ammonia, renal and liver function, albumin and blood gases
MRI brain to exclude haemorrhage, PRES, metastases or infection when the picture is atypical

case.who: 22-year-old male university student from Khon Kaen receiving ifosfamide and doxorubicin for a pelvic Ewing sarcoma
case.story: Eighteen hours into the second day of infusion he became sleepy, talked about seeing cats on the wall and then could not answer simple questions.
case.exam: Drowsy but rousable, disoriented, coarse asterixis and multifocal myoclonic jerks; no focal deficit, no meningism.
case.tests: Albumin 2.6 g/dL, creatinine mildly raised, sodium and glucose normal; EEG shows generalised slowing with frequent triphasic waves, no electrographic seizures.
case.q: What is the likely cause and how should it be managed?
case.a: Ifosfamide-induced encephalopathy; stop the infusion, give supportive care with hydration and correction of metabolic factors, consider IV methylene blue and thiamine, monitor EEG for non-convulsive seizures, and reassess dosing before any future course.

det.patho: Ifosfamide is a prodrug that hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes convert to its active form; side-chain oxidation produces chloroacetaldehyde, which crosses the blood–brain barrier and interferes with mitochondrial electron transport and fatty acid oxidation, and depletes glutathione. Low albumin, renal impairment and hepatic or drug interactions increase free metabolite levels. The result is a reversible metabolic disruption of cortical and subcortical function rather than structural damage.
det.clinical: Encephalopathy affects roughly one in ten to one in four patients and usually starts within the first day or two of a course. Mild forms cause sleepiness, inattention, mood change and hallucinations; moderate forms add asterixis, myoclonus and disorientation; severe forms reach stupor, coma and seizures. Cerebellar signs, cranial neuropathies and extrapyramidal features are less common. Recurrence with later courses is likely in those affected once.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the temporal link with ifosfamide and exclusion of other causes, particularly sepsis, hyponatraemia, hepatic or renal failure, opioid excess, brain metastases and seizures. EEG is key, showing diffuse slowing and triphasic waves and occasionally non-convulsive status, which changes treatment. Imaging is usually normal. Severity is graded clinically, for example with CTCAE or Meyers grades.
det.treatment: Stop or interrupt the infusion; this alone leads to recovery within two to three days in most patients. Methylene blue (commonly 50 mg IV every 4–6 hours) is widely used for treatment and secondary prevention, based on observational evidence; thiamine is also given. Seizures and non-convulsive status are treated with benzodiazepines and non-sedating antiseizure drugs, and haemodialysis is reserved for severe or refractory cases. Before rechallenge, correct albumin and renal factors, consider dose reduction, prolonged infusion or prophylactic methylene blue.
det.prognosis: Usually fully reversible within days; rare fatal or persistent cases occur with severe encephalopathy and delayed recognition.
pearls: Confusion within 24–48 hours of ifosfamide is drug toxicity until proven otherwise — check an EEG.
Low albumin is the strongest bedside predictor of ifosfamide encephalopathy.
Stopping the drug is the main treatment; methylene blue is supportive and used for prevention.

name: Asparaginase-associated cerebral venous thrombosis
formal: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis arising during treatment of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia with asparaginase, which depletes antithrombin, plasminogen and other hepatic proteins, usually in the induction phase together with corticosteroids; it presents with headache, seizures, focal deficits or venous haemorrhage and is treated with low-molecular-weight heparin, with cautious asparaginase re-exposure in most patients.
simple: A leukaemia drug, asparaginase, lowers the body's natural clot-blockers, so a clot can form in the brain's draining veins and cause headache, seizures or weakness.
th: asparaginase ที่ใช้รักษา ALL ลดการสร้าง antithrombin และโปรตีนต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือดจากตับ ทำให้เกิดหลอดเลือดดำในสมองอุดตัน มักเกิดช่วง induction ร่วมกับ steroid มีปวดศีรษะ ชัก อ่อนแรง หรือเลือดออกจาก venous infarct รักษาด้วย LMWH
tempoNote: Usually during induction or early intensification, days to weeks after asparaginase doses; symptoms evolve over hours to days
feat: Child, adolescent or young adult on ALL induction with new or progressive headache, vomiting or seizures
Focal deficit or drowsiness from venous infarction or haemorrhage; papilloedema with raised intracranial pressure
Superior sagittal and transverse sinuses most often affected; cortical vein thrombosis possible
Low antithrombin and fibrinogen, often with thrombocytopenia from leukaemia or chemotherapy
Higher risk in adults, with concomitant steroids, central venous catheters and inherited thrombophilia
inv: MRI with MR venography or CT venography; susceptibility imaging for cortical vein thrombus
Platelets, fibrinogen, antithrombin activity, PT and aPTT
Exclude CNS leukaemia, infection and PRES as alternative causes of seizures and headache

case.who: 16-year-old male high-school student from Phitsanulok on day 24 of induction for B-cell ALL
case.story: He has had worsening headache for two days and this morning had a focal seizure of the left arm and face that generalised.
case.exam: Drowsy after the seizure, mild left hemiparesis, bilateral papilloedema; blood pressure normal.
case.tests: Platelets 68 × 10⁹/L, fibrinogen 0.9 g/L, antithrombin 42%; MRI with MRV shows superior sagittal sinus and right cortical vein thrombosis with a small right parietal haemorrhagic venous infarct.
case.q: What caused this event and how should anticoagulation and leukaemia therapy be handled?
case.a: Asparaginase-associated cerebral venous thrombosis; start therapeutic LMWH despite the small haemorrhagic infarct (adjusting dose if platelets fall below 50 × 10⁹/L), consider antithrombin replacement when very low, give antiseizure medication, and in most cases resume asparaginase under LMWH once stable.
