det.patho: Asparaginase hydrolyses circulating asparagine, which halts protein synthesis in leukaemic lymphoblasts but also in hepatocytes. Hepatic synthesis of antithrombin, plasminogen, protein C, protein S and fibrinogen falls, tipping the balance towards thrombosis, while corticosteroids raise factor VIII and other procoagulants. Pegylated forms prolong exposure. Central venous catheters, inherited thrombophilia and older age add risk, so adults on paediatric-inspired regimens have more events than children.
det.clinical: Cerebral venous thrombosis is the most dangerous thrombotic complication of ALL therapy and typically appears during induction. Headache is the first symptom; seizures, focal deficits, encephalopathy and papilloedema follow as venous infarcts and raised intracranial pressure develop. Symptoms may be wrongly attributed to chemotherapy, intrathecal treatment, infection or leukaemic meningitis. Deep venous system involvement causes reduced consciousness and bilateral thalamic oedema.
det.diagnosis: MR venography or CT venography confirms the diagnosis, and susceptibility-weighted imaging detects isolated cortical vein thrombosis. Blood tests document low antithrombin and fibrinogen and set the baseline for anticoagulation in thrombocytopenia. CSF examination for leukaemic relapse should be deferred or done with care when anticoagulated. Thrombophilia testing is of limited acute value and is distorted by asparaginase.
det.treatment: Therapeutic LMWH is preferred; small haemorrhagic venous infarcts are not a contraindication. Platelet transfusion support or dose reduction is used when platelets fall below about 50 × 10⁹/L, and antithrombin concentrate may be considered when levels are very low and heparin seems ineffective. Asparaginase is paused during the acute phase, but cohort data show most patients can resume it safely under anticoagulation, which matters because omitting asparaginase worsens leukaemia outcomes. Anticoagulation usually continues for at least three months and until asparaginase therapy is complete; prophylactic LMWH or antithrombin is used in some adult protocols.
det.prognosis: Most patients recover with little residual deficit; seizures and focal deficits can persist after large haemorrhagic infarcts.
pearls: Headache or seizure during ALL induction is CVT until MR venography says otherwise.
A small haemorrhagic venous infarct does not prevent LMWH — the clot causes the bleed.
Most patients can resume asparaginase under LMWH once stable; omitting it harms leukaemia control.

name: Thalassaemia, neurological complications
formal: Nervous system complications of alpha- and beta-thalassaemia syndromes, including spinal cord or root compression by paravertebral extramedullary haematopoiesis, overt and silent cerebral infarction and venous thrombosis related to hypercoagulability (especially after splenectomy in non-transfusion-dependent disease), and toxicities of iron overload and chelation such as hearing loss, retinopathy and neuropathy.
simple: Thalassaemia, a common inherited anaemia in Thailand, can cause spinal cord pressure from extra blood-making tissue, silent strokes and nerve or hearing problems from iron and its treatment.
ab: ธาลัสซีเมีย ภาวะแทรกซ้อนทางระบบประสาท
th: ธาลัสซีเมียโดยเฉพาะชนิด HbE/β-thalassaemia และกลุ่มที่ไม่ต้องให้เลือดประจำ อาจมีเนื้อเยื่อสร้างเม็ดเลือดนอกไขกระดูกกดไขสันหลัง เกิด silent infarct หรือ stroke จากภาวะเลือดแข็งตัวง่ายหลังตัดม้าม และพิษจากเหล็กเกินหรือยาขับเหล็กต่อการได้ยินและสายตา
tempoNote: Cord compression from extramedullary haematopoiesis progresses over weeks to months; silent infarcts accumulate over years
feat: Young adult with HbE/beta-thalassaemia or thalassaemia intermedia, often splenectomised and infrequently transfused, with slowly progressive spastic paraparesis
Smooth, lobulated paravertebral or epidural masses in the thoracic spine that match marrow signal on MRI
Silent white-matter infarcts on MRI, sometimes with cognitive slowing; overt ischaemic stroke or CVT is less common
High-frequency sensorineural hearing loss and retinopathy with deferoxamine; renal and liver issues with deferasirox
Skeletal deformity (frontal bossing, maxillary overgrowth), splenomegaly or splenectomy scar, bronze skin
inv: MRI thoracic and lumbar spine with contrast; avoid biopsy of typical masses because of bleeding risk
Hb typing (HPLC), FBC with nucleated red cells, ferritin and cardiac/liver iron MRI
Brain MRI with vascular imaging for unexplained neurological symptoms; audiometry and eye examination on chelation

case.who: 28-year-old female office worker from Roi Et with HbE/beta-thalassaemia, splenectomised at 12 and transfused only occasionally
case.story: Over three months she noticed stiffness and weakness of both legs and tightness around the lower chest; she now needs a cane.
case.exam: Spastic paraparesis 4−/5, sensory level at T6, brisk reflexes and bilateral Babinski signs; frontal bossing and pale, mildly icteric sclerae.
case.tests: Hb 6.8 g/dL, ferritin 1,450 ng/mL; MRI shows bilateral lobulated paravertebral masses from T4 to T8 with an epidural component compressing the cord, signal similar to marrow and mild homogeneous enhancement.
case.q: What is the cause of her myelopathy and what are the treatment options?
case.a: Spinal cord compression by extramedullary haematopoiesis; start hypertransfusion to suppress erythropoiesis, low-dose radiotherapy (highly effective), hydroxyurea, and steroids for oedema, with surgical decompression reserved for rapid or severe deficit; manage iron overload.

det.patho: Ineffective erythropoiesis in thalassaemia drives marrow expansion and, when transfusions are sparse, haematopoietic tissue grows outside the marrow, especially in paravertebral regions where it can extend through foramina into the epidural space. Haemolysis, phosphatidylserine-exposing red cells, platelet activation and loss of splenic filtration after splenectomy create a hypercoagulable state that favours silent cerebral infarcts and occasionally stroke or CVT. Iron overload and its chelation add ototoxic, retinal and neuropathic effects. Thailand has one of the highest carrier frequencies for HbE and alpha-thalassaemia in the world.
det.clinical: Extramedullary haematopoiesis compressing the cord typically causes slowly progressive thoracic myelopathy with back pain or girdle sensations, though sudden worsening may follow haemorrhage into a mass. Silent infarcts are common in older splenectomised patients with non-transfusion-dependent thalassaemia and may contribute to subtle cognitive problems; overt strokes are less frequent. Peripheral neuropathy, myopathy and hearing loss occur in heavily transfused or chelated patients, and pituitary iron causes endocrine failure.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows smooth lobulated masses with intermediate T1 and T2 signal similar to marrow and mild enhancement; older lesions may show fatty or iron-laden change. In a known thalassaemia patient the appearance is characteristic, so biopsy is usually avoided because the tissue is highly vascular. Haemoglobin analysis confirms the genotype. Brain MRI with vascular imaging evaluates stroke, and audiological and ophthalmic screening are part of chelation monitoring.
det.treatment: For cord compression, hypertransfusion suppresses erythropoiesis and shrinks masses; low-dose radiotherapy is highly effective and often used first in significant deficit, with hydroxyurea and steroids as adjuncts and decompressive surgery for rapidly progressive or severe cases. Luspatercept can enlarge extramedullary masses and is used with caution in patients known to have them. Stroke prevention in high-risk non-transfusion-dependent patients includes transfusion programmes and, in some, aspirin after splenectomy with thrombocytosis. Chelation dosing is adjusted to limit toxicity, with regular hearing and eye checks.
det.prognosis: Cord compression responds well to transfusion and radiotherapy if treated before severe deficit; recurrence is common without ongoing marrow suppression.
pearls: In a thalassaemia patient with paraparesis and smooth paravertebral masses, think extramedullary haematopoiesis — and avoid biopsy.
Splenectomised, rarely transfused patients carry the highest risk of silent infarcts and thrombosis.
Deferoxamine can cause high-frequency hearing loss and retinopathy — audiometry and eye checks are routine.
det.thd: ธาลัสซีเมียพบมากในประเทศไทย ผู้ป่วยกลุ่มที่ไม่ต้องให้เลือดประจำโดยเฉพาะหลังตัดม้ามมีการสร้างเม็ดเลือดนอกไขกระดูกเป็นก้อนข้างกระดูกสันหลังส่วนอกจนกดไขสันหลังได้ MRI เห็นก้อนผิวเรียบสัญญาณเหมือนไขกระดูก ไม่ควรตัดชิ้นเนื้อ รักษาด้วยการให้เลือดจำนวนมาก ฉายรังสีขนาดต่ำ hydroxyurea และผ่าตัดในรายรุนแรง ผู้ป่วยยังเสี่ยง silent infarct และพิษจากยาขับเหล็กต่อการได้ยินและจอตา

name: Haemophilia-associated intracranial haemorrhage
formal: Intracranial bleeding — subdural, epidural, intraparenchymal or subarachnoid — in people with congenital factor VIII (haemophilia A) or factor IX (haemophilia B) deficiency, often after trivial or delayed-recognition trauma, which is the most lethal bleed in haemophilia and requires immediate factor replacement before imaging.
simple: In people born with haemophilia, even a small bump to the head can cause a serious brain bleed, so the missing clotting factor must be given straight away.
ab: ฮีโมฟีเลีย เลือดออกในสมอง
th: ผู้ป่วยฮีโมฟีเลีย A (ขาด factor VIII) และ B (ขาด factor IX) เสี่ยงเลือดออกในกะโหลกศีรษะแม้ได้รับบาดเจ็บเพียงเล็กน้อย เป็นภาวะเลือดออกที่อันตรายที่สุด ต้องให้ factor ทดแทนทันทีก่อนส่ง CT
tempoNote: Symptoms may begin hours to several days after a minor head injury; neonatal bleeds occur around delivery
feat: Boy or man with known haemophilia, often after minor head trauma, developing headache, vomiting, drowsiness or seizures
Neonates: subgaleal or intracranial bleeding after delivery, especially instrumental
Subdural haematoma is the commonest type; parenchymal bleeds increase with age and hypertension
Higher risk with severe deficiency (factor level below 1%), inhibitors, and absence of prophylaxis
Spinal epidural haematoma and iliopsoas haematoma with femoral neuropathy are other neurological bleeds
inv: Factor replacement first, then urgent non-contrast CT
Factor VIII or IX level and inhibitor (Bethesda) titre; FBC and coagulation profile
Repeat imaging for delayed expansion; MRI spine if back pain with leg symptoms

case.who: 9-year-old boy from Nakhon Si Thammarat with severe haemophilia A on emicizumab prophylaxis
case.story: He hit his head on a classroom desk two days ago; today he has a headache, vomited twice and seems unusually sleepy.
case.exam: GCS 14, small scalp haematoma over the right parietal region, no focal deficit.
case.tests: Factor VIII inhibitor history negative; CT after factor VIII concentrate shows a 6 mm right acute subdural haematoma without midline shift.
case.q: What is the key principle of management and how is his emicizumab handled?
case.a: Haemophilia-associated intracranial haemorrhage: give factor VIII concentrate immediately to reach about 100 IU/dL and maintain high levels for about two weeks with neurosurgical review; emicizumab is continued, and it interferes with aPTT-based assays, so chromogenic assays with bovine reagents are used to monitor factor VIII.

det.patho: Haemophilia A and B are X-linked deficiencies of factor VIII or IX, the key cofactors of the intrinsic tenase complex that amplifies thrombin generation on activated platelets. Without this amplification, clots form slowly and are unstable, so bleeding from torn bridging veins or small parenchymal vessels continues and may restart days after an injury. Severity tracks the factor level: severe below 1%, moderate 1–5% and mild 5–40%. Neutralising alloantibodies (inhibitors) make standard replacement ineffective.
det.clinical: ICH can occur at any age but peaks in newborns and in older adults, in whom hypertension and vascular disease add risk. Symptoms may lag behind a trivial injury by hours or days, and young children may present only with irritability, vomiting or seizures. Subdural haematoma is most frequent, followed by intraparenchymal, epidural and subarachnoid bleeds. Survivors may develop epilepsy, motor deficit or cognitive impairment.
det.diagnosis: Any head trauma or unexplained headache in a person with haemophilia is treated as a possible ICH: give replacement first, then scan. Factor levels and inhibitor titres guide dosing. Monitoring on emicizumab requires chromogenic factor VIII assays because the drug distorts aPTT and one-stage assays. In a newborn with ICH and no family history, a factor VIII or IX level should be checked.
det.treatment: Give factor concentrate immediately to target about 80–100 IU/dL, maintain trough levels high (often above 50 IU/dL) for one to two weeks and then step down, with neurosurgery under factor cover when needed. Patients with inhibitors receive bypassing agents (recombinant activated factor VII; activated prothrombin complex concentrate used cautiously with emicizumab because of thrombotic microangiopathy risk). Long-term, prophylaxis with extended half-life factors, emicizumab, or newer agents such as concizumab, marstacimab and fitusiran reduces bleeding, and gene therapy is available in some countries; secondary prophylaxis after ICH is strongly recommended. Blood pressure control matters in older patients.
det.prognosis: Mortality has fallen with early replacement and prophylaxis but remains significant, and many survivors have lasting deficits or epilepsy.
pearls: Treat first, image later: give factor before the CT in any haemophilia head injury.
Delayed presentation days after a minor knock is typical — ask about trauma in the last week.
On emicizumab, aPTT is misleadingly normal; use chromogenic assays and avoid high-dose aPCC.

name: Immune thrombocytopenia with intracranial haemorrhage (ITP-ICH)
formal: Spontaneous or trauma-provoked intracranial bleeding in primary or secondary immune thrombocytopenia, a rare but leading cause of death in ITP that occurs mostly with platelet counts below 10–20 × 10⁹/L and requires combined emergency platelet transfusion, intravenous immunoglobulin and high-dose corticosteroids, with thrombopoietin receptor agonists and neurosurgery as indicated.
simple: In immune thrombocytopenia the body destroys its own platelets; when counts are extremely low a brain bleed can occur and needs platelets, immunoglobulin and steroids all at once.
th: ITP คือภาวะภูมิคุ้มกันทำลายเกล็ดเลือด เลือดออกในสมองพบไม่บ่อยแต่เป็นสาเหตุเสียชีวิตสำคัญ มักเกิดเมื่อเกล็ดเลือดต่ำกว่า 10–20 × 10⁹/L ต้องให้เกล็ดเลือด IVIG และ steroid ขนาดสูงพร้อมกันทันที

Intraparenchymal haemorrhage most common; subdural and subarachnoid bleeding possible

FBC, smear (exclude pseudothrombocytopenia, schistocytes, blasts), PT, aPTT, fibrinogen

case.who: 71-year-old male retired civil servant from Chachoengsao with chronic ITP who stopped prednisolone a month ago
case.story: Two days of gum bleeding and tiny red spots on the legs; this morning he developed a severe headache and right-hand clumsiness. He takes aspirin after a coronary stent.
case.exam: BP 168/92, petechiae on legs and palate, blood blisters on the buccal mucosa, mild right arm weakness and expressive dysphasia.
case.tests: Platelets 4 × 10⁹/L, Hb and WBC normal, smear without schistocytes, PT and fibrinogen normal; CT shows a 15 mL left frontal lobar haematoma.
case.q: How should the platelet count be raised in this emergency?
case.a: ITP with intracranial haemorrhage: stop aspirin, give repeated or continuous platelet transfusions together with IVIG 1 g/kg and IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily, control blood pressure, start a thrombopoietin receptor agonist, and involve neurosurgery; emergency splenectomy or recombinant factor VIIa are rare last resorts.

det.patho: In ITP, autoantibodies against platelet glycoproteins and cytotoxic T cells shorten platelet survival in the spleen and liver and also suppress megakaryocyte production, while thrombopoietin levels are inappropriately normal. Once counts are extremely low, small vessels lose their haemostatic plug, and trauma, hypertension or antiplatelet drugs tip the balance towards intracranial bleeding. Secondary ITP accompanies SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome, HIV, hepatitis C, H. pylori, CLL and some drugs and vaccines.
det.clinical: ICH occurs in well under 1% of children and in somewhat more adults with ITP, mostly during periods of severe thrombocytopenia, with older age the strongest risk factor. Warning signs are mucosal (wet) bleeding and haematuria rather than skin petechiae alone. Presentation follows the haemorrhage type: headache, vomiting, focal deficit, seizures or reduced consciousness. Children with newly diagnosed ITP are most at risk in the first weeks, often after head trauma.
det.diagnosis: ITP remains a diagnosis of exclusion: isolated thrombocytopenia with a normal smear apart from large platelets, and no other cause. In the emergency the critical step is excluding TTP, DIC, leukaemia and HIT, because their treatment differs. CT confirms bleeding; MRI and vascular imaging are considered later to exclude an underlying lesion or venous thrombosis.
det.treatment: All three first-line agents are given together: platelet transfusion (often a large bolus followed by repeated or continuous infusion), IVIG 1 g/kg for one to two days, and high-dose methylprednisolone or dexamethasone. Thrombopoietin receptor agonists (romiplostim, eltrombopag, avatrombopag) are started early to sustain counts, and rescue options include recombinant factor VIIa and emergency splenectomy. Antiplatelet and anticoagulant drugs are stopped, blood pressure is controlled and neurosurgical evacuation is undertaken once haemostasis is achievable. Longer term, fostamatinib, rituximab or splenectomy are options for chronic disease.
det.prognosis: Mortality after ITP-related ICH is substantial, especially in older adults; survivors usually remain at risk while thrombocytopenia persists.
pearls: Wet purpura and haematuria signal higher bleeding risk than dry skin petechiae.
For ITP with ICH, give platelets, IVIG and high-dose steroids simultaneously — not sequentially.
Exclude TTP before transfusing platelets: look for schistocytes and haemolysis.
det.thd: ITP คือการที่ภูมิคุ้มกันทำลายเกล็ดเลือด เลือดออกในสมองเกิดเมื่อเกล็ดเลือดต่ำมาก โดยเฉพาะผู้สูงอายุ ผู้ที่ได้รับบาดเจ็บศีรษะ หรือใช้ยาต้านเกล็ดเลือด การรักษาฉุกเฉินคือให้เกล็ดเลือด IVIG และ steroid ขนาดสูงพร้อมกัน ร่วมกับยากลุ่ม TPO receptor agonist หยุดยาต้านเกล็ดเลือด คุมความดัน และปรึกษาศัลยแพทย์ ต้องแยก TTP ก่อนเสมอ

case.who: 33-year-old male rice mill worker from Chainat with a history of mild aplastic anaemia
case.story: For a week he has had worsening headache, and today he had a seizure; he has noticed cola-coloured urine on waking for months and pain when swallowing.
case.exam: Pale and slightly jaundiced, drowsy after the seizure, bilateral papilloedema, mild left leg weakness.
case.tests: Hb 7.4 g/dL, platelets 92 × 10⁹/L, LDH 2,100 U/L, haptoglobin undetectable, direct antiglobulin test negative; MRV shows superior sagittal sinus thrombosis; flow cytometry shows a 68% FLAER-negative granulocyte clone.

det.patho: A somatic PIGA mutation in a haematopoietic stem cell blocks synthesis of the GPI anchor, so the clone's progeny lack CD55 and CD59, which normally restrain complement. Red cells are destroyed intravascularly by the membrane attack complex, releasing free haemoglobin that scavenges nitric oxide and causes smooth muscle spasm and endothelial dysfunction. Platelet activation, microparticles, neutrophil activation and impaired fibrinolysis create a strongly prothrombotic state. PNH clones commonly expand in aplastic anaemia, where immune pressure favours GPI-deficient cells.
det.clinical: Most deaths in untreated PNH are due to thrombosis, which favours unusual veins: hepatic, portal, mesenteric, dermal and cerebral sinuses. Cerebral venous thrombosis causes headache, seizures, papilloedema and focal deficits; arterial strokes are rarer. Classical haemoglobinuria is seen by only a minority, so fatigue, dysphagia, abdominal pain and cytopenias may be the main clues. Breakthrough haemolysis can occur with infection or pregnancy.
det.diagnosis: Flow cytometry with FLAER and lineage markers on granulocytes and monocytes is the diagnostic test and quantifies clone size; red-cell CD59 analysis underestimates the clone after transfusion or haemolysis. Testing is recommended in unexplained CVT or splanchnic thrombosis, Coombs-negative haemolysis, and aplastic anaemia or MDS. Brain imaging with venography confirms CVT, and abdominal imaging looks for concurrent hepatic or portal vein thrombosis.
det.treatment: Acute CVT is anticoagulated with heparin, and complement inhibition is started as soon as possible because it sharply reduces recurrent thrombosis. Options include C5 inhibitors (eculizumab, ravulizumab, crovalimab) and proximal inhibitors (pegcetacoplan, oral iptacopan, danicopan as add-on), all requiring meningococcal vaccination and often antibiotic prophylaxis. Anticoagulation is usually continued long term after thrombosis. Allogeneic stem cell transplantation is reserved for severe marrow failure or refractory disease.
det.prognosis: Complement inhibitors have brought life expectancy near normal, though cerebral and hepatic thrombosis remain causes of serious morbidity, especially before diagnosis.
pearls: Unexplained CVT plus haemolysis or cytopenia: order PNH flow cytometry.
Most patients never see dark urine — rely on LDH, haptoglobin and flow cytometry.
Vaccinate against meningococcus before or alongside any complement inhibitor.

Aspirin or iron alone does not address the mechanism, and splenectomy does not control intravascular haemolysis.

det.patho: IGHMBP2 encodes an RNA helicase that supports translation and the survival of lower motor neurons, and loss of its function leads to degeneration of anterior horn cells, particularly those serving distal muscles and the diaphragm. Peripheral nerve axons and, in some patients, autonomic and sensory fibres are also affected. Residual enzyme activity from hypomorphic variants explains the milder, later-onset phenotype sometimes called distal HMN type VI or CMT2S. The disease is distinct from SMN-related SMA at the gene, protein and distribution level.
det.clinical: A normal start is followed in the first months by weakness of the feet and hands, reduced spontaneous movement and eventually diaphragm failure, which often triggers presentation with a respiratory infection. Breathing appears paradoxical and diaphragmatic ultrasound shows reduced excursion. Bulbar function and cognition are initially preserved, which makes the child interactive despite severe weakness. Over time autonomic dysregulation, constipation, sweating abnormalities and pain insensitivity may develop. Without ventilatory support, death occurs in infancy or early childhood.
det.diagnosis: Suspect the condition in an infant with distal weakness and diaphragmatic palsy or elevated hemidiaphragm. Because SMN1 testing is negative, a motor neuron gene panel or exome should include IGHMBP2, and both sequence and copy-number analysis are required. Nerve conduction studies usually show a motor axonopathy with small compound muscle potentials. Congenital myopathies, congenital myasthenic syndromes, phrenic nerve injury and mitochondrial disease are the main alternatives.
det.treatment: Management is supportive: early noninvasive or tracheostomy ventilation after family discussion, airway clearance, nutrition support, orthopaedic and physiotherapy care. Gene replacement therapy targeting IGHMBP2 with an AAV9 vector has shown improved survival and motor milestones in early-phase studies and is being evaluated in regulatory pathways, so referral to a centre with trials or expanded access should be considered. Decisions about long-term ventilation must be made with palliative care input and with realistic discussion of prognosis.
det.prognosis: Classic infantile onset is life-limiting without ventilation; some milder or later-onset genotypes have survived into childhood and beyond.
pearls: Respiratory failure with distal-predominant weakness and a normal SMN1 result should prompt IGHMBP2 testing.
Diaphragm weakness before intercostal weakness is the reverse of the pattern in SMN1 SMA.
Preserved alertness and social engagement can mislead clinicians about disease severity.

det.patho: Fukutin participates in glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan, which anchors cell membranes to the extracellular matrix via laminin binding. Defective glycosylation weakens the basement membrane of myofibres and neuron migration surfaces, causing both muscular dystrophy and abnormal neuronal migration with cobblestone cortex. A single ancestral retrotransposon insertion in the FKTN 3' untranslated region explains why the disorder is very common in Japan and rare elsewhere. Other FKTN variants cause a spectrum from severe congenital disease to adult limb-girdle weakness with cardiomyopathy.
det.clinical: Weakness is present from early infancy, with facial and truncal involvement, calf hypertrophy and early contractures. Motor development plateaus: many children sit but few walk without support, and most lose gains in later childhood. Seizures and global developmental delay are common. Swallowing difficulty, restrictive lung disease and cardiomyopathy appear in the second decade and determine longevity. Eye findings are milder than in other severe dystroglycanopathies.
det.diagnosis: The combination of very high CK, dystrophic biopsy with absent or reduced glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan, and cobblestone brain MRI strongly suggests the diagnosis. Genetic confirmation can be done by targeted FKTN analysis in patients of Japanese ancestry or by a dystroglycanopathy panel or exome elsewhere. Distinguishing it from WWS, MEB and other CMDs depends on the degree of eye and brain involvement.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying treatment is approved. Multidisciplinary care includes seizure management, physiotherapy, contracture prevention, swallowing assessment and gastrostomy, nocturnal ventilation when indicated, and periodic echocardiography with early cardiac therapy. Corticosteroids have limited and non-standard use. Trials of glycosylation-enhancing approaches and gene therapy are early-stage, so genetic counselling for recurrence risk is an important part of care.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is reduced, often with death in childhood or the second decade from respiratory or cardiac failure, although milder FKTN phenotypes survive to adulthood.
pearls: Cobblestone cortex on MRI with high CK is a dystroglycanopathy until proved otherwise.
The FKTN founder variant explains the high prevalence in Japan; look for it in patients with Japanese ancestry.
Cardiomyopathy and respiratory decline need scheduled surveillance even when the child is clinically stable.

det.patho: Maternal IgG antibodies to the acetylcholine receptor cross the placenta in the third trimester and bind fetal and neonatal end-plates, reducing receptor number and impairing neuromuscular transmission. Fetal-type receptors contain a gamma subunit that is replaced by an epsilon subunit after birth, so antibodies to the fetal form can cause arthrogryposis in the unborn child. Weakness resolves as maternal IgG is catabolised, over weeks.
det.clinical: Symptoms start within the first few days, with a weak cry, poor suck and swallow, hypotonia and a poorly expressive face, and sometimes respiratory difficulty. Extraocular involvement is less prominent than in older patients. Feeding assistance is the commonest need. Infants whose mothers have severe or active disease are at higher risk, but the correlation is imperfect and previous affected siblings increase risk.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, in the context of a maternal history of myasthenia and a time course typical of passive transfer. A supervised neostigmine test dose can support the diagnosis. Decrement on repetitive stimulation is helpful when available, and antibody testing can document the maternal source. Other causes of neonatal hypotonia such as sepsis, metabolic disease and genetic myopathies must be considered, particularly if recovery is delayed.
det.treatment: Most infants need observation in a centre with neonatal intensive care for at least 48-72 hours. Support feeding by tube or cup and ensure airway monitoring. Short courses of oral or subcutaneous neostigmine or pyridostigmine, given before feeds, are used for significant weakness. Respiratory support is given for apnoea or poor ventilation, and IVIG or plasma exchange is reserved for severe or prolonged cases. Maternal therapy should be continued through pregnancy and the obstetric and neonatal teams informed in advance.
det.prognosis: Excellent: recovery is complete, usually within a few weeks, with no persistent weakness.
pearls: Ask every floppy newborn's mother about myasthenia, even when she is in remission or has had a thymectomy.
A positive response to a neostigmine test dose in the first days supports the diagnosis.
Persistent weakness beyond 3 months should prompt a search for congenital myasthenic syndrome.

name: Arthrogryposis multiplex congenita (fetal akinesia deformation sequence)
formal: A descriptive term for multiple joint contractures present at birth, resulting from reduced fetal movement of neurogenic, myopathic, junctional, connective tissue or maternal origin, and often forming part of a fetal akinesia deformation sequence.
simple: A baby is born with several stiff, fixed joints because it moved too little in the womb; the underlying cause may be nerve, muscle or other.
ab: ข้อติดแต่กำเนิดหลายข้อ
th: ภาวะที่ทารกเกิดมามีข้อติดแข็งหลายข้อ เนื่องจากการเคลื่อนไหวของทารกในครรภ์น้อยลง สาเหตุอาจมาจากเส้นประสาท กล้ามเนื้อ รอยต่อประสาทกล้ามเนื้อ หรือพันธุกรรมต่าง ๆ จึงต้องหาสาเหตุทุกราย
tempoNote: Present from birth; many types are non-progressive, but those due to neuromuscular disease may evolve
feat: Fixed contractures of two or more joints at birth, often symmetric, with clubfeet, flexed elbows or extended knees
Reduced fetal movements and polyhydramnios in pregnancy; small jaw, pulmonary hypoplasia and short umbilical cord in severe cases
Neurogenic pattern: absent reflexes and fasciculations; myopathic pattern: hypotonia with preserved reflexes and elevated CK
Associated central nervous system anomalies, congenital heart defects or abdominal wall defects in syndromic forms
Hypotonia at birth with respiratory problems helps point to a neuromuscular cause
inv: Detailed prenatal and family history, maternal myasthenia, maternal drugs and infection exposure
Serum CK, brain and spinal cord MRI, nerve conduction studies and EMG
Genetic testing: chromosomal microarray, exome or gene panel including muscle-nerve genes, SMN1 where appropriate
Muscle biopsy for unexplained hypotonic cases

case.who: Term newborn girl at a provincial hospital in Nakhon Ratchasima, first child of healthy parents
case.story: The mother noticed few movements in late pregnancy and the obstetrician found polyhydramnios; the baby is born with stiff elbows, wrists and knees and bilateral clubfeet.
case.exam: Hypotonic, mildly low-set ears and small jaw, weak cry, abdominal breathing; absent reflexes, tongue fasciculation not seen; no ptosis.
case.tests: CK normal; chest X-ray shows small lungs; nerve conduction shows low motor amplitudes with normal sensory responses; exome identifies a variant in a motor neuron gene.
case.q: What approach should be taken to the underlying cause and what clues point to a neurogenic origin?
case.a: Treat arthrogryposis as a symptom of reduced fetal movement; absent reflexes, normal CK, low motor amplitudes and normal sensory studies indicate an anterior horn or peripheral motor nerve origin and guide genetic testing.

read.where: 11. The Diagnostic Approach to the Hypotonic and Weak Infant

det.patho: Fetal joints need movement to develop normally; reduced intrauterine movement leads to periarticular fibrosis and fixed contracture. The causes include motor neuron or nerve disease, myopathies and dystrophies, neuromuscular junction disorders such as fetal acetylcholine receptor syndromes, connective tissue abnormalities, crowding in the uterus, and maternal factors such as myasthenia or drug exposure. A large group has a genetic aetiology that overlaps with congenital neuromuscular diseases, which is why modern exome testing identifies a cause in a substantial share of children.
det.clinical: Babies show fixed joint contractures, often symmetrical, with reduced skin creases and muscle bulk. The pattern of joint involvement, hypotonia, reflexes and associated features guides the differential. Pulmonary hypoplasia, swallowing problems and feeding difficulty are the main early threats. Distal arthrogryposis syndromes typically involve hands and feet with normal strength, whereas generalised contractures with hypotonia suggest a neuromuscular disease.
det.diagnosis: Start by separating a central nervous system, a peripheral neuromuscular and a non-neuromuscular origin. CK, nerve conduction studies, EMG, brain and spine imaging and genetic testing are the core steps; muscle biopsy is added when a myopathy is suspected. Maternal antibody testing for myasthenia is required whenever the mother has weakness or the infant has features of fetal receptor inactivation. Prenatal ultrasound may suggest the diagnosis, and a precise genetic diagnosis allows recurrence-risk counselling.
det.treatment: Early orthopaedic management with serial casting, bracing and, if needed, surgery, along with intensive physiotherapy, improves function. Respiratory and feeding support are given as needed, and a multidisciplinary team follows growth, scoliosis and hip stability. When a treatable cause is found, such as congenital myasthenia or maternal myasthenia, targeted therapy is started. Genetic counselling and options for future pregnancies are discussed.
det.prognosis: Depends on the cause: isolated amyoplasia and distal forms often walk, whereas neuromuscular or syndromic forms may be severe or lethal.
pearls: Arthrogryposis is a sign, not a final diagnosis; always look for a neuromuscular cause.
Normal reflexes with distal contractures favour distal arthrogryposis; absent reflexes favour neurogenic disease.
Ask about maternal myasthenia in every infant with congenital contractures.
det.thd: Arthrogryposis multiplex congenita คือข้อติดหลายข้อตั้งแต่เกิดจากการเคลื่อนไหวของทารกในครรภ์ลดลง ไม่ใช่การวินิจฉัยสุดท้าย ต้องหาสาเหตุจากระบบประสาทและกล้ามเนื้อ เช่น SMA โรคกล้ามเนื้อ หรือแม่เป็น myasthenia ตรวจ CK, NCS/EMG, MRI และตรวจพันธุกรรม การรักษาเน้นการเข้าเฝือก ออร์โธปิดิกส์ และกายภาพบำบัด ร่วมกับดูแลการหายใจและการกิน

Maternal myasthenia; hypotonia and feeding weakness without fixed contractures, resolving over weeks
Contractures are uncommon at birth; weakness and tongue fasciculation develop after birth with SMN1 deletion

name: Congenital fibre type disproportion (CFTD)
formal: A congenital myopathy defined histologically by type 1 fibres that are at least 35-40% smaller than type 2 fibres in the absence of other specific structural lesions, caused by variants in genes such as TPM3, RYR1, ACTA1, SEPN1 and others.
simple: A muscle disease present from early life in which one type of muscle fibre is much smaller than the other under the microscope.
ab: ภาวะกล้ามเนื้อแต่กำเนิดชนิดเส้นใยขนาดไม่สมดุล
th: โรคกล้ามเนื้อแต่กำเนิดที่ตัดชิ้นเนื้อพบเส้นใยกล้ามเนื้อ type 1 เล็กกว่า type 2 อย่างชัดเจน ทารกมีอ่อนแรง ลักษณะหน้ายาว เพดานโค้งสูง และข้อติด มียีนก่อโรคหลายชนิด เช่น TPM3 RYR1 ACTA1 ผลมีตั้งแต่เล็กน้อยจนต้องใช้เครื่องช่วยหายใจ
tempoNote: Onset in infancy or early childhood; usually static or slowly progressive, with respiratory involvement in some genotypes
feat: Neonatal or infant hypotonia with proximal, often facial, weakness
Long thin face, high-arched palate, micrognathia and thin muscle bulk
Joint contractures, hip dislocation, scoliosis and foot deformity
Breathing muscles may be disproportionately affected relative to the limbs in some genotypes, notably TPM3
CK is normal or mildly raised; cognition is typically normal
inv: Muscle biopsy with ATPase fibre typing: type 1 fibre diameter at least 12% smaller than type 2 in the absence of rods or cores
Genetic panel for congenital myopathy including TPM3, RYR1, ACTA1, SEPN1 and MYH7
Spirometry, sleep study and echocardiography
Exclude neurogenic and central causes with EMG, MRI brain and SMN1 testing

case.who: 8-year-old boy followed in a paediatric neuromuscular clinic in Songkhla
case.story: He was floppy in infancy, walked at 22 months, falls often and now has difficulty climbing stairs; he had two admissions for pneumonia with poor cough.
case.exam: Long narrow face, high palate, bilateral scapular winging, proximal weakness with Gowers sign, absent ankle jerks, mild scoliosis.
case.tests: CK 180 U/L; spirometry shows FVC at 60% predicted; biopsy shows type 1 fibres much smaller than type 2 without rods or cores; TPM3 variant confirmed.
case.q: What is the pathological feature and why are respiratory studies important in this child?
case.a: Marked hypotrophy of type 1 fibres without other specific lesions; respiratory weakness can be disproportionate and cause nocturnal hypoventilation, so FVC and sleep studies should be monitored.

det.patho: The histological pattern, type 1 fibre hypotrophy without structural abnormalities, appears to be a final common pathway rather than a single disease. Variants in sarcomeric proteins (TPM3, ACTA1, MYH7), the ryanodine receptor (RYR1) and other genes can produce this pattern, and some of the same genes cause rod, core or myosin storage lesions in other patients. Impaired muscle fibre development with reduced contractile function in slow fibres is the proposed mechanism.
det.clinical: Infants present with hypotonia and generalised weakness that tends to be static or slowly progressive. Facial weakness, a long narrow face and high palate are common. Contractures, scoliosis and hip subluxation develop in childhood. Respiratory weakness may be disproportionate, particularly with TPM3 variants, and nocturnal hypoventilation can occur before it is clinically obvious.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on histology showing type 1 fibre hypotrophy of at least 12% relative to type 2 fibres without rods, cores or other specific changes, together with exclusion of neurogenic disease. Because the pattern is non-specific, a gene panel or exome is used to establish aetiology, which is clinically useful for predicting respiratory risk and possible malignant hyperthermia susceptibility in RYR1 cases. A mildly raised or normal CK is typical.
det.treatment: No cure exists, and care is supportive: physiotherapy, orthopaedic management for scoliosis and contractures, regular lung function and sleep monitoring with noninvasive ventilation when needed, swallowing assessment, nutrition and cardiac review. Cough assistance and vaccination reduce respiratory infections. RYR1-related cases need anaesthetic precautions for malignant hyperthermia. Genetic counselling is provided for the family.
det.prognosis: Generally non-progressive or slowly progressive, but respiratory involvement can be life-limiting and varies by genotype.
pearls: Fibre-type disproportion is a pattern, not a diagnosis; always look for the gene.
Always check FVC and sleep studies, because respiratory weakness can outpace limb weakness.
In RYR1-positive children flag malignant hyperthermia risk before any anaesthetic.
det.thd: CFTD เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้อแต่กำเนิดที่ตัดชิ้นเนื้อพบเส้นใย type 1 เล็กกว่า type 2 อย่างน้อย 12% โดยไม่พบ rods หรือ cores ผู้ป่วยมีอ่อนแรง ใบหน้ายาว เพดานโค้งสูง ข้อติด และอาจมีกล้ามเนื้อหายใจอ่อนแรงมาก ควรตรวจสมรรถภาพปอดและการนอนหลับ และตรวจยีน เช่น TPM3 RYR1 ACTA1 การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง

ddx.pt: Rods on Gomori trichrome or electron microscopy; also facial and neck weakness with hypotonia
Central nuclei with radial sarcoplasmic strands on oxidative stains; ptosis and ophthalmoparesis in some forms
Umbrella group, with different lesions on histology; CFTD can be a nonspecific pattern shared across genotypes

name: Rippling muscle disease (caveolinopathy)
formal: A mechanically triggered, electrically silent muscle hyperexcitability disorder, typically due to CAV3 variants, in which stretch or percussion produces propagating rolling waves of muscle contraction, mounding and stiffness.
simple: A muscle disorder where stretching or tapping the muscle makes visible ripples run across it and causes stiffness.
ab: โรคกล้ามเนื้อเป็นคลื่น
th: โรคกล้ามเนื้อที่เกิดจากยีน CAV3 กล้ามเนื้อถูกยืดหรือเคาะแล้วเกิดคลื่นการหดตัววิ่งเป็นริ้ว มีตะคริวและแข็งเกร็ง โดย EMG เงียบ (electrically silent) ต่างจาก myotonia ที่มี myotonic discharges
tempoNote: Onset in childhood or adolescence with lifelong, mostly non-progressive or slowly progressive symptoms
feat: Rolling waves of contraction that travel laterally across a muscle after stretch, often visible rather than painful
Mounding of muscle on percussion that lasts several seconds and is stable on repeated tapping
Muscle stiffness, cramps and exertional pain, worse with cold or after rest
Muscle hypertrophy; proximal weakness, toe-walking or calf tightness in some patients
Mild to moderate CK elevation; may coexist with LGMD or hyperCKemia in the same family
inv: Clinical test: percussion causing mounding and stretch-induced rolling waves
Needle EMG: electrical silence during rippling and mounding, no myotonic discharges
CK, often 2-10 times normal
CAV3 sequencing; muscle biopsy with caveolin-3 immunostaining showing reduced or mislocalised protein

case.who: 22-year-old male university student from Chonburi referred for stiffness after exercise
case.story: Since adolescence his thigh and forearm muscles ripple and feel tight after sitting, and he sees the muscle surface moving when he stretches; his mother has the same signs.
case.exam: Visible waves rolling over the quadriceps on passive stretch, tapping the biceps causes a ridge of muscle lasting several seconds, normal strength, brisk reflexes.
case.tests: CK 1,200 U/L; EMG shows silent muscle during rippling, no myotonia; CAV3 shows a heterozygous pathogenic missense variant.
case.q: How is the pattern differentiated from myotonia electrically and what gene is implicated?
case.a: Rippling is electrically silent whereas myotonia shows repetitive discharges with waxing and waning; CAV3 variants are the usual cause.

read.where: Scoping Review on ADCY5-Related Movement Disorders

det.patho: Caveolin-3 is a membrane protein of muscle caveolae that interacts with ion channels, nitric oxide synthase and signalling molecules. Loss of caveolin-3 function disturbs excitation-contraction coupling and calcium handling, producing excess mechanical excitability without electrical depolarisation. Dominant-negative variants cause misfolded protein retained in the Golgi. The same gene is linked to LGMD R25, distal myopathy, hyperCKemia and cardiomyopathy, so a family may have different phenotypes.
det.clinical: Patients describe tight, stiff muscles after rest or exercise and may notice visible rippling when they stretch. Examination reveals mounding with percussion and rolling contractions after stretch. Strength is usually normal, though some develop proximal weakness or muscle hypertrophy. Cold and exercise worsen stiffness. Some patients have very mild symptoms and are found because of elevated CK.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical and confirmed by EMG showing no electrical activity during rippling and mounding. CAV3 genetic testing is the definitive step. Muscle biopsy is not routinely required but shows reduced caveolin-3 staining in many cases. Family screening is useful given autosomal dominant inheritance. Acquired forms associated with myasthenia gravis or thymoma have been described and should be sought in new-onset adults.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying therapy. Stretching, gradual warm-up, avoiding cold exposure and heavy eccentric exercise reduce symptoms. Sodium-channel blockers have little benefit given the electrically silent mechanism, but carbamazepine, phenytoin or mexiletine can be trialled when cramp or pain is troublesome. Cardiac evaluation, including ECG, is advisable because caveolinopathy can affect the heart. Counsel on anaesthesia and rhabdomyolysis risk as for other channel-linked myopathies.
det.prognosis: Usually benign, with stable symptoms; some patients develop mild weakness later.
pearls: Rippling is a mechanical phenomenon with silent EMG; do not mistake it for myotonia.
CAV3 variants cause LGMD, rippling, distal myopathy and hyperCKemia within one gene.
New adult-onset rippling should prompt a search for acquired myasthenia or thymoma.
det.thd: Rippling muscle disease เกิดจากยีน CAV3 เมื่อยืดกล้ามเนื้อจะเห็นคลื่นหดตัววิ่งเป็นริ้ว และเมื่อเคาะจะนูนค้างหลายวินาที โดย EMG เงียบ ไม่มี myotonic discharges การรักษาคือหลีกเลี่ยงความเย็นและการออกกำลังหนักช่วงแรก ใช้ยา carbamazepine หรือ mexiletine ในรายที่มีตะคริวมาก และตรวจหัวใจเป็นระยะ

name: Hereditary myopathy with early respiratory failure (HMERF)
formal: An autosomal dominant myofibrillar myopathy caused by missense variants in the fibronectin-3 domain of the titin gene TTN, presenting in adulthood with proximal and distal weakness and early ventilatory failure out of proportion to limb weakness.
simple: An inherited adult muscle disease in which breathing muscles weaken early, sometimes before the arms and legs are severely affected.
ab: Hereditary myopathy with early respiratory failure
โรคกล้ามเนื้อทางพันธุกรรมกับการหายใจล้มเหลวระยะแรก
th: โรคกล้ามเนื้อถ่ายทอด autosomal dominant จากยีน TTN ผู้ป่วยวัยผู้ใหญ่อ่อนแรงทั้งส่วนต้นและส่วนปลาย และมีกล้ามเนื้อหายใจอ่อนแรงเร็วมาก บางรายต้องใช้เครื่องช่วยหายใจก่อนที่จะเดินไม่ได้ การตัดชิ้นเนื้อพบ cytoplasmic bodies
tempoNote: Onset typically in the third to fifth decade; weakness progresses over years, and ventilatory failure can appear early
feat: Adult with progressive proximal and distal limb weakness, trunk and neck flexor weakness
Dyspnoea, orthopnoea, morning headache and nocturnal hypoventilation, with early respiratory failure
Foot drop or difficulty rising from a chair as presenting limb symptoms
Family history compatible with dominant inheritance, though de novo cases occur
CK normal to moderately elevated; muscle MRI shows selective involvement of the posterior thigh and calf muscles
inv: FVC upright and supine, sniff nasal pressure, overnight oximetry/capnography
Muscle MRI showing selective fatty replacement, notably of semitendinosus, vastus lateralis and tibialis anterior
Muscle biopsy with cytoplasmic bodies and rimmed vacuoles; sarcomere disorganisation on electron microscopy
TTN testing focusing on the A-band fibronectin-3 domain; broader neuromuscular panel or exome

case.who: 46-year-old woman clerk from Udon Thani admitted with hypercapnic respiratory failure
case.story: Over 18 months she had worsening breathlessness lying flat, morning headaches and difficulty with stairs; her father needed home ventilation in his fifties.
case.exam: Paradoxical abdominal movement when supine, neck flexion weakness, moderate hip girdle and ankle dorsiflexion weakness, absent hypertrophy.
case.tests: ABG shows chronic hypercapnia; FVC drops by over 30% supine; CK 410 U/L; MRI shows fatty replacement of hamstrings and tibialis anterior; biopsy with cytoplasmic bodies; TTN missense in the fibronectin-3 domain.
case.q: What feature would make you suspect this disorder instead of ALS or acid maltase deficiency in an adult with ventilatory failure?
case.a: Early respiratory failure with myopathic limb weakness, selective muscle MRI pattern, cytoplasmic bodies on biopsy and an autosomal dominant family history point to a TTN fibronectin-domain myopathy.

det.patho: Titin is the giant sarcomeric protein that provides passive tension and a scaffold for the myofibrillar architecture. HMERF-causing missense variants cluster in the fibronectin-3 domain of the A-band, destabilising the protein and leading to aggregates that disrupt sarcomere assembly. Muscle fibres show cytoplasmic and reducing-body-like inclusions, rimmed vacuoles and myofibrillar disorganisation. Respiratory muscles, including the diaphragm, appear to be especially susceptible, explaining the early ventilatory failure.
det.clinical: Adults present with proximal and distal weakness, trunk weakness and symptoms of nocturnal hypoventilation such as morning headache, daytime sleepiness and orthopnoea. Respiratory failure may precede significant limb disability and may be the initial presentation, sometimes requiring emergency admission. Progression is variable but steady, and cardiac involvement is rare in classic HMERF.
det.diagnosis: Consider HMERF in any adult with myopathy and unexplained respiratory failure. Muscle MRI shows a characteristic pattern in the posterior thigh and lower leg. Biopsy shows cytoplasmic bodies and rimmed vacuoles and excludes acid maltase deficiency. Genetic confirmation requires TTN analysis, and clinicians should be aware that many TTN variants are of uncertain significance outside the known fibronectin-3 hotspot, so genetic interpretation involves a specialist laboratory.
det.treatment: There is no specific treatment. Regular monitoring of FVC, supine drop and nocturnal gas exchange allows early noninvasive ventilation, which prolongs survival and improves symptoms. Management also includes physiotherapy, cough assistance, vaccination against pneumococcus and influenza, nutrition review and genetic counselling. Cardiac evaluation is performed at baseline. Avoid sedatives that suppress ventilation.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive limb disease, but respiratory failure largely determines morbidity; outcomes are better when ventilatory support starts early.
pearls: Think of HMERF in an adult with myopathy plus hypercapnia and a dominant family history.
Check supine FVC and nocturnal gas exchange, not only sitting spirometry.
Acid maltase deficiency must be excluded because it has enzyme therapy.
det.thd: HMERF เป็นโรค myofibrillar myopathy จากยีน TTN ถ่ายทอด autosomal dominant ผู้ใหญ่มีอ่อนแรงส่วนต้นและส่วนปลายร่วมกับกล้ามเนื้อหายใจล้มเหลวเร็ว ควรตรวจ FVC ท่านอน ออกซิเมทรีและแก๊สกลางคืน MRI กล้ามเนื้อพบรูปแบบเฉพาะ ตัดชิ้นเนื้อพบ cytoplasmic bodies การรักษาคือเริ่ม NIV เร็ว กายภาพบำบัด และให้คำปรึกษาด้านพันธุกรรม

name: King-Denborough syndrome
formal: A rare congenital myopathy with dysmorphic features, short stature, skeletal anomalies and susceptibility to malignant hyperthermia, usually from RYR1 variants, with onset of hypotonia in infancy.
simple: A rare inherited muscle disease with unusual facial features and short stature in which anaesthesia can trigger dangerous overheating.
ab: myopathy with dysmorphism and malignant hyperthermia
ซินโดรมคิง-เดนโบโรห์
th: กลุ่มอาการหายากของโรคกล้ามเนื้อแต่กำเนิดที่มีใบหน้าลักษณะเฉพาะ ตัวเตี้ย กระดูกผิดรูป และเสี่ยงต่อภาวะ malignant hyperthermia เมื่อได้รับยาสลบ ส่วนใหญ่เกี่ยวข้องกับยีน RYR1
tempoNote: Hypotonia from infancy, then static or slowly progressive weakness; malignant hyperthermia risk is lifelong
feat: Dysmorphic face with ptosis, down-slanting palpebral fissures, low-set ears and micrognathia
Short stature, pectus deformity, scoliosis and cryptorchidism
Mild proximal myopathy with delayed motor milestones
Malignant hyperthermia reaction to volatile anaesthetics or succinylcholine
CK normal or slightly raised, and biopsy with nonspecific myopathic features
inv: RYR1 sequencing; consider a broader congenital myopathy panel
Muscle biopsy with nonspecific myopathic changes, sometimes cores or type 1 predominance
CK, baseline ECG, and skeletal survey for scoliosis
In-vitro contracture testing only when genetics is inconclusive and expertise is available

case.who: 6-year-old boy scheduled for strabismus surgery in a university hospital in Bangkok
case.story: He has delayed walking, short stature and mild ptosis; during a previous dental anaesthetic he developed a fever and rigid muscles that settled with cooling.
case.exam: Down-slanting eyes, micrognathia, pectus excavatum, mild proximal weakness, short stature below the 3rd percentile.
case.tests: CK 260 U/L; RYR1 heterozygous pathogenic variant; biopsy shows a mild myopathy with type 1 predominance.
case.q: What precautions are essential before anaesthesia?
case.a: Treat as malignant hyperthermia susceptible: use a trigger-free total intravenous technique, prepare dantrolene, clean the machine, and monitor temperature and end-tidal carbon dioxide.

det.patho: King-Denborough syndrome is considered a severe RYR1 or related excitation-contraction coupling disorder in which dysregulated calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum causes myopathy and malignant hyperthermia susceptibility. The syndromic features are thought to reflect early developmental effects of altered calcium signalling. The genetic basis was historically unclear, and many cases are now explained by RYR1 variants, though some remain unsolved.
det.clinical: Infants present with hypotonia, mild proximal weakness and characteristic facial and skeletal anomalies such as ptosis, micrognathia, scoliosis and cryptorchidism. Motor development is delayed but many children walk. The most important clinical event is a malignant hyperthermia crisis triggered by anaesthesia, with rigidity, tachycardia, hypercarbia, rhabdomyolysis and fever.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis rests on three features occurring together (congenital myopathy, dysmorphism and malignant hyperthermia susceptibility), supported by RYR1 testing. Biopsy shows nonspecific myopathy. Contracture testing is reserved for equivocal cases. All close relatives should be counselled and offered genetic testing.
det.treatment: Prevention is critical: avoid volatile anaesthetics and succinylcholine, use total intravenous anaesthesia, and ensure dantrolene is available. Provide a medical alert card and inform the surgical and anaesthetic teams. Supportive care includes physiotherapy, orthopaedic management for scoliosis and respiratory monitoring. Acute reactions are treated with immediate trigger withdrawal, dantrolene, cooling and supportive care.
det.prognosis: Generally good if malignant hyperthermia is prevented; the myopathy is mild and non-progressive for most.
pearls: Dysmorphism plus congenital myopathy plus anaesthetic fever suggests KDS.
Use a trigger-free anaesthetic and keep dantrolene ready in every operating theatre.
Test relatives; susceptibility is usually autosomal dominant.

name: STAC3 disorder (Native American myopathy)
formal: An autosomal recessive congenital myopathy caused by STAC3 variants, first described in Lumbee people of North Carolina, with congenital weakness, cleft palate, ptosis, kyphoscoliosis, arthrogryposis-like contractures and malignant hyperthermia susceptibility.
simple: A rare inherited muscle disease starting at birth, linked with cleft palate, droopy eyelids, short stature and a risk of overheating after anaesthesia.

case.who: 9-year-old girl evaluated for scoliosis surgery in a tertiary hospital, with consanguineous parents
case.story: She was floppy at birth, had a cleft palate repaired at one year, and has droopy eyelids; an uncle died after an anaesthetic fever.

case.tests: CK 150 U/L; exome shows homozygous STAC3 pathogenic variant; biopsy is mildly myopathic.

det.patho: STAC3 encodes an adaptor protein of the skeletal muscle excitation-contraction coupling machinery that stabilises the dihydropyridine receptor and ryanodine receptor interaction. Variants impair calcium release, causing weakness and a predisposition to uncontrolled calcium release when exposed to triggers, which explains malignant hyperthermia susceptibility. The founder variant p.Trp284Ser is common in the Lumbee population, but other variants have been described worldwide.
det.clinical: Children are hypotonic at birth with ptosis, facial weakness, cleft palate and short stature. Contractures, kyphoscoliosis and pectus anomalies are frequent. Weakness often improves or stabilises in childhood. The most dangerous complication is malignant hyperthermia during anaesthesia, which can be fatal.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is made by recognising the pattern of congenital myopathy with cleft palate and skeletal anomalies in a child of consanguineous or founder-population parents, and confirmed by STAC3 sequencing. Biopsy is nonspecific. It is crucial to alert the surgical and anaesthetic teams once the condition is first considered, even before genetic confirmation.
det.treatment: Management includes anaesthetic precautions, physiotherapy, orthopaedic care for scoliosis and contractures, speech and feeding support after cleft repair, and respiratory monitoring. Dantrolene must be available for acute reactions. Genetic counselling is offered for recurrence risk.
det.prognosis: Weakness is stable or improves, and outcome is good provided malignant hyperthermia is avoided.
pearls: Cleft palate plus ptosis plus congenital myopathy suggests STAC3.
Treat as malignant hyperthermia susceptible before genetic confirmation.
Look for STAC3 variants in non-Native American patients too.

name: Oculopharyngodistal myopathy (OPDM)
formal: A rare adult-onset myopathy with ptosis, ophthalmoparesis, bulbar weakness and distal limb weakness with rimmed vacuoles, caused by CGG repeat expansions in genes such as LRP12, GIPC1, NOTCH2NLC and RILPL1.

case.who: 52-year-old woman farmer from Nan with progressive ptosis and swallowing difficulty
case.story: Over 8 years her eyelids have drooped and she coughs with meals; recently her feet drag and she cannot grip tools. Her sister has similar symptoms.
case.exam: Bilateral ptosis, limited upgaze and abduction, facial weakness, weak finger extension and foot dorsiflexion.
case.tests: CK 380 U/L; EMG myopathic; biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles; repeat-primed PCR confirms CGG expansion in LRP12.
case.q: How does this differ from oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy and why does repeat testing matter?
case.a: OPDM adds early distal weakness and involves different CGG repeat genes; standard exome misses repeat expansions so targeted repeat analysis is needed.

det.patho: OPDM is a repeat expansion disease, with CGG repeats in the 5' untranslated regions or noncoding regions of several genes (LRP12, GIPC1, NOTCH2NLC, RILPL1). RNA from the expanded repeats forms toxic RNA foci and polyglycine-containing proteins, which form intranuclear inclusions that disrupt nuclear function. Some repeat disorders, particularly NOTCH2NLC, overlap with neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease, which explains the leukoencephalopathy in some patients.
det.clinical: Ptosis and limited eye movements begin first, followed by dysphagia, dysarthria and facial weakness. Distal limb weakness appears later or concurrently, with foot drop and finger extensor weakness. Progression is slow, but aspiration and respiratory involvement can occur late. Heterogeneity is considerable: genotype influences age at onset and associated features.
det.diagnosis: Suspect in adults with combined ocular, bulbar and distal weakness. Muscle biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles and intranuclear inclusions, and imaging helps define pattern. The definitive diagnosis requires repeat expansion detection, because conventional sequencing misses these variants. Testing should address the known genes in sequence, and family members can be counselled.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy exists. Management is supportive: swallowing therapy, nutritional support or gastrostomy for severe dysphagia, ptosis surgery or crutch glasses, ankle-foot orthoses and physiotherapy, and respiratory surveillance. Genetic counselling is offered because inheritance is dominant for most genes.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; dysphagia and aspiration are the main causes of morbidity.
pearls: Ptosis, dysphagia and distal weakness together raise OPDM above OPMD.
Order repeat-expansion testing; standard sequencing misses CGG repeats.
Rimmed vacuoles on biopsy are common to several of these myopathies.

det.patho: The oculomotor fascicles run forward from the nucleus through the tegmentum and leave the midbrain on the medial side of the cerebral peduncle, so one small ventral lesion catches both. The territory is fed by paramedian and peduncular perforators arising from P1 and the basilar apex, which are end-arteries vulnerable to lipohyalinosis, branch atheroma and emboli. Because the corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres in the peduncle have not yet crossed, the weakness is contralateral.
det.clinical: Onset is typically abrupt with diplopia or a closed eye and weakness of the opposite limbs. Fascicular palsies can be complete or partial, and the pupil is involved more often than in microvascular peripheral palsies. Dysarthria and central facial weakness are common because corticobulbar fibres travel in the same peduncle. Extension of the infarct into the thalamus, red nucleus or the other side changes the picture, so serial examination is useful. Slowly evolving Weber syndrome should prompt a search for a tumour or aneurysm.
det.diagnosis: MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging is the key test; a lesion of only a few millimetres may be seen solely on thin axial or coronal slices. Vessel imaging assesses P1, the basilar tip and possible aneurysm, and determines whether the mechanism is branch atheromatous disease, embolism or small vessel disease. A pupil-involving third nerve palsy without hemiparesis is a different problem that needs urgent angiography for aneurysm.
det.treatment: Manage as acute ischaemic stroke: intravenous thrombolysis if within the time window and eligible, and thrombectomy only if a large vessel such as the basilar artery is occluded. Secondary prevention follows the mechanism — antiplatelet therapy (short-term dual therapy for minor stroke), high-intensity statin, blood pressure control, or anticoagulation for cardioembolism. Eye patching or prisms help diplopia, and physiotherapy addresses the hemiparesis.
det.prognosis: Hemiparesis usually improves considerably; ptosis and ophthalmoparesis recover more slowly and may leave residual diplopia.
pearls: Third nerve palsy on one side plus hemiparesis on the other = ventral midbrain (Weber) until proven otherwise.
Add contralateral tremor or chorea and think Benedikt; add contralateral ataxia without weakness and think Claude.
Thin-slice DWI through the midbrain is needed; small perforator infarcts are easily missed on routine slices.

det.patho: The superior cerebellar peduncle carries output from the dentate nucleus; it crosses in the lower midbrain and then ascends past and through the red nucleus to the thalamus. A paramedian tegmental lesion above the decussation therefore damages fibres that began in the opposite cerebellar hemisphere, giving ataxia on the side opposite the lesion and opposite the third nerve palsy. The region is supplied by paramedian mesencephalic perforators from P1 and the basilar apex, also called thalamoperforating or interpeduncular branches.
det.clinical: Patients present with sudden diplopia, ptosis and clumsiness of the opposite limbs. Limb ataxia and intention tremor dominate; strength is preserved or only slightly reduced. Some patients have elements of vertical gaze palsy when the lesion extends dorsally, and overlap with Benedikt and Nothnagel syndromes is common because the territories abut. Pure fascicular oculomotor palsies may show unusual patterns, such as isolated inferior division weakness.
det.diagnosis: Diffusion MRI confirms a small paramedian tegmental infarct at the level of the red nucleus; haemorrhage, demyelination and tumour are other causes. Vascular imaging looks for basilar tip disease, and cardioembolic sources are common when the infarct is in a perforator from the top of the basilar. A careful bedside examination of ocular motility and limb coordination places the lesion before imaging.
det.treatment: Acute ischaemic stroke treatment applies, including thrombolysis when eligible. Secondary prevention depends on mechanism — anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation, antiplatelets and statin for atherosclerotic or small vessel disease. Rehabilitation focuses on coordination and gait; prisms or occlusion manage diplopia.
det.prognosis: Most patients improve over months; residual ataxic tremor and diplopia can persist.
pearls: A midbrain lesion rostral to where the superior cerebellar peduncle crosses produces ataxia on the opposite side.
Weber = weakness, Benedikt = involuntary movements, Claude = clumsiness (ataxia).
Pupil-involving third nerve palsy can be central; it is not always an aneurysm.

det.patho: The tectum lies dorsal to the aqueduct, close to the oculomotor nuclear complex and the superior cerebellar peduncles as they cross and ascend. A mass pushing down on the quadrigeminal plate, or an infarct supplied by the long circumferential branches of the PCA and SCA, can reach both structures, and midline lesions may affect both oculomotor complexes at once. Pineal region tumours (germinoma, other germ cell tumours, pineal parenchymal tumours) and tectal gliomas are the classic causes; vascular cases are less common.
det.clinical: Ophthalmoparesis is usually incomplete and may be bilateral; nuclear lesions can produce bilateral ptosis because the central caudal nucleus is a single midline structure. Ataxia mainly affects gait, and limb ataxia may be on either side. Dorsal midbrain signs (upgaze palsy, convergence–retraction nystagmus, pseudo-Argyll Robertson pupils, Collier sign) frequently accompany it. Tumours also cause hydrocephalus with headache and papilloedema, and germ cell tumours may produce diabetes insipidus or precocious puberty.
det.diagnosis: Contrast MRI is essential to separate tumour from infarct and to assess hydrocephalus. For pineal region masses, serum and CSF AFP and beta-hCG help classify germ cell tumours, and CSF cytology looks for seeding; biopsy is often needed. In vascular cases, DWI shows the infarct and vessel imaging assesses the distal basilar and proximal PCA. Exclude Miller Fisher syndrome, Wernicke encephalopathy and myasthenia when imaging is normal.
det.treatment: Treatment targets the cause: CSF diversion (endoscopic third ventriculostomy) for obstructive hydrocephalus, histology-directed therapy for tumours (germinomas are highly radiosensitive and chemosensitive), and standard acute stroke care and secondary prevention for infarcts. Supportive care includes prisms for diplopia and gait rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: Depends on the cause; germinoma has an excellent cure rate, while infarcts typically improve partially.
pearls: Ophthalmoplegia plus ataxia plus upgaze palsy in a young man: image the pineal region.
Midline oculomotor nuclear lesions give bilateral ptosis because the levator subnucleus is unpaired.
Check AFP and beta-hCG in serum and CSF before operating on a pineal region mass.
det.thd: Nothnagel syndrome คือรอยโรคที่ dorsal midbrain ซึ่งทำให้มี CN III palsy ข้างเดียวหรือสองข้างร่วมกับ ataxia จาก superior cerebellar peduncle มักมีอาการแบบ Parinaud ร่วมด้วย สาเหตุคลาสสิกคือเนื้องอกบริเวณ pineal หรือ tectum และพบจาก infarct ของ long circumferential branch ของ PCA ได้ ตรวจ MRI with contrast และ tumour marker แล้วรักษาตามสาเหตุ

name: Millard–Gubler syndrome
formal: A ventral caudal pontine syndrome in which a lesion of the basis pontis catches the fascicles of the facial (and often abducens) nerve together with the corticospinal tract, producing ipsilateral lower motor neuron facial palsy with or without lateral rectus weakness and contralateral hemiplegia.
simple: A stroke in the lower front part of the pons that weakens the face on one side, plus the arm and leg of the other side.
ab: กลุ่มอาการ Millard-Gubler
th: รอยโรคที่ basis pontis ส่วนล่าง ทำลาย fascicle ของ CN VII (และมักรวม CN VI) ร่วมกับ corticospinal tract ผู้ป่วยมีใบหน้าอ่อนแรงแบบ LMN และอาจกลอกตาออกนอกไม่ได้ข้างเดียวกับรอยโรค ร่วมกับอ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกด้านตรงข้าม มักเกิดจากอุดตันของ paramedian perforator ของ basilar
tempoNote: Sudden with infarction or haemorrhage; gradual with pontine tumours or demyelination
feat: Ipsilateral lower motor neuron facial weakness involving forehead and lower face
Ipsilateral abduction failure when the abducens fascicle is involved, with horizontal diplopia
Contralateral hemiparesis sparing the face (face is weak on the lesion side instead)
Conjugate horizontal gaze is preserved, unlike Foville syndrome
Usually a basilar paramedian perforator infarct; warning of possible evolving basilar disease
inv: MRI brain with DWI including thin axial slices through the caudal pons
CTA or MRA of the basilar artery for branch atheroma or stenosis
Standard stroke mechanism work-up

case.who: 70-year-old retired farmer from Roi Et with hypertension and dyslipidaemia
case.story: He noticed his right eye would not close and his left leg dragged; his wife saw his mouth drooping to the right side.
case.exam: Right complete LMN facial palsy, right abduction deficit with horizontal diplopia on right gaze, left hemiparesis 3/5 with brisk reflexes; horizontal saccades to the right otherwise intact in the left eye.
case.tests: DWI: right paramedian ventral caudal pontine infarct; CTA shows moderate mid-basilar stenosis.
case.q: Why is this not Bell palsy?
case.a: The facial palsy is accompanied by an abducens palsy and contralateral hemiparesis — a crossed brainstem (Millard–Gubler) syndrome from a basilar perforator infarct.

det.patho: In the caudal pons the facial and abducens fascicles pass ventrally through the basis pontis, beside the descending corticospinal fibres. Paramedian perforators from the basilar artery supply this wedge, so occlusion of one perforator, often from branch atheromatous disease at the basilar wall, injures all three. The corticospinal fibres have not yet crossed, so the limb weakness is contralateral while the cranial nerve deficits are ipsilateral.
det.clinical: The classic picture is a crossed palsy: the face on one side and the limbs on the other. The original descriptions varied, and some patients have only the facial fascicle involved, while others have abducens and facial deficits. Dysarthria and ataxic features can occur. A stuttering or progressive course over hours suggests basilar branch disease and carries a risk of evolution to locked-in syndrome.
det.diagnosis: Diffusion MRI shows a paramedian ventral pontine infarct, often extending to the basal surface (a sign of branch atheromatous disease). Vessel imaging and, where available, high-resolution vessel wall MRI assess the basilar artery. Mimics include pontine haemorrhage, demyelination, pontine glioma and metastasis.
det.treatment: Standard acute ischaemic stroke treatment, with attention to fluctuating deficits; endovascular therapy is reserved for basilar occlusion. Secondary prevention with antiplatelet therapy (short-course dual antiplatelets when suitable), high-intensity statin and blood pressure control. Eye care with lubricants and taping for lagophthalmos prevents exposure keratopathy.
det.prognosis: Limb weakness often improves; facial palsy recovers variably and may leave synkinesis.
pearls: LMN facial palsy plus contralateral hemiparesis localises to the pons, not to the hemisphere.
Isolated abduction weakness = fascicle or nerve; horizontal gaze palsy = nucleus or PPRF (Foville).
Progressive pontine branch infarcts can become locked-in syndrome — monitor closely.
det.thd: Millard–Gubler syndrome เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ basis pontis ส่วนล่าง ทำลาย fascicle ของ CN VII และ CN VI กับ corticospinal tract ผู้ป่วยมีใบหน้าอ่อนแรงแบบ LMN และกลอกตาออกนอกไม่ได้ข้างเดียวกับรอยโรค ร่วมกับอ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกด้านตรงข้าม แยกจาก Bell palsy ได้เพราะมีอาการแขนขาร่วม สาเหตุส่วนใหญ่คือ basilar perforator infarct ควรเฝ้าระวังการลุกลาม

Weber and Benedikt syndromes are midbrain lesions with third nerve involvement, and Wallenberg is lateral medullary.

name: Foville syndrome
formal: A dorsal caudal pontine tegmental syndrome in which a lesion of the abducens nucleus or paramedian pontine reticular formation and the facial fascicle produces ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy and lower motor neuron facial palsy, often with contralateral hemiparesis when the lesion extends ventrally.
simple: A stroke in the back of the lower pons that stops both eyes looking to one side and weakens that side of the face.
ab: facial colliculus syndrome with gaze palsy
กลุ่มอาการ Foville
th: รอยโรคที่ dorsal pontine tegmentum ส่วนล่าง ทำลาย abducens nucleus หรือ PPRF และ fascicle ของ CN VII ทำให้ตาทั้งสองข้างมองไปด้านรอยโรคไม่ได้ (horizontal gaze palsy) และใบหน้าอ่อนแรงแบบ LMN ข้างเดียวกัน ถ้ารอยโรคลามลงด้านหน้าจะมีอ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกด้านตรงข้าม อาจมี Horner และ INO ร่วม

feat: Ipsilateral conjugate horizontal gaze palsy (neither eye moves past midline toward the lesion), vertical gaze spared
Ipsilateral LMN facial palsy from the facial fascicle looping around the abducens nucleus
Contralateral hemiparesis when the lesion reaches the basis pontis
Possible ipsilateral Horner syndrome, facial numbness, hearing loss or INO (one-and-a-half pattern)
Causes: basilar perforator or long circumferential branch infarct, pontine haemorrhage, MS, tumour
inv: MRI brain with DWI and FLAIR, with attention to the dorsal pons beside the fourth ventricular floor
Vessel imaging of the basilar artery
Contrast MRI and CSF if demyelination or tumour is suspected in a young patient

case.who: 52-year-old female market vendor from Chiang Rai with uncontrolled hypertension
case.story: She developed a sudden headache, could not look to the left, and her left face felt heavy and drooped.
case.exam: Neither eye moves to the left beyond midline, including with doll's eye manoeuvre; right eye cannot adduct on right gaze either; left LMN facial palsy; right hemiparesis 4/5; left miosis and mild ptosis.
case.tests: CT shows a small left dorsal pontine haemorrhage; BP 210/120 mmHg.
case.q: Which two horizontal-gaze structures are affected, and what is the syndrome?
case.a: The left abducens nucleus/PPRF (left gaze palsy) and left MLF (left INO), plus the facial fascicle — Foville syndrome with a one-and-a-half pattern from a hypertensive pontine haemorrhage.

det.patho: The abducens nucleus contains both motor neurons for the ipsilateral lateral rectus and interneurons that cross to the opposite MLF to drive the medial rectus; damage to the nucleus or PPRF therefore abolishes conjugate gaze to that side. Facial nerve fibres wrap around the abducens nucleus (the facial colliculus) before exiting, so a dorsal lesion adds a peripheral-type facial palsy. Ventral extension reaches the corticospinal tract, and lateral extension may involve the descending sympathetic fibres, trigeminal nucleus or auditory pathways.
det.clinical: The patient cannot look toward the lesion with either eye, and vestibulo-ocular reflexes do not overcome a nuclear lesion (they may overcome a pure PPRF lesion). The face is weak on the same side, including forehead. Hemiparesis, if present, is contralateral. Associated INO creates the one-and-a-half syndrome; when facial palsy is added the combination is sometimes called eight-and-a-half syndrome.
det.diagnosis: MRI with DWI and FLAIR identifies infarct or demyelination in the dorsal pons; CT is good for haemorrhage. Testing the vestibulo-ocular reflex helps separate nuclear (fixed) from supranuclear or PPRF palsies. Young patients without vascular risk need evaluation for MS, cavernoma or neoplasm.
det.treatment: Acute stroke care according to the lesion type: thrombolysis for eligible infarcts, blood pressure lowering and reversal of anticoagulation for haemorrhage. Secondary prevention and rehabilitation follow. Eye protection for the facial palsy; head turning strategies and prisms are of limited help for gaze palsy.
det.prognosis: Gaze palsy often improves partially over months; small haemorrhages and lacunes generally have a good functional outcome.
pearls: Foville = gaze palsy; Millard–Gubler = lateral rectus palsy — test both eyes looking to the affected side.
Abducens nucleus lesion causes conjugate gaze palsy, not isolated abduction weakness.
Gaze palsy plus INO plus facial palsy on one side is the eight-and-a-half syndrome.
det.thd: Foville syndrome เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ dorsal pons ส่วนล่าง ทำลาย abducens nucleus/PPRF และ facial fascicle ผู้ป่วยมีตาทั้งสองข้างมองไปด้านรอยโรคไม่ได้ ร่วมกับใบหน้าอ่อนแรงแบบ LMN ข้างเดียวกัน อาจมีอ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกด้านตรงข้าม Horner หรือ INO ร่วม แยกจาก Millard–Gubler ที่มีเพียงกล้ามเนื้อ lateral rectus อ่อนแรง สาเหตุคือ infarct เลือดออก หรือ MS

name: Marie-Foix syndrome (lateral pontine syndrome)
formal: A lateral caudal pontine syndrome from occlusion of long circumferential basilar branches, combining ipsilateral limb ataxia (middle cerebellar peduncle) with contralateral hemiparesis and contralateral pain–temperature loss, sometimes with ipsilateral facial weakness or numbness.
simple: A stroke on the side of the pons that makes one arm clumsy, while the other half of the body is weak and loses pain sensation.
ab: กลุ่มอาการ Marie-Foix
th: รอยโรคที่ด้านข้างของ pons ส่วนล่าง จากการอุดตันของ long circumferential branch ของ basilar ทำให้ ataxia ของแขนขาข้างเดียวกับรอยโรค (middle cerebellar peduncle) ร่วมกับอ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกและการรับรู้ปวด/อุณหภูมิลดลงด้านตรงข้าม อาจมีใบหน้าชาหรืออ่อนแรงข้างเดียวกัน

feat: Ipsilateral limb ataxia from the middle cerebellar peduncle
Contralateral hemiparesis from corticospinal involvement
Contralateral loss of pain and temperature from the spinothalamic tract
Variable ipsilateral facial weakness, facial numbness or Horner syndrome
Hearing is spared, which helps separate it from AICA infarction
inv: MRI DWI covering the pons together with the middle cerebellar peduncle
CTA or MRA of the basilar artery and AICA
