case.who: 66-year-old male rice mill owner from Kamphaeng Phet with diabetes
case.story: He suddenly found his right hand would not hold a spoon steadily and his left leg felt weak.
case.exam: Right finger–nose dysmetria, mild right LMN facial weakness, left hemiparesis 4/5, reduced pinprick and cold over the left arm, trunk and leg; hearing normal.
case.tests: DWI: right lateral caudal pontine infarct extending into the middle cerebellar peduncle; basilar wall plaque on CTA.
case.q: Which pontine territory is involved, and which finding argues against AICA syndrome?
case.a: The lateral pons supplied by long circumferential basilar branches (Marie-Foix syndrome); normal hearing argues against AICA/labyrinthine artery involvement.

det.patho: Long circumferential branches of the basilar artery wrap around the pons to supply its lateral part, including the middle cerebellar peduncle, the spinothalamic tract and, when deep enough, the corticospinal tract. Branch atheromatous disease or emboli occluding one of these vessels produce the syndrome. The cerebellar fibres here have not crossed in a way that changes sides relative to the cerebellum they reach, so ataxia is ipsilateral, while the long tracts give contralateral signs.
det.clinical: The defining combination is ataxia on one side and weakness and spinothalamic sensory loss on the other. The original description emphasised ipsilateral ataxia, contralateral hemiparesis and contralateral hemi-hypoalgesia, with occasional facial involvement. Vertigo is mild or absent, and the absence of hearing loss is a useful bedside discriminator from AICA occlusion. Severity ranges from a minor deficit to a disabling stroke.
det.diagnosis: DWI confirms the infarct in the lateral pons and middle cerebellar peduncle. Vessel imaging assesses the basilar artery and AICA; involvement of the cerebellum or labyrinth suggests AICA rather than a pontine branch. Audiometry is worth doing if hearing is in doubt.
det.treatment: Acute ischaemic stroke protocols, followed by mechanism-based secondary prevention (antiplatelets, statin, blood pressure and diabetes control, anticoagulation if cardioembolic). Rehabilitation addresses both ataxia and weakness.
det.prognosis: Generally favourable for small infarcts; residual ataxia is the most common lasting deficit.
pearls: Ataxia on one side, weakness on the other = lateral pons (Marie-Foix).
Check hearing: deafness points to AICA/labyrinthine artery territory.
Ataxic hemiparesis from a lacune has ataxia and weakness on the same side.
det.thd: Marie-Foix syndrome คือ lateral pontine syndrome จากการอุดตันของ long circumferential branch ของ basilar ผู้ป่วยมี ataxia ข้างเดียวกับรอยโรค ร่วมกับอ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกและการรับรู้ปวด/อุณหภูมิลดลงด้านตรงข้าม การได้ยินปกติช่วยแยกจาก AICA infarction วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI DWI และรักษาแบบ ischaemic stroke

case.who: 59-year-old male truck driver from Nakhon Ratchasima with diabetes and heavy smoking
case.story: Over two days he had brief spells of right ear buzzing and spinning; this morning he developed persistent vertigo, vomiting and could not hear on the right.
case.exam: Right sensorineural deafness, right LMN facial weakness, reduced right facial pinprick, right Horner syndrome, right limb ataxia, reduced pinprick over the left body; abnormal right head impulse test with direction-changing nystagmus.
case.tests: DWI: right lateral pontine and middle cerebellar peduncle infarct with small anterior inferior cerebellar infarcts; CTA shows severe distal basilar–AICA origin stenosis.
case.q: Why did the abnormal head impulse test not exclude stroke?
case.a: AICA supplies the labyrinth through the internal auditory artery, so labyrinthine ischaemia can make the head impulse abnormal; new hearing loss with vertigo is a stroke warning (HINTS-plus).

Chapter 27: Acute Vestibular Syndrome Following Anterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (AICA) Occlusion

det.patho: AICA usually arises from the lower basilar artery and runs toward the cerebellopontine angle, where it gives off the internal auditory artery to the cochlea and vestibule before supplying the flocculus, anterior inferior cerebellum, middle cerebellar peduncle and lateral pontine tegmentum. Occlusion is most often from basilar atherosclerosis at the AICA origin or branch disease, less often from embolism. Because the labyrinth is an end-organ with little collateral supply, audiovestibular loss can precede the brainstem infarct as a prodrome.
det.clinical: The core features are acute vestibular syndrome plus ipsilateral hearing loss, with facial palsy, facial numbness, Horner and limb ataxia on the same side and spinothalamic loss on the opposite side. Partial syndromes are common, and isolated sudden deafness with vertigo may be the only sign of impending AICA infarction. Conscious level is usually preserved unless swelling or basilar extension occurs.
det.diagnosis: MRI is the test of choice, but small infarcts can be DWI-negative in the first 48 hours, so a strong clinical picture warrants repeat imaging. HINTS-plus (adding a bedside hearing test) increases sensitivity, since the head impulse can be abnormal in labyrinthine infarction. Vascular imaging assesses the basilar artery and AICA origin; audiometry documents sensorineural loss.
det.treatment: Treat as acute ischaemic stroke, including thrombolysis when eligible; endovascular therapy is relevant when the basilar artery is occluded. Close monitoring for basilar progression and cerebellar oedema is advisable. Secondary prevention (antiplatelets, intensive statin, risk factor control) plus vestibular rehabilitation and hearing rehabilitation, including hearing aids or cochlear implant evaluation for persistent deafness.
det.prognosis: Brainstem and cerebellar signs often improve well, but hearing loss is frequently permanent.
pearls: Vertigo plus new unilateral hearing loss is AICA stroke until proven otherwise.
An abnormal head impulse does not exclude AICA infarction; add a hearing test to HINTS.
Facial palsy and deafness separate AICA from PICA (lateral medullary) infarction.

name: Medial medullary syndrome (Dejerine syndrome)
formal: Infarction of the paramedian medulla, usually from vertebral artery or anterior spinal artery branch disease, producing hemiparesis on the opposite side that spares the face, impaired vibration and proprioception on the opposite side, and hypoglossal palsy on the same side.
simple: A stroke in the middle of the lowest brainstem that weakens the opposite arm and leg, numbs them to vibration, and weakens one side of the tongue.

case.who: 71-year-old female former teacher from Lampang with hypertension and diabetes
case.story: Over a day her left arm and leg became progressively weak and her speech slurred; her face felt normal.
case.exam: Left hemiparesis 2/5 sparing the face, impaired left vibration and joint position sense, pinprick normal; tongue deviates to the right on protrusion with mild right-sided fasciculation.
case.tests: DWI: right medial medullary infarct; CTA: severe right intracranial vertebral artery stenosis.
case.q: Why is the face spared while the tongue deviates to the right?
case.a: The lesion is in the right medulla below the facial nucleus, injuring the right pyramid (left hemiparesis), medial lemniscus and right hypoglossal fascicle — medial medullary syndrome.

det.patho: The medial medulla holds the pyramid, the medial lemniscus and the exiting hypoglossal fascicles, supplied by paramedian branches from the intracranial vertebral artery and the anterior spinal artery. The usual cause is atherosclerosis of the vertebral artery occluding these branches; dissection and embolism are less common. The pyramids cross just below, so a lesion above the decussation gives contralateral weakness, while the hypoglossal deficit is ipsilateral.
det.clinical: Hemiparesis is the most frequent sign and the face is classically spared. Lemniscal sensory loss is common but may be missed if only pinprick is tested. The full triad with tongue weakness occurs in a minority, so many cases look like a pure motor stroke. Progressive worsening over the first days is typical. Bilateral lesions produce quadriplegia, anarthria and sometimes respiratory failure, mimicking locked-in syndrome or high cord lesions.
det.diagnosis: MRI DWI is required, often repeated because early scans may be negative; bilateral involvement produces a Y or heart-shaped lesion. Vessel imaging looks for intracranial vertebral stenosis, occlusion or dissection. The examination should include vibration, joint position and tongue testing whenever a pure motor stroke spares the face.
det.treatment: Acute ischaemic stroke treatment, with attention to early neurological deterioration. For intracranial vertebral atherosclerosis, short-term dual antiplatelet therapy, high-intensity statin and blood pressure control are standard; stenting is not first-line. Swallowing assessment and respiratory monitoring are important, especially in bilateral lesions.
det.prognosis: Unilateral cases usually recover partially; bilateral infarction carries high morbidity and mortality.
pearls: Hemiparesis sparing the face + lemniscal loss on the same side = medial medulla.
Tongue deviates toward the lesion; limbs are weak on the opposite side.
Heart-shaped DWI lesion in the upper medulla = bilateral medial medullary infarction.

case.who: 48-year-old male taxi driver from Bangkok with hypertension
case.story: His wife found him unrousable at 6 a.m.; he had gone to bed well. In the ED he opens his eyes only to pain.
case.exam: GCS 8, no lateralised limb weakness, pupils small and sluggish, absent vertical eye movements to doll's eye manoeuvre with preserved horizontal movements.
case.tests: CT brain and CTA normal including the basilar tip; glucose 6.2 mmol/L; MRI DWI 3 hours later shows symmetric bilateral paramedian thalamic and rostral midbrain restriction with a V-shaped midbrain lesion.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and why did CTA miss it?
case.a: Artery of Percheron infarction; the artery is a single small perforator from one P1 and is not resolved by CTA.

det.patho: The paramedian thalami are usually supplied by small perforators from each P1 segment. In a minority of people a single trunk, the artery of Percheron, arises from one P1 and splits to supply both paramedian thalami and sometimes the rostral midbrain. Occlusion, typically from cardioembolism or small vessel disease, therefore produces simultaneous bilateral infarcts. Damage to the intralaminar and dorsomedial nuclei disrupts arousal and memory circuits, and rostral midbrain involvement injures the riMLF and interstitial nucleus of Cajal.
det.clinical: Classic patterns are bilateral paramedian thalamic infarcts with or without the rostral midbrain, sometimes with the anterior thalamus. The presentation is abrupt decreased consciousness, often mistaken for intoxication, seizure or metabolic coma. As arousal improves, patients show vertical gaze palsy, amnesia, confusion, apathy and occasionally behavioural change or hyperphagia. Limb weakness is minimal unless the cerebral peduncles are involved.
det.diagnosis: Early CT and CTA are frequently normal; MRI DWI shows symmetrical paramedian thalamic lesions, and the V sign on axial FLAIR at the midbrain level is highly suggestive. The differential includes top-of-basilar occlusion, deep cerebral venous thrombosis, Wernicke encephalopathy, osmotic demyelination, primary CNS lymphoma, gliomatosis and flavivirus or other encephalitis. In comatose patients without a structural cause on CT, early MRI is the key step.
det.treatment: If recognised in the window, intravenous thrombolysis can be given for this ischaemic stroke; thrombectomy is not applicable because the artery is too small. Airway protection and supportive care are often needed. Secondary prevention follows the mechanism: anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation, antiplatelets and statin otherwise; PFO evaluation in young patients. Cognitive rehabilitation and, for persistent apathy, dopaminergic agents may be tried.
det.prognosis: Consciousness usually recovers, but persistent amnesia, executive dysfunction and gaze palsy are common, especially when the midbrain is involved.
pearls: Sudden unexplained coma with normal CT and CTA: think artery of Percheron and get an MRI.
V sign on FLAIR along the interpeduncular fossa = midbrain involvement in AOP infarction.
Coma + vertical gaze palsy + no hemiparesis localises to the bilateral paramedian thalamus–rostral midbrain.

det.patho: The SCA originates close to the basilar apex, occasionally from the PCA, and supplies the superior surface of the cerebellum, the superior vermis, the dentate nucleus and the rostral lateral pontine tegmentum and superior cerebellar peduncle. Its proximal course makes it a common destination for emboli travelling up the basilar artery, so cardioembolism is the leading cause. Proximal occlusions produce brainstem plus cerebellar signs; distal branch occlusions give pure cerebellar infarcts. Small infarcts in the border zones between SCA, AICA and PICA usually reflect hypoperfusion or showers of microemboli.
det.clinical: Ataxia of limbs and gait with dysarthria is the commonest presentation, while vertigo is usually less dramatic than in PICA infarction. A complete SCA syndrome includes ipsilateral Horner syndrome, ipsilateral ataxia, contralateral spinothalamic loss and contralateral fourth nerve palsy. Associated top-of-basilar infarcts may add visual field loss, confusion or vertical gaze palsy. Large infarcts can swell and compress the fourth ventricle.
det.diagnosis: MRI confirms the territory and reveals additional posterior circulation infarcts that support embolism. CT can miss cerebellar ischaemia because of bone artefact. Vascular imaging assesses the basilar artery and vertebral arteries; cardiac monitoring and echocardiography look for an embolic source. For multiple small cerebellar border-zone infarcts, search for vertebrobasilar stenosis, hypotension, hypercoagulable states and vasculitis.
det.treatment: Standard acute ischaemic stroke treatment; basilar occlusion is a thrombectomy target. Monitor for oedema and hydrocephalus in large infarcts, with neurosurgical review for ventricular drainage or suboccipital decompression if consciousness falls. Secondary prevention is mechanism-specific — usually anticoagulation (DOAC) for atrial fibrillation, otherwise antiplatelets and statin.
det.prognosis: Usually good functional recovery for isolated SCA infarcts; outcome worsens with associated brainstem or bilateral involvement.
pearls: Dysarthria and limb ataxia with little vertigo point to the SCA territory; severe vertigo points to PICA.
SCA infarcts are often embolic — look for other top-of-basilar lesions and atrial fibrillation.
Multiple tiny cerebellar border-zone infarcts suggest haemodynamic failure or artery-to-artery microemboli.

det.patho: Head rotation occurs mainly at the atlantoaxial joint, where the vertebral artery loops between C1 and C2; in some people normal-range rotation kinks or stretches the artery contralateral to the turn. Subaxial osteophytes, disc herniation, fibrous bands or anomalous transverse foramina can compress the artery on the same or opposite side. Symptoms appear only when the compressed vessel is the dominant supply because the other vertebral artery is hypoplastic, stenosed or ends in PICA. Repeated compression can damage the intima and cause thrombus formation and embolic infarcts.
det.clinical: The typical patient describes stereotyped attacks of dizziness, visual dimming, tinnitus or syncope reproducibly triggered by turning the head to one side, resolving within seconds of returning to neutral. Some present only after a cerebellar or brainstem infarct. Elderly patients with cervical spondylosis and younger people with craniovertebral anomalies or ligamentous laxity are at risk. The classic name refers to archers turning their head to aim.
det.diagnosis: The key is to reproduce flow interruption with the head turned: duplex or transcranial Doppler shows loss of flow, and dynamic angiography (catheter or CT) demonstrates the site of compression and the collateral pattern. CT of the spine identifies the offending osteophyte or bony anomaly. MRI detects silent infarcts. Exclude BPPV, orthostatic hypotension, cardiac arrhythmia and carotid sinus hypersensitivity.
det.treatment: Initial management includes avoiding the provoking rotation, a cervical collar, and antiplatelet therapy, particularly if infarcts or intimal injury are present. Definitive treatment is surgical: decompression of the vertebral artery (removing an osteophyte or band) or C1–C2 fusion for atlantoaxial compression, which removes rotation at that level. Endovascular stenting or occlusion is reserved for selected patients. Postoperative dynamic imaging confirms patency.
det.prognosis: Surgical decompression or fusion relieves symptoms in most patients; untreated cases risk recurrent posterior circulation infarcts.
pearls: Reproducible vertigo or syncope on turning the head with normal neutral exam: think rotational vertebral artery occlusion.
Atlantoaxial compression is contralateral to the rotation; subaxial osteophyte compression is usually ipsilateral.
Dynamic imaging is essential — static CTA in neutral position is often normal.

case.who: 57-year-old male bus driver from Ratchaburi with hypertension and smoking
case.story: He had sudden left arm weakness together with double vision and unsteadiness.
case.exam: Left hemiparesis 4/5, right gaze-evoked nystagmus, right limb ataxia.
case.tests: DWI: right MCA cortical infarcts plus right cerebellar and pontine infarcts; CTA shows 70% right ICA origin stenosis with irregular plaque and a large right persistent trigeminal artery filling the basilar artery, with hypoplastic vertebral arteries.
case.q: How can one carotid plaque explain both anterior and posterior circulation infarcts?
case.a: Emboli from the right ICA plaque reach the basilar territory through the persistent trigeminal artery; urgent carotid revascularisation is indicated.

det.patho: In the 4–5 mm embryo, transient carotid–basilar anastomoses (trigeminal, otic, hypoglossal and proatlantal arteries) supply the developing hindbrain before the vertebral arteries and posterior communicating arteries mature; they normally regress within a few weeks. The trigeminal artery is the last to regress and the most likely to persist. Saltzman type I supplies the distal basilar territory with absent or small posterior communicating arteries; type II fills the SCAs while the PCAs come from the carotid via PComm; variants feed a cerebellar artery directly. Persistent hypoglossal and proatlantal arteries are the next most common types.
det.clinical: Most people never know they have it. Clinical relevance includes posterior circulation ischaemia from carotid sources, aneurysm formation at the anastomosis or elsewhere, compression of the trigeminal or ocular motor nerves, and direct carotid–cavernous fistula. During carotid endarterectomy, stenting, transsphenoidal surgery or carotid balloon occlusion, the anastomosis can transmit emboli or alter collateral flow to the brainstem.
det.diagnosis: Recognised on CTA, MRA (the sagittal tau sign) or angiography. When a stroke spans carotid and vertebrobasilar territories, look specifically for a carotid–basilar anastomosis before assuming a cardiac source. Angiography clarifies the Saltzman type, coexisting aneurysms and the role of the vessel in basilar supply.
det.treatment: No treatment is needed for incidental variants. When symptomatic, treat the associated condition — carotid revascularisation for a stenosis feeding the basilar through the anastomosis, endovascular treatment for aneurysms or fistulas, microvascular decompression for neuralgia. Procedure planning must account for the brainstem supply through the anastomosis.
det.prognosis: Benign as an isolated variant; outcome depends on the associated aneurysm, fistula or stroke.
pearls: Simultaneous carotid and basilar infarcts: look for a persistent trigeminal artery before blaming the heart.
Sagittal MRA 'tau sign' marks a persistent trigeminal artery.
Vertebral arteries are often hypoplastic, so the carotid may be the main basilar supply — critical before carotid occlusion or surgery.

name: Fetal-type posterior cerebral artery (fetal PCA)
formal: A common circle of Willis variant in which the posterior cerebral artery is supplied mainly or entirely from the internal carotid artery through an enlarged posterior communicating artery, with a hypoplastic or absent P1 segment, so that the occipital lobe belongs functionally to the anterior (carotid) circulation.
simple: A normal variation where the artery to the back of the brain is fed from the carotid artery in the neck instead of the basilar artery.
ab: persistent fetal circulation of the PCA
th: fetal-type PCA เป็นรูปแบบปกติของ circle of Willis ที่ PCA ได้เลือดหลักจาก ICA ผ่าน posterior communicating artery ที่ใหญ่ ขณะที่ P1 เล็กหรือไม่มี ทำให้สมองส่วน occipital อยู่ในระบบ carotid จึงเกิด occipital infarct จากโรคของ carotid หรือ emboli ใน ICA ได้
tempoNote: Lifelong anatomical variant; matters when stroke, aneurysm or a carotid procedure occurs
feat: Present unilaterally or bilaterally in a substantial minority of people (roughly 1 in 10 to 1 in 4 in imaging series)
Ipsilateral carotid stenosis or dissection can cause occipital (PCA territory) infarction with homonymous hemianopia
Concurrent MCA and PCA infarcts from a single carotid source may mimic multi-territory cardioembolism
Limits posterior-to-anterior collateral flow; associated with posterior communicating artery aneurysms
Relevant in thrombectomy planning and in carotid endarterectomy or balloon test occlusion
inv: CTA or MRA of the circle of Willis, noting P1 calibre and posterior communicating artery size
Carotid duplex or CTA for stenosis or dissection when a PCA infarct is ipsilateral to the variant
Standard stroke work-up for cardioembolism

case.who: 68-year-old male retired soldier from Lop Buri with diabetes
case.story: He bumped into door frames on his left side for a day and then noticed his left hand was clumsy.
case.exam: Left homonymous hemianopia, mild left arm drift and cortical sensory loss.
case.tests: DWI: right occipital and right posterior parietal infarcts; CTA shows a right fetal PCA (absent right P1, large PComm) and an 80% symptomatic right ICA origin stenosis; basilar artery normal.
case.q: How does the anatomy change the stroke mechanism and management?
case.a: The right PCA territory is fed by the right ICA through a fetal PCA, so the occipital infarct is a carotid stroke; urgent right carotid revascularisation is indicated.

det.patho: Early in development the PCA arises from the internal carotid artery via the posterior communicating artery; as the vertebrobasilar system matures the P1 segment normally enlarges and takes over. When P1 remains small or absent, the carotid continues to supply the PCA (fetal configuration). Partial forms with both P1 and PComm contributing also exist. With a full fetal PCA, the occipital lobe, much of the thalamus and posterior temporal lobe depend on the carotid circulation.
det.clinical: The variant itself is silent. Its importance is in stroke localisation: an occipital infarct with homonymous hemianopia may come from carotid disease on the same side, and combined MCA plus PCA infarcts may come from one carotid lesion. It also reduces the ability of the posterior circulation to compensate for carotid occlusion, and PComm aneurysms occur more often at enlarged fetal-type PComm origins.
det.diagnosis: Identification relies on CTA, MRA or catheter angiography; look for an absent or thread-like P1 and a PComm of similar calibre to the PCA. Whenever a PCA infarct is found, assessing the ipsilateral carotid and circle of Willis configuration avoids missing a carotid source.
det.treatment: No treatment for the variant. For stroke, follow the identified mechanism: carotid endarterectomy or stenting for symptomatic stenosis, antithrombotic therapy for dissection, anticoagulation for cardioembolism. Endovascular teams consider the fetal PCA when retrieving ICA terminus clots or performing balloon occlusion tests.
det.prognosis: Benign variant; outcomes depend on the associated vascular disease.
pearls: Occipital infarct + ipsilateral carotid stenosis + fetal PCA = carotid stroke, treat the carotid.
MCA and PCA infarcts on the same side can come from one carotid lesion when the PCA is fetal.
Check P1 calibre on every CTA of a posterior cerebral infarct.
det.thd: Fetal-type PCA เป็นรูปแบบปกติที่ PCA ได้เลือดจาก ICA ผ่าน PComm ขนาดใหญ่ โดย P1 เล็กหรือไม่มี ทำให้ occipital infarct อาจเกิดจากโรคของ carotid ข้างเดียวกัน และ infarct ทั้ง MCA กับ PCA ข้างเดียวกันอาจมาจาก carotid lesion เดียว ควรดู P1 และ PComm ใน CTA ทุกครั้งที่พบ PCA infarct และรักษาตามกลไก เช่น carotid revascularisation

name: Crossed cerebellar diaschisis (CCD)
formal: Reduced blood flow and metabolism in the cerebellar hemisphere contralateral to a supratentorial lesion (stroke, tumour, haemorrhage or seizure focus), caused by interruption of the corticopontocerebellar pathway rather than by a cerebellar lesion; seen on PET, SPECT, CT or MR perfusion.
simple: After damage to one side of the cerebrum, the opposite side of the cerebellum shows less blood flow on scans even though it is not injured itself.
th: crossed cerebellar diaschisis คือการที่ cerebellum ด้านตรงข้ามกับรอยโรคของ cerebrum มีเลือดไปเลี้ยงและ metabolism ลดลงจากการขาดสัญญาณผ่าน corticopontocerebellar pathway ไม่ใช่ infarct ของ cerebellum พบใน PET, SPECT หรือ perfusion imaging หลัง stroke เนื้องอก หรือชัก ส่วนใหญ่ไม่มีอาการเฉพาะ
tempoNote: Appears within hours to days of a supratentorial lesion and may persist; long-standing cases can lead to crossed cerebellar atrophy
feat: Contralateral cerebellar hypoperfusion on CT perfusion, ASL MRI, SPECT or FDG-PET after an MCA-territory stroke or other hemispheric lesion
No cerebellar infarct on DWI; the cerebellar tissue is structurally normal early
Often clinically silent; any ataxia is usually attributable to the supratentorial lesion itself
Degree correlates with the size and corticopontine involvement of the hemispheric lesion and with poorer outcome
Seizures or status epilepticus may cause crossed cerebellar hyperperfusion or hypoperfusion depending on phase
inv: Perfusion imaging (CT perfusion, ASL) — interpret cerebellar asymmetry in light of the supratentorial lesion
MRI DWI to confirm that the cerebellum has no infarct
FDG-PET or SPECT in research or epilepsy work-up

case.who: 65-year-old female school cook from Chon Buri with a left MCA occlusion treated by thrombectomy
case.story: Post-procedure CT perfusion was performed to look for residual hypoperfusion.
case.exam: Right hemiparesis and aphasia improving; no cerebellar signs on the left limbs.
case.tests: CT perfusion shows reduced CBF in the right cerebellar hemisphere as well as the left frontal cortex; MRI DWI shows infarct in the left insula and frontal operculum only, with a normal cerebellum.
case.q: How should the right cerebellar hypoperfusion be interpreted?
case.a: As crossed cerebellar diaschisis from the left hemispheric infarct, not a second infarct; no change in management is needed.

det.patho: The cerebral cortex projects through the corticopontine fibres to the pontine nuclei, which send crossing fibres through the middle cerebellar peduncle to the opposite cerebellar hemisphere. A supratentorial lesion removes this excitatory input, so synaptic activity, glucose metabolism and coupled blood flow fall in the contralateral cerebellum (functional deafferentation). With time, transneuronal degeneration can produce crossed cerebellar atrophy. Status epilepticus can produce the reverse — cerebellar hyperperfusion during ictal activity.
det.clinical: CCD is an imaging phenomenon, typically without specific symptoms, although the extent of diaschisis correlates with the size of the hemispheric lesion and with worse motor outcome in some studies. It is relevant because it appears on perfusion maps used for acute stroke decisions and on PET or SPECT used in epilepsy and tumour work-up. The concept of diaschisis, from von Monakow, also describes reversible dysfunction in remote connected regions such as the thalamus.
det.diagnosis: Recognise a cerebellar perfusion deficit opposite a supratentorial lesion, with no DWI abnormality in the cerebellum and no vertebrobasilar occlusion. Automated perfusion software may label the area as hypoperfused, so reports should comment on it. In epilepsy, ictal and interictal SPECT patterns of cerebellar hyperperfusion or hypoperfusion can support lateralisation.
det.treatment: No specific treatment; manage the primary lesion. Avoid misinterpreting CCD as an additional infarct or as a reason for vertebrobasilar intervention.
det.prognosis: Often partially reversible as the primary lesion recovers; persistent or severe CCD signals a larger network injury.
pearls: Cerebellar hypoperfusion opposite a hemispheric infarct with normal cerebellar DWI = CCD, not a second stroke.
The pathway is cortex → pons → crossed middle cerebellar peduncle → opposite cerebellum.
Long-standing CCD can produce unilateral crossed cerebellar atrophy on MRI.

name: Ondine’s curse (acquired central hypoventilation syndrome)
formal: Loss of automatic (metabolic) control of breathing with preserved voluntary breathing, caused by lesions of the medullary respiratory network or its descending bulbospinal pathways, leading to hypoventilation and apnoea mainly during sleep; the acquired counterpart of PHOX2B-related congenital central hypoventilation syndrome.
simple: Damage to the breathing centre in the lowest brainstem means the person breathes when awake and thinking about it, but stops breathing properly when asleep.
ab: ภาวะหยุดหายใจเมื่อหลับจากก้านสมอง
th: Ondine’s curse คือการสูญเสียการหายใจแบบอัตโนมัติขณะยังหายใจตามใจสั่งได้ จากรอยโรคที่ศูนย์ควบคุมการหายใจใน medulla หรือ bulbospinal pathway ทำให้หายใจไม่พอและหยุดหายใจขณะหลับ พบได้หลัง lateral หรือ dorsal medullary infarct สองข้าง เนื้องอก หรือ rhombencephalitis ชนิดแต่กำเนิดสัมพันธ์กับยีน PHOX2B
tempoNote: Acute after medullary stroke, haemorrhage or encephalitis; chronic or progressive with tumours, MSA or congenital forms
feat: Breathing adequate while awake and attentive but hypoventilation or apnoea during sleep or sedation
Hypercapnia with blunted ventilatory response to CO2, often without dyspnoea

Causes: extensive or bilateral lateral/dorsal medullary infarction, medullary haemorrhage or tumour, demyelination, Chiari malformation, enterovirus or Listeria rhombencephalitis, MSA

inv: Arterial blood gas awake and asleep; overnight transcutaneous or end-tidal CO2
Polysomnography showing central apnoeas and sleep-related hypoventilation
MRI brainstem with DWI and contrast
PHOX2B genetic testing in children or unexplained adult-onset cases

case.who: 67-year-old male rubber tapper from Trang with a large right lateral medullary infarct from vertebral artery occlusion
case.story: On day 3 he talks normally and his oxygen saturation is fine awake, but nurses find him cyanosed and unresponsive with slow shallow breaths each time he falls asleep.
case.exam: Awake: alert, breathing 16/min on request; asleep: respiratory rate 4/min with pauses of 30 seconds; right Horner, dysphagia, crossed sensory loss.
case.tests: Overnight ABG pCO2 72 mmHg; MRI shows the right lateral medullary infarct extending medially to the dorsal medulla with a small left dorsal medullary lesion.
case.q: What is the mechanism of the sleep apnoea and how should he be managed?
case.a: Damage to the medullary automatic respiratory centres (Ondine's curse); he needs nocturnal ventilatory support (NIV or mechanical ventilation) and avoidance of sedatives.

det.patho: Automatic breathing is generated by the medullary respiratory network — the pre-Bötzinger complex and ventral respiratory group, the dorsal respiratory group in the nucleus tractus solitarius, and CO2-sensitive cells near the retrotrapezoid nucleus — and is carried to phrenic and intercostal motor neurons by bulbospinal pathways. Voluntary breathing uses separate corticospinal pathways. Lesions that destroy the automatic system bilaterally, or a large unilateral lesion in a vulnerable patient, abolish breathing during sleep when cortical drive falls. The congenital form arises from PHOX2B mutations affecting autonomic neuron development.
det.clinical: Patients may breathe normally when awake and talking yet stop or slow breathing on falling asleep, under sedation or after opioids. Hypercapnia, morning headache, polycythaemia, pulmonary hypertension and unexpected respiratory arrest are presentations. In stroke units it is seen after extensive lateral or bilateral medullary infarcts; it is also described after medullary tumours, demyelination, brainstem encephalitis (including enterovirus 71 in children) and neurosurgery near the fourth ventricle.
det.diagnosis: Document hypoventilation during sleep with blood gases, capnography and polysomnography, and show a blunted hypercapnic ventilatory response. MRI identifies the medullary lesion. Exclude neuromuscular respiratory failure, obesity hypoventilation, chronic lung disease and drug effects. Test PHOX2B in suspected congenital or late-onset idiopathic cases.
det.treatment: Ventilatory support during sleep — non-invasive ventilation with a backup rate, or tracheostomy and mechanical ventilation in severe cases; diaphragm pacing is an option for long-term dependence. Avoid sedatives, opioids and high-flow oxygen without ventilation, which worsen hypercapnia. Respiratory stimulants have little role. Many stroke-related cases improve over weeks to months, so reassess regularly.
det.prognosis: Acquired cases after stroke may recover partially; persistent cases need lifelong ventilatory support, and unrecognised cases risk sudden death in sleep.
pearls: Normal breathing awake but apnoea asleep after medullary stroke = Ondine's curse — monitor CO2 overnight.
Oxygen alone can mask hypoventilation on pulse oximetry while CO2 climbs.
Congenital central hypoventilation is caused by PHOX2B mutations and may present in adults.

name: Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) — neurological involvement
formal: Neurological complications of systemic sclerosis, an autoimmune disease of small-vessel vasculopathy and fibrosis of skin and organs, which mainly affect the peripheral nervous system and muscle (trigeminal sensory neuropathy, entrapment and axonal neuropathies, myositis, autonomic dysfunction) and rarely the brain, often through renal crisis or vasculopathy.
simple: Scleroderma, which hardens the skin and organs, can also damage nerves (especially the face nerve for feeling) and muscles.
ab: โรคหนังแข็งกับระบบประสาท

case.who: 46-year-old female garment factory worker from Samut Prakan with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis and anti-Scl-70
case.story: Over six months she developed numbness of both cheeks and the chin, then difficulty climbing stairs; she was started on prednisolone 40 mg daily by another clinic two weeks ago.
case.exam: Sclerodactyly, digital pitting scars, reduced pinprick over both V2–V3 distributions with normal facial power, proximal weakness 4/5; today BP 198/112 mmHg and she is confused.
case.tests: Creatinine risen from 0.8 to 2.6 mg/dL, schistocytes on smear; CK 1,800 U/L; MRI shows bilateral parieto-occipital vasogenic oedema.
case.q: What acute complication explains her confusion and what is the key treatment?
case.a: Scleroderma renal crisis with PRES, likely precipitated by high-dose prednisolone; start an ACE inhibitor (e.g. captopril) promptly and minimise glucocorticoid dose.

det.patho: Systemic sclerosis combines endothelial injury and small-vessel obliteration, immune activation with specific autoantibodies, and fibroblast-driven fibrosis. Nerves can be damaged by microvascular ischaemia, by entrapment within fibrotic tissue (median nerve at the wrist), or by immune mechanisms, while muscle shows inflammatory myositis or fibrosis. Brain involvement is uncommon and usually secondary — to renal crisis with malignant hypertension and PRES, to vasculopathy or to coexisting conditions.
det.clinical: Facial numbness from trigeminal sensory neuropathy is a characteristic but uncommon complaint; it is more often seen in overlap or anti-U1-RNP disease. Carpal tunnel syndrome may be an early feature. Distal neuropathy, small-fibre pain and autonomic symptoms (gastrointestinal dysmotility, erectile dysfunction, orthostatic intolerance) occur. Myopathy presents with proximal weakness and is associated with cardiac involvement and overlap antibodies. Renal crisis, more frequent in early diffuse disease and with anti-RNA polymerase III, presents with severe hypertension, headache, visual disturbance, seizures and encephalopathy.
det.diagnosis: Systemic sclerosis is classified using the 2013 ACR/EULAR criteria (skin thickening of fingers, Raynaud, capillaroscopy changes, specific antibodies, ILD or pulmonary hypertension). Neurological work-up is guided by the syndrome: nerve conduction and blink reflex studies for neuropathy, CK, MRI and biopsy for myopathy, and urgent blood pressure, renal function and MRI for encephalopathy. Exclude drug toxicity, diabetes, B12 deficiency and coexisting Sjögren syndrome.
det.treatment: Renal crisis is treated with an ACE inhibitor started immediately and titrated, plus other antihypertensives as needed; high-dose glucocorticoids (over about 15 mg prednisolone daily) should be avoided as they precipitate it. Myositis responds to modest glucocorticoids with methotrexate, mycophenolate or IVIG. Neuropathic pain is managed with gabapentinoids, SNRIs or tricyclics; entrapments may need surgical release. Disease-modifying therapy (mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide, rituximab, tocilizumab, nintedanib for ILD) is directed by the rheumatologist.
det.prognosis: Trigeminal neuropathy tends to persist but rarely progresses to motor loss; myopathy and renal crisis carry higher morbidity and mortality.
pearls: Bilateral facial numbness with sclerodactyly or Raynaud: think connective tissue trigeminal neuropathy (SSc/MCTD).
Seizures or encephalopathy with severe hypertension in SSc = renal crisis/PRES — give an ACE inhibitor, not more steroid.
Avoid high-dose prednisolone in early diffuse SSc; it precipitates renal crisis.

name: Rheumatoid craniovertebral instability (atlantoaxial subluxation)
formal: Cervical spine instability in rheumatoid arthritis from synovitis and pannus eroding the atlantoaxial and facet joints and their ligaments, producing anterior or other atlantoaxial subluxation, vertical subluxation (cranial settling, basilar invagination) or subaxial subluxation, with risk of cervical myelopathy, brainstem compression and sudden death.
simple: Long-standing rheumatoid arthritis loosens the joints at the top of the neck so the bones can slip and press on the spinal cord or brainstem.
th: ใน rheumatoid arthritis ที่เป็นมานาน synovitis และ pannus ทำลายข้อและเอ็นที่ C1–C2 และ facet joints ทำให้เกิด atlantoaxial subluxation, cranial settling (basilar invagination) หรือ subaxial subluxation ซึ่งกดไขสันหลังส่วนคอหรือก้านสมอง ทำให้ปวดท้ายทอย อาการ myelopathy หรือเสียชีวิตเฉียบพลันได้ ต้องระวังเป็นพิเศษก่อนใส่ท่อช่วยหายใจ
tempoNote: Progresses over years of active disease; acute deterioration can follow minor trauma, falls or neck manipulation during intubation
feat: Occipital and upper neck pain (C2 distribution), often radiating to the vertex or ear
Myelopathy: hand clumsiness, hyperreflexia, Hoffmann sign, spastic gait, Lhermitte phenomenon; may be masked by joint deformity
Vertical subluxation can cause brainstem signs, vertebrobasilar ischaemia, lower cranial neuropathies or sudden death
Subaxial subluxation causes radiculopathy or a staircase pattern of slips below C2
Risk factors: long-standing erosive seropositive RA, high RF and anti-CCP, peripheral erosions, steroid use; less common in the biologic era
inv: Lateral cervical radiographs in flexion and extension: anterior atlantodental interval over 3 mm abnormal; posterior atlantodental interval under 14 mm signals cord risk
MRI cervical spine (with flexion views when safe) for pannus, cord compression and signal change
CT of the craniovertebral junction for erosions and vertical subluxation (Ranawat, Redlund-Johnell, Clark station measurements)
Pre-operative cervical imaging before general anaesthesia in long-standing RA

case.who: 61-year-old female former seamstress from Phitsanulok with 22 years of seropositive erosive RA on methotrexate and intermittent prednisolone
case.story: She has had increasing occipital pain for a year, and over three months her hands have become clumsy with buttons and she has fallen twice; she gets electric shocks down her back on bending her head.
case.exam: Ulnar deviation and swan-neck deformities; hyperreflexia in all limbs, bilateral Hoffmann signs, extensor plantars, spastic gait.
case.tests: Flexion radiograph: anterior atlantodental interval 9 mm, posterior interval 11 mm; MRI shows retro-odontoid pannus compressing the cord at C1 with T2 signal change.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what is the definitive treatment?
case.a: Rheumatoid anterior atlantoaxial subluxation with cervical myelopathy; surgical stabilisation (C1–C2 fusion, or occipitocervical fusion if there is vertical subluxation) with optimisation of RA therapy.

det.patho: The atlantoaxial joint complex is lined by synovium, and rheumatoid pannus erodes the dens, the lateral masses and the transverse ligament. Ligament laxity allows the atlas to slide forward on the axis (anterior subluxation, the commonest type). Erosion of the lateral masses lets the skull settle onto the spine so the dens migrates upward into the foramen magnum (vertical subluxation or cranial settling). Facet and uncovertebral erosion below C2 causes subaxial slips. Pannus itself also occupies the canal and compresses the cord or medulla.
det.clinical: Many patients with radiographic instability are asymptomatic. Neck and occipital pain is the commonest symptom. Myelopathy is often recognised late because hand deformities, joint pain and immobility mask weakness and clumsiness; reflex change, Hoffmann sign and Lhermitte phenomenon are useful clues. Vertical subluxation adds risk of medullary compression with dysphagia, apnoea, vertebrobasilar symptoms and sudden death. Neurological function is graded by the Ranawat classification.
det.diagnosis: Flexion–extension lateral radiographs show dynamic instability; the posterior atlantodental interval (space available for the cord) correlates better with neurological risk than the anterior interval. MRI defines pannus, cord compression and myelomalacia, and CT shows erosions and vertical migration. Patients with long-standing RA should have cervical imaging before elective surgery requiring intubation.
det.treatment: Controlling synovitis with DMARDs and biologics reduces new instability. Asymptomatic, mild instability can be observed with periodic imaging and patient education about neck precautions. Surgery (posterior C1–C2 fusion, or occipitocervical fusion with or without decompression for vertical subluxation) is indicated for myelopathy, intractable pain, posterior atlantodental interval under about 14 mm, or progressive vertical migration. Early surgery before severe myelopathy gives better results. Anaesthetists use fibreoptic or video-assisted intubation with in-line stabilisation.
det.prognosis: Untreated myelopathy progresses and carries significant mortality; surgery stabilises or improves function, best when performed before advanced deficits.
pearls: Every patient with long-standing RA needs cervical spine assessment before general anaesthesia.
Posterior atlantodental interval under 14 mm predicts cord compression better than the anterior interval.
Hand deformities hide myelopathy — check reflexes, Hoffmann sign and gait in RA clinic.
det.thd: ผู้ป่วย RA ที่เป็นมานานอาจมี atlantoaxial subluxation จาก pannus ทำลายเอ็นและกระดูกที่ C1–C2 ทำให้ปวดท้ายทอยและมี cervical myelopathy ซึ่งมักถูกบดบังด้วยข้อผิดรูป ชนิด vertical subluxation (cranial settling) กดก้านสมองและอาจเสียชีวิตเฉียบพลัน ตรวจด้วย flexion-extension x-ray, MRI และ CT รักษาด้วยการคุมโรค RA และผ่าตัด fusion เมื่อมี myelopathy หรือ PADI < 14 mm ต้องประเมินคอก่อนใส่ท่อช่วยหายใจ

qx.stem: A 60-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has suboccipital pain and electric sensations down the spine on neck flexion. She has brisk reflexes in the legs and a wide-based gait. Dynamic cervical films show an increased atlantodens interval.
qx.q: What is the most important next step?
opts: Reassure her and continue the current disease-modifying therapy
Start botulinum toxin
Urgent MRI and spinal surgical referral, with a collar and care during intubation
Repeat nerve conduction studies
Lumbar puncture
qx.why: Symptomatic atlantoaxial subluxation with myelopathic signs risks cord compression, so MRI and surgical opinion are needed; anaesthetists must be warned about neck extension. Systemic therapy alone does not reverse mechanical instability.

name: Rheumatoid meningitis
formal: A rare inflammatory leptomeningitis and/or pachymeningitis in rheumatoid arthritis, usually in long-standing seropositive disease, characterised pathologically by plasma cell and lymphocytic meningeal infiltration with rheumatoid nodules or necrotising granulomas, and presenting with headache, seizures, encephalopathy, cranial neuropathies or recurrent stroke-like focal deficits.
simple: In rheumatoid arthritis the coverings of the brain can become inflamed, causing headaches, fits or short episodes of weakness or numbness.
ab: เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบจาก rheumatoid
th: rheumatoid meningitis เป็นภาวะที่พบน้อยใน RA ที่เป็นมานานและ seropositive มีการอักเสบของ leptomeninges และ/หรือ dura ผู้ป่วยมาด้วยปวดศีรษะ ชัก สับสน cranial neuropathy หรืออาการอ่อนแรง/ชาเป็นพักๆ คล้าย TIA MRI เห็น meningeal enhancement และ FLAIR/DWI สูงในร่องสมอง ต้องแยกจากการติดเชื้อ TB และมะเร็ง วินิจฉัยแน่นอนด้วย meningeal biopsy
tempoNote: Subacute over weeks, often with recurrent transient focal episodes; can occur even when joint disease is quiet or occasionally before arthritis is diagnosed
feat: Long-standing seropositive (high RF, anti-CCP) RA, sometimes with inactive joints; reported during TNF inhibitor or other biologic therapy
Headache, seizures, confusion, behavioural change and cranial neuropathies
Recurrent stereotyped transient focal motor or sensory episodes mimicking TIA
MRI: leptomeningeal and/or dural enhancement over the convexities, often unilateral frontoparietal, with sulcal FLAIR and DWI hyperintensity
CSF: raised protein, mild lymphocytic pleocytosis, sometimes low glucose; CSF anti-CCP or RF may be elevated
inv: MRI brain with contrast, FLAIR and DWI
CSF cell count, protein, glucose, cytology and flow cytometry, TB PCR/culture, fungal antigen, CSF anti-CCP
Serum RF, anti-CCP, IgG4, ANCA, ACE; chest CT for TB, sarcoid and malignancy
Meningeal and cortical biopsy when infection and malignancy cannot be excluded

case.who: 64-year-old male retired policeman from Khon Kaen with 15 years of seropositive RA on methotrexate and recently started adalimumab
case.story: Over five weeks he had six brief episodes of tingling and weakness of the left hand lasting 10–20 minutes, then a generalised seizure; he also reports a constant right-sided headache.
case.exam: Alert, mild left pronator drift, chronic hand deformities, no fever or neck stiffness.
case.tests: MRI: right frontoparietal leptomeningeal and dural enhancement with sulcal FLAIR and DWI hyperintensity, no infarct; CSF 28 lymphocytes/µL, protein 1.1 g/L, glucose normal, TB PCR and cytology negative, CSF anti-CCP elevated; meningeal biopsy shows plasma cells and necrotising rheumatoid nodules.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the usual treatment?
case.a: Rheumatoid meningitis; after excluding infection and malignancy, high-dose glucocorticoids plus a steroid-sparing drug, for example rituximab or cyclophosphamide, and review of the TNF inhibitor.

read.where: Rheumatoid arthritis — rheumatoid meningitis and CNS nodules

det.patho: The meninges can be infiltrated by the same immune processes that form rheumatoid nodules: plasma cells, lymphocytes, palisading histiocytes and necrotising granulomas, sometimes with small-vessel vasculitis. Inflammation of the leptomeninges irritates the underlying cortex, explaining seizures and transient focal episodes, while dural involvement causes headache and cranial neuropathies. Intrathecal production of anti-CCP and RF has been described. Biologic therapy, especially TNF inhibition, may unmask or trigger the disease in some reports.
det.clinical: It typically occurs in older patients with long-standing, seropositive, often nodular RA, but joint disease may be quiescent. Presentations include subacute headache, encephalopathy, seizures, cranial nerve palsies and characteristic recurrent stereotyped focal episodes resembling TIA or focal seizures. Fever is usually absent. A minority present before or around the time of RA diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows leptomeningeal and/or pachymeningeal enhancement, commonly over the frontoparietal convexities and sometimes unilateral, often with sulcal FLAIR and diffusion hyperintensity. CSF shows inflammation without organisms; elevated CSF anti-CCP supports the diagnosis. Because tuberculosis, fungal infection, lymphoma, carcinomatous meningitis, IgG4-related disease and methotrexate-associated lymphoproliferative disorder look similar, biopsy is often needed for confirmation.
det.treatment: There are no trials; practice is based on case series. High-dose glucocorticoids (often IV methylprednisolone followed by oral taper) produce rapid improvement in most patients, combined with a steroid-sparing agent — rituximab, cyclophosphamide, methotrexate or azathioprine. Review and often stop a TNF inhibitor if the disease appeared during it. Antiseizure medication for seizures. Monitor with MRI and treat infection risk.
det.prognosis: Most respond to immunosuppression, though relapses occur and untreated cases can be fatal.
pearls: Recurrent stereotyped TIA-like spells with convexity meningeal enhancement in RA: think rheumatoid meningitis.
Always exclude TB and lymphoma before immunosuppression; biopsy when in doubt.
Elevated CSF anti-CCP is a useful supporting clue.
det.thd: Rheumatoid meningitis พบน้อย เกิดใน RA ที่เป็นมานานและ seropositive อาจเกิดแม้ข้อสงบหรือขณะได้ยา anti-TNF ผู้ป่วยมีปวดศีรษะ ชัก สับสน หรืออาการทางระบบประสาทเป็นพักๆ คล้าย TIA MRI เห็น leptomeningeal/dural enhancement บริเวณ convexity CSF มีการอักเสบและ anti-CCP สูง ต้องแยก TB เชื้อรา และ lymphoma ก่อน และอาจต้องตัดชิ้นเนื้อ รักษาด้วย steroid ขนาดสูงร่วมกับ rituximab หรือ cyclophosphamide

name: Subependymoma
formal: A slow-growing ependymal tumour (CNS WHO grade 1 in the WHO CNS5 2021 classification) arising beneath the ventricular lining, most often at the floor of the fourth ventricle or in the lateral ventricles near the septum pellucidum and foramen of Monro.
simple: A small, very slow, benign tumour stuck to the wall of a brain fluid space, usually found by chance on a scan.
ab: เนื้องอก subependymoma ในโพรงสมอง
th: เนื้องอกกลุ่ม ependymal ที่โตช้ามาก (CNS WHO grade 1) เกิดใต้ผนังโพรงสมอง มักพบที่โพรงสมองที่สี่หรือโพรงสมองข้างใกล้ septum pellucidum ส่วนใหญ่พบโดยบังเอิญในชายวัยกลางคนถึงสูงอายุ
tempoNote: Indolent for years; usually incidental, symptomatic only when it blocks CSF flow and causes hydrocephalus
feat: Typically a middle-aged or older man, frequently discovered incidentally on MRI or at autopsy
Small, well-circumscribed, lobulated intraventricular nodule attached to the ventricular wall
Bright on T2/FLAIR with little or no enhancement and no restricted diffusion; may contain tiny cysts or calcification
Symptoms, when present, come from obstructive hydrocephalus: headache, gait unsteadiness, vomiting
Fourth-ventricle lesions sit at the obex or floor and rarely spread through the foramina, unlike ependymoma
inv: MRI brain with contrast and DWI; look for hydrocephalus and the point of attachment
CT for calcification and acute ventricular size
Histology after resection when needed; mixed tumours with ependymoma areas are graded by the ependymoma component

case.who: 63-year-old retired rice-mill owner from Suphan Buri referred after a fall
case.story: CT done in the emergency department for minor head trauma showed a small mass in the fourth ventricle; he has no headache, vomiting or imbalance.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination; no papilloedema.
case.tests: MRI: 1.6 cm lobulated T2-bright nodule at the obex, a few punctate cysts, faint patchy enhancement, no diffusion restriction, normal ventricular size.
case.q: What is the most likely lesion and how should it be managed?
case.a: Subependymoma; with no hydrocephalus or symptoms, serial MRI surveillance is reasonable, reserving resection for growth or CSF obstruction.

det.patho: Subependymomas are benign glial tumours thought to come from subependymal glia or tanycytes; histology shows clusters of small uniform nuclei in a dense fibrillary background with microcysts. WHO CNS5 groups them with ependymal tumours as CNS WHO grade 1 and recognises posterior fossa, supratentorial and spinal subependymoma, each with distinct methylation profiles. Mitoses are rare, and many lesions never grow.
det.clinical: Most patients have no symptoms and the lesion is an incidental finding. When symptoms occur they reflect blocked CSF pathways: headache, nausea, gait disturbance, and occasionally cranial nerve or cerebellar signs from a fourth-ventricle mass. Lateral ventricle tumours near the foramen of Monro can cause unilateral or bilateral ventricular enlargement. Rarely, intratumoural haemorrhage produces sudden deterioration.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows a sharply marginated, lobulated nodule attached to the ventricular wall, hyperintense on T2 and FLAIR, with absent or mild patchy enhancement and no restricted diffusion. Fourth-ventricle subependymomas tend to stay within the ventricle rather than extruding through its outlets. Strong enhancement, restricted diffusion, oedema or parenchymal invasion should raise concern for ependymoma, neurocytoma, metastasis or another tumour. Definite diagnosis requires histology if the lesion is removed.
det.treatment: Asymptomatic small tumours can be observed with serial MRI, often yearly at first. Symptomatic lesions or those causing hydrocephalus are removed surgically; gross total resection is usually curative. Adjuvant radiotherapy is not needed after complete removal and is rarely used even after partial resection. CSF diversion may be required if hydrocephalus persists.
det.prognosis: Excellent; recurrence after complete resection is uncommon and survival is normal for age.
pearls: Older man, T2-bright, non-enhancing nodule at the floor of the fourth ventricle: think subependymoma first.
Subependymomas stay inside the ventricle; extension through the foramina favours ependymoma.
Mixed subependymoma-ependymoma is graded according to the ependymoma part.
det.thd: Subependymoma เป็นเนื้องอกชนิดไม่ร้าย (CNS WHO grade 1) โตช้ามาก เกิดที่ผนังโพรงสมอง มักพบโดยบังเอิญในชายสูงอายุ ภาพ MRI เป็นก้อนเล็กขอบชัด T2 สว่าง เพิ่มสารทึบรังสีน้อยหรือไม่เพิ่ม ไม่มี diffusion restriction หากไม่มีอาการให้ติดตาม MRI หากอุดกั้นทางเดินน้ำไขสันหลังจนเกิด hydrocephalus จึงผ่าตัดออก ซึ่งมักหายขาด

name: Atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumour (AT/RT)
formal: A highly malignant embryonal CNS tumour (CNS WHO grade 4) of early childhood defined by loss of SMARCB1 (INI1) or, rarely, SMARCA4 (BRG1) expression, often arising in the posterior fossa and frequently disseminated at diagnosis.
simple: A very aggressive brain cancer of babies and toddlers caused by loss of a tumour-control gene.

feat: Usually under 3 years old; vomiting, lethargy, enlarging head, developmental regression or cranial nerve palsy
Large heterogeneous mass, about half infratentorial, often off-midline in the cerebellopontine angle or cerebellar hemisphere
Cysts, haemorrhage and calcification common; solid parts are dense on CT and restrict diffusion
Thick wavy peripheral band of enhancement around a cystic centre is a suggestive pattern
Leptomeningeal spread present in a sizeable minority at diagnosis

Histology with loss of nuclear INI1 (SMARCB1) or BRG1 staining; DNA methylation for subgroup (TYR, SHH, MYC)

CSF cytology after surgery

case.who: 14-month-old boy from Udon Thani brought to the regional hospital
case.story: Three weeks of morning vomiting, stopped standing alone and became irritable; his head circumference crossed two centile lines.
case.exam: Bulging fontanelle, sunsetting eyes, left facial weakness and truncal ataxia.
case.tests: MRI: 5 cm heterogeneous left cerebellopontine angle mass with cysts, haemorrhage and restricted diffusion in solid parts, wavy rim enhancement and nodular enhancement along the spinal cord surface; histology shows loss of INI1 nuclear staining.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and which further test matters for the family?
case.a: AT/RT (SMARCB1-deficient); germline SMARCB1 testing, because rhabdoid tumour predisposition syndrome alters surveillance and counselling for siblings.

det.patho: AT/RT is defined by biallelic inactivation of SMARCB1 (rarely SMARCA4), core subunits of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodelling complex, which leaves the tumour genome otherwise remarkably quiet. Methylation profiling separates three groups with different ages and locations: ATRT-TYR (infants, often infratentorial), ATRT-SHH (supra- and infratentorial) and ATRT-MYC (often supratentorial, somewhat older). About a third of patients carry a germline variant (rhabdoid tumour predisposition syndrome), who may also develop renal or soft-tissue rhabdoid tumours. Histology shows rhabdoid cells mixed with primitive neuroectodermal, mesenchymal and epithelial elements.
det.clinical: Most children are under three. Infants present with nonspecific signs of raised intracranial pressure: vomiting, irritability, lethargy, macrocephaly and loss of milestones. Cerebellopontine angle tumours cause facial or abducens palsies; supratentorial tumours cause seizures or hemiparesis. Growth is rapid, so symptoms usually span only weeks. Adults are rarely affected.
det.diagnosis: Imaging cannot reliably separate AT/RT from medulloblastoma, but large size, off-midline position, haemorrhage, calcification, cysts and an undulating band of rim enhancement favour it. Solid tissue is hyperdense on CT and restricts diffusion. Stage the whole neuraxis with MRI before surgery to avoid postoperative artefact. Diagnosis rests on loss of nuclear INI1 or BRG1 immunostaining; methylation profiling confirms subgroup, and germline testing is recommended for every patient.
det.treatment: Management is in a paediatric neuro-oncology centre: maximal safe resection followed by intensive multi-agent chemotherapy, often with high-dose chemotherapy and autologous stem-cell rescue, and intrathecal therapy in some protocols. Focal or craniospinal radiotherapy is given where age and protocol allow, with growing acceptance of focal irradiation in young children. Targeted agents (e.g. EZH2 inhibitors such as tazemetostat) are under study. Germline carriers need tumour surveillance and family counselling.
det.prognosis: Poor but improving: contemporary intensive protocols achieve roughly 40–50% long-term survival in selected patients; young age, metastases and incomplete resection worsen outcome.
pearls: Infant with a large off-midline posterior fossa mass with haemorrhage and restricted diffusion: ask the pathologist for INI1 staining.
Every AT/RT patient should be offered germline SMARCB1/SMARCA4 testing.
Image the whole spine before surgery; leptomeningeal spread is common at presentation.
det.thd: AT/RT เป็นเนื้องอกสมองร้ายแรงในเด็กเล็ก เกิดจากการสูญเสียยีน SMARCB1 (INI1) ภาพ MRI เป็นก้อนใหญ่ไม่สม่ำเสมอ มีถุงน้ำ เลือดออก หินปูน และ diffusion restriction มักอยู่ด้านข้างของ posterior fossa ต้องทำ MRI ทั้งสมองและไขสันหลังก่อนผ่าตัด ยืนยันด้วยการย้อม INI1 ที่หายไป รักษาด้วยผ่าตัด เคมีบำบัดขนาดสูง และฉายรังสี ควรตรวจยีนแบบ germline ในผู้ป่วยทุกราย

Fourth-ventricle tumour that extrudes through the foramina, less diffusion restriction, INI1 retained
Intraventricular, frond-like, intensely enhancing; carcinomas in infants may be confused but keep INI1

name: Solitary fibrous tumour of the CNS (formerly haemangiopericytoma)
formal: A dural-based mesenchymal tumour of fibroblastic origin defined by the NAB2-STAT6 gene fusion, graded CNS WHO 1–3 in WHO CNS5 2021, which unified the former solitary fibrous tumour and haemangiopericytoma under one name; it mimics meningioma but recurs and metastasises outside the CNS more often.
simple: A tumour on the brain's covering that looks like a meningioma on scans but tends to come back and can spread to bone, lung or liver.
ab: Solitary fibrous tumour of the CNS
เนื้องอกเยื่อหุ้มสมองชนิด SFT
th: เนื้องอกของเนื้อเยื่อเกี่ยวพันที่ติดกับเยื่อดูรา มี gene fusion NAB2-STAT6 ตาม WHO CNS5 2021 รวมชื่อเดิม haemangiopericytoma ไว้ในกลุ่มนี้ ภาพคล้าย meningioma แต่กลับเป็นซ้ำบ่อยและแพร่กระจายไปกระดูก ปอด ตับได้
tempoNote: Grows over months to years; local recurrence and distant metastasis may appear more than a decade after surgery
feat: Adults in their 40s–60s with headache, seizures or focal deficits from a dural-based mass
Lobulated, often narrow-based mass with prominent flow voids and vigorous heterogeneous enhancement
No calcification or hyperostosis; adjacent skull may be eroded rather than thickened
Mixed dark and bright areas on T2 within the same tumour and very high perfusion on perfusion MRI
Brisk bleeding at surgery; tendency to recur locally and to metastasise to bone, lung and liver
inv: MRI with contrast, perfusion and MR spectroscopy (raised myo-inositol supports SFT over meningioma)
CT for bone erosion versus hyperostosis; angiography for supply and preoperative embolisation
Histology with nuclear STAT6 immunostaining (or NAB2-STAT6 fusion) and mitotic count for grade
Long-term surveillance MRI and periodic body imaging (CT chest/abdomen, bone scan or PET as indicated)

case.story: Four months of right-sided headache and two focal seizures with left-arm jerking; scan first reported as meningioma.
case.exam: Mild left pronator drift and brisk left reflexes.
case.tests: MRI: 4.5 cm lobulated right parietal dural mass with large flow voids, patchy T2 dark and bright areas, intense heterogeneous enhancement and erosion of the inner skull table without hyperostosis; histology shows strong nuclear STAT6.
case.q: Which diagnosis does the STAT6 result establish, and what follow-up is needed after resection?
case.a: CNS solitary fibrous tumour (previously haemangiopericytoma); lifelong MRI surveillance and body imaging for late metastases, with adjuvant radiotherapy if grade 2–3 or subtotal removal.

det.patho: SFT is a fibroblastic tumour driven by an intrachromosomal inversion on 12q13 that fuses NAB2 and STAT6, producing a transcriptional activator that shows up as strong nuclear STAT6 staining. WHO CNS5 dropped the separate term haemangiopericytoma and grades the tumour 1–3 according to mitotic count and necrosis. Tumours with a 'staghorn' branching vascular pattern and high cellularity correspond to the older haemangiopericytoma label. Unlike meningioma, it is not of arachnoid cap cell origin.
det.clinical: Patients are usually adults of middle age with headache, seizures, focal weakness or visual symptoms depending on site; the falx, tentorium, skull base and spinal dura are common locations. Symptoms develop slowly. The key behaviour is relapse: local recurrence is frequent and extracranial metastases to bone, lung and liver may appear many years, even decades, after the original surgery.
det.diagnosis: Imaging suggests SFT when a dural mass is lobulated or mushroom-shaped, has large flow voids, mixed T2 signal, very high cerebral blood volume, no calcification and erodes rather than thickens bone; a dural tail can still occur. MR spectroscopy may show a high myo-inositol peak. Final diagnosis requires histology with nuclear STAT6 positivity, which separates it from meningioma, schwannoma and other spindle-cell tumours. Grade is set by mitoses and necrosis.
det.treatment: Gross total resection is the main treatment; preoperative embolisation can reduce blood loss in vascular tumours. Adjuvant radiotherapy (or stereotactic radiosurgery for small residuals) is generally recommended for grade 2–3 tumours or incomplete resection and improves local control. Recurrences are treated with repeat surgery or radiation; systemic options such as anti-angiogenic agents (e.g. pazopanib, temozolomide-bevacizumab) are used for metastatic disease. Surveillance should continue for well over ten years.
det.prognosis: Long-term survival is common, but recurrence and late metastasis are frequent in higher-grade tumours, so cure cannot be declared early.
pearls: A 'meningioma' with flow voids, no calcification and bone erosion instead of hyperostosis should prompt STAT6 staining.
Haemangiopericytoma is no longer a separate WHO diagnosis; it is solitary fibrous tumour, CNS WHO grade 2–3.
Follow these patients for decades; metastases to bone, lung and liver can appear very late.
det.thd: Solitary fibrous tumour ของระบบประสาทเป็นเนื้องอกที่ติดเยื่อดูรา มี NAB2-STAT6 fusion ตาม WHO CNS5 รวมชื่อเดิม haemangiopericytoma ภาพ MRI คล้าย meningioma แต่มี flow void มาก ไม่มีหินปูน กัดกร่อนกระดูกแทนที่จะหนาตัว ยืนยันด้วยการย้อม STAT6 รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัดออกให้หมดและฉายรังสีเสริมในเกรดสูง ต้องติดตามระยะยาวเพราะกลับเป็นซ้ำและแพร่กระจายนอกสมองได้แม้ผ่านไปหลายปี

name: Intracranial epidermoid cyst
formal: A congenital extra-axial inclusion cyst lined by stratified squamous epithelium and filled with keratin and cholesterol debris, most often in the cerebellopontine angle or parasellar region, which insinuates around nerves and vessels and shows marked restricted diffusion on MRI.
simple: A slow-growing, pearly sac of skin-type cells inside the skull that wraps around nerves and can cause face pain or twitching.
ab: ถุงน้ำ epidermoid ในกะโหลก
th: ถุงน้ำแต่กำเนิดที่มีผนังเป็นเยื่อบุผิวชนิด squamous และมี keratin อยู่ภายใน มักพบที่ cerebellopontine angle ค่อย ๆ แทรกตัวห่อหุ้มเส้นประสาทและหลอดเลือด ภาพ MRI สัญญาณคล้ายน้ำไขสันหลังแต่สว่างมากบน DWI
tempoNote: Grows slowly over years like skin shedding inward; symptoms usually begin in the 20s to 50s
feat: Adult with trigeminal neuralgia, hemifacial spasm, hearing loss or tinnitus from a cerebellopontine angle lesion
Lobulated, cauliflower-like extra-axial mass that creeps into cisterns and encases vessels and nerves rather than displacing them
Close to CSF on CT, T1 and T2, but incompletely suppressed on FLAIR and very bright on DWI
No enhancement (thin rim at most); new nodular enhancement suggests rare malignant change
Rupture can cause recurrent chemical (aseptic) meningitis
inv: MRI with DWI, FLAIR and contrast; DWI separates it from arachnoid cyst
CISS/FIESTA high-resolution T2 to map involved cranial nerves before surgery
Audiometry for CPA lesions; postoperative DWI to detect residual or recurrence

case.story: One year of brief electric-shock pains in the right cheek triggered by chewing; carbamazepine helps partly; he is younger than typical for classic trigeminal neuralgia.
case.exam: Mildly reduced right corneal reflex; otherwise normal.
case.tests: MRI: lobulated right cerebellopontine angle lesion following CSF on T1 and T2, encasing the trigeminal nerve and superior cerebellar artery, incompletely dark on FLAIR and markedly bright on DWI, without enhancement.
case.q: What lesion is this and what imaging feature confirms it?
case.a: Intracranial epidermoid cyst causing secondary trigeminal neuralgia; marked restricted diffusion distinguishes it from an arachnoid cyst.

det.patho: Epidermoid cysts arise from ectodermal cells trapped during closure of the neural tube in weeks 3–5 of gestation. The squamous lining keeps desquamating keratin into the cyst, so it enlarges linearly like skin, filling cisterns and following the path of least resistance. The contents are solid flaky keratin with cholesterol crystals, giving a pearly appearance. Dermoid cysts differ by containing skin appendages and fat and by favouring the midline.
det.clinical: Symptoms appear in young to middle adulthood and depend on location. Cerebellopontine angle lesions cause trigeminal neuralgia, hemifacial spasm, hearing loss, tinnitus or imbalance; parasellar lesions can cause visual loss or seizures; fourth-ventricle lesions cause hydrocephalus. Leakage of keratin can cause repeated aseptic meningitis. Malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma is rare.
det.diagnosis: MRI is diagnostic in most cases: signal similar to CSF on T1 and T2, incomplete suppression and 'dirty' texture on FLAIR, striking hyperintensity on DWI with low or near-normal ADC, and no enhancement. On CT the lesion is low density and may scallop bone. Encasement of arteries and nerves rather than displacement is a useful sign. An enhancing nodule or rapid growth should prompt concern for carcinoma.
det.treatment: Symptomatic cysts are removed microsurgically; the contents are evacuated easily but the capsule is often adherent to nerves and vessels, so subtotal removal is common to avoid deficits. Residual capsule can regrow slowly, so follow-up DWI MRI is used over years. Perioperative steroids reduce chemical meningitis from spilled keratin. Small asymptomatic lesions can be observed.
det.prognosis: Generally good; recurrence after subtotal removal is common but slow, often over a decade.
pearls: Looks like CSF everywhere except DWI and FLAIR: epidermoid until proven otherwise.
Trigeminal neuralgia in a young adult warrants MRI for a secondary cause such as an epidermoid.
Epidermoids wrap around vessels and nerves; arachnoid cysts push them away.
det.thd: Epidermoid cyst ในกะโหลกเป็นถุงน้ำแต่กำเนิดที่มี keratin อยู่ภายใน โตช้า มักอยู่ที่ cerebellopontine angle ทำให้ปวดใบหน้าแบบ trigeminal neuralgia ใบหน้ากระตุก หรือการได้ยินลดลง ภาพ MRI คล้ายน้ำไขสันหลังแต่สว่างมากบน DWI และ FLAIR ไม่ดำสนิท จึงแยกจาก arachnoid cyst ได้ รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัด แต่เปลือกถุงมักติดเส้นประสาทจึงกลับเป็นซ้ำได้ช้า ๆ

Vestibular schwannoma and meningioma enhance solidly; schwannoma widens the internal auditory canal
Racemose cysticercosis in basal cisterns is grape-like, may enhance and does not restrict diffusion

name: Intracranial lipoma
formal: A congenital malformation in which mature adipose tissue persists within the subarachnoid cisterns because the embryonic meninx primitiva failed to resorb normally, most often in the pericallosal interhemispheric fissure and frequently accompanied by callosal dysgenesis.
simple: A harmless patch of fat inside the skull that has been there since before birth, usually found by chance.
ab: ก้อนไขมันในกะโหลก
th: ความผิดปกติแต่กำเนิดที่มีเนื้อไขมันอยู่ในช่องใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมอง มักพบเหนือ corpus callosum และอาจพบร่วมกับ corpus callosum เจริญไม่สมบูรณ์ ส่วนใหญ่ไม่มีอาการและไม่ต้องผ่าตัด
tempoNote: Present from fetal life and does not grow; symptoms, if any, reflect associated malformations or nerve involvement
feat: Usually an incidental finding on CT or MRI done for headache or head injury
Fat density on CT (strongly negative Hounsfield units), T1 bright and suppressed with fat saturation
Pericallosal lipomas: tubulonodular anterior type with calcified rim and callosal dysgenesis, or thin curvilinear posterior type
Other sites: quadrigeminal and ambient cisterns, suprasellar/tuber cinereum, cerebellopontine angle, sylvian fissure
Vessels and cranial nerves run through the lipoma rather than around it
inv: CT confirms fat attenuation and rim calcification
MRI with fat-suppressed T1 to separate fat from blood or proteinaceous material; look for corpus callosum and other anomalies
Audiometry if a cerebellopontine angle or internal auditory canal lipoma is found

case.who: 22-year-old female university student from Chiang Rai
case.story: CT after a minor scooter fall showed a strange dark midline mass; she has no seizures, normal school performance and only occasional tension headaches.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination.
case.tests: CT: nodular midline mass of about −90 HU above the genu of the corpus callosum with curvilinear rim calcification; MRI: T1-bright lesion that disappears on fat-saturated images, with a hypoplastic anterior corpus callosum; anterior cerebral arteries pass through the mass.
case.q: What is the lesion and what management is appropriate?
case.a: Tubulonodular pericallosal lipoma with callosal dysgenesis; no surgery, reassurance and no routine follow-up imaging.

det.patho: The meninx primitiva is the mesenchyme that normally differentiates into the leptomeninges and resorbs to form the cisterns. If it persists and differentiates abnormally into fat, a lipoma forms within the subarachnoid space. Because this happens while midline structures are developing, interhemispheric lipomas often coexist with partial or complete callosal agenesis, and arteries and nerves passing through the area become incorporated into the fat.
det.clinical: Most lipomas cause no symptoms. Large interhemispheric lipomas with callosal anomalies may be associated with seizures, developmental delay or other midline defects such as frontal cephaloceles. Cerebellopontine angle and internal auditory canal lipomas can produce hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo or facial symptoms. Hypothalamic lipomas are usually silent.
det.diagnosis: CT shows uniformly very low (fat) attenuation, often with rim or nodular calcification in tubulonodular lesions. MRI shows T1 and T2 hyperintensity, chemical shift artefact at the borders, and loss of signal on fat-suppressed sequences, which separates fat from methaemoglobin or proteinaceous fluid. Look carefully for the vessels and nerves running through it and for associated brain malformations. Biopsy is unnecessary.
det.treatment: Lipomas are left alone; resection is risky because of incorporated vessels and nerves and does not improve outcome. Treat associated epilepsy in the usual way. For cerebellopontine angle lipomas, symptomatic management and observation are preferred over surgery, which carries a high risk of facial and hearing nerve injury.
det.prognosis: Excellent for the lipoma itself; outcome depends on any accompanying malformations.
pearls: T1-bright lesion that vanishes on fat-saturated images is fat, not blood.
A pericallosal lipoma should prompt a look for callosal dysgenesis.
Never operate on a CPA lipoma for diagnosis; the nerves run through it.
det.thd: Intracranial lipoma คือก้อนไขมันแต่กำเนิดในช่องใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมอง เกิดจาก meninx primitiva เจริญผิดปกติ พบมากที่เหนือ corpus callosum CT เป็นความหนาแน่นไขมัน MRI สว่างบน T1 และหายไปเมื่อใช้ fat suppression มักพบร่วมกับ corpus callosum เจริญไม่สมบูรณ์ ไม่ต้องผ่าตัดเพราะมีหลอดเลือดและเส้นประสาทวิ่งผ่าน

name: Vein of Galen aneurysmal malformation (VGAM)
formal: A congenital high-flow arteriovenous fistula, formed between weeks 6 and 11 of gestation, between choroidal arteries and the persistent embryonic median prosencephalic vein (of Markowski), which dilates into a midline varix and presents in neonates with high-output heart failure or in infants with macrocrania and hydrocephalus.
simple: A large abnormal connection between arteries and a deep vein at the centre of a baby's brain that overloads the heart and fluid system.
ab: ความผิดปกติของ vein of Galen
th: ความผิดปกติแต่กำเนิดที่หลอดเลือดแดงต่อตรงกับหลอดเลือดดำ median prosencephalic vein ซึ่งโป่งพองกลางสมอง ทารกแรกเกิดมีหัวใจล้มเหลวจากเลือดไหลเวียนมาก ทารกโตขึ้นมีศีรษะโตและ hydrocephalus รักษาด้วยการอุดหลอดเลือดทางสายสวน
tempoNote: Present before birth; neonatal heart failure in the first days, or macrocrania and developmental delay over the first year
feat: Newborn with high-output cardiac failure, pulmonary hypertension and a cranial bruit
Infant with enlarging head, hydrocephalus, prominent scalp and facial veins, failure to thrive
Large midline varix behind the third ventricle draining into a persistent falcine sinus; straight sinus often absent
Choroidal type (many feeders, worse) versus mural type (few feeders, better tolerated)
Untreated venous hypertension causes brain atrophy, calcification and progressive damage ('melting brain')
inv: Prenatal Doppler ultrasound or fetal MRI showing a midline flow-filled structure; echocardiography
Postnatal MRI/MRA for brain injury, venous anatomy and hydrocephalus
Catheter angiography at the time of planned embolisation
Bicêtre neonatal evaluation score (cardiac, cerebral, respiratory, hepatic, renal function) to decide timing

case.who: 3-day-old girl born at term in a provincial hospital in Nakhon Ratchasima
case.story: Tachypnoea and poor feeding from day one, worsening despite oxygen; referred with suspected congenital heart disease.
case.exam: Loud continuous bruit over the anterior fontanelle, bounding neck pulses, hepatomegaly.
case.tests: Echocardiography: structurally normal heart with dilated right side, high-output state and reversed diastolic flow in the descending aorta; cranial ultrasound: large midline anechoic lesion showing turbulent flow on Doppler; MRI shows a midline varix draining into a falcine sinus.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what is the key treatment?
case.a: Vein of Galen aneurysmal malformation (choroidal type) with neonatal heart failure; staged transarterial endovascular embolisation, urgently if heart failure cannot be medically controlled.
