det.patho: The median prosencephalic vein drains the embryonic choroid plexus and normally regresses as the internal cerebral veins form. In VGAM, direct fistulas from choroidal, pericallosal and collicular arteries keep it open and enlarged. The huge left-to-right shunt overloads the heart and steals blood from the brain, while high venous pressure impairs CSF resorption and venous drainage, producing hydrocephalus, white matter injury and calcification. Some cases are linked to RASA1 or EPHB4 variants.
det.clinical: Presentation depends on shunt volume. Neonates develop high-output heart failure, pulmonary hypertension and multiorgan dysfunction within days. Infants present with macrocephaly, hydrocephalus, dilated facial veins, developmental delay or seizures. Older children and adults are rarely diagnosed, with headache or haemorrhage. Prenatal diagnosis is now common on third-trimester ultrasound.
det.diagnosis: Fetal ultrasound or MRI reveals a midline varix with flow. After birth, MRI and MRA define the fistulas, venous drainage (persistent falcine sinus, absent straight sinus, sinus stenoses) and brain injury; signs of 'melting brain' or extensive parenchymal damage indicate a poor outlook. Echocardiography gauges cardiac load. Angiography is reserved for treatment. The Bicêtre score helps decide whether to embolise urgently, delay, or withhold treatment.
det.treatment: Medical stabilisation of heart failure in a neonatal ICU is followed by staged transarterial embolisation with glue or coils; ideal timing for stable infants is around 4–6 months, while uncontrolled heart failure forces neonatal intervention. Ventricular shunting should be avoided or delayed, because hydrocephalus often improves after embolisation and shunting can worsen venous problems. In utero transuterine embolisation has been reported since 2023 in selected high-risk fetuses. Care requires an experienced paediatric neurointerventional team.
det.prognosis: With modern staged embolisation many children have normal or near-normal development; untreated neonatal VGAM is usually fatal, and established brain damage predicts poor outcome.
pearls: Neonatal heart failure with a structurally normal heart: listen over the head for a bruit.
A dilated vein of Galen draining a pial AVM is not a true VGAM; the true lesion drains into the embryonic median prosencephalic vein.
Embolise first, shunt last: hydrocephalus is a venous problem in VGAM.
det.thd: VGAM เป็นความผิดปกติแต่กำเนิดที่หลอดเลือดแดง choroidal ต่อตรงกับหลอดเลือดดำตัวอ่อน median prosencephalic vein จนโป่งเป็นก้อนกลางสมอง ทารกแรกเกิดมีหัวใจล้มเหลวแบบ high-output ทารกที่โตขึ้นมีศีรษะโต hydrocephalus และพัฒนาการช้า วินิจฉัยด้วย ultrasound/MRI ก่อนและหลังคลอด รักษาด้วยการอุดหลอดเลือดทางสายสวนเป็นระยะ ควรหลีกเลี่ยงการใส่ shunt ก่อนอุดหลอดเลือด

name: Carotid–cavernous fistula (CCF)
formal: An abnormal arteriovenous shunt into the cavernous sinus, either direct from the internal carotid artery (high-flow, usually traumatic or from a ruptured cavernous aneurysm) or indirect from dural branches arising from either the external or internal carotid artery (low-flow, usually spontaneous), causing orbital venous congestion and cranial nerve palsies.
simple: A leak between the carotid artery and a vein pool behind the eye, making the eye bulge, turn red and see double.
ab: ฟิสทูล่าระหว่าง carotid กับ cavernous sinus
th: การเชื่อมต่อผิดปกติระหว่างหลอดเลือดแดง carotid กับ cavernous sinus แบบตรง (มักหลังอุบัติเหตุ เลือดไหลแรง) หรือแบบอ้อม (ผ่านแขนงเยื่อดูรา มักเป็นเองในหญิงสูงอายุ) ทำให้ตาโปน ตาแดง เยื่อบุตาบวม เห็นภาพซ้อน และความดันลูกตาสูง

feat: Proptosis, chemosis and dilated tortuous (corkscrew) episcleral vessels; pulsatile proptosis and bruit in direct fistulas
Diplopia from abducens or oculomotor palsy; raised intraocular pressure and possible visual loss

Enlarged superior ophthalmic vein and bulging cavernous sinus on CT or MRI

case.who: 26-year-old male delivery rider from Chon Buri
case.story: Three weeks after a motorcycle crash with skull base fracture he noticed a whooshing noise in his head, a bulging red left eye and double vision.
case.exam: Pulsatile left proptosis, marked chemosis, corkscrew conjunctival vessels, ocular bruit, left abducens palsy, intraocular pressure 32 mmHg.
case.tests: CTA: enlarged left superior ophthalmic vein and cavernous sinus with arterial-phase filling; angiography: direct high-flow fistula from the cavernous internal carotid artery.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the preferred treatment?

det.patho: Direct CCFs result from a tear in the cavernous internal carotid artery after blunt or penetrating trauma, or from rupture of a cavernous carotid aneurysm, and carry high flow. Indirect CCFs are dural arteriovenous fistulas fed by meningeal branches of the internal and/or external carotid arteries; risk factors include older age, female sex, hypertension, pregnancy and venous sinus thrombosis. Arterial pressure transmitted into the cavernous sinus reverses flow into the orbital veins, causing congestion, and may also reroute into cortical veins, which risks haemorrhage or venous infarction.
det.clinical: The classic triad is proptosis, chemosis and orbital bruit. Diplopia comes from abducens, oculomotor or trochlear involvement or from congested extraocular muscles. Raised orbital venous pressure elevates intraocular pressure and can cause glaucoma, retinal venous stasis and optic neuropathy. Indirect fistulas present insidiously with a red eye and are often treated for months as conjunctivitis. Danger signs include falling vision, very high intraocular pressure, rapidly worsening proptosis and cortical venous drainage.
det.diagnosis: CT or MRI shows an enlarged superior ophthalmic vein, proptosis, swollen extraocular muscles and a convex cavernous sinus; CTA, TOF-MRA and dynamic MRA show early sinus filling. Catheter angiography is the reference test, defining feeders (Barrow A direct; B, C and D dural from ICA, ECA or both), flow rate and venous drainage routes, including cortical reflux. Compare both eyes, because drainage across the intercavernous sinus can make findings contralateral or bilateral.
det.treatment: Direct fistulas need endovascular closure, using detachable coils or liquid embolic through a transarterial or transvenous route, covered stents or flow diverters, with parent artery sacrifice only when necessary. Indirect low-flow fistulas without dangerous features may close spontaneously and can be watched with ophthalmic care; transvenous embolisation via the inferior petrosal sinus or superior ophthalmic vein is used when symptoms are significant. Stereotactic radiosurgery is an option for some indirect fistulas. Treat raised intraocular pressure promptly.
det.prognosis: Endovascular cure rates are high, and eye signs usually improve within weeks; delayed treatment risks permanent visual loss.
pearls: A chronic red eye that never clears with drops: think indirect CCF and look at the superior ophthalmic vein.
Cortical venous drainage converts a benign-looking fistula into an urgent one.
Findings can be on the opposite side because the cavernous sinuses communicate across the midline.

det.patho: FMD is an idiopathic disorder of arterial wall cell growth, most often of the media (medial fibroplasia), producing webs and aneurysmal outpouchings that give the beaded appearance; intimal fibroplasia gives focal tubular narrowing. Genetic contributors include a common PHACTR1 variant, and smoking and female hormones appear to modify risk. It is not inflammatory or atherosclerotic. The weakened wall predisposes to dissection and aneurysm.
det.clinical: Many patients are asymptomatic or have headache, pulsatile tinnitus, neck pain or dizziness. Cerebrovascular events include TIA and ischaemic stroke, usually from dissection or embolism, and subarachnoid haemorrhage from intracranial aneurysm. Hypertension from renal FMD, flank pain from renal infarction and spontaneous coronary artery dissection may coexist. It is often found incidentally on imaging done for other reasons.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is radiological: the multifocal beaded pattern in mid-to-distal cervical arteries is characteristic, whereas atherosclerosis affects the bulb and origin. Standing-wave artefact on angiography is regular and transient and should not be mistaken for FMD. The 2019 international consensus recommends head-to-pelvis cross-sectional imaging once in every patient, because multivessel involvement and aneurysms are common. Consider vasculitis or connective tissue disorders if there are systemic or syndromic features.
det.treatment: Most patients receive low-dose aspirin to reduce thromboembolic risk, unless contraindicated. Dissection is managed with antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy as for other dissections. Blood pressure control, smoking cessation and treatment of significant intracranial aneurysms are central. Angioplasty or stenting of cervical FMD is reserved for recurrent ischaemia despite medical therapy; renal angioplasty without stenting is effective for renovascular hypertension.
det.prognosis: Generally favourable with medical therapy; recurrent dissection and aneurysm growth are the main risks and justify periodic surveillance.
pearls: Beading at C1–C2 with a normal bulb is FMD; plaque at the bulb is atherosclerosis.
One FMD bed found means look at all beds, including intracranial aneurysms.
Pulsatile tinnitus in a middle-aged woman: consider cervical FMD.

name: Brain death (death by neurologic criteria)
formal: The irreversible loss of all functions of the brain, including the brainstem, established clinically by coma, absent brainstem reflexes and apnoea after excluding confounders, and legally recognised as death; described in the 2023 AAN/AAP/CNS/SCCM consensus as brain death/death by neurologic criteria (BD/DNC).
simple: The brain, including the part that controls breathing, has permanently stopped working, so the person has died even though a ventilator keeps the heart beating.
ab: determination of death by neurological criteria
ภาวะสมองตาย
th: ภาวะที่สมองทั้งหมดรวมถึงก้านสมองหยุดทำงานอย่างถาวร วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจพบว่าไม่รู้สึกตัว ไม่มี brainstem reflex และไม่หายใจเองจากการทดสอบ apnoea หลังแยกปัจจัยรบกวนออก ถือว่าผู้ป่วยเสียชีวิตตามกฎหมาย

case.who: 39-year-old male construction worker from Samut Prakan

case.q: Does the leg movement exclude brain death, and is an ancillary test required?
case.a: No; triple flexion is a spinal reflex compatible with brain death. With confounders excluded and a completed examination and apnoea test, no ancillary test is needed; death is declared according to national criteria.

det.patho: Brain death results when intracranial pressure exceeds arterial pressure or when global injury is so complete that cerebral and brainstem circulation and function cease. Common causes are traumatic brain injury, massive intracerebral or subarachnoid haemorrhage, large infarction with herniation and hypoxic-ischaemic injury after cardiac arrest. Once the brainstem is destroyed, spontaneous breathing, cranial reflexes and central autonomic regulation are lost; the heart can beat only with ventilatory and haemodynamic support. Diabetes insipidus and haemodynamic instability are frequent accompaniments.
det.clinical: The patient is apnoeic on the ventilator, unresponsive and without brainstem reflexes. Spinal reflexes such as triple flexion, plantar responses, finger flexion, undulating toe movements or the Lazarus sign may occur and do not exclude the diagnosis. Hypotension, hypothermia and polyuria from diabetes insipidus are common. Conditions that can mimic it include high cervical cord injury, severe polyneuropathy (fulminant GBS), hypothermia and intoxication with barbiturates, baclofen or other sedatives.
det.diagnosis: Prerequisites are an established irreversible cause consistent with imaging and the exclusion of confounders (temperature, blood pressure, drugs, metabolic disorders, neuromuscular blockade). After an appropriate observation period, one complete examination is sufficient in adults under the 2023 consensus (two in children), followed by an apnoea test. Ancillary tests are used only when part of the examination or apnoea test cannot be done safely; the 2023 guideline accepts catheter angiography, radionuclide perfusion studies and TCD, and does not endorse EEG or CT/MR angiography in adults. In Thailand, determination follows the Medical Council of Thailand announcement on brain death, which specifies who may certify and how.
det.treatment: There is no treatment once the criteria are met; death is declared. Before testing, optimise physiology so that confounders are removed. Families should be told clearly and compassionately that brain death means the person has died. If organ donation is possible, the donation team (Thai Red Cross Organ Donation Centre) is contacted separately from the treating team, and somatic support continues for donor management.
det.prognosis: Brain death is death; there are no documented recoveries when criteria are correctly applied.
pearls: Spinal reflexes such as triple flexion or the Lazarus sign do not exclude brain death.
Exclude confounders first: hypothermia, hypotension, sedatives (especially thiopental) and neuromuscular blockade.
Ancillary tests support but do not replace the clinical examination; EEG and CTA are not recommended ancillaries in the 2023 consensus.
det.thd: ภาวะสมองตายคือการที่สมองและก้านสมองหยุดทำงานถาวรจากสาเหตุที่ทราบชัด ต้องแยกปัจจัยรบกวนก่อน ได้แก่ อุณหภูมิกายต่ำ ความดันต่ำ ยานอนหลับหรือยาหย่อนกล้ามเนื้อ และความผิดปกติทางเมตาบอลิก แล้วตรวจไม่พบการตอบสนอง ไม่มี brainstem reflex และไม่หายใจเองจาก apnoea test ส่วน reflex ไขสันหลังยังพบได้ การตรวจเสริมใช้เมื่อตรวจทางคลินิกไม่ครบ ประเทศไทยวินิจฉัยตามประกาศแพทยสภา และถือว่าผู้ป่วยเสียชีวิตแล้ว

Check only for pupillary reaction and the cough reflex

det.patho: The skull and dural folds divide the intracranial space into compartments. When a mass, haematoma or oedema raises pressure in one compartment, tissue shifts toward lower pressure: under the falx, through the tentorial incisura (lateral uncal or central), upward through the incisura from the posterior fossa, or down through the foramen magnum. The shifted tissue compresses cranial nerves, the midbrain and medulla, and arteries such as the anterior and posterior cerebral arteries, while stretching of paramedian pontine and midbrain perforators causes Duret haemorrhages. External herniation can occur through a craniectomy defect.
det.clinical: Uncal herniation typically begins with a dilating ipsilateral pupil and ptosis, then declining consciousness, hemiparesis and extensor posturing. Central herniation causes gradual drowsiness, small reactive pupils, Cheyne–Stokes breathing and then progressive brainstem failure. Posterior fossa masses cause upward or tonsillar herniation with headache, neck stiffness, vomiting, sudden apnoea and bradycardia. The Cushing response (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing) signals advanced compromise. Paradoxical herniation after craniectomy can follow lumbar puncture or dehydration.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical and confirmed by CT, which shows midline shift (measured at the septum pellucidum), effacement of the basal cisterns, medial temporal lobe displacement, trapped contralateral ventricle, and complications such as posterior cerebral artery infarct or brainstem haemorrhage. The degree of cistern effacement predicts outcome better than shift alone. Lumbar puncture must not be done when imaging shows mass effect.
det.treatment: Immediate measures: secure airway, head of bed 30°, keep the neck straight, normothermia, adequate sedation and analgesia. Give hyperosmolar therapy (mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg or hypertonic saline); short-term hyperventilation to PaCO2 about 30–35 mmHg is only a bridge. Definitive treatment targets the cause: evacuation of haematoma, external ventricular drain for hydrocephalus, tumour steroids (dexamethasone for vasogenic oedema) or decompressive craniectomy. Correct coagulopathy and hyponatraemia.
det.prognosis: Depends on cause and speed of reversal; Duret haemorrhage and prolonged bilateral fixed pupils carry a very poor outlook.
pearls: A dilating pupil in a drowsy patient with a mass is uncal herniation until proven otherwise.
Kernohan notch produces ipsilateral hemiparesis, a false-localising sign.
Never perform lumbar puncture before imaging in a patient with focal signs or reduced consciousness.

simple: Serious brain injury in a baby caused by someone shaking or hitting them.

th: การบาดเจ็บของสมองในทารกหรือเด็กเล็กจากการถูกเขย่าหรือกระแทกอย่างรุนแรง ลักษณะสำคัญคือเลือดออกใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมอง เลือดออกที่จอประสาทตา และสมองขาดออกซิเจน ประวัติมักไม่สอดคล้องกับการบาดเจ็บ ต้องแจ้งทีมคุ้มครองเด็ก
tempoNote: Acute collapse, seizures or apnoea, sometimes after earlier unrecognised episodes; injuries of differing ages may coexist
feat: Usually under 1 year (peak 2–4 months, when crying peaks); presents with lethargy, vomiting, seizures, apnoea or collapse
History absent, changing or incompatible with the infant's development or the injuries
Thin subdural haematomas over the convexities and along the falx or tentorium, sometimes of mixed density
Extensive multilayer retinal haemorrhages reaching the periphery, with or without retinoschisis
Associated fractures (posterior ribs, classic metaphyseal lesions), bruising in a non-mobile infant, cervical ligament injury
inv: Non-contrast CT head initially; MRI brain with DWI and SWI plus MRI cervical (whole) spine
Dilated fundoscopy by an ophthalmologist within 24–72 h
Skeletal survey (repeat after about 2 weeks), coagulation screen, vitamin K status, liver enzymes, urine organic acids for glutaric aciduria type I
Child protection team and multidisciplinary assessment; document carefully

case.who: 3-month-old boy brought at night to a district hospital in Lop Buri by his father
case.story: The father says the baby suddenly went limp after feeding; there is no history of a fall. The baby has cried a lot over the past weeks.
case.exam: Drowsy, bulging fontanelle, two small bruises on the chest; focal seizure of the right arm.
case.tests: CT: thin bilateral convexity subdural collections of mixed density and interhemispheric blood; MRI: DWI changes in both hemispheres and bridging vein thrombosis; fundoscopy: numerous multilayer retinal haemorrhages to the ora serrata; skeletal survey: two healing posterior rib fractures; coagulation normal; urine organic acids normal.
case.q: Which diagnosis fits best, and what else needs to be done apart from treatment?
case.a: Abusive head trauma; the hospital child protection team must be involved and the case reported under Thai child protection law, ensuring the infant's and siblings' safety.

det.patho: Infants have large heads, weak neck muscles and incompletely myelinated brains. Violent acceleration–deceleration with or without impact tears bridging veins, producing subdural haemorrhage, and causes retinal and optic nerve sheath haemorrhages. The dominant cause of death and disability is secondary hypoxic-ischaemic injury, related partly to apnoea from craniocervical junction injury, together with seizures and brain swelling. Repeated episodes are common before diagnosis.
det.clinical: Presentation ranges from irritability, poor feeding and vomiting to seizures, apnoea, coma and death. Mild cases are often misdiagnosed as gastroenteritis or sepsis. Clues include a history that changes or does not fit, delay in seeking care, sentinel injuries such as bruises in a non-mobile baby, and unexplained fractures. Survivors frequently have epilepsy, cerebral palsy, visual impairment and intellectual disability.
det.diagnosis: AHT is a multidisciplinary diagnosis made after excluding medical mimics. Neuroimaging (CT then MRI with DWI and SWI and spine MRI) documents subdural haemorrhage, hypoxic-ischaemic injury, bridging vein thrombosis and spinal ligament injury. Ophthalmology, skeletal survey, coagulation and metabolic tests (including glutaric aciduria type I and vitamin K deficiency bleeding, relevant where neonatal prophylaxis may be missed) are essential. Mixed-density subdurals are not reliably datable by imaging alone, and birth-related subdurals normally resolve within the first month.
det.treatment: Treat the injury: airway, seizures, raised intracranial pressure and neurosurgical drainage when needed. Notify the hospital child protection team immediately and report according to Thai law (Child Protection Act B.E. 2546), while ensuring safety of siblings. Follow-up includes rehabilitation, vision and developmental services and long-term epilepsy care. Prevention programmes that teach parents about normal infant crying (e.g. the Period of PURPLE Crying approach) reduce risk.
det.prognosis: Poor overall: mortality is roughly 15–25%, and most survivors have lasting neurological or cognitive disability.
pearls: Subdural haemorrhage plus extensive multilayer retinal haemorrhages in an infant with no adequate history is AHT until proven otherwise.
Bruising in a baby who cannot yet cruise is a sentinel injury; investigate.
Exclude glutaric aciduria type I, coagulopathy and vitamin K deficiency bleeding, but do not let the search delay protection.
det.thd: Abusive head trauma คือการบาดเจ็บของสมองทารกจากการเขย่าหรือกระแทก พบบ่อยในทารกอายุ 2–4 เดือน มีเลือดออกใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมอง เลือดออกที่จอประสาทตาหลายชั้น สมองขาดออกซิเจน และกระดูกซี่โครงหักโดยประวัติไม่สอดคล้อง ต้องตรวจ CT/MRI ตรวจตา skeletal survey การแข็งตัวของเลือด และแยกโรค glutaric aciduria type I แจ้งทีมคุ้มครองเด็กตาม พ.ร.บ.คุ้มครองเด็ก พ.ศ. 2546 ผลการรักษามักไม่ดีและมีความพิการระยะยาว

name: Septo-optic dysplasia (SOD)
formal: A congenital disorder defined by any two of optic nerve hypoplasia, midline forebrain anomalies (absent septum pellucidum and/or callosal dysgenesis) and hypothalamic–pituitary hypoplasia with hormone deficiency; also called de Morsier syndrome.
simple: A birth condition where the eye nerves are small, a thin wall in the middle of the brain is missing, and the pituitary gland may not make enough hormones.
ab: optic nerve hypoplasia with absent septum pellucidum
th: ความผิดปกติแต่กำเนิดที่มีอย่างน้อยสองในสามอย่าง ได้แก่ เส้นประสาทตาเล็กผิดปกติ ไม่มี septum pellucidum หรือ corpus callosum ผิดปกติ และต่อมใต้สมองเจริญไม่ดีจนขาดฮอร์โมน ทำให้ตามองเห็นไม่ดี ตาสั่น และน้ำตาลต่ำในทารก
tempoNote: Present from birth; endocrine deficiencies may appear or evolve throughout childhood
feat: Infant with poor visual fixation, roving or pendular nystagmus and small pale optic discs (double-ring sign)
Neonatal hypoglycaemia, prolonged jaundice, micropenis, later short stature or delayed puberty
Risk of adrenal crisis and diabetes insipidus
MRI: small optic nerves and chiasm, absent septum pellucidum with box-shaped frontal horns, small anterior pituitary, ectopic posterior pituitary bright spot
Often born to young mothers; 'SOD-plus' when combined with schizencephaly or cortical malformation
inv: MRI brain with thin-section orbits and pituitary
Endocrine testing: cortisol, thyroid, GH/IGF-1, gonadotropins, sodium and urine osmolality; repeat over time
Ophthalmology with visual assessment; genetic testing (HESX1, SOX2, SOX3, OTX2) in selected cases

case.who: 6-week-old girl, first child of a 17-year-old mother in Mae Hong Son
case.story: Recurrent low blood glucose in the first days of life and prolonged jaundice; parents notice her eyes 'wander' and she does not follow faces.
case.exam: Pendular nystagmus, no fixation, small pale optic discs with a peripapillary halo bilaterally.
case.tests: MRI: thin optic nerves and chiasm, absent septum pellucidum, small anterior pituitary with ectopic posterior pituitary bright spot at the median eminence; morning cortisol low.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what is the most urgent management concern?
case.a: Septo-optic dysplasia with hypopituitarism; start hydrocortisone replacement with stress-dose education to prevent adrenal crisis and hypoglycaemia, then assess other pituitary axes.

read.where: Chapter 9 Congenital Disorders of the Brain and Spine — congenital optic nerve hypoplasia

det.patho: SOD reflects abnormal development of the anterior midline forebrain and hypothalamic–pituitary axis in early pregnancy. Most cases are sporadic and linked with young maternal age, first pregnancy and possibly environmental factors; a minority carry variants in transcription factor genes such as HESX1, SOX2, SOX3 or OTX2. The clinical spectrum is broad, and only a minority have all three components.
det.clinical: Visual impairment ranges from near-normal to blindness, with nystagmus often the first sign at 1–3 months. Neonates may have hypoglycaemia, conjugated jaundice and micropenis. Growth hormone deficiency is the most common hormone loss, followed by TSH and ACTH deficiency; diabetes insipidus is less common. Developmental delay, autism traits, epilepsy and hypothalamic problems (sleep, temperature, appetite) occur especially in SOD-plus.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis needs two of the three components. MRI shows optic nerve and chiasm hypoplasia, absent or deficient septum pellucidum (flat-roofed frontal horns pointing inferiorly on coronal images), hypoplastic anterior pituitary and ectopic posterior pituitary. Fundoscopy shows small discs, sometimes with a double-ring sign. Endocrine testing must be repeated because deficiencies evolve. Look for associated cortical malformations.
det.treatment: Hormone replacement as indicated (hydrocortisone with stress dosing, levothyroxine after cortisol, growth hormone, sex steroids at puberty, desmopressin for diabetes insipidus). Early visual intervention and developmental services improve function. Families need emergency plans for adrenal crisis. Manage epilepsy and behavioural or sleep problems as they arise.
det.prognosis: Highly variable; endocrine and visual problems are lifelong, and hidden ACTH deficiency is a preventable cause of death.
pearls: Neonatal hypoglycaemia plus nystagmus: look at the optic discs and image the pituitary.
An absent septum pellucidum on imaging should trigger examination of optic nerves and pituitary.
Repeat endocrine testing over time — normal results in infancy do not exclude later deficiency.
det.thd: Septo-optic dysplasia (de Morsier) คือภาวะแต่กำเนิดที่มีเส้นประสาทตาเล็ก ไม่มี septum pellucidum และต่อมใต้สมองบกพร่องอย่างน้อยสองอย่าง ทารกมีตาสั่น มองไม่เห็น น้ำตาลต่ำ ตัวเหลืองนาน อวัยวะเพศเล็ก MRI เห็นเส้นประสาทตาเล็ก ไม่มี septum และ posterior pituitary อยู่ผิดตำแหน่ง ต้องตรวจฮอร์โมนซ้ำเป็นระยะ ให้ hydrocortisone และฮอร์โมนอื่นตามที่ขาด และฟื้นฟูการมองเห็นตั้งแต่เนิ่น ๆ

name: Agenesis of the corpus callosum (ACC)
formal: Complete or partial failure of the corpus callosum to form, occurring in isolation or with other brain malformations or genetic syndromes, with characteristic imaging of parallel, widely separated lateral ventricles, colpocephaly, a high-riding third ventricle and Probst bundles.
simple: The thick band of nerve fibres that joins the two halves of the brain did not form, completely or partly, before birth.
ab: partial agenesis of the corpus callosum
ภาวะไม่มี corpus callosum แต่กำเนิด
th: ภาวะแต่กำเนิดที่ corpus callosum ไม่เกิดขึ้นทั้งหมดหรือบางส่วน อาจพบเดี่ยว ๆ หรือร่วมกับความผิดปกติอื่นและกลุ่มอาการทางพันธุกรรม ผู้ป่วยแบบเดี่ยว ๆ จำนวนมากมีพัฒนาการปกติหรือผิดปกติเล็กน้อย
tempoNote: Present from fetal life; often detected on prenatal ultrasound or later imaging for delay or seizures
feat: Prenatal ultrasound: absent cavum septi pellucidi, colpocephaly or mild ventriculomegaly
MRI: parallel non-converging lateral ventricles, enlarged occipital horns, high-riding third ventricle, Probst bundles indenting the frontal horns
Medial hemispheric sulci radiate to the third ventricle with an absent cingulate gyrus
Associated: interhemispheric cyst, lipoma, heterotopia, polymicrogyria, Dandy–Walker spectrum
Isolated cases often have normal or mildly affected intelligence; syndromic cases have epilepsy and developmental delay
inv: Fetal MRI after ultrasound suspicion; postnatal MRI brain
Chromosomal microarray, then exome or genome sequencing
Ophthalmology for chorioretinal lacunae (Aicardi syndrome in girls); metabolic tests if indicated (glycine, lactate)

case.who: Primigravida, 32 years old, at 22 weeks' gestation in a Bangkok antenatal clinic
case.story: Routine anomaly scan could not see the cavum septi pellucidi and noted mildly enlarged posterior horns.
case.exam: Fetal biometry otherwise normal; no other anomalies on detailed ultrasound.
case.tests: Fetal MRI: complete absence of the corpus callosum with parallel lateral ventricles, colpocephaly and Probst bundles; no cortical malformation; amniocentesis microarray normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and how should counselling be framed?
case.a: Isolated complete agenesis of the corpus callosum; most isolated cases have normal or mildly impaired development, but a minority have significant delay, and exome sequencing and postnatal MRI help refine prognosis.

read.where: Chapter 9 Congenital Disorders of the Brain and Spine — agenesis of the corpus callosum
18. Disorders of Cranial Volume and Shape

det.patho: The corpus callosum forms between about 10 and 20 weeks' gestation, guided by midline glial structures; disruption of axon guidance or midline patterning prevents commissural fibres from crossing. The axons that cannot cross turn and run front to back along the medial ventricles as Probst bundles. Causes include chromosomal abnormalities, single-gene disorders (more than a hundred genes, e.g. DCC, ARX, L1CAM, ZEB2), Aicardi syndrome, metabolic disorders (non-ketotic hyperglycinaemia, pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency) and teratogens such as alcohol.
det.clinical: Isolated ACC may be clinically silent or cause mild problems with processing speed, social cognition and complex problem-solving; some show subtle disconnection signs on testing. Complex ACC with other malformations or syndromes presents with developmental delay, intellectual disability, epilepsy, hypotonia or macrocephaly. Mirror movements suggest DCC variants. Girls with infantile spasms and chorioretinal lacunae point to Aicardi syndrome.
det.diagnosis: Prenatal ultrasound raises suspicion, and fetal MRI confirms and searches for associated anomalies, which strongly influence prognosis. Postnatal MRI shows absent or partial corpus callosum, Probst bundles, colpocephaly, vertical hippocampi and radiating medial sulci; partial agenesis usually spares the anterior parts. Genetic testing (microarray, then exome) is advised in all cases. Mild ventriculomegaly alone is not diagnostic.
det.treatment: There is no treatment to restore the callosum. Care is supportive: developmental surveillance, early therapy services, educational support, management of epilepsy and treatment of associated conditions. Genetic counselling guides recurrence risk.
det.prognosis: Isolated ACC carries a good prognosis in the majority (roughly three-quarters normal or mildly affected); associated anomalies or syndromes predict poorer outcome.
pearls: Absent cavum septi pellucidi on an anomaly scan should prompt a look for callosal agenesis.
Parallel ventricles plus colpocephaly plus high third ventricle = ACC on axial imaging.
Girl with infantile spasms, callosal agenesis and chorioretinal lacunae: Aicardi syndrome.
det.thd: Agenesis of the corpus callosum คือภาวะที่ corpus callosum ไม่เกิดขึ้นทั้งหมดหรือบางส่วน ตรวจพบได้ตั้งแต่ ultrasound ระหว่างตั้งครรภ์ ภาพ MRI เห็นโพรงสมองข้างขนานกัน colpocephaly โพรงสมองที่สามอยู่สูง และ Probst bundles ถ้าเป็นเดี่ยว ๆ ส่วนใหญ่พัฒนาการปกติหรือผิดปกติเล็กน้อย ถ้ามีความผิดปกติอื่นร่วมมักมีชักและพัฒนาการช้า ควรตรวจพันธุกรรม การดูแลเป็นแบบประคับประคอง

name: Hemimegalencephaly (HME)
formal: A hamartomatous malformation of cortical development in which all or part of one cerebral hemisphere is enlarged with dysplastic cortex and white matter, usually caused by somatic mosaic variants in the PI3K–AKT–mTOR pathway, presenting with early-onset drug-resistant epilepsy, hemiparesis and developmental delay.
simple: One half of the baby's brain grows too big and abnormal, causing very hard-to-control seizures.
ab: สมองซีกเดียวโตผิดปกติ
th: ความผิดปกติของการเจริญของเปลือกสมองที่ทำให้สมองซีกหนึ่งโตและเปลือกสมองผิดปกติ มักเกิดจากการกลายพันธุ์ในบางเซลล์ของ mTOR pathway ทารกมีชักรุนแรงตั้งแต่ขวบปีแรก ดื้อยา แขนขาอ่อนแรงข้างหนึ่ง และพัฒนาการช้า
tempoNote: Present from birth; seizures often begin in the first weeks or months and escalate
feat: Neonatal or infant-onset focal seizures or epileptic spasms resistant to medication
Macrocephaly with an enlarged hemisphere, contralateral hemiparesis and hemianopia, developmental delay
MRI: thick dysplastic cortex with broad gyri, blurred grey–white junction, abnormal white matter signal, enlarged ipsilateral ventricle with a straightened, pointed frontal horn
EEG: asymmetric burst-suppression or hemihypsarrhythmia over the affected side
May be isolated or part of a syndrome (linear sebaceous naevus, hypomelanosis of Ito, PIK3CA-related overgrowth, Proteus, NF1, tuberous sclerosis)
inv: MRI brain with high-resolution volumetric T1/T2 sequences; FDG-PET and EEG for surgical planning
Skin examination for naevi and pigmentary lines; body examination for overgrowth
Genetic testing on resected brain tissue (somatic PIK3CA, AKT3, MTOR) and blood for germline causes

case.who: 5-week-old boy at a university hospital in Songkhla
case.story: Seizures with left-sided stiffening and eye deviation from the second week, now dozens a day despite phenobarbital and levetiracetam.
case.exam: Head circumference above the 97th centile, poor left-sided movement, no skin lesions.
case.tests: MRI: enlarged right hemisphere with thick cortex, broad gyri, blurred grey–white boundary, abnormal T2 signal in white matter and an enlarged right lateral ventricle with a pointed frontal horn; EEG: burst-suppression mostly over the right hemisphere.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what treatment offers the best chance of seizure control?
case.a: Hemimegalencephaly; early hemispheric disconnection surgery (functional hemispherotomy or anatomical hemispherectomy) at an experienced paediatric epilepsy centre.

read.where: Chapter 9 Congenital Disorders of the Brain and Spine — abnormalities of neuronal migration

det.patho: Hemimegalencephaly results from somatic (post-zygotic) gain-of-function variants in genes of the PI3K–AKT–mTOR pathway, such as PIK3CA, AKT3 and MTOR, arising in neural progenitors of one hemisphere; the proportion of mutant cells influences extent. Increased mTOR signalling causes overgrowth of neurons and glia, abnormal neuronal migration and lamination, dysmorphic neurons and balloon cells, similar to focal cortical dysplasia type II. Germline causes and overgrowth syndromes account for some cases.
det.clinical: Most children present in the first months with frequent focal seizures, epileptic spasms or early-infantile developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. Macrocephaly, contralateral hemiparesis and visual field loss are typical, and development is usually delayed, worse with uncontrolled seizures. Some have skin naevi, pigmentary mosaicism or body overgrowth. The contralateral hemisphere usually develops normally if seizures are controlled early.
det.diagnosis: MRI is diagnostic: an enlarged hemisphere with abnormal cortex (pachygyria, polymicrogyria or dysplasia), blurred grey–white junction, white matter signal change (sometimes accelerated myelination in infancy) and an enlarged, abnormally shaped ipsilateral lateral ventricle. Careful review of the 'normal' side matters, because bilateral abnormalities affect surgical outcome. EEG and FDG-PET confirm lateralisation. Tissue testing after surgery often finds the somatic variant.
det.treatment: Antiseizure medication rarely controls seizures. Early hemispheric surgery (functional hemispherotomy, or anatomical hemispherectomy in very young infants) gives seizure freedom in about 60–70% of well-selected patients and improves development. Surgery in the first months requires specialised anaesthesia and blood management, sometimes staged or preceded by embolisation. mTOR inhibitors (sirolimus, everolimus) and PI3K inhibitors such as alpelisib are being explored. Rehabilitation addresses hemiparesis and visual field loss.
det.prognosis: Without surgery, epilepsy is typically intractable with severe developmental impairment; early surgery substantially improves seizure and developmental outcomes.
pearls: Enlarged hemisphere plus enlarged ipsilateral ventricle with a pointed frontal horn: hemimegalencephaly.
Refer early for hemispherotomy; waiting for more drug trials costs development.
Check the skin: linear naevi or mosaic pigmentation point to a syndromic form.
det.thd: Hemimegalencephaly คือภาวะที่สมองซีกหนึ่งโตผิดปกติพร้อมเปลือกสมองผิดรูป มักเกิดจาก somatic variant ใน mTOR pathway ทารกมีชักรุนแรงตั้งแต่ขวบปีแรก ดื้อยา ศีรษะโต อ่อนแรงข้างตรงข้าม MRI เห็นซีกสมองโต เปลือกสมองหนา และโพรงสมองข้างเดียวกันขยาย การผ่าตัด hemispherotomy ตั้งแต่เนิ่น ๆ ช่วยให้หยุดชักได้ราวสองในสามและพัฒนาการดีขึ้น

name: Septic cavernous sinus thrombosis
formal: Infective thrombosis of the cavernous sinus, usually from spread of sphenoid or ethmoid sinusitis, facial ('danger triangle') infection, dental or orbital infection, most often due to Staphylococcus aureus, presenting with fever, headache, chemosis, proptosis and painful ophthalmoplegia that frequently becomes bilateral.
simple: A blood clot with infection in the vein pool behind the eyes, usually spread from a sinus or face infection, causing fever, swollen bulging eyes and eyes that cannot move.
ab: septic thrombophlebitis of the cavernous sinus
ลิ่มเลือดติดเชื้อใน cavernous sinus
th: การติดเชื้อร่วมกับลิ่มเลือดใน cavernous sinus มักลามจากไซนัส sphenoid/ethmoid ฝีหรือสิวอักเสบบริเวณกลางใบหน้า หรือฟันผุ ผู้ป่วยมีไข้ ปวดศีรษะ ตาบวมแดงโปน กลอกตาไม่ได้ และมักลามไปอีกข้างใน 1–2 วัน ต้องให้ยาปฏิชีวนะทางหลอดเลือดทันที
tempoNote: Evolves over days; contralateral eye involvement within 24–48 hours is characteristic
feat: Fever, severe retro-orbital or frontal headache and systemic toxicity
Periorbital oedema, chemosis and proptosis that spreads to the opposite eye
Painful ophthalmoplegia (VI often first), ptosis, sensory loss in V1/V2 and a sluggish pupil
Recent sphenoid or ethmoid sinusitis, facial furuncle, dental abscess or orbital cellulitis
Complications: meningitis, ICA narrowing or infarct, pituitary failure, sepsis
inv: Contrast MRI with MR venography or contrast CT: enlarged cavernous sinus with filling defects, thrombosed superior ophthalmic vein, sinusitis source
Blood cultures before antibiotics; culture of sinus or abscess material
Lumbar puncture when meningitis is suspected and imaging allows
Glucose/HbA1c and immune status; consider fungal infection (mucormycosis, Aspergillus) in diabetes or immunosuppression

case.who: 38-year-old woman from Surin with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes
case.story: She squeezed a boil beside her nose a week ago; for two days she has had fever, a pounding headache and a swollen right eye, and today the left eye is also puffy.
case.exam: Temperature 39.4 °C, bilateral chemosis and proptosis worse on the right, right complete ophthalmoplegia with ptosis, left VI palsy, reduced right forehead sensation; neck slightly stiff.
case.tests: Contrast MRI: both cavernous sinuses expanded with non-enhancing filling defects and thrombosed superior ophthalmic veins; blood cultures grow methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what is the cornerstone of treatment?
case.a: Septic cavernous sinus thrombosis; urgent high-dose IV anti-staphylococcal antibiotics (with Gram-negative/anaerobic cover until cultures are known), drainage of the source, and therapeutic anticoagulation in most cases.

det.patho: The cavernous sinuses receive valveless facial, ophthalmic and pterygoid venous drainage, so infection can travel backwards into them; the two sinuses connect through intercavernous channels, explaining rapid bilateral spread. Thrombus and pus compress the oculomotor, trochlear, abducens and first two trigeminal divisions (III, IV, VI, V1, V2) and narrow the cavernous ICA. Staphylococcus aureus causes most cases; streptococci, Gram-negatives, anaerobes and, in diabetes or neutropenia, fungi account for the rest.
det.clinical: Most patients look ill, with fever and headache preceding eye signs by a day or two. Chemosis, lid oedema and proptosis then appear with painful ophthalmoplegia; abducens palsy often comes first because the nerve lies free within the sinus. Involvement of the second eye strongly favours CST over orbital cellulitis. Altered consciousness may signal meningitis, cerebritis or ICA infarction, and late hypopituitarism is described.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical plus imaging. Contrast MRI with venography shows an enlarged, irregular, poorly enhancing sinus, convex lateral walls, a dilated thrombosed superior ophthalmic vein and the infective source; CT with contrast is acceptable when MRI is not available. Blood cultures are positive in many. Distinguish orbital cellulitis (unilateral, no cavernous filling defect) and aseptic causes of a painful cavernous sinus.
det.treatment: Begin IV antibiotics immediately: an anti-staphylococcal agent (with vancomycin if MRSA is possible) plus a third-generation cephalosporin and metronidazole for sinus or dental sources, refined by cultures and continued for 3–4 weeks or longer. Drain the source (sphenoid sinus surgery, abscess or dental drainage). Anticoagulation with heparin is widely used and associated with lower morbidity in observational series, after excluding intracranial bleeding. Corticosteroids are reserved for pituitary insufficiency or selected cases; antifungal therapy and debridement are required for fungal infection.
det.prognosis: Mortality has fallen to around 10–20% with antibiotics, but up to half of survivors keep cranial nerve palsies, visual loss or pituitary dysfunction.
pearls: Spread to the second eye within a day or two separates CST from orbital cellulitis.
Abducens palsy is often the first ocular motor sign because VI floats within the sinus.
In a diabetic with black nasal crusts think mucormycosis rather than bacterial CST.

name: Superior semicircular canal dehiscence syndrome (SSCDS)

case.who: 46-year-old female temple choir singer from Ayutthaya

det.patho: Normally the inner ear has two compliant windows (oval and round), so sound energy travels through the cochlea. A bony defect over the superior canal creates a third, lower-impedance window: sound and pressure shunt fluid through the canal, stimulating its ampulla, while bone-conducted sound is heard better and air-conducted sound worse. Thin bone is likely developmental, with symptoms unmasked by ageing, trauma or straining; posterior canal dehiscence and other third windows cause similar features.
det.clinical: Patients describe sound- or pressure-induced vertigo, autophony, pulsatile or gaze-evoked sounds in the ear, fullness and imbalance; many have only auditory symptoms. Nystagmus evoked by loud tones, Valsalva or tragal pressure lies in the plane of the affected canal. Dehiscence may be bilateral. Coexisting migraine and persistent dizziness are common and influence outcome after surgery.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on three elements: compatible symptoms, physiological evidence of a third window (low cVEMP thresholds or high oVEMP amplitudes, a low-frequency air–bone gap with intact reflexes, or pressure/sound-evoked nystagmus) and high-resolution CT confirming the defect in reconstructions along the canal. Thin bone on routine axial CT is often over-called, so imaging must match the physiology; incidental dehiscence on CT without symptoms is not treated.
det.treatment: Explanation and trigger avoidance suffice for mild cases; treat coexisting migraine. Disabling symptoms justify surgical plugging or resurfacing of the canal, via a middle fossa craniotomy or a transmastoid approach, which relieves sound/pressure vertigo and autophony in most patients. Round window reinforcement is a less invasive option with less predictable results. Vestibular rehabilitation helps residual imbalance.
det.prognosis: Not progressive in most; canal plugging gives durable symptom relief in about 80–90%, with a small risk of hearing loss or transient vestibular hypofunction.
pearls: Air–bone gap with intact stapedial reflexes is a third window, not otosclerosis.
Hearing one's own eyeballs move is almost pathognomonic of a third window.
Confirm the defect on reformats in the plane of the superior canal; axial CT overestimates dehiscence.

qx.stem: A 50-year-old male tour guide from Kanchanaburi complains that his own voice sounds loud in his left ear and that the ground seems to move briefly when a bus horn sounds. qx.why: A bony defect over the superior canal acts as a third window: VEMPs show abnormally low thresholds and large amplitudes, and the air–bone gap occurs with preserved reflexes. Symptoms must match physiology because thin bone is over-called on CT. Caloric and head-impulse deficits indicate vestibular hypofunction, Dix–Hallpike nystagmus indicates posterior canal BPPV, and absent reflexes would point to otosclerosis.

name: Skull base osteomyelitis (necrotising otitis externa)

case.who: 71-year-old male rice farmer from Roi Et with type 2 diabetes for 20 years

det.patho: Pseudomonas aeruginosa invades the external canal skin at the bony–cartilaginous junction, often after minor trauma such as cotton-bud cleaning or ear syringing, and spreads through the fissures of Santorini to the stylomastoid foramen, jugular foramen, hypoglossal canal and clivus. Diabetic microangiopathy and impaired neutrophil function allow the infection to persist. Fungi (Aspergillus, Candida), Staphylococcus aureus and other Gram-negatives cause a minority, and 'central' skull base osteomyelitis can arise from sinus or deep neck sources without ear disease.
det.clinical: Severe, relentless ear pain out of proportion to the findings, worse at night, is the hallmark; discharge and granulation tissue follow. Facial palsy is the commonest neuropathy, followed by glossopharyngeal, vagal, accessory and hypoglossal involvement as the jugular foramen and hypoglossal canal are reached (Vernet or Collet–Sicard patterns). Headache, VI palsy and trigeminal pain suggest petrous apex or clival spread. Systemic signs are often minimal, which delays diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: Combine clinical setting, inflammatory markers and imaging. CT shows cortical bone erosion but changes lag behind infection; MRI is more sensitive, showing marrow replacement, enhancing soft tissue in the infratemporal and parapharyngeal spaces and nerve foramina, and venous sinus thrombosis. Deep biopsy is important both for culture (rising fluoroquinolone resistance, fungi) and to exclude squamous cell carcinoma or nasopharyngeal carcinoma, which can look identical.
det.treatment: Prolonged culture-guided antibiotics are the mainstay: IV antipseudomonal beta-lactam (ceftazidime, cefepime, piperacillin–tazobactam or a carbapenem), with step-down to oral ciprofloxacin when sensitive, for at least 6 weeks and often 8–12. Antifungal therapy (voriconazole) is needed for Aspergillus. Tight glycaemic control, local debridement and analgesia are essential; surgery is limited to biopsy, debridement or abscess drainage. Monitor CRP/ESR and repeat MRI; anticoagulation is considered for venous sinus thrombosis.
det.prognosis: Cure is achievable with prolonged therapy, but relapse occurs in up to 15–20%; cranial nerve palsies often persist and mortality remains significant in frail patients with multiple palsies.
pearls: Night-time ear pain in an elderly diabetic with otorrhoea is necrotising otitis externa until proven otherwise.
Always biopsy — carcinoma of the ear canal or nasopharynx can masquerade as skull base osteomyelitis.
Facial palsy appears first; IX–XII involvement means the jugular foramen region is reached.

det.patho: Facial nerve schwannomas are WHO grade 1 nerve sheath tumours made of Schwann cells, usually sporadic and occasionally part of NF2-related schwannomatosis. They may involve any segment from the cerebellopontine angle to the parotid, often spanning several segments, with the geniculate ganglion most frequently affected. Because the tumour displaces rather than infiltrates fascicles, function can remain good for a long time.
det.clinical: Presentation depends on the segment: proximal tumours mimic vestibular schwannoma with hearing loss; tympanic tumours cause conductive loss and a middle-ear mass; geniculate tumours cause facial weakness, twitching and sometimes extend into the middle cranial fossa; parotid tumours present as a neck or parotid lump. Some patients present with recurrent ipsilateral palsies or a palsy that never recovers. Many small tumours are found incidentally on MRI.
det.diagnosis: Gadolinium MRI shows a well-defined tubular or beaded enhancing lesion along the nerve, sometimes with a 'dumbbell' shape across the geniculate ganglion into the middle fossa. CT demonstrates smooth bony canal enlargement, unlike the destructive change of malignancy or paraganglioma. Distinguish from facial nerve venous malformation (haemangioma), which has bony spicules on CT, perineural tumour spread from parotid malignancy, and inflammatory enhancement in Bell's palsy or Ramsay Hunt syndrome.
det.treatment: Because surgery usually sacrifices the nerve and requires grafting (best result House–Brackmann III), small tumours with good function are observed with serial MRI. Stereotactic radiosurgery achieves good tumour control with preserved function in most series. Resection with cable grafting is reserved for poor facial function (HB IV or worse), large or growing tumours or brainstem compression; decompression of the bony canal is an option to slow functional decline. Eye protection and rehabilitation of synkinesis complete care.
det.prognosis: Usually slow growth; long-term facial outcome depends on function at the time of treatment.
pearls: Recurrent ipsilateral or slowly progressive 'Bell's palsy' should always be imaged with gadolinium MRI.
Twitching before weakness points to a tumour rather than idiopathic palsy.
Do not resect early when function is good — surgery usually leaves at best moderate facial weakness.

Steroid–antiviral treatment is for idiopathic palsy, parotidectomy is irrelevant to a geniculate lesion, and botulinum toxin only treats spasm.

name: Endolymphatic sac tumour (ELST)
formal: A rare, slow-growing but locally destructive papillary adenomatous tumour arising from the endolymphatic sac and duct within the posterior petrous bone, sporadic or associated with von Hippel–Lindau disease, causing sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, vertigo and facial palsy, with a retrolabyrinthine lytic mass containing calcific spicules on CT.
simple: A rare slow tumour of a small inner-ear fluid sac, often in people with von Hippel–Lindau disease, that can cause sudden or gradual deafness, ringing and dizziness.
ab: low-grade adenocarcinoma of endolymphatic sac origin
เนื้องอก endolymphatic sac
th: เนื้องอกหายากของ endolymphatic sac ในกระดูกขมับ พบได้บ่อยขึ้นในผู้ป่วย von Hippel–Lindau ทำให้หูดับหรือหูตึงข้างเดียว มีเสียงในหู เวียนศีรษะคล้าย Ménière และอาจหน้าเบี้ยว CT เห็นการกัดกร่อนกระดูกหลัง labyrinth มีจุดแคลเซียม ผู้ป่วย VHL ควรได้ MRI หูชั้นในเป็นระยะ
tempoNote: Slow growth over years; hearing can be lost suddenly from intralabyrinthine haemorrhage or hydrops
feat: Unilateral (or bilateral in VHL) sensorineural hearing loss, sometimes sudden and irreversible
Tinnitus, aural fullness and episodic vertigo that mimic Ménière's disease
Facial palsy or other cranial neuropathies when large
Associated haemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma or pancreatic cysts in VHL
inv: CT temporal bone: permeative retrolabyrinthine lytic lesion with central bony spicules and a thin calcified rim
MRI: heterogeneous T1 hyperintense foci (blood products), avid enhancement, intralabyrinthine haemorrhage
Audiometry; VHL germline testing in every patient
Angiography and preoperative embolisation for larger hypervascular tumours

case.who: 31-year-old man from Chanthaburi who had a cerebellar haemangioblastoma removed at 26
case.story: He woke with sudden deafness in the left ear eight months ago, and since then has had episodes of spinning vertigo and constant tinnitus.
case.exam: Left profound hearing loss on tuning-fork tests, right-beating nystagmus during an episode, retinal haemangioblastoma on fundoscopy.
case.tests: CT shows a lytic retrolabyrinthine mass with internal bony spicules on the left; MRI shows a heterogeneously T1-bright enhancing lesion with high signal in the vestibule; germline VHL pathogenic variant.
case.q: What is the lesion, and what surveillance would have helped?
case.a: Endolymphatic sac tumour in von Hippel–Lindau disease; regular MRI of the internal auditory canals and audiometry in VHL carriers allow removal of small tumours before hearing is lost.

det.patho: ELST is a low-grade papillary epithelial tumour arising from the endolymphatic sac or duct on the posterior surface of the petrous bone. Most are sporadic, but about 10–15% of people with VHL disease develop one, sometimes bilaterally; tumours in VHL show loss of the VHL tumour suppressor and HIF-driven hypervascularity. Hearing loss results from intralabyrinthine haemorrhage, endolymphatic hydrops from sac obstruction, or direct invasion.
det.clinical: Patients, typically young or middle-aged adults, report unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus and episodic vertigo; sudden irreversible deafness can occur even with a tiny tumour. Larger tumours erode into the cerebellopontine angle, middle ear or jugular foramen, causing facial palsy and lower cranial neuropathies. The course is slow, and metastasis is extremely rare, but local destruction can be extensive.
det.diagnosis: CT shows a permeative, 'moth-eaten' lesion in the retrolabyrinthine petrous bone between the internal auditory canal and the sigmoid sinus, with intratumoral bone spicules and posterior rim calcification. MRI shows heterogeneous T1 high signal from haemorrhage, avid enhancement and flow voids in large tumours; T1 high signal in the labyrinth indicates haemorrhage. Histology confirms; every patient should have VHL genetic testing and screening for other VHL tumours.
det.treatment: Complete surgical resection, often after embolisation, is the treatment of choice and is most likely to preserve hearing when the tumour is small. Radiosurgery or radiotherapy is used for residual or unresectable disease. Belzutifan, an oral HIF-2α inhibitor approved for VHL-associated tumours, has shown activity against several VHL lesions and is an option within multidisciplinary VHL care. VHL surveillance protocols include periodic audiometry and IAC MRI.
det.prognosis: Excellent survival; hearing and facial outcomes depend on size at diagnosis, and incomplete removal leads to recurrence.
pearls: Sudden deafness or 'Ménière-like' attacks in a VHL carrier mean MRI of the IAC, not just steroids.
A retrolabyrinthine lytic mass with bony spicules on CT is the signature of ELST.
T1-bright signal inside the labyrinth indicates intralabyrinthine haemorrhage.

name: Spinal epidural lipomatosis (SEL)
formal: Pathological overgrowth of unencapsulated epidural fat that compresses the thecal sac, most often in the lumbar spine, associated with exogenous or endogenous glucocorticoid excess, obesity and metabolic syndrome, causing neurogenic claudication, radiculopathy or, rarely, cauda equina or thoracic myelopathy.
simple: Too much fat builds up around the spinal nerves inside the spine, usually from steroids or obesity, and squeezes them, causing leg pain and weakness on walking.
ab: ไขมันในช่อง epidural มากผิดปกติ
th: ไขมันในช่อง epidural ของกระดูกสันหลังเพิ่มขึ้นจนกด thecal sac มักพบที่ระดับเอว สัมพันธ์กับการใช้ steroid นาน (รวมถึงยาสมุนไพรปน steroid) ภาวะ Cushing และโรคอ้วน อาการคือขาปวดชาเมื่อเดิน (neurogenic claudication) หรือปวดร้าวลงขา MRI เห็น thecal sac รูปตัว Y
tempoNote: Gradual over months; faster progression with high-dose steroids, sometimes improving within months after steroid withdrawal or weight loss
feat: Neurogenic claudication or back pain with radicular symptoms, often bilateral
History of long-term glucocorticoids (including adulterated herbal medicines), Cushing syndrome, obesity or metabolic syndrome
Thoracic involvement (more common with steroids) can cause myelopathy
Rarely acute cauda equina or cord compression
inv: MRI: excess T1-bright epidural fat compressing the dural sac into a 'Y' or stellate shape, suppressing on fat-saturated sequences
Grade severity by ratio of dural sac to epidural fat at the narrowest level
Screen for endogenous or exogenous hypercortisolism (drug history, dexamethasone suppression test); weight, glucose and lipids

case.who: 58-year-old woman from Suphan Buri who has taken a 'joint-pain herbal powder' bought at a temple fair for two years
case.story: Over six months she can walk only 100 metres before both calves ache and her feet go numb; sitting on a bench relieves it.
case.exam: Cushingoid face, central obesity and abdominal striae; power normal at rest, ankle jerks reduced, no sensory level.
case.tests: Morning cortisol suppressed and ACTH low (exogenous steroid); lumbar MRI shows abundant epidural fat from L4 to S1 squeezing the thecal sac into a Y shape with minimal disc disease.
case.q: What is the cause of her claudication and first-line management?
case.a: Spinal epidural lipomatosis from exogenous glucocorticoid in adulterated herbal medicine; careful tapering of the steroid with adrenal cover, weight reduction and follow-up, reserving decompression for severe or progressive deficits.

read.where: Chapter 17 Nondegenerative Diseases of the Spine — Epidural lipomatosis

det.patho: Glucocorticoids and insulin resistance promote hypertrophy of epidural adipocytes, so fat expands within the fixed bony canal, mainly at the lumbosacral levels where epidural fat is normally abundant, and in the thoracic spine with high steroid exposure. Obesity has become the commonest association, while endogenous Cushing syndrome, steroid-containing herbal remedies, protease inhibitor use and epidural steroid injections are other triggers. Compression is gradual, so roots adapt and symptoms may be modest relative to imaging.
det.clinical: Most patients have back pain with neurogenic claudication or radicular leg pain; weakness and sphincter problems are less common. Thoracic SEL, seen mainly with high-dose steroids (for example after transplantation), may cause a progressive spastic paraparesis. Look for Cushingoid features and ask specifically about traditional or herbal medicines, which in Thailand frequently contain dexamethasone or prednisolone.
det.diagnosis: MRI is diagnostic: thick T1-hyperintense, fat-suppressing epidural fat with a 'Y'-shaped or polygonal dural sac on axial images, without an enhancing mass. Severity grades relate the dural sac diameter to epidural fat. CT also shows fat density. Evaluate for endogenous or exogenous cortisol excess and metabolic disease, and exclude coexisting degenerative stenosis, which often contributes.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: taper exogenous steroids gradually with adrenal-insufficiency precautions, treat Cushing syndrome, and aim for weight loss through diet, exercise or bariatric surgery; fat volume and symptoms often improve over months. Analgesia and physiotherapy support recovery. Surgical decompressive laminectomy with fat debulking is reserved for severe or progressive deficits, cauda equina syndrome or failure of conservative care, bearing in mind higher surgical risk in obese or immunosuppressed patients.
det.prognosis: Often improves with removal of steroid exposure and weight loss; surgery helps most with refractory compression, although recurrence can occur if the driver persists.
pearls: A 'Y'-shaped thecal sac on axial MRI is the classic sign of lumbar epidural lipomatosis.
Ask about herbal medicines — hidden steroids are a frequent Thai cause.
Stop steroids slowly to avoid adrenal crisis.
det.thd: SEL คือไขมันในช่อง epidural มากผิดปกติจนกดเส้นประสาท สาเหตุหลักคือโรคอ้วน การใช้ steroid นาน (รวมถึงยาลูกกลอนหรือยาสมุนไพรที่ผสม steroid) และ Cushing syndrome อาการคือขาปวดชาเมื่อเดินหรือปวดร้าวลงขา MRI เห็นไขมันหนาและ thecal sac รูปตัว Y รักษาด้วยการลด steroid อย่างค่อยเป็นค่อยไปและลดน้ำหนัก ผ่าตัดเมื่ออาการรุนแรงหรือแย่ลง

name: Idiopathic spinal cord herniation (ISCH)
formal: Herniation of the thoracic spinal cord through a ventral or ventrolateral dural defect, usually at T2–T8, causing slowly worsening spastic paraparesis or a Brown-Séquard picture, with characteristic MRI kinking of the cord anteriorly and widening of the dorsal subarachnoid space.
simple: Part of the spinal cord in the chest region slips through a small hole in its covering and gets stuck, slowly weakening one leg and numbing the other.
ab: ไขสันหลังเลื่อนผ่านรูของเยื่อดูรา
th: ไขสันหลังส่วนอกเลื่อนผ่านรูที่เยื่อ dura ด้านหน้า ทำให้เกิดอาการแบบ Brown-Séquard ที่ค่อย ๆ เป็นมากขึ้น เช่น ขาข้างหนึ่งอ่อนแรงและอีกข้างชาต่อความเจ็บและอุณหภูมิ MRI เห็นไขสันหลังหักงอไปชิดด้านหน้าและมีช่องด้านหลังกว้าง ต้องแยกจาก arachnoid cyst ด้านหลัง
tempoNote: Insidious progression over months to years, typically in middle age, with occasional stepwise worsening
feat: Progressive Brown-Séquard pattern: ipsilateral spastic weakness and dorsal column loss, contralateral pain/temperature loss
Mid-thoracic level (T2–T8), middle-aged adults, more often women
May progress to spastic paraparesis with sphincter dysfunction
Associated superficial siderosis or CSF leak in some patients
inv: MRI: focal anterior displacement and kinking of the thoracic cord abutting the ventral dura, with an enlarged dorsal CSF space and no visible cyst wall
Thin-slice heavily T2-weighted (CISS/FIESTA) imaging to show the defect and absence of an arachnoid membrane
CT myelography to confirm continuous dorsal CSF flow when MRI is ambiguous
Look for ventral osteophyte or disc calcification that may have eroded the dura

case.who: 49-year-old female nurse from Nakhon Si Thammarat
case.story: Over three years her right leg has become stiff and she trips, and she cannot tell hot from cold water on her left leg.
case.exam: Right spastic leg weakness with brisk reflexes, right extensor plantar and loss of vibration and joint position on the right; pain and temperature reduced on the left below T7.
case.tests: MRI thoracic spine: at T5–T6 the cord is sharply angled forward against the ventral dura with a C-shaped deformity and a widened dorsal subarachnoid space; CISS shows no membrane; cord shows faint T2 signal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis, and how is it distinguished from a dorsal arachnoid cyst?
case.a: Idiopathic ventral spinal cord herniation; the cord is pulled into a ventral dural defect with a smooth focal kink and no cyst wall or flow block, while a dorsal arachnoid cyst pushes the cord forward over a longer segment with a membrane and flow obstruction.

read.where: Chapter 17 Nondegenerative Diseases of the Spine — Transdural Spinal Cord Herniation

det.patho: The cord herniates through a defect in the ventral dura, either congenital (dural duplication), acquired from prior trauma or surgery, or from erosion by a calcified disc or osteophyte. Normal thoracic kyphosis keeps the cord close to the ventral dura, and CSF pulsation gradually pulls more tissue through the hole, where it becomes tethered and ischaemic. Some patients also have a ventral CSF leak with spontaneous intracranial hypotension or superficial siderosis.
det.clinical: The typical patient is a middle-aged adult with slowly worsening, asymmetric leg symptoms that evolve into a Brown-Séquard syndrome and later spastic paraparesis. Back pain is variable. The diagnosis is often delayed for years, and the MRI is frequently misread as a dorsal arachnoid cyst. Superficial siderosis can add hearing loss and ataxia.
det.diagnosis: Sagittal MRI shows an abrupt anterior kink of the thoracic cord touching the ventral dura over one or two segments, with a widened dorsal subarachnoid space but no mass effect on the dorsal cord surface. Axial images may show the 'C-shaped' or ventrally displaced cord; high-resolution T2 shows continuity of dorsal CSF and absence of a cyst wall, and CT myelography confirms free dorsal flow. Look for associated disc calcification and siderosis.
det.treatment: Surgery is recommended for progressive deficits: the cord is reduced back into the canal and the dural defect is repaired with a patch or widened, preventing re-herniation. Surgery more reliably stops progression than reverses long-standing deficits, but many patients improve, particularly with motor symptoms of shorter duration. Stable, mildly affected patients may be followed with clinical and MRI review.
det.prognosis: Most operated patients stabilise or improve; outcomes are better when surgery is performed before severe paraparesis develops.
pearls: A slowly progressive thoracic Brown-Séquard syndrome in a middle-aged adult suggests ventral cord herniation.
Sharp focal ventral kinking without a dorsal mass is the key MRI clue; arachnoid cysts compress over a longer segment.
Check for superficial siderosis and CSF leak, which can coexist.
det.thd: ISCH คือไขสันหลังส่วนอกเลื่อนผ่านรูของเยื่อ dura ด้านหน้า พบในผู้ใหญ่วัยกลางคน อาการเป็นแบบ Brown-Séquard ที่ค่อย ๆ เป็นมากขึ้นเป็นปี MRI เห็นไขสันหลังหักงอชิดด้านหน้าในช่วงสั้น ช่องด้านหลังกว้างโดยไม่มีผนังถุงน้ำ ต่างจาก dorsal arachnoid cyst ผู้ที่อาการแย่ลงควรผ่าตัดดึงไขสันหลังกลับและซ่อมรูที่ dura

qx.stem: A 52-year-old female pharmacist from Songkhla has three years of slowly worsening left leg stiffness and loss of temperature sensation in the right leg. Sagittal T2 MRI of the thoracic spine shows the cord sharply kinked forward against the ventral dura at T4–T5 over one segment, with a widened dorsal CSF space. High-resolution T2 imaging shows no membrane in the dorsal space, and CT myelography shows free contrast flow behind the cord.
qx.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Dorsal thoracic arachnoid cyst
Thoracic disc herniation with cord compression
Spinal cord ependymoma
Multiple sclerosis plaque
Ventral transdural spinal cord herniation
qx.why: A progressive Brown-Séquard picture with an abrupt one-segment anterior kink of the thoracic cord and a dorsal CSF space that contains no membrane and flows freely indicates herniation of the cord through a ventral dural defect. A dorsal arachnoid cyst compresses the cord over a longer segment with a membrane and flow block. Surgical reduction and dural repair are offered when deficits progress.

name: Tarlov cyst (perineural cyst)
formal: A CSF-filled cyst of the dorsal root ganglion region formed between the endoneurium and perineurium of a spinal nerve root, most often at S2–S3, usually incidental but occasionally symptomatic through root compression, sacral erosion or CSF leak.
simple: A fluid bubble on a nerve root at the bottom of the spine that is usually harmless but sometimes presses on nerves and causes buttock or leg pain or bladder problems.
ab: ถุงน้ำ Tarlov ที่รากประสาทกระเบนเหน็บ
th: ถุงน้ำ CSF ที่เกิดบริเวณรากประสาทระดับกระเบนเหน็บ (มัก S2–S3) ส่วนใหญ่พบโดยบังเอิญจาก MRI และไม่ก่ออาการ บางรายกดรากประสาททำให้ปวดก้นหรือฝีเย็บ ปวดร้าวลงขา หรือปัสสาวะผิดปกติ ต้องประเมินว่าอาการตรงกับตำแหน่งถุงน้ำจริงก่อนพิจารณาผ่าตัด
tempoNote: Usually stable for years; symptoms, when present, are chronic and may worsen with standing, coughing or sitting
feat: Incidental finding on lumbosacral MRI in a few percent of adults, more often women
Symptomatic cases: sacral, perineal or buttock pain worse on sitting, standing or Valsalva, relieved by lying down
Sacral radiculopathy, sensory change, bladder, bowel or sexual dysfunction
Large cysts can erode the sacrum or cause a CSF leak with orthostatic headache
inv: MRI: CSF-signal cyst along a sacral root, often multiple and bilateral, with root fibres in the wall
CT myelography (delayed images) shows communication with the subarachnoid space
Urodynamics and pelvic floor/sacral electrophysiology when sphincter symptoms are present

case.story: For two years she has had deep buttock and perineal pain that is worse after sitting at her desk and eases when she lies flat; a recent MRI for back pain reported 'sacral cysts'.
case.exam: Reduced pinprick in the left S3 dermatome, normal leg power and reflexes, normal anal tone.
case.tests: MRI shows a 2.5 cm left S2–S3 perineural cyst with root fibres in its wall and smooth sacral remodelling; small incidental cysts on the right; delayed CT myelogram shows contrast entering the left cyst.
case.q: What principle guides whether she should have surgery?
case.a: Tarlov cysts are usually incidental; surgery (cyst fenestration and imbrication or sealing) is considered only when symptoms clearly match a large cyst on the appropriate root and conservative care fails, after excluding other pelvic and spinal causes.

read.where: Chapter 17 Nondegenerative Diseases of the Spine — Cystic Lesions (Tarlov Cyst)

det.patho: Tarlov cysts develop at the junction of the dorsal root ganglion and posterior root, where CSF accumulates between perineurial and endoneurial layers; a one-way valve or pulsatile CSF pressure may enlarge them. They are classified as type II spinal meningeal cysts because the wall contains nerve fibres. Connective tissue disorders and raised CSF pressure may predispose to multiple cysts.
det.clinical: Most cysts never cause symptoms. When they do, patients have sacral, coccygeal, perineal or buttock pain, positional worsening with sitting or standing, sciatica-like pain, sensory changes in sacral dermatomes and sometimes bladder, bowel or sexual dysfunction. Very large cysts may erode bone and occasionally present with sacral fracture or spontaneous intracranial hypotension from a leak.
det.diagnosis: MRI demonstrates CSF-signal cysts on sacral roots; CT myelography with delayed imaging shows filling and may predict symptomatic cysts. The key clinical step is correlation: cysts over 1.5 cm, on the symptomatic side and level, with positional symptoms, are more likely to be responsible. Exclude disc disease, pelvic pathology, pudendal neuralgia and functional pelvic pain before attributing symptoms to the cyst.
det.treatment: Conservative care comes first: neuropathic pain medicines, physiotherapy and cushioning. For carefully selected patients, image-guided aspiration with fibrin glue injection or microsurgical fenestration with imbrication or wall resection and dural sealing can relieve symptoms; simple aspiration usually recurs. Complications include CSF leak, infection and worsened root symptoms, so surgery should be performed in experienced centres.
det.prognosis: Incidental cysts rarely change; selected surgical patients often improve, but persistent pain is not uncommon.
pearls: Most Tarlov cysts are incidental — match the cyst to the patient's root and positional symptoms before blaming it.
Root fibres in the cyst wall distinguish it from an extradural arachnoid cyst.
Pain worse with sitting and better lying flat suggests a symptomatic perineural cyst.
det.thd: Tarlov cyst เป็นถุงน้ำ CSF บนรากประสาทระดับ S2–S3 ส่วนใหญ่พบโดยบังเอิญไม่ต้องรักษา บางรายปวดก้น ฝีเย็บ หรือปวดร้าวลงขาเมื่อนั่งหรือยืนนาน ดีขึ้นเมื่อนอนราบ อาจมีปัสสาวะผิดปกติ ก่อนรักษาต้องแน่ใจว่าอาการตรงกับขนาดและตำแหน่งถุงน้ำและแยกสาเหตุอื่นออก รักษาแบบประคับประคองก่อน ผ่าตัดหรือฉีด fibrin glue ในรายที่เลือกแล้ว

ab: ganglion cyst of the ligamentum flavum
ถุงน้ำจากข้อต่อ facet กระดูกสันหลังส่วนเอว
th: ถุงน้ำที่งอกจากข้อต่อ facet ของกระดูกสันหลังส่วนเอวที่เสื่อม มักที่ L4–L5 ร่วมกับกระดูกเคลื่อน ทำให้ปวดร้าวลงขาตามแนวรากประสาทหรือเดินแล้วปวดขา ถ้ามีเลือดออกในถุงน้ำอาการจะเป็นเฉียบพลัน MRI เห็นถุงน้ำติดกับข้อต่อ facet ด้านหลังข้างของช่องไขสันหลัง
tempoNote: Usually gradual radicular pain over weeks to months; sudden worsening with intracystic haemorrhage
feat: Older adults with lumbar spondylosis, often degenerative spondylolisthesis at L4–L5
Unilateral radicular pain (often L5) or neurogenic claudication
Acute severe radiculopathy if the cyst bleeds
Rarely cauda equina compression; cervical and thoracic cysts may cause myelopathy
inv: MRI: round posterolateral extradural cyst contiguous with an arthritic facet, T2 bright or mixed with a dark rim, peripheral enhancement
Flexion–extension radiographs for instability (spondylolisthesis)
CT may show rim calcification or gas in the facet and cyst

case.story: Three months of burning pain from the right buttock to the top of the foot, worse when standing and walking; one week ago it suddenly became much more severe after lifting a sack of rice.
case.exam: Weak right great toe extension (4/5), reduced sensation over the right dorsum of foot, positive straight leg raise at 60°.
case.tests: MRI: 12 mm cyst arising from an arthritic right L4–L5 facet, with T1 hyperintense contents and a dark rim, compressing the right L5 root in the lateral recess; grade I degenerative spondylolisthesis, slip increases on flexion films.
case.q: What is the lesion, and what surgical option is often preferred given the slip?
case.a: Haemorrhagic lumbar facet synovial cyst compressing L5; if conservative care fails, decompression with cyst excision — often with fusion when there is mobile spondylolisthesis, as cysts recur after decompression alone in unstable segments.

read.where: Chapter 16 Anatomy and Degenerative Diseases of the Spine — Synovial cysts
Companion to Peripheral Neuropathy: chapters (see text)

det.patho: Facet joint degeneration and instability raise capsular pressure and cause myxoid change, so synovial fluid herniates through capsular defects into the canal; histologically a lining may or may not be present (ganglion versus synovial cyst), and clinicians group them as juxtafacet cysts. L4–L5 is the most mobile degenerative segment, which explains its predilection. Haemorrhage into the cyst, sometimes with antiplatelet drugs, causes sudden expansion.
det.clinical: Patients present like lateral recess stenosis or disc herniation, with unilateral radicular pain, numbness and weakness or bilateral claudication. Acute severe pain suggests intracystic bleeding. Large cysts occasionally compress the cauda equina, and less common cervical or thoracic cysts can cause myelopathy.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows a smooth extradural cyst at the posterolateral canal attached to the facet joint, with variable signal depending on protein and blood content and a thin enhancing rim; facet effusion and spondylolisthesis are common companions. CT can show calcified rims or gas. Differentiate from sequestered disc fragments, nerve sheath tumours and epidural abscess by location and enhancement pattern.
det.treatment: Analgesia, physiotherapy and epidural or facet injections help some; CT-guided cyst aspiration or rupture gives relief in a proportion but recurrence is common. Persistent radiculopathy or neurological deficit is treated with surgical decompression and excision of the cyst; fusion is often added when there is dynamic spondylolisthesis or extensive facet resection, reducing recurrence. Urgent surgery is required for cauda equina syndrome.
det.prognosis: Surgery relieves radicular pain in most patients; recurrence is uncommon after fusion.
pearls: A cyst hugging an arthritic facet at L4–L5 with spondylolisthesis is the classic picture.
Sudden worsening suggests haemorrhage into the cyst.
Consider fusion when the segment is unstable, because cysts tend to recur after decompression alone.
det.thd: Lumbar facet synovial cyst เป็นถุงน้ำจากข้อต่อ facet ที่เสื่อม มักที่ L4–L5 ร่วมกับ spondylolisthesis กดรากประสาทให้ปวดร้าวลงขาหรือเดินแล้วปวดขา ถ้าเลือดออกในถุงน้ำจะปวดฉับพลันรุนแรง MRI เห็นถุงน้ำติดข้อต่อ facet ด้านหลังข้าง รักษาแบบประคับประคองหรือเจาะถุงน้ำ ถ้าไม่ดีขึ้นผ่าตัดเอาออกและมักเชื่อมกระดูกถ้ามีความไม่มั่นคง

name: Spinal extramedullary haematopoiesis (thalassaemia-related cord compression)
formal: Compensatory formation of haematopoietic tissue outside the bone marrow, presenting as paravertebral or epidural masses in chronic haemolytic or ineffective erythropoiesis — especially non-transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia and HbE/β-thalassaemia — that can compress the thoracic spinal cord or roots.
simple: In some people with thalassaemia, the body makes blood in lumps outside the bones, and a lump inside the spine can press on the spinal cord and weaken the legs.
ab: การสร้างเม็ดเลือดนอกไขกระดูกกดไขสันหลัง
th: ในผู้ป่วยธาลัสซีเมีย โดยเฉพาะ HbE/β-thalassaemia ที่ไม่ได้รับเลือดสม่ำเสมอ ร่างกายสร้างเม็ดเลือดนอกไขกระดูกเป็นก้อนข้างกระดูกสันหลังหรือในช่อง epidural ส่วนอก อาจกดไขสันหลังทำให้ขาอ่อนแรง ชา และมี sensory level พบได้ในประเทศไทย รักษาด้วยการให้เลือด ฉายรังสี hydroxyurea หรือผ่าตัด
tempoNote: Weeks to months of progressive paraparesis; may worsen quickly with haemorrhage into the mass or when anaemia deepens
feat: Young adult with non-transfusion-dependent thalassaemia (often HbE/β-thalassaemia), splenomegaly or prior splenectomy
Progressive spastic paraparesis, thoracic sensory level and back pain
Smooth lobulated bilateral paravertebral or posterior epidural masses, usually mid-thoracic
Thalassaemic facies, skull 'hair-on-end' changes, iron overload features
inv: MRI: lobulated epidural/paravertebral masses isointense to marrow, mild enhancement; fat-rich or iron-laden masses in older lesions
Haemoglobin, haemoglobin typing, iron studies and ferritin
Biopsy only if imaging is atypical, as masses are vascular; technetium marrow scan can support the diagnosis

case.who: 26-year-old male rubber tapper from Trang with HbE/β-thalassaemia who rarely attends for transfusion
case.story: Over two months his legs have become stiff and weak and he now needs a stick; he has back ache and recently started to strain to pass urine.
case.exam: Pallor, frontal bossing, massive splenomegaly; spastic paraparesis (MRC 3/5), bilateral extensor plantars and a sensory level at T8.
case.tests: Hb 6.1 g/dL, ferritin 1,800 ng/mL; MRI shows bilateral smooth paravertebral masses at T5–T9 with a posterior epidural component compressing the cord, signal similar to marrow.
case.q: What is the cause of his myelopathy, and which treatments can be combined?
case.a: Spinal extramedullary haematopoiesis from HbE/β-thalassaemia; hypertransfusion to suppress erythropoiesis plus low-dose radiotherapy, with hydroxyurea and corticosteroids, and surgical decompression if the deficit is severe or rapidly progressive.

read.where: Chapter 17 Nondegenerative Diseases of the Spine — Intensity Abnormalities of Vertebral Marrow (anemia)
