det.patho: Severe ineffective erythropoiesis raises erythropoietin drive, so haematopoietic tissue expands from marrow or arises from embryonic rests, forming masses that extend from vertebral bodies and rib heads into the paravertebral and epidural spaces. It is seen mainly in thalassaemia intermedia (now non-transfusion-dependent thalassaemia) and HbE/β-thalassaemia — common in Thailand — and less often in sickle cell disease, myelofibrosis and other chronic haemolytic states. Regular transfusion suppresses it, so poorly transfused or splenectomised patients are most at risk.
det.clinical: Paravertebral masses are often asymptomatic incidental findings on chest imaging. Epidural extension causes back pain, progressive spastic paraparesis, sensory level and sphincter dysfunction, usually in the mid-thoracic cord; radiculopathy and cauda equina presentations occur. Haemorrhage into the mass can cause sudden deterioration. Features of the underlying thalassaemia — anaemia, splenomegaly, bone changes, iron overload — are usually evident.
det.diagnosis: MRI shows smooth, lobulated, bilateral masses with signal close to red marrow, little bone destruction and mild enhancement; older lesions may become fatty or iron-laden (dark on T2). In a known thalassaemic patient the imaging is usually diagnostic, and biopsy is avoided because of bleeding risk unless malignancy remains a concern. Check haemoglobin, ferritin and transfusion history.
det.treatment: Management is multimodal and individualised: start or intensify transfusion to suppress erythropoiesis, low-dose radiotherapy (masses are highly radiosensitive), hydroxyurea to stimulate fetal haemoglobin and reduce marrow drive, and corticosteroids for oedema. Luspatercept may help anaemia in non-transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia but its effect on established masses is uncertain. Decompressive laminectomy is reserved for rapidly progressive or severe deficit, with risk of bleeding and recurrence. Iron chelation is needed once transfusion is regular.
det.prognosis: Neurological recovery is good in most patients when treatment starts early; recurrence occurs if erythropoietic drive is not controlled.
pearls: Paraparesis in a young Thai patient with thalassaemia — think extramedullary haematopoiesis first.
Masses that look like marrow on every MRI sequence and spare the bone are characteristic.
Radiotherapy and transfusion often avoid surgery; avoid biopsy because of bleeding.
det.thd: Spinal extramedullary haematopoiesis พบในผู้ป่วยธาลัสซีเมียที่ไม่ได้รับเลือดสม่ำเสมอ โดยเฉพาะ HbE/β-thalassaemia ซึ่งพบบ่อยในไทย ก้อนสร้างเม็ดเลือดข้างกระดูกสันหลังส่วนอกอาจลามเข้าช่อง epidural กดไขสันหลังทำให้ขาอ่อนแรงและมี sensory level MRI เห็นก้อนเรียบหลายก้อนสัญญาณเหมือนไขกระดูก รักษาโดยให้เลือด ฉายรังสีขนาดต่ำ hydroxyurea และ steroid ผ่าตัดเมื่ออาการรุนแรงหรือแย่ลงเร็ว

qx.stem: A 23-year-old woman from Sisaket with HbE/β-thalassaemia, splenectomised at 12 and transfused only occasionally, presents with six weeks of progressive leg weakness and a T6 sensory level. Hb is 6.5 g/dL. MRI shows smooth, lobulated, bilateral paravertebral and posterior epidural masses from T4 to T8 with signal similar to vertebral marrow on all sequences, mild enhancement and no vertebral destruction.
qx.q: Which management plan is most appropriate?
opts: CT-guided biopsy of the epidural mass before any treatment
Hypertransfusion and low-dose radiotherapy, with hydroxyurea and steroids; surgery if the deficit is severe or progressing
Empirical anti-tuberculous therapy
High-dose chemotherapy for presumed lymphoma
Iron chelation alone and review in three months
qx.why: Marrow-like, smooth bilateral paravertebral and epidural masses without bone destruction in a poorly transfused thalassaemic patient are extramedullary haematopoiesis. Suppressing erythropoietic drive with transfusion, together with highly effective low-dose radiotherapy, hydroxyurea and steroids, usually decompresses the cord, with laminectomy reserved for severe or rapid deficits. Biopsy carries bleeding risk and is needed only when imaging is atypical; chelation alone does not relieve compression.

name: Central sleep apnoea (CSA)
formal: Sleep-related breathing disorder in which airflow stops because respiratory effort is absent, defined in ICSD-3 by a central apnoea-hypopnoea index of at least 5 per hour with central events making up more than half of all events; subtypes include Cheyne–Stokes breathing, medical, drug-induced, high-altitude, primary and treatment-emergent forms.
simple: During sleep the brain briefly forgets to send the signal to breathe, so breathing stops without any chest effort.
ab: หยุดหายใจขณะหลับชนิดสมองส่วนกลาง
th: ภาวะหยุดหายใจขณะหลับเพราะไม่มีแรงพยายามหายใจ (central event > 50% ของเหตุการณ์ทั้งหมด) พบในหัวใจล้มเหลว หลอดเลือดสมอง ยาเสพติดกลุ่ม opioid หรือโรคก้านสมอง การรักษาคือแก้ที่ต้นเหตุ และระวังการใช้ ASV ในผู้ป่วย HFrEF
tempoNote: Usually chronic and tracks the underlying cause; may appear transiently at altitude or after starting CPAP and then resolve
feat: Witnessed pauses in breathing with no visible chest or abdominal movement, often in a crescendo-decrescendo waxing and waning pattern
Frequent awakenings, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea and unrefreshing sleep; snoring is usually less prominent than in obstructive apnoea
Typical settings: heart failure, atrial fibrillation, stroke, chronic opioid use, brainstem or high cervical lesions, ascent to altitude
Daytime sleepiness may be mild; patients with heart failure often complain of fatigue and insomnia instead
inv: Attended polysomnography with oronasal flow and effort belts (home tests may misclassify central events)
Echocardiography, natriuretic peptide and rhythm monitoring when heart failure or atrial fibrillation is suspected
Review all medicines, especially opioids and sedatives; MRI of the brainstem and craniocervical junction when no cause is found
Daytime arterial or venous blood gas to separate a hypocapnic form from a hypoventilation form

case.who: 68-year-old retired rice farmer from Roi Et with ischaemic cardiomyopathy and atrial fibrillation
case.story: His wife describes a pattern of breathing that gets louder then fades to silence for half a minute, repeated through the night; he wakes breathless and has stopped snoring.
case.exam: BMI 23, jugular venous distension, bibasal crackles, no pharyngeal crowding; awake oxygen saturation 95%.
case.tests: Echo shows LVEF 30%; polysomnography shows 38 central apnoeas and hypopnoeas per hour in a waxing-waning pattern with arousals at the peak of each hyperpnoea.
case.q: Which therapy should be avoided as a first move and why?
case.a: Adaptive servo-ventilation: in symptomatic heart failure with LVEF of 45% or less and predominant central apnoea it increased cardiovascular death in SERVE-HF; optimise heart failure therapy first, then consider oxygen, CPAP or phrenic nerve stimulation.

read.where: Chapter 18 Central sleep apnea and hypoventilation syndromes

det.patho: Breathing during sleep depends on the chemical drive from arterial carbon dioxide. When the controller is too sensitive, as in heart failure with prolonged circulation time and hyperventilation, the carbon dioxide level falls under the apnoeic threshold and breathing stops until it rises again, which produces cycling Cheyne–Stokes breathing. Other mechanisms are depressed medullary drive from opioids or brainstem lesions, and a transient hypocapnic overshoot after switching from wakefulness to sleep or after starting CPAP.
det.clinical: Most patients are middle-aged or older men with heart failure, atrial fibrillation or a prior stroke. Bed partners report quiet pauses and a cyclic breathing pattern; the patient notices night-time breathlessness, fragmented sleep and tiredness more than overt sleepiness. Opioid users show an ataxic irregular pattern, often with coexisting obstructive events. Primary CSA is uncommon and idiopathic, and treatment-emergent CSA appears during CPAP titration and usually fades over weeks.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis rests on polysomnography showing at least 5 central apnoeas or hypopnoeas per hour with central events more than half of the total, plus symptoms or a recognised associated condition. Cheyne–Stokes breathing requires at least three consecutive cycles of crescendo-decrescendo change in airflow amplitude. Look for the cause: cardiac assessment, opioid history, brainstem and craniocervical imaging, and blood gas to detect hypercapnia. Home sleep tests can undercount central events, so they should not be used to exclude CSA in heart failure.
det.treatment: Treat the driver first: optimise heart failure, rate and rhythm control, reduce or stop opioids and sedatives, and descend or use oxygen at altitude. CPAP can suppress central events in some heart failure patients, and nocturnal oxygen is an alternative. Adaptive servo-ventilation is contraindicated when LVEF is 45% or less and central apnoea predominates, because SERVE-HF showed higher cardiovascular mortality. Transvenous phrenic nerve stimulation is licensed for moderate to severe CSA and is chosen in selected patients; acetazolamide is used short term in altitude periodic breathing.
det.prognosis: In heart failure the presence of Cheyne–Stokes breathing marks a worse outlook but is regarded as a marker as much as a cause; in treatment-emergent and drug-induced forms the course is generally favourable once the trigger is removed.
pearls: Central apnoea means no effort at all on the belts; always check the effort channel before calling an event obstructive.
Do not start adaptive servo-ventilation in HFrEF with predominant central apnoea.
New central events during CPAP titration often settle without any change in therapy.
det.thd: CSA คือภาวะหยุดหายใจขณะหลับที่ไม่มีแรงพยายามหายใจเลย เกิดจากระบบควบคุมการหายใจไม่ทำงาน เช่น หัวใจล้มเหลว (Cheyne–Stokes) หลอดเลือดสมอง ยา opioid หรือรอยโรคก้านสมอง วินิจฉัยด้วย polysomnography ที่มี central event มากกว่าครึ่งและ AHI ≥ 5 การรักษาคือแก้สาเหตุ ลดยา opioid ปรับยาหัวใจ ใช้ CPAP ออกซิเจน หรือ phrenic nerve stimulation และห้ามใช้ ASV ใน HFrEF ที่ LVEF ≤ 45%

qx.stem: A 69-year-old man from Buriram with ischaemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 28%) has waxing and waning breathing with 40 events an hour on polysomnography, almost all central, without upper airway obstruction. He is on optimal heart failure medication.
qx.q: Which therapy is contraindicated in this patient?
opts: Nocturnal oxygen
CPAP titration
Transvenous phrenic nerve stimulation in selected cases
Adaptive servo-ventilation
Rhythm and rate optimisation
qx.why: In SERVE-HF, adaptive servo-ventilation increased cardiovascular mortality in patients with symptomatic heart failure and LVEF of 45% or less with predominant central apnoea, so it is contraindicated. Treating the heart failure, oxygen, CPAP or phrenic nerve stimulation are acceptable alternatives. Heart failure is the cause of this Cheyne–Stokes pattern.

name: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS)
formal: Chronic sleep-related hypoventilation in people with obesity (BMI 30 kg/m2 or more) who have awake daytime hypercapnia (PaCO2 above 45 mmHg), after exclusion of other causes of hypoventilation; most also have obstructive sleep apnoea.
simple: In some people with severe obesity, breathing is too shallow day and night so carbon dioxide builds up, causing sleepiness, morning headache and leg swelling.
ab: chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure of obesity
ภาวะหายใจล้มเหลวเรื้อรังจากโรคอ้วน
th: ภาวะอ้วนร่วมกับ CO2 คั่งตอนตื่น (PaCO2 > 45 mmHg) โดยไม่มีสาเหตุอื่น ส่วนใหญ่มี OSA ร่วมด้วย อาการ ง่วงมาก ปวดศีรษะตอนเช้า บวมเท้า รักษาด้วย PAP (CPAP หรือ BPAP) ลดน้ำหนัก และหลีกเลี่ยงยากดประสาท
tempoNote: Develops over years with weight gain; may present for the first time as acute-on-chronic respiratory failure
feat: Severe obesity with loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas and marked daytime sleepiness
Morning headache, poor concentration and dyspnoea on exertion
Signs of cor pulmonale: leg oedema, raised JVP, plethora
Elevated serum bicarbonate and awake hypercapnia with low awake oxygen saturation
Sustained sleep-related hypoxaemia not limited to apnoeic events
inv: Serum bicarbonate (a level of 27 mmol/L or more is a good screen), then arterial blood gas to prove PaCO2 above 45 mmHg
Polysomnography with CO2 monitoring (transcutaneous or end-tidal) and titration of positive airway pressure
Spirometry, chest imaging, thyroid function and echocardiography to exclude other causes and assess pulmonary hypertension
Review for sedatives and opioids

case.who: 52-year-old female market vendor from Nakhon Ratchasima
case.story: Gradual weight gain to 108 kg, falling asleep while selling, daily morning headaches and swollen ankles for a year; recent visit to emergency for confusion after a night of cough and cold syrup with codeine.
case.exam: BMI 41, awake SpO2 89% on room air, pitting oedema to the knees, loud second heart sound.
case.tests: Venous bicarbonate 34 mmol/L; arterial PaCO2 56 mmHg; polysomnography shows severe obstructive apnoea and sustained desaturation in REM sleep.
case.q: What is the first-line long-term treatment, and what must be avoided?
case.a: Positive airway pressure (CPAP, or bilevel if hypercapnia persists) plus supervised weight loss; avoid sedatives, opioids and uncontrolled oxygen alone.

read.where: Chapter 18 Central sleep apnea and hypoventilation syndromes

det.patho: Excess mass load on the chest wall and abdomen reduces compliance and raises the work of breathing, while leptin resistance and a blunted central ventilatory response prevent the compensatory increase in drive. Repeated obstructive events prevent CO2 clearance during the short hyperventilation that follows each apnoea, so a rise in bicarbonate accumulates and carries into wakefulness. Hypoxaemia and hypercapnia then promote pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure.
det.clinical: Most present between about 40 and 60 years of age, with severe obesity (often BMI above 40), disabling sleepiness and morning headaches. Some patients are diagnosed only when they develop acute hypercapnic respiratory failure, typically after a respiratory infection or sedatives. Hypertension, type 2 diabetes, atrial fibrillation and heart failure are frequent. Compared with simple OSA, mortality and hospital use are higher when untreated.
det.diagnosis: All three elements are needed: obesity, awake hypercapnia (PaCO2 above 45 mmHg), and sleep-disordered breathing, with other causes of hypercapnia excluded, including COPD, neuromuscular disease, chest wall deformity, hypothyroidism and drugs. A normal or low bicarbonate makes OHS unlikely, so it is the practical screen in a sleep clinic. Polysomnography with CO2 monitoring defines whether obstructive apnoea dominates and guides pressure titration.
det.treatment: Positive airway pressure is the cornerstone: CPAP is enough for most patients with severe OSA, and bilevel pressure or volume-assured modes are used if hypercapnia or desaturation persists after CPAP. Patients hospitalised with acute hypercapnic failure should leave hospital on PAP with early follow-up. Weight loss, ideally 25–30% of body weight through bariatric surgery or intensive lifestyle programmes, can reverse the syndrome. Avoid sedatives, opioids and unsupervised oxygen supplementation.
det.prognosis: Good when adherent to PAP; untreated disease carries a high risk of hospitalisation, pulmonary hypertension and death.
pearls: A serum bicarbonate under 27 mmol/L makes OHS unlikely; above that, obtain an arterial blood gas.
Most OHS patients have OSA, but OSA alone does not cause daytime hypercapnia.
Never give oxygen alone to a hypercapnic obese patient without ventilatory support.
det.thd: OHS คือภาวะอ้วนมากที่มี PaCO2 > 45 mmHg ขณะตื่น ร่วมกับการหายใจผิดปกติขณะหลับ ผู้ป่วยมักง่วงมาก ปวดศีรษะตอนเช้า บวมเท้า ตรวจ serum bicarbonate และ ABG วินิจฉัยโดยแยกโรคปอด โรคกล้ามเนื้อและ hypothyroidism รักษาด้วย PAP การลดน้ำหนัก และหลีกเลี่ยงยากดประสาทหรือการให้ออกซิเจนเพียงอย่างเดียว

qx.stem: A 48-year-old woman from Sakon Nakhon with BMI 44 attends a sleep clinic for severe daytime sleepiness, morning headaches and ankle swelling. Awake SpO2 is 90% on room air. Serum bicarbonate is 32 mmol/L, and the home test shows severe obstructive apnoea.
qx.q: Which investigation is needed next to establish the diagnosis?
opts: Overnight oxygen therapy trial alone
Awake arterial blood gas on room air
Brain MRI
Multiple sleep latency test
Muscle biopsy
qx.why: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome requires awake hypercapnia (PaCO2 above 45 mmHg) in an obese patient after other causes are excluded; an elevated bicarbonate is the screening clue and a blood gas confirms it. Oxygen alone can worsen hypercapnia. Positive airway pressure and weight loss are the treatments once confirmed.

name: Shift work disorder (SWD)
formal: Circadian rhythm sleep–wake disorder in which insomnia or excessive sleepiness, with reduced sleep time, is linked to a recurring work schedule that overlaps the usual sleep period and persists for at least three months.
simple: People who work nights or rotating shifts cannot get enough good sleep at the times they need it and feel sleepy on the job.
ab: shift work type circadian rhythm disorder
ความผิดปกติของการนอนหลับจากการทำงานเป็นกะ
th: นอนไม่หลับหรือง่วงมากในผู้ที่ทำงานกะดึก/หมุนเวียน อย่างน้อย 3 เดือน เพราะเวลางานทับกับช่วงเวลานอน ปรับด้วยตารางกะที่ดี แสงสว่างตอนทำงาน การงีบ เมลาโทนินก่อนนอนกลางวัน และ modafinil/armodafinil ในรายง่วงรุนแรง
tempoNote: Present for at least three months of exposure to the work schedule and fluctuating with the shift pattern; improves after return to day work
feat: Reduced and fragmented sleep during the day after night shifts, usually 1–4 hours shorter than on a day-work pattern
Severe sleepiness during the night shift, with lapses of attention and microsleeps
Accident risk on the commute home and at work
Gastrointestinal complaints, mood disturbance and reliance on caffeine or hypnotics
Sleep returns to normal after a few days off or a switch to day work
inv: Two weeks of sleep diary and actigraphy that include both work and rest days
Epworth Sleepiness Scale and work-schedule history

case.who: 34-year-old male nurse working rotating shifts at a Bangkok hospital
case.story: After eight months of rotating night duties he sleeps four hours after each night shift, is exhausted on duty and nearly drove into a lamp-post on the way home; on holidays he sleeps normally.
case.exam: BMI 24, normal examination, Epworth score 15.
case.tests: Actigraphy shows fragmented short sleep after night shifts and normal consolidated sleep on days off; no sleep apnoea on a home test.
case.q: Which combination of measures is most appropriate?
case.a: Planned naps and bright light early in the night shift, dark bedroom and sunglasses for the drive home, low-dose melatonin before daytime sleep, a stable schedule where possible, and modafinil or armodafinil only for persistent severe sleepiness.

det.patho: The circadian system is anchored by light and cannot shift as fast as a rapidly changing schedule, so night workers sleep at a circadian phase that promotes wakefulness and work at a phase that promotes sleep. Daytime sleep is shorter, lighter and interrupted by noise and light. Long-term misalignment also disrupts metabolic and cardiovascular regulation.
det.clinical: Roughly a quarter of night workers have clinically significant symptoms. Sleepiness peaks in the early morning hours and may cause medical errors, industrial and driving accidents. Long-term shift work is linked to metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, depression, and some cancers, and the International Agency for Research on Cancer lists night shift work as probably carcinogenic. Tolerance varies; morning types, older workers and those with caring duties are affected more.
det.diagnosis: ICSD-3 requires symptoms of insomnia or excessive sleepiness related to a work period that overlaps the usual sleep time, for at least three months, supported by sleep logs or actigraphy over at least 14 days that show circadian misalignment and sleep disturbance. Other sleep disorders must not explain the picture, so screening for sleep apnoea and restless legs is important. Questions about drivers' safety and caffeine use are a part of the assessment.
det.treatment: Behavioural measures come first: consistent sleep and wake times, a dark quiet bedroom, naps before and during the shift, limited caffeine early in the shift, and scheduling that rotates forward (day to evening to night) with enough rest between blocks. Bright light early in the night shift and sunglasses on the way home help phase delay. Melatonin before the daytime sleep is useful, and modafinil or armodafinil can be considered when sleepiness persists despite behavioural change. Hypnotics are for short periods only.
det.prognosis: Symptoms ease with a suitable schedule; chronic exposure carries long-term health risks, so counselling about screening and metabolic risk is worthwhile.
pearls: Sleepiness while driving home after a night shift is a safety emergency; arrange a ride, nap first or use public transport.
Normal sleep on days off and holidays points to a schedule problem rather than chronic insomnia.
Forward-rotating shifts are better tolerated than backward-rotating ones.
det.thd: Shift work disorder เกิดจากตารางงานที่ทับช่วงนอนปกติ ทำให้นอนไม่พอและง่วงมากขณะทำงานกะดึก ต้องมีอาการ ≥ 3 เดือน และยืนยันด้วย sleep diary/actigraphy ≥ 14 วัน แยกจาก OSA, RLS และ narcolepsy การรักษาคือจัดตารางกะให้หมุนไปข้างหน้า แสงสว่างตอนทำงาน งีบ เมลาโทนินก่อนนอนกลางวัน และใช้ modafinil/armodafinil เมื่อยังง่วงรุนแรง

name: Jet lag disorder
formal: Circadian rhythm sleep–wake disorder with insomnia or daytime sleepiness and impaired function that follows rapid travel across at least two time zones, with symptoms beginning within one to two days of the journey.
simple: After a long flight across time zones, the body clock is still on home time, so sleep and alertness are out of step with the local day.
ab: อาการเจ็ตแลก
th: นอนไม่หลับและง่วงกลางวันหลังเดินทางข้ามเขตเวลาตั้งแต่ 2 โซนขึ้นไป เพราะนาฬิกาชีวิตยังเป็นเวลาบ้าน บินไปทางตะวันออกจะแย่กว่า ปรับด้วยแสงและเมลาโทนินตามเวลาที่เหมาะสม
tempoNote: Starts within 1–2 days of arrival and resolves by itself, typically about a day per time zone crossed westward and slightly longer eastward
feat: Difficulty sleeping at the new local night and sleepiness during the new local day
Poor concentration, irritability, headache and gastrointestinal upset
Worse after eastward flights that require advancing the body clock
Severity increases with the number of time zones crossed and with age
Self-limited, with symptoms depending on the direction rather than only the distance
inv: Clinical history of travel dates, time zones and sleep pattern
Sleep diary; no routine laboratory test is needed
Consider sleep apnoea, depression or medicine effects if symptoms persist beyond a week or two after arrival

case.story: Flew from Bangkok to London for a conference; he fell asleep at 5 p.m. local time, awakened at 1 a.m. unable to sleep and was sleepy during morning meetings for the first four days.
case.exam: Normal examination with no focal neurological signs.
case.tests: None required; sleep diary shows early wake-up fixed at Bangkok time.
case.q: What advice is best for the return trip, and which flight direction is easier?
case.a: Westward travel is easier because the body clock tolerates delay better than advance; for eastward trips, seek morning light and take melatonin at the target bedtime for a few days after arrival.

read.where: Chapter 21 Shift work sleep disorder and jet lag

det.patho: The suprachiasmatic clock follows light and keeps its previous timing for days after the environment changes, so the circadian drive for sleep and wakefulness is mismatched with the local day. Because the human clock runs slightly longer than 24 hours, delaying (westward) is easier than advancing (eastward). Sleep loss during the flight adds to the problem.
det.clinical: Difficulty falling asleep at night after eastward flights, early awakening after westward flights, daytime fatigue, impaired performance, gut symptoms and mood change are the commonest complaints. Recovery needs roughly one day per time zone westward and up to one and a half days per zone eastward. Short trips of fewer than two or three days are best managed by staying on home time.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical. ICSD-3 requires sleep disturbance with impaired daytime function that follows travel across at least two time zones, with onset within one to two days, and cannot be attributed to a different sleep or medical condition. Persistent symptoms beyond several weeks should prompt reassessment.
det.treatment: Plan before the trip by shifting bedtime gradually toward destination time, then time light exposure to the direction of travel: after eastward flights seek light in the late morning and avoid it in the first hours of the local morning, and after westward flights seek light in the late afternoon and evening. Melatonin 0.5–5 mg at the destination bedtime for several nights speeds adaptation. Short-acting hypnotics can help for a few nights and caffeine may be used strategically. Stay hydrated, avoid alcohol and take short naps (under 30 minutes) only.
det.prognosis: Self-limited; a few days to two weeks depending on the number of time zones and direction.
pearls: Eastward is harder than westward.
Light and melatonin are time-dependent: the same dose can advance or delay the clock depending on when it is taken.
For stays of one or two days, keep home time.
det.thd: Jet lag เกิดจากนาฬิกาชีวิตยังเป็นเวลาที่บ้านหลังบินข้าม ≥ 2 เขตเวลา ทำให้นอนไม่หลับกลางคืนและง่วงกลางวัน บินไปทางตะวันออกแย่กว่าตะวันตก วินิจฉัยจากประวัติ แก้ได้ด้วยการจัดแสงให้ถูกเวลา เมลาโทนิน 0.5–5 มก. ก่อนนอนตามเวลาปลายทาง และงีบสั้น ๆ

name: Irregular sleep–wake rhythm disorder (ISWRD)
formal: Circadian rhythm sleep–wake disorder with a lack of any clearly defined circadian rhythm: sleep is broken into at least three separate bouts across 24 hours, with the longest bout usually under four hours, causing insomnia or sleepiness; seen mainly in neurodegenerative disease and neurodevelopmental disorders.
simple: Sleep is split into short naps scattered through day and night rather than one long night sleep.
ab: การนอนไม่เป็นเวลา
th: แบบแผนการนอนไร้จังหวะ นอนเป็นช่วงสั้น ๆ ≥ 3 ช่วงใน 24 ชม. ไม่มีช่วงนอนหลักยาว พบบ่อยในโรคสมองเสื่อม ผู้ป่วยพัฒนาการล่าช้าและผู้ที่ถูกจำกัดแสงหรือกิจกรรม รักษาด้วยการจัดตารางประจำวัน แสงและกิจกรรมตอนกลางวัน และเมลาโทนินในเด็ก
tempoNote: Persistent and usually progressive in neurodegenerative disease; lifelong in neurodevelopmental disorders
feat: At least three sleep periods in 24 hours with no single main sleep bout
Night wandering, nocturnal agitation and daytime napping that exhaust carers
Typical in advanced Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, intellectual disability and after brain injury
Total sleep time per day is often normal, but is mistimed and fragmented
Often worse with little daylight exposure, inactivity or in hospital and nursing-home settings
inv: Sleep diary kept by carers and actigraphy for at least 7 days (preferably 14)
Review of medicines, pain, urinary symptoms and mood disorder
Polysomnography when sleep apnoea or periodic limb movements is suspected
Cognitive assessment and brain imaging as part of the primary neurological evaluation

case.who: 81-year-old retired schoolteacher with Alzheimer's dementia, living with her daughter in Phitsanulok
case.story: She naps repeatedly through the day and wanders at night; her daughter has had little sleep for months, and the neurologist has increased lorazepam.
case.exam: Moderate dementia, no focal signs, sitting in a dim room most of the day.
case.tests: Seven-day actigraphy shows five sleep bouts per 24 hours with none longer than three hours.
case.q: What is the best first-line approach?
case.a: Structured daytime routine with morning outdoor light and activity, limit daytime naps, treat pain and nocturia and stop benzodiazepines; avoid hypnotics and routine melatonin in dementia.

read.where: Chapter 35 Neurological diseases and their effects on the sleep–wake cycle

det.patho: Degeneration of the suprachiasmatic nucleus and its inputs, reduced retinal light exposure and loss of social and activity cues flatten the circadian rhythm. In neurodegenerative disease, neuronal loss in the clock is associated with reduced amplitude of core temperature and melatonin rhythms. In children with neurodevelopmental disorders, abnormal clock entrainment and low melatonin secretion contribute.
det.clinical: Patients nap around the clock and are awake and agitated at night; carer burden and nursing-home admission are major consequences. Daytime sleepiness and nocturnal wandering increase falls and medication use. Sundowning, evening confusion, often coexists. ISWRD is common in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, traumatic brain injury and severe intellectual disability.
det.diagnosis: ICSD-3 requires chronic or recurrent disorganised sleep–wake pattern with at least three irregularly timed sleep episodes per 24 hours, lasting at least three months, with insomnia at night and sleepiness during the day. Sleep logs or actigraphy across at least a week demonstrate the pattern. Other sleep disorders, pain, drugs and environment must be excluded or treated.
det.treatment: Non-drug measures are the treatment of choice: regular meal, exercise and social times, morning bright light or outdoor time, minimise daytime napping, a dark quiet room at night and treat nocturia and pain. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine advises against sleep-promoting medicines for dementia patients with ISWRD; benzodiazepines and sedating antipsychotics raise mortality and the risk of falls. Melatonin may help children and adolescents with neurodevelopmental disorders. Structured light plus melatonin in dementia has not shown consistent benefit.
det.prognosis: Often persistent and following the course of the underlying condition; carer education and environmental changes provide the main benefit.
pearls: Count the sleep bouts with a carer diary: three or more irregular bouts and no main sleep period define the disorder.
Do not escalate benzodiazepines or antipsychotics for night wandering in dementia.
Daylight and daytime activity are the most effective treatment.
det.thd: ISWRD คือการนอนกระจายเป็นช่วงสั้น ๆ ≥ 3 ช่วงใน 24 ชม. โดยไม่มีช่วงนอนหลัก พบบ่อยในผู้ป่วยสมองเสื่อมและโรคพัฒนาการ ใช้ sleep diary/actigraphy ≥ 7 วันช่วยวินิจฉัย การรักษาหลักคือจัดกิจวัตรประจำวัน ให้ได้รับแสงตอนเช้า ลดการงีบ แก้ปวดและปัสสาวะกลางคืน และหลีกเลี่ยงยานอนหลับ

name: Nightmare disorder
formal: REM-related parasomnia with repeated, well-remembered, extended dysphoric dreams centred on danger to survival or security, with full alertness on waking and distress or impairment during the day.
simple: Frightening dreams happen again and again, the person wakes up fully alert and remembers them, and then has trouble going back to sleep.
ab: ฝันร้ายบ่อย
th: ฝันร้ายซ้ำ ๆ ที่จำเนื้อหาได้ดี ตื่นขึ้นมาตื่นเต็มที่และกลัว มักเกิดช่วงท้ายคืนใน REM พบในผู้ป่วย PTSD ผู้ที่เลิกยาบางชนิด หรือใช้ยา เช่น beta-blocker รักษาด้วย imagery rehearsal therapy
tempoNote: Episodes cluster late in the sleep period; recurrent and persistent after trauma or medicine exposure, with onset usually in childhood
feat: Vivid, elaborate dreams of threat, chasing, falling or harm to self or loved ones
Awakening with clear orientation and detailed recall, with fear, anger or sadness
Arises when REM periods are longest, towards morning
Dread of sleep, insomnia, daytime fatigue and anxiety
Little vocalisation or motor activity, unlike REM sleep behaviour disorder
inv: Clinical sleep history and review of medicines and substances
Screen for post-traumatic stress disorder, depression and anxiety
Video-polysomnography when dream-enacting behaviour, injuries or suspected epilepsy needs to be excluded
Screen for sleep apnoea if sleep is fragmented

case.story: Three months after a bus crash rescue she has three to four dreams a week replaying the scene, waking sweating and unable to return to sleep before dawn.
case.exam: Normal examination; hyperarousal and avoidance on mental state.
case.tests: No video-polysomnography required; PTSD checklist elevated; screening for apnoea negative.
case.q: Which treatment has the best evidence for her nightmares?
case.a: Imagery rehearsal therapy (with trauma-focused treatment for PTSD); prazosin may be considered but evidence is mixed.

det.patho: Nightmares arise from REM sleep, when limbic circuits including the amygdala are active and prefrontal regulation is weaker. Hyperarousal after trauma, REM rebound after drug withdrawal and disturbed emotional memory processing are all thought to contribute. Genetic factors and personality traits such as high sensitivity to anxiety raise vulnerability.
det.clinical: Nightmares begin in childhood in many cases and are common in adults under stress. Frequent nightmares cause fear of falling asleep, insomnia and daytime anxiety, and are linked to suicidal thinking in PTSD. Drugs that can trigger them include beta-blockers, some antidepressants, levodopa and dopamine agonists, and abrupt withdrawal of REM-suppressing agents such as alcohol, benzodiazepines and antidepressants. Nightmares in older adults with new dream enactment should prompt consideration of RBD.
det.diagnosis: ICSD-3 requires repeated extended and well-remembered disturbing dreams, with prompt full alertness on awakening and impaired sleep or daytime function. The history carries the diagnosis; polysomnography is not needed unless the history suggests RBD, seizures, apnoea or another parasomnia. Always look for PTSD, depression and drugs.
det.treatment: Imagery rehearsal therapy, in which the patient rewrites the nightmare and rehearses the new version while awake, has the best evidence; cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia and trauma-focused therapy help when relevant. Treat sleep apnoea or other sleep disorders and adjust provoking medicines. Prazosin has been used for PTSD-related nightmares, but a large trial did not confirm benefit, so it is an individual decision.
det.prognosis: Often chronic if untreated, but behavioural treatment brings substantial and durable improvement in most patients.
pearls: Full alertness and detailed recall point to a nightmare; confusion and amnesia point to a NREM parasomnia.
Always ask about new drugs and recent drug withdrawal.
In an older man, nightmares with shouting and limb movements should prompt a search for RBD.
det.thd: Nightmare disorder คือฝันร้ายที่จำได้ละเอียดและเกิดซ้ำ ผู้ป่วยตื่นเต็มที่และกลัว เกิดช่วงท้ายคืนใน REM พบหลังเหตุการณ์สะเทือนใจ (PTSD) หรือจากยา เช่น beta-blocker และการหยุดยาบางชนิด วินิจฉัยจากประวัติ ตรวจ video-PSG เมื่อสงสัย RBD หรือโรคลมชัก รักษาด้วย imagery rehearsal therapy ปรับยา และรักษา PTSD ร่วมด้วย

name: Sleep bruxism
formal: Sleep-related movement disorder characterised by rhythmic (phasic) or sustained (tonic) masticatory muscle activity, with tooth grinding or clenching, that may cause tooth wear, jaw pain or headache; in ICSD-3 it is described as a sleep-related movement disorder, with current consensus viewing it as a behaviour with risk, not a disease, in otherwise healthy people.
simple: Grinding or clenching the teeth during sleep, which can wear teeth and cause jaw and head pain.
th: การกัดหรือขบฟันขณะหลับจากการทำงานของกล้ามเนื้อบดเคี้ยวเป็นจังหวะ (RMMA) ทำให้ฟันสึก ปวดกราม หรือปวดศีรษะตอนเช้า พบร่วมกับ OSA ความเครียด ยา SSRI แอลกอฮอล์และคาเฟอีน รักษาด้วยเฝือกสบฟัน และแก้สาเหตุ
tempoNote: Episodes recur through the night, mostly in light NREM sleep with arousal; may persist for years and often lessens with age
feat: Grinding noises heard by a bed partner, at least three times a week in typical cases
Tooth wear, cracked fillings, hypertrophied masseters
Morning jaw stiffness, masticatory muscle pain or temporal headache
Temporomandibular joint clicking or limited opening
Occurs at transitions to lighter sleep with micro-arousals
inv: Dental examination for wear facets, scalloped tongue and masseter hypertrophy
Polysomnography with masseter EMG and audio-video (not required for routine cases)
Screen for obstructive sleep apnoea, reflux, medicine use (SSRI) and alcohol, caffeine and smoking

case.who: 25-year-old female graduate student in Chiang Mai
case.story: Her roommate hears grinding every night; she wakes with a temple headache and tired jaw, particularly during exam weeks, and drinks four cups of coffee daily.
case.exam: Flattened incisal edges, tender masseters and normal neurological examination.
case.tests: Dental assessment shows enamel wear; polysomnography is not required.
case.q: Which first-line management is appropriate?
case.a: Protective occlusal splint, reduce caffeine, alcohol and stress and treat any sleep apnoea; avoid routine medicines.

det.patho: Rhythmic masticatory muscle activity occurs in association with transient arousals from light NREM sleep, driven by a brief rise in autonomic and cortical activation that precedes the jaw activity. Sympathetic surges, neurotransmitter mechanisms involving dopamine and serotonin, genetic factors and airway events are all implicated. It is not simply an occlusal problem.
det.clinical: Sleep bruxism affects up to one in ten adults, falls with age, and is often reported by bed partners. Risk factors are anxiety, smoking, alcohol, caffeine, sleep-disordered breathing and some drugs, particularly SSRIs, and it is common in children. Complications include tooth wear and fractures, jaw pain and headache. Many with bruxism have no symptoms.
det.diagnosis: A practical diagnosis uses an international consensus: possible bruxism from self-report, probable bruxism with clinical findings such as wear, and definite bruxism with instrumental confirmation (EMG with audio-video polysomnography). RMMA is scored when there are at least three bursts in a rhythmic series. Other sleep disorders and neurological causes such as dyskinesias, epilepsy and drugs should be excluded.
det.treatment: The treatment aims to protect teeth and relieve symptoms rather than to abolish grinding. A custom occlusal splint, sleep hygiene, stress management and reduction of caffeine, alcohol and smoking are the foundation. If obstructive sleep apnoea coexists, treating it (CPAP or mandibular advancement) lowers bruxism. Botulinum toxin injections into the masseters are used off-label for severe or refractory pain; short courses of clonazepam are rarely needed.
det.prognosis: Benign and often improves with age; complications are dental and musculoskeletal.
pearls: Treat the consequences and risk factors; grinding itself cannot be reliably stopped.
Check for obstructive sleep apnoea in adults with bruxism.
SSRIs may cause or worsen bruxism.
det.thd: Sleep bruxism คือการขบหรือบดฟันระหว่างหลับ เกิดจากกล้ามเนื้อบดเคี้ยวทำงานเป็นจังหวะ (RMMA) ร่วมกับ micro-arousal พบร่วมกับความเครียด OSA คาเฟอีน แอลกอฮอล์ และยา SSRI ทำให้ฟันสึก ปวดกราม ปวดศีรษะ ใช้เฝือกสบฟันป้องกัน แก้ปัจจัยเสี่ยง รักษา OSA และอาจฉีด botulinum toxin ในรายรุนแรง

name: Sleep-related groaning (catathrenia)
formal: Parasomnia in which expiratory groaning occurs during sleep, typically in long clusters of prolonged exhalation after a deep breath, without the patient's awareness and without changes in oxygenation.
simple: A person makes a long, moaning sound while breathing out in sleep; the bed partner is disturbed but the sleeper does not know.
ab: ละเมอครางเสียงยาว
th: ครางเสียงยาวขณะหายใจออกระหว่างหลับ ผู้ป่วยไม่รู้ตัว คนข้างเตียงได้ยิน ไม่ใช่ลมชักหรือ OSA ส่วนใหญ่ไม่อันตราย รักษาด้วยการให้ความมั่นใจ บางรายตอบสนองต่อ CPAP
tempoNote: Starts in childhood or young adulthood and recurs most nights, often in clusters through the night
feat: Monotonous groan during expiration lasting 2–20 seconds, often repeated in clusters
Patient unaware; the bed partner or family complains
Occurs in all sleep stages though classically in REM
Eyes closed and no movement or awakening, with normal oxygen saturation
inv: Video-polysomnography with audio recording if the diagnosis is uncertain
Screen for obstructive sleep apnoea and for nocturnal epilepsy
ENT assessment if sleep apnoea or laryngeal pathology is suspected

case.story: His roommate complains of a moaning sound many nights; the student is unaware and wakes refreshed.
case.exam: BMI 22, normal ENT and neurological examination.
case.tests: Video-polysomnography shows clusters of prolonged expiratory groaning during REM sleep, preceded by deep inspiration, normal oxygen saturation and no epileptiform activity.
case.q: What is the reasonable management?
case.a: Reassurance, since it is benign; treat coexisting sleep apnoea and consider CPAP if the noise disturbs others.

read.where: Chapter 134: Circadian Disorders, Insomnia, and Parasomnias

det.patho: The mechanism is unclear. Prolonged expiration against a partly closed glottis during a slowed breathing pattern, possibly arising from a disturbance of the brainstem respiratory rhythm generator, is suggested. It is not a seizure and not a sleep-related breathing event.
det.clinical: The groan is heard once per breath over several minutes, repeated through the night, with onset often in the teens or twenties. The patient is usually unaware, and the disorder can cause relationship and social difficulties. There is no excessive sleepiness in most. It is not dangerous.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis depends on bed-partner history and is confirmed by video-polysomnography with audio, showing an inspiration followed by a prolonged expiration with groaning, without respiratory disturbance, arousal or epileptiform activity. Sleep apnoea, nocturnal seizures and RBD must be excluded.
det.treatment: No treatment is needed for health reasons. Counselling and noise management (separate sleeping spaces, earplugs) address social impact. CPAP has reduced the groaning in some patients, and mandibular advancement devices or surgery for associated sleep apnoea help others. Medicines have no proven role.
det.prognosis: Benign and often persistent, with no harm to health.
pearls: Groaning on expiration without desaturation is catathrenia; snoring on inspiration is not.
It is not a seizure, but video-polysomnography may be needed to say so.
The sleeper is not troubled; the partner is.
det.thd: Catathrenia คือการครางเสียงยาวขณะหายใจออกระหว่างหลับ ผู้ป่วยไม่รู้ตัวและไม่ง่วงกลางวัน สาเหตุไม่ชัด ไม่ใช่โรคลมชักหรือ OSA วินิจฉัยด้วย video-PSG ที่มีเสียง ไม่ต้องรักษาถ้าไม่รบกวนคนอื่น ถ้าจำเป็นลอง CPAP หรืออุปกรณ์ดันขากรรไกรเมื่อมี OSA ร่วม

name: Insufficient sleep syndrome
formal: Hypersomnolence disorder in which a person persistently obtains less sleep than needed for normal alertness, usually through voluntary behaviour, for at least three months, and symptoms resolve when sleep is extended.
simple: Daytime sleepiness caused simply by not sleeping enough, which goes away when the person sleeps longer.
ab: นอนไม่เพียงพอเรื้อรัง
th: ง่วงกลางวันจากการนอนน้อยกว่าที่ร่างกายต้องการเป็นเวลา ≥ 3 เดือน ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจากพฤติกรรม เช่น เรียนหนัก เข้าเวร ใช้จอก่อนนอน นอนชดเชยวันหยุดมาก อาการหายเมื่อนอนเพิ่ม 1–2 สัปดาห์ ต้องแยกจาก narcolepsy และ OSA
tempoNote: Present for at least three months and resolving once sleep is extended; typically worse on workdays than on weekends
feat: Habitual sleep much shorter than needed, such as 5–6 hours in an adult needing 8
Daytime sleepiness, irritability, poor attention and memory complaints
Sleeps much longer on weekends and holidays or when allowed
Rapid sleep onset in bed and, if tested, short latency on the multiple sleep latency test
Sleepiness improves after sleep extension
inv: Sleep diary and actigraphy over two weeks that include workdays and free days
Epworth Sleepiness Scale and driving or safety history
Polysomnography the night before an MSLT, with minimum 6 hours of sleep, if narcolepsy or idiopathic hypersomnia is considered
Therapeutic sleep extension trial of 1–2 weeks

case.who: 27-year-old male surgical resident in Chiang Mai
case.story: He sleeps five hours per night during the week and nine to ten hours on days off, and falls asleep during morning rounds; he suspects narcolepsy.
case.exam: BMI 25, normal examination, Epworth score 16.
case.tests: Actigraphy shows five hours on workdays and ten hours at weekends; no cataplexy; a home test shows no apnoea.
case.q: What is the best next step before an MSLT?
case.a: Two weeks of enforced adequate sleep with actigraphy confirmation, because chronic sleep restriction itself shortens sleep latency and can mimic narcolepsy on testing.

det.patho: Sleep need accumulates as homeostatic pressure with each hour awake, and prolonged restriction keeps the pressure high. Chronic partial sleep loss impairs prefrontal attention networks and increases microsleeps, while the person may no longer recognise the impairment. Social, occupational and technological demands are the usual cause.
det.clinical: Typical patients are adolescents, students, shift workers and healthcare staff who have a persistent shortfall of sleep but compensate on days off. They report sleepiness, low mood, irritability and performance errors, and some are drowsy while driving. Consequences include accidents, weight gain, hypertension and mood problems. Patients often underestimate their sleepiness.
det.diagnosis: ICSD-3 requires daily sleepiness for at least three months, a documented sleep time shorter than expected for age (by diary or actigraphy), and relief of symptoms by sleep extension. Other sleep disorders must be excluded. If tests are needed, the multiple sleep latency test should follow at least a week of documented sufficient sleep, because insufficient sleep can produce short latency and sleep-onset REM periods.
det.treatment: Education and a plan to extend sleep by at least an hour, with fixed bedtime, protected sleep opportunity and reduced evening screen use and caffeine, solve most cases. Short planned naps help while sleep is being extended. Stimulants are not appropriate. Where the schedule cannot change, explain the driving and safety risk, and review work patterns with the employer.
det.prognosis: Excellent if the behaviour changes; relapse follows return to restricted sleep.
pearls: Test for narcolepsy only after a documented sleep extension.
A big difference between weekday and weekend sleep suggests accumulated sleep debt.
Ask about driving; people with sleep debt consistently overestimate their alertness.
det.thd: Insufficient sleep syndrome คือง่วงเพราะนอนน้อยกว่าที่ร่างกายต้องการติดต่อกัน ≥ 3 เดือน มักพบในนักศึกษา แพทย์ประจำบ้านและคนทำงานเป็นกะ นอนชดเชยวันหยุดมาก ใช้ sleep diary/actigraphy ยืนยัน และก่อนตรวจ MSLT ต้องให้นอนเพียงพออย่างน้อย 1–2 สัปดาห์ เพราะการอดนอนทำให้ผล MSLT คล้าย narcolepsy ได้ รักษาโดยเพิ่มเวลานอน

name: Parasomnia overlap disorder
formal: Clinical overlap of NREM disorders of arousal (such as sleepwalking or sleep terrors) with REM sleep behaviour disorder in the same patient, often beginning in young adulthood and showing both features on video-polysomnography; a related extreme is status dissociatus, in which sleep stages cannot be separated.
simple: A person with both sleepwalking-type episodes and dream-acting episodes, which can lead to injuries.
th: ผู้ป่วยมีทั้งพฤติกรรมแบบ NREM parasomnia (เดินละเมอ ตื่นกลัวหลับ) และ RBD ในรายเดียวกัน มักเริ่มในวัยหนุ่มสาวและบาดเจ็บบ่อย ต้องทำ video-PSG ให้ความปลอดภัยในห้องนอน รักษาด้วย clonazepam หรือ melatonin และแก้ปัจจัยกระตุ้น
tempoNote: Variable nights per week; long-term in idiopathic young-onset cases, or acute-subacute when secondary to autoimmune or neurodegenerative disease
feat: Complex behaviours in sleep, with both early-night sleepwalking-like events and late-night dream-enacting events
Self-injury and injury to bed partners are common
Amnesia for some episodes and dream recall for others
May appear in childhood sleepwalkers who later develop REM sleep without atonia
Secondary forms occur with narcolepsy, medicines, post-traumatic or autoimmune disease
inv: Video-polysomnography with extended EMG montage and a full set of EEG channels
Screen for sleep apnoea and other triggers that provoke arousals
Review medicines (SSRIs, sedative-hypnotics) and alcohol
MRI and, when subacute, autoimmune antibodies including IgLON5

case.story: Since childhood he has sleepwalked early in the night, and in the last two years he has also shouted and punched in the early morning while dreaming; he once broke his hand on a bedside table.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination.
case.tests: Video-polysomnography shows confusional arousals from slow-wave sleep and, later, REM sleep without atonia with punching movements and a recalled dream; AHI 3 per hour.
case.q: Which strategy is best?
case.a: Treat as parasomnia overlap: make the bedroom safe, avoid triggers, and start clonazepam or melatonin, after excluding sleep apnoea and autoimmune causes.

read.where: Chapter 134: Circadian Disorders, Insomnia, and Parasomnias

det.patho: Both sleep systems that suppress motor output during sleep appear to fail: incomplete arousal from slow-wave sleep and loss of REM atonia can coexist, likely through instability of state boundaries in the brainstem and thalamocortical circuits. Genetic predisposition, sleep deprivation, obstructive sleep apnoea, alcohol and medicines may trigger episodes. Secondary forms occur with narcolepsy, brain injury and autoimmune encephalitis.
det.clinical: Many patients are young adults, often male, with a childhood history of sleepwalking. Episodes may be violent, with injuries to the patient or partner, and can have forensic implications. The two patterns of behaviour occur at different times in the night. A few have an older onset linked to neurodegeneration.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis needs history from a witness and video-polysomnography showing features of both disorders: arousals from slow-wave sleep and REM sleep without atonia. The ICSD-3 diagnosis is used for each component. Search for provoking factors and in subacute or older-onset cases consider autoimmune and neurodegenerative disease.
det.treatment: Safety first: remove sharp or hard objects, lock windows, place a mattress on the floor, and separate the bed partner if needed. Eliminate triggers such as sleep deprivation, alcohol and provoking drugs, and treat sleep apnoea. Clonazepam at bedtime is first-line for violent episodes and melatonin is an alternative; evidence is from case series. Address forensic and legal risk by documenting the diagnosis.
det.prognosis: Variable; many improve with trigger control and medicines, and attention to safety prevents most injuries.
pearls: Always ask both partners whether the early-night and late-night behaviours differ.
Young-onset RBD should prompt a search for secondary causes.
Sleep apnoea treatment alone can end the events.

name: Post-traumatic sleep–wake disturbance
formal: Persistent insomnia, excessive sleepiness, circadian disruption or sleep-disordered breathing that begins or worsens after traumatic brain injury; in ICSD-3, sleepiness after head injury is coded as hypersomnia due to a medical disorder.
simple: Sleep problems, either not sleeping or sleeping too much, that begin after a head injury.
ab: hypersomnia due to medical disorder after head trauma
นอนผิดปกติหลังบาดเจ็บศีรษะ
th: ปัญหาการนอนหลังบาดเจ็บสมอง (TBI) ได้แก่ นอนไม่หลับ ง่วงมากผิดปกติ จังหวะการนอนเสีย หรือหยุดหายใจขณะหลับ พบได้ประมาณครึ่งหนึ่งของผู้ป่วย ตรวจ sleep diary, actigraphy และ PSG/MSLT รักษาตามสาเหตุ
tempoNote: Begins within days to weeks of the injury; often persists for years, with hypersomnia more typical of moderate-to-severe injury and insomnia of mild injury
feat: Insomnia with sleep-onset and maintenance difficulty, often linked to pain, anxiety or depression
Excessive daytime sleepiness and increased sleep need, sometimes for more than ten hours
Delayed or irregular sleep timing, reduced alertness and fatigue
Sleep apnoea and periodic limb movements that were not present before the injury
More frequent after moderate to severe TBI and with loss of consciousness
inv: Detailed sleep history with a pre-injury baseline and screening for depression, PTSD, pain and medicines
Sleep diary and actigraphy for two weeks
Polysomnography, followed by MSLT if sleepiness persists without a cause
Brain MRI; hypocretin measurement is research-based or reserved for narcolepsy-like pictures

case.who: 33-year-old male motorbike delivery rider from Udon Thani
case.story: Four months after a motorcycle crash with a loss of consciousness for 10 minutes and a frontal contusion, he sleeps 11 hours a night, still naps twice a day and cannot concentrate.
case.exam: Normal cranial nerves and strength; mild inattention.
case.tests: Polysomnography shows a sleep efficiency of 94% with no apnoea; MSLT mean latency is 5 minutes with no sleep-onset REM periods; MRI shows frontal gliosis.
case.q: What is the most appropriate management?
case.a: Treat as post-traumatic hypersomnia: sleep hygiene and scheduled naps, address mood and pain, and consider modafinil or other wake-promoting agents after other causes are excluded.

read.where: Chapter 32 Sleep after traumatic brain injury

det.patho: Diffuse axonal injury and focal injuries to the hypothalamus, brainstem reticular activating system and thalamus disturb sleep–wake regulation. Loss of hypocretin neurons has been found after severe TBI. Mood disorders, pain, medicines, neuroendocrine changes and altered light exposure add to the problem.
det.clinical: Up to half of patients with TBI have a persistent sleep–wake problem. Insomnia predominates after mild TBI, whereas post-traumatic hypersomnia and increased sleep need are more typical after moderate to severe injury. Circadian delay, sleep apnoea, periodic limb movements and parasomnias also occur. Sleep disturbance slows cognitive and functional rehabilitation and worsens fatigue and pain.
det.diagnosis: Compare pre- and post-injury sleep, and use diary and actigraphy for objective patterns. Polysomnography excludes apnoea and limb movements; MSLT is used when sleepiness is unexplained. ICSD-3 uses hypersomnia due to a medical disorder when sleepiness follows an injury with an objective demonstration, and the diagnosis needs exclusion of other sleep disorders. Screen for depression, PTSD, medicines and substance use.
det.treatment: Treat the specific disorder: CBT for insomnia, CPAP for apnoea, and timed bright light and melatonin for circadian problems. For persistent sleepiness, modafinil or armodafinil has trial evidence and methylphenidate is another choice; sedative hypnotics should be minimised because they impair cognitive recovery. Plan naps, regular schedule, caffeine control and education. Manage pain, mood and sleep-disrupting drugs.
det.prognosis: Improves in many during the first year, but a substantial minority has persistent symptoms for years.
pearls: Ask about sleep before the injury; this is the baseline.
Look for newly unmasked sleep apnoea in any patient with poor recovery.
Avoid benzodiazepines when possible after TBI.
det.thd: ปัญหาการนอนหลังบาดเจ็บสมองพบได้ถึงครึ่งหนึ่ง ได้แก่ นอนไม่หลับ ง่วงมาก นอนยาว จังหวะนอนเสีย และ OSA การบาดเจ็บของ hypothalamus และ brainstem ทำให้ระบบควบคุมการตื่น-หลับเสีย วินิจฉัยด้วยประวัติเทียบก่อนบาดเจ็บ sleep diary/actigraphy และ PSG/MSLT รักษาตามสาเหตุ เช่น CBT-I, CPAP, แสงสว่าง/เมลาโทนิน และ modafinil เมื่อง่วงต่อเนื่อง

name: Sleep-disordered breathing after stroke
formal: Obstructive, central or mixed sleep apnoea (apnoea-hypopnoea index of at least 10 per hour in most studies) found in most patients after a stroke or TIA, both as a risk factor for and a consequence of cerebrovascular disease, and associated with worse recovery.
simple: After a stroke, many people also stop breathing repeatedly in sleep, which can slow recovery and raise the risk of another stroke.
ab: หยุดหายใจขณะหลับหลังโรคหลอดเลือดสมอง
th: ผู้ป่วยหลอดเลือดสมองส่วนใหญ่ (ราว 60–70%) มี sleep-disordered breathing ทั้ง OSA และ central apnoea เป็นทั้งปัจจัยเสี่ยงและผลของโรค ทำให้ฟื้นตัวช้าและเสี่ยงซ้ำ ควรตรวจ sleep study และรักษาด้วย CPAP เท่าที่ทนได้
tempoNote: Present in the first days after stroke in most patients; some improve in weeks to months as central events resolve, whereas obstructive apnoea tends to persist
feat: Snoring, witnessed apnoeas and restless sleep before or after the stroke
Excess daytime sleepiness, fatigue, low mood or poor rehabilitation participation
Nocturnal hypoxaemia, early-morning headache, delirium or worsening stroke deficits at night
Hypertension, atrial fibrillation and obesity as comorbidities
Both obstructive and central events, with central events more common in early or brainstem stroke
inv: Screening questionnaires (STOP-BANG, Epworth) have limited accuracy after stroke; overnight oximetry and home sleep testing are practical
Polysomnography when home testing is inconclusive or central apnoea is suspected
Cardiac evaluation for atrial fibrillation and heart failure
Timing: a repeat study 2–3 months after stroke if early testing shows predominantly central events

case.who: 63-year-old male retired policeman from Surat Thani
case.story: Three weeks after a right MCA infarct he is making slow progress in rehabilitation, is sleepy during therapy and his wife says he snores and stops breathing at night.
case.exam: BMI 31, BP 156/94 mmHg, left hemiparesis; Epworth score 14.
case.tests: Home sleep test: AHI 34 per hour, predominantly obstructive, nadir SpO2 78%.
case.q: What is the best management?
case.a: Offer CPAP with education and adherence support (benefit is for symptoms, mood and BP rather than proven recurrence reduction), together with weight and BP control and standard secondary prevention.

det.patho: Sleep apnoea increases stroke risk through intermittent hypoxia, sympathetic surges, endothelial dysfunction, hypertension, atrial fibrillation and impaired cerebral autoregulation. Conversely, stroke may cause apnoea by impairing pharyngeal muscle tone or brainstem respiratory control, and by causing Cheyne–Stokes breathing in the setting of heart failure. Most obstructive apnoea in stroke patients predates the stroke.
det.clinical: In studies, around two-thirds of patients with ischaemic stroke or TIA have AHI of 10 or more, and about 30% have a severe form. The typical stroke patient is less sleepy and less obese than the typical sleep-clinic patient, so clinical suspicion alone misses many. Untreated apnoea is associated with delirium, longer hospital stay, poorer functional outcome, depression and a higher risk of recurrent stroke and death.
det.diagnosis: Testing should be considered in all stroke and TIA patients, since symptoms are unreliable. A home sleep apnoea test or oximetry is practical in rehabilitation, and polysomnography is preferred if central apnoea, hypoventilation or a complex case is suspected. Early central events often fade, so treatment decisions can be re-examined after a few weeks. The 2021 AHA/ASA secondary prevention guideline considers sleep study reasonable in stroke or TIA patients.
det.treatment: CPAP is the treatment of choice for obstructive apnoea. Adherence after stroke is lower than in other patients, so early introduction, mask fitting and support are important. In SAVE, CPAP did not reduce cardiovascular events in people with moderate-to-severe apnoea and established vascular disease, but improved sleepiness, mood and blood pressure in adherent users. Weight loss, positional therapy, mandibular advancement and treatment of heart failure or atrial fibrillation are also used. Avoid sedatives and alcohol.
det.prognosis: Untreated sleep-disordered breathing predicts worse recovery and higher mortality; treating it is aimed at symptoms, rehabilitation and blood pressure.
pearls: Absence of sleepiness does not exclude sleep apnoea after stroke.
Early central events often resolve; obstructive disease persists.
Offer CPAP for symptom and rehabilitation benefit, not as proven stroke recurrence prevention.
det.thd: ผู้ป่วยโรคหลอดเลือดสมองมี sleep-disordered breathing ประมาณ 60–70% ทั้ง OSA และ central apnoea ที่เป็นทั้งปัจจัยเสี่ยงและผลของโรค ทำให้ฟื้นตัวช้า เสี่ยง delirium และ stroke ซ้ำ อาการเดิมอาจไม่ชัด จึงควรตรวจ home sleep test หรือ PSG รักษาด้วย CPAP ร่วมกับควบคุมน้ำหนักและความดัน แม้ SAVE ไม่พบว่าลดเหตุการณ์หลอดเลือดซ้ำ แต่ช่วยอาการง่วง อารมณ์ และความดัน

qx.stem: A 63-year-old man from Surat Thani, three weeks after a right middle cerebral artery infarct, is making slow progress in rehabilitation and is sleepy in therapy. A home sleep test shows an AHI of 34 per hour, predominantly obstructive. His wife says the snoring existed for years before the stroke.
qx.q: Which statement is most accurate?
opts: The apnoea is probably long-standing; CPAP is offered for symptoms, mood and blood pressure, although SAVE did not show fewer recurrent events
Apnoea is rare after stroke and the result is likely wrong
Central events will always dominate in hemispheric stroke
CPAP has been proven to halve recurrent stroke
The test should not be repeated or acted upon until six months
qx.why: Obstructive sleep apnoea is very common after stroke and usually precedes it. CPAP adherence is lower in stroke patients, and while SAVE showed no reduction in cardiovascular events in the intention-to-treat analysis, CPAP improved sleepiness, mood and blood pressure. Early central events may fade, but obstructive disease persists and is treated now to support rehabilitation.

ddx.pt: Same disorder in the general population; stroke makes it more common and may add central apnoea
Central events dominate in heart failure, brainstem stroke and early after stroke
Not a differential but a coexisting driver; sleep apnoea raises recurrence and mortality

name: Blunt cerebrovascular injury (BCVI)
formal: Injury to the carotid or vertebral arteries after blunt head, face or neck trauma, ranging from intimal irregularity to dissection, pseudoaneurysm, occlusion or transection, graded on the Denver (Biffl) scale; it may be clinically silent until a delayed ischaemic stroke.
simple: A tear or bruise in a neck artery after a blunt injury, which can hide for hours and then cause a stroke.
ab: หลอดเลือดแดงคอฉีกหลังอุบัติเหตุ
th: การบาดเจ็บของหลอดเลือด carotid หรือ vertebral จากแรงกระแทกที่ศีรษะ ใบหน้า หรือคอ ผู้ป่วยอาจไม่มีอาการจนเกิดเส้นเลือดสมองตีบภายหลังเป็นชั่วโมงถึงวัน จึงต้องมีเกณฑ์คัดกรองด้วย CTA และรักษาด้วยยาต้านเกล็ดเลือดหรือยากันเลือดแข็งตัว
tempoNote: Injury is instantaneous but stroke is often delayed; most ischaemic events occur within the first 72 hours and many within a day of arrival
feat: Often no symptoms at presentation (latent period); neurological deficit that does not match the head CT should prompt vascular imaging
Cervical bruit, expanding neck haematoma, Horner syndrome, seat-belt mark or neck pain after high-energy trauma
Delayed hemispheric or posterior circulation stroke, TIA or amaurosis, sometimes after an initially normal examination

Screening triggers: cervical spine fracture (especially C1–C3 or foramen transversarium extension), skull base fracture involving the carotid canal, Le Fort II/III fracture, hanging or clothesline injury, GCS under 8 with unexplained deficit

MRI with fat-suppressed T1 and MRA or DSA to confirm equivocal findings
Brain CT/MRI with diffusion imaging to find embolic infarcts
Follow-up CTA at 7–10 days and later to document healing or pseudoaneurysm change

case.who: 26-year-old male motorcycle courier from Bangkok brought in after a collision with a truck
case.story: He had a fractured left clavicle and a C2 lateral mass fracture; GCS was 15 and he was kept for orthopaedic surgery. Eighteen hours later the nurse finds he cannot lift his right arm.
case.exam: Right arm weakness 2/5, mild right facial droop, motor aphasia; left Horner syndrome; a faint left cervical bruit.
case.tests: Initial head CT normal. CTA neck shows an abrupt tapered narrowing of the left internal carotid artery 2 cm above the bifurcation with a flame-shaped taper; MRI diffusion shows scattered left MCA-territory embolic infarcts.
case.q: What is the injury and how is it graded and treated?
case.a: Blunt carotid injury (Denver grade II/IV depending on residual flow) causing artery-to-artery emboli; give antithrombotic therapy (antiplatelet or anticoagulant after weighing intracranial bleeding), manage the orthopaedic bleeding risk and repeat CTA.

det.patho: A shearing, hyperextension or rotational force stretches the internal carotid artery over the cervical transverse processes or against the skull base, or a hinge injury compresses it behind the mandible or sphenoid. The intima tears, blood enters the wall (intramural haematoma) or the lumen narrows, and platelet-fibrin thrombus forms on the exposed surface. Emboli, or flow-limiting stenosis, produce infarction. The vertebral artery is injured at the foramina transversaria, especially with C1–C3 fractures or subluxation.
det.clinical: Most patients are neurologically intact on arrival, which is the central danger. A delayed deficit usually arises within hours to days, though some strokes appear weeks later. Associated findings include Horner syndrome, neck pain, a bruit or an expanding neck haematoma, but the head CT is frequently unrevealing. Posterior circulation injury may present as vertigo, ataxia or drowsiness and is easily blamed on concussion or sedation.
det.diagnosis: Screening in all patients with high-risk injury patterns, using expanded Denver or Memphis criteria, catches far more lesions than screening based on symptoms. CTA of head and neck is the usual first test; DSA remains the reference for equivocal findings and for treating pseudoaneurysms. The Denver scale (grades I–V) guides therapy and follow-up. Imaging should be repeated at 7–10 days because grade I–II lesions often heal but pseudoaneurysms may enlarge.
det.treatment: Antithrombotic therapy reduces stroke risk when started early: either antiplatelet or heparin followed by warfarin/DOAC have been used, with no clear difference in observational data, and the choice depends on intracranial, solid organ and spinal bleeding risk. Grade I–II lesions are usually treated for 3–6 months, then reassessed. Endovascular stenting or coiling is reserved for enlarging pseudoaneurysms or failure of medical therapy, and grade V injuries need endovascular or surgical occlusion. Early involvement of trauma, neurosurgery and neurointerventional teams is important in polytrauma.
det.prognosis: With early screening and treatment the stroke rate in grade I–II injuries is low, whereas untreated lesions carry a stroke risk of a quarter or more; grade IV and V injuries have higher morbidity.
pearls: A normal head CT with a deficit that fits a single arterial territory after trauma means vascular imaging, not observation.
Fractures through the foramen transversarium or carotid canal are the cue to image the neck arteries.
Repeat the CTA at about a week — pseudoaneurysms can appear or grow after an initially mild grade.

qx.stem: A 33-year-old motorcyclist arrives in the resuscitation bay following a road traffic collision. He is alert, with a C2 fracture extending into the foramen transversarium. Head CT is normal. He has no focal deficit.
qx.q: What is the next step?
opts: No further imaging, since there is no deficit
Admit and wait for symptoms before imaging
CTA from aortic arch to vertex to screen for blunt cerebrovascular injury
Carotid duplex ultrasound only
Lumbar puncture
qx.why: Cervical fractures involving the foramen transversarium, C1–C3, or subluxation are screening triggers for BCVI, because many injuries are silent and cause delayed stroke. CTA is the first-line screening modality, and waiting for symptoms misses the window for prevention. Duplex ultrasound has poor sensitivity for the skull base and vertebral arteries.

qx.stem: CTA in a patient with a seat-belt neck injury shows a focal outpouching, 5 mm across, arising from the right cervical internal carotid at the C2 level, with mild irregular narrowing of the adjacent lumen; there is no occlusion and no extravasation.
qx.q: Which Denver (Biffl) grade does this lesion represent?
opts: Grade I
Grade II
Grade III
Grade IV
Grade V
qx.why: A pseudoaneurysm is Denver grade III, whereas grade I is intimal irregularity or dissection with under 25% stenosis, grade II is intraluminal thrombus or dissection with 25% or more stenosis, grade IV is occlusion and grade V is transection with extravasation. Grade III warrants antithrombotic therapy and endovascular repair if it enlarges or persists.

name: Cerebral fat embolism syndrome (CFES)
formal: Cerebral involvement of fat embolism syndrome, in which fat globules released after long-bone or pelvic fracture or orthopaedic surgery reach the brain through the circulation and cause an acute encephalopathy with a characteristic starfield pattern of small diffusion-restricting lesions on MRI.
simple: After a big bone break, tiny fat droplets travel to the brain and cause confusion, with a 'starry sky' pattern on MRI.
ab: ไขมันอุดตันหลอดเลือดสมอง
th: ภาวะที่หยดไขมันจากไขกระดูกหลังกระดูกยาวหักหรือผ่าตัดกระดูกเข้าสู่หลอดเลือดสมอง ทำให้สับสน ซึม ชัก หลังบาดเจ็บ 12–72 ชั่วโมง มักมี petechiae และหายใจเร็วร่วมด้วย MRI พบจุดเล็ก ๆ กระจายแบบ starfield บน DWI
tempoNote: Latent interval of about 12–72 hours after fracture or surgery, then abrupt encephalopathy; recovery usually over days to weeks

Hypoxaemia and tachypnoea, fever and tachycardia
Non-blanching petechiae over the axillae, anterior chest, neck or conjunctivae
Seizures, focal deficits or decerebrate posturing in severe cases; often a normal head CT
MRI diffusion shows innumerable tiny restricted-diffusion foci in deep and cortical white matter, a starfield pattern; T2*/SWI may show petechial microbleeds (the 'tulip' sign in the corpus callosum)
inv: MRI brain with DWI and SWI; head CT is often normal
Arterial blood gas, chest imaging (bilateral infiltrates), platelet count and haemoglobin
Transcranial Doppler or echocardiography for patent foramen ovale in unexplained cases
Screen for mimics: hypoxic injury, sepsis, drug effect, Wernicke encephalopathy, intracranial haemorrhage

case.who: 34-year-old male construction worker from Chonburi with a closed femoral shaft fracture after a fall
case.story: He was alert on arrival and was placed in skeletal traction. On the second night he became drowsy, short of breath and febrile, with a new rash in the armpits.
case.exam: Drowsy, opens eyes to voice, no focal weakness; tachypnoea with SpO2 88% on air; non-blanching petechiae over the chest and axillae.
case.tests: Head CT normal; MRI shows many tiny bright foci on diffusion across both hemispheres and the corpus callosum; platelets fall from 220 to 110; chest radiograph shows bilateral patchy opacities.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and what is the main treatment?
case.a: Fat embolism syndrome with cerebral involvement; supportive care with oxygenation and ventilation, early fracture fixation and avoiding further reaming, as no specific drug is proven.

det.patho: Marrow fat enters torn veins around the fracture or is pressed in during intramedullary reaming and travels to the lungs. When it crosses a patent foramen ovale or deforms through pulmonary capillaries, it lodges in the brain's small arterioles. Both mechanical obstruction and the toxic action of free fatty acids released by lipase cause endothelial injury, capillary leak and microinfarction. Platelet activation and local inflammation amplify the process.
det.clinical: The classic triad is respiratory distress, neurological change and petechial rash, arising after a free interval. Neurological signs vary from mild confusion to coma, seizures, focal deficit or a locked-in state, and can be present without a major respiratory component. Fever, retinopathy, thrombocytopenia and anaemia are common supportive findings. Because the head CT is normal, the encephalopathy is easily blamed on sedation, opioid use or alcohol withdrawal.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical, using criteria such as Gurd's or Schonfeld's score, supported by MRI. DWI shows numerous punctate high-signal foci in the white matter, basal ganglia, thalami and cerebellum in a starfield distribution, and SWI may show microhaemorrhages. Cerebral lesions can be present even if the lungs are spared. Exclusion of hypoxaemia, sepsis, drug effects and structural injury is required.
det.treatment: No specific therapy has been proven; management is supportive with oxygen or ventilation, haemodynamic support, early stabilisation and definitive fixation of long-bone fractures, and prevention of secondary brain injury. Steroids have been used prophylactically with mixed evidence and are not routine. Anticonvulsants are given for seizures, and agitation is managed without heavy sedation where possible. Intramedullary nailing technique and avoiding reaming in high-risk patients may reduce the embolic load.
det.prognosis: The majority recover gradually over one to several weeks, often better than the MRI burden suggests, though a minority have lasting cognitive or motor deficits and severe cases can be fatal.
pearls: A confused patient with petechiae 1–3 days after a long-bone fracture and a normal head CT should have an MRI.
Starfield DWI foci with preserved large vessels distinguish fat embolism from thromboembolic stroke.
The brain can be affected even without lung involvement — do not wait for hypoxia.
det.thd: Cerebral fat embolism พบหลังกระดูกยาวหักหรือผ่าตัดกระดูกประมาณ 12–72 ชั่วโมง ผู้ป่วยสับสนหรือซึม หายใจลำบาก มีจุดเลือดออกตามผิวหนัง CT มักปกติ แต่ MRI DWI พบจุดเล็ก ๆ กระจายแบบ starfield การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง ให้ออกซิเจน และผ่าตัดยึดกระดูกให้เร็ว ผู้ป่วยส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นใน 1–3 สัปดาห์

name: Non-hepatic hyperammonaemic encephalopathy
formal: Acute encephalopathy caused by high blood ammonia from causes other than liver failure, such as valproate, urea cycle defects unmasked in adults, urease-producing urinary infection, portosystemic shunts, chemotherapy (5-fluorouracil, asparaginase), bariatric surgery, parenteral nutrition and organ transplantation, with brain oedema and bilateral insular and cingulate cortical injury on MRI.
simple: Confusion and coma from too much ammonia in the blood even though the liver is working, for example from valproate, chemotherapy or an unusual infection.
ab: insular cortex sparing of perirolandic cortex
ภาวะแอมโมเนียสูงโดยไม่มีโรคตับ
th: สมองเสื่อมเฉียบพลันจากแอมโมเนียในเลือดสูงที่ไม่ได้เกิดจากตับวาย เช่น valproate เคมีบำบัด 5-FU ติดเชื้อทางเดินปัสสาวะที่สร้าง urease หรือผู้ป่วยหลังผ่าตัดลดน้ำหนัก MRI พบความผิดปกติของ insular และ cingulate cortex ทั้งสองข้าง ต้องตรวจระดับแอมโมเนียทุกครั้งที่ซึมสับสนไม่ทราบสาเหตุ
tempoNote: Evolves over hours to a few days; may recur with each trigger such as high-protein meals, infection or valproate re-exposure
feat: Fluctuating confusion, lethargy, vomiting and asterixis progressing to stupor or coma, with normal liver tests
Seizures or non-convulsive status epilepticus; EEG shows generalised slowing and sometimes triphasic waves
Cerebral oedema with raised intracranial pressure in rapid cases
MRI: symmetric T2/FLAIR high signal and diffusion restriction in the cingulate and insular cortex, relatively sparing the perirolandic cortex; may extend to frontal and temporal cortex

Triggers: valproate, 5-fluorouracil, L-asparaginase, topiramate, Proteus or Klebsiella UTI with urinary retention, TIPS or other portosystemic shunt, gastric bypass, high-dose steroids, post-transplant state
inv: Arterial or free-flowing venous ammonia drawn on ice and analysed promptly, with liver function tests
MRI brain with DWI and FLAIR; EEG
Plasma amino acids, urine orotic acid and genetic testing if an adult-onset urea cycle defect is suspected
Urinalysis and culture, imaging for portosystemic shunt, and a drug and nutrition history

case.who: 52-year-old female teacher from Nakhon Ratchasima with a gastric cancer on chemotherapy
case.story: On day 3 of infusional 5-fluorouracil she becomes sleepy and confused, and then vomits repeatedly. Liver enzymes are normal.
case.exam: Drowsy, disoriented, mild asterixis, no focal signs.
case.tests: Ammonia 280 µmol/L (normal under 50); ALT and bilirubin normal; MRI shows bilateral insular and cingulate hyperintensity with restricted diffusion, sparing the perirolandic cortex.
case.q: What should be done after confirming this diagnosis?
case.a: Stop the offending drug, give a protein-restricted diet with IV glucose, start lactulose or rifaximin and arginine/sodium benzoate as indicated, and consider haemodialysis if ammonia is very high or the patient is deteriorating.

det.patho: Ammonia is normally cleared by the liver through the urea cycle. When it is raised by drug inhibition of the cycle (valproate, 5-FU), heavy production by urease-splitting bacteria, bypass of the liver by a shunt, or a hereditary enzyme defect, astrocytes take up the excess and convert it with glutamate to glutamine. Intracellular glutamine accumulation draws water, causing astrocyte swelling, cytotoxic oedema and impaired neurotransmission. The insular and cingulate cortices appear selectively vulnerable on imaging.
det.clinical: Presentation resembles hepatic encephalopathy: drowsiness, confusion, vomiting, flapping tremor, and in severe cases coma and seizures. Because liver tests are normal, the diagnosis is easily missed unless ammonia is measured. Symptoms often follow starting valproate, a chemotherapy cycle, an infection with retention, or a surgical event such as bariatric surgery or transplantation. Raised intracranial pressure may occur if ammonia rises quickly.
det.diagnosis: Measure ammonia in any unexplained encephalopathy; a sample that is slow or warm gives false elevations. MRI shows the characteristic insular and cingulate cortical oedema with diffusion restriction, sparing the perirolandic region. EEG shows generalised slowing, and the cause is sought by reviewing drugs, urine cultures, shunts and nutrition. Genetic studies and plasma amino acids are needed when a hereditary urea cycle defect is suspected.
det.treatment: Remove the trigger by stopping valproate or the chemotherapeutic drug and treating infection or shunts. Reduce nitrogen load with protein restriction and adequate glucose calories, and use lactulose or rifaximin for gut-derived ammonia. Nitrogen scavengers (sodium benzoate, sodium phenylacetate) and arginine are indicated for severe or urea cycle-related cases, and renal replacement therapy is used early for ammonia above about 400 µmol/L or deterioration. L-carnitine is given for valproate toxicity. Monitor for cerebral oedema in coma.
det.prognosis: Prompt ammonia lowering can lead to full recovery, but delay of more than a day or so in a deeply comatose patient risks permanent brain damage or death.
pearls: Normal liver tests do not exclude ammonia encephalopathy — measure ammonia.
Insular and cingulate cortical oedema with sparing of the perirolandic cortex is the imaging fingerprint.
Valproate, 5-FU, urinary infection with urease-producing organisms and shunts are the common triggers.
