name: Traumatic dural venous sinus injury
formal: Injury to a dural venous sinus (most often the superior sagittal, transverse or sigmoid sinus) after head trauma, usually from an overlying skull fracture, causing sinus laceration, compression by an epidural haematoma or thrombosis.
simple: A skull fracture damages or squeezes one of the large venous channels in the brain, which can bleed or clot.

case.exam: Alert, bruising behind the right ear, no focal weakness; early bilateral papilloedema is not seen.
case.tests: CT shows a right occipital fracture crossing the transverse sinus groove with a thin epidural haematoma above and below the tentorium; CT venography shows an absent right transverse sinus signal with a filling defect.
case.q: What is the injury and what is the management approach?

det.patho: A fracture that crosses a dural venous sinus may lacerate its thin wall, producing slow low-pressure bleeding that strips the dura and forms a venous epidural haematoma. Alternatively, depressed bone or an overlying haematoma compresses the sinus and slows flow, while endothelial damage and stasis promote thrombus. Because the sinuses drain a large part of the brain, occlusion can cause raised pressure, venous infarction or haemorrhage, particularly when collateral cortical veins are insufficient.
det.clinical: Many patients are mildly affected or asymptomatic for hours. Common symptoms are persistent headache, vomiting, drowsiness and, with posterior fossa collections, neck stiffness or ataxia. Delayed venous thrombosis can manifest days later with seizures, focal deficits or papilloedema. Large sinus laceration may cause sudden deterioration, and torcular and vertex lesions may bleed massively at surgery.
det.diagnosis: The CT skull base and vault bone windows identify fractures over the sinus. A venogram (CT or MR) is recommended when a fracture crosses a major sinus or a haematoma lies adjacent to it. Venography shows a filling defect, non-opacification, a flow gap or an irregular contour, and helps distinguish a normal hypoplastic sinus from injury. Follow-up imaging detects haematoma expansion or recanalisation.
det.treatment: Most small venous epidural haematomas without mass effect are managed conservatively with serial imaging, since venous bleeding tamponades. Surgery is considered for large collections, mass effect, neurological decline or hydrocephalus; the surgeon must be prepared for sinus bleeding. Anticoagulation for post-traumatic sinus thrombosis is individualised, weighing venous infarction against intracranial bleeding and other injuries, and is often started cautiously after stable follow-up imaging. Endovascular stenting is considered in rare cases of symptomatic stenosis.
det.prognosis: Generally good if recognised; delayed recognition of a sinus laceration at surgery or extension of thrombosis with venous infarction worsens outcome.
pearls: Look for a fracture line crossing a sinus groove on bone windows and ask for a venogram.
Posterior fossa or vertex epidural haematomas are often venous and enlarge slowly.
Sinus thrombosis can appear days after trauma with new headache, seizures or papilloedema.

det.patho: The underlying cause is unknown. Biopsy of surgically explored cases showed non-specific inflammatory infiltrates in the arterial adventitia. It is thought to be a localised, self-limited perivascular inflammation, sometimes after infection. The carotid wall itself and the lumen are not affected. Because the pain generators in the adventitia and the nearby sympathetic and sensory fibres are irritated, pain spreads to the face and head.
det.clinical: Patients present with unilateral throat or neck pain, tenderness over the carotid bifurcation and radiation to the jaw or ear. The pain is aggravated by movement, chewing, or swallowing. There may be low-grade fever and a modest rise in inflammatory markers. Neurological examination is normal. Symptoms usually abate over two weeks, though some take a month, and recurrences are rare.
det.diagnosis: Imaging is what defines TIPIC. ICHD-3 requires acute unilateral neck pain with carotid tenderness, imaging showing wall thickening or perivascular infiltration without luminal stenosis, and resolution within 14 days of onset or on treatment, and exclusion of a better explanation. The alternative causes are dissection, arteritis, thyroiditis, infection, carotid web and tumour. Follow-up imaging that shows regression supports the diagnosis.
det.treatment: Treatment is symptomatic with NSAIDs and, for severe pain, a short course of oral prednisolone, to which the syndrome responds promptly. Antithrombotics are not required unless another vascular diagnosis is found. Patients should be advised to report new neurological symptoms. Recurrent or steroid-dependent cases should be re-examined for large vessel vasculitis or other causes.
det.prognosis: Excellent; symptoms resolve completely, and persistent changes should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis.
pearls: Always exclude dissection and arteritis first — carotidynia is a diagnosis of exclusion.
Perivascular sleeve with normal lumen and resolution within weeks is the pattern.
ICHD-3 now calls it TIPIC (transient perivascular inflammation of the carotid artery).

name: Developmental venous anomaly (DVA)
formal: A congenital variant of venous drainage composed of dilated medullary veins that converge on a single enlarged collecting vein draining to a cortical or deep venous system (caput medusae pattern); usually asymptomatic and benign, with symptoms arising mainly from an associated cavernous malformation or from thrombosis or outflow obstruction.
simple: A normal-but-unusual cluster of brain veins shaped like a jellyfish that is usually harmless and found by chance on MRI.

th: ความผิดปกติแต่กำเนิดของการระบายเลือดดำในสมอง ลักษณะคล้ายหัวแมงกะพรุน (caput medusae) ส่วนใหญ่ไม่มีอาการและพบโดยบังเอิญ ไม่ต้องรักษา ปัญหาที่พบได้คือมี cavernous malformation ร่วม ทำให้เลือดออกหรือชัก หรือเกิดลิ่มเลือดอุดตันใน collector vein
tempoNote: Lifelong and usually stable; complications are rare and occur at any age
feat: Incidental finding on MRI in most people; one of the commonest cerebral vascular malformations
Seizures or haemorrhage usually reflect an associated cavernous malformation (present in a minority) rather than the DVA itself
Headache, venous infarction or haemorrhage rarely if the collecting vein thromboses or is compressed
Contrast MRI or CT: many thin radial medullary veins converging on a large collector vein draining to a sinus or ependymal vein, with a normal intervening parenchyma
Cerebellar and frontal deep white matter locations are common; SWI shows the venous stellate pattern
inv: Contrast-enhanced MRI with SWI; MR venography or CT venography
Search for an associated cavernous malformation on susceptibility imaging
Catheter angiography only when arteriovenous shunting or another lesion is suspected
EEG if seizures, to localise the epileptogenic lesion

case.who: 33-year-old female nurse from Songkhla with new headaches

det.patho: The condition is believed to result from interruption of normal venous development, so that medullary veins drain to an enlarged transcortical or subependymal collector. These veins drain normal brain, so removing the DVA risks venous infarction. Chronic high-flow turbulence and local hypertension may predispose to cavernous malformation formation next to the DVA, and rare thrombosis or outflow stenosis may precipitate haemorrhagic venous infarction.
det.clinical: Almost all DVAs are asymptomatic and found incidentally. Seizures or haemorrhage when present are nearly always due to a coexistent cavernous malformation or to a different cause. Headache is common among patients who get scanned but rarely related. Symptomatic DVAs are uncommon and include venous infarction after thrombosis, trigeminal neuralgia from vascular compression, or hydrocephalus when a DVA compresses the aqueduct.
det.diagnosis: Contrast MRI or CT shows the caput medusae with a single collector vein; SWI is excellent for detecting the veins and any cavernous malformation. Conventional angiography shows a normal arterial phase and a venous-phase 'palm tree' pattern but is rarely needed. A DVA with an associated cavernoma, a large haemorrhage or an atypical enhancing lesion warrants further evaluation, including DSA if arteriovenous shunting is suspected.
det.treatment: No treatment is needed for an incidental DVA. The DVA must not be removed or embolised because it provides venous drainage for the surrounding brain. Where a cavernous malformation causes haemorrhage or epilepsy, surgery may be offered for the cavernoma with preservation of the DVA. Venous thrombosis is managed like cortical vein thrombosis with anticoagulation when appropriate. Seizures are treated with standard antiseizure medicines.
det.prognosis: Excellent; the annual risk of haemorrhage is very low unless a cavernous malformation is present.
pearls: Do not resect or embolise a DVA — it drains normal brain.
If there is a bleed, look for the cavernous malformation next to the DVA.
Caput medusae pattern on contrast MRI with no arteriovenous shunt is the signature.

name: Radiation-induced cerebral vasculopathy
formal: Delayed arteriopathy of intracranial and cervical vessels within or near a prior radiation field, presenting months to decades later as stenosis or occlusion causing ischaemic stroke, accelerated atherosclerosis, moyamoya-like collaterals, aneurysm, cavernous malformation or microbleeds.
simple: Arteries that were in the path of radiotherapy slowly narrow or weaken years later, causing strokes or bleeding.

det.patho: Radiation injures endothelium, accelerates atherosclerosis in large vessels, and causes fibrosis of the media and adventitia with intimal thickening and hyalinisation of the small vessels. Obliteration of vasa vasorum leads to ischaemic arterial wall damage, and fragile telangiectatic small vessels explain delayed cavernous malformations and microbleeds. Higher dose, young age at treatment, parasellar location, concurrent chemotherapy and conventional vascular risk factors increase the risk.
det.clinical: Presentations include ischaemic stroke, TIA, cognitive decline from chronic ischaemia, or haemorrhage from a cavernoma or ruptured aneurysm. After neck irradiation, carotid stenosis can be asymptomatic or lead to stroke years later. In children treated for suprasellar tumours, progressive moyamoya-type narrowing can emerge within a few years. A late stroke can be the first clue that radiotherapy is responsible.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis rests on history of radiotherapy, location of vessel disease within the field, and exclusion of other causes. CTA or MRA shows stenosis or occlusion, often long-segment or at unusual sites, and vessel wall MRI shows concentric enhancement. SWI shows radiation-associated cavernomas and microbleeds. Differentiation from tumour recurrence and radiation necrosis may require perfusion imaging.
det.treatment: Treatment follows the principles for stroke secondary prevention: antiplatelets, high-intensity statins and control of blood pressure and diabetes. Symptomatic carotid stenosis after neck irradiation may be treated with stenting rather than endarterectomy because of difficult surgical access, though the best option is individualised. Moyamoya-type patients with haemodynamic failure may need direct or indirect bypass. Cavernomas are observed unless bleeding or intractable seizures occur, and survivors should have lifelong vascular risk modification and surveillance.
det.prognosis: Variable; progressive stenosis can lead to repeated strokes, but early recognition and risk-factor treatment, with revascularisation where needed, improves outcome.
pearls: Ask any young stroke patient about previous cranial or neck radiotherapy.
Stenosis confined to the radiation field, with moyamoya-like collaterals, is the clue.
Radiation cavernomas can appear years later; screen with SWI.

qx.why: Long-segment carotid stenosis in a radiation field years later is typical of radiation vasculopathy. name: Traumatic intracranial pseudoaneurysm
formal: A false aneurysm of an intracranial or skull-base artery caused by penetrating or blunt head trauma, in which a vessel wall tear is contained by haematoma and surrounding tissue, with a risk of delayed rupture, epistaxis or intracerebral or subarachnoid haemorrhage.

det.patho: A pseudoaneurysm arises when the arterial wall is breached by a laceration, bone fragment, penetrating object or shear force, and extravasated blood is contained by a clot and surrounding tissue instead of a true three-layer wall. Its thin wall is prone to enlarging and rupturing as the clot lyses. Skull base locations are exposed to adjacent bone, while peripheral cortical branches may be torn by penetrating injuries or skull fractures.
det.clinical: Most lesions are discovered because of delayed haemorrhage, a new headache, a cranial neuropathy, or severe epistaxis in a patient with a recent skull base fracture. Intracranial haemorrhage may occur after an interval of days or weeks. Some are found incidentally on screening angiography. Delayed neurological decline after trauma that is not explained by early CT should prompt vascular imaging.
det.diagnosis: Because the sac may be small and slow to appear, an early negative CTA does not exclude it; imaging should be repeated at 1–3 weeks in high-risk patients. DSA is the reference test and shows a pouch with a broad or absent neck and delayed washout. High-risk patterns include penetrating injuries, fractures crossing the carotid canal or sphenoid, and unexplained delayed haemorrhage.
det.treatment: Because spontaneous resolution is unpredictable and rupture mortality is high, most pseudoaneurysms are treated. Endovascular options include parent-vessel occlusion with coils or liquid embolic agents, flow-diverting or covered stents for large-vessel lesions, and coiling when anatomy allows. Surgical trapping, clipping or excision is an alternative in accessible peripheral lesions with haematoma. The need for antithrombotic therapy in the presence of an associated blunt cerebrovascular injury should be weighed carefully.
det.prognosis: Rupture carries high mortality; with early identification and treatment, outcome is determined mainly by the severity of the original trauma.
pearls: Delayed haemorrhage after trauma means looking for a pseudoaneurysm — repeat the angiogram.
Massive epistaxis after a skull base fracture suggests a cavernous or petrous ICA pseudoaneurysm.
A normal first CTA does not exclude it.

case.who: 58-year-old male retired soldier from Surin treated for oropharyngeal squamous carcinoma with chemoradiation and later salvage laryngectomy
case.story: Four weeks after surgery a pharyngocutaneous fistula develops. He then has a small bright-red bleed from the neck wound that stops spontaneously.
case.exam: Haemodynamically stable, wound exposed with slough overlying the right carotid; a soft pulsatile mass.

det.patho: Radiation damage to the vasa vasorum causes ischaemic necrosis and fibrosis of the arterial wall, which is then weakened further by exposure to saliva and bacteria from a fistula, wound breakdown, or tumour invasion. A pseudoaneurysm forms before rupture, and thrombus can partially seal the defect to produce the herald bleed. External carotid branches are less critical and may be sacrificed more easily than the common or internal carotid.
det.clinical: Patients are typically heavily treated cancer patients with a non-healing wound. A small herald bleed should be taken seriously, as it precedes a major blowout in a large proportion of cases. When rupture occurs, bleeding is brisk and arterial and may obstruct the airway. Survivors may develop ipsilateral stroke from carotid thrombosis, emboli or hypoperfusion after ligation or occlusion.
det.diagnosis: Clinical risk recognition is key. CTA identifies pseudoaneurysms and exposed artery, and DSA confirms and allows treatment. When the patient is stable, balloon test occlusion assesses whether the carotid can be sacrificed; this guides the choice between occlusion and stent. Distinguishing threatened (exposed artery or herald bleed), impending (pseudoaneurysm) and acute (active haemorrhage) blowout guides urgency.
det.treatment: Emergency management is airway protection, direct pressure and volume resuscitation. Endovascular treatment is now first line: covered stent placement preserves flow but carries infection risk, and parent-vessel occlusion with coils or plugs is used when test occlusion permits or in the external carotid system. Surgical ligation has high stroke rates. Healing of the wound, with vascularised flap coverage and antibiotics, is necessary to reduce recurrence. Palliative planning is important in advanced cancer.
det.prognosis: Mortality and stroke rates are significant even with treatment; outcome depends on prompt recognition of herald bleeding and the underlying cancer status.
pearls: A small neck bleed in an irradiated patient is a sentinel bleed until proven otherwise.
Cover or protect the exposed artery and do not delay imaging.
Test occlusion helps decide between sacrifice and a covered stent.

name: Spinal cavernous malformation
formal: A cavernous malformation of the spinal cord or vertebral column, a well-circumscribed cluster of sinusoidal vascular channels without intervening neural tissue, causing slow stepwise myelopathy or acute haemorrhage, with a 'popcorn' appearance and haemosiderin rim on MRI.
simple: A small berry-like cluster of leaky blood vessels in or beside the spinal cord that can bleed and cause sudden or stepwise weakness and numbness.
ab: เนื้องอกหลอดเลือดคาเวอร์นัสในไขสันหลัง
th: ก้อนหลอดเลือดผิดปกติชนิด cavernous ในไขสันหลังหรือกระดูกสันหลัง ทำให้เกิดอัมพาตหรือชาแบบเป็นขั้นบันได หรือเลือดออกเฉียบพลัน MRI พบลักษณะ popcorn และขอบ haemosiderin ใน T2 และ gradient echo พบได้น้อยกว่าชนิดในสมอง

Acute severe back pain or myelopathy at the time of haemorrhage, often mimicking transverse myelitis or ischaemia
Progressive myelopathy with partial remission between episodes
MRI: reticulated core with mixed signal ('popcorn') and hypointense haemosiderin rim on T2 and GRE/SWI; minimal contrast enhancement and little oedema
May coexist with cerebral cavernous malformations in familial forms (CCM1–3) and with developmental venous anomalies

Brain MRI with SWI to look for multiple cavernomas and familial disease
Genetic testing for CCM1 (KRIT1), CCM2 and CCM3 if multiple lesions or family history

case.story: She suddenly develops a band of burning pain around the chest and numbness of the left leg, with partial recovery in a month. Four months later the numbness returns with leg weakness.
case.exam: Mild left leg spastic weakness 4/5, impaired left leg proprioception, right-sided pinprick loss below T6 (Brown–Séquard pattern).
case.tests: MRI T-spine: a 12 mm round intramedullary lesion at T5 with mixed T1/T2 signal, a dark haemosiderin rim on GRE and surrounding mild oedema; brain SWI shows two small cerebral cavernomas.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and how should it be treated?

det.patho: Cavernous malformations are low-flow clusters of dilated, thin-walled sinusoidal vessels lined by endothelium, with no interposed neural parenchyma and little arterial feeding. Repeated microhaemorrhage leaves haemosiderin and gliosis around the lesion. Familial forms follow loss-of-function mutations in CCM1, CCM2 or CCM3 with a two-hit mechanism, and are associated with multiple lesions.
det.clinical: Intramedullary spinal cavernous malformations occur less often than brain lesions. Presentation is commonly with sudden or stepwise myelopathy due to haemorrhage, accompanied by neck or back pain, sensory loss and weakness. Lesions in the cervical and thoracic cord are common. Recovery between events is typical, but repeated haemorrhage causes cumulative disability. Epidural or vertebral lesions cause radicular or compressive features.
det.diagnosis: MRI is diagnostic. The core shows heterogeneous T1 and T2 signal from blood products of different ages, with a hypointense rim on T2 and prominent blooming on GRE or SWI. There is typically little contrast enhancement and only mild oedema. Differential diagnosis includes haemorrhagic tumours and AV shunts. A brain MRI with SWI and family history identify multiple or familial disease.
det.treatment: Asymptomatic lesions are observed with serial MRI. For symptomatic patients with a lesion reaching the pial surface and progressive deficit or repeated bleeding, microsurgical resection is the standard approach and often yields stabilisation or improvement, especially when done soon after a haemorrhage, with neurophysiological monitoring. Radiosurgery is not established. Patients with familial disease need genetic counselling and brain surveillance. Rehabilitation supports recovery.
det.prognosis: Natural history is variable with a risk of repeat haemorrhage in symptomatic lesions; surgical results are best when symptoms are recent and the lesion lies near the pial surface.
pearls: Stepwise cord syndrome with a dark-rimmed popcorn lesion points to a cavernoma, not a tumour.
Always scan the brain with SWI — multiple lesions mean familial CCM.
Resect only symptomatic, accessible lesions.

name: Reye syndrome
formal: An acute non-inflammatory encephalopathy with fatty liver and hyperammonaemia that follows a viral illness, classically influenza or varicella, in a child who was given aspirin; it is now rare, and most children suspected of it turn out to have an inborn error of fatty acid oxidation or the urea cycle.
simple: A rare, dangerous brain and liver reaction in children who take aspirin during a virus infection, causing repeated vomiting, confusion and swelling of the brain.
ab: acute encephalopathy with fatty degeneration of the viscera
th: กลุ่มอาการ Reye เป็นภาวะสมองและตับผิดปกติเฉียบพลันในเด็กหลังติดเชื้อไวรัส เช่น ไข้หวัดใหญ่หรืออีสุกอีใส ที่ได้รับแอสไพริน ทำให้อาเจียนซ้ำ สับสน ชัก ตับโตจากไขมัน แอมโมเนียสูง และสมองบวม ปัจจุบันพบน้อยมากเพราะหลีกเลี่ยงแอสไพรินในเด็ก

feat: Child recovering from influenza, varicella or another viral illness who develops sudden persistent vomiting
Progressive change in behaviour, delirium, then stupor and coma, sometimes with seizures
Hepatomegaly without jaundice; raised transaminases and ammonia but normal or only mildly raised bilirubin
Hypoglycaemia in young children, and signs of raised intracranial pressure
Staging by depth of coma (Lovejoy stages) predicts outcome
inv: Blood ammonia, glucose, liver enzymes, prothrombin time and lactate
Urine organic acids, plasma acylcarnitines and amino acids to find an inborn metabolic cause
CT or MRI brain for cerebral oedema; liver biopsy only if the diagnosis stays uncertain
Salicylate level and a careful drug history

case.who: 7-year-old girl from Udon Thani admitted to a provincial hospital
case.story: Four days into an influenza-like illness treated at home with a pharmacy fever tablet containing aspirin, her fever settled, then she started vomiting repeatedly and became sleepy and irritable.
case.exam: Drowsy and confusable, rapid deep breathing, liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin, no jaundice, no meningism.
case.tests: Ammonia 210 umol/L, ALT 6 times normal, glucose 3.0 mmol/L, bilirubin normal; CT brain shows diffuse swelling; acylcarnitines are normal.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and which preceding exposure matters?
case.a: Reye syndrome after a viral infection with aspirin exposure; stop aspirin, treat as raised intracranial pressure and hyperammonaemia in an ICU, and still exclude an inherited metabolic disease.

read.where: Chapter 16: Neurologic Manifestations of Acute Hepatic Failure

det.patho: Mitochondrial injury in liver and brain is thought to follow the combination of a viral trigger and salicylate, which impairs beta-oxidation and oxidative phosphorylation. The result is microvesicular fat in hepatocytes, failure of urea synthesis and hyperammonaemia, and astrocyte swelling with cytotoxic cerebral oedema. A subset of children labelled with Reye syndrome in the past carried an undiagnosed fatty acid oxidation defect such as MCAD deficiency, urea cycle disorder or carnitine disorder, where the infection and fasting were the precipitant.
det.clinical: The typical child is school age and has had influenza or chickenpox. After a short recovery, relentless vomiting is followed by lethargy, agitation and delirium, then progressive depression of consciousness with decorticate or decerebrate posturing in advanced stages. Liver enlargement is common but jaundice is absent. Death usually arises from intracranial hypertension and herniation, and infants may present with seizures and hypoglycaemia instead of vomiting.
det.diagnosis: There is no single test; the diagnosis rests on acute non-inflammatory encephalopathy with hepatic dysfunction (raised aminotransferases or ammonia) and fatty change, after excluding other causes. CSF is acellular with normal protein, and a lumbar puncture is not done until brain imaging excludes herniation risk. Metabolic work-up on the first sample, taken before treatment, is essential because most modern cases prove to be inborn errors. Salicylate exposure should be documented from the history and levels.
det.treatment: Management is supportive in a paediatric ICU: intravenous glucose to keep glucose normal, correction of coagulopathy with vitamin K or plasma, nutrition without protein load while ammonia is high, and measures against intracranial hypertension such as head elevation, osmotherapy and controlled ventilation. Severe hyperammonaemia may need nitrogen scavengers or haemodialysis. Any aspirin or salicylate is stopped, and if a metabolic disease is found, disease-specific therapy and fasting avoidance follow. Public health advice is to avoid aspirin for fever in children and teenagers.
det.prognosis: Mortality has fallen sharply with early intensive care, and survivors of mild stages recover fully while deep coma at presentation carries a high risk of death or lasting neurological deficits.
pearls: In a child with vomiting then encephalopathy after a virus, send ammonia and glucose and ask specifically about aspirin.
Collect urine organic acids and acylcarnitines before treatment, because an inborn error of metabolism is now the commoner explanation.
Avoid lumbar puncture until imaging excludes brain swelling.
det.thd: Reye syndrome พบในเด็กที่ได้รับแอสไพรินระหว่างติดเชื้อไวรัสเช่นไข้หวัดใหญ่หรืออีสุกอีใส ทำให้ไมโทคอนเดรียในตับและสมองเสียหาย แอมโมเนียสูงและสมองบวม เด็กจะอาเจียนไม่หยุด ซึม สับสน และอาจหมดสติ ตรวจพบตับโตแต่ไม่เหลือง รักษาแบบประคับประคองในหอผู้ป่วยวิกฤตเด็ก ควบคุมน้ำตาลและความดันในกะโหลก และต้องตรวจโรคเมตาบอลิกแต่กำเนิดร่วมด้วย ควรหลีกเลี่ยงแอสไพรินในเด็ก

name: Paediatric acute-onset neuropsychiatric syndrome (PANS/PANDAS)
formal: A syndrome of abrupt, dramatic onset of obsessive-compulsive symptoms or severe restriction of food intake with accompanying emotional lability, anxiety, tics, regression or sleep disturbance in a child, hypothesised to reflect post-infectious or other immune-mediated basal ganglia dysfunction; PANDAS is the subset linked to group A streptococcal infection, and the entity remains debated.
simple: A disputed condition in which a child suddenly develops severe obsessions, compulsions, tics, anxiety or refusal to eat, sometimes after a sore throat, and the cause may be an immune reaction.
ab: paediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorders associated with streptococcal infections
th: PANS/PANDAS คือกลุ่มอาการทางจิตประสาทที่เริ่มเฉียบพลันในเด็ก ได้แก่ย้ำคิดย้ำทำรุนแรง หรือปฏิเสธอาหาร ร่วมกับวิตกกังวล อารมณ์แปรปรวน ติก และพฤติกรรมถดถอย อาจสัมพันธ์กับการติดเชื้อสเตรปโตคอกคัสกลุ่ม A และกลไกภูมิคุ้มกัน แต่ยังเป็นที่ถกเถียงและต้องแยกโรคอื่นก่อน

feat: Overnight onset of severe obsessions or compulsions, or sudden refusal to eat or drink, in a previously well child
Marked anxiety, separation fear, emotional lability, irritability or aggression
Motor or vocal tics, handwriting change, choreiform movements or urinary frequency

Exclude other causes: MRI brain, EEG, ESR/CRP, thyroid function, urine toxicology, copper studies if suggestive
Consider autoimmune encephalitis antibodies (including anti-NMDAR) and CSF when features are atypical
Structured assessment of OCD, tics and eating by a child psychiatrist

case.who: 9-year-old boy from Bangkok seen in a paediatric neurology clinic
case.story: Over a single week after a febrile sore throat he began washing his hands until they bled, could not go to bed without lengthy rituals, started blinking and throat-clearing, and stopped eating school lunch.
case.exam: Anxious, distressed, mild motor tics, normal tone, gait and fundi.
case.tests: ASO titre raised, throat culture negative, MRI brain normal, EEG normal, thyroid and ESR normal, anti-NMDAR antibody negative.
case.q: What is the working diagnosis and what should happen before immune therapy is considered?
case.a: PANS with possible post-streptococcal (PANDAS) trigger; exclude encephalitis and other causes, start CBT and SSRI-based OCD care, treat active infection, and reserve immunotherapy for severe cases under specialist supervision.

read.where: Considerations about the diagnosis of antibody-negative autoimmune encephalitis

det.patho: The leading hypothesis is molecular mimicry: antibodies raised against group A streptococcal antigens cross-react with neuronal targets in the basal ganglia, possibly through dopamine receptor signalling in cholinergic interneurons, with inflammatory activation of microglia. Support for this is limited and inconsistent, and the larger PANS construct accepts other infectious or inflammatory triggers such as mycoplasma, influenza and COVID-19. The reproducibility of animal and antibody findings is modest, so the condition is regarded as a clinical syndrome rather than a defined disease.
det.clinical: Children usually aged 4 to 12 years show a striking change from baseline, with severe OCD or restricted eating as the core, plus at least two of anxiety, emotional lability, irritability or rage, developmental or behavioural regression, school deterioration, sensorimotor abnormalities including tics, and somatic signs such as sleep problems or enuresis. Some episodes are followed by near-complete recovery and others relapse. Parents often describe the child as unrecognisable. Neurological examination is usually normal apart from tics or fine motor change.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, using the PANS research criteria, and relies on excluding other disease rather than on a marker. Streptococcal serology only shows exposure, since many children carry titres. MRI, EEG, and when features suggest it CSF and neuronal antibodies are used to exclude encephalitis, Sydenham's chorea, Wilson disease, lupus and substance effects. Because the construct is contested, a cautious label such as probable PANS is acceptable while follow-up proceeds.
det.treatment: Core treatment is the same as for primary OCD: cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention, and an SSRI started low and increased slowly. Active streptococcal infection is treated with penicillin or another antibiotic, but long-term prophylaxis and tonsillectomy are not supported by trial evidence. Immune therapies such as NSAIDs, steroids, IVIG or plasma exchange are used in severe, disabling cases under specialist care, with weak evidence. Family support, school plans and nutrition rehabilitation are important.
det.prognosis: Many children improve over months with psychiatric treatment, but relapses are common and a minority have lasting OCD or tics.
pearls: A very abrupt onset is the key feature; ASO titres alone neither prove nor exclude the diagnosis.
Always rule out autoimmune encephalitis when there is any seizure, altered awareness or abnormal EEG.
Do not give long-term antibiotics or immunotherapy as routine; CBT and SSRI are first-line.

qx.stem: An 8-year-old girl from Khon Kaen is brought in because, within ten days of a febrile sore throat, she began tapping objects in sets of four, refusing most foods, crying with separation fear and showing new throat-clearing sounds. She had been well and top of her class. Examination, MRI brain and EEG are normal; ASO titre is raised.
qx.q: Which initial management is best supported?
opts: Start long-term monthly benzathine penicillin and plan tonsillectomy
Give IVIG immediately for all such presentations
Assess for infection and exclude other causes, then offer cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention and a cautiously titrated SSRI

name: Cerebral hyperperfusion syndrome (after carotid revascularisation)
formal: A syndrome of ipsilateral headache, seizures and focal deficits, with or without intracerebral haemorrhage, caused by a marked rise in cerebral blood flow after restoration of flow through a severely stenosed carotid artery, when autoregulation in the chronically hypoperfused hemisphere cannot constrict the downstream vessels.

case.who: 68-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension from Songkhla
case.story: On day 5 after left carotid endarterectomy for 90% symptomatic stenosis he developed a severe left-sided headache, then a focal right-arm seizure that spread to a generalised convulsion.
case.exam: Drowsy, BP 190/100 mmHg, mild right hemiparesis and word-finding difficulty; wound is clean.
case.tests: CT shows left hemisphere sulcal effacement and a small frontal haemorrhage; transcranial Doppler shows left MCA velocity at 2.5 times the pre-operative value; CTA confirms an open endarterectomy site.
case.q: What is the mechanism and the key immediate treatment?
case.a: Cerebral hyperperfusion syndrome; control blood pressure strictly (for example labetalol or clevidipine), treat the seizure, avoid anticoagulant or antiplatelet loading if there is haemorrhage, and watch for progression.

det.patho: In long-standing high-grade stenosis, distal arterioles dilate maximally to maintain flow, and cerebrovascular reserve is exhausted. When the stenosis is relieved, autoregulation fails to constrict the dilated bed fast enough, so cerebral blood flow can rise to more than twice baseline. Raised perfusion pressure damages the endothelium and blood-brain barrier, causing vasogenic oedema and, at the extreme, haemorrhage. Impaired baroreflex function after carotid manipulation and postprocedural hypertension aggravate the process.
det.clinical: The syndrome occurs in a few percent of carotid revascularisations, a little more often after stenting than endarterectomy. The ipsilateral headache is typically followed by seizures and focal deficits, and impaired consciousness. Intracerebral haemorrhage is the most feared complication and carries the highest mortality. A neurological change after a carotid procedure is an emergency, since thrombosis, embolism and hyperperfusion need opposite treatments.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis combines timing after revascularisation, the clinical syndrome and evidence of increased flow: transcranial Doppler velocity rise, or perfusion imaging showing relative hyperperfusion. Imaging must also exclude acute infarction and a new stent or flap thrombosis. Pre-procedural predictors such as poor reserve on perfusion studies or poor collaterals help select patients for tight monitoring.
det.treatment: Prevention is the main strategy: monitor and strictly control systolic blood pressure for days after the procedure, using a lower target in high-risk patients (often below 140 mmHg or lower), and avoid hypertension surges. Established CHS is treated with intravenous antihypertensives, anti-seizure medication, head elevation and osmotherapy for malignant oedema, and antiplatelets are balanced against haemorrhage risk. Free radical scavengers such as edaravone are used in some countries. Staged angioplasty can be considered for very tight stenoses.
det.prognosis: Cases without haemorrhage often recover well; haemorrhage in this setting has a high death and disability rate.
pearls: Ipsilateral headache after carotid revascularisation is hyperperfusion until proved otherwise.
Tight blood pressure control after the procedure is the best prevention.
A transcranial Doppler rise of more than twofold predicts the syndrome.
det.thd: Cerebral hyperperfusion syndrome เกิดหลังเปิดหลอดเลือดแดงคาโรติดที่ตีบรุนแรง เพราะหลอดเลือดสมองที่ขยายอยู่นานปรับตัวไม่ทัน เลือดจึงไหลเข้าสมองมากเกินไป ผู้ป่วยปวดศีรษะข้างเดียวกัน ชัก อ่อนแรงหรือพูดลำบาก และอาจมีเลือดออกในสมอง ตรวจ transcranial Doppler หรือ perfusion imaging จะพบการไหลเวียนที่เพิ่มขึ้น การป้องกันและการรักษาหลักคือควบคุมความดันโลหิตอย่างเข้มงวด ให้ยากันชัก และติดตามอย่างใกล้ชิด

name: Autonomic dysreflexia
formal: A potentially life-threatening syndrome of sudden severe hypertension with reflex bradycardia, headache, flushing and sweating above the lesion, triggered by a noxious stimulus below a spinal cord injury level of T6 or higher, in which unopposed spinal sympathetic outflow cannot be damped by supraspinal control.
simple: In people with a high spinal cord injury, an irritation below the injury such as a full bladder triggers a sudden surge in blood pressure with pounding headache, which can cause a stroke if not treated quickly.
ab: mass reflex of the sympathetic system
sympathetic hyperreflexia in spinal cord injury
th: Autonomic dysreflexia เกิดในผู้ป่วยไขสันหลังบาดเจ็บระดับ T6 ขึ้นไป เมื่อมีสิ่งกระตุ้นใต้ระดับรอยโรค เช่น กระเพาะปัสสาวะเต็ม ท้องผูก หรือแผลกดทับ ทำให้ความดันโลหิตสูงพุ่ง ปวดศีรษะรุนแรง หน้าแดงและเหงื่อออกเหนือรอยโรค ชีพจรช้า เป็นภาวะฉุกเฉินที่ต้องหาและกำจัดตัวกระตุ้นทันที
tempoNote: Attacks begin within minutes of a trigger and resolve when the trigger is removed; recurrences are typical
feat: Systolic blood pressure rise of 20 to 40 mmHg or more above the patient's usually low baseline
Pounding headache, nasal congestion, blurred vision and anxiety
Flushing, sweating and goosebumps in skin territories rostral to the injury, with pallor caudal to it
Reflex bradycardia, although tachycardia or arrhythmia may occur
Common triggers: bladder distension or blocked catheter, faecal impaction, pressure ulcers, ingrown toenails, menstruation or labour
inv: Immediate blood pressure and pulse monitoring while sitting the patient up
Clinical search for triggers: bladder scan, catheter check, rectal examination, skin and nails
Urinalysis, abdominal imaging or cystoscopy if no trigger is found
ECG and neurological review if the attack is severe or atypical

case.who: 34-year-old man with T4 complete spinal cord injury from a motorcycle accident 2 years ago, in Chiang Rai
case.story: While travelling home by bus he developed a pounding headache, flushing of the face and neck, and sweating; his caregiver notes the urine bag has been empty for hours.
case.exam: BP 196/110 mmHg (usual 100/60), pulse 48/min, flushed face, goosebumps on the arms, a tense lower abdomen.
case.tests: Bladder scan 850 mL; catheter is kinked.
case.q: What is the first management step?
case.a: Sit him upright, loosen tight clothing, and remove the trigger by unkinking or replacing the catheter; recheck BP every few minutes and give a short-acting antihypertensive such as nifedipine or glyceryl trinitrate only if it stays high.

det.patho: Below a lesion at T6 or higher the splanchnic sympathetic outflow is disconnected from inhibitory brainstem control. Noxious or distending stimuli enter the cord and drive a massive, unopposed sympathetic discharge that constricts the splanchnic and peripheral vascular beds and raises blood pressure. Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus respond with vagal slowing and vasodilation above the lesion, which produces the flushing and sweating but cannot overcome the constriction below. Because baseline pressure is already low, an apparently moderate reading can still be a crisis.
det.clinical: Attacks often follow bladder or bowel events, so patients and carers learn to recognise the pounding headache and sweating. Symptoms may be minimal in some people, a so-called silent form, in which hypertension is found only on measurement. Persistent severe hypertension risks intracranial haemorrhage, seizures, retinal haemorrhage, pulmonary oedema and death. It also occurs during procedures such as cystoscopy, labour or surgery under inadequate anaesthesia.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical: an acute rise in systolic pressure of at least 20 to 40 mmHg above baseline with typical symptoms in someone with a lesion at or above T6. The work is finding the trigger, and the bladder is the most common source, followed by bowel and skin. Patients should carry a wallet card with their usual blood pressure and instructions for emergency staff.
det.treatment: First sit the patient upright, loosen clothing and abdominal binders, and measure blood pressure every 2 to 5 minutes. Look for and remove the noxious cause immediately, starting with the bladder (empty or change the catheter, using lidocaine gel if instrumentation is needed), then the bowel, then skin. If systolic pressure stays at or above 150 mmHg, give a fast-acting agent such as nifedipine, glyceryl trinitrate or captopril and keep monitoring. Recurrent attacks may need alpha-blockers, and anaesthesia is used before procedures and labour.
det.prognosis: Prompt removal of the trigger resolves nearly all attacks, but unrecognised episodes can cause stroke or death.
pearls: In tetraplegia, a normal-looking blood pressure may be dangerously high relative to the usual baseline of about 90-100 systolic.
The bladder is the first place to look, then the bowel.
Do not lie the patient flat; sitting up lowers pressure.
det.thd: Autonomic dysreflexia พบในผู้ป่วยไขสันหลังบาดเจ็บระดับ T6 หรือสูงกว่า เมื่อมีสิ่งระคายเคืองใต้ระดับรอยโรค เช่น กระเพาะปัสสาวะเต็มหรือสายสวนอุดตัน ทำให้ระบบประสาทซิมพาเทติกทำงานมากจนความดันโลหิตพุ่งสูง ปวดศีรษะ หน้าแดงและเหงื่อออกเหนือรอยโรค ชีพจรช้า ต้องให้ผู้ป่วยนั่งตัวตรง หาและกำจัดสาเหตุทันที เริ่มจากกระเพาะปัสสาวะ แล้วลำไส้ และผิวหนัง ถ้าความดันยังสูงให้ยาลดความดันออกฤทธิ์เร็ว

qx.stem: A 29-year-old woman with a complete T4 spinal cord injury is admitted in early labour at 39 weeks. As contractions strengthen, her blood pressure rises from her usual 95/55 to 185/105 mmHg with a pounding headache, flushing above the chest and a heart rate of 50/min.
qx.q: What is the best measure for preventing and treating this complication during labour?
opts: Withhold analgesia so as not to mask labour
Epidural (neuraxial) analgesia with close monitoring, sitting her upright, and short-acting antihypertensives if blood pressure stays high
Systemic opioids alone
Atropine for the bradycardia only
Immediate caesarean section under general anaesthesia without other measures
qx.why: Uterine contractions are a noxious stimulus below T6 that trigger autonomic dysreflexia. Early neuraxial blockade abolishes the afferent stimulus and is the standard preventive and therapeutic measure, along with an upright posture, vigilance for other triggers and a fast-acting antihypertensive when pressure stays elevated. Bradycardia is reflexive, so treating the rate alone leaves the cause.

name: Drowning (submersion) brain injury
formal: Hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury caused by respiratory impairment from submersion or immersion in liquid, in which the duration of submersion, water temperature, resuscitation quality and the presence of cardiac arrest determine neurological outcome; the term near-drowning is no longer recommended.
simple: Brain damage from lack of oxygen after a person has been under water, where how long they were under, how cold the water was and how quickly breathing was restored decide the outcome.
th: สมองบาดเจ็บจากการจมน้ำเกิดจากขาดออกซิเจนและเลือดไปเลี้ยงสมองเมื่อจมอยู่ใต้น้ำ ผลลัพธ์ขึ้นกับระยะเวลาที่จมน้ำ อุณหภูมิน้ำ และคุณภาพการช่วยฟื้นคืนชีพ เด็กเล็กและผู้ที่จมในน้ำเย็นจัดอาจรอดโดยสมองเสียหายน้อยกว่าที่คาด
tempoNote: Injury occurs within minutes of submersion; secondary deterioration from oedema, seizures and pneumonia evolves over the next 24-72 hours
feat: Submersion with apnoea, cyanosis or cardiac arrest, followed by coma of variable depth
Seizures and myoclonus in the first days; hypoxic brain swelling
Aspiration pneumonitis and hypoxaemia, which complicate neurological recovery
Hypothermia may protect the brain in cold water, but warm tropical water drowning has a worse outlook
Cervical spine injury should be suspected after diving or high-energy trauma
inv: Blood gas, glucose, electrolytes, toxicology, lactate
CT then MRI brain: loss of grey-white differentiation, deep grey matter and cortical diffusion restriction
Continuous EEG and somatosensory evoked potentials in comatose patients
Cervical spine imaging if injury is possible; chest radiograph

case.who: 4-year-old boy from Ayutthaya found face down in a village pond
case.story: He was submerged for an estimated 8 minutes in warm water, and bystanders started compressions before ambulance arrival; return of spontaneous circulation took 12 minutes.
case.exam: GCS 5, fixed dilated pupils at first, myoclonic jerks at 12 hours, temperature 34 C on arrival.
case.tests: ABG pH 7.05, lactate 12 mmol/L; CT at 6 hours shows loss of grey-white differentiation and effaced sulci; EEG shows burst-suppression.
case.q: What is the management goal and what predicts a poor outcome?
case.a: Supportive care with oxygenation, normothermia or controlled temperature, seizure control and avoiding secondary insults; prolonged submersion with poor resuscitation, early diffusion restriction and absent brainstem reflexes predict a poor outcome.

det.patho: Water in the airway causes laryngospasm, then aspiration, hypoxaemia and acidosis, followed by hypoxic cardiac arrest. The brain suffers global ischaemia and reperfusion injury with excitotoxicity, mitochondrial failure and cytotoxic oedema, affecting the cortex, hippocampus, basal ganglia and watershed zones. Very cold water in small children may lower metabolic demand and protect the brain if cooling precedes hypoxia. Secondary harm arises from hypoxaemia, fever, hyperglycaemia and pulmonary complications.
det.clinical: Presentations range from a child who cried and coughed to coma with cardiac arrest. Survivors may show myoclonus, seizures, spasticity and movement disorders such as dystonia and choreoathetosis, cortical visual loss, cognitive and behavioural problems. In the Thai setting, ponds, canals and rice-field ditches claim many Thai children under five, and drowning in flood events affects older people.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is by history and the clinical course. Prognosis is assessed with a combination of examination, EEG background, evoked potentials, brain MRI done between day 2 and 7 and biomarkers such as neuron-specific enolase, rather than any single test. Prognostication should be delayed until at least 72 hours after rewarming, and sedation and hypothermia must be accounted for. Always screen for cervical spine injury in diving and trauma settings.
det.treatment: The most important intervention is immediate ventilation, as soon as possible, starting in the water if the rescuer is trained, followed by CPR with early rescue breaths. Hospital care follows post-cardiac arrest principles: oxygenation to a normal range, ventilation with lung-protective settings, mean arterial pressure maintenance, seizure treatment and avoidance of fever, with targeted temperature management aiming to prevent hyperthermia. Prophylactic steroids and barbiturate coma are not beneficial. Rehabilitation, including for spasticity and cognition, begins early.
det.prognosis: Children who are awake on arrival usually recover fully, whereas those requiring prolonged resuscitation with coma and fixed pupils mostly die or survive with severe disability.
pearls: Early ventilation in the water or at the shore is the highest-yield intervention.
Submersion longer than 10 minutes and CPR longer than 25 minutes carry a very poor prognosis, but cold water can be the exception.
Withhold prognostic decisions until at least 72 hours after normothermia and off sedation.
det.thd: สมองบาดเจ็บจากการจมน้ำเกิดจากภาวะขาดออกซิเจนและขาดเลือดไปเลี้ยงสมองหลังจมน้ำ พบมากในเด็กเล็กที่จมบ่อ คลอง หรือสระ ผลลัพธ์ขึ้นกับระยะเวลาที่จมน้ำ อุณหภูมิของน้ำ การช่วยหายใจโดยเร็ว และภาวะหัวใจหยุดเต้น การรักษาคือช่วยหายใจและกู้ชีพทันที ดูแลแบบหลังหัวใจหยุดเต้น ควบคุมอุณหภูมิ ชัก ภาวะปอด และไม่ควรตัดสินพยากรณ์โรคเร็วเกินไป ภายใน 72 ชั่วโมง

name: Electrical injury and lightning strike neurological complications
formal: Neurological injury from the passage of electrical current through the body, with cardiorespiratory arrest, seizures, central and peripheral nerve damage, and delayed spinal cord syndromes; lightning produces transient keraunoparalysis and autonomic effects as well as direct brain and cardiac injury.
simple: Nerve and brain damage after a high-voltage shock or lightning strike, which can cause immediate collapse, temporary paralysis, memory problems, nerve injury and sometimes a late spinal cord problem.
ab: delayed neurological sequelae of electric shock
th: การบาดเจ็บทางระบบประสาทจากไฟฟ้าแรงสูงหรือฟ้าผ่า อาจทำให้หัวใจหยุดเต้น หมดสติ ชัก อัมพาตชั่วคราวจากฟ้าผ่า (keraunoparalysis) ปลายประสาทบาดเจ็บ และภาวะไขสันหลังอักเสบแบบเกิดช้าหลังเหตุการณ์ได้ ผู้ป่วยหลายรายมีปัญหาความจำและอารมณ์ตามมา
tempoNote: Immediate collapse and seizures, lightning paralysis lasting hours, then delayed myelopathy or neuropathy appearing days to months later
feat: Immediate cardiac or respiratory arrest, loss of consciousness, seizures and amnesia
Lightning: transient limb paralysis with cold, pulseless, mottled limbs (keraunoparalysis) that usually recovers in hours
Burns at contact points; compartment syndrome and rhabdomyolysis with high-voltage current
Peripheral nerve injury, often median or ulnar, and complex regional pain syndrome
Delayed spinal cord syndrome, tinnitus, tympanic membrane rupture, cataract and cognitive or mood problems
inv: ECG and cardiac monitoring, troponin; CK, urine myoglobin, renal function
CT head and spine for traumatic injury after falls or blast effect; MRI brain and cord when deficits persist
EEG for seizures; nerve conduction studies and EMG for peripheral nerve injury after 2-3 weeks
Neuropsychological testing and audiology and eye examination in survivors

case.who: 45-year-old rice farmer from Roi Et struck by lightning while working in the field
case.story: He collapsed, was unconscious for 10 minutes and, once awake, could not move his legs; a neighbour noticed they were cold and pale.
case.exam: Alert, legs flaccid with absent pulses and mottling, burn marks on the chest and left foot, left tympanic membrane ruptured; pulses and power returned 3 hours later.
case.tests: ECG sinus tachycardia, CK 4,200, CT head normal; at 6 weeks he complains of memory loss and a tingling left hand with a normal MRI brain.
case.q: What explains the early leg paralysis, and what follow-up is needed?
case.a: Lightning-related keraunoparalysis from transient vasospasm and autonomic stimulation, which usually resolves; arrange cognitive, mood, hearing and nerve follow-up.

det.patho: Current passing through tissue produces thermal injury and electroporation of cell membranes, which damages nerve, muscle and vessels along the current path. High-voltage contact injures peripheral nerves and may cause cord injury through direct current, vascular thrombosis or demyelination, whereas lightning delivers an enormous brief direct current that depolarises the entire myocardium and brainstem, often causing cardiac arrest from asystole with spontaneous recovery of the heart. Lightning paralysis is attributed to sympathetic vasospasm and transient spinal and peripheral nerve dysfunction. The mechanisms of delayed myelopathy are not settled.
det.clinical: Survivors of lightning commonly have a brief loss of consciousness, confusion and amnesia, and later headache, memory and concentration problems, sleep disturbance and mood symptoms. Keraunoparalysis tends to affect the legs, resolve in hours and be accompanied by autonomic signs. High-voltage industrial or power-line injury produces deep tissue necrosis, compartment syndrome and rhabdomyolysis in addition to neuropathies. Delayed cord syndromes can mimic transverse myelitis or ALS-like features days to months later.
det.diagnosis: The history is decisive. Initial work-up addresses life-threatening cardiac, renal and traumatic injuries, not just neurological ones. Imaging is often normal despite symptoms, and MRI helps in delayed myelopathy. Electrodiagnosis defines peripheral nerve injury, and neuropsychological testing documents cognitive sequelae that may be missed in routine examination.
det.treatment: Follow reverse triage in a lightning mass casualty: resuscitate those in cardiac arrest first, since many recover with prompt CPR. Treatment includes cardiac monitoring, fluids for rhabdomyolysis, fasciotomy when compartment syndrome occurs, burn care, seizure management and spinal precautions after falls. Delayed myelopathy has no proven treatment, though steroids have been tried. Rehabilitation, pain management, psychological support and hearing and eye follow-up are the mainstay.
det.prognosis: Lightning survivors have a lower mortality than the initial scene suggests if CPR is given promptly, but many have chronic cognitive, pain and mood problems.
pearls: In a lightning mass casualty, treat the apparently dead first, because those in cardiac arrest can be resuscitated.
Transient cold, pulseless, paralysed limbs after lightning are usually reversible keraunoparalysis.
A normal CT does not exclude persistent cognitive and neuropsychiatric sequelae.
det.thd: การบาดเจ็บจากไฟฟ้าแรงสูงหรือฟ้าผ่าอาจทำให้หัวใจหยุดเต้น หมดสติ ชัก และความจำเสื่อมชั่วคราว ผู้ถูกฟ้าผ่าอาจมีอัมพาตของขาที่เย็นและคลำชีพจรไม่ได้แต่หายได้เองเรียกว่า keraunoparalysis ระยะต่อมาอาจเกิดเส้นประสาทบาดเจ็บ ไขสันหลังอักเสบแบบเกิดช้า ปัญหาความจำและอารมณ์ การดูแลคือกู้ชีพและเฝ้าระวังหัวใจ ไต กล้ามเนื้อสลาย และติดตามระยะยาว

name: Neurological complications of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO)
formal: Acute brain injury in patients on venoarterial or venovenous ECMO, most often intracranial haemorrhage, ischaemic stroke, hypoxic-ischaemic injury, seizures and cerebral oedema, arising from anticoagulation, coagulopathy, emboli, abrupt changes in carbon dioxide and blood pressure and the severity of the underlying illness.
simple: Patients supported by a heart-lung machine for severe heart or lung failure can suffer bleeding or clots in the brain, and the injury is easily missed because they are sedated.
ab: Neurological complications of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation
th: ผู้ป่วยที่ใช้เครื่อง ECMO อาจเกิดเลือดออกในสมอง สมองขาดเลือด ขาดออกซิเจนต่อสมอง ชัก หรือสมองบวม จากยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือด ความผิดปกติของการแข็งตัวของเลือด ลิ่มเลือด และความดันหรือ CO2 ที่เปลี่ยนเร็ว มักตรวจพบยากเพราะผู้ป่วยถูกให้ยาสงบ
tempoNote: Most events occur in the first days of support or around cannulation and decannulation, and many are silent until sedation is lightened
feat: New pupil asymmetry, loss of reflexes or failure to wake when sedation is reduced
Intracranial haemorrhage (parenchymal, subarachnoid or subdural) in roughly one in ten adults, more in children
Ischaemic stroke from emboli, left ventricular thrombus, or differential hypoxaemia (north-south syndrome) with peripheral VA ECMO
Seizures, often non-convulsive, and watershed infarcts after rapid correction of hypercapnia
Brain death may need special consideration because of circuit flow and sedation
inv: Daily neurological examination with sedation holds, and pupillometry
Early head CT whenever there is a change, plus bedside transcranial Doppler and near-infrared spectroscopy
Continuous or repeated EEG; MRI is difficult with the circuit in place
Platelets, fibrinogen, anti-Xa or ACT, and review of anticoagulation targets

case.who: 52-year-old man from Phitsanulok on peripheral VA-ECMO for cardiogenic shock after a large myocardial infarction
case.story: On day 3 the team notes that when sedation is paused the team sees that his right pupil is wider than the left, and he does not follow commands.
case.exam: Right pupil 5 mm, sluggish; left 3 mm; no grimace to pain on the left; heparin infusion running with anti-Xa in range.
case.tests: CT shows an acute right frontal intraparenchymal haemorrhage with midline shift of 4 mm; platelets 62,000.
case.q: What is the immediate management step?
case.a: Hold anticoagulation, correct platelets and fibrinogen, discuss neurosurgical options, and continue ECMO with a heparin-free strategy while maintaining blood pressure control.

det.patho: Systemic heparin, consumptive coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, acquired von Willebrand deficiency and platelet dysfunction make bleeding likely. Emboli from the circuit, heart and aorta, hypoxaemia and sudden large changes in PaCO2 produce ischaemia and disturb cerebral autoregulation. Cannulation of neck vessels in VV ECMO may impair venous drainage and with carotid cannulation cause hemispheric injury. Inflammatory activation by the circuit and the underlying illness adds to the damage.
det.clinical: Events are often found because of a failure to wake, unequal pupils, or seizures, but on deep sedation and paralysis the first sign may be a CT done for another reason. Intracerebral haemorrhage is the most frequent severe lesion, with ischaemic stroke and hypoxic injury next. Risk factors include female sex, pre-ECMO cardiac arrest, rapid fall in PaCO2, low platelets, renal failure and VA support. Brain injury is the commonest cause of withdrawal of care.
det.diagnosis: Surveillance depends on frequent neurological examination, pupillometry and a low threshold for CT scanning, since transport on ECMO is hazardous and requires planning. EEG, transcranial Doppler and NIRS help in unexaminable patients. Brain death determination requires specific adaptations, such as apnoea testing by adjusted sweep gas, ancillary perfusion imaging and attention to sedatives.
det.treatment: Haemorrhage requires stopping or lowering anticoagulation, reversing coagulopathy, correcting platelets, and discussion between neurosurgery, ECMO team and family about continued support; some centres run heparin-free circuits. Ischaemic stroke is managed by reviewing the source and tailoring anticoagulation, with thrombectomy considered selectively. Avoid abrupt PaCO2 falls and hypotension, treat seizures and prevent fever. Early rehabilitation and cognitive follow-up are part of survivorship care.
det.prognosis: Brain injury roughly doubles in-hospital mortality, and survivors often carry cognitive and mood sequelae.
pearls: Pause sedation daily and look at the pupils; the neurological examination is the cheapest screen.
Lower the PaCO2 gradually after cannulation to avoid haemorrhage and watershed injury.
Brain death testing on ECMO needs modified apnoea testing and ancillary studies.
det.thd: ภาวะแทรกซ้อนทางระบบประสาทของ ECMO ได้แก่เลือดออกในสมอง สมองขาดเลือด ขาดออกซิเจน ชัก และสมองบวม จากยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือด เกล็ดเลือดต่ำ ลิ่มเลือด และ CO2 ที่เปลี่ยนเร็ว ผู้ป่วยมักได้รับยาสงบจึงต้องหยุดยาสงบวันละครั้งเพื่อตรวจรูม่านตาและการตอบสนอง ส่ง CT ทันทีเมื่อสงสัย และปรับยาต้านการแข็งตัวของเลือดร่วมกับทีมประสาทศัลยแพทย์

name: Propofol infusion syndrome (PRIS)
formal: A rare, frequently fatal complication of prolonged or high-dose propofol infusion, typically more than 4 mg/kg/h for over 48 hours, that presents with refractory metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperlipidaemia, cardiac failure with arrhythmia and renal failure through impaired mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation.
simple: A dangerous reaction to long, high-dose propofol sedation in intensive care, where the body's cells cannot use fat for energy, causing acid build-up, muscle breakdown and heart failure.
th: Propofol infusion syndrome เกิดจากการได้รับ propofol ขนาดสูงหรือนานเกิน 48 ชั่วโมง ทำให้การใช้ไขมันในไมโทคอนเดรียผิดปกติ ผู้ป่วยมีภาวะเลือดเป็นกรดดื้อต่อการรักษา กล้ามเนื้อสลาย ไขมันในเลือดสูง หัวใจล้มเหลวหรือเต้นผิดจังหวะ และไตวาย พบบ่อยในผู้ป่วยบาดเจ็บสมองที่ใช้ propofol ควบคุมความดันในกะโหลกหรือชัก
tempoNote: Develops within hours to days of high-dose infusion and can deteriorate rapidly
feat: Unexplained high anion gap metabolic acidosis with rising lactate in a patient on propofol
Rhabdomyolysis with high creatine kinase, myoglobinuria and hyperkalaemia
New Brugada-like ST elevation in V1-V3, bradyarrhythmia or refractory cardiac failure
Hypertriglyceridaemia, fatty liver and acute kidney injury
Risk groups: head injury, status epilepticus, high-dose catecholamine or steroid use, children and critical illness with low carbohydrate intake
inv: Arterial blood gas, lactate, triglycerides, CK, myoglobin, potassium and creatinine
12-lead ECG and echocardiography
Urine colour and myoglobin; liver function
Acylcarnitine profile if a fatty acid oxidation defect is a concern

case.who: 29-year-old man from Chon Buri with severe traumatic brain injury in the ICU
case.story: Propofol at 5 mg/kg/h has been used for 3 days to control intracranial pressure, and he is now hypotensive with dark urine and a new ECG change.
case.exam: Sedated, HR 48/min, BP 80/40 mmHg despite noradrenaline, no spontaneous movement, brown urine.
case.tests: pH 7.15, lactate 9 mmol/L, CK 38,000 U/L, triglycerides 11 mmol/L, K 6.4 mmol/L; ECG shows coved ST elevation in V1-V2.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the first step?
case.a: Propofol infusion syndrome; stop propofol immediately, switch sedation to a benzodiazepine or other alternative, provide carbohydrate calories, correct hyperkalaemia and acidosis, and consider haemofiltration or ECMO for refractory cardiac failure.

det.patho: Propofol inhibits entry of long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria and interferes with the respiratory chain at complexes I and II. Cells that rely on fatty acid oxidation, myocytes in heart and skeletal muscle, switch to anaerobic glycolysis, so lactate rises, energy runs out, and muscle cells break down. Catecholamines and steroids further promote lipolysis, and low carbohydrate intake makes the cells more dependent on fat. The lipid load from the emulsion adds to triglyceride accumulation.
det.clinical: The syndrome is rare but the case fatality is high. Often the first sign is unexplained metabolic acidosis, followed by bradycardia, widening QRS or Brugada-type ST changes and refractory hypotension. Rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalaemia and kidney failure follow, with fatty liver and hepatomegaly. It is more common in patients receiving neuro-ICU sedation for raised intracranial pressure or refractory seizures, and in children.
det.diagnosis: There is no confirmatory test; recognition depends on the combination of risk factors, dose and duration and the characteristic features. Clinicians must keep the possibility in mind, and measurement of lactate, CK and triglycerides in patients on prolonged propofol allows early detection. Other causes of acidosis and shock, such as sepsis, ischaemic gut and ongoing seizures, must be excluded.
det.treatment: Treatment is to stop propofol at the first suspicion and substitute another sedative such as a benzodiazepine, dexmedetomidine or a barbiturate where appropriate. Supportive care includes giving glucose as an energy substrate, managing hyperkalaemia, arrhythmia and cardiac failure, haemofiltration or haemodialysis for severe acidosis and renal failure, and mechanical circulatory support in refractory shock. Prevention means keeping propofol below 4 mg/kg/h and for as short a time as possible, monitoring lactate, CK and triglycerides daily, and giving adequate carbohydrate calories.
det.prognosis: Mortality is high, historically above one third, particularly if the infusion is not stopped early.
pearls: Unexplained lactic acidosis in a patient receiving propofol is propofol infusion syndrome until proved otherwise.
Avoid propofol above 4 mg/kg/h or beyond 48 hours where alternatives exist.
Brugada-like ST elevation is a late warning sign.
det.thd: Propofol infusion syndrome เกิดจากการให้ propofol ขนาดสูงและนานกว่า 48 ชั่วโมง ทำให้ไมโทคอนเดรียใช้กรดไขมันไม่ได้ ผู้ป่วยมีเลือดเป็นกรดจากแล็กเตต กล้ามเนื้อสลาย โพแทสเซียมสูง ไขมันในเลือดสูง หัวใจล้มเหลวหรือ ST ยกคล้าย Brugada และไตวาย ต้องหยุด propofol ทันที เปลี่ยนยาสงบ ให้พลังงานจากคาร์โบไฮเดรต แก้ภาวะโพแทสเซียมสูงและกรด และอาจต้องล้างไตหรือใช้เครื่องช่วยหัวใจ

qx.stem: A 17-year-old boy from Rayong in refractory status epilepticus has been sedated with propofol at about 6 mg/kg/h for three days. Overnight he becomes hypotensive and bradycardic, his urine turns dark, and blood tests show pH 7.12, lactate 10 mmol/L, potassium 6.5 mmol/L, CK 45,000 U/L and triglycerides 12 mmol/L. The ECG shows coved ST elevation in V1-V2.
qx.q: What is the most important immediate action?
opts: Increase the propofol dose to suppress the seizures more deeply
Give dantrolene for malignant hyperthermia
Add sodium bicarbonate and continue the propofol at the same rate
Start high-dose methylprednisolone
Stop propofol, switch to another sedative or anaesthetic, correct hyperkalaemia and acidosis and consider renal replacement or circulatory support
qx.why: The combination of high-dose prolonged propofol, lactic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hypertriglyceridaemia, Brugada-type ECG change and shock is propofol infusion syndrome. Early cessation is life-saving, with substitution of another sedative, glucose supplementation and organ support. Malignant hyperthermia follows volatile agents or succinylcholine and is treated with dantrolene; continuing propofol is dangerous.

name: Baclofen toxicity and withdrawal
formal: Two opposite syndromes of the GABA-B agonist baclofen: overdose or accumulation (especially in renal impairment) causing encephalopathy, coma, respiratory depression, hypotonia and seizures, and abrupt interruption of oral or intrathecal therapy causing rebound spasticity, hyperthermia, delirium, autonomic instability and, in severe cases, rhabdomyolysis and multi-organ failure.
simple: Baclofen, a muscle relaxant, can cause confusion, floppiness and coma if too much builds up, and stopping it suddenly can cause severe stiffness, fever, hallucinations and seizures.
th: Baclofen เป็นยาคลายกล้ามเนื้อที่ออกฤทธิ์ผ่านตัวรับ GABA-B การได้รับเกินขนาดหรือสะสมในผู้ป่วยไตเสื่อมทำให้สับสน ซึม กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนปวกเปียก หยุดหายใจ และชัก ส่วนการหยุดยาทันที โดยเฉพาะปั๊มฉีด baclofen เข้าไขสันหลังขัดข้อง ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อเกร็งมาก ไข้สูง สับสน ประสาทหลอน ความดันไม่คงที่ และอาจเสียชีวิต
tempoNote: Toxicity over hours to days; withdrawal begins 6-72 hours after interruption of intrathecal or high-dose oral baclofen
feat: Toxicity: confusion, coma with preserved but sluggish pupils, flaccid hypotonia, areflexia, bradycardia, hypothermia and respiratory depression
Seizures and myoclonus are possible, and EEG may show triphasic waves or burst suppression
Withdrawal: itching, increased spasticity, rebound spasms, agitation, hallucinations and seizures
Severe withdrawal: high fever, hypertension or hypotension, tachycardia, rhabdomyolysis, DIC and multiorgan failure resembling NMS or autonomic dysreflexia
Triggers: renal failure with oral dosing, pump malfunction, catheter kink or disconnection, empty reservoir, refill errors
inv: Creatinine and eGFR; CK, electrolytes, lactate, and toxicology to exclude co-ingestants
Baclofen level is rarely available quickly and does not guide emergency care
For pump patients: check the pump interrogation, reservoir volume, catheter by X-ray, CT or nuclear catheter study
EEG if the patient is unresponsive or has myoclonus

case.who: 58-year-old man from Nakhon Ratchasima with spastic paraplegia after cervical myelopathy on oral baclofen 60 mg daily
case.story: He developed acute kidney injury from dehydration, and two days later his family found him drowsy, then unresponsive with shallow breathing.
case.exam: GCS 7, bradycardia, limp limbs with absent reflexes, pupils reactive; no focal signs.
case.tests: Creatinine 4.1 mg/dL, normal CT brain, EEG with triphasic waves, urine toxicology negative.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and how is it treated?
case.a: Baclofen toxicity from renal accumulation; stop baclofen, give supportive airway and ventilation as needed, and use haemodialysis in severe renal impairment, since baclofen is dialysable.

det.patho: Baclofen is largely excreted unchanged by the kidney, so toxicity develops with acute kidney injury or chronic kidney disease even at usual doses. Excess GABA-B stimulation depresses brainstem and spinal reflexes and respiratory drive. In withdrawal, receptors that adapted to chronic stimulation are suddenly unopposed, releasing spinal reflex excitability and a sympathetic surge. Intrathecal baclofen withdrawal is more severe because oral baclofen does not cross as readily and the drug has a short half-life in cerebrospinal fluid.
det.clinical: Toxicity is increasingly seen in older people with kidney disease and in patients taking baclofen for alcohol use disorder at high doses or self-poisoning. It appears as alternating agitation and coma, with ventilatory failure, and the clinical picture can be mistaken for brain death because of absent reflexes. Withdrawal begins with itching and increased tone and may escalate to hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis and shock within a day or two. Patients with intrathecal pumps and their carers must know the warning signs.
det.diagnosis: Both are clinical diagnoses based on the temporal link to dose change or kidney function. Exclude structural lesions with CT, infection with cultures and other toxins. Drug levels are rarely helpful in time. When a pump is involved, immediate interrogation and imaging of the catheter and reservoir are needed to find the cause, and a fault means urgent replacement.
det.treatment: For toxicity, supportive care with airway protection and ventilation is the mainstay; haemodialysis removes baclofen efficiently and is considered in severe cases or renal failure. Flumazenil and physostigmine are not recommended. For withdrawal, the most important step is to restore baclofen at once: resume oral or enteral baclofen and benzodiazepines as a bridge, and repair or replace the pump or give intrathecal baclofen by lumbar catheter. Treat hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis and autonomic instability as in an ICU.
det.prognosis: Toxicity usually resolves in days with ventilation or dialysis, and untreated intrathecal withdrawal can be fatal.
pearls: Unexplained coma with flaccid areflexia in a kidney-failure patient on baclofen is baclofen toxicity.
Treat suspected intrathecal baclofen withdrawal as an emergency and give baclofen and benzodiazepines immediately.
Baclofen is removed by haemodialysis.
det.thd: Baclofen ถูกขับทางไต ผู้ป่วยไตเสื่อมจึงเสี่ยงต่อพิษ มีอาการสับสน ซึม กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนปวกเปียก รีเฟล็กซ์หาย หายใจช้า และชัก ส่วนการหยุดยาเฉียบพลัน โดยเฉพาะปั๊ม baclofen เข้าไขสันหลังขัดข้อง ทำให้เกร็งมาก ไข้สูง สับสน ความดันผันผวน และกล้ามเนื้อสลายคล้าย NMS รักษาพิษด้วยการประคับประคองและล้างไตในรายรุนแรง ส่วนอาการถอนยาต้องให้ baclofen และเบนโซไดอะซีปีนทันที และแก้ไขปั๊ม

qx.stem: A 33-year-old man with spastic multiple sclerosis and an intrathecal baclofen pump is brought in after two days of severe itching, increasing spasms and fever of 39.4 C. He is agitated, hallucinating, and has generalised rigidity. CK is 12,000 U/L, and pump interrogation shows the reservoir is empty after a missed refill.
qx.q: What is the most important management step?
opts: Treat as neuroleptic malignant syndrome with haloperidol
Wait for infection cultures before any specific treatment
Give dantrolene alone
Restore baclofen immediately, using benzodiazepines and enteral baclofen as a bridge while the pump is refilled or temporary intrathecal access is arranged, with supportive ICU care
Remove the pump permanently and give anticholinergic drugs
qx.why: Intrathecal baclofen withdrawal is an emergency with rebound spasticity, hyperthermia, delirium and rhabdomyolysis that can mimic NMS or sepsis. The cure is to restore GABA-B stimulation quickly: benzodiazepines and enteral baclofen as a bridge, and rapid refill or intrathecal re-establishment. Antipsychotics such as haloperidol worsen the picture, and dantrolene alone does not address the cause.

name: Metronidazole-induced encephalopathy
formal: A rare toxic syndrome of cerebellar dysfunction, encephalopathy, seizures or peripheral neuropathy during prolonged or high cumulative-dose metronidazole therapy, associated with characteristic reversible T2 hyperintensities in the dentate nuclei, splenium of the corpus callosum and brainstem.
simple: A rare side effect of long or high-dose metronidazole, causing unsteadiness, slurred speech and confusion, which usually clears after stopping the drug.
th: ภาวะสมองและสมองน้อยเป็นพิษจาก metronidazole ที่ใช้นานหรือขนาดสะสมสูง ทำให้เดินเซ พูดไม่ชัด ตากระตุก สับสน ชัก หรือปลายประสาทอักเสบ MRI พบสัญญาณ T2 สูงที่ dentate nucleus และ splenium ของ corpus callosum ซึ่งมักหายเมื่อหยุดยา
tempoNote: Appears after weeks of therapy or a cumulative dose over about 40 g, and improves over days to weeks after stopping
feat: Gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria and nystagmus
Confusion, encephalopathy, seizures or psychiatric symptoms
Distal sensory neuropathy with numbness and burning feet in prolonged courses
Occurs in patients treated for liver abscess, Clostridioides difficile, Crohn disease or brain abscess; risk higher in liver disease
Symmetric dentate, splenial and brainstem lesions on MRI
inv: MRI brain: T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the dentate nuclei, corpus callosum splenium, midbrain and pons, often with restricted diffusion
Review cumulative dose and duration; liver function
Exclude Wernicke encephalopathy with thiamine response and clinical context; EEG if seizures
Nerve conduction studies if neuropathy is suspected

case.who: 49-year-old woman from Nonthaburi treated for a large liver abscess
case.story: After 6 weeks of oral metronidazole 500 mg three times daily she noticed clumsy hands, slurred speech and unsteady walking; she then became mildly confused.
case.exam: Gaze-evoked nystagmus, scanning speech, bilateral dysmetria, wide-based gait.
case.tests: MRI shows symmetric T2 hyperintensity in both dentate nuclei and the splenium; B12 and thiamine are normal; liver abscess is improving.
case.q: What is the cause and what should be done?
case.a: Metronidazole-induced encephalopathy; stop or switch the drug if possible (shortening the course or using an alternative), expect the lesions to regress over weeks, and give thiamine if there is any doubt.

det.patho: The mechanism is uncertain. Proposed pathways include binding of metronidazole metabolites to neuronal RNA, inhibition of protein synthesis, GABA-A receptor modulation, and formation of free radicals that cause axonal swelling and intramyelinic oedema. The symmetrical lesions in the dentate nuclei and splenium suggest a vulnerability of areas with high metabolic turnover. Lesions are usually reversible, consistent with vasogenic and intramyelinic oedema rather than infarction.
det.clinical: Cerebellar signs dominate, with ataxia, dysarthria and nystagmus, and cognitive slowing, encephalopathy and seizures may accompany them. Peripheral neuropathy occurs separately, mainly after prolonged courses, and can be permanent. Patients may have been taking the drug for weeks for abscesses, C. difficile colitis or inflammatory bowel disease. It may be missed as hepatic encephalopathy in patients with cirrhosis.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on temporal association and the characteristic MRI pattern, with exclusion of alternatives such as thiamine deficiency, posterior circulation stroke, demyelination and infection. Improvement after cessation confirms it. Liver impairment lowers clearance and increases risk.
det.treatment: The mainstay is to stop metronidazole or substitute a different agent, depending on the infection being treated. Most cerebellar symptoms and MRI changes improve within days to a few weeks, though neuropathy and some cerebellar signs may persist. There is no antidote; supportive care, seizure treatment and physiotherapy are used. Empirical thiamine is cheap and safe if Wernicke encephalopathy is possible. Keep courses as short as possible and be careful in liver disease.
det.prognosis: Encephalopathy and ataxia usually recover after drug withdrawal, but the neuropathy can be slow or incomplete.
pearls: Dentate and splenial lesions on MRI in a patient on long-course metronidazole suggest this diagnosis.
Consider the cumulative dose, not only the daily dose.
Stopping the drug leads to recovery in most patients.
det.thd: ภาวะพิษทางสมองจาก metronidazole พบในผู้ที่ใช้ยานานหรือได้ขนาดสะสมสูง เช่น ผู้ป่วยฝีในตับ มีอาการเดินเซ พูดไม่ชัด ตากระตุก สับสน หรือชัก MRI พบสัญญาณ T2 สูงที่ dentate nucleus และ splenium ของ corpus callosum การรักษาคือหยุดหรือเปลี่ยนยา ส่วนใหญ่อาการและภาพ MRI ดีขึ้นภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์ แต่ปลายประสาทอักเสบอาจหายช้า ควรให้ thiamine หากแยก Wernicke ไม่ได้

qx.stem: A 41-year-old man from Pathum Thani with Crohn's perianal fistulae has taken metronidazole 750 mg three times a day for ten weeks. He now has slurred speech, clumsy hands, a wide-based gait and horizontal nystagmus, and he feels mildly confused. B12 and thiamine levels are normal. MRI shows symmetric T2 hyperintensities in the dentate nuclei and in the callosal splenium.
qx.q: Which management is most appropriate?
opts: Increase the metronidazole dose
Stop metronidazole (or switch to an alternative) and monitor, expecting improvement of the cerebellar signs and MRI changes over days to weeks
Start high-dose IV methylprednisolone for acute demyelination
Begin plasma exchange
Perform a cerebellar biopsy
qx.why: Dentate and splenial T2 lesions with cerebellar signs after prolonged, high cumulative metronidazole exposure indicate metronidazole-induced encephalopathy. Recovery usually follows drug cessation. Peripheral neuropathy may persist, and thiamine can be given if Wernicke encephalopathy is still possible. Steroids, plasma exchange or biopsy are unnecessary.

ddx.pt: Alcohol or malnutrition, ophthalmoplegia and mammillary body or periaqueductal change, with a response to thiamine
Posterior-column and corticospinal signs with low B12 and cervical cord T2 change, without dentate lesions
Similar pan-cerebellar syndrome but in chemotherapy for leukaemia, appearing in days
