name: Cefepime-induced neurotoxicity
formal: An encephalopathy with myoclonus, non-convulsive status epilepticus or generalised seizures caused by accumulation of cefepime, most often in patients with reduced renal function, in which an EEG with triphasic waves or periodic discharges and prompt recovery after stopping the drug characterise the syndrome; the wider term beta-lactam neurotoxicity includes other cephalosporins and carbapenems.
simple: A fourth-generation antibiotic that, when not cleared by weak kidneys, builds up in the body and causes confusion, jerking and seizures, which often disappear after the drug is stopped.
th: ภาวะสมองเป็นพิษจากยา cefepime เกิดเมื่อยาคั่งในผู้ป่วยไตเสื่อมหรือไตวายเฉียบพลันที่ไม่ได้ปรับขนาดยา ทำให้สับสน กล้ามเนื้อกระตุก ชักหรือภาวะชักต่อเนื่องแบบไม่เห็นการชักชัด EEG พบ triphasic waves หรือ periodic discharges และอาการมักดีขึ้นเมื่อหยุดยา หรือล้างไตเมื่อรุนแรง
tempoNote: Begins 1 to 10 days after starting cefepime (median about 4 days) and resolves within 2-7 days after cessation
feat: Fluctuating confusion, agitation or drowsiness in a patient on cefepime
Multifocal myoclonus, asterixis-like jerks and hallucinations
Generalised tonic-clonic seizures or non-convulsive status epilepticus presenting as coma
Renal impairment without dose adjustment, advanced age, brain injury and high doses are risk factors
EEG with triphasic waves, generalised periodic discharges or NCSE
inv: EEG, ideally continuous, in any unexplained encephalopathy on cefepime
Creatinine, eGFR and drug dosing review; ammonia, electrolytes and glucose
Neuroimaging to exclude structural causes (CT or MRI brain)
Cefepime plasma levels where available (trough > 20 mg/L are associated with toxicity)

case.who: 71-year-old man from Surat Thani with pneumonia and chronic kidney disease
case.story: He was started on cefepime 2 g every 8 hours; on day 4 he became drowsy, then jerked in both arms and did not respond to commands.
case.exam: Stuporous, multifocal myoclonus, no focal deficit, no fever; creatinine has risen to 2.8 mg/dL.
case.tests: EEG shows generalised periodic triphasic discharges with an improvement after a test dose of lorazepam; MRI is normal; CSF is bland.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what should be done?
case.a: Cefepime-induced neurotoxicity; stop cefepime (change to a non-neurotoxic antibiotic), give a benzodiazepine or antiseizure medication for NCSE, and consider haemodialysis, which removes cefepime.

det.patho: Cefepime is mostly eliminated by the kidney, so reduced clearance leads to high cerebrospinal fluid concentrations. The drug is a competitive antagonist at GABA-A receptors, and beta-lactam structure also increases glutamatergic excitability, leading to myoclonus and seizures. Blood-brain barrier injury in sepsis or brain disease increases CSF penetration. Cefepime is the most neurotoxic cephalosporin, and similar problems occur with imipenem, penicillin G and piperacillin.
det.clinical: Delirium is the common first sign, then myoclonus, seizures or NCSE with stupor and coma. Patients are often older, in the ICU, and have kidney failure, but toxicity can occur at standard doses, with normal creatinine in some. The condition is underrecognised as sepsis-associated or uraemic encephalopathy. EEG is needed because non-convulsive seizures cannot be seen.
det.diagnosis: Suspect the syndrome when encephalopathy appears days after cefepime is started or the dose is not renally adjusted. EEG with triphasic waves or periodic discharges and NCSE strongly supports it. Cefepime levels, when available, help. Improvement after stopping the drug confirms the diagnosis, and structural, infectious, metabolic and other drug causes must be considered.
det.treatment: Stop cefepime promptly and switch to an alternative with similar spectrum but lower neurotoxicity, taking care with carbapenems such as imipenem. Dose adjustment for renal function, with extended infusion adapted to eGFR, is the key preventive measure. Treat seizures or NCSE with benzodiazepines and antiseizure drugs, and consider haemodialysis, which clears cefepime, in severe cases or advanced kidney disease. Recovery over days is typical.
det.prognosis: Most patients recover fully within a week of stopping, though NCSE that is recognised late carries higher mortality.
pearls: Unexplained encephalopathy with myoclonus in a patient on cefepime with kidney disease needs an EEG and a drug change.
Cefepime is dialysable; haemodialysis speeds recovery.
Always adjust beta-lactam dose for renal function and monitor in ICU.
det.thd: Cefepime-induced neurotoxicity เกิดจากยาสะสมในผู้ป่วยไตเสื่อม ทำให้สับสน กล้ามเนื้อกระตุก ชัก หรือภาวะชักต่อเนื่องแบบ NCSE โดย EEG มักพบ triphasic waves หรือ periodic discharges ควรปรับขนาดยาตามการทำงานของไต เมื่อสงสัยให้หยุดยา เปลี่ยนยาปฏิชีวนะ ให้ยากันชักหรือเบนโซไดอะซีปีน และล้างไตในรายรุนแรง ส่วนใหญ่ฟื้นภายในไม่กี่วันหลังหยุดยา

qx.stem: A 66-year-old woman with diabetic kidney disease (eGFR 22) is treated for hospital-acquired pneumonia with cefepime 2 g every 8 hours. On day 5 she becomes stuporous with multifocal myoclonus. CT head is normal, CSF is acellular, and EEG shows generalised periodic triphasic discharges with fluctuating amplitude.
qx.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Stop cefepime, change to a non-neurotoxic antibiotic with renal dosing, treat any non-convulsive seizures and consider haemodialysis if the encephalopathy is severe
Continue cefepime and add levetiracetam alone
Start intravenous acyclovir and repeat the lumbar puncture
Give IV immunoglobulin for presumed autoimmune encephalitis
Increase cefepime to a meningitic dose because of CNS infection
qx.why: Unadjusted cefepime in renal impairment accumulates and antagonises GABA-A receptors, producing encephalopathy, myoclonus and non-convulsive status with a triphasic or periodic EEG. Recovery usually follows withdrawal of the drug, and haemodialysis clears cefepime in severe cases. Adding an antiseizure drug alone while continuing the cause fails, and the normal CSF makes encephalitis unlikely.

name: Limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy (LATE)
formal: A common amnestic neurodegenerative disorder of advanced age, defined neuropathologically by TDP-43 proteinopathy that begins in the amygdala and spreads to the hippocampus and middle frontal gyrus (LATE-NC), often with hippocampal sclerosis and usually coexisting with Alzheimer neuropathology, producing a slowly progressive amnestic dementia that mimics Alzheimer disease.
simple: A common cause of memory loss in people over 80, caused by a buildup of the protein TDP-43 in memory areas of the brain, often together with Alzheimer disease, and currently diagnosable only after death.
th: LATE เป็นภาวะสมองเสื่อมแบบความจำเสื่อมในผู้สูงอายุมาก เกิดจากการสะสมโปรตีน TDP-43 เริ่มที่ amygdala และ hippocampus มักพบร่วมกับพยาธิสภาพ Alzheimer และ hippocampal sclerosis อาการช้าและคล้ายโรค Alzheimer แต่ผลตรวจ amyloid อาจเป็นลบ ปัจจุบันวินิจฉัยแน่ชัดได้จากการตรวจศพเท่านั้น
tempoNote: Slowly progressive over years, usually slower than typical Alzheimer disease
feat: Age over 80 with gradual, mostly amnestic cognitive decline
Prominent hippocampal and medial temporal atrophy disproportionate to the degree of cortical atrophy
Negative amyloid and, often, negative tau biomarkers, or only mild Alzheimer pathology
Frequent coexistence with Alzheimer disease, vascular disease and Lewy body pathology in the oldest old
Slower decline than in Alzheimer disease; hippocampal sclerosis may show asymmetric atrophy
inv: Neuropsychology: amnestic profile with relatively preserved other domains early
MRI: medial temporal atrophy, hippocampal volume loss; FDG-PET shows medial temporal hypometabolism
Amyloid PET, CSF or plasma p-tau217 to separate AD from LATE-NC (negative or low in LATE alone)
No validated in-life TDP-43 biomarker yet; diagnosis is confirmed at autopsy

case.story: Her family describe 5 years of slowly worsening memory for recent conversations, while language, judgement and personality have remained intact; she lives with her daughter.
case.exam: MoCA 19/30 with poor delayed recall and normal naming and visuospatial tasks; neurological examination is normal.
case.tests: MRI shows marked bilateral hippocampal atrophy; plasma p-tau217 and amyloid PET are negative.
case.q: Which label fits best, and what does the negative biomarker result imply for therapy?
case.a: Probable LATE (amnestic dementia with negative AD biomarkers); this is an exclusion-based clinical label as TDP-43 cannot yet be measured in life, and it is not suitable for anti-amyloid therapy.

det.patho: LATE-NC is characterised by abnormal phosphorylated TDP-43 inclusions in neurons and glia, staged from amygdala only (stage 1) to hippocampus (stage 2) and then middle frontal gyrus (stage 3). Risk genes include TMEM106B, GRN, ABCC9 and APOE, which implicate lysosomal and neuroinflammatory pathways. The proteinopathy is distinct from frontotemporal lobar degeneration with TDP-43 and ALS in distribution and age. Co-pathologies such as amyloid plaques, neurofibrillary tangles, cerebral small vessel disease and Lewy bodies are found in a majority of those with LATE-NC.
det.clinical: The condition affects roughly a quarter of people aged over 80 at autopsy. Alone it causes a slowly progressive amnestic syndrome with preserved judgement, language and personality, and in combination with Alzheimer disease, it accelerates decline. Clinically, the pace is slower than typical Alzheimer disease. Because the presentation overlaps with Alzheimer disease, it is often labelled as Alzheimer dementia.
det.diagnosis: A consensus working group set neuropathological criteria in 2019, but there is no validated biomarker in life. A probable clinical diagnosis rests on age over 80, a slowly progressive amnestic syndrome, disproportionate hippocampal atrophy and negative amyloid or tau biomarkers. As blood biomarkers of Alzheimer pathology (p-tau217) become widely available, they will identify amyloid-negative patients who need alternative explanations. TDP-43 seed amplification and PET ligands are under development.
det.treatment: There is no disease-specific therapy, and patients with negative amyloid biomarkers are not candidates for anti-amyloid antibodies. Management follows general dementia care: cholinesterase inhibitors may be tried although evidence is limited, along with vascular risk control, hearing and vision correction, exercise, social engagement, caregiver support and advance care planning. Clinical trials aimed at TDP-43 are beginning.
det.prognosis: The course is slow, typically a few years longer than Alzheimer disease, but the combination with Alzheimer pathology is associated with faster decline.
pearls: An amyloid- and p-tau-negative amnestic dementia in a person over 80 should raise LATE.
LATE and Alzheimer disease frequently coexist; one does not exclude the other.
Diagnosis in life is still presumptive until TDP-43 biomarkers are validated.
det.thd: LATE คือภาวะสมองเสื่อมแบบความจำเสื่อมในผู้สูงอายุมาก เกิดจากโปรตีน TDP-43 สะสมที่ amygdala และ hippocampus มักพบร่วมกับโรค Alzheimer ผู้ป่วยมีความจำเสื่อมช้า ๆ MRI พบ hippocampus ฝ่อชัดแต่ผลตรวจ amyloid และ p-tau อาจเป็นลบ ปัจจุบันยังไม่มีตัวบ่งชี้ TDP-43 ในผู้ป่วยมีชีวิต จึงวินิจฉัยโดยการตัดโรคอื่นและยืนยันจากการตรวจศพ ไม่เหมาะกับยาต้าน amyloid และดูแลตามหลักโรคสมองเสื่อม

qx.stem: A neuropathologist reviewing the brain of an 88-year-old woman with slowly progressive amnestic dementia finds modest Alzheimer-type changes but dense phosphorylated TDP-43 inclusions in the amygdala and hippocampus, and hippocampal sclerosis. Her amyloid PET five years earlier was negative.
qx.q: Which description of this disorder is correct?
opts: It is the neuropathological basis of behavioural-variant FTD in people aged 55
It is a prion disease with rapid course
It is a pure disorder that never coexists with other pathology
It is a common disorder of advanced age with TDP-43 pathology that begins in the amygdala, mimics Alzheimer dementia, and often coexists with it
It responds to anti-amyloid antibodies
qx.why: This entity is a frequent cause of slowly progressive amnestic dementia over age 80. TDP-43 pathology starts in the amygdala, extends to the hippocampus and then the frontal cortex, often with hippocampal sclerosis, and coexists with Alzheimer pathology in many cases. There is no antemortem biomarker yet, and anti-amyloid therapy is ineffective for it.

name: Kernicterus (bilirubin encephalopathy)
formal: Chronic bilirubin encephalopathy resulting from deposition of unconjugated bilirubin in the basal ganglia (especially globus pallidus), brainstem nuclei and cerebellum of neonates with severe hyperbilirubinaemia, producing athetoid dyskinetic cerebral palsy, sensorineural hearing loss, upgaze palsy and dental enamel hypoplasia; the acute phase is called acute bilirubin encephalopathy.
simple: Brain damage in newborns from very high jaundice levels that causes stiff or writhing movements, deafness and eye movement problems, and is completely preventable with timely phototherapy.
th: Kernicterus หรือสมองถูกทำลายจากบิลิรูบินในทารกแรกเกิด เกิดเมื่อ unconjugated bilirubin สูงมากจนเข้าสมอง โดยเฉพาะ globus pallidus ก้านสมอง และสมองน้อย ทำให้เกร็ง ตัวแอ่น หูหนวก ตามองขึ้นบนไม่ได้ และ cerebral palsy ชนิดเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติ ป้องกันได้ด้วยการตรวจติดตามเหลืองและให้การส่องไฟ แลกเปลี่ยนเลือดโดยเร็ว
tempoNote: Acute phase within the first days to a week of life; chronic sequelae become evident over the first year and persist
feat: Early: lethargy, poor suck and hypotonia in a jaundiced newborn
Intermediate: irritability, high-pitched cry, hypertonia with retrocollis and opisthotonus, fever
Advanced: apnoea, seizures, coma; chronic: athetosis or dystonia, sensorineural deafness, vertical gaze palsy and enamel hypoplasia
Risk factors: G6PD deficiency, ABO or Rh incompatibility, prematurity, sepsis, delayed discharge without bilirubin follow-up
T2 hyperintensity of the globus pallidus on MRI in the chronic phase and T1 hyperintensity in the acute phase
inv: Total and direct serum bilirubin, with bilirubin-to-albumin ratio and plotting on hour-specific nomograms
Direct antiglobulin test, blood group, G6PD assay, haemoglobin and reticulocytes
Auditory brainstem response (ABR), which is often abnormal with auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder
MRI brain: pallidal and subthalamic signal change in the acute and chronic stages

case.who: 6-day-old term boy from Surin, discharged on day 2 and breast-fed at home
case.story: His mother noticed deepening yellow colour, sleepiness and weak feeding, and later that he arched his back when stimulated.
case.exam: Deeply jaundiced to the legs, lethargic, high-pitched cry, hypertonic with arching of the neck and trunk.
case.tests: Total bilirubin 32 mg/dL, G6PD enzyme activity is markedly low, Coombs test negative.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what is the emergency treatment?
case.a: Acute bilirubin encephalopathy from G6PD deficiency; intensive phototherapy and urgent exchange transfusion with intravenous fluids, avoiding drugs that displace bilirubin from albumin.

det.patho: Unbound free bilirubin crosses an immature or injured blood-brain barrier and enters neurons and glia, particularly in the globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, brainstem auditory nuclei, cranial nerve III and VIII nuclei and cerebellum. It interferes with mitochondrial energy metabolism, induces excitotoxicity and apoptosis. Risk depends on free bilirubin rather than total level, so acidosis, sepsis, low albumin, prematurity and drugs such as sulfonamides raise vulnerability. G6PD deficiency can cause rapid haemolysis and sudden rises in bilirubin.
det.clinical: Acute bilirubin encephalopathy evolves through lethargy and hypotonia, then irritability with hypertonia and arching, and finally apnoea, seizures and death. Survivors develop the chronic tetrad of athetoid or dystonic movements, sensorineural hearing loss (often with auditory neuropathy), upward gaze limitation and dental enamel dysplasia, with intellect often spared. Milder bilirubin-induced neurologic dysfunction may cause isolated hearing or motor problems. Incidence is higher where G6PD deficiency is prevalent, including Southeast Asia.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is by clinical staging combined with the bilirubin level and the neonatal history, and by characteristic MRI pallidal changes. ABR is the best test for auditory involvement. Universal pre-discharge bilirubin screening with age-specific nomograms and a plan for follow-up within 48 hours are the core of prevention. Determine the cause of hyperbilirubinaemia, particularly haemolysis, G6PD deficiency and sepsis.
det.treatment: Prevention and rapid treatment are crucial: intensive phototherapy, intravenous hydration and treating the cause, with exchange transfusion when bilirubin approaches the exchange threshold or when acute encephalopathy signs appear. Intravenous immunoglobulin is used in isoimmune haemolysis. Avoid drugs that displace bilirubin and check G6PD status. For chronic disease, management is multidisciplinary: hearing aids or cochlear implants (with caution in auditory neuropathy), physiotherapy, oral drugs or deep brain stimulation for dystonia and speech and communication support.
det.prognosis: Early recognition and exchange transfusion can reverse acute signs, but established chronic bilirubin encephalopathy is permanent.
pearls: Total bilirubin on the nomogram, not skin colour, determines the risk.
G6PD deficiency is a leading cause of severe neonatal jaundice and kernicterus in Thailand.
Deafness with preserved cognition and athetosis in a child suggests prior kernicterus.
det.thd: Kernicterus เกิดจากบิลิรูบินชนิดไม่จับคู่สูงมากในทารกแรกเกิดจนเข้าสมองและทำลาย globus pallidus ก้านสมอง และสมองน้อย ระยะเฉียบพลันทำให้ซึม ตัวอ่อน ต่อมาแอ่นหลัง ชัก และระยะเรื้อรังเกิด athetoid cerebral palsy หูหนวก ตามองขึ้นบนลำบาก และฟันผิดปกติ สาเหตุที่พบบ่อยในไทยคือ G6PD deficiency การป้องกันคือติดตามระดับบิลิรูบินตามเกณฑ์ ส่องไฟอย่างเข้มข้น และแลกเปลี่ยนเลือดทันทีเมื่อมีสัญญาณสมองได้รับผลกระทบ

qx.stem: A 3-year-old girl from Mae Hong Son has normal intelligence but writhing movements of the limbs and face, bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and difficulty looking upward. She was discharged on day 1 after birth, returned with deep jaundice at day 5 and required a prolonged hospital stay. A G6PD assay later showed severe deficiency.
qx.q: Which MRI finding is most characteristic of her condition?
opts: Bilateral hippocampal sclerosis
Periventricular leukomalacia only
Pontine central T2 hyperintensity
Multiple cortical tubers
Symmetric T2 hyperintensity of the globus pallidus bilaterally
qx.why: Athetoid movements, high-frequency hearing loss, vertical gaze limitation and a history of severe neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia from G6PD deficiency indicate chronic bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus). Bilirubin selectively injures the globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus and brainstem auditory nuclei, producing symmetric pallidal T2 hyperintensity on MRI. Periventricular leukomalacia is typical of preterm spastic diplegia, and tubers belong to tuberous sclerosis.

name: Pufferfish (tetrodotoxin) and ciguatera poisoning
formal: Marine neurotoxin poisonings that present after eating fish: tetrodotoxin (pufferfish, some other marine animals) blocks voltage-gated sodium channels and causes perioral paraesthesia followed by ascending flaccid paralysis and respiratory failure with preserved consciousness, whereas ciguatera (reef fish carrying ciguatoxins) opens sodium channels and causes gastrointestinal illness, cold allodynia and painful paraesthesias, bradycardia and prolonged neurological symptoms.
simple: Two kinds of fish poisoning that affect nerves: pufferfish poison can paralyse breathing within hours, and ciguatera from reef fish causes diarrhoea and a strange burning sensation to cold that can last weeks.
th: พิษ tetrodotoxin จากปลาปักเป้าปิดช่องโซเดียมทำให้ชาปากและลิ้น อ่อนแรงแบบอัมพาตจากปลายไปส่วนต้น และหยุดหายใจโดยที่ยังรู้สึกตัว ส่วนพิษ ciguatera จากปลาแนวปะการังทำให้ท้องเสีย ปวดแสบและรู้สึกเย็นเป็นร้อน ชีพจรช้า และอาการยาวนานเป็นสัปดาห์ ทั้งสองอย่างรักษาแบบประคับประคอง
tempoNote: Tetrodotoxin symptoms start within 20 minutes to a few hours and peak by 6-24 hours; ciguatera starts within 1-12 hours with sensory symptoms lasting weeks to months
feat: Tetrodotoxin: perioral and tongue numbness, dysarthria, ataxia, ascending flaccid paralysis with absent reflexes
Tetrodotoxin: hypotension, bradycardia, respiratory failure while the patient stays alert in severe cases
Ciguatera: vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain followed by cold allodynia (cold objects feel hot or burning)
Ciguatera: itching, arthralgia, myalgia, bradycardia and hypotension, with fatigue lasting weeks
Cluster of illness in people sharing a meal of pufferfish, barracuda, grouper or snapper
inv: Detailed food history and recovery of food remnants for toxin testing (LC-MS/MS, mouse bioassay or immunoassay)
ECG and continuous monitoring; spirometry or negative inspiratory force with progressive weakness
Electrolytes, CK and creatinine; nerve conduction studies show reduced conduction velocity and amplitude in severe tetrodotoxin poisoning
Exclude GBS, botulism and organophosphate poisoning

case.who: 38-year-old man from Samut Sakhon who ate home-prepared dried fish said to be a pufferfish
case.story: An hour later his lips and tongue tingled, then he developed trouble speaking and walking and felt his arms become weak, while remaining fully alert.
case.exam: Alert, dysarthric, flaccid proximal weakness, reflexes absent, BP 80/50 mmHg, breathing becoming shallow.
case.tests: Single-breath count down to 8, normal CSF protein if taken, CK normal, ECG sinus bradycardia.
case.q: What is the likely cause and what treatment is needed?
case.a: Tetrodotoxin poisoning; intubate and ventilate early, support circulation and give activated charcoal if he presents within an hour, because no antidote exists and recovery follows after 24-48 hours.

det.patho: Tetrodotoxin, concentrated in the liver, ovaries and skin of pufferfish and produced by symbiotic bacteria, binds the pore of voltage-gated sodium channels and blocks action potential generation in nerve and muscle, sparing the central nervous system in life-threatening poisoning, so patients stay conscious while paralysed. Ciguatoxins, produced by dinoflagellates and concentrated in predatory reef fish, bind sodium channels at a different site and keep them open, causing spontaneous firing. The toxins are heat-stable, so cooking does not make the fish safe.
det.clinical: Tetrodotoxin illness progresses through four grades: perioral numbness and gastrointestinal symptoms, then ataxia and paralysis, then respiratory failure and hypotension, then coma-like paralysis with fixed pupils that can be mistaken for death. Deaths mainly occur within the first 24 hours. Ciguatera causes a combination of gastrointestinal, neurological and cardiovascular symptoms with reversal of hot and cold sensation, and chronic fatigue or recurrence after eating fish or alcohol. In Thailand pufferfish poisoning is a recognised cause of paralysis.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical, based on the meal and the characteristic early symptoms. Exposure is confirmed by detection of toxin in food remnants, blood or urine in reference laboratories. Public health notification and food recovery matter because cases cluster. Exclusion of other paralysing illnesses depends on the speed of onset and the absence of CSF abnormality.
det.treatment: Management for tetrodotoxin is supportive: secure the airway early, ventilate until the toxin is cleared, give fluids and vasopressors, and decontaminate with activated charcoal if the patient is seen early. Neostigmine and anticholinesterases have been suggested but are not proven. For ciguatera, treat symptoms with antiemetics and fluids, and intravenous mannitol has been used though evidence is limited. Amitriptyline, gabapentin or pregabalin ease neuropathic symptoms, and patients should avoid fish, alcohol and nuts for some weeks.
det.prognosis: Patients who survive the first day of tetrodotoxin poisoning recover fully, and ciguatera symptoms usually fade over weeks but may last months.
pearls: Preserved consciousness with flaccid paralysis after a fish meal is tetrodotoxin until proven otherwise.
Reversal of hot and cold sensation points to ciguatera.
Cooking does not destroy either toxin.

name: Canavan disease (aspartoacylase deficiency)
formal: An autosomal recessive leukodystrophy caused by ASPA variants, in which loss of aspartoacylase lets N-acetylaspartate accumulate and the white matter becomes spongy; infants develop hypotonia, macrocephaly, optic atrophy and later spasticity.
simple: A rare inherited brain disease of babies in which the brain's white matter breaks down, causing floppiness, a growing head, poor vision and loss of skills.
th: โรค Canavan เป็นโรคเนื้อขาวสมองเสื่อมถ่ายทอดแบบยีนด้อย จากการขาดเอนไซม์ aspartoacylase ทำให้ N-acetylaspartate คั่ง ทารกจะตัวอ่อนปวกเปียก ศีรษะโต ตามองไม่เห็นจากประสาทตาฝ่อ และพัฒนาการถดถอยก่อนอายุ 6 เดือน
tempoNote: Normal or only mildly delayed in the first weeks; hypotonia and arrest of development in the first months, then relentless regression over years
feat: Poor head control, feeding difficulty and irritability in early infancy, with initial hypotonia that changes to spasticity
Head circumference climbing across percentiles, evident by about 6 months and levelling off in the third year
Optic atrophy with visual inattention or blindness during the first year
Opisthotonic-type posturing on handling, seizures in many, and severe global delay without peripheral nerve involvement
Milder juvenile or late-onset phenotypes exist with slower decline
inv: Urine N-acetylaspartic acid markedly raised; aspartoacylase activity low in fibroblasts
MRI shows diffuse symmetric white matter signal change, often with thalamus and globus pallidus involvement with relative sparing of the cerebellar white matter
Proton MR spectroscopy with a very large N-acetylaspartate peak
ASPA gene sequencing; CSF and peripheral nerve conduction normal

case.who: 5-month-old girl from Nakhon Ratchasima, first child of unrelated parents
case.story: The mother notices she cannot hold her head up, feeds slowly and cries inconsolably; the health-volunteer growth chart shows head size jumping from the 50th to above the 97th percentile in two months.
case.exam: Marked head lag with floppy trunk, increasing leg stiffness when pulled, poor visual following, large head.
case.tests: MRI shows symmetric diffuse white matter T2 hyperintensity; urine N-acetylaspartate is many times normal; ASPA has two pathogenic variants.
case.q: What enzyme is missing and what is the supportive plan?
case.a: Aspartoacylase deficiency (Canavan disease); care is supportive with feeding, seizure and spasticity management, and genetic counselling for the family.

read.where: 5. Psychomotor Delay and Regression - Progressive Encephalopathies With Onset Before Age 2

det.patho: Aspartoacylase, expressed in oligodendrocytes, splits N-acetylaspartate into acetate and aspartate, and the acetate is needed for myelin lipid synthesis. When ASPA variants abolish the enzyme, N-acetylaspartate accumulates in brain and urine, and myelin is poorly formed and then vacuolated, giving a spongy white matter. Water retention in the swollen white matter contributes to the large head. The disease is autosomal recessive and more frequent in certain founder populations.
det.clinical: Infants look normal at birth, and the first signs are poor head control, weak sucking and low awareness between 3 and 6 months. Early floppiness is replaced by spasticity with an extended-leg, flexed-arm posture. Macrocephaly appears within months, seizures are common and vision fails through optic atrophy. Severe infantile disease usually leads to death in childhood or adolescence, whereas mild forms present later with speech and motor delay.
det.diagnosis: The distinctive biochemical finding is a high urinary N-acetylaspartic acid, and proton spectroscopy shows a prominent N-acetylaspartate peak, which separates the condition from other infantile leukodystrophies on a single scan. MRI shows diffuse, symmetric white matter involvement with early subcortical U-fibre change and deep grey nuclei changes. Enzyme assay and ASPA sequencing confirm the diagnosis and allow carrier testing and prenatal counselling.
det.treatment: Management remains supportive, including gastrostomy feeding when swallowing is unsafe, anticonvulsants, tone management with baclofen and physiotherapy, and attention to respiratory care and sleep. Experimental gene therapy using AAV vectors delivering the ASPA gene has been given in small trials and is not standard care. Genetic counselling for parents and siblings is essential.
det.prognosis: Severe disease causes progressive disability and early death, while mild forms have a variable and slower course.
pearls: Macrocephaly plus regression plus optic atrophy in an infant should prompt urine N-acetylaspartate and MR spectroscopy.
A huge N-acetylaspartate peak on spectroscopy is almost specific for Canavan disease.
Peripheral nerves and CSF are normal, which separates it from Krabbe disease.

name: Megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts (MLC)
formal: A white matter disorder, usually autosomal recessive from MLC1 or GLIALCAM (HEPACAM) variants, with macrocephaly from infancy, swollen cerebral white matter with subcortical cysts, and a surprisingly slow decline in motor function with relatively preserved cognition.
simple: A rare inherited condition in which a child has an unusually large head from infancy and swollen brain white matter on MRI, yet often stays mentally well for years while movement slowly worsens.
ab: vacuolating megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts
th: โรค MLC เป็นโรคเนื้อขาวสมองผิดปกติที่ทำให้ศีรษะโตตั้งแต่ขวบแรก MRI พบเนื้อขาวบวมและมีถุงน้ำใต้เปลือกสมอง เด็กมักเริ่มเดินช้า มีอาการเกร็ง เสียการทรงตัวและชักบางราย แต่สติปัญญามักเสื่อมช้าและเล็กน้อย อาการอาจแย่ลงชั่วคราวหลังศีรษะกระแทกเล็กน้อยหรือติดเชื้อ
tempoNote: Macrocephaly in the first year; slow motor deterioration over years to decades, with sudden worsening after minor head injury or fever
feat: Head circumference well above the 98th percentile in the first year, then growth parallels the curve
Mild early motor delay, followed by progressive ataxia and spasticity, sometimes with dystonia
Epilepsy in a proportion of patients, and late mild cognitive decline
Marked clinical worsening or even coma after minor head knocks or febrile illness
Some variants (dominant MLC2B or remitting MLC2A) show macrocephaly with improving MRI and normal development
inv: MRI: diffusely swollen, T2-hyperintense cerebral white matter with subcortical cysts, especially anterior temporal and frontoparietal, with less occipital involvement
MLC1 and GLIALCAM (HEPACAM) sequencing, with parental testing when dominant disease is suspected
Routine metabolic tests, CSF and MR spectroscopy are non-diagnostic and used to exclude Canavan and Alexander disease

case.who: 3-year-old boy from Surin whose parents are first cousins
case.story: A large head has been noted since 6 months; he walked at 20 months, is clumsy and fell and became very drowsy for a day after a minor head bump at nursery.
case.exam: Head circumference above the 98th percentile, mild spastic-ataxic gait, normal language and social interaction.
case.tests: MRI shows swollen cerebral white matter with bilateral anterior temporal cysts; MLC1 shows biallelic pathogenic variants.
case.q: What advice should the family receive after the diagnosis?
case.a: Supportive care with seizure and tone management, helmet and head-injury precautions, and genetic counselling; cognition may remain relatively good.

read.where: 18. Disorders of Cranial Volume and Shape - Megalencephaly

det.patho: MLC1 and GLIALCAM encode astrocyte proteins that sit at astrocyte junctions around blood vessels and regulate ion and water movement and volume regulation. Loss of function leads to intramyelinic vacuoles and astrocyte swelling, producing swollen, vacuolated white matter and subcortical cysts. Biallelic variants cause the classic form, and a dominant GLIALCAM variant causes a remitting phenotype with normalising MRI.
det.clinical: Children present with macrocephaly in the first year, often before any other problem, and early development is normal or mildly slow. During childhood a gait with cerebellar ataxia and spasticity gradually emerges, followed by dystonia or other extrapyramidal signs in some. Seizures occur in many but are usually controlled, and intellectual decline is late and mild. Marked worsening, even coma, may follow minor head injuries or infections, and some patients walk independently for decades.
det.diagnosis: The combination of macrocephaly and an MRI with diffusely swollen white matter containing subcortical cysts in an otherwise well child is characteristic. Genetic testing of MLC1 identifies the cause in a majority, and GLIALCAM testing is added when MLC1 is negative. The main steps are to exclude Canavan disease, Alexander disease, vanishing white matter disease and hydrocephalus.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying treatment exists. Physiotherapy, antiepileptic drugs and spasticity management are provided as needed, and families are counselled to avoid head trauma, use protective headgear for active children and treat fevers promptly. Genetic counselling is offered; clinical trials of substances that act on astrocyte ion regulation are in early stages.
det.prognosis: The course is slowly progressive, and function is often preserved into adulthood, though some patients die in the teens or twenties after trauma or infection.
pearls: A big head with a swollen white matter MRI in a child who is cognitively well suggests MLC.
Warn families that minor head injury can trigger a major setback.
Order MLC1 first, then GLIALCAM if negative or if the MRI improves with time.

name: CDKL5 deficiency disorder (CDD)
formal: An X-linked developmental and epileptic encephalopathy caused by pathogenic CDKL5 variants, with seizures starting within the first months, profound developmental delay, cortical visual impairment and hand stereotypies, without the head growth deceleration typical of Rett syndrome.
simple: A rare gene disorder, mainly in girls, in which a baby has hard-to-control seizures from the first weeks of life and severe delay in development and vision.
ab: early seizure variant of Rett syndrome
X-linked infantile spasms with STK9 variants
th: CDKL5 deficiency disorder เป็นโรคสมองและลมชักเริ่มเร็วจากความผิดปกติของยีน CDKL5 บนโครโมโซม X พบในเด็กหญิงมากกว่า ทารกชักตั้งแต่ช่วงสัปดาห์แรก ๆ ตัวอ่อน พัฒนาการช้ามาก มองไม่ติดตามจากความผิดปกติของการมองเห็นที่สมอง และมีการเคลื่อนไหวมือซ้ำ ๆ โดยศีรษะมักไม่เล็กเหมือน Rett

feat: Seizures beginning at a median of about 6 weeks, nearly all by 3 months, often tonic or spasm-like and explosive at onset
Marked hypotonia, severe global delay and cortical visual impairment
Hand stereotypies, other movement disorders and disturbed sleep
Infantile spasms in many, evolving to refractory focal, tonic and myoclonic seizures
Microcephaly is not a typical feature, which helps to separate it from Rett syndrome
inv: CDKL5 sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis, or an epilepsy gene panel / exome as first-line in infantile-onset seizures
EEG: initially often normal interictally, then multifocal discharges and hypsarrhythmia if spasms occur
MRI is normal or shows non-specific atrophy; metabolic work-up excludes treatable mimics

case.story: Daily stiffening and jerking spells began at 5 weeks, resistant to phenobarbital and levetiracetam; she does not fix or follow faces and is floppy.
case.exam: Head circumference normal, hypotonic with poor head control, no visual following, hand clasping movements.
case.tests: MRI normal; EEG shows multifocal epileptiform discharges; epilepsy panel finds a de novo pathogenic CDKL5 variant.
case.q: Which drugs may worsen seizures, and what newer option exists?
case.a: Sodium channel blockers such as carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine can aggravate seizures; ganaxolone is approved for seizures in CDKL5 deficiency disorder in older children.

read.where: 5. Psychomotor Delay and Regression - Progressive Encephalopathies With Onset Before Age 2

det.patho: CDKL5 encodes a serine-threonine kinase that is highly expressed in neurons and phosphorylates targets involved in synapse formation, dendritic growth and microtubule dynamics. Loss of function disturbs excitatory synapses and network excitability. The gene is on the X chromosome, females are affected more often than males, and most variants arise de novo.
det.clinical: Seizures arise in the first weeks to months, with a median onset near 6 weeks, and tonic seizures and spasms are frequent. After an initial stormy period there may be a short seizure-free interval before refractory multifocal and myoclonic seizures return. Children show severe motor and cognitive delay, a minority learn to walk or speak, and cortical visual impairment is common. Sleep fragmentation, gastrointestinal problems, scoliosis and hand stereotypies are frequent, and caregiver burden is high.
det.diagnosis: Consensus criteria require seizure onset in the first year, developmental and motor delay, and a pathogenic CDKL5 variant. Genetic testing is therefore the confirmatory step, and next-generation epilepsy panels or exome sequencing now capture most cases early in the work-up of infantile-onset epilepsy. EEG and MRI help to describe the epilepsy and exclude structural or metabolic causes.
det.treatment: Broad-spectrum antiseizure medicines such as valproate, clobazam, levetiracetam and topiramate are used, vigabatrin or steroids for spasms, and the ketogenic diet helps some children. Carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine can worsen seizures and are usually avoided. Ganaxolone, a neuroactive steroid, has been approved for seizures in CDKL5 deficiency disorder in children over two years of age. Multidisciplinary care covers vision, feeding, sleep, orthopaedics and palliative support.
det.prognosis: Most children have lifelong severe disability and ongoing seizures, but survival into adulthood is common.
pearls: Refractory seizures starting before 3 months with severe hypotonia and visual inattention warrant an early gene panel.
Absence of microcephaly and onset of seizures before regression separate CDKL5 deficiency disorder from classic Rett syndrome.
Avoid sodium channel blockers if the diagnosis is confirmed.

name: Perinatal arterial ischaemic stroke
formal: A focal arterial infarct, most often in the middle cerebral artery territory, arising at any time from the 28th week of pregnancy to the 28th day after birth; it presents with neonatal focal seizures or later with early hand preference, and is a leading cause of congenital hemiparetic cerebral palsy.
simple: A stroke in a baby around the time of birth that blocks a brain artery, often shown by seizures in one arm or leg in the first days or by a weak side noticed months later.
th: โรคหลอดเลือดสมองตีบในทารกรอบคลอดคือภาวะสมองขาดเลือดจากหลอดเลือดแดงอุดตันระหว่างอายุครรภ์ 28 สัปดาห์ถึง 28 วันแรกหลังเกิด มักเกิดที่หลอดเลือดสมองส่วนกลาง ทารกมักชักแบบเฉพาะที่ที่แขนหรือขาข้างตรงข้าม หรือพบภายหลังจากการใช้มือข้างเดียวก่อนวัยอันควร
tempoNote: Acute presentation in the first days (symptomatic) or silent until months later when hand preference or delayed milestones appear (presumed perinatal stroke)
feat: Focal motor seizures in the first 1 to 3 days in a term infant who is otherwise well or only mildly lethargic
Contralateral hemiparesis not evident at first, with early handedness before about 12 months as a late sign
The left hemisphere and the MCA branches are involved most often
Risk factors: pre-eclampsia, chorioamnionitis, maternal thrombophilia, difficult or instrumental delivery, congenital heart disease and polycythaemia
Later epilepsy, cognitive or language problems and cerebral palsy
inv: Cranial ultrasound as a first screen, then MRI with diffusion imaging, MR angiography and MR venography to define artery or vein involvement
EEG for suspected seizures; echocardiogram, placental histology and thrombophilia testing in selected cases
Repeat imaging at follow-up shows porencephalic cavity or ex vacuo ventricular enlargement

case.who: Term male infant from Chiang Rai, day 2 of life
case.story: Born by emergency Caesarean section after prolonged rupture of membranes; at 40 hours he has repeated twitching of the right arm and leg.
case.exam: Alert but jittery, reduced spontaneous movement of the right arm, no dysmorphism.
case.tests: Diffusion MRI shows an acute left middle cerebral artery territory infarct; MR venography is normal; EEG confirms focal seizures.
case.q: How should he be managed and followed up?
case.a: Treat seizures, correct hypoxia, dehydration and anaemia, look for risk factors (infection, heart disease), avoid thrombolysis, and follow motor and language development for cerebral palsy and epilepsy.

det.patho: Most perinatal strokes are arterial ischaemic infarcts caused by embolism of placental or cardiac clot, vessel wall disease or occlusion triggered by haemodynamic stress during labour. Contributing factors include maternal infection and pre-eclampsia, polycythaemia and neonatal thrombophilia, and genetic arteriopathy such as COL4A1 variants. The brain may be more vulnerable to seizures but remarkably plastic, and many infants reorganise motor representation to the opposite hemisphere.
det.clinical: Acute symptomatic stroke typically shows up as focal motor seizures within the first week in a term infant who feeds and looks well, though some are lethargic or irritable. Many infants are not recognised until months later, when hand preference before one year, a hemiparetic gait or delayed milestones prompt imaging. Left MCA infarcts are commonest. Later complications include hemiparetic cerebral palsy, epilepsy including infantile spasms, and language, cognitive and attention problems.
det.diagnosis: Cranial ultrasound can miss early or cortical infarcts, so MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging is preferred and is combined with MR angiography and venography to separate arterial from venous stroke. Risk factor evaluation includes maternal history, placental pathology, blood count and echocardiography, while thrombophilia testing in neonates is difficult to interpret and results need confirmation later. EEG documents seizures that may be subclinical.
det.treatment: Management is supportive with oxygenation, correction of dehydration and anaemia, glucose control and treatment of seizures. Thrombolysis is not used because evidence is lacking and onset time is unclear, and thrombectomy is limited by infant size. Low-molecular-weight heparin is considered in cerebral sinovenous thrombosis, congenital heart disease or documented thrombophilia. Early rehabilitation, including constraint-induced movement therapy and family-centred programmes, supports motor recovery.
det.prognosis: Many survivors have hemiparesis, and about one in four to one in three develop epilepsy or cognitive problems; recurrence is rare.
pearls: A well-looking term newborn with focal seizures needs diffusion MRI, not just EEG and a septic screen.
Early hand preference before one year may be the first sign of an unrecognised perinatal stroke.
Treatment is supportive; neonates do not receive thrombolysis.
det.thd: Perinatal arterial ischaemic stroke เกิดเมื่อหลอดเลือดแดงสมองของทารกอุดตันระหว่างช่วงใกล้คลอดถึง 28 วันแรก ส่วนใหญ่ที่หลอดเลือดสมองส่วนกลาง ทารกมักชักเฉพาะที่แขนหรือขาข้างหนึ่งภายใน 1-3 วัน หรือถูกพบภายหลังเมื่อใช้มือข้างเดียวก่อน 1 ปี วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI แบบ diffusion ร่วมกับ MRA/MRV รักษาแบบประคับประคองและควบคุมชัก ไม่ใช้ยาละลายลิ่มเลือด และติดตามภาวะอัมพาตครึ่งซีก ลมชัก และพัฒนาการ

Thrombolysis is not used because of lack of evidence and uncertain onset time, and thrombectomy is limited by infant size. Low-molecular-weight heparin is reserved for sinovenous thrombosis, known thrombophilia or congenital heart disease. Treat seizures and follow the child for hemiparesis and epilepsy.

name: Duane retraction syndrome
formal: A congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder in which the abducens nerve is hypoplastic or absent and the lateral rectus is partly innervated by the oculomotor nerve, producing limited abduction and/or adduction with globe retraction and palpebral fissure narrowing on attempted adduction.
simple: A birth condition in which one eye cannot turn outward well, and the eye pulls back into its socket and the eyelid narrows when the person looks toward the nose.
th: Duane retraction syndrome เป็นความผิดปกติแต่กำเนิดของการเคลื่อนไหวตา ประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 6 ไม่เจริญ และกล้ามเนื้อตรงด้านนอกรับเส้นประสาทผิดทางจากคู่ที่ 3 ทำให้ลูกตากลอกออกด้านนอกไม่ได้ และเมื่อมองเข้าใน ลูกตาจะหดถอยและช่องตาแคบลง ผู้ป่วยมักเอียงหน้าเพื่อใช้ตาสองข้างพร้อมกัน
tempoNote: Present from birth and stable; noticed in infancy or childhood when a head turn or squint is seen
feat: Limited abduction, adduction or both in one eye, left eye more often involved than right
Globe retraction and narrowing of the palpebral fissure on attempted adduction, sometimes with upshoot or downshoot
Compensatory head turn toward the affected side to keep binocular single vision
Huber types I to III: type I (most common) has marked loss of abduction with mildly limited adduction
May accompany other anomalies (deafness, Goldenhar, radial ray defects) and some familial cases
inv: Orthoptic assessment of ductions, deviation in primary position, head posture and amblyopia
Forced duction testing or traction test when the diagnosis against abducens palsy is unclear
MRI of brain stem and orbits showing absent or hypoplastic sixth nerve when atypical or bilateral
Genetic testing (CHN1, SALL4) when familial or accompanied by systemic anomalies

case.who: 6-year-old girl from Nonthaburi referred for a head turn
case.story: Her teacher noticed that she turns her face to the left when copying from the board, and her left eye seems to sink in when she looks to the right.
case.exam: Left eye cannot abduct beyond the midline, left palpebral fissure narrows on adduction, no ptosis, vision 6/6 in each eye.
case.tests: Prism cover test shows orthophoria in primary position; MRI shows a thin left abducens nerve and otherwise normal brain.
case.q: How does this differ from an acquired sixth nerve palsy?
case.a: It is congenital, with retraction and fissure narrowing on adduction and a stable head turn without diplopia, unlike an acquired abducens palsy with esotropia and diplopia.

det.patho: Duane syndrome is a congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder in which the abducens nucleus or nerve fails to develop, and branches of the oculomotor nerve that supply the medial rectus reach the lateral rectus. Both muscles then contract together on adduction, pulling the globe back and narrowing the fissure, while abduction is poor. Electromyography shows the paradoxical co-innervation. Most cases are sporadic, and dominant forms occur through CHN1 and SALL4 variants.
det.clinical: Patients are usually healthy children with a head turn or apparent squint and often no diplopia, since suppression or a compensatory head posture preserves binocular vision. Eye movements show reduced abduction, adduction or both, with retraction of the globe and narrowing of the palpebral fissure on adduction. The commonest pattern, Huber type I, shows marked abduction loss and mildly limited adduction, and vertical up- or downshoots (A or V patterns) may occur. Associated anomalies include hearing loss, vertebral and radial defects and Goldenhar spectrum.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical, based on the characteristic pattern of ductions with retraction, supported by orthoptic measurement and by exclusion of acquired palsy. Forced duction testing helps in uncertain cases, and MRI showing absent abducens nerve is confirmatory in atypical or bilateral cases. Children should have a vision and amblyopia assessment, and syndromic features prompt hearing and systemic evaluation.
det.treatment: Many patients need no treatment. Refractive error and amblyopia are treated, and prisms may help small head turns. Surgery is considered for a significant abnormal head posture, a deviation in primary position or cosmetically disturbing upshoots, and consists of recession of the medial rectus, sometimes with the lateral rectus. Resection of the affected lateral rectus and transposition procedures are generally avoided because they can worsen retraction.
det.prognosis: The condition is stable for life, binocular function is usually good, and many patients need no intervention.
pearls: Narrowing of the palpebral fissure with globe retraction on adduction is the hallmark that separates Duane syndrome from sixth nerve palsy.
A congenital head turn without diplopia suggests a developmental cause.
Avoid strengthening surgery on the tight lateral rectus.
det.thd: Duane syndrome พบตั้งแต่กำเนิดจากการเจริญผิดปกติของเส้นประสาทคู่ที่ 6 ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อตรงด้านนอกถูกเลี้ยงโดยเส้นประสาทคู่ที่ 3 บางส่วน ตาข้างนั้นกลอกออกนอกไม่ได้ และเมื่อกลอกเข้าใน ลูกตาจะถอยเข้าหลังและช่องตาแคบลง เด็กมักเอียงหน้าโดยไม่เห็นภาพซ้อน แตกต่างจากอัมพาตเส้นประสาทคู่ที่ 6 ที่เกิดภายหลัง การรักษาทำเมื่อมีท่าทางศีรษะผิดปกติมาก โดยผ่าตัดถอยกล้ามเนื้อ และเลี่ยงการตัดสั้นกล้ามเนื้อตรงด้านนอก

qx.stem: A 7-year-old boy from Nonthaburi keeps his face turned to the right when reading. His right eye cannot abduct past the midline, and when he looks to the left the right eye sinks into the orbit and the palpebral fissure narrows. He has no double vision and sees 6/6 in each eye.
qx.q: What mechanism explains the retraction?
opts: Fibrosis of the inferior oblique tendon sheath limiting elevation in adduction
Acute ischaemia of the abducens nerve in the cavernous sinus
Autoantibodies against the acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction
A hypoplastic abducens nerve with aberrant oculomotor fibres innervating the lateral rectus, so both horizontal recti contract on adduction
Orbital myositis of the lateral rectus
qx.why: Duane retraction syndrome is a congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder: the abducens is hypoplastic and the lateral rectus is partly supplied by branches of the oculomotor nerve, so on adduction the medial and lateral recti co-contract, retracting the globe and narrowing the fissure. A stable head turn without diplopia points to a developmental origin, unlike an acquired sixth nerve palsy. Surgery, when needed for head posture, weakens the tight muscles; resection of the lateral rectus is avoided.

name: Acute idiopathic blind spot enlargement (big blind spot syndrome)
formal: A self-limited acute unilateral condition, mostly in young women, with a visual-field scotoma around an enlarged physiological blind spot, a hyperaemic and swollen optic disc with venous congestion, and preserved visual acuity and colour vision; it is considered a mild venous or inflammatory disorder of the peripapillary retina and optic nerve head.
simple: A short-lived problem, usually in one eye of a young adult, where a dark spot appears in the field of vision beside the normal blind spot and the optic disc looks swollen, yet reading vision stays good.
th: Big blind spot syndrome (AIBSE) คือภาวะที่จุดบอดทางสายตาขยายใหญ่เฉียบพลันในตาข้างเดียว มักพบในหญิงอายุน้อย จอประสาทตาส่วนหัวขั้วประสาทตาบวมแดงและหลอดเลือดดำคั่ง แต่สายตาและการรับสีมักปกติ อาจหายเองหรือหายเร็วขึ้นด้วยสเตียรอยด์ และต้องแยกจากภาวะหัวขั้วประสาทตาบวมจากความดันในกะโหลกสูง
tempoNote: Awareness of a spot over days; recovery in weeks to months, spontaneously or with steroids
feat: Sudden awareness of a scotoma or blurred area in one eye, sometimes with photopsia or mild headache
Visual acuity, colour vision and critical fusion frequency are normal or near normal
Optic disc swelling with hyperaemia, venous dilatation and peripapillary striate haemorrhages
Perimetry: enlarged blind spot (often 10 to 20 degrees), sometimes with an arcuate or upper quadrant extension
Usually no relative afferent pupillary defect; neurological and systemic examination normal
inv: Automated perimetry documenting enlargement of the blind spot and its recovery
Fundus examination, OCT of the peripapillary nerve fibre layer and fluorescein angiography for venous leakage
MRI brain and orbits and lumbar puncture only if bilateral, atypical or papilloedema is suspected (to exclude raised pressure)
Screen for inflammatory, infective and haematological causes in atypical cases

case.story: Four days ago she noticed a dark smudge beside the centre of vision in her right eye when reading, with no pain and no recent infection.
case.exam: Visual acuity 6/6 both eyes, normal colour plates, no afferent pupil defect; right disc swollen and red with dilated veins and a few flame haemorrhages; left disc normal.
case.tests: Perimetry shows a big right blind spot; MRI and CSF opening pressure are normal; fluorescein angiography shows disc leakage.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and expected course?
case.a: Acute idiopathic blind spot enlargement syndrome (papillophlebitis); recovery over weeks to months, spontaneous or faster with local or oral steroids, with follow-up perimetry.

det.patho: The mechanism is not settled. The fundus appearance of a swollen, hyperaemic disc with engorged veins and haemorrhages suggests a venous or low-grade inflammatory disorder of the peripapillary retina and optic nerve head, and an autoimmune component has been proposed because some patients have autoimmune or allergic histories. The syndrome is thought by some authors to form a spectrum with partial retinal vein occlusion.
det.clinical: Young adults, more often women, present with a unilateral paracentral dark spot or blurred patch lasting days. Acuity, colour vision and flicker fusion are usually preserved, there is no afferent pupillary defect and neurological examination is normal. The disc looks swollen and hyperaemic with dilated veins and a few peripapillary haemorrhages. Perimetry shows an enlarged blind spot, occasionally with an additional quadrant defect. Recurrence is rare.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis depends on the characteristic combination of unilateral disc swelling with normal visual acuity and an enlarged blind spot on perimetry in a patient without systemic or intracranial disease. The key task is to exclude raised intracranial pressure, optic neuritis, ischaemic optic neuropathy, compressive and infective causes, so imaging and CSF pressure are measured when bilateral, atypical or accompanied by headache. OCT and angiography document disc swelling and leakage, and repeat perimetry confirms recovery.
det.treatment: The disorder often settles on its own within weeks to months. Local or systemic corticosteroids have been used in case series and may hasten recovery, but there are no controlled trials. Patients with persistent disc swelling or field loss are reassessed for inflammatory, vascular or infective causes. Follow-up with perimetry until the field and disc normalise is recommended.
det.prognosis: Recovery is complete in most patients, usually without residual disc pallor.
pearls: Normal acuity with a swollen disc and a big blind spot suggests this condition rather than optic neuritis.
Always exclude raised intracranial pressure before accepting a benign local cause.
Perimetry follow-up documents recovery.
det.thd: AIBSE หรือ big blind spot syndrome คือจุดบอดขยายใหญ่เฉียบพลันในตาข้างเดียว มักพบในหญิงอายุน้อย ตรวจพบหัวขั้วประสาทตาบวมแดงและเส้นเลือดดำโป่ง แต่สายตาและการแยกสีปกติ ไม่มี RAPD ควรแยกจากความดันในกะโหลกสูง ประสาทตาอักเสบ และ NAION โดยตรวจลานสายตา OCT และ MRI ร่วมกับวัดความดันน้ำไขสันหลังเมื่อจำเป็น โรคมักหายเองหรือเร็วขึ้นด้วยสเตียรอยด์และต้องติดตามลานสายตา

qx.stem: A 27-year-old woman from Chiang Mai noticed a dark smudge next to the centre of vision in her right eye four days ago. There is no pain and no systemic illness. Fundoscopy shows a swollen red disc with dilated veins and a few flame haemorrhages on the right; the left is normal.

Normal acuity and colour vision with no relative afferent pupillary defect, and an enlarged blind spot on perimetry

Optic neuritis lowers acuity and colour vision and causes an afferent defect; ischaemic optic neuropathy gives altitudinal loss; bilateral swelling with headache raises concern for raised intracranial pressure. The condition often settles spontaneously or with steroids.

name: Skew deviation and ocular tilt reaction
formal: A disorder of the gravity-sensing vestibular pathway in which the two eyes sit at different heights (skew deviation), occurring alone or with ocular torsion and a head tilt, the triad being the ocular tilt reaction; it reflects a lesion of otolith-ocular pathways from the labyrinth through the pons and midbrain.
simple: A problem in which one eye sits higher than the other, causing vertical double vision, often with a tilted head and a tilted sense of vertical, after a lesion in the brainstem or balance pathways.
ab: tilt of the subjective visual vertical
th: Skew deviation คือภาวะที่ตาสองข้างเหลื่อมกันในแนวดิ่งจากรอยโรคในทางเดินการทรงตัวของก้านสมอง เมื่อพบร่วมกับการบิดของตาและเอียงศีรษะเรียกว่า ocular tilt reaction ผู้ป่วยมักเห็นภาพซ้อนแนวตั้ง ศีรษะเอียง และรู้สึกว่าแนวดิ่งเอียง พบบ่อยในโรคหลอดเลือดสมองก้านสมองหรือสมองน้อย
tempoNote: Usually sudden with a brainstem or cerebellar stroke or acute vestibular lesion; may improve over weeks
feat: Vertical diplopia with a vertical deviation that is not explained by a single cranial nerve or muscle palsy
Head tilt toward the lower eye and a tilted subjective visual vertical
Cyclotorsion in the classic pattern: the higher eye intorted and the lower eye extorted
Often accompanied by other brainstem signs such as internuclear ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus or ataxia
Direction of the tilt helps to localise: ipsilateral eye lower for pontomedullary lesions, contralateral for pontomesencephalic lesions
inv: Alternate cover and three-step test; cover test in upright and supine positions (the deviation often lessens when lying down)
Ophthalmoscopy or photographs for torsion and subjective visual vertical bucket test
MRI brain with diffusion imaging and vessel imaging for stroke in acute onset
Vestibular function testing and ocular motor examination

case.who: 63-year-old man from Samut Prakan with hypertension and diabetes
case.story: Woke with vertical double vision, vomiting and an urge to tilt his head to the right, with right hand clumsiness.
case.exam: Left hypertropia of 5 prism dioptres, head tilted to the right, right (lower) eye extorted and left eye intorted, mild right hypometric saccades, no Horner syndrome.
case.tests: MRI diffusion shows an acute right dorsolateral medullary infarct; the deviation falls to 1 prism dioptre when supine.
case.q: How is this different from a fourth nerve palsy and what does it suggest?
case.a: A vertical deviation that falls when supine, with the higher eye intorted, the lower eye extorted and the head tilted toward the lower eye, indicates a skew deviation / OTR from a brainstem lesion rather than an isolated trochlear palsy.

det.patho: The otolith-ocular reflex pathway runs from utricle and saccule via vestibular nuclei to the contralateral medial longitudinal fasciculus, interstitial nucleus of Cajal and oculomotor nuclei, and keeps the eyes aligned with gravity. A unilateral lesion produces a mismatch in the graviceptive tone, resulting in the lower eye on the lesion side for peripheral or pontomedullary lesions, and the opposite arrangement above the crossing. The three components, skew, torsion and head tilt, are the ocular tilt reaction.
det.clinical: Patients report vertical or oblique diplopia, a tilted view of the world and an urge to tilt the head, with disorientation while walking or reading. Examination shows a vertical misalignment that is not explained by one muscle, a torsional change and a head tilt. Skew deviation is the commonest vertical misalignment in cerebrovascular disease, often with INO, nystagmus or ataxia, and may follow cerebellar lesions, demyelination, tumours or trauma. A peripheral vestibular lesion can also produce transient OTR.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical, based on the pattern of vertical misalignment, torsion and head tilt, and on a negative pattern for a single palsy. The upright-supine test, in which the vertical deviation falls by more than half when lying flat, favours a skew deviation over trochlear palsy. The subjective visual vertical is tilted. MRI with diffusion imaging identifies the lesion in acute cases, and the HINTS examination helps to differentiate central from peripheral causes in acute vestibular syndrome.
det.treatment: Treatment targets the underlying lesion, with secondary stroke prevention when ischaemic. Symptomatic care includes occlusion of one eye or prism glasses for diplopia, and strabismus surgery is considered only if the deviation persists for six to twelve months. Skew deviation often improves spontaneously over weeks to months.
det.prognosis: Many deviations improve within months, and persistent cases are managed with prisms; prognosis relates to the underlying brainstem lesion.
pearls: A vertical deviation that falls in the supine position favours skew deviation over a fourth nerve palsy.
Vertical diplopia with head tilt and torsion in an acute vestibular syndrome is a central sign.
Look for associated INO or lateral medullary signs to localise.
det.thd: Skew deviation เกิดจากรอยโรคทางเดินการทรงตัวในก้านสมอง ทำให้ตาสองข้างเหลื่อมกันแนวดิ่ง ผู้ป่วยเห็นภาพซ้อนแนวตั้ง เมื่อมีตาบิดและเอียงศีรษะร่วมด้วยเรียก ocular tilt reaction พบบ่อยในโรคหลอดเลือดสมองก้านสมองและสมองน้อย ต่างจากอัมพาตเส้นประสาทคู่ที่ 4 ตรงที่ความเหลื่อมแนวดิ่งลดลงเมื่อนอนราบ ควรทำ MRI และรักษาสาเหตุ ใช้ปริซึมหรือปิดตาเพื่อลดภาพซ้อน

qx.stem: A 58-year-old man from Samut Prakan with hypertension wakes with vertical diplopia, vomiting and a tilted head. The left eye is 6 prism dioptres higher than the right while upright, but only 2 prism dioptres when supine. Fundus photographs show the higher eye intorted and the lower eye extorted.
qx.q: Which pattern favours a skew deviation over an isolated fourth nerve palsy?
opts: A deviation that falls markedly when lying down, with the higher eye intorted and the lower eye extorted
A hypertropia that grows when the head is tilted toward the higher eye, with extorsion of that eye
A constant deviation in every gaze position and posture
Ptosis with a dilated pupil and adduction weakness
Hypertropia only on looking down and in, with normal torsion
qx.why: Skew deviation is a supranuclear (otolith-ocular) vertical misalignment that can be accompanied by torsion and head tilt as the ocular tilt reaction. It often falls when the patient lies down and the higher eye is intorted, while in trochlear palsy the hypertropic eye is extorted and the deviation increases on tilt toward that side and does not change with posture. Localising clues are associated brainstem signs and the side of the lower eye. Stroke is the usual cause.

name: Hemispatial neglect (unilateral spatial neglect)
formal: A disorder of spatial attention, most often after right hemisphere (parietal, frontal or subcortical) injury, in which the patient fails to report, respond to or orient toward stimuli on the contralesional side of space or body, despite intact primary sensation and vision, and often without awareness of the deficit.
simple: After a stroke, most often in the right hemisphere, a person ignores things on their left, eating from only half the plate or bumping into objects, without realising it.
th: Hemispatial neglect คือภาวะละเลยพื้นที่หรือร่างกายด้านตรงข้ามกับรอยโรคในสมอง พบบ่อยหลังโรคหลอดเลือดสมองซีกขวา ผู้ป่วยกินอาหารเฉพาะครึ่งจาน ชนสิ่งของด้านซ้าย แต่งตัวไม่ครบข้าง โดยการมองเห็นและความรู้สึกพื้นฐานยังปกติและมักไม่รู้ตัวว่าผิดปกติ ต้องแยกจากการมองเห็นครึ่งซีกเสียและส่งผลให้ฟื้นฟูช้า
tempoNote: Maximal in the first days after a right hemisphere stroke, then improves over weeks to months, with residual extinction or subtle neglect
feat: Eyes and head deviated to the ipsilesional side, with reduced exploration toward the neglected side
Leaves food on one side of the plate, shaves or dresses one side only, collides with objects
Line bisection displaced toward the intact side, cancellation tasks missing targets on the neglected side, drawings that are incomplete
Extinction to double simultaneous stimulation (visual, tactile or auditory)

inv: Bedside tests: line bisection, letter or star cancellation, clock or figure drawing, reading words

Behavioural scale such as the Catherine Bergego Scale to rate everyday impact
MRI or CT to define the lesion (right MCA territory, inferior parietal or temporoparietal junction)

case.story: Right MCA infarct 5 days ago; the nurses find her eating only the right half of her rice and she turns her head right when addressed from the left.
case.exam: Left hemiparesis, normal visual acuity, full fields to single stimuli but she misses the left finger when both sides move; line bisection is shifted far to the right; she denies any weakness.
case.tests: MRI shows an acute right frontoparietal infarct.
case.q: What is the syndrome and why is it important for rehabilitation?
case.a: Left hemispatial neglect with anosognosia; it predicts a longer recovery and falls, so scanning training, prism adaptation and structured feedback are added to rehabilitation.

det.patho: Spatial attention is distributed in a network of posterior parietal, frontal, cingulate and subcortical regions, with right-hemisphere dominance for directing attention across both hemispaces. Right-sided injury leaves the left side poorly represented and the rightward bias unopposed. Neglect can be egocentric (relative to the body) or allocentric (relative to an object), and can affect personal, peripersonal or extrapersonal space, and vision, hearing or touch.
det.clinical: Neglect is among the commonest cognitive consequences of right hemisphere stroke, and patients may fail to dress or wash the left side, read only the right part of words, eat from half the plate, or bump the left side of their body. Eye movements are biased to the right and hemiparesis, hemisensory loss and hemianopia often coexist. The deficit worsens with fatigue and distraction. Anosognosia is common and makes patients unsafe for driving and crossing roads.
det.diagnosis: A bedside battery of line bisection, cancellation and drawing, supplemented by double simultaneous stimulation, identifies neglect and its type. The key distinction is from homonymous hemianopia: patients with neglect can detect isolated stimuli in the affected field but ignore them when both sides are stimulated, and they do not compensate with head turns. Functional rating scales capture everyday impact, and imaging locates the lesion.
det.treatment: Treatment is rehabilitation-based, starting with awareness training and feedback, and includes visual scanning training, limb activation, prism adaptation, neck vibration and, in some centres, non-invasive brain stimulation. No drug is established, and dopaminergic agents have been tried with inconsistent results. Safety advice about driving and walking in crowded areas is essential, and caregivers are trained to cue patients to the neglected side.
det.prognosis: Most improvement occurs in the first three months, but persistent neglect is associated with poor functional outcome and long hospital stays.
pearls: Test with both sides at once: extinction reveals neglect when single stimuli are seen.
If a patient ignores the left half of the plate and denies weakness, think right hemisphere stroke.
Neglect slows motor rehabilitation and raises fall risk.

Neglect, mainly right hemisphere, slows recovery and raises fall risk, so scanning training, awareness feedback and safety advice are added to rehabilitation.

name: Listeria monocytogenes meningitis
formal: A bacterial meningitis or meningoencephalitis caused by Listeria monocytogenes, a foodborne Gram-positive bacillus that targets neonates, pregnant women, people over 60 and the immunocompromised, is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins, and may involve the brainstem (rhombencephalitis).
simple: A serious brain infection from a germ found in contaminated food, mostly affecting newborns, pregnant women, older adults and people with weak immunity, which needs ampicillin because the usual meningitis antibiotic does not work.
th: Listeria meningitis คือเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบจากเชื้อ Listeria monocytogenes ที่ติดจากอาหารปนเปื้อน พบในทารกแรกเกิด หญิงตั้งครรภ์ ผู้สูงอายุ และผู้ที่ภูมิคุ้มกันบกพร่อง เชื้อดื้อต่อ cephalosporin จึงต้องเติม ampicillin หรือ amoxicillin ในยาเริ่มต้น บางรายมีสมองก้านสมองอักเสบ ชัก และอาการทางระบบประสาทเฉพาะที่
tempoNote: Fever and headache evolving over 1 to 3 days, sometimes subacute with brainstem signs or seizures
feat: Fever, headache and altered consciousness, sometimes with a preceding gastroenteritis
Brainstem involvement: cranial neuropathies, ataxia, hemiparesis or biphasic course
Seizures and movement disorders more often than in pneumococcal disease
Risk groups: age over 60, pregnancy, transplant, malignancy, diabetes, cirrhosis, alcohol misuse, advanced HIV, immunosuppressive drugs, neonates
Gram stain may show Gram-positive bacilli or coccobacilli; CSF pleocytosis can be lymphocytic or mixed
inv: CSF Gram stain, cell count with differential, protein, glucose, culture and PCR; blood cultures before antibiotics
MRI with contrast for rhombencephalitis, abscess or ventriculitis
Susceptibility testing, and food and exposure history for public-health reporting

case.who: 71-year-old woman from Ayutthaya on methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis
case.story: Three days of fever, headache and unsteady gait after eating pre-packed salad and soft cheese; she became drowsy on day 3.
case.exam: Temperature 38.6 C, mild neck stiffness, left sixth nerve palsy and gait ataxia.
case.tests: CSF 380 cells with mixed polymorphs and lymphocytes, protein high; Gram stain shows Gram-positive rods; MRI shows pontine enhancement.
case.q: What must be added to the empirical regimen, and for how long is therapy continued?
case.a: Add ampicillin or amoxicillin to ceftriaxone, then give penicillin-class therapy for about 21 days with MRI follow-up for brainstem or abscess involvement.

det.patho: Listeria is acquired through contaminated ready-to-eat foods, survives refrigeration, crosses the intestinal barrier and spreads by an intracellular cycle that uses actin tails to pass between cells. In cell-mediated immune deficiency it disseminates to the blood and the central nervous system, where it can infect the meninges and the brainstem via cranial nerves. Pregnancy also impairs cellular immunity and can lead to transplacental infection.
det.clinical: Adults present with fever, headache, confusion and meningism, often with seizures, focal deficits or movement disorders. Rhombencephalitis shows a biphasic febrile illness with asymmetric cranial neuropathies, ataxia and respiratory failure. Neonatal disease may be early (septicaemia) or late (meningitis). Brain abscess occurs in a minority.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on CSF and blood cultures with PCR support. In Gram-stained CSF the presence of Gram-positive bacilli or coccobacilli suggests Listeria. CSF may show only a modest pleocytosis with a mixed picture. MRI is advised when brainstem signs are present. The WHO meningitis guideline recommends adding ampicillin or amoxicillin to the empirical regimen in people with listeria risk factors, including age over 60, pregnancy and immunosuppression.
det.treatment: Cephalosporins are inactive, so treatment is ampicillin or amoxicillin (or penicillin G) for a total of about three weeks, as in the WHO table; some clinicians add gentamicin for synergy in severe cases, and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the usual alternative for serious penicillin allergy. Corticosteroids started with the empirical regimen can be stopped once Listeria is identified, since benefit is restricted to pneumococcal and Haemophilus disease. Immunosuppressants are reviewed and food safety advice is given.
det.prognosis: Mortality remains substantial, around one in five, and survivors may have cranial nerve palsies and cognitive deficits.
pearls: Gram-positive bacilli in CSF mean Listeria until proved otherwise.
Ceftriaxone alone never covers Listeria: add ampicillin in people over 60, pregnant women and the immunocompromised.
Rhombencephalitis with a biphasic course is a classic neurolisteriosis pattern.
det.thd: Listeria meningitis เกิดจากเชื้อ Listeria monocytogenes ที่ติดจากอาหารสำเร็จรูปหรือชีสนมดิบ พบในทารก หญิงตั้งครรภ์ ผู้สูงอายุ และผู้ที่ภูมิคุ้มกันต่ำ เชื้อดื้อ cephalosporin จึงต้องเติม ampicillin หรือ amoxicillin ในยาเริ่มต้นและให้ยากลุ่มเพนิซิลลินประมาณ 3 สัปดาห์ ผู้ป่วยบางรายมีสมองก้านสมองอักเสบ ย้อม Gram พบแท่งแกรมบวก อัตราตายยังสูง

WHO advises adding ampicillin or amoxicillin to the empirical regimen in people with risk factors, including age over 60, pregnancy, diabetes and immunosuppression, and its table lists penicillin G, ampicillin or amoxicillin for 21 days for Listeria. Corticosteroids can be stopped once a non-pneumococcal, non-Hib pathogen is found.

name: Group B streptococcal meningitis
formal: A bacterial meningitis caused by Streptococcus agalactiae, principally affecting neonates and infants under 3 months, either early (first week, vertically acquired) or late (after the first week), and less often pregnant or elderly adults and people with chronic conditions.
simple: A dangerous brain-lining infection in newborns and young babies caused by a germ that mothers often carry harmlessly, treated with penicillin-type antibiotics.
th: Group B streptococcal meningitis คือเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบจากเชื้อ Streptococcus agalactiae พบมากในทารกแรกเกิดและทารกอายุต่ำกว่า 3 เดือน ทั้งแบบเกิดเร็วใน 7 วันแรกซึ่งติดจากแม่ และแบบเกิดช้า ทารกซึม ไม่ดูดนม มีไข้หรือตัวเย็น ชัก และกระหม่อมโป่งตึง ต้องให้ยาปฏิชีวนะทางหลอดเลือดดำทันที
tempoNote: Hours to a day in early-onset disease; days in late-onset disease
feat: Poor feeding, lethargy, irritability, fever or low temperature in a young infant
Apnoea, respiratory distress and sepsis in early-onset disease
Seizures and bulging fontanelle; neck stiffness is often absent
Late-onset disease in infants up to 3 months, sometimes with focal infection or bacteraemia
Complications: hydrocephalus, subdural collections, infarcts, hearing loss and developmental delay
inv: Blood culture, CSF analysis (white cells with neutrophils, high protein, low glucose), CSF Gram stain, culture and PCR
Cranial ultrasound or MRI for ventriculitis, subdural effusion, infarcts and hydrocephalus
Maternal GBS screening results and intrapartum prophylaxis history; inflammatory markers

case.who: 12-day-old boy from Songkhla, born at term
case.story: Fever, refusal to feed and a brief seizure on day 12; mother had no antenatal GBS screening.
case.exam: Lethargic, temperature 38.3 C, tense anterior fontanelle, floppy.
case.tests: CSF shows 1,800 cells mostly neutrophils with low glucose; Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in chains; culture grows Streptococcus agalactiae.
case.q: What is the antibiotic choice and treatment length, and what follow-up is needed?
case.a: Penicillin G or ampicillin for 14 to 21 days, followed by hearing and neurodevelopmental assessment before and after discharge.

det.patho: Group B streptococci colonise the maternal gastrointestinal and genital tracts and pass to the infant during delivery or from caregivers. Bacteraemia in a newborn with poor immunity leads to seeding of the meninges. Inflammation of the leptomeninges and ventricles causes cerebral oedema, vasculitis and infarction, and a thickened subarachnoid space can obstruct CSF flow.
det.clinical: Early-onset disease (first 6 days) presents as sepsis and respiratory distress, with meningitis in a minority. Late-onset disease at one week to three months presents mainly as meningitis, with fever, irritability, poor feeding, lethargy, seizures and bulging fontanelle. Signs are subtle in neonates, so a low threshold for lumbar puncture applies. Hydrocephalus, cerebral infarction, sensorineural hearing loss and neurodevelopmental impairment occur in a substantial minority of survivors.
det.diagnosis: A lumbar puncture with Gram stain, culture and PCR is obtained as soon as the infant is stable, together with blood culture, but treatment must not be delayed. Neutrophilic pleocytosis, raised protein and low CSF glucose support bacterial meningitis, and Gram-positive cocci in chains point to GBS. Imaging is used for complications. Strictly, the WHO 2025 guideline covers children over one month; neonatal practice relies on national paediatric guidance.
det.treatment: Penicillin G, ampicillin or amoxicillin is the preferred definitive therapy and is given for 14 to 21 days according to the WHO table, with empirical coverage in the first line for suspected neonatal sepsis according to local protocols. The role of adjunctive steroids is restricted to pneumococcal and Haemophilus type b disease, so they can be stopped after GBS is identified. Prevention rests on screening or risk-based intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis. Follow-up includes audiology and developmental surveillance.
det.prognosis: Mortality is falling but survivors have a high rate of neurological sequelae, so follow-up is essential.
pearls: A well-appearing baby can have meningitis: low threshold for lumbar puncture under 3 months.
Gram-positive cocci in chains in infant CSF are group B streptococci until proved otherwise.
Do not forget hearing screening and developmental follow-up after discharge.

qx.q: What definitive treatment and duration does the WHO table list?

name: Hearing loss after bacterial meningitis
formal: Sensorineural (and sometimes transient conductive) hearing impairment arising during or after acute bacterial meningitis, most often pneumococcal, due to labyrinthitis and cochlear injury; it is the commonest long-term sequela and requires formal audiological screening before discharge or within four weeks.
simple: Loss of hearing that can follow meningitis because the infection harms the inner ear, which is why every survivor needs a hearing test soon after leaving hospital.
