feat: Reduced hearing or failure to respond to sound, noticed after the acute illness
More frequent after pneumococcal meningitis than other bacterial causes
Transient conductive loss may occur; permanent loss reflects cochlea, labyrinth or eighth nerve injury
Dizziness, imbalance and tinnitus in some; children show speech delay and poor school performance
Risk of cochlear ossification if cochlear implant evaluation is delayed
inv: Formal audiology before discharge or within 4 weeks: otoacoustic emissions, auditory brainstem response and behavioural or pure-tone audiometry
MRI of the inner ears for labyrinthine enhancement or early ossification; CT for ossification
Repeat testing in those who pass the first screen, as hearing can decline later

case.who: 4-year-old girl from Buriram after pneumococcal meningitis
case.story: Discharged after 10 days of ceftriaxone and dexamethasone; two weeks later the mother notes that she does not respond when called from behind and turns up the television.
case.exam: Normal tympanic membranes, no other cranial nerve findings, steady gait.
case.tests: ABR shows bilateral severe sensorineural loss; MRI shows early cochlear signal loss.
case.q: What is the urgent next step to protect hearing outcomes?
case.a: Refer urgently for hearing rehabilitation and cochlear implant assessment before the cochlea ossifies, with hearing aids in the meantime and speech therapy.

read.where: Recommendations - C. Management of sequelae (C.4 Hearing loss)

det.patho: Bacteria and inflammatory mediators spread from the subarachnoid space to the perilymph through the cochlear aqueduct or internal auditory canal, causing suppurative labyrinthitis, damage to hair cells and the spiral ganglion, and later fibrosis and new bone formation (labyrinthitis ossificans). Ototoxic antibiotics and other drugs may add to injury. Early dexamethasone reduces hearing loss in some bacterial meningitis.
det.clinical: Deafness is likely the commonest lasting complication of bacterial meningitis at any age, and it is seen most with pneumococcal infection. It may be present on admission or appear during the illness, affects one or both ears, and is mostly permanent when sensorineural. Younger children may be recognised only through delayed speech or behaviour. Vestibular symptoms, tinnitus and balance problems may coexist.
det.diagnosis: The WHO guidance advises a formal hearing test for every survivor of meningitis, whatever the organism, ideally before discharge and otherwise within four weeks. Otoacoustic emissions and auditory brainstem response suit infants, and age-appropriate audiometry suits others. MRI and CT assess cochlear patency, and individuals found to have loss need referral for hearing rehabilitation and evaluation for cochlear implantation without delay.
det.treatment: Management consists of hearing aids for mild to moderate loss, cochlear implantation for severe to profound bilateral loss, speech and language therapy and educational support. Early referral is important because the cochlea may ossify within weeks to months, reducing implant feasibility and results. Prevention depends on vaccination, early appropriate antibiotics and adjunctive dexamethasone when indicated. Those who pass a first test should be rechecked, as loss can emerge later.
det.prognosis: Outcomes with early implantation are good, whereas delayed detection leads to lasting speech and learning disability.
pearls: Test hearing before the child leaves hospital or within 4 weeks, whatever the cause of meningitis.
Pneumococcal meningitis carries the highest risk of deafness.
Delay can lead to cochlear ossification and limit implant options.

Exclude vascular parkinsonism, NPH and drug-induced causes; CSF and autonomic tests as needed

case.who: 66-year-old retired bus driver from Ubon Ratchathani
case.story: Four years of right-hand slowness and rest tremor, improved initially with levodopa; in the last year he has had two backward falls and trouble looking down at his plate.
case.exam: Mild asymmetric parkinsonism, axial rigidity, slowed vertical saccades with square-wave jerks, positive pull test.
case.tests: MRI shows mild midbrain atrophy; DaT SPECT bilaterally reduced.
case.q: Which clinical diagnosis fits and why is it easy to miss early?
case.a: PSP with predominant parkinsonism, because the early picture and levodopa response mimic PD until vertical gaze and postural features emerge.

read.where: 14 Progressive Supranuclear Palsy and Corticobasal Degeneration
Case 31 Woman with gait impairment and difficulty reading

det.patho: Like other forms of PSP, this phenotype is a 4-repeat tauopathy with neuronal and glial tau deposition affecting the substantia nigra, subthalamic nucleus, globus pallidus and brainstem. The relatively milder involvement of the midbrain tegmentum and cerebral cortex early on, with nigrostriatal loss dominating, accounts for the Parkinson-like picture and the partial levodopa response.
det.clinical: Patients present with asymmetric bradykinesia, rigidity and sometimes a tremor, and respond to levodopa, so the diagnosis is usually Parkinson disease at first. Over time, usually after three or more years, vertical gaze slows, falls begin and axial rigidity, dysarthria and swallowing problems appear. Bruno and co-authors note that the PSP-P phenotype, along with MSA-P, DLB and some other disorders, can respond to levodopa, and that all phenotypes tend to converge toward Richardson syndrome in late stages.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is difficult early and relies on recognising atypical features: early postural instability, falls, vertical gaze slowing, square-wave jerks, symmetrical onset, axial greater than limb rigidity and poor sustained response to levodopa. MDS-PSP clinical criteria assign possible or probable PSP-P, and MRI measures of midbrain atrophy support the diagnosis. DaT scanning cannot distinguish PSP from PD. A patient often fulfils more than one PSP phenotype.
det.treatment: Management is symptomatic. Levodopa is trialled at adequate dose and continued if it helps, and amantadine may be tried. Physiotherapy for balance and falls, speech and swallowing therapy, botulinum toxin for blepharospasm and dystonia, and advance care planning are the mainstays. Disease-modifying therapies are under study. Deep brain stimulation is not recommended.
det.prognosis: Survival is longer than for Richardson syndrome, often exceeding ten years from onset.
pearls: PSP-P is the PSP that looks like PD and can respond to levodopa early.
Look for slow vertical saccades and square-wave jerks in any patient with unexpectedly rapid decline.
A normal DaT scan argues against PSP-P, but an abnormal scan does not distinguish it from PD.
det.thd: PSP-P เป็นรูปแบบของ PSP ที่เริ่มด้วยอาการคล้ายพาร์กินสัน คือเคลื่อนไหวช้า แข็งเกร็งและสั่นไม่สมมาตร และตอบสนองต่อ levodopa ได้ในช่วงแรก ภายหลังหลายปีจึงเริ่มมีการกลอกตาลงล่างช้า หกล้มบ่อยและเกร็งที่ลำตัว ทำให้วินิจฉัยช้า ดำเนินโรคช้ากว่า Richardson syndrome MRI พบฝ่อของสมองส่วนกลาง ส่วน DaT SPECT แยกจากพาร์กินสันไม่ได้

qx.stem: A 66-year-old man from Ubon Ratchathani has had four years of asymmetric slowness and rest tremor with a good early response to levodopa, which has faded. He has recently fallen backward twice and has trouble looking down at his plate. Vertical saccades are slow and square-wave jerks are frequent.
qx.q: Which statement about this phenotype is correct?
opts: A levodopa response excludes any form of PSP
DaT scanning reliably separates it from Parkinson’s disease
Early levodopa responsiveness can occur, resembling Parkinson’s disease, and over time the phenotypes tend to converge toward Richardson syndrome
Early falls and vertical gaze palsy are mandatory for the diagnosis
MRI is always normal in the early stage
qx.why: PSP has several phenotypes beyond Richardson syndrome, and PSP-parkinsonism may respond to levodopa, mimicking PD until postural instability and slowed vertical saccades develop. Dopamine transporter imaging is abnormal in both and cannot separate them. Signs such as midbrain atrophy (hummingbird, Mickey Mouse and morning glory signs) support PSP, and the consensus emphasises recognising the range of phenotypes since formal criteria are not validated for all.

name: Progressive supranuclear palsy with progressive gait freezing (PSP-PGF)
formal: A PSP phenotype, formerly labelled pure akinesia with gait freezing (or primary progressive gait freezing), in which a progressive hesitation, start difficulty and freezing of gait dominates for years before limb rigidity, vertical gaze palsy and cognitive features develop.
simple: A type of progressive supranuclear palsy in which the first and main problem for years is that the feet get stuck to the floor when starting to walk or turning, without much tremor or stiffness.
ab: Progressive supranuclear palsy with progressive gait freezing
th: PSP-PGF เป็นรูปแบบของ PSP ที่อาการเด่นคือก้าวเท้าไม่ออก เริ่มเดินลำบาก และเท้าติดพื้นเมื่อหมุนตัว ทั้งที่ไม่มีอาการสั่นหรือแข็งเกร็งมากในช่วงแรก มักตอบสนองต่อ levodopa ไม่ดี ต่อมาจึงมีการกลอกตาลงล่างช้า หกล้ม และอาการอื่นของ PSP โรคดำเนินช้าและวินิจฉัยได้ยาก
tempoNote: Gait freezing and start hesitation worsen over years as the isolated presentation; supranuclear gaze palsy and falls come late
feat: Start hesitation, freezing in doorways and during turns, with feet seeming glued to the floor
Soft speech or micrographia sometimes accompany the gait problem
Little or no tremor, mild limb rigidity and poor response of freezing to levodopa
Supranuclear gaze palsy, postural instability and cognitive or frontal changes may take 5 or more years to appear
Falls are late compared with Richardson syndrome
inv: MRI brain: look for midbrain atrophy and exclude vascular lesions, hydrocephalus and structural causes of gait failure
DaT SPECT often reduced, so it does not distinguish from PD or other parkinsonism
Trial of high-volume lumbar puncture for suspected NPH and vascular risk assessment
Oculomotor examination of vertical saccades; neuropsychology if cognitive change

case.who: 71-year-old woman from Nakhon Si Thammarat, previously active farmer
case.story: Three years of progressive freezing on starting to walk and at doorways, with stuttering gait but no tremor; levodopa 600 mg daily has not helped.
case.exam: Gait initiation failure and freezing on turning, small steps, mild neck rigidity, vertical saccades slightly slow, speech soft.
case.tests: MRI shows mild midbrain atrophy without hydrocephalus or significant white matter disease; large-volume lumbar puncture does not help.
case.q: Which diagnoses are considered and what is the likely one?
case.a: PSP with progressive gait freezing; vascular parkinsonism and normal pressure hydrocephalus have been excluded and levodopa-resistant freezing with slow vertical saccades supports PSP.

read.where: 14 Progressive Supranuclear Palsy and Corticobasal Degeneration

det.patho: PSP-PGF is a tauopathy in which pathological tau accumulates predominantly in the pallidum, subthalamic nucleus and midbrain locomotor regions, including the pedunculopontine area, which disturbs the initiation and scaling of gait with relative sparing of the cortex early on. This explains the isolated gait failure and the poor response to dopaminergic treatment.
det.clinical: Patients present with a progressive inability to start walking and freezing during turns and in narrow places, often with soft speech and little else. Falls are late, in contrast to Richardson syndrome. Over several years, vertical gaze slowing, axial rigidity and cognitive or frontal changes develop and the phenotype converges with other PSP forms. The 2024 CurePSP consensus lists PSP with progressive gait freezing among the recognised phenotypes of PSP.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical, by the MDS-PSP criteria, and requires careful exclusion of vascular parkinsonism, normal pressure hydrocephalus, Parkinson disease with freezing, frontal lobe disease and other causes. MRI looks for midbrain atrophy, white matter vascular change and ventricular size. Large-volume lumbar puncture or drainage tests for NPH. DaT imaging is abnormal and does not separate PSP from PD. Formal certainty criteria for this phenotype are limited, and overlap with other PSP phenotypes is frequent.
det.treatment: A therapeutic levodopa trial is reasonable but freezing seldom responds. Treatment is mainly rehabilitative, using cueing strategies (visual and auditory cues, a walking stick with a laser line), physiotherapy, gait aids and fall prevention. Amantadine or other agents are occasionally tried. Swallowing, speech and eventually palliative care needs are addressed.
det.prognosis: Progression is slower than Richardson syndrome in many cases, although later disability resembles other forms of PSP.
pearls: Isolated levodopa-resistant freezing of gait for years should prompt consideration of PSP-PGF.
Exclude NPH and vascular parkinsonism with MRI and a CSF tap trial.
Cueing and physiotherapy help more than drugs.
det.thd: PSP-PGF เริ่มด้วยการก้าวเท้าไม่ออกและเท้าติดพื้นขณะเริ่มเดินหรือหมุนตัว โดยมีอาการสั่นหรือแข็งเกร็งน้อย ไม่ตอบสนองต่อ levodopa และหกล้มช้ากว่า Richardson syndrome ต่อมาจึงมีการกลอกตาลงล่างช้า ต้องแยกจากโรคหลอดเลือดสมองที่ทำให้เกิดพาร์กินสันและโรคน้ำในโพรงสมองโตแต่ความดันปกติ ด้วย MRI และการเจาะน้ำไขสันหลังปริมาณมาก รักษาด้วยกายภาพและวิธีกระตุ้นการก้าวเท้า

qx.stem: A 71-year-old woman from Nakhon Si Thammarat has three years of progressive start hesitation and freezing at doorways and in turns, with soft speech but no tremor. Levodopa 600 mg daily has not helped. MRI shows mild midbrain atrophy.
qx.q: Which step is most important before accepting PSP with gait freezing?
opts: A DaT scan to separate it from Parkinson’s disease
Exclude normal pressure hydrocephalus and vascular parkinsonism, for example with MRI review and a large-volume lumbar puncture
Further dopamine agonist titration to prove levodopa resistance
Autonomic testing as the primary diagnostic test
Whole-exome sequencing as the first investigation
qx.why: Isolated, levodopa-resistant gait freezing is a recognised PSP phenotype but mimics normal pressure hydrocephalus, vascular parkinsonism and other gait disorders, which are treatable or preventable and must be excluded. Dopamine transporter scanning is abnormal in PSP and PD alike. Management is rehabilitative, using cueing strategies, physiotherapy and fall prevention.

name: Pharyngeal-cervical-brachial variant of Guillain-Barre syndrome
formal: A regional variant of Guillain-Barre syndrome in which rapidly progressive weakness is confined to the oropharyngeal, neck and upper-limb muscles, with relatively spared legs, often associated with anti-GT1a (and GQ1b/GD1b) IgG antibodies after infection.
simple: A form of Guillain-Barre syndrome in which the throat, neck and arms become weak within days while the legs stay fairly strong.
th: Pharyngeal-cervical-brachial variant ของ Guillain-Barré syndrome คืออัมพาตอ่อนแรงเฉียบพลันที่กล้ามเนื้อคอหอย คอ และแขน โดยขามักแข็งแรงกว่า ผู้ป่วยกลืนลำบาก พูดไม่ชัด คออ่อน แขนอ่อนแรง และรีเฟล็กซ์แขนลดลง มักสัมพันธ์กับแอนติบอดี anti-GT1a หลังการติดเชื้อ ควรแยกจาก botulism และรักษาด้วย IVIG หรือแลกเปลี่ยนพลาสมาแบบ GBS
tempoNote: Progresses over days to under 4 weeks, nadir within about 2 to 4 weeks, often after an upper respiratory or gastrointestinal infection
feat: Dysphagia, dysarthria and facial or ocular weakness within days
Neck flexor and shoulder girdle weakness with arm weakness greater than leg weakness
Reduced or absent reflexes in the arms, with variable paraesthesia
Respiratory failure can occur, so vital capacity and bulbar function are monitored
Overlap with Miller Fisher syndrome and Bickerstaff encephalitis in some patients
inv: Nerve conduction studies show axonal or demyelinating changes in arm nerves, and sometimes reversible conduction failure
CSF albuminocytologic dissociation (may be normal in the first week)
Serum anti-GT1a, GQ1b and GD1b IgG antibodies
Brain and cervical spine MRI to exclude brainstem stroke, myelopathy and bulbar mimics; repetitive nerve stimulation or botulinum tests if botulism is suspected

case.story: After a sore throat and diarrhoea for 3 days, he developed nasal speech, choking on liquids, neck weakness and then inability to lift his arms over 5 days.
case.exam: Bilateral facial and palatal weakness, neck flexion 3/5, shoulder abduction 3/5, leg power 5/5, absent biceps and triceps jerks, normal pupils.
case.tests: CSF protein 85 mg/dL with 2 cells; nerve conduction studies show low-amplitude arm CMAPs; anti-GT1a IgG positive.
case.q: What treatment and what monitoring does he need?
case.a: IVIG at a total of 2 g/kg given across five days, or plasma exchange, with respiratory and swallowing monitoring; corticosteroids do not help.

det.patho: The syndrome results from antibody-mediated attack on peripheral nerve gangliosides after infection, typically with Campylobacter jejuni or a respiratory pathogen, through molecular mimicry and complement activation. The associated antibodies target GT1a (expressed in glossopharyngeal and vagal nerves), GQ1b and GD1b, which explains the oropharyngeal, neck and arm distribution. Pathology is axonal, demyelinating or reversible conduction failure.
det.clinical: Weakness begins in the throat and neck and spreads to the shoulders and arms within days, with prominent dysphagia, dysarthria and facial weakness, while leg strength and reflexes are relatively spared. Arm reflexes are reduced or absent, and mild sensory symptoms are common. Dysautonomia and respiratory insufficiency may occur and need intensive care. Overlap with Miller Fisher syndrome and Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis occurs through shared antibodies.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis rests on the characteristic distribution, evolution of fewer than four weeks, arm hyporeflexia, albuminocytologic dissociation and neurophysiology. Electrodiagnostic findings may show reduced CMAP amplitudes in the arms with preserved leg nerves, and reversible conduction failure may appear in sensory and motor nerves. Anti-GT1a antibodies support but are not required. Brainstem stroke, botulism, myasthenia gravis, diphtheria, poliomyelitis-like illnesses and cervical cord lesions must be excluded.
det.treatment: Treatment follows the standard approach for GBS: IVIG (2 g/kg over five days) or plasma exchange are equally effective in patients who cannot walk unaided, and corticosteroids are not helpful. Patients are monitored for bulbar failure and respiratory insufficiency with serial vital capacity, and early intubation is preferred over emergency intubation. Dysphagia needs nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding. Rehabilitation continues after discharge.
det.prognosis: Most patients recover well, although bulbar and arm strength can take many months to return and a few patients need prolonged ventilation.
pearls: Bulbar, neck and arm weakness with arm areflexia after an infection is PCB-GBS until proved otherwise.
Distinguish from botulism, which has pupillary involvement and a descending course without sensory change.
Monitor vital capacity, because bulbar weakness often accompanies respiratory failure.
det.thd: PCB variant ของ GBS มีอาการอ่อนแรงที่คอหอย คอ และแขนอย่างรวดเร็ว โดยขาแข็งแรงกว่า มักเกิดหลังการติดเชื้อ ผู้ป่วยกลืนลำบาก พูดเสียงขึ้นจมูก ยกแขนไม่ขึ้น และรีเฟล็กซ์แขนลดลง อาจพบ anti-GT1a ตรวจน้ำไขสันหลังพบโปรตีนสูงแต่เซลล์ไม่มาก รักษาด้วย IVIG หรือแลกเปลี่ยนพลาสมาและเฝ้าระวังการหายใจ ต้องแยกจาก botulism และ myasthenia gravis

qx.stem: A 44-year-old man from Chonburi, a week after a diarrhoeal illness, has nasal speech, dysphagia, neck flexor weakness and difficulty lifting his arms. Biceps and triceps reflexes are absent while leg strength is normal. CSF protein is raised with few cells.
qx.q: Which antibody profile is most associated with this regional variant?
opts: IgM against myelin-associated glycoprotein
IgG against GM1 only, causing pure motor axonal disease
IgG against LM1 and galactocerebroside
Antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor

qx.why: Regional variants of GBS are named after the muscle groups affected, and the pharyngeal-cervical-brachial form targets gangliosides GT1a, GD1b and GQ1b, which are expressed in the glossopharyngeal and vagal nerves. It overlaps with Miller Fisher syndrome. Treatment is as for GBS, with monitoring of respiratory and bulbar function, and botulism and myasthenia gravis must be excluded.

name: SOD1-related amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
formal: A genetic form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis caused by pathogenic variants in SOD1, typically autosomal dominant, with limb-onset weakness and a variable course depending on the variant, and the target of the antisense oligonucleotide tofersen.
simple: A type of ALS caused by a fault in the SOD1 gene, often running in families, for which one specific gene-lowering treatment now exists.
th: SOD1-ALS คือโรคกล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงจากเซลล์ประสาทสั่งการเสื่อมที่เกิดจากความผิดปกติของยีน SOD1 มักถ่ายทอดแบบข้ามรุ่น เริ่มด้วยอ่อนแรงที่แขนหรือขา ความเร็วของโรคขึ้นกับชนิดของการกลายพันธุ์ ปัจจุบันมียา tofersen ซึ่งเป็น antisense oligonucleotide ฉีดเข้าช่องไขสันหลังเพื่อลดโปรตีน SOD1 สำหรับผู้ป่วยกลุ่มนี้
tempoNote: Progressive over months to years; rate varies with the specific variant, from rapid to slowly progressive
feat: Asymmetric limb weakness and wasting with fasciculations, often lower limb or distal onset
Upper motor neuron signs may be subtle in some variants; bulbar involvement is relatively uncommon at onset
Family history in a proportion, but sporadic-looking cases occur because of reduced penetrance or de novo variants
Cognitive impairment and frontotemporal dementia are less typical than with C9orf72
Variant-dependent course: some pathogenic variants cause very rapid disease while others cause slow progression
inv: EMG showing active and chronic denervation in multiple regions
Genetic counselling and testing for ALS genes (C9orf72, SOD1, TARDBP, FUS) in familial cases and offered to all patients
Neurofilament light chain in serum or CSF to follow disease activity
MRI and laboratory studies to exclude mimics

case.who: 49-year-old woman from Phayao, whose father died of a motor neuron disease
case.story: Six months of right foot drop spreading to the left leg, cramps and muscle twitching, with no swallowing problems.
case.exam: Bilateral foot drop, thigh and calf wasting, fasciculations, brisk knee jerks, no bulbar signs.
case.tests: EMG shows widespread acute and chronic denervation; ALS gene panel finds a pathogenic SOD1 variant; neurofilament light chain is raised.
case.q: What treatment is specific to this genotype and what monitoring does it need?
case.a: Tofersen, an intrathecal antisense oligonucleotide, lowers SOD1 protein; start with neurologic review, CSF cell count and protein monitoring, and standard multidisciplinary ALS care.

det.patho: SOD1 encodes copper-zinc superoxide dismutase. Most variants cause a toxic gain of function by misfolded and aggregated protein rather than loss of enzyme activity, as shown by the SOD1 inclusions in affected motor neurons. Antisense therapy lowers production of the gene product. SOD1 accounts for a minority of familial ALS and a small percentage of apparently sporadic cases, and its prevalence differs by population.
det.clinical: Presentation resembles typical ALS with asymmetric limb weakness, wasting and fasciculations, but lower limb and distal onset is common and bulbar involvement and cognitive change are less prominent. The rate of progression depends on the variant; some, such as A4V in North America, cause very rapid disease, whereas other variants allow survival beyond a decade. Penetrance may be incomplete, so a family history is sometimes absent.
det.diagnosis: ALS is diagnosed by clinical and electrophysiological criteria after excluding mimics. Genetic testing is recommended when there is a family history and is increasingly offered to all patients, since individual gene-based treatments exist. Results are interpreted in the context of the variant's known behaviour, and genetic counselling is provided to relatives. Neurofilament light chain assists in monitoring.
det.treatment: All patients receive riluzole and, where available, edaravone, and above all multidisciplinary clinic care, noninvasive ventilation, nutrition and symptom management. Tofersen, approved in 2023 for adults with SOD1 variants, is an intrathecal antisense oligonucleotide: the phase 3 trial did not meet its primary clinical endpoint but reduced SOD1 protein and neurofilament light chain, and extension data suggest slowing of progression. Monitoring includes lumbar puncture procedure safety and watch for myelitis or radiculitis. Genetic counselling is essential.
det.prognosis: The course is highly variant-dependent, and tofersen may slow progression in some patients.
pearls: Test for SOD1 in every ALS patient with a suggestive family history, because tofersen is available only for this genotype.
Neurofilament light chain is a useful marker of treatment effect.
Course depends on the specific variant, so counsel accordingly.
det.thd: SOD1-ALS เกิดจากยีน SOD1 กลายพันธุ์ ทำให้โปรตีนพับผิดและเป็นพิษต่อเซลล์ประสาทสั่งการ ผู้ป่วยมีอ่อนแรงที่แขนหรือขา กล้ามเนื้อลีบและกระตุก มักเริ่มที่ขาและอาการทางเดินกลืนหรือสมองเสื่อมพบน้อยกว่า C9orf72 ความเร็วของโรคแตกต่างตามชนิดของการกลายพันธุ์ ควรตรวจยีนในผู้ป่วยที่มีประวัติครอบครัว ยา tofersen ฉีดเข้าช่องไขสันหลังเพื่อลดโปรตีน SOD1 ใช้เฉพาะกลุ่มนี้ร่วมกับการดูแลแบบสหสาขา

qx.stem: A 49-year-old woman from Phayao has progressive bilateral foot drop and fasciculations. Her father died of a motor neuron disease. A gene panel reveals a pathogenic SOD1 variant and her neurologist discusses a new gene-directed option.
qx.q: Which statement about tofersen is correct?
opts: It is an oral glutamate antagonist that prolongs survival in all ALS
It is an intrathecal antisense oligonucleotide that lowers SOD1 protein production, and it is approved only for patients with SOD1 variants
It is an AAV gene replacement that restores SMN protein
It is a monoclonal antibody against complement C5
It is a free radical scavenger given intravenously to all patients
qx.why: Tofersen reduces SOD1 mRNA through an antisense mechanism and was approved in 2023 for SOD1-ALS. The phase 3 trial missed its primary clinical endpoint but lowered SOD1 protein and neurofilament light chain, and long-term data suggest slowing. Riluzole (glutamate modulation) and edaravone (free radical scavenging) are approved for all ALS, and SMN gene therapy is for spinal muscular atrophy.

name: Immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated myopathy
formal: An immune-related adverse event of PD-1, PD-L1 or CTLA-4 inhibitors presenting as subacute proximal, bulbar or axial muscle weakness with raised creatine kinase and a necrotising or inflammatory muscle biopsy, frequently overlapping with myasthenia gravis and myocarditis.
simple: Muscle weakness that appears in weeks to months after starting cancer immunotherapy such as pembrolizumab, sometimes affecting the eyelids, swallowing, neck and breathing.

feat: Subacute proximal limb and neck extensor weakness, dropped head, and myalgia
Ptosis, diplopia, facial and bulbar weakness (dysphagia, dysarthria) resembling myasthenia
Respiratory muscle weakness and hypercapnic failure in severe cases
Concurrent myocarditis or myasthenia gravis (the overlap of myositis, myocarditis, myasthenia)
Rapid worsening is possible, and the syndrome can follow only one or two doses
inv: Creatine kinase, aldolase, troponin and ECG/echo screening for myocarditis
Acetylcholine receptor, anti-striational and myositis antibody panel (including anti-HMGCR and SRP)
EMG with repetitive stimulation: myopathic units with irritability and exclusion of neuromuscular transmission defect
MRI of muscles and muscle biopsy showing multifocal necrosis or inflammatory infiltrates

case.who: 72-year-old man from Chonburi with metastatic melanoma
case.story: Two doses of pembrolizumab, then a week of drooping eyelids, double vision, difficulty swallowing and a head that falls forward.
case.exam: Bilateral ptosis, restricted eye movements, facial and tongue weakness, neck flexor weakness, proximal 4/5 weakness without fatiguability.
case.tests: CK 1,240 U/L; striational antibodies strongly positive; AChR antibody negative; EMG shows myopathic units; repetitive stimulation shows no decrement; biopsy shows multifocal necrosis.
case.q: What are the first actions and what should be screened for?
case.a: Stop the checkpoint inhibitor, start high-dose corticosteroids and consider IVIG or plasma exchange, and urgently screen for myocarditis (troponin, ECG, echo) and respiratory failure.

det.patho: Checkpoint inhibitors release T-cell inhibition, which can unmask autoimmunity against muscle and sometimes the heart, neuromuscular junction and nerve. Shared antigens in tumour and muscle, T-cell clonal expansion and cytokine release are thought to cause immune-mediated muscle necrosis and inflammation. The biopsy can show multifocal clusters of necrotic fibres with little inflammation, distinct from scattered necrosis in antibody-mediated necrotising myopathy.
det.clinical: Weakness appears after a median of a few weeks, often within the first two or three doses, and is typically proximal, with prominent ocular, bulbar and neck extensor involvement that mimics myasthenia. Respiratory failure, myalgia, rhabdomyolysis and concurrent myocarditis are major threats. Severe cases progress rapidly and are fatal in a substantial minority.
det.diagnosis: CK is usually markedly elevated, EMG shows myopathic units with irritability, and repetitive stimulation excludes decrement unless myasthenia coexists. Muscle biopsy or MRI of muscle shows necrosis or inflammation. Cardiac screening with troponin, ECG and echocardiography, and an antibody panel including AChR, anti-striational, HMGCR and SRP, should be done in every patient. Differential diagnoses include steroid myopathy, hypothyroid myopathy and cancer-related disorders.
det.treatment: The checkpoint inhibitor is held or permanently stopped according to severity, and high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (then oral prednisolone) is first-line. IVIG or plasma exchange is added for severe, bulbar, respiratory or cardiac involvement, and abatacept or other immunotherapy may be used in refractory cases according to recent expert guidance. Patients with respiratory compromise need intensive monitoring. Oncology and neurology teams decide jointly about re-challenge.
det.prognosis: Early recognition improves recovery, but severe bulbar-respiratory forms have high mortality.
pearls: Ptosis, diplopia and dropped head after checkpoint inhibitors can be myositis, myasthenia or both.
Always screen for myocarditis with troponin and ECG.
Stop the drug and treat early; prognosis hinges on how fast therapy begins.

High-dose steroids with IVIG or plasma exchange are used, but this fulminant case continued to worsen and developed hypercapnic failure. Cardiac and respiratory surveillance is therefore mandatory in every case.

name: Hemiconvulsion–hemiplegia–epilepsy (HHE) syndrome
formal: A rare childhood syndrome in which a prolonged, usually febrile, unilateral clonic seizure is followed at once by hemiplegia from acute hemispheric injury, and weeks to years later by focal epilepsy and hemiatrophy of the affected hemisphere.
simple: A toddler has a very long one-sided fit with fever, wakes up with a weak arm and leg on that side, and later develops epilepsy.
th: กลุ่มอาการ HHE เกิดในเด็กเล็กที่ชักเกร็งกระตุกครึ่งซีกนานจากไข้ แล้วตามด้วยอัมพาตครึ่งซีกทันที ต่อมามีสมองซีกนั้นฝ่อและเกิดโรคลมชักแบบเฉพาะที่
tempoNote: A prolonged febrile hemiclonic seizure in the first 4 years, hemiplegia immediately afterwards, then focal seizures emerging after a latent interval of months to a few years
feat: Onset in a child under about 4 years of age, typically during a febrile illness, with a unilateral clonic seizure lasting from many minutes to hours
Flaccid, then spastic, hemiparesis noticed when the seizure ends, sometimes with aphasia if the left hemisphere is involved
A seizure-free interval, then focal seizures (often of temporal or frontotemporal origin) in most children, with a drug-resistant course in many
Persistent hemiparesis, cognitive and behavioural difficulty, and later asymmetry with a smaller affected side of the head and body
Much less common today because prolonged febrile seizures are treated quickly
inv: Acute MRI shows swelling of one hemisphere with restricted diffusion in cortex and subcortical white matter, often sparing deep grey nuclei
Follow-up MRI shows unilateral hemispheric atrophy with gliosis and ventricular enlargement
EEG shows early slowing of the affected hemisphere, later focal epileptiform discharges
Infection, metabolic and vascular tests are done to exclude other causes of the acute event (CSF, glucose, electrolytes, vascular imaging)

case.story: A day of fever is followed by a seizure of the right arm and leg that continues for about two hours until treated in the provincial hospital; afterwards the right side is limp.
case.exam: Drowsy, right hemiparesis with reduced tone, no neck stiffness; the weakness slowly turns spastic over the following month.
case.tests: MRI on day 2 shows swelling and diffusion restriction of the left hemisphere; at 8 months the same hemisphere is smaller; CSF is normal; at age 3 he starts having focal seizures.
case.q: How is this sequence named and what is the main lesson for acute care?
case.a: Hemiconvulsion-hemiplegia-epilepsy syndrome; the lesson is to stop prolonged febrile seizures early and, if epilepsy later becomes drug resistant, to evaluate for hemispheric surgery.

read.where: 9. Terminology for Seizures and Epilepsies - special syndromes (febrile convulsions)

det.patho: A long unilateral seizure in a febrile young child is thought to produce excitotoxic and metabolic injury of the hemisphere that is seizing, causing cytotoxic oedema and later atrophy. Genetic or inflammatory susceptibility may explain why only some prolonged seizures cause the syndrome. Older reports describe it as the sequel of unattended febrile status in under-resourced settings, and it has become rarer with early benzodiazepine treatment. The epilepsy phase reflects the damaged hemisphere as an epileptogenic focus.
det.clinical: The first stage is the hemiconvulsion, a long clonic seizure of one side that often evolves to generalised activity. The second is the hemiplegia, noticed as soon as the child recovers, accompanied by drowsiness and sometimes language loss. The third stage, after a symptom-free period that can last months to about three years, is recurrent focal epilepsy, often with temporal lobe semiology. Some children also show behavioural disorder and intellectual impairment, and the affected limbs remain paretic with contracture risk.
det.diagnosis: The history of a prolonged febrile hemiclonic seizure followed by hemiplegia is the starting point. Early MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging shows hemispheric swelling and restricted diffusion, while later images show unilateral atrophy and gliosis. The work-up must exclude meningoencephalitis, stroke, hypoglycaemia and other structural causes of the acute event, and long-term EEG and MRI help to define the epileptogenic zone. The diagnosis is largely retrospective once the typical stages are known.
det.treatment: Treatment of the acute event is to stop the seizure promptly with a benzodiazepine and a second-line intravenous antiseizure medicine, treat the fever and the infection, and give supportive neurocritical care. Epilepsy is managed with antiseizure medicines selected for focal seizures, and rehabilitation targets the hemiparesis, language and learning. If seizures remain drug resistant, hemispherotomy or a smaller resection can be considered by an epilepsy surgery centre, with good seizure outcomes in selected children whose hemisphere is already non-functional.
det.prognosis: Hemiparesis is usually permanent, and most children develop epilepsy that is often hard to control. Cognitive outcome varies from near normal to severe impairment, and surgery can offer seizure freedom.
pearls: Hemiplegia that appears right after a long one-sided febrile seizure should make you think of this sequence, not of simple Todd paralysis that clears in hours.
The three stages are hemiconvulsion, hemiplegia and then epilepsy after a latent period.
Early treatment of febrile status is the only effective prevention.
det.thd: HHE syndrome เริ่มจากเด็กอายุน้อยกว่า 4 ปีมีไข้และชักกระตุกครึ่งซีกนานผิดปกติ หลังชักหยุดจะพบแขนขาข้างนั้นอ่อนแรงถาวร MRI ระยะแรกพบสมองซีกนั้นบวมและมี diffusion restriction ต่อมาฝ่อลง หลังช่วงที่ไม่ชักนานหลายเดือนถึงไม่กี่ปีจะเกิดโรคลมชักแบบเฉพาะที่ ซึ่งมักดื้อยา การป้องกันที่ดีที่สุดคือหยุดชักจากไข้ที่นานให้เร็ว และพิจารณาผ่าตัด hemispherotomy ในรายที่ดื้อยา

qx.stem: A 5-year-old boy from Lampang had, at 20 months, a right-sided clonic seizure with fever lasting nearly two hours, followed by right hemiparesis that never fully recovered. MRI at the time showed swelling of the left hemisphere; the left hemisphere is now smaller. Since age 3 he has had frequent focal seizures despite three antiseizure medicines, and the right hand is nearly useless.
qx.q: What should be done next?
opts: Add a fourth antiseizure drug and re-assess in two years
Refer to an epilepsy surgery centre to assess for hemispherotomy
Start immunotherapy for presumed Rasmussen encephalitis
Repeat lumbar puncture for herpes simplex PCR
Prescribe steroids for presumed cerebral vasculitis
qx.why: The sequence of a prolonged febrile hemiclonic seizure, immediate hemiplegia, hemispheric atrophy and later drug-resistant focal epilepsy is the hemiconvulsion-hemiplegia-epilepsy syndrome. With a non-functional, atrophic hemisphere and drug resistance after two to three appropriate drugs, early referral for hemispherotomy gives the best chance of seizure freedom. Rasmussen encephalitis shows progressive, not abrupt, deficits, and there is no evidence for infection or vasculitis.

name: Reading epilepsy
formal: A reflex epilepsy in which seizures, typically perioral reflex myoclonia or jaw jerks that may progress to a generalised convulsion, are precipitated by reading, especially aloud, in a young person with a normal examination and brain imaging.
simple: A rare form of epilepsy in which reading, particularly reading aloud, sets off jaw twitching and sometimes a full fit.
th: โรคลมชักจากการอ่าน (reading epilepsy) เป็นโรคลมชักชนิด reflex ที่การอ่านหนังสือ โดยเฉพาะอ่านออกเสียง กระตุ้นให้ขากรรไกรกระตุกและอาจชักทั้งตัวถ้าอ่านต่อ
tempoNote: Seizures only while reading or doing related language tasks, with onset in the teens and no events at other times in the primary form
feat: Onset in late childhood to the twenties, most often between about 12 and 25 years
Brief jaw jerks, clicking or twitching of the lips and tongue while reading, often with a feeling of the words being hard to read
A generalised tonic-clonic seizure if the person keeps reading after the first warning
Triggers include reading aloud, silent reading of hard text, and sometimes speaking, writing or typing
Normal development, examination and MRI; a family history of epilepsy in some
inv: Routine EEG is normal; during reading, spikes or sharp theta appear over the dominant temporoparietal region or as generalised discharges
Video-EEG with reading tasks of increasing difficulty reproduces the events and is the confirmatory test
MRI brain is normal in the primary form and is done mainly to exclude a lesion in secondary cases

case.story: She has noticed her jaw clicking and her mouth twitching when she reads English passages aloud for exam practice; last week she lost awareness and convulsed after reading for 40 minutes.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination; during reading aloud of a long text the examiner sees rhythmic perioral twitching that stops when she puts the page down.
case.tests: Interictal EEG normal; video-EEG during reading shows left temporoparietal sharp theta followed by generalised spike-wave; MRI is normal.
case.q: What is the practical advice for the school period?
case.a: Explain the trigger, advise stopping reading when the jaw jerks begin, split reading into short sessions, and start an antiseizure medicine such as valproate, levetiracetam or clonazepam only if the events persist or she wants to read freely; avoid valproate in girls of childbearing potential if alternatives suit.

read.where: 22. Epilepsy With Reflex Seizures - Seizures Induced by Reading and Language

det.patho: Reading epilepsy is a reflex epilepsy in which a cognitive-motor activity, rather than a simple sensory stimulus, triggers a seizure. Functional imaging has shown that reading activates a network over language and orofacial motor areas in the dominant hemisphere, and the seizure appears when enough of this network is recruited. The primary form behaves like an idiopathic reflex epilepsy and may be familial, and a secondary form occurs with structural lesions and spontaneous seizures. The ILAE groups it among the reflex epilepsies.
det.clinical: Most patients are adolescents or young adults who notice that reading produces perioral twitching, jaw clicking or a sense of being unable to read. These events are brief if reading stops, but continued reading can build up into a generalised convulsion. Patients may report that thick or demanding text, loud reading or long sessions are worse. Some also react to speaking, writing or typing, and the picture then overlaps with language-induced reflex epilepsy. The secondary form shows spontaneous seizures and an abnormal baseline EEG.
det.diagnosis: The history of jaw jerks provoked by reading is highly characteristic. Interictal EEG is often normal, so the test should be video-EEG during standardised reading tasks, which can show temporoparietal discharges or generalised spike-wave and reproduce the clinical events. MRI is usually normal, and a lesion or spontaneous seizures suggest the secondary form. Other reflex epilepsies, juvenile myoclonic epilepsy and tics should be considered.
det.treatment: The simplest measure is to stop reading when the jaw jerks start and to use short reading periods with breaks. Antiseizure medicines used in practice include valproate, levetiracetam, lamotrigine and clonazepam, selected by sex, comorbidity and cognitive side effects, and valproate should be avoided in people who may become pregnant. Counselling about school accommodations, such as extra time and recorded material, is useful. Epilepsy surgery is not relevant in the primary form.
det.prognosis: The primary form usually has a benign course with good control, although the trigger tends to persist. Secondary cases follow the underlying cause.
pearls: Ask every teenager with unexplained jaw twitching or episodes at school whether they happen while reading.
A normal routine EEG does not exclude it; test with reading during the recording.
Stopping reading at the first jaw jerk is the key warning step that prevents convulsions.
det.thd: Reading epilepsy พบในวัยรุ่นถึงผู้ใหญ่ตอนต้น ผู้ป่วยมีอาการกรามกระตุกหรือริมฝีปากสั่นขณะอ่านหนังสือ โดยเฉพาะอ่านออกเสียง และถ้าฝืนอ่านต่ออาจชักเกร็งกระตุกทั้งตัว EEG ปกติระหว่างไม่มีอาการ ต้องทำ video-EEG ขณะให้อ่านจึงเห็นคลื่นผิดปกติบริเวณ temporoparietal ด้านเด่น การรักษาคือหยุดอ่านเมื่อเริ่มมีอาการ พักเป็นช่วงสั้นๆ และใช้ยากันชักเมื่อจำเป็น

qx.stem: A 16-year-old girl from Chiang Mai notices twitching of her jaw and lips when she reads English textbooks aloud. Yesterday, after reading for about 30 minutes, she lost awareness and had a generalised convulsion. Her neurological examination and brain MRI are normal, and a routine 20-minute EEG recorded at rest shows no abnormality.
qx.q: Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
opts: Repeat routine EEG after sleep deprivation only
Ambulatory EEG limited to sleep
Video-EEG recorded while she performs graded reading tasks aloud and silently
Photic stimulation at 5 to 30 Hz with eyes closed
Lumbar puncture for oligoclonal bands

Video-EEG during standardised reading reproduces the jaw jerks and records the discharge. Photic stimulation tests for photosensitivity, not language triggers, sleep recordings miss task-bound activity, and CSF testing has no role in a normal-MRI reflex epilepsy.

name: Hot water epilepsy
formal: A reflex epilepsy in which focal or generalised seizures are triggered by immersion in or pouring of hot water over the head, reported worldwide but most often in southern India and Turkey, usually beginning in childhood or adolescence.
simple: A type of epilepsy where a seizure happens when hot water is poured over the head or the body is put in a hot bath.
ab: epilepsy induced by hot water bathing
th: โรคลมชักจากน้ำร้อน (hot water epilepsy) เป็นโรคลมชักชนิด reflex ที่การราดน้ำร้อนบนศีรษะหรือแช่น้ำอุ่นจัดกระตุ้นให้เกิดอาการชักแบบเฉพาะที่หรือชักทั้งตัว พบมากในอินเดียและตุรกี

feat: Seizures begin during or just after head-bathing or immersion in hot water, with a complex focal seizure (blank stare, automatisms, impaired awareness) or tonic-clonic activity
In Indian series most patients are boys with onset around early adolescence, and the trigger is pouring jugs of hot water over the head
In younger European and Japanese children, seizures can begin as soon as the child enters the bath, and sensitivity often fades with time
Some patients, especially those with later onset, also develop spontaneous seizures with temporal lobe features
Normal examination in most; vasovagal and startle events can look similar

MRI brain is usually normal; it is done to look for hippocampal sclerosis or another focal lesion, especially if spontaneous seizures occur
A careful witness history of temperature, water pouring site and other triggers is the main diagnostic step

case.story: Three times in two months he has stared and fumbled with his hands, then collapsed, within a minute of his mother pouring warm water over his head during the morning bath.
case.exam: Normal examination between events; no seizures when he washes with lukewarm water.
case.tests: Interictal EEG shows rare right temporal sharp waves; MRI of the brain is normal.
case.q: What is the first step in management?
case.a: Teach lukewarm bathing with water poured over the body and not the head, avoid very hot water and prolonged immersion, supervise bathing, and start a focal-onset antiseizure drug only if events continue or spontaneous seizures appear.

read.where: 22. Epilepsy With Reflex Seizures - Seizures Induced by Hot Water

det.patho: The mechanism is unknown. A defect in thermoregulation, a lowered seizure threshold to a rapid rise in scalp or body temperature, or activation of an excitable temporal network have all been suggested. Startle and vasovagal reactions can mimic or add to the events. The high frequency in some regions suggests that a cultural bathing practice meets a susceptible group. Some patients later show spontaneous seizures, which fits an underlying focal epilepsy.
det.clinical: The seizure typically starts within seconds to a few minutes of the water contact, often during head-bathing in the morning. The commonest event is a complex focal seizure with an epigastric or fearful aura, staring and automatisms, followed by confusion, and generalised convulsions occur in a minority. Patients can describe the trigger clearly when asked, but families may not link seizures to the bath unless prompted. In young children the first event may occur in a bathtub, which also raises safety concerns about drowning.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis rests on a history that the seizures are consistently triggered by hot water, with a normal temperature of the water ruled out. Interictal EEG may show temporal abnormalities, and MRI should be done for focal lesions. Because syncope, startle responses and, in infants, breath-holding can imitate the events, the clinician should seek an eyewitness account of the exact sequence and, when possible, home video.
det.treatment: Avoidance of the trigger is the main treatment. Patients should use lukewarm water, avoid pouring hot water over the head, shorten bathing, and bathe with someone nearby or take showers rather than tub baths to lower drowning risk. An antiseizure drug effective for focal seizures is used if seizures persist or occur spontaneously, and some clinicians use short-term clobazam before bathing in selected patients. Families should be counselled about water safety and about avoiding saunas and very hot pools.
det.prognosis: Outcome is generally good with trigger avoidance, though a minority develop spontaneous seizures and need long-term treatment.
pearls: Ask patients from regions with ritual head-bathing about the temperature of the water and where it is poured.
Bathtub immersion in a child with this reflex is a drowning risk, so supervision is part of the treatment.
A spontaneous seizure later does not rule out the diagnosis; it means a broader focal epilepsy.

name: KCNQ2 developmental and epileptic encephalopathy
formal: A neonatal-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathy caused by usually de novo, dominant-negative or gain-of-function variants in KCNQ2, which encodes the Kv7.2 potassium channel subunit; tonic seizures start in the first week of life, often with burst-suppression or multifocal EEG, and developmental impairment persists even when seizures remit.
simple: A gene change in a brain potassium channel causes hard-to-control fits in the first days of life and long-term developmental problems.
th: KCNQ2 encephalopathy เกิดจากความผิดปกติของยีน KCNQ2 มักเกิดใหม่ในผู้ป่วย ทารกชักเกร็งในสัปดาห์แรกและมีพัฒนาการล่าช้า ซึ่งต่างจาก benign familial neonatal seizures จากยีนเดียวกันที่ชักหายเองและพัฒนาการปกติ
tempoNote: Seizures start in the first days of life, are often drug resistant for weeks to months and may settle by early childhood; developmental disability is chronic
feat: Tonic seizures, sometimes with autonomic changes and apnoea, from the first week of life
Often multifocal EEG with burst-suppression pattern in the early weeks
Hypotonia, poor feeding and reduced alertness, followed by global developmental delay and intellectual disability
Seizures often decrease in the first years of life, but motor and cognitive disability remain
Same gene as benign familial neonatal seizures, but the family history is absent in most children with the encephalopathy
inv: Video-EEG shows burst-suppression or multifocal epileptiform activity in neonates
MRI brain may be normal or show basal ganglia and thalamic T1 hyperintensity in the neonatal period, which fades later
Epilepsy gene panel or exome sequencing identifies the KCNQ2 variant, and parental testing shows de novo origin in most
Metabolic and infectious screening is done to exclude treatable causes of neonatal seizures

case.story: She has had daily stiffening episodes with eye deviation and brief apnoea since day 2; cultures and glucose are normal and phenobarbital gives only partial relief.
case.exam: Hypotonic, poor suck, repeated tonic posturing seen on the ward.
case.tests: EEG shows multifocal sharp waves with a burst-suppression pattern; MRI shows mild basal ganglia T1 hyperintensity; the epilepsy panel returns a de novo missense variant in KCNQ2.
case.q: Which antiseizure drug class is often most useful?
case.a: Sodium channel blockers such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine or phenytoin often help, and the family should be counselled that developmental problems may persist even after seizures settle.

det.patho: Kv7.2 and Kv7.3 subunits form the neuronal M-channel, a slowly activating potassium current that limits repetitive firing. Heterozygous loss of function (haploinsufficiency) produces benign familial neonatal seizures, whereas missense variants in functionally critical regions can act in a dominant-negative way or sometimes by a gain-of-function mechanism, producing the encephalopathy. Most variants arise de novo. The difference in mechanism helps explain the wide span from benign seizures to severe developmental disability.
det.clinical: Seizures begin in the first week with tonic events, often asymmetric, and may include autonomic changes. Burst-suppression or multifocal EEG patterns can lead to an initial label of Ohtahara-like syndrome. Many babies are hypotonic and feed poorly, and they later develop moderate to severe developmental delay, with spasticity in some. Seizures frequently abate in the first years of life, but other seizure types can appear later. A few variants cause milder phenotypes.
det.diagnosis: A genetic diagnosis is made by an epilepsy gene panel, exome or genome sequencing, interpreted along with the clinical picture and the variant location. Neonatal seizures need immediate exclusion of hypoglycaemia, electrolyte problems, infection and hypoxic-ischaemic injury, and a structural MRI to identify malformations. Early genetic testing is increasingly done in neonates with unexplained seizures because it affects drug choice and counselling.
det.treatment: Sodium channel blocking drugs, including carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine and phenytoin, are commonly reported to reduce seizures, and many centres use them early when a KCNQ2 variant is found. Phenobarbital and levetiracetam are often tried first but may help less. Gain-of-function variants may respond better to different treatment strategies, so variant-specific advice from an epilepsy genetics team is valuable. Retigabine (ezogabine), a Kv7 opener, has been withdrawn from the market, and newer Kv7 openers are under study. Early developmental therapy and family counselling are part of care.
det.prognosis: Seizure control often improves with time, but intellectual disability and motor impairment remain in most children.
pearls: The same gene can cause either benign neonatal seizures or a severe encephalopathy, depending on the variant.
Neonatal tonic seizures with burst-suppression EEG should prompt early gene testing.
Sodium channel blockers are the drug class to consider first once the diagnosis is known.
det.thd: KCNQ2 developmental and epileptic encephalopathy เกิดจากยีนที่สร้างช่องโพแทสเซียม Kv7.2 ผิดปกติ ทารกจะชักเกร็งในสัปดาห์แรกของชีวิต คลื่นสมองมักเป็น burst-suppression และตามด้วยพัฒนาการล่าช้า การวินิจฉัยใช้การตรวจยีน เมื่อพบแล้วยากลุ่ม sodium channel blocker เช่น carbamazepine หรือ phenytoin มักช่วยลดชักได้ แม้ชักจะดีขึ้นแต่ความพิการทางพัฒนาการมักคงอยู่

qx.q: Which drug class is most often reported to help at this stage?
opts: Benzodiazepines as the sole long-term therapy
ACTH given from the second week of life
Potassium channel openers such as retigabine, which remain widely available
Vigabatrin as first-line treatment
Sodium channel blockers such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine or phenytoin
qx.why: KCNQ2 encephalopathy produces neonatal tonic seizures with a burst-suppression or multifocal EEG, and sodium channel blockers are commonly reported to reduce seizures once the variant is known. Retigabine was withdrawn from the market, and ACTH, vigabatrin and benzodiazepines are not the targeted choice. Seizures often settle by early childhood, but developmental disability usually remains, so families need early counselling.

name: Suprascapular neuropathy
formal: An entrapment or traction mononeuropathy of the suprascapular nerve at the suprascapular or spinoglenoid notch, causing deep posterior shoulder pain with weakness and wasting of supraspinatus and infraspinatus, but no cutaneous sensory loss.
simple: A pinched nerve at the shoulder blade that gives deep shoulder pain and wasting of the muscles on the back of the shoulder.
th: ภาวะเส้นประสาท suprascapular ถูกกดทับหรือถูกดึงรั้ง ทำให้ปวดลึกที่หัวไหล่ด้านหลัง กล้ามเนื้อ supraspinatus และ infraspinatus ลีบอ่อนแรง โดยไม่มีอาการชาที่ผิวหนัง
tempoNote: Pain and weakness develop over weeks to months with repetitive overhead activity or after trauma; compressive cysts give a gradual course
feat: Deep, dull pain along the upper border of the scapula and shoulder, aggravated by cross-body arm movement
Weak shoulder abduction (the first degrees) and external rotation, often less disabling than expected because other muscles compensate
Visible hollowing of the infraspinatus fossa, and of the supraspinatus fossa if the lesion is proximal
No numbness, because the nerve has no skin territory; a distal lesion at the spinoglenoid notch causes painless infraspinatus wasting only
Common in overhead athletes, weight lifters and after large rotator cuff tears
inv: Needle EMG shows denervation and reinnervation in supraspinatus and infraspinatus, with normal deltoid, biceps, triceps and cervical paraspinals
Supraspinatus and infraspinatus motor conduction from Erb's point shows reduced amplitude or delayed latency, if technically feasible
Upper-trunk-related sensory studies (lateral antebrachial cutaneous, median to thumb, radial) are normal, excluding a plexopathy
Shoulder MRI or ultrasound looks for a ganglion cyst at the spinoglenoid notch, a rotator cuff tear or a mass

case.story: For eight months he has had a dull ache behind the left shoulder and noticed that the muscle behind the shoulder blade has shrunk; his bench press is unchanged but overhead lifts feel weaker.
case.exam: Wasting of the left infraspinatus fossa, mild weakness of external rotation, normal deltoid and biceps, no sensory loss, normal neck movement.
case.tests: EMG shows fibrillations and reduced recruitment in left supraspinatus and infraspinatus only; shoulder MRI shows a small paralabral cyst at the spinoglenoid notch.
case.q: Why is there no sensory loss and what is the usual treatment?
case.a: The suprascapular nerve has no cutaneous branch; treat the cause (cyst decompression, activity change and physiotherapy, or surgical release of the notch if conservative care fails).

2. Entrapment Neuropathies of the Upper Extremity

det.patho: The suprascapular nerve leaves the upper trunk of the plexus (C5-C6), passes under the transverse scapular ligament at the suprascapular notch to supply the supraspinatus, and then curves around the spinoglenoid notch to reach the infraspinatus. It carries deep sensory fibres from the shoulder joint, but no skin fibres. Compression at either notch occurs from ganglion cysts, tumours, ligament thickening or repetitive scapular movement, and traction can follow large retracted rotator cuff tears. Weight lifting, volleyball, baseball pitching and certain operative positions are known risk settings.
det.clinical: A proximal lesion at the suprascapular notch causes deep boring pain in the posterior shoulder and weakness of both supraspinatus and infraspinatus. A lesion at the spinoglenoid notch spares the supraspinatus, usually causes little pain and produces isolated infraspinatus wasting. Patients may be surprised by the visible hollow behind the shoulder blade. Weakness of abduction and external rotation can be subtle because the deltoid and teres minor take over.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis combines the pattern of weakness and wasting with needle EMG showing denervation limited to the suprascapular muscles and normal paraspinals, deltoid and biceps. Sensory nerve studies of upper trunk-related nerves should be normal. MRI or ultrasound is used to look for cysts, tumours and rotator cuff pathology, because identifying a compressive lesion changes treatment. Cervical radiculopathy, rotator cuff disease, brachial neuritis and upper trunk plexopathy are the main alternatives.
det.treatment: Conservative care includes rest from provocative activity, scapular stabiliser rehabilitation and treatment of the cause. Compressive ganglion cysts can be aspirated or decompressed arthroscopically, and a retracted rotator cuff tear is repaired. Surgical release of the transverse scapular ligament is considered when pain and weakness persist for months despite conservative care or when a lesion is found. Early referral matters when a mass is detected.
det.prognosis: Most patients improve after the compressive cause is removed or activity is changed, although wasted muscle may recover slowly and incompletely.
pearls: Wasting plus weakness with no sensory loss at the shoulder points to this nerve.
Painless infraspinatus-only wasting suggests a lesion at the spinoglenoid notch, often a ganglion cyst.
A normal EMG of deltoid, biceps and paraspinals separates it from C5 radiculopathy and upper plexopathy.

qx.stem: A 27-year-old volleyball player from Chonburi has a hollow below the spine of her right scapula and weakness of external rotation, but no shoulder pain and no sensory loss. Deltoid, biceps and brachioradialis strength are normal.
qx.q: Which needle EMG pattern best localises the lesion to the spinoglenoid notch?
opts: Denervation in supraspinatus and infraspinatus with normal deltoid
Denervation in the infraspinatus only, with a normal supraspinatus
Denervation in deltoid and teres minor with sparing of infraspinatus
Denervation in supraspinatus, deltoid, biceps and cervical paraspinals
Denervation in serratus anterior and rhomboids
qx.why: The suprascapular nerve passes the suprascapular notch before supplying supraspinatus and then curves around the spinoglenoid notch to infraspinatus, so a distal lesion spares the supraspinatus and is often painless. Involvement of both muscles places the lesion at the proximal notch, deltoid and teres minor are axillary nerve muscles, and findings across deltoid, biceps and paraspinals indicate root or plexus disease.

name: Long thoracic neuropathy
formal: A mononeuropathy of the long thoracic nerve (C5-C7) that paralyses the serratus anterior, causing medial scapular winging that is most obvious on forward elevation of the arm, with shoulder pain at onset in many cases.
simple: Injury to the nerve that holds the shoulder blade against the chest, so the shoulder blade sticks out like a wing when the arm is raised forward.
ab: winged scapula due to serratus palsy
th: ภาวะเส้นประสาท long thoracic เสียหาย ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อ serratus anterior อ่อนแรง กระดูกสะบักยื่นออกทางด้านหลังคล้ายปีกเมื่อยกแขนไปข้างหน้า บางรายมีอาการปวดไหล่นำมาก่อน
tempoNote: Pain over days to weeks, then painless winging; trauma and surgery cause sudden onset, and recovery takes months
feat: Medial scapular winging that worsens when the arms are pushed forward against a wall or raised in front of the body
Difficulty raising the arm above shoulder height, fatigue with overhead tasks, and shoulder or neck-shoulder ache
Isolated serratus anterior weakness, with normal sensation because the nerve has no skin territory
Causes include neuralgic amyotrophy, direct blows, carrying heavy loads on the shoulder, surgery (for example mastectomy or thoracotomy) and sports
Often isolated, but weakness of other C5-C7 muscles points to a wider process
inv: Needle EMG of serratus anterior (inserted over a rib in the mid-axillary line to avoid pneumothorax) shows denervation, with other C5-C7 muscles normal
Biceps, deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, triceps and cervical paraspinals are tested to exclude radiculopathy or plexopathy
Sensory studies of upper and middle trunk nerves are normal in an isolated lesion
MRI of the brachial plexus or shoulder is used if the history suggests brachial neuritis, a mass or trauma

case.who: 34-year-old woman, a nurse from Khon Kaen
case.story: Nine days after a viral illness she had a week of severe right shoulder pain; when the pain eased she noticed her right shoulder blade sticking out and that she could not lift her arm to hang a drip stand.
case.exam: Medial winging of the right scapula, much worse when she pushes against a wall, with normal strength of the biceps and deltoid and no sensory loss.
case.tests: EMG shows active denervation in the right serratus anterior only; cervical spine MRI is normal.
case.q: What is the most likely cause and the prognosis?
case.a: Neuralgic amyotrophy involving the long thoracic nerve; most patients improve over many months with physiotherapy, with scapular stabilisation exercises while waiting.

det.patho: Formed directly by roots C5 to C7 ahead of the plexus proper, the long thoracic nerve runs down the lateral chest wall and supplies a single muscle, the serratus anterior. Its length and superficial position make it vulnerable to traction during sports, direct pressure, heavy carrying and surgery. The commonest medical cause is neuralgic amyotrophy, in which it may be affected alone. Without serratus anterior pull, the scapula is displaced towards the spine, especially during forward elevation.
det.clinical: Many patients first have severe shoulder pain for days or weeks, followed by painless winging that is easy to miss until the patient lifts the arm forward. Overhead reaching is weak, and the shoulder girdle tires quickly. Because the serratus anterior stabilises the scapula, the deltoid and other shoulder muscles may seem weak. Sensation is normal and reflexes are intact.
det.diagnosis: Examination with the patient pushing against a wall or raising the arms forward shows medial winging, which differs from the lateral winging of trapezius weakness. EMG confirms denervation in serratus anterior and must exclude involvement of other C5-C7 muscles and the cervical roots. Needle placement needs care to avoid the pleura. If the history suggests brachial neuritis, plexus imaging and a search for preceding infection or immunisation are reasonable.
det.treatment: Neuralgic amyotrophy is managed with analgesia, early short-course corticosteroid in selected patients and rehabilitation that protects range of motion and trains the scapular stabilisers. Compressive or post-surgical causes need a review of the mechanism, and nerve exploration or transfer is considered for traumatic lesions that do not recover. A scapular brace is sometimes used for comfort. Patients should avoid heavy overhead loading until strength returns.
det.prognosis: Most idiopathic cases recover over six to twenty-four months, while traumatic cases are less predictable.
pearls: Medial winging worsens with forward push; lateral winging from trapezius worsens with abduction.
A painful onset before winging suggests neuralgic amyotrophy.
Insert the EMG needle over the rib, not the interspace, to avoid pneumothorax.

qx.stem: A 30-year-old man from Samut Prakan has painless winging of the left scapula that is worse when he pushes against a wall. Two weeks earlier he had severe shoulder pain for several days. You plan needle EMG of the serratus anterior.
qx.q: Which technique is safest and most reliable?
opts: Insert the needle in the posterior axillary fold directly toward the lung
Sample only the rhomboids as a surrogate for the serratus
Insert at the lateral thoracic wall in an intercostal space to reach the muscle
Avoid needle EMG and rely on the nerve conduction study of the long thoracic nerve alone
Insert over a rib in the mid-axillary line, or beneath the inferior angle of the scapula, avoiding the intercostal space
qx.why: The serratus anterior arises from the ribs, and a needle placed over a rib (mid-axillary line) or under the inferior scapular angle reaches the muscle while protecting the pleura. Entering an intercostal space or aiming at the lung risks pneumothorax. The long thoracic nerve has no routine sensory study, and rhomboids are supplied by a different nerve, so they cannot substitute. Other C5 to C7 muscles are also sampled to exclude plexus or root disease.

name: Spinal accessory neuropathy
formal: A mononeuropathy of cranial nerve XI, most often injured in the posterior cervical triangle during neck surgery or biopsy, causing trapezius weakness with shoulder drop, lateral scapular winging, limited abduction and shoulder pain.
simple: Injury to the nerve that powers the shoulder-shrugging muscle, leaving a drooping shoulder that is painful and hard to lift.
th: ภาวะเส้นประสาท spinal accessory (CN XI) เสียหาย มักเกิดหลังผ่าตัดหรือตัดชิ้นเนื้อบริเวณคอด้านข้าง ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อ trapezius อ่อนแรง ไหล่ตก ยกแขนไม่ขึ้น และปวดไหล่
tempoNote: Sudden after neck surgery or trauma; spontaneous cases and delayed diagnosis are common, and symptoms evolve over months
feat: Drooping of the shoulder with the scapula displaced down and out, and loss of the normal neck-shoulder slope
Weak shoulder abduction above about 90 degrees and impaired shrugging because the trapezius cannot fix the scapula

A proximal lesion also weakens the sternocleidomastoid, reducing head turning to the opposite side

Trapezius motor conduction stimulating at the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid gives a CMAP amplitude compared with the other side
Other shoulder muscles and upper-trunk sensory nerves are tested to exclude plexopathy or radiculopathy
Ultrasound or MRI of the posterior triangle is used when no surgical cause is known

case.who: 52-year-old man, a rubber-plantation owner from Trang
case.story: Four months after excision of a lymph node in the right side of the neck he has noticed that the right shoulder droops, the arm will not go overhead and it aches at night.
case.exam: Right shoulder lower than the left, wasted upper trapezius, lateral winging on abduction, normal serratus pattern on pushing a wall, intact sensation.
case.tests: EMG shows reduced trapezius motor units with active denervation, sternocleidomastoid normal; ultrasound shows scar tissue at the surgical site.
case.q: What is the next step if there is no recovery?
case.a: Early surgical exploration with nerve repair or graft is considered for iatrogenic injury, with shoulder physiotherapy and, if needed, a later tendon transfer such as the Eden-Lange procedure.

13 Cranial Nerve XI (The Spinal Accessory Nerve)

det.patho: The spinal accessory nerve arises from the upper cervical cord (C1-C4), enters the skull through the foramen magnum and leaves again via the jugular foramen. It supplies the sternocleidomastoid and then crosses the posterior cervical triangle just under the skin on its way to the trapezius. That superficial course explains most injuries, which are iatrogenic during lymph node biopsy, neck dissection or cannulation. Nerve loss destabilises the scapula and creates traction on the plexus and, rarely, vascular compression at the thoracic outlet.
det.clinical: Patients have a shoulder that droops and aches, with limited abduction and impaired lifting. Because the weak trapezius also disturbs scapular fixation, other shoulder movements seem weak, and the diagnosis is commonly delayed for months and mistaken for adhesive capsulitis or cervical radiculopathy. With a proximal lesion, the sternocleidomastoid is also weak. Pain and paraesthesia can arise from traction on the plexus.
det.diagnosis: Inspection of shoulder height, trapezius bulk and scapular winging on abduction is key. EMG of the trapezius, in several portions, and of the sternocleidomastoid, with confirmation of needle position by shrugging, shows denervation, and a motor study allows side-to-side comparison. Other shoulder muscles should be normal. Imaging looks for a mass or surgical scar, and cervical or plexus lesions are excluded.
det.treatment: Treatment depends on the cause. Iatrogenic injuries seen early may need exploration and repair, graft or neurotisation, as outcomes are better when done within a few months. Physiotherapy keeps the shoulder mobile and strengthens the remaining shoulder muscles, and analgesia and a shoulder support help pain. If recovery fails, tendon transfers or scapular stabilisation procedures are options.
det.prognosis: Recovery is variable: incomplete after surgical transection, but good in many stretch or compressive injuries.
pearls: Unexplained shoulder pain after a neck operation should prompt examination of the trapezius.
Confirm the EMG needle is in the trapezius by asking the patient to shrug.
Shoulder drop and lateral winging distinguish it from serratus anterior palsy.

qx.stem: A 58-year-old man from Surat Thani developed a drooping right shoulder and pain after a lymph node biopsy in the neck. The upper trapezius looks wasted, and you are concerned that the needle may pass through it into the underlying supraspinatus.
qx.q: How can you confirm that the needle is in the trapezius?
opts: Ask the patient to shrug the shoulder and check that motor units are recruited
Ask the patient to rotate the chin away from the lesion
Stimulate the nerve at Erb's point and watch for a twitch
Ask the patient to push the palm against a wall
Ask the patient to flex the elbow against resistance
qx.why: Shrugging activates the trapezius and the needle should show motor units; if none appear in a severely atrophic muscle, the needle may have passed into a muscle below, which could be misread as normal. Head turning tests the sternocleidomastoid, wall pushing tests the serratus anterior and elbow flexion tests the biceps, so none confirms trapezius placement.

name: Tarsal tunnel syndrome
formal: An entrapment neuropathy of the tibial nerve or its medial plantar, lateral plantar or calcaneal branches beneath the flexor retinaculum behind the medial malleolus, causing burning pain and paraesthesia in the sole and toes with normal ankle reflexes.
simple: A pinched nerve at the inside of the ankle that gives burning, tingling and numbness in the sole of the foot.
ab: posterior tibial neuropathy at the ankle
tibial nerve entrapment at the ankle
th: Tarsal tunnel syndrome คือการที่เส้นประสาท tibial หรือแขนง plantar ถูกกดทับหลังตาตุ่มด้านใน ทำให้ปวดแสบ ชา และเสียวที่ฝ่าเท้าและนิ้วเท้า โดยรีเฟล็กซ์ข้อเท้าปกติ
tempoNote: Gradual burning pain over the sole, worse after walking or standing; sometimes after ankle fracture or sprain
feat: Burning, tingling or numb sole and toes, often worse at night or after long walking
Tinel sign and tenderness behind the medial malleolus, with pain that may spread up the calf
Sensory loss over the sole with sparing of the lateral foot (sural) and dorsum (superficial peroneal), and normal ankle reflex
Intrinsic foot muscle wasting or toe weakness in advanced cases
Causes include ankle fracture, sprain, flat foot deformity, ganglion or varicosity; true cases are uncommon and often over-diagnosed
inv: Bilateral distal tibial motor studies to abductor hallucis and abductor digiti quinti pedis, with side-to-side comparison
Plantar (medial and lateral) mixed or sensory potentials are the most sensitive part of the test, but are technically hard and are often absent in healthy older people
Sural and superficial peroneal sensory responses, together with tibial and peroneal motor conduction and F-wave latencies, exclude a polyneuropathy
Needle EMG of intrinsic foot muscles is hard to interpret; compare with the other side and sample proximal tibial muscles

case.who: 41-year-old woman, a market vendor from Nakhon Pathom
case.story: Four months after a minor right ankle fracture she has persistent burning pain in the right sole, worse when she stands all day.
case.exam: Mild atrophy of intrinsic foot muscles, reduced pinprick and temperature over the sole but intact sensation on the lateral foot and dorsum, normal ankle jerks.
case.tests: Plantar mixed nerve responses are smaller and slower on the right than the left, sural and superficial peroneal responses are normal; ultrasound is normal.
case.q: Why does a normal sural response and ankle reflex matter?
case.a: They place the lesion below the ankle, making polyneuropathy, S1 radiculopathy and a proximal tibial or sciatic lesion less likely.

read.where: 18. FOCAL NEUROPATHIES: NERVE INJURIES, ENTRAPMENTS, AND OTHER MONONEUROPATHIES

det.patho: The tibial nerve passes behind the medial malleolus beneath the flexor retinaculum, where it divides into medial and lateral plantar nerves and gives off calcaneal branches. In this fibro-osseous tunnel it can be compressed by trauma, scar, a flat foot with heel valgus, ganglia, varicose veins or other masses. True idiopathic cases are uncommon, and repetitive overuse seldom causes it, unlike carpal tunnel syndrome. Many patients labelled with this syndrome in fact have a polyneuropathy or a local orthopaedic cause.
det.clinical: Patients describe burning pain, paraesthesia or numbness in the sole, toes or heel, often worse on standing and at night. Symptoms may radiate proximally to the calf. Examination can show a positive Tinel sign over the tunnel and altered sensation in the plantar distribution, with a normal lateral foot and dorsum. The ankle reflex is normal. Foot muscle wasting is a late sign, and is seen in some people without disease.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis combines the clinical picture with electrodiagnosis that compares the symptomatic and normal side: distal motor latencies and amplitudes for the two plantar branches, and plantar sensory or mixed potentials. Because the plantar potentials are tiny and often absent in healthy older people, only a marked difference between the two feet carries weight. Polyneuropathy must be excluded with sural, superficial peroneal and tibial studies, and a tarsal tunnel diagnosis is almost impossible when polyneuropathy is present. Imaging of the tunnel finds masses.
det.treatment: Initial care is activity modification, supportive footwear or orthoses to correct heel valgus, anti-inflammatory measures, neuropathic pain medicines and sometimes a corticosteroid injection. Surgical decompression of the tunnel, including release of the flexor retinaculum, is reserved for confirmed cases with a clear focal cause or persistent disabling symptoms. Results are better when a mass lesion is removed.
det.prognosis: Outcome is good when there is a definite compressive cause and poorer when the diagnosis is uncertain, as the symptoms may come from another disorder.
pearls: A normal ankle reflex and normal lateral foot sensation keep the lesion distal to the ankle.
Do not diagnose tarsal tunnel syndrome from absent plantar potentials alone, particularly in older patients.
Always screen for polyneuropathy before accepting the diagnosis.
det.thd: Tarsal tunnel syndrome เกิดจากเส้นประสาท tibial หรือแขนง medial/lateral plantar ถูกกดที่ใต้ flexor retinaculum หลังตาตุ่มใน ทำให้ปวดแสบและชาที่ฝ่าเท้าและนิ้วเท้า โดยรีเฟล็กซ์ข้อเท้าและความรู้สึกที่ด้านนอกและหลังเท้าปกติ การตรวจนำไฟฟ้าต้องเทียบสองข้าง เพราะศักย์ไฟฟ้า plantar เล็กมากและอาจไม่พบในผู้สูงอายุปกติ ต้องแยก polyneuropathy ก่อนเสมอ รักษาด้วยการปรับรองเท้า ยาลดปวดเส้นประสาท และผ่าตัดเมื่อมีสาเหตุชัดเจน

qx.stem: A 45-year-old woman from Phetchaburi has burning pain and numbness under the right foot for six months after an ankle sprain. Pinprick is reduced over the sole but normal on the lateral foot and dorsum, and both ankle jerks are present. Sural and superficial peroneal sensory responses are normal.
qx.q: Which electrodiagnostic result would best support a tarsal tunnel lesion?
opts: Absent plantar sensory potentials on both sides
Plantar mixed nerve potentials clearly smaller and slower than on the asymptomatic side, with a normal H reflex
Prolonged tibial F-wave latency with fibrillations in the gastrocnemius
Reduced sural amplitude with distal axonal changes in the extensor digitorum brevis

qx.why: Tarsal tunnel syndrome is a distal tibial lesion, so the abnormality should be restricted to the plantar branches, with a clear difference from the other foot and normal sural, superficial peroneal and H-reflex studies. Bilaterally absent plantar potentials are common in healthy older people and are not diagnostic. Abnormal F waves, proximal muscles, the sural response or paraspinal denervation point to proximal tibial, sciatic, polyneuropathy or root disease.
