name: Optic disc drusen
formal: Acellular, often calcified deposits within the optic nerve head, present in up to 2 percent of people and usually bilateral, that elevate the disc margin (pseudopapilloedema), can cause slowly progressive peripheral visual field loss and rarely cause ischaemic complications.
simple: Small chalky deposits inside the optic nerve head that make the disc look swollen even though pressure in the head is normal.
ab: hyaline bodies of the optic disc
th: Optic disc drusen คือก้อนสะสมแคลเซียมในหัวขั้วประสาทตา ทำให้จานประสาทตาดูนูนเหมือนบวมทั้งที่ความดันในกะโหลกปกติ บางรายมีลานสายตาแคบลงช้าๆ
tempoNote: Present from childhood, becoming more visible in the teens; slow progression of field loss over years
feat: Usually asymptomatic, found during routine fundus examination; present in about 2 percent of people and often bilateral
Buried drusen give a lumpy, elevated disc without a cup and with anomalous branching vessels; exposed drusen look like pale pearls
Arcuate or nasal field defects and blind spot enlargement in many, progressing slowly
Transient visual obscurations in some, and occasional acute loss from anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy
Associations include a small crowded disc, retinitis pigmentosa, angioid streaks and Alagille syndrome
inv: Fundus autofluorescence shows drusen as bright foci; ultrasonography B-scan shows calcified high-reflective bodies
Optical coherence tomography with enhanced-depth imaging shows hyporeflective, round or oval structures within the nerve head and thinning of the retinal nerve fibre layer
Visual fields document defects and are used for monitoring
Neuroimaging and lumbar puncture are not needed unless features suggest true papilloedema

case.who: 11-year-old girl from Ayutthaya referred by her school nurse
case.story: A vision check showed slightly blurred peripheral vision in the left eye; she has no headache, vomiting or double vision.
case.exam: Visual acuity 6/6, both discs raised with scalloped margins and no cup, no haemorrhages, venous pulsations absent in the left eye, a slightly enlarged blind spot.
case.tests: B-scan ultrasound shows calcified bodies at both discs; OCT shows nerve fibre layer thinning in the left eye; MRI is normal.
case.q: Does she need a lumbar puncture?
case.a: No; the findings define pseudopapilloedema from optic disc drusen, which needs follow-up of fields and OCT, not investigation for raised intracranial pressure.

read.where: 19. Neuro-ophthalmology - Optic nerve: congenital anomalies (optic disc drusen)
Chapter 18: Differential Diagnosis of Visual Field Deficits at the Bedside

det.patho: Drusen are thought to form from axonal metabolic by-products in a small scleral canal, where axoplasmic transport is impaired and calcium accumulates. They are usually sporadic, and a dominant inheritance with variable penetrance is described in some families. Disc crowding may cause transient vascular compromise. Over time, the nerve fibre layer thins and field defects appear.
det.clinical: Most patients have no symptoms and the problem is found by an optician or a physician who sees a swollen-looking disc. Children often have buried drusen, which become visible by the early teens. Visual field defects, usually inferonasal or arcuate, are present in many and progress slowly, but severe loss of central vision is rare. Complications include peripapillary choroidal neovascularisation, retinal vascular occlusion and anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy.
det.diagnosis: Direct visualisation of exposed drusen, or autofluorescence, B-scan ultrasound and OCT showing buried drusen, establishes the diagnosis. The key clinical task is to separate it from true papilloedema, using the absence of hyperaemia, haemorrhage and venous distension, the presence of a no-cup elevated disc and imaging. Other causes of disc swelling should be considered when symptoms or signs do not fit.
det.treatment: No treatment reverses the deposits. Patients are monitored with fields and OCT every one to two years, and it is reasonable to check intraocular pressure and to avoid unnecessary neurological investigation. Neovascular complications are treated with anti-VEGF injections, and some specialists lower intraocular pressure when fields progress, although evidence is limited. Patients should be told to report sudden vision loss quickly.
det.prognosis: Vision is usually preserved, with slowly progressive peripheral field loss in some.
pearls: A lumpy elevated disc without a cup in a child is drusen until proven otherwise.
Ultrasound B-scan is the quick way to show calcified drusen.
Drusen can coexist with true papilloedema, so judge the picture in clinical context.

name: Diabetic papillopathy
formal: A self-limited, usually mild unilateral or bilateral optic disc swelling in people with diabetes, often younger and with a crowded disc, causing little or no visual loss and resolving over months; it is regarded as a variant of anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy.
simple: Swelling of the optic nerve head in a person with diabetes that usually causes only mild blurring and goes away on its own.
th: Diabetic papillopathy คือจานประสาทตาบวมในผู้ป่วยเบาหวาน มักมองเห็นเบลอเล็กน้อยหรือไม่มีอาการ ส่วนใหญ่หายเองใน 2 ถึง 10 เดือน พบในผู้ป่วยอายุน้อยที่มีจานประสาทตาเล็กและแออัด
tempoNote: Disc swelling appears over days to weeks, persists for weeks, and settles over several months, sometimes leaving mild pallor
feat: Mild painless blurring of vision or an asymptomatic finding on screening
Hyperaemic disc swelling with small telangiectatic vessels on the surface, often bilateral
A small crowded cup in the fellow eye
Visual acuity 6/12 or better in most, and a small relative afferent pupillary defect if asymmetric
Younger diabetic patients, often type 1, and may coexist with diabetic retinopathy
inv: Dilated fundus examination, OCT of the disc and macula and colour photographs to document swelling
Fluorescein angiography shows early disc hyperfluorescence and leakage with telangiectasia
Visual fields show an enlarged blind spot or mild arcuate defects
Blood pressure, glycaemic control and exclusion of raised intracranial pressure (MRI/MRV and lumbar puncture) in bilateral cases

case.who: 23-year-old man with type 1 diabetes for 12 years, from Nonthaburi
case.story: He noticed slight blurring in the right eye for two weeks after intensifying his insulin regimen; there is no pain or eye movement discomfort.
case.exam: Visual acuity 6/9, mild right disc oedema with surface telangiectasia, a crowded cup in the left eye, mild background retinopathy.
case.tests: OCT shows peripapillary retinal thickening; MRI and venography are normal; fields show enlarged blind spot; the swelling resolves over 4 months leaving slight temporal pallor.
case.q: What condition does this resemble and what is the management?
case.a: It resembles anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy but with a benign course; optimise glycaemic control and blood pressure, exclude raised intracranial pressure and follow up without steroids.

det.patho: The pathogenesis is unclear. It is thought to reflect small-vessel disease and chronic hyperglycaemia affecting the optic nerve head perfusion in an anatomically crowded disc, with transient vascular leakage and axonal swelling. It resembles a mild form of anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy. Rapid lowering of glycaemia after long poor control has been associated with some cases.
det.clinical: Patients are often younger than the usual NAION patient and describe mild blurred vision or no symptoms. The disc is hyperaemic and swollen, with fine telangiectatic vessels that can be mistaken for neovascularisation. Bilateral swelling is common, and the fellow disc is often small with a minimal cup. Visual acuity is generally good, and fields show blind spot enlargement or mild defects.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical in a person with diabetes and painless disc swelling after excluding raised intracranial pressure, optic neuritis, infiltration, compressive causes and infection. Bilateral swelling requires neuroimaging and often lumbar puncture. OCT and fluorescein angiography document the swelling and the leakage, and the benign course on follow-up supports the diagnosis. Papillophlebitis and retinal vein occlusion are separated by more extensive retinal haemorrhages.
det.treatment: No treatment is proven. The usual approach is optimisation of glycaemia, blood pressure and lipids, treatment of coexisting retinopathy and observation, with the avoidance of rapid large falls in glucose where possible. Intravitreal anti-VEGF or steroid has been tried in selected cases, but evidence is limited. Patients are reviewed until the swelling resolves.
det.prognosis: Swelling resolves over several months, and vision is 6/12 or better in most, subject to diabetic retinopathy.
pearls: Bilateral disc swelling in a diabetic still needs raised intracranial pressure excluded.
Surface telangiectasia on the swollen disc is a clue and should not be treated as neovascularisation.
The prognosis is much better than in typical NAION.
det.thd: Diabetic papillopathy คือจานประสาทตาบวมในผู้ป่วยเบาหวาน มักไม่เจ็บ การมองเห็นลดเล็กน้อย พบจานประสาทตาบวมแดงมีเส้นเลือดฝอยขยาย มักมีจานประสาทตาอีกข้างเล็กและแออัด ต้องแยกจากสาเหตุอื่น เช่น ความดันในกะโหลกสูง และ optic neuritis โดยเฉพาะเมื่อบวมสองข้าง ไม่มีการรักษาเฉพาะ ควบคุมน้ำตาลและความดันโลหิต และติดตามจนบวมยุบ ซึ่งมักใช้เวลาหลายเดือน

Because the swelling is bilateral, raised intracranial pressure must be excluded with imaging and, if needed, lumbar puncture. The telangiectasia is not neovascularisation, and steroids, laser or surgery are not indicated.

name: Convergence insufficiency
formal: A binocular vergence disorder with a remote near point of convergence and reduced fusional convergence, causing asthenopia, intermittent diplopia and blurred near vision during reading or screen use, which may be primary or follow concussion, Parkinsonian disorders or other neurological disease.
simple: The eyes have trouble turning inward together for close work, so reading causes eye strain, headaches and double or blurred print.
th: Convergence insufficiency คือภาวะที่ตาสองข้างหมุนเข้าหากันเพื่อมองใกล้ได้ไม่ดี ทำให้เมื่อยตา ปวดศีรษะ เห็นภาพซ้อนหรือเบลอเวลาอ่านหนังสือหรือใช้หน้าจอนาน
tempoNote: Symptoms appear after sustained near work and ease with rest; can persist for years if untreated, or begin after head injury
feat: Eye strain, headache and tiredness during reading or screen use that ease with rest
Intermittent horizontal diplopia or blurred print at near, increasingly bothersome by evening
Reduced near point of convergence on examination, with the eye drifting out at near
Poor fusional convergence amplitude on prism testing, and often a normal range of ocular movements
Primary form often affects students; secondary causes include concussion, Parkinson disease, myasthenia, thyroid eye disease and midbrain lesions
inv: Near point of convergence measured with an accommodative target or a ruler; a break beyond about 6 to 10 cm is abnormal
Cover tests at distance and near, and prism-measured fusional convergence amplitudes
Accommodative amplitude and refraction are checked, as accommodative insufficiency often coexists
Neurological assessment and neuroimaging are used only when other signs suggest a structural cause (for example after head injury or with other oculomotor signs)

case.story: Revising for exams, he gets headaches and words 'double up' after about 15 minutes of reading, but he is fine looking across the room.
case.exam: Near point of convergence breaks at 14 cm, exophoria at near, normal eye movements, pupils and fundi.
case.tests: Prism fusional convergence amplitude is low; refraction and accommodation are normal; MRI is not needed.
case.q: What is the first-line treatment?
case.a: Office-based and home vergence exercises (orthoptic exercises) for several weeks, with prisms only if symptoms persist.

read.where: 8 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System

det.patho: Convergence relies on a midbrain and brainstem network that drives medial rectus contraction, accommodation and pupillary constriction (the near triad). In convergence insufficiency the fusional convergence reserve is insufficient to maintain single binocular vision at near, so the visual system either suppresses one image or uses extra effort that results in asthenopia. Prolonged near demand, reduced amplitude after trauma or neurodegeneration, and uncorrected refractive errors all contribute.
det.clinical: Patients describe eye strain, a pulling sensation, headaches, blurred print, words that move or run together, and double vision during near work. Symptoms are absent at distance. The condition is most often noticed in school-age and young adult people with heavy near demands. Examination shows a receded near point and exophoria at near, with normal versions.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis rests on a symptomatic patient with a remote near point of convergence, an exophoria greater at near than at distance and reduced positive fusional vergence. Cycloplegic refraction and accommodation testing are required, since accommodative insufficiency commonly coexists. Neurological causes are sought when onset follows head injury, when there are other brainstem signs, or when the pattern fits myasthenia gravis, Parkinson disease or thyroid eye disease. Divergence insufficiency and sixth nerve palsy are esotropic disorders worth separating.
det.treatment: Vergence exercises are the standard treatment: pencil push-ups and computerised or orthoptic programmes done regularly over several weeks improve both the near point and symptoms. Base-in prisms or small reading glasses are useful when exercises fail or are not tolerated, and any refractive error is corrected. Surgery is rarely indicated. Secondary cases are treated by managing the underlying disease, with vergence training adapted for the situation.
det.prognosis: Most people improve with exercises; symptoms can recur with heavy near work and may need booster training.
pearls: Symptoms with reading but not at distance, plus a remote near point, are the core pattern.
Always check accommodation and refraction, as the two problems often coexist.
New convergence weakness after head injury or in Parkinson disease should prompt a neurological look.
det.thd: Convergence insufficiency คือภาวะที่ตาเข้าหากันขณะมองใกล้ได้ไม่ดี ทำให้ปวดตา ปวดศีรษะ เห็นตัวหนังสือเบลอหรือซ้อนเมื่ออ่านนานๆ ตรวจพบจุดใกล้สุดที่ตา convergence ได้ห่างขึ้นและมี exophoria เวลามองใกล้ รักษาด้วยการฝึกตา (vergence exercises) ใช้ปริซึมเมื่อไม่ดีขึ้น และหากเกิดหลังบาดเจ็บศีรษะหรือมีโรคทางประสาทอื่นร่วมต้องหาสาเหตุ

name: Infantile nystagmus syndrome
formal: A group of early-onset conjugate nystagmus with a pendular or jerk waveform, no oscillopsia, a null zone with a compensatory head posture and dampening on convergence, which may be motor in origin or secondary to poor early vision (sensory) or to a central nervous system disorder.
simple: Constant, regular shaking of both eyes that begins in the first months of life, usually without the child seeing the world as moving.
th: Infantile nystagmus syndrome คือตากระตุกสองข้างที่เริ่มตั้งแต่ช่วงอายุไม่กี่เดือนแรก อาจเกิดจากการเห็นภาพไม่ชัดตั้งแต่เล็กหรือเป็นความผิดปกติของระบบควบคุมตาเอง ผู้ป่วยมักไม่รู้สึกว่าภาพสั่น และมีท่าเอียงหน้าเพื่อให้ตาสั่นน้อยที่สุด
tempoNote: Appears between roughly 2 and 3 months of age, persists through life, and may change slowly in waveform
feat: Onset at about 2 to 3 months of age with horizontal, uniplanar pendular or jerk nystagmus that stays horizontal in upgaze and downgaze
A null point where nystagmus is least, with a compensatory head turn or tilt
Dampening on convergence, worsening with fixation effort and anxiety, absence during sleep, and no oscillopsia
Reduced vision of variable degree, better in the motor form (often 6/12 to 6/36) than in sensory forms
Sensory causes include congenital cataract, albinism, macular hypoplasia, achromatopsia, optic nerve hypoplasia and Leber congenital amaurosis; X-linked motor forms are common
inv: Full ophthalmic examination including dilated fundus, refraction and iris transillumination
Visual electrophysiology (electroretinogram, visual evoked potentials) and OCT of the macula and disc to find retinal and optic nerve causes
MRI brain and orbits when neurological signs are present, the nystagmus is asymmetric, vertical or atypical, or optic nerve or chiasm disease is suspected
Genetic testing, such as FRMD7 for X-linked nystagmus or panels for albinism and retinal dystrophies

case.story: His mother noticed shaking of both eyes since about 10 weeks of age, and he turns his face to the right when looking at toys; his maternal uncle has a similar eye movement.
case.exam: Bilateral horizontal pendular nystagmus that dampens on convergence, a null point in right gaze, normal pupils, no iris transillumination and a normal fundus.
case.tests: ERG normal, OCT shows a normal macula, MRI brain not needed; a FRMD7 variant is found.
case.q: How should this infant be followed up?
case.a: Treat refractive error, monitor vision, discuss head-posture surgery or medication when needed later, and offer genetic counselling given X-linked inheritance.

det.patho: Infantile nystagmus is thought to result from instability of the ocular motor system during the critical period of visual development, either from sensory deprivation that prevents calibration of the gaze-holding network or from a primary defect in the motor control of eye position. Many motor cases are X-linked, with FRMD7 variants common. Dampening with convergence and a null zone reflect partial stabilisation of the control signal. The waveform often has foveation periods that allow acceptable vision.
det.clinical: Parents see regular oscillation of both eyes, usually in the first three months. The nystagmus is conjugate and horizontal, often pendular at first and jerk later, and follows the same direction in vertical gaze. Children do not have oscillopsia and compensate with a head posture. The visual outcome depends on whether a sensory disease is present, and a search for ocular and systemic associations is essential in every new case.
det.diagnosis: Assessment starts with a careful eye-movement recording by observation, then identification of afferent causes by refraction, fundus examination, electrophysiology, OCT and, where appropriate, genetic testing. MRI is reserved for atypical features, such as asymmetry, vertical or see-saw patterns, neurological signs, optic disc abnormalities or an abnormal visual evoked response. Other early-onset eye movement disorders, including spasmus nutans and latent nystagmus, should be distinguished.
det.treatment: Management begins with correcting refractive error with glasses or contact lenses and treating the sensory cause when possible. Prisms or surgery on the extraocular muscles shift the null zone and improve head posture. Medications such as gabapentin, memantine or baclofen are used in some adults, mostly with limited evidence. Families need counselling about vision, school support and inheritance.
det.prognosis: Vision is usually fair in motor forms and variable in sensory forms; the nystagmus persists but may become less disturbing with age.
pearls: Absence of oscillopsia and dampening on convergence are typical of infantile, not acquired, nystagmus.
Every infant with nystagmus needs a retinal and optic nerve search before calling it idiopathic.
Asymmetric, vertical or see-saw nystagmus with neurological features calls for MRI.
det.thd: Infantile nystagmus syndrome คือตากระตุกสองข้างที่เริ่มประมาณ 2 ถึง 3 เดือนหลังเกิด ลักษณะสม่ำเสมอในแนวนอน ลดลงเมื่อตาเข้ามองใกล้ มีจุดนิ่ง (null point) ที่ทำให้เด็กเอียงหน้า และไม่มีอาการภาพสั่น (oscillopsia) ต้องตรวจหาสาเหตุทางตา เช่น ต้อกระจกแต่กำเนิด albinism และ optic nerve hypoplasia การรักษาคือแก้สายตา ใช้ปริซึมหรือผ่าตัดกล้ามเนื้อตาเพื่อลดท่าเอียงหน้า และให้คำปรึกษาด้านพันธุกรรม

qx.stem: A mother brings her 4-month-old son from Buriram because both eyes have shaken since he was about ten weeks old. He turns his face to the right to look at toys. The movement is horizontal, remains horizontal in upgaze, lessens when he converges and stops in sleep. The fundi and pupils are normal.
qx.q: Which feature of this nystagmus is most typical of the infantile form?
opts: Oscillopsia reported by older children
Torsional beats that fatigue
Pure downbeat nystagmus in primary gaze
Direction that changes with the direction of gaze
A null zone with compensatory head posture, dampening on convergence and no oscillopsia
qx.why: Infantile nystagmus is conjugate, usually horizontal and uniplanar, has a null point with a head turn, dampens on convergence and disappears in sleep, and patients do not experience oscillopsia. Gaze-evoked direction change, vertical downbeat and torsional patterns suggest acquired or central disease. Even so, retinal and optic nerve causes (albinism, achromatopsia, optic nerve hypoplasia, congenital cataract) need to be excluded, with MRI when atypical features appear.

name: Leukoencephalopathy with brainstem and spinal cord involvement and lactate elevation (LBSL)
formal: An autosomal recessive leukoencephalopathy caused by biallelic DARS2 variants (mitochondrial aspartyl-tRNA synthetase), presenting in childhood or adulthood with slowly progressive spastic ataxia, dorsal column sensory loss and sometimes cognitive change, with MRI white matter, dorsal column, pyramidal tract and cerebellar involvement and raised lactate on MR spectroscopy.
simple: A rare inherited disease in which the brain's white matter, parts of the brainstem and spinal cord slowly break down, causing stiff, unsteady legs and loss of position sense.
ab: Leukoencephalopathy with brainstem and spinal cord involvement and lactate elevation
leukoencephalopathy with brain stem and spinal cord involvement
th: LBSL เป็นโรคเนื้อขาวสมองเสื่อมถ่ายทอดแบบยีนด้อยจากยีน DARS2 ผู้ป่วยมีการเดินเซแบบเกร็ง สูญเสียการรับรู้ตำแหน่งข้อต่อ และ MRI พบความผิดปกติของ white matter, brainstem และไขสันหลัง ร่วมกับ lactate สูงใน MR spectroscopy
tempoNote: Onset in childhood or early adulthood with slowly progressive gait disorder over years; adult cases may be mild
feat: Progressive spastic ataxia with leg stiffness and gait unsteadiness, usually beginning in childhood or early adulthood
Impaired vibration and position sensing in the feet from dorsal column involvement
Bulbar dysfunction with dysarthria and dysphagia in some, and palatal myoclonus is suggestive when present
Cognition often preserved; some adults develop cognitive decline, neuropathy or seizures
Extremely variable severity, including near-normal adults found because of MRI
inv: MRI shows symmetric periventricular and deep white matter signal change, with selective involvement of the pyramidal tracts, medial lemniscus, trigeminal tracts, cerebellar peduncles and deep cerebellar white matter, and spinal cord dorsal column and lateral corticospinal tract signal
MR spectroscopy shows an elevated lactate peak in affected white matter
DARS2 gene sequencing confirms the diagnosis, typically compound heterozygous with an intron 2 splicing variant in many patients
Serum and urine lactate may be mildly raised in some, and nerve conduction studies are used if neuropathy is suspected

case.story: Since adolescence she has had stiff legs and clumsy walking that has slowly progressed; she cannot feel her feet in the dark and has needed a stick for the past year.
case.exam: Spastic paraparesis with brisk reflexes and extensor plantars, loss of vibration and joint position in the legs, mild cerebellar dysarthria, normal cognition.
case.tests: MRI shows symmetric periventricular white matter change with brainstem pyramidal and lemniscal tract signal and dorsal column signal in the cervical cord; spectroscopy shows lactate; DARS2 sequencing finds two pathogenic variants.
case.q: What is the genetic mechanism and counselling point?
case.a: Autosomal recessive DARS2 deficiency of a mitochondrial tRNA synthetase; siblings have a 25 percent risk, and management is supportive with spasticity therapy, rehabilitation and swallowing care.

det.patho: DARS2 encodes the mitochondrial aspartyl-tRNA synthetase that attaches aspartate to its tRNA for mitochondrial protein synthesis. Biallelic hypomorphic variants, frequently one splicing variant that retains some activity, impair mitochondrial translation selectively in the tissues affected, even though the enzyme is ubiquitous. The reason for the preference for pyramidal tracts, dorsal columns and cerebellar connections is not fully known. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
det.clinical: Most patients present in late childhood to early adulthood with slowly progressive spastic gait, ataxia and impaired vibration sense, and sometimes dysarthria. Many keep normal cognition for years. Later features include neuropathy, cognitive decline, seizures and, rarely, bulbar failure. The phenotype is wide, and adult-onset or mild cases are now identified because of widespread MRI and exome sequencing.
det.diagnosis: MRI pattern recognition is central: involvement of the periventricular and deep white matter, the pyramidal tracts, medial lemniscus, trigeminal tract, cerebellar peduncles, deep cerebellar white matter and spinal cord, with lactate on MR spectroscopy. Sequencing of DARS2 confirms the diagnosis. Diagnostic criteria based on clinical, imaging and genetic features exist. Hereditary spastic paraplegia, multiple sclerosis, Alexander disease and other adult leukodystrophies are the main mimics.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying therapy. Management is supportive: antispastic drugs such as baclofen or tizanidine, botulinum toxin for focal spasticity, physiotherapy, orthoses and swallowing and speech therapy. Seizures are treated with standard antiseizure medicines, avoiding valproate where mitochondrial disease is suspected. Genetic counselling for the family and attention to bladder and bowel symptoms are part of care.
det.prognosis: Disease progression is slow in many; some patients lose independent walking in adulthood while others remain stable.
pearls: Spastic ataxia with dorsal column loss and a distinctive MRI of white matter plus brainstem and cord tracts suggests DARS2 disease.
MR spectroscopy lactate supports the diagnosis even when blood lactate is normal.
Look for compound heterozygosity with an intron 2 splice variant.
det.thd: LBSL เกิดจากความผิดปกติของยีน DARS2 ซึ่งทำหน้าที่ใน mitochondrial translation ผู้ป่วยมักเริ่มมีอาการในวัยเด็กถึงผู้ใหญ่ตอนต้น มีขาเกร็ง เดินเซ และสูญเสียการรับรู้การสั่นสะเทือนและตำแหน่งข้อต่อ MRI พบความผิดปกติของ white matter, brainstem และไขสันหลังเป็นแบบเฉพาะ และ MR spectroscopy พบ lactate สูง ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคองและให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

qx.stem: A 24-year-old woman from Phayao has slowly progressive stiff legs and loss of position sense in the feet since age 15, with normal cognition. MRI shows symmetric white matter change with signal in the pyramidal tracts, medial lemnisci, cerebellar peduncles and the dorsal columns of the cervical cord. MR spectroscopy shows a lactate peak.
qx.q: Which gene is most likely responsible?
opts: DARS2
LMNB1
GFAP
ABCD1
ARSA
qx.why: Selective brainstem, cerebellar and spinal cord tract involvement with white matter change and lactate on spectroscopy is the pattern of LBSL, an autosomal recessive disease due to DARS2 (mitochondrial aspartyl-tRNA synthetase). LMNB1 duplication causes adult-onset dominant leukodystrophy with autonomic failure, GFAP variants cause Alexander disease, ABCD1 causes X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy and ARSA causes metachromatic leukodystrophy.

name: Leukoencephalopathy with calcifications and cysts (Labrune syndrome)
formal: A rare autosomal recessive cerebral microangiopathy caused by biallelic SNORD118 variants, producing a leukoencephalopathy with intracranial calcifications, enhancing parenchymal cysts and a tendency to progressive neurological decline, usually presenting in childhood or young adulthood.
simple: A rare inherited brain small-vessel disease that causes white matter damage, calcium deposits and fluid-filled cysts in the brain.
ab: cerebroretinal microangiopathy with calcifications and cysts
th: Labrune syndrome หรือ leukoencephalopathy with calcifications and cysts เกิดจากยีน SNORD118 ผิดปกติ ทำให้หลอดเลือดฝอยในสมองเสียหาย พบ white matter ผิดปกติ หินปูนในสมอง และถุงน้ำที่มี enhancement ผู้ป่วยอาจมีชัก ท่าเดินผิดปกติ และสติปัญญาถดถอย
tempoNote: Slowly progressive course over years with possible subacute deterioration when cysts expand or bleed
feat: Onset from infancy to adulthood, most often in childhood or the young adult years
Seizures, headaches, pyramidal signs, ataxia and dystonia, with cognitive and motor decline
Asymmetric lesions that may enhance and look like tumours or inflammatory masses
Intracranial calcifications on CT, often in the thalamus, basal ganglia and subcortical white matter, with multiple cysts
Retinal vasculopathy is variable, and the disorder is considered distinct from Coats plus syndrome
inv: CT shows symmetric or asymmetric calcifications that MRI may not show well
MRI shows diffuse white matter T2 or FLAIR hyperintensity, cysts, contrast-enhancing foci and susceptibility artefacts from calcification
Genetic testing finds biallelic SNORD118 variants (a small nucleolar RNA gene, sometimes missed by standard panels)
Fundus examination and blood tests are done to exclude Coats plus, infection and calcium disorders

case.story: He had seizures from age 18 and now has progressive clumsiness; a CT scan done after a new seizure shows calcified spots and a cyst in the right frontal lobe.
case.exam: Mild spastic gait, dystonic posture of the left arm and slowed thinking; fundi are normal.
case.tests: MRI shows asymmetric white matter change, a cystic frontal lesion with enhancing foci and basal ganglia and thalamic calcifications; exome sequencing reveals two SNORD118 variants.
case.q: What is the likely mechanism and how is it treated?
case.a: A SNORD118-related cerebral microangiopathy; treatment is supportive, with antiseizure medicines and consideration of bevacizumab or surgical drainage for symptomatic expanding cysts.

det.patho: SNORD118 encodes the U8 small nucleolar RNA, required for ribosome biogenesis and the maturation of ribosomal RNA. Biallelic loss of function leads to a cerebral microangiopathy with vascular calcification, leakage, and cystic and white matter damage. Why the brain vasculature is especially affected is unclear, and the disorder is autosomal recessive.
det.clinical: Children or young adults present with seizures, headaches, gait disturbance, dystonia and cognitive regression, often over years. Some have an episode of sudden deterioration associated with cyst growth or haemorrhage. Systemic features may include anaemia, gastrointestinal bleeding or hair and nail changes in related Coats plus syndrome, while the brain-restricted syndrome has little outside the nervous system. Penetrance and phenotype vary within families.
det.diagnosis: CT detects calcifications that MRI under-represents, and MRI shows leukoencephalopathy with cysts and enhancing foci. Genetic confirmation requires sequencing of SNORD118, which may not be included on all exome analyses and so should be requested specifically. Brain biopsy is rarely needed. Calcium, parathyroid, infectious and inflammatory causes, tumours and other calcifying leukoencephalopathies must be considered.
det.treatment: No cure exists. Seizures, spasticity and dystonia are treated symptomatically. For symptomatic enlarging cysts, case series have reported benefit from stereotactic drainage and from anti-VEGF therapy with bevacizumab, which reduces leakage. Genetic counselling should be offered, and families should be supported through a complex, variable condition.
det.prognosis: The course ranges from slow progression to severe disability, with early bleeding or cyst expansion as risks.
pearls: Calcifications plus cysts plus enhancing lesions in a young person suggests this rather than a tumour.
Request SNORD118 specifically when exome is negative, as noncoding genes can be missed.
Bevacizumab has been reported to shrink enhancing lesions in selected patients.
det.thd: Labrune syndrome (LCC) เกิดจากความผิดปกติของยีน SNORD118 ถ่ายทอดแบบยีนด้อย ทำให้หลอดเลือดฝอยในสมองผิดปกติ พบ white matter เสื่อม หินปูนในสมอง และถุงน้ำที่ enhance ได้ ผู้ป่วยอาจมีชัก ขาเกร็ง ท่าทางผิดปกติ และความจำถดถอย CT เห็นหินปูนชัดกว่า MRI การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง บางรายที่ถุงน้ำโตอาจใช้ bevacizumab หรือระบายถุงน้ำตามดุลยพินิจของผู้เชี่ยวชาญ

PLP1

name: L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria
formal: An autosomal recessive neurometabolic disorder due to L2HGDH variants in which L-2-hydroxyglutarate accumulates in body fluids, causing slowly progressive developmental delay, cerebellar ataxia, seizures and macrocephaly with subcortical-predominant leukoencephalopathy and signal change in the dentate nuclei and basal ganglia.
simple: A rare inherited metabolic disease in which a chemical builds up in the brain, causing slow development, unsteadiness, fits and a large head.
th: L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria เป็นโรคเมแทบอลิกถ่ายทอดแบบยีนด้อยจากยีน L2HGDH ทำให้ L-2-hydroxyglutarate คั่งในร่างกาย ผู้ป่วยมีพัฒนาการล่าช้า เดินเซ ชัก ศีรษะโต และ MRI พบเนื้อขาวใต้เปลือกสมองผิดปกติร่วมกับ dentate nucleus
tempoNote: Early or static developmental delay, then slow cerebellar and cognitive decline over years; some adults present late
feat: Mild early delay of milestones, then progressive cerebellar ataxia and intellectual disability, appearing in infancy to adolescence
Seizures in many patients and macrocephaly in a large share
Extrapyramidal signs such as dystonia and chorea may appear later
Rarely, hearing loss and an association with brain tumours (medulloblastoma or glioma) have been reported
Some patients appear asymptomatic or have a static encephalopathy for a long time
inv: Urine organic acids show a high L-2-hydroxyglutaric acid, and the chiral analysis confirms the L-isomer; plasma and CSF levels are raised
MRI shows subcortical white matter T2 or FLAIR hyperintensity, initially focal and then confluent, with periventricular sparing; globus pallidus, caudate, putamen and dentate nuclei signal change
L2HGDH gene sequencing confirms the diagnosis
Serial MRI and development assessments to monitor progression, and surveillance for brain tumours has been advised in some programmes

case.story: His speech and walking were mildly delayed, and for two years he has been progressively unsteady; he had two generalised seizures and his head circumference is on the 98th percentile.
case.exam: Cerebellar ataxia, intention tremor, moderate intellectual disability, no spasticity.
case.tests: MRI shows subcortical white matter hyperintensity with sparing of the periventricular region and signal change in the dentate nuclei and globus pallidus; urine organic acids reveal L-2-hydroxyglutaric acid; L2HGDH has two pathogenic variants.
case.q: Which urine test establishes the diagnosis and what should be avoided in the work-up?
case.a: Urine organic acids with chiral analysis for L-2-hydroxyglutarate; do not rely on total 2-hydroxyglutarate alone, since the D-isomer represents separate disorders.

det.patho: L2HGDH encodes the mitochondrial L-2-hydroxyglutarate dehydrogenase, which converts L-2-hydroxyglutarate to alpha-ketoglutarate. L-2-hydroxyglutarate is a metabolite of damage repair, formed by promiscuous enzyme activity, and when it accumulates it is toxic, possibly by epigenetic and mitochondrial effects. The condition is autosomal recessive. The link with brain tumours is thought to relate to the oncometabolite properties of 2-hydroxyglutarate.
det.clinical: Children appear normal in the first months or have mild delay, and then slowly develop cerebellar signs, intellectual disability and often seizures. Macrocephaly is frequent. Disease course is highly variable, and adults with milder disease are described. Extrapyramidal features may emerge with time.
det.diagnosis: Urine organic acid analysis with chiral separation demonstrating L-2-hydroxyglutaric acid is the key test, and levels can be checked in plasma and CSF. MRI pattern, with subcortical white matter and dentate nuclei involvement and periventricular sparing, supports the diagnosis. L2HGDH sequencing confirms it and allows family counselling.
det.treatment: No specific treatment is proven. Supportive care includes antiseizure medicines, physiotherapy, education support and treatment of movement disorders. Riboflavin and L-carnitine have been used empirically in some patients without reliable evidence. Because of a reported tumour risk, some centres follow children with periodic MRI, and families should be told to report new neurological changes.
det.prognosis: The course is slowly progressive with variable severity, and survival into adulthood is common.
pearls: Cerebellar ataxia with macrocephaly and subcortical leukoencephalopathy should lead to urine organic acids.
The L- and D- forms are different diseases, so chiral analysis matters.
Dentate nucleus signal change is a useful MRI clue.
det.thd: L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria เกิดจากเอนไซม์ L2HGDH บกพร่อง ทำให้ L-2-hydroxyglutarate คั่งในร่างกาย ผู้ป่วยมีพัฒนาการช้า เดินเซ ชัก และศีรษะโต MRI พบเนื้อขาวใต้เปลือกสมองผิดปกติเว้นรอบโพรงสมอง และ dentate nucleus ผิดปกติ ตรวจปัสสาวะหา organic acids แบบแยกไอโซเมอร์ และยืนยันด้วยยีน L2HGDH การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง และบางศูนย์ติดตามด้วย MRI เพราะอาจเกิดเนื้องอกสมอง

qx.stem: A 10-year-old boy from Udon Thani has mild speech delay, progressive cerebellar ataxia, two seizures and a head circumference at the 98th percentile. name: CSF HIV escape
formal: A neurological syndrome in people living with HIV on antiretroviral therapy, in which HIV RNA is detectable in CSF despite suppressed plasma viral load, or exceeds plasma RNA by more than one log, with new or progressive cognitive, motor or sensory deficits, CSF pleocytosis or raised protein and white matter change on MRI.
simple: The virus hides in the brain fluid and keeps replicating even though blood tests show HIV is under control, causing new brain or nerve symptoms.
th: CSF HIV escape คือภาวะที่ตรวจพบ HIV RNA ในน้ำไขสันหลังทั้งที่ viral load ในเลือดควบคุมได้ด้วยยาต้านไวรัส ผู้ป่วยมีอาการทางระบบประสาทใหม่หรือแย่ลง เช่น ความคิดช้า เดินเซ อ่อนแรง หรือชา และ MRI พบ white matter ผิดปกติ
tempoNote: Symptoms usually evolve over weeks to a few months in patients with long-treated HIV; a few present acutely
feat: New cognitive slowing, memory or attention problems, gait disturbance, weakness, ataxia or sensory symptoms in a person with HIV who is on ART with controlled blood viral load
Subacute onset and progression over weeks to months, with variable severity and sometimes a history of very low nadir CD4 count
Often treated for years on a regimen that includes protease inhibitors, with possible drug resistance in the CSF virus
CD4 count is relatively preserved at presentation
Other opportunistic or non-HIV causes of encephalopathy are absent
inv: Paired CSF and plasma HIV RNA: CSF RNA detectable with plasma below 50 copies/mL, or CSF more than 1 log above plasma
CSF shows mild pleocytosis or raised protein in most; CSF neopterin is raised; CSF cultures, PCR for JC virus, EBV, CMV, cryptococcal antigen and syphilis serology exclude other causes
MRI shows diffuse or patchy T2/FLAIR white matter hyperintensity, sometimes focal lesions, in most patients
HIV genotypic resistance testing on CSF virus when RNA is high enough, to guide regimen change

case.who: 49-year-old man in Chiang Rai, HIV positive for 17 years
case.story: He has been on a boosted protease inhibitor regimen with undetectable plasma HIV RNA for two years, but over 6 weeks has become forgetful, slow and unsteady on stairs.
case.exam: Slowed thinking, impaired attention and recall, mild gait ataxia, brisk reflexes, no fever or neck stiffness.
case.tests: CD4 540, plasma HIV RNA below 50; CSF protein 98 mg/dL, 12 cells, HIV RNA 3,500 copies/mL, negative for JC virus, cryptococcus and syphilis; MRI shows diffuse white matter hyperintensity.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the key management step?
case.a: CSF HIV escape; check CSF genotype and revise the antiretroviral regimen to agents with good activity and CNS exposure, then repeat CSF RNA.

det.patho: Within the central nervous system, HIV can replicate in a compartment with different drug penetration and immune pressure. In some people on ART, CNS-adapted virus or drug-resistant virus replicates in the CSF while plasma stays suppressed, driving inflammation and white matter injury. A history of very low CD4 nadir and prior CNS infection may predispose. The syndrome may also reflect poor CNS penetration of the regimen or partial adherence.
det.clinical: Patients present with a subacute decline in thinking, gait or motor function, and some have sensory complaints. Examination may show psychomotor slowing, ataxia, pyramidal signs and neuropathy. Because plasma viral load is controlled and the CD4 count is acceptable, the diagnosis is easy to miss and is often attributed to ageing, depression or drug toxicity. Prompt recognition matters because the condition is potentially reversible.
det.diagnosis: The core definition is discordance between CSF and plasma HIV RNA, with detectable CSF RNA when plasma is below 50 copies/mL, or CSF exceeding plasma by more than 1 log, in a patient with compatible neurological findings. CSF abnormalities, raised neopterin and an MRI with diffuse white matter change support the diagnosis. Other causes of encephalopathy, such as infection, syphilis, lymphoma, medications, metabolic problems and CD8 encephalitis, are excluded. CSF genotyping, where available, informs treatment.
det.treatment: Treatment is optimisation of antiretroviral therapy based on prior resistance data, CSF genotype and drugs with good CNS activity, together with adherence support. In the case series, most patients improved clinically after regimen change, and CSF RNA fell on repeat testing. Corticosteroids are considered only for coexisting immune reconstitution or CD8 encephalitis under specialist advice. Follow-up includes repeat CSF HIV RNA and MRI.
det.prognosis: Most patients improve after regimen optimisation, though MRI changes can lag clinical recovery, and some do not respond.
pearls: Always pair CSF HIV RNA with plasma RNA drawn at the same time.
New neurological decline despite undetectable blood viral load is CSF escape until proven otherwise.
Exclude opportunistic infections and CD8 encephalitis before changing therapy.
det.thd: CSF HIV escape พบในผู้ป่วย HIV ที่กินยาต้านไวรัสและ viral load ในเลือดต่ำมาก แต่ตรวจน้ำไขสันหลังพบ HIV RNA สูงกว่าในเลือดอย่างชัดเจน ผู้ป่วยมีอาการทางสมองหรือเส้นประสาทใหม่ เช่น คิดช้า เดินเซ อ่อนแรง การวินิจฉัยต้องตรวจน้ำไขสันหลังคู่กับเลือด ตัดการติดเชื้อฉวยโอกาสอื่น และพิจารณาตรวจ genotype ในน้ำไขสันหลัง การรักษาคือปรับสูตรยาต้านไวรัสให้ครอบคลุมเชื้อดื้อยาและเข้าสู่ระบบประสาทได้ดี ผู้ป่วยส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้น

Over six weeks he has become slow and unsteady. CSF shows 14 cells, protein 100 mg/dL and negative testing for JC virus, cryptococcus and syphilis.
qx.q: Which CSF result would establish CSF viral escape?
opts: CSF HIV RNA detectable (for example 3,000 copies/mL) while plasma RNA is below 50 copies/mL, or at least 1 log higher in CSF than in plasma
CSF HIV RNA undetectable with an elevated protein
CSF white cell count above 5 with no virus detected
CSF HIV antibody positive
CSF neopterin normal

A raised protein or pleocytosis is common but not diagnostic, CSF antibodies are positive in any chronic HIV infection, and CSF neopterin is typically raised in this condition.

qx.q: What is the best management step?

Continuing the same regimen allows ongoing replication, steroids do not treat the virus, and stopping treatment risks systemic rebound and further CNS injury. Intrathecal chemotherapy has no role.

name: Subclinical thyroid dysfunction and cognitive impairment
formal: Cognitive complaints or measurable deficits in people with an abnormal TSH and normal free thyroid hormones; evidence links subclinical hypothyroidism to cognitive decline mainly in people younger than about 75 with higher TSH, and subclinical hyperthyroidism to higher dementia risk, but causality and benefit from treatment remain uncertain.
simple: Mild thyroid hormone imbalance, with a normal T4 but abnormal TSH, that may contribute to forgetfulness or slowed thinking in some people.
th: ภาวะต่อมไทรอยด์ผิดปกติแบบ subclinical (TSH ผิดปกติแต่ free T4 ปกติ) อาจสัมพันธ์กับความจำและสมาธิบกพร่อง โดย subclinical hypothyroidism มีความสัมพันธ์ชัดในคนอายุน้อยกว่า 75 ปีที่ TSH สูง ส่วน subclinical hyperthyroidism อาจเพิ่มความเสี่ยงสมองเสื่อม
tempoNote: Mild stable or slowly progressive cognitive complaints over months to years; most subclinical states are discovered by blood testing
feat: Mild difficulty with attention, concentration, memory or processing speed, often with tiredness or low mood
Subclinical hypothyroidism: TSH raised, free T4 normal, with annual progression to overt disease of a few percent
Subclinical hyperthyroidism: TSH suppressed, free T4 and T3 normal, with risk of atrial fibrillation and bone loss in older people
Overt thyroid disease causes the clearer cognitive syndromes, with apathy, slowing and psychosis (myxoedema madness) in hypothyroidism or restlessness and poor attention in hyperthyroidism
Data on cognition are mixed, so thyroid status is one of several contributing factors
inv: Retest TSH with free T4 about two to three months later to confirm persistence, and exclude recovery from non-thyroidal illness or thyroiditis and drug effects (amiodarone, lithium)
Anti-TPO antibodies to assess autoimmune thyroid disease and the risk of progression
Standard dementia work-up (B12, glucose, calcium, depression screen, brain MRI) to look for other causes
Cognitive screening or neuropsychological testing before and after any treatment to judge effect

case.story: She complains of slower thinking and trouble concentrating at work for a year; her TSH is 11 mIU/L with normal free T4 on two checks 3 months apart.
case.exam: Normal general neurological examination, MoCA 25/30 with lowered attention and delayed recall, mild dry skin.
case.tests: Anti-TPO positive; B12, glucose and calcium are normal; MRI shows mild white matter change only.
case.q: Should levothyroxine be started and what should be expected?
case.a: A trial of levothyroxine is reasonable at this age with TSH of 10 or more, but it may not restore cognition, so other contributors (mood, sleep, vascular risk) should still be addressed.

det.patho: Thyroid hormones act on receptors throughout the brain, including the hippocampus, affecting synaptic plasticity, cholinergic signalling, glucose metabolism and cerebral blood flow. Overt hypothyroidism is linked in experiments to tau phosphorylation and reduced hippocampal plasticity, and hyperthyroidism to vascular effects such as atrial fibrillation and to neuronal injury. Whether the mild changes in subclinical disease cause cognitive impairment is uncertain, and associations may reflect shared vascular risk and age.
det.clinical: Patients may complain of mental slowing, poor concentration and fatigue, which are non-specific and often put down to depression. Overt hypothyroidism may cause apathy, somnolence, confusion and psychosis, while hyperthyroidism causes anxiety, irritability and poor attention, with apathetic presentations in older people. Subclinical states are typically found by testing and may be asymptomatic. Cardiac risk, bone loss and lipid changes are other consequences.
det.diagnosis: Subclinical disease is defined biochemically by an abnormal TSH with normal free T4, confirmed by repeat testing after 2 to 3 months to exclude transient causes. Anti-TPO antibodies identify autoimmune disease. A cognitive evaluation should look for other causes of impairment, including depression, vitamin B12 deficiency, sleep apnoea, medications and neurodegenerative or vascular disease. Pooled studies show the link between a raised TSH and poorer cognition mainly in those below 75 years, and in those with the higher TSH values.
det.treatment: Treatment follows thyroid guidelines. In subclinical hypothyroidism, levothyroxine is generally advised for people up to about 70 with TSH of 10 or more, or with symptoms and positive antibodies, and monitoring alone is acceptable for mild elevations, especially in older adults. In subclinical hyperthyroidism, treatment is recommended for people aged 65 and older, postmenopausal women and those with TSH of 0.1 or less, according to cause and cardiovascular risk. Cognitive benefit from treatment is unproven, so cognitive problems should still receive a full evaluation.
det.prognosis: Many subclinical abnormalities remain stable or normalise, and cognitive outcome mostly depends on other brain and vascular factors.
pearls: Always repeat an abnormal TSH after a few months before diagnosing subclinical disease.
Check thyroid function in every cognitive work-up, but do not expect levothyroxine to reverse dementia.
Look for amiodarone, lithium and recovery from illness as causes of transient TSH changes.

name: IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura), neurological involvement
formal: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis (IgA vasculitis, formerly Henoch–Schönlein purpura) that affects skin, gut, joints and kidneys, and rarely the nervous system, causing headache, seizures, encephalopathy (often as PRES), focal ischaemic or haemorrhagic lesions, or neuropathy.
simple: A small-blood-vessel inflammation, mostly in children with a purple rash, belly pain and kidney problems, that can occasionally affect the brain or nerves.

Neurological involvement in a small minority: headache, seizures, confusion and visual disturbance

Infarcts, intracerebral haemorrhage, chorea, cerebral venous thrombosis or Guillain-Barré-like and mononeuropathies are rarely described
Uraemia, hypertension, electrolyte disturbance and steroid use are common contributors to central symptoms

det.patho: IgA vasculitis is an immune-complex disorder in which galactose-deficient IgA1 forms circulating complexes that deposit in small vessels of skin, gut, joints and glomeruli. Neurological involvement is uncommon and mostly secondary to hypertension, uraemia, electrolyte changes or medications, so PRES is the commonest central pattern. Direct cerebral vasculitis is rare. Peripheral nerve involvement can occur through vasculitis of vasa nervorum.
det.clinical: Most children have a self-limited illness with palpable purpura, colicky abdominal pain and joint swelling, and one third to half have renal involvement. A few develop headache, seizures, altered consciousness, visual loss, hemiparesis, chorea or cranial nerve palsy. Peripheral neuropathies, including Guillain-Barré-like illnesses, are reported. Intestinal complications such as intussusception are the main non-neurological emergency.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical (EULAR/PRINTO/PReS criteria: palpable purpura with abdominal pain, arthritis or arthralgia, renal involvement or typical IgA deposits on biopsy). In a patient with neurological signs, urgent blood pressure measurement and renal assessment are essential, followed by MRI with diffusion and venous imaging, EEG, and exclusion of infection, metabolic disturbance and other vasculitides. CSF is usually non-specific, and brain biopsy is rarely required.
det.treatment: Most neurological events relate to hypertension, so control of blood pressure, treatment of seizures and correction of renal and electrolyte problems come first. Systemic glucocorticoids, sometimes with cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate or rituximab, are used for severe vasculitis and for significant nephritis according to nephrology and rheumatology advice. Antithrombotic therapy is chosen only for proven thrombosis. A paediatric nephrologist should follow renal outcome long term.
det.prognosis: Neurological involvement usually resolves, especially PRES, but residual deficits can follow haemorrhage or infarction, and long-term outcome mostly depends on kidney disease.
pearls: In IgA vasculitis, new headache or seizure should prompt checking blood pressure and kidney function first.
PRES is the most frequent central complication.
Neuropathy and Guillain-Barré-like presentations are rare but recognised.

name: Hypertrophic olivary degeneration (HOD)
formal: A form of transneuronal degeneration in which the inferior olivary nucleus enlarges, rather than shrinks, after a lesion interrupts its input within the dentato-rubro-olivary pathway (the Guillain–Mollaret triangle, made up of the opposite dentate nucleus, the red nucleus and the central tegmental tract on the same side); it appears on MRI as a non-enhancing T2/FLAIR-hyperintense, enlarged olive in the medulla weeks to months after the causative brainstem or cerebellar lesion, and is classically linked to symptomatic palatal tremor, with oculopalatal tremor and Holmes tremor as other associated movement disorders.
simple: A delayed effect of damage elsewhere in the brainstem or cerebellum. Weeks to months later, a small nucleus at the front of the medulla (the inferior olive) swells and lights up on MRI. Many people have no symptoms; some develop rhythmic flickering of the soft palate, wobbling eyes or a slow, large tremor of the arm.
th: Hypertrophic olivary degeneration คือภาวะที่ inferior olivary nucleus ที่ medulla บวมโตและสว่างขึ้นบน MRI T2/FLAIR โดยไม่ติดสารทึบรังสี เกิดหลังมีรอยโรคที่ตัดการเชื่อมต่อใน Guillain–Mollaret triangle (dentate nucleus ฝั่งตรงข้าม red nucleus และ central tegmental tract ฝั่งเดียวกัน) มักเกิดหลังรอยโรคหลายสัปดาห์ถึงหลายเดือน และอาจแสดงเป็น palatal tremor, oculopalatal tremor หรือ Holmes tremor แต่ผู้ป่วยจำนวนมากไม่มีอาการ
tempoNote: MRI signal can appear within the first months after the causative lesion; olivary enlargement peaks around 8 to 18 months, then the olive shrinks over years while T2 signal may persist; palatal tremor usually starts months after the injury
feat: Trigger: a lesion in the contralateral dentate nucleus or superior cerebellar peduncle, or in the ipsilateral red nucleus or central tegmental tract of the pons; lesions of the olive's own outflow are said to rarely cause it
Pattern depends on lesion site: brainstem tegmental lesion gives ipsilateral HOD, cerebellar (dentate or peduncle) lesion gives contralateral HOD, a paramedian pontine lesion can give bilateral HOD
Palatal tremor: rhythmic 1–3 Hz soft-palate contractions, typically appearing about 10–11 months after the lesion; about one third of reviewed cases had it

Other movement disorders: oculopalatal tremor (pendular nystagmus with oscillopsia), dentatorubral/Holmes tremor (slow rest, postural and intention tremor, sometimes wing-beating), synchronous movements of neck muscles or diaphragm
Often asymptomatic: the radiological sign can be found years after the primary lesion in patients with no tremor; absence of palatal tremor does not exclude HOD
Pooled series of 151 reported cases: more men than women (90 men, 57 women), 89% adults; vascular lesions 63% (cavernous malformation 28%, pontine haemorrhage 18%, infarction 16%) and tumours 21%
inv: MRI brain with T2/FLAIR and contrast: enlarged, non-enhancing hyperintense olive confined to the medulla, plus the remote lesion in the dentate, red nucleus, tegmentum or superior cerebellar peduncle
Follow-up MRI: olive size falls over years and the dentate nucleus opposite the affected olive may atrophy; this temporal behaviour separates HOD from tumour and infection
Diffusion tensor imaging (research): changes along all arms of the triangle; fractional anisotropy and radial diffusivity reflect demyelination in late disease
Bedside: examine the palate, pharynx, larynx and eye movements whenever the MRI shows an olivary change
Look for the cause when none is evident: mitochondrial disease (POLG, SURF1), neuro-Behçet syndrome, Wilson disease, NMOSD, infection

case.story: Pontine haemorrhage from long-standing hypertension was treated conservatively with good recovery. About ten months later he notices a clicking sound in his ears and blurred, bobbing vision when reading.
case.exam: Rhythmic soft-palate elevation about twice a second, continuing when he stops talking; pendular vertical nystagmus; mild gait ataxia; no limb tremor.
case.tests: MRI: old dorsal pontine haemorrhage on the left; the left inferior olive is enlarged and T2-hyperintense without gadolinium enhancement; the dentate nuclei appear normal.
case.q: Which pathway explains an olivary change on the side opposite or the same as the lesion, and does he need a biopsy of the olive?
case.a: No biopsy: this is HOD, and the diagnosis rests on the typical MRI plus a remote lesion in the Guillain–Mollaret triangle. A tegmental pontine lesion interrupts the central tegmental tract and produces HOD in the olive of the lesioned side; a lesion of the dentate or superior cerebellar peduncle produces it on the opposite side. Management is symptomatic, and the olive will shrink over years whatever the tremor does.

det.patho: The inferior olive is driven chiefly by the opposite dentate nucleus, whose fibres leave through the superior cerebellar peduncle, the decussation in the midbrain, the ipsilateral red nucleus and the central tegmental tract, and projects back to the dentate across the inferior cerebellar peduncle. When the inflow is cut, the olivary neurons lose their input and respond by swelling instead of dying: vacuolar degeneration, enlarged neurons and astrocytes and later gliosis. Post-mortem staging describes no change in the first day, degeneration of the olivary capsule within days, neuronal enlargement from about three weeks, maximum enlargement around eight to nine months, a pseudohypertrophic stage with gemistocytic astrocytes after about ten months, and atrophy after three to four years.
det.clinical: Many patients never develop a movement disorder, and the incidence after brainstem injury is not known. When symptoms do occur, symptomatic palatal tremor is the classic one, driven by the central tegmental tract's links with the nucleus ambiguus; it may be accompanied by ear clicks, pendular nystagmus, synchronous neck or diaphragmatic contractions, cerebellar signs or a Holmes tremor. The syndrome is delayed, usually months after the causative stroke, haemorrhage, tumour surgery or trauma.
det.diagnosis: The key is the combination of a non-enhancing, T2/FLAIR-hyperintense enlarged olive and a remote lesion in the dentato-rubro-olivary pathway. The olive may be hyperintense without enlargement early and after atrophy, so timing matters. Tumour, inflammation and infection are distinguished by contrast uptake and by progression; infarction of the medulla usually involves the posterolateral rather than the anterior olive; chronic multiple sclerosis does not enlarge the olive.
det.treatment: Usually self-limiting and treated symptomatically; many patients need no treatment. For palatal tremor the reported options are valproate, carbamazepine, clonazepam, trihexyphenidyl or tryptophan, with unsatisfactory results, and botulinum toxin to the tensor veli palatini in severe, bothersome clicking. Holmes tremor responds poorly to drugs; clonazepam, levodopa, dopamine agonists and levetiracetam have been tried, and deep brain stimulation or thalamotomy is reserved for disabling tremor.
det.prognosis: The olive eventually shrinks over several years, but the tremor, once established, tends to persist; the underlying lesion usually determines overall disability.
pearls: Olivary hypertrophy is a delayed sign: look at the MRI weeks to months after a brainstem or cerebellar insult, not on day one.
Ipsilateral lesion, ipsilateral olive; cerebellar lesion, opposite olive. A paramedian pontine lesion can give both.
Non-enhancing and confined to the olive: that is what separates HOD from tumour, MS and infection.
Bilateral HOD without a structural lesion should raise the question of mitochondrial disease.
det.thd: HOD คือการที่ inferior olive บวมโตหลังรอยโรคใน Guillain–Mollaret triangle ซึ่งมักเป็นก้านสมองตีบหรือเลือดออก cavernous malformation หรือหลังผ่าตัดเนื้องอก ผู้ป่วยบางรายไม่มีอาการ แต่บางรายมี palatal tremor 1–3 ครั้งต่อวินาที หูมีเสียงคลิก ตากระตุกแบบ pendular หรือ Holmes tremor MRI จะเห็น olive โตและสว่างบน T2 โดยไม่ติดสารทึบรังสี การรักษาเป็นแบบตามอาการ ยาได้ผลไม่ดีนัก และ olive จะฝ่อลงเองในเวลาหลายปี

qx.stem: A 47-year-old woman from Ubon Ratchathani had a haemorrhage from a cavernous malformation in the right dorsal pons treated surgically 9 months ago. She now reports clicking in both ears. Examination shows rhythmic elevation of the soft palate about twice a second. MRI shows a T2-hyperintense, enlarged olive in the medulla that does not enhance.
qx.q: On which side is the enlarged olive expected, relative to the pontine lesion?
opts: On the left, because the olivary fibres cross at the pyramids
On the right, ipsilateral, because the central tegmental tract runs uncrossed from the red nucleus to the olive
Always bilateral regardless of lesion site
On the left, because the dentate-rubral fibres cross at the midbrain
No olivary change is possible from a pontine lesion
qx.why: A lesion of the ipsilateral central tegmental tract cuts the input to the olive on the same side, so the olive on the lesion side enlarges. The decussation that makes the olive contralateral applies to cerebellar (dentate or superior cerebellar peduncle) lesions. A paramedian pontine lesion affecting both tracts can cause bilateral change, but a lateral tegmental lesion usually gives ipsilateral HOD.

qx.stem: A 60-year-old man has a routine MRI six months after a left cerebellar haemorrhage in the dentate region. It shows a T2-hyperintense, mildly enlarged right inferior olive. There is no contrast enhancement and no brainstem symptoms.
qx.q: What should be done next?
opts: Stereotactic biopsy of the olive
Immediate high-dose corticosteroids for demyelination
Lumbar puncture and empiric antituberculous treatment
Recognise hypertrophic olivary degeneration, examine the palate and eye movements, and reassure without treatment unless symptoms appear
Repeat MRI with contrast weekly for six months
qx.why: A non-enhancing, olive-confined hyperintensity on the side opposite a dentate lesion is the typical picture of HOD, which is often asymptomatic and self-limiting. Biopsy, steroids or antituberculous drugs are not needed, and short-interval contrast scans add nothing; clinical examination of the palate and eyes and follow-up are enough.

qx.stem: A resident asks when, after a brainstem infarct, the inferior olive would first look enlarged on MRI, and when it would eventually shrink.
qx.q: Which timeline is the best summary?
opts: Enlargement within hours, atrophy within a week
No change for the first weeks; enlargement over the following months with a peak at about the first one to one and a half years; shrinkage over several years while hyperintensity may persist
Enlargement only after five years, never atrophy
Enlargement and atrophy both complete within 30 days
Olive enlarges permanently and never changes in size
qx.why: Neuronal and astrocytic hypertrophy builds from about three weeks, olivary enlargement is maximal at roughly eight to eighteen months, and the olive then shrinks over about three to four years while T2 hyperintensity can remain. HOD is therefore a delayed finding and is easy to miss on an early scan.

qx.stem: A 9-year-old boy from Surin has bilateral enlargement of the inferior olives and progressive ataxia, ophthalmoparesis and neuropathy. There is no brainstem or cerebellar structural lesion on MRI and no history of surgery or trauma. His lactate is raised.
qx.q: Which investigation is the most useful next?
opts: Gene panel including POLG and SURF1 for mitochondrial disease
Repeat MRI in one year and no other tests
Serum copper only, to exclude Wilson disease, and nothing else
Brainstem biopsy
Anti-aquaporin-4 antibody only, with no other testing
qx.why: Bilateral HOD without a structural lesion has been reported in mitochondrial disease, especially POLG and SURF1 variants (for example SANDO or Leigh syndrome), so genetic testing is the productive next step. Wilson disease and NMOSD are rarer causes and could be checked too, but they are not the single best choice given ophthalmoparesis, neuropathy and high lactate.

ddx.pt: Palatal tremor is the movement disorder; HOD is the imaging substrate of the symptomatic form, whereas the essential form has no olivary change
Pendular nystagmus with palatal movements and an enlarged olive, a late consequence of the same triangle lesion
Slow rest, postural and intention tremor from midbrain or thalamic lesions; HOD may coexist but the olive change is not required
Demyelinating medullary lesions show enhancement when active and are not confined to an enlarged olive
A posterior fossa tumour may itself be the trigger (or its surgery); olivary signal appears later and does not enhance
Brainstem inflammation can cause HOD, so a pontine lesion with mouth ulcers or uveitis should prompt this cause
Bilateral HOD without a structural lesion may be a clue to mitochondrial disease (POLG, SURF1)

name: Antiphospholipid syndrome (2023 ACR/EULAR classification)
formal: A research classification system, replacing the revised Sapporo criteria, that identifies antiphospholipid syndrome by first requiring a clinical event and a positive antiphospholipid antibody test within three years of each other, then adding weighted points from six clinical and two laboratory domains, with at least three points needed in each group.
simple: A scoring checklist that lets researchers decide whether a person with clots or pregnancy complications and positive antiphospholipid blood tests can be counted as having APS in a study; it is not a bedside rule for diagnosis.
th: เกณฑ์จำแนกโรค APS ปี 2023 ของ ACR/EULAR ใช้ระบบคะแนนถ่วงน้ำหนัก ต้องมีเหตุการณ์ทางคลินิกร่วมกับผลตรวจ antiphospholipid antibody บวกภายใน 3 ปี และได้คะแนนอย่างน้อย 3 คะแนนทั้งด้านคลินิกและด้านห้องปฏิบัติการ ออกแบบเพื่องานวิจัยที่เน้นความจำเพาะสูง ไม่ใช่เกณฑ์วินิจฉัยผู้ป่วยรายบุคคล
tempoNote: A classification tool rather than a disease course; the underlying syndrome produces sudden thrombotic events on a background of persistently positive antibodies
feat: Entry step comes first: at least one clinical criterion plus a positive aPL test (lupus anticoagulant, or moderate- or high-titre aCL or anti-β2GPI) falling within three years of each other

Eight domains, six clinical (venous thrombosis, arterial thrombosis, microvascular, obstetric, cardiac valve, haematology) and two laboratory (coagulation-based and solid-phase assays); only the highest-weighted item in each domain is counted
Classification needs three or more clinical points and three or more laboratory points; individual item weights run from 1 to 7
A thrombosis that has a ready alternative explanation (surgery, cancer, severe hypertension, diabetes, kidney disease) is down-weighted, so an unprovoked stroke in a young adult scores highest

Neurological fit: stroke counts as arterial thrombosis, cerebral venous thrombosis as venous thrombosis, and broken livedo racemosa as suspected microvascular disease; chorea, cognitive decline, migraine and MS-like lesions are not scored
inv: Lupus anticoagulant by the ISTH three-step method using two screening systems (dRVVT and a sensitive aPTT); read with caution on anticoagulants, during acute thrombosis and in pregnancy

IgG and IgM anticardiolipin and anti-β2GPI by standardised ELISA, with moderate titre defined as 40–79 units and high titre as 80 units or more; automated platforms are not interchangeable with ELISA for classification
Persistence means two positive results at least 12 weeks apart; a single LA result or IgM-only positivity earns only a point
Echocardiography for valve thickening or vegetations, platelet count, urine protein and skin inspection to capture the remaining domains

case.who: 34-year-old female bank clerk from Nakhon Ratchasima, non-smoker
case.story: Sudden right hand weakness and word-finding difficulty one morning; no recent surgery, travel, hormones or high blood pressure. She has noticed an irregular violaceous skin pattern on her thighs for years.
case.exam: Mild right hemiparesis and non-fluent aphasia; broken, asymmetric livedo racemosa over thighs and buttocks that does not fade with warming.
case.tests: MRI: left MCA branch infarct. Lupus anticoagulant positive twice, 14 weeks apart; IgG anticardiolipin and anti-β2GPI both above 80 ELISA units on both occasions; platelets 118,000/µL; ANA negative.
case.q: Does she reach the 2023 classification threshold, and which long-term anticoagulant fits best?
case.a: Yes. Clinical side: unprovoked arterial thrombosis 4, livedo racemosa 2 and thrombocytopenia 2 (the highest item per domain counts); laboratory side: persistent LA 5 and high-titre dual IgG positivity 7. Long-term warfarin (INR 2–3) is preferred over a DOAC in this triple-positive arterial case.

Section 6 Systemic Disorders That Also Involve the Cerebrovascular System

det.patho: The clinical syndrome is driven by antibodies against β2-glycoprotein I and related phospholipid-binding proteins, which activate endothelium, platelets and complement. This entry concerns the framework built around that biology. The international group started from a long list of candidate features, trimmed it by expert surveys and consensus, set weights by pairwise comparison of real-world case profiles, and tested the final rules in two validation cohorts of roughly 280 patients each. Specificity was the stated priority, so that studies and drug trials enrol people with a convincing syndrome rather than a mixed antibody-positive group.
det.clinical: At the bedside the system shows which findings carry the most weight. A thrombotic event with no competing explanation counts far more than one that follows surgery, cancer, severe hypertension or diabetes. Stroke sits in the arterial domain, cerebral venous thrombosis in the venous domain, and persistent broken livedo racemosa in the suspected-microvascular domain, whereas regular, cold-reversible livedo reticularis earns nothing. Pregnancy morbidity is reorganised around severe pre-eclampsia and placental insufficiency before 34 weeks, and valve thickening, vegetations and low platelets receive modest weights. Neurological problems common in aPL-positive patients, such as chorea, cognitive decline, migraine and MS-like white matter lesions, are outside the score, so a patient may have genuine aPL-related neurological disease and still fall short of classification.
det.diagnosis: Apply the entry step, take the single highest-weighted item in each domain, and add the points; at least three clinical and three laboratory points are required. Laboratory weights favour persistent lupus anticoagulant and high-titre IgG antibodies, with the largest weight for high-titre IgG anticardiolipin and anti-β2GPI together, while a single LA result or IgM-only positivity earns one point. Items with an equal or likelier alternative cause, for example thrombocytopenia during heparin treatment or pre-eclampsia in active lupus, are not scored. In validation the criteria were about 99% specific and 84% sensitive, against 86–91% specificity and near-complete sensitivity for the revised Sapporo set, so some people a clinician reasonably treats as having APS will not be classified. Where risk-factor data are missing in retrospective work, the lowest non-zero thrombosis weight is assigned.
det.treatment: Classification rules do not dictate treatment, and a patient who falls short can still be managed as APS by the treating team. After arterial events including stroke, long-term warfarin with an INR of 2–3 remains the standard, with higher intensity or added low-dose aspirin considered by specialists after recurrence on treatment. Direct oral anticoagulants are avoided in triple-positive and arterial APS because trials of rivaroxaban and apixaban showed more thrombotic events, especially stroke, than warfarin; they are sometimes accepted for single-positive venous disease when warfarin is impractical. Hydroxychloroquine is a frequent add-on, and acute stroke follows the usual pathway. Pregnancy needs heparin with aspirin under specialist care, and oestrogen-containing contraception is avoided.
det.prognosis: Not applicable to a classification tool; outcome depends on the antibody profile, recurrence of thrombosis and control of other vascular risk factors.
pearls: Check the entry step first: one clinical event plus a positive antibody result, both inside a three-year window.
Provoked thrombosis and one-off positive tests earn few points, so strictness is deliberate; the score is for cohorts, not for denying treatment.
Broken, fixed livedo racemosa counts; uniform livedo reticularis that fades with warmth does not.
det.thd: เกณฑ์จำแนก APS ปี 2023 ของ ACR/EULAR เริ่มจากด่านแรกคือต้องมีเหตุการณ์ทางคลินิกและผล aPL บวกภายใน 3 ปี จากนั้นนับคะแนนถ่วงน้ำหนักจาก 8 กลุ่ม (คลินิก 6 กลุ่ม ห้องปฏิบัติการ 2 กลุ่ม) โดยนับเฉพาะรายการที่คะแนนสูงสุดในแต่ละกลุ่ม ต้องได้อย่างน้อย 3 คะแนนทั้งสองด้าน ลิ่มเลือดที่มีสาเหตุอื่นชัดเจนจะได้คะแนนน้อยลง เกณฑ์นี้จำเพาะสูงมากแต่ไวน้อยกว่าเกณฑ์เดิม จึงใช้จำแนกผู้ป่วยในงานวิจัย ส่วนการรักษาในผู้ป่วยที่มี stroke จาก APS ยังเลือก warfarin มากกว่ายากลุ่ม DOAC โดยเฉพาะในผู้ที่ผลบวกทั้งสามชนิด

qx.stem: A rheumatology and neurology team is screening patients for a multicentre APS trial using the 2023 ACR/EULAR system. A 40-year-old woman has a positive lupus anticoagulant, but her only clinical event, a stroke, happened six years before the antibody was first detected.
qx.q: Which step of the classification process does she fail?
opts: The entry rule that a clinical event and a positive antibody result sit inside a three-year window
The requirement for three clinical points
The requirement that aCL must be of IgM isotype
The requirement for livedo racemosa
The requirement that the lupus anticoagulant be tested only on warfarin
qx.why: Before any points are counted, the clinical event and the antibody result must fall inside a three-year window, which makes classification more certain than the older five-year window. Failing this step excludes her whatever her later score. Livedo, IgM isotype and anticoagulant status are not entry requirements, and LA testing is preferably done off anticoagulants.

qx.stem: A 39-year-old man developed a calf DVT two weeks after major orthopaedic surgery under general anaesthesia. A lupus anticoagulant screen was positive once and was never repeated; anticardiolipin and anti-β2GPI ELISAs are negative. He has no other clinical features.
qx.q: Which statement best describes his status under the 2023 ACR/EULAR criteria?
opts: He is classified because any thrombosis plus any positive aPL test is sufficient
He is classified because the DVT is a venous event in the highest-weighted domain
He is not classified: a provoked DVT earns few clinical points and a single LA result few laboratory points
He is not classified only because DVT is not a criterion
He is classified once the platelet count is checked
qx.why: A venous event with a high-risk profile such as recent major surgery is down-weighted to one point, and a single positive LA test also earns just one laboratory point, so neither group reaches three. The system is deliberately strict to keep research cohorts homogeneous. Venous thrombosis is a scored domain, and platelet count adds points only if thrombocytopenia is present.

name: Mumps meningitis and encephalitis
formal: Central nervous system infection by mumps virus, a paramyxovirus, ranging from very common benign lymphocytic meningitis to rare encephalitis, cerebellitis, myelitis, hydrocephalus and sensorineural deafness, occurring with or without parotitis.
simple: The mumps virus, which swells the cheek glands, can also inflame the lining of the brain; it is usually mild but can sometimes cause deafness or brain swelling.
th: การติดเชื้อไวรัสคางทูมในระบบประสาท ส่วนใหญ่เป็นเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบแบบลิมโฟไซต์ที่หายเอง อาจเกิดก่อน พร้อม หรือหลังต่อมน้ำลายอักเสบ หรือไม่มีต่อมน้ำลายบวมเลย ภาวะแทรกซ้อนที่สำคัญคือหูหนวกข้างเดียวแบบ sensorineural ป้องกันได้ด้วยวัคซีน MMR
tempoNote: Meningitis usually 4-10 days after parotitis begins, but it may precede parotitis by up to a week or occur without it
feat: Fever, headache, vomiting and neck stiffness in a child, adolescent or young adult, with a strong male predominance for CNS disease
Parotid or other salivary gland swelling in many but not all; orchitis or pancreatitis are additional clues
Encephalitis is uncommon: drowsiness, seizures, hemiparesis or ataxia (cerebellitis)
Sudden, usually unilateral and often permanent sensorineural hearing loss
Outbreaks occur even in vaccinated populations as immunity wanes, typically in schools, universities and dormitories
inv: CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis, sometimes above 1,000 cells, normal or mildly raised protein; glucose mildly low in a minority
Mumps RT-PCR on CSF, saliva or buccal swab (best within the first days of parotitis) and serum IgM; IgM may be absent in vaccinated people
Serum amylase if parotid swelling is uncertain; audiometry in every patient with hearing complaints
MRI if encephalitic or ataxic, and to look for hydrocephalus

case.who: 19-year-old male university student in a dormitory in Phitsanulok, vaccination record uncertain
case.story: Swelling of both cheeks for five days, then fever, severe headache and vomiting; several dormitory friends had swollen glands last week.
case.exam: Bilateral tender parotid swelling, neck stiffness, alert; left testis tender and swollen; he reports ringing and muffled hearing in the right ear.
case.tests: CSF 700 cells (90% lymphocytes), protein 0.6 g/L, glucose 2.6 mmol/L (blood 5.5); Gram stain negative; buccal swab mumps RT-PCR positive; audiometry shows right severe sensorineural loss.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what follow-up is most important?
case.a: Mumps meningitis with orchitis and mumps-related sensorineural hearing loss; supportive care, isolation for 5 days after parotitis onset, notification and outbreak vaccination, and ENT and audiology follow-up because the deafness is often permanent.
