Chapter 5 Viral Meningitis and Aseptic Meningitis Syndrome - mumps virus
Part II: Viral Pathogens: Pathogenesis, Pathology, Diagnosis and Treatment

det.patho: Mumps virus spreads by respiratory droplets and saliva, replicates in the upper airway and lymph nodes, and then becomes viraemic, seeding salivary glands, gonads, pancreas and the CNS. It reaches the CSF through the choroid plexus and infects ependymal cells, which explains the very frequent CSF pleocytosis even without symptoms. Ependymal injury may lead to aqueduct stenosis and hydrocephalus. Deafness results from viral injury of the cochlea, particularly the organ of Corti and stria vascularis.
det.clinical: CNS involvement is so common that it is considered part of the natural history of mumps, but most of it is mild meningitis lasting about a week. Encephalitis is rare and carries the main risk of sequelae such as seizures, hemiparesis or behavioural change. Hearing loss may appear with or after the meningitis and does not correlate with its severity. In the vaccine era, cases have shifted to adolescents and young adults, many of whom have had one or two vaccine doses.
det.diagnosis: In an outbreak with parotitis the diagnosis is clinical, but confirmation by RT-PCR from a buccal swab or CSF is preferred, because IgM can be negative after vaccination. The CSF shows lymphocytes, sometimes with a mild drop in glucose that should not be mistaken for TB. Parainfluenza and other viruses can also cause parotitis, and serological cross-reaction among paramyxoviruses complicates antibody tests. Always assess hearing.
det.treatment: There is no specific antiviral; care is supportive with analgesia, hydration and antiemetics. Patients are isolated for five days after parotitis begins and contacts' vaccination status is checked, with a third MMR dose sometimes recommended in outbreaks. Sudden sensorineural loss should be referred urgently; corticosteroids are often tried, though evidence is weak, and cochlear implantation is an option for profound bilateral loss. Hydrocephalus may require CSF diversion.
det.prognosis: Meningitis recovers fully; encephalitis can leave deficits and has a small mortality, and mumps deafness is frequently permanent.
pearls: Meningitis can come before parotitis or without it; ask about outbreaks and orchitis.
Mild hypoglycorrhachia is possible in mumps meningitis, a benign mimic of TB meningitis.
Test hearing in every patient with mumps CNS infection, as unilateral deafness is easily missed.
det.thd: ไวรัสคางทูมเข้าสู่ระบบประสาทบ่อยมาก ส่วนใหญ่ทำให้เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบแบบลิมโฟไซต์ที่หายเองภายในราวหนึ่งสัปดาห์ อาจเกิดก่อน พร้อม หรือหลังต่อมน้ำลายบวม และอาจมีอัณฑะอักเสบร่วม ภาวะแทรกซ้อนสำคัญคือหูหนวกแบบ sensorineural ข้างเดียวที่มักถาวร และสมองอักเสบที่พบน้อย วินิจฉัยด้วย RT-PCR จาก buccal swab หรือน้ำไขสันหลัง รักษาตามอาการ แยกผู้ป่วย และป้องกันด้วยวัคซีน MMR สองเข็ม

name: Human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) encephalitis
formal: Encephalitis caused by human herpesvirus 6 (mainly HHV-6B), classically post-transplant acute limbic encephalitis with amnesia, seizures and SIADH in allogeneic stem cell, especially cord blood, transplant recipients, and less often encephalitis or febrile status epilepticus with primary infection in infants.
simple: A common childhood virus that usually causes a rash with fever (roseola) can wake up after a bone marrow transplant and inflame the memory areas of the brain, causing confusion, memory loss and seizures.
th: สมองอักเสบจากไวรัส HHV-6 ที่กำเริบหลังปลูกถ่ายไขกระดูก โดยเฉพาะจากเลือดสายสะดือ ประมาณ 2-6 สัปดาห์หลังปลูกถ่าย มาด้วยสับสน ความจำใหม่เสีย ชัก และโซเดียมต่ำจาก SIADH MRI เห็นสัญญาณผิดปกติที่ mesial temporal รักษาด้วย ganciclovir หรือ foscarnet
tempoNote: Post-transplant form develops around neutrophil engraftment, about 2-6 weeks after transplant, over a few days
feat: Allogeneic haematopoietic cell transplant, highest risk with cord blood, HLA mismatch, acute graft-versus-host disease or early high-dose steroids
Acute confusion with prominent anterograde amnesia, insomnia, agitation or hallucinations
Seizures, often focal from the temporal lobe or only seen on EEG
Hyponatraemia from SIADH is common
In infants: primary infection (roseola) can cause febrile seizures, febrile status epilepticus and, rarely, encephalitis
inv: MRI: T2/FLAIR swelling of the hippocampus, amygdala and uncus, unilateral or bilateral, usually without enhancement; may be normal early
CSF HHV-6 PCR with plasma quantitative PCR; CSF cells and protein are often only mildly abnormal in cytopenic hosts

Consider chromosomally integrated HHV-6 (persistently high DNA in blood and every cell) before attributing a positive PCR to active infection; test hair follicle or nail DNA or donor and recipient cells
EEG for non-convulsive seizures; sodium and osmolality; exclude HSV, CMV, toxoplasma, calcineurin inhibitor toxicity and PRES

case.who: 48-year-old man from Bangkok, 3 weeks after a double cord blood transplant for acute myeloid leukaemia
case.story: As his neutrophils recover he becomes confused, cannot remember his doctors' visits from hour to hour and sleeps poorly; his wife notices brief staring spells.
case.exam: Disoriented, severe anterograde amnesia, no focal weakness, no neck stiffness.
case.tests: Sodium 124 mmol/L with SIADH pattern; MRI shows bilateral hippocampal and amygdala FLAIR hyperintensity without enhancement; EEG shows left temporal seizures; CSF HHV-6 PCR positive with high plasma HHV-6 DNA; tacrolimus level in range; HSV PCR negative.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and treatment?
case.a: HHV-6 post-transplant acute limbic encephalitis; IV foscarnet or ganciclovir for at least 3 weeks (foscarnet often preferred to spare the engrafting marrow), antiseizure medication, correction of hyponatraemia and cognitive rehabilitation.

read.where: Chapter 13 Human Herpesvirus-6 - CNS complications of primary infection and of reactivation, treatment

det.patho: Almost everyone acquires HHV-6B in early childhood, and the virus stays latent in monocytes, lymphocytes and brain cells, especially astrocytes of the hippocampus. Profound T-cell immunodeficiency after transplant allows reactivation, which peaks near engraftment; high-level viraemia is associated with encephalitis. Infection of hippocampal astrocytes disturbs glutamate handling and neuronal survival, producing amnesia and seizures. About 1 in 100 people carry the whole viral genome in their chromosomes, which gives high viral DNA levels without disease.
det.clinical: The typical patient is a cord blood or HLA-mismatched transplant recipient who becomes confused, amnestic and sleepless a few weeks after the graft, with seizures and hyponatraemia. Fever is not always present. Untreated or late-treated cases can progress to coma and death, and survivors may have lasting memory deficits or temporal lobe epilepsy. In infants, primary infection is a frequent cause of febrile seizures and is found in a notable share of febrile status epilepticus, a recognised antecedent of mesial temporal sclerosis.
det.diagnosis: Combine the clinical syndrome, mesial temporal MRI changes and HHV-6 DNA in CSF, with plasma viral load supporting reactivation. Because HHV-6 DNA is also detected in latent infection and in inherited chromosomal integration, interpret a positive PCR in context and exclude integration when levels are persistently high. EEG is important since many seizures are subclinical. Other causes in transplant patients, including HSV, CMV, toxoplasma, drug toxicity, PRES and metabolic encephalopathy, must be excluded.
det.treatment: Antiviral therapy is ganciclovir or foscarnet for at least 3 weeks, continued until CSF or plasma DNA clears; foscarnet avoids marrow suppression but needs renal and electrolyte monitoring, and cidofovir is a second-line option. Aciclovir is not adequate. Seizures are treated with drugs chosen for minimal interactions (for example levetiracetam), SIADH with fluid restriction or careful sodium correction, and immunosuppression is reduced where possible. Pre-emptive monitoring or prophylaxis in very high-risk cord blood recipients is used in some centres.
det.prognosis: Mortality is substantial in some series and many survivors keep memory impairment or epilepsy; early treatment improves outcome.
pearls: Amnesia plus hyponatraemia a few weeks after a cord blood transplant: think HHV-6 and start foscarnet or ganciclovir.
Aciclovir does not treat HHV-6, because the virus lacks the thymidine kinase that activates it.
A very high HHV-6 DNA level in a well person may be chromosomal integration, not infection.
det.thd: HHV-6 เป็นไวรัสที่คนส่วนใหญ่ติดตั้งแต่เด็ก (ไข้ผื่น roseola) และแฝงอยู่ในสมอง หลังปลูกถ่ายไขกระดูก โดยเฉพาะจากเลือดสายสะดือ ไวรัสอาจกำเริบช่วงไขกระดูกเริ่มทำงาน ทำให้สับสน ความจำใหม่เสีย ชัก และโซเดียมต่ำ MRI เห็นสัญญาณผิดปกติที่ hippocampus และ amygdala วินิจฉัยด้วย PCR ในน้ำไขสันหลังร่วมกับ viral load ในเลือด และต้องคิดถึง chromosomal integration รักษาด้วย ganciclovir หรือ foscarnet อย่างน้อย 3 สัปดาห์ ยา acyclovir ไม่ได้ผล

qx.stem: Three weeks after a cord blood stem cell transplant, a 39-year-old woman becomes confused and cannot form new memories. Sodium is 125 mmol/L, MRI shows bilateral hippocampal FLAIR hyperintensity without enhancement, and EEG shows left temporal seizures. CSF HSV PCR is negative.
qx.q: Which treatment is most appropriate while awaiting further results?
opts: IV aciclovir
IV methylprednisolone
IV foscarnet
Oral valacyclovir
Rituximab
qx.why: Amnesia, seizures and SIADH around engraftment after cord blood transplant suggest HHV-6 post-transplant acute limbic encephalitis. HHV-6 lacks the viral thymidine kinase needed to activate aciclovir, so foscarnet or ganciclovir is used, and foscarnet spares the engrafting marrow. Steroids and rituximab treat autoimmune limbic encephalitis, which is less likely here.

name: B virus (Macacine herpesvirus 1) encephalomyelitis
formal: Zoonotic infection with Macacine alphaherpesvirus 1 (herpes B virus), carried latently by macaque monkeys, transmitted by bites, scratches, mucosal splashes or tissue exposure and causing an ascending myelitis and encephalomyelitis with high mortality unless antiviral treatment is given early.
simple: A herpes virus that monkeys such as macaques carry harmlessly can pass to people through a bite or scratch and cause a rare but very dangerous infection of the spinal cord and brain.
th: ไวรัสเริมของลิงแสมและลิงวอก (macaque) ติดสู่คนทางการกัด ข่วน หรือของเหลวกระเด็นเข้าตา ทำให้ไขสันหลังอักเสบแบบลามขึ้นและสมองอักเสบ อัตราตายสูง ต้องล้างแผลทันทีอย่างน้อย 15 นาที และพิจารณาให้ valacyclovir ป้องกัน ร่วมกับวัคซีนพิษสุนัขบ้า
tempoNote: Incubation usually 3-7 days (up to about a month); local wound symptoms then neurological signs that progress over days
feat: Exposure to a macaque: bite or scratch by temple, tourist-site or pet monkeys, laboratory and veterinary work, needlestick or splash from monkey tissue or fluids
Vesicles, pain, itching, tingling or numbness at the wound and regional lymphadenitis
Fever, myalgia and headache followed by ascending flaccid weakness, sensory loss, areflexia and urinary retention
Brainstem and cerebral involvement: diplopia, dysphagia, respiratory failure, seizures and coma
Without treatment most patients with encephalitis die and survivors often have severe deficits
inv: PCR (and culture in a specialised containment laboratory) of wound, conjunctival swabs, vesicle fluid, CSF and blood; samples from the animal where possible
Serology is hard to interpret because of cross-reaction with HSV; use a reference laboratory
CSF: lymphocytic or mixed pleocytosis, raised protein
MRI of brain and spine: T2 changes in cord, brainstem and cerebellum

case.who: 29-year-old tourist bitten on the hand by a long-tailed macaque at a temple in Lop Buri
case.story: He washed the wound briefly and received rabies vaccine and immunoglobulin, but no other treatment; 9 days later the bitten hand tingles and blisters, and over 3 days numbness and weakness climb from his legs to his chest.
case.exam: Vesicles around the healed bite, flaccid paraparesis with areflexia, sensory level at T6, urinary retention, mild diplopia.
case.tests: CSF 120 cells (80% lymphocytes), protein 1.2 g/L; MRI shows longitudinally extensive cord T2 change and a pontine lesion; vesicle and CSF PCR positive for B virus at the reference laboratory; rabies tests negative.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what should have happened at the time of the bite?
case.a: B virus ascending encephalomyelitis; treat at once with IV ganciclovir (or high-dose IV aciclovir) followed by lifelong oral valacyclovir suppression. At the time of the bite, the wound needed thorough cleansing with soap and water for at least 15 minutes and post-exposure valacyclovir for a high-risk exposure, alongside rabies prophylaxis.

read.where: Chapter 14 B Virus - nervous system disease, diagnosis, prevention and treatment

det.patho: B virus is an alphaherpesvirus closely related to HSV that infects most adult macaques, which have mild or no lesions and shed virus intermittently in saliva, eye and genital secretions. In humans it replicates at the entry site, then travels along peripheral nerves to the spinal cord and ascends to the brainstem and brain, causing haemorrhagic necrotising inflammation. Viraemia and visceral lesions also occur. Long-tailed and rhesus macaques, common at Thai temples and tourist sites, are potential sources.
det.clinical: Fewer than a hundred human cases are documented, mostly in laboratory workers, and the fatality rate before antivirals was about 70-80 per cent. Symptoms start at the wound with vesicles, pain or paraesthesia, then a febrile flu-like phase. Neurological disease begins as ascending myelitis or encephalomyelitis, leading to respiratory failure and coma within days. A few cases of human-to-human transmission to close contacts have been reported.
det.diagnosis: The key is the exposure history; any neurological illness after a macaque injury should be treated as B virus until excluded. PCR of lesions, mucosal swabs, CSF and blood is the main test, but must be done by specialised laboratories with biosafety facilities. Serology is unreliable because of cross-reactivity with HSV antibodies. Rabies testing should be done in parallel because the exposure is identical.
det.treatment: Prevention after exposure is critical: wash or irrigate the wound or eye immediately for 15 minutes with soap and water or saline, assess risk, and give a 14-day course of valacyclovir, 1 g thrice daily (or oral aciclovir at 800 mg five times each day), for high-risk exposures; rabies post-exposure prophylaxis and tetanus cover are also needed in Thailand. Established disease is treated with IV aciclovir 12.5-15 mg/kg 8-hourly, or IV ganciclovir 5 mg/kg 12-hourly once the CNS is involved, continued until symptoms resolve and cultures are negative, then lifelong oral valacyclovir suppression. Intensive care for respiratory and autonomic failure is often required.
det.prognosis: Untreated encephalitis is usually fatal; early antiviral treatment has allowed survival, sometimes with full recovery, but many survivors have severe disability.
pearls: A macaque bite in Thailand needs two prophylaxes: rabies PEP and consideration of B virus PEP with valacyclovir.
Proper wound cleansing within minutes is the most effective single step.
Ascending myelitis with vesicles at an old monkey bite is B virus until proven otherwise.
det.thd: B virus เป็นไวรัสเริมของลิง macaque เช่น ลิงแสมและลิงวอก ซึ่งพบมากตามวัดและแหล่งท่องเที่ยวในไทย ติดสู่คนทางการกัด ข่วน หรือของเหลวกระเด็นเข้าเยื่อบุ แล้วเดินทางตามเส้นประสาทขึ้นไขสันหลังและสมอง ทำให้มีตุ่มน้ำที่แผล ไขสันหลังอักเสบแบบลามขึ้น และสมองอักเสบที่ตายสูง เมื่อถูกลิงกัดต้องล้างแผลด้วยสบู่และน้ำอย่างน้อย 15 นาที ให้วัคซีนพิษสุนัขบ้า และพิจารณา valacyclovir 14 วัน ถ้ามีอาการแล้วให้ acyclovir หรือ ganciclovir ทางหลอดเลือดดำทันที

qx.stem: A 24-year-old backpacker is bitten deeply on the forearm by a macaque at a temple in central Thailand. She arrives at the emergency department 30 minutes later. She has had no previous rabies vaccination.
qx.q: In addition to thorough wound washing for 15 minutes, which combination is most appropriate?
opts: Rabies vaccine and rabies immunoglobulin plus oral valacyclovir for 14 days
Rabies vaccine only, because monkeys do not carry other dangerous viruses
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate only
Oral valacyclovir only, since rabies is rare in monkeys
Observation and treatment only if symptoms appear
qx.why: A macaque bite is a category III rabies exposure in Thailand and also a high-risk exposure to B virus, which causes an often fatal ascending encephalomyelitis. Post-exposure valacyclovir (or aciclovir) is recommended for deep bites, alongside full rabies prophylaxis. Waiting for symptoms loses the window for prevention.

name: Mycoplasma pneumoniae-associated encephalitis
formal: Encephalitis and related CNS syndromes linked to Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection, either early (within about a week of respiratory symptoms, with organisms in CSF, suggesting direct invasion) or late (more than a week later, immune mediated, overlapping ADEM, transverse myelitis, Guillain-Barre syndrome, striatal necrosis and stroke).
simple: A common bacterium that causes walking pneumonia in school children can, uncommonly, inflame the brain either directly or by stirring up the immune system a week or two later.
th: สมองอักเสบที่สัมพันธ์กับเชื้อ Mycoplasma pneumoniae พบบ่อยในเด็กวัยเรียน แบ่งเป็นชนิดเกิดเร็วภายในหนึ่งสัปดาห์หลังอาการทางเดินหายใจ (เชื้อเข้าสมองโดยตรง) และชนิดเกิดช้า (ภูมิคุ้มกัน) ที่ซ้อนกับ ADEM, transverse myelitis และ GBS วินิจฉัยด้วย PCR จากคอและน้ำไขสันหลังร่วมกับ serology
tempoNote: Early form within about 5-7 days of cough or sore throat; late form more than a week after the respiratory illness, which may have been mild or absent
feat: School-age children and young adults with a preceding or concurrent cough, sore throat or atypical pneumonia; epidemics recur every few years, including the 2023-2024 global wave
Encephalopathy, seizures, behavioural change, focal deficits or ataxia; fever variable
Late immune forms: ADEM, transverse myelitis, Guillain-Barre syndrome, acute striatal necrosis, optic neuritis and arterial ischaemic stroke
Extra-neural clues: mucositis or Stevens-Johnson rash, haemolytic anaemia with cold agglutinins, otitis
Respiratory symptoms may be absent in up to a fifth of patients
inv: PCR for M. pneumoniae on throat or nasopharyngeal swab and on CSF; CSF PCR positivity favours the early direct-invasion form
Serology (IgM, or paired IgG showing seroconversion or fourfold rise) supports recent infection; IgM alone is not specific
CSF: normal or mild pleocytosis and raised protein; MRI may be normal or show cortical, white matter, basal ganglia or cord lesions
Chest X-ray, MOG and AQP4 antibodies in demyelinating presentations; EEG; exclude HSV and other encephalitides

case.story: Ten days of cough and low fever treated at a clinic with amoxicillin, then a day of irritability, slurred speech and a focal seizure.
case.exam: Drowsy, right hemiparesis, bilateral extensor plantars, scattered crackles in the left lower chest.
case.tests: Chest X-ray left lower patchy infiltrate; throat swab M. pneumoniae PCR positive, serum IgM positive with high cold agglutinins; CSF 25 lymphocytes, protein 0.7 g/L, Mycoplasma and HSV PCR negative; MRI multifocal T2 white matter and thalamic lesions; MOG antibody negative.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and how should she be treated?
case.a: Late-onset (immune-mediated) Mycoplasma-associated encephalitis with an ADEM pattern; high-dose IV methylprednisolone (IVIG or plasma exchange if no response), plus a CNS-penetrating anti-Mycoplasma antibiotic such as azithromycin or, given her age and macrolide resistance concerns, doxycycline.

read.where: Chapter 25 Mycoplasmal and Ureaplasmal Infections - neurologic manifestations of Mycoplasma pneumoniae, diagnosis and treatment

det.patho: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a small wall-less bacterium spread by droplets. Neurological disease arises in two ways: early direct invasion of the CNS, sometimes with local cytokine release, and later molecular mimicry, in which antibodies against mycoplasmal glycolipids cross-react with galactocerebroside and gangliosides of myelin and nerve. A vasculopathy or procoagulant state explains some strokes. Because many children carry the organism asymptomatically in the throat, causation must be argued from timing and several tests together.
det.clinical: Mycoplasma is among the most frequently identified causes of childhood encephalitis in several series, although CNS complications occur in only a small fraction of infections. The early form presents within a week of respiratory symptoms with encephalopathy and seizures. The late form follows a gap of more than a week and resembles ADEM, transverse myelitis or Guillain-Barre syndrome, sometimes with striatal necrosis or stroke. Outcomes range from full recovery to persistent deficits, especially in the late form.
det.diagnosis: Testing both the throat (PCR) and CSF (PCR) and pairing it with serology gives the best evidence; IgM can persist for months and PCR can be positive in carriers. CSF PCR is positive mainly in the early form. MRI pattern guides classification: cortical or normal in early disease, multifocal demyelination, striatal or cord lesions in late disease. MOG and AQP4 antibodies are checked when demyelination is seen, because they change long-term management.
det.treatment: Give an antibiotic that reaches the CNS and is active against mycoplasma: doxycycline or a fluoroquinolone penetrate the CSF better than macrolides, and macrolide resistance is common in East Asia, so doxycycline is now widely used even in young children for short courses. Immune-mediated late disease is treated with high-dose corticosteroids, then IVIG or plasma exchange if needed. Seizures, raised pressure and respiratory illness receive standard supportive care. Antibiotic benefit is uncertain in purely immune forms, but most experts treat while organisms may still be present.
det.prognosis: Most children recover, but a substantial minority, especially with the late immune form, striatal necrosis or stroke, keep neurological sequelae.
pearls: Ask about cough two weeks earlier in a child with ADEM, myelitis or striatal necrosis.
A positive throat PCR alone does not prove causation, because carriage is common; combine timing, PCR and serology.
Amoxicillin and cephalosporins do not act on Mycoplasma, which lacks a cell wall.
det.thd: Mycoplasma pneumoniae เป็นแบคทีเรียไม่มีผนังเซลล์ที่ทำให้ปอดอักเสบในเด็กวัยเรียน บางรายเกิดสมองอักเสบได้สองแบบ คือเกิดเร็วภายในหนึ่งสัปดาห์จากเชื้อเข้าสมองโดยตรง และเกิดช้าหลังหนึ่งสัปดาห์จากภูมิคุ้มกัน ซึ่งคล้าย ADEM, transverse myelitis หรือ GBS วินิจฉัยด้วย PCR จากคอและน้ำไขสันหลังร่วมกับ serology รักษาด้วยยาที่เข้าสมองได้ดี เช่น doxycycline หรือ fluoroquinolone และให้สเตียรอยด์ขนาดสูง IVIG หรือ plasma exchange ในชนิดภูมิคุ้มกัน

ddx.pt: The same picture after other infections or vaccines; Mycoplasma is one trigger to look for
Temporal lobe involvement and CSF HSV PCR positive; aciclovir until excluded
Rapid coma after influenza or other viral illness with symmetric thalamic necrosis and high transaminases

name: Jumping disorders (culture-bound startle syndromes)
formal: A group of socially shaped startle syndromes in which an exaggerated jump to a sudden stimulus is followed by stereotyped learned behaviour such as shouting, swearing, striking out, echolalia, echopraxia or automatic obedience to commands; described in specific communities and regarded as behavioural rather than a structural brainstem disorder.
simple: People in certain communities who, when startled, jump a lot and then copy words or actions or obey shouted orders without thinking; it is a learned behaviour pattern, not brain damage.
th: Jumping disorders เป็นกลุ่มอาการสะดุ้งเกินที่ผูกกับวัฒนธรรม เช่น latah ในมาเลเซีย/อินโดนีเซีย และ bah-tschi ในไทย เมื่อถูกทำให้ตกใจจะสะดุ้งแรงแล้วพูดตาม ทำท่าตาม หรือทำตามคำสั่งโดยอัตโนมัติ ถือเป็นพฤติกรรมที่เรียนรู้ทางสังคม ไม่ใช่รอยโรคในก้านสมอง
tempoNote: Brief episodes provoked by sudden noise, touch or a shouted command, recurring for years; usually begins in adolescence or adulthood after repeated teasing within the group
feat: An exaggerated jump to an unexpected sound, poke or shout, followed by automatic actions that the person says they cannot hold back
Echolalia (repeating words), echopraxia (copying movements), coprolalia-like outbursts and forced obedience, e.g. throwing an object when told to throw
Episodes are often deliberately provoked by friends or co-workers, and the behaviour is accepted or even entertaining within the community
Normal neurological examination between episodes; no stiffness in infancy, no falls with injury, no response to stimulus repetition pattern typical of hyperekplexia
Reported among French-Canadian lumberjacks, Cajuns, Malay and Javanese women (latah), Siberian groups (myriachit) and Thai adults (bah-tschi)
inv: Mainly clinical; video of a provoked episode and the social history are the most useful data
Neurological examination and, if doubt remains, MRI brain to exclude a structural brainstem or frontal lesion
Startle EMG studies (if available) show a startle reflex that is not abnormally large or that habituates, unlike hereditary hyperekplexia
Genetic testing for GLRA1/SLC6A5 only if onset was neonatal or there is a family history of stiffness and falls

case.who: 52-year-old woman who sells fruit at a market in Pattani
case.story: Since her twenties, whenever a neighbour claps behind her she jumps, shouts a rude word and copies the neighbour's gestures; if someone shouts 'drop it' she drops whatever she is holding. Her stall-mates provoke this for fun.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination, no stiffness, normal tone and reflexes; a surprise clap produces a jump followed by repetition of the examiner's last phrase.
case.tests: MRI brain normal; no family history of neonatal stiffness.
case.q: What is the best label for this behaviour and what distinguishes it from hyperekplexia?
case.a: A culture-bound jumping disorder (latah type); after the jump come learned echo and obedience behaviours, which do not occur in hyperekplexia, where the startle is a stiff reflex with falls and onset in infancy.

1 - Clinical overview and phenomenology of movement disorders

det.patho: These syndromes are thought to arise when a normal startle reaction is repeatedly provoked and rewarded inside a close social group, so that a learned behavioural sequence becomes attached to the jump. The startle reflex itself is usually physiologically normal or only mildly enlarged. Cultural expectations, dissociation and operant conditioning are proposed mechanisms, and no consistent structural lesion or gene has been found.
det.clinical: Onset is usually in adolescence or adult life, often after years of being teased. A sudden stimulus causes a jump, a shout or swear word, and then copying of speech or movements, or immediate obedience to an order even if it is embarrassing or dangerous. The person is aware and may be distressed, but episodes are often tolerated or encouraged by the group. Examination between attacks is normal, and the condition is lifelong but not progressive.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis rests on the history, the social setting and observation of a provoked episode. The key step is to separate it from hyperekplexia (infant onset, stiffness, falls, glycine pathway genes), startle epilepsy (EEG change, structural lesion) and tics. Brain imaging and EMG are used only when the picture is atypical. Labelling it as culture-bound rather than as a brainstem disease avoids unnecessary drugs.
det.treatment: Explanation and reassurance, asking family and co-workers to stop provoking episodes, and simple behavioural approaches are the main tools. Cognitive behavioural therapy can reduce distress and automatic responses. Clonazepam is not routinely helpful because the reflex is not the core problem. Safety advice is important when obedience behaviour could lead to injury.
det.prognosis: Benign and non-progressive; episodes may lessen when provocation stops.
pearls: Jump followed by echolalia, echopraxia or forced obedience points to a jumping disorder; jump followed by stiffness and a fall points to hyperekplexia.
Ask who provokes the episodes; social reinforcement is a defining feature.
A Thai form (bah-tschi) has been described, so this can be met in Thai clinics.
det.thd: Jumping disorders เช่น latah และ bah-tschi เกิดจากการสะดุ้งปกติที่ถูกกระตุ้นซ้ำ ๆ ในกลุ่มสังคมจนกลายเป็นพฤติกรรมที่เรียนรู้ เมื่อตกใจผู้ป่วยจะสะดุ้งแล้วพูดตาม ทำท่าตาม หรือทำตามคำสั่ง ตรวจร่างกายปกติ ต่างจาก hyperekplexia ที่เริ่มตั้งแต่ทารก ตัวแข็งและล้มเมื่อสะดุ้ง การรักษาหลักคืออธิบาย ขอให้คนรอบข้างเลิกแกล้ง และใช้พฤติกรรมบำบัด

qx.stem: A 47-year-old woman from Songkhla is brought by her daughter because, for twenty years, any sudden tap on her shoulder makes her leap, shout an obscene word and then imitate whatever the person nearby is doing. Market friends startle her on purpose. She has never fallen stiffly, and her neurological examination and MRI brain are normal.
qx.q: Which feature best separates her condition from hereditary hyperekplexia?
opts: Onset in adult life after repeated provocation
A normal brain MRI
Learned echo and obedience behaviour after the jump
A strong startle to unexpected noise
Response of the jump to clonazepam
qx.why: In culture-bound jumping disorders (latah, bah-tschi) the jump is followed by stereotyped learned behaviour such as echolalia, echopraxia and forced obedience, which hyperekplexia never shows. Hyperekplexia begins in infancy with stiffness and falls and is linked to glycine receptor pathway genes. A normal MRI and an exaggerated startle occur in both, and clonazepam helps hyperekplexia rather than jumping disorders.

name: Jumpy stump
formal: Involuntary jerks, spasms or chaotic writhing movements of an amputation stump that persist long after surgery, usually accompanied by stump or phantom pain, attributed to abnormal afferent input from injured nerves and secondary reorganisation of spinal and cortical motor circuits.
simple: After a limb amputation, the remaining stump keeps jerking or twitching by itself, often with pain, sometimes for many years.
th: Jumpy stump คือการกระตุกหรือเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติของตอแขนขาหลังตัดออก มักมาพร้อมอาการปวดตอหรือปวด phantom limb อาจเป็นต่อเนื่องหลายปี เชื่อว่าเกิดจากเส้นประสาทที่ถูกตัดส่งสัญญาณผิดปกติเข้าไขสันหลังและสมอง
tempoNote: Brief jerking soon after amputation is common and settles in weeks; the true syndrome starts weeks to months later and can last for decades
feat: Repetitive jerks, tonic spasms or irregular chaotic movements of an upper or lower limb stump, sometimes exhausting and disturbing sleep
Usually preceded or accompanied by severe stump pain, neuroma pain or phantom limb pain
Movements can be triggered by touching the stump, by voluntary movement or by emotional stress
Onset is delayed after the amputation, distinguishing it from the short-lived postoperative stump jerking that resolves spontaneously
A drug-induced phantom dyskinesia (for example after dopamine-blocking antiemetics) is a rare variant
inv: Clinical observation and video; examine the stump for neuroma, infection, ill-fitting prosthesis and skin breakdown
Ultrasound or MRI of the stump to look for a neuroma or local pathology
Surface EMG to characterise the jerks (segmental myoclonus pattern versus dystonic spasms)
Spinal MRI if there are other segmental signs suggesting a cord or root lesion

case.story: His right leg was amputated above the knee after a road accident two years ago. For the past 18 months the stump has jerked many times an hour, worse at night and when he fits his prosthesis, with burning stump pain.
case.exam: Irregular flexion jerks of the stump at rest, provoked by tapping a tender point at the distal scar; no other neurological signs.
case.tests: Ultrasound shows a 9 mm neuroma of the sciatic nerve stump; surface EMG shows brief irregular bursts in the hip flexors.
case.q: What is this syndrome and what treatment is reasonable?
case.a: Painful jumpy stump; treat the pain generator (neuroma management, neuropathic pain drugs) and consider botulinum toxin into the jerking muscles or clonazepam, with prosthetic and rehabilitation input.

1 Clinical overview and phenomenology of movement disorders - Jumpy stumps

det.patho: Section of a peripheral nerve produces abnormal ectopic firing from the nerve end and neuroma, which bombards the spinal segment that supplied the lost limb. Loss of normal sensory input, axonal sprouting and plastic reorganisation in the spinal cord and sensorimotor cortex are thought to produce involuntary motor output, explaining the close tie with phantom pain. Some cases behave like peripherally induced segmental myoclonus and others like dystonic spasms.
det.clinical: Patients describe jerks, spasms or flailing movements of the stump that start weeks to months after the amputation and may last for decades. Pain usually comes first and the movements often worsen as the pain flares. Touch, prosthesis use, voluntary movement or stress can trigger them. They interfere with prosthesis fitting, sleep and quality of life and should be separated from the normal brief jerks of the first postoperative weeks.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by video and surface EMG. The stump should be examined for neuroma, infection, bone spur or poorly fitting socket, with ultrasound or MRI as needed. Spinal imaging is done if segmental signs suggest a cord or root lesion, and functional features should be sought because functional movements can follow injury too.
det.treatment: Treatment targets both pain and movement. Options include neuropathic pain medicines (gabapentinoids, tricyclics), neuroma management (injection, revision or targeted muscle reinnervation in specialist centres), clonazepam or levetiracetam for myoclonic jerks and botulinum toxin injected into the overactive stump muscles. Mirror therapy and graded motor imagery may help phantom pain. Results are variable, and a multidisciplinary amputee rehabilitation team is ideal.
det.prognosis: Often chronic and difficult to treat; partial improvement is common when the pain source is controlled.
pearls: Ask about stump pain and neuroma in any amputee with jerking of the stump; pain usually comes first.
Early postoperative stump twitching usually settles, whereas delayed-onset jumpy stump tends to persist.
It is classed with the peripherally induced movement disorders, alongside painful legs and moving toes.
det.thd: Jumpy stump เกิดหลังตัดแขนขาไปแล้วหลายสัปดาห์ถึงหลายเดือน ตอแขนขากระตุกหรือเกร็งเอง มักมีอาการปวดตอหรือ phantom pain นำมาก่อน กลไกคือเส้นประสาทที่ถูกตัดและ neuroma ส่งสัญญาณผิดปกติ ทำให้วงจรไขสันหลังและสมองปรับตัวผิดปกติ ควรตรวจหา neuroma และปัญหาเบ้าขาเทียม รักษาด้วยยาแก้ปวดประสาท จัดการ neuroma ยา clonazepam หรือฉีด botulinum toxin ร่วมกับทีมฟื้นฟู

name: Pisa syndrome
formal: A lateral flexion of the trunk of at least about 10 degrees, which typically worsens while sitting or walking and largely corrects when lying supine or with passive mobilisation, seen in Parkinson disease, atypical parkinsonism and after exposure to antipsychotics or cholinesterase inhibitors.
simple: The body leans to one side like the Leaning Tower of Pisa, usually in Parkinson disease or as a side effect of certain medicines, and straightens when lying down.
th: Pisa syndrome คือลำตัวเอียงไปด้านข้างอย่างน้อยราว 10 องศา เป็นมากขึ้นเวลานั่งหรือเดิน และหายหรือดีขึ้นเมื่อนอนหงาย พบใน Parkinson disease, MSA และเป็นผลข้างเคียงของยาต้านโรคจิตหรือยากลุ่ม cholinesterase inhibitor
tempoNote: Acute or subacute after starting or increasing a drug (days to weeks), or slowly progressive over months to years in parkinsonian disorders
feat: Lateral bending of the trunk, often away from the side of worse parkinsonism in PD (direction varies), worse when standing and walking
Corrects partly or fully when supine or with passive pushing, unlike fixed scoliosis
Back pain, imbalance and difficulty with daily activities; may coexist with camptocormia or antecollis
Drug-associated forms follow antipsychotics, cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine), antidepressants or dopaminergic changes
An early severe Pisa posture is a red flag for multiple system atrophy
inv: Clinical measurement of the lateral flexion angle standing and supine (photographs or a wall goniometer)
Medication review and timing relative to any new drug
Spine radiographs or MRI to exclude fixed scoliosis, vertebral fracture or disc disease
EMG of paraspinal and abdominal oblique muscles to identify overactive muscles before botulinum toxin, and muscle MRI if myopathy is suspected

case.who: 71-year-old retired teacher from Chiang Mai with Parkinson disease for 8 years
case.story: Three weeks after donepezil was added for memory decline, her family notice she leans increasingly to the right when sitting and walking, with low back pain.
case.exam: Asymmetric parkinsonism worse on the left; trunk leans about 20 degrees to the right when standing, almost fully corrected when lying supine.
case.tests: Spine radiograph shows mild degenerative change but no fixed scoliosis.
case.q: What is the posture and what is the first step in management?
case.a: Pisa syndrome, probably drug-associated; reduce or stop the cholinesterase inhibitor, review dopaminergic therapy and start physiotherapy, considering botulinum toxin if it persists.

det.patho: The mechanism is debated: asymmetric basal ganglia output leading to axial dystonia, impaired vestibular and proprioceptive integration of body verticality, and secondary paraspinal myopathy all contribute. Drugs that alter dopaminergic or cholinergic balance in the striatum can trigger it acutely. In longstanding cases soft-tissue changes and spinal degeneration make the posture less reversible.
det.clinical: It occurs in a minority of people with Parkinson disease and more often in multiple system atrophy and dementia with Lewy bodies. The tilt becomes more obvious with fatigue and walking, causes back pain and impairs balance and reaching. Drug-induced cases can appear within days to weeks of a new medicine. Patients are often unaware of the tilt until others point it out.
det.diagnosis: International consensus (2016) defines it as lateral trunk flexion of at least 10 degrees that can be almost fully corrected by passive mobilisation or lying supine. Measure the angle standing and supine, review all drugs, image the spine to exclude fixed scoliosis or fracture and use EMG to map overactive paraspinal and oblique muscles. Distinguish it from camptocormia and from structural scoliosis.
det.treatment: First remove or reduce causative drugs and optimise dopaminergic therapy; drug-related cases often improve within weeks. Intensive physiotherapy and postural rehabilitation are the mainstay. EMG-guided botulinum toxin into overactive lumbar paraspinal or oblique muscles combined with rehabilitation can help selected patients. The effect of deep brain stimulation on Pisa syndrome is inconsistent, and spinal surgery is reserved for fixed deformity because of high complication rates.
det.prognosis: Early drug-induced cases are often reversible; chronic cases in neurodegenerative disease tend to become fixed.
pearls: Ask what was started recently: cholinesterase inhibitors and antipsychotics are classic triggers.
If it straightens when supine, it is Pisa syndrome rather than fixed scoliosis.
A severe early Pisa posture is a supportive red flag for MSA in the MDS criteria.
det.thd: Pisa syndrome คือลำตัวเอียงไปข้างหนึ่งเกิน 10 องศาซึ่งแก้ได้เมื่อนอนหรือดันกลับ พบใน PD, MSA และหลังใช้ยาต้านโรคจิตหรือ donepezil/rivastigmine ควรทบทวนยาที่เพิ่งเริ่ม ถ่ายภาพกระดูกสันหลังเพื่อแยก scoliosis และใช้ EMG หากล้ามเนื้อที่เกร็ง การรักษาคือลดยาต้นเหตุ ปรับยา dopaminergic กายภาพบำบัด และพิจารณาฉีด botulinum toxin

qx.stem: A 74-year-old man with Parkinson disease for nine years developed visual hallucinations and memory decline, so rivastigmine patches were started and quetiapine added. One month later he leans about 25 degrees to the left when seated and walking, but lies straight on the examination couch. Spine films show no fixed scoliosis.
qx.q: What should be done first?

Bilateral subthalamic deep brain stimulation

DBS has inconsistent effects on this posture and spinal surgery is reserved for fixed deformity. Simply increasing levodopa does not address the trigger.

name: Hemimasticatory spasm
formal: A rare peripheral movement disorder with paroxysmal, painful, unilateral contractions of jaw-closing muscles (masseter, temporalis, sometimes medial pterygoid) caused by ectopic excitation of the motor branch of the trigeminal nerve, frequently associated with localised scleroderma or progressive hemifacial atrophy.
simple: Sudden painful clenching of the jaw on one side, a bit like hemifacial spasm but in the chewing muscles, often in people with one-sided facial skin and fat shrinkage.
th: Hemimasticatory spasm คือการเกร็งกระตุกของกล้ามเนื้อเคี้ยว (masseter, temporalis) ข้างเดียวเป็นพัก ๆ และปวด อาจกัดลิ้นหรือฟันหัก เกิดจากเส้นประสาทสมองคู่ที่ 5 ส่วน motor ถูกกระตุ้นผิดปกติ มักพบร่วมกับ morphea หรือ Parry–Romberg
tempoNote: Brief spasms of seconds to minutes, triggered by chewing or talking, recurring over years; usually begins in young or middle adult life
feat: Sudden unilateral jaw closure with brief twitches or longer tonic spasms, often painful, sometimes causing tongue biting, dislocation or broken teeth
Triggered by chewing, biting, speaking or yawning; may occur in sleep
Masseter or temporalis hypertrophy on the affected side
Often with ipsilateral facial hemiatrophy or localised scleroderma (morphea en coup de sabre / Parry–Romberg)
Facial expression muscles and eyelids are spared, unlike hemifacial spasm
inv: EMG of masseter and temporalis showing irregular high-frequency bursts during spasms; the masseter inhibitory (silent) period may be absent during spasms
Blink reflex and facial nerve studies normal, helping to separate it from hemifacial spasm
MRI of brain and trigeminal pathway to exclude compression, tumour or demyelination
Dermatology review and skin biopsy if morphea is suspected; ANA or other autoimmune work-up as indicated

case.story: For three years the left side of her jaw suddenly clamps shut while eating or talking, lasting a few seconds and very painful; once she cracked a molar. She also has a slowly deepening groove on the left forehead.
case.exam: Hypertrophied left masseter; a linear area of skin atrophy on the left forehead; no eyelid or mouth-corner twitching; trigeminal sensation normal.
case.tests: EMG shows irregular high-frequency bursts in left masseter and temporalis during spasms; blink reflex normal; MRI shows no compressive lesion.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the best symptomatic treatment?
case.a: Hemimasticatory spasm associated with localised scleroderma (morphea en coup de sabre); botulinum toxin injection into the left masseter and temporalis is the most effective treatment.

det.patho: The likely mechanism is focal injury to the trigeminal motor root, possibly from deep tissue changes of localised scleroderma, leading to ephaptic transmission and ectopic discharges, much like facial nerve hyperactivity in hemifacial spasm. The jaw-closing muscles supplied by that branch therefore contract involuntarily. Vascular compression has been proposed in a few cases without skin disease.
det.clinical: It is rare and usually begins in young to middle adults, women more than men. Spasms are unilateral, sudden and often painful, ranging from twitches to sustained clenching lasting minutes, and are set off by chewing or talking. Chronic spasms cause masseter hypertrophy, dental damage and temporomandibular problems. A careful look at the face often reveals ipsilateral hemiatrophy or a linear scleroderma lesion.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, confirmed by EMG showing irregular bursts in masseter and temporalis and changes in the masseter inhibitory reflex, with normal facial nerve studies. MRI excludes structural lesions of the trigeminal pathway. Dermatological assessment for morphea is important because it changes management and prognosis.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin injected into the overactive masseter and temporalis is the treatment of choice and usually gives marked relief for several months. Carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, clonazepam or gabapentin can help partially. Dental protection with a night guard reduces tooth damage. Microvascular decompression of the motor trigeminal root has been reported in selected refractory cases; active morphea is treated by dermatology.
det.prognosis: Chronic but benign; repeated botulinum toxin keeps most patients comfortable.
pearls: Think of it as hemifacial spasm of the jaw: trigeminal motor, not facial nerve.
Look at the face for morphea or Parry–Romberg hemiatrophy.
Botulinum toxin into masseter and temporalis is first-line.
det.thd: Hemimasticatory spasm เป็นภาวะที่กล้ามเนื้อเคี้ยวข้างเดียวหดเกร็งเป็นพัก ๆ และปวด เกิดจากเส้นประสาท trigeminal ส่วน motor ถูกกระตุ้นผิดปกติ มักพบร่วมกับ localised scleroderma หรือ Parry–Romberg ต่างจาก hemifacial spasm ที่เป็นกล้ามเนื้อใบหน้า วินิจฉัยด้วย EMG และ MRI รักษาด้วยการฉีด botulinum toxin ที่ masseter และ temporalis ร่วมกับเฝือกฟัน

Botulinum toxin into the overactive masticatory muscles is the most effective treatment. Facial nerve decompression treats hemifacial spasm, and anticholinergics or levodopa target dystonia rather than this peripheral disorder.

name: Obsessional slowness
formal: A disabling slowness of everyday goal-directed activities in obsessive-compulsive disorder, caused by repeated checking, perfectionism, mental rituals and the need to do things in an exact order, sometimes with mild parkinsonian-like signs but without true bradykinesia (no decrement) or nigrostriatal dopamine loss.
simple: A person with severe obsessive-compulsive disorder takes hours to wash, dress or eat because they must do each step in a precise way, so they look slow like Parkinson disease, but the cause is the obsessions.
th: Obsessional slowness คือการทำกิจวัตรช้ามากในผู้ป่วยโรคย้ำคิดย้ำทำ เพราะต้องทำทีละขั้นตอนอย่างถูกต้องและตรวจซ้ำ ดูคล้าย Parkinson แต่ไม่มี bradykinesia แท้ (ไม่มี decrement) และ DaT scan ปกติ
tempoNote: Gradual onset in adolescence or early adulthood, often with longstanding obsessive-compulsive symptoms; course fluctuates with stress
feat: Extremely slow washing, dressing, eating or walking through doorways because of rituals, checking and the need for exactness
Long pauses and hesitations before or during actions, with repeated restarts
May show reduced arm swing, hypomimia or flexed posture, but finger and foot tapping show no progressive decrement
Associated obsessions about symmetry, order or doing things just right; insight may be limited
Can coexist with tics or Tourette syndrome
inv: Careful psychiatric assessment with a structured OCD scale (Y-BOCS)
Neurological examination focused on decrement, rigidity and rest tremor to separate it from parkinsonism
DaT-SPECT is normal when a neurodegenerative cause is genuinely in doubt
MRI brain to exclude basal ganglia or frontal lesions in atypical or late-onset cases

case.story: Over two years he has become so slow that a morning shower takes three hours and dressing another hour; he must step over the bathroom threshold with the right foot first and restart if interrupted. His mother fears Parkinson disease.
case.exam: Long pauses before starting tasks, reduced facial expression and slow gait, but finger tapping is slow to start without decrement; no rigidity or tremor.
case.tests: MRI brain normal; Y-BOCS shows severe OCD; DaT-SPECT normal.
case.q: What explains his slowness and what treatment is appropriate?
case.a: Obsessional slowness in severe OCD; treat with cognitive behavioural therapy (exposure with response prevention plus prompting and pacing) and a high-dose SSRI or clomipramine, with neurosurgery only in refractory cases.

det.patho: Obsessional slowness reflects dysfunction of cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loops involving orbitofrontal and anterior cingulate cortex and the caudate, the same network implicated in OCD. Patients have trouble initiating and completing goal-directed sequences because each step is interrupted by doubt, checking and perfectionism. The nigrostriatal dopamine system is intact, which is why dopaminergic drugs do not help.
det.clinical: It is an uncommon but severe form of OCD that mostly affects young men. Patients spend hours on routine tasks, and the slowness is selective for ritualised activities. They may appear parkinsonian with reduced spontaneous movement and arm swing, but motor examination lacks decrement and true rigidity. Insight is often poor and associated depression and functional disability are common.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is made by recognising underlying obsessive-compulsive symptoms and showing that slowness is linked to rituals rather than to a motor deficit. Structured scales such as Y-BOCS help. In older patients or atypical cases, brain imaging and DaT-SPECT help exclude a neurodegenerative or structural cause.
det.treatment: Cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention, adapted with prompting, shaping and time targets, is the core treatment. Serotonergic drugs at full dose (SSRIs or clomipramine) are added, and antipsychotic augmentation may be used in partial responders. In expert centres, very refractory OCD is sometimes treated with DBS targeting the ventral capsule and adjacent striatum. Levodopa is not useful.
det.prognosis: Chronic with partial response in many patients; intensive behavioural treatment can produce meaningful functional gains.
pearls: Slowness without decrement, linked to rituals, is not parkinsonism.
Ask what the patient is thinking during the pauses; the answer often reveals checking or doubt.
DaT-SPECT is normal, which reassures when Parkinson disease is feared.

name: THAP1 dystonia (DYT6)
formal: Autosomal dominant isolated dystonia with reduced penetrance caused by pathogenic variants in THAP1, a transcription factor that regulates TOR1A; typically begins in childhood or adolescence in the cranial, cervical or arm muscles with prominent laryngeal and oromandibular involvement and variable spread.
simple: An inherited dystonia, first found in Amish-Mennonite families, that usually starts in the neck, face, voice box or arm of a young person and may later involve other body regions.
th: THAP1 dystonia (DYT6) เป็นโรค dystonia ทางพันธุกรรมถ่ายทอดแบบเด่นที่ penetrance ไม่สมบูรณ์ มักเริ่มในเด็กโตหรือวัยรุ่นที่คอ ใบหน้า กล่องเสียง หรือแขน มีปัญหาการพูดเด่น แล้วอาจลามไปส่วนอื่น
tempoNote: Onset usually in childhood to early adulthood (mean mid-teens), progressing over years to segmental or generalised dystonia in many
feat: Onset in the cranial-cervical region or an arm, rather than the leg as in TOR1A (DYT1) dystonia
Prominent speech involvement: spasmodic dysphonia, oromandibular and lingual dystonia causing dysarthria
Spread to segmental or generalised dystonia in a large proportion; legs often relatively spared
Autosomal dominant with reduced penetrance (about 60%) and variable expression within families
Normal cognition and no other neurological signs (isolated dystonia)
inv: Genetic testing for THAP1 (and TOR1A, GNAL, KMT2B, ANO3) using a dystonia gene panel or exome in early-onset isolated dystonia
MRI brain is normal and is done to exclude acquired or degenerative causes
Levodopa trial to exclude dopa-responsive dystonia in young-onset cases
Copper studies and slit-lamp examination to exclude Wilson disease

case.who: 16-year-old high-school student from Nakhon Si Thammarat
case.story: Over two years her voice has become strained and broken and her head pulls to the left; recently her right hand cramps when writing. Her father has had a mild neck tilt for years.
case.exam: Adductor spasmodic dysphonia, left torticollis, jaw-opening dystonia when speaking and dystonic posturing of the right hand when writing; legs normal; cognition normal.
case.tests: MRI brain and copper studies normal; no response to a 1-month levodopa trial; a dystonia gene panel finds a heterozygous pathogenic THAP1 variant, also present in the father.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and how does it influence counselling about DBS?
case.a: THAP1 (DYT6) dystonia; GPi-DBS can help limb and neck dystonia, but benefit is usually less complete than in TOR1A dystonia and speech or laryngeal symptoms often respond poorly.

det.patho: THAP1 encodes a zinc-finger transcription factor that binds DNA and regulates the expression of genes including TOR1A, linking two major forms of isolated dystonia through shared pathways. Pathogenic variants (missense, truncating) cause dystonia with reduced penetrance through altered gene regulation in motor circuits involving the basal ganglia and cerebellum. First mapped in Amish-Mennonite families, it is now found in many populations including Asians.
det.clinical: Onset is commonly in late childhood or adolescence, though adult onset occurs. Cranial-cervical onset is typical, and laryngeal, oromandibular and tongue involvement give a characteristic speech disorder. Many patients progress to segmental or generalised dystonia, with legs least affected. Family members carrying the same variant may have mild focal dystonia or none, so a negative family history does not exclude it.
det.diagnosis: In MDS nomenclature it is DYT-THAP1, an isolated dystonia confirmed by genetic testing, usually within a multi-gene panel or exome for early-onset or familial dystonia. MRI brain is normal. A levodopa trial and copper studies are standard to exclude treatable dopa-responsive dystonia and Wilson disease. Genetic counselling should mention reduced penetrance.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin treats focal targets such as the neck, larynx and jaw. Oral trihexyphenidyl in gradually increasing doses can help young patients, with baclofen or clonazepam as additions. GPi deep brain stimulation is used for disabling segmental or generalised dystonia; it improves limb and trunk dystonia but outcomes are more variable than in TOR1A dystonia, and speech often improves least. Speech therapy and physiotherapy support function.
det.prognosis: Variable; many have lifelong segmental dystonia with speech disability, while some family members remain mildly affected.
pearls: Early-onset dystonia with voice and jaw involvement should prompt THAP1 testing.
TOR1A dystonia starts in a limb and spares the face; THAP1 dystonia favours the cranial and cervical region.
Counsel that GPi-DBS benefit is less predictable and speech may not improve.
det.thd: THAP1 dystonia (DYT6) เป็น dystonia ทางพันธุกรรมแบบเด่นที่ penetrance ไม่สมบูรณ์ มักเริ่มช่วงวัยรุ่นที่คอ กราม ลิ้น หรือกล่องเสียง จึงมีปัญหาการพูดเด่น แล้วลามเป็น segmental หรือ generalised dystonia วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีน หลังแยก DRD และ Wilson แล้ว รักษาด้วย botulinum toxin ยา trihexyphenidyl และ GPi-DBS ซึ่งได้ผลน้อยกว่า DYT1 โดยเฉพาะอาการพูด

Examination shows no other neurological signs. MRI brain and copper studies are normal and a levodopa trial gives no benefit.
qx.q: Which gene is the most likely cause?

GCH1
SGCE
THAP1

TOR1A dystonia usually starts in a limb and spares the voice, GCH1 causes levodopa-responsive dystonia, SGCE causes myoclonus-dystonia and ATP1A3 causes rapid-onset dystonia-parkinsonism.

name: Motor impersistence
formal: Inability to sustain a voluntary movement or posture, for example holding the eyelids shut, the tongue out, the gaze to one side or the hand grip firm, despite adequate strength and an initial good effort; a bedside marker of frontal, right-hemisphere or disconnecting lesions and of neurodegenerative disease such as Huntington's disease.
simple: A person starts an action correctly, such as sticking out the tongue or squeezing a hand, but cannot keep it going and lets go after a few seconds even though the muscles are strong.
th: Motor impersistence คือการที่ผู้ป่วยทำท่าตามสั่งได้ตอนแรกแต่ไม่สามารถคงท่านั้นไว้ เช่น ปิดตาแน่น แลบลิ้น หรือบีบมือ ทั้งที่กำลังกล้ามเนื้อปกติ พบในรอยโรคสมองส่วนหน้าและซีกขวา corpus callosum หรือ thalamus และในโรคเสื่อมของระบบประสาท เช่น Huntington’s disease เป็นสัญญาณที่ตรวจง่ายแต่มักถูกมองข้าม
tempoNote: Acute after a focal stroke or injury; chronic and slowly worsening in neurodegenerative disease such as Huntington's disease
feat: Eyelids drift open, gaze returns to the midline, the tongue slips back into the mouth or the mouth closes, or the grip loosens and tightens in waves although each movement began well
Everyday form: clumsiness, dropping objects and unsteady handshake, which patients sometimes find more troublesome than chorea itself
Seen with right frontal and central lesions, callosal disconnection, thalamic lesions and widespread network disease; isolated basal ganglia lesions rarely produce it
Often accompanies Huntington's disease, Alzheimer's disease and subcortical vascular cognitive impairment, and can track progression in Huntington's disease
Salient targets can reduce it: a patient who loses a moving finger may still follow a face or banknote, so inability to follow even the interesting target means more severe impersistence
inv: Bedside tasks held for 10–20 seconds: sustained eye closure, lateral gaze, tongue protrusion or mouth opening, arm extension and hand grip, noting how long the action lasts and how often it breaks
In Huntington's disease the tongue protrusion task is graded 0–4 in the UHDRS total motor score, but inter-rater reliability for subtle findings is poor
Quantitative tongue-force recording (glossomotography) detects mild cases and improves reliability in research settings
MRI brain for right frontal, callosal or thalamic lesions and for atrophy; HTT CAG repeat testing when chorea, psychiatric change or family history are present

case.who: 49-year-old male taxi driver from Khon Kaen, brought by his wife
case.story: Eighteen months of irritability, dropped cups and restless fidgeting; his father died in a psychiatric hospital in his fifties.
case.exam: Cannot keep the tongue out for more than a couple of seconds, which darts in repeatedly; hand grip surges and fades; eyes open spontaneously during eye closure; mild chorea of the fingers; saccades are slow to start.
case.tests: MRI shows caudate and putamen atrophy; HTT CAG repeat of 43 on the abnormal allele.
case.q: What does the bedside finding indicate, and what is the next step?
case.a: Motor impersistence reflects failure of the attentional-intentional motor network and, with chorea and a family history, points to Huntington's disease; confirm with genetic testing after pre-test counselling and plan multidisciplinary care.

read.where: Clinical description and elicitation; Pathophysiology and anatomical correlates; Validity, sensitivity and specificity
1 - Clinical overview and phenomenology of movement disorders

det.patho: Early writers linked impersistence to the right hemisphere and to a disturbed basic state of alertness, whereas later work described a failure to use sensory feedback to keep a movement going. The attention-intention model treats it as the motor counterpart of lost sensory vigilance. More recent imaging in subcortical vascular cognitive impairment relates it to thinning of dorsal frontoparietal, orbitofrontal and medial prefrontal cortex, which favours a distributed network disorder over a single hemispheric centre. Callosal and thalamic lesions can disrupt the same network, whereas pure basal ganglia lesions rarely cause it.
det.clinical: The patient can follow the instruction at first but cannot maintain it for even a few seconds: the eyes open, the gaze drifts back, the tongue retracts or the grip fluctuates. Patients complain of clumsiness and dropped objects rather than of weakness. It appears after focal right frontal, central, callosal or thalamic lesions from stroke, tumour or trauma, and in neurodegenerative disease including Huntington's disease and Alzheimer's disease. In Huntington's disease it is often an early motor sign, sometimes more disabling than the chorea.
det.diagnosis: Ask the patient to hold each posture for about 10 to 20 seconds, with clear repeated instructions, and time how long the action is sustained. Use several tasks (eye closure, lateral gaze, tongue protrusion, arm extension and grip) because sensitivity varies with technique and the examiner's experience. Normal strength, normal comprehension and attention to the task separate it from weakness, apraxia and inattention. A positive result is a prompt to look for structural or degenerative brain disease with MRI, and in the right setting with genetic testing, because the sign is relatively specific for brain pathology though not for one disease.
det.treatment: The sign itself has no targeted therapy; management is directed at the cause, such as secondary stroke prevention, tumour treatment or multidisciplinary care in Huntington's disease. Occupational therapy can help with dropped objects, safe handling and adaptive grips. Explaining the problem to families helps them recognise that it is neurological and not poor effort or lack of attention. Chorea treatment, where needed, is separate and uses VMAT2 inhibitors.
det.prognosis: Course follows the underlying cause: it may improve after a focal lesion recovers, and tends to worsen as neurodegenerative disease advances.
pearls: Motor impersistence is cheap to test: ask for eye closure, tongue out and a firm grip for 10–20 seconds.
Normal power with a failure to keep going separates impersistence from weakness, and starting well separates it from apraxia.
A positive bedside test warrants imaging or genetic work-up; do not dismiss it as poor cooperation.
det.thd: Motor impersistence คือการไม่สามารถคงการเคลื่อนไหวหรือท่าทางไว้ได้ เช่น หลับตาแน่น แลบลิ้น มองไปด้านข้าง หรือบีบมือ แม้กำลังกล้ามเนื้อปกติและเริ่มทำได้ดีตอนแรก พบจากรอยโรคสมองส่วนหน้าและซีกขวา corpus callosum thalamus และโรคเสื่อม เช่น Huntington’s disease ตรวจโดยให้ผู้ป่วยคงท่า 10–20 วินาที ถ้าพบควรหาสาเหตุด้วย MRI และตรวจพันธุกรรมตามบริบท การรักษาคือรักษาโรคต้นเหตุและให้กิจกรรมบำบัดช่วยเรื่องการหยิบจับ

name: Parkinsonism–hyperpyrexia syndrome
formal: A life-threatening syndrome of fever, severe rigidity, autonomic instability and impaired consciousness in a person with Parkinson’s disease, usually triggered by withdrawal, reduction or poor absorption of dopaminergic treatment; it resembles neuroleptic malignant syndrome without a dopamine blocker.
simple: When someone with Parkinson’s disease suddenly stops or cannot absorb their medicines, they can become extremely stiff, feverish and confused, and need emergency care.
ab: neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome in Parkinson’s disease
th: Parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome คือภาวะฉุกเฉินในผู้ป่วย Parkinson’s disease ที่ขาดยากลุ่มโดพามีนอย่างกะทันหัน ทำให้มีไข้สูง กล้ามเนื้อแข็งมาก สับสน และระบบอัตโนมัติรวน คล้าย neuroleptic malignant syndrome แต่ไม่ได้ใช้ยาต้านโดพามีน ต้องให้ยา levodopa ซ้ำทันที (ผ่านสายให้อาหารถ้าจำเป็น) ร่วมกับให้น้ำและลดไข้
tempoNote: Starts 18 hours to a week after dopaminergic drugs are cut or stopped; fever and confusion usually follow within about 3 to 4 days
feat: Abrupt worsening of rigidity and tremor to an immobile state, followed by fever (sometimes above 41 °C), sweating and tachycardia
Altered consciousness from agitation and confusion to stupor, with mutism in some; seizures or myoclonus occasionally

Triggers: stopping or skipping levodopa, dose reductions after deep brain stimulation, switching formulations, unabsorbed doses during illness or surgery, tolcapone withdrawal, dopamine blockers in a parkinsonian patient

Raised CK (often modest), leucocytosis and dehydration; complications include aspiration pneumonia, venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, kidney failure, and permanent worsening of Parkinson’s disease
Compared with true NMS, onset is slower, CK and white count rise less, and the patient is older, but both are potentially fatal
inv: Review of exact dopaminergic medicines and doses taken in the last week; check whether the patient could swallow or absorb them (surgery, nil by mouth, vomiting, high-protein meals)
CK, renal function, electrolytes (especially sodium), full blood count and blood gas; urine for myoglobin
Infection work-up (blood and urine cultures, chest X-ray, CSF if meningism) because sepsis and aspiration pneumonia cause or accompany the syndrome
ECG, chest imaging or CT pulmonary angiogram if breathlessness suggests embolism, and a swallowing assessment before oral restart

case.who: 71-year-old woman from Lampang with Parkinson’s disease for ten years, treated with levodopa five times a day
case.story: Admitted for a hip fracture, she was kept nil by mouth and her levodopa was omitted for two days. On the third day she became extremely rigid, hot and drowsy.
case.exam: Temperature 39.4 °C, pulse 118, blood pressure 150/95 mmHg, profuse sweating, board-like rigidity, coarse tremor, responds only to loud voice.
case.tests: CK 3,800 U/L, white count 17,000/µL, urea raised; chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation; CSF not needed.
case.q: What is the first step in treatment?
case.a: Restart levodopa immediately, through a nasogastric tube if she cannot swallow, with intravenous fluids, cooling, antibiotics for aspiration pneumonia, thromboprophylaxis and ICU-level monitoring; a dopamine agonist patch or dantrolene may be added in severe cases, and the omission of levodopa should be investigated and prevented.

det.patho: The syndrome is a state of acute central dopamine deficiency. In Parkinson’s disease the striatum depends on exogenous dopaminergic drugs, so withdrawal removes the supply to the nigrostriatal system and also to the hypothalamic dopamine pathways that regulate temperature and to mesolimbic circuits that govern mental state. Patients who developed it had lower cerebrospinal fluid homovanillic acid than comparison patients, which suggests a narrow safety margin in some people. The result is the same hypodopaminergic state that underlies NMS and malignant catatonia.
det.clinical: Rigidity and tremor grow within a day or two, followed by fever, sweating, fast heart rate, confusion and mutism. Some patients have no change in medication but have an intercurrent illness, dehydration or a switch from immediate-release to controlled-release levodopa. Deep brain stimulation can reduce levodopa needs, and abrupt stopping of medication afterwards has caused fatal cases. Death occurs through hyperthermic coma, pulmonary embolism, aspiration or renal failure, and survivors often have more severe parkinsonism than before.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical: fever, rigidity and altered consciousness in a Parkinson patient whose dopaminergic therapy was reduced, interrupted or not absorbed. If there is no change in medication, search for an alternative cause, including dopamine-blocking antiemetics or antipsychotics, infection, serotonin syndrome and catatonia. CK and white count support but are not required. Always look for infection and venous thrombosis.
det.treatment: The key is to restore dopaminergic therapy at once, by nasogastric tube if the patient cannot swallow, and to treat as for NMS: ICU care, fluids, cooling, antimicrobials, nutrition, thromboprophylaxis and airway protection. In more severe cases the book added oral bromocriptine and intravenous dantrolene; today a rotigotine patch or apomorphine is a more practical dopamine agonist route for non-swallowing patients, and dantrolene is used with caution. A trial of three days of pulse methylprednisolone was reported to shorten the course. Prevent recurrence by never stopping dopaminergic drugs abruptly, by giving levodopa on time in hospital (including through a tube), and by avoiding dopamine blockers other than quetiapine or clozapine.
det.prognosis: With early dopaminergic restart, symptoms often reverse in hours to a week, though hospital stays of 1 to 3 weeks are common. Deaths occur, and a number of survivors have a lasting step down in motor function.
pearls: In hospitalised Parkinson patients, give levodopa on time or lose the patient: omissions kill.
Fever plus rigidity after levodopa withdrawal needs levodopa first, not dantrolene first.
No dopamine blockers in Parkinson’s disease, apart from low-dose quetiapine or clozapine.
det.thd: Parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome เกิดในผู้ป่วย Parkinson’s disease ที่หยุดหรือลดยา levodopa กะทันหัน หรือดูดซึมยาไม่ได้ เช่น งดน้ำงดอาหารระหว่างผ่าตัด ผู้ป่วยแข็งเกร็งมาก มีไข้สูง เหงื่อออก สับสน CK อาจสูง ต้องให้ levodopa ซ้ำทันที ผ่านสายให้อาหารได้ ร่วมกับให้น้ำ ลดไข้ รักษาการติดเชื้อ ป้องกันลิ่มเลือด และดูแลในไอซียู การป้องกันคือห้ามหยุดยาโดพามีนอย่างกะทันหันและหลีกเลี่ยงยาต้านโดพามีน

qx.stem: A 68-year-old woman with Parkinson's disease for 12 years is admitted for bowel obstruction. Her levodopa is omitted for three days because she is nil by mouth. She now has temperature 39.1 °C, pulse 122, extreme rigidity, a coarse tremor and confusion. CK is 2,700 U/L and white count 16,000/µL. Chest X-ray and cultures are pending.
qx.q: Which action should be taken first?
opts: Give intravenous haloperidol to control the confusion
Start dantrolene alone and continue to withhold levodopa until the fever settles
Reinstate levodopa immediately by nasogastric tube, with fluids, cooling and a search for infection
Start a serotonin antagonist
Administer intravenous immunoglobulin
qx.why: Fever, rigidity and altered consciousness after withdrawal of dopaminergic therapy in Parkinson's disease is the parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome. The priority is rapid restoration of dopaminergic treatment, via a tube if she cannot swallow, plus intensive supportive care, treatment of infection and prevention of thrombosis. Dopamine blockers such as haloperidol worsen it, dantrolene is an adjunct and not a substitute for levodopa, and serotonin antagonists or IVIG do not address the cause.

name: Hemichorea–hemiballismus associated with non-ketotic hyperglycaemia
formal: A hyperkinetic syndrome of acute hemichorea or hemiballismus in people with severe, often long-standing, uncontrolled hyperglycaemia, characterised by T1-hyperintense signal in the contralateral putamen on MRI and usually resolving after glucose is corrected.
simple: Very high blood sugar can cause one arm and leg to flail or jerk involuntarily, and the movements often stop once the sugar is brought down.
th: Hemichorea-hemiballismus จากน้ำตาลในเลือดสูงแบบ non-ketotic (diabetic striatopathy) พบบ่อยในผู้สูงอายุหญิงเอเชียที่เป็นเบาหวานควบคุมไม่ดี มีการเหวี่ยงแขนขาครึ่งซีกเฉียบพลัน MRI พบความเข้ม T1 สูงที่ putamen ด้านตรงข้าม การรักษาหลักคือลดน้ำตาลและแก้ภาวะ hyperosmolar ส่วนใหญ่หายภายในวันถึงสัปดาห์ และใช้ haloperidol, risperidone หรือ tetrabenazine ถ้าอาการรุนแรง
tempoNote: Appears over hours to days with the hyperglycaemic episode; most resolve within days to weeks after glucose control, though a minority persist beyond 3 months
feat: Acute or subacute involuntary movements of one arm and leg, from small flowing chorea to violent proximal ballism, with alertness and normal strength
Typical patient is elderly, female and Asian with type 2 diabetes, severe hyperglycaemia and often a hyperosmolar state, but ketosis is absent in most
T1 hyperintensity of the contralateral putamen, sometimes with the caudate or globus pallidus, with matching CT hyperdensity; T2 and diffusion changes in about two thirds
Usually improves within hours to days as glucose is corrected; about one in five has mild symptoms beyond 3 months
Second most common cause of hemiballismus worldwide in the book, after small-vessel stroke; relapses occur with later hyperglycaemia
inv: Plasma glucose, HbA1c, osmolality, ketones, sodium and renal function at presentation
MRI brain with T1, T2, SWI and diffusion sequences; CT head to see putaminal hyperdensity and exclude haemorrhage
Stroke and secondary-cause work-up where imaging does not match: lupus, antiphospholipid antibodies, thyroid function, HIV
Repeat imaging after recovery to confirm resolution of the signal change

case.who: 73-year-old woman from Nakhon Sawan with type 2 diabetes who had stopped her medicines
case.story: Four days of constant jerking and flinging of the left arm and leg, with extreme thirst and weight loss.
case.exam: Alert; left hemichorea with intermittent ballism of the shoulder; no weakness; dry mucosa.
case.tests: Glucose 29 mmol/L, ketones negative, osmolality raised, HbA1c 15%; CT shows slight hyperdensity of the right putamen; MRI T1 hyperintensity of the right putamen.
case.q: What is the treatment priority and what is the expected course?
case.a: Correct dehydration and hyperglycaemia with fluids and insulin, avoiding rapid osmolar shifts; add a low-dose dopamine blocker or tetrabenazine only if the movements disturb sleep or injure her. The movements usually fade within days to weeks, and the imaging change clears later.

det.patho: The mechanism is not settled. Autopsy in two patients months after recovery showed gliosis with gemistocytic astrocytes in the striatum, a reaction not typical of infarction, and no blood vessel abnormalities. Hyperglycaemia may switch brain metabolism to the anaerobic use of GABA and acetate, depleting inhibitory output, and hyperviscosity may impair striatal perfusion. Petechial bleeding, calcium and manganese deposition and astrocyte-related paramagnetic effects have been proposed to explain the T1 hyperintensity.
det.clinical: Presentation is with hemichorea or hemiballismus on the side opposite the striatal change, though both sides can occasionally be affected. Women predominate and the disorder is described most from East and Southeast Asia, so the Thai clinician should expect it. The patient is awake with normal strength, and the movements stop in sleep. Many are not known to be diabetic at the time. Recurrent episodes may follow later hyperglycaemia.
det.diagnosis: Take a glucose measurement in every patient with new hemichorea or hemiballismus. The diagnosis rests on severe hyperglycaemia, typical striatal T1 signal on MRI (or hyperdensity on CT) and exclusion of stroke, tumour, infection and autoimmune disease. Lesions on diffusion imaging may be absent or mild. The picture can be reproduced by non-hyperglycaemic causes of striatal injury, so atypical features, bilateral disease or a normal glucose should prompt a wider search.
det.treatment: The first treatment is metabolic: rehydration, insulin and monitoring of electrolytes and osmolality. Neuroleptics (haloperidol, risperidone) or dopamine depleters (tetrabenazine) give relief in severe cases; valproate, clonazepam and other agents are used when these cannot be given. Protect the limb from injury and watch for exhaustion and rhabdomyolysis. Surgery is almost never required. After recovery set a clear diabetes plan, since relapse can follow poor control.
det.prognosis: Most patients recover within days to a few weeks after the glucose is corrected, although about one in five has mild persistent movements beyond 3 months. Recurrence is possible with further hyperglycaemia.
pearls: Measure glucose first in any new unilateral chorea or ballism.
T1-bright putamen without a vascular lesion on MRI should suggest hyperglycaemic hemichorea.
Treat the sugar, not only the movement.
det.thd: Hemichorea-hemiballismus จากภาวะน้ำตาลสูง non-ketotic พบบ่อยในผู้ป่วยเบาหวานสูงอายุหญิงเอเชีย ผู้ป่วยมีแขนขาครึ่งซีกกระตุกเหวี่ยงเฉียบพลันแต่ยังรู้ตัวดีและกำลังปกติ MRI พบ T1 สูงที่ putamen ด้านตรงข้าม ให้ตรวจน้ำตาลทุกรายที่มี chorea หรือ ballism ใหม่ การรักษาคือให้น้ำและ insulin ลดน้ำตาล ให้ haloperidol, risperidone หรือ tetrabenazine เมื่อรบกวนมาก ส่วนใหญ่หายภายในวันถึงสัปดาห์ และควรควบคุมเบาหวานเพื่อป้องกันกลับเป็นซ้ำ

qx.stem: A 70-year-old woman from Roi Et with untreated type 2 diabetes has had three days of flinging and jerking movements of the left arm and leg. She is alert, strength is normal, and the movements stop in sleep. Glucose is 31 mmol/L without ketones. CT shows a mildly hyperdense right putamen, and MRI shows T1 hyperintensity of the same structure without restricted diffusion.
qx.q: What is the best initial treatment?
opts: Pallidotomy
Thrombolysis for acute stroke
Rehydration and insulin to correct hyperglycaemia, adding a low-dose dopamine blocker only if the movements are disabling
High-dose valproate as the sole treatment
Levodopa trial
qx.why: Acute unilateral chorea-ballism with severe hyperglycaemia and a T1-bright putamen is the hyperglycaemic form, common in older Asian women. Correcting the metabolic state often resolves the movements within days to weeks. Dopamine blockers or depleters can be added if symptoms are severe, whereas thrombolysis is wrong without an infarct, surgery is reserved for rare persistent cases and levodopa would aggravate the movements.

ddx.pt: Diffusion restriction in the infarct territory and abrupt onset at a vascular event without hyperglycaemia
Includes other causes such as lacunar infarct, mass lesion or HIV-associated toxoplasmosis where glucose is not extreme
Younger woman with antiphospholipid antibodies, other organ involvement and bilateral chorea
