name: Tic emergencies
formal: Urgent situations arising from tic disorders and Tourette syndrome: severe exacerbations, injury to nerves, spinal cord or eye from violent tics, tic-related pain syndromes, abrupt tics from acute brain disease, and new movements (akathisia, dystonia) caused by anti-tic drugs.
simple: Most tics are mild, but a tic disorder can become an emergency when the tics suddenly flare up, injure the person, or are caused or mimicked by a new illness or medicine.
th: Tic emergencies คือภาวะฉุกเฉินจากโรค tic หรือ Tourette syndrome ได้แก่ tic กำเริบรุนแรง tic แรงจนบาดเจ็บ (เช่น radiculopathy หรือ cervical myelopathy) ปวดจาก tic tic ที่เกิดใหม่เฉียบพลันจากโรคสมอง และการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติใหม่จากยารักษา tic เช่น akathisia ต้องหาตัวกระตุ้น หยุดยาที่ทำให้ tic แย่ลง แยกภาวะอื่น และเลือกยา aripiprazole, risperidone, alpha-agonist หรือ botulinum toxin ตามความเหมาะสม
tempoNote: A flare or a complication develops over days to weeks on a background of chronic tics; secondary tics from encephalitis or stroke appear abruptly
feat: Severe exacerbation of an existing tic disorder, commonly at the start of school, with fatigue, stress, infection or tic-aggravating drugs (stimulants, decongestants, some antidepressants and anticonvulsants)
Neurological injury from violent tics: nerve root or peripheral nerve compression, and cervical myelopathy from whiplash-type neck tics
Painful tic syndromes from the tic itself, from striking objects, from the effort of suppression, or from self-injury
Abrupt tics in an older patient, or with neurological signs, point to encephalitis, post-streptococcal disease, stroke, head injury, drug effect or a functional disorder
New akathisia, dystonia or tardive movements from anti-tic drugs are often mistaken for a tic flare and treated with more of the same drug
inv: Review of drug history and recent changes (stimulants, antihistamines, decongestants, antipsychotics) and of sleep, stress and infection
MRI of the neck and EMG when there is weakness, sensory loss or pain from neck, hip or limb tics
Throat swab, ASO titre and inflammatory markers when an abrupt childhood onset follows streptococcal infection; EEG, brain MRI and CSF if encephalopathy
ECG and QT interval before pimozide or other QT-prolonging drugs

case.who: 14-year-old boy from Pathum Thani with Tourette syndrome since the age of 7
case.story: For three months his head has jerked backward violently dozens of times an hour; now both hands are tingling and he drops pencils.
case.exam: Frequent forceful neck extension tics, hyperreflexia in the arms and brisk knee jerks, mild spastic gait, clumsy hand function.
case.tests: MRI cervical spine shows narrowing of the canal at C4–C5 with intramedullary T2 hyperintensity; EMG normal.
case.q: What is the emergency and the plan?
case.a: Cervical myelopathy from violent neck tics. Treat the tics urgently (for example aripiprazole or risperidone, botulinum toxin to neck muscles, and a cervical collar for protection), involve spinal surgeons and avoid neck manipulation.

det.patho: Tics arise from dysfunction of cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits that releases unwanted sensorimotor programs; premonitory urges and relief on performing a tic are characteristic. The pattern waxes and wanes, with a peak between 7 and 15 years. Physical injury results from the repetitive forceful movements of a tic, and secondary tics from encephalitis or stroke reflect striatal damage. Drug-induced movement disorders reflect dopamine blockade.
det.clinical: Most patients never need emergency care, but an acute exacerbation can reach a point where school, sleep or safety are in jeopardy. Severe neck-extension tics may cause radiculopathy, myelopathy or vertebral artery injury, and hip-thrusting tics have caused sciatic nerve compression. Pain may arise from the tic, from suppression effort or from self-injury. Abrupt onset in an adult or a child with fever, confusion or focal signs calls for investigation. Drugs prescribed for tics can produce akathisia, acute dystonia and tardive syndromes that are misread as tic flares.
det.diagnosis: Define the pattern: age at onset, premonitory urge, ability to suppress, variability and family history. Identify exacerbating factors, including drugs. For injury, image the relevant spine or limb and perform EMG. For abrupt tics, look for infection, autoimmune disease, stroke, head injury, toxic and metabolic causes, and consider functional tic-like behaviour when complex movements begin suddenly in adolescence. Distinguish new akathisia or dystonia, which the patient perceives as involuntary and which does not improve with distraction.
det.treatment: Remove triggers, restore sleep and treat comorbid anxiety, ADHD and OCD. Education and comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics (habit reversal) are first-line for many patients. When drugs are needed, alpha-2 agonists (clonidine, guanfacine), aripiprazole or risperidone are widely preferred today, with tetrabenazine, valbenazine or deutetrabenazine as alternatives; pimozide, which the book favoured, is now used rarely because of QT prolongation. Botulinum toxin suits focal disabling tics, and deep brain stimulation is for severe refractory adults. When a tic-related injury is present, protect the spine, treat the tics aggressively and involve surgeons.
det.prognosis: Tics typically improve in late adolescence, and emergencies are self-limited when triggers are removed. Neurological injury can be permanent if not recognised early.
pearls: A new involuntary movement after starting an anti-tic drug may be akathisia, not a worse tic.
Violent neck tics can cause myelopathy; image the spine.
Stimulants and decongestants commonly worsen tics.
det.thd: Tic emergencies คือภาวะฉุกเฉินในผู้ป่วย tic หรือ Tourette เช่น tic กำเริบรุนแรงจนไปโรงเรียนไม่ได้ tic แรงทำให้เกิดการบาดเจ็บของรากประสาทหรือไขสันหลังส่วนคอ ปวดจาก tic tic ใหม่ที่เกิดฉับพลันจากโรคสมอง และการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติจากยา เช่น akathisia ที่มักถูกเข้าใจผิดว่าเป็น tic แย่ลง ต้องหาตัวกระตุ้น ปรับยา ทำ MRI คอเมื่อมีอาการชาหรืออ่อนแรง ใช้ aripiprazole, risperidone, clonidine หรือ botulinum toxin ตามความเหมาะสม

qx.stem: A 17-year-old boy with Tourette syndrome was started on pimozide three weeks ago, and the dose was doubled last week because his legs seemed 'worse'. He now cannot sit still, shifts his weight constantly, says he feels an unbearable inner restlessness and paces the corridor. His tics are unchanged in frequency.
qx.q: What is the most likely explanation and next step?
opts: Tic exacerbation; increase the pimozide further
Akathisia induced by the dopamine blocker; reduce the dose or change drug and consider propranolol, a benzodiazepine or an anticholinergic
Sydenham's chorea; start penicillin
Functional movement disorder; stop all medicines and refer to psychiatry
Oculogyric crisis; give intravenous diphenhydramine only
qx.why: New inner restlessness and leg movements soon after starting and raising a dopamine blocker, with unchanged tics, are acute akathisia, the commonest drug-induced movement disorder mistaken for a tic flare. The response is to lower the dose or switch drug and give propranolol, benzodiazepine or an anticholinergic. Raising the dose would worsen it, and nothing in the history points to chorea, a functional disorder or dystonia.

name: Malignant phonic tics
formal: Severe, frequent and disabling vocal tics in Tourette syndrome, including loud screaming, barking and refractory coprolalia, that resist usual treatment, lead to social, occupational or physical harm and may respond to botulinum toxin injection of the laryngeal muscles.
simple: Some people with Tourette syndrome have vocal tics so loud, frequent or offensive that they cannot work, study or stay safe, and ordinary tic drugs do not help.
th: Malignant phonic tics คือเสียง tic ที่รุนแรง ดัง ถี่ หรือหยาบคาย (coprolalia) ใน Tourette syndrome จนผู้ป่วยทำงานหรือเรียนไม่ได้ เสี่ยงถูกทำร้ายหรือบาดเจ็บ และไม่ตอบสนองต่อยามาตรฐาน อาจรักษาด้วยยากลุ่ม dopamine blocker หรือ tetrabenazine และฉีด botulinum toxin เข้ากล้ามเนื้อสายเสียง (thyroarytenoid) ซึ่งลดเสียงและความรู้สึกอยากทำ tic ได้
tempoNote: A chronic tic disorder with severe vocal tics that can persist or intensify for months to years, typically after the usual teen peak; the crisis is the degree of disability, not abrupt onset
feat: Loud, repetitive barking, screaming, grunting or yelping, or complex vocalisations such as echolalia, palilalia and coprolalia
Preceded by a premonitory urge, usually felt in the throat or chest, and relief on performing the tic; transient suppression is possible
Coprolalia occurs in a minority of patients with Tourette syndrome (reports vary from under 10% to over a half in clinic series) and persists into adulthood in a few
Consequences: school or job loss, fights and assaults, isolation, depression, anxiety, and sometimes self-injury and physical harm from forceful tics
Often accompanied by obsessive-compulsive disorder, ADHD, rage attacks and self-injurious compulsions
inv: Clinical diagnosis; confirm tic phenomenology and exclude functional or drug-induced causes
Review of medicines already tried (dopamine blockers, tetrabenazine, alpha-agonists, SSRIs) and their doses and side effects
ENT or laryngeal evaluation with flexible laryngoscopy and EMG guidance before toxin injection
Screening for depression, suicidality, OCD and ADHD; ECG before QT-prolonging drugs

case.who: 19-year-old man from Chiang Rai, a university student with Tourette syndrome since childhood
case.story: Over the past year his loud barking and shouted obscenities worsened until he was banned from lectures and was beaten by a stranger on the bus. Risperidone and clonidine have reduced his motor tics but not the vocal ones.
case.exam: Frequent loud barks and shouted words several times a minute, heard in the next room; vocal cord movements normal, with strong urge felt in the throat.
case.tests: ECG normal; no evidence of structural brain disease; mood and anxiety screening show moderate depression.
case.q: What further options are available?
case.a: Malignant phonic tics. Offer habit-reversal therapy and treat depression, optimise the antipsychotic or add another approved anti-tic agent, and consider EMG-guided botulinum toxin injection into one thyroarytenoid muscle, accepting a transient weak voice and mild swallowing difficulty.

det.patho: Phonic tics are motor tics of respiratory, laryngeal, pharyngeal, oral or nasal muscles. They are thought to arise from disinhibition of cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loops, with limbic and ventral basal ganglia input generating aberrant impulses. Premonitory sensations are the driver, and tics are often described as semi-voluntary responses to those urges. Coprolalia is not a simple learned behaviour but a complex tic.
det.clinical: Phonic tics are often the most disabling feature of Tourette syndrome. They range from sniffing and throat clearing to screaming, barking and obscene shouts. The social effects can be dramatic, with exclusion, violence directed at the patient and legal trouble. Pain, hoarseness and breathing strain follow forceful vocalisation, and severe self-injury has been reported in the same patients with severe tics. The prevalence and severity vary between series, and most patients improve after adolescence.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical and depends on the typical features of tics: premonitory urge, suppressibility, waxing and waning, and variation. Screen for coexisting disorders that worsen disability. Distinguish from functional tic-like behaviour and from vocalisations in schizophrenia, stereotypy or Huntington’s disease. Laryngoscopy can document normal anatomy before injection.
det.treatment: Start with education, behavioural treatment and treatment of OCD and ADHD, and remove aggravating drugs. Dopamine-blocking drugs (aripiprazole, risperidone, fluphenazine) and VMAT2 inhibitors are the main drug options; pimozide and haloperidol were the main choices when the book was written. Alpha-2 agonists are milder. For loud vocal tics that resist drugs, EMG-guided botulinum toxin injected into the thyroarytenoid muscle reduces the loudness and also the premonitory urge, with a typical benefit for around 20 weeks and side effects of weak voice and mild swallowing difficulty. Deep brain stimulation is reserved for the most severe cases.
det.prognosis: Many patients improve in young adulthood, and the toxin approach allows some to work and socialise again. Risk of depression and self-harm requires monitoring.
pearls: Botulinum toxin into the thyroarytenoid can help refractory phonic tics, including coprolalia.
Doses that are too low may fail; moderate unilateral dosing is the usual start.
Screen for depression and self-harm in anyone with disabling tics.
det.thd: Malignant phonic tics คือ vocal tic ที่รุนแรง เสียงดังหรือถี่มาก เช่น กรีดร้อง เห่า หรือพูดคำหยาบ (coprolalia) ใน Tourette syndrome จนส่งผลต่อการเรียน การทำงาน และความปลอดภัย ผู้ป่วยมักมีความอยากทำ tic ที่คอ รักษาด้วยการให้ความรู้ พฤติกรรมบำบัด ยา เช่น aripiprazole, risperidone, tetrabenazine และถ้าไม่ดีขึ้นพิจารณาฉีด botulinum toxin เข้ากล้ามเนื้อสายเสียงใต้คำแนะนำของ EMG ซึ่งอาจทำให้เสียงแผ่วและกลืนลำบากชั่วคราว

Strained or breathy voice only during speech, not sudden unwanted noises
Sudden-onset, variable and socially modelled tic-like behaviours in older children or adolescents without a premonitory urge

name: Acute spinal rigidity
formal: A syndrome of continuous, uniform muscle stiffness with superimposed spasms, myoclonus and posturing caused by loss of inhibitory interneuron control over the spinal motor neurons, due to structural, ischaemic, inflammatory or paraneoplastic myelopathy, or by stiff-person-spectrum disease.
simple: A rare problem in which the trunk or legs become hard and stiff, with painful spasms, because the spinal cord’s braking circuits have been damaged.
ab: rigidity and spasms of spinal origin
th: Acute spinal rigidity คือภาวะกล้ามเนื้อแข็งเกร็งสม่ำเสมอพร้อมกับ spasm และ myoclonus จากการสูญเสีย interneuron ยับยั้งในไขสันหลัง พบจากเนื้องอก ไขสันหลังขาดเลือด การอักเสบ paraneoplastic หรือ stiff-person spectrum ผู้ป่วยมักมีอาการไขสันหลังอื่นร่วมด้วย ต้องทำ MRI ไขสันหลัง ตรวจ anti-GAD และ EMG รักษาตามสาเหตุและให้ baclofen, benzodiazepine หรือ tizanidine
tempoNote: Rigidity and spasms develop over days to months after a spinal lesion, or evolve as part of stiff-person-spectrum disease; abrupt worsening can follow stopping baclofen
feat: Continuous, plastic-like rigidity of the trunk and legs (or arms) that is uniform through the range of movement, with fixed postures and contracture
Painful spasms and jerky myoclonus on top of the rigidity; stimuli may trigger them, and they continue in sleep
Usually accompanied by signs of a myelopathy: segmental wasting, reflex change, extensor plantar response and a sensory level
Causes: intramedullary tumour or cyst, trauma and syrinx, ischaemia, necrotising or inflammatory myelitis, paraneoplastic myelopathy
Stiff-person syndrome, PERM and the stiff-limb syndrome are important non-structural causes; abrupt withdrawal of baclofen can trigger crisis with autonomic failure
inv: MRI of the whole spinal cord with contrast, to look for intramedullary lesions, syrinx or compression
EMG with persistent firing of opposing muscle pairs at rest and exaggerated cutaneomuscular reflexes
Anti-GAD65, glycine receptor, amphiphysin and paraneoplastic antibodies; CSF cell count and oligoclonal bands
CT or PET for cancer in those with antibodies or progression, and breast imaging in a woman with arm rigidity

case.who: 47-year-old man from Phitsanulok, 8 months after surgery for a thoracic intramedullary ependymoma
case.story: Gradual stiffness of both legs with painful flexor spasms triggered by touching the skin and when walking.
case.exam: Markedly increased tone in both legs with palpable muscle contraction at rest, hip and knee flexion postures, brisk reflexes, extensor plantars, sensory level at T10.
case.tests: MRI shows post-operative myelomalacia and a small cyst at T9–T10 without compression; EMG shows continuous motor unit firing; anti-GAD65 negative.
case.q: What kind of rigidity is this and how should it be managed?
case.a: Spinal rigidity with flexor spasms from damaged spinal interneurons. Manage with baclofen (consider intrathecal delivery if oral doses fail), a benzodiazepine or tizanidine, botulinum toxin for focal problems and physiotherapy; never withdraw baclofen abruptly.

det.patho: Experimental work shows that ischaemic loss of interneurons in the central and posterior grey matter, with sparing of anterior horn cells, causes continuous firing of alpha motor neurons and rigidity with co-contraction of antagonist muscles. The rigidity persists after dorsal root section and is largely independent of afferent input. Loss of reciprocal inhibition explains why opposing muscles contract together. In humans similar lesions follow tumours, trauma, myelitis, ischaemia and paraneoplastic disease; stiff-person syndrome is a related but more diffuse disorder of inhibitory circuits.
det.clinical: The rigidity is unlike parkinsonian lead-pipe rigidity or spasticity in being continuous and relatively uniform and in producing fixed postures and contractures. Stimulus-sensitive spasms, segmental myoclonus and tremor are common. The pattern of the limb posture varies, and in some cases the patient cannot activate the muscle voluntarily. In most reported cases there are segmental motor and sensory signs, which direct attention to the cord. A leg that is rigid with brisk reflexes and no myelopathy on imaging should raise the possibility of stiff-person syndrome or stiff-limb syndrome.
det.diagnosis: Image the entire spinal cord first. Use EMG to demonstrate continuous motor unit activity and enhanced cutaneomuscular reflexes. Send anti-GAD and paraneoplastic antibodies and examine the CSF. Differentiate basal ganglia rigidity (lead-pipe with tremor), spasticity (velocity-dependent), frontal gegenhalten, neuromyotonia and myotonia. Tetanus and strychnine poisoning must always be considered when spasms are acute and stimulus-triggered.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: decompression or resection of a mass, immunotherapy for inflammatory or autoimmune myelopathy, treatment of the cancer. Symptomatic drugs include baclofen, diazepam or clonazepam, tizanidine or clonidine, gabapentin, valproate and botulinum toxin for focal problems. Large doses may be needed, and intrathecal baclofen is more efficient. Stop none of these drugs abruptly; withdrawal of baclofen can provoke a severe crisis. Immunotherapy including IVIG is used in stiff-person syndrome.
det.prognosis: Depends on the underlying lesion. Structural lesions may leave chronic rigidity with contractures, whereas immune-mediated forms can respond to treatment.
pearls: Rigid legs with brisk reflexes and a sensory level: image the spinal cord.
Rigidity without any cord signs and with stimulus-sensitive spasms: think stiff-person syndrome.
Never stop intrathecal or oral baclofen suddenly.
det.thd: Acute spinal rigidity คือภาวะที่กล้ามเนื้อลำตัวหรือขาแข็งเกร็งสม่ำเสมอ มี spasm และ myoclonus เจ็บเมื่อถูกกระตุ้น เกิดจากรอยโรคที่ทำลาย interneuron ในไขสันหลัง เช่น เนื้องอก ไขสันหลังขาดเลือด การอักเสบ หรือ paraneoplastic บางรายเป็น stiff-person syndrome หรือ PERM ต้องทำ MRI ไขสันหลังทั้งแนว ตรวจ EMG และแอนติบอดี GAD แล้วรักษาตามสาเหตุ ให้ baclofen, benzodiazepine หรือ tizanidine และห้ามหยุด baclofen ทันที

Trismus, risus sardonicus and generalised spasms after a wound; autonomic storms; clinical diagnosis in unvaccinated patients

name: Cryptococcus neoformans (pathogen)
formal: An encapsulated basidiomycetous yeast found worldwide in soil, decaying vegetation and bird (especially pigeon) droppings; inhaled spores reach the lung and, in people with defective cell-mediated immunity, spread to the CNS to cause subacute meningoencephalitis with very high intracranial pressure, cryptococcomas and pseudocysts. It is the leading cause of fungal meningitis in advanced HIV and a major cause of HIV-related death in Southeast Asia and Africa.
simple: A yeast from soil and bird droppings that most people breathe in without harm; when the immune system is weak, especially in advanced HIV, it causes a slow, high-pressure meningitis that damages vision and consciousness.
th: Cryptococcus neoformans เป็นยีสต์มีแคปซูลที่พบในดินและมูลนก โดยเฉพาะนกพิราบ ติดต่อทางการหายใจ ก่อโรคเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบกึ่งเฉียบพลันที่มีความดันในกะโหลกสูงมากในผู้ป่วย HIV ระยะท้าย ผู้ปลูกถ่ายอวัยวะ และผู้ได้สเตียรอยด์ ตรวจ CrAg ได้เร็วในเลือดและ CSF
tempoNote: Headache and malaise build over 1-4 weeks; deterioration is driven by intracranial pressure
feat: Habitat and geography: worldwide in soil and pigeon droppings; heavy burden in Southeast Asia (including Thailand), sub-Saharan Africa and India where late HIV presentation persists

Host risk: advanced HIV (about two thirds of cases), transplant, corticosteroids, diabetes, haematological cancer, idiopathic CD4 lymphopenia, anti-GM-CSF autoantibodies; 5-20% of CNS cases are in apparently immunocompetent people
CNS syndromes: subacute meningoencephalitis with very high pressure (often 25 cm CSF or more), cryptococcomas, pseudocysts, hydrocephalus, cranial neuropathies
Extra-CNS clues: pneumonia or nodules, umbilicated skin papules, positive blood CrAg
Distinguish from other fungi: yeast capsule gives no beta-D-glucan signal; CrAg is positive; contrast Cryptococcus gattii (pathogen) which favours healthy hosts and large masses
inv: Lumbar puncture with opening pressure; CSF CrAg lateral flow (quick, accurate); CSF fungal culture for relapse and susceptibility; serum CrAg
CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis with raised protein and low-normal glucose, but may be almost normal in deep immunosuppression
Beta-D-glucan usually negative; galactomannan not used
MRI: dilated perivascular spaces, gelatinous pseudocysts in basal ganglia, meningeal enhancement, cryptococcomas, hydrocephalus

case.who: 41-year-old woman, factory worker from Samut Prakan, HIV diagnosed after admission, no ART yet
case.story: Five weeks of headache, nausea and low fever, then dim vision in both eyes.
case.exam: Drowsy, visual acuity 6/18 bilaterally, bilateral papilloedema, mild neck stiffness.
case.tests: CD4 19 cells/µL; serum CrAg positive; CSF opening pressure 45 cm, 8 cells, CrAg titre 1:1024; culture later grows an encapsulated yeast.
case.q: Name the organism and the treatment steps that protect her sight.
case.a: Cryptococcus neoformans: induction with liposomal amphotericin B and flucytosine plus fluconazole, daily therapeutic lumbar punctures until pressure is 25 cm CSF or lower, no steroids, and ART deferred 4-6 weeks.

det.patho: Spores about 5 micrometres across are inhaled and cleared in most people. In weak cell-mediated immunity the yeast survives in macrophages, disseminates in blood and seeds the brain. The polysaccharide capsule blunts immunity, and capsular material with yeast clogs the arachnoid granulations so pressure rises far above that of ordinary meningitis; the brain tissue is almost always involved, so meningoencephalitis is the correct term. Disease is often reactivation of dormant infection.
det.clinical: Most patients have headache, fever, nausea and altered mental state over weeks; vision loss, diplopia and coma signal high pressure. Cryptococcomas occur in a minority; lungs, skin and prostate may be involved. In HIV, IRIS can follow ART start. Outside HIV, steroid therapy and organ transplant are leading predispositions, and presentation is slower and more inflammatory.
det.diagnosis: CrAg lateral flow on CSF (or serum) is the main test, with high sensitivity and specificity, rapid result and low cost; it replaced India ink. Fungal culture is slow but useful in relapse since CrAg can stay positive for months. Measure opening pressure at every tap. Screening serum CrAg in HIV with CD4 below 100-200 permits pre-emptive treatment. Titres should not be used to monitor response.
det.treatment: Induction: liposomal amphotericin B with flucytosine, now often as a single high dose of the liposomal drug with 14 days of flucytosine and fluconazole; longer induction (4-6 weeks) for high burden, cryptococcoma or slow response. Then fluconazole consolidation and 6-12 months of lower-dose maintenance. Drain CSF repeatedly until pressure is 25 cm or lower or symptoms resolve. Reduce immunosuppression where possible and avoid steroids. In HIV, delay ART for 4-6 weeks if not already started; in transplant recipients taper immunosuppression gradually to protect the graft and reduce IRIS.
det.prognosis: Mortality is considerable despite treatment, especially with coma, high fungal load or uncontrolled pressure; permanent visual loss or hydrocephalus can follow.
pearls: Opening pressure and CrAg on day one; therapeutic lumbar puncture is life- and sight-saving.
A negative beta-D-glucan is expected and does not argue against Cryptococcus.
See Cryptococcal meningoencephalitis for the disease page and Cryptococcus gattii (pathogen) for the sister species.
det.thd: Cryptococcus neoformans เป็นยีสต์ที่มีแคปซูล พบในดินและมูลนก ติดต่อโดยการหายใจ ก่อโรคเยื่อหุ้มสมองและสมองอักเสบกึ่งเฉียบพลัน ส่วนใหญ่ในผู้ป่วย HIV ระยะท้าย ผู้ปลูกถ่ายอวัยวะ หรือผู้ได้สเตียรอยด์ อาการคือปวดศีรษะนาน เห็นภาพซ้อน ตามัว ซึม จากความดันในกะโหลกสูง วินิจฉัยด้วย CrAg ใน CSF หรือเลือด วัด opening pressure และเพาะเชื้อ รักษาด้วย liposomal amphotericin B ร่วมกับ flucytosine และ fluconazole เจาะหลังระบายซ้ำ ไม่ให้ steroid และเริ่ม ART ช้ากว่าปกติ 4-6 สัปดาห์

qx.stem: A 36-year-old man from Khon Kaen with newly diagnosed HIV (CD4 15 cells/µL) has had four weeks of headache, vomiting and blurred vision. Examination shows bilateral papilloedema and a left sixth nerve palsy without marked neck stiffness. CT head is normal. Lumbar puncture records an opening pressure of 40 cm CSF.
qx.q: Which action is most important alongside starting antifungal induction therapy?
opts: Start dexamethasone to reduce brain swelling
Give acetazolamide to lower CSF production
Start antiretroviral therapy the same day
Drain CSF by repeated therapeutic lumbar punctures until pressure is 25 cm CSF or lower
Wait for the culture result before treating
qx.why: Raised pressure from yeast clogging the arachnoid granulations drives blindness and death, so repeated lumbar puncture is part of treatment. Steroids and acetazolamide have no proven benefit, early ART raises the risk of IRIS-related death, and treatment should not wait for culture because CrAg gives the diagnosis within minutes.

qx.stem: A 50-year-old woman on long-term prednisolone for lupus has had subacute headache for three weeks. Cerebrospinal fluid shows 25 lymphocytes, raised protein and CSF cryptococcal antigen positive. Serum beta-D-glucan returns negative.
qx.q: How should the negative serum beta-D-glucan be interpreted?
opts: It is expected, because Cryptococcus does not produce a beta-D-glucan signal
It excludes fungal meningitis and the CrAg is a false positive
It means the infection is caused by Aspergillus instead
It indicates candidaemia from a central line
It means that amphotericin should be avoided
qx.why: Cryptococcus, Mucorales and Blastomyces are all negative for serum beta-D-glucan, so a negative result does not argue against the diagnosis. A positive CSF CrAg is highly sensitive and specific and decides the diagnosis. The other options misread the assay.

name: Cryptococcus gattii (pathogen)
formal: The second pathogenic species complex of Cryptococcus, associated with eucalyptus and other trees in tropical and temperate regions (including the Vancouver Island and Pacific Northwest outbreak) and more often infecting apparently immunocompetent people; compared with C. neoformans it forms larger lung and brain masses (cryptococcomas), needs longer therapy and more often requires surgery.
simple: A tree-associated cousin of the usual cryptococcus yeast that can infect healthy people and tends to make large lumps in the lungs and brain rather than only meningitis.
th: Cryptococcus gattii เป็นเชื้อรากลุ่ม cryptococcus ที่สัมพันธ์กับต้นไม้ เช่น ยูคาลิปตัส และก่อโรคได้ในคนที่ภูมิคุ้มกันปกติ มักเป็นก้อน cryptococcoma ในปอดและสมอง มีภาวะแทรกซ้อนทางระบบประสาทและความดันในกะโหลกสูงมากกว่า ต้องรักษานานกว่าและบางรายต้องผ่าตัด
tempoNote: Weeks to months; large mass lesions and hydrocephalus can evolve slowly even after drug therapy begins
feat: Habitat and geography: eucalyptus and other trees; tropical and subtropical regions (Australia, Papua New Guinea, Southeast Asia, Africa, South America) and an outbreak from Vancouver Island that extended into the United States; uncommon in Thailand compared with C. neoformans
Host: often immunocompetent adults, men more than women; HIV or transplant also possible
CNS syndromes: meningoencephalitis, large cryptococcomas, hydrocephalus, cranial neuropathy, raised intracranial pressure; lungs often involved
Compared with C. neoformans: more mass lesions, more surgery, longer therapy and more residual neurological deficit
Diagnostics identical (CrAg, culture); species identification needs culture and molecular typing
inv: CSF and serum CrAg; may be positive in the setting of a mass with relatively little meningitis; culture with species identification
Opening pressure at lumbar puncture once imaging excludes a mass lesion that makes a tap unsafe
MRI with contrast: single or multiple cryptococcomas, hydrocephalus, meningeal enhancement
Chest CT for pulmonary masses

case.who: 49-year-old man, rubber-plantation owner from Trat, previously healthy and HIV negative
case.story: Two months of cough and then three weeks of morning headaches and unsteady gait.
case.exam: Papilloedema, left cerebellar ataxia, no fever or meningism.
case.tests: Chest CT: 4 cm right lower lobe mass; MRI: 3 cm ring-enhancing left cerebellar lesion with hydrocephalus; serum and CSF CrAg positive; culture identifies Cryptococcus gattii.
case.q: How does management differ from usual HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis?
case.a: He needs a longer induction course (liposomal amphotericin B with flucytosine for 4-6 weeks), pressure control with CSF diversion for hydrocephalus, neurosurgical review for the cerebellar mass, and prolonged fluconazole consolidation and maintenance; there is no HIV-driven ART timing issue.

det.patho: C. gattii is acquired by inhaling spores from trees and soil, not from bird droppings. Healthy hosts mount a granulomatous response that contains the organism, producing mass-like cryptococcomas in lung and brain rather than diffuse meningitis; the same containment is thought to explain larger mass lesions than with C. neoformans. Outbreaks on Vancouver Island since 1999 showed that it can spread outside the tropics.
det.clinical: Presents as pulmonary mass or nodules and/or CNS disease with headache, focal deficits, hydrocephalus and raised pressure over weeks to months. Neurological complications such as hydrocephalus, deafness, blindness and persistent deficits are more frequent than with C. neoformans. Skin and other organ involvement are uncommon.
det.diagnosis: CrAg and culture establish cryptococcosis; species is confirmed on culture with molecular tests, which has treatment and prognostic implications. Imaging typically shows enhancing masses and hydrocephalus. Because tissue is often needed for large lesions, biopsy or resection may give the diagnosis.
det.treatment: Antifungal treatment follows the same drug logic as C. neoformans (liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine induction, then fluconazole) but is extended: longer induction (4-6 weeks or until lesions shrink), prolonged consolidation and maintenance for many months to a year or more, guided by imaging and response. Hydrocephalus may need a shunt or external drain, and large or accessible masses may need resection; drain CSF repeatedly for raised pressure. Steroids are only used for IRIS or severe mass effect with specialist advice.
det.prognosis: Worse neurological outcome than C. neoformans in some series, with prolonged illness and more sequelae.
pearls: Cryptococcosis in a healthy person with a lung or brain mass: think C. gattii.
Expect longer treatment and a bigger role for surgery and CSF diversion than in C. neoformans.
See Cryptococcus neoformans (pathogen) and the disease page Cryptococcal meningoencephalitis.
det.thd: Cryptococcus gattii เป็นเชื้อรา cryptococcus ที่เกี่ยวข้องกับต้นไม้ เช่น ยูคาลิปตัส พบในคนที่ภูมิคุ้มกันปกติได้ มักเกิดเป็นก้อน cryptococcoma ในปอดและสมอง มีโพรงสมองโตและความดันในกะโหลกสูง วินิจฉัยด้วย CrAg เพาะเชื้อและตรวจระบุชนิด การรักษาใช้ยากลุ่มเดียวกับ C. neoformans คือ liposomal amphotericin B ร่วมกับ flucytosine แล้วต่อด้วย fluconazole แต่ต้องรักษานานกว่า บางรายต้องผ่าตัดก้อนหรือใส่ shunt

qx.stem: A 45-year-old HIV-negative man, previously healthy, lives near a eucalyptus plantation in northern Australia. He has two months of cough followed by headache and unsteady gait. Chest imaging shows a 4 cm lung mass, and MRI shows a ring-enhancing cerebellar lesion with early hydrocephalus. CSF cryptococcal antigen is positive.
qx.q: Which statement best distinguishes this species from the usual HIV-associated cryptococcal infection?
opts: It never affects the brain parenchyma
It is resistant to all antifungal drugs
It is acquired only from pigeon droppings
It causes disease only in neutropenic patients
It typically infects healthy hosts, forms larger masses and needs longer therapy and more surgery
qx.why: C. gattii is linked to trees such as eucalyptus, often affects apparently immunocompetent people and tends to form cryptococcomas with more neurological complications, requiring prolonged antifungal therapy and sometimes surgery or CSF diversion. Pigeon droppings are the typical source of C. neoformans. It remains treatable with the usual agents.

name: Aspergillus species (pathogen)
formal: Ubiquitous soil moulds (chiefly A. fumigatus, A. flavus, A. terreus and A. niger) with septate hyphae that branch at acute angles; inhaled conidia colonise the lung and, in neutropenia, transplant, steroid or kinase-inhibitor therapy, invade blood vessels to cause haemorrhagic infarcts and abscesses in the brain, or invade the CNS directly from the sinuses.
simple: A common mould found in soil and dust that is harmless to most people but, in someone with a very weak immune system, spreads from the lungs or sinuses to the brain and blocks small blood vessels, causing strokes, bleeds and abscesses.
th: Aspergillus เป็นราที่พบทั่วไปในดินและฝุ่น ไม่ก่อโรคในคนปกติ แต่ในผู้ป่วย neutropenia ปลูกถ่ายอวัยวะ ได้สเตียรอยด์หรือยากลุ่ม tyrosine kinase inhibitor เชื้อจะแพร่จากปอดหรือไซนัสไปสมอง บุกรุกหลอดเลือด ทำให้เกิดฝี สมองขาดเลือดและเลือดออก
tempoNote: Days to weeks in neutropenia; granulomatous sino-orbital forms may take months
feat: Habitat and geography: found worldwide in soil, compost and dust; A. flavus is prominent in hot, dry climates of South Asia and the Middle East; hospital construction dust and water can be sources

Host risk: haematological malignancy, stem-cell or solid organ transplant, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, steroids, genetic neutrophil defects, severe influenza or COVID-19, diabetes (sinus disease); about a third of CNS cases have no known predisposition
CNS syndromes: multiple abscesses (about 70%), haemorrhagic infarction, mycotic aneurysm, cavernous sinus thrombosis, skull base granuloma; meningitis uncommon
Extra-CNS clues: lung nodules with halo sign, sinusitis, positive serum galactomannan
Distinguish from other fungi: septate hyphae at acute angles and galactomannan-positive, unlike Mucorales (pathogen); voriconazole responsive, unlike Mucorales and Lomentospora
inv: CSF Aspergillus PCR (most useful), CSF and serum galactomannan, beta-D-glucan; serum galactomannan sensitivity for CNS disease is low and false positives occur
MRI with SWI: ring lesions with haemorrhage, restricted diffusion, infarcts at grey-white junctions and basal ganglia
Tissue: narrow septate hyphae with acute-angle branching; culture for species and azole resistance
CSF may show lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein and low glucose, or be unremarkable

case.who: 28-year-old woman with acute myeloid leukaemia, day 18 of neutropenia after induction at a Bangkok hospital
case.story: Persistent fever on broad-spectrum antibiotics and pleuritic chest pain, then sudden right arm weakness and a focal seizure.
case.exam: Febrile, drowsy, right hemiparesis and expressive aphasia; no neck stiffness.
case.tests: Chest CT: nodules with halo; MRI: three left basal ganglia and frontal lesions with haemorrhage and rim enhancement; serum galactomannan index 2.6.
case.q: What is the likely organism and drug of choice?
case.a: Aspergillus: voriconazole with trough monitoring; alternatives are isavuconazole or liposomal amphotericin B; add neurosurgical review for accessible abscesses and neutrophil recovery.

det.patho: Conidia are inhaled in daily life. Where neutrophil or macrophage function is impaired, they germinate and invade vessel walls, causing thrombosis, haemorrhage and abscess, and they may seed the CNS by blood or spread directly from sinusitis or the orbit. Mycotic aneurysms form where hyphae weaken arterial walls.
det.clinical: CNS involvement is often late in a patient already treated for lung disease; headache and focal deficits dominate. Meningitis, infarction, haemorrhage and cavernous sinus syndromes are less common than abscess. Sino-orbital A. flavus disease in apparently healthy or diabetic hosts presents with proptosis and cranial neuropathies over weeks.
det.diagnosis: A highly specific CSF PCR may spare a biopsy. Serum galactomannan is specific for Aspergillus but poorly sensitive for CNS disease (about 20%), and false positives (about 6%) arise from beta-lactam antibiotics, galactomannan-rich foods and parenteral nutrition; it can cross-react with Histoplasma and Talaromyces. Tissue examination and culture remain definitive.
det.treatment: Voriconazole is first-line for several months (duration not defined), with therapeutic drug monitoring because of variable levels and toxicity (vision change, hepatitis, hallucinations). Liposomal amphotericin B is second-line; isavuconazole is an alternative. Surgical drainage of accessible lesions, reduction of immunosuppression and prophylaxis (posaconazole or voriconazole) in prolonged neutropenia are recommended. Echinocandins penetrate CSF poorly and are only adjuncts.
det.prognosis: Poor, especially in immunocompromised or obtunded patients; better with solitary resectable lesions in immunocompetent hosts.
pearls: Haemorrhagic infarcts plus fever in neutropenia: angioinvasive mould until proven otherwise.
Use CSF PCR rather than serum galactomannan to look for CNS disease.
Disease page: Central nervous system aspergillosis; look-alike: Mucorales (pathogen).
det.thd: Aspergillus เป็นราที่พบทั่วไปในดินและฝุ่น ผู้ป่วยภูมิคุ้มกันต่ำ เช่น neutropenia ปลูกถ่ายอวัยวะ หรือได้สเตียรอยด์ อาจติดเชื้อทางปอดหรือไซนัสแล้วแพร่ไปสมอง เชื้อบุกรุกหลอดเลือดทำให้เกิดฝีหลายตำแหน่ง สมองขาดเลือดและเลือดออก อาการคือปวดศีรษะ อ่อนแรง ชัก ตรวจ MRI, galactomannan, CSF PCR และตัดชิ้นเนื้อ ยาหลักคือ voriconazole โดยติดตามระดับยา ร่วมกับผ่าตัดระบายฝีเมื่อทำได้ และลดยากดภูมิ

qx.stem: A 55-year-old woman with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia on a tyrosine kinase inhibitor has headache and right arm weakness for ten days, plus a cough. MRI shows a ring-enhancing frontal abscess with haemorrhage. Serum galactomannan is negative, and the team asks which test best supports CNS aspergillosis without a brain biopsy.
qx.q: Which test is most useful?
opts: Serum beta-D-glucan alone
CSF Aspergillus PCR
India ink preparation of CSF
Serum Histoplasma antigen
CSF Gram stain
qx.why: Serum galactomannan has low sensitivity (about 20%) for CNS aspergillosis, so a negative result does not exclude it; CSF PCR is highly specific and may avoid biopsy. India ink targets Cryptococcus, and Gram stain targets bacteria. Voriconazole would be the treatment once the diagnosis is made.

name: Candida species (pathogen)
formal: Commensal budding yeasts of the gut, skin and genitourinary tract (C. albicans commonest; C. parapsilosis, C. tropicalis, C. glabrata and the multidrug-resistant C. auris increasingly) that reach the CNS through candidaemia or neurosurgical devices to cause meningitis, meningoencephalitis with cerebral microabscesses, ventriculitis and, rarely, macroabscesses or mycotic aneurysms.
simple: A yeast that normally lives on our skin and in our gut and causes brain infection when it gets into the blood, usually in newborns, patients on chemotherapy or long ICU stays, or after brain surgery with drains or shunts.
th: Candida เป็นยีสต์ที่อยู่ปกติบนผิวหนังและทางเดินอาหาร ก่อโรคในสมองเมื่อเข้ากระแสเลือด โดยเฉพาะทารกเกิดก่อนกำหนด ผู้ป่วย neutropenia ผู้ป่วย ICU ระยะยาว ผู้ใช้สารเสพติดทางหลอดเลือด หรือผู้มี shunt/drain ทำให้เกิดเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ ฝีเล็ก ๆ หลายจุด หรือ ventriculitis
tempoNote: Meningitis in days to weeks; microabscess encephalopathy often subacute; device infection indolent
feat: Habitat and geography: global commensal; increasing non-albicans and resistant species in hospitals
Host risk: neutropenia, prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics, parenteral nutrition, central lines, intravenous drug use, prematurity and extremes of age, neurosurgical devices; HIV in some
CNS syndromes: meningoencephalitis with microabscesses (basal ganglia and cerebellum), device-related ventriculitis, rare macroabscess, mycotic aneurysm, stroke
Extra-CNS clues: candidaemia, endophthalmitis (retinal exam is mandatory), endocarditis, skin and renal involvement

Distinguish from other fungi: yeast and pseudohyphae in CSF with sensitive CSF culture (about 80%); beta-D-glucan positive, unlike Cryptococcus; fever and meningism are common, unlike Cryptococcus (pathogen)
inv: CSF Gram stain, microscopy and culture (sensitivity about 80%); CSF pleocytosis (mixed or lymphocytic), raised protein, glucose often normal
CSF and serum beta-D-glucan (CSF values useful); blood cultures; Candida PCR is species-limited
MRI: multiple small ring or punctate lesions at grey-white junction, basal ganglia and cerebellum, sometimes normal early; dilated fundoscopy for endophthalmitis
Susceptibility testing, particularly for non-albicans species and C. auris

case.who: 51-year-old woman recovering from chemotherapy-induced neutropenic sepsis on ICU in Chiang Mai, with a central line and total parenteral nutrition
case.story: On day 10 she becomes drowsy and febrile despite broad-spectrum antibiotics.
case.exam: GCS 11, mild neck stiffness, no focal deficit; fundoscopy shows chorioretinal white lesions.
case.tests: Blood and CSF cultures grow Candida; CSF 120 cells, protein 1.0 g/L, glucose normal; MRI: multiple small enhancing foci in basal ganglia and cerebellum.
case.q: What is the antifungal regimen and which non-drug step is essential?
case.a: Liposomal amphotericin B with or without flucytosine, tailored by species; remove the infected central line and any devices, treat the eye if involved, and step down to fluconazole if the isolate is susceptible after clinical response.

det.patho: Candida enters the bloodstream from gut, lines or surgical sites. Prolonged candidaemia seeds the brain with tiny abscesses at the grey-white junction, basal ganglia and cerebellum; devices allow direct seeding of ventricles. Broad-spectrum antibiotics and parenteral nutrition promote overgrowth and translocation.
det.clinical: Fever, drowsiness and low Glasgow Coma Scale score are typical; meningeal signs and headache are less common than in bacterial meningitis (headache alone in about a third). Focal deficits arise from larger abscesses or mycotic aneurysm. Concurrent endophthalmitis, endocarditis, skin or renal involvement may signal dissemination.
det.diagnosis: Suspect CNS candidiasis even when blood cultures and early imaging are negative. CSF culture and microscopy are the mainstay, CSF beta-D-glucan is increasingly used, and PCR is species-limited. Every patient with candidaemia needs dilated fundoscopy. Remove or replace infected devices.
det.treatment: Liposomal amphotericin B (3-5 mg/kg daily) with or without flucytosine is preferred, because both reach brain and CSF better than echinocandins; fluconazole is used as step-down for susceptible isolates. Remove infected lines, shunts or drains and drain collections. Duration is several weeks and continues until CSF and imaging abnormalities resolve; short courses relapse. Echinocandins are adjuncts only because CNS penetration is poor, and resistant C. auris requires specialist input.
det.prognosis: Mortality is considerable and varies with host, species and device removal.
pearls: Candida is the main fungal pathogen of CSF devices and neonates; ask about lines and shunts.
Beta-D-glucan is positive in Candida but negative in Cryptococcus and Mucorales.
Always do a dilated eye exam in candidaemia.
det.thd: Candida เป็นยีสต์ที่อยู่ในร่างกายตามปกติ แต่เข้ากระแสเลือดได้ในผู้ป่วย neutropenia ผู้ใช้ยาปฏิชีวนะกว้างนาน ผู้ได้สารอาหารทางหลอดเลือด ทารกคลอดก่อนกำหนด หรือผู้ที่มีสาย central line และ shunt ทำให้เกิดเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบและฝีเล็กหลายจุดในสมอง ตรวจเพาะเชื้อ CSF และเลือด ตรวจจอประสาทตา รักษาด้วย liposomal amphotericin B ร่วมกับ flucytosine ถอดสายหรืออุปกรณ์ที่ติดเชื้อ แล้วต่อด้วย fluconazole ตามผลความไวของเชื้อ

name: Mucorales (pathogen)
formal: An order of fast-growing, broad, ribbon-like, pauci-septate moulds (Rhizopus, Mucor, Lichtheimia, Rhizomucor and others) found in soil, compost and rotting vegetation; in diabetic ketoacidosis, steroid or haematological immunosuppression they invade sinus mucosa and arteries to cause rhino-orbital-cerebral infection with necrosis, cavernous sinus thrombosis and carotid occlusion, or haematogenous brain abscess.
simple: Common bread-mould-type fungi that explode in growth in people with very high sugar and acid levels (DKA) or heavy steroid use, destroying the nose, eye socket and brain within days.

feat: Habitat and geography: global, especially humid environments; India and South Asia carry the largest burden, with a COVID-era surge; Thai reports include cerebral mucormycosis in people who inject heroin
Host risk: diabetes and DKA, steroids, haematological malignancy, transplant, deferoxamine and iron overload, injection drug use, trauma; sometimes none

CNS syndromes: rhino-orbital-cerebral disease (facial pain, eschar, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia), cavernous sinus thrombosis, internal carotid occlusion with infarct, frontal cerebritis, isolated brain abscess
Extra-CNS clues: sinusitis without fever, palatal ulcer, pulmonary mucormycosis
Distinguish from other fungi: broad aseptate hyphae at right angles, beta-D-glucan and galactomannan negative, voriconazole inactive, versus Aspergillus species (pathogen)
inv: Endoscopic biopsy and direct microscopy (KOH or calcofluor): ribbon-like aseptate hyphae with vessel invasion; culture and tissue PCR are useful
Contrast MRI of brain, orbits and sinuses; CT sinuses for bone erosion; MRA or CTA for carotid
CSF: mixed pleocytosis, raised protein, glucose often normal; CSF rarely grows the organism
Glucose, ketones, blood gas; ocular examination; beta-D-glucan and galactomannan unhelpful

case.who: 63-year-old man, retired gardener from Nakhon Pathom, type 2 diabetes with HbA1c 14% and recent high-dose prednisolone for a rash
case.story: Facial pain and a bloody nasal discharge for four days, then a falling left upper lid with diplopia.
case.exam: Left ptosis, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia and decreased vision, black discoloured area on the palate, glucose 480 mg/dL.
case.tests: MRI: left ethmoid-sphenoid sinus disease with orbital apex involvement and cavernous sinus thrombosis; nasal biopsy shows broad aseptate hyphae; galactomannan negative.
case.q: Which two interventions matter most besides blood glucose control?
case.a: Liposomal amphotericin B at high dose and urgent surgical debridement of necrotic tissue, with reduction of steroids and later isavuconazole or posaconazole as step-down or adjunct; voriconazole is not effective.

det.patho: Spores enter via inhalation, ingestion or skin inoculation. In ketoacidosis, free iron and acidity impair neutrophils and favour fungal growth (the fungus has a ketone reductase), and hyphae invade artery walls, causing thrombosis and tissue death. The ethmoid and sphenoid sinuses drain towards the orbit and cavernous sinus, so these sites carry a high risk of intracranial spread. Neutropenic patients usually get pulmonary or disseminated disease with metastatic brain abscess.
det.clinical: Fever may be absent. Facial pain, swelling and numbness, nasal discharge and dark mucosa are the usual first signs; eschar is late. Ptosis, proptosis, visual loss and ophthalmoplegia reflect orbital apex or cavernous sinus disease, and hemiparesis suggests carotid occlusion. Cerebral involvement without sinus disease is uncommon and linked to intravenous drug use.
det.diagnosis: Tissue is the key: direct microscopy shows aseptate hyphae, culture is often negative, PCR on tissue is highly useful. Neither beta-D-glucan nor galactomannan helps. MRI and CT define extent; ocular examination excludes retinal disease.
det.treatment: Liposomal amphotericin B (high dose, up to 10 mg/kg in CNS disease in some centres) with early, repeated debridement; isavuconazole or posaconazole, continued for 6 months or longer, as adjunct or step-down guided by imaging; manage DKA, stop steroids and deferoxamine. Treatment may take weeks to months for imaging and CSF to resolve. Deferasirox did not improve survival in a trial and is not recommended.
det.prognosis: High mortality, increased by continued steroid use and cerebral involvement; survivors often have severe morbidity.
pearls: DKA plus facial pain, orbital signs or palatal necrosis is mucormycosis until proven otherwise.
Voriconazole is no use against Mucorales.
Disease page: Rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis.
det.thd: Mucorales เป็นกลุ่มราที่พบในดินและพืชเน่า ก่อโรครุนแรงในผู้ป่วยเบาหวานที่มี DKA ผู้ได้สเตียรอยด์ หรือผู้ป่วยมะเร็งเม็ดเลือด เชื้อบุกรุกหลอดเลือดทำให้เนื้อเยื่อตายสีดำ ลามจากไซนัสสู่เบ้าตา cavernous sinus และสมองภายในไม่กี่วัน วินิจฉัยโดยตัดชิ้นเนื้อพบเส้นใยขนาดใหญ่ไม่มีผนังกั้น ตรวจ beta-D-glucan และ galactomannan ไม่ช่วย รักษาด้วย liposomal amphotericin B ขนาดสูง ผ่าตัดเนื้อตาย แก้ DKA และลดสเตียรอยด์ แล้วต่อด้วย isavuconazole หรือ posaconazole

qx.stem: A 60-year-old man whose diabetes is poorly controlled, with recent high-dose steroids has five days of facial pain, bloody nasal discharge and now sudden loss of vision with proptosis and ophthalmoplegia on the left. MRI shows ethmoid sinus disease invading the orbit and cavernous sinus. Serum galactomannan and beta-D-glucan are both negative.
qx.q: What is the best immediate management?
opts: Voriconazole alone, awaiting biopsy
Observation, because both fungal markers are negative
Liposomal amphotericin B with urgent surgical debridement and control of glucose and steroids
Oral fluconazole and nasal decongestants
Intravenous caspofungin as monotherapy
qx.why: Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is a surgical-medical emergency in which negative fungal markers are typical, and delay is fatal. Liposomal amphotericin B, debridement and reversal of the predisposing factors are the pillars. Voriconazole, fluconazole and echinocandins do not reliably treat Mucorales.

name: Histoplasma capsulatum (pathogen)
formal: A thermally dimorphic fungus found in soil enriched by bird and bat droppings (caves, mines, old buildings) in the Americas, Africa and Asia; inhaled spores convert to intracellular yeasts in macrophages and, in HIV, haematological malignancy or TNF-alpha inhibitor therapy, disseminate to cause subacute or chronic meningitis, ring-enhancing histoplasmomas and cerebritis.
simple: A fungus from bird and bat droppings in caves and old buildings that most people clear as a mild chest illness, but that can spread to the brain in people with advanced HIV or immune-suppressing drugs.
th: Histoplasma capsulatum เป็นราชนิด dimorphic ที่พบในมูลนกและค้างคาว ในถ้ำ เหมือง หรืออาคารเก่า ติดโดยหายใจเอาสปอร์ ส่วนใหญ่ไม่มีอาการ แต่ในผู้ป่วย HIV ระยะท้าย ผู้ป่วยมะเร็งเม็ดเลือด หรือผู้ใช้ยากลุ่ม TNF inhibitor อาจแพร่ไปสมองทำให้เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบเรื้อรังหรือเกิดก้อน histoplasmoma
tempoNote: Weeks to months of headache and cranial neuropathy; relapse after short therapy
feat: Habitat and geography: Mississippi and Ohio valleys, Central and South America, Africa, and foci in Asia including Thailand and Southeast Asia, particularly in people with HIV
Host risk: advanced HIV, haematological malignancy, TNF-alpha inhibitors, other immunosuppression; only 5-20% of disseminated cases involve the CNS
CNS syndromes: chronic meningitis, histoplasmoma (ring-enhancing masses), cerebritis, spinal lesions, stroke
Extra-CNS clues: fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, adrenal and gastrointestinal lesions, oral ulcers resembling cancer

Distinguish from other fungi: urine and serum Histoplasma antigen is positive (cross-reacts with Aspergillus galactomannan); beta-D-glucan positive; versus Talaromyces marneffei (pathogen) which has skin lesions and positive blood culture
inv: Histoplasma antigen on urine, serum and CSF (urine most sensitive in disseminated disease); CSF antibodies; CSF culture is poor
CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein, low glucose
MRI: ring-enhancing lesions (histoplasmoma), meningeal enhancement, occasional infarcts
Tissue histopathology of marrow, lymph node, oral ulcer or brain: small intracellular yeasts

case.who: 44-year-old man, cave guide from Kanchanaburi, HIV positive and non-adherent to ART
case.story: Five weeks of fever, weight loss, headache and then drooping of the face on one side.
case.exam: Febrile, cachectic, oral ulcer, left facial palsy, mild neck stiffness, hepatosplenomegaly.
case.tests: Urine Histoplasma antigen strongly positive; CSF 60 lymphocytes, protein 1.4 g/L, low glucose; MRI: meningeal enhancement and a ring-enhancing lesion; CrAg negative.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and treatment sequence?
case.a: CNS histoplasmosis: liposomal amphotericin B for 4-6 weeks, then itraconazole for at least a year (some continue lifelong in HIV), restart or optimise ART after the antifungal is established.

det.patho: Microconidia inhaled from contaminated soil convert to yeasts at body temperature and are taken up by macrophages, in which they multiply. Host cellular immunity controls the infection; when it fails, parasitised macrophages spread through the reticuloendothelial system and sometimes cross into the CNS. About one in 2000 acute infections disseminate, and 5-20% of those involve the nervous system.
det.clinical: The CNS picture is usually a chronic meningitis with headache, altered cognition and cranial neuropathies, or one or more ring-enhancing histoplasmomas causing seizures and focal deficits. Healthy adults can disseminate to a single organ (meningitis or hepatitis). In HIV, fever, cytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly and mucosal ulcers are frequent clues.
det.diagnosis: Antigen detection in urine, serum and CSF is the most useful tool, and CSF antibodies add yield; culture is slow and CSF culture and beta-D-glucan are not helpful. Aspergillus galactomannan can cross-react. Histopathology of marrow, lymph node or brain is useful when rapid diagnosis is needed. The 2026 review reports most CNS cases have abnormal MRI.
det.treatment: Induce with liposomal amphotericin B for 4-6 weeks (about 5 mg/kg daily), then itraconazole at least 12 months, with drug-level monitoring; some patients with HIV need ongoing suppression. Restart or continue ART, delaying if ART-naive. Reduce other immunosuppression where possible.
det.prognosis: Serious disease with relapse after incomplete treatment; outcomes depend on host immunity and early therapy.
pearls: Ask about caves, bats, old buildings and bird roosts in anyone with HIV, fever and chronic meningitis.
Urine antigen is the quickest bedside lead; CSF culture is often negative.
Aspergillus galactomannan can be falsely positive in histoplasmosis (see Aspergillus species (pathogen)).

name: Coccidioides species (pathogen)

feat: Habitat and geography: arid soil in Arizona, California Central Valley, northern Mexico and parts of South America; not endemic to Thailand or Southeast Asia, so suspect it only with travel or work in those areas

MRI: basilar enhancement, hydrocephalus, infarcts, dural or sinus thrombosis

case.who: 46-year-old Thai engineer who worked on solar farms in Arizona for three years, now back in Chonburi

det.patho: Arthroconidia in disturbed soil are inhaled and transform into spherules in tissue. Dissemination to the meninges produces dense basal exudate, hydrocephalus and arteritis of penetrating vessels.
det.clinical: Persistent headache is typical, with fever, confusion and gait disturbance. Hydrocephalus is the most common complication, and vasculitis can cause lacunar strokes. Valley fever may precede CNS disease, but not always.
det.diagnosis: A travel history is essential. CSF eosinophilia suggests the diagnosis; CSF antigen is highly sensitive and specific in the 2026 review, serology is weaker, and culture is poor. Direct visualisation of organisms is rare.
det.treatment: Fluconazole at moderately high dose is first line (800-1200 mg daily is commonly used), continued lifelong given the high relapse rate. Alternative azoles are used for failure; intrathecal amphotericin B is reserved for refractory disease. Hydrocephalus is shunted, and dexamethasone treats vasculitic complications.
det.prognosis: Fatal if untreated; good survival on lifelong azole, with hydrocephalus and infarcts the main problems.
pearls: Desert dust and a chronic basal meningitis: ask about travel, even years ago.
CSF eosinophils are a diagnostic clue.

feat: Habitat and geography: soil and bamboo-rat burrows in rural Thailand (north), Vietnam, southern China, north-east India; cases cluster in the rainy season among agricultural workers

Host risk: advanced HIV (CD4 below 100) in most; second only to tuberculosis and cryptococcosis as HIV opportunistic infection in endemic areas; also other immunodeficiency and anti-interferon-gamma antibodies

case.tests: Skin smear shows yeasts with central septa; blood culture grows mould-phase fungus with red pigment; CrAg negative; CSF few cells, culture positive.
case.q: What is the antifungal plan?
case.a: Talaromycosis with CNS involvement: amphotericin B (liposomal where available) for 4-6 weeks and then itraconazole or voriconazole, with ART after the antifungal is established and secondary prophylaxis until CD4 recovers.

det.clinical: Most patients have fever, weight loss and skin lesions, with lung, liver and marrow involvement. det.diagnosis: Culture and microscopy of tissue or fluid remain the gold standard. Serum beta-D-glucan is commonly positive, but specific ELISA, serology and PCR are not widely validated for CNS infection.
det.treatment: Published CNS experience is very limited: amphotericin B (liposomal) for 4-6 weeks and then itraconazole or voriconazole for about ten weeks has been used successfully. Itraconazole prophylaxis continues until immune recovery.

name: Scedosporium and Lomentospora (pathogen)
formal: Hyaline septate soil and sewage moulds (Scedosporium apiospermum complex, formerly Pseudallescheria boydii, and Lomentospora prolificans) that cause brain abscess, often frontal, after near-drowning in polluted water, craniofacial trauma or neurosurgery or in immunocompromised hosts; they are histologically similar to Aspergillus, frequently resistant to amphotericin B and other drugs, and have very high mortality.
simple: Moulds from polluted water and soil that cause brain abscesses after near-drowning, injuries or immune suppression; they look like Aspergillus under the microscope but resist many drugs.
th: Scedosporium (Pseudallescheria boydii) และ Lomentospora prolificans เป็นราที่พบในดิน น้ำเสีย และน้ำเน่า ก่อฝีในสมองหลังเกือบจมน้ำ ได้รับบาดเจ็บบริเวณศีรษะและใบหน้า หรือผ่าตัดสมอง และในผู้ป่วยภูมิคุ้มกันต่ำ จุลพยาธิวิทยาคล้าย Aspergillus แต่ดื้อต่อ amphotericin B และยาหลายชนิด อัตราตายสูง
tempoNote: Abscess signs 2-4 weeks after near-drowning; weeks in immunocompromised hosts
feat: Habitat and geography: polluted water, sewage, manure and soil worldwide; near-drowning in floods and tsunami-type events is a classic exposure
Host risk: near-drowning, craniofacial trauma, neurosurgery, haematological malignancy, transplant, immunodeficiency; also immunocompetent hosts
CNS syndromes: frontal-predominant solitary or multiple abscesses, meningoencephalitis, rare ventriculitis
Extra-CNS clues: pneumonia, sinusitis, mycetoma (Madura foot) or metastatic skin lesions

Distinguish from other fungi: looks like Aspergillus on histology but often resists amphotericin B and echinocandins; Lomentospora is the most resistant (Aspergillus species (pathogen) and Fusarium species (pathogen))
inv: Tissue (abscess aspirate or biopsy) culture with susceptibility testing is essential; blood culture for L. prolificans in disseminated disease
CSF can be normal or show pleocytosis and raised protein
MRI or CT: solitary or multiple ring-enhancing abscesses, frontal predominance
Beta-D-glucan is variably positive; galactomannan is negative

case.who: 34-year-old man, rice-field worker from Phitsanulok, nearly drowned in a flooded irrigation canal three weeks ago

det.patho: Spores enter by aspiration of contaminated water (pneumonia, haematogenous spread), by direct trauma, via catheters or from contiguous sinus infection. Like other moulds they invade vessels, forming abscesses with a granulomatous capsule; about half of CNS cases have no other site.
det.clinical: Headache, fever and focal deficits suggest an abscess, with symptoms emerging 2-4 weeks after near-drowning. Immunocompromised patients may have concurrent lung or skin lesions; CSF can be unremarkable.
det.diagnosis: Tissue culture is needed; histology cannot distinguish from Aspergillus. Susceptibility testing matters because resistance is widespread. The 2026 review notes CSF may be normal or show pleocytosis, and ventriculitis is rare.
det.treatment: Voriconazole is the base, often combined with liposomal amphotericin B, and neurosurgical drainage or debridement is usually needed; Lomentospora prolificans is resistant to most agents and new drugs (olorofim, fosmanogepix) are investigational. Immunosuppression should be reduced if possible.
det.prognosis: Mortality has historically been above 75% and resistance is rising; single lesions with surgery do better.

Do not rely on amphotericin B alone.
It looks like Aspergillus but is not the same disease; see Aspergillus species (pathogen).

name: Fusarium species (pathogen)

Extra-CNS clues: cutaneous lesions after a foot or thorn injury, lung disease

case.who: 47-year-old male farmer from Surin on prednisolone after a kidney transplant, recently returned from working in India
case.story: Three weeks of headache, seizures and sleepiness after he injured his foot with a pitchfork.
case.exam: Drowsy, left hemiparesis.
case.tests: MRI: a 3 cm thick-walled right temporal abscess; aspirate shows dark brown septate hyphae and grows Cladophialophora bantiana.
case.q: What is the cornerstone of treatment?
case.a: Early complete excision of the abscess with antifungal therapy (liposomal amphotericin B and/or voriconazole, guided by susceptibility; flucytosine adjunct in some regimens), then prolonged azole (itraconazole more than 12 months) and reduction of immunosuppression; terbinafine is not useful because it does not penetrate CSF.

det.patho: These fungi contain melanin that protects them from the immune system, and they enter by inhalation or injury, then spread by blood to the brain. Cladophialophora bantiana is notably neurotropic and mostly affects otherwise healthy people.
det.clinical: Headache, seizures and focal deficits over weeks to months suggest a mass; most present with a solitary abscess. In outbreak settings, meningitis follows contaminated epidural steroid injection.
det.diagnosis: Definitive diagnosis is by tissue culture showing dark brown septate hyphae; molecular methods are promising. CSF culture is gold standard in meningitis.
det.treatment: Early complete excision plus antifungal therapy: amphotericin B and/or voriconazole guided by susceptibility testing, with itraconazole for more than 12 months commonly used. Terbinafine has no role. Flucytosine has been used.
det.prognosis: Mortality is high; survivors usually had complete resection of an encapsulated lesion.
pearls: Brain abscess in a healthy farmer with a negative bacterial work-up: ask for fungal stains.
Complete surgical excision improves survival.
Terbinafine does not reach the CSF.

name: Paracoccidioides (pathogen)
formal: Thermally dimorphic fungi (P. brasiliensis complex and P. lutzii) acquired exclusively in Latin America, predominantly Brazil, by inhalation of conidia from rural soil; after pneumonitis and lymphatic spread they reactivate months to years later and, unlike most mycoses, involve the CNS commonly (about 30% of invasive disease), mostly in immunocompetent men, as multiple granulomatous pseudotumours.
simple: A fungus of rural soil in South America that mainly affects farm workers and can form several granuloma-like lumps in the brain, even in people with normal immunity.
th: Paracoccidioides เป็นราชนิด dimorphic ที่ติดจากดินในพื้นที่ชนบทของละตินอเมริกา โดยเฉพาะบราซิล ติดโดยหายใจเอาสปอร์ แล้วอยู่เงียบก่อนกำเริบหลายเดือนถึงหลายปี พบการติดเชื้อสมองบ่อยกว่าราชนิดอื่น มักในผู้ชายวัยทำงานที่ภูมิคุ้มกันปกติ ทำให้เกิดก้อน granuloma หลายก้อนในสมอง ในไทยพบเฉพาะผู้มีประวัติเดินทาง
tempoNote: Weeks to months; reactivation can occur years after leaving the endemic area
feat: Habitat and geography: rural soil in Latin America, mostly Brazil; not endemic to Thailand, so suspect with a history of travel, jungle or farm work
Host risk: rural soil exposure, smoking and alcohol; men more than women (above 90%); many immunocompetent
CNS syndromes: pseudotumoural granulomas (often multiple), headache, focal deficits, seizures, ataxia; meningitis occasionally
Extra-CNS clues: chronic form in people over 30 with lung disease and lymphadenopathy; acute form with fever, hepatosplenomegaly and marrow involvement
Distinguish from other fungi: CSF non-diagnostic and immunodiffusion performs poorly; biopsy shows multiple-budding yeast; versus Histoplasma capsulatum (pathogen)
inv: Brain biopsy with microscopy and culture is the most practical test; CSF protein raised, glucose normal, mild pleocytosis
MRI: multiple granulomatous lesions with ring enhancement, T1 hyperintense and T2 hypointense core, meningeal enhancement, ischaemic lesions
Serology is of limited value in CNS disease
Chest imaging and lymph node assessment

case.who: 48-year-old man who worked as a coffee-farm labourer in Brazil for ten years, living in Bangkok for one year
case.story: Two weeks of progressive left arm weakness and headache; he smokes and drinks daily.
case.exam: Left arm weakness 4/5, no fever, lymphadenopathy in the neck.
case.tests: MRI: three ring-enhancing lesions in the right hemisphere; brain biopsy shows yeast with multiple buds.
case.q: What treatment is used and for how long?
case.a: Paracoccidioidomycosis of the CNS; long-term trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or fluconazole (years), with amphotericin B added for severe or disseminated disease; duration guided by response.

det.clinical: Two forms exist: an acute/subacute juvenile form and a chronic adult form with pulmonary symptoms, lymphadenopathy and CNS lesions. CNS lesions are usually multiple pseudotumours at any location.

det.prognosis: Guarded; relapse is common with short treatment.
pearls: A man with prior rural Latin American work and multiple ring lesions: consider Paracoccidioides.
CNS involvement is more frequent here than in other endemic mycoses.

name: Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour (MPNST)
formal: A high-grade sarcoma growing out of a peripheral nerve or out of a pre-existing nerve sheath tumour, most often a plexiform neurofibroma in neurofibromatosis type 1, showing Schwann-cell lineage features, frequent loss of H3 K27 trimethylation and a strong tendency to local recurrence and lung metastasis.
simple: A cancer that grows from the covering of a nerve; in people with NF1 it often starts inside an old, soft nerve lump that suddenly grows and hurts.
th: MPNST เป็นมะเร็ง sarcoma ของปลอกหุ้มเส้นประสาทส่วนปลาย ครึ่งหนึ่งเกิดในผู้ป่วย NF1 โดยเปลี่ยนมาจาก plexiform neurofibroma ที่โตเร็ว ปวดมาก และมีอ่อนแรงใหม่
tempoNote: Weeks to months of rapid growth, new constant pain and progressive deficit, often in a nerve mass that had been stable for years
feat: A deep mass on a large nerve trunk (sciatic, brachial or lumbosacral plexus, paraspinal roots) that enlarges quickly
Persistent pain, often waking the patient at night, with a new or worsening motor or sensory deficit in that nerve's territory
About half occur in NF1, usually younger adults, from a plexiform or atypical neurofibroma; others are sporadic or follow earlier radiotherapy
Hard, fixed mass with Tinel-like tingling, and sometimes lung metastases already present at diagnosis
Highly aggressive: local recurrence and pulmonary spread are common and NF1 patients fare worse
inv: Contrast MRI of the whole lesion: size over about 5 cm, irregular margins, perilesional oedema, heterogeneous enhancement and central necrosis raise suspicion, but none is specific
FDG-PET/CT to separate a malignant focus from benign plexiform neurofibroma and to guide the biopsy target
Image-guided core or open multi-site biopsy at a sarcoma centre; histology with loss of H3K27me3 and patchy or absent S100/SOX10
Staging with CT of the chest (lungs are the main metastatic site) before definitive surgery

case.who: 29-year-old man from Nakhon Ratchasima with NF1 (café-au-lait spots and many skin neurofibromas)
case.story: A soft lump behind his right knee, known since his teens, has doubled in size over three months and now aches all night; he has begun to catch his right toes when walking.
case.exam: Firm, tender 7 cm popliteal mass that cannot be moved from side to side; weak ankle dorsiflexion and eversion, reduced feeling on the top of the foot, brisk Tinel sign over the mass.
case.tests: MRI shows a heterogeneous enhancing mass with central necrosis along the sciatic nerve bifurcation; FDG-PET has one intensely avid area; core biopsy from that area shows a high-grade spindle-cell sarcoma with loss of H3K27me3; chest CT is clear.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what treatment gives the best chance of cure?
case.a: MPNST arising in a plexiform neurofibroma; wide en-bloc resection with clear margins at a sarcoma centre (accepting nerve sacrifice), usually with pre- or postoperative radiotherapy, and anthracycline-ifosfamide chemotherapy considered for high-risk or metastatic disease.

det.patho: MPNST is a soft tissue sarcoma of Schwann-cell or perineurial lineage, making up a few percent to about one tenth of all soft tissue sarcomas. Roughly half arise in NF1, where loss of the NF1 gene in a plexiform or atypical neurofibroma is followed by CDKN2A/B deletion and then inactivation of the PRC2 complex (SUZ12 or EED), which removes H3 K27 trimethylation; the remainder are sporadic or radiation-associated. Atypical neurofibromatous neoplasm of uncertain biological potential (ANNUBP) represents the premalignant step. Divergent differentiation can occur, for example rhabdomyoblastic elements in malignant triton tumour, which is high grade.
det.clinical: The usual story is a deep nerve mass that suddenly grows, with constant or nocturnal pain and a new deficit, in a young adult with NF1 or in an older adult without a syndrome. Major trunks and plexuses of the limbs, buttock, trunk and paraspinal region are typical, while dermal neurofibromas do not become malignant. People with NF1 carry a lifetime risk of roughly one in ten, much higher than the general population, and a large internal plexiform tumour burden raises this risk further. Lung metastases may be the first sign, and spinal or paraspinal tumours can cause cord or root compression.
det.diagnosis: Any change in a known plexiform neurofibroma, such as fast growth, new pain, hardness or new weakness, needs MRI and FDG-PET, which together guide where to biopsy. Because these tumours are heterogeneous, the biopsy should target the most metabolically active or necrotic region, and several areas may need sampling; it should be planned with the sarcoma surgeon to avoid contaminating future resection planes. No single marker is diagnostic: S100 and SOX10 are often lost in about half, while complete loss of H3K27me3 is a helpful supportive marker. Pathology must separate MPNST from cellular schwannoma, ANNUBP, synovial sarcoma and other spindle-cell sarcomas.
det.treatment: Management belongs to a sarcoma multidisciplinary team, and the goal is cancer control rather than sparing the nerve. Wide en-bloc resection with negative margins is the main curative step, even if a major nerve must be sacrificed, and radiotherapy before or after surgery improves local control for high-grade or marginally resected tumours. Doxorubicin with ifosfamide is used for unresectable or metastatic disease and is sometimes given before surgery, with modest response rates. MEK inhibitors such as selumetinib, and mirdametinib approved in 2025, shrink inoperable plexiform neurofibromas in NF1 but do not treat established MPNST; clinical trials target PRC2 loss and MEK-CDK4/6 combinations.
det.prognosis: Five-year survival is roughly one third to one half and worse than most soft tissue sarcomas; size over 5 cm, high grade, positive margins, truncal site and NF1 association predict a poor outcome. Pulmonary metastasis is the usual cause of death.
pearls: In NF1, a painful plexiform neurofibroma that is growing fast is MPNST until proven otherwise; skin neurofibromas never undergo this change.
Biopsy the PET-hot part of the tumour, because a sample from the benign part gives a falsely reassuring result.
Loss of H3K27me3 on immunohistochemistry supports MPNST, while normal staining does not exclude it.
det.thd: MPNST เป็นมะเร็งของปลอกหุ้มเส้นประสาทส่วนปลาย ราวครึ่งหนึ่งเกิดในผู้ป่วย NF1 โดยเปลี่ยนจาก plexiform neurofibroma ก้อนจะโตเร็ว ปวดตลอดเวลาหรือปวดกลางคืน และมีอ่อนแรงหรือชาใหม่ การวินิจฉัยใช้ MRI ร่วมกับ FDG-PET เพื่อเลือกตำแหน่งตัดชิ้นเนื้อที่ถูกต้อง และตรวจย้อมพบการสูญเสีย H3K27me3 การรักษาหลักคือผ่าตัดเอาก้อนออกทั้งหมดพร้อมขอบปลอดเนื้องอกแม้ต้องเสียเส้นประสาท ร่วมกับฉายรังสี ส่วนเคมีบำบัด doxorubicin และ ifosfamide ใช้ในรายลุกลาม พยากรณ์โรคไม่ดีเพราะแพร่ไปปอดบ่อย

qx.stem: A 26-year-old woman from Nakhon Si Thammarat with neurofibromatosis type 1 has a plexiform neurofibroma in the left buttock that has been stable for ten years. Over two months it has grown, she has night pain down the leg, and new weakness of foot plantar flexion. MRI shows a heterogeneous region with central necrosis within the mass.

Fine-needle aspiration from the most superficial part

Because the tumour is heterogeneous, PET guides biopsy toward the malignant focus, and the biopsy should be planned with the surgeon who will do the wide resection. Superficial aspirates often miss the malignant part, and MEK inhibitors treat benign plexiform neurofibroma, not MPNST.

name: Traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI)
formal: Acute mechanical damage to the spinal cord, from fracture-dislocation, disc extrusion, hyperextension in a stenotic canal or penetrating injury, classified by neurological level and by the ASIA/ISNCSCI impairment scale (A complete to E normal), with early priorities of avoiding secondary injury through airway, perfusion, alignment and timely decompression.
simple: A serious injury to the spinal cord after an accident that causes weakness or paralysis and loss of feeling below the injured level, plus bladder, bowel and blood pressure problems.
th: การบาดเจ็บไขสันหลังจากอุบัติเหตุ ทำให้อ่อนแรงและชาต่ำกว่าระดับที่บาดเจ็บ กลั้นปัสสาวะอุจจาระไม่ได้ ความดันต่ำและชีพจรช้า (neurogenic shock) จัดระดับด้วย ASIA impairment scale A–E การดูแลเบื้องต้นคือตรึงกระดูกสันหลัง ดูแลทางเดินหายใจ รักษาความดันเฉลี่ย (MAP) 85–90 mmHg ผ่าตัดลดการกดทับเมื่อเหมาะสม และให้ฟื้นฟูสภาพ
tempoNote: Maximum deficit at impact; spinal shock lasts days to weeks, then spasticity emerges; most neurological recovery occurs in the first 3 to 6 months
feat: Complete injury: no motor or sensory function in the lowest sacral segments (S4–5); incomplete injury preserves sacral sensation or voluntary anal contraction, which is the best predictor of recovery

Level is defined by the key muscles (C5 elbow flexors, C6 wrist extensors, C7 triceps, C8 finger flexors, T1 little finger abductors, L2 hip flexors, L3 knee extensors, L4 ankle dorsiflexors, L5 long toe extensors, S1 plantar flexors) and by the pinprick and light-touch sensory level

Spinal shock: flaccid paralysis with loss of reflexes (including bulbocavernosus) below the lesion for days to weeks, then spasticity; neurogenic shock is a separate state of hypotension and bradycardia from loss of sympathetic tone in injuries above T6

Complications: respiratory failure (C3–5 injury affects the diaphragm), pressure sores, venous thromboembolism, neurogenic bladder and bowel, autonomic dysreflexia, pain and spasticity, heterotopic ossification

Incomplete syndromes: central cord (arms worse than legs), anterior cord (motor and pain loss with preserved dorsal columns), Brown-Séquard (ipsilateral motor and position loss, contralateral pain and temperature loss) and posterior cord
inv: Trauma CT of the spine with reconstructions for bony injury (a high-sensitivity first test); MRI as soon as safe for cord haemorrhage, oedema, disc, ligament and epidural haematoma
ISNCSCI examination (motor score of 100, sensory levels, anal sensation and contraction) at admission and repeated at 72 hours and later for prognosis; check bulbocavernosus and anal wink reflexes
CT angiography of the neck for vertebral artery injury in cervical fractures and dislocations; chest, blood gases and vital capacity monitoring in cervical injury

case.who: 29-year-old man, a rubber plantation worker from Trang
case.story: He fell 4 metres from a tree and landed on his head; he cannot feel or move below the shoulders.
case.exam: Alert, BP 82/50 and heart rate 48, flaccid quadriparesis with elbow flexion 3/5 but no wrist extension, sensory level C5, absent reflexes, no voluntary anal contraction but preserved perianal sensation.
case.tests: CT shows a C5–6 bilateral facet dislocation; MRI shows cord compression with intramedullary haemorrhage and a disc fragment.
case.q: What are the priorities and what is the AIS grade?
case.a: Neurogenic shock with a cervical injury at C5, AIS B (sensory but no motor function below the level, with sacral sparing of sensation). Maintain neutral alignment, secure the airway if breathing fails, use vasopressors to hold the MAP in the 85–90 mm Hg range for several days, reduce the dislocation and decompress early, and avoid high-dose methylprednisolone.
