det.patho: The initial mechanical injury (contusion, laceration, compression or transection) is followed by secondary damage over hours and days from haemorrhage, ischaemia, oedema, excitotoxicity, free radicals and inflammation. Preserving cord perfusion and removing ongoing compression are the main modifiable factors. Spinal shock is a transient loss of all cord function below the lesion including reflexes; neurogenic shock comes from interruption of sympathetic outflow above T1 to T6 and produces vasodilatation and bradycardia.
det.clinical: Road traffic collisions, falls from height, assaults and sports are the main causes, and in much of Asia falls from trees and motorcycle crashes are common. Presentation is loss of voluntary movement, sensation and sphincter control below the injury, sometimes with priapism, hypotension and bradycardia. Respiratory compromise increases with higher level. Distinguishing complete from incomplete injury requires testing sacral function; the bulbocavernosus reflex indicates when spinal shock has resolved. Recovery of a complete injury beyond spinal shock is unusual, whereas incomplete injuries often improve.
det.diagnosis: Follow trauma protocols with in-line immobilisation; do not clear the neck clinically if there is distracting injury, intoxication or deficit, but use validated rules (NEXUS, Canadian C-spine rule) or CT. Document the ISNCSCI examination and AIS grade (A complete, B sensory incomplete, C motor incomplete with less than half of key muscles at grade 3 or more, D with at least half, E normal) because it guides prognosis. MRI shows cord signal change and haemorrhage and informs prognosis, and CT angiography screens for vertebral artery injury in cervical injury.
det.treatment: Prehospital and emergency care aims at spinal alignment, airway, ventilation and avoiding hypotension (systolic below 90 mm Hg) and hypoxia. Monitor in an ICU, and keep the mean arterial pressure within 85–90 mm Hg during roughly the first 5 to 7 days. High-dose methylprednisolone is not recommended because of weak evidence and complications; guidelines either advise against or only weakly suggest it within 8 hours. Early surgical decompression and stabilisation, preferably within 24 hours for cervical injuries with incomplete deficits, is suggested by observational and pooled data (STASCIS); closed or open reduction of facet dislocations is done urgently. Prevent thromboembolism with early prophylaxis, pressure sores with turning and padding, manage bladder with intermittent catheterisation and start rehabilitation early. Neuroprotective and regenerative trials (riluzole, hypothermia, cell therapy) remain experimental.
det.prognosis: Recovery depends on the AIS grade and sacral sparing: most with AIS A remain complete, while most with AIS D regain walking. Life expectancy is reduced mainly by respiratory and urinary infection.
pearls: Sacral sparing (perianal sensation or voluntary anal contraction) means the injury is incomplete.
Treat hypotension in cord injury as neurogenic only after bleeding has been excluded; maintain MAP 85–90 mm Hg early.
Return of the bulbocavernosus reflex marks the end of spinal shock; do not declare a complete injury before then.
det.thd: การบาดเจ็บไขสันหลังเกิดจากอุบัติเหตุ เช่น ตกจากที่สูงหรือรถจักรยานยนต์ ผู้ป่วยอ่อนแรงและชาต่ำกว่าระดับที่บาดเจ็บ ปัสสาวะและอุจจาระไม่ได้ อาจมีความดันต่ำและชีพจรช้าจาก neurogenic shock ต้องแยก spinal shock ซึ่งคือภาวะรีเฟล็กซ์หายชั่วคราว ตรวจและให้เกรดด้วย ASIA impairment scale A–E ดูแลโดยตรึงกระดูกสันหลัง ช่วยหายใจถ้าจำเป็น ควบคุม MAP 85–90 mmHg ผ่าตัดลดการกดทับและยึดตรึงกระดูกสันหลังตั้งแต่เนิ่น ๆ ไม่แนะนำการให้ methylprednisolone ขนาดสูงเป็นมาตรฐาน และฟื้นฟูสภาพทันที

qx.stem: A 34-year-old motorcyclist in Khon Kaen is brought in after a high-speed crash. He has no movement or sensation below the nipples, flaccid legs, absent reflexes and no sacral sensation. Blood pressure is 82/44 mmHg with heart rate 48 per minute, and his skin is warm. FAST ultrasound and pelvic X-ray are normal, and CT shows a T3-T4 fracture-dislocation.
qx.q: Which statement best describes his circulatory state and its management?
opts: Haemorrhagic shock; transfuse to haemoglobin over 12 g/dL before any imaging
Spinal shock; it explains the low blood pressure and needs no treatment
Cardiogenic shock; start dobutamine and diuretics
Septic shock; take cultures and start meropenem
Neurogenic shock from lost sympathetic tone; give fluids, then a vasopressor such as noradrenaline to keep mean arterial pressure about 85 mmHg
qx.why: Low blood pressure with bradycardia and warm skin after a high thoracic or cervical cord injury is neurogenic shock from loss of sympathetic outflow. Guidelines suggest keeping mean arterial pressure around 85-90 mmHg for the first days with fluids and vasopressors, after bleeding is excluded. Spinal shock is a different term describing loss of reflexes below the injury, not hypotension.

name: Raised intracranial pressure
formal: Sustained elevation of intracranial pressure above about 20 to 22 mm Hg in adults from a mass, oedema, haemorrhage, hydrocephalus, venous outflow obstruction or diffuse swelling, lowering cerebral perfusion pressure and risking herniation; managed by cause-directed treatment and tiered measures guided by ICP, CPP and the clinical examination.
simple: Too much pressure inside the skull from swelling, bleeding, a tumour or blocked fluid pathways, which can squeeze the brain and cut its blood supply.
th: ความดันในกะโหลกศีรษะสูง (ICP > 20–22 mmHg) จากก้อนเนื้อ เลือดออก สมองบวม น้ำคั่งโพรงสมอง หรือเส้นเลือดดำอุดตัน ทำให้ปวดศีรษะ อาเจียน ซึมลง จอประสาทตาบวม และอาจเกิดสมองเคลื่อน (herniation) การรักษาเริ่มจากยกศีรษะ 30 องศา หลีกเลี่ยงภาวะความดันต่ำและขาดออกซิเจน ใช้ยาเพิ่มความเข้มข้นพลาสมา (mannitol หรือ hypertonic saline) ระบายน้ำไขสันหลัง และผ่าตัดหาสาเหตุหรือเปิดกะโหลก
tempoNote: Over minutes to hours with a haematoma, swelling or acute hydrocephalus; days to weeks with tumours, abscesses or venous thrombosis
feat: Headache worse on lying, waking or straining, vomiting, drowsiness, papilloedema and visual obscurations; sixth nerve palsies are a false-localising sign
Cushing response (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respiration) and unilateral dilated pupil, or posturing, signal herniation and need immediate action
Monro-Kellie doctrine: brain (about 1400 mL), blood (150 mL) and CSF (150 mL) share a rigid skull; once compensation by CSF and venous shift is exhausted a small volume gives a large pressure rise
Cerebral perfusion pressure equals mean arterial pressure minus ICP; in severe TBI aim for a CPP of about 60 to 70 mm Hg and ICP under 22 mm Hg

Causes include traumatic and spontaneous haemorrhage, infarction with swelling (malignant MCA), tumour with vasogenic oedema, abscess, hydrocephalus, venous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, hepatic failure and status epilepticus
inv: Urgent CT head: mass effect, midline shift, effaced basal cisterns, hydrocephalus, sulcal effacement; MRI/MRV for venous thrombosis or posterior fossa disease

Invasive ICP monitoring with an external ventricular drain (allows drainage) or intraparenchymal probe in comatose patients with a plausible risk of intracranial hypertension; ICP waveform and compliance analysis
Noninvasive adjuncts: optic nerve sheath diameter by ultrasound, transcranial Doppler pulsatility, pupillometry; brain tissue oxygen and cerebral microdialysis in specialised units
Never perform lumbar puncture before imaging when a mass lesion or obstructive hydrocephalus is possible

case.who: 54-year-old man from Surin, a driver with hypertension
case.story: A left hemispheric intracerebral haemorrhage of 60 mL is found on CT after sudden headache and right weakness; six hours later he becomes drowsy and vomits.
case.exam: GCS 9 (E2 V2 M5), left pupil 5 mm and sluggish, right hemiplegia, blood pressure 190/100 with pulse 52.
case.tests: Repeat CT shows haematoma expansion to 85 mL with 9 mm midline shift and obliterated left basal cisterns.
case.q: What is the sequence of management?
case.a: Raised ICP with early herniation. Raise the head to 30 degrees, secure the airway and normoxia, give hyperosmolar therapy (mannitol 0.5–1 g/kg or 3% saline bolus) as a bridge, place ICP monitoring or an external ventricular drain if there is hydrocephalus, and arrange urgent surgical evacuation. Avoid hypotension while controlling blood pressure.

det.patho: The cranium holds brain, blood and CSF in a nearly fixed volume, so an added volume is first buffered by displacing CSF and venous blood; once reserve is spent, compliance falls and small increments produce steep pressure rises. High ICP lowers cerebral perfusion pressure and, if autoregulation is lost, causes ischaemia, while pressure gradients between compartments drive herniation. Pathological waveforms include plateau (Lundberg A) waves of 50 mm Hg or more lasting 5–20 minutes, which signal critically low compliance. The relevant target is adequate cerebral blood flow, not ICP alone.
det.clinical: Chronic or subacute elevation presents with headache, vomiting, papilloedema, visual blurring and drowsiness. Acute elevation causes falling consciousness, pupillary change, hypertension and bradycardia (Cushing response), irregular breathing and posturing, which are signs of impending herniation. The signs of the cause (focal deficit in haemorrhage, fever in meningitis, papilloedema in venous thrombosis) usually guide the diagnosis. Infants show a tense fontanelle, sunsetting eyes and rapid head growth.
det.diagnosis: Neuroimaging is urgent; lumbar puncture only after imaging. In comatose patients with a mass lesion, severe TBI or hydrocephalus, ICP monitoring allows treatment thresholds (usually above 20–22 mm Hg) and CPP targets to be applied; an external ventricular drain also treats hydrocephalus but carries risks of infection and haemorrhage. Waveform analysis and autoregulation indices are research tools. Look for causes that need specific treatment, such as hydrocephalus, venous thrombosis, abscess, seizures and hepatic failure.
det.treatment: Start with basic measures: elevate the head to 30–45 degrees with the neck neutral, avoid jugular compression, maintain normal oxygenation, euvolaemia, normal blood pressure and normothermia, treat pain, agitation and seizures, keep sodium in the high-normal range and avoid hyperglycaemia and hypotonic fluids. Step up to CSF drainage, hyperosmolar therapy (mannitol 0.25–1 g/kg, or 3% saline infusions or bolus; hold if serum osmolality is above 320 mOsm/L) and short-term moderate hyperventilation to a PaCO2 of 30–35 mm Hg only as rescue. Refractory pressure calls for repeat CT to exclude a surgical lesion, then deep sedation, barbiturate coma, decompressive craniectomy or controlled hypothermia in selected cases; RESCUEicp showed that late craniectomy lowers mortality but increases survival with severe disability, so patient values matter. Steroids help vasogenic oedema from tumours and abscess but are harmful in head injury (CRASH trial).
det.prognosis: Outcome depends on cause and on the duration of pressure above threshold; sustained intracranial hypertension carries high mortality and disability.
pearls: Treat the cause: a surgical mass or hydrocephalus needs drainage or removal, not just osmotherapy.
Lumbar puncture is contraindicated until imaging excludes a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus.
Prophylactic hyperventilation lowers cerebral blood flow and is harmful; use it only as a short rescue.
det.thd: ความดันในกะโหลกศีรษะสูงเกิดเมื่อสมอง เลือด หรือน้ำไขสันหลังมีปริมาตรเกินพื้นที่ที่จำกัดของกะโหลก จากก้อนเนื้อ เลือดออก สมองบวม หรือน้ำคั่งในโพรงสมอง ผู้ป่วยปวดศีรษะ อาเจียน ซึมลง จอประสาทตาบวม และเมื่อรุนแรงมีรูม่านตาข้างเดียวขยาย ความดันสูง ชีพจรช้า (Cushing response) ต้องส่ง CT ก่อนเจาะหลัง ดูแลโดยยกศีรษะ 30 องศา ให้ออกซิเจนและความดันเหมาะสม ใช้ mannitol หรือ 3% saline ระบายน้ำไขสันหลัง และผ่าตัดเอาสาเหตุออก เช่น ก้อนเลือด หรือผ่าตัดเปิดกะโหลก (decompressive craniectomy) เมื่อรักษาอื่นไม่ได้ผล

qx.stem: A 23-year-old man in a Bangkok trauma ICU has a severe head injury with diffuse swelling on CT. He is intubated and sedated, the head of the bed is at 30 degrees, PaCO2 is 37 mmHg, and he has received a mannitol bolus. An external ventricular drain shows ICP of 28 mmHg for 20 minutes, and CSF drainage gives only brief relief.
qx.q: Which is the most appropriate next measure?
opts: Give a bolus of hypertonic saline and keep the treatment tiers going toward decompressive craniectomy if ICP stays high
Prolonged hyperventilation to PaCO2 of 25 mmHg
High-dose dexamethasone
Lay him fully flat to improve cerebral perfusion
Stop sedation to allow a neurological examination
qx.why: ICP above 22 mmHg after first-tier measures needs escalation: hyperosmolar therapy with hypertonic saline or more mannitol, then higher tiers such as barbiturates or decompressive craniectomy. Prolonged hyperventilation risks ischaemia, steroids are harmful in traumatic brain injury, and lying flat or stopping sedation tends to raise ICP.

name: Cerebral salt wasting (CSW)
formal: Renal sodium loss with extracellular volume depletion and hyponatraemia caused by intracranial disease, most often aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage, traumatic brain injury or neurosurgery; biochemically similar to SIADH but distinguished by hypovolaemia and negative sodium balance, which makes fluid restriction harmful.
simple: After a brain bleed or injury the kidneys lose too much salt and water, leaving the blood sodium low and the patient dry; treatment is to give salt and fluid, not to restrict fluid.
th: Cerebral salt wasting คือภาวะที่ไตเสียโซเดียมและน้ำมากหลังโรคทางสมอง โดยเฉพาะหลังเลือดออกใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมองจากหลอดเลือดโป่งพอง ทำให้โซเดียมต่ำและร่างกายขาดปริมาตรน้ำ ต่างจาก SIADH ที่ปริมาตรปกติหรือเกิน การรักษาคือให้เกลือและน้ำชดเชย ห้ามจำกัดน้ำ เพราะอาจทำให้เกิดสมองขาดเลือดจาก vasospasm
tempoNote: Appears in the first days to two weeks after a brain insult and usually resolves in weeks
feat: Hyponatraemia with high urine sodium and urine osmolality, clinical or measured hypovolaemia (low central venous pressure, orthostasis, dry mucosae, rising haematocrit and urea) and polyuria in a neurosurgical or SAH patient
Typically after aneurysmal SAH, severe TBI, craniotomy, tumour surgery or meningitis; peaks around days 3 to 10 after SAH, overlapping the vasospasm window
Serum and urine chemistries can look identical to SIADH, so volume status and sodium balance are the discriminators; high or normal-high potassium argues against SIADH
Features of hyponatraemia range from headache and nausea to confusion, seizures and coma when the fall is rapid
Its importance is that fluid restriction, the treatment of SIADH, worsens hypovolaemia, thickens the blood and increases the risk of delayed cerebral ischaemia
inv: Serum sodium and osmolality, urine sodium and osmolality, potassium, urea, uric acid, glucose and haematocrit, repeated every 6 to 12 hours initially
Estimate volume status: weight trend, input-output charts, central venous pressure or echo-derived indices; plasma volume measurement is a research tool
Exclude adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, diuretic effect, hyperglycaemia and iatrogenic hypotonic fluids; check cortisol if shock or refractory course

case.who: 52-year-old woman from Khon Kaen on day 6 after coiling for a ruptured posterior communicating aneurysm
case.story: Her sodium has fallen from 139 to 126 mmol/L over two days while she is drowsy; she is passing 3.5 litres of urine a day and was placed on 1 litre fluid restriction yesterday.
case.exam: Dry tongue, orthostatic drop in blood pressure, weight down 2.5 kg, mild new left leg weakness.
case.tests: Urine sodium 78 mmol/L, urine osmolality 510 mOsm/kg, serum urea and haematocrit rising; TCD velocities in the right ACA and MCA are climbing.
case.q: What is the correct management?
case.a: Cerebral salt wasting with volume depletion and a vasospasm risk. Stop the fluid restriction, give isotonic saline and extra salt, consider fludrocortisone, aim for euvolaemia and a sodium rise below 8–10 mmol/L per day, and continue nimodipine and vasospasm surveillance.

read.where: Chapter 5 General and Neurology — Hyponatremia; Cerebral salt wasting
Chapter 28 Disorders of Consciousness and Intensive Care Neurology

det.patho: Intracranial disease causes the kidney to lose sodium, possibly through impaired sympathetic renal input, natriuretic peptides such as brain and atrial natriuretic peptide and ouabain-like factors. The resulting loss of sodium and water contracts the extracellular volume, which then stimulates antidiuretic hormone release and may thereby perpetuate hyponatraemia. CSW and SIADH can coexist or be difficult to separate on laboratory grounds alone.
det.clinical: CSW usually appears within the first week or two after SAH, TBI or neurosurgery, with a falling sodium, high urine output and signs of volume depletion. The decline in sodium may precede or accompany delayed cerebral ischaemia. Symptoms of hyponatraemia (headache, nausea, confusion, seizures) overlap those of the primary disease and are easily attributed to it. Hypovolaemia also impairs perfusion in patients at risk of vasospasm.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis rests on documenting hyponatraemia with natriuresis plus a negative fluid balance or reduced extracellular volume; urine sodium above about 40 mmol/L with concentrated urine does not distinguish CSW from SIADH. Clinical assessment, trends in weight, haematocrit, urea and uric acid, fluid balance and central venous pressure matter most, and an elevated serum potassium is incompatible with SIADH. Exclude adrenal insufficiency and diuretic effect.
det.treatment: Restore and maintain euvolaemia with isotonic saline, and give enteral sodium chloride tablets or hypertonic saline (1.5 or 3%) for symptomatic or severe hyponatraemia, targeting a rise in sodium of 0.5 mmol/L per hour or less and no more than 8–10 mmol/L in 24 hours, with sodium checks every 4 hours. Fludrocortisone (0.1–0.2 mg twice daily) reduces natriuresis and is commonly used after SAH; hydrocortisone is an alternative. Avoid fluid restriction, hypotonic fluids and over-rapid correction (osmotic demyelination), and monitor for hyperchloraemic acidosis. Continue nimodipine and watch for vasospasm.
det.prognosis: Usually self-limited over one to three weeks with appropriate replacement; unrecognised volume depletion can worsen neurological outcome.
pearls: Hyponatraemia after SAH should be treated as salt wasting until proven otherwise: assess volume, do not restrict fluid.
Hyperkalaemia with hyponatraemia cannot be SIADH.
Correct sodium slowly, no faster than 8–10 mmol/L in 24 hours.
det.thd: Cerebral salt wasting เกิดหลังโรคสมอง โดยเฉพาะหลัง SAH จากหลอดเลือดโป่งพองแตก การบาดเจ็บสมอง หรือผ่าตัดสมอง ไตขับโซเดียมและน้ำมากเกินไปจนร่างกายขาดน้ำและโซเดียมต่ำ ปัสสาวะออกมาก น้ำหนักลด ผลเลือดและปัสสาวะคล้าย SIADH แต่ต่างตรงที่ผู้ป่วยขาดปริมาตรน้ำ การรักษาคือให้ น้ำเกลือ เกลือรับประทาน หรือ hypertonic saline และอาจให้ fludrocortisone ห้ามจำกัดน้ำ เพราะอาจเกิดสมองขาดเลือดจาก vasospasm และต้องแก้โซเดียมช้า ๆ ไม่เกิน 8–10 mmol/L ใน 24 ชั่วโมง

qx.stem: A 45-year-old man in a Songkhla ICU is on day 5 after a ruptured aneurysm was clipped. Serum sodium has fallen from 139 to 126 mmol/L. He is producing 4 L of urine per day, urine sodium is 140 mmol/L, he is tachycardic with dry mucous membranes, his weight has dropped 2 kg and haematocrit has risen.
qx.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Replace volume and salt with isotonic or hypertonic saline, adding fludrocortisone if needed
Restrict fluid to 800 mL per day
Start tolvaptan and restrict fluid
Give furosemide with 3% saline
Observe; sodium will correct once the vasospasm window ends
qx.why: Heavy natriuresis with clinical volume depletion points to cerebral salt wasting rather than SIADH, which is euvolaemic. Treatment is sodium and volume replacement, with fludrocortisone as an adjunct. Fluid restriction, the standard treatment of SIADH, would cause hypovolaemia and raise the risk of delayed cerebral ischaemia after subarachnoid haemorrhage.

name: Craniosynostosis
formal: Premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures, either isolated (nonsyndromic, most commonly sagittal) or part of a genetic craniofacial syndrome (FGFR-related Apert, Crouzon and Pfeiffer), producing characteristic head shapes, restricted skull growth, and in some children raised intracranial pressure, visual and developmental problems; treated surgically in the first year.
simple: The soft joints between a baby's skull bones close too early, so the head grows in an abnormal shape and sometimes cannot make enough room for the growing brain.
th: Craniosynostosis คือรอยต่อกะโหลกศีรษะของทารกปิดเร็วกว่าปกติ ทำให้รูปศีรษะผิดปกติ เช่น ศีรษะยาวแคบจาก sagittal synostosis ถ้าปิดหลายรอยต่อหรือเป็นกลุ่มอาการ (Apert, Crouzon) อาจมีความดันในกะโหลกสูง จอประสาทตาบวม และพัฒนาการช้า ตรวจดูรูปศีรษะ คลำสันกระดูก ถ่าย CT 3 มิติ และผ่าตัดแก้ไขในช่วงขวบปีแรก เพื่อให้สมองเจริญเติบโตและรูปศีรษะดีขึ้น
tempoNote: Present at birth or evident in the first months as the head shape evolves; raised ICP may emerge over months to years if untreated
feat: Sagittal synostosis is the commonest single-suture form (boys more than girls) and gives a long narrow boat-shaped head (scaphocephaly) with a palpable midline ridge and frontal bossing

Metopic synostosis gives trigonocephaly (pointed forehead and narrow temples); unilateral coronal synostosis gives anterior plagiocephaly with a flat forehead and a raised orbit (harlequin eye sign); lambdoid synostosis gives a flat trapezoid occiput with a ridge

Multiple suture involvement and syndromic forms (Apert with syndactyly, Crouzon with midface hypoplasia and proptosis, Pfeiffer) often have raised ICP, hydrocephalus, Chiari malformation, airway obstruction and exposure keratopathy
Raised ICP occurs in about 10% with a single suture and in a larger share of multiple sutures, with papilloedema, poor head growth, irritability, developmental delay and sleep-disordered breathing
Positional (deformational) plagiocephaly is far more common, is a parallelogram rather than a trapezoid, and improves with repositioning
inv: Clinical assessment: ridge over the suture, head shape from above, failure to move the bones against each other, ear position, fontanelle and measurement of head circumference
Low-dose CT with 3D reconstruction confirms fused sutures and associated anomalies (ultrasound may screen in infants); MRI or MRV when hydrocephalus, Chiari or venous outflow disease is suspected
Fundoscopy or OCT for papilloedema, genetic testing (FGFR1–3, TWIST1, TCF12, ERF) in syndromic or multi-suture cases, sleep study and ophthalmology review

case.who: 3-month-old boy from Samut Prakan, first child
case.story: Parents notice the head has become long and narrow with a prominent forehead; he feeds and develops normally and has had no vomiting.
case.exam: Scaphocephaly with a hard keel along the sagittal suture, wide anterior fontanelle closed prematurely at the posterior end, normal fundi, head circumference at the 60th centile.
case.tests: Low-dose CT with 3D reconstruction shows a fused sagittal suture, no hydrocephalus and no other fused sutures.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and when should surgery be offered?
case.a: Nonsyndromic sagittal craniosynostosis. Offer surgical correction in the first 6 to 12 months (strip craniectomy, spring-assisted or cranial vault remodelling depending on age) by a craniofacial team, to normalise skull shape and prevent raised ICP.

read.where: Chapter 15 Primary Intracranial Anomalies — Craniosynostosis; Craniofacial dysmorphic syndromes
18. Disorders of Cranial Volume and Shape
Chapter 9: Congenital Disorders of the Brain and Spine

det.patho: Sutures normally remain open to accommodate brain growth, and premature fusion restricts growth perpendicular to the suture and causes compensatory growth at the open sutures. Most single-suture cases are sporadic and nonsyndromic, with a minority having a genetic cause; FGFR2, FGFR3, TWIST1, TCF12 and other mutations underlie syndromic forms, most inherited as autosomal dominant. Multiple fused sutures reduce intracranial volume and can raise ICP, and venous hypertension, Chiari malformation and airway obstruction add to it.
det.clinical: Parents or clinicians notice the shape of the head at birth or in the first months. Sagittal synostosis is the commonest, then coronal (more often girls and in syndromes), metopic and lambdoid. Scaphocephaly has a reduced biparietal diameter with a close to normal circumference, so head circumference can mislead. Unilateral coronal synostosis can cause amblyopia from the elevated orbit. Syndromic children have midface hypoplasia, proptosis, airway and hearing problems. Developmental delay is more related to the syndrome and raised ICP than to a single suture.
det.diagnosis: Distinguish from positional plagiocephaly by shape (trapezoid with ipsilateral ear displaced backward in lambdoid synostosis vs parallelogram with ear forward in positional), a palpable ridge or trough, immobile sutures and imaging. Observation with repositioning for 6 to 8 weeks resolves positional cases. CT is the definitive investigation, and a radiograph showing 'beaten copper' pattern, sutural diastasis or sellar erosion suggests raised pressure. Raised ICP is suspected from papilloedema, falling head growth or developmental slowing.
det.treatment: Surgery is the treatment for functional or cosmetic reasons and for raised ICP. For sagittal synostosis, a strip craniectomy or endoscopic suturectomy with helmet moulding before about 4 months, or spring-assisted expansion, or a cranial vault remodelling after that, are options; the aim is to correct shape and give room for growth. Syndromic and multisutural cases need staged work by a neurosurgeon and craniofacial surgeon, with attention to hydrocephalus, Chiari, airway and eye protection. Blood loss and transfusion are significant risks in infants; ICP and fundi are monitored afterwards.
det.prognosis: Early surgery gives good cosmetic results and normal development in most nonsyndromic cases; outcome in syndromic forms depends on the syndrome and associated problems.
pearls: Fused sagittal suture: boat-shaped head with a ridge; the circumference can be normal.
A trapezoid head means lambdoid synostosis, a parallelogram means positional plagiocephaly.
Multiple fused sutures or a syndrome: check for raised ICP, Chiari and airway obstruction.
det.thd: Craniosynostosis คือรอยต่อกะโหลกของทารกปิดก่อนเวลา ทำให้ศีรษะมีรูปร่างผิดปกติตามรอยต่อที่ปิด เช่น sagittal synostosis ทำให้หัวยาวแคบแบบเรือ (scaphocephaly) metopic ทำให้หน้าผากแหลม coronal ทำให้หน้าผากด้านหนึ่งแบน ถ้าปิดหลายรอยต่อหรือเป็นกลุ่มอาการ เช่น Apert และ Crouzon ความดันในกะโหลกอาจสูง ตรวจโดยดูรูปศีรษะ คลำสันกระดูก และ CT 3 มิติ แยกจาก positional plagiocephaly ซึ่งดีขึ้นเมื่อจัดท่านอน การผ่าตัดทำในช่วงขวบปีแรก

name: Skull fractures (linear, depressed and basal)
formal: Fractures of the calvaria or skull base classified as linear, diastatic, depressed, open (compound) or basal; most linear fractures need no surgery, whereas open or markedly depressed fractures, those with dural tear or contamination, and basal fractures with CSF leak or cranial nerve injury need targeted management and surveillance for infection and vascular injury.
simple: A crack or dent in the skull bone after a head injury; most cracks heal on their own, but dents, open wounds and skull-base fractures may cause bleeding, nerve injury or CSF leak and infection.
th: กะโหลกศีรษะแตกแบ่งเป็นแตกเป็นเส้น (linear) กดบุ๋ม (depressed) แผลเปิด (compound) และแตกที่ฐานกะโหลก (basal) กะโหลกแตกเป็นเส้นส่วนใหญ่ไม่ต้องผ่าตัด แต่ควรตรวจหาก้อนเลือดและบาดเจ็บสมอง ส่วนแตกกดบุ๋มลึกกว่าความหนากะโหลกหรือแผลเปิดมักต้องผ่าตัด ฐานกะโหลกแตกอาจมีรอยช้ำหลังหู (Battle) ช้ำรอบตา น้ำไขสันหลังรั่วจากจมูก/หู หรือเส้นประสาทสมอง VII/VIII บาดเจ็บ
tempoNote: Injury is immediate; CSF leak, facial palsy, meningitis or vascular complications can appear within hours to weeks
feat: About 90% of paediatric calvarial fractures are linear; diastatic fractures separate a suture and are more common in young children

Depressed fractures that sink more than the thickness of the adjacent skull, open fractures with dural tear, gross contamination, frontal sinus involvement or underlying haematoma are usually elevated and debrided

Basal fractures usually extend from the vault: periorbital ecchymosis, mastoid (Battle) sign, haemotympanum, CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea, anosmia and cranial nerve palsies (VII, VIII, and III to VI in clival fractures)
Temporal bone fractures: longitudinal (70–90%) spare the facial nerve and cochlea but may disrupt ossicles; transverse fractures more often cause facial palsy and sensorineural deafness
Clival and skull base fractures can injure carotid and vertebrobasilar arteries and cause traumatic aneurysm, dissection or diabetes insipidus
inv: Non-contrast CT head with bone windows (and thin-cut skull base reconstruction) is the investigation of choice; plain films are of limited value and can mislead because vessel grooves and sutures mimic fractures
CT angiography when a fracture crosses the carotid canal, clivus or foramen magnum, or neurology suggests vascular injury (blunt cerebrovascular injury)
CSF leak confirmation by beta-2 transferrin or beta-trace protein, high-resolution CT or MR cisternography; audiometry and facial electroneuronography for temporal bone injury

case.who: 25-year-old man, a motorcycle rider from Chiang Mai who was not wearing a helmet
case.story: He had a collision with a pickup truck, was confused for a few minutes and then talks normally; there is clear fluid dripping from the right ear and his right face droops.
case.exam: GCS 15, right periauricular bruising (Battle sign), haemotympanum with a visible tear in the external canal, immediate-onset right lower motor neurone facial palsy, hearing loss on the right.
case.tests: CT shows a transverse right petrous fracture, a small temporal contusion and no extra-axial haematoma; CT angiography of the carotid canal is normal.
case.q: What is the management of the facial palsy and the CSF leak?
case.a: Basal skull fracture (transverse temporal bone) with immediate facial palsy. Observe and monitor with serial neuro examination, ENT and audiology consultation, with steroids often used for facial palsy and facial electroneuronography (surgical decompression is considered if function does not recover). Most CSF otorrhoea stops in days with head elevation; avoid routine prophylactic antibiotics, give pneumococcal vaccination, and counsel on meningitis symptoms.

read.where: Chapter 54 Skull Fractures — Depressed skull fractures; Basal skull fractures; temporal bone and clival fractures

det.patho: A skull fracture indicates substantial force; its importance depends on the underlying brain, vessel and dural injury more than on the bone injury itself. Fractures that cross the middle meningeal groove tear the artery and cause extradural haematoma; those over venous sinuses can cause sinus laceration or thrombosis. Fractures that tear dura over paranasal sinuses, mastoid or petrous bone open a pathway between the CSF space and the environment, with risk of meningitis. In infants a dural tear with an expanding fracture can lead to a growing skull fracture (leptomeningeal cyst).
det.clinical: Examine the scalp wound, palpate for step deformity, and look for signs of skull base injury: bruising around the eyes or behind the ear, haemotympanum, bleeding from the ear, CSF leak, loss of smell, hearing loss, vertigo and facial palsy. A clival or longitudinal fracture can be accompanied by vascular injury and delayed traumatic aneurysm. Posttraumatic seizures relate to the brain injury, not to the fracture or its elevation. Facial palsy that is immediate suggests nerve disruption and delayed palsy suggests oedema.
det.diagnosis: CT is diagnostic and essential, with bone windows and thin skull base slices. Skull radiographs add little. Depth of depression is compared with the adjacent bone thickness, and any dural penetration (pneumocephalus, bone fragments in brain) changes the plan. Confirm CSF leaks with beta-2 transferrin. Evaluate hearing and facial nerve function in temporal bone fractures and vascular imaging for fractures across arterial canals. In children, consider non-accidental injury when a fracture does not match the history.
det.treatment: Simple linear fractures need analgesia, observation and head injury advice. Open or depressed fractures deeper than the skull thickness, or those with dural tear, contamination or haematoma, are elevated and debrided early, with antibiotics for compound fractures and watertight dural repair; fractures over a major venous sinus are managed conservatively if the patient is stable. Nonsurgical management of a depressed fracture is possible when there is no dural penetration, depression is under 1 cm, no frontal sinus involvement, infection or deformity. Most traumatic CSF leaks stop spontaneously within a week with head elevation; persistent leaks need lumbar drainage or surgical repair, and prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended routinely. Facial palsy and hearing loss are managed with ENT. Rare growing fractures require dural repair and cranioplasty.
det.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the brain injury; isolated linear fractures heal well, and persistent CSF leak or vascular injury are the main avoidable complications.
pearls: A fracture is a marker of force: look for an underlying extradural haematoma or vascular injury.
Depressed fractures: operate for depression greater than the skull thickness, open wound or dural tear; elevation does not prevent epilepsy.
Battle sign, raccoon eyes and clear nasal or ear fluid after trauma mean a basal fracture.
det.thd: กะโหลกแตกแบ่งเป็น linear, depressed, compound และ basal ส่วนใหญ่แตกเป็นเส้นและหายได้เอง แต่ต้องตรวจ CT หาเลือดออกหรือบาดเจ็บสมอง การแตกกดบุ๋มลึกกว่าความหนาของกะโหลก แผลเปิด หรือเยื่อดูราฉีก มักต้องผ่าตัดยกกระดูกและทำความสะอาด ฐานกะโหลกแตกอาจมีรอยช้ำหลังหู ช้ำรอบตา น้ำไขสันหลังรั่วจากจมูกหรือหู เส้นประสาทสมองบาดเจ็บ หรือหลอดเลือดบาดเจ็บ การรั่วส่วนใหญ่หยุดเองภายใน 1 สัปดาห์ ไม่ควรให้ยาปฏิชีวนะป้องกันเป็นประจำ แต่ต้องเฝ้าระวังเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ

name: Burner (stinger) and transient cervical cord neurapraxia
formal: Two sport-related cervical injuries: the burner or stinger, a unilateral brachial plexus or nerve root traction injury causing transient burning pain and weakness in an arm, and cervical cord neurapraxia, a transient bilateral or four-limb sensory and motor disturbance (burning hands when bilateral) from cord compression or concussion in the canal, usually resolving within minutes to hours; return-to-play depends on canal size, imaging and recurrence.
simple: After a tackle or collision an athlete feels a sudden burning, tingling or weakness in one arm (burner) or sometimes in both arms or all four limbs (cord neurapraxia), which usually clears within minutes but can signal a narrow neck canal or an injury needing assessment.
ab: Burner  and transient cervical cord neurapraxia
th: Burner หรือ stinger คือการบาดเจ็บของข่ายประสาทแขนหรือรากประสาทที่คอจากการกระแทกหรือดึงรั้งในกีฬา ผู้เล่นรู้สึกแสบร้อนและชาที่แขนข้างเดียว อาจอ่อนแรง ส่วน cervical cord neurapraxia คือไขสันหลังคอถูกกระทบเฉียบพลัน ทำให้ชาแสบหรืออ่อนแรงหลายแขนขาชั่วคราว (burning hands เมื่อสองแขน) มักหายภายใน 15 นาที แต่ต้องตรวจหาช่องไขสันหลังแคบและความไม่มั่นคง ก่อนกลับเล่น
tempoNote: Pain and weakness begin at impact and usually clear within seconds to minutes; cord neurapraxia typically resolves in under 15 minutes, occasionally up to 48 hours
feat: Burner: unilateral burning dysaesthetic pain from the shoulder to the hand, with C5 or C6 weakness (shoulder abduction, elbow flexion), after a tackle that depresses the shoulder while the neck is bent to the other side or extended and rotated to the same side
Mechanisms: stretch of the brachial plexus upper trunk, or compression of the root in the foramen; most recover within minutes, but weakness lasting more than a day suggests axonal injury
Burning hands syndrome: bilateral burning in the hands with variable arm weakness, probably a mild central cord injury

Cervical cord neurapraxia: transient sensory change, with or without weakness or paralysis, involving all four limbs in about 80%, with full recovery; a narrow cervical canal (low Torg-Pavlov ratio) predisposes and recurrence on return to contact play is common
Spear tackler’s spine: head-first tackling in a stiff, straightened cervical spine increases risk of fractures and quadriplegia; the technique is banned
inv: Immediate sideline assessment: remove from play, immobilise the neck if any neck pain, bilateral symptoms, altered consciousness or persisting deficit; leave the helmet on at the scene unless removal is essential and staff are trained
Cervical MRI after any episode of cord neurapraxia, a burner that is recurrent, persistent or bilateral; flexion-extension films or CT for instability and canal diameter
Electrodiagnostic studies (EMG) at about 2 to 3 weeks if weakness or sensory loss persists, to distinguish root from plexus injury and gauge axonal loss

case.story: After a tackle he fell, felt sudden burning and numbness in both arms and legs and could not move for about ten minutes; all symptoms then settled.
case.exam: Now normal motor examination and reflexes, full neck movement, no midline tenderness.
case.tests: MRI shows a congenitally narrow cervical canal with cord contact at C3–4 but no cord oedema or ligament injury; flexion-extension views are stable.
case.q: What is the advice about return to play?
case.a: Cervical cord neurapraxia in a narrow canal. After a single episode with resolved symptoms and a normal MRI without cord signal change or instability a relative restriction may be discussed with a spine specialist, but contact sport is contraindicated if there is cord oedema or defect, instability, symptoms lasting longer than 36 hours or repeated episodes; shared decision making is needed.

read.where: Chapter 59 Spine Trauma — Sports-related spinal cord injuries; Football-related cervical spine injuries; Return to play
8 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System

det.patho: A burner results from forceful depression of the shoulder with lateral flexion of the head to the opposite side, which stretches the plexus upper trunk, or from forced extension and ipsilateral rotation compressing the root in its foramen; it is not a spinal cord injury. Cord neurapraxia is thought to result from a transient pincer effect on the cord in a narrow canal, with temporary conduction block rather than structural injury. Burning hands syndrome probably represents a mild central cord injury.
det.clinical: A burner presents with sudden unilateral burning pain, numbness or weakness of the arm, usually from C5 or C6, and the athlete often holds the arm still and shakes it. Symptoms commonly resolve within minutes, and recurrent burners may predispose to chronic weakness. Cord neurapraxia affects both arms, or arms and legs, with burning, tingling or temporary paralysis that typically lasts under 15 minutes. Head-down tackling leads to vertebral fractures and quadriplegia in some, while carotid or vertebral dissection may follow a neck blow.
det.diagnosis: Distinguish root and plexus from cord injury at the sideline: unilateral arm symptoms with a normal neck examination suggest a burner, whereas bilateral symptoms, neck pain, leg involvement or any persistent deficit demand immobilisation and cord imaging. MRI looks for canal stenosis, cord signal change, disc herniation and ligamentous injury. Canal width is assessed on lateral radiographs or MRI; a narrow canal predisposes but is not an absolute predictor of injury. EMG after two to three weeks clarifies axonal injury in persistent burners.
det.treatment: Remove the athlete from play. For a burner, allow return to play only after complete symptom resolution with full painless neck movement and normal strength; persistent weakness requires rest, rehabilitation and investigation. Prevent recurrence with neck and shoulder strengthening, proper tackle technique and, in some sports, cervical collars or shoulder padding. For cord neurapraxia, refer for MRI and specialist advice; return to contact sport is generally not advised if there is a structural cord abnormality, instability, persisting symptoms or more than one episode. Uncomplicated single episodes with a normal MRI may be allowed to return after counselling, but decisions are individual.
det.prognosis: Both usually recover completely; recurrence is frequent, particularly in those with a narrow canal.
pearls: Unilateral arm symptoms: burner. Bilateral arms or four limbs: cord injury until proven otherwise.
Any neck pain or persistent deficit after impact: immobilise and image.
Narrow canal plus repeated episodes is the main reason to stop contact sport.
det.thd: Burner (stinger) คือการบาดเจ็บของข่ายประสาทแขนหรือรากประสาทคอจากการกระแทกหรือดึงรั้งในกีฬา ทำให้แสบร้อนและชาที่แขนข้างเดียว อาจอ่อนแรงที่ C5–C6 และมักหายภายในไม่กี่นาที ส่วน cervical cord neurapraxia คืออาการทางไขสันหลังชั่วคราว ชาแสบหรืออ่อนแรงหลายแขนขา มักหายภายใน 15 นาที ต้องตรวจ MRI หาช่องไขสันหลังแคบ ความไม่มั่นคง หรือ cord oedema ก่อนตัดสินใจกลับไปเล่น หากอาการอยู่นาน เกิดซ้ำ หรือภาพรังสีผิดปกติ ควรหลีกเลี่ยงกีฬาปะทะ

name: Empty sella syndrome
formal: A sella turcica largely filled with CSF because the arachnoid herniates through the diaphragma sellae and flattens the pituitary against the sellar floor, either primary (often in obese, hypertensive women, linked to raised CSF pressure) or secondary to pituitary surgery, radiotherapy, infarction or raised intracranial pressure; usually incidental, but headache, mild pituitary dysfunction, visual deterioration from chiasm herniation or CSF rhinorrhoea can occur.
simple: The bony saddle that holds the pituitary gland looks empty on scans because it is filled with spinal fluid and the gland is squashed flat; it is often harmless but can be linked to headaches, hormone problems or raised head pressure.
ab: empty sella and idiopathic intracranial hypertension
th: Empty sella syndrome คือ sella turcica ถูกเติมด้วยน้ำไขสันหลังและต่อมใต้สมองแบนติดพื้นหลุม พบทั้งชนิดปฐมภูมิ (ไม่มีประวัติรักษาเนื้องอก มักในหญิงอ้วนความดันสูง) และทุติยภูมิ (หลังผ่าตัด รังสีรักษา เลือดออก หรือความดันในกะโหลกสูง) ส่วนใหญ่ไม่มีอาการ แต่บางรายปวดศีรษะ ฮอร์โมนต่ำ ตามัวจาก chiasm เลื่อน หรือน้ำไขสันหลังรั่วจากจมูก ต้องตรวจฮอร์โมนและหา IIH
tempoNote: Usually silent for years and found incidentally; symptoms, if any, evolve slowly
feat: Often an incidental MRI finding, with a flattened pituitary against the floor and the infundibulum crossing the middle of the sella (infundibulum sign)
Primary form is commoner in women, obesity and hypertension, and is frequent in idiopathic intracranial hypertension and in patients with pituitary tumours

Headache is the commonest symptom; clinically evident endocrine disease is uncommon, but up to a third have subtle abnormalities (reduced growth hormone reserve, mild hyperprolactinaemia, low ADH reserve)
Secondary forms follow trauma, pituitary surgery or radiotherapy, apoplexy or Sheehan syndrome, and chronic raised pressure (IIH, Chiari malformation, hydrocephalus)
Complications: visual loss from the optic chiasm kinking or sagging down into the sella, CSF rhinorrhoea, and hypopituitarism when the underlying cause is destructive
inv: MRI pituitary protocol with sagittal and coronal views; CSF signal in the sella and a thin rim of flattened gland; look for tumour remnant, chiasm herniation and signs of raised pressure (flattened globes, distended optic sheaths, transverse sinus stenosis)
Pituitary hormone panel (prolactin, IGF-1, morning cortisol, TSH and free T4, LH/FSH and sex steroids, sodium and osmolality), with dynamic testing if hypopituitarism is suspected
Visual fields, fundoscopy and, where indicated, lumbar puncture opening pressure; CT cisternography or MRI for CSF leak

case.who: 34-year-old woman with obesity (BMI 36) from Nakhon Si Thammarat
case.story: Chronic daily headache, transient visual obscurations on standing and irregular periods; MRI done for headache reports an empty sella.
case.exam: Blood pressure 138/88, bilateral papilloedema, normal acuity, enlarged blind spots on perimetry, no focal signs.
case.tests: MRI: empty sella with flattened pituitary, flattened posterior globes and bilateral transverse sinus narrowing; prolactin 48 ng/mL, other hormones normal; lumbar puncture opening pressure 34 cm H2O with normal CSF.
case.q: What does the empty sella suggest and how is it managed?
case.a: Secondary empty sella from idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Treat the raised pressure (weight loss, acetazolamide, visual monitoring, and, if vision is threatened, surgery such as CSF shunting or fenestrating the optic nerve sheath), and recheck the pituitary axes; no sella-specific treatment is needed.

read.where: Chapter 47 Pseudotumor Cerebri and Empty Sella Syndrome — Empty sella syndrome

det.patho: In the primary form, the diaphragma sellae is incomplete, and repeated transmission of CSF pulsations pushes arachnoid and CSF into the sella, enlarging it and compressing the pituitary against its floor. Raised intracranial pressure from IIH, hydrocephalus or Chiari malformation promotes this and a partially empty sella is common in the general population. Secondary forms follow loss of pituitary tissue after surgery, radiotherapy, infarction (including Sheehan syndrome) or tumour shrinkage with arachnoid prolapse into the space.
det.clinical: Most patients are middle-aged women who are overweight and hypertensive and have a normal examination or non-specific headache. Pituitary dysfunction, usually mild, can be found when tested. Visual deterioration due to chiasm descent into the sella is seen mainly with secondary forms and following tumour shrinkage. CSF rhinorrhoea is a rare presentation, and a shunt for hydrocephalus in such cases can draw in air (tension pneumocephalus). Hyperprolactinaemia with amenorrhoea-galactorrhoea is occasionally reported.
det.diagnosis: MRI is the investigation of choice; the sella is filled with CSF signal and the stalk is central. The infundibulum sign helps: in an empty sella the stalk crosses the sella, whereas an arachnoid cyst inside the sella pushes it aside. Endocrine testing is advised because clinical and laboratory evidence of hypopituitarism may be present. Look for causes: IIH, hydrocephalus, Chiari, prior treatment, Sheehan syndrome. Visual fields and fundoscopy are essential, and lumbar puncture opening pressure is measured when raised pressure is suspected.
det.treatment: No treatment is needed for an incidental finding. Treat the underlying cause (IIH, hydrocephalus) and any hormone deficiency; hyperprolactinaemia interfering with gonadal function can be treated with a dopamine agonist. Surgery is generally not indicated except for CSF rhinorrhoea, which requires work-up for raised pressure and cause, and repair (often transsphenoidal with lumbar drainage) because simple shunting risks tension pneumocephalus. Visual loss from chiasm herniation may be treated by chiasmapexy, using fat, muscle or cartilage to elevate the chiasm, mainly by an endoscopic transsphenoidal approach, with better results for field than acuity.
det.prognosis: Benign in most; outcome is determined by the underlying cause such as IIH or prior pituitary disease.
pearls: An empty sella in a headache patient should prompt a check of fundi and CSF pressure for IIH.
The infundibulum sign (stalk in the midline) separates empty sella from a cystic mass.
Test the pituitary axes: up to a third have a subtle deficit.
det.thd: Empty sella syndrome คือภาวะที่ sella turcica ถูกเติมด้วยน้ำไขสันหลัง ทำให้ต่อมใต้สมองแบนติดพื้นหลุม มักพบโดยบังเอิญใน MRI ผู้ป่วยมักเป็นหญิงอ้วนที่ความดันโลหิตสูง และอาจมีปวดศีรษะ ชนิดทุติยภูมิเกิดหลังผ่าตัดหรือฉายแสงต่อมใต้สมอง หรือจากความดันในกะโหลกสูง เช่น IIH หรือ Chiari ควรตรวจฮอร์โมนต่อมใต้สมอง ตรวจจอประสาทตาและลานสายตา และวัดความดันน้ำไขสันหลังถ้าสงสัย IIH โดยทั่วไปไม่ต้องรักษาเฉพาะ ยกเว้นน้ำไขสันหลังรั่วหรือตามัวจาก chiasm ถูกดึงลงในหลุม

An intrasellar or suprasellar cyst displaces the infundibulum, unlike empty sella where the stalk lies in the midline

name: Sporadic fatal insomnia (sFI; MM2-thalamic sporadic CJD)
formal: A rare sporadic prion disease (MM2-thalamic subtype of sporadic CJD, about 2% of cases) in which progressive insomnia leads, with ataxia and dementia, to death within 1–1.5 years; it has no PRNP mutation and shows damage mostly in the thalamus and inferior olives with little spongiform change.
simple: A rare, non-inherited cousin of fatal familial insomnia: the person stops being able to sleep, then becomes unsteady and confused. Genetic testing is normal.
th: sFI เป็นโรคพรีออนแบบเกิดเองชนิดย่อย MM2-thalamic พบประมาณ 2% ของ sCJD เริ่มด้วยนอนไม่หลับ ต่อมาเดินเซและสมองเสื่อม ไม่มีการกลายพันธุ์ของ PRNP พยาธิสภาพอยู่ที่ thalamus และ inferior olive เป็นหลัก
tempoNote: Insomnia over weeks to months, then ataxia and dementia; median duration about 1–1.5 years, longer than classic sCJD
feat: Insomnia, often with fragmented or dream-like sleep, as the presenting problem, then ataxia and later dementia
Methionine homozygosity at codon 129 with a type 2 protease-resistant fragment (MM2-thalamic); PRNP has no mutation
Pathology confined mainly to thalamus and inferior olives, with very little vacuolation
Overlaps with fatal familial insomnia in symptoms and pathology but without the D178N mutation or family history
Insomnia is not unique: other sporadic prion subtypes can start with sleep disturbance
inv: PRNP sequencing: no pathogenic variant, codon 129 MM; this separates sFI from FFI
MRI is frequently unremarkable early; FDG-PET may show thalamic and cingulate hypometabolism and polysomnography shows loss of normal sleep architecture
CSF RT-QuIC is less sensitive than in classic sCJD, and periodic EEG complexes are uncommon
Exclude autoimmune insomnia syndromes (anti-IgLON5, Morvan), sleep apnoea, psychiatric insomnia and thalamic structural disease

case.story: Three months of being unable to sleep more than two hours; she acts out dreams at night and is anxious by day, then becomes unsteady. No relative had a similar illness.
case.exam: Inattentive, mild gait ataxia, fluctuating confusion; heart rate and blood pressure mildly raised.
case.tests: Polysomnography shows markedly reduced total sleep with loss of spindles; MRI normal; FDG-PET thalamic hypometabolism; PRNP wild type and codon 129 MM; CSF RT-QuIC weakly positive; autoimmune panel negative.
case.q: How does this differ from fatal familial insomnia, and why does the distinction matter?
case.a: It is a sporadic prion disease (MM2-thalamic) without a PRNP mutation; the clinical picture matches FFI, but there is no inherited risk for her children, whereas FFI would need genetic counselling of relatives.

read.where: Chapter 95 Prion Diseases — Sporadic Prion Disease: Molecular classification (MM2-thalamic)

det.patho: Sporadic fatal insomnia corresponds to the MM2-thalamic (MM2T) subtype of sporadic prion disease, in which the codon 129 MM genotype and a type 2 prion lead to loss of neurons and gliosis mostly in thalamus and inferior olives, with little of the usual cortical vacuolation. Thalamic damage explains the loss of sleep architecture. It occurs in about 2% of sporadic prion disease and is not inherited. Some prion researchers use the term sporadic fatal insomnia because of the overlap with FFI.
det.clinical: Insomnia dominates the early course and is followed by ataxia and then dementia, so patients are often first seen by sleep or psychiatry services. Autonomic features can occur but are less prominent than in FFI. Duration is usually 1–1.5 years, longer than the classic MM1 form. Younger-onset sporadic prion disease also tends to present with sleep and mood complaints.
det.diagnosis: Because the standard tests are less informative in this subtype, diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, a normal PRNP sequence, supportive PET or polysomnography changes, a mimic work-up and, when positive, RT-QuIC. A negative RT-QuIC and normal diffusion MRI do not exclude it. Definite diagnosis requires neuropathology with Western blot typing.
det.treatment: No effective treatment exists. Hypnotics and sedatives give little lasting benefit, so sleep is managed supportively, with treatment of agitation and autonomic symptoms and early palliative care. Handle surgical instruments and tissue under prion precautions.
det.prognosis: Median survival around 1–1.5 years; fatal.
pearls: Progressive insomnia with ataxia and dementia plus a normal PRNP points to sFI rather than FFI.
Treat the autoimmune insomnia mimics (anti-IgLON5, Morvan) first, because they may respond to immunotherapy.
Normal MRI and negative RT-QuIC do not exclude MM2-thalamic disease.
det.thd: sFI คือโรคพรีออนแบบเกิดเองชนิดย่อย MM2-thalamic ผู้ป่วยเริ่มด้วยนอนไม่หลับมากขึ้นเรื่อย ๆ ต่อมาเดินเซและสมองเสื่อม ใช้เวลาประมาณ 1-1.5 ปี ไม่มีการกลายพันธุ์ของ PRNP จึงไม่ถ่ายทอดทางพันธุกรรม พยาธิสภาพอยู่ที่ thalamus MRI และ RT-QuIC อาจปกติหรือไม่ชัดเจน ควรแยกจาก FFI และโรคภูมิต้านทานตนเองที่ทำให้นอนไม่หลับก่อน ยังไม่มียารักษาให้หาย

name: Variably protease-sensitive prionopathy (VPSPr)
formal: An extremely rare sporadic prion disease, probably under-diagnosed, in which most PrPSc is protease-sensitive and shows an atypical five-band Western blot with no diglycosylated band; it runs about 2.5 years with psychiatric, language and frontal features and is poorly detected by RT-QuIC, MRI, EEG and 14-3-3.
simple: A very rare, slower sporadic prion disease that looks like a frontotemporal or other dementia, and that the usual prion tests often miss.
ab: sporadic prion disease with protease-sensitive PrPSc
th: VPSPr เป็นโรคพรีออนแบบเกิดเองที่พบน้อยมาก PrPSc ส่วนใหญ่ไวต่อโปรตีเอส ดำเนินช้ากว่า sCJD ราว 2.5 ปี มักเริ่มด้วยอาการทางจิตเวช ภาษา และ frontal lobe และตรวจ RT-QuIC, MRI, EEG ได้ผลน้อย ทำให้วินิจฉัยยาก
tempoNote: Gradual decline over about 2.5 years on average, much slower than sCJD; presentation can mimic frontotemporal dementia or motor neuron disease
feat: Mean onset in the late 60s, similar to classic sCJD, but a mean duration of about 2.5 years
Psychiatric symptoms, speech and language difficulty and frontal dysfunction are common at onset; ALS/FTD-spectrum presentations are reported
Fewer than 50 cases in the literature; probably 0.7–1.7% of sporadic prion disease
Codon 129 distribution differs from sCJD: about 65% VV, 24% MV, 11% MM
Diagnosis is difficult because standard antemortem prion tests are often normal
inv: RT-QuIC, MRI diffusion, EEG periodic complexes and CSF 14-3-3 have low sensitivity in this form
PRNP sequencing excludes a genetic prion disease

Neuropathology with Western blot is the key: protease-sensitive PrPSc, a five-band pattern without the diglycosylated band, and special immunohistochemistry because the usual protease-resistant core stain is insufficient
Broad dementia work-up (frontotemporal, Alzheimer, autoimmune, vascular) because the prion tests are unhelpful

case.story: Two years of progressive word-finding difficulty, apathy and poor judgement, treated first as depression and then as behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia; mild gait imbalance appeared last year.
case.exam: Non-fluent speech with phonemic errors, disinhibition, mild limb ataxia; no myoclonus.
case.tests: MRI shows only mild frontal and cerebellar atrophy with no restricted diffusion; CSF RT-QuIC negative twice and 14-3-3 negative; PRNP wild type with codon 129 VV; autopsy later shows protease-sensitive PrPSc with a five-band blot.
case.q: Why can this disease go undetected, and what confirms it?
case.a: Its PrPSc is largely protease-sensitive and seeds poorly, so RT-QuIC, MRI and EEG are often normal; neuropathology with Western blot typing makes the diagnosis.

read.where: Chapter 95 Prion Diseases — Variably Protease-Sensitive Prionopathy

det.patho: The usual hallmark of prion disease is a protease-resistant core of PrPSc, but in VPSPr most PrPSc is cleaved by proteases, so standard immunohistochemical methods that depend on resistance miss it. Western blot shows five bands and lacks the diglycosylated band normally seen. The pathology differs from sCJD, with fewer spongiform changes and a distinct deposit pattern. The estimated prevalence is under 2% of sporadic prion disease.
det.clinical: Patients are in their late 60s and the illness progresses over about 2.5 years. Many present with psychiatric symptoms, speech and language disturbance and frontal lobe dysfunction. The spectrum keeps widening, including patients with ALS/FTD-type illness. Because it looks like a slowly progressive dementia, it is often missed until neuropathology.
det.diagnosis: Suspect VPSPr in a patient with a slow, atypical dementia and cerebellar or parkinsonian features who has a normal PRNP sequence and negative RT-QuIC, MRI diffusion, EEG and 14-3-3. These ancillary tests are insensitive, perhaps because of poor seeding activity. Confirmation needs brain tissue with Western blot and special immunohistochemistry. Always exclude other common neurodegenerative causes.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy exists and care is supportive, with palliative planning and caregiver support. Treat depression, agitation and psychosis symptomatically, and arrange speech, swallowing and mobility support as the illness advances. Because the diagnosis is usually retrospective, apply prion precautions whenever brain biopsy or neurosurgery is considered in an undiagnosed, steadily declining patient. Research on PrPC-lowering therapy is expected to include slower sporadic forms.
det.prognosis: Average duration around 2.5 years; fatal.
pearls: A negative RT-QuIC does not exclude a prion disease if the course is slow and atypical.
Codon 129 VV is more frequent here than in classic sCJD.
Think of VPSPr when a presumed FTD or ALS-FTD patient has an unusual cerebellar sign.
det.thd: VPSPr เป็นโรคพรีออนแบบเกิดเองที่พบน้อยมาก มี PrPSc ส่วนใหญ่ไวต่อโปรตีเอส ผู้ป่วยอายุราว 60 ปลายและมีอาการทางจิตเวช ภาษา และ frontal lobe ใช้เวลาเฉลี่ยราว 2.5 ปี จึงคล้าย FTD การตรวจ RT-QuIC, MRI, EEG และ 14-3-3 มักให้ผลปกติ ต้องอาศัยชิ้นเนื้อสมองและ Western blot ในการวินิจฉัย ยังไม่มียารักษา

qx.stem: A 68-year-old man had 2.5 years of apathy, progressive word-finding difficulty and later mild ataxia, treated as behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia. Repeated EEG, MRI diffusion, CSF RT-QuIC and 14-3-3 were all unremarkable and PRNP was wild type with codon 129 VV. Post-mortem examination suggested a prion disease.
qx.q: Which Western blot finding fits the final diagnosis?
opts: A type 2B pattern with a prominent diglycosylated upper band
A protease-resistant core with strong diglycosylated band, identical to MM1 sCJD
Absence of any abnormal protein on the blot
A single 21 kD band only, confirming kuru
Largely protease-sensitive PrPSc with a five-band pattern lacking the diglycosylated band
qx.why: Variably protease-sensitive prionopathy has PrPSc that is mostly cleaved by proteases, so standard methods that rely on the resistant core miss it; Western blot shows five bands without the diglycosylated band. The 2B pattern belongs to variant CJD, and the usual antemortem prion tests are often normal in VPSPr because of poor seeding.

name: Kuru
formal: An acquired, now almost extinct prion disease of the Fore people of the Papua New Guinea highlands, spread through ritual endocannibalism, with a mean incubation of about 12 years (up to 50 or more) and a subacute cerebellar syndrome with tremor, ataxia and emotional lability leading to death in roughly a year.
simple: The 'shaking' disease once seen in a New Guinea tribe, spread by eating the brains of dead relatives in funeral rites. It caused tremor and loss of balance and was fatal. It is the first proof that a brain disease can be transmitted by prions.
ab: acquired prion disease of Papua New Guinea
th: Kuru เป็นโรคพรีออนที่ได้รับจากภายนอก พบในชนเผ่า Fore ของปาปัวนิวกินี จากพิธีกินศพญาติ มีระยะฟักตัวเฉลี่ย 12 ปี (นานได้ถึง 50 ปี) อาการสั่น เดินเซ และอารมณ์แปรปรวน เสียชีวิตภายในราว 1 ปี ปัจจุบันแทบไม่พบแล้ว
tempoNote: Incubation about 12 years (range up to 50 or more); clinical course roughly 11 months from tremor and ataxia to death
feat: Subacute cerebellar syndrome of tremor and gait ataxia in all patients, with later inability to walk or sit
Emotional lability, including inappropriate laughter, gives the old name laughing sickness (noted in board summaries)
Fore word kuru means to shake or tremble; women and children were affected most because they ate the brain and organs
Essentially eliminated after ritual cannibalism stopped; very rare cases with incubation up to 50 years, longer in codon 129 heterozygotes
Kuru-type amyloid plaques in about 75% at autopsy; lymphoreticular PrPSc unlikely
inv: Diagnosis rests on exposure history and clinical syndrome in a member of an affected community
PRNP codon 129 genotype is informative: heterozygotes have longer incubation; protective alleles have been found in the Fore
Brain pathology shows spongiform change, gliosis and kuru plaques
Modern cases would be assessed with MRI, RT-QuIC and PRNP sequencing as for other prion diseases

case.who: 71-year-old retired teacher, born in a Papua New Guinea highland village and now living in Chiang Mai
case.story: Eight months ago he developed trembling hands and a staggering gait and can no longer walk unaided. He grew up in a village where funeral feasts that included the dead relative's tissues were still practised, five to six decades ago.
case.exam: Truncal and limb ataxia, coarse tremor, dysarthria, labile mood with inappropriate laughing; cognition fairly preserved early.
case.tests: MRI cerebellar atrophy; EEG slow without periodic complexes; PRNP codon 129 MV; CSF RT-QuIC pending.
case.q: Which acquired prion disease does this suggest, and why is the incubation so long?
case.a: Kuru; heterozygosity at codon 129 is associated with very long incubation, here several decades after childhood exposure.

read.where: Chapter 95 Prion Diseases — Acquired Prion Disease: Kuru

det.patho: Kuru was the first human disease shown to be transmissible by a prion, and it probably began when a Fore person with sporadic CJD was eaten. Infection came through consumption of brain and other tissue, and because women and children took the parts with the highest prion load, they were affected most. Plaques of amyloid occur in about three-quarters of cases and the disease tends to spare the lymphoreticular system. Genetic risk factors and, more recently, protective alleles have been found in the Fore.
det.clinical: Patients developed tremor and gait ataxia, with cerebellar dysfunction in all and emotional lability including inappropriate laughing. Disease progressed to inability to sit or walk, with later cognitive failure and death in about 11 months on average. The Fore word kuru means to tremble. Cases have fallen to rare, extremely late ones, with incubation times of 50 years or longer, particularly in people heterozygous at codon 129.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis today depends on the cultural and exposure history and a cerebellar-led syndrome, supported by modern prion tests; EEG periodic complexes are not typical. Neuropathology confirms spongiform change and plaques. PRNP codon 129 genotype helps explain incubation length.
det.treatment: No treatment exists and care is supportive. Elimination of mortuary cannibalism ended the epidemic. Standard prion precautions apply to any neurosurgical procedure.
det.prognosis: Fatal within about a year of the first symptoms.
pearls: Kuru shows that a protein can transmit disease and that incubation can last decades.
Ataxia and tremor with preserved cognition early are typical; dementia comes later.
Codon 129 heterozygosity protects against early disease and lengthens incubation.
det.thd: Kuru คือโรคพรีออนที่ติดต่อผ่านพิธีกินเนื้อเยื่อของผู้เสียชีวิตในชนเผ่า Fore ของปาปัวนิวกินี มีระยะฟักตัวนานเฉลี่ย 12 ปี และอาจนานถึง 50 ปี ผู้ป่วยมีสั่น เดินเซ และอารมณ์แปรปรวน เสียชีวิตภายในราว 1 ปี พบ plaque ของ amyloid ในสมองประมาณ 75% พิธีกรรมนี้หยุดแล้ว จึงเกือบไม่พบโรคนี้ ยังไม่มียารักษา

Another acquired prion disease but with psychiatric onset, painful sensory symptoms and the pulvinar sign

name: CSF RT-QuIC (prion seeding assay)
formal: A real-time quaking-induced conversion assay, the only seed amplification assay in clinical use for prion disease: CSF (or other tissue) is shaken with recombinant prion protein substrate so that trace PrPSc templates fibril growth that is read by fluorescence; second-generation protocols have specificity of about 98% or more and sensitivity of roughly 85–95% for sporadic CJD.
simple: A spinal-fluid test that detects the abnormal prion protein itself by multiplying it in the laboratory. A positive result in the right patient is almost proof of CJD; a negative one cannot exclude it.
th: RT-QuIC เป็นการตรวจที่ขยายสัญญาณ PrPSc ในน้ำไขสันหลังจนตรวจพบด้วยแสงฟลูออเรสเซนซ์ ชนิดรุ่นที่สองมีความจำเพาะราว 98% ขึ้นไป และความไวประมาณ 85-95% ใน sCJD ผลบวกในบริบทที่เหมาะสมช่วยวินิจฉัยได้แทบแน่นอน แต่ผลลบไม่ตัดโรคออก โดยเฉพาะชนิดที่ดำเนินช้า
tempoNote: Positive early in rapidly progressive sCJD (often within weeks of onset); results come back in days
feat: Principle: recombinant PrPC substrate plus repeated shaking and rest cycles; PrPSc in the sample seeds fibril formation, detected as rising fluorescence in real time
Second-generation protocol (truncated hamster PrPC substrate, in US clinical use since 2015): specificity about 98% or higher, sensitivity about 85–95% (about 90% in the UCSF cohort)
Clinical sample is CSF (and brain tissue); olfactory mucosa brushings are used in Italy, and skin, eye, extraocular muscle and tears are still research; blood is not suitable
False negatives occur with blood-contaminated CSF, some molecular subtypes and slow forms (GSS, FFI, 5–7 octapeptide repeats, stop codons, VPSPr)
Incorporated into the UK 2017, CDC 2018 and European 2021 criteria: a progressive neurological syndrome plus a positive RT-QuIC is probable sCJD even without the classic clinical signs
inv: Collect a clear CSF sample by lumbar puncture, avoid blood contamination and send to a laboratory that runs the second-generation assay; availability in Thailand may require a reference laboratory abroad
Interpret with MRI (DWI and ADC), total tau and a mimic work-up, because combining them beats RT-QuIC alone
If RT-QuIC is negative but suspicion remains, repeat after interval, send PRNP sequencing and consider tissue testing

case.story: Five weeks of being forgetful, then imbalance and sudden jerks; a rapid dementia work-up in a university hospital is sent.
case.exam: Disoriented, limb ataxia, startle myoclonus; no fever.
case.tests: MRI DWI shows cortical ribbon and caudate restriction; CSF cells 1/µL, protein 48 mg/dL; autoimmune panel negative; CSF RT-QuIC positive (second-generation).
case.q: How does the RT-QuIC result change diagnosis under current criteria?
case.a: Together with a progressive neurological syndrome and no alternative explanation, a positive CSF RT-QuIC establishes probable sporadic CJD; the family should be counselled, infection control informed and surveillance notified.

read.where: Chapter 95 Prion Diseases — Ancillary diagnostic tests: Cerebrospinal fluid (RT-QuIC)

det.patho: RT-QuIC exploits the self-templating property of PrPSc: a tiny amount of seed in CSF converts recombinant PrPC substrate into amyloid fibrils during shaking, and the fibrils are detected with an amyloid-binding fluorescent dye. It is analogous to PCR for nucleic acids but amplifies misfolded protein, not DNA. The second-generation protocol uses a truncated hamster substrate to improve sensitivity and specificity. Seeding depends on prion strain and host codon 129 genotype, which explains different sensitivity across subtypes.
det.clinical: Clinicians order RT-QuIC in rapidly progressive dementia, ataxia or atypical parkinsonism with suspected prion disease, ideally with MRI results in hand. It is positive in the majority of sCJD, including early cases, and in many fast genetic variants such as E200K and V210I. It is often negative in slow forms (GSS, FFI, some insertions and stop-codon variants) and in VPSPr. The test is most useful when the pre-test probability is reasonable, because widespread testing in low-probability patients could create false positives.
det.diagnosis: Treat a positive result in a compatible patient as strongly supportive, and under UK, CDC and European criteria sufficient for probable sCJD with a progressive neurological syndrome and no alternative explanation. Treat a negative result as non-exclusionary: sensitivity is about 90%, so MRI with DWI and ADC, CSF total tau, EEG and PRNP sequencing remain necessary. Do not use blood-stained CSF. Older criteria that depended on 14-3-3 are superseded for practical use, and 14-3-3 is retained only as a supportive option.
det.treatment: The test does not change drug treatment, as none is effective, but a positive result triggers counselling, palliative care involvement, prion precautions for neurosurgical instruments and notification of surveillance. Standard bedside precautions suffice for CSF handling, with laboratory staff informed of the suspicion. A negative result should not stop the search for treatable mimics, and in a very suggestive case the test is repeated or other tissue sampled. Offer PRNP sequencing in parallel so that a genetic cause is not missed.
det.prognosis: A positive result carries the prognosis of the underlying prion disease; in classic sCJD median survival is about 4.5–6 months.
pearls: RT-QuIC detects the prion, not the neuronal damage, which is why it is far more specific than 14-3-3 or tau.
A negative RT-QuIC never excludes slow prion disease; check MRI and PRNP.
Bloody CSF can make RT-QuIC falsely negative; repeat the tap if needed.
det.thd: RT-QuIC ตรวจหา prion โดยตรงโดยขยายปริมาณ PrPSc ในน้ำไขสันหลังให้มากพอจนวัดด้วยแสงฟลูออเรสเซนซ์ได้ รุ่นที่สองมีความจำเพาะราว 98% ขึ้นไปและความไวราว 85-95% ใน sCJD ผลบวกร่วมกับอาการที่เข้ากันช่วยวินิจฉัย probable sCJD ได้ตามเกณฑ์ปัจจุบัน แต่ผลลบไม่ตัดโรคออก โดยเฉพาะ GSS FFI และ VPSPr ต้องอ่านร่วมกับ MRI DWI/ADC, total tau และการตรวจยีน PRNP น้ำไขสันหลังที่มีเลือดปนอาจทำให้ผลลบเทียม

qx.stem: A 60-year-old bus driver from Lampang has two months of imbalance and memory loss. MRI shows caudate and putamen restricted diffusion with matching low ADC, and the autoimmune panel is negative. The CSF RT-QuIC is reported negative, but the laboratory notes that the sample was visibly blood-stained.
qx.q: Which interpretation is most appropriate?
opts: Prion disease is excluded because a negative RT-QuIC has a negative predictive value of 100%
The result does not exclude prion disease, since blood contamination and imperfect sensitivity cause false negatives; repeat on a clear sample and continue the work-up
The MRI should be disregarded in favour of the negative CSF assay because RT-QuIC is more reliable than imaging
Brain biopsy is mandatory before any other action is taken
A positive 14-3-3 would be required to override the negative RT-QuIC
qx.why: Second-generation RT-QuIC is highly specific but only about 85–95% sensitive, and blood-contaminated CSF can give false negatives. A typical diffusion MRI keeps prion disease high on the list, so repeat the test on a clean sample, send t-tau and PRNP sequencing, and exclude mimics. 14-3-3 is poorly specific and is not used to override RT-QuIC, and biopsy is not first-line.

name: CSF 14-3-3 protein
formal: A family of intracellular neuronal proteins released into CSF by rapid neuronal injury; the 14-3-3 assay (Western blot, or the more accurate gamma-isoform ELISA) was the first CSF surrogate marker for CJD but is poorly specific because it is raised in many non-prion conditions, and RT-QuIC-based criteria have superseded older 14-3-3-based ones.
simple: A spinal-fluid test showing that brain cells are dying fast. It is often positive in CJD but also in stroke, seizures, encephalitis and other conditions, so a positive result alone does not prove CJD.
th: 14-3-3 เป็นโปรตีนในเซลล์ประสาทที่หลุดออกมาในน้ำไขสันหลังเมื่อเซลล์ตายเร็ว เคยเป็นตัวตรวจ CSF ตัวแรกของ CJD แต่ไม่จำเพาะ เพราะสูงขึ้นในโรคอื่น เช่น หลอดเลือดสมอง ชัก และสมองอักเสบ ปัจจุบันเกณฑ์ที่ใช้ RT-QuIC เข้ามาแทนเกณฑ์เดิมที่พึ่ง 14-3-3 เป็นหลัก
tempoNote: Rises during rapid neuronal loss, so it is most often positive in the first months of fast sCJD and less so in slow forms
feat: Marker of neuronal injury and not of prion: it is raised in many conditions with rapid cell loss

Proposed as the first surrogate CSF marker for sCJD in 1996; the older Western blot is less reproducible than the 14-3-3 gamma-isoform ELISA, which had sensitivity or specificity of 85% or more in some European series
North American cohorts with Western blot reported lower performance (about 50–80%), and sensitivity and specificity vary between laboratories and countries
False positives arise from stroke, seizures, autoimmune encephalopathies and other rapidly progressive disease that recover and never reach autopsy
Included in WHO 1998 criteria (with a duration under 2 years) and still listed in some current tables as an option, but RT-QuIC-based criteria have replaced reliance on it
inv: If sent, use the gamma-isoform ELISA where available, and always interpret with RT-QuIC, MRI diffusion and total tau
Do not use it alone to diagnose or exclude CJD
A mimic work-up (autoimmune antibodies, infection, lymphoma, metabolic causes) is needed whenever 14-3-3 is positive

case.story: Four weeks of confusion and a generalised seizure; a CSF 14-3-3 sent from a community hospital returns positive and the family is told it is 'mad cow disease'.
case.exam: Drowsy, disoriented, no myoclonus; right hemiparesis.
case.tests: MRI shows an acute left MCA territory infarct with restricted diffusion; CSF RT-QuIC negative; CSF 14-3-3 positive; EEG focal slowing.
case.q: What is the right interpretation of the 14-3-3 result?
case.a: It reflects acute neuronal injury from the stroke and seizure and is a recognised false positive; RT-QuIC is negative and MRI explains the findings, so CJD is not supported.

det.patho: 14-3-3 proteins are abundant intracellular regulatory proteins in neurons that leak into CSF when neurons die quickly. The assay therefore measures the intensity of neuronal loss and not prion seeding. The assumption that sCJD produces a degree of injury unmatched by other diseases is only partly true, which limits specificity. The original Western blot has been supplemented by the 14-3-3 gamma ELISA.
det.clinical: It was ordered in suspected CJD and rapid dementias, often from community hospitals, and positive results frequently led to unnecessary alarm. Elevations are common in stroke, seizures, autoimmune encephalopathies and other acute injury. In slow prion disease such as GSS, FFI or VPSPr it is often normal. Many dementia experts now regard it as a marker of rapid neuronal injury rather than of CJD.
det.diagnosis: Studies that restrict controls to autopsy-proven cases overestimate specificity, because nonprion rapid decliners who recover are never counted. The 14-3-3 gamma ELISA performs better than Western blot but still varies between laboratories. Total tau is generally the better surrogate, and CSF RT-QuIC, which detects the prion itself, is more specific. Older criteria (WHO 1998) that depended on 14-3-3 and periodic EEG were designed for surveillance and are superseded for practice, although 14-3-3 remains an optional item in some current tables.
det.treatment: The assay is not a treatment, but a positive 14-3-3 should lead to a broader work-up and not to premature palliation. Exclude treatable mimics such as autoimmune encephalitis, infection and lymphoma, and treat seizures if present. Share the result with the family with clear caveats about its poor specificity. If CJD is later confirmed, manage as for any prion disease with symptomatic and palliative care.
det.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the underlying disease; a positive 14-3-3 itself is not prognostic.
pearls: A positive 14-3-3 only says that neurons are dying; it does not say why.
A normal 14-3-3 does not exclude slow prion disease.
If you must choose one CSF surrogate, choose total tau over 14-3-3.
det.thd: 14-3-3 เป็นโปรตีนในเซลล์ประสาทที่รั่วเข้าน้ำไขสันหลังเมื่อเซลล์ประสาทตายเร็ว จึงสูงได้ทั้งใน CJD หลอดเลือดสมองตีบ ชัก และสมองอักเสบ ทำให้ไม่จำเพาะ ชนิด gamma ELISA ดีกว่า Western blot แต่ผลยังต่างกันตามห้องปฏิบัติการ เกณฑ์วินิจฉัยเดิมที่พึ่ง 14-3-3 ถูกแทนด้วยเกณฑ์ที่ใช้ RT-QuIC ควรอ่านผลร่วมกับ MRI และ RT-QuIC เสมอ

qx.stem: A 71-year-old woman from Ayutthaya had a generalised seizure and a right hemiparesis three days ago. MRI shows an acute left MCA infarct with restricted diffusion. A CSF sample sent from the referring hospital reports a positive 14-3-3 protein, and her family has been told it could be mad cow disease. CSF RT-QuIC is negative.
qx.q: How should the 14-3-3 result be interpreted?
opts: It confirms variant CJD because 14-3-3 is specific for BSE prions
It confirms sporadic CJD and the infarct is an incidental finding
It indicates iatrogenic CJD from a previous hospital procedure
It proves autoimmune encephalitis because 14-3-3 is an antibody
It reflects acute neuronal injury from stroke and seizure and is a recognised false positive, so CJD is not supported
qx.why: 14-3-3 is released by any rapid neuronal damage and is raised in stroke, seizures and autoimmune encephalopathies, so its specificity for CJD is poor. The negative RT-QuIC, the acute infarct on MRI and the abrupt time course point away from CJD. 14-3-3 is not an antibody and does not distinguish variant from sporadic disease.
