name: CSF total tau (t-tau)
formal: The concentration of total tau protein in CSF, a general marker of neuronal destruction that reaches very high levels in sporadic CJD; of the surrogate CSF markers it is probably the best single one for CJD, especially when interpreted with phosphorylated tau (p-tau181) or amyloid-beta 42, but it is not specific and never approaches the diagnostic value of brain MRI.
simple: A spinal-fluid measurement of how many brain cells are being damaged. It is extremely high in CJD, but it also rises after stroke, seizures and encephalitis, and moderately in Alzheimer disease.
th: Total tau ในน้ำไขสันหลังสะท้อนการทำลายเซลล์ประสาท สูงมากใน sCJD และเป็นตัวบ่งชี้ทดแทนที่ดีที่สุดตัวเดียวในกลุ่ม แต่ไม่จำเพาะ เพราะสูงได้ในหลอดเลือดสมอง ชัก สมองอักเสบ และสูงปานกลางใน Alzheimer ควรอ่านร่วมกับ p-tau181 หรือ Aβ42 รวมทั้ง MRI และ RT-QuIC
tempoNote: Rises with fast neuronal loss, so values are highest in rapid forms and lower in slow types such as GSS
feat: A nonspecific marker of neuronal injury: very high in sCJD, high in acute stroke, encephalitis and seizures, moderately raised in Alzheimer disease
Probably the best single CSF surrogate marker for sCJD, particularly with p-tau181 or Aβ42; in sCJD, p-tau is typically low relative to t-tau, so the t-tau:p-tau ratio is informative
Other surrogate markers: neuron-specific enolase and S100B; neurofilament light and GFAP are nonspecific and being studied for prognosis
Sensitivity in slow genetic forms (GSS, FFI) and most atypical subtypes is lower; surrogate markers reach roughly 40–75% sensitivity there
Less informative than DWI-ADC MRI and RT-QuIC, but cheap and widely available
inv: Send t-tau with p-tau181 and Aβ42 in the same CSF sample as RT-QuIC
Use the laboratory's cut-off (commonly in the range of 1000–1400 pg/mL; lab-specific) and interpret trajectory, not a single value
Interpret in context of timing: tau is raised for weeks after a stroke or status epilepticus

case.who: 66-year-old man, retired civil servant from Nakhon Pathom
case.story: Eight weeks of forgetfulness, trouble with numbers and a stumbling gait; initial MRI read as normal.
case.exam: Disoriented, mild ataxia, no myoclonus yet.
case.tests: CSF total tau markedly raised with low p-tau181 and Aβ42 abnormal; RT-QuIC positive; repeat MRI with DWI and ADC shows cortical ribboning.
case.q: How should the very high total tau be interpreted?
case.a: It supports rapid neuronal destruction and, combined with a low p-tau ratio, positive RT-QuIC and repeat DWI/ADC MRI, fits sporadic CJD; by itself, it cannot distinguish CJD from stroke or encephalitis.

det.patho: Tau is a microtubule-associated protein of axons; when neurons die in large numbers it is released into CSF. In sCJD, the explosive neuronal loss produces some of the highest CSF t-tau values seen in any disease, while phosphorylated tau stays relatively low, so the ratio separates it from Alzheimer disease. Tau is not specific for prions: any acute destructive process raises it.
det.clinical: Clinicians use t-tau as part of a CSF panel in rapidly progressive dementia, usually alongside RT-QuIC. A markedly raised level with a positive RT-QuIC and diffusion MRI makes CJD very likely, whereas moderately raised levels in a slow course point to Alzheimer or other neurodegeneration. The test is also used to monitor in research, as a prognostic marker in some prion cohorts.
det.diagnosis: Among surrogate markers t-tau, especially with p-tau181 or Aβ42, may outperform 14-3-3, but it is far less useful than brain MRI and RT-QuIC. Studies vary in methodology and not all included the same markers, so published cut-offs are not interchangeable. Timing matters because tau rises after any acute brain injury, and elevated values in someone with stroke, seizures or encephalitis do not suggest CJD. In slow or genetic prion disease the sensitivity of surrogate markers is only about 40–75%.
det.treatment: No treatment decision rests on tau alone; a high value should prompt MRI with DWI and ADC, RT-QuIC and a mimic work-up so that treatable causes (autoimmune encephalitis, lymphoma, infection) are found before palliation. If a treatable cause is identified, treat it and repeat the tau later, since values fall as injury settles. If prion disease is confirmed, care is symptomatic and palliative.
det.prognosis: Very high values may track with faster decline in some cohorts, but individual prognosis relies on prion subtype and clinical course.
pearls: High t-tau plus low p-tau in a fast dementia fits CJD better than Alzheimer disease.
Tau is raised after stroke and status epilepticus, so check timing before interpreting.
Do not rely on tau alone; it never replaces diffusion MRI or RT-QuIC.
det.thd: Total tau ในน้ำไขสันหลังเป็นตัวบ่งชี้การทำลายเซลล์ประสาท จะสูงมากใน sCJD ขณะที่ p-tau181 ค่อนข้างต่ำ จึงช่วยแยกจาก Alzheimer ได้ และเป็นตัวบ่งชี้ทดแทนที่ดีที่สุดตัวเดียวสำหรับ CJD แต่ก็สูงได้ใน stroke ชัก และสมองอักเสบ จึงต้องอ่านร่วมกับ MRI DWI/ADC และ RT-QuIC เสมอ ค่าจะต่ำกว่าในชนิดที่ดำเนินช้า เช่น GSS และ FFI

name: DWI/FLAIR cortical ribboning and basal ganglia signal (CJD MRI pattern)
formal: The characteristic MRI picture of sporadic CJD: restricted diffusion (bright DWI with matching dark ADC) in the cortical ribbon and/or caudate and putamen, sparing the perirolandic cortex, with a decreasing anterior-to-posterior striatal gradient; DWI is more sensitive than FLAIR and when read together with ADC the pattern reaches sensitivity and specificity in the mid-to-high 90s.
simple: A brain MRI pattern, best seen on diffusion scans, where the outer layer of the cortex and the deep grey nuclei light up. When read properly, it is the most informative single test for CJD.
ab: DWI/FLAIR cortical ribboning and basal ganglia signal
th: รูปแบบ MRI ของ sCJD คือ DWI สว่างพร้อม ADC มืดตามแนว cortical ribbon และ/หรือ caudate-putamen โดยเว้น perirolandic cortex ความไวและความจำเพาะระดับสูงราว 90 กลาง ๆ ขึ้นไป DWI ไวกว่า FLAIR และต้องยืนยันด้วย ADC ส่วน vCJD มี pulvinar sign และ double hockey stick sign
tempoNote: Present at the time of the first scan in most patients and may progress as the disease evolves; FLAIR changes alone are common and nonspecific
feat: Reduced diffusion (DWI bright, ADC dark) in the cortical ribbon and in caudate and putamen, in more than 92–95% of sCJD; FLAIR shows the same regions less clearly
Typical sparing of the perirolandic cortex, especially the central sulcus, and an anterior-to-posterior gradient in the striatum
Mechanism: restricted water movement inside vacuolated dendrites, not infarction
vCJD: pulvinar brighter than anterior putamen on FLAIR/T2 (pulvinar sign) with dorsomedial thalamic signal (double hockey-stick sign), also seen in some sporadic subtypes such as MV2K and VV2
Cerebellar atrophy and isolated thalamic restriction are not part of sCJD criteria; frontal, insular, cingulate and hippocampal signal was excluded in older European criteria because of artefact
inv: Always obtain DWI, ADC (and eADC) in a rapidly progressive dementia; ask the radiologist about CJD, as many scans are misread
Confirm restricted diffusion with ADC and acquire in a second plane (axial and coronal), using multishot EPI, RESOLVE or turbo-spin-echo sequences to reduce air-brain artefact
Compare against T2 shine-through, seizure-related, hypoxic, metabolic and encephalitic causes

case.who: 65-year-old woman, retired nurse from Chiang Rai
case.story: Six weeks of progressive confusion and visual blurring; the first scan at a provincial hospital was reported as 'mild atrophy'.
case.exam: Disoriented, left homonymous quadrantanopia, limb ataxia, rigidity.
case.tests: Repeat MRI: DWI bright ribbon in right temporo-parieto-occipital cortex and both caudate heads with matching low ADC; central sulcus spared; FLAIR shows fainter change; CSF RT-QuIC positive.
case.q: What did the first reading miss, and which sequences secure the diagnosis?
case.a: The diffusion pattern; DWI with ADC confirmation (and a second plane) shows true restriction in cortex and striatum, which, with RT-QuIC, supports probable sCJD.

det.patho: Diffusion restriction in CJD arises from water trapped in vacuoles within the dendritic tree of neurons, with neuronal loss and gliosis, not from cytotoxic oedema of infarction. The cortex and striatum are most affected in typical sCJD, while molecular subtypes vary, for example deep nuclei in VV2 and MV2 and cortical in MM2C. In vCJD the posterior and dorsomedial thalamus is hit.
det.clinical: MRI is the single most informative test in suspected sCJD and sensitivity and specificity are in the mid-to-high 90s. Early reports described basal ganglia signal on T2, then cortical gyral signal on FLAIR and finally DWI as the best. DWI is brighter than FLAIR, easier to read and more sensitive. However, most CJD scans are misread, including at academic centres, so a direct request for review is useful. It is also helpful to differentiate molecular subtypes.
det.diagnosis: UCSF, UK, CDC and European criteria include MRI (caudate/putamen, or at least two cortical regions among temporal, parietal and occipital, without subcortical white matter involvement) and the newest European version requires true restricted diffusion on DWI and ADC. FLAIR hyperintensity alone is insufficient because FLAIR ribboning appears on some scanners in nonprion patients and deep-nuclei T2/FLAIR signal occurs in metabolic and autoimmune disease. DWI alone can mislead because of T2 shine-through, so ADC is mandatory. Mimics with cortical or basal ganglia signal include seizures, hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, autoimmune encephalitis (LGI1), Hashimoto encephalopathy, Wernicke and toxic causes.
det.treatment: The scan itself leads to no treatment change, but a CJD-pattern MRI should be read together with RT-QuIC and the clinical syndrome; if the pattern is atypical, exclude treatable mimics such as autoimmune encephalitis before concluding. Positive imaging triggers infection control planning for any neurosurgery or biopsy. Seizure-related restriction should be treated with antiseizure medication and the scan repeated.
det.prognosis: Cortical-predominant versus deep-nuclear pattern, and number of regions involved, correlate with subtype and speed of progression in cohort studies.
pearls: In a rapid dementia, order DWI plus ADC and ask for a second plane before calling the scan normal.
Spared central sulcus with adjacent cortical ribboning and an anterior-to-posterior striatal gradient are classic.
Pulvinar brighter than the anterior putamen, not merely a bright thalamus, defines the pulvinar sign.
det.thd: MRI เป็นการตรวจที่ให้ข้อมูลมากที่สุดใน sCJD โดย DWI จะสว่างและ ADC มืดตามแนว cortical ribbon และ caudate-putamen โดยเว้น perirolandic cortex ความไวและความจำเพาะราว 90 กลาง ๆ ขึ้นไป ต้องดู ADC ยืนยันเสมอ เพราะ DWI อย่างเดียวอาจหลอกจาก T2 shine-through และควรถ่ายอีกระนาบหนึ่ง ส่วน vCJD มี pulvinar sign และ double hockey stick sign MRI มักถูกอ่านพลาด จึงควรแจ้งรังสีแพทย์ว่าสงสัย CJD

qx.stem: A 66-year-old woman has had six weeks of progressive confusion and startle-induced jerks. Brain MRI shows bright DWI signal along the frontal and insular cortex and the interhemispheric margin, and the radiologist cannot tell whether this is real restriction or a susceptibility artefact at the CSF-brain interface.
qx.q: Which imaging should be done next?
opts: Repeat the scan with gadolinium, since enhancement would separate artefact from prion disease
Obtain MR spectroscopy of the frontal lobes and treat the lactate peak as diagnostic
Accept the FLAIR hyperintensity alone, because FLAIR is more specific than DWI for CJD
Check the ADC map and repeat diffusion in a second plane with an artefact-reduced technique
Arrange FDG-PET and defer the diagnosis until cortical hypometabolism is shown
qx.why: True restricted diffusion needs a bright DWI signal with a matching dark ADC; DWI alone can be bright through T2 shine-through, and artefacts near CSF spaces can be reduced by a second plane and special EPI or turbo-spin-echo sequences. FLAIR is less specific and cortical ribboning can appear on FLAIR in non-prion patients. Gadolinium, spectroscopy and PET add little to this specific question.

name: PRNP codon 129 genotype and PRNP sequencing
formal: Sequencing of the prion protein gene on chromosome 20, which identifies pathogenic PRNP variants of genetic prion disease (E200K, V210I, V180I, P102L, D178N and others) and defines the common methionine/valine polymorphism at codon 129 (MM, MV or VV) that shapes susceptibility, phenotype, prion type and the speed of sporadic and acquired disease.
simple: A blood or saliva gene test that checks the prion gene for disease-causing mutations and tells which genetic type (MM, MV, VV) a patient has at one key position. It separates inherited from sporadic prion disease and helps explain how fast disease runs.
th: การตรวจลำดับยีน PRNP ใช้หาการกลายพันธุ์ที่ก่อโรคพรีออนทางพันธุกรรม (เช่น E200K, V210I, V180I, P102L, D178N) และบอกจีโนไทป์ที่ codon 129 (MM, MV, VV) ซึ่งมีผลต่อความเสี่ยง รูปแบบอาการ และความเร็วของโรค ควรเสนอตรวจในผู้ป่วยโรคพรีออนทุกราย หลังให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม เพราะราว 47% ไม่มีประวัติครอบครัว
tempoNote: Genotype is fixed from birth; it explains phenotype and speed (rapid vs slow) but the test is done once at diagnosis
feat: Detects pathogenic PRNP variants: more than 60 described; E200K, V210I, V180I, P102L and D178N account for about 85% of genetic prion disease
Codon 129 genotype: normal population about 51% MV, 37% MM, 12% VV; in sCJD about 66–72% MM; in vCJD more than 99% MM; heterozygosity (MV) is somewhat protective and tends to slow disease
Samples: blood, saliva or buccal swab in life; DNA from frozen autopsy brain in some countries
Penetrance matters: nearly 100% for most variants, about 10% for V210I, 1% for V180I and 0.1% for M232R, which also occur in healthy people
Genetic panels can miss octapeptide repeat insertions or deletions; D178N plus 129M gives FFI while D178N plus 129V gives genetic CJD
inv: Offer PRNP sequencing to every patient with prion disease after genetic counselling, even with no family history (47% have none)
Request specific testing for octapeptide repeat insertions or deletions if the phenotype suggests them
Variant classification follows published guidelines for causality; low-penetrance variants need cautious interpretation

case.who: 55-year-old man, builder from Nakhon Si Thammarat
case.story: Three months of memory loss and gait imbalance with sudden jerks; his phenotype looks identical to sporadic CJD and he has no known family history.
case.exam: Disoriented, ataxic gait, myoclonus; MRI cortical ribboning and CSF RT-QuIC positive.
case.tests: PRNP sequencing after counselling: E200K mutation with codon 129 MM.
case.q: Why was sequencing useful despite a classic CJD picture, and what follows?
case.a: It shows genetic CJD, not a sporadic one, so each first-degree relative has a 50% chance of carrying it; offer genetic counselling to relatives before any predictive testing, and discuss reproductive options such as preimplantation genetic diagnosis.

det.patho: PRNP, located on chromosome 20p, encodes the 253-residue prion protein. Pathogenic variants make the protein prone to misfolding (point mutations, octapeptide repeat insertions, deletions, stop codons), producing genetic prion disease. The common M129V polymorphism (like a Q219K polymorphism, it is not itself pathogenic) alters susceptibility and phenotype; methionine/valine heterozygosity is somewhat protective and slows decline, whereas VV or MM homozygosity is associated with faster progression.
det.clinical: Genetic prion disease makes up about 10–15% of prion diseases and often looks like sCJD, with no family history in nearly half. Most variants begin in the 40s–60s. Genotype helps explain unusual courses: D178N-129M (FFI) vs D178N-129V (genetic CJD), long incubation in kuru and iatrogenic cases in heterozygotes, and the almost uniform MM genotype in clinical vCJD. In East Asian populations MM is much more frequent than in Europeans.
det.diagnosis: Order PRNP sequencing in all suspected prion cases after pre-test counselling, ideally from blood. A pathogenic variant in a patient with a compatible syndrome establishes genetic prion disease. For low-penetrance variants (V210I, V180I, M232R), a positive result may not be causal, and the clinical picture and CSF tests must be considered. Genotyping at codon 129 is part of every sCJD work-up, because it predicts rate of decline and helps subtype. If the laboratory uses a gene panel, ask whether octapeptide repeats are covered.
det.treatment: Results guide genetic counselling for relatives, predictive testing protocols, and reproductive options (preimplantation genetic diagnosis). There is no genotype-specific treatment, but PrPC-lowering antisense oligonucleotides and doxycycline prophylaxis in FFI carriers are being tested in research. Handle the diagnosis sensitively because a dominant fatal disease is distressing for the whole family.
det.prognosis: Genotype and mutation predict the likely speed of disease: months for E200K genetic CJD, about 18 months for FFI and years for GSS; homozygous codon 129 predicts faster sporadic decline.
pearls: Send PRNP in every prion case; nearly half of genetic cases have no family history.
Counsel before testing: a positive result commits relatives to a fatal dominant diagnosis.
Codon 129 is not a mutation but a normal polymorphism that modifies phenotype.
det.thd: การตรวจลำดับยีน PRNP หาการกลายพันธุ์ที่ก่อโรคพรีออนทางพันธุกรรม และบอกจีโนไทป์ที่ codon 129 (MM, MV, VV) ซึ่งมีผลต่อรูปแบบและความเร็วของโรค เช่น D178N ร่วมกับ 129M ให้ FFI แต่ร่วมกับ 129V ให้ genetic CJD ควรเสนอตรวจในผู้ป่วยทุกราย แม้ไม่มีประวัติครอบครัวเพราะราวครึ่งหนึ่งไม่มี และต้องให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรมก่อนส่งตรวจ ผลมีผลต่อญาติและทางเลือกการมีบุตร

qx.stem: Two unrelated patients carry the same PRNP D178N mutation. One has eight months of intractable insomnia, drenching sweats and tachycardia, and polysomnography shows loss of sleep spindles. The other has a rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus resembling sporadic CJD.
qx.q: What best explains the difference between them?
opts: Codon 129 on the mutant allele is methionine in the first patient and valine in the second
The first patient has a stop-codon mutation and the second has an octapeptide insertion
The second patient has acquired disease from a contaminated dura graft
Only the second patient has a pathogenic mutation, as D178N alone is benign
The first patient has a sporadic form, which always starts with insomnia
qx.why: D178N with methionine on the same allele (129M) gives fatal familial insomnia, whereas D178N with valine (129V) causes genetic CJD. Stop-codon and octapeptide variants are different mutations. Acquired disease would not carry D178N, and D178N is pathogenic in both.

D178N with codon 129 methionine; the same variant with 129 valine gives genetic CJD
Nearly all patients are MM at codon 129; sequencing excludes a mutation, but the diagnosis rests on clinical and MRI features and tissue

name: Alcohol withdrawal syndrome
formal: A predictable syndrome of autonomic overactivity, tremor, anxiety, insomnia and, in severe cases, hallucinations, seizures and delirium that follows a fall or stop in heavy, prolonged alcohol intake, caused by unopposed glutamatergic and noradrenergic activity after chronic GABA-A enhancement.
simple: When someone who has been drinking heavily for a long time suddenly stops, the brain becomes over-excited, causing shaking, sweating and anxiety, and sometimes fits or severe confusion.
th: กลุ่มอาการถอนสุราเกิดเมื่อผู้ดื่มหนักเป็นเวลานานหยุดหรือลดการดื่ม มีมือสั่น เหงื่อออก ใจสั่น นอนไม่หลับ อาจมีประสาทหลอน ชัก และ delirium tremens ซึ่งอันตรายถึงชีวิต รักษาด้วย benzodiazepine และ thiamine
tempoNote: Tremor and autonomic signs begin 6–24 hours after the last drink; hallucinosis 12–48 hours; seizures usually within 6–48 hours; delirium tremens typically 48–96 hours, lasting several days
feat: Coarse tremor, sweating, tachycardia, hypertension, nausea, anxiety and insomnia within a day of stopping or reducing heavy drinking
Alcoholic hallucinosis: mainly visual or auditory hallucinations with a clear sensorium and preserved orientation
Withdrawal seizures: generalised tonic-clonic, often single or in a short cluster, without a focal onset
Delirium tremens: fluctuating confusion, hallucinations, agitation, fever and autonomic instability, with real mortality if untreated
Risk factors for severe withdrawal: prior seizures or delirium tremens, heavy daily intake, older age, comorbid illness and low platelets or potassium
inv: CIWA-Ar (or a similar validated scale) to grade severity and guide symptom-triggered treatment; blood alcohol level
Glucose, sodium, potassium, magnesium, phosphate, liver tests, CBC and CK; ECG
CT brain after a first seizure, a focal seizure, head injury or failure to recover; consider CSF and EEG if fever, focal signs or prolonged confusion

case.who: 49-year-old male construction worker from Sing Buri who drinks a bottle of rice whisky daily
case.story: Admitted for a leg fracture, he becomes tremulous and sweaty on day 2, then has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure; on day 3 he is picking at the bedsheets, sees insects on the wall and pulls out his drip.
case.exam: Temperature 38.2 °C, pulse 128, BP 170/100, coarse tremor, disoriented to time and place, no neck stiffness, no focal deficits, horizontal nystagmus.
case.tests: CIWA-Ar 28; glucose 5.8 mmol/L; potassium 3.0, magnesium 0.55 mmol/L; platelets 90,000; CT brain normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the immediate management?
case.a: Alcohol withdrawal delirium (delirium tremens) after a withdrawal seizure; give IV benzodiazepine in escalating doses titrated to calm sedation, high-dose IV thiamine, correct potassium and magnesium, monitor in a high-dependency setting and consider phenobarbital or ICU care if benzodiazepines fail.

read.where: Chapter 33 Alcohol and the Nervous System

det.patho: Chronic alcohol enhances GABA-A inhibition and blocks NMDA glutamate receptors; the brain adapts by down-regulating GABA-A function and up-regulating NMDA receptors and noradrenergic tone. When alcohol is withdrawn, the unopposed excitatory state produces tremor, autonomic overactivity, seizures and delirium. Repeated detoxifications appear to sensitise the brain (kindling), so each later withdrawal tends to be worse.
det.clinical: Minor withdrawal with tremor, sweating, nausea, anxiety and insomnia starts within hours. Hallucinosis may appear while orientation is intact. Seizures are usually generalised and occur early; a focal seizure or a seizure after several days should raise other causes. Delirium tremens develops in a small minority, typically on days 2 to 4, with confusion, vivid hallucinations, agitation, fever and cardiovascular instability, and complications include aspiration, arrhythmia and injury.
det.diagnosis: DSM-5-TR requires cessation or reduction of heavy prolonged drinking followed by at least two features among autonomic hyperactivity, tremor, insomnia, nausea, hallucinations, agitation, anxiety and seizures. Severity scales such as CIWA-Ar guide treatment but need an alert, communicative patient. Always look for coexisting head injury, infection, hypoglycaemia, electrolyte disturbance, Wernicke encephalopathy and withdrawal from other sedatives.
det.treatment: Benzodiazepines are first line, given by a symptom-triggered or front-loaded approach; long-acting agents (diazepam, chlordiazepoxide) suit most patients, while lorazepam is preferred in significant liver disease or old age. Phenobarbital is an alternative or adjunct for benzodiazepine-resistant withdrawal, and dexmedetomidine may calm autonomic features but does not prevent seizures. Give thiamine before or with glucose-containing fluids, at high IV dose if Wernicke encephalopathy is possible, and replace magnesium, potassium and phosphate. Antiseizure medicines such as phenytoin do not prevent withdrawal seizures; after recovery, offer relapse-prevention medicine (acamprosate, naltrexone if liver allows, or baclofen) and psychosocial support.
det.prognosis: Most withdrawal is mild and settles within a week; treated delirium tremens has a mortality of about 1–5%, much higher if recognised late.
pearls: Withdrawal seizures are generalised and early; a focal or late seizure needs a search for another cause such as subdural haematoma.
Phenytoin does not prevent alcohol withdrawal seizures; benzodiazepines do.
Give thiamine to every patient in alcohol withdrawal, but never delay glucose in a hypoglycaemic patient.
det.thd: กลุ่มอาการถอนสุราเกิดหลังหยุดหรือลดการดื่มในผู้ที่ดื่มหนักเป็นเวลานาน ภายใน 6–24 ชั่วโมงมีมือสั่น เหงื่อออก ใจสั่น ความดันสูง อาจชักแบบทั้งตัวใน 6–48 ชั่วโมง และบางรายเกิด delirium tremens ในวันที่ 2–4 ซึ่งสับสน เห็นภาพหลอน มีไข้ และอาจเสียชีวิต ประเมินความรุนแรงด้วย CIWA-Ar รักษาด้วย benzodiazepine ให้ thiamine ขนาดสูง แก้ไขแมกนีเซียมและโพแทสเซียม และต้องหาสาเหตุอื่นที่พบร่วม เช่น เลือดออกใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมองหรือการติดเชื้อ

qx.stem: A 52-year-old male fisherman from Chumphon who drinks heavily every day is admitted for pneumonia. Thirty hours after his last drink he is tremulous and sweating and has a single generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 1 minute. He wakes within 20 minutes with no focal deficit. Glucose is normal and CT brain shows only mild atrophy.
qx.q: Which medicine best prevents further withdrawal seizures?
opts: Intravenous phenytoin loading
A benzodiazepine such as diazepam
Oral levetiracetam for 6 months
Haloperidol
Intravenous magnesium alone
qx.why: Alcohol withdrawal seizures arise from loss of GABA-A inhibition and are prevented by cross-tolerant GABAergic drugs, so benzodiazepines are the treatment of choice. Phenytoin does not prevent them and long-term antiseizure medicine is not indicated after a typical early generalised withdrawal seizure. Haloperidol lowers the seizure threshold, and magnesium should be replaced but does not replace a benzodiazepine.

name: Psychosis due to a neurological condition
formal: Hallucinations or delusions judged to be the direct physiological consequence of a neurological disorder, such as epilepsy, Parkinson disease and Lewy body disease, stroke, Huntington disease, multiple sclerosis, encephalitis or brain tumour, occurring outside delirium and not better explained by a primary psychotic illness or a drug.
simple: Seeing or hearing things that are not there, or holding fixed false beliefs, because of a disease of the brain such as epilepsy, Parkinson disease or encephalitis, rather than schizophrenia.
ab: psychotic disorder due to another medical condition
th: โรคจิตที่เกิดจากโรคระบบประสาทโดยตรง เช่น โรคลมชัก พาร์กินสัน สมองอักเสบ stroke หรือเนื้องอก มีประสาทหลอนหรือหลงผิดโดยไม่ได้อยู่ในภาวะ delirium ต้องหาสาเหตุและรักษาโรคต้นเหตุ
tempoNote: Postictal psychosis follows a seizure cluster after a lucid interval of hours to about 3 days and lasts days; interictal psychosis is chronic; Parkinson disease psychosis builds up over months to years
feat: Late-onset or atypical psychosis with visual hallucinations, confusion, seizures, focal signs, headache or movement disorder points to a neurological cause
Postictal psychosis: after a cluster of seizures, a clear interval of 12–72 hours, then delusions, hallucinations and mood change for days
Interictal psychosis: schizophrenia-like illness after years of drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy; forced normalisation is a rare variant when seizures stop
Parkinson disease psychosis starts with minor phenomena (presence, passage, illusions), then well-formed visual hallucinations and delusions, often unmasked by dopaminergic drugs
New psychosis with seizures, dyskinesias or autonomic signs in a young adult suggests autoimmune encephalitis, especially anti-NMDAR
inv: MRI brain, EEG (including prolonged or video-EEG when seizures are suspected) and screening blood tests (glucose, sodium, calcium, thyroid, B12, HIV, syphilis)
CSF with cell count, protein, viral PCR and neuronal antibodies (serum and CSF) in acute or subacute onset
Medication review (levodopa, dopamine agonists, amantadine, anticholinergics, steroids, levetiracetam, topiramate) and urine toxicology

case.who: 41-year-old female accountant from Ubon Ratchathani with drug-resistant left temporal lobe epilepsy
case.story: After four focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures in one night from missed doses, she is back to normal for 2 days, then becomes convinced that neighbours are poisoning her food, hears voices and barely sleeps.
case.exam: Alert and oriented, attention normal, frightened and suspicious; no focal deficits; no fever.
case.tests: Video-EEG shows left temporal interictal discharges but no ongoing seizures; MRI shows left hippocampal sclerosis; bloods and toxicology are normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and how should it be managed?
case.a: Postictal psychosis; ensure safety, give a short course of a benzodiazepine and low-dose atypical antipsychotic, restore seizure control, and refer for epilepsy surgery evaluation because recurrence is common.

read.where: 10.5 Other Cognitive and Mental Disorders due to Another Medical Condition

det.patho: Psychosis arises when neurological disease disrupts dopaminergic, glutamatergic or limbic networks. In epilepsy, repeated temporal limbic discharges and postictal changes in perfusion and neurotransmission are thought to drive psychotic episodes. In Parkinson and Lewy body disease, Lewy pathology in visual and limbic areas, cholinergic loss and dopaminergic treatment combine. Autoimmune encephalitis, Huntington disease, multiple sclerosis, strokes in the right hemisphere or thalamus, and tumours can all produce similar pictures.
det.clinical: Clues to a neurological cause include onset after 40, visual or tactile rather than purely auditory hallucinations, cognitive impairment, seizures, focal signs, abnormal movements and rapid change. Postictal psychosis is the most common epilepsy-related form and has a characteristic delay after a seizure cluster. Interictal psychosis resembles schizophrenia but with preserved affect and fewer negative symptoms. Parkinson disease psychosis affects a large share of patients over time and predicts dementia and nursing-home placement.
det.diagnosis: DSM-5-TR uses a secondary psychotic disorder category, attributed to the medical illness, when history, examination or tests show a causal medical illness and delirium is absent. The work-up covers MRI, EEG, metabolic and infective screening, CSF and neuronal antibodies in acute onset, and a careful drug review. In epilepsy, distinguish postictal from ictal (non-convulsive status) and interictal psychosis, and consider drug-induced psychosis from levetiracetam, topiramate or perampanel.
det.treatment: Treat or remove the cause first: restore seizure control, reduce anticholinergics, amantadine and dopamine agonists in Parkinson disease, and start immunotherapy for autoimmune encephalitis. When antipsychotics are needed, use low doses of agents with little dopamine D2 blockade: quetiapine or clozapine (with blood monitoring) in Parkinson and Lewy body disease, and pimavanserin where available; avoid haloperidol and risperidone in these patients. In epilepsy, most atypical antipsychotics are safe at usual doses, while clozapine needs care because it lowers seizure threshold. Postictal psychosis responds to short-term benzodiazepines and antipsychotics.
det.prognosis: Outcome depends on the underlying disease; postictal psychosis usually clears within days to weeks but tends to recur, whereas Parkinson disease psychosis signals a more advanced illness.
pearls: A lucid interval of hours to 3 days after a seizure cluster is the signature of postictal psychosis.
In Lewy body or Parkinson disease, haloperidol can cause severe rigidity or death; use quetiapine, clozapine or pimavanserin.
New psychosis with seizures or abnormal movements in a young woman needs NMDAR antibody testing.
det.thd: โรคจิตจากโรคระบบประสาทคือประสาทหลอนหรือหลงผิดที่เกิดจากโรคสมองโดยตรง เช่น หลังชักหลายครั้ง (postictal psychosis ซึ่งมีช่วงปกติ 12–72 ชั่วโมงก่อนเกิด) ลมชักเรื้อรังของ temporal lobe พาร์กินสันและ Lewy body disease สมองอักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกัน หรือ stroke ควรสงสัยเมื่อเริ่มเป็นหลังอายุ 40 ปี เห็นภาพหลอน มีชัก หรือมีอาการทางระบบประสาท ตรวจ MRI EEG เลือด และน้ำไขสันหลังตามความเหมาะสม รักษาโรคต้นเหตุก่อน และถ้าต้องใช้ยาต้านโรคจิตในพาร์กินสันให้เลือก quetiapine หรือ clozapine หลีกเลี่ยง haloperidol

qx.stem: A 36-year-old male mechanic from Lampang has drug-resistant right temporal lobe epilepsy from hippocampal sclerosis. After running out of medicine he has five convulsive seizures over one night, recovers fully and returns to work. Two days later he stops sleeping, believes his wife is plotting to kill him and hears his dead father talking. He is oriented and attentive, and EEG shows no ongoing seizures.
qx.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Non-convulsive status epilepticus
Interictal schizophrenia-like psychosis
Postictal psychosis
Levetiracetam-induced psychosis
Postictal delirium
qx.why: Postictal psychosis typically follows a seizure cluster after a lucid interval of about 12 to 72 hours and presents with paranoid delusions, hallucinations and mood change with clear awareness. A normal ongoing EEG argues against non-convulsive status, and preserved attention excludes delirium. Interictal psychosis is a chronic illness without this tight link to a seizure cluster, and he has had no drug change.

qx.stem: A 74-year-old woman from Nakhon Pathom has had Parkinson disease for 9 years, treated with levodopa, pramipexole and trihexyphenidyl. Over 2 months she has begun to see children sitting on her sofa and accuses her husband of stealing her jewellery. She has mild cognitive slowing but normal attention. Bloods, urine and chest X-ray are normal.
qx.q: After stopping trihexyphenidyl, what is the best next step?
opts: Add haloperidol at night
Increase levodopa to improve her motor state
Start risperidone 2 mg daily
Reduce or withdraw pramipexole, then add low-dose quetiapine if symptoms persist
Start electroconvulsive therapy
qx.why: In Parkinson disease psychosis, drugs are removed in order of risk and least motor benefit: anticholinergics first, then dopamine agonists and amantadine, keeping levodopa where possible. If symptoms persist, quetiapine, clozapine or pimavanserin are used because they barely block striatal D2 receptors. Haloperidol and risperidone worsen parkinsonism and can provoke severe reactions in Lewy body disease.

name: Anxiety disorders
formal: A group of psychiatric disorders characterised by excessive fear, anxiety and avoidance, including panic disorder, generalised anxiety disorder, agoraphobia, social anxiety disorder and specific phobia, which are frequent mimics and comorbidities of neurological conditions such as seizures, vestibular disorders, stroke and Parkinson disease.
simple: Conditions where fear or worry is much stronger or longer than the situation deserves; panic attacks can feel like a stroke, a seizure or heart trouble.
th: โรควิตกกังวล เช่น panic disorder และ generalised anxiety disorder มีความกลัวหรือกังวลมากเกินเหตุ อาการ panic อาจคล้าย stroke ชัก หรือเวียนศีรษะ และพบร่วมบ่อยในโรคระบบประสาท
tempoNote: Panic attacks peak within minutes and settle within about 30 minutes; generalised anxiety disorder needs worry on most days for at least 6 months; post-stroke anxiety often starts within months and can persist for years
feat: Panic attack: abrupt surge of fear peaking within minutes with palpitations, breathlessness, chest tightness, dizziness, perioral and hand tingling, trembling and fear of dying or losing control
Generalised anxiety disorder: persistent hard-to-control worry with feeling keyed up, tiring easily, trouble focusing, irritability, tense muscles and broken sleep
Common after stroke, in Parkinson disease (including OFF-period anxiety), epilepsy, multiple sclerosis and migraine, and a driver of persistent dizziness
Hyperventilation can cause bilateral or one-sided paraesthesia, light-headedness and even carpopedal spasm
Red flags for a neurological mimic: stereotyped brief events with altered awareness, focal deficits, onset after 45, or attacks from sleep
inv: Screen with GAD-7 or HADS; ask about panic, avoidance, alcohol, caffeine and substance use
ECG, glucose, thyroid function and medication review (stimulants, steroids, salbutamol, levothyroxine, SSRI start-up)
EEG, MRI or vestibular testing only when features suggest focal seizures, TIA or a vestibular disorder

case.who: 33-year-old female bank teller from Udon Thani
case.story: Over 4 months she has had sudden spells of pounding heart, chest tightness, tingling in both hands and around the mouth, and fear that she is having a stroke; each peaks within 10 minutes and fades in 20, and she now avoids crowded malls.
case.exam: Normal neurological and cardiovascular examination between attacks; voluntary hyperventilation for 2 minutes reproduces the tingling.
case.tests: ECG, glucose, TSH and electrolytes are normal; GAD-7 is 14; no imaging is needed.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the first-line treatment?
case.a: Panic disorder with agoraphobia; explain the bodily symptoms, offer CBT with interoceptive exposure and an SSRI started at low dose, and avoid regular benzodiazepines.

read.where: 14.2 Clinical Features of the Anxiety Disorders

det.patho: Anxiety disorders involve an overactive threat circuit (amygdala, insula, anterior cingulate) with weaker prefrontal regulation, interacting with noradrenergic and serotonergic systems. In neurological disease, lesions of frontal or basal ganglia circuits, loss of noradrenergic and serotonergic neurons in Parkinson disease, and the unpredictability of seizures or falls all raise risk. Interoceptive sensitivity explains why bodily symptoms escalate into panic.
det.clinical: Panic disorder brings recurrent unexpected attacks with persistent worry about further attacks or avoidance. Generalised anxiety disorder is chronic worry with physical tension and insomnia. After stroke, anxiety affects around a quarter of survivors, frequently alongside depression; in Parkinson disease it may fluctuate with OFF periods. Panic attacks commonly present to neurology as numbness, dizziness or suspected TIA, while ictal fear from temporal lobe seizures can be misread as panic.
det.diagnosis: DSM-5-TR criteria define each disorder, and a panic attack specifier can be added to any condition. GAD-7 and HADS help screening. Features favouring epilepsy over panic include very brief, highly stereotyped events, altered awareness, automatisms and postictal confusion; features favouring TIA include focal negative deficits without autonomic surge. Exclude thyroid disease, arrhythmia, hypoglycaemia, phaeochromocytoma, drug effects and alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal.
det.treatment: CBT, including interoceptive exposure for panic, is first line. SSRIs and SNRIs are the main drugs, started low because early jitteriness can worsen anxiety, with pregabalin as an alternative for generalised anxiety. Benzodiazepines are for short-term crisis use only because of dependence, falls and cognitive effects, particularly in older or neurologically ill patients. In Parkinson disease, smoothing OFF periods can reduce anxiety; in epilepsy, SSRIs are safe at usual doses.
det.prognosis: Often chronic and fluctuating, but most patients improve substantially with CBT and medication; untreated anxiety worsens neurological rehabilitation and quality of life.
pearls: Bilateral perioral and hand tingling during a fear surge suggests hyperventilation, not a stroke.
Very short, identical events with déjà vu or automatisms are focal seizures until proven otherwise.
Avoid regular benzodiazepines in older neurological patients; prefer SSRIs and CBT.
det.thd: โรควิตกกังวลประกอบด้วย panic disorder, generalised anxiety disorder และโรคกลัวชนิดต่างๆ อาการ panic เกิดเร็วภายในไม่กี่นาที ใจสั่น แน่นหน้าอก ชารอบปากและมือ กลัวตาย ซึ่งอาจคล้าย stroke หรือชัก พบบ่อยหลัง stroke ในพาร์กินสัน โรคลมชัก และผู้ที่เวียนศีรษะเรื้อรัง ต้องแยกจากชักแบบ focal TIA น้ำตาลต่ำ และโรคไทรอยด์ การรักษาหลักคือ CBT และยา SSRI หรือ SNRI ส่วน benzodiazepine ใช้ระยะสั้นเท่านั้น

qx.stem: A 31-year-old female call-centre worker from Chonburi has had 10 attacks in 3 months. Each begins with a rising feeling from the stomach and a strong sense of having lived the moment before, lasts about 40 seconds and is followed by a minute of lip smacking that she does not remember. Her husband says she looks frightened at the start. She has been told she has panic disorder.
qx.q: Which step should come next?
opts: Increase her SSRI dose
EEG and epilepsy-protocol MRI for suspected focal seizures
Start regular clonazepam
Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy only
Arrange a cardiac event monitor only
qx.why: Very brief, stereotyped events with epigastric rising, déjà vu and automatisms with amnesia are typical of focal impaired awareness seizures from the mesial temporal lobe, where fear can be the ictal emotion. Panic attacks last minutes, build more gradually and do not cause automatisms with loss of awareness. EEG and epilepsy-protocol MRI are needed before treating this as an anxiety disorder.

Daily non-spinning dizziness worse upright and in busy visual surroundings, often triggered by a vestibular event and sustained by anxiety
Sweating, tremor and anxiety with confusion that resolve with glucose; low measured glucose

name: Apathy syndrome
formal: A syndrome of reduced goal-directed behaviour, cognition and emotional responsiveness caused by disease of frontal-subcortical motivational circuits, common after stroke and in Parkinson disease, small vessel disease, dementia, traumatic brain injury and Huntington disease, and distinct from depression.
simple: The person loses drive and interest and stops starting things, but does not necessarily feel sad; it comes from damage to the brain's motivation circuits.
th: ภาวะเฉยเมย (apathy) คือการขาดแรงจูงใจ ไม่ริเริ่มทำสิ่งต่างๆ และอารมณ์ตอบสนองลดลง เกิดจากรอยโรควงจรสมองส่วนหน้าและ basal ganglia พบบ่อยหลัง stroke ในพาร์กินสันและสมองเสื่อม ต่างจากโรคซึมเศร้าที่มีความเศร้า
tempoNote: Appears in the weeks after a stroke or brain injury, or develops gradually with neurodegenerative and small vessel disease; usually persistent if untreated
feat: Reduced initiative and goal-directed activity, lack of interest in new things and dependence on others to prompt daily tasks
Blunted emotional response to good or bad news, often without sadness, guilt or hopelessness
Linked with lesions of the anterior cingulate, medial frontal cortex, ventral striatum, globus pallidus and medial thalamus, and with diffuse white matter disease
Common in Parkinson disease (worse after reducing dopaminergic drugs or after subthalamic DBS), bvFTD, Alzheimer disease, Huntington disease and after TBI
Severe form is abulia; the extreme is akinetic mutism
inv: Apathy scales (Apathy Evaluation Scale, Starkstein Apathy Scale, Lille Apathy Rating Scale in Parkinson disease) with a caregiver report
Screen separately for depression (PHQ-9, HADS) and cognitive impairment
MRI to define frontal-subcortical lesions or small vessel disease; check thyroid, B12 and sedating drugs

case.story: Six weeks after bilateral caudate head infarcts he sits in front of the television all day, no longer visits the temple or his friends and eats only when his daughter puts food in front of him; he denies feeling sad.
case.exam: Slow to answer but accurate when prompted, flat facial expression, no mood-related guilt or hopelessness; mild gait slowing; no paresis.
case.tests: PHQ-9 is 6 with low scores on sadness items; Apathy Evaluation Scale is high; MRI shows bilateral caudate lacunes and moderate white matter hyperintensities; TSH and B12 normal.
case.q: How should his problem be named, and how does it change management?
case.a: Post-stroke apathy rather than major depression; use structured activity scheduling, caregiver prompting and goal-based rehabilitation, consider a trial of methylphenidate or a dopaminergic drug, and avoid relying on SSRIs, which may worsen apathy.

read.where: 2.2 Neuropsychiatric Aspects of Cerebrovascular Disorders - Apathy

det.patho: Motivation depends on circuits linking the anterior cingulate and medial orbitofrontal cortex with the ventral striatum, ventral pallidum and medial thalamus, modulated by mesolimbic dopamine. Damage anywhere along this loop, or diffuse disconnection by small vessel disease, reduces the conversion of goals into action. In Parkinson disease, mesolimbic dopamine loss and its unmasking when dopaminergic drugs are reduced are key.
det.clinical: Apathy shows as reduced behavioural initiative, reduced cognitive curiosity and reduced emotional response. It affects roughly a third of stroke survivors and a similar share of people with Parkinson disease, and is very common in dementia. It is often mistaken for depression, laziness or poor cooperation with therapy, and it predicts poorer rehabilitation and functional outcome. Families may describe a placid person who is pleasant but does nothing unless asked.
det.diagnosis: International consensus criteria (revised in 2018) require loss or reduction of goal-directed behaviour, cognitive activity and emotion, present for most of the time over at least 4 weeks and causing impairment, not explained by physical disability, reduced consciousness or substances. Rating scales and caregiver reports help. Depression is screened for separately, since the two can overlap; the absence of sadness, guilt and hopelessness favours apathy. Hypothyroidism, sedating drugs, hypoactive delirium and akinetic mutism are other considerations.
det.treatment: Non-drug approaches come first: explanation to families, structured routines, external cues, activity scheduling, exercise and goal-focused rehabilitation. Methylphenidate improved apathy in Alzheimer disease trials and is used off-label after stroke and TBI with cardiovascular monitoring. In Parkinson disease, optimising dopaminergic therapy, particularly dopamine agonists, can help, and apathy after subthalamic DBS may respond to dopaminergic adjustment. SSRIs can blunt motivation further, so their use should be reconsidered if apathy, not depression, is the main problem.
det.prognosis: Often persistent, particularly with progressive disease, but structured support and selected drugs can improve participation and caregiver burden.
pearls: Apathy without sadness is not depression, and SSRIs may make it worse.
Bilateral caudate, medial frontal or medial thalamic strokes are classic causes of abulia.
New apathy after subthalamic DBS or after cutting dopamine agonists in Parkinson disease suggests a dopamine withdrawal state.
det.thd: Apathy คือภาวะขาดแรงจูงใจ ไม่ริเริ่มทำกิจกรรม และอารมณ์ตอบสนองลดลง แต่ไม่จำเป็นต้องรู้สึกเศร้า เกิดจากรอยโรควงจรสมองส่วนหน้า cingulate และ basal ganglia พบบ่อยหลัง stroke ในพาร์กินสัน สมองเสื่อม และหลังบาดเจ็บสมอง ประเมินด้วย Apathy Evaluation Scale และตรวจซึมเศร้าแยกต่างหาก การรักษาเน้นจัดกิจกรรมเป็นโครงสร้าง ให้ญาติช่วยกระตุ้น ฟื้นฟูแบบมีเป้าหมาย อาจลองยา methylphenidate หรือยากลุ่ม dopamine และระวังว่า SSRI อาจทำให้เฉยเมยมากขึ้น

qx.stem: A 70-year-old woman from Ratchaburi had bilateral anterior cerebral artery territory infarcts 2 months ago. She now stays in bed unless prompted, rarely speaks spontaneously but answers correctly, and shows no sadness or guilt. Her PHQ-9 is 5. She was started on sertraline by another doctor and the family feels she is now even less engaged.
qx.q: Which approach is most appropriate?
opts: Double the sertraline dose
Add a benzodiazepine for agitation
Recognise apathy rather than depression, review the SSRI, and use structured activity with a trial of methylphenidate
Start haloperidol for negative symptoms
Arrange electroconvulsive therapy for depressive stupor
qx.why: Medial frontal and cingulate damage produces apathy or abulia, a loss of motivation without depressed mood. SSRIs can blunt motivation further, so their benefit should be reconsidered. Structured routines, caregiver prompts, goal-based rehabilitation and stimulant or dopaminergic drugs are the usual options, while antipsychotics and benzodiazepines would worsen the picture.

ddx.pt: Sadness, guilt, hopelessness or suicidal ideation are present; apathy can coexist but is not the same syndrome
The extreme end: awake and tracking but almost no speech or movement, usually from bilateral medial frontal or diencephalic lesions
Apathy with disinhibition, loss of empathy, compulsions and dietary change that progress over years

name: Sleep enuresis
formal: Involuntary passing of urine in sleep on two or more nights weekly beyond 5 years of age; primary if the child has never been consistently dry, secondary if it returns after at least 6 months of dryness.
simple: Bedwetting in a child old enough to be dry at night; new bedwetting after a dry spell needs a search for a cause.
th: การปัสสาวะรดที่นอนขณะหลับอย่างน้อย 2 ครั้งต่อสัปดาห์ในเด็กอายุเกิน 5 ปี ถ้ากลับมาเป็นหลังจากแห้งมาอย่างน้อย 6 เดือนต้องหาสาเหตุ เช่น OSA เบาหวาน โรคไต หรือชัก
tempoNote: Primary enuresis is lifelong from infancy and fades with age; secondary enuresis starts after at least 6 months of dryness and follows its cause
feat: Wetting in sleep on two or more nights weekly beyond age 5, for 3 months or longer
Primary form is common, more frequent in boys, often familial, and becomes less common each year of childhood
Mechanisms: nocturnal polyuria, small functional bladder capacity and a high arousal threshold
Secondary form suggests OSA, diabetes mellitus or insipidus, chronic kidney disease, constipation, urinary infection, seizures or emotional stress
Daytime wetting, weak stream or back and leg signs suggest a bladder or spinal cause
inv: Bladder diary and urinalysis (glucose, infection, specific gravity) in all children
Ask about snoring and apnoeas; sleep study if OSA suspected
Kidney function, glucose and urine osmolality for secondary enuresis
Spine examination, and MRI of the lumbosacral spine if neurological signs or daytime symptoms suggest tethered cord

case.story: He was dry at night from age 4 but started wetting the bed 5 nights a week 3 months ago; he snores loudly, breathes through his mouth and is sleepy in class.
case.exam: Large tonsils, BMI at the 97th centile; spine and lower-limb neurology normal.
case.tests: Urinalysis normal, no glucose; home video and PSG show obstructive apnoea with AHI 9 per hour.
case.q: Which condition explains the return of wetting, and how should it be treated?
case.a: Obstructive sleep apnoea; adenotonsillectomy and weight management often resolve both the apnoea and the wetting.

read.where: Chapter 134: Circadian Disorders, Insomnia, and Parasomnias

det.patho: Primary enuresis reflects delayed maturation of three systems: the nocturnal rise in vasopressin that reduces urine output, bladder capacity and inhibition, and the ability to wake to a full bladder. Strong family inheritance is typical. Secondary enuresis is usually caused by a condition that increases urine volume, irritates the bladder, damages its nerve supply or deepens sleep.
det.clinical: Children with primary enuresis are otherwise well and usually wet once a night, often early in sleep. The impact on self-esteem and family life is significant, and stress may worsen it but rarely causes it. In OSA, the wetting often improves after airway treatment. In adults, new bedwetting should raise concern for nocturnal seizures, prostate or bladder disease, diabetes, heart failure or neurological disease.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical once a child older than 5 wets in sleep on two or more nights weekly. A bladder and fluid diary, urinalysis and examination of the abdomen, spine, genitalia and lower-limb neurology are the core assessment. Secondary or adult-onset enuresis needs targeted tests for diabetes, kidney disease, OSA and seizures. Daytime symptoms point to bladder dysfunction rather than simple enuresis.
det.treatment: Start with reassurance, avoiding blame, regular daytime voiding, reduced fluids in the evening and treatment of constipation. An enuresis alarm is the most effective long-term treatment for motivated families and needs several weeks of consistent use. Desmopressin at bedtime reduces urine output and works quickly, with fluid restriction around the dose to avoid hyponatraemia. Imipramine is no longer recommended because of cardiac toxicity, and secondary enuresis is treated by managing the cause.
det.prognosis: Primary enuresis resolves spontaneously in about 15% of children each year, and very few remain wet into adulthood.
pearls: New bedwetting in a snoring child should prompt evaluation for OSA.
Alarm therapy cures more often than desmopressin, which mainly controls symptoms.
Check urine glucose in any child with new bedwetting and thirst.
det.thd: Sleep enuresis คือการปัสสาวะรดที่นอนขณะหลับอย่างน้อย 2 ครั้งต่อสัปดาห์ในเด็กอายุเกิน 5 ปี ชนิด primary คือไม่เคยแห้งต่อเนื่อง มักเป็นกรรมพันธุ์และหายเองตามอายุ ชนิด secondary คือกลับมาเป็นหลังแห้งมาแล้ว 6 เดือน ต้องหาสาเหตุ เช่น OSA เบาหวาน โรคไต ท้องผูก หรือชัก การรักษาหลักคือ enuresis alarm และ desmopressin โดยไม่แนะนำ imipramine อีกต่อไป

qx.stem: An 11-year-old girl from Suphan Buri was dry at night from age 4 until 2 months ago, when she began wetting the bed most nights. She is thirsty, drinks large volumes of water and has lost 3 kg. Examination is normal apart from dry mucous membranes; she does not snore.
qx.q: What is the most important initial test?
opts: Overnight polysomnography
Urine dipstick for glucose and blood glucose
MRI of the lumbosacral spine
Trial of desmopressin before any testing
Referral for family therapy
qx.why: This is secondary enuresis with polydipsia and weight loss, which points to new diabetes mellitus causing polyuria, so urine and blood glucose are the urgent first tests. Secondary enuresis always needs a search for a cause before symptomatic treatment such as desmopressin. PSG would be relevant if she snored, and spinal MRI if there were neurological or daytime bladder signs.

ddx.pt: Snoring, apnoeas and sleepiness; OSA raises nocturnal urine output and arousal threshold
Wetting with tongue biting, confusion or witnessed stereotyped events

name: Menstrual-related hypersomnia
formal: A rare recurrent hypersomnia in which episodes of excessive sleep, sometimes with behavioural change, occur in relation to the menstrual cycle, usually in the days before menstruation; regarded as a menstrual subtype of recurrent (Kleine–Levin-type) hypersomnia.
simple: A young woman becomes extremely sleepy for several days each month around her period and is normal for the rest of the cycle.
th: ภาวะหลับมากผิดปกติเป็นช่วง ๆ สัมพันธ์กับรอบเดือน มักเป็นหลายวันก่อนมีประจำเดือน ระหว่างรอบปกติดี พบน้อย ถือเป็นกลุ่มเดียวกับ recurrent hypersomnia และอาจตอบสนองต่อยาคุมกำเนิด
tempoNote: Episodes of a few days to about a week, recurring with menstrual cycles, typically starting within the first years after menarche
feat: Recurrent episodes of severe sleepiness and prolonged sleep linked to the menstrual cycle, often premenstrual
May include cognitive slowing, apathy, irritability or increased appetite during episodes, as in Kleine–Levin syndrome
Normal sleep and behaviour between episodes
Onset usually in adolescence; familial clustering with Kleine–Levin syndrome has been reported
inv: Sleep and menstrual diary over at least three cycles to show timing
Actigraphy during and between episodes
Exclude anaemia, hypothyroidism, depression, OSA and premenstrual dysphoric disorder
MRI brain and EEG if neurological signs or atypical features

case.story: For a year she has slept 14–16 hours a day for 5 days before each period and missed school, while being alert and active for the rest of the month.
case.exam: Normal neurological and gynaecological examination.
case.tests: Three months of diary and actigraphy show prolonged sleep only in the premenstrual week; full blood count and TSH normal.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and a reasonable treatment trial?
case.a: Menstrual-related hypersomnia; a trial of continuous combined hormonal contraception to suppress ovulation, with neurology review if features change.

det.patho: The mechanism is unknown; changes in reproductive hormones, particularly in the luteal phase, are thought to trigger hypothalamic dysfunction in susceptible individuals. Its link with Kleine–Levin syndrome, including affected siblings of both types, suggests a shared predisposition.
det.clinical: Episodes begin around menarche and occur in step with the cycle, usually in the late luteal phase. Patients sleep most of the day and may show slowed thinking and apathy. Between episodes they are entirely well. The pattern is easily missed unless sleep and periods are charted together.
det.diagnosis: There are no specific tests; diagnosis requires recurrent hypersomnia clearly linked to menses over several cycles, with normal function between. Sleep diary and actigraphy alongside a menstrual calendar establish the timing. Exclude anaemia from heavy periods, thyroid disease, depression and premenstrual dysphoric disorder, and investigate further if neurological features occur.
det.treatment: Suppressing ovulation with combined hormonal contraception has been reported to stop episodes in many patients. Stimulants may help alertness during episodes. If hormonal therapy fails, management follows that of Kleine–Levin syndrome, including consideration of lithium. Safety advice about driving during episodes is important.
det.prognosis: Limited data; many patients respond to hormonal therapy and episodes may lessen with time.
pearls: Chart sleep against the menstrual calendar when a young woman has monthly bouts of sleepiness.
Response to ovulation suppression supports the diagnosis.
det.thd: Menstrual-related hypersomnia เป็นภาวะหลับมากเป็นช่วง ๆ ที่สัมพันธ์กับรอบเดือน มักเกิดหลายวันก่อนมีประจำเดือน ระหว่างรอบปกติดี เชื่อว่าเกี่ยวกับฮอร์โมนเพศและอยู่ในกลุ่มเดียวกับ Kleine–Levin syndrome วินิจฉัยด้วยการบันทึกการนอนคู่กับรอบเดือนและตัดสาเหตุอื่น เช่น โลหิตจาง ไทรอยด์ หรือซึมเศร้า การรักษาที่มีรายงานว่าได้ผลคือยาคุมกำเนิดเพื่อกดการตกไข่

ddx.pt: Recurrent hypersomnia with derealisation and hyperphagia, not tied to the menstrual cycle
Daily sleepiness without symptom-free intervals
Premenstrual or cyclical mood change with hypersomnia as a secondary feature

name: Sleep-related hallucinations
formal: Mostly visual false perceptions arising while falling asleep (hypnagogic) or while waking up (hypnopompic), recognised as unreal after full awakening; classified in ICSD-3-TR among the other parasomnias, including complex nocturnal visual hallucinations.
simple: Seeing or hearing things that are not there while falling asleep or waking up, often frightening but usually harmless.
th: การเห็นภาพหรือได้ยินเสียงที่ไม่มีจริงช่วงกำลังหลับ (hypnagogic) หรือช่วงตื่น (hypnopompic) เกิดจากภาพฝันของ REM แทรกเข้าช่วงตื่น พบในคนทั่วไปเมื่ออดนอนและพบบ่อยใน narcolepsy
tempoNote: Brief experiences lasting seconds to minutes at sleep–wake transitions, occurring sporadically or in runs
feat: Vivid visual, auditory or tactile perceptions at sleep onset or on waking, often of people, animals or a presence
Insight returns once fully awake; frequently combined with sleep paralysis
Common in healthy young adults, especially with sleep deprivation, irregular schedules or anxiety
Frequent and early-onset hallucinations with daytime sleepiness suggest narcolepsy
Complex visual hallucinations on waking in older adults raise Lewy body disease, visual loss (Charles Bonnet) or medicine effects
inv: Detailed history: timing, insight, sleepiness, cataplexy, vision and cognition
PSG and MSLT if daytime sleepiness or cataplexy is present
Eye examination, cognitive screening and medicine review (dopaminergic drugs, beta-blockers) in older adults
EEG if events are stereotyped or associated with altered awareness

case.story: After a month of rotating night shifts she sees a dark figure at the foot of the bed as she falls asleep, sometimes unable to move; she knows it is not real once awake.
case.exam: Normal; no daytime sleep attacks, no weakness with laughter, normal vision.
case.tests: None needed at this stage.
case.q: What is the likely explanation and when would further testing be needed?
case.a: Hypnagogic hallucinations from sleep deprivation and circadian disruption; reassure and stabilise sleep, and test for narcolepsy only if sleepiness or cataplexy develops.

read.where: Chapter 133: Hypersomnias and Sleep-Related Movement Disorders

det.patho: Hypnagogic and hypnopompic hallucinations arise when dream imagery from REM or transitional sleep appears while the person is partly awake. Early REM onset, as in sleep deprivation and narcolepsy, makes them more likely. Complex nocturnal visual hallucinations in older people may involve visual pathway and cholinergic dysfunction rather than simple REM intrusion.
det.clinical: Experiences are short and vivid, and often include a threatening presence, figures in the room or voices, sometimes with sleep paralysis. People recognise them as unreal after waking, which separates them from psychosis. Isolated episodes are very common in students and shift workers. Recurrent frightening episodes can lead to fear of sleep and insomnia.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, based on timing at sleep transitions and preserved insight after awakening. Ask about sleepiness and cataplexy and arrange PSG with MSLT if they are present. In older adults, evaluate vision, cognition, parkinsonism and medicines. Consider occipital seizures if the hallucinations are stereotyped and simple, and psychiatric illness if insight is lost.
det.treatment: Reassurance and an explanation of the mechanism, regular sufficient sleep and avoiding triggers such as alcohol and shift misalignment are first line. Treat underlying narcolepsy, which also reduces hallucinations, for example with oxybate or pitolisant. In older adults, review dopaminergic and other provoking medicines and treat the underlying cause.
det.prognosis: Usually benign and decreases with better sleep; prognosis otherwise follows the underlying disorder.
pearls: Preserved insight on awakening separates sleep-related hallucinations from psychosis.
Hypnagogic hallucinations alone do not make a diagnosis of narcolepsy.
New complex hallucinations on waking in an older adult deserve a search for Lewy body disease or visual loss.
det.thd: Sleep-related hallucinations คือการเห็นหรือได้ยินสิ่งที่ไม่มีจริงช่วงกำลังหลับหรือกำลังตื่น เกิดจากภาพฝันของ REM แทรกเข้ามา ผู้ป่วยรู้ว่าไม่จริงเมื่อตื่นเต็มที่ พบในคนอดนอนหรือทำงานเป็นกะ และเป็นอาการหนึ่งของ narcolepsy ถ้ามีง่วงกลางวันหรือ cataplexy ให้ตรวจ MSLT ในผู้สูงอายุต้องนึกถึง Lewy body disease ตาบอด หรือยา การรักษาคือให้ความมั่นใจ นอนให้พอ และรักษาโรคต้นเหตุ

name: Hypnagogic foot tremor and alternating leg muscle activation
formal: Benign sleep-related movement patterns seen on polysomnography at the wake–sleep transition or in light NREM sleep: hypnagogic foot tremor is rhythmic movement of one or both feet, and alternating leg muscle activation (ALMA) is brief activation alternating between the legs; both are normal variants rather than disorders.
simple: Rhythmic foot or leg twitching while drifting off to sleep that shows up on a sleep study and is usually harmless.
ab: rhythmic feet movements while falling asleep
th: การเคลื่อนไหวของเท้าหรือขาเป็นจังหวะช่วงกำลังหลับหรือหลับตื้น ตรวจพบจาก PSG ได้แก่ hypnagogic foot tremor และ ALMA ถือเป็นลักษณะปกติที่ไม่ต้องรักษา
tempoNote: Short trains of seconds to minutes at sleep onset or in N1–N2 sleep, recurring nightly in some people
feat: Hypnagogic foot tremor: rhythmic foot or toe movements at about 0.3–4 Hz in trains of at least four bursts
ALMA: brief anterior tibialis bursts alternating between legs at about 0.5–3 Hz, in runs of at least four
Usually unnoticed by the patient; seen by a bed partner or found on PSG
More frequent with antidepressants, and in people with OSA, PLMS or RLS, which can cause arousals
inv: PSG with leg EMG and video identifies and scores the patterns
Look for coexisting OSA, PLMS and RLS that may need treatment
No specific blood tests; ferritin if RLS symptoms coexist

case.story: He had a sleep study for snoring; he has no leg discomfort and no daytime problems from movements, but his wife notices his feet shake as he falls asleep. He takes venlafaxine.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination.
case.tests: PSG: AHI 18 per hour; trains of rhythmic left-foot EMG bursts at about 1.5 Hz during N1, and short runs of alternating leg bursts without arousal.
case.q: How should the leg findings be managed?
case.a: Hypnagogic foot tremor and ALMA, benign variants possibly enhanced by the SNRI; no treatment beyond addressing the OSA.

det.patho: These patterns probably reflect rhythmic spinal or brainstem motor generators released as wakefulness gives way to light sleep. They are related to other sleep-transition phenomena and may be enhanced by serotonergic antidepressants and by arousal-causing disorders.
det.clinical: Most people have no symptoms, and the patterns are found when sleep is studied for another reason. Bed partners may notice rhythmic foot shaking at sleep onset. Rarely, frequent runs coincide with arousals or insomnia, but a causal link is uncertain.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is by PSG with leg EMG. Hypnagogic foot tremor consists of trains of at least four EMG bursts of about 0.25–1 second at roughly 0.3–4 Hz, and ALMA of at least four brief bursts alternating between legs at about 0.5–3 Hz. Distinguish them from periodic limb movements, which recur every 5–90 seconds, and from rhythmic movement disorder.
det.treatment: No treatment is needed for the patterns themselves. Reassure the patient and treat associated OSA, RLS or PLMS where present. If movements seem linked to an antidepressant and to symptoms, a medicine review is reasonable.
det.prognosis: Benign.
pearls: Rhythmic leg bursts at 1–2 Hz are not periodic limb movements, which repeat about every 20–40 seconds.
These are PSG findings and normal variants; avoid starting dopaminergic drugs for them.
det.thd: Hypnagogic foot tremor และ alternating leg muscle activation (ALMA) เป็นการเคลื่อนไหวของเท้าหรือขาเป็นจังหวะเร็วประมาณ 0.5–4 ครั้งต่อวินาทีช่วงกำลังหลับหรือหลับตื้น ตรวจพบจาก PSG ต่างจาก PLMS ที่กระตุกทุก 20–40 วินาที ถือเป็นลักษณะปกติ อาจเพิ่มขึ้นเมื่อใช้ยาต้านซึมเศร้า ไม่ต้องรักษา นอกจากรักษาโรคร่วมเช่น OSA หรือ RLS

ddx.pt: Periodic leg flexions every 5–90 seconds rather than rhythmic bursts at 0.5–4 Hz
Large-amplitude head or body rocking at sleep onset, mostly in young children
Axial jerks spreading from the trunk during relaxed wakefulness before sleep

name: Unruptured intracranial aneurysm (UIA)
formal: An intracranial arterial wall outpouching, most often saccular and at a bifurcation of the circle of Willis, that has not bled; usually silent and found incidentally, with management balancing a small but cumulative risk of subarachnoid haemorrhage against the risks of endovascular or surgical repair.
simple: A weak, ballooned spot on a brain artery that has not burst; most are found by chance on a scan, and the decision is whether to watch it or to repair it.

case.who: 52-year-old woman from Chiang Mai with hypertension, 15-pack-year smoking and a brother who had SAH at 49
case.story: MRA for recurrent left-sided headache shows a 5-mm saccular aneurysm of the internal carotid–posterior communicating junction with a small daughter sac. She has no third nerve palsy and no thunderclap episodes.
case.exam: Blood pressure 148/92 mm Hg, normal pupils and eye movements, no focal deficit.
case.tests: CTA confirms the aneurysm with an irregular dome; DSA is arranged for planning. PHASES-type tools give a modest score, but the family history, smoking and morphology are not captured by them.
case.q: What is the best way to approach management?
case.a: A multidisciplinary shared decision: control blood pressure, stop smoking, explain warning symptoms, and discuss repair (often endovascular) because of the irregular shape, family history and her young age; if she prefers observation, repeat imaging at 6–12 months. det.patho: Aneurysms form where haemodynamic stress and inflammation degrade the internal elastic lamina and injure the endothelium, most often at arterial bifurcations. Smoking and hypertension are independent and additive risks, and their combination multiplies the risk in women. Genetic contributions include common variants in CDKN2B-AS1, EDNRA and SOX17, and heritable conditions including dominantly inherited polycystic kidney disease, aortic coarctation, Ehlers–Danlos syndrome, glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism, moyamoya disease and thoracic aortic aneurysm. A first-degree family history raises the risk of formation about three to four times and the risk of rupture by roughly 2.5 times.
det.clinical: Most patients are asymptomatic and the aneurysm is found while investigating headache, dizziness or a different condition. Headaches are common but often unrelated; sudden severe pain demands urgent imaging for SAH. A downward-pointing PComA aneurysm may cause a painful third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil, and giant or fusiform basilar aneurysms may compress the brainstem or optic chiasm. Aneurysmal thrombus can embolise and cause TIA or stroke. Anxiety and depression are frequent regardless of whether the aneurysm is watched or treated.
det.diagnosis: CTA and MRA are preferred for detection and follow-up because they are sensitive and noninvasive, with DSA reserved for small lesions, discordant findings or treatment planning. Natural history is uncertain: annual rupture risk for small anterior circulation aneurysms without prior SAH may be well under 1%, around 0.5% per year for those under 7 mm in Japanese data and 1–2% or more for 7 mm and above, particularly in the posterior circulation. PHASES stratifies 5-year rupture risk from roughly 0.4% at the lowest scores to about 18% at the highest; ELAPSS predicts growth; UIATS adds treatment risk. Irregular shape, a daughter sac, multiplicity, ICA or basilar location and arteriovenous malformation raise risk, as does uncontrolled hypertension, which also raises the risk of growth.
det.treatment: Small (under 7 mm) asymptomatic aneurysms are usually managed conservatively with smoking cessation, blood pressure control, education about warning symptoms and scheduled imaging; growth of 0.5 mm or more over three years is a reason for closer follow-up or reconsideration. Repair is considered for symptomatic, growing, larger (about 7 mm or more) or anterior circulation lesions with extra risk factors, and thresholds are falling as safer devices appear. Endovascular options include coiling, balloon- or stent-assisted coiling, flow diversion and intrasaccular devices; they carry lower procedural harm but more residual or recurrent aneurysm than surgical clipping, which gives more durable occlusion with more neurological deficits and longer admission. Complex lesions may need bypass. After either approach, long-term imaging checks for recurrence and new aneurysms, and antiplatelet therapy is planned around stents and flow diverters.
det.prognosis: Most small aneurysms never rupture, but a rupture is devastating, so decisions rest on cumulative risk, age and life expectancy, and treatment risk.
pearls: Painful pupil-involving third nerve palsy means a PComA aneurysm until proven otherwise: image urgently.
PHASES omits smoking, family history and shape; treat the patient, not only the score.
Control blood pressure and stop smoking in every patient, whether the aneurysm is watched or repaired.

qx.stem: A 50-year-old man with treated hypertension and a 10-pack-year smoking history has headaches that are clearly tension-type. MRA obtained for another reason shows a 4-mm smooth saccular aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery. He has no family history and no neurological signs.
qx.q: Which management plan is most appropriate?
opts: Immediate clipping because any aneurysm in the anterior circulation should be repaired
Lifelong avoidance of exercise and no further imaging
Flow-diverter placement within one week
Cessation of smoking, blood pressure control and scheduled follow-up imaging, with warning symptoms explained
Repeat lumbar puncture every year to look for xanthochromia
qx.why: Small (under 7 mm), smooth, asymptomatic aneurysms carry a low annual rupture risk and are usually managed conservatively, with smoking cessation, good blood pressure control, education about thunderclap headache and cranial nerve palsy, and repeat CTA or MRA at 6–12 months and then at longer intervals. Repair carries procedural risk that outweighs the benefit here. Lumbar puncture and exercise restriction have no role.

qx.stem: A 45-year-old woman asks about screening after her mother and her maternal aunt both died of subarachnoid haemorrhage. She has no symptoms and normal blood pressure. Her sister, aged 40, has autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.
qx.q: What is the best advice for this woman?
opts: No screening, because population screening for aneurysms is recommended against in everyone
Offer noninvasive vascular imaging (CTA or MRA) after counselling, since two affected relatives place her in a screening group
Perform lumbar puncture to look for old blood
Start prophylactic aneurysm clipping without imaging
Repeat transcranial Doppler yearly
qx.why: Having two or more relatives with aneurysm or SAH is a recognised indication to offer CTA or MRA screening after counselling about benefits and downsides, whereas screening the general population does more harm than good. Imaging comes before any treatment decision, and lumbar puncture or Doppler cannot detect unruptured aneurysms reliably.

qx.stem: A resident calculates a PHASES score for a 55-year-old hypertensive smoker whose brother had an SAH, and who has a 6-mm aneurysm with an irregular outline and a daughter sac. The score looks only moderate, and the resident wonders why the team still leans towards repair.
qx.q: Which statement correctly explains the discrepancy?
opts: PHASES is validated only for ruptured aneurysms
PHASES includes smoking, family history and shape, so the resident miscounted
PHASES does not capture smoking, family history or aneurysm morphology, which can raise the real risk
PHASES scores range from 0 to 100, so moderate scores are not informative
PHASES applies only to aneurysms of the vertebral artery
qx.why: PHASES was derived post hoc from pooled cohorts using population, hypertension, age, size, earlier SAH and site; it leaves out smoking, family history and shape. A moderate score therefore may underestimate risk, which is why scores must be combined with morphology and patient factors. It applies to unruptured aneurysms, its range is 0 to 22, and it is not specific to one artery.

qx.stem: A 68-year-old man with COPD and coronary artery disease has an incidental 9-mm ICA aneurysm in the anterior circulation. The team agrees that treatment is justified. The surgeon explains that a randomised comparison of clipping and endovascular treatment found different strengths for each.
qx.q: Which statement best matches the evidence for this patient?
opts: Clipping gives more complete and durable occlusion but more neurological deficits and a longer stay, so endovascular repair is attractive for him
Endovascular repair is better in every respect
Clipping is safer and so is always preferred in the elderly
The two techniques have identical occlusion and complication rates
Bypass surgery is the first-line choice for ICA aneurysms
qx.why: In the randomised comparison, clipping left fewer failures of occlusion or residual aneurysm, whereas endovascular treatment caused fewer neurological deficits and shorter admissions. For an older patient with cardiopulmonary comorbidity, lower procedural risk usually outweighs the higher recurrence, so endovascular treatment is favoured with follow-up imaging. Bypass is for complex lesions not suited to standard approaches.

qx.stem: A 62-year-old man is under surveillance for a 4-mm MCA aneurysm. Over three years the aneurysm has enlarged by about 1.5 mm, and his clinic blood pressure remains around 170/100 mm Hg despite two drugs. He has no symptoms.
qx.q: What is the most appropriate response?
opts: Stop imaging because the aneurysm is still under 7 mm
Intensify blood pressure control, shorten the imaging interval and ask the neurovascular team to reconsider repair
Begin anticoagulation to prevent aneurysm thrombosis
Perform lumbar puncture
Switch to ultrasound surveillance
qx.why: Growth is a marker of instability, and growth of about 0.5 mm over three years prompts closer monitoring; uncontrolled hypertension is also associated with a much higher chance of growth. Stopping imaging ignores both, and size alone does not make growth benign. Anticoagulation, lumbar puncture and ultrasound do not address the aneurysm.

name: Anti-LGI1 encephalitis
formal: Autoimmune limbic encephalitis driven by IgG4-predominant antibodies to LGI1, a secreted protein of the VGKC complex, presenting in older adults with memory loss, faciobrachial dystonic seizures and frequent hyponatraemia; tumours are uncommon.
simple: An immune attack on a brain protein that mostly affects people over 50, causing memory trouble, brief arm-and-face jerks and low blood sodium; it usually improves with immune treatment.

feat: Faciobrachial dystonic seizures: very short, frequent tonic posturing of one arm and the same side of the face, sometimes the leg, often dozens a day
Rapidly worsening short-term memory, disorientation and mood or sleep change
Hyponatraemia in roughly two thirds of patients (inappropriate ADH)
Focal seizures with piloerection, autonomic or emotional auras

CSF frequently normal or shows only mild protein rise; EEG may miss FBDS

case.story: For six weeks his wife has seen his left arm and face stiffen for a second or two, up to forty times a day. In the past two weeks he forgets conversations and gets lost in his own village.
case.exam: Oriented to person only; delayed recall 0/3. During the visit his left hand abruptly flexes with a grimace for about one second. No focal weakness.
case.tests: Na 126 mmol/L. MRI: right mesial temporal FLAIR hyperintensity. CSF: 2 cells, protein 48 mg/dL. EEG unremarkable during an attack.
case.q: Which antibody should be requested, and why treat the jerks quickly?
case.a: Anti-LGI1. The brief arm-face attacks are faciobrachial dystonic seizures; they respond far better to immunotherapy than to antiseizure drugs, and treating them early can prevent the full cognitive syndrome.
