det.patho: LGI1 is secreted by neurons and links presynaptic ADAM23 to postsynaptic ADAM22, tuning Kv1 potassium channel and AMPA receptor function. Patient antibodies, mainly IgG4, block this protein–protein bridge rather than activating complement, which raises neuronal excitability and impairs hippocampal plasticity. There is a strong HLA class II association (DRB1*07:01), supporting a non-paraneoplastic origin in most.
det.clinical: Typical patients are in their sixth or seventh decade. FBDS can precede cognitive symptoms by weeks and are often mistaken for movement disorders or functional events. Later come amnesia, confusion, insomnia, depression and temporal lobe seizures; a smaller group has a slowly progressive dementia-like course. Paroxysmal dizzy spells, bradycardia from ictal asystole and psychiatric presentations are well described.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on a compatible syndrome plus LGI1 antibodies on cell-based testing; serum is usually positive while CSF can be negative. MRI and CSF are frequently unremarkable, so a normal workup does not exclude it. Hyponatraemia plus FBDS in an older person is a strong clue. Exclude infection, prion disease and neurodegenerative dementia.
det.treatment: First-line therapy is high-dose corticosteroids, often combined with IVIG or plasma exchange; FBDS frequently stop within days of steroids. Patients with incomplete response or relapse can receive rituximab. Antiseizure drugs help focal seizures but rarely control FBDS alone; carbamazepine-class agents may cause rash more often in this group. Correct sodium cautiously and check for thymoma when clinically suggested.
det.prognosis: Most patients regain independence, but residual memory deficits and hippocampal atrophy are common; relapse occurs in roughly a quarter to a third. Early treatment is linked to better cognitive outcome.
pearls: Stereotyped one-second arm-face jerks in an older adult: think LGI1 and treat with immunotherapy.
Low sodium plus new amnesia should prompt an antibody panel.
Normal CSF and MRI are common and do not argue against the diagnosis.

qx.stem: A 67-year-old retired policeman from Ubon Ratchathani has up to 60 brief attacks a day in which his left face grimaces and his left arm stiffens for about two seconds. Over a month he has become forgetful and irritable. Serum sodium is 127 mmol/L. MRI shows mild right hippocampal T2 hyperintensity. Levetiracetam and then carbamazepine have not reduced the attacks. Serum LGI1-IgG is positive.
qx.q: Which management step should come next?
opts: Add a third antiseizure medication and reassess in a month
Treat the hyponatraemia with fluid restriction alone and observe
Start immunotherapy promptly, for example IV methylprednisolone with or without IVIG
Arrange whole-body PET and defer treatment until a tumour is excluded
Refer for right temporal lobectomy
qx.why: These are faciobrachial dystonic seizures with hyponatraemia, the signature of LGI1 antibody encephalitis. FBDS respond poorly to antiseizure drugs but well to immunotherapy, and treating early may prevent progression to established cognitive impairment. Tumours are uncommon with LGI1 (unlike CASPR2 with thymoma), so screening should not delay treatment, and surgery has no role.

name: Anti-GABA-B receptor encephalitis
formal: Autoimmune limbic encephalitis caused by antibodies to the B1 subunit of the metabotropic GABA-B receptor, characterised by early prominent seizures or status epilepticus with memory and behavioural change; about half of cases are paraneoplastic, mainly with small-cell lung cancer.
simple: An immune attack on a calming receptor in the brain that causes hard-to-control seizures and confusion, often in older smokers with lung cancer.

feat: New-onset seizures that cluster or progress to status epilepticus, frequently the first sign
Short-term memory loss, confusion and behavioural change of limbic type
Older patients (median about 60), many with heavy smoking history
Small-cell lung cancer in roughly half; often coexisting SOX1 or KCTD16 antibodies
Less often ataxia, opsoclonus-myoclonus or brainstem features

case.who: 63-year-old man, rice farmer and 40-pack-year smoker from Suphan Buri
case.story: Brought in after three generalised seizures in one morning; relatives report two weeks of repetitive questioning and forgetting meals.
case.exam: Drowsy, disoriented, with intermittent right-sided facial twitching; no fever, no neck stiffness.
case.tests: MRI: bilateral mesial temporal FLAIR hyperintensity. CSF: 18 lymphocytes, protein 72 mg/dL, HSV PCR negative. CT chest: right hilar mass with mediastinal nodes.
case.q: Which neuronal-surface antibody fits, and what is the tumour likely to be?
case.a: GABA-B receptor antibodies; the hilar mass is most likely small-cell lung cancer, so biopsy and oncology treatment run in parallel with immunotherapy.

det.patho: GABA-B receptors are G-protein-coupled inhibitory receptors pre- and postsynaptically; antibodies against the B1 subunit block receptor function without major internalisation, reducing inhibition and lowering seizure threshold. Paraneoplastic cases arise because small-cell lung tumours, of neuroendocrine origin, express the receptor. Non-tumour cases tend to be younger and may follow a more favourable course.
det.clinical: The picture is limbic encephalitis with unusually severe and early seizures, often refractory or progressing to status. Memory and behaviour change follow, and some patients present with rapidly progressive cognitive decline. Rarer presentations include cerebellar ataxia and opsoclonus-myoclonus. Weight loss and smoking history should raise concern for an occult lung primary.
det.diagnosis: Test serum and CSF on a cell-based assay; CSF positivity is more specific. MRI, EEG and CSF support an inflammatory process but are nonspecific. A tumour search is mandatory, and repeated screening is advised if the first is negative. Exclude infectious encephalitis and metabolic causes of seizures.
det.treatment: Give corticosteroids with IVIG or plasma exchange, and treat seizures aggressively, often needing several antiseizure drugs. Cancer therapy (chemotherapy or chemoradiation for SCLC) is essential in paraneoplastic cases and improves neurological outcome. Escalate to rituximab or cyclophosphamide when response is incomplete.
det.prognosis: Seizures and cognition often improve with treatment, but overall survival in paraneoplastic cases is limited by the lung cancer; non-paraneoplastic patients do better.
pearls: Seizure-dominant limbic encephalitis in an older smoker: GABA-B antibodies and a chest scan.
Seizures respond to immunotherapy far better than to antiseizure drugs alone.
KCTD16 co-antibodies strongly point to an underlying tumour.

det.patho: GFAP is an intermediate filament inside astrocytes, out of reach of circulating antibody, so GFAP-alpha IgG is best viewed as a marker of the immune response rather than its cause; biopsies show perivascular cuffs of T and B cells with plasma cells in the Virchow–Robin spaces and microglial activation, and cytotoxic CD8 T cells are thought to do the damage. Selective loss of astrocytes has not been convincingly shown (GFAP and AQP4 staining were lost together, or not at all, in the few biopsies studied), which is why some experts prefer 'GFAP antibody-associated meningoencephalomyelitis' to 'astrocytopathy' and contrast it with AQP4 disease, where the antibody is pathogenic. The perivascular focus of inflammation explains the radial enhancement along medullary veins and the overlap with CLIPPERS-like steroid dependence. Reported triggers include preceding viral infections (including HSV), checkpoint inhibitor therapy and tumours. Tumour figures depend on the cohort: Mayo series found neoplasms in about a fifth to a quarter (teratoma the commonest single type, usually with coexisting NMDAR antibodies), whereas only about 7% of 102 patients had a non-teratoma cancer within two years, so most cases are not paraneoplastic.
det.clinical: Most patients are middle-aged (median mid-40s, any age, no clear sex bias) and develop a subacute meningoencephalitis, encephalomyelitis or myelitis over days to weeks after a flu-like prodrome with fever and headache. Confusion, somnolence, psychiatric change, tremor, myoclonus and ataxia are common, as are autonomic features — urinary retention above all, sometimes constipation or orthostatic hypotension; optic disc swelling resembling papilloedema reflects optic perivascular inflammation. Severe cases develop hyponatraemia, central hypoventilation and coma. Roughly a third have coexisting NMDAR or AQP4 antibodies, in which case the phenotype follows those antibodies and the GFAP result adds little. A monophasic course is usual, but around 10–20% relapse, typically while steroids are being withdrawn.
det.diagnosis: Look for GFAP-alpha IgG in CSF and confirm it with two methods (cell-based assay plus tissue immunostaining, which gives a radial glial pattern); in about half of true cases the antibody is detectable only in CSF, whereas antibody found only in serum, or at low titre with a non-matching syndrome, is weak evidence because around 2% of people with other neurological disorders or none carry it. CSF is inflammatory in most — lymphocytic pleocytosis (often >100 cells), raised protein, oligoclonal bands and sometimes low glucose — so the profile overlaps closely with TB, fungal and viral meningitis. Brain MRI shows periventricular T2 lesions and, in perhaps a third to a half, linear radial perivascular enhancement running away from the ventricles, sometimes with leptomeningeal or brainstem enhancement; this sign is suggestive but neither specific (it occurs in lymphoma, sarcoid, CLIPPERS, infection) nor sensitive. Spinal MRI often shows long, faint lesions with central canal or punctate enhancement. Exclude infection thoroughly, test for NMDAR and AQP4 antibodies, image the pelvis for teratoma (particularly in young women or when NMDAR antibodies coexist), and screen the body for other tumours according to age and risk.
det.treatment: Once infection is reasonably excluded, give a 3–5-day pulse of IV methylprednisolone (usually 1 g a day), then oral prednisolone around 1 mg/kg/day for roughly 2–3 months, then taper slowly over the following months; around four in five respond, often within days, which is better than most T-cell-mediated encephalitides. Add IVIG or plasma exchange for severe, ventilated or incompletely responsive patients. Relapses, which tend to occur as steroids are withdrawn, justify a steroid-sparing agent such as rituximab, mycophenolate or azathioprine. Remove any tumour, and in checkpoint-inhibitor cases manage jointly with oncology.
det.prognosis: Most patients recover to mild or no disability (median mRS below 2 in published series), but relapses occur in 10–20%, and outcomes are worse with severe myelitis, prolonged ventilation, delayed treatment or associated cancer.
pearls: Fever plus lymphocytic CSF plus radial perivascular enhancement: think GFAP antibody disease before committing to a TBM label.
Test CSF, not just serum — serum-only GFAP IgG is a weak and sometimes misleading result.
Tremor, myoclonus and urinary retention in a meningoencephalitis are useful bedside clues.
If NMDAR or AQP4 antibodies coexist, treat and screen according to those antibodies.

In a 2026 Chinese series of 29 patients, men predominated, tremor and bladder/bowel dysfunction each affected over half, two-thirds had abnormal thyroid tests (mostly low T3) tracking with severity, no tumour was found, and most recovered with immunotherapy — oral and pulse steroids worked about equally, with rituximab or efgartigimod for relapses.

A transient oval splenial (corpus callosum) lesion — the RESLES pattern — can be the MRI face of GFAP autoimmunity; urinary retention, refractory hyponatraemia, low CSF glucose and spinal leptomeningeal enhancement favour GFAP astrocytopathy over viral encephalitis, so send CSF GFAP IgG.

name: Anti-IgLON5 disease
formal: Neurological disorder with antibodies to the neuronal adhesion molecule IgLON5 and features of both autoimmunity and neurodegeneration (neuronal tau deposits in brainstem and hypothalamus), presenting with a distinctive parasomnia and obstructive sleep breathing, bulbar dysfunction, gait instability, movement disorders and cognitive change.
simple: A rare, slowly worsening illness in which an antibody targets a nerve-cell surface protein, causing abnormal movements and breathing in sleep, swallowing problems and unsteady walking.
th: โรคจากแอนติบอดีต่อ IgLON5 ที่มีทั้งภูมิต้านทานและการเสื่อมแบบ tauopathy — ละเมอผิดปกติ หายใจผิดปกติตอนหลับ กลืนลำบาก เดินเซ และการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติ

Bulbar dysfunction: dysphagia, dysarthria, laryngeal stridor, sometimes central hypoventilation

case.story: Over two years his wife notices loud noisy breathing at night, arm movements as if eating or handing over objects while asleep, choking on rice, and progressive unsteadiness.
case.exam: Mild dysarthria, slow vertical saccades, wide-based gait with falls on pull test, occasional facial chorea; cognition near normal.
case.tests: MRI brain normal. Polysomnography: stridor, obstructive apnoeas and undifferentiated NREM sleep with finalistic movements. Serum and CSF IgLON5 IgG positive.
case.q: What clue on sleep study separates this from simple REM sleep behaviour disorder?
case.a: Abnormal behaviours arise in disorganised NREM sleep together with stridor and obstructive apnoea; this pattern, plus bulbar and gait signs, suggests anti-IgLON5 disease rather than isolated RBD.

read.where: Considerations about the diagnosis of antibody-negative autoimmune encephalitis

det.patho: IgLON5 belongs to a family of neuronal cell-adhesion molecules. Antibodies cause irreversible internalisation of IgLON5 from the neuronal surface in culture, and autopsies show a novel neuronal tauopathy concentrated in the tegmentum of the brainstem and hypothalamus, without the typical inflammation of encephalitis. Whether autoimmunity triggers the neurodegeneration or vice versa remains debated; the strong HLA link supports a primary immune mechanism.
det.clinical: Four main patterns are recognised: sleep-dominant, bulbar-dominant, PSP-like gait disorder, and cognitive decline with or without chorea, but most patients combine several. Stridor and central hypoventilation create a risk of sudden nocturnal death. Fasciculations, cramps and dysautonomia may also appear. Diagnosis is often delayed because the pieces are attributed to separate disorders.
det.diagnosis: Detect IgLON5 IgG in serum or CSF by cell-based assay in a compatible clinical picture. Video-polysomnography is highly informative. Routine MRI and CSF are usually unremarkable. Consider it in any atypical PSP, MSA or motor neuron disease presentation with sleep breathing problems.
det.treatment: Immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG, plasma exchange, rituximab) helps a proportion of patients, particularly when started early, before neurodegeneration is established, and when CSF shows inflammation. Respiratory support with CPAP or tracheostomy for stridor and apnoea, and nutritional support such as gastrostomy, are often essential. Treat the movement disorder symptomatically.
det.prognosis: Historically progressive with substantial mortality, often from sudden death or aspiration; earlier recognition and immunotherapy have improved outcomes in some series.
pearls: Stridor plus parasomnia plus bulbar signs: send IgLON5 antibodies.
A disorder bridging autoimmunity and tauopathy.
Secure the airway at night; sudden death in sleep is a major risk.
det.thd: Anti-IgLON5 disease เป็นโรคที่มีแอนติบอดีต่อ IgLON5 ร่วมกับการสะสม tau ในก้านสมองและ hypothalamus อาการค่อย ๆ เป็นนานหลายปี ได้แก่ ละเมอทำกิจกรรมขณะหลับในช่วง NREM หายใจเสียงดัง (stridor) และหยุดหายใจขณะหลับ กลืนลำบาก พูดไม่ชัด เดินเซหกล้มคล้าย PSP และการเคลื่อนไหวผิดปกติ ตรวจ polysomnography และแอนติบอดีช่วยวินิจฉัย รักษาด้วยยากดภูมิร่วมกับการดูแลทางหายใจและการกลืน

It mimics PSP, MSA or prion disease, but those tests would not capture the antibody-defined disorder, which may respond partly to early immunotherapy.

name: Immune checkpoint inhibitor-related encephalitis
formal: Immune-related adverse event of the CNS after treatment with PD-1, PD-L1 or CTLA-4 inhibitors, presenting as meningitis, limbic or diffuse encephalitis, cerebellar or brainstem syndromes, sometimes with paraneoplastic antibodies (Ma2, Hu, NMDAR), usually within weeks to months of starting therapy.
simple: Brain inflammation caused by modern cancer immunotherapy drugs that wake up the immune system, leading to confusion, seizures or unsteadiness during cancer treatment.
th: สมองอักเสบเป็นผลข้างเคียงของยา immune checkpoint inhibitor (เช่น anti-PD-1) — สับสน ชัก เดินเซ หรือเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ ระหว่างรักษามะเร็ง
tempoNote: Usually within the first 3–4 months of therapy (median about 2 months), evolving over days to weeks
feat: Confusion, altered behaviour, headache, fever or reduced consciousness during ICI therapy
Seizures, aphasia, or limbic syndrome with memory loss
Cerebellar or brainstem phenotypes (ataxia, diplopia), especially with Ma2 or Hu antibodies
Frequent concurrent irAEs: myositis, myocarditis, myasthenia, colitis, hepatitis, thyroiditis
Most often with PD-1 inhibitors or combined PD-1 plus CTLA-4 therapy

CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein; cytology and infectious PCR (HSV, VZV)
Neuronal antibody panel in serum and CSF (Ma2, Hu, NMDAR, GAD and others)

case.who: 61-year-old man with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma, treated in Khon Kaen
case.story: Seven weeks after starting pembrolizumab he develops headache, fever and two days of increasing confusion and word-finding difficulty.
case.exam: Temperature 38.0 °C, disoriented, fluent aphasia, mild neck stiffness, no focal weakness.

case.a: ICI-related encephalitis (with concurrent thyroiditis); hold pembrolizumab and give high-dose IV methylprednisolone, escalating to IVIG, plasma exchange or rituximab if there is no improvement.

Encephalitis seminar: clinical features in autoimmune encephalitis (checkpoint inhibitor and CAR T-cell related); management
Original article: institutional cohort of 14 patients and literature review of 132 — presentation, CSF/MRI/antibody findings, treatment, relapse and rechallenge
Review: autoimmune encephalitis and aseptic meningitis as irAEs; onconeural (Ma2, Hu) versus surface antibodies

det.patho: CTLA-4 dampens T-cell priming in lymph nodes, and PD-1 binding to PD-L1 switches off effector T cells in tissues; blocking these checkpoints releases antitumour immunity but also lets self-reactive T cells escape control. In some patients the drug amplifies a pre-existing, subclinical paraneoplastic response, so onconeural antibodies (Ma2, Hu, and others) appear, particularly with small-cell or neuroendocrine lung cancer and other tumours that express neuronal antigens; experimental models show checkpoint blockade can turn tolerated neuronal-antigen responses into destructive CD8 T-cell attack. Most CNS cases, however, are antibody-negative meningitis or encephalitis presumed T-cell mediated, and occasional patients carry glial antibodies such as GFAP. An autopsy of a fatal case found dense CD4 and CD8 T-cell infiltrates in both temporal lobes and the striatum, and in pooled reports neuronal antibodies — when sought — were found in close to half, mostly against intracellular targets (Ma2 the most frequent, then Hu, GAD65 and GFAP), while surface-receptor antibodies such as NMDAR are uncommon. Combination PD-1 plus CTLA-4 therapy carries the highest overall rate of immune-related adverse events (irAEs), and Japanese pharmacovigilance has flagged an unexpectedly high encephalitis rate with atezolizumab in Asian patients.
det.clinical: Neurological irAEs affect about 1.5% of treated patients, with serious events in under 1%; most involve nerve, junction and muscle, and CNS events are rarer — pharmacovigilance data suggest roughly 0.5% for encephalitis and about 0.15% for meningitis — but can be fatal. Onset is typically within the first few months (median about 2 months, range under a day to well over a year); encephalitis is linked more with PD-1/PD-L1 agents and aseptic meningitis more with CTLA-4 blockade, the latter usually 10–30 days after the first dose with fever leading and headache and meningism following over several days. Confusion, memory loss or altered consciousness is the dominant complaint in nearly nine in ten, with gait imbalance, headache, fever, psychiatric change and seizures (about a quarter) common; because meningeal and parenchymal inflammation usually coexist, 'meningoencephalitis' is often the better label. Phenotypes include aseptic meningitis (headache, fever, meningism), diffuse encephalitis with confusion, reduced consciousness, seizures and focal signs, limbic encephalitis, rhombencephalitis, cerebellar ataxia, myelitis and demyelination. Other irAEs often run alongside — thyroiditis, hypophysitis, colitis, hepatitis — and the myositis–myocarditis–myasthenia overlap is the most lethal combination.
det.diagnosis: It is a diagnosis of exclusion with a supportive temporal link: rule out brain or leptomeningeal metastases, CNS infection (send HSV/VZV PCR and start acyclovir until negative), PRES, metabolic, endocrine (hypophysitis, adrenal crisis, hyponatraemia) and drug causes, non-convulsive seizures and radiation effects. Contrast MRI is abnormal in roughly two-thirds (limbic, multifocal white matter or dural/leptomeningeal change) but can be normal at first and evolve, so repeat it if the picture persists; CSF usually shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis with raised protein (normal cell counts in about a fifth), plus cytology or flow cytometry to exclude malignant meningitis, and a raised CSF adenosine deaminase does not prove TB, which still must be excluded. EEG detects seizures or encephalopathy. Test a neuronal and glial antibody panel in serum and CSF, because Ma2 or Hu positivity changes prognosis, and remember that a negative panel, normal MRI or bland CSF does not exclude the diagnosis. Grade severity with oncology irAE criteria (CTCAE), and check CK, troponin, ECG, thyroid, cortisol and liver tests for coexisting organ inflammation.
det.treatment: Hold the checkpoint inhibitor at the first suspicion. For mild symptoms with infection excluded, oral prednisolone or IV methylprednisolone around 1–2 mg/kg/day may suffice; for moderate to severe encephalitis give pulsed IV methylprednisolone (1 g a day for 3–5 days), then taper over at least 4–6 weeks. Add IVIG or plasma exchange if there is no improvement within a few days, and consider rituximab (or occasionally other agents) for refractory or antibody-positive disease; in pooled reports almost all received steroids, about a quarter IVIG, a tenth plasma exchange and an eighth rituximab. Treat seizures and support the airway as needed, and watch closely during the steroid taper, when most relapses occur. Rechallenge is a shared decision with oncology: guidelines advise permanent discontinuation after moderate–severe encephalitis, and in the few patients re-exposed after recovery almost half relapsed, so it is reserved for selected mild cases (such as brief aseptic meningitis) with close neurological monitoring.
det.prognosis: About four in five improve, often within 1–3 weeks and within a day for purely meningeal cases, and relapse occurs in about a tenth; however, around a third are left with cognitive deficits or epilepsy, and roughly one in ten dies of the encephalitis. Limbic encephalitis on MRI and onconeural (Ma2 or Hu) antibodies predict poor recovery, and long-term survival depends mainly on the cancer, which often keeps responding to the ICI already given.
pearls: Ask every confused cancer patient whether they receive immunotherapy and when it started.
Check CK, troponin and ECG — concurrent myocarditis can kill.
Exclude HSV and metastases quickly, but do not let the work-up delay steroids once they are reasonably ruled out.
A positive Ma2 or Hu antibody means a paraneoplastic-type course with poorer recovery.

name: Childhood absence epilepsy (CAE)
formal: An idiopathic generalised epilepsy syndrome of otherwise normal school-age children, characterised by many brief daily typical absence seizures with abrupt loss and return of awareness and 3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave discharges on EEG.

Dozens to hundreds of episodes per day, often first noticed by a teacher as daydreaming or falling school marks

case.exam: Normal examination. Asked to blow a paper pinwheel for 3 minutes, she stops, stares and blinks for about 8 seconds, then continues blowing.
case.tests: EEG: repeated 3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave bursts of 6–12 seconds during hyperventilation; background normal.
case.q: Which first drug is preferred, and which commonly used drug may make these seizures worse?
case.a: Ethosuximide (best balance of efficacy and attention side effects); carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine can aggravate absences.

det.patho: CAE is a genetically complex generalised epilepsy in which abnormal oscillation in thalamocortical circuits produces spike-and-wave discharges. T-type calcium channels in thalamic relay neurons drive this rhythm, which is why ethosuximide, a T-channel blocker, works. Most cases are polygenic; it affects girls slightly more often and accounts for a sizeable minority of school-age epilepsy.
det.clinical: A well child aged roughly 4–10 has frequent short absences that start and stop abruptly; a seizure longer than about 30 seconds or with postictal drowsiness should make you rethink. Generalised convulsions are uncommon during the active years and their early presence suggests another syndrome. Features that argue against CAE include prominent eyelid or limb myoclonus, strong photosensitivity and absences that leave awareness partly intact. Attention problems and learning difficulty are common even with seizure control and deserve screening.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical-electrographic: a hyperventilation-provoked absence with regular 3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave on an otherwise normal EEG is close to diagnostic, and an EEG without discharges during proper over-breathing makes untreated CAE unlikely. MRI is optional in typical cases. Onset under 4 years, drug resistance or movement disorder should prompt testing for GLUT1 deficiency. Distinguish from inattentive daydreaming, which can be interrupted by touch or voice.
det.treatment: Ethosuximide is the preferred first agent; valproate is equally effective but carries more attentional and systemic side effects, and lamotrigine is less effective though better tolerated. Valproate is favoured if generalised tonic-clonic seizures also occur, since ethosuximide does not cover them. Avoid carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, gabapentin and vigabatrin, which can worsen absences. Repeat EEG with hyperventilation to confirm control, and consider withdrawal after about two seizure-free years.
det.prognosis: Most children remit by adolescence, but a minority later develop convulsions or evolve into juvenile myoclonic epilepsy; school and attention difficulties may persist.
pearls: Ask the child to over-breathe in clinic — a provoked absence is a bedside diagnosis.
Ethosuximide does not protect against tonic-clonic seizures.
Absence onset before age 4: think GLUT1 deficiency.
det.thd: CAE เป็นโรคลมชักชนิด generalized ที่พบในเด็กวัยเรียนพัฒนาการปกติ เกิดจากวงจร thalamus–cortex ที่สั่นผิดจังหวะ เด็กจะเหม่อหยุดนิ่งไม่กี่วินาทีวันละหลายครั้งแล้วทำต่อได้ทันที การให้หายใจเร็ว 3–5 นาทีกระตุ้นอาการได้ EEG พบ spike-wave 3 Hz ยาแรกคือ ethosuximide (valproate ใช้ได้ถ้ามีชักเกร็งกระตุกร่วม) ควรเลี่ยง carbamazepine ส่วนใหญ่หายได้เมื่อเข้าวัยรุ่น

qx.stem: A 6-year-old girl in Grade 1 is described by her teacher as daydreaming dozens of times a day, stopping mid-sentence for a few seconds with eyelid flutter, then carrying on. Development and examination are normal. During the clinic visit, blowing a pinwheel for two minutes provokes an episode; EEG shows symmetric 3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave lasting 9 seconds on a normal background.
qx.q: Which is the preferred initial medication?
opts: Ethosuximide
Carbamazepine
Phenytoin
Gabapentin
Vigabatrin
qx.why: This is childhood absence epilepsy. In the comparative trial of ethosuximide, valproate and lamotrigine, ethosuximide matched valproate for seizure freedom with fewer attentional side effects, and both beat lamotrigine. Carbamazepine, phenytoin, gabapentin and vigabatrin can aggravate absences.

name: Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (SeLECTS)
formal: A common self-limited focal epilepsy of childhood presenting with brief sleep-related hemifacial sensorimotor seizures with speech arrest and drooling, and centrotemporal spikes activated by sleep on EEG, with remission by adolescence.
simple: A common childhood epilepsy where the child has brief seizures twitching the face and mouth on one side, mostly during sleep, which go away by the teenage years.
ab: benign childhood epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes
th: เด็กอายุ 4–10 ปีชักกระตุกมุมปากหน้าข้างเดียว น้ำลายไหล พูดไม่ได้ แต่รู้ตัว มักเกิดตอนหลับ EEG เป็น centrotemporal spikes หายเองเมื่อโต
tempoNote: Onset usually 4–10 years; infrequent seizures, mostly in sleep, remitting by mid-teens
feat: Tingling then twitching of one side of the face, lips, tongue or throat, with gurgling sounds and drooling
Speech arrest or slurred speech while the child remains aware
Mostly on falling asleep or just before waking; may spread to a nocturnal bilateral tonic-clonic seizure
Normal development and examination; seizures usually few in number
inv: EEG including drowsiness and sleep: high-amplitude diphasic centrotemporal spikes, often bilateral independent, markedly increased in sleep
MRI only if atypical features (abnormal examination, developmental problems, unusual seizures or EEG)
Neuropsychology or school assessment if language, reading or attention difficulties are reported

case.story: Twice his mother found him at dawn with the right corner of his mouth jerking, saliva running and making throaty noises; he nodded but could not speak for a minute.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination and school performance.
case.tests: Sleep EEG: frequent left centrotemporal spikes with a horizontal dipole, increasing greatly in drowsiness; background normal.
case.q: Is long-term antiseizure medication mandatory?
case.a: No. For children with this self-limited rolandic-type epilepsy (SeLECTS), many families choose no drug when seizures are rare and nocturnal; treatment (e.g. levetiracetam or sulthiame) is reserved for frequent or daytime seizures or family preference.

read.where: Multiple Choice Questions for Part V

det.patho: SeLECTS is the most frequent focal epilepsy of childhood, reflecting an age-related, genetically influenced hyperexcitability of the lower Rolandic (sensorimotor) cortex that controls the face and oropharynx. Inheritance is complex; GRIN2A and other genes contribute in the atypical spectrum. Centrotemporal spikes are also seen in some healthy children who never have seizures.
det.clinical: Seizures are brief, focal and involve the face, mouth and throat with speech arrest; awareness is generally kept, and nocturnal events may become bilateral convulsions. Most children have fewer than ten seizures in total. Subtle language, reading and attention problems are recognised during the active phase. Red flags for an atypical course include daytime clusters, negative myoclonus, falls, or new regression, which may signal evolution to epileptic encephalopathy with spike-wave activation in sleep.
det.diagnosis: A typical history plus centrotemporal spikes that increase in sleep on a normal background is enough; sleep-deprived EEG improves yield. Imaging is not required for a classic picture. Consider structural focal epilepsy if examination is abnormal, seizures are prolonged or the EEG focus is fixed with focal slowing.
det.treatment: Many children need no treatment because seizures are infrequent, nocturnal and self-limiting; education and reassurance matter most. When treatment is chosen, levetiracetam, sulthiame or carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine are options, although sodium-channel drugs occasionally worsen the EEG and lead to atypical evolution. Treatment can usually stop after 1–2 seizure-free years or by mid-adolescence.
det.prognosis: Remission by about age 15 is near universal; most children have normal adult cognition, though some benefit from support for transient learning difficulties.
pearls: Drooling, gurgling and speech arrest at night with intact awareness: Rolandic.
The spikes far outlast the seizures — do not treat the EEG.
New regression or daytime drops means look for EE-SWAS.
det.thd: SeLECTS หรือ Rolandic epilepsy เป็นโรคลมชักเฉพาะที่ที่พบบ่อยที่สุดในเด็ก อายุ 4–10 ปี เด็กจะชักกระตุกที่มุมปากหรือใบหน้าข้างเดียว น้ำลายไหล พูดไม่ได้แต่ยังรู้ตัว มักเกิดตอนหลับหรือใกล้ตื่น EEG พบ centrotemporal spikes ที่มากขึ้นตอนหลับ ส่วนใหญ่ชักไม่กี่ครั้งและหายเองก่อนอายุ 15 ปี จึงอาจไม่ต้องใช้ยา ถ้าชักบ่อยหรือกลางวันอาจให้ levetiracetam หรือ sulthiame

qx.stem: An 8-year-old boy is found by his mother at 5 am making gurgling sounds, with the right corner of his mouth twitching and saliva drooling; he is aware but cannot speak for a minute. He has had two such events in a year. Development and MRI are normal. Sleep EEG shows frequent high-amplitude diphasic spikes over the left central-midtemporal region with a horizontal dipole, increasing markedly in sleep.
qx.q: Which counselling is most accurate?
opts: Lifelong medication is required because spikes are frequent in sleep
Urgent epilepsy surgery evaluation is warranted
A ketogenic diet is the first-line option
Seizures typically remit by mid-adolescence and treatment may not be needed if events are infrequent
He will probably develop juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
qx.why: Nocturnal hemifacial sensorimotor seizures with speech arrest and drooling plus sleep-activated centrotemporal spikes with a tangential dipole are typical of SeLECTS. Seizures are usually few and remit by puberty; spike frequency does not mandate treatment. Atypical features such as cognitive regression or near-continuous spikes in sleep would prompt re-evaluation.

name: Self-limited epilepsy with autonomic seizures (Panayiotopoulos syndrome)
formal: A self-limited focal epilepsy of early childhood in which infrequent, often prolonged seizures are dominated by autonomic features, especially vomiting, with variable eye deviation and impaired awareness, and an EEG showing shifting multifocal, often occipital, spikes.
simple: A childhood epilepsy where seizures mainly cause vomiting, paleness and staring, often during sleep, and which usually stops on its own within a year or two.
th: เด็กเล็ก 3–6 ปีชักแบบอาเจียน ซีด ตาเหลือก ซึม นานเป็นสิบนาทีจนดูเหมือนติดเชื้อสมอง แต่ชักน้อยครั้งและหายเอง
tempoNote: Onset 1–14 years, peak 3–6; seizures often last more than 30 minutes but are few, with remission within 1–2 years
feat: Nausea, retching and vomiting at seizure onset, often from sleep
Pallor, sweating, pupillary change, incontinence, and occasionally ictal syncope with limpness
Eye or head deviation and gradually reduced responsiveness; may end in a hemiclonic or generalised seizure
Seizures commonly prolonged (autonomic status epilepticus) yet the child recovers fully after sleep
Normal development and examination between events
inv: EEG: multifocal high-amplitude spikes, frequently occipital, that shift location and increase in sleep; normal background
Blood glucose, electrolytes and, if febrile or slow to recover, CSF to exclude infection
MRI if features are atypical

case.story: An hour after going to bed she woke, vomited three times, became pale and floppy with eyes turned to the left, and did not respond for about 40 minutes. She was afebrile and after a long sleep was back to normal.
case.exam: Normal next morning; no meningism, no focal deficit.
case.tests: Glucose and electrolytes normal. EEG: high-voltage spikes over the right occipital region, and over left centrotemporal leads on a second recording.
case.q: Why is this commonly misdiagnosed, and is long-term medication usually required?
case.a: The vomiting, pallor and unresponsiveness mimic encephalitis, syncope, migraine or gastroenteritis. Most children have only a few seizures and need no daily drug; a rescue benzodiazepine plan for prolonged events is usually sufficient.

det.patho: Panayiotopoulos syndrome is thought to reflect an age-related, diffuse cortical hyperexcitability whose discharges, wherever they start, readily activate the central autonomic network, producing emetic and other autonomic symptoms. It is one of the commoner childhood epilepsies, accounting for a few percent of children with seizures, and shares an overlapping spectrum with Rolandic epilepsy.
det.clinical: Typical children are aged 3 to 6 and well; seizures start from sleep with vomiting and other autonomic changes, then eye deviation and reduced awareness. Many last more than half an hour, qualifying as autonomic status epilepticus, yet leave no deficit. Ictal syncope-like episodes with unresponsiveness and limpness can occur. About a third have a single seizure and most fewer than five.
det.diagnosis: Recognition is clinical, supported by an EEG with shifting multifocal spikes, often occipital, on a normal background; a normal EEG does not exclude it. Because the first event resembles encephalitis, metabolic crisis or gastroenteritis, appropriate acute exclusion of infection and hypoglycaemia is reasonable. Unlike late-onset visual occipital epilepsy, visual hallucinations and migraine-like headache are not central.
det.treatment: Daily antiseizure treatment is usually unnecessary; parents should be taught to recognise events and given buccal or intranasal midazolam (or rectal diazepam) for prolonged seizures. If seizures are frequent, a drug such as levetiracetam or carbamazepine may be used and later withdrawn. Explaining the benign outlook is important because episodes are frightening.
det.prognosis: Remission usually occurs within 1–2 years of onset; development is normal, though a small proportion later have Rolandic or other focal seizures.
pearls: Ictal vomiting from sleep in a well preschool child: think Panayiotopoulos.
Long seizure duration does not mean a bad prognosis here.
Shifting multifocal spikes on EEG are typical; occipital is the commonest site.
det.thd: Panayiotopoulos syndrome (SeLEAS) เป็นโรคลมชักที่หายเองในเด็กเล็กอายุ 3–6 ปี อาการเด่นคืออาเจียน ซีด เหงื่อออก ตาเหลือกข้างหนึ่ง และซึมไม่ตอบสนอง มักเกิดตอนหลับและอาจนานเกิน 30 นาที จึงถูกวินิจฉัยผิดเป็นสมองอักเสบหรือกระเพาะลำไส้อักเสบ EEG พบ spike หลายตำแหน่งที่ย้ายไปมา มักบริเวณ occipital ส่วนใหญ่ชักไม่กี่ครั้งและหายใน 1–2 ปี มักไม่ต้องกินยาประจำ ให้ยาฉุกเฉินเช่น midazolam ไว้ใช้เมื่อชักนาน

qx.stem: A 4-year-old girl wakes at night pale and vomiting repeatedly, then becomes unresponsive with eyes deviated to the right for 35 minutes before rescue buccal midazolam is given. She recovers fully after sleeping. CT and MRI are normal. EEG shows high-amplitude spikes shifting between occipital and frontal regions, increasing in sleep.
qx.q: Which statement about the most likely diagnosis is correct?
opts: The episode is best explained by encephalitis and requires 3 weeks of acyclovir
Prognosis is excellent with few seizures, despite long autonomic events
This is the onset of Lennox–Gastaut syndrome
Vomiting excludes an epileptic cause
Visual hallucinations are the cardinal feature
qx.why: Prominent ictal autonomic features (emesis, pallor), deviation of the eyes and prolonged nocturnal events in a preschooler with multifocal sleep-activated spikes indicate Panayiotopoulos syndrome. Despite autonomic status the outlook is excellent, and many children need only rescue medication. Elementary visual hallucinations characterise childhood occipital visual epilepsy instead.

name: Febrile seizures
formal: Seizures occurring with fever of 38 °C or higher in children aged about 6 months to 5 years without CNS infection, metabolic disturbance or prior afebrile seizures; classified as simple (brief, generalised, single in 24 hours) or complex (focal, prolonged beyond 15 minutes, or recurrent within 24 hours).
simple: A seizure that happens in a young child during a fever, usually short and harmless, and not caused by an infection of the brain.
th: เด็ก 6 เดือน–5 ปีชักขณะมีไข้โดยไม่มีการติดเชื้อในสมอง แบ่งเป็น simple และ complex — ส่วนใหญ่ไม่อันตราย แต่ต้องคิดถึง meningitis ก่อนเสมอ
tempoNote: Single brief events during the first day of a febrile illness; recurrence in about a third, outgrown by age 5–6
feat: Generalised tonic-clonic or atonic seizure, usually under 5 minutes, early in a febrile illness such as URI or roseola
Brief postictal drowsiness then return to normal behaviour
Complex features: focal onset, duration over 15 minutes, or more than one in 24 hours
Family history of febrile seizures common
No meningism, persistent encephalopathy or focal deficit
inv: Find the fever source clinically; routine EEG, imaging and blood tests are not required after a simple febrile seizure
Lumbar puncture if meningeal signs, persistent drowsiness, prior antibiotics masking signs, or age under 12 months with incomplete Hib/pneumococcal vaccination
Glucose and electrolytes if vomiting, dehydration or prolonged seizure; EEG/MRI considered after complex or recurrent focal events

case.who: 18-month-old boy brought to a district hospital emergency room in Ayutthaya
case.story: On the first day of a 39.4 °C fever and runny nose he had a 2-minute generalised jerking seizure at home. He was drowsy for 20 minutes and is now playing.
case.exam: Red throat and ears, alert, no neck stiffness, bulging fontanelle or rash; normal neurological examination. Fully vaccinated.
case.tests: None needed beyond a bedside glucose (5.1 mmol/L).
case.q: Does he need antipyretic prophylaxis or a daily antiseizure drug to prevent recurrence?
case.a: No. Antipyretics improve comfort but do not prevent recurrence, and continuous drugs are not recommended for simple febrile seizures; reassure, teach first aid and consider a rescue benzodiazepine only for a prolonged-seizure history.

det.patho: Fever lowers the seizure threshold of the immature brain through temperature-sensitive ion channels and cytokine (e.g. IL-1β) effects. Susceptibility is strongly familial and polygenic; some families carry variants in SCN1A and other genes within the GEFS+ spectrum. Febrile seizures affect roughly 2–5% of children in Western series and higher proportions in parts of Asia.
det.clinical: Peak age is 12–18 months. Most seizures are simple and occur on the first day of fever, sometimes as the first sign of illness. Complex seizures are focal, longer than 15 minutes or repeated within 24 hours; febrile status (over 30 minutes) is uncommon but needs urgent treatment. Recurrence risk is higher with onset before 18 months, a first-degree relative with febrile seizures, low temperature at the time of seizure and short fever-to-seizure interval.
det.diagnosis: This is a diagnosis made after excluding CNS infection and acute symptomatic causes. A well, fully vaccinated child after a simple febrile seizure needs only a search for the fever source. Lower your threshold for LP in infants, partially treated illness, or slow recovery. Remember that a seizure with fever in a child over 5 or with persistent deficits is not a febrile seizure until proven otherwise.
det.treatment: Treat a seizure lasting over 5 minutes with a benzodiazepine (buccal/intranasal midazolam or rectal/IV diazepam) as for status epilepticus. Parents need first-aid education: place on the side, do not put anything in the mouth, time the event. Antipyretics are for comfort only. Long-term antiseizure drugs are not justified for simple febrile seizures; a home rescue benzodiazepine may be offered to families with prolonged or frequent events.
det.prognosis: Simple febrile seizures do not harm development or intelligence; later epilepsy risk is about 1–2%, rising modestly with complex features, neurodevelopmental problems or family history of epilepsy.
pearls: Simple = generalised, under 15 minutes, once in 24 hours.
Antipyretics do not prevent febrile seizure recurrence.
Prolonged lateralised febrile seizures in infancy: think Dravet.
det.thd: ชักจากไข้พบในเด็กอายุ 6 เดือนถึง 5 ปี เกิดขณะมีไข้โดยไม่มีการติดเชื้อในสมอง แบ่งเป็นแบบ simple (ชักทั้งตัว สั้นกว่า 15 นาที ครั้งเดียวใน 24 ชม.) และ complex สิ่งสำคัญคือแยก meningitis โดยดูอาการคอแข็ง ซึมนาน หรือทารกที่ยังไม่ได้วัคซีนครบ ไม่ต้องตรวจ EEG หรือ CT ในแบบ simple การให้ยาลดไข้ไม่ป้องกันการชักซ้ำ และไม่ต้องให้ยากันชักระยะยาว ถ้าชักเกิน 5 นาทีให้ benzodiazepine โอกาสเป็นลมชักต่อมาต่ำ

name: Self-limited familial neonatal epilepsy (SeLFNE)
formal: An autosomal dominant self-limited epilepsy of otherwise healthy term neonates, usually due to KCNQ2 (less often KCNQ3) variants, with brief focal tonic seizures and autonomic features beginning in the first week of life and remitting within months.
simple: An inherited epilepsy in healthy newborn babies, causing short stiffening seizures in the first days of life that usually go away within a few months.
th: ทารกครบกำหนดแข็งแรงดีชักเกร็งสั้น ๆ ตั้งแต่วันที่ 2–7 หลังคลอด มีประวัติครอบครัวคล้ายกัน ยีน KCNQ2 — หายเองในไม่กี่เดือน
tempoNote: Onset day 2–7 of life, often many brief seizures daily for days to weeks; remission usually by 6 months
feat: Healthy term newborn who feeds and behaves normally between seizures
Brief focal tonic posturing, often asymmetric, followed by clonic jerks, with apnoea, desaturation or other autonomic change
Seizures can cluster many times a day in the first weeks
Parent or other relative had similar newborn seizures (autosomal dominant)
Normal examination and development
inv: First exclude acute causes: glucose, calcium, magnesium, sodium, sepsis screen and CSF, cranial ultrasound/MRI
Video-EEG to confirm electrographic seizures; interictal background normal or mildly abnormal
Genetic testing for KCNQ2 and KCNQ3 (parental testing clarifies inheritance)

case.who: 4-day-old term girl, born at a provincial hospital in Chachoengsao
case.story: Since day 3 she has brief episodes of stiffening of the right arm and face with a short pause in breathing, about 10 per day. Feeding well. Her father had 'newborn fits' that stopped in infancy.
case.exam: Alert, normal tone and reflexes between episodes; no dysmorphism.
case.tests: Glucose, calcium, magnesium, sodium, CBC, CRP and CSF normal; MRI normal. Video-EEG: focal onset seizures with normal background. KCNQ2 heterozygous variant, also present in father.
case.q: Which drug is often strikingly effective, and what is the expected course?
case.a: Low-dose carbamazepine (a sodium-channel blocker) often stops seizures quickly; seizures usually remit within weeks to months and development is typically normal, though later epilepsy occurs in a minority.

det.patho: KCNQ2 and KCNQ3 encode subunits of the voltage-gated potassium channel that generates the M-current, which stabilises neuronal membrane potential. Heterozygous variants that partially reduce this current cause transient hyperexcitability in the neonatal brain, which improves as other inhibitory mechanisms mature. Interestingly, different (often de novo, dominant-negative) KCNQ2 variants instead produce a severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathy.
det.clinical: Seizures start in the first week of life, most commonly days 2 to 7, in term babies with normal pregnancy and delivery. Events are brief tonic, often asymmetric, with apnoea, colour change and later clonic movements; they may be frequent at first. The baby is well between seizures. A related infantile form (self-limited familial infantile epilepsy, often PRRT2) begins at a few months of age.
det.diagnosis: This is a diagnosis made after excluding acute symptomatic neonatal seizures such as hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy, haemorrhage, infection and metabolic disturbance. Video-EEG confirmation is important because neonatal events are easily over- or under-called. Family history and genetic testing confirm it; a de novo KCNQ2 variant with abnormal EEG or examination points instead to the encephalopathic form.
det.treatment: Seizures respond well to sodium-channel blockers, particularly carbamazepine (or oxcarbazepine), often better than to phenobarbital, which is used first in many neonatal units. Treatment can usually be withdrawn after a few months. Families need counselling about the dominant inheritance and the small risk of later seizures.
det.prognosis: Most infants remit within six months and develop normally; about 10–15% have later seizures in childhood or adult life.
pearls: Well term baby, seizures from day 2–7, parent with newborn seizures: KCNQ2.
Carbamazepine is often the most effective drug for KCNQ2 seizures.
Same gene, different variant: KCNQ2 can also cause a severe DEE.
det.thd: SeLFNE (เดิมเรียก benign familial neonatal seizures) เป็นโรคลมชักถ่ายทอดแบบ autosomal dominant ส่วนใหญ่จากยีน KCNQ2 ทารกครบกำหนดแข็งแรงดีจะชักเกร็งสั้น ๆ ร่วมกับหยุดหายใจในช่วงวันที่ 2–7 หลังคลอด และมักมีพ่อแม่เคยชักตอนแรกเกิด ต้องตรวจแยกสาเหตุเฉียบพลันก่อน เช่น น้ำตาลต่ำ แคลเซียมต่ำ ติดเชื้อ หรือสมองขาดออกซิเจน ยา carbamazepine ได้ผลดีมาก ส่วนใหญ่หายภายใน 6 เดือนและพัฒนาการปกติ

qx.stem: A healthy-appearing girl born at 39 weeks feeds well but on day 3 starts having brief episodes of apnoea with stiffening of one side followed by clonic jerks, up to 15 times a day. Glucose, calcium, sodium, cranial ultrasound and MRI are normal, and the interictal EEG background is normal. Her father and paternal aunt had similar episodes as newborns that stopped within a few months.
qx.q: Which statement about her most likely condition is correct?
opts: Mutations in KCNQ2 or KCNQ3 are most likely; sodium-channel blockers such as carbamazepine usually work well
Inheritance is X-linked and only boys are affected
Pyridoxine dependency is likely; lifelong vitamin B6 is required
Severe developmental impairment is expected even if seizures stop
The interictal EEG typically shows burst suppression
qx.why: Neonatal-onset seizures in a well baby with a normal background and an autosomal dominant family history point to self-limited familial neonatal epilepsy, usually due to KCNQ2 (less often KCNQ3) variants. Seizures often respond promptly to carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine and remit within months, with mostly normal development. Burst suppression and poor outcome suggest a KCNQ2 developmental and epileptic encephalopathy instead.

ddx.pt: De novo KCNQ2 or other variants with abnormal tone, burst-suppression or very abnormal EEG and developmental impairment
Drug-resistant seizures with encephalopathy and abnormal EEG, responding to pyridoxine; ALDH7A1 variants

name: Early-onset generalized TOR1A dystonia (DYT1)
formal: Autosomal dominant isolated dystonia caused by a GAG deletion in TOR1A (torsinA), usually beginning in a limb in childhood or adolescence and spreading to other body parts, with reduced penetrance.
simple: An inherited dystonia that starts in a child's leg or arm, causing twisting postures that can spread through the body, while thinking stays normal.
th: dystonia ทางพันธุกรรมจากยีน TOR1A เริ่มที่แขนหรือขาในวัยเด็กแล้วลามทั้งตัว สติปัญญาปกติ ตอบสนองดีต่อ DBS ที่ GPi
tempoNote: Onset usually 5–20 years in a limb, spreading over about 5 years, then stable
feat: Action dystonia of a leg (foot inversion when walking) or arm (writing) in an otherwise healthy child
Spread to trunk and other limbs over a few years; craniocervical muscles usually spared
Twisting postures may be relieved by walking backwards or running at first
Normal intellect, reflexes and MRI; no parkinsonism
Autosomal dominant with about 30% penetrance, so family history is often silent
inv: TOR1A testing for the c.907_909delGAG variant (now usually within a dystonia gene panel)
MRI brain normal (excludes acquired causes)
Levodopa trial to exclude dopa-responsive dystonia

case.story: His right foot twists inward when he walks to school but not when he runs; over a year his right hand writing became cramped and his trunk now twists sideways. An uncle had a stiff, turned foot.
case.exam: Right foot inversion and toe flexion on walking, right arm posturing on writing, truncal torsion; strength, reflexes, eye movements and cognition normal.
case.tests: MRI brain normal; copper studies normal; no levodopa response after 3 months; TOR1A GAG deletion detected.
case.q: Which treatment offers the best long-term chance of improvement if medicines fail?
case.a: Bilateral GPi deep brain stimulation; DYT1 dystonia responds particularly well, with gains building over months.

read.where: Chapter 11 Dystonia: Phenomenology, classification, etiology, pathology, biochemistry, and genetics

det.patho: A three-base GAG deletion in TOR1A removes one glutamate from torsinA, an AAA+ ATPase in the endoplasmic reticulum and nuclear envelope. The result is a neurodevelopmental circuit disorder affecting striatal cholinergic signalling and cerebello-thalamo-cortical pathways, without neurodegeneration. Penetrance is only about 30%, and the variant is more common in Ashkenazi Jewish families through a founder effect.
det.clinical: Dystonia usually starts in a limb as action-specific posturing and then generalises, especially when onset is early and in the leg. Later onset (over about 25) tends to stay focal or segmental in the arm. Cranial and cervical involvement is less prominent than in other genetic dystonias. Severe cases can develop status dystonicus, a medical emergency with rhabdomyolysis risk.
det.diagnosis: Suspect DYT1 in isolated limb-onset dystonia before 26 years, or in a relative of a known carrier. Genetic testing confirms it; gene panels also capture THAP1, GNAL and others. Before testing, exclude acquired causes with MRI, give a levodopa trial and test copper metabolism. Normal neurological examination apart from dystonia is expected.
det.treatment: High-dose trihexyphenidyl, titrated slowly, is the main oral drug and is well tolerated by children; baclofen, clonazepam and tetrabenazine are add-ons. Botulinum toxin helps troublesome focal components. Bilateral GPi DBS gives large, durable improvement in many patients, often better than in non-genetic generalized dystonia. Status dystonicus needs ICU care, sedation and early DBS consideration.
det.prognosis: Generalised disability can be severe without treatment, but life expectancy is normal and many patients regain independence after DBS.
pearls: Limb-onset dystonia in a child with normal brain MRI: test TOR1A and try levodopa.
Earlier and leg onset predicts spread; adult arm onset tends to stay focal.
DYT1 is among the best responders to pallidal DBS.
det.thd: DYT1 dystonia เกิดจากการขาดหายของ GAG ในยีน TOR1A ถ่ายทอดแบบ autosomal dominant แต่แสดงอาการเพียงราว 30% เด็กเริ่มมีเท้าหรือมือบิดเกร็งขณะใช้งาน แล้วลามไปลำตัวและแขนขาอื่น สติปัญญาและ MRI ปกติ ต้องลอง levodopa และตรวจ Wilson ก่อน รักษาด้วย trihexyphenidyl ขนาดสูง botulinum toxin และ DBS ที่ GPi ซึ่งได้ผลดีมาก

qx.stem: A 16-year-old boy began with right-hand writing difficulty at age 10; over six years the dystonia spread to both legs and the trunk, and he now needs a wheelchair outside the house. Cognition is normal, MRI is normal and a levodopa trial for three months gave no benefit. Genetic testing shows the TOR1A three-base-pair GAG deletion. High-dose trihexyphenidyl causes memory complaints without useful motor gain.
qx.q: Which treatment offers the best chance of substantial, lasting improvement?
opts: Bilateral GPi deep brain stimulation
Unilateral thalamotomy contralateral to the worst limb
Intrathecal baclofen pump as first choice
Botulinum toxin injected into all affected muscle groups
Long-term tetrabenazine at maximal dose
qx.why: Isolated generalized dystonia, especially TOR1A-positive and with onset in childhood, responds well to bilateral GPi DBS, with improvement that often builds over months and persists for years. Toxin is limited to focal or segmental targets by dose, lesional thalamotomy is outdated for generalized disease, and intrathecal baclofen or VMAT2 inhibitors are adjuncts with weaker evidence. Under the consensus classification, this is an isolated, early-onset, generalized, progressive dystonia of genetic aetiology.

name: Ataxia with vitamin E deficiency (AVED)
formal: Autosomal recessive spinocerebellar disorder caused by TTPA variants that impair hepatic alpha-tocopherol transfer protein, producing very low serum vitamin E despite normal fat absorption and a Friedreich-like ataxia; lifelong high-dose vitamin E halts or slows progression.
simple: An inherited condition in which the liver cannot keep vitamin E in the blood, causing Friedreich-like unsteadiness that can be stopped with vitamin E capsules.
ab: Friedreich-like ataxia with vitamin E deficiency
th: ataxia ยีนด้อยที่เหมือน Friedreich มากแต่รักษาได้ — vitamin E ในเลือดต่ำมากทั้งที่ดูดซึมไขมันปกติ ให้ vitamin E ขนาดสูงตลอดชีวิต
tempoNote: Usually starts between 5 and 20 years, progressing slowly over years if untreated
feat: Sensory–cerebellar ataxia with lost proprioception and positive Romberg
Areflexia with extensor plantar responses, as in Friedreich ataxia
Head titubation or tremor and dystonia are more common than in Friedreich ataxia
Retinitis pigmentosa or reduced night vision in some
Cardiomyopathy and diabetes much less frequent than in Friedreich ataxia
inv: Serum vitamin E markedly low (often below 2.5 mg/L); interpret with lipids — lipid profile is normal
Lipid panel and smear normal (no acanthocytes), excluding abetalipoproteinaemia
MRI: little or no cerebellar atrophy; cervical cord may be thin
TTPA sequencing; check siblings' vitamin E levels

case.story: Two years of worsening clumsiness and a nodding head tremor; an older sister has the same walk.
case.exam: Gait ataxia, positive Romberg, absent ankle and knee jerks, upgoing toes, loss of joint position sense in toes, gentle head titubation; fundi normal.
case.tests: FXN GAA repeat analysis negative. Serum vitamin E 1.1 mg/L; cholesterol and triglycerides normal; ECG normal.
case.q: What is the likely cause, and what should you do for the sister?
case.a: AVED from TTPA variants; start high-dose oral vitamin E for him and measure the sister's vitamin E (and test TTPA) so she can be treated early.

read.where: Review: Autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxias for which treatment is available; Biomarkers; Table 3

det.patho: TTPA encodes the liver protein that loads alpha-tocopherol into VLDL for export. Without it, dietary vitamin E is absorbed but rapidly excreted, so tissue levels stay very low. Chronic oxidative injury damages long sensory axons, dorsal columns and Purkinje cells. AVED is especially frequent in North Africa and the Mediterranean, where a founder TTPA frameshift is common, but it occurs in many populations.
det.clinical: The picture closely mirrors Friedreich ataxia: progressive gait ataxia, dysarthria, areflexia, proprioceptive loss and extensor plantars, starting in late childhood or the teenage years. Head titubation, dystonia and retinopathy are relative pointers to AVED, whereas heart and glucose involvement are uncommon. Mild missense variants can produce adult onset or slower courses.
det.diagnosis: Measure serum vitamin E in every patient with a Friedreich-like syndrome in whom FXN testing is negative, and ideally at the same time. Very low levels with normal lipid absorption and no malabsorption or cholestasis point to AVED; confirm by TTPA sequencing. Acquired deficiency from cystic fibrosis, cholestatic liver disease, short bowel or bariatric surgery must be excluded.
det.treatment: Lifelong oral vitamin E, commonly 800–1500 mg/day (or about 40 mg/kg/day in children) in divided doses with meals, aiming for high-normal serum levels; monitor levels every few months at first. Treatment arrests progression and can partly improve ataxia if begun early, so presymptomatic siblings should be tested and treated. Supportive rehabilitation continues alongside.
det.prognosis: With early, sustained treatment many patients remain ambulant and stable; established deficits improve only partly.
pearls: Always send vitamin E with the FXN test — AVED is a treatable Friedreich mimic.
Head titubation in a 'Friedreich' patient is a clue to AVED.
Screen siblings; treatment before symptoms gives the best outcome.
det.thd: AVED เกิดจากยีน TTPA ทำให้ตับเก็บ vitamin E ไว้ในเลือดไม่ได้ ระดับ vitamin E ต่ำมากแม้ดูดซึมไขมันปกติ อาการเหมือน Friedreich ataxia คือเดินเซ reflex หาย Babinski บวก แต่มักมีศีรษะสั่นและหัวใจปกติ วินิจฉัยด้วยระดับ vitamin E และตรวจยีน รักษาด้วย vitamin E ขนาดสูงตลอดชีวิต ยิ่งให้เร็วยิ่งดี และควรตรวจพี่น้องด้วย

name: Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis (CTX)
formal: Autosomal recessive bile acid synthesis disorder caused by CYP27A1 (sterol 27-hydroxylase) deficiency, leading to cholestanol accumulation with infantile diarrhoea, juvenile cataracts, tendon xanthomas and a progressive spastic-ataxic syndrome with cognitive decline; chenodeoxycholic acid replacement is effective if started early.
simple: An inherited problem making bile acids, so a cholesterol-like fat builds up in the brain, tendons and eyes; a bile acid tablet can prevent much of the damage.
th: โรคยีนด้อยสร้างกรดน้ำดีไม่ได้ ทำให้ cholestanol สะสม — ท้องเสียเรื้อรังตั้งแต่เด็ก ต้อกระจกในวัยรุ่น ก้อนไขมันที่เอ็นร้อยหวาย และขาเกร็งร่วมเดินเซ รักษาได้ด้วย CDCA
tempoNote: Systemic clues from childhood; neurological decline usually from the late teens or 20s, progressing over decades
feat: Chronic diarrhoea since infancy or childhood
Bilateral cataracts in childhood or adolescence
Tendon xanthomas, especially Achilles, appearing in the 2nd–3rd decade (may be absent)
Spastic paraparesis with cerebellar ataxia and dysarthria; peripheral neuropathy
Learning difficulty, later dementia or psychiatric symptoms; epilepsy and early osteoporosis
inv: Plasma cholestanol raised with normal or low cholesterol; urine bile alcohols increased
MRI: symmetric T2 hyperintensity of the dentate nuclei and cerebellar white matter; may extend to cerebral white matter and corticospinal tracts
Achilles ultrasound or MRI for xanthomas; NCS; bone density
CYP27A1 sequencing

case.story: Loose stools since childhood, cataract surgery at 17, now stiff legs, unsteady walking and forgetfulness over five years.
case.exam: Firm swellings over both Achilles tendons, spastic-ataxic gait, brisk reflexes with extensor plantars, MoCA 22/30.
case.tests: MRI: bilateral dentate nucleus T2 hyperintensity; cholestanol five times normal; total cholesterol normal.
case.q: Which treatment should be started without delay?
case.a: Chenodeoxycholic acid (adult dose usually 750 mg/day in three doses) for cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis, confirmed by CYP27A1 testing.

det.patho: Loss of mitochondrial sterol 27-hydroxylase (CYP27A1) blocks the normal side-chain oxidation step in bile acid synthesis. Chenodeoxycholic acid is deficient, feedback on cholesterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase is lost, and the pathway is diverted to cholestanol and bile alcohols, which deposit in brain, tendons, lens and bone. Lipids may look normal on a standard panel.
det.clinical: The sequence is often infantile cholestasis or diarrhoea, juvenile cataracts, then xanthomas and neurological disease in early adulthood. Neurological features include spasticity, cerebellar ataxia, neuropathy, parkinsonism, seizures, psychiatric illness and progressive cognitive decline. A 'spinal' form with slowly progressive spastic paraparesis is recognised. Diagnosis is often delayed by many years.
det.diagnosis: Measure plasma cholestanol (and urine bile alcohols) in any young adult with spastic ataxia or leukodystrophy plus cataract, chronic diarrhoea or tendon swelling. Dentate nucleus T2 signal is a valuable imaging pointer. Confirm with CYP27A1 sequencing; screen siblings.
det.treatment: Oral chenodeoxycholic acid restores feedback inhibition and lowers cholestanol; usual adult dose is 750 mg/day divided, with about 15 mg/kg/day in children. It is approved in Europe and, since 2025, in the US. Early treatment can prevent or stabilise neurological disease, while advanced deficits respond poorly. Monitor cholestanol and liver tests; statins have been used as adjuncts. Cataract surgery and bone protection are also needed.
det.prognosis: Excellent when treated in childhood; untreated, progressive disability and dementia develop, and some die in middle age.
pearls: Childhood cataract + chronic diarrhoea + later spastic ataxia: check cholestanol.
Normal cholesterol does not exclude CTX.
Bilateral dentate T2 hyperintensity in a young adult is a clue.
det.thd: CTX เกิดจากยีน CYP27A1 ทำให้สร้างกรดน้ำดีไม่ได้และ cholestanol สะสมในสมอง เอ็น และเลนส์ตา ผู้ป่วยมีท้องเสียเรื้อรังตั้งแต่เด็ก ต้อกระจกตั้งแต่วัยรุ่น ก้อนไขมันที่เอ็นร้อยหวาย ต่อมามีขาเกร็ง เดินเซ และความจำเสื่อม MRI พบ dentate nucleus สว่างสองข้าง ตรวจ cholestanol สูง รักษาด้วย chenodeoxycholic acid ยิ่งเริ่มเร็วยิ่งได้ผลดี

name: Marinesco–Sjögren syndrome
formal: Autosomal recessive disorder, usually due to SIL1 variants affecting an endoplasmic reticulum chaperone co-factor, characterised by early-onset cerebellar ataxia with cerebellar atrophy, congenital or early bilateral cataracts, progressive vacuolar myopathy and variable intellectual disability.
simple: A rare inherited condition of childhood that combines unsteadiness, cataracts in both eyes, weak muscles and learning difficulty.
ab: cerebellar ataxia with cataract and myopathy
th: โรคยีนด้อยจาก SIL1 ในเด็ก — เดินเซจากสมองน้อยฝ่อ ต้อกระจกสองข้างแต่เล็ก กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรงจาก myopathy และพัฒนาการช้า

case.exam: Short stature, aphakic glasses, nystagmus, truncal ataxia, intention tremor, proximal and distal weakness with thin limbs, reflexes reduced.

det.patho: SIL1 encodes a nucleotide exchange factor for BiP, the main chaperone of the endoplasmic reticulum. Its loss disturbs protein folding, triggering ER stress in Purkinje cells, lens fibres and skeletal muscle. A minority of clinically typical cases lack SIL1 variants, implying other genes.
det.clinical: Babies are hypotonic and late to sit and walk; ataxia becomes evident in early childhood. Cataracts are either congenital or form rapidly. Myopathic weakness progresses slowly and many patients lose walking in adulthood. Learning difficulty, short stature, hypogonadism, strabismus and scoliosis are common.
det.diagnosis: The combination of cerebellar atrophy, early cataract and myopathy is distinctive. Supportive findings are raised CK, myopathic EMG and characteristic vacuolar and perinuclear membrane changes on muscle biopsy. Confirm with SIL1 testing; consider CTX, congenital disorders of glycosylation and mitochondrial disease when SIL1 is negative.
det.treatment: There is no specific treatment. Early cataract surgery is vital for visual development, followed by physiotherapy, orthoses, scoliosis care, educational support and endocrine management of hypogonadism. Offer genetic counselling.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is near normal, but disability from ataxia and myopathy increases over time.
pearls: Ataxia + cataract + myopathy in a child: Marinesco–Sjögren syndrome.
Raised CK in an ataxic child should prompt thoughts of a coexisting myopathy.
Like ARSACS, it reflects a chaperone defect.

name: Cardioembolic stroke (atrial fibrillation and other cardiac sources)
formal: Ischaemic stroke or TIA caused by thrombus or other material travelling from the heart (or across a right-to-left shunt), most often from the left atrial appendage in atrial fibrillation, and also from ventricular thrombus, valve disease, endocarditis or cardiac tumours.

det.patho: Cardioembolism causes about one-fifth to one-quarter of ischaemic strokes. Atrial fibrillation (paroxysmal or persistent) is the leading source: stasis in the left atrial appendage forms red-cell-rich thrombus that lodges in large intracranial arteries. Other high-risk sources include LV thrombus after anterior MI or with low ejection fraction, mechanical valves, rheumatic mitral stenosis (still important in Thailand), infective and non-bacterial endocarditis, and atrial myxoma. Lower-risk or uncertain sources include patent foramen ovale with paradoxical embolism, atrial septal aneurysm, atrial cardiopathy and complex aortic arch plaque.
det.clinical: Onset is typically abrupt with maximal deficit, frequently with cortical signs or large vessel occlusion, giving severe strokes with higher early mortality than other subtypes. Simultaneous infarcts in different territories, a top-of-basilar syndrome, or isolated hemianopia/Wernicke aphasia suggest embolism. Rapid recovery can occur when the embolus breaks up. Paroxysmal AF is often missed on the admission ECG and becomes apparent only with prolonged monitoring. Fever, splinter haemorrhages or new murmur point to endocarditis.
det.diagnosis: Search systematically: ECG, at least 24–72 h of rhythm monitoring, and echocardiography. When no source is found after standard work-up and the infarct is non-lacunar, the stroke is classed as ESUS; extended monitoring with an insertable cardiac monitor detects AF in a substantial minority. TOE is preferred when endocarditis, LA appendage thrombus or PFO in young patients is suspected. Use the RoPE score to judge whether a PFO is likely causal. Exclude large artery and small vessel causes, as patients may have more than one.
det.treatment: Acute care follows standard reperfusion pathways (thrombolysis if eligible and not anticoagulated, thrombectomy for large vessel occlusion); thrombolysis is contraindicated in suspected endocarditis. For non-valvular AF, start a DOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban or dabigatran) in preference to warfarin; recent trials support early initiation — within about 48 h for minor-to-moderate strokes and around day 6–7 for large infarcts. Warfarin remains necessary for mechanical valves and moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis. Left atrial appendage occlusion is an option when long-term anticoagulation is contraindicated. Endocarditis needs antibiotics and early cardiac surgical review, not anticoagulation. PFO closure plus antiplatelet benefits selected patients under 60 with ESUS and a high-risk PFO. Anticoagulation is not superior to aspirin in unselected ESUS.
det.prognosis: Cardioembolic strokes are more disabling and more often fatal than other subtypes; untreated AF carries a recurrence rate of about 5–10% per year after stroke, reduced by roughly two-thirds with anticoagulation.

Never anticoagulate or thrombolyse a stroke from infective endocarditis.

det.patho: The dorsolateral medulla receives small branches from the intracranial (V4) vertebral artery and from the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA); occlusion of the vertebral artery — atherothrombotic, embolic or from dissection — is the culprit more often than isolated PICA disease. The infarct strikes the vestibular nuclei (vertigo, nystagmus, ocular tilt), the spinal trigeminal tract and nucleus (ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss), the lateral spinothalamic tract (contralateral body pain and temperature loss), the descending sympathetic pathway (Horner syndrome), nucleus ambiguus (dysphagia, hoarseness, palatal weakness) and the inferior cerebellar peduncle with spinocerebellar fibres (ipsilateral ataxia and lateropulsion). The pyramids and medial lemniscus lie medially and are spared, so strength and joint position sense are preserved. Dissection is a leading cause in younger adults, while atherosclerosis and cardioembolism dominate in older patients.
det.clinical: Onset is usually abrupt with vertigo, vomiting, staggering and difficulty sitting or standing unaided, often preceded by neck or occipital pain when the cause is dissection. The body is pushed toward the lesion side, and the eyes are pulled the same way: saccades overshoot toward the lesion and fall short away from it (ipsipulsion), with an ipsiversive ocular tilt reaction and tilt of the perceived vertical. Crossed sensory loss, ipsilateral Horner syndrome, hoarseness, dysphagia, hiccups and limb ataxia appear in varying combinations, and partial forms — rostral lesions with prominent dysphagia, caudal lesions with prominent vertigo and ataxia — are common. Severe dysphagia with aspiration is the main early danger, while respiratory failure, central sleep apnoea and autonomic instability are rarer. Weeks later, burning or icy dysaesthetic pain may appear in the face or opposite body as central post-stroke pain.
det.diagnosis: Crossed pain–temperature loss together with vertigo and Horner syndrome localises reliably to the lateral medulla at the bedside. MRI with thin-slice axial and coronal DWI confirms the infarct, but small medullary lesions can be invisible in the first 24–48 hours, so repeat MRI if suspicion remains. In an isolated acute vestibular syndrome, a central HINTS pattern (normal head impulse, direction-changing or gaze-evoked nystagmus, skew deviation) and severe truncal ataxia point to stroke, although a lesion involving the vestibular nucleus or nerve root entry zone can give an abnormal head impulse. CTA or MRA, with fat-suppressed T1 to look for intramural haematoma, identifies vertebral occlusion, stenosis or dissection, and the usual cardiac work-up applies. A formal swallow assessment is required before any oral intake, and an accompanying PICA cerebellar infarct needs repeat imaging if consciousness declines.
det.treatment: Manage as acute ischaemic stroke: IV thrombolysis within 4.5 hours of onset (extended windows per local imaging-based protocols) and thrombectomy when there is a vertebrobasilar large vessel occlusion. For vertebral dissection, antiplatelet therapy and anticoagulation performed similarly in trials, and antiplatelets are usually chosen; atherosclerotic disease is treated with antiplatelets, high-intensity statin and risk-factor control, with short-term dual antiplatelet therapy considered after minor stroke. Keep the patient nil by mouth until swallowing is tested, use nasogastric or later gastrostomy feeding as needed, and protect the airway; persistent hiccups may respond to baclofen, chlorpromazine or metoclopramide. Monitor PICA cerebellar infarcts for swelling, with suboccipital decompression for deterioration. Early vestibular and swallowing rehabilitation speed recovery, and central post-stroke pain may need amitriptyline, a gabapentinoid or lamotrigine.
det.prognosis: Mortality is low and most patients regain independent walking, though swallowing can take weeks to recover; recurrence risk depends on the underlying vessel lesion, and a minority are left with chronic facial or body pain, imbalance or hoarseness.
pearls: Crossed face–body sensory loss without weakness localises to the lateral medulla.
The culprit is more often the vertebral artery than PICA itself.
Hiccups and hoarseness with vertigo should never be called peripheral.
Eyes and body both drifting toward the lesion side (lateropulsion) is a medullary sign, not a labyrinthine one.
det.thd: Lateral medullary syndrome หรือ Wallenberg syndrome เกิดจากสมองขาดเลือดที่ medulla ด้านข้าง มักเกิดจาก vertebral artery อุดตันหรือฉีกขาด (dissection ในคนอายุน้อย) มากกว่า PICA เอง ผู้ป่วยเวียนศีรษะ คลื่นไส้ ตาสั่น กลืนลำบาก เสียงแหบ สะอึก มี Horner และเซหรือถูกดึงไปข้างเดียวกับรอยโรค (ทั้งลำตัวและการกลอกตา) ชาเจ็บและอุณหภูมิที่หน้าด้านเดียวกันแต่ที่ลำตัวด้านตรงข้าม แขนขาไม่อ่อนแรงเพราะ pyramid อยู่ด้านในไม่ถูกทำลาย วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI DWI แบบชิ้นบาง (ช่วง 24–48 ชั่วโมงแรกอาจปกติ) และตรวจหลอดเลือดด้วย CTA/MRA รักษาแบบ acute ischaemic stroke ให้งดน้ำงดอาหารจนตรวจการกลืน ระวังสำลัก และเฝ้าระวังสมองน้อยบวมถ้ามี PICA infarct ร่วม

qx.stem: A 49-year-old motorcycle mechanic from Lampang develops sudden vertigo, vomiting, hoarseness and difficulty swallowing after a week of right occipital neck pain. He has a right Horner syndrome, reduced pain sensation on the right face and the left arm and leg, right limb ataxia and a weak gag on the right. Limb strength is normal.
qx.q: Which lesion best explains these findings?
opts: Left lateral pontine infarct from an AICA occlusion
Right medial medullary infarct from an anterior spinal artery branch
Right thalamic infarct from a thalamogeniculate branch
Right lateral medullary infarct, here likely from right vertebral artery dissection
Left midbrain infarct from a posterior cerebral artery branch
qx.why: Ipsilateral facial pain loss (spinal trigeminal nucleus), ipsilateral Horner syndrome (descending sympathetic fibres), dysphagia and hoarseness (nucleus ambiguus), ipsilateral ataxia and crossed limb spinothalamic loss localise to the lateral medulla on the side of the facial signs. Preceding neck pain suggests vertebral dissection, a common cause in younger adults. Medial medullary lesions cause contralateral weakness and tongue deviation, and AICA infarcts typically add facial palsy and hearing loss.

qx.stem: A 58-year-old Bangkok taxi driver with diabetes wakes with vertigo, hoarseness and hiccups. He is drowsy-free and strong in all limbs. Right paramedian pons
Right dorsolateral medulla
Right ventral midbrain

Strength is spared because the pyramid lies medially. A left-sided lesion would reverse the pattern, and a pontine or midbrain lesion would not produce hiccups and hoarseness from nucleus ambiguus involvement.

Ventral pontine infarcts cause motor weakness, and AICA infarcts add facial weakness and hearing loss.

qx.stem: A 46-year-old badminton coach has abrupt vertigo, vomiting and a hoarse voice after a neck-twisting smash. On examination he leans to the right, has reduced pinprick and cold sensation on the right face and the left arm and leg, and his right limbs are ataxic. Limb strength is full. qx.why: Descending sympathetic fibres travel through the dorsolateral medulla, so an ipsilateral Horner syndrome is part of the lateral medullary picture, as are crossed pain-temperature loss, ipsilateral ataxia and dysphagia or hoarseness from nucleus ambiguus involvement. Pyramidal weakness, hypoglossal palsy and dorsal-column loss belong to the medial medullary syndrome. A neck-twisting injury in a young patient should prompt a search for vertebral artery dissection.
